Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (betaine, N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is an osmolyte that is synthesized in prokaryotes |CITS: [10896953][17098399]|, plants |CITS: [20946588]| and animals |CITS: [12031467]| where it is accumulated to high cytoplasmic concentrations and acts as an osmoprotectant in response to osmotic stress (see the pathways in class |FRAME: Betaine-Biosynthesis|)., While the conversion of |FRAME: CHOLINE| to |FRAME: BETAINE| for the purpose of accumulating |FRAME: BETAINE| as an osmoprotectant is considered to be biosynthetic, the conversion of |FRAME: CHOLINE| to |FRAME: BETAINE| for the purpose of further catabolism should be considered as a |FRAME: Choline-Degradation| pathway. Several such pathways have been demonstrated. In the first pathway |FRAME: CHOLINE| is degraded to |FRAME: BETAINE| using a combination of two different dehydrogenases (see |FRAME:CHOLINE-BETAINE-ANA-PWY|). In the second a single enzyme, choline oxidase, is used (see |FRAME: PWY-3721|). In the third, |FRAME: CHOLINE| is degraded to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| by lyase cleavage (see |FRAME: PWY-7167|). In the fourth, both choline oxidase and betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase participate (this pathway)., About This Pathway, In addition to pathway |FRAME: PWY-3721| that is found in some fungi |CITS: [23221722]|, another fungal variant of choline degradation has been demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-451804| in which both |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.17| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8| participate. , Choline oxidase catalyzes the oxidation of choline to glycine betaine, with betaine aldehyde as an intermediate, and the reduction of molecular oxygen to hydrogen peroxide using FAD as cofactor |CITS: [23563483]|. Based on kinetic analysis, an enzymatic mechanism was postulated in which |FRAME: BETAINE_ALDEHYDE| is released from the active site of choline oxidase and undergoes rapid reversible hydration to |FRAME: BETAINE-ALDEHYDE-HYDRATE| (gem-diol choline). The latter compound is likely to be the actual substrate for continued catalysis by choline oxidase, which further oxidizes it to |FRAME: BETAINE|. , The |FRAME: BETAINE_ALDEHYDE| intermediate can also be oxidized to |FRAME: BETAINE| by |FRAME: NAD|-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8| |CITS: [23563483]|., Characterization of mutant phenotypes from single and double deletion mutants of genes CHOA (encoding choline oxidase) and BADH (encoding betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase) suggested that in |FRAME: TAX-451804| |FRAME: BETAINE| functions exclusively as a metabolic intermediate in the catabolism of |FRAME: CHOLINE|, rather than as a stress protectant. The growth of the mutants was not affected by stress conditions including osmotic stress and reactive oxygen species. A high |FRAME: NACL| concentration did not affect expression of the two genes |CITS: [23563483]|.

Summary: Adenosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: AMP| (AMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| , which is converted to AMP by the action of, |FRAME: ASL-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6126|). Note that the free base |FRAME: ADENINE| or the ribonucleoside |FRAME: ADENOSINE| are not produced via the de novo pathway., Many organisms can also recycle adenosine nucleotides by a combination of degradation and salvage pathways. The degradation pathways are responsible for the conversion of the nucleotides to the nucleoside (|FRAME: ADENOSINE|) and free base form (|FRAME: ADENINE|), and further degradation to compounds that can be catabolized to basic building blocks (for example, see |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|)., A key reaction in |FRAME: ADENINE| salvage is the phosphoribosylation of adenine to |FRAME: AMP|, a reaction that is common to all organisms. However, the interconversion of |FRAME: ADENINE| to |FRAME: GMP| involves several steps and different pathways in different organisms., Several bacterial species and lower eukaryotes have been shown to possess an enzyme that is able to directly deaminate adenine to |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|. These organisms include |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [6408059]|, |FRAME: TAX-354| |CITS: [6017742 ]|, |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [11440125]|, |FRAME: TAX-4903| |CITS: [6017742]|, |FRAME: TAX-4896| |CITS: [Pourquie71]|, |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [1577682][ 6392474 ]|, |FRAME: TAX-5656|, and four |FRAME: TAX-38568| species |CITS: [291031]|. In addition, a homolog of the |FRAME: BSU14520| gene was discovered in the genomes of hundreds of additional bacteria and archaebacteria., In |FRAME: TAX-1423|, when preformed purines are present in the growth medium, they are readily taken up by specific transport systems and used for nucleotide synthesis. Under these conditions, de novo purine synthesis is shut down. Mutants of |FRAME: TAX-1423| defective in |FRAME: BSU14520-MONOMER| are not able to grow with adenine., Adenine deamination was also shown to be an essential step in the utilization of adenine as the total purine source in, |FRAME: TAX-4896| |CITS: [Pourquie71]| and |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [1577682]|.

|FRAME: 1-2-Beta-D-Glucans "β-1,2-Glucan"| is a homopolymer composed of glucose residues connected by β(1,2) linkages., This type of glucan has been reported from some Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-357|, |FRAME: TAX-379|, |FRAME: TAX-28105|, and |FRAME: TAX-234|, where it exists mainly in cyclic form |CITS: [Hisamatsu82][2117876][8078434][15880113][22583376]|. Cyclic β-1,2-glucans have been reported to play a role in osmotic regulation |CITS: [3941890][2318812][10779706]|, but were also reported to act as commensal factors in |FRAME: TAX-379| |CITS: [18052882]| and as infectious factors in |FRAME: TAX-235| |CITS: [11401996]|., Cyclic β-1,2-glucans are usually found with a degree of polymerization (DPs) around 20, although a much longer glucan (DPs of around 40) has been reported from |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [Koizumi84]|., Linear β-1,2-glucans have been found in |FRAME: TAX-434| and |FRAME: TAX-338| |CITS: [Amemura85][3540204]|, and linear glucans with β-1,6-glucosyl branches was reported in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-317| (see |FRAME: CPD-16398|) |CITS: [3941890][7961404][10779706]|., In Brucella the cyclic glucan acts on host cell membranes at the level of lipid rafts controlling vacuole maturation, avoiding lysosome fusion, and allowing Brucella to reach the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [15880113]|., The |FRAME: BAB_RS16445-MONOMER| (Cgs) of |FRAME: TAX-235| is a 320-kDa integral inner membrane protein that catalyzes the synthesis CβG |CITS: [9721274][29624823]|. The enzyme contains an N-terminal inverting processive β-1,2-glucosyltransferase domain (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.391|), a central cyclic β-1,2-glucan glucanotransferase domain (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.397|), and a C-terminal β-1,2-glucoside hydrolase domain (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.333|). The first domain binds a glucose molecule, donated by |FRAME: CPD-12575|, to an uncharacterized amino acid, and elongates it to form a β-1,2-glucan attached to the enzyme. The central domain catalyzes cyclization, and the third domain controls chain length |CITS: [38300345]|., The Brucella glycan is further modified by the addition of two succinyl residues per glucan molecule at C-6 positions |CITS: [16816173]|.

Summary: General Background, Saponins are glycosides of triterpenoid (this pathway) or steroidal aglycones (see |FRAME:PWY-2541|) with a varying number of sugar side chains. Saponins are especially enriched in plant epidermal cells forming a protective surfactant that forms a soapy froth when mixed with water |CITS: [12188349]|., Found among a wide variety of plants legumes constitute a major source of saponins |CITS: [WALLER96B]| |CITS: [12644640]|. The saponins isolated from soybean and other legumes, also referred to as soyasaponins, are derived from triterpenoid aglycones such as soyasapogenol A, B, E, medicagenic acid, hederagenin and bayogenin which have been identified through metabolic profiling |CITS: [11830145]|., Saponins possess a number of biological activities that have been intensively investigated over the last few decades. Extracts of plants rich on saponins have been demonstrated to have allelopathic, antiflammatory, hemolytic |CITS: [WALLER96B]|, cholesterol lowering |CITS: [SAUVAIRE96]| |CITS: [10540988]| and anticancer properties |CITS: [15134504]| but are also known to reduce the digestibility in ruminants |CITS: [ 8726748][CHEEKE96][10552705]| and to be generally toxic to cold blooded animals and insects |CITS: [TAVA96]|., The diversity in conjugation of saponins increases the biological activity of those compounds compared to their aglycone (sapogenin) complements |CITS: [11344312]|. In addition, saponin has been successfully tested as a cleaning agent for remediation of heavy metal contaminated soils |CITS: [12365835]|. However, the physiological significance of saponins in plants remains poorly understood and requires further research., About This Pathway, The first committed step in the biosynthesis of triterpenoid saponins is the cyclization of 2,3-oxidosqualene, a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of terpenoids that marks both a branching point for phytosterols and triterpenoid biosyntheses |CITS: [11510484]| and primary (sterols) and secondary (triterpenoids) metabolism |CITS: [9746369]|. The reaction is carried out by a specific oxidosqualene cyclase (OSC), i.e. β-amyrin synthase (bAS) that catalyzes the formation of β-amyrin and is inducible upon treatment with methyljasmonate |CITS: [12721381]|. β-amyrin is the central compound that represents another branch point in the saponin biosynthesis and can be converted into at least five different triterpenoid aglycones in legumes |CITS: [12492844]|.The cyclization of 2,3-oxidosqualene can generate more than 80 different skeleton types leading to tetra- and pentacyclic compounds via multiple (8-10) asymmetric centres , in one single enzymatic step |CITS: [14751299]|. That clearly indicates the high stereospecificity of the enzyme involved in a series of intermediate reactions which mechanism has been thoroughly investigated |CITS: [9746369]|., The further decoration of β-amyrin towards the synthesis of soyasaponins involves hydroxylation and glycosylation reactions. In analogy to a series of similar oxidative reactions involved in the biosynthesis of brassinosteroids (|FRAME:PWY-699|, |FRAME:PWY-2582|) the involvement of cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases have been expected for the formation of soysaponin |CITS: [12644640]| |CITS: [14751299]|., The characterization of a 24-hydroxylase being able to hydroxylate both β-amyrin to form olean-12-ene-3beta,24-diol and sophoradiol to generate soyasapogenol B has been reported |CITS: [16478469]|. The next activity, which forms soyasapogenol, is also carried out by a cytochrome P450 |CITS: [22039103]|., The remaining reaction of the pathway concerns the attachment of glycosidic residues to the sapogenin, leading to the formation of a saponin. The first step is the attachemnt of β-glucuronate, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-7612|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-12198| (UGASGT). This is followed by attachment of β-galactose and L-rhamnose, forming |FRAME: CPD-13255| |CITS: [20350545]|.

Summary: |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE "4-Aminobenzoate"| is an important metabolic intermediate, leading to the biosynthesis of various products such as |FRAME: All-Folates folates|, |FRAME: Ubiquinones ubiquinone| (in eukaryotes), and various bacterial antibiotics (e.g. |FRAME: Candicidins|)., In this pathway |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| is produced from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| in two steps. In the first step |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.85|, synthesizes |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXYCHORISMATE| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| and |FRAME: GLN|. The enzyme is composed from two subunit, PabA and PabB (in some organisms they are fused together into a bifunctional protein). PabA functions as a glutaminase, but only when in complex with PabB. PabB is an aminodeoxychorismate synthase that utilizes chorismate and ammonia (derived from glutamine hydrolysis by PabA) as substrates. In the absence of PabA PabB can utilize added ammonia at a reduced rate |CITS: [2251281][AndersonK91][1637823]|., During the reaction chorismate binds to PabB by a transitory covalent bond between the ε-amino group of a lysine residue (K274 in the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-582|) and position C-2 of chorismate, resulting in loss of the hydroxyl group at position C-4. This intermediate is then attacked by the ammonia molecule generated by PabA, resulting in release of the product |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXYCHORISMATE| |CITS: [15770625][16605270]|., In the second step |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.38| (PabC) forms the final product. The reaction involves the elimination of pyruvate from 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate with concomitant aromatization of the cyclohexadiene ring. The enzyme is classified as an α,β-lyase of the fold-type IV family, and requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate for activity |CITS: [11011151]|.

Summary: While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]|, it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|., The most common mechanism for retreiving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination,, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves, the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid., In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|)., In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central, metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich, pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the, corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde., Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced, (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols",, or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids (fusel acids) |CITS: [15933030]|., |FRAME: ILE| is one of the three protein-building branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), along with, |FRAME: VAL| and |FRAME: LEU|., The metabolism of BCAA in yeast is different than in other eukaryotes. While most other eukaryotes, (as well as many prokaryotes) catabolize |FRAME: ILE| through a succession of acyl-coA derivatives, to metabolites that can enter the TCA cycle (see |FRAME:ILEUDEG-PWY|), providing the organism, with carbon as well as nitrogen, yeast are not able to use, |FRAME:ILE| as a carbon source, and process it through the Ehtlich pathway to |FRAME:CPD-7033|, |CITS: [10753893]|., Initial work performed by Ehrlich and others suggested that the catabolism of |FRAME:ILE| in, |FRAME: TAX-4932| first involves transamination using |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| (similar to the, first step of the pathway found in other eukaryotes), but continues with decarboxylation of the keto acid, to produce an aldehyde that is then reduced to |FRAME:CPD-7033| |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. Later work, by Dickinson et al suggests that the product of |FRAME: ILE| transamination,, |FRAME:2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE|, can be decarboxylated by any one of a family of, decarboxylase enzymes encoded by the genes |FRAME:YLR044C|, |FRAME: YLR134W|, |FRAME:YGR087C|,, |FRAME: YDL080C|, and |FRAME: YDR380W| |CITS: [10753893]|., The final step in this pathway can be catalyzed by any of the yeast alcohol dehydrogenases, |CITS: [12499363]|

Summary: General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose |CITS: [12065209]|. , In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosil α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein)., In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation and no internal hydrogen bond formation. The combination of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms trehalose can be used as external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|. In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|. The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood |CITS: [11081789]|., About This Pathway, Several organisms are capable of synthesizing trehalose directly from maltodextrin, independently of the presence of the phosphate compounds trehalose-6-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate. In some of these organisms this is the only trehalose biosynthesis pathway, while in others (such as mycobacteria and C. glutamicum) several trehalose biosynthesis pathways coexist |CITS: [12890033][10658666]|., In this pathway trehalose is formed by the action of several enzymes. An |FRAME: MONOMER-5703| (also known as glycogen- or starch-debranching enzyme) hydrolyzes the α-1,6-glucosidic linkages in glycogen or other polysaccharides such as starch to produce |FRAME: Maltodextrins|. A |FRAME: MONOMER-5701| (MTS) then catalyzes the conversion of maltodextrin to maltooligosyl-trehalose by forming an α,α-1,1-glucosidic linkage using a mechanism of intermolecular transglucosylation., A third enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-5702| (MTH), hydrolyzes the product to form trehalose and a maltodextrin which is shorter by two glucosyl residues |CITS: [8980629]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-1718|, which possess three different pathways for the biosynthesis of trehalose, this is the main route for trehalose biosynthesis. Recently it has been shown that this pathway is present in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1704|, |CITS: [11055902]| and is prevalent in |FRAME: TAX-82115|, including |FRAME: TAX-375|, |FRAME: TAX-29448|, |FRAME: TAX-394|, |FRAME: ORG-6005|, |FRAME: TAX-398|, |FRAME: TAX-387| , |FRAME: TAX-386|, and |FRAME: TAX-7|, |CITS: [10528404]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes, ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8 Ubiquinone 8| (Q-8) is a common form of ubiquinone among bacteria. Most of the Gram-negative facultative anaerobes, such as the enterobacteria, produce Q-8 (in addition to |FRAME: CPD-9728| and |FRAME: DEMETHYLMENAQUINONE|). Q-8 has been documented in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [13673033]|, |FRAME: TAX-546|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, |FRAME: TAX-554|, |FRAME: TAX-584|, |FRAME: TAX-585| |CITS: [4886765]| and |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [Bezborodov69]|, as well as in the non-enterobacteria |FRAME: TAX-644|, |FRAME: TAX-648| |CITS: [4886765]| and |FRAME: TAX-51367| |CITS: [Collins81]|. It is also common in aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-354| |CITS: [13673033][4288128]|, |FRAME: TAX-353| |CITS: [13869492]|, |FRAME: TAX-107673| |CITS: [Denis75]|, |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [4351160]|, |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [Yamada68]|, and various |FRAME: TAX-338| strains |CITS: [Ikemoto80]|. Q-8 was also found to be the major quinone in an unidentified strain of the gliding bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1021| |CITS: [Carr67]| and in some phototrophic bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1049| |CITS: [14240125]|, |FRAME:TAX-1053|, |FRAME: TAX-28068| |CITS: [Carr65][5727384]|, and a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1081| |CITS: [5727384]|. Q-8 is often found as a secondary quinone in |FRAME: TAX-286| strains |CITS: [4886765]|., The best studied ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway is that of |FRAME: TAX-83333|, which produces a |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8|. The first committed step of the pathway is the conversion of chorismate to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| by |FRAME: CHORPYRLY-MONOMER|. The enzyme retains and is efficiently inhibited by the product of the reaction, 4-hydroxybenzoate, which may present a control mechanism for the ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway or a mechanism for delivery of 4-hydroxybenzoate to the membrane |CITS: [11455603][11825618]|., The second step in the pathway is the transfer of the polyisoprenoid tail onto |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| by the membrane-bound |FRAME: 4OHBENZOATE-OCTAPRENYLTRANSFER-MONOMER|. This is followed by the, decarboxylation of the ring structure by |FRAME: CPLX0-301| to form |FRAME: 2-OCTAPRENYLPHENOL|. Under anaerobic conditions, this compound accumulates in the membrane and is not converted into ubiquinone. Further steps in the pathway require the presence of dioxygen |CITS: [361395]|., Following is the alternating introduction of three hydroxyl- and three methyl groups. With the exception of the methyltransferase that catalyzes both of the O-methyltransferase reactions, UbiG, none of the enzymes have been studied biochemically and their substrate and cofactor requirements are still unknown. The hydroxylation reactions are catalyzed by different types of enzymes in different bacterial clades. Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, have three enzymes, each dedicated to one of the three hydroxylation events. In some organisms two hydroxylases catalyze the three reactions, yet in some organism a single enzyme, encoded by the ubiM gene, catalyzes all three reactions |CITS: [27822549]|. , Because the octaprenyl tail of Q-8 is attached early in this pathway, it was long thought that the subsequent steps take place in the membrane. However, most of the biosynthetic enzymes do not show features of membrane proteins. It has now been shown that the biosynthetic steps take place within a soluble metabolon that shields the octaprenyl tail from the aqueous environment of the cytoplasm |CITS: [30686758]|. , For the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8| in yeast, see |FRAME: PWY-5870|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13893 "Lincomycin A"| was isolated for the first time in 1962 from a soil bacterium near Lincoln, Nebraska, which gave its name to both the species (|FRAME: TAX-1915|) and the compound |CITS: [Mason62]|., It is a lincosamide antibiotic that blocks protein synthesis in sensitive bacterial strains by inhibiting the peptidyltransferase reaction on the 50S ribosomal subunit |CITS: [14762701]|., It was subsequently shown that lincomycin is produced not only by |FRAME: TAX-1915| but also by other actinomycetes. Together with the semi-synthetic derivative |FRAME: CPD-13892|, it is a medically important chemotherapeutic., A gene cluster containing 27 genes involved in lincomycin biosynthesis has been isolated and characterized |CITS: [8577249]|. The cluster, which is about 35 kb, has been incorporated into the chromosome of a non-producing strain, resulting in low-level production of lincomycin |CITS: [19085073]|., Lincomycin A is composed of two building blocks, |FRAME: CPD-13894| (propyl-L-hygric acid) and |FRAME: CPD-13896|, which are synthesized by separate branches. As such it belongs to a group of structurally different and functionally diverse natural compounds that contain a 4-alkyl-L-proline building unit, which is derived from |FRAME:TYR|., Sequence analysis of the lmb gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1915| revealed that the products of genes |FRAME: G-34548|, |FRAME: G-34551|, |FRAME: G-34549| and |FRAME: G-34550| have amino acid sequence similarities with those involved in NDP-heptose biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-143495| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6478| and |FRAME: PWY0-1241|). These lmb genes were shown to catalyze reactions resulting in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-17019|, starting with intermediates of the pentose phosphate cycle |CITS: [Brahme84][22989310][24380627]|., The path leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-13894| starts with the |FRAME: G-14828| and |FRAME: G-14829| products, which convert |FRAME: TYR| to |FRAME: CPD-13901| |CITS: [9531633][15355345][18817745][21919439][31710815]|. This intermediate is cleaved, releasing an |FRAME: OXALATE| moiety, and C-methylated. There has been some disagreement regarding the order of C-C bond cleavage and C-methylation. A 2016 paper reported that purified recombinant |FRAME: G-80611 LmbW| methyltransferase acts on |FRAME: CPD-13901|, suggesting that methylation preceeds the C-C bond cleavage reaction |CITS: [27014201]|. The 2017 paper that characterized the C-C bond cleavage activity of |FRAME: G-80612 LmbA| claimed that C-C bond cleavage occurs first |CITS: [28706296]|. A subsequent paper published in 2018 argued that C-C bond cleavage cannot precede C-methylation |CITS: [30093642]|. However, a rebuttal argued that bond cleavage does precede C-methylation |CITS: [30093620]|. Since no further communication regarding this topic has been published, the MetaCyc pathway shows cleavage preceding C-methylation. The pathway continues with the |FRAME: G-80613| isomerase and |FRAME: G-80614| reductase, whose combined activities produce the |FRAME: CPD-13894| building block |CITS: [27014201]|., The later part of the pathway, which brings together the two building blocks, was found to be far more complex than expected and to include some processes that have not been described previously., |FRAME: CPD-13894| is activated by adenylation and is attached to a peptidyl-carrier protein (the N-terminal domain of the bifunctional LmbN protein) |CITS: [25741696]|, while the other buidling block, |FRAME: CPD-17019|, undergoes an unusual exchange of the GDP moiety with the small-molecule thiol |FRAME: Ergothioneine|. Ergothioneine serves as a carrier, channeling the lincosamine unit and mediating its condensation with |FRAME: CPD-13894|, which is dettached from its carrier protein in the process. Next the |FRAME: Ergothioneine| moiety is replaced by a different small thiol, |FRAME: CPD1G-2|, which serves as a sulfur donor, as it is eventually cleaved, leaving its sulfur incorporated in the product |CITS: [25607359]|. Following N-deacetylation |CITS: [32786288]| and N-methylation, a carbon-sulfur bond is cleaved by |FRAME: G-80618 LmbF|, leaving a sulfhydryl group. The last cleavage activates the molecule, which becomes toxic. However, the sulfhydryl group is highly unstable, and is immediately N-methylated to form the final product |CITS: [28791100]|.

Summary: |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE Sulfoacetaldedhyde| is a central intermediate of organosulfate degradation |CITS: [12471498]|., In this pathway, originally studied in the human gut bacterium |FRAME: TAX-35833|, |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-3745| by an NADH-dependent reductase. |FRAME: CPD-3745 Isethionate| is then cleaved to |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: ACETALD| by a glycyl radical enzym, |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.38| (|FRAME: G-80414|) |CITS: [30718429]|., Active glycyl radical enzymes contain a glycyl radical in the active site. They are translated in an inactive state and require a dedicated activase enzyme (which in this case is encoded by islB). A reduced [4Fe-4S]+1 cluster of the activase transfers an electron to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, forming |FRAME: MET| and a |FRAME: CPD-15400|, which subsequently activates the glycyl radical enzyme by stereospecific abstraction of a C-2 pro-S H atom from a highly conserved glycine residue. The glycyl radical in turn abstracts an H atom from a conserved cysteine residue in the active site, forming a thiyl radical that attacks the substrate. Once activated, the enzyme can catalyze many reactions since the radical is restored at the end of the catalytic process. IslA is the first glycyl radical enzyme reported to catalyze cleavage of a sulfur-carbon bond |CITS: [30718429]|., The |FRAME: ACETALD| produced is oxidized by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.10|, to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which is converted via |FRAME: ACETYL-P| to |FRAME: ACET| that is excreted from the cells. The |FRAME: SO3| is reduced to |FRAME: HS| by |FRAME: EC-1.8.1.22| (as described in the latter section of |FRAME: DISSULFRED-PWY|). |FRAME: HS "Hydrogen sulfide"| has many effects in the human gut. On one hand it is a potent genotoxin and may contribute to the onset of colorectal cancer |CITS: [20120018]|. It can also reduce disulfide bonds in the mucus layer of the gut epithelium, disrupting its barrier function and potentially playing a role in inflammatory bowel disease |CITS: [26852376]|. On the other hand |FRAME: HS| produced by gut microbes may also act as a signaling molecule in the host, potentially leading to beneficial effects, such as cardioprotection |CITS: [27682122][27869680]|. , Searches for putative genes encoding |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.38|, in sequenced microbial genomes revealed more than 250 sequences, predominantly in Deltaproteobacteria, but also in Firmicutes, Gammaproteobacteria, and Bacteroidetes, suggesting that the pathway may be quite common |CITS: [30718429]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Phytobilins Phytobilins| are tetrapyrrole molecules that are synthesized by plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Major classes of phytobilins are:, 1. |FRAME: Phycobilins Phycobilins|, which are the chromophores of |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins| |CITS: [16663825]| and some algal phytochromes |CITS: [8616213]|, 2. |FRAME: Phytochromobilins Phytochromobilins|, which are the chromophores of higher plants |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| |CITS: [1634523][7744741]|., |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins Phycobiliproteins| are light-harvesting accessory pigments of cyanobacteria, red algae and cryptophytes, and |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| are photoreceptors that respond to red and far-red light in photosynthetic organisms., Phytochromes are dimeric proteins with each monomer covalently attached with a bilin chromophore |CITS: [16387836][20534495]|. The plant bilin chromophore, |FRAME: CPD-15004|, is synthesized from heme in the chloroplast. The assembly of phytochrome occurs in the cytoplasm., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathways for the production of the four cyanobacterial |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-3702| pathway for |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| biosynthesis, have been elucidated. These five chromophores share a common precursor, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, which is the product of heme macrocycle cleavage by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18|. |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is subsequently reduced by one of several possible ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases., The committed step in phytochromobilin biosynthesis is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18 "heme oxygenase"| (HO). Although HOs with other regiospecificities were known from bacteria and insects (see for example |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.48|), the |FRAME: TAX-3702| HOs were shown to only produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| (BV) isomer from heme |CITS: [19860740]|. BV is subsequently reduced in plants to (3Z)- and (3E)-phytochromobilin |CITS: [7744741]|. It's not clear whether the isomerization of (3Z) to (3E)-phytochromobilin is enzyme catalyzed or spontaneous., Different BV reductases with unique double bond specificities found in different organisms divert BV to distinct end products, such as |FRAME: BILIRUBIN| in mammals, |FRAME: Phycocyanobilins phycocyanobilin| and |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins phycoerythrobilin| in cyanobacteria and red algae, and |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| in plants and green algae |CITS: [11283349]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THR| is an indispensable amino acid. It is degraded by a complex network of pathways and regulatory signals |CITS: [9871012]|., Two of the major routes for the degradation of L-threonine are known to occur both in mammals and in microorganisms., In the first route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREDEHYDCAT-CPLX| (EC 4.3.1.19) to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, which is rapidly and irreversibly converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5437|). A biosynthetic version of this enzyme has also been reported in certain anaerobic bacteria (see |FRAME:ILEUSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [13405870]|., In the second route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREODEHYD-CPLX| (EC 1.1.1.103) to form |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT|, which is mainly cleaved by |FRAME: AKBLIG-CPLX|, forming glycine and acetyl-CoA (see |FRAME:THREONINE-DEG2-PWY|). In the absence of the latter activity |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT| is spontaneously converted to |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|, which is further metabolized into |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| (see |FRAME: THRDLCTCAT-PWY|)., A third route has been demonstrated in several bacteria and fungi. This route is based on the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7266| (EC 4.1.2.5), which cleaves threonine directly into |FRAME:GLY| and |FRAME:ACETALD| (see |FRAME:PWY-5436|)., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: THREODEHYD-CPLX|-based pathway is the primary route of L-threonine degradation in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. |FRAME: THREODEHYD-CPLX| catalyzes the oxidation of threonine by |FRAME:NAD| to |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT|. The later is converted by |FRAME:AKBLIG-CPLX| into glycine and acetyl-CoA |CITS: [5821726]|. The pathway is widespread in nature, and has been described in archaea |CITS: [16817900]|, bacteria |CITS: [334738]|, fungi |CITS: [6428467]|, birds |CITS: [11558922]|, and mammals |CITS: [728468]|. Threonine dehydrogenase has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS: [6780553]|, a psychrophilic Cytophaga sp. KUC-1 |CITS: [12867457]|,, |FRAME: TAX-1511| |CITS: [7763136]|, chicken liver mitochondria |CITS: [7028754]|, goat liver mitochondria |CITS: [3888978]|, and porcine liver mitochondria |CITS: [7827500]|., In a study of 75 soil bacteria capable of growth on L-threonine, the threonine dehydrogenase pathway was predominant, being the main route in 46 organisms |CITS: [5076220]|. Another study of seven bacterial genera capable of growth on L-threonine found that threonine degradation via this pathway was predominant in all cases , with glycine further metabolized to pyruvate via L-serine |CITS: [942418]|., In bacteria |FRAME:GLY| is further converted to |FRAME: SER|, which acts as a nitrogen donor, permitting the organisms to grow on threonine as the sole source for both carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [334738][6782087]|.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1392| is a Gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium that can cause serious disease and fatalities in humans, and animals. This organism produces two types of catechol siderophores under iron-limiting conditions - |FRAME: CPD-9985| and |FRAME: CPD-9984| |CITS: [17189355]| (see also |FRAME: PWY-5903|)., While most catechol siderophores, including |FRAME: CPD-9984| and |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN|, use |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| as the active building block, |FRAME: CPD-9985| chelates ferric iron through the rare 3,4-isomer of dihydroxybenzoate - |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9985| requires six genes, namely, |FRAME: G-11392|, |FRAME: G-11391|, |FRAME: G-11393|, |FRAME: G-11395|, |FRAME: G-11394| and |FRAME: G-11390|, which are located in a single operon |CITS: [17189355]|. , The proposed pathway for |FRAME: CPD-9985| biosynthesis has gone through several revisions as data became available. An initial pathway was proposed in 2007 based on analysis of mutations in |FRAME: G-11392| and |FRAME: G-11391| and the identification of intermediates accumulated by the mutants |CITS: [17189355]|. A more detailed pathway was proposed following the purification of the proteins encoded by, |FRAME: G-11393|, |FRAME: G-11395| and |FRAME: G-11394| |CITS: [17346033]|. A revised version was published after the protein encoded by |FRAME: G-11391| was purified |CITS: [18758617]|. Finally, a missing step in the pathway was filled with the isolation of |FRAME: G-11390| |CITS: [18955706][18975921]|., The three main inputs into the pathway are |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME: CIT|. Before |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| can participate in the pathway, it must be activated by adenylation and binding to |FRAME: Holo-AsbD-Proteins|, an aryl-carrier protein, in a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-11393|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14943|., The next steps of the pathway involve combining two molecules of activated |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| (in the form of |FRAME: 34-DHB-AsbD-Proteins|), one |FRAME: CPD-11479| molecule, and a second |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|. This is achieved in three steps, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-11391|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14941| and the |FRAME: G-11394|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14944|. There are two routes, depending which enzyme acts first, but routes proceed via |FRAME: CPD-11481| to |FRAME: CPD-9985| |CITS: [18758617]|., asb: anthrax siderophore biosynthesis |CITS: [14756782]|, Review: |CITS: [27425635]|

General Background, |FRAME:MALONATE Malonate| is found in small amounts in plants |CITS: [13013230]| and is produced by some bacteria |CITS: [786256]|. Most of the malonate in the environment, however, comes from industrial production. The dimethyl and diethyl forms, in particularly, are produced at more than 12,000 tons per year (1995) |CITS: [11902724]|., Several strains of bacteria are able to utilize malonate as sole source of carbon and energy. Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, In most plants, purine nucleotides are completely degraded to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| via the ureides |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|. This degradation proceeds via the intermediates |FRAME: XANTHINE| and |FRAME: URATE|., The initial step of AMP degradation is the conversion of AMP to IMP, which is converted to xanthine in two alternative routes, via |FRAME: XANTHOSINE| or |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|. , The product of this pathway, |FRAME: URATE|, is converted to to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as described in |FRAME: PWY-5691|., The plant pathway is very similar to that found in mammals. However, mammals do not have the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-11783| (EC 3.5.4.15) |CITS: [14725335]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6353|).

Summary: General Background, Polyunsaturated long- and very-long-chain fatty acids (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear. While PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants and are not synthesized by animals, they are also produced by a narrow group of predominately marine γ-proteobacteria, which includes (among others) species of the |FRAME: TAX-22|, |FRAME: TAX-657|, |FRAME: TAX-58050|, |FRAME: TAX-28228| and |FRAME: TAX-662| genera |CITS: [4197274][Johns77][16347037][16535638][11777566][12594015]|. Since these organisms are associated with growth in low temperatures and often high pressure, it has been suggested that PUFA synthesis by these organisms is an important adaptation for countering the effects of elevated hydrostatic pressure and low temperature on membrane fluidity or phase. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that in strains that have been analysed, PUFA synthesis is temperature-dependent and, for deep-sea isolates, pressure-dependent |CITS: [10671446]|., |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Eicosapentaenoate| (EPA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains five cis double bonds, one of which is located at the third carbon from the omega end, which makes it an omega-3 fatty acid. EPA is produced by microalgae and is common in fish who eat the algae, although the fish can not produce it. It is also produced by fungi, mosses and ferns, but is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. EPA is also produced by some marine bacteria |CITS: [10220156]|. The pathways used by microalgae and bacteria are completely different. In the aerobic pathway, used in mosses, saturated fatty acids synthesized by fatty acid synthase are desaturated and elongated to PUFAs in many enzymatic reactions, some of which oxygen-requiring. In the anaerobic pathway utilized by bacteria, PUFAs are anaerobically synthesized from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by PUFA synthases., About this Pathway, Even though the exact mechanism of the bacterial PUFA synthases has not been defined, it is well documented that these complexes are encoded by four or five genes |CITS: [9274025][11104010]|, which have been designated pfaEABCD |CITS: [12055309]|. The genetic structure of the PUFA biosynthetic genes consists of a four-gene operon that includes pfaABCD, while pfaE, which encodes the phosphopantetheinyl transferase required for catalytic activation of acyl carrier protein domains, may be found elsewhere in the genome |CITS: [21105981]|., PUFA synthases capable of synthesizing |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) were found in several marine bacteria including |FRAME: TAX-314092| |CITS: [11452122][8729138]| and |FRAME: TAX-298386| |CITS: [12055309]|. A synthase responsible for synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) was identified in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-90736| |CITS: [16988784]|, and a synthase capable of producing |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| was identified in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-365033| |CITS: [25263707]|., |FRAME: TAX-314092|, which was isolated from the intestinal contents of the Pacific mackerel, produces EPA as the sole polyunsaturated fatty acid, amounting to 24-40% of the total fatty acid in the cell. EPA exists as phospholipid in this organism, and was found in the sn-2 position of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE phosphatidylethanolamine| and |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE phosphatidylglycerol|. The gene cluster encoding the eicosapentaenoate synthase was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, resulting in the production of EPA |CITS: [8729138 ]|. The enzyme has been documented in a number of other bacterial strains including the deep-sea bacterium |FRAME: TAX-298386| |CITS: [12055309]| and |FRAME: TAX-211586| |CITS: [Lee06]|.

The pentitols |FRAME: RIBITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-355| are common in nature, while the pentitols |FRAME: XYLITOL| and |FRAME: L-ARABITOL| are rare or absent., Pentitols and other neutral polyols can be taken up by bacteria and serve as a carbon and energy source. Gram-negative bacteria and Actinobacteria import the polyol intact, convert them into a keto sugar by a polyol hydrogenase, and then phosphorylate the keto sugar and metabolize it via the pentose phosphate or glycolytic pathways (see |FRAME: RIBITOLUTIL-PWY||). Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1582| |CITS: [118163]| and |FRAME:TAX-33945| |CITS: [12467497]|, transport polyols into the cell using a phosphotransferase system, resulting in their phosphoylation. The polyol phosphates are then oxidized by polyol phosphate dehydrogenases (this pathway)., |FRAME: TAX-1582| strains 64H and BL23 (but not ATCC 334) are able to ferment |FRAME: RIBITOL|. The organism employes a |FRAME: CPLX-85405| system to import |FRAME: RIBITOL| into the cell. Once imported, the phosphorylated compound is oxidzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-124217| to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, which enters the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [23564164]|.

General Background, Arginase-mediated |FRAME: ARG| degradation is widely distributed in the biosphere and is found in all primary kingdoms |CITS: [8759304]|. The first step in this process, catalyzed by the enzyme arginase, is the hydrolysis of |FRAME:ARG| to form |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME:UREA|., There are many variations of the arginase pathway, since the fate of the products of the arginase reaction may be different in different organisms. Variants of arginase-based |FRAME: ARG|-degradation pathways include |FRAME: ARGASEDEG-PWY|, |FRAME:ARG-PRO-PWY|, and |FRAME: ARG-GLU-PWY|., About This Pathway, The preferred nitrogen sources of |FRAME: TAX-4932| are |FRAME: AMMONIA|, |FRAME: ASN|, and |FRAME: GLN|. However, if these sources are not available, |FRAME: TAX-4932| is able to utilize arginine as its sole nitrogen source., Earlier work has established that |FRAME: TAX-4932| converts |FRAME: ARG| via |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| to |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, which undergoes a spontaneous cyclization reaction, forming |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| (P5C). This sequence of reactions is identical to the "classical" arginase pathway (see |FRAME: ARGASEDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [14263163]|. However, while in the "classical" pathway P5C is cnoverted to |FRAME: GLT|, it was shown that in |FRAME: TAX-4932| it is converted to |FRAME: PRO| by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.2| |CITS: [6997271]|. The |FRAME: PRO| that is formed is then catabolized to |FRAME: GLT| by the normal |FRAME: PRO| degradation pathway (see |FRAME: PROUT-PWY|)., Since P5C is also an intermediate in the |FRAME: PRO| degradation pathway, it occurs twice in the path from |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: GLT|. Thus P5C can be converted to either |FRAME: GLT| (by the enzyme |FRAME: YHR037W-MONOMER|) or to |FRAME: PRO| by P5C reductase |CITS: [6997271]|. Futile cycling between |FRAME: PRO| and P5C is prevented by subcellular compartmentalization - while |FRAME: YHR037W-MONOMER| is a mitochondrial enzyme, P5C reductase is located in the cytoplasm |CITS: [7009582]|., The first two enzymes in this pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-6892| and |FRAME: YLR438W-MONOMER|, are inducible by |FRAME: ARG|. |FRAME: CPLX-6891| is constitutive, and the last two enzymes (|FRAME: YLR142W-MONOMER| and, |FRAME: YHR037W-MONOMER|) are inducible by |FRAME: PRO|., There has also been a report that the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148| utilizes the same pathway, catabolizing |FRAME: ARG| into |FRAME: PRO|, which is eventually converted to |FRAME: GLT| |CITS: [10648527]|. The authors suggest that the bacteria utilize this pathway as part of the process of conversion of the cyanobacterial storage compound cyanophycin (multi-L-arginyl-poly-L-aspartate) into |FRAME: GLN|, a preferred nitrogen source.

|FRAME: CPD-26140 "Macrocyclic archaeol"| is a rare archaeal lipid that has been reported from only a few species, including |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [17773336][6549008]|, |FRAME: TAX-667126|, and |FRAME: TAX-647113| |CITS: [Baumann18]|., The enzyme responsible for formation of macrocyclic archaeol is |FRAME: EC-1.21.98.5|. In most species it forms |FRAME: Antiparallel-GDGT-Phospholipids "glycerol dibiphytanyl glycerol tetraether phospholipids"| (GDGTs), although it has been shown that when the |FRAME: TAX-42879| or |FRAME: TAX-2214| genes encoding the enzyme were expressed in |FRAME: TAX-39152|, the recombinant enzymes formed a small amount of macrocyclic archaeol even though the compound has not been reported from these organisms |CITS: [35318330]|.,  The reaction catalyzed by the enzyme is challenging since it necessitates the coupling of two completely inert sp<sup>3</sup>-hybridized carbon centers. The enzyme is a radical SAM enzyme that contains three [Fe<sub>4</sub>S<sub>4</sub>] clusters and one mononuclear rubredoxin-like iron ion, each found in a separate domain. It forms a |FRAME: CPD-15400| and utilizes it to activate its substrate. The reaction involves an intermediate bond between the substrate carbon and a sulfur of one of the [Fe<sub>4</sub>S<sub>4</sub>] clusters |CITS: [35882349]|., The enzyme acts specifically on fully saturated substrates, following the action of |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.11|.

Names: protein N-glycosylation processing of proteins targeted for retention in cellular organelles (cis-Golgi, yeast)
Summary: General Background, N-linked glycosylation is an important process found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria., During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. It has been shown that the glycosylation is essential for the proper folding of some eukaryotic proteins., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes consists of three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7918|)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (several pathways exist, including this one)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., About This Pathway, Following the removal of the three glucosyl residues and several mannosyl residues from the |FRAME: CPD-18077 tetradecasaccharide|, the N-glycosylated proteins in the yeast ER are in the form of |FRAME: Man8GlcNAc2-protein-A123B13| |CITS: [12090241]|., Upon transfer of the proteins from the ER to the cis-Golgi, the core N-linked glycans receive an α-1,6-linked mannose by the transferase |FRAME: G3O-30552| |CITS: [1628616][8253757]|. The next phase of processing splits into two different pathways. In one pathway, which applies to cell wall proteins and periplasmic proteins, the α-1,6 mannosyl residue is extended into a very large polymer, as described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-8323|., The second pathway, described here, applies to proteins targeted for retention in cellular organelles. In this pathway the newly added α-1,6 mannosyl residue is extended by only two mannosyl residues - an α-1,2 residue, capped by an α-1,3-linked residue. While the α-1,2-mannosyltransferase remains unknown as of 2021, |FRAME: YER001W| has been identified as a GT-71 mannosyltransferase that attaches the terminal α-1,3-linked mannose |CITS: [2185468]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Brassinosteroids Brassinosteroids| are steroidal phytohormones that regulate various important physiological and developmental processes, such as cell elongation and division, pollen fertility, photomorphogenesis, differentiation of vascular elements, and stress resistance |CITS: [Mandava88][15012241]|. Brassinosteroids, which have structural similarity to |FRAME: ECDYSONE|, the molting hormone of insects, are C27, C28 and C29 steroids depending on their C-24 alkyl substituents. More than 70 free, naturally occurring brassinosteroids have been identified in plants. The C28 brassinosteroid |FRAME: CPD-697| (BL) is the most biologically active and together with its C28 congeners is distributed widely in the plant kingdom |CITS:[15012241]|., The biosynthesis pathway of brassinolide was initially elucidated using cultured |FRAME:TAX-4058| cells. Extensive metabolic studies suggested that brassinosteroids biosynthesis occurs along a metabolic grid where broad substrate specificities of the participating enzymes allow metabolite flow via multiple pathways, depending on the order in which the enzymes act. Two such pathways, named the early and late C-6 oxidation pathways, were the first to be described |CITS: [9121728][10982435][14502988]| (see |FRAME:PWY-699|). A third route, named the early C-22 oxidation branch (depicted here) was also demonstrated |CITS:[12376657]|., The existence of this alternative biosynthesis branch has been postulated from the study of the Arabidopsis thaliana sax1 (|FRAME: AT5G05690|) and det2 (|FRAME: AT2G38050|) mutants. The sax1 phenotype could be rescued by application of synthetic |FRAME: CPD-3945| and |FRAME: CPD-3946|, compounds that were later detected in planta |CITS:[12376657][11489171]|. This complementation could also occur in the dark, suggesting that the C22α-hydroxy pathway is active in dark conditions |CITS: [10377996]|., The Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT3G50660| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: AT3G50660-MONOMER|, was subsequently cloned |CITS: [11319239][11489171]|, as were the |FRAME: AT4G36380| and |FRAME: AT3G13730| genes, which encode redundantly functioning (22S)-22-hydroxysteroid 23-monooxygenases |CITS: [17138693]|., In vitro kinetic analysis of |FRAME: AT3G50660| showed that |FRAME: CPD-707| is its major substrate (the catalytic efficiency (Kcat/Km) for |FRAME: CPD-707| was 325 times higher than that for |FRAME: CPD-710| |CITS: [16460510]|), suggesting that the C-22 hydroxylation branch is the main route of brassinosteroid biosynthesis in plants (at least in Arabidopsis) |CITS: [16460510]|. This conclusion was supported by a later study that performed detailed kinetic analysis of |FRAME: AT5G05690| and |FRAME: AT2G38050| |CITS: [22822057]|., As of 2021, several reaction steps remain unelucidated: the enzymes forming |FRAME: CPD-698| from |FRAME: CPD-707|, the 3-dehydrogenase converting |FRAME: CPD-709| to |FRAME: CPD-710|, the C-6 oxidation step of |FRAME: CPD-710|, |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.M54|, and |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.M2| |CITS: [30363110]|.

Summary: |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN "Riboflavin"| is the precursor for the essential flavin cofactors |FRAME:FMN| and |FRAME:FAD|, which are used in a wide variety of redox reactions. Riboflavin is also known as vitamin B2, because it is an essential nutrient and can not be synthesized by mammals., The biosynthesis of one riboflavin molecule requires one molecule of |FRAME: GTP| and two molecules of, |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| as substrates., The imidazole ring of GTP is hydrolytically opened, yielding a 4, 5-diaminopyrimidine which is converted to, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| by a sequence of deamination, side chain reduction, and dephosphorylation. Condensation of |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| with, |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-BUTANONE-P| obtained from |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| results in the formation of, |FRAME: DIMETHYL-D-RIBITYL-LUMAZINE|., Dismutation of the lumazine derivative yields |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN| and, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE|, which is recycled in the pathway |CITS: [10940330]|., The riboflavin biosynthesis pathway and its enzymes are well understood, although the enzymes catalyzing the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-1086| has been identified only recently |CITS: [24123841]|. , Several bifunctional enzymes are involved in this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-1423|., One bifunctional enzyme catalyzes the two steps required for converting |FRAME: DIAMINO-OH-PHOSPHORIBOSYLAMINO-PYR| to |FRAME: CPD-1086|. Another such enzyme catalyzes the last two steps of the pathway, |FRAME:ENZRXN-16078| and |FRAME:ENZRXN-16079|., In addition, in both |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |FRAME: CPLX8J2-124| is a bifunctional enzyme complex, that catalyzes the two steps leading from |FRAME:AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| and, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-BUTANONE-P| to |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN| via |FRAME:DIMETHYL-D-RIBITYL-LUMAZINE|., This complex consists of a core of three α subunits and 60 β subunits arranged in an icosahedral, capsid around the α trimer in the central core |CITS: [7473709]|., Different variations of the pathway are found in the different kingdoms of life., The enzymes catalyzing the fungal pathway are similar to the bacterial/plant ones, but there is a difference in the order in which they act. Two enzymatic steps are required to convert |FRAME: DIAMINO-OH-PHOSPHORIBOSYLAMINO-PYR| to |FRAME: CPD-1086| - a demaination and a reduction., In bacteria and plants, the deaminase acts first, followed by the reductase (although both steps are catalyzed by a single, bifunctional enzyme in some organisms) |CITS: [15208317]|, while in fungi the reductase acts first, followed by the deaminase (see |FRAME: PWY-6168|). The archaeal pathway also differs in several steps (see |FRAME: PWY-6167|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that is abundant in many vegetable oils, especially safflower and sunflower oils. It is an essential dietary requirement for all mammals, that lack the Δ12 desaturase that produces it. A few animals are able to synthesize |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6001|., Linoleate is an ω-6 fatty acid, referring to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid., In all plant tissues, the major glycerolipids are first synthesized using only palmitoyl (16:0) and oleoyl (18:1) acyl groups, the products of plastidic saturated fatty acid synthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5971|, |FRAME: PWY-5989| and |FRAME: PWY-5147|). Subsequent desaturation of the fatty acids to the highly unsaturated forms typical of the membranes of plant cells is carried while they are already attached to lipids., About This Pathway, Most of the oleoyl-[acp] is released from the [acp]-moiety and exported from the plastid to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and is converted to |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA| in the process by the plastidic |FRAME: AT1G77590-MONOMER|. The |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA| is incorporated into lipids, forming |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE phosphatidylglycerols|, |FRAME: Diacylglycerides diglycerides|, and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholines|., Further desaturation of the oleoyl groups to linoleoyl groups in the ER occurrs while incorporated into lipids, and is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.22||, encoded by the |FRAME: AT3G12120| gene., A smaller portion of the oleoyl-[acp] molecules can be incorporated into |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE phosphatidylglycerols| and |FRAME: Diacylglycerides diglycerides| within the chloroplast. In this case, the desaturation to |FRAME: Linoleoyl-groups| occurs by a plastidic desaturase (|FRAME: EC-1.14.19.23|), which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-10795| gene., Envelope membranes isolated from chloroplasts of spinach (|FRAME: TAX-3562|) could desaturate oleoyl groups in monogalactosyl diacylglycerol to linoleoyl groups. The desaturation required NADPH in combination with ferredoxin, and was also observed with other biosynthetic intermediates such as phosphatidates |CITS: [11607123]|.

|FRAME:TAX-65409| (Baikal skullcap), a species of the Lamiacea family, belongs to the 50 most important medicinal herbs used in traditional Chinese medicine. Especially the roots of this plant are rich on flavones which are characteristic tracer compounds in |FRAME:TAX-4139| plants. The flavone aglycones and glucuronides |FRAME:CPD-12725|, |FRAME:CPD-12724|, |FRAME:CPD-12728| and |FRAME:CPD-12727| (see |FRAME:PWY-7213|) are the most extensively studied flavones from |FRAME:TAX-4139| and have shown interesting pharmacological properties |CITS: [20708926]|. |FRAME:CPD-12724 Baicalein| is more effective than |FRAME:CPD-12725| and has demonstrated antibacterial |CITS:[7312987]|, antiviral |CITS:[1313232]| and anticancer |CITS:[9066718]| properties. In addition |FRAME:CPD-12724| was shown to stimulate the chloride secretion in marine vertebrates |CITS:[8390669]| and activates transcription factors involved in signaling pathways |CITS:[23339711]|. , The metabolism of |FRAME:CPD-12724| comprises 7-O-glucurosylation |CITS:[10724177]|, deglucuronidation |CITS:[Morimoto95]|, |CITS:[8593473]|, |CITS: [10858442]| |CITS:[Zhang05]| and 7-O-glucosylation |CITS:[10872235]| reactions. Notably, the baicalin glucurosidase will generate more |FRAME:CPD-12724|, which is usually present in |FRAME:TAX-4139| at much lower concentrations than |FRAME:CPD-12725| and might be a first plant defense response to deter pathogens |CITS:[20708926]|. Moreover, it appears that the baicalin glucurosidase reaction is involved in a novel |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| detoxification pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-7214|).

|FRAME: D-tagatose| is a ketohexose that is a C-4 epimer of D-fructose. It is a low-calorie natural sugar present in small amounts in fruits and milk products, and can replace sucrose in food, since their taste, cooking, and texture properties are very similar. Its low glycemic index and its antihyperglycemic effect make D-tagatose a promising sweetener., Some bacterial species are able to use |FRAME: D-tagatose| as a carbohydrate source by transporting into the cell by phosphotransferase uptake systems |CITS: [15257457][23524682]|. The resulting |FRAME: CPD-23692| is then phosphorylated again by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.234|, and the product is split by |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.40|, forming the glycolytic intermediates |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|. The pathway was originally demonstrated in Gram-negative enteric bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-571|, |FRAME: TAX-573|, and |FRAME: TAX-28901| |CITS: [1525745]|, but later shown to exist in some Gram-positive bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1402| |CITS: [23524682]|., |FRAME: D-tagatose| exists primarily in the pyranose form in solution |CITS: [Freimund96]|, and its 1-phosphorylated form was also shown to exist primarily in a pyranose form |CITS: [26159072]|. However, only the furanose form can be phosphorylated at the C6 position. Thus it has been proposed that the kinase TagK binds its substrate in a pyranose form, but its mechanism involves opening of the ring and formation of a furanose structure prior to the phosphorylation |CITS: [26159072]|.

General Background, In general, the majority of betacyanins are derived from |FRAME: CPD-8652| (cyclo-DOPA, see pathway |FRAME:PWY-5399|) |CITS: [12620337][16669781]|. However, there are few exceptions that have demonstrated the alternative route , of betacyanins derived from catecholamine dopamine such as |FRAME: CPD-8854| and derivatives thereof , |CITS: [PIATTELLI70][10198080]|., Betaxanthins have been reported to be biosynthesized via dopamine (|FRAME:PWY-5426|, |FRAME:PWY-5403|) , and a existing competition of the pigment pathways and the dopamine biosynthesis in response to light has been , reported |CITS: [Endress84]|. Dopamine-derived betacyanins |CITS: [11261575]|, for example 2-descarboxybetanidin has to share parts , with those betaxanthin pathways indicating interconnected biosyntheses. Nevertheless, although those compounds , are rare and only minor betalains in plants they represent the only aglycones among the usually glucosylated and/or , acylated betacyanins |CITS: [12620337]|. , About This Pathway, Tyrosinases have been shown to accept L-Dopa and dopamine catalyzing the formation , of dopaquinone and dopaminequinone, respectively |CITS: [Mueller96]|. The subsequent cyclization to 2-descarboxy-cyclo-dopa , and condensation with betalamic acid to 2-descarboxy-betanidin is non-enzymatic |CITS: [10198080]|, the latter , standing for the decisive step in that biosynthesis.

Fungal peptidyl alkaloids derived from the nonproteinogenic β-amino acid |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| are secondary metabolites produced predominantly in the fungi family Aspergillaceae |CITS:[22064917]|. Indole alkaloids produced by fungi such as fumiquinazoline (see |FRAME:PWY-7542|) , acetylaszonalenin (see |FRAME:PWY-7532|) and ardeemins (this pathway) exhibit interesting biological activities which triggers in-depth research of this molecules in the fields of pharmacology, biochemistry and molecular biology and guided efforts for the total synthesis of such alkaloids, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-16985| |CITS:[19007134]| . Ardeemins are named after their displayed properties, i.e. Ability to Reverse Drug insensitivity |CITS:[23330675]|. |FRAME:CPD-16986 N-acetylardeemin| and other intermediates of the pathway have been shown to be promising assets for cancer research as potential therapeutics because they reverse effects on multi-drug resistant cancer cells |CITS:[8478256] [24858827] [24443428]| by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein-mediated drug efflux |CITS:[10397452]|. This results, for instance, in a more than 700-fold sensitization towards vinca antitumor alkaloids |CITS:[9653193]|. , The three gene biosynthetic gene cluster (ardABC) for |FRAME:PWY-7543| has been identified in Neosartorya fischeri and two of the three genes have been genetically and biochemically characterized |CITS:[23330675]|. The starting reaction of the pathway, i.e. the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16984| from the nonproteinogenic β-amino acid |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and the proteinogenic amino acids |FRAME:TRP| and |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is catalyzed by the trimodular nonribosomal synthetase (NPRS) encoded by ardA. ArdA has been identified using the specific code of the anthranilate-activating module for NPRS's |CITS:[20225828]|. The formed product |FRAME:CPD-16984| is a regioisomer of |FRAME:CPD-16968| produced in the |FRAME:PWY-7542|. Although both NPRS's use the exact same set of nonproteinogenic and proteinogenic amino acids different compounds are produced which has been proposed to be due to a changed amino acid residue binding sequence and the epimerization of |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| in the E domain of module 2 of ardA which changes the L- amino acid to its D-configuration |CITS:[23330675]|. The following prenylation step is catalyzed by the ardeemin FQ prenylase (ardB) which formed the hexacyclic |FRAME:CPD-16985| via an allylic cation at the C-2 of the indole moiety of the tryptophan side-chain of |FRAME:CPD-16984| |CITS:[23330675]|. The enzyme for the last step, a putative acetyltransferase has not yet been biochemically characterized, but the product of this enzymatic reaction, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16986| has been found in biochemical assays carried out with the fully functional gene cluster indicating its probable molecular function. In addition, ardC has been found to share high amino acid homology with the aszonalenin acetyltransferase (AnaAT) in the, with regard to compound structures and enzymatic conversions, closely related |FRAME:PWY-7532| |CITS:[23330675]|.

Many bacterial species can ferment |FRAME: PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| via several intermediate compounds,, including |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|, |FRAME: CPD-10353|, and |FRAME: DIACETYL|.  Not all species carry the process all the way through - some may stop earlier, accumulating some of the intermediates. Thus this pathway only describes the production of |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| from |FRAME: CPD-10353|. Pathways leading to the production of |FRAME: ACETOIN| are described in |FRAME: Acetoin-Biosynthesis|., |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| is of commercial interest, mostly as an antifreeze agent due to to its low freezing point and high boiling point |CITS: [Magee87]|.  One of its well known applications is the formation of methyl ethyl ketone, by dehydration, which can be used as a liquid fuel additive |CITS: [11234948]|., The metabolic function of 2,3-butanediol is not yet known, although it may play a role in preventing intracellular, acidification by changing the metabolism from acid production to the formation of a neutral compound, |CITS: [6298028]|.  In addition, the pathway might participate in regulation of the NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio, in the bacteria |CITS: [8444801]|., There are three isomeric forms of 2,3-butanediol (BD ) - |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|, |FRAME: CPD-346| and |FRAME: CPD-12004|, and two isomeric forms of acetoin - |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: CPD-255|., The conversion of acetoin to 2,3-butanediol, which is reversible, is performed by the enzyme acetoin reductase (AR), also known as 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenase (BDH). , 4 types of AR activities have been identified, differing in substrate specificity; a R-acetoin reductase forming, |FRAME: CPD-12004|, an S-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: CPD-12004|, an S-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: CPD-346|, and an R-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| |CITS: [Ui84]|., Several enzymes have been shown to form |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| from |FRAME: CPD-10353| |CITS: [13837186]|. Such enzymes have been reported in several organisms, including the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-442|, |FRAME: TAX-1406| and |FRAME: TAX-554| |CITS: [25056]| and the baker's yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|. The enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1406|  |CITS: [25056]| and |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [2222122]| were purified and characterized.

Summary: Caffeine, 1,3,7-trimethylxanthine, is one of the best known purine alkaloids and also the most abundant one in nature, followed by theobromine, the immediate precursor of caffeine (3,7-dimethylxanthine) |CITS: [14977593]|. Caffeine presents , in high concentrations in many coffea plants and tea plants. It can accumulate up to 2% dry weight in seeds and young expanding leaves of Coffea arabica, and up to 3% dry weight in young leaves of tea (|FRAME:TAX-4442|). The exact physiological role of endogenous purine alkaloids in plants is undetermined. Their hypothetic roles include being a defense chemical where high concentrations of caffeine accumulated in young leaves, fruits and flower buds help protect these soft tissues from predators, or being an autotoxic chemical where caffeine released from seed coats into the soil inhibits germination of other seeds. However there is little evidence supports the hypothesis., The depicted pathway herein illustrates the major route of caffeine biosynthesis, from xanthosine. It involves three SAM-dependent N-methyltransferase activities, namely xanthosine N-methyltransferase, 7-methylxanthine N-methyltransferase, and theobromine N-methyltransferase. 7-methylxanthosine synthase of coffee was shown have the specific xanthosine N-methyltransferase activity. It specifically converts xanthosine to 7-methylxanthosine (the first methylation step). XMP is not an effective substrate. Theobromine synthase has also been characterized from coffee which has the specific 7-methylxanthine N-methyltransferase activity. It converts 7-methylxanthine to theobromine (the second methylation step). Caffeine synthase has been characterized from both coffee and tea. Caffeine synthase is a dual function enzyme. It has both the 7-methylxanthine N-methyltransferase and the theobromine N-methyltransferase activities. It converts 7-methylxanthine to theobromine and theobromine to caffeine, the second and the third methylation steps. Immature fruits are the major sites of caffeine biosynthesis in coffee plants, where high levels of transcripts of genes encoding the three methyltransferation activities are also found |CITS: [12746542]|.  , Free purine nucleotides are the major resources of xanthosine. Xanthosine is derived from salvage of adenine and guanine nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-6607|). Newly synthesized IMP from de novo purine biosynthesis, and adenosine released from the SAM cycle (see |FRAME: PWY-5041|) may also be converted to xanthosine and enter the caffeine biosynthesis pathway.  , In addition to the major route, caffeine may also be synthesized via a few minor routes such as from 7-methylxanthine via paraxanthine (see |FRAME: PWY-5038|).

Summary: The arginine deiminase (ADI) pathway is widely distributed among prokaryotic organisms. It has been detected in many organisms, including lactic bacteria |CITS: [10359490][10733246][15939575]|, Bacilii |CITS: [4436643][690081]|, |FRAME:TAX-286| species |CITS: [6438064][3129535]|, |FRAME:TAX-642| species |CITS: [6303241]|, Clostridia |CITS: [12999794][5335895]|, |FRAME:TAX-2093| secies |CITS: [5911610][126306][6438064][3806049]|, Sterptococci |CITS: [2843090][12406748]|, |FRAME:TAX-2132| secies |CITS: [Igwebe78]|, Spirochaetes |CITS: [977548]|, and cyanobacteria |CITS: [100070]|. It was also demonstrated in the halophylic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2242| |CITS: [5903088]|., In addition, the pathway is also present in some primitive eukaryotic protozoans, including |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [6312311]|, |FRAME: TAX-56690| |CITS: [7866382]|, |FRAME: TAX-28002| |CITS: [12706792]|, and |FRAME: TAX-5741|, in which it plays a significant role in energy metabolism, providing a route for anaerobic substrate level phosphorylation |CITS: [2228433]|. , The enzymes of this pathway have also been found in |FRAME: ORG-5993|, and it was shown that |FRAME:TAX-3701| chloroplasts can metabolize arginine and citrulline all the way to CO2. However, since |FRAME:TAX-3701|, rarely encounters exogenous arginine or citrulline, it is assumed that in this organism this pathway may serve as a means for extracting nitrogen from endogenous sources |CITS: [8278506]|., Organisms that employ this pathway use the enzyme arginine deiminase to convert arginine to |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. Citrulline is degraded further (see |FRAME: CITRULLINE-DEG-PWY|), forming ATP, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, and |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| |CITS: [8759859] [10733246]|. The arginine deiminase pathway provides the organisms with energy, carbon, and nitrogen. In addition, it has been suggested that the pathway can also protect some bacteria from acidic conditions, by the production of ammonia., Indeed, the arginine deiminase system can function at very low pH. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-2133| FA-1, the pH at which arginolysis was reduced to 10% of the maximum was between 2.1 and 2.6, or more than 1 full pH unit below the minimum for glycolysis (pH 3.7), and more than 2 units below the minimum for growth in complex medium (pH 4.7) |CITS: [2843090]|. The arginine deiminase pathway is thought to be a critical factor in oral biofilm pH homeostasis that may inhibit the emergence of a cariogenic flora |CITS: [11094270]|., The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway are often found in an operon, which may also include the arcD gene, encoding a membrane-bound arginine-ornithine antiporter, as well as a putative aminopeptidase-encoding arcT gene and a regulator-encoding arcR gene |CITS: [1311296][9696763][12450828]|.
