Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathway derives in part from the central metabolic precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from oxaloacetate, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here differs from other pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotides de novo biosynthesis pathways by including the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.30 "dCTP deaminase (dUMP-forming) (EC 3.5.4.30)"|, an archaeal enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of dCTP to dUMP in one step. Most organisms catalyze this conversion in two steps, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.13 "dCTP deaminase (EC 3.5.4.13)"| and |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.23 "dUTP diphosphatase (EC 3.6.1.23)"|, as can be seen in |FRAME: PWY-7187|., The enzyme, which releases dUMP, ammonia, and pyrophosphate, has been discovered in the methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [12538648]|.

Summary: Pyrimidine, purine, and pyridine nucleotide synthesis all require phosphoribosylpyrophosphate (PRPP) as a precursor.  PRPP is utilized by both the de novo pathways and the auxiliary or salvage pathways by which endogenously formed or exogenously added pyrimidine, purine, or pyridine bases are converted to the corresponding ribonucleoside monophosphates by phosphoribosyltransferases. PRPP is also used in the histidine and tryptophan biosynthesis pathways. PRPP thus may be regarded as a precursor for the synthesis of nucleic acids, proteins, and for the NAD(P) coenzymes. The formation of PRPP therefore is subjected to strict metabolic control |CITS:[3009477]|.

β-Alanine is a naturally occurring β-amino acid found in animals, plants |CITS: [5762452]|, and , microorganisms. It differs from L-alanine (an α-amino acid) in the position of the amino group on the , β carbon, rather than the α carbon. In the pathway shown here, β-alanine is converted to , malonate semialdehyde by transamination of pyruvate to L-alanine, in a pyruvate-dependent reaction. , α-Ketoglutarate (2-oxoglutarate) cannot be substituted for pyruvate |CITS: [13712439]|. Malonate , semialdehyde is then converted to acetyl-CoA and CO2 in an oxidative decarboxylation step. Both , of the enzymes have been purified and characterized |CITS: [13712439]| and their reactions have been established , as the route of β-alanine degradation in this organism |CITS: [13712439]|. These authors demonstrated , stoichiometric quantities of malonate semialdehyde and L-alanine formed from β-alanine and pyruvate; and , acetyl-CoA and CO2 formed from malonate semialdehyde and CoA., In the malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase reaction, the authors noted that this enzyme simultaneously catalyzes , the dehydrogenation and decarboxylation of malonate semialdehyde to a thioester CoA derivative. However, their , data ruled out acetaldehyde and malonyl-CoA as free intermediates, as well as the participation of a malonyl , semialdehyde-CoA intermediate |CITS: [13712439]|. Therefore, intermediates in this reaction are hypothetical. The , formation of CO2 was demonstrated using β-alanine-1-C14. Radioactive , CO2 was formed from the carbonyl carbon of malonate semialdehyde |CITS: [13712439]|. Using the , same strain of P. fluorescens, β-alanine degradation was shown to be an inducible pathway when , P. fluorescens was grown with β-alanine as a sole carbon and nitrogen source. The two reactions were , identified as EC 2.6.1.18 and EC 1.2.1.18 |CITS: [5489438]|., Unlike L-alanine, β-alanine is not incorporated into proteins. In microorganisms and plants, β-alanine is , used in the biosynthesis of the vitamin pantothenate which is then used for coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein , biosynthesis. Animals lack this pathway and must obtain the vitamin in their diet. In microorganisms, β-alanine , is generally synthesized by decarboxylation of L-aspartate |CITS: [6767707]|., It should be noted that the strain of P. fluorescens in which this β-alanine degradation pathway was , extensively studied |CITS: [13712439]| has been classified as P. putida by the American Type Culture , Collection (ATCC) under deposit number 11250., A mammalian pathway for β-alanine degradation in rat liver is described in MetaCyc pathway β-alanine , degradation I.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-14866 Quercetagetin| is the 6-hydroxylated derivative of |FRAME:CPD-520|. Although |FRAME:CPD-14866| itself is not utilized by any enzyme of this pathway it signifies the pathway that branches off the |FRAME:PWY-7150| by introducing a hydroxyl group to the 6-position (A-ring) of the flavonol |FRAME:CPD-520| |CITS:[Ibrahim05]| |CITS:[Ibrahim89]|. The polymethylated |FRAME:CPD-14866| glucoside pathway accumulates four major glucosides in |FRAME:TAX-36749| |FRAME:CPD-14886| and |FRAME:CPD-14887| and the two main glucosides of the pathway, i.e. the 2'-hydroxy derived |FRAME:CPD-14863| and |FRAME:CPD-14864| |CITS:[Collins81a]|. The intermediate metabolites are below the detection limit in the corresponding plant tissues which required meticulous in vitro experiments to characterize their biosynthesis. , The formation of the polymethylated |FRAME:CPD-14866| glucosides are carried out in a coordinated and highly ordered sequence. The first committed step of this pathway is the 6-hydroxylation of partial methylated quercetins such as |FRAME:345-TRIHYDROXY-37-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE| and |FRAME:CPD-10510| |CITS:[11068865]| |CITS:[15596008]| which established the |FRAME:CPD-14866| character of the compounds. A series of 3'-, (|CITS: [DE82]| |CITS:[3994393]|) 6, (|CITS: [DE82]| |CITS:[3994393]|) and 4'-O-specific methyltransferases (|CITS:[3994393]| |CITS:[3994394]|) lead to |FRAME:CPD-14856| which is a metabolite that stands between the quercetagetins of the upstream and the 2'-hydroxy quercetagetins of the downstream portion of the pathway. The catalytic action of the putative 2'-monooxygenase, which remains to be characterized, yields |FRAME:CPD-14861| which in turn is the starting metabolite to produce |FRAME:CPD-14863| and |FRAME:CPD-14864| in either a catalytic sequence of 3'-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[16663104]| |CITS:[Latchinian87]| |CITS:[6236078]| followed by a 2'-O-specific methyltransferase |CITS:[Khouri87]| or a metabolic sequence that proceeds vice versa. All of the above enzymes are highly substrate- and position-specific catalyzing only the corresponding A-, (6) and B-ring (2',3',4') positions and exclusively accept only the respective di-, tri-, tetra-, or pentamethylated flavonols. , The final polymethylated glucosides of |FRAME:CPD-520| could be localized in the cell walls of leaf epidermal and mesophyll cells utilizing immunofluorescence |CITS:[Lamoureux86]| |CITS:[Brisson86]|, immunogold labeling |CITS:[Marchand87]| and electron microscope observations |CITS:[Charest86]|. Immunogold labeling was also employed to pinpoint the location of the 3'-O-glucosyltransferase to the periplasmic region of cells, which appears to be loosely associated with membrane structures and vesicles of ER |CITS:[1832846]|. The highly coordinated and stepwise sequence of methylation, hydroxylation and glucosylation of the pathway as well as the location of final products prompted the proposal of a multienzyme system. This multienzyme complex is localized at the ER where the pathway is executed and from which vesicles transport and eventually excrete the final products into or near the cell wall |CITS:[Ibrahim87]|. , Note regarding the numbering of the B-ring, The usual consecutive numeration of the C-atoms of the B-ring is clockwise, starting on the C-atom connected to the side-chain. The 3'- and 5'-position are similar as they are both in meta-position to the side-chain. However, when the 2'-position is substituted the 3'-position is often designated as 5'-position in the literature. In order to maintain consistency and to avoid confusion all compounds and enzymes of the pathway are depicted and named according to the consecutive, clockwise numeration of the B-ring whether or not the 2'-position is substituted, i.e. 3' is not replaced by 5' in neither structure nor naming.

|FRAME: CPD-10437 "Dimethyl sulfone"| is a major product of the chemical oxidation in the atmosphere of the principal biogenic sulfur gas,, |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS). It is also produced by enzymatic oxidation of DMS (see |FRAME: PWY-6059|)., Several methylophilic organisms can utilize |FRAME: CPD-10437| as the only carbon and energy substrate, |CITS: [10896224]|., Three such organisms, namely |FRAME: TAX-121291|, |FRAME: TAX-121292| and |FRAME: TAX-121290|, have been isolated, based on this ability. These organism possess a |FRAME: MONOMER-14331| enzyme that reduces |FRAME: CPD-10437| to, |FRAME: DMSO| (DMSO)., Reduction of DMSO to |FRAME: CPD-7670| is followed by monooxygenation to produce |FRAME: CPD-7671| and, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6047|), which is incorporated into the cell carbon. The |FRAME: CPD-7671|, is oxidized to yield a second molecule of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. The sulfide that is produced is oxidized to sulfate,, and used as a sulfur source for biosynthesis |CITS: [11807567]|.

|FRAME: INDICAN Indican| is the β-D-glucoside of |FRAME: INDOXYL|, and is found in several plant families, the most important being Acanthaceae, Asclepiadaceae, Apocynaceae, Fabaceae, and Polygonaceae. The function of |FRAME: INDICAN| in plants is still unknown., After enzymic or chemical hydrolysis, |FRAME: INDICAN| can converted back to |FRAME: INDOXYL|, which can spontaneously dimerize (in the presence of oxygen) to |FRAME: CPD-10525|. Indigo was one of the most important dye compounds in the past, and is still an esteemed dye today., The pathway for |FRAME: PWY-6068| diverts from that of |FRAME: TRP| at |FRAME: INDOLE|, which is produced from |FRAME: INDOLE-3-GLYCEROL-P| by the |FRAME: MONOMER-3561|. Indole is converted by dioxygenase systems (enzyme complexes that form cis-dihydrodiols) to |FRAME: CPD-10523|, which spontaneously eliminate a water molecule to form |FRAME: INDOXYL|. While dioxygenase enzymes from the plants that are konwn to produce |FRAME: CPD-10525| have not been studied yet, bacterial enzymes, such as |FRAME:CPLX-7256| from |FRAME: TAX-303|, have been used successfully for the production of |FRAME: INDICAN| in strain of |FRAME:TAX-562| engineered to produce |FRAME: CPD-10525| |CITS: [6353574]|., In the plant, |FRAME: INDOXYL| is converted to |FRAME: INDICAN| by |FRAME: MONOMER-14292|. This enzyme has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-222567| |CITS: [10680172]| and |FRAME: TAX-96455| |CITS: [10795317]|. However, as mentioned above, in the absence of this enzyme |FRAME: INDOXYL| can dimerize spontaneously to |FRAME: CPD-10525|.

Summary: |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE "Androst-4-ene-3,17-dione"| (androstenedione) is a key intermediate of microbial steroid metabolism. It is a naturally occurring steroid hormone produced in the gonad or ovary, and an immediate precursor of |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| in males and |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRONE| in females |CITS: [18329874]|. , The compound was first isolated in 1931 from a male policeman's urine and named androsterone (andro = male, ster = sterol, one = ketone) |CITS: [Butenandt34]|. The chemical structure of androsterone was reported soon after |CITS: [Ruzicka34]|., The pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| was proposed already in 1968 based on analysis of the compounds produced in culture of testosterone-grown |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [Coulter68]|. , |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE "Androst-4-en-3,17-dione"| undergoes Δ1-dehydrogenation followed by a 9α-hydroxylation to produce |FRAME: CPD-13680|, an unstable compound that rearranges spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-13708|, a structure that misses the B ring., The opening of the A ring is achieved by the successive actions of a hydroxylase that hydroxylates the C4 position and a meta-cleavage dioxygenase that opens the ring |CITS: [11739769]|. A hydrolase (|FRAME: G185E-7847|) then breaks the product into two parts - |FRAME: CPD-13711| (which still contains the intact C and D rings) and |FRAME: CPD-13712| |CITS: [12676694][16151114]|. The latter is believed to be processed by three enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-14747|, |FRAME: G-14748| and |FRAME: G-14749|, into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [16151114]|., The degradation of the last two steroid rings, starting with |FRAME: CPD-13711|, was shown to begin with the removal of the side chain in the form of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by one β-oxidation cycle |CITS:[Lee67][Miclo90][Miclo92]| in a process that involves the |FRAME: G185E-7838| and |FRAME: G-14760| genes |CITS: [21901092][23146019]|. However, the complete pathway was described only in 2017 |CITS: [28377529]|. The genes involved in this part of the pathway are regulated by the KstR2 regulator. The 5-member D ring is first hydrolyzed by an enoyl-CoA hydratase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7827| gene, followed by hydrolysis of the 6-member C ring by a hydrolase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7828| and |FRAME: G185E-7829| genes |CITS: [29581275]|. Following another round of β-oxidation, which results in the release of another |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, the remaining product is split into |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [28377529]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamin-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., |FRAME: THIAMINE Thiamine| is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., Thiamin biosynthesis is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-6893|)., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the synthesis of the pyrimidine moiety of |FRAME: THIAMINE|. Starting with |FRAME: 5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-5-AMINOIMIDAZOLE|, an intermdiate in purine biosynthesis, two enzymatic steps, catalyzed by |FRAME: THIC-MONOMER "ThiC"| and |FRAME: HMP-P-KIN-CPLX "ThiD"|, produce |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP|., The first reaction is one of the most complicated rearrangement reactions known. The ThiC enzyme belongs to the radical SAM family, all members of which utilize |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) to generate an 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical that in turn serves as an oxidant for a wide variety of enzymatic reactions |CITS: [18953358]|. The first stage of catalysis is the reduction of SAM to produce |FRAME: MET| and a 5-deoxyadenosyl radical, which is generated at the active site. The radical reacts directly with the substrate to catalyze a complex rearrangement reaction that includes two iterative hydrogen atom abstractions (which necessitates the regeneration of the radical following the first abstraction). C1' and C3' of the substrate, which are not inorporated into the product, are converted to formate and carbon monoxide, respectively |CITS: [20886485]|., The second enzyme, ThiD, is a simple kinase. It is a bifunctional enzyme, and can also phosphorylate |FRAME: HMP|, as a part of a thiamin salvage pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6897|) |CITS: [14973012]|.

Summary: General Background, The pentavalent organic arsenical |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE| (MMAV) is currently used as an herbicide on cotton fields or for postemergence control of crabgrass and other turf weeds in the United States |CITS: [28936873]|. |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE "Methylarsonate| has been shown to be reduced by bacteria, producing the highly toxic |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| (MMAIII) |CITS: [21272184]|., |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE "Methylarsonous acid"| is also generated in vivo by methylation of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.137| (see |FRAME: PWY-8266|). The enzyme, which is named ArsM in prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbes and AS3MT in animals, can catalyze one to three methylations of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and its initial product is |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| |CITS: [16102566]|., It has been proposed that organisms produced |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| as a primitive antibiotic before the atmosphere became oxidizing. In today's oxidizing atmosphere the compound is oxidized spontaneously to the relatively nontoxic |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE|. However, even today some soil organisms have been shown to reduce |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE| back to |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, continually regenerating the toxic species |CITS: [21272184]|., Organisms have developed several ways to cope with the toxicity of |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, including its export, oxidation, and cleavage of the carbon-arsenic bond., About This Pathway, An enzyme catalyzing the cleavage of the arsenic-carbon bond in certain trivalent organic arsenical compounds has been described from |FRAME: TAX-1501233|, a bacterium isolated from a Florida golf course soil. The gene encoding the enzyme was identified as |FRAME: G-80527|, a gene previously reported from arsenic resistance operons, although its function has not been known |CITS: [24821808]|. , The enzyme is a nonheme iron-dependent dioxygenase that can break the carbon-arsenic bond. When expressed in an arsenic-hypersensitive strain of |FRAME: TAX-562|, the organism acquired the ability to demethylate the compound, resulting in |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| resistance. Purified recombinant ArsI catalyzed Fe2+-dependent |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| demethylation, and could cleave the C-As bond in several other trivalent aromatic arsenicals, including |FRAME: CPD-22656|, |FRAME: CPD-24364| and |FRAME: CPD-24366| |CITS: [24821808]|., ArsI homologs are widely distributed in prokaryotes.

General Background, The biosynthesis of several important metabolites involves the consumption of |FRAME: MET| through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), in a reaction that releases |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA). , These metabilites include polyamines (see |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME:BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-1303|), |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|), and bacterial auto-inducers (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration is tightly regulated. Several pathways that recycle MTA back to |FRAME: MET| have been described., A pathway known as the universal methionine salvage pathway (|FRAME: PWY-4361|) is present with some variations in almost all eukaryotes and some bacteria |CITS: [19946895]|. However, a limiting factor to the distribution of that pathway is that it contains an oxygen-requiring step (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|), and is thus present only in aerobic organisms. Alternative pathways exist in anaerobic organisms and are described here and in |FRAME: PWY-8132|., About This Pathway, Work with |FRAME: TAX-1085| has revealed a pathway that links MTA metabolism with isoprenoid biosynthesis |CITS: [23042035]|., In this pathway MTA is converted into |FRAME: CPD-444| (as described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6756|) followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-1063| catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-15512|-encoded |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.23|. At this point an unusual enzyme, |FRAME: EC-5.3.3.23|, which is related to the RubisCO proteins, catalyzes the isomerization to |FRAME: CPD-15020|., This compound is split into two by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.8.4.6|. One product, |FRAME: CPD-7671|, is recycle to |FRAME: MET| while the other one, |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P|, enters the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| for generating isoprenoids, thus generating a link between methionine salvage and isoprenoids biosynthesis |CITS: [23035785]|., This pathway, which does not require oxygen, is performed by the facultative anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-1085|, which does not possess the enzymes of the |FRAME: PWY-4361 "universal methionine salvage pathway"|, under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions |CITS: [23042035][27406564]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-395598| is the most abundant organism in a four-member community that was isolated by continuous, culture enrichment based on the ability to grow on |FRAME: CPD-10576| as a sole carbon source |CITS: [11207732]|., When grown in monocultures, the organism can use |FRAME: CPD-110|, |FRAME: CPD-10576| and |FRAME: CPD-10663|, as the sole source of carbon and energy., During growth on chlorosalicylates there is no expression of enzymes of the chlorocatechol pathway,, but the strains shows a high level of |FRAME: CPLX-7717| |CITS: [11207732]|., The pathway for degradation of chlorosalicylates by this strain comprises an interesting patchwork of enzymes known, to be involved in the 3-oxoadipate pathway and in the chlorocatechol pathway, as well as |FRAME: CPLX-7717|, |CITS: [14617643]|., Chlorosalicylates are transformed by a |FRAME: MONOMER-14434| into |FRAME: CPD-9152|, which is subject to ring, cleavage by |FRAME: MONOMER-14435| to yield |FRAME: CPD-279|., The next enzyme in the pathway is |FRAME: MONOMER-14436|. This enzyme catalyzes the transformation of, |FRAME: CPD-279| to |FRAME: CPD-10640|, a dead-end metabolite that is rather toxic., However, this reaction proceeds via an intermediate - |FRAME: 2-CL-5-OXO-2-5-DIH-FURAN-2-ACETATE|., The enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7717| acts on this intermediate, converting it to |FRAME: CPD-294| in high efficiency,, and preventing |FRAME: CPD-10640| formation. |FRAME: CPD-294| is reduced to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| by, |FRAME: MONOMER-14438| |CITS: [14617643]|, and the later is converted to TCA cycle intermediates, (see |FRAME: PWY-2361|)., The genes encoding the first three enzymes of this pathway were found in a single gene cluster that is, expressed during growth on salicylate and chlorosalicylate |CITS: [17172348]|. Three three genes were cloned,, and their products were purified and characterized. These enzymes proved to be highly adapted towards, 4-methylsalicylate transformation, having the highest affinities to intermediates of methylsalicylate degradation, |CITS: [17172348]|. The gene encoding |FRAME: CPLX-7717| was discovered in a different part of the chromosome,, and the purified protein was characterized as well |CITS: [18789896]|., In a different study of the degradation of two monochlorodibenzofurans by a bacterial consortium, it was found, that one organism degraded the monochlorodibenzofurans to chlorosalicylates, which were excreted, while, another organism, identified as |FRAME: TAX-395599|, mineralized the released chlorosalicylates by a pathway, that included |FRAME: CPD-9152| and |FRAME: CPD-10640| |CITS: [11423955]|., Since no enzyme that can degraded |FRAME: CPD-10640| is known, it is possible that it was only a byproduct,, and that the degradation proceeded via the pathway described here |CITS: [14617643]|.

General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic formaldehyde is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms. , In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central, intermediate., It has been suggested that the formaldehyde concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph, would rise to 100mM in less than 1 minute if formaldehyde consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|., Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by, unrelated or distantly related genes. , About This Pathway, This pathway involves a |FRAME: CPLX-3423| that does not require a thiol cofactor for its activity., This enzyme has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [12445786]|,, and homologs of this enzyme were found in the genomes of several organisms |CITS: [7926692]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| (CoA) is a ubiquitous compound found in archaea, bacteria, plants, and animals. It is a common acyl carrier in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and is required for a multitude of reactions for both biosynthetic and degradative pathways, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids |CITS: [16415216]|., The biosynthesis of CoA occurs via different pathways in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes, and thus enzymes specific for the bacterial pathway are targets for antibacterial drug discovery., About This Pathway, The first compound in this pathway, |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE|, is produced by phosphorylation of |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|, as described in |FRAME: PANTO-PWY|. Only microorganisms and plants (including some eukaryotic microbes, such as |FRAME: TAX-4932|) can synthesize |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| de novo - animals must obtain it in their diet, giving it the name vitamin B5., The first step in this pathway is the ligation of |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| with |FRAME: CYS|. Prokaryotic organisms utilize a CTP dependent enzyme - |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.5|. This is the only difference between the prokaryotic pathway and the eukaryotic pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7851|), since eukaryotes utilize an ATP-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-6.3.2.51|)., The pathway continues by decarboxylation to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.36|. The next step consists of the transfer of an adenyly group from ATP to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|, forming |FRAME: DEPHOSPHO-COA|. The ultimate reaction is a phosphorylation catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.24|, producing |FRAME: CO-A|. All of the enzymes of this pathway are essential for growth.

Summary: This pathway shows the reactions that constitute one turn of a cycle that lengthens the chain of an acyl-[acyl-carrier protein] molecule by two carbons. The pathway is fed acetoacetyl-[acp] (see Pathway |FRAME: FASYN-INITIAL-PWY|), which is a substrate of the second reaction shown here., The products of multiple turns of this cycle are drawn off to become components of fatty acid-containing compounds, such as phospholipids, lipid A, and lipoproteins. They comprise saturated fatty acids such as |FRAME: DODECANOATE| (dodecanoate), |FRAME: CPD-7836| (tetradecanoate), |FRAME: PALMITATE| (hexadecanoate), and |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| (octadecanoate)., In |FRAME: TAX-562|, of the four reactions involved in a cycle of fatty-acid elongation, two are catalyzed by more that one enzyme. These function preferentially on substrates of different chain length. They also act differentially on saturated and unsaturated substrates |CITS: [8910376]|., The first reaction in the sequence, the condensation reaction, is catalyzed in |FRAME:TAX-562| by three enzymes, FabB, FabF, and FabH. However, FabH initiates fatty-acid synthesis: it uses only acetyl-[acp] as a substrate, and is thus not included in this pathway (see Pathway |FRAME: FASYN-INITIAL-PWY|) |CITS: [14523010]|. Other organisms may use other initiation enzymes, such as |FRAME: G-15300 FabY|., Bacteria such as |FRAME:TAX-562| also contain unsaturated fatty acids. These are formed by a pathway that branches at the level of the 10-carbon intermediate (see |FRAME:PWY0-862|) |CITS: [14527277][8246839]|., FabB, but not FabF, participates in the synthesis of unsaturated fatty acids |CITS: [11566998]|. The activity of FabF, and hence the fraction of fatty acids that are saturated, is modultated by temperature. However, the distribution of the flow of synthesis that proceeds to saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids is determined mostly by the activities of FabA and FabZ |CITS: [8910376]|., The final step of the cycle, the reductase, is known to be catalzed by enzymes that utilize either NADH, or NADPH, or both |CITS: [9022698]|. The |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: EG11528 FabI| can use both cofactors, although the activity with NADH was shown to be over 17-fold higher than with NADPH |CITS: [9022698]|. |FRAME: G-15301 FabV| and |FRAME: G-15302 FabK| are NADH-specific. FabV enzymes are common in Gram-negative bacteria, and have been described from multiple organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-208964| |CITS: [19933806]|, |FRAME: TAX-13373| |CITS: [20055482]|, |FRAME: TAX-347| |CITS: [22039545]|, |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [22232178]|, and |FRAME: TAX-632| |CITS: [22244758]|. FabK enzymes are found only in some Gram-positive bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [10910344][12487627]| and |FRAME: TAX-837| |CITS: [22820244]|. Another isoform, |FRAME: BSU08650 FabL|, which is found in |FRAME: TAX-1423| and some other Gram-positive bacteria, uses only NADPH |CITS: [11007778]|.

Summary: |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP) is an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|., Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS:[12124622][17068264]|., DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|., Two main routes are known for DMSP degradation. In the first route DMSP is cleaved, producing |FRAME: CPD-7670|, (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6046| and |FRAME: PWY-6056|). |FRAME: CPD-7670| is exchanged between the ocean and the atmosphere and is the main atural source of sulfur to the atmosphere., In the second route (this pathway) DMSP is a demethylated to form |FRAME: CPD-7672| (MTPA) in a, reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7772|., A study of Caribbean Sea populations estimated that 5 to 66% of the total DMSP degraders were using, the demethylation pathway |CITS: [Visscher92]|., Demethylating bacteria have been isolated from both aerobic |CITS: [16348607][7811100]| and anaerobic, |CITS: [16347732][vanderMaarel93][8899985]| environments. Several sulfate-reducing bacteria have been, shown to catalyze the reaction. It is speculated that they use the removed methyl group as an input into, the oxidative acetylCoA/CO dehydrogenase pathway (a |FRAME: CODH-PWY| running in the reverse, direction) |CITS: [8899985]|., A gene encoding |FRAME:CPLX-7772| was discovered in the marine aerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-89184|, and named |FRAME: G-10859|. A homologous gene from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-335992|, (which is considered the most abundant bacterium on the planet) was cloned and successfully expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|,, enabling it to convert DMSP to MPTA., Sequence analysis of environmental samples suggest that about a third of the bacteria in surface, ocean waters possess genes similar to the |FRAME: G-10859| gene,  and may participate in DMSP, demethylation |CITS: [17068264]|., The proteins from both |FRAME: TAX-89184| and |FRAME: TAX-335992| have been purified and investigated., These enzymes were found to have a high Km for DMSP (> 5 mM), which can be explained by the fact that the, bacteria accumulate DMSP intracellularly to concentrations as high as 70 mM |CITS: [18849431]|., In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-449288| |CITS: [vanderMaarel93]| MTPA is a final product, and a dead-end metabolite. In others it is processed by either further demethylation to, |FRAME: CPD-7673| (see |FRAME: PWY-6045|) or by cleavage to |FRAME: CPD-7671| and, |FRAME: ACRYLATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6048|)., In anaerobic environments |FRAME: CPD-7672| is also used as a substrate for methanogens (see, |FRAME: PWY-5260|).

In |FRAME: TAX-9606| the skin of the underarm (axilla) is a unique niche for bacteria. It is nutrient-rich thanks to secretions of various glands that open onto the skin or into hair follicles, and hosts a unique microbial community |CITS: [18494895]|., The chemical composition of the secreted nutrients is complex. The sebaceous gland secretes esterified fatty acids and other lipids; the eccrine glands produce a dilute salt solution with lactate and other organic solutes |CITS: [Bovell15]|; and the apocrine gland secretes an odourless lipid-rich viscous secretion (only with the onset of puberty). , The malodour that is typical to the axilla is produced by metabolism carried out by the axillary microbiota, the main members of which are |FRAME: TAX-1279|, |FRAME: TAX-1912216|, |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-165779| and |FRAME: TAX-162289| |CITS: [19478181][21428987][25653852]|., Three types of compounds have been linked with the malodour - 16-androstene steroids |CITS: [8142319][23278215]|; a series of structurally-unusual medium-chain (C6-C10) acids originating from N-acylglutamine precursors |CITS: [12468539][17193210]|; and thioalcohols (also called sulfanylalkanols) |CITS: [17191898][17191839]|., The thioalcohols are particularly pungent and can be detected at extremely low concentrations. The most abundant and pungent of these thioalcohols is |FRAME: CPD-21078| (3M3SH). An odourless precursor of this compound, |FRAME: CPD-21107| (also known as 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol-[Cys-Gly] conjugate, or Cys-Gly-3M3SH), is produced by the human host and secreted from the apocrine glands in the axilla |CITS: [17192014]|., About This Pathway, The dominant genera colonizing the axilla are |FRAME: TAX-1279|, |FRAME: TAX-1912216|, |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-165779| and |FRAME: TAX-162289| |CITS: [19478181][21428987][25653852]|. However, only a limited number of axillary staphylococcal species take up and metabolize |FRAME: CPD-21107|. , Due to its dipeptide moiety the compound enters the cell through a proton-coupled transporter (POT) for oligopeptide di-/tripeptides (DtpT), which is conserved across all staphylococcal species (althuogh not all strains are able to decompose it) |CITS: [29966586]|. These POT transporters belong to the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) and use the proton electrochemical gradient across the membrane to drive the uptake of di- and tri-peptides across the cell membrane |CITS: [12905028]|., Once inside the cell, the compound is cleaved by a dipeptidase such as |FRAME: MONOMER-20503| of |FRAME: ORG-6356|, releasing a glycine |CITS: [18515361]|. The cleavage product, |FRAME: CPD-21108|, is then cleaved further by |FRAME: CPLX-9655|, an enzyme that is present only in |FRAME: CPD-21078|-producing species. The enzyme is rather specific for its substrate and is distinct from C-S lyases acting on a broad range of cysteine-conjugated ligands |CITS: [32719469]|.

Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., |FRAME: MANNITOL| is the most abundant polyol in nature, and is found in bacteria, fungi, algae, lichens and vascular plants., All three naturally-occurring hexitols can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., Each of these hexitols enters the cell via a specific phosphotransferase system, so the first intracellular species is the 6-phospho-derivative |CITS: [1100608]| (note that due to symmetry of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|, their phosphorylation at either end produces the same molecule. When these molecules are phosphorylated at the 6 position by the PTS system, the resulting molecules are named |FRAME: MANNITOL-1P| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, respectively, by conventional nomenclature rules)., In all three cases this sugar alcohol phosphate becomes the substrate for a dehydrogenase that oxidizes its 2-alcohol group to a keto group. In the cases of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: SORBITOL|, the resulting keto sugar phosphate is |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, an intermediate of glycolysis, and hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy |CITS: [6384188][2111176]|.

Summary: General Background - Respiration, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., Bacterial Nitrate Respiration, Many bacteria are able to respire in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative electron acceptors. Due to the low redox potential of the nitrate/nitrite pair, nitrate is one of the preferred alternative electron acceptors. Bacterial anaerobic nitrate respiration can proceed along two different pathways. One pathway is the denitrification process, in which nitrate is sequentially reduced through nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and finally to dinitrogen (see |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY|). In the second pathway, nitrate is first reduced to nitrite and the latter is subsequently converted in a six-electron reduction step to ammonia, which is secreted from the cell., This six-electron reduction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: NRFMULTI-CPLX|, a periplasmic complex made of several proteins. The catalytic subunit of this complex is |FRAME: CYTOCHROMEC552-MONOMER|, a hexaheme c-type cytochrome encoded by the |FRAME: EG11781| gene |CITS: [7309757][3002798][2833168]|., The dissimilatory nitrite reductases are different from the assimilatory nitrite reductases in several ways, including their induction by nitrate under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [4405508]| and the fact that they are not suppressed by the presence of ammonium |CITS: [5726295]|., Four classes of nitrate reductases are known - a eukaryotic class, and three prokaryotic classes. The eukaryotic nitrate reductases are found in plants, algae and fungi, and are involved in assimilation of nitrate. They are composed of two identical subunits, and contain a |FRAME: CPD-15870| and an |FRAME:FAD| prosthetic group. In general, plant enzymes prefer NADH as the electron donor (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.1"|) and fungal enzymes prefer NADPH (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.3"|), although some enzymes were reported, to accept either of these compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPORNOPH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.2"|) |CITS: [14209328]|., Example for eukaryotic enzymes include the |FRAME: CPLX-7198| from |FRAME: TAX-3702| and the, |FRAME: CPLX-7498| from |FRAME: TAX-5141|. , Prokaryotic nitrate reductases are divided into three classes, including a class of assimilatory enzymes and two classes of respiratory enzymes. All of them include a |FRAME: CPD-582| cofactor, but differ in their substructures, cellular location, and cofactor requirement. Variabillity among enzymes is also found within the classes. Assimilatory prokaryotic nitrate reductases (NAS) are involved in the assimilation of nitrogen from nitrate for incorporation into protein. Despite their, relatedness, these enzymes vary in their substructures and cofactors. For example, |FRAME: CPLX-7499| from |FRAME:TAX-290336| is a heterodimer that utilizes NAD(P)H, while |FRAME: MONOMER-13441| from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1140| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13440| from the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-354| are monomeric and utilize ferredoxin (|FRAME: 1.7.7.2-RXN "E.C. 1.7.7.2"|) and flavodoxin, respectively., Respiratory nitrate reductases use nitrate as the electron acceptor of an anaerobic respiratory chain which, usually starts with the quinone pool (|FRAME: RXN0-6369 "EC 1.7.99.4"|)., One of these classes (NAR) consists of membrane-bound enzymes that are composed of three different subunits. These enzymes, which include |FRAME: CPLX-7502| from |FRAME: TAX-316| and the |FRAME:TAX-83333| enzymes |FRAME:NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX| and |FRAME:NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX|, are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane, with the active site facing the cytoplasm., The second class of bacterial respiratory nitrate reductases (NAP) consists of periplasmic enzymes, which are usually heterodimers, although monomeric forms have been reported. Examples for enzymes belonging to this class include |FRAME:NAP-CPLX| from |FRAME:TAX-83333| (|FRAME: RXN0-6369 "EC 1.7.99.4"|) and |FRAME:CPLX-7500| from |FRAME: TAX-668| (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-CYTOCHROME-RXN "EC 1.9.6.1"|)., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| anaerobic respiratory chain formed by formate dehydrogenase and nitrate reductase the transfer of electrons from formate to nitrate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force (pmf) across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [4905536], [4616697], [5996], [6255943]|. The formate to nitrate respiratory chain in E. coli generates pmf (H+/e- = 2) by a redox loop mechanism as first described by Peter Mitchell |CITS: [5329743]|. Two electrons are transferred from the formate oxidation site in the periplasm to the site of nitrate reduction in the cytoplasm by a menaquinone pool which drives proton translocation in the opposite direction. , E. coli K-12 contains two respiratory formate dehydrogenases. Formate dehydrogenase N (FDH-N) is induced by anaerobiosis and the presence of nitrate |CITS: [12923080], [2168848]| whereas aerobic conditions, and to a lesser extent nitrate under anaerobic conditions, induce expression of formate dehydrogenase O (FDH-O) |CITS: [8522521]|. Formate dehydrogenase N contributes to the generation of proton potential (H+/e- = 1); oxidation of formate in the periplasm is accompanied by menaquinone reduction at the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane |CITS: [Jones80] [11884747]|. , E. coli K-12 also contains two energy conserving (H+/e- = 1) nitrate reductases. Expression of nitrate reductase A (NRA) occurs in response to high levels of nitrate in the environment whereas expression of nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is not dependent on nitrate levels or anaerobiosis |CITS: [10464201]|. , FDH-N and NRA are coupled together in the anaerobic formate to nitrate electron transfer pathway when levels of nitrate are high. FDH-O and NRZ also couple together to catalyse formate dependent nitrate reduction - this pathway operates when cell suspensions from aerobically grown cultures are placed under anaerobic conditions and thus its physiological importance may be in the transition to anaerobiosis |CITS: [1504073] [8522521]|. , Nitrate reduction and Parkinson disease, Nitrate respiration by gut Enterobacteriaceae was shown to lead to the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+, creating an oxidizing redox potential. These oxidizing conditions enable the formation of dopamine-derived quinones, which induce aggregation of the α-synuclein protein. α-synuclein aggregation has been associated with Parkinson's disease etiology |CITS: [38517270]|.

The products of ureide catabolism are re-assimilated and utilized in nitrogen metabolism., Early reports about allantoin degradation in |FRAME: TAX-3847| found that different cultivars were, utilizing different routes |CITS:[16664492][16664133][16665292][16666035][10944160]|. However, a later, study concluded that the previous investigations may have been misled by side effects of the enzyme, inhibitor used, and that both cultivars were utilizing the same degradation pathway. In both cases the, route from |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| to |FRAME: CPD-1091| involved the production of, |FRAME: AMMONIA|, while |FRAME: UREA| was produced later in the pathway, by ureidoglycolate, urea-lyase (EC 4.3.2.3) |CITS: [15020640]|. Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, In most plants, purine nucleotides are completely degraded to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| via the ureides |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|. This degradation proceeds via the intermediates |FRAME: XANTHINE| and |FRAME: URATE|., The initial step of GMP degradation in this pathway is the conversion of GMP to |FRAME: GUANOSINE|, which is degraded to |FRAME: XANTHINE| via |FRAME: XANTHOSINE|. A different route from |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME: XANTHINE| is described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6606|., Studies in tea leaves and cultured |FRAME: TAX-4058| cells showed that guanosine deaminase activity was much higher than that of guanine deaminase |CITS: [Ashihara97]|, indicating that degradation of GMP via the pathway depicted here is likely to be the major route in this plant. However, the guanosine deaminase enzymatic activity has not been reported from other sources., Regardless of the exact steps leading to its formation, |FRAME: XANTHINE| is converted to |FRAME:URATE| by xanthine dehydrogenase |CITS: [14726515]|, and the latter is converted to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as described in |FRAME: PWY-5691|.

General Backround, Polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|), a group of positively charged small molecules present in virtually all living organisms, have been implicated in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [4873311][3157043][2185470][1409623]|. Although polyamines are clearly necessary for optimal cell growth, a surplus of polyamines can cause inhibition of growth and protein synthesis |CITS: [8223591]|, and thus a balance is desired between the production and breakdown of polyamines., About This Pathway, Several metabolic pathways for the degradation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| are known. The first |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| degradation pathway was found in in 1985 |CITS:[3897201]| (see |FRAME:PUTDEG-PWY |). That pathway is dedicated to the degradation of intracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. A second pathway was found in |FRAME: TAX-83333| twenty years later. This pathway seems to be dedicated to the degradation of extracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| |CITS: [15590624]|., The pathway was discovered following the discovery of a cluster of seven unassigned genes on the |FRAME: TAX-83333| chromosome. In addition to a putrescine transporter, encoded by the puuP gene, the cluster contains four genes that encode the enzymes involved in this pathway, and two additional genes (puuE and puuR) that encode an enzyme involved in the catabolism of GABA (see |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY|) and a regulator |CITS: [15590624]|., In this pathway, |FRAME:PUTRESCINE | is γ-glutamylated at the expense of an ATP molecule. The resulting |FRAME: GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-PUTRESCINE| is oxidized to |FRAME:GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-GAMMA-AMINOBUTYRALDEH|, which is then dehydrogenated into |FRAME: CPD-9000|. In the last step, the γ-glutamyl, group is removed by hydrolysis, generating |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|., The key difference between this pathway and |FRAME:PUTDEG-PWY| is the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. In the other pathway, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is degraded directly to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|. However, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE| is unstable, and tends to form the cyclic form |FRAME: CPD-6124| nonenzymatically via the reaction |FRAME: RXN-6423|. The authors suggest that the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| potentially facilitates its catabolism by preventing this cyclization |CITS: [15590624]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycogen is a highly branched glucose polymer that serves as a form of energy storage in animals and fungi. It resembles plant-produced |FRAME: Starch starch| and is sometimes called "animal starch"., Glycogen is formed of small chains of 8 to 12 glucose molecules linked together by α (1->4) bonds. These small chains, also known as |FRAME: Maltodextrins maltodextrins|, are in turn linked together by α (1->6) bonds. The α-1,4 linkages make up approximately 95% of the total molecule. The α-1,6 branches accounts for 7-10% of the linkages and are evenly distributed within the glycogen particle., Since each chain (with the exception of the outer unbranched chains) supports two branches, glycogen particles grow spherically by adding tiers (a tier corresponds to the spherical space separating two consecutive branches from all chains located at similar distance from the center of the particle)., Mathematical modelling predicts a maximal value for the particle size above which further growth is impossible as there would not be sufficient space for interaction of the chains with the catalytic sites of glycogen metabolism enzymes. This generates a particle consisting of 12 tiers corresponding to a 42 nm maximal diameter including 55 000 glucose residues. 36% of this total number rests in the outer (unbranched) shell and is thus readily accessible to glycogen catabolism without debranching |CITS: [12179957]|., Although glycogen and starch are two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide, starch is solid semi-crystalline while glycogen particles are entirely hydrosoluble |CITS: [21220783]|., Glucose is polymerized within the polysaccharides thanks to its activation in the form of a nucleotide-sugar through the action of NDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase. All eukaryotes known synthesize glycogen from |FRAME: CPD-12575| while all Gram-negative glycogen accumulating bacteria use |FRAME:ADP-D-GLUCOSE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5067| and |FRAME:GLYCOGENSYNTH-PWY|)., About This Pathway, Unlike |FRAME: CPD-12575|, which is used by all living cells to synthesize a large number of different molecules, |FRAME:ADP-D-GLUCOSE| is devoted to the synthesis of glycogen in bacteria (and also to the synthesis of the osmoprotectant glucosylglycerol in cyanobacteria). Thus, the synthesis of ADP-glucose defines the first committed step of glycogen synthesis in bacteria while glucan elongation defines the first committed step of eukaryotic glycogen synthesis. The enzyme catalyzing this reaction, |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.27|, is rate-limiting for the pathway. , The glucose from the glycosyl-nucleotide is transferred to the non-reducing end of either a maltodextrin or a glycogen primer forming a new α-1,4-glucosidic linkage in an elongation reaction catalysed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.21 "EC 2.4.1.21, glycogen synthase"|., After chain elongation the formation of the branched α-1,6-glucosidic linkages is catalyzed by the glycogen branching enzyme. Branching proceeds differently through an hydrolytic cleavage of a pre-existing α-1,4-linked glucan synthesized through glycogen synthase and an intra or intermolecular transfer of a segment of chain in the α-1,6 position.

Summary: Glucosinolates are 1-thio-β-D-glucosides. They are found prominently in the order Capparales, which include cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, broccoli, and the model plant Arabidopsis. Many glucosinolate-producing plants have typical sharp taste and odor that are caused by their glucosinolates. , The glucosinolates play an important role in plant defense. Upon herbivore attack glucosinolates are hydrolyzed and broken down to toxic compounds in a process that starts with the action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147 "EC 3.2.1.147, myrosinase|. The myrosinases are S-glycosidases that remove the sugar moiety from glucosinolates, leaving unstable thiohydroximate-O-sulfate products that undergo spontaneous hydrolysis to form |FRAME: ISOTHIOCYANATES isothiocyanates|. The resulting isothiocyantaes are bioactive, and have been shown to have antimicrobial and insecticidal activities., In the presence of specific plant proteins, some glucosinolate hydrolysis products are diverted away from isothiocyanate. |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5 "Nitrile-specifier proteins (NSPs, EC 4.8.1.5)"| are known to catalyze the formation of nitriles. |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.6 "Epithiospecifier proteins (ESPs, EC 4.8.1.6)"| are responsible for the formation either nitriles or epithionitriles, depending on the structure of the parent glucosinolate (see |FRAME: PWY-5267|), and |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.7 "thiocyanate-forming proteins (TFPs, EC 4.8.1.7)"| are known to catalyze the formation of thiocyanates |CITS: [17139450]|., About This Pathway, Most species in the Brassicaceae produce one or more indole glucosinolates. In addition to the parent |FRAME: CPD-1863| (indol-3-ylmethylglucosinolate), other commonly encountered indole glucosinolates are |FRAME: CPD-19470|, |FRAME: 1-METHOXY-3-INDOLYLMETHYL-GLUCOSINOLATE| (1-methoxy-glucobrassicin), and |FRAME: 4-METHOXY-3-INDOLYLMETHYL-GLUCOSINOLATE|., While the identity of the myrosinase involved in the pathway has not been determined, it has been shown not to be the product of the |FRAME: AT5G26000| or |FRAME: AT5G25980| genes, since a tgg1/tgg2 double mutant excreted a similar metabolite profile as the wild type plants |CITS: [18346197]|. It may be the product of the |FRAME: AT2G44490| gene, which is known to act on |FRAME: CPD-1863| |CITS: [19095900]|., Unlike aliphatic and aromatic glucosinolates, the immediate degradation of indole glucosinolates upon herbivore attack results in formation of only nitriles and isothiocyanates. The main glucosinolate of |FRAME: TAX-3702| and most Brassica species, |FRAME: CPD-1863|, is thus converted enzymatically to |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD| by |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5|, and non-enzymatically to |FRAME: CPDQT-429|. , The isothiocyanate is highly reactive and can react with water, ascorbate, glutathione, amino acids, and other plant metabolites to produce a variety of physiologically active indole compounds. Upon releasing the thiocyanate ion, it forms a carbonium ion that converts spontaneously to the alcohol |FRAME: CPDQT-428| |CITS: [Chevolleau97]|. The alcohol in turn oligomerizes to form the dimer |FRAME: CPDQT-424| |CITS: [Gmelin61]| as well as higher order oligomers, up to the pentamer, in reactions that liberate |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| |CITS: [1643248][Agerbirk96]|. When |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is present, the carbonium ion acts with it preferentially, forming |FRAME: CPDQT-426| |CITS: [Agerbirk98][10869675]|., A study on the effect of the indole glucosinolate breakdown products on |FRAME: TAX-13164| (green peach aphid) has shown that the most active compound was |FRAME: CPDQT-427|, which forms by the spontaneous reaction of |FRAME: CYS| with |FRAME: CPDQT-428| within the aphid |CITS: [18346197]|. A non-enzymatic reaction of |FRAME: CPDQT-428| with glutathione has also been reported |CITS: [11849035]|., In |FRAME: TAX-3711| (turnip) roots, the most common degradation products were |FRAME: INDOLE-3-CARBOXALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: CPD-13135| |CITS: [11867093]|. Although it hasn't been proved, it is likely that these compounds were formed from |FRAME: CPDQT-428| |CITS: [Agerbirk09]|. Oxidation of |FRAME: CPDQT-428| to |FRAME: INDOLE-3-CARBOXALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: CPD-13135| has been reported in mammalian systems |CITS: [8832811][11849035][15297427]|., |FRAME: CPD-13135 "Indole-3-carboxylate"| was also observed in |FRAME: TAX-3709| (rutabaga). However, in that plant it was shown that |FRAME: CPD-13135| was derived from the nitrile via |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN|. The exact path from |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| to |FRAME: CPD-13135| has not been determined, but is likely to involve chain shortening similar to fatty acid β-oxidation |CITS: [18075646]|. , It should be noted that a different indole glucosinolate metabolism pathway operates in intact cells, resulting in the production of several unusual metabolites, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWYQT-4477|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, also known as vitamin C, fulfils multiple essential roles in both plants and animals., Being a strong reducing agent, it functions as the primary water soluble antioxidant in cells, interacting with reactive oxygen species generated during oxidative stress and protecting cell constituents from oxidative damage |CITS: [ 10727845]|. It also functions as a cofactor for several enzymes, which are involved in many important pathways, including collagen hydroxylation, carnitine biosynthesis, norepinephrine biosynthesis, and hormone and tyrosine metabolism., In plants L-ascorbate is also implicated in defense against pathogens and in control of plant growth and development., A significant proportion of a plant's ascorbate is found in the apoplast (the aqueous solution permeating the cell walls) |CITS: [15608627]|., While most organisms synthesize L-ascorbate, not all do. Examples for organisms that are not able to synthesize L-ascorbate include simians and humans., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has been industrially produced for around 70 years. The first chemical process was achieved in 1933, from |FRAME: CPD-14964| |CITS: [Haworth33]|. One year later a method was developed for the production of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| from |FRAME: D-Glucose| |CITS: [Reichstein34]|. This method, known as the Reichstein process, is still used despite its complexity. The process begins with the chemical hydrogenation of |FRAME: D-Glucose| to form |FRAME: SORBITOL|. D-sorbitol is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9569| in a biological reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: TAX-442|. This conversion utilizes a microbial system since only the L-isomer is biologically active. L-sorbose is then crystallized and after condensation with acetone, sorbose-diacetone is formed, which is afterwards oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-13059| using a platinum catalyst. After enolization and lactonization, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is obtained with a final yield of about 50% |CITS: [1366548]|., This cumbersome process can be greatly simplified by the biological process described in this pathway. A large part of the pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: D-Glucose| to |FRAME: 25-DIDEHYDRO-D-GLUCONATE|, occurs naturally in some bacteria. The strain that is used traditionally is |FRAME: TAX-549|. The product of this process can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-13059| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8596| |CITS: [16346005]|, which has been cloned from several |FRAME: TAX-1716| strains |CITS: [12436304]| and introduced to |FRAME: TAX-549|, generating a single strain that can produce |FRAME: CPD-13059| from D-glucose |CITS: [17842676]|. The final dehydration of |FRAME: CPD-13059| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is still performed chemically |CITS: [Bremus06]|.

|FRAME: Salmochelins Salmochelins| are C-glucosylated |FRAME: Siderophore siderophores| related to |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN| that are produced by |FRAME: TAX-590| species, uropathogenic and avian pathogenic |FRAME: TAX-562| strains, and certain |FRAME: TAX-570| strains. Mono- (MGE), di- (DGE), and triglucosylated (TGE) forms have been reported |CITS: [12655053][15259369][15598734]|., These compounds were initially reported to confer protection against Salmonella when included in the diet of mice, and were named "Salmonella Resistance Factors" (SRF) or "Salmonellosis pacifarins" |CITS: [5288264][1090527]|, although today siderophores are considered virulence factors |CITS: [23959718]|. The most commonly observed salmochelin is the diglucosylated form, which is known as |FRAME: CPD-21578 "salmochelin S4"|. Macrolactone-opened derivatives have also been isolated |CITS: [15259369]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8022|)., The glucosylation is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.369| (|FRAME: G-58802|), which transfers glucosyl groups from |FRAME: CPD-12575| to carbon C5 of one, two, or three of the 2,3-dihydroxybenzoyl units of |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN| |CITS: [15598734]|., The glucosylation has been interpreted as a bacterial evasion mechanism that prevents sequestration of the siderophore by the mammalian host's serum albumin |CITS: [6234017]| or the catecholate siderophore-binding protein siderocalin |CITS: [12453412]|.

Organosulfonate compounds are found in the environment as both natural products and xenobiotics. They are catabolized by microorganisms that utilize the carbon and sulfur moieties. Aliphatic C3 sulfonates are widespread natural products found in the environment and are derived from microbial, plant and animal sources. The bacterial catabolism of C3 sulfonates such as |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| (racemic sulfolactate), |FRAME: CPD-380|, and |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| has been studied. The work has focused on the catabolism of the carbon moiety, the fate of the sulfonate group, and the transport systems necessary for organosulfonates to cross the cell membrane. Bioinformatics analyses have shown a diversity in pathways of sulfonate degradation in bacteria from both marine and terrestrial environments (in |CITS: [20007648]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16341843]|)., To date, three desulfonation pathways have been proposed for the degradation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| including:, (1) |FRAME: PWY-6616|: direct desulfonation of |FRAME: CPD-367| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-8144|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12191| and |FRAME: G-12192| genes. |FRAME: CPD-11799| is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-367| via |FRAME: CPD-380| by two dehydrogenases of opposite stereochemistry, encoded by |FRAME: G-12189| and |FRAME: G-12190|., (2) |FRAME: PWY-6637|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), followed by decarboxylation of sulfopyruvate to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by the |FRAME: CPLX-8153| encoded by the |FRAME: G-12226| and |FRAME: G-12227| genes, desulfonation to acetyl phosphate by |FRAME: G-12229|, and conversion of acetyl phosphate to acetyl-CoA., (3) |FRAME: PWY-6638|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), transamination of |FRAME: CPD-380| to |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE|, racemization of |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| to |FRAME: CPD-28271|, and desulfonation of |FRAME: CPD-28271| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| by the product of the |FRAME: G-12230| gene., In all of these pathways the |FRAME: HSO3| or |FRAME: SO3| produced by the desulfonation reaction is proposed to be transported through the cell membrane and oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| by a periplasmic enzyme, possibly the product of genes sorAB in some organisms |CITS: [19581363][20150239] [16341843]|., In each of these pathways a different enzymatic desulfonation mechanism is used., In |FRAME: PWY-6616| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: CPD-367| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.24| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8146| from |FRAME: ORG-6160| and |FRAME: CPLX-8144| from |FRAME: TAX-290398| for examples |CITS: [15758220]|., In |FRAME: PWY-6637| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15|. See |FRAME: MONOMER-15909|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12229| gene in |FRAME: TAX-89187| for example |CITS: [19581363][20150239]|., In |FRAME: PWY-6638| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.25|. See |FRAME: CPLX-8147| from |FRAME: TAX-246200| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15910| from |FRAME: TAX-89187| for examples |CITS: [19581363][16302849]|.

In |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: CPD-69| can occur inside the cell as a result of nonenzymatic decomposition, of |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|, and in the environment due to dissociation of |FRAME: UREA| and photooxidation of, |FRAME: HCN|., Although cyanate at high concentrations is toxic to |FRAME:TAX-562|, it can serve as a sole source of nitrogen due to, the production of |FRAME: AMMONIA| by |FRAME: CYANLY-CPLX| |CITS: [3034861]|.  The cyanate degradation pathway therefore, serves the dual purpose of detoxification and nitrogen utilization |CITS: [7768821]|.  , Cyanase catalyzes the first step of the pathway, producing |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and the unstable compound, |FRAME: CARBAMATE|, which spontaneously decomposes to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|,, thus producing a source of nitrogen for growth., The second enzyme of this pathway, carbonic anhydrase, is an essential component of the pathway.  In the, absence of carbonic anhydrase at atmospheric concentrations of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, non-enzymatic hydration of, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| is not sufficient to prevent depletion of the intracellular |FRAME: HCO3| pool due to rapid, diffusion of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [8444806]|., |FRAME: TAX-294| NCIB 11764 is also capable of utilizing cyanate as a sole source of nitrogen for growth, |CITS: [2495763]|. The induced enzymatic activity of extracts of cyanate grown |FRAME: TAX-294| NCIB, 11764 cells was shown to be bicarbonate dependent and specific for cyanate, resembling, the enzymatic activity of cyanase as described in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [2495763]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Omega-3-Fatty-Acids "ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids"| are known to be essential for proper neuronal and immune function. Deficiencies in these important fatty acids are associated with mental dysfunction, cardiovascular disorders, cancer and other diseases., Resolvins (resolution phase interaction products) are a class of lipid based anti-inflammatory mediators derived from the ω 3 fatty acids |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) and |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA). Those derived from DHA are termed the D-series resolvins |CITS: [15726828]|. These endogenous mediators have a wide distribution in leukocytes, brain and glial cells., |FRAME: CPD-524 Aspirin| has well known anti-inflammatory, antipyretic functions and anticoagulant functions. It is often prescribed long-term, at low doses, to help prevent heart attacks, strokes, and blood clot formation in high risk patients. Aspirin may also prevent the occurrence of certain types of cancer. Aspirin exerts its actions by the inhibition of both |FRAME: HS01815| (COX1) and |FRAME: HS01115| (COX2) which has a negative effect on prostaglandin synthesis. It irreversibly acetylates COX-2 which loses the ability to generate prostaglandin intermediates. However, COX-2 retains oxygenase activity, which results in the production of various types of anti-inflammatory mediators., About this Pathway, Unesterified DHA is released from phosphatidylethanolamine and converted via aspirin-acetylated COX-2 to |FRAME: CPD-17452 (17R)-hydroxy-DHA| |CITS: [15726828]|. This has been observed in human microvascular endothelial cells. , |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, then inserts a hydroperoxy moiety at either the 4 or 7 positions, resulting in the formation of two intermediates that are rapidly converted to the 4,5 epoxide and 7,8 epoxide, respectively, giving rise to the (17R)-series resolvins |CITS: [12590139]|., During ischemic conditions like stroke or coronary thrombosis there are leukocyte infiltration and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines which contribute to tissue damage. Ischemia also causes release of DHA from membrane phospholipids. Aspirin mediated biosynthesis of the (17R)-series resolvins facilitates the inhibition of both leukocyte infiltration and cytokine expression |CITS: [15726828]|. , In the absence of aspirin there is a de novo biosynthesis of (17S)-resolvins - see |FRAME: PWY66-397|.

|FRAME: CPD-13056 Toyocamycin| is |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines| antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1927|., The compound was first isolated in 1956 and shown to have anti-fungal properties |CITS: [13345725]|., It was later shown that toyocamycin also inhibits the growth of bacteria and animal tumors. It has been suggested that toyocamycin is incorporated into RNA (internal and terminal positions) and DNA |CITS:[5582755]|, and that it inhibits the synthesis of rRNA |CITS: [5815146][4322403][4359880][318864][560201][88041][6944069]|. It was also shown to inhibit phosphatidylinositol kinase |CITS: [2177464]|., The biosynthesis of toyocamycin has been studied by radio tracers |CITS: [5418715][5498424]|, genetic studies |CITS: [18721750]| and NMR |CITS: [21298182]|. While early studies suggested that adenine is incorporated into toyocamycin, later studies suggested that the pathway starts with GTP, and proceeds via the intermeidate |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, which is also an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the 7-deazapurine nucleosides |FRAME: CPD-13057| and |FRAME: CPD-13053| |CITS: [18721750]|., A gene cluster involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13056| and |FRAME: CPD-13052| has been identified based on sequence information derived from |FRAME: CPLX-8239|, the enzyme that converts |FRAME: CPD-13056| to |FRAME: CPD-13052|. Two of the enzymes encoded by genes from the cluster, |FRAME: GTP-CYCLOHYDRO-I-RXN "EC 3.5.4.16, GTP cyclohydrolase I"| and |FRAME: CPLX-8239|, have been characterized biochemically. The rest of the enzymes were characterized only by their sequence. The similarity between these genes and well-known genes involved in purine metabolism (such as  |FRAME: GMP-REDUCT-RXN "EC 1.7.1.7, GMP reductase"|, |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCCINATE-SYNTHASE-RXN "EC 6.3.4.4, adenylosuccinate synthase"| and  |FRAME: AMPSYN-RXN "EC 4.3.2.2, adenylosuccinate lyase"|) suggests obvious roles for their products |CITS: [18721750]|.

Carvone is a monocyclic monoterpene ketone, which is produced by over 70 different plants., It exists in two stereoisomeric forms; |FRAME: CPD-1089|, which is the main component in the, essential oil of spearmint (|FRAME: TAX-29719|) (see |FRAME: PWY-3061|, and |FRAME: CPD-10037|,, which is the main component in the essential oils of caraway (|FRAME: TAX-48032|) and dill, (|FRAME: TAX-40922|)., Both compounds are natural flavours widely applied by the flavour and fragrance industry., In plants, carvone is formed in a biosynthetic pathway from limonene via hydroxylation at the C6 position,, forming carveol, and subsequent oxidation of carveol to carvone |CITS: [9017926]|.

Summary: General Background, At the time of this review, 136 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity. Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is, the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana., GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and GA4 enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs,, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed. It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis.Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme, production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). During active growth, the plant will maintain gibberellin homeostasis by metabolizing most gibberellins by rapid hydroxylation to inactive conjugates. Active |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed in the disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen produces large amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Inactive conjugates might be stored or translocated via the phloem and xylem before their release (activation) at the proper time and in the proper tissue., About This Pathway, GA12, the first true gibberellin is synthesized in plastids (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|). It is then further oxidized in the cytosol to a wide range of gibberellins. Depending on the sequence of hydroxylation at the 3β- and 13-positions, parallel pathways branch from GA12 to the C19-GAs, the number and prevalence of these branch pathways varying from species to species. The presence of the early 13-hydroxylation branch pathway, a pathway originating from GA12 via GA53 and leading to the hydroxylated C19 GA1 has been demonstrated in many species including maize, rice, pea and Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[10557253],[11117879],[9154988],[7630935]|. So far, however, there is no evidence that these gibberellins exist in |FRAME: TAX-3208| or green algae |CITS: [JOHRI08][18930434][ANTEROLA08]|., Enzymes: The reactions of this pathway are catalyzed by 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases. The first step of this pathway is performed by a gibberellin 13-hydroxylase. This enzyme allows for the conversion of GA12 to GA53. The following enzyme of this pathway, gibberellin 20-oxidase, catalyzes the removal of C-20, thereby forming the C19-skeleton in GA20. This enzyme performs the sequential oxidation of C-20 to the alcohol and aldehyde, followed by the removal of the C atom through formation of the 4, 10-lactone ring. The alcohol intermediate (GA44) must be in its open lactone form (free alcohol) to be catalyzed by the enzyme. It is however extracted from plants in its closed δ-lactone form (|FRAME: CPD-638|) which is no longer oxidized by GA20-oxidases. Although it is not certain whether this form occurs naturally in planta or is an artifact of the extraction procedure, it is interesting to note that spinach cell-free extracts contain an enzyme able to catalyze the conversion of the δ-lactone form to its free alcohol form |CITS:[WARD97]|. Additional oxidation reactions leading to the formation of growth-active GAs such as GA1 are performed by gibberellin 3-oxidases which, depending on the species, are varyingly regiospecific |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|.
