Summary: Phaseollin, one of the major phytoalexins in bean (|FRAME:TAX-3885|), belongs to the complex types of pterocarpans., Such compounds are characterized by side attachments involving cyclic or acyclic structures derived from , dimethylallyl (prenyl) or geranyl groups |CITS: [Tahara95]|. The biosynthesis of phaseollin parallels the biosynthesis , of gluceollins, the prenylated pterocarpans in soybean (|FRAME:TAX-3847|). However, the last committed reaction in glyceollin , biosynthesis, the dehydration and cyclization of the dimethylallyl intermediates (glyceollidin I and II) has been , enzymatically clarified whereas the corresponding step in bean (phaseollidin to phaseollin) remains to be investigated, |CITS: [Woodward80]| |CITS: [Dewick82]|., The limited distribution of prenyltransferases has resulted in a smaller number of plants being able to synthesize complex , isoflavonoids. The prenylated pterocarpans are even restrictively distributed throughout the legumes |CITS: [Tahara95]|., Phaseollin was the first antifungal isoflavonoid identified from bean and is believed to play an important role in host plant , defense. It has been found that pterocarpans containing the prenyl substituent in the D-ring (phaseollidin, phaseollin) are , the most effective feeding deterrents, hence efforts have been attempted to transfer prenyltransferase genes to important , forage crops (e.g. white clover). , It has been confirmed that prenylation occurred after the basic skeleton of pterocarpans (or other classes of isoflavonoids) , has been constructed |CITS: [Dewick82]|. As most of the enzymes involved in phytoalexin biosynthesis the prenyltransferase , activity was significantly increased by biotic and abiotic elicitors (yeast extract, CuCl2 treatment) |CITS: [Biggs87]|., Bean cultivars resistant and susceptible to |FRAME:TAX-290576| fungus showed different responses to CuCl2 , treatment. Phaseollin production was significantly higher in the resistant cultivars than in the susceptible ones establishing , a positive correlation between resistance and susceptibility to |FRAME:TAX-290576|, the causing agent of anthrachnose , disease in bean |CITS: [Durango02]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:S-ALLANTOIN "(S)-(+)-allantoin"| is a common product of purine degradation. Allantoin is rich in nitrogen, and many organisms are able to degrade and recycle it. Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1458|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, do so under aerobic conditions, while others such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: ORG-5985| and |FRAME: TAX-587| do so only anaerobically., S-Allantoin degradation is not limited to bacteria. Ureide-transporting plants convert fixed nitrogen in their roots to |FRAME:S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|, which are then transported to upper parts of the plant, where they are degraded to release the nitrogen. In addition, some fungi and animals also degrade allantoin., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-64|, comprises the hydrolysis of the internal amide bond of |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN|, forming |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| |CITS: [786256]|. This enzyme turned out to be common to all organisms that can degrade allantoin, and is the first step in all allantoin degradation pathways., |FRAME: ALLANTOATE "Allantoate"| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1091| via one of two routes. Summary: |FRAME: SER| biosynthesis is a major metabolic pathway in many organisms. Its end product, |FRAME: SER|, is not only used in protein synthesis, but also as a precursor for the biosynthesis of glycine, cysteine, tryptophan, and phospholipids. In addition, it directly or indirectly serves as a source of one-carbon units for the biosynthesis of various compounds. Many organisms from all domain of life are able to convert |FRAME: SER| to |FRAME: D-SERINE| by racemization., In bacteria racemization usually takes place for the sake of degradation. Some organisms can use |FRAME: D-SERINE| as the sole carbon and nitrogen sources (see |FRAME: PWY0-1535|). More recently it has been shown that the ability to utilize and/or detoxify D-serine plays a role in pathogenesis |CITS: [12823810][17088369][17785472][19674114]|., In other cases racemization evolved as an antibiotic resistance mechanism. Resistance to vancomycin that originated in |FRAME: TAX-1350| (collectively called VRE, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus), but eventually spread to other organisms depends on D-ala-D-ala ligases with altered specificity that incorporate either |FRAME: D-LACTATE| or |FRAME: D-SERINE| instead of the second |FRAME: D-ALANINE|. When incorporated into peptidoglycan, these modified peptides do not bind glycopeptide antibiotics |CITS: [10209740][10878136]|., D-serine was thought to exist only in bacteria until it was found to serve as a signaling molecule in the vertebrate brain. D-Serine, which is synthesized in neurons by the bifunctional serine racemase/D-serine dehydratase, serves as a neuromodulator by coactivating NMDA receptors, making them able to open if they then also bind glutamate. D-serine is a potent agonist at the glycine site (NR1) of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)-type glutamate receptor (NMDAR). For the receptor to open, glutamate and either glycine or D-serine must bind to it |CITS: [20106978]|.

General Background, In adult female moths, species-specific sex pheromones are released from the pheromone gland in order to attract males of the same species (conspecific males). These pheromones are synthesized de novo in this gland from precursors derived from fatty acid biosynthesis. Many different sex pheromones have been chemically characterized. Moth Type I sex pheromones are C10-C18 primary alcohols, aldehydes, or acetate esters usually containing several double bonds. Type II are unsaturated hydrocarbons or hydrocarbon epoxides. Sex pheromones are usually produced as multicomponent mixtures (blends) (reviewed in |CITS: [22160231][20139627]|)., |FRAME: TAX-7109| is a widespread, polyphagous pest of Mediterranean countries. An analysis of the sex pheromones produced by the female moth identified a complex of four pheromones - |FRAME: CPD-17818|, |FRAME: CPD-17810|, |FRAME: CPD-17812|, and |FRAME: CPD-17804| |CITS: [4516592]|. A later study detected a fifth compound - |FRAME: CPD-17808| |CITS: [2295634]|., About This Pathway, The pathway was studied using deuterium-labeled fatty acids, which were fed to the pheromone glands |CITS: [2295634]|. Label from |FRAME: PALMITATE| was incorporated into all of the pheromone acetates, as well as all acyl-CoA intermediates, indicating that the starting compound is |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA|, the standard product of the fatty acid synthase (see |FRAME: PWY-5994|)., The fate of palmitoyl-CoA in the pheromone gland depends on the order of events. When β-oxidation occurs first, palmitoyl-CoA is shortened by two carbons to form |FRAME: TETRADECANOYL-COA|. This intermediate can be desaturated into either |FRAME: E-11-TETRADECENOYL-COA| or |FRAME: Z-11-TETRADECENOYL-COA|, presumably by the same enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-19261| |CITS: [Navarro97][10563812]|., Alternatively, palmitoyl-CoA could first be desaturated, generating |FRAME: CPD-16001|, which is then shortened by one cycle of β oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-17464| |CITS: [2295634]|., |FRAME: E-11-TETRADECENOYL-COA| is the subject of a different desaturase, |FRAME: MONOMER-19262|, which introduces a second double bond, generating |FRAME: CPD-17804| |CITS: [11378415]|., While this has not been studied in |FRAME: TAX-7109|, studies in another moth, |FRAME: TAX-7091|, showed that the acyl-CoA precursors of the pheromones are mainly found incorporated into |FRAME: Triacylglycerols "triacylglycerols"| in the cytoplasmic lipid droplets of pheromone gland cells (this step in not shown in this pathway, see |FRAME: PWY-7423|). When adult females emerge from pupation, signaling events initiated by the neurohormone pheromone biosynthesis-activating neuropeptide (PBAN) regulate lipolysis of the stored |FRAME: Triacylglycerols "triacylglycerols"|, releasing the compounds for their final processing, which includes reduction to alcohols, and, in the case of |FRAME: TAX-7109|, acetylation |CITS: [9063992][22649392][23955937]|., All four products are presumably converted to the corresponding alcohols by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.84| (FAR), which is located in the pheromone gland |CITS: [12871998]|. The last step is the acetylation of the alcohols by an uncharacterized acetylase, producing the final pheromone acetates., With the exception of the desaturases, the pathway has been studied only using deuterium-labeled compounds, and thus most of the enzymes involved have not been studied or identified in |FRAME: TAX-7109| |CITS: [2295634]|.

General Background, Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|. Bioluminescence is particularly predominant in the marine environment, in members of planktonic bacteria and protozoa, many invertebrates, and vertebrates with specialized light producing organs that harbor symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-7723|). The requirement for oxygen suggests that bioluminescence evolved after oxygen levels began to rise through the activities of early oxygenic phototrophic cyanobacteria., |FRAME: TAX-6625| is a luminescent small squid that lives in the deep sea and is indigenous to northern Japan. It is named after Watase, who first described its luminescence in 1905 |CITS: [Watase05]|. The squid emits light from three different types of photophores, the brightest of which are three large organs found on the tips of each of the fourth pair of arms. Five smaller light organs are positioned in a row along the ventral margin of each eye, and hundreds of minute photophores are scattered across the ventral integument of the mantle, funnel, head, and arms |CITS: [16593580]|. The squid arm tip photophores are densely packed with protein microcrystals that catalyze the bioluminescent reaction |CITS: [21821032]|. The crystals contain three proteins, all members of the ANL superfamily of adenylating enzymes that also includes the firefly luciferase, with which the squid proteins share 19 to 21% sequence identity |CITS: [27279452]|. Like the firefly, the squid produces bright blue flashes (470 nm), and is popularly called firefly squid., Like many other marine organisms, including coelenterates and ctenophores, shrimps, fishes, and some chaetognaths |CITS: [Shimomura80][Campbell90][20972255]|, the luciferin used by the squid is |FRAME: Coelenterazines|, an imidazopyrazinone derivative. The biosynthetic origin of coelenterazine is not known, but it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it and is dependent on a dietary supply |CITS: [11572972]|. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| |CITS: [Thomson95]|. The specific coelentrazine used by the squid is a disulfated version, |FRAME: LUCIFERIN| |CITS: [Goto74][Inoue75][Inoue76]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: TAX-6625| bioluminescence reaction was shown to require ATP and magnesium |CITS: [16593580]|, |FRAME: LUCIFERIN|, a membrane-bound luciferase, and molecular oxygen |CITS: [12101012]|. A potential pathway was suggested in which |FRAME: LUCIFERIN| is activated by ATP to form an adenylate. The AMP group leaves, trigerring oxygenation by molecular oxygen, forming an unstable dioxetanone intermediate. The dioxetanone ring collapses, releasing CO2 and generating the energy required to form an |FRAME: CPD-20265|. The product then emits a photon as it returns to its ground state. Based on studies of similar systems from other organisms, the light emitter was presumed to be the amide anion in the singlet excited state bound to luciferase |CITS: [16165097]|. The proposed pathway was confirmed 12 years later by the use of density functional theory (DFT) |CITS: [28032762]|., The squid arm tip photophores contain numerous densely packed, tiny rod-shaped objects that catalyze the bioluminescent reaction |CITS: [Shima27]|. These structures were shown to be protein microcrystals. When the crystals were purified by centrifugation on a sucrose gradient and analysed by SDS-PAGE, they were found to contain a major 63 kDa protein and a minor 81 kDa protein (in a mass ratio of about 8 to 1) |CITS: [21821032]|. , A later study identified three different proteins in the crystals |CITS: [27279452]|. The three proteins are paralogous, and all are members of the ANL superfamily of adenylating enzymes, which also includes the firefly luciferase |CITS: [27279452]|. Despite the fact that they act on very different substrates, both the firefly and the squid luciferases require ATP and produce bright blue flashes (470 nm), suggesting convergent evolution.

The legume-specific pterocarpans medicarpin and maackiain have been originally thought not to be converted into , malonylglucosides but to exist exclusively as de novo formed aglycones. In addition, trifolirhizin (maackiain-3-O-glucoside), maackiain- and medicarpin , malonyl glucosides together with afrormosin malonyl glucoside have been established as constitutive compounds in , red clover |CITS: [McMurchy84]| |CITS: [11413204]| and alfalfa |CITS: [Kessmann90]|, respectively., Upon elicitation not only the aglycones medicarpin and maackiain increased in cell cultures of chickpea but a delayed , and significant higher amount of their conjugates also occurred. The accumulation of maackiain and medicarpin , conjugates was especially noticeable when a first burst in aglycone accumulation has passed |CITS: [Weidemann91]|., The pterocarpan malonyl glucosides are found predominantly in vacuoles |CITS: [Mackenbrock92]| whereas the , de novo cytoplasmatic synthesized aglycones (medicarpin, maackiain) are often excreted. This has been discussed , as a metabolic channeling preventing aglycone conjugation and reflecting a tight regulation of pools |CITS: [Barz92]|, spatially separated in cytoplasm (pterocarpan aglycones) and vacuoles (pterocarpan conjugates). , All enzymes necessary to catalyze the conversion of the aglycones to the conjugated metabolites exist and function , in chickpea, and their activities upon elicitation have been measured |CITS: [Daniel88]|. The enzymes catalyzing the , formation of the pterocarpan malonylglucosides were highly induced at lower elicitor level. Increasing elicitation caused , a strong repression of those enzymes but increased the activities of the enzymes involved in the catabolism of the , malonylglucosides towards the aglycones |CITS: [Barz92]| |CITS: [11413204]|., Experiments with the phenylalanine-ammonia-lyase (PAL) specific inhibitor AOPP (α-amino-β-phenylpropionic acid) , under elicitor conditions resulted in the channeling of formononetin released from the corresponding malonylglucosides , into the biosynthetic route of medicarpin/maackiain formation underlining the regulatory importance of this pathway |CITS: [Barz89]|., The isoflavone conjugate cycle is discussed as an anapleurotic sequence for legumes, when a high demand for , phytoalexin formation exists and the de novo biosynthesis is delayed because of insufficient amounts of early precursors. , It has also been argued that the conjugation prevents the excessive formation of medicarpin in alfalfa, which inhibits , nodulation through its phytotoxity to |FRAME:TAX-379| species |CITS: [Kessmann90]|., Research in leguminous plants has revealed the existence of the conjugate interconversion for many intermediates , involved in the biosynthesis of phytoalexins. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12380 Pheomelanin| is a common type of melanin pigment, which is found in hair and skin. Pheomelanin imparts a pink to red hue and is accordingly found in large quantities in red hair. In skin pheomelanin is particularly concentrated in the lips, nipples, glans of the penis, and vagina., Chemically, pheomelanin consists mostly of benzothiazine units, which are degraded to benzothiazole units to some extent |CITS: [4210254]|. It is difficult to specify the exact structure of melanin polymers, since they are composed of many different, units that are connected through strong carbon-carbon bonds., The pathway starts with tyrosinase (|FRAME: HS01248|), which catalyzes the initial, rate-limiting step of melanogenesis, forming |FRAME: DOPAQUINONE|. This compound is extremely reactive, and in the presence of |FRAME: CYS| reacts spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-20260| and |FRAME: CPD-15154| |CITS: [61113][408183]|. These reactions are rapid, and continue as long as cysteine is present |CITS: [10952395]|. In an experiment conducted with a tyrosinae from the mushroom |FRAME: TAX-5341| the ratio beween |FRAME: CPD-15154| and |FRAME: CPD-20260| was 5:1 |CITS: [408183]|., It should be noted that in the absence of |FRAME: CYS|, |FRAME: DOPAQUINONE| undergoes several spontaneous rearrangements, generating |FRAME: CPD-8652| and |FRAME: L-DOPACHROME|, leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-12379| (see |FRAME: PWY-6498|). Thus, the presence of |FRAME: CYS| is a key determinant for the production of either |FRAME: CPD-12379| or |FRAME: CPD-12380| |CITS: [9367182]|., Once the |FRAME: CYS| concentration decreases to 30 times lower than the |FRAME: CPD-15154| concentration, another reaction becomes predominant - the oxidation of the S-cysteinyldopa compounds by |FRAME: DOPAQUINONE| generating their quinone forms (|FRAME: CPD-20261| and |FRAME: CPD-20262|, respectively). |FRAME: DOPAQUINONE Dopaquinone| is reduced to |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| |CITS: [10952395][12753395]|., Once the S-cysteinyldopaquinones are formed, they rapidly cyclize (via an attack of the cysteinyl side-chain amino group on the carbonyl group) to give cyclic o-quinonimine intermediates that tautomerize to a benzothiazine intermediates, which then react to form |FRAME: CPD-12380| |CITS: [11744399]|.

Summary: The formation of the two heterocycles involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| (vitamin B1), i.e. the thiazole (see |FRAME:PWY-6908|) and pyrimidine moiety (this pathway), in |FRAME:TAX-4932| diverge significantly from their bacterial counterparts (see |FRAME:PWY-6892|, |FRAME:PWY-6890|) |CITS:[18161008]|. Whereas the biosynthetic route of the thiazole heterocycle is conserved between plants and fungi, the pyrimidine component, i.e. |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYL-PYR-P| is biosynthesized differently even between plants and fungi |CITS:[12777485] [14570482] [Himmeldirk98] [Ishida08]|. , In dependence on physiological conditions |FRAME:TAX-4932| appears to employ two different pathways leading to the pyrimidine moiety of |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. In the presence of oxygen (aerobic branch - this pathway) radioactive labeling clearly indicated |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| as a main intermediate in the generation of the pyrimidine heterocycle of |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| |CITS:[8528151] [Ishida08]|. In the absence of oxygen (anaerobic conditions) radioactive |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| is not incorporated into |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| |CITS:[10706422] [10705981]| and the THI5 gene family, encoding a key enzyme in the aerobic branch of the pyrimidine moiety, is not involved at all |CITS:[12777485]|. However, the pathway has not yet been investigated in detail and remains to be elucidated. , Under aerobic conditions the pathway proceeds from |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE|, which is imported into the cells by the |FRAME: G3O-30671| pyridoxine transporter |CITS: [12649274]|. From |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| the biosynthesis of |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, a main co-substrate for the HMP-P synthase forming |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYL-PYR-P|, may proceed via different routes. The reaction sequence has not been determined but the enzymes, i.e. pyridoxine/pyridoxal kinase |CITS:[17696614]|, pyridoxine 5'-phosphate oxidase |CITS:[Tsuge80] [7896706]| and pyridoxine 4-dehydrogenase/pyridoxal reductase |CITS:[3076441]| have been shown to be involved in the biosynthetic route towards |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. Several pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-6466|, |FRAME:PWY-6910|) involved in synthesizing |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYL-PYR-P| precursors may feed into the |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYL-PYR-P| pathway |CITS:[10383756] [15614489]| but have been considered salvage or independent pathways with only marginal effects on the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| |CITS:[18028398]|., A number of authors reported conclusive proofs that |FRAME:HIS| constitutes one of the main components forming |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYL-PYR-P|, however the source of |FRAME:HIS| remained elusive |CITS:[3048267] [8528151] [14570482] [12777485] [Ishida08]|. More recently this puzzle could be resolved by demonstrating in |FRAME:TAX-5475| and |FRAME:TAX-4930| that in an unprecedented biochemical process the 4-amino-2-methyl-5-phosphomethylpyrimidine synthase (THI5) catalyzes the last step in the pathway as a single-turnover (suicide) enzyme donating an internal |FRAME:HIS| residue (His-66) to the reaction |CITS:[22568620] [23048037]|.

Rhizoma Coptidis (the rhizome of |FRAME: TAX-261450|) has been employed in traditional oriental medicine for the treatment of various diseases, such as gastroenteritis, ulcer and inflammation for two thousand years.The active ingredients in the rhizomes are protoberberine-type alkaloids, including |FRAME: BERBERINE|, |FRAME: PALMATINE|, |FRAME: CPD-21760|, |FRAME: CPD-21762|, and |FRAME: CPD-19603|, with |FRAME: BERBERINE| being the most abundant., Modern pharmacological studies suggest that |FRAME: CPD-21762| has broad biological activity, including antihyperlipidemic |CITS: [26119076][27045983][26593426][26848702][26876917]| and antihyperglycemic |CITS: [2177949][19023536][21968062][25137652][26027757]| effects as well as anti-inflammatory |CITS: [25540292][27239206]|, anti-Alzheimer and antioxidant effects |CITS: [19652386]|. A study of the inhibitory affect of protoberberines on |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.5|, has found that |FRAME: CPD-21762| is the most potent urease inhibitor |CITS: [28167234]|. |FRAME: CPD-21762 Epiberberine| also interacts with human organic cation transporters and cytochrome P-450 enzymes |CITS: [26134304][21425377]|. In addition, studies have shown that its toxicity is lower than that of the other coptis alkaloids |CITS: [23159469][24856764]|., A pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-21762| biosynthesis has been propsed based on studies of |FRAME: TAX-261450|, althuogh the enzymes catalyzing the steps have not been identified |CITS: [29915609]|., Like many other benzylisoquinoline alkaloids, including the protoberberine, benzophenanthridine, and morphinan alkaloids, the pathway towards |FRAME: CPD-21760| passes through the central intermediate |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| (for its biosynthesis, see |FRAME: PWY-3581|). |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| is converted to |FRAME: S-SCOULERINE| by |FRAME: EC-1.21.3.3|, also known as berberine bridge enzyme, or BBE |CITS: [8972604][16728404]|., Based on the proposed pathway, scoulerine is O-methylated at C2, forming |FRAME: CPD-20734|. A berberine bridge enzyme forms a methylenedioxy bridge, generating |FRAME: CPD-21761|, which is then oxidized by |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.8|, forming |FRAME: CPD-21762| |CITS: [29915609]|.

The dioxins, including dibenzofuran, dibenzo-p-dioxin, and biphenyl, are created as by-products during industrial processes such as incineration, paper bleaching, and chemical synthesis. Dibenzofuran, in particular, has also been used as an insecticide, and is formed from the photolysis of chlorinated biphenyl ethers. These compounds are extremely stable in the environment, and their accumulation in soils poses a serious environmental concern. , Several species of bacteria capable degrading dibenzofuran have been identified, including |FRAME:TAX-286|, |FRAME:TAX-338|, |FRAME:TAX-53355|, |FRAME:TAX-33882|, and |FRAME:TAX-1827|. |FRAME:TAX-13687| sp. RW1 is able to utilize dibenzofuran as a sole source of carbon and energy. The first step of the bacterial degradation of dibenzofuran, the angular dioxygenation of dibenzofuran, is catalyzed by a four component class IIa dioxygenase, dibenzo 4,4a-dioxygenase. The product of this initial step, 4,4a-dihydro-4,4a-dihydroxybenzofuran, spontaneously rearomatizes to yield 2,2',3-trihydroxybiphenyl. Ring-cleavage of 2,2',3-trihydroxybiphenyl is then catalyzed by extradiol dioxygenases yielding 2-hydroxy-6-oxo-2,4-hexadienoic acid, which is then hydrolyzed to form 2-oxopent-4-enoate and salicylate. The end products of this pathway, salicylate and 2-oxopent-4-enoate, are further degraded via separate pathways |CITS: [10348858] [9683494] [8981980]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-183 "Gallate"| and structurally related compounds are widely distributed in nature. Plant lignin and tannins are major sources of these compounds, which are degraded by soil microorganisms as part of the terrestrial carbon cycle. , Gallate is also used industrially in inks and paints, and gallate esters are used as food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical antioxidants. Gallate and its derivatives are also of interest in drug development (reviewed in |CITS: [12769668]|. , Gallate and related compounds contain a benzene nucleus and at least 2 phenolic hydroxyl groups. Under aerobic conditions the benzene ring is cleaved by varioius dioxygenases (see |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-II-PWY| and |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|)., An anaerobic pathway for gallate degradation is described here., About This Pathway, Multiple microorganisms, including |FRAME: TAX-549| |CITS: [9835557]|, |FRAME: TAX-1351| |CITS: [Nakajima91]|, |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [Nakajima91]|, |FRAME: TAX-315405| |CITS: [12054261]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [23645198]|, are able to nonoxidatively decarboxylate |FRAME: CPD-183| to |FRAME: PYROGALLOL|, but do not possess the enzymes required to degrade pyrogallol further., |FRAME: ORG-5904| is an anaerobe that can grow fermentatively on the trihydroxylated mononuclear aromatic compounds |FRAME: CPD-183|, |FRAME:PYROGALLOL| and |FRAME:CPD-16|. Unlike the organisms mentioned earlier, this bacterium is able to fully degrade these compounds, producing acetate and butyrate in the process., Exogenous |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| or formate is required as an electron donor |CITS:[ArchMicr144-8][3571153] [3372475] [2925649] [8423143][8014845]|.

General Background, There are two main sources for acetone production in organisms: the decarboxylation of |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE| (EC 4.1.1.4) and the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| (EC 1.1.1.80)., Acetoacetate decarboxylation is the major source of acetone in mammals, and arises from either lipolysis or amino acid degradation |CITS: [12726989]|. Acetoacetate decarboxylation may happen either enzymatically or non-enzymatically., The enzyme responsible for this reaction, |FRAME:CPLX-102|, was first identified in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1488|. However, the existence of this enzymatic activity in mammals, including rat and humans has been documented |CITS: [4624981][963888]|., The conversion of isopropanol to acetone is catalyzed by the class I isozymes of the hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase family |CITS: [4358273][12726989]|. Over the years, differences in the activity of enzymes from different sources have been noted |CITS: [6389978]|. For example, horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase could not react with isopropanol |CITS: [Theorell51]|., About This Pathway, Once acetone is formed, it can be metabolized in several pathways. One of these pathways involves its conversion to |FRAME:METHYL-GLYOXAL| in two consecutive steps via acetol as intermediate., The production of methylglyoxal from acetone was proposed in 1984, based on studies of acetone metabolism in the rat |CITS: [6706932]|. The possible role of cytochrome P450s in acetone metabolism was recognized in 1980 |CITS: [ 6928621]|, and cytochrome P450 2E1 was identified as both the acetone and acetol monooxygenases in liver microsomes from rabbit, rat and mouse |CITS: [4055750][3943633][10424765]|., This pathway is inducible, and can be induced by several agents (acetone, ethanol, pyrazole, imidazole, etc.) or under different physiological and pathological circumstances, such as fasting or diabetes mellitus |CITS: [2806080]|.

This can occur in two ways: via a direct reaction catalyzed by the, mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, or via an indirect route, involving pyruvate decarboxylase,, acetaldehyde dehydrogenase and acetyl-coenzyme A synthetase |CITS: [13522696][8012582]|, Pyruvate decarboxylase, of which several forms are available, generates |FRAME:ACETALD|,, which is then converted to |FRAME:ACET| by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Although |FRAME: TAX-4932|, possess several forms of this enzyme, it is only the constitutive cytosolic form, encoded by, |FRAME: G-10420|,  that is thought to be involved in the production of |FRAME:ACET| from which, cytosolic |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| is synthesized |CITS: [9392076]|., This proposal is supported by the fact that pyruvate decarboxylase is required for growth on glucose, even under nonfermentative conditions, suggesting that the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase, complex cannot function as the sole source of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| during growth of |FRAME: TAX-4932|, on glucose |CITS: [8904337]|.

Summary: General Background, Plants contain significant amounts of hydroxy fatty acids in their sphingolipids. Hydroxy fatty acids are used extensively by several industries. The importance of hydroxylated fatty acids for commercial and nutritional purposes resulted in efforts to develop metabolic engineered pathways for these compounds |CITS:[Somerville96] [11800570]|., Most of the enzymes involved in the formation of hydroxylated fatty acids have been characterized from species of the |FRAME:TAX-3700| family, which contains a high percentage of hydroxylated fatty acids in their seed oil. , Biosynthesis of hydroxylated fatty acids takes place at the endoplasmatic reticulum, and includes the microsomal fatty acid elongation (FAE) system and desaturase enzymes |CITS:[Browse91] [11743108]|. It should be noted that while the elongase system accepts only coenzyme-A esters |CITS:[2029543]|, other enzymes such as desaturases and hydroxylases act on fatty acids esterified to a glycerolipid backbone (usually to the sn-2 position of the membrane lipid phosphatidylcholin) |CITS:[1747126] [8784737]|. This requires the reversible transfer of fatty acids between lipids and coA-esters, which is essential part of the pathway., It should also be noted that although acyl-CoA hydrolases exist to release fatty acids from |FRAME:CO-A|, free fatty acids are considered toxic and therefore are very rare inside the cell (Ed Cahoon 2013, personal communication)., About This Pathway, The seeds of |FRAME:TAX-3701| |CITS:[11171267]| and |FRAME: TAX-3987| |CITS:[16661734]| accumulate the hydroxylated fatty acid |FRAME:CPD-12193|. The seeds of species of |FRAME:TAX-98028| contain high amounts of |FRAME:CPD-12170| as well as the more more desaturated |FRAME:CPD-12192| and |FRAME:CPD-12191| |CITS:[Hayes95][Dierig04]|., The pathway in |FRAME:TAX-98028| shown here, which is based on labeling studies |CITS:[12223689]|, starts with formation of |FRAME:CPD-12193| by an oleate 12-hydroxylase |CITS:[9680976][Dauk07]|, followed by desaturation to |FRAME:CPD-12192| |CITS:[9680976][Engeseth96]|., The further steps towards the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-12170| may occur either through the elongation of |FRAME:CPD-12193| or the hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-12189| |CITS:[8784737] [9085577]|. The elongation of |FRAME:OLEOYL-COA| to form |FRAME:CPD-15363| has been demonstrated in various species |CITS:[2029543][11743108][11341960]|. The final reactions leading to |FRAME:CPD-12191| remain to be demonstrated.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) can occur via two distinct routes: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway, such as this pathway) and the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (MEP pathway). In the former, IPP is synthesized from the condensation of three acetyl-CoA molecules; in contrast, in the MEP pathway IPP is synthesized via the condensation of pyruvate and D-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate., For many years, the MVA pathway was considered to be the sole source of IPP in all living organisms, until several inconsistencies led to the discovery of the MEP pathway in bacteria and plants. The MEP pathway is present in most eubacteria, in unicellular green algae, in the chloroplasts of phototrophic organisms and in some unicellular eukaryotes related to photosynthetic phyla, such as the Plasmodium parasites. , The mevalonate pathway is found in animals, fungi, the cytoplasm of phototrophic organisms, archaea, and some, eubacteria. A considerable variability exists among archaea, and at least four different variants of the MVA pathway have been described from that kingdom. The |FRAME: PWY-922 "eukaryotic variant"| is rare in archaea, but occurs in members of the order |FRAME: TAX-2281|, such as |FRAME: TAX-2287| |CITS: [23378249]|. While most archaea posses a variant now known as the |FRAME: PWY-8125 "archaeal pathway"| |CITS: [30224495]|, a |FRAME: PWY-6174 "third variant"| has been described from halophilic archaea such as |FRAME: TAX-2246| |CITS: [24375100]| (that pathway was also found in the eubacterium |FRAME: TAX-120962| |CITS: [24327557]|), and a |FRAME: PWY-7524 "fourth variant"| has been described from archaea of the order |FRAME: TAX-2301| |CITS: [24755225][25636853]|., About This Pathway, In eukaryotic cells, the mevalonate pathway leads to |FRAME:PWY-2541|, |FRAME: PWY-6075| and dolichol biosynthesis via the formation of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP). IPP from this pathway is also used to synthesize cytosolic |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (GGPP), which is used (along with FPP) for the prenylation of proteins. In plants, the mevalonate pathway is also a source of isoprene units for the biosynthesis of a variety of terpenoids (e.g. cytokinins, brassinosteroids, sesquiterpenes, polyprenoids)., The enzymes of this pathway have all been isolated and characterized from bacteria. Additionally, a number of plant homologues have been demonstrated to be fully functional, largely through functional complementation of bacterial and yeast mutant strains.

The pathway desribes the degradation of glycerophosphodiesters into an alcohol and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|. The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.46|, removes a hydrophilic alcohol, including choline, ethanolamine, glycerol, inositol and serine |CITS:[2829735]|. The second enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.3|, oxidizes |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, transferring the electrons to the membrane quinone pool., |FRAME:TAX-562| K12 possesses two systems the salvage of |FRAME: Glycerophosphodiesters "glycerophosphoryl diesters"|, the Glp system and the Ugp system. , In the Glp system, the |FRAME: EG10399| gene encodes a periplasmic glycerophosphoryl diester phosphodiesterase (periplasmic GDP) which hydrolyzes deacylated phospholipids to an alcohol and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|. The latter is then transported into the cell by the GlpT transporter. Periplasmic GDP is specific for the glycerophospho- moiety of the substrate, while the alcohol can be any one of several alcohols. This provides the cell with the capability of channeling a wide variety of glycerophosphodiesters into the glpQT-encoded dissimilatory system., In the Ugp system the diesters are hydrolyzed during transport at the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane to |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| and an alcohol by a cytoplasmic GDP, an enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: EG11050| gene. , Globin proteins are ubiquitous in living organisms and carry out a variety of functions related to the ability of their prosthetic heme group to bind gaseous ligands, such as oxygen, |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| (NO), and |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE|. In mammals NO is mainly produced by NO synthases (see |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.39| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.47|). Mammalian hemoglobins including myoglobin, blood cell hemoglobin, neuroglobin, and cytoglobin, were all shown to reduce nitrite to form nitric oxide, but with very slow rate constants, making it unlikely that they contribute significantly to NO production., On the other hand, hemoglobins from plants and cyanobacteria, which are not oxygen transporters, have been shown to catalyze this conversion at much higher rates, up to 10-fold higher than animal hemoglobins |CITS: [21495624]|. These organisms, when under hypoxic conditions, contain much higher (millimolar) nitrite concentrations (resulting from their assimilatory nitrogen metabolism). These rate constants, along with the relatively high concentrations of nitrite present during hypoxia, suggest that plant and cyanobacterial hemoglobins could serve as anaerobic nitrite reductases in vivo., While the fate of NO is not yet known with certainty, it has been shown that the plant and cyanobacterial enzymes can also reduce |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| to |FRAME: AMMONIUM|, at rates 100-2500 times faster than animal hemoglobins |CITS: [22080728]|. General Background, The process of oxidative phosphorylation is vital for the conservation of energy for growth and development in most organisms. This spontaneous process involves the thermodynamically favorable transfer of an electron from a donor to an acceptor through a series of electron carriers in a respiratory chain |CITS: [12792025]|. Concomitantly, protons are pumped across the membrane which enables energy to be conserved via the chemiosmotic coupling of a proton motive force (pmf). The pmf is used to couple proton transfer back across the membrane for ATP synthesis from ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) by ATP synthase |CITS: [12792025]|. , Fermentative microbes synthesize ATP via substrate level phosphorylation, whereby ADP is directly phosphorylated using high energy phosphate compounds such as phosphoenolpyruvate produced by the oxidative metabolism of sugars and amino acids. , Some anaerobes have been shown to utilize a membrane-bound hydrogenase as part of a rudimentary respiratory chain for energy conservation. The most readily available electron acceptor for this respiratory system is a proton. Thus, in |FRAME: TAX-2261|, |FRAME: TAX-119072| and some other thermophilic microbes, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| is produced as a waste product from proton reduction and this is coupled to ATP synthesis by a unique membrane-bound hydrogenase |CITS: [12792025]|., About This Pathway, This pathway couples |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production from reducing equivalents generated during fermentation of glucose to acetate, ethanol and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| with proton transport and energy conservation. It is mediated by a membrane bound [NiFe] hydrogenase that has been characterized in several bacteria and archaea |CITS: [15168611]|. , The redox protein ferredoxin is reduced during primary metabolism by a number of oxidoreductases such as |FRAME: MONOMER-11816| and |FRAME: CPLX-1868|. Reduced ferrodoxin is crucial as the electron donor for the membrane-bound hydrogenase. The hydrogenase catalyzes the reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| and concomitantly translocates protons, one proton per molecule of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolved in |FRAME: TAX-2261| |CITS: [12792025]|. A chemiosmotically coupled ATP synthase utilizes the proton gradient to bring protons back into the cell and generate ATP.

Summary: Inositol is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is the physiologically most common tereoisomer and is abundantly (but not universally) distributed throughout much of the biological system., |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is an essential polyol in eukaryotes, where its phospholipid derivative |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols phosphatidylinositol| (PI) is an important constituent of phospholipid membranes. PI is also cleaved by phospholipase C to generate inositol phosphate (IP) and diacyglycerol, both of which are central cell signalling molecules., In prokaryotes inositol is not as widely spread as in eukaryotes. While it is commonly found in archaea, where its derivatives serve an important role in osmotic protection at high temperatures |CITS: [12220406]|, it is absent (or present in very low amounts) from most eubacteria, with the exception of the Actinomycetales group, which includes the streptomycetes, corynebacteria and mycobacteria. In these organisms a phosphorylated inositol is an intermediate in the synthesis of a major thiol called |FRAME: CPD1G-2| |CITS: [11544359]|. Mycothiol is important in maintaining the redox balance in the cell, in protection from oxidative stress, and in cysteine storage., In addition, the corynebacteria and mycobacteria produce several cell wall lipoglycans from PI. In these compounds the lipid moieties which are attached to the PI act as anchors in the cell envelope., PI-containing molecules have been shown to be essential for growth of the fast-growing species |FRAME: TAX-1772|, as mutants lacking PI synthase are not viable |CITS: [10889206]|., In most other eubacteria inositol compounds (small soluble molecules or lipids) are undetected or represent very minor components. Earlier work found that various strains of |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME:TAX-90371| and |FRAME:TAX-286| sp. did not contain any PI |CITS: [4552305][844323]|. Later work discovered readily measurable amounts of PI and PI synthase in |FRAME:TAX-317|, |FRAME:TAX-549|, and Ice+ strains of |FRAME:TAX-562| (these are, strains that promote ice-nucleation) |CITS: [1848220]|., However, phosphatidylinositol in these |FRAME:TAX-562| strains represents less than 0.01% of total phospholipid in the cells |CITS: [1848220]|., In all myo-inositol-producing organisms studied to date myo-inositol is produced via dephosphorylation of L-myo-inositol 1-phosphate, which is generated from glucose 6-phosphate in a rate-limiting step by L-myo-inositol 1-phosphate synthase (MIPS).

Summary: General Background, Oxidative stress in plants often occurs in response to biotic and abiotic stresses. The reactive oxygen species that form under oxidative stress can damage numerous biomolecules, including proteins and lipids. The chloroplast, an organelle often subject to oxidative stress, contains a high proportion of |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID linolenic| and |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID linoleic acids| in its membrane. When these prevalent fatty acids undergo lipid peroxidation, a variety of short-chain carbonyls may be formed. A subset of these, α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, such as |FRAME: ACROLEIN| are known to cause damage to cells and tissues. In chloroplasts, this damage can threaten to disrupt to vital process of photosynthesis |CITS: [18538576][19578873][12694595]|. Therefore, several mechnisms for detoxifying these reactive carbonyl compounds are present in chloroplasts |CITS: [21169366]|. Glutathione-S-transferase (GST)-based modification of toxic compounds is one robust system that is supported by high levels of glutathione in the chloroplast. But, there is evidence that compounds such as |FRAME: ACROLEIN| reduce the rate of photosynthesis when glutathione needed for detoxification in not available to allow the function of several Calvin cycle enzymes |CITS:[19578873]|. The NADPH-dependent set of reactions depicted in this metabolic cluster provide another means for reducing the toxicity of reactive eletrophilic carbonyl compounds in the chloroplast |CITS: [21169366][19616008]|., Similar pathways for detoxification are likely to exist in the mitochondria and cytosol, but, they will be carried out by a set of related enzymes present in those compartments |CITS: [21169366]|., About This Pathway, Two different type of enzymatic activities that can be used to minimize the threat posed by reactive carbonyl compounds are shown in this metabolic cluster., |FRAME: AT1G23740| acts to reduce the the unsaturated bond on α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, leading to the production of saturated ketones and aldehydes. Although the action of this enzyme is important, it cannot detoxify the whole assortment of reactive carbonyl compounds on its own. First, it does not show strong activity against α,β-unsaturated carbonyls that have more than 5 carbons. Second, the saturated aldehydes produced by |FRAME: AT1G23740| can also be dangerous to the plant. Therefore, additional enzymes with over-lapping substrate specificities, namely, a chloroplastic |FRAME: AT2G37770 aldo-keto reductase| and chloroplastic |FRAME: AT1G54870-MONOMER aldehyde reductase| contribute to the protection of this organelle by reducing the carbonyl groups on toxic compounds to yield the corresponding alcohols |CITS: [21169366][19616008]|.

Summary: Many prokaryotic species, as well as all eukaryotes, do not have the full genetic information required for de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, but can synthesize |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| from |FRAME: CPD-1829 "cobalamin"|. These organisms are capable of |FRAME: CPD-1829 "cobalamin"| transport into the cell, or they can synthesize it de novo from |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| in an uncharacterized route |CITS: [14351147][8770581]|., The actual substrate for the adenosylation reaction is |FRAME: COB-I-ALAMIN|, in which the cobalt ion has a valency of +1. However, |FRAME: COB-I-ALAMIN| is very reactive, and, if left unprotected, is rapidly oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-1829|. Thus, before the enzyme can act on the substrate, it needs to reduce it to +1 valency. This poses a problem, as the midpoint redox potential of the Co2+/Co1+ couple is -610 mV, which is is too low for any known cellular reductant |CITS: [4489]|. Remarkably, the adenosyltransferase enzymes are able to overcome this thermodynamic barrier. After binding |FRAME: CPD-1829| an aromatic amino acid residue displaces the |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| lower ligand |CITS: [19236001]|, generating a four-coordinate |FRAME: CPD-1829| intermediate, the reduction potential of which is higher by >250 mV, bringing it within physiological range |CITS: [15954777][15913339][18672897]|. The cobalt is subsequently reduced to the +1 valence. The source of the electron used for the reduction of the enzyme-bound |FRAME: CPD-1829| to |FRAME: COB-I-ALAMIN| in vivo has not been established. However, CobA was shown to interact in vitro with flavodoxin A (FldA), and reduced FldA was shown to efficiently drive the adenosylation of cob(II)alamin |CITS: [11408479][16207720]|. Furthermore, free reduced flavins and non-specific flavoproteins can also reduce cob(II)alamin bound in the active site of the enzyme, leading to the suggestion that bona fide cobalamin reductases may not be necessary |CITS: [19933577]|., Once the intermediate is reduced to the (I) valence, it attacks the adeonyl group of the bound ATP, resulting in its transfer to the cobalamin to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| |CITS: [8550510][7592411][ColiSalII]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAURINE Taurine| is a sulfonated amino acid. The name comes from Taurus (Latin for bull), as it was first isolated from ox bile. It is found in high abundance in the tissues of many animals (especially sea animals) and, in lesser abundance, in plants, fungi, and some bacterial species., Taurine plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many species. The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis., Taurine is produced from |FRAME: CYS| in multiple pathways. Two pathways have been described in mammals: the "cysteinesulfinate pathway" (see |FRAME: PWY-5331|), which proceeds via |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| and |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| |CITS: [4297098]|, and the "cysteamine pathway" (see |FRAME: PWY-7850|), which proceeds via |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE|, |FRAME: CPD-239|, and |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| |CITS: [Cavallini76][Scandurra78]|. A third pathway that involves |FRAME: SO3| (see |FRAME: PWY-8359|) has been described from Sauropsida |CITS: [32601391]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME:CYS| is rapidly oxidized in rat liver cystosol to its S-oxidation product, |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-8844|. The product of this reaction, |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE|, lies at a metabolic branch point. It can enter the mitochondria, where it is transaminated to give |FRAME: 3-SULFINYL-PYRUVATE| (see the pathway |FRAME: CYSTEINE-DEG-PWY|), or it may stay in the cytosol and be decarboxylated to |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE|, as shown in this pathway. It can also be oxidized to produce |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| (although this is less common)., |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE "Hypotaurine"| exists in low concentrations in liver and brain of adult mammals, and at least 90% of it is readily oxidized to |FRAME: TAURINE| |CITS: [Osman97]|. The evidence for an enzyme that is responsible for this conversion has been controversial for 55 years |CITS: [13979247][5408877][4713187][7295801][4059226]| until it was shown in 2020 that the reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-80650|, one of the isozymes of |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.8| |CITS: [32156684]|., Evidence for taurine biosynthesis in bacteria, Although |FRAME: TAURINE| is the major product of |FRAME: CYS| metabolism in mammals, some evidence for a similar pathway in bacteria has been presented based on the discovery of a substrate selectivity motif in amino acid decarboxylases |CITS: [23972067]|. Human |FRAME: CPLX66-437| was shown to contain a three residue substrate recognition motif X1aa19X2aaX3 within its active site that coordinates |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| (cysteine sulfinic acid). This motif was also identified in human glutamic acid decarbxylase for its corresponding substrate. Interestingly, the motif was also found in some marine bacterial genes that were annotated as glutamate decarboxylases |CITS: [23972067]|. , It was shown that |FRAME: TAX-91464| contains a specific cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase and that the organism accumulated |FRAME: TAURINE| in the cytosol under physiological conditions. HPLC analysis of lysates from cells grown with |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| showed disappearance of this compound and accumulation of a peak corresponding to |FRAME: TAURINE|. Although |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| could not be clearly identified, it may have been oxidized to |FRAME: TAURINE| in the lysates. The presence of |FRAME: TAURINE| was also suggested by ESI/MS data. Together with the observation that in |FRAME: TAX-91464| and |FRAME: TAX-313594| cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase homologs are found within putative operons that also contain cysteine dioxygenase homologs, the data suggest that marine bacteria may contain a |FRAME: TAURINE| biosynthetic pathway. The physiological role of |FRAME: TAURINE| in such bacteria is unclear |CITS: [23972067]|.

Summary: General Background, The transition element molybdenum (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. There are several molybdenum cofactors, including |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT), |FRAME: CPD-582| (MGD), |FRAME: CPD-23445|, or others |CITS: [1587808]|., Though not as common, some bacterial and archaeal enzymes use tungsten cofactors. The molybdenum and tungsten cofactors share the same structure |CITS: [11848842]|., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of molybdenum/tungsten cofactors have been investigated in detail in bacteria |CITS: [7836363][8514783][8514782][1587808][14761975]| and plants |CITS: [16669776][16784786][12147719][16234918][9421926]|. All of the different cofactors are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT). The variability of the molybdenum cofactors found in bacteria is achieved by the attachment of GMP, AMP, IMP, or CMP to the phosphate group of MPT, and by attachment of different ligands (different number of oxo and sulfo groups, or amino acids from the enzyme) to the metal., The MPT structure is conserved in all organisms and it has been demonstrated that its biosynthesis is preserved in bacteria and eukaryotes alike. It is produced from |FRAME: GTP| via |FRAME: PRECURSOR-Z| (precursor Z) in three steps catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.22|, |FRAME: EC-4.6.1.17|, and |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.12| |CITS: [7890743][23627491]|., About This Pathway, The small subunits of MPT synthases from different organisms (such as the bacterial |FRAME:EG11597-MONOMER "MoaD"| protein) contain a double glycine motif at the C terminus. The free carboxylate group of the terminal glycine is activated by an accessory protein (|FRAME:EG10154-MONOMER "MoeB"| in bacteria, |FRAME: HS04742| in humans and Cnx5 in plants) to a carboxy-adenylate form, which is then sulfurylated by the action of two sulfurtransferase, one of which is a rhodanese, resulting in a thiocarboxylate. Each small subunit in the complex donates the sulfur atom of the thiocarboxylate to |FRAME: PRECURSOR-Z|, resulting in formation of |FRAME: CPD-4| |CITS: [11459846]|., The insertion of Mo or W into molybdopterin is described in |FRAME: PWY-8171| and |FRAME: PWY-8167|, respectively.

The basidiomycete model fungus |FRAME: TAX-71150| forms symbiotic associations (called ectomycorrhizae) with, various trees including spruce, pine, birch, poplar, and beech. A crucial part of the symbiosis is the decomposition of litter material, making nutrients embedded in recalcitrant organic matter complexe accessible to the host plant |CITS: [25524234]|., The fungus, like many other members of the |FRAME: TAX-68889| order, produces brightly colored aromatic pigments, including |FRAME: CPD-27628 "pulvinic acids"| and the |FRAME: 25-Diarylcyclopentenones 2,5-diarylcyclopentenones|. These pigments display redox activity and are assumed to play a crucial role in the reduction of Fe3+ during the Fenton-based decomposition of litter material |CITS: [21764756]|., Both the pulvinic acids and the 2,5-diarylcyclopentenones are synthesized from a single precursor intermediate - |FRAME: CPD-14619|. |FRAME:CPD-14619 Atromentin| is one of the earliest fungal secondary metabolites which were extracted and structurally elucidated |CITS:[Thoerner78]|., The pathway of atromentin biosynthesis originates from the amino acid |FRAME:TYR|. |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.5, |, which has been characterized from the basidiomycete |FRAME: TAX-80604|, forms |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, the substrate for the next enzyme |CITS:[18805498]|. , |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.10|, is a non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS)-like enzyme that comprises three domains: an adenylation (A) domain, an acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain, and a thioesterase (TE) domain. The enzyme activates the monomeric substrate, attaches it via a thioester bond, condenses two monomers, and releases the finalized molecule |CITS:[18805498]|. A phosphopantetheinyl (Ppant) transferase that converts the apo-enzyme into a holo-enzyme is required for enzyme activity |CITS:[12828367]|., In |FRAME: TAX-80604| and |FRAME: TAX-71150| a gene encoding an aminotransferase is found just downstream of the gene encoding atromentin synthase. This is not the case in the basidiomycete |FRAME: TAX-5382| |CITS:[22730234]|., Atromentin synthase is one of only a limited number of biochemically characterized NRPS-like enzymes that accept an aromatic α-keto acid |CITS:[22730234]|., Terphenylquinones such as |FRAME:CPD-14619| have been reported to inhibit HIV-replication enzymes |CITS:[14714192]|, human src protein tyrosine kinase |CITS:[15787429]| and the enoyl-acyl carrier protein (ACP) reductase of Streptococcus pneumonia |CITS:[17323650]|, making them promising candidates for biomedical research.

Names: UDP-β-L-arabinose biosynthesis II (from β-L-arabinose) // UDP-L-arabinose biosynthesis (salvage pathway) // UDP-L-arabinose biosynthesis II (from L-arabinose)
Summary: General Background, L-Arabinose, the 4-epimer of D-xylose, is a monosaccharide found primarily in plants. It is mainly present in cell wall polymers such as pectic (rhamnogalacturonan I, rhamnogalacturonan II) and hemicellulosic (xylan, xyloglucan) components, as well as in the glycosyl-moieties of proteins such as arabinogalactan proteins and extensions |CITS:[10517829],[10640355]|. Although little is known of the incorporation of arabinose into these polymers or the contribution of the arabinosyl-substituents to the functions of the wall polymers, it has been demonstrated that arabinose-containing polymers are derived from UDP-L-arabinose, the activated sugar used by arabinosyltransferases |CITS:[FEINGOLD80]|., The formation of UDP-L-arabinose occurs via two routes: a) a salvage pathway leading to the formation of UDP-L-arabinose from free arabinose (this pathway), and b) a de novo synthesis route involving the epimerisation of UDP-D-xylose by a UDP-D-xylose 4-epimerase (|FRAME:PWY-63|). , In plants, the primary role of the sugar salvage pathways is presumed to be in the recycling of sugars derived from the turnover of macromolecules such as polysaccharides, galactolipids and proteoglycans, which have sugar components. , Key Notes on the Enzymes: Numerous bacterial, fungal, and mammalian sugar kinase genes have been isolated and have led to the identification of three evolutionarily distinct gene families: hexokinase, ribokinase and galactokinase families. In plants, few enzymes of the galactokinase have been described: both galactokinase and arabinokinase activities have been reported in cell-free preparations from seedlings of |FRAME:TAX-3916| |CITS:[14426659],[165743]|; additionally, the Arabidopsis thaliana ARA1 gene encoding an arabinose kinase (its activity was detected in crude extracts) has been cloned |CITS:[DOLEZAL91]|. The formation of UDP-L-arabinose at the end of the salvage pathway is achieved by a UDP-L-arabinose pyrophosphorylase. An enzyme with such activity has been purified from pea sprouts. This enzyme (USP for 'UDP-sugar pyrophosphorylase') was shown to have a broad range of monosaccharide substrates |CITS:[15326166]|., Important Note: In cell wall the majority of arabinose is in a furanose, not pyranose, configuration.

Summary: General Background, Antibiotics belonging to the |FRAME: Tetrahydroisoquinolines tetrahydroisoquinoline| class have been isolated from various soil bacteria as well as some marine invertebrates such as sponges and ascidians, where they are most likely produced by symbiotic bacteria. These antibiotics exhibit remarkable antitumor activity and share several common structural features |CITS: [11996547]|., Some of the compounds included in this class are |FRAME: CPD-16513| |CITS: [567065]|, |FRAME: CPD-18026| |CITS: [16314293]|, |FRAME: CPD-18027| |CITS: [7174530]| and |FRAME: CPD-18028| |CITS: [6860429]|. Among them, |FRAME: CPD-18026| exhibits the most potent antitumor activity and has been approved as an anticancer drug for use in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma |CITS: [25273374]|., The saframycins, a family of antibiotics prduced by |FRAME: TAX-1914|, were discovered during the course of screening for antitumor antibiotics |CITS: [591455]|. |FRAME: CPD-16513 "Saframycin A"| has potent antiproliferative effects in leukemia- and tumor-derived cells. A structure has been assigned in 1980 |CITS: [7418832]|., |FRAME: CPD-16513 "Saframycin A"| was shown to preferentially block RNA synthesis |CITS: [567065]|. When reduced in situ with NADPH. saframycin A causes single-strand breaks in DNA |CITS: [7066293][2131839]|., It has been shown that upon binding to duplex DNA |FRAME: CPD-16513| forms complexes with the |FRAME: HS03433| protein, which, in addition to its role as |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.12|, also functions as a key transcriptional coactivator necessary for entry into S phase. The formation of the complex induces a toxic response in cells |CITS: [15079082]|., About This Pathway, Early studies of |FRAME: CPD-16513| biosynthesis established that its biosynthetic precursors are one |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, one |FRAME: GLY|, and two |FRAME: TYR| residues |CITS: [3880741]|. Studies of the biosynthesis of the related |FRAME: CPD-18037| by |FRAME: TAX-34| showed the involvement of several |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "non-ribosomal peptide synthases"| (NRPS) |CITS: [8936303]|. This was further supported by heterologous production of |FRAME: CPD-18036|, normally produced by a strain of |FRAME: TAX-294|, in several other Pseudomonas strains after introduction of the biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS: [15773985]|., Based on the sequence similarity to known genes from other organisms, Liu and coworkers isolated the complete |FRAME: CPD-16513| biosynthetic gene cluster, which comprises 62 kb and 30 genes |CITS: [17981978][19494690]|., The cluster contains three large non-ribosomal peptide synthases, named |FRAME: MONOMER-19341 SfmA|, |FRAME: MONOMER-19339 SfmB| and |FRAME: MONOMER-19340 SfmC|, whose adenylation domains were shown to be specific for |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: GLY|, and |FRAME: CPD-18029|, respectively. It was later shown that an additional acyl-carrier protein domain of SmfA binds a fatty acid |CITS: [23034225]|. In addition, SfmA contains an N-terminal acyl-CoA ligase domain, usually found in lipopeptide NRPSs, which is predicted to activate a long-chain fatty acid , and SfmC contains a highly unusual Pictet Spengler domain |CITS: [20453862][22409961][23034225]|., According to the proposed pathway, SfmA attached the fatty acid to L-alanine and transfers it to the activated glycine bound to SfmB, producing an acyl-L-alanylglycine moiety. This acylated moiety is reduced to an aldehyde by the reduction domain of SfmC, then transferred to the modified tyrosine residue bound to SfmC, where it is acted upon by the Pictet-Spengler (PS) domain. A Pictet Spengler reaction is a chemical reaction in which a β-arylethylamine undergoes ring closure after condensation with an aldehyde or ketone. Following an additional reduction a bicyclic aldehyde intermediate is formed. At this point SfmC is reinstated with a second modified tyrosine residue, and the process repeats itself, resulting in formation of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-18030| that possess the tetrahydroisoquinoline core structure |CITS: [23034225]|., The building block |FRAME: CPD-18029| is generated from |FRAME: TYR| in three steps, by enzymes that have been described |CITS: [19494690][22187429]|. Several tailoring enzymes convert |FRAME: CPD-18030| to |FRAME: CPD-16513|, but these enzymes have not been characterized yet |CITS: [17981978]|., Experiments have shown that acylation by a long-chain fatty acid is required for synthesis. Since tetrahydroisoquinoline antibiotics do not contain a long acyl chain, deacylatiuon must occur later in the pathway. A peptidase-like gene, sfmE, is found in the cluster and is putatively assigned the role of hydrolysis of the cryptic acyl chain during the maturation process |CITS: [17981978]|.

Summary: The biosynthesis of several important metabolites involves the consumption of |FRAME: MET| through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) in a reaction that releases |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA)., These metabilites include polyamines (see |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME:BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-1303|), |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|), and bacterial auto-inducers (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration is tightly regulated through the methionine salvage cycle, where MTA is recycled through a series of reactions back to |FRAME: MET|., The methionine salvage pathway, also called the Yang cycle, is present with some variations in all types of organisms |CITS: [19946895]| (|FRAME: TAX-562| is a notorious exception). It has been partially characterized from a number of organisms, including bacteria |CITS:[8227039][7852397][8694776][9880484][11371200]|, plants |CITS: [Baur72][Murr75][Kushad83][Miyazaki87]|, yeast |CITS: [3906034]|, protozoal parasites |CITS: [8585735][ 11443076]| and rat |CITS: [7007366][7068632][7852397]|. The pathway was best studied in the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-573|., While most of the pathway is conserved among all organisms, several variants exist that differ in the initial steps of the pathway, between |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) and |FRAME: CPD-1063| (MTRP). These variants, describing bacteria and plants, higher eukaryotes, and protozoa, are described by several pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|., This metabolic differences in the early steps of the methionine salvage pathway are being exploited for developing new drugs targeted against pathogenic microorganisms |CITS: [2854458][2153115][1929327]|., Several variants of the methionine salvage cycle are available in MetaCyc. The pathway shown here operates in higher eukaryotes and includes polyamine biosynthesis., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here depicts the formation of MTA by the production of the polyamine |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, although MTA is also formed during the biosynthesis of other polyamines., Unlike in plants and bacteria, where the recycling of MTA to methionine starts with a two step conversion of MTA to |FRAME: CPD-444| via |FRAME: CPD-560| , in higher eukaryotes this is achieved in a single step catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.28| (see |FRAME: PWY-6756|)., Once |FRAME: CPD-444| is formed, it is recycled back to L-methionine in 6 steps, comprising an isomerase, a dehydratase, an enolase, a phosphatase, an oxygenase, and a transaminase. The last enzyme, a glutamine-dependent transaminase, produces the byproduct |FRAME: 2-KETO-GLUTARAMATE|, which is believed to be toxic |CITS: [15016471]|. Thus an additional enzyme, an ω-amidase that converts the latter to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, is also considered a part of the pathway |CITS: [24837359]|., A few notes of interest about the enzymes of this pathway, The reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|, can occur non-enzymatically in the presence of air. It is yet unknown whether the non-enzymatic reaction occurs in vivo |CITS: [7852397]|., If the enzyme that usually catalyzes this reaction binds a Ni2+ instead of Fe2+, it catalyzes a different reaction (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.53|), forming a shunt of the methionine salvage pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5389|) |CITS:[7852397] [9880484][11371200]|. While the purpose of this shunt is yet unknown, it has been suggested that it may provide a mechanism for regulating |FRAME: MET| levels in vivo |CITS: [11371200]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The structure of the O-antigen of |FRAME: ORG-6228| is very similar to that of the human |FRAME: B-antigen "B antigen"|, the determinant of blood type group B. As a result, the organism has high blood group B activity, and additional weak blood group A activity |CITS: [2471591]|. , The entire |FRAME: ORG-6228| O antigen gene cluster has been sequenced, and all the genes responsible for the synthesis of this O antigen have been identified by sequence comparative analysis |CITS: [15713070]|. The pathway belongs to the family of Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways. In a subsequent study, the |FRAME: ORG-6228| oligosaccharide repeating unit was assembled in vitro starting with chemically prepared |FRAME: CPD-15430| |CITS: [20418877]|., Biosynthesis is initiated on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane with the transfer of a sugar phosphate residue to an undecaprenyl phosphate anchor, catalyzed by an integral membrane protein (|FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33|) |CITS: [14670712]|. This is followed by the sequential assembly of the pentasaccharide repeating units by four glycosyltransferases (WbnH, WbnJ, WbnK and WbnI). Following the assembly of the core repeating units of the O-antigen they are translocated by the flippase Wzx to the periplasmic side of the membrane |CITS: [8606190]|, where the polymerase Wzy catalyzes their polymerization from the nonreducing end by means of a block-transfer mechanism |CITS: [5289031][20418877]|.

Summary: Phenylpropanoid compounds are abundant in natural environments, and can originate from putrefaction of proteins in soil or as breakdown products of plants materials such as lignin, various oils, and resins (for the biosynthesis of phenylpropanoid compounds, please see |FRAME: PHENYLPROPANOID-SYN|)., Microbial catabolism of phenylpropanoid compounds plays an important role in the natural degradation of these compounds. In addition, the degradation of several phenylpropanoid compounds is important for industrial applications such as wine making, aging, and storage |CITS: [9143125]|. , This is one of only two aromatic-ring-cleavage pathways found in |FRAME:TAX-562|. That |FRAME:TAX-562| can degrade aromatic acids suggests a wider natural distribution for |FRAME:TAX-562| than the anaerobic environment of the animal gut |CITS: [6345502]|., In the utilization of aromatic acids as a carbon and energy source, |FRAME:TAX-562| employs a branched meta-cleavage pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYPHENYL-PROPIONATE|.  Degradation of these two compounds ultimately yields |FRAME: SUC|, |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|.  Acetaldehyde is further metabolized to yield |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (the second part of this pathway is escribed in |FRAME: PWY-5162|).  , The pathway (including the portion that is described in |FRAME: PWY-5162|) has eight known steps, which makes it among the longest catabolic sequences in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [3531186][8399388][9098055]|., The pathway's enzyme are also able to metabolize |FRAME: CPD-674| and |FRAME: CPD-10797|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6690|.

Names: citronellol degradation // acyclic terpene utilization pathway
Summary: General Background, The plant-derived acyclic monoterpenol |FRAME: Citronellols| is used in the food and perfume industries and is also a natural insect repellent. Both |FRAME: CPD-7980| and |FRAME: CPD-12877| isomers are found in nature and vary in proportion depending upon the plant species (in |CITS: [14971495]|). Degradation of |FRAME: Citronellols| has been studied in some members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-286|. In early work, |FRAME: TAX-53408| was shown to utilize |FRAME: Citronellols| and related compounds as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [14445211]|. In contrast, |FRAME: TAX-160488| was unable to grow on |FRAME: Citronellols| or |FRAME: Citronellates| and lacks the atu gene cluster (see below) |CITS: [16820476]|., Based on mutant analysis, degradation of the related acyclic monoterpenol |FRAME: GERANIOL| in |FRAME: TAX-53408| and |FRAME: TAX-287| has been suggested to occur in separate steps, independent from |FRAME: Citronellols| oxidation (cited as unpublished data in |CITS: [20490788]|). However |FRAME: GERANIOL| degradation (not shown) converges with the |FRAME: PWY-6670| pathway at |FRAME: CPD-1827|., About This Pathway, This pathway has been functionally divided into four phases. Phase one is the upper acyclic terpene utilization pathway that results in |FRAME: CO-A| activation of |FRAME: Citronellates|. Phase two is the lower acyclic terpene utilization pathway in which the β-methyl group is removed in several steps, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-12897| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (as shown in the pathway link to |FRAME: PWY-6672|). These reactions are catalyzed by enzymes encoded in the atuABCDEFGH gene cluster (see below). Phase three involves two rounds of β-oxidation converting |FRAME: CPD-12897| to |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA|. Phase four involves further metabolism of |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA| via the |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY| pathway to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, as shown in the pathway link from |FRAME: PWY-6672| and in the subsequent pathway link to |FRAME: ACETOACETATE-DEG-PWY|. Phase four enzymes are encoded by the leucine/isovalerate utilization gene cluster liuABCDE with allows utilization of both |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME: ISOVALERATE| after its conversion to |FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA| (reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]|)., The initial step involves oxidation of |FRAME: Citronellols| first to its corresponding aldehyde |FRAME: Citronellals| and then to an acid |FRAME: Citronellates|. However, the alcohol dehydrogenases that are active on these methyl-branched substrates have not been positively identified and may include NAD(P)-dependent and/or PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases. The acid is activated by formation of its |FRAME: CO-A| ester. |FRAME: CPD-12896| is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-1827| by the dehydrogenase AtuD. The β-methyl group of this compound must be removed before the β-oxidation steps can occur. Geranyl-CoA carboxylase is a key enzyme in the conversion of the β-methyl group to an acetate group that is then removed by double bond hydration and lyase cleavage, as shown in the pathway link to |FRAME: PWY-6672|., Two rounds of β-oxidation follow and the resulting |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA| is thought to be degraded via the |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY| pathway. Note that in the β-oxidation steps it is uncertain whether the enzymes used are the same as those used for fatty acids, or whether enzymes specific for methyl-branched substrates are used (therefore, partial EC numbers are shown here). Overall, one molecule of |FRAME: Citronellols| yields six molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, and two molecules of carbon dioxide (as |FRAME: HCO3|) are fixed during the four phases of this pathway. In |CITS: [16000717]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]| and in |CITS: [12658511]|., The acyclic terpene utilization (atuABCDEFGH) gene cluster is highly similar in |FRAME: TAX-53408| and |FRAME: TAX-287|. Highly similar gene clusters are also found in |FRAME: TAX-300| and |FRAME: TAX-220664| and |FRAME: TAX-205922|, although |FRAME: TAX-220664| lacks atuG and atuH and is unable to utilize |FRAME: GERANIOL|. Evidence suggests that the genes are regulated by atuR and they are not expressed during growth on unrelated substrates, or substrates of the |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY| pathway. In addition, other genes involved in acyclic monoterpene utilization include exaA encoding a PQQ-dependent ethanol dehydrogenase, aceA encoding isocitrate lyase, mqoB encoding malate:quinone oxidoreductase, and moeA2 which is necessary for molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis. Notably, it appears that utilization of |FRAME: GERANIOL|, but not |FRAME: Citronellols|, is molybdenum-dependent which suggests that oxidation of |FRAME: GERANIOL| and |FRAME: Citronellols| requires different enzymes (reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]|).
