Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is an important and ubiquitous structural component of eukaryotic cell membranes. Many bacterial species possess the capability to metabolize cholesterol and can survive on cholesterol as a single carbon source. The exact taxonomy of some species or genera recognized to catabolize cholesterol has changed over time. Two of the strains that were studied extensively, Nocardia restrictus ATCC 14887 and |FRAME:TAX-1702| ATCC 21387, are now classified as strains of |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [874450][12843070]|. In general, the mycolate-containing nocardioform actinomycetes, which include the genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-2053|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-1827| and |FRAME: TAX-2060|, have all been shown to catabolize cholesterol and plant sterols |CITS: [19843168]|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1883| have also been shown to decompose different steroids, including cholesterol |CITS: [Arima69]|. There have also been some reports of Proteobacteria that can degrade cholesterol |CITS: [4628510][9572974]|., Prior to their degradation, sterols are actively transported into the actinobacterial cells by the Mce4 steroid transporter |CITS: [18955493]|., The microbial degradation of cholesterol is challenging because of its complex chemical structure, low solubility in water, low number of functional groups and the presence of four alicyclic rings and two quaternary carbon atoms. A preliminary cholesterol degradation pathway has been proposed based on metabolites of cholesterol that have been identified in several actinomycete strains |CITS: [17345852]|, and is still being updated as new information becomes available. In general, cholesterol catabolism yields four molecules of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, four molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, one |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, and one |FRAME: SUC-COA|, which can feed the citric acid cycle and generate ATP, or feed biosynthetic pathways such as lipid biosynthesis |CITS: [Murohisa93][28377529]|., Cholesterol-regulated genes are usually located in gene clusters that are induced by cholesterol. In |FRAME: TAX-101510|, for example, the cluster contains 82 genes, whose proposed functions mostly fit the predicted pathway |CITS: [17264217]|., About This Pathway, Generally, microbial degradation of cholesterol starts with oxidation of the cholesterol 3β-hydroxyl moiety and isomerization of the structure from Δ5 into Δ4. This transformation is catalyzed by either |FRAME: MONOMER-16891| or |FRAME: G185E-5271-MONOMER|, depending on the species, and results in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-323|., Following the initial reaction, the cholesterol degradation pathway involves two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. While it becomes clear that different organisms perform these processes in different order, the order in specific organisms is still not well known. It has been suggested that the side chain is eliminated first in |FRAME: TAX-101510|, while in |FRAME:TAX-1773| the two processes may occur simultaneously |CITS: [21987574]|. The pathway depicted here follows a route where the side chain is degraded completely before the steroid rings are opened., Side-chain degradation starts with |FRAME: RHA1_RO04679 Cyp125|, a P450 cytochrome that catalyzes the C-27 hydroxylation of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and subsequently oxidizes the hydroxylation product to |FRAME: CPD-13689| via an aldehyde intermediate |CITS: [19843222]|. Degradation proceeds via two cycles of a β-oxidative type process. The first step is activation of the molecule by forming a coenzyme A ester, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-14719|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-16899| |CITS: [21602385]|. The first β-oxidation cycle removes a |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety, while the second cycle removes |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. The exact identity of many of the enzymes involved in these two cycles has been reported |CITS: [Griffin11][Wipperman14][Yang15]|., The degradation of the side chain is completed by the removal of a second |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety in a process that involves three enzymes, all of which encoded by genes in the intracellular growth (igr) operon |CITS: [Thomas11]|. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenation of the 2'-propanoate side chain, followed by enoyl-CoA hydration, produce a quaternary alcohol, which then undergoes a retroaldol C1-C2' cleavage reaction catalyzed by a third enzyme, producing |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| and liberating another |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| molecule |CITS: [Thomas11][25203216][Yang15]|., The opening of the B ring is achieved by the successive actions of |FRAME: G-14723 KstD| (3-ketosteroid-Δ1-dehydrogenase) and |FRAME: CPLX-8371 KshA| (3-ketosteroid 9α-monooxygenase). |FRAME: G-14723 KstD| catalyzes the trans-axial elimination of the C1 and C2 hydrogen atoms of the A-ring |CITS: [18031290]|, while |FRAME: CPLX-8371 KshA| catalyzes the hydroxylation of the carbon at the C9 position |CITS: [19561185]|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-13680|, is unstable, and rearranges spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-13708|, a structure that misses the B ring., The opening of the A ring is achieved by the successive action of a hydroxylase (|FRAME: G185E-7848|) that hydroxylates the C4 position |CITS: [20448045]|, and a dioxygenase (|FRAME: G185E-7846|) that opens the ring |CITS: [19300498]|. A hydrolase (|FRAME: G185E-7847|) then breaks the product into two parts - |FRAME: CPD-13711| (which still contains the intact C and D rings) and |FRAME: CPD-13712| |CITS: [19875455]|. The latter is believed to be processed by three enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-14732|, |FRAME: G-14734| and |FRAME: G-14733|, into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|. The three proteins have not been characterized from a cholesterol-degrading organism yet, and this prediction is based on their similarity to the tesEFG genes of |FRAME: ORG-6191|, which catalyze the same activities as part of the |FRAME: PWY-6937 "testosterone and androsterone degradation"| pathway of that organism |CITS: [16151114]|., The degradation of the last two steroid rings, starting with |FRAME: CPD-13711|, was shown to begin with the removal of the side chain in the form of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by one β-oxidation cycle |CITS:[Lee67][Miclo90][Miclo92]| in a process that involves the |FRAME: G185E-7838| and |FRAME: G-14760| genes |CITS: [21901092][23146019]|. However, the complete pathway was described only in 2017 |CITS: [28377529]|. This part of the pathway is catalyzed by the, KstR2-regulated genes. The 5-member D ring is first hydrolyzed by an enoyl-CoA hydratase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7827| gene, followed by hydrolysis of the 6-member C ring by a hydrolase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7828| and |FRAME: G185E-7829| genes |CITS: [29581275]|. Following another round of β-oxidation, which results in the release of another |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, the remaining product is split into |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [28377529]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Antimycins Antimycins| are a family of natural products produced by various |FRAME: TAX-1883| species and share a common structural skeleton: a nine-membered dilactone ring substituted with one alkyl moiety (at C-7), one acyl moiety (at C-8), two methyl moieties (at C-4 and C-9), and an amide linkage (C-3) connecting to a 3'-formamidosalicylic acid., The first antimycin was isolated in 1949 |CITS: [Dunshee49]|, and since then more than 40 antimycin-type compounds varying in their alkyl and acyl chains have been reported |CITS: [16161485][15813185][19662084][20300130][22611362]|., Antimycins exhibit significant bioactivities, including antifungal, insecticidal, and nematocidal properties. They inhibit the mitochondrial electron transport chain by binding to |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.8| |CITS: [4346389]|, and |FRAME: CPD-5744|, more commonly known simply as antimycin A, is classified as an extremely hazardous substance in the United States. This compound was registered for use as a fish toxicant in 1960 and is the active ingredient in the piscicide Fintrol®, which is used to eliminate invasive species in areas where resident species are threatened, providing a complete kill at 25 ppb |CITS: [14082250][4430813]|., Antimycins were also reported to have potent and selective inhibition of Bcl2/BclXL related antiapoptotic proteins, making them candidates for new anticancer agents |CITS: [11175751][17620436]|., The biosynthetic gene cluster for antimycin was identified in |FRAME: TAX-861065|, a symbiont of |FRAME: TAX-64783| leaf-cutter ants that use the antibiotic as a weedkiller against microfungal weeds that infect their fungal gardens |CITS: [21857911]|. The biosynthetic pathway has been elucidated |CITS: [22861048][22971101][24367419][25275920]|., About This Pathway, Antimycins are synthesized via a hybrid non-ribosomal peptide synthase/polyketide synthase (NRPS/PKS) pathway. The starter unit is an unusual |FRAME: CPD-25685| |CITS: [5042448]| which is synthesized from |FRAME: TRP| |CITS: [5663531]| by the antFGHIJKLNO genes |CITS: [22971101]|., The starter unit is loaded on the |FRAME: CPLX-9755|, which extends it using |FRAME: THR| and pyruvate before transferring it to the |FRAME: CPLX-9756|. An enzyme similar to |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.85|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107869| gene, converts 2-enoyl-CoAs to 2-carboxy-CoAs, which are used by AntD as extending units. AntD does not contain a ketoreductase domain, and a necessary reduction of an oxo group is performed by a stand-alone ketoreductase encoded by the |FRAME: G-107867| gene, while the compound is still attached to AntD |CITS: [34151573]|. Following the reduction, the PKS's thioesterase domain releases the product, forming the nine-membered dilactone ring. The last reaction in the pathway is catalyzed by the |FRAME: MONOMER-22119 "AntB acyltransferase"|, a promiscuous enzyme with a broad substrate specificity |CITS: [23772837]|., The combined promiscuity of |FRAME: G-107869 AntE|, |FRAME: CPLX-9756 AntD|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-22119 AntB| results in incorporation of a large variety of short chain alkyl and acyl residues, leading to the many different forms of antimycins.

|FRAME: XYLITOL Xylitol| is a naturally occurring pentitol sugar alcohol. It is found in low concentrations in the fibers of many fruits and vegetables, and can be extracted from various berries, oats, and mushrooms, as well as fibrous material such as corn husks, sugar cane bagasse and birch |CITS: [16242318]|. , Xylitol is roughly as sweet as sucrose, and is used as a diabetic sweetener. Since it is symmetrical, there are no D or L forms of xylitol. |FRAME: XYLITOL Xylitol|, like |FRAME: L-ARABITOL|, is rather rare in nature, compared with the much more abundant pentitols |FRAME: RIBITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-355|., Pentitols and other neutral polyols can be taken up by bacteria and serve as a carbon and energy source. Gram-negative bacteria and Actinobacteria import the polyol intact, convert them into a keto sugar by a polyol hydrogenase, and then phosphorylate the keto sugar and metabolize it via the pentose phosphate or glycolytic pathways (see |FRAME: LARABITOLUTIL-PWY|). Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1582| |CITS: [118163]| and |FRAME:TAX-33945| |CITS: [12467497]|, transport polyols into the cell using a phosphotransferase system, resulting in their phosphoylation. The polyol phosphates are then oxidized by polyol phosphate dehydrogenases (this pathway)., Firmicutes transport pentitols via a phosphoenolpyruvate:glycose phosphotransferase system (PTS) either of the galactitol or the mannose family. In this pathway, |FRAME: XYLITOL| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-496| as it is transported into the cell, and the latter is oxidized into |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which can enter the pentose phosphate pathway. |FRAME: TAX-1639| is able to grow with |FRAME: XYLITOL| as the sole carbon source. While the transport reaction was verified, the second reaction could not be verified since |FRAME: CPD-496| is not available commercially |CITS: [27553222]|.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of, polymerizations to form various polyisoprenoids., There are two different pathways for the biosynthesis of IPP. Bacteria that possess ubiquinone generally, use the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (MEP), while the eukaryotic microorganisms use the, |FRAME: PWY-922|. However, exceptions exist - for example, some eukaryotic microbes, like the green, algae and the malarial parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833|, appear to utilize the MEP pathway,, and some bacteria utilze the mevalonate pathway |CITS:[11173292][15197467]|., In |FRAME: TAX-83333| the initial addition of two isoprenyl units to form |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is, catalyzed by |FRAME: FPPSYN-MONOMER|, and further polymerizations are carried out by additional, enzymes, depending on the configuration., Additions in the trans configuration are carried out by |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|, while addition in, the cis configuration is catalyzed by |FRAME: UPPSYN-CPLX|., In |FRAME:TAX-562|, the trans-polyisoprenoid pathway continues to form, |FRAME: OCTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE|, which is utilized in the |FRAME: UBISYN-PWY| and, |FRAME: MENAQUINONESYN-PWY| pathways for formation the inner membrane electron carriers, ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone., The cis,trans-polyisoprenoid pathway continues to form, |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE|, the precursor for |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P|, which, functions as the carrier lipid in the biosynthesis of peptidoglycan, enterobacterial common antigen, and lipopolysaccharides (LPS).

General Background, |FRAME: Lignins "Lignin"| is the most abundant aromatic compound in nature, and its mineralization is an important step in the terrestrial, carbon cycle. Lignin is broken down to various biaryl and monoaryl compounds such as |FRAME: BIPHENYL|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|., Complex lignin is resistant to most bacterial enzymes, and its degradation is usually initiated by white rot fungi, which secrete extracellular degradation enzymes such as |FRAME: MONOMER-14338 "lignin peroxidase"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14335 "manganese peroxidase"|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14334 "laccase"| |CITS: [8246842]|. The resulting low-molecular-weight lignin can be further degraded and mineralized by bacteria |CITS: [1785937]|., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-303| and |FRAME: TAX-101510|, have also been shown to degrade complex lignin |CITS: [20567767]|., Many bacterial species are able to grow on many of the lower complexity compounds that are formed by the fungal peroxidases as their sole sources of carbon and energy. |FRAME: TAX-502559| is known to degrade lignin-derived compounds possessing guaiacyl (4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl) and syringyl (4-hydroxy-3,5-dimethoxyphenyl) moieties to |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|, respectively, and is able to completely mineralize these two compounds as described in the |FRAME: PWY-6338| and |FRAME: PWY-6339| pathways., A similar ability was demonstrated for other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-101510| |CITS: [22057861]|, but those organisms utilize somewhat different enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7098|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: VANILLIN "Vanillin"| and |FRAME: VANILLATE| are important intermediate metabolites of lignin-derived aromatic compounds. |FRAME: TAX-502559| converts |FRAME: VANILLIN| to |FRAME: VANILLATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15120| (encoded by |FRAME: G-11556|) |CITS: [17928721]|., |FRAME: VANILLATE "Vanillate"| is converted in |FRAME: TAX-502559| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| by a tetrahydrofolate-dependent demethylase, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.341|, encoded by |FRAME: G-11548| |CITS: [9501423]|., When the enzyme was discovered, it represented a novel type of vanillate demethylation, since previously characterized enzymes that catalyzed this reaction were monooxygenases (|FRAME: RXN-10891 "EC 1.14.13.82, vanillate monooxygenase"|)., The methyl-carrier |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"|, which is formed by this reaction, can transfer the methyl group to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is used for |FRAME: MET| biosynthesis, or to other folates, in which case it can be used for guanosine nucleotide biosynthesis via |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| and |FRAME: IMP| |CITS: [27634497]|., |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "Protocatechuate"| is degraded by this organism into central metabolism intermediates using the |FRAME: P184-PWY "meta cleavage pathway"| |CITS: [4143957]|., |FRAME: TAX-101510|, which also degrades |FRAME: VANILLIN| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7098|), utilizes the |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY "ortho cleavage pathway"| to degrade protocatechuate to central metabolism intermediates |CITS: [22057861]|.

General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, also known as vitamin C, fulfils multiple essential roles in both plants and animals., Being a strong reducing agent, it functions as an antioxidant and a redox buffer. It is also a cofactor for several enzymes, which are involved in many important pathways, including collagen hydroxylation, carnitine biosynthesis, norepinephrine biosynthesis, and hormone and tyrosine metabolism., In plants L-ascorbate is also implicated in defense against pathogens and in control of plant growth and development., A significant proportion of a plants ascorbate is found in the apoplast (the aqueous solution permeating the cell walls) |CITS: [15608627]|., Under aerobic conditions L-ascorbate is oxidized in cells to |FRAME: CPD-13907 dehydroascorbate| (via the radical |FRAME: CPD-318|), which can be recycled back to ascorbate by the |FRAME: PWY-2261|. However, once formed, dehydroascorbate can be further broken down in vivo by irreversible reactions, escaping the |FRAME: PWY-2261|., Several pathways for the irreversible catabolism of ascorbate have been described. Facultatively aerobic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-573| degrade L-ascorbate by different pathways under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6961| and |FRAME: PWY0-301|). The anaerobic pathway begins with phosphorylation of ascorbate (mediated by a PTS-type transporter), while the aerobic pathway proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-334|. Both pathways produce |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a centeral metabolite that is fed into the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [18708499]|., Plants from the |FRAME: TAX-3602| family (e.g. grapes) metabolize ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-13059| and |FRAME: L-IDONATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6704|). The tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 1-4 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 4 and 5 |CITS: [Loewus99][16567629]|. , The geraniaceous plant |FRAME: TAX-1417776| metabolizes ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| and |FRAME: OXALATE| via a different pathway, with |FRAME: L-THREONATE|, rather than L-idonate, as an intermediate (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6960|). In this case the tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 3-6 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 2 and 3 |CITS:[Loewus99][15862089]|. Grapes are also known to accumulate |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [DeBolt04]|, and thus may be using both pathways to generate tartrate., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-334| (DKG) has been a well established degradation product of |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| (DHA) for a long time, although the pathway it is involved in was not well characterized |CITS: [16659288][10727845]|., The first part of this pathway, up to |FRAME: CPD-13912|, was described by a careful study that evaluated the different chemical reactions involved in DHA catabolism in the plant apoplast |CITS: [21846329]|. It was reported that under non-enzymatic, non-oxidative conditions, DKG was formed slowly and converted to |FRAME: CPD-13913|, which was reversibly de-lactonized to |FRAME: CPD-13912|. There was little evidence for enzyme activity for any of the described steps |CITS: [21846329]|., However, a 2020 paper reported that the pathway occurrs in hundreds of bacterial species, including important pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: TAX-470|. The new study extended the pathway all the way to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, and assigned enzymes to the different steps |CITS: [31917558]|., Note that while the pathway shown here ends with |FRAME: CPD0-1198|, continued processing as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7516| is mandatory for the ability of the organism to grow on |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, as |FRAME: TAX-381666| mutants defective in |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.176| or |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.43| were not able to grow on |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [31917558]|.

Cytokinins, which are N6-substituted purine derivatives, are a class of plant hormones that plays important physiological roles in plants, from promotion of cell division, to release of lateral buds from apical dominance or delay of senescence. Cytokinin homeostasis is regulated by the rate of biosynthesis, import, conjugation (mainly in the form of glycosides) and degradation. Cytokinins are irreversibly degraded by cytokinin oxidases which catalyse cleavage of the N6-isopentenyl-side chain resulting in formation of adenine-type compounds. Cytokinins isopentenyladenine, zeatins and their ribosides are cleaved in a single enzymatic step by oxidative side chain cleavage. This activity has been recorded in many plants and is thought to plant a key role in controlling cytokinin levels in plants.

Summary: Mycobacteria produce an unusually complex array of sulfated structures, including |FRAME: CPD1G-2| |CITS: [8076641]|,  sulfolipids (see |FRAME: PWY-7746|) |CITS: [820371][21919534]|, sulfated glycopeptidolipids |CITS: [1445849][10092667]|, and sulfated quinones |CITS: [16537518]|., The principal menaquinone of Mycobacteria is |FRAME: CPD-9849|, which contains a 9-prenyl unit side chain with one isoprenyl unit (at the β position) saturated. The molecule is often referred to as MK-9(H<sub>2</sub>) |CITS: [5942654][6035490][6035491]|., In addition, several organisms have been shown to produce an |FRAME: CPD-18196 "ω-sulfated form of the quinone"|. This compound,  previously known as S881, resides in the outer membrane and is involved in the regulation of virulence. The presence of the compound results in attenuation in virulence, and significantly increased the mean time to death in infected mice |CITS: [16537518]|. , Sulfation is achieved by the action of two enzymes - an ω-hydroxylase that introduces a hydroxyl group at the terminal carbon, and a sulfotransferase |CITS: [18928249][27933784]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipopolysaccharides that comprise all three regions are called |FRAME: Smooth-Form-LPS "smooth (S)-form LPS"|, while LPS lacking the O-antigen are named |FRAME: LOS "rough (R)-form LPS"| or lipooligosaccharide (LOS)., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., The core oligosaccharides are conceptually divided further into two regions: inner core and outer core. The inner core is highly conserved, contains |FRAME: KDO| (Kdo) and |FRAME: CPD-21358| (Hep) residues, and is often phosphorylated. The inner core oligosaccharide plays a critical role in essential barrier function of the outer membrane. The outer core comprises a tri-hexose backbone modified with varying side-branch substitutions of hexose and acetamidohexose residues. The outer core provides an attachment site for O-antigen., About This Pathway, The completed |FRAME: KDO2-LIPID-A "Kdo2-lipid A"| serves as the acceptor on which the core oligosaccharide chains are assembled by sequential glycosyl transfer from nucleotide sugar precursors. This process involves a co-ordinated complex of membrane-associated glycosyltransferases acting at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane. Many of the enzymes are predicted to be peripheral proteins. , |FRAME:TAX-590| mutants that lack the heptose region of the inner core display "deep rough" phenotypes that contain only lipid A decorated with Kdo. This phenotype causes instability of the outer membrane, resulting in loss of expression of pili and flagella and secretion of hemolysin with reduced activity. Mutations that eliminate synthesis of the outer core result in enhanced susceptibility to some hydrophobic compouns due to an indirect effect on core phosphorylation., The chromosomal waa region of |FRAME: TAX-28901| contains the major core-oligosaccharide assembly operons |CITS: [12045108][17362200]|. The region was previously known as the rfa region, but is now named according to the nomenclature system proposed originally in |CITS: [9004408]| and |CITS: [9791168]|., Once synthesized, the rough-type LPS, composed of lipid A and the completed core, is transported across the inner membrane into the periplasmatic space. The flipping of the lipid A coupled LPS core is carried out by |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.6| (MsbA), an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein |CITS: [9575204]|., In mutants that do not produce O-antigen the lipidA-core molecules are directly inserted into the outer leaflet of the outer bacterial membrane. In organisms that do produce O-antigen, the O-antigen is ligated to the core in the periplasmatic space by the |FRAME: STM3713-MONOMER| (WaaL) before being shuttled to the outer membrane by |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.5|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the pyrimidine ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, mono- or diphosphorylated forms of pyrimidine nucleotides activate other molecules, as in |FRAME: CMP-KDO|, |FRAME: CPD-12575|, and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., The de novo biosynthetic pathways of pyrimidine nucleotides consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. Salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides, and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways to form other nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|).However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level. These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The de novo pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthetic pathway converts |FRAME: HCO3|, |FRAME: GLN|,, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to |FRAME: UMP| (uridine 5'-monophosphate), a pyrimidine nucleotide that can be subsequently converted to all other pyrimidine nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7176|)., The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.5|, forms |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|, which is not only an intermediate of pyrimidine synthesis but also a precursor for the synthesis of amino acids such as |FRAME: ARG|, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: CANAVANINE|. The pathway continues with the condensation of |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| with |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to form |FRAME: CARBAMYUL-L-ASPARTATE| |CITS: [8041358]|. The products is cyclized to, |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE|, the first intermediate that contains a pyrimidine ring., The next step, the oxidation of |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| to |FRAME: OROTATE| is carried out by different enzymes in different organisms. In general, Gram-positive bacteria and fungi contain class 1 enzymes, which are cytosolic, include |FRAME: FMN| cofators, and use |FRAME: FUM| or NAD(P)+ as electron acceptors (|FRAME: EC-1.3.98.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.14|, or |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.15|). Gram-negative bacteria and eukaryotes possess class 2 enzymes, which are membrane bound and use |FRAME: Quinones| as electron acceptor (|FRAME: EC-1.3.5.2 "EC 1.3.5.2"|) |CITS: [Jensen98]|., The final two steps, the condensation of |FRAME: OROTATE| with PRPP forming |FRAME: OROTIDINE-5-PHOSPHATE|, (OMP) followed by the decarboylation of OMP to UMP, are carried out by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.10|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.23|. The last step is considered the rate-limiting step of the overall de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [7579161]|., In plants, the two initial enzymatic reactions of this pathway occur in the plastids, while all of the remaining reactions occur in the cytosol and mitochondria |CITS: [22474184]|. This implies that |FRAME: CARBAMYUL-L-ASPARTATE| must be exported from the plastids. A plastidic nucleobase transporter specific for uracil (a precursor for pyrimidine salvage pathways) has been reported |CITS: [22474184]|. Since the reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: DIHYDROOROTOX-MONOMER "dihydroorotate dehydrogenase"| occurs in the mitochondria, transporters for both |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| and |FRAME: OROTATE| must exist, although they have not been identified yet., The de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides appears to be one of the most ancient biochemical pathways, as it is evolutionary conserved in all species. Although the enzymatic steps in this pathway are conserved throughout all organisms (with the exception of the oxidation of |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| to |FRAME: OROTATE|), some differences in the enzymes do exist. For example, in plants and bacteria the three steps leading from |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| to |FRAME: OROTATE| are catalyzed by three different proteins, while in mammals they are catalyzed by the single multifunctional |FRAME: CPLX-6703| |CITS: [8619816]|., Similarly, the last two steps of the pathway are carried out by a bi-functional enzyme (|FRAME: AT3G54470-MONOMER|) in plants and animals |CITS: [2876681][7579161][9878395]| whereas bacteria express two separate proteins for that purpose.

General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, At least four alternative routes have been reported in plants. , The pathway depicted here depends on two N-methylations with phospho-base phosphoethanolamine and phospho-N-methylethanolamine, followed by a downstream N-methylation on phosphatidyl-base phosphatidyl-N-imethylethanolamine., Radio tracer experiments with crude cell extracts suggested such a pathway in carrot |CITS: [16666464]| and in olive |CITS: [7998981]|.

Summary: General Background, The staple vegetable crops tomato (|FRAME: TAX-4081|) and potato (|FRAME: TAX-4081|) are a significant part of the daily diet worldwide. However, despite their importance as source for starch (energy), protein, fiber and vitamins, these vegetables also contain specialized (secondary) metabolites with adverse nutritive properties |CITS:[17090106]|. The steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-17696| and derivatives thereof described in this pathway are typically found in the |FRAME: TAX-4070| family |CITS:[Ripperger98]| and labeled as antinutritional compounds |CITS:[23788733]| which cannot completely be removed from food |CITS:[17090106]|. By exceeding certain concentrations in the diet steroidal glycoalkaloids may become toxic, causing digestive problems and impede the absorption of nutrients |CITS:[22069686] [25556315]|. |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-Tomatine| and derivatives have been found to disrupt the integrity of membranes causing the leakage of electrolytes and subsequent depolarization of membrane potential |CITS:[Steel88] [1390841]|. , However, steroidal alkaloids have also been reported to serve as phytoanticipins and provide a protective shield against a broad range of pathogens including bacteria and fungi. They have also been shown to be effective against herbivorous animals and may act as phytoalexins against competing plants |CITS:[Guntner97] [18944982] [18624637] [Hoagland09]|. A number of fungal and bacterial pathogens have developed a detoxifying response towards steroidal glycoalkaloids by attacking the |FRAME:CPD-18735| moiety of |FRAME:CPD-17696|, a modification which may reduce the toxicity for the attackers (see |FRAME: PWY18C3-5|) |CITS:[18944982] [10477313]|. Moreover, tomato steroidal alkaloids such as the aglycon |FRAME:CPD-18644|, the glycosylated |FRAME:CPD-17696| and other |FRAME: TAX-4070| glycoalkaloids have been proven to possess many beneficial traits for humans and exhibit anticarcinogenic, cardioprotective and immunostimulating properties (summarized in |CITS:[24079774] [25821990]|)., More than 120 steroidal glycoalkaloids (SGAs) have been observed in various organs of tomato and potato |CITS:[18266924][19053181][18441227][23941899][20113441]|. The high diversity found in SGAs is also due to the presence or absence of a 5,6-double bond in the B-ring, which influences the toxicity of the respective SGAs. Whereas |FRAME:CPD-9214| and |FRAME:CPD-9211| are the principal glycoalkaloids found in |FRAME: TAX-4113| (see |FRAME:PWY-5666|), |FRAME:CPD-17696| is the major steroidal glycoalkaloid in green tissues (leaves and fruits) of |FRAME: TAX-4081| |CITS:[15053555]|. The tomato pathway(s) that, with the onset of fruit maturation, lead to further decorated steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-18747| are largely unknown but a number of derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-17696| have been identified by metabolic profiling |CITS:[23788733] [19415927]|., About This Pathway, The characterization of the |FRAME: G18C3-402| protein in potato and tomato clarified the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-22267| to |FRAME:CPD-17697|. The GAME25 protein belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family and exhibits three different activities of 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, Δ5,4 isomerase, and 3-oxosteroid reductase |CITS:[29784829][30892648]|. GAME25 starts by catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-22266| from |FRAME:CPD-22267|. Following the reduction of the 5,6 double bond by |FRAME: MONOMER-21176| |CITS: [31983879]|, GAME25 catalyzes an additional reaction, reducing the 3-oxo group it formed previously. Silencing GAME25 results in redirection of the biosynthetic route from saturated SGAs (such as |FRAME:CPD-17696|) to unsaturated SGAs, of which |FRAME:CPD-22267| represents the branch point. The unsaturated compounds are more toxic, inhibiting mycelial growth and germination of the pathogenic fungi |FRAME: TAX-474922| and |FRAME: TAX-40559| |CITS:[29784829]|., The |FRAME: G18C3-8|-encoded tomatidine 3-O-galactosyltransferase |CITS: [Zimowski98][22180624][23788733]| first adds |FRAME:ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE|, which is followed by two glucosylations carried out by the |FRAME: G18C3-9| and |FRAME: G18C3-10| encoded tomatine galactoside glucosyltransferase and γ-tomatine glucosyltransferase, respectively |CITS:[23788733]|. The last step in the pathway that generates the final product |FRAME:CPD-17696| is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G18C3-11|-encoded β1-tomatine xylosyltransferase |CITS:[23788733]|. The in vitro activity of all the glycosyltransferases have been demonstrated with recombinant proteins expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| and in vivo in mutants devoid of the respective GAME genes |CITS:[22180624][23788733]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The lipopolysaccharide of |FRAME: TAX-34054| consists of repeat units containing |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine|, |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: MANNOSE|, |FRAME: L-fucoses|, and the unusual sugar |FRAME: CPD-23290|., Bioinformatic analysis of the genome sequence identified the O-antigen gene cluster, and predicted the involvement of 4 enzymes in the conversion of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| to |FRAME: CPD-23288| |CITS: [9004221]|., In a later study the last two enzymes of the pathway, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80684| and |FRAME: G-80685| genes, were purified, and their activity was verified by a coupled spectrophotometric assay, starting with |FRAME: CPD-658| and monitoring oxidation of NADPH |CITS: [26174084]|.

Summary: Pinitol is a methylated cyclic sugar alcohol (cyclitol). It has been found in bacteria, fungi, algae and plants. It plays an important role in osmoregulation and osmoprotection. In the salt-tolerant plant M. crystallinum (common ice plant), pinitol can accumulate up to 70% of total soluble carbohydrate, or 10% of plant dry weight under water stress conditions. In salt-tolerant plants pinitol was found located in the cytosol and chloroplast. In angiosperms, pinitol biosynthesis proceeds via ononitol (1D-4-O-methyl myo-inositol) |CITS: [1600940]|, whereas in gymnosperms, it proceeds via sequoyitol (1D-5-O-methyl myo-inositol) |CITS: [Dittrich72]|., Epimerization of sequoyitol to pinitol proceeds via a keto intermediate, D-5-O-methyl-2,3,5/4,6-pentahydroxycyclohexanone. The conversion of sequoyitol to the keto intermediate was catalyzed by a NAD-specific dehydrogenase activity, whereas the conversion of the keto to pinitol was catalyzed by a NADP-dependent dehydrogenase activity. In Trifolium incarnatum, both enzyme activities were detected in a partially purified protein fraction from leaves, however the authors were not able to distinguish between the possibilities of the two activities being reside in one protein or in two proteins |CITS: [4389340]|.

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, Arsenite is more toxic than arsenate, yet many arsenate detoxification pathways proceed via arsenite, since no arsenate efflux carriers or pumps have been identified. This pathway of arsenate resistance is unusual in that it does not involve reduction to arsenite. The pathway involves biosynthesis and extrusion of the unusual pentavalent organoarsenical |FRAME: CPD1YI0-1|., The pathway's enzymes are encoded by two genes that are present next to each other in the genome and are transcribed together. The gap3 gene encodes an enzyme very similar to the typical |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.12| (GAPDH), the cytosolic NAD-dependent enzyme found in all organisms so far studied. In the presence of arsenate the enzyme incorporates it into |FRAME: GAP| instead of phosphate, producing |FRAME: CPD1YI0-1|. The steady state rate of GAPDH activity with phosphate is very low compared with the same concentration of arsenate, presumably due to the fact that the two products have three orders of magnitude difference in stability. While |FRAME: DPG| builds up and becomes inhibitory, |FRAME: CPD1YI0-1| never accumulates |CITS: [26991003]|., The |FRAME: G-80623| gene product is a novel MFS membrane protein. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-287| contains 10 transmembrane spanning segments, and is specific for |FRAME: CPD1YI0-1|. Since the half-life of this compound is less than 2.5 s, it must be generated in situ |CITS: [26991003]|., The pathway has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-287|. However, more than 2000 genomes, primarily from gamma proteobacteria, were found to contain arsJ homologs. A number of eukaryotic algae, including |FRAME: TAX-3055|, also have arsJ genes |CITS: [26991003]|. Although it is most often linked with pneumonia and bacteremia, it is also associated with other infections such as necrotizing fasciitis and urinary tract and wound infections., Like other pathogens, |FRAME: TAX-470| depends on siderophores for its supply of iron. Several strains of |FRAME: TAX-470|, including some clinical isolates, produce a siderophore named |FRAME: CPD-21002|, which is composed of equimolar quantities of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, |FRAME: THR| and |FRAME: CPD-21001| |CITS: [7802543]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Heme-b Heme| (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. While the heme biosynthetic pathway produces |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives are also formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., About This Pathway, The classic pathway for heme biosynthesis comprises an ordered and sequential decarboxylation of the majority of the acidic side chains of |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, followed by oxidation and ferrochelation, as described in |FRAME: HEME-BIOSYNTHESIS-II|., Analysis of completely sequenced archaeal and |FRAME: TAX-213115| genomes revealed that these organisms possess the genes that encode enzymes for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, but lack any of the genes necessary for the conversion of uroporphyrinogen into |FRAME: PROTOHEME| through the classical pathway |CITS: [12177321][18808173]|., In addition, several studies have revealed the presence of several intermediates, such as |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN|, |FRAME: CPD-17068|, |FRAME: CPD-17070| and |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX|. Thus, it has been suggested that sulfate-reducing bacteria and archaea synthesize heme via a completely different pathway |CITS: [9560192][19267692][21197080]|., The pathway has not been well understood until the discovery of homologs of |FRAME: G-34569 nirD| and |FRAME: G-34568|, enzymes that participate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Heme-d1| from |FRAME: SIROHEME|, in sulfate-reducing bacteria and archaea |CITS: [21969545]|. Since sulfate-reducing bacteria and archaea do not produce |FRAME: Heme-d1|, the discovery led the way to deciphering the alternative heme biosynthesis pathway, which also proceeds via |FRAME: SIROHEME| |CITS: [21969545]|. As a matter of fact, the first reaction, generating |FRAME: CPD-17068|, is common to both pathways. This reaction is catalyzed in sulfate reducing bacteria and archaea by a heterodimeric |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.111|. The genes encoding the two subunits of this enzyme, |FRAME: G-34572| and |FRAME: G-34573|, are often fused in Archaebacteria. The enzymes involved in the pathway have been studied in detail from the sulfur-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-876| |CITS: [21969545][24865947]| and the methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2208| |CITS: [24669201]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: CPD-21965 mitomycins| are a family of antitumor agents of extraordinary potency, and are used against various disorders associated with the growth and spread of cells. The first members of the family, |FRAME: CPD-17519| and |FRAME: CPD-17521|, were discovered in cultures of |FRAME: TAX-53502| in 1956, with other members reported from different Streptomyces strains in subsequent studies |CITS: [13385186][24544727][1906109][Remers05]|. They have been classified into the mitomycin A, B and G types based on the nature and stereochemistry of the side chains at C-9. The antimicrobial and antitumor activities of the mitomycins result from their alkylation of DNA. They also haves various oxygen tension-dependent cytotoxic effects on cells, including the cross-linking of DNA |CITS: [16526821]|. The most active anticancer agent is |FRAME: CPD-17518|, which was launched as an anticancer drug in Japan |CITS: [9383461]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-10231| was identified as the specific precursor of the mitomycin aromatic chromophore, including the attached methyl group, which arises from the carboxyl group |CITS: [Anderson80]|. Other compounds, including |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|, and |FRAME: MET|, were also reported to be efficiently incorporated into mitomycins |CITS: [5120255][Hornemann71][4810575][1184475]|., Cloning and sequencing of the mitomycin C gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-1914| revealed 47 genes in a 55 kb DNA region |CITS: [10099135]|. Seven of these genes are likely to be involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10231|. Three genes, |FRAME: G-63018|, |FRAME: G-63019|, and mitR are propsoed to encode a ligase, a glycosyltransferase, and a putative C–C bond forming enzyme, respectively, that are responsible for the formation of the mitosane skeleton. The inactivation of any of these genes abolished or severely reduced mitomycin production |CITS: [10094699][19161340]|., The cluster also contains three genes encoding SAM-dependent methyltransferase. The |FRAME: G-63021| gene was shown to encode |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.316|, forming the 6-O-methyl group found in |FRAME: CPD-17519| and |FRAME: CPD-17521| |CITS: [17461583][21538548]|., The products of four reductase genes (mitH, mitK, mmcI and mmcJ) and a SAM-independent methyltransferase gene (mmcE) were proposed to be involved in the reduction of the C-6 carboxyl to a methyl, although the mechanism of this process remains unknown. The |FRAME: G-63020| gene encodes an enzyme that is homologous to O-carbamoylation enzymes and is proposed to catalyze the carbamoylation of the C-10 hydroxyl group using |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| derived from |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| |CITS: [10099135]|., As of 2019, the pathway remains poorly characterized.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the first segment, up to the intermediate lipid IVA., In many Gram-negative bacteria lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., This pathway includes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor lipid IVA. Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. One exception is |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.54|, which is known to be catalyzed by three completely different types of enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: EG12666| |CITS: [12000770]|, |FRAME: G-55034| |CITS: [20608695]|, and |FRAME: G-55035| |CITS: [27006461]| genes., About This Pathway, While some bacteria have a highly conserved lipid A structure, the intracellular pathogen |FRAME: TAX-837|, which plays a key role in adult periodontitis, produces a highly variable lipid A. The different lipid A isoforms can exert opposite effects on the activation of the human Toll-like receptors TLR2 and TLR4, enabling the organism to orchestrate its virulence to control the host's innate immune pathway activation and biofilm dysbiosis |CITS: [19552698][29503705]|., The initial structure synthesized by |FRAME: TAX-837| is that of a |FRAME: CPD-24240 "penta-acylated and bisphosphorylated lipid A"|. This structure was found to already contain variability due to incorporation of different fatty acids by the O- and N-acyltransferases encoded by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS03565| and |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS03555| genes, respectively |CITS: [7721702]|., Later on, the organism uses three lipid A-modifying enzymes (|FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M10|, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M11|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.77 "EC 3.1.1.77, lipid A deacylase"|) to form additional variations on the structures |CITS: [17335558][19552698]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (ascorbic acid, vitamin C) is a reducing agent and antioxidant biosynthesized by plants, eukaryotic algae, some bacteria and many, but not all vertebrates.|FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it. These species rely on mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries. Reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|., In photosynthesizing plants and eukaryotic algae |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has roles in metabolism, electron transport, the cell cycle and responses to pathogens and abiotic stress. When coupled with its redox system, the ascorbate/glutathione cycle, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| can effectively regulate cellular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| levels (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-2261|) |CITS: [18460785]|. Interestingly, |FRAME: TAX-1117| do not possess any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis, and minimize photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases, suggesting that the use of ascorbate evolved after the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote |CITS: [23109712][25768426]|., Ascorbate Biosynthesis in Plants, Four different pathways for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| have been described in plants., • The first plant pathway was suggested in 1998 by Wheeler et al |CITS: [9620799]|. The pathway starts from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| and proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-Galactopyranose| and |FRAME: CPD-330| (see |FRAME: PWY-882|)., • A second pathway, known as the L-gulose pathway, also starts with |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. However, that pathway proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-gulopyranose| and |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS:[12954627]| (see |FRAME: PWY4FS-11|)., • A third pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-3747| (strawberry). In that pathway |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is formed from |FRAME: CPD-330|, as in the first pathway. However, the pathway starts from |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, and proceeds via |FRAME: CPD0-1083| |CITS:[13363799][12524550]|. Tracer and feeding studies have also shown conversion of |FRAME: CPD-23305| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [Loewus63]|. (see |FRAME: PWY-8143|)., • A fourth pathway suggested that |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| can also be channeled towards the production of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: EC-1.13.99.1|, based on the effect of overexpressing the |FRAME: AT4G26260| gene. According to that proposal, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is reduced to |FRAME: L-GULONATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS: [14976233]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8142|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.18|, converts |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| not only to |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE|, an intermediate in the L-galactose pathway, but also to |FRAME: CPD-7078| |CITS: [12954627]|. This finding prompted the proposal of the L-gulose pathway. Furthermore, feeding Arabidopsis cells with |FRAME: L-Gulose| or |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| increased ascorbate level, supporting the existence of the L-gulose route., Initially, an argument against the existence of the gulose pathway was the lack of enzymes dedicated to catalyze the last two steps. The L-galactose dehydrogenase purified from pea was shown active with L-gulose, although the enzyme's substrate specificity with L-gulose (Km= 3.7 mM) was very low compared with its preferred substrate L-galactose (Km= 0.43 mM) |CITS:[12047629]|. The activity of |FRAME: EC-1.3.2.M1|, was reported in potato tubers, in both the mitochondrial and cytosolic cell fractions |CITS:[12954627]|. Further support was obtained with the characterization of |FRAME: GQT-4735| and |FRAME: GQT-4288|, which showed that they are specific for |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS: [20622436][30112455]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763 "Rhodophyta (red algae)"|, mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-143 Nitroglycerin| (glycerol trinitrate) has been used for more than a century as an explosive. It is also used as a vasodilator in the treatment of angina |CITS: [10779131]|., During its production large quantities of wastewaters are transferred to lagoons or soakaways, often resulting in contamination of soils. Nitrate esters such as nitrogycerin are known to persist in the environment for long periods of time and their biodegradation presents a challenge to microorganisms due to the rarity of naturally occurring analogs., Several bacterial strains that can biodegrade nitroglycerin have been isolated |CITS: [8919782][9371434][7618866][White96][16535244]|. Complete denitration has been demonstrated previously in mixed bacterial populations |CITS: [9726874][103501]|., Exceptions are a Rhodococcus species that was shown to achieve complete denitration |CITS: [11375172]|, as well as cultures of |FRAME: TAX-70792| Dierckx |CITS: [9143106]|.

Summary: General Background, Most pathogenic bacteria have an absolute requirement for iron, which is scarce within their host environment. In vertebrates the majority of the iron is found in the form of heme. Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. In general, the bacteria express outer membrane proteins that bind heme compounds, extract heme from them, and transport the heme into the cell, where it is degraded to release the iron |CITS: [1425573][7783623][9157245]|. The most common heme-degradation systems utilize heme oxygenase enzymes that degrade heme to yield iron, carbon monoxide, and biliverdin., Several forms of bacterial heme oxygenases are known, and they are described in the various heme degradation pathways in MetaCyc. The enzymes consume three molecules of oxygen and a total of seven electron equivalents to break the tetrapyrrole ring and liberate the iron. However, while some enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), others produce different unusual isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| (|FRAME: PWY-7844|), |FRAME: CPD-18928| (|FRAME: PWY-7843|), |FRAME: CPD-19710| (|FRAME: PWY-7846|), |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| (|FRAME: PWY-7847|) and |FRAME: CPD-19716| and |FRAME: CPD-19715| (|FRAME: PWY-7848|)., About This Pathway, Similarly to other pathogenic bacteria, the acquisition of iron is required for infectivity and pathogenicity of |FRAME: TAX-1773|. Iron is scarce within their host environment, and is found mostly in the form of heme., All mycobacteria posses a heme-oxygenating enzyme known as MhuD (for mycobacterial heme utilization, degrader)., Unlike other heme oxygenases, the dimeric enzyme was shown to be able to bind two heme molecules per monomer. However, only the monoheme complex is enzymatically active |CITS: [19917297]|., The crystal structure shares overall structural similarities with |FRAME: G-54980 IsdG| and |FRAME: G-54981 Isd|I of |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [19917297]|.However, unlike those enzymes or the canonical heme oxygenases, MhuD does not release formaldehyde or carbon monoxide. Instead, it forms unique products, named micobilins, that retain the α-meso-carbon at the ring cleavage site as an aldehyde group |CITS: [23420845]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHITIN Chitin|, a long-chain polymer of a |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, is the second most abundant biologically produced polymer (|FRAME: CELLULOSE| is the most abundant). Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is a commercially important alkaloid produced by some plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5037| and |FRAME: PWY-5038|). |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation pathways have been reported in yeast, filamentous fungi, some plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6552| and |FRAME: PWY-6553|), bacteria and animals. Although the overall scheme of demethylation and oxidation reactions is similar, the main pathways, enzymes used, and some of the products vary. In humans |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is degraded by cytochrome P-450, N-acetyltransferase and xanthine oxidase enzymes |CITS: [15013152]|, whereas the bacterial pathways appear to involve enzymes different from these. The bacterial enzymes are of interest in bioremediation of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-containing waste from coffee and tea processing, the conversion of such waste to animal feed, the development of biodecaffination techniques, as well as their use in the development of pharmaceuticals and biofuels. Although these pathways are relatively well characterized, the demethylation enzymes have generally been unstable during purification. Work on gene cloning and recombinant enzyme purification and characterization is in progress |CITS: [22328667]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [14977550] [17009088]| and |CITS: [8919637]|., Although |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| in high concentrations is toxic to bacteria, some develop the ability to catabolize it. This includes strains of |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-507| and an unnamed strain of |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [MAZZA96]|). |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading strains have been isolated from the soil under coffee trees and in the laboratory by enrichment procedures involving |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| addition to the growth media. |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading bacteria use both N-demethylation and oxidation for |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| catabolism, as shown in this pathway and in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6632| and |FRAME: PWY-6633|. In the N-demethylating pathway, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is thought to be initially degraded by an oxidative demethylation mechanism. This mechanism involves N-demethylating monooxygenases that utilize NAD(P)H, producing dimethylxanthines, followed by monomethylxanthines and |FRAME: XANTHINE|. This mechanism has been supported by the creation of EC 1.14.13.128. |FRAME: XANTHINE| is degraded by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to |FRAME: URATE|, which is then degraded as shown in the pathway link. In these reactions the methyl groups are oxidized to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and its derivatives may also be oxidized by caffeine oxidases or dehydrogenases to their corresponding methylurate derivatives as shown in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6632| and |FRAME: PWY-6633| (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550]| and |CITS: [17009088]|)., Although most studies report an oxidative demethylation mechanism for |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and its derivatives as shown here, an early study by |CITS: [1158847]| proposed a hydrolytic demethylation mechanism (not shown). It was suggested that |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is metabolized by a demethylating enzyme capable of hydrolyzing each of the three methyl groups and converting them to |FRAME: METOH|. |FRAME: METOH| was proposed to be oxidized by dehydrogenases to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| via |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550] [17009088]|., Bacteria have not been reported to demethylate |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| to |FRAME: CPD-12479| (1,3-dimethylxanthine), a reaction found in |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading fungi and plants (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6552|). However, it has been shown that |FRAME: ORG-6144| was able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| as sole carbon and nitrogen source, in addition to |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE|. |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| were metabolized to |FRAME: XANTHINE| via N-demethylation. |FRAME: CPD-12479| and its |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-9025| derivatives were also metabolized by oxidation to methylurates although these did not appear to be further metabolized. Growth of |FRAME: ORG-6144| on either |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: CPD-12479|, or the N-demethylated metabolites of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| resulted in coexpression of enzymes involved in the N-demethylation pathways of both |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12479| |CITS: [19447909]|. More recently, enzymes degrading both |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12479| have been characterized |CITS: [22328667][20966097]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6999|)., The inducible nature of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading enzymes in |FRAME: TAX-286| strains has been demonstrated |CITS: [18720498] [7461603]|. Recent studies of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation done with whole cells, or cell-free extracts include |CITS: [20495941] [19229573] [19447909] [18720498] [17554468]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17009088]|., About This Pathway, In some |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading bacteria the major route of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) catabolism appears to be via initial demethylation to |FRAME: 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| (3,7-dimethylxanthine), followed by demethylation to |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE|, and then |FRAME: XANTHINE|. |FRAME: XANTHINE| is further degraded by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to |FRAME: URATE|, with subsequent catabolism to central metabolites (as shown in the pathway link, which is in turn linked to pathway |FRAME: PWY-5694|. Another route of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation is via initial demethylation to |FRAME: 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| (1,7-dimethylxanthine) followed by |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: XANTHINE|. In |FRAME: ORG-6144|, a soil bacterium isolated by enrichment on |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| was reported to be a minor route |CITS: [19447909]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17009088]|., More recently, in |FRAME: ORG-6144| genes ndmA and ndmB encoding N-demethylases of the |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation pathway have been identified, cloned, and their recombinant enzyme products characterized. These N-demethylases allow this organism to utilize |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|. They represent a new class of Rieske non-heme iron monooxygenase and have the potential to produce useful products from caffeine-containing coffee and tea waste. The monooxygenase genes ndmA and ndmB as well as an essential FMN NAD(P)H reductase encoded by ndmD were located on a 13.2 kB fragement of genomic DNA that also contained a gene encoding a formaldehyde dehydrogenase |CITS: [22328667]|. Contrary to a previous report |CITS: [20966097]|, the products of ndmA and ndmB are separate enzymes with distinct substrate specificities |CITS: [22328667]|. , Eariler evidence suggested that another gene ndmC encodes a N-demethylase specific for |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE|, although the enzyme was not purified and the possible involvement of NdmD was not confirmed |CITS: [22328667]|. However, later work showed that a NdmCDE complex catalyzes the final demethylation reaction (see |FRAME: CPLX-8855|) |CITS: [23813729]|., |FRAME: ORG-6145| was shown to degrade caffeine by the demethylation pathway, but it also oxidized |FRAME: 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE| to their corresponding methyluric acids |FRAME: CPD-12482|, |FRAME: CPD-12483| and |FRAME: CPD-12481| via a broad substrate specificity |FRAME: CPLX-8094|. The methyluric acids did not support growth of the organism |CITS: [YAMAOKA99]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6632|)., |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| can also be oxidized directly by caffeine oxidase or caffeine dehydrogenase to |FRAME: CPD-12480| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6633|).

As derivatives of the |FRAME:PWY-361| coumarins (1,2-benzopyrone) are widespread in higher plants and can be found in all parts of a plant. Coumarins occur frequently as glucosides and are as such involved in metabolic sequences whereas free coumarins are less commonly found in plants |CITS:[Seigler98]| |CITS: [Mitova96]| |CITS:[11830165]|. The biosynthetic route of dihydrocoumarins such as |FRAME:CPD-14427| and |FRAME:CPD-8097| has been a matter of debate for some time because in vitro experiments with phenoloxidase demonstrated a fast conversion of caffeic acid to esculetin |CITS:[Sato67]|. However, tracer experiments clearly established a biosynthetic sequence via |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:CPD-8186| instead of caffeic acid as an intermediate (see |FRAME:PWY-6982|) |CITS:[Sato72]|, |CITS:[Brown86]|, |CITS:[Brown86a]|, |CITS:[Bourgaud06]|., |FRAME:DAPHNIN Daphnin| (7-(β-D-glucopyranosyloxy)-8-hydroxycoumarin) is hydrolyzed by the action of a transglucosylase which expresses both hydrolase and transglucosylase activity, to form |FRAME:CPD-14427| and |FRAME:CPD-14428|, respectively. Similarly, the glucosyltransferase catalyzing the glucosylation reaction of daphnetin to rebuild daphnin has been shown to express strict position specificity towards the 7-hydroxyl group of daphnetin but converted also esculetin and with lesser efficiency |FRAME:SCOPOLETIN| |CITS:[Ibrahim80]|. Summary: General Background, Cyanobacteria are able to conduct both photosynthesis and respiration and have evolved a electron transport pathways that operate under both conditions. Another important electron transfer pathway these organisms must operate is cyclic electron flow, which allows them to generate proton motive force without producing reducing power. An additional requirement the organisms face is the ability to dissipate excess electron flow, which could happen when light and environmental conditions change rapidly., Like most cyanobacterial species, |FRAME: TAX-84588| possesses two membrane systems: the cytoplasmic membrane and a series of internal thylakoid membranes. The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes, as does a resipratory electron chain, while an additional respiratory electron transfer chain is localized in the cytoplasmic membrane., The only electron-transfer quinone found in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone| (PQ), which is shared among the photosynthetic light reactions and the respiratory electron chain. Three other components - |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76|, the small copper protein |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER|, are also shared between the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transfer chains., It has been shown that the major electron source for the respiratory pathways is |FRAME: SUC|, which feeds into |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-18| (SDH), an enzyme complex that contributes to the proton gradient |CITS: [11418566]|. It is less clear whether the organisms utilize NADPH or NADH as an electron source. Two types of NAD(P)H dehydrogenase-like enzymes are present - NDH-1, of which several different complexes are present |CITS: [1907569]| and |FRAME: TX72_RS01490-MONOMER NDH-2| |CITS: [11418566]|. An emerging understanding of these enzymes suggests that NDH-1 complexes are only involved in cyclic electron flow |CITS: [30573545][32060291]|, and questions the role of NDH-2 enzymes in respiration as well |CITS: [10383967][30847494]|., The genome of |FRAME: TAX-84588| encodes several terminal oxidases. The main one is a |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-27 "cytochrome aa3-type cytochrome c oxidase"| (CtaI), and is encoded by the |FRAME: TX72_RS09370|, |FRAME: TX72_RS09375|, and |FRAME: TX72_RS09380| genes. A second oxidase, predicted to be a |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-26 "cytochrome bo-type quinol oxidase"|, is known as the "alternative oxidase" (CtaII) and is encoded by the |FRAME: TX72_RS07680|, |FRAME: TX72_RS07685|, and |FRAME: TX72_RS07690| genes. A third terminal oxidase that accepts palstoquinone is encoded by the |FRAME: TX72_RS04385| gene., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the transfer of electrons from succinate to oxygen in a chain that includes |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-18| (SDH), |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone|, |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76|, |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-27|., The electrons from SDH are transferred to PQ, which diffuses through the membrane and can deliver the electrons to different components, depending on the needs of the organism. The electrons can be transferred directly to a |FRAME: TX72_RS04385-MONOMER| |CITS: [19067963][Mackey08]| (see |FRAME: PWY1YI0-7|), to an alternative |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-26 "cytochrome bo-type quinol oxidase"| |CITS: [9922162]| (see |FRAME: PWY1YI0-8|), or to the |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76| as shown here., From the |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76| the electrons are transferred to |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-27| by either |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER|, as shown here, or, under copper limitation, by |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER| |CITS: [22749908]| (see |FRAME: PWY1YI0-2|). In cyanobacteria, |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER| and |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER| are able to replace each other as redox carriers in the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transport chains, with the synthesis of one or another protein being regulated by the copper concentration in the culture medium |CITS: [1326543][10050775][14660567]|., Despite their intrinsic different conformations, |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER| and |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER| share a number of similar physicochemical and structural features that allow them to interact with the same redox partners with equivalent kinetic efficiency and replace each other inside the cells |CITS: [7547859][11013249]|.

Summary: Even though the membrane lipids of archaea contain isoprenoid-based hydrocarbon chains instead of fatty acids (see pathways under |FRAME: Archaeal-Lipid-Biosynthesis|), small amounts of fatty acids and derivatives have been detected in archaeal cells |CITS: [5672876][26880868]|. When grown on 13C-labeled glycerol, |FRAME: TAX-2285| produced mainly |FRAME: CPD-195| and |FRAME: CPD-3617|, and a smaller amount of |FRAME: DODECANOATE|. When |FRAME: TAX-2246| was fed the labeled glycerol, it produced mainly |FRAME: PALMITATE|, with trace amounts of |FRAME: CPD-3617|, |FRAME: DODECANOATE|, |FRAME: CPD-7836|, and |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| also detected |CITS: [Schmerling24]|. The role fatty acids play in archaea is not known., Many archaeal genomes have bacterial-like genes encoding components of fatty acid synthase type II (FAS-II) systems and/or β-oxidation enzymes, raising the possibility that a biosynthetic pathway, possibly a β-oxidation pathway operating in the reverse direction, exists in certain archaeal species |CITS: [22718911][24818264]|., A 2019 study confirmed the existence of a functional β-oxidation pathway in |FRAME: TAX-2285|, but did not determine whether that pathway can function in the reverse direction |CITS: [30948713]|. In 2024 it was shown that the β-oxidation pathway functions only in the catabolic direction, and that a different set of genes encode enzymes that enable the biosynthesis of fatty acids. Three of the four enzymes combine to form a |FRAME: CPLX-85499|. The pathway enables the biosynthesis of fatty acyl-CoAs from an acetyl-CoA starter molecule in an acyl-carrier-protein-independent manner |CITS: [Schmerling24]|., Homologs of the |FRAME: TAX-2285| fatty acid synthesis genes are commonly found in monophyletic groups within the Crenarchaeota. No closely related homologs could be found in other archaea, such as Thermococcales or Halobacteriales (although fatty acids have been detected in |FRAME: TAX-2246|).
