Summary: General Background, Poly-γ-glutamate (PGA) is a natural polymer that is synthesized by several bacteria (all Gram-positive), archaea and (so far) one eukaryote (|FRAME: TAX-6073|). PGA polymers of 10 to more than 1000 kDa have been described. PGA has many industrial uses in wastewater treatment, medicine, the food industry, cosmetics, agriculture, and more |CITS: [25288645]|., PGA plays diverse roles in the producing organisms, depending on the organism and its environment. Pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-1392| use it to produce a capsule that protects them from host defense systems |CITS: [2984311]|. Soil bacteria use released PGA for the sequestration of toxic metal ions |CITS: [16348371]|. The bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1371| and |FRAME: TAX-1570|, as well as the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-64602| (the only archaea known to produce PGA) use it to decrease high local salt concentrations |CITS: [Kandler83][11411682]|. |FRAME: TAX-6073| use PGA to trigger the explosion of nematocysts, stringing cells used to capture prey, for locomotion and for defence |CITS: [1693614]|., PGA was first described in |FRAME: TAX-1392| at the start of the 20th Century |CITS: [Ivanovics37]|. This organism produces a capsule that is composed solely of PGA. The capsule enables the bacteria to escape phagocytosis, and therefore acts as a virulence factor. The |FRAME: TAX-1392| capsule is composed exclusively of the D enantiomer, making it non-immunogenic. However, other bacteria may produce PGA that contains either only D, only L, or a mixture of the two |CITS: [16689787]|. γ-PGA is also found in the mucilage of natto (fermented soybeans a traditional food in Japan), which contains a mixture of γ-PGA and fructan produced by Bacillus subtilis Sawamura |CITS: [11499575]|., About This Pathway, Some Bacillis species such as |FRAME: TAX-1392| possess a capsule consisting of pure |FRAME: Poly-Gamma-D-Glutamate|. Only a few bacteria, mostly from the genus |FRAME: TAX-1386|, have been reported to possess the genes required for |FRAME: Poly-Gamma-Glutamates| (PGA) synthesis. In |FRAME: TAX-1392| the genes are carried by the plasmid pXO2 |CITS: [3926644][2984311]|. Two genes - |FRAME: GBAA_PXO2_0066| and |FRAME: GBAA_PXO2_0065|, are reponsible for polyglutamate synthesis. Two other genes, |FRAME: GBAA_PXO2_0064| and |FRAME: GBAA_PXO2_0062|, encode a transporter that exports the polymer from the cytoplasm through the plasma membrane. A fifth gene, |FRAME: GBAA_PXO2_0063|, encodes an enzyme that attaches the capsular filaments to the bacterial envelope by cleaving the capsule and generating amide bonds with the peptidoglycan tetrapeptides |CITS: [19017271]|. The proteins are believed to interact and form a complex |CITS: [10486244][16689787]|., The genes were given different names in different organisms - cap in |FRAME: TAX-1392| |CITS: [2536679]|, pgs in |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [11606194]|, and ywsC and ywtAB in |FRAME: TAX-224308| |CITS: [11751809]|. , The exact mechanism by which |FRAME: GLT| is isomerized to |FRAME: D-GLT| and added to the polymer is still not known, although it is established that ATP is required. Studies in |FRAME: TAX-1423| have shown that while a PgsBCA complex produces PGA with a D-glutamate to L-glutamate ratio of 75/25, a PgsBC complex produced a polymer with a D/L ratio of 5/95, indicating that PgsA plays an important role in the isomerization process |CITS: [29971620]|., The CapB protein harbours a Walker A sequence typically found in ATPases and is the polymerase subunit |CITS: [9166795]|. CapC is also believed to be directly involved in PGA synthesis |CITS: [11606194][16267300]|. CapA has been classified as an A1-type anchor protein located on the outer cell surface |CITS: [10532392][16391053]|.

Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and protein modification, where fatty acyl moieties of proteins modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., |FRAME: PALMITATE Palmitate| is one of the most common saturated fatty acids found in animals and plants. It was discovered by Edmond Fremy in 1840 in saponified palm oil, of which it is a major component, and hence its name. Palmitate is synthesized by stepwise condensation of C2 units to a growing acyl chain. Each elongation cycle results in the addition of two carbons to the acyl chain, and consists of four separate reactions. The first step is the condensation of a C2 unit with the nascent [acp]-bound acyl, forming a |FRAME: B-KETOACYL-ACP| and releasing CO2. This step is followed by reduction to |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP|, dehydration to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-ACP|, and a final reduction to form the elongated fatty acid-[acp]. This chain of event repeats itself several times, until the final product, |FRAME:Palmitoyl-ACPs|, is formed., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II. The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|). The pathway catalyzed by the type I systems is available at |FRAME: PWY-5994|., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., Unlike the type I system that accepts |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of the two-carbon units, the type II systems accept only |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|. The final product of the pathway is |FRAME:Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl group bound to the acyl-carrier protein"|. It is released from the [acp] moiety and converted to a free acid or a CoA-derivative., In plant systems |FRAME:Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"| is often extended to form |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5989|). Thus, in most plants the primary products of fatty acid biosynthesis are both |FRAME:Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"| (16:0-ACP) and |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| (18:0-ACP). In addition, the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7072|, which is ubiquitous in plants, introduces the first double bond in |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| (while still bound to ACP), producing |FRAME: Oleoyl-ACPs oleoyl-acp|. The palmitate and oleate products can either be utilized within the plastid for lipid assembly and further desaturation, or exported to allow further desaturation in the endoplasmic reticulum, as well as incorporation into lipids., The fatty acids that are exported out of the chloroplast are first cleaved from ACP by thioesterases, followed by activation to fatty acyl-CoAs by an outer envelope |FRAME: AT1G77590| activity. Once activated to acyl-CoAs, they are exported to the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [14973169]|.

Summary: General Background, Deoxyribonucleotides are synthesised de novo at the diphosphate level through reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group of the corresponding ribonucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|). This reduction is mediated by the key enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|., The de novo synthesis of ribonucleotides is very expensive, and organisms have adapted to salvage potential precursors from their environment. Since nucleotides can not be imported into the cell due to the negative charge of the phosphate groups, salvage is limited to free bases and nucleosides. , Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. It has been shown that in quiescent or terminally differentiated mammalian cells, resting in the G0 phase, ribonucleotide reductase is not produced due to a block during transcription and the cells rely on salvage for deoxyribonucleotides for DNA repair |CITS: [3044582][1696835]|. Similarly, the salvage pathway is the sole provider of deoxyribonucleotides to be used in DNA repair or mitochondrial DNA replication in G1 cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|., The deoxyribonucleosides enter through the cell membrane by facilitated diffusion via a low affinity, high capacity, non-concentrative nucleoside carrier protein with a wide specificity, possessed by almost all animal cells |CITS: [3048401]|. The next step in the salvage pathway is the phosphorylation of the nucleosides to monophosphates. Once phosphorylation occurs, the nucleotides are trapped intracellularly due to their negative charge., About This Pathway, Deoxyribonucleoside kinases salvage deoxyribonucleosides by phosphorylating them at the 5' position. The key enzymes in the salvage of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleosides are |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.21 "thymidine kinase (EC 2.7.1.21)"|, (which also phosphorylates deoxyuridine) and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.74 "deoxycytidine kinase (EC 2.7.1.74)"|., This salvage pathway is well characterized in bacteria |CITS: [402352]|, mammals |CITS: [7494863]|, and plants |CITS: [22897443]|., Mammalian cells contain both of these kinases. In humans |FRAME: CPLX-8618| is encoded by the |FRAME: HS08100| gene, while two isozymes, encoded by |FRAME: HS09657| and |FRAME: HS09420|, catalyze thymidine kinase activity |CITS: [6281270][8380161]|., |FRAME: TAX-3702| posseses two thymidine kinase genes (|FRAME: AT3G07800| and |FRAME: AT5G23070|), and a broad substrate range |FRAME: AT1G72040-MONOMER| encoded by a single |FRAME: AT1G72040| gene that can phosphorylate both |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE| |CITS: [22897443]|., Most eubacteria also employ this salvage pathway. However, some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-90370|, lack the enzyme that phosphorylates deoxycytidine |CITS: [EcoSal]|. The yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| does not have any deoxyribonucleoside kinases, and thus does not possess this pathway., In addition to these two kinases, the pathway also shows how |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE| can be salvaged for the synthesis of deoxythymidine nucleotides. This is enabled by deamination to |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE|, followed by phosphorylation by thymidine kinase to form dUMP. The latter can be converted directly to |FRAME: TMP| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase (EC 2.1.1.45)"|., Once formed, the monophosphates are phosphorylated further to form the triphosphates that are required for DNA synthesis. |FRAME: TMP| is phosphorylated to the diphosphate form by a specific |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.9 " dTMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.9)"|, while |FRAME: DCMP| is phosphorylated in eukaryotes by the |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.14 "bifunctional UMP/CMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.14)"| and in prokaryotes by a dedicated |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.25 "(d)CMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.25)"|. Both diphosphates, |FRAME: DUDP| and |FRAME: DCDP|, are phosphorylated to the triphosphate forms by the broad-substrate range |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.6 "nucleoside-diphosphate kinase (EC 2.7.4.6)"|.

Summary: Polyunsaturated |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "long chain fatty acids"| (PUFAs) have18 or more carbon atoms containing more than one double bond in its backbone. The PUFAs that have 2 or more cis double bonds separated from each other by a single methylene group are generally either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, and are considered essential fatty acids for mammals., PUFAs accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|. They are also produced by some marine bacteria, but are not commonly found in higher plants. , |FRAME: CPD-10244 Docosahexanoate| (DHA) is a 22-carbon long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (LCPUFA) with 6 methylene interrupted cis double bonds |CITS: [15292371]|. DHA and other LCPUFAs like |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID arachidonate| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE eicosapentaenoate| are precursors of different classes of eicosanoid effectors involved in the regulation of many important mammalian functions |CITS: [14704315]|. , In algae, fungi and lower plants DHA is synthesized de novo from acetate. Mammals are not able to synthesis DHA de novo, and instead synthesize it from the essential fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (which they obtain in their diet) via alternating steps of microsomal aerobic desaturation and elongation |CITS: [11397798][14704315]| followed by a peroxisomal β-oxidation step |CITS: [10903473]|., Another method of DHA synthesis is described in some marine bacteria and primitive eukaryotes utilizing the polyketide syntase systems |CITS: [12835316]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7585|)., About this Pathway, Unlike lower eukaryotes that synthesize DHA via a pathway that involves a 4-desaturation step (see |FRAME: PWY-7053|), the most common mammalian pathway for DHA biosynthesis is a 4-desaturase-independent pathway, involving two rounds of elongation and a 6-desaturation step in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by a two carbon shortening via limited β-oxidation in the peroxisome |CITS: [10903473]| (although a 4-desaturation pathway appears to function as well |CITS: [26065859]|). This process is very slow, particularly in males |CITS: [16188209]|., For simplicity, this pathway begins with |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|, in its CoA-activated form, which is the form found in mammalian cells. Mammals produce this 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid from |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| obtained in the diet, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7049|., |FRAME: CPD-14018 Icosapentaenoyl-CoA| goes through two rounds of elongation by the |FRAME: ENSG00000096256-MONOMER|, encoded in humans by the |FRAME: ENSG00000096256| gene, forming |FRAME: CPD-17331 tetracosapentaenoyl-CoA|. This C24 compound then undergoes a 6-desaturation by |FRAME: HS05918-MONOMER| to yield |FRAME: CPD-17385 tetracosahexaenoyl-CoA|., Finally, |FRAME: CPD-17385 tetracosahexaenoyl-CoA| is transferred to the peroxisome, where it is shortened by two carbons via a single β-oxidation cycle, producing DHA.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Galactolipids galactolipids| |FRAME: D-Galactosyl-12-diacyl-glycerols monogalactosyldiacylglycerol| (MGDG) and |FRAME: Galactosyl-galactosyl-diacyl-glycerols digalactosyldiacylglycerol| (DGDG) are prevalent membrane, lipids in organisms that carry out oxygenic photosynthesis, such as land plants, algae, and cyanobacteria |CITS: [Dormann01]|. MGDG and DGDG constitute about 50% and 30%, respectively, of the total lipids in the majority of photosynthetic membranes., Crystallographic analysis of photosystem complexes revealed that stoichiometric amounts of both types of galactolipids are bound in the interior of photosystem complexes |CITS: [16963124][21499260]|, and it has been shown that a galactolipid-deficient mutant of |FRAME: TAX-3702| lacks photosynthetic activity |CITS: [17940034]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of galactolipids in plants is localized to the envelope membranes of chloroplasts. Thus both MGDG and DGDG have to be transported to the thylakoid membranes during chloroplast development., The glycosylglycerides are synthesized using |FRAME: DIACYLGLYCEROL diacylglycerol| (DAG) as the starting compound. The first enzyme of galactolipid synthesis, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.46|, was isolated from cucumber seedlings |CITS: [8990209]|. This enzyme transfers a galactose residue from |FRAME: CPD-14553| onto diacylglycerol. The enzyme inverts the anomeric configuration of the galactose, resulting in a β bond to DAG. Three genes encoding MGDG synthases were isolated from Arabidopsis |CITS: [11553816]|. However, only |FRAME: AT4G31780| is crucial for the synthesis of most of the MGDG lipid required for thylakoid membrane assembly in chloroplasts. |FRAME: AT5G20410| and |FRAME: AT2G11810| are only expressed in certain plant organs or under specific conditions such as phosphate limitation |CITS: [18808455]|., The second enzyme involved is |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.241|. Arabidopsis contains two genes encoding the enzyme - |FRAME: AT3G11670| and |FRAME: AT4G00550| |CITS: [10381884]|. Both are UDP-galactose-dependent galactosyltransferases that transfer galactose from |FRAME: CPD-14553| onto MGDG with retention of the anomeric configuration of the sugar moiety., In addition to MGDG and DGDG, plants contain low amounts of oligogalactolipids with three or four galactose residues in their head groups. The synthesis of these oligogalactolipids is independent of DGDG synthases |FRAME: AT3G11670| and |FRAME: AT4G00550|, and is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.184| (GGGT) |CITS: [12743031]|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: AT3G06510| gene |CITS: [20798281]|. GGGT is not related to glycosyltransferases and belongs to the family of glycosylhydrolases. The enzyme acts on MGDG, converting it into di-, tri-, and tetragalactosyldiacylglycerol during low temperature stress. The galactosyl linkages are all in β form |CITS: [12743031]|. The GGGT activity provides an important mechanism for the stabilization of the chloroplast membranes during freezing and drought stress. SFR2 is essential for the adaptation of Arabidopsis to freezing stress |CITS: [15258268][18466306]|

General Background, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| (also known as heparitin sulfate) binds to specific proteins such as antithrombin and several growth factors, thereby regulating various biological processes including anticoagulation and angiogenesis |CITS: [9151776]|. The unique sulfation pattern of a monosaccharide sequence within HS is believed to be critical for binding to the target protein., Heparan sulfate is a member of the |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| family. It consists of a variably sulfated repeating disaccharide unit which is composed of a hexuronic acid and a hexosamine., The most common repeating unit, which makes up around 50% of the total disaccharide units in heparan sulfate, is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12541|. In other units |FRAME: CPD-12521| may be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12515| or its sulfated form |FRAME: CPD-12518|, and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| may be sulfated to |FRAME: CPD-12565|, or may be substituted by |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine| or |FRAME: CPD-12533|., The structure of heparan sulfate is very similar to that of |FRAME: HEPARIN|. Heparan sulfate contains lower amounts of sulfate and less iduronic acid than heparin |CITS: [5484472]|. In addition, heparan sulfates disaccharide units are organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains, while heparin disaccharides are sulfated randomly |CITS: [15047699]|. |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| chains comprise three different types of domains: S-domains that contain contiguous N-sulfated residues, unmodified N-acetyl-rich regions, and mixed transition zones between the S-domains and the unmodified segments. Only the S-domains have binding capacities for growth factors and other proteins |CITS: [11489926]|., About This Pathway, This heparan sulfate degradation pathway has been elucidated in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-984|, which is capable of degrading it to its basic constituents., The pathway starts with |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.8|, which degrades heparan sulfate to mono-sulfated disaccharides. The lyase acts by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disaccharides. , The mono-sulfated unsaturated disaccharides are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-19229|, which cleaves the disaccharide generating an unsaturated uronic acid and |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine|. The sulfate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.10.1.1|, yielding free |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE| and inorganic sulfate |CITS: [4730325]|., The unsaturated uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-13122|, is degraded to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP| as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6507|.

|FRAME: MEVALONATE| is an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of polyisoprenoids such as sterols ands dolichols (see |FRAME:PWY-922| and |FRAME:PWY66-341|). It is produced from |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA| (HMG-CoA) by the enzyme |FRAME: YML075C-MONOMER "3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase"| (HMG-CoA reductase)., Several microorganisms are able to grow on |FRAME:MEVALONATE| as the sole carbon source |CITS: [4289807][4321764]|. In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-32044|, |FRAME:MEVALONATE| enters the cells by an inducible active transport system |CITS: [6434521]|. Internalized |FRAME:MEVALONATE| is then oxidatively deacylated by the first enzyme of this pathway, |FRAME:CPLX-7002|, to |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA|, which is also an intermediate in the degradation of |FRAME: LEU| (see |FRAME:LEU-DEG2-PWY|). The reaction is the reversal of that catalyzed by the biosynthetic enzyme, |FRAME: 1.1.1.34-RXN "EC 1.1.1.34, hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA reductase (NADPH)"|., The second enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-8421|, one of the key enzymes in |FRAME: LEU| degradation, splits |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA| into |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE| and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [4289807]|., In |FRAME: TAX-32044|, the genes encoding the two enzymes, |FRAME: G-9192| and |FRAME:G-9191|, respectively, reside  in a single operon, which is coinduced with the transport system. The genes have been cloned, and the two enzymes have been overexpressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|  |CITS: [2687236]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Nitriles Nitriles"| are used extensively in the chemical industry. Synthetic nitrile compounds are used in benzonitrile herbicides, as precursors for the synthesis of polyacrylonitrile plastics, and as organic solvents. |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE "Acrylonitrile"| is the primary component in the manufacture of acrylonitrile-butadienestyrene (ABS) resin. It is also used as a precursor of acrylic fibers. The CN triple bond that defines nitriles makes many of them very toxic and generally non-biodegradable. Some compounds, such as acetonitrile, were shown to be carcinogenic in rodents |CITS: [16270753]|. Indiscriminate discharge of improperly treated nitrile wastes into a natural water body can cause serious problems and severe impacts on the aquatic ecology |CITS: [15242125]|., While the cyano group is very resistant, some bacteria are able to degrade nitriles, using two different routes. Some organisms possess nitrilases (|FRAME: EC-3.5.5.1| and |FRAME: EC-3.5.5.7|) that can hydrolyze nitriles to the corresponding carboxylic acids in a single step, forming ammonia in the process (see |FRAME: PWY-7309|). Other organisms utilize a two step process, as described in this pathway. |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.84|, forms amides from the nitriles, and |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.4|, hydrolyzes the amids to carboxylic acids., About This Pathway, Several species, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-1663|, |FRAME: TAX-85007|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-286| |CITS: [Watanabe87]|, |FRAME: TAX-1827| |CITS: [10347869][1390687]|, |FRAME: TAX-12916|, |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS:[15242125]|, |FRAME: TAX-469| |CITS: [7772945]| and |FRAME: TAX-546| |CITS:[14672363]| are able to degrade |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE| to acrylate, using it as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen. Some of these strains have been used successfully for the removal of acrylonitrile from soils |CITS: [14672363]|, wastewater |CITS:[7772945][15242125 ]| and gasses |CITS: [14755563]|. Among the species shown to possess enzymes of the nitrile hydratase route are |FRAME:ORG-6132| |CITS: [3830164]| and |FRAME: ORG-5980| |CITS: [2920826][2001397]|., This pathway is used in the commercial production of acrylamide and acrylate |CITS: [2659343][1368882][17022452]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, A few bacterial phyla appear to possess menaquinones with very long prenyl side chains. Several members of the |FRAME: TAX-976| phylum, which consists of obligate anaerobes, were reported to produce |FRAME: CPD-9719| as either their main quinone (as in the case of |FRAME: TAX-28123| |CITS: [6102980][6363375]| and |FRAME: TAX-823| |CITS: [Skerman80]|), or in combination with |FRAME: CPD-9723|, as reported for |FRAME: TAX-28111| |CITS: [6363375]|,, |FRAME: TAX-817| |CITS: [6363375][7118751][7462123]|, |FRAME: TAX-28132| |CITS: [6102980] [6363375]|, |FRAME: TAX-28116| |CITS: [6363375]|, |FRAME: TAX-28134| strains 5540, G9a-C2 and 7880, |FRAME: TAX-818|, and |FRAME: TAX-821| |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|., In addition, several members of the |FRAME: TAX-201174| have been reported to contain major amounts of |FRAME: CPD-9719|, including |FRAME: TAX-1658| |CITS: [119033]|, |FRAME: TAX-2014| |CITS: [Yamada77a]|, |FRAME: TAX-144185| |CITS: [Yamada76b]|, |FRAME: TAX-59737| and |FRAME: TAX-33888| |CITS: [107269]|.

Summary: As their name implies, |FRAME: Steroid-Hormones "steroid hormones"| are steroids that act as hormones. Steroid hormones are divided into five groups based on the receptors to which they bind: |FRAME: Glucocorticoids glucocorticoids|, |FRAME: Mineralocorticoids mineralocorticoids|, |FRAME: Androgens androgens|, |FRAME: Estrogens estrogens|, and |FRAME: Progestogens progestogens|. Certain vitamin D derivatives (e.g. |FRAME: CALCITRIOL|) are sometimes considered a sixth steroid hormone group., The natural steroid hormones of mammals are generally synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| in the gonads and adrenal glands., Cholesterol is released from lipid droplets or endosomes and transported to the mitochondria by carrier proteins. The rate limiting step for steroid hormone synthesis is the transport of cholesterol from the outer to inner mitochondrial membrane by the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR) |CITS: [16973755]|., Once in the mitochondrial inner membrane cholesterol is converted in the into the pre-hormone |FRAME: PREGNENOLONE| in three distinct reactions all catalyzed by a single cytochrome P450 encoded by |FRAME: HS06719|., |FRAME: PREGNENOLONE| can be metabolized to either the |FRAME: Progestogens progestogen| |FRAME: PROGESTERONE| or the |FRAME: Androgens androgen| |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| as described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-7299| and |FRAME: PWY66-378|, respectively., |FRAME: PROGESTERONE Progesterone| is modified into |FRAME: Glucocorticoids glucocorticoids| and |FRAME: Mineralocorticoids mineralocorticoids| such as |FRAME: CORTICOSTERONE|, |FRAME: ALDOSTERONE| and |FRAME: CORTISOL|, while |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| is modified to the |FRAME: Androgens androgens| |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| and |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| and the |FRAME: Estrogens astrogens| |FRAME: ESTRONE| and |FRAME: CPD-352|.

Summary: Brassinosteroids (BR) are growth-promoting plant hormones. Brassinolide is the most active BR, whereas 26-hydroxybrassinolide is an inactive hormone |CITS: [14605216]|. Two CYP450s have been identified in Arabidopsis to inactivate BR, however via different biochemical mechanisms. CYP734A1 (previously called CYP72B1) was shown, biochemically and genetically, to be a C-26 hydroxylase that inactivates BR by converting brassinolide and castasteron to 26-hydroxybrassinolide and 26-hydroxycastasterone, respectively |CITS: [14605216]|. CYP72C1 is a homolog of CYP734A1. Although metabolite analysis of CYP72C1 over-expression mutant indicated that brassinolide, castasterone, 6-deoxocastasterone, 3-dehydro-6-deoxoteasterone, 6-deoxotyphasterol and typhasterol are all potential substrates of CYP72C1, no corresponding C-26 hydroxylation products was found |CITS: [15773851]|. The mode of action for CYP72C1 is unclear., In addition to 26-hydroxylation, BR may be inactivated by 23-O-glucosulation. Over-expression of the Arabidopsis UDP-glucosyltransferase UGT73C5 in Arabidopsis plants led to BR-deficient phenotypes. Feeding the UGT73C5-overexpressing plants with castasterone (CS) and brassinolide (BL) caused a two orders of magnitude increase of 23-O-glucosides of CS and BL. The results suggested a role of glucosylation by UGT73C5 in BR homeostasis |CITS: [16214889]|. , A brassinosteroid sulfotransferase activity was also found in Arabidopsis which indicating another possible route of BR-inactivation |CITS: [17039368]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Factor-420 "Factor 420"| (also known as coenzyme F420, or simply F420) is a redox-active compound well-known for its role in methanogenesis. Although playing a crucial role in methanoarchaeal metabolism, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage., F420 was first isolated as a cosubstrate involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-19258| in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1960 |CITS: [McCormick82]| (see |FRAME: EC-1.3.98.4|). It is currently known to be involved in the biosynthesis of a number of secondary metabolites |CITS: [8577249]|, the degradation of nitroaromatics |CITS: [10217752]|, and activation of nitroimidazofurans |CITS: [10879539]|. Mycobacterium and Nocardia contain an |FRAME: EC-1.1.98.2 "F420-dependent glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase"| |CITS: [8997717][8631674]|, and an F420-containing photolyase has been discovered in a number of microorganisms |CITS: [2110564]|. However, F420 is best known for its role in methanogenesis (see |FRAME:CPLX-341| and |FRAME:CPLX-323|)., The structure of factor 420 from |FRAME: TAX-145262| was elucidated by Eirich et al, who showed that it was an [N-(N-L-lactyl-γ-L-glutamyl)-L glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin] |CITS: [728375]|. That compound contained two glutamate residues, with the terminal glutamate bound through an amide bond to the γ position of the other glutamate. Subsequent work revealed variation in the polyglutamylation of F420 among different organisms, with up to a total of seven γ-linked glutamates, sometimes capped by a terminal α-linked glutamate (see |FRAME:PWY-5199|) |CITS: [12867481]|., About This Pathway, Genome sequencing projects suggested that some Gram-negative bacteria have acquired the genes for factor 420 biosynthesis by horizontal transfer. These predictions were verified by fluorescence microscopy and analytical chemistry |CITS: [27505347][28049838]|. Such a gene cluster has been studied in more detail from the proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-412963|, which is an intracellular endosymbiont of the phytopathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-58291| |CITS: [31469543]|., The genes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and were found to encode the biosynthesis of a new variant of factor 420, which is derived from |FRAME: G3P| instead of |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE| (as in archaea) or |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| (as in mycobacteria). The specific reaction catalysed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.28|, was found to depend on the availability of substrate, which is determined by the type of CofC enzyme present in the organism - |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.68|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.105|, or |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.106|.|CITS: [31469543]|., The new variant, which was named |FRAME: CPD-22708 "3PG-factor 420"|, was shown to be able to substitute for the canonical factor 420 for several enzymes. Like in the case of the canonical factor, 3PG-factor 420 is polyglutamylated by CofE, which adds up to six L-glutamate residues |CITS: [31469543]|.

Studies have shown that the capacity to use hydrocarbons as sole carbon and energy source, is very common, and not restricted to any particular group of microorganisms., Examples were found in a wide range of prokaryotic and eukaryotic genera including Gram-negative, and Gram-positive bacteria, yeasts, fungi, and even some achlorophyllous algae |CITS: [7532480]|., One of these organisms is the Gram negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-301|,  isolated from, machine shop cutting oil |CITS: [16560407]|, which can grow on intermediate chain length n-alkanes, (C<sub>6</sub> to C<sub>12</sub>). , This pathway describes the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-148| by this organism., The key enzyme in this pathway is the |FRAME: CPLX-3202|, which is encoded by the OCT plasmid, |CITS: [4515610]|. The |FRAME: CPLX-3202| system introduces molecular oxygen in the terminal carbon, atom of the hydrocarbons at the expense of NADH |CITS: [4403503]| to yield primary alcohols, |CITS: [7592483]|. It is composed of three components - a |FRAME: MONOMER-3842|, a, |FRAME: MONOMER-3844|,  and a |FRAME: MONOMER-1021|., The NADH-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-1021| transfers the electrons from NADH, via the electron, carrier |FRAME: MONOMER-3844|, to the monooxygenase, which reduces the other oxygen atom., The product of the hydroxylase system, |FRAME: OCTANOL|, is then further catabolized by an, |FRAME: MONOMER-1081|, an |FRAME: MONOMER-1082| and an |FRAME: MONOMER-1083|., The final product, |FRAME: CPD-196|, enters the β-oxidation-cycle, and can be utilized, as a carbon and energy source |CITS: [1453953][7532480]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamin diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamin-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamin is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, Since the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| is a very complex process, many organisms possess various salvage pathways thart enable them to rescue thiamin fragments obtained from the environment. This pathway describes the salvage of |FRAME: HMP| (HMP), a degradation product of thiamin that can be generated by |FRAME: BSU11650-MONOMER thiaminase| enzymes., The salvaged HMP is phosphorylated to form |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP|, which is incorporated into the de novo thiamin biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [18054064]|. In most cases the salvage reaction is catalyzed by the biosynthetic enzyme that catalyzes the following reaction, which is part of the de novo pathway.

Several antibiotics produced by Streptomyces species, including mureidomycin, cirratiomycin, and pacidamycins, contain the unusual amino acid |FRAME: CPD-27226| [(2S,3S)-DABA]., The pathway leading to its production was reported only in 2024, when the gene cluster encoding cirratiomycin biosynthesis was described. The production of |FRAME: CPD-27226| from |FRAME: THR| requires 4 enzymes. Homologous genes were found in the genomes of other organisms known to produce the compound |CITS: [38456538]|., The pathway starts with phosphorylation of L-threonine at the O3 position. The next enzyme catalyzes the transfer of the activated L-threonyl moiety to the Nβ nitrogen of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, forming |FRAME: CPD-27227|. This is followed by a lyase that breaks a C-N bond, releasing |FRAME: FUM| and forming |FRAME: CPD-27228|., In many organisms this is the end result, as (2S,3R))-DABA is also found as a component of many secondatry products, including totopotensamide, malacidin, and friulimicin. However, in organisms that produce ((2S,3S)-DABA a 4th enzyme, an epimerase, converts (2S,3R)-DABA to (2S,3S)-DABA |CITS: [38456538]|.

Summary: General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: |FRAME: Penams penams| (e.g. penicillins), |FRAME: Cephems ceph-3-ems| (e.g. cephalosporins, cephamycins), |FRAME: Clavams clavams| (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| (e.g. thienamycins) and |FRAME: Monolactams monolactams| (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while clavams, carbapenems and monolactams are produced by bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|. The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem (see |FRAME: PWY-5737|) and clavam (this pathway) antibiotics differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). The pathway for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially elucidated and the order of some known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., The clavam |FRAME: CPD-9261| is biosynthesized as a secondary metabolite in |FRAME: TAX-1901| and is produced industrially in this organism by fermentation. Although it has only weak antibiotic activity, it is a potent inhibitor of Class A serine β-lactamases produced by some bacteria (see |FRAME: MONOMER-13427| and |FRAME: EG10040-MONOMER|). It is used clinically in combination with β-lactam antibiotics to combat resistance in bacterial pathogens. The 3R,5R stereochemistry is required for its inhibitory activity. Other species of |FRAME:TAX-1883| do not produce |FRAME: CPD-9261|, but do produce other clavam metabolites with 5S stereochemistry., About This Pathway, In this pathway, |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: GAP| condense to form the β-amino acid |FRAME: L-N2-2-CARBOXYETHYLARGININE|. The β-lactam ring is formed in the second reaction (click on the More Detail button to see compound structures). A single enzyme clavaminic acid synthase catalyzes three of the four reactions leading to the bicyclic intermediate |FRAME: CLAVAMINATE|. This compound is a proposed branch point for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9261| and the 5S clavams. The conversion of |FRAME: CLAVAMINATE| to the unstable intermediate |FRAME: CPD-9260| through an apparent double-epimerization and oxidative deamination remains uncharacterized, although it involves an |FRAME: CPD-24202| intermediate |CITS: [16251194]| and an |FRAME: CPD-24203| intermediate |CITS: [30194098]|. Steps leading to the conversion of |FRAME: CLAVAMINATE| to the 5S clavams also remain uncharacterized. A gene named cpe, encoding a β-lactamase-related protein, has been suggested as a candidate for catalyzing the epimerization of 5S precursors to the 5R configuration, although this has not been experimentally proven yet |CITS: [23897479][31013337]|. The final step is known to be a reduction of |FRAME: CPD-9260| to |FRAME: CPD-9261| |CITS: [FULSTON01]|., Current literature suggests that the clavulanate biosynthesis gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-1901| comprises genes involved in its synthesis, transport and regulation. A second clavam gene cluster contains several paralogous genes including cas1 and ceaS1. The clavaminate synthase isozyme products of paralogous genes cas1 and cas2 are both functional and are nutritionally regulated. Some of the other genes in this second gene cluster are involved only in the synthesis of 5S clavams and others are of unknown function. In |CITS: [16251194] [15342599] [12413541]|.

|FRAME: CPD-8204 Dimorphecolate| (9-OH-18:2Δ10trans,12trans) is the major fatty acid found in seeds of |FRAME: TAX-13490| species. It is a conjugated fatty acid that has three unusual structural features: , 1) a C-9 hydroxyl group , 2) conjugated Δ10,Δ12 double bonds, and, 3) two trans double bonds, rather than the much more common cis bonds. , This special fatty acid has potential values in industrial applications such as the manufacture of paints, inks, lubricants, plastics, and nylon., |FRAME: CPD-8204 Dimorphecolate| is derived from |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| by the concerted activity of two desaturase enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-9662| and |FRAME: G-9663| genes |CITS: [14718523]|., cDNAs of both enzymes have been cloned. Ectopic expression in yeast and soybean somatic embryo cells demonstrated that |FRAME: G-9662| encodes a oleate 12(E)-desaturase, able to convert |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| (18:1Δ9cis) to |FRAME: CPD-8203| (18:2Δ9cis,12trans). The ectopic expression experiments also demonstrated that |FRAME: G-9663| encodes a Δ9 fatty acid conjugase-like enzyme that is able to introduce a hydroxyl group at C9 while simultaneously converting the cis Δ9 double bond to a trans Δ10 double bond |CITS: [14718523]|.

Summary: General Background, The genus |FRAME: TAX-26496| is the most important genus of the |FRAME: TAX-26468| family, which comprises approximately 190 species of trees and lianas. |FRAME: CPD-21554 Strychnine| is a terpene indole alkaloid belonging to the Strychnos family of Corynanthe alkaloids and was the first alkaloid to be identified in plants of the |FRAME: TAX-26496| genus. It is found in the seeds and bark of many plants in this genus., |FRAME: TAX-28545| is a tree native to the tropical forests on the Malabar Coast in Southern India, Sri Lanka and Indonesia. It has an orange-colored fruit that contains five seeds. The toxic effects of these seeds have been well known from the times of ancient India, although the chemical compound itself was not identified., In 1819, Pelletier and Caventou reported the isolation of strychnine, in pure form, as the principal toxin from |FRAME: TAX-28545| and |FRAME: TAX-1037790| |CITS: [Pelletier19]|. The correct structure was reported in 1946 |CITS: [Briggs46][Holmes46]|. The absolute stereochemistry of strychnine was established by Peerdeman in 1956 with X-ray crystallographic analysis |CITS: [Peerdeman56]|. Strychnine is one of the most complex natural products of its size, with twenty-four skeletal atoms arranged in seven rings, resulting in six contiguous stereogenic centers., Strychnine is a powerful toxin (a lethal dose of strychnine for an adult human is in the range of 30-100 mg). It is an antagonist of glycine and acetylcholine receptors and affects primarily the motor nerve fibers in the spinal cord which control muscle contraction. It binds noncovalently to the same receptor as glycine, preventing the inhibitory effects of glycine on the postsynaptic neuron and resulting in activation of the motor neurons |CITS: [5443256][5093729][3023812][8939452]|. This activation causes spastic muscle contractions and eventually death by asphyxiation |CITS: [4067548]|., About This Pathway, While the pathway that leads to |FRAME: CPD-21554| biosynthesis has been studied for many years, the definitive pathway has been proposed, and the enzymes involved identified, only in 2022 |CITS: [35794473]|. Earlier work has identified |FRAME: CPD-27135| as an intermediate |CITS: [Heimberger73]|, but the steps leading to its formation or eventual conversion to |FRAME: CPD-21554| remained unknown., The initial steps of the pathway, which are not shown here, involve the condensation of |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| with |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD| to form |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5290|) and the conversion of |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| to |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE|, which is the common biogenetic intermediate for all monoterpenoid indole alkaloids |CITS: [28827772]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8519|)., The first commited step of the pathway is carried out by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.80|, which catalyzes an oxidative cyclization involving C16, forming |FRAME: CPD-21559|. The next step involves the loss of the methoxycarbonyl group from |FRAME: CPD-21559| to give |FRAME: CPD-24090|. Hydroxylation, followed by stereospecific reduction of the endocyclic double bond, provides the |FRAME: CPD-27135|, which was first isolated by Heimberger and Scott in 1973 |CITS: [Heimberger73]|, although previously synthesized by Wieland and Gumlich in 1932 |CITS: [Wieland32]|., To complete the strychnidine backbone two additional carbons are required. Early work has shown that they originate from acetate |CITS: [Anet53][Schlatter69]|. It is now known that the carbons are added by malonylation, forming |FRAME: CPD-24092|, which converts in a slow and un-catalyzed reaction to |FRAME: CPD-21554| |CITS: [35794473]|., Many of the plants that produce |FRAME: CPD-21554| also synthesize |FRAME: CPD-24093|, a less toxic 9,10-dimethoxy derivative of |FRAME: CPD-21554|.

General Background, Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|., Bioluminescence is particularly predominant in the marine environment, in members of planktonic bacteria and protozoa, many invertebrates, and vertebrates with specialized light producing organs that harbor symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria. However, terrestrial bioluminescent fungi are spread throughout the globe. The bioluminescent fungi, which comprise around 80 different species, belong to four known lineages of the |FRAME: TAX-5338| order of basidiomycete fungi - the Armillaria, the Omphalotus, the Mycenoid , and the Lucentipes lineages |CITS: [Chew15]|. All of the bioluminescent fungi appear to share a single bioluminescent system |CITS: [22495263]|., About This Pathway, The enzymatic nature of the fungal bioluminescence system was proposed already in the 1960s |CITS: [13859816][14234795]|. However, the involvement of a luciferase was proved only in 2009 |CITS: [19789811]|. The system was shown to require a luciferin, a NAD(P)H-dependent reductase, NADPH or NADH, and a luciferase. Hot and cold extracts (representing luciferin and luciferase-containing extracts, respectively) prepared from members of all four lineages can cross-react, indicating that all fungi use the same luciferin/luciferase system |CITS: [22495263]|., The identity of the fungal luciferin was discovered only in 2015. It was shownd to be |FRAME: CPD-20572|, derived from the known fungal and plant secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-6989|. The fungal luciferin does not share structural similarity with the other eight known luciferins |CITS: [26094784]|. While the fungal luciferase has not been identifed or purified yet, incubation of microsomal preparations of a luciferase fraction with purified the luciferin resulted in its oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-20573 oxyluciferin|, which was subsequently hydrolyzed enzymatically into |FRAME: CPD-676|. The enzyme could also act on several analogs such as |FRAME: CPD-20619| |CITS: [28508049]|., The researchers propose that upon reaction with molecular oxygen the enzyme forms a high energy intermediate that contains an endoperoxide within the α-pyrone ring. The decomposition of the endoperoxide leads to release of a CO2 molecule and the formation of the oxyluciferin in the electronically excited state. Decay to the ground state emits light. There is currently no evidence for the formation of a 1,2-dioxetanone, as is the case in many other bioluminescence systems |CITS: [28508049]|.

General Background, |FRAME: TOLUENE Toluene| is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic compounds can be degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus |FRAME:TAX-286| and closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward bioremediation of environmental pollutants by metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|). Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various species that involve different initial monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these pathways converge in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-111| (2,3-dihydroxytoluenel) |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound is a substrate for ring cleavage enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission pathway, resulting in the formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-3-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-DIOL-PWY|). , About This Pathway, A degradative plasmid, TOM, containing an operon for the inducible toluene ortho-monooxygenase pathway has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-292| G4. The operon, tomA012345, encodes toluene ortho-monooxygenase and catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, which allow this organism to grow on toluene and related compounds as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [7538275]|, and in |CITS: [11751810]|. This pathway for toluene degradation via |FRAME: CPD-111| in |FRAME: TAX-292| (previously known as Pseudomonas cepacia) is shown here., In this pathway, toluene is sequentially hydroxylated by the |FRAME: CPLX-6483| system. The first hydroxylation is at the ortho position yielding |FRAME: CPD-109| (2-hydroxytoluene) as an intermediate, and the second is at the meta position yielding |FRAME: CPD-111| |CITS: [7578004]|. , Ring fission of |FRAME: CPD-111| is catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase to produce |FRAME: 2H6OH2-4DIENOATE|. This compound is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, or its tautomeric dienol form |FRAME: CPD-6761|. This tautomerization occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|. It is not known which tautomeric form is produced by the hydrolase, and which form is used by the hydratase of |FRAME: TAX-292|. However, it has been suggested that the |FRAME:TAX-303| hydratase uses the dienol form as a substrate |CITS: [2681159]|, and there is evidence that the |FRAME:TAX-562| hydratase also uses the dienol form as substrate, producing a ketonized intermediate in the reaction mechanism |CITS: [9492273]|., The enzymes catalyzing the last three reactions in this pathway, as well as the intermediates, were not directly demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-292|. However, their existence in this organism is inferred by work in Pseudomonas |CITS: [8063106]|. The products of the pathway are pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and acetaldehyde, which may be converted by acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, a central metabolite |CITS: [8063106][8419288]|.

|FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| is frequently released in the effluent from explosives manufacture as well, as in the manufacture of organic chemicals and plastics. It is the primary starting material for the, manufacture of |FRAME: ANILINE|, a compound used in the production of polyurethane, |CITS: [8368838]|., The pollution potential of |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| is very large, and it is listed among the U.S., Environmental Protection Agency priority pollutants |CITS: [Callahan79]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-58226|, which was isolated from an industrial waste treatment plant in New, Jersey, can utilize |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| as the sole source for carbon, nitrogen and energy, |CITS: [16535050]|. |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| is converted to |FRAME: CATECHOL| by the enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-3981|, a large complex that belongs to the family of Rieske nonheme iron oxygenases, |CITS: [11823201]|., The |FRAME: CATECHOL| is then degraded by a meta-cleavage pathway via, |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [10382261]|., A different pathway for the degeradation of |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| is described in, |FRAME: PWY-5637|.

Names: NAD biosynthesis from nicotinamide I (amidated pathway) // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide biosynthesis // amidated NAD salvage pathway
Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, Members of the family |FRAME:TAX-712| do not possess either the NAD de novo biosynthesis pathway or the NAD salvage pathway, and rely on the presence of NAD or related compounds in the growth medium. They have been classified into two distinct classes based on their specific requirement: members of the so called "V-factor-dependent" class, which includes the pathogen |FRAME:TAX-727|, require supplements in which the pyridine nucleotide source must possess an intact pyridine-ribose bond and the pyridine-carbonyl group must be amidated. Thus, they require either NAD, |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE| (NMN) or |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE| (NR). On the other hand, members of the "V-factor-independent" class possess the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.12|, which converts |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| to NMN, and are thus able to to synthesize NAD from |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| as well |CITS: [2946387]|., In 1973 Kasarov and Moat reported the presence of |FRAME: MONOMER-8262| in |FRAME: TAX-733| |CITS: [4356297]|. Almost three decades later, Martin et al were able to clone the gene encoding the enzyme from pNAD1, a plasmid of |FRAME: TAX-730| which confers V-factor independence on that strain |CITS: [14742562][11157928]|. , The presence of this gene, named |FRAME: G-6261|, was shown to confer V-factor independence on other strains, , including |FRAME:TAX-727| and |FRAME: TAX-715| |CITS: [11157928]|., While a similar gene has not been found in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [12446641]|, genes with significant sequence homology were found in many other organisms, including the human pre-B-cell colony enhancing factor PBEF and the bacterial species |FRAME:TAX-2097|, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Shewanella putrefaciens, Synechocystis sp., |FRAME:TAX-1299|, |FRAME:TAX-747|, and Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans |CITS: [11157928]|. The human pre-B-cell colony enhancing factor has been purifed and shown to be a nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase |CITS: [12555668][15381699]|., Unlike the reaction catalyzed by NadV, the second reaction in this pathway is not unique. It is part of an NAD salvage pathway found in many organsms including |FRAME:TAX-562| (see |FRAME: NAD-BIOSYNTHESIS-II|). In these organisms the reaction is catalyzed by the fusion protein |FRAME: MONOMER-8322| encoded by the |FRAME:G-6302| gene., In some cases, such as the case of |FRAME: TAX-730|, both NadV and NadR exist simultaneously, and combined they catalyze this pathway |CITS: [12446641]|., Yet in other organisms the second reaction is catalyzed by a different protein, encoded by the nadM gene which (in these organisms) is usually found in the same operon as the nadV gene. nadM encodes a bifunctional enzyme similar to both archaeal |FRAME: CPLX-7107| and archaeal 'Nudix' (nucleoside diphosphate linked moiety X) hydrolases (enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of a phosphate from ADP sugars, such as |FRAME:ADENOSINE_DIPHOSPHATE_RIBOSE|)., It has been suggested that in these organisms this pathway is responsible for the recycling of endogenous nicotinamide, which may be generated by the hydrolysis of NAD to nicotinamide and ADP-ribose by a documented but not characterized enzyme |CITS: [7768863][16585762]|. Such a pathway would provide an explanation for the Nudix hydrolase portion of the fusion protein.

General Background, Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and its name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes (including plants) and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. In eukaryotes, among other roles, it is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The physiological role of carnitine in bacteria is still unknown |CITS: [9037756]|. , |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| is a much rarer form. However, some bacterial species are capable of metabolizing it as well. Several mechanisms for the metabolism of D-carnitine have been discovered. |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-303| can convert D-carnitine to L-carnitine by the action of carnitine racemase |CITS: [7815937][Monnich95]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7472|). |FRAME:TAX-357| has |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.254|, a dedicated enzyme that acts only on D-carnitine, converting it to 3-dehydrocarnitine (see |FRAME: PWY-7471|), while |FRAME:TAX-471| has a monooxygenase that can accept both L- and D-carnitine as substrates |CITS: [9214773]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3641|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-29440| can grow on |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| as its sole source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy |CITS: [monnich95]|., The organism possesses a |FRAME: MONOMER-18571| that converts |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| into |FRAME: CARNITINE|. In addition, During growth on either L- or D-camitine an L-carnitine dehydrogenase is induced. No D-carnitine dehydrogenase could be found, suggesting the degradation of D-carnitine involves its initial racemization to L-carnitine, followed by the dehydrogenation of the latter |CITS: [monnich95]|., A similar racemase was also described in |FRAME: ORG-6255| |CITS: [9830124]|., The later part of the pathway, which includes the breakdown of |FRAME: 3-DE-H-CARNITINE| to |FRAME: BETAINE|, and potentially to glycine, is not as well characterized. Early reports suggested that 3-dehydrocarnitine is broken down to acetate and glycine-betaine |CITS: [5334176]|, while later research implicated trimethylaminoacetone and glycine betaine as intermediates |CITS: [5438040]|. The reactions have not been characterized, and the enzymes responsible for them have not been identified. The authors |CITS: [5438040]| found that NAD+ was required for the formation of trimethylaminoacetone, and that NAD+, ATP and coenzyme A were required for the formation of glycine betaine.

Names: L-ascorbate biosynthesis III (D-sorbitol pathway) // L-ascorbic acid biosynthesis III // vitamin C biosynthesis
Summary: L-Ascorbate (L-ascorbic acid, vitamin C) can be biosynthesized by plants, many vertebrates, and by some bacteria starting from certain sugars and sugar alcohols (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-882| and |FRAME: PWY3DJ-35471|). L-ascorbate is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic , preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries. L-Ascorbate is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and some other vertebrates (teleost fishes, paseriform birds, bats and guinea pigs) that cannot biosynthesize it. It has roles in collagen synthesis, as an antioxidant, as a cofactor in reactions catalyzed by some metal-dependent mono- and dioxygenases and may be involved in cell signaling reactions and transcription factor , activation. A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy (reviewed in |CITS: [16516325]| and |CITS: [17222174]|). , Most of the commercial production of this compound is via the Reichstein method that combines chemical and biotechnological steps. However, it is inefficient and more cost-effective biotechnological methods are being investigated. Single-strain and mixed culture microbial processes involve conversion of D-glucose, D-sorbitol, or L-sorbose to the key intermediate 2-keto-L-gulonate (|FRAME: CPD-377|). This intermediate is then converted to L-ascorbate by chemical , esterification and lactonization (reviewed in |CITS: [16516325]|)., The pathway shown here has been proposed for the direct enzymatic production of L-ascorbate from D-sorbitol and L-sorbose by |FRAME: TAX-92945| (previously known as as Gluconobacter oxydans DSM 4025) |CITS: [ASAKURA99]|. D-sorbitol and L-sorbose are naturally occurring plant carbohydrates (see |FRAME: PWY-5054| and |CITS: [13181867]|). L-ascorbate was produced by growing cells from the substrates L-sorbose and D-sorbitol via a proposed L-sorbosone intermediate. Varying amounts of L-ascorbate were also produced by resting cells from L-sorbosone, L-gulose, L-sorbose and D-sorbitol (|CITS: [15785002] [16461703]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16516325]|). The identity of the L-ascorbate product has been confirmed by HPLC, NMR and mass analyses (cited as a personal communication from Sugisawa in the review |CITS: [16516325]|)., In the L-sorbose to L-sorbosone conversion in |FRAME: TAX-92945|, the open chain form of the product L-sorbosone can hypothetically lactonize to either a furanose form (1.4-lactone), or a pyranose form (2,6-lactone) (in |CITS: [16461703]|). The 1,4-lactone form of L-sorbosone was proposed to explain the direct conversion of L-sorbosone to L-ascorbate by isoforms of a novel enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-13211| (SNDH1), encoded by gene sndH. The 2,6-lactone form of L-sorbosone was proposed to be converted to 2-keto-L-gulonate in several undefined steps involving the enzymes shown here and aldehyde dehydrogenase. The demonstration of the direct enzymatic conversion of L-sorbosone to L-ascorbate by L-sorbosone dehydrogenase has potential for the economical, biotechnological production of L-ascorbate |CITS: [16461703]|.

Many anthocyanins found in ornamental plant flowers are polyacylated, many of them with a signature 6"-O-malonylation at the 3-glucosyl moiety of the respective anthocyanin |CITS:[12481098]|. The wide variety of such polyacylated anthocyanins in the plant kingdom and the discernable high specificities of the catalyzing aromatic and aliphatic acyltransferases for the acyl donors and acceptors underline the extensive diversity of the participating enzymes |CITS:[Nakayama03]|. The anthocyanins have been recognized for their roles in attracting pollinators, UV-protection of plants and to confer valuable qualities such as color and nutritional additives for the benefit of human food (see reviews |CITS:[11287230] [11130659]|)., It has been shown that the orange to blue coloration of plant flowers is provided through anthocyanins and that anthocyanins contribute to pigment stabilization and solubility. Malonylation appears to be a common step in enhancing pigment solubility |CITS:[Strack94]| but also plays a role in stabilizing the pigment by protecting the glucosyl moiety from β-glucosidase attacks and degradation |CITS:[12481098]|. , In the Compositae family often dimalonylated anthocyanins are predominant such as the |FRAME:CPD-7700| which has been found to accumulate as a major pigment in Chrysanthemum x moriflorum, one of the most important ornamental plants in the world |CITS:[Nakayama97]|. The first step in the depicted pathway is carried out by a cyanidin 3-O-glucoside 6"-O-malonyltransferase which regiospecifically transfer the malonyl group to the 6"-hydroxyl group of the 3-O-glucosyl moiety yielding the corresponding anthocyanidin 3-O 6"-O-malonylglucoside |CITS:[12481098] [Suzuki03a] [Suzuki04]|. The consecutive second malonylation to form |FRAME:CPD-7700| has been found in Chrysanthemum where a second malonyltransferase has been identified which exhibits dual enzyme activities and also acts as anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside 3",6"-dimalonyltransferase |CITS:[Suzuki04]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| is synthesized by C-2 epimerisation of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.14|), and |FRAME: UDP-MANNACA| is synthesized by dehydrogenation of |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.336|., The pathway was first established as part of the synthesis of the enterobacterial common antigen (ECA), which contains the modified sugar |FRAME: CPD-15664| (see |FRAME: ECASYN-PWY|), but the gene was subsequently identified in the polysaccharide biosynthesis gene clusters of other bacteria, such as the Vi cluster of |FRAME: ORG-6239| and the capsule biosynthesis cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1280|, in which |FRAME: CPD-15664| participates in the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen| and the capsule glycoprotein, respectively.., Originally named |FRAME: EG11452|, the recommended name for the gene is now mnaB |CITS: [14670712]|.

General Background, The antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-15417|, |FRAME: CPD-15421|, and |FRAME: CPD-15504| (known as the aminocoumarin antibiotics) bind type II topoisomerases, including DNA gyrase, with an extremely high affinity, with equilibrium dissociation constants in the 10 nM range |CITS: [8231802]|. They compete with ATP for binding to the B subunit of DNA gyrase and thus inhibit the ATP-dependent DNA supercoiling catalysed by gyrase., The three antibiotics, which are produced by different microorganisms (|FRAME: TAX-2893586|, |FRAME: TAX-149682| and |FRAME: TAX-68264|, respectively), share several characteristics., All three contain a 7-hydroxy-2-aminocoumarin core (ring B). The phenolic 7-hydroxyl group of the bicyclic aminocoumarin scaffold is attached to an |FRAME: CPD-15426| sugar moiety (ring C), while the 2-amino group is ligated to a prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit (in |FRAME: CPD-15417| and |FRAME: CPD-15421|) or to a methylpyrroledicarboxylic acid that links two aminocoumarin moieties (in |FRAME: CPD-15504|) (ring A). The noviosyl sugar is then methylated at the 4-OH position and acylated at the 3-OH position to produce the mature, active antibiotic. |FRAME: CPD-15421 Clorobiocin| and |FRAME: CPD-15504| are both decorated at the 3 position of ring C by a 5-methylpyrrole-2-carboxyl moiety, whereas the corresponding modification in |FRAME: CPD-15417| is a carbamoyl group |CITS: [16868863]|., , The pharmacophore of these antibiotics is the decorated noviosyl sugar, which is presented by the planar aminocoumarin to the ATP binding site of the GyrB subunit of gyrase to interdict DNA replication |CITS: [8635474][9144789]|., About This Pathway, The pathway for the synthesis of the aminocoumarin core is found in all three organisms. Unfortunately the orthologous genes were named differently in each organism - for example, novH/cloH/couH. In this representation, we would use the names of the genes from the |FRAME: CPD-15417| producer |FRAME: TAX-2893586|., The aminocoumarin core is synthesized from |FRAME: TYR|, which has to be bound to |FRAME: NovH-proteins|. That protein contains two domains - an adenylation (A) domain and a thiolation (T) domain, similat to initiation modules in nonribosomal peptide synthetase assembly lines. The A domain activates |FRAME: TYR| to tyrosine-AMP and then covalently tethers the aminoacyl moiety to the thiol of a phosphopantetheine prosthetic group in the T domain |CITS: [11325587]|. All subsequent modifications leading to formation of the aminocoumarin core occur on this covalently tethered entity., The enzyme-bound tyrosine is first hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-15492| by a |FRAME: G-16078|-encoded cytochrome P450-type monooxygenase |CITS: [11325587]|. The next step is oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-15507|, which is catalyzed by a heterotetrameric hydrogenase encoded by |FRAME: G-16075| and |FRAME: G-16076| |CITS: [16171397]|., The last part of this pathway is still not characterized. It is believed that the next step is a 2-hydroxylation, but the enzyme that introduces this 2-hydroxy group is still unknown. Following this hydroxylation a final lactonization results in the release of the aminocoumarin core from the peptidyl-carrier protein.

Summary: The homoserine biosynthesis pathway is a three-step pathway that converts L-aspartate into homoserine. Some of the enzymes that catalyze the first step in this pathway are bifunctional, also serving to catalyze the final step in the pathway., The final product of this pathway, homoserine, feeds into biosynthetic pathways for both threonine and methionine. Fittingly, this pathway is regulated by the outputs of both of those pathways. metL is repressed by abundant methionine. thrA is regulated by threonine- and isoleucine-dependent attenuation, and both the aspartate kinase and homoserine dehydrogenase activities of ThrA are inhibited by threonine. The middle enzymatic activity, aspartate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, is subject to some form of repression by both methionine and threonine.

Nicotinate (niacin, vitamin B3, 3-pyridinecarboxylate) is a pyridine ring-containing compound., Microorganisms have multiple ways of degrading pyridine and its derivatives, and degradation of these compounds , is relevant to both biological and industrial processes. The degradation of nicotinate by both aerobic and anaerobic , organisms involves the initial formation of 6-hydroxynicotinate, but the pathways diverge after that. Among aerobic , organisms, the pathway in |FRAME:TAX-286| is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-722|. A similar , inducible, aerobic pathway proposed for |FRAME:TAX-86668| is shown here (this organism was earlier described , as Bacillus sp., |CITS: [NAGEL90]|). Nicotinate can be used by B. niacini as a sole carbon and nitrogen , source, and synthesis of the first two enzymes was shown to be coordinately induced by 6-hydroxynicotinate , |CITS: [5079068]| and reviewed in |CITS: [8840783]|., Following the initial enzymatic conversion of nicotinate to 6-hydroxynicotinate, the second enzyme catalyzes the , formation of 2,6-dihydroxynicotinate. However, unlike the |FRAME:TAX-286| pathway, the enzyme that cleaves , the pyridine ring converting 2,6-dihydroxynicotinate to maleamate was not demonstrated in this organism, nor was , the isomerase that converts malate to fumarate. Evidence for the latter part of this pathway derives from oxidation , of maleamate and maleate by extracts of cells grown on nicotinate |CITS: [14216418]|. 2,3,6-Trihydroxypyridine , and N-formylmaleamate are proposed intermediates in the conversion of 2,6-dihydroxynicotinate to , maleamate. Non-enzymatic oxidation of 2,3,6-trihydroxypyridine is thought to give rise to the blue pigment , produced by nicotinate grown cells |CITS: [14216418]|. , In the first reaction of this pathway, it has been shown that the oxygen of the hydroxyl group is derived from water, , rather than molecular oxygen |CITS: [5128335]|. The second hydroxylation reaction is followed by oxidative ring , cleavage, hydrolytic deamination and isomerization. The fumarate produced enters the TCA cycle |CITS: [5079068]|, , as indicated by the pathway link.
