Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13284 "Helvolic acid"| is a fusidane-type antibiotic that was isolated from the pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-746128| as part of the 1940s war effort to develop antibiotics |CITS: [17755578]|., Fusidane-type antibiotics are a group of fungi-derived 29-nor-protostane triterpenoid antibiotics that are characterized by a Z-configured double bond between C17 and C20, a C21 carboxylic acid, and a 16-O acetyl group in the protostadienol framework., Fusidane-type antibiotics are the only known clinically used antibiotics that target elongation factor G (EF-G) to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. Owing to their unique mechanism of action, they have little cross-resistance with other commonly used antibiotics |CITS: [4900137][4945809][24336183]|., A nine gene cluster encoding |FRAME: CPD-13284| biosynthesis was identified from the genome sequence of |FRAME: TAX-330879| in 2009, and the function of some of the involved enzymes was studied |CITS: [19216560][19415934]|. However, the complete pathway was reported only in 2017 |CITS: [29158519]|. At the time, the cluster was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-5062|, resulting in production of |FRAME: CPD-13284|., About This Pathway, The pathway begins with |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.32|, which converts the common precursor |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| to |FRAME: CPD-13283|. Next, a cytochrome P450 encoded by |FRAME: G-124764| catalyzes three successive oxidations of the C-4β methyl group, resulting in a carboxylate at that position., The pathway continues with hydroxylation at position 16, catalyzed by a second P450 enzyme (encoded by |FRAME: G-124765|), acetylation of the new hydroxyl group by the acetyltransferase |FRAME: G-124766 HelD2|, and introduction of a second carboxylate at position C20, which is catalyzed by a third P450 enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-124767|., At this point, a hydrogenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124768| gene oxidizes the 3β-ol group to a carbonyl group, which triggers decarboxylation of the 4β carboxylate, forming |FRAME: CPD-27370|. The HelB1 and HelC enzymes form a system that removes one methyl group from the C-4 position of the 4,4-dimethylated steroid substrate. This system acts preferentially on the 4β-methyl group, which is similar to the bacterial enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.246|, and differs from the animal/fungal enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.9|, and the plant enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.10| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.11|. In those systems that act on the 4α carbon, the remaining methyl group isomerizes from β to α configuration, enabling the enzymes to remove the second methyl group. However, in fusidane-type antibiotics, the remaining 4α methyl is unlikely to change configuration, and thus the compounds retain one methyl group at that position., In the next step of the pathway a fourth P450 enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124769| gene, hydroxylates two different positions - it introduces a hydroxyl group at position 6, and an oxo group at position 7. This is followed by acetylation of the hydroxyl at position 6 (catalyzed by |FRAME: G-124770 HelD1|), and finally, a reduction of the 1(2) bond of the first ring, catalyzed by |FRAME: G-124771 HelE|, to afford |FRAME: CPD-13284| |CITS: [29158519]|., It should be noted that some of the pathway's enzymes can act at a different order, generating different intermediates than those shown here, though the final product is the same.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-347| (PDO) is produced in nature by a large number of bacteria, including Citrobacter, Clostridium,, Enterobacter, Klebsiella and Lactobacillus species, via the fermentation of |FRAME: GLYCEROL|., A common problem with anaerobic growth is the generation of excess reducing equivalents in the form of NADH, whose reoxidation to NAD+ requires formation of a by-product that can serve as an electron sink. In the case of glycerol, the process comprises two steps - the rearrangement of glycerol to |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL|, followed by its NADH-dependent reduction to |FRAME: CPD-347|, which is excreted from the cell., PDO is used for the production of poly(propylene terephtalate), a polyester prepared from |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| and PDO that has highly desired properties for some large volume markets (such as fibers used in apparel and carpet applications). This pathway describes the production of PDO from D-glucose in an engineered |FRAME: TAX-562| strain that incorporates glycerol fermentation enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-573| and |FRAME: TAX-4932|., The early part of the pathway involves native |FRAME: TAX-562| enzymes of glycolysis, up to the splitting of a |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| molecule into |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|., Two major changes were engineered into the |FRAME: TAX-562| host strain: the deletion of the PTS system, forcing the transport and phosphorylation of glucose to be performed by the |FRAME: EG12148| galactose permease and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.2|, respectively, which is more energetically efficient than the PTS system, and the down-regulation of |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.12| (gap), resulting in less carbon being directed towards the TCA cycle, is thus more carbon available for fermentation to glycerol., The conversion of |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: GLYCEROL| is carried out by two |FRAME: TAX-4932| enzymes: |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.8| (encoded by the |FRAME: YDL022W| gene) and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.21| (encoded by |FRAME: YER062C|)., The conversion of |FRAME: GLYCEROL| to |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL| is catalyzed by the coenzyme-B12-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-3581| from |FRAME: TAX-573|. The enzyme undergoes rapid "suicidal" inactivation by glycerol during catalysis resulting in damaged coenzyme B12, and requires a reactivation factor for continuous activity |CITS: [6997273]|. That factor is a heterotetramer containing two elongated 63 kDa alpha subunits (encoded by the dhaF gene) and two globular 14 kDa beta subunits (encoded by dhaG) |CITS: [10383983][12517345]|. Thus the introduction of the enzyme requires five genes - three genes encoding |FRAME: CPLX-3581| and two genes encoding its reactivation factor., The last enzyme in the pathway is an |FRAME: TAX-562| enzyme - the |FRAME: CPLX0-7667| encoded by |FRAME: G7564|. Unlike the enzymes dedicated to the conversion of |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL| to |FRAME: CPD-347|, which utilize NADH, this enzyme utilizes NADPH, and results in higher titers of PDO |CITS: [14580573]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASN "Asparagine"| (Asn) was the first amino acid to be isolated, back in 1806. It was isolated from from asparagus juice, hence its name. Asn is not an essential amino acid in humans, which synthesize it from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, as shown in |FRAME: ASPARAGINE-BIOSYNTHESIS|. The amide group carries no charge under physiological pH and is readily hydrolyzed, converting |FRAME: ASN| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|. This process is thought to be one of several, related to the molecular basis for aging. Asparagine has a high propensity to hydrogen-bond and is a common site of attachment for carbohydrates in N-linked glycosylation., About this Pathway, There are at least three human enzymes capable of hydrolyzing the amino acid |FRAME: ASN| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|. The most studied is the lysosomal |FRAME: CPLX66-523| (AGA) which removes carbohydrate groups linked to asparagine, in the final step of cell surface glycoprotein degradation |CITS: [8846222]|. It also has asparagine hydrolase activity., The enzymes |FRAME: HS15413-MONOMER| and |FRAME: CPLX66-530| catalyze the hydrolysis of |FRAME: ASN| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: AMMONIUM| |CITS: [22861376]|. The latter enzyme also exhibits β-aspartyl peptidase activity consistent with enzymes designated as plant-type asparaginases, cleaving a β-linked Asp residue from the N-terminus of a polypeptide., The enzyme |FRAME: CPLX66-371| catalyzes the transamination of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| which can subsequently enter either the |FRAME: PWY66-398| or |FRAME: PWY66-399|., Asparaginases play a prominent role in chemotherapy, as cancer cells are dependent on the availability of extracellular |FRAME: ASN| (ASN). ASN depletion by administration of bacterial asparaginases interferes with the metabolism of the cancer cell leading to apoptosis |CITS: [22861376]|. None of the three human asparaginases have the required intrinsic kinetic property (low Km) for replacing bacterial asparaginases in chemotherapy. Recombinant |FRAME: CPLX66-530| could be a substitute for the bacterial enzymes, if it can be modified to have enhanced catalytic activity |CITS: [24768817]|. , The |FRAME: HS08648-MONOMER| may act synergistically with |FRAME: HS04385-MONOMER| to relieve accumulation of potentially toxic isoaspartyl peptides in mammalian brain and other tissues |CITS: [19839645]|. Formation of isoaspartyl peptide bonds occurs via the spontaneous degradation of peptides and proteins. This can decrease the biological activity of a protein, altering its susceptibility to proteolytic degradation and elicit autoimmunity |CITS: [10708396]|.

General Background, (+)-Sesamin belongs to the furofuran group of lignans and is widespread among vascular plants. |FRAME:TAX-4182| is broadly cultivated throughout the world because it contains high amounts of sesame oil in its seeds, a natural product which is highly valued because of its antioxidant properties. It has been found that these properties can be attributed to the furfuran lignans present in this oil such as piperitol, sesamin and sesamolin |CITS: [Lewis99]| |CITS: [DAVIN03]|. , There are many biological effects reported that connect to (+)-sesamin and derivatives thereof which are beneficial , for humans from the viewpoint of health care |CITS: [MacRae84]|. (+)-Sesamin was shown to provide protection , against liver damage |CITS: [12617602]|, decreased lipid peroxidation |CITS: [14598914]| as a result of elevating , the concentration of vitamin E |CITS: [11983822]|, and exhibited anti-inflammatory effects |CITS: [10966903]| and , inhibition of vascular superoxide production |CITS: [14646174]|., About This Pathway, All the lignans that are formed during the course of (+)-sesamin biosynthesis can be found in later phases of the seed development but not in leaves or early stages of seed development indicating a narrow window of corresponding biosynthetic activities |CITS: [16785429]|. , The enzymatic activity successively converting (+)-pinoresinol to (+)-piperitol and (+)-sesamin has been identified , in microsomes of |FRAME:TAX-4182| seeds |CITS: [Kato98]| |CITS: [Jiao98]|. The enzyme, a cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenase (CYP81Q1) catalyzes the methylenedioxy bridge formation on different aromatic rings on both ends of (+)-pinoresinol, hence acting as a bifunctional protein |CITS: [16785429]|. The cloning of the gene and characterization of the enzyme provided insight into the mode of action and dismissed the previously proposed mechanism of two independently acting cytochrome P450's involved in those steps |CITS: [Jiao98]|., Alternative routes that circumvent (+)-sesamin and form (+)-sesamolin via (+)-sesamolinol have been proposed but remain to be experimentally verified (|CITS: [Lewis99]| |CITS: [Kato98]|).

General Background, In adult female moths, species-specific sex pheromones are released from the pheromone gland in order to attract males of the same species (conspecific males). These pheromones are synthesized de novo in this gland from precursors derived from fatty acid biosynthesis. Many different sex pheromones have been chemically characterized. Moth Type I sex pheromones are C10-C18 primary alcohols, aldehydes, or acetate esters usually containing several double bonds. Type II are unsaturated hydrocarbons or hydrocarbon epoxides. Sex pheromones are usually produced as multicomponent mixtures (blends) (reviewed in |CITS: [22160231][20139627]|)., Many tortricids within the |FRAME: TAX-81687| subfamily have Δ8-unsaturated, Δ10-unsaturated, or Δ8,10 doubly unsaturated pheromone components., The major pheromone component of the codling moth |FRAME: TAX-82600| was identified as |FRAME: CPD-17798| |CITS: [17778064]|. The pathway leading to production of this pheromone was studied by topically applying Deuterium-labeled fatty acids to the pheromone gland, and monitoring their incorporation into pheromone alcohols |CITS: [24276140]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA|, produced by the regular fatty acid biosynthesis pathway. |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA "Palmitoyl-CoA"| is shortened by two rounds of β-oxidation, first to |FRAME: TETRADECANOYL-COA|, then to |FRAME: LAUROYLCOA-CPD|., The latter is then the subject of two desaturases: a 9-desaturase introduces the first double bond at opsition 9, generating |FRAME: CPD-17795|. A conjugase enzyme then converts this single double bond into two conjugated trans double bonds at positions 8 and 10 |CITS: [24276140]|., By analogy to data obtained by studying the biosynthesis of the pheromone |FRAME: CPD-16004| by the moth |FRAME: TAX-7091|, the |FRAME: CPD-17798| precursor |FRAME: CPD-17797| is mainly found as a |FRAME: Triacylglycerols "triacylglycerol"| ester in the cytoplasmic lipid droplets of pheromone gland cells. When adult females emerge from pupation, signaling events initiated by the neurohormone PBAN (pheromone biosynthesis-activating neuropeptide) regulate lipolysis of the stored |FRAME: Triacylglycerols "triacylglycerols"|, releasing |FRAME: CPD-17797| for its final reductive modification (see |FRAME: PWY-7423|)., The |FRAME: TAX-7091| pheromone gland fatty acyl reductase (FAR) is an alcohol-generating long-chain FAR that is homologous to the |FRAME: TAX-3999| (jojoba plant) enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.84| |CITS: [12871998]|. It is assumed that a similar enzyme acts in |FRAME: TAX-82600| to generate |FRAME: CPD-17798|., The pathway has so far been studied only using deuterium isotopes, and thus no specific information is available about the enzymes.

Summary: General Background, The p-hydroxycinnamates |FRAME: COUMARATE| (p-coumarate), |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| and |FRAME: CAFFEATE| are phenylpropanoid compounds produced by green plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY1F-467| and |FRAME: PWY-2181|). These compounds are degraded by soil bacteria. An aerobic pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| has been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-502559| |CITS: [12200295]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6343|). A similar pathway operates on |FRAME: COUMARATE|, as shown here., It has been suggested that the ability to degrade hydroxy-cinnamic acids contributes to bacterial wilt virulence by facilitating root entry and by protecting the pathogen from the toxicity of these compounds |CITS: [25423265]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-674 "Cinnamate"| derivatives, including |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| and |FRAME: COUMARATE|, play important roles in the cross-linking of the cell walls of various grasses and represent up to 1.5% of the weight of their cell walls., In the first step of the pathway |FRAME: MONOMER-15132| catalyzes the transfer of CoA to the carboxyl group of |FRAME: COUMARATE|, generating |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA|. In the second and third steps, both catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15133|, |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| is hydrated to form |FRAME: CPD-12199|, which is then cleaved to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [8987621][9579070][11152072]|., Once formed, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| is converted via |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and processed to central metabolism intermediates, as described in the pathway |FRAME: P184-PWY|.

|FRAME:CPD-15300 Lampranthin I| and |FRAME:CPD-15297| belong to the compound class of acylated betacyanins which are widespread among the |FRAME:TAX-3524| |CITS:[Minale66]| |CITS:[Piattelli69]|. In this order the red and yellow betacyanin pigments replace the anthocyanins in flowers and fruits usually present in most of the other plant families. Betalains are valued because of their antioxidant and radical scavenging properties and are therefore often used as food accessories (reviewed in |CITS:[12620337]|). The exact structures of the lampranthins had been a matter of debate for some time. However, |FRAME:CPD-15297| has been isolated from |FRAME:TAX-188832| and Phytolacca and structurally elucidated |CITS:[Strack88]| |CITS:[8688183]|. , Acyltransferases can either utilize acyl-CoA's which usually belong in the BAHD family |CITS:[16616872]| or employ acyl-glucose as acyl donor |CITS:[18471436]| (see as an example |FRAME:PWY-7261|). The formation of |FRAME:CPD-15300| and |FRAME:CPD-15297| is catalyzed by the action of aromatic acyl transferases, i.e. |FRAME:MONOMER-18008|. The enzyme has been identified an partially characterized from petals of Lampranthin sociorum and shown to exhibit a rather narrow and specific substrate spectrum with regard to acyl-donor and acyl-acceptor |CITS:[Bokern88]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, |FRAME:TAX-1511| can grow on |FRAME: ARG| by converting it to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE|, which is processed via both the oxidative and reductive branches of the Stickland reaction. The oxidation branch leads to production of acetyl-CoA and generates ATP, while producing 4 reducing equivalents (see |FRAME: PWY-6344|). The reductive branch utilizes these reducing equivalents by production of |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| via |FRAME: PRO| |CITS: [Brock97][10220161]|., Following the conversion of |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE|, the reductive route proceeds by formation of |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, which converts spontaneously to |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|. |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.2|, forms |FRAME: PRO| at the expense of one reducing equivalent (NADH or NADPH)., |FRAME: PRO| is converted further into |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| is a process that consumes another reducing equivalent, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8186|. Further metabolism of |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| has not been described in |FRAME: TAX-1511|. However, in |FRAME: TAX-47246| and |FRAME: TAX-1527| it is fermented to ammonia, |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: VALERATE| in a pathway involving |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYPENTANOYL-COA| and |FRAME: CPD-20685| |CITS: [3597403][2085413][11759672]|., The pathway was initially thought to exist only in |FRAME: TAX-1239|, but a later study found the genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway in organisms that also belong to the |FRAME: TAX-201174 Actinobacteria| and |FRAME: TAX-200918 Thermotogae| phyla |CITS: [19251850]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is the second most abundant biologically produced polymer (|FRAME: CELLULOSE| is the most abundant). |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is found in the cell walls of fungi, yeast and green algae, as well as the exoskeletons of crustaceans (including planktonic types) and insects. In the marine environment |FRAME: CHITIN| is an abundant polysaccharide that is a source of carbon and nitrogen for marine organisms. Its degradation by several genera of marine chitinolytic bacteria is part of the cycling of nutrients in ocean water. In addition to ocean water, chitinase genes have been identified in bacteria from freshwater and saline lakes, estuaries, and soil. Within bacteria, the ability to degrade chitin appears to be limited to the |FRAME: TAX-1224|, |FRAME: TAX-976|, |FRAME: TAX-201174| and |FRAME: TAX-1239| (in |CITS: [17933912]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21607543]|). Some bacterial species have been shown to contain multiple chitinase genes to efficiently utilize different forms of |FRAME: CHITIN| and some of its by-products |CITS: [16535505]|., |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| degradation is also important in the terrestrial environment where it is degraded by chitinolytic enzymes in plants, fungi, insects and mammals, as well as other bacteria. The pathway shown here is the beginning of the chitin catabolic pathway as studied in the family |FRAME: TAX-641| (the later part of the pathway is described in |FRAME: PWY-6906|. However, since the enzymes |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.14| and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.52| are also found in many other organisms, this segment of the pathway is potentially present in a wide taxonomic range., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CHITIN| catabolic pathway has been studied in species of the genus |FRAME: TAX-662| |CITS: [1761533][11850417][17933912][19553519]|. The proposed pathway shown here for |FRAME: TAX-666| and |FRAME: TAX-29494| involves a core set of genes that appear to be conserved in members of the family |FRAME: TAX-641|. The predicted gene functions are based on a combination of biochemical evidence in |FRAME: TAX-662| species, microarray expression data, experimental evidence, and bioinformatic predictions |CITS: [17933912]|. Overall, |FRAME: CHITIN| utilization is a highly complex process that has been divided into several stages (sensing, attachment, extracellular degradation, uptake and catabolism) and involves many genes |CITS: [14699052][14983042]|., The overall pathway spans the extracellular space, periplasm, and cytosol. This pathway shows reactions that can occur in the extracellular space and periplasm, as proposed and summarized in |CITS: [17933912]|. The cytosolic reactions are shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6906| as indicated by the pathway link., Several extracellular chitinases break down the |FRAME: CHITIN| polymer into chitodextrins greater than two residues in length (N-acetyl-D-glucosamine oligosaccharides, GlcNAcn) |CITS: [9791107][14983042][16535505]|. These oligosaccharides are transported into the periplasm via a specific outer membrane known as chitoporin |CITS: [10913115]|. Any GlcNAc monomers (|FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|) or GlcNAc dimers (|FRAME: CHITOBIOSE|) are believed to enter via nonspecific outer membrane porins (not shown) |CITS: [17933912]|., In the periplasm, chitodextrinases |CITS: [8969204]| and β-N-acetylglucosaminidases |CITS: [8969205]| degrade the GlcNAc oligosaccharides to monomers and dimers. The dimer (|FRAME: CHITOBIOSE|) is transported across the inner membrane into the cytosol by an ABC-type transporter (as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6906|) |CITS: [14699052][8969203][17933912]|. The monomer (|FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|) can be transported across the inner membrane into the cytosol with concomitant phosphorylation to |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| by a PTSGlcNAc transporter (as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6906|) |CITS: [8969209][14699052][17933912]|. The |FRAME: TAX-29494| GlcNAc/Glc PTS permease has been partially characterized |CITS: [8969209]|., Although not shown in this pathway, it has been suggested that because some forms of natural |FRAME: CHITIN| can contain deacetylated residues (see |FRAME: MONOMER-16910| and |CITS: [16878976]|) partially deacetylated chitooligosaccharides might also be found in the periplasm (|CITS: [17933912]|). For example, the disaccharide GlcNAc-GlcN (|FRAME: CPD-12274|) was proposed to be catabolized in the periplasm by a deacetylase (VC1280) |CITS: [17933912]|. However, the VC1280 enzyme (see |FRAME: FY484_RS06480-MONOMER|) was shown by |CITS: [17884842]| to be secreted into the extracellular medium. It was specific for the penultimate GlcNAc moiety at the nonreducing end of chitooligosaccharides, but its action on substrate GlcNAc-GlcN was not experimentally tested. If the proposed product (GlcN)2 (|FRAME: CPD-13545|) is present in the periplasm, it could undergo PTS transport into the cytosol with concomitant phosphorylation |CITS: [14983042][17933912]| as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6906|., Some other |FRAME: TAX-662| species such as |FRAME: TAX-670| and |FRAME: TAX-663|, contain a gene that encodes an extracellular chitin disaccharide deacetylase, EC 3.5.1.105 (see |FRAME: MONOMER-16793| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15495| for these organisms, respectively). These enzymes hydrolyze the acetamide bond at the reducing end residue of |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE| (the major hydrolysis product of extracellular chitinase) to produce extracellular GlcNAc-GlcN (|FRAME: CPD-12274|). This latter compound has been shown in |FRAME: TAX-670| to be a specific inducer of chitinolytic enzyme synthesis and also a chemotactic attractant in these organisms |CITS: [19553519][21575022]|., Carnivorous Plants, A few plants have specialized their physiology to consume and digest insects as a source of nutrients |CITS: [20009546]|. Several species of carnivorous plants are known, including |FRAME: TAX-4375|, popularly known as the pitcher plant. These plants produce pitchers, specialized morphological adaptations geared to trap, retain and digest insects |CITS: [21135573 ]|. The pitchers contain a highly acidic fluid rich in digestive enzymes., Studies have shown that when a prey is trapped the pH in the pitcher fluid drops due to the activity of proton pumps |CITS: [11525511]|. Several enzymes have been reported in the pitcher fluid, including β-D-xylosidase, β-1,3-glucanase and chitinases. The chitinases are essential for the degradation of the hard chitin exteriors of the insect prey |CITS: [18183948]|.

Summary: General Background, A new metabolic pathway for complex-type N-glycan degradation by intestinal anaerobic bacteria has been proposed. It is based on the characterization of a unique |FRAME: CPLX-8946| in |FRAME: TAX-226186|. This enzyme would allow these bacteria to conserve |FRAME: ATP| by directly phosphorylating |FRAME: MANNOSE|, which can enter glycolysis as shown here. In contrast, conventional degradation of |FRAME: CPD-16181| would occur via a β-mannosidase and phosphorylation of |FRAME: MANNOSE| by an |FRAME: ATP|-dependent kinase |CITS: [23943617]|., The initial portion of this pathway shown in |CITS: [23943617]| is hypothetical and therefore it is not shown here. It would begin with the release of complex-type glycan moieties of host N-linked glycoproteins by a secreted endo-β-N-acetylhexosaminidase (BT1038) that hydrolyzes the β(1,4) bond between the Asn-attached |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| residue and the adjacent |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| residue. The released glycan would be transported into the periplasm by the transporter homologs of SusC (BT1040) and SusD (BT1039). In the periplasm multiple endo-glycosidases would cleave the glycan, including an α-mannosidase (BT1032) with α(1,6) and α(1,3) specificity which would release the core |FRAME: CPD-16181|. The latter compound would be transported from the periplasm into the cytoplasm via predicted MFS transporter BT1034 |CITS: [23943617]|., About This Pathway, As described above, in the cytoplasm |FRAME: CPD-16181| could be efficiently degraded via inverting phosphorolytic cleavage by BT1033-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-8946| to produce |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| and |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P|. This unique phosphorylase was heterologously expressed in Escherichia coli, purified and characterized. It was also found to hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-17261|, producing |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE| and |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P|. The |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P| is metabolized further by α-phosphomannomutase (predicted BT1548 or BT3950), and mannose 6-phosphate isomerase (predicted BT0373) as shown, with |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| entering the glycolyitc pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5484|). Amino sugars are metabolized as shown in |FRAME: PWY-6517| and |FRAME: PWY-6902| |CITS: [23943617]|.

Summary: Although β-oxidation is the major route for fatty acid degradation, fatty acids can also be subject to α- and, ω-oxidation., There are several forms of α-oxidation. In this pathway a fatty acid is oxidized at the α-position (C-2) to give rise to a 2-hydroperoxy fatty acid. A different type of α-oxidation, used for the degradation of β-methyl-branched fatty acids, is described at |FRAME: PWY66-387|., 2-hydroperoxy fatty acids are chemically unstable and are quickly converted to chain-shortened (by one carbon) fatty aldehydes through decarboxylation, or to 2-hydroxy fatty acids. The chain-shortened fatty aldehydes are further oxidized to free fatty acids which can enter the next round of α-oxidation. The conversion of the intermediate 2(R)-hydroperoxy fatty acids to 2(R)-hydroxy fatty acids may be spontaneous or catalyzed by a peroxidase |CITS: [12432929]|. , It was reported that pea α-dioxygenase catalyzes both the dioxygenation and the peroxidation activities |CITS: [10938370]|. The conversion of the chain-shortened aldehydes to corresponding fatty acids may be spontaneous or catalyzed by an NAD+ oxidoreductase. An enzyme with such activity, described as "a 50 kDa subunit of α-dioxygenase" was described from pea |CITS: [10938370]|., Both polysaturated and unsaturated fatty acids are effective substrates in the pathway. Among the tested substrates are laurate, palmitate, stearate, oleate, linoleate, linolenate, and arachidonate., The physiological role of fatty acid α-oxidation in plants is not clear, but the process has been correlated with responses to both biotic and abiotic stresses, such as wounding and plant-pathogen interactions |CITS:[12060227] [14522973]|. It has also been noted that α-dioxygenase in pea is induced only during seed germination |CITS: [10938370]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14140 "Butirosins A"| and |FRAME: CPD-14193| are naturally occurring derivatives of the |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "2-aminoglycoside antibiotics"| |FRAME: CPD-14196| and |FRAME: CPD-14143|, respectively, produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1397| and discovered in the early 1970s |CITS: [4207954][4670491][4670492]|., The butirosins are unique among naturally occurring aminoglycosides since they contain an (S)-4-amino-2-hydroxybutyrate (AHBA) side-chain at the C-1 amine of the central 2-deoxystreptamine ring. This modification has been shown to confer resistance against several aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (the C-1 amine is a frequent target of aminoglycoside N-acyltransferases). As a result, the butirosins are active toward many aminoglycoside-resistant strains., Although the butirosins are not themselves clinically useful drugs, the properties of their side-chain have led to successful synthetic alteration of |FRAME: CPD-4822| and |FRAME: CPD-14161| to produce |FRAME: CPD-14197| and |FRAME: CPD-14162|, respectively |CITS: [62814][Watanabe87a]|., About This Pathway, For discussion of the portion of the pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-14143|, please see the pathways |FRAME: PWY-7022| and |FRAME: PWY-7015|. For discussion of the |FRAME: TAX-1397| genes involved in that portion of the pathway please see |CITS: [11132962][16156513][17206729]|., The biosynthesis of AHBA side chain from L-glutamate proceeds via intermediates tethered to a specific acyl carrier protein, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15063| gene. The L-glutamate is first activated and tethered to BtrI via a thioester linkage between its γ-carboxyl group and the terminal sulfhydryl group of the 4'-phosphopantethein arm of holo-BtrI |CITS: [15975512]|., Decarboxylation and α-hydroxylation, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-15059| and the |FRAME: G-15060| gene products, respectively, occur sequentially while the intermediates are still linked to the carrier protein, resulting in |FRAME: 2-H-4-G-glutamylamino-butanoyl-BtrI| |CITS: [15975512]|. A transferase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15061| gene, transfers the side-chain, still capped by a terminal γ-glutamyl group, to |FRAME: CPD-14143|, and the pathway is completed by the removal of the terminal glutamyl, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-15062| gene product |CITS: [17462573]|.

|FRAME: CPD-5561 Lovastatin| is a polyketide produced by the filamentous fungus |FRAME: TAX-33178|., Lovastatin is an inhibitor of the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.34| (HMGR) that catalyzes the reduction of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA| to |FRAME: MEVALONATE|, a key step in |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| biosynthesis, and is widely prescribed (along with the semisynthetic derivative |FRAME: CPD66-17|) as a hypercholesterolemia drug., The compound exists in two forms. The fungal enzyme produces the biologically active |FRAME: CPD-16924|. The commercial drug is produced as |FRAME: CPD-5561|, which is hydrolyzed to the active form upon ingestion., Two highly reducing iterative type I polyketide synthases (PKS) play central roles in the biosynthesis of lovastatin acid. The lovastatin nonaketide synthase (LNKS, encoded by |FRAME: G-34490|), together with the dissociated enoylreductase encoded by |FRAME: G-34489|, are responsible for the assembly of |FRAME: CPD-16907| |CITS: [10381407][10334994]|. Since LovB lacks a thiesterase domain, a dedicated thiesterase, encoded by |FRAME: G-34491|, is required for the release of this product from the PKS |CITS: [23653178]|. , |FRAME: CPD-16907 "Dihydromonacolin L acid"|, the first free intermediate in the pathway, is then modified by the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (encoded by |FRAME: G-34492|) through hydroxylation and dehydration to produce |FRAME: CPD-16905|, which is then hydroxylated at C-8 by the same enzyme to produce |FRAME: CPD-16908| |CITS: [21495633]|., In a parallel branch, the α-methylbutanoyl side chain is synthesized by a second PKS enzyme, the lovastatin diketide synthase (LDKS) encoded by |FRAME: G-34497| |CITS: [21069965]|., The ultimate step of the pathway comprises the transfer of the side chain from LovF to the C-8 hydroxy group of |FRAME: CPD-16908| by an acyl transferase encoded by |FRAME: G-34493|, generating |FRAME: CPD-16924| |CITS: [17113998][19530726]|.

About this Pathway, |FRAME: PROGESTERONE Progesterone| is a C-21 steroid hormone involved in the female menstrual cycle, pregnancy and embryogenesis of humans and other species. Progesterone is the major naturally occurring human progestogen., In animals, progesterone is produced in the ovaries (by the corpus luteum), the adrenal glands, and, during pregnancy, in the placenta. In addition, progesterone is also produced by some plant species, such as |FRAME: TAX-51240| |CITS: [20108949]|, Like other steroid hormones, progresterone is synthesized from |FRAME: PREGNENOLONE|, which in turn is made from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| (see |FRAME: PWY66-377|). The conversion is carried out in two separate, sequential reactions, first the dehydrogenation of the 3β-hydroxy steroid, producing pregn-5-ene-3,20-dione, followed by an isomerization to progesterone |CITS: [7673125]|. This is carried out by the multi-functional enzyme pregnenolone 3-dehydrogenase/progesterone isomerase encoded by |FRAME: HS08829| and |FRAME: HS10943|, which differ in their expression patterns.

Summary: General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives. These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|. The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two broad categories - oxidative and reductive. In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, Aerobic metabolism of |FRAME: CPD-9168| via |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: CATECHOL| was originally reported in 1966 in several strains of bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-37919 "Rhodococcus opacus (previously described as Nocardia opaca)"| |CITS: [5912586]|. A similar pathway was reported much later in |FRAME: ORG-5994|, an organism that can utilize |FRAME: CPD-9168| as the sole carbon, nitrogen, and energy source |CITS: [10623604]|. This organism also posseses a second pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE|., Thus, in |FRAME: ORG-5994| |FRAME: CPD-9169|, the first intermediate in the pathway, is a branching point: it can be converted to either |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| by a mutase (see |FRAME: PWY-5647|), or to |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| by a reductase (this pathway) |CITS: [14680704]|. An identical branching pathway has been described in the proteobacterium |FRAME: ORG-5996| |CITS:[17213670]|., A study that investigated the growth response and physiological changes of |FRAME: ORG-5994| towards high concentrations of |FRAME: CPD-9168| found that the organism could utilize 30mM |FRAME: CPD-9168| as sole source of carbon and energy, and was capable of growth on up to 200mM when the cells were pre-exposed to lower concentrations of the compound |CITS: [17391368]|., The enzymes that participate in the pathway have not been purified from |FRAME: ORG-5994|, but it was shown that the genes encoding them are located on a 65 kb plasmid |CITS: [10623604]|., Thin-layer chromatography, gas chromatography and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry identifed |FRAME: CPD-9169|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| as intermediates in the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-9168| by |FRAME: ORG-5994| |CITS: [10623604]|. This study also verified that |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| was produced as a major intermediate in the pathway, and not in a side reaction, as reported in the earlier studies. The mechanism by which |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| is cleaved to form |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| in this organism has not been determined |CITS: [10623604]|. In |FRAME: ORG-5996|, on the other hand, |FRAME:CATECHOL| and |FRAME: CIS-CIS-MUCONATE| were clearly identified as intermediates, suggesting that at least in this organism |FRAME:CATECHOL| is the terminal aromatic intermediate, and is further degraded via the meta cleavage pathway |CITS: [17213670]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of sulfated |FRAME:CPD-12557| and |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues. The |FRAME: CPD-12557| residues are substituted to varying degrees with sulfate linked to 4- and/or 6-hydroxyl positions, forming |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, and to a lesser extent the uronic acid residues may be substituted with sulfate at the 2-hydroxyl position forming |FRAME: CPD-12527|. The uronic acid residues may also be substituted with sulfate at the 3-hydroxyl positions, although this substitution is quite rare., The following names have been used to define different sulfation states:, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A "Chondroitin sulfate A"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C "Chondroitin sulfate C"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12565|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-D "Chondroitin sulfate D"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12527| and |FRAME: CPD-12565|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-E "Chondroitin sulfate E"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12526|, The term "chondroitin sulfate B" has been used in the past to refer to |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, but is not used any more., The chondroitin chains vary in size up to a hundred or more disaccharide repeating units. They are usually found attached to assorted core proteins as part of a proteoglycan complex. Chondroitin sulfate is a major component of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but is also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors., About This Pathway, Chondroitin sulfate chains are synthesized in situ on the protein chain. They are attached to the core protein via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the "glycoaminoglycan-protein linkage region", which is formed by sequential stepwise additions of the sugar residues to specific core proteins. The synthesis of the linkage region is described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|., The linkage region may be extended into mutiple kinds of glycosaminoglycans. However, the addition of an |FRAME: CPD-12557| residue prevents the formation of |FRAME: HEPARIN| or |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and commits the molecule to become chondroitin or dermatan. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase. Humans have two isoforms of this enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: HS07428| and |FRAME:HS10013| genes |CITS: [11788602][12716890][12433924]|., Once the linkage region has been formed and committed, the polymerzation of the chondroitin/dermatan chain proceeds by the alternate addition of |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-3604| from activated precursors to the non-reducing end of the elongating chain. The addition of both residues is catalyzed by the bifunctional chondroitin sulfate synthases., Humans possess three isoforms of this bifunctional enzyme (|FRAME: HS13400|, |FRAME: HS13103| and |FRAME: HS11959|), plus an additional enzyme that can catalyze only the addition of |FRAME: CPD-12521| (|FRAME: HS12080|) |CITS:[11514575][12907687][12145278]|. It has been suggested that chondroitin polymerization is achieved by multiple combinations of the different enzymes and that each combination may play a unique role in the biosynthesis of chondroitin or dermatan sulfate |CITS:[17253960][18316376]|., Further control over the exact nature of the chondroitin sulfate is determined by the modifications performed during the later part of the pathway. These modifications include the sulfation of the |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME:CPD-12557| residues at different positions by a number of sulfotransferases with strict specificities. The modifications are performed by several types and isoforms of enzymes, and the exact combination depends on the environment and type of the cell that produces the molecule., The sulfation of |FRAME:CPD-12557| at the 4-hydroxyl position is catalyzed by three enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: HS10284|, |FRAME: HS06130| and |FRAME: HS11524| genes |CITS: [10722746][10781601][12080076]|. The sulfation of |FRAME:CPD-12557| at the 6-hydroxyl position is catalyzed by enzymes encoded by the |FRAME:HS04610| and |FRAME: HS07394| genes |CITS: [9883891][9714738][10781596][10956661]|. Another enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: HS11694|, catalyzes the sulfation at the C6 position of residues already sulfated at the C4 position |CITS: [11572857]|., The C2 position of |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues is also often sulfated in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: ENSG00000111962-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS03488| gene |CITS: [10187838]|., The very first reaction in this pathway, the addition of a xylose molecule to a serine residue of the core protein, is performed at the endoplasmic reticulum. The rest of the pathway occurs at the Golgi apparatus.

General Background, At the time of this review, 136 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity. Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana. GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and GA4 enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed. It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis., Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). During active growth, the plant will maintain gibberellin homeostasis by metabolizing most gibberellins by rapid hydroxylation to inactive conjugates. Active |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed in the disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen produces large amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Inactive conjugates might be stored or translocated via the phloem and xylem before their release (activation) at the proper time and in the proper tissue., About This Pathway, GA12, the first true gibberellin is synthesized in plastids (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|). It is then further oxidized in the cytosol to a wide range of gibberellins. Depending on the sequence of hydroxylation at the 3β- and 13-positions, parallel pathways branch from GA12 to the C19-GAs, the number and prevalence of these branch pathways varying from species to species. The presence of the early C3-hydroxylation branch pathway, a pathway originating from GA12 and leading to the hydroxylated C19 GA4 via formation of GA14 has been demonstrated in particular in the developing seedlings and endosperm of the pumpkin |FRAME:TAX-3661| |CITS:[6126862],[9286114]|. It was also shown that GA15 could be the subject of C3-hydroxylation, thereby linking the C-3 hydroxylation pathway to the |FRAME:PWY-5070|., Enzymes: The reactions of this pathway are catalyzed by 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases. The first enzyme, gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of the C-3 carbon of GA12 or GA15. These enzymes generally have broad spectrum of substrates and do not therefore specifically catalyze the early C-3 hydroxylation but also the 3β-hydroxylation reactions of late C-3 hydroxylation pathways. (Note: one pumpkin enzyme encoded by |FRAME:G-9087|, however, was shown to specifically catalyze the late C-3 hydroxylation of GA9 to GA4). Gibberellin 20-oxidase, catalyzes the removal of C-20, thereby forming the C19-skeleton in GA4. This enzyme performs the sequential oxidation of C-20 to the alcohol and aldehyde, followed by the removal of the C atom through formation of the 4, 10-lactone ring. The alcohol intermediates (GA15 and GA37) must be in their open lactone form (free alcohol) to be catalyzed by the enzyme. Those gibberellins are however extracted from plants in their closed δ-lactone form (|FRAME:CPD-6971| and |FRAME:CPD-6974|) which is no longer oxidized by GA20-oxidases. Although it is not certain whether this form occurs naturally in planta or is an artifact of the extraction procedure, it is interesting to note that spinach cell-free extracts contain an enzyme able to catalyze the conversion of the δ-lactone form to some free alcohol forms |CITS:[WARD97]|.

Summary: The organic volatile |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| is one of the more than 400 identified volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in plants detected so far |CITS: [9881368]| which play important roles in defining taste and aroma in fruits such as tomato |CITS:[24692651]|. But VOCs also represent compounds involved in plant defense through luring predators to plants preyed on by pests |CITS:[23955880] [26197563] [16222805]| and reproductive biology by attracting pollinators |CITS:[11960742] [20462477] [23383981] [12921438]|. Although hundreds of VOCs have been found in tomato, |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| belongs to the few aroma and flavor forming volatile compounds which are above the range of olfactory threshold perceivable by humans |CITS:[Buttery87] [Buttery93]|. |FRAME:CPD-6442 Methylsalicylate| is the principal compound (98%) found in essential oil of the perennial plant wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens) |CITS:[Middleton93]| and has been frequently used as food and medicinal additive claimed to have contributed to a drop in cardiovascular mortality in the United States |CITS:[Janssen96]|. On the other side, |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| has also been under investigation because of potential poisoning effects on humans |CITS:[8880210]|. , The catalyzing enzyme, i.e. salicylate 1-O-methyltransferase has been first characterized from Clarkia breweri |CITS:[Ross99]| which is also a member of a new methyltransferase family referred to as SABATH |CITS: [DAuria03]|. |FRAME:CPD-110 Salicylate| is known as an hormone that is involved in systemic disease resistant in plants, also referred to as systemic acquired resistance (SAR) |CITS:[17810266] [15283665] [17904410]| but growing evidence points to |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| as the transmitted signal |CITS:[17916738] [17916698] [19131332] [21311035]|. However, in order to initiate SAR |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| must be converted back to |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| at the target location because in many cases O-methylester of plant hormones have been shown to be ineffective (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-24 methylsalicylate degradation|) |CITS:[Schulaev97]|., In tomato, a cDNA encoding a salicylate O-methyltransferase (SAMT1) has been identified, cloned and expressed in E. coli and subsequently subjected to biochemical assays to determine catalytic properties of the enzyme |CITS:[20070566]|. It could be demonstrated that the SAMT1 encoded protein was very specific for |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| forming |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate|, hence acting as a salicylate 1-O-methyltransferase. This finding was confirmed by in vivo experiments with sense and antisense transgenic plants either producing significantly more |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| than control plants or significantly less of the |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| product |CITS:[20070566]|. In addition, silencing SAMT1 resulted in a higher infection rate by spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) in tomato because this plant pest became virtually undetectable for their predators. The switching-off of SAMT1 also made tomato plants more prone towards the root fungus Fusarium oxysporum indicating that SAMT1 and its encoded enzyme is able to interfere with direct and indirect plant defense reactions |CITS:[20059742]|.

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., About This Pathway, There are at least two types of IAA conjugates: ester and amide conjugates. The ester conjugates are formed with sugars or polyols through an oxygen bridge, whereas the amide conjugates are formed with amino acids or polypeptides through , an amide bond., The content of conjugates varies among different plants. Arabidopsis leaves contain predominantly amide conjugates while maize has been shown to possess various ester conjugates., IAA-polypeptides are proposed to constitute the bulk fraction of amide conjugates in Arabidopsis. A 35kDa protein covalently linked with IAA was detected using the bean IAP1 protein probe |CITS: [11830675]|., In addition to the amide conjugates IAA-glucose has been detected in Arabidopsis leaves. It is thought IAA-glucose is an intermediate in IAA metabolism. Unlike what is known in maize, the next coupling reaction has not been identified for IAA-glucose., Although considerable studies (esp. radio tracer experiments) have been carried out in the area of IAA amide conjugate biosynthesis in Arabidopsis, enzymes and enzymatic reactions are poorly characterized.

HK4", were described in 1994 (without the sequences) in a patent application |CITS: [Zimmermann94]|. The first and the key enzyme in this pathway is γ-butyrobetainyl CoA synthetase (BcoA), which was characterized in 2016 from |FRAME: TAX-1763573| |CITS: [27125317]|. The rest of the genes were characterized from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-382| (strain 3D0a2; DSMZ-30135), which is capable of utilizing |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| as its sole carbon and nitrogen source. Since the genome of that strain has not been sequenced, the authors idetified the genes in |FRAME: TAX-1286640| (which were 100% identical).

Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, This superpathway combines multiple routes in which some organisms (including bacteria, yeast and plants) can salvage the pyrimidine ribonucleosides |FRAME: CYTIDINE| and |FRAME: URIDINE| and convert them to the ribonucleotide |FRAME: UMP|, which can serve as a precursor for the synthesis of all other pyrimidine nucleotides., Since most of the salvage enzymes have higher activity with |FRAME: URIDINE|, most of the available |FRAME: CYTIDINE| is coverted to |FRAME: URIDINE| by cytidine deaminase, |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.5|., |FRAME: URIDINE Uridine| is then converted to UMP in one of two routes. In the first route, this transformation is achieved in a single step by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.48 "uridine kinase (EC 2.7.1.48)"|. In most organisms this enzyme is also active with |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, and thus can form |FRAME: CMP| as well (although this has not been shown yet for the plant enzymes)., In the second route, |FRAME: URIDINE| is first hydrolyzed to the nucleobase |FRAME: URACIL| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.3 "uridine nucleosidase (EC 3.2.2.3)"|, and the nucleobase is phosphoribosylated to UMP by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.9 "uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (EC 2.4.2.9)"|., Mammals have not been included in this superpathway, since they do not have the enzyme uridine nucleosidase and thus can not convert uridine to uracil. They do utilize a nucleoside kinase-based pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7183|).

In mammals, |FRAME: HS| (H2S) is primarily produced by the two enzymes of the trans-sulfuration pathway - |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.22| (|FRAME: HS08461|) and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.1| (|FRAME: HS04050|) (see |FRAME: PWY66-426|). A third enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.2| (|FRAME: HS05177|) can also contribute to endogenous |FRAME: HS| production using |FRAME: 3-MERCAPTO-PYRUVATE| as a substrate (see |FRAME: PWY-5329|)., The steady-state concentration of |FRAME: HS| is estimated to be in the low nanomolar range in most tissues |CITS: [18799635][22229551]| with the exception of aorta, where it is ~20- to 100-fold higher |CITS: [20812866]|. Kinetic studies have shown that the flux of sulfur into |FRAME: HS| is high and comparable to that directed into |FRAME: GLUTATHIONESYN-PWY| in the liver |CITS: [22229551]|. Thus, the low steady-state concentration of |FRAME: HS| reflects a highly active oxidation pathway. , An increase of |FRAME: HS| concentrations to as little as 0.3 μM in cell homogenates and ~20 μM in intact cells results in inhibition of |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.9| |CITS: [21028947][15996823]|. It has been estimated that |FRAME: HS| concentrations of 10-20 nM in the vicinity of mitochondria or 0.5–1 μM outside the cell stimulate its catabolism |CITS: [21028947]|., Sulfide at sublethal concentrations is rapidly oxidized in mammals |CITS: [4647068]|. The dominant sulfide oxidation products vary in a tissue-specific manner. It has been shown to be |FRAME: SULFATE| in liver and kidney |CITS: [4647068]| and |FRAME: S2O3| in colonic mucosa and lung |CITS: [11389886]|., The sulfide oxidation pathway, which resides in the mitochondrion, starts with |FRAME: EC-1.8.5.8| (SQOR). This membrane-bound enzyme, located at the inner mitochondrial membrane, catalyzes the oxidation of |FRAME: HS| to persulfide, transferring the electrons to the electron transport chain via an FAD cofactor and reduced quinones. Unlike the bacterial homologs (|FRAME: EC-1.8.5.4|), which repeats the catalytic cycle without releasing the product, producing a polysulfide (the reaction stops when the maximum length of the polysulfide that can be accommodated in the sulfide oxidation pocket is achieved), the eukaryotic enzyme transfers the persulfide to an acceptor at the end of each catalytic cycle |CITS: [18494801]|. While the enzyme can transfer the sulfur to several acceptors, including glutathione, sulfite, and cysteine |CITS: [22852582]|, kinetic modeling suggests that the former is by far the most important acceptor in vivo |CITS: [25225291]|., The product, |FRAME: CPD-11281|, is oxidized by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.18| to |FRAME: CPD-17866|, which hydrolyzes spontaneously into |FRAME: SO3| |CITS: [19136963][23144459]|. People with mutations in the gene encoding this enzyme (|FRAME: HS12604|) suffer from ethylmalonic encephalopathy, an autosomal recessive fatal disorder characterized by early-onset encephalopathy, microangiopathy, chronic diarrhea, defective cytochrome c oxidase in muscle and brain, high concentrations of C4 and C5 acylcarnitines in blood, and high excretion of ethylmalonic acid in urine |CITS: [14732903][16183799][18593870]|. , Finally, depending on the tissue, |FRAME: SO3| can be directed into two different routes. The first route is oxidation by |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.1|. This metallohemoprotein, which contains molybdenum and protoheme as prosthetic groups, is active mostly in the liver, where it catalyzes the oxidation of |FRAME: SO3| to |FRAME: SULFATE| |CITS: [14956][9242907][9428520]|. Sulfite oxidase deficiency is a lethal genetic disease that results from defects either in the genes encoding proteins involved in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis or in the |FRAME: HS06627| gene |CITS: [16048997]|., The second route is the transfer of a second sulfur originating from |FRAME: CPD-11281| (the product of |FRAME: EC-1.8.5.8|), converting |FRAME: SO3| to |FRAME: S2O3|. This reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.1|, better known as rhodanese |CITS: [18494801][25225291]|.

|FRAME: TAX-198620| is a dominant bacterial species found within the rhizosphere. The organism was shown to selectively inhibit growth of other bacterial species growing in soybean root exudates by producing and secreting a family of bacterial tetrahydropyridine alkaloids known as koreenceines (|FRAME: CPD-28062|, |FRAME: CPD-28061|, |FRAME: CPD-28063|, and |FRAME: CPD-28064|). The first three of these metabolites are analogs of the plant alkaloid |FRAME: CPD-9424|, which is responsible for the toxicity of the poison hemlock |CITS: [30877115]|. In pairwise interactions, the koreenceine biosynthetic cluster was shown to be responsible for 85 and 22% of differentially regulated genes in |FRAME: TAX-986| and |FRAME: TAX-1396|, respectively |CITS: [35435700]|., The koreenceine biosynthetic cluster of |FRAME: TAX-198620| (named kecA-K) was discovered by screening a transposon mutants library. The cluster suggests a similar biosynthetic pathway to that of the plant alkaloid |FRAME: CPD-9424|. Deletion of the cluster abolished koreenceine production |CITS: [30877115]|., The first five genes of the cluster, kecABCDE, encode a type II polyketide synthase system: kecA encodes an acyl carrier protein, kecB and kecD encode β-ketoacyl synthases (KSα), and kecC and kecE encode partial β-ketoacyl synthases with conserved thiolase domains (chain length factor [CLF] or KSβ). It has been proposed that two heterodimeric systems, KecB-KecC and KecD-KecE, catalyze polyketide elongation of a starter molecule bound to KecA, using |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| as extension units |CITS: [30877115]|., The type of starter molecule determines the type of product. |FRAME: CPD-28062 "Koreenceine A"|, |FRAME: CPD-28061|, and |FRAME: CPD-28063| can be produced from |FRAME: CPD-21018|, |FRAME: CPD-3617|, or |FRAME: CPD-21098|, respectively. |FRAME: CPD-28064 "Koreenceine D"| is likely derived from |FRAME: CPD-28063| by an unidentified halogenase reaction |CITS: [30877115]|., The triketide product undergoes β-keto reductive modifications catalyzed by the KecG and KecH reductases. A bifunctional enzyme encoded by kecF is predicted to catalyze the reduction of the [acp]-bound intermadiate, releasing an aldehyde, followed by transamination of the aldehyde intermediate, which leads to spontaneous cyclization, generating the koreenceine product |CITS: [30877115]|., The last three genes in the cluster, kecIJK, are predicted to participate in the translocation of the koreenceine molecules outside the cell |CITS: [30877115]|.

Summary: Isoprene, a gaseous hydrocarbon, is emitted in substantial quantities by many different plant species from mosses to poplar trees |CITS: [17921528]|. Isoprene can affect atmospheric chemistry, and, under particular conditions, can contribute to ozone and aerosol formation in the atmosphere |CITS: [17921528]|. Ozone and aerosols both pose health threats to humans |CITS: [17921528]|, and plant growth can also be reduced by elevated ozone levels |CITS: [17084004]|., There are a few potential biological explanations for isoprene emissions by plants. Isoprene appears to help protect plants against sun flecks that can rapidly raise leaf temperatures |CITS: [11299379][VELIKOVA05]|. In addition, isoprene-emitting plants have increased tolerance to ozone and other reactive oxygen species (ROS) |CITS: [11743121][11457950][12011357][19324699]|. But, the molecular mechanisms of these isoprene-mediated stress responses are still under investigation. One hypothesis is that isoprene stabilizes lipid membranes |CITS: [17125733]|., Levels of isoprene emission are affected by plant developmental stage, circadian rhythms |CITS: [16899082][17122071]|, and several environmental stimuli (reviewed in |CITS: [17921528]|). Notably, isoprene emissions rise in response to higher temperatures and are light-dependent |CITS: [SANADZE69][17921528]|. The level of isoprene synthase (IspS) activity is correlated with the levels of isoprene emission, indicating that this enzyme is a key regulator of isoprene production. Its activity seems to be largely determined by transcript abundance. Isoprene emissions can also be affected by the level of DMAPP substrate availability, the level of reducing power and ATP, competition with PEP carboxylase for CO<sub>2</sub> |CITS: [LORETO07]|, and other factors (reviewed in |CITS: [17921528]|)., Isoprene biosynthesis occurs in the chloroplasts and isoprene synthase can be detected in this organelle in a |FRAME:TAX-80863| hybrid |CITS: [16052321]| but extra-chloroplastic sources of DMAPP can also be utilized |CITS: [15286296]|., Developing a better understanding of isoprene emissions is necessary for understanding plant development and for predicting atmospheric conditions in the short and long term.

Summary: Oil is a major carbon reserve in most plant seeds. Conversion of carbohydrates to oil generally starts by glycolysis (either |FRAME:GLYCOLYSIS "mitochondrial"| or |FRAME:PWY-1042 "cytosolic"|). |FRAME: PYRUVATE "Pyruvate"|, the end product of glycolysis, is further decarboxylated to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, the precursor for fatty acid and oil biosynthesis. In the process, one-third of carbon is lost as |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. An elegant experiment illustrated the existence of a Rubisco shunt |CITS: [15592419]|. Comparing to glycolysis, the Rubisco shunt results in an increase of carbon conversion efficiency, yielding 20% more |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| with 40% less carbon loss. In oilseed rape, the Rubisco shunt is responsible for the production of 37% -75% of phosphoglycerate in the developing embryo. , There are three stages in the Rubisco shunt. , Stage I is composed of the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (in reverse direction of what is shown in |FRAME:NONOXIPENT-PWY|), where a series of re-arrangements of the carbon skeleton convert the six-carbon sugar , |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| to the five-carbon sugar |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, which is further converted to |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|. The net change is:, 5 |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| = 6 |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|, Stage II is catalyzed by the carboxylase activity of Rubisco, which fixes one molecule of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| with one molecule of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|, yielding two molecules three-carbon |FRAME: G3P|. The net change is: , 6 |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| + 6 |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| = 12 |FRAME: G3P|, In stage III |FRAME: G3P| is converted to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| via the later steps of glycolysis. Pyruvate is further metabolized to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| which fuels fatty acid biosynthesis (|FRAME:PWY-4381|) and seed oil (|FRAME:TRIGLSYN-PWY|) accumulation. The net change is: , 12 |FRAME: G3P| = 12 |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| + 12 |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, Overall, the net carbon stoichiometry via the Rubisco shunt is:, 5 |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| = 12 |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| + 6 |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, Comparing to glycolysis (5 |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| = 10 |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| + 10 |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|), the Rubisco shunt allows the conversion of carbohydrate into 20% more |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| than glycolysis, and has 40% less carbon loss as |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|., Note that there is no active |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY| following the Rubisco step in developing seeds. This allows the continuation of Rubisco shunt to stage III., The whole pathway is located in the plastid.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Kauralexins Kauralexins| are a class of |FRAME: CPD1F-128|-related diterpenoid defense compounds found in maize. They are produced in response to a variety of biotic threats, including the larvae of the European corn borer |FRAME: TAX-29057| and fungi such as |FRAME: TAX-58291| and |FRAME:TAX-5518|. Jasmonic acid and ethylene can also work synergistically to promote kauralexin production. Kauralexins can also be detected in the scutella of 19 diverse maize inbred lines suggesting that these compounds are broadly or universally expressed among all maize varieties |CITS: [21402917]|. , Importantly, at low concentrations, |FRAME: CPD-13541| and |FRAME: CPD-13544| reduce the growth of |FRAME: TAX-58291| and |FRAME:TAX-5518|. In addition, in choice and nonchoice assays |FRAME: TAX-29057| consume less tissue treated with these compounds than untreated control tissue, indicating that kauralexins also have anti-feedant properties |CITS: [21402917]|. , About This Pathway, Although many of the compounds in this pathway have been identified experimentally, notably kauralexin A1, A2, A3, and B1, B2, and B3 |CITS: [21402917]| the overall pathway scheme is proposed largely based on the sequence of enzymatic activities observed in other terpenoid biosynthetic routes, such as |FRAME: PWY-6575|., Several lines of evidence suggest that kauralexin production depends on the activity of An2, including the increased level of An2 transcripts that accumulate prior to kauralexin accumulation |CITS: [21402917]|., Tranformation of ent-CPP to ent-kaurene and ent-isokaurene likely requires the activity two different synthases. In rice, these labdane-related diterpene cyclases show show quite stringent specificity. For example, OsKS1 (kaurane synthase 1) produces ent-kaurene whereas OsKSL5/6 (kaurane-synthase-like 5/6) appears to primarily catalyze the formation of ent-isokaurene |CITS: [17141283]|. Maize may have similarly stereospecific kaurene synthases. , The remainder of the reactions in the pathway are likely catalyzed by one or more cytochrome p450 enzymes and the predicted NADPH cofactors and oxygen inputs have been included on that basis. It is likely that these p450 enzymes would catalyze the formation of an alcohol and then its conversion to an aldehyde and finally a carboxylic acid to give rise to |FRAME: CPD-13539| and |FRAME: CPD-13542|. The same series of reactions would likely be repeated on a different carbon atom to produce first two alcohols (not shown) followed by aldehydes |FRAME: CPD-13541| and |FRAME: CPD-13544| and finally the dicarboxylates |FRAME: CPD-13540| and |FRAME: CPD-13543|. This series of reactions has been observed for several other p450 enzymes that act in plant secondary metabolism, such as those that participate in |FRAME:PWY-6540| and gibberellin metabolism |CITS: [12127586][20351109][11722763]|., Identification of all of the unknown enzymes and the intermediate compounds that participate in kauralexin biosynthesis will lead to a better understanding of this overall pathway and its role in maize defense against fungi, herbivory, and other biotic threats.

Summary: The diterpenoid |FRAME:CPD-14501| is the aglycone precursor of the sweet compounds produced by the plant |FRAME:TAX-55670|, and is thus the entry compound in the steviol glucoside biosynthesis pathway. Steviol has also been reported to show promise as cancer preventive agent in various in vitro anticancer tests |CITS:[19131254]|, and to offer therapeuthic benefits through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions |CITS:[19000919]|. In the plants, steviol is involved in the regulation of growth processes |CITS:[18329674]|, but is generally considered less efficient than the corresponding glucosides (see |FRAME:PWY-7071|). , Up to the formation of |FRAME: CPD1F-132|, the |FRAME:PWY-7070| pathway shares its reactions with the biosynthesis of the diterpenoid plant hormone |FRAME:CPD1F-95| (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|). Therefore, the C-13 hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD1F-132| is not only the first committed step towards the formation of the various steviol glucosides by a number of glucosyltransferases, but also an important divergence point away from gibberellin biosynthesis., There has been some controversy with regard to the characterization of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.M48|. The enzyme was reported to have been purified to homogeneity from the stroma of |FRAME:TAX-55670| and shown to catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-14501| from |FRAME: CPD1F-136| |CITS:[8806729]|. However, other authors, e.g. |CITS:[14561506]| |CITS:[17397883]| have argued that the nature of the reported enzyme is inconsistent with other oxidases in the pathway with regard to cell localization and that the reported N-terminal sequence was actually that of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.13|. Various genes were later deposited in the Genbank database as encoding kaurenoic acid 13-hydroxylases, though none of them was characterized at the time. In 2016 the genes were tested for their activity by expression in an |FRAME: TAX-562| host, and only one of them was found to have activity, which was very low |CITS: [26358188]|. As of 2020, the highest activity for the conversion of |FRAME: CPD1F-136| to |FRAME: CPD-14501| is obtained with a recombinant |FRAME: TAX-3702| enzyme (CYP714A2) |CITS: [32013995]|. An enzyme similar to the Arabidopsis protein was identified in |FRAME: TAX-55670| and named KAHn2. However, a recombinant version of that enzyme still has a much lower activity than the Arabidposis enzyme |CITS: [26358188]|.
