Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS Sphingolipids| are a class of lipids derived from the unsaturated aliphatic amino alcohol |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| that are essential components of the plasma membrane in all eukaryotic cells. Sphingolipids concentrate with sterols (|FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| in animals and |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| in yeast) to form lipid rafts, specialized membrane microdomains implicated in a variety of cellular processes, including sorting of membrane proteins and lipids, as well as organizing and regulating signaling cascades |CITS: [12452424]|., The sphingosine backbone of sphingolipids (often referred to as the |FRAME: Sphingoids "sphingoid base"|) is amide-linked to an acyl group, such as a fatty acid, and is often also O-linked to a head group. In yeast the head group is inositol, which in some cases is modified further by the addition of a mannose sugar and a second inositol., The sphingoid bases often consists of modified forms of sphingosine. When the double bond at position 4 is saturated, it is named |FRAME: CPD-13612|. In yeast the sphingoid base is a C4-hydroxylated sphinganine, known as |FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE|, and the |FRAME: Ceramides ceramides| that it forms are known as |FRAME: Phytoceramides phytoceramides|., The preferred acyl-CoA substrates for the yeast enzyme have been reported to be C24:0 (|FRAME: CPD-10280|) and C26:0 (|FRAME: CPD1G-277|) compounds, which are produced by the very-long-chain elongase system (see |FRAME: PWY-7036|)., A thorough analysis of ceramide biosynthesis in yeast, which involved in vitro assays using |FRAME: CPD-13612|, |FRAME: CPD-13611|, |FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-22075| as sphingoind bases, and 16:0, 18:0, 20:0, 22:0, 22:1, 24:0, 24:1, and 26:0 acyl-CoAs as the acyl donors, has observed a strong preference for |FRAME: CPD-22075| as the sphingoid base and for 20:0, 22:0, and 24:0 CoAs as the acyl moieties. The most common acyl moiety used was C24:0 followed by C22:0, C20:0, C24:1, C26:0, C22:1 and C18:0. The most common sphingoid base was by far |FRAME: CPD-22075|, followed by |FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-13612|, with a very minor fraction of |FRAME: CPD-13611| |CITS: [25725359]|., About This Pathway, De novo sphingolipid biosynthesis is required for survival, and loss of the pathway affects growth and viability., Even though mammals and |FRAME: TAX-4932| produce structurally and chemically different types of sphingoid bases, ceramides, and complex sphingolipids, the early steps in their sphingolipid synthesis pathways, up to formation of ceramides, are similar. The earlier part of the pathway, up to ceramide formation, occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). , |FRAME: TAX-4932| cells make three complex sphingolipids: |FRAME: IPC "inositol-phosphoceramide"| (IPC), |FRAME: MIPC "mannose-inositol-phosphoceramide"| (MIPC), and |FRAME: MIP2C "mannosyl-diinositol-phosphorylceramide"| [MIP2C] |CITS:[12069845]|. The latter makes about 75% of the total sphingolipid content, while the other 25% are divided evenly among the other two |CITS: [12484746]|. The complex sphingolipids are made in the Golgi apparatus, and this part of the pathway does not have a mammalian counterpart. The most common acyl chain lengths in the yeast sphingolipids are C24 and C26., It should be noted that the complex sphingolipids are not the only sphingolipids that have biological activity. Several intermediates in sphingolipid biosynthesis have been shown to play important roles on their own as signaling molecules and growth regulators. Both the sphingoid base |FRAME: CPD-13612| and the |FRAME: Phytoceramides phytoceramides| have been implicated as secondary messengers in signaling pathways that regulate heat stress response |CITS: [9405471][11967828]|. , In addition, externally-provided sphingoid bases are phosphorylated by dedicated enzymes, forming |FRAME: CPD-649| and |FRAME: PHTYOSPHINGOSINE-1-P|, both of which have been shown to be components of a tightly-controlled system that regulates cell growth |CITS: [12684378]|. The phosphates can be dephosphorylated back to sphingoid bases (see |FRAME: PWY-7119|), which then enter the de novo biosynthetic pathway., Since phosphoinositol-containing sphingolipids are not found in mammals, enzymes that catalyze the later steps of this pathway are considered a target for antifungal drugs |CITS: [9092515][15578972]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is a reducing acidic sugar that often forms a hexapyranose ring structure. It is common in carbohydrate chains of proteoglycans and is part of mucous animal secretions (such as saliva), cell glycocalyx and intercellular matrix. The hexapyranosic form |FRAME: CPD-12521| is found in the glycosaminoglycans |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates|, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: Hyaluronan|., In animals D-glucuronate is degraded as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5525|. Bacteria degrade |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by three different pathways: the isomerase pathway, which is found in enterobacteria (see |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY|), an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-17141| (see |FRAME: PWY-6501|), and an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, Enteric bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| can use β-D-glucuronides and the hexuronates |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| and |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| as the sole sources of carbon for growth. β-D-glucuronides are detoxification products that are excreted into the mammalian gut in the bile. |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is found in animal mucus and at low levels in plant tissues. The enzymes of this pathway were first described in a series of publications by Ashwell et al |CITS: [13584413][13794771][14401695][13831814][13813474]|., The initial step in the degradation of β-glucuronides is hydrolysis by |FRAME: CPLX0-7662| to yield |FRAME: GLUCURONATE|, which is subsequently isomerized to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| by D-glucuronate isomerase, an enzyme which can also carry out an analogous function in the |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY| pathway., D-fructuronate is then metabolized to central metabolism intermediates, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7242|.

General Background, Arginase-mediated |FRAME: ARG| degradation is widely distributed in the biosphere, and is found, in all primary kingdoms |CITS: [8759304]|. The first step in this process, catalyzed by the enzyme, arginase, is the hydrolysis of |FRAME:ARG| to form |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME:UREA|., There are many variations of the arginase pathway, since the fate of the products of the arginase, reaction may be different in different organisms., Variants of arginase-based |FRAME: ARG|-degradation pathways include |FRAME: ARGASEDEG-PWY|,, |FRAME:ARG-PRO-PWY| and |FRAME: ARG-GLU-PWY|., About This Pathway, Upon infection of wounded plants, |FRAME: TAX-358| transfers oncogenic fragments of DNA (T-DNA), from plasmids (called Ti plasmids) into the nucleus of host plant cells., Once in the plant cells, the T-DNA genes integrate into the plant genome and start directing the plants, to synthesize opines, such as |FRAME: CPD-309| and |FRAME: CPD-308|., The opines, which are secreted into the environment, are transported into the bacteria, where, they are catabolized to provide the cells with carbon, nitrogen, and energy |CITS:[9244272][9791116], [10869063] [16195384]|. The first step in the catabolism of the opines is their conversion into, |FRAME: ARG| (see |FRAME: OCTOPINEDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: NOPALINEDEG-PWY| pathways)., |FRAME: ARG| is then degraded into |FRAME: GLT| via this variant of |FRAME: ARG| degradation, pathway., In addition to the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-358|, the pathway was also found in the facultative, parasite |FRAME: TAX-29459|, which can survive and reproduce inside mammalian cells |CITS: [9375792]|., Like other arginase-based pathways, the pathway starts with an |FRAME: CPLX-6896|-mediated, conversion of |FRAME:ARG| to |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME:UREA|., However, the next step utilizes the unusual enzyme, ornithine cyclodeaminase, which converts |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| directly to |FRAME: PRO|, with the, release of |FRAME: AMMONIA|., This enzyme is cosidered uncommon, and apart from |FRAME: TAX-358| has been reported in only, two |FRAME:TAX-286| strains, some strains of |FRAME:TAX-1485| |CITS: [3281832]|, and in, |FRAME: TAX-29459| |CITS: [9375792]|., However, similar genes have been identified in the genome of many organisms, suggesting that, the distribution of this enzyme may be much wider than previously believed., In |FRAME: TAX-358| the genes encoding arginase and ornithine cyclodeaminase are found on Ti, plasmids |CITS: [3957872][8606160][8981973]|., The |FRAME: PRO| formed is degraded via a common catabolic route for this amino acid, (see |FRAME: PROUT-PWY|).

General Background, Organosulfonate compounds are found in the environment as both natural products and xenobiotics. They are catabolized by microorganisms that utilize the carbon and sulfur moieties. Aliphatic C3 sulfonates are widespread natural products found in the environment and are derived from microbial, plant and animal sources. The bacterial catabolism of C3 sulfonates such as |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| (racemic sulfolactate), |FRAME: CPD-380|, and |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| has been studied. The work has focused on the catabolism of the carbon moiety, the fate of the sulfonate group, and the transport systems necessary for organosulfonates to cross the cell membrane. Bioinformatics analyses have shown a diversity in pathways of sulfonate degradation in bacteria from both marine and terrestrial environments (in |CITS: [20007648]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16341843]|)., To date, three desulfonation pathways have been proposed for the degradation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| including:, (1) |FRAME: PWY-6616|: direct desulfonation of |FRAME: CPD-367| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-8144|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12191| and |FRAME: G-12192| genes. |FRAME: CPD-11799| is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-367| via |FRAME: CPD-380| by two dehydrogenases of opposite stereochemistry, encoded by |FRAME: G-12189| and |FRAME: G-12190|., (2) |FRAME: PWY-6637|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), followed by decarboxylation of sulfopyruvate to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by the |FRAME: CPLX-8153| encoded by the |FRAME: G-12226| and |FRAME: G-12227| genes, desulfonation to acetyl phosphate by |FRAME: G-12229|, and conversion of acetyl phosphate to acetyl-CoA., (3) |FRAME: PWY-6638|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), transamination of |FRAME: CPD-380| to |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE|, racemization of |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| to |FRAME: CPD-28271|, and desulfonation of |FRAME: CPD-28271| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| by the product of the |FRAME: G-12230| gene., In all of these pathways the |FRAME: HSO3| or |FRAME: SO3| produced by the desulfonation reaction is proposed to be transported through the cell membrane and oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| by a periplasmic enzyme, possibly the product of genes sorAB in some organisms |CITS: [19581363][20150239] [16341843]|., In each of these pathways a different enzymatic desulfonation mechanism is used., In |FRAME: PWY-6616| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: CPD-367| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.24| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8146| from |FRAME: ORG-6160| and |FRAME: CPLX-8144| from |FRAME: TAX-290398| for examples |CITS: [15758220]|., In |FRAME: PWY-6637| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15|. See |FRAME: MONOMER-15909|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12229| gene in |FRAME: TAX-89187| for example |CITS: [19581363][20150239]|., In |FRAME: PWY-6638| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.25|. See |FRAME: CPLX-8147| from |FRAME: TAX-246200| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15910| from |FRAME: TAX-89187| for examples |CITS: [19581363][16302849]|.

General Background, In terms of both frequency and magnitude of plant biomass accumulation, the transfer of the glycosyl moiety is one of the most important biochemical reactions known. Two-thirds of the biosphere`s carbon existing as carbohydrates is due to this kind of reaction. Transfer of the glycosyl moiety from sugar nucleotides to a large number and molecular diversity of acceptors is catalyzed by glycosyltransferases |CITS: [SINNOTT90]|. , Glucosyltransferases as one subclass of glycosyltransferases are involved in the glucosylation of a broad variety of secondary plant metabolites, amongst them monolignols involved in the metabolic sequence of lignin biosynthesis |CITS: [IBRAHIM77][FOERSTER99]|. Modifying enzymes such as the multigene family of glucosyltransferases contribute to the plasticity of metabolism where corresponding products are either involved in a particular biosynthetic route or may act as gateways into different metabolic pathways |CITS: [11042211]| |CITS: [10973093]|., The presence and significance to lignification of glucosylated cinnamyl alcohols in the cambium of woody plants were, emphasized several decades ago by Freudenberg |CITS: [FREUDENBERG63]| |CITS: [5593877]|. Although gucosyltransferases in general may cover a broad substrate spectrum it has been demonstrated that certain glucosyltransferases exhibit a rather strict specificity towards their substrates |CITS: [4731963]| |CITS: [11430981]| |CITS: [15907484]|., About This Pathway, The most prominent monolignol glucoside accumulating in a variety of plants is the 4-O-β-D-glucopyranoside of trans-coniferyl alcohol, i.e. coniferin (|FRAME:PWY-116|). The enzyme catalyzing the formation of coniferin has been purified from different plant sources |CITS: [10853]| and appears to be most active in developing xylem of gymnosperms |CITS: [6210530]| |CITS: [11430981]|., The UDPG:coniferyl alcohol glucosyltransferase (CAGT) also glucosylates sinapyl alcohol with high efficiency in pine cambium |CITS: [SAVIDGE98]| |CITS: [FOERSTER00]| and cell cultures of |FRAME:TAX-55182| and |FRAME:TAX-3764| spec., |CITS: [IBRAHIM77]| |CITS: [10853]|. In addition, coniferyl and sinapyl aldehydes have been converted with comparable , catalytic efficiency |CITS: [6210530]| |CITS: [11430981]| |CITS: [10853]|. Recent investigation of the multigene family encoding enzymes conjugating lignin monomers in |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [15907484]| revealed a single gene expressing a CAGT highly specific for coniferyl and sinapyl aldehydes. The recombinant expressed enzyme significantly differs from the other members of this gene family with regard to substrate preference as they specifically encode enzymes for the glucosylation of the monolignol alcohols. These findings confirm the long assumed incorporation of aldehydic components into lignin because the phloroglucinol-HCl lignin specific dye reaction depends on the presence, of aldehyde groups |CITS: [FREUDENBERG68]|., Additionally, it has been demonstrated that dihydroconiferyl alcohol, a monomer isolated from developing xylem of |FRAME:TAX-3339| |CITS: [SAVIDGE87]| but usually not regarded as an important component of the lignin biosynthetic pathway had also been converted into the 4-O-β-D-glucopyranoside |CITS: [11430981]|. Moreover, the catalytic activity for the formation of dihydroconiferyl alcohol has been found in the microsomal fraction of developing pine xylem |CITS: [11430982]|., In addition, this rare monolignol has been determined as a major component in lignin of a mutant loblolly pine accounting , for around 30% per unit |CITS: [9211851]| emphasizing the metabolic plasticity of monomeric components involved in lignin biosynthesis.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA Cinnamoyl-CoA| and the closely related compound, |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| are important precursors to a number of compound classes, including phenylpropanoids, flavonoids, and volatile benzenoids in plants and polyketides in plants and bacteria |CITS: [12502351][19258320]|. Members of these classes can play many roles, for instance as defense, signaling, pigment, and aroma compounds., About This Pathway, Both |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA| and |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| are derived from |FRAME: CPD-674| produced from |FRAME: PHE| by the activity of a phenylalanine ammonia lysase (PAL). Their only structural difference is the presence of a hydroxyl group in the 4-position on the benzene ring. If the hydroxyl group is added directly to |FRAME: CPD-674|, then |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| can be made without a |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA| intermediate (see |FRAME: PWY1F-467| and |FRAME: PWY-361|). However, as shown in this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-674| can be also be a direct substrate for a CoA ligase. In some cases, the |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA| generated by this enzyme may be used directly in secondary metabolic pathways (e.g. |FRAME: PWY-6443|, |FRAME: PWY-5059|), however, it may also be used to produce |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| through a late hydroxylation (e.g. |FRAME: PWY-6432|)., Although PAL has been well-characterized in plants since its initial discovery in 1961 |CITS: [14458851]|, it wasn't until much later than an enzyme believed to be responsible for catalyzing the second step in this pathway was first identified in bacteria |CITS: [12502351]|. , In plants, the first step in this pathway is often rate limiting, for example, in the production of flavonoids. Therefore, expression levels and activity levels of PAL are often highly regulated and changes are induced by different stresses (rev. in |CITS: [17612622]|, ex. in |CITS: [16456646]|).

General Background, The |FRAME: Furanocoumarins furanocoumarins| are one of the main groups of coumarins. Their synthesis starts with thecoupling of |FRAME: CPD-4211| to the coumarin |FRAME: CPD-8186|, leading to formation of a skeleton that contains a furan ring fused with coumarin., Furanocoumarins are minor constituents in plants belonging to |FRAME: TAX-4037|, |FRAME: TAX-3803|, |FRAME: TAX-3487|, and |FRAME: TAX-23513| families. They are natural toxins that protect the plants from insects, herbivory, and microbes. Production is triggered by several types of stresses, including fungal infections |CITS: [6682038][8062387]| and stresses such as wounding |CITS: [Zangerl90]| or acid fog |CITS: [Dercks90]| . , Furanocoumarins are also toxic to humans. Direct contact with the sap from some plants containing furanocoumarins (such as |FRAME: TAX-380077|) causes inflammation, burns and irritating sensitivity to sunlight |CITS: [ 33174568]|. Some naturally occurring methoxy derivatives of furanocoumarins have been applied clinically, coupled with exposure to sunlight, to cure dermatological diseases for more than 2000 years. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12695 "5-Nitroanthranilate"| is an amino-nitroaromatic compound. It is produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1930| (the predominant causal agent of common scab of potato in North America), and can be degraded by another soil bacterium, |FRAME: TAX-722413| (also isolated from potato farm soil)., The degradation of |FRAME: CPD-12695| is initiated by a deamination reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15902| |CITS: [20081004]|. The next step, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-17373|, involves fission of the ring by dioxygenation . The ring opening leads to the elimination of the nitro group (either during the ring fission or immediately following it) and to spontaneous lactonization |CITS: [21498645]|. The |FRAME: G-15153|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17374| catalyzes the hydrolysis of the lactone to produce |FRAME: CPD-1070|, a key intermediate in the biodegradation of 5-substituted salicylates, including |FRAME: CPD-633| and 5-halosalicylates., The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-1070| to central intermediates is likely to proceed via |FRAME: CPD-277|, as a transient accumulation of |FRAME: FUM| is observed during the degradation process. The gene that encodes the isomerase that converts |FRAME: CPD-1070| to |FRAME: CPD-277| has not been discovered yet, but a gene that is likely to encode the next enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-17375|, has been observed, and as it contains a domain with similarity to isomerases, may also encode the missing isomerase |CITS: [21498645]|., The key enzyme of this pathway is |FRAME: MONOMER-17373|, an enzyme that is able to attack and cleave the aromatic ring without the requirement for prior removal of the nitro group. The elimination of a nitro group during the subsequent spontaneous lactone formation establishes a novel mechanism for denitration of nitro aliphatic compounds.

Names: Salmonella enterica serotype O:54 O antigen biosynthesis // group O:54 Salmonella O antigen biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The synthesis of the group O:54 antigen is the only known example for a Salmonella O antigen that is produced by the synthase-dependent pathway. This antigen is a homopolymer of N-acetylmannosamine (ManNAc) with alternating β-(1→3) and β-(1→4) linkages. Most of the genes encoding enzymes that participate in the pathway (|FRAME: G-80967|, |FRAME: G-80968|, and |FRAME: G-80969|) are encoded on the 6.9-kb ColE1-based mobilizable plasmid pWQ799 |CITS: [7545154]|., The pathway begins on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane with the transfer of N-acetylglucosamine 1-phosphate to |FRAME: CPD-9646| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA), which is encoded by a chromosomal gene. WecA is not unique to this pathway, as it participates in the |FRAME: ECASYN-PWY| pathway., |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.14| (MnaA) converts UDP-GlcNAc to UDP-ManNAc, the precursor needed for synthesis of the O:54 glycan. The plasmid-encoded MnaA is a functional homolog of the chromosomally-encoded WecB, which participates in the ECA biosynthesis pathway. , The first committed step is catalyzed by WbbE, which transfers the first ManNAc residue to |FRAME: ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINYLDIPHOSPHO-UNDECAPRE|. This residue is considered an adaptor on which chain extension can occur |CITS: [8910488]|. The rest of the pathway is catalyzed by WbbF, a bifunctional glycosyltransferase that catalyzes the polymerization of the O:54 O antigen by extending the nonreducing end by the repeating motif (1→3)-β-D-ManNAc-(1→4)-β-D-ManNAc-. WbbF also acts as a flippase, flipping the polymerized chain from the cytosol to the periplasm, where it could be transferred to lipid A-core to form the complete lipopolysaccharide.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Denitrification is a respiratory process in which nitrate is used as the ultimate electron acceptor for electrons that are derived from the quinone pool. Denitrification occurs only in oxygen depletion conditions since oxygen is a more favorable electron acceptor than nitrate. It is an important part of the global nitrogen cycle, returning biological nitrogen to the atmosphere and maintaining the balance of the nitrogen budget. In four reactions, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME:EC-1.7.5.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.5| and |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.4|, |FRAME: NITRATE| is successively reduced to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE|, with the nitrogen being transformed to the next lower oxidation state in each successive reaction. The oxidized nitrogen compounds that are produced during denitrification are also used as alternative electron acceptors for energy production |CITS:[2005866][9667932][10320675][10368138]|. , Denitrifying ability has been found in microorganisms belonging to numerous groups of bacteria and archaea |CITS:[12359326]| as well as some fungi |CITS: [9409151][MOROZKINA07]|. At least 30 genera of bacteria are known to denitrify |CITS: [17070915]|. However, most of the current knowledge has been acquired from a small number of organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-316|, |FRAME: TAX-266| and |FRAME: TAX-287|., The first enzyme in the pathway is nitrate reductase. In Gram-negative bacteria this enzyme is located at the cytoplasmic membrane, and as the reaction it catalyzes consumes protons (forming water), it faces the cytoplasmic side. The product of the enzyme, nitrite, is highly toxic. It is transported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm by dedicated nitrate/nitrite exchangers (such as the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10642 NarK| and |FRAME: EG12153 NarU|). Once nitrite is transported to the periplasm, it can be reduced to ammonium by the periplasmic nitrite reductase |CITS: [23934766]|, In fungi the first two reactions occur in the mitochondrion, and the rest of the pathway occurs in the cytoplasm |CITS: [Morozkina07]|., In addition to the four enzymes shown here many other genes are involved in the pathway, encoding electron donors, electron carriers, chaperonins and proteins involved in metal processing. There are 33 genes involved in denitrification in |FRAME: TAX-316| |CITS:[12359326]|., The onlly difference between this pathway and |FRAME:PWY-6748| is the third enzyme. In this pathway this reaction is catalyzed by a cytochrome c-dependent enzyme, while in |FRAME:PWY-6748| it is catalyzed by a quinol-dependent enzyme.

General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, In heterotrophic organisms carotenoids protect against singlet oxygen as well as against peroxy radicals., Certain strains of the yellow-pigmented, non-photosynthetic genus |FRAME: TAX-53335|, including |FRAME: TAX-549 "Pantoea agglomerans (previously known as Erwinia herbicola)"| and |FRAME: TAX-553 "Pantoea ananatis (previously known as Erwinia uredovora)"|, form carotenoids such as hydroxylated |FRAME: CPD1F-129| derivatives and corresponding glycosides., The main pigments produced in these strains are |FRAME: CPD-11472|, |FRAME: CPD-11470| and |FRAME: CPD-11471| |CITS:[2254247][1946693]|., A gene fragment from |FRAME: TAX-549| was cloned and expressed in an |FRAME:TAX-562| host, conferring carotenoid biosynthesis on the host. Nucleotide sequencing, mutagenesis, and identification of carotenoid intermediates accumulated in the |FRAME:TAX-562| host defined six clustered genes (crtB, crtE, crtI, crtX, crtY, and crtZ) involved in the biosynthetic pathway from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| to the final product |FRAME: CPD-11471| |CITS:[2040425][1946693][7808389]|., Overexpression of |FRAME: TAX-53335| crtB, crtE, crtI, |FRAME: G-11389|, |FRAME: G-11388|, and |FRAME: G-11387| in |FRAME: TAX-562| or |FRAME: TAX-358| has confirmed their proposed biosynthetic activities |CITS:[1400305][1409639][1599492][1555761][8422926][8215396][8275101][8645170][9593819]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycolysis, which was first studied as a pathway for the utilization of glucose, is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, the other two being the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| and the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. Glycolysis is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces six of the 13 precursor metabolites that are the starting materials for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules (the six compounds are |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:G3P|, |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). Glycolysis can be found, if at least in part, in almost all organisms., Even though glycolysis is often described starting with glucose, other hexoses (e.g. fructose) can also serve as input (as its name implies - glycose is a general term for simple sugars)., Glycolysis has evolved to fulfill two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) being an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism), it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy., This switching of direction is possible because all but two of the enzymatic reactions comprising glycolysis are reversible, and the conversions catalyzed by the two exceptions are rendered functionally reversible by other enzymes (|FRAME:F16B-CPLX "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase"| and |FRAME:PEPSYNTH-CPLX|) that catalyze different irreversible reactions flowing in the opposite direction., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-2261| is a strict anaerobic archaeon, capable of utilizing pyruvate, sugars and complex organic compounds as carbon and energy sources. It is a hyperthermophilic facultative sulfur-reducing species that is able to grow in the absence of sulfur by fermentation of peptides, carbohydrates and pyruvate, as indicated by the pathway link. |FRAME: TAX-2261| employs a modified glycolytic pathway for the catabolism of sugars that contains three unique enzymes., Two are ADP-dependent kinases, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.147| and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.146|, and the third is a tungsten-containing |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.6| (GAPOR). GAPOR converts glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate into 3-phosphoglycerate in a single reaction, by passing ATP formation by substrate-level-phosphorylation via phosphoglycerate kinase., The initial degradation of polysaccharides to oligosaccharides by |FRAME: TAX-2261| involves specific extracellular glycosyl hydrolases. The oligosaccharide products are transported into the cell by ABC-type or secondary transporters. Further hydrolysis is accomplished by specific intracellular glycoside hydrolases. The final glucose monomers are metabolized to pyruvate by the pathway shown here. Since the organism spends two high energy phosphate bonds early in the pathway and produces only two ATP molecules, the main gain of this pathway is reducing power, in the form of reduced ferredoxin., The pyruvate that is formed is further fermented to acetate, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen |CITS: [11133967] [9783166][Kengen96][10762259][9119024][8530474][8830684][7721730][16233230]|., Regulation of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-2261| remains poorly understood |CITS: [12921536][28425930]|. Genomic and biochemical data suggest that other species of |FRAME:TAX-2260| also have this pathway |CITS:[12921536][Kengen96][10493919]|.
Level 1: Generation of precursor metabolites and energy

Common-Name-Taxa: Burkholderia sp. JB1,Pseudomonas sp. CA10,Rhizorhabdus wittichii,Terrabacter sp. DPO360,Pseudomonas sp. HH69
Summary: Dibenzo-p-dioxins are produced as byproducts during the manufacturing of a variety of compounds,, including herbicides, fungicides, and insecticides, during the process of paper pulp bleaching, and, during the combustion of solid waste in incinerators or in accidental fires., These xenobiotics are chemically stable, thus posing a serious health concern due to their accumulation, in the environment.  Several microorganisms have been shown to grow on dibenzo-p-dioxin as a sole, carbon source, including |FRAME: ORG-5969|, |FRAME: TAX-392499|, |FRAME: TAX-135214|, |FRAME: TAX-48070|, and |FRAME: TAX-80621| |CITS: [11959434]|., The first step in the degradation of dibenzo-p-dioxin is the dihydroxylation, of one of the aromatic rings by a three-component enzyme system, which leads to a spontaneous, rearomatization to more stable compounds |CITS: [9683494]|., This dioxin dioxygenase enzyme system is composed of a heterodimeric terminal oxygenase and an, electron-transfer system involving a [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin. |CITS: [9654094]| Both end products shown, here, catechol and 2-hydroxymuconate can be further catabolized via separate pathways, |CITS: [10348858] [9683494]|.

Names: 1D-myo-inositol hexakisphosphate biosynthesis I (from Ins(1,4,5)P3) // phytate biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| (phytate, phytic acid) is one of the most prevalent forms of phosphorylated inositols in the eukaryotic cell, with a total concentration of 15-100 μM |CITS:[3426614][1684044][8435066]|. It's cellular distribution is not completely known - some of it is soluble, some is "wall-papered" around membranes, while some is bound to proteins |CITS: [9838040]|. In plant seeds, large amount of phytate are complexed with cations and deposited as globular inclusions in membrane-bound storage bodies |CITS: [15700415]|., The compound has been proposed to have a number of signaling roles, including regulation of insulin exocytosis |CITS: [9114007]|, regulation of nuclear mRNA export |CITS:[10390371][10683435]|, binding of the clathrin assembly proteins AP2 and AP3 |CITS: [1849645][1371119]|, inhibition of clathrin cage assembly |CITS: [7814377][7829485]|, and inhibition of serine and threonine protein phosphatases that are thought to regulate L-type Ca2+ channels |CITS: [9334307]|., Phytate in Plants, In plant cells phytate serves as a storage form of myo-inositol, phosphate and mineral nutrients for utilization during seed germination and seedling growth. It is deposited within single-membrane storage organelles referred to as protein bodies and is usually present as mixed complexes with different cations, including |FRAME: K+|, |FRAME: MG+2|, |FRAME: CA+2|, |FRAME: FE+2|, and |FRAME: ZN+2|, known as phytin |CITS:[11590064][8744268]|., Although phytin only makes up about 1% of the seed weight, it may contain up to 80% of the total seed phosphorus |CITS:[15700415]|. Phytate is also present in other plant tissues and organs such as pollen, roots, tuber and turions in smaller quantities |CITS:[14568069]|. , About This Pathway, The main function of |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| in yeast is related to regulation of mRNA export from the nucleus |CITS: [10390371][10720331][10683435 ]|., The biosynthetic pathway found in yeast and plants proceeds from |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (produced by phospholipase C as described in |FRAME: PWY-6351|) by a series of successive phosphorylations carried out by only two enzymes., In yeast, |FRAME: G3O-24| encodes |FRAME: MONOMER3O-64|, a versatile enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorylation of |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| at both the 3- and 6-positions, resulting in formation of both |FRAME: CPD-506| and |FRAME: INOSITOL-1456-TETRAKISPHOSPHATE|. Similarly, the enzyme phosphorylates both of these compounds to |FRAME: CPD-1107| |CITS: [10683435]|., In |FRAME: TAX-3702| very similar enzymes exist. The plant has two isoforms of |FRAME: G3O-24|, encoded by |FRAME: AT5G07370| and |FRAME: AT5G61760| |CITS: [12226109]|., |FRAME: CPD-1107| is substrate for the |FRAME: YDR315C|-encoded |FRAME: YDR315C-MONOMER|, which adds a phosphate group at position 2, resulting in |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE|. This enzyme is found in all eukaryotes, from yeast to mammals., Yeast cells lacking |FRAME: YDR315C| are deficient in |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| production and exhibit lethality when combined with a gle1 (encoding the nuclear pore protein GLE1, which is involved in RNA export from the nucleus) mutant allele |CITS: [10960485]|. Plant |FRAME: AT5G61760| gene can rescue this mutant |CITS: [12226109]|., Humans and monogastric animals lack hydrolytic phytases in their digestive tract, and are unable to extract the minerals from it. Undigested phytate in animal waste is a major contributor to eutrophication and environmental phosphorus pollution |CITS:[11590064][11906835]|.

General Background, The p-hydroxycinnamates |FRAME: COUMARATE| (p-coumarate), |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| and |FRAME: CAFFEATE| are phenylpropanoid compounds produced by green plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY1F-467| and |FRAME: PWY-2181|). These compounds are degraded by soil bacteria. An aerobic pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| has been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-502559| |CITS: [12200295]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6343|). A similar pathway operates on |FRAME: CPD-676|, as shown here., It has been suggested that the ability to degrade hydroxy-cinnamic acids contributes to bacterial wilt virulence by facilitating root entry and by protecting the pathogen from the toxicity of these compounds |CITS: [25423265]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-674 "Cinnamate"| derivatives, including |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: COUMARATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-676|, play important roles in the cross-linking of the cell walls of various grasses and represent up to 1.5% of the weight of their cell walls., In the first step of the pathway |FRAME: MONOMER-15132| catalyzes the transfer of CoA to the carboxyl group of |FRAME: CPD-676|, generating |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA|. In the second and third steps, both catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15133|, |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA| is hydrated to form |FRAME: CPD-21376|, which is then cleaved to |FRAME: CPD-7616| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [8987621][9579070][11152072]|., Once formed, |FRAME: CPD-7616| is converted to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and processed to central metabolism intermediates, as described in the pathway |FRAME: P184-PWY|.

Colchicine is an antimitotic agent that has been traditionally used as drug for gout. It is also a FAO approved drug for the treatment of the gout disease |CITS: [RUEFFER98]|. Many derivatives of colchicine are also potential anticancer drugs in various stages of testing for efficacy |CITS: [SCOTT60][HAYASHI88]|. It is extensively used in cytological research |CITS: [BARKER98]|, |CITS: [SHELDRAKE98][WOODHOUSE98]|., The unusual tropolone ring of these compounds makes chemical synthesis a difficult task |CITS:[SIVAKUMAR04]|. The biosynthesis is poorly understood in terms of characterizing single reaction steps and corresponding enzymes, though the entire enzyme complement required to carry out the main biosynthetic sequence seems to be present in the microsome preparations |CITS: [Nasreen97][RUEFFER98]|. , The main reaction steps in the pathway have been identified through labeled compounds shown to be involved as intermediate precursors in the making of |FRAME:CPD-9785|. The first reaction is the para-para phenol oxidative coupling of |FRAME:CPD-9790| |CITS:[Nasreen96][Maier97]| which forms |FRAME:CPD-9789|. |FRAME:CPD-9789 Isoandrocymbine| is O-methylated followed by NADPH-dependent oxidations and amide hydrolysis (loss of the formyl group) which generates the very unusual tropane structure by ring expansion of the tyrosine-derived aromatic ring |CITS: [RUEFFER98][Dewick02]|. The last steps in the pathway comprise oxidative demethylation of |FRAME:CPD-9787| followed by the N-acetylation of the resulting |FRAME:CPD-9786| which finally yields |FRAME:CPD-9785|. All the reactions have been demonstrated in the microsomal fraction obtained from seeds of |FRAME:TAX-45005| but pinpointing the late steps of the pathway to corresponding enzymes remain to be done |CITS: [Nasreen96][Nasreen97][RUEFFER98][Dewick02]|.

Names: gondoate biosynthesis (anaerobic) // cis-11-icosenoate biosynthesis // (11Z)-icos-11-enoate biosynthesis // (11Z)-icosenoate biosynthesis // gondoic acid biosynthesis // 11-eicosenoic acid biosynthesis
Summary: The saprophytic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1377| produces the unusual monounsaturated fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-12189| |CITS: [23972938]|. While |FRAME: CPD-12189| is also found in plants, it is produced in bacteria in an anaerobic pathway that does not involve oxygen-dependent desaturase enzymes., The pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1377| is similar to the pathway used by many bacteria to produce |FRAME: CPD-17910| (see |FRAME: PWY0-862|). The key enzyme of that pathway is |FRAME: EC-5.3.3.14| (|FRAME: EG10273 FabA|), which has the unique ability of converting some of the |FRAME: Trans-D2-decenoyl-ACPs "(2E)-dec-2-enoyl-[acp]"| (an intermediate the |FRAME: PWY-5971 "palmitate biosynthesis"| pathway) to |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acp]"|, which is then elongated in the usual fatty acid elongation process to form |FRAME: Cis-Delta5-dodecenoyl-ACPs "(5Z)-dodec-5-enoyl-[acp]"|. , In the case of bacterial gondoate prduction (which involves oleate as an intermediate), the key step in the pathway is a similar isomerization, but of a later intermediate of the palmitate biosynthesis pathway, |FRAME: Dodec-2-enoyl-ACPs|, which contains a longer acyl chain (note that the reaction is not shown in this pathway, but in |FRAME: PWY-7664|, which describes earlier steps in the process). The enzyme catalyzing the isomerization reaction in |FRAME: TAX-1377| is a unique hydratase/isomerase, encoded by |FRAME: G-44009|, which fulfills the roles of both |FRAME: EG11284| (the hydratase involved in the fatty acid elongation process) and |FRAME: EG10273|, which is essential for production of unsaturated fatty acids |CITS: [23972938]|., Another key enzyme in bacterial anaerobic unsaturated fatty acids biosynthesis is the enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of the FabA (or FabQ) product with malonyl-[acp], thus allowing the fatty acid elongation enzymes to continue the extension of the unsaturated fatty acid by two carbons. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this activity is provided by |FRAME: EG10274 FabB|. In |FRAME: TAX-1377|, which lacks FabB, this activity is carried out by a trifunctional |FRAME: G-44012 FabF| enzyme, which catalyzes the activities of the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG10277| and |FRAME: EG12606| |CITS: [23972938]|., Three rounds of the sequential action of FabF - FabG - FabQ - FabK generate |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| (see |FRAME: PWY-7664|). A fourth round extends the fatty acid to |FRAME: CPD-12189|.

Names: toluene degradation to 2-hydroxypentadienoate (via toluene-cis-diol) // toluene degradation via toluene-cis-diol
Summary: Toluene is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic compounds can be , degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus |FRAME:TAX-286| and , closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward bioremediation of environmental pollutants by , metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|). , Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various species that involve different initial , monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these pathways converge in the formation , of 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound is a substrate for ring cleavage , enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission pathway, resulting in the , formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and MetaCyc pathways , |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-3-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-2-OH-PWY|). , The chromosome of |FRAME:TAX-303| F1 contains a gene cluster encoding enzymes that allow this , organism to grow on toluene and related compounds as sole carbon and energy source , |CITS: [2670929], [1916282], [8063106]|. Other strains of P. putida may contain plasmid-encoded genes for , toluene degradation (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|). The inducible toluene , dioxygenase enzyme hydroxylates toluene to its dihydrodiol derivative by incorporating both atoms of an oxygen , molecule into the aromatic nucleus. The dihydroxylated derivative is dehydrogenated to a catechol. Ring fission , of the catechol 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) is catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase to produce , cis,cis-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate. This compound is hydrolyzed to 2-oxopent-4-enoate, , or its tautomeric dienol form cis-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate. This tautomerization occurs spontaneously , in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|. It is not known which tautomeric form is produced by the hydrolase, , and which form is used by the hydratase of P. putida F1 in this pathway. However, it has been suggested , that the |FRAME:TAX-303| mt-2 hydratase, encoded by the TOL plasmid pWW0, uses the dienol form , as a substrate |CITS: [2681159]|, and there is evidence that the |FRAME:TAX-562| hydratase also uses the , dienol form as substrate, producing a ketonized intermediate in the reaction mechanism |CITS: [9492273]|. The , products of the pathway are pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and acetaldehyde, which may be converted , by acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, a central metabolite |CITS: [8063106]|.

In chemolithoautotrophic ammonia-oxidizing bacteria ammonia oxidation to nitrite is performed in two steps. Ammonia is first converted to hydroxylamine by ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), and hydroxylamine is then oxidized to nitrite by a hydroxylamine oxidoreductase (HAO). In the process the bacteria are able to generate sufficient energy for growth and maintenance reactions, including the reductive fixation of carbon dioxide., Many heterotrophic bacteria can also oxidize ammonia to nitrite. There are several key differences between heterotrophic and autotrophic ammonia oxidation. Firstly, heterotrophic ammonia oxidation usually does not generate energy (although there has been a report about a |FRAME:TAX-286| strain which utilizes hydroxylamine oxidation as an additional energy source |CITS: [9049019]|). It has been suggested that in these bacteria nitrification is used as a sink for excess reducing, power generated by oxidative metabolism |CITS: [Robertson88][8253206]|., It has been shown that many heterotrophs couple ammonia oxidation to aerobic denitrification |CITS: [2181927][8253206][9765887][12460428][12889035]|. In this process the nitrite produced by ammonia oxidation is reduced to nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and possibly to nitrogen gas. By coupling the two pathways, the bacteria end up disposing of excess reducing power, even though the ammonia oxidizing pathway on its own generates, rather than consumes, reducing power., Secondly, while the second step of the pathway (the oxidation of hydroxylamine to nitrite) is catalyzed in autotrophs only by enzymes with hydroxylamine oxidoreductase activity, heterotrophs may apply alternative routes, as demonstrated in this pathway |CITS: [8674977]|., Although the nitrification rate in heterotrophs is very low compared to the rate in nitrifying autotrophs, the sum of their activities on the earth is very significant as the global mass of the heterotrophs is very large., |FRAME: TAX-511| cells can oxidize ammonia to nitrite and various organic acids |CITS: [7765476 ]|. An enzyme which participated in the oxidation of hydroxylamine to nitrite was partially purified from |FRAME: TAX-511| and was found to be a pyruvic oxime dioxygenase |CITS: [8674977]|., Hydroxylamine, in the presence of pyruvate, can form pyruvic oxime in a spontaneous, non enzymatic reaction. In this organism the pyruvic oxime is oxidized aerobically to nitrite in the presence of hydroxylamine or ascorbate by a pyruvic oxime dioxygenase, in a reaction that consumes molecular oxygen in equimolar amounts to the nitrite formed |CITS: [8674977]|., This pathway is not limited to a single organism, as the oxidation of pyruvic oxime to nitrite was also demonstrated for, whole cells of |FRAME:TAX-222| sp.  |CITS: [14944588]|., In addition, Otte et al |CITS: [10091333]| have shown that during hydroxylamine oxidation |FRAME: TAX-511| produces |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE| gas, some of which is subsequently reduced to dinitrogen gas. Further experiments showed that the source for the |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE| was not denitrification of nitrite. The authors concluded that the nitrous oxide was most likely produced as a by-product of hydroxylamine oxidation., The authors also partially purified a small (20 kDa) non-heme hydroxylamine oxidoreductase from |FRAME: TAX-511|, similar in size to the HAOs purified from other ammonia-oxidizing heterotrophs |CITS: [8253206][9082922]|., Since it has been shown that |FRAME: TAX-511| cells can oxidize ammonia to nitrite |CITS: [7765476 ]|, the bacterium is likely to also possess an ammonia-oxidizing enzyme like AMO. However, such an enzyme has not been discovered yet.

|FRAME: CPD-18772 Gadusol| is a UV-absorbing compound structurally related to the mycosporines. It was initially isolated from cod (|FRAME: TAX-8049|) roe |CITS: [7200360]|, but also found in roes of other marine fish |CITS: [Arbeloa10]|, sea urchin eggs |CITS: [Chioccara86]|, cysts and nauplii of brine shrimp |CITS: [Grant85]|, mantis shrimp crystalline cones |CITS: [24998530]|, and sponges |CITS: [Bandaranayake97]|., While |FRAME: CPD-18772| has often been reported from fish and other marine animals, it has been thought that its accumulation is of dietary or symbiont origin |CITS: [Arbeloa10][21963801][25137589]|. However, in 2015 it was found that most egg-laying vertebrates actually have the genes that are required to produce |FRAME: CPD-18772| from the common metabolite |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| |CITS: [25965179]|., The pathway, which has been characterized in the zebra fish (|FRAME: TAX-7955|), is composed of three reactions catalyzed by two enzymes. The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.152|, is well-known from microbes. The second enzyme, which was novel, is a bifunctional enzyme composed of two domains: an N-terminal S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferase which O-methylates the second position of |FRAME: CPD-9663|, and a C-terminal NAD+-dependent oxidoreductase that introduces a double bond in the core ring, forming |FRAME: CPD-18772| |CITS: [25965179]|., Homologous genes have been found in amphibians, reptiles, and birds.

Analysis of the genomic sequence of |FRAME: TAX-162425| reveals the presence of 32 biosynthetic gene clusters having polyketide synthase genes. Some of the clusters are located near the telomeres of chromosomes, where transcription is controlled by epigenetic regulation., One of the mechanisms for such regulation is methylation of lysine 4 on histone H3, which is catalyzed by the COMPASS (complex associated with Set1) complex. Knocking out the cclA gene, which encodes a component of the COMPASS complex, resulted in activation of clusters responsible for production of |FRAME: CPD-23470| and other |FRAME: CPD-8215| derivatives |CITS: [20139316]|., Based on gene deletion experiments, five genes (|FRAME: G-125084|, |FRAME: G-80807|, mdpJ,|FRAME: G-125082| and |FRAME: G-125086|) were identified as necessary for the formation of |FRAME: CPD-23470| from |FRAME: CPD-8215| |CITS: [20139316]|. A pathway has been proposed at the time, but was later found incorrect., In 2012 an alternative route was proposed, which proceeds via the deoxygenation of |FRAME: CPD-8215| to |FRAME: CPD-8216| prior to oxidative ring cleavage |CITS: [22730213]|. However, some details of that pathway were also found incorrect., The pathway starts with MdpK. Based on its similarity to |FRAME: G-80800|, it was initially suggested that MdpK plays a role in rearrangement of an epoxide intermediate in the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-8215| to |FRAME: CPD-23470| |CITS: [15771506][20139316]|. However, later findings indicated that MdpK catalyzes the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-8215| to |FRAME: CPD-23469| |CITS: [30746079][ 36222427]|. This proposal is supported by earlier observations that disruption of MdpK also leads to an accumulation of emodin and emodin analogs |CITS: [20139316][21351751]|., The next enzyme in the pathway is MdpC. The purified enzyme was shown to reduce either of the hydroquinone tautomers to |FRAME: CPD-23461| |CITS: [22909031]|. Dehydration of the product, carried out by the dehydratase MdpB, forms |FRAME: CPD-28149|, which tautomerizes to |FRAME: CPD-28151|. , The last reaction, oxygenation that results in ring cleavage, is carried out by MdpL. Based on sequence homology, MdpL was originally described as a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase that acts on a quinone intermediate to form |FRAME: CPD-23470| |CITS: [20139316]|. However, based on additional understanding, gained mostly from studies of the related enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-17514|, MdpL is now predicted to be a non-heme dioxygenase |CITS: [36222427]|.

Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) have been recognized as important metabolites involved in the chemical warfare of plants against pathogenic organisms and herbivores. VOCs represent transmitters of biological signals to communicate within the ecosystem of plants to trigger responses from predators of such pests |CITS:[19246460]|. In addition, VOCs also have considerable value in commercial products, for instance tea, by influencing the aroma of this beverage. Tea belongs to the most consumed beverages worldwide and the sup-tropical plant Camellia sinensis constitutes the source for all non-herbal teas which are differentiated in dependence of fermentation processes into black, green and oolong tea |CITS:[Bliss03] [1614995] [9447270]|. However, important tea plant VOCs such as |FRAME:GERANIOL| and others |CITS:[Kawakami95]| are stored as glycosidic compounds such as acuminoside and β-vicianoside |CITS:[11087494] [11308343]| or β-primeverosides |CITS:[7763947] [7522061] [7765491]| (this pathway) which need to be cleaved by e.g. β-primeverosidases to be released as respective volatiles (see |FRAME:PWY-7114|). , β-Primeverosides (β-D-xylopyranosyl-β-D-glucopyranoside) are the most prevalent aroma diglycoside storage forms found in Camellia sinensis. Their biosyntheses are elusive and have only been partially elucidated. The pathway for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-14731| has been established by utilizing a glucosyltransferase coexpression analysis carried out in Arabidopsis thaliana which identified a glucosyltransferase (UGT85A3) able to catalyze the glucosylation of monoterpene- and aliphatic alcohols. The gene UGT85A3 was used as probe for screening of a cDNA library generated from leaves, stem and roots of Camellia sinensis which led to the identification of an orthologous gene in this plant |CITS:[25922059]|., The identified gene (85K11) was cloned and expressed in E. coli to reveal the in vitro activity of the enzyme. It could be demonstrated that the 85K11 encoded glucosyltransferase preferentially glucosylated |FRAME:GERANIOL| yielding |FRAME:CPD-18262| with |FRAME:CPD-12575| as the most efficient sugar donor. The more pathway-specific glycosyltransferase however, was the xylosyltransferase involved in the Camilla sinensis β-primeveroside pathway. The heterologously expressed and purified enzyme encoded by 94P1 xylosylated in vitro with high specificity |FRAME:CPD-18262| yielding |FRAME:CPD-14731| and only accepted |FRAME:UDP-D-XYLOSE| as sugar donor. Homology modelling indicated one special amino acid residue (Ile-114) which solely was responsible for the specificity of the geraniol glucoside 6'-O-xylosyltransferase. This was confirmed by site-directed mutagenesis which led to the loss of specificity for |FRAME:UDP-D-XYLOSE| favoring |FRAME:CPD-12575| instead, which indicated that 94P1 may have been evolved from a glucosyltransferase after acquiring the critical Ile-141. The expression pattern for both the geraniol glucosyltransferase (85K11) and the geraniol glucoside 6'-O-xylosyltransferase (94P1) coincided with the accumulation pattern of |FRAME:CPD-14731| in primarily young leaves suggesting a possible involvement in the chemical defense against pathogens in this susceptible young organ |CITS:[25922059]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8718 Taxol| (paclitaxel) is a highly effective anticancer drug extensively used in the treament of various carcinomas, melanomas and sarcomas |CITS: [11707604]|. Taxol was first isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew tree (|FRAME: TAX-46220|). Limited supply prompted intensive research efforts to find alternate sources including isolation from renewable foliage tissues. Currently, biosynthesis in tissue culture systems from renewable plantation-grown |FRAME: TAX-25628| species, along with semi synthesis of taxol and its analogs from advanced taxane diterpenoid metabolites, remain the main source for this potent chemotherapeutic agent |CITS: [8621577]|. However, total synthesis is not yet a commercially viable option, and as a result, the demand for |FRAME: CPD-8718| greatly exceeds the supply from both natural sources and semisynthesis., The biosynthetic pathway of taxol is complicated and is stil not fully understood (see |FRAME: PWY-5660|). |FRAME: TAXA-411-DIENE "Taxa-4,11-diene"| (taxadiene) is the first dedicated intermediate in |FRAME: CPD-8718| biosynthesis, and there have been several efforts to produce it recombinantly., About This Pathway, This pathway details the production of |FRAME: TAXA-411-DIENE| in an |FRAME: TAX-562| host, as described in |CITS: [11553461]|. Like all terpenes, |FRAME: TAXA-411-DIENE| is formed from |FRAME: CPD-4211| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, which are produced natively in |FRAME: TAX-562| via the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|., One molecule of |FRAME: CPD-4211| is combined with three molecules of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| to form |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This process consists of three reactions, via the formation of the intermediates |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| and |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. The first two reactions can be catalyzed by the bifunctional |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10508 IspA| enzyme. The third one is catalyzed in this pathway by a recombinant |FRAME: MONOMER-18246| enzyme from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-549|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-17754| gene., |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP "All-trans-geranylgeranyl diphosphate"| is cyclyzed to |FRAME: TAXA-411-DIENE| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.17|, cloned from the yew tree |FRAME: TAX-46220|., Early versions of this engineered pathway in both |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-4932| resulted in titers of less than 10mg/liter |CITS: [11553461][18485776]|. A later attempt to optimize the pathway in |FRAME: TAX-562| increased the titer to approximately 1g/liter |CITS: [20929806]|. In that study, the next pathway enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.176|, has also been cloned.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD0-1308 Glyphosate| is a broad-spectrum systemic herbicide used to kill weeds. It was initially patented and sold by the Monsanto Company in the 1970s under the tradename Roundup, and has become the most used herbicide in the world |CITS: [21668647]|., Glyphosate's mode of action is to inhibit the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.19|, which catalyzes the transfer of the enolpyruvyl moiety of |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: SHIKIMATE-5P| to form |FRAME: 3-ENOLPYRUVYL-SHIKIMATE-5P|. This is a key reaction in the |FRAME: ARO-PWY "shikimate pathway"|, leading to synthesis of aromatic amino acids via |FRAME: CHORISMATE| in plants, fungi, bacteria, and apicomplexan parasites |CITS: [7396959]|., While little degradation of glyphosate has been reported in plants (most likely due to contaminating microbes), glyphosate degradation in soils is extensive and rapid |CITS: [Torstensson85]|. Three degradation pathways have been described so far, two of which involve production of |FRAME: CPD0-1074| (AMPA) |CITS: [16347639][Monsanto95]|, a phosphonate that can be metabolized by a wide variety of microorganisms |CITS: [14088788][14302415][618850][Daughton79][Daughton79a][453832][3804975]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7805|). , A number of pure cultures of bacteria have been identified that degrade glyphosate by one of the known routes |CITS: [16346357][Talbot84][2430939][16346999][2442160][3804975][2439330][16347356][Hallas88][3997803][3223761][16347639][Quinn88][Lerbs90][2339877][16348512]|., Pure cultures capable of degrading glyphosate to AMPA have been reported for a |FRAME: TAX-237| sp. |CITS: [16346999]|, for a |FRAME: TAX-286| sp. |CITS: [3223761]| and for |FRAME: TAX-37927| |CITS: [16347639]|, and a large number of isolates that convert glyphosate to AMPA have been identified from industrial activated sludges that treat glyphosate wastes |CITS: [Hallas88]|., About This Pathway, The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-37927| ATCC 13752 appears to degrade glyphosate solely by oxidation with formation of AMPA |CITS: [16347639]|. Glyphosate oxidase activity has been demonstrated with the FAD-dependent glycine oxidase (ThiO) of |FRAME:TAX-1423|. The activity of the wild-type enzyme with glyphosate is low due to a very high Km (87 mM). However, a mutant containing three point mutations (G51S/A54R/H244A) reaches an up to a 210-fold increase in catalytic efficiency compared with the wild-type enzyme |CITS: [19864430]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamin diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, The thiamine biosynthesis pathway illustrated here has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-1423|. There are several differences between the pathways employed by |FRAME: TAX-1423| and by |FRAME: TAX-562| (see |FRAME: THISYN-PWY|). , Thiamine biosynthesis in bacteria is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|. A final phosphorylation reaction yields the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. , The biosynthesis of the thiazole moiety is complex. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| it involves six proteins, the products of the |FRAME: BSU29590|, |FRAME: BSU11700|, |FRAME: BSU11680|, |FRAME: BSU11670|, |FRAME: BSU11690| and |FRAME: BSU11660| genes. , The process begins when the |FRAME: ThiF-Proteins "ThiF protein"| activates |FRAME: Thi-S| by adenylation of its carboxy terminus, generating |FRAME:Adenylated-ThiS-Proteins|. |FRAME: BSU29590-MONOMER IscS|, a protein that is also involved in the biosynthesis of iron-sulfur clusters, catalyzes the transfer of a sulfur atom from cysteine to the adenylated ThiS, generating |FRAME: ThiS-CoASH-proteins|., In a parallel reaction, |FRAME: CPLX-8352| (ThiO) forms |FRAME: CPD-12279| from |FRAME: GLY|., The main reaction in the thiazole synthesis pathway is a very complex reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: BSU11690-MONOMER| (ThiG), that requires three inputs: |FRAME: ThiS-CoASH-proteins|, |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| (DXP) and |FRAME: CPD-12279|., For many years the product of this reaction was assumed to be |FRAME: THZ| (thiazole). However, recent work performed with the thiazole synthase from |FRAME: TAX-1423| has shown that the actual product is the thiazole tautomer |FRAME: CPD-13575| |CITS: [19216519]|. A dedicated |FRAME: BSU11660-MONOMER| converts this product into a different tautomer, |FRAME: CPD-13576|, which is the actual substrate for the thiamine-phosphate diphosphorylase enzyme |CITS: [21534620]|., The biosynthesis of the pyrimidine moiety of thiamin is also not simple. The first step is one of the most complicated rearrangement reactions known. The ThiC enzyme belongs to the radical SAM family, all members of which utilize |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) to generate an 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical that in turn serves as an oxidant for a wide variety of enzymatic reactions |CITS: [18953358]|. The first stage of catalysis is the reduction of SAM to produce |FRAME: MET| and a 5-deoxyadenosyl radical, which is generated at the active site. The radical reacts directly with the substrate to catalyze a complex rearrangement reaction that includes two iterative hydrogen atom abstractions (which necessitates the regeneration of the radical following the first abstraction). C1' and C3' of the substrate, which are not inorporated into the product, are converted to formate and carbon monoxide, respectively |CITS: [20886485]|., The second enzyme, ThiD, is a simple kinase, and produces |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP| |CITS: [14973012]|., The last part of the pathway consists of the coupling of the two moieties of thiamin, forming |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|, and its phosphorylation to the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. , Although it is not absolutely clear at this time, it is possible that |FRAME: BSU38290-MONOMER| acts in vivo on different substrates in different organisms |CITS: [21534620]|.

|FRAME:CPD-16846 Terrequinone A| and related asterriquinones are fungal bisindole alkaloids and belong to the compound family of bisindolylquinones |CITS:[DMELLO97]|. The cytotoxic bisindolylquinones display a broad range of bioactivities which are exploited for drug development and applied as potent agents for a variety of human diseases. Asterriquinones have been shown to cause genomic DNA degradation, arrest the cell cycle and induce apoptosis of murine leukemia tumor cells |CITS:[9413222]|. Moreover, intermediates of the pathway such as |FRAME:CPD-16844| have been reported to possess anti-HIV |CITS:[9207909]| and anti-diabetic |CITS:[15833894]| activities. , The anti-tumor compound |FRAME:CPD-16846| has been found to be synthesized via an biosynthetic gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-162425| identified through a genome-wide transcriptional profiling screen |CITS:[16426969]|. The ascertainment and demarcation of this cluster has been realized utilizing the transcriptional regulator protein LaeA which exercises control of gene expression of secondary (specialized) metabolite gene clusters |CITS:[17291795]|. In-depth in silico analysis provided evidence that five genes are involved in the terrequinone A gene cluster (tdi - tryptophan derived) which have been named tdiA through tdiE |CITS:[16426969]|. All five genes of the terrequinone A gene cluster have been recombinant expressed in E. coli, purified to homogeneity and characterized with regard to their molecular function within the pathway. , The committing step of the pathway, the formation of |FRAME:INDOLE_PYRUVATE| from |FRAME:TRP|, is catalyzed by the L-tryptophan:phenylpyruvate aminotransferase encoded by tdiD. The substrate preference of the tdiD encoded aminotransferase has been determined in vitro |CITS:[17704773] [17584611]| and its affiliation to the gene cluster proven by complementing a terrequinone A null phenotype with the tdiD gene which reconstituted |FRAME:CPD-16846| to almost wild type levels |CITS:[17584611]|. The following reactions of the pathway are catalyzed by enzymes which stand out because of their unique properties. The formation of the central intermediate of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16844| from |FRAME:INDOLE_PYRUVATE| is carried out by a nonribosomal peptide synthetase encoded by tdiA. In general, nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS) are characterized by unique structural features accommodating the assembly of molecules in question along a line of domains which possess distinctive enzymatic activities |CITS:[19374989]|. TdiA consists of an adenylation- (A), thiolation- (T) and thioester cleavage (TE) domain. The A-domain recognizes and activates the two monomer |FRAME:INDOLE_PYRUVATE| molecules which are then bound as thioesters through the T-domain. Finally, the TE-domain catalyzes the unusual C-C bonding and subsequent release of the head-to-tail dimerized product, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16844|. The whole reaction sequence is nonoxidative and independent of cofactors |CITS:[17704773] [17584611]|., The next reactions have been proposed in a divergent manner by the two research groups working independently on the pathway |CITS:[17704773] [18029206]| based on their experimental findings regarding the bisindolylquinone prenyltransferase encoded by tdiB. One route is proposed via |FRAME:CPD-16845| which is generated by reverse prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-16844| with |FRAME:CPD-4211|. The subsequent prenylation to form |FRAME:CPD-16846| was also discussed but not demonstrated |CITS:[18029206]|. The second possible biosynthetic route towards |FRAME:CPD-16846| was shown by iterative prenylation (normal and reverse) of |FRAME:CPD-16848| by the bisindolylquinone prenyltransferase (tdiB). The latter compound has been produced through the reduction of |FRAME:CPD-16844| catalyzed by the didemethylasterriquinone D reductase encoded by tdiC |CITS:[17704773]|. The function of the remaining gene, i.e. tdiE remains to be verified but experiments with the combined expression of tdiC, tdiB and tdiE indicates a probable role for tdiE as a chaperone to prevent the generation of shunt products |CITS:[ 17704773]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-9382 Serinol| is a free amine that has been found in sugarcane leaf surface. Water-wash of sugarcane leaves containing serinol was found to activate toxin production in |FRAME: TAX-48696|, a fungal pathogen that causes the eyespot disease of sugarcane |CITS: [16592362]|. This discovery suggests that pathogenic organisms can use host metabolic intermediates as compounds to regulate aspects of their pathogenicity, such as toxin production |CITS: [16592362]|., In addition to plants, serinol is also found in the α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-29448|. The serinol derivatives |FRAME: CPD-20104| and |FRAME: CPD-20103| were reported to play a positive role in symbiosis between Bradyrhizobium strains and their host legumes by reducing the amount of ethylene synthesized by the hosts and thus decreasing the negative effect of ethylene on nodulation |CITS: [14711685]|., N-Acylated serinol was shown to induce apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells, indicating a therapeutic potential of N-acylated serinol for treatment of cancer in the nervous system |CITS: [10617602]|. Serinol was also indicated as a good monomer for synthetic polyester production |CITS: [15588891]|., About This Pathway, In sugarcane, serinol is biosynthesized from dihydroxyacetone phosphate via a two-step pathway. Enzyme activities catalyzing both of the reactions have been detected in sugarcane cell free extracts |CITS: [16660234]|.
