Summary: |FRAME: CPD-403 "3-Hydroxy-4-methylanthranilate"| occurs exclusively in the actinomycete family of bacteria, and serves as a building block of several secondary metabolites including the |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN actinomycin| phenoxazinone chromophore |CITS: [20945860]|., |FRAME: CPD-403 "3-Hydroxy-4-methylanthranilate"| is synthesized from |FRAME: TRP|, and the genes encoding its biosynthesis are present in the actinomycin biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1892|. This cluster contains two large inverted repeats (which probably arose by gene duplication of a primordial actinomycin biosynthesic gene cluster) and thus nine of the cluster genes are duplicated |CITS: [20304989]|., Two such paralogous genes are |FRAME: G-44205| and |FRAME: G-44206|, which encode methyltransferases that exclusively methylate |FRAME: CPD-18443| to |FRAME: CPD-18438| |CITS: [20945860]|. Curiously, the enzymes are highly specific for the D-isomer of this compound, even though they are active (at a 5-fold lower level) on |FRAME: TRP|. It is not known yet when and how is the L-isomer |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE|, which is presumably produced from L-tryptophan, converted to a D-form. It is worth noting that no enzyme capable of converting |FRAME: CPD-14736| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| has been found in |FRAME: TAX-1892|, opening the possibility for the existence of a novel enzyme that produces |FRAME: CPD-18438| directly., The product of these enzymes, |FRAME: CPD-18438|, is a substrate for the enzymes encoded by two other paralogous genes in the cluster, |FRAME: G-44207| and |FRAME: G-44208|. These enezymes, which resemble hydroxykynureninase, were initially shown to have a substrate preference for |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| |CITS: [20304989]|, but were later shown to be active on the methylated form, producing |FRAME: CPD-403| |CITS: [20945860]|.

General Background, Nevadensin is a lipophilic methylated flavonoid found in sweet basil (|FRAME: TAX-39350|). Flavonoids are found throughout the plant kingdom where they play diverse and important physiological roles |CITS: [21880658]|. Many of these structurally diverse compounds also have an impact on human health and the enzymes involved in their production are attractive candidates for metabolic engineering |CITS: [21732240]|., To date, the end product of this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-15468|, has only been reported in a small number of |FRAME: TAX-91827| species, such as in the |FRAME: TAX-255818| and |FRAME: TAX-39173| genuses |CITS: [Suksamrarn03][11281133]|, but, it may be found in additional plant species in the future. Regiospecific O-methylations as well as the hydroxylations at positions 6 and 8 of the A ring of |FRAME: CPD-15468| are distinctive features of this compound and several related compounds that may contribute to their lipophilicity. Given the phylogenetic dispersion of these compounds efforts are underway to determine if they are synthesized in the same manner in diverse species |CITS: [23184958]|. , About This Pathway, Flavone metabolism in basil appears to occur in complex manner. |FRAME: CPD-15468 Nevadensin| is formed via |FRAME: CPD-15477|, which is formed from |FRAME: CPD-431| in multiple routes, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7325|. |FRAME: CPD-15477 Salvigenin| is 8-hydroxylated by a Rieske-type oxygenase (|FRAME: G-124265|) to |FRAME: CPD-15476| |CITS: [25139498]|., Next |FRAME: CPD-15476| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-15468| by O-methylation of position 8 of the A ring and O-demethylation at the 7 position of the same ring.The 7-O-demethylase involved in the production of |FRAME: CPD-15468| is a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase |CITS: [25378691]|. While a candidate for the gene encoding the methyltranferase has been identified, its activity was not verified experimentally because its substrates were not available at the time |CITS: [23747095]|.

Summary: The heme degradation pathway that is found in animals is based on the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18| |CITS: [4386763]|. This enzyme catayzes the opening of the tetrapyrrole macrocycle of |FRAME: Heme-b|, forming |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, |FRAME: FE+2|, and |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE|. The enzyme uses heme as both a substrate and a cofactor, and has been purified from many animals, including humans |CITS: [4390967][96115][438202][1929402][10467099]|. After the enzyme binds ferric-heme, one electron is donated by |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4|, converting the heme-iron to the ferrous state. Molecular oxygen then binds the reduced pentacoordinate heme to form a meta-stable oxy complex. A one electron reduction and protonation yields a ferric-hydroperoxo complex that self-hydroxylates at the α-meso carbon. The ferric |FRAME: CPD-19720| is then converted to biliverdin through multiple oxidoreductive steps and a |FRAME: CPD-19719| intermediate |CITS: [10467099][17534530]|., It should be noted that a very similar enzyme also occurs on some bacteria, although the electron donor for the bacterial enzyme is different |CITS: [9422739][11073924]|., In animals |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| is reduced to |FRAME: BILIRUBIN| by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.24|. This cytosolic enzyme was originally discovered in Guinea pig liver |CITS: [4378982]|, and has been characterized from several mammals, including rat and humans |CITS: [8424666][8631357]|. Two forms of biliverdin-IX α reductase and two forms of biliverdin-IX β reductase have been purified from human liver |CITS: [7929092]|., Bilirubin is an effective chain-breaking antioxidant in vitro |CITS: [3029864]|, although it has been questioned whether if fulfills this role in vivo |CITS: [8033927]|. Proposed roles for bilirubin in vivo include a scavenger of nitric oxide |CITS: [14637193]| and an endogenous modulator of neurotrophin redox signaling |CITS: [18338802]|. , Unconjugated bilirubin is extremely water insoluble. It is carried (mostly by albumin) to the liver, where it is converted to glucuronides, which are water soluble. The glucuronides are eventually excreted in bile. Glucuronated forms include two positional isomers of a monoglucuronoside (|FRAME: CPD-20932| and |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-GLUCURONOSIDE|) as well as |FRAME: BILIRUBIN-BISGLUCURONOSIDE| |CITS: [5145912][949313][7378044]|. Two glucuronosyltransferases, encoded by the UGT1A1 and |FRAME: HS11970| genes, have been associated with this process. Both catalyze the formation of both monoglucuronoside isomers as well as the bisglucuronoside., It should be noted that while most of the bilirubin in adult humans is the α form, it is the β form that predominates in fetal bile. Other enzymes are responsible for the degradation of the β form |CITS: [7929092][8799475]|.

Summary: The term |FRAME: CPD-5242 tunicamycin| refers to a mixture of related nucleoside antibiotics targeting bacterial teichoic acid and peptidoglycan biosynthesis at the steps of |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.13|, respectively. Tunicamycins cannot be used clinically since they are also acive against the eukaryotic enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.15|, which is involved in an early step of |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS "protein N-glycosylation"|. The compounds bind specifically to the active site of the enzymes, blocking their activity and terminating the biosynthesis of the polymers at the first commited step |CITS: [ 444447]|., The first tunicamycin compound was originally isolated in 1957 under the name mycospocidin |CITS: [13513523]| (it was shown to be a tunicamycin much later |CITS: [Tkacz78]|). A few years later more tunicamycin compounds were isolated from cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1079983|, this time under the name tunicamycin, and initially described as anti-viral agents, although they were subsequently shown to be also active against yeasts, fungi and Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5572750]|. Tunicamycins were later isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1901| |CITS: [468729]| and |FRAME: TAX-1969|, in which they accumulate to much higher concentrations. The process for tunicamycin preparation was patented 1980 with |FRAME: TAX-1079985| |CITS: [Hamill80]|., All tunicamycins contain |FRAME: URACIL|, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|, a unique 11-carbon 2-aminodialdose called |FRAME: CPD-19359|, and a fatty acid linked to the amino group of the tunicamine. The various members of the tunicamycin group, all of which appear to have antimicrobial activity, differ only in the structure of their fatty acyl chain |CITS: [Takatsuki77]|., Isotopic labeling experiments suggested that tunicamycin is produced from two molecules of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and one molecule of |FRAME: URIDINE| |CITS: [12093793]|., Three simultaneous independent genome mining studies of |FRAME: TAX-1901| and |FRAME: TAX-1969| have identified gene clusters that encodes tunicamycin biosynthesis. |CITS: [21153459][Wyszynski10][Karki11]|. When a minimal gene cluster was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-1969| and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1902|, the recombinant host produced tunicamycins, indicating that the minimal cluster contained all of the required genes |CITS: [Wyszynski10]|. Based on the predicted function of the genes in the cluster, both groups suggested rather similar pathways for tunicamycin biosynthesis., The initial steps of the pathway were later studied in more detail, revealing very unusual exo-glycal intermediates, which have not been described in biology previously |CITS: [22717438]|.

Summary: General Background, Six pathways are now recognized in bacteria, most algae, fungi and higher plants for the biosynthesis of lysine. They are divided into two groups - the diaminopimelate (DAP) pathways, and the |FRAME:CPD-468| pathways., In the pathways that belong to the DAP group, lysine is produced from aspartate (along with methionine, threonine and isoleucine). All of the DAP group pathways share the upper segments, which include the four steps required for conversion of L-aspartate to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|. They also share the last step, which is the conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (D,L-DAP, or meso-DAP) to lysine., However, these pathways differ in the routes leading from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|. The four variations include:, (I) the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|), which involves succinylated intermediates. In this route |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is coverted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in four enzymatic steps., (II) the acetylase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2941|), which involves acetylated intermediates. This route also involves four enzymatic steps for the conversion of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|., (III) the dehydrogenase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2942|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in a single enzymatic step. , (IV) the diaminopimelate-aminotransferase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5097|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in two steps., In addition to lysine, all of the pathways in this group also produce |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is an important metabolite on its own (for example, as a constituent of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan)., The two other pathways belong to the |FRAME: CPD-468| group. They are found in organisms that have no requirement for |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, as it is not a component of their cell walls. These pathways also share the first segments, leading to the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-468| (α-aminoadipate)., However, in yeast and fungi, as well as |FRAME: TAX-3038|, the pathway continues with the key enzyme |FRAME: YBR115C-MONOMER|, leading to the intermediate |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see |FRAME: LYSINE-AMINOAD-PWY|), while in prokaryotes the pathway continues in a path similar to bacterial arginine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., Most of the bacteria that have been investigated in detail appear to utilize only one of these pathways |CITS: [1906065]|. A few exceptions include |FRAME: TAX-44252|, in which variants (II) and (III) seem to coexist |CITS: [BARTLETT85]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, in which variant (I) and (III) coexist |CITS: [1906065]|., Lysine is one of the 10 essential amino acids that mammals are unable to synthesize, and must therefore acquire in their diets. , About This Pathway, Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1718|, Brevibacterium, lactofermentum and |FRAME:TAX-1421|, can convert tetrahydrodipicolinate to, meso-diaminopimelate in a single enzymatic step, catalyzed by the enzyme diaminopimelate dehydrogenase., In some organisms, such as B. sphaericus, this is the only lysine biosynthesis pathway |CITS: [White83]|, , while in others, such as C. glutamicum, it exists in parallel with alternative pathways., Even though the conversion of tetrahydrodipicolinate to meso-diaminopimelate, involves a single enzymatic step, the full reaction is composed of two steps. In the first step, which is presumably, spontaneous, tetrahydrodipicolinate loses a water molecule, and opens to its acyclic form,, L-α-amino-ε-keto-pimelate. The second step is the enzymatic conversion to, meso-DAP |CITS: [762012]|.

|FRAME: ITACONATE Itaconate| is an unsaturated acid with conjugated double bonds and two carboxyl groups. The acid was discovered in 1837 |CITS: [Baup37]|, and was named |FRAME: ITACONATE| as an anagram of |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE|, from which it was first derived by Crasso in 1840 |CITS: [Turner41]|. Because of its unique structure and characteristics, itaconate and its ester are useful materials for the bioindustry. It is used for the synthesis of fiber, resin, plastic, rubber, paints, surfactant, ion-exchange resins and lubricant |CITS: [17451943]|., |FRAME: ITACONATE Itaconate| inhibits |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.1|, the key enzyme of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate shunt"|, which is essential for bacterial growth under specific conditions |CITS: [17593]|. Its production by mammalian macrophages can inhibit the growth of pathogenic bacteria and is considered an immune defense |CITS: [23610393]|., The production of |FRAME: ITACONATE| by fungi was first observed in |FRAME: TAX-36638| in 1929 |CITS: [Kinoshita31]|, but was studied the most in the organism |FRAME: TAX-33178| |CITS: [16747058] [13438853][13438855][13911957][8227940]|, which is also used for the industrial production of |FRAME: ITACONATE| |CITS:[11548996][12146646][17451943][17697977]|., The pathway presented here has been elucidated by studies of whole cells of |FRAME: TAX-33178| |CITS: [7768868]|. The metabolites were identified by HPLC, by the incorporation of <sup>14</sup>C-labelled  compounds into itaconate, and by <sup>13</sup>C NMR. The experiments showed that itaconate was synthesized from the TCA cycle intermediates |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CIT| and |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE|., Following the removal of a water molecule from |FRAME: CIT| by |FRAME: MONOMER-13634| |CITS: [Winskill83]|, which occurs in the mitochondrion, |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE| moves to the cytosol, where it is converted to |FRAME: ITACONATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-13632|, an enzyme that catalyzes a decarboxylation accompanied by a 1,3-allylic rearrangement |CITS:[13438855][Jaklitsch91]|.

General Background, Many organisms including bacteria, fungi, metazoa, and plants can degrade glucose polymers derived from |FRAME: Starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6724|, |FRAME: PWY-842|, |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5941|). Some hyperthermophilic archaea have also been shown to produce |FRAME: Starch|-degrading enzymes, and pathways for the utilization of |FRAME: Starch| and its derivatives, such as |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|, |FRAME: Maltodextrins|, and |FRAME: MALTOSE| have been proposed. These hyperthermophilic archaea can utilize |FRAME: Starch| and its degradation products as primary carbon sources during anaerobic growth. Thermostable starch-degrading enzymes produced by hyperthermophpilic organisms are of industrial interest |CITS: [16513741] [11489857] [17921308] [11702074]|., The hyperthermophilic, sulfate-reducing archaeon |FRAME: ORG-6178| has been shown to degrade |FRAME: Starch| via a unique pathway involving cyclodextrin intermediates (see |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|) as described below in About This Pathway |CITS: [17921308] [11702074]|. Cyclodextrins (cyclomaltodextrins) are cyclic oligosaccharides composed of α-1,4-linked glucose units. Early literature referred to them as Schardinger dextrins. Cyclodextrins corresponding to 6-12+ glucose units have been characterized (in |CITS: [5758537]|) (see |FRAME: CPD-3782|, |FRAME: CPD-3781|, |FRAME: CPD-3783|). The physicochemical properties of cyclodextrins give them broad applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries (in |CITS: [11489857]|)., The hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-186497| was shown to degrade |FRAME: Starch| mainly via maltodextrins in a pathway involving an extracellular amylopullulanase, a transporter, an intracellular 4-α-glucanotransferase, and a maltodextrin phosphorylase. These enzymes produce |FRAME: GLC| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| that are converted to |FRAME: GLC-6-P| and degraded in pathway |FRAME: P341-PWY| (|CITS: [16513741]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6737|)., In the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-91619| evidence suggested a |FRAME: Starch| degradation pathway via formation of cyclodextrins from |FRAME: Starch| extracellularly by a |FRAME: MONOMER-16282|, transport of cyclodextrins into the cell, and their degradation by a |FRAME: MONOMER-16283| to the end products |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| (|CITS: [11489857]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6735|)., Among bacteria |FRAME:TAX-562| cannot utilize |FRAME: Starch|, but it can metabolize short, linear maltodextrins (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY|). However the enterobacterium |FRAME: TAX-290336| can utilize |FRAME: Starch| as a sole source of carbon and energy. Mutant analysis suggested that it metabolizes |FRAME: Starch| by two pathways. The first was a proposed maltose/maltodextrin pathway involving extracellular degradation of |FRAME: Starch| by pullulanase and the disproportionation activity of cyclodextrin glucanotransferase to form linear maltodextins. After transport into the cell they are degraded to |FRAME: GLC| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by the products of malP, malQ and malZ. The second was a proposed cyclodextrin pathway involving extracellular conversion of |FRAME: Starch| to cyclodextrins (see |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|) by cyclodextrin glucanotransferase, transport into the cell, linearization by |FRAME: MONOMER-16314| (CymH) |CITS: [8599539]|, and further catabolism as in the maltose/maltodextrin pathway |CITS: [8594196] [9573146]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-6178| is a sulfate-reducing, hyperthermophilic archaeon that was shown to utilize |FRAME: Starch| and |FRAME: SULFATE| as sources of carbon and energy. |FRAME: Starch Starch| was incompletely oxidized to |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| via a glycolysis pathway that was enzymatically similar to the |FRAME: P341-PWY| pathway shown in the pathway link. |FRAME: SULFATE Sulfate| was reduced to |FRAME: HS| (see pathway |FRAME: DISSULFRED-PWY|). The enzymes in this proposed pathway have been characterized as shown here. In contrast, it was noted that another strain, |FRAME: TAX-224325|, does not contain sugar utilization genes and is therefore unable to utilize sugars |CITS: [17921308]|., This pathway of |FRAME: Starch| degradation begins with the extracellular production of cyclodextrins (see above) from |FRAME: Starch| by the membrane-associated enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8244|. Cyclodextrins are proposed to be taken into the cell by an as yet uncharacterized transport system. Inside the cell they are hydrolyzed to |FRAME: Maltodextrins| (maltooligosaccharides) by |FRAME: MONOMER-16275|. |FRAME: GLC-1-P| is produced from |FRAME: Maltodextrins| (maltooligosaccharides) by |FRAME: CPLX-8245|. |FRAME: GLC-1-P| is converted by |FRAME: CPLX-8246| to |FRAME: ALPHA-GLC-6-P|. This compound can enter glycolysis |CITS: [17921308]|, possibly after spontaneous or enzymatic conversion to its epimer |FRAME: GLC-6-P|. Whether the α, β, or both α and β epimers are used depends upon the anomeric specificity of the glycolytic enzyme involved.

Papaverine is a benzylisoquinoline alkaloid that was first discovered in 1848. It is usually found a minor component in most of the opium poppy varieties. Papaverine has several medicinal activities such as antispasmodic |CITS: [6529614]| and vasodilatory. It has been used in clinic treatment of cerebral vasospasm |CITS: [15990041]|. Its biosynthetic route was initially proposed almost a century ago however is still controversial and under debate. Mainly there are two proposed routes, the N-demethylation pathway starting from (S)-reticuline as supported by a recent radio tracer study |CITS: [20494383]|, and the (S)-coclaurine-derived pathway, supported by comparative transcriptome evidence |CITS: [23738019]|. Only three enzymes of the proposed routes have been identified and characterized, namely 7OMT in the N-demethylation pathway, N7OMT in the (S)-coclaurine-derived pathway, and an oxidase catalyzes the last step shared by both routes.

Summary: The stilbene compound |FRAME: CPD-83| is a phytoalexin produced by a number of plants as a defense response compound to microbial pathogenic attacks. It has been studied for a range of pharmocological activities including reversing the ageing process and anticancer effects. The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-83| is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-84|. , This pathway describes the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-83|. The enzyme responsible for its degradation was cloned  from the pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-5270| |CITS: [21073977]|. This fungus is the causative agent of corn smut, and is a model organism for the elucidation of molecular mechanisms underlying fungal dimorphism |CITS: [18502157]|, |CITS: [17352901]| and the study of fungal-plant host interactions |CITS: [12535072]|. It produces a range of secondary metabolites to enable it to negotiate diverse environments and survive competition for accessing suitable plant hosts |CITS: [18585066]|. |FRAME: TAX-5270| produces the precursor molecules of retinal; β-carotene and tetraterpene pigment along with the members of the ubiquitous carotenoid cleavage enzymes |CITS: [19584000]|, |CITS: [21073977]|. , The carotenoid cleavage enzymes catalyze the cleavage of conjugated double bonds by introducing molecular oxygen |CITS: [18478524]|. These enzymes are known to help in the establishment of plant-fungal interaction such as arbuscular mycorrhiza |CITS: [18716794]|. Also, they help in degrading stilbene compounds like |FRAME: CPD-83| |CITS: [21073977]| as shown in this pathway.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD0-1198| is a sugar acid of the aldonic acid family |CITS: [422572]|. |FRAME: TAX-208964| is able to use |FRAME: CPD0-1198| as a carbon source. The |FRAME: CPD0-1198| catabolic pathway initiated by L-lyxonate dehydratase (LyxD) has been elucidated |CITS: [24831290]|., About This Pathway, Enzymes with the activity of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.176| (LyxD) were identified from |FRAME: TAX-391735| and |FRAME: TAX-398580|. Site-directed mutagenesis studies of conserved residues H316 and R179 showed that both residues were essential for activity. An enzyme with 70% sequence identity and conserved active site residues was identified in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-208964| and was further characterized |CITS: [24831290]|. , |FRAME: TAX-208964| was shown to grow on minimal medium containing |FRAME: CPD0-1198|, but not on |FRAME: CPD-16836| or |FRAME: CPD0-1197| suggesting a pathway for |FRAME: CPD0-1198| utilization. There was also no growth on |FRAME: L-Lyxose|, |FRAME: D-Gulose|, or |FRAME: L-mannose|, suggesting that the common oxidation pathway (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5517|) was not utilized. The pathway shown here was suggested by the proximity in the genome of the genes encoding the three pathway enzymes and by the up-regulation of these enzymes when the organism was grown on |FRAME: CPD0-1198| as carbon source, as determined by transcriptomic analysis |CITS: [24831290]|., Orthologous genes were later identifed in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-381666| and all three activities were confirmed using recombinant enzymes |CITS: [31917558]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-837| is an etiological agent of chronic periodontitis. Like most Gram-negative bacteria it displays lipopolysaccharides (LPS) on the cell surface. However, unlike many other orgnaisms |FRAME: TAX-837| has two different O-polysaccharides - a conventional O-polysaccharide (named O-LPS), which is described here, and an anionic O-polysaccharide (named A-LPS) consisting of a repeating unit with a yeast mannan-like structure formed by α-(1→6) and α(1→2) mannosyltransferases |CITS: [18263730]|. Several studies have suggested that A-LPS may contain additional structural sugars such as |FRAME: D-Galactose| and |FRAME: CPD-14608| in addition to mannose residues |CITS: [23717416][24852504]|. Both O-polysaccharides are covalently attached to the lipid A-core., The structure of the O-LPS repeat unit was described in 2001 |CITS: [11532006]|. It's biosynthesis is believed to begin with the formation of |FRAME: CPD-191| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.6|, encoded by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01470| gene. |FRAME: TAX-837| has a second paralog of that enzyme, encoded by wbaP, which appears to start the biosynthesis of A-LPS |CITS: [23509024]|., The three glycosyl transferases necessary for the synthesis of the O-LPS repeat unit are encoded by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01445|, |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01440|, and |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01405| genes |CITS: [28972686]|. Following the formation of the repeat unit it is flipped across the inner membrane to the periplasmic side by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS08880|-encoded flippase. In the periplam the units are assembled into a longer polysaccharide by an |FRAME: CPLX-9616| encoded by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01430| gene, and eventually transferred to the lipid A core by an O antigen ligase |CITS: [19525343]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: GERANIOL "Geraniol"| is a linear monoterpene that occurs in many terpene-containing essential oils derived from plants. It has a flowery, rose-like scent and is found in large quantities in palmrosa, geranium and rose oils. Citrol is a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-7978| and |FRAME: GERANIOL|. Citral is a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-9762| (cis-citral) and |FRAME: GERANIAL| (trans-citral) and is widely used in the flavor, fragrance and other industries. |FRAME: CPD-7969| (methylheptenone) has been described as having a green citrus-like odor and a bittersweet taste (in |CITS: [11778886]| and in |CITS: [12444979]|)., The biotransformation of |FRAME: GERANIOL| to |FRAME: CPD-7969| (methylheptenone) by fungi and bacteria has been previously documented and pathways have been proposed, but they were not substantiated biochemically. However more recent biochemical studies have elucidated the pathway for this biotransformation in spore extracts of |FRAME: ORG-6174|. This work was based on enzymatic studies as well as substrate degradation and product formation studies. This novel pathway involves citrol dehydrogenase and a novel citral lyase |CITS: [11778886] [12444979]|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: GERANIOL "Geraniol"| is converted to |FRAME: GERANIAL| by |FRAME: NAD|-dependent citrol (geraniol and nerol) dehydrogenase, which also converts |FRAME: CPD-7978| to |FRAME: CPD-9762|. |FRAME: GERANIAL| (trans-citral) can undergo non-enzyme catalyzed cis-trans isomerization to produce |FRAME: CPD-9762| (cis-citral) in the presence of amino acids |CITS: [11087492]|. Likewise, |FRAME: CPD-9762| can also undergo this isomerization to |FRAME: GERANIAL|. The mixture of |FRAME: GERANIAL| and |FRAME: CPD-9762| (known as citral) formed is deacetylated by citral lyase to form |FRAME: CPD-7969| (methylheptenone) and |FRAME: ACETALD|. Further metabolism of |FRAME: CPD-7969| was not reported in this paper, although a pseudomonad has been shown to degrade it |CITS: [612543]|., |FRAME: GERANIAL "Geranial"| can also be transformed to |FRAME: CPD-7618| (geranic acid) by |FRAME: NAD|-dependent citral dehydrogenase activity. Whole spores could catalyze the reverse reaction converting |FRAME: CPD-7618| to citral (|FRAME: GERANIAL| and |FRAME: CPD-9762|). Over time, all reactants were converted to |FRAME: CPD-7969| (methylheptenone) and |FRAME: ACETALD| by citral lyase activity. Citral lyase catalyzes a novel enzymatic activity involving the deacetylation of an α,β-unsaturated aldehyde |CITS: [11778886]|.

Summary: General Background, The main CO2 fixation enzyme in plants, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39 "EC 4.1.1.39, ribulose-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase"| (RuBisCO), has both carboxylase (photosynthetic CO2 fixation) and oxygenase (photorespiration) activities. The carboxylase activity is favored at high CO2/O2 ratio, whereas the oxygenase activity predominates at a decreased CO2/O2 ratio., At the time when RuBisCO first evolved, atmospheric CO2 concentration was very high and thus the enzyme's carboxylase activity was favored. However, later in evolution, atmospheric O2 concentration began to rise and RuBisCO's oxygenase activity increased at the expense of the carboxylase activity. In temperate climates and under moderate light levels, when the stomata are fully open, diffusion from the atmosphere is fully sufficient to ensure an ample supply of CO2 and C3 photosynthesis is rather efficient. However, in hot climates and under high light levels, the plants need to close their stomata to avoid water loss, restricting the ability of the CO2 to diffuse. Under these conditions the CO2 levels can go down to the point where photorespiration becomes a serious problem, reducing photosynthesis by more than 40%. The C4 system, which is found only in plants growing in conditions that require closure of the stomata, has evolved to address this problem., C4 plants have evolved to respond to lowered CO2 levels. The C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle starts with carbon fixation in the mesophyll cells by a combination of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.1 "EC 4.2.1.1, carbonic anhydrase"|, which converts the gasous CO2 to soluble |FRAME: HCO3|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31|, which incorporates the latter, forming the C4 acid |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|. Oxaloacetate or a derivative thereof (|FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|) is then transported from the mesophyll cells to bundle sheath cells. Once inside the bundle sheath cells, CO2 is released from the C4 acids, generating a micro-environment with a much higher concentration of CO2, suitable for an efficient carboxylation by RuBisCO., Three variations of the C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle have been described in plants, namely the |FRAME: PWY-241 "NADP-ME"| (NADP-malic enzyme), |FRAME: PWY-7115 "NAD-ME"| (NAD-malic enzyme), or |FRAME: PWY-7117 PEPCK| (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) types. The NADP-ME variant does not involve L-aspartate and utilizes an NADP-dependent malic enzyme to releases CO2 from |FRAME: MAL|. The NAD-ME variant does involve L-aspartate and utilizes an NAD-dependent malic enzyme. The PEPCK variant contains an additional route for CO2 release by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49|, which usually operates to supplement the NADP-ME variant., However, some research suggests that different C4 decarboxylation pathways may cooccur in plants that were previously considered to belong to exclusively one C4 photosynthetic type |CITS:[24609651]|. For instance, |FRAME: TAX-4577| has been shown to use both |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| for the generation of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[Chapman81]|. In addition, it has been demonstrated that maize leaves require the activity of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1| to maintain an efficient flow-rate. Moreover, the |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49 "phosphoenol carboxykinase"| (PEPCK), considered the hallmark of the PEPCK pathway, is also active in maize and shown to support |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE|-driven photosynthesis |CITS:[22186372]|. Similar results have been reported from the NADP-ME type plant |FRAME: TAX-4224|, which also utilizes both |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| equally and demonstrates aspartate aminotransferase activity |CITS:[Meister96]|. In general, current discussion of the C4 photosynthetic pathway types moves in a direction favoring the existence of only two subtypes, i.e. NADP-ME and NAD-ME, both of which may contain a supplementary PEPCK cycle |CITS:[24609651]|., About This Pathway, C4 photosynthesis basically represents a |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| concentrating mechanism (CCM). The system evolved independently more than 60 times, indicating a strong evolutionary drive to optimize photosynthetic |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation as an tool to keep pace with an ever-changing environment |CITS:[21631531]|. This MetaCyc pathway describes the NAD-ME (NAD-malic enzyme) variant. Note that the pathway spans two cell types, mesophyll and bundle sheath cells. , The roles and sub-cellular locations of carbonic anhydrases (CA) in plants differ and are metabolically integrated in a rather complex manner regardless of the seemingly simple reaction they catalyze, i.e. the reversible hydration of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:HCO3| |CITS:[Badger03] [Moroney01]|. In C3 plants CA's are ambivalent enzymes and contribute to increased |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| concentration in micro-compartments creating a more efficient environment for the carbon fixating role of RuBisCO in the chloroplast, and also have non-photosynthetic functions as in lipid biosynthesis and operating as antioxidant |CITS:[24146374]|. However, in C4 plants β-carbonic anhydrases operating in the cytoplasm of mesophyll cells are considered essential for the operation of the pathway by providing the PEP-carboxylase substrate |FRAME:HCO3| for |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation into |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| |CITS:[16666063]|. Corresponding β-carbonic anhydrases characterized in Zea mays, i.e. CA2 |CITS:[20933433] [Burnell97]| and in Flaveria bidentis |CITS:[17496111]|, i.e. CA3 are part of a small CA family in this plants where only one member is directly involved in the first reaction of C4 photosynthesis |CITS:[23414801] [Burnell90]| (see |FRAME:PWY-241| and |FRAME:PWY-7117|). However, it appears that even those β-carbonic anhydrases have only a limited role in C4 photosynthesis under current climate conditions and are more essential when C4 plants are stressed by high temperature and drought |CITS:[24706552]|. There is currently no report of a characterized β-carbonic anhydrase from a NAD-ME type plant., The initial CO2 fixation occurs in the mesophyll cells, forming |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|e. Aspartate enters the bundle sheath cells and is converted to |FRAME: MAL|. CO2 is released from malate by a NAD-dependent malic enzyme. Pyruvate is converted to alanine and alanine returns to the mesophyll cells, where it is converted to pyruvate and subsequently replenishes phosphoenolpyruvate. Importantly, the Asp/Ala shuttle between the two cell types maintains the ammonia balance between mesophyll and bundle sheath cells.

Summary: General Background, Thiols play a major role in the detoxification of stress-inducing factors., |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE "Glutathione"| (GSH) is the major thiol in eukaryotic organisms, Gram negative bacteria and the majority of Gram positive bacteria, but it is not universal. In some organisms other thiols have taken its role, including |FRAME: CoM|, |FRAME: TRYPANOTHIONE|, ergothioneine, and the ovothiols. , The major thiol found in |FRAME: TAX-2037| is |FRAME: CPD1G-2| (MSH) |CITS: [8076641]|. This thiol, which is unique to these organisms, has the structure (1-D-myo-inosityl-2(N-acetyl-L-cysteinyl)amino-2-deoxy-α-D-glucopyranoside. Although it, contains the cysteine nucleus as the active moiety, it has the molecular framework of a disaccharide containing, myo-inositol (Ins) and glucosamine (GlcN) |CITS: [15730267]|., Like GSH, MSH has several functions: it functions as a reserve of cysteine, it is used for the detoxification of alkylating agents, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and antibiotics, and it acts as a thiol buffer, maintaining the highly reducing environment within the cell |CITS: [18772286]|., About This Pathway, A pathway for the biosynthesis of mycothiol has been proposed based on the isolation of various intermediates in wild type as well as mutants of |FRAME: TAX-1772| |CITS: [9271081][9804803]|, and was further supported (with one exception) by the identification and isolation of several of the enzymes catalyzing the reactions., The pathway consists of five steps, starting with |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| (the original proposal suggested that the pathway starts with |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, but this assumption was found incorrect |CITS: [18390549]|)., In the first step, |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| and |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| are, joined to create |FRAME: CPD-11975| (or GlcNAc-Ins-P) in a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: G18NG-9958|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-7952|. The phosphate is then removed by a phosphatase whose identity is still not known, resulting in |FRAME: CPD1G-1|., In the next step an acetyl group is removed by the |FRAME: G185E-5339|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-7953| , forming the deacetylated disaccharide |FRAME: CPD1G-0|. It is believed that this enzyme is important is regulating the pathway |CITS: [11092856]|. The |FRAME: G-7321|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-5721| then adds a cycteine residue, forming |FRAME: CPD1G-120| |CITS: [12033919]|., In the last reaction, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-4968| -encoded |FRAME: G185E-4968-MONOMER|, an acetyl group is added to the α-amino group of the cysteine, forming |FRAME: CPD1G-2| |CITS: [12375100]|., The genes encoding the different enzymes that are involved are scattered throughout the genome, and do not form, an operon., The bacteria that synthesize |FRAME: CPD1G-2| use it as a protectant against electrophilic compounds as well as for detoxification of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species |CITS: [15730267]|. More information about the detoxification mechanism of |FRAME: CPD1G-2| is discussed in the pathways |FRAME: PWY1G-1| and |FRAME: PWY1G-170|., When mycothiol is oxidized by a reactive species, it forms a disulfide called |FRAME: MYCOTHIONE|. The oxidized form is recycled back to mycothiol by a dedicated reductase (see the pathway |FRAME: PWY1G-126|).

Summary: The [Fe]-hydrogenase from methanogenic archaea (|FRAME: EC-1.12.98.2|), one of three types of hydrogenases, reversibly catalyzes the cleavage of H2 and the subsequent transfer of the hydride ion to methenyltetrahydromethanopterin |CITS: [Shima10]|. For the activation/production of H2, the enzyme contains an iron guanylylpyridinol (FeGP) cofactor, which is composed of guanylylpyridinol and an iron center with two CO ligands. The pyridinol ring is ligated to the iron center through its nitrogen atom and an acyl carbon atom - the only natural acyl-organometallic iron compound that has been described (as of 2025)|. The iron atom is also ligated to an L-cysteine residue of the enzyme and to an "unknown" ligand |CITS: [14686932][15127449][15506791][16028957][16887798][18653896]|., When exposed to UV-A/blue light, the cofactor decomposes to guanylylpyridinol with a 6-carboxymethyl group, Fe2+ and two molecules of CO |CITS: [28294213]|. Stable-isotope labeling experiments indicated that the origins of both CO groups are CO2 molecules |CITS: [22260087]|., Seven genes, named hcg for hmd co-occurring genes (the hmd gene encodes the hydrogenase), were reported to be required for the cofactor biosynthesis. In addition, an Hmd paralog known as HmdII was suggested to function as a scaffold for biosynthesis of the cofactor, although it was reported to not be required for biosynthesis of the cofactor |CITS: [20235826][23551135]|., The first intermediate in the biosynthetic pathway that has been identified is |FRAME: CPD-27516|, which is formed by the radical SAM enzyme HcgA from unidentified precursors |CITS: [36264001]|. This compound is then 3-methylated by the HcgC methyltransferase |CITS: [27391308]|. HcgB is a guanylyltransferase that catalyzes the guanylation of the dimethylated compound, forming |FRAME: CPD-27517| |CITS: [24249552][28294213]|. The carboxy group of this compound is activated by binding an adenosine monophosphate (AMP) moiety in a reaction catalyzed by HcgE |CITS: [25882909]|. The guanylylpyridinol is then transferred to an L-cysteine residue of the HcgF protein |CITS: [25882909]|. The final reactions that form the cofactor have not been characterized as of 2025, although the HcgD protein was proposed to act as an iron chaperone, and a second radical SAM enzyme, HcgG, has been proposed as the enzyme responsible for the reaction |CITS: [36264001]|.

Summary: About 20% of the |FRAME: MET| pool is used as a building block of proteins. The rest is converted to, |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), the major methyl donor in the cell., When SAM donates its methyl group, it is converted to |FRAME: ADENOSYL-HOMO-CYS|. This molecule can be, recycled back to SAM via the S-adenosyl-L-methionine cycle, also known as the activated methyl cycle (AMC)., There are two main variations of this pathway, one found mostly in prokaryotes, while the other is found predominantly, but not exclusively, in eukaryotes. The main difference between the variants is the processing of |FRAME: ADENOSYL-HOMO-CYS| (SAH), the immediate product of the methylation reactions., In the first pathway (described in |FRAME: PWY-6151|) SAH is first hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-564| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.9|, followed by conversion to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.21|. In the second pathway, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-5041|, SAH is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| in a single step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.13.2.1|., The cycle continues with the methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| to |FRAME: MET| using a methyl group from a methylated folate. In some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-9606|, this reaction is catalyzed by a, |FRAME: HOMOCYSMETB12-MONOMER| (EC 2.1.1.13). In other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|,, the reaction is catalyzed by a |FRAME: G18NG-10711-MONOMER| (EC 2.1.1.14). Yet some organisms,, such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, have both enzymes, as described in the pathway, |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|. In |FRAME: TAX-562| the reaction catalyzed by the B12-dependent enzyme is more, than 100-fold faster than the reaction catalyzed by the B12-independent isoenzyme |CITS: [15215334]|., Finally, the cycle is completed with the regeneration of SAM by |FRAME: CPLX-7754|.

Summary: In both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, sugar and amino sugar residues are converted to sugar nucleotides prior to their incorporation into structural polysaccharides via UDP-sugar transferases. UDP-N-acetyl-D-galactosamine (UDP-GalNAc) is the amino sugar nucleotide donor of N-acetyl-D-galactosamine (GalNAc) residues for the biosynthesis of cell surface structures., In some bacteria, some fungi (but not yeast), and metazoa, UDP-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) can be converted to UDP-N-acetyl-D-galactosamine by UDP-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine 4-epimerase. N-Acetyl-D-galactosamine is a component of several different kinds of cell surface structures and glycosylated proteins, as described below. Reviewed in |CITS: [16408321]|., In |FRAME:TAX-1423| the gne gene product was shown to have UDP-GlcNAc 4-epimerase activity, catalyzing the formation of |FRAME: CPD-14795|, a substrate for the formation of the cell wall anionic polymer (strain 168 minor teichoic acid) |CITS: [14597172]|. In |FRAME:TAX-1308| GalNAc is found in the exopolydaccharide as a result of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 4-epimerase activity |CITS: [11525994]|. In |FRAME:TAX-630| serotype O:8 and |FRAME:TAX-562| serotype O86:B7, one of the sugars of the lipopolysaccharide O-antigen is GalNAc, produced by UDP-N-acetylgalactosamine 4-epimerase, the product of gene gne |CITS: [12107146] [17105195]|. In |FRAME:TAX-287| serotype O:6 and |FRAME:TAX-703| serotype O17, the UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 4-epimerase product of genes wbpP and wbgU respectively, is involved in lipopolysaccharide O-antigen biosynthesis |CITS: [15752069] [12484781]|. In |FRAME:TAX-197| GalNAc residues are present in the three major cell surface carbohydrates of this , organism. Their biosynthesis involves the UDP-GalNAc 4-epimerase product of gene gne which also has UDP-GlcNAc activity |CITS: [15509570]|., In eukaryotes, nucleotide sugars are biosynthesized in the cytosol and translocated into the Golgi apparatus by nucleotide sugar transporters. In the lumen of the Golgi, nucleotide sugars are sugar donors for protein glycosylation (in |CITS: [17060606]|). In glycoproteins of animals and higher plants, mucin-type O-glycosylation is a widespread post-translational modification. The carbohydrate chains are initiated by O-linked GalNAc (via serine and threonine residues) and are structurally more complex than N-linked carbohydrate chains (in |CITS: [11308013]|). The carbohydrate chains of mucin-type O-glycans are involved in cell differentiation and transformation (in |CITS: [16650853]|).

|FRAME: PWY-6745 "Phytochelatins"|, (Glu-Cys)n-Gly where n=2-11, are the principle heavy metal-detoxifying compounds in the plant kingdom. Isophytochelatins are isoforms of phytochelatins in which the terminal amino acid consists of serine, glutamate, glutamine or beta-alanine. Isophytochelatins occur in only those plants that contain glutathione isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-211 "homoglutathione"| and hydroxymethylglutathione. Legumes are unique in that they are able to synthesize homoglutathione and thus homophytochelatins, (Glu-Cys)n-betaAla where n=2-11.  Soybean produces exclusively homophytochelatins whereas Lotus is able to synthesize both phytochelatins and homophytochelatins. , Homophytochelatins are synthesized from glutathione and homoglutathione. In both the initial reaction and the following polymerization process, glutathione serves as the donor molecule of γ-glutamylcysteine unit. Homoglutathione or homophytochelatins are the acceptor molecules. Previsouly identified phytochelatin synthase from Lotus was shown to also have homophytochelatin synthase activity |CITS: [16489135]|.  Interestingly, although the Arabidopsis plants accumulate only phytochelatins not homophytochelatins, the Arabidopsis phytochelatin synthase was shown to have homophytochelatin synthase activity in vitro |CITS: [16489135]|.

Names: coenzyme A biosynthesis III (archaea) // CoA biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| (CoA) is a ubiquitous compound found in archaea, bacteria, plants, and animals. It is a common acyl carrier in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and is required for a multitude of reactions for both biosynthetic and degradative pathways, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids |CITS: [16415216]|., The biosynthesis of CoA occurs via different pathways in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes, and thus enzymes specific for the bacterial pathway are targets for antibacterial drug discovery., About This Pathway, The first compound in this pathway, |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE|, is produced by the archaeal-specific enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.36|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6654|. Only microorganisms and plants (including some eukaryotic microbes, such as |FRAME: TAX-4932|) can synthesize |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| de novo - animals must obtain it in their diet, giving it the name vitamin B5., The first step in this pathway is the ligation of |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| with |FRAME: CYS|. Prokaryotic organisms utilize a CTP dependent enzyme - |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.5| (eukaryotes utilize the ATP-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.51|). The pathway continues by decarboxylation to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.36|. Studies with several archaeal species, including |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [16371361]|, and |FRAME: TAX-311400| |CITS: [31337720]|, have shown that in these organisms the two steps are catalyzed by a single, bifunctional enzyme, as is the case in most bacteria., The next step consists of the transfer of an adenyly group from ATP to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|, forming |FRAME: DEPHOSPHO-COA|. The enzyme has been studied from |FRAME: TAX-29292| and was found to resemble the eukaryotic enzyme. However, although only distantly related, secondary structure prediction indicated that the archaeal and eukaryotic enzymes belong to the same nucleotidyltransferase superfamily of the bacterial enzyme |CITS: [12756245]|,, The ultimate reaction is a phosphorylation producing |FRAME: CO-A|. In bacteria and eukarya this reaction is catalyzed by the ATP-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.24|. However, a study of the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-311400| has shown that the archaeal enzyme is GTP-dependent |CITS: [31337720]|.

The discovery of |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| (NO) as a crucial signal in plants has enhanced and redirected our understanding of many processes in plant physiology. There has been a surge in investigative studies to understand the biosynthesis of NO in both plants and animals. Plant NO biosynthesis appears to be more complex than animal NO synthesis, as it includes nitrite and |FRAME: ARG|-dependent mechanisms. In animals, NO synthases are the main sources of |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|, these complex enzymes oxidize |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| and |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| |CITS: [16356941]|. The plant NOS isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3702| has no sequence similarity with animal NOS, but its role in NO production has been demonstrated. The Arabidopsis mutant AtNOS1 encodes a distinct nitric oxide synthase that regulates growth and hormonal signaling in plants |CITS: [14526079 ]|. , Evidence has accumulated that the NOS in plants are targeted to plastids and are required for ribosome functions, and also indicates it to be a GTPase |CITS: [19168714]|. In other studies, it was demonstrated that the disruption of NOS dependent NO synthesis is associated with salt tolerance in plants like |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [17351048]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-4081|, NOS generated NO acts downstream of auxin and is involved in regulating Fe-deficiency-induced responses as shown in this study |CITS: [21511908 ]|. However, the exact relationship between NO and IAA is not yet clear.

General Background, |FRAME: SO3 Sulfite| plays a key role in oxidative sulfur metabolism. It is derived from multiple sources: First, sulfite is the main intermediate in the oxidation of sulfur compounds to |FRAME: SULFATE| |CITS: [11557133]|., In purple sulfur bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1049|, the oxidation of |FRAME: HS| and |FRAME:S2O3| results in formation of intracellular sulfur globules, which are oxidized to sulfite by the Dsr system (see |FRAME: PWY-6676|)., A second source for sulfite is the desulfonation of organic compounds by enzymes like |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15| (Xsc) (see |FRAME: PWY-1281|)., A third source of sulfite is extracellular sulfite retrieved from the environment. Free sulfite in the periplasm (which most likely exists as bisulfite) is bound to the |FRAME: SoxY-Protein "SoxYZ"| protein complex in the form of |FRAME: SoxY-Systeine-Sulfinate|. The binding acts to shield components of the periplasm from chemical reactions with sulfite, and may also be required for delivering the sulfite to a transporter that exports it into the cytoplasm for oxidation |CITS: [24030319]|., , Some microorganisms (such as |FRAME: TAX-60136| species) can use sulfite as their sole electron source |CITS: [Sorokin95][10319472 ]|. , Enzymes that catalyze the direct oxidation of sulfite to sulfate are molybdenum hydroxylases, and belong to the sulfite oxidase family, which includes both sulfite-oxidizing enzymes and plant assimilatory nitrate reductases (such as the |FRAME: CPLX-7196| of |FRAME: ORG-5993|). The best characterized members of this family are sulfite oxidases, from avian and mammalian sources. However, these enzymes differ from the bacterial enzymes in that they can use oxygen as an electron acceptor (see |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.1|)., Some sulfite oxidizing enzymes are located in the periplasm. The best characterized enzyme from this group is |FRAME: EC-1.8.2.1| (SOR) from |FRAME: TAX-921|, which contains a molybdopyranopterin cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-5276|). Another well-characterized periplasmic enzyme is the |FRAME:CPLX-882| (such as that from |FRAME: TAX-82367|). It has been shown that this system can oxidize sulfite independently from the presence of the |FRAME:CPLX-7150| component (a molybdohemoprotein), but it is not clear whether the Sox system functions in vivo as a sulfite-oxidizing enzyme |CITS:[10940005][Lu84][11425697]|)., Other enzyme systems that oxidize sulfite are located in the cytoplasm. Two general mechanisms for sulfite oxidation in the cytoplasm have been described: a direct oxidation by a membrane-bound iron-sulfur molybdoprotein (|FRAME: EC-1.8.5.6|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7457|), and an indirect, AMP-dependent oxidation via the intermediate |FRAME:APS| (APS) (see |FRAME:PWY-5279| and |FRAME:PWY-5278|) |CITS: [11557133]|. The direct oxidation route is much more prevalent, but the two mechanisms are present simultaneously in many organisms, including β and γ proteobacteria (|FRAME: TAX-931|, |FRAME: TAX-1049|, |FRAME: TAX-36861|, |FRAME: TAX-1021|), green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1091|), Gram-positive bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-28034|) and even archaea (|FRAME: TAX-2283|) |CITS: [11557133]|., While many organisms possess only the direct mechanism, the only examples for organisms that possess only the non-direct mechanism are found in the bacterial endosymbionts of invertebrates |CITS: [Nelson95]|., About This Pathway, The enzyme responsible for the direct oxidation of sulfite to sulfate in the cytoplasm is a membrane-bound, cytoplasmically oriented iron-sulfur molybdoprotein encoded by three genes - |FRAME: G-17994|, |FRAME: G-17995| and |FRAME: G-17996|. The SoeABC (named for Sulfite-Oxidizing Enzyme) complex was initially reported to be responsible for sulfite oxidation in the organosulfonate-degrading chemotrophic α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-89184| |CITS: [Lehmann12]|, and later studied in |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [24030319]|., The complex consists of an |FRAME: EG11947|/|FRAME: G-9658|-like membrane anchor (SoeC) and two cytoplasmic subunits: an iron-sulfur protein (SoeB) and a molybdoprotein with an N-terminal [Fe4S4] iron-sulfur cluster binding site (SoeA). Even though SoeA is a molybdoenzyme, it belongs to a completely different family than the the periplasmic Sor-type sulfite dehydrogenases (such as the |FRAME: CPLX-7139| from |FRAME: TAX-921|)., In |FRAME: TAX-1049| this enzyme plays a major role in the cytoplasmic oxidation of sulfite, with |FRAME: CPLX-8193| (which catalyzes the indirect oxidation) playing a secondary role |CITS: [24030319]|., It should be noted that entrance of externally supplied sulfite into the cytoplasm is dependent on the |FRAME: CPLX-8197| complex. It is suggested that binding of sulfite to the complex in the periplasm may be necessary for its transport into the cytoplasm |CITS: [24030319]|.

Summary: General Background, Starch and glycogen, megadalton-sized glucose polymers, are the major reservoir of readily available, energy and carbon compounds in most living organisms, ranging from archaea, eubacteria and yeasts,, up to higher eukaryotes including plants and animals |CITS: [20192737][21185717]|. Only parasites seem to lack enzymes, for the metabolism of these compounds |CITS: [12175798]|., The structure of |FRAME: Starch| in higher plants differs from that of its counterpart |FRAME: Glycogens| in animals and bacteria. |FRAME: Starch Starch| is a complex α-glucan that can be very difficult to adequately describe. |FRAME: Starch Starch| contains at least two different major sub-classes of α-glucans: |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses amylose| and |FRAME: CPD-7043|. |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses Amylose| contains up to several thousand α-glucosyl units linked almost exclusively in α(1->4) linkage with very few branches of α(1->6) linkage., |FRAME: CPD-7043 Amylopectin|, on the other hand is a much more branched, molecule with many α(1->6) linkages and contains up to several million glucosyl residues. At least twelve different types of starch with different branching patterns and chain lengths have been reported |CITS: [ROBYT13]|. To further complicate the situation, |FRAME: Starch starch| can appears in different crystalline and soluble forms which are difficult to define and depict using standard chemical structures., It has been reported that cyanobacteria synthesize glycogen while red algae produce floridean-starch with structure that is intermediate between starch and glycogen, and that green algae accumulate amylopectin-like polysaccharides. However, some cyanobacteria (classified into group 5 by Honda et al |CITS: [10229577]| have distinct α-polyglucans (which were designated as semi-amylopectin), making them a transition point between glycogen and starch biosynthesis |CITS: [Wing-Ming94][15695453]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Starch Starch| is synthesized in plastids, including chloroplasts in photosynthetic tissues and amyloplasts in, non-photosynthetic tissues such as seeds, roots, and tubers. Starch synthesized in, chloroplasts of photosynthetic tissues is degraded to maltose and glucose during the dark period (see |FRAME: PWY-6724|)., These sugars are exported to the cytosol and used in |FRAME: PWY-7238 sucrose synthesis|., Sucrose can be readily transported to non-photosynthetic tissues to support plant growth or for starch synthesis in amyloplasts., The |FRAME: Starch| biosynthesis pathway depicted here includes both chloroplast and amyloplast pathways., The starting point for the chloroplast pathway is fructose-6-phosphate, a product of photosynthetic carbon, fixation. The starting point for amyloplast pathway is glucose-1-phosphate, a product of sucrose, degradation. Studies from potato, pea, and maize indicate that glucose-6-phosphate, in addition to, glucose-1-phosphate, can be imported into the amyloplast and can serve as the starting point for, starch biosynthesis |CITS: [10929100]|., The role of plastidial α-phosphorylase enzymes (|FRAME: RXN-1826 2.4.1.1)| in starch biosynthesis remain controversial and may differ between species |CITS: [23393426][BALL09]|. For example, mutations in the |FRAME: AT3G29320| gene of Arabidopsis have no effect on starch biosynthesis |CITS: 15173560|., Following the initial production of |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE|, |FRAME:Starch| biosynthesis appears to involve reactions catalyzed by at least three classes of enzymes, i.e. starch synthases, starch branching enzymes and, starch debranching enzymes |CITS: [BALL09]|. However, the exact steps involved and the order in which they are required for the formation of different types of starch may differ between species and even between different types of cells within the same species |CITS: [15743447]|. , There is also evidence that |FRAME: TAX-3055| might involve an additional enzyme in |FRAME:PWY-622|, namely, a disproportionating enzyme, |FRAME: GIO2-442|. However the corresponding enzyme, |FRAME: AT5G64860-MONOMER DPE1| in Arabidopsis has been shown to play a part in |FRAME: PWY-6427 starch degradation| instead |CITS: [BALL09][23393426]|., Developing a better understanding of starch biosynthesis and its regulation is an active area of research.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Furanocoumarins furanocoumarins| are one of the main groups of coumarins. Their synthesis starts with thecoupling of |FRAME: CPD-4211| to the coumarin |FRAME: CPD-8186|, leading to formation of a skeleton that contains a furan ring fused with coumarin., Furanocoumarins are minor constituents in plants belonging to |FRAME: TAX-4037|, |FRAME: TAX-3803|, |FRAME: TAX-3487|, and |FRAME: TAX-23513| families. They are natural toxins that protect the plants from insects, herbivory, and microbes. Production is triggered by several types of stresses, including fungal infections |CITS: [6682038][8062387]| and stresses such as wounding |CITS: [Zangerl90]| or acid fog |CITS: [Dercks90]| . , Furanocoumarins are also toxic to humans. Direct contact with the sap from some plants containing furanocoumarins (such as |FRAME: TAX-380077|) causes inflammation, burns and irritating sensitivity to sunlight |CITS: [ 33174568]|. Some naturally occurring methoxy derivatives of furanocoumarins have been applied clinically, coupled with exposure to sunlight, to cure dermatological diseases for more than 2000 years. Linear furanocoumarins such as |FRAME: CPD-13042| and |FRAME: 5-METHOXYFURANOCOUMARIN| are used in the clinic in combination with UV radiation to treat several diseases, such as mycosis fungoides, vitiligo and psoriasis. Several clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate furanocoumarins potential to treat additional conditions, such as graft versus host disease, Crohn's disease, and several cancer types |CITS: [33174568]|., A well documented toxicity of furanocoumarins is related to their inhibition of cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes |CITS: [14769198]|. An example is the interaction of furanocoumarins produced by grapefruit with |FRAME: HS08544-MONOMER| (CYP3A4), an enzyme that is involved in the bioinactivation of about 50% of all drugs currently used, resulting in enhanced systemic drug concentration through impaired drug metabolism, and leading to recommendation to avoid grapefruit while taking drugs |CITS: [23184849]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of all furanocoumarin starts with the coumarin |FRAME: CPD-8186|. The pathway starts with |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.139|, which attaches |FRAME: CPD-4211|. The prenyl group can be attached to C-6 of |FRAME: CPD-8186|, leading to linear furanocoumarins as described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5365|, or it could be attached to C-8, leading to formation of the angular fucocoumarins as described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-8476|. The enzymes catalyzing the prenylation were shown to have different specificities - some prefer the C-6 position, while others prefer the C-8 position |CITS: [24354545][Munkata16]|., Following the prenyltransferase step, the products are first cyclized, then converted to |FRAME: PHYTOALEXIN-CMPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9815|, respectively, by two cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases. Further modifications by P-450 monooxygenases and SAM-dependent methyltransferase lead to production of several compounds, ending at |FRAME: CPD-15049| and |FRAME: CPD-9834|, respectively |CITS: [33174568]|., While the pathways are rather well understood, many of the involved enzymes have not been identified as of 2023.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Triterpenes Triterpenoids| are an important class of compounds found in prokaryotes and eukaryotes that participate in diverse biological processes. Triterpenoids and their derivatives can act as lipid membrane components (e.g. |FRAME: Sterols|, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|, |FRAME: CPD-4162|, etc.), hormones (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-697|), and defense compounds, especially in plants (e.g. |FRAME: PWY-5756 saponins|) |CITS: [19575586][22105807][CHAPPELL95]|. In addition, numerous triterpenoids, or their downstream products have medical applications |CITS: [2991440][4828716][SZAKIEL05]|., Triterpenoids originate from |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| (oxidosqualene). This compound can be converted into an amazing number of structurally diverse backbones, including over 100 identified in plants alone |CITS: [20610397][14751299]|. These transformations are typically carried out by members of two large families of enzymes collectively know as oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) or squalene-hopene cyclases (SHCs). Research to understand structure-function relationships based on the sequences of these proteins and their product(s) is ongoing |CITS:[14751299][15525992][12081472]|. , About This Pathway, The different tritepenoids that are produced by OSCs can be further sub-divided based on several criteria, including the number of rings present. The reactions present in this metabolic cluster portray the biosynthesis of a subset of the triterpenes, namely, the pentacyclic triterpenes that have five rings. Some of the OSCs that catalyze the formation of these compounds appear to produce only one product, such as |FRAME: MONOMER-17974 TTS1| from tomato |CITS: [21059824]|, however, others are multifunctional, such as |FRAME: MONOMER-17973 GLS| from |FRAME: TAX-23013| |CITS:[20610397]|. Different numbers of carbocation rearrangements are required to form the different triterpene structures. |FRAME: CPD-13047 Friedelin| formation likely requires at least ten rearrangements, the highest number observed to date |CITS: [20610397]|.

General Background, |FRAME: HIS| can be catabolized by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms in two principal routes., The main difference between these two routes is the first step, which is performed by either, a |FRAME: CPLX-6924| (as in this pathway) or a histidine transaminase (|FRAME: HISTDEG-PWY| and, |FRAME: PWY-5031|)., At least three different flavors of |FRAME: CPLX-6925|-based pathways have been found so far., All proceed in a similar manner up to the intermediate |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE|., Three steps, catalyzed by distinct enzymes, lead to this intermediate., In the first step |FRAME: HIS| is split into |FRAME: UROCANATE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| by, a |FRAME: CPLX-6925| |CITS: [14367318][12980948]|; Next |FRAME: UROCANATE|, is converted to |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-981|, |CITS: [13587518][13821933]|; and finally, |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| is converted to, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| by |FRAME: HUTIBACSU-MONOMER| |CITS: [13587518], [13739526]|., In all three flavors |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is further degraded to |FRAME: GLT|., However, the mechanism of |FRAME: GLT| production is different in the three pathways. , In several Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-90371|,, |FRAME: TAX-573|, |FRAME: TAX-548| and |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE|, is split into |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: FORMAMIDE| |CITS: [14367318]| ; the latter compound, does not appear to be metabolized further (|FRAME: HISDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [13416179]|. , In fluorescent Pseudomonads, including |FRAME: TAX-303|, |FRAME: TAX-294| and |FRAME: TAX-287|,, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is first hydrolyzed to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and , |FRAME: CPD-600|, which in turn is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: FORMATE|, (|FRAME: PWY-5028|) |CITS: [13211593][4290562]|; the |FRAME: FORMATE| can serve the cell as, a source of single carbon compounds |CITS: [13563517]|. , Finally, in the livers of mammals |FRAME: GLT| is generated by the transfer of the formimino group to, |FRAME: THF| (|FRAME: PWY-5030|). |FRAME: THF| is metabolized further, transferring, the formyl moiety to the pool of single carbon compounds |CITS: [13672973]|., About This Pathway, Urocanic acid was first isolated in 1874 by the chemist M. Jaffe from the urine of a dog, hence the name, (latin: urina = urine, and |FRAME:TAX-9611| = dog) |CITS: [7944380]|., Unfortunately the dog escaped before Jaffe was able identify the structure., The identity and structure of the substance was eventually revealed in 1912 by Hunter, who was the first, to suggest that it is an intermediate in the catabolism of |FRAME: HIS| |CITS: [Hunter12]|., Edlbacher identified the locus of histidine degradation as the liver of various animals, and named the, enzyme that degrades |FRAME: HIS| to |FRAME: GLT| "histidase" |CITS: [Edlbacher26][Edlbacher30]|., In 1930 Kauffmann and Mislowitzer defined histidase more correctly, as the enzyme that converts, |FRAME: HIS| to |FRAME: UROCANATE| |CITS: [Kauffmann30]|., After a lengthy debate concerning the nature of the third intermediate, it was finally, shown conclusively that it is |FRAME:N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE | by Borek and Waelsch, |CITS: [13117923]|., In Pseudomonads, unlike other bacterial species, an additional intermediate was observed., This intermediate was identified by Tabor and Mehler as |FRAME: CPD-600|, demonstrating that in these, organisms |FRAME: HIS| catabolism includes one additional step |CITS: [13211593]|., Finally, Revel and Magasanik identified the last intermediate as, |FRAME:4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| |CITS: [13587518]|, a suggestion which, was confirmed with the isolation of the substance |CITS: [13804907]|, establishing the complete pathway., The additional step in the degradation of |FRAME: HIS| in Pseudomonads results in the formation, of |FRAME: FORMATE| instead of |FRAME: FORMAMIDE|. Apparently, this difference enables the, bacteria to use this single carbon for biosynthesis of purines. Bacteria which produce, |FRAME: FORMAMIDE| are not able to do so |CITS: [13563517]|., As in other bacteria, the pathway is repressed by carbon sources such as |FRAME: GLC| and, |FRAME: SUC|, and induced by the presence of |FRAME:UROCANATE|.,

General Background, In prokaryotes and eukaryotes, heme (protoheme IX, protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation. Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as protoheme IX, different derivatives of protoheme IX can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including the way it is bound to the protein, such as heme o, heme a, heme c, and heme d., In various organisms, important branch points within the heme biosynthetic pathway lead to the biosynthesis of other important compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P381-PWY|), coenzyme F430 (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5196|), siroheme (see EcoCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5194|), heme D (see EcoCyc reaction |FRAME: RXN-8073|), and bacteriochlorophyll (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|)., In Escherichia coli, heme biosynthesis begins with L-glutamate and proceeds through 5-amino-levulinate (the universal tetrapyrrole precursor) to uroporphyrinogen III as shown in the |FRAME: PWY-5188| pathway. Uroporphyrinogen III is converted to protoheme IX in the pathway shown here. Subsequent reactions that produce heme o and heme d are shown in the reaction links. In E. coli, hemes c, d, and o function as the prosthetic groups for c-type cytochromes, cytochrome bd, and cytochrome bo, respectively. The c-type cytochromes are synthesized only anaerobically in the presence of nitrogenous electron acceptors. Cytochrome bd and cytochrome bo are O2-reducing terminal oxidase complexes. , Although regulation of heme biosynthesis is not well studied in E. coli, evidence suggests that the cellular level of free protoheme IX controls the rate of heme synthesis at the level of formation of glutamate-1-semialdehyde by glutamyl-tRNA reductase encoded by hemA (see EcoCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5188|)., Review: Beale, S.I. (2007) "Biosynthesis of Hemes" EcoSal 3.6.3.11 |CITS: [ecosal]|, Reviews: |CITS: [13680202][12177321][16093570][19721088][20506125]|, About This Pathway, The pathway shown here from uroporphyrinogen III to protoheme IX is a segment of the overall heme biosynthetic pathway. The pathway links at the beginning and end of this pathway show the preceding and succeeding steps. This pathway describes the aerobic route for protoheme IX biosynthesis. It involves the enzyme coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (HemF), which requires molecular oxygen for the conversion of coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX., In this pathway the four acetate groups of uroporphyrinogen III are sequentially decarboxylated, and the methyl groups from these four acetates remain in coproporphyrinogen III. Two propionate groups at positions 3 and 8 of coproporphyrinogen III are oxidatively decarboxylated to vinyl groups by the O2-requiring HemF, producing protoporphyrinogen IX |CITS: [12975365]|. In the facultatively aerobic E. coli and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium, an O2-independent enzyme, coproporphyrinogen dehydrogenase (HemN) can function under anaerobic conditions. HemN contains an O2-sensitive iron-sulfur cluster |CITS: [14633981]| (see pathway |FRAME: HEMESYN2-PWY|)., In the next step, six electrons are removed from protoporphyrinogen IX by a membrane-associated oxidase (HemG), forming protoporphyrin IX. In E. coli under aerobic conditions, this enzyme uses ubiquinone as electron acceptor coupled to cytochrome—ubiquinol oxidases with oxygen as the final electron acceptor, while under anaerobic conditions, the enzyme receives the electrons from menaquinone, and oxidation is coupled to the reduction of nitrate or fumarate |CITS: [20484676]|. The final step forming heme (protoheme IX) is catalyzed by ferrochelatase, which inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX. , Review: Beale, S.I. (2007) "Biosynthesis of Hemes" EcoSal 3.6.3.11 |CITS: [ecosal]|

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "Protocatechuate"| is one of the key intermediate metabolites in the microbial degradation of various aromatic compounds, including phthalates, hydroxybenzoates, and lignin-derived aromatic compounds such as |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|., The key step in these degradation pathways, the fission of the protocatechuate aromatic ring, can be catalyzed by one of the three distinct dioxygenases - |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, |FRAME: CPLX-2721| and |FRAME: CPLX-7915|., The fission products, and thus the degradation pathways, depend on the type of dioxygenase employed. The three pathways are described in |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6336|, respectively., About This Pathway, This pathway has been reported initially in some Bacilli |CITS: [163224][931947]|, and eventually studied in more detail in the thermophile |FRAME: TAX-649508|, which was isolated from a 50 °C hot spring |CITS: [453834]|., The key enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7915|, has been purified several times from |FRAME: TAX-649508| cells grown on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| and characterized |CITS: [453834][2280722][8392511]|. The rapid disappearance of the immediate ring fission product |FRAME: CPD-11842| in cell extracts and the accumulation of |FRAME: HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD| indicated a very rapid enzymatic decarboxylation of the former. This and other observations lead to the prediction of the pathway as presented here |CITS: [453834]|., A gene cluster encoding all of the enzymes involved in this pathway (along with the enzyme for conversion of |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|) was identified and characterized |CITS: [19717587]|. The genes were cloned into |FRAME:TAX-562| individually and their function was confirmed. In addition, introduction of the full cluster into |FRAME:TAX-562| confer the ability to grow on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| as the sole carbon source |CITS: [19717587]|.
