Summary: Please note: This pathway does not represent a single organism. Rather, it is a superpathway assembled , from pathways found in several different organisms. Its purpose is to provide an overview of the diversity of ways , that organisms can biosynthesize β-lactam antibiotics. , Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common , biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are , classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: penams (e.g. penicillins), ceph-3-ems (e.g. , cephalosporins, cephamycins), clavams (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), carbapenems (e.g. thienamycins), and monolactams , (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by , both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while the remaining three classes of beta-lactams are produced by bacteria. , Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|. The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem , and clavam antibiotics differ from this classic β-lactam pathway (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5737| , and |FRAME: PWY-5679|). The pathway for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially , elucidated and the order of some known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A , biosynthesis have been purified and characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., Penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins are produced , by different organisms from branches of the common β-lactam pathway shown here. The pathway branches at , isopenicillin N to form penicillins and branches again at deacetylcephalosporin to form cephalosporins and , cephamycins. The antibacterial mechanism of action of β-lactam antibiotics involves inhibition of the , transpeptidation reaction during bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which leads to cell lysis. This reaction is , catalyzed by class A and class B penecillin binding proteins. It is specifically inhibited by penicillin and , other β-lactam antibiotics via formation of a covalent complex with the active serine of the transpeptidation , domain of penicillin binding proteins. This prevents crosslinking and weakens the peptidoglycan polymer , (in |CITS: [12867450]|). See pathways |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5265|. Bacterial , resistance to β-lactam antibiotics can involve alterations in penicillin binding proteins, reduced antibiotic , permeation across the membrane, or the production of β-lactamase enzymes (in |CITS: [12195735]|). See , enzymes |FRAME: EG10040-MONOMER|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13427| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13428|.

|FRAME: CPD-19877| is a four-carbon acid sugar that can be used by some bacteria as the sole carbon source., The pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-19877| was found by a bioinformatic analysis of genes clustered with a D-threonate-binding protein (SBP), which is a part of a TRAP (tripartite ATP-independent permease) transporter for the compound |CITS: [25540822]|., Following import into the cell, |FRAME: CPD-19877| is phosphorylated to form |FRAME: ERYTHRONATE-4P| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.220|. The enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55076| gene, is one of the first members of a large family of enzymes, known as DUF (domain of unknown function) 1537, to which a function has been assigned |CITS: [27402745]|., Following phosphorylation, the compound is dehygrogenated at position 3 by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.409|. This dehydrogenase, with has some similarity to |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.262|, catalyzes a dehydrogenation, generating an unstable product that undergoes a decarboxylation to yield the central metabolite |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS: [27402745]|.

|FRAME: CREPENYNATE "Crepenynate"| (crepenynic acid) is an unusual fatty acid containing a triple acetylenic bond. It is found in high concentration (70%) incorporated into triacylglycerol in |FRAME: TAX-72610| seed oil. Crepenynic acid can be converted by alkali isomerization to |FRAME: CPD-17615| and |FRAME: CPD-14381|, which are valuable in the production of high quality coatings and lubricants |CITS: [9572738]|., |FRAME: CREPENYNATE "Crepenynate"| production is not limited to plants, as it has also been reported from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-75102| (Pacific golden chanterelle) |CITS: [20606235]|., An enzyme responsible for converting |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (incorporated into triacylglycrol) to |FRAME: CREPENYNATE| has been described from mirosomal preparations of |FRAME: TAX-72610| |CITS: [Banas97]|., The enzyme was later shown to be a member of the desaturases family. These enzymes are known to utilize |FRAME: Cytochromes-b5| as the electron donor, and require molecular oxygen for the desaturation activity |CITS: [9572738][17329262]|.

Sesquiterpenes are a large family of C15 isoprenoids, found in bacteria, fungi, insects and plants. They are derived from , farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) or nerolidyl diphosphate by the action of enzymes called sesquiterpene synthases. The synthesis , of sesquiterpenes from FPP is localized in the cytosol/endoplasmic reticulum boundary. E-bF occurs in a number of plants , and is known to play a role in chemical communication. The well studied farnesene in aphids acts as a pheromones and , deters predators. The biosynthesis of EbF in Mentha presents the possibility of engineering the EbS gene into other plants. , The production of aphid deflecting farnesene products would provide the much needed defence against aphid infestation of , plants |CITS: [16083926]|., The cis-calamenene sesquiterpenoids are found in the foliage of Cupressus bakeri as natural products. They are also isolated , from Madagascan shrub Tarenna madagascariensis (Rubiaceae) |CITS: [17365697]|.,

Summary: General Background, The transfer of one-carbon units is essential in several pathways of cellular metabolism. In many of these processes, one-carbon transfers are mediated by the coenzyme |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| (THF). Modified derivatives of THF supply the activated one-carbon units required for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Purines purines|, |FRAME: TMP thymidylate|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: HIS|, |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|,, and formylmethionyl-|FRAME: Initiation-tRNAmet tRNAfmet|., Various catabolic reactions generate specific one-carbon derivatives of THF, which are then interconverted between different oxidation states. The enzymes involved are |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.3|, |FRAME:EC-3.5.4.9|, and |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.5|. In many eukaryotes (plants excluded) these three activities are catalyzed by a single trifunctional enzyme known as the |FRAME: CPLX-6934 "C1-THF synthase"|., In the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| it has been shown that two forms of this enzyme exist - a cytosolic enzyme, and a mitochondrial enzyme |CITS: [2836393]|., About this pathway in methylotrophs, Methylotrophic bacteria produce very large amounts of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which serves as a central intermediate in biosynthesis. It has been suggested that the formaldehyde concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph would rise to 100mM in less than 1 minute if formaldehyde consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by unrelated or distantly related genes. In a pathway of major importance in methylotrophs, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| is converted to |FRAME: FORMATE| by enzymes that utilize the "archaea-like" cofactor |FRAME: THMPT| (H4MPT) (see |FRAME: PWY-1723|). The formate is then directed to the |FRAME:PWY-1622 "serine cycle"| for biosynthesis of metabolic building blocks., This pathway is utilized in methylotrophs for the assimilation of the |FRAME: FORMATE| into |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate"|, which is fed to the |FRAME:PWY-1622 "serine cycle"| |CITS: [14645277]|., Note that the |FRAME: THF-GLU-N "tetrahydrofolate"|-based pathway shown here is a major biosynthetic pathway, while the |FRAME: THMPT| pathway is used mostly for the generation of reducing power and ATP.

While |FRAME:HYDANTOIN-5-PROPIONATE| is not metabilized in mammals any further,, and is excreted in the urine, some bacteria are able to utilize it as the sole source of carbon for growth,, by hydrolyzing it first to |FRAME: N-CARBAMYL-L-GLUTAMATE|, and then to |FRAME: GLT| |CITS: [14085380]|., Two additional metabolites that are formed from |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| were shown, to be formed non-enzymatically. These are |FRAME: FORMYL-ISOGLUTAMINE|, which is further, converted to |FRAME: ISOGLUTAMINE|, and |FRAME: 4-OXOGLUTARAMATE|, which is formed, from |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| non enzymatically along with |FRAME:AMMONIA|, and |FRAME:FORMATE|. |FRAME: 4-OXOGLUTARAMATE| is degraded non-enzymatically into, |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS: [13804906][13960897]|.

Summary: Aerobic bacteria that can utilize |FRAME: ACETYLENE| for growth have been reported several times in the literature, although not often |CITS: [Birch32][37235][DeBont80][Tam83][Germon88][9084145]|. Certain anaerobic bacteria are also able to utilize |FRAME: ACETYLENE| for growth |CITS: [16345714]|. Several strains of strictly anaerobic bacteria that can use  |FRAME: ACETYLENE| as a sole carbon and energy source were purified from marine and freshwater sediments, and were described as a new species in the genus |FRAME:TAX-18| |CITS: [Schink1985]|., In all cases where the pathway has been investigated, |FRAME: ACETALD| was shown to be an intermediate, and |FRAME:ACET| a product |CITS: [DeBont80]|. |FRAME: TAX-29542| converts |FRAME: ACETYLENE| to |FRAME: ACETALD| by a unique tungsten-containing enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-941|. Exposure of this enzyme to oxygen results in conversion of its [4Fe-4S] cluster to a truncated [3Fe-4S] cluster and loss of activity |CITS: [7592321][10447686]|. Other acetylene hydratase enzymes from aerobic organisms have been shown to be molybdenum enzymes that do not cross-react with antibodies raised against the |FRAME: TAX-29542| enzyme, suggesting that acetylene hydratases are a biochemically heterogenous group of enzymes |CITS: [9084145]|., |FRAME: ACETALD Acetaldehyde| is only an intermediate in the pathway, and is subsequently converted to other compounds. In all cases that have been studied |FRAME:ACET| is formed. In the case of |FRAME: TAX-29542|, |FRAME: ACETALD| is also converted to |FRAME:ETOH| |CITS: [Schink1985]|. Though the hydration of acetylene to acetaldehyde is highly exergonic, studies on cell yield in this organism showed that only the free energy of the |FRAME: MONOMER-13297| reaction (0.5 mol ATP per mol acetylene) is used for growth |CITS: [Schink1985]|., Other substrates that are utilized by |FRAME: TAX-29542| include |FRAME: ACETOIN|, |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME: CHOLINE|, |FRAME: DL-12-Propanediol| and |FRAME:GLYCEROL| |CITS: [Schink1985]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-16801 "3,5,6-Trichloro-2-pyridinol"| (TCP) is the main degradation product of some herbicides and insecticides such as |FRAME: CPD-8963|, and is a widespread pollutant |CITS: [24422434][24833556]|. TCP can be degraded by several genera of bacteria |CITS: [23850940][23131657][20457514][19297093 ][19082866][XUIBB08][12057943][16535719][16143458]| and fungi |CITS: [23553803][23073111][23056611][17609859]| but in most cases the genes involved have not been characterized. However, |FRAME: TAX-657395| was shown to degrade |FRAME: CPD-16801| with high efficiency and two gene clusters tcpRXA and dhpRIJK involved in its degradation has been cloned and characterized |CITS: 24056464|., About This Pathway, In the tcpRXA gene cluster TcpA is a |FRAME: FADH2|-dependent monooxygenase that is closely related to the |FRAME: REUT_A1585-MONOMER| from |FRAME: TAX-264198| (see |FRAME: REUT_A1585-MONOMER|). TcpR is a LysR type transcriptional regulator that is activated by TCP. TcpX is is a flavin reductase that can deliver protons from |FRAME: NADH| to |FRAME: FAD| to produce |FRAME: FADH2| |CITS: 24056464|. , Expression of the tcpRXA gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in the ability of this organism to transform |FRAME: CPD-16801| to |FRAME: CPD-16803|. However, expression of tcpA alone in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in no |FRAME: CPD-16803| production, indicating TcpX is essential for this activity |CITS: 24056464|., Mutants deficient in the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-16803| were also obtained and the dhpRIJK gene cluster was cloned. Genes dhpI and dhpJ were expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|. The product of dhpJ was shown to be a 3,6-dihydroxypyridine-2,5-dione hydrolase that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-16803| to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-16804|, which is further degraded by the 5-amino-2,4,5-trioxopentanoic acid hydrolase DhpI to unidentified products, and the remaining reactions in the pathway were not determined., The product of dhpR was found to be closely related in sequence to the AraC family of transcriptional regulators, and that of dhpK to the MFS family of transporters |CITS: 24056464|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-Galactose| is a rare hexose present in plant and animal glycans |CITS: [9403992][1672824][23802881]|. Members of the |FRAME: TAX-816| found in the human gut microbiome are known to encode a large number of glycoside hydrolases and polysaccharide lyases which can degrade poorly digestible plant polysaccharides. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-435590| is prevalent in the human gut and a cluster of genes putatively involved in carbohydrate degradation has been identified in this organism. Using bioinformatic and functional analyses, three new enzymes encoded by genes |FRAME: G-34623|, |FRAME: G-34624| and |FRAME: G-34625| were identified, cloned and shown to catalyze the reactions of a novel |FRAME: L-Galactose| catabolic pathway |CITS: [24963813]|. In addition to several gut commensals, bioinformatics analysis suggested the presence of this pathway in the free-living organisms |FRAME: TAX-185294| and |FRAME: TAX-294710| |CITS: [24963813]| (see the species list above)., About This Pathway, A novel metabolic pathway for the conversion of |FRAME: L-Galactose| to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| has been demonstrated in the human gut bacterium |FRAME: TAX-435590|. In the first reaction, |FRAME: L-Galactopyranose| (which was shown by the authors to be the predominant form in solution) is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-17157| by the product of gene |FRAME: G-34623|. This lactone can spontaneously convert to the more stable |FRAME: CPD-330| (see |FRAME: RXN-15925|). Both lactones can be hydrolyzed by the gene |FRAME: G-34624|-encoded lactonase to the acid |FRAME: CPD0-1083|. However, NMR spectroscopy data showed that the product of gene |FRAME: G-34624| preferentially hydrolyzes |FRAME: CPD-17157| 300 times faster than |FRAME: CPD-330|, making |FRAME: CPD-17157| the physiological substrate |CITS: [24963813]|., As shown in the link to pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1306|, |FRAME: CPD0-1083| is then oxidized to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| by the product of gene |FRAME: G-34625|. |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| is further degraded as shown in the link to pathway |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|, and in the subsequent link to the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY| |CITS: [24963813]|.

Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., |FRAME: MANNITOL| is the most abundant polyol in nature, and is found in bacteria, fungi, algae, lichens and vascular plants., Many higher plants are known to contain mannitol. In several plant species (including |FRAME:TAX-4045| (celery), Ligustrum vulgare L. (privet), Fraxinus Americana L. (white ash), and Syringa vulgaris L. (lilac)mannitol is a major photoassimilate that is translocated through the phloem and stored in various sink tissues. Mannitol is thought to serve as a C storage compound or for storage of reducing power due to its capacity to be oxidized to its respective aldose or ketose sugar in a process that generates NADH |CITS:[1416989][loescher87][stacey74]|, thus giving a higher net ATP yield than the catabolism of an equal amount of sucrose |CITS:[pharr95]|., In vascular plants, mannitol is oxidized directly to mannose by the catalytic activity of NAD-dependent mannitol dehydrogenase (MTD; to date, the best characterized enzyme of the pathway |CITS:[11725947]|), a 1-oxidoreductase. This enzyme differs from microbial mannitol dehydrogenases (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.67|), which are 2-oxidoreductases converting mannitol or mannitol-1-phosphate to fructose or fructose-6-phosphate, respectively. MTD catalyzes the first committed step of translocated mannitol to the central metabolism.

Summary: General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on C1 compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on, |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-45353|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 "Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| |CITS: [12595136]|., In these organisms |FRAME:METOH| is oxidized to |FRAME:FORMALDEHYDE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7392| (AOD) in a reaction that produces |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5506|). To avoid damage to the cell by these very active compounds, this reaction occurs in peroxisomes, where |FRAME: ENZRXN-14009| decomposes the hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen |CITS: [17023065]|., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branchpoint, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (this pathway), or a dissimilatory pathway, which provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|) |CITS: [17023065]|., About This Pathway, Methylotrophs usually assimilate carbon by converting three C1 molecules into a single C3 compound via a cyclic pathway, similar to the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY| used in photosynthesis. In prokaryotes, two such pathways are known, including the ribulose monophosphate cycle (|FRAME: PWY-1861|) and the serine pathway (|FRAME:PWY-1622|). In methylotrophic yeast only one such pathway exists, the |FRAME:P185-PWY| |CITS: [Vandijkens78]|., Three molecules of formaldehyde, generated in the peroxisome by |FRAME:CPLX-7392|, are processed by this pathway into a single molecule of |FRAME:GAP|, which is shuttled into the core biosynthetic pathways., The key step of this pathway is the transfer of a glycoaldehyde group from |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, forming |FRAME:DIHYDROXYACETONE| and |FRAME:GAP|. This reaction is catalyzed by, |FRAME:CPLX-7394| (DHAS), another peroxisomal enzyme |CITS: [2987872]|. DHAS). The products of this reaction leave the peroxisome and are rearranged in the cytoplasmic in a pathway that involves many of the enzymes of the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY|, in a way that regenerates |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| and, for every three cycles, generates one net molecule of |FRAME:GAP| that is directed towards biosynthesis |CITS:[vanDijkens78][Anthony82]|., Since the diagram does not represent this pathway with clarity, more information is provided here:, For every molecule of |FRAME:GAP| that is incorporated into biomass, three molecules of |FRAME:FORMALDEHYDE| are fixed, generating three molecules of |FRAME:DIHYDROXYACETONE|, and consuming three molecules of |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| (X5P). Two of the |FRAME:DIHYDROXYACETONE| molecules are condensed with two molecules of |FRAME: GAP| to produce two molecules of |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE|, while the third, one is converted to |FRAME: GAP|, |FRAME:DPG| and finally |FRAME:G3P|, and routed to biosynthesis., Each of the three molecules of X5P that are utilized is regenerated in a different route. First, the two molecules of |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| mention above are dephosphorylated into two molecules of |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| by the enzyme EC 3.1.3.11. One molecule of X5P is regenerated directly from |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| by EC 2.2.1.3, in a reaction that also generates a molecule of |FRAME:ERYTHROSE-4P|., The second X5P molecule is generated from the other |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| molecule in a different route, consuming the |FRAME:ERYTHROSE-4P| and generating |FRAME:D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| (catalyzed by EC 2.2.1.2), which is then converted to X5P by EC 2.2.1.1, in a reaction that also generates |FRAME:RIBOSE-5P|., Finally, the |FRAME:RIBOSE-5P| molecule is converted to |FRAME:RIBULOSE-5P| by EC 5.3.1.6, which is then converted to the third X5P molecule by EC 5.1.3.1 |CITS: [Anthony82]|.

Carotenoid cleavage dioxygenases (CCD) catalyze the oxidative cleavage of C-C double-bonds in carotenoids forming apocarotenoids |CITS: [16616608], [20670614]|. Apocarotenoids is a diverse class of compounds that play important physiological roles. For example, vitamin A (retinol and retinal) is required for vision in animals, abscisic acid is required for seed development in plants, and many small volatile aroma compounds such as beta-ionone give the characteristic of fruits and flowers. , Some CCDs recognize specific carotenoid substrates, whereas others act upon a broad range of substrates. Some cleave specific double bonds while others can cleave double bonds at different positions. So far the best characterized plant CCDs include CCD1, CCD2, CCD4, CCD7, CCD8, ZCD and LCD., CCD1 and CCD4 have been isolated from a number of plant species |CITS: [11316814], [19264332], [15584954], [19120446], [18611853]|. They generally show promiscuity in choice of substrates. For example, the rice CCD1, like the Arabidopsis CCD1, cleaves both linear and cyclic carotenoids at the 9,10 and 9',10' positions. , In addition, the rice CCD1 also cleaves 5',6' and 7',8' double bonds in combination with cleavage at the 9,10 double bond |CITS: [19120446]|. The Arabidopsis CCD7 catalyzes a specific asymmetric 9,10-cleavage of beta-carotene to produce beta-ionone (C13) and 10'-apo-beta-carotenal (C27) |CITS: [15342640]|. 10'-apo-beta-carotenal is further cleaved by CCD8 |CITS: [15342640]|. ZCD from Crocus sativus is a zeaxanthin-specific CCD that cleaves 7,8(7',8') double bonds |CITS: [12509521]|. LCD from Bixa orellana is a lycopene-specific CCD that recognizes 5,6(5',6') double bonds |CITS: [12829782]|., Besides CCDs, Nine-cis-epoxy-carotenoid dioxygenases (NCEDs) is another enzyme class that catalyzes the oxidative cleavage of carotenoids. They specifically cleave the 11,12(11',12') double bond of 9-cis-violaxanthin or 9-cis-neoxanthin which leads to the |FRAME: PWY-695 "synthesis of abscisic acid"| in plants |CITS: [11532178]|.

Summary: In both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, sugar and amino sugar residues are converted to sugar nucleotides prior to their incorporation into structural polysaccharides via UDP-sugar transferases. |FRAME: CPD-14795| (UDP-GalNAc) is the amino sugar nucleotide donor of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine| (GalNAc) residues for the biosynthesis of cell surface structures., Most organisms, from bacteria to eukarya, synthesize |FRAME: CPD-14795| from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.7| (see |FRAME: PWY-5512|). While the acido- and thermophilic crenarchaeon |FRAME: TAX-111955| can synthesize |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| via the |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY| pathway, it does not have |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.7|., Instead, the organism was found to produce |FRAME: CPD-14795| via a novel pathway that utilizes several enzyme activities that have not been observed previously |CITS: [29507091]|., Many of the enzymes that participate in |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| biosynthesis are promiscious in |FRAME: TAX-111955| and are able to act on the comparable galactosamine substrate., Like the |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY| pathway, this pathway starts with |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|, which is converted to |FRAME: D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| by the actions of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.9| and |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.16|. However, instead of being converted to |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE-1P|, |FRAME: D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| is epimerized into |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| by a novel enzyme, |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.42|., The rest of the pathway is catalyzed by enzymes that also participate in |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| biosynthesis. |FRAME: MONOMER-20593 "Phosphohexosamine mutase"| (which also catalyzes the activity of |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.10|) catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: CPD0-1646|. This is followed by the action of the |FRAME: MONOMER-20592|, which catalyzes both acetylation and activation by UTP, thus forming the final product |FRAME: CPD-14795|. As the enzyme upstream, this enzyme also catalyzes the homologous reactions with glucosamine-based substrates during |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| biosynthesis., The key enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.42|, has been found only in the |FRAME: TAX-28889 Crenarchaeota| |CITS: [29507091]|.

Summary: Oryzalexine such as |FRAME:CPD-7093|, |FRAME:CPD-16613|, |FRAME:CPD-16614| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-16612| and |FRAME:CPD-16611| (see |FRAME:PWY-7478|) are inducible phytoalexins occurring in rice (Oryza sativa) which originate from |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| formed via the MEP-pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5121|) |CITS:[17634747]|. They belong to the labdane-related diterpenoids |CITS:[20890488]| which have become an well researched subject because of the genetic clusters in rice which coordinate their biosyntheses |CITS:[20921179]| and are still considered a rare occurrence in the plant kingdom |CITS:[19662496]|. |FRAME:CPD-7093 Oryzalexin A|, |FRAME:CPD-16613| and |FRAME:CPD-16614| has been isolated from rice and shown to inhibit spore germination and germ tube growth of the blast fungus Pyricularia oryzae (now renamed to Magnaporthe grisea) |CITS:[Akatsuka85]|., Rice is one of the most important food plant in the world and the principal food crop in the lower-income countries |CITS:[Seck12]| which is mirrored in the extensive scientific literature, the sequencing of the genome of its two cultivars indica |CITS:[11935017]| and japonica |CITS:[11935018]| and the existence of curated databases involved in the annotation of genes, enzymes and pathways |CITS:[16381966]|., The |FRAME:PWY-7489| pathway has been the subject of a PhD thesis |CITS:[Wu 2012]| which has not yet been published in peer reviewed journals and remains to be substantiated by the scientific community. However, the results are in line with published data |CITS:[17872948] [12005050]| and have been obtained by methods and materials used in other publications of the author (e.g. |CITS:[21985968] [23795884]|). The pathway describes the identification, purification, recombinant expression and biochemical characterization of oryzalexin synthases involved in the ketonization of |FRAME:CPD-16612| towards the formation of |FRAME:CPD-7093|, |FRAME:CPD-16613| and |FRAME:CPD-16614|. The enzymes in question have been codon optimized, N-terminally modified for bacterial expression and introduced to an modular metabolic engineered system in E. coli |CITS:[17480080]|. The three short chain dehydrogenase/reductases (SDR), i.e. MAS and its two paralogs MASL1 and MASL2 characterized in the study have the distinctive motifs typical for SDR's. , MAS and MASL1 are also located in the gene cluster on chromosome 4 which coordinates the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-7092|. MAS was shown to carry out the dehydrogenation of |FRAME:CPD-9905| at the 3-position yielding |FRAME:CPD-7092| as it has been shown before |CITS:[17872948] [12005050]| but was also able to catalyze the dehydrogenation of |FRAME:CPD-16612| and |FRAME:CPD-7093| at the 3-position yielding |FRAME:CPD-16613| and |FRAME:CPD-16614|, respectively. The same reactions are catalyzed by MASL1 indicating for the first time that genes (MAS, MASL1) of the momilactone biosynthetic gene cluster can act outside of a designated cluster. In contrary to MAS and MASL1 being restricted to the C3α-ketonization, MASL2 can carry out the hydroxyl oxidation at the C3α and C7β position of |FRAME:CPD-16612| yielding the respective ketone derivatives |FRAME:CPD-16613| and |FRAME:CPD-7093|. Moreover, MASL2 can further ketonize the 7β hydroxyl group of |FRAME:CPD-16613| and the 3α-hydroxyl group of |FRAME:CPD-7093|, in both cases forming |FRAME:CPD-16614| |CITS:[Wu 2012]|.

Monoterpene such as |FRAME:CPD-8785|, |FRAME:CPD-260| and |FRAME:CPD-10037| are responsible for the characteristic odor of caraway or dill and differ in that context remarkably from the corresponding (-) or (R)-enantiomers found in spearmint to which they confer a more sweetish odor |CITS:[DeCarvalho06]|. The biotransformation of the limonene enantiomers can be observed in bacteria, fungi and plants |CITS:[12743755]| and are scientifically interesting and economically relevant because the elucidation of how the involved regiospecificity can be controlled bears the potential for discovering new reactions and designing more specific drugs |CITS:[17192005] [12743459]|., Monoterpenes have been shown to possess beneficial effects on human health |CITS:[12743459]| and are widely used as fragrance and flavor |CITS:[DeCarvalho06]|. In addition, monoterpenes such as |FRAME:CPD-8785| have been reported to act as defense against pest insects and pollinator inductor |CITS:[Harborne91]|. Moreover, the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-10037| was introduced as an effective sprouting inhibitor of potatoes |CITS:[Oosterhaven95]|., The monoterpene |FRAME:CPD-10037| highly accumulates in fruits of Carum carvis (caraway) which is extensively used in human food and alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks |CITS:[Morton76]|. The formation of the (+)-enantiomer of carvone in caraway follows the same steps as elucidated for the (-)-enantiomer in spearmint |CITS:[16666709]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5928|). The three step pathway consists of the cyclization of |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| to form |FRAME:CPD-8785| which is catalyzed by a highly region- and stereospecific (+)-limonene synthase |CITS:[9662532] [11305598]|. The second step of the pathway is the rate-limiting step of the pathway catalyzed by the (+)-limonene 6-monooxygenase |CITS:[9662532] [Bouwmeester99]| yielding |FRAME:CPD-260| which in turn is oxidized to |FRAME:CPD-10037| by the action of a |FRAME:NAD|-dependent (+)-trans-carveol dehydrogenase |[Bouwmeester99]|. The activity of the enzymes in the pathway are dependent upon the stage of fruit development which may lead either to the accumulation of |FRAME:CPD-8785| in early or |FRAME:CPD-10037| in later phases of fruit maturity |[9662532]|

Names: colupulone and cohumulone biosynthesis // bitter acid biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, The ripe cones of the hop (|FRAME:TAX-3486|) plant are covered with glandular hairs containing a mixture of essential oil and |FRAME: BITTER-ACIDS "bitter acids"|. These compounds are commercially important. In addition to their great importantce for the beer brewing industry, having a major effect on the final aroma and taste of beer, they also have antimicrobial, antifungal and antifeedant activities |CITS:[mizobuchi85a]|., The bitter acids that are synthesized by the hop fall into two types: the |FRAME: ALPHA-ACIDS "α acids"|, which contain two prenyl side chains, and the |FRAME: BETA-ACIDS "β acids"|, which contain three such chains. The former group is of particular importance for the brewing industry as they are transformed during the brewing process into |FRAME: Iso-Alpha-Bitter-Acids "iso-α bitter acids"|, such as |FRAME:CPD-7116| and |FRAME:CPD-7115|, which contribute to the bitter taste of beer |CITS:[15953717]|., About This Pathway, The pathway described here shows the biosynthesis of the α acid |FRAME: CPD-7108| and the β acid |FRAME: CPD-7111|. The first commited step of the pathway, leading to the formation of the 2-acyl-phloroglucinol derivative |FRAME: CPD-7104|, is catalyzed by the chalcone synthase-like enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.156|, using |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA| as the starter molecule. The |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA| was shown to be derived from |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-20125|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55018| gene |CITS: [23300257]|., The next steps consist of prenylations catalyzed by two different prenyltransferases |CITS: [22166201][25564559]|. The prenyl moieties are provided by |FRAME: CPD-4211| that predominantly originates from the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY|, although a small fraction has been shown to derive from the |FRAME:PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| |CITS:[10406953]|. Following an initial prenylation at position 4 by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.136|, a second prenylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.137|, adds a second prenyl side chain at position 6. If the same enzyme adds a third prenyl chain at position 6, |FRAME: CPD-7111| is formed. If, instead, a monooxygenation occurs, |FRAME: CPD-7108| is formed. Since the identity of the oxygenase is not known yet, this last step of the pathway is not well understood.

General Background, |FRAME: METHYLNICOTINATE Trigonelline|, the N-methyl conjugate of |FRAME: NIACINE|, was first isolated from seeds of fenugreek (|FRAME: TAX-78534|) |CITS: [JAHNS85]| and has been found since in many other plant species including pea, hemp, coffee, soybean and potatoes |CITS: [FODOR85]|. Trigonelline is often classified as a pyridine alkaloid |CITS: [DEWICK97]| |CITS: [SEIGLER98]|. As a direct derivative of nicotinic acid trigonelline belongs to the so-called 'pseudoalkaloids' which may be the reason that other authors do not list this compound as an alkaloid but rank it more generic among nitrogen containing compounds |CITS: [HARBORNE93]|., Trigonelline is regarded as a physiological active compound in plants inducing leaf movements |CITS: [10777626]|, accumulating upon stress |CITS: [CHO99]| and acting as an osmoprotectant |CITS: [RAJASEKARAN01]|. Moreover, trigonelline has been found to function as a hormone that is involved in the control of the cell cycle in plants and animals. It was established that trigonelline was capable of promoting specific G2 cellular arrest |CITS: [TRAMONTANO82]|. The molecular reason for that seems to be a specific interference of trigonelline with the DNA replication process causing an elongated cell cycle and impair root elongation |CITS: [10923713]|. The G2 cellular arrest caused by trigonelline was found to depend on the age of the organism. Older seedlings of |FRAME:TAX-3888| produce an unusual substituted pyrrole that has been identified as an endogenous control factor that could override trigonelline induced cellular arrest |CITS: [LYNN87]|. , About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of trigonelline has been investigated in connection with nicotinic acid (niacin) biosynthesis and NAD recycling in plants (similar to |FRAME:PYRIDNUCSAL-PWY| and |FRAME:PWY-5381|) |CITS: [ARDITTI79][ZHENG04]|. The N-methylation of nicotinic acid forming trigonelline is catalyzed by the nicotinate N-methyltransferase (EC 2.1.1.7) which has been first investigated in seeds of |FRAME:TAX-3888| |CITS: [13790768]|. This enzyme was later purified and characterized demonstrating a high preference for nicotinic acid as substrate but not for nicotinamide which has been often observed with partially purified enzymes |CITS: [3364975]|., Trigonelline has long been considered as a metabolic dead-end product but continuous research revealed that this nicotinic acid conjugate rather constitutes a kind of a storage form of niacin which can be re-converted to nicotinic acid, hence feeding the pyridine nucleotide cycle |CITS: [14029718]| |CITS: [6347195]|. The conversion back to nicotinic acid is due to a demethylating activity which is predominantly non-oxidative |CITS: [185134]| but the responsible enzyme and the methyl group acceptor remains to be characterized. However, the relatively slow demethylation of trigonelline to nicotinate has caused doubt on the notion of trigonelline being a true storage compound |CITS: [Upmeier88a]|. Instead, it was proposed that the formation of trigonelline may rather represent the detoxification of excess nicotinate and nicotinamide released from the pyridine nucleotide cycle |CITS: [15837705]|.

Summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., LTAs have been grouped into different types (type I through V) based on their chemical structures. Type I LTA is found in a large range of Firmicutes. It has an unbranched 13 linked glycerol phosphate (GroP) backbone, and is usually linked to the bacterial membrane via a glycolipid anchor. The hydroxyl groups at the C-2 position of the GroP repeating units are modified with D-alanyl or glycosyl groups to varying degrees. It should be noted that not all type I LTAs are glycosylated, and variations in the type of sugar exist. For example, some |FRAME: TAX-1386 Bacillus| strains lack glycosyl groups, some contain |FRAME: CPD-12541|, and some contain |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| |CITS: [3733670][2914853]|. The LTA of all |FRAME: TAX-1639| strains investigated to date is glycosylated with |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| |CITS: [6415040][3093460]|, and the LTA of |FRAME: TAX-1280| strain H is glycosylated with |FRAME: CPD-12541| |CITS: [6268617]|., LTAs can be very abundant. In |FRAME: TAX-1280| every ninth lipid on the outer leaflet of the membrane is an LTA molecule, and the average length is 25 GroP units |CITS: [6697992]|. Although the exact role of LTA is unknown, mutants display significant growth and physiological defects. Teichoic acids are proposed to serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1313| and related species form an unusually complex teichoic acid, which is used as both a wall teichoic acid (attached to peptidoglycan) and lipoteichoic acid (attached to the membrane). The latter is known as type IV LTA., Both polymers share a common cytoplasmic pathway of precursor synthesis, and differ only in the last step, during which the polymer is transferred from the undecaprenyl diphosphate membrane anchor that was used during biosynthesis to either peptidoglycan or to |FRAME: 12-DIACYL-3-O-ALPHA-D-GLUCOPYRANOSYL| (Glc-DAG) glycolipid embedded in the external leaf of the membrane., The repeating units are rather complex pentamers, and contain the rare amino sugar |FRAME: CPD-19333| (AATGal), |FRAME: Glucopyranose glucose| (Glc), |FRAME: CPD-372 "ribitol phosphate"| (modified with |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine| and |FRAME: D-ALANINE|), and two |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine| residues, each of which carries a |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| (P-Cho) moiety., |FRAME: TAX-1313| is not able to synthesize |FRAME: CHOLINE|, and thus its growth depends on exogenous choline, which is exclusively metabolized to decorate the teichoic acid chains |CITS: [4381896]|. Before it could be added to the polymer, choline needs to be phosphorylated and activated to |FRAME: CDP-CHOLINE|. Choline plays an important role in pathogenicity, and mutants with no choline in their cell wall are completely avitulent |CITS: [18621904]|., The pathway starts with the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-19333| to a membrane anchor, |FRAME: CPD-9646| (see |FRAME: PWY-7467|) |CITS: [18245291]|. The next residues of the repeating unit are then added in succession - glucose, ribitol phosphate, and two units of N-acetyl-D-galactosamine. Two dedicated enzymes add the phosphorylcholine residues to the last two residues., It has been thought initially that teichoic acids of |FRAME: TAX-1313| are not glycosylated. However, the use of a milder extraction method revealed that the ribitol units are indeed decorated with N-acetyl-D-galactosamine, as is common with other types of LTA |CITS: [16943191]|., A polymerase catalyzes the trasfer of additional repeating units to the nascent polymer until the maximal length is reached. The full structure is then flipped through the membrane by a flippase enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-44719| gene. Once it faces the external side of the membrane, ribitol units are D-alanylated by a complex system encoded by the dlt operon (in the common laboratory strain R6 a mutation in the |FRAME: G-44720| gene results in lack of D-alanylation) |CITS: [16885447]|., The last step in the pathway is the transfer of the complete polymer either to peptidoglycan or to a glycolipid anchor |CITS: [11294844]| by the action of LCP enzymes |CITS: [22432711]|., The synthesis of the teichoic acid repeating unit requires the products of at least 16 known and hypothetical genes, present in four regions: the 8-gene lic1/lic2 region (licA, licB, licC, licD1, licD2, tarI, tarJ, and tacF); the five genes in the lic3 region (licD3, spr1221, spr1222, spr1223, and spr1224); and two 2-gene regions, spr0091-spr0092 and spr1645-spr1655 |CITS: [22432701]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation, and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. , The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|,, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism, |CITS: [8676868]|. , Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been, shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|. , Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria, and certain fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. , The biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail in bacteria. Sequencing analysis and some experimental evidence suggests that the steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, derived from a |FRAME: CPD-205|-like structure. The early steps of the pathway are responsible for the synthesis of the precursor pimelate moiety, and are described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-6519| and |FRAME: PWY-6578|. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described here., The pathway described here is different from that described in |FRAME: PWY0-1507| since the |FRAME: TAX-1423|enzyme that catayzes the first step cannot use |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as an amino-group donor, and uses |FRAME:LYS| instead |CITS: [15880481]|. The rest of the pathway is identical: |FRAME: EC-6.3.3.3| catalyzes the first ring closure by a carboxylation reaction that does not require biotin as a prosthetic group, forming |FRAME: DETHIOBIOTIN| |CITS: [4921568]|. This intermediate is then converted to the final product by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.6|. This enzyme inserts a sulfur atom between C6 and C9 of dethiobiotin in a |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent reaction. It has not been possible to reconstitute a catalytic reaction of this enzyme in vitro, and there is some uncertainty regarding the reaction mechanism, cofactor requirements, and the source of the sulfur atom |CITS: [15850974]|. However, recent experiments have suggested that a |FRAME: CPD-6| of the enzyme is the source of the sulfur atom. Consistent with its proposed role as the sulfur donor, degradation of the [2Fe-2S] cluster |CITS: [14967042]| as well as exchange of sulfur atoms between the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] clusters |CITS: [16533066]| is observed during turnover of the enzyme., Another difference between the biosynthetic pathways of Gram-negative bacteria (|FRAME: BIOTIN-BIOSYNTHESIS-PWY|) and Gram-positive bacteria (|FRAME: PWY-5005|) is upstream of the precursor |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE|. Gram-positive bacteria generate |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| from |FRAME:CPD-205| as described in |FRAME: PWY-6578|, while in Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| is synthesized from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| in a pathway described in |FRAME: PWY-6519| |CITS: [20693992]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Candicidins Candicidin| is an aromatic polyene macrolide antibiotic produced by some species of |FRAME: TAX-1883|. It has a complex structure composed of a macrolide ring, the amino sugar |FRAME: CPD-16768|, and an aromatic moiety, |FRAME: CPD-16769|. Lechevalier first described this antibiotic as C135 and it was renamed candicidin due to its strong action against |FRAME: TAX-5475| species including one of the most common human fungal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-5476| |CITS: [13159187]|. Like other polyene macrolide antibiotics, candicidin interacts strongly with ergosterol, the predominant sterol component in the plasma membrane of fungi. The increased susceptibility of immunocompromised patients to fungal attacks has stimulated research efforts to isolate effective antifungal agents (reviewed in |CITS: [19362642][12664141]|). , The same compound was isolated independently from |FRAME: TAX-206662|, and named FR-008. Despite initial reports that FR-008 is different from candicidin, it was later shown that the two compounds are in fact identical |CITS: [18559273]|. Structural elucidation of candicidin revealed that it consists of three components named |FRAME: CPD-13108|, |FRAME: CPD-17190|, and |FRAME: CPD-17191|. All structural variants have been characterized (|CITS: [18559273]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19362642]|)., In the candicidin gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1911| 21 contiguous ORFs have been identified. Sequencing studies have shown that the gene clusters in both |FRAME: TAX-1911| and |FRAME: TAX-206662| are essentially identical in nucleotide sequence |CITS: [14652074]|., About This Pathway, This pathway starts with the synthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-16769| moiety. |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.85| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-12529| gene) synthesizes |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXYCHORISMATE| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| and |FRAME: GLN| (see |FRAME: PWY-6543|). In |FRAME: TAX-1911| and |FRAME: TAX-206662| the enzyme is a fused, bifunctional protein with aminotransferase and 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate synthase activities. PabAB has been partially purified and characterized |CITS: [3930655 ]| and its encoding gene has been cloned |CITS: [6420235]|. Another gene pabC-1 was found near pab in |FRAME: TAX-206662|. It was shown to encode a |FRAME: MONOMER-18662| that releases |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. A second pabC-2 gene with |FRAME: MONOMER-18663| activity was also identified |CITS: [19389784]|., Subsequent reactions in candicidin biosynthesis involve a type I polyketide synthase (PKS) encoded in the gene cluster by six ORFs that contain 21 modules. In |FRAME: TAX-206662| the initial activation of |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| to its |FRAME: CO-A| derivative occurs on the PKS, catalyzed by the product of |FRAME: G-43689|. FscA contains a loading module with a putative |FRAME: ATP|-dependent carboxylic acid:CoA ligase and an acyl carrier protein domain. The |FRAME: CPD-13109| precursor is then loaded to start the synthesis of the polyketide chain |CITS: [11782498][14652074]|. Genes |FRAME: G-12529| and |FRAME: G-43689| (named canP1 in |FRAME: TAX-1911|) are likely form a transcriptional unit that is in opposite orientation to the other polyketide synthase genes (reviewed in |CITS: [19362642]|)., The polyketide is further elongated by the polyketide synthase proteins encoded by |FRAME: G-43691|, |FRAME: G-43692|, |FRAME: G-43693|, |FRAME: G-43694|, and |FRAME: G-43695| that contain three, six, six, four and one modules, respectively. |FRAME: CPD-13109 "4-Aminobenzoyl-CoA"| acts as the starter unit for the head-to-tail condensation of four |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| and 15 |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| units to produce a polyketide aglycone (|CITS: [11782498]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19362642][12664141]|)., The resulting polyketide aglycone is modified by tailoring enzymes and the attachment of the deoxysugar |FRAME: CPD-16768| to form |FRAME: CPD-13108|. , The gene cluster also contains genes encoding proteins involved in regulation and export (|CITS: [11782498]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19362642][12664141]|).

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-20999 Pseudomonine| is an isoxazolidone siderophore that was initially characterized from |FRAME: TAX-294| AH2, a strain isolated from a Nile perch caught in Lake Victoria |CITS: [Anthoni95]|. |FRAME: CPD-20999 Pseudomonine| is similar to |FRAME: Pyochelin|, consisting of |FRAME: CPD-110| and two heterocyclic amino acid moieties., The genes encoding the pseudomonine biosynthetic enzymes were localized in |FRAME: TAX-294| |CITS: [11222588]| and |FRAME: TAX-384676| |CITS: [18710233]|. The 21 kb pms cluster contains seven genes encoding three non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs) (PmsG,D,E) and four additional enzymes (PmsA,B,C,F)., The pathway starts with the formation of |FRAME: CPD-110| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| as described in |FRAME: PWY-6406| |CITS: [11222588]|. |FRAME: CPD-110 Salicylate| is then activated by the adenylation domain of |FRAME: MONOMER-20463 PmsE|, which binds it at its aryl-carrier domain. The much larger, three-domain NRPS |FRAME: G-58253 PmsD| activates an |FRAME: ARG| molecule and transfers it to a peptidyl-carrier domain of PmsG. The Cy2 domain of PmsD proceeds to transfer the salicyl moiety from PmsE to the L-threonyl group attached to PmsG, while the Cy1 domain of PmsD performs a cyclodehydration on the product, forming a salicylmethyloxazolinyl group still attached to PmsG., In a second branch of the pathway, the histidine decarboxylase PmsA and histamine N-monooxygenase |FRAME: G-58254 PmsF| convert |FRAME: HIS| to |FRAME: CPD-21001|. The final activity of |FRAME: G-58253 PmsD| is the transfer |FRAME: CPD-21001| to salicylmethyloxazolinyl-[PmsG], forming the oxazoline hydroxamate condensation product |FRAME: CPD-21000|, which is released by PmsG. The latter compound is unstable, and rearranges non-enzymatically to form |FRAME: CPD-20999| |CITS: [18710233]|., The PmsD, E and G proteins were shown to be highly promiscuous. |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE 2,3-Dihydroxybenzoate| can substitute for |FRAME: CPD-110|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-21002|, a siderophore produced by |FRAME: TAX-470|. |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: CYS| can substitute for |FRAME: THR|. When |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| and |FRAME: CYS| substitute for |FRAME: CPD-110| and |FRAME: THR|, respectively, the pseudomonine synthase assembly line produces |FRAME: CPD-9990|, a siderophore known from |FRAME: TAX-55601| |CITS: [19320483]|.

Summary: Archaeal tRNA contains |FRAME: CPD-13057| (often referred to as G*), a 7-deazaguanosine modified nucleoside unique to Archaea |CITS: [7683667]|. Archaeosine is found in the majority of archaeal tRNAs specifically at position 15 of the dihydrouridine loop (D-loop) |CITS: [2470031]|, a position not modified in either eukaryotic or bacterial tRNA., The presence of the positively charged formamidine group of archaeosine and its location at the interface of the D-loop/T-stem in the tertiary structure of the tRNA are thought to be important in structural stabilization of the tRNA through electrostatic interactions with the anionic phosphates |CITS: [7683667]|. This is assumed to be a critical role in thermophiles, protecting tRNA from thermal denaturation., The pathway leading to production of the intermediate |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is common to the archaea and bacteria, and is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6703|., While in bacteria |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is converted to |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| prior to incorporation in tRNA (see |FRAME: PWY-6700|), in archaea |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is incorporated directly by the archaeal |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.48|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12503| gene |CITS: [20129918]|., Once incorporated, the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.97| catalyzes the direct addition of an ammonia group, generated from, glutamine or asparagine hydrolysis, to the nitrile of |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, a previously unknown amidinotransferase chemistry, generating |FRAME: CPD-13057| within the tRNA |CITS: [20129918]|., In Euryarchaeota the enzyme is encoded by the |FRAME: G-12502| gene. Many Crenarchaeota that produce |FRAME: CPD-13057| do not have the arcS gene, and instead contain the |FRAME: G-55183| gene (which is very similar to the bacterial |FRAME: G7452| gene) |CITS: [22032275]|, whose product catalyzes the same activity as ArcS |CITS: [27802572]|.

Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose joined by an α(1,2) glycosidic linkage. Some microorganisms can utilize sucrose by transporting it into the cell via specific permeases. It can then undergo hydrolysis (as shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SUCUTIL-PWY|), or phosphorolysis as shown here. This pathway occurs in the genus |FRAME:TAX-1678|. These saccharolytic, obligate anaerobes are commensals in the gut of humans and animals, and are thought to contribute to health |CITS: [15660210]|., The genes for the initial steps of sucrose degradation have been shown to be organized into an operon in |FRAME:TAX-302911| and Bifidobacterium longum. This includes a transporter scrT (predicted to be a solute-cation symporter), sucrose phosphorylase scrP, and a repressor scrR (reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]|). An additional sucrose hydrolyzing enzyme, the product of gene bfrA has been reported in |FRAME:TAX-302911| |CITS: [12732943]|., In this pathway, after sucrose is transported into the cell, it is cleaved by sucrose phosphorylase. The product fructose is phosphorylated by fructokinase |CITS: [15375133]|. A gene pgm encoding phosphoglucomutase, which catalyzes reaction EC 5.4.2.2, has been predicted in Bifidobacterium longum |CITS: [12381787]|. The α-D-glucose-6-phosphate product of this reaction can spontaneously and reversibly convert to the beta anomer and form an equilibrium mixture (EC 5.1.3.15). This conversion has also been shown to be catalyzed by an epimerase in other organisms |CITS: [11946648] [1092547]|. β-D-Glucose-6-phosphate can be isomerized to D-fructose-6-phosphate (EC 5.3.1.9). A gene encoding glucose-6-phosphate isomerase has been predicted in Bifidobacterium longum |CITS: [12381787]|. , Interestingly, a fructose-6-phosphate phosphoketolase (F6PPK) pathway (bifidobacterial shunt) has been described in bifidobacteria for the metabolism of glucose (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P124-PWY|). The fructose-6-phosphate produced in the pathway shown here is further metabolized via this pathway, as indicated by the pathway link. In the F6PPK pathway, phosphoketolase catalyzes the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to D-erythrose-4-phosphate and acetyl-phosphate. In some species it can also act on xylulose-5-phosphate (in |CITS: [11292814]|). This enzyme, along with a transaldolase and a transketolase, catalyzes the formation of other central metabolic intermediates which the organism can ferment to acetate and lactate |CITS: [16077128] [15375133]|.

Summary: The obligate anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1520|, the saprophytic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1377|, and the purple non-sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-272943| produce the unusual monounsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-17289| and |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| |CITS: [14498314][5554109][6886674][12583708][23972938][Granafei15]|. While |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| is a common fatty acid in other organisms, where it is produced by oxygen-dependent desaturase enzymes, it is unusual in bacteria., The pathway used by the bacteria to produce these fatty acids has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-1377| |CITS: [23972938]|. It is similar to the pathway used by many bacteria to produce |FRAME: CPD-17910| (see |FRAME: PWY0-862|). The key enzyme of that pathway is |FRAME: EC-5.3.3.14| (|FRAME: EG10273 FabA|), which has the unique ability of converting some of the |FRAME: Trans-D2-decenoyl-ACPs "(2E)-dec-2-enoyl-[acp]"| (an intermediate the |FRAME: PWY-5971 "palmitate biosynthesis"| pathway) to |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acp]"|, which is then elongated in the usual fatty acid elongation process to form |FRAME: Cis-Delta5-dodecenoyl-ACPs "(5Z)-dodec-5-enoyl-[acp]"|. , In the case of bacterial oleate prduction, the key step in the pathway is a similar isomerization, but of a later intermediate of the palmitate biosynthesis pathway, |FRAME: Dodec-2-enoyl-ACPs|, which contains a longer acyl chain. The enzyme catalyzing the isomerization reaction in |FRAME: TAX-1377| is a unique hydratase/isomerase, encoded by |FRAME: G-44009|, which fulfils the roles of both |FRAME: EG11284| (the hydratase involved in the fatty acid elongation process) and |FRAME: EG10273|, which is essential for production of unsaturated fatty acids |CITS: [23972938]|., The enzyme responsible for the isomerization in |FRAME: TAX-1520| is still unknown, as it has been shown that the fabZ homolog in that organism is unable to perform the isomerization reaction |CITS: [19493359]|., Another key enzyme in bacterial anaerobic unsaturated fatty acids biosynthesis is the enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of the FabA (or FabQ) product with malonyl-[acp], thus allowing the fatty acid elongation enzymes to continue the extension of the unsaturated fatty acid by two carbons. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this activity is provided by |FRAME: EG10274 FabB|. In |FRAME: TAX-1377|, which lacks FabB, this activity is carried out by a trifunctional |FRAME: G-44012 FabF| enzyme, which catalyzes the activities of the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG10277| and |FRAME: EG12606| |CITS: [23972938]|., Three rounds of the sequential action of FabF - FabG - FabQ - FabK generate |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|, as shown in this pathway. In |FRAME: TAX-1377| alone a fourth round generates |FRAME: CPD-12189| (see |FRAME: PWY-7663|).

Summary: General Background, Organophosphate pesticides such as |FRAME: PARATHION| and |FRAME:CPD-8973|have been used, extensively as insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides. , Methyl parathion is used primarily to kill insects on farm crops, especially cotton., It can no longer be used on food crops commonly consumed by children., Methyl parathion is a cholinesterase inhibitor, and exposure to very high levels for a short period in air, or water may cause death. Changes in mental state may last several months after exposure has ended., EPA regulations allow 0.002 mg/L of methyl parathion in drinking water., About This Pathway, A few organisms can degrade methyl-parathion and completely mineralize it., A |FRAME: TAX-303| strain has been documented to degrade both both methyl parathion as a sole, carbon and phosphorus source |CITS: [7704828]|. This organism hydrolyzed methyl-parathion to, |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL|, which was subsequently degraded via hydroquinone and 1,2,4-benzenetriol, to maleyl-acetate., A |FRAME:TAX-286| strain designated |FRAME: TAX-486399| can use methyl-parathion as a sole, carbon, energy, and phosphorus source |CITS: [10394616]|. The |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| provided, carbon and energy, while the other cleavage product, |FRAME:CPD-8974|, was used as a phosphorus, source., |FRAME: TAX-165468| can utilize methyl-parathion as a sole carbon, energy, and nitrogen source, |CITS: [16039612]|. The genes encoding the required enzymes are carried on a 70 kb plasmid, designated pZWL0. The |FRAME:G-9915| gene encoding the methyl-parathion hydrolyzing enzyme, has been cloned from this organism and succssfully expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. Interestingly, this gene, is completely different from the opd genes encoding parathion hydrolases., The key enzyme in methyl-parathion degradation is methyl-parathion hydrolase, which has been, described in a variety of bacteria., Unlike the organisms mentioned above, an organism identified as |FRAME: TAX-153154| is able to, hydrolyze methyl-parathion to p-nitrophenol, but is not able to degrade p-nitrophenol, further. The gene encoding the methyl-parathion hydrolyzing enzyme in this organism has been cloned, and succssfully expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [1157204]|. It is almost identical to the plasmid-borne, |FRAME:G-9915| gene cloned from |FRAME: TAX-165468|, but is located on the chromosome., According to at least one publication, |FRAME:CPD-8974| is degraded to methane, phosphate, and sulfate, enabling the organism to utilze |FRAME:CPD-8973| as the sole phosphorus source, |CITS: [10394616]|. The exact path for this degradation is not known.

Summary: Flavonol 3-glucosides esterified with hydroxycinnamic acids have been found very effective compounds in screening out ultraviolet-B radiation (280-320 nm). In |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles the most abundant UV-B protective pigments are mono- and diacylated flavonol 3-glucoside which are esterified with |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| on the 3" and 6"-position of the glucose molecule |CITS:[Schnitzler96]| |CITS:[Fischbach99]|. Especially the last acylation step generating the 3",6"-diacylated flavonol glucosides confers the molecule structures to efficient UV-B radiation absorbing compounds |CITS:[Jungblut95]|. , The soluble and cell-wall bound flavonol acylglucosides are accumulating in the epidermal layer of the needles, hence efficiently shielding and protecting the mesophyll cells from UV-B radiation |CITS:[Schnitzler96]|. Based on data obtained from UV experiments on |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles it appears that the soluble flavonol glucosides are first generated within the cell and then transported to the cell wall where the acylation with |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| and association with cell wall components takes place |CITS:[16898012]|. UV-B radiation induces the formation of diacylated flavonol glucosides. |FRAME:CPD-14982 Kaempferol 3-O-(3",6"-O-di-p-coumaroyl)-glucoside| was strongly induced in primary needles after exposure to UV-B radiation |CITS:[Jungblut95]| whereas the content of hydroxycinnamic acids remained unchanged |CITS[Schnitzler96]|. The biosynthesis of acylated flavonol glucosides appears to occur in a seasonal fashion. The soluble flavonol glucosides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-453|, |FRAME:CPD-14969| and |FRAME:CPD1F-437| peak in June at the beginning of needle development and act at this time as the prominent UV-screening pigments. In July the more effective diacylated flavonol glucosides, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-14982| are formed and resume the role of UV-protective pigments (see also |FRAME:PWY-7171|, |FRAME:PWY-7172|) |CITS:[Fischbach99]|. , Three hydroxycinnamoyl transferases (HCT) have been identified and characterized in cell extracts of |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles. The HCT's catalyze the addition of |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| in a position-specific manner and have been characterized as 3"-, 4"- and 6"-HCT's |CITS:[15752358]|. The 6"-HCT was inducible by UV-B radiation and present in the first year needle's development whereas the 3"-HCT was constitutively expressed and showed high values throughout a 2 year period of needle development |CITS:[16898012]|. The 4"-acylation was an unexpected activity as 4"-acylated compounds have not yet been identified in Pinus species. However, similar flavonol acylglucoside with the 4"-pattern have been found in broadleaf species such as oak |CITS:[Romussi83]| indicating the potential occurrence of minor flavonol acylglucoside in other species as well.

Summary: General Background, Sulfur is an essential nutrient for all life forms. Plants, fungi, and many bacteria reduce inorganic sulfate to sulfide to cover their need for the element. Before the sulfur can be assimilated into biosynthetic pathways it needs to be reduced to |FRAME:HS|. Pathways catalyzing the reduction of sulfate to sulfide for the purpose of incorporation into newly synthesized molecules are called pathways of assimilatory sulfate reduction., In addition, certain organisms can use sulfate as an alternative electron acceptor in the absence of oxygen. Pathways of sulfate reduction for the purpose of energy production are called pathways of dissimilatory sulfate reduction., The reduction of sulfate to sulfite requires two electrons at a standard redox potential (E0') of -516 mV, which is too high for physiological electron carriers |CITS: [860983]|. The problem is solved by the activation of the sulfate, by forming a mixed anhydride between phosphate and sulfate as in |FRAME:APS| (APS) or |FRAME:PAPS| (PAPS). This linkage lowers the potential to E0' = -60 mV, which is easilly covered by thiols or pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [14627706]|., About This Pathway, In many bacteria and lower eukaryotes, assimilatory sulfate reduction proceeds via activation of |FRAME: SULFATE| to APS by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4| (also known as ATP sulfurylase). This enzyme has an unfavorable equilibrium (Keq ~ 10-7 M) in the direction of APS formation, and it has been postulated that the reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of PPi by a ubiquitous inorganic pyrophosphatase |CITS: [2821345]|. In |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was found that the enzymes couples the formation of APS to hydrolysis of GTP |CITS: [8117661]|., Following sulfate activation, the pathway consists of phosphorylation of APS to PAPS, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.25| (APS kinase), reduction to |FRAME: SO3|, which is catalyzed by the thioredoxin (or glutaredoxin)-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.8| (PAPS reductase), and a final reduction of sulfite to sulfide, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.8.1.2|.
