Summary: |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is an essential cofactor for carboxyl group transfer enzymes such as, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, and is required by all forms of life |CITS: [ColiSalII]|. , Despite the importance and prevalance of biotin, its detailed biosynthetic pathway remained enigmatic for over 70 years. The first complete pathway for biotin synthesis was suggested for its synthesis in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [20693992]|., Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, derived from a |FRAME: CPD-205|-like structure. The early steps of the pathway, which are described here, are responsible for the synthesis of the precursor of the pimelate moiety in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described in |FRAME: PWY0-1507|., The origins of the biotin carbon atoms in |FRAME: TAX-562| are known from 13C NMR analysis of products labeled in vivo |CITS: [8125118][Indrajit94]|. The C3, C5 and C7 carbons are derived from carbon C1 of acetate, while the C2, C4 and C6 carbons are derived from carbon C2 of acetate. The C1 carbon originates from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. This labeling pattern indicated that the pimeloyl moiety of biotin is formed by head-to-tail incorporation of three intact acetate units, similar to the synthesis of fatty acids |CITS: [Indrajit94]|. As the biotin C1 and C7 atoms show different labeling patterns, free pimelic acid (a symmetrical molecule) could not be an intermediate, and thus it has been assumed that |FRAME: CPD-558| is the precursor |CITS: [Webb07]|., The elucidation of the pathway proved difficult, mostly since only two genes, |FRAME: EG10119| and |FRAME: EG10122|, were implicate in the synthesis of the pimeloyl moiety |CITS: [4563978][8830257][4877129]|., Based on these finding, there have been several suggestions that enzymes of the fatty acid biosynthesis pathway are involved, although none of these suggestions could explain the full process |CITS: [Indrajit94][13930373]|. An inclusive model was finally suggested in 2010 |CITS: [20693992]|. Based on this model, |FRAME: EG10119 "BioC"| converts the free carboxyl group of a |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| thioester to its methyl ester by transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|.The newly acquired methyl group mimics the methyl ends of normal fatty acyl chains, and enables the esterified |FRAME: CPD-12454| to enter the fatty acid synthetic pathway., Two reiterations of the fatty acid elongation cycle (see |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY|) produce |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACP-methyl-esters "pimeloyl-[acp] methyl ester"|, which is cleaved by |FRAME: EG10122 "BioH"| to give |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs "pimeloyl-[acp]"|. The [acp] protein is then removed in a complex reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EG10121 "BioF"|, forming |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE|, the first intermediate in biotin ring assembly., It should be noted that many organisms that have a |FRAME: EG10119| gene do not have a homolog of the |FRAME: EG10122| gene. A remarkable diversity was found in the enzymes catalyzing this step, with different, non-related genes found in different organisms, including |FRAME: G-17965| from |FRAME: TAX-401614| |CITS: [23152908]|, |FRAME: G-15494| from |FRAME: TAX-93059| |CITS: [23152908]|, |FRAME: G-15495| from |FRAME: TAX-71421| |CITS: [24313380]|, and |FRAME: HP0287| from |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [26868423]|., The next step in the pathway involves the unusual use of the common methyl-group donor |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as an amino-group donor, a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: EG10117|-encoded |FRAME: DAPASYN-CPLX| |CITS: [1092681][1092682][12379100]|. This product of this reaction, |FRAME: DIAMINONONANOATE|, is the target of a unique carboxylase, the |FRAME: EG10120|-encoded |FRAME: DETHIOBIOTIN-SYN-CPLX|. This enzye catalyzes the first ring closure by a carboxylation reaction that does not require biotin as a prosthetic group, forming |FRAME: DETHIOBIOTIN| |CITS: [4921568]|., The ultimate step in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: BIOTIN-SYN-CPLX|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10118|., This enzyme inserts a sulfur atom between C6 and C9 of dethiobiotin in a |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent reaction. It has not been possible to reconstitute a catalytic reaction of this enzyme in vitro, and there is some uncertainty regarding the reaction mechanism, cofactor requirements, and the, source of the sulfur atom |CITS: [15850974]|. However, recent experiments have suggested that a |FRAME: CPD-6| of the enzyme is the source of the sulfur atom. Consistent with its proposed role as the sulfur donor, degradation of the [2Fe-2S] cluster |CITS: [14967042]| as well as exchange of sulfur atoms between the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] clusters |CITS: [16533066]| is observed during turnover of the enzyme., According to this model, the introduction of the methyl ester early in the pathway disguises the biotin synthetic intermediates so that they become substrates for the fatty acid synthetic pathway. When the synthesis of the pimeloyl moiety is complete and disguise is no longer needed, the methyl group is removed to free the carboxyl group that will eventually be used to attach biotin to its target metabolic enzymes., An in vitro system that uses dialyzed cell extracts was used in combination with several mutant strains and purified proteins to verify the proposed pathway |CITS: [20693992]|.

General Background, Organophosphate pesticides such as |FRAME: PARATHION| and |FRAME:CPD-8973| have been used, extensively as insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides. , Parathion, which is a cholinesterase inhibitor (see EC 3.1.1.7 and 3.1.1.8 for cholinesterases), is, extremely toxic to most animals including humans (in which LD50 is 5 to 10 mg/kg), and may cause, death by inducing respiratory failure., The use of Parathion is banned in many countries due to its toxicity and pollutant properties., About This Pathway, Some bacterial strains are able to degrade parathion and related compounds. A mixed culture of at least, 9 isolates was able to grow on parathion as a sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [8005][9901]|,, although so far no single organism was shown to use parathion as the sole carbon source, |CITS:[16039612][4727806]|., Two organisms that have been studied in detail are |FRAME: TAX-336203| |CITS: [4727806]| and, |FRAME: TAX-293| |CITS: [2555328]|. In both cases parathion degradation starts with the hydrolysis of, parathion to |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| and |FRAME:DIETHYLTHIOPHOSPHATE|, followed by a, second hydrolysis of |FRAME: DIETHYLTHIOPHOSPHATE| to |FRAME:DIETHYLPHOSPHATE|, |CITS: [8005]|., In these organisms, |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| (PNP) was not degraded further, and was, released into the environment. The rate of this enzymatic hydrolysis was more than 2000 fold faster, than the chemical reaction, as catalyzed by 0.1N sodium hydroxide |CITS: [9901]|., This initial hydrolysis of parathion reduces the toxicity by nearly 120-fold |CITS:[42449]|., The key enzyme in parathion degradation is parathion hydrolase, which has been described in, a variety of bacteria. In the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-336203| and |FRAME: TAX-293| the enzyme is encoded, by related opd plasmid-borne genes |CITS:[3015022][2834339][3202637][12732518]|., Similar enzymes have been purified from additional organisms, and are apparently encoded by genes, non-related to the opd genes |CITS: [2541658]|. , Parathion hydrolases often have broad substrate range, broad temperature and pH optima,, and high stability |CITS:[255328][2541058]|., Both products of this pathway, |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| and |FRAME:DIETHYLTHIOPHOSPHATE|,, can be degraded by microorganisms. Two pathways of |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| degradation have, been described (see |FRAME: PWY-5487| and |FRAME: PWY-5488|), and the degradation of, |FRAME:DIETHYLTHIOPHOSPHATE| has been described in several mixed cultures |CITS:[16347763], [16987656]|. However, the exact nature of this degradation pathway is not known yet., It should be mentioned that in the case of the related compound |FRAME:CPD-8973|, complete, mineralization by a single organism has been reported several times., For more details, see |FRAME: PWY-5489|., This pathway was curated based on a pathway curated in the UM-BBD database |CITS: [Cornett97]|.

|FRAME: CPD-9562 Hypericin| is a napthodianthrone isolated from |FRAME: TAX-65561| (St John's Wort), a medicinal herb. It occurs as a red dye and forms hypercinate salts with sodium and potassium. |FRAME: TAX-65561| is , known to cause photo sensitivity. The mechanism of |FRAME: CPD-9562| action is explained by its ability to absorb , in the UV and visible range along with the production of singlet oxygen, indicative of |FRAME: CPD-9562| being an , effective phototoxic agent in the eye capable of damaging both the lens and retina., |FRAME: CPD-9562 Hypericin| is a natural photosensitizer with numerous biological activities that are enhanced upon exposure to light. It is a potent antiretroviral agent and also known to induce photogenerated intracellular drop in pH. , This property makes |FRAME: CPD-9562| a prime candidate for clinical application in the treatment of human glioma , tumors |CITS: [9865736]|. Remarkably, the one gene encoding Hyp-1 protein which soley catalyzes |FRAME: CPD-9562| from |FRAME: CPD-8215| shows homology to Bet.v.1 class allergens |CITS: [12799379]|. |FRAME: CPD-9562 Hypericin| is reported to interact with DNA in vitro and in intact cells and in a DNA unwinding assay it created a torsional strain on the DNA that did not allow topoisomerase II DNA binding activity. Further, |FRAME: CPD-9562| was several times more potent than topo II poisons and brought about complete antagonism of drug-stabilized cleavage complexes |CITS: [11597574]|. , |FRAME: CPD-9562 Hypericin| biosynthesis occurs in the polyketide pathway and little is known about the genes involved, , except that the precursor molecule is |FRAME: CPD-8215| and |FRAME: CPD-9562| is formed by the dimerization of |FRAME: CPD-23474| via phenolic oxidation |CITS: [15979315]|. Hyp-1 gene has been isolated and shows a direct , and specific bioconversion of |FRAME: CPD-8215| to |FRAME: CPD-9562| in the dark. This involves a condensation reaction followed by dehydration and sequence of oxidative cyclizations to yield |FRAME: CPD-9562|. It is hypothesized that Hyp-1 catalyzes an initial condensation reaction between |FRAME: CPD-8215| and |FRAME: CPD-23474| followed by a dehydration to form |FRAME: CPD-9558|. Emodin dianthrone eventually undergoes phenolic oxidation to , |FRAME: CPD-9561|, either by photoactivation or by Hyp-1 itself |CITS: [12799379]|. , Addendum, However, it should be noted that neither the intermediates depicted in the pathway above nor the reaction sequences have been experimentally established. The Hyp-1 gene product was recombinant expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, purified and crystallized and its structure determined. It could be shown that the protein belongs to the family of pathogenesis-related class 10 (PR-10) which members with only two exceptions have no clearly understood biological role. In addition, the attempt to catalyze the formation of |FRAME:CPD-9562| from |FRAME:CPD-8215| was not successful although the size and shape of the protein cavity was suited to bind either two |FRAME:CPD-8215| or one |FRAME:CPD-9562| molecule(s). Several possibilities for the role of Hyp-1 were discussed: 1) some factors are missing necessary for Hyp-1 activity or additionally required for complementing the reaction steps 2) Hyp-1 is not directly involved in the biosynthetic route but serves as a transport vehicle to the dark glands |CITS:[19853038]|. The former is supported by the report that other enzymes than Hyp-1 maybe involved in the overall pathway |CITS:[18647343]| and the latter has merit by the finding that the expression of Hyp-1 in roots is much higher than in the expected biosynthetic site of |FRAME:CPD-9562| in the dark glands of leaves which may then only serve as storage facilities |CITS:[16988829]|. It appears that the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-9562| may be more complicated than previously thought and more research is necessary to determine all factors involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-9562|. , ,

The filamentous fungus Beauveria bassiana has been intensively and systematically studied due to its insect pathogenic properties. It was one of the first discovered entomopathogenic fungi which caused the white muscardine disease in the domesticated silk worm (Bombyx mori) which had devastating consequences on the European silkworm industry in the 18th century (summarized in |CITS:[Rehner05]|. The pathogenic principle of Beauveria bassiana is based on the production of mycotoxins and toxic proteins which upon secretion affect numerous insects |CITS:[15209284] [20674578]|. In turn, these entomopathogenic properties also furthered the development of biological pest control with Beauveria bassiana as a cost-effective mycoinsecticide. In order to gain insight into the underlying pathways and virulence factors the genome of Beauveria bassiana was sequenced which cleared the way for exploring potential biosynthetic secondary metabolite pathways and toxic protein production |CITS:[22761991]|., Amongst the yellow pigments found in Beauveria bassiana are the derivatives originated from highly reduced (HR) polyketides and amino acids |FRAME:CPD-17122| (this pathway) and the closely related |FRAME:CPD-17134| (see |FRAME:PWY-7563|) |CITS:[Wat77]|. It has been shown that |FRAME:CPD-17122| inhibits membrane ATPase activity in erythrocytes causing varying degrees of cell lysis |CITS:[Jeffs97]|. However, it appears that |FRAME:CPD-17122| is not involved in insect pathogenesis because |FRAME:CPD-17122|-knock-out mutants and the wild-type of Beauveria bassiana exhibit the same pathogenicity |CITS:[17216664]|. , The genetic cluster involved in |FRAME:PWY-7561| has been discovered and shown to consist of basically four genes, named TenS, TenC, TenA and TenB |CITS:[17216664]|. TenS encodes for the tenellin synthetase, a hybrid of polyketide synthase (PKS) and nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) which are often encountered in fungal polyketide metabolites biosyntheses |CITS:[17581644] [17369821] [20111804]|. However, it appears that the enoyl reductase (ER) domain in the N-terminal PKS of TenS is inactive and the necessary enoyl reduction must be carried out by the co-expressed trans-acting enoyl reductase TenC. TenC has a similar function than lovC in the |FRAME:PWY-7535| and shows a high sequence similarity to this protein. Together the two genes TenS and TenC realize the first reaction of the pathway forming |FRAME:CPD-17124| from |FRAME:MALONYL-COA|, |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| via an pentaketide intermediate, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17125| generated by the highly reducing PKS of TenS in tandem with TenC |CITS:[17216664] [18266306] [20575135]|. The following unusual oxidative ring expansion of the tetramic |FRAME:CPD-17124| into the 2-pyridone compound |FRAME:CPD-17123| is carried out by the cytochrome P450 dependent pretenellin A oxidase encoded by TenA |CITS:[19067514]|. The last step, the N-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17123| to form the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17122| is catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 dependent pretenellin B N-monooxygenase encoded by TenB. N-hydroxylation carried out by a cytochrome P450 dependent protein is very rare and TenB appears to be the only member of this class in either bacteria and fungi |CITS:[19067514]|., A later study has shown that both |FRAME: CPD-17122| and |FRAME: CPD-25622| can chelate iron, which could benefit B. bassiana to outcompete other fungui in cocultures and to adapt to iron-replete and -depleted conditions |CITS: [34903054]|.

Summary: Plant-derived sterols (also known as phytosterols), such as |FRAME: CPD-4143| and |FRAME: CPD-707|, are abundant naturally occurring sterols. While the bacterial degradation of the animal-derived |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| has been studied comprehensively (see |FRAME: PWY-6945| and |FRAME: PWY-6946|), the degradation of phytosterols is not nearly as well documented., Early studies showed that many species of the genera |FRAME:TAX-1663|, Bacillus, |FRAME:TAX-1696|, |FRAME:TAX-1716|, |FRAME:TAX-33882|, |FRAME:TAX-1763|, |FRAME:TAX-1817|, Protoaminobacter, Serrattia and |FRAME:TAX-1883| were able to degrade sitosterol, and that in the presence of the enzyme inhibitor |FRAME: CPD-8819| they accumulated |FRAME: CPD-13704|, indicating complete removal of the sitosterol side-chain independently of the sterol rings opening |CITS: [Arima69]|., Several intermediates in the side-chain degradation pathway were reported over the years from different strains, including Nocardia sp. M29 |CITS: [Martin76]|, |FRAME: TAX-36822 "Gordonia rubripertincta (previously known as Norcardia corallina IF0 3338)"| |CITS: [Arima78]|, |FRAME: TAX-1766| |CITS: [7210061]| and |FRAME: TAX-1795| |CITS: [Fujimoto82]|., It was concluded that the mode of microbial degradation of the sitosterol side chain proceeds via hydroxylation at C26, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-13797|. In the next step |FRAME: HCO3| is incorporated onto the C28 position, followed by carbon-carbon bond fission, liberating |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and forming |FRAME: CPD-13696|, an intermediate that is also formed during |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| degradation |CITS: [Fujimoto82a]|., The rest of the pathway is predicted to proceed analogously to cholesterol degradation. Side-chain degradation is completed by liberation of a second molecule of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| followed by one molecule of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, resulting in the common sterol-degradation intermediate |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| |CITS:[1529708] [18329874]|. For the complete degradation of the latter, see |FRAME: PWY-6944|., A model for the side chain cleavage by |FRAME: ORG-6197| was provided by |CITS: [4046606]|. The model, which was based on the identification of several intermediates, suggested that prior to side-chain cleavage the 3-hydroxy A-ring of the sterol has to be oxidized to a 3-oxo-5-ene structure (a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-17008|). Once this is achieved, side-chain degradation can start. This observation has also been confirmed for the degradation of other sterols, as well as bile acids. The model was later revised by |CITS: [Szentirmai90]|, and the revised model is used as the basis of the pathway shown here.

Summary: This pathway, which is known best as the Ljungdahl-Wood pathway, describes autotrophic production of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| from two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules., The pathway has been documented in several types of organisms, and is best studied in homoacetogenic bacteria |CITS:[Jansen82]| (a related pathway exists in methanogens - see |FRAME: PWY-7784|). Homoacetogenic bacteria are strict anaerobes that can synthesize acetate from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [7747932] [3096193]|., Two key enzymes in this pathway activate |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. The first enzyme reduces |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:FORMATE|. While originally it was reported that |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.10|, is responsible for this function, more recently it was shown that different organisms utilize different variations of this activity, including |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.M4|, and |FRAME: EC-1.17.98.5|. The second enzyme is |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.4|, which reduces |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE|., The formate formed is incorporated into |FRAME:THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|, and goes through a series of rearrangements resulting in the formation of a methyl group, in the form of |FRAME:5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"|. This methyl group then reacts with the CO formed by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.4|, producing |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, which is then converted to |FRAME:ACET| (see |FRAME: Acetate-Formation|)., The pathway ends with the formation of acetate from acetyl-CoA via acetyl phosphate in an ATP-generating reaction (see |FRAME: PWY0-1312|). Since all of the ATP that is formed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.2.1| is consumed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.3|, growth with H2 and CO2 is only possible if the pathway is coupled to electron-transport phosphorylation. Of the redox reactions involved only the reduction of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate| to |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N 5-methyltrahydrofolate| (E0' = -200 mV) |CITS: [Wohlfarth91]| with H2 (E0' = -414 mV) is exergonic enough to be coupled with energy conservation |CITS: [2094291][22800682]|., In |FRAME: TAX-1497| the MetVF proteins interact with ferredoxin |CITS: [6381490]|. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-33952| shows methylene-H4F reductase activity with NADH |CITS: [Buchenau01]|, and the |FRAME: G-80884|/|FRAME: G-80885| genes that encode methylene-H4F reductase in that organism are clustered with the |FRAME: G-80886| gene, which encodes an NADH dehydrogenase |CITS: [25733614]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1525| the MetVF proteins form a complex with |FRAME: CPLX-8900| and |FRAME: MONOMER-18816| proteins, suggesting some sort of electron bifurcation |CITS: [25002540]|. Thus, it seems that different acetogens, although all of them use the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway of CO2 reduction to acetic acid, have evolved different ways to directly or indirectly conserve the energy associated with methylene-H4F reduction |CITS: [25002540]|., This pathway operates in the opposite direction in sulfate reducing bacteria, where electrons originating from organic molecules are shuttled via acetyl-CoA to NADH, oxidizing |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [Rabus06]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9991 "Yersiniabactin"| is a siderophore naturally produced by |FRAME: TAX-632| (the causative agent for bubonic plague) during times of iron starvation., The compound is biosynthesized intracellularly by the modular |FRAME: CPLX-7973|, a large complex composed of four primary enzymes - |FRAME: MONOMER-15295| (YbtE), |FRAME: MONOMER-15298|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15297| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15296| (YbtU), encompassing seventeen functional domains, twelve catalytic domains, and five carrier modules. The complex is able to select, activate, and incorporate one molecule of |FRAME: CPD-110|, three |FRAME: CYS| molecules, and one |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| into a single |FRAME: CPD-9991| molecule |CITS: [11927258]|., The process begins by the activation of |FRAME: CPD-110| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15295 "YbtE"|, which generates a |FRAME: CPD-12084| |CITS: [9709002]|. . , The second enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15298 "HMWP2"| (High Molecular Weight Protein 2), consists of two multidomain nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) modules. The first module accepts the activated salicylate unit through an aryl carrier protein. The second module is an adenylation domain that attaches two cysteine units through thioester bonds to two peptidyl carrier proteins. , HMWP2 then catalyzes the successive addition and cyclization of each cysteine unit to the growing product chain, and then transfers it to |FRAME: MONOMER-15297 "HMWP1"| |CITS: [10769129]|., HMWP1 contains both a polyketide (PKS) and nonribosomal peptide (NRPS) modules |CITS: [11516308]|. The ketosynthase domain initially accepts the partial yersiniabactin chain from HMWP2. The PKS portion of HMWP1 then catalyzes the addition of a malonate unit (preloaded onto an acyl carrier protein through the acyltransferase domain). The resultant enzyme-tethered product is reduced through an NADPH-dependent ketoreductase domain and methylated through a methyltransferase domain using |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as a substrate. The HMWP1 NRPS module catalyzes the addition, cyclization, and methylation of a final cysteine unit. Finally, a thioesterase domain catalyzes the release of yersiniabactin from HMWP1. The last enzyme,|FRAME: MONOMER-15296 "YbtU"|, is a reductase that reduces the second thiazoline ring of the growing enzyme-tethered product sometimes during biosynthesis., The biosynthesis of yersiniabactin has been reconstituted in vitro in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [11927258]|. The rate of one turnover, which comprises 22 chemical operations, was determined at 1.4 min(-1).

Names: Kaede-type red fluorescent protein chromophore biosynthesis // RFP chromophore biosynthesis
Summary: |FRAME: GFP "Green fluorescent proteins"| (GFPs) are proteins that exhibit bright green fluorescence when exposed to light in the blue to ultraviolet range. GFPs form a part of the bioluminesence systems of many marine organisms, and the first such protein, from the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100|, was described already in 1962 |CITS: [13911999]|., Some other species, including non-bioluminesent species, encode homologs of GFP. Many |FRAME: TAX-6101| species exhibit bright fluorescent colors, and while the most common color is green, other colors are also found |CITS: [Catala59][Mazel95]|. The fluorescence in these species is assumed to provide protection from strong solar radiation |CITS: [Kawaguti44]|. A different function has been proposed for organisms living in deeper habitats - the conversion of blue light into a longer wavelength that is more suitable for photosynthesis by the algal endosymbionts |CITS: [28313957]|., In a 1999 study genes encoding remote homologs of the |FRAME: G-55175| gene of |FRAME: TAX-6100| were cloned from six non-bioluminescent reef corals and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified. Despite a low overall identity with GFP (26-30%), all of the proteins fluoresced, and two of them (from |FRAME: TAX-105401| and |FRAME: TAX-86599| species) were found to fluoresce at the yellow and red wavelengths, respectively |CITS: [10504696]|. It is now recognized that the family of GFP-like proteins includes |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent proteins"| (GFP), |FRAME: PWY-8514 "red fluorescent proteins"| (RFP), |FRAME: YFP-Chromophore "yellow fluorescent proteins"| (YFP), |FRAME: CFP-Chromophore "cyan fluorescent proteins"| (CFP) and |FRAME: BCP-Chromophore "purple-blue non-fluorescent chromoproteins"| (CP) |CITS: [18648549]|., All of these proteins share the same β-can fold first observed in GFP, but most are not associated with bioluminescence. While the fluorophores of previously-described GFPs are formed autocatalitically from  the three amino acids Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly, later identified proteins have significant variability in the first position, containing Gln, Lys, His, or Asn |CITS: [10504696][12271129]|., Three years after discovery of the |FRAME: RFP-Chromophore "DsRed-type red fluorescent protein"|, a different type of red fluorescent protein was reported from the stony coral |FRAME: TAX-196280|. This protein is formed in the dark as a green-fluorescent protein, but when exposed to UV or violet light it begins to emmit bright red fluorescence. The protein was named Kaede (maple leaf in Japanese) |CITS: [12271129]|., The gene encoding the protein was cloned, showing that the three amino acids that form the chromophore are His-Tyr-Gly. The protein was expressed in HeLa cells, and when subjected to maximal illumination, the ratio of red-to-green signal increased 2,000-fold |CITS: [12271129]|., Similar proteins were discovered shortly afterwards from the soft coral |FRAME: TAX-191210| (DendFP), the great star coral |FRAME: TAX-63558|, the corallimorph |FRAME: TAX-165100| |CITS: [11929996]|, the stony coral |FRAME: TAX-46758| (EosFP) |CITS: [15505211]|, and the coral |FRAME: TAX-1869259| (KikG) |CITS: [15731765]|., Like other members of the GFP family, the Kaede-type red fluorescent proteins feature a β barrel structure and form homotetramers |CITS: [19942137]|., The histidine residue is critical for the formation of the red chromophore, because its imidazole ring is ultimately incorporated into the three-ring π-system of the mature chromophore. A mechanism for the formation of the chromophore has been proposed. According to the mechanism, the first steps are similar to those forming the green fluorescent protein (see |FRAME: PWY-8513|), and in the absence of an appropriate light source the green form is the final state of protein self-processing. This form experiences a protonation-deprotonation equilibria, and only the neutral non-fluorescent form can be converted further. , Exposure of the non-fluorescent form to UV or violet light triggers electronic excitation of the neutral GFP-like chromophore which results in scission of the main protein chain. The N-terminal part of the protein initially contains a hydroxyimino group, which undergoes isomerization, forming a stable terminal amide group. Subsequent deprotonation of the β-carbon of the histidine residue forms the mature red-fluorescing chromophore |CITS: [14580354][ 15505211][15964985][19942137]|.

Names: (S)-propane-1,2-diol degradation // propylene glycol degradation // L-1,2-propanediol degradation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| (propylene glycol) is produced from |FRAME: LACTALD| during the bacterial degradation of |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-Fucopyranoses| (see |FRAME: PWY0-1315| and the associated pathway links) (in |CITS: [18805996]|). |FRAME: TAX-28901| can utilize |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| as a carbon source and its metabolism may be a virulence factor |CITS: [10498708]|. Under fermentative conditions, |FRAME: CPD-665| (propionaldehyde) is formed and converted to |FRAME: PROPANOL| and |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate), |FRAME: ATP| is produced, and |FRAME: NAD| is regenerated (in |CITS: [18805996]|). The reactions forming |FRAME: CPD-665| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| occur within a specialized bacterial microcompartment known as a metabolosome (see the About This Pathway section below). , The first enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: CPLX1R65-171|, a diol dehydratase composed of polypeptides PduCDE. This enzyme is dependent upon |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| (vitamin B12), which requires anaerobic conditions for its de novo biosynthesis (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5507|). Initially it was thought that |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| utilization required oxygen, leading to an apparent |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| paradox. This paradox was resolved by the discovery that |FRAME: TAX-28901| can use |FRAME: CPD-14| as an alternative electron acceptor during anaerobic degradation of both |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| and |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| |CITS: [11274105]|., The adenosyl group of the |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| cofactor of |FRAME: CPLX1R65-171| is unstable in vivo and can be converted to |FRAME: CPD0-1256| in a reaction that inactivates the enzyme |CITS: [20656910]|. Active enzyme can be regenerated within the microcompartment by the combined action of a reactivase PduGH |CITS: [10498708]| (biochemically characterized in |FRAME: TAX-571| |CITS: [21040475]|), a dedicated |FRAME: STM2050-MONOMER| |CITS: [11160088]|, and a cobalamin reductase PduS, that together regenerate |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|. Thus, the microcompartment contains a complete |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| recycling system |CITS: [20656910]| (and in |CITS: [21821773]|)., Under aerobic conditions, exogenously added |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| (or its precursor |FRAME: COBINAMIDE|) can be imported into the cell to allow use of |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| as a carbon and energy source via the |FRAME: PWY0-42| as shown in the pathway link |CITS: [11274105][10482501]| and in |CITS: [18805996]|., There is also evidence for the production of |FRAME: PROPANOL| and |FRAME: PROPIONATE| via this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1637| species, although the |FRAME: PWY0-42| may not be present in these organisms |CITS: [18805996]|. In addition to the organisms shown here, genes for |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|-dependent propanediol utilization have also been identified in species of |FRAME:TAX-620|, |FRAME:TAX-629|, |FRAME:TAX-1578| and |FRAME:TAX-1357|, as well as |FRAME:TAX-562| E24377A (reviewed in |CITS: [18937343]|)., About This Pathway, The first two reactions of this pathway occur within the lumen of a bacterial microcompartment (BMC), a capsid-like shell composed of multiple proteins that is analogous to the carboxysome of cyanobacteria. The |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|-dependent |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| utilization (Pdu) microcompartment consists of major polypeptides PduABB'CDEGHJKOPTU which includes enzymes PduCDE, PduGH, PduO and PduP, as well as BMC-domain containing proteins PduABB'JKNTU |CITS: [21239588]|. A structural proein (PduM) has also been described |CITS: [22343294]|. The proposed function of this microcompartment is to sequester toxic |FRAME: CPD-665| (propionaldehyde). The remaining reactions occur in the cytosol (reviewed in |CITS: [18937343]| and |CITS: [21315581]|)., The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-665| to |FRAME: PROPANOL| is catalyzed within the compartment by an alcohol dehydrogenase/aldehyde reductase encoded by the |FRAME: STM2052| gene, which provides ample supply of NAD+ to |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.87| (|FRAME: STM2051 PduP|) |CITS: [10498708][23077559]|., The |FRAME: PROPIONATE| formed can be activated to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| by the reversible reactions catalyzed by PduW and PduL. |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA Propanoyl-CoA| can also be formed from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| by the Acs and PrpE enzymes in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-42| (see |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.17|). |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA Propanoyl-CoA| is thus an intermediate in the catabolism of both |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| (this pathway) and |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-42|) and is necessary for expression of the prpBCDE genes of the |FRAME: PWY0-42| during growth on |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| |CITS: [12700259]|., The genes of this pathway are clustered and are located adjacent to the cbi/cob gene cluster needed for |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthesis. Both clusters are regulated by the pocR gene (|CITS: [1312999][8071226]| and in |CITS: [18805996]|)., The 21 gene regulon encoding the pdu organelle and propanediol degradation enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-546| was cloned and expressed successfully in |FRAME: TAX-562|, allowing |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| utilization |CITS: [18332146]|.

Names: glycolipid desaturation // fatty acid desaturation // polyunsaturated glycolipid biosynthesis
Summary: Fatty acids constitute a major component of plant membranes in the form of glycerolipids, mainly phosphoglycerolipids and glycosylglycerolipids. The majority of them have C16 or C18 carbon chains and are attached to the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of the glycerol backbone. In Arabidopsis, the major fatty acids are C16:0, C16:1, C16:2, C16:3, C18:1, C18:2, and C18:3. Unsaturated fatty acids are significant to membrane functions such as photosynthesis and cold tolerance. C16:3 and C18:3 together make up more than 90% of the fatty acid content of monogalactosyldiacylglycerol (MGDG), a major glycosylglycerolipid of leaf chloroplast membranes |CITS: [arabidopsis94]|.   , C18:1 is desaturated from C18:0 in the form of stearoyl-ACP (|FRAME: PWY-5147|) and is subsequently incorporated into glycerolipids. The rest of the unsaturated fatty acids, C16:1, C16:2, C16:3, C18:2 and C18:3, on the other hand, are desaturated from C16:0 or C18:1 after C16:0 and C18:1 are incorporated into glycerolipids. These latter desaturation processes are catalyzed by membrane-bound fatty acid desaturases, and occur in chloroplasts and ER. Fatty acid desaturation is best studied in Arabidopsis using desaturase mutants. , The depicted glycosylglyceride desaturation pathway illustrates the biosynthesis of 18:3-16:3-MGDG and 18:3-18:3-DGDG, the two most abundant glycosylglycerolipid found in chloroplast membranes. It is noteworthy that desaturation occurs on both sn-1 and sn-2 acyl chains, and that the order of the desaturation steps on one chain versus the other is not known. Here, all the possible steps are presented.

Ginseng is the famous oriental medicinal herb Panax sps used as a drug since ancient times. The active ingredients in ginseng are glycosylated triterpene saponins called ginsenosides |CITS: [12920566]|. More than 30 kinds of ginsenosides are known. Based on the aglycone skeleton they are classified into two groups; the dammarenediol-type and oleanane-type |CITS: [16962103]|. The ginsenosides differ from one another only by the type, the number, the sites of attachment of sugar moieties and the number of hydroxyl groups |CITS: [Yue05]|. However, the biological activities of the ginsenosides differ extensively. , The pharmacological activities of various ginsenosides include cardio-protective, immuno-modulatory, anti-fatigue, antitumour |CITS: [11748374]| and hepato-protective effects |CITS: [Yue05]|. The roots of |FRAME: TAX-4054| contain the triterpene saponins and undergo specific developmental changes to function as an organ that synthesizes the ginsenosides |CITS: [LUO05]|. The various types of ginsenosides accumulate with age |CITS: [15356323]|. , The chemical synthesis of ginsenosides has not been feasible and little is known about the genes and biochemical pathways. The ginsenoside backbones are synthesized from the |FRAME: POLYISOPRENSYN-PWY| by cyclization of |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| |CITS: [15356323]|. The cyclization leads to a branch point for the sterol and triterpene pathways. Based on the aglycone backbone they are classified into 3 types: protopanaxdiol-type, protopanaxtriol-type, and oleanane-type saponins |CITS: [12920566]|. The triterpene backbone undergoes various modifications, such as oxidation, substitution, and glycosylation to give the characteristic ginsenosides. , The most extensively researched ginseng compounds are Rb1, Rb2, Rc, Rd, Rg1, Rg2, |FRAME: CPD-12102|, Re, Rf, Rh1 and |FRAME: CPD-12104|, |CITS: [18557901]|. |FRAME: CPD-12102| has been isolated from Panax ginseng, its precursor and enzyme catalyzing its formation in the plant has not been identified. As its application in anti cancer research is immense, it has been isolated from bacteria and fungi depicted in this pathway. , In this pathway, the downstream product of |FRAME: CPD-12102| has been identified as |FRAME: CPD-12104| and the enzyme catalyzing this reaction has been isolated and characterized |CITS: [11456082]|. |FRAME: CPD-12104| has been studied for its effect of cell cycle arrest in breast cancer studies |CITS: [19629651]|, anti tumour activity |CITS: [19160799]| and several other drug effects.

Names: arsenite to oxygen electron transfer (via azurin) // arsenite oxidation II (respiratory)
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Arsenic is ubiquitous in the environment, and is present in four oxidation states: 0 (elemental), -3 (arsine), +3 (arsenite) and +5 (arsenate). The two soluble forms of arsenic, arsenite and arsenate, are toxic to biological systems, with arsenite considered 100 times more toxic., Since the first report of bacterial arsenite oxidation |CITS: [Green18]|, several arsenite-oxidizing bacteria have been isolated from various environments including gold mines |CITS: [10618208]|, sewage |CITS: [10837]|, hyper-saline lake |CITS: [12324322]|, soil |CITS: [Osborne76]|, cattle dip fluid |CITS: [Green18][13229843]|, geothermal springs |CITS: [Salmassi02]| and arsenic-contaminated ground water |CITS: [10406083]|., Both chemolithoautotrophic and heterotrophic arsenite-oxidizing bacteria have been identified, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-76588| |CITS: [Leblanc95]|, |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [Leblanc95]|, |FRAME: TAX-204773| |CITS: [12486049]|, |FRAME: TAX-511| |CITS: [1331097]|, |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [7219219]|, |FRAME: TAX-47420| |CITS: [15178476]|, and |FRAME: TAX-286| |CITS: [7219219]|, as well as the thermophiles |FRAME: TAX-271| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [11642444]|. Chemolithoautotrophic As(III)-oxidizing bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1125847|, use As(III) as the electron donor, oxygen as the electron acceptor, and carbon dioxide-bicarbonate as the carbon source |CITS: [10618208]|., Since arsenate is far less toxic than arsenite, the oxidation of arsenite can be considered a detoxification process. However, the oxidation of As(III) to As(V), when coupled to the reduction of oxygen to water, is an exergonic process, and it has been suggested that at least some bacteria may derive energy out of this process |CITS: [15178476]|., The most common arsenite oxidase is encoded by the |FRAME: G-8323| and |FRAME: G-8324| genes (AioAB). The enzyme was first purified from |FRAME: TAX-511| in 1992 |CITS: [1331097]|, and was further charaqcterized from different As(III) oxidizers, such as |FRAME: TAX-204773| and |FRAME: TAX-1125847| |CITS: [10618208][12486049][28496149][28801050]|. Homologs of the genes encoding AioAB have been found in phylogenetically diverse strains including members of α-,β-,γ-Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Aquificae, Bacteroidetes, Chlorobi, Chloroflexi, Crenarchaeota, Deinococcus-Thermus, Firmicutes and Nitrospira |CITS: [24507904]|., AioBA is a heterotetramer consisting of a large catalytic subunit (AioA) and a small subunit (AioB) located on the periplasmic surface of the inner membrane. AioA is divided into four domains, in which domain I contains a bound [3Fe-4S] cluster and a Rieske subunit and domains II-IV contain bound molybdenum |CITS: [11250197]|. AioB contains a Rieske [2Fe-2S] domain, which is homologous to |FRAME: CPLX-8219|, |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.6| (cytochrome b6f) and |FRAME: EC-1.14.12.12| |CITS: [11250197]|., During the initial purification of the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-511| it was reported that it can transfer the electrons to either an azurin or a c-type cytochrome |CITS: [1331097]|. The activity with azurin was classified as |FRAME: EC-1.20.9.1|, while activity with c-type cytochrome was classified as |FRAME: EC-1.20.2.1|. Subsequent work with the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-375569| identified only a c551-type cytochrome as the dedicated electron acceptor |CITS: [15178476]|, and a study of the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-1125847| also found only a periplasmic c-type cytochrome (c552) that serves as the electron acceptor for the enzyme |CITS: [17306216][23891971]|., Disruption of the gene encoding the cytochrome c550 in |FRAME: TAX-1315272| did not completely block bacterial As(III) oxidation, leading to the discovery of a novel protein involved in As(III) oxidation electron transport, which was named |FRAME: MONOMER-21714 AioE| |CITS: [28128323]|. The protein (Uniprot accession I6R3V7) has been originally annotated as an FAD-dependent pyridine nucleotide-disulfide oxidoreductase. The redox potential gradient is AioBA > AioE > CytC550, leading to the suggestion that AioE functions as the direct electron acceptor for AioAB. Deletion of aioE resulted in a null As(III) oxidation phenotype and decreased the production of NADH |CITS: [28128323]|. The authors reported that AioE belongs to the TrkA family, and speculated that because of that AioE may reduce NAD+ to NADH and H+ in addition to transfering electrons to the cytochrome, due to the presence of an NAD(P)-binding domain |CITS: [28128323]|.

Summary: The pentitols |FRAME: CPD-355| (D-arabinol) and |FRAME: RIBITOL| are common in nature, while the pentitols |FRAME: XYLITOL| and |FRAME: L-ARABITOL| are rare or absent., Pentitols and other neutral polyols can be taken up by bacteria and serve as a carbon and energy source. Gram-negative bacteria and Actinobacteria import the polyol intact, convert them into a keto sugar by a polyol hydrogenase, and then phosphorylate the keto sugar and metabolize it via the pentose phosphate or glycolytic pathways (this pathway). Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1582| |CITS: [118163]| and |FRAME:TAX-33945| |CITS: [12467497]|, transport polyols into the cell using a phosphotransferase system, resulting in their phosphoylation. The polyol phosphates are then oxidized by polyol phosphate dehydrogenases (see |FRAME: PWY-8392|). , Several species of enteric bacteria have been shown to have naturally occurring D-arabitol degradation pathways as indicated here. Approximately 85% of |FRAME:TAX-570| strains and 10% of |FRAME:TAX-562| strains can degrade D-arabitol and ribitol (|FRAME:TAX-562| K-12 and B strains do not utilize these compounds) (|CITS: [1097416]| and in |CITS: [9639934]|). The genes form an operon encoding an NAD-dependent dehydrogenase, an ATP-dependent kinase, and a specific H+ symporter controlled by a repressor, with D-arabitol as the inducer (in |CITS: [9639934]|). In |FRAME:TAX-294| a putative operon contains genes for an ABC-type transport complex, a polyol dehydrogenase, and two kinases for the transport and utilization of D-arabitol and the hexitols |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: SORBITOL|. The mannitol dehydrogenase encoded by mtlD has a broad substrate specificity, oxidizing all three polyols to the corresponding keto sugars (in |CITS: [9666063]|). , In this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-355| is transported into the cell, converted to the ketopentose |FRAME: D-XYLULOSE|, and then phosphorylated. |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a common intermediate in pentose and pentitol metabolism, can enter the pentose phosphate pathway., Examples of other pentitol degradation pathways include |FRAME: RIBITOLUTIL-PWY| and |FRAME: LARABITOLUTIL-PWY|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-183 "Gallate"| and structurally related compounds are widely distributed in nature. Plant lignin and tannins are major sources of these compounds, which are degraded by soil microorganisms as part of the terrestrial carbon cycle. , Gallate is also used industrially in inks and paints, and gallate esters are used as food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical antioxidants. Gallate and its derivatives are also of interest in drug development (reviewed in |CITS: [12769668]|. , Gallate and related compounds contain a benzene nucleus and at least 2 phenolic hydroxyl groups. Under aerobic conditions the benzene ring is cleaved by varioius dioxygenases. The benzene nucleus can be cleaved by ortho or meta fission enzymes, leading to different degradation pathways. Several distinct pathways of aerobic aromatic catabolism can be initiated by these dioxygenases, and their distribution among bacteria is complex |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|. Examples of these oxidative pathways are shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|, |FRAME: METHYLGALLATE-DEGRADATION-PWY|, , |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY-2504|., An anaerobic pathway for gallate degradation is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P3-PWY|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME:CPLX-8177 "Gallate dioxygenase"| is a ring-cleavage dioxygenase found in several gallate-degrading organisms that acts specifically on |FRAME: CPD-183| to produce the keto-tautomer of 4-oxalomesaconate |CITS:[16030014][Nogales10]|. The enzyme shares a common ancestor with |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, and has a two-domain architecture that might have evolved from the fusion of the large and small subunits of the latter. In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-285|, it has been shown that |FRAME: CPLX-2701| can catalyze the same reaction, although with lower efficiency |CITS: [5048285]|., The product of the ring cleavage is the keto tautomer of 4-oxalomesaconate, |FRAME: 4-OXALOMESACONATE| |CITS: [Nogales10]|. While it can form the enol form, |FRAME: CPD-185|, spontaneously, it has been shown that in |FRAME: TAX-160488| a dedicated enzyme, |FRAME: G1G01-2697-MONOMER|, catalyzes this conversion |CITS: [Nogales10]|. , The enol form is the substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-2781| |CITS: [11092855]|, and the product of this enzyme, |FRAME: 4-OH-4-ACETYL-2-OXOGLUTARATE|, is cleaved by an aldolase to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, which enter central metabolism |CITS: [12486039]|., Fluorescent pseudomonads, such as |FRAME:TAX-303|, can also cleave gallate by the ortho cleavage enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-2721|, resulting in formation of the lactone |FRAME: CPD-184| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|).

Oryzalide such as |FRAME:CPD-16665| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-16735| are diterpenoid phytoalexins found in rice |CITS:[Kono91] [Watanabe90]| where they are formed in response to phytopathogenic attacks |CITS:[14527276]|. |FRAME:CPD-16665 Oryzalide A|, |FRAME:CPD-16735| and other oryzlide-related compounds such as oryzadione |CITS:[15184015]| and acidic derivatives of oryzalide |CITS:[Watanabe92]| accumulate especially in lesion areas after infestation |CITS:[Watanabe96]| indicating the involvement of oryzalide and derivatives in the defense system of Oryza sativa. The elucidation of the biosynthesis of the various phytoalexins in rice has become the focus of research for two reasons: 1) Rice belongs to the most important food plants in the world and provides the staple food for half of the world's population |CITS:[Seck12]| and 2) the emerging theme of biogenetic clusters in plants |CITS:[20921179]| which are usually only a common feature in microbes |CITS:[18216259]| but appear to exist on two chromosomes (2 and 4) in rice |CITS:[19662496]|., The oryzalide biosynthesis starts like all the other subclasses of rice diterpenoid phytoalexins (see |FRAME:PWY-7477|, |FRAME:PWY-7478|, |FRAME:PWY-7489| and |FRAME:PWY-7484|) with the bicyclization of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (see |FRAME:PWY-2981|) |CITS:[17634747]|. Oryzalide derive from |FRAME: ENT-COPALYL-DIPHOSPHATE| but only a few steps of the pathway have been described so far. Most of the enzymes characterized in rice and involved in the biosynthesis of the various diterpenoid phytoalexins have been codon optimized, N-terminally modified for bacterial expression using and introduced to an modular metabolic engineered system in E. coli |CITS:[17480080]| and the enzymes involved in |FRAME:PWY-7481| are no exception., Labdane-related diterpene synthases exhibit a high degree of stereospecificity |CITS:[20890488]|. The enzymes catalyzing the committed step in oryzalide biosynthesis, i.e. |FRAME:MONOMER-18622| forming |FRAME:CPD-11534| from |FRAME: ENT-COPALYL-DIPHOSPHATE| |CITS:[17141283] [16861806]| are very stereospecific. However, it has been shown that a singular switch of an amino acid residue in the active site of the enzyme will fundamentally change the product outcome from the same substrate. Whereas the enzyme of the indica group of Oryza sativa will produce |FRAME:CPD-11534| the same enzyme from the japonica group of rice will not and produces |FRAME:CPD-7097| instead |CITS:[17456599]|. The next and last known reaction in the biosynthetic route is catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-18621| which very specifically hydroxylates |FRAME:CPD-11534| at C-2α forming the respective |FRAME:CPD-13920| which is an presumed intermediate in |FRAME:PWY-7481| |CITS:[21985968] [17634747]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium Selenium| is an essential micronutrient for animals and humans but has not yet been proven to be an essential micronutrient for land plants |CITS: [11683552][16307305]|. There is evidence, however, of Chlamydomonas proteins that contains a |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| residue suggesting that algal species might also require |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [17105189][12110581]|. The health requirement of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for humans and animals can be met by crops and forage plants that contain selenocompounds. |FRAME: TAX-4232| among the oilseed crops was shown to be a good source for this micronutrient |CITS: [15012198]|. In addition, there is evidence that certain seleno-compounds, including |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12024|, have anti-carcinogenic properties |CITS: [14748935]|. , Despite its importance as a micronutrient, higher concentrations of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| are toxic to humans, other animals, and plants largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064][12753978][16661781]|. , In general, plants take up both |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE| from soil. A series of |FRAME: PWY-6932 reduction steps| converts |FRAME: SELENATE| to |FRAME: SE-2| / |FRAME: CPD-678| and this is assimilated into the seleno-amino acids |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19309459]|., In Se accumulator plants, these seleno-amino acids may be modified to create storage compounds that are presumably sequestered in the vacuoles. Seasonal weeds like |FRAME: TAX-3575| and |FRAME: TAX-83445| along with perennial weeds like |FRAME: TAX-41550| employ this strategy and accumulate high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| in organic seleno-compounds |CITS: [19800657]|. Se accumulation can help to protect plants against attacks by prairie dogs, insects, and fungi (see refs in |CITS: [21628258]|)., Other plants, like |FRAME: ORG-5993| generate seleno-compounds as well, but rather than storing them, they transform them into less toxic volatile compounds, such as |FRAME: CPD-12005| (DMSe) that can then be released from the plants |CITS: [10759525]|. This process is also called phytovolatilization |CITS: [19656903]|. , While these strategies directly benefit the plants that employ them, they can also be put to use for the phytoremediation of seleniferous soils that contain dangerously high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium|. Numerous insights into endogenous seleno-compound metabolism in plants have been gained through efforts to engineer plants that show improved selenium phytoremediation abilities |CITS: [15005814][19800657][19893365][17445958][10759525]|., About This Pathway, To reduce the risk of misincorporating |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| into proteins, this compound can be methylated to form the non-coding seleno-amino acid |FRAME: CPD-12025|. Some Se hyperaccumulating plants may sequester this compound., Both Se-non-accumulators and accumulators may also further metabolize |FRAME: CPD-12025| to produce the volatile |FRAME: CPD-12005|. This could occur in at least two manners. In the hyperaccumulator |FRAME:TAX-15853| species, this may occur in a |FRAME: PWY-6935 four-step process| that involves the formation of the intermediate compound |FRAME: CPD-13720|. However, this intermediate is not likely produced in Arabidopsis and many other plants. Therefore, this one-step variant has been proposed. Formation of |FRAME: CPD-12005| may be catalyzed by a putative methylmethionine / Se-methyl-Se-methionine hydrolase in Arabidopsis thaliana and other plants, but no such enzyme has been identified or characterized yet, particularly with respect to seleno-compound metabolism |CITS: [12376649]|. It is also possible that this reaction may happen spontaneously through chemical decomposition, but this would be expected to occur very slowly at physiological pH., Roots may be the primary site of |FRAME: CPD-12005| production (see citations in |CITS: [9701603]|).

Nitroaromatic compounds are found in many pesticides, dyes, explosives, and solvents,, and they also serve as precursors for the production of aminoaromatic derivatives., Because of their common usage, nitroaromatic compounds have become pollutants in rivers,, wastewaters, groundwaters, pesticide-treated soils, and the atmosphere., |FRAME: CPD-258| (ONP) and |FRAME: CPD-8179| have been listed as priority pollutants by the, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Degradation of |FRAME: CPD-258| by Pseudomonas has been reported several times in the literature, |CITS:[13093710][14114131]|., A |FRAME:TAX-303| strain that grew on |FRAME: CPD-258| and |FRAME: CPD-9127| as sole sources, of carbon and nitrogen was isolated from soil by Zeyer and Kearney |CITS: [Zeyer84]|., Growing and resting cells degraded |FRAME: CPD-258| and released |FRAME: NITRITE|., Experiments with a cell-free system demonstrated that the organism possessed an inducible enzyme, that degraded |FRAME: CPD-258| to |FRAME: NITRITE| and |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [Zeyer84]|., The later was further degraded via |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| by the ortho-cleavage system, (see |FRAME: PWY-5417| |CITS: [3752997]|., The responsible enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-13318|, has been purified and characterized, |CITS: [3350791]|.

Several different enzymes convert |FRAME: LYS| to |FRAME: ALLYSINE|, as shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5298|, |FRAME: PWY-5314| and |FRAME: PWY-5324|., |FRAME: ALLYSINE| spontaneously cyclizes in solution to form |FRAME: CPD-7682| |CITS: [6801024]|. , A novel, inducible |FRAME: MONOMER-12465| has been characterized in the industrially relevant , yeast |FRAME: TAX-4929 "Meyerozyma guilliermondii (anamorph Candida guilliermondii)"|. This enzyme specifically uses L-lysine as amino group donor and pyruvate as amino group acceptor to produce |FRAME: ALLYSINE| and L-alanine. The organism is able to use L-lysine as a sole nitrogen source, but not as a sole carbon source. When |FRAME: TAX-4929| is grown with ammonia as the sole nitrogen source the enzyme is present in very low amounts, but it increases over 100-fold when cells are grown with L-lysine as the sole nitrogen source. , The high inducibility of L-lysine:pyruvate:aminotransferase by L-lysine, the absence of any other lysine-degrading enzyme activities in this organism, and the isolation of regulatory mutants of this enzyme that are unable to use L-lysine as sole nitrogen source, provides evidence that L-lysine:pyruvate:aminotransferase plays an important role as the first step in lysine catabolism in |FRAME: TAX-4929| |CITS: [87SCHMIDT] [88SCHMIDT]|., Further metabolism of |FRAME: CPD-7682| has not been described in |FRAME: TAX-4929|, although this compound is metabolized via |FRAME: CPD-468| to glutarate by |FRAME: TAX-303| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5283|).

Summary: Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins, including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. , In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in, transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as, |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in, modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|,, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., The protoheme biosynthetic pathway shown here is found in some bacteria (including, |FRAME: TAX-83333|), archaea, and plants. In these organisms the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway, starts with glutamate (see |FRAME: PWY-5188|)., In many other organisms, including animals, fungi, apicomplexan protozoa (such as the malaria parasite, |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [15144063]|), and members of the α-proteobacteria, the tetrapyrrole, biosynthesis pathway starts with glycine and succinyl-CoA (see |FRAME:PWY-5189|)., Both the glycine and glutamate pathways are present in the chloroplast-containing |FRAME: TAX-3039|, (reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [15576047], [12051904], [16093570]|)., Both tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathways merge at the intermediate |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE|., However, a branch point at |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| leads to biosynthesis of different, compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|),, |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|),, and heme D biosynthesis., A second branch point at |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| leads to biosynthesis of chlorophyll, in plants and bacteriochlorophyll in photosynthetic bacteria (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|)., In eukaryotes, heme biosynthesis spans the mitochondrial (or plastid) and cytosol compartments., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [12177321], [16093570]|.

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., IAA (indole-3-acetic acid), one of the most common active forms of the phytohormone auxin, is often, present in conjugated forms. Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. Meanwhile, conjugated forms of auxin play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., About This Pathway, The maize degradation pathway depicted here is based on in-vivo feeding experiments and in-vitro assays with plant extracts. The genes and enzymes involved in the pathway are still unknown.

Names: 9-lipoxygenase and 9-hydroperoxide lyase pathway // 9-LOX and 9-HPL pathway // 9-oxo-nonanoate biosynthesis
Summary: Lipoxygenases (LOX) are nonheme iron-containing enzymes that catalyze the dioxygenation of fatty acids with a 1,4-pentadiene structure, generating hydroperoxy fatty acids. The enzymes are ubiquitous among eukaryotes. In plants, LOX enzymes are known to insert oxygen at position C-9 (9-LOX) (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.58|) or position C-13 (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.12|) of |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, the most abundant fatty acids in plant membrane lipids |CITS: [12452441]|., The oxygen is inserted into one of the carbons that participate in the cis double bonds of the substrate. During the process that bond is moved to a neighboring carbon and changes to a trans configuration. So, for example, |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| ((9Z,12Z)-octadeca-9,12-dienoate) becomes |FRAME: CPD-8677| (9(S)-hydroperoxy-10(E),12(Z)-octadecadienoate) via 9-LOX activity, and |FRAME: 13-HYDROPEROXYOCTADECA-911-DIENOATE| via 13-LOX activity (see |FRAME: PWY-5410|). In plants, most reported LOXs are 13-LOXs, which catalyze the first reaction in |FRAME: PWY-735|., The hydroperoxide intermediates can be converted to aldehydes and oxoacids by hydroperoxide lyases (HPL). HPLs are divided into two groups, 9-HPL and 13-HPL, depending on their substrate preferences, either being 9-hydroperoxides, or 13-hydroperoxides. The aldehydes produced by 9-HPL are known as defense compounds, as well as imparting special flavors. For example, (2E)-nonenal gives the cardboard flavor of aged beer, and the off-flavor of aged milled rice. 9-HPL activity has only been reported from a few plant species including rice and cucumber.

Names: GDP-L-fucose biosynthesis II (from L-fucose) // GDP-L-fucose biosynthesis (salvage pathway)
Summary: General Background, L-Fucose is an important monosaccharide found in a diverse array of organisms. It is a carbohydrate component of bacterial lipopolysaccharides, mammalian and plant glycoproteins (such as the human antigenic glycoproteins or glycolipids of erythrocyte membranes) and various plant cell wall polysaccharides. It is found in xyloglucans and rhamnogalacturonans I and II. Fucosylation is performed by fucosyltransferases which require the activated form GDP-L-fucose (GDP-Fuc) as the donor substrate., The formation of UDP-Fuc occurs via two routes: a) a salvage pathway leading to the formation of UDP-Fuc from free L-fucose (this pathway), and b) a de novo synthesis route from GDP-D-mannose (|FRAME:PWY-66|). , In plants, biosynthesis of GDP-L-fucose is thought to occur mainly through de novo synthesis. The primary role of the sugar salvage pathways is presumed to be in the recycling of sugars derived from the turnover of macromolecules such as polysaccharides, galactolipids and proteoglycans, which have sugar components. Although the presence of GDP-L-fucose pyrophosphorylase activity in sycamore cell cultures and corn roots has been suggested |CITS:[5704313],[646802]| no enzyme of this pathway have yet been described in plants.

General Background, The two acyclic homoterpenes |FRAME:CPD-8844| (DMNT) and |FRAME:CPD-8846| (TMTT) are widespread constituents of flower fragrances |CITS:[boland89][gabler91],[donath95]|. These homoterpenes are released from the foliage of many plant species following herbivore damage |CITS:[boland92],[dicke94]|, and are part of the arsenal used in plant tritrophic 'indirect defense', which uses the volatile compounds to attract predators of the herbivores and help them locate their prey so that they do less damage to the host plants |CITS:[Dicke99][10517823][16723271]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-8844| is known to be produced from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-5434|. However, an unexpected second route for its production has been discovered., In this route, whic occurs in roots, the compound is produced from the C30 triterpene diol |FRAME: CPD-10307| by the action of a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase encoded by the |FRAME: AT4G15330| gene |CITS: [25724638]|., The |FRAME: AT4G15330| gene clusters with the arabidiol synthase gene |FRAME: AT4G15340|, and both genes are coexpressed constitutively in the root stele and meristematic tissue |CITS: [25724638]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFAs) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes. The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in the |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived compounds (though the term is often used to include metabolites of 18- and 22-carbon PUFAs). , This pathway describes how |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| is liberated from common glycerophopholipids and sterols in the cell, and how it is converted to some of the more common icosanoids.

Names: phosphatidylinositol biosynthesis I (bacteria) // L-1-phosphatidyl-inositol biosynthesis I (bacteria)
Summary: |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "L-1-phosphatidylinositols"| (PI) are glycerophospholipids that serve as a a minor component in the cytosolic side of eukaryotic cell membranes., Phosphatidylinositol lipids are known as inositides or phosphoinositides. The most common fatty acids of mammalian phosphatidylinositols are |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| in the sn-1 position and |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| in the sn-2 position., Inositol, the polar head of PI, is commonly found in archaebacteria, where its derivatives serve an important role in osmotic protection at high temperatures |CITS: [12220406]|, but is absent (or present in very low amounts) from most eubacteria, with the exception of the Actinomycetales group, which contains the streptomycetes, corynebacteria and mycobacteria., These organisms use inositol for the synthesis of a major thiol called mycothiol |CITS: [11544359]| (see |FRAME: PWY1G-0|), and for production of |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "phosphatidylinositol"|, which is used in several cell wall lipoglycans. In these compounds the lipid moieties of PI act as anchors in the cell envelope. PI-containing molecules have been shown to be essential for growth of the fast-growing species |FRAME: TAX-1772| |CITS: [10889206]|., In Eukaryotes PI is synthsized from |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL| in a single step, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: YPR113W-MONOMER| (see|FRAME: PWY-7625|). Bacteria do not possess this enzyme. Instead, they use a |FRAME: G185E-6855-MONOMER|, which uses |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| rather than |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| as a substrate. The product of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-177|, is converted to |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "phosphatidylinositol"| by a phosphatase |CITS: [20798167]|., While the pathway was initially studied in mycobacteria |CITS: [20798167]|, it was later shown to be universal in bacteria that contain inositol phospholipids. Phosphatidylinositol phosphate synthase enzymes have been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-33903|, |FRAME: TAX-1747|, |FRAME: TAX-1718|, and |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [24269814]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Strigolactones Strigolactones| are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi., The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635 "Gossypium hirsutum (cotton)"| infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels |CITS: [17780042]|., Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| |CITS: [Hauck92]|, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| |CITS: [Mueler92]| and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) |CITS: [Yokota98]|., The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis |CITS: [15944687]|., The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone |CITS: [Mosse73]|., Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interaction between the fungi and the roots., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-28130 Sorgomol| is a strigol-type strigolactone hormone identified in 2008 from sorghum (|FRAME: TAX-4558|) and shown to act as germination stimulant for root parasitic plants from the |FRAME: TAX-4169| and |FRAME: TAX-36747| genera. Its structure was found to be very similar to that of |FRAME: CPD-14652|, with hydroxylation on C-9 |CITS: [Xie8]|. The compound was later identified in root exudates from other plants, such as |FRAME: TAX-3870| (white lupin) |CITS: [19222028]|, |FRAME: TAX-16752| |CITS: [23290861]|, |FRAME: TAX-4232| (sunflower) |CITS: [26252191]|, and |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) |CITS: [29294064][30363087]|. It was reported to be produced from |FRAME: CPD-14652| by hydroxylation carried out by a cytochrome P450 enzyme |CITS: [23597492]|., The enzyme was identified in 2021 by performiong RNA-seq analysis on root tissue from sorghum grown in conditions that are known to favor strigolactone production. The enzyme was purified and shown to catalyze the reaction in vitro and also ex vivo when overexpressed in hairy roots of |FRAME: TAX-34305| |CITS: [33793911]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22470 "Kainate"| is an ionotropic glutamate receptor agonist that has been used to discover and characterize several classes of ionotropic glutamate receptors. The |FRAME: TAX-2763 "red algae lineage"| has been observed to contain gene clusters for |FRAME: PWY-8080|., About This Pathway, Kainate biosynthesis starts with the prenylation of |FRAME: GLT| with |FRAME: CPD-4211| to produce |FRAME: CPD-22469|. |FRAME: CPD-22469 "Prekainate"| is then cyclized to produce |FRAME: CPD-22470| and |FRAME: CPD-22472|. Presence of all compounds produced by the proposed kainate biosynthesis pathway was confirmed through LCMS analysis of |FRAME: TAX-945030| aqueous extract |CITS: [30995339]|.

General Background, Plants often store carbohydrates by synthesizing |FRAME: Cyclitols|, such as |FRAME: CPD-8056|, due to their high solubility and metabolically inert characteristics |CITS: [29281092]|. A highly studied example of cyclitols biosynthesis is |FRAME: PWY-6738|, which |FRAME: PWY-8078| is similar to. , About This Pathway, The gene for |FRAME: MONOMER-20881|, |FRAME: G-80444|, was found by screening the |FRAME: TAX-151069| genome for genes with sequence homology to |FRAME: MONOMER-16307|, an enzyme that catalyzes a similar methyltransferase reaction found in the |FRAME: PWY-6738| pathway. When |FRAME: G-80444| was heterologously expressed and purified, the recombinant enzyme demonstrated inositol methyltransferase activity in vitro. , Concentrations of |FRAME: 1-METHYL-MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-8056| were reduced in mature leaves when |FRAME: MONOMER-20881| expression was silenced using virus-induced gene silencing, demonstrating that its activity is important for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-8056| in the |FRAME: TAX-151069| plant. The last step for quebrachitol biosynthesis, |FRAME: RXN-20799 "the epimerization of D-bornesitol to L-quebrachitol"|, has not been fully elucidated as of 2018 |CITS: [29281092]|.

Cyclic hydroxamic acids and particularly their aglycone forms have been reported to be involved in the defense of plants against a wide range of pathogens and insects. The aglycone forms are autotoxic and are generally found stored in plants in their 2-O-β-D-glucoside form |CITS:[CAMBIER99]|., The toxic aglycone is enzymatically released by the action of β-glucosidases (the origin of which can be from the compromised plant or the pathogen itself).
