Summary: |FRAME: CPD-15747| is a 2,3,6-trideoxysugar found in several antibiotics, such as |FRAME: CPD-14693| and |FRAME: CPD-12245|, the antibiotic of choice against |FRAME: CPD-9220|-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA). The emergence of vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) strains has focused research on understanding the nature of the binding of these antibiotics to their substrates, leading to modifications that may overcome the resistance, and their biosynthesis, in the hope of being able to alter the pathway to introduce the desired modifications., The biosynthetic pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-15747| has been studied in the |FRAME: CPD-14693|-producer |FRAME: TAX-31958|. The gene cluster encoding |FRAME: CPD-14693| production has been sequenced and found to contain 39 genes which are involved in the biosynthesis of the heptapeptide backbone and |FRAME: CPD-15747|, and the additional chlorination and oxidation reactions that are involved. Of the 39 genes, four (orf23-orf26, now |FRAME: G-17927|, |FRAME: G-17931|, |FRAME: G-17928| and |FRAME: G-17930|, respectively) were proposed to be involved in biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15746|, the activated form of the sugar |CITS: [9545426]|., A subsequent study has identified an additional gene (orf14, now evaC) that is involved. The five genes were cloned, heterogeniously expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified to near-homogeneity and studied |CITS: [11035791]|. The five enzymes reconstituted the complete biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15746| from |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in a process that involves C-2 deoxygenation, C-3 amination and methylation, C-5 epimerization, and C-4 ketoreduction. The final product's identity was confirmed by mass spectrometry and NMR |CITS: [11035791]|., These enzymes were also used to produce |FRAME: CPD-15746 | in a study of |FRAME: CPLX-8810|, an enzyme from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47853| that modifies the amino group of the sugar to a nitoso group, leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-16419|, a component of the octasaccharide antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-16431| produced by that organism |CITS: [20866105]|.

The term |FRAME: Vitamin-E| (tocochromenols) is a collective term for the eight forms of |FRAME: Tocotrienols tocotrienols| and |FRAME: Tocopherols tocopherols|, each existing as α, β, γ, and δ species., Structurally tocotrienols and tocopherols differ only in the degree of unsaturation of their side-chain. The tocotrienol chain comprises three trans-double bonds, whereas the tocopherol chain is fully saturated. In addition, the α, β, γ, and δ species of both compound groups vary in the methylation pattern of the chromanol ring |CITS:[12897790]|., The tocotrienols are mostly found in monocots |CITS:[Padley94]| and a few dicots |CITS:[17110122]| whereas tocopherols are wider spread in the plant kingdom and dominate in the dicots |CITS:[8827691]|. Tocotrienols are known as potent antioxidant and because of that have been appreciated for their nutritive value in human food and animal fodder |CITS:[8464850]|. Moreover, health-promoting assets of tocotrienols such as anticancer properties |CITS:[22095072]| made this compound group commercially interesting as nutraceuticals., The biosynthetic pathway of tocotrienols (this pathway) only differs in one step from the biosynthesis of tocopherols (see |FRAME:PWY-1422|). The first committed step of the pathway catalyzed by the homogentisate geranylgeranyl transferase (HGGT) is characterized by the high acceptance of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| over the similar |FRAME:PHYTYL-PYROPHOSPHATE| which leads the way into tocopherol biosynthesis |CITS:[12897790] [21223386]|. All other enzymes after this step, i.e. tocopherol cyclases |CITS:[18810749] [23733887]| and tocopherol methyltransferases |CITS:[22763462]| can work with either one of the precursors and produce either tocotrienols, tocopherols or a mixture of both. This could also be demonstrated by introducing barley HGGT to species which do not produce tocotrienols, e.g. Arabidopsis, corn and tobacco. As a result of the transformation the transgenic plants produced predominantly tocotrienols and enhanced the overall production of vitamin E in those species |CITS:[12897790] [21223386] [18810749] [526275]|.

General Background, The inorganic sulfur compound |FRAME: S2O3| contains two sulfur atoms: a sulfone-sulfur (oxidation state +V), and a sulfane-sulfur (oxidation state -I). At low pH thiosulfate decomposes spontaneously to |FRAME: SO3| and elemental sulfur, |CITS: [4552952]|. At neutral pH the compound is relatively stable, but several types of bacteria can catalyze its disproportionation in a process in which thiosulfate serves as both an electron donor and an electron acceptor. , Several types of enzymes have been described that are able to catalyze the disproportionation of thiosulfate. These enzymes have been differentiated based on the nature of the electron donor: some enzymes require thiols for this purpose, some utilize cytochrome c3, which receives the electrons from molecular hydrogen via a hydrogenase, some accept the electrons from the quinone pool, and some have only been active in vitro when coupled to cyanide. These four classes of enzymes are described in the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5277|, |FRAME:PWY-5352|, |FRAME: PWY-7813|, and |FRAME:PWY-5350|, respectively., About This Pathway, Thiol-dependent thiosulfate reductases occur in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms of different phyla |CITS: [13654229][14484816][5658075][3480285][16535035][10959561]|., A |FRAME: TAX-4932| enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of thiosulfate to sulfide and sulfite has been described as early as 1959 |CITS: [13654229]|. The enzyme, which was named |FRAME: G3O-33772-MONOMER| (official name thiosulfate-thiol sulfurtransferase), requires the presence of thiols, such as |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE|, |FRAME:CYS| and |FRAME:HOMO-CYS| |CITS: [6849932]|., The reaction with glutathione was investigated in much detail, and kinetic studies showed that a |FRAME: CPD-11281| intermmediate was formed. The authors concluded that the enzyme only catalyzed the transfer of the sulfane sulfur to the thiol, forming sulfite and a persulfide, and that spontaneous reaction of the persulfide with excess thiol released the free, |FRAME:HS| as the final product |CITS: [3309558]|., The formal mechanism of the reaction has been described as rapid equilibrium-ordered with glutathione as the leading substrate |CITS: [6361026]|. It is still not known which thiols are the natural substrates for the enzyme., The reduction of thiosulfate in the presence of glutathione was described in bacteria as well. A 1959 paper describes the formation of polythionates from thiosulfate and glutathione in |FRAME: TAX-930|. The reaction required the presence of glutathione |CITS: [16590379]|. A few years later Peck et al. suggested the participation of a thiol-dependent thiosulfate reductase in the oxidation of thiosulfate by the Gram-negative sulfur-oxidizing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-931| |CITS: [16590712][14484816]|. These authors also found that glutathione was necessary for activity., The distinction between thiosulfate reductase and rhodanese (|FRAME: EC-2.8.1.1|) is not always straight forward. For example, Aird et al. purified an enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-471| that could catalyze either reaction under different conditions |CITS: [3480285]|.

Summary: Phenylpropanoid compounds are abundant in natural environments, and can originate from putrefaction of proteins in soil or as breakdown products of plant materials such as lignin, various oils, and resins (for the biosynthesis of phenylpropanoid compounds, please see |FRAME: PHENYLPROPANOID-SYN|)., Microbial catabolism of phenylpropanoid compounds plays an important role in the natural degradation of these compounds. In addition, the degradation of several phenylpropanoid compounds is important for industrial applications such as wine making, aging, and storage |CITS: [9143125]|. , The degradation of |FRAME: CPD-674 "cinnamate"|, |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE|, and their hydroxylated derivatives has been reported in several bacteria, including an Acinetobacter sp. |CITS: [5881653]|, a Pseudomonas sp. |CITS: [3777934][4348920]|, an Arthrobacter sp. |CITS: [4348920]|, |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [6345502]|, and |FRAME: TAX-33008| |CITS: [9324265]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| this pathway is one of only two aromatic-ring-cleavage pathways that are found in the organism. The fact that |FRAME:TAX-562| can degrade aromatic acids suggests a wider natural distribution for |FRAME:TAX-562| than the anaerobic environment of the animal gut |CITS: [6345502]|. The enzymes of this pathway can metabolize |FRAME: CPD-674| and |FRAME: CPD-10796| as well as |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYPHENYL-PROPIONATE| (see |FRAME: HCAMHPDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [9603882]|., The pathway ultimately yields |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, which is further degraded to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as described in |FRAME: PWY-5162|. The pathway, including the portion that is described in |FRAME: PWY-5162|, has eight steps, making it one of the longest catabolic sequences known in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [3531186][8399388][9098055]|.

Names: meso-butanediol biosynthesis I // (R,S)-butylene glycol fermentation // (R,S)-butanediol fermentation // (R,S)-butanediol biosynthesis
Summary: Many bacterial species can ferment |FRAME:PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2,3-butanediol"| via several intermediate compounds, including |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|, |FRAME: DIACETYL| and |FRAME: ACETOIN|. Not all species carry the process all the way from pyruvate to 2,3-butanediol - some may stop earlier, accumulating some of the intermediates., There are two isomeric forms of acetoin - |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: CPD-255|, and three isomeric forms of 2,3-butanediol (BD ) - |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|, |FRAME: CPD-346| and |FRAME: CPD-12004|. Different organisms produce different forms, or different combinations of the different forms. This pathway describes the production of |FRAME: CPD-12004| from |FRAME: CPD-10353|., The conversion of acetoin to 2,3-butanediol, which is reversible, is performed by the enzyme acetoin reductase (AR), also known as 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenase (BDH)., 4 types of AR activities have been identified, differing in the substrate and product stereo-specificity. One of these activities is the production |FRAME: CPD-12004| from |FRAME: CPD-10353| |CITS: [Ui84]|. Enzymes that catalyze this activity have been characterized from several organisms including |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [Ui97]| and |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS: [8879540]|., The metabolic function of 2,3-butanediol is not yet known, although it may play a role in preventing intracellular, acidification by changing the metabolism from acid production to the formation of a neutral compound, |CITS: [6298028]|.  In addition, the pathway might participate in regulation of the NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio, in the bacteria |CITS: [8444801]|.

General Background, |FRAME: HIS| can be catabolized by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms by two principal routes. The main difference between the two routes is the first step, which is performed by either, a histidase (see |FRAME: HISDEG-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-5028| and, |FRAME: PWY-5030|) or a histidine transaminase (|FRAME: HISTDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5031|). , Two different histidine transaminase-based pathways have been found so far. The prokaryotic, pathway uilizes a |FRAME: HISTTRANSAM-MONOMER| for the first step, while the eukaryotic pathway utilizes a |FRAME: CPLX-6920| for this purpose., About This Pathway, This pathway was detected only in the enterobacterium |FRAME: TAX-37762|, where it appears to be, the only |FRAME: HIS| catabolic pathway |CITS: [13172251][13198941][14081727]|. , The better characterized |FRAME: TAX-83333| does not appear to have the ability to degrade |FRAME: HIS|, at all. , In the first step, |FRAME: HIS| is deaminated to |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE| by the action of a, |FRAME: HISTTRANSAM-MONOMER| |CITS: [4234165]|. In the following reaction,, |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE| is reduced to |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| by a dedicated enzyme,, |FRAME: IMILACTDEHYDROG-MONOMER| |CITS: [4385322][4237631]|. , These two reactions are the only ones that have been characterized in the pathway. , |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| is further metabolized through a ring-opening step into several, undefined acyclic compounds |CITS: [HeregaardBBRC25335]|. , The two enzymes of this pathway have been discovered in other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-80866|, and |FRAME: TAX-285|. However, in these organisms the pathway appears to operate in the opposite direction, converting |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| to |FRAME: HIS|, which is then degraded in the regular, histidase-mediated pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5029 |) |CITS: [4236463]|.

Names: L-glutamate degradation II // L-glutamate - L-aspartate pathway // L-aspartate degradation
Summary: General Background, The first enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1|, catalyzes a reversible reaction that functions in both the biosynthesis and degradation of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| in prokaryotes and eukaryotes (see pathways |FRAME: ASPARTATE-DEG1-PWY|, |FRAME: MALATE-ASPARTATE-SHUTTLE-PWY| and |FRAME: ASPARTATESYN-PWY|). It also functions in the bacterial pathway for |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| degradation shown here (see About This Pathway below). Other routes for |FRAME: GLT| degradation in prokaryotes and eukaryotes are indicated in the glutamate degradation pathway variant links on this page., The second enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.1| (aspartase), also catalyzes a reversible reaction, but its physiological role in most bacteria appears to be in the |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| degradation (deamination) direction as shown here. In |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| auxotrophy requires mutations in both aspC and tyrB, encoding aspartate aminotransferase and tyrosine aminotransferase, respectively (reviewed in Reitzer, L. (2004) "Biosynthesis of Glutamate, Aspartate, Asparagine, l-Alanine, and d-Alanine" EcoSal 3.6.1.3 |CITS: [ecosal]|). In |FRAME: TAX-1423| aspartase was shown to be required for growth on |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| as sole carbon source |CITS: [403177]|. , Literature reports have raised the possibility that aspartase may also function in vivo in an |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| biosynthetic (amination of |FRAME: FUM|) direction in some organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-294| |CITS: [1331036] [804298]|. Industrially, the intracellular aspartase in immobilized whole cells of |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [4598223] [39611] [7763346]| and |FRAME: TAX-92706| |CITS: [TERASAWA85] [7789816]| has been used as a biocatalyst to synthesize |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| under optimized strain and bioprocess conditions. Purified aspartase from |FRAME: TAX-562| is also used industrially for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| |CITS: [39611] [17650675]|., Interestingly, a 1963 report showed that growing or resting cells of Bacterium cadaveris ATCC 9760 (|FRAME: TAX-569|) were able to utilize |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| via the activity of aspartase. Partially purified aspartase from this organism catalyzed the condensation of the strong nucleophile |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| with |FRAME: FUM| to produce |FRAME: CPD-13364| |CITS: [14087356]|. More recently, the thermotolerant aspartase from |FRAME: TAX-96471| (AspB) was shown to utilize various alternative amine substrates in the amination reaction in vitro to produce N-substituted aspartic acids that are of interest in industrial applications |CITS: [19490103] [18844200]| and |CITS: [10334861]|., About This Pathway, The primary pathway using |FRAME: GLT| as a carbon source in |FRAME: TAX-83333| involves transamination with |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, yielding |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS:[13710926] [4888774]|. The reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME:ASPAMINOTRANS-DIMER|., The |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| thus formed is converted to |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| by |FRAME:ASPARTASE-CPLX|, also known as aspartase. The |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| needed to continue the reaction is regenerated through the |FRAME: TCA|., Mutants unable to form either of these two enzymes lost the ability to utilize |FRAME: GLT| as a carbon source |CITS: [4898223]|. The same pathway has been shown to exist in |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [28074]|.

Names: estradiol biosynthesis II // estrogen biosynthesis II
Summary: |FRAME: Estrogens Estrogens| are steroid hormones synthesized in the ovaries, breasts, adipose and other tissues that are critical for sexual development and function. They can also act as inducers of tumour growth in estrogen dependent cancerous tissues and as such are targets for widely used anti-cancer therapies, such as |FRAME: CPD-4541| and |FRAME: HS06413 aromatase| inhibitors. Estrogen levels at baseline and when increased during pregnancy correlate with breast cancer risk, so enzymes in this pathway are targets of existing or potential cancer therapies., The main estrogens in humans are |FRAME: ESTRONE|, |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRIOL|, which differ in the number of hydroxyl groups (one for |FRAME: ESTRONE|, two for |FRAME: CPD-352| and three for |FRAME: ESTRIOL|). |FRAME: CPD-352| is about 10 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRONE| and about 80 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRIOL| in its estrogenic effect., |FRAME: CPD-352| is the predominant estrogen in non-pregenant women during their reproductive years in terms of serum levels. |FRAME: ESTRONE Estrone| is the predominant circulating estrogen in women during menopause and |FRAME: ESTRIOL| is the predominant circulating estrogen during pregnancy., In premenapausal women 17β-estradiol is produced by the granulosa cells of the ovaries by the aromatization of |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| (via |FRAME: ESTRONE|) as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY66-380|. However, ||FRAME: CPD-352| is also produced as an active metabolic product of testosterone as described here. This pathway is the main pathway for |FRAME: CPD-352| synthesis in males, which contain the hormone at roughly the same concentration as postmenopausal women. , The key enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: HS06413| (aromatase), which is required for all estrogen production. This enzyme, which acts an a monooxygenase to make the first carbon ring aromatic, is the target of the aromatase inhibitors which are given to post-menopausal breast cancer patients.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-18054 Fusarin C| is a mycotoxin produced from various species across the fungal genus Fusarium, for instance Fusarium verticillioides |CITS:[22652150]|, Fusarium venenatum |CITS:[15368570]|, Fusarium graminearum |CITS:[16278459]|, Fusarium oxysporum |CITS:[10427735]| and Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[22865073]|. Most of the various Fusarium species have been found on different host plants including important agricultural crops. For example, |FRAME:CPD-18054| has been verified in 40 out of 50 different corn samples |CITS:[21894895]| and therefore classified a contamination risk for human food and livestock feed., It has been shown that |FRAME:CPD-18054| is mutagenic after metabolic activation |CITS:[6623491] [Wiebe81]| and is easily converted to stereoisomers when exposed to UV-light |CITS:[Gelderblom84]|. Its toxicity towards mammalian cell lines has been shown, but no mutagenic or clastogenic effects had been recorded when |FRAME:CPD-18054| was applied without the S-9 mix (an liver tissue homogenate used for biological assays) |CITS:[4006077]|. On the other side |FRAME:CPD-18054| exhibits mycoestrogenic activities and stimulated breast cancer cells |CITS:[21683775]| and also showed cytostatic activity against LI210 and HL60cells |CITS:[9207916]|., |FRAME:CPD-18054 Fusarin C| (this pathway) belongs to a group of substituted 2-pyrrolidinones isolated from various fungi which produce for instance |FRAME:CPD-17992| (see |FRAME:PWY-7669|) or further ring-extended 2-pyridones such as |FRAME:CPD-17122| (see |FRAME:PWY-7561|). Although the mechanisms of the reactions in the |FRAME:PWY-7673| remain to be confirmed in vitro and in vivo and not all reactions have been elucidated in detail, the sequencing of the genome |CITS:[23825955]|, the discovery of the respective gene cluster |CITS:[23932525]| and the results of single and multiple gene deletions combined with cocultivation and metabolic profiling |CITS:[22865073] [23932525] [15368570] [22877497]| have allowed to propose a likely sequence of the reaction steps and respective gene and enzyme assignment in the |FRAME:PWY-7673|. Interestingly, the nine genes forming the fus gene cluster are expressed under nitrogen sufficient conditions, of which only four genes are required for the synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-18054|. The genes of the fus cluster have been shown to be co-regulated by the velvet complex in Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[23932525]| as demonstrated before for the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites in this species |CITS:[20572938]|., The hybrid polyketide synthase (PKS)-nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) |CITS:[22289777]| encoded by Fus1 (or FusA) produces the heptaketide |FRAME:CPD-18059| (PKS part of Fus1) and incorporates |FRAME:HOMO-SER| to the pentaene side chain (NRPS part of Fus1) |CITS:[15368570] [22865073] [23932525]|. The latter was shown to be added to the heptaketide moiety using labeled |FRAME:HOMO-SER| |CITS:[17121404]| whereas the polyketide formation had been demonstrated by feeding labeled acetate to Fusarium verticillioides |CITS:[Steyn85]|. Very likely the reaction products of the Fus1 encoded fusarin C synthetase and the Fus8 encoded fusarin cytochrome P450 monooxygenase are the open ring forms of |FRAME:CPD-18058| and |FRAME:CPD-18057|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18067| and |FRAME:CPD-18068|, respectively |CITS:[23932525]|. However, the occurrence of multiple stereoisomers and the instability of the intermediate(s) may require further investigation to clarify the exact reaction mechanism.

Summary: General Background, Bacteriochlorophylls are photosynthetic light harvesting pigments found in photosynthetic bacteria. There are many different types of bacteriochlorophylls, including |FRAME: Bacteriochlorophyll-a "bacteriochlorophyll a"|, |FRAME:CPD-9091|, |FRAME:CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME:CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"|, |FRAME:CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| and |FRAME:CPD-9095| |CITS: [9442890]|, with vaying structures |CITS: [Senge95]|. In additions, while most of the bacteriochlorophylls contain a |FRAME: MG+2| ion, there are varieties that contain a |FRAME: ZN+2| ion |CITS: [Wakao96]|., Much of the knowledge about bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis comes from the organisms |FRAME: TAX-1061| and |FRAME: TAX-1063|, which produce mainly |FRAME:CPD-9067|, the most common form of the bacteriochlorophylls., Most of the bacteria that synthesize bacteriochlorophyll are anoxygenic species that belong to the proteobacteria (and specifically to the |FRAME: TAX-41295|, |FRAME: TAX-1046| and |FRAME: TAX-191412|, also known as the purple non-sulfur bacteria, the purple sulfur bacteria, and the green sulfur bacteria, respectively). The purple bacteria are named due to the color of the pigment. These species mostly photosynthesize under anaerobic conditions. However, bacteriochlorophylls are also present in some groups of aerobic bacteria, such as members of the |FRAME: TAX-522| genus |CITS: [Wakao93]|. For a complete list of aerobic bacteria that contain bacteriochlorophyll, see |CITS: [12483616]|., |FRAME:CPD-9067 "Bacteriochlorophyll a"| functions not only as a light-harvesting pigment in antenna complexes, but also acts as a "special pair" to drive the photosynthetic electron transfer in the reaction center., A related compound, |FRAME: CPD-9096| (which is essentially bacteriochlorophyll without the metal ion) is found as an accessory pigment in the reaction centers of green and purple photosynthetic bacteria |CITS:[6808895][11872709]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-9067| is a complex multienzymatic process, and involves at least 15 steps starting at |FRAME:5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5529|). The early part of the biosynthetic pathway (up to |FRAME:PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX|) is shared with heme biosynthesis, while the later part, which starts with the insertion of a |FRAME: MG+2| ion into the porphyrin ring, is specific to |FRAME:CPD-9067|., In the purple bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1061| and |FRAME: TAX-1063| all genes of the later part of the pathway are clustered in several tightly linked operons. The region, which is called the photosynthesis gene cluster, is also linked to some other genes involved in photosynthesis |CITS: [16571720]|., A certain complication in the pathway is the fact that chlorophyll intermediates such as |FRAME:MG-PROTOPORPHYRIN|, |FRAME:MG-PROTOPORPHYRIN-MONOMETHYL-ESTER|, |FRAME: MONO-VINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|, and |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| occur in two different forms: a monovinyl and a divinyl (the divinyl forms have a C-8 vinyl substituent, which is reduced to an ethyl group in the monovinyl forms). The pool of monovinyl and divinyl intermediates differ among species, and (in plants) with the age of tissue and light regime. Three enzyme are known to catalyze the reduction of the 8-vinyl group: |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.75| (encoded in phototrophic bacteria by the |FRAME: G-10101| gene), |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.13| (encoded by the |FRAME: SGL_RS12255| gene), and also |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.15|, which catalyzes this activity as a latent activity. While the reduction could occur at different stages along the pathway, in MetaCyc it is depicted at the level of |FRAME: DIVINYLCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|., Three enzymes, |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.15| (COR), and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.396| (BchC), and |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.165| (BchF), are involved in the conversion of |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| to |FRAME: CPD-9066|. The enzymes can act in multiple orders, resulting in the formation of different intermediates, but the final product of the cumulative action of the three enzymes is always |FRAME:CPD-9066|., Once formed, a variety of alcohols can be esterified to the propanoate group at position 17 of |FRAME:CPD-9066|, including |FRAME: CPD-9087|, |FRAME: PHYTOL|, |FRAME: Farnesols|, |FRAME: CPD-348|, |FRAME: CPD-7873| and |FRAME: CPD-18893| |CITS: [16228437]|. However, the in vivo reaction involves |FRAME: CPD-9087| |CITS: [10809697]|. This side chain is then reduced in three steps by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.111|, to form |FRAME: CPD-9067| |CITS: [7947681]|.

Sorbitol (D-glucitol) is a polyol found in many fruits (see |FRAME: PWY-5054|). It is used commercially as a sweetener, , humectant, texturizer, softener, and is a precursor of other products of commercial interest including vitamin C , (see |FRAME: PWY-5521|). It is produced by mainly chemical methods. The Gram-negative, fermentative, , α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-542| has been shown to biosynthesize sorbitol and gluconolactone , from glucose and fructose in a one-step enzymatic reaction catalyzed by a unique enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7444|. This , reaction has potential for the biotechnological production of sorbitol. Reviewed in |CITS: [SPRENGER96]| and |CITS: [15304760]|., This reaction takes place in the periplasm. Periplasmic glucose and fructose are derived from sucrose in the , environment via extracellular levan sucrase (LevU) and sucrase (invertase, InvB) secreted by this organism. , Glucose and fructose enter the cell by a facilitated diffusion system. These extracellular enzymes , allow Z. mobilis to utilize sucorse from sugar-rich plant saps, or honey as an energy source |CITS: [10333527]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [SPRENGER96]| and |CITS: [15304760]|., Glucono-δ-lactone in the periplasm is converted to gluconate by a lactonase. Sorbitol and gluconate are , transported into the cytosol via sorbitol and gluconate carriers. Sorbitol is not metabolized further. It accumulates , in the cytosol and may serve as an osmoprotectant when the organism grows in , environments of high external osmolarity created by high concentrations of sugars, such as in saps from dessicated , plants (in |CITS: [8002594]| and reviewed in |CITS: [SPRENGER96]|). Gluconate is converted to , 6-phosphogluconate, which enters the Entner-Doudoroff pathway, as shown by the pathway link. Pyruvate , produced by this pathway, or by subsequent glycolytic reactions (see the pathway link , in |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|) is fermented anaerobically to mainly ethanol and carbon dioxide , (see |FRAME: PWY-5486|). Reviewed in |CITS: [SPRENGER96]| and |CITS: [15304760]|. , Glucose and fructose can also directly enter the cytosol via facilitators and are fermented anaerobically to mainly , ethanol and carbon dioxide. Aerobically, acetaldehyde and acetate are also produced. |FRAME:TAX-542| , is a source of biotechnologically produced ethanol (in |CITS: [9805385]|). Reviewed in |CITS: [SPRENGER96]| and |CITS: [15304760]|.

The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-14538| and its stereospecific precursor isomers |FRAME:CPD-1901| and |FRAME:CPD-1907| is one of the grisan-type compound producing pathways primarily found in fungi. The spiro structure of these compounds allows for different regio- and/or stereospecific isomers which may exhibit altered biological functions and play divergent roles within metabolic pathways., |FRAME:CPD-14538 Asterric acid| the end-product of this pathway has been reported to inhibit vascular endothelial growth and acted as antifungal and antimicrobial agent |CITS:[1473998]| |CITS:[12195960]| |CITS:[18720971]| while the +/- stereoisomers of bisdechlorogeodin have been shown to display herbicidal activity |CITS:[8968402]|., It is interesting that at a time only one of the two stereosisomers are being produced in differenct species, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-1901| in |FRAME:TAX-5073| |CITS:[7049104]| |CITS:[8820909]| and |FRAME:CPD-1907| in Oospora |CITS:[7049104]| despite only minor differences in molecular properties between the two catalyzing enzymes.

Names: thiazole component of thiamine diphosphate biosynthesis IV
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the |FRAME: THIAMINE|-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|. Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820 Plasmodium|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, |FRAME: THIAMINE-P "Thiamine phosphate"| is formed by the coupling of two moieties, the pyrimidine |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP| and the thiazole |FRAME: THZ-P|, which are produced by two different pathways. This pathway describes the formation of the thiazole moiety in some archaea., Unlike the bacterial pathway, which involves many enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-6892|), the pathway found in plants, fungi, and archaea requires only one enzyme. Unlike the homologous enzyme from plants, fungi, and halobacteria (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.60|), which uses an intrinsic cysteine as sulfur donor and is thus a single turn-over enzyme, the enzymes from the |FRAME: TAX-183939| |FRAME: TAX-2190| and |FRAME: TAX-2189| were shown to utilize sulfide as the sulfur source |CITS: [26928142]|., A later study looking for orthologs of the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-2190| identified orthologous enzymes in 96 organisms that are taxonomically and ecologically diverse, belonging to three archaeal and nine bacterial phyla including mesophiles, thermophiles, aerobes, microaerophiles, and anaerobes. The enzymes from two of those, |FRAME: TAX-113287| and |FRAME: TAX-228745|, were able to complement a thiamine auxotroph mutant of |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [30337452]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-27002 Indigoidine| is a dimeric blue 3,3'-bipyridyl pigment biosynthesized from two molecules of |FRAME: GLN|, that imparts blue color to bacterial colonies. Its production has been reported in phytopathogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-33014|, |FRAME: TAX-1914|, and |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [16349687]| and in saprophytic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-37927| and |FRAME: TAX-45465| |CITS: [Elazari-Volcani39][13595813][13856051][14106078][14347925][5345987]|. It's biological role is not currently understood., Based on its pronounced blue color, production of |FRAME: CPD-27002| has been developed as a reporter system in bacterial and mammalian cells |CITS: [ 22543310][25801098][33118808][34371757][37184703]|., The enzyme producing indigoidine was first described from |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [11790734]| and later studied in |FRAME: TAX-204038| |CITS: [19879116]| and |FRAME: TAX-1914| |CITS: [17237222]|. It is a nonribosomal peptide synthase (NPRS) that contains an L-glutamine-specific adenylation (A) domain, a peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domain, an FMN-dependent oxidation (O) domain that is integrated into the A domain, and a thioesterase (TE) domain |CITS: [17237222]|., Two mechanisms have been proposed for the enzyme's activity: according to one mechanism, |FRAME: ARG| is first cyclyzed and released from the NRPS, followed by oxidation of the free molecule by the oxidation domain |CITS: [11790734][17237222]| (this is the mechanism depicted here). According to the second proposed mechanism the flavin-dependent oxidation of L-glutamine occurs on the carrier protein prior to cyclization and dimerization |CITS: [23051833]|. In both proposed mechanisms the final product of the enzyme is |FRAME: CPD-27005|, which auto-oxidizes to generate the blue pigment, similar to the formation of |FRAME: CPD-10525| from |FRAME: INDOXYL| (see |FRAME: PWY-6069|).

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Naphthomycins naphthomycins| belong to the family of the |FRAME: Ansamycins ansamycin| antibiotics, whose characteristic structure comprises an aromatic moiety bridged at nonadjacent positions by an aliphatic chain. The |FRAME: Naphthomycins naphthomycins| are 29-membered ansamacrolactams with the largest ring reported so far in the ansamycin family. The ring contains a characteristic triene. Some of them have chlorination on the 3-amino-5-hydroxybenzoate ring., The naphthomycins display signifcant antibacterial, antifungal, and antitumor activities that are different from those of the |FRAME: Rifamycins rifamycins| and |FRAME: Streptovaricins streptovaricins| |CITS: [3997667]|. They have been reported from several |FRAME: TAX-876169|, including |FRAME: TAX-42236|, |FRAME: TAX-1910|, |FRAME: TAX-42684|, |FRAME: TAX-876169| |CITS: [4988744][ 6874565][4030505][9820235][17965482][22742732]|. The structure of |FRAME: CPD-21917| was elucidated in 1975 |CITS: [805115]|, and its absolute configuration was reported in 1984 |CITS: [6511662]|., About This Pathway, Like all ansamycins, the biosynthesis of the naphthomycins backbone starts with |FRAME: CPD-10231|, which is adenylated by the loading module of the first polyketide synthase protein and loaded onto its acyl-carrier protein (acp) domain. , The earlier steps of of ansamycins biosynthesis follow a common root. A type I modular polyketide synthase (PKS) initiates the polyketide chain with a |FRAME: CPD-10231| starter unit, followed by multiple steps of chain elongation with various extender units on subsequent modules of the PKS. In the case of naphthomycins, the starter unit is extended by seven propionate and six acetate extender units |CITS: [Lee94]|. The extended chain is then released from the PKS and cyclized by an amide synthase. A more detailed description of these steps is provided in |FRAME: PWY-5984|. The enzymes involed in this part of the pathway, the |FRAME: CPLX-9389| (which includes the |FRAME: G-63010|-|FRAME: G-63015| gene products), |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.M73| (|FRAME: G-63011|), and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.M75| (|FRAME: G-63016|), are very similar to the |FRAME: TAX-33910| enzymes that participate in |FRAME: PWY-5984| |CITS: [21614382]|., A portion of the naphthomycin biosynthetic cluster, which included the complete set of |FRAME: CPD-10231| biosynthetic genes, the |FRAME: G-63016| gene, and a part of the |FRAME: G-63015| gene were cloned from |FRAME: TAX-42684| in 1999 |CITS: [10103039]|. The sequence of the complete biosynthetic cluster, which spans about 106 kb, was reported in 2011 |CITS: [21614382]|., Compared to other ansamycins, the post-PKS modifications of naphthomycins are relatively simple, and mostly concern substitution at the C-30 carbon. An as yet unknown enzyme catalyzes the dehydration of |FRAME: CPD-21923|, forming |FRAME: CPD-21922|. The |FRAME: G-63009| gene encodes an FAD-dependent halogenase that catalyzes the chlorination of |FRAME: CPD-21922| at C-30 to form |FRAME: CPD-21917| |CITS: [21614382]|. The enzyme responsible for the formation of other naphthomycins have not been characterized as of 2019.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of, polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl, diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-83333| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|, or the human |FRAME: CPLX-7582|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme., Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the, polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a, preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone, molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length., However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain, length. For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|.

This pathway has been reported in bacteria from the |FRAME: TAX-186801| class, which possess the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.83|., In the first part of the pathway |FRAME: TYR| is transaminated to |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| and then oxidized/decarboxylated to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYPHENYLACETATE|. This portion of the pathway has also been documented in the |FRAME: TAX-201174 Actinobacteria| phylum, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5151|., However, only |FRAME: TAX-186801| have so far been shown to posses an enzyme that can decarboxylate the latter to |FRAME: CPD-108| (p-cresol). When this occurs in the gut or the colon of a mammal, the resulting |FRAME: CPD-108| is absorbed into the blood and arrives to the liver, where it is sulfated by a liver enzyme (see |FRAME: HS11091-MONOMER|). The product, |FRAME: CPD-16819|, is normally removed in the urine. However, in people that suffer from uremia (chronic renal failure) it accumulates in the blood. Since it is bound to proteins in the blood, it can not be removed efficiently by dialysis. 4-methylphenyl is considered to be a uremic toxin; It has been linked to cardiovascular disease and oxidative injury, and is the major component of urinary MBPLM (myelin basic protein-like material) |CITS: [21343587]|.

Summary: This pathway describes late steps in the biosynthesis of B12 vitamins, starting with |FRAME: CPD-689| - the step where the early-insertion and late-insertion pathways combine. It ends with the formation of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP|, a compound that can be used to synthesize different forms of the vitamin, depending on the lower case ligand that is attached to it., The first major event in this pathway the attachment of the upper ligand, 5'deoxyadenosine, by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.17| |CITS: [2403541][1917862][7916712]|., In the next step, |FRAME: CPD-690| is converted step-wise to the hexa-amide |FRAME: CPD-691| by four amidation reactions, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.10| |CITS: [1917839]|. |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.10|, catalyzes the addition of |FRAME: R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE|, producing a |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| structure. Initially it was assumed that |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| was the substrate, but it is now accepted that the phosphorylated form, |FRAME:R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE|, is likely to be the real substrate in vivo |CITS: [Blanche95]|., This is followed by addition of |FRAME: GMP| to the phosphate group, generating |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP|. The reaction is catalyzed by a bifunctional protein, that also catalyzes the activity of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.156| |CITS: [1655696][10869342][15939305]|.

|FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| is a normally occurring metabolite of |FRAME:HIS| that is excreted in the urine of a number of mammals |CITS:[ 13563454]| (see pathway |FRAME:PWY-5031|). |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| arises from the reduction of |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE|, which is formed from |FRAME:HIS| by transamination |CITS:[13990226]|. This can occur either by mammalian enzymes (|FRAME:PWY-5031|) or by gut bacteria (|FRAME:HISTDEG-PWY|). Once formed, |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| does not appear to be degraded further by mammalian systems., Westley and Ceithaml found that both |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| and |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE| satisfy the growth requirements of a large number of histidine auxotrophs of |FRAME: TAX-566546|. They concluded that the |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| in the growth medium was converted via |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE| into |FRAME:HIS|, in a set of reactions that are the reversal of those reported for the histidine catabolic pathway of |FRAME: TAX-37762| (see pathway |FRAME: HISTDEG-PWY|) |CITS:[ 13283604]|., By using enrichment culture techniques, Coote and Hassall were able to isolate several non-fluorescent Pseudomonads that were able to use |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| as the sole source of carbon and energy for growth |CITS:[4146796]|. They demonstrated that in |FRAME: TAX-285|, following the conversion of |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| via |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE| to  |FRAME:HIS|, |FRAME:HIS| is degraded into |FRAME:GLT| in the usual histidine catabolic pathway found in fluorescent Pseudomonads (see |FRAME: PWY-5028|)., The enzymes converting |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-LACTATE| to |FRAME:IMIDAZOLE-PYRUVATE|, and the later to |FRAME:HIS|, namely imidazole-lactate-NADP oxidoreductase and |FRAME: MONOMER-11647|, respectively, were not purified from these organisms. However, their activity was demonstrated in cell-free extracts of both |FRAME: TAX-80866| |CITS:[4303364]| and |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [4146796]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP) is an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]| (see |FRAME:Dimethylsulfoniopropionate-Biosynthesis|)., Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS: [17068264]|. , DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|., Two main routes are known for DMSP degradation, one leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-7670| (as described in this pathway and in |FRAME: PWY-6056|) and the other leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-7672| (see |FRAME: PWY-6052|)., |FRAME: CPD-7670 "Dimethylsulfide"|, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere,, and is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to sulfuric and methanesulfonic acids, which attract water and promote cloud formation |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, most of the DMS in the oceanic environment is degraded biologically (see |FRAME: PWY-6047|)., About This Pathway, The bacterial cleavage of DMSP to DMS and acrylate was described already in 1962 |CITS: [14004329]|. Since then it has been described in anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [14004329][Marc06]|, aerobic bacteria |CITS:[Ledyard93][16534905][Van-der-Maarel96][Visscher92][10473380]|, a heterotrophic dinoflagellate |CITS: [Kadota68]|, algae |CITS:[13366990][Stefels93][De-Souza96][Stefels96][Steinke98][Nishiguchi95]|, and marine fungi, such as |FRAME: TAX-5523| |CITS: [16349475]|., A |FRAME: MONOMER-14221| enzyme was initially described from the red alga |FRAME: TAX-1261582| |CITS:[13366990]|, and subsequently purified from several other organisms, including the microaerophilic bacterium |FRAME:ORG-6049| |CITS:[16534905]|, the red alga |FRAME:TAX-282368| |CITS:[Nishiguchi95]|, the green alga |FRAME: TAX-135247| |CITS: [De-Souza96]| and the anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1121434| |CITS: [Marc06]|., The first gene encoding such an enzyme was found only in 2008, in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-52598|, |CITS: [18237308]|. When the |FRAME: G-10872| gene was cloned and expressed in an |FRAME:TAX-562| strain, it conferred high levels of DMSP-dependent DMS production on the host. Homologues of DddL were found in the marine bacteria |FRAME: TAX-314267|, |FRAME: TAX-314232|, |FRAME: TAX-384765|, |FRAME: TAX-398580|, |FRAME: TAX-252305|, |FRAME: TAX-314271|, and |FRAME: TAX-314231|, and in the two |FRAME: TAX-1060| strains |FRAME: TAX-272943| and |FRAME: TAX-349101| |CITS: [18237308]|. The source of the last two strains is not known, but they may be marine as well., Curiously, several additional genes, |FRAME: G-11961|, |FRAME: G-12534| and |FRAME: G-12535|, were found to encode unrelated enzymes that possess the same activity |CITS: [19220400][Kirkwood10][20880330][21248856]|. DddP genes were found in many marine bacteria (they are more abundant than the |FRAME: G-10872| genes in the Global Ocean sampling dataset), as well as some fungi |CITS: [19776768]| and marine phages |CITS: [20045332]|, while |FRAME: G-12534| appears to be limited to the Roseobacter clade, and |FRAME: G-12535| is limited to several microaerophilic genera. The remarkable diversity of these enzymes suggests that they have evolved in different environments, to address different needs and conditions, and emphesizes the importance of DMSP in the marine environment., A second DMSP cleavage pathway, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-10871|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14240|, is described in |FRAME: PWY-6056|.

Summary: The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleosides |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE| can be degraded by phosphorylases that remove the |FRAME: DEOXY-D-RIBOSE-1-PHOSPHATE| moiety, leaving the free pyrimidine nucleobases |FRAME: THYMINE| and |FRAME: URACIL|, respectively. , There are several types of enzymes that can perform this reaction: the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1422| possesses the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8610| (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.2 "EC 2.4.2.2"|) that can accept not only |FRAME: THYMIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE|, but also |FRAME: URIDINE|. Humans, as well as the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|, possess the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8611| (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.4 "EC 2.4.2.4"|), which is also able to catalyze the reaction with |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE|. Some organisms (humans included) have the enzyme |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "uridine phosphorylase"| (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.3 "EC 2.4.2.3"|), which is specific for |FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE|, and does not accept |FRAME: THYMIDINE|., Neither of these enzymes is able to accept |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE|, and thus this nucleoside is converted into |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8612| (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.5 "EC 3.5.4.5"|)., The nucleobases that are formed by the phosphorylases can be degraded further, as described in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6430| and |FRAME: PWY-3982|, or reused to synthesize a new nucleoside., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|, which can utilize all three deoxyribonucleosides as total sources of carbon and energy, |FRAME: DEOXY-D-RIBOSE-1-PHOSPHATE| is converted to |FRAME: DEOXY-RIBOSE-5P| by a |FRAME: PPENTOMUT-MONOMER|. A specific aldolase splits D-deoxyribose-5-phosphate, yielding |FRAME: GAP|, which enters central metabolism through the glycolytic pathway, and |FRAME: ACETALD|, which must be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| before it can enter central metabolism via the TCA cycle., The amino nitrogen that is removed from |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE|, but not the ring-nitrogen of |FRAME: URACIL| or |FRAME: THYMINE|, can serve as a total nitrogen source for |FRAME: TAX-562| over its entire temperature range of growth. The ring nitrogens are available to serve as total nitrogen sources at room temperature via the pathway encoded by genes in the rut operon (see |FRAME: PWY0-1471|) |CITS: [16540542]|. , Plants and yeast do not appear to have either EC 2.4.2.2, EC 2.4.2.4 or EC 2.4.2.23, and thus do not have this pathway.

Summary: General Background, Protein glycosylation is an important process found in all kingdoms of life. N-glycosylation is found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria. During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. In eukaryotes, the nascent proteins that are synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane where they acquire the initial carbohydrate chains on specific asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes can be divided into the following three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7919|)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (this pathway)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and use somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathway is in general similar to the eukaryotic one, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7658|)., About This Pathway, The oligosaccharides attached to plant N-glycans are less complex and less diverse than those produced by mammals (see |FRAME: PWY-7426|). For example, they are less branched and are not decorated with sialic acid. Instead, they contain different modifications (xylosylation, fucosylation, and |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a-type"| structures). Even though complex N-glycans are not essential for the development and reproduction of plants when grown under standard environmental conditions |CITS: [8278542][15013764]|, these modifications are conserved in higher plants and found even in distantly related mosses |CITS: [11358875][14566560]|, indicating that they serve important, though not yet understood, functions., Starting with the five mannose N-glycan |FRAME: Mannosyl5-N-Glycans|, the formation of complex and hybrid N-glycans is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.101| (|FRAME: AT4G38240|), which catalyzes the addition of GlcNAc in β1-2 linkage to the Manα(1-3) terminus of the five-mannose structure. , Immediately after the action of |FRAME: AT4G38240|, alternative processing reactions can take place in plants because |FRAME: Mannosyl5-N-acetyl-glucosamine2-R| serves as substrate for at least three different N-glycan processing enzymes., One possible route, which is identical to the one found in animals, is the cleavage of two mannose residues by mannosidase II (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.114 "EC 3.2.1.114"|, |FRAME: AT5G14950|). This removal exposes the Manα(1-6) terminus that serves as a substrate for |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.143| (|FRAME: G-55182|), which acts next., Alternatively, the hybrid |FRAME: Mannosyl5-N-acetyl-glucosamine2-R| glycan can be modified in the medial-Golgi by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.38| (|FRAME: AT5G55500|) or medial- to trans-Golgi by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.214| (|FRAME: AT3G19280| or |FRAME: AT1G49710|). These enzymes are ubiquitous in plants, but not present in mammals., While |FRAME: AT5G55500| and |FRAME: AT3G19280|/|FRAME: AT1G49710| can utilize the same acceptor, preceding fucosylation prevents subsequent xylosylation |CITS: [15686448]|, while on the other hand xylosylation enhances subsequent fucosylation |CITS: [15013764][18346095][21478158]|. Thus, it is possible that |FRAME: AT5G55500| acts first in vivo., The last known step in the plant N-glycan processing pathway is the generation of |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a"| structures. First, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.86| (|FRAME: AT1G26810|) transfers a galatosyl residue in β1,3-linkage to terminal GlcNAc residues, resulting in the synthesis of |FRAME: Core1| structures. Next, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.65| (|FRAME: GQT-3947|) transfers a fucosyl residue in α1,4-linkage to the GlcNAc, completing the synthesis of the Lewis a structure., No additional elongation or modification of terminal GlcNAc residues has been identified in plants |CITS: [26911286]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Recently an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate, which proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-10477|, has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|. Initial analysis of sequenced genomes suggested that the pathway might be present in a variety of organisms |CITS: [19557031]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6262|). However, further analysis revealed that the newly discovered pathway is not identical among all of these organisms. A related, yet different route, has been described in |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-197| |CITS: [21489995]|., This route is similar to the |FRAME: PWY-6262 "futalosine pathway"|, but proceeds via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-13324| rather than |FRAME: CPD-10477|. The two pathways differ from each other only by the enzymes that form and hydrolize |FRAME: CPD-13324| and |FRAME: CPD-10477|, respectively. , In this pathway |FRAME: CHORISMATE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-13324| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-16550| (|FRAME: G-12801|), which incorporates |FRAME: ADENOSINE| rather than |FRAME: INOSINE|. This intermediate is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16549| to form |FRAME: CPD-10484|, which is a common intermedaite to both pathways |CITS: [21489995]|., The other enzymes in this pathway have not been characterized yet from |FRAME: TAX-210| or |FRAME: TAX-197|.

Summary: The conversion of |FRAME: TYR| to |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| by an aminotransferase, is a common reaction, found in most organisms., In some organisms it is part of degradative pathways (as in |FRAME: TYRFUMCAT-PWY|) while in, others it is part of biosynthetic pathways (as in |FRAME: PWY-1581|)., |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| is an central precursor, which is used for the synthesis, of primary metabolites such as |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE-9| and |FRAME: Vitamin-E|,, both important quinones found in all oxygenic photosynthetic organisms, as well as secondary, metabolites, such as |FRAME: CPD-6981|.

Summary: The sequence of reactions in the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway may vary.  This pathway shows one possible , variant of cholesterol biosynthesis.  This and other alternate routes exist because reduction of the , carbon 24,25 double bond on the hydrocarbon side chain of the sterol ring structure by sterol , Δ<sup>24</sup>-reductase can occur at multiple points in the pathway, giving rise to different , intermediates.  These intermediates, with or without a double bond in the hydrocarbon side chain, can serve , as substrates for the other enzymes in the pathway.  However, there is evidence that the preferred point of , carbon 24,25 double bond reduction is directly after the isomerization of zymosterol |CITS: [9291139]|, as shown , in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-341|.  In |CITS: [11519011]| and reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|., In the pathway shown here reduction of the carbon 24,25 double bond in the hydrocarbon side chain occurs , at the point of lanosterol, producing |FRAME: CPD-8606|.  This compound is a substrate for the next , enzyme in the pathway lanosterol 14 α-demethylase (cytochrome P450 51 protein) , (reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|, in |CITS: [1872829] [2799854] [3409414] [13965665]|).  Carbon monoxide has , been shown to inhibit this enzyme, causing lanosterol and 24,25-dihydrolanosterol to , accumulate |CITS: [5073750] [9291139]| .  The antimycotic drugs ketoconazole and miconazole have also been , shown to inhibit lanosterol 14 α-demethylase, resulting in an accumulation of 24,25-dihydrolanosterol , |CITS: [2043135] [9291139] [3356951]|.  Other azoles, oxygenated lanosterol derivatives, and their analogs, , that inhibit this enzyme (as well as HMG-CoA reductase from the |FRAME: PWY-922|) have been studied , as possible cholesterol-lowering drugs |CITS: [7626636] [3409414] [8161528] [1940622]|.

Summary: Tetrapyrrole compounds include four rings of the pyrrole type, generally linked, together by single-atom bridges between the α positions of the five-membered pyrrole rings., Tetrapyrroles usually function as a metal-binding cofactor in many important enzymes, proteins and pigments,, such as heme, chlorophyll, cobalamine (vitamin B12), siroheme, and cofator F430., The tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway shown here beginning, with glycine and succinyl-CoA (a TCA cycle intermediate) is found in animals, fungi, apicomplexan protozoa (such, as the malaria parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [15144063]|), and members of the, α-proteobacteria.  In other bacteria (including |FRAME:TAX-562|) and archaea, tetrapyrrole biosynthesis, begins with glutamate instead of glycine (see |FRAME: PWY-5188|). Plants, who biosynthesize, tetrapyrrole for use as heme and chlorophyll, also synthesize it from glutamate., Interestingly, the chloroplast-containing protozoan |FRAME: TAX-3039| possesses both pathways., Regardless whether the starting point is glycine or glutamate, both pathways converge at the intermediate, |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| and proceed through the important intermediate, |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, which is a major branch point that leads to biosynthesis of different, tetrapyrrole compounds, such as the corrinoid cobalamine, (vitamin B<sub>12</sub>) (see MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: P381-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5507|),, the methanogenic coenzyme F<sub>430</sub> (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME|, (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|), and heme D., This pathway has been studied in the photosynthetic purple nonsulfur α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1063|, which posesses two chromosomes and five additional replicons. In this organism there are two genes encoding  5-aminolevulinate synthase, |FRAME: G-9025| and |FRAME:G-10074|, that are present on chromosomes 1 and 2, respectively., Biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole cofactors |FRAME: Hemes|, |FRAME: CPD-9067|, |FRAME: SIROHEME| and |FRAME: COB-I-ALAMIN| in this organism is highly regulated and is dependent upon expression of these two isozymes (in |CITS: [7592416], [10491185]|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|, is also the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]|. It was first identified in 1948 in the red alga |FRAME: TAX-1261582| |CITS: [18101461]|, and is found in the highest concentrations in |FRAME: TAX-2864| (dinoflagellates) and |FRAME: TAX-2608131| (haptophytes). However, DMSP is produced by many more organisms including diatoms, green algae, some higher plants like |FRAME: TAX-4547| (sugarcane) and the coastal angiosperms |FRAME: TAX-15853| and |FRAME: TAX-101473|, bacteria, and some coral species |CITS: [31231779]|., Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS: [17068264]|., Biological degradation of DMSP is the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6046|). The degradation of DMSP to DMS and subsequent exchange of DMS across the ocean-atmosphere boundary is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. The flux of DMS from the ocean to the atmosphere is estimated at about 1.5 x 10(13) g of sulfur annually. Once in the atmosphere, DMS plays a major part in cloud formation and potentially in climate regulation., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway for DMSP was first studied in the green plant |FRAME: TAX-101473|, and found to start with |FRAME: MET| and include the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-397| and |FRAME: CPD-10472|. |FRAME: CPD-397| is converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-10472| in a single reaction catalyzed by an as yet uncharacterized enzyme complex |CITS: [12223879]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6054|). , The pathway in the Gramineae |FRAME: TAX-29706| (previously known as Spartina alterniflora) was shown to contain one additional intermediate - |FRAME: CPD-10471| |CITS: [9576797]|. The presence of this intermediate necessitates the presence of two new enzymes, and the corresponding activities were indeed identified in |FRAME: TAX-29706| leaf extracts using specific radioassays |CITS: [10889264]|. The first, |FRAME: MONOMER-14238| (SDC), strongly prefers the L-enantiomer |FRAME: CPD-397|, is |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|-dependent, generates equimolar amounts of CO2cand |FRAME: CPD-10471|, and has a high apparent Km (approximately 18 mM) for its substrate., The second enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-14239| (DOX), requires molecular oxygen for activity, and shows a lower apparent Km for its substrate (1.8 mM)., Enzyme assays conducted with grasses that lack DMSP biosynthesis capabilities showed none or very little SDC or DOX activity, supporting a role for these enzymes in DMSP biosynthesis |CITS: [10889264]|., The first and last enzymes of the pathway, on the other hand, are not unique to dimethylsulfoniopropanoate producers. The first enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.12| (MMT) occurs in all flowering plants and participates in other functions in other plants (e.g. Sin phloem sulfur transport |CITS: [10449582]|). Similarly, the last step is catalyzed by the multifunctional enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8| (BADH) . When the enzyme from sugar beet (|FRAME: TAX-161934|) was expressed in tobacco (|FRAME: TAX-4097|) it demonstrated, in addition to BADH activity, three other aldehyde dehydrogenase activities, acting on 3-|FRAME: CPD-10472|, |FRAME: CPD-6082|, and |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, suggesting that BADH is a broad substrate range enzyme with multiple parallel activities |CITS: [12223684]|. In another work it was shown that |FRAME: CPD-10472| is a better substrate for BADH from amaranth (|FRAME: TAX-28502|) than |FRAME: BETAINE_ALDEHYDE| |CITS: [8990271]|., A 2017 paper reported finding the gene sequences for the enzymes that participate in this pathway. Unfortunately the actual data was included in supplementary information that was not made available |CITS: [28694102]|.

Taken together lignins and lignans count for about 30% of carbon in vascular plants |CITS: [Lewis99]|. , Cell suspension cultures of |FRAME: TAX-35941| accumulate the arylnaphthalene lignan |FRAME: CPD-13456| which is a glycoside of |FRAME: CPD-13455|, |CITS: [16872135]|. There is growing interest in lignans like |FRAME: CPD-13455| and |FRAME: CPD-13456| and their synthetic derivatives due to their application in cancer chemotherapy and other pharmacological effects |CITS: [11809070 ]|. |FRAME: CPD-13456| and its derivatives are putative remedies for topical chronic inflammatory disorders such as dermatitis and psoriasis. An acetylapioside derivative of diphyllin is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor |CITS: [11988863]|. , The dihydroarylnaphthalenes are mostly concentrated in the aerial part of  |FRAME: TAX-4005| plant. The enzyme justicidin B 7-hydroxylase  was isolated and characterized. This enzyme catalyzes the last step in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13456| by introducing a hydroxyl group in position 7 of |FRAME: CPD-13455| |CITS: [17997463]|.

Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many type of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CTP| is one of the building blocks of RNA. It is synthesized de novo from |FRAME: UTP| (see |FRAME: PWY-7176|)., However, when |FRAME: CMP| is available via salvage of cytidine nucleosides, it can be phosphorylated to CTP by the action of two kinases., The first phosphorylation, from |FRAME: CMP| to |FRAME: CDP|, is catalyzed in prokaryotes by a dedicated |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.25 "(d)CMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.25)"| and in eukaryotes by the bifunctional |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.14 "UMP/CMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.14)"|., The second phophorylation, from |FRAME: CDP| to |FRAME: CTP|, is catalyzed in all organisms by the broad-substrate range |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.6 "nucleoside diphosphate kinase (EC 2.7.4.6)"|.

Aurachin alkaloids were originally isolated from the myxobacterium |FRAME: TAX-675526| in the 1980s |CITS: [3106289]|. They are potent inhibitors of mitochondrial respiration through blockage of NADH oxidation, presumably because of their significant structural similarity to |FRAME: Menaquinones menaquinone| |CITS: [7827023][20335999]|. |FRAME: CPD-7733 "Aurachin C"| is a particularly effective inhibitor of the two terminal oxidases of |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: CYT-O-UBIOX-CPLX "cytochromes bo"| and |FRAME: CYT-D-UBIOX-CPLX "cytochrome bd"|, whereas |FRAME: CPD-15909| displays a selectivity for inhibition of cytochrome bd |CITS: [7827023]|., Beside |FRAME: TAX-40|, only one other producer species has been discovered - the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6248|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-15906| |CITS: [19168983]|. Despite the fact that these two organisms are phylogenetically unrelated, the genes that encode the biosyntheric enzymes share some similarity |CITS: [23677853]|., In order to identify the genes that are involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15906|, a transposon mutant of |FRAME: TAX-1833| that lost its ability to produce the antibiotic has been constructed. Sequebnce analysis of the area around the transposon insertion revealed a locus with 11 open reading frames, some of which similar to the gene from |FRAME: TAX-675526| |CITS: [23677853]|., Mutants in each of the genes shown in this pathway were constructed, and in every case the mutation prevented the formation of |FRAME: CPD-15906|. In addition, when all of the genes from the cluster were cloned and and expressed together in a non-producing strain of |FRAME: TAX-1833|, the host was able to form |FRAME: CPD-15906|, indicating that the proposed pathway is valid |CITS: [23677853]|., Curiously, one of the required enzymes, which is proposed to catalyze the hydroxylation of C9' in the prenyl chain of |FRAME: CPD-15909|, is not found in the cluster (and its function must have been substituted by a native enzyme in the transformed host). In addition, no gene encoding a resistance mechanism against the antibiotic has been found in the cluster. The last step of the pathway, the hydroxylation of the nitrogen atom in the quinoline ring, is carried out by a cytochrome P450. In cotrast, the same step is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-675526| by the |FRAME: G-17847| gene product, which is a Rieske [2Fe-2S] oxygenase.

Summary: General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various, insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are, believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness, of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans, was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose, |CITS: [12065209]|. , In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits, of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosil α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus, nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, , including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects, and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein). , In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity,, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation and no internal hydrogen bond formation. , The combinatrion of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms trehalose can be used as external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute, (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a, structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|., In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as, a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|., The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood, |CITS: [11081789]|., About This Pathway, While |FRAME: CPD-12575| is the most common substrate for the biosynthesis of trehalose (by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.15|) in most organisms, there are cases where a different modified nucleotide is used as a substrate. A |FRAME: GDP-D-GLUCOSE|-dependent trehalose phosphate synthase has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1912| |CITS: [6022837][5726304]|, and demonstrated in many other streptomycetes |CITS: [Elbein67b]|. It is not clear why the streptomycetes are using this variation., Trehalose is synthesized in streptomycetes throughout colony development, but is preferentially stored in aerial hyphae and spores. A protective role for trehalose has been postulated in dormant spores under dehydration conditions, where it acts as a substitute for water |CITS: [4355488][11164305]|.
