General Background:, In several species of filamentous fungi gene clusters containing both functionally orthologous and unique genes produce a variety of bioprotective indole-diterpene metabolites from |FRAME: CPD-16741| including |FRAME: CPD-16744| in |FRAME: TAX-70109| |CITS: [17428785][23311903][23525886][23949005]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7493|), |FRAME: CPD-16963| in |FRAME: TAX-5059| |CITS: [25087641][19801473][24038699][15528556]| (this pathway), terpendoles in |FRAME: TAX-124418| |CITS: [23261604]| (see |FRAME: MONOMER-18795|), and lolitrems in |FRAME: TAX-73839| |CITS: [16765617]| and |FRAME: TAX-35717| |CITS: [22750140]|., The pathogenic soil fungus |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces the tremorgenic mycotoxin |FRAME: CPD-16963| and its isomer |FRAME: CPD-16966| |CITS: [TEPASKEMR92][19801473]|. Two gene clusters encoding enzymes for |FRAME: CPD-16963| biosynthesis have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-5059|. The first cluster ATM1 contains genes atmG, atmC and atmM. The second cluster ATM2 contains genes atmD, atmQ, atmB, atmA and atmP. Transcript levels for these genes were shown to increase at the onset of |FRAME: CPD-16963| synthesis |CITS: [24038699]|., About This Pathway, Reconstitution experiments using a |FRAME: TAX-70109| gene paxP deletion mutant showed that |FRAME: TAX-5059| gene atmP can complement paxP and that the |FRAME: MONOMER-18805 "AtmP"| gene product is a functional ortholog of |FRAME: MONOMER-18638 "PaxP"| that can convert |FRAME: CPD-16741| to |FRAME: CPD-16743| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7493|). However, similar experiments using a |FRAME: TAX-70109| gene paxQ deletion mutant showed that the |FRAME: TAX-5059| |FRAME: MONOMER-18803 "AtmQ"| gene product is not a functional ortholog of |FRAME: MONOMER-18639 "PaxQ"|. Instead, |FRAME: MONOMER-18803 "AtmQ"| converted |FRAME: CPD-16743| to |FRAME: CPD-16961| and |FRAME: CPD-16962| (this pathway). The latter two intermediates are proposed to be unique to the |FRAME: CPD-16963| biosynthesis pathway. These intermediates were also identified in wild-type cultures of |FRAME: TAX-5059| |CITS: [19801473]|. , The product of |FRAME: TAX-5059| gene atmD was proposed to be a prenyltransferase. |FRAME: CPLX-8895 "AtmD"| was suggested to function as a "reverse" prenyltransferase which links |FRAME: CPD-4211| via its C-3, rather than via its C-1 or C-2 as for "regular" prenyltransferases. The identification of three isomers (|FRAME: CPD-16963|, |FRAME: CPD-16966| and a possible prenylated derivative of |FRAME: CPD-16962|) differing in the positions and/or arrangements of the prenyl groups on the indole moiety suggested catalytic promiscuity for this enzyme |CITS: [19801473]|., In subsequent work |FRAME: CPLX-8895 "AtmD"| was experimentally shown to be a prenyltransferase. Recombinant |FRAME: CPLX-8895 "AtmD"| showed 32% amino acid sequence identity to |FRAME: CPLX-8856 "PaxD"|. Characterization of its substrate specificity revealed its differing regiospecificities and prenylation mode specificities |CITS: [24038699]|. In addition, the |FRAME: CPD-16963| biosynthetic pathway was reconstituted by introduction of heterologous genes into |FRAME: TAX-5062| and the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-16963| was demonstrated |CITS: [25087641]|.

General Background, Osmoprotectants or compatible solutes are small organic molecules with neutral charge and low toxicity that act as osmolytes and help organisms survive extreme osmotic stress. Most microorganisms capable of osmotic adaptation accumulate compatible solutes in response to increases in the levels of salts or sugars in the environment., |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it is accumulated at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant. In addition to its osmoprotectant activity, glycine betaine is also a potent protectant against mutagenic compounds |CITS: [12730887][15802867]| and radiation-induced damage |CITS: [12841603]|., |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| can either be taken up directly from the environment, or synthesized. A common biosynthesis pathway for glycine betaine is from |FRAME: CHOLINE|, utilizing a two-step pathway with |FRAME: BETAINE_ALDEHYDE| as intermediate. This pathway is conserved in bacteria and plants, but shows divergence in the enzymes involved. Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive bacteria and higher plants all use |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8|, to catalyze the conversion of betaine aldehyde to glycine betaine. The choline-to-betaine aldehyde reaction, however, is divergent: Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-287|, and |FRAME: TAX-382| utilize |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.1| (see |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|), Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, use an alcohol dehydrogenase (see |FRAME: PWY-3722|), while high plants use |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.7| (see |FRAME: PWY1F-353|)., Certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1677| and |FRAME: TAX-1665|, as well as the fungus |FRAME: TAX-109805|, use yet another enzyme to catalyze this conversion: they use a soluble |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.17|, that catalyzes both steps (see |FRAME: PWY-3721|). , There exists at least one more variation for the synthesis of glycine betaine, which is found in several halotolerant bacteria. The pathway was found in |FRAME: TAX-1052| and several other organisms, which synthesize glycine betaine from glycine through a series of methylation reactions |CITS: [10896953]| (this pathway). However, since methylation reactions are expensive (due to the cost of regenerating S-adenosylmethionine), this pathway is less common., General Background, Glycine betaine (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it is accumulated at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant. In addition to its osmoprotectant activity, glycine betaine is also a potent protectant against mutagenic compounds |CITS: [12730887][15802867]| and radiation-induced damage |CITS: [12841603]|., Glycine betaine can either be taken up directly from the environment, or synthesized. Common biosynthesis pathways for glycine betaine start with either choline (see |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-3722| and |FRAME: PWY1F-353|) or glycine (see |FRAME: P541-PWY|)., Glycine betaine synthesis from glycine, which was originally described in several halotolerant bacteria, involves a series of methylation reactions |CITS: [10896953]|. Summary: Vitamin K-dependent proteins are modified by carboxylation of clusters of glutamate residues to carboxylated glutamate as they transit through the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [12475254]|. The modified proteins are diverse in both structure and function and are found in many cell and tissue types, including several proteins of the blood-clotting system. The carboxylation is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.90|, an enzyme that uses various vitamin-K hydroquinones, including menaquinol, as co-substrates that are epoxidated during the reaction, generating |FRAME: 23-EPOXY-23-DIHYDRO-2-METHYL-14-NAPHTHOQ|. Plasma concentrations of |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| in healthy fasting people are of the order of only 0.5 nM. Tissue reserves are low as well - the median total liver pool of |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| measured in British adults was estimated at about 20 nmol. Menaquinone concentration is higher, up to 200-300 nmol |CITS: [8785182]|. While the majority of vitamin K reserves in the liver comprise long chain forms (|FRAME: CPD-9718| through to |FRAME: CPD-9721|), extrahepatic tissues contain mainly |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| and/or |FRAME: CPD-9726| |CITS: [7947656][8785182][8632229]|., The main reason for the low concentration of |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| is that much of it is rapidly catabolized |CITS: [4617407]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8000|). The polyisoprenoid side chain is shortened to two major carboxylic acid aglycones with 7- and 5-carbon side chains, respectively, which are excreted in bile and urine, mainly as glucuronides |CITS: [4617407][7306367][18841274]|. The catabolic pathway involves ω-hydroxylation by |FRAME: HS02675| |CITS: [19297519][23505319]|., In several tissues, such as brain, kidney, and pancreas, |FRAME: CPD-9726| is the predominant quinone form. In 2010 it was found that |FRAME: CPD-21305| is formed from |FRAME: MENADIOL| by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.M22|, an enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: HS04454| gene. The gene is homologous to the bacterial |FRAME: EG11880| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.74| |CITS: [20953171]|., Although many cell lines readily convert |FRAME: CPD-3766| to |FRAME: CPD-21305| |CITS: [9446847][16469140][18083713][22437559]|, the same cell lines show either no |CITS: [9446847][16469140][22437559]| or much reduced |CITS: [9446847][18083713]| capacity to utilize |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| as a substrate, indicating that a different enzyme is responsible for the removal of the side chain from the latter. Additional observations using labelled precursors suggested that this enzyme forms |FRAME: CPD-3766| |CITS: [22437559]|. Studies in rats confirmed that dietary |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-3766| in the intestine and transported to tissues, where it is prenylated to form |FRAME: CPD-21305| |CITS: [24085302]|. Since |FRAME: HS04454| accepts only the |FRAME: MENADIOL| form, an as-yet unidentified redox enzyme in the tissues must carry out the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-3766| to |FRAME: MENADIOL| |CITS: [24085302][24489112]|.

Summary: The catecholamines |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE norepinephrine|, |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE epinephrine| and |FRAME: DOPAMINE| are synthesized  in the central nervous system (CNS), sympathetic nerves and in the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. Nonneuronal cells in the gastrointestinal tract and the kidneys are among other tissues capable of producing  catecholamines., In the CNS, dopamine and norepinephrine are widely distributed, whereas epinephrine is found in the mammalian brain in relatively low concentrations. In the periphery, norepinephrine is the transmitter of the postganglionic sympathetic nervous system and dopamine is involved in the regulation of renal and gastrointestinal function. The main source of epinephrine outside of the CNS are the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla., Dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine are synthesized by a series of enzymes with cytoplasmic and vesicular locations.  This biosynthetic pathway was first postulated in 1939 |CITS: [13667411]|, and the rate-limiting step was, experimentally confirmed in1964  |CITS:[5836553][14216443]|  Synthesis of dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine ends at different points in the pathway depending on the availability of the various biosynthetic enzymes , involved in each step.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12379 "Eumelanin"| is a common type of |FRAME: MELANIN| pigment, which is found in hair and skin. , There are two types of eumelanin, black and brown, which differ by their pattern of polymer bonds., A small amount of black eumelanin in the absence of other pigments causes grey hair, while a small amount of brown eumelanin in the absence of other pigments causes yellow (blond) color hair., Spectroscopic studies of the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12379| showed that it takes place in three chromophoric phases. Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, Shiga toxin producing |FRAME: TAX-562| strains of serogroup O:111 are the most frequently isolated non-O157 strains causing outbreaks of gastroenteritis with hemolytic-uremic syndrome |CITS: [2213982][1976876][8784557]|. An O111 clone was the first |FRAME: TAX-562| strain implicated as a cause of outbreaks of gastroenteritis |CITS: [Bray45][14770850]|., The structure of the |FRAME: CPD-23782| was reported already in 1978 |CITS: [Eklund78]|. It was later found that members of group O of Salmonella enterica (serotype O:35) such as |FRAME: TAX-29473| produce an identical O-antigen repeat unit |CITS: [6339053][23848592]|. A similar repeat unit is produced by E. coli O55 and S. enterica serovar greenside., The O antigen biosynthetic cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1055535| was cloned an expressed in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, resulting in production of the |FRAME: CPD-24109| |CITS: [1722559]|. At the time, about half of the cluster was sequenced. In a subsequent publication the authors reported the sequence of the remainder of the gene cluster |CITS: [9774562]|. The cluster contains genes encoding the enzymes necessary for |FRAME: CPD-9391| biosynthesis, an O antigen flippase, an O antigen polymerase, and three glycosyltransferases involved in the pathway |CITS: [9774562]|., Another study has determined the precise roles of the individual glycosyltranferases. In that study the full cluster was introduced to an E. coli host in which the genes responsible for enterobacterial common antigen (ECA), O-antigen, and colanic acid (CA) synthesis were deleted. By disabling each of the glycosyltransferases and analyzing the resulting O antigens produced by the mutant it was possible to show that |FRAME: G-81055| encodes an α-1,3-galactosyltransferase, |FRAME: G-81056| encodes an α-(1,4)-glucosyltransferase, and |FRAME: G-81057| encodes a colitosyltransferase that transfers both colitosyl residues |CITS: [18156323]|.

Summary: General Background, Curcumin (dihydroferuloylmethane) is a yellow pigment found in turmeric (|FRAME:TAX-136217|). It is used in many ways, as an ingredient in food such as a colorant of spices (e.g. curry powder) and mustard. Curcumin also has a long history in the traditional medicine of Asian countries. Recently, curcumin has been investigated with respect to its potent anti-inflammatory and ant-leishmanial properties |CITS: [11878200]|, anti-cancer activity and a possible clinical application for treatment of Alzheimer's disease (|CITS:[18573304]| and referenced in |CITS: [15178322]|)., Although curcumin offers a significant potential as a novel medicine or lead compound its bioavailability is dramatically decreased due to the extremely limited solubility of curcumin aglycones in watery solutions. However, it has been found that the solubility of curcumin can be enhanced considerably by means of glucosylation |CITS:[14644434]|. Hence the pharmacological exploration of those compounds is considered a major attempt to further explore the practical applications of pharmacologically useful curcumin glucosides |CITS: [15178322]|. , About This Pathway, The pathway displayed here reflects a more applied aspect of secondary plant metabolism. Although curcumin has been metabolized in |FRAME:TAX-4058| the compound and its derivatives have not been reported in this plant. The occurrence of curcumin and metabolites thereof are mainly restricted to monocots, more specifically to the order of Zingiberales |CITS: [GANG06]|. Therefore the glucosyltransferases identified in |FRAME:TAX-4058| may also be involved in the detoxification of xenobiotics |CITS:[15926195]| which is supported by the up-regulation of enzyme activity after treatment with |FRAME:CPD1F-2| |CITS:[17940060]|. , Testing 10 different plant cell suspension cultures |FRAME:TAX-4058| turned out to be the only one to produce a wide variety of glucosylated curcumin species. Curcumin was not only converted to simple glucosides by introducing glucose residues onto the two phenolic hydroxyl groups (curcumin monoglucoside - CMG, curcumine diglucoside - CDG) but also by forming L-1,6-glycosidic linkages, leading to the gentiobioside derivatives (curcumin gentiobioside - CGB, curcumin gentiobiosyl glucoside - CGG, curcumin digentiobioside - CDGB). The corresponding curcumin glucoside 1,6-glucosyltransferase has been purified and biochemically characterized |CITS:[17940060]|. In addition to that, the flavonoid 1,6-glucosyltransferase catalyzing the sequential elongation of the gentioside chain to form not only gentiobioside but also gentiotrioside and gentiotetraside of |FRAME:CPD-6602| has been cloned from |FRAME:TAX-4058| and the catalytic properties of the recombinant protein determined |CITS:[19561332]|, The solubility of the curcumin glucosides has been enhanced dramatically. The solubility increased 230-fold for CMG, 10.000-fold for CDG and reached over 20 million-fold for CDGB compared to the curcumin aglycone |CITS: [14644434]|. The glucosides obtained by an enzymatic reaction in the cell cultures have been much more effective in terms of solubility than other approaches, e.g. the formation of cyclodextrin complexes of curcumin which resulted in a 26.000-fold solubility increase |CITS: [12204572]|., A UDPG:glucosyltransferase (UGT) was identified in |FRAME:TAX-4058| (CaUGT2) that was able to carry out the first two glucosylations to the curcumin mono and diglucoside in a sequential manner |CITS: [15178322]|. The other glucosylation steps have not yet been assigned to a special UGT. The substrate specificity of CaUGT2 was relatively broad glucosylating esculetin as well. However, the formation of a diglucoside of esculetin was not detected. Therefore, it was proposed that CaUGT2 may possess certain position specificity for the hydroxyl group to be glucosylated |CITS: [15178322]|., The expression of the CaUGT2 was rapidly induced under the influence of methyl jasmonate and salicylic acid. It was proposed that the UDPG:glucosyltransferase of |FRAME:TAX-4058| may represent a defense related enzyme involved in the detoxification of xenobiotica and/or biosynthesis of defense molecules.

|FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|). The β-oxidation of saturated fatty acids is a straightforward process which requires the participation of three enzymes, i.e. acyl-CoA oxidase (POX1), the multifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase (FOX2) and the thiolase (POT1). At the end of the process stands a saturated fatty acid shortened by 2 carbon units (|FRAME:ACETYL-COA|) which is further metabolized in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-5690|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7292| and |FRAME:PWY-7307|). , The major pathway for the break-down of |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD| via β-oxidation is the isomerase-dependent pathway depicted here. This pathway only requires the catalytic activity of one additionally auxiliary enzyme, i.e. Δ3,Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase after which the pathway has been named. After two cycles of β-oxidation the double bond of |FRAME:OLEOYL-COA| is moved from Δ9 into the Δ5 position and has additionally been received a trans-double bond at position 2 by the catalytic action of |FRAME:YGL205W-MONOMER| (POX1) |CITS:[2189786] [8685242] [19830908]|. The intermediate |FRAME:CPD0-1162| goes through another cycle of β-oxidation after which |FRAME:CPD-7221| is isomerized by |FRAME:CPLX-8706| to form |FRAME:CPD-7222|. The resulting |FRAME:CPD-7222| is now a proper substrate for further β-oxidation in the cycle. As all the enzymes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation also the auxiliary Δ3,Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) is inducible by fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD|) |CITS:[9837886] [9813046]| which also causes increased proliferation of the peroxisomal compartment |CITS:[5325972] [3332968]|. In addition to fatty acids with double bonds on odd-numbered positions ECI1 also is discussed as an requirement for the break-down at even-numbered double bonds of fatty acids |CITS:[9813046]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Flavonoids Flavonoids| are secondary metabolites formed from phenylpropanoid and fatty acid derivatives and have important functions, acting as UV-B protectors |CITS:[11724379]|, attractors of pollinators and seed dispersers, insect feeding attractors, anti-feedants, signal molecules in legume-rhizobium bacteria interactions |CITS:[3738520]|, and , fungicides. Flavonoids have also received a lot of attention due to their effect of human health. In some plant species, flavonoids are required for fertility, but this is not the case in |FRAME:TAX-3701| |CITS:[8672888]|., |FRAME: Flavonoids Flavonoids| constitute a relatively diverse family of aromatic molecules that are derived from phenylalanine and malonyl-coenzyme A (via the fatty acid pathway) |CITS: [11402179]|. There are six major subgroups found in most higher plants: the |FRAME: Chalcones chalcones|, |FRAME: Flavones flavones|, |FRAME: Flavanols flavonols|, |FRAME: Flavonols flavanols|, |FRAME: Anthocyanins anthocyanins|, and |FRAME: PA-N condensed tannins| (proanthocyanidins); a seventh group, the |FRAME: AURONE aurones|, is not ubiquitous., |FRAME: Isoflavonoids Isoflavonoids| are found mostly in legumes but also in a small number of non-legume plants. Another specialized form of flavonoids, the phlobaphenes (monomers: 3-deoxyanthocyanins) have been detected in only a few species so far. Stilbenes, closely related to flavonoids, are synthesized by yet another group of unrelated species., Biosynthesis is thought to occur in the cytoplasm through enzymes that are associated with the endoplasmatic reticulum membranes |CITS:[3321063]| where the enzymes form a large, macromolecular complex |CITS:[10536025]|. Interestingly, the pathway also accommodates bifunctional enzymes that are involved in more than the presented flavonoid pathway above. For instance the naringenin 3-dioxygenases from Citrus unshiu (CuFLS) |CITS:[12180990] [12620339]| and the gymnosperm Ginkgo biloba (GbFLS1) |CITS:[21643949]| can also act as flavonol synthase in the |FRAME:PWY-3101|. In addition, the recombinant Citrus naringenin 3-dioxygenase (FLS) had been shown to be able to accept the unusual substrate |FRAME:CPD-14042| to form the (-) isomer of |FRAME:DIHYDROKAEMPFEROL-CMPD|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15886| |CITS:[12620339]|. , The structure of the major flavonoids in |FRAME:TAX-3701| have recently been described |CITS:[10514319]|. Under greenhouse conditions, only kaempferol glycosides accumulate in |FRAME:TAX-3701|. With higher UV exposure, quercetin metabolites can be detected as well |CITS:[10514319]|. Most flavonoids accumulate in the vacuole, the cuticular wax and in the cell wall |CITS:[10975502]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| (phytate, phytic acid) is one of the most prevalent forms of phosphorylated inositols in the eukaryotic cell, with a total concentration of 15-100 μM |CITS:[3426614][1684044][8435066]|. It's cellular distribution is not completely known - some of it is soluble, some is "wall-papered" around membranes, while some is bound to proteins |CITS: [9838040]|. In plant seeds, large amount of phytate are complexed with cations and deposited as globular inclusions in membrane-bound storage bodies |CITS: [15700415]|., The compound has been proposed to have a number of signaling roles, including regulation of insulin exocytosis |CITS: [9114007]|, regulation of nuclear mRNA export |CITS:[10390371][10683435]|, binding of the clathrin assembly proteins AP2 and AP3 |CITS: [1849645][1371119]|, inhibition of clathrin cage assembly |CITS: [7814377][7829485]|, and inhibition of serine and threonine protein phosphatases that are thought to regulate L-type Ca2+ channels |CITS: [9334307]|., About This Pathway, In plant cells phytate serves as a storage form of myo-inositol, phosphate and mineral nutrients for utilization during seed germination and seedling growth. It is deposited within single-membrane storage organelles referred to as protein bodies and is usually present as mixed complexes with different cations, including |FRAME: K+|, |FRAME: MG+2|, |FRAME: CA+2|, |FRAME: FE+2|, and |FRAME: ZN+2|, known as phytin |CITS:[11590064][8744268]|., Although phytin only makes up about 1% of the seed weight, it may contain up to 80% of the total seed phosphorus |CITS:[15700415]|. Phytate is also present in other plant tissues and organs such as pollen, roots, tuber and turions in smaller quantities |CITS:[14568069]|. , One phytate biosynthetic pathway found in plants proceeds from |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (produced by phospholipase C) as described in |FRAME: PWY-6361| by a series of successive phosphorylations carried out by only two enzymes., A second, indirect pathway, has been suggested to occur via |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE|. The pathway is indirect because |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| itself is produced from |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6364|). However, once formed, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| can be phosphorylated by |FRAME: AT5G16760-MONOMER| (|FRAME: AT5G16760|), an enzyme that does not recognize |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| as substrate |CITS: [14568069]|. The products of |FRAME: AT5G16760| are then phosphorylated further by the same enzymes used in |FRAME: PWY-6361|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-17343 "Anditomin"| is |FRAME: CPD-17353|. These complex organo-oxygen natural products are produced by fungi from polyketide and terpenoid precursors. They have unique, highly oxygenated structures containing a complex bridged-ring system. The elucidation of the biosynthetic pathway for the meroterpenoid |FRAME: CPD-17343| in |FRAME: TAX-1549217| provides an opportunity for future construction of novel scaffolds for use in drug discovery |CITS: [25216349]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CPD-17343| biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1549217| was identified by bioinformatic analysis and the and gene products were functionally characterized (note that NCBI Taxonomy merged the Emericella variecolor and Aspergillus stellifer entries). The early-stage and late-stage biosynthetic steps were determined by expression of recombinant enzymes in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-5062| followed by analysis of products by HPLC, 1H NMR, 13C NMR and mass spectrometry. The mid-stage biosynthetic steps were elucidated using feeding experiments to predict the sequence of tailoring enzymes. In the case of AndA and AndF, recombinant enzyme was expressed in Escherichia coli, purified and characterized |CITS: [25216349]|., The pathway begins with a polyketide synthase encoded by gene andM that produces |FRAME: CPD-17316| as its final product. AndK is a bifunctional P450 monooxygenase and hydrolase fusion protein that produces the phthalide compound |FRAME: CPD-17317|. AndD is a prenyltransferase that incorporates the farnesyl moiety. AndE is an epoxidase that forms the (S)-epoxide |FRAME: CPD-17325|. The terpene cyclase AndB then forms |FRAME: CPD-17333| |CITS: [25216349]|. , The mid-stage biosynthetic steps include AndA, AndJ and AndI. The nonheme iron-dependent dioxygenase AndA was shown to catalyze two reactions, the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: CPD-17334| to produce the enone |FRAME: CPD-17335| that contains a Δ1,2-conjugated double bond, and an isomerization involving an unprecedented skeletal rearrangement that results in the bridged-ring of |FRAME: CPD-17336|. This is in contrast to a previously proposed DielsAlder reaction. AndA thus generates the scaffold of the andilesins class of secondary metabolites. AndJ is a |FRAME: FAD|-dependent Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase that generates a seven-membered lactone ring from |FRAME: CPD-17336|. AndI is a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) that appears to reduce |FRAME: CPD-17337| to |FRAME: CPD-17339| |CITS: [25216349]|. , In the late-stage biosynthetic steps acetyltransferase AndG attaches an acetyl group to the hydroxyl group of |FRAME: CPD-17339|. This acetyl group is then lost in a spontaneous reaction. AndH is another SDR reductase that catalyzes reduction of the C-6 double bond of |FRAME: CPD-17341| to produce |FRAME: CPD-17342|. Finally AndF, another nonheme iron-dependent dioxygenase like AndA, oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-17342| to |FRAME: CPD-17343|. Based on the cofactor requirements for the production of both |FRAME: CPD-17336| by AndA and |FRAME: CPD-17343| by AndF, as well as the analogous FtmF reaction (see |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.38|), detailed reaction mechanisms for AndA and AndF were proposed |CITS: [25216349]|.

|FRAME: CPD-20101| (also known as L-2-amino-4-methoxy-trans-3-butenoic acid or AMB) is a toxin produced by the opportunistic pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287|. It is a non-proteinogenic amino acid belonging to a small group of natural compounds known as |FRAME: CPD-20107 oxyvinylglycines|, which irreversibly inhibit enzymes that require |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| as a co-factor |CITS: [Berkowitz06]|., Isolated originally by its ability to inhibit the growth of |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [4624612]| and |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [4205653]|, |FRAME: CPD-20101| was shown to inhibit |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1| in pigs |CITS: [4210878][6451]| and in rat hepatocytes |CITS: [7294799][6466297]|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.20| in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [1164442]|, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.37| in rats |CITS: [763076]|, and |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1| in Walker carcinoma |CITS: [7460079]|. The compound also inhibits L-methionine tRNA aminoacylation |CITS: [16660951]|, and was shown to inhibit the growth of important plant and animal pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-552| |CITS: [23757135]| and |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [25814981]|., The enzymes involved in |FRAME: CPD-20101| metabolism are encoded in two transcriptional units. The first transcriptional unit, ambA, encodes a putative LysE-type transporter and is poroposed to encode an AMB transporter responsible for its secretion. The second transcriptional unit encodes four proteins involved in AMB biosynthesis. Two of these, AmbB and AmbE, are large |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "non-ribosomal peptide synthetases"| (NRPSs) while the other two, ambC and ambD, belong to the family of Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases (EC 1.14.11) |CITS: [20543073][23757135]|., The number of thiolation domains in AmbB and AmbE NRPSs indicates that AMB biosynthesis proceeds via a tripeptide precursor. AmbB contains an L-alanine adenylation domain, a corresponding thiolation domain (for loading the adenylated alanine onto a phosphopantetheine arm attached at a conserved serine), and a condensation domain that transfers the alanine to a glutamate residue attached to the |FRAME: G-55158 AmbE| protein., AmbE contains an L-glutamine adenylation domain, two thiolation domains (for loading adenylated amino acids onto a phosphopantetheine arm attached at a conserved serine), a condensation domain, a methyltransferase domain, and a thioesterase domain. An additional domain of unknown function may be located at the N-terminal end of AmbE., Assays with purified reconstructed holo proteins showed that an L-glutamate residue is adenylated by AmbE and transfered to the T1 domain. An L-alanine is then transfered from |FRAME: G-55157 AmbB| to the glutamate. A second L-alanine, presumably adenylated by AmbB, is transferred to the T2 domain of AmbE, and the L-glutamyl-L-alanine dipeptide is transferred to the second alanine, forming an L-alanyl-L-glutamyl-L-alanine tripeptide |CITS: [25814981]|., Further modifications, which convert the L-glutamate residue to |FRAME: CPD-20101|, occur while the tripeptide is still tethered to AmbE. These modifications are catalyzed by the methylation domain of AmbE and by the ambC and ambD oxygenases, but have not been characterized yet. Following these modifications, the peptide is released by the action of the thioesterase domain, followed by cleavage of the two alanines, forming a free |FRAME: CPD-20101| |CITS: [25814981]|., The role of the two flanking L-alanine residues is not clear. They may prevent AMB toxicity before it is exported out of the cell.

Summary: About This Pathway, |FRAME: SER| biosynthesis is a major metabolic pathway in many organisms. Its end product, |FRAME: SER|, is not only used in protein synthesis, but also as a precursor for the biosynthesis of glycine, cysteine, tryptophan, and phospholipids. In addition, it directly or indirectly serves as a source of one-carbon units for the biosynthesis of various compounds., In the pathway described here, which operates in archaea |CITS: [17071763]|, bacteria |CITS: [11354602]|, yeast, some protists, plant plastids and animals, serine is derived from |FRAME: G3P|, an intermediate of glycolysis., Regulation of the pathway is mainly accomplished by feedback inhibition of the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.95|. The second enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.52|, requires |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| (PLP) as a cofactor and is also required for the biosynthesis of PLP itself. Thus the cell must ensure that the supply of PLP is adequate. Little biochemical work has been done on the final enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.3|., Serine Biosynthesis in Plants, |FRAME: SER| biosynthesis in plants proceeds by three pathways. The pathway described here, which is called the phosphorylated pathway, operates in plastids. The phosphorylated pathway is thought to contribute to serine biosynthesis mostly in the dark or in non-photosynthetic tissues. Since the genes of the phosphorylated pathway are upregulated by high salinity, flood and cold, it is thought that the phosphorylated pathway is also important in supplying serine under, environmental stresses., A second pathway, which has not been studied much, operates in the cytosol and is described in |FRAME: PWY-8011|., However, the best studied and arguably the most important serine biosynthesis pathway in plants, which is called the glycolate pathway, is part of the |FRAME: PWY-181 photorespiration| pathway. In that pathway |FRAME: SER| is formed |from glycolate via glycine. The glycolate pathway dominates in the photosynthetic tissues. Most of the serine produced in the phosphorylated pathway is fed into with the photorespiration pathway as input for |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, and its carbon is directed to the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY "Calvin cycle"| via |FRAME: OH-PYR| and |FRAME: GLYCERATE|.

The stigma of solanaceous species is covered by large amounts of exudate, a substance that is primarily lipidic, although other compounds such as proteins, sugars, and pigments are also present., The lipidic component of the exudate comprises estolide, a lipid-based polyester |CITS: [18481134]|. Estolide is rich in ω-hydroxy fatty acids (fatty acids containing a hydroxy group on the terminal or ω carbon)., The exudate of |FRAME: TAX-4102| stigma contains up to 96% ω-hydroxy fatty acids mainly in the form of |FRAME: 18-HYDROXYOLEATE| and |FRAME: CPD-17376|., The ω-hydroxy fatty acid monomers are thought to be attached to a glycerol backbone, forming |FRAME: Diacylglycerides| or |FRAME: Triacylglycerides|, and then iteratively esterified such that the ω-hydroxyl of one fatty acid is esterified to a carboxyl group of another to ultimately form the estolide., In the pathway shown here a |FRAME: CPD-12262| is shown, containing 4 fatty acids. In tobacco stigma, estolides are formed as tetra-, penta-, hexa-, and hepta-acyl glycerides, and are capped by normal fatty acids |CITS: [Matsuzaki83]|., Despite the important role that the stigmatic exudate plays in the pollination process, little is known about the enzymes involved. A cytochrome P450 enzyme that is responsible for the hydroxylation of the fatty-acyl CoAs has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-4102| |CITS: [19940120]|.

Summary: General Background, This pathway and the two linked pathways depict parts of the pathways for the N-linked glycosylation of certain protein |FRAME: ASN| residues in some |FRAME: TAX-194| species, and the O-linked glycosylation of certain protein |FRAME: SER| residues in |FRAME: TAX-482| species (see |FRAME: PWY-7031| and |FRAME: PWY-7037|, respectively). Protein O-linked glycosylation has been also described in |FRAME: TAX-287| strains |CITS: [16740931][17085575]|, |FRAME: TAX-817| |CITS: [21115495]|, and possibly other genera |CITS: [22391990]|, although the pathways have not been shown., Until the mid-1970s, protein glycosylation was thought to occur only in eukaryotes. However, prokaryotic N-linked and O-linked protein glycosylation was later found in a restricted set of archaea and bacteria, including pathogens and commensals. The prokaryotic glycans can include both common and rare monosaccharides (reviewed in |CITS: [18694827][9076508]|). The biological role of protein glycosylation in prokaryotes is not yet fully elucidated, but it is thought to be involved in host interactions such as adherence and pathogenicity (|CITS: [19681908]|, in |CITS: [22389484]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [12687605][14659687][20948550][20371512]|). Prokaryotic protein glycosylation may also enhance protein stability |CITS: [19154179]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-197| is a pathogen of the human gut mucosa that is associated with gastroenteritis (reviewed in |CITS: [9025274]|). The pgl gene cluster in this organism was identified as being involved in protein N-linked glycosylation |CITS: [10361304]|. It was shown that the pgl gene cluster could be functionally transferred from |FRAME: TAX-197| to |FRAME:TAX-562| resulting in glycosylation of two periplasmic proteins with a heptasaccharide |CITS: [12459590]|. Expression of the genes in this cluster in |FRAME:TAX-562| followed by mutational analysis and structural analysis of the glycans produced suggested the functional roles of the genes |CITS: [15752194]|. Subsequent biochemical analyses confirmed their functions in the pathway |CITS: [16356848][16186480]|., The pathway is initiated by enzymes PglF, PglE and PglD which transform |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| into |FRAME: CPD-14248| as shown in this pathway. The N,N'-diacetylbacillosamine residue is an unusual sugar that is found in some bacteria (reviewed in |CITS: [17717023]|). It ultimately becomes the carbohydrate-peptide linking monosaccharide. As depicted in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7031|, enzymes PglA, PglC, PglH, PglI and PglJ are glycosyltransferases that assemble the heptasaccharide on the membrane-bound lipid anchor |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| (reviewed in |CITS: [21506607]|)., The PglF-catalyzed C-6 dehydratase reaction produces the UDP-4-keto sugar intermediate |FRAME: CPD-13847|. This 4-keto sugar intermediate is used by PglE as its primary substrate |CITS: [17087520]|., The in vitro synthesis of the complete lipid-linked heptasaccharide, including this initial portion of the pathway, has been demonstrated |CITS: [17087520]|., This pathway is also found in |FRAME: TAX-482| species which contain pgl genes with similar molecular functions. However, the genes are arranged differently on the chromosome and the product of pglB is bifunctional in |FRAME: TAX-482|, having both amino-acetylase and phosphoglycosyltransferase activity |CITS: [21542610]|.

Fumitremorgins are tremorgenic mycotoxins |CITS:[5122678]| and represent a group of prenylated indole alkaloids which are mostly found in the genera Aspergillus and Penicillium of the fungi kingdom |CITS:[11245401] [23467716] [20024094]||. Aspergillus fumigatus, a main producer of tremorgins, is the foremost cause for fungal diseases with a high mortality rate in immunocompromised humans |CITS:[20618330] [21102391]|. Aspergillus fumigatus preliminary invades the sinopulmonary tract and lung |CITS:[17890370]| inducing chronic diseases such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis which often has a lethal outcome |CITS:[19403905] [22640845] [23889240]|. Therefore, Aspergillus fumigatus has been in the focus of researchers for some time now which, amongst others, resulted in the deciphering of its genome |CITS:[16372009] [16371993]| and the elucidation of gene clusters involved in the making of fungal secondary metabolites exhibiting numerous activities of physiological importance |CITS:[16322742]|. , |FRAME:CPD-15266 Fumitremorgin C| and various intermediates of the pathway such as |FRAME:CPD-15263| and |FRAME:CPD-15262| have been found to be candidates for promising anticancer drugs. |FRAME:CPD-15262 Tryprostatin B| and |FRAME:CPD-15262| inhibit the mammalian cell-cycle progression |CITS:[8698634]| through disruption of microtubule assembly |CITS:[9677311] [11058035]| and have been demonstrated to express growth inhibitory properties in certain human cancer types such as breast, lung, and prostate cancer |CITS:[11931609]|. Special notice deserves the research done with |FRAME:CPD-15266| with respect to its inhibition of an breast cancer resistant protein (BCRP) |CITS:[10646850]| which represents an drug transporter conferring drug resistance to its host by extruding a wide variety of structurally divergent drugs across cell membranes |CITS:[16402910]|. Hence, |FRAME:CPD-15266| indicates its potential as a lead compound for investigating the molecular and biochemical principles of this BCRP transporter and for the development of novel drugs designed for pioneering cancer treatments |CITS:[10646850]|. , The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-15266| originates from the formation of cyclic dipeptides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15265| catalyzed by the brevianamid F synthase which synthesizes the peptide bond between |FRAME:TRP| and |FRAME:PRO| |CITS:[16755625] [Williams00]|. The formed cyclic |L-Trp-L-Pro| undergoes prenylation and the type of prenylation, i.e. 'regular' versus 'reverse' at position C-2 directs the pathway either to compound classes such as fumitremorgins and spirotryprostatins (regular prenylation) or compound classes such as brevianamides and notoamides (reverse prenylation) |CITS:[20024094] [20722388]|. The brevianamide F prenyltransferase catalyzes the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15263| from |FRAME:CPD-15265| using |FRAME:CPD-4211| |CITS:[16000710] [21105662]| and was also shown to be able to prenylate the C-3 of the indole nucleus |CITS:[23090579]| indicating the capability to produce an even wider spectrum of cyclic dipeptide intermediates., Further chemical modifications of the diketopiperazine core include the 6-hydroxylation of the indole ring of |FRAME:CPD-15263| yielding |FRAME:CPD-15264| which is then further methylated to generate |FRAME:CPD-15262|. The molecular functions of the respective enzymes, i.e. tryprostatin B 6-hydroxylase |CITS:[19226505]| and 6-hydroxytryprostatin B methytransferase |CITS:[19226505] [23649274]| have been demonstrated in direct assays as well as in functional complementation and mutant knock-outs. Finally, the formation of cyclization products, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15266| and |FRAME:CPD-15267| is realized via the formation of a C-N bond catalyzed by the first described fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme carrying out that reaction, i.e. fumitremorgin C synthase |CITS:[19226505]|. It remains to be shown whether |FRAME:CPD-15267| represents a shunt-product or a variant in the |FRAME:PWY-7525|. The further metabolism of |FRAME:CPD-15266| in Aspergillus fumigatus and related species is depicted in |FRAME:PWY-7526| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7537|).

|FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate "3-Sulfopropanediol"| (2,3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate, DHPS) is a widespread intermediate in plant and algal transformations of |FRAME: CPD-10247| from the plant sulfolipid |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL| |CITS: [7626014]| (see |FRAME: PWYQT-4427|). It is also recovered quantitatively during bacterial degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10247| |CITS: [14602597]|, and is secreted by all diatoms |CITS: [5085579]|. , A gene cluster encoding enzymes involved in |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| degradation has been discovered in several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-264198|, |FRAME: TAX-89187| and |FRAME: TAX-246200|. The gene cluster also includes genes required for the downstream degradation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate 3-sulfolactate| |CITS: [19581363]|., Based on the assumed gene functions, a pathway has been proposed. The main enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-8154| (|FRAME: G-12216|), catalyzes the 3-hydrogenation of only one of the the enantiomers, |FRAME: CPD-12692|, to |FRAME: CPD-367|, which is degraded further by different pathways in different organisms. In |FRAME: TAX-264198| sulfolcatate is desulfonated by |FRAME: RXN-11691 "(R)-sulfolactate sulfo-lyase"|, while in |FRAME: TAX-89187| it is degraded by a |FRAME: PWY-6641 "bifurcated pathway"| (see the different pathways under |FRAME: Sulfolactate-Degradation|)., The other enantiomer, |FRAME: CPD-12693|, is converted to the (R) form via |FRAME: CPD-12694| by the successive action of two dehydrogenases, |FRAME: MONOMER-15898| (|FRAME: G-12217|) and |FRAME: MONOMER-15899| (|FRAME: G-12218|) |CITS: [20150239]|., The enzymes of this pathway were purified from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-264198| and shown to catalyze the predicted activities |CITS: [20150239]|.

Arginine and agmatine are metabolized via the |FRAME: ARGDEGRAD-PWY "arginine deiminase pathway"| and |FRAME: PWY2S1Y-3 "agmatine deiminase pathway"|, respectively., Both pathways start with a deiminase reaction (|FRAME: EC-3.5.3.6| and |FRAME: EC-3.5.3.12|, respectively), followed by a carbamoyltransferase reaction (|FRAME: EC-2.1.3.3| and |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.6|, respectively), forming |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME:TAURINE| (2-aminoethanesulfonate), a natural occuring amino acid analogue of, |FRAME:B-ALANINE|, plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many, species., The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation,, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular |FRAME: CA+2| homeostasis., While plants or animals cannot degrade taurine, several species of bacteria and fungi are capable of, doing that., For example, |FRAME: ORG-5927| can grow on taurine as the sole source of carbon,, nitrogen, sulfur and energy |CITS: [113035]|., Some anaerobic bacteria can use taurine for respiration as either an electron acceptor (eg., |FRAME: ORG-5878|) or an electron donor (eg. |FRAME: TAX-56119|, |FRAME: ORG-5923|,, |FRAME: TAX-82367| NKNCYSA). Others can use it as a fermentative substrate (eg. |FRAME: ORG-5898|), |CITS: [12471498][9297467]|., The different species often utilize different pathways, resulting in conversion of taurine into different, sulfur compounds. For example, |FRAME: ORG-5927| converts taurine to, |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| |CITS: [11082195]|, which is cleaved to |FRAME: SO3|, |CITS: [11160104]|, and eventually converted to |FRAME:HS| by a sulfite reductase |CITS: [9143131]|., |FRAME: TAX-56119| |CITS: [9202468]|, |FRAME: ORG-5923| (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), and, |FRAME: TAX-82367| NKNCYSA (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), all convert taurine to, |FRAME: SULFATE| (additional products are ammonia and CO2), while, |FRAME: ORG-5898| converts taurine to thiosulfate, ammonia and acetate |CITS: [9297467]|., Taurine degradation is known to be initiated by at least three different types of reactions: transamination,, which appears to be the most widespread |CITS: [113035][5058441][5012173][629994]|, oxidation, |CITS: [5551654]|, and oxygenation |CITS: [9287300]|. In the first two cases sulfoacetaldehyde is an, intermediate, whereas in the third case taurine is converted to sulfite and aminoacetaldehyde, |CITS: [9287300]|., About This Pathway, Two aminotransferases involved in taurine dissimilation have been described,, |FRAME:MONOMER-3663| in |FRAME: ORG-5927| and |FRAME: ORG-5878| (see |FRAME:PWY-1263|), |CITS: [113035][11082195]| and |FRAME:MONOMER-2966| in |FRAME: ORG-5857| (this pathway) |CITS: [5058441][5012173][629994]|., Experimental evidence for |FRAME:MONOMER-2966| suggested that taurine may be degraded via this enzymatic route; however, initially this pathway has not been substantiated by further evidence, and |FRAME:MONOMER-2966| activity is induced by |FRAME:B-ALANINE|, but not taurine |CITS: [3003495]|. Furthermore, the organism from which this enzyme has been purified (|FRAME: ORG-5857|) is not capable of growth on taurine |CITS: [5058441][12471498]|., Cook and Denger |CITS: [12471498]| speculated that the physiological role of |FRAME:MONOMER-2966| in this organism may be the transamination of β-alanine rather than taurine., Further evidence for the pathway was obtained from the organisms |FRAME: ORG-6177| and |FRAME: TAX-290398|, both of which can utilize |FRAME: TAURINE| as the nitrogen source, and both of which posses only |FRAME: MONOMER-16211| |CITS: [20133363]|.

Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, The key enzyme in this salvage pathway is uridine-cytidine kinase (also known as uridine kinase, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.48 "EC 2.7.1.48"|). This enzyme catalyzes the phosphorylation of the nucleosides |FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE| to their monophosphate forms., The enzyme is found in archaea, bacteria, fungi, plants and animals, although some differences exists among the enzymes. For example, the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-562| prefers GTP as the phosphate donor |CITS: [211379]|, while the mammalian enzyme prefers ATP. The enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-3702| are dual-domain proteins, with the second domain resembling |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.9 "EC 2.4.2.9, uracil phosphoribosyltransferase"|, although they were shown to lack such activity |CITS: [19563437]|., Another enzyme that participates in the salvage of nucleosides is cytidine deaminase (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.5 "EC 3.5.4.5"|). It has been shown in |FRAME: TAX-562| that exogenously supplied |FRAME: CYTIDINE| is not directly converted to CMP. Instead, a very active |FRAME: CYTIDEAM-CPLX| converts it rapidly to |FRAME: URIDINE|, which is phosphorylated to UMP, and eventually converted to UTP and CTP. However, exogenously supplied cytidine will be phosphorylated to CMP if cytidine deaminase is blocked by mutation |CITS: [ColiSalII]|., This pathway was shown to be the exclusive pyrimidine ribonucleoside salvage pathway operating in potato tubers |CITS: [12244448]|.

Summary: Although organophosphorus insecticides are banned in most developed countries, they are still widely applied in developing countries for the control of major agricultural pests. |FRAME: CPD-8963 Chlorpyrifos| is an organophosphorus insecticide that has been commercially used since the 1960s to control foliar insects on cotton, paddy, pasture, and vegetable crops. It is still widely used in some countries to control gall midge, plant hoppers, and other crop pests. The insecticide inhibits |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.7|, in an irreversible manner and causes insect death ,and is also toxic to non-target organisms such as mammals |CITS: [15177657]|., The half-life of chlorpyrifos degradation varies from 10 to 120 days in soil depending on the soil type, pH, moisture, and initial concentrations., Many organisms have been reported to be able to degrade |FRAME: CPD-8963|, including both bacterial and fungal, strains. Genes responsible for the phenotype have been studied in a few cases. Several different, non-related enzymes have been shown to be able to catalyze the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-8963|., The enzyme methyl parathion hydrolase (MPH), encoded by |FRAME: G-80424| gene, has been reported numerous times to hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-8963| to |FRAME: CPD-16801| (TCP) |CITS: [17107423][17306510][22805954][23131657]|., An esterase (|FRAME: G-80425|) that hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-8963| efficiently has been reported from from |FRAME: TAX-1580| WCP902 |CITS: [20405842]|. A fungal chlorpyrifos-hydrolyzing enzyme (CPH) was identified from |FRAME: TAX-29917| Hu-01. The enzyme required no cofactors  and was strongly inhibited by Hg<sup>2+</sup>, Fe<sup>3+</sup>, DTT, β-mercaptoethanol and SDS |CITS: [22693630]|., The product of hydrolysis, |FRAME: CPD-16801| (TCP), shows relatively high antimicrobial effects on microorganisms, and often interferes with further degradation, although some organisms are capable of degrading both |FRAME: CPD-8963| and |FRAME: CPD-16801|. TCP is listed as a persistent and mobile pollutant by the US Environmental Protection Agency. It is mobile in soil as well as leachable into groundwater and surface water |CITS: [Manclus95]|.

Summary: The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-168695| produces a family of potent 20S-proteasome inhibitors. Originally three members of the family were isolated - |FRAME: CPD-12674|, |FRAME: CPD-12685|, and |FRAME: CPD-27917| |CITS: [19590008]|. Later additional compounds - |FRAME: CPD-12686| through |FRAME: CPD-27921| |CITS: [ 17243724]| and |FRAME: CPD-27922| |CITS: [21154492]|. These related compounds possess a unique bicyclic structural element, composed of a tightly fused |FRAME: Gamma-Lactams "γ-lactam"| and |FRAME: Beta-lactones "β-lactone"| rings. The salinosporamides bind irreversibly to the proteosome with great affinity, and |FRAME: CPD-12674| is used as an anticancer agent. It entered phase I human clinical trials for the treatment of multiple myeloma only three years after its discovery |CITS: [15916417]|., Similar compounds, the |FRAME: Cinnabaramides cinnabaramides|, which are produced by a terrestrial Streptomyces strain, share the same structure, but contain a C2 hexyl chain., Feeding experiments with stable isotopes established that salinosporamides are biosynthesized from three biosynthetic building blocks, namely, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME: CPD-12684|, and |FRAME: CPD-12675| |CITS: [17274624]|., Genome sequencing of |FRAME: TAX-369723| revealed a biosynthetic 41 kb, 29 ORFs gene cluster (sal) that encodes a hybrid PKS-NRPS pathway responsible for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12674| |CITS: [17563368]|. Pathways leading to the synthesis of the two complex building blocks have been studied., The subset of genes involved in the biosynthesis of the nonproteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: CPD-12684| has been identified |CITS: [18512922]|. This proposed pathway proceeds via a shunt in the phenylalanine pathway at the stage of |FRAME: PREPHENATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6628|). |FRAME: CPD-12684| is incorporated into the final product by nonribosomal peptide synthetase biochemistry in which the amino acid selection and activation is conducted by the adenylation-peptidyl carrier protein (A-PCP) protein SalB. Following its tethering to the PKS-NRPS complex it undergoes β-hydroxylation, putatively catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 SalD. The β-hydroxy amino acid unit is then primed for condensation with the diketide product of the bimodular polyketide synthase SalA protein for final assembly into |FRAME: CPD-12674| |CITS: [18512922]|., The pathway for synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12675|, the C2 group in |FRAME: CPD-12674|, starts with |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19590008]|. The first enzyme in that pathway, an |FRAME:CPLX-8149| (|FRAME:G-12198|), halogenates SAM with chloride, producing |FRAME: CPD-12676| and |FRAME: MET| |CITS: [18059261]|. Further modifications, catalyzed by seven independent enzymes, lead to formation of |FRAME: CPD-12675| |CITS: [19590008]|., The final assembely is catalyzed by the large |FRAME: CPLX-8150|, encoded by |FRAME: G-12211| and |FRAME: G-12212|. This hybrid PKS-NRPS enzyme binds |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as a starter unit, along with two other building blocks - |FRAME: CPD-12675| and |FRAME: CPD-12684|, and combines them to form the final product, |FRAME: CPD-12674|. Alternatively, the enzyme can bind other C2 groups instead of |FRAME: CPD-12675|, leading to synthesis of other salinosporamides. The selection of the C2 unit is performed by the SalA protein  |CITS: [19601645][19590008]|.

Names: Escherichia coli serotype O:9a O antigen biosynthesis // polymannose O-polysaccharide biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The O-polysaccharides of |FRAME: TAX-1010796|, |FRAME: TAX-1010797|, and |FRAME: ORG-6346| are a family of related structures comprising linear homopolymers of mannopyranose. Their biosynthetic pathways are considered prototypes for the ABC transporter-dependent pathway., In all three serotypes the O-antigen is composed of an |FRAME: CPD-12541| residue that serves to link the polysaccharide to its |FRAME: CPD-9646| membrane anchor during its biosynthesis, a short adapter region comprising three mannose residues connected in α(1→3) linkages, and a long repeat unit domain, which consists of many repeats of a serotype-specific repeat unit. The chain is terminated by either a methyl phosphate or a methyl group that is recognized by the ABC transporter., The first 4 residues are identical among the three serotypes, and are synthesized by identical enzymes (WecA, WbdC, and WbdB). The repeat unit differs among the serotypes, and is synthesized by serotype-specific multifunctional WbdA enzymes. Chain termination is catalyzed by WbdD proteins. WbdDO8 is a membrane-associated methyltransferase, whereas WbdDO9/O9a is a bifunctional kinase/methyltransferase., The O-polysaccharide of |FRAME: ORG-6346| is identical to that of |FRAME: ORG-6347|, and the genetic loci encoding the involved enzymes are highly conserved between the two species and likely reflect lateral gene transfer., The pathway begins with the transfer of |FRAME: CPD-12541| to the 55-carbon polyisoprenoid lipid acceptor |FRAME: CPD-9646|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). WecA is part of the machinery for |FRAME: ECASYN-PWY "biosynthesis of the enterobacterial common antigen glycan"|, and the wecA gene is not located in the O-polysaccharide locus |CITS: [6183115][7514591]|., |FRAME: ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINYLDIPHOSPHO-UNDECAPRE| is committed to the polysaccharide biosynthesis by the action of WbdC and WbdB, two GDP-mannose-dependent mannosyltransferases that transfer one and two α-(1,3)-linked mannose residues, respectively, forming the trimannosyl adapoter region |CITS: [22875852]|. These enzymes and the resulting structure are conserved in E. coli serotypes O9a, O9, and O8, which produce structurally related O-polysaccharides that differ only in the type and sequence of linkages in their repeat units |CITS: [22475157]|., The adapter domain is then extended by a serotype-specific multidomain polymerizing mannosyltransferase (WbdA) |CITS: [22475157][22989876]|. In |FRAME: ORG-6346| the polymerase contains two glycosyltransferase active sites - the, N-terminal domain possesses α-(1,2)-mannosyltransferase activity |CITS: [22875852]|, while the C-terminal domain is an α-(1,3)-mannosyltransferase |CITS: [25422321]|. The enzyme keeps transfering two mannose rediues in α-(1,2) linkage, followed by two mannose residues in α-(1,3) linkage. Polymerization is halted by the peripheral membrane protein WbdD, which terminates polymerization by adding a methyl phosphate to the non-reducing end of the nascent polymer |CITS: [15184370][21990359][22970759]|. This terminal modification is then recognized by a dedicated ATP-binding cassette transporter that exports the completed polysaccharide across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [15980069][ 18032609]|. After export, the polysaccharide is transferred to the |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|-core portion of LPS, translocated to the cell surface, and inserted into the outer membrane |CITS: [12045108][24580642]|., WbdD plays two roles - in addition to terminating the elongation, it also recruits the polymerase WbdA to the membrane |CITS: [19734145]|. The stoichiometry of the two proteins active complexes is a critical factor in establishing the chain length distribution of the resulting glycan, as complexes with different stoichiometries have different physical sizes that generate a range of glycan chain lengths |CITS: [24733938]|.

Names: abscisic acid degradation to phaseic acid // abscisate degradation I // abscisic acid degradation I // ABA hydroxylation pathway // abscisic acid hydroxylation pathway // 8'-hydroxylation pathway
Summary: General Background, The plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) is involved in the regulation of several crucial physiological and developmental processes in plants, as well as in the adaptative responses to environmental stresses |CITS:[zeevaart88]|. The regulation of these processes hinges on the size of the bioactive ABA pool. This pool is thought to be maintained through a finely tuned equilibrium between ABA biosynthesis and catabolism. Among the ABA catabolic pathways, the 8'-hydroxylation pathway leading to the formation of phaseic acid (this pathway) appears to be the major regulation point (but see also |FRAME:PWY-7640| and |FRAME:PWY-7642|). Phaseic acid (PA) and its derivative dihydrophaseic acid (DPA) are inactive forms of the hormone., About This Pathway, The inactivation of ABA to PA involves two steps: the 8'-hydroxylation of ABA to 8'-hydroxy-ABA (8'-OH-ABA) which is in turn converted to PA. Several cytochrome P450 monooxygenases have been described in the literature that can catalyze the conversion of ABA to 8'-OH-ABA |CITS:[9808729],[15064374],[15044947]|. So far, these enzymes have demonstrated a requirement for NADPH as electron donor |CITS:[15044947],[15064374]|. A certain amount of doubt remains as to whether the conversion of 8'-OH-ABA to phaseic acid occurs spontaneously or is the result of an enzymatic activity: indeed, although the reaction appears to occur quickly in vitro, the reaction might require an enzyme in vivo |CITS:[milborrow88]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17433 Chaetoglobosin A| belongs to the cytochalasans, a highly diversified group of fungal metabolites which display a broad range of bioactive properties |CITS:[4200278] [20411198]|. Cytochalasans have been shown to act as phytoalexins |CITS:[4200278]|, hamper cholesterol synthesis |CITS:[6251046]|, interfere with glucose transport in human erythrocyte membranes |CITS:[7356953]| and inhibit the secretion of thyroid hormones |CITS:[4334139]|. Cytochalasans have also been recognized as facilitators for fungal virulence |CITS:[25350301]| and major contaminants of food |CITS:[15080656]| but are also discussed as mediators in symbiotic liaisons between fungi and plants |CITS:[11548053]|. However, the first and foremost reason that cytochalasans have been investigated intensively is the cytostatic activity expressed from all metabolites in this group. The name cytochalasan has been derived from the Greek terms kytos (= cell) and chalasis (= relaxation) indicating their ability to influence the cytoskeleton, more precisely to act on actin filaments in the cell |CITS:[3312229]|. It has been shown that cytochalasans applied in suboptimal concentrations result in increased, multinucleated cells whereas cytotoxic amounts of cytochalasans produce cells without nucleus, an effect which is exploited in cellular process studies |CITS:[12498880]|., Cytochalasans are characterized by a common tricyclic scaffold formed by a macrocycle connected to an isoindolone system |CITS:[4200278]|. The different members of the cytochalasan compound group are formed by octa- or nonaketides derived from acetate and methionine units and assembled by the polyketide synthetase part (PKS) of the polyketide synthetase (PKS)-nonribosomal petide synthetase (NRPS) enzyme(s) involved in cytochalasan biosynthesis, whereas the NPRS moiety of the hybrid enzyme attaches an amino acid to the polyketide chain, i.e. |FRAME:PHE| for zygosporins |CITS:[5751331]|, |FRAME:TRP| for cytochalsins |CITS:[Probst81]| and chaetoglobosins |CITS:[15080656]|, |FRAME:TYR| for pyrichalsins |CITS:[14695792]| and |FRAME:LEU| for aspochalasins |CITS:[Chapman08]|., The |FRAME:PWY-7612| has been elucidated after identifying the respective gene cluster in Penicillium expansum |CITS:[17636916]| and Chaetomium globosum |CITS:[23611317]|. |FRAME:CPD-17433 Chaetoglobosin A| |CITS:[Sekita73]| and other metabolites expected to be part of the biosynthetic route such as |FRAME:CPD-17428| |CITS:[Oikawa91]|, |FRAME:CPD-17432| |CITS:[Oikawa93]|, |FRAME:CPD-17429| |CITS:[20225834] [24426105]| and |FRAME:CPD-17430| |CITS:[Sekita82]| have all been identified in Chaetomium. Summary: General Background, Grass pea (|FRAME: TAX-3860|) is a major source of protein for regions in South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, especially during times of drought |CITS: [28264526]|. However, overconsumption of the crop, which contains the non-proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: N3-OXALYL-L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE| in its seeds, may lead to neurolathyrism, a paralysis of the lower limbs. The exact mechanism by which |FRAME: N3-OXALYL-L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE| causes neurodegeneration is still unkown |CITS: [28094806]|. However, the compound is known to excite a subgroup of glutamate receptors, known as the AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptors |CITS: [6258722]|. , About This Pathway, Within the plant, |FRAME: N3-OXALYL-L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE| has been reported to carry out a multitude of functions, such as acting as a zinc ion carrier |CITS: [8053001]|, or a protector from oxidative stress |CITS: [20510333]|., |FRAME: N3-OXALYL-L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE| is biosynthesized from the heterocyclic amino acid |FRAME: CPD-16449| (BIA) that is only abundantly present at the seedling stage of grass pea. BIA is also found in seedlings of the garden pea (Pisum sativum) and lentil (Lens culinaris), where, in contrast with grass pea, it is not further metabolized, into a-ODAP |CITS: [Kuo98]|. Biosynthesis was found to be co-regulated with the nitrogen and sulfur metabolisms., |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.9| was identified as the key enzyme |CITS: [1814634][29112818]|. More recently, a novel cysteine, synthase (LsCSase) gene from grass pea has been identified and characterized. The gene regulation matched the expression patterns of BIA production |CITS: [29247850]|.

Summary: General Background, Bixin, also known as 'annatto', is a pigment synthesized naturally by a single terrestrial plant, |FRAME:TAX-66672|, native from the tropical Americas (and widely cultivated and naturalized elsewhere in the tropics). The annatto tree produces this carotenoid-based dye which is extracted from its seeds. Mayas and Aztecs used the annatto extract to dye textiles and use as cosmetic (body dye and lipstick); it was also used as a food colorant in the cocoa drink, cacahuatl. Additionally, annatto was being used in traditional medicine to cure diabetes, as an antimicrobial, against snake bites or sunburns. In its current applications, annatto is used mostly as a food colorant of cheese and other dairy products such as margarine and butter. It is also still used in the cosmetic industry for body care products. The pigments are found on the surface of the seeds where they accumulate in a resinous, oily substance. This covering contains a variety of pigments including |FRAME:CPD-7973| and a variety of apocarotenoid; however, the two main constituents of industrial relevance are the water-soluble apocarotenoid |FRAME:CPD-7971| and the oil-soluble apocarotenoid ester |FRAME:CPD-7972|. The former is a strong colorant: one liter of a 1% norbixin solution is sufficient for the coloring of 16 tonnes of cheese |CITS:[14624856]|; the latter is also used for the coloring of dairy products, but more specifically those with high contents of fatty acids, it is also used in the cosmetic industry and as a dye for leather., About This Pathway, All the genes and enzymes required for the biosynthesis of the compounds aforementioned have been identified |CITS:[12829782]|. The biosynthesis of the apocarotenoid ester bixin from lycopene requires three enzymatic steps involving a |FRAME:MONOMER-12416|, |FRAME:MONOMER-12424| and a |FRAME:MONOMER-12425|. Although these enzymes have been demonstrated to catalyze the required reactions, no specific kinetic studies have been performed to date.

Summary: The first purine nucleotide that is synthesized de novo is |FRAME: IMP| (IMP). IMP is converted to |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| by the enzyme |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCCINATE-SYN-DIMER|, and the latter is converted to the first adenosine nucleotide, |FRAME: AMP| (AMP), by the action of |FRAME:AMPSYN-ENZRXN|., AMP is phosphorylated to ADP and subsequently to ATP. However, a major source for this conversion is the |FRAME: CPLX490-3510 ATP synthase| complex, which is membrane bound and utilizes the proton gradient across membranes to phosphorylate ADP. This is the reaction depicted in this pathway., ADP can also be converted to the deoxy form |FRAME: DADP| (dADP) by the enzyme nucleoside diphosphate reductase. Once formed, dADP can be phosphorylated into the DNA building block |FRAME: DATP dATP| by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX|., In bacterial systems genetic studies indicate that the majority of de novo purine biosynthetic genes are unlinked but may act as a single unit of regulation controlled by the `purR' repressor protein |CITS:[2404765]|.
