Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is an important and ubiquitous structural component of eukaryotic cell membranes. Many bacterial species possess the capability to metabolize cholesterol and can survive on cholesterol as a single carbon source. The exact taxonomy of some species or genera recognized to catabolize cholesterol has changed over time. Two of the strains that were studied extensively, Nocardia restrictus ATCC 14887 and |FRAME:TAX-1702| ATCC 21387, are now classified as strains of |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [874450][12843070]|. In general, the mycolate-containing nocardioform actinomycetes, which include the genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-2053|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-1827| and |FRAME: TAX-2060|, have all been shown to catabolize cholesterol and plant sterols |CITS: [19843168]|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1883| have also been shown to decompose different steroids, including cholesterol |CITS: [Arima69]|. There have also been some reports of Proteobacteria that can degrade cholesterol |CITS: [4628510][9572974]|., Prior to their degradation, sterols are actively transported into the actinobacterial cells by the Mce4 steroid transporter |CITS: [18955493]|., The microbial degradation of cholesterol is challenging because of its complex chemical structure, low solubility in water, low number of functional groups and the presence of four alicyclic rings and two quaternary carbon atoms. A preliminary cholesterol degradation pathway has been proposed based on metabolites of cholesterol that have been identified in several actinomycete strains |CITS: [17345852]|, and is still being updated as new information becomes available. In general, cholesterol catabolism yields four molecules of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, four molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, one |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, and one |FRAME: SUC-COA|, which can feed the citric acid cycle and generate ATP, or feed biosynthetic pathways such as lipid biosynthesis |CITS: [Murohisa93][28377529]|., Cholesterol-regulated genes are usually located in gene clusters that are induced by cholesterol. In |FRAME: TAX-101510|, for example, the cluster contains 82 genes, whose proposed functions mostly fit the predicted pathway |CITS: [17264217]|., About This Pathway, Generally, microbial degradation of cholesterol starts with oxidation of the cholesterol 3β-hydroxyl moiety and isomerization of the structure from Δ5 into Δ4. This transformation is catalyzed by either |FRAME: MONOMER-16891| or |FRAME: G185E-5271-MONOMER|, depending on the species, and results in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-323|., Following the initial reaction, the cholesterol degradation pathway involves two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. While it becomes clear that different organisms perform these processes in different order, the order in specific organisms is still not well known. It has been suggested that the side chain is eliminated first in |FRAME: TAX-101510|, while in |FRAME:TAX-1773| the two processes may occur simultaneously |CITS: [21987574]|. The pathway depicted here follows a route where the side chain is degraded completely before the steroid rings are opened., Side-chain degradation starts with |FRAME: RHA1_RO04679 Cyp125|, a P450 cytochrome that catalyzes the C-27 hydroxylation of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and subsequently oxidizes the hydroxylation product to |FRAME: CPD-13689| via an aldehyde intermediate |CITS: [19843222]|. Degradation proceeds via two cycles of a β-oxidative type process. The first step is activation of the molecule by forming a coenzyme A ester, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-14719|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-16899| |CITS: [21602385]|. The first β-oxidation cycle removes a |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety, while the second cycle removes |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. The exact identity of the enzymes involves in these two cycles is not known with certainty, but they are thought to include |FRAME: G185E-4366| (|FRAME: G185E-4366-MONOMER|), |FRAME: G185E-5233| (|FRAME: G185E-5233-MONOMER|), |FRAME: G185E-7779| (|FRAME: G185E-7779-MONOMER "3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase"|), and |FRAME: G185E-7823| (|FRAME: G185E-7823-MONOMER|) |CITS: [Griffin11]|., The degradation of the side chain is completed by the removal of a second |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety in a process that involves three enzymes, which have been studied in |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [Thomas11]|. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenation of the 2'-propanoate side chain, followed by enoyl-CoA hydration, produce a quaternary alcohol, which then undergoes a retroaldol C1-C2' cleavage reaction catalyzed by a third enzyme, producing |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| and liberating another |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| molecule |CITS: [Thomas11]|. Homologous genes are found in the chromosomes of other cholesterol-degrading organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-685727|., The opening of the B ring is achieved by the successive actions of |FRAME: G-14723 KstD| (3-ketosteroid-Δ1-dehydrogenase) and |FRAME: CPLX-8371 KshA| (3-ketosteroid 9α-monooxygenase). |FRAME: G-14723 KstD| catalyzes the trans-axial elimination of the C1 and C2 hydrogen atoms of the A-ring |CITS: [18031290]|, while |FRAME: CPLX-8371 KshA| catalyzes the hydroxylation of the carbon at the C9 position |CITS: [19561185]|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-13680|, is unstable, and rearranges spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-13708|, a structure that misses the B ring., The opening of the A ring is achieved by the successive action of a hydroxylase (|FRAME: G185E-7848|) that hydroxylates the C4 position |CITS: [20448045]|, and a dioxygenase (|FRAME: G185E-7846|) that opens the ring |CITS: [19300498]|. A hydrolase (|FRAME: G185E-7847|) then breaks the product into two parts - |FRAME: CPD-13711| (which still contains the intact C and D rings) and |FRAME: CPD-13712| |CITS: [19875455]|. The latter is believed to be processed by three enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-14732|, |FRAME: G-14734| and |FRAME: G-14733|, into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|. The three proteins have not been characterized from a cholesterol-degrading organism yet, and this prediction is based on their similarity to the tesEFG genes of |FRAME: ORG-6191|, which catalyze the same activities as part of the |FRAME: PWY-6937 "testosterone and androsterone degradation"| pathway of that organism |CITS: [16151114]|., The degradation of the last two steroid rings, starting with |FRAME: CPD-13711|, was shown to begin with the removal of the side chain in the form of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by one β-oxidation cycle |CITS:[Lee67][Miclo90][Miclo92]| in a process that involves the |FRAME: G185E-7838| and |FRAME: G-14760| genes |CITS: [21901092][23146019]|. However, the complete pathway was described only in 2017 |CITS: [28377529]|. This part of the pathway is catalyzed by the, KstR2-regulated genes. The 5-member D ring is first hydrolyzed by an enoyl-CoA hydratase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7827| gene, followed by hydrolysis of the 6-member C ring by a hydrolase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7828| and |FRAME: G185E-7829| genes |CITS: [29581275]|. Following another round of β-oxidation, which results in the release of another |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, the remaining product is split into |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [28377529]|.

Triterpene compounds are plant secondary metabolites that are often involved in plant defense and, may also have beneficial effects when ingested by humans. They arise from numerous different, cyclizations of 2,3-oxidosqualene catalyzed by various oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs), |CITS:[16581287][ 17446857][10536024]|. Attempts to determine the functional specificity of, members of the OSC family of enzymes in Arabidopsis led to the discovery that THAS produces, thalianol when expressed in yeast |CITS:[15208422]|. Later studies with plants confirmed that this metabolite, is present at low levels in Arabidopsis roots, and that THAS is required for its synthesis, |CITS: [18356490]|. Characterization of plants with mutations in the two adjacent genes coding, for enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-3700|-specific families of P450 proteins demonstrate that, THAH and THAD further modify thalianol. Like the avenacin gene cluster found in oats, this, set of three genes forms another operon-like group of metabolically-related, enzymes |CITS: [18356490]|. , The functional importance of this pathway is still under investigation., The three thalianol-related metabolites can be identified in Arabidopsis roots and, an accumulation of thalianol and thalian-diol can increase root growth |CITS: [18356490]|., But, despite the expected role for triterpenes in plant defense, roots of thas, thad,, and thah mutants do not appear more susceptible to a few strains of bacterial and plant, pathogens that have been tested |CITS: [18356490]|. In addition, over-expression, of THAS and THAD, leading to the ectopic production of thalianol and thalian-diol in aerial, tissues can cause stunted plant growth |CITS: [18356490]|. Further work should help clarify, the biological role of thalianol and its derivatives in Arabidopsis thaliana and related species.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, An important branch-point in the biosynthesis of carotenoids lies in the cyclization of the linear, pink |FRAME:CPD1F-114| into carotenes with all-β-, all-ε- or mixed β and ε rings (|FRAME: CPD1F-118|). The cyclization reactions are catalyzed by lycopene β- or ε-cyclases. These cyclases all share a conserved amino acid sequence signature and bind dinucleotides such as FAD and NADP |CITS:[8837512]|, but otherwise share little resemblance., Several classes of lycopene cyclases have been identified in bacteria: the CrtY-type β-cyclases are found in many carotenogenic proteobacteria, Streptomyces spp., and the Chloroflexi; the CrtL cyclases include both β- and ε-cyclases of some cyanobacteria and plants; the heterodimeric cyclases (CrtYc/CrtYd) are found in some Gram-positive bacteria, and are related to the lycopene cyclases of archaea and halophilic bacteria; and the CruA/CruP cyclases are found in green sulfur bacteria and cyanobacteria that do not possess CrtY or CrtL cyclases., A single cyclization of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| performed by |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.19|, adds a β ring at one end, resulting in |FRAME: CPD1F-126|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf., Chlorophyll functions as the main light harvesting pigment in photosynthesis, capturing photons and transfering them to the reaction centers. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-18895|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, |FRAME: CPD-10335|, |FRAME: CPD-18896|, |FRAME: CPD-18897| and |FRAME: CPD-18898|)., |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLL-A "Chlorophyll a"| is found in all green plants, cyanobacteria, euglenozoa, and all photosynthetic algae. In these organisms, the pigment is found mostly in its monovinyl form (a vinyl group at C-3 and an ethyl group at C-8). However, its biosynthetic pathway involves largely divinyl intermediates (vinyl groups at both C-3 and C-8). Two different enzymes are known to catalyze the reduction of the C-8 vinyl group. This pathway describes |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.13|, which is found in most of the cyanobacteria, in eukaryotic algae such as the red alga |FRAME: TAX-280699|, the diatom |FRAME: TAX-296543| and the green algae |FRAME: TAX-242159| and |FRAME: TAX-3055|, the purple bacteria |FRAME: TAX-258594| and |FRAME: TAX-1085|, and in the green sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-290317| |CITS: [18715956]|., The last step in the biosynthesis of chlorophyll is the esterification of a side chain. The enzyme responsible for the esterification reaction (|FRAME: EC-2.5.1.62|) prefers phytyl diphosphate, but can also use geranylgeranyl diphosphate, in which case the geranylgeranyl side-chain is subsequently reduced to a phytyl chain by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.83|.

General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-20679 Fucoxanthin|, its modified forms, and |FRAME: CPD-20680|, are the major carotenoids in the macroalgae |FRAME: TAX-2870| (brown algae) and the microalgae |FRAME: TAX-33849| (diatoms) |CITS: [22888128]|., Carotenoids such as fucoxanthin extend the spectral range of photosynthetic light harvesting by enabling the efficient absorption of blue-green light, which prevails in many marine habitats. As a result, algae containing these carotenoids are brown colored. Fucoxanthin species are present only in algae with "complex" plastids that were acquired by secondary or higher-order endosymbiosis involving an early red alga. , The fucoxanthin-containing diatoms and brown algae and the hexanoyloxy- and butanoyloxy-fucoxanthin-containing haptophytes are among the most abundant algal groups in marine environments and are estimated to contribute more than, half of the global marine primary production |CITS: [9657713][17765976][19622724][26929361]|., Fucoxanthin was first isolated from the marine brown seaweeds |FRAME: TAX-3011|, |FRAME: TAX-2875 Dictyota|, and |FRAME: TAX-33637| in 1914 |CITS: [Willstatter14]|. The complete structure including chirality was determined only in 1990 |CITS: [Englert90]|. Fucoxanthin has an unusual allenic bond that is responsible for its very high antioxidant activity |CITS: [10227153][17894451]|. Fucoxanthin has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, anti-obese, antidiabetic, antiangiogenic and antimalarial activities, and has been shown to have protective effects on the liver, blood vessels of the brain, bones, skin, and eyes |CITS: [22072997]|., Many of the enzymes involved in this pathway have not been discovered as of 2023. A tentative pathway was proposed in 2012 |CITS: [22888128]|. However, the later discovery of two of the enzymes involved and characterization of intermediates produced by knockout mutants in these enzymes has led to the proposition of a modified pathway |CITS: [36095219]|. The 2023 discovery of the |FRAME: G-124891| hydratase resulted in an additional modification of the pathway |CITS: [37100425]|., It should be noted that brown algae (|FRAME: TAX-2870|) or golden-brown algae (|FRAME: TAX-2825|) do not possess orthologs of |FRAME: G-124432| and |FRAME: G-124433| and must synthesize fucoxanthin via an alternative route |CITS: [31744163][36095219]|.

Summary: General Background, A broad variety of volatile ester compounds have been found to constitute components , of complex cocktails in numerous plants emitted to serve in both reproductive and vegetative processes. More , than 1.000 low-molecular-weight organic compounds have been identified to date |CITS: [15326281]|, most of , them components of floral scents. The flower volatiles function as pollinator attractants but may also be involved , in defense mechanism, such as airborne signals to attract natural predators of herbivores |CITS: [12732318]|, to, directly repel herbivores |CITS: [GERSHENZON91]| or to activate defense-related genes in neighboring plants , or healthy tissue in infected plants (Shulaev et al. 1997). , Although phenylpropanoid derivatives are not usually volatile, some of them with a reduced carboxyl group at C9 , (e.g. aldehydes, alcohols) or those containing alkyl additions to the hydroxyl groups of the benzyl ring or to the , carboxyl group (i.e. esters, ethers) are volatile |CITS: [10712525]|. Methyl(iso)eugenol, methylchavicol and , methylcinnamate are frequently found and investigated in floral scents of |FRAME:TAX-36903| and Ocimum , basilicum. Together with benzenoid esters, terpenoids, fatty acid derivatives, C5-branched compounds, and , various nitrogen and sulfur containing compounds |CITS: [15326281]| cinnamoic esters form the core of , physiologically active volatiles in plants. Certain volatiles such as methylsalicylate and methyl jasmonate (|FRAME:PWY-735|) , are also thought to be involved in cell-to-cell signaling |CITS: [SHULAEV97]|., Special information: The methyltransferases involved in the reactions of the pathway (e.g. IEMT - isoeugenol , methyltransferase) share high identities at the amino acid level with other methyltransferases involved in the , lignin biosynthetic pathway (COMT - caffeic acid/5-hydroxyferulic acid O-methyltransferase). However, they , express a distinct substrate specificity and methylation regiospecificity which is caused by only a few amino acid, changes |CITS: [10415125]| |CITS: [9439593]|. It was also shown that the gene encoding IEMT in fragrant and , non-fragrant lines of |FRAME:TAX-36903| exhibits flower-specific and temporal expression patterns , |CITS: [9159948]| indicating the importance of those processes for the evolution of new scents., Gang and coworkes |CITS: [11884690]| demonstrated that a single amino acid change discriminates the substrate , specificity between CVOMT1 (chavicol-O-methyltransferase) and EOMT1 (eugenol-O-methyltransferase) in Ocimum , basilicum. It was concluded that the relative ease and interconvertibility of this event leading to new specific , enzymatic activities may constitute a factor facilitating convergent evolution.

Both plants and fungi produce high concentrations of gallate |CITS: [9325260]|, while bacteria are known to produce small amounts., An early intermediate of the shikimate pathway, |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE|, has been implicated as a potential precursor for gallate synthesis in plants |CITS: [15474568]|. A careful study has revealed that gallate is formed from |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE| by the action of |FRAME: AT3G06350-MONOMER|, a multifunctional enzyme that also catalyzes the reversible reduction of |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE| to |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| |CITS: [Muir11]|. In the presence of NADPH the enzyme catalyzes reduction of |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE|, and in the presence of NADP+ it catalyzes its oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-13085|, an unstable compound that undergoes a spontaeous and rapid rearrangement to |FRAME: CPD-183|., This observation has been confirmed by several methods. Overexpression of cloned shikimate dehydrogenase from |FRAME: TAX-51240| in |FRAME: TAX-4097| resulted in increase of over 500% in the accumulation of gallate. In addition, shikimate dehydrogenase enzymes that were purified from several plants, as well as the bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, were shown to produce gallate in vitro |CITS: [Muir11]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ALGINATE Alginate| is a major component of the cell walls of |FRAME: TAX-2870| (brown algae), and can make up to 45% of the total algal material. It is a linear polysaccharide of (1-4)-linked |FRAME: CPD-15205|, with variable amounts of its C-5 epimer |FRAME: CPD-15204| |CITS: [Schmidt26]|. The |FRAME: CPD-15205| (M) and |FRAME: CPD-15204| (G) residues are arranged in homopolymeric regions of M and G blocks, interspaced with regions of alternating structure (MG blocks). The physicochemical properties of alginate depend on both the overall M to G ratio and the relative proportions of the three block types in the chain. G block-rich alginate forms a high-strength gel in presence of divalent cations such as calcium, and is found in more rigid parts of the alga. Alginates rich in M or MG blocks are more flexible. The composition varies among species, and within an organism according to the nature and the age of the tissues as well as to the season and to the growing area. Depending on its composition, alginate can absorb 200-300 times its own weight in water, forming a viscous gum., Historically, alginate extracted from seaweed has had a wide variety of uses. Its unique physical properties enable it to be used as a stabilizer, viscosifier, and gelling agent in the food and beverage, paper and printing, biomaterials,, and pharmaceutical industries |CITS:[9283015][9393029][11018131][12149954][16183570][20581859][25300542]|. Commercial varieties of alginate are extracted from several species, including the giant kelp |FRAME: TAX-35122|, |FRAME: TAX-52969|, and various types of |FRAME: TAX-33637|., The alginates formed by brown algae are non-acetylated. An acetylated form of alginate is produced by bacteria that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-352| genera. The higher the degree of O-acetylation, the higher the viscosity and pseudoplastic rheology of the alginate |CITS: [Skjak-Braek88]|., The biological function of alginates differs between the two genera. In |FRAME: TAX-286| alginate is associated with biofilms, promoting bacterial adherence to target cell walls |CITS: [3155514]|, while in |FRAME: TAX-352| alginate is a structural element in the wall of the cyst, a desiccation-resistant capsule that is formed under adverse environmental conditions |CITS: [16912921]|. See pathway |FRAME: PWY-6082| for the biosynthesis of bacterial alginate., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of alginate in brown algae has been studied early, although not at the level of detail in which the pathway was studied in the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287|. The first step consists of oxidation of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-1828| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.132|, followed by polymerization to form a |FRAME: Poly-beta-D-Mannuronate| polymer, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.33| |CITS: [5954796]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5659| for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|). This is followed by epimerization of some D-mannuronosyl residues into L-guluronosyl residues within the polymer chain, a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.37| |CITS: [4778911][14526115]|., Sequence analysis suggests that |FRAME: TAX-80365| features at least 21 different mannuronan C-5-epimerase genes |CITS: [14526115]|. The presence of so many different genes for mannuronan C-5-epimerases suggests that, even though they fulfill the same biochemical function, the enzymes may be involved in a variety of biological functions. Depending on the season, the age of the plant, and the tissue type, different epimerases are likely to be required to specifically tailor the relative contents and distributions of G blocks, M blocks, and MG blocks in alginate chains |CITS: [14526115]|.

Summary: General Background, Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|. Bioluminescence is particularly predominant in the marine environment, in members of planktonic bacteria and protozoa, many invertebrates, and vertebrates with specialized light producing organs that harbor symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-7723|). The requirement for oxygen suggests that bioluminescence evolved after oxygen levels began to rise through the activities of early oxygenic phototrophic cyanobacteria., Many coelenterates and ctenophores, such as the sea pansy |FRAME: TAX-6134|, the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6099|, the hydroid |FRAME: TAX-32569|, and the ctenophore |FRAME: TAX-27922|, are bioluminescent. The luciferin in these organisms is |FRAME: Coelenterazines coelenterazine|, an imidazopyrazinone derivative that is also found in distantly related types of luminous organisms such as squids, shrimps, fishes, and some chaetognaths |CITS: [Shimomura80][Campbell90][20972255]|, as well as in many nonluminous organisms |CITS: [9336010]|. The biosynthetic origin of coelenterazine is not known. However, it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it, and is dependent on a dietary supply of this luciferin for bioluminescence |CITS: [11572972]|. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| |CITS: [Thomson95]|., Even though many different types of organisms use |FRAME: RENILLA-LUCIFERIN coelenterazine| as the luciferin, the enzymes employed are not the same. For example, the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100| uses the Ca2+-regulated photoprotein aequorin (see |FRAME: PWY-7915|), while the sea pansy |FRAME: TAX-6134| uses a luciferase as shown here., About This Pathway, Upon binding coelenterazine, the luciferase enzyme catalyzes a monooxygenation, producing a very short-lived peroxide that cyclizes into a dioxetanone structure, which collapses, releasing a CO2 molecule. The spontaneous breakdown of the dioxetanone releases the energy (about 50 kcal/mole) that is necessary to generate the excited state of oxyluciferin |CITS: [27179]|., Studies of the soft coral |FRAME: TAX-6136| showed that the bioluminescence is located in specialized membrane-enclosed subcellular particles known as the lumisomes |CITS: [4144548]|, which are clustered in intracellular organelles that were named luminelles |CITS: [233975]|. Several descriptions of the luciferin's structure were published over the years, with the final structure reported in 1977 |CITS: [4397765][4401724][16592045][4147978][16592444]|., Early on it was reported that in addition to the luciferase and luciferin the system requires oxygen and ATP |CITS: [13695546]|. However, shortly after it was found that the system requires |FRAME: 3-5-ADP| rather than ATP |CITS: [13881360]|. This requirement was clarified with the discovery that the luciferin is stored in a sulfated form, named |FRAME: LUCIFERYL-SULFATE| |CITS: [4382092]|. Before the luciferin can be used as a substrate for the luciferase the sulfate group needs to be removed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.2.10|, in a reaction that involves |FRAME: 3-5-ADP| |CITS: [4392153]|., In 1974 the coelenterazine-binding protein was discovered. This crucial member of the bioluminescence system binds coelenterazine and protects it from auto oxidation. The protein has three Ca2+-binding sites. Upon an increase in the calcium ions concentration the protein releases the coelenterazine, making it available for the luciferase. This discovery explained an earlier observation that light emission could be triggered by calcium |CITS: [4149963][33174][18385886][18655070]|., The final component in the Renilla system is a |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent protein"| (GFP). In the absence of the GFP the excited oxyluciferin emit a photon of blue light. However, in vivo the excited oxyluciferin transfers the excitation energy to GFP, which then emits a green photon |CITS: [33175][36127][17980388]|., The identification of all the components of the bioluminecensce system in |FRAME: TAX-6134| clarified the mechanism. The sulfokinase removes a sulfate from the storage form of coelenterazine, generating free coelenterazine, which is then bound by the coelenterazine-binding protein |CITS: [7480150]|. Following a triger event the Ca2+ concentration goes up in the lumisomes, causing the release of coelenterazin and its oxidation by the luciferase. The reaction involves the release of a CO2 group and formation of oxyluciferin in an excited state |CITS: [27179]|. The energy is then transferred to the green fluorescent protein (GFP), which emits a green photon (λmax ~509 nm)., It should be noted that some organisms lack GFP, in which case the luciferase-bound excited coelenteramide emits blue light (λmax ~480 nm).

Summary: Protein substrates of the |FRAME: Ubiquitins ubiquitin| (Ub) system, which controls the levels of many intracellular proteins, are conjugated to ubiquitin through the action of |FRAME: E3-independent-Ubiquitin-carrier-E2 "E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes"| or |FRAME: E3-ubiquitin-carrier-proteins "E3 ubiquitin transferases"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7511|). , |FRAME: E3-ubiquitin-carrier-proteins "E3 ubiquitin transferases"| recognize their substrates by specific degradation signals, known as degrons |CITS: [11017125][14744430][15688063][15950869]|. Once recognized, the protein substrate is ubiquitylated and degraded by the 26S proteasome |CITS: [9476896][15571806]|., One class of degrons, called N-degrons, is the substrate's N-terminal residue. Certain residues (named "destabilizing residues") are recognized by the ubiquitin system and mark the protein for degradation. The set of destabilizing residues in a given cell type yields a rule, called the N-end rule, which relates the in vivo half-life of a protein to the identity of its N-terminal residue |CITS: [3018930]|., |FRAME: ARG| is a primary N-terminal destabilizing residue (Ndp). When present at the N-terminal of a protein, it is recognized directly by UBR-type |FRAME: E3-ubiquitin-carrier-proteins "E3 ubiquitin transferases"| (such as |FRAME: HS08405|), and the (ubiquitylated) protein is directed to the proteasome. , In eukaryotes, |FRAME: HS03017|-encoded arginyl-transferases (RD,E,C*-transferases) conjugate an N-terminal arginine residue to two or three types of N-terminal residues (known as the secondary N-terminal destabilizing residues, or Nds). The yeast enzyme recognizes N-terminal |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (D) and |FRAME: GLT| (E), while the mammalian enzyme also recognizes oxidized forms (sulfinates and sulfonates) of |FRAME: CYS| (C*). , The Nds targets are produced via different mechanisms. Oxidized |FRAME: CYS| is produced by the removal of the initiator |FRAME: MET| from the freshly synthesized protein (in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.4.11.18|), followed by oxidation of the exposed cysteine by either |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| or reactive oxygen species |CITS: [16222293]|., In the case of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (D) and |FRAME: GLT| (E), they are formed from |FRAME: ASN| (N) and |FRAME: GLN| (Q) by dedicated enzymes. In yeast, a single enzyme, NTA1, can deamidate both substrates. In mammals, the deamidation of |FRAME: ASN| (N) and |FRAME: GLN| (Q) is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.121| (|FRAME: HS14648|) and |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.122| (|FRAME: HS14634|), respectively. , N and Q, which have been named teritiary N-terminal destabilizing residues (Ndt), are exposed after the initiator methionine is acetylated by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.254| and subsequently removed by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.1| (|FRAME: HS08997|)., The arginylation branch of the N-end rule pathway mediates, in particular, the cardiovascular development, the fidelity of chromosome segregation, and the control of signaling by |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| |CITS: [21276945]|. By acting on cysteine residues that were oxidized by nitric oxide, the pathway acts as a nitric oxide sensor that functions through its ability to destroy specific regulatory proteins bearing N-terminal cysteine, at rates controlled by nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species |CITS: [16222293]|.

|FRAME: CPD0-1227 Triclosan| is an antibacterial and antifungal agent. At lower concentrations triclosan appears bacteriostatic and targets bacteria mainly by inhibiting fatty acid synthesis via its binding to the bacterial |FRAME: ENOYL-ACP-REDUCT-NADH-MONOMER|, a key enzyme in the |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY "fatty acid elongation cycle"|., In many bacteria the enzyme is encoded by the |FRAME: EG11528| gene. Triclosan forms a tight, non-covalent ternary complex with the oxidized NADH cofactor in the active site of FabI, thus inactivating the enzyme |CITS: [10196195]|., However, some bacteria are naturally resistant to triclosan due to the presence of triclosan-resistant enoyl-ACP reductase isoforms. Some Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1313|, possess the |FRAME: G-15302| gene that encodes a triclosan-resistant enzyme |CITS: [10910344]|, while some Gram-negative bacteria, like |FRAME:TAX-666|, have a non-related triclosan-resistant isoform encoded by |FRAME: G-15301| |CITS: [18032386]|., Some Gram-positive organisms have yet a different isoform encoded by |FRAME: BSU08650|. FabL is inhibited by triclosan in a reversible manner, but does not form a stable NAD-triclosan ternary complex like FabI |CITS: [11007778]|.

General Background, |FRAME: PHYTOL "Phytol"| is a metabolite of chlorophyll. The |FRAME: PHYTOL phytol| side chain of chlorophyll is esterified to the porphyrin ring via an ester bond (for example see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A chlorophyll a|). Although humans cannot cleave |FRAME: PHYTOL phytol| from the porphyrin ring of chlorophyll, |FRAME: PHYTOL phytol| can be cleaved by other organisms, such as rumen bacteria in ruminants, and converted to |FRAME: PHYTANATE phytanate| (a 3-methyl-branched fatty acid). |FRAME: PHYTANATE "Phytanate"| derived from the diet can be metabolized by humans as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-387 fatty acid α-oxidation II|. However, it has been shown that humans can also metabolize dietary |FRAME: PHYTOL phytol| to |FRAME: CPD-206 phytanoyl-CoA| as shown in this pathway. |FRAME: CPD-206 "Phytanoyl-CoA"| is also further metabolized as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-387 fatty acid α-oxidation II| (reviewed in |CITS: [16799769]| and |CITS: [21683154]|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: PHYTOL "Phytol"| was originally thought to be metabolized to |FRAME: PHYTANATE phytanate| |CITS: [15110319]| although subsequent work showed that it is actually metabolized to its coenzyme A derivative, |FRAME: CPD-206 phytanoyl-CoA| |CITS: [15866875]|. The first step involves oxidation of |FRAME: PHYTOL phytol| to the aldehyde |FRAME: CPD-14926 phytenal| by an as yet unidentified alcohol dehydrogenase. The aldehyde is then oxidized to the acid |FRAME: CPD-14927 phytenate| by an aldehyde dehydrogenase that was identified as the product of human gene |FRAME: HS01061| |CITS: [15110319][15866875]|. An as yet unidentified acyl-CoA synthase(s) convert |FRAME: CPD-14927 phytenate| to its coenzyme A derivative |FRAME: CPD-14928 phytenoyl-CoA|. This activity(ies) was detected in both the microsomal and peroxisomal fractions in rat liver |CITS: [15866875]|. The |FRAME: CPD-14928 phytenoyl-CoA| is then reduced to |FRAME: CPD-206 phytanoyl-CoA| by the peroxisomal enzyme product of human gene |FRAME: HS03889|. Details of the presumed entry of |FRAME: CPD-14928 phytenoyl-CoA| into the peroxisome remain to be determined, as does the role of mitochondrial phytenoyl-CoA reductase activity |CITS: [16546181]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [16799769]| and |CITS: [21683154]|.

Names: D-cycloserine inhibition of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate // D-cycloserine inhibition of PLP
Summary: |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE "Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate"| (PLP, vitamin B6) is an essential cofactor in all living systems |CITS: [7748903]|. It is one of the most versatile cofactors and participates in transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, Cα-Cβ cleavage and α-β elimination reactions. PLP plays an important role in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism and has been implicated in singlet oxygen resistance |CITS: [10687384]|., In most enzymes the aldehyde group of PLP forms a Schiff-base linkage (internal aldimine) with the ε-amino group of a specific lysine residue at the active site., |FRAME: CPD-2482| is an antibiotic substance produced by several |FRAME:TAX-1883| species |CITS: [Merck89]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7274|). The compound, which is a cyclic analog of |FRAME: D-ALANINE|, is known as an inhibitor of some PLP-dependent enzymes, such as |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1| |CITS: [6065087]|, |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.1| |CITS: [4555420]|, and |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.4| |CITS: [14479178]|. The last two enzymes are particularly useful targets, as they are necessary for the biosynthesis of the bacterial cell wall. |FRAME: CPD-2482| is clinically used as a second-line of defense against |FRAME: TAX-1773|, especially when the bacterium is resistant to other antituberculosis antibiotics |CITS: [10488174]|., Inactivation of the enzymes is caused by the detachment of the PLP cofactor from the active site lysine residue due to the formation of a |FRAME: CPD-24778| adduct between |FRAME: CPD-2482| and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|. Once formed, the adduct can undergoe a series of spontaneous transformations leading to two products - one of the routes results in the irreversible formation of the aldoxime compound |FRAME: CPD-24783|, while the other route leads to the reversible formation of |FRAME: CPD-24780| |CITS: [32203411]|., The presence of the irreversible route results in incomplete inactivation of alanine racemase, which has been described in mycobacteria |CITS: [24478820]|. In the irreversible route hydrolysis of the isoxazolidinone ring of the aldimine intermediate leads to ring opening and subsequent intramolecular transaldimination to generate a stable oxime product. As a result, a fraction of the active sites (estimated to be up to 10% after 24 h) is left in an apo state and can be reconstituted with free PLP, regenerating active enzyme |CITS: [32203411]|.

Names: hydrogen production VIII // photosynthetic hydrogen generation
Summary: Background, Unicellular green algae can utilize molecular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| in the dark to drive cellular metabolism, or evolve |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| in the light with electrons derived from the photosynthetic oxidation of water |CITS: [11706159]|. |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| is produced anaerobically when mitochondrial respiration is inhibited, and this permits electron flow through the electron transport chain with the concommitant generation of ATP |CITS: [11102662]|. , Molecular oxygen suppresses expression of the genes associated with |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production and also inhibits the hydrogenase enzyme, hence under aerobic conditions, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| is not evolved |CITS: [16143840]|. A prior anaerobic incubation of the algae in the dark can remove this inhibition and induces expression of a [FeFe] hydrogenase. A subsequent illumination then drives |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolution for a short period of time, till the release of photosynthetic |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| inhibits the process. Photosystem II (PSII) mediates the light driven reaction of splitting water molecules into |FRAME: PROTON| and |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE|., About This Pathway, During eukaryotic photosynthesis, electron transport is driven by photons captured by the antenna proteins LHCII/LHCI bound to PSII and PSI respectively. Linear photosynthetic electron transport originating from water oxidation, proceeds via PSII, cytochrome b6-f and PSI to the chloroplast ferredoxin |CITS: [21605544]|. Ferredoxin can pass electrons to several further acceptors. Under aerobic conditions, most of the electrons are used to reduce NADP+ to NADPH by ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase (FNR). The NADPH is then consumed by reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| assimilation in the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|., The catalytic site, also known as the "hydrogen cluster" (HC) of [FeFe] hydrogenase accepts electrons from reduced ferredoxin |CITS: [10631256]|. The HC generates molecular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| utilizing protons as a sink for these high potential-energy electrons |CITS: [17721788]|., Under conditions that inhibit photosynthesis and generate anoxia, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production naturally occurs. This requires a fully active PSI for electron transfer to ferredoxin. PSII activity is partially inhibited by a block in turnover of the D1 protein causing a reduction in photosynthetic oxygen evolution |CITS: [11006346]|. However, PSII still retains a low level of water oxidation activity, which can feed some electrons into the electron transport chain. When the level of oxygen evolved by PSII drops below respiratory consumption, the cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and express the hydrogenase., The majority of the electrons required for |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolution during anoxia come from the redox equivalents of fermentative metabolism. These are supplied into the electron transport chain by an NAD(P)H-plastoquinone-oxidoreductase through non-photochemical PQ reduction. Prior aerobic PSII activity is crucial for build up of the starch and protein required for this. , During prolonged fermentative metabolism in |FRAME: TAX-3055|, formate and ethanol are generated. This creates alternate sources for reduced ferredoxin, which feeds directly into |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production at the level of the [FeFe] hydrogenase.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) can occur via two distinct routes: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway, such as this pathway) and the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (MEP pathway). In the former, IPP is synthesized from the condensation of three acetyl-CoA molecules; in contrast, in the MEP pathway IPP is synthesized via the condensation of pyruvate and D-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate., For many years, the MVA pathway was considered to be the sole source of IPP in all living organisms, until several inconsistencies led to the discovery of the MEP pathway in bacteria and plants. The MEP pathway is present in most eubacteria, in unicellular green algae, in the chloroplasts of phototrophic organisms and in some unicellular eukaryotes related to photosynthetic phyla, such as the Plasmodium parasites. , The mevalonate pathway is found in animals, fungi, the cytoplasm of phototrophic organisms, archaea, and some, eubacteria. A considerable variability exists among archaea, and at least four different variants of the MVA pathway have been described from that kingdom. The |FRAME: PWY-922 "eukaryotic variant"| is rare in archaea, but occurs in members of the order |FRAME: TAX-2281|, such as |FRAME: TAX-2287| |CITS: [23378249]|. While most archaea posses a variant now known as the |FRAME: PWY-8125 "archaeal pathway"| |CITS: [30224495]|, a |FRAME: PWY-6174 "third variant"| has been described from halophilic archaea such as |FRAME: TAX-2246| |CITS: [24375100]| (that pathway was also found in the eubacterium |FRAME: TAX-120962| |CITS: [24327557]|), and a |FRAME: PWY-7524 "fourth variant"| has been described from archaea of the order |FRAME: TAX-2301| |CITS: [24755225][25636853]|., About This Pathway, All other variants of the mevalonate pathway include |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.36|, an enzyme that converts |FRAME: MEVALONATE| to |FRAME: CPD-499|. Extreme acidophiles of the |FRAME: TAX-2301| order have developed a new variant of the pathway that involves two novel enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.185|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.186|. These enzymes catalyze two successive phosphorylations, generating |FRAME: MEVALONATE-DP| |CITS: [24914732][24755225]|. This compound is then decarboxylated by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.110|, an enzyme that evolved from |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.33|, but has lost its phosphorylation ability |CITS: [28004831]|., The novel enzymes have been discovered in the extreme acidophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2303|, but exist in other members of the |FRAME: TAX-2301| order. The last part of the pathway, the phosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-10818| to the universal isoprenoid precursor |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, proceeds as in other archaea, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.26| |CITS: [24914732][24755225]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-5691|, one of the causative agents of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), alternates during its life cycle between the bloodstream of its mammalian host and the blood-feeding tsetse fly, Glossina. The parasite exists in different forms during its life cycle. In the mammalian bloodstream it exists as long, slender-forms, while in the insect it appears as stubby forms known as procyclic cells. Profound differences exist in the metabolism of the two forms., The long slender bloodstream form depends entirely on glycolysis for energy generation and excretes pyruvate as the major end product of carbohydrate metabolism. In the procyclic stage, the end product of glycolysis, pyruvate, is not excreted but further metabolized inside the mitochondrion. |FRAME: PYRUVATE Pyruvate| enters the mitochondrion and is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|, into |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| (see |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|). The acetyl-CoA is not degraded to carbon dioxide via the |FRAME:TCA|, but is converted into |FRAME:ACET| |CITS: [15326192]|., Acetate is the main end product of glucose metabolism in a number of other trypanosomatides, such as |FRAME: TAX-5671| and |FRAME: TAX-5665| |CITS: [9501211]|., Acetate formation is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.18| (ASCT), an enzyme that transfers the CoA group from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME:SUC|, producing |FRAME: SUC-COA|. Since |FRAME: SUC-COA| can be restored to |FRAME:SUC|, the pathway has been named ASCT cycle., A knockout mutant of |FRAME: TAX-5691| depleted for ASCT showed a reduced acetate production, supporting the role of this enzyme in acetate production. However, ASCT mutants still excrete acetate from glucose metabolism, implying that ASCT is not the only acetate-producing pathway in this parasite |CITS: [15326192]|., Occurrence of the ASCT cycle in mitochondria is very restricted; it has only been found in trypanosomatids and some parasitic helminths such as |FRAME: TAX-6192| |CITS: [5721923][681067][421954][8885873]|. However, the pathway was also found in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-33011|, and phylogenetic analysis suggests it occurs in other bacterial species that belong to 5 different phyla (Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Proteobacteria) |CITS: [33931420]|. , ASCT is also found in several eukaryotes that do not have mitochondria, including the hydrogenosome-containing trichomonads (such as |FRAME: TAX-56690| and |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [3090435]|) and the anaerobic fungus |FRAME: TAX-73818| |CITS: [8257282]|. However, since these organisms do not have |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|, they use a different pathway variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5538|).

Names: thiamine diphosphate salvage V // thiamin salvage V
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-13576| (cHET-P) is formed as an intermediate of the de novo |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| biosynthetic pathway by some organisms (see |FRAME: PWY-6891|). The compound and its non-phosphorylated form, |FRAME: CPD-26488| (cHET), are found in environments as different as sea water and the mammalian intestine |CITS: [29654239]|. , Some organisms are not able to synthesize the thiazole component of thiamine de novo and utilize salvage pathways in which they recover an external source for that component. While many organisms have been shown to utlize |FRAME: THZ| (HET) for this purpose, marine picophytoplankton such as |FRAME: TAX-70448| and |FRAME: TAX-1764204| were found to be unable to utilize HET, but to utilize the carboxylated form cHET very efficiently. The compound appears to be phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.50| (ThiM), which serves as a substrate for |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.3| (ThiE) |CITS: [JAmChemSoc1172351]|., Further experiments performed with mutants of the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| and the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| that were not able to produce the thiazole component of thiamine showed that these organisms were also capable of utilizing cHET as a precursor. The findings were interpreted to say that cHET is an important contributor to the production of |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|, particularly for prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms |CITS: [29654239]|.

General Background, |FRAME: D-APIOSE| is the only plant cell wall monosaccharide with a branched carbon skeleton. In higher plants it is mainly found as a component of the |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RGII) pectin fraction of the primary cell walls. In this pectic polysaccharide D-apiose acts as an attachment point for two complex side chains |CITS:[8798473]|. The linkage occurs through the formation of a cyclic diester between the hydroxyl groups of the furanose ring of D-apiose and borate. The two remaining hydroxyl groups of the RGII-bound borate diester react with a second D-apiose residue from another RGII chain to form a borate tetraester |CITS:[8798473],[10224062]|. The exact pathway leading to the incorporation of D-apiose into RGII remains largely unknown, although it is known that apiose is transferred from its activated form |FRAME: UDP-APIOSE|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UDP-APIOSE| is formed by the decarboxylation of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE|. This conversion occurs in a single enzymatic reaction that involves decarboxylation followed by re-arrangement of the carbon skeleton and ring contraction. The mechanism of formation of UDP-D-apiose has been proposed in |CITS:[12969423]|., The enzyme responsible for this reaction is bifunctional and also catalyze the decarboxylation of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| to |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE|, and has thus been named UDP-apiose/UDP-xylose synthase |CITS:[12969423]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-837| is an etiological agent of chronic periodontitis. Like most Gram-negative bacteria it displays lipopolysaccharides (LPS) on the cell surface. However, unlike many other orgnaisms |FRAME: TAX-837| has two different O-polysaccharides - a conventional O-polysaccharide (named O-LPS, described in |FRAME: PWY-8228|), and an anionic O-polysaccharide (named A-LPS) consisting of a repeating unit with a yeast mannan-like structure formed by α-(1→6) and α(1→2) mannosyltransferases |CITS: [18263730]|. Several studies have suggested that A-LPS contains additional structural sugars such as |FRAME: D-Galactose| and |FRAME: CPD-14608| in addition to mannose residues |CITS: [23717416][24852504]|. Both O-polysaccharides are covalently attached to the lipid A-core., |FRAME: TAX-837| uses a type IX secretion system to secrete cargo proteins to the cell surface, where they are anchored, via A-LPS. A study of the anchoring mechanism has shown that the C terminus of each cargo protein is amide-bonded to |FRAME: CPD-24136|, which serves as a linking sugar |CITS: [32873758]|., Among the secreted cargo proteins are the gingipains, extracellular proteases that play the most significant role in the virulence of the organism. Since the gingipains are required to accumulate the heme pigment on the cell surface, mutants lacking A-LPS are unable to produce black pigmented colonies on blood agar., |FRAME: CPD-24136 3-Acetamido-2,3-dideoxy-2-(seryl)amino-α-D-glucuronamide| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-10313| by the action of three enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS04650|, |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS04655|, and |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01465| genes |CITS: [32873758]|. |FRAME: CPD-10313| is produced from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| in four steps catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-15292|, |FRAME: G-15293|, |FRAME: G-15295|, and |FRAME: G-15294| genes (see |FRAME: PWY-7090|). All of these genes have been shown to be required for A-LPS biosynthesis |CITS: [15731033][24852504][32873758]|. The exact functions of |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS04650|, |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS04655|, and |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS01465| were discovered in 2020 |CITS: [32873758]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 Salicylate| is a key phenolic compound biosynthesized by many plants and some microorganisms. It is a member of an important anti-inflammatory drug class used widely in human medicine. In microorganisms |FRAME: CPD-110| is a biosynthetic precursor of secondary metabolites and siderophores, and a regulator of antibiotic efflux |CITS: [15837391]|. In plants |FRAME: CPD-110| may be converted by glucosylation, esterification, or methylation to physiologically active derivatives |CITS: [11607533]|. The source of the name |FRAME: CPD-110| (salicylic acid) comes from the name of the willow tree, |FRAME:TAX-40685|, from whose bark it can be obtained., For examples of salicylate biosynthetic pathways, see |FRAME: PWY-6408|, |FRAME: PWY-6407|, |FRAME: PWY-6406|, |FRAME: PWY-981|, |FRAME: PWY-6621|, |FRAME: PWY-6624| and |FRAME: PWY-4203| |CITS: [20020317]|., In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-110| can be degraded through several pathways including oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6183|), oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-633| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6224|), direct fission of |FRAME: CPD-110| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8159|), and degradation after CoA derivative formation (this pathway). |FRAME: CPD-110| is also an intermediate in |FRAME: PWY-5427|., In yeast, earlier work on |FRAME: TAX-5554| showed |FRAME: CPD-110| oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [7364712] [6539772]|. In a more recent report using |FRAME: ORG-6162| a novel pathway of |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation via |FRAME: PHENOL| was elucidated (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6636|) |CITS: [20020317]|., About This Pathway, A novel pathway for |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation has been demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-235278| in which |FRAME: CPD-110| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-633| through |FRAME: CPD-12112| and |FRAME: CPD-12703|. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-110| to |FRAME: CPD-12112| involves a postulated |FRAME: CPD-12084| intermediate. A |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation gene cluster sdgABCDEFGHR was identified in |FRAME: TAX-235278| the expression of which was inducible by |FRAME: CPD-110| |CITS: [15006746]|., Gene sdgA was required for the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-110| to |FRAME: CPD-12112| with cofactors |FRAME: ATP| and |FRAME: CO-A|. The product of gene sdgA was suggested to be a salicylyl-CoA ligase although it showed amino acid sequence similarity to an AMP-ligase by BLAST analysis. It was experimentally shown to be essential for the production of |FRAME: CPD-12112|. A |FRAME: CPD-12084| intermediate was postulated, although it was not detected. The product of gene sdgB was also proposed to be involved in |FRAME: CO-A| addition, although this could not be demonstrated under the experimental conditions used. |FRAME: CPD-12112| was produced by SdgA in the presence or absence of SdgB |CITS: [15006746]|., |FRAME: CPD-12112| was converted by the product of gene sdgC, a salicylyl-CoA 5-hydroxylase, to |FRAME: CPD-12703|. This compound appeared to spontaneously hydrolyze under the experimental conditions used, thus this reaction may or may not be enzyme-catalyzed. The product of sdgD converted |FRAME: CPD-633| to |FRAME: CPD-1070|., The fate of |FRAME: CPD-1070| was not determined, although two possibilities were suggested. One was direct cleavage to |FRAME: MALEATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and the other was isomerization to |FRAME: CPD-277| and hydrolysis to |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6223|). The functions of the remaining genes were not determined |CITS: [15006746]|.

Sucrose (table sugar) is an important dietary nutrient both as an energy storage molecule and by providing an aesthetic component to food, sweetness. Sucrose is widely produced by plants and when ingested by humans is degraded in the small intestine by the sucrase component of a |FRAME: CPLX66-547 "bifunctional sucrase/isomaltase"| attached to the lumenal membrane of enterocytes |CITS: [807575]|. This bi-functional enzyme is encoded by the SI gene, which produces a single polypeptide that is proteolytically cleaved into two monomers which maintain a very stable heterodimeric configuration., Glucose, as a metabolite of starch or sucrose degradation, is taken up into small intestine enterocytes by the Na+/glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) expressed on the lumenal membrane |CITS: [12885248]|. Human mutations in the SGLT1 gene have been shown to cause Glucose-Galactose Malabsorption (GGM) resulting in neonatal onset of diarrhea leading to death unless glucose and galactose are removed from the diet |CITS: [8563765]|., Fructose is another common sweetener that is degraded by this pathway as well. Fructose, as metabolite of sucrose degradation or as dietary nutrient, is absorbed by the GLUT5 transporter on the brush border membrane of enterocytes of the small intestine |CITS: [1550217]|. The efflux transporter, GLUT2, resides in the basolateral membrane of intestinal cells and transports fructose into the bloodstream |CITS: [8457197]|, where it is carried throughout the body and metabolized by three closely related, tissue-specific enzymes. Fructose has been used for intravenous feeding to trauma victims in hospitals, but very high plasma levels carry risks of lactic acidosis and are detrimental to the liver so this procedure is generally avoided.

Summary: |FRAME:THIAMINE Thiamine| (vitamin B1) is an essential molecule that is required in all living organisms but is only produced in prokaryotes, yeasts and plants |CITS:[Rapala-Kozik11]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| and its biological active derivate |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| is complex and can be achieved via different pathways in the various organisms (for instances see |FRAME:PWY-6894| |FRAME:PWY-6908| |FRAME:PWY-7356|) |CITS:[18161008] [22449018]||. Besides |FRAME:THIAMINE| and it's well characterized diphosphorylated derivative three more |FRAME:THIAMINE| phosphates have been shown to exist, i.e. |FRAME:THIAMINE-P|, |FRAME:CPD-611| and |FRAME:CPD0-1095| |CITS:[17334376] [19490098]|. , Although |FRAME:CPD-611| is found in most cells across all kingdoms its biosynthesis and biological role has only been partially elucidated and remains to be researched in more detail |CITS:[12943234]|. There is only insufficient knowledge about the biological role of |FRAME:CPD-611|. It appears that unlike |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:CPD-611| does not act as an coenzyme but has been shown to be involved in the activation of anion channels and protein phosphorylation in vertebrates and acting as mediator (alarmone) in signaling pathways, e.g. under stress conditions like amino acid starvation in bacteria |CITS:[19490098] [14769791] [18215312] [8114078]|., |FRAME:CPD-611 Thiamine triphosphate| has also been found in Saccharomyces cerevisiae |CITS:[13111284]| and its biosynthesis studied |CITS:[3034239]|. The corresponding enzyme, i.e. thiamine diphosphate kinase catalyzing the transfer of a phosphor from |FRAME:ATP| to |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| yielding |FRAME:CPD-611| and |FRAME:ADP| has been isolated and biochemically characterized in Saccharomyces cerevisiae but its coding gene has not been identified yet. Although the oligomeric nature of the protein could be demonstrated the correct number and molecular weight of the subunits remains to be verified |CITS:[3034239]|. In contrast to the finding in yeast the bacterial biosynthetic route to |FRAME:CPD-611| originates from |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| and |FRAME:Pi|, a reaction which appears to be fueled by the chemiosmotic force of the respiratory chain |CITS:[23323214]|. The reverse reaction from |FRAME:CPD-611| to |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| catalyzed by a thiamine triphosphatase has been shown to exist in bacteria |CITS:[3026493] [3039089]| and vertebrates |CITS:[4335862]| (reviewed in |CITS:[24021036]|) but reminds to be demonstrated in yeast.

Summary: Although the deoxyhexose rhamnose is found in glycoconjugates of bacteria and plants (but not animals), the rare D-isoform is found only in the outer cell surface of bacteria.  |FRAME: CPD-13829| is a constituent of the lipopolysaccharide of the plant pathogens |FRAME: TAX-339| and |FRAME: TAX-317| and the animal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-287|, |FRAME: TAX-292|, |FRAME: TAX-196| and |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [10477307][11096116][11856318][14739333]|., |FRAME: CPD-353| is the nucleotide-activated donor of D-rhamnose units to the A-band lipopolysaccharide in |FRAME:TAX-287|.  This gram-negative organism synthesizes two variants of lipopolysaccharide, designated A-band and B-band.  The O-antigen of the A-band lipopolysaccharide is a homopolymer of D-rhamnose residues arranged in repeating trisaccharide units, whereas the O-antigen of the B-band is a heteropolymer containing many different monosaccharides.  |FRAME:ORG-5927| is a pathogen that causes opportunistic infections in animals and plants, and the lipopolysaccharide of the outer membrane contributes to its virulence |CITS: [10477307][11856318][14739333]|., The biosynthesis of the O-antigen in |FRAME:TAX-562| is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: OANTIGEN-PWY|, although its composition is different from that of |FRAME:ORG-5927|. , |FRAME: ORG-6194| also has D-rhamnose residues on its surface. However, they are in the S-layer, a crystalline protein layer found on the outermost cell surface of many bacteria and archaea. The S-layer of this Gram-positive, thermophilic bacterium is glycosylated with identical repeats of D-rhamnose and |FRAME: CPD-13886| units (in |CITS: [11096116]|)., In this pathway, the final product is the D-rhamnose donor, |FRAME: CPD-353|. It is synthesized from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| in two steps, involving a dehydratase and a reductase. The precursor |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE| is also a common intermediate for the synthesis of other GDP-monodeoxyhexoses such as:  |FRAME: CPD-13118|, |FRAME: CPD-354|, and |FRAME: CPD-20462|; the GDP-dideoxyhexose |FRAME: CPD-9391|; and the GDP-dideoxy amino sugar |FRAME: CPD-9387| |CITS: [11096116][11856318][14739333]|.  The biosynthesis of the starting substrate, |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|, is shown in the pathway link.

This ethanol degradation pathway begins with conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde by |FRAME: CPLX66-121 "peroxisomal catalase"| |CITS: [SALWAYJG2002]|. The resulting acetaldehyde passes from the peroxisome to the cytoplasm and into the mitochondrial compartment where it is converted to acetate (by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase). Should acetate be activated to acetyl-CoA within the liver, it would not be oxidized by the Krebs cycle because of the prevailing high ratio of NADH + H / NAD+ within the liver mitochondrial matrix. Consequently, acetate leaves the mitochondrial compartment and the hepatocyte to be metabolised by extra-hepatic tissues |CITS: [SALWAYJG2002]|. Extrahepatic tissues take up acetate where it is converted to acetyl-CoA |CITS: [11420176]|., Four distinct human ethanol degradation pathways have been described - three oxidative pathways and one nonoxidative pathway.  All oxidative pathways mediate the oxidation of ethanol to acetaldehye which is then oxidized to acetate for subsequent extra-hepatic activation to acetyl-CoA |CITS: [11420176]|. Oxidative pathways are differentiated based on the enzyme/mechanism by which ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde., The present pathway utilizes |FRAME: CPLX66-121 "peroxisomal catalase"| with the other two oxidative pathways utilizing endoplasmic reticulum |FRAME: HS05414-MONOMER "Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System"| (MEOS) (|FRAME: PWY66-161|) and |FRAME: CPLX66-101 "cytoplasmic alcohol dehydrogenase"| (|FRAME: PWY66-21|), respectively. The nonoxidative pathway is less well characterized but produces fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEEs) as primary end products |CITS: [12456329]|., Oxidative and nonoxidative pathways have been demonstrated in a range of tissues including gastric, pancreatic, hepatic and lung. Inhibition of oxidative ethanol degradation pathways raises both hepatic and pancreatic FAEE levels demonstrating that oxidative and nonoxidative pathways are alternative metabolically linked pathways. Pancreatic ethanol metabolism occurs predominantly by the nonoxidative pathway but oxidative routes to acetaldehyde have also been demonstrated in the pancreas - the cytochrome P450 2E1 and alcohol dehydrogenase pathways |CITS: [12870777]|., Ethanol metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver and the resulting oxidative metabolite acetaldehyde is thought to play a role in alcohol induced liver injury. Additionally, there is now solid evidence that FAEEs also play a role in alcoholic pancreatitis |CITS:[12065293]|. Blood and organ levels of FAEEs are raised by ethanol consumption with the highest concentration observed in the pancreas. FAEE generation from ethanol is greater in the pancreas than in any other organ suggesting that the pancreatic pathway contributes to raised blood and organ FAEE levels |CITS: [12065293]|., Under conditions of acute ethanol consumption, the majority of ethanol is degraded by the hepatic oxidative pathways predominantly the alcohol dehydrogenase mediated pathway. However, under conditions of chronic ethanol consumption, hepatic MEOS activity and nonoxidative pathways are induced and quantitatively make a greater contribution to ethanol catabolism. The stimulatory effect of ethanol on Cytochrome P450 2E1 levels results in increased oxygen consumption, production of excess free radicals and increased metabolism of ethanol, vitamin A and testosterone - the chronic effects of which contribute to depletion of antioxidative activity. Antioxidative deficiency (glutathione, vitamin E, phosphatidylcholine) and excess free radicals are believed to subsequently contribute to the progression of alcoholic liver disease |CITS: [12901271]|., Polymorphic loci for genes encoding enzymes of ethanol degradation pathways have been identified and resulting variant isoenzymes characterized and found to exhibit distinct kinetic properties. Indeed, genetically determined differences in ethanol metabolism may, in part, account for the variability of individual susceptibility to the physical complications of alcohol abuse |CITS: [3519419]|.
