Summary: General Background, The three aromatic amino acids, |FRAME: TRP|, |FRAME: TYR|, and |FRAME: PHE|, derived from the common precursor , |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, are constituents of proteins, and precursors of many plant secondary metabolites., , Two steps are required for conversion of |FRAME: PREPHENATE| to |FRAME: TYR|: a dehydrogenation/decarboxylation, and a transamination., Two possible routes for this conversion are known. In the route described in |FRAME: TYRSYN| the, decarboxylation occurs first, resulting in the intermediate |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, followed by, a transamination to |FRAME: TYR|. In the second route, described here, transamination occurs first, resulting in formation of, |FRAME: CPD-659|, which is subsequently decarboxylated to |FRAME: TYR|., While the first route has been confirmed in many microorganisms, including E.coli and yeast, , some other bacteria, including cyanobacteria, as well as many plants, employ the arogenate route |CITS: [4206476][3298985]|., The two routes have been reported to co-exist in many microorganisms. In addition, the, |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| route cannot be completely ruled out for plants based on these facts: , 1) early studies detected prephenate dehydrogenase activity in mung bean shoots |CITS: [4379953]|,, 2) the Arabidopsis arogenate dehydrogenase TyrAAT2 presents a weak prephenate dehydrogenase , activity |CITS: [12354106]|, even though the high Km for prephenate and low specific activity of prephenate , dehydrogenase reaction indicates the reaction is unlikely physiologically significant., Two types of arogenate dehydrogenase are known, that utilze either NADP+ or NAD+. These two types, are described by the pathways |FRAME: PWY-3461| and |FRAME: PWY-6120|, respectively., About This Pathway, The two key reactions in this pathway are catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-8101| and, |FRAME: AT5G34930-MONOMER|, respectively., Arogenate is the branch-point and the immediate precursor for the synthesis of both tyrosine and phenylalanine. , Arogenate dehydrogenase is the key enzyme channeling arogenate towards tyrosine synthesis. Its activity is , strongly feedback inhibited by tyrosine. , The Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT5G34930-MONOMER| |CITS:[12354106]|, as well as the enzyme from the cyanobacterium, |FRAME: TAX-1148| |CITS: [15171683]|, are strictly NADP-dependent (see |FRAME: PWY-3461|)., The enzymes from maize |CITS:[Byng1981]| and the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1866|, |CITS:[2590341]| are strictly NAD-dependent.

General Background, |FRAME: Neomycins Neomycins| are a family of broad-spectrum highly toxic antibiotics produced by |FRAME: TAX-1906|. They were discovered in 1949 by Waksman and Lechevalier (Waksman later received the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physiology and medicine) |CITS: [17782716]|., Neomycin usually exists as a complex composed of two stereoisomers, |FRAME: CPD-14142| and |FRAME: CPD-14141|, which are the two active components. A third component, |FRAME: CPD-14137 "neomycin A"|, which is a degradation product, is present in small quantities., Neomycin was originally used as a treatment for tuberculosis, but serious side effects soon became apparent, including ototoxicity |CITS: [8170691]|, which sometimes developed to complete loss of hearing, and nephrotoxicity. Thus systemic use of neomycin is limited, and the most common mode of use is via topical application |CITS: [6224608]|., About This Pathway, The early parts of the neomycin biosynthesis are similar to those of related antibiotics - please see the pathways |FRAME: PWY-7014| and |FRAME: PWY-7015|. The enzymes that are unique to neomycin biosynthesis are those catalyzing the last five steps, starting with |FRAME: CPD-14143|. The |FRAME: G-15047|-encoded glycosyltransferase adds an acetyl-glucosaminyl moiety, resulting in the four-ring structure of neomycin. The acetate residue is removed by a dual-function deacetylase (encoded by |FRAME: G-15045|), and the C-6''' position of the the glucosamine moiety is aminated by the successive action of an oxidase (|FRAME:G-15024|) and an aminotransferase (|FRAME: G-15025|), resulting in |FRAME: CPD-14141|., The last step described here is the epimerization reaction at C-5''' of |FRAME: CPD-14141| to |FRAME: CPD-14142|. However, at this time neither the timing of the epimerization nor the identity of the responsible enzyme are known.

|FRAME: Mycofactocins Mycofactocin| (MFT) was first identified by a bioinformatic analysis that demonstrated the co-occurrence of the genes mftABCDEF in over 600 bacterial species, including pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1764|, and |FRAME: TAX-1809|. It was also noted that genes encoding for three different dehydrogenase families (TIGR03971, TIGR03989, and TIGR04266) were found only in the genomes of organisms that contained the mft genes. This led to the proposal that MFT is an important cofactor for the enzymes that belong to these families |CITS: [21223593]|., Strengthening this proposal was the fact that knocking out the mftA-D and mftF genes abolished ethanol assimilation in |FRAME: TAX-1772|, a similar result to knocking out the msmeg_6242 gene, which encodes an iron-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase that belongs to the TIGR04266 family |CITS: [31113891]|., The similarity of the mftA, mftB and mftC genes to the |FRAME: G-11752|, pqqD, and |FRAME: G-11753| genes, which are required for the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: PQQ "pyrroloquinoline quinone"| (PQQ) cofactor, has led to a hypothesis that MFT is synthesized from the conserved C-terminal region on the precursor peptide MftA |CITS: [21223593]|. This hypothesis was confirmed by two independent studies that reported that MftC catalyzes the |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent oxidative decarboxylation of the C-terminus on MftA, in the presence of MftB, resulting in an unsaturated tyramine structure |CITS: [27312813][27158836]|. Additional research revealed that MftC catalyzes an additional activity, forming a five-membered lactam ring from the penultimate valine residue |CITS: [28634235]|., Subsequent work has shown that MftE is a peptide hydrolase that releases the modified C-terminal residues (AHDP) from the precursor protein |CITS: [28077628][30183269]|, and that MftD catalyzes an oxygen-dependent oxidative deamination of the phenyl ring of AHDP to generate |FRAME: CPD-22872|, a compound that was shown to have redox activity, and could be used by an MFT-dependent carveol dehydrogenase |CITS: [31381312]|., Further undertanding of the pathway was gained later the same year, when a number of glucosylated species of mycofactocin were detected in |FRAME: TAX-1772|. It was shown that the enzyme encoded by the last gene in the cluster, MftF, catalyzes the transfer of up to nine glucosyl residues in β(1→4) configuration to |FRAME: CPD-22872|. In addition, most of the compounds were found to contain 2-O--methylation on the second glucosyl residue |CITS: [Pena-Ortiz19]|. As of 2020, the identity of the methyltransferase is not known. The appearance of glycosylated, AHDP species in the wild type together with a drastic decrease of aglycons in Δ|FRAME: G-80624| mutants can be interpreted in a scenario where either glycosylation or the MftF protein itself are essential for the MftD step to efficiently take place in vivo |CITS: [Pena-Ortiz20]|., Assays performed with |FRAME: CPLX-7608| showed that both the aglycone |FRAME: CPD-22872| and all of the oligoglucosylated and methylated/glucosylated species were completely turned over by the enzyme, confirming that all of them are bona-fide mycofactocins with full cofactor function |CITS: [Pena-Ortiz19]|.

|FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|). The β-oxidation of saturated fatty acids is a straightforward process which requires the participation of three enzymes, i.e. acyl-CoA oxidase (POX1), the multifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase (FOX2) and the thiolase (POT1). At the end of the process stands a saturated fatty acid shortened by 2 carbon units (|FRAME:ACETYL-COA|) which is further metabolized in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-5690|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291| and |FRAME:PWY-7292|). , By employing auxiliary enzymes in addition to the classic enzymes of fatty acid β-oxidation in peroxisomes of |FRAME:TAX-4932| alternative processing routes are opened up for unsaturated fatty acids which would otherwise form an metabolic block in the β-oxidative break-down |CITS:[10709656]|. The intermediate |FRAME:CPD0-1158| can take different metabolic directions (compare |FRAME:PWY-7292|), one of which is forming |FRAME:CPD-15566| (this pathway) which is catalyzed by Δ3,5,Δ2,4-dienoyl-CoA isomerase (DCI1) |CITS:[10381339] [10455114]|. , However, the debate about whether or not DCI1 encodes the dienoyl-CoA isomerase or what role the reductase-dependent pathway in the in vivo degradation of |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD| plays is ongoing and further research is required to solve the matter |CITS:[10455114] [19830908]|. Unquestionable however is the existence and molecular function of the 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase which is encoded in |FRAME:TAX-4932| by the gene SPS19 |CITS:[1738316] [9268358]| catalyzing the NADPH-dependent conversion of 2,4-dienoyl-CoA's into 3-enoyl-CoA's. The latter compounds are substrates for the catalytic action of Δ3,Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) transforming 3-trans-enoyl-CoA's into 2-trans-enoyl-CoA's which in turn qualify as proper substrates for further metabolization in the β-oxidation cycle. Taken together the occurrence of SPS19 in yeast and its localization to the peroxisomes |CITS:[9268358]| is indicative for a functioning reductase-dependent pathway in this organism which has been found before as a minor pathway in mammals |CITS:[8300563] [9417087]|.

Storage proteins of pulses are protected by the presence of enzymes that convert O-diphenols to O-quinones. This helps prolong the storage of the legumes seeds for longer periods. Many legumes that lack these oxidation enzymes result in having a very small shelf storage time and in economic loss |CITS: [19525325]|. , This pathway shows the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-11724|, a caffiec-malic ester that accumulates in red clover (|FRAME: TAX-57577|) up to several micrograms/gram of fresh weight. The enzymes underlying this pathway are targets for engineering into other legumes that lack them. , |FRAME: CPD-11724 Phaselate| is an endogenous substrate for the polyphenol oxidase of red clover, and the seasonal variation of phaselic acid has been studied and evaluated for correlation of enzyme and substrate levels |CITS: [18361497]|. The combination of PPO and diphenols protect red clover storage protein from proteolysis during ensiling.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-12245 "Vancomycin"| is a glycopeptide that is often used for treating patients infected with antibiotic-resistant bacteria (especially Streptococcal and Staphylococcal infections) and patients who are allergic to penicillins |CITS: [10232990]|. The widespread prevalence of methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA) has made vancomycin the antibiotic of last resort for eliminating multi-drug-resistant Gram-positive bacteria., Glycopeptide antibiotics such as |FRAME: CPD-12245| and |FRAME: CPD-12251| inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to the |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| end of the peptidoglycan pentapeptide (see |FRAME: CPD-7695| for the structure of the petidoglycan monomer). These residues are added to the peptidoglycan precursor as a |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide, produced by |FRAME: CPLX-8013|., During maturation of the bacterial cell wall the terminal |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue of the pentapeptide is cleaved by the D,D-transpeptidases that form the peptide crosslinks between adjacent glycan threads. These enzymes, which are known as |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin-binding proteins"| (PBPs), must hydrolyze the D-Ala-D-Ala bond for their activity (for example, see the |FRAME: TAX-1280| PBPs |FRAME: MONOMER-15471|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15456|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15472|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15473|, and the methicillin-resistant |FRAME: MONOMER-15469|)., The binding of the antibiotics to the terminal |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide blocks the binding transpeptidases and inhibits the transglycosylation and transpeptidation reactions of peptidoglycan assembly., After three decades of vancomycin use resistant mutants appeared. Resistance initially appeared in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1350| (collectively called VRE, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus), but eventually spread to other organisms. The resistant strains have D-ala-D-ala ligases with altered specificity, resulting in incorporation of either |FRAME: D-LACTATE| or |FRAME: D-SERINE| instead of the second |FRAME: D-ALANINE|. When incorporated into peptidoglycan, these modified peptides do not bind glycopcptide antibiotics., The spread of vancomycin resistance is a major biomedical concern, especially strains of methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA) which acquired vancomycin resistance (sometimes referred to as "superbugs")., Three types of ligases that incorporate |FRAME: D-LACTATE| have been documented. |FRAME:CPLX-8016 "VanA"| is carried on a transposon and confers high-level inducible resistance to both vancomycin and teicoplanin, |FRAME:CPLX-8014 "VanB"| is also carried on a transposon and confers variable levels of inducible resistance to vancomycin only, and |FRAME:CPLX-8019 "VanD"| is carried on the chromosome and confers constitutive resistance to high levels of vancomycin and low levels of teicoplanin., Four type of ligases that incorporate |FRAME: D-SERINE| have been described so far (see |FRAME: PWY-6455|). Low-level intrinsic resistance is provided by by VanC-type |FRAME: CPD-12249| ligases, found in |FRAME: TAX-1353| (VanC1) and |FRAME: TAX-37734| (|FRAME: CPLX-8015 "VanC2"|). In addition, |FRAME: CPLX-8020 "VanE"| and |FRAME: CPLX-8021 "VanG"| have been found in the chromosomes of several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1351|., About This Pathway, Bacteria that become resistant to vancomycin by incorporating |FRAME: D-LACTATE| in their peptidoglycan acquire a gene cluster that contains genes that encode for a number of proteins, five of which are essential for the high-level resistance phenotype. The five essential gene products are called VanR, VanS, VanH, VanX, and either VanA, VanB, or VanD., . , VanR and VanS make up a two-component signal transduction system that regulates the expression of the other three genes and appears to be stimulated by the presence of vancomycin |CITS: [8161518][10985787]|., |FRAME: G-11858| encodes a |FRAME: CPLX-8017 "D-ala-D-ala dipeptidase"| that hydrolyzes |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptides prior to their incorporation into peptidoglycan. |FRAME: G-11851 "VanH"| encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-15467| that converts |FRAME: PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: D-LACTATE|, and |FRAME: G-11850|, |FRAME: EF_RS10940| and |FRAME: G-11861| encode an enzyme that ligates the |FRAME: D-LACTATE| to |FRAME: D-ALANINE|, producing |FRAME: CPD-12247| depsipeptides. The depsipeptides are incorporated in the peptidoglycan pentapeptide instead of the |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide., Since |FRAME: CPD-12245| has very little affinity to the depsipeptide, the resulting peptidoglycan is immune to vancomycin binding, but is still a good substrate for the transpeptidases that form the crosslinking between peptidoglycan threads., It has been shown that in response to |FRAME: CPD-12245| the ratio of |FRAME: CPD-12247| to |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| in peptidoglycan of |FRAME: TAX-1352| is 49:1. Following insertional inactivation of |FRAME: G-11858| the ratio went down to 1:1 |CITS: [7854121]|.

Names: palmitoleate biosynthesis IV (fungi and animals) // palmitoleic acid biosynthesis // monounsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis // unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis
Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| (16:1Δ9) is a common unsaturated fatty acid, found in bacteria, fungi |CITS: [8294460]|, plants |CITS: [7548115]| and animals |CITS:[14321753] [6030882]|. It comprises from 10% to 65% of the seed oil of several plants., |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| can be formed directly from the saturated fatty acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| by the action of Δ9 desaturase enzymes. Such enzymes have been reported from cyanobacteria |CITS: [7929259][10937442][16689682][17385315]|, fungi |CITS: [2674136][12055292]|, higher plants |CITS: [12208502][8861937]|, , fish |CITS: [11170264]| and mammals |CITS: [16443825]|., Desaturase enzyme do not operate on a free acid substrate. Three types of desaturases are known, that act on acyl-CoA, acyl-[acp], and acyl-lipid conjugates, respectively., In many bacteria and some plants |FRAME: CPD-9245| is derived from |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs| |CITS: [9154992]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5366|). In mammals the enzyme acts only on CoA-derivatives |CITS: [16443825]|, as shown in this pathway, and in some plants and cyanobacteria the desaturase acts on fatty acids embedded within the structure of lipids |CITS: [7929259]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7589|)., The sole |FRAME: TAX-4932| Δ9 fatty acid desaturase is |FRAME: YGL055W|, an ER membrane-bound protein that is required for the production of monounsaturated fatty acids |CITS: [1978720]|. Ole1p catalyzes the formation of a double bond between carbons 9 and 10 (denoted by Δ9) in the cis configuration. Other fungi and eukaryotes have additional fatty acid desaturases that can produce double bonds in the Δ12 and Δ15 positions., The Ole1p sequence is similar to homologs in rat and human (SCD1) over the majority of the protein, including a cluster of histidine residues that coordinate the binding of a diiron-oxo prosthetic group within the catalytic site (reviewed in |CITS: [16920014]|). The rat and yeast proteins are similar enough that exogenously expressed rat protein can rescue an ole1 null mutant |CITS: [1978720]|. However, Ole1p has an additional C-terminal, 113 amino acid extension (relative to the rat protein), which encodes a cytochrome b5-like domain not found in mammalian desaturases. In animal cells, cytochrome b5 is thought to be the electron donor for fatty acid desaturation. In contrast, the yeast cytochrome b5 (Cyb5) is dispensable for the synthesis of unsaturated fatty acids because Ole1p contains inherent electron donor activity. The rat protein is unable to rescue an ole1 cyb5 double mutant |CITS:[8530368]|.

General Background, The mycotoxins |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of the B-group and G-group aflatoxins, which constitute the major groups of naturally occurring aflatoxins. The production of aflatoxins by some strains of several |FRAME:TAX-5052| species has been extensively studied. However many species, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425 "Emericella nidulans (previously known as Aspergullus nidulans)"|, produce only |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| as a final product (in |CITS: [18486503]|). |FRAME: TAX-5067| produces both B- and G-group aflatoxins from |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587|, while |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces only B-group aflatoxins. The biological role of these mycotoxins in fungi remains unclear (in |CITS: [17620135] [18246345]| and, reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|)., Aflatoxins are highly toxic and carcinogenic crop contaminants that create major economic and public health problems worldwide. Much research has been focused on identifying compounds that inhibit aflatoxin biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-4592| is metabolized by mammalian liver cytochrome P450 enzymes to a mutagenic epoxide that covalently binds to DNA. Its genotoxic mechanism of action has been studied in yeast |CITS: [8968101] [9771940]|. Other species, such as |FRAME: TAX-5062| and |FRAME:TAX-41058|, are unable to produce aflatoxins and are used in food fermentation |CITS: [17665189]|., Most of the aflatoxin biosynthetic genes are clustered in Aspergilli and are positively regulated by gene aflR (in |CITS: [17620135] [16448506] [16108793] [15094053] [7618880] [16535712]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]| and |CITS: [15006741]|). The enzyme reactions and biosynthetic intermediates in the aflatoxin biosynthetic pathway have been reviewed in detail |CITS: [15022028]|. See MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5954|, |FRAME: PWY-5955|, |FRAME: PWY-5956|, |FRAME: PWY-5960| and |FRAME: PWY-5961|., About This Pathway, In this segment of the aflatoxin biosynthesis pathway, a second O-methyltransferase catalyzes a, |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent methylation of |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN|. |FRAME: CPD-7157|, is the last stable intermediate in the biosynthesis of aflatoxins B1 and G1, which are, independently produced from it. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-7157| to |FRAME: CPD-4592| involves several, transformations that have been proposed to be catalyzed by a single microsomal cytochrome P-450 enzyme, the product of gene, ordA (|CITS: [11996570]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|). In an initial oxidative cycle, production of a, 11-hydroxy O-methylsterigmatocystin intermediate has been demonstrated |CITS: [11996570]|. This is, followed by aryl ring cleavage, demethylation, dehydration, decarboxylation and rearrangement to produce, |FRAME: CPD-4592| |CITS: [11996570]|. , |FRAME: CPD-7157| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-10178| in a series of uncharacterized steps, shown here, as a triple arrow, that involve the products of genes aflQ (ordA), aflU (cypA) and, nadA |CITS: [18486503] [15528514] [11996570]|. Strains of |FRAME: TAX-5059| are thought to produce only, aflatoxins B1 and B2, while strains of |FRAME: TAX-5067| produce all four major, aflatoxins (B1, B2, G1 and G2). Aflatoxins are excreted from, mycelia and their biosynthetic intermediates accumulate in cells. No aflatoxin export system has been, identified yet. Reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8 Ubiquinone-8| (Q-8) is common in yeast species (but not in |FRAME: TAX-4932|, which produces |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-6|). Q-8-forming species are distributed in the genera |FRAME: TAX-5475|, |FRAME: TAX-36908|, |FRAME: TAX-36910|, |FRAME: TAX-4917|, |FRAME: TAX-4919|, |FRAME: TAX-4943| and, |FRAME: TAX-29828| |CITS: [Suzuki98][Goto86][Phaff86][2589855][Walt89][Yamada76a]|. The length of the polyprenyl tail of ubiquinone has been used for phylogenetic classification of these organisms |CITS:[12469316][12501366]|., Recent findings suggest that some |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8| forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|. No homologs of the decarboxylase |FRAME: EG11396 UbiD|, as well as |FRAME: EG11044 UbiX|, which forms the |FRAME: CPD-18260| cofactor for UbiD, were identified in |FRAME: TAX-340|. Similarly, no gene for decarboxylation has been identified in yeast. Both the bacterium and yeast use the same type of |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.60| (|FRAME: G-80759| and |FRAME: YOR125C|, respectively) which are diiron enzymes that differ from the common bacterial enzyme |FRAME: G6365 UbiF|. In addition, deletion of ubiJ, ubiB, and ubiK in |FRAME: TAX-340| resulted in an accumulation of the intermediate |FRAME: 3-OCTAPRENYL-4-HYDROXYBENZOATE|, while deletion of the orthologous |FRAME: TAX-562| genes led to an accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-23381|, suggesting that the decarboxylation reaction during ring modification may occur later in the pathway, as it is in the eukaryotic pathway |CITS: [30681910]|., For the regular bacterial Q-8 biosynthesis pathway, see |FRAME: UBISYN-PWY|.

Fumitremorgins are tremorgenic mycotoxins |CITS:[5122678]| which have been named after their tremor inducing effect on the central nervous system in mice |CITS:[14107473]|. These compounds represent a group of prenylated indole alkaloids which are mostly found in the genera Aspergillus and Penicillium of the fungi kingdom |CITS:[11245401] [23467716] [20024094]||. Aspergillus fumigatus, a main producer of tremorgins, is the foremost cause for fungal diseases with a high mortality rate in immunocompromised humans |CITS:[20618330] [21102391]|. Because of their considerable impact on human health, Aspergillus fumigatus has been in the focus of researchers for some time now which, amongst others, resulted in the deciphering of its genome |CITS:[16372009] [16371993]| and the elucidation of gene clusters involved in the making of fungal secondary metabolites exhibiting numerous activities of physiological importance |CITS:[16322742]|. , In spite of their food poisoning and lung disease causing properties fumitremorgins and their pathway intermediates also exhibit a variety of interesting pharmacological activities which makes them promising candidates for drug improvement and cancer treatments. Aspergillus fumigatus has been reported to produce at least 226 bioactive secondary metabolites many of which possess such novel traits |CITS:[18763205]|. |FRAME:CPD-15260 Fumitremorgin B| and |FRAME:CPD-15259| efficiently inhibit mammalian cell-cycle progression |CITS:[8698634] [22575049]| and have been generally classified as genotoxic |CITS:[14627292]|. , The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-15261| appears not to have the necessary genetic make-up in the wild-type of Aspergillus fumigatus |CITS:[23109474] [16755625]| but other Aspergillus fumigatus strains |CITS:[6988091] [Horie81]| and close relatives such as Neosartorya fischeri |CITS:[3415223]| have been shown to produce |FRAME:CPD-15261|. For this reason various authors |CITS:[19763315] [21063425]| have proposed |FRAME:CPD-15259| as the final product of the pathway for Aspergillus. One of the possible reasons for finding |FRAME:CPD-15261| only in a few strains of Aspergillus fumigatus might be that the gene encoding verruculogen prenyltransferase catalyzing the last step of the pathway, is not part of the tremorgin biosynthetic cluster in Aspergillus fumigatus but is located on another chromosome |CITS:[23109474]| and may have been lost or rendered inactive in certain Aspergillus strains. , The substrate of the first committed reaction of the |FRAME:PWY-7526|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15266| has been produced previously (see |FRAME:PWY-7525| and also |FRAME:PWY-7537|) and is hydroxylated in both the C-12 and C-13 position of the indole ring by the cytochrome P450 dependent fumitremorgin C hydroxylase |CITS:[19226505]| yielding the next intermediate of the pathway - |FRAME:CPD-15268|. After the C-prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-15268| by the 12α,13α-dihydroxyfumitremorgin C prenyltransferase |CITS:[18683158]| forming |FRAME:CPD-15260|, the following reaction, the formation of an endoperoxide bond between the two prenyl moieties generating the cyclic |FRAME:CPD-15259| is considered the key reaction of the pathway. The catalyzing enzyme, i.e. verruculogen synthase, is a α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase able to insert both oxygen atoms from molecular |FRAME:OXYGEN-MOLECULE| and the first one of its kind reported for fungal pathways |CITS:[19763315] [21404415]|. The last step of the pathway, as mentioned above, is catalyzed by an verruculogen specific O-prenyltransferase generating the final pathway product |FRAME:CPD-15261| |CITS:[23109474]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CHORISMATE Chorismate| is an important intermediate that leads to the biosynthesis of several essential metabolites,, including aromatic amino acids, vitamins E and K, ubiquinone and certain siderophores |CITS: [2279393]|., |FRAME: CHORISMATE| is synthesized in 5 steps from |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6163|)., In most organisms, |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| is synthesized from |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| in two steps, (see |FRAME: PWY-6164|). However, the genomes of the archaea contain no orthologs for the genes that encode, these two enzymes. Instead, at least the euryarchaeota appear to utilize an alternative pathway in which, |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| is synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-10791| and, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| |CITS: [15182204]|. These two compounds are first condensed to form, |FRAME: CPD-10792|, which cyclizes to |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE|., From |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| and on to |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, the archaeal pathway appears to be identical, to the bacterial pathway |CITS: [15262931][17010158 ]|., It has been shown that the source for |FRAME: CPD-10791| is glycolytic |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE|,, which is condensed with |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [17014089]|., The latter is believed to be produced by a spontaneous reaction from |FRAME: GAP|, which is known to be unstable at, temperatures above 60°C, and to decompose to |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [2021650][17014089]|.

General Background, Sterols are isoprenoid-derived molecules that have essential functions in eukaryotes. In vertebrates |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| is by far the major sterol, whereas a mixture of various sterols is present in higher plants, including |FRAME: CPD-4143| (usually predominant), |FRAME: CPD-4162|, |FRAME: CPD-707|, |FRAME: CPD-4127|, |FRAME: CPD-4161| and |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. Sterols are present in three forms: free sterols (the major form with a free 3β-hydroxyl), steryl esters, and steryl glucosides., Free sterols are integral components of the membrane lipid bilayer and thus interact with some molecular species of, phosphoglycero(sphingo) lipids. The extent of this interaction plays a functional role in the regulation of membrane fluidity and permeability. Sterols have also been shown to play important roles in embryonic development of vertebrates and the formation of membrane microdomains (rafts), which may constitute signaling centers for multiple pathways |CITS:[11278759]|., Finally, sterols are precursors of compounds with a high physiological activity such as brassinosteroids, an important class of plant hormones involved in growth and development |CITS: [8602526]|, ecdysteroids in invertebrates |CITS:[7791536]| and plants |CITS:[Coriot93]|, and antheridiol and oogoniols, sexual pheromones of aquatic fungi belonging to, the saprolegniale class |CITS:[1913877]|., About This Pathway, Diatoms possess sterols that are typical for both plants and animals |CITS: [Rampen09]|. For example, the bloom-forming species |FRAME: TAX-267567| and |FRAME: TAX-29204| synthesize |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and |FRAME: DESMOSTEROL-CPD|, which are typical for animals; |FRAME: CPD-8134| and |FRAME: CPD-706|, which are typical for plants; |FRAME: CPD-22095|, commonly found in algae; and |FRAME: CPD-24178|, which is often found in marine invertebrates |CITS: [32144288]|., Molecular studies in the diatom |FRAME: TAX-2850| suggested the existence of a mixed plant and fungal pathway, but that proposal was questioned due to the fact that diatoms do not produce |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|, the typical fungal sterol |CITS: [24996048]|. The complete biosynthetic pathway of sterols in |FRAME: TAX-267567| and |FRAME: TAX-29204| was reported in a study that involved transcriptomics, labelling methods, and GC-MS profiling |CITS: [32144288]|., Like the pathways in in plants and algae, sterol biosynthesis starts in diatoms with |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL|, which is derived from mevalonate. The diatom cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, which is described here, is almost identical to the pathway characterized from the rhodophyte |FRAME: TAX-2769| (see |FRAME: PWY-8191|). The two pathways share the the beginning and the end portions. However, they differ in the section between |FRAME: 4-METHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL| and |FRAME: 5-ALPHA-CHOLESTA-724-DIEN-3-BETA-OL|, which in the diatom involves a |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL| intermediate and enzymes usually found in animals and fungi |CITS: [32144288]|., See |FRAME: PWY-8238| for biosynthesis of other strols in diatoms, and |FRAME: PWY-8240| for the combined biosynthesis of all sterols in diatoms.

Summary: General Background, Six pathways are now recognized in bacteria, most algae, fungi and higher plants for the biosynthesis of lysine. They are divided into two groups - the diaminopimelate (DAP) pathways, and the |FRAME:CPD-468| pathways., In the pathways that belong to the DAP group, lysine is produced from aspartate (along with methionine, threonine and isoleucine). All of the DAP group pathways share the upper segments, which include the four steps required for conversion of L-aspartate to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|. They also share the last step, which is the conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (D,L-DAP, or meso-DAP) to lysine., However, these pathways differ in the routes leading from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|. The four variations include:, (I) the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|), which involves succinylated intermediates. In this route |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is coverted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in four enzymatic steps., (II) the acetylase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2941|), which involves acetylated intermediates. This route also involves four enzymatic steps for the conversion of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|., (III) the dehydrogenase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2942|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in a single enzymatic step. , (IV) the diaminopimelate-aminotransferase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5097|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in two steps., In addition to lysine, all of the pathways in this group also produce |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is an important metabolite on its own (for example, as a constituent of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan)., The two other pathways belong to the |FRAME: CPD-468| group. They are found in organisms that have no requirement for |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, as it is not a component of their cell walls. These pathways also share the first segments, leading to the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-468| (α-aminoadipate)., However, in yeast and fungi, as well as |FRAME: TAX-3038|, the pathway continues with the key enzyme |FRAME: YBR115C-MONOMER|, leading to the intermediate |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see |FRAME: LYSINE-AMINOAD-PWY|), while in prokaryotes the pathway continues in a path similar to bacterial arginine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., Most of the bacteria that have been investigated in detail appear to utilize only one of these pathways |CITS: [1906065]|. A few exceptions include |FRAME: TAX-44252|, in which variants (II) and (III) seem to coexist |CITS: [BARTLETT85]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, in which variant (I) and (III) coexist |CITS: [1906065]|., Lysine is one of the 10 essential amino acids that mammals are unable to synthesize, and must therefore acquire in their diets., About This Pathway, The pathway of prokaryotic lysine biosynthesis via |FRAME: CPD-468| was discovered in the hyper-thermophilic Gram-negative eubacterium |FRAME: TAX-274|, and most of the research has been done with this organism |CITS:[10074061][10613839][9868782]|. Most of the genes involved in this pathway are present in a single cluster in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-274|. Similar genes have been discovered in the related eubacterium |FRAME: TAX-1299| |CITS: [12213936]|, and in several archaebacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-29292|, |FRAME: TAX-53953|, |FRAME: TAX-2287|, |FRAME: TAX-111955| and |FRAME: TAX-56636| |CITS: [15063502]|., In the first half of this pathway |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-468| by the same enzymatic reactions that occur in lower eukaryotes. However, the second half of the pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-468| to |FRAME: LYS|, is completely different. While in lower eukaryotes this conversion occurs through an adenylated derivative and saccharopine intermediates, in prokaryotes the corresponding conversion occurs in a manner similar to a portion of the arginine biosynthetic pathway and to a portion of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle |CITS: [10613839][12095615]|. The first step is the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-468| to a dedicated carrier protein, encoded by the lysW gene |CITS: [19620981]|. The compound is covalently linked to the γ-carboxyl group of the last C-terminal residue of LysW by a dedicated enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-5207| gene. The C-terminal part of LysW is acidic, and is easily recognized by the subsequent enzymes, all of which have a basic environment around their active sites. In this way all subsequent transformations leading to |FRAME: LYS| occur while the amino acid is attached to LysW, and the |FRAME: CPD-468| side chain is converted to a C-terminal lysyl side chain in the LysW-conjugated form. Eventually, a dedicated enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-5222| gene releases the mature amino acid |CITS: [19620981]|.

The |FRAME: PWY-6422| pathway was first characterized in |FRAME: TAX-287| by Jann et al |CITS: [3141581]|., The pathway was shown to utilize a |FRAME: MONOMER-11563|, which can only accept |FRAME:CPD-220| as substrate. The products of this enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-824| and |FRAME: AMMONIUM|, are converted to |FRAME:ARG| by the |FRAME: MONOMER-15372|, and L-arginine is catabolized via the |FRAME: AST-PWY| or |FRAME: PWY-5742| pathways., Thus, the combined action of the |FRAME: MONOMER-11563| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15372| provides a two-component arginine racemase, which enables the organism to catabolize |FRAME: CPD-220| via the |FRAME: ARG| catabolic pathways |CITS: [19139398]|., The two enzymes that participate in this pathway are encoded by genes that reside in a single operon |CITS: [19139398]|, and are induced by growth on |FRAME: CPD-220| and |FRAME: CPD-824|, but not on |FRAME: ARG| |CITS: [3141581]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: RETINOATE "All-trans retinoic acid"|, one of the forms of vitamin A, is a metabolite of |FRAME: CPD-13524| that mediates the functions of vitamin A required for growth and development, and is required in all chordate animals., During early embryonic development, retinoic acid generated in a specific region of the embryo helps determine position along the embryonic anterior/posterior axis by serving as an intercellular signaling molecule that guides development of the posterior portion of the embryo |CITS: [18805086]|. It acts through Hox genes, which ultimately control anterior/posterior patterning in early developmental stages |CITS: [17495912]|., In the adult, the normal growth and differentiation of the epidermis require an adequate supply of |FRAME: RETINOATE|, which is responsible for most of the activity of vitamin A, save visual pigment effects which require |FRAME: RETINAL| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6861|), and some cell metabolism effects that may require |FRAME: CPD-13524|., Retinoic acid controls the expression of retinoid-responsive genes via interactions of the retinoic acid/nuclear receptor complexes at specific DNA sequences in their control regions. , About This Pathway, The cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8347| (which also exists in a second form known as |FRAME: CPLX-8148|) generates |FRAME: RETINOATE| from |FRAME: CPD-13524| in human mammary epithelial cells. The substrate must be bound to |FRAME: Cellular-Retinol-Binding-Proteins|., Both forms of the protein can form retinoate, although via different mechanisms. The |FRAME: CPLX-8148| form can generate |FRAME: RETINOATE| directly, as shown here |CITS: [18569334]|. The |FRAME: CPLX-8347| form catalyzes two reactions - the oxidation of |FRAME: CRPB-all-trans-Retinol| to |FRAME: CRPB-all-trans-Retinal|, followed by oxidation of the latter to |FRAME: RETINOATE| |CITS: [11697048][17847715]|., This biological significance of this observation is not completely understood, but it may represent a cytosolic pathway for production of |FRAME: RETINOATE|. It has been reported that 6 to 20% of cellular retinal-generating capacity occurs in the cytosol |CITS: [21621639]|.

Summary: Plant phytoalexins such as |FRAME:CPD-3944|, |FRAME:CPD-4884|, |FRAME:CPD-3402| and |FRAME:CPD-3631| formed in response to pathogenic attacks |CITS:[8071365] [Dixon95]| can be rendered inactive by phytopathogenic fungi exhibiting enzyme activities involved in the dissimilation of fungicidal plant defense compounds |CITS:[20214490]|. The above mentioned pterocarpans are the major phytoalexins found in various legumes such as Medicago sativa (|FRAME:CPD-3402|, see |FRAME:PWY-2463|) |CITS:[Paiva94]|, Cicer arietinum (|FRAME:CPD-3631|, see |FRAME:PWY-2464|) |CITS:[Lucy88]|, Pisum sativum (|FRAME:CPD-3944|, see |FRAME:PWY-2467|) |CITS:[Banks82]| and Phaseollus vulgaris (|FRAME:CPD-4884|, see |FRAME:PWY-3042|) |CITS:[Dewick82]|. , Two major fungal phytopathogens, i.e. Nectria haematoccoca (anthromorph Fusarium solani) causing stem and root rot diseases in legumes and Didymella rabiei, the causal agent for chickpea blight in Cicer arietinum have been investigated focusing on the ability of the fungi to inactivate phytoalexins with antimicrobial activities. The latter is based on a set of fungal enzymes being able to convert phytoalexins to less fungitoxic compounds. In addition, fungi with the enzymatic capability to detoxify phytoalexins are often also more virulent |CITS:[Smith84]|. For example, the Nectria haematococca gene MAK1encoding a pterocarpan 1α-hydroxylase able to convert |FRAME:CPD-3402| and |FRAME:CPD-3631| into the less toxic 1α-hydroxy derivatives |FRAME:CPD-17458| and |FRAME:CPD-17457| |CITS:[8709942] [11485199]| is highly virulent, whereas related genes (MAK3 and 4) also detoxifying |FRAME:CPD-3402| and |FRAME:CPD-3631| are not |CITS:[16348672] [16348671] [Denny82]|. Similar results have been observed for |FRAME:CPD-3944| detoxification catalyzed by the pisatin demethylase encoded by PDAT9 |CITS:[3065148] [8208242] [9683653]| (highly virulent) or PDA6-1 |CITS:[8076822] [9683653]| (not virulent) in Nectria haematococca |CITS: [Ciufetti96] [Delserone99] [Kistler84] [Tegtmeier82]|. Also the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17459| from |FRAME:CPD-4884| by the respective phaseollin 1α-hydroxylase |CITS:[Kistler81]| has been proposed to be connected to virulence |CITS:[VanEtten75]|. , Interestingly, the pterocarpan 1α-hydroxylases described for the hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-3402| and |FRAME:CPD-3631| may belong to different protein families such as cytochrome P450 dependent enzymes identified in Nectria haematococca |CITS:[8709942] [11485199]| or the |FRAME:FAD|-dependent monooxygenase isolated from Didymella rabiei |CITS:[Tenhaken91]|. The latter organism also revealed a second route of phytoalexin inactivation, i.e. the reduction of |FRAME:CPD-3402| and |FRAME:CPD-3631| by a |FRAME:NADPH|-dependent oxidorecutase forming the corresponding 2'-hydroxyisoflavans, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17501| and |FRAME:CPD-17502| |CITS:[Hohl]|. The further oxidative conversion to |FRAME:CPD-17503| and |FRAME:CPD-17504| has been shown in experiments, however the catalyzing enzyme remains to be identified |CITS:[Hohl]|. In addition, phytoalexins formed in Phaseolus vulgaris such as |FRAME:CPD-4884| and |FRAME:CPD-4885| are detoxified in different ways, the former through hydroxylation at the 1α-position by a phaseollin hydroxylase generating the less toxic |FRAME:CPD-17459| |CITS:[Denheuvel74][Kistler81]| and the latter by hydration of the prenyl moiety of |FRAME:CPD-4885| catalyzed by the phaseollidin hydratase which not only detoxifies this particular phytoalexin but may also interfere with the host's general ability for phytoalexin biosynthesis through the product of the reaction |FRAME:PHASEOLLIDIN-HYDRATE| |CITS:[1521768]|.

Summary: D-Amino acids are synthesized by amino acid racemases. In bacteria D-serine is produced by the general-specificity |FRAME:EC-5.1.1.18 |. Eukaryotes have a serine-specific enzyme, |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.10|, |CITS: [19249065]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8140|)., Many bacterial species, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, are able to utilize |FRAME: D-SERINE| as the sole source of arbon and nitrogen for growth |CITS: [1090588]|. D-serine also has a bacteriostatic effect due to its effect on the biosynthesis of L-serine and pantothenate |CITS: [4574697]|. Detoxification of D-serine and its utilization as a carbon and nitrogen source are accomplished by a single enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.18| |CITS: [14216615]|. D-serine ammonia-lyase, which is induced by D-serine, catalyzes the deamination of D-serine to form pyruvate and ammonia |CITS: [13271312][14216615][14216616]|. Recently, it has been shown that the ability to utilize and/or detoxify D-serine plays a role in pathogenesis by certain pathogenic bacteria |CITS: [12823810][17088369][17785472][19674114]|., The vertebrate brain contains significant amounts of |FRAME: D-SERINE| which has a role in N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor function. In the mammalian brain |FRAME: D-SERINE|, produced from |FRAME: SER| by a bifunctional serine racemase/D-serine dehydratase, is mainly degraded by |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.3|. Plants, like mammals, have a bifunctional serine racemase/D-serine dehydratase |CITS: [16483618]|. , In the avian brain D-amino acid oxidase is not expressed and |FRAME: D-SERINE| is degraded by |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.18|. In other avian tissues both enzymes are present |CITS: [17254537][21676877]|. D-serine dehydratase has also been identified in yeast |CITS: [17937657]|.

Summary: Sulfoacetaldedhyde is a central intermediate of organosulfate degradation, including taurine, and, isoethionate |CITS: [12471498]|., The facultative bacterium, |FRAME: TAX-56119| oxidizes |FRAME: TAURINE| with nitrate as the terminal, electron acceptor. In the first step of the pathway, taurine is transaminated to, |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE|., Several studies suggested that sulfoacetaldehyde was desulfonated to |FRAME:SO3| and, |FRAME:ACET| by a sulfoacetaldehyde sulfo-lyase (Sly)(EC 4.4.1.12). However, Ruff et. al., |CITS: [12358600]| demonstrated that sulfoacetaldehyde was desulfonated to sulfite and, |FRAME:ACETYL-P| by |FRAME: CPLX-3062| (Xsc) in |FRAME: TAX-56119|., The desulfonation reaction catalyzed by Xsc, as well as the presence of an xsc gene, were also, confirmed in |FRAME: ORG-5995| and |FRAME: ORG-5898|., This evidence, along with additional experimental results, suggested that the desulfonation enzymes, purifed from |FRAME: ORG-5995| and |FRAME: ORG-5898|, which were formerly called Slys,, were actually Xsc enzymes as well., Acetylphosphate is converted to either acetyl CoA (by a |FRAME: MONOMER-3661|) or to acetate by an, acetate kinase., At least in |FRAME: ORG-5878|, sulfite is reduced to sulfide by a dissimilatory sulfite reductase, (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|) |CITS: [9990724][9143131]|., In addition, in |FRAME: ORG-5878| sulfite or thiosulfate serves as an electron acceptor for anaerobic, respiration with formate as the electron donor |CITS: [9143131]|.

In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of, polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl, diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme., Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the, polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a, preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone, molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length., However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain, length. For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|., Long chain menaquinones, such as |FRAME: CPD-9723|, |FRAME: CPD-9722| and |FRAME: CPD-9721|, are not common, but have been documented in several bacterial species, belonging to the, |FRAME: TAX-171552| and |FRAME: TAX-85023| families |CITS: [6102980][7462123][2223612]|.

Pyruvate is , transported into the mitochondrion where it is oxidatively decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex , to carbon dioxide and acetyl-CoA (as shown in the pathway link).  Acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle ., Biosynthetically, pyruvate is involved in gluconeogenesis (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY|) , and is also a precursor of the pyruvate family of amino acids:  alanine, valine, leucine and isoleucine., In plants and bacteria, it is also a precursor of isoprenoids (see MetaCyc pathway, |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|).  , Alanine aminotransferase is a commonly used diagnostic marker in humans.  It is produced mainly in the , liver and its presence in serum is an indicator of liver disease |CITS: [1992953]|.  The enzyme is present as , isozymes in both the cytosol and mitochondrion.  Expression of the isozymes varies among tissues and is , species-specific (in |CITS: [16495081]|).   , In bacteria, alanine is converted to pyruvate by oxidative deamination (|CITS: [Gottschalk1986]|) , (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY1-2|).  An alanine aminotransferase has been identified in the , archaeon |FRAME:TAX-2261| and is thought to function biosynthetically, transaminating pyruvate with , glutamate |CITS: [10762259]| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5096|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS Sphingolipids| are a class of lipids derived from the unsaturated aliphatic amino alcohol |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| that are essential components of the plasma membrane in all eukaryotic cells. Sphingolipids concentrate with sterols (|FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| in animals and |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| in yeast) to form lipid rafts, specialized membrane microdomains implicated in a variety of cellular processes, including sorting of membrane proteins and lipids, as well as organizing and regulating signaling cascades |CITS: [12452424]|., The sphingosine backbone of sphingolipids (often referred to as the |FRAME: Sphingoids "sphingoid base"|) is amide-linked to an acyl group, such as a fatty acid, and is often also O-linked to a head group. In yeast the head group is inositol, which in some cases is modified further by the addition of a mannose sugar and a second inositol., The sphingoid bases often consists of modified forms of sphingosine. When the double bond at position 4 is saturated, the compound is named |FRAME: CPD-13612|. In yeast the sphingoid base is a C4-hydroxylated sphinganine known as |FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE|, and the |FRAME: Ceramides ceramides| that it forms are known as |FRAME: Phytoceramides phytoceramides|., |FRAME: TAX-4932| cells make three complex sphingolipids: |FRAME: IPC "inositol-phosphoceramide"| (IPC), |FRAME: MIPC "mannose-inositol-phosphoceramide"| (MIPC), and |FRAME: MIP2C "mannosyl-diinositol-phosphorylceramide"| (M(IP)2C) |CITS:[12069845]|. For a review of their synthesis, see |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPID-SYN-PWY|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: YER019W| gene of |FRAME: TAX-4932| encodes an enzyme that catalyzes the removal of the head group from the three complex sphingolipids of yeast (|FRAME: IPC|, |FRAME: MIPC| and |FRAME: MIP2C|), leaving |FRAME: Alpha-hydroxyphytoceramides| |CITS: [ 9516416][11006294]|., The ceramides can be cleaved back into sphingoid bases and free (hydroxylated) fatty acids by the ceramidases |FRAME: YBR183W| and |FRAME: YPL087W| |CITS: [10900202][10702247]|. In mammals these enzymes (see |FRAME: CERAMIDASE-RXN "EC 3.5.1.23"|) are important since they are required to generate |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE|, the precursor for |FRAME: CPD3DJ-11366|, which is a very important signaling molecule |CITS: [16997623]| (see |FRAME: PWY3DJ-11470|). However, the role of the yeast enzymes is still not well understood., The two ceramidases differ in their specificity: |FRAME: YBR183W| preferentially hydrolyzes phytoceramides, whereas |FRAME: YPL087W| prefers dihydroceramides. Neither enzyme hydrolyzes unsaturated mammalian-type ceramides |CITS: [10900202]|., The |FRAME: YOR171C| and |FRAME: YLR260W| genes encode lipid kinases that catalyze the phosphorylation of the sphingoid long chain bases |FRAME: CPD-13612| and |FRAME: PHYTOSPINGOSINE| to form |FRAME: CPD-649| and |FRAME: PHTYOSPHINGOSINE-1-P|, respectively. The genes are not essential, and deletion of both genes causes no changes in vegetative growth |CITS: [9677363]|. However, these enzymes are essential for utilization of externally provided sphingoid bases, as it has been shown that externally provided sphingoid bases are always phosphorylated. Phosphorylated long chain bases have been implicated in stress responses |CITS: [12684378]| and their accumulation results in cell growth inhibition |CITS: [11102354]|. , The phosphorylated sphingoid bases have two potential fates - they can be dephosphorylated back to sphingoid bases (by phosphatases encoded by the |FRAME: YJL134W| and |FRAME: YKR053C| genes) and directed towards sphingolipid biosynthesis (see |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPID-SYN-PWY|), or they can be cleaved by the enzyme |FRAME: YDR294C-MONOMER| (|FRAME: YDR294C|) to produce |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| and |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes| |CITS: [9334171]|. This cleavage is the only reaction that is known to actually degrade sphingoid intermediates and remove them from the sphingoid compounds pool.

|FRAME: CPD-684| is a diterpene hydrocarbon that is synthesized in castor |FRAME: TAX-3988| plants, within the young seeds |CITS: [8954576]|. It has been observed that |FRAME: CPD-684| is biosynthesized as a response to fungal infection, particularly |FRAME: TAX-4846|. This fungus breaks down the plant cell wall and the fragments of oligogalactouronide are recognized as signal molecules |CITS: [16662367]|. General Background, Sterols are isoprenoid-derived molecules that have essential functions in eukaryotes. In vertebrates |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| is by far the major sterol, whereas a mixture of various sterols is present in higher plants, including |FRAME: CPD-4143| (usually predominant), |FRAME: CPD-4162|, |FRAME: CPD-707|, |FRAME: CPD-4127|, |FRAME: CPD-4161| and |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. Sterols are present in three forms: free sterols (the major form with a free 3β-hydroxyl), steryl esters, and steryl glucosides., Free sterols are integral components of the membrane lipid bilayer and thus interact with some molecular species of, phosphoglycero(sphingo) lipids. The extent of this interaction plays a functional role in the regulation of membrane fluidity and permeability. Sterols have also been shown to play important roles in embryonic development of vertebrates and the formation of membrane microdomains (rafts), which may constitute signaling centers for multiple pathways |CITS:[11278759]|., Finally, sterols are precursors of compounds with a high physiological activity such as brassinosteroids, an important class of plant hormones involved in growth and development |CITS: [8602526]|, ecdysteroids in invertebrates |CITS:[7791536]| and plants |CITS:[Coriot93]|, and antheridiol and oogoniols, sexual pheromones of aquatic fungi belonging to, the saprolegniale class |CITS:[1913877]|., About This Pathway, Diatoms possess sterols that are typical for both plants and animals |CITS: [Rampen09]|. For example, the bloom-forming species |FRAME: TAX-267567| and |FRAME: TAX-29204| synthesize |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and |FRAME: DESMOSTEROL-CPD|, which are typical for animals; |FRAME: CPD-8134| and |FRAME: CPD-706|, which are typical for plants; |FRAME: CPD-22095|, commonly found in algae; and |FRAME: CPD-24178|, which is often found in marine invertebrates |CITS: [32144288]|., Molecular studies in the diatom |FRAME: TAX-2850| suggested the existence of a mixed plant and fungal pathway, but that proposal was questioned due to the fact that diatoms do not produce |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|, the typical fungal sterol |CITS: [24996048]|. The complete biosynthetic pathway of sterols in |FRAME: TAX-267567| and |FRAME: TAX-29204| was reported in a study that involved transcriptomics, labelling methods, and GC-MS profiling |CITS: [32144288]|., Like the pathways in in plants and algae, sterol biosynthesis starts in diatoms with |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL|, which is derived from |FRAME: MEVALONATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-922|). A large part of the pathway described here is similar to the pathway found in plants (see |FRAME: PWY-2541|). Both pathways form |FRAME: CPD-8134| (also called Δ22-dihydrobrassicasterol) using the same enzymatic steps., A split point in both the plant pathway and the diatom pathway is |FRAME: CPD-4101|, which can be either oxygenated, leading to |FRAME: CPD-8134|, or methylated. In plants, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.143|, forms |FRAME: CPD-4124|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-4143| and |FRAME: CPD-4162|. However, the methylase in diatoms forms |FRAME: CPD-24186|, leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-22095| and |FRAME: CPD-24178|., See |FRAME: PWY-8239| for cholseterol biosynthesis in diatoms, and |FRAME: PWY-8240| for the combined biosynthesis of all sterols in diatoms.

Summary: |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| is one of the building blocks of DNA and is released when cells die and their DNA degrades. It is released from 2'-deoxyribonucleosides by the action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.M2| |CITS: [468819][2026165]|., A well-documented enzyme that can process |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| is |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.229| (|FRAME: G-63084|) |CITS: [13563487]|. This 3-oxo acid is then cleaved by a β-keto acid cleavage enzyme into |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE| and |FRAME: CPD-22292|., The former product is converted to acetyl-CoA, while the latter is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCERATE| and phosphorylated to |FRAME: 2-PG|, both of which are intermediates of central metabolism |CITS: [30746495]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13053 Queuosine| is a modified nucleoside that is present in certain tRNAs in bacteria and most eukaryotes (but not in yeast) |CITS: [ 12697167]|. Queuosine, which is |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines|, occupies the first anticodon position of tRNAs for |FRAME: HIS|, |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: ASN| and |FRAME: TYR| |CITS: [ 4550561]|. This anticodon position pairs with the third "wobble" position in codons, and queuosine improves accuracy of translation |CITS: [ 2988936][11532950]|. The base in queuosine is called |FRAME: QUEUINE|., Eukaryotes are not able to synthesize |FRAME: QUEUINE|. They receive it in their diet, and incorporate it directly in tRNA using the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.64| as shown here., Most bacteria perform de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13053| [see |FRAME: PWY-6700|]. However, the process is costly, as it starts from GTP and requires many cofactors. Thus salvage pathways exist for recycling |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, |FRAME: QUEUINE|, or |FRAME: CPD-13053|. Recycling pathways are found both in organisms that can synthesize |FRAME: CPD-13053| de novo and in organisms that can't., About This Pathway, Phylogenomic analyses suggested that an eukaryotic-type salvage pathway (direct incorporation of |FRAME: QUEUINE|) must exist in bacteria such as Chlamydia, Wolbachia, Corynebacterium, Actinomyces, and Bifidobacterium species, as they possess a TGT encoding gene and sometimes predicted |FRAME: CPD-13053| precursor transporters, but lack all of the other genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-13053| biosynthetic enzymes |CITS: [28208705]|. Summary: |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation |CITS: [8490246]|. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces., Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| |CITS: [25969757]|., The core structure that defines the |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs "gala series"| is Galα(1,4)Galβ-Cer. The most common gala-series glycosphingolipids in humans are |FRAME: A-GALACTOSYLCERAMIDE "β-D-galactosyl-N-acylsphingosine"| (GalCer) and |FRAME: Monogalactosylceramide-Sulfate "galactosylceramide sulfate"| (sulfatide), which are found in oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, kidney, testis, and intestine. They are also present in high concentrations in the multilamellar layers of myelin, where they are required for glial adhesion |CITS: [19815855]| via interaction between the carbohydrate head groups of sulfatide and GalCer on different myelin layers |CITS: [19941861]|., Like other myelin lipids, the ceramides of gala-series glycosphingolipids are enriched in 2-hydroxy-fatty acids, which may contribute to carbohydrate-carbohydrate interactions between them |CITS: [8399212]|., Another gala-series glycosphingolipid, |FRAME: Digalactosylceramides digalactosylceramide|, was documented in kidney |CITS: [5443698][3818564][3782312]|, meconium |CITS: [6782103]|, and muscle |CITS: [7057112]|. It was shown to be the receptor for staphylococcal enterotoxin-B |CITS:[7655170][9056214][17895522][23180309]|., A uniquer member of the gala-series glycosphingolipids is |FRAME: Ganglioside-GM4 "ganglioside GM4"|. Most gangliosides are biosynthetically derived from |FRAME: Glucosyl-acyl-sphingosines β-D-glucosyl-N-acylsphingosine"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7836|), and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GM4 "ganglioside GM4"| is the only human ganglioside that is derived from GalCer., Ganglioside GM4 has been discovered as a minor component of human brain gangliosides |CITS: [14175998]|, where it is, localized within myelin |CITS: [4754859]|. It also occurs in additional tissues, such as erythrocytes, kidney, and in the intestine, and is abundant in some fish species. Currently Little is known about its function., The first step in the pathway, ceramide galactosylation, occurs at the ER membrane by a type I transmembrane protein with a catalytic domain facing the luminal side of the ER |CITS: [9748263]|. The other steps (formation of |FRAME: Monogalactosylceramide-Sulfate sulfatide|, |FRAME: Digalactosylceramides digalactosylceramide|, and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GM4 "ganglioside GM4"|) take place in the lumen of the Golgi apparatus |CITS: [8601603]|.

Summary: General Background, In cassava, rapid post-harvest physiological deterioration (PPD) causes significant losses for farmers each year. Cassava is an important staple food crop in developing countries and serves as the second highest source of calories in sub-Saharan Africa. Unfortunately, around a quarter of the annual cassava crop can be lost due to PPD in Africa |CITS: [21526968]|. Therefore, efforts are underway to characterize the biochemical pathways that contribute to PPD. The formation of scopolin,scopoletin, esculin, and esculetin begins in cassava plants shortly after they are cut and there is strong evidence that scopoletin contributes to the deterioration of cassava tubers |CITS: [WHEATLY85] [HUANG01]|., |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN Scopoletin| (7-hydroxy-6-methoxy coumarin) is a hydroxycoumarin. It is found in a number of plant species including Arabidopsis, cassava, sweet potato, sunflower, cotton and tobacco |CITS: [19004461], [18547395]|. Scopoletin is thought to be involved in plant defense responses. In tobacco, accumulation of scopoletin was shown to strongly correlate with tobacco mosaic virus-induced localized acquired resistance |CITS: [12060240]|. Scopoletin appears to have many pharmacological effects as well, such as antidepressant |CITS: [20599906]|, anti-arthritic |CITS: [21078410]|,and anti-gastro-esophageal inflammatory |CITS: [21163341]|. It may also help to ameliorate insulin resistance |CITS: [20886413]| treat of hypertriglyceridemia |CITS: [17786283]|. In addition, it was also shown to have antitermite activity |CITS: [20563628]|., About This Pathway, Despite the importance of this pathway for plant and human health, many details on the reactions and enzymes involved in scopolin and scopoletin biosynythesis remain unclear, and may differ between different species. The first reaction, presumably catalyzed by a phenylalanine ammonia lyase in cassava, is likely found in all species. However, the downstream reactions including hydroxylations, isomerizations, etc., are generally less-well characterized and likely less conserved. For instance, genetic and biochemical evidence in Arabidopsis support the conclusion that in this species scopoletin is derived from feruloyl-CoA, not ferulate |CITS: [18547395]|, as shown in the |FRAME: PWY-6792| parthway. However, experiments carried out using isotopically labeled substrates did not reveal a CoA dependence for scopolin biosynthesis in cassava as depicted in this pathway |CITS: [19004461]|., At least three different biosynthetic routes for scopolin have been suggested |CITS: [19004461]| however, isotopic feeding experiments reveal that the dominant pathway for scopolin biosynthesis proceeds through |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|. In contrast, esculetin and esculin are primarily made via 2'4'-dihydroxycinnamate. Only a small amount of esculetin is methylated to form scopoletin in |FRAME: TAX-3983| |CITS: [19004461]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathway derives in part from the central metabolic precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from oxaloacetate, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, This superpathway illustrates the universal do novo biosynthetic route for producing pyrimidine ribonucleotides (|FRAME: CDP| and |FRAME: UDP|), and the most common route in which these ribonucleotides are converted to the deoxyribonucleotides, including the DNA-specific thymine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate |FRAME: TTP|. This pathway is universal, and is found in archaea, bacteria, fungi, plants and animals., Deoxyribonucleotides are synthesized by reduction of ribonucleotides at the C2' position, which in this pathway is catalyzed by the rate-limiting enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "EC 1.17.4.1, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|. Since this enzyme, which plays a central role in DNA replication and repair, can only perform the reduction of nucleoside-diphosphates, the conversion of the product of de novo biosynthesis, |FRAME: UMP|, to a deoxyuridine form requires phosphorylation to |FRAME: UDP| followed by reduction to |FRAME: DUDP|. Likewise, reduction of the first cytidine-nucleotide that is formed de novo, |FRAME: CTP|, to a deoxycytidine form requires dephosphorylation to |FRAME: CDP| followed by reduction to |FRAME: DCDP|., Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase"| (EC 2.1.1.45)., The enzyme only accepts the mono-phosphorylated form |FRAME: DUMP|. Thus, the first deoxyuridine nucleotide that is formed, |FRAME: DUDP|, needs to be converted to the monophosphate form. This is done in two steps - phosphorylation to |FRAME: DUTP|, followed by the removal of a diphosphate group, resulting in |FRAME: DUMP|., Once |FRAME: TMP| is formed, two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: HS11626-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: CPLX66-1052|., In organisms that contain the enzyme |FRAME: DCTP-DEAM-CPLX| (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.13 EC 3.5.4.13"|), a second route forms |FRAME: DUMP| from |FRAME: DCDP|. |FRAME: DCDP| is phosphorylated to |FRAME: DCTP|, followed by deamination to |FRAME: DUTP| and hydrolysis to |FRAME: DUMP| (see |FRAME: PWY-7187|).

|FRAME:CPD-8097 Esculetin| and its glucosidic derivatives such as |FRAME:CPD-14429| amd |FRAME:CPD-14461| have been first isolated from inflorescences of |FRAME:TAX-13427| and Solanum pinnatisectum. The co-occurrence of all three metabolites in such different plant families (Asteracea, Solanaceae) was considered of biogenetic importance indicating that esculetin is a common precursor for further glucosidic metabolization and that the enzymes involved are not restricted to certain plant families |CITS:[14399695]|. , The biosynthesis of esculetin and related coumarins such as daphnetin and scopoletin had been the focus of research for some time. The first proposed pathway to esculetin as depicted in |FRAME:PWY-5349| does not occur in planta despite the fact that caffeic acid was readily converted into esculetin by plant phenoloxidases in crude extracts |CITS:[Sato67]|. Instead, the biosynthetic route proceeds via p-coumaric acid |CITS:[Sato72]|, |CITS:[Brown86]|, |CITS:[Brown86a]| and umbelliferone |CITS:[Bourgaud06]| |CITS:[19035613]| as has been shown through tracer feeding experiments in various plants (see |FRAME:PWY-6982|). , Similarly to the |FRAME:MONOMER-17430| in the |FRAME:PWY-7056| pathway the |FRAME:TAX-13426| transglucosylase exhibits dual activities (hydrolase and transglucosylase) catalyzing the formation of esculin via esculetin from cichoriin. However, in contrast to the only enzyme found in |FRAME: TAX-329675|, there are two enzymes with transglucosylase characteristics present in |FRAME:TAX-13427| |CITS:[Sato72a]|. Whether those enzymes represent isozymes with different hydrolase/transglucosylase (HD/TG) ratios or are of the same enzyme undergoing conformational and functional changes has not been established and remains to be investigated. In agreement with the high substrate specificity of the β-glucosidase activity of the transglucosylase found in |FRAME: TAX-329675| the |FRAME:TAX-13427| transglucosylase expressed an even higher hydrolytic specificity for coumarins. , The back reaction from esculetin forming cichoriin is carried out by UDPG dependent 7-O-glucosyltransferases which are multi-substrate enzyms but biotransform esculetin with the highest turn-over rate |CITS:[Ibrahim80]| |CITS:[10940474]|.

Studies in the 1950s have shown that |FRAME: GAPOXNPHOSPHN-RXN "glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase"| slowly catalyzes the formation of a hydrated form of NADH, called |FRAME: NADHX|, from NADH |CITS: [Rafter54]|. The equilibrium of this hydration reaction is in favor (100/1) of the hydrated form |CITS: [3061454]|, making the reaction virtually irreversible. In addition, NADHX can be formed spontaneously from NADH under slightly acidic conditions., NADHX and NADPHX are inhibitors of several dehydrogenases |CITS: [ 9851831]| and it is thus important to eliminate them. This is achieved by the enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000153481-MONOMER| which has been originally described from yeast |CITS: [Meinhart56]|. Upon identification of the yeast enzyme it was found that homologs are found in the overwhelming majority of eukaryotes and prokaryotes. The human and yeast enzymes also accept (S)-NADPHX, with higher maximal activity |CITS: [21994945]|., Since both |FRAME: CPD0-2472| and |FRAME: CPD-653| are formed, but |FRAME: ENSG00000153481-MONOMER| can only accept the S-form, the R form needs to be epimerized to the S-form before it can converted back to NADH. This is achieved by the enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000163382-MONOMER| |CITS: [21994945]|. , The two enzymes are encoded by two different genes in yeast and humans. Many prokaryotes possess an ADP-dependent bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both reactions |CITS: [21994945]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6938-1|).
