Summary: |FRAME:CPD-18421 Deoxynivalenol| is a type B trichothecene produced in certain strains of Fusarium graminearum (telemorph Gibberella zeae) which represent an specific chemotype inside the species. In general, trichothecene are sequiterpenoids characterized by a varying pattern of oxygen and ester groups on a core tricyclic skeleton bearing an epoxide function which is commonly referred to as 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene (EPT) structure |CITS:[Grove07]|. More than 200 trichothecene have been identified from various genera of fungi and classified into four groups (type A to D) according to the substitution pattern on the basic EPT core |CITS:[Ueno80] [Betina89] [Alexander09] [22069741]|. Trichothecene are considered mycotoxins which are phytotoxic |CITS:[22295175]|, contaminate food and animal feed, have been reported to cause vomiting, skin dermatitis, and hemorrhagic lesions |CITS:[3158480] [8246841]| and interfere with complex developmental processes |CITS:[23667578]|. The toxicity of |FRAME:CPD-18421| (also referred to as vomitoxin) |CITS:[8637056]| is well documented and numerous studies are carried out to elucidate the multifaceted effects of trichothecenes to counteract the significant losses caused by Fusarium pathogens worldwide |CITS:[18791024] [19385728] [5816375] [15762554] [25680507]|. The contribution of trichothecenes to virulence of Fusarium graminearum has also been investigated with due regard and obtained data support the involvement of trichothecene as shown in Δtri5 mutants and complementation experiments |CITS:[Proctor02] [9274012] [10931910]|. Interesting is also the note that efforts have been made to convert |FRAME:CPD-18421| to |FRAME:CPD-18419| as an fuel ethanol co-product in yeast by expressing Fusarium trichothecene 3-O-acetyltransferase |CITS:[21888629]|., As mentioned above Fusarium species can be grouped into certain chemotypes. The two main chemotypes are associated with species which either produce |FRAME:CPD-18421| or |FRAME:CPD-18427| |CITS:[Miller91]|, the former being further divided into an |FRAME:CPD-18419| (3-ADON) and an |FRAME:CPD-18420| (15-ADON) chemotype |CITS:[21216300]|. It has been demonstrated that the genetic difference between |FRAME:CPD-18421| and |FRAME:CPD-18427| chemotypes lies in the functionality of two genes, i.e. TRI13 coding for a trichothecene 4-hydroxylase and TRI7 encoding for a trichothecene 4-acetyltransferase. Both genes are present but nonfunctional in |FRAME:CPD-18421|-producing Fusarium chemotypes |CITS:[11352533] [11976083]|. In this respect it is alarming to see reports about an evolutionary shift of chemotypes which drives the spread of more toxigenic Fusarium graminearum in the US and worldwide with severe consequences for food safety and production |CITS:[20205536] [18035565] [19843228] [17451976] [Waalwijk03]|., The proteins catalyzing the biosynthesis of the various trichothecene are organized in biosynthetic cluster (TRI) |CITS:[14998528] [12650935]| where most of the genes appear to be coordinately expressed and regulated |CITS:[12080147]|. The pathway leading to |FRAME:CPD-18421| continues from the core pathway, i.e. |FRAME:PWY-7711| at |FRAME:CPD-18411| which is also a branch point for the |FRAME:PWY-7730|. The cytochrome P450 dependent trichothecene 7,8-dihydroxylase (TRI1) has been demonstrated to catalyze the first step into the |FRAME:PWY-7712|. The hydroxylation of both C-7 and C-8 of |FRAME:CPD-18411| results in the generation of |FRAME:CPD-18417| |CITS:[15066795 ] [16604118]|. The following transformation to |FRAME:CPD-18418| which bears the carbonyl at C-8, signifying the compound as a type B trichothecene, remains to be shown. The following deacylation of |FRAME:CPD-18418| then defines the two sub-chemotypes inside the |FRAME:CPD-18421|-producing chemotyp, i.e. 3-ADON (|FRAME:CPD-18419|) or 15-ADON (|FRAME:CPD-18420|). Fusarium graminearum strain Z3639 belongs to the |FRAME:CPD-18420|-producing chemotype, i.e. the TRI8 encoded trichothecene esterase deacylates at the C-3 position hence producing |FRAME:CPD-18420| |CITS:[12039755] [21216300]|. On the other side, Fusarium graminearum strain 70E1 belongs to the |FRAME:CPD-18419|-producing chemotype, i.e. removing the acyl group from the C-15 position. Accordingly the TRI8 encoded protein produces |FRAME:CPD-18419| acting as trichothecene C-15 esterase |CITS: [21216300]|. Chimeric constructs of Tri8's from |FRAME:CPD-18420|-producing and |FRAME:CPD-18419|-producing Fusarium strains revealed that a sequence variation between amino acid residues 216-312 is responsible for the trichothecene esterase activity to be either express trichothecene C-3 esterase activity or trichothecene C-15 esterase activity |CITS:[21216300]|. The protein(s) catalyzing the remaining deacylation of either C-3 (|FRAME:CPD-18419|) or C-15 (|FRAME:CPD-18420|) to form |FRAME:CPD-18421| remain to be elucidated.

General Background, This pathway represents the oxidative degradation of flavonols such as |FRAME: RUTIN| (a glycoside) and |FRAME: CPD-520| by fungi. Flavonols are secondary metabolites found in abundance in plant tissues and exudates. This pathway for |FRAME: RUTIN| degradation (commonly named the rutin catabolic pathway) was first studied in fungi over fifty years ago |CITS: [13844170][13852047]| and the entire pathway was enzymologically characterized in the mold |FRAME: TAX-5059| |CITS: [13844170][13784623 ][13905544][13784624][CHILD63]|. More recent research in this area has focused on the enzyme quercetin 2,3-dioxygenase (quercetinase) (|CITS: [11839311][18206655]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20419500]|)., This pathway has been strictly proven only in molds (filamentous fungi). Various molds, including those from the genera |FRAME: TAX-5052| and |FRAME: TAX-5073| can use |FRAME: RUTIN| as a sole source of carbon and energy via this pathway. In molds all three enzymes have been characterized and their enzymatic activities are found extracellularly. The pathway is also probable in yeast-like fungi and yeasts based on metabolite detection studies, although the enzymatic activities were shown to be intracellular (|CITS: [13852047][5950962]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20419500]|)., In bacteria, this pathway is less likely. Bacterial homologs of quercetinase have been characterized, such as the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-375060| |CITS: [18950192][18681865][17516049]| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [14741339][15039076][15628860][16411777]|. A pirin protein homolog yhhW in |FRAME:TAX-562| was shown to possess quercetinase activity |CITS: [15951572]| (see |FRAME: G7756-MONOMER|). However, the bacterial quercetinases may function in detoxification rather than catabolism, and the remaining two enzymes of the pathway have not been reported in prokaryotes (reviewed in |CITS: [20419500][16562863]|)., About This Pathway, In the first step of this pathway a glycosidase hydrolyzes the disaccharide |FRAME: CPD-12733| from the glycosylated flavonol |FRAME: RUTIN|, producing the flavonol aglycone |FRAME: CPD-520| and |FRAME: CPD-12733|. Because the second enzyme quercetinase cannot utilize 3-glycosylated flavonols, a glycosidase capable of deglycosylating a glycosylated flavonol is necessary. A glycosidase (rutinase) from |FRAME: TAX-5059| has been characterized |CITS: [13905544]| and a β-rutinosidase from |FRAME: TAX-121627| has also been characterized |CITS: [10923813]|. Both glycosidases were produced extracellularly. Other known extracellular glycosidases that could also potentially participate in this pathway, but have not been proven to participate, include β-glucosidase, α-L-rhamnosidase, and quercitrinase (EC 3.2.1.66) (reviewed in |CITS: [20419500]|)., The second enzyme in the rutin catabolic pathway is quercetin 2,3-dioxygenase (quercetinase) which catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-520| to a depside (|FRAME: 2-PROTOCATECHUOYLPHLOROGLUCINOLCARBOXYLA|) and |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| (see |CITS: [5003249]| for a definition of depside). This enzyme has been relatively well studied (reviewed in |CITS: [20419500]|). Summary: General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various, insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are, believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness, of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans, was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose, |CITS: [12065209]|. , In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits, of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosil α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus, nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, , including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein). , In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity,, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation and no internal hydrogen bond formation. , The combinatrion of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms trehalose can be used as external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute, (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a, structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|., In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as, a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|., The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood, |CITS: [11081789]|., About This Pathway, Several organisms are capable of synthesizing trehalose directly from maltose, independently of the presence of, the phosphate compounds trehalose-6-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate. In some of these organisms, this is the only trehalose biosynthesis pathway, while in others (such as mycobacteria and |FRAME: TAX-1718|), several trehalose biosynthesis pathways coexist |CITS: [12890033][10658666]|., In this reaction, trehalose is formed by intramolecular rearrangement of the α-1,4 bond of maltose to the, α-1-1 bond of trehalose |CITS: [12791289]|. Some of the enzymes produce glucose and/or , α,β-trehalose as a by-product, while others, such as the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-316| CJ38, produce, trehalose alone |CITS: [15654636]|., It was postulated that in |FRAME: TAX-1718| this pathway may work in the opposite direction, compensating for the, absence of a trehalase enzyme, by dconverting excess trehalose into maltose, making it available as a carbon, source |CITS: [12890033]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is an essential trace element for many (but not all) organisms. For example mammals require selenium, but some protists, such as |FRAME:TAX-5691|, do not |CITS: [19279205]|. The green alga |FRAME: TAX-3055| contains selenoproteins, but land plants and yeast do not |CITS: [12110581]|. The best studied biological form of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is the amino acid |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| (sec). Examples for selenoproteins include |FRAME: EC-1.12.98.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.12.98.3|, |FRAME: EC-1.12.2.1| and |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.12|. For more selenoproteins see MetaCyc pages for |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| and |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE|, which contain links to enzymes for which |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is functionally important. |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is also present in selenonucleosides that have been identified in bacterial tRNAs (reviewed in |CITS: [19344749]|)., In |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| the thiol group of |FRAME: CYS| is replaced by a selenol group. |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| is considered to be the 21st genetically encoded amino acid because it is co-translationally inserted into nacent polypeptide chains at an in-frame UGA nonsnense codon in the mRNA. This is done by a decoding mechanism that involves a selenocysteine insertion sequence (SECIS) element in the mRNA and coordinated interactions between RNA-protein complexes. A model for the role of these cytoplasmic and nuclear supramolecular complex interactions in |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| biosynthesis has been proposed |CITS: [16508009]|. The function of |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| in proteins remains to be completely defined, although its occurrence in the active site of some redox-active enzymes suggests a role in their catalytic mechanism. There are two known pathways for selenocysteine biosynthesis. One is found in bacteria (see pathway |FRAME: PWY0-901|) and the other is found in archaea and eukaryotes (this pathway), which has interesting phylogenetic implications (reviewed in |CITS: [19344749]|)., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| is an essential constituent of 3 proteins: |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGN-CPLX|, |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGO-CPLX|, and |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGH-MONOMER|; each of them contains one selenocysteine residue |CITS: [2941757]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| is unique among amino acid biosyntheses because its defining step occurs while attached to a tRNA molecule. The tRNA molecule, tRNA,sec, serves only to insert |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| into these proteins |CITS: [1702199]|., tRNAsec has an anticodon that recognizes the stop codon UGA; it also has properties that allow it to be charged with |FRAME: SER| by serS-encoded seryl-tRNA synthetase. But it cannot insert serine at an UGA codon. Only after it has been converted to selenocysteinyl-tRNAsec by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.9.1.1| can it recognize certain UGAs as sense codons and insert selenocysteine there |CITS: [1474891]|. Recognition of UGA as a sense codon and insertion of selenocysteine depends on adjacent sequences in mRNA termed SECIS (selenocysteine insertion sequence) and a special elongation factor termed SELB, the product of the |FRAME: EG10942| gene, which acts in place of EF-Tu in this special case |CITS: [1396569][8483932]|., |FRAME: SEPO3 Selenophosphate| donates the selenium to seryl-tRNAsec thereby converting it to selenocysteinyl-tRNAsec. The physiological source of its selenium, shown here as |FRAME: SE-2|, is not known for certain. |FRAME: SE-2 Selenide| is synthesized, via |FRAME: SELENITE|, from |FRAME: SELENATE| by the same enzymes that reduce sulfate, via sulfite, to sulfide |CITS: [8811175]|.

Summary: General Background, Protein glycosylation is an important process found in all kingdoms of life. N-glycosylation is found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria. During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. In eukaryotes, the nascent proteins that are synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane where they acquire the initial carbohydrate chains on specific asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes can be divided into the following three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (this pathway)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7426|)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and use somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathway is in general similar to the eukaryotic one, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7658|)., About This Pathway, Processing of the N-linked oligosaccharides begins immediately following the transfer of the tetradecasaccharide from its dolichol-bound form to nascent proteins. The first step in the processing is the removal of the terminal α-1,2-linked glucose, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.106| (α-glucosidase I) |CITS: [9363442][11971867]|. , This is followed by the removal of the two α-1,3-linked glucose residues, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.207| (α-glucosidase II) |CITS: [8910335][16373354]|. It has been shown that trimming of the glucose residues is identical in |FRAME: TAX-4932| and in mammalian cells. The removal of glucosyl residues is concomitant with completion of both glycosylation and folding of the target protein |CITS: [7881169]|. Furthermore, it has been shown that incompletely folded proteins must present a single glucose moiety to be recognized by the folding chaperone calnexin |CITS: [8302866][7915231][7736594][7592804]|. Thus, by removing the first α-1,3-linked glucose residue, glucosidase II allows nascent polypeptides to interact with calnexin, and by removing the innermost glucose residue, it regulates the dissociation of folded proteins from calnexin and allows their exit from the ER., Following the removal of the three glucosyl residues, α-mannosidases remove some or all of the α-1,2-linked mannose residues. In |FRAME: TAX-4932| only one specific α-mannosidase has been found. The enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: YJR131W| gene, primarily trims a single α-1,2-linked mannose residue from Man9GlcNAc2 to produce Man8GlcNAc2 |CITS: [12090241]|. In mammalian cells more enzymes exist. |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.209| (|FRAME: HS11144|), which is located in the ER, removes only one mannose residue. Three other mannosidases (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.113|, |FRAME: HS03480|, |FRAME: HS05846|, and |FRAME: HS04162|), which are located in the Golgi, remove all four mannosyl residues. The enzymes, which are expressed in different tissues, remove the residues in different orders, forming different intermediates, but end up producing the same Man5GlcNAc2 heptasaccharide |CITS: [8054711][9878780][10915796]|., |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.130| (|FRAME: HS16090|) provides an alternative route by removing a disaccharide, rather than a single nucleotide |CITS: [3818665]|., Following the removal of glucose and mannose residues, Golgi glycosyltransferases add different sugars in a species- and cell-specific manner, leading to production of complex glycans. One such route is described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7426|., It should be mentioned that misfolded glycoproteins are handled in the ER mostly by the cytoplasmic |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.52|, resulting in free N-glycans. A cytosol/vacuole α-mannosidase, (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.24 "EC 3.2.1.24"|) then trims these free glycans, eventually forming the trisaccharide |FRAME: CPD-20274|, which at least in yeast is not catabolized any further |CITS: [26264652]|.

General Background, Chlorotoluenes are important intermediates in many chemical processes, and are still produced in large amounts., Due to their chemical stability and recalcitrance to degradation they tend to accumulate in the environment., Only a few bacterial strains that can mineralize chlorinated toluenes are known, and only a few of those can degrade, dichlorotoluenes. One of these organisms is |FRAME: TAX-393999|, a strain that is known to mineralize a broad spectrum, of chloro-substituted benzenes, as well as |FRAME: CPD-10654|, |FRAME: CPD-7697|, |FRAME: CPD-10836|,, |FRAME: CPD-10837| and |FRAME: CPD-10838| |CITS: [16348484]|. , The key to the metabolic versatility of |FRAME: TAX-393999| is the presence of two enzymes - a broad-substrate-spectrum, |FRAME: CPLX-7696|, known as TecA, and a similarly broad spectrum |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, known as TecB., Together these two enzymes catalyze the initial steps in the metabolism of all of these compounds, converting, them to modified catechols. The modified catechols are then processed by modified ortho-cleavage pathways, that utilize enzymes specilized in the degradation of chloro-substituted aromatic compounds., About This Pathway, The degradation of the different chlorinated toluenes by |FRAME: TAX-393999| utilizes the same enzymes,, although the pathways follow different routes |CITS: [12218011]|., |FRAME: CPD-10836| is initially activated by dioxygenation, catalyzed by the broad spectrum |FRAME: CPLX-7696|,, followed by rearomatization catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-10854|., Ring opening of the catechol proceeds via a modified ortho cleavage pathway, employing |FRAME: CPLX-7713|., The product of this reaction, |FRAME: CPD-10852|, is subject to both 1,4- and 3,6-cycloisomerization by, |FRAME: CPLX-7712|, and thus is degraded via a branched metabolic route., The product of the 3,6 cycloisomerization, |FRAME: CPD-10847|, as well as the product of the 1,4 cycloisomerization,, |FRAME: CPD-10849| (generated in two steps - a lactonization to |FRAME: CPD-10850|, followed by dehalogenation),, are hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-10844| and |FRAME: CPD-10845|, respectively, by |FRAME: MONOMER-14658|., The intermediates of the proposed pathway were isolated and identified by HPLC and NMR analyses. In addition,, the individual enzymes were completely or partially purified, and their activities confirmed |CITS: [12218011]|., The end products of this pathway are assumed to be further degraded to TCA cycle intermediates by a modified, |FRAME: PWY-2361| pathway that has not been characterized in this organism |CITS: [12218011]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| (phytate, phytic acid) is one of the most prevalent forms of phosphorylated inositols in the eukaryotic cell, with a total concentration of 15-100 μM |CITS:[3426614][1684044][8435066]|. It's cellular distribution is not completely known - some of it is soluble, some is "wall-papered" around membranes, while some is bound to proteins |CITS: [9838040]|. In plant seeds, large amount of phytate are complexed with cations and deposited as globular inclusions in membrane-bound storage bodies |CITS: [15700415]|., The compound has been proposed to have a number of signaling roles, including regulation of insulin exocytosis |CITS: [9114007]|, regulation of nuclear mRNA export |CITS:[10390371][10683435]|, binding of the clathrin assembly proteins AP2 and AP3 |CITS: [1849645][1371119]|, inhibition of clathrin cage assembly |CITS: [7814377][7829485]|, and inhibition of serine and threonine protein phosphatases that are thought to regulate L-type Ca2+ channels |CITS: [9334307]|., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge about |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| biosynthesis concerns lipid-dependent pathways, where the inositol phosphate precursor originates from a phospholipid, as described in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6361| and |FRAME: PWY-6362|. However, information exists that suggests that certain organisms synthesize this compound from |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| or |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| that do not originate from phospholipids., To date such pathways have only been studied in two organisms - the aquatic monocotyledonous plant |FRAME: TAX-29656| |CITS:[8660287]| (see |FRAME: PWY-4661|), and the slime mold |FRAME:TAX-44689| (described here) |CITS: [2198472]|. It should be noted that the metabolism of inositol phosphates in Dictyostelium is very complex, and several other pathways operate in parallel to this one |CITS: [9247119]|., The sequence of conversions from |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| to |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| in |FRAME:TAX-44689| has been illucidated mostly by the use of radiolabeled compounds. No enzymes have been well characterized from this organism, although two enzymes have been partially purified - a |FRAME: MONOMER-15196| that catalyzes the phosphorylation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| to |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P|, and an |FRAME: MONOMER-15197| that catalyzes the phosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-505| to |FRAME: CPD-1107|., The studies clearly implicated |FRAME: CPD-11930| and |FRAME: CPD-6681| as intermediates in the pathway., Characterization of the five-phosphorylated compound was more diffucult, as three such compounds were identified. However, in whole cells incubated with labeled |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, the radioactivity of |FRAME: CPD-1107| was much higher than that of the other two compounds. In addition, the two other compounds, but not |FRAME: CPD-1107|, could be formed by dephosphorylation of |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE|. The authors thus concluded that |FRAME: CPD-1107| is the most likely intermediate |CITS: [2198472]|.

Summary: General Background, The proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: GLY| can biosynthesized via several different pathways. The main pathway in most organisms is the production of glycine from |FRAME:SER| via |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|. Eukaryotic organisms have both a cytosolic enzyme (SHMT2) and a mitochondrial enzyme (SHMT1) (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-PWY|). The two isoforms were reported to work in opposite directions depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [9398220]|., A less well described glycine production pathway is acheived by the operation of the |FRAME: CPLX-7302| in reverse (see |FRAME: GLYCINE-SYN2-PWY|)., In a third pathway glycine is formed from |FRAME: GLYOX|, a product of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-ALA-PWY|)., And finally, glycine can also be formed from |FRAME:THR| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.48| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-THR-PWY|)., About This Pathway, In eukaryotes glycine can be biosynthesized by the reverse reactions of the mitochondrial |FRAME: CPLX-7302| (for glycine cleavage pathway detail see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GLYCLEAV-PWY|). Glycine biosynthesis by reversal of the glycine cleavage complex reactions has been demonstrated in vivo in the yeast |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS: [11298766] [1390656]| and in vitro in |FRAME:TAX-9031| (chicken) |CITS: [4648867]| and |FRAME:TAX-10116| (rat) |CITS: [4460882]|. In |FRAME:TAX-4932|, there is evidence for the reversibility of the glycine cleavage complex reactions in both aerobic and anaerobic central metabolism |CITS: [11298766]|. , As shown in the reaction link to |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, the glycine produced can be used in serine biosynthesis via glycine hydroxymethyltransferase. Glycine can also be biosynthesized from serine by the reverse of the glycine hydroxymethyltransferase reaction, as shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GLYSYN-PWY| |CITS: [12350229]|. , In addition to its use in protein biosynthesis, glycine is used in the biosynthesis of other compounds such as tetrapyrroles and purines, as shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: DENOVOPURINE2-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-841|). Along with serine, glycine is an important donor of one-carbon units via the tetrahydrofolate pathways, as shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-2161|, |FRAME: PWY-2201|, |FRAME: 1CMET2-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-3841|., Glycine can also be produced by glyoxylate aminotransferase acting on glyoxylate and alanine (see MetaCyc reaction |FRAME: ALANINE--GLYOXYLATE-AMINOTRANSFERASE-RXN|) |CITS: [12899834]|, glyoxylate and glutamate (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-181|), or glyoxylate and serine (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-1622|). , In bacteria and fungi, glycine can be biosynthesized from threonine by threonine aldolase (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5436|).

|FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, which is relatively abundant in nature, being a constituent of chitosan, chitin, the, cell walls of fungi as well as the cell walls, capsular polysaccharides, and outer membranes of bacteria, is an excellent total source of carbon, energy and nitrogen., In some organisms |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| is transported into the cell by a PTS system which phosphoylates it to |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| (see |FRAME: GLUAMCAT-PWY|). In other organisms the compound is transported by different types of transporters, without being phosphorylated. In these cases phosphorylation occurs intracellularly by the enzyme |FRAME: G6576-MONOMER|. Following the sequential removal of its acetyl and amino groups, it enters glycolysis as |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| and hence flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy |CITS: [20081036]|.

Summary: |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN| is a non-proteinogenic amino acid that is a structural analogue of |FRAME: GLT| . As such, it is a potent inhibitor of glutamine synthetase, an enzyme central to nitrogen regulation in many bacterial and plant species |CITS: [5010035][Lea84]|. It is the active ingredient in several nonselective systemic herbicides, including Basta, Rely, Finale, Challenge and Liberty., |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN "Phosphinothricin"| is currently the only known naturally occurring compound in which a C-P-C bond motif (phosphorus linked to two carbons) is found., |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN| is produced by at least three species of actinomycetes as a component of non-ribosomally synthesized peptides. These include |FRAME: CPD-11749|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-2065| |CITS: [6480502]| and |FRAME: CPD-10013| (PTT), also known as bialaphos, which is produced by some strains of |FRAME: TAX-1912| |CITS: [7166539]| and |FRAME: TAX-1938| |CITS: [5010035]|., The peptides are potent antibiotics and herbicides, transported into cells via the oligopeptide transport system, and hydrolyzed intracellularly by peptidases, releasing the toxic |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN|., Studies of |FRAME: CPD-10013| biosynthesis in either of these two organisms suggest that it involves no less than 18 discrete enzymatically catalyzed reactions, starting from the common metabolite |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|. These enzymatic steps have been linked to a chromosomal gene cluster about 35 kb in length that includes at least 24 genes that are essential for the process |CITS:[15574905][15616300]|. Most of the steps have been ellucidated, and many of the enzymes have been identified |CITS: [8593056][9673017][11472937][15616300][17632514][19516340]|., The pathway includes several unusual transformations, including a C(sp<sup>3</sup>)-C(sp<sup>3</sup>) bond cleavage by the |FRAME: G-11481|-encoded dioxygenase, the formation of two phosphorus-carbon bonds by |FRAME: MONOMER-15034| (|FRAME: G-11474|) and |FRAME: MONOMER-15054| (|FRAME: G-11494|), and the assembley of the peptide backbone by three nonribosomal peptide sythetases, encoded by |FRAME: G-11498|, |FRAME: G-11499| and |FRAME: G-11500|., Different iterations of the pathway have been published over the years. A major revision of the upper part of the pathway, specifically the portion from |FRAME: CPD-551| to |FRAME:1-CARBOXYVINYL-CARBOXYPHOSPHONATE|, has been suggested in 2007 by |CITS: [17632514]|. A role for two small thioesterase-like genes (|FRAME: G-44318| and |FRAME: G-44319|) was proposed in 2015 |CITS: [26328935]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipoarabinomannans Lipoarabinomannan| (LAM) and |FRAME: Lipomannans lipomannan| (LM) are lipoglycans found anchored in the plasma membrane of |FRAME: TAX-1763| species via a phosphatidyl-myo-inositol moiety |CITS: [9218490][20560059]|. Holes in the cell envelope poles, which have been described as kettle holes, allow the surface exposure of plasma membrane anchored LAM |CITS: [1871433][9451020]|., Lipomannans and lipoarabinomannans are biosynthesized by extending the phosphatidylinositol mannoside |FRAME: Phosphatidyl-myo-inositol-Man-6-acyl-Man "2-O-(6-O-acyl-α-D-mannosyl)-6-O-(α-D-mannosyl)-1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol"| (AcPIM2). That structure is extended by a linear α-1,6-linked mannan backbone made up of 20-25 mannopyranose residues. Different acyl groups, including |FRAME: PALMITATE|, |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|, |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-18581|, are attached to the glycerol and inositol residues. Most of the backbone residues are elaborated by single α-1,2-linked mannopyranose units., Lipomannan is converted to lipoarabinomannan by the attachment of a single large branched D-arabinan structure, very similar to that found in |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "mycobacterial arabinogalactan"|. The arabinan is attached to single mannose residue in the α-1,6-D-mannan backbone. The major LAM glycoforms contain about 50 arabinofuranose residues |CITS: [29443974]|., The non-reducing termini of the arabinogalactan chains in LAM are often capped by a structure that is species-specific. Several species, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, produce mannoside caps made of one to three α-(1→2) linked mannopyranose residues that may be further substituted with an α-(1→4)-linked methylthio-D-xylose (MTX) residue |CITS: [16608340]|. This sugar was the first thiosugar described from a bacterial polysaccharide |CITS: [22575989]|., The addition of the two mannosyl residues to the cap is described in |FRAME: PWY185E-9|. The methylthioxylose residue is added by a transferase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-4674| gene |CITS: [29443974]|, which is part of a five-gene cluster that also encodes the biosynthesis of the MTX |CITS: [29443974]| (see |FRAME: PWY185E-5|)., Note that the chain lengths shown in this diagram have been significantly shortened. The actual molecule contains about 110 glycosyl residues. In addition, some modifications found in LAM such as succinylation of some arabinofuranose residues are not shown.

Summary: General Background, The rifamycins are members of the ansamycin family of antibiotics. |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B Rifamycin B| is produced as an end product by the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-33910| (previously known as Streptomyces mediterranei and Nocardia mediterranei)". Rifamycin production is controlled by a single gene cluster containing structural, resistance, export and regulatory genes |CITS: [9512878]|. |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B Rifamycin B| is less potent as an antibiotic than its precursor |FRAME: CPD-10236|, which has been used clinically. Many analogs of rifamycin have been produced, with |FRAME: CPD-18727| being widely used to treat mycobacterial infections. Due to the rapid development of resistance to rifampicin, it is used in combination with other agents such as |FRAME: ISONIAZIDE|, or other analogs such as |FRAME: CPD-21871| can be used (reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|). Rifamycins inhibit DNA-dependent RNA synthesis by binding tightly to prokaryotic DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. The mechanism of rifampicin inhibition has been studied in detail |CITS: [11290327]|. The majority of mutations leading to resistance are found in the RNA polymerase β subunit, although other mechanisms including impeded uptake and antibiotic modification are known. Autoresistance of |FRAME: TAX-33910| is due to the insensitivity of its DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to the antibiotic it produces. A rifamycin export protein, the product of gene rifP, has been identified and is thought to prevent the accumulation of rifamycin within the cell |CITS: [17351715]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|., About This Pathway, The backbone of |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B| is formed by the |FRAME: CPLX-9376|, a type I modular polyketide synthase encoded by five genes, |FRAME: G-10772|, |FRAME: G-10773|, |FRAME: G-10774|, |FRAME: G-10775| and |FRAME: G-10776|. Each gene product encodes a subunit that contains one or more modules, with each module composed of several functional domains (reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|). The pathway starts when the loading module activates the unusual starter unit |FRAME: CPD-10231| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5979|) by adenylation and links it to the [acyl carrier protein] domain of RifA |CITS: [11352749][11955082] [14599196]|., For simplification, the extension of the polyketide chain is shown in this pathway diagram in an abbreviated form, divided into only two main steps that are separated by the formation of the second ring, which occurs after the first module (RifA) has formed a tetraketide but before the next module (RifB) forms a pentaketide. The individual chain extension steps are illustrated and described in |CITS: [11352749]| and |CITS: [15700959]|., Once |FRAME: G-10772 RifA| has formed a tetraketide, a flavin-dependent hydroxylase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58867| gene, hydroxylates the ring, followed by oxidation of the dihydroxylated ring to a quinone, which is catalyzed by an as-yet unidentified enzyme |CITS: [16079331]|. The next extension (catalyzed by |FRAME: G-10773 RifB|) results in cyclization, forming a second ring. It has been shown that if ring closure does not occur due to an introduced mutation, module 4 does not process the tetraketide (referred to as |FRAME: CPD-21872 "P8/1-OG"|) and it is released |CITS: [15700959]|., Following formation of the cyclized pentaketide, six more chain extension steps involving modules 5-10 (the products of genes |FRAME: G-10773|, |FRAME: G-10774|, |FRAME: G-10775| and |FRAME: G-10776| of the |FRAME: CPLX-9376|) produce the final [acyl carrier protein]-bound product, a linear undecaketide with a naphthoquinone ring. The product of gene |FRAME: G-10783|, an amide synthase, catalyzes both its release from the polyketide synthase and intramolecular amide formation, resulting in the first cyclic macrolactam product, |FRAME: CPD-10241| (|CITS: [16079331][10430893] [10627035]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|)., |FRAME: CPD-10241 Proansamycin X| undergoes a series of complex post-polyketide synthase modification reactions to finally produce |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B|. First, formation of a double bond at position 7,8 of the second ring (this reaction is attributed in some papers to RifT; however, a study that used complementation of a rifT mutant concluded that the enzyme is not involed directly in rifamycin B biosynthesis |CITS: [20726561]|) and hydroxylation of C-34α by an unknown enzyme form |FRAME: CPD-10243|. This is followed by a very complex oxygenation catalyzed by the cytochrome P-450 enzyme |FRAME: G-58871| that generates |FRAME: CPD-10239| |CITS: [16079331]|. Three additional modifications transform this compound into |FRAME: CPD-10236| |CITS: [12623077][15791687]|., The hydroquinone |FRAME: CPD-10236| is spontaneously oxidized to the quinone |FRAME: CPD-21864| by ambient O2, and this transformation is dramatically accelerated by the presence of divalent metal ions. It is possible that an enzyme catalyzes this reaction in vivo |CITS: [29904078]|., In the next step |FRAME: CPLX-9377|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10784| and |FRAME: G-58870| genes, forms |FRAME: CPD-21865|, which is oxidized by another cytochrome P-450 enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58872| gene, to |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-O|. The last reaction is this pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-O| to |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B|, occurs spontaneously in the presence of NADPH |CITS: [29904078]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-16760 "Linuron"| is a phenylurea herbicide that is widely used in agriculture. Bacterial strains, bacterial consortia, and fungi have been identified that can either partially degrade |FRAME: CPD-16760|, or mineralize it as a sole source of carbon, nitrogen and energy. Biodegradation is a major contributor to |FRAME: CPD-16760| dissipation in the environment |CITS: [23811502][20603879 ][17991021][5119200][19464778]|. In bacteria |FRAME: CPD-16760| degradation is initiated by amide hydrolysis to produce |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: CPD-16759|. |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE "3,4-Dichloroaniline"| is then degraded to |FRAME: CPD-10626| (4,5-dichlorocatechol) and further to TCA cycle intermediates as shown in the pathway link. |FRAME: CPD-16759 "N,O-Dimethylhydroxylamine"| has been described as easily degraded to simple compounds |CITS: [22003008]|., Early studies using |FRAME: TAX-1421 "Lysinibacillus sphaericus (previously known as Bacillus sphaericus)"| showed that a partially purified, |FRAME: CPD-16760|-inducible acylamidase can degrade |FRAME: CPD-16760| and other acylanilide and phenylurea herbicides and fungicides. |FRAME: CPD-16760 "Linuron"| was degraded to |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: CPD-16759| |CITS: [5119200][5021977]|. |FRAME: ORG-6261| degraded several substituted phenylurea herbicides including |FRAME: CPD-16775| and |FRAME: CPD-16760| utilizing a plasmid-encoded phenylurea hydrolase |FRAME: CPLX-8861 "PuhA"|. |FRAME: ORG-6262| was also shown to hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-16775|, |FRAME: CPD-16760| and a range of other phenylurea substrates utilizing phenylurea hydrolase |FRAME: CPLX-8860 "PuhB"|. However |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE| was accumulated in both of these organisms suggesting that the compounds were not mineralized |CITS: [11319111][19000034]|. In subsequent work the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-16760| by bacterial consortia was studied and |FRAME: TAX-207745| was identified as a |FRAME: CPD-16760| degrader |CITS: [12620840][17991021][18373685]|., About This Pathway, Strains of |FRAME: TAX-34072| are important |FRAME: CPD-16760| degraders that provide the initial hydrolysis step as well as subsequent steps. In |FRAME: TAX-282217| the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-16760| to |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE| is catalyzed by a hydrolase encoded by the libA gene. |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE "3,4-Dichloroaniline"| is then oxidized by a multicomponent dioxygenase complex encoded in the dcaQTA1A2BR gene cluster that degrades it to |FRAME: CPD-10626| (4,5-dichlorocatechol). The latter compound is further degraded by genes in the ccdRCFDE cluster via a modified ortho-cleavage pathway (as shown in the pathway link) |CITS: [22003008]|., Other |FRAME: CPD-16760|-degrading |FRAME: TAX-34072| strains such as |FRAME: TAX-207745| do not contain a libA homolog. This |FRAME: CPD-16760|-mineralizing strain initiates |FRAME: CPD-16760| hydrolysis using the product of gene hylA. |FRAME: CPLX-8858 "HylA"| has properties distinct from |FRAME: MONOMER-18671 "LibA"|, and from the phenylurea-hydrolyzing enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-8861 "PuhA"| and |FRAME: CPLX-8860 "PuhB"| that are found in the Gram-positive bacteria |FRAME: ORG-6261| and |FRAME: ORG-6262|, respectively., In spontaneous mutants of |FRAME: TAX-207745| that are defective in |FRAME: CPD-16760| hydrolysis, gene hylA is absent. However hylA is present in strains that lack libA (|FRAME: TAX-207745| and |FRAME: TAX-434008|). Both hylA and libA are associated with gene modules that encode enzymes for |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE| degradation |CITS: [23811502][22003008][20146937]|. Thus, in different species of |FRAME: TAX-34072| evolutionarily distinct but isofunctional |FRAME: CPD-16760| hydrolase genes initiate |FRAME: 34-DICHLOROANILINE| degradation which suggests the occurrence of divergent evolution and independent acquisition of genetic modules |CITS: [23811502]|.

General Background, Many organisms including bacteria, fungi, metazoa, and plants can degrade glucose polymers derived from |FRAME: Starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6724|, |FRAME: PWY-842|, |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5941|). Some hyperthermophilic archaea have also been shown to produce |FRAME: Starch|-degrading enzymes, and pathways for the utilization of |FRAME: Starch| and its derivatives, such as |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|, |FRAME: Maltodextrins|, and |FRAME: MALTOSE| have been proposed. These hyperthermophilic archaea can utilize |FRAME: Starch| and its degradation products as primary carbon sources during anaerobic growth. Thermostable starch-degrading enzymes produced by hyperthermophpilic organisms are of industrial interest |CITS: [16513741] [11489857] [17921308] [11702074]|., In the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-91619| enzymatic evidence suggested a |FRAME: Starch| degradation pathway via formation of cyclodextrins from |FRAME: Starch| by an extracellular cyclodextrin glucanotransferase, transport into the cell, and linearization by cyclodextrinase |CITS: [11489857]|. In this organism, the cyclodextrinase appeared to hydrolyze cyclodextrins to the end products |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| as described below in About This Pathway (|CITS: [11489857]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|). Cyclodextrins (cyclomaltodextrins) are cyclic oligosaccharides composed of α-1,4-linked glucose units. Early literature referred to them as Schardinger dextrins. Cyclodextrins corresponding to 6-12+ glucose units have been characterized (in |CITS: [5758537]|) (see |FRAME: CPD-3782|, |FRAME: CPD-3781|, |FRAME: CPD-3783|). The physicochemical properties of cyclodextrins give them broad applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries (in |CITS: [11489857]|)., The hyperthermophilic, sulfate-reducing archaeon |FRAME: ORG-6178| has been shown to degrade |FRAME: Starch| via a unique pathway involving cyclodextrin intermediates |CITS: [17921308] [11702074]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6731|). , The hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-186497| was shown to degrade |FRAME: Starch| mainly via maltodextrins in a pathway involving an extracellular amylopullulanase, a transporter, an intracellular 4-α-glucanotransferase, and a maltodextrin phosphorylase. These enzymes produce |FRAME: GLC| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| that are converted to |FRAME: GLC-6-P| and degraded in pathway |FRAME: P341-PWY| (|CITS: [16513741]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6737|)., Among bacteria |FRAME:TAX-562| cannot utilize |FRAME: Starch|, but it can metabolize short, linear maltodextrins (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY|). However the enterobacterium |FRAME: TAX-290336| can utilize |FRAME: Starch| as a sole source of carbon and energy. Mutant analysis suggested that it metabolizes |FRAME: Starch| by two pathways. The first was a proposed maltose/maltodextrin pathway involving extracellular degradation of |FRAME: Starch| by pullulanase and the disproportionation activity of cyclodextrin glucanotransferase to form linear maltodextins. After transport into the cell they are degraded to |FRAME: GLC| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by the products of malP, malQ and malZ. The second was a proposed cyclodextrin pathway involving extracellular conversion of |FRAME: Starch| to cyclodextrins (see |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|) by cyclodextrin glucanotransferase, transport into the cell, linearization by |FRAME: MONOMER-16314| (CymH) |CITS: [8599539]|, and further catabolism as in the maltose/maltodextrin pathway |CITS: [8594196] [9573146]|., About This Pathway, The hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-91619| was shown to possess a gene cluster containing genes for the degradation of |FRAME: Starch| via the synthesis, transport and degradation of cyclodextrins derived from |FRAME: Starch|. A unique extracellular |FRAME: MONOMER-16282| encoded by gene cgtA was purified from culture broth and characterized |CITS: [10223990]|. This enzyme catalyzed predominantly the formation of |FRAME: CPD-3782| from |FRAME: Starch|, with only small amounts of |FRAME: CPD-3781| and |FRAME: CPD-3783|) formed. The organism also produced an extremely thermostable intracellular |FRAME: MONOMER-16283| encoded by gene cgtB and a cyclodextrin binding protein encoded by gene cgtC that were also purified and characterized. In addition, genes cgtD and cgtE were found to encode putative cyclodextrin binding protein-dependent permease proteins |CITS: [11489857] [10223990]|., A unique metabolic pathway involving extracellular cyclodextrin synthesis from |FRAME: Starch| by |FRAME: MONOMER-16282|, a cyclodextrin transport system, and intracellular cyclodextrin degradation was proposed. Intracellular cyclodextrins were shown to be hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16283| to the end products |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| via initial hydrolysis to linear maltodextrins, followed by further hydrolysis to smaller maltodextrins and then to |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| |CITS: [11489857]|. The exact route of metabolism of these end products was not described.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "Protocatechuate"| is one of the key intermediate metabolites in the microbial degradation of various aromatic compounds, including phthalates, hydroxybenzoates, and lignin-derived aromatic compounds such as |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|., The key step in these degradation pathways, the fission of the protocatechuate aromatic ring, can be catalyzed by one of the three distinct dioxygenases - |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, |FRAME: CPLX-2721| and |FRAME: CPLX-7915|., The fission products, and thus the degradation pathways, depend on the type of dioxygenase employed. The three pathways are described in |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6336|, respectively., About This Pathway, This pathway has been reported initially in some Bacilli |CITS: [163224][931947]|, and eventually studied in more detail in the thermophile |FRAME: TAX-649508|, which was isolated from a 50 °C hot spring |CITS: [453834]|., The key enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7915|, has been purified several times from |FRAME: TAX-649508| cells grown on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| and characterized |CITS: [453834][2280722][8392511]|. The rapid disappearance of the immediate ring fission product |FRAME: CPD-11842| in cell extracts and the accumulation of |FRAME: HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD| indicated a very rapid enzymatic decarboxylation of the former. This and other observations lead to the prediction of the pathway as presented here |CITS: [453834]|., A gene cluster encoding all of the enzymes involved in this pathway (along with the enzyme for conversion of |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|) was identified and characterized |CITS: [19717587]|. The genes were cloned into |FRAME:TAX-562| individually and their function was confirmed. In addition, introduction of the full cluster into |FRAME:TAX-562| confer the ability to grow on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| as the sole carbon source |CITS: [19717587]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SKATOLE Skatole|, or 3-methylindole, is a heterocyclic compound derived from |FRAME: TRP|. In mammals it is formed by intestinal bacteria in the digestive tract, and is responsible for the distinct fecal malodor |CITS: [36586563]|. It is detectable at a threshold concentration as low as 0.56 ppb. , Skatole has also been detected in some plants, including orange blossoms, jasmine, and beetroot |CITS: [Osborne75]|., In ruminants skatole has been reported to be oxidized in the lungs, generating a reactive electrophilic metabolite that causes pulmonotoxicity |CITS: [5019784]|., , Skatole also acts as an oviposition cue for Culex mosquitoes, contributing to the transmission of mosquito-borne diseases such as filariasis, Japanese encephalitis, and West Nile fever |CITS: [15274442][20623327]|., In humans gut bacteria-derived skatole functions as a pneumotoxin |CITS: [2519817][2181487]|., About This Pathway, The pathway for skatole biosynthesis appears to be chimeric, meaning that different reactions in the pathwya are catalyzed by different organisms. For example, |FRAME: TAX-1299998|, which has been shown to produce the enzyme catalyzing the last step, appears to lack the enzyme needed to catalyze the second step., The pathway is initiated by |FRAME: TRP| deamination, mediated by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.27| |CITS: [7811697]|. The product, |FRAME: INDOLE_PYRUVATE|, is decarboxylated to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETALDEHYDE| by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.74|, which has been characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-550| |CITS: [1639814][32283770]|. The aldehyde undergoes a dehydrogenation process and is converted to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA). This reaction has been observed with |FRAME: TAX-1598| and |FRAME: TAX-1579| |CITS: [29143823][28775213]| and characterized in vitro for the |FRAME: TAX-83333| enzyme PuuC |CITS: [ 31272146]|. The final step is IAA decarboxylation by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.115|, which has been found documented from several fermenting bacteria in the |FRAME: TAX-186802| and |FRAME: TAX-84999| orders |CITS: [30310076]|.

Furthermore, |FRAME: TAX-1488| is a slow growing organism which is not as well understood as some other microorganisms, making it an arduous task to optimize |FRAME: BUTANOL| production |CITS: [17942358]|. , About this Pathway, The |FRAME:TAX-1485| |FRAME: BUTANOL| biosynthesis pathway was reconstructed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, a well studied organism |CITS: [17942358]|. Summary: Many of the secondary metabolites accumulating in plants during organ development are anthocyanidin glycosides, for instance cyanidin galactosides detected in red kiwifruits |CITS:[19203266]| and apple skins |CITS:[19652996]| or acylated anthocyanidin glycosides found in carrots |CITS:[1368363]|. The attachment of glycosides to anthocyanidins, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-591| confers color to the pigments and subsequent glycosylation and acylation is known to stabilize this effect |CITS:[Brouillard83] [12358498]|. The importance of glycosylation is emphasized by the observation that glycosyltransferases have been shown to belong to the most regulated steps in anthocyanin modification pathways |CITS:[18258692]|. , Whereas in Actinidia (kiwi) |CITS:[19203266]|, Malus (apple) |CITS:[19652996]| and Diospyros (persimmon) |CITS:[19641937]| anthocyanindin glycosides such as |FRAME:CPD-15012| dominate carrot cell suspensions continue the anthocyanidin modification and further acylate anthocyanidin glycosides. The first committed, and probably rate-limiting step in the pathway is the galactosylation of |FRAME:CPD-591| which is subsequently followed by the xylosylation of the resulting |FRAME:CPD-14998| |CITS:[8717136] [21175894] [19641937]|. The formation of the anthocyanidin triglycoside which is supposedly carried out by a UDP-glucose:glucosyltransferase has not yet been described in the literature. However, the anthocyanidin triglycoside, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14999| is the substrate for the anthocyanidin glycoside acyltransferase(s) which accept either |FRAME:1-O-SINAPOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE|, |FRAME: CPD-15281| or |FRAME:CPD-8674| to form the corresponding acylated anthocyanidin triglucosides such as for instance |FRAME:CPD-15000| |CITS:[24186789] [9684371]|.

|FRAME: CPD-16900 Ccetylaszonalenin| is a mycotoxin that was initially isolated from an unidentified Aspergillus species |CITS: [ 4761386]|. Together with its non-acetylated form |FRAME: CPD-16898| it was subsequently identified in various fungal strains, including |FRAME: TAX-41063| |CITS: [Kimura82]|, |FRAME: TAX-746128| |CITS: [17617730]|, |FRAME: TAX-41282| |CITS: [12945765]|, and |FRAME: TAX-36630| |CITS: [Wakana06]|. Their stereoisomers |FRAME: CPD-18325| and |FRAME: CPD-18326| were isolated from |FRAME: TAX-340412| |CITS: [Rank06]|. Fungal prenylated indol derivatives such as |FRAME:CPD-16900| constitute a fusion of aromatic and isoprenoid moieties |CITS:[20024094][21063425]| that seems to occur predominantly in the fungal family |FRAME: TAX-1131492| |CITS:[Williams00] [Stocking00]|. , A biosynthetic gene cluster for the production of |FRAME:CPD-16900| comprising a set of three genes encoding a nonribosomal peptide synthetase (AnaPS), a prenyltransferase (AnaPT) and a acetyltransferase (AnaAT) has been identified by genomic mining in |FRAME: TAX-36630| |CITS:[19001367]| and subsequently genetically and biochemically characterized., The nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) AnaPS catalyzed the formation of the cyclic dipeptide (|FRAME:CPD-16899|) from the nonproteinogenic aromatic β-amino acid |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME:TRP|. It is one of the remarkable features of fungal NRPS's to accept rather unusual amino acids which do not belong to the group of proteinogenic amino acids |CITS:[18663394] [23659680]|. The molecular function of AnaPS was demonstrated in various experimental approaches, first the activation and loading of |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| by the first module of the bimodular AnaPS |CITS:[20225828]| and second the expression of the holoprotein AnaPS in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae system |CITS:[22902615]| in which the catalysis of |FRAME:CPD-16899| was verified. Deviant from fungal NRPS's which often terminate the reaction through a condensation (CT) domain AnaPS releases the product via an epimerization (E) domain |CITS:[22902615]|. , The following step, the reverse prenylation at position C-3 of the indole ring is carried out by the benzodiazepinedione prenyltransferase AnaPT |CITS:[19001367]|. AnaPT is promiscuous in terms of accepting various other tryptophan-containing cyclic dipeptides |CITS:[19421461] [20165805]| and as an exception from members of the |FRAME:CPD-4211| prenyltransferase (DMATS) superfamily also used |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| |CITS:[24014429]| and |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| |CITS:[24430210]| producing the respective geranylated and farnesylated products. Remarkably, in those cases the enzyme changed its regioselectivity and prenylated C-6 or C-7 instead of C-3 |CITS:[24014429]| probably enabled by an unusually enlarged binding site |CITS:[24239009]|. The final step of the pathway, the N-acetylation of |FRAME:CPD-16898| yielding |FRAME:CPD-16900| was demonstrated using the recombinant, His-tag purified AnaAT |CITS:[19001367]|.

Anthocyanidins are core pigments for the flower coloration of plants. When glycosylated the more stable anthocyanins are formed |CITS:[Davies09] [Yonekura-Sakakibara09]|. The only six types of anthocyanin aglycones form a plethora of thousands of anthocyanin derivatives by modifying their core structure through glycosylation, hydroxylation, acylation and methylation |CITS:[18476875]|. Acylation of anthocyanin molecules is realized by either aromatic or aliphatic acyl moieties. Aromatic acylation has been suggested to contribute to more bluer colors |CITS:[10846752]| while aliphatic acylation has been considered as a factor to stabilize the structure of anthocyanins |CITS:[12481098]|. , There are two types of anthocyanin acyltransferases carrying out the acylation, the ones that utilize acyl-CoA's which belong to the BAHD family |CITS:[16616872]| and the other type that employ acyl-glucoses as acyl donors as first described in |FRAME:TAX-4039| |CITS:[Glaessgen92]|. , Among the many acylated anthocyanins found in plants only |FRAME:TAX-3570| possesses anthocyanins acylated with |FRAME:MAL| |CITS:[Terahara86] [Terahara86a] [11140528]|. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of anthocyanidin malylglucosides catalyzed by a |FRAME:MONOMER-17999| (AMalT). The AMalT employs a aliphatic acyl-glucose, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15286| and accepts only anthocyanidin 3-glucosides forming basic pigments involved in the flower coloration of |FRAME:TAX-3570| |CITS:[18471436]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| (CoA) is a ubiquitous compound found in archaea, bacteria, plants, and animals. It is a common acyl carrier in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and is required for a multitude of reactions for both biosynthetic and degradative pathways, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids |CITS: [16415216]|., The biosynthesis of CoA occurs via different pathways in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes, and thus enzymes specific for the bacterial pathway are targets for antibacterial drug discovery., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1423| is able to produce |FRAME: CO-A| de novo, as described in the pathway |FRAME: COA-PWY|, which relies on the biosynthesis of |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|. However, the organism is able to synthesize |FRAME: CO-A| when grown on complex medium even in the absence of |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| synthesis, due to the presence of a salvage pathway in which |FRAME: CPD-27132| is used as the starting material., This compound is thought to arise outside the cell by spontaneous condensation of |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: CPD-511|. The latter is a degradation product of the phosphopantetheine moiety of acyl carrier proteins., |FRAME: CPD-27132 Cysteinopantetheine| enters the cell via the |FRAME: CPLX8J2-67|. Once inside the cell, it undergoes reduction by an as-yet uncharacterized process, forming |FRAME: CPD-511| and |FRAME: CYS|. |FRAME: CPD-511 Panthetheine| is phosphorylated by the |FRAME: BSU23760-MONOMER|, forming |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| and joining the do novo biosynthetic route |CITS: [Warneke24]|.

General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [Shellhammer90][15012185][11706201]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.15|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.4|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|. Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria and certain fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. While the biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail only in bacteria, ongoing success in sequencing whole genomes from other organisms has provided evidence that the general steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Despite the importance and prevalance of biotin, its detailed biosynthetic pathway remained enigmatic for over 70 years. Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, and is derived from |FRAME: CPD-205|. The early steps of the pathway, which are described here, are limited to the synthesis of the precursor pimelate moiety. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described in |FRAME: PWY0-1507|., The Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1423| uses different enzymes/pathways for synthesizing the pimelate moiety either by salvage or de novo. In the salvage pathway, externally-provided pimelate is activated to |FRAME: CPD-558| (see |FRAME: PWY-6578|). In the de novo pathway, which is described here, the pimelate moiety can be generated from a range of |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-ACPs long-chain acyl-[acp]"| molecules. , The key enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: BSU30190-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU30190| gene. This P450 enzyme catalyzes the oxidative C-C bond cleavage of long chain acyl-[acp]s, forming |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs pimeloyl-[acp]| |CITS: [11368323][20658980]|. Like other cytochrome P450 enzymes, BioI uses the cysteine-ligated active site heme to activate molecular oxygen by two flavodoxin-mediated reductions with NADPH. The proposed mechanism involves four sub-reactions, during which two oxygen atoms are incorporated at position 7 and 8 of the acyl-[acp] molecule, followed by cleavage and incorporation of a third oxygen atom to form |FRAME: 7-Oxoheptanoyl-ACPs "7-oxoheptanoyl-[acp]"|, and its subsequent oxidation to |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs "pimeloyl-[acp]"| (it is still not clear whether the last reaction is spontaneous or catalyzed by the enzyme). The mechanism is similar to that of |FRAME: 1.14.15.6-RXN "EC 1.14.15.6, cholesterol monooxygenase (side-chain-cleaving)"| |CITS: [20658980]|. Although free fatty acids can be processed by BioI in vitro, the physiological substrates are thought to be acyl-[acp]s |CITS: [11368323]|.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., In some anaerobic organisms the pathway can also operate in the reverse direction, functioning as an autotrophic CO2 fixation pathway, see more about it below., The input to the oxidative cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn this variant of the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, reduces one |FRAME: NAD|, two |FRAME: NADP|, one |FRAME: Quinones quinone| and two ferredoxins to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH|, |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol| and reduced ferredoxins, respectively, and phosphorylates one molecule of ADP to ATP., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105|, a key member of the "standard" TCA cycle that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: SUC-COA|, is absent, or not expressed, in many organisms, including obligately autotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria and archaea |CITS: [15449607]|, as well as mycobacteria |CITS: [16045627]|. Most cyanobacteria also lack a gene encoding the enzyme |CITS: [4963789][15449607][21282404]|., The absence of this enzyme could in theory result in incomplete oxidative or reductive TCA cycles that supply biosynthetic intermediates in response to growth conditions (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P42-PWY|). However, in some cases other enzymes substitute for the missing activity and complete the cycle. For example, in some archaeal and bacterial species the role of 2-oxoglutarate dehydorgenase is replaced by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3| (this pathway, and see also |FRAME: REDCITCYC|) |CITS: [22174252][10091606]|. , Succinate can also be formed by a reductive TCA half-cycle, or by the glyoxylate bypass (in |CITS: [16027371]|) (see |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|). , The pathway is believed to operate in several types of mycobacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1772| and |FRAME: TAX-1765| |CITS: [16027371][19936047][21561773]|, and has been described from the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2277| |CITS: [16740941]|. A similar, yet somewhat different pathway occurs in helicobacteria (see |FRAME: REDCITCYC|)., The pathway in the reverse direction, The key enzyme of this pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3|, can also participates in a reductive TCA cycle, where the pathway operates in the reverse direction. See |FRAME: P23-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5392|.

Summary: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the first segment, up to the intermediate lipid IV<sub>A</sub>., In many bacterial species lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., This pathway includes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor lipid IV<sub>A</sub>. Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. One exception is |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.54|, which is known to be catalyzed by three completely different types of enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: EG12666| |CITS: [12000770]|, |FRAME: G-55034| |CITS: [20608695]|, and |FRAME: G-55035| |CITS: [27006461]| genes., There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

Summary: The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15731|, the deoxyaminosugar moiety of the antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-13962| and |FRAME: CPD-13973|, involves several enzymes encoded by a single gene cluster. The genes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15731| have been named dnm, while the gene involved in the biosynthesis of the rest of the |FRAME: CPD-13962| molecule were named dnr or dau, depending on the strain., The first two steps of the pathway, the activation of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by dTDP and 4,6 dehydration, are common to the biosynthesis of many dTDP-sugars. Strong sequence similarity to well-characterized genes indicates these reactions are catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-1950| by the products of the |FRAME: G-44655| and |FRAME: G-44656| genes, respectively |CITS: [8932700]|. The |FRAME: G-44656| gene from strain ATCC 29050 contains a frameshift mutation that causes the premature termination of translation |CITS: [8932700]|. In that organism the reaction appears to be catalyzed by another dehydratase, which has been purified and partially sequenced earlier |CITS: [1588310]|. , The next steps are catalyzed by a 3,5-epimerase (|FRAME: G-44657|) |CITS: [9209071]|, a 2,3-dehydratase (|FRAME: G-44658|) |CITS: [8955419]|, and a 3-aminotransferase (|FRAME: G-44660|) |CITS: [7868593]|. , Finally, the 4-ketoreductase encoded by |FRAME: G-44659| reduces the C-4 ketone to a hydroxyl group to produce |FRAME: CPD-15731| |CITS: [9209071]|.

The fungus |FRAME: TAX-29910| produces the cyclosporins, a group of neutral cyclic oligopeptides composed of 11 amino acids. While the native function of the compounds is to act as antifungals against competing fungi, they were found to have multiple biological effects. |FRAME: CPD-20532 "Cyclosporin A"|, the main metabolite, is a potent, specific immunosuppressant., One of the 11 amino acids that compose the cyclosporines is |FRAME: CPD-26317| (2-Bmt), the presence of which is essential for high immunosuppressive activity;, Early experiments with [<sup>13</sup>C]acetate, labeled either at the methyl or the carboxyl group, demonstrated that the carbon skeleton of the compound is built up by head-to-tail coupling of four acetate units, whereas the C-methyl in position 4 originates from methionine |CITS: [6873239]|. The exact structure of the compound was reported following the generation of cyclosporin non-producing mutant that accumulated it |CITS: [2116402]|., Subsequent studies have shown that the unusual amino acid is produced via a polyketide pathway, utilizing acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA, NADPH, and S-adenosylmethionine |CITS: [8253730][8679598]|. Sequencing of the |FRAME: TAX-29910| genome identified the cyclosporin biosynthetic gene cluster, and suggested candidates for the genes that are involved in 2-Bmt biosynthesis |CITS: [23818858]|. A later study has asigned specific roles for the products of the |FRAME: G-124396|, |FRAME: G-124397|, and |FRAME: G-124398| genes, which encode a polyketide synthase, a cytochrome P450, and an aminotransferase, respectively. Mutations in each of the genes abolished production of 2-Bmt |CITS: [30279281]|.

Summary: Several microorganisms have been isolated which are capable of degrading toluene via various mechanisms. , |FRAME:TAX-300| KR1 is capable of using toluene as a sole carbon and energy source, converting, toluene to protocatechuate which is then oxidized to form substrates of the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Unlike the other , pathways of microbial toluene degradation which involves meta cleavage of the aromatic ring, the enzymes , in this degradation pathway degrade toluene by a sequence of ortho ring cleavage reactions. |CITS: [2019564]| The initial step, in this reaction involves the hydroxylation of toluene by a toluene-4-monooxygenase system to form p-cresol.|CITS: [1885512]|, p-cresol is subsequently converted to p-hydroxybenzaldehyde by a flavocytochrome, p-cresol, methylhydroxylase.|CITS: [3790500]| p-hydroxybenzaldehyde is then oxidized by an NAD+-dependent , dehydrogenase to form p-hydroxybenzoate.|CITS: [2722739]| Hydroxybenzoate is then subsequently, hydroxylated to form protocatechuate, which is then completely dissimilated by an ortho cleavage pathway. |CITS: [2019564]|

Summary: General Background, The reductive tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle is a carbon dioxide fixation pathway found in autotrophic eubacteria and archaea (there is a report of the pathway also operating in a strain of the green algae |FRAME: TAX-3055| |CITS: [16668673]|). It is considered to be a primordial pathway for production of starting organic molecules for biosynthesis of sugars, lipids, amino acids, pyrimidines and pyrroles |CITS: [11540925][9084754][15340153]|., Other pathways for carbon dioxide fixation are listed under |FRAME: CO2-Fixation|., The reductive TCA cycle is largely the oxidative, catabolic |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| in reverse. Most of the enzymes of the TCA cycle work reversibly and could catalyze both directions. Only two counteracting enzyme pairs are thought to determine the oxidative or reductive direction of the cycle. These two enzymes are |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.8|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3| (the enzymes listed here are those catalyzing the reductive direction) |CITS: [SCHAUDER87][SHIBA85][15028704]|. It should be noted that these enzymes may participate in other pathways (for example, |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3| also participates in the |FRAME: REDCITCYC "oxidative TCA cycle"| found in |FRAME: TAX-72293|). Nonetheless, the presence of these enzyme activities in autotrophically grown bacteria and archaea is considered indicative of the presence of the reductive TCA cycle., Activities of the key enzymes in the reductive TCA cycle have been demonstrated in many autotrophic bacteria and archaea including the following: the green sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1092| |CITS: [FUCHS80][11248686]|; the δ proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-2291| |CITS: [SCHAUDER87]|; the α proteobacterium strain MC-1 |CITS: [16461683]|; the ε proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-39766| and |FRAME: TAX-162154| |CITS: [15838028]|; seven other ε proteobacteria isolated from deep-sea hydrothermal environments |CITS: [16269773]|; the aquificales |FRAME: TAX-940| and |FRAME: TAX-2714| |CITS: [SHIBA85][BEH93]|; and the Crenarchaeota |FRAME: TAX-70771| |CITS: [2506014] [BEH93]|, and |FRAME: TAX-2277| |CITS: [12610721]|. In additon, the genes of the reductive TCA cycle have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1097| TLS |CITS: [12093901]|, and |FRAME: TAX-2271| |CITS: [15028704]|., In a few cases, the presence of both the oxidative and reductive TCA cycles has been shown in the same organism, as in |FRAME: TAX-2271| and |FRAME: TAX-2277| |CITS: [Selig94][12610721][15028704]|., About This Pathway, The pathway described here was first discovered in the green sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-115852| |CITS: [5219700]|., The key step of converting citrate to oxaloacetate and acetyl-coA is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.8|., The basic cycle results in the fixation of two molecules of carbon dioxide and the production of one molecule of acetyl-CoA |CITS: [15028704][15838028][16269773]|., Another molecule of carbon dioxide can be fixed by the carboxylation of acetyl-coA to pyruvate |CITS: [11248686]|. Pyruvate can be converted to phosphoenolpyruvate, which can enter |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis| |CITS: [BEH93]|, or, as shown here, can alternatively assimilate a fourth carbon dioxide molecule by carboxylation to oxaloacetate. This carboxylation is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31| |CITS: [5219700][SCHAUDER87][11540925][9084754][11248686]|.
