Summary: Wild chicory (|FRAME:TAX-13427|) is a blue-flowered composite plant that has spread all over the world from the Mediterranean and east Asia. Since the seventeenth century it has been cultivated (var sativum) for its bitter roots that were roasted and used in hot coffee-like beverages. Although the use of these roots was displaced by genuine coffee from |FRAME: TAX-13443|, sprouts of the plant that are grown in the dark became popular as a vegetable (Belgian endive) halfway through the nineteenth century, and are widely used in Mediterranean cuisine., Chicory roots contain a number of bitter-tasting compounds called sesquiterpene lactones that are postulated to originate from a common germacranolide, |FRAME: CPD-9410|. Sesquiterpenoid lactones are a major class of plant secondary metabolites mainly found in |FRAME: TAX-4210|. The sesquiterpene lactones in chicory act as antifeedants towards insects and also suspected to act as antifungal and antibacterial agents |CITS: [FRANSSEN05]|. Several thousand sesquiterpenoid lactones are known, all of them contain either guaiane, eudesmane, or a germacrane structure of which |FRAME: CPD-9410| is structurally the simplest and is generally accepted as the parent compound of guaianolides, eudesmanolides, or germacranolides |CITS: [12011356]|. , Most of the enzymatic steps of |FRAME: PWY-6540| have been experimentally proven |CITS: [11299372][12011356]|. In Chicory the most abundant lactones are guaianolides called lactucin and lactucopicrin. The biosynthesis of lactucin is suggested to occur via the |FRAME: CPD-9410| pathway |CITS: [FRANSSEN05]|. The costunolide synthase in Lactuca sativa was shown to produce |FRAME:CPD-16700| from |FRAME:CPD-9413| which is then non-enzymatically converted to |FRAME:CPD-9410|. The homolog identified in Helianthus annuus catalyzes the 8β-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-9413| which yielded the corresponding |FRAME:CPD-16701|. It remains to be shown if this compound can be further metabolized to |FRAME:CPD-9410| catalyzed by a yet unknown costunolide synthase or if |FRAME:CPD-16701| represents the entrance compound into sesquiterpene lactones (STLs) other than |FRAME:CPD-9410| |CITS:[21515683]|. , Three of the steps of this pathway are catalyzed by the same enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.95| (GAO1). The pathway is evolutionarily conserved in the three main subfamilies of |FRAME: TAX-4210| as well as the basal phylogenetic species; |FRAME: TAX-171760|. The authors also demonstrated the capacity of GAO1 enzymes to catalyze the non-natural substrate amphordiene to artemisinic acid. The amorphodiene oxidase enzyme showed little activity towards the oxidation of germacrene A, indicating that the ancestral GAO1 retained catalytic plasticity, whereas the diverged AMO1 had lost that capacity |CITS: [20351109]|.

Summary: The term |FRAME: Vitamin-E| (tocochromenols) is a collective term for the eight forms of |FRAME: Tocotrienols tocotrienols| and |FRAME: Tocopherols tocopherols|, each existing as α, β, γ, and δ species., Structurally tocotrienols and tocopherols differ only in the degree of unsaturation of their side-chain. The tocotrienol chain comprises three trans-double bonds, whereas the tocopherol chain is fully saturated. In addition, the α, β, γ, and δ species of both compound groups vary in the methylation pattern of the chromanol ring |CITS:[12897790]|. , Vitamin E compounds are synthesized only by photosynthetic organisms, although they are essential dietary components for animals (including humans), where they act primarily as antioxidants. Their presumed role in plants involve protection of chloroplast lipids and chlorophylls against oxidative damages. The tocotrienols are mostly found in monocots |CITS:[Padley94]| and a few dicots |CITS:[17110122]|, whereas tocopherols are wider spread in the plant kingdom and dominate in the dicots |CITS:[8827691]|., The |FRAME: Tocopherols tocopherols| include |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL|, |FRAME: BETA-TOCOPHEROL|, |FRAME: GAMA-TOCOPHEROL| and |FRAME:DELTA-TOCOPHEROL|, which differ only in the number and position of methyl groups on the chromanol ring. |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| has been shown to possess the highest vitamin E, activity., The genes encoding all the of pathway enzymes have been cloned from Arabidopsis.

Summary: The |FRAME: Mammalian-GPI-Anchors "glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor"| is a glycolipid structure that is added posttranslationally to the C-terminus of many eukaryotic proteins (roughly 1% of all proteins encoded by eukaryotic genomes, and ~10-20% of all membrane proteins that enter the secretory pathway after being targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum). It anchors the attached protein in the outer leaflet of the cell membrane. , The GPI anchor is preassembled by enzymes attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). For a full description of the GPI anchor biosynthesis in the ER see |FRAME: PWY-8601|. Following the transfer of the GPI anchor to target proteins in the ER, a post-attachment remodeling phase begins, which prompts an ER-to-Golgi transport of the GPI-anchored proteins, where they continue the modification and eventually sorted out of the Golgi to their final location |CITS: [24784135][38167496]|., The first modification process is the removal of the acyl chain linked to the 2-OH position of inositol ring, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.M30| (|FRAME: G66-46571|) |CITS: [24784135][38167496]|. Next, The product of the |FRAME: HS08014| gene (also referred to as PGAP5), a metallophosphoesterase, catalyzes the removal of the phophoethanolamine (pEtN) side-chain from the second mannose. This activity was reported to be a prerequisite for the efficient exit of GPI-APs from the ER |CITS: [19837036]|., At this point the processed GPI-anchored proteins are transported from the ER to the Golgi in vesicles formed by coat protein complex II (COPII). These vesicles bud off from the ER at specialized sites and then fuse with the Golgi apparatus. Specific proteins, including those of the p24 family, are involved in packaging GPI-attached proteins into these vesicles., The processing of the GPI anchor continues in the Golgi. The sn-2 position of the diacylglycerol moiety of the GPI anchor, which originally contains an unsaturated fatty acid, is removed by |FRAME: HS14861| (previously known as PERLD1) |CITS: [17314402]|. |FRAME: HS07576|, a 2-lyso-GPI anchor O-acyltransferase, then replaces it with a saturated C18:0 fatty acid |CITS: [16407401]|., A second enzyme with the same enzymatic activity as |FRAME: HS14861| was shown to be encoded by the |FRAME: HS05317| gene. Unlike |FRAME: HS14861|, |FRAME: HS05317| plays an important role during early embryonic development |CITS: [ 27881714]|., Some mammalian proteins carry GPI anchors with additional modifications to the anchors such as a GalNAc residue attached to the first mannosyl residue by a β(1,4) linkage |CITS: [2897081]|. The GalNAc residue may be elongated further by a β(1,3) linked galactose, and the galactose can be modified in turn by sialic acid |CITS: [1350920]|. The physiological roles of these side-chains are largely unknown., The enzyme responsible for transferring the GalNAc residue to the first mannose is a Golgi-located N-acetylgalactosamine transferase encoded by the |FRAME: HS15293| gene |CITS: [29374258]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-205 Pimelate| is a seven-carbon linear saturated dicarboxylic acid. In Gram-positive organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, pimelate is used as a precursor to |FRAME: BIOTIN| |CITS: [28196402]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5005|)., Pimelate is also used as an organic chemical raw material, altthough at much smaller quantities than |FRAME: ADIPATE|. At present, pimelate is produced industrially mainly through the cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-110|, which has disadvantages of requiring strict reaction conditions and an expensive catalyst., About This Pathway, As of 2025, the biosynthetic pathway of pimelate is still unknown, though an engineered pathway for its production has been reported |CITS: [35352865]|., A patent application from 2011 described an engineered pathway, termed the "reverse adipate degradation pathway" (RADP), in which the enzymes involved in |FRAME: PWY-8354 "adipate degradation"| were used to catalyze its production under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [Burgard11]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8347|). In 2014 the pathway was tested successfully by cloning enzymes from multiple organisms and expressing them in |FRAME: TAX-562|, though the yield was rather low, at 0.7mg adipate per liter |CITS: [24895214]|., In 2015 the pathway was unexpectedly found to function in the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-57106| |CITS: [26189483]|. |FRAME: ORG-57106| is an engineered strain constructed to produce |FRAME: PROPANOL|. The native celR gene (encoding |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.4|) was replaced by the |FRAME: G-12174| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1488|, which encodes a bifunctional |FRAME: MONOMER-15847| |CITS: [21757023][26227414]|. When grown on glucose (5 g/L) the organism was found to produce 0.18 g/L adipate |CITS: [26189483]|. In later work the pathway was reconstructed in |FRAME: TAX-562| by cloning all of the |FRAME: TAX-2021| genes. Overexpression of the |FRAME: G-107676| gene, combined with deletion of the succinate-CoA ligase gene to promote accumulation of succinyl-CoA, resulted in production of 68.0 g/L adipate |CITS: [29625225]|., The first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-21927| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-107673| gene), was found to have a broad substrate spectrum, and could catalyze the Claisen condensation of multiple acyl-CoAs to produce different, dicarboxylic acids. One of the combinations catalyzed by the enzyme is the condensation of |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to form |FRAME: 3-OXOPIMELOYL-COA|. The remaining 4 enzymes of the pathway appear to have a broad substrate range as well, and by feeding |FRAME: GLUTARATE| to the cells, pimelate was produced. Further improvements that included deletion of the bioF gene and introduction of a glutarate transporter resulted in production of 21.8 mg/L of pimelate. Replacement of two of the enzymes with different isozymes increased production to 36.7 mg/L |CITS: [35352865]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|). Analogs of these pathways are also found in the metabolism of deoxyhexoses such as |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-fucoses| (see |FRAME: RHAMCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|). The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]|.
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|). The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimnberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]|.
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees |CITS: [Pingman57]|). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. Free arabinose is formed during the degradation of complex polymers, as in |FRAME: PWY-6790|, |FRAME: PWY-8006|, and |FRAME: PWY-6813|., This pathway has been studied in detail in |FRAME:TAX-562|. Because L-arabinose enters |FRAME:TAX-562| either by a low-affinity proton-driven transporter (AraE) or a high-affinity ATP-driven system (AraFGH), its first intracellular form is unphosphorylated. An isomerase and a kinase convert it to |FRAME: L-RIBULOSE-5-P|, which is convereted by an epimerase to |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|., |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| enters the pentose phosphate pathway, which produces multiple key precursor metabolites as well as reducing power and metabolic energy.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis, (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|),, and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is, highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for, a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes, that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase, enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal, dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, The glyoxalase system is probably the most common pathway that catalyzes the conversion of methylglyoxal to a less toxic product. In this pathway, |FRAME:METHYL-GLYOXAL| is converted to |FRAME:D-LACTATE| via the intermediate, |FRAME:S-LACTOYL-GLUTATHIONE| by 2 enzymes:, |FRAME:GLYOXI-CPLX| isomerizes the hemithioacetal that is formed non-enzymatically from |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| and |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| to |FRAME:S-LACTOYL-GLUTATHIONE|. |FRAME:GLYOXII-MONOMER| hydrolyzes the thioester to |FRAME:D-LACTATE| regenerating the glutathione in the process., The fate of |FRAME:D-LACTATE| has been less well characterized. The most likely scenario is its conversion to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| by the action of |FRAME:DLACTDEHYDROGFAD-MONOMER|, a flavoprotein specific to the D-form of lactate |CITS: [497162][12127981]|., The pathway is ubiquitous in biological life, taking place in the cytosol of prokaryotes and the mitochondria of eukaryotes |CITS: [15987839]|.

General Background, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is a reducing acidic sugar that often forms a hexapyranose ring structure. It is common in carbohydrate chains of proteoglycans and is part of mucous animal secretions (such as saliva), cell glycocalyx and intercellular matrix. The hexapyranosic form |FRAME: CPD-12521| is found in the glycosaminoglycans |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates|, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: Hyaluronan|., In animals D-glucuronate is degraded as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5525|. Bacteria degrade |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by three different pathways: the isomerase pathway, which is found in enterobacteria (see |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY|), an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-17141| (see |FRAME: PWY-6501|), and an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, Both oxidative pathways begin with the oxidation of |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by the inducible |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.203| to |FRAME: CPD-12595| |CITS: [19060141][19921179]|. The lactone was initially thought to hydrolyze only by a spontaneous reaction |CITS: [2471][19897761]|. Later |FRAME: EC-5.4.1.4| was found, an enzyme that converts |FRAME: CPD-17138| to the 1,4-lactone, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6486|. Though that enzyme was not tested for its activity with |FRAME: CPD-12595|, enzymatic conversion of that compound is likely. However, the isomerase, as well as the enzyme that processes its products, are not found in genomes of members of the |FRAME: TAX-135621|, |FRAME: TAX-119060|, and |FRAME: TAX-80864|. Instead, these organisms have dedicated enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124194| and |FRAME: G-124195| genes, that hydrolyze the 1,5-lactones directly to a linear product as shown here |CITS: [30249705]|., With the help of three additional enzymes, two dehydratases and a dehydrogenase, the pathway proceeds to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6499|), which can be metabolized via the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| or used in many other pathways.

Both purine and pyrimidine deoxyribonuclosides can be degraded by phosphorylases that removes the |FRAME: DEOXY-D-RIBOSE-1-PHOSPHATE| moiety, leaving the free nucleobases. , In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: DEOXY-D-RIBOSE-1-PHOSPHATE| is converted to |FRAME: DEOXY-RIBOSE-5P| by a |FRAME: PPENTOMUT-MONOMER|.  A specific |FRAME: DEOXYRIBOSE-P-ALD-MONOMER| splits D-deoxyribose-5-phosphate, yielding |FRAME: GAP|, which enters central metabolism through the glycolytic pathway, and |FRAME: ACETALD|, which must be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| before it can enter central metabolism via the TCA cycle., Although |FRAME: TAX-562| is able to utilize the deoxyribose moiety of deoxyribonucleosides, unlike the closely related organism |FRAME: TAX-90371| it is unable to utilize exogenously supplied deoxyribose, due to lack of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.229|.

Summary: The yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| can directly assimilate inorganic sulfur for the biosynthesis of, sulfur-containing amino acids., Detailed description of the pathway converting |FRAME: SULFATE| to |FRAME: HS| is provided in, the pathway |FRAME:SO4ASSIM-PWY|., |FRAME:HOMO-SER| is biosynthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which in turn is synthesized, from |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|, a TCA cycle intermediate., Homoserine is activated through esterification to form the O-acetyl ester by the enzyme, |FRAME:MONOMER-9423|., |FRAME: HS|, which is the end result of sulfate assimilation, reacts with, |FRAME:CPD-667|, replacing the acetyl group and forming |FRAME:HOMO-CYS|., Finally, |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| can be converted to |FRAME: CYS| via |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|, by a reversible transsulfuration pathway. , In contrast to enteric bacteria and mammals, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has two transsulfuration pathways, employing two separate sets of enzymes |CITS: [9409150]|.

The ketocarotinoid |FRAME:CPD-7847| has been found in bacteria, fungi and a number of unicellular algae |CITS:[Goodwin80]| where its biosynthesis in the various organisms has been characterized to some extend (see |FRAME:PWY-5288|). |FRAME:CPD-7847 Astaxanthin| and |FRAME:CPD-7847| mono- and diester have also been discovered in plants but so far only in the flower petals of a few species of the genus Adonis such as Adonis aestivalis |CITS:[Neamtu66] [Kamata87] [21263199]| and Adonis annua |CITS:[14445279] [Egger65]|. This ketocarotenoid had also been reported as an autumn carotenoid present in Metasequoia glyptostroboides |CITS:[Czeczuga87]| but later studies could not confirm the findings |CITS:[Ida91]|. The pigment |FRAME:CPD-7847| and some other signature ketocarotinoids such as |FRAME:CPD-7849| accumulate in the petals and provide the blood red color of flowers in those Adonis species., |FRAME:CPD-7847 Astaxanthin| is an sought-after additive to feed fish and crustaceans bred in captivity which is imperative for attaining their natural coloration, and in poultry feed (summarized in |CITS:[Amaya14]|) as well as a neutraceutical for the benefits of humans |CITS:[3524619] [8660397] [10740262] [24402174]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-7847| has become an candidate for cardiovascular therapies |CITS:[Fassett11]|, shown potential in cancer chemoprevention |CITS:[22418926] [12549764]| and has promise as an ant-inflammatory and antioxidant agent which may also be able to modulate gene activities |CITS:[15479561]|. For that reasons the elucidation of the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-7847| is not only an research project for academics but also reflects strong economic interests. Although the synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-7847| in the lab has long been achieved |CITS:[Leftwick67]| and is the currently cheapest way to produce this ketocarotinoid, there is strong interest in producing |FRAME:CPD-7847| biosynthetically in order to meet the high level of demand. The most promising candidates for that venture is currently the green algae Haematococcus pluvialis |CITS:[10740262]| and the red yeast Xanthophyllomyces dendrorhous (also known as Phaffia rhodozyma) |CITS:[21046372] [12898396]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5288|), but attempts have also been made to include higher plants |CITS:[16957020] [18992217] [Misawa09] [21398427]|. However, in order to successfully establish a profitable |FRAME:CPD-7847|-targeted biosynthesis, the complete biosynthetic sequence, catalyzing enzymes and the pathway's regulation and interconnectivity must first be elucidated |CITS:[Farre10]|. , It appears that the biosynthetic order, ancestry of involved enzymes, reaction catalysis and respective enzymatic nomenclature of the |FRAME:CPD-7847| biosynthesis in Adonis differs significantly from the ones observed in bacteria, fungi and green algae (see |FRAME:PWY-5288|). The key reaction in the |FRAME:PWY-7636| is the successive 4- and 4'-hydroxylation of the two β-rings of |FRAME:CPD1F-129| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17650| and |FRAME:CPD-7853|, respectively. This reaction is catalyzed by two carotenoid β-ring 4-dehydrogenases encoded by cbdf1 and 2 which also catalyze the subsequent 3,4-desaturation of the β-rings producing the ketocarotenoid pathway intermediates |FRAME:CPD-17651| and |FRAME:CPD-7854| |CITS:[15659105]| (see also |FRAME:PWY-5291|). The latter is substrate for the carotenoid 4-hydroxy-β-ring 4-dehydrogenases ketonizing the 4-hydroxyl groups encoded by hbdf1 and 2 forming |FRAME:CPD-17652| and subsequently |FRAME:CPD-7851| |CITS:[21862704]|. Interestingly, the final step(s) of the pathway, i.e. the 3- and 3'-hydroxylation of the β-rings is carried out by the same enzyme(s) that catalyzed the initial reaction of the pathway, i.e. the carotenoid β-ring 4-dehydrogenases encoded by cbdf1 and 2 forming the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-7847| via |FRAME:CPD-7849| |CITS:[21862704]|. In contrary to the |FRAME:CPD-7847| biosynthesis in bacteria, cyanobacteria, fungi and green algae the corresponding pathway in Adonis appears to be linear along the reaction chain of symmetric 4 (4')-hydroxylation, 3,4 (3',4')-desaturation, 4 (4')-ketolation and 3 (3')-hydroxylation |CITS:[15659105] [21862704]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Gangliosides "Gangliosides"| are molecules composed of |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids| (|FRAME: Ceramides| and |FRAME: Oligosaccharides|) with one or more sialic acids (usually |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) linked to the sugar chain. They are components of the cell plasma membrane that modulates cell signal transduction events, and appear to concentrate in lipid rafts., The name ganglioside is derived from the ganglion cells of the brain, from which the first gangliosides were isolated by the German scientist Ernst Klenk in 1942 |CITS: [Klenk42]|. Indeed, gangliosides dominate the composition of the glycocalyces of most of the cells of the vertebrate nervous system. Although gangliosides with various glycan structures are found in every vertebrate tissue, they are markedly more abundant in the nervous system, where each cell has on average about 10 million cell surface gangliosides |CITS: [27261254]|. Typical concentrations in adult brain range from 2 to 14 μg lipid-bound sialic acid/mg protein, and the concentration in the grey matter is about 5-fold higher than in white matter |CITS: [6470716]|. Ganglioside expression in the brain correlates with neurogenesis, synaptogenesis, synaptic transmission, and cell proliferation |CITS: [7755881][19575597][26007338]|., Variations in the sialoglycan and lipid components of the gangliosides result in hundreds of distinct ganglioside structures with a variety of functions that ranges from regulating receptor tyrosine kinases to directing cell-cell communication, cell-substrate interaction, adhesion, and protein targeting |CITS: [17991443]|. Mammalian brain gangliosides, however, are dominated by only four types of gangliosides - |FRAME: CPD-7188 "ganglioside GM1a|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1a "ganglioside GD1a"|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1b "ganglioside GD1b"| and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1b "ganglioside GT1b"| |CITS: [22735313]|. The ceramide lipid components of brain gangliosides are dominated by a single fatty acid (|FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|) attached to one of two sphingoid bases, |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-19684| |CITS: [21113547]|., While many non-human mammals synthesize gangliosides that contain two types of sialic acids - |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| and |FRAME: CPD-273|, mammalian brain gangliosides almost exclusively carry the former., Like other glycosphingolipids, gangliosides are biosynthesized in the Golgi apparatus stepwise by a series of glycosyltransferases that use nucleotide sugar donors to first glucosylate ceramide and then elongate the saccharide chain. They are formed at intracellular membranes, from which they are transported to the plasma membrane by exocytotic membrane flow |CITS: [21698755]|., |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| |CITS: [10320813]|., The ceramide lipid of glycosphingolipids is embedded in the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, with the glycan extending 2-2.5 nm outward, perpendicular to the plane of the lipid bilayer |CITS: [19056784]|. What makes gangliosides different from other glycosphingolipids is the incorporation of sialic acids. With a mean Pka value of around 2.6, sialic acids are more acidic than the majority of carboxylic acids and negatively charged at most physiological pH values., The sialic acids are added by a family of glycosyltransferases called sialyltransferases, which catalyze the transfer of a sialic acid from |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| to the acceptor carbohydrate. All mammalian sialyltransferases characterized to date have type II transmembrane topology and contain highly conserved motifs called sialyl motifs L (long), S (short), and VS (very short) |CITS: [8448381][7685014][9134419]|. Sialyl motif L is characterized by a 45-60-amino acid region in the center of the protein, and it is involved in binding |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| |CITS: [7829476]|. Sialyl motif S, which is located in the carboxy-terminal region and consists of a 20-30-amino acid stretch, is involved in binding both the donor and acceptor substrates |CITS: [9545292]|. Sialyl motif VS is also located in the carboxy-terminal region, and is thought to be involved in the catalytic process |CITS: [9134419][11278664]| (reviewed in |CITS: [11980897]|)., About the nomenclature of gangliosides, Ganglioside naming is somewhat complex. Two ganglioside nomenclature systems are currently in use. The most commonly used is a short-hand nomenclature suggested by Svennerholm, which was initially based on the migration order of |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio-series"| gangliosides in chromatography |CITS: [14066623]|. The more comprehensive system formulated by IUPAC |CITS: [9826173]| is applied much less frequently., A typical ganglioside name using the old system looks like |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"|., The first letter refers to the glycosphingolipid series. For example, the "G" stands for the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|. The next letter describes the number of sialic acid residues: (A = 0, M =1, D = 2, T = 3, Q = 4, P = 5, H = 6, S = 7). The following number describes the number of the non-sialic residues, and is derived in a rather complex manner. It was initially assumed that the number of such residues does not exceed 5. The number in the name was calculated as (5 - the number of uncharged carbohydrates)., In addition, several sub-series of gangliosides have been defined based on the number of sialic acids attached to the galactose residue of the lacosylceramide core. If no sialic residues are present at that position, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: 0-Series-Ganglioside "0-series"|. Those with one sialic acid at that position are named the |FRAME: A-Series-Gangliosides "a-series"|, those with two sialic acids belong to the |FRAME: B-Series-Gangliosides "b-series"|, and so on. |FRAME: C-Series-Gangliosides "C-series"| or higher gangliosides are rare in adult mammals and birds, but are abundant in fish and amphibians. Confusingly, GM1b and GD1c are both 0-series gangliosides, despite having a "b" and "c" in their names., So, for example, the |FRAME: Ganglioside-GQ1b "ganglioside GQ1b"| is named as follows: G = belongs to the ganglio series, Q = 4 sialic acids, 1 = 4 non-sialic residues, and b = belongs to the b-series, meaning two of the sialic acids are attached to the inner galactose.

Summary: General Background, This pathway and the linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-7028| depict parts of the pathway for the O-linked glycosylation of certain |FRAME: SER| residues in proteins such as pilin in |FRAME: TAX-482| species |CITS: [21542610]|. An analogous pathway leading to N-linked glycosylation of certain protein |FRAME: ASN| residues in |FRAME: TAX-194| species is shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7031| (reviewed in |CITS: [21506607]|. Protein O-linked glycosylation has also been described in |FRAME: TAX-287| strains |CITS: [16740931][17085575]|, |FRAME: TAX-817| |CITS: [21115495]|, and possibly other genera |CITS: [22391990]|, although the pathways have not been shown. Pathways for archaeal O-linked protein glycosylation remain undefined (reviewed in |CITS: [20976295][21506607]|)., Until the mid-1970s, protein glycosylation was thought to occur only in eukaryotes. However, prokaryotic N-linked and O-linked protein glycosylation was later found in a restricted set of archaea and bacteria, including pathogens and commensals. The prokaryotic glycans can include both common and rare monosaccharides (reviewed in |CITS: [18694827][9076508]|). The biological role of protein glycosylation in prokaryotes is not yet fully elucidated, but it is thought to be involved in host interactions such as adherence and pathogenicity (|CITS: [19681908]|, in |CITS: [22389484]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [12687605][14659687][20948550][20371512]|). Prokaryotic protein glycosylation may also enhance protein stability |CITS: [19154179]|., Eukaryotic N-linked glycosylation has been extensively studied in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|). Archaeal N-linked glycosylation was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-2242| |CITS: [1270419][4455689]|. Bacterial N-linked glycosylation was discovered in the Gram-negative |FRAME: TAX-197| (|CITS: [10361304]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [15738950][12781527]|)., Although the overall process of protein N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes, archaea and bacteria is similar (reviewed in |CITS: [16510493][21506607]|), this pathway for O-linked protein glycosylation is unique. It involves polyprenyl-linked intermediates, whereas most other O-linked protein glycosylation pathways involve sequential transfer of monosaccharides from activated donors |CITS: [21542610]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-482| species the pgl genes can produce glycans with variable structures. The trisaccharide shown here becomes a pilin glycan in |FRAME: TAX-485| and |FRAME: TAX-487|. The disaccharide is an alternative glycan produced by the product of gene pglH in |FRAME: TAX-482| species |CITS: [21542610][21606362]|., Analogous to the bacterial N-glycosylation pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7031|), this pathway begins on the cytosolic side of the cell membrane and ends with the glycosylation reaction (shown in the reaction link) on the periplasmic side. A putative flippase encoded by pglF translocates the lipid-linked glycan into the periplasm (not shown) |CITS: [21542610]|., The phosphoglycosyltransferase function of PglB attaches phospho-N,N'-diacetylbacillosamine to the membrane bound |FRAME: CPD-9646| carrier. Then, either PglA and PglE may act sequentially to transfer two galactosyl residues, or PglH may transfer a glucosyl residue. Following the flippase-catalyzed translocation, the oligosaccharyltransferase PglO transfers the oligosaccharide "en bloc" to certain protein |FRAME: SER| residues forming an O-linkage with the serine hydroxyl group |CITS: [21542610]|.

This Pathway in Bacteria:, |FRAME: TAX-83333| can synthesize glutamate from ammonia in two pathways., In addition, if complex sources of nitrogen are available, other pathways (see below) become active and, take over glutamate synthesis. , The pathway shown here synthesizes |FRAME:GLT| directly from |FRAME: AMMONIA|,, |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, and |FRAME: NADPH|. , The other is a cyclic pathway, which consists of two steps and requires ATP, and is described at, |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY|)., Unlike the cyclic pathway, the pathway shown here does not require ATP to drive the reaction., The Km for ammonia of this reaction is much higher than that of the, ATP-driven cyclic pathway., Expression of the two ammonia-to-glutamate pathways is regulated so that they operate under different, environmental circumstances. The ATP-independent pathway functions when ammonia is abundant; the, ATP-driven pathway functions when concentrations of ammonia are low. The ATP-independent pathway, offers significant energy savings over the ATP-driven pathway, as the latter uses over 10, percent of the cell's total expenditure of ATP when it is active |CITS: [11807064]|., If complex sources of nitrogen are available, glutamate can be synthesized from arginine, (|FRAME: AST-PWY|) or proline (|FRAME: PROUT-PWY|) or from α-ketoglutarate by, transamination of the amino group from arginine or aspartate. , The complexity of glutamate biosynthesis reflects the quantitatively central role that the amino acid plays, in the metabolism of |FRAME:TAX-562|. It is a major constituent of E. coli's proteins and because it is, a major nitrogen donor for other biosyntheses, about 80% of the cell's nitrogen flows through glutamate, when |FRAME:TAX-562| is growing on a medium containing ammonia as the total source of nitrogen. , This Pathway in Yeast:, Like |FRAME: TAX-83333 | yeast cells contain 2 pathways for the synthesis of glutamate. , One of the pathways, shown here, is mediated by two isoforms of glutamate dehydrogenase, encoded by, |FRAME: YOR375C| and |FRAME: YAL062W| |CITS: [2989290][9287019]| (this pathway), while the second, pathway is driven by the combined activities of glutamine synthetase and glutamate synthase,, encoded by |FRAME: YPR035W| and |FRAME: YDL171C|, respectively |CITS: [2570348][8923741]|, (see |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY|)., Studies of |FRAME: YOR375C| and |FRAME: YAL062W| regulation indicate that the cell uses these, isoforms under different growth conditions |CITS: [11562373]|. Expression of GDH3 is induced by ethanol, and repressed by glucose, whereas GDH1 expression is high in either carbon source. Gdh1p uses, α-ketoglutarate at a higher rate than Gdh3p., Thus, under fermentative growth conditions, Gdh1p drives glutamate biosynthesis, whereas in, nonfermentable or limiting carbon sources, Gdh3p is the key isoform involved in balancing distribution of, α-ketoglutarate to glutamate biosynthesis and energy metabolism.

General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase I (NDH-1) and fumarate reductase (FRD) the transfer of electrons from NADH to fumarate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. Two electrons are transferred from the NADH oxidation site of NDH-1 to the fumarate reduction site of FRD by a menaquinone pool. , Anaerobic growth of E. coli K-12 with fumarate operates preferentially with NDH-I. Electron transport from NADH to fumarate decreases significantly in a strain lacking NDH-I compared to wild-type. No significant decrease occurs in a strain lacking NADH dehydrogenase II (NDH-II) |CITS: [9063459]| , By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is believed to function as a proton pump translocating 4 H+ per NADH oxidized (2e-), however, a lower ratio of 3H+/2e- has also been proposed |CITS: [22392981]|. The H+/e- ratio for NDH-1 is at least 1.5 |CITS: [8892824]|. Fumarate reductase does not contribute to the generation of proton potential |CITS: [10373108]|. Proton pumping by NDH-I is the only mechanism for PMF generation in the NADH to fumarate electron transport chain |CITS: [9063459]| , Expression of the nuo operon, encoding NDH-1 is stimulated by fumarate |CITS: [9063459]|. Expression of the frd operon is repressed by the preferred electron acceptors, oxygen and nitrate and induced by fumarate |CITS: [2999070], [3298218] [3035558]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14177 Paromomycin| is |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics|, first isolated from |FRAME: TAX-68185| in the 1950s |CITS: [18947845]|. Like other aminoglucoside antibiotics, it inhibits protein synthesis by binding to 16S ribosomal RNA |CITS: [11587639]|., Paromomycin is active against not only Gram-negative and many Gram-positive bacteria, but also some protozoa and cestodes. It is the only aminoglycoside with clinically important antileishmanial activity. While it is not used anhy more against bacteria, it is still used clinically to treat some intestinal infections such as cryptosporidiosis, amoebiasis, and leishmaniasis |CITS: [13812394][8036682][18447603]|. In 2007 it was licensed in India as an effective, well tolerated and affordable treatment for visceral leishmaniasis |CITS: [18947845]|., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-282216| paromomycin is modified further into the antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-14176| |CITS: [21689223]|., About This Pathway, For information about the pathway leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-14125|, please see |FRAME: PWY-7014|., The original organism in which |FRAME: CPD-14177| was discover, |FRAME: TAX-68185|, has been studied little and no sequence information related to antibiotic biosynthesis is available for it. The pathway leading from |FRAME: CPD-14125| to |FRAME: CPD-14177| has been studied to a certain level in |FRAME: TAX-282216|. However, even in this organism most of the enzymes were not studied in detail, and their function is deduced from sequence similarity to related enzymes used in the biosynthesis of other aminoglycoside antibiotics. The first two enzymes in this pathway, encoded by |FRAME: G-15051| and |FRAME: G-15052|, are similar to the |FRAME: G-15040 BtrL| and |FRAME: G-15041 BtrP| enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1397|, which have been studied as part of |FRAME: CPD-14140| biosynthesis |CITS: [17482823]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7015|)., The next two enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-15053| and |FRAME: G-15054|, are similar to the |FRAME: G-15047 NeoK| and |FRAME: G-15045 NeoL| enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1906|, which have been studied as part of |FRAME: PWY-7016| |CITS: [18311744]|., Finally, the last two enzymes in this pathway have been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-282216| itself |CITS: [21689223]|.

Summary: The strictly anaerobic δ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-316277| is able to ferment |FRAME: BENZOATE| and |FRAME: CROTONATE| in the presence and in the absence of a hydrogen-consuming partner. When a suitable partner is present, the reducing equivalents that are formed during the fermentation process can be released as hydrogen gas or formate, which are readily consumed by the synthrophic partner for CO<sub>2</sub> or sulfate reduction |CITS: [18707608]|., However, when the organism grows in pure culture, the release of reducing equivalents as H<sub>2</sub> or formate is not thermodynamically favorable. The organism solves the problem by fermenting the substrates to |FRAME: ACET| with the concomitant production of the unusual metabolite |FRAME: CPD-575|, which is excreted from the cell (see also |FRAME: PWY-7402|). Thus, the redox equivalents produced during oxidation of |FRAME: BENZOATE| or |FRAME: CROTONATE| to |FRAME: ACET| are recycled via the production of |FRAME: CPD-575|. The formation of |FRAME: CPD-575| is a unique fermentation process that has been described so far only in |FRAME: TAX-316277| |CITS: [18707608][11282627]|., In the case of |FRAME: CROTONATE| fermentation, it is first activated to |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA|, which acts as a branch point. While some of it is fermented to acetate by the enzymes of the late part of the |FRAME: CENTBENZCOA-PWY "anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway"|, the rest is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-575|. The formation of cyclohexane carboxylate from crotonate is believed to involve many of the enzymes used for the same benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway operating in the reverse direction. Those enzyme follow a reversed route up to |FRAME: CYCLOHEXA-15-DIENE-1-CARBONYL-COA|, which is converted in two steps to |FRAME: CPD-577|. The two enzymes that catalyze these steps have been identified, purified, and characterized. |FRAME: CPD-577| is converted by an as-yet unidentified enzyme to |FRAME: CPD-575| |CITS: [23667239]|.

Summary: Cresols (|FRAME: CPD-109|, |FRAME: CPD-112| and |FRAME: CPD-108|, also known as ortho-, meta-, and para-cresol, respectively) are phenolic compounds commonly found in sites of fuel processing activities such as coal gasification and the fractionation of coal, tar, and petroleum. Cresols are commonly used in disinfectants, surfactants, and wood preservatives, and are intermediates in the manufacture of pesticides and resins. Despite their similarity, the different isomers of cresol are degraded through different pathways, and in some cases, the same isomer can be degraded by more than one pathway., The pathway for |FRAME: CPD-108| degradation was reported already in 1957. The researchers showed that a non-fluorescent Pseudomonad initiates the degradation by oxidation of the methyl group with the successive formation of |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE|, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| and |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| |CITS: [13445676]|., The degradation starts with the hydroxylation of the methyl group by a tetrameric α2β2 flavocytochrome, |FRAME: EC-1.17.9.1| |CITS: [3790500]|. The enzyme oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-108| (p-cresol) to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| in two steps, via |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-BENZYL-ALCOHOL| |CITS: [3460061]|., The product, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE|, is oxidized by the NADP+-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.96| to form |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| |CITS: [10565539][23736872]|. Hydroxybenzoate is subsequently hydroxylated to form |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, which is completely dissimilated by an ortho cleavage pathway., The enzymes that participate in this pathway are also involved in the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-18280| (see |FRAME: PWY-7703|).

Summary: General Background, Plants accumulate and mobilize |FRAME: Starch| in both photosynthetic tissue (leaves) and non-photosynthetic storage tissues (such as tuber and seed endosperm). In leaves, starch is synthesized during the light period and is degraded during the dark period, as depicted in this pathway. In storage tissues, starch is degraded during tuber sprouting and seed germinating. Except for seed endosperm where starch degradation occurs in an acellular tissue (see |FRAME: PWY-842|), starch degradation generally occurs in the plastids (chloroplast of leaves and amyloplast of tubers) where starch accumulates. Isoforms of the starch degradation enzymes are also found and in many cases abundant in extra-plastidic subcellular locations in leaves and tubers. Their physiological functions are not well understood |CITS: [20192737]|., About This Pathway, In leaves, starch biosynthesis leads to the formation of granules in the chloroplast stroma during the light period and the granules are degraded during the dark period. The starch granules have very complex structures. |FRAME: Starch Starch| is composed of two different polyglucan chains, |FRAME: CPD-7043 amylopectins| and |FRAME: Alpha-Amyloses α-amyloses|. The |FRAME: CPD-7043 amylopectin| chains form double helices that are tightly packed in layers of crystalline lamellae. Starch degradation must proceed from the outside of these granules and requires the disruption of the tight association between amylopectin chains |CITS: [20192737]|., Recent work has helped to reveal multiple enzymes that are involved in making the exterior polyglucan chains on the starch polymers more accessible to hydrolytic degradation. Notably, in Arabidopsis two enzymes, |FRAME: AT1G10760-MONOMER| (GWD) |CITS: [16914145][17666166]| and |FRAME: AT5G26570-MONOMER| (PWD) |CITS: [15686522][15618411]| sequentially catalyze the addition of phosphate to the C6 and then the C3 residues of glucosyl residues in the amylopectin chains to move them from an insoluble to a soluble state |CITS: [19325165][20192737]|. , The SEX4 |FRAME: AT3G52180-MONOMER| can help to make these soluble chains better substrates for the hydrolytic activity of β-amylases by removing the phosphates residues |CITS: [20192737]|. , β-amylases such as |FRAME: AT4G17090-MONOMER BAM3| remove maltose units from the α-1,4-linked unbranched chains of the amylopectin. Maltose is then transported out of the chloroplast for inclusion in various cytosolic sugar metabolism pathways |CITS: [14704427]|., As |FRAME: AT4G17090-MONOMER BAM3| and other chloroplastic β-amylases release maltose from the exposed chains, they eventually encounter branch points introduced by α-1,6-linked glucosyl residues. Glucoses linked in this manner are not substrates for β-amylases so these enzymes cannot act on the exposed chains again until a debranching enzyme, such as |FRAME: AT4G09020-MONOMER isoamylase 3| (ISA3) removes the α-1,6 linkages. Chloroplastic β-amylases can then continue to release maltose units for export. Malto-oligosaccharide chains containing fewer than four glucosyl residues can be acted on by |FRAME: AT5G64860-MONOMER DPE1| or other chloroplastic disproportionating enzymes to release glucose. This glucose can also be transported to the cytosol for use in sugar metabolism |CITS: [20192737]|., Though it is not depicted in this pathway, Chloroplastic β-amylases enzymes also likey act on any α-1,4-linked-malto-oligosaccharide chains that are free in the stroma that contain at least four glucose residues |CITS: [20192737]|. , In some species, including |FRAME: TAX-3055| |CITS: [17018036]|and |FRAME: TAX-4530| (rice) |CITS: [18621947]|, the |FRAME: Linear-Malto-Oligosaccharides malto-oligosaccharides| may also be broken down to |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by malto-oligosaccharide phosphorylase enzymes (see |FRAME: RXN-12392 reaction|). Although a chloroplastic enzyme with this activity can be found in Arabidopsis (|FRAME: AT3G29320-MONOMER PHS1|), there is no evidence that it actually participates in starch degradation in that species |CITS: [15173560]|. In general, the potential in planta role of these enzymes in starch degradation remains a matter of on-going debate and investigation |CITS: [20192737]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HEPARIN "Heparin"| is a glycosaminoglycan polymer with a molecular weight ranging from 3 to 30 kDa. It is composed of a variable sulfated repeating disaccharide units composed of hexuronic (either iduronic or glucuronic) acid and glucosamine residues, in which the 2 position of the hexuronic acid and the 2, 3, or 6 positions of glucosamine may be sulfated. The two residuces within a disaccharide are linked by a (1->4) bond, as are the disaccharides to each other., The main disaccharide unit consists of |FRAME: CPD-12518| and |FRAME: CPD-12533| [it is often referred to as IdoA(2S)-(1->4)-GlcNS(6S)]. However, |FRAME: CPD-12518| can be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12521|, and |FRAME: CPD-12533| can be replaced by |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: CPD-12545| or |FRAME: CPD-12565|., The basic IdoA(2S)-(1->4)-GlcNS(6S) disaccharide accounts for at least 85% of heparin isolated from beef lung and about 75% of heparin from porcine intestinal mucosa |CITS: [Casu89][Gatti79]|., Variations in the extent and location of sulfation, as well as the conformation of the alternating hexuronic acid residues, lead to a high degree of heterogeneity. By convention, heparin refers to molecules which possess a high sulfate content and large amounts of iduronic acid., The structure of |FRAME: HEPARIN| is very similar to that of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| (also known as heparitin sulfate). Heparan sulfate contains lower amounts of sulfate and less iduronic acid than heparin |CITS: [5484472]|. In addition, heparan sulfates disaccharide units are organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains, while heparin disaccharides are sulfated more uniformly |CITS: [15047699]|., About This Pathway, This heparin degradation pathway has been elucidated in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-984|, which is capable of degrading heparin to its basic constituents., The pathway starts with |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.7|, (also known as heparinase), which degrades heparin to trisulfated disaccharides. The lyase acts by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disaccharides. , The trisulfated unsaturated disaccharides are desulfated by |FRAME: EC-3.1.6.13|, yielding a disulfated disaccharide., This enzyme also occurs in mammals, and mutations in the human enzyme (endcoded by the |FRAME: CPLX-8124 IDS| gene) cause the serious disorder mucopolysaccharidosis type II (MPS II, Hunter syndrome). Patients with MPS II store and excrete large amounts of partially degraded |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, and the disease often results in significant developmental defects and death before the age of 10 |CITS:[1901826][9147653][11462244]|., This desulfated product is a substrate for |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.56|, which cleaves the disaccharide generating an unsaturated uronic acid and |FRAME: N6-O-disulfo-D-glucosamine|., The unsaturated uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-13122|, is degraded to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP| as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6507|., In the last steps of the pathway the sulfate groups are then removed from |FRAME: N6-O-disulfo-D-glucosamine| by the sequential activities of |FRAME: EC-3.1.6.11| and |FRAME: EC-3.10.1.1|, yielding free |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE| and inorganic sulfate |CITS: [4730325]|.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms. As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called |FRAME: Siderophore siderophores|, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions. The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane. In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, Pyoverdines are a group of structurally related siderophores produced by fluorescent |FRAME: TAX-286| species under iron starvation conditions. While many Pseudomonads make more than one type of siderophore molecules, pyoverdines are always the primary iron uptake system., Pyoverdines are species-specific, and the structures of more than 100 different pyoverdines from different strains and species of Pseudomonas have been determined |CITS: [15079896][18221784]|. All of these compounds possess similar structure composed of three parts: a conserved fluorescent dihydroxyquinoline chromophore, a variable acyl side chain (either dicarboxylic acid or amide) bound to the amino group of the chromophore, and a variable peptide chain linked by an amide group bound to the C1 (rarely C3) carboxyl group of the chromophore |CITS: [17118662]|. The peptide chains vary greatly, but consist of 6-19 amino acid residues containing one or more hydroxamates. The pyoverdine chromophore is derived from |FRAME:TYR| |CITS: [Nowak-Thompson94]| and |FRAME: CPD-470| |CITS: [Bockmann97]|., The best studied pyoverdine is |FRAME: CPD-12096| (PVDI), which is produced by the opportunistic pathogen |FRAME: TAX-208964|. In this molecule the peptide chain consists of the eight amino acid residues |FRAME: D-SERINE|-|FRAME: ARG|-|FRAME: D-SERINE|-|FRAME: CPD-12097|-c(|FRAME: LYS|-|FRAME: CPD-12097|-|FRAME: THR|-|FRAME: THR|). The last four amino acids form a cycle |CITS: [19787431]|. Even though the pathway has not been fully characterized, much is known about it., The major part of synthesis is carried out in the cytoplasm by four large non ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-11722|, |FRAME: G-11723|, |FRAME: G-11724| and |FRAME: G-11725|, that together synthesize the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-12098|., The first NRPS enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15310|, contains modules for the binding of |FRAME: GLT|, |FRAME:TYR| and |FRAME: CPD-470| |CITS: [12354233]|. The latter is produced from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| by |FRAME: CPLX-7978|, encoded by |FRAME: G-11721| |CITS: [15317763]|. |FRAME:TYR| is epimerized to |FRAME: D-TYROSINE| and condensed with |FRAME: CPD-470| into a tetrahydropyrimidine ring which is later modified to form the dihydroxyquinoline chromophore. |FRAME: GLT| forms the attachment point of an acyl side chain, and is later modified to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, |FRAME: CPD-22398| or |FRAME: CPD-22399| (the last two are often hydrolyzed to |FRAME: SUC| and |FRAME: RS-Malate malate|, respectively) |CITS: [15079896]|. A fourth module of PvdL catalyzes acylation by myristate, which is later removed (after translocation of the compound into the periplasm) by the acylase |FRAME: G-11155 PvdQ| |CITS: [12354233][19778968]|., The second NRPS enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15311|, contains four modules that bind (in this order) an |FRAME:SER|, an |FRAME: ARG|, a second |FRAME:SER|, and an |FRAME: CPD-12097|. The latter is produced from |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| by the combined action of |FRAME: MONOMER-15307| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15308|, encoded by |FRAME: G-11719| and |FRAME: G-11720|, respectively |CITS: [8106324][11390682]|. These amino acids are added to the molecule, forming the first part of the peptide moiety. During the process, the serine residues are epimerized to a D configuration., The nascent molecule is transferred to the third NRPS enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15312|, which adds an |FRAME: LYS| and a second |FRAME: CPD-12097|, and then to the fourth NRPS enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15313|, which adds the final two |FRAME: THR| residues. The last L-threonine forms a bond with the second |FRAME: CPD-12097|, resulting in a cyclic structure. The product, known as |FRAME: CPD-12098|, is released from the complex and transported to the periplasm for maturation. This transport is mediated by a transporter encoded by pvdE |CITS: [19787431]|., The process of maturation, which is carried out in the periplasm, starts with removal of the acyl chain, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-11155|. Next, a tyrosinase-like enzyme, |FRAME: G-80437 PvdP|, catalyzes two successive oxidations, forming |FRAME: CPD-22393|. An additional oxidation catalyzed by |FRAME: G-80439 PvdO|, possibly in conjunction with other proteins, produces |FRAME: CPD-12096|., The last steps in the pathway involve side-chain modifications that transform the original |FRAME: GLT| side chain to either |FRAME: CPD-22398| (catalyzed by |FRAME: G-80440 PvdN|) or to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (catalyzed by |FRAME: G-80441 PtaA|). The modified pyoverdines are then secreted via various transport systems such as PvdRT-OmpQ, and bind outside ferric iron |CITS: [30386787]|., The mature pyoverdines are exported from the periplasm by two efflux systems - the ABC-type pyoverdine exporter PvdRT-OmpQ and the MdtABC-OpmB pyoverdine efflux system |CITS: [30346656]|. After chelating iron, the ferric siderophore is transported back into the cells via the outer membrane FpvA-TonB ferric-pyoverdine transporter system |CITS: [8335619][15733922][18221784]|. Once in the periplasm the ferric-pyoverdine complex is probably first scavenged by the periplasmic FpvC-FpvF complex |CITS: [23009327]|. In the next step the iron is reduced by the FpvG ferric-pyoverdine reductase, in a process that involves several other proteins, including the the inner membrane protein FpvH |CITS: [28192658]|. The reduced iron ions are released and transported into the cytoplasm by the ABC-type Fe2+ transporter FpvDE, although the exact process is still not well understood |CITS: [17148441][23009327]|. The siderophore is recycled by being exported back out of the cell by the two efflux pumps described above |CITS: [Yeterian09][30386787]|., The pvd genes are expressed only under iron starvation, and expression requires the alternative sigma factor PvdS |CITS: [12207687]|.

|FRAME: CPD-14130 "2-Exo-hydroxy-1,8-cineole"| (also known as 6-endo-hydroxycineole) is the first metabolite of |FRAME: CPD-4261|, a cyclic monoterpene containing an internal ether linkage. The trivial name of 1,8-cineole is eucalyptol. It is found in the oil from the leaves of Eucalyptus radiata var. Australiana and is used in the fragrance and flavor industries. Microorganisms metabolizing 1,8-cineole as sole carbon source must cleave both the ring and ether linkages. A role for a biological Baeyer-Villiger oxygenation mechanism had been proposed in this cleavage. This mechanism inserts an oxygen atom between the ketone carrying carbon and the adjacent carbon carrying a methyl group (reviewed in |CITS: [1368150]|)., When |FRAME:TAX-1827| sp. strain C1 was grown with 1,8-cineole as sole carbon source, two metabolites, 6-endo-hydroxycineole and 6-oxocineole were produced. These were purified and identified by GLC, GLC-MS, NMR and optical rotation. |FRAME:TAX-1827| grown with 1,8-cineole was also able to utilize either of these two metabolites as sole carbon source, whereas succinate grown cells could not utilize them, suggesting enzyme induction |CITS: [DRWILLIAMS]|., Two enzymes, 6-endo-hydroxycineole dehydrogenase and 6-oxocineole oxygenase were identified in crude extracts of 1,8-cineole grown cells. Reversible NAD-dependent dehydrogenation of 6-endo-hydroxycineole to 6-oxocineole was shown. The 6-oxocineole oxygenase activity was unstable during purification attempts and its initial oxygenation product could not be characterized. However, crude extracts of 1,8-cineole grown cells showed substrate stimulation of oxygen consumption when incubated with 6-oxocineole and NADPH. This reaction produced the lactone (R)-5,5-dimethyl-4-(3'-oxobutyl)-4,5-dihydrofuran-2(3H)-one (represented in the pathway as 4,5-dihydro-5,5-dimethyl-4-(3-oxobutyl)furan-2(3H)-one). However, this lactone was believed to be an artifact formed from an acid metabolite during the acidification and extraction procedure. The product of oxygenation was hypothesized to be the acid metabolite produced by Baeyer-Villiger oxygenation and spontaneous lactone cleavage reactions |CITS: [DRWILLIAMS]|. , Due to the lack of purified 6-oxocineole oxygenase, a known Bayer-Villiger enzyme 2,5-diketocamphane 1,2-monooxygenase from |FRAME:TAX-303| was studied using several related substrates including 6-oxocineole. With 6-oxocineole as substrate, a lactone was formed and pH stat studies suggested spontaneous lactone cleavage. It was also shown that a chemical Baeyer-Villiger oxygenation of 6-oxocineole produced the same lactone, (R)-5,5-dimethyl-4-(3'-oxobutyl)-4,5-dihydrofuran-2(3H)-one, as the biological oxygenation of 6-oxocineole. This suggested that 6-oxocineole is degraded by a biological Baeyer-Villiger oxygenation reaction |CITS: [DRWILLIAMS]|. , In the proposed pathway for 6-endo-hydroxycineole degradation, a putative 1,8-cineole 6-endo-hydroxylase forms 6-endo-hydroxycineole. Support for the existence of such an enzyme is based on accumulation of 6-endo-hydroxycineole and induction of the dehydrogenase. A ring oxygen insertion into 6-oxocineole by a Baeyer-Villiger reaction is hypothesized to produce the strained lactone 1,6,6-trimethyl-2,7-dioxobicyclo-[3.2.2]nonan-3-one. This lactone spontaneously forms a hemiacetal and further spontaneous cleavage of the ether linkage forms an acyclic hydroxyacid, followed by ring closure to form the lactone 4,5-dihydro-5,5-dimethyl-4-(3-oxobutyl)furan-2(3H)-one. The route of further metabolism of the acyclic hydroxyacid intermediate was not reported |CITS: [DRWILLIAMS]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [1368150]|.

Summary: Many bacterial species are capable of oxidizing cyclic alcohols and ketones to the corresponding, dicarboxylic acids., The growth of microorganisms with cyclohexane as carbon and energy source was reported already, in 1948 in |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [Imelik48]|. Later work has documented metabolism of, |FRAME: CPD-8923| and |FRAME: CYCLOHEXANOL| in several strains, including |FRAME: TAX-469|,, |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-279| species |CITS: [1261][Tanaka77][Stirling77][Anderson80], [16346796][14568154]|., Cyclohexane is first oxidized to cyclohexanol |CITS: [Stirling77][16346796]|. A pathway for the, degradation of cyclohexanol to |FRAME:ADIPATE| was first suggested in |FRAME: TAX-1818| |CITS: [5119767]|, and later described in detail in |FRAME: TAX-40214| |CITS: [1261]|. It seems to be common to many, different strains |CITS: [10940013][10224025][12021799]|., The five enzyme that catalyze this pathway are encoded by the ChnABCDE genes , |CITS: [10940013]|, which are found in one or more operons, although the structure of the operons, can differ significantly among species |CITS: [12021799]|., The product of this pathway, |FRAME:ADIPATE|, is likely processed via β-oxidation to, |FRAME:SUC-COA| and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, which enter intermediary metabolism |CITS: [5916393], [4962165]|.

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) is involved in the regulation of several crucial physiological and developmental processes in plants, as well as in the adaptative responses to environmental stresses |CITS:[zeevaart88]|. The regulation of these processes hinges on the size of the bioactive ABA pool. This pool is thought to be maintained through a finely tuned equilibrium between ABA biosynthesis and catabolism. Among the ABA catabolic pathways, the 8'-hydroxylation pathway leading to the formation of phaseic acid (PA) appears to be the major regulation point. In addition, the catabolic sequence of the formation of |FRAME:CPD-7729| via 9'-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-693| (see |FRAME:PWY-7640|) and the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17688| (see |FRAME:PWY-7642|) are also considered to be involved in the cellular regulation of this phytohormone. Another important ABA catabolic route operates through the conjugation of ABA (or its hydroxylated derivatives such as PA) with glucose. One of the most widespread conjugates is |FRAME:CPD-7727| (ABA-GE) |CITS:[16662451]|. ABA conjugates are thought to be physiologically inactive and to accumulate in vacuoles as the plant matures |CITS:[16664479],[lehmann86]|. Recently, however, ABA-GE was postulated to be involved in the long-distance transport of ABA through the vascular system |CITS:[11741037],[hansen99]|., About This Pathway, The glucosylation of ABA to form ABA-GE has been shown to be catalyzed by a number of glucosyltransferases from Adzuki bean and Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[12114582],[lim05]|. These enzymes require UDP-glucose as substrate for the reaction. They tend to be able to use a variety of substrates such as indole-3-acetate or trans-cinnamate. The existence of a β-glucosidase able to catalyze the release of ABA from ABA-GE has been reported in crude extracts of barley leaves, more specifically in the intercellular washing fluid |CITS:[10948220]|., The anabolic reaction resulting in |FRAME:CPD-7727| (ABA-GE) catalyzed by various abscisic acid glucosyltransferases and the catabolic sequence releasing |FRAME:CPD-693| from the ABA-GE by abscisic acid glucose ester β-glucosidases appears to be fine-tuned to the localized and overall cellular regulation of |FRAME:CPD-693|. In contrast to the 7'-, 8'- and 9'-hydroxylation pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-7642|, |FRAME:PWY-5271| and |FRAME:PWY-7640|, respectively) which irreversibly degrade |FRAME:CPD-693|, the metabolism of |FRAME:CPD-7727| reflects an pathway which can quickly remove or add |FRAME:CPD-693| in response to the respective requirements of the cell. The interaction of anabolic and catabolic enzymes in the pathway to contribute to the fine-tuning of |FRAME:CPD-693| in the cell has been demonstrated. , The |FRAME:AT3G21780-MONOMER| together with two homolog UDP-glucosyltransferases is involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-7727|, hence lower the cellular |FRAME:CPD-693| concentration and shown, when knocked down by RNAi in transgenic Arabidopsis plants, to affect |FRAME:CPD-693| responses by interfering with the expression of genes involved in the 8'-hydroxylation pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5271|). This expression-repression pattern is inversed, i.e. when the glucosyltransferase(s) are suppressed the expression of the 8'-hydroxylation pathway (Cyp707A1 - A4) is induced and vice versa |CITS:[24676855]|. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that the CYP707A enzymes are also involved in the 9'-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-693|, hence the |FRAME:PWY-7640| is also directly affected by the functional status of the glucosyltransferase(s) |CITS:[21414645]|. Along the same line of experimental evidence it has been demonstrated that the abscisic acid glucose ester β-glucosidases in Arabidopsis encoded by BG1 |CITS:[16990135]| and BG2 |CITS:[22582100]| releasing |FRAME:CPD-693| from |FRAME:CPD-7727| are also in sync with the expression behavior of the glucosyltransferase(s) |CITS:[24676855]|. Interestingly, the β-glucosidases are located in different cell organelles, BG1 is localized to the endoplasmatic reticulum (ER) whereas BG2 is situated in the vacuole. The fact that BG2 can rescue Δbg1 mutant plants indicates the existence of an regulatory network for the homeostasis of |FRAME:CPD-693| across cellular organelles, which along with the glucosyltransferase(s) located in the cytosol provide a net of |FRAME:CPD-693| receptors which may be involved in adjusting the required concentration of |FRAME:CPD-693| more locally rather than on an overall cellular level by coordinating catabolic and anabolic pathways of |FRAME:CPD-693| |CITS:[24676855] [22582100]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, also known as vitamin C, fulfils multiple essential roles in both plants and animals., Being a strong reducing agent, it functions as an antioxidant and a redox buffer. It is also a cofactor for several enzymes, which are involved in many important pathways, including collagen hydroxylation, carnitine biosynthesis, norepinephrine biosynthesis, and hormone and tyrosine metabolism., In plants L-ascorbate is also implicated in defense against pathogens and in control of plant growth and development., A significant proportion of a plant's ascorbate is found in the apoplast (the aqueous solution permeating the cell walls) |CITS: [15608627]|., Under aerobic conditions L-ascorbate is oxidized in cells to |FRAME: CPD-13907 dehydroascorbate| (via the radical |FRAME: CPD-318|), which can be recycled back to ascorbate by the |FRAME: PWY-2261|. However, once formed, dehydroascorbate can be further broken down in vivo by irreversible reactions, escaping the |FRAME: PWY-2261|., Several pathways for the irreversible catabolism of ascorbate have been described. Facultatively aerobic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-573| degrade L-ascorbate by different pathways under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6961| and |FRAME: PWY0-301|). The anaerobic pathway begins with phosphorylation of ascorbate (mediated by a PTS-type transporter), while the aerobic pathway proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-334|. Both pathways produce |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a centeral metabolite that is fed into the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [18708499]|., Plants from the |FRAME: TAX-3602| family (e.g. grapes) metabolize ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-13059| and |FRAME: L-IDONATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6704|). The tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 1-4 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 4 and 5 |CITS: [Loewus99][16567629]|. , The geraniaceous plant |FRAME: TAX-1417776| metabolizes ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| and |FRAME: OXALATE| via a different pathway, with |FRAME: L-THREONATE|, rather than L-idonate, as an intermediate (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6960|). In this case the tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 3-6 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 2 and 3 |CITS:[Loewus99][15862089]|. Grapes are also known to accumulate |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [DeBolt04]|, and thus may be using both pathways to generate tartrate., About This Pathway, Under anaerobic conditions |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-573| degrade |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: L-ASCORBATE-6-PHOSPHATE| utilizing the enzymes encoded by the ula regulon (see |FRAME: PWY0-301|). Under aerobic conditions L-ascotbate is auto-oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-334|, which can not be degraded by the anaerobic pathway. A different set of enzymes, encoded by the yiaK-S operon, enables the cells to catabolize L-ascorbate under aerobic conditions as well |CITS: [18708499]|., The yiaK-S operon, which is controled by the YiaJ repressor, encodes two unique proteins - a reductase (|FRAME: EG12279|) and a kinase (|FRAME: EG12284 yiaP|) as well as three proteins that are paralogous to ula operon proteins: a carboxylase (|FRAME: EG12285 yiaQ|) and two epimerases (|FRAME: EG12287 yiaS| and |FRAME: EG12286 yiaR|) (note tha many of these genes are now known under different names). YiaK and YiaP convert |FRAME: CPD-334| to |FRAME: CPD-2343|, which can be processed by the rest of the enzymes to |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a centeral metabolite that is fed into the pentose phosphate pathway., Curiously, the yia regulon is also regulated by |FRAME: L-ASCORBATE-6-PHOSPHATE|, a metabolite that can only be produced by the |FRAME: EIISGA|, which is encoded by the ula regulon. Thus, efficient aerobic metabolism of L-ascorbate is dependent on the presence of both systems. In addition, the expression of the yiaK-S operon, but not the expression of the ula regulon, is regulated by oxygen availability. General Background, |FRAME: D-APIOSE| is a unique branched-chain pentose found principally in plants. It is a key component of structurally complex cell wall polysaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| (RG-II) in the cell walls of higher plants and in apigalacturonan in the cell walls of aquatic monocots, and is a building block of a large number of naturally occurring secondary metabolites., The name "apiose" is derived from the flavonoid glycoside |FRAME: 7-O-BETA-D-APIOFURANOSYL-12-BETA-D-GLU apiin|, from which it was first obtained |CITS: [Vongerichten01]|. Apiin itself is named after parsley (|FRAME: TAX-4043|), which at the time was known as Apium petroselinum |CITS: [26848180]|., About This Pathway, The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway were found by first identifying genes encoding D-apiose-specific substrate binding proteins (SBPs), since SBPs, which are components of certain types of transporters, are often clustered with catabolic genes that metabolize the compound the SBPs bind to., The pathway has been characterized using enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1042878| and |FRAME: TAX-78245|, and was predicted to be present in 108 bacterial species.
