Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, The yellow carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-15033| is a poly-hydroxy derivative of |FRAME: CPD1F-129| isolated only from some prokaryotes, including some species of cyanobacteria |CITS: [18794175]|, the |FRAME: CPD-9067|-containing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210512| [|CITS: [16585705 ]|, the moderately thermophilic aerobic photosynthetic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-60454| |CITS: [9103629]|, the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1113698| |CITS: [16085816]|, the soil-residing |FRAME:TAX-41276| |CITS:[16781830]|, the strictly aerobic photosynthetic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1044| |CITS: [Takaichi90]|, and most |FRAME: TAX-13687| species |CITS: [Jenkins79]|., The necessary genes required to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-15033| from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, namely crtB, crtI, crtY, crtZ and crtG, have been identified from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-1113698|, |FRAME: TAX-41276|, |FRAME: TAX-197221| and |FRAME: TAX-179878| |CITS: [18794175][16085816][16781830][22509387]|., When the |FRAME:G-15521| gene of |FRAME: TAX-179878| was introduced to |FRAME: CPD1F-130|- and |FRAME: CPD1F-129|-accumulating |FRAME:TAX-562| cells, the transformants produced |FRAME: CPD-15033| and |FRAME: CPD-15034|, respectively, confirming that the gene encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-17879|, and demonstrating that the enzyme can also accept β-carotene as substrate |CITS: [22509387]|. However, not all crtG genes from the various bacteria encode enzymes exhibiting the same substrate preference. For instance, in spite of the very high sequence similarity between the crtG's of Brevundimonas SD212 and Brevundimonas DC263 (79% amino acid identity) the crtG from SD212 encoded a carotenoid 2-hydroxylase operating on both |FRAME:CPD1F-130| and ketocarotinoids (see|FRAME:PWY-7637|) whereas the same enzyme from DC263 could only 2- and 2'-hydroxylate |FRAME:CPD1F-130| forming |FRAME:CPD-15033| via |FRAME:CPD-15032| and was unable to metabolize xanthophylls with ketonized β,β-ionone rings (this pathway) |CITS:[16781830]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Phytobilins Phytobilins| are tetrapyrrole molecules that are synthesized by plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Major classes of phytobilins are:, 1. |FRAME: Phycobilins Phycobilins|, which are the chromophores of |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins| |CITS: [16663825]| and some algal phytochromes |CITS: [8616213]|, 2. |FRAME: Phytochromobilins Phytochromobilins|, which are the chromophores of higher plants |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| |CITS: [1634523][7744741]|., |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins Phycobiliproteins| are light-harvesting accessory pigments of cyanobacteria, red algae and cryptophytes, and |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| are photoreversible light signal-transducing pigments of plants, some algae, and some cyanobacteria., One of the major class of phycobiliproteins in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: Phycocyanins phycocyanins|, and its chromophore is called |FRAME: Phycocyanobilins phycocyanobilin|. There are two stereoisomers of phycocyanobilin, but apparently only |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN| is produced initially, with the second isomer potentially produced, by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathways for the production of the four cyanobacterial |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-3702| pathway for |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| biosynthesis, have been elucidated. These five chromophores share a common precursor, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, which is the product of heme macrocycle cleavage by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18|. |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is subsequently reduced by one of several possible ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases., |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN| is biosynthesized from heme in a pathway that begins with the opening of the tetrapyrrole macrocycle of protoheme to form |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: SGL_RS03350-MONOMER| |CITS: [9744099]|. In at least some cyanobacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1148|, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| is converted to |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN| by a single enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-13954|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10655| gene |CITS: [11283349]|. The same conversion is apparently catalyzed by multiple enzymes in the red algae |FRAME:TAX-2771| |CITS: [2505754]|., There are two stereoisomers of phycocyanobilin, |FRAME: CPD-17222| and |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN|. While |FRAME: CPD-17222| is the major pigment that is released from phycobiliproteins by methanolysis |CITS: [1634523]|, only |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN| is produced initially |CITS: [11283349]|, with the second isomer produced either spontaneously or by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1280| is natural inhabitant of the skin and mucous membranes of mammals, able to cause disease in humans ranging from mild wound infections to more serious ailments including septic shock, endocarditis, and osteomyletis., |FRAME: TAX-1280| is known to produce four siderophores: |FRAME: CPD-12589| |CITS: [2139423]|, |FRAME: CPD-12590| |CITS: [8400765]|, |FRAME: CPD-21048| |CITS: [14688077]|, and |FRAME: CPD-21049| |CITS: [9125585]|., |FRAME: CPD-12590 "Staphyloferrin B"| is an α-hydroxycarboxylate siderophore comprised of L-2,3-diaminopropanoate, citrate, 1,2-diaminoethane and 2-oxoglutarate moieties |CITS: [8400765]|. Its biosynthesis involves three different NRPS-independent siderophore (NIS) synthase enzymes, which catalyze condensation reactions with units of dicarboxylic acids, diamines, and/or amine alcohols to form the final siderophore structure. The NIS enzymes differ from the non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPS) in that intermediates and enzymes are freely dissociable from one another during assembly., The sbnA–I operon that encodes |FRAME: CPD-12590| biosynthesis has been reported first in 2004. Insertional inactivation of the |FRAME: G1I0R-73| gene or deletion of the entire operon eliminated production of the siderophore and resulted in decreased growth in iron-starved media |CITS: [14688077][15547261][19400778 ]|. The biochemical, characterization of the enzymes catalyzing the later part of the pathway - the NIS synthases |FRAME: G1I0R-73 SbnE|, |FRAME: G1I0R-74 SbnF| and |FRAME: G1I0R-71 SbnC|, and the decarboxylase |FRAME: G1I0R-73 SbnE|, was reported in 2009 |CITS: [19775248]|. Later papers described the activity of SbnA and SbnB |CITS: [21906287][24485762][26794841]| and SbnI |CITS: [29483190]|, whose combined action produces |FRAME: L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE| from |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: GLT|.

|FRAME: CPD-8186 Umbelliferone| is a coumarin found in all higher plants and an important intermediate in the synthesis of more complex derivatives, such as poly-hydroxylated/methoxylated/prenylated coumarins, furanocoumarins and pyranocoumarins |CITS: [Bourgaud06]|., Early tracer experiments performed with |FRAME: TAX-286619 "Anthoxanthum nitens (vanilla grass)"| and |FRAME: TAX-47083| |CITS: [13805037][Ellis71]| and with |FRAME: TAX-39329 "Lavandula angustifolia (lavender)"| |CITS: [13873722]| showed that |FRAME: CPD-674 cinnamate| is incorporated into coumarin and 7-hydroxycoumarins and that para-hydroxylation was a prerequisite for ortho-hydroxylation. These observations lead to proposing that |FRAME: CPD-8186| is formed after the ortho-hydroxylation of |FRAME: COUMARATE| that leads to synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-14005|, and that the latter is subsequently transformed into umbelliferone by the spontaneous closure of the lactone ring, which occurs under acidic or neutral conditions (reviewed in |CITS: [Bourgaud06]|)., |FRAME: MONOMER-17096|, a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase enzyme that catalyzes this hydroxylation, was identified much later from the common rue, |FRAME: TAX-37565| |CITS: [22168819]|. The purified enzyme could not accept |FRAME: COUMARATE|, but catalyzed the hydroxylation of the activated form |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA|, producing |FRAME: CPD-14010| which undergoes spontaneous lactonization to form |FRAME: CPD-8186|., The same enzyme can also hydroxylate |FRAME: FERULOYL-COA|, forming |FRAME: CPD-13328| that lactonizes spontaneously to form |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN| |CITS: [22168819]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6792|).

Gossypol is a yellow pigment. It presents in roots, foliar tissues and seeds of cotton. Gossypols and related terpenoids are stored in the gossypol glands which are characteristic of all cotton plants. Gossypol along with its precursors hemigossypol and desoxyhemigossypol, are dominant phytoalexins protecting cultivated cotton plants against economically important diseases such as verticillium wilt caused by fungi. Co-existing with gossypol is its methyl ether. The methyl ethers of gossypol and its related terpenoids are less toxic to pathogens and herbivorous insects. Gossypol has also been known toxic to monogastric animals (non-ruminants) for long time. In more recent years, it was also found , toxic and causes death of ruminants live stocks |CITS: [2667706]|. The toxicity of gossypol in cotton seeds renders their value as a feed which is a misfortune given that cotton seed contains over 30% proteins and 30% oils. Gossypol also holds medicinal potentials as a male antifertility agent, and as antitumour, antiviral and antioxidant drugs |CITS: [16255680]|., (+)-δ-cadinene synthase catalyzes the first committed step in gossypol biosynthesis, converting FPP to (+)-δ-cadinene. (+)-δ-cadinene is consequently hydroxylated at the C-8 position leading to 8-hydroxy-(+)-δ-cadinene. Via yet uncharacterized steps, 8-hydroxy-(+)-δ-cadinene is converted to desoxyhemigossypol, which is a branching point leading to both gossypol and methylated gossypol. Methylation of desoxyhemigossypol is catalyzed by a , highly specific methyltransferase, desoxyhemigossypol-6-O-methyltransferase. Modulation at this enzyme by the cotton plant may present a control for the relevant level of methylated and unmethylated terpenoids that affects the plant's resistance to pathogens and insects |CITS: [12009981]|.

Summary: General Background, The S-layer (surface layer) is a ubiquitous component of the cell envelope in many bacteria and archaea |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. It is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble |FRAME: O-Antigens "O-antigens"| of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides| of Gram-negative organisms |CITS: [11741945]|., The backbone of the glycan chain of the S-layer protein of |FRAME: ORG-6194| (DSM 10154) is built by four |FRAME: CPD-13829| units, with two of them substituted by α-1,2-linked |FRAME: CPD-13886| units |CITS: [12740380]|. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15596|, the thymidine diphosphate activated molecule that serves as a donor for the assembly of the glycan chain., About This Pathway, Like several other modified sugar nucleotide biosynthetic pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-6942| for an example), the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15596| starts with |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is activated by |FRAME: TTP| and converted to |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps. These steps are also involved in the synthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| (see |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|). However, the last three steps of this pathway are catalyzed by unique enzymes. These enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-14823|, |FRAME: G-14825|, and |FRAME: G-14826| genes, catalyze isomerization, transamination, and transacetylation, respectively, producing |FRAME: CPD-15596|. The five genes included in this pathway are located in a single operon |CITS: [12740380]|., In the case of |FRAME: TAX-318161|, it has been shown that the third and fifth reactions are catalyzed by a |FRAME: CPLX-8948| comprising an amino-terminal N-acetyltransferase domain connected by a flexible loop to the carboxy-terminal isomerase domain |CITS: [24128043]|.

Organic compound volatiles are main factors of aroma in fruits and vegetables. The cultivated tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) has been shown to biosynthesize more than 400 such compounds of which, however, only a small number exceed the olfactory threshold which is discernible by humans |CITS:[Buttery87] [9881368]|. For the economically important crop tomato it has been shown that the composition of the volatiles released by tomato fruits influences the preference and, consequently, purchase behavior of consumers |CITS:[22633806] [22677284]|. Varieties of tomato effuse different amounts of an aroma referred to as 'smoky' which originates from the glycosidic cleavage of phenylpropanoid related diglycosides. Volatile aglycones conjugated with a hexosepentose moiety to give off the 'smoky' aroma are |FRAME:CPD-400 guaiacol| |CITS:[9881368]| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-23 guaiacol biosynthesis|) but also |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-22 methylsalicylate biosynthesis|) and |FRAME:CPD-6481 eugenol| |CITS:[19889876]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5859 eugenol and isoeugenol biosynthesis|). Especially the release of |FRAME:CPD-400 guaiacol| has been associated with the attribute 'smoky' from various food products |CITS:[14690393] [17090925] [18052239]| which can be determined by a number of methods amongst them the use of trained sensory panels |CITS:[Menendez12] [9881368]|. , Glycosylation of specialized metabolites is a major biochemical conversion observed in plants which confers properties such as better solubility, faster transport within cells, converting reactive to more inert compounds for storage, deactivation and detoxification of xenobiotica |CITS:[15241472] [16669774]|. Moreover, biological activities, taste, and color are also known to be associated with glycosylation of specialized metabolites in plants |CITS:[21845280] [25088478]|. Phenylpropanoid volatiles (PhP-V) have been found in tomato fruits as cleavable diglycosides and non-cleavable triglycosides |CITS:[19889876]|. In particular, the PhP-V digycosides |FRAME:CPD-19216 guaiacol O-β-D-xylopyranosyl-(1->6)-O-β-D-glucopyranoside|, |FRAME:CPD-19215 methylsalicylate O-β-D-xylopyranosyl-(1->6)-O-β-D-glucopyranoside| and |FRAME:CPD-14737 eugenol O-β-D-xylopyranosyl-(1->6)-O-β-D-glucopyranoside| and their non-volatile triglycoside counterparts |FRAME:CPD-19196 guaiacol 2-O-β-D-glucopyranosyl-(1 -> 2)-[O-β-D-xylopyranosyl-(1 -> 6)]-O-β-D-glucopyranoside|. |FRAME:CPD-19197 methylsalicylate 2-O-β-D-glucopyranosyl-(1 -> 2)-[O-β-D-xylopyranosyl-(1 -> 6)]-O-β-D-glucopyranoside| and |FRAME:CPD-19194 eugenol 2-O-β-D-glucopyranosyl-(1 -> 2)-[O-β-D-xylopyranosyl-(1 -> 6)]-O-β-D-glucopyranoside| have been identified there |CITS:[20574729]|. In tomato the amount of nonvolatile glycoconjugated phenylpropanoid compounds has been found to surpass the volatiles from the same compound class |CITS:[17902628] [20014855]|. , The biochemistry which occurs during fruit ripening is very complex and much remains to be learned about the underlying physiology and molecular biology |CITS:[Robards99] [Aivalakis08]|. Although progress has been made over time regarding the elucidation of pathways, genes and enzymes addressing valued traits in tomato |CITS:[24446507]| not much is known about glycosylated volatile biosynthetic pathways |CITS:[24692651]|. This pathway depicts the conversion of volatile phenylpropanoid diglycosides to their non-volatile phenylpropanoid triglycosid complements which is an important step towards control and manipulation of aroma traits in tomato. The catalyzing glucosyltransferase encoded by NSGT1 in Solanum lycopersicum was identified using a combinatorial approach including complementary metabolomics, trait locus mapping, tomato genome sequence data and untargeted gene expression analysis. The expression of NSGT1 was well correlated with the glycosylation pattern in tomato fruits and biochemical assays with crude recombinant protein extracts confirmed the substrate specificity of the protein to glucosylate phenylpropanoid volatile diglycosides forming the corresponding triglycosides responsible for the 'smoky' aroma of the fruits (respective compounds are specified above) |CITS:[23956261]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HS "Hydrogen sulfide"| is acknowledged as a toxic gas with an odor of rotting eggs, and its existence in biological tissues has been known for over 300 years |CITS: [22314625]|. However, it is has only recently been identified as a physiologic messenger molecule. The gasotransmitter elicits a range of physiological effects, including modulation of blood pressure, reduction of ischemia reperfusion injury and inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain |CITS: [1894850][15845845][17878306]|. , Hydrogen sulfide acts as an endothelial derived relaxing factor that regulates normal blood pressure by acting through ATP-sensitive potassium channels, and participates in various phases of the inflammatory process, in an anti-inflammatory capacity. Hydrogen sulfide has emerged as the third endogenous gaseous mediator in the central and peripheral nervous system. , Two other gases, |FRAME: CPD-15028| and |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE|, are also endogenously produced and have been proposed as neuronal messengers in the brain. In the CNS, hydrogen sulfide is generated mainly in astrocytes and neurons, and may participate in cognition, memory and neuroprotection |CITS: [8558235]|. In the peripheral nervous system, hydrogen sulfide may be involved in autonomic control of the cardiopulmonary and gastrointestinal functions, and regulate pain and inflammation |CITS: [21275894]|., Currently, the most advanced efforts to develop therapeutic agents involve the combination of hydrogen sulfide donors with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Hydrogen sulfide provides cytoprotection to gastric mucosa adversely affected by NSAIDs, while in combination with the inhibition of |FRAME: PWY66-374 "prostaglandin synthesis"| has potential synergistic anti-inflammatory influences |CITS: [22314625]|., About this Pathway, In mammalian tissues |FRAME: HS| is produced endogenously mostly from |FRAME: CYS| and/or |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|. The two pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzymes |FRAME: CPLX66-335| and |FRAME: CPLX66-336|, are key in the synthesis of this metabolite via transsulfuration reactions |CITS: [21275900]|. In mammals, the activity of |FRAME: CPLX66-335| is highly regulated. The enzyme contains a heme cofactor that functions as a redox sensor and utilizes |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as an allosteric activator |CITS: [19531479]|. Impaired |FRAME: CPLX66-335| activity causes hyperhomocystinuria and hyperhomocysteinemia, both risk factors for cardiovascular diseases. , Impaired activity of |FRAME: CPLX66-336| causes cystathioninuria, hypercystathioninemia and increase the risk of developing atherosclerosis and bladder cancer. This trans-sulfuration pathway yields novel thioether metabolites. The γ-replacement reaction, which condenses two molecules of homocysteine, yields |FRAME: CPD66-96|, a novel biomarker, which has been reported in the urine of homocystinuric patients. The β-replacement reaction, which condenses two molecules of cysteine, generates |FRAME: CPD-3736|. Excessive production of hydrogen sulfide in hyperhomocysteinemia may contribute to the associated cardiovascular pathology |CITS: [19261609]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NIACINE "Nicotinate"| (niacin, 3-pyridinecarboxylate) is a carboxylic derivative of |FRAME: PYRIDINE| that is found in nature as part of pyridine cofactors (e.g., NAD and NADP) and alkaloids (e.g., |FRAME: NICOTINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12317|). Nicotinate is an essential compound for those organisms that are not able to synthesize it, and is thus also called vitamin B3. In addition, nicotinate is also a carbon and nitrogen source for different bacteria and some fungi., Microorganisms have multiple ways of degrading pyridine and its derivatives, and degradation of these compounds , is relevant to both biological and industrial processes. The degradation of nicotinate by both aerobic and , anaerobic organisms involves the initial formation of |FRAME: 6-HYDROXY-NICOTINATE|, but the pathways diverge after that. , This pathway describes the degradation of |FRAME: NIACINE| as performed by the aerobic bacteria |FRAME: TAX-294| and |FRAME: TAX-303|., The pathway was originally studied in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-303| and |FRAME:TAX-294|, such as |FRAME: ORG-6130| and |FRAME: ORG-6129| |CITS: [13475371][5578917]|. The segment of the pathway beginning with |FRAME: 2-5-DIHYDROXYPYRIDINE| has also been shown in two strains of |FRAME:TAX-222| sp. grown on |FRAME: 2-HYDROXYPYRIDINE| or |FRAME: CPD-12318| |CITS: [4455192][4664939]|., A much more recent study of |FRAME: TAX-160488| identified the genetic determinants of the pathway |CITS: [18678916]|., This study also found that the conversion of |FRAME: 2-5-DIHYDROXYPYRIDINE| to |FRAME: MALEAMATE| is a two step process via |FRAME: CPD-12278|, catalyzed by two distinct enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G1G01-4210| and |FRAME: G1G01-4208|, and not a single step as was assumed until then., The pathway starts with two hydroxylation reactions. The first enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-11618|, derives the oxygen from water, rather than molecular oxygen. The Pseudomonas enzyme is unusual in having three c-type cytochromes rather than FAD, which is the usual cofactor of enzymes in this family. The cytochromes enable the enzyme to interact directly with respiratory chain, most likely transferring the electrons to an oxygen-dependent terminal oxidase |CITS: [13546162][18678916][19118407]|. The second hydroxylation is catalyzed by |FRAME: G1G01-4209-MONOMER|, a dioxygen-dependent enzyme., The next reaction, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G1G01-4210|-encoded |FRAME: G1G01-4210-MONOMER|, cleaves the ring structure. Following a deformylation to |FRAME: MALEAMATE|, a |FRAME: G1G01-4206-MONOMER| enzyme catalyzes hydrolytic deamination, a step that liberates |FRAME: AMMONIUM| and enables |FRAME: NIACINE| to serve as a sole nitrogen source for the organisms., The final reaction of the pathway is isomerization to |FRAME: FUM|, a TCA cycle intermediate |CITS: [13475371][8840783]|.

Summary: |FRAME:TAX-36749|, a small semi-aquatic herb of the |FRAME:TAX-3792| family does not biosynthesize lignins but accumulates a number of tri- to tetramethylated |FRAME:CPD-520| glucosides (this pathway) and tri- to pentamethylated |FRAME:CPD-14866| glucosides (see |FRAME:PWY-7151|) instead. The elucidation of the two pathways which includes the identification and characterization of five O-methyltransferases, two O-glucosyltransferases and one |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent dioxygenase has been accomplished by Ragai K. Ibrahim and colleagues (reviewed in |CITS:[Ibrahim05]| |CITS:[Ibrahim89]|). , Only two 2'-hydroxy derived polymethylated quercetin glucosides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14856| and |FRAME:CPD-14859| representing the final products of this pathway, are found in |FRAME:TAX-23242| whereas the intermediate precursors do not accrue to any detectable amount |CITS:[Collins81a]|. The biosynthesis of these intermediates had to be investigated in detail in in vitro experiments. The formation of the polymethylated quercetin glucosides are carried out in a coordinated and highly ordered sequence. The catalytic properties obtained from in vitro characterization of quercetin 3-O-methyltransferase (see |FRAME:PWY-6064|) |CITS:[De82]|, 3-quercetin 7-O-methyltransferase |CITS:[3994393]| |CITS:[3415239]| and 3,7-dimethylquercetin 4'-O-methyltransferase |CITS:[3994393]| |CITS:[3994394]| strongly point to the ordained methylation sequence: |FRAME:CPD-520| - |FRAME:3457-TETRAHYDROXY-3-METHOXYFLAVONE| - |FRAME:345-TRIHYDROXY-37-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE| - |FRAME:CPD-10510|. |FRAME:345-TRIHYDROXY-37-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE 3,7-Dimethylquercetin| is the main metabolite from which the |FRAME:CPD-14866| derived glucoside series branches off but |FRAME:CPD-10510| is also accepted by the 6-hydroxylase, hence channeling partial methylated |FRAME:CPD-520| derivatives into the polymethylated |FRAME:CPD-14866| glucoside biosynthetic pathway. All of the above enzymes are highly substrate- and position-specific catalyzing only the corresponding A-, (3, 7) and B-ring (4') positions and exclusively accept either the unmethylated or the respective mono- or dimethylated flavonols. , The further metabolism of the partial methylated quercetins involves a yet to be determined monooxygenase which introduces the 2'-hydroxy group to the B-ring yielding |FRAME:CPD-14853|. The final products of the pathway are catalyzed by a sequence of a position-specific 2'-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[16663104]| |CITS:[Latchinian87]| |CITS:[6236078]| followed by a 3'-O-specific methyltransferase |CITS:[9002616]| |CITS:[9747535]| or a sequence which goes the other way around. , The final polymethylated glucosides of |FRAME:CPD-520| could be localized in the cell walls of leaf epidermal and mesophyll cells utilizing immunofluorescence |CITS:[Lamoureux86]| |CITS:[Brisson86]|, immunogold labeling |CITS:[Marchand87]| and electron microscope observations |CITS:[Charest86]|. Immunogold labeling was also employed to pinpoint the location of the 2'-O-glucosyltransferase to the periplasmic region of cells, which appears to be loosely associated with membrane structures and vesicles of ER |CITS:[1832846]|. The highly coordinated and stepwise sequence of methylation, hydroxylation and glucosylation of the pathway as well as the location of final products prompted the proposal of a multienzyme system. This multienzyme complex is localized at the ER where the pathway is executed and from which vesicles transport and eventually excrete the final products into or near the cell wall |CITS:[Ibrahim87]|. , Note regarding the numbering of the B-ring, The usual consecutive numeration of the C-atoms of the B-ring is clockwise, starting on the C-atom connected to the side-chain. The 3'- and 5'-position are similar as they are both in meta-position to the side-chain. However, when the 2'-position is substituted the 3'-position is often designated as 5'-position in the literature. In order to maintain consistency and to avoid confusion all compounds and enzymes of the pathway are depicted and named according to the consecutive, clockwise numeration of the B-ring whether or not the 2'-position is substituted, i.e. 3' is not replaced by 5' in neither structure nor naming.

A menaquinone with partially saturated isoprenyl moieties was reported as early as 1963 |CITS: [13946232]|. This type of substitution was later reported from a wide range of bacterial species. The location of the reduced double bond differs among different species - In mycobacteria the reduced double bond is often in the β-isoprene unit, in some Gram-negative organisms it is often located more distally from the naphthoquinone moiety, and in Gram-positive organisms the modification is found in both area, depending on the species |CITS: [7022156]|., In mycobacteria, the predominant menaquinone is |FRAME: CPD-9849| |CITS: [6035490][5635783][4201898]|, although a further modified version exists as well (see |FRAME: PWY-7781|)., The enzyme catalyzing the reduction, |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.38| (|FRAME: G185E-4694|), has been discovered in 2015 in |FRAME: TAX-83332| and |FRAME: TAX-246196|, and appears to be highly conserved throughout the mycobacteria. Conserved genes were also identified in other Gram-positive species with partially saturated menaquinones of known structure such as |FRAME: TAX-1717|, Nocardia spp., and Streptomyces species |CITS: [26436137]|., The role and importance of this modification is not well understood. However, it has been shown that the small structural changes can cause dramatic changes in the properties of the molecules |CITS: [14531689]|. More recent experiments suggested that |FRAME: CPD-9849| is 3-fold more efficient than |FRAME: CPD-9720| in electron transport. In addition, deletion of the |FRAME: G185E-4694| gene reduces |FRAME: TAX-83332| survival in macrophages |CITS: [26436137]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ILE| is almost always synthesized from |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|. In the most common pathway, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is generated from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| via |FRAME: THR| (see |FRAME:PWY-3001|). The key enzyme in that pathway is |FRAME:THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10493| gene., In addition to the standard pathway, microorganisms have developed several alternative pathways for |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis. |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be synthesized from |FRAME: GLT| via |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5103|) |CITS: [4550817]|, from |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5101|) |CITS: [4607875][4808901][15292141]|, and from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| by carboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-5104|) |CITS: [5800441][1212197][Eikmanns83a]|)., In addition, there are several reports that under anaerobic conditions some anaerobic bacteria can carboxylate, |FRAME: CPD-7076| to |FRAME: ILE| via |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| (this pathway) |CITS: [5813342][6726176][6440485 ]|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-7076|, which is often found in the form of its coenzyme A derivative, |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|, is a volatile fatty acid abundant in the rumen of animals, produced in part by the microbial flora during the anaerobic digestion of complex organic substrates. It is also produced by anaerobic parasites (see |FRAME: PWY-5109|). , The connection between |FRAME:CPD-7076| and the biosynthesis of |FRAME:ILE| was suggested early on |CITS:[14946192]|. A study performed in 1969 found that several ruminal archaea and bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-83816| and |FRAME: TAX-839|, extensively incorporated |FRAME: CPD-7076| into |FRAME: ILE| in a manner that suggested this may be the main |FRAME: ILE| biosynthetic pathway in these organisms |CITS: [5813342]|., This finding was reproduced in 1984 by a study of |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-1509| |CITS: [6726176]|, and by another study that found that |FRAME: TAX-839|, as well as the anaerobic pathogen |FRAME: TAX-817|, synthesized |FRAME: ILE| from |FRAME: CPD-7076| by incorporating the intact |FRAME: CPD-7076| carbon skeleton into the |FRAME: ILE| molecule |CITS: [6440485]|. The authors suspected that the organisms were capable of synthesizing |FRAME: ILE| in multiple pathways, and that this pathway was preferred under the fatty-acid rich, anaerobic environment of the rumen. Additional studies have expanded the observation to the methanogenic archaea |FRAME: TAX-2203|, |FRAME: TAX-2161| and |FRAME: TAX-2173|, which were shown to synthesize |FRAME: ILE| in multiple pathways, from either |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5104|) or |FRAME:CPD-7076| |CITS: [Ekiel84]|. A definite preference in these organisms for using |FRAME:CPD-7076| as the precursor has been noted., The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-7076| (via its CoA-derivative) to |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| depends on a reductive carboxylation reaction, which is only possible in highly reduced environments because of the requirement for a very electronegative electron donor such as reduced ferredoxin |CITS: [Buchanan72]|. While an enzyme catalyzing this reaction has not been isolated specifically from the organisms mentioned above, |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| is known to be a substrate for |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|, which is found in |FRAME: TAX-145262|, where it is thought to participate in the biosynthesis of amino acids from fatty acids |CITS: [9108258]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HYGROMYCIN-B Hygromycin B| is an aminocyclitol antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-1912|. It is unusual in that it is active against both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. It obstructs protein synthesis |CITS: [18567815]| by targeting 30S ribosomal subunits in bacteria |CITS: [11014183][12709313][17043113]| and the elongation of nascent chains during the translation of polysomes in eukaryotic cells |CITS: [367435][6433789]|., Hygromycin B was discovered in 1958 |CITS: [Mann58]|. Structurally it has a trisaccharide scaffold assembled from 2-deoxysteptamine (ring I), D-talose (ring II), and destomic acid (ring III) that are linked sequentially by glycoside bonds |CITS: [5498836]|., Hygromycin B has been produced on an industrial scale |CITS: [5298042]| and used to treat parasite infection in poultry and livestock |CITS: [14405260][14405258][4167359][5629634][5629663]| as well as in research, as a selection agent for genetic manipulation in biological studies |CITS: [6098829][24130756][24751825]|., About This Pathway, Considering the common use of |FRAME: HYGROMYCIN-B| since the early 60s, it is somewhat surprising that its biosynthetic pathway has not been studied much until 2015. In 2006 the hygromycin B biosynthetic gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-68042| was deposited into GenBank by Piepersberg et al. (accession no. AJ628642). However, prior to 215 the only component whose biosynthetic route was deciphered was the |FRAME: CPD-10151| ring, as it is also a component of |FRAME: CPD-14125|, a common moiety of several |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| including |FRAME: CPD-14177|, |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin|, |FRAME: Lividomycins lividomycin| and certain forms of |FRAME: Kanamycins kanamycin| |CITS: [16506694]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7014|)., In 2015 a study has identified |FRAME: G-107818 HygX|, the enzyme responsible for the formation of the unique orthoester linkage between D-talose (ring II) and destomic acid (ring III) |CITS: [26240321]|. The enzyme was further studied in 2018, in a study that also characterized the activities of |FRAME: G-107819 HygF| and |FRAME: G-107820 HygM|, which are responsible for disaccharide formation and N-3 methylation, respectively |CITS: [29878752]|. Another 2018 study focused on the formation of the heptose motif in ring III, showing that it is derived from |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| and providing a partial pathway for its biosynthesis |CITS: [ 29483275]|. Most of the remaining activities of the pathway were studied only in 2020 using CRISPR-Cas9-associated base editing, which enables mutations without relying on homologous recombination |CITS: [32275383]|., It was found that the pathway can proceed via parallel branches, which are linked by N-3-methylation performed by the very promiscuous methyltranferase HygM. For the sake of simplicity, only a part of the parallel branches is shown here.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety. Their oxidized forms are depicted here as |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| due to the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring. Their reduced forms are referred to as |FRAME: NADH| and |FRAME: NADPH|., These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes"., The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form., |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|)., Despite their importance, the regulation of |FRAME: NAD| phosphorylation and dephosphorylation remains incompletely defined. Earlier work on the kinetics of pyridine nucleotide metabolism in |FRAME:TAX-562| demonstrated that the ratio of |FRAME: NADP| to |FRAME: NAD| results largely from the rates of |FRAME: NADP| and |FRAME: NAD| interconversion (in |CITS: [4146187]|)., In |FRAME:TAX-562| the reversible reduction of both |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| is carried out by the two transhydrogenase isoforms shown in the reaction links. The PntAB complex, encoded by the pntA and pntB genes, is located in the inner membrane and also functions as a proton pump. Its physiological function is to catalyze energy-dependent reduction of |FRAME: NADP| with |FRAME: NADH|. The soluble product of gene sthA is thought to function mainly in the reoxidation of |FRAME: NADPH| with |FRAME: NAD|. The expression of these two isoforms is modulated by the redox state of cellular metabolism |CITS: [14660605]|. In |CITS: [5543676]| and reviewed by Penfound, T. and J.W. Foster in |CITS: [ColiSalII]| (see below). , About This Pathway, NAD kinases have been characterized in organisms from a variety of taxonomic groups including archaea, eubacteria and eukaryotes (reviewed in |CITS: [18391451]|). The NAD kinase of |FRAME:TAX-28901| has been shown to be essential for growth |CITS: [16682646]| and evidence for its essentiality in |FRAME:TAX-562| has been presented |CITS: [12142426]|., In contrast, NADP phosphatases (NADPases) remain poorly characterized despite their important role. Although an NAD kinase homolog in the archaeon |FRAME:TAX-2190| was shown to also have NADP phosphatase activity, NADP phosphatases from eubacterial and eukaryotic sources still require identification of the genes encoding them and further study of their enzymatic properties. In |FRAME:TAX-562| the product of cysQ showed high NADP and NADPH phosphatase activities, but kinetic studies of the purified enzyme suggested that it is not the true NADP phosphatase of this organism. Reviewed in |CITS: [18391451] [17295611]|., Reviewed in Penfound, T. and J.W. Foster (1996) "Biosynthesis and Recycling of NAD", chapter 48, pp. 721-730, in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13955 Mithramycin| is an aureolic acid-type anticancer agent that has been used in the treatment of testicular cancer |CITS:[14224214][7700186]|, Paget's disease of bone |CITS: [12846580]|, and the management of hypercalcemia. It also possesses antibiotic activity against Gram-positive but not Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [9150235]|., Mithramycin is an aromatic polyketide containing a three-ring chromophoric aglycon derived from the condensation of 10 acetate molecules, which is modified by a trisaccharidal chain [D-olivosyl-(3→1)-D-oliosyl-(3→1)-D-mycarosyl] and a disaccharidal chain [D-olivosyl-(3→1)-D-olivosyl], attached at the 2 and 6 positions of the aglycon, respectively. Thus, one molecule of |FRAME: CPD-13955| contains 3 molecules of |FRAME: D-Olivose|, one molecule of |FRAME: CPD-13963|, and one molecule of |FRAME: CPD-13964|., The three sugars are synthesized in the activated dTDP forms from a single intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-13381|, which is produced from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| in 4 steps. The first three steps are catalyzed by the products of the genes |FRAME: G-14873|, |FRAME: G-14874| and |FRAME: G-14875| |CITS: [9150235][11254130]| (the 4th one has not been identified yet, but is orthologous to the |FRAME: G-14868| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1890| |CITS: [21960454]|)., Interestingly, a single protein, encoded by the |FRAME: G-14876| gene, can catalyze both methyltransferase and reductase reactions on this substrate |CITS: [11254130][21960454]|. Reduction produces |FRAME: CPD-11916|, while methyl transfer, followed by a reduction catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-14878| gene product, produces |FRAME: CPD-13957| |CITS: [11853433]|. A different reductase, encoded by |FRAME: G-14877|, that has a different stereo specificity, generates |FRAME: CPD-13956| |CITS: [21960454]|.

Like |FRAME:CPD-18421|, the trichothecene compound |FRAME:CPD-18427| is a type B trichothecene produced in certain strains of Fusarium graminearum (telemorph Gibberella zeae) which stand for an specific chemotype inside the species. Trichothecene are characterized as sequiterpenoids with an varying pattern of oxygen and ester groups on a core tricyclic skeleton bearing an epoxide function which is commonly known as 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene (EPT) structure |CITS:[Grove07]|. A considerable number of trichothecene have been identified from various genera of fungi and classified into four groups (type A to D) according to the substitution pattern on the basic EPT core |CITS:[Ueno80] [Betina89] [Alexander09] [22069741]|. Trichothecene are mycotoxins which display phytotoxic activities |CITS:[22295175]|, are the origin of contaminated food and animal feed, and have been reported to cause vomiting, skin dermatitis, and hemorrhagic lesions |CITS:[3158480] [8246841]|. Numerous studies have been carried out to elucidate the many effects of trichothecenes and to investigate the underlying pathways in order to counteract the significant losses caused by Fusarium pathogens worldwide |CITS:[18791024] [19385728] [5816375] [15762554] [25680507]| which threaten the existence of farms and whole rural communities |CITS:[18944567]|. , The two main chemotypes in the genus of Fusarium are linked to species which either produce |FRAME:CPD-18421| (see |FRAME:PWY-7712|) or |FRAME:CPD-18427| (this pathway) |CITS:[Miller91]|. It has been demonstrated that the genetic difference between |FRAME:CPD-18421| and |FRAME:CPD-18427| chemotypes lies in the functionality of two genes, i.e. TRI13 coding for a trichothecene 4-hydroxylase and TRI7 encoding for a trichothecene 4-acetyltransferase. Both genes are present but nonfunctional in |FRAME:CPD-18421|-producing Fusarium chemotypes |CITS:[11352533] [11976083]|. There are some alarming reports about an evolutionary shift of chemotypes which drives the spread of more toxigenic Fusarium graminearum in the US and worldwide with severe consequences for food safety and production |CITS:[20205536] [18035565] [19843228] [17451976] [Waalwijk03]|. Compared with its congenial type B partner |FRAME:CPD-18421|, |FRAME:CPD-18427|, which is more prevalent in Asia, contaminates cereals at higher levels and induces more severe acute and chronic toxicities |CITS:[3209016] [20882466]|. , It is known that in fungi biosynthetic clusters are employed for producing secondary or specialized metabolites |CITS:[25784900]|. Accordingly, the proteins catalyzing the biosynthesis of the various trichothecene are also organized in biosynthetic cluster (TRI) |CITS:[14998528] [12650935]| where most of the genes appear to be coordinately expressed and regulated |CITS:[12080147]|. The pathway generating |FRAME:CPD-18427| can be fed through intermediates of two other trichothecene pathways, i.e. |FRAME:PWY-7712| and |FRAME:PWY-7730|. Summary: General Background, This pathway is a continuation of the linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-7383|. Please see the General Background section in that pathway summary. Both pathways are shown together in |FRAME: PWY-7389|., About This Pathway, In marine invertebrates and parasitic helminths |FRAME: MAL| produced by anaerobic reactions in the cytosol (as shown in the linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-7383|) is transported into the mitochondrion where it is both reduced to |FRAME: FUM| in one branch, and oxidized to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| in the other branch, as shown here. This has been referred to as malate dismutation. In this split pathway, these two compounds are anaerobically metabolized to |FRAME: SUC|, |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate) and |FRAME: ACET|, which accumulate., The two reactions that convert |FRAME: MAL| to |FRAME: SUC| are the reverse of those that occur in the TCA cycle. The reduction of |FRAME: FUM| via the electron transfer chain consumes the |FRAME: NADH| produced in the oxidative branch to maintain redox balance (see |FRAME: CPLX-8764|). In addition, mitochondrial |FRAME: MAL| can also be oxidized to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and enter the TCA cycle which may function at a low rate during anaerobiosis (|CITS: [FELBECKH80]| and reviewed in |CITS: [7984874][12594928]| (see |FRAME: PWY66-398|)., Radiotracer studies in marine molluscs have shown that most of the carbon skeleton of cytosolic |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| appears in mitochondrial |FRAME: SUC| during anaerobiosis |CITS: [DEZWAANA73][COLLICUTJM77]|. In the mitochondrion |FRAME: MAL| is dehydrated to |FRAME: FUM| by fumarase. |FRAME: FUM "Fumarate"| is an important compound in this anaerobic pathway. In the absence of oxygen, |FRAME: FUM| plays the role of electron acceptor and is reduced to |FRAME: SUC| via the |FRAME: CPLX-8764|. |FRAME: FUM "Fumarate"| reduction is coupled to the electron transfer chain (see below) which requires the low redox potential |FRAME: Rhodoquinols "rhodoquinol"| as electron donor to fumarate reductase |CITS: [8537365]| and reviewed in |CITS: [7984874][22688819]| (see related pathway |FRAME: PWY-8570|)., The reaction sequence to |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate) formation is catalyzed by an acyl-CoA transferase (propionyl-CoA:succinate CoA transferase), methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase, and propionyl-CoA carboxylase. One mole of |FRAME: ATP| is formed during the decarboxylation of |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| (D-methylmalonyl-CoA) to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [SCHROFFG80][6450565][SCHOTTLERU84]|. The |FRAME: CO-A| moiety is not split by thiolytic cleavage, but is transferred to |FRAME: SUC| to regenerate |FRAME: SUC-COA|., The oxidative branch that produces |FRAME: ACET| generates |FRAME: NADH| which is oxidized by respiratory complex I to |FRAME: NAD|, producing electrons for the fumarate reductase complex and protons to drive ATP synthase. |FRAME: ACET "Acetate"| is formed in anaerobic mitochondria by acetate:succinate CoA-transferase (reviewed in |CITS: [7984874][ 12594928][20085767]|). Note that this enzyme has been referred to as |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.8| |CITS: [20085767]| but it is described by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.18| in a more recent Enzyme Commission entry. The |FRAME: SUC-COA| formed by this enzyme can then be converted back to |FRAME: SUC| with the concomitant production of |FRAME: ATP| catalyzed by a TCA cycle enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.5| (reviewed in |CITS: [20085767]|)., Overall, the terminal reactions of anaerobic mitochondria have been referred to as the NADH-fumarate reductase system which is composed of complex II (rhodoquinol-fumarate reductase) and complex I (NADH-rhodoquinone reductase). Thus electron transfer from |FRAME: NADH| to |FRAME: FUM| is coupled to |FRAME: ATP| synthesis. (reviewed in |CITS: [9693724][23333273]|., The formation and excretion of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate) as end products of |FRAME: Glycogens "glycogen"| breakdown during prolonged environmental hypoia has been experimentally demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-6550| |CITS: [SCHULZTKF83][KLUYTMANSJH83]|., The adult forms of the parasitic worms |FRAME: TAX-6252|, |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6192| have similar mitochondrial anaerobic energy metabolism pathways except that in |FRAME: TAX-6251| |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| (propionyl-CoA) are condensed and reduced to the branched chain fatty acid end products |FRAME: CPD-7076| (2-methylbutanoate) and |FRAME: CPD-15866| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5109|). In |FRAME: TAX-6192| |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: ACET| are the accumulated products. Mitochondria of the lugworm |FRAME: TAX-6344| are also able to oxidize environmental |FRAME: CPD-7046| (sulfide) to |FRAME: S2O3| (|CITS: [8631334]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22688819]|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation, and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|. Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria, and certain archaea and fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. The biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail in bacteria. Sequencing analysis and some experimental evidence suggests that the steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, derived from a |FRAME: CPD-205|-like structure. The early steps of the pathway are responsible for the synthesis of the precursor pimelate moiety, and are described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-6519| and |FRAME: PWY-6578|. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described here., The first step in this part of the pathway involves the unusual use of the common methyl-group donor |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as an amino-group donor, a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: EG10117|-encoded |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.62| |CITS: [1092681][1092682][12379100]|. This product of this reaction, |FRAME: DIAMINONONANOATE|, is the target of a unique carboxylase, the |FRAME: EG10120|-encoded |FRAME: EC-6.3.3.3|. This enzye catalyzes the first ring closure by a carboxylation reaction that does not require biotin as a prosthetic group, forming |FRAME: DETHIOBIOTIN| |CITS: [4921568]|., The ultimate step in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.6|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10118|. This enzyme inserts a sulfur atom between C6 and C9 of dethiobiotin in a |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent reaction. It has not been possible to reconstitute a catalytic reaction of this enzyme in vitro, and there is some uncertainty regarding the reaction mechanism, cofactor requirements, and the source of the sulfur atom |CITS: [15850974]|. However, recent experiments have suggested that a |FRAME: CPD-6| of the enzyme is the source of the sulfur atom. Consistent with its proposed role as the sulfur donor, degradation of the [2Fe-2S] cluster |CITS: [14967042]| as well as exchange of sulfur atoms between the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] clusters |CITS: [16533066]| is observed during turnover of the enzyme., Recently detailed analysis of biotin biosynthetic genes was done with several additional bacterial species, as well as in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-497727| |CITS: [30218044]|. There is much variation in the organization of the genes involved: In some cases all of the bio genes are organized within a single transcription unit (such as |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [8763940]| and |FRAME: TAX-381| |CITS: [11320134]|), while in other cases the genes are organized in multiple operons, sometimes at different locations in the chromosome., Some organisms even lack some of the genes - for example, |FRAME: TAX-1718| seems to lack the bioC, bioH, and bioF genes |CITS: [8161820]|., The difference between the biosynthetic pathways of Gram-negative bacteria (|FRAME: BIOTIN-BIOSYNTHESIS-PWY|) and Gram-positive bacteria (|FRAME: PWY-5005|) is upstream of the precursor |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE|. Gram-positive bacteria generate |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| from |FRAME:CPD-205| as described in |FRAME: PWY-6578|, while in Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| is synthesized from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| in a pathway described in |FRAME: PWY-6519| |CITS: [20693992]|., About This Pathway in Plants, The biotin pathway has been investigated using biotin-auxotroph mutants of Arabidopsis thaliana. It could be shown that two enzymes correspond to certain mutations - |FRAME: G-12146|, which has been shown to encode the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-8566| |CITS: [8676868]|, and |FRAME: AT2G43360|, which encodes the |FRAME: AT2G43360-CPLX| |CITS: [8680961][0009501126]|. , Biotin synthase is the only enzyme of the pathway which has been investigated in plants on the molecular level |CITS: [8680961][9428635][11706201][12714594]|., Biotin synthase activity could be clearly demonstrated in Arabidopsis utilizing the synthase and accessory proteins from |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [11706201]|. It has been shown that mitochondrial components are necessary for the function of the enzyme, acting similar to the flavodoxin reduction system found in |FRAME:TAX-562|. The mitochondrial components identified were adrenodoxin, adrenodoxin reductase and cystein desulfurase (Nfs1) which proved to be essential for the plant biotin synthase reaction and accommodates the cellular location of the enzyme |CITS: [12714594]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.1|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.1|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.2| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., Thiamine biosynthesis is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| (see |FRAME: PWY-6893|)., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the last part of the thiamine biosynthesis pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1280| - the coupling of the two moieties of thiamine, the thiazole and the pyrimidine, forming |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|, and its phosphorylation to the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|., While most bacteria achieve this phosphorylation in a single step, catalyzed by |FRAME: THI-P-KIN-MONOMER| (|FRAME: G6234|) (see |FRAME: PWY-6893|), |FRAME: TAX-1280| lacks that enzyme., An analysis of its genome suggested that this bacterium may be utilizing a pathway similar to the eukaryotic pathway, where |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| is first dephosphorylated to |FRAME: THIAMINE|, which is then diphosphorylated to |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: THISYNARA-PWY|) |CITS: [19888457]|., The genes involved in the thiamine biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: TAX-1280| have been cloned from |FRAME: ORG-6189| and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. Many of them were purified. Biochemical analysis confirmed that the final steps in the pathway were indeed similar to those utilized by eukaryotes |CITS: [19888457]|., The |FRAME: G-14648| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1280|, which encodes the enzyme that catalyzes the last step, |FRAME: MONOMER-16817|, has been identified based on its similarity to eukaryotic enzymes. The gene resides in an operon that also contains a phosphatase-encoding gene (|FRAME: G-14649|), that was shown to have a broad substrate range and to be able to act on |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| |CITS: [19888457]|. However, genes encoding a specific |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.100|, were later identified in |FRAME: TAX-169435|, |FRAME: TAX-88431|, and |FRAME: TAX-863|, and were shown to have efficient in vivo activity |CITS: [26537753]|.

The presence of methyl groups shifts the midpoint potential (E<sub>M</sub>) value for the first reduction step to more negative potentials of about 40 to 80 mV per methyl group., |FRAME: 7-8-Dimethylmenaquinones 7,8-dimethylmenaquinone| (DMMK) is a menaquinone derivative of uncertain function that is restricted to species of the class |FRAME: TAX-84998| (phylum |FRAME: TAX-201174|), and is used as a coriobacterial biomarker. , It is assumed that DMMK plays a part in anaerobic low-potential electron transport chains, which are electron transport chains that use a terminal electron acceptor whose redox potential is more negative than that of menaquinone. However, this has not been proven yet., Formation of DMMK requires two successive methylations of menaquinone. One of the enzymes involved, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.350|, has been described in 2017 from |FRAME: TAX-844| |CITS: [28164386]|. The second enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.M96|, was described the following year from |FRAME: TAX-446660| |CITS: [29408546]|. Both enzymes are class C radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) methyltransferases.

Summary: |FRAME: PENTACHLOROPHENOL Pentachlorophenol| (PCP) is a a polychlorinated aromatic compound that has been released into the environment as a wood preservative and broad spectrum biocide |CITS:[Kaufman77][Crosby81]|. This compound is a major environmental pollutant due to its toxicity and recalcitrance, and it is regulated as one of the priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |CITS: [Middaugh94]|. Microorganisms have been used to remove PCP from the environment |CITS: [16535458]|, and several aerobic PCP-degrading bacteria have been isolated from contaminated soils |CITS: [11423949]|. |FRAME: TAX-46429 "Sphingobium chlorophenolicum (previously known as Sphingomonas chlorophenolica)"| strain ATCC 39723 is one of the bacteria capable of completely mineralizing PCP |CITS: [4091568]|, The degradation pathway in |FRAME: TAX-46429| starts with |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.50|, an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME:PENTACHLOROPHENOL| to |FRAME: CPD-19762|, followed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.404|, which reduces the latter to |FRAME: TETRACHLOROHYDROQUINONE|. The next enzyme, a glutathione transferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-263| gene, catalyzes the next two steps, resulting in |FRAME: 26-DICHLORO-P-HYDROQUINONE|. PcpC is susceptible to oxidative damage, and the damaged PcpC produces glutathionyl (GS) conjugates which it can't process further. These conjugates can be rescued by the action of another glutathione transferase encoded by |FRAME: G-55001|, which completes the reduction reaction and removes the glutathione moiety., The next enzyme, |FRAME:26DICHDIOXFLAVO-MONOMER|, cleaves the ring, resulting in the non-aromatic product |FRAME:2-CHLOROMALEYLACETATE| |CITS: [10526172][8619798][7765838]|. This compound is dehalogenated in two steps by |FRAME: MONOMER-14670|, resulting in |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, a common intermediate in the degradation of aromatic compounds, which is further degraded into central metabolism intermediates., The genes responsible for degradation of |FRAME: PENTACHLOROPHENOL| are found on a secondary chromosome that encodes primarily genes that appear to be involved in environmental adaptation |CITS: [22179583]|. The first and third enzymes in this pathway (|FRAME:CPLX-9185| and |FRAME:26DICHDIOXFLAVO-MONOMER|) may have originated from enzymes in a pathway for degradation of a naturally occurring chlorinated phenol. The second enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-1581|, may have evolved from a maleylacetoacetate isomerase (for example, see |FRAME:MONOMER-12045|) which is normally involved in degradation of tyrosine |CITS: [10838562]|. These three genes were acquired fairly recently via two different horizontal gene transfer events, while the genes encoding the final two enzymes were acquired earlier |CITS: [22179583]|., The pathway is not very effective - |FRAME:CPLX-9185| is very slow, and |FRAME:CPLX-1581| is subject to severe product inhibition, further suggesting that the pathway has evolved recently |CITS: [10838562]|.

|FRAME: Quinolones Quinolone| alkaloids are found in diverse types of organisms and exhibit a variety of biological activities, including antibacterial, antimalarial, antiviral and antitumor activities |CITS: [19442143][22365088]|., Fungi such as |FRAME: TAX-60167| are known for biosynthesizing |FRAME: Quinolones quinolones| such as |FRAME:CPD-18297| (see |FRAME:PWY-7704|) in the hyphae, in sync with the formation of conidia |CITS:[Luckner62] [Luckner80]|. The quinolone strucutre is of major pharmaceutical interest and its biosynthesis has been well studied. The closely-related quinolone |FRAME:CPD-18302| is produced in |FRAME: TAX-162425| |CITS: [17036148]| and the responsible gene cluster as well as the catalyzing enzymes have been elucidated |CITS:[25251934]|. , It has been known for a long time that the quinolone-producing fungi also produce |FRAME: Benzodiazepine-Alkaloids "benzodiazepine alkaloids"| such as |FRAME:CPD-18377| |CITS:[24773150]|, and it was established early on that the |FRAME: Benzodiazepines "benzodiazepines"| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of quinolones |CITS:[Smith69]|., The benzodiazepinedione structure originates from the condensation of |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and an amino acid |CITS:[Luckner62][5823102]| by nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) (summarized in |CITS:[23659680]|). The NRPS cyclopeptine synthetase from |FRAME: TAX-162425|, encoded by the asqK gene, has been identified and overexpressed in this organism and shown to produce |FRAME:CPD-18299| from |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME:CPD-18298|. , The complex following steps, catalyzed by the AsqJ dioxygenase, have also been studied. The transormation catalyzed by AsqJ consists of two oxidation reactions, a desaturation that produces a double bond, and a monooxygenation on that double forming an epoxide |CITS:[25251934]|. Although the AsqJ dioxygenase also accepted the respective intermediates of the |FRAME:CPD-18297| biosynthesis, its activity towards the 4'-methoxy intermediates was significantly better, indicating that those compounds may be the true substrates for the dioxygenase. , The unusual epoxide formed by AsqJ affords the rearrangement of the 6,7-bicyclic |FRAME: Benzodiazepines benzodiazepines| structure into the 6,6-bicyclic |FRAME: Quinolones quinolone| structure, which is catalyzed by the AsqI cyclopenase |CITS:[30026518]|. The first quinolone compound, |FRAME: CPD-18302|, is thought to be modified in two steps (a methyltransferase and a monooxygenase) into |FRAME: CPD-25947|. However, as of 2022 the identity of these enzymes has not been established., Further processing is described in pathways |FRAME: PWY-8389| and |FRAME: PWY-8388|.

Summary: General Background, L-Arabinose, the 4-epimer of D-xylose, is a monosaccharide found primarily in plants. It is mainly present in cell wall polymers such as pectic (rhamnogalacturonan I, rhamnogalacturonan II) and hemicellulosic (xylan, xyloglucan) components, as well as in the glycosyl-moieties of proteins such as arabinogalactan proteins and extensions |CITS:[10517829],[10640355]|. Although little is known of the incorporation of arabinose into these polymers or the contribution of the arabinosyl-substituents to the functions of the wall polymers, it has been demonstrated that arabinose-containing polymers are derived from UDP-L-arabinose, the activated sugar used by arabinosyltransferases |CITS:[FEINGOLD80]|., This Pathway in Plants:, The formation of UDP-L-arabinose occurs via two routes: a) the de novo synthesis route (this pathway) involves the epimerisation of UDP-D-xylose by a UDP-D-xylose 4-epimerase, and b) a salvage pathway leading to the formation of UDP-L-arabinose from free arabinose (|FRAME:PWY-82|). , Key Notes on the Enzymes: Few UDP-D-xylose 4-epimerases have been described in the literature although this enzymatic activity has been described for several plants |CITS:[192218],[192219],[13821949],[5483919]|. One has been purified from wheat germ extract. When the enzymatic activity of this enzyme was tested, the reversible conversion of UDP-L-arabinose (UDP-L-Ara) to UDP-D-xylose (UDP-D-Xyl) was achieved with an equilibrium constant of 1.25 |CITS:[5483919]|. More recently, the Arabidopsis thaliana MUR4 mutant was described which was shown to be affected in its ability to epimerize UDP-D-Xyl to UDP-L-Ara |CITS:[10517829],[12566589]|. Although the MUR4 protein was expressed in transgenic yeast cells and shown to possess UDP-D-xylose 4-epimerase activity, the corresponding enzyme has not yet been fully purified., Important Note: In cell wall the majority of arabinose is in a furanose, not pyranose, configuration., This Pathway in Bacteria:, There is also evidence for this pathway in plant-associated bacteria belonging to the family |FRAME: TAX-82115|. Rhizobia are soil bacteria that fix nitrogen in the root nodules of some leguminous plants. In |FRAME: TAX-266834| an operon was identified that contains genes uxe and uxs1 encoding UDP-xylose 4-epimerase and UDP-xylose synthase 1, respectively. Data from real-time 1H-NMR spectroscopy demonstrated the conversion of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| to |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE|, and |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-12513|. These UDP-sugars are then used for the biosynthesis of xylose-containing and arabinose-containing cell surface glycans. Their pathways and the roles that they play in nodulation are only beginning to be elucidated |CITS: [20847005]|., Two orthologs of each gene encoding active enzymes were also identified in other rhizobial species including |FRAME: TAX-216596| (loci R10559 and R10078 for uxe, R10560 and R10077 for uxs). These observations were cited in |CITS: [20847005]| as unpublished data.

|FRAME: CPD-22422 Gingkotoxin| is one of the components of the seed of the |FRAME: TAX-3311| plant. When ingested at a high dose it is known to cause seizures, paralysis, and sometimes death |CITS: [26819944]|. The compound is a competitive inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.35| |CITS: [17250738][22879864][22857512][26092494]|. This inhibition depletes the brain of phosphorylated B6 vitamers, and may result in the downregulation of glutamate decarboxylation., |FRAME: CPD-22422 Gingkotoxin| is produced by methylation of |FRAME: PYRIDOXINE| |CITS: [10691705]|, which is likely produced from |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|. |FRAME: TAX-3311| has a copy of a pdx1 gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-4.3.3.6|. This is the key enzyme of the |FRAME: PWY-6466| pathway, which is found in archaea, fungi, plants, and most bacteria. Thus it is believed that the precursor of |FRAME: CPD-22422| in |FRAME: TAX-3311| is |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| formed by the |FRAME: PWY-6466| pathway., It was postulated that |FRAME: PYRIDOXINE| is derived from |FRAME: PYRIDOXINE-5P|, which is generated from |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| by a dehydrogenase reaction. However, as of 2019 none of the enzymes of this pathway has been identified |CITS: [20041670]|.

Summary: The fungus Penicillium aethiopicum is known for producing complex secondary metabolites such as the polyketides |FRAME:CPD-17869| (see |FRAME:PWY-7660|), |FRAME:CPD-17786| (see |FRAME:PWY-7653|) and |FRAME:CPD-17868| (this pathway) which are distinctive metabolites for this fungus and serve as chemotaxonomic marker for the species |CITS:[Frisvad04]|. |FRAME:CPD-17868 Viridicatumtoxin| has been first isolated and structurally elucidated from Penicillium viridicatum |CITS:[Kabuto76]| and first biosynthetic steps proposed by feeding radioactive labeled precursors |CITS:[Jesus82]|. This hybrid polyketide-isoprenoid compound has been linked to kidney damages (nephrotoxicity) |CITS:[4122267]| and shown to exhibit moderate antitumor activity whereas its 11-O-beta glucoside, the main product of microbial biotransformation, was found completely inactive |CITS:[Raju82]|. In addition, it has been demonstrated that |FRAME:CPD-17868| was a very potent growth inhibitor of the antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a known pathogenic bacterium causing various skin and respiratory infections in humans |CITS:[19168978]|., A number of fungal polyketide pathways have been detected by identifying the corresponding polyketide synthase (PKS) genes |CITS:[17390002] [23368997] [23758576]| and new technologies such a s genome mining |CITS:[17369821] [16426969]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7565|; |FRAME:PWY-7520|) and next-generation sequencing |CITS:[25642215]| allowed to unravel cryptic or silent gene clusters of fungal secondary metabolites of interest. The gene cluster for both the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17868| (vrt) and |FRAME:CPD-17786| (grf) (see |FRAME:PWY-7653|) in Penicillium aethiopicum have been detected utilizing an approach of bioinformatics PKS genes mining and genomic comparative analysis with an close relative, i.e. Penicillium chrysogenum known not to produce those polyketide derivatives |CITS:[20534346]|. The vtr cluster has also been detected in an insect pathogen Metarhizium acridum |CITS:[21253567]| and the human pathogen Aspergillus ustus |CITS:[25706180]|. , The identification of genes in the |FRAME:CPD-17868| (vrt) cluster and characterization of the respective enzymes for key reactions in the pathway have resulted in the discovery of the most probable biosynthetic route as shown above. The PKS, encoded by vrtA, catalyzed the synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17877| from |FRAME:CPD-17870| and 8 molecules of |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| which was demonstrated by targeted gene deletion and RNA silencing |CITS:[20534346]|. Other crucial pathway reactions such as the 5-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17873| to gain |FRAME:CPD-17874| encoded by VrtE and the cytochrome P450 dependent oxygenase VrtK catalyzing the cyclization of the spirobicyclic ring of |FRAME:CPD-17871| to yield the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17868| |CITS:[24161266]| as well as the prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-17875| catalyzed by the 5-hydroxyanthrotainin geranyltransferase (VrtC) |CITS:[22590971]| have been ascertained by gene deletion and assays of heterologously expressed and purified protein. The latter reaction depends on the availability of |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| which is provided through the action of the VrtD encoded geranyl diphosphate synthase |CITS:[20534346]|. , Two of the reactions in the pathway have been associated by bioinformatics analysis revealing similarity to homologues in other organisms, i.e. the malonamate-CoA ligase encoded by VrtB and the VrtF encoded 5-hydroxy-desmethylanthrotainin 8-O-methyltransferase |CITS:[20534346]|. The remaining two reactions presumably carried out by proteins encoded by VrtG (12a-deshydroxy-desmethylanthrotainin thioesterase) and VrtH (12a-deshydroxy-desmethylanthrotainin 12a-hydroxylase) have also been predicted by bioinformatics analysis |CITS:[20534346]| but have some experimental support through homologues of Aspergillus niger which carry out the same type of reactions as expected for the corresponding steps in the |FRAME:PWY-7659| |CITS:[21866960]|.

Several bacterial species, such as the Gram-negative denitrifying bacterium |FRAME: TAX-59406| , the Gram-positive |FRAME: TAX-1422| and the proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-266265| are able to utilize benzoate , aerobically as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [8335640][12399500][18462753]|. Unlike many other aerobic microorganisms, which degrade benzoate via catechol (see |FRAME: PWY-2503|), these organisms degrade benzoate via |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| |CITS: [8335640][11222587][11306574][12399500]|, similar to the first step in anaerobic benzoate degradation |CITS: [7592432][12897012]|.  , A unique feature of this benzoate degradation pathway is that each intermediate is processed as a coenzyme A (CoA) thioester, up to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPYL-COA| , which is converted to the central intermediates |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: SUC-COA| by β-ketoadipyl-CoA thiolase., The cleavage of the aromatic ring occurs in two steps. First, the ring is epoxylated at positions 2 and 3 by the |FRAME: G-2241|- and |FRAME: G-2242|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-2682|, resulting in formation of a ring that contains two double bonds and an epoxy group |CITS: [ 20452977]|. The product is then cleaved by the |FRAME: G-11804|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-8006| in a hydrolytic reaction that releases formate |CITS: [15916608]|., The next enzyme in the pathway is the |FRAME: G-11807|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-8007|, which forms |FRAME: CIS-34-DEHYDROADIPYL-COA| |CITS: [16585753]|., The rest of the pathway is not as well characterized, but intermediates that have been idetified in these organisms suggest that the pathway proceeds via |FRAME: TRANS-23-DEHYDROADIPYL-COA| and |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYADIPYL-COA|., The genes that encode the pathway's enzyme have been founds found in a single cluster. In |FRAME: TAX-59406| they are named Box for Benzoyl-CoA Oxidation. The genes are induced in the presence of benzoate  |CITS: [12399500]|.
