Summary: Background, (S) and (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate serve as precursors for the synthesis of polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), vitamins, antibiotics, pheromones, and flavor compounds |CITS: [10066830]||CITS: [23333586]|. PHAs are a microbially produced class of polyesters that can serve as renewable plastics, see |FRAME: PWY1-3|. However, microbial production of PHAs is a costly affair, and engineering microbes to produce hydroxyalkanoates is significantly cheaper. Furthermore, hydroxyalkanoates are small molecules which can be secreted into the extracellular millieu as opposed to PHAs which accumulate intracellularly as insoluble granules |CITS: [23333586]|. , While |FRAME: CPD-335| monomer units can be synthesized by depolymerization of microbially synthesized poly-(R)-3-hydroxybutyric acid (PHB), due to stereospecific constraints the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-1843| from PHB is not possible |CITS: [19304817]|. This pathway allows for the synthesis of both entantiomers of 3-hydroxbutyrate., About this Pathway, Photosynthetic organisms such as cyanobacteria use sunlight to generate reducing equivalents and incorporate |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into organic molecules |CITS: [19915552]|. With the ongoing problems of global climate change, they are good candidates to produce renewable compounds by recycling |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. |FRAME: PWY-7216| was previously engineered into |FRAME: TAX-511145| for the production of two enantiomers of 3-hydroxybutyrate, precursors in the synthesis of poly-hydroxyalkanoates which serve as renewable plastics. Engineering the pathway into |FRAME: TAX-1148| allows the synthesis of these compounds photosynthetically from sunlight and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Given the increasing concerns about global warming and the environment, this would be an ecologically tolerable method of producing required precursors for the synthesis of plastics., |FRAME: TAX-1148| is a photosynthetic cyanobacterium, and this pathway constitutes a link between photosynthesis and 3-hydroxybutyrate production, utilizing |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| as the carbon source., It should be noted that wild type |FRAME: TAX-1148| naturally produces polyhydroxybutyrates. The most significant step in engineering this pathway was to clone the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10995| gene, which encodes a thioesterase capable of cleaving coenzyme A from|FRAME: CPD-650| and |FRAME: S-3-HYDROXYBUTANOYL-COA|, which resulted in the extracellular accumulation of 3-hydroxybutyrate. Almost all the cloned genes for the last part of the pathway were under the control of a strong promoter Ptac |CITS: [8251644]|.

Summary: Please note: This pathway utilizes a single compound (monobromobimane, mBBr) as an example for this, general detoxification pathway. The same mechanism applies for the detoxification of a broad spectrum of toxins and, antibiotic compounds, including rifamycin, N-ethylmalemide, iodoacetamide, chlorodinitrobenzene, menadione,, plumbagin, and streptomycin |CITS: [15342574]|., General Background, Thiols play a major role in the detoxification of stress-inducing factors. In mammals, the major, thiol is the tripeptide glutathione (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly, known as GSH). , Toxins are conjugated to GSH in the liver by a dedicated enzyme, resulting in a, cysteine-toxin conjugate. The conjugate is acetylated in the kidney to form mercapturate, which is then excreted, out of the body |CITS: [8145281]|., Pathogenic bacteria live in a particularly hostile environment, in which the host deliberately generates toxins,, including reactive oxygen species, to destroy the invading organism. Thus thiols are particularly important for, the survival of these organisms. While GSH is the major thiol in eukaryotic organisms, Gram negative, bacteria and the majority of Gram positive bacteria, mycobacteria and some other Actinomycetales utilize, |FRAME: CPD1G-2| (MSH) as the major thiol |CITS: [8076641]|. , About This Pathway, Monobromobimane (mBBr) is an alkylating agent which forms a stable fluorescent derivative (mycothiol-, monobromobimase conjugate, or MSmB) with mycothiol (MSH) and is utilized in the quantitative determination of, thiols. When cells of |FRAME:TAX-1772| are exposed to mBBr, the alkylating, agent enters the cells and reacts non-enzymatically with MSH, forming MSmB. , This conjugate is then cleaved by the Mca (|FRAME: MONOMER-9708|) enzyme to |FRAME: CPD1G-0|, (GlcN-Ins - a precursor of mycothiol - see the pathway |FRAME: PWY1G-0|) and the bimane derivative of, N-acetylcysteine (AcCySmB), a mercapturate. , Within minutes all of the mercapturate is exported to the medium, while the GlcN-Ins is retained in the cells, and, recycled back into MSH |CITS: [10978158]|., This pathway is believed to be used in many organisms that produce MSH, including antibiotics-producing, actinomycetes. It is similar to the GSH-mediated detoxification pathway which operates in mammals, but is, simpler and quicker |CITS: [12420157]|. The Mca enzyme is highly specific to mycothiol, but is promiscuous, with respect to the structure of the attached toxin molecule |CITS: [10978158]|, and is thus capable of detoxifying, many different compounds, including the antibiotics angucycline, ansamycin, γ-lactam, naphthoquinone,, phenoxazinone, and phenazine (as determined by the presence of marcapturate forms of these compounds in, culture media) |CITS: [12420157]|.

General Background, Ubiquinone (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, Coenzyme Q6 (ubiquinone, |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30|) is involved in the mitochondrial respiratory chain in yeast (|FRAME:TAX-4932|) and has been also demonstrated to function as an membrane antioxidant, cofactor of uncoupling proteins and functional modulator of membrane transition pores |CITS:[20494114]|. Eleven genes (COQ1-9, ARH1, YAH1) encoding for proteins directly or indirectly involved in the biosynthetic sequence of the proposed 9 reaction steps to form |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| have been identified and characterized. A characteristic feature of |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| biosynthesis is that the catalysis of the various steps is realized through an multi-subunit complex. For eight of the participating polypeptides (COQ1-3, COQ5-7, ARH1, YAH1) an enzymatic function has been established |CITS:[17482885] [10375636] [9818721][26260787]| whereas the functions of COQ4, COQ9 |CITS:[22593570]| and COQ8 |CITS:[18801050] [21944752] [22593570]| is still under investigation., However, utilizing COQ knock-out mutants and functional complementation tools point out that COQ8 is very probably a kinase that phosphorylates various COQ's and is essential for the assembly and integrity of the Q6 biosynthetic complex |CITS:[19002377]|. COQ4 has been shown to affect the first methylation reaction in the pathway catalyzed by COQ3 but also appears to have a general role in the multi-subunit complex acting in the pathway. Furthermore, COQ9 affects the functionality of COQ6 and COQ7 |CITS:[22593570]|., The discovery that besides |FRAME:4-hydroxybenzoate| also the 4-amino-substituted |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| serves as a precursor of |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| biosynthesis has extended the scope of this pathway considerably |CITS:[20534343] [20592037]|. The reason that |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| as a natural substrate of the pathway has been overlooked lies in the fact that this compound is a constitutive component of the glucose synthetic medium for yeast cultivation and has therefore never been tested as a substrate. In addition, only after the role of a novel ferredoxin/ferredoxin reductase (YHD1/ARH1) system essential for the first hydroxylation step of the pathway had been detected |CITS:[20534343]| a targeted investigation for intermediates of affected reactions became possible. It has been shown that COQ2 and COQ6 accept both 4-hydroxy and 4-amino substituted precursors in the biosynthetic route towards |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| |CITS:[20534343] [20592037]|., Through feeding of labeled |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| and the recapturing of the label in the benzoquinone ring of |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| its validity of serving as in vivo precursor had been demonstrated |CITS: [20534343]|. In 2015 it has been found that |FRAME: YGR255C|, which catalyzes the C-5 hydroxylation in the pathway starting with |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, is a bi-functional enzyme, also catalyzing the hydroxylation/deamination of the C-4 position in the pathway starting with |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE|. The C4-hydroxylation/deamination reaction is believed to occur immediately after the C-5 hydroxylation |CITS: [26260787]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Arsenic is ubiquitous in the environment, and is present in four oxidation states: 0 (elemental), -3 (arsine), +3 (arsenite) and +5 (arsenate). The two soluble forms of arsenic, arsenite and arsenate, are toxic to biological systems, with arsenite considered 100 times more toxic., Arsenate respiration (i.e. the oxidation of organic carbon, hydrogen or sulfide coupled with the reduction of arsenate to arsenite) can theoretically generate enough energy to support bacterial growth, but the toxicity of the resulting arsenite made it seem like an unlikely scenario. However, in 1994 Ahmann et al |CITS: [7935832]| reported the identification of a bacterium that reduces arsenate to arsenite and gains energy for growth., Since that initial discovery many more microorganisms that can reduce arsenate to arsenite have been discovered |CITS: [10425777][11722908][12324322][13129615][15128527][15545465][15919992]|., In 2003 the genes encoding arsenate reductase were discovered in the arsenate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-94122| (Shewanella arsenana). The two genes, arrA and arrB, comprise an operon which is controlled by an anaerobic transcription factor |CITS: [12939408]|., Following that discovery similar genes were discovered in many other organisms. The arrA gene is well conserved, having 60-100% similarity when compared with seven phylogenetically diverse arsenate-respiring bacteria |CITS: [15486292]|, and can be used as a reliable marker for As(V) respiration., Sequence analysis of the arsenate reductase proteins show that they share many characteristics with |FRAME: EC-1.20.2.1| (often referred to as arsenite oxidase). Like the arsenite oxidases they are heterodimeric periplasmic proteins consisting of a large molybdopterin-containing subunit (ArrA) that contains an iron-sulfur center and a smaller [Fe-S] center protein (ArrB). One difference is that the iron-sulfur center in ArrB is not homologous to the Rieske center of arsenite oxidase |CITS: [15691908]|.
Level 1: Generation of precursor metabolites and energy

Summary: General Background, Aryl carotenoids that contain φ-type rings were first discovered in the Japanese sea sponge |FRAME: TAX-6062|, which at the time was known as Reniera japonica |CITS: [Yamaguchi57]| (in retrospect they were most likely produced by bacterial endosymbionts of the sponge). Thus the first compounds to be defined from that organism were named |FRAME: CPD-20646| (φ,χ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi57a]| and |FRAME: CPD-20624| (φ,φ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi58][Yamaguchi59]|. Aryl carotenoids were subsequently identified in most non-oxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (green and purple sulfur bacteria) as well as some non-photosynthetic species of the |FRAME: TAX-1763| and |FRAME: TAX-1883| genera |CITS: [5711189][5781524][Schmidt70][4635689]|. , In green sulfur bacteria (GSB) most of the aryl carotenoids are found in chlorosomes. These obligately anaerobic photoautotrophs can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph (up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight |CITS: [Overmann92]|) due to their chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. The chlorosome consists of mostly |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"|, or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| that self-aggregate into large oligomers, but also contains up to 10% carotenoids., The main carotenoid produced by GSB species with |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| or |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| as the primary antenna component is the monocyclic |FRAME: CPD-20625|, while the main carotenoids produced by brown-colored green sulfur bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-274537|), which contain |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| as their primary antenna bacteriochlorophyl are the dicyclic |FRAME: CPD-20626| and |FRAME: CPD-20624| (see |FRAME: PWY-7941|), as well as small quantities of |FRAME: CPD-20627| and |FRAME: CPD-20629| |CITS: [15115301][18676669]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7940|)., About This Pathway, Soon after the discovery of aryl carotenoids it was proposed that the aryl ring systems are formed by the aromatization and accompanying methyl migration of the common β ring systems |CITS: [Cooper63]|. Inhibitor studies of the system in |FRAME: TAX-1092| suggested that |FRAME: CPD-20625| is formed from |FRAME: CPD1F-114| via |FRAME: CPD1F-126| |CITS: [526104]|., This proposed pathway was eventually confirmed, and shown to involve two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.19|, which forms a β-type ring at one end of lycopene, and |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.39|, which converts the ring to a φ-type ring., Four different enzyme families are known to catalyze the former reaction (CrtY-type, CrtL-type, heterodimeric enzymes, and CruA type lycopene β-cyclases). The enzymes found in GSB (the first of which was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1097|) belong to the last family. It is a monocyclase, and only acts on one of the ends of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| |CITS: [17606904]|. , The second activity is encoded in GSB by the |FRAME: G-58136| gene. This type of enzymes was discovered in actinobacteria (specifically, in |FRAME: TAX-1911|) |CITS: [10395965]|. The GSB enzyme is similar to the actinobacterial enzyme, but differs by having a Rieske iron-sulfur domain of 116 amino acids in the middle of the sequence that is not found in the actinomycete enzyme |CITS: [15292122]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Phosphoinositides "Phosphoinositides"| play a key role in signal transduction in the eukaryotic cell, transmitting signals from the cell surface to modulate intracellular processes. One well known phosphoinositide pathway produces the secondary messengers |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: DIACYLGLYCEROL "diacylglycerol"| and is described in |FRAME: PWY-6351|., The 3-phosphoinositide pathway described here is another one of the major pathways of intracellular signal transduction. At the center of this pathway are the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases (PI 3-kinases), enzymes that produce the monophosphate |FRAME: CPD-177 "phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate"|, the bisphosphate |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH "phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate"| and the trisphosphate |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE "phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate"|, all important compounds in , signaling cascades that influences a wide variety of cellular functions., The 3-phosphoinositide pathway has been implicated in growth factor-dependent mitogenesis, membrane ruffling and glucose uptake, cell proliferation, oncogenic transformation, cell survival, cell migration, and intracellular protein trafficking. |CITS: [8086005]|. Some of the products of the PI 3-kinases, namely |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH "phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate"| and the trisphosphate |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE "phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate"|, are almost absent in quiescent cells but are produced rapidly upon stimulation by a variety of factors, suggesting a likely function as second messengers. In addition, these compounds do not seem to be substrates for phospholipases C |CITS: [2553693]|, and it has been proposed that they may act via the activation of certain protein kinases such as Akt/RAC/PKB and certain protein kinase C isoforms |CITS: [ 8181054][7798235]|., The enzymes responsible for the generation of 3' phosphoinositides, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases, have been assigned to three classes based on structural similarity, substrate specificity, and probable mechanism of activation |CITS: [9247130]|. , Class I is composed of heterodimeric enzymes, each containing one catalytic subunit, encoded by |FRAME: HS04527|, |FRAME: HS00644|, |FRAME: HS02818| or |FRAME: HS10353|, and one regulatory subunit, encoded by |FRAME: HS07270|, |FRAME: HS02779|, |FRAME: HS04135|, |FRAME: HS13887| or |FRAME: HS16294|. Even though all class I enzymes can phosphorylate in vitro |FRAME:L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "phosphatidylinositol"|, |FRAME: CPD-1108| and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA|, only the later is beleived to be the in vivo substrate (|FRAME:2.7.1.153-RXN "EC 2.7.1.153"|)., Class II enzymes are monomeric proteins that are distinguished by a carboxy-terminal C2 (CalB) |FRAME: CA+2|-binding domain |CITS: [9632630]|, and are encoded by |FRAME: HS00315|, |FRAME: HS05725| and |FRAME: HS06583|. They accept several types of substrates, and are the only mammalian enzyme thought to catalyze |FRAME:2.7.1.154-RXN "EC 2.7.1.154"|. , Class III enzymes are heterodimeric, composed of a catalytic subunit (|FRAME: HS01275|) and a regulatory subunit (|FRAME: HS03788|). These enzymes, which are homologs of the yeast Vps34p protein, can only phosphorylate |FRAME:L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols| (|FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-3-KINASE-RXN "EC 2.7.1.137"|).

General Backround, Polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME:SPERMINE|), a group of positively charged small molecules present in virtually all living organisms, have been implicated in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [4873311][3157043][2185470][1409623]|. Although polyamines are clearly necessary for optimal cell growth, a surplus of polyamines can cause inhibition of growth and protein synthesis |CITS: [8223591]|, and thus a balance is desired between the production and breakdown of polyamines. Several metabolic pathways for the degradation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| are known., About This Pathway, The unique feature of this variation is the enzyme catalyzing the first step, |FRAME: CPLX-26|. While similar pathways in other bacteria utilize an aminotransferase for the oxidation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, |FRAME: TAX-1275| posseses a |FRAME: CPLX-26|, catalyzing a |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| generating reaction similar to other diamine oxidases. However, this enzyme differs strikingly from animal and plant diamine oxidases in both its substrates and inhibitor specificities |CITS: [Adachi66][4341347]|., The original literature focused on |FRAME: CPLX-26| rather than the putrescine degradation pathway of |FRAME: TAX-1275|, and as a result, the downstream steps are not known. The enzyme was shown to generate |FRAME: CPD-6124| in vitro. This compound is spontaneously formed from |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, which is assumed to be the real product of this enzyme. The fate of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, though, is unclear. It is likely that |FRAME: TAX-1275|, like most other bacteria, posseses a 4-aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase that can convert it to, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, but there is no data to support it.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here illustrates the most common route in which pyrimidine ribonucleotides (|FRAME: CDP| and |FRAME: UDP|) are converted to their corresponding deoxyribonucleotides, and the DNA-specific thymine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate |FRAME: TTP| is formed. It is found in archaea, bacteria, fungi, plants and animals., The pathway also includes |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.15|, which is found in eukaryotes and some bacteria. However, many bacterial species lack this enzyme and form CDP in other routes. , Deoxyribonucleotides are synthesized by reduction of ribonucleotides at the C2' position, which in this pathway is catalyzed by the rate-limiting enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "EC 1.17.4.1, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|. Since this enzyme, which plays a central role in DNA replication and repair, can only perform the reduction of nucleoside-diphosphates, the conversion of the product of de novo biosynthesis, |FRAME: UMP|, to a deoxyuridine form requires phosphorylation to |FRAME: UDP| followed by reduction to |FRAME: DUDP|. Likewise, reduction of the first cytidine-nucleotide that is formed de novo, |FRAME: CTP|, to a deoxycytidine form requires dephosphorylation to |FRAME: CDP| followed by reduction to |FRAME: DCDP|., Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase, EC 2.1.1.45"| (some organisms have an alternative enzyme, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6545|)., The enzyme only accepts the mono-phosphorylated form |FRAME: DUMP|. Thus, the first deoxyuridine nucleotide that is formed, |FRAME: DUDP|, needs to be converted to the monophosphate form before it can be reduced/methylated. This is achieved in two steps - phosphorylation to |FRAME: DUTP|, followed by the removal of a diphosphate group, resulting in |FRAME: DUMP|., Once |FRAME: TMP| is formed, two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: HS11626-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: CPLX66-1052|., In organisms that contain the enzyme |FRAME: DCTP-DEAM-CPLX| (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.13 EC 3.5.4.13"|), a second route forms |FRAME: DUMP| from |FRAME: DCDP| (see |FRAME: PWY-7187|).

Summary: General Background, The superpathway of anthocyanin biosynthesis that originates from cyanidin and cyanidin 3-O-glucoside comprises the formation of compounds such as rose anthocyanin, anthocyanidin sophoroside and shisonin. Those anthocyanins are flower pigments that contribute to a wide variation of colors in many species representing various structures that range from simple anthocyanin diglucosides to more complex polyacylated anthocyanins., Rose anthocyanins are based on the simple structure of cyanidin 3,5-diglucoside. This anthocyanin is obviously potent enough to provide the wide spectrum of colors found in roses. Like the anthocyanidin 3-glucoside in other plants (compare |FRAME:PWY-5125|, |FRAME:PWY-5153|) the anthocyanidin 3,5-diglucoside constitutes the first stable anthocyanin in roses and contributes to its solubility in the vacuole |CITS: [Heller94][11960739]|. Insofar the pathway described here is unique to the rose family., Antocyanidins often occur as sophorosides, i.e. diglucosides that consist of glucose attached to the 2''-O-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of anthocyanidins. The anthocyanidin that confers the bright blue color to |FRAME:TAX-35883| (a member of the Convolvulacea) is a sophoroside that forms a complex with several caffeoyl residues, known as |FRAME:CPD-7841| (HBA). Reddish-brown flowers of dusky mutants of |FRAME:TAX-35883| contain |FRAME:CPD-7840| (WBA) representing the most favorite flower hue for Japanese floriculturists |CITS: [15842621]|. , Shisonin, a mono-malonylated anthocyanin, has been found in high amounts in Labiatae. Together with the bi-malonylated anthocyanin salvianin (|FRAME:PWY-5268|) shisonin constitutes a major flower pigment in that genus |CITS: [11809447]|. Both anthocyanins occur predominantly in different species, i.e. shisonin in Perilla |CITS: [12590125]| and salvianin in Salvia |CITS: [Kondo89]| and share key enzymatic steps of their respective biosyntheses comprising glucosylation and aromatic and aliphatic acylation., About This Pathway, Rose anthocyanin: The formation of cyanidin 3,5-diglucoside in roses is catalyzed by a distinctive enzyme that is able to glucosylate both the flavonoid A-ring 5-O-position and the 3-O-position of the flavonoid C-ring. In contrast to the two single glucosyltransferases involved in the generation of anthocyanin 3,5-diglucoside in other plants this unique enzyme possesses both catalytic activities and also changes the order of glucosylation |CITS: [15944692]|. The first intermediate in this pathway is the unstable anthocyanidin-5-O-glucoside which is subsequently further glucosylated to form the stable cyanidin 3,5-diglucoside., Anthocyanin sophoroside: The crucial step in the formation of anthocyanidin sophoroside as precursors for HBA and WBA in Ipomoea is catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside 2-O''-glucosyltransferase (3GGT). , The enzyme adds glucose to anthocyanidin 3-glucosides at the 2''-O-position of the glucose moiety forming the corresponding sophorosides. Although the enzyme accepts all three major anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside, anthocyanidin 3,5-diglucoside are not suitable substrates for the 3GGT |CITS: [15842621]|., Shisonin: The formation of shisonin, the precursor for the aliphatic acylation with malonyl-CoA to form malonylshisonin is carried out by 3-aromatic acylation of cyanindin 3-O-glucoside with p-coumaric acid |CITS: [Fujiwara98]| |CITS: [10845463]| followed by the 5-O-glucosylation of the anthocyanin. The exact biosynthetic route towards shisonin is still a matter of debate and the actual succession of 5-O-glucosylation and 3-O-acylation remains to be demonstrated. The anthocyanin-5-O-glucoside-6'''-O-malonyltransferase |CITS: [12578391]| that produces malonylshisonin expresses a high affinity towards both pelargonidin (salvianin biosynthesis) and cyanidin (shisonin biosynthesis) derived anthocyanidin intermediates forming the corresponding aromatic and aliphatic , acylated compounds.

The plethora of monoterpene molecules follows the evolution and diversification of monoterpene synthases. , |FRAME: +-bornyl-diphosphate (+)-Bornyl diphosphate| is one of the monoterpenes from sage plants (|FRAME: TAX-38868|) that produces numerous other cyclic monoterpenes. This enzyme has become a model to decipher the mode of cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| and product formation via monoterpene synthases in general |CITS: [9614092]|.

General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the, synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives., These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere, |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms,, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|. |FRAME: CPD-701| is a precursor to the explosive |FRAME: CPD-9138| (TNT),, which is a major product of the explosives industry. Many sites are contaminated by TNT and by, mono- and dinitrotoluenes |CITS: [8245826]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation, pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|., The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two, broad categories - oxidative and reductive., In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or, di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and, |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is, released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-5960| can metabolize |FRAME: CPD-701| via |FRAME: CPD-704| to, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, which is subsequently broken down to central metabolites., The first part of this process (up to |FRAME: CPD-704|) is very similar to the process with which, P. putida catabolizes toluene via a set of enzymes encoded by the xyl genes,, which are present on the TOL plasmid (see the pathway |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|)., In fact, toluene is an alternative substrate for this pathway., Three of the genes encoding enzymes in this pathway (|FRAME: G-1843|, |FRAME: G-1842| and, |FRAME: G-1841|) are very similar to the xylAMC genes |CITS: [9555884]|. However, a fourth , gene in this operon, encoding |FRAME:ENZRXN-2203| (ntnB), which was originally, similar to the |FRAME: G-2063| gene, has been disrupted by foreign DNA and lost its functionallity., This function has been replaced in strain TW3 by a novel NAD(P)+-independent alcohol, dehydrogenase, which is encoded by |FRAME: G-1461|, a gene that bears no resemblence to the, |FRAME: G-2063| gene |CITS: [10809692]|., An almost identical pathway is found |FRAME: ORG-5973| |CITS: [8357257]|. Strains, TW3 and 4NT differ only in that the novel 4-nitrobenzyl alcohol dehydrogenase in strain TW3 is not, dependent on the cofactors NAD+ or NADP+, whereas the enzyme from, strain 4NT (which has no insertion, and thus is almost identical to the |FRAME:ENZRXN-3107|, XylB from the TOL pathway) is NAD+ dependent . , In this pathway, P. putida retains the nitro group during a sequential oxidation of the methyl, group to form |FRAME: CPD-704|. The nitro group is subsequently released as ammonia during, protocatechuate formation (see the pathway "4-nitrobenzoate degradation").

General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common , biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are , classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: penams (e.g. penicillins), ceph-3-ems (e.g. , cephalosporins, cephamycins), clavams (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), carbapenems (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9377|, thienamycins) and monolactams , (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by , both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while the remaining three classes of beta-lactams are produced by bacteria. , Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|., Penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins are produced by different organisms from branches of a common , pathway. The pathway branches at isopenicillin N to form penicillins and branches again at deacetylcephalosporin , to form cephalosporins and cephamycins (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|)., The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem and clavam antibiotics see |FRAME: PWY-5737| , and |FRAME: PWY-5679|) differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). The pathway , for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially elucidated and the order of some , known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and , characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., The antibacterial mechanism of action of β-lactam antibiotics involves inhibition of the transpeptidation reaction , during bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which leads to cell lysis. This reaction is catalyzed by class A and , class B penecillin binding proteins. It is specifically inhibited by penicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics via , formation of a covalent complex with the active serine of the transpeptidation domain of penicillin binding proteins. , This prevents crosslinking and weakens the peptidoglycan polymer (in |CITS: [12867450]|). See pathways , |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5265|. Bacterial resistance to β-lactam antibiotics , can involve alterations in penicillin binding proteins, reduced antibiotic permeation across the membrane, or the , production of β-lactamase enzymes (in |CITS:[12195735]|). Shikonin is a red naphthoquinone, naturally accumulated in the roots of various Boraginaceae species, , such as Lithospermum erythrorhizon. The dried root of Lithospermum erythrorhizon, called zicao, is a , Chinese herbal medicine. The various bioactivities of shikonin, the major component of zicao, include , anti-tumor, enhancement of wound healing, and inhibition of HIV. Shikonin has also been used as textile , dyes, food colorants and cosmetics. Due to its high industrial value and high yield in cell culture, , shikonin is the first plant secondary metabolite to be commercially produced via plant cell culture. , The production of shikonin is inhibited by light and induced by methyl jasmonate |CITS: [9640665]|. Shikonin , is derived from two precursors, 4-hydroxybenzoate, produced from phenylalanine via the phenylpropanoid , pathway, and geranyl diphosphate, produced via the mevalonate pathway. The first reaction, a , prenylation step catalyzed by a geranyltransferase, is analogous to that of the prenyltransferase in |FRAME: UBISYN-PWY|. p-hydroxybenzoate geranyltransferase has strict substrate specificity , for GPP |CITS: [11744717]|. The transcriptional regulation of this enzyme directly affects shikonin production, , indicating that the enzyme plays an important role in the regulation of shikonin biosynthesis at the , gene expression level |CITS: [11744717]|., The biosynthesis of shikonin occurs in the small vesicles derived from ER. Shikonin is eventually , secreted into the cell wall after fusion of the vesicles with the plasma membrane.

General Background, Sialic acids are a family of polyhydroxylated α-keto acids that contain nine carbon atoms. Most sialic acids, are derivatives of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, or |FRAME: CPD-21259| (KDN). , |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is the most common sialic acid in mammals (see pathway, |FRAME: PWY-6138|), while KDN is abundant in lower vertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Their core, structures can be modified at the hydroxyl groups, lactonized, or hydroxylated at the acetamido group, generating, many derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-262| is a derivative of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| (this, pathway). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Sialic acids are found mainly in vertebrates and a few higher invertebrates (ascidians and echinoderms). These, acidic sugars are usually the terminal sugar residue in the glycan chains of vertebrate glycoconjugates (mostly, glycoproteins and glycolipids, but also proteoglycans and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors). They function in, mediating cellular recognition and adhesion events for many important processes such as development, the immune, and inflammatory responses, and oncogenesis. Sialic acid occurs rarely in invertebrates. Endogenous sialylation, has been shown to occur in |FRAME: TAX-7215|, but details of sialic acid biosynthesis in this organism remain to, be determined |CITS: [18568399]|. However, it is possible the sialic acids might be biosynthesized by other, eukaryotes in a species and/or life cycle-dependent manner. In |CITS: [7841794]| and reviewed in, |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Most bacteria do not biosynthesize sialic acids, but some pathogenic, or symbiotic bacteria biosynthesize sialic, acids as a means of evading a host's immune system (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6139|). The sialic acid is, displayed on the bacterial cell surface (in capsular polysaccharides) in order to mimic mammalian cells. Pathogens, that biosynthesize sialic acids include |FRAME: TAX-487|, |FRAME: TAX-1392869| and |FRAME: TAX-197|. In, addition, the human gut symbiont |FRAME: TAX-818| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-21259|, |CITS: [18804026]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Whether or not archaea contain sialic acids remains to be, determined. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Other sialic acid-like sugars biosynthesized by bacteria include the nonulosonic acids |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [16751642]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|) and legionaminic acid |CITS: [18275154]|., Protists are thought to lack the ability to biosynthesize sialic acids although more genome data are needed to confirm, this. Sialic acids have been thought to be absent in plants but some studies raise the possibility, |CITS: [18258224]|. Fungi appear to lack any known sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, although strain-specific, or, novel pathways could exist. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Also, see |FRAME: PWY-6145|., About This Pathway, The occurrence of |FRAME: CPD-273| in glycoconjugates varies with animal species, tissue and stage of, development. It is produced by the action of a hydroxylase specific for the substrate, |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| and thus plays a key role in regulation of glycoconjugate sialylation, with |FRAME: CPD-273| (in |CITS: [8647250]|). Humans lack this enzyme. In humans, the CMAH gene encoding, this enzyme is a pseudogene due to a deletion in exon 6 that occurred approximately 3.2 million years ago, |CITS: [16272417] [9675135]|., The hydroxylation of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| to |FRAME: CPD-262| is proposed to be mediated, by an electron transport enzyme system. The cytosolic |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| hydroxylase, (monooxygenase) requires cytochrome b5, |FRAME: NADH|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14527| (see, |FRAME: CPLX-7746|).

General Background, Polysaccharide capsules are ubiquitous structures found on the cell surface of a broad range of bacterial species. They are thick mucous-like layers of polysaccharides that form a cap around the bacterial surface. They are an important factor in the virulence of many animal and plant pathogens, where they protect the bacteria from opsonophagocytosis and complement-mediated killing by the host., Capsular polysaccharides are linear and consist of regularly repeating subunits of one to six monosaccharides. They have molecular weights on the order of 100-2000 kDa, and are linked to the cell surface of the bacterium via covalent attachments to phospholipids, lipid-A molecules, or peptidoglycan. The composition allows for a remarkable variability - over 80 different capsular polysaccharides (also known as K antigens) have been described for |FRAME: TAX-562| alone., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1396| is a foodborne, spore-forming pathogenic bacterium that is present in soil, dust, water, plants, and the intestinal tract of insects and mammals. The organism can exist as a planktonic vegetative cell, a spore, or as a member of a biofilm community., In the planktonic phase and in late stage biofilm, the organism synthesizes an unusual cell wall polysaccharide composed of the repeating trisaccharide subunit |FRAME: Bacillus-Cereus-HF-PS-Polysaccharide "→6)Gal(α1→2)(2-R-hydroxyglutar-5-ylamido)Fuc2NAc4N-(α1→6)GlcNAc(β1→"|, where galactose is linked to the hydroxyglutarate moiety of the rare monosaccharide |FRAME: CPD-19694| (FucNAc-4-amido-(2)-hydroxyglutarate), which has so far not been observed elsewhere |CITS: [21784857]|., This pathway describes the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-19694|, which is produced as the activated form |FRAME: CPD-19693|. The first key enzyme is |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.92|, which has been described previously from |FRAME: TAX-272559|, in which it is incorporated into the capsular polysaccharide as well as |FRAME: Lipoteichoic-Acids "lipoteichoic acids"| |CITS: [23458065]|. The second enzyme, which has not been described previously, is |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.65|, a ligase that condenses |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| with |FRAME: CPD-16606| at the expense of ATP hydrolysis |CITS: [25368324]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14140 "Butirosins A"| and |FRAME: CPD-14193| are naturally occurring derivatives of the |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "2-aminoglycoside antibiotics"| |FRAME: CPD-14196| and |FRAME: CPD-14143|, respectively, produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1397| and discovered in the early 1970s |CITS: [4207954][4670491][4670492]|., The butirosins are unique among naturally occurring aminoglycosides since they contain an (S)-4-amino-2-hydroxybutyrate (AHBA) side-chain at the C-1 amine of the central 2-deoxystreptamine ring. This modification has been shown to confer resistance against several aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (the C-1 amine is a frequent target of aminoglycoside N-acyltransferases). As a result, the butirosins are active toward many aminoglycoside-resistant strains., Although the butirosins are not themselves clinically useful drugs, the properties of their side-chain have led to successful synthetic alteration of |FRAME: CPD-4822| and |FRAME: CPD-14161| to produce |FRAME: CPD-14197| and |FRAME: CPD-14162|, respectively |CITS: [62814][Watanabe87a]|., About This Pathway, For discussion of the pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-14143|, please see the pathways |FRAME: PWY-7014| and |FRAME: PWY-7015|., The biosynthesis of AHBA side chain from L-glutamate proceeds via intermediates tethered to a specific acyl carrier protein, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15063| gene. The L-glutamate is first activated and tethered to BtrI via a thioester linkage between its γ-carboxyl group and the terminal sulfhydryl group of the 4'-phosphopantethein arm of holo-BtrI |CITS: [15975512]|., Decarboxylation and α-hydroxylation, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-15059| and the |FRAME: G-15060| gene products, respectively, occur sequentially while the intermediates are still linked to the carrier protein, resulting in |FRAME: 2-H-4-G-glutamylamino-butanoyl-BtrI| |CITS: [15975512]|. A transferase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15061| gene, transfers the side-chain, still capped by a terminal γ-glutamyl group, to |FRAME: CPD-14143|, and the pathway is completed by the removal of the terminal glutamyl, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-15062| gene product |CITS: [17462573]|.

Alizarin is a red pigment found in the roots of the madder (Rubia tinctorum) plant. It was used traditionally , as a dye. The biosynthesis of alizarin in plant cell culture can be induced by oomycetes elicitor, , suggesting a biological role of alizarin in plant defense |CITS: [Tegelen99]|. In addition to alizarin, the madder , plant also accumulates many other anthraquinones, with the major ones being munjstin, and the , C-ring glycosides lucidin primeveroside and ruberythric acid. , The A ring and B ring of these madder anthraquinones are derived from isochorismate and , alpha-ketoglutarate via 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate, which is also a precursor for the biosynthesis of , naphthoqionones such as juglone and lawsone. Radio tracer studies showed that the C ring is derived , from DMAPP (dimethylallyldiphosphate) of the MEP pathway, but not the MAV , pathway |CITS: [Eichinger99], [11754943]|. The reactions leading from DMAPP and 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate to , the anthraquinones are not well characterized. Multiple steps may be involved., It should be pointed out that some plants as well as fungi can synthesize anthraquinones in a different , route, specifically, from acetyl-CoA via the polyketide pathway (cited in |CITS: [Eichinger99]|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-693 "Abscisic acid"| (ABA) is an isoprenoid plant hormone that was initially thought to be a signaling molecule whose accumulation induces the abscission of leaves (abscission is the process by which a plant drops one or more of its parts, such as a leaf, fruit, flower or seed), hence its name. Now, however, it is known that abscission is usually regulated by ethylene, and abscisic acid is involved in the process only in a small number of plants., In most plants the accumulation of ABA appears to be a signal for other processes., In seeds, ABA plays a dual role in embryo growth during developmen. In early embryogenesis ABA prevents seed abortion and promotes embryo growth |CITS: [12417697][14716564]|. In contrast, during late embryogenesis, when the hormone level increases, ABA blocks the embryo growth by counteracting the action of gibberellin to promote germination |CITS: [10759503][11124119]|., In other tissues ABA-mediated signalling plays an important part in plant responses to environmental stress and plant pathogens, such as development of desiccation tolerance |CITS:[10611388][11842158][11779861][12221975]|, suppression of vivipary |CITS: [10753527][11124119][15363412]|, and water stress-induced closure of stomata |CITS: [11559734][12834401]|., In plants, abscisic acid is synthesized from C40 carotenoids. The C15 backbone of ABA is formed after the oxidative cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-7424|, and the final molecule is formed by two additional reactions, a dehydrogenase and an oxidoreductase, as described in this pathway |CITS: [12692318][15862093]|., In some plant pathogenic fungi ABA is synthesized a different biosynthetic route that involves the direct cyclization of C15 terpenoid (sesquiterpene) |CITS: [10945263][11129578][15618629][15464154][15240257]|.

Summary: General Background, In plants, a large amount of the cell-wall biomass is derived from the precursor UDP-glucuronate (UDP-GlcA) through the complex interconversion of nucleotide sugars (for review see |CITS:[15134748]|). UDP-GlcA is converted to a number of other sugars including UDP-galacturonate, UDP-xylose and UDP-arabinose. UDP-GlcA is synthesized in plants via two independent routes. The more predominant route involves the direct oxidation of UDP-glucose by UDP-glucose dehydrogenase (see |FRAME:EC-1.1.1.22|). A second pathway (this pathway) however has been described in plants and relies on the oxygenation of myo-inositol. Free myo-inositol is synthesized from glucose-6-phosphate, phytate or acquired from exogenous sources., Key Notes on the Enzymes: Within the inositol oxygenase pathway, myo-inositol is converted into free GlcA by myo-inositol oxygenase (MIOX, EC 1.13.99.1). This enzyme is a key committing step in the pathway as it catalyzes the thermodynamically irreversible oxygenative cleavage of myo-inositol to GlcA. The second step of the pathway involves the conversion of GlcA into GlcA 1-phosphate. This reaction is catalyzed by a glucuronokinase in the presence of ATP and Mg2+. This catalytic activity has been reported in several plants (for example, |FRAME:TAX-4577|, |FRAME:TAX-4097|, and |FRAME:TAX-3847| |CITS:[DICKINSON82]|). It was first characterized in more detail only in |FRAME:TAX-3916| and Lilium longifolium |CITS:[192151],[13661996]|, but work on the latter enzyme eventually allowed for the identification of a full-length functional |FRAME: AT3G01640-MONOMER| in |FRAME:ORG-5993| |CITS: [19951951]|. The last step of the pathway is catalyzed by enzymes with UDP-glucuronate pyrophosphate activity. One enzyme partially purified from barley seedlings was shown to catalyze the conversion of GlcA 1-phosphate into UDP-GlcA |CITS:[5570433]|. The study of this enzyme suggested that the production of UDP-GlcA from myo-inositol might be the predominant route in young barley seedlings. A second enzyme isolated from pea sprouts was also shown to catalyze this reaction. Interestingly, this enzyme was able to convert a wide range of monosaccharides 1-phosphate to their activated UDP-sugar form. This enzyme was postulated to be involved in the formation of UDP-sugars at the end of salvage pathways in higher plants |CITS:[15326166]|.

Summary: General Background, Methylated amines are ubiquitous in the environment, especially in the marine ecosystem. They are produced by the degradation of proteins and of quartenary amines such as |FRAME: BETAINE|, |FRAME: DL-CARNITINE carnitine|, |FRAME: CHOLINE|, and |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|, which are common osmolytes of many marine organisms., The most methylated form, |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA), can be converted to |FRAME: CH4| by methanogenic archaea via methanogenesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5250|). In addition, some microorganisms are able to use TMA as the sole source for carbon, nitrogen and energy. TMA is first converted in several steps to |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| (MMA), which can be oxidized further by multiple mechanisms, depending on the bacteria., Bacteria that possess the enzyme methylamine dehydrogenase (|FRAME: RXN-2841 "EC 1.4.9.1"|), can oxidize |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and ammonia is a single reaction (see |FRAME: PWY-6967|). MMA-degrading bacteria that lack that enzyme can achieve the same outcome by a pathway that proceeds via two unusual amino acids - |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-404|, as described here. , The microbial oxidation of methylated amines is an important component of environmental cycling of carbon and nitrogen, as well as an essential step in preventing formation of methane, the second most important greenhouse gas, following carbon dioxide |CITS: [19943898]|., About This Pathway, The intermediates of this pathway were discovered in the 1960s and a preliminary pathway has been proposed |CITS: [5905132]|. The original pathway involved two key enzymes, |FRAME: MONOMER-17025| (EC 2.1.1.21) and |FRAME: MONOMER-17027| (EC 1.5.99.5). The first enzyme was believed to convert methylamine into |FRAME: CPD-404| |CITS: [5905132][5562354]| and the second to cleave the latter to formaldehyde and glutamate |CITS:[4399353][5028076]|. In a parallel route, an enzyme that converts methylamine into |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| (|FRAME: CPLX-8403|, EC 6.3.4.12) has also been reported |CITS: [5800436]|. The relation between these two branches has not been clear. A potential solution has been proposed in a much later study involving the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-199596|, according to which the actual in vivo substrate of EC 2.1.1.21 is |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| rather than methylamine |CITS: [20472738]|. This proposal is supported by the observation that |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-404|, as determined by radiotracer work in |FRAME: TAX-83| |CITS: [940497]|. Based on this proposal, all three enzymes form a linear route, with methylamine first converted to |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: CPD-404| and oxidized to formaldehyde and glutamate |CITS: [20472738]|., The methyl groups are released in this pathway in the form of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which can be assimilated via the |FRAME: PWY-1622 "serine pathway"| or |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation "oxidized to CO2"|. The nitrogen is released in the form of ammonia and can be assimilated via the |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY "GS/GOGAT pathway"|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:ACET Acetate| production from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| can occur via several distinct pathways, which are found in different organisms., Many bacterial and archaeal species produce acetate from acetyl CoA via a two-step pathway in which |FRAME:ACETYL-P| occurs as an intermediate (see |FRAME:PWY0-1312|) |CITS: [21941]|. The second reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME:EC-2.7.2.1|, results in the generation of ATP from ADP., In most archaea |CITS: [8830684]|, some eubacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-971| |CITS: [Michel90]| and |FRAME: TAX-1108| |CITS: [24164217]|), and amitochondriate protists (such as |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [13076]| and |FRAME: TAX-5741| |CITS: [8557109]|) acetate is produced from acetyl CoA in a single step via the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.2.1.13|. In this process, the formation of acetate from acetyl CoA concomitantly produces ATP from ADP (see |FRAME:PWY-5535|)., A third pathway was described from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-316277|, where acetate is produced from acetyl CoA in a single step via the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.2.1.1|. Unlike in the previous pathway, ATP is produced from AMP (see |FRAME:PWY-8328|)., A fourth variant (|FRAME:PWY-5536|) is found in a diverse group of organisms, which includes some bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-33011| |CITS: [33931420]|), the hydrogenosome-containing trichomonads (such as |FRAME: TAX-56690| and |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [3090435]|), some anaerobic fungi (such as |FRAME: TAX-73818| |CITS: [8257282]|), the parasitic helminth |FRAME: TAX-6192| |CITS: [681067][421954][8885873]| and the trypanosomatides |CITS: [9501211][15326192]|. These organisms produce acetate from acetyl CoA by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.18| (ASCT), an enzyme that transfers the CoA group from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME:SUC|, producing |FRAME: SUC-COA|. |FRAME: SUC-COA| is restored to |FRAME:SUC| by |FRAME:CPLX-7458|, a TCA cycle enzyme that generates ATP from ADP., About This Pathway, The thermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2261| is a strict anaerobe, capable of utilizing pyruvate, sugars and complex organic compounds as carbon and energy sources. When sulfur is available, the organism uses it as an electron acceptor for anaerobic respiration. Summary: While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]| it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|. The most common mechanism for retrieving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid. In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde. Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols", or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids ("fusel acids") |CITS: [15933030]|., Aromatic amino acids, such as |FRAME:PHE|, can be used as a nitrogen source, but not as a carbon source. Following the transamination of |FRAME: PHE| to |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE|, the 2-oxo acid is converted to |FRAME:PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| and eventually |FRAME:CPD-7035|, which is excreted from the cell |CITS: [12902239]|. The first step is performed by either of two aromatic amino acid transaminases. |FRAME: YHR137W-MONOMER| is the main catabolic enzyme, and accepts |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, or |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, but not |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, as the amino acceptor |CITS: [6763508][9491082]|. However, a reaction utilizing |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| as the amino acceptor has also been demonstrated, and is likely catalyzed by |FRAME: YGL202W-MONOMER| |CITS: [6763508][9491082][9491083]|., Once transaminated, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated by either of four decarboxylases, although recent results suggest that the main decarboxylase performing this reaction in vivo is the |FRAME:CPLX3O-71|, encoded by the |FRAME: YDR380W| gene, whose expression increased 30-fold when |FRAME:PHE| replaced |FRAME: AMMONIA| as the culture's nitrogen source |CITS: [15933030]|., The last step of this pathway can be performed by any of the yeast alcohol dehydrogenases |CITS: [12499363]|.

|FRAME: CPD-8959 Podophyllotoxin| is a non-alkaloid toxin lignan extracted from the roots and rhizomes of |FRAME: TAX-1461176| species. It is used without modifications as a topical treatment of external warts, including genital warts caused by some types of the human papillomavirus (HPV). However, its main importance comes from semisynthetic derivatives that are used in a variety of medical applications as purgative, vesicant, antirheumatic, antiviral, and antitumor agents. These derivatives include |FRAME:CPD-16754|, |FRAME:CPD-16755| and |FRAME:CPD-17609|, which are used in various chemotherapies, including lung cancer, lymphomas, and genital tumors. These compounds induce DNA breakage through inhibition of topoisomerase II., |FRAME: CPD-8959 Podophyllotoxin| is produced from |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL| via a complex pathway, which is described in MetaCyc in three parts - |FRAME: PWY-5466|, |FRAME: PWY-7748| and |FRAME: PWY-7749|. While the upper portion of the pathway has been well understood since the 1990s, the lower part of the pathway was only discovered in 2015 |CITS: [26359402]|., To find the missing enzymes, the scientists looked for specific types of enzymes (methyltransferases, cytochrome P450 hydroxylases, oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and polyphenol oxidases) by analyzing RNA sequencing data from the |FRAME:CPD-8959|-producer |FRAME: TAX-93608|, looking for genes that are highly expressed in rhizome, stem, and leaf tissues (the typical expression pattern of genes involved in |FRAME: CPD-8959| biosynthesis) |CITS: [26359402]|., Candidate enzymes were tested initially by |FRAME: TAX-357|-mediated transient expression in |FRAME: TAX-4100|. Combinatorial expression was accomplished by coinfiltrating multiple |FRAME: TAX-357| strains, each harboring a different expression construct. Since the host did not produce sufficient amounts of the starting compound |FRAME: CPD-8912|, this compound was also infiltrated into leaves expressing the different constructs. Using this technique, the researchers were able to identify sixnew  enzymatic steps and to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-17595|, |FRAME: CPD-8958| and even |FRAME: CPD-18757|, the |FRAME: CPD-16754| aglycone, in the tobacco plant |CITS: [26359402]|., An enzyme that produces |FRAME: CPD-8959| has not been discovered. The intermediate |FRAME: CPD-17595| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-8958| by an oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase, which catalyzes the closing of the central six-membered ring in the aryltetralin scaffold. However, this compound (which could in theory be converted to |FRAME: CPD-8959| in a single hydroxylation step) was found to be demethylated, and the subsequent hydroxylation is catalyzed by an enzyme with a different stereochemical preference, leading to the formation of |FRAME: CPD-18757| |CITS: [26359402]|. While unexpected, this latter compound is the direct precursor to |FRAME: CPD-16754| |CITS: [1988106]|. Thus, the discovery of the new enzymes opened up the possibility of recombinant biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-16754| and its derivatives instead of the current semisynthetic process.

Sativan is an isoflavan derived from medicarpin, a pterocarpan plant defense compound found in a, number of leguminous plants including |FRAME: TAX-3879| |CITS: [Dewick79]|, and several species from, the genus Trigonella |CITS: [Ingham76]|. Medicarpin, sativan, and vestitol, an isoflavan intermediate, in the sativan biosynthetic pathway, have all been classified as phytoalexins that are up-regulated, by fungal attacks or other stresses. All three exhibit anti-fungal properties, with both vestitol and, sativan inhibiting H. carbonum mycelial growth slightly better than medicarpin |CITS: [Ingham77]|., Vestitol was also identified as a major feeding deterrent for Costelytra zealandica larvae in Lotus, pedunculatus |CITS: [Russell78]|., The specific reactions involved in generating sativan and its isoflavan precursor, vestitol, have, remained uncharacterized for some time even though a hypothetical pathway connecting them, was proposed many years ago |CITS: [Ingham76]|. Labeling studies confirmed that both of these isoflavans, could be produced from medicarpin in |FRAME: TAX-3879| |CITS: [Dewick79]|. But, the first enzyme in this, pathway, pterocarpan reductase (PTR), was only recently characterized in Lotus corniculatus var., japonicus (|FRAME: TAX-34305|). Although some early studies were not able to find any evidence of medicarpin, within the family Loteae |CITS: [Ingham77]|, (-)-vestitol, the biologically relevant enantiomer, was produced, by recombinant purified PTR protein |CITS: [16996502]|. Interestingly, the genes encoding this enzyme, were found by sequence similarity to phenylcoumaran benzylic ester reductase (PCBER) from, Populus trichocarpa , (AJ005803) based on the recognition that the cleavage of the dihydrofuran ring, of medicarpin resembles the cleavage of a comparable ring in lignan |CITS: [16996502]| catalyzed by, PCBER |CITS: [10066819]|., There is evidence for the reverse reaction, and labeled forms of vestitol can also be converted into, medicarpin in |FRAME: TAX-3879| |CITS: [Dewick79]|. However, preliminary evidence suggests that a different, enzyme might perform this function since this activity was not observed in recombinant |FRAME: TAX-34305| PTR, protein |CITS: [16996502]|., The next hypothesized step in sativan biosynthesis requires the activity of a 2'-O-methyltransferase, to directly convert vestitol to sativan. To date, a few type I O-methyltransferases (IOMTs) isolated, from |FRAME: TAX-3880| act on vestitol in vitro. However, they appear to prefer to methylate at the, 4'-position and 7-position, and there is no conclusive proof that they can methylate at the 2'-position, of vestitol |CITS: [17001495]|. Consequently, additional work may be needed to identify the enzymes that, perform this task in vivo. , There is clear evidence that vestitol and sativan levels rise in response to specific biological, insults, such as Helminthosporium turcicum Pass. inoculation of Lotus corniculatus and application, of an elicitor from the non-pathogenic Verticillium albo-atrum to |FRAME: TAX-3879| |CITS: [Tang01]|. Several, enzymes that act upstream of medicarpin show increased activity in response to biotic stress, |CITS: [16667295], [11164575]|, which could explain the elevated levels of these defensive isoflavan, compounds. But, direct regulation of enzymes downstream of medicarpin could also contribute., One of the IOMTs from |FRAME: TAX-3880| that might possibly convert vestitol to sativan, MtIOMT5, is, transcriptionally up-regulated following treatment with the fungal leaf spot pathogen Phoma, medicaginis |CITS: [17001495]| but further work will be required to characterize the expression and activity, patterns of PTR proteins.

Summary: General Background, Arginine biosynthesis is notable for its complexity and variability at the genetic level, and by its connection with several other pathways, such as pyrimidine and polyamine biosynthesis, and certain degradative pathways. The initial steps of the arginine biosynthetic pathways proceed via N-acetylated intermediates. The presumed reason for this is that the acetylation prevents the spontaneous cyclization of glutamate derivatives, which leads to proline biosynthesis, thus keeping the two pathways separate |CITS: [12633501]|. A variation of the pathway found in some archaebacteria and hyperthermophilic bacteria utilizes a dedicated carrier protein to protect the intermediates instead of acetylation., Several alternative arginine biosynthetic pathways have evolved in bacteria:, In |FRAME:ARGSYN-PWY|, which is not very common, the key intermediate |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG) is formed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1|. A second key intermediate downstream, |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE|, is hydrolyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.16|, releasing acetate, and forming the arginine precursor |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|., In |FRAME:ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|), which is found in most of the prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbes investigated up to now, the two reactions mentioned above are linked: the acetyl group which is removed from |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is recycled onto glutamate, regenerating |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG)., This recycling is performed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35|. This pathway is considered more evolved, since the overall reaction is energetically more favorable |CITS: [3534538]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-5154| is found in several eubacteria. While in the two pathways mentioned above |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is deacetylate to |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, which is subsequntly transcarbamoylated to form |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|, in this variant |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is not deacetylated. Instead, it is, transcarbamoylated directly by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.9|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-7224|. The enzyme |FRAME:ACETYLORNDEACET-CPLX| can accept |FRAME: CPD-7224| as a substrate, and deacetylates it into |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| |CITS: [16585758]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-7400|, which has been described in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2285|, involves early intermediates that are protected not by acetylation but by a carrier protein (the LysW |FRAME: LysW|), which participates in the biosynthesis of both |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: LEU| in these organsims |CITS: [23434852]|., About This Pathway, This pathway was discovered much later than the first two variants, and was elucidated after the discovery of a key enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7070| (AOTCase) |CITS: [15731101]|. This enzyme belongs to a group of proteins that are similar to members of the family of ornithine transcarbamylases (OTCases), but lack the SMG amino acid motif, which is essential for the recognition of ornithine as a substrate., An analysis of 474 sequences that were annotated as OTCases revealed that over 10% of them are more likely to be AOTCases |CITS: [16585758]|., Only two of the |FRAME: TAX-339| enzymes involved in this pathway have been purified and characterized. Thus, only these enzymes appear in this pathway diagram. However, it is most likely that the rest of the pathway in |FRAME: TAX-339| is similar to the linear variant depicted in |FRAME:ARGSYN-PWY|, as no homolog of the |FRAME:G-289| gene could be found in this organism (M. Hiroki, personal communication).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CARNITINE| is a zwitterionic, quaternary amine carboxylate that has essential and diverse roles in intermediary metabolism in all living kingdoms., Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and the name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes, plants, and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. , In animals and yeast carnitine is best known for its contribution to fatty acid intracellular trafficking |CITS: [2199593]|. In plants L-carnitine is also associated with fatty acid metabolism, although its exact function is less well understood |CITS: [17988884][30080631]|. In bacteria carnitine is an important osmoprotectant, and can also enhance thermotolerance, cryotolerance and barotolerance |CITS: [25787873]|., |FRAME: CARNITINE| is used in pharmaceutical and nutritional preparations and methods have been described for its production and separation from its |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| enantiomer |CITS: [12191705 ] [9830124]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17910757]|., In mammals carnitine is obtained both by endogenous biosynthesis and from the diet. Its homeostasis is also maintained by re-absorption in the kidney. The best characterized role of carnitine is in aiding the transport of activated, long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for β-oxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-6111|). It also transfers products of peroxisomal β-oxidation into mitochondria for oxidation by the TCA cycle (see |FRAME: PWY-5690|). Other functions include modulation of acyl-CoA/CoA ratios, energy storage as acetylcarnitine, and excretion of poorly metabolized acyl groups as carnitine esters (reviewed in |CITS: [11802770]|)., The |FRAME: CARNITINE| biosynthetic pathway has been characterized in mammals (reviewed in |CITS: [11802770]|) and fungi |CITS: [144128]|. Several bacterial carnitine degradation pathways have been characterized (see |FRAME: CARNMET-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-3602|, and |FRAME: PWY-3641|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CARNITINE| is biosynthesized from |FRAME: N6N6N6-TRIMETHYL-L-LYSINE|. This compound does not appear to be synthesized by the tri-methylation of free L-lysine. Rather, certain lysine residues within some proteins are methylated post-translationally in S-adenosyl-methionine-dependent reactions. Proteins modified in this way include calmodulin, myosin, actin, ribulose-bisphosphate-carboxylase/oxygenase, fructose-bisphosphate aldolase, cytochrome c and histones (see |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.127| for an exapmple). When these proteins are degraded in lysosomes, |FRAME: N6N6N6-TRIMETHYL-L-LYSINE| is released. The rate of carnitine biosynthesis depends upon the availability of |FRAME: N6N6N6-TRIMETHYL-L-LYSINE| in the mitochondrial matrix at the site of |FRAME: CPLX-7715| activity. A transport system for this substrate and the product |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-N6N6N6-TRIMETHYL-L-LYSINE| has been postulated |CITS: [17944936]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [11802770]| and |CITS: [15363636]|., The pathway involves C3 hydroxylation of |FRAME: N6N6N6-TRIMETHYL-L-LYSINE| by an enzyme found in kidney, liver, heart, muscle and brain mitochondria. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (vitamin C) is required to maintain the iron cofactor of this enzyme in the ferrous state. A cytosolic aldolase activity, located in liver and various other tissues, then produces |FRAME: 4-TRIMETHYLAMMONIOBUTANAL|. , It has been shown that the enzyme catalyzing the aldolase reaction is the |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1 "cytosolic serine hydroxymethyltransferase"| (EC 2.1.2.1) (reviewed in |CITS: [11802770]|. In mouse, a different enzyme (threonine aldolase; Tha1) catalyzes the reaction more efficiently. It has been suggest that humans have lost the gene originally involved in carnitine biosynthesis, and that serine hydroxymethyltransferase partially compensates for the lost activity |CITS: [38615009]|., After dehydrogenation to |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| in the cytosol, this compound enters the circulation and is actively transported primarily into the kidney and liver. In these organs a cytosolic enzyme hydroxylates this compound at C3 to produce |FRAME: CARNITINE|. In this reaction, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is again required to maintain the ferrous iron cofactor. |FRAME: CARNITINE| enters the circulation and is taken up by other tissues via active, sodium-dependent transporters (reviewed in |CITS: [15363636]|).

General Background, Chlorobenzoates are a group of compounds that occur in the environment in large amounts either because of their release, as herbicides or as products of bacterial degradation of polychlorinated biphenyls |CITS: [7217013]|., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation seems to have evolved recently as a result, of their widespread release to the environment., About This Pathway, It has been shown that some bacterial species degrade |FRAME: CPD-3486| via |FRAME: CPD-633|, |CITS: [Johnston72][8779583]|., While the enzyme(s) that catalyzes the first step in the pathway has not been characterized, evidence suggests that, |FRAME: CPD-3486| is converted to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYBENZOATE|, which is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-633|, by the well-characterized |FRAME:CPLX-7833 "3-hydroxybenzoate 6-hydroxylase"|. Gentisate is then processed to TCA cycle intermediates, as, described in |FRAME: PWY-6223|., Organisms that employ this pathway have been isolated both under low oxygen concentration |CITS: [8779583]| and, high oxygen concentrations |CITS: [10779619]|. However, these organisms appear to compete better under conditions of, slow growth and nutrient limitation |CITS: [Krooneman98][10779619]|.

|FRAME: CPD-10247 Sulfoquinovose| is a major component of organo-sulfur compounds in nature |CITS: [428677]|. It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes |CITS: [15012227][17334828]|., Bacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated, and multiple degradation pathways have been described |CITS: [Liu21]|., About this pathway, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.199|, hydrolyzes terminal non-reducing α-sulfoquinovoside residues in |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL "α-sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerides"| and |FRAME: CPD-19111 "α-sulfoquinovosyl glycerol"|. The gene encoding it, |FRAME: EG11843|, has been found in association with all three sulfoglycolytic pathways that were reported first. It was thus employed to search for novel sulfoglycolytic pathways., A search for genes clustered in the neighborhood of this gene identified several Sequence Similarity Networks (SSNs) that were different from the three pathways known at the time. These SSNs were found to be associated with three additional sulfoglycolytic pathways |CITS: [Liu21]|., This pathway, found in several members of the α-proteobacteria, involves a homolog of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.5| (SsuD) and and a member of the aldo-keto reductase family. The monooxygenase was shown to catalyze the oxygenolytic C-S cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-10247| to sulfite and 6-dehydro-D-glucose, and the reductase was shown to catalyze the reduction of that product to |FRAME: Glucopyranose|. D-Glucose is then degraded further via the Entner-Duodoroff pathway |CITS: [Liu21]|., The pathway's enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1176649| were described in much detail in a subsequent 2022 study.
