Summary: |FRAME: CPD-16942 4-Oxopentanoate| (commonly known as levulinate) is readily obtained from biomass through non-enzymatic acid hydrolysis of a wide range of feedstock. The compound is considered important commercially, as it can be used as a renewable feedstock for the production of fuel additives, flavors, fragrances, and polymers., Calcium levulinate is used as a common oral and parenteral source of calcium., A study of levulinate degradation in perfused rat livers and live rats that were given calcium levulinate suggested the existence of three degradation pathways, all of which involved CoA thioesters. Two of those produced lactate, while the third (this pathway) produced |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [21126961]|., In addition, some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-160488| can metabolize |FRAME: CPD-16942| as their sole carbon source. Studies of |FRAME: CPD-16942| catabolism identified |FRAME: CPD-20688| and |FRAME: CPD-12765| (or their CoA thioesters) as pathway intermediates |CITS: [18938201]| and suggested that it is likely processed via CoA thioesters |CITS: [21821073]|. Transposon mutagenesis of |FRAME: TAX-160488| identified 3 genes essential for |FRAME: CPD-16942| degradation that are clustered together on the chromosome. Analysis of that region showed a cluster of seven genes that are cotranscribed. By constructing mutant strains for each of these genes and analyzing the products they produce while growing on |FRAME: CPD-16942| it was found the the bacterium utilizes a pathway similar to the rat liver pathway that produces |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [28947739]|., Following the reduction of the oxo group at position 4 to a hydroxyl group, the main task of the pathway is to move the hydroxyl group to position 3, making it a substrate for the β-oxidation pathway. This is achieved by phosphorylation, followed by formation of a double bond at positions 3,4, migration of the double bond to positions 2,3, and eventually hydration to form the hydroxyl at position 3. The phosphorylation step likely generates a better leaving group and makes the subsequent dehydration more thermodynamically favourable., The lva operon is highly conserved among the various Pseudomonas species, and can be found in a variety of α-, β- and γ-proteobacteria.

|FRAME: CPD-13804 "Erythromycin A"| is a macrolide antibiotic with an antimicrobial spectrum similar to or slightly wider than that of penicillin. The antibiotic was isolated in 1952 from |FRAME: TAX-1836| by scientists from the Lilly research laboratories |CITS:[McGuire52]|. It was given the trade name "Ilotycin", but the name erythromycin was introduced the same year in an editorial announcing this antibiotic |CITS: [12984186]|, Erythromycin A is used in clinical medicine against infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria. It is also used for many pulmonary infections such as Legionnaire's disease and as an alternative for patients allergic to penicillins |CITS: [11851474]|., Erythromycin contains a 14-membered lactone ring with ten asymmetric centers (the aglycon is called |FRAME: CPD-13947|) and two sugars (|FRAME: CPD-13969| and |FRAME: CPD-13780|). The structure was elucidated in 1957 |CITS: [Wiley57]|, and the absolute stereochemistry was assigned by X-ray crystallography in 1965 |CITS: [14295195]|., The biosynthesis of erythromycin starts with the polyketide synthase (PKS) |FRAME: CPLX-8415| (DEBS). This modular PKS is composed of three subunits that contain a loading module that binds |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and six additional modules, each extending the nascent molecule by incorporating a molecule of |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| and releasing CoA and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [2024119][1618327]|. Following rearrangment, the final product of the synthase is |FRAME: CPD-428|, which is oxygenated by a monooxygenase to form the erythromycin aglycon, |FRAME: CPD-13947| |CITS: [2446657][1840640][1732208]|., Two glycosyl transferases, encoded by |FRAME: G-14884| and |FRAME: G-14883|, transfer the deoxysugars |FRAME: CPD-13969| and |FRAME: CPD-13780| to the aglycone, respectively, resulting in the first compound with antibiotic activity, |FRAME: CPD-13806| |CITS: [9353926]|., In most organisms |FRAME: CPD-13806| is modified to generate more active compounds. In |FRAME: TAX-1836| additional steps generate  |FRAME: CPD-13804| (see |FRAME: PWY-7108|). In |FRAME: TAX-47868| a third modified deoxysugar, |FRAME: CPD-14692|, is added to create |FRAME: CPD-12966| (see |FRAME: PWY-7109|).

In this pathway |FRAME:GLT| is deaminated by an NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenase, forming, |FRAME:AMMONIA| and |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, which is then fed to the |FRAME:TCA|., The deamination of |FRAME: GLT| is a key reaction not only in the degradation of |FRAME: GLT|,, but also in the degradation of several other amino acids.  |FRAME:ARG|, |FRAME:GLN|, |FRAME:HIS|,, and |FRAME:PRO| are all converted to |FRAME:GLT| during their catabolism |CITS[3289795]|., The enzymes catalyzing the deamination of |FRAME: GLT| are the ubiquitous glutamate dehydrogenases, (GDHs). , GDHs catalyze a reversible reaction, and are involved in both the anabolic function of, glutamate biosynthesis and the catabolic function of glutamate utilization, depending on the organism, and the conditions.  In some organisms, a single enzyme can catalyze both functions under different, physiological conditions., The mammalian GDHs, which are located in the mitochonrial matrix, are capable of using both NAD+, and NADP+ as cofactors (EC 1.4.1.3). , Most of the prokaryotic enzymes can use either NAD+ (EC 1.4.1.2)  (see, |FRAME: GLUTAMATE-DEG1-PWY|) or NADP+ (EC 1.4.1.4) (see |FRAME: GLUTSYNIII-PWY|), |CITS:[4147773]|, but some prokaryotic GDHs, like |FRAME: CPLX-6821| of |FRAME: TAX-1423| strain PCI, 219, have dual cofactor specificity |CITS:[14949]|., Although the NADP+-specific enzymes are capable of catalyzing a reversible reaction, they are believed, to take part only in the anabolic reactions of glutamate biosynthesis (see |FRAME: GLUTSYNIII-PWY|)., Plants have multiple forms of GDH enzymes, but so far they appear to be specific to either NADH, (localized in the mitochondria) or to NADPH (in chloroplasts) |CITS: [Srivastava87][9112779]|, and are, thus not listed in this pathway.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn this variant of the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, reduces a total of four molecules of either |FRAME: NAD|, |FRAME: NADP|, or |FRAME: Quinones quinone| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively, and phosphorylates one molecule of nucleotide diphosphate (ADP or GDP) to nucleotide triphosphate (ATP or GTP)., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, This is a common variation of the pathway that occurs in many bacteria and archaea., There are a few small differences between this prokaryotic version of the cycle and the version found in most eukaryotes (see |FRAME: PWY-5690|). In this pathway, an NADP-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: ISOCITDEH-RXN "EC 1.1.1.42"|) catalyzes the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: THREO-DS-ISO-CITRATE| to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, while eukaryotes employ an NAD+-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: ISOCITRATE-DEHYDROGENASE-NAD+-RXN "EC 1.1.1.41"|). Another difference is that while in most eukaryotes the conversion of |FRAME: MAL| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| is catalyzed only by the NAD-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37|, some prokaryotes that employ this variation of the TCA cycle possess the alternative quinone-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.4|. , While the pathway is most common in heterotrophic bacteria and archaea, there is evidence for its presence in some facultatively autotrophic archaea when growing under heterotrophic conditions., In |FRAME: TAX-562|, when acetate is the carbon source, citrate synthase is rate-limiting for the TCA cycle |CITS: [3889909][3332995]|.

Summary: An abscisic acid (ABA) biosynthesis shunt was proposed from radio tracer experiments conducted in wild type tomato leaves and in ABA-aldehyde oxidation mutants |CITS: [16668451]|. In this ABA shunt pathway, instead of forming ABA directly from ABA-aldehyde by |FRAME: EC-1.2.3.14|, ABA-aldehyde is first reduced to ABA-alcohol, which is subsequently oxidized to ABA by the action of cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases. The involvement of P-450 monooxygenases is supported by the fact that the formation of ABA from ABA-alcohol is inhibited by CO |CITS: [16668451]|., This is a minor ABA synthesis route, which was also found in potato and barley. It may play an important role in mutants which are impaired in the major ABA synthesis pathway.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-25885 Sulfazecin| is a monobactam antibiotic, discovered in the early 1980s in |FRAME: TAX-1912599|. The structure of |FRAME: CPD-25885| was found to be 3(R)-3-D-glutamyl-γ-D-alanylamino-3-methoxyazetidin-2-one-1-sulfonate. The name 'sulfazecin' was given to denote the fact that sulfonic acid is structurally unique in its direct link to the nitrogen atom of azetidin-2-one. The organism also produced a related compound, |FRAME: CPD-25892|, in which the D-alanine moiety was replaqced with an L-alanine |CITS: [7007891][7024230]|., Like many other monobactam antibiotics, |FRAME: CPD-25885| is resistant to β-lactamases and is thus a promising lead compound for the development of β-lactamase-resistant antibiotics |CITS: [3878359]|. Several reports were made concerning modifications of |FRAME: CPD-25885| to improve its antibacterial activity |CITS: [6358173][6499083][4008329]|., The sulfazecin biosynthetic gene cluster has been identified only in 2017, using transposon mutagenesis, and lead to the proposed pathway described here |CITS: [28017601]|. The pathway involves two non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs), a methyltransferase, a sulfotransferase, and a dioxygenase. One of the NRPS enzymes is monomodular (|FRAME: MONOMER-124143 SulI|) while the other one is bimodular (|FRAME: CPLX-85395 SulM|) |CITS: [28017601]|., The SulI A1 domain was shown to activate |FRAME: D-GLT| with stereochemical accuracy, while the A2 and A3 domains of SulM are specific for |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and |FRAME: L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE|, respectively. Once bound, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is epimerized to |FRAME: D-ALANINE| by an epimerization domain. The non-proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE| eventually forms the core of the β-lactam ring |CITS: [28017601]|., Following the formation of the tripeptide, the free amine group of the 2,3-diaminopropanoyl moiety is sulfonated by the SulN sulfotransferase, followed by formation of the bactam ring and release from the NRPS, both of which are catalyzed by the thioesterase domain of SulM |CITS: [29155429]|., The processes completes by introdution of a hydroxyl group at position 3 of the bactam ring, a reaction catalyzed by the SulO dioxygenase, followed by methylation of the hydroxy group forming a methoxy group, which catalyzed by the methyltransferase SulP |CITS: [29155429]|, It is worth noting that this pathway is very different from the |FRAME: PWY-7797 "pathway for the biosynthesis of the monobactam nocardicin A"|, in which the β-lactam ring is formed from |FRAME: SER|.

One of the numerous cytosolic inositol polyphosphates that serve special fiunctions in the cell, |FRAME: CPD-178| has been characterized as a receptor-generated negative intracellular regulator of one or more types of apical |FRAME: CA+2|-activated chloride channels (CaCCs) in epithelial cells |CITS: [7935818][8816834][11279175]|, and specifically of the ClC-3 chloride channel, which is involved in tumor cell migration, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses |CITS:[18951024]|., Elevated cytosolic |FRAME: CA+2| activates CaCC phosphorylation by Ca2+/calmodulin-activated kinase II (CaMKII), increasing the sensitivity of CaCC to Ca2+-triggered opening, and sometimes triggers CaCC opening in some other manner as well.  , |FRAME: CPD-178| is normally present in cells at a concentration of about 1 μ. However, its concentration slowly increases during sustained stimulation of G-protein-coupled receptors that activate phospholipase C and elevate cytosolic |FRAME: CA+2| |CITS: [1530578]|. As its concentration rises into the 3–10 μM range, |FRAME: CPD-178| progressively inhibits the |FRAME: CA+2|-triggered opening of CaCC |CITS: [7935818][8816834][11279175]|., The stimulated increase in the concentration of |FRAME: CPD-178| appears to be a result of 1-dephosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-1107|, a molecule that is relatively abundant in cells and has no effect on CaCC function. Inactivation is achieved by phosphorylation back to |FRAME: CPD-1107|. Remarkably, these two reactions are carried out by the same enzyme, |FRAME: HS02123-MONOMER|, which is also responsible for the phosphorylation of an earlier intermediate in the pathway, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [HO02]|. The versatility of the enzyme, which can phosphorylate its substrate at different positions, arise from the fact that substrates can approach the active site in up to three different orientations |CITS: [11042108]|., Increased expression of |FRAME: HS02123-MONOMER| enhanced the receptor-activated |FRAME: CPD-178| accumulation, as well as the responsiveness of cells to |FRAME: CPD-178|-mediated negative regulation of CaCC |CITS: [8999935][Ho02]|.

Summary: |FRAME: EC-5.1.2.1|, which is encoded by the larA gene, allows organisms to interconvert different isomers of lactate |CITS: [16166538]|. The transfer of the sulfur to the substrate converts these cysteine residues to hydroalanine, effectively inactivating the enzyme |CITS: [27114550]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7928|)., A study of LarE from |FRAME: TAX-2336| has found a different mechanism for the introduction of the sulfur atoms. The sulfur atom is transferred to the fourth iron site of the cluster, forming a temporary {4Fe-5S] cluster. The sulfur atom then attacks the activated substrate for sulfur transfer |CITS: [35700827]|.

Summary: Please note: This pathway does not represent a single organism. Rather, it is a superpathway, assembled from pathways found in different organisms. Its purpose is to provide an overview, of the ways that they degrade pentoses and pentitols., Pentose sugars and pentitol sugar alcohols can be grouped into several basic catabolic pathways. These , pathways are relevant to the degradation of plant material in the environment. Bacteria have been shown to , degrade pentoses using isomerases, kinases and epimerases; and pentitols using dehydrogenases and kinases. The L- or D-xylulose 5-phosphate formed is metabolized through the pentose phosphate pathway. , Some bacteria and archaea use an oxidative, nonphosphorylative pathway for pentoses involving dehydrogenases, , lactonases and dehydratases, yielding the central metabolite α-ketoglutarate. In some organisms, an , aldolase can yield pyruvate and glycolaldehyde, or glycolate (see Summary in |FRAME: PWY-5517|). , Fungi commonly use reductases, dehydrogenases and kinases to metabolize these substrates through , D-xylulose 5-phosphate and the pentose phosphate pathway. The fungal D-xylose and L-arabinose degradation , pathways join at xylitol |CITS: [16849334]| and |CITS: [16321042]|.

Summary: |FRAME: ACRYLATE "Acrylate"| is a product of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP) and |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE| degradation (see |FRAME: PWY-6046| and |FRAME: P344-PWY|). Some organisms are able to utilize acrylate as sole carbon source., The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-246200| possesses two general pathways for metabolism of DMSP. One of the pathways is described here, while the other is described in |FRAME: PWY-6373|., In this pathway |FRAME: ACRYLATE| is transformed into |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.17| (other unidentifed acyl-CoA ligases appear to catalyze this transformation as well). Acryloyl-CoA is then reduced to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.84| (AcuI). In addition, |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA| is also rapidly hydrated to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONYL-COA| by acryloyl-CoA hydratase (AcuH) |CITS: [23815737]|., The dehydration of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONYL-COA| to |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA| followed by reduction to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| was also described from |FRAME: TAX-1063| |CITS: [22056933]|., Study of the key enzymes from the typical DMSP-catabolizing Roseobacters |FRAME: TAX-246200|, |FRAME: TAX-55218|, and |FRAME: TAX-215813| has determined that this pathway represents an effective detoxification system for |FRAME: ACRYLATE| catabolism. The genes encoding these enzymes are conserved in many organisms across all domains of life, suggesting that this detoxification system is likely relevant to metabolic processes and environments beyond DMSP catabolism |CITS: [28598523]|.

General Background, Most pathogenic bacteria have an absolute requirement for iron, which is scarce within their host environment. In vertebrates the majority of the iron is found in the form of heme. Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. In general, the bacteria express outer membrane proteins that bind heme compounds, extract heme from them, and transport the heme into the cell, where it is degraded to release the iron |CITS: [1425573][7783623][9157245]|. The most common heme-degradation systems utilize heme oxygenase enzymes that degrade heme to yield iron, carbon monoxide, and biliverdin., Several forms of bacterial heme oxygenases are known, and they are described in the various heme degradation pathways in MetaCyc. The enzymes consume three molecules of oxygen and a total of seven electron equivalents to break the tetrapyrrole ring and liberate the iron. However, while some enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), others produce different unusual isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| (|FRAME: PWY-7844|), |FRAME: CPD-18928| (|FRAME: PWY-7843|), |FRAME: CPD-19710| (|FRAME: PWY-7846|), |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| (|FRAME: PWY-7847|) and |FRAME: CPD-19716| and |FRAME: CPD-19715| (|FRAME: PWY-7848|)., About This Pathway, Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. One such system is the iron-regulated surface determinant (Isd) system, which is dedicated to heme-iron acquisition from host hemoglobin |CITS: [12574635]|. The system, which was characterized in |FRAME: TAX-1280|, includes nine proteins that are responsible for the binding of hemoglobin, removal of the heme cofactor, its transport into the bacterium, and its degradation to release the iron |CITS: [15101396]|., The degradation step is catalyzed by two paralogous heme oxygenases, the products of the |FRAME: G-54980| and |FRAME: G-54981| genes. The two proteins belong to a family of heme oxygenases that is distinct from the canonical eukaryotic and prokaryotic heme oxygenases. Despite sharing 64% sequence identity at the amino acid level and having very similar crystal structures |CITS: [18713745]|, the two enzymes are not functionally redundant, as both are required for staphylococcal growth with heme as a sole iron source |CITS: [18643935]|. Unlike canonical heme oxygenases that form |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, the IsdG/I enzymes form a mixture of β- and δ-isomers of oxo-bilirubins that were named |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| |CITS: [20180905]|., In addition, the enzymes produce |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and not |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE|, indicating that their mechanism is significantly different from that of the cannonical heme oxygenases |CITS: [23600533]|.

General Background, The thiol redox system of |FRAME:TAX-562| consists of the thioredoxin pathway (shown here) and the glutathione/glutaredoxin pathway (see |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY|). Electrons from |FRAME: NADPH| flow through these pathways via gradients in redox potentials. Thioredoxin and glutaredoxin reduce disulfide bonds by a thiol-disulfide exchange mechanism involving two active site cysteine residues in the motif CXXC (where X is any amino acid) that form either a disulfide or a dithiol. In addition to the importance of thiol redox potential |CITS: [10464247]|, other important factors in the thiol redox system are cellular location |CITS: [9724776]| and the overall redox state of the cell. Both the thioredoxin and glutathione pathways appear to operate in parallel. Genetic studies in |FRAME:TAX-562| have shown the two pathways to be functionally redundant during aerobic growth, although inactivation of both pathways results in unviability. Reviewed in |CITS: [17659286] [18423382] [11544348]|. , The thioredoxin pathway is involved in reducing important cytoplasmic enzymes such as the essential ribonucleotide reductase, as well as 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate reductase and methionine sulfoxide reductases A and B. |FRAME:TAX-562| thioredoxin also binds to bacteriophage T7 DNA polymerase and serves as its processivity factor for polymerization during phage growth (|CITS: [20080681]| and in |CITS: [9440688]|). In addition, many other proteins that may interact with thioredoxin have been identified |CITS: [15502869] [15004283]|. Thioredoxin is also involved in a pathway for the trans-membrane transfer of reducing potential from the cytoplasm to the periplasm to reduce the protein disulfide isomerase DbsC |CITS: [9352906] [19258316]|. After acting as a reductant, disulfide-containing oxidized thioredoxin is reduced back to a dithiol by thioredoxin reductase, an FAD-containing, NADPH-dependent enzyme. Reviewed in |CITS: [17659286]|. , The thiol redox system is present in taxonomic groups from archaea to man. However, despite structural and mechanistic similariteis between prokaryotic and eukaryotic thiol redox systems, their overall cellular functions differ (reviewed in |CITS: [17659286]| and |CITS: [11012661]|). , About This Pathway, In this pathway diagram, clicking on the protein class named "a reduced thioredoxin" will display a page showing two instances of this class named reduced thioredoxin 2 and reduced thioredoxin 1. These proteins are the products of |FRAME:TAX-562| genes trxC and trxA, respectively. Clicking on either of the instance names will display a page showing some structural and functional properties of the respective protein., Again in the pathway diagram, clicking on the protein class named "an oxidized thioredoxin" will display a page showing two instances of this class named oxidized thioredoxin 1 and oxidized thioredoxin 2. Note that in the gene-reaction schematic shown on this page the reduced thioredoxins are considered to be the direct gene products and their oxidized forms are shown separately as modified forms of the gene products., In |FRAME:TAX-562| TrxA is a more well studied thiol-disulfide oxidoreductase than TrxC (Trx2). TrxC was identified later as a novel thioredoxin that forms a subfamily of the TrxA protein family. The gene encoding TrxC is under control of the transcriptional regulator OxyR which responds to oxidative stress, although the biological role of TrxC remains to be fully elucidated |CITS: [9388228] [12952960]|.

This pathway is found in several sulfur-oxidizing organisms, including the facultative chemolithotroph |FRAME: TAX-921| and the acidophilic thiobacilli. Acidithiobacilii are prominent bacteria that catalyze the oxidation of inorganic sulfur compounds under acidic conditions (pH 1 to 3) and ambient temperatures. Important members include the Acidithiobacillus and Acidiphilium spp., which can grow chemolithoautotrophically with sulfide, elemental sulfur, thiosulfate or polythionates |CITS: [9828441][10758854]|., Extracellular elemental sulfur most likely enters the periplasmic space by binding to thiol groups of special outer-membrane proteins and being transported as persulfide sulfur |CITS: [12855721]|. The thiol-bearing membrane proteins have not been identified conclusively, but candidates include a sulfide-binding protein isolated from |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [Sugio91]| as well as several outer-membrane proteins which have been associated with sulfur oxidation in this organism |CITS: [Buonfiglio93][10406099][8824625]|., In all cases of elemental sulfur oxidation, an activation reaction is assumed to take place prior to oxidation. Elemental sulfur consists of two main forms: rings and linear chains. The thermodynamically most stable form is the cyclic orthorombic form (also called cyclo-octasulfur), which contains 8 sulfur atoms per ring. However, other polysulfane rings (such as S6, S7, and even much larger rings, such as S50 ) also exist. Both ring sulfur and linear polymeric sulfur are not soluble in water |CITS: [Steudel00][17379736]|. A recent study showed that the puple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| is capable of uptaking only polymeric linear sulfur |CITS: [17379736]|., Many studies of sulfur oxidation by acidophilic bacteria showed that the first step of the pathway depends on low-molecular-mass thiols such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (GSH) for activity |CITS:[Suzuki66][4968764]|. Similar GSH-dependent activity has also been detected in |FRAME: TAX-28034| |CITS: [15029700]|., In a study by Rohwerder and Sand |CITS: [12855721]| it was shown that cell-free systems from several members of the Acidithiobacillus and Acidiphilium spp. oxidized elemental sulfur only via |FRAME: CPD-11281| (GSSH), a non-enzymic reaction product from glutathione (GSH) and elemental sulfur. While GSH (and possibly other cellular thiols) plays a crucial role in elemental sulfur activation, it is not consumed during the enzymic sulfane sulfur oxidation. The enzyme that oxidizes the sulfur, the periplasmic |FRAME:CPLX-7137|, restores the glutathione while converting |FRAME: CPD-11281| to |FRAME: SO3|., The enzyme cannot accept sulfur or sulfide, but is specific for the sulfane sulfur of monoorganylpolysulfanes (RSnH, where n>1), and predominantly persulfides (where n=2), which is oxidized to sulfite in the presence of molecular oxygen and water. Organic persulfides such as |FRAME: CPD-11281| could not be replaced by other sulfane-sulfur-containing compounds (thiosulfate, polythionates, bisorganylpolysulfanes or monoarylthiosulfonates) as sulfur donor., The product of |FRAME: CPLX-7137| activity was shown to be |FRAME:SO3|, which is subsequently oxidized to |FRAME:SULFATE| by a |FRAME: MONOMER-12334| |CITS: [11557133]|. These molybdenum-containing enzymes use cytochromes c as electron acceptors |CITS: [5142118][Nakamura95][deJong2000]|, with the exception of an enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-920|, which uses |FRAME: FE+3| (see |FRAME:FESULFOX-PWY|)., For a discussion of sulfide oxidation by this system, see |FRAME:PWY-5285|.

Summary: General Background, Linear alkylbenzenesulfonates are the major commercial laundry surfactants in worldwide use. They can be completely degraded (mineralized) by heterotrophic bacterial communities. These mixtures of congeners are first degraded into multiple sulfophenylcarboxylates which are then mineralized. It is known that many different organisms are required to degrade linear alkylbenzenesulfonates due to the narrow substrate spectrum utilized by each species |CITS: [23001656]|., As an example, it has been shown that a pair of heterotrophic bacteria |FRAME: TAX-402881| and |FRAME: TAX-399795| are able to degrade the linear alkylbenzenesulfonate surfactant |FRAME: CPD-16869|. |FRAME: TAX-402881| utilized |FRAME: CPD-16869| as a carbon and energy source by uptake and side chain shortening via activation by ω-oxygenation, oxidation to the corresponding sulfophenylcarboxylate, and rounds of β-oxidation to produce a major sulfophenylcarboxylate product |FRAME: CPD-16865|, which was excreted |CIT: [15240283][17557839][19915037]|. |FRAME: TAX-399795| was shown to take up and mineralize |FRAME: CPD-16865| |CITS: [23001656][19915037]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-399795| the upper part of this pathway leading to the production of |FRAME: CPD-16866| remains incompletely defined. After uptake of |FRAME: CPD-16865| the pathway is thought to involve the removal of a two-carbon unit from the four-carbon side chain of |FRAME: CPD-16865| by reactions analogous to β-oxidation, thus generating |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| for the TCA cycle (see pathways |FRAME: FAO-PWY| and |FRAME: TCA|). , However, two enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-399795| involved in the mineralization of |FRAME: CPD-16865| have been characterized. The first enzyme is an inducible Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase, |FRAME: MONOMER-18731| that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-16866| to |FRAME: CPD-16867|. The second enzyme is an inducible |FRAME: MONOMER-18732| that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-16867| to |FRAME: CPD-16868|. Reconstitution experiments using purified enzymes quantitatively demonstrated the reaction sequence from |FRAME: CPD-16866| via |FRAME: CPD-16867| to |FRAME: CPD-16868| |CITS: [23001656]|., Mineralization of |FRAME: CPD-16868| likely occurs via its monooxygenation to |FRAME: CPD-10418| followed by ring cleavage, desulfonation, oxidation of |FRAME: SO3|, and extrusion of |FRAME: SULFATE|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: WATER| |CITS: [23001656][19915037]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6041|.

Selenium is an essential trace element that is crucial for the normal development of bacteria and animals. High concentrations of selenium are however toxic, largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064]|. In humans the safety threshold between acute selenium poisoning (>400 μg/day) and selenium deficiency (<40 μg/day) is very narrow. , The natural forms of selenium include |FRAME: SELENATE| [Se(VI)], |FRAME: SELENITE| [Se(IV)], |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| [Se(0)], and |FRAME: SE-2| [Se(-II)]. Selenite is the most toxic, while elemental selenium is insoluble and is generally considered to be non-toxic |CITS: [25631289]|. However, selenium rarely occurs in its elemental state in nature. , |FRAME: SELENATE Selenate| can be used by some bacterial species as a respiratory terminal electron acceptor to support anaerobic growth. The key enzyme for this process is selenate reductase, which reduces selenate to selenite. Two such enzymes have been described - a periplasmic |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.9|, which receives its electrons from s soluble cytochrome c, and |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.14|, which is a membrane-bound enzyme that receives its electrons directly from the membrane quinone pool. Both enzymes are molybdoenzymes, though the former is a type II molybdoenzyme, while the latter is a type I., The latter enzyme has been studied from the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-388741|, which has been isolated from the effluent sediment of a glass manufacturing plant |CITS: [Fujita97]|., The product, |FRAME: SELENITE|, is presumed to be reduced in the cytoplasm, forming intracellular selenium nanospheres that are ultimately secreted into the surrounding medium.

Names: nitrate reduction VII (denitrification) // denitrification // nitrate respiration
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Denitrification is part of the global nitrogen cycle, returning biological nitrogen to the atmosphere and maintaining the balance of the nitrogen budget. In four reactions, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME:ENZRXN-2541|, |FRAME: CPLX-1701|, |FRAME: CPLX-1741| and |FRAME: CPLX-1742|, |FRAME: NITRATE| is successively reduced to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE|, with the nitrogen being transformed to the next lower oxidation state in each successive reaction. , The first reaction occurs in the cytoplasm. In Gram-negative bacteria nitrite is then transported to the periplasm, where the rest of the process occurs. In fungi the first two reactions occur in the mitochondrion, and the rest of the pathway occurs in the cytoplasm |CITS: [Morozkina07]|, Denitrification is also part of cellular bioenergetics. The oxidized nitrogen compounds are used as alternative electron acceptors for energy production |CITS:[10320675][10368138][9667932][2005866]|., In addition to the four enzyme, many other genes are involved in the pathway, encoding electron donors, electron carriers, chaperonins and proteins involved in metal processing. There are 33 genes involved in denitrification in |FRAME: TAX-316| |CITS:[12359326]|., Denitrifying ability has been found in microorganisms belonging to numerous groups of bacteria and archaea |CITS:[12359326]| as well as some fungi |CITS: [9409151][MOROZKINA07]|. However, most of the current knowledge has been acquired from a small number of organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-316|, |FRAME: TAX-266| and |FRAME: TAX-287|., The first enzyme in the pathway is nitrate reductase. In Gram-negative bacteria this enzyme is located at the cytoplasmic membrane, and as the reaction it catalyzes consumes protons (forming water), it faces the cytoplasmic side. The product of the enzyme, nitrite, is highly toxic. It is transported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm by dedicated nitrate/nitrite exchangers (such as the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10642 NarK| and |FRAME: EG12153 NarU|). Once nitrite is transported to the periplasm, it can be reduced to ammonium by the periplasmic nitrite reductase |CITS: [23934766]|, In fungi the first two reactions occur in the mitochondrion, and the rest of the pathway occurs in the cytoplasm |CITS: [Morozkina07]|., The onlly difference between this pathway and |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY| is the third enzyme. In this pathway this reaction is catalyzed by a menaquinol-dependent enzyme, while in |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY| it is catalyzed by a cytochrome c-dependent enzyme.

Names: adenosine nucleotides degradation III // adenosine ribonucleotide/ribonucleoside metabolism
Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, The pathway that is described here is a degradation pathway found in some bacteria, that typically feeds into a salvage pathway. In |FRAME: TAX-83333| this is the major route of AMP catabolism. AMP degradation is not used necessarily for energy production, but is often required for maintaining the ATP to AMP ratio at relatively constant levels in the face of declining absolute levels of ATP. Thus partial degradation of AMP to a product that can be recycled to the nucleotide later is desired. , The enzyme |FRAME: AMP-NUCLEOSID-CPLX| (|FRAME: AMP-NUCLEOSID-RXN "EC 3.2.2.4"| Can convert AMP into |FRAME: ADENINE| in a single step |CITS: [7000783]|. The |FRAME: ADENINE| that is produced in the nucleosidase reaction can be reincorporated into the purine pool via the salvage pathways |CITS: [7000783] [2690948]|.

Names: ubiquinol biosynthesis (early decarboxylation, generic) // ubiquinone biosynthesis (early decarboxylation, generic)
Summary: |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). In prokaryotes ubiquinone participates in various respiratory pathways, mostly aerobic. The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|, which feeds isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10). This pathway uses generic reactions in which the number of isoprenoid subunits is not specified., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation precede decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized.

Summary: The |FRAME: Sphingofungins sphingofungins| are a group of structurally related compounds produced by fungi that specifically inhibit |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.50|, the enzyme that catalyzes the initial step in sphingolipid biosynthesis., The first four sphingofungins (A-D) were discovered and isolated from the human pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-746128| in 1992 |CITS: [1500351]|. This was followed shortly by the discovery of two additional sphingofungins (E and F) from |FRAME: TAX-264951| |CITS: [1474000]|, and later two other sphingofungins (G and H) from |FRAME: TAX-41959| |CITS: [29745730]|., Sphingofungin biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-746128| starts with a polyketide synthase (PKS) that extends the starter molecule |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| using 8 |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender units. The PKS lacks thioesterase domain, and thus the C18 polyketide product (which contains two double bonds at positions 4 and 10) remains bound to its acyl-carrier domain. This product is released from the PKS by the next enzyme,  the SphA aminomalonate transferase, which condenses it with the uncommon substrate |FRAME: AMINOMALONATE|, forming |FRAME: CPD-26579| |CITS: [35023724]|., Following reduction of the 3-oxo group, a cytochrome P-450 enzyme hydroxylates position C14, and presumably reduces the double bond at position C12 (although the reduction of a C=C double bond is an unusual activity for a cytochrome P-450 enzyme). An additional hydroxylation performed by the SphC dioxygenase forms the first sphingofungin - |FRAME: CPD-26567|. Acetylation at position O-5 produces |FRAME: CPD-26568| |CITS: [35023724]|. Spontaneous migration of the acetyl group to the nitrogen results in |FRAME: CPD-26569| |CITS: [1500351][35023724]|., |FRAME: CPD-26570 "Sphingofungin E"| and |FRAME: CPD-26571|, which are produced by |FRAME: TAX-264951|, are formed in a similar pathway, with the only difference being the specificity of the SphA aminoacyltransferase homolog, which is that organism accepts |FRAME: CPD-26581| and |FRAME: CPD-26582| instead of |FRAME: AMINOMALONATE| |CITS: [35023724]|.

Summary: Some organisms utilize organic substrates (such as fatty acids, alcohols, esters, as well as waxes, alkenes, and methylated compounds) that are metabolized via |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|. These organisms need to find a way to convert |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, a 2-carbon compound, to a 4-carbon compound that could feed their anaplerotic reactions (reactions that form metabolic intermediates for biosynthesis). , A common solution to the problem is the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, a modified version of the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"| that bypasses those steps in the cycle that lead to a loss of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Acetyl-CoA enters the cycle at two steps, and since no carbon escapes it in the form of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, the output is the 4-carbon compound succinate., However, many bacteria are known to not contain |FRAME:EC-4.1.3.1|, the key enzyme of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|. These organisms include many purple nonsulfur bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1063|, and |FRAME: TAX-1085|, and other α-proteobacteria, such as the methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-272630| and the facultative denitrifier |FRAME: TAX-34007|. These organisms require a different solution to the problem., One such solution, the |FRAME:PWY-5741|, has been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1063|. Condensation of glyoxylate and another molecule of acetyl-CoA yields |FRAME: MAL|, while propionyl-CoA is carboxylated to |FRAME:SUC| via |FRAME: PROPIONMET-PWY "a dedicated pathway"|., The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-7544|, which simultaneously carboxylates and reduces the 4-carbon compound |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA|, forming the 5-carbon compound |FRAME: CPD-9406|., Another pathway that addresses the same needs, the |FRAME: PWY-6728|, operates in |FRAME: TAX-183963| |CITS: [21252347]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-14496 Ursolate| is a pentacyclic triterpenoic acid that occurs naturally in many plants. As many other triterpenoids ursolate (ursolic acid) has been reported to exhibit a variety of pharmacological effects such as antibacterial and cytotoxic activity |CITS:[18835348]|, preventing and treatment of various cancers |CITS:[22427843]| |CITS:[22549898]|, anti-human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) activities |CITS:[19520182]| and is considered as potential anti-Alzheimer's disease therapeutic |CITS:[22430119]|. , The cyclization of 2,3-oxidosqualene to form |FRAME:CPD-8250| in this pathway is catalyzed by a oxidosqualene cyclase (α-amyrin synthase). In Catharanthus roseus the amyrin synthase has been found to catalyze the formation of both |FRAME:CPD-8250| and |FRAME:CPD-6948| from |FRAME:EPOXYSQUALENE| in a ratio of 2.5 : 1, hence being able to operate in two pathways, the |FRAME:PWY-7068| (this pathway; also see |FRAME:PWY-5377|) and the formation of |FRAME:CPD-9459| (see |FRAME:PWY-7069|) |CITS:[22837051]|. , A microsomal cytochrome P450-dependent oxidase (CYP716A12) catalyzes a series of oxidation reactions at C-28 of the α-amyrin backbone which results in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-14496| through the intermediates |FRAME:CPD-14494| and probably |FRAME:CPD-14495|. The multifunctional α-amyrin 28-oxidase (CYP716A12) was not only able to carry out the three sequential oxidation steps from α-amyrin towards ursolate but was also found to catalyze the three-step-oxidation of both |FRAME:CPD-90| to form |FRAME:CPD-14493| (acting as lupeol 28-oxidase, see |FRAME:PWY-7067|) and |FRAME:CPD-6948| to biosynthesize |FRAME:CPD-9459| (acting as β-amyrin 28-oxidase, see |FRAME:PWY-7069|) |CITS:[22039103]|. In a similar fashion did the α-amyrin 28-monooxygenase (CYP716AL1) identified in Cathanranthus roseus catalyze the formation of |FRAME:CPD-14496| which has been shown to accumulate in the epidermis of Catharanthus leaves |CITS:[18326827]|., Besides the multifunctional |FRAME:TAX-3877| lupeol 28-oxidase another cytochrome P450-dependent oxidase (CYP716A15) has been identified in |FRAME:TAX-29760| through coexpression analysis and shown to catalyze the same series of oxidations on C-28 of the α-amyrin core structure to form |FRAME:CPD-14496| |CITS:[22039103]|. Such multifunctional cytochrome P450's functionalizing substrate backbones with a series of oxidative steps have also been reported in the formation of another triterpenoid, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14483| (see |FRAME:PWY-7066|) where β-amyrin 11-oxidase (CYP88D6) and 11-oxo-β-amyrin 30-oxidase (CYP72A154) have been shown to carry out a sequential two (on C-11) and three-step substrate oxidation (on C-30), respectively |CITS:[18779566]| |CITS:[22128119]|.

General Background, |FRAME: B-ALANINE| is an important precursort of |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| biosynthesis. In both bacteria |CITS: [7037743]| and archaea |CITS: [24891443]| the main route of |FRAME: B-ALANINE| synthesis is the single step decarboxylation of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (it has been shown that in |FRAME: TAX-37762| |FRAME: B-ALANINE| can be synthesized from |FRAME: URACIL| as well |CITS: [3553866]|)., |FRAME: B-ALANINE| biosynthesis by |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| decarboxylation appears to be exclusive to prokaryotes., Eukaryotes employ alternative multi-step pathways to achieve the same goal (see |FRAME: PWY-3981|, |FRAME: PWY-3941| and |FRAME: PWY-3982|)., The bacterial enzyme catalyzing the decarboxylation of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.11|, is one of a small class of enzymes that use a covalently bound pyruvoyl prosthetic group. The pyruvoyl group is thought to act analogously to a pyridoxal phosphate cofactor by forming a Schiff base with the amino group of the substrate and then serving as an electron sink to facilitate the decarboxylation |CITS: [2018773]|., Interestingly, the archaeal enzyme (as characterized from |FRAME: TAX-2190|) is pyridoxal phosphate-dependent. It is also known to decarboxylate |FRAME: TYR| for |FRAME: Methanofurans methanofuran| biosynthesis |CITS: [15715981]|.

Summary: |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (UDP-GlcNAc) is an essential precursor of cell wall peptidoglycan,, lipopolysaccharide and enterobacterial common antigen.  This situates UDP-GlcNAc at a branch point in metabolism,, each fork leading to synthesis of a major envelope component of the cell |CITS: [ColiSalII]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN (Indole-3-yl)acetate| (IAA) is a well-known phytohormone. Several biosynthetic routes have been reported in higher plants (see |FRAME: PWY-581|). In addition, several plant-associated bacteria and fungi also have the ability to produce IAA, which they use to force plants to produce compounds that provide the bacteria with carbon, nitrogen, and energy sources. The production of plant hormones such as IAA and cytokinin seems to be essential for the virulence of these bacteria., About This Pathway, The phytopathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29438| causes olive and oleander knot disease. The bacterium induces the formation of tumorous galls by the synthesis and secretion of the plant hormones |FRAME: CPD-4208| |CITS: [3515320]| and |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) |CITS: [7204339]| into host intercellular spaces., |FRAME: TAX-29438| synthesizes |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| from L-tryptophan in two steps. The first is the oxidative decarboxylation of |FRAME: TRP| to form |FRAME: CPD-237| (IAM) |CITS: [14059783]|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.12.3|. The second step is the conversion of IAM to IAA, catalyzed by, 3-indoleacetamide hydrolase. The |FRAME: TAX-29438| tryptophan 2-monooxygenase has been purified and characterized as early as 1966 |CITS: [5916389]|., In olive isolates the iaa operon, encoding the two enzymes, is located on the chromosome; in oleander isolates the operon is located on plasmids. A strain isolated from an American oleander harbored a 52 kb plasmid, called pIAA1 |CITS: [7204339]|, while a strain isolated from oleanders in Italy harbored a 72 kb plasmid, named pIAA2 |CITS: [7909615]|., The |FRAME: G-5821| and |FRAME: G-5841| genes, encoding the monooxygenase and hydrolase, have been cloned and overexpressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [6274847][2644217]|., Another plant pathogen, |FRAME: TAX-358|, also possesses the genes encoding this pathway on a plasmid, within the T-DNA region of the Ti plasmid |CITS: [INZE84]|. However, |FRAME: TAX-358| does not produce IAA intracellularily. Instead, the T-DNA region of the Ti plasmid is transferred into the cells of its plant host, where it is stably integrated into the plant's genome |CITS: [6962315]|. The genes are then expressed, producing IAA within the plant tissue.

Summary: 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes convert 2-oxo acids to the corresponding acyl-CoA derivatives and produce NADH and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an irreversible reaction., Five members of this family are known at present, including the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| (PDHC - this pathway), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| (OGDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| (BCDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| (GDHC), and the |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190| (ADHC). They all function at strategic points in (usually aerobic) catabolic pathways and are subject to stringent control |CITS: [9655933]|., Acetoin, along with diacetyl, is one of the compounds that give butter its characteristic flavor. It is natuarally found in many plants, including apples, asparagus, black currants, blackberry, wheat, broccoli, brussels sprouts, and cantaloupe., Many bacteria can grow on acetoin. Both aerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [10368162]|,  |FRAME:TAX-381666| |CITS: [2061286]| and |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [7813883]|, as well as anaerobes, such as |FRAME: TAX-33954| |CITS: [8206840]| and |FRAME: TAX-338963| |CITS: [8110297]|, were shown to degrade acetoin by a direct cleavage to |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190|., The products, |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, can be channeled to either respiration or fermentation, depending on the organism and conditions., The substrate range for growth of the strict anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-338963| is restricted to |FRAME: ACETOIN|,, |FRAME: CPD-10354|, |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2,3-butanediol"|, and |FRAME: GLYCOL| |CITS: [Oppermann88]|., During fermentation, acetoin is degraded to equimolar amounts of acetate and ethanol |CITS: [Schink84]|. The key enzyme in this degradation pathway is the |FRAME: CPLX-7659|, a large enzyme complex that belongs to the 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complex family, which also includes |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| (PDHC), |FRAME: 2OXOGLUTARATEDEH-CPLX|, |FRAME: CPLX8J2-279| and |FRAME: GLYCLEAV-PWY| (GDHC)., The formation of the acetoin dehydrogenase complex is induced during growth on acetoin, and the, induction was demonstrated in several related species, including |FRAME: TAX-44672|, |FRAME: TAX-29542|, |FRAME: TAX-29543|, |FRAME: TAX-52690|, and |FRAME: TAX-33954| |CITS: [8110297]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| (CoA) is a cofactor of ubiquitous occurrence in plants, bacteria, and animals needed in, a large number of enzymatic reactions central to intermediary metabolism, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids. Coenzyme A is the common acyl carrier in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells required for a multitude of reactions for both biosynthetic and degradative pathways amongst others forming derivatives that are key intermediates in energy metabolism |CITS: [16415216]|., Pantothenate (vitamin B5) is the universal precursor for the synthesis of the 4'-phosphopantetheine moiety of CoA and of acyl carrier proteins. Only plants and microorganisms can synthesize pantothenate de novo. In contrast to the bacterial biosynthesis of pantothenate (|FRAME:PANTO-PWY|), plant pathways for pantothenate formation are incomplete., Coenzyme A (CoA), derived from pantothenate is a cofactor of ubiquitous occurrence in plants, bacteria and animals needed in a large number of enzymatic reactions central to intermediary metabolism, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids., About This Pathway, Feeding studies in |FRAME:TAX-3888| leaf discs support the existence of a similar biosynthesis pathway of pantothenate via pantoate: when fed with [14C]valine, the radiolabel was incorporated into α-oxoisovalerate, oxopantoate and pantoate |CITS:[jones94]|. The last enzyme of the pathway: pantothenate synthetase catalyzes the formation of pantothenate from pantoate and β-alanine. The origin of plant β-alanine is uncertain but appears to be different from that of bacteria which synthesize it from L-aspartate. Instead plants seem to produce β-alanine from a variety of other sources, like polyamines, uracil and propionate (see |FRAME:PWY-3941|)., The biosynthesis of CoA is carried out from pantothenate in five enzymatic steps. All of the enzymes involved have been recently identified in Arabidopsis thaliana and the metabolic sequence confirmed in vitro by combining the recombinant enzymes |CITS: [12860978]|., Pantothenate kinase, the enzyme catalyzing the first step, phosphorylates 4'-phosphopantothenate to 4'-phosphopantothenate followed by the addition of cysteine resulting in the formation of (R)-4'-phospho-N-pantothenoylcysteine (PPC). PPC is decarboxylated in the next reaction to 4'-phosphopantetheine and then in two successive reactions converted to CoA by the enzymatic action of 4'-phosphopantetheine adenylyltransferase and dephospho-CoA kinase |CITS: [12860978]| |CITS: [12614618]|. The reactions in the biosynthetic route towards CoA parallel the reaction sequence obtained in bacteria but differ regarding the functionality of the involved enzymes. In plants every step is catalyzed by single monofunctional enzymes, whereas in bacteria and mammals bifunctional enzymes are, employed |CITS: [16415216]|.

Breeding programs for economical important crops have been mainly directed towards improving yield, shelf life, color and resistance against stress factors of biotic and abiotic nature |CITS:[17717024]|. However, perfecting flavor has been proved to be much more difficult because of the large number of different compounds involved. For instance, the flavor of tomato is comprised of sugars, acids and more than 30 volatiles |CITS:[19241574] [20456053] [22633806]|. The volatile organic compound (VOC) |FRAME:CPD-400 guaiacol| is one of the distinct aroma forming compounds which gives off an smoky bouquet |CITS:[12644227]| which has been labeled as a undesirable property for many fruits |CITS:[19346240]| (see also |FRAME:PWY18C3-21 "phenylpropanoid volatiles glycoconjugation (tomato)"| and a summary of the topic at |FRAME:PWY18C3-25 "superpathway of methylsalicylate metabolism"|). Nevertheless, |FRAME:CPD-400 guaiacol| is contained in a number of processed food, for instance wine, coffee, tea and cocoa |CITS:[10554288] [12952431] [20092321]|. , A class of O-methyltransferases characterized by their specificity for ortho-diphenolic substrates and inducibility by pathogens or elicitors has been attributed to the methylation of |FRAME:CATECHOL catechol| to |FRAME:CPD-400 guaiacol| |CITS:[7518088]|. In tomato species such as Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum pennellii the O-methyltransferase encoded by CTOMT1 exhibited a very high affinity towards |FRAME:CATECHOL| both in vitro and in vivo. Transgenic tomato plants which either overexpressed CTOMT1 or had the gene eliminated showed a corresponding enhanced or reduced production of |FRAME:CPD-400| |CITS:[22103597]|., Tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) contains three such ortho-diphenolic O-methyltransferases - OMT I, II, and III, which exhibit different substrate specificities |CITS:[Collendavelloo81]|. OMT I was shown to be involved in the lignin biosynthetic pathway whereas OMT II and III were pathogen-inducible |CITS:[24408651]| and shown to methylate |FRAME:CATECHOL| to form |FRAME:CPD-400| |CITS:[Collendavelloo81][7518088]|. OMT II and III are isoforms encoded by the same gene and modified post-translationally, resulting in small differences in their molecular weights and digestibility by proteases |CITS:[7518088]|. The OMT gene encoding the enzymes was identified through immuno-detection screening an expression library obtained from tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) infected Nicotiana tabacum leaves |CITS:[7518088]| with a purified antibody raised against OMT III |CITS:[3566281]|. A genomic DNA analysis of wild type tobacco species suggested that the Nicotiana tabacum gene evolved from predecessor genes in Nicotiana sylvestris and Nicotiana tomentosifromis |CITS:[7518088]|. , Interestingly, the catechol O-methyltransferase encoded by OMT in Nicotiana tabacum also displayed a pronounced activity towards |FRAME:CAFFEOYL-COA trans-caffeoyl-CoA| forming |FRAME:FERULOYL-COA feruloyl-CoA| |CITS:[10482677]|. It has been reported previously that hydroxylated cinnamate derivatives are increasingly deposited into the cell wall as a barrier in response to pathogen attacks |CITS:[Nicholson92]|. These results would be in line with the reported enhanced expression of the gene following pathogenic infection or elicitor treatment |CITS:[5012655] [24408651]|.

|FRAME: CPD-21553 Akuammicine| is a monoterpene indole alkaloid of the Vinca sub-group, produced by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4056| family of plants, including |FRAME: TAX-4058|, |FRAME: TAX-52846|, |FRAME: TAX-60093|, and members of the |FRAME: TAX-84858|., |FRAME: CPD-21553 Akuammicine| was first isolated in 1927 from tree seeds forwarded by the Department of Agriculture in the Gold Coast Colony to the Kew Royal Botanic Gardens in England. The tree, referred to as "Akuamma", was identified by the gardens director as Picralima Klaineana, now known as |FRAME: TAX-52846| |CITS: [Henry27] [Henry32]|. The seeds are used for the treatment of malaria |CITS: [8302957][Okunji05]| and diarrhoea, and as a painkiller.|CITS: [24418074]|. The structure of |FRAME: CPD-21553| was reported in the 50s |CITS: [Robinson54a][Aghoramurthy57][Smith60][Bernauer60][Edwards61]| and confirmed by X-ray crystallography in 2017 |CITS: [29152344]|., Like other monoterpene indole alkaloids, the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-21553| starts with the production of |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| (see |FRAME: PWY-5290|), and continues via the common intermediate |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8519|). Production of |FRAME: CPD-21553| from |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| requires only a single enzyme, the cytochrome P450 |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.80|, and involves several spontaeous rearrangements |CITS: [28827772][29511102]|.

Summary: General Background, Fusidane-type antibiotics are a group of fungi-derived 29-nor-protostane triterpenoid antibiotics that are characterized by a Z-configured double bond between C17 and C20, a C21 carboxylic acid, and a 16-O acetyl group in the protostadienol framework. All of the fusidane-type antibiotics exhibit potent bacteriostatic activity against Gram-positive bacteria, targeting elongation factor G (EF-G) to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis |CITS: [4900137][16489743][19833919]|. Since they are the only known clinically used antibiotics that target EF-G, they have little cross-resistance with other commonly used antibiotics |CITS: [4900137][4945809][24336183]|., Despite of its name, |FRAME: CPD-27364| is a steroidic acid and not |FRAME: Cephalosporins|. It was named this way because it was isolated from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5044|, which used to be named Cephalosporium acremonium |CITS: [14904388][14878978][Chou69]|. It is also known by the more appropriate name acremonic acid., |FRAME: CPD-27364 "Cephalosporin P1"| is active mostly against Gram-positive organisms, with particularly potent activity against |FRAME: TAX-1280|, including methicillin-sensitive S. aureus, methicillin-resistant S. aureus and vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus |CITS: [12461002]|., The genes encoding the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-27364| were identified in the sequenced genome of the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5044| in 2020 and found to comprise two separate gene clusters. One cluster consists of the six conserved genes, common to the biosynthesis of fusidane-type antibiotics, which produce the common intermediate |FRAME: CPD-27370|. The other cluster contains three genes that convert that intermediate to |FRAME: CPD-27364| |CITS: [31860257]|., About This Pathway, The pathway begins with |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.32|, which converts the common precursor |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| to |FRAME: CPD-13283|. Next, a cytochrome P450 encoded by |FRAME: G-124782| catalyzes three successive oxidations of the C-4β methyl group, resulting in a carboxylate at that position., The pathway continues with hydroxylation at position 16, catalyzed by a second P450 enzyme (encoded by |FRAME: G-124783|), acetylation of the new hydroxyl group by the acetyltransferase |FRAME: G-124784 CepD1|, and introduction of a second carboxylate at position C20, which is catalyzed by a third P450 enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-124785|., At this point, a hydrogenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124786| gene oxidizes the 3β-ol group to a carbonyl group, which triggers decarboxylation of the 4β carboxylate, forming |FRAME: CPD-27370|. Thus the CepB1 and CepC1 enzymes form a system that removes one methyl group from the C-4 position of the 4,4-dimethylated steroid substrate. This system acts preferentially on the 4β-methyl group, which is similar to the bacterial enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.246|, and differs from the animal/fungal enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.9|, and the plant enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.10| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.11|. In those systems that act on the 4α carbon, the remaining methyl group isomerizes from β to α configuration, enabling the enzymes to remove the second methyl group. However, in fusidane-type antibiotics, the remaining 4α methyl is unlikely to change configuration, and thus the compounds retain one methyl group at that position., The pathway is completeted by the action of three additional enzymes. A fourth P450 enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124787| gene, introduces two hydroxyl groups at positions 6 and 7, respectively, followed by acetylation of the hydroxyl at C6 by an acetyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124788| gene. The last reaction of the pathway is the reduction of the carbonyl group at position 3 to an α-hydroxyl group by |FRAME: G-124789 CepC2| |CITS: [31860257]|., The last three enzyme are rather promiscuous and can act in a different order than the one shown here, resulting in formation of several other products. However, based on the kinetic properties of the enzymes and the amount of the different products formed, the authors proposed that the main biosynthetic route is the one shown here |CITS: [31860257]|.

Summary: General Background, The biogenic amines |FRAME: TYRAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-58| are relatively abundant in invertebrates (protostomes and some lower detuerostomes |CITS: [PFLUGERHJ05]|), whereas in vertebrates they are found in only trace amounts. In invertebrates |FRAME: TYRAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-58| are the predominantly important biogenic amines and they function independently as neuroactive compounds. |FRAME: CPD-58 "Octopamine"| has a role in modulating many physiological and behavioral processes and is found in both neuronal and non-neuronal tissues of most invertebrates studied. Evidence is also accumulating that |FRAME: TYRAMINE| has diverse physiological roles in invertebrates (|CITS: [20026245]| and reviewed in |CITS: [10515667][15355245][18588893][20621695]|). , |FRAME: CPD-58 "Octopamine"| was discovered in the salivary glands of the octopus |CITS: [14934361]|. In insects |FRAME: CPD-58| has been shown to function as a neuromodulator, a neurotransmitter and a neurohormone. Its metabolism is highly regulated. It binds to specific receptors that are not found in vertebrates, making them potential targets for insecticide development (reviewed in |CITS: [20621695]|). In the nematode |FRAME: TAX-6239| the succinylation of biogenic amine neurotransmitters such as |FRAME: CPD-58| is an important aspect of their metabolism. Summary: |FRAME: PA-N Proanthocyanidins| are a class of polyphenols present in leaves, seeds, barks and fruits of many, plants, where they provide protection against predation and pathogen attack |CITS: [15720617]|. They are flavonoid oligomers obtained by the condensation of two or more units of |FRAME: Flavan-3-ols flavan-3-ols|. Many proanthocyanidins are oligomers of |FRAME: CPD-1961| and |FRAME: CPD-7630| and their gallic acid esters., Natural procyanidins are highly diverse in size and composition, and the monomers are usually lined up by C-4/C-8 or C-4/C-6 linkages |CITS: [12788945]|. More complex polyphenols, made of the same polymeric building blocks, form the group of tannins., Initial studies of proanthocyanidin biosynthesis were done with "transparent testa" (tt) and "tannin deficient seed" (tds) mutants of |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [12376625][10677433][11402179]|. These mutants have a pale yellow seed coat due to lack of oxidized proanthocyanidin and their analysis revealed mutations in biosynthetic genes, transcription factors and transporters., In tea (|FRAME: TAX-4442|) leaves |FRAME: Flavan-3-ols flavan-3-ols| make up to 30% of the total dry weight. A further 3% is composed of proanthocyanidins and their polymers |CITS: [23288883]|., |FRAME: Flavan-3-ols Flavan-3-ol monomers| are synthesized via two distinct branches of the general flavonoid pathway. Both branches proceed from |FRAME: CPD-19093 leucoanthocyanidins|, which are |FRAME: Flavanols flavonols| with hydroxy groups at positions 3 and 4., In one branch leucoanthocyanidins are reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.3| (LAR) directly to |FRAME: CPD-10359 "(2R,3S)-flavan-3-ols"| (also known as 2,3-trans-flavan-3-ols). In the other branch, leucoanthocyanidins are first oxidized by |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.4| (ANS) to anthocyanidins, which are then reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.77| (ANR) to |FRAME: CPD-10414 "(2R,3R)-flavan-3-ols"| (also known as 2,3-cis-flavan-3-ols)., It should be noted that even though most flavan-3-ols fall into these two classes , some anthocyanin reductases were shown to possess intrinsic epimerase activity, and can generate |FRAME: 2S-3S-Flavan-3-ols "(2S,3S)-flavan-3-ols"| and |FRAME: 2S-3R-Flavan-3-ols "(2S,3R)-flavan-3-ols"| |CITS: [19690377][20030585]|., LAR, ANS and ANR are soluble cytoplasmic enzymes |CITS: [17885080]|. Proanthocyanidin monomer formation and proanthocyanidin polymerization likely occur after transport into the vacuole |CITS: [14675436][16669768]|. Since transporters appear to be dedicated to glycosylated forms of the flavan-3-ol monomer, it has been suggested that the monomeric units are glycosylated before being transported into the vacuole |CITS: [19684242]|. Summary: General Background, The bisindole alkaloid compounds |FRAME: CPD-7858| and |FRAME: CPD-19894| are anticancer drugs naturally produced by |FRAME: TAX-4058| (Madagascar periwinkle) leaves. Their anticancer activity is a result of their binding to |FRAME: Tubulins tubulin|, thereby inhibiting the assembly of microtubules and resulting in cell cycle arrest., The anti-proliferative properties of the compounds were discovered by serendipity. A tea made from |FRAME: TAX-4058| has been used for a long time as a folk-remedy for diabetes. When the tea was tested in a lab in 1949, it failed to show any effect on diabetes. However, when the extract was injected into rats, they died within a few days from a bacterial infection. Further research has found that administering the extract by injection resulted in severely reduced white blood cell count and bone marrow depression. An effort to identify the active compound started in 1955, and partially enriched material was shown to possess carcinostatic activity against transplantable mammary adenocarcinoma |CITS: [13627916]|. The structure of |FRAME: CPD-7858|, originally named vincaleukoblastine, was reported in 1958 |CITS: [Noble58]|, and its anticancer effects were confirmed shortly after |CITS: [13719013][13842983][14407465]|. |FRAME: CPD-19894 Vincristine| was isolated a few years later |CITS: [14070392]|., The compounds are used extensively in cancer chemotherapy and are very valuable., Their complicated structures make the total chemical synthesis difficult and expensive and thus they are still harvested, from cultivated plants, despite the fact that they only accumulate in trace amounts. Initially one ton of dried leaves were used to produce one ounce of pure |FRAME: CPD-19894| |CITS: [1489402]|. Attempts to produce them using cell or tissue culture have failed, prompting extensive efforts to study their biosynthetic pathway, to enable either increased production in planta or their production in engineered microorganisms., About This Pathway, The pathway leading to the production of |FRAME: CPD-7858| and |FRAME: CPD-19894| is very complicated, and some of its enzymes were identified only in 2018. |FRAME: CPD-7858 Vinblastine| is formed by the condensation of the aspidosperma-type monoterpenoid indole alkaloid (MIA) |FRAME: VINDOLINE| and the iboga-type MIA |FRAME: CPD-7859|. Both compounds are derived from |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| in parallel branches., The pathway leading to production of |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| is described in |FRAME: PWY-5290|, and the pathway leading to conversion of |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| to the common intermediate |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| is described in |FRAME: PWY-8519|. , This pathway proceeds from |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| by the action of several enzymes, including a cytochrome P-450 oxidase and two dehtydrogenases, which generate a succession of unstable intermediates until |FRAME: CPD-21546| is formed and immediately acetylated by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.323|. The acetylation is believed to confer stability, preventing the spontaneous deformylation that would have occured otherwise |CITS: [29511102]|., The oxygen-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.21.3.11|, forms |FRAME: CPD-21551|, a compound that contains a nine-carbon ring. This is followed by reduction of a double C-C bond to form |FRAME: CPD-21550|, which tautomerizes to |FRAME: CPD-21549|, a branching point in the pathway |CITS: [29724909]|., Two hydrolases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58789| and |FRAME: G-58790| genes, can act on |FRAME: CPD-21549|, generating |FRAME: CPD-7859| or |FRAME: TABERSONINE|, respectively. Both hydrolases cleave the nine-carbon ring, generating |FRAME: CPD-21545|, but the cleavage is followed by different cyclization patterns by the two enzymes, resulting in formation of the iboga- and aspidosperma-type skeletons, respectively |CITS: [29511102][29724909]|., |FRAME: TABERSONINE Tabersonine| is further modified to form |FRAME: VINDOLINE| in a seven-steps pathway. The modifications include hydroxylation and O-methylation to produce |FRAME: CPD-7164|, oxygenation at C-3, reduction of the C-1/C-2 bond, N-methylation, hydroxylation at C-4, and acetylation at O-4 |CITS: [25918424]|. If the first two steps of this sub-pathway are skipped, |FRAME: CPD-19895| (a compound similar to |FRAME: VINDOLINE| but lacking a methoxyl group) is formed instead |CITS: [25918424]|., The next enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-12365|, has not been identified genetically, although it was reported to be a peroxidase |CITS: [Sottomayor97]|. The enzyme using a radical mechanism to condense |FRAME: CPD-7859| and |FRAME: VINDOLINE| to form |FRAME: CPD-13001|, which hydrolyzes, presumably spontaneously, to form |FRAME: CPD-7858| |CITS: [14513315]|. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-7858| to |FRAME: CPD-19894| has not been characterized as of 2018., The enzyme activities are almost exclusively restricted to germinating seedlings and young leaves of |FRAME: TAX-4058|. In addition, the enzyme activities are light-induced. Dark-grown seedlings have no enzyme activities and are thus not capable in producing |FRAME: VINDOLINE|. Most of the enzymes involved in this pathway are localized in leaf epidermis |CITS: [18053006][24108213][25918424]|. However, the last two enzymes (D4H and DAT) leading to |FRAME: VINDOLINE| production are localized in two different types of biochemically-specialized leaf mesophyll cells known as idioblasts and laticifers, respectively |CITS: [10330473]|. As a result |FRAME: VINDOLINE| is found within the specialized internal leaf cells that preferentially express the terminal pathway reactions |CITS: [10330473][20696903]|. |FRAME: CPD-7859 Catharanthine|, on the other hand, accumulates entirely in the wax exudates on the leaf surface |CITS: [20696903]|.

Summary: Adenosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: AMP| (AMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| , which is converted to AMP by the action of, |FRAME: ASL-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6126|). Summary: The structure of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol| (PG) was determined in 1958 from lipid isolates of single-cell green algae from the |FRAME: TAX-3087| genus |CITS: [13510267]|. Its structure is analogous to phosphatidylinositol (PI), but with a glyceryl moiety replacing the inosityl moiety of PI. , Within a decade it has been found in higher plants |CITS: [Benson61]|, Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4868364][4295332]| and mammals |CITS: [5660098]|. It was later discovered in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2246|, indicating that it is produced by all three domains of life. The biosynthetic pathway was elucidated in the early 60s |CITS: [14033231]|, and a laboratory synthesis was completed a few years later |CITS: [5916374]|., The abundance of PG is relatively low compared with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in prokaryotes or with either PE or phosphatidylcholine (PC) in eukaryotes |CITS: [18216768][20671299][21172818]|. It is typically more concentrated in plant systems than in animals, forming 1.5-4·5% of the lipid fraction |CITS: [23532185][3592680]|, Since its discovery, biochemical research into PG has been dominated by its roles in the surfactant of lung tissue (PG is the second largest lipid constituent of lung surfactant in almost all mammals), chloroplast membranes (PG is the only phospholipid found in chloroplast thylakoids) and in both bacterial and mammalian systems., In plants PG biosynthesis can occur at three subcellular locations - chloroplast, mitochondrion and ER. In the plastid (described here), phosphatidylglycerol is assembled de novo from the newly synthesized fatty acids, and acyl-ACPs are the acyl donors |CITS: [16774646]|. In the non-plastidic pathway (|FRAME: PWY4FS-8|) acyl-CoA are used as the acyl-donor |CITS: [Moore82]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE Naphthalene| is the simplest fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, and is abundant in soils., Several bacterial species are able to grow on naphthalene as the sole cource of carbon and energy |CITS:[4423716][10433976][10620687]|., Naphthalene is catabolized through |FRAME: CIS-12-DIHYDRONAPHTHALENE-12-DIOL|, |FRAME: SALICYLALDEHYDE|, and |FRAME: CPD-110|. The later is converted into either |FRAME: CATECHOL|, which is then degraded by either the meta or the ortho cleavage pathways to TCA cycle intermediates |CITS: [1245462]|, or to |FRAME: CPD-633|, which is degraded by a different pathway to TCA cycle intermediates |CITS: [9573207]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6183| and |FRAME: PWY-6224|, respectively)., Several different models have been proposed for this pathway, due to the difficulty working with the unstable intermediate |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE-12-DIOL|, which is rapidly and spontaneously oxidized in water to |FRAME:CPD-4895|. However, some organisms, such as |FRAME: ORG-5978|, carry these genes on their chromosome |CITS: [10433976]|. Transcription of the genes in this operon is regulated by a salicylate-dependent transcription regulator (such as NahR for the operon located on the NAH plasmid) |CITS: [3028396], [3007442]|.
