General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees |CITS: [Pingman57]|). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. Free arabinose is formed during the degradation of complex polymers, as in |FRAME: PWY-6790|, |FRAME: PWY-8006|, and |FRAME: PWY-6813|., The initial steps in this pathway, which belongs to the second type of pentose sugars degradation, involve reduction and oxidation reactions that produce |FRAME: XYLITOL|, which is degraded as shown in the pathway |FRAME: LARABITOLUTIL-PWY|., Deletion analysis studies concluded that the first step is catalyzed in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5061| by three different enzymes: a reductase encoded by the |FRAME: G-12470| gene, which has a preferred specificity for |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and two reductases with a preference for |FRAME: D-Xylose|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10035| and |FRAME: G-107617| genes |CITS: [33666344]|. In |FRAME: TAX-51453| the first step appears to be mainly catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16170|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12473| gene, which also catalyzes the first steps in |FRAME: D-Xylose| and |FRAME: D-Galactose| catabolism (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5516| and |FRAME: PWY-6693|). , The reduction of |FRAME: L-XYLULOSE| to |FRAME: XYLITOL| has been shown to be catalyzed by the product of gene |FRAME: G-12471| in |FRAME: TAX-5061| and by the product of gene |FRAME: G-34472| in |FRAME: TAX-51453|, with both enzymes being phylogenetically distinct |CITS: [20654618][21212945][23506391]|.

|FRAME: CPD-20899 Valinomycin| is a cyclooligomer |FRAME: Depsipeptides depsipeptide| produced by several Streptomyces strains |CITS: [Brockmann55][Brockmann57][2345137][9835560][10400343]|. It has diverse biological activities including antifungal |CITS: [21278263]|, antibacterial |CITS: [10400343]|, insecticidal-nematocidal |CITS: [Patterson70]|, antiparasitic |CITS: [20390111]|, antiviral |CITS: [15226499]|, and antitumor |CITS: [16595926]| activities. Of particular interest is that valinomycin demonstrated a high potency against SARS-CoV in infected Vero E6 cells with an EC50 of 0.85 μm |CITS: [15226499]|. |FRAME: CPD-20899 Valinomycin| forms an ionophore that specifically modulates potassium ion transport across biological membranes, which may explain some of its biological activity |CITS: [5411177][786156]|., |FRAME: CPD-20899 Valinomycin| is a dodecadepsipeptide assembled from 3 identical copies of the tetradepsipeptide |FRAME: CPD-25315|, which contains alternating amide and ester bonds |CITS: [5660414][4368457][913608]|. Interestingly, a very similar compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-1892|, |FRAME: CPD-25325|, is a cyclic octadepsipeptide consisting of two copies of the same tetradepsipeptide |CITS: [10400343]|., The biosynthetic gene cluster of valinomycin has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-285482|, and a model for its biosynthesis has been proposed |CITS: [16511823][ 16910662]|. Valinomycin is synthesized by the tetramodular |FRAME: CPLX-9693|, which is composed of two non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) subunits encoded by the |FRAME: G-107626| and |FRAME: G-107627| genes., The Vlm1 protein contains two modules. Module 1 contains an adenylation domain (A1), a ketoreductase domain (KR1), and a peptidyl-carrier protein domain (PCP1). The module adenylates and binds |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| (an intermediate of valine biosynthesis), reduces it to |FRAME: CPD-25314| and transfers it to the PCP1 domain., Module 2 contains a condensation domain (C2), an adenylation domain (A2), a peptidyl-carrier protein domain (PCP2), and an epimerase domain (E2). This module binds and adenylates an |FRAME: VAL| molecule, and the epimerase domain converts it to |FRAME: CPD-3642|, which is loaded on the PCP2 domain. The condensation domain accepts the (2R)-2-hydroxy-3-methylbutanoyl moiety from PCP1 and condenses it with the PCP2-bound D-valine |CITS: [16511823]|., The Vlm2 protein contains two additional modules. Module 3 contains a condensation domain (C3), an adenylation domain (A3), a ketoreductase domain (KR3), and a peptidyl-carrier protein domain (PCP3). The module adenylates and binds a pyruvate molecule. The KR3 domain reduces it to |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, which is loaded on the PCP3 domain, and the condensation domain transfers the intermediate from PCP2 to the lactoyl residue. The last module contains a condensation domain (C4), an adenylation domain (A4), a peptidyl-carrier protein domain (PCP4) and a thioesterase domain (TE). This module adenylates and binds an |FRAME: VAL| molecue and transfers it to PCP4, and the condesation domain transfers the intermediate chain from PCP4, forming a tetradepsipeptide, which is transferred to the TE domain |CITS: [16511823]|. , The enzyme goes through 3 rounds of synthesis, each time transferring the tetradepsipeptide to the TE domain, which condenses the three products to a dodecadepsipeptide. Once the full length is achieved, the TE domain cleaves off the linear product and catalyzes the head-to-tail cyclization that produces the mature |FRAME: CPD-20899| |CITS: [30542153]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-27481 Avaroferrin| is a cyclic dihydroxamate siderophore that was originally described as a by-product produced by artificially perturbed siderophore biosynthesis of |FRAME: TAX-24| |CITS: [22976977]|. However, the siderophore was found to be produced by heterologous expression of deep-sea metagenomic DNA |CITS: [25222668]| and was shown to be the main siderophore produced by |FRAME: TAX-38313| |CITS: [24615751]|., |FRAME: TAX-38313|, which was isolated from the red seaweed |FRAME: TAX-2769|, produces three related siderophores - |FRAME: CPD-11970|, |FRAME: CPD-11967|, and |FRAME: CPD-27481| at a ration of 1:1:2. The first two comprise a symmetric ring composed of two identical subunits, derived from |FRAME: CADAVERINE| and |FRAME: CPD-11967|, respectively, while |FRAME: CPD-27481| is a chimeric product resulting from the condesation of the two building blocks used for the synthesis of the other two siderophores. |FRAME: TAX-38313| was found to inhibit the swarming behavior of a strain of |FRAME: TAX-663| that was isolated from the same red seaweed as |FRAME: TAX-38313|, by making iron(III) unavailable to it |CITS: [24615751]|., The avaroferrins biosynthetic gene cluster is a mashup of putrebactin and bisucaberin biosynthetic genes |CITS: [24615751]|. A later study has found that the siderophore synthase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124848| gene, is capable of synthesizing all three siderophores. In vitro the enzyme preferred the |FRAME: CADAVERINE|-derived precursor and produced more |FRAME: CPD-11970|. The favored production of |FRAME: CPD-27481| in vivo is determined by the availability of the substrates |CITS: [28434877]|.

Summary: General Background, Polyamines are found in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes and are necessary for normal cellular physiology. They include the diamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, the triamines |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (sym-norspermidine) and |FRAME: CPD-1821| (homospermidine), and the tetraamine |FRAME: SPERMINE| (in |CITS: [20194510]| and in |CITS: [19196710]|)., Several independent pathways have been identified for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|. In pathway |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE| (decarboxylated |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|) donates an aminopropyl group to |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| to form |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| in a reaction catalyzed by spermidine synthase. This pathway is found in most eukaryotes and archaea and in many bacteria., In this pathway variant, |FRAME: PWY-6559|, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| donates a carboxyaminopropyl group to |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| to form |FRAME: CPD-10012|. This reaction is catalyzed by either carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase (CANSDH) or carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase (CASDH) depending upon species. Likewise, the subsequent decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-10012| to produce |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| is catalyzed by either carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine decarboxylase (CANSDC) or carboxyspermidine decarboxylase (CASDC) |CITS: [19196710][22025614]| and in |CITS: [20194510]|., A |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthetic pathway found in hyperthermophiles involves |FRAME: CPD-13489| as an intermediate |CITS: [20675472][15983049]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6834|). In addition, some bacteria biosynthesize the triamine |FRAME: CPD-1821| rather than |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| |CITS: [20194510]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5907|)., About This Pathway, This |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthetic pathway is based on both bioinformatic and genetic analysis |CITS: [19196710][22025614]|. In this pathway |FRAME: TAX-666| is thought to utilize |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| derived from either pathway |FRAME: PWY-40| or |FRAME: PWY-46| |CITS: [19196710]|. |FRAME: TAX-197| was shown to utilize |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| derived from pathway |FRAME: PWY-43| |CITS: [22025614]|. , Some bacteria lack orthologs for the |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthetic enzymes S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.50) and spermidine synthase (EC 2.5.1.16) (see pathway |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY|). Instead, |FRAME: TAX-666| was shown to possess carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase (CANSDH) and carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine decarboxylase (CANSDC). A clustered pair of genes encoding CANSDH and CANSDC was found to be widespread in the α-, β-, γ-, δ- and ε-proteobacteria, firmicutes and a candidate division TG-1, suggesting that this pathway for |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthesis may be widely used. In |FRAME: TAX-666| these enzymes were shown to be utilized for the biosynthesis of both |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| (this pathway) and |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6562|) |CITS: [19196710]|., In |FRAME: TAX-197| however, the CANSDH and CANSDC orthologs were identified as carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase (CASDH) and carboxyspermidine decarboxylase (CASDC). |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| was the only polyamine found in this organism, leading to the conclusion that |FRAME: TAX-197| does not synthesize |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|. Orthologs of CASDH and CASDC were also identified in many other bacterial phyla which include important human pathogens, human gut microbiome species, and deep sea hydrothermal vent species. These orthologs were often found to be clustered with |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| biosynthetic genes, which also suggests their role in |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthesis rather than |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| biosynthesis |CITS: [22025614]|., It was shown that in |FRAME: TAX-197|, CASDC activity is critical for growth. It was also shown that the function provided by |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| in cell proliferation can be replaced by |FRAME: CPD-1821| (or to a lesser extent |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|). Deletion mutants of all except one enzyme in the pathway abolished |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthesis. The exception was CASDH, which showed a large accumulation of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|. It was suggested that a metabolic bypass was operative and that CASDH is a rate-limiting enzyme that regulates |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| levels. It was also noted that the multiple |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthetic pathways found in bacteria offer an opportunity for antimicrobial drug development |CITS: [22025614]|.

Summary: General background, Maintenance of genomic and transcriptomic integrity is a vital goal of all organisms. Cells are often subjected to reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as |FRAME: CPD-12377|, that arise due to oxidative stress, ionizing radiation, and certain aspects of normal cellular metabolism. These ROS can modify nucletide bases and cause problems during DNA replication and RNA transcription. This damage can occur on free nucleotides or in the context of DNA or RNA macromolecules. Organisms have evolved several strategies for combating the damage that can be caused by oxidative stress, including this pathway that is involved in eliminating a source of potentially mutagenic nucleotides before they can be used for DNA replication or mRNA transcription |CITS: [Rogacheva08]|., Oxidation of the free nucleotides |FRAME: GTP| and |FRAME: DGTP| can occur spontaneously in cells when a hydroxyl radical attacks the C8 position of the purine base |FRAME: GUANINE| |CITS: [16863995]|. If |FRAME: 8-Oxo-dGTP| is incorporated into DNA it can pair with a C or an A and lead to G:C ->T:A or A:T -> C:G transversions, respectively, although the A:T to C:G transversion seems to be more common in vivo (|CITS: [1309939] [Rogacheva08]|). Similarly, an |FRAME: CPD-12366| can be incorrectly incorporated opposite an adenosine residue during RNA transcription |CITS: [17804481]|. To prevent these errors, Nudix hydrolase-type enzymes act to remove one or two phophate groups from the oxidized nucelotides, rendering them incompetent for incorporation into DNA or RNA |CITS: [Rogacheva08]|. It is important to note that there is evidence from humans that |FRAME: CPD-12365| cannot be re-phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.8| |CITS: [7819228]|. , Oxidized (d)GTP is a major source of genetic lesions. Both bacteria and eukaryotes show marked increases in DNA and RNA errors when this pathway is blocked. The errors caused by the failure of this pathway may be linked to cancer and other DNA-damage related diseases |CITS: [1309939][17804481][Rogacheva08]|. , About this pathway, The ROS-induced oxidation shown in this pathway occurs spontaneously. The subsequent detoxification of the damaged free nucleotides is carried out by members of the Nudix family of hydrolases. |FRAME: EG10626 MutT| from |FRAME: TAX-562| was the first characterized protein shown to have this protective pyrophosphatase activity |CITS: [9311918]|. Homologs of this protein have been functionally characterized in species as distantly related as humans |CITS: [1332067]|, the yeast S. cerevisiae |CITS: [15475388]|, and Arabidopsis plants |CITS: [15878881][17804481]|, suggesting that this is a widely conserved pathway., In humans, |FRAME: CPD-12365| is dephosphorylated further into |FRAME: CPD-12381|, which can exit through the cell membrane and end up in the urine. It's urine concentration is used as a diagnostic indicator of oxidative stress |CITS: [7819228]|. It is unclear what downstream steps are used to remove or recycle |FRAME: CPD-12367| or |FRAME: CPD-12365| in other organisms.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-6341| is an enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) strain that was recognized for causing acute diarrhea in infants |CITS: [14392127][14397827][13664001][13969771]|. Some strains of this serotype produce a Shiga toxin, resulting in intestinal bleeding and occlusion |CITS: [10962819][17066335]|. One specific strain, |FRAME: TAX-574521|, has been used worldwide as a prototype strain to study EPEC biology, genetics, and virulence |CITS: [18952797]|. , The structure of the O antigen repeat unit of |FRAME: ORG-6341| was originally reported in 1993 |CITS: [7693348]|. In the initial study it was observed that the repeat unit contains about one acetyl group per unit, but that the acetyl group is present at several, unspecified locations. A later study has confirmed the structure and located the acetyl groups to positions O3 and O4 of the fucosyl residue, with a distribution of ~65% at O3 and ~35% at O4 |CITS: [ 20594547]|. The O127 unit is very similar to the |FRAME: CPD-24138|, only differing in the presence of a GalNAc residue in place of the GlcNAc residue at the first position and having O-acetylation at the fucosyl residue., The O antigen gene cluster of |FRAME: ORG-6341| was sequenced in 2007 and found to contain 11 ORFs, including five genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-13118| biosynthesis enzymes, three genes encoding glycosyltransferases, one gene encoding an acetyltransferase, and genes encoding an O antigen repeat unit flippase and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [15778030][17634307][20594547]|. Most of the genes are very similar the corresponding genes in |FRAME: ORG-6228| and |FRAME: ORG-57078|, reflecting the similarity between the O antigens of these organisms. However, only the cluster of |FRAME: ORG-6341| contains a gene encoding an acetyltransferase.

The phenylpropanoids are a large family of compounds, mostly found in plants, that are synthesized from |FRAME: PHE| and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: TYR|. The pathway that starts from |FRAME: PHE| forms |FRAME: COUMARATE| as a main intermediate. The name "phenylpropanoid" is derived from this compound, which consists of an aromatic phenyl group and a propene tail. Further processing results in the biosynthesis of many types of compounds, including |FRAME: Lignols monolignols| (precursors to |FRAME: Lignins lignin| and lignocellulose), |FRAME: Flavonoids flavonoids|, |FRAME: Coumarins coumarins|, |FRAME: Stilbenoids stilbenoids|, and phenolic acids., Phenylpropanoids are found throughout the plant kingdom, where they serve as essential components of a number of structural polymers, provide protection from ultraviolet light, defend against herbivores and pathogens, and also mediate plant-pollinator interactions as floral pigments and scent compounds., This pathway contains the initial reactions of the phenylpropanoid pathway, from |FRAME: PHE| to |FRAME: COUMARATE|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Cobamides that contains |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE| were originally produced by growing |FRAME: TAX-562| cells in the presence of |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|. The authors were able to purify the cobamide and test its activity in cultures of |FRAME: TAX-88167|, reporting an activity of about 36% of that of cobalamin |CITS: [14351147]|. A similar assay was conducted a few years later with cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1553| grown in the presence of |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|. Comparative assays conducted with |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.1| and purified cofactors found that the benzimidazolylcobamide had the highest affinity for the enzyme and resulted in the highest activity, followed by adenosylcobalamine (dimethylbenzimidazolylcobamide) and adeninylcobamide. The coenzyme was also able to fully support the growth of an |FRAME: TAX-562| B12-requiring mutant |CITS: [13796809]|. The first report of naturally-produced benzimidazolyl cobamides was made only in 2013. HPLC analysis of corrinoid extracts from |FRAME: TAX-29466| revelaed the presence of benzimidazolyl cobamides |CITS: [24055007]|. , This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20845|. The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the lower ligand base is activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (CobT) by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide or a related compound to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphoribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) to form the cobamide. The enzymes that operate in this pathway are the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis. Studies of the specificity of these enzymes have suggested that the nature of the lower ligand is controlled by metabolic factors |CITS: [11441022]| as well as by the specificity of CobT |CITS: [24055007]|.

Summary: General Background, The transition element molybdenum (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. There are several molybdenum cofactors, including |FRAME: CPD-582| (MGD), |FRAME: CPD-23445|, and others |CITS: [1587808]|., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of molybdenum cofactors have been investigated in detail in bacteria |CITS: [7836363][8514783][8514782][1587808][14761975]| and plants |CITS: [16669776][16784786][12147719][16234918][9421926]|. All of the different cofactors are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT). The variability of the molybdenum cofactors found in bacteria is achieved by the attachment of GMP, AMP, IMP, or CMP to the phosphate group of MPT, and by attachment of different ligands (different number of oxo and sulfo groups, or amino acids from the enzyme) to the metal., The MPT structure is conserved in all organisms and it has been demonstrated that its biosynthesis is preserved in bacteria and eukaryotes alike. It is produced from |FRAME: GTP| via |FRAME: PRECURSOR-Z| (precursor Z) in three steps catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.22|, |FRAME: EC-4.6.1.17|, and |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.12| |CITS: [7890743][23627491]|., About This Pathway, All the molybdenum cofactors are derived from |FRAME: CPD-4|, whose biosynthesis is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6823|., The insertion of Mo into molybdopterin, forming the biologically active prosthetic group, is catalyzed in eukaryotes by a multifunctional two-domain protein. The protein first activates |FRAME: CPD-4| to |FRAME: CPD-8122| |CITS: [15504727][ 9341109][11554796][12590921][10823911]| and then inserts molybdate into the cofactor in a step that involves AMP cleavage |CITS: [16636046][15504727]|. In a somewhat analogous manner, in |FRAME:TAX-562| the MoeA protein mediates ligation of Mo to molybdopterin while the MogA protein enhances this process in an ATP-dependent manner |CITS: [17198377]|., The insertion of Mo coincides with the release of copper bound to the molybdopterin dithiolate sulfur |CITS: [15306815]| which seems to play a more stabilizing role of |FRAME: CPD-8122| than being actively involved in Mo insertion |CITS: [16636046]|., One difference between the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways is that some of the eukaryotic enzymes are fusion proteins with two functional domains, each catalyzing a different step in the pathway, while the bacterial proteins are single domain enzymes and catalyze only a single step.

Enzymes of pathway: CPLX66-1722 // CPLX-85568 // CPLX66-2051 // ENSG00000069943-MONOMER // ENSG00000060642-MONOMER // MONOMER66-43644 // CPLX66-2052 // G66-32357-MONOMER // HS03111-MONOMER // CPLX66-1721 // CPLX-7855 // CPLX66-13 // ENSG00000138688-MONOMER
Summary: The |FRAME: Mammalian-GPI-Anchors "glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor"| is a glycolipid structure that is added posttranslationally to the C-terminus of many eukaryotic proteins (roughly 1% of all proteins encoded by eukaryotic genomes, and ~10-20% of all membrane proteins that enter the secretory pathway after being targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum). It anchors the attached protein in the outer leaflet of the cell membrane., The GPI anchor has a complex structure that includes a phosphoethanolamine linker, glycan core, and phospholipid tail. It is considered the most complex and metabolically expensive of the lipid posttranslational modifications described so far., Different components of the anchor were reported beginning in 1985, but the first detailed structural analysis of a GPI, anchor was reported 1988, for the variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) from parasitic protozoan |FRAME: TAX-5691| |CITS: [3340856]|. Analyses of the structures of protein-bound GPIs from mammals, protozoa, and yeast reveal that they have a conserved core structure: protein-CO-NH2-CH2-CH2-PO4-6-α-D-Man-(1→2)-α-D-Man-(1→6)-α-D-Man-(1→4)-α-D-GlcN-(1→6)-myo-inositol phospholipid., The GPI core in yeast and mammals is modified during its biosynthesis by the addition of a palmitoyl group to the 2-OH of the inositol moiety and by the addition of up to three ethanolamine phosphate (Etn-P) moieties to specific positions on the first three mannoses. Addition of a fourth, α(1,2)-linked mannose to the third mannose is obligatory in yeast but not in mammalian cells, although a fourth mannose may be added in a tissue-specific manner., The GPI anchor is preassembled by enzymes attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The pathway is initiated on the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane and completed in the ER lumen, necessitating transbilayer flipping of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1113 "6-(α-D-glucosaminyl)-1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol"|. The flippase responsible for this transfer is the only enzyme that has not been identified, and may be identical to the flippase responsible for transferring |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE phosphatidylethanolamine| into the ER. The complete GPI anchor is transferred to target proteins in the lumen of the ER. Following the transfer, a post-attachment remodeling phase begins, resulting in an ER-to-Golgi transport of the GPI-anchored proteins, where they continue the modification and eventually sorted out of the Golgi to their final location |CITS: [24784135][38167496]|., Mutations in the genes involved in the pathway cause rare inherited GPI deficiencies (IGDs) resulting in genetic disorders mainly characterized by intellectual disability, developmental delay, cerebellar atrophy, seizures, hypotonia, and dysmorphic features. Some patients also display hyperphosphatasia, deafness, and anomalies in various organs |CITS: [32466763]|.

Many nitroalkane compounds are used in the chemical industry as intermediate compounds in chemical , syntheses. Some of them are toxic or carcinogenic and their biodegradation is of considerable interest. , Nitroalkane compounds are also biosynthesized by microorganisms and plants as defense chemicals , (in |CITS: [1217935] [16682407]|). Bacteria, yeasts, fungi and higher plants have been shown to oxidize nitroalkane , compounds to their corresponding aldehydes or ketones, and nitrite. Industrially, oxidation of nitroalkanes to less , toxic species can be used in bioremediation. Biologically, these oxidations can counter the production of toxic , nitroalkanes by other organisms, or protect the producing organism |CITS: [16430210]|., A nitroalkane degrading enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7188|, from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5507|, has been , extensively studied and its crystal structure has been determined |CITS: [16430210]|. This |FRAME: FAD|-containing , flavoprotein catalyzes the oxidation of primary nitroalkanes to aldehydes, and secondary nitroalkanes to ketones, , along with the production of |FRAME: NITRITE|. Primary nitroalkanes are the best substrates. Its action on |FRAME: CPD-12077| is shown in this pathway. In contrast to other nitroalkane oxidizing enzymes (see below), this enzyme acts on neutral nitroalkanes rather than nitroalkanes in their anionic (nitronate) form (such as |FRAME: CPD-320|), and electrons are transferred to oxygen to form hydrogen peroxide (in |CITS: [10684620]|). The physiological relevance of this enzyme is suggested by its induction upon growth of the organism in media containing |FRAME: CPD-12077|, and its use of neutral rather than anionic nitroalkanes as substrates. This also suggests that nitroethane is a physiological substrate |CITS: [22538]|, in |CITS: [8769086]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15581574]|. , Further catabolism of the |FRAME: ACETALD| product in this organism has not been reported, although it may be , metabolized by NADPH-aldehyde reductase/NADP-alcohol dehydrogenase. This enzyme reduces , carbonyl compounds to the corresponding alcohols in fungi, yeasts and animals (in |CITS: [16233633]|). Nitrite , may reduced to ammonia by nitrite reductase and used in nitrogen-containing biomolecules |CITS: [1217935]|. , These are indicated by the reaction links. , Another nitroalkane degrading enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-482| EC 1.13.12.16 (formerly 2-nitropropane dioxygenase EC 1.13.11.32), has been studied in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [9501443] [15582992]| and the yeast |FRAME: TAX-1004253 "Cyberlindnera mrakii (previosuly known as Hansenula mrakii)"| |CITS: [11214] [7813473]|. Recombinant nitronate monooxygenase (formerly 2-nitropropane dioxygenase) from |FRAME:TAX-287| has also been produced and its crystal structure determined |CITS: [16682407]|. Nitronate monooxygenase oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-320| to |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: NITRITE| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-723|). However, this enzyme differs from nitroalkane oxidase in its mechanism, its preference for the anionic form of the substrate, and it does not produce hydrogen peroxide as a product (reviewed in |CITS: [15581574]|). , Several other flavoenzymes from microorganisms have been shown to oxidize nitroalkanes including: nitroalkane , dioxygenase from Streptomyces ansochromogenes |CITS: [12473127]|; 3-nitropropionate oxidase , (EC 1.7.3.5) from Penicillium atrovenetum |CITS: [3667582]|; and glucose oxidase from , |FRAME:TAX-5061| |CITS: [16930]|. In mammals, nitroethane oxidation by D-amino acid oxidase , from pig kidney has been shown |CITS: [4145800]|. Unlike nitroalkane oxidase, these enzymes also react with the anionic form of the nitro-containing substrate.

Summary: General Background, The sulfonation of biological compounds (sulfoconjugation) is a fundamental metabolic process, in which a sulfate group is added to an oxygen moiety to form a sulfate ester bond. The sulfonation of biomolecules occurs widely and results in a dramatic change in the physicochemical property of the sulfonated compounds |CITS: [Huxtable86]|., Sulfonated macromolecules such as |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans|, |FRAME: HEPARIN| or |FRAME:Glucosinolates| are involved in many important processes, such as cell adhesion, hemostasis, the viscoelastic properties of connective tissue, and plant defense mechanisms. The sulfonation of tyrosine residues has been established as a post-translational modification for many secretory and membrane proteins (see |FRAME: HS10030-MONOMER|) and sulfated versions of lipids such as sphingolipids and galactoglycerolipids are found in the brain, peripheral nerves, and reproductive, tissues of mammals., In addition, sulfoconjugation is important in the biotransformation of many low molecular weight compounds such as neurotransmitters and hormones, including catecholamines, iodothyronines, and steroids, and in the production of plant secondary metabolites, such as glucosinolates., Another role for sulfonation is the detoxification and removal of drugs and xenobiotics compounds |CITS: [9668121]|., About This Pathway, In the course of sulfonation, inorganic sulfate must be activated prior to being transferred to an acceptor molecule |CITS: [13851709]|. In many organisms, including plants and mammals, |FRAME: PAPS| (PAPS) is used as the universal sulfonate donor for all sulfotransferase reactions |CITS: [13575436][6107250]|., The activation of inorganic sulfate to form PAPS is achieved by the concerted action of two enzymes., The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4| (also known as ATP-sulfurylase) and involves the reaction of inorganic sulfate with ATP to form |FRAME: APS| (APS) and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi). This enzyme has an unfavorable equilibrium (Keq ~ 10-7 M) in the direction of APS formation, and it has been postulated that the reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of PPi by a ubiquitous inorganic pyrophosphatase |CITS: [2821345]|. In |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was found that the enzymes couples the formation of APS to hydrolysis of GTP |CITS: [8117661]|., The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.25|, and involves the reaction of APS with ATP to form PAPS and ADP., It should be mentioned that in plants most of the APS is used for biosynthesis of |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: MET| via the further reduction of APS to sulfide (see |FRAME:SULFMETII-PWY|). In mammals, however, all of the APS is converted to PAPS and used for sulfonation., In bacteria, fungi, yeast and plants the two enzymes are found as separate polypeptide chains. In mammals the enzymes are physically linked on a single bifunctional protein |CITS: [8180221]|., For an extensive list of sulfonation reactions using |FRAME:PAPS|, please look at that compound's page.

General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the, synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives., These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere, |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms,, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation, pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|., The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two, broad categories - oxidative and reductive., In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or, di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and, |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is, released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-232721| is a proteobacterium that was isolated from nitrobenzene-contaminated soil and, groundwater. The organism can grow on |FRAME: 2-NITROTOLUENE| as the sole source of carbon,, nitrogen, and energy. |FRAME: 2-NITROTOLUENE| is rapidly metabolized during growth with, concomitant release of |FRAME: NITRITE| |CITS: [7944378]|., Extracts prepared from cells grown with |FRAME: 2-NITROTOLUENE| oxidize the compoud to, |FRAME: CPD-111| and |FRAME: NITRITE| in the presence of NAD(P)H and ferrous iron, |CITS: [8002568]|. |FRAME: CPLX-7469|, the enzyme responsible for this reaction, is a three component, dioxygenase system and has been purified and well characterized |CITS: [8002568][9495758][16000792]|., The enzymatic activities of other two enzymes of the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-13375| and, |FRAME: CPLX-7484|, were demonstrated in the extracts, but the enzymes have not been purified,, and the enzymes are not well characterized |CITS: [7944378]|.

Summary: In both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, sugar and amino sugar residues are converted to sugar nucleotides prior to their incorporation into structural polysaccharides via UDP-sugar transferases. In this pathway, UDP-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc) is the amino sugar nucleotide donor of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc) residues for the biosynthesis of glycosylated proteins and cell surface structures. Two variations of this pathway exist, one in eukaryotes and one in prokaryotes. In the eukaryotic pathway shown here, fructose-6-phosphate produced during, glycolysis (see pathway |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY|) is transaminated and isomerized to glucosamine-6-phosphate, followed by acetylation to N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate, isomerization to N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-1-phosphate, and uridylation to UDP-GlcNAc. In prokaryotes, the first and last reactions are similar to those of eukaryotes, but in the second and third reactions, glucosamine-6-phosphate is isomerized to glucosamine-1-phosphate, followed by its N acetylation to N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-1-phosphate (see pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|). Reviewed in |CITS: [16408321]|. , In eukaryotes this cytosolic pathway is highly regulated. UDP-GlcNAc donates GlcNAc residues for the biosynthesis of several classes of compounds, including N-linked glycans (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|), glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins, glycolipids, and |FRAME:CHITIN|, a , homopolymer of GlcNac (in |CITS: [14555471]|). This pathway has been well studied both genetically and biochemically in yeast. The first committed, rate-limiting, step in hexosamine de novo biosynthesis is catalyzed by glucosamine-6-phosphate synthase (glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase). It is essentially irreversible and is regulated at the transcriptional and posttranslational levels, including feedback inhibition by UDP-GlcNAc (reviewed in |CITS: [16408321]|)., This pathway has received consderable attention since it has the potential to influence both leptin production |CITS: [9641678]| and leptin responsiveness |CITS: [23493533][25446204]|., In some bacteria, some fungi (but not yeast), and metazoa, UDP-GlcNAc can be converted to UDP-N-acetyl-D-galactosamine by UDP-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine 4-epimerase. N-acetyl-D-galactosamine is a component of several different kinds of cell surface structures and glycosylated proteins (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5512|). A UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.14) produces UDP-N-acetyl-D-mannosamine for N-glycosylated mannoprotein biosynthesis. Reviewed in |CITS: [16408321]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7172 "Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol"| (THC) is the main psychoactive substance found in the cannabis plant. In 1988 it was found that the pharmacological actions of THC result from its binding to two receptors - the cannabinoid receptors CB1, located mainly in the central nervous system, and CB2, mainly present in cells of the immune system. Both receptors belong to the superfamily of membrane-bound G-protein-coupled receptors |CITS: [9336020]|., As THC is not a naturally occurring substance in the mammalian body, the existence of a specific receptor for THC implied that there should be endogenous molecules for these existing receptors (endocanabinoids). The first such molecule, |FRAME: CPD-7598| (N-arachidonoyl ethanolamine), was isolated by the Israeli scientist Raphael Mechoulam in 1992 |CITS: [1470919]|. Since then four more endocanabinoids have been reported - |FRAME: CPD-12600|, |FRAME: CPD-22217| (noladin ether), |FRAME: CPD-22218|, and |FRAME: CPD-22219| |CITS: [17227440]|., Binding of endocannabinoids (or cannabinoids) to cannabinoid receptors results in a decrease in the intracellular level of |FRAME: CAMP| and activation of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.24|, through the coupled Gi/o proteins. In addition, the activation of cannabinoid receptors modulates ion channels through Gi/o proteins, leading to the activation of A-type and inward-rectifyier potassium channels and the inhibition of N-type and P/Q-type calcium channels |CITS: [19126434]|., |FRAME: CPD-7598 Anandamide| is a fatty acid amide composed of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| coupled to |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| through an amide linkage |CITS: [7990962][19126434]|. Unlike THC, anandamide breaks down very quickly in the body, and thus does not produce the same psychoactive effect as THC., It is synthesized in areas of the brain that are important in memory and higher-thought processes. Synthesis is highest in the hippocampus, followed by the thalamus, cortex, as well as striatum, and lowest in the cerebellum, pons, and medulla |CITS: [8022836]|. |FRAME: CPD-7598 Anandamide| and other |FRAME: N-Acylethanolamines ethanolamides| are present in the maternal milk and were reported to be critical for milk ingestion and therefore the survival of the newborn., About This Pathway, There are three types of lipoxygenases that act on |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| in mammals. The enzymes, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|, insert oxygen in a regio- and stereospecific manner at positions C5, C12, or C15 of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|, respectively. The same enzymes also oxygenate |FRAME: CPD-7598|, adding O2 at different positions of their arachidonic acid backbone. The resulting hydroperoxide products are rapidly and nonenzymatically reduced in the cell to their corresponding hydroxylated derivatives |CITS: [27245907]|., |FRAME: CPD-22253| has been shown to bind to the CB1 receptor with comparable affinity as |FRAME: CPD-7598|, whereas the other two hydroxylated forms show reduced binding affinity |CITS: [12166944]|. All of the lipoxygenase products were found to be inhibitors of |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.60| (|FRAME: HS04139|) in the low to submicromolar range., The lipoxygenase metabolites haves been suggested to be involved in various physiological processes, including attenuatation of cytotoxic edema formation in a CB1 receptor-independent manner by |FRAME: CPD-22253|, and enhancement of the neuroprotective effect of |FRAME: CPD-7598| in the acute phase by |FRAME: CPD-22256| |CITS: [12764100]|.

Summary: Cyanobacteria are able to conduct both photosynthesis and respiration and have evolved a electron transport pathways that operate under both conditions. Another important electron transfer pathway these organisms must operate is cyclic electron flow, which allows them to generate proton motive force without producing reducing power. An additional requirement the organisms face is the ability to dissipate excess electron flow, which could happen when light and environmental conditions change rapidly., Like most cyanobacterial species, |FRAME: TAX-84588| possesses two membrane systems: the cytoplasmic membrane and a series of internal thylakoid membranes. The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes, as does a resipratory electron chain, while an additional respiratory electron transfer chain is localized in the cytoplasmic membrane., The only electron-transfer quinone found in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone| (PQ), which is shared among the photosynthetic light reactions and the respiratory electron chain. Three other components - |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76|, the small copper protein |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER|, are also shared between the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transfer chains., While it has been shown that the major electron source for the respiratory pathways in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: SUC| |CITS: [11418566]|, it was also shown that |FRAME: CPLX490-3523 NDH-11| and |FRAME: CPLX-9637 NDH-12| complexes are involved in respiration |CITS: [10906128]|. Active electron flow from metabolites to the PQ pool was strongly suppressed in NdhF1 mutants |CITS: [21036997]|, and deletion of either NdhP or NdhQ, which stabilize the NDH-1 complex, drastically decreased the respiratory capacity of cyanobacterial cells |CITS: [24089436][25873552]|., Because cyanobacterial NDH-11 and NDH-12 complexes use ferredoxin as their electron donor |CITS: [30573545][32060291]|, the involvement of NDH-1 in respiration requires a specific version of |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2| (FNR) that transfers electrons from NADPH to ferredoxin. It has been shown that in |FRAME: TAX-1148| translation of the petH gene results in two isoforms. While FNRL is involved in NADP+ reduction and photosynthesis, FNRS, which accumulates during heterotrophic growth, catalyzes ferredoxin reduction by NADPH and likely participates in respiration |CITS: [17116880][26735062 ]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation |CITS: [8490246]|. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces., Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| |CITS: [25969757]|., Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage., |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| |CITS: [10320813]|., About lacto-series glycosphingolipids, The lacto series gangliosides are essential to multiple physiological functions, including the control of reproductive output |CITS: [21087515]|., The core structure that defines the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"| is Galβ(1,3)GlcNAcβ(1,3)Galβ(1,4)Glcβ-Cer. The first two residues at the non-reducing end, Galβ(1,3)GlcNAcβ (N-acetyllactosamine), are also known as the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precusor disaccharide"|., Fucosylation of the 3 position of the glucosamine residue within the disaccharide yields a β-D-galactosyl-(1,3)-[(α-1,4-L-fucosyl)-N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminyl] moiety, which is known as the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a epitope"|. The related |FRAME: sLea-Antigen| "sialyl-Lewis a epitope"|, which plays an important role during embryogenesis |CITS: [6381330]|, is a ligand for E-selectin (see also the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7832|)., The key reaction that forms the core structure is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.86|, forming |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-N-ACETYL-D-GLU|. This compound was reported to be a major component of human meconium. The major fatty acids of human meconium lactotetraosylceramide were 2-hydroxy fatty acids with 16 and 20 to 24 carbon atoms, and the bases were sphingosine and phytosphingosine |CITS: [479198]|. The compound was also observed in human gastric epithelial cells, where it serves as a receptor for |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [11914375]|., α(2,3)-sialylation of this compound at the terminal galactosyl residue forms |FRAME: sLc4Cer "ganglioside 3'-isoLM1"|, and further α(2,6)-sialylation of the penultimate N-acetyl-glucosamine residue forms |FRAME: 36-isoLD1 "ganglioside 3',6'-isoLD1|. Expression of both of these compounds is restricted to the developmental period in healthy individuals |CITS: [3585330][2775765]|. However, both have been associated with glioma |CITS: [3339365][8417168][1748882]| and central nervous system |CITS: [7518092]| in adults. |FRAME: sLc4Cer "Ganglioside 3'-isoLM1"| was detected in 92% of tumour specimens collected from 44 patients with astrocytoma grade II, anaplastic astrocytoma, anaplastic oligodendrogliomas, oligodendrogliomas, and glioblastoma multiforme. |FRAME: 36-isoLD1 "Ganglioside 3',6'-isoLD1| was found in 47% of the tumour biopsies |CITS: [9088372]|. The compounds are considered ideal targets for brain tumor immunotherapy |CITS: [23924792]|.

General Background, Versicolorin B is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the mycotoxin sterigmatocystin. |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN|, and |FRAME: CPD-4587| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of the B-group and G-group aflatoxins, which constitute the major groups of naturally occurring aflatoxins. The production of aflatoxins by some strains of several |FRAME:TAX-5052| species has been extensively studied. However many species, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425 "Emericella nidulans (previously known as Aspergullus nidulans)"|, produce only |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| as a final product (in |CITS: [18486503]|). |FRAME: TAX-5067| produces both B- and G-group aflatoxins from |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587|, while |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces only B-group aflatoxins. The biological role of these mycotoxins in fungi remains unclear (in |CITS: [17620135] [18246345]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|)., Aflatoxins are highly toxic and carcinogenic crop contaminants that create major economic and public health problems worldwide. Much research has been focused on identifying compounds that inhibit aflatoxin biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-4592| is metabolized by mammalian liver cytochrome P450 enzymes to a mutagenic epoxide that covalently binds to DNA. Its genotoxic mechanism of action has been studied in yeast |CITS: [8968101] [9771940]|. Other species, such as |FRAME: TAX-5062| and |FRAME:TAX-41058|, are unable to produce aflatoxins and are used in food fermentation |CITS: [17665189]|., Most of the aflatoxin biosynthetic genes are clustered in Aspergilli and are positively regulated by gene aflR (in |CITS: [17620135] [16448506] [16108793] [15094053] [7618880] [16535712]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]| and |CITS: [15006741]|). The enzyme reactions and biosynthetic intermediates in the aflatoxin biosynthetic pathway have been reviewed in detail |CITS: [15022028]|. See MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5954|, |FRAME: PWY-5956|, |FRAME: PWY-5959|, |FRAME: PWY-5960| and |FRAME: PWY-5961|., About This Pathway, The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10167| to |FRAME: CPD-10175| appears to involve a main pathway and a side, pathway. These form a metabolic grid, or network thought to be regulated by |FRAME: NADPH| levels in the cell, |CITS: [12513978] [1770361]| . In the main pathway, a stereospecific monooxygenase converts, |FRAME: CPD-10167| to |FRAME: CPD-10168|, followed by another monooxygenase that converts this compound, to |FRAME: CPD-10170|. At least one cytosolic esterase converts |FRAME: CPD-10170| to, |FRAME: CPD-10171|. Under physiological conditions a cyclase stereospecific for the (2'S) configuration of, |FRAME: CPD-10171| converts it to the (1'R,2'S) configuration of |FRAME: CPD-10175|. The, substrates |FRAME: CPD-10168|, |FRAME: CPD-10170| and |FRAME: CPD-10171| are probably racemic. Under, physiological conditions the (2'R) configuration of |FRAME: CPD-10171| spontaneously forms the (2'S), configuration, resulting in production of optically pure (1'R,2'S) configuration of |FRAME: CPD-10175|, by the cyclase in the pathway. This compound determines the (1'R,2'S)-bisfuran configuration, of |FRAME: CPD-10176|, |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and the aflatoxins |CITS: [8368837]|. In the side, pathway, a reductase/dehydrogenase can utilize |FRAME: CPD-10168|, |FRAME: CPD-10170| and, |FRAME: CPD-10171| as substrates, the products of which are also substrates for the main pathway, enzymes. Reviewed in detail in |CITS: [15022028]|. , |FRAME: CPD-10175| is a branch point in the pathway. In one branch it can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-10176|, and subsequently to |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN|, |FRAME: CPD-4592| and |FRAME: CPD-10178|. In, the other branch it can be converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-4587| by a series of uncharacterized reactions, and then to |FRAME: CPD-10177| and |FRAME: CPD-10179| (reviewed in detail in |CITS: [15022028]|). This is, indicated by the pathway links.

General Background, Natural essential oils contain monoterpenes as one of their major constituents. The oil accumulates in glands found in leaves, petals and trichomes. |FRAME: CPD-7978 Nerol| is naturally presents in essential oils of many plants. It is one of the three terpene compounds principally responsible for the muscat aroma, and has been reported from many plants, including orange blossom, ginger, basil, cardamom, mint and mandarin., Nerol is widely used in many fields including toiletries, perfumed soaps, fine flavors and fragrances and detergents. It is recognized as a safe flavor ingredient by Flavor and Extrat Manufacturers Association states, and was approved as a flavor by the Food and Drug Administration |CITS: [18640199]|. Nerol is mainly produced by chemical synthesis, although a recombinant procedure for its biosynthesis from glucose has been published |CITS: [31076292]|., About This Pathway, The pathway has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-3847| (soybean), where the key enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.1.7.13|, has been discovered. While |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| is the widely accepted common substrate for monoterpene biosynthesis, this enzyme is specific for |FRAME: CPD-461| |CITS: [24124526]|., The substrate for this enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-461|, is produced by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.28|, an enzyme that has been known for a long time |CITS: [4303098][19487664]|

Summary: General Background, The main input of |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| (p-nitrophenol, PNP) into the environment is the hydrolysis of methyl, parathion or parathion, which are commonly used as pesticides in agriculture (see |FRAME:PARATHION-DEGRADATION-PWY |)., PNP is also found in industrial wastes since it is a precursor not only of of pesticides such as carbofuran, nitrofen, methyl parathion and parathion, but also of certain pharmaceuticals, plasticizers, azo dyes, explosives etc. In addition, diesel fuel and gasoline exhaust also contain PNP |CITS: [Tremp93]|. Because of the widespread nature of p-nitrophenol and other nitrophenols, they are considered as major pollutants by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA)., Several bacterial species have the ability to degrade |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL|. These include Nocardia, |CITS:[8250573]|, Arthrobacter |CITS: [8085840]|, |FRAME: TAX-46429| and |FRAME: TAX-262099| |CITS: [Leung97]|, Flavobacterium |CITS: [Raymond71]|, |FRAME: TAX-292| |CITS: [8702398]|, |FRAME: TAX-1421| |CITS: [9647818]|, |FRAME: ORG-6211| |CITS: [15262926]|, Pseudomonas |CITS: [8005]| and |FRAME: TAX-475| |CITS: [16348446]|., In general, aerobic degradation of PNP by Gram-negative bacteria is initiated by formation of |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5487|), while the first intermediate of PNP degradation by Gram-positive bacteria is |FRAME: CPD-158| (this pathway). Exceptions, however, do occur. For example, |FRAME: TAX-336938| is a Gram-negative organism that degrades PNP via 4-nitrocatechol |CITS: [17043828]|, and the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-633150| possesses both pathways |CITS: [22380602]|., About This Pathway, The key enzyme in this |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| degradation pathway is a two-component hydroxylase that oxidizes PNP to |FRAME: CPD-158|. The hydroxylase has been detected in several organisms, both Gram-positive and Gram-negative, including Nocardia |CITS: [6477623]|, |FRAME: TAX-1421| JS905 |CITS: [9647818]|, |FRAME: TAX-129133|, |CITS: [16233382]|, |FRAME: ORG-6211| |CITS: [15262926]| and |FRAME: TAX-336938| |CITS: [17043828]|., Memebers of this family include two components: an oxygenase, which catalyzes the oxidation of the substrates using reduced flavins, and a reductase whose role is the replenishing of the reduced flavins. A single enzyme from this family catalyzes the first two steps of this pathway |CITS: [9647818][16233382]|. The enzyme generates |FRAME:CPD-8130| and releases stoichiometric amounts of nitrite., |FRAME:CPD-8130| is then oxidized to |FRAME:CPD-294|, which is converted to |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE| and shuttled through the |FRAME:PWY-2361| pathway to central metabolism.

|FRAME: CPD-23382 "Omphalotin A"| is a cyclic peptide isolated from the basidiomycete |FRAME: TAX-72120| that shows strong and selective nematicidal activity against the plant pathogenic |FRAME: TAX-6306| with no further phytotoxic, antibacterial, or antifungal activities |CITS: [Mayer97]|. Shortly after the discovery of |FRAME: CPD-23382| three related compounds were discovered in the organism and named |FRAME: CPD-23385|, |FRAME: CPD-23383| and |FRAME: CPD-23384| |CITS: [Buchel98]| and several years later five more types were reported - |FRAME: CPD-23391|, |FRAME: CPD-23392|, |FRAME: CPD-23393|, |FRAME: CPD-23394|, and |FRAME: CPD-23396| |CITS: [Liermann09]|. Omphalotin B-I are derived from |FRAME: CPD-23382| by acetylation and hydroxylation reactions and all retain the specific activity against |FRAME: TAX-6306|, with |FRAME: CPD-23391| having the highest activity |CITS: [Liermann09]|., |FRAME: CPD-23382 "Omphalotin A"| is produced by cleavage of a precursor protein, which also functions as a methyltranferase. The enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80765| gene, self methylates its C-terminal region, which consists of the 12 residues of the cyclic peptide, followed by a conserved 6-residue follower peptide. Following the methylation, a prolyl peptidase encoded by the |FRAME: G-80766| gene releases the dodecapeptide, which cyclizes to form |FRAME: CPD-23382| |CITS: [28581484][28715095]|., The gene cluster that contains |FRAME: G-80765| and |FRAME: G-80766| contains three more genes encoding an acetyltransferase (OphC) and two cytochrome P-450 enzymes (OphM1 and OphM2) that are believed to perform the modifications that produce the other omphalotins |CITS: [28581484][28715095]|., Until the discovery of the |FRAME: G-80765 OphMA| methylase, it was thuoght that N-methylation of backbone amide bonds in peptide natural products is exclusive to non-ribosomal peptides |CITS: [28949431]|.

In whole cells of E. coli K-12 formate dependent nitrite reduction is associated with the generation of a proton motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [MOTTERAM81] [6283015]|. Nitrite reduction, by formate is dependent on menaquinone (shown in this pathway) and/or demethylmenaquinone for electron transfer |CITS: [9325429]|., Maximum nrf (nitrite reduction by formate) activity is found in cells grown anaerobically in the presence of formate and nitrite |CITS: [37075]|. E. coli K-12 contains two nitrite reductases - a periplasmic respiratory enzyme (shown in this pathway) encoded by genes from the nrf operon and a cytoplasmic NADH dependent enzyme (|FRAME: NITRITREDUCT-CPLX|) whose physiological function is proabably to detoxify nitrite. nrf expression is induced anaerobically in an Fnr-dependent manner and further regulated in response to environmental levels of nitrate and nitrite |CITS: [2173895][7854119][8057835][11004182]|. , E. coli K-12 contains three membrane assocated formate dehydrogenases. Formate dehydrogenase N (FDH-N) and formate dehydrogenase O (FDH-O) (both shown in this pathway) are respiratory enzymes while |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGH-MONOMER "formate dehydrogenase H"| (FDH-H) (not shown here) is generally considered to be active under fermentative conditions where it forms part of the formate hydrogen-lyase complex (see review by |CITS: [7747941]|). However, all three enzymes may be active in formate dependent nitrite reduction |CITS: [8409924][12923080]|. A mutant strain lacking all three enzymes is Nrf - (unable to catalyse formate dependent nitrite reduction); an ΔFDH-OΔFDH-N double mutant has less than 10% of the Nrf activity of the parent strain |CITS: [8409924]|., Nitrite reduction by other electron donors such as pyruvate, ethanol and lactate has been reported (see |CITS: [12165429]| and references within) but are thought to be be minor pathways., Please note: due to software limitations this pathway incorrectly depicts the soluble periplasmic nitrite reductase NrfA as a membrane protein.

Summary: Background, Amid rising energy costs, dwindling fossil fuel resources and accelerated global warming, there is an increasing demand for the production of biofuels from renewable sources. Microbial fermentation of biomass is a renewable method of producing fuel compounds such as ethanol but requires scalable feedstock. Corn and sugarcane can be used as industrial feedstocks for ethanol production, but they also have commercial value as food. Inedible lignocellulosic plant material can be converted to simple sugars and subsequently ethanol by microbial fermentation, but this is an expensive method for producing |FRAME: ETOH|. , Brown macroalgae are abundant in alginate, mannitol and glucan and have the potential to be an ideal feedstock for ethanol production, as they don't require arable land or fresh water for growth. However, while mannitol and glucan can be microbially converted to ethanol, this has some major limitations and industrial microbes lack the ability to metabolize alginate |CITS: [22267807]|., |FRAME: ALGINATE "Alginate"| is a linear co-polymer of two uronic acids, with the majority of the polymer consisting of 1,4-linked |FRAME: CPD-15205|, with variable amounts of its C-5 epimer |FRAME: CPD-15204| |CITS: [20507980]|. The β-D-mannuronate and α-L-guluronate can form poly-β-D-mannuronate, poly-α-L-guluronate or a heterpolymeric mixture of both β-D-mannuronate and α-L-guluronate. , The alginate degradation pathway has been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-90322| and related species. This pathway has the potential to yield ethanol and has recently been designed in a suitable platform to be genetically engineered into |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [22267807]|., About this Pathway, This alginate degradation pathway has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-90322|, a soil Gram-negative bacterium isolated from a ditch based on its ability to utilize alginate as a sole source for carbon |CITS: [Yonemoto91]|., When grown on alginate, |FRAME: TAX-90322| forms a mouth-like pit on the cell surface through the reorganization and fluidity of the pleat structures, resulting in the concentration of the external alginate in the pit |CITS: [8607879]|. The concentrated polysaccharide is imported into the periplasm, where the alginate-binding proteins AlgQ1 or AlgQ2 are expressed. AlgQ1 or AlgQ2 mediates the transfer of alginate from the outer membrane to a inner-membrane-bound ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter |CITS: [12486124][18189419][21238429][25665777]|. The ABC transporter consists of a AlgM1/AlgM2 heterodimer, which acts as a membrane-spanning domain, and an AlgS homodimer, which acts as an ATPase |CITS: [11676004][18256495]|., Once within the cytoplasm, |FRAME: ALGINATE| is endolytically cleaved by a β elimination reaction into di-, tri- and tetrasaccharides by three cytoplasmic alginate lyases (|FRAME: MONOMER-17106|, |FRAME: MONOMER-19216| and |FRAME: MONOMER-19217|), which are all derived from a common precursor protein |CITS: [16233753]|. The resulting oligosaccharides, which contain an unsaturated sugar acid at their non-reducing end, are cleaved to monosaccharides by the action of |FRAME: MONOMER-17101|., The end product of the depolymerization process, |FRAME: CPD-17705|, was initially reported to convert spontaneously into the linear α keto acid |FRAME: 4S5S-45-DIHYDROXY-26-DIOXOHEXANOATE| |CITS: [10913091]|. However, later research has uncovered a dedicated enzyme (KdgF) that catalyzes this conversion |CITS: [27185956]|., An NADPH-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-8980| reduces this α keto acid to |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| |CITS: [20685299]|. By the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.45| (which has not been characterized yet from |FRAME: TAX-90322|) this compound can be phosphorylated into |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"|., Most of the genes that are involved in alginate uptake and degradation are located in a single cluster. Expression of the genes is induced by the presence of alginate through the action of the transcription factor AlgO |CITS: [24816607]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-9459 Oleanolate| is a natural occuring triterpenoic acid that is widely distributed throughout the plant kingdom. A recent study reported |FRAME:CPD-9459| being identified in >1,620 species of about 146 plant families which include monocots and gymnosperms |CITS:[Fai09]|. As many other triterpenoids oleanolate (oleanolic acid) has been reported to exhibit a variety of pharmacological effects such as antibacterial and cytotoxic activity |CITS:[18835348]|, arresting the cell cycle and inducing apoptosis in many tumor cell lines |CITS:[22678527]| |CITS:[22549898]| and it is also considered as potential anti-Alzheimer's disease therapeutic |CITS:[22430119]|. , The cyclization of 2,3-oxidosqualene to form |FRAME:CPD-8250| in this pathway is catalyzed by a oxidosqualene cyclase (β-amyrin synthase). The close relationship of the enzyme with the biosynthesis of oleanolate in |FRAME:TAX-50768| has been demonstrated through direct correlation with oleanolate accumulation and the tissue-specific level of expression of β-amyrin synthase |CITS:[19420748]|. In Catharanthus roseus the amyrin synthase has been found to catalyze the formation of both |FRAME:CPD-8250| and |FRAME:CPD-6948| from |FRAME:EPOXYSQUALENE| in a ratio of 2.5 : 1, hence being able to operate in two pathways, the |FRAME:PWY-7069| (this pathway) and the formation of |FRAME:CPD-14496| (see |FRAME:PWY-7068|) |CITS:[22837051]|., A microsomal cytochrome P450-dependent oxidase (CYP716A12) catalyzes a series of oxidation reactions at C-28 of the β-amyrin backbone which results in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-9459| through the intermediates |FRAME:CPD-14499| and probably |FRAME:CPD-14498|. The multifunctional β-amyrin 28-oxidase (CYP716A12) was not only able to carry out the three sequential oxidation steps from β-amyrin towards oleanolate but was also found to catalyze the three-step-oxidation of both |FRAME:CPD-90| to form |FRAME:CPD-14493| (acting as lupeol 28-oxidase, see |FRAME:PWY-7067|) and |FRAME:CPD-8250| to biosynthesize |FRAME:CPD-14496| (acting as α-amyrin 28-oxidase, see |FRAME:PWY-7068|) |CITS:[22039103]|. The β-amyrin 28-monooxygenase (CYP716AL1) identified in Cathanranthus roseus also catalyzed the stepwise formation of |FRAME:CPD-9459| which has been shown to accumulate in the epidermis of Catharanthus leaves |CITS:[18326827]|., Besides the multifunctional |FRAME:TAX-3877| lupeol 28-oxidase another two cytochrome P450-dependent oxidases (CYP716A15 and CYP716A17) have been identified in |FRAME:TAX-29760| through coexpression analysis and shown to catalyze the same series of oxidations on C-28 of the β-amyrin core structure to form |FRAME:CPD-9459| |CITS:[22039103]|. Such multifunctional cytochrome P450's functionalizing substrate backbones with a series of oxidative steps have also been reported in the formation of another triterpenoid, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14483| (see |FRAME:PWY-7066|) where β-amyrin 11-oxidase (CYP88D6) and 11-oxo-β-amyrin 30-oxidase (CYP72A154) have been shown to carry out a sequential two (on C-11) and three-step substrate oxidation (on C-30), respectively |CITS:[18779566]| |CITS:[22128119]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamin diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamin-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamin is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., Thiamin biosynthesis is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| (see |FRAME: PWY-6893|)., About This Pathway, This pathway describes only the synthesis of the thiazole moiety of thiamin. Different variations of this pathway exist, this particular pathway describes the pathway that occurs in |FRAME: TAX-1423|., The biosynthesis of the thiazole moiety is complex. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| it involves six proteins, the products of the |FRAME: BSU29590|, |FRAME: BSU11700|, |FRAME: BSU11680|, |FRAME: BSU11670|, |FRAME: BSU11690| and |FRAME: BSU11660| genes. , The process begins when the |FRAME: ThiF-Proteins "ThiF protein"| activates |FRAME: Thi-S| by adenylation of its carboxy terminus, generating |FRAME:Adenylated-ThiS-Proteins|. |FRAME: BSU29590-MONOMER IscS|, a protein that is also involved in the biosynthesis of iron-sulfur clusters, catalyzes the transfer of a sulfur atom from cysteine to the adenylated ThiS, generating |FRAME: ThiS-CoASH-proteins|., In a parallel reaction, |FRAME: CPLX-8352| (ThiO) forms |FRAME: CPD-12279| from |FRAME: GLY|., The main reaction of this pathway is a very complex reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: BSU11690-MONOMER| (ThiG), that requires three inputs: |FRAME: ThiS-CoASH-proteins|, |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| (DXP) and |FRAME: CPD-12279|., For many years the product of this reaction was assumed to be |FRAME: THZ| (thiazole). However, recent work performed with the thiazole synthase from |FRAME: TAX-1423| has shown that the actual product is the thiazole tautomer |FRAME: CPD-13575| |CITS: [19216519]|. A dedicated |FRAME: BSU11660-MONOMER| converts this product into a different tautomer, |FRAME: CPD-13576|, which is the actual substrate for the thiamine-phosphate diphosphorylase enzyme |CITS: [21534620]|., There are a few differences between the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1423| (see |FRAME: PWY-6892|) and |FRAME: TAX-83333|. |FRAME: CPD-12279| is formed from |FRAME: GLY| rather than from |FRAME: TYR| |CITS: [12627963]|. The |FRAME:BSU29580 ThiI| protein of Bacillus does not seem to be essential or even participate in this pathway |CITS: [14567704]|, and |FRAME: BSU11660-MONOMER| does not exist in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [21534620]|.

|FRAME:PHE Phenylalanine| is one of the three proteinogenic aromatic amino acids that are produced only in plants and microorganisms. It is a central metabolite, and plants direct up to 30% of the carbon flux from photosynthesis towards its biosynthesis |CITS:[22554242]|. Moreover, |FRAME:PHE| is precursor of a plethora of secondary metabolites involved in plant defense (e.g. flavonoids |CITS:[11743081][22404468]|), signaling and protection (e.g. isoflavonoids |CITS:[12644640][20921162]|), reproduction (e.g. phenylpropanoids and volatiles |CITS:[20035037]|) and general plant fitness (e.g. vitamin E, plastoquinone, and suberin). , The biosynthesis of |FRAME:PHE| has been known to comprise two major pathways, a plant pathway via |FRAME:CPD-659|, which has been claimed to occur exclusively in plastids (|FRAME: PWY-3462|) and the microbial pathway via |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE| (|FRAME: PHESYN|)., However, this all-plastidal paradigm was challenged when a cytosolic |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.57| (|FRAME: G-17921|), was detected in |FRAME: TAX-4102| that significantly contributed to the cellular |FRAME:PHE| biosynthesis. The enzyme exhibited an unusual substrate preference for |FRAME:TYR| as amino donor and |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE| as the acceptor, forming |FRAME:PHE| and |FRAME:P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|. Although PPY-AT also could utilize |FRAME:GLT| for |FRAME:PHE| formation, the catalytic efficiency of that reaction was lower., The aminotransferase also catalyzed the corresponding reverse reactions, but with considerably less activity. The new cytosolic aromatic amino acid transaminase step was discussed as mediator for the interconnection of |FRAME:TYR| catabolism and |FRAME:PHE| anabolism, adding another level of complexity to |FRAME:PHE| metabolism in plants |CITS:[24270997]|., The same activities were also carried out by an aromatic amino acid transaminase from |FRAME: TAX-3656| |CITS:[24270997]|. That enzyme had been previously reported to be involved in the formation of |FRAME:PHE|-derived volatiles |CITS:[20065117]|. , The generated |FRAME:P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| produced in the forward reaction with |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE| and |FRAME:TYR| has been proposed to be involved in the formation of |FRAME:HOMOGENTISATE|, which serves as a precursor for vitamin E (tocopherols and tocotrienols) biosynthesis (e.g. |FRAME:PWY-7436|) |CITS:[24270997]|., It should be noted that the first enzymatic step in the pathway, , catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.51|, remains to be elucidated, although the catalytic activity was described in extracts from Petunia petals |CITS:[24270997]|.
