Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MET| (Met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in protein biosynthesis, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines. In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., Some bacteria can synthesize methionine using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE| with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine (|FRAME: HOMOSER-METSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [3309561]|. Plants use a modification of this pathway, where |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, instead of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting homoserine to cystathionine (|FRAME: PWY-702|)., Other bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi, can use a different route in which they directly assimilate inorganic sulfur by a sulfhydrylation (see |FRAME:HSERMETANA-PWY|). In that route |FRAME: HS|, the final product of microbial sulfate reduction (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) reacts with O-acetylated homoserine, with replacement of the acetyl group by sulfide to form |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is once again methylated to methionine (see |FRAME: PWY-5344|)., Most methanogenic archaea utilize yet a different pathway. While these organisms also use |FRAME: HS| as the sulfur source, the other precursor for |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| production is |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, produced from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (this pathway)., Methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., About This Pathway, The first genome sequencing of a methanogen (in 1996) has revealed that the organism does not utilize any of the known pathways for methionine biosynthesis. While methanogens can produce |FRAME: HOMO-SER|, most of them do not have the genes that are required for its conversion to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| |CITS: [8688087]|. , Isotopic feeding experiments in |FRAME: TAX-39152| demonstrated that the sulfur in methionine is derived from |FRAME: HS|, as is the case in the bactrerial pathway described in |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY| |CITS: [20709756]|. , However, the methanogenic pathway involves two genes that are missing in other organisms |CITS: [25315403]|. One of these proteins is an enzyme that catalyzes a sulfur transfer from |FRAME: HS| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, producing |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| |CITS: [25938369]|. The other protein is a dedicated ferredoxin that acts an an electron donor for the sulfurtransferase |CITS: [25938369]|., The last enzyme in the archaeal pathway, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58242| gene, catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from a corrinoid protein (which has not yet been identified) to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|. Unlike the bacterial enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, it is not able to use |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "5-methyltetrahydrofolate"| as a methyl donor |CITS: [10469143]|., Depite being initially characterized as a pathway used strictly by methanogenic archaea, the pathway was subsequently demonstrated in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-883| |CITS: [29324779]|.

Summary: 3-Phenylpropionate is a natural environmental compound produced by degradation of organic matter, including plant lignin. Bacterial catabolism of this aromatic compound has been studied in several genera. An |FRAME:TAX-562| K12 pathway for degradation of 3-phenylpropionate is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: HCAMHPDEG-PWY|. The organism in the pathway shown here, the aerobic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-78509|, is an extreme halophile isolated from soil contaminated with saline oil brine |CITS: [10086844]|., |FRAME: TAX-78509| is able to utilize aromatic compounds as sole carbon and energy sources. This pathway represents a proposed pathway for degrading 3-phenylpropionic acid. The unstable intermediates, 3-hydroxy-3-phenylpropionyl-CoA and 3-keto-3-phenylpropionyl-CoA, were not detected in a biochemical study, but the conversion of cinnamyl-CoA to benzoyl-CoA did occur |CITS: [10086844]|., The first segment of the pathway, converting 3-phenylpropionate to benzoyl-CoA, is similar to fatty acid β-oxidation. Three of the reactions are labeled here as hypothetical due to lack of detection of the unstable intermediates. However, the conversion of cinnamyl-CoA to benzoyl-CoA was shown to be NAD-dependent |CITS: [10086844]|., The formation of the dihydroxylated intermediate, 2,5-dihydroxybenzoate (gentisate), followed by ring cleavage by gentisate dioxygenase, is characteristic of bacterial aerobic degradation of aromatic compounds. No hydroxylase activities for the conversion of benzoyl-CoA to 3-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA, and 3-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA to 2,5-dihydroxybenzoate were detected, although the metabolites 3-hydroxybenzoate and 2,5-dihydroxybenzoate (gentisate) were identified. The two segments of the pathway are regulated separately, by inducible enzymes |CITS: [10086844]|. In |FRAME:TAX-286|, the product of the cis-trans isomerase, 3-fumarylpyruvate, has been shown to be further metabolized by hydrolysis to fumarate and pyruvate |CITS: [14461395]|.

The |FRAME: PWY-3982 "reductive pyrimidine catabolic pathway"| is the most widespread pathway for pyrimidine degradation in bacteria. In that pathway only one of the two nitrogen atoms of the |FRAME: PYRIMIDINE-RING| ring is released in a usable form (as |FRAME: AMMONIUM|). The other nitrogen atom ends up in the end product |FRAME: B-ALANINE|, which can be used for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|, but not as a nitrogen source., Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-292806|, are able to continue the pyrimidine degradation pathway by converting |FRAME: B-ALANINE| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| (via |FRAME: MALONATE-S-ALD|), transfering the second nitrogen to a |FRAME: GLT| molecule, which can be used for protein biosynthesis |CITS: [31455636]|., The pydDE genes that encodes the required enzymes are found in many Gram-positive bacteria in the classes |FRAME: TAX-91061| and |FRAME: TAX-186801|, where they are associated with the reductive pyrimidine pathway genes.

|FRAME: CPD-1001 p-Cymene| is a natural constituent of a number of essential oils. It has been identified in volatile oils from more than 100 plants, including eucalyptus, cumin, thyme, cypress, coriander, sage, star anise, and cinnamon. It is the major component in the essential oils of cumin and thyme., Several strains of |FRAME: TAX-303|, including |FRAME: TAX-351746|, |FRAME: ORG-6334|, and |FRAME: ORG-6335|, have been documented to utilize |FRAME:CPD-1001| for growth. Work performed by Ribbons et al, assisted by the isolation of mutants |CITS: [942434][7204334]|, has clarified much of the process, including the initial reactions |CITS: [845117]|, the ring cleavage mechanisms, and the subsequent reactions |CITS: [845118]|., The upper pathway of |FRAME: CPD-1001| metabolism occurs by progressive oxidation of the methyl side-chain to carboxylic acid, generating |FRAME:CPD-1004| |CITS: [Leavitt67][4240446]|. The pathway continues by degradation of the latter via |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, and overall yields |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE|, |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [4240445][4240446][845117]|., The cym and cmt operons, encoding the catabolism of |FRAME:CPD-1001| and |FRAME:CPD-1004|, respectively, were cloned and sequenced from both |FRAME: TAX-351746| |CITS: [8631713][9150211]| and |FRAME: ORG-6335| |CITS: [16728956]|. The tod operon, encoding the catabolism of toluene, is located only 2.8 kb downstream from the cmt operon |CITS: [8631713][16728956]|., The full pathway can be seen at |FRAME:PWY-5266|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-27449 Scytonemin| is a lipophilic pigment widely distributed among cyanobacteria from diverse habitats that acts as a sunscreen. It has a unique, highly conjugated heterocyclic skeleton, and is synthesized from intermediates of the |FRAME: PHE| and |FRAME: TYR| pathways in response to UV-A or UV-B exposure |CITS: [19482954]|. Scytonemin accumulates within the extracellular sheath or slime of the producing organism, forming a stable, protective layer that absorbs as much as 90% of the incident radiation |CITS: [Garcia-Pichel91]|., Although the compoud was discovered already in 1849, its structure was solved only in 1993 |CITS: [8405307]|. Depending on the redox conditions it can exist in two inter-convertible forms: a more common oxidized yellow-brown form, and a reduced form with bright red color |CITS: [Garcia-Pichel91]|., The genes encoding scytonemin biosynthesis were originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [17351042]|. The gene cluster, which contains 18 genes in that organism, was shown to be transcribed in its entirety after exposure to UV radiation |CITS: [19482954]|. Three enzymes, the products of the |FRAME: G-124809|, |FRAME: G-124808|, and |FRAME: G-124810| genes, have been implicated in the production of the ketone compound |FRAME: CPD-27475|, which is one (auto)oxidation state away from what is called the |FRAME: CPD2SK3-7| |CITS: [21501195][19780555]|., Five other genes, |FRAME: G-124812| - |FRAME: G-124816| have been implicated in the export of the |FRAME: CPD2SK3-7| to the periplasm. The oxidative dimerization that forms |FRAME: CPD-27449| is catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G-124811| gene |CITS: [30482833]|., Scytonemin is located in the exopolysaccharide matrix and must be transported accross the outer membrane to its final location. Mutation analysis showed that scyD does not effect scytonemin biosynthesis, while a scyF produces less product |CITS: [27242750]|. Whether these proteins have any role in the final export process remains unclear as of 2024.

Summary: The peptidoglycan (PG) or murein sacculus of E. coli K-12 is assembled from monomer subunits of the disaccharide pentapeptide, N-acetyl-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)muramoyl-L-alanyl-γ-D-glutamyl-meso-2,6-diaminopimeloyl-D-alanyl-D-alanine (also known as GlcNAc-MurNAc-pentapeptide) which are synthesized in the cytoplasm as lipid linked molecules (lipid II) and then flipped across the inner membrane by a flippase protein (see |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY|). Mature peptidoglycan is assembled on the outer face of the inner membrane through the action of transglycosylases, transpeptidases and peptidoglycan hydrolases. , Peptidoglycan is a heterogeneous polymer; the length of mature glycan strands varies |CITS: [2285138][3292521]| - the average degree of oligomerization is about 25 to 40 disaccharide units |CITS: [17658458]| - and may be affected by growth conditions. The length of the peptide stem also varies - di-, tri-, tetra- and pentapeptide muropeptides have all been identified - as have different levels of cross-linkage from monomeric peptides to tetrameric peptides |CITS: [3292521]|. Growing glycan chains remain linked to the lipid carrier (di-trans,octa-cis-undecaprenyl phosphate); the terminal residues of released strands are GlcNAc and 1,6-anyhdroMurNAc |CITS: [357]| however the mechanism resulting in release remains unknown - lytic transglycosylases which cleave PG producing 1,6-anyhdroMurNAc muropeptides during PG recycling and turnover do not seem to be involved (see |CITS: [22126997]|., Transglycosylases catalyse the formation of a β1 → 4 N-acetylmuramoyl-N-acetylglucosamine bond between a growing glycan chain and a newly flipped disaccharide pentapeptide monomer releasing a molecule of di-trans,octa-cis-undecaprenyl diphosphate (UPP) for recycling in the process. It is not clear whether the growing glycan chain serves as glycosyl donor and the disaccharide monomer as acceptor or vice versa; evidence for the former has been presented (|CITS: [16351056]|). Transpeptidases cross link glycan strands within newly synthesized peptidoglycan and between newly made material and preexisting peptidoglycan; they also link peptidoglycan to Braun's lipoprotein (Lpp) in the outer membrane and catalyse the exchange of carboxy terminal D-alanine residues with glycine in the peptide stem. , DD-transpeptidases catalyse the cross-linking of the glycan strands between the the D-alanine at position 4 of a pentapeptide stem and the meso-diaminopimelyl residue (m-A2pm) at position 3 of a separate tetrapeptide stem (a D-Ala → m-A2pm cross-link); LD transpeptidases catalyse the cross link between two m-A2pm residues of separate stems. E. coli K-12 contains bifunctional transglycosylases/DD transpeptidases (|FRAME: CPLX0-7717 "MrcA"| also known as penicillin binding protein 1A or PBP1A, |FRAME: CPLX0-3951 "MrcB"|/PBP1B and |FRAME: G7322-MONOMER "PbpC"|/PBP1C) |CITS: [7006606][16840781][7001458][10542235]|, monofunctional DD transpeptidases (|FRAME: EG10606-MONOMER "MrdA"|/PBP2, |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER "FtsI"|/PBP3) |CITS: [6297485][3531167]|, a monofunctional transglycosylase (|FRAME: G7668-MONOMER "MtgA"|) |CITS: [8772200]| and 2 LD transpeptidases (|FRAME: EG11253-MONOMER "LdtD"| and |FRAME: G6904-MONOMER "LdtE"|) which form m-A2pm → m-A2pm cross links within peptidoglycan |CITS: [18456808]|. A further three LD-transpeptidases (|FRAME: G7073-MONOMER "LdtA"|, |FRAME: G6571-MONOMER "LdtC"| and |FRAME: G6422-MONOMER "LdtB"|) cleave the m-A2pm-d-Ala peptide bond of a peptidoglycan donor stem and link the m-A2pm residue to the the C-terminal lysine residue of Braun's lipoprotein and catalyse the exchange of D-alanine with glycine in tetrapeptide stems |CITS: [17369299][18456808]|. , The murein of E. coli K-12 is characterised by the presence of 'free' penta-, tetra-, and tripeptide stems (ie. stems not involved in cross linkages) in varying proportions. Pentapeptide stems are converted to tetrapeptides by the action of DD carboxypeptidases (primarily |FRAME: EG10201-MONOMER "DacA or PBP5"|) which remove the C-terminal D-alanine residue |CITS: [7002918]| while tripeptide stems are formed by cleavage of the (L)-meso-A2pm →D-Ala bond of tetrapeptide stems. This latter reaction is catalysed by the LD-transpeptidase enzymes (LdtA, LdtB, LdtC, LdtD and LdtE) which also have LD-carboxypeptidase activity |CITS: [18456808]|. The amount of dipeptide subunits in isolated murein is low and the mechanism by which they might be formed is not clear., Peptidoglycan synthases are regulated by multiple protein-protein interactions and different peptidoglycan synthesis complexes appear to be active at different stages of the cell cycle; the interaction of peptidoglycan synthases with cytoskeletal proteins |FRAME: EG10608-MONOMER "MreB"| and |FRAME: EG10347-MONOMER "FtsZ"| is important during cell elongation and division (reviewed in |CITS: [26370943][22203377]|). Subcomplexes of SEDS (shape, elongation, division and sporulation) family proteins with class 2 penicillin binding proteins (transpeptidases) are proposed to be the primary peptidoglycan synthases in cell elongation and division |CITS: [27525505]| - in E. coli K-12, these roles may be fulfilled by the SEDS proteins |FRAME: EG10607-MONOMER "MrdB"| and |FRAME: EG10344-MONOMER "FtsW"| and the class 2 PBPs |FRAME: EG10606-MONOMER "MrdA"| and |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER "FtsI"| |CITS: [27643381]|. , Please note: This pathway has been designed to include many of the reactions that are involved during the assembly of nascent peptidoglycan but the heterogeneous nature of the mature polymer precludes depiction by a single pathway. This pathway does not depict the insertion of newly made peptidoglycan into the existing sacculus - several models for this process have been proposed (see |CITS: [17658458]|). The insertion of new material requires cleavage of mature peptidoglycan and E. coli contains a variety of peptidoglycan hydrolases which cleave the glycoside and amide bonds of mature peptidoglycan (reviewed in |CITS: [22126997]|). There is a significant turnover of peptidoglycan during cell growth and this is accompanied by recycling of the turnover products for reuse (see |FRAME: PWY0-1261| and |FRAME: PWY0-1546|)., Reviews: |CITS: [1779930][11320055][17658458][18081839][22126997]|

Summary: The nightshade family is known to produce unusual, specialized metabolites in glandular trichomes |CITS:[21098679]|, which are secreted onto surfaces of leaves, stems and flowers and may serve as a defense against herbivore attacks |CITS:[2652002] [Severson85]|. Such specialized metabolites are sugar derivatives, specifically acylsugars which are specialized compounds comprised of either a glucose backbone, i.e. acylglucoses |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| or a |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold, i.e. acylsucroses which are decorated with acyl groups of varying length and structure |CITS:[18931142]|. Wild tomato species have been shown to possess a greater diversity in the acylation pattern of those sugar frameworks than cultivated tomatoes |CITS:[Shapiro94] [21098679]|. The diversity is most strikingly in Solanum habrochaites (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) |CITS:[23054567]| but also Solanum pennellii acylsucroses (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)|) deviate remarkably from the acylation pattern observed in cultivated species of tomato (compare with |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)|)., Research on acylsugars and their role in the life cycle of members of the Solanaceae is ongoing but broad-spectrum insecticidal properties |CITS:[Hawthorne92] [18807203] [Maluf10] [Leckie12]| have been reported which include interactions with phytohormones |CITS:[21068365]|, interferece with feeding behavior of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94] [Liedl95]| and attracting predators of feeding pest larvae |CITS:[21518882]|. Acylsugars also have received attention because of serving in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries as non-hazardous additives |CITS:[Hill99]|., Plants have developed dynamic and complex metabolic networks producing a tremendous amount of specialized metabolites |CITS:[21275647]| which are paramount for the chemical diversity of compounds involved in plant defense and communication/signaling pathways. The high variation in the acylation pattern of acylsucroses in wild species of tomato is another example for the phenomenon of flexible biochemistry in plants. It is an interesting finding that the acylation pattern in Solanum habrochaites is strongly correlated with the geographic location of this plant |CITS:[23054567]|., For instance, the furanose moiety of the |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| frame in Solanum habrochaites was either not acylated (northern accessions), contained a single short (C4-C5) or long acyl (C10-C12) chain or even accommodated two short acyl chains (southern accessions). The reason for the high variability of acylsucroses in the species is the existence of various ASAT3-like |CITS:[25862303]| and ASAT4-like |CITS:[23054567]| sequences which encode for acyltransferases with different substrate specificities in various accession lines of Solanum habrochaites. In addition, the existence of an ASAT4 gene encoding a functional acetyltransferase in Solanum habrochaites divides C-2 bearing acylsugars in southern areas (supercluster 1) from the C-2 lacking acylsugars from accession in northern areas of Peru and Ecuador (supercluster 2) |CITS:[23054567]|., In contrary to Solanum habrochaites all acylsucroses found in Solanum pennellii lack furanose acylation which is attributed to an ASAT3 like gene encoding a acyltransferase which instead of acylating the 3'-ring position of furanose decorates the 2-position of the pyranose moiety. In vitro assays with purified recombinant ASAT3 protein demonstrated the inability of this enzyme to accept diacylsucrose metabolites as substrates. Instead, monoacylated sucrose such as |FRAME:CPD-19018 sucrose-4-isovalerate| was accepted |CITS:[25862303]|. Moreover, the results of the assays did correspond with the in vivo identified metabolites in Solanum pennellii which were shown to be not acylated on the furanose moiety and did not have a acetyl group associated to the C-2 position of the pyranose ring |CITS:[20113441]|.

The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds, including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "γ-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "γ-butenolides"|, as chemical signaling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation |CITS: [2268871]|. At least 60% of |FRAME: TAX-1883| species appear to produce γ-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011) only a small number of them have been characterized |CITS: [21090718]|., Based on their structures, these γ-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, the |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and the |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|., Each γ-butyrolactone can interact with a specific receptor |CITS: [7592371]|, which in turns binds to the promoter region of a transcriptional activator. When the concentration of the γ-butyrolactone reaches a critical threshold, it binds to receptor molecule, resulting in its dissociation from the promoter and production of the transcription activator, which then activates the transcription of a number of genes required for secondary metabolism and morphological differentiation |CITS: [24367152]|., The |FRAME: CPD1A0-6123|- and |FRAME: CPD-17025|-producing |FRAME: TAX-100226| synthesizes several |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type γ-butyrolactones"|, named |FRAME: CPD-19918|, |FRAME: CPD-19945|, and |FRAME: CPD-19946|, that control the production of these antibiotics |CITS: [10753903][19778723]|. The receptors that binds these molecules are encoded by the scbR and scbR2 genes |CITS: [11555283][26442964]|., The biosynthetic pathway for γ-butyrolactones in |FRAME: TAX-100226| is thought to be similar that of |FRAME: TAX-1911|, which was shown to proceed from 3-oxo-fatty-acyl-[acp] molecules, which are intermediates of fatty acid biosynthesis, and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of glycolysis |CITS: [17277085]|. The two molecules are condensed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.277|, which is encoded in |FRAME: TAX-100226| by the |FRAME: SCO6266| gene, forming an ester that converts spontaneously to a lactone. A second enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.113|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: SCO6267| gene, reduces the double bond. The phosphate group is removed by a phosphatase that may be a non-specific enzyme (the removal of the phosphate group could be catalyzed in vitro by the bacterial alkaline phosphatase), producing |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones| |CITS: [17277085]|. The last step, which is the only one unique to the biosynthesis of IM-2 type butanolides, is the stereospecific reduction of the 6-oxo group to an (R)-hydroxy group, which is catalyzed by a reductase encoded by the |FRAME: SCO6264| gene |CITS: [Sanchez16][29510026]|.

Summary: Note: this pathway describes a process that involves both the cytoplasmic membrane and the outer membrane. Due to current limitations in the pathway layout algorithm, the pathway is displayed using only a single membrane. Read the following text to get more information about the localization of the different components., Dissimilatory metal reduction is a microbial respiratory process in which the reduction of an oxidized metal is coupled to energy conservation under anoxic conditions. A number of species of Gram-negative bacteria can use insoluble minerals of Fe(III) as extracellular respiratory electron acceptors, and the best studied ones are members of the |FRAME: TAX-22| and |FRAME: TAX-28231| genera. In |FRAME: TAX-211586| at least five proteins have been shown to play an essential role in the electron transport from the quinone pool of the plasma membrane to extracellular Fe(III)., The |FRAME: MONOMER-20175 "tetraheme c-type cytochrome CymA"|, which is localized to the outer surface of the cytoplasmic membrane, catalyzes the transfer of electrons from menaquinol to various periplasmic electron-accepting proteins, including the |FRAME: MONOMER-124342| FccA (see |FRAME: PWY-8552|). A |FRAME: G-55066| mutant cannot grow with |FRAME: DMSO| (DMSO), |FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: FUM|, or ferric iron as terminal electron acceptors, indicating that it acts as the entry point of electrons for several electron transport pathways |CITS: [9023196][10613864][12196158][12899636]|., Three other proteins involved in dissimilatory iron reduction are encoded by the |FRAME: G-124820|, |FRAME: G-124822|, and |FRAME: G-124821| genes, which are located in an operon. The three proteins form a |FRAME: CPLX-85506 complex| |CITS: [20018742]|., MtrA is a periplasmic decaheme c-type cytochrome and is essential for ferric iron reduction. It has been shown to be reduced by CymA |CITS: [12732647][17644630][19837833]|., MtrC is a decaheme c-type cytochrome located on the extracellular face of the outer membran that acts a terminal Fe(III) reductase. An |FRAME: G-124821| deletion mutant has reduced electron transfer activity to Fe(III) and was ~70% impaired in ferric reductase activity catalyzed by the membrane fraction |CITS: [12406753]|. , MtrB is an outer membrane β-barrel porin comprising 28 transmembrane β-strands. MtrB was originally proposed to be a component of the ferric and manganese reductase |CITS: [9829939][11169112]|, though it is now known to have a different role |CITS: [12406753]|. MtrB forms a porin in the outer membrane within which MtrA and MtrC embed at the inner and outer faces of the membrane, respectively, enabling MtrA to pass the electrons to MtrC |CITS: [20018742]|., The outer membrane protein |FRAME: MONOMER-124824 OmcA| is also a decaheme cytochrome protein that was reported to directly transfer electrons to different insoluble Fe(III) oxides, including hematite |CITS: [17061851][17608722][17061851]|. When assayed with ferric nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) as the electron acceptor, both OmcA and MtrC (also named OmcB) were found to form a high-affinity complex that catalyzed the electron transfer faster than each of the proteins did separately |CITS: [16788180]|. However, it was later suggested that OmcA and MtrC are involved in the reduction of Mn(IV) rather than Fe(III) |CITS: [11133454][12039733][12039733]|., The current model proposes that electrons are transferred from the plasma membrane quinone pool to CymA, which reansfers them to MtrA, bound at the periplasmic side of the outer membrane. MtrA to MtrB, which forms a porin through the membrane. The electrons are transferred to the decaheme cytochrome MtrC, which is bound on the extracellular side of the MtrB pore. MtrC then binds directly to the surface of Fe(II) oxides and reduces them. The decaheme cytochrome OmcA, which binds to MtrC, performs a very similar task to that of MtrC, though it employes a different mode of attachment to the oxides., In addition, a bidirectional electron transfer has been observed between the fumarate reductase FccA and MtrA, suggesting that FccA may function as a transient electron storage protein that partucupates in iron reduction as well as fumarate reduction |CITS: [19837833]|.

Summary: Chloronitrobenzenes (CNBs) are widely used as intermediates in the manufacture of many chlorinated aromatic compounds, and are known to be very toxic. These compounds are generally resistant to microbial degradation due to the electron-withdrawing properties of nitro and chlorine groups |CITS: [10049867]|, and have been listed as priority pollutants by the European Economic Community and by China |CITS: [15580337]|., |FRAME: CPD-9154| (4CNB) is a relatively new anthropogenic compound, and until recently no single organism was shown to be able to degrade it. However, in recent years there have been several reports of such strains: |FRAME:TAX-283| strain LW1 |CITS: [10103229]|, |FRAME: TAX-543891| |CITS:[15580337][16517619][17526790]|, and |FRAME: ORG-5961| |CITS: [16642329][16583229]|., The genes involved in 4CNB degradation in both |FRAME: TAX-543891| and |FRAME: ORG-5961| are located on large plasmids (pCNB-1 |CITS: [17526790]| and pZWL73 |CITS: [16583229]|, respectively). In plasmid pCNB-1 the genes reside within a very large transposon, named TnCNB1 |CITS: [17526790]|., In general, the degradation pathway for 4CNB is similar to that of nitrobenzene (see |FRAME: PWY-5637|). Most of the genes are similar to the previously identified nbz, amn and nba genes from |FRAME: ORG-5945|, |FRAME: TAX-301| JS45, |FRAME: TAX-874293| and |FRAME: ORG-5935|, involved in the degradation of nitrobenzene, aminophenol and nitrobenzoate |CITS: [16517619]|.

General Background, Nitrification, the oxidation of |FRAME: AMMONIA| to |FRAME: NITRATE| by microorganisms, is a key process in the global nitrogen cycle, resulting in nitrogen loss from ecosystems, eutrophication of surface and ground waters, and the production of atmospherically active trace gases. For many years it has been thought that no one organism is capable of carrying out the whole process, with ammonia oxidizers limited to the conversion of ammonia to |FRAME: NITRITE| and nitrite oxidizers confined to the oxidation of nitrite to nitrate. However, that paradigm has been proven unfounded with the isolation of organisms capable of the full oxidation of ammonia to nirtate |CITS: [26610024][26610025]|., The "classical" ammonia-oxidizing bacteria are chemolithoautotrophs that utilize the process to generate sufficient energy for growth and maintenance reactions, including the reductive fixation of carbon dioxide. However, many heterotrophic bacteria can also oxidize ammonia to nitrite. The key difference between heterotrophic and autotrophic ammonia oxidation is that heterotrophic ammonia oxidation usually does not generate energy (although there has been a report about a |FRAME:TAX-286| strain which utilizes hydroxylamine oxidation as an additional energy source |CITS: [9049019]|). It has been suggested that in these bacteria nitrification is used as a sink for excess reducing power generated by oxidative metabolism |CITS: [Robertson88][8253206]|. , While the second step of the pathway (the oxidation of hydroxylamine to nitrite) is catalyzed in autotrophs only by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-1321|, heterotrophs may apply alternative routes, as demonstrated in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-2242| |CITS: [8674977]|., About This Pathway, Autotrophic ammonia oxidizing bacteria include the genera |FRAME: TAX-35798|, |FRAME: TAX-914| and |FRAME: TAX-1227|, all of which possess the genes encoding the two essential enzymes, ammonia monooxygenase (AMO) and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase (HAO). The best studied ammonia oxidizing organism is |FRAME: TAX-915|., The haoABC genes are clustered in the genomes of all autotrophic ammonia oxidizing bacteria with genes encoding two cytochromes, the multi-heme |FRAME: MONOMER-17537| (|FRAME: G-15261 cycA|) and the quinone/quinol-reactive |FRAME: MONOMER-17538| (|FRAME: G-15262|) |CITS: [8195067]|., Based on observations of in vitro reduction of cytochrome c554 by HAO |CITS: [1660304]| and demonstration of quinone reductase function of cytochrome cm552 |CITS: [18505274]|, a model has been proposed for the electron flow from hydroxylamine to quinone. Based on this model, the 4 electrons released in the oxidation of |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| by HAO in |FRAME: TAX-915| are channeled through cytochrome c554 to cytochrome cm552, where they are partitioned |CITS:[4372235][9808046]|. Two of the electrons are routed back to AMO, where they are used for the oxidation of ammonia, while the other two electrons are routed through the ubiquinone pool to a cytochrome oxidase, where they are used for the generation of a proton motive force, or for the production of NADH via a reverse electron flow |CITS:[11004450][12209257]|. The combined machinary involved in this process has been named "Hydroxylamine Ubiquinone Redox Module" (HURM). However, it should be noted that a redox interaction between cytochromes c554 and cm552 has not been observed yet, and thus the model is hypothetical. It can not be ruled out at the moment that HAO interacts directly with cytochrome cm552 |CITS: [19197347]| or even with a different cytochrome., The proposed electron transfer chain described in this pathway appears to be restricted to autotrophic ammonia oxidizers since all other nitrifying bacteria, such as methane-oxidizing Proteobacteria and Verrucomicrobia, lack a homologue of |FRAME: G-15262| |CITS: [22842521]|., See also pathway |FRAME: PWY-7084|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., About This Pathway, Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negatives, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) is a human host innate immune receptor that, together with its co-receptor myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD-2), recognizes lipopolysaccharides of invading bacteria by recognizing and binding lipid A. Binding of lipid A by the TLR4/MD-2 complex initiates a proinflammatory response, which leads to production of costimulatory molecules required for adaptive immunity, and eventually clearance of the infection., |FRAME: TAX-837| is unusually adept at evading the innate immune response mediated by TLR4. While the initial lipid A structure synthesized by the organism, which is |FRAME: CPD-24240 "penta-acylated and bisphosphorylated"|, is a moderate TLR4 agonist, the organism uses three lipid A-modifying enzymes (|FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M10|, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.M11|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.77 "EC 3.1.1.77, lipid A deacylase"|) whose combined action produces several alternative forms, including a tetra-acylated, non-phosphorylated structure that is inert for TLR4 activation |CITS: [17335558][19552698][21220483][28320881][30782639]|., It has been shown that the presence of high concentration of |FRAME: CPD-11678|, which is the result of increased vascular ulceration and the release of blood into gingival tissues, causes the accumulation of a tetra-acylated, mono-phosphorylated structure that is an antagonist of TLR2 and TLR4 activation |CITS: [16611234][16861633][18802645][19552698]|. It was also shown that changes in temperature can cause a shift in the lipid A form produced |CITS: [ 21220483]|. The accumulation of the mono-phopsphorylated form is achieved by inactivation of lipid A 1-phosphatase, providing a mechanism for hemin-dependent regulation of lipid A activity from TLR4 evasive to TLR4 suppressive |CITS: [19552698][24478080]|., Different lipid A forms affect interaction not only with TLR2 and TLR4, but also with a number of host systems, such as matrix metalloproteinase-3, which is highly upregulated only when the penta-acylated, bis-phosphorylated form is present |CITS: [23548063]|. Summary: General Background, Tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis. Folates also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine, play a role in histidine catabolism , |CITS: [11001804]|, and in plants are also involved in photorespiration, amino acid metabolism and chloroplastic protein biosynthesis |CITS: [11960743]| |CITS: [12644692]|., Folates are abundant in green leaves, and folic acid was initially isolated from a large amount (four tons) of spinach leaves. The name folate is derived from the Latin folium (leaf) |CITS: [3067148]|., Folates are modified by the addition of glutamate moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail. The polyglutamylated forms are usually preferred by the enzymes that use folates since the turnover rate of those compounds is markedly increased |CITS: [9190084][SCOTT00][KIRK94]|. In addition, in eukaryotic cells the glutamylated forms of folate facilitate the retention of the vitamin within the cell and its subcellular compartments |CITS: [1916088]|., The product of this pathway, |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydropteroylmonoglutamate, H4PteGlu1,, THF), is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. Members of the family differ in the oxidation state, of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions (see |FRAME: PWY-2201|), and the number of conjugated glutamate residues (see |FRAME: PWY-2161|)., About This Pathway, This pathway for the de novo biosynthesis of folates is found in bacteria, fungi, and plants., Folates are tripartite molecules and are made up of a pterin, |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| and |FRAME:GLT| moieties., The first two are synthesized from |FRAME:GTP| and |FRAME:CHORISMATE|, respectively., The first committed step catalyzed by |FRAME: FOLE-CPLX| converts GTP into |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3|., The triphosphate motif is removed by a still unknown process, and the resulting, |FRAME: DIHYDRO-NEO-PTERIN| is converted to |FRAME: AMINO-OH-HYDROXYMETHYL-DIHYDROPTERIDINE|, by |FRAME: CPLX0-3936| (FolB)., The consecutive action of the FolK, FolP, FolC, and FolA enzymes finally produces the final product, |FRAME: THF| |CITS: [12039964]|., In plants the pterin moiety is formed from GTP in the cytosol, which couples to pABA (synthesized in plastids) in mitochondria followed by subsequent glutamylation and reduction steps which may take place in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids |CITS: [11960743][11752472]|. The recent discovery that folylpolyglutamate synthases are present in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids with each of them encoded by a different gene in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [11752472]| points to the fact that at least parts of the pathway can be carried out independently in those compartments., In addition to the de novo pathway, many organisms also possess a salvage pathway that is used to re-synthesize tetrahydrofolate from breakdown products of folates in the cell, such as 5 or 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate., About Folates In Animals, While plants and many microorganisms can synthesize folate coenzymes by the de novo synthesis pathway, vertebrates are absolutely dependent on nutritional sources, making folate a vitamin. Food folates exist mainly as |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"| and |FRAME:FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (formyl-H4PteGlun) |CITS: [405403]|., Polyglutamyl folates are hydrolyzed to folylmonoglutamates by |FRAME: HS06361-MONOMER|, and metabolized within the enterocyte into 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1. This monoglutamyl folate coenzyme is the plasma form of the vitamin |CITS: [13906633][2736319]|, and is transported to peripheral tissues where it is demethylated by the vitamin B12-dependent |FRAME:ENZRXN-5465| to monoglutamyl tetrahydrofolate (H4PteGlu1)., Insufficient supply of the vitamin in vertebrates leads to anemia in adults, and has been shown to cause neural tube malformation in human embryos |CITS: [11744531]|. In addition, folate defficiency has been linked to a number of other birth defects, several types of cancer, dementia, affective disorders, Down's syndrom, and serious conditions affecting pregnancy outcome (for a review, see |CITS: [11001804]|).

|FRAME: TAX-38881|, a colony-forming, fresh water green algae, is regarded as a potential source of biofuel because of its ability to produce large amounts of hydrocarbons. Depending on the strain and growth conditions, up to 75% of algal dry mass can be hydrocarbons., Different strains of |FRAME: TAX-38881| produce different hydrocarbons |CITS: [Dayananda]|. Three races have been documented: |FRAME: TAX-869302| (A race) produces odd numbered (C25 to C31) n-alkadienes and trienes. |FRAME: TAX-869301| (B race) produces triterpenoid hydrocarbons known as botryococcenes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n–10</sub>, n = 30–37) of isoprenoid origin |CITS: [Chisti80]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6105|), and the |FRAME: ORG-6353 "L race"| produces a single hydrocarboin - the C40 tetraterpene |FRAME: CPD-13313| |CITS: [Metzger90]|., The first committed step in |FRAME: CPD-13313| biosynthesis is the condensation of two |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| molecules and the reduction of the product to |FRAME: CPD-20653|, which is carried by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.148|. The reaction is analogous to that catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.21| from two molecules of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| |CITS: [27050299]|., |FRAME: CPD-20653 Lycopaoctaene| then undergos sequential reductions that eventually produce |FRAME: CPD-13313| as the major product of the pathway. Even though the reductase enzyme(s) have not been identified yet, metabolite analysis of |FRAME: ORG-6353| has shown the presence of most expected intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-20661|, |FRAME: CPD-20660|, |FRAME: CPD-20659|, and |FRAME: CPD-20658| |CITS: [27050299]|., |FRAME: CPD-13313| biosynthesis activity was detected mainly in the microsomal fraction. This, combined with sequence analysis, suggests that lycopaoctaene synthase is localized to a membrane system, possibly the endoplasmic reticulum, as is the case for squalene synthase.

Summary: The meta-cleavage pathway of catechol is one of the major pathways for the degradation of aromatic compounds. Its importance has been well demonstrated in bacteria of many genera, including species of |FRAME: TAX-352|, |FRAME: TAX-48736| and numerous species of |FRAME: TAX-286|. , The most comprehensively studied meta-cleavage pathway is that of the TOL plasmid pWWO, which encodes a |FRAME: PWY-5178 "toluene degradation pathway"| in |FRAME: TAX-303|. The genes are located in an operon that encodes the enzymes for conversion of benzoate to catechol and catechol to the central metabolites pyruvate and acetaldehyde |CITS: [2183008]|., |FRAME: CATECHOL Catechol| itself is an intermediate in the degradation of many different aromatic compounds. In addition to |FRAME:BENZOATE|, catechol is an intermediate in the degradation of toluate, |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE|, |FRAME:CPD-110|, and |FRAME: PHENOL|, and substituted catechols are intermediates in the catabolism of methylated and chlorinated derivatives of these compounds., In this pathway, the aromatic ring of |FRAME:CATECHOL| is cleaved by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-2841| adjacent to the two catechol hydroxyls. The product of this cleavage, |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD|, is metabolized in one of two routes. In one variant (described in |FRAME:PWY-5415|), it is hydrolyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-12763|, generating the important intermediate |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| in a single step., In the second variant (this pathway), |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD| is dehydrogenated by |FRAME:CPLX-7245| to |FRAME: CPD-13339|, the enol-form of 4-oxalocrotonate, which is then isomerized to the keto form by |FRAME:CPLX-7237|, and decarboxylated by |FRAME:CPLX-7239|., The latter is in a tight complex with the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7240|. It's product, |FRAME:CPD-6761|, is an unstable tautomer of |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE|. This product is transferred to |FRAME: CPLX-7240| within the complex., Thus, the two branches, which separate at |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD|, join again at |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| (or its tautomer |FRAME:CPD-6761|) |CITS: [2681159]|., The hydrolase-based variant is the preferred route for 3-substituted catechols, while the dehydrogenase-based route is the preferred route for non-substituted and 4-substituted catechols |CITS: [7890778]|., |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| is metabolized to pyruvate and acetaldehyde (and eventually, acetyl-coA) by successive action of the enzymes |FRAME:CPLX-7240|, |FRAME:MONOMER-12778| and |FRAME:MONOMER-12780|. The last two enzymes form a |FRAME: CPLX-7250| complex, which facilitates the transfer of the toxic acetaldehyde intermediate between them |CITS: [8419288]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamin diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, The thiamine biosynthesis pathway illustrated here has been most extensively studied in |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-90371|. There are several differences between the pathways employed by |FRAME: TAX-1423| and by |FRAME: TAX-562| (see |FRAME: PWY-6895|). , Thiamine biosynthesis in bacteria is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|. A final phosphorylation reaction yields the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. , The biosynthesis of the thiazole moiety is complex and in |FRAME:TAX-562| involves six proteins, the products of the |FRAME: G1|, |FRAME: EG11587|, |FRAME: EG11589|, |FRAME: EG11590|, |FRAME: G6238|, and |FRAME: G7325| genes. , The process begins when IscS, a protein that is also involved in the biosynthesis of iron-sulfur clusters, catalyzes the transfer of a sulfur atom from cysteine to |FRAME:Sulfur-Carrier-Proteins-ThiI|, generating a |FRAME: Sulfurylated-ThiI|., In a parallel route, |FRAME: ThiF-Proteins| catalyzes a two step process: First, the activation of |FRAME: Thi-S| by adenylation of its carboxy terminus, generating |FRAME:Adenylated-ThiS-Proteins|, and second, the subsequent exchange of the adenylate with the |FRAME: Sulfurylated-ThiI "ThiI persulfide"|, generating |FRAME: ThiS-ThiI-disulfides|., The next step is a disulfide interchange, where a |FRAME: Sulfurylated-ThiF "ThiF sulfur-carrier protein"| replaces the |FRAME:Sulfurylated-ThiI "ThiI"| moiety, resulting in |FRAME:ThiS-ThiF-disulfides|., This dual-protein disulfide finally acts as the sulfur donor for thiazole formation, in a reaction that also involves |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| and |FRAME: CPD-12279|, and is catalyzed by the |FRAME: THIG-MONOMER| protein., |FRAME: CPD-12279| is formed in |FRAME:TAX-562| from |FRAME: TYR| by |FRAME: THIH-MONOMER| (ThiH), which forms a complex with |FRAME: THIG-MONOMER| |CITS:[9632726][11438688][16388576]|., The biosynthesis of the pyrimidine moiety of thiamin is not simple either. Starting with |FRAME: 5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-5-AMINOIMIDAZOLE|, an intermdiate in purine biosynthesis, two enzymatic steps, catalyzed by |FRAME: THIC-MONOMER| and |FRAME: HMP-P-KIN-CPLX "ThiD"|, produce |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP|. The first of these reactions is one of the most complex rearrangement reactions known., Finally, the two moieties are condensed together by |FRAME: THIE-MONOMER|, and phophorylated to the final form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|, by |FRAME: THI-P-KIN-MONOMER|., Thiamine and its thiazole and pyrimidine intermediates are stable under physiological conditions and are salvaged from the environment by organisms for producing thiamine. Studies with different |FRAME: TAX-562| mutants demonstrated that cocultures of Δ|FRAME: EG11585|-Δ|FRAME: EG11586| and Δ|FRAME: EG11585|-Δ|FRAME: EG11589| (but not Δ|FRAME: EG11586|-Δ|FRAME: EG11589|) mutants are able to grow in a thiamine-deficient medium |CITS: [35357164]|.

Summary: General Background, The pollen grain wall in most plant species has the same basic structure, although the size, shape and external morphology are species-specific. It consists of an outer and inner layer, called the exine and intine, respectively. The exine consists of an outer sculptured portion, the sexine, and a simpler inner layer, the nexine. The sculptured sexine is made up of radially directed rods, the bacula, which have enlarged heads that fuse to form a patterned wall, and the tectum, which is the outermost edge of the exine. The exine wall has important roles in protecting the pollen from various environmental stresses and bacterial attacks when it moves from the anther to the stigma, and in the species-specific adhesion of pollen grains to the female stigma cells |CITS: [14756310]|., The interstices of the exine are coated with a sticky hydrophobic lipidic and proteinaceous layer known as the tryphine or pollen coat. A mojor component of the tryphine is sporopollenin - a complex polymer that confers physical strength, chemical inertness and elasticity to the exine. The chemical composition of sporopollenin remains poorly characterized due to its extreme resistance to chemical and biological degradations. However limited data indicates the presence of aliphatic polyhydroxy compounds and phenolic hydroxyl groups |CITS: [14713155]|. Several genes and their encoded enzymes involved in sporopollenin biosynthesis have been identified in the recent years |CITS: [21193572][19700560][21193570][17496121][19218397]|. The genetic and biochemical data further suggest that sporopollenin components include hydroxylated fatty acids and their derived tetraketide α-pyrones. The sporopollenin components are presumably coupled with ester and ether linkages. Nonetheless, the exact chemical nature of the sporopollenin polymer and its components still remains to be elucidated. For example, although in vitro enzyme characterization supports the presence of tetraketide α-pyrones, their occurrence has not been reported in Arabidopsis., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with fatty acids synrthesized in the plastid - |FRAME: DODECANOATE|, |FRAME: PALMITATE|, |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| and |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|. These fatty acids are exported from the plastid and imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in their CoA-activated forms. Once they enter the ER, they are believed to be hydrolyzed to free fatty acids that are hydroxylated by P450 fatty acid monooxygenases. Two routes have been described. |FRAME: DODECANOATE Laurate| (C12:0) is hydroxylated at position 7 by a dedicated monooxygenase, encoded by the |FRAME: AT1G01280| gene |CITS: [17496121]|. The other three fatty acids are hydroxylated at the ω position by long-chain fatty acid ω-hydroxylase, encoded by |FRAME: AT1G69500| |CITS: [19700560]|. Once hydroxylated, the fatty acids are again esterified to coenzyme A in a reaction catalyzed by the fatty acyl-CoA synthetase encoded by |FRAME: AT1G62940| |CITS: [19218397]| and exported from the ER to the cytosol. ., The processes in the cytosol are not well understood, but a few enzymes are known to be involved. The alcohol-forming fatty acyl-CoA reductase encoded by the |FRAME: AT3G11980| gene is absoltely required, and is assumed to convert the hydroxylated fatty acyl-CoAs to fatty alcohols |CITS: [9351246]|. |FRAME: CPD-17638| is also the substrate for the tetraketide α-pyrone synthases encoded by |FRAME: AT1G02050| and |FRAME: AT4G34850|, which convert it to the tetraketide α-pyrone |FRAME: CPD-17645| |CITS: [21193570]|., The genes involved in this pathway, CYP704B1, CYP703A2, ACOS5, PKSA, PKSB, TKPR1 and TKPR2, are tightly co-expressed.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipopolysaccharides that comprise all three regions are called |FRAME: Smooth-Form-LPS "smooth (S)-form LPS"|, while LPS lacking the O-antigen are named |FRAME: LOS "rough (R)-form LPS"| or lipooligosaccharide (LOS)., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., The core oligosaccharides are conceptually divided further into two regions: inner core and outer core. The inner core is highly conserved, contains |FRAME: KDO| (Kdo) and |FRAME: CPD-21358| (Hep) residues, and is often phosphorylated. The inner core oligosaccharide plays a critical role in essential barrier function of the outer membrane. The outer core comprises a tri-hexose backbone modified with varying side-branch substitutions of hexose and acetamidohexose residues. The outer core provides an attachment site for O-antigen., About This Pathway, The completed |FRAME: KDO2-LIPID-A "Kdo2-lipid A"| serves as the acceptor on which the core oligosaccharide chains are assembled by sequential glycosyl transfer from nucleotide sugar precursors. This process involves a co-ordinated complex of membrane-associated glycosyltransferases acting at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane. Many of the enzymes are predicted to be peripheral proteins. , Strains of |FRAME: TAX-83333| normally do not synthesize the O-antigen due to mutations in the O-antigen operon that evolved during lab culturing of this strain, and thus form only rough lipopolysaccharides. However, they are capable of forming the antigen if those mutations are corrected |CITS: [7517391]|., |FRAME:TAX-562| mutants that lack the heptose region of the inner core display "deep rough" phenotypes that contain only lipid A decorated with Kdo. This phenotype causes instability of the outer membrane, resulting in loss of expression of pili and flagella and secretion of hemolysin with reduced activity. Mutations that eliminate synthesis of the outer core result in enhanced susceptibility to some hydrophobic compouns due to an indirect effect on core phosphorylation. , Once synthesized, the rough-type LPS, composed of lipid A and the completed core, is transported across the inner membrane into the periplasmatic space. The flipping of the lipid A coupled LPS core is carried out by |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.6| (|FRAME: EG10613 MsbA|), an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein |CITS: [9575204]|., In organisms that do not produce O-glycan the rough-type LPS is directly inserted into the outer leaflet of the outer bacterial membrane. In organisms that do produce O-glycan it is converted into the smooth LPS in the periplasmatic space before being shuttled to the outer membrane by |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.5|., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [9791168][12045108][15052329][17362200]|.

General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various, insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are, believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness, of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans, was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose, |CITS: [12065209]|. , In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits, of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosil α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus, nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, , including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects, and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein). , In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity,, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation, and no internal hydrogen bond formation. , The combination of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms, trehalose can be used as an external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute, (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a, structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|., In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as, a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|., The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood, |CITS: [11081789]|., About This Pathway, The hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2265| accumulates trehalose in response to high, osmolarity when grown in the presence of yeast extract that contains trehalose., Trehalose induces a high affinity ABC transporter for trehalose and maltose that is most likely responsible, for the accumulation of trehalose. The operon that contains the trasporter genes is also induced under, conditions of elevated temperature, suggesting that the accumulation of trehalose occurs in response to, osmotic, and possibly heat stress., The operon also includes the |FRAME: G-10765| gene, encoding a |FRAME: CPLX-7634|., This enzyme can produce |FRAME: TREHALOSE| from |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| and glucose in a, reversible reaction, and can also use UDP- and GDP-glucose, with less efficiency |CITS: [15364950]|., A similar pathway has been described in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-53953| |CITS: [15737605]|., A related, yet different, pathway has been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-2271|. In that pathway, the, trehalose synthase reaction is unidirectional (see |FRAME: PWY-5985|) |CITS: [18483808]|.

Research in floral scent has been intensified over the last few decades indicating its importance for biological (pollination, defense), economical (perfume) and breeding (ornamental plants) purposes. Currently, 1719 volatile compounds involved in emitting floral scent comprising 991 species from 90 families and 38 orders have been listed |CITS:[Knudsen06]|. Amongst them roses with more than 25.000 cultivars make up an important part and research on scent, color and durability has shed some light on the biosynthesis of the main scents found in roses |CITS:[12123815]| |CITS:[16233496]| |CITS:[12177504]| ., Modern roses have been derived from European and Chinese roses, all of them being different in the chemical compounds they emit as scent. Chinese roses produce aromatic compounds such as 3,5-dimethoxytoluene (DMT) (this pathway) and 1,3,5-trimethoxybenzene (TMB) (see |FRAME:PWY-5765|) whereas European roses predominantly emit |FRAME:CPD-7035| (see |FRAME:PWY-5751|) and monoterpenes. In modern roses as a result of a long and intensive history of breeding, both |FRAME:CPD-9500| and |FRAME:CPD-9502| occur emanating the typical "tea aroma' scent |CITS:[16361520]| |CITS:[18413608]|., A number of O-methyltransferases have been identified which catalyze in vitro the two steps of the DMT pathway. It has been demonstrated that in dependence of the availability of substrates the orcinol O-methyltransferases (OOMT's) carry out steps in both DMT- and |FRAME:PWY-5765| which underlines their enzymatic multifunctionality. Based upon the different catalytic properties of OOMT1 and OOMT2 from Rose x hybrid |CITS:[12177504]| the sequential methylation of |FRAME:ORCINOL-CPD| to |FRAME:CPD-9502| could be demonstrated. Interestingly, only a single amino acid polymorphism in the phenolic substrate binding site seems to be responsible for the different catalytic efficiency of OMT1 and OMT2 towards their preferred substrates |CITS: [18413608]|. Other orcinol O-methyltransferases were involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-9501| (this pathway) as well as in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-9499| (see |FRAME:PWY-5765|) |CITS:[12123815]| indicating their possible involvement in both pathways.

Summary: Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., Each of these can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., All three naturally-occurring hexitols can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., Each of these hexitols enters the cell via a specific phosphotransferase system, so the first intracellular species is the 6-phospho-derivative |CITS: [1100608]| (note that due to symmetry of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|, their phosphorylation at either end produces the same molecule. When these molecules are phosphorylated at the 6 position by the PTS system, the resulting molecules are named |FRAME: MANNITOL-1P| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, respectively, by conventional nomenclature rules)., In all three cases this sugar alcohol phosphate becomes the substrate for a dehydrogenase that oxidizes its 2-alcohol group to a keto group. In the cases of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: SORBITOL|, the resulting keto sugar phosphate is |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, an intermediate of glycolysis, and hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy |CITS: [3553176][1408350]|.

Summary: General Background, There are several alternative pathways for the degradation of trehalose., Depending on the organism, trehalose may enter the cell either through a permease, in which case it, remains unmodified, or it may be transported by a phosphotransferase system (PTS), resulting in the, phoshorylated trehalose-6-phosphate form., Degradation then proceeds by different mechanisms: , Unmodified trehalose may be degraded by a hydrolyzing trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|), or it may, be split by the action of a trehalose phosphorylase (see |FRAME: PWY-2722| and |FRAME: PWY-2723|)., Likewise, trehalose-6-phosphate may be either hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase, (see |FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) or it could be attacked by a trehalose-6-phosphate phosphorylase, (see |FRAME: PWY-2721|). , About This Pathway, Trehalose phosphorylase (TP), the key enzyme in this pathway, catalyzes the reversible synthesis, (and degradation) of trehalose from/to |FRAME: D-glucose-1-phosphates| and |FRAME: D-Glucose|. , Two varieties of TP enzymes have been characterized: One variety is specific for the α forms of, D-glucose and D-glucose-1-phosphate, while the other is specific for the β forms., Thus, the two forms catalyze different reactions, and were given different EC numbers, (see the pathway |FRAME:PWY-2722| for the enzymes that use the β form)., The glucose-1-phosphate that is formed by the phosphorylase during trehalose degradation is, subsequently converted to glucose-6-phosphate by the appropriate phosphoglucomutase (which is also, either α- or β-specific)., TP enzymes that are α-specific have been found mostly in fungi, although such an enzyme was, also dicovered in yeast (|FRAME: TAX-53655|)., Organisms from which α-specific TP enzymes were isolated include the basidiomycetous fungi , |FRAME: TAX-5334| |CITS: [10393097]|, |FRAME: TAX-5341| |CITS: [9813313 ]|,, |FRAME: TAX-38945| |CITS: [Kitamoto88]|, |FRAME: TAX-50053| |CITS: [12880768]|, |FRAME: TAX-5322|, |CITS: [12880768]| and |FRAME: TAX-5627| |CITS: [0009797287]|.

Phytocassanes constitute one of the diterpenoid phytoalexin subclasses found in rice (Oryza sativa) which are induced upon infection with pathogen fungi and inhibit its spore germination |CITS:[Koga95]|. There are five phytocassanes known to date, |FRAME:CPD-7094|, |FRAME:CPD-16671|, |FRAME:CPD-16672|, |FRAME:CPD-16673| and |FRAME:CPD-16674| which only differ in the number and position of hydroxyl and keto-groups in the A-ring. The hydroxylation of C1 present in |FRAME:CPD-16671|, |FRAME:CPD-16672| and |FRAME:CPD-16674| has been shown to be a key functional moiety associated with antifungal activity |CITS:[Koga97]|. Rice, which belongs to the most important food plants in the world and provides the staple food for half of the world's population |CITS:[Seck12]| has been intensively studied to elucidate and improve the existing defense system against phytopathogen attacks diminishing the crop yield of this vital human food resource |CITS:[16956633]|. , Like all the other subclasses of phytoalexins found in rice (see |FRAME:PWY-7477|, |FRAME:PWY-7478|, |FRAME:PWY-7489| and |FRAME:PWY-7481|) phytocassanes originate from |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| formed via the MEP-pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5121|) |CITS:[17634747]|. A pair of cyclyzation and rearrangements catalyzed by copalyl/labdadienyl diphosphate synthases (CPS) |CITS:[15341631] [15542489]| and kaurene synthase like (KSL) proteins (see |FRAME:PWY-2981|) |CITS:[17141283]| convert |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| to |FRAME:CPD-4751|, the precursor for the biosynthesis of all phytocassanes. Oryza sativa has become the focal plant in the emerging theme of genetic clusters |CITS:[20921179]| which have been reported to be common amongst microbes |CITS:[18216259]| but are rather rare in plants |CITS:[19662496]|. The formation of the rice diterpenoid phytocassanes (this pathway) originates from the biosynthetic gene cluster on chromosome 4, with another cluster for phytoalexin and allelochemical biosynthesis existing on chromosome 2 |CITS:[19662496]|. , The |FRAME:PWY-7484| has only been partially elucidated and the pathway may proceed via different routes which remain to be verified. Most of the enzymes characterized in rice and involved in the biosynthesis of the various diterpenoid phytoalexins have been codon optimized, N-terminally modified for bacterial expression using and introduced to an modular metabolic engineered system in E. coli |CITS:[17480080]|. The cytochrome P450 dependent diterpene olefin hydroxylase encoded by KOL4 (also referred to as CYP701A8) was shown to hydroxylate the C3α-position of |FRAME:CPD-4751| to form |FRAME:CPD-16689| |CITS:[22247270] [23795884]|. However, the route towards the important intermediate |FRAME:CPD-16675|, probably the branch point towards |FRAME:CPD-16672| and |FRAME:CPD-16674|, may also proceed via |FRAME:CPD-13924| which is formed through the C11β-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-4751| catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-18619| |CITS:[19825834]| and the multifunctional cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase CYP76M8 which also carries out that reaction |CITS:[22215681] [23795884]|. , Yet another route appears possible through the enzymatic action of |FRAME:MONOMER-18620| which yields |FRAME:CPD-16719| from |FRAME:CPD-4751| in vitro, hence realizing the hydroxylation at C2 which can be found in another key intermediate of phytocassane biosynthesis, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16676| |CITS:[21985968]| but the C2 hydroxylation may also appear at a later step in the biosynthesis |CITS:[16956633]|. The latter enzyme also has been demonstrated in vitro to catalyze the C2-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-16675| forming |FRAME:CPD-16676| |CITS:[21985968]| which is considered the intermediate from which the biosynthesis towards |FRAME:CPD-7094|, |FRAME:CPD-16671| and |FRAME:CPD-16673| proceeds.

Summary: |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID Stearate| is a saturated fatty acid that occurs in many animal and vegetable fats and oils. It is an important constituent of milk fats, lard, and cocoa and shea butters. Stearate was first described by Michel Eugene Chevreul in 1823, and its name comes from Greek for "hard fat", reflecting the fact that stearate forms a waxy solid |CITS: [16477801]|., De novo plant fatty acid synthesis occurs primarily in plastids and chloroplasts (it was shown that at least in Arabidopsis fatty acid synthesis also occurs in the mitochondria). The process involves a series of reactions catalyzed by fatty acid synthase (FAS) complexes that provoke the condensation of |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| and |FRAME: ACYL-ACP| (see |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY|)., In animals the last [acp]-bound intermediate appears to be |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"|, and elongation to |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| proceeds via CoA-bound intermediates in the ER (see |FRAME: PWY-5972|). In bacteria and plants elongation to stearate appears to continue via [acp]-bound intermediates, and |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| has been detected in many species |CITS: [4831331]|. , At least in plants, the elongation from |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"| to |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| is catalyzed by a dedicated β-ketoacyl-[acp] synthase, encoded by |FRAME: G-10790| (The enzyme involved in de novo fatty acid synthesis system up to |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"| is encoded by |FRAME: AT5G46290|) |CITS: [4153356][11337402]|., |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "Strearoyl-[acp]"| can be hydrolyzed by acyl-ACP thioesterase enzymes |CITS: [7734968]|. However, before the fatty acids can be exported out of the chloroplast they must be activated to fatty acyl-CoAs by an outer envelope |FRAME: AT1G77590| activity. Once activated, they are exported to the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [14973169]|., A more common route involves desaturation of |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| to |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|. Plants contain acyl-ACP desaturase enzymes, which introduce a double bond in the 9 position of |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| to generate |FRAME: Oleoyl-ACPs "oleoyl-[acp]"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5147|). Stearate is the only fatty acid that is desaturated in its ACP-bound form. All other desaturation reactions occur only after the fatty acid has been attached to a glycerolipid backbone., In cyanobacteria stearate is also often desaturated to oleate. However, unlike plants, in cyanobacteria this desaturation reaction occurs only after the incorporation of stearate into a lipid. Prior to incorporation into a lipid, the fatty acid is transferred to a coenzyme A molecule, resulting in formation of |FRAME: STEAROYL-COA|., Since the activity of the desaturase enzymes is often very high, |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| is often the main product of intraplastidial fatty acid synthesis |CITS: [8652653]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the biosynthesis of the amino acids |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: LYS|, |FRAME: THR|, and |FRAME: MET|, all of which are derived from the central metabolite |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, an intermediate of the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. The specific pathways shown here are those used by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|., The pathway starts by the reversible transamination of |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1|, providing a link between carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID Oxaloacetate|, which is consumed in this pathway, is replenished from the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|, by |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|, and in some bacteria also by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31| |CITS: [Gottschalk1986]|., |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is converted in two steps to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, which is the first branch point in this pathway. One branch leads toward |FRAME: LYS| biosynthesis, while the other continues towards the biosynthesis of the other amino acids included in this superpathway |CITS: [14929228]|. Because this step is common to all of the subsequent biosynthetic pathways, |FRAME: TAX-562| has three different enzymes that catalyze it (|FRAME: ASPKINIHOMOSERDEHYDROGI-CPLX "aspartate kinase I"|, |FRAME: ASPKINIIHOMOSERDEHYDROGII-CPLX "aspartate kinase II"|, and |FRAME: ASPKINIII-CPLX "aspartate kinase III"|), which are controlled by the available supply of |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET| and |FRAME: LYS|, respectively |CITS: [4148765]|., The L-lysine pathway shown here belongs to the diaminopimelate (DAP) group of Lysine pathways, and is known as the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|, as it involves succinylated intermediates., The rest of the |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| is converted to |FRAME: HOMO-SER| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.3|. Once again, |FRAME: TAX-562| has two different enzymes catalyzing this reaction, which are controlled by the availability of |FRAME: THR| and |FRAME: MET|, respectively |CITS: [4551091][4889171]|., |FRAME: HOMO-SER| can be isomerized to |FRAME: THR| in two steps that involved phosphorylation and de-phosphorylation |CITS: [11368768]|, or alternatively can lead to the formation of |FRAME: MET| in a 4-step pathway. , For |FRAME: MET| biosynthesis, homoserine is first activated by O-succinylation, and the product is combined with |FRAME: CYS| to form cystathionine. This compound is cleaved to homocysteine, which is subsequently methylated to produce methionine. The last reaction is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-562| by two different enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13| and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14|. Both enzymes use |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N| as the methyl donor. However, the former requires cobalamin (vitamin B12), while the latter does not |CITS: [1339288]|.

Summary: Bacteria can oxidatively deaminate amino acids for use as growth substrates. Alanine is converted to pyruvate,, a central metabolic intermediate. As shown in the pathway link, pyruvate is converted to carbon dioxide and, acetyl-CoA, which enters the TCA cycle . Alanine dehydrogenase is a NAD+-linked dehydrogenase, that occurs in several different types of bacteria |CITS: [Gottschalk1986]|. It catalyzes the reversible conversion of, alanine to its keto acid pyruvate, with reduction of NAD+ and release of ammonia. Both the degradative, and biosynthetic directions of this reaction are important to microbial carbon and nitrogen metabolism. The, enzyme is also of industrial and medical interest. It is used in the measurement of L-alanine, and in enzyme, assays (in |CITS: [9972262]|). It is also present as an antigen in pathogenic |FRAME:TAX-1773|, and is a possible target for therapeutic intervention |CITS: [10527947]|. , In |FRAME:TAX-1423|, degradation of L-alanine by alanine dehydrogenase has been shown to be important, in generating pyruvate as an energy source for sporulation |CITS: [8226620] [4204435]|. In other organisms, a, degradative role for this enzyme in vivo is suggested by its in vitro kinetics. The, |FRAME:TAX-548| enzyme has a lower Km for alanine than enzymes of the, genus Bacillus |CITS: [9972262]|. Alanine dehydrogenase from the non-nitrogen fixing, thermophilic, cyanobacterium |FRAME:TAX-32060| was suggested to play a role in deamination based on its kinetic, characteristics |CITS: [7896761]|., In a facultatively methylotrophic pseudomonad, the enzyme may have dual roles in alanine degradation and, nitrogen assimilation |CITS: [3446176]|. The alanine dehydrogenase of the phototrophic nonsulfur bacterium, |FRAME:TAX-1061| also has a dual role, depending upon the growth conditions |CITS: [2722749]|., In |FRAME:TAX-1772|, alanine dehydrogenase may have an important role in alanine, degradation and anaerobic growth |CITS: [12193615]|. In other bacteria, such as Rhizobium leguminosanum, pea bacterioids, alanine dehydrogenase plays a biosynthetic role in nitrogen assimilation |CITS: [10792736]|., Alanine dehydrogenase has also been characterized in archaea, although its amino acid sequence is, significantly different from the conserved bacterial sequences (in |CITS: [15516582]|). The physiological role(s), of this enzyme in archaea is unclear., In another pathway, alanine dehydrogenase is involved in the degradation of taurine by the anaerobe, |FRAME:TAX-35833| |CITS: [11041346]| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-1263|).

Limonene, a monocyclic monoterpene, is the most widespread terpene in the world and is formed by, more than 300 plants., |FRAME: CPD-8785|, the most widespread form of limonene, is the major constituent of citrus peel, essential oils, in which it is usually found at concentrations between 90 and 96%. Several plants form, a mixture of both enantiomers, while others produce only the |FRAME: CPD-4886| form., |FRAME: ORG-6040|, a Gram-positive bacterium, is able to grow on both |FRAME: CPD-8785| and, |FRAME: CPD-4886| as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [10224006]|. The same enzymes,, which are not stereo-selective, catalyze both |FRAME:PWY-5924| and |FRAME:PWY-5923|, |CITS: [10224006]|., Based on product accumulation studies and on the purification of several key enzymes, this degradation, pathway has been reconstructed: , The pathway starts with the attack of |FRAME: MONOMER-13976| on |FRAME: CPD-4886|,, producing |FRAME: 4S-limonene-1-2-epoxides|. Next, |FRAME: MONOMER-13975|, a unique enzyme different from, all epoxide hydrolases previously described, converts the epoxide to a |FRAME: CPD-10055|., Several alcohol dehydrogenase activities were identified in the cell extract, but only one of them, was inducible by growing the cells with limonene. That activity was attributed to |FRAME: CPLX-7608|,, an enzyme that also participates in the degradation of carveol and dihydrocarveol, that is believed to, be the main alcohol dehydrogenase involved in this pathway |CITS: [10473585]|., The product of the alcohol dehydrogenase, |FRAME: CPD-10058|, is the substrate for, |FRAME: MONOMER-13964|, another enzyme that participates in the degradation of several, monoterpenoids, including carveol and menthol |CITS: [10769172]|., The product of the monooxygenase, |FRAME: CPD-10060|, spontaneously rearranges to form, |FRAME: CPD-10063|, which is then converted in the presence of CoA and ATP to |FRAME: CPD-10066|, by |FRAME: MONOMER-13974|. This coA-derivative is then mineralized completely by β oxidation, |CITS: [10224006]|., The second enantiomer of limonene, |FRAME: CPD-4886|, is degraded by the same enzymes, as, described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-5924|.
