Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms. As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9984 Bacillibactin| is a catecholate siderophore produced by many |FRAME: TAX-91061| |CITS:[11112781]|., It is a cyclic trimeric ester made of three units of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate-glycine-threonine, joined in a cyclic structure by lactone linkages, similar to the enterobacterial siderophore |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN| |CITS: [11112781]|., The linear copmponent |FRAME:CPD-9983| (known as itoic acid after its discoverer, Takeru Ito) also has iron-chelating capabillities |CITS: [8357268]|., Bacillibactin is synthesized under iron-deficient conditions and excreted into the environment where it binds Fe(III) with high affinity and specificity. The ferrisiderophore complexes are taken up into the cell by specific transport components., Bacillibactin synthesis is divided into two parts:, 1) the conversion of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, 2) the synthesis of bacillibactin from |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, |FRAME: GLY| and , |FRAME: THR|., The second part of the pathway is a complex process catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-7603|., The process starts with the activation of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| by adenylation, and its transfer to the free thiol group of the |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| cofactor of the aryl-carrier protein domain of the DhbB protein. The reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7604|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10623| |CITS: [11112781]|., The next steps are the additions of |FRAME: GLY| and |FRAME: THR| to the activated 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate. These amino acids are activated by adenylation and then transferred to two peptidyl-carrier-protein domains of the seven-domain protein |FRAME: Holo-BSU31960-MONOMER|, which must be activated first by the binding of of two |FRAME:PANTETHEINE-P| cofactors (catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-13919|)., Two additional domains of this enzyme catalyze the transfer and condensation of the activated 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate first with the glycyl, and then with the L-threonyl groups, forming DHB-glycine-threonine attached to a peptidyl-carrier-protein domain |CITS: [11112781]|., The product is transferred to the thioesterase (Te) domain of |FRAME: Holo-BSU31960-MONOMER|, which is responsible for the trimerization of three such moieties and the release of the trilactone bacillibactin.

Summary: General Background, Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The lipid A component of pathogenic bacteria is detected by the host serum LPS-binding protein (LBP), which is dependent on two cofactors: cluster of differentiation 14 (CD14) and myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD2). The lipid A/LBP complex is subsequently recognized by the opsonic receptor CD14, forming a triple complex that activates Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). TLR4 activation triggers a signalling cascade, leading to the production of cytokines and clotting factors and the secretion of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) and other stimulatory molecules |CITS: [10963608]|. CAMP binds to negatively charged structural motifs such as the phosphate groups on lipid A, leading to cell lysis and death |CITS: [19601838]|. If the immune response is too strong sepsis and septic shock can occur, leading to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome and death |CITS: [12857774]|., In many bacterial species lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor lipid IVA. , Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. , About This Pathway, Compared with other enterobacterial lipid As, the lipid A of |FRAME: TAX-210| activates TLR4 in a much weaker form, displaying a 1000-fold lower endotoxicity compared with lipid A from |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [Yamaoka08]|. Several modifications result in this weak TLR4 elicitation: the major form of |FRAME: TAX-210| lipid A is acylated by four rather than six fatty acids, contains only a single Kdo residue, lacks the usual 4'-phosphate group, and has a phosphoethanolamine (PEtN) moiety replacing the 1-position phosphate group |CITS: [ 21903201]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Phthiocerols Phthiocerol|- and |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerol|-based lipids and glycolipids are a component of the outer layer of the cell envelope of a small number of slow-growing |FRAME: TAX-1762|, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-33894|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1777|, |FRAME: TAX-1769| and |FRAME: TAX-1809| |CITS: [3149973]|., Phthiocerols comprise a linear carbohydrate molecule to which one methoxyl group, one methyl group, and two secondary hydroxyl groups are attached. Two types of phthiocerols have been described. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-A "phthiocerol A"| the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-B "phthiocerol B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10., The related |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerols| contain a phenol group, usually decorated by glycosylation in a species-specific manner, at the ω end of the molecule |CITS: [3113946]|. The phenolphthiocerol molecules have either 35 or 37 carbon atoms., In most organisms the two hydroxyl groups of both phthiocerols and phenolphthiocerols are esterified by |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"|. In |FRAME: TAX-1781| and |FRAME: TAX-1809|, however, they are esterified by |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"| |CITS: [3149973][3113946]|., About This Pathway, Phenolphthiocerols biosynthesis starts with the lysis of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to produce |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|. This compound is activated by adenylation by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.50| (|FRAME: G-44325 FadD22|) |CITS: [20553505]|, followed by transfer to |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.261| (|FRAME: G-15015|), a polyketide synthase (PKS) enzyme that extendeds it by the addition of 8 or 9 malonyl-CoA units. Following the release from the PKS, the resulting extended compound is adenylated again, this time by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.51| (|FRAME: G-44326|) |CITS: [20553505]|, and transfered to |FRAME: CPLX-9045|, a large polyketide synthase (PKS) complex encoded by the ppsA-ppsE genes |CITS: [9201977][15749014]|., The |FRAME: CPLX-9045 "(phenol)phthiodiolenone synthase"| PKS complex extends the compound by the addition of two |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and three |FRAME: METHYL-MALONYL-COA| units, producing |FRAME: Phenolphthiodiolenone| intermediate that contains an oxo group instead of the methoxyl group found in phenolphthiocerols |CITS: [9201977][15749014]|. Because the PpsD protein is missing a required enoyl reductase domain, the product also contains a double bond between the C4 and C5 carbons. This bond is reduced by the product of the |FRAME: G185E-7207| gene |CITS: [17468241]|. The pathway is completed by reduction of the oxo group to a hydroxyl group, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-7205| gene product |CITS: [15995190]|, and its methylation to form the methoxyl group, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-7206| gene product |CITS: [15292265]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-7741|.

Summary: A new |FRAME: TRP| catabolic pathway has been described in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-216591|. In this pathway, |FRAME: TRP| is converted to |FRAME: 2-AMINO-3-3-OXOPROP-2-ENYL-BUT-2-ENEDI|, which is enzymatically degraded to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| via the intermediates |FRAME: 2-AMINO-MUCONATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-246|, a route that is commonly used by bacteria for the degradation of nitroaromatic compounds |CITS: [16267312]|., Several of the enzymes have been cloned and overexpressed, and their activity verified (these enzymes include |FRAME: CPLX-7480|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13371|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13372| and |FRAME: CPLX-7481|). Other enzymes in this pathway are predicted, based on the presence of putative genes encoding them in the same gene clusters that include the verifed enzymes. Such predicted enzymes include 4-oxalocrotonate decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.77), 2-ket-pentenoate hydratase (EC 4.2.1.80), 2-keto-4-hydroxypentenoate aldolase, and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. These genes are found in two clusters in |FRAME: TAX-216591|, but were found in a single uninterrupted cluster in |FRAME: TAX-1396| 10897, supporting the notion of a shared metabolic function of these genes in tryptophan metabolism |CITS: [16267312]|. Putative genes encoding the first three reactions in the pathway were also found in the |FRAME: TAX-216591| genome. However, no gene encoding kynurenine-3-monooxygenase (EC 1.13.14.9) was found, suggesting that the reaction is catalyzed by a nonorthologous form of the enzyme in this organism., This pathway shares the upstream set of reactions (up to |FRAME: 2-AMINO-MUCONATE|) with the tryptophan degradation pathway that is proposed to operate in mammals (see |FRAME: TRYPTOPHAN-DEGRADATION-1|). However, the downstream part of the pathway differs from the mammalian pathway, in which |FRAME: 2-AMINO-3-3-OXOPROP-2-ENYL-BUT-2-ENEDI| is converted via completely different intermediates, which include |FRAME: 2K-ADIPATE| and, |FRAME:GLUTARYL-COA|.

Summary: General Background, Like most Gram-negative bacteria, the outermost layer of the outer membrane of |FRAME: TAX-22| bacteria is primarily composed of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides| (LPS)., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The sugar |FRAME: KDO| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is the first sugar added to lipid A in the majority of Gram-negative bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-1269|). In strains of |FRAME: TAX-22| Kdo undergoes an additional modification prior to its attachment to the lipid, in which the C8 hydroxyl group is converted to a primary amine, forming |FRAME: CPD-18063| (Kdo8N), as described here |CITS: [14499575][15013415][18619581]|., Many species, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, add two Kdo sugars with a single Kdo transferase (see |FRAME: KDOSYN-PWY|), whereas others, including members of the genera |FRAME: TAX-22| and |FRAME: TAX-724|, add a single Kdo that is then phosphorylated by a separate enzyme (see |FRAME: PWY-7676|)., About This Pathway, This pathway starts with the isomerization of |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| to |FRAME: ARABINOSE-5P|, followed by its conversion to |FRAME: KDO-8P| (KDOP), which is catalyzed by a family of enzymes called |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.55| (KDOPS). The bacterial KDOPSs have been grouped in two classes, and plant KDOPSs belong to a third class |CITS:[15070398]|., In the next step the phosphate group is removed from |FRAME: KDO-8P| by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.45|, generating Kdo. Until this point the pathway is conserved among all Gram-negative bacteria. However, in members of |FRAME: TAX-22|, the next two enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-44058| and |FRAME: G-44059|, catalyze the dehydrogenation of the hydroxyl group at C8 to a keto group, followed by a transamination, respectively, generating |FRAME: CPD-18063| (Kdo8N) |CITS: [23413030]|., The last step of the pathway is the activation of Kdo8N to |FRAME: CPD-18062|, which is catalyzed by the dedicated enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.90|., When the three enzymes were expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, more than 75% of the extracted LPS produced by the recombinant host contained Kdo8N |CITS: [23413030]|.

Acute inflammation is a beneficial response to injury and infection that involves neutrophils, eosinophils, and M1-polarized macrophages, which produce bioactive molecules such as leukotrienes and prostaglandins. If successful, this response leads to clearance of invading organisms, tissue repair, and regeneration. The pro-inflammatory response eventually transitions to the pro-resolution phase of inflammation, during which M2-polarized macrophages produce potent molecules collectively known as |FRAME: SPMs "specialized pro-resolving mediators"| (SPMs). The SPMs include |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, which are derived from either |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) or |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA), and the DHA-derived |FRAME: protectins protectins| and |FRAME: Maresins maresins|., Maresins are a class of SPMs made from |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) and were first discovered in macrophage exudates. They are extremely potent oxylipins that decrease the inflammatory response as well as promote healing and homeostasis |CITS: [29674943]|. Maresins have picomolar to nanomolar potency in reducing polymorphonuclear cell infiltration, increasing macrophage phagocytosis of cellular debris, and increasing tissue regeneration in a planaria model |CITS: [19103881][22253477][35163291]|., |FRAME: CPD-24700 "Maresin 1"| (MaR1) is the first member of this family to be identified |CITS: [19103881]|, followed by |FRAME: CPD-24693| (MarR2) |CITS: [25036362]|. There are also maresin sulfido-conjugates, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8355|. In addition to its anti-inflammatory, pro-resolving |CITS: [19103881]|, tissue regenerative and anti-nociceptive actions |CITS: [22253477][23504711]|, MaR1 was also found to dampen the pro-inflammatory response to organic dust in bronchial epithelial cells |CITS: [23663457]|, and to attenuate mouse colitis |CITS: [24038091]|. MaR2 displayed potent anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving actions. At 1 ng it reduced neutrophil infiltration in mouse peritonitis by ~40%, and at 10 pM it enhanced human macrophage phagocytosis of zymosan by ~90% |CITS: [25036362]|., Maresins are biosynthesized in human macrophages from DHA in a pathway that begins with |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|. The enzyme is highly expressed in platelets and has been shown to produce 13S,14S-epoxy-DHA in a proinflammation state. However, a careful comparison of the activities of |FRAME: HS03167-MONOMER| and |FRAME: HS08621-MONOMER| with |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) has shown that while the former is responsible for the formation of the hydroperoxide |FRAME: CPD-25487|, the latter is much more active in the conversion of this compound to |FRAME: CPD-25480| (with kcat/KM value over 40 times higher) |CITS: [32324389]|., A hydrolase from neutrophils was required to make appreciable levels of MaR1 in neutrophil-platelet aggregates. The identity of the hydrolase has not been reported, though it is known not to be |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.6| |CITS: [23504711][25369934]|. The hydrolase that forms MaR2 was shown to be |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| |CITS: [25036362]|.

Summary: Alanine is an essential component of protein (as |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|) and of peptidoglycan (as a roughly 3:1 mix of |FRAME: D-ALANINE| and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|). Only about a tenth of total alanine synthesized is incorporated into peptidoglycan. |FRAME: D-ALANINE| is produced by racemization of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|., Racemization can occur not only for the sake of biosynthesis, as some organisms can use |FRAME: D-ALANINE| as the sole carbon and nitrogen sources. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-20754 Tabtoxinine-β-lactam|, also known as wild fire toxin, is a toxin produced by certain strains of |FRAME: TAX-317| that attack tobacco, beans and oats. The toxin is misrecognized as |FRAME: GLN| by the plant |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.2|, resulting in irreversible inactivation. Inhibition of glutamine synthetase leads to a rise in intracellular ammonia levels and severe chlorosis |CITS: [16662928]|., While the early stages of the pathway are still not known, a few studies relying on radioactive isoptope labeling sugggest that |FRAME: CPD-20754| is produced from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|, an intermediate of L-lysine biosynthesis |CITS: [2881927][Roth90]|. The genes involved in the production of |FRAME: CPD-20754| are located in a cluster, along with genes involved in export and inactivation. Some of the cluster genes (tabABD) have homology to lysine biosynthetic genes, supporting the proposal that the two pathways may share their early part |CITS: [1648077][16506699][8990304]|. , |FRAME: CPD-20754 Tabtoxinine-β-lactam| is biosynthesized in an inactive form, as part of the dipeptide |FRAME: CPD-20753| |CITS: [10047897][22994681]|. Upon its export from the cell, the dipeptide is hydrolyzed by a dedicated periplasmic peptidase, releasing the free |FRAME: CPD-20754|. It also appears that some of the toxin is exported as a dipeptide and imported as such by the plant, followed by its hydrolysis and activation by a plant peptidase |CITS: [Uchytil80][Durbin84][Levi86]|., In addition to its synthesis in an inactive form, the bacteria utilize additional mechanisms for defense against the toxic activity. One such mechanism is the tabtoxin resistance protein, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58179| gene, which N-acetylates |FRAME: CPD-20751|, resulting in a modified compound that is not recognized by glutamine synthetase |CITS: [Anzai89][2336364][12527305][22994681]|. Another mechanism involves adenylylation of glutamine synthetase |CITS: [2870053]|., In addition to the enzymatic mechanisms, both the toxin and the dipeptide are subject to a spontaneous chemical rearrangement that converts them into the corresponding δ-lactones. The spontaneous reaction occurs much faster under basic conditions. Both of the δ-lactones are not recognized by glutamine synthetrase |CITS: [22994681]|.

Ginger (|FRAME: TAX-94328|) is a flowering plant whose rhizome is widely used as a spice and a folk medicine. It has analgesic and gastroprotective properties and is used to treat colds, digestive diseases, and gastrointestinal congestion |CITS: [16422532][2214812][19833188][31331547]|. It has also been studied as a potential anticancer drug |CITS: [10793599][17683926][34202966][38218504]|., The sharp flavor of raw ginger is attributed to |FRAME: Gingerols gingerols|. While several forms exist, |FRAME: CPD-13494| is the main compound responsible for the pungency of ginger. [6]-Gingerol occurs as a yellow oil that can be crystallized. The flavor typical of cooked ginger is from |FRAME: CPD-27956|, which is formed from [6]-gingerol during the cooking process., [6]-Gingerol is derived from |FRAME: PHE| via the |FRAME: PWY1F-467 phenylpropanoid biosynthesis| and |FRAME: PWY-361| pathways, up to the production of |FRAME: FERULOYL-COA|. Many enzymes involved in these pathways have been evaluated for their potential role in the biosynthesis of gingerol |CITS: [16890967]|. Many of the genes have multiple copies, and expression analysis revealed that different loci have become functionally specialized in different tissues and different developmental stages of the rhizome |CITS: [30512040]|., A haplotype-resolved genome of diploid ginger was reported in 2021, and the authors proposed a backbone biosynthetic pathway of gingerol analogs, which consists of 12 enzymatic gene families, including |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.24| (PAL), |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.91| (C4H), |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12| (4CL), |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.99| (CST), |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.96| (C3'H), |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.68| (C3OMT), |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.104| (CCOMT), |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.133| (CSE), a polyketide synthase (PKS), an NADPH-dependent alkanal/one oxidoreductase (AOR), and a dehydrogenase (DHN) |CITS: [34354044]|., The first enzyme that is specific for gingerol biosynthesis is a polyketide synthase that condenses |FRAME: FERULOYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and |FRAME: HEXANOYL-COA|, forming |FRAME: CPD-27957| (replacement of |FRAME: HEXANOYL-COA| with other acyl-CoAs results in formation of the other gingerols). The pathway continues with two reduction events, forming |FRAME: CPD-13494| |CITS: [34354044]|. Each of these enzymes occurs in ginger in many isoforms, as was also shown in a ginger genome assembly published in 2024 |CITS: [38251816]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-8097 Esculetin| belongs to the compound class of dihydroxycoumarins that have their biogenetic root in the |FRAME:PWY-361| and originate more directly from the 7-hydroxycoumarin |FRAME:CPD-8186| |CITS:[Brown86]| |CITS:[19035613]|. The biosyntheses of coumarins including dihydroxycoumarins have not been investigated exhaustively even though coumarins have been reported to influence a variety of biological functions in plants such as defense actions against phytopathogens, abiotic stress response and control of oxidative strain |CITS:[Bourgaud06]| |CITS:[Matern99]|. Esculetin in particular has been reported to affect physiological processes, for example root and stalk development, germination and interfering with growth regulators, i.e. |FRAME:INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN|, cytokinin and gibberellins. In addition, scopoletin and its glucoside scopolin are known to directly inhibit a variety of enzymes involved in primary as well as secondary metabolic pathways |CITS:[Brown81]|. There are also indications that esculetin and its glucoside esculin as well as scopoletin/scopolin are involved in post-harvest physiological deterioration (PPD) in cassava roots |CITS:[20943239]|, It has been previously reported that esculetin acts as an intermediate between umbelliferone and scopoletin |CITS:[Brown86]| |CITS:[Gutierrez95]|. Tsang and Ibrahim |CITS:[Tsang79]| could isolate a multi-substrate O-methyltransferase from tobacco that acted on a number of phenylpropanoids and derivatives and specifically converted esculetin to scopoletin. More recently Kim et al. |CITS:[16717435]| characterized a O-methyltransferase that was not only able to carry out the O-methylation of esculetin to scopoletin but yielded in addition isoscopoletin and the double-methylated scoparone. However, besides the bioformation of scopoletin shown in this pathway and its formation via feruloyl-CoA (see |FRAME:PWY-6792|) other pathways for the biogenesis of scopoletin may exist that remain to be investigated |CITS:[19035613]|., The 3-O |CITS:[18487633]| and 4-O-glucosylation |CITS:[Fleuriet80]| steps depicted in the pathway are carried out by multi-substrate glucosyltransferases which also act on esculetin. However, the exact structures of the resulting products have not been determined and the compounds shown here represent only the expected structures according to the position specificity described for the corresponding glucosyltransferases. The transglucosylase (6-O-glucosyltransferase activity) converting esculetin to esculin (7-hydroxy-6-cumarinyl-glucosid) is like the |FRAME:MONOMER-17432| in the |FRAME:PWY-7055| pathway a low-energy enzyme that does not require high energy (UDP-glucose) donors. However, it differs from that enzyme in representing activities of two enzymes. Whether those activities refer to one bifunctional enzyme with shifting hydrolase (HD) /transglucosylase (TG) activity or two separate enzymes remains to be clarified |CITS:[Sato72a]|.

|FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). In prokaryotes ubiquinone participates in various respiratory pathways, mostly aerobic. The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|, which feeds isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10). This pathway uses generic reactions in which the number of isoprenoid subunits is not specified., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized.

Summary: Many microorganisms can utilize D-galactose for growth via two alternative pathways, the Leloir pathway (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-6317|), and the De Ley-Doudoroff pathway represented here and in the pathway link.  The Leloir pathway, used by most organisms including enteric bacteria, converts D-galactose to D-glucose-1-phosphate.  The De Ley-Doudoroff pathway is used by a few bacterial species and was first described in |FRAME:TAX-304| , (now |FRAME:TAX-304|) |CITS: [13462997]|.  This pathway oxidizes D-galactose to a lactone, followed by enzymatic hydrolysis of the lactone to galactonate.  The presence of D-galactono-1,4-lactone (galactono-γ-lactone) and its enzymatic hydrolysis have been demonstrated |CITS: [13462997]|.  As shown in the pathway link, galactonate is dehydrated to 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-galactonate, which is phosphorylated and then cleaved by an aldolase to D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate.  The key enzyme in the De Ley-Doudoroff pathway is the initial enzyme, galactose dehydrogenase (in |CITS: [11823194] [16349292] [3745118]|). , A similar oxidative, but non-phosphorylative, pathway for D-galactose degradation to glyceraldehyde and pyruvate has been demonstrated in extracts of |FRAME:TAX-5061| |CITS: [11427238]|.  Pseudomonads have also been shown to oxidize glucose in similar initial reactions, although further catabolism proceeds through the Entner-Doudoroff pathway to D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: DHGLUCONATE-PYR-CAT-PWY|).  A pathway for oxidation of the pentoses D- and L-arabinose in these organisms has also been described.  |CITS: [13462997] [13271422]| and in |CITS: [4149284]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Opines Opines| are a large family of low molecular weight compounds. The vast majority of opines are secondary amine derivatives resulting from the reduction of the imine formed by condensation of an amino acid, either with a keto acid or a sugar. Opines from the |FRAME: CPD-308| family are formed when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| serves as the keto substrate in the condensation reaction, while those of the |FRAME: CPD-309| family are formed when |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is involved in the condensation reaction. Opines of the |FRAME: CPD-15773| and |FRAME: CPD-26410| families are formed by the condensation of an amino acid with a sugar., A small, separate class of opines is the |FRAME: Agrocinopines agrocinopines|, which are sugar-phosphodiesters (e.g., |FRAME: CPD-15774|, which is a phosphodiester of sucrose and L-arabinose)., While opines are found in marine invertebrates, fungi, higher plants and mammals, they are most commonly found in plant crown gall tumors or hairy root tumors, where they are produced by bacteria of the genera |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379|, respectively. Biosynthesis of opines in crown gall tumors is performed by enzymes encoded by genes contained in T-DNA (transfer DNA), which is part of the Ti plasmid (in Agrobacterium) or Ri plasmid (in Rhizobium). The plasmids are inserted by the bacteria into the plant genome, where they are integrated and expressed. Those opines are used by the bacteria as energy, carbon and nitrogen sources. Each strain of Agrobacterium and Rhizobium induces and catabolizes a specific set of opines, determined by the specific Ti or Ri plasmid they possess. Over 30 different opines have been described., The enzymes catalyzing the condensation of amino acids with 2-oxo acids to form opines are known as opine dehydrogenases. These enzymes are oxidoreductases that catalyze the reversible, |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP|-dependent reductive condensation reaction between an α-keto acid and the α-amino or ω-amino group of an amino acid to form imino acids (opines) and water. They have been classified into several Enzyme Commission (EC) entries depending upon their substrate specificity. Studies have shown that opines are synthesized in plant crown gall tumors as a result of infection by |FRAME: TAX-358|, and in some marine invertebrates under hypoxic or anoxic conditions (reviewed in |CITS: [23644944][10869063][GADEG86]|)., About This Pathway, Opine dehydrogenases are cytosolic oxidoreductases that catalyze the reversible, |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP|-dependent reductive condensation reaction between an α-keto acid and the α-amino or ω-amino group of an amino acid to form imino acids (referred to as opines) and water. They have been characterized from some soil bacteria and marine invertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7351|). , In |FRAME: TAX-357| species opine dehydrogenases are encoded on Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmids which are involved in plant crown gall tumor formation. Portions of Ti plasmid DNA are transferred to a susceptible host plant cell and become integrated into its nuclear genome. Expression of these bacterial genes in the resulting plant tumor cell directs the synthesis and secretion of opines. The opines that are synthesized vary among bacterial strains. |FRAME: TAX-358| genes |FRAME: G-15382| and |FRAME: G-17722| encode enzymes that direct the synthesis of several opines (reviewed in |CITS: [10869063]|). The opines produced and secreted by the plant crown gall tumor can subsequently be used by the infecting bacteria as a carbon or nitrogen source during host colonization. They are taken up by the bacteria via permeases and degraded by opine-specific enzymes (see pathways |FRAME: OCTOPINEDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: NOPALINEDEG-PWY|)., Native nopaline synthase was purified and characterized from the crown gall tumor tissue of the sunflower |FRAME: TAX-4232| infected with |FRAME: TAX-176300| or |FRAME: TAX-176299|, both of which utilize nopaline |CITS: [476084]|.

Summary: Oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) are among the most conserved sterol bosynthetic enzymes at the sequence level, and homologues have been detected in all species capable of sterol synthesis., There are two main types of sterols-producing OSCs based on the end product of the cyclization: |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.7|, which is found in animals, fungi, choanozoa, trypanosomatids, dinoflagellates, and some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-414|; and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.8|, which is found in higher plants, red and green algae, amoebozoa, diatoms, euglenids, heterolobosea and some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-41| (see |FRAME: PWY-8028|) |CITS: [12519197][24596261]|. A rare third type is |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.47| |CITS: [21526825]|., The reaction catalyzed by OSCs is one of the most complicated biochemical reactions catalyzed by a single protein |CITS: [16754609]|. The key steps in the cyclization include:, 1. Positioning of squalene 2,3-epoxide in a prefolded configuration within the active site., 2. Protonation of the epoxide group by a catalytic acid., 3. Ring formation, during which cation intermediates are stabilized by cation–π interactions with aromatic residues of the active site, followed by migration of the cation out to C20., 4. Skeletal rearrangement via hydride- and methyl-shifts (largely spontaneous) as the proton migrates back to a region of high π-electron density around the B/C rings., 5. Deprotonation by basic residues to quench the final protosteryl cation; the position of the deprotonation determines the OSC product (lanosterol versus cycloartenol)., |FRAME: LANOSTEROL Lanosterol| is produced in vertebrates and fungi as an intermediate in the synthesis of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|, respectively. In addition, lanosterol has been found in several prokaryotes, including the |FRAME: TAX-29| species |FRAME: TAX-41| |CITS: [12519197]| and |FRAME: TAX-54| |CITS: [Kohl83]|, some aerobic methylotrophs such as |FRAME: TAX-243233|, the Planctomycete |FRAME: TAX-114| |CITS: [14660793]|, and |FRAME: TAX-51353| |CITS: [10802170]|., A prokaryotic enzyme has been cloned from |FRAME: TAX-414| and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, confirming activity |CITS: [17928701]|. The enzymatic reaction proceeded in a regio- and stereospecific fashion identical to those from eukaryotic species, implying that the bacterial gene may have been acquired from ancient eukaryotes (along with the gene encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-14485|) through lateral gene transfer |CITS: [17928701]|.

Summary: In mycobacteria, mannose is the key component of glycolipids, lipoglycans, and a number of glycosylated proteins, which makes it essential for growth and viability., All mycobacterial species, including pathogenic |FRAME: TAX-1773|, synthesize an abundant class of phosphatidylinositol mannosides (PIMs) that are essential for normal growth and viability. These glycolipids are important cell-wall and/or plasma-membrane components in their own right and can also be hyperglycosylated to form other wall components, such as lipomannan (LM) and lipoarabinomannan (LAM). PIMs, LM, and LAM all contain a common core structure, suggesting that the early steps in their biosynthesis are the same |CITS: [ 4297467]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME: AcPIM6 AcPIM6|, LM, and LAM bifurcates after the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: AcPIM4 AcPIM4| |CITS: [16803893]|., The major PIM species are PI-dimannosides (|FRAME: Phosphatidyl-myo-inositol-Man-6-acyl-Man AcPIM2| and a double-acylated variant known as |FRAME: Ac2PIM2 Ac2PIM2|) and PI-hexamannosides (|FRAME: AcPIM6 AcPIM6| and its double-acylated variant |FRAME: Ac2PIM6 Ac2PIM6|). AcPIM2 and AcPIM6 contain one fatty acid linked to the mannose residue in addition to a diacylglycerol moiety, whereas Ac2PIM2 and Ac2PIM6 contain an additional fatty acid linked to the inositol residue., The surface exposed lipoglycans, PIMs, LM, and LAM possess significant immunomodulatory effects in macrophages,, including cytokine production, inhibition of phagosome maturation, and apoptosis and also account for crossprotective, immunity of mycobacteria |CITS: [21521247]|., |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| serves as an intracellular nucleotide-derived mannose donor for the synthesis of several glycolipids and mannosylated proteins by the GT-A/B superfamily of glycosyltransferases |CITS: [12824488]|. Later steps in this pathway involve glycosyltransferases that belong to the GT-C superfamily and use |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Mannosyl-Phosphates| (PPM) as the mannose donor. GT-C mannosyltranferases also catalyze reactions in the periplasmic synthesis of larger lipoglycans such as LM, and LAM. The presence of a C50-polyprenol-based mannolipid, |FRAME: BETA-D-MANNOSYLPHOSPHODECAPRENOL|, was first reported in 1970 from |FRAME: TAX-1773|  |CITS: [4991887]|. However, additional forms including a C35 |FRAME: CPD-19968| and a C40 |FRAME: CPD-19967| were later identified in |FRAME: TAX-1772| |CITS: [9719676]|. PPM is synthesized in mycobacteria from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: G185E-6255-MONOMER| (Ppm1) |CITS: [11931640]|.

The optimal concentration of the precursors; |FRAME: CPD3O-4151|, phenylalanine and |FRAME: TYR| along with elicitor concentration was established in this study |CITS: [17329834]|., |FRAME: CPD-13354 Salidroside| is mainly found in the roots. The glycosylation of |FRAME: CPD3O-4151| is the final step of the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13354|, the glycosyltransferases responsible for salidroside biosynthesis have been isolated |CITS: [21497865]| and |CITS: [17333022]|. The isolation and over expression of a tyrosine decarboxylase resulted in the increase in |FRAME: CPD3O-4151| and |FRAME: CPD-13354| production, indicating its role in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13354| |CITS: [21538102]|. Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The O antigen structure of |FRAME: TAX-2170726| has been determined. It is composed of repeats of the pentasaccharide |FRAME: CPD-18918 "α-L-Col-(1→2)-β-D-Gal-(1→3)-β-D-GlcNAc-(1→3)-α-D-Gal-(1→3)-GalNAc"| connected by β(1,6) linkages between the GlcNAc residue and the GalNAc residue |CITS: [7030487]|. Exactly the same antigen is produced by serotype O:50 Salmonella enterica strains (group Z) such as |FRAME: TAX-297361| |CITS: [6339053]|., The O antigen biosynthesis gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2170726| has been sequenced and four postulated glycosyltransferases were identified |CITS: [11976290]|. The product of the |FRAME: G-81036| gene is 27% identical to WbbP of |FRAME: TAX-622| serotype 1 and has a similar hydrophobic profile. Summary: General Background, The vast majority of the red to violet betacyanins are derived from the aglycon |FRAME: CPD-8653|, which is produced, by the condensation of |FRAME: CPD-8651| (see |FRAME:PWY-5394|) and |FRAME: CPD-8652| (although some are derived from |FRAME: DOPAMINE| - see |FRAME:PWY-5439|). The violet color of betacyanins is based on the observed shift to the corresponding absorbance maximum (λmax 534-554 nm) of the aromatic structure after that condensation |CITS: [CHRISTINET04]|. Betacyanins are a subclass of the betalains and occur almost exclusively in the order of Caryophyllales |CITS: [12620337] [16212790][16669781]|., Betalains have also been identified in a restricted number of basidiomycetes but no betacyanin pigments have been found in those fungi whereas the biosynthesis of several betaxanthin compounds along with other derivatives of betalamic acid such as muscaflavin and muscapurpurin has been established |CITS: [Mueller97a]|., It has been demonstrated that the biosynthesis of betacyanins appears to be linked to cell division activity. The peak of betacyanin accumulation in Phytolacca suspension cells (accumulating betalains) was positively correlated with cell division activity as shown by specific inhibitors. In contrary, the anthocyanin production in Vitis cell cultures revealed a negative correlation towards cell division indicating that both pigments are not just structurally divers but differentially regulated as well |CITS: [SAKUTA94]|., About This Pathway, The observed diversity of betacyanin structures is due to the frequently observed acylation and glucosylation of the aglycone betanidin. The glucosylation of betanidin takes place in a regiospecific way resulting in either the production of betanin (via betanidin 5-O-glucosyltransferase) |CITS: [10504573]| or e.g. gomphrenin I (via betanidin 6-O-glucosyltransferase) |CITS: [11855654]|., Betacyanins are derivatives of tyrosine. The first enzyme that converts L-tyrosine to an intermediate of the betacyanin biosynthetic route i.e. dopaquinone is tyrosinase. That enzyme is bifunctional possessing both tyrosine hydroxylating activity (EC 1.14.18.1) that catalyzes the formation of L-DOPA from L-tyrosine and DOPA oxidase activity (EC 1.10.3.1) catalyzing the subsequent step to form dopaquinone |CITS: [Steiner99] [14759157]|. The consecutive conversion of dopaquinone to cyclo-DOPA occurs in a non-enzymatic cyclisation. Tyrosinases are copper-containing polyphenol oxidases (PPOs) which have been subject of numerous studies because of the loss in commercial value they cause through the browning effect in fruits and vegetables |CITS:[Mayer91]|. Although the physiological functions of PPOs in plants are mostly unknown they have been associated with pigment formation (this pathway) |CITS:[Vaughn84]| and scavenging molecular oxygen in chloroplasts |CITS:[Vaughn88]|., The crucial intermediate in this biosynthesis, i.e. cyclo-DOPA can be further metabolized via two pathways. One pathway leads to the aglycone betanidin by the spontaneous condensation of cyclo-DOPA with betalamic acid which is further 5-O-glucosylated to form betanin. The other pathway variant employs the 5-O-glucosylation of cyclo-DOPA by UDPG:cyclo-DOPA 5-O-glucosyltransferase as the first enzymatic step |CITS: [15695438]| which is succeeded by the spontaneous condensation to form betanin.

Summary: In the strictly anaerobic bacteria |FRAME: TAX-971|, |FRAME: TAX-29466| and |FRAME: TAX-82374|, |FRAME: CADAVERINE| produced by lysine decarboxylase is an essential component of its |FRAME: Selenomonas-ruminantium-peptidoglycan peptidoglycan|. In |FRAME: TAX-971|, |FRAME: CADAVERINE| is constitutively biosynthesized from |FRAME: LYS|, and has been shown to be essential for integrity of the cell envelope and for normal growth of the organism |CITS: [3084485]| and in |CITS: [11073919]|. , In some organisms such as |FRAME:TAX-562| this pathway is used to confer acid resistance. Under conditions of anaerobiosis and phosphate starvation (believed to reflect conditions in the gut) |FRAME: TAX-562| converts glucose to weak organic acids which, though they are excreted, can reenter the cell and cause bactericidal acid stress even at only moderately acidic pH., Acid resistance system 4 (AR4) is an |FRAME: LYS|-dependent acid resistance system that allows for the survival under these conditions when L-lysine is available. The system couples the transport activity of a |FRAME: CADB-MONOMER| (CadB) with |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.18| (|FRAME: EG10131 CadA|). CadB functions by exchanging external |FRAME: LYS| for internal |FRAME: CADAVERINE|. The imported L-lysine is decarboxylated inside the cell by CadA to cadaverine in a reaction that releases CO2 and consumes a proton. Cadaverine is then exported through CadB. This process effectively consumes protons within the cytoplasm, raising the pH. In addition, |FRAME: CADAVERINE| inhibits porin-mediated outer membrane permeability, which may protect the cells further from acid stress |CITS: [12486035]|., An |FRAME: PWY0-1305 "L-glutamate-dependent acid resistance system"| (AR2) is also able to provide acid resistance to E. coli growing under conditions of anaerobiosis and phosphate starvation, but to a slightly lesser degree than AR4, possibly due to the different pH optimums of their respective decarboxylase enzymes |CITS: [17209032]|. AR2 is more efficient than AR3 or AR4 as a mediator of acid resistance at low pH |CITS: [15494746]|., Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-287|, degrade |FRAME: LYS| to |FRAME: CADAVERINE|, followed by complete degradation of the later to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (see |FRAME: PWY-6328|).

Summary: Several pseudomonads are capable of using one or both enantiomers of mandelic acid as a sole carbon source. , The mandelate pathway of |FRAME:TAX-303| consists of five enzymes which convert both |FRAME: CPD-121| and |FRAME: CPD-122| to |FRAME: BENZOATE|, which is subsequently processed to acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) and succinyl-CoA in the β-ketoadipate pathway. , The first enzyme in the pathway, mandelate racemase, catalyzes the interconversion of the enantiomers of mandelate. Subsequently, (S)-mandelate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-122| to form |FRAME: PHENYLGLYOXYLATE|, which is then converted into |FRAME: BENZALDEHYDE| by benzoylformate decarboxylase in a thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent reaction. Benzaldehyde is then converted to |FRAME: BENZOATE| by two benzaldehyde dehydrogenases (one NAD+-dependent and one NADP+-dependent)., The genes encoding the first three enzymes in the pathway (MdlA, MdlB, MdlC) are organized in an operon that is induced by either enantiomer of mandelic acid. The genes encoding the benzaldehyde dehydrogenases are located upstream of this the mdlABC operon, and are transcribed independently.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In |FRAME: TAX-810| additional Kdo units are added by a (2->8) or (2->4) linkages (see |FRAME: PWY-6467|). The actual donor of Kdo units is its activated form, |FRAME: CMP-KDO|., Kdo-containing |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA| molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety., LPS are produced by all Gram-negative bacteria, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-909932| and |FRAME: TAX-53433|, which belong to the firmicutes phylum, suggesting that an ancient LPS-containing diderm cell envelope was present in the ancestor of the Firmicutes |CITS: [27580370]|. There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are also synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

Like several other inositol phosphates, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1456-TETRAKISPHOSPHATE| is a second messenger molecule that plays a critical role in cellular signaling |CITS: [11457089]|., At micromolar concentrations it inhibits IGF-1-induced thymidine incorporation in human breast cancer cells and thus prevents the ability of these cells to grow |CITS: [10834940]|. It  is also involved in nuclear processes since it is required for gene regulation and may control gene expression |CITS: [10720331]|., |FRAME: CPD-1107| exists in most mammalian cells at micromolar concentrations, and is considered one of two major inositol phosphates in the cell (along with |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE|). Unlike in yeast, where |FRAME: INOSITOL-1456-TETRAKISPHOSPHATE| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-1107| and |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE|, the human pathway proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-505|, which is phosphorylated to |FRAME: CPD-1107| by |FRAME: HS07712-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6362|) |CITS: [15531582]|. That enzyme has a clear preference for |FRAME: CPD-505| over |FRAME: CPD-506| |CITS: [12223481]|., Multiple biochemical evidence suggests that the major source for |FRAME: CPD-506| in mammals is the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-1107|, catalyzed by |FRAME: HS03025-MONOMER| |CITS: [1328236][9359836]|. Once formed, it can be deactivated by its conversion back to the petakisphosphate form by |FRAME: HS07712-MONOMER|, despite the lower affinity of this enzyme towards |FRAME: CPD-506| |CITS: [16293229]|., This pathway is manipulated by the pathogen |FRAME:TAX-28901|. Upon infection, the bacterium introduces the virulence factor |FRAME: G-11620| into the gastrointestinal cell. SopB is an inositol phosphatase and catalyzes the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-1107| to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1456-TETRAKISPHOSPHATE|. This results in an increased chloride channel activity, contributing to diarrhea in the host, and potentially facilitates bacterial entry into the cells |CITS: [11158563][9405634]|.

General Background, Acetophenones and their ring-chlorinated derivatives are produced by microbial degradation of industrial chemicals. For example, |FRAME: PHENYL| is produced from |FRAME: PWY-481| and |FRAME: CPD-10598| is produced from |FRAME: PWY-6080|. Some microorganisms have been shown to utilize acetophenones for aerobic growth. In |FRAME: ORG-6204| the pathway for aerobic mineralization of |FRAME: CPD-10598| has been elucidated and the fate of the |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| intermediate was determined |CITS: [18502868]|. Because |FRAME: ORG-6204| appears to lack hydroquinone hydroxylating activity, no hydroxyhydroquinone (|FRAME: CPD-8130|) could be formed and metabolized as in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6200|, |FRAME: PWY-5488|, and |FRAME: P343-PWY|. Instead, |FRAME: ORG-6204| oxidizes |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYMUCONIC-SEMIALDEHYDE|, which is then converted in two steps to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| (similar to pathway |FRAME: PWY-5487|) |CITS: [18502868]|. The pathway also appears to be found in |FRAME: ORG-6205| |CITS: [19251889]|., About This Pathway, Although first two reactions in the pathway had previously been characterized |CITS: [11322873][16348372]|, the subsequent conversion of |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| was studied in desalted cell extracts of |FRAME: ORG-6204|. The pathway was further studied by analyzing the degradation of difluorinated hydroquinones in cell extracts using 19F NMR spectral analysis. Both keto and enol tautomeric forms of |FRAME: CPD-294| (maleylacetate) were identified, although a previous study suggested that the keto form (|FRAME: CPD-294|) is present under physiological conditions |CITS: [11844781]|. A hydroquinone dioxygenase was partially purified from cell extracts |CITS: [18502868]|, and subsequently purified and characterized |CITS: [18502867]|. The hapCDEFGHIBA gene cluster encoding enzymes of the pathway was cloned and sequenced |CITS: [18502868]|., Several of the pathway enzymes have been characterized as shown in this pathway. In |FRAME: ORG-6204| the last two reactions were proposed to be catalyzed by the products of hapE and hapF, respectively. THe product of hapE was predicted to be a |FRAME: NAD|-dependent dehydrogenase that converts |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYMUCONIC-SEMIALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: CPD-294|. The product of hapF appeared to be an ortholog of maleylacetate reductase from |FRAME:ORG-6112|, sharing 56% amino acid sequence identity |CITS: [18502868]|.

Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and protein modification, where fatty acyl moieties of proteins modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II. The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|). The pathway catalyzed by the type I systems is available at |FRAME: PWY-5994|., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|. Unlike the type I system that accepts |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of the two-carbon units, the type II systems accept only |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|., About This Pathway, Many Gram-positive organisms, such as the bacilli, staphylococci, and streptomycetes, produce odd- and even-carbon-number branched-chain fatty acids. Branched-chain fatty acids display a lower melting point temperature than their straight-chain equivalents, and their presence in the membrane is expected to increase its fluidity, similar to the effect of unsaturation |CITS: [26300876]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| 95% of the total fatty acids are branched |CITS: [4392505][1886522]|. The most common fatty acids are |FRAME: CPD-9917| (34%), |FRAME: CPD-19657| (24%), |FRAME: CPD-18175| (13%), |FRAME: CPD-23515| (12%), |FRAME: CPD-23509| (9%), and |FRAME: CPD-19660| (4%) |CITS: [28825491]|., The substrate specificity of the FabH condensing enzyme is the determining factor in the biosynthesis of branched-chain fatty acids by type II fatty acid synthases. In organisms that produce non-branched fatty acids such as |FRAME: TAX-562| FabH is specific for |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as the starter molecule. In contrast, the FabH enzymes from organisms that produce branched-chain fatty acids, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, utilize branched-chain acyl-CoA primers much more efficiently than |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (for |FRAME: TAX-1423| the ratio is 100:1) |CITS: [1886522]|. The rest of the enzymes that form the fatty acid synthase system do not have a significant degree of selectivity for either branched-chain or straight-chain fatty acids |CITS: [10629181]|., The most common starter molecules for branched-chain fatty acids are derived from the branched-chain amino acids |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: VAL|, and |FRAME: ILE|. An aminotransferase converts these acids to the α-keto acids |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE|, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, and |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE|, respectively. A specialized α-keto acid dehydrogenase, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25|, is critical for generating the branched-chain acyl-CoA primers for the FabH enzymes (|FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA|, |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, and |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|, respectively) |CITS: [ 3142877]|., The type of primer used determines the type of the branched-chain fatty acid formed. |FRAME: Anteiso-fatty-acids "Anteiso-fatty acids"|, which are derived from |FRAME: ILE|, have an odd number of carbons and are characterized by a methyl-substituent located on the antepenultimate carbon of the carboxyalkyl chain. Anteiso-fatty acids are the most prominent fatty acids of cell membranes of some bacteria, especially of the genus Bacillus. The most relevant anteiso-fatty acids in food and bacteria are |FRAME: CPD-9917| and |FRAME: CPD-23509| |CITS: [28129363]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE "Trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline"| residues contribute to the stability of the |FRAME: Collagens collagen| triple helix, a major constituent of animal protein. It is also found in higher plants and algae. Mammals are able to degrade 4-hydroxy-L-proline to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYOX| (see |FRAME: HYDROXYPRODEG-PWY|). , About This Pathway, Bacteria can also degrade |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE|, in a different pathway. The inducible pathway, found in some species, converts |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE| to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. All enzymes of the pathway can be induced by growth on |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE| or its epimer |FRAME: CIS-4-HYDROXY-D-PROLINE| (formerly referred to as allohydroxy-D-proline) as the sole carbon and nitrogen source., Induction is not sensitive to catabolite repression by |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: SUC|, |FRAME: GLT|, or |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|., An uptake system that concentrates 4-hydroxy-L-proline intracellularly has also been described. The uptake system appears to be regulated as a unit with the degradation system and resembles sugar, rather than amino acid, transport systems. This may be due to the inability of these organisms to incorporate 4-hydroxy-L-proline into cellular protein, thus its metabolic role as a carbon and energy source |CITS: [5764334][5438054][6250440]|., More recent support for this pathway has come from both bioinformatic analysis of putative gene clusters related to 4-hydroxy-L-proline degradation, and experimental characterization of three enzymes in the pathway. These included D-hydroxyproline dehydrogenase from |FRAME: ORG-6168| and |FRAME: TAX-208964|, Δ1-pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate deaminase from |FRAME: ORG-6168|, and α-ketoglutaric semialdehyde dehydrogenase from |FRAME: ORG-6168| |CITS: [22833679]|., Interestingly, although the D-hydroxoproline dehydrogenases show similar substrate and cofactor specificity in the two species, they differ structurally. Characterization of recombinant enzymes expressed in a P. putida host showed that the |FRAME: ORG-6168| enzyme is a |FRAME: FAD|-containing putative dimer, whereas the |FRAME: TAX-208964| enzyme is a novel α4β4γ4 heterododecamer containing two molecules of |FRAME: FAD|, one of |FRAME: FMN| and a |FRAME: CPD-6|. These data suggest an example of convergent evolution for this pathway in these two species. In addition, Δ1-pyrroline-4-hydroxy-2-carboxylate deaminase from |FRAME: ORG-6168| was shown to be a unique member of the dihydropicolinate synthase/N-acetylneuraminate lyase protein family |CITS: [22833679]|.

Summary: Background, |FRAME: SEROTONIN "Serotonin"| and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| are both derived from the amino acid |FRAME: TRP|. Serotonin is a monoamine neurotransmitter found in the CNS and gut. In the CNS, it is causally involved in the regulation of mood, sleep, appetite, memory and learning |CITS: [16615082]|. Modulation of serotonin at synapses is the modus operandi of several classes of antidepressants. Serotonin in the periphery is expressed in the enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract and regulates gut motility. Released from the enterochromaffin cells, it is taken up by platelets and plays a role in primary homeostasis and cell mediated immune responses |CITS: [19630576]|. Circulating |FRAME: SEROTONIN| derived from peripheral tissues is primarily metabolized in the liver to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYINDOLE_ACETATE|, which is excreted in the urine, see |FRAME: PWY-6313|., |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE "Melatonin"| is a hormone regulating a number of different physiological functions including sleep induction, circadian rhythm, oxidative stress and immune response |CITS: [9674691]|. It is synthesized nocturnally in the pineal gland |CITS: [20478436]|. , About this Pathway, The biosynthesis of serotonin and melatonin in animals utilize some common reactions starting from L-tryptophan. |FRAME: CPLX-7488 "Tryptophan hydroxylase"| catalyzes the rate-limiting step of |FRAME: SEROTONIN| biosynthesis, the oxidation of |FRAME:TRP| to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXY-TRYPTOPHAN| |CITS: [12379098]|. The reaction, which occurs in the presence of molecular oxygen, requires |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN| as a cofactor. |FRAME: CPLX-7890 "Aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase"| is a pyridoxal 5-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the decarboxylation of |FRAME: 5-HYDROXY-TRYPTOPHAN| to the indoleamine |FRAME: SEROTONIN| |CITS: [1540578]|. , |FRAME: HS05303-MONOMER "Serotonin N-acetyltransferase"| catalyzes the N-acetylation of serotonin to N-acetylserotonin, the rate-limiting step in melatonin synthesis. It is this enzyme which controls the circadian rhythm of melatonin production by the pineal gland. In all vertebrates, enzyme activity is highest at night time and activity decreases very rapidly upon exposure to light |CITS: [9238858]|. Rhythms in the mammalian pineal gland are set by afferent information derived from the endogenous clock in the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)., |FRAME: CPLX66-309 "Acetylserotonin O-methyltransferase"| is the last enzyme of the melatonin biosynthesis pathway, catalyzing the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| onto |FRAME: N-ACETYL-SEROTONIN|, to produce |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE|. , Melatonin levels are under strong genetic influence and have heterogeneous expression among individuals |CITS: [21517957]|. Abnormal melatonin synthesis has been reported as a risk factor for a variety of medical conditions, such as diabetes and psychiatric disorders |CITS: [18516223]|.

Summary: Triterpenes are isoprenoidal natural products comprising six isoprene units, more than 200 triterpene derivatives , have been reported from ferns that have structures distinct from those found in higher plants. The most commonly , occurring triterpenes in ferns are |FRAME: HOPAN-22-OL| diplopterol, diploptene |FRAME: HOP-2229-ENE|, and fernenene , (fern-9(11)-ene). They are found in almost all ferns with a few exceptions. These triterpenes lack oxygen functionality at , C-3, which is ubiquitously found in triterpenes of flowering plants. In higher plants, cyclic triterpene skeletons are formed at the, cyclization step of the common substrate |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| by the enzyme termed oxidosqualene cyclase (OSC). Protonation, and opening of epoxide initiate polyene cyclization and subsequent electrophilic additions to the neighboring double bonds, , followed by Wagner–Meerwein rearrangements to construct varieties of triterpene skeleton. Thus, all the cyclization products, , such as |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL|, b-amyrin, and lupeol, retain epoxide oxygen as the b-hydroxyl group at C-3. In contrast, , the triterpenes of ferns are of the hydrocarbon type and lack oxygen functionality at C-3 and is reminiscent of bacterial , hopanoids produced from |FRAME: SQUALENE| |CITS: [18154734]|. This study showed the presence of the squalene , cyclase as well as the oxidosqualene cyclases in ferns.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Thaxtomins "thaxtomin phytotoxins"| are microbially produced cyclic dipeptides (2,5-diketopiperazines) formed from the condensation of |FRAME: CPD-27290| and |FRAME: PHE| groups. The 4-nitroindole moiety is essential for their phytotoxicity. Although the mechanism of action is as yet unknown, it is established that the thaxtomins exert their phytotoxicity by inhibiting cellulose biosynthesis in plants |CITS: [19269997][19467551]|., The thaxtomins were first identified in the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1930|, which attacks growing potato tubers through immature lenticels and wound sites, forming scabs |CITS: [Lambert89][King89]|. They were later shown to elicit scab symptoms on other economically important root crops such as beet, carrot, parsnip, radish, sweet potato and turnip |CITS: [16719719]|. While several different forms of thaxtomins have been detected in producing organisms, |FRAME: CPD-27279| is the major form in |FRAME: TAX-1930|, |FRAME: TAX-42234|, and |FRAME: TAX-85558| |CITS: [19467551]|. |FRAME: CPD-27281 "Thaxtomin C"| is the main thaxtomin produced by |FRAME: TAX-103232| |CITS: [King94]|., |FRAME: CPD-27279 "Thaxtomin A"| is a powerful herbicide that causes dramatic plant cell hypertrophy and seedling stunting at the nanomolar level |CITS: [11368592][Fry02][12897252][19269997]|. It has shown high selectivity for common monocot and dicot weed control in rice crops and turfgrass landscape |CITS: [17268610][25804187][Wolfe16][Wolfe16a]| and has been approved by the EPA for use as an herbicide for several crops (registration number: 84059-12)., The genes encoding the enzymes involved in thaxtomin A production are located in a cluster carried on a mobilizable pathogenicity island |CITS: [15686551]|. The gene cluster consists of seven genes, one of which encodes a regulator |CITS: [17919290]|. , About This Pathway, The pathway begins with the |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|-dependent nitration of |FRAME: TRP|, which is mediated by an NO synthase (|FRAME:G-124706 TxtD|) and an unusual cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (|FRAME: G-124707 TxtE|). TxtD forms |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| from |FRAME: ARG| |CITS: [15129284]|, while TxtE catalyzes the nitration of Trp by using the NO in the presence of O2 and reduced ferredoxin, forming |FRAME: CPD-27290| |CITS: [22941045]|., The next step involves two non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs), |FRAME: G-124709 TxtA| and |FRAME: G-124708 TxtB|, which bind |FRAME: PHE| and |FRAME: CPD-27290|, respectively. The NRPSs N-methylate their substrate, then catalyze a condensation, forming the 2,5-diketopiperazine |FRAME: CPD-27282| |CITS: [11115114][19570136]|., The last enzyme of the pathway is another cytochrome P450, |FRAME: G-124710 TxtC|. That enzyme hydroxylates two different and distant sites within the |FRAME: PHE| component of |FRAME: CPD-27282|. The reactions follow a preferred order, with hydroxylation of the α-carbon, forming |FRAME: CPD-27280|, preceding functionalization of the phenyl group, which generates |FRAME: CPD-27279|. The enzyme achieves this ability by binding distinct conformations of the substrate and monohydroxylated intermediate |CITS: [30516965]|.

|FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., Some organisms metabolize oxalate to formate, and use formate dehydrogenase to generate NADH with the electrons derived from oxalate |CITS: [14435491][14101969]|. One of these organisms is |FRAME: TAX-96344|, a facultative autotrophic bacterium that is able to grow on oxalate and formate as its sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [13108847]|. , When |FRAME: TAX-96344| is grown with formate, it derives the energy from the oxidation of formate by |FRAME: MONOMER-16181|, and shuttles the |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| that is produced to the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY| for autotrophic carbon fixation. However, when it is grown with |FRAME: OXALATE| it adapts a heterotrophic growth mode. It still derives energy from the oxidation of formate by |FRAME: MONOMER-16181| (after conversion of oxalate to formate through coenzyme A thioesters). However, the carbon from oxalate is assimilated heterotrophically through the |FRAME: GLYCOLATEMET-PWY "glycerate pathway"| |CITS:[16742593][623498]|., The pathway was also demonstrated in several methylotrophs, including |FRAME: TAX-272630| and |FRAME: TAX-82996|. However, in these organisms the |FRAME: GLYOX| that is produced in processed via the |FRAME: PWY-1622 "serine pathways"| |CITS: [5472155]|.

Summary: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the first segment, up to the intermediate lipid IV<sub>A</sub>., Many bacterial species produce lipid A molecules that contain |FRAME: CPD-24440|. This modification has been shown to increase resistance to antimicrobial peptides, and in pathogens - to dampen the host immune response. In some organisms the lipid A disaccharide is composed solely of |FRAME: CPD-24440|, as shown in this pathway, and in others, such as |FRAME: TAX-920|, the disaccharide is composed of both |FRAME: CPD-24440| and |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|., This sugar is produced from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, which is converted by two enzymes, a dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-107456|) and an aminotransferase (|FRAME: G-107457|), to |FRAME: CPD-24442|. That compound is subsequently acylated and deacetylated, resulting in acylated 2,3-diamino-2,3-dideoxy-D-glucopyranose |CITS: [15044494]|., The rest of the pathway follows similar route as other lipid IV<sub>A</sub> biosynthesis pathway. The LpxA enzyme of |FRAME: TAX-562| has been shown to acylate |FRAME: CPD-24440|, although this sugar is not produced by that organism. However, an LpxA enzyme from L. interrogans displayed no activity with |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| |CITS: [15044493]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "Fatty acids"| are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and fatty acyl moieties of proteins that modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II., Type I systems are found in lower eukaryotes and animals, while type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. Thus both systems operate in animals - the type I system in the cytosol, (see |FRAME: PWY-5994|), and the type II system in the mitochondria (this pathway)., The main difference between the two systems is that type I systems consist of one (in the case of animals) or two (in the case of fungi) large multifunctional gene products that form a single complex that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while in type II systems the different reactions are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., Fatty acid biosynthesis starts with an initiation sequence that produces |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs|, an activated molecule that is used for subsequent elongation reactions, which ultimately produce the final fatty acid products. This pathway describes only the initiation sequence that occurs in the mitochondria., About This Pathway, The contribution of the mitochondrial pathway counts for only a few percentage of the overall cellular fatty acid biosynthesis, as the bulk of endogenously derived fatty acids is synthesized in the cytosol by the type I fatty acid synthase system |CITS: [9187370]|. The mitochondrial pathway is believed to provide the octanoyl group that is required for the endogenous synthesis of |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID|. Additionally there is putative evidence suggesting its involvement in remodeling of cardiolipins |CITS: [1397269][8595652]|., The mitochondrial FAS pathway is indespensible, as demonstrated by the observation that the inactivation of any FAS II gene in yeast results in the loss of mitochondrially encoded cytochromes and ultimately in a respiratory-deficient phenotype., The first step in de novo fatty acid biosynthesis is production of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|. Malonyl-CoA can be produced in mammals by the two isoforms of |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.2|, ACC1 and ACC2. However, both enzymes have been reported to be cytosolic, and a different enzyme, |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.76|, has been found to produce malonyl-CoA in the mitochondria from malonate |CITS: [21846720]|. Surprisngly, a 2017 paper reported that an isoform of ACC1, expressed from an |FRAME: HS05598| transcript splicing variant, also provides malonyl-CoA to the mitochondrial fatty acid biosynthesis pathway |CITS: [28986507]|. , The malonyl moiety of malonyl-CoA is then transferred to the mitochondrial acyl-carrier protein by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.39|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS02028| gene |CITS: [12882974]|., The initiation of fatty acid biosynthesis requires an acetyl primer. In type I systems the acetyl group is attached to the fatty acid synthase without a need for additional enzymes. Type II systems of bacteria and plants usually require a specialized enzyme (called β-ketoacyl synthase III in prokaryotes and chloroplasts) that accepts |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as the primer. However, such an enzyme has not been identified in mitochondria, and the only mitochondrial β-ketoacyl synthase, which is encoded by the |FRAME: HS07707| gene, can only accept the acetyl primer from |FRAME: ACETYL-ACP "acetyl-[acp]"|. It has not been reported which enzyme is responsible for the acetylation of the acp protein., |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP "Malonyl-[acp]"| is used as the extender unit throughout the process of mitochondrial fatty acid biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY66-430|), with the malonyl moiety transferred to acyl-[acp] acceptors of varying lentghs. During the initiation process the malonyl group is transferred to the acetyl group primer via a decarboxylative condensation reaction. The product, |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE|, marks the end of the fatty acid biosynthesis initiation process. It is subsequently extended by several cycles of the fatty acid synthase, as described in |FRAME: PWY66-430| and |FRAME: PWY-7388|.
