Summary: |FRAME: CPD-2482| is an antibiotic substance produced by several |FRAME:TAX-1883| species |CITS: [Merck89]|., The compound, which is a cyclic analog of D-alanine, prevents the catalytic activities of both |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.1| |CITS: [4555420]| and |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.4| |CITS: [14479178]|, which are necessary for the biosynthesis of the bacterial cell wall (see |FRAME: PWY-8300|). It is clinically used as a second-line of defense against |FRAME: TAX-1773|, especially when the bacterium is resistant to other antituberculosis antibiotics |CITS: [10488174]|., |FRAME: CPD-2482| is also a candidate for the treatment of various psychological dysfunctions, since it has been shown to be a partial agonist for the |FRAME: CPD-10705| receptor |CITS: [2170997][9892252][15502972]|., The biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-2482| has been proposed based on substrate-feeding experiments |CITS: [Svensson81][Svensson82]|., A 21-kb DNA fragment containing the D-cycloserine biosynthetic gene cluster has been cloned from a |FRAME: TAX-1914| strain (ATCC 11924) |CITS: [20086163]|. In addition to eight genes involved in the biosynthesis of D-cycloserine, the cluster includes two genes that confer resistance to the antibiotic, encoding a resistant form of D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase (dscI) |CITS: [15302885]| and a D-cycloserine efflux pump (dcsJ) |CITS: [14632285]|. Expression of the cluster in the nonproducing organism |FRAME: TAX-1916| resulted in production of the antibiotic |CITS: [20086163]|., Experiments with individual enzymes that participate in the pathway have verified the predicted function of the genes and supported the proposed pathway |CITS: [20086163][22307920][22547619][23529730]|.

Summary: General Background, The antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-15417|, |FRAME: CPD-15421|, and |FRAME: CPD-15504| (known as the aminocoumarin antibiotics) bind type II topoisomerases, including DNA gyrase, with an extremely high affinity, with equilibrium dissociation constants in the 10 nM range |CITS: [8231802]|. They compete with ATP for binding to the B subunit of DNA gyrase and thus inhibit the ATP-dependent DNA supercoiling catalysed by gyrase., The three antibiotics, which are produced by different microorganisms (|FRAME: TAX-2893586|, |FRAME: TAX-149682| and |FRAME: TAX-68264|, respectively), share several characteristics., All three contain a 7-hydroxy-2-aminocoumarin core (ring B). The phenolic 7-hydroxyl group of the bicyclic aminocoumarin scaffold is attached to an |FRAME: CPD-15426| sugar moiety (ring C), while the 2-amino group is ligated to a prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit (in |FRAME: CPD-15417| and |FRAME: CPD-15421|) or to a methylpyrroledicarboxylic acid that links two aminocoumarin moieties (in |FRAME: CPD-15504|) (ring A). The noviosyl sugar is then methylated at the 4-OH position and acylated at the 3-OH position to produce the mature, active antibiotic. |FRAME: CPD-15421 Clorobiocin| and |FRAME: CPD-15504| are both decorated at the 3 position of ring C by a 5-methylpyrrole-2-carboxyl moiety, whereas the corresponding modification in |FRAME: CPD-15417| is a carbamoyl group |CITS: [16868863]|., , The pharmacophore of these antibiotics is the decorated noviosyl sugar, which is presented by the planar aminocoumarin to the ATP binding site of the GyrB subunit of gyrase to interdict DNA replication |CITS: [8635474][9144789]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-15417 Novobiocin| is known to be produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2893586 Streptomyces caeruleus (previously known as Streptomyces spheroides and Streptomyces niveus)"|., The novobiocin biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2893586| NCIB 11891 was identified by using a dNDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase gene fragments as probes, and cloned in its entirety |CITS: [10770754]|. Sequencing of the region revealed the presence of 23 putative open reading frames, including a novobiocin-resistant gyrB gene. Inactivation of the |FRAME: G-16080| gene (encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-18087|) abolished novobiocin production. A part of the cluster was cloned into |FRAME: TAX-457428|, and the transformed strain was shown to produce |FRAME: CPD-15415| |CITS: [10770754]|., The pathway can be divided into 4 parts: the synthesis of the aminocoumarin core, the noviose sugar, and the prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit, and the final decoration of the assembled product., The aminocoumarin core is synthesized from |FRAME: TYR|, which has to be bound to the |FRAME: MONOMER-18084|. That protein contains two domains - an adenylation (A) domain and a thiolation (T) domain, similat to initiation modules in nonribosomal peptide synthetase assembly lines. The A domain activates |FRAME: TYR| to tyrosine-AMP and then covalently tethers the aminoacyl moiety to the thiol of a phosphopantetheine prosthetic group in the T domain |CITS: [11325587]|. All subsequent modifications leading to formation of the aminocoumarin core occur on this covalently tethered entity., The enzyme-bound tyrosine is first hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-15492| and then oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-15507| |CITS: [16171397]|. A 2-hydroxylation is believed to take place as the next step, although the enzyme that introduces this 2-hydroxy group is still unknown. A final lactonization results in the release of the aminocoumarin core from the NovH protein., In a parallel route the prenylated 4-hydroxybenzoate moiety |FRAME: CPD-15423| is formed from |FRAME: PREPHENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-4211| by the action of three enzymes |CITS: [19557032][12777382]|. This compound is then transferred to the aminocoumarin core by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-18056| (|FRAME: G-16051|) |CITS:[10801869]|, followed by methylation to |FRAME: CPD-15415|, catalyzed by a methyltransferase encoded by |FRAME: G-16050| |CITS: [16274243]|., The third route comprises five enzymes that form |FRAME: CPD-15496| from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS: [15752721]|. The sugar is then attached to |FRAME: CPD-15415| by |FRAME: MONOMER-18054| (|FRAME: G-16049|) |CITS: [12680772]|., The final portion of the pathway consists of methylation and carbamoylation of positions 4 and 3 (respectively) of the demethylnoviosyl sugar, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-16048| and |FRAME: G-16047| genes, resulting in the final product |FRAME: CPD-15417| |CITS: [14694473]|.

Summary: General Background, Folates are required in a variety of reactions (known as one-carbon metabolism) in both bacterial and mammalian tissues, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides. , During folate biosynthesis the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.3.2.12|, adds an |FRAME:GLT| residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H2PteGlu1. This molecule in turn is reduced by |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATEREDUCT-MONOMER| to |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydrofolate, H4PteGlu1, or THF) (see |FRAME: FOLSYN-PWY|). THF can then be converted to several other folate molecules |CITS: [11501996]| (see |FRAME: PWY-2201|)., However, most folate molecules are further modified in cells by successive additions of |FRAME:GLT| residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-γ-glutamates) (see |FRAME: PWY-2161|). Most of the glutamate residues are added by γ-carboxy-linked polyglutamylation via an amide linkage to the γ-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are different from the more common α-carboxyl-linked amide bonds, they are not hydrolyzed by most peptidases or proteases. , About This Pathway, As vertebrates are not able to synthesize folate in vivo, they are absolutely dependent on nutritional sources, making folate a vitamin. Food folates exist mainly as the polyglutamylated forms |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (N5-methyl-H4PteGlun) and |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (N10-formyl-H4PteGlun) |CITS: [405403]|., In animals, during the absorption of food folates, which are usually polyglutamylated, the folate derivatives are hydrolyzed to a mono-glutamate level prior to transport by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.9|. The monoglutamylated forms are then metabolized within the enterocyte into |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF|. This monoglutamyl folate coenzyme is the plasma form of the vitamin |CITS: [13906633][2736319]|, and is transported to peripheral tissues where it is demethylated by the vitamin B12-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, to monoglutamyl tetrahydrofolate (H4PteGlu1)., γ-Glutamyl hydrolases were characterized from multiple sources, and exhibit either endo- or exopeptidase activity, depending on the organism and tissue of origin |CITS: [6547136]|. In mammals they are often lysosomal with an acidic pH optimum |CITS: [2174100]|. The enzyme is often sulfhydryl and zinc dependent |CITS: [2867095][2341911]|, may be heavily glycosylated |CITS: [1150668][8343522]|, and has molecular mass between 50 and 150 kDa.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Cobamides containing the purines |FRAME: ADENINE| and |FRAME: CPD-18323| as the lower ligand bases (known as |FRAME: CPD-20858 "pseudo-vitamin B12"| and |FRAME: CPD-20859 "factor A"|, respectively, before the nature of the lower ligands was discovered |CITS: [13159915][Dion54]|) have been reported from multiple organisms. Early studies suggested that factor A is the most common form of cobamide in bacteria |CITS: [13025519]|. More than 70 % of the cobamides in the rumen contents of calves was found to be in the form of factor A |CITS: [Ford53]|. More recently, factor A was found to be (by far) the most common type of cobamide in human feces (>60%) |CITS: [18469256]|., Adeninlyl cobamides have been reported as the predominant cobamides in |FRAME: TAX-1494| |CITS: [1315276][10940017]|, in |FRAME: TAX-1598| |CITS: [17888910]| and in some cyanobacteria |CITS: [10552882][17147452][17616007][20086323]|. They are likely to be the native cofactor of |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.7| |CITS: [4297225]| and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.1| |CITS: [1315276]|. Both cobamides were shown to be produced by |FRAME: TAX-28901| when grown anaerobically |CITS: [10648108]|. It has been shown that all three corrinoid-dependent enzymes of |FRAME: TAX-28901| can use |FRAME: CPD-20858| |CITS: [17981976]|., It has been shown that when incorporated into enzymes, these cofactors operate in the "base-off" conformation, meaning that one of the protein's amino acids displaces the the Co-coordinating lower ligand base |CITS: [Fieber02]|., This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20853|. The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the lower ligand base is activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (CobT) by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide or a related compound to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphoribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) to form the cobamide. The enzymes that operate in this pathway are the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis. Studies of the specificity of these enzymes have suggested that the nature of the lower ligand is controlled by metabolic factors |CITS: [11441022]| as well as by the specificity of CobT |CITS: [24055007]|., |FRAME: CPD-20859|, originally named vitamin B12d and later factor A, was shown to contain |FRAME: CPD-18323| already in the early 1950s |CITS: [Dion54][14351146]|. An x-ray crystal structure was reported in 1981 |CITS: [Kopf81]|. The source of |FRAME: CPD-18323| is not known. Since the only enzyme known to methylate adenine at the C2 position is |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.192|, it is possible that the source for this compound is tRNA degradation.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, (Per)chlorate-reducing bacteria use the highly oxidized chlorate ion as the sole electron acceptor for oxidation of organic matter. The reduction of chlorate occurs in a two-step reaction: |FRAME: CHLORATE| reduction to |FRAME: CHLORITE|, followed by the decomposition of the latter to |FRAME: CL-| ions and |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE|. The second step is one of the rare occasions where molecular oxygen is formed in a metabolic reaction [other examples include |FRAME: PWY-101 "photosynthesis"|, the detoxification of reactive oxygen species (see for example |FRAME: DETOX1-PWY|), and potentially the reaction catalyzed by "nitric oxide lyase" (see |FRAME: PWY-6523|)]., The two enzymes that catalyze chlorate reduction, |FRAME: CPLX-8077| and |FRAME: CPLX-8078|, are periplasmic, and have been purified from several organisms |CITS: [12957948][19361444]|. Electron transport from the bacterial inner membrane to the soluble periplasmic chlorate reductase is mediated by soluble c cytochromes |CITS: [20015627]|, while additional c cytochromes present in the periplasm appear to serve as electron donors for the terminal oxidase |CITS: [19233956]|., The oxygen that is produced in the process is believed to be used by either terminal oxidases or by monooxygenases that attack hydrocarbons, enabling the organisms to use oxygen-requiring enzymes under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [14735323]|., Perchlorate and chlorate reduction has also been observed in the archaea. However, in those organisms chlorite is not enzymatically split into chloride and oxygen. Instead, it is eliminated by an interplay of abiotic and biotic redox reactions involving sulfur compounds |CITS: [23559251]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN "Bacimethrin"| is an antibiotic that has been shown to be active against many bacteria and yeasts |CITS: [14066391]|. Its toxicity derives from its endogenous conversion to the thiamin antivitamin |FRAME: CPD0-2022| by the |FRAME: THIAMINE| biosynthetic enzymes of these microorganisms (see the pathways under pathway class |FRAME: Thiamine-Biosynthesis|). |FRAME: CPD0-2022 "2'-Methoxythiamin pyrophosphate"| inhibits some key |FRAME: THIAMINE|-dependent metabolic enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX| (in |CITS: [24654570]|)., The |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN| biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-441770| has been characterized and the biosynthesis of |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN| from |FRAME: CMP| has been demonstrated in an in vitro reconstitution system (see below) |CITS: [24654570]|. , The |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN| biosynthetic gene cluster has also been identified in other strains of |FRAME: TAX-1491| as well as in the sequenced genomes of a number of other bacteria (see the species listed above). It is of interest that in all cases another gene, bcmE encoding thiaminase-1 is also found in this gene cluster (see |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.2|). This finding suggests that the secreted thiaminase-1 may degrade any |FRAME: THIAMINE| that is present in the environment, thereby enhancing the toxicity of |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN| in a coordinated antibiotic strategy |CITS: [24654570]|. , The thiaminase-1 encoding gene bcmE from |FRAME: TAX-441770| has also been also cloned and its product expressed and shown to be specific for |FRAME: THIAMINE| as substrate |CITS: [24654570]|. In addition, an inactive bcmE C143S mutant was constructed, expressed, purified, and its crystal structure determined with bound |FRAME: THIAMINE| at 2.2 Å resolution |CITS: [24079939]|., About This Pathway, The reactions in this pathway were demonstrated in an in vitro reconstitution system by sequential addition of the purified BcmA-D enzymes. The His6-tagged proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli, purified and characterized. Their enzymatic reactions were analyzed by reverse-phase HPLC. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-15531| to |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN| by BcmC was confirmed by positive ion mode electrospray ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry analysis |CITS: [24654570]|., BcmA was shown to catalyze the methylenetetrahydrofolate-dependent hydroxymethylation of |FRAME: CMP| to produce |FRAME: CPD-17143|. BcmB then catalyzed cleavage of the N-glycosyl bond producing |FRAME: CPD-15531|. The latter compound was methylated by BcmC to produce |FRAME: BACIMETHRIN|, which was pyrophosphorylated by BcmD to produce |FRAME: CPD0-2021|. This latter compound can enter the |FRAME: THIAMINE| biosynthesis pathway to produce the antivitamin |FRAME: CPD0-2022| |CITS: [24654570]| (see the pathways under pathway class |FRAME: Thiamine-Biosynthesis|).

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-23439 "Carminic acid"| is a natural red pigment found in some scale insects including the American cochineals (|FRAME: TAX-765876|), which are mostly sessile phloem feeders, living as parasites exclusively on cacti belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-106975| genus. Carminic acid, which is thought to serve as a defense compound against predation by ants |CITS: [17779027]|, makes up to 26% of the dry weight of adult females in this species |CITS: [25195465]|., Carminic acid has been used as colorant by the Mayans, Incas, and Aztecs. During the Spanish colonial era, the dried insect powder was exported to Europe, where it became an important commodity. By the early nineteenth century, the American cochineal was introduced and reared on its cactus host outside Central and South America. Today carminic acid is widely used as a colorant in the food, textile, cosmetic, paint, and coating industry. Peru is the main producer of carminic acid from |FRAME: TAX-765876| |CITS: [29215010]|., Carminic acid production is very labor-intensive. After harvesting and drying the adult females the pigment is extracted by boiling the dried insects in an alkaline solution and removal of the insect parts. The dye can be further purified by precipitation with alum under acidic conditions to produce a more intense red aluminum salt called carmine lake., About This Pathway, The first enzyme of the pathway to be identified (and as of 2023, the only one) is |FRAME: MONOMER-21278|, which was shown in 2017 to catalyzes the last reaction in the pathway |CITS: [29215010]|. , In the following year an analysis of the chemical composition of |FRAME: TAX-765876| with the aim to discover intermediates in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-23439| detected |FRAME: CPD-23441|, suggesting that the first step is catalyzed by a polyketide synthase (PKS). Based on that finding, and on the earlier identification of the glucosyltransferase, the authors proposed the pathway shown here, which comprises a PKS, two oxidation steps (the latter of which catalyzed by a cytochrome P450) and a final glucosylation |CITS: [29551461]|., Despite the prediction for the participation of a PKS enzyme in the pathway, no PKS-encoding gene has been identified in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-765876| or its bacterial symbionts. In fact, no functional animal PKSs have ever been identified. A successful attempt to produce carminic acid heterologously utilized a plant type III polyketide synthase that formed a non-reduced linear octaketide (|FRAME: MONOMER-15013| from |FRAME: TAX-45385|), followed by subsequent folding into |FRAME: CPD-23441| by a cyclase and a aromatase from a bacterial type II PKS system (ZhuI cyclase and ZhuJ aromatase from |FRAME: TAX-140437|). When expressed in |FRAME: TAX-162425|, the recombinant enzymes formed the anthrone, which appeared to be oxidized spontaneously to |FRAME: CPD-23440|. The latter was further oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-23438| by an endogenous enzyme of the host. Addition of the |FRAME: G-80794| gene, which encodes the glucosyltransferase, resulted in |FRAME: CPD-23439| production |CITS: [30150747]|., A similar recombinant pathway was later designed using |FRAME: TAX-562| as the host, resulting in production of 0.63 mg/L of carminic acid from glucose |CITS: [33797895]|., As of 2023, the native enzymes catalyzing the first 3 steps of this pathway have not been identified.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1281 "Coenzyme B"| is one of the many unusual cofactors present in methanogens and required for methane formation. Like |FRAME: Factor-420|, |FRAME: CPD-1281| acts as an electron carrier in the metabolism of methanogens (see |FRAME: P241-PWY|)., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| functions as a methyl carrier in methanogenesis, and |FRAME: Me-CoM| has been established as the terminal intermediate of methanogenesis from all substrates (see |FRAME:METHFORM-PWY|). In addition to its role in methanogenesis, different forms of |FRAME: CoM| have physiological roles in methanogens, and are specific enzyme substrates |CITS: [2115763]|., All catabolic processes in methanogenesis lead to the formation of a mixed disulfide bond between |FRAME: CoM| and |FRAME: CPD-1281|, by a reaction in which |FRAME: CPD-1281| reduces |FRAME: Me-CoM|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CH4| and a |FRAME:CPD-1282| |CITS: [12102556]| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|)., The process in which |FRAME:CPD-1282| is reduced back to |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| has been studied extensively. There are two different enzyme systems that are capable of reducing the |FRAME:CPD-1282|. One is a membrane-bound system, encoded by the hdrDE genes, which uses |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE| as its electron donor |CITS: [15168610]|. The other is a soluble cytoplasmic system encoded by the hdrABC genes, which can use several types of electron donors, either directly, or by forming a complex with other enzymes., About This Pathway, Heterodisulfide reductases (Hdr) of the HdrABC class are ancient enzymes that existed in the prokaryotic common ancestor. The enzymes consist of a large HdrA subunit that contains FAD and multiple [4Fe-4S] clusters, a smaller catalytic HdrB subunit, and an electron transfer HdrC subunit. Electrons enter the enzyme at HdrA, and are transferred via HdrC to the active site of HdrB., In the hydrogenotroph |FRAME: TAX-39152| the cytoplasmic HdrABC is found complexed with either the |FRAME: CPLX-684 "MvhAGD hydrogenase"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7867|) or with formate dehydrogenase, forming |FRAME: EC-1.8.98.6| |CITS: [20534465]|. Either H2 or formate can donate electrons for the reduction of the heterodisulfide. When the hydrogenase was deleted from |FRAME: TAX-39152|, the mutant dispalyed growth equal to wild-type when grown on formate |CITS: [20534465]|., The three proteins also form a supercomplex with |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.12|, which catalyzes the most endergonic reaction in the methanogenesis pathway. Electron pairs donated by the hydrogenase or formate dehydrogenase are bifurcated by the HdrA subunit, and are used to reduce both the |FRAME: CPD-1282| and ferredoxin, the latter delivering its electrons to |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.12|. By this coupling, the energy of heterodisulfide reduction drives the pathway forward |CITS: [21262829]|. , It has been shown that the electrons are transferred from the formate dehydrogenase to the HdrA subunit of the reductase by an electron transfer protein orginially described as a δ subunit of the hydrogenase |CITS: [24039260]|.

Summary: In the respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase II (NDH-II) and cytochrome bd oxidase the transfer of electrons from NADH to oxygen is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. NDH-II does not contribute to the generation of proton potential |CITS: [3122832], [2679883]|; cytochrome bd oxidase translocates 1 H+/e- by means of an oriented redox loop |CITS: [1850294]|., During glucose limited aerobic growth E. coli directs electron flux through both |FRAME: NADH-DHI-CPLX "NADH dehydrogenase I"| (NDH-I) and NDH-II |CITS: [8491720]|. Electron transport from NADH to oxygen is not affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but is significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II; similarly nitrate respiration with NADH was only slightly affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II. This suggests that NDH-II is used preferentially in aerobic and nitrate respiration |CITS: [9063459]|., Cytochrome bd oxidase is expressed under oxygen-limiting conditions |CITS: [2172211], [8576043]| unlike cytochrome bo oxidase which is expressed when oxygen levels are high |CITS: [6365921]|. E. coli K-12 also contains a second bd-type cytochrome (|FRAME: APP-UBIOX-CPLX|) encoded by the appBC genes. The physiological role of cytochrome bd-II is uncertain although it is able to generate PMF via a mechanism similar to cytochrome bd-I |CITS: [21987791]|.

Summary: General Background, Manganese is the second most abundant transition metal found in the Earth's crust. In the environment, manganese is mostly found in three different oxidation states: II, III, and IV. Mn(II), primarily occurring as the soluble |FRAME: MN+2| species, is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions. Mn(III) and Mn(IV), which are commonly found in the form of various oxides and oxyhydroxides, are favored at high pH and oxic conditions (although in certain environments Mn(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands |CITS: [17008530]|). Mn(III) also occurs as a transient intermediate in the oxidation of Mn(II) to Mn(IV) oxides |CITS: [15800042]|., Mn oxides are highly reactive. They mediate redox reactions with organic and inorganic compounds (see for example |CITS: [31466008][34157973]|) and sequester a variety of metals, thus controlling the distribution and availability of many trace elements and influencing several elemental biogeochemical cycles. As the strongest environmentally relevant oxidant after oxygen, they serve as electron acceptors for anaerobic respiration by Mn-reducing organisms |CITS: [Tebo04]|., Microorganisms, especially bacteria but also fungi, are known to catalyze the oxidation of Mn(II) and the formation of Mn(III) and Mn(IV) oxide minerals. The majority of naturally occurring environmental Mn oxides are believed to be derived either directly from biogenic Mn(II) oxidation processes or from the subsequent alteration of biogenic oxides |CITS: [Tebo04]|., Despite the great importance of microbial Mn(II) oxidation, many aspects of the physiology and biochemistry of this process remain obscure |CITS: [16054815]|., Biochemical studies have shown the involvement of two types of enzymes in Mn oxidation - a peroxidase (described in |FRAME: PWY-6591|) and a multicopper oxidase (described in |FRAME: PWY-6592|). At least one organism, |FRAME: TAX-76869|, contains both types of enzymes |CITS: [27084014]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-287752| is a marine α-proteobacterium isolated from Saanich Inlet, Canada, from the interface between the bottom anoxic water and the overlying oxygenated water |CITS: [16346931][19768133]|. The organism, which belong to the |FRAME: TAX-356| order, oxidizes Mn(II) and contains an active RubisCO enzyme |CITS:[8828223][18344346]|., Analysis of proteins associated with Mn-oxidation in this strain revealed a |FRAME: SI859A1_02124-MONOMER "hemolysin-type calcium-binding outer membrane protein"| that belongs to the family of animal heme peroxidases |CITS: [18344346]|. In assays conducted with the purified protein, activity was enhanced by the addition of |FRAME: CA+2|, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and a combination of NAD+ and |FRAME: PQQ| |CITS: [19411418]|. , Interestingly, the |FRAME: SI859A1_02124| gene that encodes the enzyme is located next to an operon encoding a type II secretion machinery, on the other side of which is a gene encoding a |FRAME: SI859A1_02135-MONOMER "multicopper oxidase"| thought to be also involved in Mn-oxidation |CITS: [18344346]|., Similar manganese peroxidases were also found in |FRAME: TAX-161528|, another marine α-proteobacterium |CITS: [17673976][19411418]| and the non-marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-76869| |CITS: [27084014]|. Studies with the former suggest that quinones may play an integral role in bacterial Mn(II) oxidation |CIT:[17673976]|.

Summary: Mercury exists naturally in small amounts in the environment, though its levels have been increasing due, to anthropogenic activities such as coal burning, the use of mercurial fungicides and the use of mercury, as catalyst in industry. Mercury is extremely toxic, mostly due to its affinity to sulfhydryl groups, with, which it forms tight coordinate bonds., Mercury resistance is the most widespread antimicrobial-resistance system, and is found, in a wide variety of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, as well as archaea, |CITS:[4565536][410779][914774][350872][2626597][9168120]|., Mercury resistance is often divided into two categories: broad-spectrum (resistance to inorganic mercury, as well as a wide range of organomercurials) and narrow spectrum (resistance to inorganic mercury and, a very limited number of organomercurials)., The key enzyme in both categories is |FRAME: CPLX-2803| (MerA), which reduces the more toxic, mercuric ion (|FRAME: HG+2|) to the relatively non-toxic and volatile elemental mercury, (|FRAME: HG0|), a reaction that occurs in the cytoplasm |CITS: [2067577]|., Organisms that possess broad-spectrum resistance also utilize a second enzyme,, |FRAME:MONOMER-3304| (MerB) that breaks the mercury-carbon bond in the organomercurials, and releases the mercury in the form of |FRAME: HG+2|, which is then reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-2803|.

General Background, While the biosynthesis of C40 carotenoids (with 40-carbon backbones) is common in plants, algae, fungi, and bacteria, C30 carotenoids are relatively rare. Two types of such molecules have been described - the symmetrical 4,4'-diapocarotenoids and the asymmetrical 8'-apocarotenoids., C40 carotenoids are produced by the combination of two C20 precursors (|FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|)., The symmetrical C30 carotenoids are produced by the the conjugation of two C15 molecules (|FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|), and have a system of three conjugated double bounds at the center of the molecule. 4,4'-diapocarotenoids have been reported in a small group of bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [7275936]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5875|), |FRAME: TAX-29428| |CITS: [Kleinig79]|, |FRAME: TAX-1352| |CITS: [4212486]|, and |FRAME:TAX-2697| spp. |CITS: [9297464]|., The asymmetrical 8'-apocarotenoids are produced from the conjugation of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| and |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|. They have been described in |FRAME: TAX-192421| |CITS: [19194031]|, |FRAME: TAX-1570|, |CITS: [20414323]|, and yellow/orange Bacillus spore-formers |CITS: [21215325]|., About This Pathway, The methylotroph |FRAME:TAX-318114| produces the C(30) compound |FRAME: CPD-13152| |CITS: [Kleinig82]|., The first part of the pathway is identical to the pathway for biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280|, producing |FRAME: CPD-9906|. However, while the |FRAME: TAX-1280| |FRAME: MONOMER-13875| enzyme catalyzes only three desaturation steps, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-9911|, the |FRAME: MONOMER-16325| enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-318114| catalyzes four successive steps, producing |FRAME: CPD-13149| |CITS:[Kleinig82][15933032]|. , Both pathways continue in a similar manner - the activation of both ends of the molecule by |FRAME: MONOMER-16324|, forming aldehyde groups, followed by further oxygenation by |FRAME: MONOMER-16326|, which forms carboxylate groups |CITS:[15933032]|., The last part of the pathway, further modification forming |FRAME: CPD-13152|, has not been characterized yet.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleotides are found in all living organisms. They are essential components of nucleic acids, and play a crucial role in growth, development and reproduction, as well as in a large number of essential metabolic progressions such as interconversions from sugars to polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., The de novo pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthetic pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5686|) converts |FRAME: HCO3|, |FRAME: GLN|, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to |FRAME: UMP| (UMP). This pathway appears to be one of the most ancient biochemical pathways as it is evolutionary conserved in all species., UMP is subsequently converted to other pyrimidines, as described in this pathway. , About This Pathway, The de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides starts with |FRAME: UMP|, and proceeds via |FRAME: UDP| to |FRAME: UTP|. |FRAME: CTP| is only formed de novo by deamination of |FRAME: UTP|., The first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: UMPKI-CPLX|, catalyzes the phosphorylation of UMP to form UDP., The eukaryotic enzyme also catalyzes the phosphorylation of CMP to CDP, and was thus named |FRAME: AT5G26667-MONOMER| |CITS: [15604701]|., The next enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX| (NDK), catalyzes a reaction in which the, terminal phosphate of a nucleoside-triphosphate is transferred to a nucleoside-diphosphate - in this case, the, transfer of a phosphate from the purine ATP to the pyrimidine UDP, forming UTP. The enzyme has a broad substrate specificity, and is involved in the biosynthesis of several nucleoside-triphosphates, including formation of CTP from CDP., In the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| the enzyme is encoded by a small gene family and has been demonstrated to mediate, polar auxin transport |CITS: [15927941]| and interact with other proteins conferring stress tolerance |CITS: [12506203]|., Interconversion between thymidine and cytidine nucleotides is made possible by the glutamine (or ammonia)-dependent, enzyme |FRAME: CTPSYN-CPLX|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SUCROSE Sucrose| is the major product of photosynthesis in most plants and is known to be essential for their growth, development, carbon storage, signal transduction and stress protection |CITS: [11005202]|., Sucrose is also found in cyanobacteria, and the ability to synthesize sucrose is a widespread feature of these organisms |CITS: [21054739]|. In addition, sucrose is produced by many nonphotosynthetic aerobic methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria |CITS: [1055047][12656177][14529181][23808151][23865613]|., In photosynthetic organisms, the product of photosynthetic carbon fixation (|FRAME: GAP|) is transported from the chloroplast into the cytoplasm, where it is transformed to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| by enzymes of the |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis| pathway. In plants, |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| is used to synthesize sucrose, the form in which most fixed organic carbon is translocated from photosynthetic tissue to non-photosynthetic organs. Sucrose also provides substrates for plant storage glycosides such as |FRAME: Starch starch| and |FRAME: Fructans fructans|. Storage glycosides, including sucrose, are mobilized and utilized during seed germination and plant growth., In marine and freshwater cyanobacteria, sucrose fulfils a different role. It is often synthesized in response to salt or temperature stress and seems to maintain the osmotic balance and to stabilize protein and membrane structure and function |CITS: [Reed86][7854254]|. Methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria also synthesize sucrose as a secondary osmotic compound, along with the major compatible solute |FRAME: ECTOINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7347|)., About This Pathway, Sucrose synthesis is performed by generating the phosphorylated form, |FRAME: SUCROSE-6P| (the "F" indicates that the phosphate group is attached to the furanose moiety), followed by dephosphorylation. The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.14|, which condenses |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| with |FRAME: CPD-12575|. The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.24|, which hydrolyzes |FRAME: SUCROSE-6P| to |FRAME: SUCROSE|., In photosynthetic organisms both precursors originate from photosynthetic-derived carbon, via |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| |CITS: [20026474]|., Most plant possess another enzyme that can form sucrose - |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.13|. However, the name of this enzyme is misleading, since it has been shown that under most physiological conditions it catalyzes a sucrose cleavage reaction, and is thus involved in sucrose degradation |CITS: [plantbiochemistry97]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3801|).

General Background, |FRAME: Nitriles Nitriles"| are used extensively in the chemical industry. Synthetic nitrile compounds are used in benzonitrile herbicides, as precursors for the synthesis of polyacrylonitrile plastics, and as organic solvents. |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE "Acrylonitrile"| is the primary component in the manufacture of acrylonitrile-butadienestyrene (ABS) resin. It is also used as a precursor of acrylic fibers. The CN triple bond that defines nitriles makes many of them very toxic and generally non-biodegradable. Some compounds, such as acetonitrile, were shown to be carcinogenic in rodents |CITS: [16270753]|. Indiscriminate discharge of improperly treated nitrile wastes into a natural water body can cause serious problems and severe impacts on the aquatic ecology |CITS: [15242125]|., While the cyano group is very resistant, some bacteria are able to degrade nitriles, using two different routes. Some organisms possess nitrilases (|FRAME: EC-3.5.5.1| and |FRAME: EC-3.5.5.7|) that can hydrolyze nitriles to the corresponding carboxylic acids in a single step, forming ammonia in the process (as described in this pathway). Other organisms utilize a two step process that involves |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.84| and |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.4| (see |FRAME: PWY-7308|)., About This Pathway, Several species, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-1663|, |FRAME: TAX-85007|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-286| |CITS: [Watanabe87]|, |FRAME: TAX-1827| |CITS: [10347869][1390687]|, |FRAME: TAX-12916|, |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS:[15242125]|, |FRAME: TAX-469| |CITS: [7772945]| and |FRAME: TAX-546| |CITS:[14672363]| are able to degrade |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE| to acrylate, using it as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen. Some of these strains have been used successfully for the removal of acrylonitrile from soils |CITS: [14672363]|, wastewater |CITS:[7772945][15242125 ]| and gasses |CITS: [14755563]|., Nitrilase enzymes catalyze the hydrolysis of nitriles to carboxylic acids and ammonia without the formation of free amide intermediates. They are found in plants, animals, fungi and certain prokaryotes. The first bacterial nitrilase was isolated from a soil bacterium (possibly a Pseudomonas species) by selection for growth on the naturally occurring nitrile |FRAME: RICININE| as a sole carbon source |CITS: [14247679][14247680]|. Since then nitrilases have been characterized from a range of bacteria and fungi. Comparison of these enzymes show great differences in their substrate specificity, native structure and aggregation properties, and pH optima |CITS: [14632988]|., Most nitrilases show highest activity with aromatic nitriles, but some enzymes prefer aliphatic nitriles. A nitrilase that preferentially catalyzes the hydrolysis of aliphatic nitriles was purified from |FRAME: TAX-1829| |CITS: [2394676]|. The enzyme consisted of 15 to 16 identical subunits, and acted on aliphatic olefinic nitriles such as |FRAME:CPD-8861| and |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE| as the most suitable substrates.

Summary: |FRAME: OLEANDOMYCIN Oleandomycin| is a clinically important 14-membered macrolide antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1890|. It contains a macrolactone ring (|FRAME: CPD-13827|) modified by the attachment of two cyclic 6-deoxysugars, |FRAME: CPD-13948| and |FRAME: CPD-13780| |CITS: [16405329]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6971|). |FRAME: CPD-13948| is a methylated form of the sugar |FRAME: CPD-11912|, and it has been shown that the activated form of L-olivose, |FRAME: CPD-11915|, is the actual sugar that is attached to the ring. The attached olivose is then methylated to oleandrose. This pathway describes the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-11915|., The genes involved in the synthesis of the two deoxysugars of |FRAME: OLEANDOMYCIN| are located in a single cluster in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-1890| |CITS: [10770761]|. The genes were cloned into a plasmid and expressed in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1888| that harbors the |FRAME: G-14858| gene (encoding oleandrosyl glycosyltransferase) integrated into the chromosome. When the transformed cells were incubated in the presence of the erythromycin aglycone |FRAME: CPD-13947|, they produced 3-L-olivosyl-erythronolide B, indicating that the genes were sufficient for production of |FRAME: CPD-11912| |CITS: [10770761]|. When the |FRAME: G-14860| gene, encoding an |FRAME:CPLX-8413|, was included as well, the cells produced L-oleandrosyl-erythronolide B |CITS: [10770761]|., The pathway shown here is an integration of the original proposed pathway |CITS: [10770761]| and a later paper that looked at the synthesis of the related compound |FRAME: CPD-11916| by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-41951| |CITS: [21960454]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate "Dermatan sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of sulfated |FRAME: CPD-3604| and |FRAME: CPD-12515| (and some |FRAME: CPD-12521|) residues. The |FRAME: CPD-3604| residues are substituted to varying degrees with sulfate linked to 4- and/or 6-hydroxyl positions, forming |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, and the uronic acid residues may be substituted with sulfate at the 2-hydroxyl position forming |FRAME: CPD-12527| or |FRAME:CPD-12518|., The uronic acid residues may also be substituted with sulfate at the 3-hydroxyl positions, although this substitution is quite rare., The dermatan chains vary in size up to a hundred or more disaccharide repeating units. They are usually found attached to assorted core proteins as part of a proteoglycan complex. Dermatan sulfate is a major component of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but is also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors., The dermatan chains are synthesized in situ on the protein chain. They are attached to the core protein via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the "glycoaminoglycan-protein linkage region", which is formed by sequential stepwise additions of the sugar residues to specific core proteins. The synthesis of the linkage region is described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|, and the polymerzation of the chondroitin/dermatan chain is described in |FRAME: PWY-6566|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the later modifications in the biosynthesis of dermatan sulfate. A key reaction in the conversion of the chondroitin/dermatan precursor chain to a dermatan sulfate chain is the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues to |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: HS03472-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS03472| gene |CITS: [16505484]|., The rest of the modifications consist of sulfation reactions. The enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000169105-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS09883| gene, is a sulfotransferase that appears to be specific for sulfating the C4 position of |FRAME: CPD-3604| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues, and is thus dermatan-specific. Although a similar enzyme specific for 6-sulfation of dermatan has not been found, it has been suggested that such an enzyme exists, as the enzymes that sulfate chondroitin at the 6 position of |FRAME: CPD-3604| do not have high activity when that residue is linked to |FRAME: CPD-12515| |CITS: [9883891]|., On the other hand, the enzyme that catalyzes the 6-sulfation of |FRAME: CPD-3604| residues that are already sulfated at the C4 position is the same one that catalyzes the reaction with |FRAME:CHONDROITIN-4-SULFATE|, encoded by |FRAME: HS11694| |CITS: [11572857]|., Similarly, the enzyme that catalyzes the sulfation of the C2 position of |FRAME:DERMATAN-L-IDURONATE| is the same one that catalyzes a similar reaction with |FRAME: Chondroitin-Protein| residues, |FRAME: ENSG00000111962-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS03488|) |CITS: [10187838]|.

General Background, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-SERINE "L-1-phosphatidylserines"| are essential phospholipids in mammalian cells. They can be synthetized from |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| or |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE| by exchange of |FRAME: SER| with the |FRAME: CHOLINE| or |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| moiety respectively., In mammalian cells, this serine exchange is catalyzed by two different enzymes |FRAME: HS08129-MONOMER| and |FRAME: HS10846-MONOMER| whose substrates are |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| and |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE| respectively |CITS: [19014349]|., About This Pathway, Missense mutation in |FRAME: HS08129-MONOMER| has been found to be the cause of Lenz-Majewski syndrome, a human genetic disease associated with disturbance of phosphatidylserine metabosim., The mutant |FRAME: HS08129-MONOMER| shows a reduced end-product inhibition which causes an incresed production of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-SERINE| |CITS: [24241535]|.

|FRAME: CPD-21503 Itatartarate| (itatartaric acid) was first observed in |FRAME: TAX-33178| |CITS: [21006957]|. Early studies of its biosynthesis suggested that it was produced from |FRAME: ITACONATE| |CITS: [4166071][4836927]|. Later it was shown to accumulate with |FRAME: ITACONATE| and the lactone form |FRAME: CPD-21502| in strains of the genus |FRAME: TAX-5269|. Experiments with permeabilized cells of |FRAME: TAX-63396| suggested that |FRAME: CPD-21502| is formed from |FRAME: ITACONATE|, followed by transformation to |FRAME: CPD-21503|. At the time, the authors proposed that |FRAME: CPD-14325| was an intermediate |CITS: [Guevarra90]|., While the exact pathway is still not completely known, the characterization of the |FRAME: G-58771| gene, which is located adjacent to the itaconate biosynthesis cluster of |FRAME: TAX-5270|, clarified how |FRAME: CPD-21502| is formed |CITS: [26639528]|. The gene encodes a cytochrome P-450 enzyme that converts |FRAME: ITACONATE| directly to |FRAME: CPD-21502|, without forming |FRAME: CPD-14325|. Disruption of |FRAME: G-58771| abolished |FRAME: CPD-21502| production completely |CITS: [27750034]|., As of 2018, the transformation of |FRAME: CPD-21502| to |FRAME: CPD-21503| has not been characterized. However, The |FRAME: G-58774| gene, which is located adjacent to the itaconate biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-5270|, is predicted to encode a ring cleaving dioxygenase, and as such has been proposed as a potential candidate for the catalysis of this transformation |CITS: [27750034]|

Summary: |FRAME: Polyketide-quinones "Polyketide quinones"| are used by some organisms as a functional alternative to |FRAME: Menaquinones menaquinone| under specific conditions such as low oxygen environments or sporulation., The first study of the enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of polyketide quinone was reported in 2008 from |FRAME: TAX-67263|. The srsABC operon in this organism encodes a type III polyketide synthase (PKS), a methyltransferase, and a flavoprotein hydroxylase. Overexpression of the srs genes in the heterologous host |FRAME: TAX-1916| showed that the type III PKS SrsA is responsible for synthesis of 5-alkyl-4-methylresorcinols, SrsB methylates these products at the O1 position to yield alkylresorcinol methyl ethers, and SrsC hydroxylates the methyl ethers at position C6. SrsA was shown to synthesize 5-alkyl-4-methylresorcinol using acyl-CoAs of various chain lengths as a starter substrate, extending them using two molecules of malonyl-CoA and one molecule of methylmalonyl-CoA in a strictly controlled order |CITS: [18364359]|., While the authors reported that srs-like operons are found widely among Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, the role of the polyketide quinones was not understood at the time |CITS: [18364359]|., A new understanding of polyketide quinones was achieved in 2015, when it was reported that these molecules can serve as alternate mobile electron carriers in the respiratory electron transport chain during respiration in oxygen-deficient niches. The authors, who studied the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1772|, found that the enzymes are specifically expressed in biofilms and other oxygen-deficient niches. They also reported that the system is conserved in all mycobacteria as well as in several other Actinobacterial and a few Proteobacterial species |CITS: [26585386]|., A study of the freshwater bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1573406| has shown that the organism switches from using menaquinone to using polyketide quinone during its development cycle. The gene cluster was significantly upregulated during the dormant sporulation stage, while the menaquinone biosynthetic genes were downregulated during this period. A metabolite extract from the spores showed 10 times more polyketide quinone molecules than menaquinones |CITS: [36507669]|.

However, recent work disputes this claim, having found no |FRAME:CPD-2041|, in human blood and no |FRAME:MONOMER-11830| activity in rat liver |CITS: [3356699]|

Summary: Natural rubber is an important raw material in an enormous number of products. The backbone of natural rubber comprises a (cis)-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans-isoprene units at the ω-terminus, formed by the sequential condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) units in cis configuration onto a short all-trans prenyl diphosphate. It is very similar in structure to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichols|, but the chain length is much longer (C>1500)., Natural rubber is produced from latex - a material that makes up the cytoplasmic content of the latecifers or latex vessels of |FRAME: TAX-3981| (the Brazilian rubber tree) |CITS: [17545224]|. Although over 2000 plant species capable of producing rubber have been identified, only a few synthesize the high molecular weight rubber that is required for the production of high quality rubber products, and natural rubber is currently produced commercially only from |FRAME: TAX-3981|., Despite the enormous amounts of rubber waste materials that are released into the environment, complete degradation in nature is still rare, and rubber wastes usually remain in the environment for a very long time. There have been reports of microorganisms that can attack from many ecosystems with moderate physical parameters (temperature, pH, and salinity) |CITS: [16535106][9170260][10742254][15638519][22142727][23863290][Chia14]|. Three types of rubber-cleaving enzymes have been characterized so far. One is the rubber oxygenase |FRAME: G-55185 RoxA|, which was first isolated from |FRAME: TAX-230757| and so far found only in Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [16348100][15574940][15870336][23934498]|; the second is the latex clearing protein (|FRAME: G-55186 Lcp|), which has been reported so far only from Gram-positive Actinobacteria |CITS: [15638519][16672480][24928880][27215318]|; and the third one is |FRAME: G-55188 RoxB| from |FRAME: TAX-230757|, which has sequence similarity to RoxA, but produces the same products as Lcp |CITS: [28500046]|., RoxA is a c-type diheme dioxygenase that cleaves |FRAME: cis-14-isoprene| from its end into |FRAME: CPD-20487|, a C15 compound with a terminal keto and aldehyde groups (see |FRAME: PWY-7924|). Lcp is a b-type cytochrome and cleaves rubber to several products of different sizes (C20-C35 and higher) via an endo-type mechanism |CITS: [24907333][25819959]|. RoxB is also a c-type diheme dioxygenase, but catalyzes an endo-type reaction, producing the same products as Lcp., Despite their differences, all three enzymes are dioxygenases that catalyze an oxidative cleavage of the cis double bonds in the polymer backbone, generating carbonyl and aldehyde end groups. , Two genes (oxiA and oxiB) located downstream from the |FRAME: G-55186| gene in |FRAME: TAX-256642| seem to constitute an operon with it. The two genes encode the putative subunits of a heteromultimeric molybdenum -containing aldehyde dehydrogenase, that likely acts on the products of Lcp |CITS: [15638519][18606806]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9717 Ubiquinone-7| (Q-7) is common in yeast. Many strains of |FRAME:TAX-5475|, |FRAME:TAX-4919| and |FRAME: TAX-604195| form Q-7 |CITS: [13673033]|. As a matter of fact, ubiquinone tail length has been used for the phylogenetic classification of these organisms |CITS: [Suzuki98][12469316]|. Q-7 is much less abundant among bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-5855|).

|FRAME:TAX-562| can use both diacid sugars D-glucarate and galactarate as the sole source of carbon for growth. , The initial step in the degradation of D-glucarate is its dehydration to 5-keto-4-deoxy-D-glucarate by, |FRAME: GLUCARDEHYDRA-MONOMER|. The subsequent steps in this pathway, cleavage of, 5-keto-4-deoxy-D-glucarate into pyruvate and tartronate semialdehyde by |FRAME: CPLX0-7615|, reduction, of tartronate semialdehyde to D-glycerate by |FRAME: TSA-REDUCT-MONOMER|, and phosphorylation of, D-glycerate to form 2-phosphoglycerate by |FRAME: GKI-MONOMER|, are shared with the, |FRAME: GALACTARDEG-PWY| pathway., Review: Mandrand-Berthelot, M.-A., Condemine, G., and Hugouvieux-Cotte-Pattat, N., EcoSal Module 3.4.2, |CITS: [ecosal]|

General Background, Cyanobacterial lipids consist of glycerolipids with a C18 fatty acid esterified at position sn-1 and a C16 fatty acid esterified at position sn-2 |CITS: [Sato82]|., The cyanobacteria have been classified into four groups according to the distribution of the fatty acids in their glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|. , Strains in Group 1 are characterized by the presence of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (|FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9245|) at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively., Strains in Group 2 contain the tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| at the sn-1 position and the mono-unsaturated C16 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-9245| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 3 have a different tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid (|FRAME: CPD-8117|) at the sn-1 position and the saturated C16 acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 4 are similar to strains in Group 3 except that they have, in addition, the tri-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| and the tetra-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: CPD-12653| at the sn-1 position., |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD Oleate| (oleic acid) is a monounsaturated fatty acid produced by all cyanobacteria, although the acid is only incorporated into lipids of group 1 members (in other groups it is further desaturated into various polyansaturated products). It is produced by many other organisms, including plants and animals., About This Pathway, In cyanobacteria |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is formed bound to an acyl-carrier protein, part of the fatty acid synthase complex. Stearate is transfered to the sn-1 position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.15| |CITS: [16039611]|., As described above, glycerolipids from all cyanobacteria contain unsturated C18 fatty acids in the sn-1 position, but differ in the degree and nature of unsaturation. The desaturation occurs only after |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| has been incorporated into the glycerol backbone, and is catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes known as acyl-lipid desaturases., The first desaturation occurs at position 9, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.28|, encoded by the |FRAME: SGL_RS15040| gene |CITS: [7929259]|., It should be noted that acyl-lipid 9-desaturases have also been isolated from plants, although their role is not well understood |CITS: [8541490][9559566]|.

Summary: General Background, Sulfur is an essential nutrient for all life forms. Plants, fungi, and many bacteria reduce inorganic sulfate to sulfide to cover their need for the element. Before the sulfur can be assimilated into biosynthetic pathways it needs to be reduced to |FRAME:HS|., Pathways catalyzing the reduction of sulfate to sulfide for the purpose of incorporation into newly synthesized molecules are called pathways of assimilatory sulfate reduction. In addition, certain organisms can use sulfate as an alternative electron acceptor in the absence of oxygen. Pathways of sulfate reduction for the purpose of energy production are called pathways of dissimilatory sulfate reduction., The reduction of sulfate to sulfite requires two electrons at a standard redox potential (E0') of -516 mV, which is too high for physiological electron carriers |CITS: [860983]|. The problem is solved by the activation of the sulfate, by forming a mixed anhydride between phosphate and sulfate as in |FRAME:APS| (APS) or |FRAME:PAPS| (PAPS). This linkage lowers the potential to E0' = -60 mV, which is easilly covered by thiols or pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [14627706]|., About This Pathway, In many bacteria and lower eukaryotes, assimilatory sulfate reduction proceeds via activation of |FRAME: SULFATE| to APS by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4| (also known as ATP sulfurylase). This enzyme has an unfavorable equilibrium (Keq ~ 10-7 M) in the direction of APS formation, and it has been postulated that the reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of PPi by a ubiquitous inorganic pyrophosphatase |CITS: [2821345]|. In |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was found that the enzymes couples the formation of APS to hydrolysis of GTP |CITS: [8117661]|., Following sulfate activation, the pathway consists of phosphorylation of APS to PAPS, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.25| (APS kinase), reduction to |FRAME: SO3|, which is catalyzed by the thioredoxin (or glutaredoxin)-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.8| (PAPS reductase), and a final reduction of sulfite to sulfide, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.8.7.1|.

Summary: The |FRAME: PWY-5743| is one of few |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation pathways that are known. The pathway was discovered in the green nonsulfur phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1108| |CITS: [Holo89][8354269]|, and seems to be limited to organisms that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-1106| phylum |CITS: [17635550]|, one of the five major lineages of phototrophic bacteria., A related pathway operates in some acidophilic archaebacteria of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-28889|, such as |FRAME: TAX-41673|, |FRAME: TAX-47303| and |FRAME: TAX-43687| (see |FRAME: PWY-5789|)., Each turn of the cycle results in the net fixation of two molecules of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| (in the form of |FRAME: HCO3|) into one molecule of |FRAME:GLYOX|. The glyoxylate, which is an unconventional carbon source, is converted into |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, a central carbon precursor, by a dedicated pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5744|)., The pathway starts with |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| carboxylation to |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, catalyzed by |FRAME: ENZRXN-14489|. Under autotrophic growth conditions |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| is reduced with NADPH by |FRAME: CPLX-7550| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE|, a characteristic intermediate of this pathway., 3-Hydroxypropionate is reductively converted to |FRAME: SUC-COA| in a process in which |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| is carboxylated, fixing another molecule of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Succinyl-CoA, which has been thus formed from one |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and two |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, is used to regenerate the initial CO<sub>2</sub> acceptor molecule |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, and |FRAME:GLYOX| is released., Several of the enzymes of this pathway are multifunctional. |FRAME: MALONYL-COA "Malonyl-CoA"| is reduced to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| in two steps by the bifunctional enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7551| |CITS: [11948153]|, while |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| is converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| in a single step by a remarkable single trifunctional enzyme, a natural fusion protein that integrates a CoA ligase, an enoyl-CoA hydratase, and an enoyl-CoA reductase |CITS: [11821399]|. Some of the enzymes also participate in the |FRAME: PWY-5744| cycle, which converts the |FRAME:GLYOX| formed by this pathway into |FRAME:PYRUVATE|. These enzymes catalyze the reactions in different direction in the two cycles. In some cases, as in the case of |FRAME: CPLX-7549|, they accept a different substrate when catalyzing the reaction in the opposite direction |CITS: [12374834]|., The genes encoding several of the enzymes that participate in this pathway were identified by their sequence when the |FRAME: TAX-1108| genome was sequenced |CITS: [21714912]|. These enzymes still await purification and characterization at the biochemical level.

Summary: Chlorobenzene has been identified as a, priority pollutant, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)., The first thorough study of the pathway for |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE| degradation was performed by Reineke, and Knackmuss |CITS: [6712211]|. In that study they have isolated an organism, identified only as strain WR1306,, which could utilize |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE| as the sole source of carbon., Respiration data and enzyme activities in cell extracts, as well as the isolation of |FRAME: CPD-9151| from the, culture fluid, led to a proposed pathway. The pathway starts with a dioxygenase attack on |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE|,, generating |FRAME: CPD-10609|, which is re-aromatized to |FRAME: CPD-9151|., The catechol is then processed via a modified ortho cleavage pathway via the intermediates , |FRAME: 2-CL-MUCONATE|, |FRAME: 4-CARBOXYMETHYLENEBUT-2-EN-4-OLIDE|, and |FRAME: CPD-294|,, and the later is reduced to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which is precessed into TCA cycle intermediates (see, |FRAME: PWY-2361|)., |FRAME: TAX-393999| was originally isolated by its ability to mineralize |FRAME: 124-TCB|. However, this, organism can also grow on |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE|, all three isomerers of dichlorobenzene, and, |FRAME: CPD-10620| |CITS: [16348484][9249026]|. The genes encoding the dioxygenase and dehydrogenase in, this organism are localized on a small plasmid |CITS: [9864349]|., The bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6071| is not able to grow with |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE|, despite the fact that, including this compound in the growth medium induces several enzymes, including |FRAME: MONOMER-81|,, |FRAME: MONOMER-102| and |FRAME: MONOMER-103|. Furthermore, when the relevant enzymes were purified,, they were able to catalyze the degradation |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE| in vitro., The authors speculate that lack of growth with this compound may be the result of toxicity of one of the intermediates, involved |CITS: [9148781]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-1821 Homospermidine| is an uncommon triaminic polyamine found in bacteria, fungi, higher plants, amphibians, arthropods, and mammalian tissues. The biosynthetic pathway was initially characterized in higher plants with the isolation of the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.45| |CITS: [10476066]|., The enzyme uses an NAD cofactor and catalyzes the reaction in three steps, with some of the intermediates presumably remaining enzyme-bound: (a) NAD+-dependent dehydrogenation of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, (b) transfer of the 4-aminobutylidene group from |FRAME: CPD-14378| to |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| and (c) reduction of the imine intermediate to form |FRAME: CPD-1821|., In plants formation of homospermidine leads to the biosynthesis of pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PA), which are found in certain angiosperm families, as it is the unique precursor of necine base moiety of all PA's representing 1-hydroxmethylpyrrolizidine derivatives |CITS: [17320124]|., The HSS enzymes of |FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-18794| evolved from |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.46|. The HSS enzymes possess all the enzyme characteristics of the latter, but lost the ability to bind elF5A. The |FRAME: MONOMER-13914|, on the other hand, was able to catalyze the activity of homospermidine synthase |CITS: [10542236]|., In bacteria homospermidine is formed by a different enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.44|, which, unlike the eukaryotic enzyme, can also use |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| as the donor of the aminobutylidene group |CITS: [437275][8407874]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8149|).

Summary: General background, |FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291| and |FRAME:PWY-7292|) |CITS:[12697341] [14523547] [8685242]|., The degradation of the cis-unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME:CPD-15680| in |FRAME:TAX-4930| (this pathway) has been investigated by monitoring the formation of polyhydroxyalkanoates (see |FRAME:PWY-6657|). The commonly used method to study the degradation of unsaturated fatty acids in yeast such as observing clearing zones around colonies growing on media which provide those fatty acids as sole carbon source has its limits in detecting certain intermediates |CITS:[11566445]|. The formation of polymers from polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) had been originally developed for commercial purposes by producing protein-based polymers and elastomers as part of the efforts to produce renewable and biodegradable raw materials |CITS:[10209132] [9634754]|. However, it rapidly became apparent that the polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) polymerization method also represented a powerful tool to follow carbon fluxes, monitor substrate specificities, detect and engineer new metabolic routes and analyze quantity and quality of unusual fatty acid degradation intermediates in a variety of organisms |CITS:[9634754] [11679353] [10571864] [18657232]|. , About the pathway, By introducing a bacterial PHA synthase from Pseudomonads modified for yeast peroxisomal targeting which polymerizes the various 3-hydroxy-acyl-CoA species generated in the β-oxidation cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-7288|) it is now possible to determine the composition and amount of the substrates and intermediates in a range from 5 to 16 carbons in length |CITS:[16347790] [11679353]|. The degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15680| following the fatty acid activation to form the respective CoA derivative occurs in a pathway that combines auxiliary enzymes with core-enzymes of the β-oxidation cycle. Utilizing yeast mutants, i.e. Δeci1, Δsps19 and Δdci1 and evaluating the quantity and monomer composition of the synthesized PHA the participation of DCI1 in the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15680| could be excluded and the pathway sequence determined |CITS:[15904873]|. As mentioned above the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15680| could only be monitored via PHA polymerization to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15660| as this is the detection limit of the method |CITS:[16347790]|. , The metabolic steps as depicted in the pathway schema are catalyzed by the β-oxidation enzymes POX1 |CITS: [2189786] [11431484]|, the multifunctional enzyme FOX2 |CITS:[1551874] [10497229] [16574148]| and the 3-keto-thiolase (POT1) |CITS:[7754706] [9402066] [7812714]|. In contrast to the isomer of |FRAME:CPD-15680|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15679| which employs two pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-7338| and |FRAME:PWY-7339|) the breakdown of |FRAME:CPD-15680| is realized in one single pathway which also requires the participation of the auxiliary enzymes 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase (SPS19) |CITS:[9268358] [1738316]| and Δ3-Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) |CITS:[9837886] [9813046]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7672 3-Methylthiopropanoate| is produced by several routes: (i) catabolism of methionine |CITS:[479166]|, (ii) demethylation of dimethylsulfoniopropionate in bacteria |CITS:[8899985]| or (iii) a shunt route of the |FRAME:PWY-5389|., In the latter route, represented here, 1,2-dihydroxy-3-keto-5-methylthiopentene is oxidized to formate and 3-methylthioproprionate. The purpose of this shunt route, also known as the off-pathway reaction of methionine salvage, is yet unknown; it has been postulated that it might provide a mechanism for regulating methionine levels in vivo |CITS: [11371200]|., The enzyme responsible for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-7672| is acireductone dioxygenase. This enzyme has been found in a number of species and has been shown to be involved in the catalysis of two reactions: the Fe2+-dependent conversion of |FRAME:CPD-85| into |FRAME:CPD-479| (EC 1.13.11.53) and the Ni2+-dependent conversion of the same substrate into |FRAME:CPD-7672| (EC 1.13.11.54) |CITS:[16989860]|. This enzyme has been characterized for |FRAME:TAX-573| (see |FRAME:MONOMER-1323|) and in rice. The latter was shown to catalyze mostly the Fe2+-acireductone dioxygenase step. Indeed, this enzyme appears to have a preference for Fe2+ rather than Ni2+ suggesting it might be involved mostly in the |FRAME:PWY-4361| rather than the shunt pathway producing the cytotoxic compound 3-S-methylthiopropionate |CITS:[16297065]|., This Pathway in Plants:, In plants, the production of 3-methylthiopropionate remains uncertain. The compound is cytotoxic to plant cells and has been reported in leaves of cassava infected by |FRAME:TAX-339| as a blight-inducing toxin |CITS:[perreaux86]|. It is known to be produced by phytopathogens and by soil microorganisms, and to affect the growth of plant seedlings |CITS:[12715879]|.

Derivatives of pyridine are ubiquitous in nature. |FRAME: CPD-26209 4-Hydroxypyridine| has been identified in extracts of |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [10952545]| and |FRAME: TAX-59691| |CITS: [Davey09]| and as an unspecific detoxification product of pyridine in laboratory animals |CITS: [7147998]|. In addition, derivatives of |FRAME: CPD-26209| enter the environment from several other sources such as the degradation of the herbicide |FRAME: CPD-26217|, the radiocontrast agent |FRAME: CPD-26218|, the natural allelochemical |FRAME: MIMOSINE| |CITS: [27213712]|, and the natural antibiotics |FRAME: Caerulomycins caerulomycin| |CITS: [Divekar67]| and |FRAME: CPD0-1233| |CITS: [14527553]|., Already in 1972 it was reported that a strain of Agrobacterium (NCIB 10413) can use |FRAME: CPD-26209| as a sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [4664939]|. The pathway was reported to include a monooxygenase that forms |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPIRIDIN-CPD| |CITS: [4156169]|, a ring-opening dioxygenase, and a hydrolase. The end products were determined to be ammonia, formate, and pyruvate |CITS: [4375963]|., |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-4H-PYRID-4-ONE|, a tautomer of |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPIRIDIN-CPD|, is known to be an intermediate in the degaradation of |FRAME: MIMOSINE|, and the enzymes involved in its degradation in the mimosine-degrading bacterium |FRAME: TAX-147233| have been reported (see |FRAME: PWY-8431|). In that organisms it appears that a para-cleavage dioxygenase and a single hydrolase are sufficient for the degradation of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-4H-PYRID-4-ONE| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and |FRAME: AMMONIUM| |CITS: [15968058][17390132][20138776]|., Characterization of the |FRAME: CPD-26209| catabolic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-376808| identified the genes encoding the monooxygenase (|FRAME: G-124314|), a potential ring-opening dioxygenase (|FRAME: G-124315|), and two hydrolases (|FRAME: G-124316| and |FRAME: G-124317|). Experimental evidence was obtained for the function of most of these enzymes |CITS: [32545463]|.
