Summary: |FRAME: GFP "Green fluorescent proteins"| (GFPs) are proteins that exhibit bright green fluorescence when exposed to light in the blue to ultraviolet range. In many marine organisms GFPs form a part of the bioluminesence systems, although some non-bioluminescent organisms also possess GFPs. , The protein from the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100| was the first GFP to be described |CITS: [13911999]|. In this organism GFP is coupled to the |FRAME: Aequorins aequorin| enzyme, which catalyzes a reaction that forms |FRAME: CPD-20235|. This compound can emit blue light, which can then trigger fluorescence by GFP. However, due to coupling between aequorin and GFP, the short distance enables Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET), a much more efficient, non-radiative energy-transfer process |CITS: [4397528][4151620]|. A similar situation occurs in the soft coral |FRAME: TAX-6136|, where GFP interacts with the luciferase enzyme |CITS: [33175]|., The protein was first isolated and purified in 1974 |CITS: [4151620]|. A more thorough characterization, including molecular weight, sedimentation coefficient, extinction coefficient, diffusion coefficient, and amino acid composition, was published a few years later |CITS: [28749]|. A cDNA encoding the enzyme was isolated in 1992, suggesting multiple chromosomal genes encoding the protein |CITS: [1347277]|. Cloning and expressing GFP in bacteria and in |FRAME: TAX-6239| has suggeted that GFP could serve as a marker for studying gene expression in vivo |CITS: [8303295][8137953]|., Several studies have identified the structure of the GFP chromophore, which is produced by autocatalytic cyclization of the tripeptide Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly which involves dehydration and oxidation by air. An internal tripeptide, Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly (some species have threonine in the first position, while others have a serine in that position), forms the chromophore by nucleophilic attack of Gly-Nα on the carbonyl group of Thr or Ser, followed by dehydration and oxidation of the Cα-Cβ bond of Tyr |CITS: [Shimomura79][Ward80][McCapra88][8448132][ 7809066][9811837]|. Only the oxidized form is fluorescent |CITS: [8082767]|. Formation of the chromophore requires proper folding |CITS: [9184161]|., In a 1999 study genes encoding remote homologs of the |FRAME: G-55175| gene of |FRAME: TAX-6100| were cloned from six non-bioluminescent reef corals, expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and purified. Despite a low overall identity with GFP (26-30%), all of the proteins fluoresced, and two of them (from |FRAME: TAX-105401| and |FRAME: TAX-86599| species) were found to fluoresce at the yellow and red wavelengths, respectively |CITS: [10504696]|. It is now recognized that the family of GFP-like proteins includes |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent proteins"| (GFP), |FRAME: PWY-8514 "red fluorescent proteins"| (RFP), |FRAME: YFP-Chromophore "yellow fluorescent proteins"| (YFP), |FRAME: CFP-Chromophore "cyan fluorescent proteins"| (CFP) and |FRAME: BCP-Chromophore "purple-blue non-fluorescent chromoproteins"| (CP) |CITS: [18648549]|., All of these proteins share the same β-can fold first observed in GFP, but most are not associated with bioluminescence. While the fluorophores of previously-described GFPs are formed autocatalitically from the three amino acids Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly, later identified proteins have significant variability in the first position, containing Gln, Lys, His, or Asn |CITS: [10504696][12271129]|., Over the years GFP has become an extremely useful tool in cell and molecular biology, where it is used as an in situ reporter of expression. The scientists Roger Y. Tsien, Osamu Shimomura, and Martin Chalfie were awarded the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery and development of the green fluorescent protein.

Summary: General Background, Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gallbladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum)., The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids., Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids are produced in the liver from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. Their structures vary, as do their proportions in different species. The primary bile acids are conjugated in the liver with |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: TAURINE| before secretion into the bile. Further conversion into secondary bile acids occurs through the action of microbial enzymes in the gut., Four pathways for bile acid biosynthesis have been described. The neutral (classic) pathway begins with hydroxylation at the 7α ring position of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.23|). The acidic (alternate) pathway begins with 27-hydroxylation of the |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| side chain (|FRAME: EC-1.14.15.15|). The 24-hydroxylase (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.25|) and 25-hydroxylase (|FRAME: EC-1.14.99.38|) pathways begin with these respective side chain hydroxylations. The three side chain hydroxylations are followed by 7α hydroxylation (via |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.26| or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.29|). Hydroxylation at the 7α position is a characteristic of bile acids. All but one of these reactions are catalyzed by enzymes of the cytochrome P450 family. , The acidic, 24-hydroxylase and 25-hydroxylase pathways have only been partly illustrated in the literature (later reaction steps were omitted). It should also be noted that the exact order of reactions in all of the bile acid biosynthetic pathways remains unclear because many of the intermediates are substrates for more than one biosynthetic enzyme. In addition, the relative contributions of the different pathways may vary by species, age and physiological condition (in |CITS: [17346171]|). The neutral pathway is considered the quantitatively most important pathway in humans. The acidic pathway leads mainly to |FRAME: CPD-15189| and may be more important in rats. The 24- and 25-hydroxylase pathways, are considered minor pathways. Reviewed extensively in |CITS: [12543708] [17346171] [18815433] [11969205]|., About This Pathway, This pathway shows the neutral (classic) pathway for the biosynthesis of two possible bile acid conjugates of |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189|. It is represented here essentially as shown in |CITS: [12543708]| and as shown in part in |CITS: [17346171]| and |CITS: [15769750]|. The pathway is initiated by hydroxylation at the 7α position of the |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| ring structure, followed by reactions that further modify the |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| rings, oxidize and shorten the side chain, and conjugate the bile acid with an amino acid to increase solubility. Free |FRAME: CHOLATE| may result from regulated action of peroxisomal coenzyme A thioesterase 2 on |FRAME: CPD-202|, although the biological consequences of changes in the ratio of free and conjugated forms are not understood. More than 98% of bile acids excreted from the liver are conjugated (in |CITS: [12543708]|). Humans and rats produce both |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID| and |FRAME: CPD-3743|. Mice produce |FRAME: CPD-3743| due to difference in substrate specificity of their conjugating enzyme (|CITS: [9215542] [11673457]| and reviewed in |CITS: [12543708]|)., The enzymes in the pathway are found in multiple subcellular locations including the endoplasmic reticulum, cytosol, mitochondrion and peroxisome (as indicated on the enzyme display pages). These enzymes also function in steroid metabolism, very long chain fatty acid metabolism and vitamin D biosynthesis. Reviewed in |CITS: [12543708] [17346171] [18815433] [11969205]|. Oxysterols produced during bile acid biosynthesis also function in cholesterol homeostasis (reviewed in |CITS: [17346171]|., A branch point after the second reaction at |FRAME: CPD-1087| leads to a similar biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15189| derivatives in most mammalian species. This branch lacks the |FRAME: MONOMER-14303| step (as illustrated in |CITS: [12543708] [17346171]|). |FRAME: CHOLATE "Cholate"| differs from |FRAME: CPD-15189| by the presence of a hydroxyl group at the 12α position. The relevant enzymes in the pathway shown here are also active on the corresponding dihydroxy substrates that lead to |FRAME: CPD-15189| derivatives |CITS: [6736016] [3459552] [2848026] [9390170] [9307041] [18538142] [11146090] [9538213] [624713] [3746130]|., Other bile acids (and their derivatives) such as |FRAME: Muricholates|, |FRAME: CPD-10534| and |FRAME: CPD-7284| are also produced by mouse, bear and pig, respectively (in |CITS: [12543708]|).

Seed oils of a few plant species are enriched in conjugated fatty acids, which are fatty acids containing conjugated or non-methylene-interrupted double bonds. Because conjugated double bonds have high rates of oxidation, seed oils rich in conjugated double bonds are used commercially as drying agents in paints and varnishes., The conjugated double bonds are introduced by "conjugases", divergent forms of |FRAME: AT3G12120| (|FRAME: EC-1.14.19.22|). Conjugases act on fatty acids bound to phosphatidylcholine as substrates, as has been shown for FAD2 enzymes, and modify an existing double bond to produce the conjugated double bonds with or without introducing a new double bond., |FRAME: CPD-8228 Calendate| ((8E,10E,12Z)-octadeca-8,10,12-trienoate) is a conjugated form of |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|. It is a major fatty acid component of the seed oil of Calendula officinalis, an annual flowering plant in which |FRAME: CPD-8228| comprises more than 40% of the seed lipid fatty acids., |FRAME: CPD-8228 Calendate| is derived from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| by a fatty acid conjugase that converts a cis Δ9 double bond into a conjugated trans-trans double bond system |CITS: [11067856][11161042]|.

Developing primary leaves of Secale cereale show a very distinct compartmentation and tissue specificity of flavonoids |CITS:[Strack82a]|. C-glucosyl-apigenin-O-glucosides such as isovitexin arabinoside and galactoside have been found exclusively in the epidermal tissues of rye primary leaves |CITS:[Dellamonica83]| whereas luteolin glucuronide such as |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONIDE| and |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| accumulate only in the photosynthetically active mesophyll of the primary leaves of this plant |CITS: [Schulz85] |. It appears that a connection exists between organogenesis, i.e. the primary leaf development and tissue specific distribution and metabolism of flavonoids |CITS:[Schulz86] [Schulz88a]|. The physiological role of luteolin and its glucuronide descendants has not been fully established, however a novel function of luteolin was found in the interaction of alfalfa and Rhizobium meliloti as an inducer molecule for nodulation genes |CITS:[3738520]|. , The pathway of luteolin triglucuronide consists of three sequential steps carried out by three position specific flavone glucuronosyltransferases, i.e. luteolin-7-O-glucuronosyltransferase (LGT) which glucuronidates |FRAME:5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE| in the 7-O-position of the A-ring, the luteolin-7-O-glucuronide-2"-O-glucuronosyltransferase (LMT) which adds a further |FRAME:GLUCURONATE| to the 2"-position of the first added |FRAME:GLUCURONATE| and the luteolin-7-O-diglucuronide 4'-O-glucuronosyltransferase (LDT) which specifically glucuronidates the 4'-position of the C-ring |CITS:[Schulz88]|. The first two steps occur in the cytosol which has been confirmed by the cytosolic location of the corresponding enzymes LGT and LMT by means of cellular fractionation. The last step of the pathway is carried out in the vacuole where the final product |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| is stored and the LDT has been found to operate |CITS:[24177970]|. , The luteolin triglucuronide biosynthesis seems to occur in dependence of the age of the developing leaves. The final product |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| accumulates until day 5 of leaf development coinciding with high activities of the involved glucuronosyltransferases LGT, LMT and LDT. After day 5 a sharp drop of the luteolin trigucuronide is observed |CITS:[Schulz88] [Schulz88a]|. It appears that |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| is then transported to the apoplastic space where it is subjected to degradation (see |FRAME:PWY-7445|).

Summary: General Background, Juvenile hormones, a group of sesquiterpenoids, regulate several processes including embryonic development, metamorphosis, and reproduction in many insect species. |FRAME:CPD-8838 Juvenile hormone III| (JH III) is the most widespread juvenile hormone in insects |CITS: [15355237]|. One of the main roles of JH III is preventing metamorphosis by modulating |FRAME: ECDYSONE| action. When JH III is present, |FRAME: ECDYSONE| causes insect to repeat the most recent stage, and |FRAME: ECDYSONE| must act in the absence of JH in order for metamorphosis to be initiated. JH III is synthesized and released from the corpora allata (CA), a pair of small endocrine glands with nervous connections to the brain |CITS: [14599502]|. , The late stages of JH III biosynthesis start with |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, which is produced via the |FRAME: PWY-922 mevalonate pathway|. |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is hydrolyzed by a pyrophosphatase to |FRAME: 2-TRANS6-TRANS-FARNESOL|, then oxidized successively to |FRAME: 2-TRANS6-TRANS-FARNESAL| and |FRAME: CPD-12585| by an alcohol dehydrogenase and an aldehyde dehydrogenase, respectively., The next two steps differ depending on the insect order. In Orthoptera, Dictyoptera and mosquitoes |FRAME: CPD-12585| is methylated by a SAM-dependent methyltransferase to form |FRAME: CPD-12586|, which is converted by a P450 monooxygenase to the epoxide form |FRAME: CPD-8838| |CITS: [12728004]| (this pathway). In Lepidoptera, on the other hand, methylation follows epoxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-6650|)., Enzymes catalyzing all steps in the pathway have been cloned or characterized in insects, crustaceans or plants, including farnesyl phosphatase, farnesol and farnesal dehydrogenases and oxidases, carboxy methyltransferases, and a cytochrome P450 epoxidase |CITS: [6366103][19940247][16165084][1160503]|. Nevertheless, much remains to be learned concerning the enzymatic activities and modes of regulation associated with this pathway in various species., This Pathway in Plants, JH III has also been identified in a few plant species, including the sedge |FRAME: TAX-388567| |CITS: [11598232]| and |FRAME: TAX-489335| |CITS: [10820832 ]|. The exact role of |FRAME:CPD-8838 JH III| in plants remains under investigation. Early studies suggested that it might act as a deterrent to insect herbivory, bolstered by the finding that insects that come in contact with |FRAME: TAX-388567| have disrupted development |CITS: [TOONG88]|. However, later experiments suggested that JH III might act as an allelopathic chemical to supress the development of competing plants |CITS: [BEDE00]|. Given the fact that |FRAME: TAX-388567| is an invasive weed that can cause serious losses for rice and other crops, developing a better understanding of |FRAME:CPD-8838 JH III| biosynthesis in this species may help to explain its competitive advantage and point to a way to reduce its spread |CITS: [11598232]|., |FRAME:CPD-12586 "Methyl (2E,6E)-farnesoate"|, the compound immediately upstream of |FRAME:CPD-8838 JH III| in this biosynthetic pathway, has also been identified in several plant species (see ref in |CITS: [11598232]|) as well as in crustaceans |CITS: [10876134]|, where it plays a role in regulating development. An enzyme catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-12586|, |FRAME: AT3G44860-MONOMER FAMT| has been identified in |FRAME: ORG-5993|. Transcript levels for this enzyme are up-regulated by a fungal elicitor, as well as jasmonic acid and salicylic acid treatment, suggesting a possible involvement in plant defense |CITS: [16165084]| . Though |FRAME:CPD-12586| has not been detected in Arabidopsis in vivo, it has been observed in other plants where the biological importance of it and other JH III precursors remains to be determined |CITS: [11598232][16165084]|.

Summary: N1-methyl-N3-aminocarboxypropyl-pseudouridine (m1acp3ψ) is considered the most complex modification found in eukaryotic rRNA. The modified base is located at the tip of helix 31 of the 18S rRNA , and is strongly conserved in eukaryotes., The formation of this modified nucleotide requires three successive modification reactions. The process begins with the snR35 H/ACA snoRNP guided conversion of |FRAME: URIDINE| into |FRAME: CPD-497| |CITS: [7630735]|. In a second step, the essential SPOUT-class methyltransferase |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.260| (Nep1/Emg1) modifies the pseudouridine to |FRAME: CPD-25378| |CITS: [18208838][20047967][20972225]|, and finally |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.157| (Str3) transfers an N3-aminocarboxypropyl moiety from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, forming the final |FRAME: CPD-25379| modification |CITS: [27084949]|., The two former reactions take place early, in the nucleolus and nucleus, while the third reaction occurs late during 40S rRNA biogenesis in the cytoplasm |CITS: [629754][25200078]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| is a nucleotide sugar involved in the synthesis of diverse plant cell wall hemicelluloses (xyloglucan, xylan) and minor plant metabolites. It is also required for the synthesis of glycoproteins, animal proteoglycans and fungal polysaccharides (for review see |CITS:[12481102]|). , This Pathway in Plants:, In plants, the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| occurs both in the cytosol and in membrane-bound compartments. The major biosynthesis route occurs through the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12575| (UDP-Glc). This conversion involves two enzymatic steps: the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| (UDP-GlcA) by a |FRAME: MGI:1306785-MONOMER| and the subsequent decarboxylation to |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| by a |FRAME: AT3G53520-MONOMER|. Regulation of these enzymes is important in understanding the partitioning of carbon into hemicellulose away from starch, sucrose and cellulose, which are irreversible processes. Biochemical evidence suggests that the timing of expression of |FRAME: MGI:1306785-MONOMER| and to some extent that of |FRAME: AT3G53520-MONOMER| may control the flux of carbon into hemicellulose in vascular differentiating tissues., Key Notes on the Enzymes:, In plants, two different types of UDP-Glc dehydrogenases have been identified so far: the first type, exemplified by the UDP-Glc dehydrogenase isolated from soybean nodules |CITS:[8938413]|, has a unique catalytic activity towards UDP-Glc (EC 1.1.1.22); the second type exemplified by the mammalian-like tobacco dehydrogenase |CITS:[15821883]| has dual dehydrogenase activities towards UDP-Glc (EC 1.1.1.22) and ethanol (EC 1.1.1.1). Similarly, biochemical analysis of UDP-glucuronate decarboxylases suggests that this enzyme may come in different forms |CITS:[15821883]|., This Pathway in Bacteria:, There is also evidence for this pathway in plant-associated bacteria belonging to the family |FRAME: TAX-82115|. Rhizobia are soil bacteria that fix nitrogen in the root nodules of some leguminous plants. In |FRAME: TAX-266834| an operon was identified that contains genes uxe and uxs1 encoding UDP-xylose 4-epimerase and UDP-xylose synthase 1, respectively. Data from real-time 1H-NMR spectroscopy demonstrated the conversion of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| to |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE|, and |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-12513|. These UDP-sugars are then used for the biosynthesis of xylose-containing and arabinose-containing cell surface glycans. Their pathways and the roles that they play in nodulation are only beginning to be elucidated |CITS: [20847005]|., Two orthologs of each gene encoding active enzymes were also identified in other rhizobial species including |FRAME: TAX-216596| (loci R10559 and R10078 for uxe, R10560 and R10077 for uxs). These observations were cited in |CITS: [20847005]| as unpublished data.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TYLOSIN Tylosin| is a macrolide type antibiotic produced by several species of bacteria. It is composed of of a 16-membered branched lactone ring (|FRAME: CPD-15957|) and three sugars, |FRAME: CPD-13969|, |FRAME: CPD-13844|, and |FRAME: Mycinopyranose| |CITS: [5500229]|. While the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1906| is best known for tylosin production and is used for its commercial production |CITS: [10206653]|, some other species produce it as well, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-1927| |CITS: [4405313]| and |FRAME: TAX-1912| |CITS: [14274950]|., Tylosin has a broad spectrum of activity against Gram-positive organisms and a limited range against Gram-negative organisms |CITS: [13711004][14008169][10490072][10684178][10705553]|. It is extremely active against Mycoplasma species isolated from both mammalian and avian hosts |CITS: [14253997][4287117][3991415][8929244]|., Like other macrolides, tylosin has a bacteriostatic effect caused by inhibition of protein synthesis through binding to the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome |CITS: [412822][6662812][10995229][11090288]|., Tylosin is used in veterinary medicine to treat bacterial infections in a wide range of species and is considered very safe |CITS: [13731398][13687109][17421521][4901467][4817062][3617407][8812572]|. It has also been used as a growth promotant in some species |CITS: [4758014][9988049]|, and as a treatment for colitis in companion animals |CITS: [4496763][15756055]|., About This Pathway, The breakthrough in deciphering the biosynthetic pathway of tylosin came with the generation of |FRAME: TAX-1906| mutants blocked in many different steps of the pathway |CITS: [7283418]|. Characterization of the pathway's intermediates that accumulated in the different mutants led to an initial proposal, which was subsequently modified as more data became available. , The first step of the pathway is catalyzed by a very large polyketide synthase complex that condenses molecules of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, |FRAME: CPD-9406| and |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| into |FRAME: CPD-15948| (formerly called protylonolide), a process that is postulated to involve 21 steps |CITS: [7283418]|. The complex comprises five mega genes that span 41 kb, namely |FRAME: G-17874|, |FRAME: G-17875|, |FRAME: G-17876|, |FRAME: G-17877| and |FRAME: G-17878| (ranging from 170 to 460 kD). Each of the proteins contains one or two complete sets of chain extension, as well as fuctional group modification, domains, for a total of seven homodimeric modules. The last protein, TylGV, contains a thioesterase domain that terminates the chain elongation and cyclyzes the product. In addition, a dedicated thioesterase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-17893| gene, is believed to remove aberrant material that would otherwise block the TylG complex |CITS: [10322123]|., The first post-PKS modification is the transfer of the first sugar, a |FRAME: CPD-13844|, to the hydroxyl at position 5 |CITS: [15612702]|. Following that, two of the methyl groups of the aglycone are oxidized. The methyl group at position 20 is hydroxylated and then oxidized to an oxo group which remains intact in the final product |CITS: [7126228]|. The methyl group at position C23 is hydroxylated, and then substituted with a |FRAME: CPD-15941| sugar |CITS:[9651492]|, followed by the attachemnt of |FRAME: CPD-13969| to the 4'-OH group of the already attached |FRAME: CPD-13844| sugar |CITS: [10658660]|., The last steps of the pathway are two methylations of the |FRAME: CPD-15941| sugar which convert it to a |FRAME: Mycinopyranose| |CITS: [855999][7305323][3170602][3170601]|., The tylosin gene cluster is very large, and occupies about 1% of the |FRAME: TAX-1906| chromosome |CITS: [1186964]|. It has been sequenced in several increments, and contains not only the genes shown in this pathway, but also the genes necessary for the synthesis of the three deoxysugars, for a total of at least 44 open reading frames |CITS: [7984112][9031628][10220165][10510490][10658660][16131199]|. The cluster also contains multiple regulators and resistance genes.

Summary: L-Lysine degradation is varied among microorganisms, animals and plants. Although many initiating reactions have been studied, in some organisms not all subsequent reactions have been described. Initiating reactions include: decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.18) in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY0-461|; saccharopine dehydrogenase (EC 1.5.1.8) in |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY|; ε-N-acetylase (EC 2.3.1.32) in |FRAME: LYSDEGII-PWY|; lysine 2-monooxygenase (EC 1.13.12.2) in |FRAME: PWY-5280|; racemase (EC 5.1.1.5) in |FRAME: PWY-5283|; ε-transaminase (EC 2.6.1.36) in |FRAME: PWY-5298|; α-oxidase (EC 1.4.3.14) in |FRAME: PWY-5311|; ε-dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.1.18) in |FRAME: PWY-5314|; aminomutase (anaerobic) (EC 5.4.3.2) in |FRAME: P163-PWY|; and a novel ε-transaminase (EC 2.6.1.71) in |FRAME: PWY-5324|. Reviewed in |CITS: [10714900]|., Common intermediates leading to central metabolism include: |FRAME: ALLYSINE|/|FRAME: CPD-7682|; |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE|/|FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE|; |FRAME: CPD-468|; |FRAME: 2K-ADIPATE|; |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE|; |FRAME: CPD-280|; and |FRAME: GLUTARATE|., In addition, a L-lysine 6-monooxygenase (EC 1.14.13.59) is involved in aerobactin bioxynthesis (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: AEROBACTINSYN-PWY|). An enzyme in human liver catalyzing the deamination of the lysine α-amino group, L-lysine 2-dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.1.15), was suggested by an early paper |CITS: [4291003]| but was not subsequently verified (in |CITS: [14766574]|).

Summary: General Background, Some bacteria living in anoxic environments are able to ferment amino acids to |FRAME: AMMONIA|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: ACET| and short chain fatty acids., Proteins are initially hydrolyzed by exogenous proteases to small peptides and single amino acids, which are then taken up by the bacteria and degraded internally., Acetogenic organisms use the |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| for the synthesis of |FRAME: ACET|, while the so called "syntrophic" bacteria oxidize the short chain fatty acids to |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, provided methanogenic archaea in the environment keep the partial pressure of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| at very low values (see |FRAME:METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., At least one pathway is known for the fermentation of every one of the 20 protein-buildng amino acids. In the case of |FRAME: GLT|, at least five such pathways are known |CITS: [11759672]|., About This Pathway, The methylaspartate pathway is one of the major pathways by which glutamate is fermented and has been first described in a closely related group of soil |FRAME: TAX-186801|. It includes two documented varieties - one in which |FRAME: GLT| is degraded to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (|FRAME:GLUDEG-II-PWY|) and one in which |FRAME: GLT| is degraded into |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (|FRAME:PWY-5088|)., The methylaspartate pathway starts with several non-fermentative steps. In the first step the linear carbon chain of |FRAME: GLT| is rearranged into the branched carbon skeleton of |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE|, facilitating the subsequent elimination of |FRAME: AMMONIA| since the β-H is now activated by the adjacent carboxyl group. |FRAME:MESACONATE Mesaconate| is then hydrated to |FRAME:S-CITRAMALATE|, which is subsequently cleaved to |FRAME:ACET| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|. The pathway continues with the fermentation of pyruvate to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (see |FRAME: CENTFERM-PWY|)., The methylaspartate pathway has also been demonstrated in some enterobacteriaceae isolated from soil, including |FRAME: TAX-35703|, |FRAME: TAX-546| and |FRAME: TAX-582| |CITS: [9385136]|, and in |FRAME: TAX-81464| |CITS: [Nanninga87]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CELLULOSE "Cellulose"| is the most abundant organic polymer found in nature. It is produced by plants, some animals, algae, fungi, flagellates and bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-28448|, |FRAME: TAX-358| and |FRAME: TAX-379| spp. |CITS: [2030672]|. Cellulose is an intrinsic structural component of plant primary and secondary cell walls, building a network with other carbohydrate polymers. Bacteria generally produce cellulose as an extracellular component for mechanical and chemical protection, but it can also be used to facilitate cell adhesion to host tissue |CITS: [7462151]|., Cellulose accounts for about 20% (by weight) of the plant primary cell walls, and about 50% of the secondary cell walls., The primary structure of cellulose is a linear array of D-glucose molecules joined by β (1,4) glycosyl linkage. The biosynthesis of cellulose is catalyzed by the cellulose synthase enzyme complex located in the plasma membrane. Polymer synthesis is coupled to membrane translocation through a channel formed by the cellulose synthase. The enzyme is visualized as rosettes that are composed of six subunits, with each rosette subunit in turn composed of 6 cellulose synthases. Each individual cellulose synthase catalyzes the formation of one glucan chain which then associates with neighbor chains of the same rosette to form cellulose microfibrils |CITS: [12514238]|., About This Pathway, It was hypothesized that cellulose synthesis requires a primer, similar to glycogen biosynthesis. Work in cotton has shown that |FRAME: CPD-11608| can serve as a primer. UDP-glucose can be used to form sterol cellodextrins from |FRAME: CPD-11608|, presumably catalyzed by a cellulose synthase |CITS: [11778054]|. , Eukaryotic cellulose synthases function in macromolecular complexes containing several different enzyme isoforms. At least six cellulose synthase genes were shown to be required in cellulose synthesis in |FRAME: TAX-3701|. |FRAME: G-1681|, |FRAME: G-1682|, and |FRAME: G-1683| are involved in cellulose biosynthesis in the primary walls. |FRAME: G-1684|, |FRAME: G-1685|, and |FRAME: G-1686| are involved in cellulose synthesis in the secondary walls. Mutant and mutant complementation analysis indicate that these isoforms of cellulose synthase are not functionally redundant. The UDP-glucose is channeled in Arabidopsis from sucrose degradation., It has been shown in Arabidopsis that in addition to cellulose synthase |FRAME: MONOMER-2367| is also required in cellulose biosynthesis. It is possibly involved in trimming off defective glucans from the growing microfibrils, or cleaving off the sitosterol-β-glucose primer from the growing glucan chains |CITS: [11351091]|., Bacterial cellulose is implicated in the formation of biofilms, and its synthesis is stimulated by cyclic-di-GMP. Prokaryotic cellulose synthases associate with additional subunits to bridge the periplasm and the outer membrane. In bacteria, cellulose synthesis and translocation is catalyzed by the inner membrane-associated bacterial cellulose synthase BcsA and BcsB subunits. BcsA is the catalytically active subunit, and BcsB is a membrane-anchored subunit that is essential for catalysis.

Glyceollins are the main phytoalexins found in soybean (Glycine max). Consistent with most of the isoflavonoid-derived phytoalexins, glyceollins are induced in response to plant pathogens |CITS: [10888516][6540173]| and related stress |CITS: [12590114]|., The final enzymatic steps in glyceollin biosynthesis include the introduction of dimethylallyl groups to (-)-glycinol leading to two prenylated precursors (glyceollidin I and II) with the subsequent cyclization of those intermediates producing the three glyceollins (I - III) identified in soybean. These steps closely resemble the final biosynthetic sequence reported for phaseollin accumulation in bean |CITS: [Biggs87]|. A fourth glyceollin, the 3-O-methyl derivative of 2-dimethylallyl-trihydroxypterocarpan (2-DMA-THP) has been reported in soybean |CITS: [Lyne78]|, but has not yet been further confirmed by other researchers., Cytochrome P450 dependent enzymes are highly involved in the glyceollin biosynthesis, catalyzing five out of fourteen enzymatic steps |CITS: [Heller94]|, which convert phenylalanine to the final glyceollins. Beside of the P450's involved in, the early and intermediate steps and common to other pathways as well (cinnamte-4-hydroxylase, isoflavone synthase, isoflavone-2'-hydroxylase), the glyceollin specific P450 enzymes (3,9-dihydroxypterocarpan 6a-hydroxylase, prenylpterocarpan cyclase) are recognized as highly inducible, regarded as presumably transcriptionally regulated enzymes  |CITS: [9648734]| and useful for monitoring plant defense response on a molecular level., Prenylation of pterocarpans, and isoflavonoids in general, leads to more complex structures, improves lipid solubility and has been reported to increase their antifungal and antifeedant activity |CITS: [Tahara95]|. Plants, involving the phytoalexin , glyceollin in their defense repertoire, can obviously distinguish between different kinds of stress. Simple wounding of plant , tissues was not sufficient to increase glyceollin production, whereas elicitation with fungal pathogens resulted in a fast and , specific glyceollin accumulation |CITS: [Zahringer78]| |CITS: [Leube83]|., However, it has been shown that such a response is triggered by a complex cascade of events and depends on many different factors including the age of tissues, light and the generation of an "elicitation competency" in the responding cells |CITS: [Abbasi01]|. Glyceollins have been found to be bacteriostatic, hence influencing nitrogen-fixing soybean symbionts. However, rhizobial polysaccharides can act as antagonists in the negative regulation of defense activation |CITS: [12399178]| inducing the production of certain isoflavonoids (daidzein, genistein, isoliquiritigenin) which renders this bacterium insensitive to potentially bactericidal concentrations of glyceollin |CITS: [1622242]|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, As a general rule, most prokaryotes utilize the aspartate de novo pathway, in which the nicotinate moiety of, NAD is synthesized from aspartate (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|)., In eukaryotes, the de novo pathway starts with tryptophan (this pathway)., The role of tryptophan as a precursor in eukaryotic NAD biosynthesis was first suggested by nutritional studies, in which humans stricken with pellagra, a nicotinamide (niacine) deficiency disease, recovered after the addition, of tryptophan or niacin to their diets |CITS: [Krehl45]|. Other studies established tryptophan as a precursor of NAD, in many animal and plant systems |CITS: [6997723]|. This pathway is closely related to the catabolic pathway, of tryptophan (|FRAME: TRPCAT-PWY|), suggesting an evolutionary link between the two., , Though rare, the synthesis of NAD from tryptophan in prokaryotes has been observed in several organisms., Wilson and Henderson reported that |FRAME:TAX-56448| pv. pruni requires niacin for growth, and can use tryptophan or 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid as a substitute |CITS: [14001084]|. Some members of the , Actinomycete group were also reported to utilize tryptophan for NAD biosynthesis |CITS: [5829238]|., Recent studies based on comparative genome analysis have identified the five genes involved in the "eukaryotic", pathway in several bacterial strains, confirming that some bacteria may indeed utilize this pathway rather than the, aspartate pathway |CITS: [14700627]|., In yeast, the de novo pathway consists of six enzymatic steps (catalyzed by the products of the BNA genes), and one non-enzymatic reaction., After the last enzymatic reaction (catalyzed by Bna6p), the de novo pathway converges with the salvage, pathway |CITS: [12062417]|., In plants:, In plants current evidence strongly supports the NAD biosynthetic route from L-aspartate (|FRAME:PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|). , However, the finding of gene homologs encoding enzymes of the early steps in the kynurenine pathway (this pathway) in , the genome sequence of rice (|FRAME:TAX-4530|) does not rule out this pathway in monocotyledones and remains , to be further investigated |CITS: [16698895]| |CITS: [14977569]|.

Summary: General Background, Marine organisms, including bacteria, algae and invertebrates, contain many organobromine compounds. Over 2,200 of those, with a wide range of biological properties, have been reported by 2017. Some brominated compounds, such as |FRAME: PBDEs "polybrominated diphenyl ethers"| (BDEs) in their hydroxylated and methoxylated forms, are found across all trophic levels in marine biota, from cyanobacteria and macroalgae to whales and seabirds. In some marine sponges within the |FRAME: TAX-190525| family BDEs can exceed 10% of the sponge tissue by dry weight |CITS: [Unson94][Becerro04]|., Other compounds, such as the brominated biphenyl |FRAME: CPD-20552|, the brominated bipyrrole |FRAME: CPD-20553|, and the hybrid |FRAME: CPD-20554|, have been shown to be synthesized by several species of |FRAME: TAX-53246|, a marine γ-proteobacterial genus often associated with eukaryotic hosts |CITS: [4380876][Andersen74][12543647]|., To find the genes encoding the biosynthesis of brominated compounds, the genomes of two |FRAME: TAX-53246| species, |FRAME: TAX-1315281| and |FRAME: TAX-1353533|, were sequenced, and the genomes were searched for homologs of two genes known to be involved in the formation of chlorinated pyrroles - |FRAME: G-55300| and |FRAME: G-55299| (based on the assumption that a similar mechanism may operate in the formation of chlorinated and brominated pyrroles). The search led to the identification of a brominated marine pyrroles/phenols (bmp) biosynthetic gene cluster in both bacteria |CITS: [24974229]|., Cloning of the bmp1-8 genes and their expression in |FRAME: TAX-562| led to production of many typical brominated compounds, including brominated phenols, pyrroles, biphenyls, bipyrroles and hydbrid phenyl-pyrrole molecules. By expressing the bmp cluster with individual gene deletions it was possible to delinetate the function of the individual enzymes, and to show that the cluster encodes all of the enzymes that are necessary for production of brominated phenols, brominated pyrroles, and their derivatives |CITS: [24974229]|., About This Pathway, Early isotope feeding experiments suggested that |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is the precursor for bromophenols |CITS: [Hanefeld94]|. However, the exact pathway became known only after the bromophenol biosynthetic gene cluster was sequenced from two strains of |FRAME: TAX-53246| |CITS: [24974229]|. |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is formed from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-55295| gene. |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-20548| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.55|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-55296| gene. This unusual brominase, which resembles flavin-dependent oxygenases, catalyzes two successive brominations, the second of which also involves decarboxylation. While the enzyme has been shown in vivo to also catalyze a third bromination, forming |FRAME: CPD-20551|, the main product appears to be |FRAME: CPD-20548| |CITS: [24974229]|., In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-713587|, the synthesis of brominated phenols ends at |FRAME: CPD-20548| and possibly |FRAME: CPD-20551| and/or methoxylated forms of those. Other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1353533|, |FRAME: TAX-1315281|, and |FRAME: TAX-717774|, which possess the |FRAME: G-55297| gene encoding |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18|, are able to produce many biphenyl and biphenyl ethers formed by coupling of the basic brominated phenols (see |FRAME: PWY-7932|. In addition, organisms that have the genes required for production of both brominated phenols and brominated pyrroles (see |FRAME: PWY-7931|), as well as |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18|, can produce hybrid compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-20554| (also described in |FRAME: PWY-7932|) |CITS: [24974229]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase I (NDH-1) and cytochrome bo oxidase, the transfer of electrons from NADH to oxygen is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [3122832]|. , By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is thought to function as a proton pump translocating 4H+ per NADH oxidised (2e-) [H+/e- = 2] however a lower ratio of 3H+/2e- has also been proposed |CITS: [8892824], [22392981]|. Cytochrome bo oxidase contributes to the PMF (H+/e-=2) through its action as a proton pump (H+/e-=1) |CITS: [2544445]| and through a redox loop mechanism (H+/e-=1) (|CITS: [1850294]| and see review by |CITS: [9230919]|). , During glucose limited aerobic growth E. coli directs electron flux through both NDH-I and |FRAME: NADH-DHII-MONOMER "NADH dehydrognease II| (NDH-II) |CITS: [8491720]|. Electron transport from NADH to oxygen is not affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but is significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II which suggests that NDH-II is used preferentially in aerobic respiration |CITS: [9063459]|, Cytochrome bo oxidase is expressed when levels of oxygen are high |CITS: [6365921]| unlike the cytochrome bd oxidase which is expressed under oxygen-limiting conditions |CITS: [2172211], [8576043]|.

Summary: The polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|) are a group of positively charged organic polycations that are involved in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [3157043][4873311][1409623][2185470]|. While it is clear that polyamines are essential for normal cell growth, we still do not fully understand their specific molecular functions in vivo |CITS:[3157043]|. |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| are found in all life forms, and |FRAME:SPERMINE| is found mostly in eukaryotes. A few bacterial species that were reported to contain |FRAME:SPERMINE| include |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS:[4875413]| and |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS: [13538999]|., Unlike |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, |FRAME:SPERMINE| is not essential for viability in eukaryotes. Exogenous |FRAME:SPERMINE| supported growth of |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|-depleted cells only after its degradation into |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| |CITS: [kramer96]| and |FRAME:SPERMINE|-defficient transgenic mice, which were generated by eliminating the SpmS gene, located on the X chromosome, were viable |CITS: [ 9467015]|. Although, the lack of |FRAME:SPERMINE| biosynthesis resulted in a phenotype in affected males that included symptoms of circling behavior, hyperactivity, head shaking, inner ear abnormalities, deafness, sterility, a profound postnatal growth retardation, and a propensity to sudden death. The symptoms were eliminated when the gene was overexpressed in the mice. These results showed that |FRAME:SPERMINE| synthesis is needed for normal growth, viability, and fertility in male mice |CITS: [15459188]|., In |FRAME:TAX-4932| the lack of |FRAME:YLR146C| had no obvious manifestation on the mutant phenotype and the homozygous Δspe4 diploid cells sporulated normally indicating that |FRAME:SPERMINE| in yeast was not essential for growth and development. Hence, the role of |FRAME:SPERMINE| in yeast remains unclear and needs further research. The high amino acid identity (50%) between the |FRAME:YPR069C-MONOMER| and |FRAME:YLR146C-MONOMER| prompted the suggestion that |FRAME:YLR146C-MONOMER| may have been descended from |FRAME:YPR069C-MONOMER| by gene duplication |CITS:[9573363]|., |FRAME:SPERMINE| is formed by the addition of a propylamine moiety to |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, catalyzed by an aminopropyltransferase termed |FRAME: CPLX-6908|. The source of the propylamine group is decarboxylated |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (|FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE|) which is produced by the action of the pyruvoyl-containing enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6906|. Summary: General Background, Some bacteria living in anoxic environments are able to ferment amino acids to |FRAME: AMMONIA|,, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "short chain fatty acids"|. Proteins are initially hydrolyzed by exogenous proteases to small peptides and single amino acids, which are then taken up by the bacteria and degraded internally., Acetogenic organisms use the |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| for the synthesis of |FRAME: ACET|, while the so called "syntrophic" bacteria oxidize the short chain fatty acids to |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, provided methanogenic archaea in the environment keep the partial pressure of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| at very low values (see |FRAME:METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., At least one pathway is known for the fermentation of every one of the 20 protein-buildng amino acids. In the case of |FRAME: GLT|, at least five such pathways are known |CITS: [11759672]|., The hydroxyglutarate pathway described here is one of the major pathways by which glutamate is fermented. It falls into the category of the 2-hydroxyacid pathway, a general pathway by which approximately half of the proteinaceous amino acids are reduced via their corresponding 2-hydroxy acids. Amino acids other than glutamate that can be fermented via the 2-hydroxyacid pathway include: |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: CYS|, |FRAME: GLN|, |FRAME: HIS|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: TYR|., These amino acids, similar to |FRAME: GLT|, may also be fermented by other pathways., About This Pathway, The first step of the 2-hydroxyacid pathway involves the conversion of the amino acid to the 2-oxo (2-keto) acid via a transamination or deamination reaction. The 2-oxo acid is subsequently reduced to the corresponding 2-hydroxyacid, which is then activated to its CoA ester and dehydrated to the enoyl-CoA (in this case |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA|) |CITS: [LENGELER99]|. |FRAME:CROTONYL-COA "Crotonyl-CoA"| disproportionates to yield |FRAME:ACET| and |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID| as follows: 1 molecule of |FRAME:CROTONYL-COA| is oxidized to 2 molecules of |FRAME:ACET| (via |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|), and 1 molecule of |FRAME:CROTONYL-COA| is reduced to |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID| (via |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|) |CITS: [Gottschalk1986]|., This pathway is found in organisms living in anoxic niches within humans and animals, including members of the genera |FRAME:TAX-904|, |FRAME:TAX-1485|, |FRAME:TAX-848| and |FRAME: TAX-1257|. Another major pathway by which glutamate can be fermented is the methylaspartate pathway, which is used by several |FRAME:TAX-1485| and enterobacteria spp. That pathway also produces butanoate, but in addition produces |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| (see |FRAME:GLUDEG-II-PWY|)., Two of the most interesting reactions in this pathway are the 1) reversible dehydration of |FRAME: 2-HYDROXYGLUTARYL-COA| to |FRAME: GLUTACONYL-COA| with a syn-geometry |CITS: [7398622]|, and 2) the decarboxylation of |FRAME: GLUTACONYL-COA| to |FRAME:CROTONYL-COA|. The dehydration reaction is of interest, because the forward and reverse reactions cannot be explained by an ionic mechanism. Consequently, a radical mechanism has been postulated |CITS: [7607244]|. In the forward direction the hydrogen atom is abstracted from the non-activated β position, and in the reverse direction, a hydroxyl group from water is added to the asymmetric double bond at the C-2 position rather than at C-3 as would have been expected based on typical acid-base catalysis. The decarboxylation reaction is of interest because the free energy of decarboxylation is used to translocate sodium ions across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [6628393]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22702 Carbaryl| is acarbamate insecticide commonly sold under the brand name Sevin. Part of the carbaryl molecule resembles |FRAME: ACETYLCHOLINE|, causing it to bond to |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.7|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.8|. The binding is reversible, but the resulting carbamoylated enzymes undergo the final hydrolysis step of the catalysis very slowly (minutes) compared with the naturally-acetylated enzymes (microseconds), resulting in significant inhibition of their natural activity. As a result, carbaryl interferes with the cholinergic nervous system, as the effects of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine cannot be terminated by carbamoylated acetylcholinesterase. This results in muscle spasms and eventually death., Carbaryl is highly toxic to insects, but is detoxified and eliminated rapidly in vertebrates. Since they is neither concentrated in fat nor secreted in milk, carbaryl-based insecticides are commonly used in the US for food crops. Carbaryl is also the active ingredient in Carylderm shampoo, which is used against head lice., Although approved for more than 100 crops in the US, carbaryl is illegal in many countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Iran, Germany, and Angola, due to the fact that it kills both targeted and beneficial insects (e.g., honeybees), as well as crustaceans., About This Pathway, Carbamate pesticides such as |FRAME: CPD-22702 Carbaryl| do not persist in the environment for a long time. It was noted already in 1972 that |FRAME: CPD-22702| hydrolyzes to form |FRAME: NAPHTHOL|, |FRAME: METHYLAMINE|, and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [Vontor72]|. The enzymes that catalyze this transformation (|FRAME: EC-3.5.1.137|), have been purified and characterized from various organisms |CITS: [1785941][16348989][8407847][11445174][11872471][12149124][14612234][29079626]|. |FRAME: NAPHTHOL| is metabolized further to |FRAME: CPD-110|. Further degradation depends on the strain - some organisms metabolize it to |FRAME: CPD-633|, while others metabolize it to |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [3920177][3086270][1903914][10049857][11375667]|., Many organisms have been shown to utilize |FRAME: CPD-22702| as their sole source of carbon and energy. In addition, the |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| that is formed can be used by some of the organisms as their sole source of nitrogen |CITS: [30315077]|. , The pathway from |FRAME: NAPHTHOL| to |FRAME: CPD-110| was first investigated in 2005 in a study of three |FRAME: TAX-286| strains able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-22702| as the sole source of carbon and energy. That study found that the next intermediate is |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE-12-DIOL|, and characterized the activity of the enzyme responsible for this transformation, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.M78| |CITS: [16204509]|., The transformation from |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE-12-DIOL| to |FRAME: SALICYLALDEHYDE| was shown to be more complex than proposed in |CITS: [16204509]|. Work by Eaton and Chapman, who studied the degradation of |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE|, has established that the transformation requires three different enzymes - |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.56|, |FRAME: EC-5.99.1.4|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.45| |CITS: [1447127]|. The last activity of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.65|, has been demonstrated in several |FRAME: CPD-22702| degraders |CITS: [23728496]|., A contig containing all the |FRAME: PWY-8111| genes was isolated in 2016 from |FRAME: TAX-1586081| and the full sequence was deposited in Genbank (entry KU522233).

Summary: General Background, Cytokinins play important physiological roles in plants, from promotion of cell division, to release of lateral buds from apical dominance or delay of senescence. Although their biological activity, signal transduction and metabolism have long been studied, much remains to be uncovered of their genetics and biosynthesis |CITS: [11337393]|., The natural cytokinins are adenine derivatives and can be classified by the configuration of their N6-side chain as either isoprenoid or aromatic cytokinins. The most prevalent cytokinins by far are those with an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain, and in particular those with a trans-hydroxylated N6-side chain, such as |FRAME: CPD-4210| and its derivatives., In terms of biological activity, it would seem that, at least in the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, two cytokinin species: |FRAME: CPD-4210| (tZ) and |FRAME: CPD-4209| (iP), are considered to be active forms. By contrast, |FRAME: CPD-4441| (cZ) exhibits only low or no activity in this plant. It has been suggested that |FRAME: CPD-4441| might contribute to the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-4210| through interconversion by a zeatin cis-trans-isomerase |CITS:[12231873]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-4441| is described in |FRAME: PWY-2781|., Multiple routes have been proposed for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-4210|. One pathway is described here. A second, tRNA pathway has been proposed based on the discovery that some tRNA molecules contain an |FRAME: CPD-4207| (iPA) residue at the site adjacent to the anticodon |CITS:[402938]|. The modification is catalyzed by an enzyme that has been identified in various organisms including |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [4346747]|, |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS: [4311031]|, |FRAME:TAX-1579| |CITS: [809333]|, |FRAME:TAX-9606| |CITS: [11111046]| and |FRAME:TAX-4577| |CITS: [342386]|. , About This Pathway, The pathway thought to produce the majority of de novo cytokinins utilizes |FRAME: CPD-4211| and AMP, ADP or ATP as substrates, and proceeds via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-4205|., The isopentenyl group of |FRAME: CPD-4211| is transferred to the N6 of AMP, ADP or ATP, resulting in the production of |FRAME: CPD-4205|, |FRAME: CPD-4203| and |FRAME: CPD-4201|, respectively. These reactions are catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: AT1G68460-MONOMER|. In |FRAME: TAX-3702| seven IPT genes have been identified |CITS:[11313355][11479373][12734720]|., It has been shown that an enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-12015| gene removes the phosphoribosyl group from |FRAME: CPD-4205|, producing |FRAME: CPD-4209|, which can be converted to the active |FRAME: CPD-4210| by a single hydroxylation reaction |CITS: [17287810]|., In addition, another hydroxylase in known to act on |FRAME: CPD-4205|, |FRAME: CPD-4203| and |FRAME: CPD-4201|, converting them to trans-zeatin ribosides |CITS:[15280363]|. Following the removal of the phosphate groups from the di- and tri-phosphate forms, the product, |FRAME: CPD-4206|, is converted to the active form by the |FRAME: G-12015|-encoded phosphoribohydrolase |CITS: [17287810]|., Two possible sources exist for the prenyl group: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA) and the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (MEP). In |FRAME: TAX-3702|, the plastidic MEP pathway is at the origin of the |FRAME: CPD-4210| species, whereas the |FRAME: CPD-4441| derivatives use the cytosolic MVA pathway |CITS: [14726522]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8117| (GLA) is a polyunsaturated (18:3) ω-6 fatty acid (the 6 refers to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid). It is synthesized from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| by Δ6 desaturase enzymes. Unlike its precursor, GLA is not an essential fatty acid for animals, since almost all animals possess a Δ6 desaturase enzyme., GLA is of major importance in animal cells, being the precursor for the synthesis of several Δ6-desaturated fatty acids, such as |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5353|). Δ6-desaturated fatty acids have roles in the maintenance of membrane structure and function, in the regulation of cholesterol synthesis and transport, in the prevention of water loss from the, skin, and as precursors of eicosanoids, including prostaglandins and leucotrienes |CITS: [1334266]|., It has been documented that certain organisms, including some plants |CITS:[11170598][16718484]|, filamentous fungi |CITS:[11112411][10570972]| and cyanobacteria |CITS: [8389613][16328883]| can produce substantial portions of |FRAME: CPD-8117|. In the plant kingdom, |FRAME: CPD-8117| is only found in a few higher plants (including black currants,, evening primrose, borage and hemp), and is usually found exclusively in the seeds., About This Pathway, Mammals have desaturase and elongase enzymes that enable the synthesis of highly polyunsaturated fatty acids from simpler ones, but lack the enzymes necessary for producing the simpler fatty acids (some carnivores, such as cats, are not able to desaturate simpler fatty acids, and must obtain all polyunsaturated fatty acids in their diet |CITS: [1186900]|)., In order to produce |FRAME: CPD-8117|, mammals must obtain |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| in their diet. Once introduced and activated into its |FRAME: CPD-18| form, linoleate can be desaturated to |FRAME: GAMMA-LINOLENOYL-COA| by a 6-desaturase (in plants fatty acid desaturation generally utilizes fatty acids incorporated into lipids rather than their acyl-CoA forms, see |FRAME: PWY-5998|., Desaturation reactions in animals require oxygen, and are catalyzed by a microsomal membrane-bound three-component enzyme complex that includes |FRAME: ENSG00000166347-MONOMER|, an |FRAME: HS02015-MONOMER|, and the fatty acid desaturase. In many cases, as for the human |FRAME: HS05918-MONOMER|, the desaturases are fusion products composed of an N-terminal cytochrome b5-like domain and a C-terminal multiple membrane-spanning desaturase portion, and thus the enzyme complex does not require an additional free cytochrome b5 |CITS: [10860662]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13053 Queuosine| is a modified nucleoside that is present in certain tRNAs in bacteria and most eukaryotes (but not in yeast) |CITS: [ 12697167]|. Queuosine, which is |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines|, occupies the first anticodon position of tRNAs for |FRAME: HIS|, |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: ASN| and |FRAME: TYR| |CITS: [ 4550561]|. This anticodon position pairs with the third "wobble" position in codons, and queuosine improves accuracy of translation |CITS: [ 2988936][11532950]|. The base in queuosine is called |FRAME: QUEUINE|., Most bacteria perform de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13053| [see |FRAME: PWY-6700|]. However, the process is costly, as it starts from GTP and requires many cofactors. Thus salvage pathways exist for recycling |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, |FRAME: QUEUINE|, or |FRAME: CPD-13053|. Recycling pathways are found both in organisms that can synthesize |FRAME: CPD-13053| de novo and in organisms that can't., About This Pathway, The pathway described here is exists in organisms such as the enteropathogen |FRAME: TAX-1496|, which lack the |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| synthesis genes (|FRAME: G7431|, |FRAME: BSU13740|, |FRAME: G6245|, and |FRAME: G7452|) but harbor genes encoding the remaining enzymes of the de novo pathway. It is used to salvage |FRAME: CPD-13053| nucleosides, which are produced by degradation of tRNA. The nucleoside is either produced in vivo inside the cells, or is transported into the cell by a dedicated transporter (see |FRAME: CPLX12WB-78|). It is then hydrolized to |FRAME: QUEUINE| and |FRAME: D-Ribose| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.M3|. |FRAME: QUEUINE Queuine| is converted to |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| by the radical S-adenosyl-L-methionine (radical SAM) enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.3.99.M4| |CITS: [31481610]|. Once formed, |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is incorporated into tRNA as it does in the de novo pathway.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-10247 Sulfoquinovose| is a major component of organo-sulfur compounds in nature |CITS: [428677]|. It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes |CITS: [15012227][17334828]|., Bacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated, and multiple degradation pathways have been described |CITS: [Liu21]|., About this pathway, The first |FRAME: CPD-10247| degradation pathway was characterized in |FRAME: TAX-562| (see |FRAME: PWY-7446|). That pathway results in excretion of |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| out of the cell. A different pathway, which resembles the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"|, was found to operate in several Pseudomonas species, and ends with excretion of |FRAME: CPD-11799| |CITS: [26195800]|., The gene clusters that encode the enzymes of the first two pathway variants are found in proteobacteria, but not in Gram-positive (phylum Firmicutes) bacteria. This observation led to the discovery of a third pathway, which has been characterized from the SQ-degrading Gram-positive bacteria |FRAME: ORG-57071| and |FRAME: TAX-1404| |CITS: [32919372][33036753]|., The pathway consists of three reactions - one is shared with the glycolysis analogous pathway, one is shared with the Entner-Doudoroff pathway analogous pathway, and one is catalyzed by a novel transaldolase enzyme that produces |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| through transfer of the non-sulfonated C3-(glycerone) moiety of |FRAME: CPD-16501| to |FRAME: GAP| as acceptor molecule |CITS: [32919372]|. Like the Pseudomonas pathway, this third variant also ends with the excretion of |FRAME: CPD-11799| out of the cell |CITS: [32919372][33036753]|., All of the enzymes that participate in the pathway are encoded by genes located in a single inducible cluster. Similar clusters have been found largely in the bacterial phyla |FRAME: TAX-1239| (orders |FRAME: TAX-1385|, |FRAME: TAX-186802| and |FRAME: TAX-186826|), |FRAME: TAX-200918 Thermotogae| and |FRAME: TAX-200795 Chloroflexi| |CITS: [33036753]|.

Summary: Sulfite in excess will cause damage to the organism, by breaking disulfide bridges (sulfitolysis), forming metabolic inhibitors such as hydroxysulfonates and interfere with the availability of essential cations required for nutrition |CITS: [Heber98]|., Sulfite oxidation is different in plants and animals. In vertebrates the role of sulfite oxidation lays in the detoxification of sulfite derived from the decomposition of sulfur-containing amino acids. In addition, sulfite is formed from sulfur dioxide, an environmental pollutant, and is provided exogenously, either as a constituent of certain fruits, or as a preservative in dried fruits, vegetables and wine |CITS: [8586770]|., In plants, sulfite is produced as an intermediate during the assimilation of sulfur, by reducing sulfate via sulfite to sulfide to form cysteine. , Both animals and plants possess |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.1|, a molybdenum-containing enzyme that converts sulfite to sulate using oxygen as the electron donor. One major point of difference is the location of the enzyme, which is found in vertebrates in the mitochondria, but is localized to the peroxisome in plants |CITS: [15653809]|., In animals the enzyme is is located in the mitochondrial intermembrane space and is active mostly in the liver, where it catalyzes the terminal reaction in the oxidative degradation of the sulfur-containing amino acids cysteine and methionine (see |FRAME: PWY-5328|)., The enzyme has been isolated from different sources and exists as a homodimer of molecular weight in the range 101-110 kDa. In animals (but not plants) the enzyme also contains a heme group. Each subunit can be proteolytically cleaved into two domains |CITS:[14956]|, the smaller of which contains a b5 cytochrome, while the larger harbors the molybdenum cofactor |CITS: [9242907]|. Sulfite oxidase deficiency is a lethal genetic disease in animals. It can be caused by defects in the sulfite oxidase gene, or in genes involved in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis |CITS: [16048997]|., In plants sulfite oxidation constitutes a converse pathway to sulfate assimilation that occurrs in chloroplasts. The peroxisomal location of sulfite detoxification solves the problem of having two counteracting pathways in the same cell compartment |CITS: [16307306]|. , In contrast to its animal counterpart the plant sulfite oxidase lacks the heme domain, hence being the only known Mo enzyme that possesses no other redox-active centers |CITS: [11598126][16407262]|., While sulfite produced during the process of sulfate assimilation is converted into sulfide rapidly, sulfite oxidase has been described as a 'safety valve' to detoxify increased levels of sulfite |CITS: [16307306]|, which would be harmful to plants. Both enzymatic and non-enzymatic steps are involved in the sulfite oxidation in plants under conditions of high sulfite concentration, as the catalase in the peroxisomes is inhibited by sulfite, which would result in excess hydrogen peroxide, which oxidizes sulfite non-enzymatically |CITS: [16407262]|.

Summary: Several genera of bacteria have been shown to ferment |FRAME: LYS| as a sole source of carbon and nitrogen,, producing |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| and |FRAME:ACET| as well as |FRAME:AMMONIA|., This pathway is often referred to as the lysine fermentation pathway, or the 3-keto-5-aminohexanoate pathway, |CITS: [6811551]|., The first five reactions are distinctive to the pathway. |FRAME: LYS| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-233|, (β-lysine) which is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-1067|, followed by deamination to a keto acid and reaction with, acetyl-CoA to form |FRAME: CPD-672| and |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE|., |FRAME: CPD-672| is deaminated to |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA|, which is reduced to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|., The later reacts with |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE| to produce |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| and |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA|., |FRAME: ACETOACETYL-COA| is split into two |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| molecules. One molecule is shuttled back to |FRAME:CPLX-7527|, while the other is converted to |FRAME:ACET| through an |FRAME: ACETYL-P| intermediates |CITS: [6811551]|., Several enzymes of this pathway have been well characterized in peptide degrading members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-1485|.  The first one, |FRAME: CPLX-7525| is interesting mechanistically and the, crystal structure has been solved |CITS: [16166264]|. The presence of this pathway in the more recently, described |FRAME: TAX-100174| has been suggested by the presence of acetate and butyrate, as end products of lysine fermentation |CITS: [10843071]|., Eight of the genes involved in this pathway were known in 2007, and these genes have been identified in at least 11, bacterial genomes |CITS: [17166837]|.

Summary: Amongst the complex plant metabolic networks producing and directing hundreds of thousands of compounds often involved in defense and interaction with predators and pathogens are the glandular trichome produced acylsugars specifically found in the Solanaceae family |CITS:[21098679]|. Acylsucroses (summarized in |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)|) as well as acylglucoses |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| have been shown to exhibit broad-spectrum insecticidal properties |CITS:[Hawthorne92] [18807203] [Maluf10] [Leckie12]| through interacting with phytohormones |CITS:[21068365]| and feeding behaviors of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94] [Liedl95]|. Acylsucroses have also been found |CITS:[Severson85]| and reported to dispose of pest larvae in Nicotiana plants by serving as first food source for the larvae which in return emit volatiles that attract predators of those larvae |CITS:[21518882]|. Although limited in scope, acylsugars have also been commercially exploited as safe additives to food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical products |CITS:[Hill99]|. , The production of triacylsucroses (this pathway) and tetraacylsucroses (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-11 tetraacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|), acylsugars which predominantly accumulate in the cultivated tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) |CITS:[22988115] [24772058]|, is based on the allocation of precursors provided through monoacylated (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-8 monoacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) and diacylated (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-9 diacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) sucroses. Research on the underlying pathways of acylsugars has been driven by the widespread occurrence and diversity of those specialized metabolites which represent marker compounds for the genus Solanum |CITS:[20113441] [Leckie14]|. The availability of an increasing number of genomes from tomato species, e.g. the stress-tolerant Solanum pennellii |CITS:[25064008]| also opens paths to confer desired properties of wild tomatoes to cultivated tomato species |CITS:[Lawson97]|. The striking diversity of acylated sucrose is particularly obvious in wild species of Solanum (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) and appears to be associated with geographical locations |CITS:[Shapiro94] [23054567]|., A forward genetic screen of the cultivated Solanum lycopersicum M82 and introgression lines of Solanum lycopersicum M82 and Solanum pennellii LA0716 allowed to identify the acyltransferase (ASAT3) of the BAHD family |CITS:[16616872]| located on chromosome 11 which is able to decorate the backbone of |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| at the 3'-position of the furanose moiety. The molecular function of the ASAT3 encoded protein was demonstrated in various ways. RNAi silenced plants of Solanum lycopersicum with gradually reduced ASAT3 expression and subsequent metabolic profiling revealed a strong reduction of the overall acylsucrose production and acylsucroses lacking the acylation at the furanose 3'-position. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13804 "Erythromycin A"| is a macrolide antibiotic with an antimicrobial spectrum similar to or slightly wider than that of penicillin. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-15682| and |FRAME: CPD-15681| are constituents of O-Antigen or capsule polysaccharides in a number of pathogenic bacteria., |FRAME: CPD-15681| has been described as a constituent of the LPS of |FRAME: TAX-630| serotypes O11,23 and O11,24 |CITS: [12147463]|, |FRAME: ORG-6240| |CITS: [7530967]|, |FRAME: ORG-6241| |CITS: [9654072]|, |FRAME: ORG-6242| |CITS: [9113724]|, and |FRAME: TAX-185332| |CITS: [12575896]|, and as a consistuent of the capsule polysaccharides of |FRAME: TAX-272559| and |FRAME: ORG-6243| |CITS: [6185469]|., Like all other O-antigen sugars, these compounds are synthesized in an activated form, coulped to a nucleotide sugar. The genes were named |FRAME: G-17668|, |FRAME: G-17663|, and |FRAME: G-17662|., Two of the genes are very similar to the |FRAME: G-17655| and |FRAME: G-17657| genes of |FRAME: TAX-287|, which encode enzymes involved in |FRAME: PWY-7330| |CITS: [12464616]|. At the time the research was done, the |FRAME: G-17655| gene product was believed to catalyze this activity in |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [12464616]|, and accordingly, the |FRAME: G-17668| gene product was assigned to it as well, even though |FRAME: CPD-15642| was never detected as a product. Summary: Methoxylated aromatic compounds are important components of lignin and are found in significant amounts in the subsurface. The possibility of such compounds serving as substrates for methylotrophic methanogens was studied in 2016, revealing that strains of |FRAME: TAX-660064| are able to use them as methanogenic substrates |CITS: [27738170]|. An extensive genome analysis of |FRAME: TAX-660064| identified an operon that encodes the participating enzymes: a corrinoid protein (|FRAME: BP07_RS03260|), three methyltransferases (|FRAME: BP07_RS03240|, |FRAME: BP07_RS03255|, and |FRAME: BP07_RS03250|) and a corrinoid activator protein (mtoD). A study of |FRAME: TAX-2234| confirmed that the first part of the pathway does indeed occur in this organism. However, in the absence of |FRAME: CoM|, the methyl group of |FRAME: METHYL-THMPT| is processed by different routes., In one route |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.M4|, forms |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: ACET|, forming one molecule of ATP by substrate level phosphoylation. In a different route the methyl group is processed to CO<sub>2</sub> by the enzymes of the |FRAME: PWY-7784| pathway operating in the reverse direction. The latter route is predominant, as CO<sub>2</sub> is the main product. The reducing power that accumulates during the pathway in the form of |FRAME: Reduced-Factor-F420| is discharged by the reduction of sulfate, which acts as the terminal electron acceptor, resulting in production of sulfide |CITS: [33913565]|., Genomes of members of other archaea, such as Bathyarchaeota, Lokiarchaeota, Verstraetearchaeota, Korarchaeota, Helarchaeota and Nezhaarchaeota, encode a similar demethoxylation system, suggesting that the pathway may play an important role in the carbon cycle |CITS: [33913565]|.

Summary: Tyrosinases, widely scattered among animals, plants and fungi, are involved in many biologically essential functions such as pigmentation, sclerotization, primary immune response and host defence., The tyrosinases use molecular oxygen to catalyze two different enzymatic reactions - the ortho-hydroxylation of monophenols to ortho-diphenols (monophenolase, cresolase acticity) and the oxidation of ortho-diphenols to ortho-quinones (diphenolase, catecholase activity). They belong to the family of class 3 copper proteins, which contain two copper atoms at the active site, each stabilized by three |FRAME: HIS| residues |CITS: [10820445]|., The mammalian |FRAME: HS01248-MONOMER| is a melanocyte-specific enzyme critical for the synthesis of |FRAME: MELANIN|, which takes place in a post-Golgi compartment termed the melanosome. This molecule is subject to both enzymatic and non-enzymatic oxidation and polymerization steps that lead to formation of the many different types of melanins that are found in living organisms., Melanin production is also present in bacteria.
