Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-20049 Sinalbin| is an |FRAME: TYR|-derived glucosinolate found in the seeds of white mustard, |FRAME: TAX-3728|, and in many wild plant species |CITS: [19479767]|. In |FRAME: TAX-3728| it comprises about 93% of the total glucosinolate content |CITS: [16248567]|., Like other glucosinolates, sinalbin is a natural pesticide and contributes to the plant's defense against herbivores and, pathogens. Upon wounding sinalbin is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) forming |FRAME: CPD-20056|, a sharp, pungent, and flavored compound with strong antimicrobial and anti-insecticidal properties |CITS: [23575118]|., Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine. Thus, there is scarse information about specific enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of tyrosine-derived glucosinolates., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Summary: General Background, Some invertebrates, protists and fungi must survive prolonged exposure to hypoxia or anoxia. These facultative anaerobes may contain either mitochondria that function anaerobically, or hydrogenosomes as cellular organelles in which reactions of anaerobic respiration occur. Most anaerobic mitochondria use endogenously produced electron acceptors such as |FRAME: FUM| to generate |FRAME: SUC| via membrane-bound fumarate reductase. This enzyme is usually associated with the electron carrier |FRAME: Rhodoquinones "rhodoquinone"|, proton-pumping, and ATP synthase. The pathway shown here has been experimentally demonstrated in some marine invertebrates, but variations of it can be found in other organisms such as the parasites |FRAME: TAX-6251| and |FRAME: TAX-6192| (see below) (reviewed in |CITS: [22688819][12594928][12417132][9693724][7998964]|)., Marine invertebrates can utilize several different anaerobic energy-yielding metabolic pathways when exposed to prolonged conditions of environmental or functional hypoxia or anoxia. These include opine and/or lactate production (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-7351| and |FRAME: PWY-5481|), phosphagen utilization (see |FRAME: MONOMER-18221|), as well as this pathway and the linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-7384| (together referred to as the aspartate-succinate pathway, see |FRAME: PWY-7389|). In addition, metabolic depression can also occur during anaerobiosis resulting in reduction of metabolism below the standard metabolic rate (reviewed in |CITS: [7984874][DEZWAANA96]|., The anaerobic energy metabolism of parasites (metazoan, protozoan and fungal) has also been extensively studied (reviewed in |CITS: [22688819]|) (see pathway class |FRAME: Fermentation|). , About This Pathway, In marine invertebrates the cytosolic end product of glycolysis, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, is a substrate for opine and lactate synthesis (as indicated by the pathway links). It is also a substrate for the coupled transamination reactions in which |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is produced and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is transaminated to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| as shown here. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| transamination is thus coupled to |FRAME: Glycogens "glycogen"| fermentation |CITS: [13973395][SCHOTTLERU84]|. |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID "Oxaloacetate"| is reduced to |FRAME: MAL| by cytosolic malate dehydrogenase. |FRAME: MAL| is then transported into the mitochondrion where it is anaerobically metabolized to |FRAME: SUC|, |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate) and |FRAME: ACET| (as shown in the linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-7384|). Mitochondrial |FRAME: MAL| can also be oxidized to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and enter the TCA cycle which runs at a lower rate during anaerobiosis (|CITS: [FELBECKH80]| and reviewed in |CITS: [7984874]| (see |FRAME: PWY66-398|)., During the anaerobic degradation of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| in the cytosol, the |FRAME: NAD| produced by malate dehydrogenase allows continuous oxidation of |FRAME: GAP| in the glycolytic pathway (see pathway |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY|). Studies have shown that |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| degradation and the concomitant synthesis of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| occurs during early anaerobiosis and suggest that |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is an end product |CITS: [SCHOTTLERU84]|. Summary: General Background, The generic pathway described here is found in organisms of different ecological niches and roles., One type of organisms that employ this enzymatic reaction are the hydrogen bacteria. These organisms are able to use |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as a sole source of electrons and reducing power under aerobic conditions. They are facultative lithotrophs, and are able to reduce |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| via the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|., Most of the hydrogen bacteria possess only a membrane-bound enzyme that transfers the electrons from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| directly to the respiratory electron transfer chain, as described here (see |FRAME: CPLX-841| from |FRAME: TAX-106590|)., A smaller number of hydrogen bacteria possess a soluble hydrogenase that is able to transfer the electrons directly to NAD, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5382|., Another group of organisms that posses this type of hydrogenase are nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. These organisms need to consume the |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| produced by the |FRAME: CPLX-525| in the heterocycsts. Cyanobacteria were found to possess two types of hydrogenases - an NAD-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-8066|, and a dimeric enzyme which can only consume hydrogen, known as an |FRAME:CPLX-8068 "uptake hydrogenase"|., About This Pathway, Almost all of the hydrogen oxidizing bacteria possess a membrane-bound hydrogenase (MBH) (an exception is found in |FRAME: TAX-2074| and |FRAME: TAX-37919|, which contain only a soluble hydrogenase |CITS: [Aggag74]|)., The membrane-bound enzymes are not coupled directly to NAD, and transfer the electrons from the hydrogen to the respiratory chain. This electron transfer results in the generation of a proton motive force and the phosphorylation of ADP to of ATP. In order to generate reducing power, these organisms need to use reverse electron flow, an inefficient process that is reflected in relatively slow growth rates. , Carbon fixation by these organisms is achieved exclusively by the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|, as only anaerobic bacteria such as the methanogens, acetogens or the Chlorobiaceae have electron donors with a sufficiently negative potential, which are required for the |FRAME: CODH-PWY| |CITS: [6271040]|., The exact nature of the respiratory chain in these organismsis is not well known. Likewise, it is not clear at which step do the electrons from the hydrogen enter the system. Several studies indicated that two different routes are involved in the oxidation of NADH and hydrogen in |FRAME: TAX-106590|, with the branch point possibly at ubiquinone |CITS: [107951]|., The electron transport chain in this organism is branched, and contains three c-type cytochromes, five b-type cytochromes, two a-type hemes, one d-type heme, and four different terminal oxidases |CITS: [Koemen91]|. A bo-type oxidase has been implicated as the terminal oxidase for electrons originating from, the memberane-bound hydrogenase |CITS: [8661937]|., Initially it was believed that membrane-bound hydrogenases are composed of a catalytic heterodimer. However, more recent work has shown that the complexes include a third subunit, an integral membrane protein, which was found to be a cytochrome b |CITS: [8257102][10852874]|. The trimeric enzyme mediated electron transfer from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| to a quinone, suggesting a potential connection point between the hydrogenase and the respiratory chain |CITS: [ 1587288]|., Cyanobacteria also possess a membrane-bound hydrogenase, encoded by the genes |FRAME: G-12023| and |FRAME: G-12024|. The role of this enzyme is to consume the hydrogen gas that is produced by the |FRAME: CPLX-525| in heterocysts |CITS:[7846053][10692368]|.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of, polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl, diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme., Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the, polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a, preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone, molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length., However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain, length., Organisms whose main quinone contains a chain of 7 isoprenyl units include some Gram-negative, bacteria (for example, the gliding bacterium |FRAME: TAX-997| and the phototroph |FRAME: TAX-1049|, strain D), but mostly Gram-positive bacteria, such as many members of the |FRAME: TAX-1386|,, |FRAME: TAX-1279| and |FRAME: TAX-1637| genera.,  For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Hemes Heme| (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the common aerobic route for |FRAME: Heme-b| biosynthesis. This pathway involves the enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.3| and |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.4|, which require moelecular oxygen for their respective reactions., There are several types of protoporphyrinogen oxidases: in most eukaryotes and many aerobic or facultative bacteria, such as Firmicutes, the enzyme is a FAD-dependent ~55 kDa protein encoded by the |FRAME: BSU10140| gene. A number of γ-proteobacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-562|, have another type of oxidase, a 21 kDa protein encoded by the |FRAME: EG11485| gene. Most archaea and many other bacteria, including the majority of cyanobacteria, have a third version of the enzyme, a 24 kDa protein encoded by |FRAME: SGL_RS03055| |CITS: [20823222]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8816 "γ-Resorcylate"| and |FRAME: CPD-623| occur in nature as secondary metabolites in plants and fungi |CITS: [18427109][19795855]|. , A bacterial strain that could use |FRAME: CPD-623| as the sole source of carbon (|FRAME: ORG-5953|) was originally isolated by enrichment culture in 1976. The degradation pathway was shown to proceed via |FRAME: CPD-8130|, |FRAME: CPD-294| and |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which is degraded to acetyl-CoA via the |FRAME: PWY-2361| pathway |CITS: [1280][942589]|., The same pathway was subsequently documented in |FRAME: TAX-267998| |CITS: [17158677]|, |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [16963551]| and |FRAME: TAX-101510| |CITS: [26319878]|. While the pathway's intermediates are shared within all of these organisms, variability occurs in the enzymes that catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-623| to |FRAME: CPD-8130|. In |FRAME: TAX-267998| the reaction is catalyzed by a two-component FADH2-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.27|), in |FRAME: TAX-1718| it is catalyzed by a single-component NADPH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.219|), and in |FRAME: TAX-101510| it is catalyzed by a single-component NADH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.220|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1718| can grow on |FRAME: CPD-623| as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [16963551]|., Searching the genome for genes encoding a hydroxyquinol 1,2-dioxygenase using the sequence of the cphA gene from |FRAME: TAX-85085| |CITS: [16269679]| led to the identification of two candidates. Each of these genes resided in a cluster of several degradation genes. Mutation analysis as well as characterization of the enzymes showed that one of the clusters, which included the |FRAME: G18NG-10730|, |FRAME: G18NG-10731|, and |FRAME: G18NG-10732| genes, was essential for |FRAME: CPD-623| degradation, while the other cluster encoded redundant, but not essential, hydroxyquinol 1,2-dioxygenase and maleylacetate reductase., The |FRAME: G18NG-10730| gene was found to encode a novel single-component resorcinol 4-hydroxylase that is specific for NADPH as its electron source. No homologous gene was found in the other cluster. The reason for the redundancy is not known, but it was hypothesized that the genes in the different clusters may be expressed under different conditions |CITS: [16963551]|.

Summary: General Background, Galacturonate (GalA) is a major sugar residue of plant pectic polysaccharides |CITS:[MOHNEN02]| and a minor component of some plant arabinogalactan proteins (Darvill et al., 1980; Yates et al., 1996). GalA is also found in various cell-surface polysaccharides of different Gram negative bacteria (for review see |CITS:[15563616]|). The existence of GalA is not restricted to Gram-negative bacteria being present in the capsular polysaccharide of the Gram-positive human pathogen type-I |FRAME:TAX-1313|, as well as in certain polysaccharides, of the Cyanobacterium spp.. The synthesis of GalA-containing polymers requires UDP-α-D-galacturonate (UDP-GalA)., The formation of UDP-D-GalA occurs via two routes: a) a salvage pathway leading to the formation of UDP-D-GalA from free galacturonate (this pathway), and b) a de novo synthesis route involving the epimerisation of UDP-D-glucuronate by a UDP-D-glucuronate 4-epimerase (|FRAME:PWY-4861|). , In plants, the primary role of the sugar salvage pathways is presumed to be in the recycling of sugars derived from the turnover of macromolecules such as polysaccharides, galactolipids and proteoglycans, which have sugar components. , Key Notes on the Enzymes: The galacturonokinase and UDP-D-galacturonate pyrophosphorylase activities characterizing this pathway have been found in plants from extracts of |FRAME:TAX-3916|; unfortunately, further enzymatic characterization is not available at this time.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation |CITS: [8490246]|. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extend to the outer environment, forming an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces., Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| |CITS: [25969757]|., Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage., |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| |CITS: [10320813]|., About neolacto-series glycosphingolipids, The core structure that defines the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| is Galβ(1,4)GlcNAcβ(1,3)Galβ(1,4)Glcβ-Cer. The first two residues at the non-reducing end, Galβ(1,4)GlcNAcβ (|FRAME: BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSAMINE N-acetyllactosamine|), are also known as the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 precusor disaccharide"|. Some of the common neolacto-series compounds, specifically |FRAME: Neolactotetraosylceramides neolactotetraosylceramides|, |FRAME: Neolactohexaosylceramides neolactohexaosylceramides|, and |FRAME: Neolactooctaosylceramides neolactooctaosylceramides|, are polymers of this disaccharide. These forms were shown to mediate corneal epithelial cell migration following injury |CITS: [7775461]|., Fucosylation of the 3 position of the glucosamine residue within the disaccharide yields a β-D-galactosyl-1,4-(α-1,3-L-fucosyl)-N-acetyl-D-glucosaminyl moiety, which is known as the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| (also known as SSEA-1). The |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| has been implicated in cell-cell recognition, neurite outgrowth, and neuronal migration during development. The related |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x epitope"| plays an important role during early steps of inflammatory response by serving as a ligand to the three known selectins - E-selectin (also known as endothelial leucocyte adhesion molecules, ELAM-1), P-Selectin, and L-selectin, resulting in the capture of leucocytes from the plasma and their attachment to blood endothelial cells |CITS: [2210723][7591266]| (see also the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7831|)., The neolactoglycosphingolipids are a major glycoshingolipids group and have been reported from many different tissues, including erythrocytes |CITS: [12033406]|, brain |CITS: [3667553]|, nerve cells |CITS: [2440989]|, mature myeloid cells |CITS: [8489255]|, as well as tumor cells |CITS: [1567904]|., Sialylation of neolactoglycosphingolipids produces a small number of |FRAME: Gangliosides gangliosides|, which are contained predominantly in the extraneural tissues. These gangliosides include the α(2,3)-gangliosides |FRAME: ACETYLNEURAMINYL-23-BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ET "ganglioside LM1"|, |FRAME: Sialyl-23-neolactohexaosylceramides|, and |FRAME: Neu-23-neolactoheptaosylceramides|, which have been reported from multiple sources, including chicken muscle |CITS: [Chien80]|, rabbit muscle |CITS: [7251579]|, the human peripheral nervous system |CITS: [Chou84]|, and rat nerve cells |CITS: [3989569]|. |FRAME: ACETYLNEURAMINYL-23-BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ET "Ganglioside LM1"| is the predominant ganglioside (61%) of the peripheral nerve myelin |CITS: [3989569][1402926][10526188]|., An α(2,3)-sialyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: HS00798| gene is specific for neolacto-series substrates |CITS: [10206952]|., An α-(2,6)-sialylated neolacto ganglioside, named |FRAME: Ganglioside-6-LM1|, has been reported from human meconium |CITS: [2473071]|. Other, less well charecterized, gangliosides of the neolacto series, including disialylated forms and α(2,6) forms, have been reported |CITS: [7251579][14588011]|, but since their biosynthesis has not been defined, they are not included in this pathway.

Names: cytidylyl copper-molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis // [CuSMoO2] cluster biosynthesis
Summary: Like other aerobic carboxidotrophs, |FRAME: TAX-40137| is an aerobic Gram-negative bacterium that utilizes |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| as its sole source of carbon and energy under chemolithoautotrophic conditions. The key enzyme in the process is |FRAME: EC-1.2.5.3|, which accommodates a unique cofactor in its active site that contains a bimetallic [CuSMoO2] cluster (|FRAME: CPD-23450|). The cofactor is incorporated into the apo-enzyme as |FRAME: CPD-23445|, and is modified further post-incorporation., The 14.54-kb cox gene cluster on the circular DNA megaplasmid pHCG3 of |FRAME: TAX-40137| includes the subcluster coxMSL, which encodes the three polypeptides that make up |FRAME: EC-1.2.5.3|, and the subcluster coxDEFG, which encodes the proteins that are involved in the post-translational modifications of the |FRAME: CPD-23450| |CITS: [10433972][14644498]|., As in most other bacterial molybdoenzymes, the molybdenum ion is coordinated by a molybdopterin cytosine dinucleotide cofactor |CITS: [10430865][2275562]|. The copper ion, which is attached to the molybdenum via a sulfur atom, is also coordinated by the cysteine residue 388 of the active site loop VAYRCSFR found on the enzyme's large subunit |CITS: [10433972][ 7721710]| , The presence of copper was observed only after a structure of the enzyme was derived at a resolution of 1.1 Å (the enzyme was thought to contain selenium prior to that) |CITS: [12475995]|. The bimetallic cluster was shown to have the composition [CuISMoVI(=O)2] when oxidized, and [CuISMoIV(=O)OH2] when reduced |CITS: [12515558]|., The crystal structure of the enzyme was first determined to 2.2 Å at which time shown that the enzyme is a dimer of heterotrimers composed of three different subunbits. The large subunit contains the molybdopterin-cytosine dinucleotide cofactor, the medium subunit contains a FAD cofactor, and the small subunit contains two types of [2Fe-2S] clusters. These cofactors establish an intramolecular electron transport that delivers the electrons generated through the oxidation of |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| at the [CuSMoO2] cluster to [2Fe-2S] I, [2Fe-2S] II, and finally to FAD, from where they are fed into a respiratory chain to generate a membrane potential |CITS: [10430865]|., The cluster is assembled post-translationally, with a sulfur, then copper, added after the molybdenum is in place. These steps are slow and rate limiting in the synthesis of the enzyme |CITS: [16091936]|. Sulfur is inserted by CoxD |CITS: [19189964][23077613]| by a MgATP-dependent, reductive sulfuration of [MoVIO3] to [MoVO2SH]. The molybdenum atom is then reoxidized and Cu1+-ion is integrated. The copper is supplied by the soluble CoxF protein, which forms a complex with the membrane-bound CoxE protein. The initial copper source is Cu2+-phytate, which is mobilized through the phytase activity of CoxF and then transferred to the CoxF putative copper-binding site |CITS: [25377894]|., |CITS: [19189964]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-10614| (MCPA) is a systemic foliar herbicide used to control annual and perennial weeds in small grains,, grassland, and turf. MCPA is usually formulated as either an aqueous salt (e.g., dimethylamine, DMA or sodium salts), or as an ester (e.g., 2-ethylhexyl). Formulations of MCPA are registered world-wide for use on agricultural crops such as, cereals, grasses and pulses, and in non-crop areas |CITS: [15896442]|., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-264198|, can use |FRAME: CPD-10614| as the sole sources for carbon and energy, |CITS: [Pieper88]|. Other organisms that can degrade MPCA have been reported |CITS: [5123885][5123886]|., The genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-10614| degradation by |FRAME: TAX-264198| are located on the conjugative plasmid, pJP4. The genes on this plasmid are organized in three clusters. One cluster includes the, |FRAME: G-10972| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-14384| (so called because it is also responsible for, the degradation of the more common herbicide |FRAME: CPD-9009|)., The two other operons, named tfdI (or simply tfd) and tfdII, are very similar to each, other, and each encodes the same set of five enzymes, although not at the same order. Some differences in the function, and regulation of the proteins encoded by the two clusters have been reported |CITS: [16597983][14676989]|., The enzymes encoded by pJP4 catalyze the overall conversion of MPCA to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|., |FRAME: MONOMER-14384|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10972|, cleaves the ether bonds of |FRAME: CPD-10614| and, produces |FRAME: CPD-10615| in a |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent reaction., The chlorophenol is a substrate for the two chlorophenol hydroxylases encoded by the |FRAME: G-10973| and, |FRAME: G-10974| genes, which transform it to |FRAME: CPD-10616|. , The later is then converted to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| by the enzymes encoded by other tfd genes, (see |FRAME: PWY-6102|)., Further metabolism of |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| to tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, is encoded by chromosomal genes. , The enzymes described in this pathway also catalyze the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-9009| (2,4-D) (see, |FRAME: PWY-6085|).

Background, Nitrogen is a vital building block of amino and nucleic acids, and despite its abundance in the atmosphere is a limiting nutrient in many ecosystems. This is because the dinitrogen molecule can not be used directly for biosynthesis and must be converted to the reduced form |FRAME: AMMONIA|, to become bioavailable. The process of reductive breakage of the nitrogen-nitrogen bond to form two |FRAME: AMMONIA| molecules is called nitrogen fixation, and can be performed biologically only by certain bacteria and archaea that possess the nitrogenase enzyme system (microorganisms that fix atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia are called diazotrophs). This system is is only active under anaerobic conditions as it is extremely sensitive to molecular oxygen., Filamentous cyanobacteria perform nitrogenase activity in specialized cells known as heterocysts, which possess thicker cell envelope that allows reduced oxygen permeability. The heterocysts do not perform photosynthesis, and thus these organisms physically separate oxygen evolution from nitrogenase activity, allowing the filament to perform both processes simultaneously |CITS: [16371161]|. Non-heterocystous cyanobacteria perform these functions altrernatively during light and dark periods, separate oxygen evolution from nitrogenase activity temoprally |CITS: [1620069]|. , While most of the nitrogen-fixing organisms are free living, some exist in a symbiotic relationship with plants. A well known example is |FRAME: TAX-356|, which live within the root nodules of leguminous plants., In non-oxygenic phototrophs such as the purple non-sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1061| no oxygen is produced during photosynthesis, hence they naturally foster the anaerobic conditions required by hydrogenase and nitrogenase during photosynthesis., Nitrogen fixation is accompanied by an obligatory reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|. Of the diazotrophic microbes known to possess this function, some species of |FRAME: TAX-1117| are among the best categorized |CITS: [16371161]|. , About This Pathway, The reaction in this pathway is catalyzed by a multiprotein nitrogenase complex, comprising of a dinitrogenase reductase component and a dinitrogenase component |CITS: [1529353]|. Dinitrogenase reductase transfers electrons from the external electron donor (a ferredoxin in the case of |FRAME: EC-1.18.6.1|, or a flavoprotein in the case of |FRAME: EC-1.19.6.1|) to dinitrogenase. Dinitrogenase is a metalloprotein that reduces dinitrogen in three successive two-electron reductions: nitrogen to diimine, diimine to hydrazine, and hydrazine to two molecules of ammonia and one molecule of hydrogen. , Three types of nitrogenase systems have been described based on the metal content of the second cofactor (they also differ in their protein structures). Type I contains a molybedenum and iron cofactor (|FRAME: CPD-41 "[FeMo]-cofactor"|), type II contains vanadium and iron cofactor ([FeV]-cofactor) and type III contains only iron ([FeFe]-cofactor). Different genes and gene products are associated with the different types |CITS: [11848850]|. All diazotrophic organisms sequenced to date encode an [FeMo]-nitrogenase, but some also have one or two alternative forms. , It has been reported that of the three nitrogenases, the [FeFe] nitrogenase and [FeV] nitrogenase produce more |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| than the [Mo] nitrogenase., The reduction of nitrogen to ammonia is highly endergonic and requires metabolic energy, which is provided in the form of ATP |CITS: [17903205]|. It is accompanied by the reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [4344006]|. In a pure nitrogen atmosphere, more of the electrons are allocated for nitrogen reduction than for proton reduction and the reaction requires a minimum of 16 ATP molecules to reduce nitrogen to ammonia and hydrogen |CITS: [11875125]|. , In addition to nitrogen and protons, the nitrogenase complex can reduce |FRAME: ACETYLENE|, |FRAME: HCN|, and a number of other small molecules |CITS: [11848850]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-14447| is a common intermediate in the aerobic degradation of many aromatic compounds, including |FRAME:CATECHOL|, |FRAME:TOLUENE|, |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE| and |FRAME:CPD-926|., The degradation pathway depicted here has been described in several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-83333|. The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway are often found on plasmids, such as naphthalene catabolic plasmids (pWW60-22 |CITS: [7496535]| and pND6-1 |CITS: [15246534]|), nitrobenzene catabolic plasmids (pNB1 and pNB2, |CITS: [10633088]|) and toluene catabolic plasmids (TOL) such as pWW102 |CITS: [9611813]|., In this pathway |FRAME:CPD-14447| is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-2-KETOVALERATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:EC-4.2.1.80|. |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-2-KETOVALERATE| is broken into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ACETALD|, which is then converted to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| by |FRAME:MONOMER-354| |CITS: [2681159][7496535]|., In aqueous solutions |FRAME: CPD-14447| rapidly ketonizes to the β,γ-unsaturated ketone |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| before a much slower conversion to the α,β-unsaturated ketone |FRAME: CPD-14441|. At equilibrium, |FRAME: CPD-14441| predominates. Because of the quick transformation to |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, it has initially been thought that the latter is the actual tautomer that is formed by catabolic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.7.1.8|, |FRAME: EC-3.7.1.9|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.77|, and acts as the substrate for |FRAME:EC-4.2.1.80|. However, careful analysis has shown that the actual intermediate is |FRAME: CPD-14447| |CITS: [15301547][17902707]|.

Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, In most plants, purine nucleotides are completely degraded to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| via the ureides |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|. This degradation proceeds via the intermediates |FRAME: XANTHINE| and |FRAME: URATE|., The initial step of GMP degradation in this pathway is the conversion of GMP to |FRAME: GUANOSINE|, which can be degraded to |FRAME: XANTHINE| via |FRAME: GUANINE|. The enzyme that converts |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME: GUANINE|, guanosine deaminase, has been reported in fungi |CITS: [7551735]| and green plants |CITS: [GURANOWSKI82]|. A different route from |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME: XANTHINE| is described in |FRAME: PWY-6607|., |FRAME: XANTHINE| is converted to |FRAME:URATE| by xanthine dehydrogenase |CITS: [14726515]|, and the latter is converted to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as described in |FRAME: PWY-5691|., This plant/fungal pathway is very similar to that found in mammals. However, mammals do not have the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-11783| (EC 3.5.4.15) and instead use |FRAME: CPLX-6181| (EC 2.4.2.1) |CITS: [14725335]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6608|).

Summary: Preliminary note, It should be noted that |FRAME:CPD-1789| has been mistakenly called D-erythroascorbic acid (D-erythroascorbate) in the literature which has been remedied by the International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (IUBMB) in May 2008., About the pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-1789| from |FRAME:D-ARABINOSE| has been observed in |FRAME:TAX-4932| and other fungi |CITS:[10802179] [11281285]|. Since the occurrence of |FRAME:CPD-1789| has been reported in |FRAME:TAX-4932| and the fungus Lypomyces starkeyi |CITS:[Nick86]| its physiological function has been a matter of debate. |FRAME:CPD-1789 Dehydro-D-arabinono-1,4-lactone| is an analog of |FRAME:ASCORBATE| which performs a number of important functions in plants and animals such as an antioxidant, co-factor for Fe-containing enzymes, electron acceptor and controller of developmental processes (reviewed in |CITS:[Loewus99] [11153268]|. , Although the existence of |FRAME:ASCORBATE| has been reported in yeast |CITS:[4555845]| and the capability of |FRAME:TAX-4932| demonstrated to synthesize vitamin C under certain conditions |CITS:[10802179]| it is widely acknowledged that |FRAME:TAX-4930| produces |FRAME:CPD-1789| instead. The similarity in molecule structure, pathway sequence and catalyzing enzymes between |FRAME:ASCORBATE| biosynthesis (see for example |FRAME:PWY4FS-11|) and |FRAME:PWY3O-6| has prompted the isolation, purification and characterization of the corresponding enzymes. , The first step in the pathway is catalyzed by D-arabinose dehydrogenase (ARA). There are two D-arabinose dehydrogenases characterized in |FRAME:TAX-4932|, the NADP+-dependent enzyme ARA1 |CITS:[9920381] [17151466]| and the NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase ARA2 |CITS:[17097644]|, the latter characterized as the main contributor in the production of |FRAME:CPD-1789|. The final step in the pathway, the oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-356| yielding |FRAME:CPD-1789| is carried out by the D-arabinono-1,4-lactone oxidase (ALO1) |CITS:[10094636] [369458] [10508108]|. , The physiological significance of |FRAME:CPD-1789| in |FRAME:TAX-4932| and other fungi is not clear yet and further research is needed to resolve the question. However, it has been shown that |FRAME:CPD-1789| acts as an antioxidant |CITS:[10094636] [10508108]|, has shown vitamin C activity |CITS:[Shao93]| and is therefore considered as a fungal compound with similar properties as |FRAME:ASCORBATE| has in plants and animals.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) is a side product in the biosynthesis of several important compounds., An important case is polyamine synthesis, where |FRAME: MET| is consumed through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) in a reaction that releases MTA (see the pathway |FRAME:POLYAMINSYN3-PWY|). MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration needs to be tightly regulated., Another example is found in the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287|, where MTA is a by product in the synthesis of the autoinducer compounds |FRAME: CPD-10783| and |FRAME: CPD-10784| (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., To ensure that the pathways that produce MTA as a byproduct are not blocked, the organism must remove this compound. The most common way of achieving it is through the |FRAME: PWY-4361 "methionine salvage"| pathway, in which MTA is recycled through a series of reactions back to AMP and |FRAME: MET|., While the methionine salvage pathway is widely conserved, its initial steps, converting MTA to |FRAME:CPD-444|, differ among microorganisms and plants (such as the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [8694776]| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [12022921]|), protozoans (such as |FRAME: TAX-5741| and |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [2854458]|) and mammalian cells. The different routes employed by these organisms are described in the different pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|., About This Pathway, This pathway is found mostly in bacteria and plants. In it MTA is degraded to |FRAME:CPD-444| (MTRP) in two steps; MTA is initially cleaved to |FRAME:ADENINE| and |FRAME:CPD-560| (MTR) by |FRAME:ENZRXN-1450|, followed by phosphorylation of MTR to MTRP by |FRAME: KP1_RS07375-MONOMER|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, A reductive Stickland reaction of |FRAME: PRO| is known to serve as an electron sink that can be coupled to the oxidation of several different amino acids., |FRAME: PRO| needs to first be converted to |FRAME: D-PROLINE| by |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.4|, since only the latter can serve as a substrate for the key enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.1|., This enzyme contains a pyruvoyl prosthetic group and |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| that are essential for its catalytic activity |CITS: [JBC242-5158][1262330][659433][7372621][8203910][10085076]|. The enzyme consists of the PrdA and PrdB sububits, and also requires an additional protein encoded by the prdC gene |CITS: [Kabisch01][20937090]|., According to the proposed model, catalysis by |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.1|, begins by the binding of |FRAME: D-PROLINE| by the pyruvoyl group of the PrdA protein. The dissociated, nucleophilic selenocysteine moiety in PrdB attacks the α-C-atom of D-proline, leading to a reductive cleavage of the C-N-bond of the pyrrolidine ring and the formation of a selenoether. The selenoether is then cleaved by a cysteine moiety of PrdB, resulting in a mixed selenide-sulfide bond in the active site of PrdB., This bond is then reduced by a special terminal sulfide-selenide group of PrdC, restoring PrdB to its active state, and resulting in formation of a mixed selenide-sulfide bond in PrdC, which is then reduced to the active form by NADH., Finally, |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| is released from PrdA by hydrolysis, regenerating the pyruvoyl moiety |CITS: [20937090]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (ascorbic acid, vitamin C) is a reducing agent and antioxidant biosynthesized by plants, eukaryotic algae, some bacteria and many, but not all vertebrates.|FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it. These species rely on mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries. Reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|., In photosynthesizing plants and eukaryotic algae |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has roles in metabolism, electron transport, the cell cycle and responses to pathogens and abiotic stress. When coupled with its redox system, the ascorbate/glutathione cycle, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| can effectively regulate cellular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| levels (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-2261|) |CITS: [18460785]|. Interestingly, |FRAME: TAX-1117| do not possess any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis, and minimize photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases, suggesting that the use of ascorbate evolved after the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote |CITS: [23109712][25768426]|., Ascorbate Biosynthesis in Plants, Four different pathways for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| have been described in plants., • The first plant pathway was suggested in 1998 by Wheeler et al |CITS: [9620799]|. The pathway starts from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| and proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-Galactopyranose| and |FRAME: CPD-330| (see |FRAME: PWY-882|)., • A second pathway, known as the L-gulose pathway, also starts with |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. However, that pathway proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-gulopyranose| and |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS:[12954627]| (see |FRAME: PWY4FS-11|)., • A third pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-3747| (strawberry). In that pathway |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is formed from |FRAME: CPD-330|, as in the first pathway. However, the pathway starts from |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, and proceeds via |FRAME: CPD0-1083| |CITS:[13363799][12524550]|. Tracer and feeding studies have also shown conversion of |FRAME: CPD-23305| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [Loewus63]|. (see |FRAME: PWY-8143|)., • A fourth pathway suggested that |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| can also be channeled towards the production of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: EC-1.13.99.1|, based on the effect of overexpressing the |FRAME: AT4G26260| gene. According to that proposal, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is reduced to |FRAME: L-GULONATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS: [14976233]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8142|)., About This Pathway, Already in 1958 it was shown that |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is formed in plants by |FRAME: EC-1.3.2.3| |CITS: [13522636]|, although the role of |FRAME: CPD-330| as a physiological precursor has been disputed. A breakthrough arrived only 40 years later, when several key enzymes in the pathway were described |CITS: [9620799]|. The authors have shown that |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.18| plays a key role, converting |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE|, and characterized |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.316|, which produces the substrate for the lacton dehydrogenase. At the time there were two missing steps in the proposed pathway, for the conversion of |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| to |FRAME: L-Galactose|., The first of the missing steps,|FRAME: EC-3.1.3.93|, was filled in 2004 with the discovery of |FRAME: AT3G02870| |CITS: [15550539][16595667]|, and the last step, |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.69|, was filled in 2007, with the discovery of |FRAME: AT4G26850| and |FRAME: AT5G55120| |CITS: [17462988][18824398]|., A combination of genetic and biochemical approaches have demonstrated that the L-galactose pathway is the dominant biosynthetic route to L-ascorbate in many plants |CITS: [10097187][17877701]|., Regulation of ascorbate biosynthesis:, Ascorabte biosynthesis is regulated at multiple levels (reviewed in |CITS:[18824398]|). Jasmonates, which have been , shown to increase ascorbate levels in Arabidopsis, were found to induce expression of several genes in the ascorbate biosynthesis pathway, including |FRAME: AT2G39770|, |FRAME: AT5G28840|, and |FRAME: AT4G26850|/|FRAME: AT5G55120|., In addition, |FRAME: AT4G26850|/|FRAME: AT5G55120|, |FRAME: AT3G02870|, and |FRAME: G-80696| were shown regulated by light. The enzyme activity of |FRAME: AT5G28840| was found to be under feedback inhibition. Feedback inhibition of |FRAME: AT4G26850| was indicated at the transcriptional level. Experiments with Arabidopsis cell suspension culture indicate that the rate limiting step in ascorbate biosynthesis occurs between D-mannose and L-galactose |CITS:[10517845][16413588]|, possibly the step catalyzed by |FRAME: AT5G28840| |CITS:[16413588]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Nitriles Nitriles"| are used extensively in the chemical industry. Synthetic nitrile compounds are used in benzonitrile herbicides, as precursors for the synthesis of polyacrylonitrile plastics, and as organic solvents. |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE "Acrylonitrile"| is the primary component in the manufacture of acrylonitrile-butadienestyrene (ABS) resin.  It is also used as a precursor of acrylic fibers. The CN triple bond that defines nitriles makes many of them very toxic and generally non-biodegradable. Some compounds, such as acetonitrile, were shown to be carcinogenic in rodents |CITS: [16270753]|. Indiscriminate discharge of improperly treated nitrile wastes into a natural water body can cause serious problems and severe impacts on the aquatic ecology |CITS: [15242125]|., Some bacteria can degrade nitriles using a combination of three different groups of enzymes: Nitrilases (|FRAME: EC-3.5.5.1| and |FRAME: EC-3.5.5.7|) hydrolyze nitriles to the corresponding carboxylic acids in a single step, forming ammonia in the process, while |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.84|, forms amides from the nitriles. The amides can be subsequently hydrolyzed to carboxylic acids by amidases (|FRAME: EC-3.5.1.4 "EC 3.5.1.4"|)., Several species, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-1663|, |FRAME: TAX-85007|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-286| |CITS: [Watanabe87]|, |FRAME: TAX-1827| |CITS: [10347869][1390687]|, |FRAME: TAX-12916|, |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS:[15242125]|, |FRAME: TAX-469| |CITS: [7772945]| and |FRAME: TAX-546| |CITS:[14672363]| are able to degrade acrylonitrile to acrylate, using it as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen. Some of these strains have been used successfully for the removal of acrylonitrile from soils |CITS: [14672363]|, wastewater |CITS:[7772945][15242125 ]| and gasses |CITS: [14755563]|., In addition, nitrile hydratases are being used in the commercial production of acrylate and acrylamide |CITS: [2659343][1368882][17022452]|.

Summary: General Background, Polyamines are found in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes and are necessary for normal cellular physiology. They include the diamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, the triamines |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (sym-norspermidine) and |FRAME: CPD-1821| (homospermidine) and the tetraamine |FRAME: SPERMINE| (in |CITS: [20194510]| and in |CITS: [19196710]|). Links to their biosynthetic pathways can be found by clicking on these compounds links. See also |FRAME: POLYAMSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: POLYAMINSYN3-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6565|. In members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-662|, |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| is a major polyamine (in |CITS: [19196710]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| donates a carboxyaminopropyl group to |FRAME: CPD-313| to form |FRAME: CPD-9995| in a reaction catalyzed by carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase (CANSDH). Decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-9995| catalyzed by carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine decarboxylase (CANSDC) produces |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| is also a precursor for |FRAME: CPD-313| biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD-470| which is catalyzed by a bifunctional fusion protein L-2,4-diaminobutyrate aminotransferase/decarboxylase (DABA AT/DC) (|CITS: [3697846] [19196710]| and in |CITS: [20194510]|)., This |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| based pathway has been experimentally demonstrated in vivo in |FRAME: TAX-666| including a branch of this pathway that leads to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| as shown in the pathway link. Both pathways are shown together in |FRAME: PWY-6565|., Heterologous expression in |FRAME:TAX-562| of the genes encoding the enzymes in this pathway resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-313| and |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (which are inactive polyamines in |FRAME:TAX-562|). Deletion of the gene encoding CANSDC in |FRAME: TAX-666| resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-9995|. Deletion of the genes encoding either CANSDC or CANSDH led to loss of |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| and |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, thus identifying the gene encoding CANSDH. Interestingly, deletion of the |FRAME: TAX-666| genes encoding either CANSDH or CANSDC reduced the growth rate of planktonic cells by approximately 50% and severely reduced biofilm formation. Biofilm formation could be rescued by adding exogenous |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|, but not |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| . The pathway did not appear to be related to the infectivity of |FRAME: TAX-666|, using a mouse model |CITS: [19196710]|. Earlier work also suggested a role for |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| in biofilm formation in |FRAME: TAX-666| |CITS: [16237027]|., Bioinformatic analysis suggested that DABA AT/DC fusion proteins and their clustering with CANSDH and CANSDC were found only in the family |FRAME: TAX-641|, giving support to their role in both |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| biosynthesis in these organisms. However, a clustered pair of CANSDH and CANSDC genes was widespread in the α-, β-, γ-, δ- and ε-proteobacteria, firmicutes and a candidate division TG-1, suggesting that the pathway for |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthesis may be more widely used. However, this conclusion could not be extended to |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| biosynthesis without experimental support due to the use of |FRAME: CPD-470| in other pathways (see |FRAME: P101-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-6409| and |FRAME: PWY-761|) |CITS: [19196710]|.

Summary: General Background, Most organisms have less than 45 different tRNAs despite the fact that there are 61 different amino acid codons. The reason for this is that the third base of the codon is less discriminatory for the amino acid than the other two bases. Thus, the first base of the tRNA anticodon, which pairs with the third base of the codon, is more permissive for mismatches than the other two positions. At this position, which is known as the wobble position, 'U's and 'C's may be read by a 'G' in the anticodon. Similarly, 'A's and 'G's may be read by a 'U' or 'y' (pseudouridine) in the anticodon., The nucleotide at the wobble position is often modified, and particularly uridines, which are almost invariably modified. In yeast, 11 out of 13 wobble uridine-containing tRNAs are modified in some manner. The modifications increase the efficiency of codon reading and prevent mistranslation by limiting wobbling. In particular the 2-thiolation of the uridine is required for efficient codon recognition on the ribosome., The uridine34 wobble bases of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu are universally modified, although different modifications occur in different taxa and even in different cell compartments., In |FRAME: PWY-7891 "yeast mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19983| (τm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7889 "mammalian mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19980| (cmnm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7888 "cytoplasmic tRNAs of all eukaryotes"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19978| (mcm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7892 "the bacterium E. coli"| the modification is |FRAME: 5-METHYLAMINOMETHYL-2-THIOURIDINE| (mnm5s2U)., About This Pathay, The process starts with the modification of uridine34 to |FRAME: CPD-19979| (mcm5U) by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.229| |CITS: [21209336]|. , The subsequent 2-thiolation of the modified uridine residue is catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-9230 "CTU1/CTU2"| complex |CITS:[18391219] [19151091]|. The sulfur that is used for the thiolation originates in |FRAME: CYS|, but is transferred by a long sulfur relay chain that includes the proteins |FRAME: HS01304|, |FRAME: HS05177| (TUM1), |FRAME: HS04742|, and |FRAME: HS15524|. The human |FRAME: HS04742| protein is a branch point, being involved in both the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-4| and the thiolation of certain tRNAs |CITS: [28098827]|., MOCS3 contains an N-terminal domain similar to the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10154 MoeB| protein and a C-terminal domain displaying similarities to sulfurtransferase rhodanese enzymes. The rhodanese domain obtains a sulfur atom from the |FRAME: TUM1 "TUM1 sulfurtransferase"| (also known as MPST), which it received from the |FRAME: HS01304| L-cysteine desulfurase. MOCS3 then transfers the sulfur to either |FRAME: MONOMER-16667 MOCS2A| (for |FRAME: CPD-4| biosynthesis)| |CITS: [15073332]|, or to the ubiquitin-like protein |FRAME: URM1 URM1|, which transfers the sulfur to tRNAs| |CITS: [19145231]|. MOCS3 performs its action by catalyzing an adenylation of a glycine residue at the C-terminus of it target, followed by sulfur transfer and formation of a thiocarboxylate group |CITS: [22453920]|. The thiocarboxylated URM1 acts as the sulfur donor to the tRNA in a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-9230 "CTU1/CTU2"| complex |CITS:[18391219] [19151091]|.

General Background, Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-78245| and |FRAME: TAX-1829|, are capable of aerobic growth using aliphatic alkenes (such as |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|, |FRAME: PROPENE| and |FRAME: CPD-19063|) as source of carbon and energy., In these organisms the alkenes are oxidized to epoxides (also known as epoxyalkanes) by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7450|, a large complex similar to the aromatic monooxygenases such as |FRAME:CPLX-2181|. Epoxides contain an oxirane ring making them highly reactive electrophilic molecules, and are thus quite toxic to the cells. Depending on the organism, the epoxides are processed in several ways. Some organisms use glutathione and the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.34| to attack and open the oxirane ring |CITS: [10715003]|. Other organisms have been shown to use the unusual cofactor |FRAME:CoM| |CITS: [10411892]|, yet others use epoxide hydrolases |CITS: [25576605]|. The products of these reactions are then catabolized to central metabolites |CITS: [11352719]|., The |FRAME: PROPENE|-utilizing |FRAME: TAX-78245| has been shown to utilize |FRAME:CoM| in a pathway that eventually generates the β-ketoacid |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE|, which is chanelled to central metabolism. The pathway involves |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|-dependent carboxylation |CITS: [8631727][9555888]|., Prior to the discovery of its use in this pathway, it was believed that the roles of |FRAME: CoM| were limited to methanogenesis in methanogenic archaea. The genes encoding CoM biosynthesis enzymes, as well as the genes encoding propene degradation enzymes, are carried on the linear megaplasmid pXAUT01 |CITS: [20844868]|., About This Pathway, When acting on |FRAME: PROPENE|, |FRAME:CPLX-7450| generates two enantiomers of epoxypropane: |FRAME:R-12-EPOXYPROPANE| and |FRAME:S-12-EPOXYPROPANE|. A single zinc-dependent alkyltransferase, |FRAME:CPLX-4821|, capable of recognizing both enantiomers, adds |FRAME: CoM|, resulting in two enantiomeric intermediates,, |FRAME:2-R-HYDROXYPROPYL-COM| and |FRAME:2-S-HYDROXYPROPYL-COM|. Two different dehydrogenases, each highly specific for its substrate, are needed to metabolize both of these enantiomers to the first non-chiralic intermediate, |FRAME:2-OXOPROPYL-COM|., The last enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME:CPLX-4822|, catalyzes the actual carboxylation reaction. It is is an NADPH:disulfide oxidoreductase/carboxylase, and it reduces the thioether bond of the 2-ketoalkyl-CoM conjugate, liberating |FRAME: CoM| and carboxylating the resulting carbanion, generating (in this case) |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE|.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, Methylated thiols such as |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) and |FRAME: CPD-7672| (MMPA) can serve as methylotrophic methanogenic precursors |CITS: [16347202][10224009]|., The osmolite |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN|, which is found in many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|, is also the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]|. |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN Dimethylsulfoniopropionate| can be degraded unaerobically by either cleavage to |FRAME: CPD-7670| and |FRAME: ACRYLATE|, or by demethylation to |FRAME: CPD-7672| (see |FRAME:Dimethylsulfoniopropionate-Degradation|)., Most |FRAME: TAX-2207| species are able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-7672|, although some species, such as |FRAME: TAX-2208|, can only do so when grown on |FRAME:ACET| (but not |FRAME:METOH|) |CITS: [9371433]|. , The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., Unlike similar systems for |FRAME:CoM| methylation by |FRAME:METOH| and different methylamines, the |FRAME: TAX-2208| enzymatic complex that methylates |FRAME:CoM| with methylated thiols consists of only two types of peptides. The MtsA peptide catalyzes both methyltransferase activities, which are catalyzed in the other systems by two different methyltransferase, MT1 and MT2 |CITS: [11073950]|. The second peptide, MtsB, is a corrinoid protein, similar to the one found in the other systems. Earlier studies suggested that one corrinoid cofactor is bound per MtsA:MtsB pair, and six to seven such pairs comprise a 480 kDa complex |CITS: [8335638][8282704]|. However, later work suggested that MtsA forms dimers in solution |CITS: [11073950]|., In |FRAME: TAX-2214| A gene cluster highly upregulated during growth on |FRAME: CPD-7672| was discovered |CITS: [25691524]|. The cluster includes |FRAME: G-44585|, which encodes a methyltransferase, mtpC, encoding a corrinoid protein, mtpP, encoding a transporter, and msrH, encoding a transcriptional activator., Mutants lacking any of these genes had a normal phenotype when grown on methanol, acetate, methylamines, DMS, or methylthiol, but were severely impaired in their ability to grow on |FRAME: CPD-7672|. The authors proposed that MtpA acts as a bifunctional MT1/MT2 protein, catalyzing the transfer of the methyl group from |FRAME: CPD-7672| to the corrinoid protein MtpC and the subsequent transfer of the methyl group from methyl-MtpC to coenzyme-M |CITS: [25691524]|.

Summary: Lyngbyatoxins (|FRAME: CPD-18328|, |FRAME: CPD-18331| and |FRAME: CPD-18332|) are potent skin irritants produced by the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1155739| (originally misclassified as |FRAME: TAX-158786| |CITS: [21724952]|), and are known to cause a condition known as Swimmers Itch off the Hawaiian island of Oahu (although there are other compounds that cause the same condition, see for example |FRAME: CPD-21919| and |FRAME: CPD-21918|)., The compounds are pharmacologically related to the |FRAME: CPD-18330 teleocidin| (|FRAME: CPD-18328| is identical to teleocidin A-1) |CITS: [Takashima60][Fujiki83][2890278]| and |FRAME: CPD-18340 olivoretin| |CITS: [6525665][6439591]| metabolites isolated from the actinomycetes |FRAME: TAX-58352| and |FRAME: TAX-68246|, respectively. These compounds exert skin irritation through potent activation of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.13| (PKC), and have been shown to be potent tumor promoters |CITS: [3134123]|., An early sudy of teleocidin biosynthesis has found that all of its isomers are produced from the same intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-18327|, which is synthesized from |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: VAL| and |FRAME: TRP| via |FRAME: CPD-18333| |CITS: [Irie90]|. It has also been shown that the monoterpenoid moiety of |FRAME: CPD-18339| is synthesized via the non-mevalonate pathway |CITS: [Irie98]|., A biosynthetic gene cluster that encodes lyngbyatoxin biosynthesis was isolated from a DNA library of |FRAME: TAX-1155739| cultured from Kahala Beach, Oahu, using a probe for a non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS)-associated C-terminal reductase (Red) domain, which was assumed to be involved in the production of |FRAME: CPD-18327| |CITS: [15366877]|. The cluster, which spans a 11.3 kb region, consists of four genes, which were named |FRAME: G-44188|, |FRAME: G-44186|, |FRAME: G-44187| and |FRAME: G-44189|., The |FRAME: G-44188| gene encodes a two-module NRPS protein. The first module contains an L-valine specific adenylation (A) domain, an N-methylation domain, and a peptidyl carrier protein (PCP). The second module contains a, condensation (C) domain, an L-tryptophan specific A domain, a PCP, and a C-terminal reductase (Red) domain. The reductase domain releases |FRAME: CPD-18333| from the synthase via an NADPH-dependent reductive cleavage that forms the alcohol group rather than the usual thioesterase mechanism of NRPSs, which typically couple chain release and cyclization., Cyclization is afforded by the action of the product of the |FRAME: G-44186| gene. This unusual cytochrome P450 monooxygenase is highly similar to MbtH, a |FRAME: TAX-1773| enzyme involved in |FRAME: CPD-18345 mycobactin| biosynthesis |CITS: [9831524][15366877]|]|. In the presence of NADPH, spinach ferredoxin and spinach ferredoxin reductase, the enzyme was shown to convert |FRAME: CPD-18333| to |FRAME: CPD-18327| through the oxidation and, cyclization of the dipeptide |CITS: [20000453]|. , The |FRAME: G-44187| gene was shown to catalyze the transfer of a geranyl group from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| to |FRAME: CPD-18327| as the final step in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-18328| |CITS: [15366877]|., The |FRAME: G-44189| gene is similar to oxidase/reductase-type proteins, and was thus proposed to be involved in the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-18328| into the minor metabolites |FRAME: CPD-18331| and |FRAME: CPD-18332| |CITS: [15366877]|., Cloning and expression of the genes in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in high titers of both |FRAME: CPD-18327| and |FRAME: CPD-18328| and low amounts of |FRAME: CPD-18331| and |FRAME: CPD-18332| |CITS: [23751865]|.

Bisbenzylisoquinoline alkaloids are dimeric benzyltetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloids. The formation of the dimers is catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 enzyme, CYP80A1. The enzyme is unusual in that it is an oxidase rather than a monooxygenase. It catalyzes the region- and stereo-selective formation of a C-O phenol couple without incorporation of oxygen into the product. The CYP80A1 condenses two molecules of (R)-N-methylcoclaurine, or one each of (R)- and (S)- N-methylcoclaurine, intermediates of (S)-reticuline pathway, to form (R,R)-guattegaumerine or (R,S)-berbamunine, respectively.

Summary: General Background, The broad definition of a |FRAME: Lipoproteins lipoprotein| is a protein to which lipids are bound. Many enzymes, transporters, structural proteins, antigens, adhesins, and toxins are lipoproteins, including the high-density (HDL) and low-density (LDL) lipoproteins that carry fats in the blood stream., The lipoprotein known as |FRAME: EG10544-MONOMER| (Lpp) is considered the most abundant protein in |FRAME: TAX-562| and accounts for more than 40% of the peptidoglycan on a weight basis. It is necessary for the stabilization and integrity of the bacterial cell envelope and is thought to physically tether the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan layer |CITS:[4899922][4565677][4578317]|., Membrane-attached lipoproteins of Gram-negative bacteria and Mycobacteria are tethered to the membrane by an N-acyl-(S-diacylglyceryl)-cysteine anchor that is variably acylated depending on the genus. In many Gram-positive bacteria certain variations exist (see below)., About This Pathway, In bacteria all lipoproteins are initially translated as precursors (|FRAME: Prolipoproteins prolipoproteins|) containing an N-terminal signal peptide that contains a conserved lipobox motif sequence preceding a cysteine residue. The signal peptide is inserted into the membrane, serving as a membrane anchor for the protein |CITS: [12876315][19367716]|. Once attached the outer face of the membrane, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.145| (Lgt) attaches a diacylglycerol moiety from a phospholipid donor by a thioether bond to the cysteine residue. At this point the protein is attached to the membrane by three anchors - the two fatty acids of the diacylglycerol molecule and the signal peptide |CITS: [8051048]|., In most organisms |FRAME: EC-3.4.23.36| (Lsp) then cleaves the leader peptide, leaving the cysteine as the N-terminal amino acid of the protein |CITS: [7040395]|. Some variations exist - for example, in |FRAME: TAX-2115| the peptide is cleaved two amino acids away from the cysteine (towards the N-terminus) |CITS: [22303020]|., More variety is found in some low GC Gram-positive bacteria. Three new forms have been observed - a |FRAME: Peptidyl-Form-Lipoprotein-N-terminus "peptidyl form"| (which results from the alternative cleaving by Lsp, with two amino acids present before the lipid-modified cysteine residue), an |FRAME: N-Acetyl-Lipoprotein "N-acetyl form"|, and an N-acylated monoacyl-glyceryl form known as the |FRAME: Lyso-Form-Lipoprotein-Cysteine "lyso-form"| |CITS: [22135097][22303020][28320885]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA "Benzoyl-CoA"| is an important precursor to a number of different compounds. In plants, volatile benzenoids derived from |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, such as |FRAME:CPD-6443|, can serve as aroma compounds |CITS: [12226525][15326281][15286288]| or defense signals |CITS:[19400653][19820324]|. Meanwhile, polyketides derived from |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| in bacteria may have antibiotic and other effects |CITS: [12502351]|. , About This Pathway, Following the initial activation of trans-cinnamic acid with CoA in the |FRAME: PWY-6457| pathway, the three reactions shown in this pathway are expected to share similarities with the β-oxidation process involved in |FRAME: PWY-5136 "fatty acid metabolism"|. These reactions, from |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA| to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| will likely require the sequential activities of an enoyl-CoA hydratase, a dehydrogenase, and a thiolase |CITS: [15286288]|. , Enzymes catalyzing two of these steps have been identified in bacteria |CITS: [12502351]|, but the dehydrogenase has not yet been found. In plants, none of the enzymes predicted to participate in this pathway have been cloned or characterized to date, but radiotracer studies provide strong evidence for the existence of this pathway |CITS: [11219576]|.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn this variant of the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules and reduces a total of four molecules: one |FRAME: NAD|, two |FRAME: NADP|, and one |FRAME: Quinones quinone| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105|, a key member of the "standard" TCA cycle that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: SUC-COA|, is absent, or not expressed, in many organisms, including obligately autotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria and archaea |CITS: [15449607]| as well as mycobacteria |CITS: [16045627]|. Most cyanobacteria also lack a gene encoding the enzyme |CITS: [4963789][15449607][21282404]|., The absence of this enzyme could theoretically result in incomplete oxidative or reductive TCA cycles that supply biosynthetic intermediates in response to growth conditions (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P42-PWY|). However, in some cases other enzymes substitute for the missing activity and complete the cycle. For example, some archaea and the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| possess the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3| (see |FRAME: REDCITCYC|) |CITS: [10091606]|. , In the pathway described here, the role of the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex is replaced by two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.71| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.79 "EC 1.2.1.79, succinate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase"| |CITS: [22174252]|. Similarly to the glyoxylate shunt, this pathway bypasses the synthesis of ATP via |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.5|. Note that by avoiding the generation of ATP, this variant of the TCA cycle is not inhibited by high ATP concentration, which is typical in photosynthetic organisms., Since |FRAME: SUC-COA| is not produced by the pathway, pools of |FRAME: SUC-COA| for synthesis of |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, |FRAME: Sulfolipids sulfolipids| and |FRAME: Hemes heme| have to be derived in an energy-dependent manner, either from |FRAME: SUC| at the expense of ATP (by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.5|) or from |FRAME: METHYL-MALONYL-COA| via |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.2| |CITS: [16027371][Munoz-Elias06]|., Succinate can also be formed by a reductive TCA half-cycle, or by the glyoxylate bypass, as shown here (in |CITS: [16027371]|) (see |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|)., The 2-oxoglutarate decarboxylase and succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase reactions have been shown in |FRAME: TAX-3039| |CITS: [SHIGEOKA86][1910306]|, in some rhizobia |CITS: [10781553]|, and in cyanobacteria |CITS: [22174252]|. The pathway was also thought to exist in mycobacteria |CITS: [16027371]|, but it was later shown that the key enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.71|, is missing from those organisms |CITS: [20416504]|, and that they operate a different variation instead (see |FRAME: PWY-6969|).
