Summary: Cyanogenic glucosides are widely distributed in the plant kingdom and the pathways involved in biosynthesis and degradation of cyanogens are thought to be of ancient origin |CITS:[9431670]| |CITS:[Ganjewala10]| |CITS:[Seigler98]|. In the long-standing and ongoing warfare between plants and herbivores defense mechanisms have been developed to scare off plant predators utilizing the plethora of secondary metabolites |CITS:[21429539]|. In this regard cyanogenesis, the liberation of |FRAME:HCN| from cyanogenic glucosides belongs to the most effective deterrent pathways. However, a few insects in the way of co-evolution, have acquired the ability to metabolize and even sequester cyanogenic glucosides for their protection |CITS:[14751300]|. Beside defense function and involvement in germination |CITS:[10669009]| the bioactivation of cyanogenic glucosides has also been found to serve as N-storage in non-cyanogenic compounds and alternative source for amino acid synthesis (see |FRAME:ASPSYNII-PWY|) |CITS:[Lieberei85]| |CITS:[18842274]|., It has been argued that |FRAME:CPD-14594| co-occurs in plants containing |FRAME:LINAMARIN| although not easily detectable during the various plant developmental stages |CITS:[16665975]|. Since |FRAME:LINAMARIN| enjoys a fairly broad distribution in plants and has been proven to exist in the plant families Compositae, Euphorbiaceae, Linaceae, Papaveraceae and Fabaceae (Leguminosae) |CITS:[10669009]| |FRAME:CPD-14594| may occur in more species than originally thought. Selmar and colleagues have comprehensively studied the metabolism of |FRAME:CPD-14594| in |FRAME:TAX-3981| and as a result have delineated a general metabolic concept which they coined 'linustatin pathway' |CITS:[16665975]|. , According to this postulated pathway |FRAME:LINAMARIN| is glucosylated in the endosperm to form the cyanogenic disaccharide |FRAME:CPD-14594| |CITS:[Selmar91]| |CITS:[Selmar93]| which functions as transport metabolite in long-distance transportation towards the developing leaves |CITS:[Selmar93a]| |CITS:[19409582]|. |FRAME:CPD-14594 Linustatin| cannot be hydrolyzed by the apoplastic linamarase |CITS:[16665288]| and therefore qualifies as transport metabolite. Having reached the leaves |FRAME:CPD-14594| is either hydrolyzed by a specific linustatin diglucosidase releasing |FRAME: 2-HYDROXY-2-METHYLPROPANENITRILE| and |FRAME:CPD-3605| (|FRAME:TAX-3981|) |CITS:[16665975]| or sequentially degraded to |FRAME: 2-HYDROXY-2-METHYLPROPANENITRILE| liberating 2 molecules |FRAME:GLC| in the process (|FRAME:TAX-4006|) |CITS:[3936419]|. The |FRAME:HCN| is not released but fixed by a β-cyanoalanine synthase (see |FRAME:ASPSYNII-PWY|), hence converted to non-cyanogenic compounds. It has been reported that the 'linustatin pathway' also functions in Manihut esculenta |CITS:[Lykkesfeldt94]|, The enzymes involved in the cyanogenesis of |FRAME:CPD-14594|, i.e. β-glucosidase |CITS:[16665288]| |CITS:[3936419]|, β-diglucosidase |CITS:[16665975]| and (S)-hydroxynitrile lyases |CITS:[Selmar89]| |CITS:[8621461]| |CITS:[9094745]| have all been identified and biochemically characterized.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| is a common unsaturated fatty acid, found in bacteria, fungi |CITS: [8294460]|, plants |CITS: [7548115]| and animals |CITS:[14321753] [6030882]|. Only bacteria can produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically, and thus the key enzymes of this pathway (particularly |FRAME: EG10273| which catalyzes an early step - see |FRAME: PWY0-862|) have been targeted for development of new antibacterial agents |CITS: [22188524][23174186]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: CPD-9245| is one of only two unsaturated fatty acids (along with |FRAME: CPD-9247|), which together comprise about one-half of the total fatty acid content of the organism. |FRAME: PALMITATE Palmitate|, |FRAME: CPD-9245|, and |FRAME: CPD-9247| make up the bulk of the fatty acids found in |FRAME:TAX-562| membranes |CITS: [8246839]|., |FRAME:TAX-562| has three β-ketoacyl-ACP synthases (KAS): |FRAME: FABB-CPLX|, |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| and |FRAME: CPLX0-252|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG12606| and |FRAME: EG10277|, respectively., The extension of |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs| to |FRAME: Palmitoleoyl-ACPs| is believed to be catalyzed primarily by |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG10274|). On the other hand, overexpression of KASI leads to the overproduction of |FRAME: CPD-9247| |CITS: [6337151]|., It has been shown that the basal ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids in |FRAME:TAX-562| is controlled by the level of two enzymes - |FRAME: FABA-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG10273|) and |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG10274|) |CITS: [8246839]|. Thioredoxin reduces L-cysteine-disulfide of target proteins, modifying their activity and serving as a redox-based regulator of cellular metabolism. Thioredoxin also participates in repair of oxidatively damaged proteins. During the reaction Trx itself in oxidized, forming a disulfide bridge between two cysteine residues. In addition, Trx has been shown in some organisms to be involved in a pathway for the trans-membrane transfer of reducing potential from the cytoplasm to the periplasm |CITS: [9352906] [19258316]|.  , The thioredoxin system, which restores Trx to its reduced, active state, is composed of thioredoxins (Trx), thioredoxin reductases (TrxR), and a reductant., In most organisms the reductant used is NADPH (see |FRAME: THIOREDOX-PWY|). The disulfide-containing oxidized thioredoxin is reduced back to a dithiol by the NADPH-dependent flavoprotein thioredoxin reductase (|FRAME: EC-1.8.1.9 "EC 1.8.1.9"|)| |CITS: [17659286]|. , However, ancient methanogens such as |FRAME: TAX-2190| were found to utilizes an factor 420 (F<sub>420</sub>)-dependent thioredoxin reductase. The E'<sub>0</sub> of enzyme-bound flavin is approximately -389 mV, making electron transfer from reduced F420 to flavin endergonic. But under the high partial pressures of hydrogen present in deep-sea volcanoe environments the potential of the F<sub>420</sub>/F<sub>420</sub>H<sub>2</sub> pair can be as low as -425 mV, making the enzyme efficient |CITS: [27590343]|.

Summary: General Background, Biodegradation of aromatic compounds is a common process in anoxic environments. The many natural and synthetic aromatic compounds found in the environment are usually degraded by anaerobic microorganisms into only few central intermediates, prior to ring cleavage |CITS: [9057820]|. Benzoyl-CoA is the most important of these intermediates since a large number of compounds, including chloro-, nitro-, and aminobenzoates, aromatic hydrocarbons, and phenolic compounds, are initially converted to benzoyl-CoA prior to ring reduction and cleavage |CITS: [11282627]|., The pathways for anaerobic benzoate and benzoyl-CoA degradation have been studied primarily in two microorganisms, the phototrophic, purple, nonsulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1076| and the nitrate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-59405|., About This Pathway, Under anaerobic conditions, the denitrifying bacterium |FRAME: TAX-59405| can grow with benzoate as the sole carbon source. It is also capable of metabolizing the alicyclic acids cyclohexanecarboxylate and cyclohex-1-ene-1-carboxylate, which then enter the benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway., In both the phototroph |FRAME: TAX-1076| and denitrifying bacterium |FRAME: TAX-59405| anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation is initiated by reductive ring cleavage catalyzed by benzoyl-CoA reductase (see also |FRAME:P321-PWY|). This reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 molecules of ATP and requires reduced ferrodoxin as an electron acceptor. Whereas in |FRAME: TAX-1076| the cyclic diene is further reduced to |FRAME: CPD-533|, in |FRAME: TAX-59405| the cyclic diene is hydrated to|FRAME: 6-HYDROXYCYCLOHEX-1-ENE-1-CARBONYL-COA|. The respective products are subsequently β-oxidized to cyclic β-oxo compounds, which in turn undergo hydrolytic ring cleavage to |FRAME: CPD-558| in |FRAME: TAX-1076| and |FRAME:3-HYDROXYPIMELYL-COA| in |FRAME: TAX-59405|., These intermediates are further β-oxidized via |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA| to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [10406950] [FEMSMicRev22-439] [9683649] [9746358] [8439237]|., A gene cluster encoding all of the required enzymes has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-59405| |CITS: [9746358]|.

Summary: Some strains of |FRAME: TAX-613| and related bacteria can produce |FRAME: CPD-16992| |CITS: [13843029]|, a red linear tripyrrole antibiotic and a member of the prodiginines, a family of related compounds produced by some Serratia species, actinomycetes and other bacteria |CITS: [17109029]|., |FRAME: CPD-16992 Prodigiosin| is a classic secondary metabolite that is only produced in the stationary stage of bacterial growth |CITS: [4572893]|., The production of prodigiosin has been shown to be influenced by numerous environmental factors including inorganic phosphate availability, media composition, temperature and pH |CITS: [14332439][7765446][12436260][12519208]|., The biosynthesis of prodigiosin is controlled by a complex regulatory network, and is influenced by |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "N-acyl-homoserine lactone"| quorum-sensing |CITS: [9402023][12519208][15916601]|., While the physiological function of prodigiosin is still not known, many studies have shown that prodigiosin has antifungal, antibacterial, antiprotozoal/antimalarial, immunosuppressive and anticancer activities |CITS: [10358154][10891115][11015311][12682632][14555220][17109029][20717667]|. It has been suggested that it may be an important factor for the trypanolytic activity of |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [15208042]|., In 2004 the prodigiosin biosynthesis gene cluster (pig cluster) was cloned and sequenced from two strains of Serratia (|FRAME: ORG-6266| and |FRAME: TAX-104623|), revealing 14 and 15 ORFs, respectively |CITS: [15528645]|. The clusteres were also expressed in heterologous hosts. Based on the gene annotations, an initial scheme for the biosynthesis of prodigiosin has been proposed. The two main precursors, |FRAME: CPD-17013| (MBC) and |FRAME: CPD-17007| (MAP) are produced in parallel branches, then condensed into |FRAME: CPD-16992| in the final step., In a subsequent project, in-frame deletions or insertions were generated in every biosynthetic gene in the cluster from |FRAME: TAX-104623|, and the biosynthetic intermediates accumulating in each mutant have been analyzed by LC-MS, cross-feeding, and genetic complementation studies |CITS: [15853884]|. Based on these results a modified version of the pathway has been suggested, as is depicted here., Both branches utilize interesting chemistry. The MBC branch includes an uncommon mechanism for pyrrole biosynthesis from |FRAME: PRO|, which involves proteins with homology to the adenylation and peptidyl-carrier protein domains of |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "non-ribosomal peptide sythetases"| (similar mechanism is found in the biosynthesis of other pyrrole-containing compounds, such as |FRAME: CPD-15504|, |FRAME: CPD-17024|, and |FRAME: CPD-17025|) |CITS: [11880032]|. The MAP branch includes |FRAME: G-34530 PigD|, an enzyme that catalyzes an assymetric Stetter reaction. A homolog of this enzyme has been described in |FRAME: TAX-316|, and is involved in the synthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-842| dechlorination agent |FRAME: CPD-8207| |CITS: [11234929][15528645]|.

Summary: Polyunsaturated |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "long chain fatty acids"| (PUFAs) have18 or more carbon atoms containing more than one double bond in its backbone. The PUFAs that have 2 or more cis double bonds separated from each other by a single methylene group are generally either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, and are considered essential fatty acids for mammals., PUFAs accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|. They are also produced by some marine bacteria, but are not commonly found in higher plants. , |FRAME: CPD-10244 Docosahexanoate| (DHA) is a 22 carbon long chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (LCPUFA) with 6 methylene interrupted cis double bonds |CITS: [15292371]|. DHA and other LCPUFAs like |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID arachidonate| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE eicosapentaenoate| are precursors of different classes of eicosanoid effectors involved in the regulation of many important mammalian functions |CITS: [14704315]|. , In algae, fungi and lower plants DHA is synthesized de novo from acetate. Mammals are not able to synthesis DHA de novo, and instead synthesize it from the essential fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (which they obtain in their diet) via alternating steps of aerobic desaturation and elongation |CITS: [11397798][14704315]|., Another method of DHA synthesis is described in some marine bacteria and primitive eukaryotes utilizing the polyketide syntase systems |CITS: [12835316]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7585|)., About this Pathway, For simplicity, this pathway begins with |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE|, in its lipid-incorporated form, which is the form found in most cells. Different organisms produce this 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid by different routes, which are described by the pathway links in the diagram., Once |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| is transferred from the lipid to a coenzyme A carrier, it is elongated to |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| via a |FRAME: MONOMER-16977|. The elongated fatty acid is transferred back to a lipid, where it undergoes a 4-desaturation by |FRAME: MONOMER-16978| to yield DHA |CITS: [11397798]|., Mammals were thought to synthesize DHA only via a 4-desaturase-independent pathway, involving an additional Δ7 elongation and a 6-desaturation step in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by a two carbon shortening via limited β-oxidation in peroxisomes |CITS: [10903473]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7606|). However, that fact has been challenged following the finding that the desaturase enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: HS05918| gene can also catalyze 4-desaturation reactions |CITS: [26065859]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7727|).

General Background, Polythioesters (PTEs) are microbially-synthesized, non-biodegradable polymers containing sulfur in the thioester linkages of the backbone |CITS: [15762657]|. They accumulate as hydrophobic inclusions in the cytoplasm of bacterial cells, similarly to |FRAME: Polyhydroxyalkanoates "polyhydroxyalkanoic acids"| (PHAs) |CITS: [15468206]|., PHAs and PTEs are industrially and scientifically interesting materials because they possess some unique characteristics regarding their biodegradability, microstructure, thermal behaviour and diverse mechanical properties, and because many of them can be produced from nonpetrochemical resources, PTE heteropolymers were first detected in |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [11160796]|. That organism naturally accumulates PHAs at levels of up to more than 90% of the cell dry matter. When given |FRAME: CPD-7673|, |FRAME: CPD-16592|, |FRAME: CPD-16591|, |FRAME: CPD-16587| or |FRAME: CPD-16586| (in addition to a second compound that serves as a carbon and energy source) its unspecific |FRAME: CPLX-7357| produces various PTE heteropolymers., While PTE polymers are structural analogs of common cell metabolites, only few bacteria are able to degrade them |CITS: [16738107][19001372]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-16587 "3,3'-Thiodipropionate"| (TDP) is an organic sulfide and a precursor for the synthesis of polythioesters (PTEs) in bacteria |CITS: [12725926]|. Several strains of the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-34073| were isolated due to their ability to use the compound as a sole source of carbon and energy. The bacteria are capable of degrading the compound into the common metabolic intermediate |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [19001372]|., A pathway for the degradation of TDP in this organism was constructed based on the characterization of multiple transposon mutants that lost the ability to grow with TDP as the sole source of carbon and energy. , Two of the enzymes involved, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.91| and |FRAME: MONOMER-18547|, were identified |CITS: [19001372]|., The enzyme catalyzing the next reaction in the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-8843|, was identified in |FRAME: TAX-1247726|, a β proteobacterium that was isolated due to its ability to utilize |FRAME: CPD-16586| as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [16738107]|.

Some bacteria, such as the human gut bacteria |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-821| are able to utilize |FRAME: CPD0-1083 L-galactonate| as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS:[381020][24963813]|. , The initial step in the pathway involves conversion of L-galactonate to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| by an inducible |FRAME: RXN0-5229| |CITS:[17088549]|. Subsequent reactions generate |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, an intermediate of the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"| (as described in the pathway |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|) |CITS:[381020]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-2056315| is a verocytotoxin-producing E. coli (VTEC) [also referred to as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC)] that has been reported from cattle, goats and humans |CITS: [Blanco11][10698990]|. , The study if this O antigen is one of few cases where the O antigen gene cluster was sequenced and analyzed before the O unit structure was determined. The gene cluster was sequenced in 2005 and found to contain 13 open reading frames. The cluster includes genes required for biosynthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|, genes required for biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15644|, three glycosyltransferases, and the genes encoding an O antigen repeat unit flippase, and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [16207976]|. One of the glycosyltransferase genes, |FRAME: G-81149|, shares 96% identity with wbuB of E. coli O26, which is an L-fucosaminetransferase, and thus it was deduced that the O antigen contains this residue. The other two glycosyltransferase genes were not assigned a function at the time, though one of them was similar to a rhamnosyltransferase., The structure of the repeat unit of the |FRAME: TAX-2056315| O antigen was reported in 2011 and found to contain one GlcNAc residue, two FucNAc residues, and one rhamnosyl residue |CITS: [21867992]|. The antigen shares the →3)-α-L-FucNAc-(1→3)-β-D-GlcNAc-(1→ structural element with the O antigen from E. coli O15, resulting in some cross reactivity with anti O:15 serum., Based on the sturcture, the remaining two glycosyltransferases could be assigned a function, since |FRAME: G-81151| is similar to genes known to encode rhamnosyltransferases and is likely to encode the same type of enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-2056315|, leaving |FRAME: G-81150| to encode the second fucosaminyltransferase.

Summary: The pathway of valine biosynthesis is a four-step pathway that shares all, of its steps with the parallel pathway of isoleucine biosynthesis. These, entwined pathways are part of the |FRAME:BRANCHED-CHAIN-AA-SYN-PWY|, that generates, not only isoleucine and valine, but also leucine., As a consequence of having several of its component enzymes involved in the synthesis, of three different amino acids, the pathway of isoleucine biosynthesis is subject, to regulation by all three amino acids. The first step in the pathway is primarily, inhibited by valine, along with inhibition by isoleucine and leucine., The potential disruption this might cause to the parallel, isoleucine biosynthesis pathway step using the same enzymes is resolved by, upregulation of an earlier step that is unique to isoleucine biosynthesis, as explained, in the |FRAME:ILEUSYN-PWY| summary. In this way, valine biosynthesis can be regulated, independently of isoleucine biosynthesis, despite all four valine biosynthesis enzymes, also participating in isoleucine biosynthesis.

Triacyglycerols (TAG) from vegetable oils are a major source of essential fatty acids in human diet, namely polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) linoleate (18:2) and linolenate (18:3). In oilseeds, TAG is synthesized via the |FRAME: TRIGLSYN-PWY "Kennedy pathway"|, where the precursor diacylglycerol (DAG) is de novo synthesized from glycerol-3-phosphate. In addition to the Kennedy pathway, there are several other paths supplying DAG for TAG biosynthesis during seed development in plants |CITS: [19329563]|. Since further desaturation of 18:1 to form 18:2 and 18:3 occurs mainly in phosphatidylcholine (PC, see |FRAME: PWY-762|), together, these alternative paths in converting PC to DAG can provide enrichment of the PUFA content in TAG. , 1) reverse reaction of CDP-choline:1,2-diacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase (CPT, 2.7.8.2), Radio tracer studies using microsomes isolated from developing safflower cotyledons indicated that CPT catalyzes a reversible exchange of diacylglycerol moieties between pools of PC and DAG |CITS: [Slack85]|. The maximum activity of CPT coincides with the maximum rate of accumulation of PC and TAG. It is very plausible that the releasing of PUFA-contained DAG from PC, catalyzed by the reverse activity of CPT, may contribute to the enrichment of PUFA in TAG.  , 2) phosphatidylcholine:diacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase, A novel enzyme was recently isolated from Arabidopsis |CITS: [19833868]|. The Arabidopsis phosphatidylcholine:diacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase, encoded by ROD1, catalyzes the transfer of phosphocholine head group from PC to DAG. The interconversion of PC and DAG catalyzed by ROD1 provides a major route through which 18:1 (in DAG) enters PC for further desaturation, and in turn the PUFAs 18:2 and 18:3 (in PC) re-enter to the DAG pool for TAG biosynthesis. Arabidopsis ROD1 mutants had a 40% reduction of 18:2 and 18:3 in the seed TAG.  , It was postulated that a phospholipase C (3.1.4.3) activity may also generate DAG for TAG synthesis. However no such activity has been reported in developing seeds |CITS: [19329563]|.  , Besides the paths depicted here, an |FRAME: PWY-6803 "acyl editing mechanism"| also exists that can further enrich PUFA in oilseed TAG |CITS: [19329563]|.

Summary: Background, |FRAME: TAX-38881|, a colony-forming, fresh water green algae, is regarded as a potential source of biofuel because of its ability to produce large amounts of hydrocarbons. Depending on the strain and growth conditions, up to 75% of algal dry mass can be hydrocarbons., Different strains of |FRAME: TAX-38881| produce different hydrocarbons |CITS: [Dayananda]|. Three races have been documented: |FRAME: TAX-869302| (A race) produces odd numbered (C25 to C31) n-alkadienes and trienes. |FRAME: TAX-869301| (B race) produces triterpenoid hydrocarbons known as botryococcenes (CnH2n–10, n = 30–37) of isoprenoid origin |CITS: [Chisti80]|, and the |FRAME: ORG-6353 "L race"| produces a single hydrocarbon - the C40 tetraterpene |FRAME: CPD-13313| |CITS: [Metzger90]|., About this Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-869301| produces the linear triterpenes, squalene, botryococcene and their methylated derivatives |CITS: [12405558]|. Of these, botryococcene and its methyl derivatives account for the majority of the triterpene oils. |FRAME: CPD-10662| have a high octane rating for their highly branched structures and great potential as a renewable source of energy. They accumulate rapidly in |FRAME: TAX-869301| |CITS: [10620354][14725863]|. , For abundant C30 botrycoccenes production, |FRAME: TAX-869301| needs to efficiently generate |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) and |FRAME: CPD-4211| (DMAPP), fundamental precursors of isoprenoid synthesis. IPP is produced from the condensation of acetyl CoA via the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|. In the latter pathway, pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate are condensed into |FRAME:DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| (DOXP), which is converted to the intermediate in IPP biosynthesis, |FRAME: 2-C-METHYL-D-ERYTHRITOL-4-PHOSPHATE| (MEP) |CITS: [8645235]|., Stereochemical studies and incorporation experiments have revealed that |FRAME: CPD-465| (PSPP) is a common precursor in the synthesis of both squalene and C30 botryococcene |CITS: [15630516]|. A squalene synthase like enzyme designated SSL-3 was shown to specifically generate C30 botryococcene from PSPP |CITS: [21746901]|., By S-adenosylmethionine mediated methylation, |FRAME: CPD-10662| can go on to form its higher homologue botryococcenes |CITS: [15630516]||CITS: [10620354]|. Similarly, squalene alkylation, with methionine as the source of methyl groups, leads to the synthesis of C31-C34 higher homologues |CITS: [15630516]||CITS: [15541746]|. The production of C32 methylated squalenes and botryococcenes requires the activity of three triterpene methyl transferases 1, 2 and 3. TMT-1 and 2 seem to methylate C30 and C31 squalenes, while TMT-3 exclusively methylates C30 and C31 botryococcenes |CITS: [21746901]|., CO2 enrichment favors the formation of lower botryococcenes (C30-C32), whereas cultures with ambient air accumulate higher botryococcenes (C33-C37) |CITS: [18050944]|., Similarly, the alternate branch of the pathway downstream of presqualene diphosphate, produces squalene and its methylated derivatives monomethyl squalene and dimethyl squalene.

In some cases |FRAME: CPD-21492| appears to be a final product, while in other cases the degradation continues, to |FRAME: INDOLE-PROPIONATE| |CITS: [HOOGERHEIDE38][WOODS35][1275638]|. , Much of our knowledge of tryptophan catabolism, via |FRAME: CPD-21492|, comes from the cheese industry, since, this pathway is thought to promote the formation of aromatic compounds such as |FRAME: INDOLE| and |FRAME: SKATOLE| (3-methylindole), which imparts putrid, fecal, and unclean flavors in cheese., In |FRAME:TAX-1509|, tryptophan is catabolized via |FRAME: INDOLE_PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: CPD-21492|, and, |FRAME: CPD-11578| to |FRAME: INDOLE-PROPIONATE| |CITS: [5697992]|. Summary: General Background, The ability to reduce sulfur using |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| or organic substrates as electron, donors is widespread among thermophiles. It is mostly found in hyperthermophilic archea living in volcanic, habitats, and in mesophilic and thermophilic bacteria living in anoxic marine or brackish sediments,, fresh water sediments, bovine rumen, hot water pools from solfataric fields, and volcanic hot springs, |CITS: [FEMSMicRev22-353]|., Some methanogens, especially the thermophilic and hyperthermophilic members of the genera, |FRAME:TAX-2319|,|FRAME:TAX-2160|,|FRAME:TAX-2179|, and |FRAME:TAX-2184| are also able, to reduce elemental sulfur to |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [Stetter83]|., Some of the organisms (including members of the archaebacterial genera |FRAME:TAX-2260|,, Thermoproteus, Pyrodictum,|FRAME:TAX-12914|,|FRAME:TAX-12914|,|FRAME:TAX-41674| and |FRAME:TAX-2276|) are, able to use |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| as the sole energy source., These organisms must couple sulfur reduction to ADP phosphorylation., The majority of sulfur reducers, however, grow organotrophically, and can utilize complex substrates, such as proteins. Since some of these organisms excrete organic products such as |FRAME: ACET|, or |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|, the metabolic significance of sulfur reduction in them is less clear, |CITS: [Schauder93]|., Elemental sulfur is not a good substrate for enzymatic reactions because its solubility, in water is very low (5 μg/L at 25 °) |CITS: [Boulegue78]|. One mechanism that solves, the problem is the conversion of the sulfur ring to a more soluble sulfur intemediate (sometimes referred, to as activated sulfur) prior to reduction |CITS:[16346781][Zoephel88][Schauder93]|., This mechanism has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-844|, in which the soluble compound has, been shown to be |FRAME: Polysulfides| |CITS: [Klimmek91]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5364|)., A second possibility is the physical attachment of the microbes to the elemental sulfur, resulting in, a direct conversion of sulfur to sulfide. Such physical attachment has been shown to be important during, aerobic sulfur oxidation by |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS:[16349107][16535613]|. In addition, a recently, purified |FRAME: CPLX-7193| from the acidophilic hyperthermophile |FRAME: TAX-2283| was shown to, oxidize elemental sulfur in vitro without the need for |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [12949162]|. Since, polysulfides are unstable at low pH, it is possible that |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| is the actual substrate for acidophilic, organisms., With the exception of a few organisms, it is still not clear which of these two possible mechanisms, is used by the different sulfur reducers., About This Pathway, Hyperthermophilic chemolithoautotrophic archaea gain energy by reducing |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| to |FRAME: HS|, using electrons from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|., Sulfur reduction in these lithotrophic organisms must be coupled to ADP phosphorylation., In |FRAME: TAX-35616| the respiratory chain was found to contain a hydrogenase,, a quinone and a c-type cytochrome |CITS: [2128798][1900502][1309514]|., The electron transport chain of |FRAME: TAX-54256| differs: the nine subunit complex which makes up the, |FRAME: CPLX-1662| represents the entire respiratory chain of the organism, containing a, |FRAME:MONOMER-106|, a |FRAME:MONOMER-108|, and electron transport components,, all in one stable complex., The |FRAME:MONOMER-106|, which is of the Ni/Fe type, is not sensitive to oxygen.The, |FRAME:MONOMER-108|, on the other hand, is irreversibly damaged by it., The complex contains 50-55 mol sulfur, 50-55 mol iron and 1.6 mol nickel per mol native complex., The enzyme has a temperature optimum of about 100 ° C |CITS: [9546664][FEMSMicRev22-353]|., While quite different from the hyperthermophiles, the acidophile chemolithtroph |FRAME: TAX-920| is also capable, of reducing elemental sulfur to |FRAME:HS|. When five strains of |FRAME: TAX-920| were tested, all of them, produced hydrogen sulfide from elemental sulfur at pH 1.5., Under argon gas |FRAME: HS| production stopped after 1 day of incubation. In contrast, under , |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |FRAME:HS| production continued for 6 days, producing much more, sulfide, and suggesting that electrons from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| were used to reduce, elemental sulfur to give hydrogen sulfide |CITS: [16232841]|.

Summary: General Background, Biodegradation of aromatic compounds is a common process in anoxic environments. The many natural and synthetic aromatic compounds found in the environment are usually degraded by anaerobic microorganisms into only few central intermediates, prior to ring cleavage |CITS: [9057820]|. |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA Benzoyl-CoA| is the most important of these intermediates since a large number of compounds, including chloro-, nitro-, and aminobenzoates, aromatic hydrocarbons, and phenolic compounds, are initially converted to benzoyl-CoA prior to ring reduction and cleavage |CITS: [11282627]|., The pathways for anaerobic benzoate and benzoyl-CoA degradation have been studied primarily in two microorganisms, the phototrophic, purple, nonsulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1076| and the nitrate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-59405|., About This Pathway, Under anaerobic conditions, the phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1076| can grow with |FRAME: BENZOATE| as the sole carbon source and obtain energy from light via cyclic photophosphorylation. It is also capable of metabolizing the alicyclic acids |FRAME: CPD-575| and |FRAME: CPD-21746|, which then enter the benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway., In both the phototroph |FRAME: TAX-1076| and denitrifying bacterium |FRAME: TAX-59405| anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation is initiated by reductive ring cleavage catalyzed by benzoyl-CoA reductase (see also |FRAME:CENTBENZCOA-PWY|). This reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 molecules of ATP and requires reduced ferrodoxin as an electron acceptor. Whereas in |FRAME: TAX-1076| the cyclic diene is further reduced to |FRAME: CPD-533|, in |FRAME: TAX-59405| the cyclic diene is hydrated to|FRAME: 6-HYDROXYCYCLOHEX-1-ENE-1-CARBONYL-COA|. The respective products are subsequently β-oxidized to cyclic β-oxo compounds, which in turn undergo hydrolytic ring cleavage to |FRAME: CPD-558| in |FRAME: TAX-1076| and |FRAME:3-HYDROXYPIMELYL-COA| in |FRAME: TAX-59405|., These intermediates are further β-oxidized via |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA| to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in a segment of the pathway sometimes referred to as the "lower benzoyl-CoA pathway". The genes responsible for this segment up to |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA| are contained in a single pimFABCDE cluster and constitute an operon. The gene predicted to encode |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.259|, pimE, appears to have a frameshift in |FRAME: TAX-1076| and may not encode a functional enzyme |CITS: [15758219]|., A pim operon deletion strain is still able to grow, albeit more slowly than the wild-type, on dicarboxylic acids and |FRAME: BENZOATE|, indicating that the Pim enzymes are not the only |FRAME: TAX-1076| enzymes that can catalyze the degradation of these compounds |CITS: [15758219]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, The carotenoid pigments are synthesized in the plastids of plants where it is derived from the pathways, of isoprenoid biosynthesis (for review, see |CITS:[15012246]|). More specifically, the first committed, step of carotenoid biosynthesis is that of the formation of phytoene from geranylgeranyl diphosphate,, obtained from the |FRAME:PWY-5121|. This conversion is in fact a two-step reaction catalyzed by the, enzyme phytoene synthase., Phytoene then undergoes a series of four desaturation reactions leading to the formation of, |FRAME:CPD1F-114| via |FRAME:CPD-7408|, |FRAME:CPD1F-98|, |FRAME:NEUROSPORENE|., Although the desaturation steps use all-trans compounds in bacteria, plants accumulate small, amounts of cis-carotenes indicative of additional cis-to-trans isomerization steps, (see note below)., An important branch-point in the biosynthesis of carotenoids lies in the cyclization of the linear, pink, |FRAME:CPD1F-114| into carotenes with all-β-, all-ε- or mixed β and ε rings., Carotenoids with two ε rings are, however, rarely observed in plants and algae, and, when, detected, are usually found in trace amounts |CITS:[GOODWIN80]|; lettuce is a rare example of plants, known to accumulate substantial amounts of bicyclic ε ring carotenoids (see, |FRAME:PWY-5175|). The cyclization reaction are catalyzed by lycopene β- or ε-cyclases., These cyclases all share an amino acid sequence signature that is conserved in those enzymes and, binds dinucleotides such as FAD and NADP |CITS:[8837512]|, but otherwise share little resemblance., The formation of α-carotene from lycopene is likely to proceed by the addition of a β-ring to, |FRAME:CPD1F-115|. The alternative route (addition of an ε-ring to |FRAME:CPD1F-126|), appears unlikely as the ε-cyclase does not seem to be able to add a second ε ring to, the monocyclic δ-carotene |CITS:[8837512]|., Finally, the carotenes are oxygenated in various ways (hydroxylation, epoxydation, de-epoxidation) to, form xanthophylls which comprise most of the carotenoid pigments in the thylakoid membrane of plants., Hydroxylations play an important role in the oxygenation of carotenes and are catalyzed by hydroxylases, acting specifically onto β or ε rings., It has been postulated that the regulation of ε-cyclase, possibly through control of gene, expression, determines xanthophylls composition in leaves and other plant tissues, since its products, (δ-carotene) is destined to the α-carotene branch |CITS:[10205893]|., In photosynthetic tissues, carotenoids generally occur as their stable trans configuration., For neoxanthin, however, it would appear that the 9'-cis isomer: |FRAME:CPD-7424|, is favored in, photosynthetic tissues, while |FRAME:CPD1F-135| preferentially accumulates in non-photosynthetic, plant tissues or plants grown in the dark or under low light conditions |CITS:[11029576]|. It has been, postulated that a Δ9'-neoxanthin isomerase may exist in spinach |CITS:[10725601]|; moreover,, while both isomers were detected during the characterization of the tomato |FRAME:MONOMER-12165|,, the authors deemed the isomerization unlikely to be due to the activity of the enzyme per se, |CITS:[11029576]|.

Summary: Chlorobenzenes are used in the production of pesticides, dyes, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, rubbers, plastics,, and electric goods |CITS: [11472925]|. Their occurrence in the environment is widespread and they are, found in the atmosphere |CITS: [10864157]|, water |CITS: [3314709][16157172]|, soil |CITS: [17988797][2695324]|,, sediments |CITS: [15694470]|, vegetables |CITS:[16002141]|, and animals |CITS: [15325147]|., Chlorobenzenes are of great concern because of their toxicity, persistence and accumulation in the food chain,, and many of them have been declared, priority pollutants, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)., Aerobic microbial degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10620| is not common, but has been reported in a few strains, including, |FRAME: TAX-469561| |CITS: [16348484]|, |FRAME: TAX-393999| |CITS: [9249026]|, and |FRAME: ORG-6079|, |CITS: [10347041]|., The enzyme responsible for initiating the pathway is the broad range |FRAME:CPLX-7696|, a Class IIB dioxygenase, that contains a reductase, a ferredoxin, and a catalytic terminal dioxygenase composed of a large α-subunit and, a small β-subunit with an (αβ)n configuration |CITS: [9791099]|., This enzyme activates its substrates by catalyzing the introduction of two atoms of molecular oxygen into the aromatic, ring. In the case of |FRAME: CPD-10620|, the resulting compound, |FRAME: CPD-10621|, is unstable and rearomatizes, spontaneously, losing one of the chloride groups in the process and forming |FRAME: CPD-10622|, an intermediate that also, appears in the degradation of |FRAME:124-TCB| |CITS: [9249026]|., |FRAME: CPD-10622| is degraded further into |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| via a modified ortho cleavage, pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6094|)., A single amino acid required for dechlorination of |FRAME: CPD-10620|, as well as potentially interacting regions,, have been mapped in the |FRAME: CPLX-7696| from |FRAME: TAX-393999| |CITS: [9791099]|.

Summary: Background, Photosynthetic organisms use sunlight to generate reducing equivalents and incorporate |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into organic molecules which range from sugars to alcohols |CITS: [19915552]|. Some of these alcohols can be used as an alternative renewable fuel. With the ongoing problems of global climate change, reducing |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| emissions by recycling |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| directly into fuels would be greatly beneficial., |FRAME: TAX-1140| was engineered to over express |FRAME: CPLX2PN3-59| with the resultant enhanced production of |FRAME: CPD-7000| and |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL| from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [19915552]|. |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL| is a good substitute fuel for gasoline |CITS: [19915552]|. Another candidate biofuel replacement for gasoline is |FRAME: BUTANOL "Butanol"|. |FRAME: TAX-1488| synthesizes a mixture of |FRAME: ACETONE|, |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH| (the ABE process) from the conversion of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| via the |FRAME: PWY-6594| |CITS: [3540574]|. However, industrial production of |FRAME: BUTANOL| from |FRAME: TAX-1488| is not ideal, as the microorganism produces low yields, has limited tolerance to the products and strictly regulated pathways |CITS: [19756010]|. The |FRAME: PWY-6883| pathway from |FRAME: TAX-1488| was genetically engineered in |FRAME: TAX-562| for |FRAME: BUTANOL| production |CITS: [20143230]|. This pathway was subsequently engineered into |FRAME: TAX-1117 "cyanobacteria| for autotrophic |FRAME: BUTANOL| production., The synthesis of one molecule of |FRAME: BUTANOL| via |FRAME: PWY-101| and the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY| requires an input of 48 photons |CITS: [21569861]|. , About this Pathway, The |FRAME: BUTANOL| generating pathway is entirely engineered into |FRAME: TAX-1140| using genes from |FRAME: TAX-1488| and |FRAME: TAX-3039|. This superpathway is composed of three consecutive pathways for the production of |FRAME: BUTANOL|. The first two pathways are naturally occurring in cyanobacteria. The |FRAME: PWY-101 "photosynthesis pathway"| generates |FRAME: NADPH| which fuels the generation of |FRAME: GAP| via the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|. |FRAME: GAP| is converted to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| via glycolysis, which is in turn converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, the entry point into the third pathway. , An anaerobic environment is a prerequisite for production of |FRAME: BUTANOL|, as some of the enzymes including the product of the adhE2 gene are oxygen sensitive |CITS: [11790753]|. The pathway takes advantage of natural light cycles, with |FRAME: TAX-1140| accumulating reduced carbon during the day, and utilizing it at night to produce |FRAME: BUTANOL|., |FRAME: NADH| is the cofactor required by this pathway, and pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase can regenerate NAD+ and NADPH |CITS: [15604828]|. Overexpression of the genes pntA and pntb which code for the subunits of this protein might enhance butanol production.

Summary: General Background, Chlorotoluenes are important intermediates in many chemical processes, and are still produced in large amounts., Due to their chemical stability and recalcitrance to degradation they tend to accumulate in the environment., Only a few bacterial strains that can mineralize chlorinated toluenes are known, and only a few of those can degrade, dichlorotoluenes. One of these organisms is |FRAME: TAX-393999|, a strain that is known to mineralize a broad spectrum, of chloro-substituted benzenes, as well as |FRAME: CPD-10654|, |FRAME: CPD-7697|, |FRAME: CPD-10836|,, |FRAME: CPD-10837| and |FRAME: CPD-10838| |CITS: [16348484]|. , The key to the metabolic versatility of |FRAME: TAX-393999| is the presence of two enzymes - a broad-substrate-spectrum, |FRAME: CPLX-7696|, known as TecA, and a similarly broad spectrum |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, known as TecB., Together these two enzymes catalyze the initial steps in the metabolism of all of these compounds, converting, them to modified catechols. The modified catechols are then processed by modified ortho-cleavage pathways, that utilize enzymes specilized in the degradation of chloro-substituted aromatic compounds., About This Pathway, The degradation of the different chlorinated toluenes by |FRAME: TAX-393999| utilizes the same enzymes,, although the pathways follow different routes |CITS: [12218011]|., |FRAME: CPD-10838| is initially activated by dioxygenation, catalyzed by the broad spectrum |FRAME: CPLX-7696|,, followed by rearomatization catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-10840|., Ring opening of the catechol proceeds via a modified ortho cleavage pathway, employing |FRAME: CPLX-7713|., The product of this reaction, |FRAME: CPD-10841|, is subject to 3,6-cycloisomerization by, |FRAME: CPLX-7712|, resulting in formation of |FRAME: CPD-10842|. Finally, the lactone is hydrolyzed to, |FRAME: CPD-10843| by |FRAME: MONOMER-14658| |CITS: [12218011]|., The intermediates of the proposed pathway were isolated and identified by HPLC and NMR analyses. In addition,, the individual enzymes were completely or partially purified, and their activities confirmed |CITS: [12218011]|., The end product of this pathway is assumed to be further degraded to TCA cycle intermediates by a modified, |FRAME: PWY-2361| pathway that has not been characterized in this organism |CITS: [12218011]|.

Some of the xenobiotic sulfonates that are found in sewage originate from pharmaceutical, compounds whose active ingredients are derivatized from |FRAME: CPD-10431|, (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-10432| and |FRAME: CPD-10433|) ., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-209770| was isolated from an aerobic enrichment culture that utilized, |FRAME: CPD-10431| as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [11479707]|., Whole cells of strain EDS1 were able to desulfonate ethanedisulfonate only if molecular oxygen was, available. The ethanedisulfonate-dependent oxygen uptake of whole cells during growth rose to a, maximum before the end of growth and then sank rapidly. However, no turnover of ethanedisulfonate, was detected in cell extracts. This was interpreted as evidence for an inducible desulfonative, oxygenase that was not active in cell extracts.

Summary: Until fairly recently the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| in plants was poorly understood and only a few enzymes involved in this pathway had been characterized |CITS:[25217510]|. On the other hand, this pathway has been elucidated in much more detail in animals (see for instance |FRAME:PWY66-5|) |CITS:[21902244]|. |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| has been found in plants at much lower concentrations than in animals (i.e. 1-2% of the total sterols) but can accumulate to significant higher levels in Solanaceae |CITS:[Whitaker88] [Whitaker91] [Japelt11]|. The more prominent sterols in plants, which have been investigated in more detail are the phytosterols (C24-alkylsterols) |CITS:[Piironen00]| (see |FRAME:PWY-2541|). , The observation that |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| level and steroidal glycoalkaloid biosynthesis in potato appeared to be connected |CITS:[Bergenstrahle96]| confirmed previous results |CITS:[Tschesche80] [Heftmann67]| and laid the foundation to studies that implicated the involvement of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| in the biosynthesis of steroidal glycoalkaloids |CITS:[Ohmura95] [23473422]|. Because of their adverse effects in human diet steroidal glycoalkaloids are considered a health threat |CITS:[17090106]|, a fact which in view of the advantageous pharmaceutical properties of steroidal glycoalkaloids resulted in considerable efforts to elucidate the underlying pathways of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL|, |FRAME:CPD-17696| in tomato (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-2|, |FRAME:PWY18C3-3|) |CITS:[22180624] [23788733]| and |FRAME:CPD-9214| and |FRAME:CPD-9211| in potato (see |FRAME:PWY-5666|) |CITS:[McCue05] [16298403] [17157337]|. Furthermore, |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| is an important component of membranes and protective surface layers and gives rise to phytoecdysteroids |CITS:[11393511] [25556315]|., The finding that |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| is usually present in plants in only diminutive amounts but rises to significant higher levels in members of the Solaneceae family suggests that the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| in those species might be distinct from that of other plants. For instance, in |FRAME: TAX-4100| the level of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| reaches up to 12% of the total sterols |CITS:[26671544]|. The |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| biosynthetic pathway is the gateway to various steroids and vitamins, e.g. |FRAME:VITAMIN_D3| (see |FRAME:PWY-6076|) |CITS:[23717318]|. Metabolic intermediates such as |FRAME:CYCLOARTENOL| and |FRAME:DESMOSTEROL-CPD| are branching points that either give way to plant C-24 alkylsterols (see |FRAME:PWY-2541|) or |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL|. The flux into different pathways depends on the activity of basically two enzymes competing for those substrates, i.e. the sterol C-24 methyltransferase 1, which steers the flux of carbon towards C-24 alkylsterols and in doing so lowers |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| biosynthesis |CITS:[10852933] [12226510] [12692338]|, and the sterol side chain reductase (SSR2), which has been shown to form respective precursor and |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| by reducing the side chain of |FRAME:CYCLOARTENOL| and |FRAME:DESMOSTEROL-CPD| |CITS:[25217510]|., Using the human 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase (|FRAME: HS03985|) |CITS:[11519011]| as probe and performing BLAST searches against the potato unigene database |CITS:[11125077]| and the tomato database |CITS:[20935049]| resulted in the identification of cDNA's (SSR2) that encoded sterol side chain reductases able to carry out the reduction of |FRAME:CYCLOARTENOL| and |FRAME:DESMOSTEROL-CPD| to form |FRAME:CPD-4181| and |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL|, respectively |CITS:[25217510]|., The |FRAME: G18C3-13| cDNA of tomato was then used to identify the entire set of cholesterogenesis genes in |FRAME: TAX-4081| and |FRAME: TAX-4100| and this information lead to the entire reaction sequence required for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| in plants |CITS:[28005066] [26876023]|. It was found that the enzymes of this pathway are often promiscuous and are active in related pathways such as |FRAME:PWY-2541|. This is in accordance with the evolutionary 'patchwork' hypothesis, proposing that ancestral enzymes with low substrate specificity develop narrower specificities through duplication and diversification over time, which eventually results in the genesis of new pathways with enzymes of new catalytic properties |CITS:[4207200] [26276843]|. This is exemplified by the C4-demethylation complex formed by sterol methyl oxidases (SMO's), 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/C4-decarboxylase (3βHSD), and 3-oxosteroid reductase (SDR) |CITS:[8031136] [21902244] [21147141]|. In tomato and |FRAME: TAX-4100| SMO3 and 4 encode proteins that are specific for cholesterol biosynthesis, whereas SMO1 and 2 encode proteins that catalyze reactions in |FRAME:PWY-2541|. Since both groups of SMO's participate in a multi-enzyme complexes with the same promiscuous 3βHSD and SDR proteins, the specificity of the SMO component determines in what pathway, |FRAME:PWY18C3-1| or |FRAME:PWY-2541|, those enzyme complexes operate |CITS:[28005066] [26876023]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Cobamides Cobamides| are a family of cobalt-containing corrinoid cofactors. Cobamides contain a corrin ring with a cobalt ion in its center. Four of the six coordination sites of the cobalt ion are provided by the corrin ring, while the other two are provided by upper (β) and lower (α) ligands, which are located above and below the ring plane, respectively. The best known cobamide, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin|, contains |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand., At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described in bacteria. These ligands can be classified in three families - benzimidazolyl, purinyl, or phenolyl bases. Individual cobamide-producing bacteria typically synthesize only one type of cobamide, and most organisms studied to date are selective in their cobamide use. For example, the human gut bacterium |FRAME: TAX-818| can use benzimidazolyl and purinyl cobamides but not phenolyl cobamides |CITS: [24439897]| and |FRAME: TAX-2378| requires phenolyl cobamides |CITS: [23417488]|., De novo synthesis of cobamides requires a great deal of genetic information, which is only found in some prokaryotes. Some organisms that are not capable of producing their cobamids de novo have evolved mechanisms for cobamide remodeling - they can pick up the cobamides available in their environment, and if they are not of the type required by their enzymes, they can remove and replace the lower ligand |CITS: [22923412][24803319][27040778][31609521]|., Two enzymes are know to be envolved in cobamide remodeling. CbiZ (|FRAME: EC-3.5.1.90|) was shown in archaea and some bacterial species to hydrolyze the amide bond adjacent to the aminopropanol linker, forming a cobyrate. A set of six gene products can then attach a different lower ligand to the cobyrate |CITS: [19889098]|. The CbiR protein hydrolyzes the phosphoribosyl bond in the nucleotide loop of cobamides, producing a cobinamide phosphate |CITS: [33293380]|., The |FRAME: G-107473| gene from |FRAME: TAX-239935| was tested with 7 substrates, all with a 5'-deoxyadenosyl upper ligand, and was active with all of them, showing similar activity with benzimidazolyl and purinyl cobamides and higher activities with phenolyl cobamides |CITS: [33293380]|. Heterologous expression of |FRAME: G-107473| from |FRAME: TAX-239935| in |FRAME: TAX-562| allowed the host to remodel |FRAME: CPD-20842| (in the presence of |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|) to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| |CITS: [33293380]|., Homologs of cbiR were found in the genomes of 275 bacterial taxa and 1 archaeal taxon from diverse habitats, including aquatic environments, sewage, digesters, oil spills, bioreactors, soil, and human and animal hosts. 80% of all cbiR homologs are located adjacent to genes involved in cobamide biosynthesis, suggesting they function in cobamide remodeling.

Summary: Please note: Not all of the reactions shown in this superpathway may be found in each of the organisms listed here. Rather, this superpathway has been generated to show the diversity of jasmonyl-amino acid conjugates that are synthesized by a number of different plant species., Jasmonates are an important class of compounds, related to |FRAME:CPD-734|, found throughout the plant kingdom, as well as in fungi |CITS:[17513307]|)., These compounds may participate in a number of biological processes including resistance to herbivores and some, pathogens, protection against ozone, senescence, and reproductive development (reviewed in |CITS:[19025383][17513307]|). , Many different jasmonate precursors and jasmonate derivatives have biological activity, including jasmonyl, (JA)-amino acid conjugates. Different species may have a different array of JA-amino acid conjugates, and the, biological activity of each compound may differ between species. For example, jasmonyl-isoleucine (JA-Ile) has, been shown to have biological activity in a number of different plants, including Arabidopsis thaliana, |CITS:[15258265][18247047]|, |FRAME:TAX-49451||CITS:[17273867][17085687]|, Achyranthes bidentata, |CITS:[18812165]|, barley |CITS:[9315685]|, tomato |CITS:[18458331]|, rice |CITS:[ 9013895]| and others., In Arabidopsis thaliana, JA-Ile promotes the interaction between COI1 (an F-box) protein and the, JAZ1 repressor protein. In this manner, JA-Ile is believed, to help destabilize the JAZ1 repressor and thereby promote JA-responsive transcription |CITS:[17637677]|., COI1 and JAZ homologs have been found in other plants, such as tomato, where they also bind in a JA-Ile-dependent, manner, |CITS:[18458331]|, indicating that JA-Ile might have a similar function in other plant species. However, this has, not been studied in |FRAME:TAX-49451| to date., Interestingly, in Polygonum longisetum, a weed commonly found in Japan, a treatment of 100 uM JA-Ile fails, to stimulate the normal JA-responsive emissions of volatile sesquiterpenes |CITS:[TAMOGAMI07]| indicating that even, JA-Ile may not be similarly effective in all plants. Other differences in biological activity have been observed across species for many other conjugates including, JA-ACC, JA-leucine, and JA-valine. , The enzymes capable of synthesizing JA-amino acid conjugates are structurally related to the acyl, adenylate-forming firefly luciferase superfamily of enzymes |CITS:[12084835][15258265]|., To date, JA-amino acid synthetase enzymes have been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[15258265]|, and |FRAME:TAX-49451| |CITS:[17273867][17085687]|, but given the widespread identification of these, compounds in numerous species, homologous enzymes must exist throughout the plant kingdom. , Additional studies in Arabidopsis thaliana suggest that the specific isomeric forms of the same jasmonate can, have very different biological effects |CITS: [19349968]|., For example, initial studies suggested that (-)-JA-Ile was a biologically active phytohormone |CITS: [SEMBDER93][17291501]|. However,, later work shows that |FRAME: CPD-11259| is the biologically active form of the compound |CITS: [19349968, ]|. This compound exists at low levels in most commercial preparations of |FRAME: CPD-11232| and may explain the observed, biologically activity originally associated with the (-)-JA-Ile diastereomer. A pure preparation of (-)-JA-Ile does, does not promote JAZ/COI1 binding in vitro |CITS: [19349968]|. Interestingly, the biologically, active form, |FRAME: CPD-11259|,, more closely resembles the potent bacterial phytotoxin coronatine than |FRAME: CPD-11232| does |CITS: [19349968][19377448]|., In some species, certain JA-amino acid conjugates have no discernable biological activity, e.g. JA-Val in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[15258265]|. It is unclear whether these are storage forms of JA or catabolic intermediates. Another important, phytohormone, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), can be conjugated with several amino acids, as shown in the, |FRAME:PWY-6219| pathway. Some of these compounds, such as IAA-aspartate are targeted for further, breakdown (|CITS:[9733548]|, (see |FRAME:PWY-2021|), while others, such as, IAA-alanine may serve, as storage forms. A family of amido hydrolases can release free, active IAA from some of these, "storage" IAA conjugates |CITS:[7792259][10072397]|. But, to date, no JA-amido hydrolases (that could release free, JA from the amino acid conjugates) have been identified in plants. However, this enzymatic activity has been, detected in the fungus, Botryodiplodia theobromae |CITS:[9141491]|., Further work will be required to determine the metabolic and functional fate of the "inactive" JA-amino acid, conjugates in different species.

The |FRAME: Echinocandins echinocandins| represent a family of fungal cyclic lipo-hexapeptides characterized by their fungicidal and fungistatic properties against ascomycetes of the genera Candida and Aspergillus, respectively |CITS:[25156669]|. The effectiveness of echinocandins is based on their noncompetitive inhibition of 1,3-β-glucan synthases which are essential for fungal cell wall synthesis |CITS:[6235127]| and also cause defects in cell polarity which extend their mode of action with yet another functional quality |CITS:[24258022]|. Echinocandins have been successfully used in treatments against invasive candidiasis |CITS:[22412055]|, which accounts for one of the highest mortal infections in intensive care units (IUC) |CITS:[19952319]| and consequently has intensified the research on these fungal cyclopeptides and derivatives thereof |CITS:[23463246] [25642215]|. , After the first isolation of |FRAME:CPD-17711| in the early 1970s |CITS:[Benz74]| the importance of this antimycotic agent soon became apparent and was followed by efforts to synthesize echinocandins in the lab (for instance |CITS:[22175373]|). The application of echinocandins for human treatments was somewhat hindered by their hemolytic properties which led to the development of semisynthetic derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-17711| (this pathway) and its close relative |FRAME:CPD-17738| |CITS:[23688303]| which had been primarily modified in their fatty acid moiety. Compounds such as |FRAME:CPD-17734| |CITS:[2708131]| and |FRAME:CPD-17735| |CITS:[7650681] [17266452]| (derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-17711| - see also |FRAME:PWY-7652|) as well as |FRAME:CPD-17736| |CITS:[8083161]| and |FRAME:CPD-17737| |CITS:[10513849]| (derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-17738|) significantly reduced hemolysis but retained the bioactivity of the original compounds., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17711| is closely related to the biosynthesis of its amino acid building blocks which form the cyclic hexapeptide scaffold. This is supported by the presence of two independent gene clusters involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-17711|, i.e. the echinocandin (ecd) gene cluster and the L-homotyrosine (hyt) gene cluster |CITS:[22998630]|. Of the six amino acid residues involved four of them are nonproteinogenic and either mono-, or dihydroxylated. The first step in the biosynthesis is the activation of |FRAME:LINOLEIC_ACID| and its linkage to the six module nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) which is catalyzed by the linoleyl-AMP ligase encoded by EcdI in Emericella rugulosa |CITS:[22998630]|. The NRPS encoded by EcdA then adds successively |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, |FRAME:THR|, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE|, |FRAME:CPD-17730| (see |FRAME:PWY-7649|), again |FRAME:THR| and finally |FRAME:CPD-17747| (see |FRAME:PWY-7648|). The formed lipo-hexapeptide is then released and macrocyclized by the terminal condensation domain (CT) of the last module |CITS:[22998630]|. , In order to obtain the hydroxylation degree of |FRAME:CPD-17711| at least eight hydroxylations on the amino acid residues are required. It appears that the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17730| is encoded by genes of both gene clusters (ecd and hty) (see |FRAME:PWY-7649|) and happens before the integration of the amino acid residue to the growing peptide chain. In contrast, the dihydroxylation of the |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| residue occurs after the release of the cyclic hexapeptide, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17739| by the echinocandine D hydroxylase encoded by EcdH which iteratively hydroxylates the C-4 and C-5 position of |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| |CITS:[23451921]|. It remains to be shown the timing and catalyzing enzyme for the hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17722| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17747| and the elucidation of the final hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17740| to form the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17711|.

Summary: The macrocyclic polyketides |FRAME: CPD-10016| (FK506), |FRAME: CPD-18261| (FK520), and |FRAME: CPD-14676| are potent immunosuppressants that prevent T-cell proliferation through initial binding to the immunophilin FKBP12. Analogs of these molecules are of considerable interest as therapeutics in both metastatic and inflammatory disease., |FRAME: CPD-10016 Tacrolimus| and |FRAME: CPD-18261| are very similar to each other and are synthesized by very similar polyketide synthase/non-ribosomal peptide synthase (PKS/NRPS) systems. The two compounds differ only in the group attached to carbon 21, which is an ethyl group in |FRAME: CPD-18261| and an unusual allyl group in |FRAME: CPD-10016|., Two independent studies reported that the extender unit responsible for the allyl group, |FRAME: CPD-26199|, is synthesized by several enzymes that include a diketide system |CITS: [20194504][21175203]|., The system includes two polyketide synthases encoded by the |FRAME: G-124299| and |FRAME: G-124300| genes (also named allA and allB). TcsA binds a malonyl starter unit while TcsB accepts a propanoyl moiety from |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and transfers it to TcsA, forming a 3-oxopentanoyl group. The rest of the pathway continues while the intermediates are attached to TcsA., It is believed that two enzymes of the general fatty acid biosynthesis pathway, namely |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.100|, and |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.59|, act next, their combined action forming a (2E)-pent-2-enoyl group. Two additional dedicated enzymes encoded by genes present in the same operon as |FRAME: G-124299| and |FRAME: G-124300| complete the pathway: TcsC is a carboxylase/reductase that reduces the double bond and adds a carboxyl group at position 2 of the pentanoate skeleton, while TcsD is a dehydrogenase that oxidizes the terminal bond, forming the final product of the system, a 2-allylmalonyll group. This group is then transferred to CoA, forming |FRAME: CPD-26199|., This extender unit is incorporated into the |FRAME: CPD-10016| skeleton by the FkbB polyketide synthasei |CITS: [20194504][21175203]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1281 "Coenzyme B"| is one of the many unusual cofactors present in methanogens and required for methane formation. Like |FRAME: Factor-420|, |FRAME: CPD-1281| acts as an electron carrier in the metabolism of methanogens (see |FRAME: P241-PWY|)., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| functions as a methyl carrier in methanogenesis, and |FRAME: Me-CoM| has been established as the terminal intermediate of methanogenesis from all substrates (see |FRAME:METHFORM-PWY|). In addition to its role in methanogenesis, different forms of |FRAME: CoM| have physiological roles in methanogens, and are specific enzyme substrates |CITS: [2115763]|., All catabolic processes in methanogenesis lead to the formation of a mixed disulfide bond between |FRAME: CoM| and |FRAME: CPD-1281|, by a reaction in which |FRAME: CPD-1281| reduces |FRAME: Me-CoM|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CH4| and a |FRAME:CPD-1282| |CITS: [12102556]| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|)., The process in which |FRAME:CPD-1282| is reduced back to |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| has been studied extensively. There are two different enzyme systems that are capable of reducing the |FRAME:CPD-1282|. One is a membrane-bound system, encoded by the hdrDE genes, which uses |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE| as its electron donor |CITS: [15168610]|. The other is a soluble cytoplasmic system encoded by the hdrABC genes, which can use several types of electron donors, either directly, or by forming a complex with other enzymes., About This Pathway, Heterodisulfide reductases (Hdr) of the HdrABC class are ancient enzymes that existed in the prokaryotic common ancestor. The enzymes consist of a large HdrA subunit that contains FAD and multiple [4Fe-4S] clusters, a smaller catalytic HdrB subunit, and an electron transfer HdrC subunit. Electrons enter the enzyme at HdrA, and are transferred via HdrC to the active site of HdrB., In H2-oxidizing CO2-reducing species such as |FRAME: TAX-145262| and |FRAME: TAX-145263| the cytoplasmic HdrABC is complexed with the |FRAME: CPLX-684 "MvhAGD hydrogenase"|, forming |FRAME: EC-1.8.98.5| |CITS: [8119281]|. Electron pairs donated from the hydrogenase are bifurcated by the HdrA subunit, and are used to reduce both the |FRAME: CPD-1282| and ferredoxin |CITS: [21262829]|., It has been shown that the electrons are transferred from the hydrogenase to the HdrA subunit of the reductase by the δ subunit of the hydrogenase |CITS: [24039260]|.

The homeostasis of glycerophospholipids constitutes an indispensable element for buildup, maintenance and component dynamics of cell membranes in all organisms. The many different phospholipid molecular species found in yeast basically vary in their composition of fatty acids esterified to the sn-1 and sn-2 position of a phosphorylated |FRAME:GLYCEROL| and a head group which can either be a |FRAME:CHOLINE|, |FRAME:ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME:MYO-INOSITOL| or the one phospholipid without a head group, i.e. phosphatidate (for example |FRAME:CPD-8291|) |CITS:[14321173] [22345606]|. After the de novo synthesis of phospholipids in the Kennedy pathway (see |FRAME:TRIGLSYN-PWY|, |FRAME:PWY3O-450|) glycerophospholipids can be degraded (see |FRAME:LIPAS-PWY|) and remodeled (this pathway; see also |FRAME:PWY-7409| and |FRAME:PWY-7417|). The latter has been proposed by William E.M. Lands |CITS:[14413818]| who describes in the eponymous 'Lands cycle' a de-acylation-re-acylation process of phospholipids typically characterized by saturated acyl chains at the sn-1 and unsaturated acyl chains at the sn-2 position |CITS:[7871882]|., This remodeling process starts with the de-acylation at the sn-2 position of phospholipids catalyzed by phospholipases (e.g. phospholipase A2) generating the corresponding lyso-phospholipids. The resulting lyso-phospholipids represent the substrates for acyl-CoA dependent lyso-phospholipid acyltransferases or phospholipid transacylases which can re-acylate the sn-2 position. Generally, the Lands cycle constitutes an exchange of fatty acids at the sn-2 position which is an substantial factor in the maintenance of the homeostasis of phospholipids |CITS:[17010666]|. This de- and re-acylation process translates into many physiological functions, for example increasing membrane fluidity through a higher percentage of unsaturated acyl chains, re-esterification of exogenous lyso-phospholipids |CITS:[17726007]|, buffering excess toxic fatty acids |CITS:[22090344] [19608739]| and maintenance of the intrinsic membrane curvature necessary to preserve membrane integrity |CITS:[16339082] [31173]|., In the phosphatidylcholine remodeling pathway the de-acylation of |FRAME:1-2-DIPALMITOYLPHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| is catalyzed by the phospholipase A2 activity of the triacylglycerol lipase TGL4p |CITS:[16135509] [16267052] [20332534]| whereas the re-acylation of |FRAME:CPD-8343| is carried out by the acyl-CoA dependent lyso-phosphatidylcholine acyltransferase (TAZ1p) |CITS:[9930410] [15588229]|. Phosphatidylcholine (PC) is a very dominant phospholipid species in membranes of most eukaryotic organisms |CITS:[17010666]| and as such its homeostasis must be under a very tight control to ensure the proper functioning of cell membranes |CITS:[16339082]|.
