Summary: Please note: This is a superpathway that describes the degradation of the amino acid |FRAME: MET| in mammals., For more information about this pathway, please consult the different subpathways that make it up., |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid in mammals. It is not biosynthesized and must be obtained in the diet. It may be metabolized in the liver by several pathways, which are regulated by changes in the concentration of enzyme, substrate, and effector molecules |CITS: [3309559][15539209]|., In the degradation pathway shown here, L-methionine is first metabolized to S-adenosyl-L-methionine, a compound that mediates most biological methylations., In the next reaction, the S-methyl group is transferred to other acceptors, such as DNA shown here, in a transmethylation step. The product, S-adenosyl-homocysteine, is then hydrolyzed to homocysteine and adenine., In rats and humans approximately half of the homocysteine formed is remethylated to methionine via two salvage pathways, one involving |FRAME: MONOMER-9225| (EC 2.1.1.13), and the other involving |FRAME:CPLX-5601| (EC 2.1.1.5) (see |FRAME:ADENOSYLHOMOCYSCAT-PWY|)., The remainder of the homocysteine condenses with serine to form |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE|., |FRAME:CPLX-5163| catalyzes cleavage of the C-γ-S bond of |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE|, yielding |FRAME:CYS|, |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| and |FRAME:AMMONIA| in a transsulfuration reaction (reviewed in |CITS: [3309559], [15539209]|) (see |FRAME:HOMOCYSDEGR-PWY|). |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is transported from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix, where it is further degraded to |FRAME: SUC-COA|, which is fed to the |FRAME: TCA| (see |FRAME:PWY-5130|)., There are several degradation pathways for cysteine in mammals., The major route of cysteine degradation most likely starts by the oxidation of cysteine to, |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE|., The conversion of |FRAME: CYS| to |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| (L-cysteine sulfinic acid) forms, a branch point., In one route, |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| is transaminated by |FRAME:ENZRXN-9021| to, |FRAME: 3-SULFINYL-PYRUVATE|, which spontaneously degrades to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and, |FRAME:SO3|, as shown here |CITS: [13314623]|. Sulfite is oxidized by |FRAME:CPLX-7169| to, |FRAME: SULFATE|, which is excreted in the urine |CITS: [7491943]|, and pyruvate is converted by, |FRAME:PYRUVDEHYD-PWY| to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, which enters the |FRAME: TCA| (see, |FRAME: CYSTEINE-DEG-PWY|). This is the pathway included in the superpathway., A second route involves the decarboxylation of |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| to form, |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE|, which is further oxidized to |FRAME:TAURINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5331|)., Taurine is used in the synthesis of bile salts., In addition, cysteine can also be metabolized to pyruvate by 3-sulfinoalanine-independent pathways., These involve the cysteine desulfhydrase activity of |FRAME: CPLX-5163| (see |FRAME: LCYSDEG-PWY|), or an initial direct transamination by |FRAME:ENZRXN-13116| to form |FRAME: 3-MERCAPTO-PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5329|) |CITS: [3309559]|., The relative use of these two pathways shows species and tissue specificity (reviewed in |CITS: [3309559]|). In vitro studies of freshly isolated rat renal cortical tubules |CITS: [2111378]|, and freshly isolated rat enterocytes |CITS: [2621485]|, showed that these cell types predominantly used this 3-sulfinoalanine transmination pathway to pyruvate, rather than the decarboxylation pathway to taurine. Substantial amounts of |FRAME:MONOMER-8844| and |FRAME:CPLX-5342| activities were demonstrated in rat renal cortical tubules |CITS: [2111378]|. 3-Sulfinoalanine-independent pathways, particularly cleavage by |FRAME:CPLX-5163|, also had significant roles in these, cell types. However, in freshly isolated rat hepatocytes, the 3-sulfinoalanine-independent pathways, particularly the pathway involving cleavage by |FRAME: CPLX-5163|, had a predominant role., The hepatocytes also used the 3-sulfinoalanine decarboxylation pathway to taurine, to a lesser, extent |CITS: [3117038]|.

General Background, Anthocyanins are water-soluble, secondary plant products that constitute a major subgroup (about 15 to 20%) of flavonoids |CITS: [Andersen06]|. Almost all vascular plants possess basic anthocyanins such as pelargonidin-3-O-glucoside (this pathway) and cyanidin-3-O-glucoside (|FRAME:PWY-5125|) responsible for the red to magenta coloration of flowers and fruits and delphinidin-3-O-glucoside (|FRAME:PWY-5153|) introducing blue tones to the floral organs of plants |CITS: [11130659]|., Anthocyanins play important roles as pigments of flowers and fruits in numerous plants across the plant kingdom to attract insects for pollination and act as protectants against UV-B irradiation |CITS: [14561507]|. They also exhibit anti-oxidant activities and therefore may serve as potential anticancer |CITS: [16084717]| and anti-arteriosclerosis compounds in human health |CITS: [15282635]| |CITS: [12828368]| |CITS: [11960739]|. Anthocyanines constitute biological active metabolites that also modulate inter-species relationships being intimately connected with the co-existence of plants with, e.g. insects, mammals, and birds |CITS: [11820759]|., About This Pathway, As described for the biosynthesis of cyanidin- (see |FRAME:PWY-5125|) and delphinidin-derived anthocyanins (see |FRAME:PWY-5153|) pelargonidin-based pigments are built up in a series of two enzymes, the anthocyanidin synthase (ANS - synonym leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase - LDOX) converting |FRAME:LEUCOPELARGONIDIN-CMPD| to |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-CMPD| and the UDPG: flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferase (3-UGT) producing the first stable anthocyanin of this pathway, i.e. |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-3-GLUCOSIDE-CMPD| |CITS: [Kitamura06]| (for a more comprehensive comment see - |FRAME:PWY-5125|)., The anthocyanidin synthase has been proposed to be a component of a macromolecular complex located at the endoplasmatic reticulum. In dependence on the enzymes involved in the complex (e.g. flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylase) and their metabolic order the ANS is involved in the production of pelargonidin-derived pigments as found in strawberry |CITS: [12376640]| and recombinant petunia ANS expressed with 3-UGT in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [11316805]|. However, specific data addressing this reaction with regard to kinetic parameter and substrate specificity remain to be reported., The flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferases involved in this pathway have been found to cover a broader spectrum of anthocyanidins. This is indicated by the occurrence of |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-3-GLUCOSIDE-CMPD| in |FRAME:TAX-29760| |CITS:[19673489]| and strawberry |CITS: [11559107]| representing species containing pelargonidin-derived anthocyanins.

Summary: General Background, Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum)., The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids., Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|)., Following a meal, the bile acids are secreted into the small intestine, where they play an important role in digestion by acting as detergents. The majority (~97%) of the bile acids are reabsorbed in the ileum and returned to the liver. The rest enter the large intestine, where they are modified by bacteria into secondary bile acids. The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24-amide hydrolysis (releasing the glycine and taurine molecules) and 7α-dehydroxylation, forming |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| |CITS: [7276750]|., The bacterially-produced secondary bile acids affect host physiology in multiple ways. Some of them are ligands for the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), the liver X receptor (LXR), the G proteincoupled receptor TGR5, and the vitamin D receptor, and have been shown to trigger signaling cascades |CITS: [12016314][17823458][18670431]|. |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE Deoxycholate| production has been shown to have a positive affect by limiting the outgrowth of the enteric pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1496| |CITS: [25337874]|, while on the other hand |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| have been implicated as causative agents in colon carcinogenesis |CITS: [4427390][1255778]|., About This Pathway, The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24 amide hydrolysis and 7-dehydroxylation. Amide hydrolysis (which is described in |FRAME: PWY-8135|) is quite common and is found in many Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial species. The 7-dehydroxylation process is less common, and is found only in some species of anaerobic intestinal bacteria. The process is rather complex and consists of an oxidative part, a dehydration, and a reductive part. The enzymes involved are encoded by the bile acid-inducible (bai) operons., Gene products involved in the pathway may vary depending upon the bile acid substrate. For example, the products of |FRAME: G-44404| and |FRAME: G-44405| genes are involved in degradation of the minor 7β-hydroxy bile acid |FRAME: CPD-10534| (see |FRAME: PWY-8134|). More widespread, constitutive reactions of bile acid metabolism by intestinal bacteria are shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6518|., In |FRAME: TAX-29347| the oxidative part of the pathway begins with active transport of a bile acid across the bacterial membrane, which is mediated by the product of the baiG gene, a H+-dependent primary bile acid transporter |CITS: [8955384]|. The bile acid is activated by ligation to |FRAME: CO-A| in an |FRAME: ATP|-dependent manner by the product of |FRAME: G-139| |CITS: [1551828]|. The 3α-hydroxy group of the bile acid-CoA thioester is oxidized by either of the products of the three genes |FRAME: G-140|, |FRAME: G-141| and |FRAME: G-142|, which can utilize |FRAME: NAD| or |FRAME: NADP| and are specific for bile acid-CoA conjugates. A double bond is inserted between C-4 and C-5 by the product of |FRAME: G-12042|, an |FRAME: NAD|-dependent flavoprotein |CITS: [7766153][23836456]|., There is some uncertainty regarding at which stage the intermediates remain in the form of CoA-esters. Earlier models suggested that CoA-esters serve as substrates for most of the downstream enzymes. However, based on substrate preference of the enzymes in the later part of the pathway, it is currently believed that |FRAME: G-18017 BaiF|, a CoA-transferase, acts after |FRAME: G-12042 BaiCD|, and that the intermediates for the rest of the pathway are free bile acids rather than CoA-esters |CITS: [16299351][31092280]|., The next reaction is the rate-limiting and irreversible dehydration of the 7α-hydroxyl group, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.106| (|FRAME: G-143 BaiE)|, resulting in the introduction of a second double bond at C-6 |CITS: [8808760][26650892]|. The pathway continues by a series of three reductions, the first two of which catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.114| (|FRAME: G-58251 BaiN)| |CITS: [29217478]|, and the last one likely by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21157| |FRAME: G-80673 BaiO| |CITS: [31092280]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD Ethene| (also known as ethylene) is known in plants, fungi and bacteria. In plants, ethene is an important hormone that regulates plant growth and development. It is well-known as a fruit-ripening hormone and is biologically active in trace amounts. Ethene also plays a general role as a growth inhibitor in promoting leaf and flower senescence and abscission., All plants produce ethene from |FRAME: MET| (as described here). In addition, two alternative ethene biosynthetic pathways have been reported from microorganisms. Most microorganisms produce only trace amounts of ethene via the |FRAME: CPD-479| (KMBA) pathway |CITS: [Kazuhiro92]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6854|). In that route ethene is produced non-enzymatically by hydroxyl radicals that are produced from molecular oxygen by an |FRAME: MONOMER-16774| |CITS: [3541827][2792734]|. In the second microbial pathway, which is found mostly in members of the |FRAME: TAX-136849|, ethene is formed enzymatically from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6853|)., Being the simplest unsaturated organic molecule, ethene is the building block for synthetic polymers including plastics such as polyethylene. Large amounts of ethylene are currently produced in a chemical process from fossil fuels. It is the organic compound that has the highest annual global production. , About This Pathway, In plants, methionine is the only known precursor of ethene biosynthesis. Ethene is synthesized from |FRAME: MET| through intermediates |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) and |FRAME: CPD-68| (ACC). Ethene synthesis can be induced by environmental stress and other plant growth hormones such as auxin. Its production and action can be inhibited by specific ethene production inhibitors such as silver and high concentration of CO2. , The cloning and analysis of |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.14 "1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate synthase"| (ACC synthase, EC 4.4.1.14) genes from a number of plants show that they form a multigene family that are differentially regulated. The transcripts accumulate as a response to a variety of triggers such as ethene, hormones, wounding, ripening, senescence and pollination |CITS: [10996253]|.

It is used as a solvent for pesticides and as a heat, transfer agent with PCBs; its mixture with tetrachlorobenzene is applied in controlling shellfish predators |CITS: [361369]|., It is included in the EPA list of priority pollutants., The aerobic microbial degradation of |FRAME: 124-TCB| has been reported in several strains, including, |FRAME: TAX-65067| |CITS: [van der Meer87][1987135][9809414]|, |FRAME: TAX-469561| and, |FRAME: TAX-393999| (then reported as Pseudomonas PS12) |CITS: [16348484]|, Bordetella sp. strains E3 and F2, |CITS: [17633183]| and |FRAME: ORG-6078| |CITS: [18763518]|., Degradation of |FRAME: 124-TCB| proceeds in a manner common to all chlorobenzenes: it starts with a |FRAME: CPLX-7705|, attack, which is followed by a re-aromatization by |FRAME: MONOMER-14407|. The product of these two enzymes,, |FRAME: CPD-10622|, is degraded in a modified ortho cleavage pathway to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, (see |FRAME: CPD-10622|)., Biodegradation of |FRAME: 124-TCB| in natural samples usually occurs in very low rates, due to insufficient degradation, capacity by the indigenous microorganisms. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, The pathway depicted here depends on the direct conversion of the phosphatidyl-base phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine by successive methylations., This pathway is found in animals, yeast, and bacteria that interact with eukaryotic cells (reviewed in |CITS: [18204095][17010666][20656373]|). In the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| this is the primary pathway, but both this pathway and pathway |FRAME: PWY3O-450| can substiture for one another depending on growth conditions. The two pathways offer versatility in regulation of the molecular species composition of phosphatidylcholine in yeast |CITS: [12627972][15258140]| (in |CITS: [2198947]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17010666]|)., Among bacteria, both this pathway and pathway |FRAME: PWY-6826| are present in |FRAME: TAX-358| and |FRAME: TAX-382|. The pathway shown here is the only pathway identified in |FRAME: TAX-542|. It is the preferred pathway in |FRAME: TAX-375|, |FRAME: TAX-312252| and |FRAME: TAX-1063|. In |FRAME: TAX-235| this pathway may function under certain conditions |CITS: [16882035]|, in |FRAME: TAX-446| it appears to be a minor pathway |CITS: [17979985]| and in |FRAME: TAX-287| this pathway may be nonfunctional |CITS: [12169604]| (reviewed in |CITS: [20656373][12848422][14663079]|).

Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., Each of these can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., All three naturally-occurring hexitols can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., Each of these hexitols enters the cell via a specific phosphotransferase system, so the first intracellular species is the 6-phospho-derivative |CITS: [1100608]| (note that due to symmetry of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|, their phosphorylation at either end produces the same molecule. When these molecules are phosphorylated at the 6 position by the PTS system, the resulting molecules are named |FRAME: MANNITOL-1P| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, respectively, by conventional nomenclature rules)., In all three cases this sugar alcohol phosphate becomes the substrate for a dehydrogenase that oxidizes its 2-alcohol group to a keto group. In the cases of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: SORBITOL|, the resulting keto sugar phosphate is |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, an intermediate of glycolysis, and hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy., In the case of |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, however, the product of the dehydrogenation is |FRAME: TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE|, which becomes the substrate of a kinase and subsequently an aldolase (in a pair of reactions that parallel those of glycolysis) before it is converted into intermediates (|FRAME: GAP| and, |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|) of glycolysis |CITS: [8955298][27956522]|.

General Background, Pheromones are chemical messengers that are produced and secreted by both eukaryotes and prokaryotes |CITS: [10406089][22495567][24118108]|. They affect the behavior or physiology of other members of the same species. Pheromone production and function has been well studied in insects and has applications in pest control. Insect pheromones are synthesized from precursors that are produced by existing metabolic pathways, with one or several tissue-specific enzymes transforming the precursors into pheromones of high stereochemical and quantitative specificity (reviewed in |CITS: [10406089][22160232]|)., The pine engraver beetle |FRAME: TAX-102803| (bark beetle) infests a variety of pine trees that have been weakened or have recently died. The major component of its aggregation pheromone is ipsdienol which is synthesized via the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| in the anterior midgut of male |FRAME: TAX-102803|. A derivative compound, ipsenol, functions as an anti-aggregant. The biosynthesis of ipsdienol is stimulated by |FRAME: CPD-8838| |CITS: [16640731]|., The enantiomeric composition of ipsdienol is functionally important in different species of |FRAME: TAX-55979| and in different populations of |FRAME: TAX-102803|. For example North American western populations of |FRAME: TAX-102803| produce and respond to a blend containing >95% |FRAME: CPD-8835|, whereas eastern populations utilize an approximately 60:40 ratio of |FRAME: CPD-8835|:|FRAME: CPD-8834|. Both populations use |FRAME: CPD-15930| as an anti-aggregation signal. The |FRAME: TAX-102829| pheromone consists of >90% |FRAME: CPD-8834| (in |CITS: [19034575][22101251][23376633]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20727970]|). Such stereochemistry-bioactivity relationships in insect pheromones is a general phenomenon (reviewed in |CITS: [21633977]|)., About This Pathway, This ipsdienol de novo biosynthetic pathway is a branch of the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"|. The bifunctional enzyme geranyl diphosphate synthase/myrcene synthase (GPPS/MS) catalyzes the production of |FRAME: CPD-4888| |CITS: [15983375]|. , |FRAME: CPD-4888 "β-Myrcene"| is then hydroxylated by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes to produce the enantiomers |FRAME: CPD-8834| and |FRAME: CPD-8835|. The exact CYP gene product used depends upon the species or population of |FRAME: TAX-55979|. In a western population of North American |FRAME: TAX-102803| the product of |FRAME: G-17870| appears to function solely in pheromone biosynthesis and is coordinately regulated with other pheromone biosynthetic enzymes. However, details of the enzymatic mechanism for production of the different enantiomeric ratios of |FRAME: CPD-8834| and |FRAME: CPD-8835| by the CYPs remain unclear |CITS: [23376633]|., An |FRAME: TAX-102803| ipsdienol dehydrogenase that oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-8835| to |FRAME: CPD-15919| has also been characterized that may participate in determining the final ratio of |FRAME: CPD-8835| to |FRAME: CPD-8834| |CITS: [22101251]|., |FRAME: CPD-15919 "Ipsedienone"| may then be converted to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-15928| which is thought to be a precursor of |FRAME: CPD-15929| and |FRAME: CPD-15930|. However this part of the pathway remains hypothetical and may involve additional as yet uncharacterized oxidoreductases |CITS: [22101251]| (not shown).

Summary: General Background, Heptose sugars, mostly glycero-manno-heptoses, are found in the cell surface polymers of many bacteria., They are most common in the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of most Gram-negative bacteria |CITS:[1794130][1618845]|, but are also found in capsules |CITS: [11373120]| and O-antigens |CITS: [10512635]| of some Gram-negatives, and in the S-layer of certain Gram-positive bacteria |CITS:[8720077][10406844][12101286]|. Glycosylation of an autotransporter adhesin protein with glycero-manno-heptose residues has also been reported |CITS: [11442838]|., D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units have been found in different anomeric configurations. The core oligosaccharide of the LPS of |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-573| contain short heptan chains composed of α-configured D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units |CITS: [9346320][9507008]|, while the O-antigen of |FRAME: TAX-703| was shown to contain β-configured residues |CITS: [10712598]|., Prior to their incorporation, the heptose residues are activated by attachment to a nucleotide. Two pathways for the activation of heptose sugars have been described - |FRAME: PWY0-1241| in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and |FRAME: PWY-6478| in |FRAME: TAX-143495|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ADP-D-GLYCERO-D-MANNO-HEPTOSE| is a precursor for the inner core |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharide"| (LPS) |CITS: [11751812]|. , The genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway have been found in the genome of many important pathogens, including |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: TAX-192222|, |FRAME: TAX-71421|, |FRAME: TAX-85962| and |FRAME: TAX-208964| |CITS: [11279237]|. General Background, |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "Hapalindole-type alkaloids"| are a group of hybrid isoprenoid-indole alkaloids produced solely by members of Subsection V of the cyanobacteria, such as the |FRAME: TAX-1190| and |FRAME: TAX-162985| species. These compounds often have antibacterial, antimycotic, or antialgal activities., Since the initial isolation of |FRAME: CPD-20793| in 1984 |CITS: [Moore84]|, more than 80 members of this family have been isolated |CITS: [Moore87][Smitka92][Park92][Stratmann94][17315959][19371071]|. All of these compounds have an isonitrile- or isothiocyanate-containing indole alkaloid skeleton, with a cyclized isoprene unit. The major classes of the hapalindole-type molecules are the |FRAME: Hapalindoles hapalindoles|, the |FRAME: Fischerindoles fischerindoles|, the |FRAME: Welwitindolinones welwitindolinones|, and the |FRAME: Ambiguines ambiguines|, which differ in their core structure., |FRAME: CPD-20800 "Hapalindole H"| was shown to induce apoptosis in prostate cancer cells, acting as an inhibitor of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) |CITS: [29848677]|., About This Pathway, The first biosynthetic pathway for a hapalindole-type alkaloid was reported for |FRAME: CPD-20794|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-230521|, which was the only axenic cyanobacterial hapalindole-type-molecule producer available at the time. The genome of the organism was sequenced, and searches for putative genes encoding isonitrile synthase and prenyltransferase have identified a cluster of 32 protein-coding genes involved in ambiguine biosynthesis. This discovery was made by two different labs, which named the genes in the cluster amb and fam, respectively |CITS: [24180436][26629885]|., In addition to genes unique to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "hapalindole-type alkaloids"|, the cluster contains homologs of the trpA-E genes, which are responsible for |FRAME: TRP| biosynthesis, as well as five dedicated genes for |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, |FRAME: CPD-4211|, and |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| biosynthesis., The first committed step in the pathway is the addition of an isonitrile function to |FRAME: TRP|, which is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-230521| by two paralougous enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-58189| and |FRAME: G-58190| genes. Both genes are homologous to the |FRAME: G-58184| gene, which has been shown to encode an |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.25| |CITS: [16206308]|. The enzyme is known to use |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-20766| |CITS: [16217820]|. The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.11|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58188| gene. This enzyme catalyzes an Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent monooxygenation at C-3 of the substrate, followed by decarboxylation and dehydration to form a cis C-C double bond |CITS: [24180436][28212039]|. The third enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.146|, catalyzes geranylation of the intermediate, forming the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-20795| |CITS: [26629885]|., This intermediate is the last common intermediate in the synthesis of the different hapalindole-type alkaloids, as different organisms possess different cyclases that form different core structures while acting on it. A heterodimeric cyclase composed of the |FRAME: G-58194| and |FRAME: G-58195| gene products results in formation of |FRAME: CPD-20800|, which is then modified to other hapalinodole compounds |CITS: [28288107]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-7959|, |FRAME: PWY-8483|, and |FRAME: PWY-7958|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-10 Ubiquinone-10| (Q-10) has been described in many bacterial species that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-28211|. Species that were found to contain Q-10 as their major quinone include |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [12501289]|, |FRAME: TAX-235| |CITS: [Thiele69]| and |FRAME: TAX-29459| |CITS: [4351160]|, |FRAME: TAX-318683|, |FRAME:TAX-38307| and |FRAME:TAX-28448| |CITS:[Yamada69]|, |FRAME: TAX-266| |CITS: [14429752][4296023][12501289]|, |FRAME: TAX-375| |CITS: [Daniel79]|, and the purple bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1061|, |FRAME: TAX-1063| and |FRAME: TAX-1076| |CITS: [5862408][4147456][5727384]| and |FRAME: TAX-1085| |CITS: [172493][12501289]|., Since Q-10 is the only quinone found in humans, and since it has been suggested that administration of Q-10 has a positive effect for various diseases (for example, |CITS: [7612003]|), there has been an interest in the utilization of bacterial Q-10 producers for the manufacture of this compound |CITS: [12501289][16528515][16797569][16815062][17124579]|., Various microorganisms, including bacteria (e.g. Agrobacterium, Rhodobacter, Paracoccus) and yeasts (e.g. Candida, Rhodotorula, Saitoella) have been reported as Q-10 producers in patented laid-open applications |CITS: [Yajima03][25817210]|. A review of the biotechnological production of Q-10 is found in |CITS: [15744486]|., For the biosynthesis of Q-10 in eukaryotes see |FRAME: PWY-5872|.

Over 200 non-protein amino acids are present in plants. Many occur in free forms while some are detected in peptide conjugates. Many have toxic properties. The role of non-protein amino acids in plants has been proposed to include serving as defense compounds against predators, as storage forms of carbon and nitrogen, and as detoxification products |CITS: [wallsgrove95]|. Mimosine showed a potential defense mechanism against invading viruses by chelating the iron of ribonucleotide reductase [23], which is essential for DNA synthesis for viruses., |FRAME: MIMOSINE|, β-(3-hydroxy-4-pyridon-1-yl)-L-alanine, is a non-protein amino acid found in the legume species |FRAME: TAX-76306| and |FRAME: TAX-3866|. It acts as an iron chelator and blocks the mammalian cell cycle at the G1/S phase. Mimosine suppresses the synthesis of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3a (eIF3a or eIF p170) and, subsequently, retards the translation of α-tubulin |CITS: [Dong04]| and ribonucleotide reductase |CITS: [12972576]|. Chelation of zinc by mimosine is also suggested to affect the function of zinc finger transcription factors, which impede the transcription of cytoplasmic serine hydroxymethyltransferase (cSHMT), an essential enzyme for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis |CITS: [15531579]|., Mimosine is synthesized by a reaction mechanism comparable to the biosynthesis of cysteine (see |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.47|) in that both use |FRAME: ACETYLSERINE| as the donor of the alanyl group. Mimosine synthase has been considered an isozyme of Cys synthase |CITS: [Ikegami90]|. While it has been reported that cytosolic OASTL from |FRAME: TAX-3866| only produces |FRAME: CYS| |CITS: [24777760]|, a later study has reported that a cysteine synthase from that plant showed both |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: MIMOSINE| synthesis in extracts of overexpressing |FRAME: TAX-562| host |CITS: [29691793]|., A similar observation was made in watermelon where the cysteine synthase catalyzes not only the synthesis of cysteine but also |FRAME: CPD-670|, see: |FRAME: PWY-4961|.

General Background, The mycotoxins |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of the B-group and G-group aflatoxins, which constitute the major groups of naturally occurring aflatoxins. The production of aflatoxins by some strains of several |FRAME:TAX-5052| species has been extensively studied. However many species, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425|, produce only |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| as a final product (in |CITS: [18486503]|). |FRAME: TAX-5067| produces both B- and G-group aflatoxins from |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587|, while |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces only B-group aflatoxins. The biological role of these mycotoxins in fungi remains unclear (in |CITS: [17620135] [18246345]| and, reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|)., Aflatoxins are highly toxic and carcinogenic crop contaminants that create major economic and public health problems worldwide. Much research has been focused on identifying compounds that inhibit aflatoxin biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-4592| is metabolized by mammalian liver cytochrome P450 enzymes to a mutagenic epoxide that covalently binds to DNA. Its genotoxic mechanism of action has been studied in yeast |CITS: [8968101] [9771940]|. Other species, such as |FRAME: TAX-5062| and |FRAME:TAX-41058|, are unable to produce aflatoxins and are used in food fermentation |CITS: [17665189]|., Most of the aflatoxin biosynthetic genes are clustered in Aspergilli and are positively regulated by gene aflR (in |CITS: [17620135] [16448506] [16108793] [15094053] [7618880] [16535712]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]| and |CITS: [15006741]|). The enzyme reactions and biosynthetic intermediates in the aflatoxin biosynthetic pathway have been reviewed in detail |CITS: [15022028]|. See MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5954|, |FRAME: PWY-5955|, |FRAME: PWY-5956|, |FRAME: PWY-5959| and |FRAME: PWY-5961|., About This Pathway, In this segment of the aflatoxin biosynthesis pathway, |FRAME: CPD-10175| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-4586|, in a series of uncharacterized steps, shown here as a triple arrow, that involve the products of genes, aflX (ordB), aflY (hypA), aflM (ver-1) and aflN (verA). The next, two reactions involve two |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent O-methyltransferases. Similar, to the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-7157| to |FRAME: CPD-4592|, the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-4588| to, |FRAME: CPD-10177| involves several transformations that have been proposed to be catalyzed by a single, microsomal cytochrome P-450 enzyme, the product of gene ordA (|CITS: [11996570]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|). In, an initial oxidative cycle, production of a dihydro-11-hydroxy O-methylsterigmatocystin intermediate has been, demonstrated |CITS: [11996570]|. This is followed by aryl ring cleavage, demethylation, dehydration, decarboxylation, and rearrangement to produce |FRAME: CPD-10177| |CITS: [11996570]|., |FRAME: CPD-4588| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-10179| in a series of, uncharacterized steps, shown here as a triple arrow, that involve the products of genes aflQ (ordA),, aflU (cypA) and nadA |CITS: [18486503] [15528514] [11996570]|. The tetrahydrobisfuran, ring of |FRAME: CPD-10175| is maintained in these steps. Strains of |FRAME: TAX-5059| are thought to, produce only aflatoxins B1 and B2, while strains of |FRAME: TAX-5067| produce all four, major aflatoxins (B1, B2, G1 and G2). Aflatoxins are, excreted from mycelia and their biosynthetic intermediates accumulate in cells. No aflatoxin export system, has been identified yet. Reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, Both the D- and L- enantiomeric forms of the pentose sugar |FRAME: Arabinoses| are found in nature, although |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is more common. Both forms can be degraded by microorganisms., The pathway for |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE| degradation shown here was characterized from the aerobic, hyperthermophilic crenarchaeon |FRAME: TAX-2287|. This organism can use some pentoses, hexoses, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides as a sole carbon and energy source. The data suggested that |FRAME: TAX-2287| converts |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE| to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via an inducible set of enzymes, as shown in this pathway., One difference between this pathway and the L-arabinose oxidation pathway shown in |FRAME: PWY-5517| is the absence of an up-regulated lactonase in |FRAME: TAX-2287|. It has been postulated that there may be no need for a lactonase due to the hyperthermophilic nature of this organism. Lactone hydrolysis can occur spontaneously, but slowly at ambient temperatures. However, at 80 °C the spontaneous reaction may be rapid enough to not be rate-limiting |CITS: [16849334]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Xylans Xylan| is found in the cell walls of plants and some green and red algae, and is the major constituent of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|. The most common type of xylan is by far |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan|, a linear polymer of |FRAME: BETA-D-XYLOSE| residues linked by (1→4) glycosidic bonds. This polysaccharide backbone is often decorated by additional sugars, forming complex polymers such as |FRAME: Arabinoxylan arabinoxylan| and |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans glucuronoxylan|. , Arabinoxylans have been identified in wheat, rye, barley, oat, rice, and sorghum, as well as in some less common plants, including pangola grass, bamboo shoots and rye grass. |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans Glucuronoxylans| and |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans glucuronoarabinoxylans| are located mainly in the secondary wall and function as an adhesive by forming covalent and non-covalent bonds with |FRAME: Lignins lignin|, |FRAME: CELLULOSE cellulose|, and other polymers essential to the integrity of the cell wall., Angiosperm (hardwood) glucuronoxylans also have a high rate of substitution (70-80%) by acetyl groups, at position 2 and/or 3 of the β-D-xylopyranosyl. The degradation of cell wall is immensely important in industrial production as a supplement in animal feed, food and beverages, textiles, bleaching and production of biofuels. The main enzymes involved in xylan degradation are the xylanases. These enzymes are produced mainly by microorganisms that break down plant cell walls, but are also present in marine algae, protozoans, crustaceans, insects, snails and seeds of land plants |CITS: [9118232]|. , The principle source of xylanases for the industry are filamentous fungi, since they secrete these enzymes into the medium and their xylanase levels are very high |CITS: [15944805]|. In recent years there has been a focus on xylanases from extremophiles that can withstand high temperatures and extreme pH found during industrial processes |CITS: [21120468]|. Due to the complex structure of xylan polymers, degradation requires a number of different types of enzymes working in tandem. These include endoxylanases (|FRAME: 3.2.1.8-RXN "EC 3.2.1.8, endo-1,4-β-xylanase"|; |FRAME: 3.2.1.136-RXN "EC 3.2.1.136, glucuronoarabinoxylan endo-1,4-β-xylanase"|), β-xylosidases (|FRAME: 3.2.1.156-RXN "EC 3.2.1.156, oligosaccharide reducing-end xylanase"|; |FRAME: 3.2.1.37-RXN "EC 3.2.1.37, xylan 1,4-β-xylosidase"|), ferulate esterases (|FRAME: 3.1.1.73-RXN "EC 3.1.1.73"|), acetylxylan esterases (|FRAME: 3.1.1.72-RXN "EC 3.1.1.72"|), α-glucuronidases (|FRAME: 3.2.1.139-RXN "EC 3.2.1.139"|), arabinases (|FRAME: 3.2.1.99-RXN "EC 3.2.1.99"| and arabinofuranosidases (|FRAME: 3.2.1.55-RXN "EC 3.2.1.55"|).

General Background, The complex phenotypes of |FRAME: TAX-7215 "Drosophila"| eye color mutants have been studied for nearly a century. Two classes of pigments contribute to eye color, the pteridine red drosopterins and the brown ommochromes. They are located in pteridine or ommochrome pigment granules present in cells of the ommatidia. Ommochrome pigments such as |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN| are produced by nonenzymatic oxidation of the |FRAME: TRP| degradation product |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| |CITS: [22474291][10625213][10333572]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6309|). The drosopterins are derived from |FRAME: GTP| as shown here., In wild-type flies at least five pigment components of the red drosopterins have been identified including the major components |FRAME: CPD-16456| and isodrosopterin, and minor components neodrosopterin, |FRAME: CPD-16457| and an uncharacterized fraction. |FRAME: CPD-16457 "Aurodrosopterin"| is similar to |FRAME: CPD-16456| but lacks one amino group on the pteridine moiety. A biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-16456| and |FRAME: CPD-16457| has been proposed as shown here (|CITS: [19567870]| and reviewed in |CITS: [23436441]|)., Mutant studies have also identified other |FRAME: TAX-7227| genes that affect metabolites in or derived from, the |FRAME: CPD-16456| pathway. These include Hn (Henna) encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase |CITS: [18677598]| and ry (rosy) encoding xanthine oxidase |CITS: [18657538]|. Gene cho (chocolate) and mal (maroon-like) are unknown lesions for which a metabolomics approach has been taken to elucidate their role |CITS: [19843177]|. Genes encoding transporters for drosopterin and ommochrome pigment precurosrs have also been characterized |CITS: [10407069]|., There is also evidence for the presence of the drosopterin class of pteridine pigments in other insects, as well as higher taxa such as fish, lizards, amphibians and birds |CITS: [891751][11410150][MAANME08][22036614]|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here is based on the more recent literature |CITS: [19567870][19843177]|. As in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5663| the starting compound is |FRAME: GTP| and the first two reactions are shared by both pathways. , In the first reaction |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3| is formed by GTP cyclohydrolase encoded by gene Pu (Punch) |CITS: [6413298]|. This compound is then converted to |FRAME: 6-PYRUVOYL-5678-TETRAHYDROPTERIN| by pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase encoded by gene pr (purple) |CITS: [2110003]|. Then |FRAME: 6-PYRUVOYL-5678-TETRAHYDROPTERIN| is converted to the |FRAME: Pyrimidodiazepines "pyrimidodiazepine"| |FRAME: A-PYRIMIDODIAZEPINE| by pyrimidodiazepine synthase encoded by gene se (sepia) |CITS: [16712527][6438092][6421807]|. The cl gene (clot) encodes a protein that is an essential component of a |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| redox system for this reaction |CITS: [12589444]|., A hypothetical side chain releasing enzyme may convert |FRAME: 6-PYRUVOYL-5678-TETRAHYDROPTERIN| to |FRAME: CPD0-1718|, although it is uncertain whether this reaction occurs spontaneously, or is enzymatically catalyzed |CITS: [19567870]|. The latter compound was shown to be converted to |FRAME: CPD-16458| by the dihydropterin deaminase activity of guanine deaminase encoded by gene DhpD |CITS: [19567870]|., The remaining two steps were shown to occur nonenzymatically via spontaneous condensation reactions between |FRAME: CPD0-1718| and |FRAME: Pyrimidodiazepines| which produces |FRAME: CPD-16456|, and between |FRAME: CPD-16458| and |FRAME: Pyrimidodiazepines| which produces |FRAME: CPD-16457|. These reactions occurred under acidic conditions in vitro |CITS: [YIMJ93]|, but were also proposed to occur in vivo |CITS: [19567870]|. The stereoisomers of these two products, isodrosopterin and isoaurodrosopterin |CITS: [109114]|, are also produced |CITS: [19567870]|., A |FRAME: CPLX-8818| putatively encoded by gene lix (little isoxanthopterin) has also been described that catalyzes the oxidation of 7,8-dihydropteridines to their fully oxidized products. Its physiological role was suggested to be the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD0-1718| |CITS: [1745247][6815189]|. Its activity suggests additional routes for the formation of various |FRAME: Pterins "pterins"| |CITS: [19843177]|.

Summary: General Background, Aromatic and aliphatic biogenic amines are synthesized by the decarboxylation of amino acids. Biogenic amines have important physiological functions in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. The bacterial degradation of the aromatic biogenic amine |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE| is shown in pathways |FRAME: 2PHENDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6534|. The analogous bacterial degradation of the aromatic ring-hydroxylated biogenic amines |FRAME: CPD-58|, |FRAME: TYRAMINE|, |FRAME: DOPAMINE| and |FRAME: 1-4-HYDROXYPHENYL-2-METHYLAMINOETHAN| is shown in this pathway and the linked meta-cleavage pathway |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYPHENYLACETATE-DEGRADATION-PWY| |CITS: [3034855 ][3121590][20482587]|. , Relatively little information is available regarding the bacterial degradation of the biogenic amine |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE|, an aminoalkylindole produced by the decarboxylation of |FRAME: TRP|. However the oxidation of |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| by |FRAME: TAX-1269| and |FRAME: TAX-1386| species has been reported |CITS: [4441405][9562873][4036551]|., About This Pathway , Early work on aromatic amine degradation reported the existence of enzymes oxidizing |FRAME: TYRAMINE| and |FRAME: DOPAMINE| in several different genera of bacteria, although the remainder of the pathway was not fully elucidated |CITS: [YAMADAH67I][YAMADAH67II][179974][7007350][6830237]|., The degradation of |FRAME: 1-4-HYDROXYPHENYL-2-METHYLAMINOETHAN| by an |FRAME: TAX-1663| species designated |FRAME: ORG-6249| was shown to occur via synephrine dehydratase, with the |FRAME: HYDRPHENYLAC-CPD| product entering the meta-cleavage pathway as shown in the pathway link to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYPHENYLACETATE-DEGRADATION-PWY| |CITS: [1150621][1008837][588248][3729420]|., Subsequently, |CITS: [3034855]| described a tyramine dehydrogenase and an octopamine dehydratase (octopamine hydrolyase) activity in |FRAME: TAX-208964|, with the |FRAME: HYDRPHENYLAC-CPD| product entering the meta-cleavage pathway. This organism could also utilize |FRAME: DOPAMINE| or |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and as sole sources of carbon or nitrogen. It could utilize |FRAME: 1-4-HYDROXYPHENYL-2-METHYLAMINOETHAN| as a carbon source but poorly if at all as a sole nitrogen source. It was unable to utilize |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE|, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE|, or |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE| as a sole carbon or nitrogen source., A putative |FRAME: FAD|-containing amine oxidase (|FRAME: EC-1.4.3.4|) catalyzing |FRAME: TYRAMINE| and |FRAME: DOPAMINE| oxidation in |FRAME: ORG-6143| was demonstrated by |CITS: [20482587]|, with subsequent reactions following the meta-cleavage pathway. A copper-containing amine oxidase (|FRAME: EC-1.4.3.21|) from |FRAME: TAX-1665| has been extensively studied, although the remainder of the pathway was not characterized |CITS: [21984603]|., Note that the |FRAME: OCTOPAMINE-DEHYDRATASE-RXN "octopamine dehydratase"| and |FRAME: SYNEPHRINE-DEHYDRATASE-RXN "synephrine dehydratase"| reactions are shown as a composite reaction that is composed of an enzyme-catalyzed subreaction and two spontaneous subreactions, as shown in their respective links.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1281 "Coenzyme B"| is one of the many unusual cofactors present in methanogens and required for methane formation. Like |FRAME: Factor-420|, |FRAME: CPD-1281| acts as an electron carrier in the metabolism of methanogens (see |FRAME: P241-PWY|)., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| functions as a methyl carrier in methanogenesis, and |FRAME: Me-CoM| has been established as the terminal intermediate of methanogenesis from all substrates (see |FRAME:METHFORM-PWY|). In addition to its role in methanogenesis, different forms of |FRAME: CoM| have physiological roles in methanogens, and are specific enzyme substrates |CITS: [2115763]|., All catabolic processes in methanogenesis lead to the formation of a mixed disulfide bond between |FRAME: CoM| and |FRAME: CPD-1281|, by a reaction in which |FRAME: CPD-1281| reduces |FRAME: Me-CoM|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CH4| and a |FRAME:CPD-1282| |CITS: [12102556]| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|)., The process in which |FRAME:CPD-1282| is reduced back to |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| has been studied extensively. There are two different enzyme systems that are capable of reducing the |FRAME:CPD-1282|. One is a membrane-bound system, encoded by the hdrDE genes, which uses |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE| as its electron donor |CITS: [15168610]|. The other is a soluble cytoplasmic system encoded by the hdrABC genes, which can use several types of electron donors, either directly, or by forming a complex with other enzymes., About This Pathway, Heterodisulfide reductases (Hdr) of the HdrABC class are ancient enzymes that existed in the prokaryotic common ancestor. The enzymes consist of a large HdrA subunit that contains FAD and multiple [4Fe-4S] clusters, a smaller catalytic HdrB subunit, and an electron transfer HdrC subunit. Electrons enter the enzyme at HdrA, and are transferred via HdrC to the active site of HdrB., Many methanogens have two copies of HdrABC proteins. The |FRAME: G-55046|, |FRAME: G-55047|, and |FRAME: G-55048| genes are located in a single operon, while the |FRAME: G-55049|, |FRAME: G-55050| and |FRAME: G-55051| genes are fdound in two operons - the |FRAME: G-55049| gene is located in one operon that also contains a gene encoding a polyferredoxin, while |FRAME: G-55050| and |FRAME: G-55051| form an operon of their own. The hdrA2 gene is a fusion of an hdrA1 homolog and an mvhD homolog (mvhD encodes a hydrogenase electron-transfer subunit) |CITS: [19968794]|. In |FRAME: TAX-2214| transcription of hdrA1B1C1 was observed during growth on methanol and trimethylamine, but not on acetate, and thus HdrA1B1C1 is assumed to be involved only in methanogenesis from methyotrophic substrates in that species. On the other hand, the hdrA2B2C2 genes exhibited reporter activity under all conditions tested |CITS: [19968794]|., Studies with purified HdrA2B2C2 protein found that the enzyme could use reduced ferredoxin as the electron source for the reduction of the |FRAME: CPD-1282|. It is believed that the ferredoxin is reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.4| during methanogenesis from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|)., Interestingly, the enzyme can also use |FRAME: Reduced-Factor-F420 "reduced coenzyme F420"| as an electron donor. Using electron bifurcation, the enzyme directs the electron pairs from |FRAME: Reduced-Factor-F420| towards the reduction of both ferredoxin and |FRAME: CPD-1282| |CITS: [28174314]|. However, since coenzyme F420 is not involved in methanogenesis from acetate, it is thought that the enzyme uses ferredoxin as the electron source during this process. The enzyme may function in its coenzyme F420 electron bifurcation mode during Fe(III)-dependent anaerobic methane oxidation |CITS: [28174314]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It s involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall., The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of α-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|., Diferent components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains., Other types of pectin include chains of |FRAME: Apiogalacturonans apiogalacturonan|, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl homogalacturonan|, and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|., In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. Partially esterified pectins are often refered to as pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, as, |FRAME: PECTATE|., Phytopathogenic and saprophytic bacteria and fungi produce variety of extracellular and intracellular enzymes that de-esterify and depolymerize pectin and its derivatives. In pectinolytic bacteria the initial steps of pectin degradation to |FRAME: PECTATE pectate| and oligogalacturonides involve the action of extracellularly secreted pectin methylesterases, pectin acetylesterases, pectin lyases, pectate hydrolases and pectate lyases. Pectate degrading hydrolases and lyases are not always extracellular and are also found in the cytoplasm and periplasm., Pectinolytic enzymes vary among species and strains. Pectin-degrading enzymes are used in the food, fiber and animal feed industries. The development of inhibitors of enzymes that degrade pectin and its derivatives is of interest as a possible way to prevent crop spoilage, although none have been reported as of 2010 |CITS: [19618506][8905080][18535148]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: G-12025| gene of the plant-pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-204038 "Dickeya dadantii (previously known as Erwinia chrysanthemi)"| encodes an extracellularly secreted pectin methylesterase that catalyzes the key first step in the bacterial invasion of plant tissue. This step consists og demethylation of the methoxyl groups on pectin to produce pectate, facilitating the action of pectate lyases and and pectate hydrolases (polygalacturonases). , The pelB gene (not shown in this pathway) encodes an outer membrane lipoprotein that acts in the periplasm |CITS: [8830237]|. PelB catalyzes the deesterification of pectate to generate smaller, methylated pectin oligogalacturonides that can be imported into the cell |CITS: [17717531][8905080]|., Pectin methylesterases are also produced by plants and are important in remodeling the plant cell wall during growth and development |CITS: [17717531]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-1081|)., The periplasmic, exo-cleaving pectate lyase |FRAME: G-12031 PehX| attacks the pectin oligomers and liberates the disaccharide |FRAME: CPD-12435|. It prefers tetragalacturonate as substrate, but also cleaves longer oligomers |CITS: [10049400]|., The last enzyme included in this pathway is encoded by the |FRAME: G-12026| gene. It is a cytoplasmic oligogalacturonate lyase that cleaves both unsaturated and saturated oligogalacturonides to their monomeric components |FRAME: CPD-37| and |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|. The products of the lyase are metaobolized into componds of central metabolism as described in |FRAME: PWY-6507| and |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain. Recent, findings suggest that GABA has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well |CITS: [15003233]|. In animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: GLUTDECARBOX-RXN "glutamate decarboxylase"|., The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|. Diiferent variants of both enzymes are known. The amino-group acceptor for the transamination can be either |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|) or |FRAME:PYRUVATE| (e.g. in the plant |FRAME: ORG-5862| |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|). Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+., The action of glutamate decarboxylase, γ-aminobutyrate aminotransferase and succinate semialdehyde, dehydrogenase, combined, defines a short pathway known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. , While there is no evidence for a special role for GABA in bacteria, the capabillity to degrade it exists in many strains. GABA is present in the environment as a product of plant and animal tissue decay, and many bacteria can synthesize GABA as an intermediate in the degradation of putrescine (see |FRAME: Putrescine-Degradation "putrescine degradation"|). , The first indication for a bacterial pathway for GABA degradation was found in |FRAME: TAX-294|, |CITS:[13654294][13654295]|. While some organisms, like |FRAME: TAX-294|, can grow on GABA as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, others, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, can grow on it only as a nitrogen source |CITS: [8951816][12123465]|., About This Pathway, When the fate of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| was studied in |FRAME: TAX-1511|, a strict anaerobe isolated from North Carolina swamp mud |CITS:[14399736]|, a different pathway was observed., Among the products produced by this strain were |FRAME:4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE|, |FRAME:AMMONIA|, and |FRAME:ACET|. While the first step of the pathway was found to be identical to that in |FRAME: TAX-294|, the second, step was different: In |FRAME: TAX-1511| |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD| is converted to |FRAME:4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE|. The |FRAME:GLT| formed during the transamination of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| is converted back to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, liberating |FRAME:AMMONIA| in the process |CITS:[13952769]|., Recently the |FRAME: G-10272|, |FRAME: G-10271| and |FRAME: G-10270| genes, encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-13486|, |FRAME: CPLX-7514| and |FRAME: CPLX-7515|, respectively, were cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [11041350]|. These are the first |FRAME: TAX-33953| proteins with a known gene sequence.

Summary: |FRAME: CPLX0-3104| is a serine protease complex responsible for the ATP-dependent degradation of a number of proteins |CITS: [3049606]|. |FRAME: EG10156-MONOMER "ClpA"| functions as an ATP-dependent chaperone component and |FRAME: EG10158-MONOMER "ClpP"| as the serine protease component., In general, proteases recognize their substrates by specific degradation signals, known as degrons. One of the degrons that are recognized by ClpAP is the identity of the amino-terminal residue of the protein, known as N-degron. Certain residues (named "destabilizing residues") are recognized by the protease complex and mark the protein for degradation. The set of destabilizing residues in a given cell type yields a rule, called the N-end rule, which relates the in vivo half-life of a protein to the identity of its N-terminal residue |CITS: [3018930][1962196]|., ClpAP rapidly degrades proteins whose N-terminal amino acid is |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|, all of which are considered primary N-terminal destabilizing residues (Ndp) |CITS: [1962196]|. Although ClpAP alone can recognize N-end rule motifs, binding of the adaptor protein |FRAME: G6463-MONOMER "ClpS"| specifically enhances their turnover |CITS: [16467841]|. ClpS is the bacterial N-recognin, and binds to the Ndp residues Leu, Phe, Trp, or Tyr |CITS: [16467841]|. ClpS also binds to the ClpA subunits of ClpAP and thereby functions as an adaptor in mediating the processive degradation of N-end rule substrates by ClpAP., The ClpS-ClpAP complex recognizes an N-end motif using both a free alpha-amino group and the identity of the N-terminal residue. The identity of adjacent residues can also affect recognition, and the distance between the N-end residue and the folded portion of a protein is critical |CITS: [18550545]|., In organisms that possess |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.29|, |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: GLT| are considered secondary N-terminal destabilizing residues (Nds). When these amino acids are present at the N-terminus, they are recognized by |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.29| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-44614| gene), which attaches an |FRAME: LEU| residue to them, transforming the N-terminus to an Ndp |CITS: [16492767]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-12245 "Vancomycin"| is a glycopeptide that is often used for treating patients infected with antibiotic-resistant bacteria (especially Streptococcal and Staphylococcal infections) and patients who are allergic to penicillins |CITS: [10232990]|. The widespread prevalence of methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA) has made vancomycin the antibiotic of last resort for eliminating multi-drug-resistant Gram-positive bacteria., Glycopeptide antibiotics such as |FRAME: CPD-12245| and |FRAME: CPD-12251| inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to the |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| end of the peptidoglycan pentapeptide (see |FRAME: CPD-7695| for the structure of the petidoglycan monomer). These residues are added to the peptidoglycan precursor as a |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide, produced by |FRAME: CPLX-8013|., During maturation of the bacterial cell wall the terminal |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue of the pentapeptide is cleaved by the D,D-transpeptidases that form the peptide crosslinks between adjacent glycan threads. These enzymes, which are known as penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), must hydrolyze the D-ala-D-ala bond for their activity (for example, see the |FRAME: TAX-1280| PBPs |FRAME: MONOMER-15471|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15456|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15472|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15473|, and the methicillin-resistant |FRAME: MONOMER-15469|)., The binding of the antibiotics to the terminal |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide blocks the binding transpeptidases and inhibits the transglycosylation and transpeptidation reactions of peptidoglycan assembly., After three decades of vancomycin use resistant mutants appeared. Resistance initially appeared in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1350| (collectively called VRE, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus), but eventually spread to other organisms. The resistant strains have D-ala-D-ala ligases with altered specificity, resulting in incorporation of either |FRAME: D-LACTATE| or |FRAME: D-SERINE| instead of the second |FRAME: D-ALANINE|. When incorporated into peptidoglycan, these modified peptides do not bind glycopeptide antibiotics., The spread of vancomycin resistance is a major biomedical concern, especially strains of methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA) which acquired vancomycin resistance (sometimes referred to as "superbugs")., Three types of ligases that incorporate |FRAME: D-LACTATE| have been documented (see |FRAME: PWY-6454|). |FRAME:CPLX-8016 "VanA"| is carried on a transposon and confers high-level inducible resistance to both vancomycin and teicoplanin, |FRAME:CPLX-8014 "VanB"| is also carried on a transposon and confers variable levels of inducible resistance to vancomycin only, and |FRAME:CPLX-8019 "VanD"| is carried on the chromosome and confers constitutive resistance to high levels of vancomycin and low levels of teicoplanin., Four type of ligases that incorporate |FRAME: D-SERINE| have been described so far. Low-level intrinsic resistance is provided by by VanC-type |FRAME: CPD-12249| ligases, found in |FRAME: TAX-1353| (|FRAME: CPLX-8023 VanC1|) and |FRAME: TAX-37734| (|FRAME: CPLX-8015 "VanC2"|). In addition, |FRAME: CPLX-8020 "VanE"| and |FRAME: CPLX-8021 "VanG"| have been found in the chromosomes of several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1351|., About This Pathway, Bacteria that become resistant to vancomycin by incorporating |FRAME: D-SERINE| into their peptidoglycan are known to possess several types of D-alanine--D-serine ligases. In general, resistance requires a gene cluster that contains five essential gene products - VanR, VanS, VanH, VanX, and either VanC, VanE, or VanG., VanC is a chrosomally-encoded ligase present in |FRAME: TAX-1353| and |FRAME: TAX-37734|., This enzyme confers modest resistance to |FRAME: CPD-12245| with sensitivity retained to |FRAME: CPD-12251|., Several subtypes have been described, including |FRAME: G-11866| in |FRAME: TAX-1353| |CITS: [1551598]| and |FRAME: G-11849| and |FRAME: G-11867| in |FRAME: TAX-37734| |CITS:[9294159][12615874][19216682]|., Some strains of |FRAME: TAX-1351| possess similar ligases, known as |FRAME: G-11862| and |FRAME: G-11863|. These too confer consitutive, low level resistance towards |FRAME: CPD-12245| and no resistance towards |FRAME: CPD-12251| |CITS: [10471558][11036060][12019119][14617152][16723588]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Factor-420 "Factor 420"| (also known as coenzyme F420 or simply F420) is a redox-active compound well-known for its role in methanogenesis. Although playing a crucial role in methanoarchaeal metabolism, F420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium (see |FRAME:PWY-5198|)., The first F420 structure that was characterized contained two glutamate residues, with the terminal glutamate bound through an amide bond to the γ position of the other glutamate. Subsequent work revealed variation in the polyglutamylation of F420 among different organisms, with up to a total of seven γ-linked glutamates, sometimes capped by a terminal α-linked glutamate |CITS:[7916957][12867481]|. For example, |FRAME: TAX-2208| has F420 with four and five γ-linked glutamates |CITS: [Gorris88]|, |FRAME: TAX-1772| contain primarily five and six γ-glutamyl forms of F420 |CITS:[11479701]|, and the non-methanogen archeon |FRAME: TAX-2234| contains four γ-linked glutamates |CITS: [12867481]|., The enzyme responsible for the glutamylation is bifunctiuonal, catalyzing two distinct and independent reactions. The enzyme first attaches a glutamate via its α-NH<sub>2</sub> to F420-0 (|FRAME: EC-6.3.2.31|). After a certain amount of monoglutamylated F420-1 has accumulated, the enzyme catalyzes the ligation of additional glutamate residues at the γ position of the terminal glutamate residue (cf. |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.34|) |CITS: [17669425]|., In most bacteria the enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7536| gene, possesses a third function, the |FRAME: FMNH2|-dependent reduction of |FRAME: CPD-22327| to |FRAME: CPD-10333|. In archaea the glutamylation is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-9425| gene product, which does not catalyze the reduction |CITS: [30952857]|., In the hydrogenotrophic methanogens of the genera methanobacterium and methanococcus the common form of F420 is an unusual α-F420-3 form, in which a single α-linked glutamate residue caps the γ-linked glutamates. A study of |FRAME: TAX-2190| found the forms α-F420-3, α-F420-4, and α-F420-5, all of which capped by an α-linked glutamate residue |CITS: [12867481]|.The enzyme responsible for the addition of the α-linked residue, |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.32|, was found to be a monomeric enzyme similar to enzymes found in other organisms that are involved in the biosynthesis of glutathione, folate and the murein peptide |CITS: [12909715]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Pectin Pectin| is an important component of the plant cell wall. Pectin contains polygalacturonan as a linear component and |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| (RG-I) and |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan type II"| (RG-II) as branched chains |CITS: [16660529][9067088]|. , |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "Rhamnogalacturonan type I "| consists of repeating α-(1,2)-|FRAME:L-rhamnose|-α-(1,4)-|FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| disaccharide units. About half of the Rha residues are substituted with side chains of various neutral oligosaccharides such as arabinans, galactans, and arabinogalactans |CITS: [16661590 ]|. RG-II contains polygalacturonan as a backbone and a complex of approximately 30 monosaccharides, including rare sugars such as apiose and aceric acid as a side chain |CITS: [8798473]|., Many plant-pathogenic fungi and bacteria produce enzymes responsible for plant cell wall degradation. The degradation pathway for the polygalacturonan region in pectin has been extensively characterized in plant-pathogenic microbes such as |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [8905080]| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species |CITS: [11729262]|. A large number of polygalacturonan-degrading enzymes (i.e., pectin lyase, pectate lyase, and polygalacturonase) have also been identified from many fungi and bacteria. However, studies of the microbial degradation system for the RG region in pectin have been limited. One such system has been reported in |FRAME: TAX-5053| (see |FRAME: PWY-6769|). Another one, studied in |FRAME: TAX-224308|, is described here., About This Pathway, The saprophytic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-224308| grows well withn plant cell wall polysaccharides such as pectin, olygalacturonan, and |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I "| (RGI-) as the carbon source. The yes gene cluster is one of three clusters that are induced during growth on RG I. , Among the proteins encoded by the yes cluster, |FRAME: BSU07050| and |FRAME: BSU07060| encode two RG lyases whose combined action releases disaccharides from RG-I. YesW is a |FRAME: BSU07050-MONOMER| that is secreted by the cells, which catalyzes the initial cleavage of the RG-I main chain. The resultant oligosaccharides, which have an unsaturated saccharide at the non-reducing end, are converted to disaccharides through the extracellular enzyme |FRAME: BSU07060-MONOMER| (YesX). The disaccharides are finally degraded into their constituent monosaccharides by the reaction of two intracellular enzyme, the unsaturated galacturonyl hydrolases |FRAME: BSU07000-MONOMER YesR| and YteR |CITS: [17449691]|., The yes gene cluster is also induced in |FRAME: TAX-86029| when grown with soy beans. This is an important industrial strain used for the production of natto, a Japanese fermented soy beans dish |CITS: [17449691]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-14553| is the activated form of |FRAME: D-galactopyranose|. While it is often produced as an intermediate of galactose catabolism (see |FRAME: PWY-6317|), this nucleotide sugar is also involved in the production of many types of polysaccharides, glycans, and glycoconjugates in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., In prokaryotes, |FRAME: CPD-14553| is a common precursor for O-antigens and S-layer polysaccharides (see |FRAME: PWY-7328|), protein glycosylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7037|) and cell wall polymers (see |FRAME: PWY-6397|)., A few examples for eukaryotic polysaccharides whose biosynthesis requires |FRAME: CPD-14553| include xyloglucans (|FRAME: PWY-5936|), glycolipids (|FRAME: PWY-401|), glycosaminoglycans (|FRAME: PWY-6557|), glycoalkaloids (|FRAME: PWY-5666|), fagopyritols (|FRAME: PWY-5380|) and saponins (|FRAME: PWY-5203|).

|FRAME: CPD-27874 Isobutylmalonyl-CoA| is a rarely used extender unit for some polyketide synthases. It's use was first reported from the mangrove endophyte |FRAME: TAX-995841|, where it participates in the biosynthesis of the divergolides and the germicidins |CITS: [21506215]|., The pathway starts with the amino acid |FRAME: VAL|, which is processed into |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.42| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25|. Isobutanoyl-CoA is then elongated by a designated ketosynthase III-type enzyme (|FRAME: G-124998 DivS|) and transformed into |FRAME: CPD-18023| by the action of |FRAME: G-124997 DivT|, an enzyme similar to |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.85|. The pathway is completed by reductive carboxylation catalyzed by |FRAME: G-124996 DivR|, a crotonyl-CoA reductase-like enzyme |CITS: [21506215]|., In |FRAME: TAX-995841| the three genes are located in an operon, next to the divergolide biosynthetic gene cluster.
