Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFA) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes., The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in these compounds. The icosanoids are derived from the 20-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (AA; 20:4n-6), |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA; 20:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-8120| (DGLA; 20:3n-6)., Additional fatty acids are also oxygenated to yield bioactive products, including the the 18-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (LA; 18:2n-6) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (ALA; 18:3n-3) and the 22-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| (DPA; 22:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA; 22:6n-3). Strictly speaking, the derivatives of such acids should be named octadecanoids (for C18 compounds) and docosanoids (for 22 carbon compounds), though these compounds are often included in the icosanoids, making the definition broader than initially intended., In mammals icosanoids and related mediators mediate a wide array of critical biological processes such as ovulation, initiation of labor, bone metabolism, nerve growth and development, wound healing, kidney function, blood-vessel tone, blood coagulation, immune responses, and inflammation. Despite the great importance of these compounds, mammals are not able to form a double bond at either the n-3 or n-6 position of a fatty acyl chain and must rely entirely on dietary intake for PUFAs |CITS: [25486530]|., Three main enzyme families act on PUFAs. The first one is |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.1| (the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes), which possess dual cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activities and catalyze the oxidative cyclization of PUFAs to |FRAME: CPD-24676|, |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|, or |FRAME: CPD-26009| (depending on the starting PUFA), which are subsequently converted to a variety of prostanoids and thromboxanes by cell-specific terminal synthases and isomerases., The second family is the lipoxygenases (LOX), which catalyze the stereoselective insertion of molecular oxygen into PUFA with the formation of hydroperoxy fatty acids that are subsequently reduced to the corresponding hydroxy-fatty acids. The lipoxygenases are divided into three main form depneding on the carbon at which they oxygenate |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|: |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|., The third family is cytochrome P450 monooxygenases that catalyzes the hydroxylation and/or epoxygenation of PUFAs. In addition to producing LOX-like monohydroxy fatty acids, CYP can add a hydroxyl moiety to the ω-carbons, of PUFA to form a unique class of omega-hydroxylated fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-21314|). The epoxides that are formed by these enzymes can be hydrolyzed to the corresponding dihydroxyfatty acids by |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| (sEH).

|FRAME: NADPHX| is a hydrated form of |FRAME: NADPH|, where the hydroxyl group is attached at position 6 of the nicotinamide moiety., NAD(P)H spontaneously hydrates to both the (6S)- and (6R)- isomers. |FRAME: NADHX| and |FRAME: NADPHX| are inhibitors of several dehydrogenases |CITS: [ 9851831]| and it is thus important to eliminate them. This is achieved by a bifunctional enzyme. One of its activities, that of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.136|, converts |FRAME: CPD0-2474| back to |FRAME: NADPH|. , Since both |FRAME: CPD0-2474| and |FRAME: CPD-14133| are formed, but the enzyme can only dehydrate the S-form, the enzyme possesses a second activity, that of |FRAME: EC-5.1.99.6|, which epimerizes the R form to a 60:40 ratio of S/R forms |CITS: [21994945]|., In eukaryotes the two activities are catalyzed by two different enzymes. The dehydratase is ATP-dependent, unlike the ADP-dependent prokaryotic enzyme (see |FRAME: PWY-6938|).

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-41956|, also known as the fly agaric, is well known for its psychoactive effects, which are mediated by |FRAME: CPD-23410| and its decarboxylation product |FRAME: CPD-22030|., |FRAME: CPD-23410 Ibotenate| is a conformationally-restricted analogue of the neurotransmitter |FRAME: GLT| and acts as a non-selective agonist of the NMDA and group I (mGluR1 and mGluR5) and II (mGluR2 and mGluR3) metabotropic glutamate receptors. In addition, it also acts as a weak agonist of the AMPA and kainate receptors., |FRAME: CPD-22030 Muscimol| is an analogue of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA), and is a potent, selective agonist for the GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors with exceptionally high affinity to GABA<sub>A</sub>-δ receptors |CITS: [24473816][30565258]|. GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors are widely distributed in the brain, and so when |FRAME: CPD-22030| is administered, it alters neuronal activity in multiple regions including the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum, resulting in sedative-hypnotic, depressant and hallucinogenic psychoactivity., The structure of |FRAME: CPD-23410| was reported back in 1964 |CITS: [14266560]|. Based on co-occurring metabolites, |FRAME: CPD-48| was suggested as a precursor in 1969, even though the compound has not been detected in |FRAME: TAX-41956| |CITS: [Matsumoto69]|. Further progress toward identifying the biosynthesis pathway came only 50 years later |CITS: [32233056]|. Building on the earlier suggestion, the authors searched for enzymes that may catalyze the hydroxylation of either |FRAME: GLT| or |FRAME: GLN|. While no enzymes are known to catalyze the reaction with the free amino acids, the GloE dioxygenase from |FRAME: TAX-101852| was proposed to catalyze |FRAME: GLN| 3-hydroxylation during the biosynthesis of the non-ribosomal peptide |FRAME: CPD-23418| |CITS: [25270390]|. A similar gene, |FRAME: G-80777|, was discovered in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-41956|, leading the way to the discovery of the ibotenate and muscimol biosynthesis gene cluster |CITS: [32233056]|., As of 2020, only the product of the |FRAME: G-80777| has been characterized biochemically, and thus the pathway is still considered largely hypothetical.

|FRAME: CPD-21650 "Indole-3-carbonyl nitrile"| (ICN) is a novel secondary metabolite observed in |FRAME: TAX-3702|. The compound contains a highly reactive α-ketonitrile moiety that has not been found in any plant natural product previously |CITS: [26352477]|. The α-ketonitrile is susceptible to nucleophilic attack, leading to the displacement of a cyanide ion, a common defense mechanism in cyanogenic plants., ICN is formed from |FRAME: TRP| by the action of two cytochrome P-450 enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: AT4G39950| and |FRAME: AT2G30750| genes and a hydrogen peroxide-producing oxidoreductase encoded by the |FRAME: AT1G26380| gene. The early steps in its biosynthesis is identical to those of |FRAME: CAMALEXIN-SYN|. However, |FRAME: AT2G30750| differs from |FRAME: AT2G30770|, which participates in camalexin biosynthesis, by stopping catalysis when |FRAME: CPD-21441| is formed |CITS: [26352477]|. |FRAME: AT2G30770| appears to catalyze an additional dehydration reaction, forming |FRAME: CPD-21440| |CITS: [25953104]|., ICN is hydroxylated by another cytochrome P-450, |FRAME: AT4G31970|, to form |FRAME: CPD-21649|. This compound is presumably converted in vivo to form thiazolated compounds. However, the later part of the pathway has not been described yet |CITS: [26352477]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13015| (mannosylglucosylglycerate, MGG) is a compatible solute identified in the slightly thermophilic species |FRAME: TAX-28237| (optimum growth temperature of 55 to 60°C), a member of the order Thermotogales. Under optimum growth conditions MGG is the major solute in this organism. It plays a role during low-level osmotic adaptation only, whereas α-glutamate and, to a lesser extent, L-proline are used for osmoprotection under salt stress |CITS: [17521333]|., |FRAME: CPD-13015| is a derivative of |FRAME: CPD-9190|, identified in the free form in |FRAME: TAX-556|, in the marine cyanobacteria |FRAME: TAX-1219| and |FRAME: TAX-32049|, and in the thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-309805| (see |FRAME: PWY-5662| and |FRAME: PWY-6685|)., The pathways for MGG biosynthesis have been studied in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-69499|, which appears to possess two alternative pathways. In one of the pathways, mannosylglucosylglycerate is produced from |FRAME: G3P| and |FRAME: CPD-12575| by three enzymes, encoded by |FRAME:G-12444|, |FRAME: G-12436| and |FRAME: G-12440| (this pathway). In the second pathway, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-6687|, MGG is produced from |FRAME: GLYCERATE| and |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| by two enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-12442| and |FRAME: G-12445| |CITS: [20061481]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: G-12444| gene of |FRAME: TAX-69499| was identified by its similarity to known genes from other organisms. The |FRAME: G-12436| gene was predicted to be involved since it encodes a glycosyltransferase and is located next to |FRAME:G-12444|. The two genes were amplified by PCR and cloned, and the recombinant enzymes were characterized., The native MggB enzyme was partially purified and characterized. The enzyme was subjected to peptide mass fingerprinting analysis, and the results suggested |FRAME: G-12440| as a potential gene encoding the enzyme, although this prediction has not been proved yet |CITS: [20061481]|.

Names: pyrimidine nucleobases salvage I // uracil salvage
Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, The key enzyme in the salvage of the pyrimidine nucleobase |FRAME: URACIL| is uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (UPRT) (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.9 "EC 2.4.2.9"|), which transfers a phosphoribosyl group from |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to uracil, generating |FRAME: UMP| in a single step. The enzyme is found in archaea, bacteria, lower eukaryotes and plants |CITS: [16660311][216696][2189783][8856065][11773618][14658380]|. This pathway was shown to be the major route for uracil salvage in potato tubers |CITS: [12244448]|., Mammals lack the enzyme, and thereby are unable to perform the one-step salvage of uracil |CITS: [15685165]| and are limited to recycling pyrimidine nucleosides via uridine kinases (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|)., Some archaea, bacteria and lower eukaryotes that possess the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7932| (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.1 "EC 3.5.4.1"|) are also able to salvage exogenously supplied |FRAME: CYTOSINE| by converting it to |FRAME: URACIL| (see |FRAME: PWY-7194|).

Summary: General Background, Polyunsaturated long- and very-long-chain fatty acids (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear., These compounds are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturatedare very long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. , Polyunsaturated very long chain fatty acids are also found in mammals. For example, in humans |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (20:4Δ5,8,11,14) and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (20:5Δ5,8,11,14,17) are precursors of the regulatory molecules eicosanoids, which are involved in many cellular functions including vascular permeability, inflammation, regulation of immune system, blood clotting, neurotransmission and cholesterol metabolism., |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Eicosapentaenoate| (EPA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains five cis double bonds, one of which is located at the third carbon from the omega end, which makes it an omega-3 fatty acid. EPA is produced by microalgae and is common in fish who eat the algae, although the fish can not produce it. It is also produced by mosses and ferns, but is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. EPA is also produced by some marine bacteria, mostly those adapted to low temperatures and high pressures, via a completely different pathway |CITS: [10220156]|., About This pathway, While humans can not synthesize EPA de novo, they are able to convert the essential fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| to EPA. Humans require either |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| or EPA to produce |FRAME: CPD-10244|, a primary structural component of the human brain cerebral cortex, sperm, testicles and retina. , The biosynthesis of polyunsaturated fatty acids in animals and most fungi occurs when the compounds are activated as coenzyme A esters. Once |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| is activated to |FRAME: LINOLENOYL-COA|, the common mammalian pathway involves a Δ6 desaturation, elongation by the elongase complex (see |FRAME: PWY-7036|), and a second desaturation at the 5th position. , The Δ5 and Δ6 desaturases are front-loading desaturases and introduce the new double bonds at the fifth carbon from the carboxyl end of the fatty acid. Both genes contain a cytochrome b5 domain, and thus do not depend on external cytochrome b5 for activity., Note that an alternative pathway, which includes a Δ8 desaturation step, has also been reported (see |FRAME: PWY-7724|).

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-16888 "Mannojirimycin"| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Azasugars azasugars|, which are analogs of monosaccharides in which the ring oxygen is replaced by an imino group. Azasugars are produced by plants and microorganisms. They are known to inhibit many glycosidases and are of potential use in the pharmaceutical and agrochemical industries. , Although the biosynthetic pathway for azasugars has not been fully elucidated, a cluster of three bacterial genes gabT1, yktC1 and gutB1 involved in |FRAME: CPD-16888| biosynthesis has been identified and their products characterized. Based on these data, a pathway for the biosynthesis of the glcosidase inhibitors |FRAME: 1-DEOXYNOJIRIMYCIN| and |FRAME: CPD-16891| has been proposed in which |FRAME: CPD-16888| is a branch point leading to the two products. Although |FRAME: 1-DEOXYNOJIRIMYCIN| has been extracted from certain plants such as |FRAME:TAX-3498| (mulberry) leaves, its bacterial production on a larger scale is desirable (|CITS: [21786380]|, in |CITS: [23265519]| and reviewed in |CITS: [12851286]|)., |FRAME: TAX-1883| and |FRAME: TAX-1386| species can fermentatively produce both |FRAME: 1-DEOXYNOJIRIMYCIN| and |FRAME: 1-DEOXYXYLONOJIRIMYCIN|, with the latter stereoisomer (C2-epimer) produced in smaller amounts in |FRAME: TAX-1386| species |CITS: [23265519]|., The production of |FRAME: 1-DEOXYNOJIRIMYCIN| has been demonstrated in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1390| |CITS: [24354768][23265519]|, in |FRAME: TAX-720555| |CITS: [24354768]|, in |FRAME: TAX-886882| |CITS: [24354768]|, and in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [23265519][21717329]|. However, genes gabT1, yktC1 and gutB1 that were shown to be involved in |FRAME: 1-DEOXYNOJIRIMYCIN| production are absent in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-224308| |CITS: [21717329]|., About This Pathway, Evidence suggests that |FRAME: CPD-15709| from the glycolytic pool is transaminated to form |FRAME: CPD-16885| in a reaction catalyzed by GabT1. After dephosphorylation by YktC1, the |FRAME: NAD|-preferring amino-mannitol dehydrogenase GutB1 oxidizes the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-16886| to the acyclic aminoaldehyde intermediate |FRAME: CPD-16887| which spontaneously cyclizes to form |FRAME: CPD-16888| |CITS: [21786380][24354768]|., The remainder of the pathway to |FRAME: 1-DEOXYNOJIRIMYCIN| has been hypothesized to involve epimerization of |FRAME: CPD-16888| to |FRAME: CPD-16889|, followed by dehydration and reduction steps. Formation of |FRAME: CPD-16891| could occur without the epimerization step (|CITS: [21786380]| and illustrated in |CITS: [23265519]|). However, these steps have not yet been demonstrated and are not shown here.

Several types of cytokinins conjugation exist which render cytokinins inactive: O-xylosylation, O-glucosylation, and N-glucosylation. When plants are subjected to high levels of cytokinin application, the major conjugate that forms is the 7-N-glucoside |CITS: [15342621]|. Moreover, unlike O-glucosides, the glucosylation of which is reversible through the action of glucosidases, 7-N- and 9-N-glucosides are resistant to glucosidases |CITS: [8235622]|. This, taken with N-glucosides accumulation in plant subjected to high doses of cytokinins, has led to the suggestion that N-glucosylation is involved in detoxification |CITS: [15342621]|.

Summary: General Background, Natural, pigmented phenazine-containing compounds produced by eubacteria posses broad-spectrum antibiotic, activity, although their mode(s) of action is not completely understood. An exception is the archael, genus |FRAME:TAX-2207| which produces an unusual, membrane-bound phenazine, |FRAME: CPD-7323|, that, is used as an electron carrier in methanogenesis (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5207|). Phenazines can be simple,, or complex including isoprenylated, or carbohydrate-containing derivatives. Phenazine-producing bacteria are more, abundant in the Actinobacteria, but some proteobacteria also produce them., Fluorescent pseudomonads such as |FRAME: ORG-5929|, |FRAME: TAX-1038921 "Pseudomonas chlororaphis subsp. aureofaciens 30-84 (previously named P. aureofaciens 30-84)"| |CITS: [11114932]| and |FRAME: TAX-287| are the best studied phenazine producers. These organisms typically biosynthesize two or more phenazines, although |FRAME: ORG-5929| produces only |FRAME: CPD-9522|., This compound may be modified by methylation, transamidation, hydroxylation, or decarboxylation by the products of linked, or unlinked genes. Phenazine production by fluorescent pseudomonads makes them interesting as biological control agents to combat fungal plant pathogens in the soil. Although the physiological role of phenazines within these organisms is uncertain, they appear to give them a competitive advantage in the environment. The phenazine pyocyanin is a virulence factor for |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: CPD-9522| has been shown to be involved in |FRAME: ORG-5929| phytotoxicity. Reviewed in |CITS: [16719720]| and |CITS: [15008629]|., About This Pathway, Some, but not all strains of |FRAME: TAX-333|, produce |FRAME: CPD-9547|. In |FRAME: TAX-1038921| evidence suggests that this reaction is catalyzed by the product of gene |FRAME: G-10465|. PhzO is similar in amino acid sequence to the family of two-component nonheme flavin-diffusable bacterial aromatic monooxygenases. An as yet undefined reductase is presumably also required. Spontaneous decarboxylation of the product results in |FRAME: CPD-9546|. These and other phenazine derivatives may have improved antibiotic activity |CITS: [11114932]|.

Summary: The pentitols |FRAME: CPD-355| (D-arabinol) and |FRAME: RIBITOL| are common in nature, while the pentitols |FRAME: XYLITOL| and |FRAME: L-ARABITOL| are rare or absent., Pentitols and other neutral polyols can be taken up by bacteria and serve as a carbon and energy source. Gram-negative bacteria and Actinobacteria import the polyol intact, convert them into a keto sugar by a polyol hydrogenase, and then phosphorylate the keto sugar and metabolize it via the pentose phosphate or glycolytic pathways (see |FRAME: DARABITOLUTIL-PWY|). Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1582| |CITS: [118163]| and |FRAME:TAX-33945| |CITS: [12467497]|, transport polyols into the cell using a phosphotransferase system, resulting in their phosphoylation. The polyol phosphates are then oxidized by polyol phosphate dehydrogenases (this pathway).     , Firmicutes transport pentitols via a phosphoenolpyruvate:glycose phosphotransferase system (PTS) either of the galactitol or the mannose family. In this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-355| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-12079| as it is transported into the cell, and the latter is oxidized into |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which can enter the pentose phosphate pathway., Examples of other pentitol degradation pathways include |FRAME: RIBITOLUTIL-PWY| and |FRAME: LARABITOLUTIL-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins, including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. , In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in, transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as, |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in, modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|,, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., The protoheme biosynthetic pathway shown here is found in animals, fungi, apicomplexan protozoa, (such as the malaria parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [15144063]|), and members of the, α-proteobacteria. In these organisms the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway starts with glycine, and succinyl-CoA (see |FRAME:PWY-5189|)., In other bacteria (including |FRAME:TAX-562|) and archaea, tetrapyrrole biosynthesis begins with, glutamate instead of glycine (see |FRAME:PWY-5188|). Plants also biosynthesize heme via, glutamate for use in cytochromes and compounds derived from heme. Both the glycine and glutamate pathways are present in the chloroplast-containing |FRAME: TAX-3039| (reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [15576047], [12051904], [16093570]|)., Both tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathways merge at the intermediate |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE|., however, a branch point at |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| leads to biosynthesis of different, compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|),, |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|),, and heme D biosynthesis., A second branch point at |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| leads to biosynthesis of chlorophyll, in plants and bacteriochlorophyll in photosynthetic bacteria (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|)., In eukaryotes, heme biosynthesis spans the mitochondrial (or plastid) and cytosol compartments., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [12177321], [16093570]|. , About This Pathway, This MetaCyc pathway shows many enzymes and genes for heme biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-9606| and the photosynthetic purple nonsulfur α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1063|., |FRAME: TAX-1063| possesses two chromosomes and five additional replicons. Two genes encoding 5-aminolevulinate synthase, hemA and hemT, are present on chromosomes 1 and 2, respectively. Biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole cofactors heme, bacteriochlorophyll, siroheme and cobalamin in this organism is highly regulated and is dependent upon expression of these two isozymes (in |CITS: [7592416], [10491185]|). The hemA gene product is expressed under normal aerobic and photosynthetic conditions, under which the hemT gene product is not expressed. No activity could be demonstrated for the purified, recombinant hemT gene product in vitro |CITS: [10491185]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-1063|, no hemD gene encoding uroporphyrinogen III synthase has been identified. A , gene encoding coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (oxygen-dependent) has been identified as hemF and has amino acid sequence similarities to the eukaryotic enzyme. However, oxygen-independent , (anaerobic) hemN and hemZ encoded forms of the enzyme also exist in this organism, and there is , evidence that these two alleles were duplicated |CITS: [15028685]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1063| and many other , prokaryotes, no gene encoding protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (EC 1.3.3.4) has been definitively identified, , although the gene has been identified as hemG in |FRAME:TAX-562| and hemY , in |FRAME: TAX-1423|. Reviewed in |CITS: [12177321]|. , The ferrochelatase reaction involves incorporation of ferrous iron. In bacteria the mechanisms for acquisition of , ferrous and ferric iron depend upon which form is available in the environment and its abundance. The source , of ferrous iron for this reaction in bacteria may involve direct import by divalent metal ion transporters, more , complex mechanisms involving siderophores, other transport systems, and extracellular reductases |CITS: [12054438]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [12829269]|., In humans, the eight steps of the pathway are divided between the cytosol and the mitochondria, with the final product heme, being synthesized in the mitochondria. The pathway occurs in many cell types and is regulated in a tissue and cell specific manner. The first reaction of the pathway catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-342| or |FRAME: CPLX66-342| is considered the rate-limiting step |CITS: [23471474]|. Defects in any of the enzymes in humans, leads to a group of inherited disorders called porphyrias.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Inositols Inositol| is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers., |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is the physiologically most common stereoisomer and is distributed abundantly (but not universally) throughout the biological system. It is an essential polyol in eukaryotes, where its phospholipid derivative |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols phosphatidylinositol| (PI) is an important constituent of phospholipid membranes. PI is also cleaved by phospholipase C to generate inositol phosphate (IP) and diacyglycerol, both of which are central cell signalling molecules., |FRAME: CPD-8050 "scyllo-Inositol"| is a relatively rare form of inositol but is sometimes found in organisms. It has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-13422| buds |CITS: [10830508]| and in |FRAME: TAX-4513 barley| seeds, where it is present in phosphatidylinositol |CITS: [7755633]|. The phosphatidylinositol synthase of |FRAME: TAX-5919| can act on |FRAME: CPD-8050| |CITS: [17403152]|. In mammals, |FRAME: CPD-8050| has been shown to localize in the kidney and brain |CITS: [5644141]|, and an enzyme from bovine brain was found to interconvert |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-8050| |CITS: [1267771]|., |FRAME: CPD-8052| is a relatively rare form of inositol. Minor amounts have been found in animal and human tissue sources |CITS: [6643610]||, and it has been shown that |FRAME: CPD-8052| and |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| are components of two different inositol phosphoglycan (IPG) molecules in mammalian systems |CITS: [2833261][2517463]|. , About This Pathway, A pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| was initially characterized in |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [5905122][5905123][4328832]|. Since then many microorganisms have been reported to be able to grow on |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| as their sole carbon source, including the yeast |FRAME: TAX-54550| |CITS: [4351258]|., More recent studies in |FRAME: TAX-1423| have identified multiple genes required for |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| catabolism. The iol divergon includes the operons iolABCDEFGHIJ and iolRS |CITS: [9226270]|, and the iolT gene |CITS: [11807058]|. Seven of these genes encode the enzymes that catalyze the complete degradation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| to |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|., Characterization of the |FRAME: BSU39700|-enoded |FRAME: CPLX-8649| found that the enzyme can also act on |FRAME: CPD-8052| |CITS: [16461681]|. The product of this reaction, |FRAME: CPD-365|, can be converted by the |FRAME: BSU39680|-encoded |FRAME: BSU39680-MONOMER| to |FRAME: CPD-14808|, an intermediate in |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| degradation., Another study found that |FRAME: TAX-1423| can also grow using |FRAME: CPD-8050| as its sole carbon source |CITS: [20133360]|. The organism possesses two enzymes that can catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-8050| to |FRAME: CPD-14808|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU33530| and |FRAME: BSU10850|. However, only the NAD+-dependent IolX is involved in |FRAME: CPD-8050| catabolism. The other enzyme, which is NADP+-dependent, may be involved in |FRAME: CPD-8050| biosynthesis |CITS: [20133360]|.

Summary: Nicotine is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-4093|) |CITS: [Schmeltz77]|, where it functions as a defense compound. In the plant tissue nicotine is mostly present in the |FRAME: NICOTINE| isomeric form |CITS: [Armstrong98]|, although tobacco smoke contains up to 10% of |FRAME: R-NICOTINE|, probably due to racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|)., The aerobic soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29320| (previously known as various strains of |FRAME: TAX-1671| |CITS: [1581183]|) is able to grow on either isomer of nicotine as a sole source of carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [4186896]|. The genes encoding the enzymes required for nicotine degradation mostly reside on a 160 kb plasmid, named pAO1, and are induced during growth on nicotine |CITS: [9878353]|., Nicotine enters the cell by facilitated diffusion, driven by the nicotine concentration gradient |CITS: [19443550]|. , The first enzyme of the degradation pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-2221|, introduces a hydroxyl group into the 6-position of the pyridine ring of both isomers of nicotine |CITS: [FEMSMicLett52-13]|. Two different, stereo-specific enzymes oxidize the 6-hydroxynicotines, producing the optically inactive |FRAME:CPD-14077| that hydrolyzes spontaneously to |FRAME: CPD-107| |CITS: [4965794]|. The latter is hydroxylated at the 2-position of the pyridine ring by |FRAME: CPLX-2241| (ketone dehydrogenase), forming |FRAME: CPD-113| |CITS: [9878353]|., The next step involves |FRAME: EC-3.7.1.19|, a C-C bond hydrolizing enzyme that splits the molecule into |FRAME: CPD-123| and |FRAME: CPD-124|, both of which are processed further in parallel routes |CITS: [16321959]|., |FRAME: CPD-123| is hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-2301| |CITS: [4636328]|. This compound was thought to be further degraded to maleamate |CITS: [5835946]|. However, the recent discovery of a |FRAME: CPLX-8438| suggests that it may be hydrolyzed to |FRAME: 2-KETO-GLUTARAMATE|, and then converted to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, which can either enter the TCA or be converted to glutamate and directed to biosynthesis |CITS: [21288482]|., |FRAME: CPD-2301| is also known to dimerize spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-14081|, a blue compound that renders the bacterial cells dark blue upon nicotine degradation |CITS: [5384624]|. A dedictaed enzyme on the pAO1 plasmid reduces this compound to its hydroquinone form, presumably to protect the cells from the formation of a semiquinone radical form, which would lead to formation of harmful reactive oxygen species |CITS: [17293530]|., |FRAME: CPD-124| is converted to |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD| in two routes: either directly, by the action of |FRAME: MONOMER-17144|, or via |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, by the actions of |FRAME: MONOMER-17148| and an as-yet unidentified transaminase. |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD "Succinate aldehyde"| is oxidized to |FRAME: SUC| and enters central metabolism |CITS: [15838033][16689938]|.

Summary: General Background, Sulfolipids constitute one of the important classes of sulfated metabolites that are found in pathogenic mycobacteria |CITS: [16933356]|. The sulfolipid family consists of different forms of acylated sulfated trehaloses. The sulfolipids were first detected while searching for the reason for the observed correlation between pathogenicity of |FRAME: TAX-1773| strains and the adsorption of neutral red dye by their envelopes |CITS: [16590578]|, even though it was later shown that the sulfolipids are not responsible for this reaction |CITS: [15004126]|., Sulfolipids are the most notable sulfated metabolites of |FRAME: TAX-1773| (they account for 1% of its dry weight |CITS: [4989541]|). Many studies reported a correlation between their abundance and the strain's virulence. In addition, |FRAME: CPD-18706|, an intermediate in the sulfolipid biosynthetic pathway, has been shown to be a potent T-cell antigen presented by the nonclassical MHC molecule CD1b |CITS: [14981115]|., Sulfolipids contain a sulfated trehalose core that is tetraacylated with different types of fatty acids. One of the positions (2') is esterified to an n-fatty acid (either palmitate and stearate) while the other three sites (3', 6' and 6) are occupied by either |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"| or |FRAME: Hydroxyphthioceranic-Acids "hydroxyphthioceranic acids"|. Two major forms of sulfolipids were named |FRAME: CPD-18711| (SL-I) and |FRAME: CPD-18600| (SL-II). Additional minor forms, differing in the composition of the branched fatty acids and the acylation positions were also reported and named SL-I' [2-palmitoyl/stearoyl-3,6-bis(phthioceranoyl)-6'-hydroxyphthioceranoyltrehalose 2'-sulfate], and SL-II' [2-palmitoyl/stearoyl-4,6,6'-tris(hydroxyphthioceranoyl)trehalose 2'-sulfate]., The presence of either plamitoyl or stearoyl group at position 2, and the various combinations of different chain lengths of the hydroxyphthioceranoic acid substituents located at positions 6 and 6' of the trehalose backbone result in hundreds of different structures for each type of sulfolipid |CITS: [4989541][820371][21919534]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with the sulfation of the common disaccharide |FRAME: TREHALOSE| at the O2 position by |FRAME: EC-2.8.2.37| |CITS: [15258569]|. The sulfated disaccharide is acylated at the 2' position by either a palmitate or stearate fatty acid, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.288| (|FRAME: G185E-8116|), forming |FRAME: CPD-18715| |CITS: [17592143]|., The next steps involve acylation of the 3', 6 and 6' position by either |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids| or |FRAME: Hydroxyphthioceranic-Acids|. These acids are synthesized from palmitate or stearate by the polyketide synthase |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.287| (|FRAME: G185E-8121|, also known as pks2) |CITS: [11278910][24028583]|. As is the case in other mycobacterial polyketide synthases, the starter molecules are first activated by adenylation, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: G185E-8122 FadD23| |CITS: [17389997]|., The PKS2 synthase can catalyze extension by either seven or eight methylmalonyl-CoA externder units, resulting in formation of either hepta- or octamethylated acids. In addition, it is assumed that the enzyme also produces hydroxyphthioceranic acids, by skipping the dehydratase (DH) and enoylreductase (ER) domains during the first cycle of condensation |CITS: [17389997]|., The first addition of (hydroxy)phthioceranic acid is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.283| (|FRAME: G185E-8120|). This enzyme transfers a single acid to position 3' |CITS: [17259623][17592143]|. This is followed by two additional transfers to positions 6 and 6', which are catalyzed successively by the same enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.284| (|FRAME: G185E-8118|) |CITS: [22194604]|. While |FRAME: G185E-8120 PapA1| transfers the acid from a CoA form, |FRAME: G185E-8118 Chp1| catalyzes a transesterification reaction, transferring the acyl groups between two substrate molecules. It is selective for diacylated substrates, generating one tetraacylated molecule and two monoacylated molecule. The reaction is similar to that catalyzed by |FRAME: G185E-5353|, involved in |FRAME: PWY-7738| |CITS: [22194604]|., The process described above occurs at the cytoplasmic side of the membrane. Following its synthesis, the sulfolipid is transported to the periplasmic side of the membrane. Transport from the cytoplasm to the periplasm has been shown to be dependent on two proteins - MmpL8 and Sap. These proteins are involved not only in transport, but somehow are also involved in the biosynthesis of sulfolipids |CITS: [12724526]|, potentially by forming a scaffold onto which the other enzymes assemble |CITS: [22194604]|.

General Background, Hydrogenases catalyze the reversible reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [21900241]|. They are found in a wide variety of microorganisms and enable them to use |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as a source of reductant under either anaerobic or aerobic conditions. Fermentative microbes utilize hydrogenase to dispose of excess reductant, using protons as the terminal electron acceptor and generating |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as a waste product. , About this Pathway, The |FRAME:CPLX-8255| described in this pathway is a cytoplasmic heterotetrameric [Fe] only hydrogenase and a flavoprotein like most NAD(P)+ hydrogenases |CITS: [15256587]|. The FMN prosthetic group plays an important role in oxidizing NADH., |FRAME: TAX-119072| uses the enzymes of the |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY| to convert glucose to pyruvate, generating ATP and NADH. Pyruvate is then oxidized to acetyl CoA and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| using |FRAME: PWY-5100|. , During fermentation at low |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| pressure, glucose is completely converted to acetate, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|. Thus the oxidation of NADH is coupled to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| formation. At high |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| pressure, metabolism is shifted towards ethanol formation and 50 % of the NADH is oxidized via the reduction of acetyl CoA to ethanol.

Summary: General Background, Mycolic acids are the hallmark of the cell envelope of |FRAME: TAX-1773| and related species and genera. They comprise a homologous series of C60-C90 (2R)-alkyl-(3R)-hydroxy very long-chain fatty acids, and are found as either esters of |FRAME: Arabinogalactan| or as free lipids in the form of trehalose dimycolate (TDM). Both forms contribute to forming the two leaflets of the mycobacterial outer membrane, also called the mycomembrane, which protects the organism from antibiotics and the host's immune system |CITS: [15653820][17555433][15353567]|., There is a significant variability in the structure of mycolic acids among different species. Acids from |FRAME: TAX-1716| species contain 22-38 carbon atoms, |FRAME: TAX-697025| and |FRAME: TAX-697025| spp. contain 30-36, |FRAME: TAX-37914| spp. contain 34-38, |FRAME: TAX-1827| spp. contain 34-52 in, |FRAME: TAX-1817| spp. contain 46-60, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia| spp. contain 46-66, |FRAME: TAX-2060| spp. contain 64-78 , |FRAME: TAX-1763| spp. contain 60-90, and |FRAME: TAX-286801| spp. contain up to 100 carbon atoms |CITS: [24374164]|., The acids are formed by a Claisen-type condensation of two components - the meromycolic chain and a fatty acid., Several structural classes of mycolic acids exist. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the most apolar ones, known as α-mycolic acids, contain 74-80 carbon atoms (out of which 22-26 carbons are located in the fatty acid moiety and the rest on the mero-chain) and generally two double bonds (that can be in either cis- or trans-configuration) or two cis-cyclopropyl groups located in the meromycolic chain. The cyclopropane rings are believed to protect the organism from oxidative stress |CITS: [15653820]|. α-Mycolic acids usually comprise more than 70 percent of the total mycolic acids in the cell., Other classes are defined by additional oxygen functions located in the distal part of the meromycolic chain, and include keto-, methoxy-, wax ester-, epoxy-, and hydroxy-types. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the oxygenated mycolic acids (keto-, methoxy-, and hydroxy-types) contain ~84-88 carbon atoms, and are thus four to six carbons longer than the α-mycolic acids from the same strains., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of mycolic acids could be divided conceptually into three parts: the biosynthesis of the fatty acid moiety, the biosynthesis of the mero-acid moiety, and the condensation of both parts., Mycobacteria are quite unique in having two fatty acid synthase systems - FAS-I, a multidomain, multifunctional fatty acid synthase similar to those found in yeast and mammals, and FAS-II, a system consisting of several soluble enzymes that is similar to that found in bacteria and plants., The pathway towards mycolic acids starts with the action of the FAS-I system, which has a bimodal distribution of products - forming C14/C16 long-chain acyl-CoAs and C24/26 very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs. The C24/26 very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs are modified only by carboxylation at the C2 position, at which point they are ready for condensation with meromycolic acids to form mycolic acids. The C14/C16 products serve as starter molecules for the FAS-II system, which continues elongation to form meromycolic acids., A key enzyme is |FRAME: G185E-4666 FabH|, which acts as a link between the FAS-I and FAS-II systems, catalyzing the condensation of the FAS-I-derived C14/C16 acyl-CoAs with malonyl-[acpM]. The enzyme is most active with |FRAME: LAUROYLCOA-CPD|., During elongation by the FAS-II system, continuous introduction of 2-carbon units upstream of the the double bond at position 3 results in its "migration" farther from the carboxylate (to positions 5, 7, 9 etc). Isomerases (encoded by echA10 and echA11) act at two stages of the pathway, introducing double bonds into the compounds. One isomerase acts on |FRAME: trans-delta2-behenoyl-ACPs|, forming |FRAME: cis-delta3-behenoyl-ACPs|, and another on |FRAME: trans-D2-cis-D15-gheddoyl-ACPs|, forming |FRAME: cis-cis-D3-15-C34-2-ACPs|. The action of the second isomerase results in a branch in the pathway, where some of the acids continue with an additional double bond, while others continue without it. Both continue to be elongated by the FAS-II system. However, all of the acids that escaped isomeization at the C35 level undergo an isomerization at the level of C40., Following completion of the elongation process, the acids are modified by several additional enzymes that introduce methoxy groups and convert double bonds to cyclopropyl groups (including |FRAME: G185E-4788|, |FRAME: G185E-4787|, |FRAME: G185E-4786|, |FRAME: G185E-4785|, |FRAME: G185E-4597|, |FRAME: G185E-4635|). The final modified acids, as well as the final product of the FAS-I system, are then transferred from their [acp] and CoA carriers (respectively) to a polyketide enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-8096| gene, which catalyzes their condensation into a mycolic acid |CITS: [14695899][15042094]|., Additional enzymes catalyze the conjugation of the mycolic acids first to |FRAME: CPD1G-69| and subsequently to |FRAME: TREHALOSE-6P|. Following the removal of the phosphate, the free mycolic acid is exported to the periplasm, where it is attached to arabinogalactan in the cell wall, or to a second mycolic acid, forming a dimycolate.

Macrolide antibiotics are therapeutically important agents that are effective inhibitors of bacterial protein biosynthesis. They bind to the large 50S ribosomal subunit at or near the peptidyl transferase center and block the elongation of the peptide chain., |FRAME: OLEANDOMYCIN Oleandomycin| is a clinically important 14-membered macrolide antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1890|. It contains a macrolactone ring (|FRAME: CPD-13827|) modified by the attachment of two cyclic sugars, |FRAME: Oleandrose| and |FRAME: CPD-13780|. Oleandomycin differs from |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycins| by an exocyclic epoxide at C8, a unique feature not found in any other known polyoxo macrolide |CITS: [16405329]|., Oleandomycin biosynthesis starts with the production of the |FRAME: CPD-13827| ring. A large modular type I polyketide synthase comprising three large polypeptides, encoded by |FRAME: G-14853|, |FRAME: G-14854| and |FRAME: G-14855|, condenses one starter |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| unit and six extender |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| units to form |FRAME: CPD-13946| |CITS: [10908114]|. A P-450 monooxygenase enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-14857| catalyzes the epoxidation at positions 8 and 8a, resulting in the complete |FRAME: CPD-13827| ring |CITS: [7737473][10908114][11994157]|., A glycosyltransferase encoded by |FRAME: G-14858| transfers an olivose from the activated form |FRAME: CPD-11915| to the C3 position |CITS: [9749673][10594828][11514520]|, followed by 3-O methylation of the olivosyl to form an oleandrosyl group |CITS: [10770761][11514520]|. The process in completed by the transfer of a desosaminyl group from |FRAME: CPD-13776| to the C5 position by a second glycosyltransferase, encoded by |FRAME: G-14859| |CITS: [9749673][10594828]|., Once produced, |FRAME: OLEANDOMYCIN| could harm its producer. To protect the host against the antibiotic, oleadomycin is inactivated in the cell by two intracellular glycosyltransferases, encoded by |FRAME: G-14862| and |FRAME: G-14861|, which add a glucose molecule to the 2-OH group of the desosamine ring. Once the inactive antibiotic is secreted out of the cell, it is reactivated by an extracellular glucosidase (encoded by |FRAME: G-14863|) that removes the glucose |CITS: [9680207]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6972|).

Summary: General Background, Cell-cell communication in bacteria is accomplished through the exchange of extracellular signalling molecules called autoinducers. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., Autoinducer systems depend on two main components - the autoinducer and its receptor, which also functions as an autoinducer-dependent transcriptional regulator that binds DNA immediately upstream of the genes that are controlled., Autoinducer systems have been implicated in regulation of various systems. For example, |FRAME: G-11135|/luxR of |FRAME: TAX-668| regulate bioluminescence, luxM/luxN of |FRAME: TAX-669| regulate bioluminescence and polyhydroxybutyrate biosynthesis, |FRAME: G-11138|/lasR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates virulence factors, |FRAME: G-11136|/rhlR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates rhamnolipid synthesis as well as virulence factors, and |FRAME: G-11137|/TraR of |FRAME: TAX-358| regulates plasmid conjugal transfer |CITS: [8905097]|., Several types of autoinducers are known. Gram-negative bacteria typically use |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "acyl-homoserine lactones"|, known as type AI-1, as their autoinducers. The first autoinducer to be discovered was |FRAME: CPD-10780|, an AI-1 type compound from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [7236614]|. Many variants of AI-1 type inducers exist, differing from each other in the composition of the acyl moiety. In some cases, one organism may produce multiple types of acyl homoserine lactone type autoinducers, each produced by a dedicated synthase., A few examples are |FRAME: CPD-10781| from |FRAME: TAX-669|, |FRAME: CPD-10782| from |FRAME: TAX-358|,, |FRAME: CPD-10783| and |FRAME: CPD-10784| from |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: CPD-10780| and, |FRAME: CPD-10785| from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [8905097]|., Another very common family of autoinducers include compounds produced from |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|, which was first described from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-669|, in which it is used to control luciferase expression |CITS:[7984107][9990077]|. AI-2 type compounds are produced by a remarkably wide variety of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, leading to the proposal that AI-2 is a universal signal that functions in interspecies cell-to-cell communication |CITS: [11544353][18803868]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-666|, the causative agent of the disease cholera, does not produce an acyl-homoserine lactone autoinducer. This organism uses two other autoinducer/receptor quorum-sensing systems to regulate biofilm formation and virulence factor production: (|FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE "AI-2"|/LuxPQ (see |FRAME: PWY-6154|) and |FRAME: CPD-10786|/CqsS7) |CITS: [12176318][18004304]|., |FRAME: CPD-10786|, the major autoinducer system of the two, is produced from |FRAME: CPD-10267| in two enzymatic steps, as described in this pathway. The first enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: FY484_RS16660|, ligates |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| and |FRAME: CPD-10267| while eliminating |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| and coenzyme A, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-17488|, a potent quorum-sensing molecule on its own |CITS: [21197957]|. This compound undergoes a spontaneous hydrolytic deamination to form |FRAME: CPD-17489|, which is reduced by an oxoreductase encoded by the |FRAME: FY484_RS05405| gene to form the final product |CITS: [21197957]|.

Secondary metabolites with an 2,5-pyrrolidinedione (also referred to as tetramate) ring system (see for instance |FRAME:PWY-7555|) have piqued the interest of researchers for some time because of their reported antibiotic and antiviral activities |CITS:[Royles95] [18334299]| and by forming a scaffold which significantly expands the chemical diversity of secondary metabolites |CITS:[23729217]| (for an example see |FRAME:PWY-7660|). The two tetramate diasteromers |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285|, the synthesis of which in the laboratory has also been reported |CITS:[Helaine01]|, have been found in various marine-derived fungi such as |FRAME: TAX-371130| |CITS:[Neumann09]| and the mold-like fungus |FRAME: TAX-38033| |CITS:[16872138]|., Reported biological activities for |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285| comprise acting as inhibitors of the chemokine receptor CCR-5 involved in the immune system of humans |CITS:[16872138]| and inhibiting human leucocyte elastase (HLE) |CITS:[19413111]|, which point out the inherent potential of these compounds for the future development of pharmaceutical breakthrough drugs and treatments |CITS:[18033577]|., The identification of the gene cluster in the ascomycete |FRAME: TAX-95324| responsible for |FRAME:PWY-7702| has been achieved by searching the genome of the fungus for polyketide synthase (PKS) - nonribosomal polyketide synthetase (NRPS) proteins associated with an stand-alone enoyl reductase (ER). It was shown that the cluster consisted of 8 genes, among them the PKS-NRPS encoded by |FRAME: G-44171|, the stand-alone enoyl reductase encoded by |FRAME: G-44172|, and an aldolase encoded by tasA. The latter has been shown to be involved in the biosynthesis by providing the non-proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME:CPD-15319| (see |FRAME:PWY-7701|) as building block for the tetramic acid diastereomers |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285|. Interestingly, |FRAME:CPD-15319| had been previously found to accumulate in plants |CITS:[Grobbelaar55]| which however are not known to biosynthesize tetramic acid derivatives like |FRAME:CPD-18284|. , The biosynthetic sequence of the pathway towards |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285| has been elucidated by utilizing the Fusarium heterosporum expression platform (see |CITS:[25436464]|) which allowed the expression of each gene individually or in combination with each other. In combination with the expressed PKS-NRPS (tasS), the stand-alone enoyl reductase (tasC) and the aldolase (tasA) the final products of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285| were produced |CITS:[25885659]|., A subsequent study in |FRAME: TAX-38033| clarified the pathway further, demonstrating the activity of the lipocalin-like CghA, which facilitates a stereoselective intramolecular [4+2] cycloaddition of the poly ketide product to form the decalin core |CITS: [26360642]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into |FRAME: XYLITOL|, which is then converted to |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515| and |FRAME: PWY-5516|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|). An analog for these pathways is also found in the metabolism of the deoxyhexose |FRAME: L-rhamnose| (see |FRAME: PWY-6713|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, This D-arabinose degradation pathway, found in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, does not fall into any of the categories described above. Rather, the organism uses the enzymes of the |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY| pathway. Expression of these enzymes is normally induced by L-fucose and not by D-arabinose, and thus wild-type |FRAME:TAX-83333| can not use D-arabinose as a sole source of carbon and energy without prior induction by growth on L-fucose |CITS: [4928018]| (although growth on D-arabinose is made possible by a mutation in the transcriptional regulator FucR |CITS: [3100814]|)., D-arabinose is metabolized yielding |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of glycolysis, which thereby enters central metabolism, and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. Glycolaldehyde may be further catabolized to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| |CITS: [4928018]|., The related organism |FRAME:TAX-37762| uses a different pathway that belongs to the first type of canonical pentose degradation pathways to catabolize D-arabinose; see |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|.

Names: cyan fluorescent protein chromophore biosynthesis // CFP chromophore biosynthesis
Summary: |FRAME: GFP "Green fluorescent proteins"| (GFPs) are proteins that exhibit bright green fluorescence when exposed to light in the blue to ultraviolet range. GFPs form a part of the bioluminesence systems of many marine organisms, and the first such protein, from the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100|, was described already in 1962 |CITS: [13911999]|., Some other species, including non-bioluminesent species, encode homologs of GFP. Many |FRAME: TAX-6101| species exhibit bright fluorescent colors, and while the most common color is green, other colors are also found |CITS: [Catala59][Mazel95]|. The fluorescence in these species is assumed to provide protection from strong solar radiation |CITS: [Kawaguti44]|. A different function has been proposed for organisms living in deeper habitats - the conversion of blue light into a longer wavelength that is more suitable for photosynthesis by the algal endosymbionts |CITS: [28313957]|., In a 1999 study genes encoding remote homologs of the |FRAME: G-55175| gene of |FRAME: TAX-6100| were cloned from six non-bioluminescent reef corals and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified. Despite a low overall identity with GFP (26-30%), all of the proteins fluoresced, and two of them (from |FRAME: TAX-105401| and |FRAME: TAX-86599| species) were found to fluoresce at the yellow and red wavelengths, respectively |CITS: [10504696]|. It is now recognized that the family of GFP-like proteins includes |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent proteins"| (GFP), |FRAME: PWY-8514 "red fluorescent proteins"| (RFP), |FRAME: YFP-Chromophore "yellow fluorescent proteins"| (YFP), |FRAME: CFP-Chromophore "cyan fluorescent proteins"| (CFP) and |FRAME: BCP-Chromophore "purple-blue non-fluorescent chromoproteins"| (CP) |CITS: [18648549]|., All of these proteins share the same β-can fold first observed in GFP, but most are not associated with bioluminescence. While the fluorophores of previously-described GFPs are formed autocatalitically from the three amino acids Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly, later identified proteins have significant variability in the first position, containing Gln, Lys, His, or Asn |CITS: [10504696][12271129]|., Three Anthozoan cyan fluorescent proteins (CFPs) (amFP486, dsFP483, and cFP484) have been described and characterized in some detail in 1999 |CITS: [10504696]|. amFP486, which was cloned from the sea anemone |FRAME: TAX-105399|, is a tetrameric protein with subunit molecular mass of 25 kDa. It shows only 26% identity in amino acid sequence to |FRAME: G-55175| from |FRAME: TAX-6100|, and is much more similar to |FRAME: CPLX-85482| and |FRAME: CPLX-85484| (42% and 50% identity, respectively)., The chromophore of amFP486 is formed from the tripeptide Lys-Tyr-Gly, similarly to the |FRAME: CPLX-85484|, and is cis-coplanar like most of the fluorescent proteins. However, its post-translational modifications are different from those of the zFP538, and, except for Lys instead of Ser at the first position, they appear to be identical to those of GFP |CITS: [16120682]|., A study that investigated the basis for blue-shifted emission of CFPs by comparing sequences of several fluorescent proteins found that position 165 (amFP486 numbering) is occupied by either Ala or His in the CFPs but by Ile or Met in most other FPs. Mutation of Ala-165 to Ile or Met yielded a protein with fluorescence spectra that was intermediate between those of CFPs and GFPs |CITS: [11459517]|., In a later study amFP486 was produced recombinantly in |FRAME: TAX-562| and its high-resolution crystal structure was reported. The authors concluded that the cyan emission arises from the GFP-like chromophore due to charge distribution that is shifted toward the phenolate end of the chromophore by polar and electrostatic influences caused by the His-199 and Ala-165 residues. The function of His199 is to stabilize the fluorescent state by locking the chromophore into the cis-planar state and lowering the pKa so that the anionic (= fluorescent) state is predominant |CITS: [16120682]|. A similar conclustion was obtained from the X-ray structure of dsFP483, a cyan fluorescent protein from the coral |FRAME: TAX-105400| |CITS: [18395223]|., It should be noted that the chromophore of MiCy, a cyan fluorescent protein from an Acropora coral (UniProt ID Q6I7B1), is produced from the amino acids Gln-Tyr-Gly, indicating that the amino acid at the first position does not have to be lysine in order to produce cyan emissions |CITS: [15065984]|.
