Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-2002| is a catecholate siderophore produced exclusively by |FRAME: TAX-666|., Vibriobactin contains three molecules of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| linked either directly or through |FRAME:THR| residues to the polyamine |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| |CITS: [6706943]|., The steps leading to the synthesis of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| are identical to those found in bacteria that synthesize other catecholate siderophores, such as |FRAME: CPD-9984| and |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN|, and the |FRAME: VC0774|, |FRAME: FY484_RS04015| and |FRAME: VC0773| genes of |FRAME: TAX-666| are homologs of |FRAME: EG10259|, |FRAME: EG10260| and |FRAME: EG10261| of |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [9371453]|., However, the steps leading from |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| to |FRAME: CPD-2002| are different, although certain similarities to the biosynthesis of other siderophores do exist., The genes required for vibriobactin biosynthesis are located in two separate genetic clusters. Most of the genes ocur in one cluster, with the very large |FRAME: FY484_RS11055| gene residing in a second cluster, along with genes encoding vibriobactin transport and utilization |CITS: [10692380]|., The three |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| molecules are activated by |FRAME: FY484_RS04020| to the adenylate form, and then transferred to the free thiol of the phosphopantetheine arm of the aryl-carrier protein domain of three copies of |FRAME: MONOMER-15205|, resulting in three copies of |FRAME: CPD-11951| |CITS: [11112537]|., One of these molecules forms an amide bond with |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: VC0775|, producing |FRAME: CPD-11950| |CITS:[11160122][11112537]|. It should be stated that |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| is very rare among bacteria, but common in Vibrionales |CITS: [2059921]|., The other two |FRAME: CPD-11951| molecules are processed by two copies of VibF which have already bound an |FRAME: THR| molecules onto their peptidyl carrier domains. VibF condenses and heterocyclizes |FRAME: CPD-11951| with the bound |FRAME: THR| to form |FRAME: CPD-11949|., These enzyme-bound aryl oxazoline molecules are then successively transferred to the |FRAME: CPD-11950| mlecule, forming first the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-11952| and then |FRAME: CPD-2002| |CITS: [11112538]|., This process can be described as a single reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-7946|:, |FRAME:RXN-10988|

The degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10654| has been reported for several organisms that harbor the TOL plasmid. These, organisms utilize the |FRAME: CPLX-2521|, |FRAME: CPLX-2542| and |FRAME: CPLX-2543| enzymes, encoded by, the plasmid, for transforming the side chain of |FRAME: CPD-10654|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-3486| |CITS: [1526468]|., |FRAME: CPD-3486| can be degraded by the chlorocatechol degradation pathway enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-6088|),, and thus transformation of the 3-chlorobenzoate degrading strain |FRAME: TAX-65741| with the TOL plasmid resulted in, an engineered strain that was able to completely mineralize |FRAME: CPD-10654| |CITS: [1526468]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8647 "Raspberry ketone"| (4-hydroxybutanone) is the key metabolite among 230 volatile compounds that determine the bouquet of raspberry. In contrast to the complex nature of other aromas that alter rapidly if the composition of their multiple compounds is not maintained, raspberry ketone is the single dominant volatile that defines raspberry aroma |CITS: [16478225]|. Although it occurs only in low concentrations (between 1 to 17 μg/100g FW |CITS: [BOREJSZAWYSOCKI92]|) raspberry ketone and its glucosidic derivatives |CITS: [PABST90]| have been found across the plant kingdom |CITS: [10552430]| as well as in fungi |CITS: [12514017]| and insects |CITS: [16593321]|., Raspberry ketone acts as olfactory stimulant |CITS: [15898497]|, exerts anti-obese actions, alters lipid metabolism |CITS: [15862604][16637681]| and shows growth inhibition and antifeedant activity |CITS: [15026059]|., Raspberry ketone is a sought-after aroma that is widely used in the food industry for flavor of beverages and dairy products. The natural product, unlike synthetic adulterations, increases appeal and value for commercial purposes |CITS: [10554227]|. Because the low natural occurrence in plants it may cost up to $10.000/kg |CITS: [12514017]|., About This Pathway, The pathway for raspberry ketone biosynthesis is a short sequence of two enzymatic conversions. Benzalacetone synthase (BST), a chalcone synthase-like enzyme, catalyzes the one-step decarboxylative condensation of p-coumaroyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA to p-hydroxybenzalacetone. This step is considered rate-limiting. The enzyme has been isolated, cloned and characterized |CITS: [15026059][11389739][12724310]| and found to be different from the closely related chalcone synthase (CHS) and stilbene synthase (STS)., The polyketide type III synthase (PKS III) from Polygonum cuspidatum represents yet another type in the PKS type III superfamily. In contrast to almost all PKS III proteins which have 1 intron in their gene structure |CITS:[Schroder97]|, the PKS III encoded by PKS2 from Polygonum has 3 introns. Moreover, the highly conserved |FRAME:PHE| 'gatekeeper' residues Phe215 and Phe265 in the active site of PKS IIIs were replaced by |FRAME:LEU| and |FRAME:CYS| in PKS2. Interestingly, the PKS2 encoded protein shows a different substrate specificity in dependence on the pH conditions, at physiological normal pH (6.5-8.5) the recombinant enzyme acted as p-coumaryltriacetic lactone synthase (CTAS) forming predominantly |FRAME:CPD-6954| and |FRAME:CPD-6955| (see |FRAME:PWY-84|). In contrast to that, at a higher pH of 9.0-9.5, the PKS2 mainly catalyzed the formation of |FRAME:CPD-8636|| after only one round of condensation, hence acting as benzalacetone synthase (BAS) (this pathway) |CITS:[18998157]|., The second step in the pathway converts p-hydroxyacetone to raspberry ketone (p-hydroxybutanone). The NADPH-dependent enzyme activity that reduces the double bond in the side chain of p-hydroxybenzalacetone has been found in crude extracts of raspberry berries and cell cultures |CITS: [Borejsza-Wysocki94]|. However, the cloning and enzymatic characterization of this enzyme remains to be accomplished.

General Background, Heptose sugars, mostly glycero-manno-heptoses, are found in the cell surface polymers of many bacteria. Prior to their incorporation, the heptose residues are activated by attachment to a nucleotide (see pathways |FRAME: PWY0-1241| and |FRAME: PWY-6478|). These activated heptoses can be uniquely modified by enzymes before incorporation into the polymers. In bacterial pathogens heptose derivatives such as 6-deoxyheptoses that are not found in mammals can play an important role in virulence, as demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-633| |CITS: [18284593]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7613|). Heptose modifying enzymes are therefore of interest as potential drug targets |CITS: [19610666][18284593]|., |FRAME: TAX-197| is a commensal in poultry and cattle, but is a pathogen in humans and the main cause of food-borne disease in developed countries. Its capsular polysaccharide contains modified heptoses. Although the exact role of modified heptoses in this organism is not known, they may potentially contribute to virulence. Several of the modifying enzymes encoded in the capsular gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-354242| have been characterized as described in this pathway |CITS: [23689373][22787156][21711244]|., Note that this pathway has been shown to occur in strain |FRAME: TAX-354242|, but not in strain |FRAME: TAX-192222|. The latter strain contains 6-O-methylated substrates |CITS: [12392544]| that are thought to be generated by the action of putative methyltransferase MlghD |CITS: [23103756]|. The |FRAME: TAX-192222| in vivo pathway that likely produces GDP-6-O-methyl-L-gluco-heptose remains hypothetical, although several of the enzymes have been characterized (see |FRAME: MONOMER-19064 "MlghB"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-19065 "MlghC"| and |FRAME: MONOMER-19062 "WcaGNCTC"|) and an in vitro pathway was demonstrated using |FRAME: CPD-17406| as a surrogate starting substrate (not shown). Thus, strain-specific epimerization/reduction reactions generate variations in the capsule-linked heptoses of |FRAME: TAX-197| |CITS: [23689373]|., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-354242| pathway shown here, the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-17409| requires the sequential action of enzymes DdahA (WcbK), DadhB, and DdahC. DadhB serves as C-3 epimerase and DadhC serves as a C-4 reductase. Data suggested that the reversible epimerization step catalyzed by DdahB is rate-limiting in the pathway |CITS: [22787156]|., The C-4 reductase WcaG81176 is not part of the main pathway, but it appears to affect the pathway in a complex regulatory loop involving DdahC, WcaG81176 and |FRAME: CPD-17411|. WcaG81176 appears to divert substrate conversion to the latter compound |CITS: [22787156]|.

Names: bis(guanylyl molybdopterin) cofactor sulfurylation // sulfo-bis(guanylyl molybdopterin) cofactor biosynthesis // bis-MGD sulfulylation
Summary: General Background, The transition element molybdenum (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. This molybdenum cofactor (MoCo) consists of a unique tricyclic pterin compound (molybdopterin) containing a Mo-binding and coordinating dithiolene group. MoCo binds to diverse apoproteins and confers activity to the resulting holoproteins ubiquitously involved in essential redox reactions in the global C-, N-, and S-cycles |CITS: [11848841]| |CITS: [16307306]|., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of MoCo has been investigated in detail in bacteria, e.g. |CITS: [7836363][8514783][8514782][1587808][14761975]|., About This Pathway, Many enzymes depend on the sulfo-form of molybdenum cofactor (MoCo). The so called maturation of MoCo involves the addition of sulfur to the Mo center, replacing an oxo group. In eukaryotes this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.9| (e.g. the plant ABA3) |CITS: [11553608][15561708]|. However, prokaryotes do not have such an enzyme. In prokaryotes MoCo first binds to a chaperone (such as XdhC) before it is sulfurylated by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.7|. Many of the prokaryotic molybdoenzymes have a specific chaperone |CITS: [23201473]|. The chaperones interact with the desulfurase, so that MoCo is sulfurated while it is still bound to the chaperone and before the insertion into the target protein. Binding to the chaperone stabilizes the sulfurated form of MoCo. Once sulfurylated, the chaperone transfer the cofactor to its target protein |CITS: [17649978]|., The crystal structures of several molybdoenzymes revealed that MoCo is deeply buried inside the proteins, at the end of a funnel-shaped passage giving access only to the substrate |CITS: [9242907]|. The insertion step is believed to be catalyzed by the chaperones |CITS: [8522945][19519768]|,, An example of such a chaperone is the |FRAME: CPLX0-8175| (|FRAME: EG11859|) of |FRAME: TAX-562|, which is a specific chaperone for |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGH-MONOMER| (|FRAME: EG10285|). FdhD first binds |FRAME: CPD-15873| |CITS: [24444607][30444874]|, then acts as a sulfur transferase between the |FRAME: CPLX0-248 "L-cysteine desulfurase IscS"| and |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGH-MONOMER| |CITS: [22194618]|. IscS transfers the sulfur from |FRAME: CYS| to FdhD in form of a persulfide |CITS: [25649206]|., In addition to formate dehydrogenases, the DMSO reductase family includes many members for which an additional sulfur ligand of the molybdenum atom of bis-MGD has been reported at the catalytic site |CITS: [18327621][21419779][29334455]|., See |CITS: [32239579]| for a review.

Enzymes of pathway: MONOMER-20628 // CPLX-9343 // MONOMER-20631 // CPLX-7411 // MONOMER-20632 // MONOMER-13208
Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, The pentose |FRAME: CPD-25028| (D-xylose, wood sugar) is a major monosaccharide component of |FRAME: Xylans|, a polysaccharide found in the hemicellulose of plant cell walls., The first detailed genetic analysis on the Weimberg pathway genes was carried out with the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-192| |CITS: [16326697][16835232][16950779]| and |FRAME: TAX-190650| |CITS: [17172333]|. Since then the pathway was demonstrated in additional bacterial species such as |FRAME: TAX-29320| |CITS: [23063486]| and |FRAME: TAX-470150| |CITS: [24934825]|, and is described here., About This Pathway, This pathway is analogous to the oxidative pentose catabolic pathways proposed for the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-192| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5517|). In this pathway |FRAME: CPD-25028| was shown to be exclusively degraded to the tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate)., Enzymes biochemically characterized include |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.175| |CITS: [17172333]|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.82| |CITS: [19584053]|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.141| |CITS: [18448118]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.26|, that converts |FRAME: CPD-654| (2-ketoglutarate semialdehyde) to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS: [16835232]|., The oxidation product of the first enzyme (|FRAME: CPD-360|) can undergo spontaneous lactone ring opening. However, the hydrolysis of the lactone is facilitated by a dedicated xylonolactonase. The activity of this enzyme was confirmed by expression in |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [22709678][25073011]|., A very similar pathway has been described from many archaeal species. However, archaeons do not have an ortholog of the first enzyme of the bacterial pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.175|, and instead possess an NADP-dependent enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.179|, that bears no sequence similarity. The archaeal pathway is described in |FRAME: PWY-6760|.

|FRAME: TAX-108557| can utilize three sulfonated aromatic compounds as sole sources of carbon and energy. |FRAME:4-TOLUENESULFONATE| (TS) and |FRAME: BENZENESULFONATE| (BS) are desulfonated by the same enzyme system, the |FRAME:CPLX-7208| (B/TSDOS)., Another enzyme system, |FRAME: CPLX-7207|, can also desulfonate both TS and BS. The desulfonated products then undergo meta-ring cleavage reactions. The cleavage product of 4-methylcatechol is not shown as it is unknown whether a 1,6- or a 2,3-cleavage occurs |CITS: [8075807] [9990724]|.

General Background, Bacterial membranes typically consist of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL "phosphatidylglycerol"|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE "phosphatidylethanolamine"| and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN "cardiolipin"|. These anionic phospholipids are important for membrane biogenesis and function., The plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-340| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "phosphatidylcholine"| using a yeast-like acylation pathway |CITS: 24329598| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7470|). The presence of a phosphatidylserine decarboxylase in this organism (UniProt ID Q4UWE4) suggests that a typically bacterial |FRAME: PWY-5669| pathway is also present., However, analysis of a phosphatidylserine decarboxylase mutant suggested that an additional, phosphatidylserine decarboxylase-independent and |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|-dependent route of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE "phosphatidylethanolamine"| biosynthesis was also present in this organism. They characterized a bifunctional cardiolipin/phosphatidylethanolamine synthase that also synthesizes |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN "cardiolipin"| in a typically eukaryotic manner via this bifunctional enzyme |CITS: [24707916]| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, A bifunctional cardiolipin/phosphatidylethanolamine synthase has been characterized in the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-314565| that provides an additional |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|-dependent, phosphatidylserine decarboxylase-independent, route for |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE "phosphatidylethanolamine"| biosynthesis. In addition, the cardiolipin synthase activity of this enzyme is more typical of those found in eukarytoes, although such a cardiolipin synthase has also been described in actinobacteria |CITS: 19439403| (see |FRAME: AT4G04870-MONOMER|)., Five other putative cardiolipin synthases were also identified in |FRAME: TAX-314565| although their exact physiological role has not been determined. This bifunctional cardiolipin/phosphatidylethanolamine synthase from |FRAME: TAX-314565| was not found in |FRAME: TAX-358| or |FRAME: TAX-562|, suggesting its limited occurrence in bacteria |CITS: 24707916|.

Summary: Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., |FRAME: MANNITOL| is the most abundant polyol in nature, and is found in bacteria, fungi, algae, lichens and vascular plants., All three naturally-occurring hexitols can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., Each of these hexitols enters the cell via a specific phosphotransferase system, so the first intracellular species is the 6-phospho-derivative |CITS: [1100608]| (note that due to symmetry of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|, their phosphorylation at either end produces the same molecule. When these molecules are phosphorylated at the 6 position by the PTS system, the resulting molecules are named |FRAME: MANNITOL-1P| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, respectively, by conventional nomenclature rules)., In all three cases this sugar alcohol phosphate becomes the substrate for a dehydrogenase that oxidizes its 2-alcohol group to a keto group. In the cases of |FRAME: MANNITOL| and |FRAME: SORBITOL|, the resulting keto sugar phosphate is |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, an intermediate of glycolysis, and hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy |CITS: [6384188][2111176]|., In the case of |FRAME: GALACTITOL-1-PHOSPHATE|, however, the product of the dehydrogenation is |FRAME: TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE|, which becomes the substrate of a kinase and subsequently an aldolase (in a pair of reactions that parallel those of glycolysis) before it is converted into intermediates (|FRAME: GAP| and, |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|) of glycolysis |CITS: [8955298]|.

Names: indole-3-acetate inactivation VIII // IAA inactivation VIII // indole-3-acetic acid inactivation VIII
Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1981|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., About This Pathway, Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. IAA is often present in conjugated forms that play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others, serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., IAA-amino acid conjugates have been identified and studied in many species, including |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [15749753]|, cucumber (|FRAME: TAX-3659|) |CITS: [16664134]|, Scots pine (|FRAME:TAX-3349|) |CITS: [11154354]|, and, rice |FRAME: TAX-4530| |CITS: [17628621] [15849417]|, and IAA-O-glucosyl esters have been encountered in multiple plant species, including |FRAME: TAX-3702| and maize (|FRAME:TAX-4577|) |CITS:[15749753][4835696]|. In addition, there is evidence concerning the biosynthesis of another conjugated form of IAA in rice that has a canonical O-linked amino acid adduct, and a less common N-linked glucose attached to the indole portion of IAA |CITS: [17628621]| . , There is evidence for free IAA, |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP|, and |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-GLU| in rice |CITS: [17628621] [15849417]|. The reactions that form these two conjugates have been studied in |FRAME: TAX-3702| (|FRAME: PWY-1782|) and most likely occur in a similar manner in rice. Radiotracer studies indicate that these IAA conjugates can be incorporated into |FRAME: CPD-9568| and |FRAME: CPD-9573| |CITS: [17628621]|. Although UDP-glucose often participates in glucosyltransferase reactions, the identity of the sugar donor in these reaction remains unknown. High levels of free |FRAME: CPD-9567| are detected in rice seeds, but, this compound does not appear to be a precursor for the glucosylated IAA-amino acid conjugates |CITS:[17628621]|. In fact, it may actually be derived from these compounds through the action of an amide hydrolase. Alternatively, this compound may be produced directly by the N-glucosylation of IAA, a reaction that has been proposed to occur in Scots pine seedlings |CITS: [11154354]|., Although these experiements were conducted with only one species, the presence of IAA-N-linked hexoses and/or IAA-N-linked-hexose-amino acid conjugates in other species such as |FRAME: TAX-3702|, |FRAME: TAX-4577|, |FRAME: TAX-34305|, and Scots pine |CITS: [11154354][17628621]| suggests that these forms of auxin might be found throughout the plant kingdom. Neither |FRAME: CPD-9567| nor its amino acid conjugates show auxin activity in root and shoot elongation assays in rice |CITS: [17628621]|, and their biological role in auxin metabolism and auxin signaling needs to be clarified.

About lipoate, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| is a sulfur-containing cofactor found in many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. It is utilized by several enzymes involved in oxidative metabolism, including the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, the |FRAME: PWY-5084| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, the |FRAME: PWY-5046| |CITS: [2188967]|, and the |FRAME: GLYCLEAV-PWY| |CITS: [1655709][8444795]|., Each of these enzyme complexes is composed of multiple copies of three enzymes: a substrate-specific, decarboxylase-dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), specific for each type of complex, and a dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3), a flavoprotein, that is a common component of these multienzyme complexes., E1 catalyzes both the decarboxylation of the α-keto acid and the subsequent reductive, acylation of the lipoyl moiety, which is covalently bound to E2. E2 catalyzes, the acyl transfer step, and E3 catalyzes the reoxidation of the dihydrolipoyl moiety with NAD, as the ultimate electron acceptor |CITS: [2188967]|., The lipoate cofactor is bound to the E2 by an amide linkage between its carboxylate moiety, and a specific lysine residue in the enzyme |CITS: [8444795]|., About This Pathway, The bacterial pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1639| replicates within the cytosol of mammalian cells. The bacterium is auxotrophic for lipoate, and must scavenge it from its host. , The pathway for lipate scavenging by |FRAME: TAX-1639| includes three steps. A |FRAME: MONOMER-17108| catalyzes the cleavage of lipoate from host lipoylated proteins, releasing it as free lipoate |CITS: [21768091]|. A |FRAME: MONOMER-17111| encoded by the |FRAME: G-14912| gene catalyzes the attachment of the lipoate to |FRAME: Gcv-H| (GcvH) |CITS: [17908209]|. The enzyme appears specific for the modification of GcvH only. Finally, a third enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-14913|, releases the lipoyl moiety from the |FRAME: PROTEIN-LIPOYLLYSINE "lipoylated glycine-cleavage complex protein"| and facilitates its attachment to other metabolic enzyme complexes |CITS: [21768091]|.

General Background, Golden rice is a variety of rice (|FRAME: TAX-4530|) that has been engineered to synthesize |FRAME: CPD1F-129|, a precursor of |FRAME: Vitamin-A|, in the edible parts of rice, the endosperm., The native rice plant does produce β-carotene, but production is limited to leaves. It has been estimated that in Southeast Asia a quarter of a million children go blind each year due to vitamin A deficiency |CITS: [2643699]| and that 124 million children worldwide are deficient in vitamin A. Improved nutrition could prevent 1 million to 2 million deaths annually among children |CITS: [2669883]|., About This Pathway, The rice endosperm is capable of synthesizing the early intermediate |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. The conversion of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| to |FRAME: CPD1F-129| can be divided into three parts:, 1. The conversion of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| to |FRAME: CPD-12321|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.32|., 2. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12321| to |FRAME: CPD1F-114|, 3. The cyclization of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to |FRAME: CPD1F-129|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.19|., In carotene-producing plants, the second step (conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12321| to |FRAME: CPD1F-114|) is catalyzed by 4 enzymes - 2 desaturases and two isomerases (see |FRAME: PWY-6475| and |FRAME: PWY-5943|). However, in some bacteria the process is catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.31| (see |FRAME: PWY-5942|)., In order to simplify, the researchers have used the bacterial enzyme, reducing the number of total required foreign genes from six to three |CITS: [10634784]|. In the first version of Golden Rice the first and third parts were catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-17755| and |FRAME: G-17756| enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-39639| (daffodil), while the middle part was catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-11939| encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15564| of the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-553|. However, it was soon found that the rice |FRAME: G-17758| gene is active in the endosome, and thus the |FRAME: G-17756| gene was not required, reducing the number of required foreign genes to two |CITS: [15821145]|., The genes were transformed into the rice nuclear genome and placed under the control of an endosperm-specific promoter, so they are only expressed in the endosperm. The first version, known as SGR1, produced 1.6 μg/g of carotenoids under greenhouse conditions. However, field tests showed Golden Rice grown in the field performed far better, producing 4 to 5 times more β-carotene than when grown under greenhouse conditions., In 2005 a second version, known as Golden Rice 2, has been constructed, substituting the daffodil |FRAME: MONOMER-18247 "phytoene synthase"| with the |FRAME: GBWI-61910-MONOMER "enzyme from maize"|. This improved construct produces 23 times more carotenoids than the first version (up to 37 μg/g), and preferentially accumulates β-carotene (up to 31 μg/g) |CITS: [15793573]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-18453| (N, N'-diacetyl-8-epilegionaminate, 8eLeg5Ac7Ac) is a rarely occurring in nature sialic acid-like sugar that appears in the O-glycans of some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [3104040]|, |FRAME: TAX-59203| |CITS: [1394306 ]|, |FRAME: TAX-29486| |CITS: [7514497]| and |FRAME: ORG-6284| |CITS: [Knirel09]|. In most cases the stereochemistry of this sugar was originally misdiagnosed, and the correct stereochemistry was determined later |CITS: [8901267][8766209][11383892]|., A similar sugar, |FRAME: CPD-18469|, has been found within |FRAME: TAX-562| O antigens only once before, in |FRAME: TAX-2072457| |CITS: [10469128]|., Following the isolation of the sugar from the O-specific polysaccharide of |FRAME: ORG-6284| |CITS: [Knirel09]|, a gene cluster that encodes all of the enzymes necessary for its synthesis was identified in the organism and characterized |CITS: [20331420]|. The cluster, which is typically located between the |FRAME: G7093| and |FRAME: EG10411| genes, is the largest O-antigen cluster sequenced so far, including 18 genes (the shortest cluster, found in strain O155, contains only four genes) |CITS: [25428893]|. Most of the genes were assigned functions based on their similarity to known genes from other organisms and taking into account the |FRAME: ORG-6284| antigen structure., In general, the pathway is similar to the pathway of |FRAME: PWY-6143 "CMP-pseudaminate (Pse5Ac7Ac) biosynthesis"|, which has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-197|, and the pathway of |FRAME: PWY-6749 "CMP-legionaminate (Leg5Ac7Ac) biosynthesis"|, which has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-197|, with certain differences among the pathways:, -C6 dehydration is accompanied by C5 epimerization for synthesis of Pse5Ac7Ac and 8eLeg5Ac7Ac but not Leg5Ac7Ac;, -Removal of UDP is accompanied by C2 epimerization in the pathways of Leg5Ac7Ac and 8eLeg5Ac7Ac but not Pse5Ac7Ac. The step is catalyzed by a single bifunctional enzyme during Leg5Ac7Ac biosynthesis, but by two different enzymes during 8eLeg5Ac7Ac biosynthesis |CITS: [20331420]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: ORG-57078| serogroup is one of the six most common Salmonella serogroups in the United States (B, C1, C2, D, E, and O13). The structure of the O antigen repeat unit of this serotype was reported in 2010 from |FRAME: TAX-436295| |CITS: [20594547]|. The repeat unit is closely related to the |FRAME: CPD-23877|, which differs only in the presence of a GalNAc residue in place of the GlcNAc residue and O-acetylation at the fucosyl residue. In addition, The O13 and O43 antigens differ only in the configuration (α vs. β) and the position (1→2 vs. 1→4) of the polymerization linkage between the O units and the presence of a Gal side chain in the O43 antigen., The O antigen biosynthetic cluster from the O13 strain |FRAME: TAX-436295| was sequenced in 2007 and found to contain 10 ORFs, including five genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-13118| biosynthesis enzymes, three genes encoding glycosyltransferases, and genes encoding an O antigen repeat unit flippase and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [17634307]|. Nine of the genes shared 61% to 93% amino acid identity with the corresponding genes in |FRAME: ORG-6341|, reflecting the similarity between the O antigens of the two organisms.

Summary: General Background, The main CO2 fixation enzyme in plants, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39 "EC 4.1.1.39, ribulose-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase"| (RuBisCO), has both carboxylase (photosynthetic CO2 fixation) and oxygenase (photorespiration) activities. The carboxylase activity is favored at high CO2/O2 ratio, whereas the oxygenase activity predominates at a decreased CO2/O2 ratio., At the time when RuBisCO first evolved, atmospheric CO2 concentration was very high and thus the enzyme's carboxylase activity was favored. However, later in evolution, atmospheric O2 concentration began to rise and RuBisCO's oxygenase activity increased at the expense of the carboxylase activity. In temperate climates and under moderate light levels, when the stomata are fully open, diffusion from the atmosphere is fully sufficient to ensure an ample supply of CO2 and C3 photosynthesis is rather efficient. However, in hot climates and under high light levels, the plants need to close their stomata to avoid water loss, restricting the ability of the CO2 to diffuse. Under these conditions the CO2 levels can go down to the point where photorespiration becomes a serious problem, reducing photosynthesis by more than 40%. The C4 system, which is found only in plants growing in conditions that require closure of the stomata, has evolved to address this problem., C4 plants have evolved to respond to lowered CO2 levels. The C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle starts with carbon fixation in the mesophyll cells by a combination of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.1 "EC 4.2.1.1, carbonic anhydrase"|, which converts the gasous CO2 to soluble |FRAME: HCO3|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31|, which incorporates the latter, forming the C4 acid |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|. Oxaloacetate or a derivative thereof (|FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|) is then transported from the mesophyll cells to bundle sheath cells. Once inside the bundle sheath cells, CO2 is released from the C4 acids, generating a micro-environment with a much higher concentration of CO2, suitable for an efficient carboxylation by RuBisCO., Three variations of the C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle have been described in plants, namely the |FRAME: PWY-241 "NADP-ME"| (NADP-malic enzyme), |FRAME: PWY-7115 "NAD-ME"| (NAD-malic enzyme), or |FRAME: PWY-7117 PEPCK| (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) types. The NADP-ME variant does not involve L-aspartate and utilizes an NADP-dependent malic enzyme to releases CO2 from |FRAME: MAL|. The NAD-ME variant does involve L-aspartate and utilizes an NAD-dependent malic enzyme. The PEPCK variant contains an additional route for CO2 release by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49|, which usually operates to supplement the NADP-ME variant., However, some research suggests that different C4 decarboxylation pathways may cooccur in plants that were previously considered to belong to exclusively one C4 photosynthetic type |CITS:[24609651]|. For instance, |FRAME: TAX-4577| has been shown to use both |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| for the generation of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[Chapman81]|. In addition, it has been demonstrated that maize leaves require the activity of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1| to maintain an efficient flow-rate. Moreover, the |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49 "phosphoenol carboxykinase"| (PEPCK), considered the hallmark of the PEPCK pathway, is also active in maize and shown to support |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE|-driven photosynthesis |CITS:[22186372]|. Similar results have been reported from the NADP-ME type plant |FRAME: TAX-4224|, which also utilizes both |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| equally and demonstrates aspartate aminotransferase activity |CITS:[Meister96]|. In general, current discussion of the C4 photosynthetic pathway types moves in a direction favoring the existence of only two subtypes, i.e. NADP-ME and NAD-ME, both of which may contain a supplementary PEPCK cycle |CITS:[24609651]|., About This Pathway, C4 photosynthesis basically represents a |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| concentrating mechanism (CCM) which independently originated more than 60 times in plants indicating the evolutionary drive to optimize photosynthetic |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation as an tool to keep pace with an ever-changing environment |CITS:[21631531]|.This MetaCyc pathway describes the NADP-ME variant, found in major C4 crops such as maize, sorghum, and sugar cane., Note that the pathway spans two cell types, mesophyll and bundle sheath cells., The roles and sub-cellular locations of carbonic anhydrases (CA) in plants differ and are metabolically integrated in a rather complex manner regardless of the seemingly simple reaction they catalyze, i.e. the reversible hydration of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:HCO3| |CITS:[Badger03] [Moroney01]|. In C3 plants CA's are ambivalent enzymes and contribute to increased |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| concentration in micro-compartments creating a more efficient environment for the carbon fixating role of RuBisCO in the chloroplast, and also have non-photosynthetic functions as in lipid biosynthesis and operating as antioxidant |CITS:[24146374]|. However, in C4 plants β-carbonic anhydrases operating in the cytoplasm of mesophyll cells are considered essential for the operation of the pathway by providing the PEP-carboxylase substrate |FRAME:HCO3| for |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation into |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| |CITS:[16666063]|. Corresponding β-carbonic anhydrases characterized in Zea mays, i.e. CA2 |CITS:[20933433] [Burnell97]| and in Flaveria bidentis |CITS:[17496111]|, i.e. CA3 are part of a small CA family in this plants where only one member is directly involved in the first reaction of C4 photosynthesis |CITS:[23414801] [Burnell90]|. However, it appears that even those β-carbonic anhydrases have only a limited role in C4 photosynthesis under current climate conditions and are more essential when C4 plants are stressed by high temperature and drought |CITS:[24706552]|. , The initial CO2 fixation occurs in the mesophyll cells, producing |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| that is subsequently converted to |FRAME: MAL|. Malate is transported into bundle sheath cells and CO2 is released there by an |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.40 "NADP-dependent malic enzyme"|. Pyruvate reenters the mesophyll cells and replenishes phosphoenolpyruvate. , Experimental evidence indicates that CO2 fixation in cyanobacteria is mediated by the C3 pathway, and although C4 acids are among the initial products of photosynthesis, these organisms do not have the enzymatic capacity for the operation of a C4 pathway |CITS: [Colman89]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Chaxalactins chaxalactins| are a group of macrolactone polyketides produced by |FRAME: TAX-1437453|, an organism that was isolated from a soil sample collected from the Chaxa Lagoon, located in the Salar, de Atacama in northern Chile. Among those are two families of polyketide antibiotics, the chaxalactins |CITS: [21879726]| and the ansamycin-like |FRAME: Chaxamycins chaxamycins| |CITS: [21553813]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8036|). General Background, |FRAME: CREATINE| (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCGREAT-PWY|) is reversibly phosphorylated by creatine kinase to create a cellular pool of |FRAME: CREATINE-P| (phosphocreatine, phosphoryl-creatine). This pool stores high energy phosphate for the replenishment of |FRAME: ATP| during periods of high, or fluctuating energy demand in cells and tissues. Creatine kinase therefore plays an important role in energy homeostasis of cells such as muscle cells, that have intermittent, high energy requirements. Phosphagen kinase systems such as this are found in the tissues of most vertebrates (reviewed in |CITS: [5071177], [10893433]|). A variety of creatine kinase assays exist, due to their use as clinical indicators of myocardial and skeletal muscle disorders and as a marker for myocardial infarction (reviewed in |CITS: [15804623]|)., About This Pathway, In fast-twitch skeletal muscle cells a cytosolic pool of |FRAME: CREATINE-P| is available to immediately regenerate, |FRAME: ATP| that is needed during bursts of activity. However, in tissues and cells such as slow-twitch skeletal muscle, heart and spermatozoa, a continuous delivery of high-energy phosphate to sites of |FRAME: ATP| use is necessary. A buffer model for the former example and a transport (shuttle) model for the latter examples have been proposed for creatine kinase function. However, these models are not static and the creatine kinase system appears to be highly flexible and adaptable to the requirements of a given tissue. Reviewed in |CITS: [10893433]|., Both cytosolic and mitochondrial isoforms of creatine kinase participate in this important cellular high energy phosphate buffering and high energy phosphate transport system. The cytosolic isoforms are dimers and the mitochondrial isoforms are octamers that can dissociate into dimers. Creatine kinase is often localized at cellular sites of |FRAME: ATP| generation where it creates a pool of |FRAME: CREATINE-P|, or at sites of |FRAME: ATP| consumption where it uses |FRAME: CREATINE-P| to restore the balance of |FRAME: ATP| and |FRAME: ADP| (in |CITS: [11154064]|)., |FRAME: CREATINE-P| can undergo spontaneous conversion directly to |FRAME: CREATININE|, or to |FRAME: CPD-10788|, which can then spontaneously convert to |FRAME: CREATININE|. |FRAME: CREATININE| is normally excreted in the urine. Reviewed in |CITS: [10893433]|.

Summary: General Background, Isoflavonoids represent a subclass within the complex structured division of flavanoids , being involved in fundamental processes of plants such as growth, development and defence against pathogens. The , elaboration of the flavonoid skeleton is applied by a variety of enzymes typical for those branching pathways, most , importantly the cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases introducing hydroxyl groups to the phenylchromanone , (flavonoids) and 3-phenylchromane (isoflavonoids) structures |CITS: [Heller94]| |CITS: [WOLLENWEBER94]|. , Soybean (|FRAME:TAX-3847|) produces a variety of isoflavonoid compounds possessing 6,7-dihydroxy substitution , patterns on ring A, e.g. glycitein (|FRAME:CPD-7027|) and afrormosin (|FRAME:CPD-7026|) |CITS: [Dewick94]|. , Moreover, hydroxyl groups at position 6 of the A-ring are found in several flavonoid classes including flavones, flavonols , and anthocyanins. Therefore, it has been assumed that a flavonoid 6-hydroxylase should exist to carry out the respective , regiospecific monooxygenation on ring A |CITS: [11027686]|. , This pathway describes the formation of 6,7,4'-trihydroxyisoflavone in soybean through the catalytic activity of a , flavonoid 6-hydroxylase executing the entry reaction to a pathway which metabolic sequence parallels the formation , of 7,4'-dihydroxyflavone (daidzein) from liquiritigenin (|FRAME:PWY-2002|)., About This Pathway, The formation of 6,7,4'-trihydroxyisoflavone is mostly executed by pathway-specific , cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases and starts with the hydroxylation of the 6-position on ring A of flavanones , such as liquiritigenin, eridictyol and naringenin. The preferred substrates of the identified flavonoid-6-hydroxylase |CITS: [9648734]| , are flavanones but the enzyme also converts to a lesser extent flavones but not isoflavones to its 6-hydroxyl derivatives , |CITS: [11027686]|. , The resulting trihydroxyflavanone is converted to an intermediate 2-hydroxyisoflavanone (2,6,7,4'-tetrahydroxyisoflavanone) , by isoflavone synthase (IFS) catalyzing a unique 2,3 aryl ring migration. It has been found that the recombinant IFS , (CYP93C1v2) efficiently used 6,7,4'-trihydroxyflavanone as substrate |CITS: [11027686]|. The final step involved in , the formation of the isoflavonoid skeleton, i.e. 6,7,4'-trihydroxyisoflavone (this pathway) is the elimination of water from , the hydroxyisoflavanone intermediate which can either be catalyzed by 2-hydroxyisoflavanone dehydratase (HID) , |CITS: [15734910]| or may occur as spontaneous dehydration |CITS: [Hakamatsuka98]|.

Summary: General Background, There are several alternative pathways for the degradation of trehalose. Depending on the organism, trehalose may enter the cell either through a permease, in which case it remains unmodified, or it may be transported by a phosphotransferase system (PTS), resulting in the phoshorylated trehalose-6-phosphate form. Degradation then proceeds by different mechanisms: Unmodified trehalose may be degraded by a hydrolyzing trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|), or it may be split by the action of a trehalose phosphorylase (see |FRAME: PWY-2722| and |FRAME: PWY-2723|). Likewise, trehalose-6-phosphate may be either hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase (see |FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) or it could be attacked by a trehalose-6-phosphate phosphorylase (see |FRAME: PWY-2721|). , About This Pathway, Trehalose phosphorylase (TP), the key enzyme in this pathway, catalyzes the reversible synthesis (and degradation) of trehalose from/to |FRAME: D-glucose-1-phosphates| and |FRAME: D-Glucose|., Two varieties of TP enzymes have been characterized: One variety is specific for the α forms of D-glucose and D-glucose-1-phosphate, while the other is specific for the β forms. Thus, the two forms catalyze different reactions, and were given different EC numbers (see the pathway |FRAME:PWY-2723| for the enzymes that use the α form). The glucose-1-phosphate that is formed by the phosphorylase during trehalose degradation is subsequently converted to glucose-6-phosphate by the appropriate phosphoglucomutase (which is also either α- or β-specific)., β-specific TP enzymes have been found in various organisms, including the green algae |FRAME: TAX-3039| |CITS: [5413942][4623846]|, and various bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS: [12596853][12400680]|, |FRAME: TAX-53367| |CITS: [9614710][7557309]|, |FRAME: TAX-29323|, |FRAME: ORG-6003| |CITS: [Yoshida95]|, |FRAME: TAX-375| and the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1204| |CITS: [10564766]|.

In |FRAME: TAX-5722| |FRAME: 3-P-SERINE| appears to be produced in this route, feeding both |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: CYS| biosynthesis. Some archaea are capable of forming |FRAME: 3-P-SERINE| directly from |FRAME: SER| (see |FRAME: PWY-8009|).

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, Desferrioxamines are a group of nonpeptide hydroxamate siderophores that are produced by many |FRAME: TAX-1883| species. One member of this group, |FRAME: CPD-3764|, is marketed under the name Desferal for the treatment of iron overload in humans, but several other forms are known, including |FRAME: CPD-11957| and |FRAME: CPD-11956|., Studies of the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-3764| in |FRAME: TAX-28893| have shown that the first step is the decarboxylation of |FRAME: LYS| to yield |FRAME: CADAVERINE| |CITS: [Schupp87]|. A DNA fragment that complemented a mutant defective in this step has been isolated, and eventually a partial sequence was obtained, which contained the promoter region and two genes, which were named |FRAME: SCO2782| and |FRAME: SCO2783| |CITS: [2841191][8501033]|., Following the sequencing of the |FRAME: TAX-100226| genome a cluster of four genes has been identified and proposed to be responsible for desferrioxamine biosynthesis |CITS: [12000953]|. Unlike |FRAME: TAX-28893|, this organism produces |FRAME: CPD-11957| as its major siderophore, along witrh smaller amounts of |FRAME: CPD-11956|. The genomic sequence correlated with the partial sequence previously obtained by |CITS: [8501033]|., A plausible pathway for the complete synthesis has been proposed on the basis of comparative sequence analysis and biochemical evidence |CITS: [15600304]|. Based on the proposed pathway, which is described here, |FRAME: SCO2783| encodes a |FRAME: SCO2783-MONOMER| that produces |FRAME: CPD-11953|. |FRAME: SCO2784| encodes a |FRAME: SCO2784-MONOMER| that can use |FRAME: SUC-COA| to acylate |FRAME: CPD-11953|, forming |FRAME: CPD-11955|. It is assumed that the desC products of |FRAME: TAX-28893| and other organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD-3764| have a relaxed substrate specificity that permits them to accept |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as well as |FRAME: SUC-COA| |CITS: [15600304]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6376|)., The last enzyme in the pathway, encoded by |FRAME: SCO2785|, catalyzes the oligomerization of three |FRAME: CPD-11955| molecules to produce |FRAME: CPD-11956|, as well as cyclization to yield the final product, |FRAME: CPD-11957|., Knockout mutants of |FRAME: SCO2782| (|CITS: [17257267]| and |FRAME: SCO2785| |CITS: [15600304]| both resulted in abolishing synthesis. Transcriptional regulation of the desferrioxamine gene cluster is mediated by binding of the Fe(II)-dependent repressor DmdR1 to an iron box in the promoter of the |FRAME: SCO2782| gene |CITS: [17257267]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, The carotenoids of photosynthetic bacteria are membrane lipids that have two main roles during photosynthesis - light harvesting and protection from reactive oxygen species., More specifically, carotenoids absorb light and transmit the absorbed energy via bacteriochlorophyll to the membrane-bound photochemical reaction centers. In addition, they can interact with singlet oxygen that is produced by the interaction of molecular oxygen with bacteriochlorophyll in the triplet state., protecting the organism from the potential photooxidative damage that may result., |FRAME: TAX-1061| is a facultative phototrophic Gram-negative purple non-sulfur bacterium. This organism grows chemoheterotrophically when oxygen is abundant, but upon reduction of the oxygen tension it induces an intra-cytoplasmic photosynthetic membrane system and switches to phototrophic growth., In the absence of oxygen |FRAME: TAX-1061| accumulates the carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-11468| ( and a smaller amount of |FRAME: CPD-11467|) |CITS: [7358679]|, while in the presence of oxygen the keto-derivative |FRAME: CPD-11466| predominates |CITS: [2747617]|.

|FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFA) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes., The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in these compounds. The icosanoids are derived from the 20-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (AA; 20:4n-6), |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA; 20:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-8120| (DGLA; 20:3n-6)., Additional fatty acids are also oxygenated to yield bioactive products, including the the 18-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (LA; 18:2n-6) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (ALA; 18:3n-3) and the 22-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| (DPA; 22:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA; 22:6n-3). Strictly speaking, the derivatives of such acids should be named octadecanoids (for C18 compounds) and docosanoids (for 22 carbon compounds), though these compounds are often included in the icosanoids, making the definition broader than initially intended., In mammals icosanoids and related mediators mediate a wide array of critical biological processes such as ovulation, initiation of labor, bone metabolism, nerve growth and development, wound healing, kidney function, blood-vessel tone, blood coagulation, immune responses, and inflammation. Despite the great importance of these compounds, mammals are not able to form a double bond at either the n-3 or n-6 position of a fatty acyl chain and must rely entirely on dietary intake for PUFAs |CITS: [25486530]|., Three main enzyme families act on PUFAs. The first one is |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.1| (the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes), which possess dual cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activities and catalyze the oxidative cyclization of PUFAs to |FRAME: CPD-24676|, |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|, or |FRAME: CPD-26009| (depending on the starting PUFA), which are subsequently converted to a variety of prostanoids and thromboxanes by cell-specific terminal synthases and isomerases., The second family is the lipoxygenases (LOX), which catalyze the stereoselective insertion of molecular oxygen into PUFA with the formation of hydroperoxy fatty acids that are subsequently reduced to the corresponding hydroxy-fatty acids. The lipoxygenases are divided into three main form depneding on the carbon at which they oxygenate |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|: |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|., The third family is cytochrome P450 monooxygenases that catalyzes the hydroxylation and/or epoxygenation of PUFAs. In addition to producing LOX-like monohydroxy fatty acids, CYP can add a hydroxyl moiety to the ω-carbons, of PUFA to form a unique class of omega-hydroxylated fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-21314|). The epoxides that are formed by these enzymes can be hydrolyzed to the corresponding dihydroxyfatty acids by |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| (sEH).

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-15423| is a prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit that is attached to the 2-amino group of the aminocoumarin core of the two aminocoumarin antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-15417| and |FRAME: CPD-15421|, which are produced by the bacterial species |FRAME: TAX-2893586| and |FRAME: TAX-149682|., These antibiotics bind type II topoisomerases, including DNA gyrase, with an extremely high affinity, with equilibrium dissociation constants in the 10 nM range |CITS: [8231802]|. They compete with ATP for binding to the B subunit of DNA gyrase and thus inhibit the ATP-dependent DNA supercoiling catalysed by gyrase |CITS: [6295263]|., About This Pathway, Following the cloning and sequencing of the |FRAME: CPD-15417| biosynthesis cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2893586|, a route has been proposed for the synthesis of the prenylated 4-hydroxybenzoate moiety |CITS: [10770754]|. , |FRAME: CPD-15423| is formed from |FRAME: PREPHENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-4211| by the action of three enzymes |CITS: [19557032][12777382]|., The first enzyme, prephenate dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-16085| or cloF) catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of |FRAME: PREPHENATE| to |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| |CITS: [12736771]|., The second enzyme, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dimethylallyl transferase (|FRAME: G-16084|| or cloQ) transfers a dimethylallyl moiety from |FRAME: CPD-4211| to |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, generating |FRAME: CPD-15467| |CITS: [Steensky98]|., Finally, the third enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-16086| or cloR, is a bifunctional non-heme iron oxygenase that converts |FRAME: CPD-15467| via |FRAME: CPD-15502| to |FRAME: CPD-15423| in two consecutive oxidative decarboxylation steps |CITS: [12777382]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-57074| is an O serogroup that belongs to enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), which can cause outbreaks of gastroenteritis |CITS: [6189854]|., The structure of the |FRAME: CPD-24124| was reported in 2005 |CITS: [15620681]|. This repeat unit is unusual in having two of the residues connected by a phophodiester linkage. It is identical to the structure of the O-antigen from |FRAME: TAX-623| D12 |CITS: [18422615]|, and is similar to the O antigen repeat unit from |FRAME: ORG-57075|, which contains a similar phophodiester linkage |CITS: [15620681]|., The O antigen biosynthetic cluster of |FRAME: ORG-57074| was sequenced and published in 2008. It is almost identical to the cluster of |FRAME: TAX-623| D12 |CITS: [18422615]|., The cluster contains genes for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|, four glycosyltransferases, an O antigen repeat unit flippase, and an O antigen polymerase., Two of the glycosyltransferases have been characterized (|FRAME: G-81076| and |FRAME: G-81075|) |CITS: [18487334][31974821]|. The |FRAME: G-81077| gene encodes a Stealth protein and is very likely an α-(1,6)-GlcNAc-1-phosphoryltranferase (see |CITS: [16299590]|). The fourth gene, |FRAME: G-81078|, is thus a candidate for encoding the enzyme catalyzing the remaining glycosyltransfer reaction, that of a β-(1→4)-rhamnosyltransferase. The enzyme shares 44% identity with the product of the wegG gene of of |FRAME: TAX-1450173| |CITS: [23193180]|. The O antigen repeat units of these two serotypes share a β-L-Rha-(1→4)-D-GlcpNAc linkage, supporting the annotation of |FRAME: G-81078| as β-(1→4)-rhamnosyltransferase.

Polyunsaturated |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "long chain fatty acids"| (PUFAs) have18 or more carbon atoms containing more than one double bond in its backbone. The PUFAs that have 2 or more cis double bonds separated from each other by a single methylene group are generally either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, and are considered essential fatty acids for mammals., PUFAs accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|. They are also produced by some marine bacteria, but are not commonly found in higher plants. , |FRAME: CPD-10244 Docosahexanoate| (DHA) is a 22-carbon long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid (LCPUFA) with 6 methylene interrupted cis double bonds |CITS: [15292371]|. DHA and other LCPUFAs like |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID arachidonate| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE eicosapentaenoate| are precursors of different classes of eicosanoid effectors involved in the regulation of many important mammalian functions |CITS: [14704315]|. , In algae, fungi and lower plants DHA is synthesized de novo from acetate. Mammals are not able to synthesis DHA de novo, and instead synthesize it from the essential fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (which they obtain in their diet) via alternating steps of microsomal aerobic desaturation and elongation |CITS: [11397798][14704315]| followed by a peroxisomal β-oxidation step |CITS: [10903473]|., Another method of DHA synthesis is described in some marine bacteria and primitive eukaryotes utilizing the polyketide syntase systems |CITS: [12835316]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7585|)., About this Pathway, Since mammals do not have a 4-desaturase, they were thought to be incapable of synthesizing |FRAME: CPD-10244| using the short, 4-desaturase-based pathway utilized by lower eukaryotes (see |FRAME: PWY-7053|). Instead, the main docosahexaenoate biosynthesis pathway in mammals is believed to involve the repeated use of a fatty acid desaturase 2 (FADS2) protein to perform 6-desaturation on C24 fatty acids in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by 1 round of β-oxidation in the peroxisomes (see |FRAME: PWY-7606|). However, it has been reported that the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: HS05918| gene, originally characterized as a 6-desaturase, is also capable to perform 4-desaturation, enabling the much shorter pathwyay shown here |CITS: [26065859]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: TAX-4668| family consists of about 75 genera and 1100 species that are wide-spread in the tropics and warm temperate regions of the world. It includes ornamental plants such as |FRAME: TAX-4697| (daffodils) and |FRAME: TAX-4669| (snowdrops)., Members of this family produce a group of unique alkaloids collectively known as Amaryllidaceae alkaloids. Since the first isolation of |FRAME: CPD-19438|, more than 500 Amaryllidaceae alkaloids have been isolated. |FRAME: CPD-19430 Galanthamine| is the best known member of the family, having been used clinically for treatment of Alzheimer disease symptoms |CITS: [12875613]|, but other members of this family have documented pharmacological activities, including antitumor, antiviral, antibacterial, antifungal, and antimalarial activities, making them promising pharmaceutical agents |CITS: [24182986][He15]|. For example, |FRAME: CPD-19429|, |FRAME: CPD-19439|, and |FRAME: CPD-19438| have cancer fighting potential |CITS: [15270564][19788245][24182986]|., Continued development of Amaryllidaceae alkaloids for clinical and pharmaceutical applications requires the ability to produce them in a cost effective manner. However, the information about the genes and proteins involved in their biosynthesis is still rather limited., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of all Amaryllidacea alkaloids passes through the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-19420|, which is produced by the condensation of |FRAME: TYRAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-7616| (producing |FRAME: CPD-19419|), followed by imine reduction. |FRAME: CPD-7616 3,4-Dihydroxybenzaldehyde| is hypothesized to originate from a branch of the |FRAME: PWY1F-467 "phenylpropanoid pathway"|, as shown here, while |FRAME: TYRAMINE| is produced directly from |FRAME: TYR|., |FRAME: TYRAMINE Tyramine| and |FRAME: CPD-7616| may be condensed by the activity of an amine-aldehyde condensing enzyme such as |FRAME: EC-3.5.99.13|. However, it is also possible that the condensation occurs nonenzymatically, or in the active site of the enzyme that reduces |FRAME: CPD-19419| to |FRAME: CPD-19420|, which may be |FRAME: CPLX-9160|. It has been shown that both |FRAME: TYRAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-7616| can bind to the active site of that enzyme |CITS: [27252378]|., The last common step for all Amaryllidacea alkaloids is the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-19420| to |FRAME: CPD-19421|, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.336| |CITS: [25061748]|., Next, the two aromatic rings of |FRAME: CPD-19421| are condensed with each other in one of three ways. A para-para' condensation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.50|, produces the two enantiomers of |FRAME: CPD-19426|. A para-ortho' condensation (which was shown to be a minor activity of |FRAME: MONOMER-20066|) leads to formation of |FRAME: CPD-19432|, and an ortho-para' condensation (catalyzed by an unknown enzyme) forms |FRAME: CPD-19436| |CITS: [26941773]|., A number of tailoring enzymes, consisting mostly of oxidoreductases and methyltransferases (most of which are still unknown) convert these three intermediates into the hundreds of Amaryllidacea alkaloids. A pathway leading from |FRAME: CPD-19432| to |FRAME: CPD-19430| has been proposed based on isotope labeling experiments |CITS: [Eichhorn98]|. A pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-19429| has also been proposed |CITS: [Feinstein76][25061748]|., The last reaction in several of the branches is the formation of an oxide bridge between methoxy and hydroxy groups. While the enzymes that catalyze this activity have not been described yet, they are believed to be members of the cytochrome P-450 family, based on similar enzymes that have been characterized (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.64|, |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.65|, and |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.68|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-17158 Arginomycin| is a peptidyl nucleoside antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1295550| that shows bioactivity against Gram-positive bacteria and fungi |CITS: [3610832]|. The skeleton of arginomycin is highly similar to that of the rice blast antibiotic |FRAME: BLASTICIDIN-S|, which is produced by |FRAME: TAX-68214|. The only difference is in the L-arginine-derived guanidino side chain, which in |FRAME: CPD-17158| is |FRAME: CPD-12429|., |FRAME: CPD-12429|, a rare amino acid, was first described as a constituent of the peptide |FRAME: CPD-17167| from |FRAME: TAX-1522108|, and later shown to be produced by |FRAME: TAX-321| as an antibiotic against the related species |FRAME: TAX-318|, a plant pathogen that is responsible for bacterial blight of soybean |CITS: [18655083]|., The arginomycin biosynthetic gene cluster was identified by hybridization of a 550-bp PCR product produced by degenerate PCR primers that were designed based on sequence alignments of the |FRAME: G-34634| gene of |FRAME: TAX-68214| and some of its homologs, retrieved from the databases. The PCR product was used to screen a genomic library of |FRAME: TAX-1295550| and isolate a fosmid that contained the full |FRAME: CPD-17158| biosynthetic cluster |CITS: [24907335]|., A 29-kb DNA fragment was excised from the fosmid and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1902|. Fermentation broth of the resultant recombinant strain produced arginomycin (as verified by liquid chromatography and concordant tandem mass spectroscopy), indicating that the cluster contains all of the required genes for arginomycin biosynthesis |CITS: [24907335]|. Comparison of the cluster to that responsible for |FRAME: PWY-7570| has identifed two arginomycin-specific genes, namely, argM and argN, which are involved in the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12429|., The rest of the pathway steps and enzymes have not been studied, and are assumed to be identical to those of |FRAME: PWY-7570|. Since there are still some uncertainties in that pathway, the same uncertainties are present in this pathway. A further complication is that the oxidoreductase encoded by the |FRAME: G-34635| gene in |FRAME: TAX-68214| has no homolog in |FRAME: TAX-1295550|, leaving the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-17160| to |FRAME: CPD-17161| with no candidate enzyme |CITS: [24907335]|.
