Summary: Chlorobenzenes are used in the production of pesticides, dyes, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, rubbers, plastics,, and electric goods |CITS: [11472925]|. Their occurrence in the environment is widespread and they are, found in the atmosphere |CITS: [10864157]|, water |CITS: [3314709][16157172]|, soil |CITS: [17988797][2695324]|,, sediments |CITS: [15694470]|, vegetables |CITS:[16002141]|, and animals |CITS: [15325147]|., Chlorobenzenes are of great concern because of their toxicity, persistence and accumulation in the food chain,, and many of them have been declared, priority pollutants, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)., Two important chlrobenzene compounds, |FRAME: 124-TCB| and |FRAME: CPD-10620|, are degraded via, |FRAME: CPD-10622|. This catechol is degraded to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| in a modified ortho cleavage, pathway. The first three enzymes of the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-14402|, |FRAME: CPLX-7703|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14406|, have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-65067| and characterized, although, the fourth enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7710|, has not., It should be noted that complete degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10620| and |FRAME: 124-TCB| requires that, |FRAME: CPLX-7710| remove two chlorine atoms from |FRAME: CPD-10637|. Studies with purified |FRAME: CPLX-7708|, from several organisms showed that while these enzymes can remove both chlorine atoms, the chlorine at the 2 position is removed much more efficiently than the chlorine at the 5 position |CITS: [8407778][8550433]|.

General Background, Cyanobacterial lipids consist of glycerolipids with a C18 fatty acid esterified at position sn-1 and a C16 fatty acid esterified at position sn-2 |CITS: [Sato82]|., The cyanobacteria have been classified into four groups according to the distribution of the fatty acids in their glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|. , Strains in Group 1 are characterized by the presence of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (|FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9245|) at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively., Strains in Group 2 contain the tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| at the sn-1 position and the mono-unsaturated C16 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-9245| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 3 have a different tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid (|FRAME: CPD-8117|) at the sn-1 position and the saturated C16 acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 4 are similar to strains in Group 3 except that they have, in addition, the tri-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| and the tetra-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: CPD-12653| at the sn-1 position., |FRAME: CPD-12653 Stearidonate| (SDA) is an ω-3 fatty acid, sometimes called moroctic acid., It is also found in the seed oils of several plants, including hemp, blackcurrant, corn gromwel and echium, where it is produced from |FRAME: CPD-8117| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.25|., In mammals it is biosynthesized (in its |FRAME: CPD-14392| form) from |FRAME: LINOLENOYL-COA| by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.3|., About This Pathway, In cyanobacteria |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is formed bound to an acyl-carrier protein, part of the fatty acid synthase complex. Stearate is transfered to the sn-1 position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.15| |CITS: [16039611]|., As described above, glycerolipids from all cyanobacteria contain unsturated C18 fatty acids in the sn-1 position, but differ in the degree and nature of unsaturation. The desaturation occurs only after |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| has been incorporated into the glycerol backbone, and is catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes known as acyl-lipid desaturases., The first desaturation occurs at position 9, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS15040| encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS15040-MONOMER| |CITS: [7929259]|. This is followed by desaturation at position 12, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10130|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS10130-MONOMER| |CITS: [2118597]|. The third desaturation occurs at position 6, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-10796|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14125| |CITS: [16328883]|. Lastly, |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.36|, encoded by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10825| gene, introduces a fourth desaturation at carbon 15, generating |FRAME: CPD-12653|.

Summary: |FRAME: TRICHLOROPHENOL| (2,4,6-TCP) has been used as a wood preservative for decades around the world, resulting in severe groundwater contamination around sawmills. It is considered a priority environmental pollutant worldwide |CITS: [Sittig81]|. Several aerobic bacteria have been reported to degrade this pollutant, and in several cases to utilize it as the sole carbon source |CITS:[1892382][1599247][7737484][8573500]|., A catabolic pathway for |FRAME: TRICHLOROPHENOL| degradation has been proposed., The pathway is initiated by the conversion of |FRAME: TRICHLOROPHENOL| to |FRAME: 26-DICHLORO-P-HYDROQUINONE| and then to |FRAME: 6-CHQ|. Both steps are catalyzed by the bifunctional enzyme |FRAME: REUT_A1585-MONOMER| (|FRAME: REUT_A1585|) in combination with the |FRAME: MONOMER-20857| (|FRAME: G-80420|)., |FRAME: 6-CHQ| is transformed to |FRAME: 2-CHLOROMALEYLACETATE| by |FRAME: REUT_A1587-MONOMER|, and, |FRAME: 2-CHLOROMALEYLACETATE| is converted via |FRAME: CPD-294| to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, by a bifunctional |FRAME: REUT_A1589-MONOMER| |CITS:[7798136][8981999][10986670][12057943]|., The |FRAME: REUT_A1585|, |FRAME: G-80420|, and |FRAME: REUT_A1587| genes encoding the first three enzymes of the pathway have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-264198| in a a single operon |CITS: [12057943]|., While the last two reactions of the pathway are known to be catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-264198| by the, |FRAME: CPLX-7709| enzyme that is encoded by |FRAME: G-11000|, a gene carried on the pJP4 catabolic plasmid,, the full pathway was also demonstrated in |FRAME: ORG-6075|, a strain that has been cured from the plasmid,, demonstrating that the organism must possess a similar enzyme encoded by a chromosomal gene, |CITS:[7737484][10986670]|. Such a gene, named |FRAME: REUT_A1589|, has indeed been found downstream of the, other tcp genes |CITS: [14660355]|. Two additional genes in the operon, named tcpX and tcpY,, encode unknown functions.

Summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., The best characterized wall teichoic acids are those from |FRAME: TAX-224308| and |FRAME: TAX-655816|, in which the polymeric units are |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY "glycerol phosphate"| and |FRAME: PWY-7815 "ribitol phosphate"|, respectively |CITS: [13684313]|. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 1-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. The anomeric phosphate of the linkage unit is covalently attached to peptidoglycan (PG) via a phosphodiester bond to the C6 hydroxyl of N-acetylmuramate., It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: PWY-7819 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]|. , Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, The main form of wall teichoic acid in |FRAME: TAX-224308 "Bacillus subtilis 168"| (also known as the major teichoic acid of this strain) is a poly-glycerol phosphate polymer. This polymer is composed of about 40 repeating units, and is linked to the peptidoglycan moiety by a linkage unit consisting of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate-N-acetylmannosamine and one to three glycerol phosphate residues |CITS: [2692601]| (the convention used to be that three glycerol phosphate units are present |CITS: [416968]|, but more recent research indicates that it may be only a single unit |CITS: [11882717]|.), , The biosynthetic process can be divided into the following main steps: first, the linkage unit is synthesized, attached to a lipid carrier. Next, the polymeric chain is added, one unit at a time, and is glucosylated. The compound is then transported through the membrane to the outer cell wall, where the glycerol phosphate units are decorated with |FRAME: D-ALANINE|. Finally, the mature molecule is transferred from its lipid carrier to peptidoglycan. A more detailed description follows:, The first step is the attachment of an N-acetyl-glocasamine molecule to the lipid carrier |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P|, by the action of the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35530-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35530|, gene |CITS: [12101296]|. The N-acetyl-glucosamine has to be activated, in the form of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (for more information on the acivation of this donor molecule see the pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|)., Next, an activated |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| unit is added by the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35750-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35750| gene, to generate an N-acetyl-mannosaminyl-β-(1->4)-N-acetyl-glucosamine disaccharide, attached to the lipid., UDP-N-acetyl-mannosamine is synthesized from UDP-N-acetyl-glocasamine by |FRAME: BSU35660-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35660| gene |CITS: [1906927][12107153]|. The last step in the synthesis of the linkage unit is the addition of one glycerol phosphate unit, which is performed by a dedicated |FRAME: BSU35760-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35760|. The glycerol-phosphate unit has to be activated as well, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-606|, which is generated from glycerol-3-phosphate by |FRAME: CPLX-5322|, the product of the |FRAME: BSU35740| gene., Once the linkage unit is ready, |FRAME: BSU35720-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35720|, adds additional glycerol phosphate units successively, until the chain has achieved its final length. A |FRAME: BSU35730-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35730|, adds glucose molecules to the chain, usually attached to the C-2 hydroxyl groups of the glycerol. The glucosylated polymer is then exported (flipped) to the external side of the cytoplasmic membrane by the teichoic acid ABC transporter, which is encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35710| and |FRAME: BSU35700| genes). D-alanine is then added to some of the glycerol units by a machinery encoded by the dlt operon. Finally, the complete teichoic acid is hooked through its linkage unit on the C-6 of a MurNAc residue of a growing peptidoglycan chain in a transfer reaction catalyzed by any of three members of the LCP (LytR-CpsA-Psr) protein family (|FRAME: BSU35840|, |FRAME: BSU35650|, and |FRAME: BSU35520|), releasing the undecaprenyl anchor |CITS:[21964069]|., Most of the enzymes involved in teichoic acid biosynthesis are encoded by the tag genes which are clustered on a 50 kb region of the chromosome |CITS: [1906926]|. The absence of teichoic acid is not lethal for |FRAME: TAX-224308|, and mutations in the |FRAME: BSU35750| or |FRAME: BSU35530| genes, which encode early enzymes in the pathway, result in a morphological change of the cell from rod shape to a sphere shape. However, mutations in late enzymes in the pathway are lethal, due to the accumulation of toxic intermediates.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-470| is a pathogen implicated in a significant number of nosocomial infections in immunocompromized patients. Although it is most often linked with pneumonia and bacteremia, it is also associated with other infections such as necrotizing fasciitis and urinary tract and wound infections., Like other pathogens, |FRAME: TAX-470| depends on siderophores for its supply of iron. The best characterized siderophore produced by the organism is |FRAME: CPD-21002|, which is composed of equimolar quantities of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, |FRAME: THR| and |FRAME: CPD-21001| |CITS: [7802543]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7984|)., However, some strains of |FRAME: TAX-470|, such as |FRAME: TAX-509173|, possess a natural mutation in their |FRAME: EG10259| ortholog and cannot synthesize |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, a precursor required for the production of |FRAME: CPD-21002| |CITS: [22570720]|. Such strains have been shown to utilize a different siderophore, and a gene cluster identified in the genome of some of these strains appeared to encode the biosynthesis of a novel hydroxamate siderophore |CITS: [21144895][21342532]|., A later study has identified two hydroxamate siderophores produced by |FRAME: TAX-509173|, which were named |FRAME: CPD-21009| and |FRAME: CPD-21010|. In addition, the study has predicted the biosynthetic pathway leading to their production, and proposed the indentities of the genes and enzymes that are involved |CITS: [26235845]|. As of 2018, the enzyme activities have not been verified biochemically.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|), and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, There are several pathways for the removal of methylglyoxal. In this pathway, methylglyoxal is reduced to acetol by the action of various enymes possessing |FRAME: G7558-MONOMER| activity. , Most of the enzymes that have been characterized with this activity belong to the family of NADPH-dependent aldo-keto reductases (AKRs). For example, the human aldose reductase (EC 1.1.1.21) and aldehyde reductase (EC 1.1.1.2) are both capable of reducing methylglyoxal to acetol |CITS: [1537826]|. Other mammalian AKRs that were shown to catalyze this reaction include AKR1, AKR1A, AKR1B1, AKR7, AKR7A2 and AKR7A5 |CITS: [16919][10510318][12123834][12604212]|., Several |FRAME: TAX-83333| enzymes homologous to the mammalian AKRs have also been shown to catalyze the same reaction |CITS: [9095467]|. Overexpression of the aldo-keto reductase AKR14A1, encoded by the |FRAME:G7558| gene, leads to increased resistance to methylglyoxal |CITS: [12583903]|. In addition, three other genes (|FRAME:G6967|, |FRAME:G7565|, and |FRAME:EG11648|) were shown to encode proteins with similar activities |CITS:[16077126]|., All four proteins were purified, and shown to catalyze the reaction in vitro, in the presence of NADPH. A similar enzyme has been identified in cyanobacteria |CITS: [16804176]|., A variation has been found in the Saccharomycete fungus |FRAME: TAX-1004253|, in which an NADH-dependent methylglyoxal reductase has been documented |CITS: [Inoue92]|., Prolonged incubations of |FRAME:TAX-562| cell-free extracts with methylglyoxal resulted in conversion of acetol to |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| |CITS: [16077126]|. The enzyme proposed to catalyze this reaction is |FRAME:GLYCDEH-CPLX| |CITS: [6183251][3920199]|. A similar conversion has been observed in other microorganisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1517|, |CITS: [Cameron86]|. In bacteria |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| is a dead-end metabolite and exits the cell rapidly |CITS: [2644239]|., The same reaction has also been observed in mammalian systems, where it is catalyzed by |FRAME: HS01502-MONOMER| |CITS: [1537826]|. In mammals |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| is metabolized in the liver to L-lactate |CITS: [1537826]|.

General Background, |FRAME: D-galactofuranose| is the five-carbon ring form of |FRAME: D-galactopyranose|. In solution both forms exist in equilibrium with |FRAME: D-galactopyranose| formation favored. Although |FRAME: D-galactopyranose| is ubiquitous in cellular organisms, |FRAME: D-galactofuranose| is found only in some non-mammalian eukaryotes and in some bacteria including mycobacteria and Escherichia coli (as indicated in the pathway links and E. coli enzyme |FRAME: EG11983-MONOMER|)., |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTO-14-FURANOSE| is a nucleotide-activated form of |FRAME: D-galactofuranose| that is used by some organisms in the biosynthesis of polysaccharides and glycoconjugates. Although |FRAME: D-galactofuranose| residues are not found in mammals, higher plants and yeasts, they are found in the glycans of some bacteria and lower eukaryotes including trypanosomatids, nematodes, the free-living alga |FRAME: TAX-3055| and filamentous fungi. These groups include known pathogens. |FRAME: D-galactofuranose| residues are antigenic in humans and are therefore of interest as therapeutic targets (|CITS: [24118544]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21940757]|)., About This Pathway, In filamentous fungi |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTO-14-FURANOSE| is biosynthesized in the cytosol starting with |FRAME: CPD-12575| which is derived from |FRAME: GLC-6-P| as indicated in the pathway link. Following the epimerization of |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: CPD-14553|, |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.9| converts |FRAME: CPD-14553| to its five-carbon ring form |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTO-14-FURANOSE|. The substrate of the mutase, |FRAME: CPD-14553|, may also be formed by the Leloir pathway enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.12|. In protozoan parasites such as |FRAME: TAX-5664| which appear to lack an ortholog encoding the Leloir pathway enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-14553| can be formed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.64| |CITS: [20335578][19906649][21073876]|. The pathway product |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTO-14-FURANOSE| is then transported from the cytosol to the Golgi lumen for glycoconjugate biosynthesis (reviewed in |CITS: [21940757]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6317|). , In filamentous fungi galactomannan metabolism has been studied in both the non-pathogenic model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425| and in the opportunistic pathogen |FRAME: TAX-746128|, and relevant orthologs have been identified in these organisms. In |FRAME: TAX-162425| cytosolic UDP-glucose 4-epimerase (synonym UDP-galactose 4-epimerase) is encoded by ugeA |CITS: [20211750]|. In |FRAME: TAX-746128| uge5 encodes the dominant cytosolic UDP-glucose 4-epimerase that is essential for growth on |FRAME: D-Galactose| and the synthesis of |FRAME: D-galactofuranose|. In |FRAME: TAX-746128| a second gene uge3 with no identified ortholog in |FRAME: TAX-162425| has also been characterized. Both Uge5 and Uge3 are required for galactosaminogalactan synthesis in |FRAME: TAX-746128| |CITS: [24257745]|. In |FRAME: TAX-162425| cytosolic UDP-galactose mutase is encoded by ugmA, and in |FRAME: TAX-746128| by ugm1 (glfA) |CITS: [24257745]|. , |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTO-14-FURANOSE| is then transported from the cytosol to the Golgi lumen for galactomannoprotein biosynthesis (not shown). In |FRAME: TAX-162425| the UDP-galactofuranose transporter is encoded by ugtA |CITS: [21693196]|, and in |FRAME: TAX-746128| by ugt1 (glfB) (|CITS: [24257745]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21940757]|). In both organisms a novel, |FRAME: G-55162|-encoded, Golgi-localized, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.398|, has been characterized that is involved in synthesis of the galactofurnaose antigen of O-linked glycans. The O-glycans are then transported in vesicles to the hyphal cell surface |CITS: [24118544]|.

Names: pyruvate to cytochrome bd oxidase electron transfer // pyruvate oxidation pathway // pyruvic acid to cytochrome bd oxidase electron transfer
Summary: This pathway is one of three by which pyruvate, largely derived from glycolysis, is cleaved. Under conditions of aerobic growth, most pyruvate is cleaved by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex [see Pathway: |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|] to CO2 and acetyl-CoA. Anaerobically it is cleaved via pyruvate formate lyase (see Pathway: |FRAME: FERMENTATION-PWY|). The physiological role of this third (PoxB) route, which yields acetate and CO2, is mysterious because it yields acetate rather than acetyl-CoA and is, therefore, energetically wasteful. However, the pathway does play some useful metabolic role because mutant strains lacking PoxB activity grow more slowly and yield a lesser crop of cells |CITS: [11390679]|. PoxB expression, under the control of RpoS, is increased as cultures enter stationary phase. Greater quantities of acetate accumulate and the ace (acetate conversion to acetyl-CoA) pathway is induced. Perhaps this pathway functions as a "safety valve" to maintain acetyl-CoA at optimum intracellular levels., A respiratory chain consisting of pyruvate oxidase, ubiquinone-8 and cytochrome bd complex can be reconstituted in proteoliposomes and generates transmembrane potential |CITS: [6367818]|. The H+/e- ratio for pyruvate oxidase is not known; cytochrome bd terminal oxidase tranlocates 1 H+/e- by means of an oriented redox loop (see review by |CITS: [9230919]|.

Summary: A new antitumor antibiotic, |FRAME: CPD-10115| (TP), was isolated from |FRAME: ORG-6042|, a soil bacterium. The antibiotic inhibited the growth of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and prolonged the survival period of mice bearing leukemia L-1210, P388 and Ehrlich ascites carcinoma |CITS: [3841535]|., The gene cluster that contains the mevalonate pathway genes was isolated from this organism, and sequence analysis in the upstream region of the cluster revealed several new open reading frames (ORFs) that were suggested to encode TP biosynthetic genes |CITS: [11567009]|. Two of these reading frames, ORF11 and ORF12, encoded a protein showing similarities to eukaryotic diterpene cyclases and a eubacterial pentalenene synthase, respectively. Inactivation of these genes resulted in no production of TP, confirming their role in its biosynthesis., When the genes were expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1916| together with the GGDP synthase gene, the transformant started to produce a new compound, identified as |FRAME: CPD-10114|, that shares much of the skeleton structure of TP. When the two proteins were purified from an overexpressing strain of |FRAME:TAX-562|, they converted GGDP into terpentetriene in vitro |CITS: [11567009]|., Additional characterization of these gene products found that the ORF11 (renamed |FRAME: G-10680|) product converted GGDP into |FRAME: CPD-10113|, while the ORF12 (renamed |FRAME: G-10681|) product completed the transformation of |FRAME: CPD-10113| to |FRAME: CPD-10114|. The enzymes were named accordingly |FRAME: MONOMER-13987| and |FRAME: CPLX-7609|, respectively |CITS: [12138123]|., There is no information regarding the conversion from |FRAME: CPD-10114| to |FRAME: CPD-10115|.

Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, This pathway of guanosine nucleotides degradation begins with the conversion of GMP to |FRAME: GUANOSINE|, which is then converted to the free base |FRAME: GUANINE| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6181| (EC 2.4.2.1). |FRAME: GUANINE "Guanine"| is converted to |FRAME:URATE| via |FRAME: XANTHINE| by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-11785| and |FRAME: XANTHINE-OXIDASE| |CITS: [14726515]|., This pathway is very similar to a pathway that occurs in plants and fungi (|FRAME: PWY-6606|). However, in this pathway |FRAME: GUANOSINE| is converted to |FRAME: GUANINE| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6181| (EC 2.4.2.1) while in plants this conversion is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-15864| (EC 3.5.4.15) |CITS: [14725335]|.

General Background, Lichens are symbioses of photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria and heterotrophic fungi, joined to form a new biological entity different from its individual components. Many lichens produce unique phenolic substances known as |FRAME: Depsides depsides| and |FRAME: Depsidones depsidones|, some of which not produced by other fungi and plants. While the roles of these ompounds are not well understood, it has been proposed that they provide allelopathic defense and light screening |CITS: [10643590]|. , Hundreds of depsides and depsidones have been characterized |CITS: [Huneck96]|, and their core structure is remarkably conserved. , |FRAME: Depsides Depsides| consist of two or occasionally three aromatic rings (usually |FRAME: CPD-47| or its derivatives) joined by ester linkages. |FRAME: Depsidones Depsidones| are similar, but also have an ether linkage between the rings. It is generally accepted that depsidones come from depsides |CITS: [14077039]|. Lichen depsides and depsidones have been grouped in a β-orcinol or orcinol series, depending on the presence of a methyl group on the C3 carbon of their rings. They accumulate as semi-crystalline accretions within and above the extracellular matrix coating the lichen hyphae |CITS: [Honegger09]|., Many of these compounds show biological activities with potential pharmacological applications, mainly as antiviral agents or for dermatological treatments., The |FRAME: CPD-47|-based rings that form the depsides are generated by non-reducing plyketide synthases (NR-PKSs) |CITS: [14676319]|. The presence of one or more methyltranferase domains within the PKS determines whether the product will be |FRAME: CPD-47|, |FRAME: CPD-25030|, or |FRAME: CPD-17316|. The NR-PKS not only synthesizes the ring components, but also forms the ester bond between them |CITS: [21289108][34430202]|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-25034 "Grayanic acid"| is a depsidone produced by certain lichens. It was isolated in mount Fuji, Japan, in 1939, from the lichen |FRAME: TAX-27339|, in which it is the only major secondary metabolite known. The chemical structure was elucidated only in 1963 |CITS: [14075265]|., The |FRAME: G-107586| gene, encoding the NR-PKS that participates in the pathway, were identified using degenerate PCR primers based on the |FRAME: G-107590| gene of |FRAME: TAX-162425|, which encodes an NR-PKS that produces |FRAME: CPD-47|. The gene is located in a cluster with genes encoding a cytochrome P450 and a methyltranferase, which are the expected enzymes necessary to complete the pathway. This was the first putative biosynthetic gene cluster for a lichen depside and depsidone that has been proposed. Expression of |FRAME: G-107586| was shown to be correlated with |FRAME: CPD-25034| production. Although the evidence is indirect, it supports the proposed pathway |CITS: [21289108]|., According to the proposed pathway, PKS16 accepts two different starter units of very different lengths (C2 and C8), synthesizes two phenolic ring structures in parallel, and then joins the two rings via an ester linkage to form the depside induction |CITS: [21289108]|. The hypothesis that this type of PKSs catalyze both the synthesis of the rings and their condensation into a depside was proven in 2021 with the characterization of the |FRAME: G-107589| gene of |FRAME: TAX-136282|, which forms the depside |FRAME: ORSELDEP-CPD| |CITS: [34430202]|.

|FRAME: CPD-20726 Crotonosine| is a dienone alkaloid isolated from the plant |FRAME: TAX-912362| (Spanish Rosemary) by Haynes and his collaborators as a part of a study of the medicinal properties of plants used in Jamaican folk medicine |CITS: [Haynes63][Haynes63a]|. , Feeding experiments with |FRAME: R-COCLAURINE| and |FRAME: S-COCLAURINE|, labelled with tritium, showed that only the former is an efficient precursor of crotonosine., The oxidation of |FRAME: R-COCLAURINE| produces a dienone intermediate. The next transformation, the "flipping" of the hydroxyl and methoxyl groups, was studied using labelled compounds and appears to proceed by demethylation, followed by remethylation at a different position |CITS: [6068302]|., The pathway was deduced from the incorporation of radiactive-labelled compounds, and no information exists about the enzymes involved.

Summary: General Background, Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum)., The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids., Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|)., Following a meal, the bile acids are secreted into the small intestine, where they play an important role in digestion by acting as detergents. The majority (~97%) of the bile acids are reabsorbed in the ileum and returned to the liver. The rest enter the large intestine, where they are modified by bacteria into secondary bile acids. The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24-amide hydrolysis (releasing the glycine and taurine molecules) and 7α-dehydroxylation, forming |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| |CITS: [7276750]|., The bacterially-produced secondary bile acids affect host physiology in multiple ways. Some of them are ligands for the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), the liver X receptor (LXR), the G proteincoupled receptor TGR5, and the vitamin D receptor, and have been shown to trigger signaling cascades |CITS: [12016314][17823458][18670431]|. |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE Deoxycholate| production has been shown to have a positive affect by limiting the outgrowth of the enteric pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1496| |CITS: [25337874]|, while on the other hand |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| have been implicated as causative agents in colon carcinogenesis |CITS: [4427390][1255778]|., About This Pathway, The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24 amide hydrolysis and 7-dehydroxylation. , C24 amide hydrolysis is catalyzed by bile acid hydrolases that remove the glycine and taurine conjugants. The enzymes are widespread among Gram-positive intestinal bacteria and have been identified from commensal gut microbiota, pathogens, and free-living bacteria, as well as some archaeal species |CITS: [18757757]|. Most of them are detected in several genera of gastrointestinal autochthonous micro-organisms in animals, including |FRAME: TAX-1678| |CITS: [14762068]|, |FRAME: TAX-1578| |CITS: [18539794][22416715]|, |FRAME: TAX-1350| |CITS: [15633685]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1301| |CITS: [15613825]|., Certain pathogens like |FRAME: TAX-235| |CITS: [17088355]|, |FRAME: TAX-1639| |CITS: [12180927]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1502| |CITS: [7618863]| have also been reported to encode bile acid hydrolases. |FRAME: TAX-235| and opportunistic pathogens from the |FRAME: TAX-338| |CITS: [12039776][16307764]| and |FRAME: TAX-816| |CITS: [10993][2628421]| genera are the only Gram-negative bacteria reported to exhibit the activity., Many bile acid hydrolases have been studied since the first one was purified back in 1967 |CITS: [6016335]|. Enzymes from different sources differ in their size, optimal pHs and temperatures, molecular weights, and substrate preferences. Some prefer glyco-conjugated bile acids (|FRAME: EC-3.5.1.24|), some prefer tauro-conjugated bile acids (|FRAME: EC-3.5.1.74|), and some are similarly active with both conjugants., For a review of bile acid hydrolases, see |CITS: [30098054]|.

General Background, |FRAME: D-APIOSE| is a unique branched-chain pentose found principally in plants. It is a key component of structurally complex cell wall polysaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| (RG-II) in the cell walls of higher plants and in apigalacturonan in the cell walls of aquatic monocots, and is a building block of a large number of naturally occurring secondary metabolites., The name "apiose" is derived from the flavonoid glycoside |FRAME: 7-O-BETA-D-APIOFURANOSYL-12-BETA-D-GLU apiin|, from which it was first obtained |CITS: [Vongerichten01]|. Apiin itself is named after parsley (|FRAME: TAX-4043|), which at the time was known as Apium petroselinum |CITS: [26848180]|., About This Pathway, The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway were found by first identifying genes encoding D-apiose-specific substrate binding proteins (SBPs), since SBPs, which are components of certain types of transporters, are often clustered with catabolic genes that metabolize the compound the SBPs bind to., The pathway shown here was characterized using enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-311403| and |FRAME: TAX-396598|, and was predicted to be present in 204 bacterial species |CITS: [29867142]|. The pathway's product, |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, is an intermediate in the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|.

Summary: tRNAs are the molecular adapters that allow the synthesis of proteins based on mRNAs transcribed from protein-coding genes. The active form of tRNA is generated by a combination of nuclease-based processing, the modification of select nucleosides, and finally charging via the |FRAME: TRNA-CHARGING-PWY|., tRNA processing is a multi-step pathway carried out by a mix of endonucleases and exonucleases. Processing begins with the endonucleolytic cleavage of individual tRNA precursors from RNAs containing multiple tRNAs, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-3.1.26.12|. This initial cleavage can generate precursor molecules with a long 3' trailing end or with a short 3' extension. Precursors with a long trailer require additional exonucleolytic processing by |FRAME: EC-3.1.13.1| before the other nucleases in the pathway can act., Following this initial processing step, a suite of ribonucleases (|FRAME: EC-3.1.13.5|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.56|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.26.5|) cut down the 5' and 3' ends to yield the final, processed tRNA., Although this processing pathway can function with as a few as one of its constituent exonucleases, the final tRNA product may be "imperfect," with a 3' end that may be longer or shorter than normal.

The terpenoid |FRAME: Fenchone| is a major component of the volatile oil extracted from several plants including |FRAME: TAX-2849586| (fennel) |CITS: [7436420]| and lavender |CITS: [24943828]|. It has a structure and an odor similar to those of camphor, and is used as in food flavoring as well as in perfumery. , Fenchone's chemical structure is that of an irregular bicyclic monoterpene ketone. This pathway depicts the cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| to form |FRAME: CPD-685|, followed by dehydrogenation to |FRAME: CPD-27983|. The enzymes for this pathway have been demonstrated in the leaf extracts of |FRAME: TAX-2849586| |CITS: [7436420]|.

General Background, Most pathogenic bacteria have an absolute requirement for iron, which is scarce within their host environment. In vertebrates the majority of the iron is found in the form of heme. Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. In general, the bacteria express outer membrane proteins that bind heme compounds, extract heme from them, and transport the heme into the cell, where it is degraded to release the iron |CITS: [1425573][7783623][9157245]|. The most common heme-degradation systems utilize heme oxygenase enzymes that degrade heme to yield iron, carbon monoxide, and biliverdin., Several forms of bacterial heme oxygenases are known, and they are described in the various heme degradation pathways in MetaCyc. The enzymes consume three molecules of oxygen and a total of seven electron equivalents to break the tetrapyrrole ring and liberate the iron. However, while some enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), others produce different unusual isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| (|FRAME: PWY-7844|), |FRAME: CPD-18928| (|FRAME: PWY-7843|), |FRAME: CPD-19710| (|FRAME: PWY-7846|), |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| (|FRAME: PWY-7847|) and |FRAME: CPD-19716| and |FRAME: CPD-19715| (|FRAME: PWY-7848|)., About This Pathway, The bacterial pathogen |FRAME: TAX-83334| possesses a different enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44457| gene. Despite not being homologous to the cannonical heme oxygenases, ChuS can degrade heme in a reaction that releases carbon monoxide. Unlike traditional heme oxygenases, the reaction catalyzed by ChuS involves |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. While the initial intermediates of the reaction (a ferrous keto π neutral radical and ferric verdoheme) are in common with heme oxygenases, the next step involves the cleavage of the porphyrin ring at adjacent meso-carbons, resulting in the release of |FRAME: CPD-18928|, a |FRAME: CPD-18929| product, and ferric iron |CITS: [26598215]|., Homologs of |FRAME: G-44457| include hemS from |FRAME: TAX-630| and phuS from |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [16943192][24560694]|., Some information about this transformation is still missing - mass spectrometry of the tripyrrole suggests that it contains one more oxygen that those included in the structure shown here. The location and oxidation state of this oxygen within the tripyrrole structure are still not known |CITS: [26598215]|.

|FRAME: CPD-25752 Puerarin| is an isoflavone C-glucoside found in the roots of |FRAME: TAX-3893| (kudzu vine). It is the main ingredient of Kakkon-to, a very famous Kampo medicine (traditional medicine in China and Japan) used for the treatment of colds. Puerarin shows various pharmacological properties such as antioxidant, anticancer and anti-inflammatory activities, and attenuation of insulin resistance |CITS: [24339367]|., The |FRAME: TAX-498716| metabolizes |FRAME: CPD-25752| to |FRAME: DAIDZEIN| |CITS: [18670101][21212542]|. Enzymatic studies suggested that more than three bacterial enzymes are involved in the process |CITS: [23328408]|., A putative puerarin-metabolizing operon consisting of eight genes (dgpABCDEFGH) was reported from strain PUE, and a recombinant |FRAME: CPLX-9779|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107948| and |FRAME: G-107949| genes, was shown to cleave the C-glycosidic bond in |FRAME: CPD-25753|, but not in |FRAME: CPD-25752|, indicating that |FRAME: CPD-25753| is a reaction intermediate |CITS: [30626800]|., A search of the dgp operon for the enzyme that converts |FRAME: CPD-25752| to |FRAME: CPD-25753| suggested the |FRAME: G-107947| gene, which encodes an oxidoreductase, and its N terminus sequence matched that of a previously reported protein involved in puerarin metabolism |CITS: [23328408]|., The gene was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant protein was purified. The enzyme contains a tightly, but noncovalently, bound NAD+/NADH cofactor |CITS: [32385077]|., The enzyme was active against |FRAME: CPD-25752| only in the presence of |FRAME: 3-Dehydro-D-Glucopyranose|, which functions as the hydride acceptor |CITS: [32385077]|.

|FRAME: CPD-403 "3-Hydroxy-4-methylanthranilate"| occurs exclusively in the actinomycete family of bacteria, and serves as a building block of several secondary metabolites including the |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN actinomycin| phenoxazinone chromophore |CITS: [20945860]| and the antitumor antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-18442| |CITS: [21612226]|., |FRAME: CPD-403 "3-Hydroxy-4-methylanthranilate"| is synthesized from |FRAME: TRP|. In |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN actinomycin|-producing organisms the methyltransferase is highly specific for the D-isomer of the substrate (see |FRAME: PWY-7717|). Summary: Nitrogen is frequently the limiting nutrient for growth of many crop plants. Legumes solved this problem by establishing a symbiotic relationship with bacteria from the genus |FRAME: TAX-374|, which contain the enzyme nitrogenase., Nitrogenase catalyzes the conversion of atmospheric |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| to |FRAME: AMMONIA|, which can be used to meet the plant's metabolic nitrogen requirements (see |FRAME: N2FIX-PWY|)., The ammonia generated by the bacteria is first converted into the amino acid |FRAME:GLN| and then incorporated into |FRAME: IMP| (IMP), a purine synthesized de novo during nitrogen fixation by roots (see |FRAME: PWY-841|)., Before the fixed nitrogen can be used by the plant, it must be converted into organic forms that can be transported throughout the plant and further metabolized., There are two major forms of organic nitrogen compounds that can be transported - amides (such as |FRAME:ASN| and |FRAME:GLN|) and ureides (such as |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|)., Temperate-region legumes, such as pea, are amide exporters, while legumes of tropical origin, such as soybean, kidney bean and peanut, export nitrogen in the form of ureides (see |FRAME: URSIN-PWY|). , The pathway that is described here, the conversion of |FRAME:IMP| to |FRAME:URATE|, is part of the pathway leading to the production of ureides in plants. However, it is also a part of the degradation of purines, which is found in many organisms., Many mammals, for example, can mineralize purines completely to TCA cycle building blocks in a pathway that includes this subpathway. Humans and apes possess this pathway, but do not have the enzyne urate oxidase (|FRAME: URATE-OXIDASE-RXN "EC 1.7.3.3"|, and thus accumulate urate, which has to be disposed of via urine.

Instead, archaeabacteria appear to utilize an alternative pathway in which, |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| is synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-10791| and, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| |CITS: [15182204]|. These two compounds are first condensed to form, |FRAME: CPD-10792|, which cyclizes to |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE|., From |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| and on to |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, the archaeal pathway appears to be identical, to the bacterial pathway |CITS: [15262931][17010158 ]|., It has been shown that the source for |FRAME: CPD-10791| is glycolytic |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE|,, which is condensed with |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [17014089]|., The latter is believed to be produced by a spontaneous reaction from |FRAME: GAP|, which is known to be unstable at, temperatures above 60°C and to decompose to |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [2021650][17014089]|., The product of this pathwy, |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE|, not only feeds the shikimate pathway, but is also the source for |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE|, an important precursor for the synthesis of |FRAME: THMPT|  |CITS: [17010158]|.

Summary: There are two main sources for |FRAME: ACETONE| production in organisms: the decarboxylation of, |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE| (EC 4.1.1.4) and the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, (EC 1.1.1.80)., The conversion of |FRAME:ISO-PROPANOL| to |FRAME: ACETONE| was initially demonstrated in 1940, in a strain of the photosynthetic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-28068|, which could use, |FRAME:ISO-PROPANOL| as the sole source of carbon |CITS: [Foster40]|., Subsequent work showed that the conversion was a direct dehydrogenation |CITS: [15436443]|., Since then several strains of bacteria were shown to be able to utilize |FRAME:ISO-PROPANOL| as the, sole source of carbon and energy. Despite the fact that |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| is a toxic, solvent, some organisms are able to tolerate high concentrations of it. For example, the organism, |FRAME: TAX-1010| is able to grow in the presence of up to 38 g/li |FRAME:ISO-PROPANOL|, with the, highest degradation rate at a concentration of 7.5 g/li. This organism produces acetone as an, intermediate |CITS: [16758171]|., Despite the many years that have passed since the initial discovery, the nature of the enzyme responsible, for this conversion is still not known. Alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes that catalyze the reversible, conversion of |FRAME: ACETONE| to |FRAME:ISO-PROPANOL| have been studied in, |FRAME:ISO-PROPANOL|-producing bacteria |CITS: [16347317]| as well as mammalian tissues, |CITS: [398364]|. All of these enzyme appear to require NADP as a cosubstrate., Much more is known about the conversion of |FRAME: ACETONE| to |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE|., The involvement of carboxylation was first suggested by Kuenen and coworkers, who showed that growth, of |FRAME: TAX-82367| on acetone and propanol was dependent on the exogenous supply of, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [Bonnet-Smits88]|., The coversion of |FRAME: ACETONE| to |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE| occurs in both aerobic and, anaerobic organisms., Most of the knowledge about the aerobic reaction comes from work with the obligate aerobe, |FRAME: TAX-78245| |CITS: [8763926][9237998][12003937]|. This organism, has an inducible |FRAME:CPLX-7447|, which comprises up to 25% of the total soluble proteins in the, cell after induction |CITS: [9237998]|. The enzyme, which is composed of three different polypeptides,, has been purified and characterized, but its mechanism is still not understood well |CITS: [9477250]|., Very similar enzymes have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [12003937]| and, |FRAME: TAX-1829| |CITS: [10217764]|, and sequence analysis predicts the existence of homologs, in several strains of the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [12003937]|., Most of the evidence about anaerobic acetone degradation via carboxylation comes from whole-cell, studies. The reaction has been studied in denitrifying bacteria |CITS: [2557377][1368470]|, sulfate, reducing bacteria |CITS: [2244787][7778975]|, and photosynthetic anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [Birks97]|., An acetone carboxylase has been partially purified from anaerobically-grown |FRAME: TAX-1061|, and, was shown to be composed of at least two different polypeptides |CITS: [Birks97]|.

Summary: Some invertebrates, protists and fungi must survive prolonged exposure to hypoxia or anoxia. These facultative anaerobes may contain either mitochondria that function anaerobically, or hydrogenosomes as cellular organelles in which reactions of anaerobic respiration occur. Most anaerobic mitochondria use endogenously produced electron acceptors such as |FRAME: FUM| to generate |FRAME: SUC| via membrane-bound fumarate reductase. This enzyme is usually associated with the electron carrier |FRAME: Rhodoquinones "rhodoquinone"|, proton-pumping, and ATP synthase. The pathway shown here has been experimentally demonstrated in some marine invertebrates, but variations of it can be found in other organisms such as the parasites |FRAME: TAX-6251| and |FRAME: TAX-6192| (reviewed in |CITS: [22688819][12594928][12417132][9693724][7998964]|)., Marine invertebrates can utilize several different anaerobic energy-yielding metabolic pathways when exposed to prolonged conditions of environmental or functional hypoxia or anoxia. These include opine and/or lactate production (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-7351| and |FRAME: PWY-5481|), phosphagen utilization (see |FRAME: MONOMER-18221|), as well as the aspartate-succinate pathway shown here. In addition, metabolic depression can also occur during anaerobiosis resulting in reduction of metabolism below the standard metabolic rate (reviewed in |CITS: [7984874][DEZWAANA96]|., Fermentation pathways found in metazoan, protozoan and fungal parasites have also been extensively studied (reviewed in |CITS: [22688819]|) (see pathways under class |FRAME: Fermentation|)., The superpathway shown here spans two subcellular compartments. The |FRAME: MAL| formed in the cytosol is transported into the mitochondrion. For a more detailed description, please see the "About This Pathway" sections in the Summaries for the individual subpathways listed below.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-18512| is an unusual deoxysugar that contributes to the structure of the three aminocoumarin antibiotics -  |FRAME: CPD-15417|, |FRAME: CPD-15421|, and |FRAME: CPD-15504|, which are produced by the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-2893586|, |FRAME: TAX-149682| and |FRAME: TAX-68264|, respectively., These antibiotics bind type II topoisomerases, including DNA gyrase, with an extremely high affinity, with equilibrium dissociation constants in the 10 nM range |CITS: [8231802]|. They compete with ATP for binding to the B subunit of DNA gyrase and thus inhibit the ATP-dependent DNA supercoiling catalysed by gyrase. The noviose attaches to the 7' position of the coumarin core by a glycosidic linkage, and, after certain modifications, confers the biological activity to these compounds |CITS: [6295263]|., The influence of noviose in determining the antibacterial spectrum of coumarin antibiotics originates from the presence of three methyl groups (4'-O-methyl and 5',5'-dimethyl groups) in the sugar subunit, which sit in a pocket close to hydrophobic amino acid residues of the gyrase |CITS: [Gammon02][10522711]|., Following the cloning and sequencing of the |FRAME: CPD-15417| biosynthesis cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2893586|, a typical deoxysugar biosynthetic route has been proposed for the synthesis of noviose |CITS: [10770754]|. The proposed pathway starts with the modification of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| to |FRAME:DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps that are common to all deoxysugars biosyntheses. Subsequent epimerization, second methylation at position 5 and ketoreduction at position 4 lead to production of |FRAME: CPD-15496|. Final methylation to form |FRAME: CPD-18512| occurs only after the transfer of the sugar to the antibiotic aglycon (see |FRAME: PWY-7287|)., The proposed pathway has been validated by cloning and recombinant expression of the  |FRAME: G-16081|, |FRAME: G-16082| and |FRAME: G-16083| genes, which encode the last three steps of the pathway |CITS: [15752721]|.

General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, At least four alternative routes have been reported in plants. , The pathway depicted here depends on three consecutive N-methylation steps that are carried out on phospho-bases, phosphoethanolamine, phospho-N-methylethanolamine, and phospho-N-dimethylethanolamine. , Radio tracer experiments with crude cell extracts suggested such a pathway in Lemna and carrot |CITS: [16666464]|, but not in soybean. An Arabidopsis gene (AtNMT1) was isolated through functional complementation of a yeast mutant deficient in phosphatidylcholine. Assay of the AtNMT1 recombinant enzyme indicated that it catalyzes three sequential methylations of phosphoethanolamine to form phosphocholine |CITS: [11115895]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, and |FRAME: CPD-10335|). Non-oxygenic bacteria possess a related pigment called bacteriochlorophyll, which also exists in several variants (|FRAME:CPD-9067|, |FRAME:CPD-9091|,, |FRAME:CPD-9092|, |FRAME:CPD-9093|, |FRAME:CPD-9094| and |FRAME:CPD-9095|). This pathway describes the formation of |FRAME: DIVINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|, an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of all chlorophylls., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of chlorophylls begins with the condensation of eight molecules of |FRAME:5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| (ALA, originating from |FRAME: GLT|) to |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, the first cyclic tetrapyrrole (see |FRAME: PWY-5188|). This compound is then sequentially converted to |FRAME:PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX|, which is the branch-point intermediate to hemes and chlorophylls., The incorporation of |FRAME: MG+2| into |FRAME:PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| occurs at the next step, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:MG-PROTOPORPHYRIN| (MgP). A methyl transferase subsequently converts MgP into, |FRAME:MG-PROTOPORPHYRIN-MONOMETHYL-ESTER| (MgPMME), which is the substrate for a cyclase reaction, involving molecular oxygen. The cyclase forms |FRAME:DIVINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|, an intermediate that contains a fifth ring (ring E), characteristic of all chlorophylls. A combined action by an 8-vinyl reductase (multiple forms exist) and a protochlorophyllide reductase (multiple forms exist) results in the formation of |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|., This pathway describes the action of It should be noted that most organisms also possess a light-independent enzyme that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| from |FRAME: MONO-VINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|. That enzyme is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7159|., This biosynthetic pathway, which occurs in all aerobic photosynthetic organisms, has been described through genetic analysis of bacterial mutants and in vitro reconstitution of individual reactions |CITS:[9442890][12242396][beale99][14617630]|., Anaerobic phototrophic bacteria possess a very similar pathway. However, the cyclase found in these organisms does not require molecular oxygen. A variant of the pathway found in anaerobic bacteria is described in |FRAME:PWY-5531|.

General Background, The compound eyes of insects are composed of long hexagonal units called ommatidia. An ommatidium contains a cluster of photoreceptor cells surrounded by support cells and pigment cells. In most insects each ommatidium is innervated by one axon and thus provides the brain with one picture element. The number of ommatidia in the eye ranges from just a handful to around 30,000, depending on the species. , Most of the inner portion of the ommatidium is composed of 6 to 9 long and thin photoreceptor cells (abbreviated "R cells") that contain the visual pigments. The portion of the R cells at the central axis of the ommatidium collectively form a a transparent tube that serves as a light guide, called the rhabdom. In certain flies, the rhabdom has separated into seven independent rhabdomeres. In these organisms each ommatidium contains seven axons leading from it, rather than a single one., Not all photoreceptor cells in insects express the same type of visual pigments. Different versions of |FRAME: Rhodopsins rhodopsins| are known to exist in insects, and three different chromophores have been reported - |FRAME: CPD-881|, |FRAME: CPD-14328| and |FRAME: CPD-14329| |CITS: [8001586][Seki98]|. Most of the insect visual pigments use the (3R)-3-hydroxyretinal enantiomer, but members of the higher Diptera, the |FRAME: TAX-480117|, have been shown to synthesize and use the (3S)-3-hydroxyretinal enantiomer as chromophore |CITS: [Seki98]|., In the case of the house fly, |FRAME: TAX-7370| (3000 ommatidia) or the fruit fly, |FRAME: TAX-7227| (800 ommatidia), each of the ommatidia contains eight photoreceptors, named R1 through R8. The R1-R6 cells contain a blue/green-sensitive rhodopsin Rh1 that confers response to UV light |CITS: [3087059][3617517]|. The R7 and R8 cells express different types of rhodopsin - R7 cells express either Rh3 or Rh4, which are sensitive to UV (345 nm and 375 nm, respectively) |CITS: [2953598][2437266][2952772][1403087]|, while R8 cells express either Rh5 or Rh6, which absorb blue and green light |CITS: [8982159][9165115][9109375][10594055]|. While it is well established that Rh1 rhodopsin is associated with a |FRAME: CPD-14328| chromophore, it is still not known which chromophores are used by the other types. It has been shown that at least in |FRAME: G-15150| mutants, Rh4 rhodopsin binds |FRAME: CPD-14329| |CITS: [16464863]|., About This Pathway, One of the key questions regarding the formation of the insect chromophores was the mechanism of retinal hydroxylation, which was thought to be necessaey to generate the 3-hydroxylated forms used by the insect rhodopsins. A P450 hydroxylase has been described, and may play a role (although not shown here) |CITS: [9826202]|. However, better characterization of the |FRAME: G-15150| gene product showed that the enzyme is active on hydroxylated substrates such as |FRAME: CPD1F-130| and |FRAME: CPD-7409|, and thus capable of producing already-hydroxylated retinal molecules. Furthermore, it has been shown that the enzyme, which was originally thought to be a carotene oxygenase (|FRAME: RXN-13374 "EC 1.14.99.36"|), is actually a |FRAME: MONOMER-17370|, and isomerizes one of its products to the cis form |CITS: [19020100]|. Thus, when the substrate of the enzyme is |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, one of the products is |FRAME: CPD-14329|, the chromophore used by most insects, and potential chromophore of fruit fly Rh4 rhodopsin., The rest of this pathway describes the conversion of the other cleavage product, |FRAME: CPD-14334|, to |FRAME: CPD-14328|, the chromophore required by the Rh1 rhodopsin of higher flies. The pathway, which combines routes suggested by several investigators, continues with the binding of the free retinal molecue to the |FRAME: MONOMER-17367| |CITS: [15917458]|. The retinal is then reduced to retinol by the |FRAME: G-15147|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17368| |CITS: [20045325]| and epimerized from an (R) form to an (S) form by the |FRAME: G-15150| gene product |CITS: [16464863]|. The product, |FRAME:3R-all-trans-3-hydroxyretinol-RBPs "(3R)-all-trans-3-hydroxyretinol"| is then isomerized to a cis form by an as-yet unidentified isomerase, followed by oxidation to retinal by the |FRAME: G-15148|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17369|, forming the chromophore for the Rh1 rhodopsin |CITS: [22399771]|.

Summary: General Background, 4-Hydroxyproline (|FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE|) residues contribute to the stability of the |FRAME: Collagens "collagen"| triple helix. |FRAME: Collagens "Collagen"| is a major constituent of animal protein. Other animal proteins containing 4-hydroxyproline include |FRAME: elastin|, the complement component C1q, and acetyl cholinesterase. 4-Hydroxyproline is also found in some proteins of higher plants and algae. Most of the 4-hydroxyproline in animals is biosynthesized by post-translational modification of appropriate |FRAME: PRO| residues by proline hydroxylase during the biosynthesis and maturation of collagen. Thus, 4-hydroxyproline released during |FRAME: Collagens "collagen"| degradation cannot be reutilized, and is degraded., About This Pathway, This major mammalian pathway for 4-hydroxyproline degradation has been demonstrated in liver and kidney mitochondria. Expression of mRNA for all of the enzymes in this pathway has been demonstrated in human liver, kidney, pancreas and small intestine, as well as in HepG2 cells |CITS: [22207577]|. The first two reactions of the pathway are analogous to those of |FRAME: PRO| degradation (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PROUT-PWY|). However the first enzyme, hydroxyproline oxidase, is distinct from proline oxidase based on studies of the accumulation of free 4-hydroxyproline, but not |FRAME: PRO|, in the plasma and urine of individuals with a deficiency of this enzyme |CITS: [9063421]|. Those deficient in proline oxidase do not show elevated 4-hydroxyproline levels. The two enzyme activities can also be differentially destroyed by chemical, physical, or enzymatic treatment (reviewed in |CITS: [6250440][18806117]|). , The second enzyme, pyrroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase, appears to be shared by both the |FRAME: PROUT-PWY| and |FRAME: HYDROXYPRODEG-PWY| pathways |CITS: [500817] [13681370]|. The bovine enzyme has been shown to catalyze the dehydrogenation of both |FRAME: PYRROLINE-HYDROXY-CARBOXYLATE| and |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| |CITS: [13681370]|. The substrate |FRAME: PYRROLINE-HYDROXY-CARBOXYLATE| exists in spontaneous equilibrium with its open chain form |FRAME: L-4-HYDROXYGLUTAMATE_SEMIALDEHYDE| (4-hydroxy-glutamic-4-semialdehyde) |CITS: [12660328]|. Evidence suggested that the bovine enzyme binds the ring form |CITS: [13681370]| and reviewed in |CITS: [6250440]|. However later work on the human enzyme suggested that it binds the open-chain form |CITS: [3944130][22516612]|. After the deamination step, the hydroxyl group of |FRAME: D-4-HYDROXY-2-KETO-GLUTARATE| permits an aldol cleavage to produce |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYOX|., |FRAME: GLYOX Glyoxylate| is a reactive compound that is enzymatically converted to less active derivatives. There is evidence that it may be reduced to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| by glyoxylate reductase, converted to |FRAME: GLY| by serine:pyruvate/alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase, or oxidized to |FRAME: OXALATE| by lactate dehydrogenase. Production of excess |FRAME: OXALATE| is physiologically undesirable and regulatory mechanisms have been suggested. Mutations in the gene encoding human glyoxylate reductase (GRHPR) lead to primary hyperoxaluria type 2 (|CITS: [14635115] [16198644] [12660328] [15849464]| and reviewed in |CITS: [6250440]|)., Bacteria can also degrade 4-hydroxyproline. An inducible pathway has been shown for this compound in |FRAME: TAX-286| species |CITS: [5764334]|. See MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5159|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE Plastoquinones| (PQ) are benzoquinone electron carriers that can function as acceptor/donor for either one or two electrons. They are analogs of |FRAME: Ubiquinones "ubiquinones"| (Coenzyme Q), with two methyl groups substituting the methoxy groups found in Q. The fully reduced form is called |FRAME: Plastoquinols|., Plastoquinones are found in the chloroplasts of higher plants, red, brown and green algae, and in cyanobacteria, and are important members of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, where they carry electrons from |FRAME: CPLX490-3506| to the |FRAME: CPLX-9022|. Plastoquinones also serve as a membrane-associated two-electron carriers in other respiratory electron transport chains. In fact, it has been shown that in cyanobacteria essentially all electron transport through unbound quinones proceeds via PQ in cyanobacterial thylakoids. Apart from PQ the only quinone found in thylakoids is |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1), which is associated with PS I |CITS: [Vermaas01]|., Plastoquinones also serve as cofactors involved in the desaturation of |FRAME: CPD-12321| in the synthesis of carotenoids (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|)., Plastoquinone was isolated originally in 1946 from alfalfa, but was not identified at the time. It was rediscovered in 1959 and its structure was described in the same year (see |CITS: [7022156]|)., About This Pathway, The pathway for the biosynthesis of plastoquinone in plants starts with |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE|. |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE| is a branching point in the formation of plastoquinones and |FRAME: Vitamin-E tocopherols|. The committed step in plastoquinone biosynthesis is condensation of |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE| and |FRAME: CPD-21340|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-3784|., A different enzyme (|FRAME: AT2G18950-MONOMER|) catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE| with |FRAME: PHYTYL-PYROPHOSPHATE|, the committed step for biosynthesis of tocopherols (see |FRAME: PWY-1422|)., The plastoquinone biosynthesis in cyanobacteria is different than that of plants (see |FRAME: PWY-6978|).

|FRAME: CPD-19390 Chlorzoxazone| is a precursor, as well as a degradation product, of |FRAME: CPD-19392| (FE), a postemergence aryloxyphenoxy propionate herbicide that is used to control annual and perennial weeds in crops. It is highly toxic to microorganisms and difficult to degrade |CITS: [19199602]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1481731| was isolated from an enriched FE-degrading consortium based on its ability to degrade |FRAME: CPD-19390|. Incubation of the bacterium with 0.2 mM of |FRAME: CPD-19390| resulted in removal of 98% of the compound within 72 hours |CITS: [Dong15]|., The enzyme responsible for the initial attack on this compound, |FRAME: CPLX-9157|, has been identified, purified, and characterized. Hydrolysis by the enzyme produces |FRAME: CPD-19391|, which is unstable and undergoes spontaneous decarboxylation to |FRAME: CPD-9158| |CITS: [Dong15]|., The rest of the degradation pathway is identical to the later part of the pathway for |FRAME: CPD-9154| degradation (see |FRAME: PWY-5645|). A |FRAME: CPD-9158| metabolic gene cluster surrounded by two IS1071 transposable elements was discovered in the |FRAME: TAX-1481731| genome, and shares 99% identity with the clusters from |FRAME: TAX-543891| and |FRAME: ORG-5961|, which are known to degrade |FRAME: CPD-9154| |CITS: [Dong15]|.

Summary: General Background, Plants contain significant amounts of hydroxy fatty acids in their sphingolipids. |FRAME:CPD-12193 Ricinoleate| occurs throughout the plant kingdom and is common in some species in particular. Castor oil extracted from |FRAME:TAX-3988| (castor bean) contains almost 90% |FRAME:CPD-12193|. |FRAME:CPD-12193 Ricinoleate| is produced in large scale and used to produce |FRAME:CPD-3623|, which is used in the production of some types of nylon and for production of high temperature greases for jet engines. , About This Pathway, The seeds of |FRAME:TAX-3701| |CITS:[11171267]| and |FRAME: TAX-3987 Ricinus| |CITS:[16661734]| accumulate the hydroxylated fatty acid |FRAME:CPD-12193|. The key enzyme in |FRAME:CPD-12193| biosynthesis is |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.4| |CITS:[9680976][Dauk07]|., The enzyme was originally characterized from |FRAME: TAX-3988|. It is only expressed in developing seeds |CITS: [17672910][22319559]| and is very similar to membrane-bound desaturases |CITS: [7624314]|., The in vivo substrate for the enzyme is |FRAME: 1-ACYL-2-OLEOYL-SN-GLYCERO-3-PHOSPHOCHOL "1-acyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine"| |CITS: [8784737]|. Although enzymes that liberate free fatty acids from their lipid and CoA derivatives exist in the cell, free fatty acids are considered toxic and therefore are very rare inside the cell.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Despite the fact that cobamides containing phenolic lower ligand bases comprise about 16% of the total cobamides isolated from gut microbiome of humans |CITS: [18469256]|, not much information is available about the organisms that produce them. One organism that is known to produce both |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108| as lower ligand bases of biologically active cobamides is the homoacetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2378| |CITS: [3350008][Stupperich89]|. Other organisms that were shown to produce 4-methylphenolylcobamides nclude the human gut bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29466| |CITS: [21696461]| and |FRAME: TAX-1122947|, which, when grown in lactate-amended, B12-free medium, produces both phenolylcobamide and 4-methylphenolylcobamide |CITS: [24463969]|., Unlike other common cobamide lower ligand bases, |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108| cannot establish a coordination bond with the cobalt ion of the ring. The lack of this coordination bond limits the use of these cofactors to enzymes that use cobamide coenzymes in their base-off conformation |CITS: [Stupperich89a]|, The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the phenolic lower ligand bases (both |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108|) are activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.55|, a heterodimeric enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-44074| and |FRAME: G-44075| genes |CITS: [21696461]|, by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphoribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) to form the cobamide. The last two enzymes that operate in this pathway are believed to be the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis., Enzymes of |FRAME: TAX-2378| appear to have a preference for the phenolyl cobamides. The addition of benzimidazoles to cultures results in a decrease in growth rate when grown on |FRAME: METOH|, |FRAME: CPD-20857|, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| plus |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, or |FRAME: BETAINE| |CITS: [23417488]|.

Summary: General Background, 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes convert 2-oxo acids to the corresponding acyl-CoA derivatives and produce NADH and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an irreversible reaction., Five members of this family are known at present, including the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| (PDHC - this pathway), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| (OGDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| (BCDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| (GDHC), and the |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190| (ADHC). They all function at strategic points in (usually aerobic) catabolic pathways and are subject to stringent control |CITS: [9655933]|., With the exception of GDHC, the 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes share a common structure. They consist of three main components, namely a 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3)., In Gram-positive bacteria and mitochondria, the E1 component is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, while in Gram-negative bacteria it is made of a single type of subunit., In all cases described so far, many copies of each subunit assemble to form the full complex. For example, the |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| comprises 24, 24, and 12 units of the E1, E2, and E3 components, respectively., The core of the complex is made of either 24 (Gram-negative bacteria) or 60 (mitochondria) E2 units, which contain the lipoyl active site in the form of lipoyllysine, as well as binding sites for the other two subunits. E1, which contains a |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| cofactor, catalyzes the binding of the 2-oxo acid to the lipoyl group of E2, which then transfers an acyl group (the nature of the acyl group depends on the particular enzyme) to |FRAME: CO-A|, forming an acyl-CoA. During this transfer, the lipoyl group is reduced to dihydrolipoyl. E3 then transfers the protons to NAD, forming NADH and restoring the dihydrolipoyllysine group back to lipoyllysine., Cryoelectron microscopy of PDHC from |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS:[12411477]| and ox kidney |CITS: [11752427]| has revealed that the E2 inner core is surrounded by an outer shell of E1 and E3 components, with the lipoyl domains confined to the annular space between them where they must make successive journeys between the three types of active sites (E1-E3), which are physically far apart |CITS: [12795594]|., About This Pathway, The pathway illustrated here presents the reactions catalyzed by the |FRAME:2OXOGLUTARATEDEH-CPLX|, a key enzyme of the |FRAME: TCA|. These reactions can be summarized by the general reaction, |FRAME: 2OXOGLUTARATEDEH-RXN|, which is the form commonly found in the TCA cycle.
