Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17600 Arctigenin| is a lignan with an astounding spectrum of documented pharmacological activities. It has been reported to possess antitumor activities, acting selectively against cancer cells under glucose deprivation |CITS:[16452235] [20232300]|. Interestingly, it could be demonstrated that only the (-)-enantiomer of |FRAME:CPD-17600| expressed the cytotoxicity that inhibited nutrient-starved human pancreatic PANC-1 cancer cells |CITS:[24660468]| pointing out a seminal strategy to develop more potent drugs |CITS:[23287053]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-17600| has also been considered a lead structure for the development of inhibitors of human immunodeficiency virus type-1 integrase, the protein responsible for integrating retroviral DNA into host cell chromosomal DNA |CITS:[8568830]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-17600| exhibits antiproliferative |CITS:[Ryu95]|, hepatoprotective |CITS:[12913279]|, anti-inflammatory |CITS:[18180122]| and pain-relieving activities |CITS:[16636966]|, the latter considered promising for developing treatments of rheumatic arthritis and gynopathic disorders. Remarkable are also the reported suppressive activities against a variety of enzymes such as the cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase |CITS:[6280885]| and the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase associated with tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) expression |CITS:[15313439]|. |FRAME:CPD-17600 Arctigenin| also activated AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) involved in glucose and lipid metabolism which is potential useful in treatments of type 2 diabetes |CITS:[22095235]|., On a plant physiological level |FRAME:CPD-17600| had been reported to be involved in stimulatory allelopathy as it was identified as growth-promoting factor secreted from germinating Arctium lappa (burdock) seeds which significantly increased the shoot growth of Celosia cristata (cockscomb) |CITS:[Higashinakasu05]|. The lignan |FRAME:CPD-17600| is also a component frequently found in heartwood |CITS:[11142847]| where it is proposed to contribute, together with a variety of norlignans (see |FRAME:PWY-7632|), to the prevention of heart rot caused by heart-rot fungi |CITS:[Suzuki01] [Suzuki02] [15599432] [Suzuki07]| and appears to be wide-spread amongst plants |CITS:[Suzuki82] [Ozawa93] [Umezawa03b]|. In general, the biosynthetic routes of lignans often display unique stereochemical particularities which is illuminating for bioorganic synthesis of chiral pharmaceuticals |CITS:[23161544]| and biomimetic chemistry |CITS:[Suzuki07]| highlighting the impressive diversity in the biosynthesis of lignans |CITS:[12162547] [Umezawa03]|., |FRAME:CPD-8912 Matairesinol| which is the branch point towards |FRAME:PWY-7629| (yatein) and |FRAME:PWY-7630| (pluviatolide), both proposed to be involved in the making of the antitumor compound |FRAME:CPD-8959| (see |FRAME:PWY-5479|), is also substrate for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17600| and |FRAME:CPD-17601|. The regioselectivity and substrate enantiomer specificity of the respective O-methylation reaction(s) involved is very distinctive and dependent on the plant species. The matairesinol 4'-O-methyltransferase characterized from Carthamus tinctorius (ctmromt) |CITS:[Umezawa13] [Ragamustari14]| and Anthriscus sylvestris (MROMT) |CITS:[Ragamustari13] [Ragamustari14]| only accepts the (-)-enantiomer out of a racemic mix of (+/-)-matairesinol forming |FRAME:CPD-17600|. However, the matairesinol 4-O-methyltransferase isolated from Forsythia koreana (FkOMT72) |CITS:[Ozawa93] [Ragamustari14]| yielded |FRAME:CPD-17601| from the same racemic mix of (+/-)-matairesinol, hence differing significantly from the product formation of the MROMT (Anthriscus sylvestris) and ctmromt (Carthamus tinctorius) encoded matairesinol 4'-O-methyltransferases.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN "Adenosylcobalamin"| (also known as vitamin B12 or coenzyme B12) was discovered in the 1920s after Minot and Murphy reported that they could cure the symptoms of pernicious anaemia by feeding patients with crude liver extract |CITS: [Minot26]| (they received the Nobel prize in 1934 for this discovery)., The unknown factor has been isolated and subsequently crystallized in 1948 |CITS:[Lester48][Rickes48]|, and was given the name vitamin B12 and, as it was shown to contain a cobalt ion, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin| (although this term is used to describe a family of related compounds) |CITS: [12195810]|., Cobalamins are some of the most structurally complex small molecules made in Nature. They contain a contracted porphinoid ring with a cobalt ion ligated at its center and further held in place by a lower axial base (|FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|) and a methyl or adenosyl group that function as an upper axial ligand. Their biosynthesis is similarly complex, and requires more than thirty genes. Cobalamin biosynthesis is confined to only some bacteria and archaea |CITS: [11935176]|., Two main pathways are known for |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthesis - an aerobic pathway (this pathway) and an anaerobic pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5507|). The main differences between these pathways are the timing of the |FRAME: CO+2| ion insertion and the ring-contraction mechanism (for more about ring contraction, see |CITS: [16592942]|). |FRAME: CO+2| is inserted early on in the anaerobic pathway, and rather late in the aerobic pathway., The two different routes then merge at |FRAME: CPD-689|, and the later part of the pathway is identical, or at least very similar., About This Pathway, The best characterized aerobic |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthetic pathway is that of the aerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-43306|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| starts with the biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole intermediate |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, which is a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of several important compounds, such as |FRAME: Hemes heme| and |FRAME: Chlorophylls chlorophyl|. |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III "Uroporphyrinogen III| is converted to a corrin ring by a complex process that involves (among other things) the attachment of eight methyl groups, all derived from |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM). During the process the ring contracts via bonding of carbons C-1 and C-19 to each other, eliminating carbon C-20 from the ring. Both the C-20 carbon and the added C-20 methyl group are lost in the form of |FRAME: ACET|., The intermediates formed prior to the formation of the corrin ring are called precorrins. The precorrins are numbered corresponding to the number of methyl groups that have been already introduced. If two different intermediates have the same number of methyl groups, they are also labeled by A or B (as in |FRAME:CPD-675|). If there is still some uncertainty about an intermediate, it is given a temporary designation of X or Y., The first committed step in this pathway is the addition of a methyl group to carbon C-20 of the tetrapyrrole ring to give |FRAME: CPD-642|. This intermediate, which contains three additional methyl groups (compared with |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|), is oxidized by |FRAME:MONOMER-84|, using molecular oxygen, to |FRAME:CPD-643|, an intermediate that has been described as "spring-loaded for contraction" |CITS: [12195810]|., This intermediate, which has a hydroxy group at carbon C-20, forms a lactone between carbons C-1 and C-2. However, the ring is not contracted until the next enzyme (another methyltransferase) adds a methyl group to carbon C-17., At this point the ring contracts, forming the next intermediate, |FRAME:CPD-651|., Following the addition of four more methyl groups (at positions C-11, C-1, C-5 and C-15) and the release of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, the final precorrin intermediate, |FRAME:CPD-686|, is formed. This intermediate is the substrate for the enzyme |FRAME:MONOMER-115|, which finally converts it to a true corrin ring compound, |FRAME:CPD-687|., This corrin ring intermediate still requires an extensive modification. Successive amidation reactions transfer two amide groups from two |FRAME: GLN| molecules to the carboxy groups a and c, resulting in |FRAME:CPD-689|, and a |FRAME: CO+2| ion is inserted into the ring by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-327|, forming |FRAME: CPD-689| - the point where the early-insertion and late-insertion pathways combine., The |FRAME: CO+2| ion is immediately reduced to |FRAME: CO+1| and is adenosylated to form |FRAME:CPD-690|. Additional amidation of carboxy groups b, d, e and g generates |FRAME:CPD-691|., At this point the lower ligand base is synthesized and tethered to the corrin ring via a structure known as the nucleotide loop, which is composed of some form of |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| and |FRAME:DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|., More information about the biosynthesis of these side chains is provided in the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5443| and |FRAME:PWY-5523|., There is some uncertainty about the order in which some of the final reactions of the pathway occur. Depending on the order of the reactions, different intermediates may form. It was initially assumed that |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| serves as substrate for the enzyme that attaches it to |FRAME: CPD-691|. However, the Km value for |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| is very high (20mM), suggesting this may not be the natural substrate. Recent findings in |FRAME: TAX-90371| suggest that the natural substrate is actually |FRAME:R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE|. In this case the product of the reaction is, |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P|, which is further phosphorylated by GTP to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| |CITS: [9446573]|. Even though this has not been proven in |FRAME: TAX-43306|, we have decided to present the pathway using this route. , Another uncertainty concerns the addition of |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP|. The |FRAME:MONOMER-144| enzyme isolated from |FRAME: TAX-43306| accepts both |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| and |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| as substrates |CITS: [1917841]|. It is not clear whether |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| is added directly, generating |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P|, followed by dephosphorylation to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| (as shown here), or whether the phosphate group is first removed from |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P|, in which case |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| is added, and the product is |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|. We have chosen to use the first option in this pathway diagram.

Summary: General Background, Quinomycin-type antibiotics are C2-symmetric cyclic depsipeptides with a pair of intercalative chromophores that show potent antibacterial, anticancer and antiviral activities. These antibiotics have potent DNA binding affinities at a level between nM and mM with different sequence selectivities. Reflecting these distinct affinities, quinomycin antibiotics show different inhibitory activities against various enzymes, such as DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase, and topoisomerase |CITS: [16408310]|. Most members of this family of compounds are toxic to mammalian cells., Quinomycin class peptide antibiotics have characteristic chromophores, which are essential for their biological activities. Among more than 20 congeners of this class of antibiotics, only two major chromophores have been identified - |FRAME: CPD-18534| and |FRAME: CPD-18533|. The former is found, among other compounds, in |FRAME: CPD-18530| produced by |FRAME: TAX-324833|, and |FRAME: CPD-18541|, which is produced by |FRAME: TAX-45399|., About This Pathway, Early studies have suggested that the precursor for |FRAME: CPD-18534| biosynthesis is |FRAME: TRP| |CITS: [670441]|., When the |FRAME: CPD-18530| biosynthetic gene cluster was isolated from the |FRAME: TAX-324833| linear plasmid, sequence analysis revealed the presence of eight genes that were candidates for encoding the enzymes of |FRAME: CPD-18534| biosynthesis |CITS: [16799553]|., Based on the predicted functions of these gene products, it has been suggested that |FRAME: CPD-18534| biosynthesis parallels the first stage of |FRAME: CPD-18548| biosynthesis, in which a cytochrome P450 enzyme hydroxylates an L-histidine bound to the thiolation domain of a peptidyl-carrier protein |CITS: [11841943]|, with the notable difference that in this case the amino acid is |FRAME: TRP| and not |FRAME: HIS|. The product is released by a dedicated thioesterase, and is then subjected to two transformations similar to those that occur during L-tryptophan degradation to |FRAME: CPD-14736| (see |FRAME: PWY-6309|). First, oxidative ring opening is catalyzed by a dioxygenase, followed by hydrolysis leading to the departure of a formate group and generation of |FRAME: CPD-18532|., The rest of the pathway is believed to be a mix of enzyme-catalyzed reactions and spontaneous reactions. Oxidative cyclization accompanied by hydrolysis is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44288| gene product, followed by oxidation of the product by the |FRAME: G-44287| gene product, produce |FRAME: CPD-18545|.This unstable compound can undergo spontaneous decarboxylation, cyclic imine formation, and oxidative aromatization to yield |FRAME: CPD-18534| |CITS: [16799553]|., An indirect proof for this pathway was obtained by cloning all of the genes necessary for |FRAME: CPD-18530| biosynthesis (including the ecm16 gene that confers resistance to the antibiotic) and expressing them in |FRAME: TAX-562|. After 8 days of fed-batch fermentation in minimal medium the recombinant strain was found to produce |FRAME: CPD-18530| with a yield of 0.3 mg per 1 liter of culture |CITS: [16799553]|., It should be noted that up to the formation of |FRAME: CPD-18532| the pathway is identical to that leading to |FRAME: CPD-18533| biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-7733|).

Summary: Chlorobenzenes are used in the production of pesticides, dyes, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, rubbers, plastics,, and electric goods |CITS: [11472925]|. Their occurrence in the environment is widespread and they are, found in the atmosphere |CITS: [10864157]|, water |CITS: [3314709][16157172]|, soil |CITS: [17988797][2695324]|,, sediments |CITS: [15694470]|, vegetables |CITS:[16002141]|, and animals |CITS: [15325147]|., Chlorobenzenes are of great concern because of their toxicity, persistence and accumulation in the food chain,, and many of them have been declared, priority pollutants, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)., |FRAME: O-DICHLOROBENZENE| is used primarily as a high-boiling solvent for waxes, gums, resins, tars, rubbers, and oils., It is a preferred solvent in reactions involving fullerenes, and is also used as a degreasing agent for metals, leather and wool., In addition, it is used as an insecticide for termites and locust borers., Animal studies with rats and mice have shown |FRAME: O-DICHLOROBENZENE| to induce acute hepatotoxic effects., It has been identified as an EPA priority pollutant., A few bacterial species were reported to be able to utilize |FRAME: O-DICHLOROBENZENE| as the sole source of carbon., These include an unidentified Pseudomonas sp. |CITS: [3281582]|, |FRAME: TAX-65067| |CITS: [1987135]|,, |FRAME: TAX-393999| |CITS: [11526005]| and |FRAME: TAX-1288| |CITS: [Ziagova07]|. , |FRAME: O-DICHLOROBENZENE| is degraded via |FRAME: CPD-10624| to |FRAME: CPD-10626|,, which is subject to ring opening via a modified ortho cleavage pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6093|)., The genes encoding the two enzymes that are responsible for this conversion,, |FRAME: CPLX-7696| and |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, have been cloned from |FRAME: TAX-393999| and expressed, in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [11526005]|.

Summary: General Background, Six pathways are now recognized in bacteria, most algae, fungi and higher plants for the biosynthesis of lysine. They are divided into two groups - the diaminopimelate (DAP) pathways, and the |FRAME:CPD-468| pathways., In the pathways that belong to the DAP group, lysine is produced from aspartate (along with methionine, threonine and isoleucine). All of the DAP group pathways share the upper segments, which include the four steps required for conversion of L-aspartate to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|. They also share the last step, which is the conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (D,L-DAP, or meso-DAP) to lysine., However, these pathways differ in the routes leading from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|. The four variations include:, (I) the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|), which involves succinylated intermediates. In this route |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is coverted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in four enzymatic steps., (II) the acetylase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2941|), which involves acetylated intermediates. This route also involves four enzymatic steps for the conversion of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|., (III) the dehydrogenase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2942|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in a single enzymatic step. , (IV) the diaminopimelate-aminotransferase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5097|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in two steps., In addition to lysine, all of the pathways in this group also produce |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is an important metabolite on its own (for example, as a constituent of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan)., The two other pathways belong to the |FRAME: CPD-468| group. They are found in organisms that have no requirement for |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, as it is not a component of their cell walls. These pathways also share the first segments, leading to the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-468| (α-aminoadipate)., However, in yeast and fungi, as well as |FRAME: TAX-3038|, the pathway continues with the key enzyme |FRAME: YBR115C-MONOMER|, leading to the intermediate |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see |FRAME: LYSINE-AMINOAD-PWY|), while in prokaryotes the pathway continues in a path similar to bacterial arginine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., Most of the bacteria that have been investigated in detail appear to utilize only one of these pathways |CITS: [1906065]|. A few exceptions include |FRAME: TAX-44252|, in which variants (II) and (III) seem to coexist |CITS: [BARTLETT85]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, in which variant (I) and (III) coexist |CITS: [1906065]|., Lysine is one of the 10 essential amino acids that mammals are unable to synthesize, and must therefore acquire in their diets., About This Pathway, Lysine biosynthesis in plants was thought to be identical to the prokaryotic DAP (diaminopimelate) pathway that uses N-succinylated intermediates (|FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|) |CITS: [15652176]|. However the Arabidopsis genome does not contain a homolog of |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.117|. Furthermore, the Arabidopsis homologs of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.17|, and |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.18|, are not likely to function in lysine biosynthesis |CITS: [15652176]|. It was thus suggested that plants may synthesize lysine via an enzyme that bypasses the three reactions by directly converting tetrahydrodipicolinate to L,L-diaminopimelate. An Arabidopsis enzyme that catalyzes this reaction, |FRAME: AT4G33680-MONOMER|, was indeed discovered |CITS: [16361515]|. Despite the fact that the forward reaction (towards lysine biosynthesis) seems to be unfavorable, the enzyme was shown to be involved in lysine biosynthesis under physiological conditions by functional complementation of an |FRAME: TAX-562| lysine biosynthesis double mutant of dapD and dapE., The key enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.83|, was discovered not only in green plants, but also in bacteria belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-1117| and |FRAME: TAX-1783257| |CITS: [17093042]|, and in archaea of the |FRAME: TAX-183925| and the |FRAME: TAX-183939| classes |CITS: [18371309][20418392]|. Soon after it was reported that a diverged form of the enzyme is also common in many other bacterial phyla |CITS: [18310350]|. Phylogenetic analyses suggested that two lateral gene transfers occurred in the DapL genes, one from archaea to bacteria, forming the DapL2 group, and one from bacteria to archaea, forming the DapL1 group |CITS: [20418392]|., The first committed enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.3.3.7|, is feedback regulated by lysine |CITS: [8000011]|. Its catalyzed reaction is the rate-limiting step for lysine biosynthesis. |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.83|, may impose another regulation point of lysine biosynthesis - using maize cultured embryo cells, it was shown that the overall rate of lysine synthesis is in the same range of the forward reaction catalyzed by this enzyme |CITS: [16361515]|., Lysine biosynthesis in plants occurs within chloroplasts. No evidence exists for extra plastidic location of the pathway |CITS: [15652176]|.

General Background, Many organisms including bacteria, fungi, metazoa, and plants can degrade glucose polymers derived from |FRAME: Starch| or |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6724|, |FRAME: PWY-842|, |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5941|). Some hyperthermophilic archaea have also been shown to produce |FRAME: Starch|-degrading enzymes, and pathways for the utilization of |FRAME: Starch| and its derivatives, such as |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|, |FRAME: Maltodextrins|, and |FRAME: MALTOSE| have been proposed. These hyperthermophilic archaea can utilize |FRAME: Starch| and its degradation products as primary carbon sources during anaerobic growth. Thermostable starch-degrading enzymes produced by hyperthermophilic organisms are of industrial interest |CITS: [16513741] [11489857] [17921308] [11702074]|., |FRAME: TAX-186497| was shown to degrade |FRAME: Starch| mainly via maltodextrins in a pathway involving an extracellular amylopullulanase, a transporter, an intracellular 4-α-glucanotransferase, and a maltodextrin phosphorylase, as described below in About This Pathway (|CITS: [16513741]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|)., The sulfate-reducing archaeon |FRAME: ORG-6178| has been shown to degrade |FRAME: Starch| via a unique pathway involving cyclodextrin intermediates |CITS: [17921308] [11702074]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6731|)., In the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-91619| evidence suggested a |FRAME: Starch| degradation pathway via formation of cyclodextrins from |FRAME: Starch| extracellularly by a |FRAME: MONOMER-16282|, transport of cyclodextrins into the cell, and their degradation by a |FRAME: MONOMER-16283| to the end products |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| (|CITS: [11489857]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6735|)., Among bacteria |FRAME:TAX-562| cannot utilize |FRAME: Starch|, but it can metabolize short, linear maltodextrins (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY|). However the enterobacterium |FRAME: TAX-290336| can utilize |FRAME: Starch| as a sole source of carbon and energy. Mutant analysis suggested that it metabolizes |FRAME: Starch| by two pathways. The first was a proposed maltose/maltodextrin pathway involving extracellular degradation of |FRAME: Starch| by pullulanase and the disproportionation activity of cyclodextrin glucanotransferase to form linear maltodextins. After transport into the cell they are degraded to |FRAME: GLC| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by the products of malP, malQ and malZ. The second was a proposed cyclodextrin pathway involving extracellular conversion of |FRAME: Starch| to cyclodextrins (see |FRAME: Cyclodextrins|) by cyclodextrin glucanotransferase, transport into the cell, linearization by |FRAME: MONOMER-16314| (CymH) |CITS: [8599539]|, and further catabolism as in the maltose/maltodextrin pathway |CITS: [8594196] [9573146]|., About This Pathway, The hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-186497| is an obligately anaerobic heterotroph that is able to utilize a variety of sugars as a primary carbon source. Its genome encodes many glycosyl hydrolases and transferases, the physiological function of which are unclear. Using global transcriptional profiling data and biochemical studies |CITS: [16513741]| have defined the pathway for starch metabolism in |FRAME: TAX-186497|. This pathway involves an |FRAME: MONOMER-16303| (PF1935*) acting extracellularly, and |FRAME: MONOMER-16304| (PF0272), |FRAME: MONOMER-16305| (maltodextrin phosphorylase) (PF1535) and phosphoglucomutase (PF0588) acting intracellularly. Although other candidates for |FRAME: Starch| degrading enzymes were annotated in the |FRAME: TAX-186497| genome, they did not appear to be functionally involved in |FRAME: Starch| degradation (|CITS: [16513741]| and in |CITS: [17921308]|)., In this pathway |FRAME: Starch| is degraded extracellularly by |FRAME: MONOMER-16303| which has both pullulanase and α-amylase activity. Products of its α-amylase activity include maltodextrins (see |FRAME: Maltodextrins|), |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: D-Glucose| |CITS: [15599521] [9293009]|. Two active transporters Mal-II and Mal-I transport maltodextrins and |FRAME: MALTOSE| respectively, into the cell |CITS: [15803655]|. A |FRAME: MONOMER-16304| generates |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| from |FRAME: MALTOSE| and maltodextrins. |FRAME: MONOMER-16305| (maltodextrin phosphorylase) converts maltodextrins to |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS: [16513741]|., The |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| produced in the pathway are proposed to enter the novel glycolytic pathway of this organism after conversion of the latter compound to |FRAME: ALPHA-GLC-6-P| by phosphoglucomutase (EC 5.4.2.2) |CITS: [16513741]|. In aqueous solution the epimers |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| and |FRAME: GLC| spontaneously interconvert, forming an equilibrium mixture |CITS: [FRANKS87]|. Likewise, |FRAME: ALPHA-GLC-6-P| exists in equilibrium with its epimer |FRAME: GLC-6-P|. These reactions can also be enzyme-catalyzed. Whether the α, β, or both α and β epimers are used depends upon the anomeric specificity of the enzymes that utilize these compounds.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| is a non-standard amino acid that is not normally incorporated into proteins, during protein synthesis., The name citrulline was coined in 1930 from |FRAME:TAX-3653|, the Latin name of the watermelon, from which it was, first isolated., Free citrulline is formed mainly by catabolism of amino acids in the small intestine (see, |FRAME:CITRULBIO-PWY|), as an intermediate in the conversion of ammonia to urea in the, |FRAME:PWY-4984|, and as a by-product during the production of nitric oxide (see, |FRAME:PWY-4983|)., In addition, citrulline is also formed by modification of arginine residues in proteins (see, |FRAME: PWY-4921|)., About This Pathway, Free citrulline metabolism involves three key enzymes: nitric oxide synthase (NOS, EC 1.14.13.39), which catalyzes, the production of nitric oxide from arginine, generating citrulline as a by-product, |FRAME:CPLX-6662|, (OCT, EC 2.1.3.3), which produces citrulline by condensing carbamoyl phosphate and L-ornithine,, and |FRAME: CPLX-6641| (ASS, EC 6.3.4.5), which converts citrulline into argininosuccinate., The tissue distribution of these enzymes results in three orthogonal metabolic routes for citrulline in, mammals, all of which are depicted in this pathway:, 1. In the liver, citrulline is locally synthesized by the combined action of |FRAME:CPLX-6621|,, |FRAME: HS00415-MONOMER| and |FRAME:CPLX-6662|, and, metabolized by |FRAME: CPLX-6641| and |FRAME:CPLX-6661| back to arginine., The main purpose of this cycle is the production of urea, and it is described in greater detail in the pathway, |FRAME:PWY-4984|. , 2. In most of the tissues producing NO, citrulline is generated from arginine in a single step by NOS,, and then recycled back into arginine via |FRAME: CPLX-6641| and |FRAME:CPLX-6661|., The main purpose of this cycle is the production of NO, and it is described in greater detail in the, pathway |FRAME:PWY-4983|. , 3. In the gut citrulline is synthesized from glutamine and other amino acids (such as proline) by the, combined action of many enzymes, including, |FRAME:CPLX-6761|, |FRAME: HS00730-MONOMER|, |FRAME: HS01958-MONOMER|,, |FRAME:CPLX-6747| and |FRAME:CPLX-6662|., Citrulline is then released into the blood, and converted back into arginine in the kidneys by, |FRAME: CPLX-6641| and |FRAME:CPLX-6661|., The main purpose of this pathway is the transport of arginine in the blood, avoiding captation by the liver,, and it is described in the pathway |FRAME:CITRULBIO-PWY|., Citrulline has long been administered in the treatment of inherited urea cycle disorders, and recent studies, suggest that it may be used to control the production of NO., In plants, citrulline has additional roles. It has been shown that in, drought-tolerant wild watermelon leaves citrulline functions both as a compatible solute and ahydroxyl, radical scavenger |CITS: [11728468][12102508]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13804 "Erythromycin A"| is a macrolide antibiotic with an antimicrobial spectrum similar to or slightly wider than that of penicillin. The antibiotic was isolated in 1952 from |FRAME: TAX-1836| by scientists from the Lilly research laboratories |CITS:[McGuire52]|. It was given the trade name "Ilotycin", but the name erythromycin was introduced the same year in an editorial announcing this antibiotic |CITS: [12984186]|, Erythromycin A is used in clinical medicine against infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria. It is also used for many pulmonary infections such as Legionnaire's disease and as an alternative for patients allergic to penicillins |CITS: [11851474]|., Erythromycin contains a 14-membered lactone ring with ten asymmetric centers (the aglycon is called |FRAME: CPD-13947|) and two sugars (|FRAME: CPD-13969| and |FRAME: CPD-13780|). The structure was elucidated in 1957 |CITS: [Wiley57]|, and the absolute stereochemistry was assigned by X-ray crystallography in 1965 |CITS: [14295195]|., The biosynthesis of erythromycin starts with the polyketide synthase (PKS) |FRAME: CPLX-8415| (DEBS). This modular PKS is composed on three subunits that contain a loading module that binds |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and six additional modules, each extending the nascent molecule by incorporating a molecule of |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| and releasing CoA and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [2024119][1618327]|. Following rearrangment, the final product of the synthase is |FRAME: CPD-428|, which is oxygenated by a monooxygenase to form the erythromycin aglycon, |FRAME: CPD-13947| |CITS: [2446657][1840640][1732208]|., Two glycosyl transferase, encoded by |FRAME: G-14884| and |FRAME: G-14883|, transfer the deoxysugars |FRAME: CPD-13969| and |FRAME: CPD-13780| to the aglycone, respectively, resulting in the first compound with antibiotic activity, |FRAME: CPD-13806| |CITS: [9353926]|. , Two additional steps are required to generate the most active compound, |FRAME: CPD-13804| - an oxygenation |CITS: [8416893]| and a methylation |CITS: [2185226]|, catalyzed by enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-14865| and |FRAME: G-14864|, respectively. Depending on the order in which these two enzymes act, two other active intermediates are formed - |FRAME: CPD-13805| and |FRAME: CPD-13951|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylate"| is an aromatic compound that is is common throughout the plant kingdom and is also found in some bacteria. Salicylate is an important phytohormone, mediating both local and systemic defense responses in plants. It induces flowering and is involved in resistance against pathogen infection through the systematic acquired resistance mechanism |CITS: [12873532][15283665]|., Two pathways have been described for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-110| in plants. In Arabidopsis, the majority of |FRAME: CPD-110| is derived from|FRAME: CHORISMATE| via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8321|. However, salicylate can also be synthesized via |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA|, and |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|. Isotope feeding experiments in tobacco and other higher plants, including rice, demonstrated that free benzoate can serve as the direct precursor of salicylate |CITS: [12231938][9765542]|., Benzoate is synthesized by cinnamate chain shortening reactions via a β-oxidation process analogous to fatty acid β-oxidation |CITS: [11219576]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6458|). Benzoate is then converted to salicylate by benzoate 2-hydroxylase (BA2H) |CITS: [7479795]|. As of 2021, no gene has been specified for encoding this enzyme |CITS: [32362901]|., More recent studies in tobacco indicated that conjugated forms of benzoate - CoA thioesters or glucose esters, are more likely to be the precursors of salicylate |CITS: [11154339]|.

Summary: |FRAME:TAX-562| can utilize alkanesulfonates as a sulfur source for growth.  Utilization of alkanesulfonate as well as, methanesulfonate and L-cysteate requires the two-component alkanesulfonate monooxygenase system consisting, of an NAD(P)H-dependent FMN reductase and an FMN-dependent alkanesulfonate monooxygenase, |CITS: [10480865][11750815]|., Flavin cofactors are usually bound to proteins through strong covalent or non-covalent interactions; in this system,, however, the flavin serves as a substrate for both enzymes and is not bound as a prosthetic group.  Thus, the, transfer of the reduced flavin between the FMN reductase and the monooxygenase must be tightly controlled to, prevent generation of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, superoxide, or hydroxyl radicals.  Recent studies showed, kinetic interactions between the FMN reductase and the monooxygenase |CITS: [15882995]| and the formation of a, stable complex between the two enzymes |CITS: [16997955]|.  These results support a model for direct transfer of the, reduced flavin., Review: |CITS: [11479697]|

Cyanogenesis is the process that enables plants to release |FRAME:HCN| from cyanogenic glucosides (α-hydroxynitrile β-glucosides) upon tissue disruption as a chemical defense against herbivores and predators. Therefore the liberation of the respiratory poison |FRAME:HCN| can be defined as a bio-activation process of deterring compounds resulting from the interaction of cyanogenic glucosides and their cleaving enzymes (β-glucosidases,,  α-hydroxynitrile lyases) which are otherwise spatially separated in plant tissues |CITS:[16667728]|. The cleavage of cyanogenic glucosides comprises the sequential release of sugar and |FRAME:HCN| and is catalyzed either by a cyanogenic glucoside-specific β-glucosidase and a α-hydroxynitrile lyase (pH < 6) or the spontaneous dissoziation of |FRAME:HCN| from the aglycone (pH > 6) |CITS:[Ganjewala10]|., Among the edible plants humans use for food (maize, wheat, sorghum, cassava, sugarcane, many legumes) over two-thirds are cyanogenic. In spite of this apparent contradiction the occurrence of cyanogenic compounds in plants might have represented a favorable trait for selective domestication by the first farmers. Those plants were singled out because they were observed to be free of pests and food competitors and only humans developed over time the ability to overcome the poisonous effects by proper food processing |CITS:[9431670]|., It has been found that β-glucosidases involved in plant cyanogenesis are usually very specific and recognize both aglycone and glycone structure of the substrates |CITS:[17548373]|. The degradation of |FRAME:CPD-14589| and |FRAME:CPD-1103|, the endogenous cyanogenic glucosides in |FRAME:TAX-55501| is realized by two different β-glucosidases. Although those cyanogenic glucosides share most of the pathway and are very similar in structure and distribution within the plant the particular β-glucosidase only accepts its corresponding natural substrate |CITS:[NAHRSTEDT79]|  |CITS:[240769]|  |CITS:[411729]|. That seems to be different for cyanogenic β-glucosidases isolated from fungi as they display activity against a broad spectrum of cyanogenic substrates |CITS:[10380623]|.

Summary: |FRAME:TAX-562| is able to utilize either glycolate or glyoxylate as a sole source of carbon and energy. , There are two routes of this metabolism, the one shown here in which metabolism flows into the TCA, cycle and an alternate route (|FRAME: GLYCOLATEMET-PWY|) in which it flows into glycolysis.  The, alternate route (|FRAME: GLYCOLATEMET-PWY|) is apparently essential for |FRAME:TAX-562| to be able to, grow on either of these two substrates because a mutational block in its key enzyme (glyoxylate, carboligase) precludes growth on either substrate.  This pathway (|FRAME: GLYOXDEG-PWY|) appears, to play an ancillary role because a mutational block in its key enzyme (malate synthase G) has no, detectable effect on the utilization of either substrate, although it must be significant because malate, synthase is strongly induced by the presence of glyoxylate.  (|FRAME:TAX-562| has two malate synthases,, this one, called G and another, called A, which participates in the glyoxylate cycle.)  The essentiality of, the other pathway (|FRAME: GLYCOLATEMET-PWY|) may reflect the fact that that it feeds into, glycolysis and therefore becomes a source of acetyl-CoA which is essential for this pathway, (|FRAME: GLYOXDEG-PWY|). , In addition to the utilization of exogenous glycolate and glyoxylate, these pathways also allow, |FRAME:TAX-562| to utilize glyoxylate that was endogenously generated as a by-product of purine metabolism and, DNA repair. , Review: Clark, D.P. and J. Summary: Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman's net, with each cell of the mesh defined by two segments of parallel, glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks, which allow the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|. These peptide crosslinks are usually composed of two pentapeptides, each attached in one end to one of the glycan segment and extending towards (but not reaching) the other one. The two pentapeptides can form a crosslink with each other in more than one way., The composition and structure of peptidoglycan varies among different bacterial species, but in general consists of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues. The pentapeptide is bound through its N terminus to the carboxyl group of muramate., The pentapeptide is formed through the action of soluble enzymes that couple ATP-hydrolysis to the ligation of the amino acid monomers. This ATP-dependent coupling of amino acid monomers and elongating peptides by soluble enzymes is very unusual, as oligopeptides are usually formed either by ribosomes or by |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "nonribosomal peptide synthases"|. A similar mechanism is also found in the |FRAME: GLUTATHIONESYN-PWY "biosynthesis of glutatione"|., The pentapeptide, which contains alternating L and D amino acids, reveals considerable variation among species, with the greatest variation found in the third position. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: UDP-NAcMur-Peptides "UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-pentapeptide"| found in most of the Gram-positive organisms, which contains |FRAME:LYS| in the third position., For a complete peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway that incorporates this variation of pentapeptide, see |FRAME: PWY-5265|.

In addition to serving as an intermediate for the medicinal alkaloid berberine synthesis,, |FRAME: S-TETRAHYDROCOLUMBAMINE| can be converted to |FRAME: PALMATINE| via either, |FRAME: TETRAHYDROPALMATINE| or |FRAME: COLUMBAMINE|.

|FRAME:CPD-16664 Ophiobolin F| is a member of 25 ophiobolins identified to date in various genera of fungi |CITS:[10968403]|. Like |FRAME:CPD-18556| (see |FRAME:PWY-7736|) ophiobolins belong to the terpenoid class of sesterterpenoids which are formed by a homologous series of five isoprene units (C25) and thus stand between diterpenoids (C20) and triterpenoids (C30) with four and six isoprene units, respectively |CITS:[Crews85] [23385977]|. , The first ophiobolin was identified and purified from Bipolaris oryzae (formerly referred to as Helminthosporium oryzae) and named cochliobolin |CITS:[Orsenigo57]|, which was however later renamed to ophiobolin |CITS:[Nakamura58]|. The best known ophiobolin is |FRAME:CPD-18465| because of its reported ability to arrest the cell cycle |CITS:[25890975]|, hence showing promise as anticancer agent |CITS:[26212208] [23538442]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-18465| has been shown to constitute a natural inhibitor of calmodulin and as such interferes with the function of essential enzymes |CITS:[6321479] [12145198]|. Other ophiobolins have been demonstrated to exhibit mycoherbicide activities |CITS:[16962149]|, show potential as anti-tumor drug |CITS:[25603341]| and also displayed antifungal and antiprotozoal activities |CITS:[25812930]|., It is known that many specialized metabolites in fungi reside in silent biosynthetic gene clusters which under certain cultural conditions are inactive and do not produce any products |CITS:[20433937] [23178386]|. The biosynthesis of the sesterterpenoid |FRAME:CPD-16664| has been identified in Aspergillus clavatus by an genome mining approach utilizing |FRAME:MONOMER-14878| (see |FRAME:PWY-6659|) as probe. The specifically developed expression system for specialized metabolites in Aspergillus oryzae allowed to elucidate the biosynthetic steps towards |FRAME:CPD-16664|. The Aspergillus clavatus sesterterpene synthase encoded by OS was shown to consist of two domains, i.e. a C-terminal prenyltransferase (PT) domain and an N-terminal terpene cyclase (TC) domain. The two domains enable the OS encoded protein to act as a bifunctional enzyme hence prenylate |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| and form |FRAME:ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| via |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, whereas the terpene cyclase (TC) part of the enzyme catalyzed the cyclization reaction to form |FRAME:CPD-16664| from |FRAME:ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE|, hence forming the 5-8-5-membered tricyclic fused structure which is characteristic for ophiobolins |CITS:[23324037]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-11749 "Phosalacine"| is a herbicidal antibiotic containing |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN| produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2065|., It is believed that phosalacine is decomposed in vivo to provide |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN|, which has the actual antibiotic and herbicidal effect, by mimicking L-glutamate and inhibiting the enzyme glutamine synthetase |CITS: [6480502][6480509]|., |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN| is produced by at least three species of actinomycetes as a component of non-ribosomally synthesized peptides. These include |FRAME: CPD-11749|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-2065| |CITS: [6480502]| and |FRAME: CPD-10013| (PTT), which is produced by some strains of |FRAME: TAX-1912| |CITS: [7166539]| and |FRAME: TAX-1938| |CITS: [5010035]|., The peptides are potent antibiotics and herbicides, transported into cells via the oligopeptide transport system, and hydrolyzed intracellularly by peptidases, releasing the toxic |FRAME: L-PHOSPHINOTHRICIN|., Studies of |FRAME: CPD-10013| biosynthesis in either of these two organisms suggest that it involves no less than 18 discrete enzymatically catalyzed reactions, starting from the common metabolite |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|. These enzymatic steps have been linked to a chromosomal gene cluster about 35 kb in length that includes at least 24 genes that are essential for the process |CITS:[15574905][15616300]|. Most of the steps have been ellucidated, and many of the enzymes have been identified |CITS: [8593056][9673017][11472937][15616300][17632514][19516340]|., The pathway includes several unusual transformations, including a C(sp3)-C(sp3) bond cleavage by the |FRAME: G-11481|-encoded dioxygenase, the formation of two phosphorus-carbon bonds by |FRAME: MONOMER-15034| (|FRAME: G-11474|) and |FRAME: MONOMER-15054| (|FRAME: G-11494|), and the assembley of the peptide backbone by three nonribosomal peptide sythetases, encoded by |FRAME: G-11498|, |FRAME: G-11499| and |FRAME: G-11500|., Even though most of the sudies focused on |FRAME: CPD-10013| biosynthesis, the pathway for |FRAME:CPD-11749| biosynthesis is essentially identical up to the last five steps, where an |FRAME: LEU| residue substitutes for an |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| residue in the third position of the tripeptide., Different iterations of the pathway have been published over the years. A major revision of the upper part of the pathway, specifically the portion from |FRAME: CPD-551| to |FRAME:1-CARBOXYVINYL-CARBOXYPHOSPHONATE|, has been suggested in 2007 by |CITS: [17632514]|. A role for two small thioesterase-like genes (|FRAME: G-44318| and |FRAME: G-44319|) was proposed in 2015 |CITS: [26328935]|.

Summary: Jasmonates, including the conjugate |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"| (JA-ILe), are an important class of compounds, related to |FRAME:Jasmonic-Acids "jasmonic acid"|, found in many, if not all, plant species. These compounds may participate in a number of biological processes including resistance to herbivores and some pathogens, senescence, reproductive development, and protection against ozone |CITS:[16807821][17513307][19025383]|. , The hormonal action of jasmonate is controlled by the precise balance between its biosynthesis and inactivation. One of the main inactivation pathways is the oxidation of jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine at the C-12 position. Three successive oxidation steps, catalyzed by cytochromes P450 |FRAME: AT3G48520| and |FRAME: AT2G27690|, can convert the compound to |FRAME: CPD-13420| (12-OHJA), |FRAME: CPD-19811| and |FRAME: CPD-19812| |CITS: [22215670][26164240]|., The biological role of 12-OHJA is ambiguous. It has been shown to induce tuber formation in potatoes |CITS:[Helder93]|. It appears not to effect root growth and germination in tomato |CITS:[17995915]|, although it does prompt distinct sets of transcriptional changes in that plant |CITS:[17995915]|. 12OH-JA-Ile is less effective than JA-Ile in promoting COI1-JAZ interaction, although it still maintains some activity as a receptor ligand |CITS: [21576464]|. 12COOH-JA-Ile, on the other hand, is completely inactive in promoting COI1-JAZ interaction |CITS: [25210037]|., A branching point exists at the level of |FRAME: CPD-13420| due to the action of hydrolases encoded by the |FRAME: G-3181| and |FRAME: AT1G44350| genes, which liberate the isoleucyl group, generating |FRAME: CPD-11260|, which so far appears to be inactive., |FRAME: CPD-11260| is known to be sulfated into |FRAME: 12-Hydroxyjasmonate-Sulfates| (12-OHJA) |CITS:[ 17995915]| and glucosylated into |FRAME: CPD-19813| |CITS: [24467969]|. No biological activity has been attributed to the sulfated 12-OHJA derivative. Unlike methyl JA, |FRAME: 12-Hydroxyjasmonate-Sulfates| does not inhibit germination or root elongation in tomato seedlings |CITS: [17995915]|. Its fate is also not clear, but it is not likely to be a hydrolyzable storage form of hydroxyjasmonate because the Arabidopsis genome is not predicted to encode sulfatases |CITS:[12637544]|.

Summary: General Background, Phytoalexins are low-molecular weight compounds that are synthesized and accumulated in plants after exposure to microorganisms. They have been suggested to serve as plant antibiotics in the defense systems of plants |CITS: [11149940]|. Biosynthesis of phytoalexins is induced in infected leaves of rice plants. Four structurally distinct types of polycyclic diterpenes, oryzalexins A-F, (-)-phytocassanes A-E, momilactones A and B, and oryzalexin S, have been identified as phytoalexins in the infected rice leaves. The diterpenes ent-cassa-12,15-diene, ent-sandaracopimara-8(14),15-diene, 9β-pimara-7,15-diene and stemar-13-ene are thought to be the precursors to phytocassanes A-E, oryzalexins A-F, momilactones A and B and oryzalexin S, respectively |CITS: [14675427]|., About This Pathway, This branched pathways starts with the cyclization of geranylgeranyl diphosphate into ent-copalyl diphosphate and syn-copalyl diphosphate. The catalytic conversion of these two compounds into the four diterpene hydrocarbons is achieved by diterpene cyclases thought to play key roles in the biosynthesis of rice diterpenoid phytoalexins. The metabolic fate of the ambiguous |FRAME:CPD-9907| remains to be elucidated. However, it has been demonstrated that the cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase (CYP99A3) (see |FRAME:PWY-7477|) was able to catalyze the successive oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-9907| yielding |FRAME:CPD-16681|. This oxidation cascade comprised the conversion of the C19 methyl group (|FRAME:CPD-9907|) into a carboxylic acid group (|FRAME:CPD-16681|) via the intermediate alcohol (|FRAME:CPD-16679|) and aldehyde (|FRAME:CPD-16680|). Although those compounds have not yet been identified in Oryza the metabolic activity of CYP99A3 indicates the direction of possible biosynthetic pathways |CITS:[21175892]|.

Summary: The Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1534| is a non-saccharolytic anaerobic organism that can ferment |FRAME:ETOH| and |FRAME:ACET| to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID|, |FRAME: HEXANOATE| (caproate), and molecular hydrogen |CITS:[16588706][Bornstein48][4055746]|. In additon, this organism can utilize |FRAME:SUC| , |FRAME: CROTONATE|, |FRAME: VINYL-ACETATE|, and |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE| |CITS: [Kenealy85]|., In this pathway, |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, which is derived from |FRAME:ETOH| (see |FRAME: ETOH-ACETYLCOA-ANA-PWY|) can be processed in two routes. In the first route, acetyl-CoA is converted  to |FRAME:ACET| via |FRAME: ACETYL-P|. This conversion generates ATP, which is required for growth, by substrate-level phosphorylation |CITS: [5655494 ]|., In the second route, the reducing power which accumulates during the conversion of ethanol to acetyl-CoA is dispensed via a cycle that results in the excretion of |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (or |FRAME: HEXANOATE|)., The cycle starts with the condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules to form acetoacetyl-CoA. This compund then proceeds in a cycle via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-650| and |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA|, forming |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|., The later reacts with |FRAME:ACET| via a transacylation reaction. Acetate is acylated to acetyl-CoA, while |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is converted to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID|, which is secreted from the cell. The acetyl-CoA that is formed can re-enter the pathway at the condensation step. Thus, the four electrons obtained from the oxidation of ethanol are balanced with the four necessary to reduce the four-carbon moiety formed from one ethanol and one acetate |CITS: [4055746]|., The same cycle can operate with different CoA donors for the condensation reaction. When |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| or |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| are the donors, the cycle intermediates are different, and the secreted compound is not butyrate but |FRAME: VALERATE| or |FRAME: HEXANOATE|, respectively., A very similar pathway has been described in a related organism, |FRAME: TAX-155865|. The only difference is that the source of acetyl-CoA in this organism is not ethanol, but rather pyruvate, derived from amino acids |CITS: [15347751]|., The main difference between this pathway and the one described in |FRAME: CENTFERM-PWY| is the last step. In the other pathway, |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is converted to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| in an energy conserving route via |FRAME: BUTYRYL-P|. In this pathway, the conversion is a single-step transacylation reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-6|. This reaction yields the CoA donor for a subsequent condensation reaction, and is thus responsible for the cyclical nature of this pathway.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [Shellhammer90][15012185][11706201]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.15|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.4|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|. Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria and certain fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. While the biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail only in bacteria, ongoing success in sequencing whole genomes from other organisms has provided evidence that the general steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Despite the importance and prevalance of biotin, its detailed biosynthetic pathway remained enigmatic for over 70 years. Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, and is derived from |FRAME: CPD-205|. The early steps of the pathway, which are described here, are limited to the synthesis of the precursor pimelate moiety. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described in |FRAME: PWY0-1507|., Distinct pimelate synthesis pathways have been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| (see |FRAME: PWY-6519| and |FRAME: PWY-7147|). However, the α-proteobacteria lack the genes necessary for those pathways. Instead, they encode a different gene in their biotin bisynthesis operons, which is similar to |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.180| (FabH). The gene has been named bioZ |CITS: [11320134]|., In 2020 it has been shown that BioZ indeed catalyzes a reaction similar to that carried out by FabH. However, while FabH uses |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as a primer for elongation with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP malonyl-[acp]|, BioZ uses |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA|, an intermediate in lysine degradation, as the primer. By condensing |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP malonyl-[acp]| the enzyme forms |FRAME: 3-oxopimeloyl-ACPs 3-oxopimeloyl-[acp]|. The three fatty acid biosynthesis enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.100|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.59|, and |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.9|, (FabG, FabA, and FabI) complete the conversion of this compound to |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs pimeloyl-[acp]| |CITS: [33154364]|., The last step of the pathway, which is common to all biotin biosynthetic pathways described so far, is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.47| (BioF), which converts |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs pimeloyl-[acp]| to |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE|.

Summary: General Background, The mitochondrial |FRAME: CARNITINE| shuttle pathway is part of the cellular |FRAME: CARNITINE| system that regulates pools of |FRAME: CO-A| derivatives. This system is comprised of membrane proteins that transport |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and carnitine acyltransferase enzymes (found in mitochondria, peroxisomes and the endoplasmic reticulum) that catalyze a freely reversible equilibrium between |FRAME: ACYL-COA| and |FRAME: O-Acyl-L-Carnitines|. Acyl-L-carnitine esters provide transport of acyl groups between cellular compartments, provide a source of activated acyl groups, and provide a vehicle for excreting excess acyl groups. Reviewed in |CITS: [11257506]|. See pathway |FRAME: PWY-6100|., In mammalian mitochondria, |FRAME: CARNITINE| provides transport of fatty acids into the lumen for energy production via β-oxidation. Trans-esterification of fatty acid CoA esters (|FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs|) to |FRAME: CARNITINE| is essential because fatty acid CoA esters cannot cross the mitochondrial membranes. Reviewed in |CITS: [11257506]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway, referred to as the carnitine shuttle, long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs (such as |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA|, produced by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.3|, are trans-esterified to |FRAME: CARNITINE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-14439| (one of three possible tissue isoforms) at the mitochondrial outer membrane. Genes encoding mammalian liver, muscle and brain isoforms of this enzyme have been identified as |FRAME: G-11015|, Cpt1b and Cpt1c, respectively |CITS: [18248603]|. This rate-limiting enzyme is a key regulatory step for fatty acid β-oxidation due to its sensitivity to inhibition by |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| produced during fatty acid biosynthesis (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-4381|). It is also of interest as a target for anti-obesity and anti-diabetes drugs |CITS: [17458181] [16615913]|. A specific carrier, the |FRAME: MONOMER-14443|, then transports the long-chain O-acyl-L-carnitine esters through the inner mitochondrial membrane. Reviewed in |CITS: [11257506] [11802770]|., On the mitochondrial lumen side, the O-acyl-L-carnitine esters are trans-esterified back to their |FRAME: CO-A| esters by |FRAME: MONOMER-14441| (Cpt2), using intramitochondrial |FRAME: CO-A|. Released |FRAME: CARNITINE| can leave the mitochondrion via the |FRAME: MONOMER-14443| and be available to shuttle more fatty acids into the mitochondrion. Reviewed in |CITS: [11257506] [11802770]|., Intramitochondrial |FRAME: CARNITINE| can also be transesterified to |FRAME: O-ACETYLCARNITINE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-14440| (EC 2.3.1.7) using |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, the product of fatty acid β-oxidation (see pathway |FRAME: FAO-PWY|). |FRAME: O-ACETYLCARNITINE| can then leave the mitochondrion via the |FRAME: MONOMER-14443|. Similarly, |FRAME: CO-A| derivatives of short-chain fatty acids can also be trans-esterifed by this enzyme and leave the mitochondrion. All of these reversible acylations provide a mechanism for modulation of intracellular |FRAME: CO-A| and acyl-CoA concentrations. Reviewed in |CITS: [11257506] [11802770]|.

|FRAME: CPD-18280 2,4-Xylenol| is a byproduct of the coal gas industry and has been listed in the Priority Pollutants List by the US Environmental Protection Agency for its environmental toxicity., The first report of bacterial degradation of |FRAME: CPD-18280| was made in 1962 |CITS: [Leibnitz62]|. That organism, an unidentified Pseudomonad, oxidized |FRAME: CPD-18280| to |FRAME: CPD-18291|, but complete degradation was not reported at that time., Complete degradation into |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| was reported in 1968 by another Pseudomonas strain, later named |FRAME: ORG-6283| |CITS: [4387388]|. Several additional intermediates were observed - |FRAME: CPD-18294| and |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and a complete route (as shown here) has been suggested., According to the proposed pathway, |FRAME: CPD-18280| degradation is initiated by oxidation of the para-methyl group to a carboxyl group via an alcohol and an aldehyde intermediates, forming |FRAME: CPD-18291|. In the next stage, the ortho-methyl group in |FRAME: CPD-18291| is also oxidized to a carboxyl group, again via an alcohol and an aldehyde termediates, producing |FRAME: CPD-18294|. Finally, 4-hydroxyisophthalate is converted to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, entering the |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY "ortho ring-cleavage pathway"| for further metabolism |CITS: [4387388]|., Two of the pathway's enzymes, |FRAME: MONOMER-19471| |CITS: [ElMansi90]| and |FRAME: MONOMER-19472| |CITS: [18349]|, were purified from |FRAME: ORG-6283| and characterized, although their encoding genes were not reported., The enzymes catalyzing the first part of the pathway (the oxidation of the para-methyl group to a carboxyl group) were shown to be identical to those involved in |FRAME: PWY-7700| by the same organism |CITS: [23736872]|. The first enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.17.9.1|), encoded by the |FRAME: G-44167| and |FRAME: G-44168| genes, catalyzes the hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-18280| to |FRAME: CPD-18289| and its subsequent dehydrogenation to |FRAME: CPD-18290|. The second enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.2.1.96|), encoded by |FRAME: G-44179|, hydroxylates the aldehyde to a carboxylate., Another strain (originally reported as Paracoccus sp. strain U120, but eventually classified as |FRAME: TAX-200254| |CITS: [Mechichi02]|) was also reported to degrade |FRAME: CPD-18280| |CITS: [1904702]|. However, that organism performed the degradation anaerobically, using nitrate as the electron acceptor, and the pathway diverged from the pathway shown here at the stage of |FRAME: CPD-18291|, which was converted to a CoA ester.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-633 Gentisate| and substituted gentisates serve as key intermediates in the aerobic pathways for the, metabolism of a large number of aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYBENZOATE| |CITS: [1427003], [2256782]|, substituted phenols |CITS: [907340][6995451]|, |FRAME: CPD-110| |CITS:[Ohmoto91][8645313]|,, |FRAME: CPD-11248| |CITS: [9696766]|, and |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE| |CITS: [9573207][1622263][2988437]|., Two pathway variants are known for the degradation of gentisate. Both pathways start with the ring-cleavage oxidation of gentisate to yield |FRAME: CPD-1070|. However, in one pathway variant (the isomerization route) maleylpyruvate is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-277|, with the subsequent hydrolysis to |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6223|), while in the other variant (the direct hydrolysis route) maleylpyruvate is hydrolyzed directly to |FRAME: MALEATE| and pyruvate |CITS: [5704827]|., About This Pathway, In the pathway described here maleylpyruvate is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-277|. This conversion is performed by either a |FRAME: MONOMER-14770| |CITS: [11133965]| or by a |FRAME: G18NG-12642-MONOMER| |CITS: [16481315]|, depending on the species. In the last step of the pathway |FRAME: CPD-277| is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which enter central metabolism at the TCA cycle |CITS: [7400101][907340][2256782][14461395][8760924]|.

The compound |FRAME: CPD-6959| is a stilbene produced by a number of plants as a defense response compound. Its localization varies in different plant species, it is commonly found in leaves and fruits such as |FRAME: TAX-29760| and blueberries, in the heartwood of sandalwood trees, and in barks of Guibourtia tessmanii |CITS: [ 12150803]|. |FRAME: CPD-6959| has been subjected to a number of pharmacological studies because of their known medicinal properties in folk medicine. Its chemical structure is very similar to |FRAME: CPD-83|, but because of its double methylated nature it carries higher bioavailability |CITS: [21116625]|, and thus has a higher transport rate into cells. Based on animal studies, |FRAME: CPD-6959| has been shown to be effective as an antineoplastic |CITS: [21056131]| antiinflammatory as well as anti-oxidant agent and all these properties are reviewed in this monograph |CITS: [20807001]|., In this pathway, the methyltransferase enzymes responsible for the formation of |FRAME: CPD-6959| from the precursor |FRAME: CPD-83| via |FRAME: CPD-12871| has been cloned |CITS: [18799660]|.

C-glycosides are widespread in the plant kingdom and have been shown to occur in at least 20 families of angiosperms |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. Moreover, they have also been found in insects and microbes |CITS:[17404902]| and are attributed to a broad range of biological activities. They act as antioxidants |CITS:[Ramarathnam89]| |CITS:[1824129]|, show antimicrobial activity |CITS:[16651765]|, facilitate mycorrhizal symbioses |CITS:[12026171]|, screen and protect from UV |CITS:[Les90]| and are valuable agents in preventing lipoprotein oxidation |CITS:[Kim2005]| and cancer development |CITS:[11172671]| in humans. , C-glycosideflavonoids represent the largest group of C-glycosides in plants and are especially dominant in cereals such as maize, wheat and rice |CITS:[17404902]| |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. The special attachment of the aglycone directly to the C1 of the pyranose ring of a sugar confers high structural stability to the C-glycosides which even withstand acidic treatment., The pathway has been shown to proceed via 2-hydroxyflavanone precursors |CITS:[Kerscher87]| |CITS:[Kerscher88]|. This first committed reaction of the pathway is catalyzed by a flavanone 2-hydroxylase which hydoxylates the corresponding flavanones |CITS:[20647377]|. The C-glycosyltransferase only acts on the open form of the 2-hydroxyflavanones, i.e. dibenzoylmethane tautomers which are glycosylated at position 6 of the A ring |CITS:[19411659][Kerscher88]|. In vitro experiments showed that upon acidic treatment the 2-hydroxyflavanone glucosides were dehydrated to the corresponding flavones forming a mixture of 6C and 8C-glycosylflavones. However, in planta experiments demonstrated the existence of a C-glycosylflavanone dehydratase which preferentially catalyzed the formation of 6C-glycosylflavones |CITS:[19411659]|. C-glycosylflavones extracted from rice revealed a pattern of |FRAME:GLC| attached to 6C and |FRAME:CPD-12049| attached to 8C of the A-ring |CITS:[Besson85]| whereas in wheat the pattern was |FRAME:GLC| in 6C and |FRAME:BETA-D-XYLOSE| in the 8C position |CITS:[16494903]|. To date the characterized C-glycosyltransferases only act on |FRAME: CPD-12575| in vitro |CITS:[19411659]| and the question whether or not one or more C-glycosyltransferases are involved in the pathway remains to be shown. Besides |FRAME:CPD-15084| and |FRAME:CPD-15087| various other C-glycosylflavones in cereals are produced from either |FRAME:NARINGENIN-CMPD| (see |FRAME:PWY-6602|) or |FRAME:CPD-6994| (see |FRAME:PWY-7188|).

The H+/e- ratio of proline dehydrogenase has not been determined; cytochrome bo oxidase catalyses both vectorial and scalar proton translocation |CITS: [1850294]|. , Proline dehydrogenase functions as both a membrane associated bifunctional dehydrogenase and a cytosolic transcriptional repressor, switching between the two functions in response to proline availability (reviewed in |CITS: [18324349]|). Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Vitamins-B6 Vitamin B6| is a group term for |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| (PL), |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| (PN), |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| (PM) and their 5'-phosphorylated derivatives |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| (PLP), |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE-5P| (PNP) and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP), which are also referred to as vitamers. Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) is the biochemically active form, and is an essential cofactor in all living systems |CITS: [7748903]|. It plays an important role in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism and has been implicated in singlet oxygen resistance. Most bacteria, archaebacteria, fungi, and plants synthesize PLP in a single reaction, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6466|, although some bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, use a longer, more complex pathway (|FRAME: PYRIDOXSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [9696782][12896974]|. Animals do not synthesize this compound, making it an essential nutrient in their diet., PLP is an essential cofactor of numerous metabolic enzymes, predominantly in amino acid metabolism. It is one of the most versatile cofactors and participates in transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, Cα-Cβ cleavage and α-β elimination reactions. In humans this vitamin has a role in numerous functions ranging from modulation of hormone function to potent antioxidant activity., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of this vitamin was thoroughly studied in |FRAME:TAX-562| and involves two branches with seven enzymatic steps. In one branch, the sequential action of the enzymes Epd, PdxB and SerC results in the convesrion of erythrose 4-phosphate into 4-phosphohydroxy-L-threonine. The latter then undergoes oxidation and decarboxylation by PdxA to form 3-hydroxy-1-aminoacetone phosphate. In the other branch, deoxyxylulose 5-phosphate (DXP) is derived from glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (GAP) and pyruvate by the action of Dxs. The products of the two branches, i.e. 3-hydroxy-1-aminoacetone phosphate and DXP, are then condensed by PdxJ to form PNP, which enters the salvage pathway to undergo oxidation by PdxH to form the PLP cofactor., From the six pdx genes, two of them, epd and serC, are involved in other metabolic processes, but pdxA, pdxB, pdxJ and pdxH are unique for PLP biosynthesis |CITS: [1537800]|. PdxJ, the PNP synthase is the key ezyme that catalyzes a multistep ring closure yielding PNP and inorganic phosphate (Pi). This is the last step in the de novo synthetic pathway., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [17822383][15242009][12686115]|., An alternative DXP-independent pathway for PNP biosynthesis is described at |FRAME: PWY-6466|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7172 "Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol"| (THC) is the main psychoactive substance found in the cannabis plant. In 1988 it was found that the pharmacological actions of THC result from its binding to two receptors - the cannabinoid receptors CB1, located mainly in the central nervous system, and CB2, mainly present in cells of the immune system. Both receptors belong to the superfamily of membrane-bound G-protein-coupled receptors |CITS: [9336020]|., As THC is not a naturally occurring substance in the mammalian body, the existence of a specific receptor for THC implied that there should be endogenous molecules for these existing receptors (endocanabinoids). The first such molecule, |FRAME: CPD-7598| (N-arachidonoyl ethanolamine), was isolated by the Israeli scientist Raphael Mechoulam in 1992 |CITS: [1470919]|. Since then four more endocanabinoids have been reported - |FRAME: CPD-12600|, |FRAME: CPD-22217| (noladin ether), |FRAME: CPD-22218|, and |FRAME: CPD-22219| |CITS: [17227440]|., Binding of endocannabinoids (or cannabinoids) to cannabinoid receptors results in a decrease in the intracellular level of |FRAME: CAMP| and activation of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.24|, through the coupled Gi/o proteins. In addition, the activation of cannabinoid receptors modulates ion channels through Gi/o proteins, leading to the activation of A-type and inward-rectifyier potassium channels and the inhibition of N-type and P/Q-type calcium channels |CITS: [19126434]|., |FRAME: CPD-7598 Anandamide| is a fatty acid amide composed of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| coupled to |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| through an amide linkage |CITS: [7990962][19126434]|. Unlike THC, anandamide breaks down very quickly in the body, and thus does not produce the same psychoactive effect as THC., It is synthesized in areas of the brain that are important in memory and higher-thought processes. Synthesis is highest in the hippocampus, followed by the thalamus, cortex, as well as striatum, and lowest in the cerebellum, pons, and medulla |CITS: [8022836]|. |FRAME: CPD-7598 Anandamide| and other |FRAME: N-Acylethanolamines ethanolamides| are present in the maternal milk and were reported to be critical for milk ingestion and therefore the survival of the newborn., About This Pathway, Unlike classical neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, endocannabinoids are not stored in vesicles in the cell, and are produced on demand from membrane phospholipids. The phospholipid precursor of |FRAME: CPD-7598| is, |FRAME: N-arachidonoyl-PE "N-arachidonoyl phosphatidylethanolamine"| (NAPE), which is produced from |FRAME: 1-arachidonoyl-PC "1-arachidonoyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine"| by an N-acyltransferase enzyme |CITS: [12052034]|., While the most common pathway for |FRAME: CPD-7598| formation is via multiple routes originating in |FRAME: N-arachidonoyl-PE "N-arachidonoyl-phosphatidylethanolamine"| (see |FRAME: PWY-8051|), an alternative pathway originating from |FRAME: N-Ara-Ethanolamine-Plasmalogen "N-(arachidonoyl)ethanolamine plasmalogen"| has also been described |CITS: [21801852]|., Plasmalogen-type phospholipids constitute 65% of the total N-arachidonoylethanolamine phospholipids in rat brain, suggesting that N-acylethanolamine plasmalogens (pNAPEs) are a major class of N-acylethanolamine phospholipids in the brain |CITS: [17957091]|. , Schmid et al. reported that pNAPE is a good substrate of |FRAME: HS14850| in rat heart microsome, forming N-acylethanolamines directly |CITS: [6308001]|. In addition, Diether-type analogs of NAPEs were reported to be substrates of the enzyme |CITS: [16818490][19715685]|., |FRAME: HS14850|-independent biosynthesis of N-acylethanolamines from pNAPEs has also been reported |CITS: [21801852]|. The study, which took place in |FRAME: HS14850|-defficient mice, concluded that pNAPEs are hydrolyzed at the sn-2 position, forming |FRAME: 2-Lyso-N-Acyl-Plasmalogens "2-lyso-(N-acyl)ethanolamine plasmalogen"| (lyso-pNAPEs). The resulting lyso-pNAPEs cannot be hydrolyzed at the sn-1 position owing to the presence of an ether bond, and thus are acted on by |FRAME: HS06258-MONOMER|, forming N-acylethanolamines. The enzyme appears to be non-specific regarding the N-acyl species, as formation of |FRAME: CPD-7598|, |FRAME: CPD-20399|, and |FRAME: CPD-20398| was observed |CITS: [21801852]|.

Summary: Tryptophan biosynthesis in microbes involves five enzymes, encoded by 7 genes. The genes (trpA,B,C,D,E,F) , are usually arranged in a single cluster |CITS: [2679363]|, and form an operon whose transcription , is negatively regulated by tryptophan |CITS: [7007895]|. Additional regulation mechanisms exist at the translational and , post-translational levels, presumably because tryptophan synthesis is very expensive (78 mol ATP for each mol, of tryptophan produced)., In addition, hyperthermophilic organisms usually have an additional gene, trpB2, which is located outside of the , tryptophan operon. This gene encodes an additional enzyme which is similar to a subunit of tryptophan synthase., The two last steps in this pathway are catalyzed by a single enzyme, tryptophan synthase, which, is composed of two α and two β subunits (E.C. reaction 4.2.1.20). , However, it has been shown that each of the subunits is responsible for catalyzing an individual step, and is able , to catalyze that step on its own. Thus, the activity of tryptophan synthase was divided into , two individual steps in the pathway, each catalyzed by the corresponding subunit.

|FRAME: ASCORBATE| (vitamin C) production was estimated at 110,000 tons per year in 2001 |CITS: [11307843]|. , Most of the commercial production of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is via the Reichstein method that combines chemical and biotechnological steps. Since the process is inefficient, more cost-effective biotechnological methods are being investigated. Microbial processes that are in use involve conversion of |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, or |FRAME: CPD-9569| to the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-13059|, which is then converted to L-ascorbate by chemical esterification and lactonization |CITS: [16516325]|., The pathway shown here has been described in several genera, including |FRAME:TAX-286|, |FRAME:TAX-434| and |FRAME:TAX-441| |CITS: [Isono68]|. In this pathway, |FRAME: SORBITOL| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9569| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7573|. Several forms of this enzyme have been isolated and characterized, most of them from the genus |FRAME:TAX-441| |CITS: [11866120][16232778]|., In the conversion of L-sorbose to |FRAME: L-SORBOSONE| the open chain form of the product can hypothetically lactonize to either the furanose form |FRAME: CPD-9055|, or the pyranose form |FRAME: CPD-9056| |CITS: [16461703]|. The 2,6-lactone form was proposed to be converted to |FRAME: CPD-13059| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7574|.
