Summary: |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE "Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate"| (PLP, vitamin B6) is an essential cofactor in all living systems |CITS: [7748903]|. It is one of the most versatile cofactors and participates in transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, Cα-Cβ cleavage and α-β elimination reactions. PLP plays an important role in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism and has been implicated in singlet oxygen resistance |CITS: [10687384]|. , Most bacteria, archaebacteria, fungi, and plants synthesize PLP de novo in a single reaction, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6466|. Some bacteria use a longer, more complex pathway (see |FRAME: PYRIDOXSYN-PWY|). However, PLP is often synthesized by salvage pathways., This pathway described how PLP can be salvaged from |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL|, |FRAME: PYRIDOXINE| and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE|, which are taken up from the environment. The salvage of these three compounds involves only two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.35| and |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.5|.

General Background, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that contains a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide., Lipoate is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme systems involved in oxidative metabolism, including |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| |CITS: [2188967]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| |CITS: [1655709][8444795]|., Each of these enzyme complexes is composed of multiple copies of three enzymes: a substrate-specific, decarboxylase-dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), specific for each type of complex, and a dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3). , The (E2) proteins have a dedicated lipoyl domain. In order for the complex to be active, lipoate must be attached to the lipoyl domain by an amide linkage between its carboxylate moiety and a specific lysine residue in the enzyme |CITS: [8444795]|., E1 catalyzes a reaction in which the substrate is attached to the lipoate cofactor and decarboxylated. During this reaction, the lipoate cofactor is reduced to dihydriolipoate., E2 then catalyzes an acyl transfer step, in which the product of the reaction is released. Finally, E3 catalyzes the oxidation of the dihydrolipoyl cofactor back to lipoyl form, with NAD being the ultimate electron acceptor |CITS: [2188967]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of lipoate is unusual, and shares the same mechanism as the biosynthesis of biotin., The |FRAME: EG11796-MONOMER| (LplA) was initially described as acting only on lipoate that has, been imported from outside the cell (see |FRAME: PWY0-522|) |CITS: [8002607]|., However, a new role for this enzyme was found, following the observation that |FRAME:TAX-562| lipB mutants (defective in |FRAME:EG11591-MONOMER|), grew well with |FRAME: CPD-195| instead of |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID|., Octanoate growth required both |FRAME:EG11796-MONOMER| and |FRAME:CPLX0-782|, the enzyme, that converts octanoyl side chains to lipoyl side chains, suggesting that |FRAME:EG11796-MONOMER|, attached octanoate to the enzyme domain, and |FRAME:CPLX0-782| converted the octanoate to lipoate, |CITS: [14700636]|., The first enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: EG11591-MONOMER|, transfers octanoate to specific lysyl, residues in lipoate-dependent enzymes, resulting in the formation of octanylated domains, The next enzyme in the pathway, lipoate synthase, catalyzes the conversion of the octanoyl side chain, to an active lipoyl, generating a fully active lipoylated domain., The enzyme is an iron-sulfur protein that requires the presence of the molecule S-adenosyl-L-methionine (AdoMet) |CITS: [8444795][11106496]|., An electron which originates from the [4Fe-4S] cluster of the enzyme serves to split at least two, molecules of AdoMet into a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical and methionine |CITS: [11834738]|., The radical then abstracts a hydrogen from a C-H bond of thew octanoyl side chain, becoming, 5'-adenosine in the process. , The newly-formed unstable octanoyl radical then reacts directly with the Fe-S center of the enzyme., Two sulfur atoms from the center enter the structure of the octanoyl side chain, producing lipoyl, which, dissociates from the enzyme along with excess iron, leaving it with a [2Fe-2S] center., Thus, in this unusual reaction, the iron-sulfur center of the enzyme is not just a catalytic accelerator, but, also a substrate, donating the two sulfur atoms |CITS: [11153271]|. , It should be noted that while this process has been well documented in vitro |CITS: [11106496]|,, there is still a possibility that there exists another sulfur donor in vivo, and that the Fe-S center, acts as sulfur donor only in the absence of this natural donor |CITS: [11395404]|., Lipoate Biosynthesis in Other Organisms, Genes encoding LipA and LipB have been identified in mammalian genomes, and it has been shown that, mammalian cells are capable of synthesizing |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| in mitochondria |CITS: [11389890]|., However, their significance is not fully understood because it is generally believed that mammals, primarily rely on salvaged |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| (see |FRAME: PWY0-522|)., Lipoate biosynthesis has also been demonstrated in plants |CITS: [10671542]|., It is not clear whether Archaea utilize lipoate. No clear evidence is available, although the genes, encoding a putative 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complex have been reported in |FRAME: TAX-2246|, |CITS: [10832633]|.

Summary: General Background, Vitamin D refers to a group of fat-soluble secosteroids responsible for enhancing intestinal absorption of calcium, iron, magnesium, phosphate and zinc., In humans, the most important compounds in this group are |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3| (cholecalciferol), which is produced in animal skin from |FRAME: CPD-4187| after exposure to |FRAME: UV-Light| and |FRAME: Heat|, and |FRAME: VITAMIN_D2| (ergocalciferol), which is produced in plants and fungi from |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| after exposure to |FRAME: UV-Light|., In its activated form (|FRAME: CALCITRIOL|), vitamin D is necessary for optimal absorption and regulation of dietary |FRAME: CA+2| and |FRAME: Pi|. This nutrient is essential for the prevention of rickets, a bone-softening disease (reviewed in |CITS: [15585789][15951480][16563471]|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3 "Vitamin D3"|, a secosteroid pro-hormone, is produced in the skin by the action of |FRAME: UV-Light| and |FRAME: Heat| on |FRAME: CPD-4187| (pro-vitamin D3), a |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| biosynthetic intermediate (as shown in the pathway link). The initial product of photolysis is |FRAME: CPD-10570|, which is converted by thermal equilibration to the thermodynamically favored 5,6-isomer, |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3| |CITS: [194588]|. Under normal conditions, |FRAME: VITAMIN_D3| is transported to the liver via the plasma vitamin D binding protein where it is hydroxylated to |FRAME: CALCIDIOL| (25-hydroxy vitamin D3). This compound is transported to the kidney where it is further hydroxylated to the active metabolite |FRAME: CALCITRIOL| (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3). This metabolite is considered to be a hormone. Its binding to the nuclear vitamin D receptor is followed by a complex series of events that regulate gene expression. It also has non-genomic effects mediated by a membrane receptor and second messengers. Evidence is accumulating that |FRAME: CALCITRIOL| has many other functions, including cancer prevention, immune system modulation and endocrine system regulation. Reviewed in |CITS: [15951480] [16563471] [15585789] [12520537] [15544953]|., The identity of the liver enzyme catalyzing the hydroxylation of vitamin D3 at carbon 25 to form |FRAME: CALCIDIOL| has not been firmly established, although current evidence suggests that microsomal |FRAME: HS17721-MONOMER| is the most likely candidate for this function (in |CITS: [15951480]| and in |CITS: [15465040]|). However, studies in pig suggest that both liver microsomal CYP2D25 and mitochondrial |FRAME: MONOMER-14308| (EC 1.14.13.15, see |FRAME: PWY-6061|) can hydroxylate vitamin D3 to calcidiol |CITS: [12670492]|., The key, rate-limiting enzyme in the pathway appears to be kidney mitochondrial |FRAME: MONOMER-14354| (P450C1) (EC 1.14.13.13), based on studies in mouse, human and rat. It is negatively regulated by |FRAME: CALCITRIOL| at the transcriptional level (reviewed in |CITS: [15544953]|. However, based on pig studies it has been suggested that 1α hydroxylation of calcidiol in kidney can be accomplished by mitochondrial |FRAME: MONOMER-14308|, or a microsomal enzyme, as well as |FRAME: MONOMER-14354| (reviewed in |CITS: [11172626]|)., Catabolism (inactivation) of excess hormone |FRAME: CALCITRIOL| is an important regulatory point. It is catabolized in the kidney by pathways involving species-dependent side chain C24, or C23 hydroxylation. The C24 pathway is initiated by |FRAME: MONOMER-14357| which catalyzes initial side chain hydroxylation (|FRAME: MONOMER-14357|). In the C24 pathway the final metabolite |FRAME: CPD-10578| is excreted. The C23 pathway produces a side chain lactone end product (in |CITS: [17646648]|). The expression of both |FRAME: MONOMER-14354| and |FRAME: MONOMER-14357| is modulated by |FRAME: CALCITRIOL| and a variety of cellular regulatory agents including parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, and |FRAME: CA+2| and |FRAME: Pi| levels (reviewed in |CITS: [12520537] [15544953]|). An additional pathway involving a C3 epimerization of the A-ring has been described |CITS: [17196157]|. Summary: The |FRAME: Mammalian-GPI-Anchors "glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor"| is a glycolipid structure that is added posttranslationally to the C-terminus of many eukaryotic proteins (roughly 1% of all proteins encoded by eukaryotic genomes, and ~10-20% of all membrane proteins that enter the secretory pathway after being targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum). It anchors the attached protein in the outer leaflet of the cell membrane., The GPI anchor has a complex structure that includes a phosphoethanolamine linker, glycan core, and phospholipid tail. It is considered the most complex and metabolically expensive of the lipid posttranslational modifications described so far., Different components of the anchor were reported beginning in 1985, but the first detailed structural analysis of a GPI, anchor was reported 1988, for the variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) from parasitic protozoan |FRAME: TAX-5691| |CITS: [3340856]|. Analyses of the structures of protein-bound GPIs from mammals, protozoa, and yeast reveal that they have a conserved core structure: protein-CO-NH2-CH2-CH2-PO4-6-α-D-Man-(1→2)-α-D-Man-(1→6)-α-D-Man-(1→4)-α-D-GlcN-(1→6)-myo-inositol phospholipid., The GPI core in yeast and mammals is modified during its biosynthesis by the addition of a palmitoyl group to the 2-OH of the inositol moiety and by the addition of up to three ethanolamine phosphate (Etn-P) moieties to specific positions on the first three mannoses. Addition of a fourth, α(1,2)-linked mannose to the third mannose is obligatory in yeast but not in mammalian cells, although a fourth mannose may be added in a tissue-specific manner., The GPI anchor is preassembled by enzymes attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The pathway is initiated on the cytoplasmic face of the ER membrane and completed in the ER lumen, necessitating transbilayer flipping of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1113 "6-(α-D-glucosaminyl)-1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol"|. The flippase responsible for this transfer is the only enzyme that has not been identified, and may be identical to the flippase responsible for transferring |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE phosphatidylethanolamine| into the ER. The complete GPI anchor is transferred to target proteins in the lumen of the ER. Following the transfer, the acyl group attached to the 2-OH of the inositol moietyis removed. This removal initiates a post-attachment remodeling phase of the anchored protein and prompts an ER-to-Golgi transport of the GPI-anchored proteins |CITS: [24784135][38167496]|., Post attachment remodeling in yeast involves conversion of the diacylglycerol, which originally contains C16 and C18 fatty acids, to ceramides. A minor fraction contains a modified diacylglycerol containing C26:0 in position sn-2 |CITS: [8253761][9218792]|. In addition, an α(1,2) or α(1,3)-linked mannose can be added to mannose 4 in the Golgi by as yet unknown transferases |CITS: [7649981]|.

More recently, evidence has been obtained for a novel meta-cleavage pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| in |FRAME: TAX-395598| |CITS: [22609919]| as shown in this pathway., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-395598| can utilize |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| as a sole carbon source. Many nitroalkane compounds are used in the chemical industry as intermediate compounds in chemical syntheses. , Some of them are toxic or carcinogenic and their biodegradation is of considerable interest. Nitroalkane compounds , are also biosynthesized by microorganisms and plants as defense chemicals (in |CITS: [1217935] [16682407]|). , Bacteria, yeasts, fungi and higher plants have been shown to oxidize nitroalkane compounds to their corresponding , aldehydes or ketones, and nitrite. Industrially, oxidation of nitroalkanes to less toxic species can be used in , bioremediation. Biologically, these oxidations can counter the production of toxic nitroalkanes by other organisms, , or protect the producing organism |CITS: [16430210]|., Nitroalkanes such as |FRAME: CPD-12077| can undergo ionization of their α-carbon atoms producing the anionic alkyl nitronate (|FRAME: CPD-320|) form of the neutral nitroalkane (|FRAME: CPD-12077|) (reviewed in |CITS: [19577534]|). The enzyme nitronate monooxygenase (EC 1.13.12.16) was formerly referred to as 2-nitropropane dioxygenase (EC 1.13.11.32). This flavin-dependent enzyme uses |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| to oxidize anionic alkyl nitronates (and in the case of the |FRAME: TAX-5141| enzyme, neutral nitroalkanes), producing the corresponding carbonyl compounds and |FRAME: NITRITE|. The reaction mechanism of the enzyme which involves anionic flavosemiquinone intermediates, as well as its structural properties, are under investigation (reviewed in |CITS: [19577534]|)., As shown in this pathway, nitronate monooxygenase (formerly 2-nitropropane dioxygenase) oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-320| to |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: NITRITE|. The enzymes from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [9501443] [15582992]| and the yeast |FRAME: TAX-1004253 Cyberlindnera mrakii (previously known as Hansenula mrakii)"| |CITS: [11214] [7813473]| differ in their prosthetic groups, the former containing |FRAME: FMN| and the latter containing |FRAME: FAD|. The |FRAME: NITRITE| produced can subsequently be reduced to |FRAME: AMMONIA| by nitrite reductase and used in nitrogen-containing biomolecules |CITS: [1217935] [8096840]|., Recombinant |FRAME: FMN|-containing nitronate monooxygenase (formerly 2-nitropropane dioxygenase) from |FRAME: TAX-287| has also been produced and its crystal structure determined |CITS: [16682407]|. However, denitrifying bacteria reduce |FRAME: NITRITE| (from |FRAME: NITRATE|) via a different pathway (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY|)., Another |FRAME: FAD|-containing nitroalkane degrading enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7188|, from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5507|, has been extensively studied and its crystal structure has been determined |CITS: [16430210]|. The enzyme differes from nitronate monooxygenase in its mechanism, and in the production of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| as a product (reviewed in |CITS: [15581574]|). The reaction was designated as EC class 1.7.3 by |CITS: [22538]| and is described by EC 1.7.3.1 with |FRAME: CPD-12077| as substrate (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5355|)., Several other flavoenzymes from microorganisms have been shown to oxidize nitroalkanes including: nitroalkane , dioxygenase from Streptomyces ansochromogenes |CITS: [12473127]|; 3-nitropropionate oxidase (EC 1.7.3.5) , from Penicillium atrovenetum |CITS: [3667582]|; and glucose oxidase from |FRAME:TAX-5061| |CITS: [16930]|. In mammals, |FRAME: CPD-12077| oxidation by D-amino acid oxidase from pig kidney has been shown |CITS: [4145800]|. With the exception of nitroalkane oxidase from |FRAME: TAX-5507|, these enzymes react with the anionic form of the nitro-containing substrate. Nitroalkane oxidase prefers the neutral form (in |CITS: [16430210]|).

General Background, Bacteria often accumulate |FRAME: CHOLINE| because it can be easily converted to |FRAME: BETAINE|, a common osmoprotectant in bacteria |CITS: [LeRudulier84]|. Choline is also an essential nutrient for higher organisms, including humans, contributing to cell membrane function, methyl transfer events, and neurotransmission., Many organisms can catabolize choline via glycine betaine and utilize it as a sole source for both carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [3290197] [6406829]|. Two such pathways have been described from aerobic microbes (see |FRAME:CHOLINE-BETAINE-ANA-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-3721| and |FRAME: PWY-3661|). Other organisms are capable of anaerobic degradation of choline via |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE|, as described in this pathway., About This Pathway, Bacterial conversion of |FRAME: CHOLINE| to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| was first reported in 1910 |CITS: [Ackermann10]|. Subsequent experiments with whole cells and cell-free extracts of choline-fermenting anaerobic bacteria revealed that the pathway involves an initial C-N bond cleavage of choline to produce |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: ACETALD| |CITS: [13852193][14400373][13712528]|. The enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CHOLINE| to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.99.4|, was identified more than a hundred years later (in 2012) in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-207559| |CITS: [23151509]|. The enzyme utilizes a glycine radical to cleave the C-N bond in |FRAME: CHOLINE|., It is well known that symbiotic gut microbes in humans |CITS: [14832377][6842395][15975041]| and other vertebrates |CITS: [646798][1736035][11959019]| generate |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| from |FRAME: CHOLINE|. In humans, |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| is further processed to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| (TMAO) by the liver enzyme flavin-dependent monooxygenase 3 (|FRAME: HS00223|) |CITS: [15922018]|. TMAO both enhances atherosclerosis in animal models and is associated with cardiovascular risks in clinical studies, and thus inhibiting its production may serve as a potential therapeutic approach. One such approach is the use of |FRAME: CPD-20998|, a potent non-lethal inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-4.3.99.4| |CITS: [26687352]|., In marine sediments |CITS: [16346162][16346640]| and in the gastrointestinal tracts of ruminants |CITS: [646798]| choline-derived |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| is an important substrate for methanogenesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5250|).

Summary: Propionic acid bacteria (also known as propionibacteria) are Gram-positive, anaerobic bacteria,, found as saprophytes on animals (including humans) and in dairy products (such as Swiss cheese)., Propionibacteria produce large amounts of |FRAME:PROPIONATE| as the end product of glucose, fermentaion., The first work of importance on the chemistry of propionate fermentation was published as early, as 1878 |CITS:[Fitz78]|., For a long time propionibacteria were assumed to form propionate by the direct decarboxylation, of |FRAME:SUC-COA| to |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |CITS: [13271286][Wood56]|. A similar mechanism (in the opposite direction) was believed to catalyze, propionate degradation |CITS: [13100070]|., However, in 1957 it was shown that during propionate catabolism in animal cells the primary, product of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| carboxylation was not |FRAME:SUC-COA|, but, methylmalonyl-coA |CITS: [13502357]|. That discovery prompted a re-evaluation of the, pathway of propionate fermentation., A careful analysis revealed that |FRAME:SUC-COA| is not decarboxylated, but is converted to, |FRAME:METHYL-MALONYL-COA|, and that it is the latter compound (after racemization) that is cleaved,, transfering a C1 unit to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| |CITS: [16590594]|., This reaction, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7155|, generates |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA|, and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|., The |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA| that is formed acts as a |FRAME:CO-A| donor for a different step, of this cycle, where it is transferred to |FRAME:SUC|. This reaction, catalyzed by, |FRAME: MONOMER-13083|, forms |FRAME:SUC-COA| and |FRAME:PROPIONATE|, the final product, of this cycle., Even though the pathway was investigated mostly in propionibacteria, many other species, including, |FRAME: TAX-894| |CITS: [Stams84]|, |FRAME: TAX-29543| |CITS: [Schink87]| and |FRAME: TAX-865|, |CITS: [Tholozan94]| use it as well., Another propionate fermentation pathway is the acrylate pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5494 |).

Summary: General Background, This background summary covers this pathway and related pathways |FRAME: PWY-7008|, |FRAME: PWY-7010| and |FRAME: PWY-7011|. Yet neither |FRAME: CPD-1281| nor |FRAME: CoM| is produced by sulfur oxidizers. The HdrAB1B2C1C2 proteins have been co-purified from the non-methanogenic, hyperthermopilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-63363| in 2016, though no functional role was assigned at that time |CITS: [27284018]|. Based on the methanogenic complex structure (HdrA<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>) and the crystal structure of an sHdrA homodimer from |FRAME: TAX-53399|, a sHdrAA'C1B1C2B2 stoichiometry was predicted  for the sHdr complex |CITS: [32750208]|., The role of this system was first demonstrated in 2018, using the |FRAME: CPD-7670| degrader |FRAME: TAX-53399|. The final enzyme of the DMS degradation pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.4|, is located in the periplasm. It has been proposed that the sulfide produced by that enzyme is transported to the cytoplasm, where it is transferred by a relay of sulfur-carrying proteins until it reaches the |FRAME: TusA "TusA sulfur-carrier protein"|, which delivers it to the |FRAME: CPLX-85529| (sHdr system) |CITS: [29930335][38747384]|., Analysis of |FRAME: TAX-53399| cells grown with DMS has shown a significant increase in the transcription of the genes encoding the sHdr system. The authors proposed that the sHdr system oxidizes sulfide, provided by TusA, to sulfite, which is exported back to the periplasm |CITS: [29930335]|. The four electrons released by the reaction are transferred to a dedicated lipoyl protein, |FRAME: LbpA-Proteins LbpA| |CITS: [30004385]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8572|). The electrons are then transferred to NAD+ |CITS: [33460586]|., The genes encoding the sHdr proteins, the sulfur carriers, the lipoyl protein, and the enzymes that produce the lipoyl group are all located in the same gene cluster., The fate of the sulfite in the periplasm is less clear. In a 2018 publication it was proposed that sulfite reacts with hydrogen sulfide released by |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.4|, generating thiosulfate, which is oxidized to sulfate by the Sox system |CITS: [29930335]|. In a 2023 publication it was proposed that sulfite is oxidized directly to sulfate, potentially by the products of the Hden_1145/45 genes |CITS: [36367491]|. In a 2024 manuscript it was suggested that the sulfite is oxidized to sulfate either directly by |FRAME: EC-1.8.5.6|, or indirectly by |FRAME: EC-1.8.99.2|, which converts it to |FRAME: APS|, followed by oxidation by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4| |CITS: [38631440]|., Mutants lacking a functional sHdr complex can not grow on DMS, most likely due to the accumulation of sulfide, which is inhibitory for |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.4| |CITS: [29930335]|.

Summary: General Background, Some bacteria are capable of aerobic growth using aliphatic alkenes (such as |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|, |FRAME: PROPENE| and |FRAME: CPD-19063|) as source of carbon and energy., In these organisms the alkenes are oxidized to epoxides (also known as epoxyalkanes) by the |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.69|, a large complex similar to the aromatic monooxygenases such as |FRAME:CPLX-2181|. Epoxides contain an oxirane ring making them highly reactive electrophilic molecules, and are thus quite toxic to the cells. Depending on the organism, the epoxides are processed in one of several ways. Some organisms use glutathione and the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.34| to attack and open the oxirane ring |CITS: [10715003]|. Other organisms have been shown to use the unusual cofactor |FRAME:CoM| and an enzyme such as |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.23| |CITS: [10411892]|, yet others use epoxide hydrolases |CITS: [25576605]|. The products of these reactions are then catabolized to central metabolites |CITS: [11352719]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-19009 2-Methylpropene| (isobutylene) is one of four butene isomers and is the simplest branched alkene. In excess of 10 million tons of this gas are produced worldwide annually, mainly from cracking of petroleum. 2-Methylpropene is used as feedstock for the production of high-volume petrochemicals, including ether fuel oxygenates such as |FRAME: CPD-19011| (MTBE); high-octane gasoline blending components such as |FRAME: CPD-19039| (isooctane); and butyl rubber (a copolymer of |FRAME: CPD-19009| with |FRAME: CPD-9436|) |CITS: [22234536]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1547487| was isolated from sediment from a shallow freshwater stream by enrichment culture based on its ability to utilize |FRAME: CPD-19009| as the sole source of carbon and energy. The organism is not able to grow on most other C2 to C5 straight-chain, branched, or chlorinated alkenes, but is able to grow slowly on |FRAME: CPD-19045| and |FRAME: CPD-19046| |CITS: [25576605]|., In addition to |FRAME: CPD-19009|, |FRAME: TAX-1547487| also grows well on |FRAME: CPD-19010| and |FRAME: CPD-19013|, suggesting that these compounds are intermediates in the degradation pathway. Production of |FRAME: CPD-19010| implies that the first step in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.69|, as is the case in other alkene degradation pathways. While |FRAME: CPD-19010| could not be detected in the cells, feeding the cells with |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (not a growth substrate) resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-19003|, confirming that such a monooxygenase is indeed present |CITS: [25576605]|., When cells were incubated with |FRAME: CPD-19010|, the compound was consumed rapidly, and stoichiometric amounts of |FRAME: CPD-19013| were formed, suggesting that the the epoxide is hydrolyzed., Upon continued incubation, the product was oxidized further, resulting in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-19014|. These observations suggests that the organism possesses an epoxide hydrolase and a dehydrogenase enzyme that acts on |FRAME: CPD-19013| in a sequential manner, converting the alcohol function to a carboxylate function via an aldehyde intermediate |CITS: [25576605]|., The rest of the pathway appears identical to the pathway proposed for |FRAME: PWY-7779| |CITS: [22433853][25576605]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for O antigen synthesis are often present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The lipid A-core oligosaccharide and the O-antigens are synthesized in the cytoplasm, exported to the periplasm, and combined by the |FRAME: STM3713-MONOMER|, forming lipopolysaccharides (LPS) attached to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane. The LPS are then transferred from the inner membrane to the outer membrane and through it, remaining attached to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane., In |FRAME: TAX-590| the system responsible for transporting lipopolysaccharides from the inner membrane to the outer membrane consists of seven Lpt proteins - LptA through LptG. Together these proteins form a transenvelope bridge that transports LPS from the inner membrane, across the periplasm, to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane., LptB2FG is an ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter which, together with LptC, extracts the lipid A-core oligosaccharide from the inner membrane. LptA is a periplasmic protein that acts as a bridge between the inner membrane and the outer membrane. LptDE is an outer membrane protein complex that functions to anchor the oligosaccharide at the cell surface.The Lpt system acts downstream from |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.6|, which is responsible for flipping the lipid A-core structure across the inner membrane.

The lignan |FRAME:CPD-17595| is a typical component of heartwood in angiosperm trees |CITS:[Erdtman79]| that serves as long-term protectant against pathogen attacks and significantly contributes to the robustness, hence lifespan, of the trees |CITS:[20371107]|. In addition, yatein is a key intermediate in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-8959| and its derivatives (see |FRAME: PWY-7749|), which are important precursors for anti-cancer drugs such as |FRAME:CPD-16754|, |FRAME:CPD-16755| and |FRAME:CPD-17609| |CITS:[Umezawa03][15378293]|., The upper part of the pathway, describing the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8912| from |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL|, is described in |FRAME: PWY-5466|. The next enzyme, identified in 2013, is a cytochrome P450 that catalyzes the formation of the methylenedioxy bridge in |FRAME: CPD-17597| |CITS:[23161544]|., The rest of the pathway's enzymes were identified in a single study two years later. The scientists looked for potential genes involved in the pathway by analyzing RNA sequencing data from the |FRAME:CPD-8959|-producer |FRAME: TAX-93608| for specific types of enzymes (methyltransferases, cytochrome P450 hydroxylases, oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and polyphenol oxidases) that are highly expressed in rhizome, stem, and leaf tissues (the typical expression pattern of genes involved in |FRAME: CPD-8959| biosynthesis) |CITS: [26359402]|., Candidate enzymes were tested initially by |FRAME: TAX-357|-mediated transient expression in |FRAME: TAX-4100|. Combinatorial expression was accomplished by coinfiltrating multiple |FRAME: TAX-357| strains, each harboring a different expression construct. Since the host did not produce sufficient amounts of the starting compound |FRAME: CPD-8912|, this compound was also infiltrated into leaves expressing the different constructs. Using this technique, the researchers were able to identify the next six enzymatic steps (the last three are described in |FRAME: PWY-7749|) and to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-17595|, |FRAME: CPD-8958| and even |FRAME: CPD-18757|, the |FRAME: CPD-16754| aglycone, in the tobacco plant |CITS: [26359402]|.

The tripeptide glutathione plays an important role in cellular redox control and detoxification of heavy metals, electrophilic xenobiotics, and toxic side products of normal plant metabolism. In some legume tissues, homoglutathione can partially or completely replace glutathione |CITS: [14601672]|. The initial step of homoglutathione biosynthesis resembles that of |FRAME: GLUTATHIONESYN-PWY "glutathione biosynthesis"|. Once the dipeptide γ-glutamylcysteine was formed in the initial reaction, a β-alanine residue is added to form homoglutathione.

|FRAME: CANAVANINE| was first discovered and isolated in 1929 from jack bean (|FRAME: TAX-3823|) |CITS: [Kitagawa29]|. Its occurrence is limited to legumes |CITS: [331385]|, where it often serves as the main nitrogen storage compound in seeds, with a content of up to 12% of the seeds dry weight |CITS: [Rosenthal77]|., |FRAME: CANAVANINE| accumulates in many leguminous plants as a nitrogen storage compound and as an antimetabolite of |FRAME: ARG| involved in plant defense. The toxic effects of canavanine originate from the mimicry of arginine, thereby interfering with arginine metabolism and protein functions when incorporated during translation. Arginyl-tRNA synthetases are usually not able to discriminate between |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: CANAVANINE|, resulting in the incorporation of the latter into nascent polypeptide chains and in the formation of dysfunctional proteins |CITS: [3455753][9122181]|., Upon germination |FRAME: CANAVANINE| is degraded to |FRAME: L-CANALINE| and |FRAME: UREA|, which can be further degraded to |FRAME: HOMO-SER|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIUM| |CITS: [16667673]|. |FRAME: L-CANALINE| forms stable oximes with 2-oxoglutarate and other carbonyl-containing compounds, causing deleterious effects in the tricarboxylic acid cycle |CITS: [6486804]|. In addition, the formation of canaline-pyridoxal phosphate oxime with pyridoxal phosphate inhibits pyridoxal phosphate-containing enzymes. , Arginase catalyzes the first step of canavanine degradation by plants. The reaction releases the stored nitrogen as urea which is further degraded to ammonia by urease. Since the product |FRAME: L-CANALINE| is toxic, it does not accumulate in plants, but is irreversibly converted by canaline reductase to |FRAME: HOMO-SER| and ammonia |CITS: [1542671]|. |FRAME: HOMO-SER| supports the biosynthesis of other protein-forming amino acids. , |FRAME: L-CANALINE| can also be detoxified to canaline-glyoxylate oxime or 3-oxoproprionate (reviewed in |CITS: [Rosenthal90]|).

Summary: General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: penams (e.g. penicillins), ceph-3-ems (e.g. cephalosporins, cephamycins), clavams (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), carbapenems (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9377|, thienamycins) and monolactams (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while the remaining three classes of beta-lactams are produced by bacteria (reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|)., Penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins are produced by different organisms from branches of a common pathway. The pathway branches at isopenicillin N to form penicillins and branches again at deacetylcephalosporin to form cephalosporins and cephamycins (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|)., The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem and clavam antibiotics see |FRAME: PWY-5737| and |FRAME: PWY-5679|) differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). The pathway for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially elucidated and the order of some known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., The antibacterial mechanism of action of β-lactam antibiotics involves inhibition of the transpeptidation reaction during bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which leads to cell lysis. This reaction is catalyzed by class A and class B penecillin binding proteins. It is specifically inhibited by penicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics via formation of a covalent complex with the active serine of the transpeptidation domain of penicillin binding proteins. This prevents crosslinking and weakens the peptidoglycan polymer (in |CITS: [12867450]|). See pathways |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5265|. Bacterial resistance to β-lactam antibiotics can involve alterations in penicillin binding proteins, reduced antibiotic permeation across the membrane, or the production of β-lactamase enzymes (in |CITS:[12195735]|). See enzymes |FRAME: EG10040-MONOMER|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13427| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13428|., About This Pathway, Isopenicillin N is a branch point in the pathway that leads to the biosynthesis of penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins (as shown in the pathway links). The two reactions shown here are common to the biosynthesis of all three antibiotics. Reviewed in |CITS: [15719552]| |CITS: [10422579]| and |CITS: [9729600]|. 2-Aminoadipate (α-aminoadipate, L-2-aminohexanedioate) is a non-proteinogenic amino acid derived from L-lysine metabolism and is one of the three precursor amino acids in the pathway. In the first reaction the three L-amino acids condense to form the tripeptide δ-(L-α-aminoadipyl)-L-cysteinyl-D-valine (ACV). This reaction is catalyzed by ACV synthetase, a nonribosomal peptide synthetase which also epimerizes L-valine to D-valine. The reaction represents a connection point between primary and secondary metabolism (in |CITS: [9355751]|). The second reaction involves oxidative ring closure catalyzed by isopenicillin-N synthase leading to the formation of isopenicillin N. Isopenicillin N has weak antibiotic activity and is the first bioactive intermediate in the pathway (reviewed in |CITS: [12749845]| and |CITS: [9729600]|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-18237 "Zwittermicin A"| (ZmA) is a linear aminopolyol antibiotic that was originally identified in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1396| as the agent suppressing disease caused by the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-54510| |CITS: [16348145]|. , It was later shown to have activity not only against protists, but also against certain Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and some fungi |CITS: [9625782][18798190]|. ZmA was also reported to potentiate the activity of the toxin protein of |FRAME: TAX-1428| against insects |CITS: [Broderick03]|. The chemical structure of ZmA was initially reported in 1994 |CITS: [He94]|, and the exact stereo configuration was reported in 2007/2008 |CITS: [17249781][18798190]|., ZmA is a very unusual molecule, and is one of only a few linear aminopolyol natural products to be identified. Its core is formed from ethanolamine and glycolyl moieties that are rarely seen in natural products, and contains an unusual 2-aminosuccinamide moiety that is derived from |FRAME: CPD-18251|. In addition, its N terminus contains a D-serine residue, even though the precursor is L-serine. Based on the current understanding of its biosynthwetic pathway, ZmA is synthesized as a larger construct that is cleaved on both sides to produce ZmA, |FRAME: CPD-18252| and |FRAME: CPD-18253| |CITS: [19098220]|., The biosynthesis of ZmA involves both nonribosomal peptide synthases (NRPS) and polyketide synthases (PKS) |CITS: [16983083]|. The synthesis of the large precursor requires the condensation of the amino acids |FRAME: ASN|, |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, and |FRAME: L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE|, along with the carboxylic acid precursors |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, |FRAME: Aminomalonyl-PCP "aminomalonyl-[seryl-carrier protein]"|, and |FRAME: 2-Hydroxymalonyl-ACP "(2R)-2-hydroxymalonyl-[acp]"|. However, the products of |FRAME: ASN|, as well as the products of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME: MET|, are eventually cleaved off, so ZmA is actually synthesized from only five precursors: |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE|, |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, |FRAME: Aminomalonyl-PCP "aminomalonyl-[seryl-carrier protein]"|, and |FRAME: 2-Hydroxymalonyl-ACP "(2R)-2-hydroxymalonyl-[acp]"|., Biosynthetic gene clusters that include NRPS and PKS were discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1396| and |FRAME: TAX-1428| |CITS: [14711631][17225146][18446411]|, and the complete gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1396| has been sequenced and characterized in 2009 |CITS: [19098220]|., Seven genes encodes the large NRPS and PKS complex: |FRAME: G-44146|, |FRAME: G-44147|, |FRAME: G-44148|, |FRAME: G-44149|, |FRAME: G-44150|, |FRAME: G-44151| and |FRAME: G-44152|. Combined, these proteins contain 34 domains |CITS: [19098220]|., Other genes encode systems that produce |FRAME: Aminomalonyl-PCP "aminomalonyl-[seryl-carrier protein]"| from |FRAME: SER| (|FRAME: G-44142|, |FRAME: G-44140|, |FRAME: G-44143|); |FRAME: CPD-18251| from |FRAME: SER| (|FRAME: G-44144| and |FRAME: G-44145|); and |FRAME: 2-Hydroxymalonyl-ACP "(2R)-2-hydroxymalonyl-[acp]"| from |FRAME: DPG| (|FRAME: G-44139|, |FRAME: G-44140|, |FRAME: G-44141|). An enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-44153| catalyzes the oxidative cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-18258| from the polyketide complex, while an enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-44154| catalyzes the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-18252| from |FRAME: CPD-18258|, and its exportation out of the cell |CITS: [19098220]|.

Summary: General Background, Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are fatty acid that have 13 or more carbon atoms and contain more than one double bond in their backbone. The PUFAs that have 2 or more cis double bonds separated from each other by a single methylene group generally belong to the essential fatty acids which are all either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, meaning that there will be a double bond at carbon 3 or 6, respectively, from the end of the molecule., PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturated long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. They are produced in many algae, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|., |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID "Arachidonate"| (arachidonic acid) is a polyunsaturated ω-6 fatty acid with a 20-carbon chain and four cis-double bonds. It is produced de novo at high levels by mosses, by some lower eukaryotes (e.g. Euglena), and by some marine bacteria adapted to low temperatures and high pressures., About this Pathway, Some fungi, such as the filamentous fungus |FRAME: TAX-64518|, are capable of producing a large amount of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| de novo |CITS: [Yamada87]|. |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID Arachidonate| production by certain species of moss is also well documented ., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| in the moss |FRAME: TAX-3218| starts with |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (18:2Δ9,12) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|(18:3Δ9,12,15), respectively, and involves sequential Δ6 desaturation, elongation, and Δ5 desaturation. The desaturases and elongases involved in long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids biosynthesis require that the substrates are esterified to coenzyme A |CITS: [12835316]|. Fatty acid elongase complexes comprise of the β-keto-acyl-CoA synthase, ketoacyl-CoA reductase, hydroxyacyl-CoA reductase and the enoyl-CoA reductase enzyme activities |CITS: [15292371]|., An acyl-lipid 6-desaturase was identified and cloned in |FRAME: TAX-3218| |CITS: [9744093]|, as were a Δ6-acyl-CoA elongase |CITS: [12164806]| and an acyl-lipid 5-desaturase |CITS: [16728405]|. The Δ5 and Δ6 desaturases are front-loading desatrurases, and introduce the new double bonds between the carboxyl end of the fatty acid and an existing double bond. Unlike mamalian Δ5 and Δ6 desaturases, which act on acyl-coAs, the enzymes from lower plants, fungi, worms and algae prefer to act on fatty acids that are incorporated at the sn-2 position of glycerolipids |CITS: [12835316]|. The elongase, on the other hand, acts on coenzyme A-linked substrates. Thus, following the Δ6 desaturation the fatty acids have to be transferred from a lipid to CoA for elongation, after which they are transferred back to a lipid for the Δ5 desaturation |CITS: [12835316]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-6958|.

The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds, including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "γ-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "γ-butenolides"|, as chemical signaling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation |CITS: [2268871]|. At least 60% of |FRAME: TAX-1883| species appear to produce γ-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011) only a small number of them have been characterized |CITS: [21090718]|., Based on their structures, these γ-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, the |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and the |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|., The prototypic A-factor is |FRAME: CPD-10135|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-1911| and known to control |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| production, |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| resistance, and aerial mycelium formation |CITS: [5622968][6292150][3112126]|. This A-factor interacts with the ArpA receptor |CITS: [7592371]|, which binds to the promoter region of a transcriptional activator known as AdpA. When the concentration of the A-factor reaches a critical threshold, it binds to ArpA, resulting in its dissociation from the promoter and transcription of AdpA. AdpA then activates the transcription of a number of genes required for secondary metabolism and morphological differentiation |CITS: [24367152]|., The biosynthesis of this A-factor was shown to proceed from |FRAME: 8-methyl-3-oxononanoyl-ACP|, an intermediate of fatty acid biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-1911|, and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of glycolysis. The two molecules are condensed by the product of the |FRAME: G-55082| gene, forming an ester that converts spontaneously to a lactone. A second enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55084| gene, reduces the double bond, forming a phosphorylated version of the A-factor. Finally, the phosphate group is removed by a phosphatase, forming the final |FRAME: CPD-10135| molecule. Since the removal of the phosphate group was catalyzed by the bacterial alkaline phosphatase, it may not be catalyzed by a dedicated enzyme in vivo |CITS: [17277085]|., It should be noted that the A-factor can also be produced by an alternative pathway, in which the phosphate group is removed directly from |FRAME: CPD-19890|, and the dephosphorylated ester is converted nonenzymatically to a butenolide, which is then reduced by a reductase different from BprA (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7881|). Because introduction of |FRAME: G-55082| alone into |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in production of an A-factor analogue, the reductase and phosphatase involved in the alternative pathway are not specific to A-factor biosynthesis, and it is believed that the pathway described here is the relevant route for A-factor biosynthesis in vivo |CITS: [17277085]|.

Summary: The intermediate role of |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE| in the oxidative metabolism of aromatic compounds, by bacteria was first suggested by Kilby, who reported its accumulation in cultures of, |FRAME:TAX-475| growing on phenol |CITS: [Kilby48]|., This observation was confirmed by the demonstration that cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-303|,, induced by growth on aromatic precursors, can convert both catechol or protocatechuate, to |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE| |CITS: [15421941]|., The pathway is widely distributed among bacteria |CITS: [4599397]|. It consists of two parallel branches, for the dissimilation of |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| and |FRAME:CATECHOL|., While the enzymes of the pathway from different microorganisms share common ancestry, |CITS:[4199895][4199896][4215816]|, many different gene organizations, and forms of regulation have evolved |CITS: [1624453]|.

Summary: General Background, Flavonole such as kaempferol (this pathway) and quercetin and their glucosidic , derivatives (compare |FRAME:PWY-5321|) are the major flavonoids found in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [10514319]| , |CITS: [16939316]|. Metabolic mutants of Arabidopsis were found to express a different profile of flavonols , emphasizing the value of metabolic profiling for the exploration of the underlying pathways |CITS: [GRAHAM98]|. , The third main flavonol, |FRAME:MYRICETIN| bearing three hydroxyl groups on the flavonoid B-ring has not , been discovered in Arabidopsis indicating that the corresponding biosynthetic branch does not operate in , this plant |CITS: [8528278]|., The occurrence of the two main flavonols kaempferol and quercetin is predominant in different tissues. Quercetin , appears to be the main flavonoid in seeds and kaempferol is more prominent in flowers of Arabidopsis |CITS: [ 9112784]|, |CITS: [8528278]|. Beside the glycosylated monomeric flavonols, dimers and oligomers of flavonols have been , identified in Arabidopsis which again accumulate in a spatially and temporally controlled manner that is , dependent of seed development and maturation of seeds |CITS: [16395586]|., The biological function of flavonoids including flavonols such as UV-protection, defense and resistance against , biological and non-biological agents and interacting with plant hormones |CITS: [11960739]| has been investigated , in depth. However, flavonols also have a significant impact on human health as that they are an important component , of the daily diet. Flavonols are involved in the prevention of cancer and cardiovascular diseases that have , attracted researchers to reveal the causal molecular principles (e.g. |CITS: [16176136]| |CITS: [16097445]|., About This Pathway, Glycosylation is one of the most widespread modifications of plant secondary , metabolites that can alter properties and functions of the modified compound |CITS: [16214386]|. The variety , of glycosyltransferases and their substrate specificity is impressive and has been reviewed in several papers , |CITS: [11469580]| |CITS: [10973093]|. 120 putative UDP-glucose: glycosyltransferases alone have been , predicted from the genome of Arabidopsis but for only a few their molecular function has been verified , experimentally |CITS: [16214386]|. , The glycosyltransferases acting in Arabidopsis thaliana have been demonstrated to preferentially , transport sugars to the 3-OH and 7-OH position of the C and the A-ring of the flavonol, respectively. The , regioselectivity of 91 recombinant glycosyltransferase enzymes in Arabidopsis has been investigated displaying , the in vitro range of monoglucosylated (3-O-, 7-O-, 3'-O-, 4'-O-monoglucosides) , and diglucosylated (3,7-di-O-glucoside, 7,3'-di-O-glucoside) flavonols |CITS: [15352060]|. , The enzymes catalyzing the 3-O and 7-O-glucosylation have been purified from Arabidopsis , |CITS: [Kim06]| |CITS: [16794327]| |CITS: [14697269]|. Quercetin- and kaempferol-3-rhamnoside are the most , abundant flavonols reported and the corresponding enzymes have been purified and characterized via a functional , genomic approach just recently |CITS: [12900416]|. The kaempferol biosynthesis as displayed reflects the , currently known enzymatic steps and the results of metabolic profiling |CITS: [16939316]| |CITS: [16395586]| , but some of the enzymes catalyzing the formation of the |FRAME:CPD-14847| or |FRAME:CPD-8067| remain to be characterized. The identification of the flavonol 7-O-rhamnosyltransferase responsible for the formation of major kaempferol and quercetin glycosides in |FRAME:TAX-3701| has been achieved by utilizing transcriptome expression analysis. The molecular function of the flavonol 7-O-rhamnosyltransferase (UGT89C1) was confirmed through T-DNA mutants knocked out for the UGT89C1 in which rhamnosylated flavonols could not be found in the metabolic profile. In addition, the recombinant expressed GST-fusion protein demonstrated the very specific 7-rhamnosylation for flavonol mono- and diglucosides |CITS:[17314094]|.

Names: superpathway of 4-aminobutanoate degradation to succinate // γ-amino-butyrate shunt // GABA degradation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain. Recent, findings suggest that GABA has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well |CITS: [15003233]|. In animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: GLUTDECARBOX-RXN "glutamate decarboxylase"|., The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|. Diiferent variants of both enzymes are known. The amino-group acceptor for the transamination can be either |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|) or |FRAME:PYRUVATE| (e.g. in the plant |FRAME: ORG-5862| |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|). Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+., The action of glutamate decarboxylase, γ-aminobutyrate aminotransferase and succinate semialdehyde, dehydrogenase, combined, defines a short pathway known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. , While there is no evidence for a special role for GABA in bacteria, the capabillity to degrade it exists in many strains. GABA is present in the environment as a product of plant and animal tissue decay, and many bacteria can synthesize GABA as an intermediate in the degradation of putrescine (see |FRAME: Putrescine-Degradation "putrescine degradation"|). , The first indication for a bacterial pathway for GABA degradation was found in |FRAME: TAX-294|, |CITS:[13654294][13654295]|. While some organisms, like |FRAME: TAX-294|, can grow on GABA as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, others, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, can grow on it only as a nitrogen source |CITS: [8951816][12123465]|., About This Pathway, Many organisms have more than one variant of the enzymes involved in GABA degradation., In |FRAME: TAX-83333| the first reaction of this pathway, the transfer of the amino group from GABA to 2-ketoglutarate, can be catalyzed by two independently expressed 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferases. Likewise, two dehydrogenases with differing cosubstrate requirements catalyze the second step. Regulation of expression of the gab enzymes in this pathway is complex and may involve post-transcriptional control mechanisms |CITS: [14731280]|. , Wild-type strains of |FRAME: TAX-83333| cannot grow on GABA as the sole source of either nitrogen or carbon, even though the enzymes necessary for this pathway are present in the organism |CITS:[4550821]|. , GABA degradation is prevented by supression of these enzymes by a regulator, which also limits the the import of external GABA. The regulator (encoded by gabC |CITS:[4590473]|), is found in the same operon as the genes encoding |FRAME:GABATRANSAM-CPLX| (|FRAME:EG10361|) and succinate dehydrogenase (|FRAME:EG11329|) |CITS:[2188954][12446648]|, along with a |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| permease (encoded by gabP |CITS:[28310][374339]|)., Mutants in the gab operon are still able to grow on putrescine, due to the presence of an alternative putrescine degradation pathway (|FRAME: PWY0-1221|), as well as an alternative |FRAME: G6646-MONOMER|, (which is encoded by the |FRAME: G6646| gene)., Schneider et al |CITS:[12446648]| showed that while all nitrogen sources induce this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, it does not contribute to the catabolism of any other nitrogen source but GABA. The authors speculate that the main purpose of this pathway is to keep putrescine concentrations in check during nitrogen-limited growth |CITS:[12446648]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD0-1099 "Colanic acid"| is an exopolysaccharide secreted by |FRAME: TAX-562| and a number of other |FRAME: TAX-543| that encapsulates the organism, resulting in a mucoid appearance |CITS: [13963285]|. Colanic acid is thought to promote biofilm formation and to protect the organism when exposed to harsh environments such as acidic conditions |CITS: [11371548][16706906]|., Even though it wasn't identified as such, colanic acid was first described in 1927 by Dorothea Smith, who isolated a polysaccharide from a mucoid strain of |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [19869322]|. Fourteen years later, in a study on the antigens of the Enterobacteriaceae, it was noticed that one antigen was common to several mucoid strains of |FRAME: TAX-57045| |CITS: [Kauffmann41]|. It was soon reported that the same antigen, which was named "M" antigen, is produced by mucoid Escherichia coli strains |CITS: [15406247]|. In 1954 Kauffmann reported that the antigen was common to all mucoid Salmonella species |CITS: [Kauffmann54]|., Similar exopolysaccharides were reported from a number of mucoid strains and species |CITS: [13475241][13641209][13963285][14073028][5324934]|. In the early 60s it was reported that a large number of Salmonella and Escherichia strains that are not normally mucoid can be induced to form slime exopolysaccharides when grown at 15 to 20°C in high phosphate concentration |CITS: [Anderson61][Anderson63]|, and the exopolysaccharide was named "colanic acid" after |FRAME: TAX-562| from which it was isolated |CITS: [13963285]|. In a paper describing the discovery of the same polysaccharide in |FRAME: TAX-83333| it was suggested that colanic acid and the "M antigen" reported in the earlier studies are identical |CITS: [14206589]|. A confirmation was obtained in 1969 when it was shown that colanic acid of identical composition is produced by strains from the genera Salmonella, Escherichia, and Aerobacter. At that time the exact structure was not known, though it was known that the polysaccharide contains glucose, galactose, fucose, and glucuronate, as well as some O-acetyl groups |CITS: [ 4902806]|., A structure for colanic acid isolated from Salmonella typhimurium was derived from mass spectrometry and published in 1971 |CITS: [4939458]|. Additional structural studies have shown that colanic acid from different organisms is very similar, with the polysaccharide composed of a hexasaccharide repeating unit consisting of glucose, two fucoses, two galactoses, and glucuronate. In addition, one fucose and one galactose may be acetylated to varying degrees, and the terminal galactose residue is modified. The repeat units are connected by a linkage between the first and third residues, with the remaining three residues forming a side chain |CITS: [4311825][4902692]|. Differences are found in the modifications of the terminal galactose residue, which was found to contain a 4,6-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-pyruvoyl group, a 3,4-ethylidene group, or a 4,6-methylene group in different strains |CITS: [4941627]|. While colanic acid was considered exclusively an exopolysaccharide that is only loosely associated with the cell surface, a 2007 study also found that colanic acid can be attached to the lipid A core of lipopolysaccharide instead of the O antigen, forming a novel type of lipopolysaccharide which was named |FRAME: CPD0-1101 MLPS| |CITS: [17227761]|. The structure shown here, reported in the same study, was derived by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis of one colanic acid subunit attached to lipid A-core, and includes several modifications of the structure reported earlier |CITS: [17227761]|., About This Pathway, Like |FRAME: O-Antigens "O antigens"|, the colanic acid repeat is assembled on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane, linked to the membrane by the lipid anchor |FRAME: CPD-9649|. The precursors are provided in their activated form (|FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CPD-13118|, |FRAME: CPD-14553| and |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE|), and added to the oligosaccharide by a series of glycosyl transferases., Once assembled by glycosyltransferases, acetyltransferases, and a pyruvoyltransferase, the single repeat unit is flipped by a Wzx-type flippase across the inner membrane to the periplasmic side, where it is polymerized by a Wzy-type polymerase. Following polymerization, the colanic acid polymer is cleaved from the undecaprenyl membrane anchor, transported across the periplasm, and excreted into the extracellular space. Alternatively, it can be ligated to the lipid A core, forming a type of lipopolysaccharide., The gene cluster encoding colanic acid biosynthesis was located in 1984 |CITS: [6090411]| and sequenced in 1996, and found to contain 19 genes. The cluster contains the genes encoding the enzymes necessary for |FRAME: CPD-13118| biosynthesis, six glycosyltransferases, two acetyltransferases, a Wzx-type repeat unit flippase, and a Wzy-type polymerase |CITS: [8759852]|. The first three genes of the cluster encode the members of a complex that exports colanic acid from the periplasm |CITS: [16030241]|. Expression of colanic acid biosynthesis is regulated by the rcs (regulator of capsule synthesis) genes, |FRAME: EG10820|, |FRAME: EG10821|, and |FRAME: EG10822| |CITS: [1943696]|., While the general pathway was suggested based on the cluster's sequence |CITS: [8759852]|, surprisingly the specific role of the glycosyltransferases was deciphered only in 2019 |CITS: [30821147]|. The activity of four of the glycosyltransferases and the two acetyltransferases was demonstrated by in vitro assays using purified proteins. As of 2020, the activity of two of the enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G7095| and |FRAME: G7096| gene, which are expected to encode a galactosyltransferase and a pyruvoyltransferases, has not been demonstrated experimentally.

Names: L-ascorbate biosynthesis VI (plants, myo-inositol pathway) // L-ascorbic acid biosynthesis VI
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (ascorbic acid, vitamin C) is a reducing agent and antioxidant biosynthesized by plants, eukaryotic algae, some bacteria and many, but not all vertebrates.|FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it. These species rely on mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries. Reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|., In photosynthesizing plants and eukaryotic algae |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has roles in metabolism, electron transport, the cell cycle and responses to pathogens and abiotic stress. When coupled with its redox system, the ascorbate/glutathione cycle, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| can effectively regulate cellular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| levels (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-2261|) |CITS: [18460785]|. Interestingly, |FRAME: TAX-1117| do not possess any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis, and minimize photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases, suggesting that the use of ascorbate evolved after the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote |CITS: [23109712][25768426]|., Ascorbate Biosynthesis in Plants, Four different pathways for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| have been described in plants., • The first plant pathway was suggested in 1998 by Wheeler et al |CITS: [9620799]|. The pathway starts from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| and proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-Galactopyranose| and |FRAME: CPD-330| (see |FRAME: PWY-882|)., • A second pathway, known as the L-gulose pathway, also starts with |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. However, that pathway proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-gulopyranose| and |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS:[12954627]| (see |FRAME: PWY4FS-11|)., • A third pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-3747| (strawberry). In that pathway |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is formed from |FRAME: CPD-330|, as in the first pathway. However, the pathway starts from |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, and proceeds via |FRAME: CPD0-1083| |CITS:[13363799][12524550]|. Tracer and feeding studies have also shown conversion of |FRAME: CPD-23305| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [Loewus63]|. (see |FRAME: PWY-8143|)., • A fourth pathway suggested that |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| can also be channeled towards the production of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: EC-1.13.99.1|, based on the effect of overexpressing the |FRAME: AT4G26260| gene. According to that proposal, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is reduced to |FRAME: L-GULONATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS: [14976233]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8142|)., About This Pathway, A metabolic profiling analysis of |FRAME: TAX-3702| has shown the presence of |FRAME: L-GULONATE|, a known intermediate of vertebrate |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis |CITS: [12590116]|., A paper published in 2004 reported that |FRAME: ASCORBATE| levels increased 2- to 3-fold in homozygous |FRAME: TAX-3702| lines overexpressing the |FRAME: AT4G26260| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-1.13.99.1|, prompting the suggestion that this enzyme may be involved in L-ascorbate biosynthesis in plants rather than UDP-sugar biosynthesis |CITS:[14976233]|. Very similar results were obtained with tomato, where over-expression of the MIOX4 gene resulted in a significant increase in total ascorbate in leaves and red fruits |CITS: [32252624]|., The proposed pathway, which is shown here, involves three additional enzymes, two of which, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.17|, have not been reported from plants. Thus, the pathway is still speculative. A more recent study has shown that in tomato the overexpression of |FRAME: AT4G26260| led to increased expression of the genes encoding |FRAME: PWY-882|. Thus, it is possible that the contribution of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: EC-1.13.99.1| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis is implemented via enhancing a different pathway |CITS: [32252624]|.

Names: benzoylanthranilate biosynthesis // dianthalexins biosynthesis // N-benzoyl-4-methoxyanthranilic acid biosynthesis
Summary: The carnation plant |FRAME: TAX-3570| is susceptible to disease caused by the fungi |FRAME: TAX-4792| and |FRAME: TAX-171631|. When cell suspensions of carnation cells were infected with the fungi, the cells accumulated anthranilate-derived defense compounds known as phytoalexins, specifically dianthalexin and dianthramides, which are nitrogen containing phytoalexins |CITS: [2817901]|., The resistance response is dependent on the rapid transformation of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| as a precursor to phytoalexins. This pathway shows the first committed step of the production of dianthramides, the formation of |FRAME: CPD-423|. The pathway is believed to proceed via |FRAME: N-BENZOYL-4-METHOXYANTHRANILATE|. This route indicates that shikimate pathway could be crucial in disease response in carnation |CITS: [9426598]|. Carnation encodes a small family of genes encoding |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.144| |CITS: [9426598]|. Analysis of the expression of one of the genes (|FRAME: G-11502|) showed that several sequence motifs scattered over a wide range of the 5'-flanking region and in the exon sequence are responsible for the full elicitor regulation of the gene |CITS: [9869425]|.

Apocarotenoids are terpenoid pigments derived from carotenoid pathways, they usually pigment organisms in bright yellow to orange color. They are products of carotenoid cleavage reactions generally mediated by carotenoid oxygenases. These enzymes constitute a new non-heme iron enzyme family found in all taxa |CITS: [19007949]|. , The apocarotenoids perform several important functions in organisms such as the retinal chromophore in fungi, the plant hormone, ABA, and the fungal pheromone, trisporic acid. The pigmentation of fungal and plant parts is due to the accumulation of apocarotenoids |CITS: [18812228]|. , |FRAME: CPD-12930 Neurosporaxanthin| is a β-apo-4'-carotenoid (C35) that represents the end-product of the carotenoid pathway in |FRAME: TAX-5141|. Neurosporaxanthin biosynthesis requires the activity of the albino gene products (AL-1, AL-2 and AL-3), which yield |FRAME: CPD-7953| |CITS: [18627463]|. , |FRAME: CPD-12930 Neurosporaxanthin| is synthesized in three sequential steps. The order of these steps was initially thought to consist of cyclization of |FRAME: CPD-12932| (C40), cleavage of the product, |FRAME: CPD-7953|, to form |FRAME: CPD-12935| (C35) |CITS: [17610084]|, and oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-12935| as the final step. However, the isolation of mutants lacking these enzymes showed an accumulation of intermediates other than β-apo-4'-carotenal. The compounds were identified as |FRAME: CPD-12936| and apo-4'-lycopenol, indicating the presence of an alternative pathway, in which cyclization is the last step |CITS: [18812228]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Names: propanethial S-oxide biosynthesis // onion lachrymatory factor biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-40553| family have been valued both for flavor and medicinal purposes throughout the world., The domestic Alliums (such as onion, garlic, chives and leek) contain high concentrations of organic sulfur compounds especially in their bulbs and leaves. These compounds consist mostly of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| such as |FRAME: CPD-9269|, |FRAME: CPD-9307|, and |FRAME: CPD-9277|, as well as γ-glutamyl peptides (together these compounds make up over 70% of the total sulfur in garlic |CITS: [ Lawson96]|)., These compounds, which are found in the cytoplasm, are produced constitutively. The S-alkyl cysteine S-oxides are substrates for the alliinase enzymes (|FRAME: EC-4.4.1.4|), which convert them to |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|. However, the enzymes are kept in vacuoles, and are thus sequestered from their substrates |CITS: [Lancaster81][19463015]|. Only when the tissue is injured, the alliinase enzymes are released from the vaculoes and interact with their substrates, producing |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|., |CITS: [16010345]|. Once formed, S-alkylsulfenates are very active and tend to condense spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-17425 thiosulfinates| |CITS: [21905712]|. Depending on the Allium species, and under differing conditions, the thiosulfinates can decompose to form additional sulfur constituents including diallyl, methyl allyl, and diethyl mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, and hexasulfides, vinyldithiins, and (E)- and (Z)-ajoene |CITS: [16010345]|., In some species, dedicated enzymes commonly known as "lachrymatory-factor synthases" act on the S-alkylsulfenates rapidly, before they condense, producing volatile compounds that cause the eyes of animals to tear (lachrymatory factors) - a further defense mechanism against herbivory., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-4679| (onion) contains S-methyl and S-propanoyl cysteine S-oxides and their S-1-propenyl derivatives, but not the S-2-propenyl(allyl) derivatives |CITS: [9799098]|., It is well known that when onions (|FRAME: TAX-4679|) are chopped, they release a volatile compound that causes tearing in animals. This compound, commonly referred to as a lachrymatory-factor, was shown to be |FRAME: CPD-9305| |CITS: [5546155]|., |FRAME: CPD-9305| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-9307| by the action of two enzymes - |FRAME: MONOMER-13505| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13498| (often referred to as lachrymatory-factor synthase) |CITS: [12384686]|., The path of synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9307| is still speculative. An early research paper reported that γ-glutamyl peptides are not the immediate precursors for its synthesis |CITS: [Edwards94]|. However, later work has suggested that the pathway does involve γ glutamyl peptides, starting with glutathione and a carboxypropyl source. Radiolabeled |FRAME: VAL| has been shown to give rise to to radiolabeled |FRAME: CPD-13859| |CITS: [Granroth70]|, and thus L-valine degradation is a potential source for the side group of the S-alk(en)yl-L-cysteine S-oxides |CITS: [15234988][15652575]|., As described above, |FRAME: CPD-9307| is constitutively present in the cytoplasm of onion cells, but is sequestered from the |FRAME: MONOMER-13505|, which is kept in vacuoles. Upon injury alliinase is released, converting it to |FRAME: CPD-9304| |CITS: [10759524]|, which is rapidly converted to the lachrymatory-factor |FRAME: CPD-9305| by |FRAME: MONOMER-13498|. In the absence of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-9304| dimerizes spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-9306| |CITS: [21905712]|.
