Summary: General Background, Deoxyribonucleotides are synthesised de novo at the diphosphate level through reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group of the corresponding ribonucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|). This reduction is mediated by the key enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|., The de novo synthesis of ribonucleotides is very expensive, and organisms have adapted to salvage potential precursors from their environment. Since nucleotides can not be imported into the cell due to the negative charge of the phosphate groups, salvage is limited to free bases and nucleosides. , Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. It has been shown that in quiescent or terminally differentiated mammalian cells, resting in the G0 phase, ribonucleotide reductase is not produced due to a block during transcription and the cells rely on salvage for deoxyribonucleotides for DNA repair |CITS: [3044582][1696835]|. Similarly, the salvage pathway is the sole provider of deoxyribonucleotides to be used in DNA repair or mitochondrial DNA replication in G1 cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|., The deoxyribonucleosides enter through the cell membrane by facilitated diffusion via a low affinity, high capacity, non-concentrative nucleoside carrier protein with a wide specificity, possessed by almost all animal cells |CITS: [3048401]|. The next step in the salvage pathway is the phosphorylation of the nucleosides to monophosphates. Once phosphorylation occurs, the nucleotides are trapped intracellularly due to their negative charge., About This Pathway, Deoxyribonucleoside kinases salvage deoxyribonucleosides by phosphorylating them at the 5' position. The key enzymes in the salvage of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleosides are |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.21 "thymidine kinase (EC 2.7.1.21)"| (which also phosphorylates deoxyuridine) and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.74 "deoxycytidine kinase (EC 2.7.1.74)"|., This salvage pathway is well characterized in bacteria |CITS: [402352]|, mammals |CITS: [7494863]|, and plants |CITS: [22897443]|., Mammalian cells contain both of these kinases. In humans |FRAME: CPLX-8618| is encoded by the |FRAME: HS08100| gene, while two isozymes, encoded by |FRAME: HS09657| and |FRAME: HS09420|, catalyze thymidine kinase activity |CITS: [6281270][8380161]|., |FRAME: TAX-3702| posseses two thymidine kinase genes (|FRAME: AT3G07800| and |FRAME: AT5G23070|), and a broad substrate range |FRAME: AT1G72040-MONOMER| encoded by a single |FRAME: AT1G72040| gene that can phosphorylate both |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE| |CITS: [22897443]|., Most eubacteria also employ this salvage pathway. However, some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-90370|, lack the enzyme that phosphorylates deoxycytidine |CITS: [EcoSal]|. The yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| does not have any deoxyribonucleoside kinases, and thus does not possess this pathway., In addition to these two kinases, the pathway also shows how |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE| can be salvaged for the synthesis of deoxythymidine nucleotides. This is enabled by deamination to |FRAME: DEOXYURIDINE|, followed by phosphorylation by thymidine kinase to form dUMP. The latter can be converted directly to dTMP by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase (EC 2.1.1.45)"|.

General Background, N-linked glycosylation is an important process found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria., During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein, which are located in sequons (Asn-X-Ser or Asn-X-Thr). It has been shown that the glycosylation is essential for the proper folding of some proteins., In eukaryotes, most N-linked oligosaccharides derive from a branched 14-residue sugar (tetradecasaccharide) attached to a |FRAME: DOLICHOLP dolichol phosphate|. The structure of this precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and even the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor |CITS: [6088086][DeLaCanal][15665075]| (see |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathways are in general similar to the eukaryotic ones, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]|., About This Pathway, The archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2188| is a marine methanogen that generates N-linked glycoproteins with a unique trisaccharide composed of |FRAME: CPD-17867|. Several |FRAME: TAX-2188| proteins modified with this trisaccharide have been described, including the four proteins that make up the flagellum and the S-layer protein |CITS: [15723834]|., Genetic analyses identified a number of genes that are involved in the biosynthesis and assembly of the glycans |CITS: [16824110][18178736][18978056]|. Inactivation of some of these genes (named agl for archaeal glycosylation) affected flagella assembly., A major difference between this archaeal pathway and the eukaryotic/bacterial pathways is in the earliest membrane-committed step. In eukarya and bacteria this step is catalyzed by a phosphoglycosyl transferase, which forms an α-linked polyprenyl-diphosphate monosaccharide. In the archeal pathway this step is catalyzed by a glycosyl transferase (|FRAME: G-43973|), resulting in formation of a polyprenyl-monophosphate monosaccharide |CITS: [23624439]|., The next two monosaccharides are transferred to the nascent glycan by glycosyltransferases encoded by the |FRAME: G-43974| and |FRAME: G-43976| genes |CITS: [16824110][18978056][23624439]|. Following the translocation of the glycan to the exterior of the membrane via an as yet unknown flippase enzyme, the trisaccharide is transferred to L-asparagine residues in the target proteins by the |FRAME: MONOMER-19266| encoded by |FRAME: G-43977| |CITS: [16824110][23624439]|.

|FRAME: ORG-5891| can utilize |FRAME: 4-TOLUENESULFONATE| as a sole source of carbon and energy., The enzymes of the pathway attack the methyl group of the toluene, oxidizing it sequentially to an alocohol, an aldehyde, and eventually to a carboxylate group. The carboxylated intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-257|, is converted to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| in a single step catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7483|. |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, the final product of this pathway, is subject to meta ring cleavage (see pathway |FRAME: P184-PWY|) |CITS: [Microbiol141-1891][8828208]|., The degradation into the intermediate |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| is a common strategy in this organism, which has been shown to degrade at least eight aromatic compounds in this way |CITS: [15650824]|., The first three reactions in this pathway are catalyzed by enzymes that do not discriminate between sulfonates and carboxyl substituents, and thus also participate in the |FRAME: 4TOLCARBDEG-PWY| pathway. The last reaction, on the other hand, is catalyzed by an enzyme specific for |FRAME: CPD-257|., The enzymes of this pathway are encoded by genes that are present on conjugative plasmids. Different strains may have different versions of the plasmids, and some plasmids contain only a part of the genes, limiting the metabolic variability of the strains |CITS: [8828208][9172362]|, |CITS: [9990724][2614395] [2012609] [2050632] [9006050]|.

The occurrence of (R)-configured tetrahydroprotoberberine alkaloids such as |FRAME:R-CANADINE| is very rare and has been reported only for a few species in the Papaveraceae family |CITS:[Kametani68]|. The bulbs of Corydalis cava have been shown to be especially enriched with |FRAME:R-CANADINE| |CITS:[Spaeth31]| which was the reason to choose this particular plant as useful resource for elucidating the respective biosynthesis. The tetrahydroberberine extracted from the tubers of Corydalis have been demonstrated their use as an relaxant when suffering from gastrointestinal dysfunctions and shown potential as therapeutics for functional dyspepsia |CITS:[21659472]|. The development of efficient drugs has high priority considering the about 15% of the western world population which are affected by this chronic disorder of the digestive tract |CITS:[16886913]|., Cell free extracts from bulbs of Corydalis cava have been used to carry out in vitro experiments to elucidate the formation of |FRAME:R-CANADINE|. In addition, radioactive labelled precursors were administered to track the stepwise chemical conversion of the substrates in vivo. The experiments unequivocally showed that |FRAME:BERBERINE| was iteratively reduced via the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-16870| to form |FRAME:R-CANADINE| which disproved former notions about precursors with the same (R)-chirality. The second part of the reaction, i.e. the enantioselective reduction of the dehydro precursor |FRAME:CPD-16870| yielding |FRAME:R-CANADINE| appears to be the rate-limiting step of the pathway. Because the experiments were carried out with unpurified protein extracts it remains an open question whether or not one or more reductases are involved in the reaction |CITS:[Bauer91a]|.

General Background, The existence of a biosynthetic pathway from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| leading to the formation of |FRAME: B-ALANINE| has been shown to exist in bacteria and plants |CITS:[stadtman55][13905315],[rathina02]|. In several plants, the synthesis of |FRAME: B-ALANINE| from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| has been shown by radiotracer ([14C]-propionate) experiments |CITS:[13905315][rathina02]|. The exact intermediate steps of the biosynthesis are uncertain and almost no enzyme information is available for this pathway at the time of this review.

General Background, |FRAME: HIS| can be catabolized by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms in two principal routes. The main difference between these routes is the first step, which is performed by either a |FRAME: CPLX-6925| (as in this pathway) or a histidine transaminase (|FRAME: HISTDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5031|)., At least three different flavors of |FRAME: CPLX-6925|-based pathways have been found so far. All proceed in a similar manner up to the intermediate |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE|. Three steps, catalyzed by distinct enzymes, lead to this intermediate. In the first step |FRAME: HIS| is split into |FRAME: UROCANATE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| by, a |FRAME: CPLX-6925| |CITS: [14367318][12980948]|; Next |FRAME: UROCANATE| is converted to |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-981| |CITS: [13587518][13821933]|; and finally, |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| is converted to |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| by |FRAME: HUTIBACSU-MONOMER| |CITS: [13587518][13739526]|., In all three flavors |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is further degraded to |FRAME: GLT|. However, the mechanism of |FRAME: GLT| production is different in the three pathways. In several Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-90371|, |FRAME: TAX-573|, |FRAME: TAX-548| and |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is split into |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: FORMAMIDE| |CITS: [14367318]| ; the latter compound does not appear to be metabolized further (|FRAME: HISDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [13416179]|. In fluorescent Pseudomonads, including |FRAME: TAX-303|, |FRAME: TAX-294| and |FRAME: TAX-287|, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is first hydrolyzed to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: CPD-600|, which in turn is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (|FRAME: PWY-5028|) |CITS: [13211593][4290562]|; the |FRAME: FORMATE| can serve the cell as a source of single carbon compounds |CITS: [13563517]|. Finally, in the livers of mammals |FRAME: GLT| is generated by the transfer of the formimino group to |FRAME: THF|, which is metabolized further, transferring the formyl moiety to the pool of single carbon compounds |CITS: [13672973]|., About This Pathway, Sera and Yada were the first to show that |FRAME:HIS| is converted to |FRAME: UROCANATE| in mammalian livers |CITS: [Sera39]|. Following a period of controversy, it was shown that the histidase-catalyzed reaction is part of the major pathway for |FRAME: HIS| degradation in mammals |CITS: [13061415]|. The pathway is similar to the one found in some bacteria ((|FRAME: HISDEG-PWY|), but differs in the fate of the intermediate |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE|., Early observations of increased urinary excretion of |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| in rats defficient in |FRAME: THF| suggested that the later had a role in |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| metabolism |CITS: [13563480]|. It was subsequently shown that |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| was a very effective formylating agent in the enzymatic synthesis of formyl-folate in liver preparations |CITS: [13475326]|, and a liver enzymatic system has been described as catalyzing the following reaction:, |FRAME:N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| + |FRAME:THF| = |FRAME:GLT| + |FRAME:10-FORMYL-THF| + |FRAME:AMMONIA| |CITS: [13475327]|., A few years later Tabor and Wyngarden published that this "reaction" was actually the sum of three separate reactions, carried out by the enzymes glutamate formimidoyltransferase, formimidoyltetrahydrofolate cyclodeaminase, and methenyltetrahydrofolate cyclohydrolase |CITS: [13672973]|. Yet in 1976 it was discovered that in Eukaryotes the first two reactions are actually catalyzed by a single bifunctional enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-6933| (FTCD), that has both a formiminotransferase (FT) and a cyclodeaminase (CD) domains |CITS: [999878]|. Each of these domains has sequence similarity to the corresponding eubacterial genes encoding the corresponding mono-functional enzyme |CITS: [ 7654689][10773664]|. The FT activity transfers the formimino group from |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| to the N5 position of |FRAME: THF| (THF) producing |FRAME: CPD-671| and |FRAME: GLT|. |FRAME: CPD-671| is then channeled to the deaminase catalytic site, where it undergoes cyclization to produce |FRAME: 5-10-METHENYL-THF| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|., |FRAME: 5-10-METHENYL-THF| is an important precursor for coenzymes such as |FRAME:5-FORMYL-THF| and |FRAME: 10-FORMYL-THF|, and for the biosynthesis of several nucleotides and other molecules, including |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| and |FRAME: N-FORMYLMETHIONINE| tRNA |CITS: [15272307]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CANAVANINE| was first discovered and isolated in 1929 from jack bean (|FRAME: TAX-3823|) |CITS: [Kitagawa29]|. Its occurrence is limited to legumes |CITS: [331385]|, where it often serves as the main nitrogen storage compound in seeds, with a content of up to 12% of the seeds dry weight |CITS: [Rosenthal77]|., |FRAME: CANAVANINE| also serves as an antimetabolite of |FRAME: ARG| involved in plant defense. The toxic effects of canavanine originate from the mimicry of arginine, thereby interfering with arginine metabolism and protein functions when incorporated during translation. Arginyl-tRNA synthetases are usually not able to discriminate between |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: CANAVANINE|, resulting in the incorporation of the latter into nascent polypeptide chains and in the formation of dysfunctional proteins |CITS: [3455753][9122181]|., Despite the toxicity of L-canavanine, it has been shown to also act as a signaling molecule for free-living symbiotic bacteria to onset their symbiosis with the legume plant, and as a nutrient for both symbiotic and non-symbiotic, bacteria in the rhizosphere. The legume |FRAME: TAX-74613| exudes |FRAME: CANAVANINE| in order to support symbiotic events with rhizobia |CITS: [19602148]|. A study of hairy vetch (|FRAME: TAX-3911|) has shown that canavanine is exudated by the roots during early plant development impacting the composition and metabolic activity of the microbial soil community |CITS: [34646244]|., |FRAME: TAX-2842348|, an organism isolated from bean rhizosphere |CITS: [35072599]|, can grow with |FRAME: CANAVANINE| as its sole carbon source. A pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CANAVANINE| to |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: CPD-10150| in this organism has been characterized and is described here |CITS: [Hauth22]|. The key enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.43|, has been found only in members of the Pseudomonas and Rhizobium genera.

General Background, Phytate (phytic acid) is the most abundant myo-inositol phosphate (hexakisphosphate) in, plant cells. Phytate serves as a storage form of myo-inositol, phosphate and mineral nutrients, for utilization during seed germination and seedling growth. It is deposited within single-membrane, storage organelles referred to as protein bodies and is usually present as mixed complexes with minerals, (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+, Zn2+), known as phytin |CITS:[11590064],[8744268]|. Up to 80% of the total seed phosphorus is stored in, phytin |CITS:[15700415]|. Although phytate is found in large quantities in seeds, it is also present in, other plant tissues and organs such as pollen, roots, tuber and turions (for review see |CITS:[14568069]|). The potential of phytate to form very stable complexes with mineral and proteins confers upon this molecule its notorious antinutritional properties. Humans and monogastric animals lack the hydrolytic phytases in their digestive tract. Therefore, the high concentrations of phytate in food grains and its ability to chelate mineral cations compromise mineral absorption. Undigested phytate in animal waste also contributes to eutrophication and environmental phosphorus pollution |CITS:[11590064],[11906835]|. The degradation of phytate is achieved by a group of enzymes called phytases which have been mostly studied in microorganisms and plants. Phytases belong to a special class of phosphomonoesterases and are capable of initiating the stepwise release of phosphate from phytate. Phytases are used to reduce the level of phosphate pollution in areas of intensive animal production. Addition of adequate amounts of microbial phytases in animal feed improves the utilization of phosphate from phytate, allowing, for a reduction in inorganic phosphate supplementation in the diets for simple-stomached animals., As a result, the fecal phosphate excretion of these animals may be reduced by up to 50%. Finally,, phytases can improve the nutritional value of plant-based foods (especially grains) by increasing the, availability of the minerals chelated in phytin., This Pathway in Plants:, The degradation of phytate into myo-inositol phosphate intermediates and, finally,, myo-inositol, is performed by phytases which catalyze the removal of all the phosphate residues, of the phytate molecule in a sequential order. Each myo-inositol intermediate is released from, the enzyme and may become a substrate for further hydrolysis |CITS:[12405789]|. Unlike the better, characterized phytate degradation pathway from cereals and legumes (see |FRAME:PWY-4702|), which, has been confirmed by metabolic profiling as well as enzymatic information, this pathway results mainly, from the activity of the |FRAME:TAX-3885| phytase activity. This enzyme was shown to degrade, phytate through the sequential removal of phosphates: D-6 followed by D-5, then D-4 or D-1 and finally, D-3 |CITS:[MAITI74]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|, is also the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]|. It was first identified in 1948 in the red alga |FRAME: TAX-1261582| |CITS: [18101461]|, and is found in the highest concentrations in |FRAME: TAX-2864| (dinoflagellates) and |FRAME: TAX-2608131| (haptophytes). However, DMSP is produced by many more organisms including diatoms, green algae, some higher plants like |FRAME: TAX-4547| (sugarcane) and the coastal angiosperms |FRAME: TAX-15853| and |FRAME: TAX-101473|, bacteria, and some coral species |CITS: [31231779]|., Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS: [17068264]|., Biological degradation of DMSP is the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6046|). The degradation of DMSP to DMS and subsequent exchange of DMS across the ocean-atmosphere boundary is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. The flux of DMS from the ocean to the atmosphere is estimated at about 1.5 x 10(13) g of sulfur annually. Once in the atmosphere, DMS plays a major part in cloud formation and potentially in climate regulation., About This Pathway, Initial studies performed with the green macroalga |FRAME: TAX-63410| showed that |FRAME: MET| was the source of the sulfur atom and both methyl groups in DMSP, and that the α carbon of methionine was the source of the carboxyl group |CITS: [Greene62][Kahn64]|. However, the exact sequence of reactions was not determined until much later, when the pathway for DMSP biosynthesis in the related alga |FRAME: TAX-3116| was confirmed by in vivo isotope labelling |CITS: [9202120]|., Starting from methionine, the pathway includes transamination, reduction, and S-methylation (in this order) producing the novel sulfonium compound |FRAME: CPD-10470|, which is oxidatively decarboxylated to DMSP. The pathway intermediates were found in several other species, including the prymnesiophyte |FRAME: TAX-2903|, the diatom |FRAME: TAX-35125|, and a species of |FRAME: TAX-3164|, a prasinophyte |CITS: [9202120]|. The stereoconfiguration of the two intermediates |FRAME: CPD-10468| and |FRAME: CPD-10470| was shown in a study of the pathway in |FRAME: TAX-3116| |CITS: [Summers98]|., A 2011 study attempted to identify the genes encoding the enzymes that participate in this pathway from the diatom |FRAME: TAX-186039|. However, the only gene from this study that was eventually tested was found not be be involved |CITS: [22034629]|., Somewhat surprisingly, in 2017 it was reported that many marine heterotrophic bacteria, specifically from the |FRAME: TAX-28211| class, also produce DMSP using this pathway. The pathway was studied in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-187304|, and the |FRAME: G-80710| gene encoding the methyltransferase in that organism was identified - the first DMSP biosynthesis gene to be identified in any organism |CITS: [28191900]|. , DsyB protein-coding genes were predicted to be present in up to 0.5% of bacteria sampled in the Tara Oceans and Global Ocean Sampling (GOS) marine metagenomes, but were absent in terrestrial metagenomes |CITS: [28191900]|. Following the discovery of the bacterial gene, eukaryotic orthologs were found in many phytoplankton and corals species, including all marine prymnesiophytes, most dinoflagellates, some corals and ~20% of diatoms and Ochrophyta |CITS: [29483657]|.

|FRAME:CPD-6442 Methylsalicylate| is an organic volatile compound (VOC) of which more than 400 have been detected in plants |CITS: [9881368]| and known to play important roles in defining taste and aroma in fruits such as tomato |CITS:[24692651]|. For the economically important crop tomato it has been shown that the composition of the volatiles released by tomato fruits influences the preference and, consequently, purchase behavior of consumers |CITS:[22633806] [22677284]|. Although hundreds of VOCs have been found in tomato, |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| belongs to the few aroma and flavor forming volatile compounds which are above the range of olfactory threshold perceivable by humans |CITS:[Buttery87] [Buttery93]|. , The hydroxylated benzoic acid derivatives |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| and |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| like many VOCs are involved in many developmental processes in plants including defense against pests |CITS:[23955880] [26197563] [16222805]|, reproductive biology |CITS:[11960742] [20462477] [23383981] [12921438]| and are also used as food and medicinal additives for the benefit of humans |CITS:[Janssen96]|. Most importantly, |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| is known as an hormone that is involved in systemic disease resistant in plants, also referred to as systemic acquired resistance (SAR) |CITS:[17810266] [15283665] [17904410]|. It has been proposed to be involved in the activation of plant defensive actions at both the infection as well as distal, uninfected sites, hence acting systemically |CITS:[Dempsey99]|. In addition, growing evidence points to |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| as the transmitted signal |CITS:[17916738] [17916698] [19131332] [21311035]|., Plant defense is based on the interaction between pathogen and host on the molecular level, often referred to as gene-for-gene interaction |CITS:[2088175]| which elicits a response such as ion flux changes, increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) or the release/production of |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate|, nitric oxide and increased expression of pathogen related (PR) genes |CITS:[11459065]|. There are still many open questions regarding the SAR immune response in plants but a clearer picture of the process has been obtained over the last years (reviewed in |CITS:[7858199] [Vidhyasekaran15]|). |FRAME:CPD-110 Salicylate| can be biosynthesized (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-22 methylsalicylate biosynthesis|) and metabolized in plants in various ways and may occur as a methylated |CITS:[Shulaev97] [9489012]| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-22 methylsalicylate biosynthesis|) or glucose conjugated compound |CITS:[12297650]| (compare with |FRAME:PWY18C3-21 phenylpropanoid volatiles glycoconjugation (tomato)|)., With regard to the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-22 methylsalicylate biosynthesis|) a cDNA encoding a salicylate O-methyltransferase (SAMT1) has been identified in tomato and shown that the SAMT1 encoded protein was very specific for |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| forming |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate|, hence acting as a salicylate 1-O-methyltransferase |CITS:[20070566]|. The silencing of SAMT1 made tomato plants more prone towards the root fungus Fusarium oxysporum and a higher infection rate by spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) was observed, indicating that SAMT1 and its encoded enzyme is able to interfere with direct and indirect plant defense reactions |CITS:[20059742]|. The formed |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| can be degraded to |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-24 methylsalicylate degradation|) by the action of a methylsalicylate esterase, e.g. SABP2 which was studied in Nicotiana tabacum with respect to local and systemic resistance against the tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) |CITS:[12223676] [14673096]| and in Solanum tuberosum in which the MES1 encoded methylsalicylate esterase was shown to elicit SAR in this plant |CITS:[20687805]|. The mechanism through which |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| operates in the SAR immune response appears to be via |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate|, which functions as a mobile signal in the phloem |CITS:[17916738]| and is re-converted to |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| at the target issues by the action of the methylsalicylate esterase. The released |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| then initiates the SAR response and induces the expression of NPR genes |CITS:[15337097]|. , In summary, it was demonstrated that the SABP2 encoded methylsalicylate esterase does not act as receptor in the SAR immune response but rather as a biochemical mediator in the SAR signaling pathway |CITS:[20621100]|. Consequently, |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| may not act as an receptor in the traditional sense but rather through many targets in various developmental processes related to biochemistry, physiology and pathology in plants and animals (|CITS:[14673096] [25584724]| and summarized in |CITS:[27303403]|)., Finally, conjugated |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| derivatives are responsible for the aroma of tomato fruits referred to as 'smoky' which originates from the glycosidic cleavage of phenylpropanoid related diglycosides. Volatile aglycones conjugated with a hexosepentose moiety to give off the 'smoky' aroma are |FRAME:CPD-400 guaiacol| |CITS:[9881368]| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-23 guaiacol biosynthesis|) but also |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-22 methylsalicylate biosynthesis|) and |FRAME:CPD-6481 eugenol| |CITS:[19889876]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5859 eugenol and isoeugenol biosynthesis|).. Phenylpropanoid volatiles (PhP-V) have been found in tomato fruits as cleavable diglycosides and non-cleavable triglycosides |CITS:[19889876]| which defines the release and storage of PhP-Vs in the fruits. The catalyzing glucosyltransferase encoded by NSGT1 in Solanum lycopersicum was well correlated with the glycosylation pattern in tomato fruits and biochemical assays confirmed the substrate specificity of the protein to glucosylate phenylpropanoid volatile diglycosides to form the corresponding non-cleavable triglycosides |CITS:[23956261]|.

Names: indole-3-acetate inactivation VII // IAA inactivation VII // indole-3-acetic acid inactivation VII
Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., About This Pathway, Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. IAA is often present in conjugated forms that play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others, serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., When various forms of auxin are applied to the ~1 mm-thick colored epicarp (flavedo) of oranges (|FRAME:TAX-2711|) they can have differential impacts on the coloration and longevity of the fruit. This is likely due to the different levels of metabolism that these auxins undergo in oranges (see refs in |CITS:[11382233]|). , Radiotracer studies demonstrate the existence of at least two pathways for IAA metabolism in the intact flavedo of orange |CITS:[11382233]|. First, IAA can be used to generate |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| through a series of reactions found in several other plants, including |FRAME: TAX-3702| (|FRAME:PWY-2021|), poplar (|FRAME:PWY-1962|), and beans (|FRAME:PWY-1981|). Second, a novel compound, |FRAME: Dioxindole-3-Acetyl-3-O-hexoses|, is also formed. Glucose is the most likely hexose present in this compound in orange, but galactose, mannose, and lactose cannot be excluded |CITS:[11382233]|. , Feeding experiments using radiolabeled immediate precursors support all of the reactions depicted in this pathway, but no enzymes involved have been identified in oranges |CITS:[11382233]|., A quantitative comparison suggests that in green fruit, during the first 48 hours after treatment with radiolabeled IAA, approximately 50-60% of the IAA is shunted towards the |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETIC-ACID| branch of the pathway, 10-25% is utilized in the |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| pathway, and the remaining 5-10% is involved in the formation of an uncharacterized metabolite |CITS:[11382233]|., Though the biological activity of the intermediate and end products of this pathway are not characterized in orange, similar oxidized and Asp-conjugated forms of IAA appear to be inactive in other plant species (reviewed in |CITS:[15749753]|).

Bacterial sterol production was first discovered in the aerobic methanotroph |FRAME: TAX-243233|. |FRAME: TAX-243233| produces several modified lanosterol products including |FRAME: 44-DIMETHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-8610|, |FRAME: 4-METHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-4184| and |FRAME: CPD-21732| |CITS: [4929985][999649]|. Subsequent studies have demonstrated the production of similar sterols in other aerobic methanotrophs of the |FRAME: TAX-135618| order within the γ-proteobacteria |CITS: [10802170][26483502]|., Note that this pathway diagram starts with |FRAME: LANOSTEROL|. The reactions leading to its production are described separately in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-5670| and |FRAME: PWY-6132|., Homologs of the first two dedicated enzymes, |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.17| (ERG1) and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.7| (ERG7) have been found in |FRAME: TAX-414| |CITS: [17567593][17928701]|. Like homologs from other sterol-producing bacteria such as members of the |FRAME: TAX-113| and |FRAME: TAX-40| genera, the |FRAME: G-11059| gene of |FRAME: TAX-414| is closely related to its eukaryotic counterpart, potentially indicating an ancient horizontal gene transfer |CITS: [17923113][17928701]|., The presence of C-14 demethylated sterols in the methylotrophs suggested that they possess enzymes that can remove a methyl group from this position. Indeed, a homolog of the eukaryotic cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.154| (|FRAME: YHR007C|) has been found in the |FRAME: TAX-414| genome. The enzyme, which was named |FRAME: G-58813 CYP51|, uses ferredoxin as its electron donor |CITS: [12235134]|., Likewise, the presence of C-4 monomethylated sterols in the methylotrophs suggested that they also possess enzymes that can remove one of the two methyl group found at this position in |FRAME: LANOSTEROL|. However, no homologs of the eukaryotic enzymes (|FRAME: YGR060W|, |FRAME: YGL001C| and |FRAME: YLR100W|) have been found in the genome. In 2018 it was discovered that the methylotrophs possess a set of unrelated genes, |FRAME: G-58811| and |FRAME: G-58812|, which provide the same functionality, indicating convergent evolution |CITS: [29784781]|. , Even though SdmA and SdmB catalyze similar oxidative reactions, there are significant distinctions between the eukaryotic and bacterial C-4 demthylation systems. The bacterial system comprises only two proteins rather than three, and removes the 4β methyl group as opposed to the eukaryotic enzymes that remove the 4α methyl group. In addition, the bacterial system can remove only one methyl group from the 4,4-dimethylated lanosterol, leaving a monomethylated product, while the eukaryotic systems can remove both methyl groups |CITS: [29784781]|., As of 2018, the enzyme that is responsible for the unusual desaturation at C-8(14), leading to |FRAME: CPD-21732|, has not been identified.

Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|). An analog for these pathways is also found in the metabolism of the deoxyhexose |FRAME: L-rhamnose| (see |FRAME: PWY-6713|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees |CITS: [Pingman57]|). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. Free arabinose is formed during the degradation of complex polymers, as in |FRAME: PWY-6790|, |FRAME: PWY-8006|, and |FRAME: PWY-6813|., |FRAME: TAX-2287| and |FRAME: TAX-2285| can utilize the pentoses |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028| as carbon sources. The |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| degradation pathway shown here proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-1134| to |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|., Three additional enzymes have been included in this pathway, a glycolaldehyde oxidoreductase, a glyoxylate reductase (glycolate dehydrogenase), and a malate synthase, that combined catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: MAL|, which feeds into the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| (|CITS: [20736170]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21612976]|., It is not clear whether the lactonase reaction (|FRAME: EC-3.1.1.15|) is enzymatically catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-2281|. Although two |FRAME: TAX-2287| genes have been identified as lactonases, they are not differentially expressed. It has been postulated that there may be no need for a lactonase due to the hyperthermophilic nature of this organism. Lactone hydrolysis can occur spontaneously but slowly at ambient temperatures. However at 80 °C the spontaneous reaction may be rapid enough to not be rate-limiting |CITS: [16849334]|., Similar pathways exist for the degradation of |FRAME: D-Xylose| and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, see |FRAME: PWY-7294| and |FRAME: DARABCATK12-PWY|.

The organosulfinate |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| and the organosulfonate |FRAME: TAURINE| function as high concentration (0.25 M) osmolytes in certain organisms, such as deep-sea invertebrates. |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE Hypotaurine| is the precursor of taurine in the taurine biosynthetic pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5331|)., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-318586| can utilize |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| as a carbon, nitrogen, and energy source. A proteomic analysis of cells grown with |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| showed two highly expressed genes - |FRAME: G-17746| and |FRAME: G-17748|. Enzymatic assay of the purified product of the |FRAME: G-17746| gene confirmed that it encodes a bifunctional taurine/hypotaurine--pyruvate aminotransferase with a preference for |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE|. The product of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-15830|, is very unstable and decomposes spontaneously to |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: ACETALD|. The latter is oxidized to  |FRAME: ACET| by the product of the |FRAME: G-17748| gene |CITS: [23603744]|.

Names: ent -kaurene biosynthesis II // ent -kaurene biosynthesis in bryophyta // ent -kaurene biosynthesis in fungi
Summary: ent -kaurene is an important hydrocarbon precursor of |FRAME: Gibberellins gibberelin| biosynthesis. It is formed by the two step cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| via copalyl diphosphate. These compunds are produced by a number of fungi, and have been isolated and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-1214568| |CITS: [18391465]|, |FRAME: TAX-5127| |CITS: [9745028]|, |CITS: [10803977]|, as well as in higher plants (see |FRAME: PWY-5032|). However the phyllogentic analysis of the gene clusters of the above pathway in different organisms shows that the enzymes have evolved in an interesting manner. In lower forms like fungi and moss the key enzyme is a bifunctional enzyme that cyclizes the |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| directly to the ent kaurene products |CITS: [17064690]|, in higher plants two distinct enzymes carry out the cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| in a two step reaction |CITS: [16861806]|

Names: cyclohexane-1-carboxylate degradation II (anaerobic) // anaerobic cyclohexane carboxylate degradation // anaerobic cyclohexane-1-carboxylate degradation
Summary: |FRAME: CPD-575 Cyclohexane-1-carboxylate| is formed by oxidative microbial degradation of n-alkylcycloparaffins and anaerobic degradation of benzoate. It also occurs in nature as a functional group in more complex compounds (e.g. polyketide antibiotics from Streptomyces species). Several pathways for its degradation, both aerobic and anaerobic, have been described., The first anaerobic degradation pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-1076|, in which the compound is degraded via |FRAME: CPD-558| and modified β-oxidation steps that yield three acetyl-CoA molecules and one CO2 molecule |CITS: [10781543]| (see |FRAME: PWY-301|). However, that pathway is rather rare., A different anaerobic pathway variant was described from |FRAME: TAX-28232|. This pathway variant, whichis much more common, is found in most anaerobic bacteria that degrade |FRAME: CPD-575|. The pathway includes |FRAME: EC-3.7.1.21|, which catalyzes the addition of one molecule of water to the double bond of |FRAME: 6-OXOCYCLOHEX-1-ENE-1-CARBONYL-COA| prior to the hydrolytic C-C cleavage of the alicyclic ring, which forms |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYPIMELYL-COA| instead of |FRAME: CPD-558|. |CITS: [25112478]|.

Names: superpathway of fatty acid biosynthesis initiation
Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes and are determinants of intracellular communication, in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]|, and fatty acyl moieties of proteins that modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid (FAS) biosynthesis mechanisms. The type I system is found in mammals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex, (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|)., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., The best studied pathway is that of |FRAME: TAX-83333|, from which all the enzymes have been purified and crystalized. In plants fatty acid synthesis occurs mainly in plastids of leaf mesophyll cells, seeds, and oil-accumulating fruits. Although most of the synthesis occurrs in plastids, it has been shown that mitochondria are also capable of synthesizing fatty acids |CITS: [14660674]|., Fatty acid biosynthesis starts with an initiation sequence that produces |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs|, an activated molecule that is used for subsequent elongation reactions, which ultimately produce the final fatty acid products. This superpathway describes only the initiation sequence, subsequent elongation reactions are described in the pathways |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-862|., About This Pathway, There are several different routes in which an organism can produce acetoacetyl-ACP. The pathway shown here shows three such routes using different combinations of β-ketoacyl-ACP synthases (KAS) (in the case of |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: FABB-CPLX|, |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| and |FRAME: CPLX0-252|, which are encoded by |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG12606| and |FRAME: EG10277|, respectively)., In general, the |FRAME: EG10277|-encoded enzyme is responsible for the initiation of fatty acid elongation, utilizing acyl-coA primers, while the |FRAME: EG10274|/|FRAME: EG12606| products are responsible for the subsequent rounds of elongation, condensing malonyl-ACP with different length acyl-ACPs to extend the acyl chain by two carbons |CITS: [15952903][18384517]|., Three pathways for the initiation of fatty acid biosynthesis have been proposed |CITS: [1551888]|., In the first pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-4381|) |FRAME: CPLX0-252| catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| to yield |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs|., In the second pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5966|) the acetate moiety is first transferred from |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: ACETYL-ACP| by |FRAME:ACP-S-ACETYLTRANSFER-ENZRXN| (this is a second function of |FRAME: CPLX0-252|; it is not clear whether an additional dedicated enzyme exists in the organism). The acetyl-ACP is then condensed with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| by |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| (or alternatively |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX|)., The third pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5965|) involves the decarboxylation of |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| by |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| to form |FRAME: ACETYL-ACP| followed by subsequent condensation with a second |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|., It is now believed that |FRAME: CPLX0-252| is the key enzyme in the initiation of fatty acids biosynthesis |CITS: [15952903]|. It selectively catalyzes the formation of acetoacetyl-ACP and specifically uses CoA thioesters rather than acyl-ACP as the primer. The products tend to be shorter than the products of KASI and II, which are involved primarily in elongation reactions, and unlike the other two enzymes, KASIII cannot participate in the terminal elongation steps of fatty acid biosynthesis., While |FRAME: FABB-CPLX| and |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| have been shown in vitro to utilize substrates with short acyl moieties, forming acetoacetyl-ACP, the importance of these enzyme for initiation of fatty acid biosynthesis in vivo is not clear |CITS: [15952903]|.

Summary: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|).

Names: caffeine degradation IV (bacteria, via demethylation and oxidation)
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is a commercially important alkaloid produced by some plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5037| and |FRAME: PWY-5038|). |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation pathways have been reported in yeast, filamentous fungi, some plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6552| and |FRAME: PWY-6553|), bacteria and animals. Although the overall scheme of demethylation and oxidation reactions is similar, the main pathways, enzymes used, and some of the products vary. In humans |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is degraded by cytochrome P-450, N-acetyltransferase and xanthine oxidase enzymes |CITS: [15013152]|, whereas the bacterial pathways appear to involve enzymes different from these. The bacterial enzymes are of interest in bioremediation of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-containing waste from coffee and tea processing, the conversion of such waste to animal feed, the development of biodecaffination techniques, as well as their use in the development of pharmaceuticals and biofuels. Although these pathways are relatively well characterized, the demethylation enzymes have generally been unstable during purification. Work on gene cloning and recombinant enzyme purification and characterization is in progress |CITS: [22328667]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [14977550] [17009088]| and |CITS: [8919637]|., Although |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| in high concentrations is toxic to bacteria, some develop the ability to catabolize it. This includes strains of |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-507| and an unnamed strain of |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [MAZZA96]|). |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading strains have been isolated from the soil under coffee trees and in the laboratory by enrichment procedures involving |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| addition to the growth media. |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading bacteria use both N-demethylation and oxidation for |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| catabolism, as shown in this pathway and in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6538| and |FRAME: PWY-6633|. In the N-demethylating pathway, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is thought to be initially degraded by an oxidative demethylation mechanism. This mechanism involves N-demethylating monooxygenases that utilize NAD(P)H, producing dimethylxanthines, followed by monomethylxanthines and |FRAME: XANTHINE|. This mechanism has been supported by the creation of EC 1.14.13.128. |FRAME: XANTHINE| is degraded by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to |FRAME: URATE|, which is then degraded as shown in the pathway link. Reviewed in |CITS: [17009088]|., About This Pathway, In some |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading bacteria the major route of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) catabolism appears to be via initial demethylation to |FRAME: 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| (3,7-dimethylxanthine), followed by demethylation to |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE|, and then |FRAME: XANTHINE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6538|). |FRAME: XANTHINE| is further degraded by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to |FRAME: URATE|, with subsequent catabolism to central metabolites (as shown in the pathway link, which is in turn linked to pathway |FRAME: PWY-5694|. |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID Lipoate| is an essential sulfur-containing cofactor of various multienzyme complexes and responsible in Saccharomyces cerevisiae for the lipoylation of the E2 subunits of three mitochondrial proteins, i.e. pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH) and the glycine cleavage enzyme (GCV) |CITS:[2007123] [19570983]|. Those enzymes have been shown to play pivotal roles in mitochondrial maintenance and respiratory growth |CITS:[10839818] [20226757]|. Moreover, a protective role of |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| against hydrogen peroxide has been reported indicating its properties as antioxidant and antimutagenic agent |CITS:[14599473]|. , Fatty acid biosynthesis in eukaryotic organisms is carried out in independent, dual cellular locations, the cytosol with fatty acid synthase (FAS) complexes (FAS I type) synthesizing fatty acids (for example |FRAME:PWY-5994|) and the mitochondria where monofunctional enzymes catalyze the various steps of fatty acid biosynthesis (FAS II type) |CITS:[19028688]|. The latter resembles the bacterial FAS II system (see |FRAME:PWY0-501|, |FRAME:PWY0-1275|) but except for |FRAME:CPD-195|, the precursor for |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| (compare |FRAME:PWY-7388|), the functions of other final products made by the pathway remain unclear and require further research |CITS:[19028688]|., This pathway summarizes the two branches of lipoate biosynthesis and incorporation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The pathway describes the lipoylation of the subunit (GVC3) of the glycine cleavage system in yeast |CITS:[9020168]|, which catalyzes the cleavage of |FRAME:GLY| to |FRAME:AMMONIA| and C1 units and is accountable for the utilization of this amino acid as exclusive source of nitrogen. It has been shown that glycine cleavage activity is not required for lipoylation. However, the lipoylated GVC3 subunit is a prerequisite for the lipoylation of the E2 subunits of PDH and KGDH and as such essential for endogenous |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| biosynthesis and attachment |CITS:[19570983]|. The first step in the pathway is catalyzed by a lipoyl/octanoyl transferase (LIP2) in Saccharomyces which utilizes |FRAME:OCTANOYL-ACP| (see |FRAME:PWY-7388|) to modify GCV3 forming the respective octanoylated molecule |CITS:[11356580]|. In the second step of the pathway a mitochondrial lipoyl synthase (LIP5) catalyzes the insertion of two sulfur into |FRAME:CPD-195| |CITS:[8349643] [11106496]|, hence forming the lipoylated GCV3 molecule., It appears that octanylated GCV3 is a checkpoint for the |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| biosynthesis and incorporation |CITS:[23960015]|. Once all GCV3 has been octanoylated a so far elusive octanoyl-ACP:CoA transferase carries out the formation of |FRAME:CPD-196| from |FRAME:OCTANOYL-ACP|. |FRAME:CPD-196 Octanoyl-CoA| has been found to be the substrate for the octanoyl-CoA:protein transferase (LIP3 also referred to as AIM22) which transfers the octanoyl group to both the E2 subunits of pyruvate dehydrogenase (LAT1) and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGD2), respectively, forming the corresponding octanoylated proteins |CITS:[19570983] [23960015]|. In the following step of the pathway a mitochondrial lipoyl synthase (LIP5) catalyzes the insertion of two sulfur into |FRAME:CPD-195| |CITS:[8349643] [11106496]|, hence forming the lipoylated PDH and KGDH molecules. In this branch of the lipoate biosynthesis and attachment the lipoylation of the E2 subunits of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH) is depicted, describing the role of the enzymes which catalyze the oxidative decarboxylation of glycolysis end product |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and TCA cycle intermediate |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, hence connecting cytosolic glycolysis with mitochondrial respiration.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The 6-deoxy sugar |FRAME: CPD-15696| is present in the O-antigens of |FRAME: TAX-287| serotypes O5 and O11. It is synthesized as the activated form |FRAME: CPD-15648| from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|., The wbp gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-287| serotype O5 has been studied |CITS: [7687320][8939432]|. The cluster includes, among others, the two biosynthetic genes |FRAME: G-17661| and |FRAME: G-17659| which are responsible for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15696|., The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.135| (encoded by |FRAME: G-17659|) catalyzes a dehydration reaction in which the hydroxyl group at C6 is lost, and the hydroxy group at position C4 is oxidized to a keto group. This enzyme maintains the stereo configuration at carbon C5 [unlike |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.115|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-17655| gene in different serotypes of |FRAME: TAX-287|, which catalyzes a similar reaction that also includes inversion of the C5 bond]. The product, |FRAME: CPD-13847|, can be a substrate for two similar enzymes that reduce the C4 keto group, resulting in different stereo configurations. |FRAME: G-17661 WbpK| generates |FRAME: CPD-15648|, while |FRAME: G-17660 WbpV| generates |FRAME: CPD-15647| (see |FRAME: PWY-7334|).

Summary: |FRAME: STIPIT-CPD "Stipitatic acid"| is a fungal metabolite isolated from |FRAME: TAX-28564| in 1942 |CITS: [16747484]|. At the time, its structure presented a challenge to the researchers. The structure was described a few years later, presenting an unprecedented type of nonbenzenoid aromatic system |CITS: [Dewar45]|. Dewar named this seven-membered ring system |FRAME: CPD-7024| |CITS: [14780257]|., |FRAME: STIPIT-CPD "Stipitatic acid"| and other fungal tropolones continue to stimulate interest. For example |FRAME: CPD-18154| possesses potent antiplasmodial activity and is considered a candidate for an antimalarial drug |CITS: [21063422]|., In 1963 it was shown that the precursors of |FRAME: STIPIT-CPD| are acetate, malonate, and a C1 unit |CITS: [13967549]|, and later |FRAME: CPD-18145| was reported to be an early intermediate |CITS: [4819765]|. It has also been shown that the source of the oxygen incorporated into the tropolone skeleton during ring expansion is molecular oxygen |CITS: [Osullivan95]|., The later part of the pathway was proposed to proceed via via |FRAME: CPD-18151| |CITS: [Holik73]|, |FRAME: CPD-18153|, and |FRAME: CPD-45| |CITS: [Doi06]|. The last step of the pathway has been described early on as a decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-45| |CITS: [14109225]|., Better characterization of the polyketide synthase that starts the pathway was first acheived from a different organism - the fungal plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-5046|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-18146|, a non-tropolone compound. It has been shown that |FRAME: CPD-18145| is the product of the synthase, and the gene encoding it was identified |CITS: [17912413]|. The gene's sequence was used to identify the homologous gene in |FRAME: TAX-28564|, which participates in |FRAME: STIPIT-CPD| biosynthesis |CITS: [22508998]|. Both enzymes contain the same domains - starter unit acyl transferase, ketoacylsynthase, acyl transferase, product template, acyl carrier protein, C-methyl transferase, and acyl CoA thiolester reductase domains., Identification of the polyketide synthase gene in |FRAME: TAX-28564| led to the discovery of neighboring genes that encode other enzymes that are involved in the pathwy. As of 2015, only three additional enzymes have been characterized. These enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-44096|, |FRAME: G-44097|, and |FRAME:G-44098|, catalyze the next three steps in the pathway |CITS: [22508998]|., Sequence analysis suggests that tropolone biosynthetic clusters exist in at least 10 other organisms

Summary: General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms. , In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central intermediate. , It has been suggested that the |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph, would rise to 100 mM in less than 1 minute if |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by, unrelated or distantly related genes. , About This Pathway, Even though |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| is almost a universal thiol, present in eukaryotes, Gram negative bacteria, and several Gram positive bacteria, there are some organisms that produce alternative thiols. One such group is the actinomycetes, including the mycobacteria, which produce the unique compound |FRAME: CPD1G-2| as their main thiol (see the pathway |FRAME: PWY1G-0| and |CITS: [12420157]|). In these organisms a new type of formaldehyde dehydrogenase was discovered, which is specific to |FRAME: CPD1G-2| as its cofactor |CITS: [3160586][1597190][9202149]|. This enzyme catalyzes a very similar reaction to the |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|-dependent enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-3381|., |FRAME:S-HYDROXYMETHYLMYCOTHIOL|, which is formed spontaneously by |FRAME: CPD1G-2| and |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD1G-121| in the presence of |FRAME: NAD|. The product is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: CPD1G-2| |CITS: [12809551]|. It is still not known whether the hydrolysis is catalyzed enzymatically.

In the respiratory chain formed by hydrogenase and fumarate reductase, the oxidation of hydrogen in the periplasm of E. coli K-12 is coupled to the reduction of fumarate in the cytoplasm. H2-dependent reduction of fumarate in spheroplasts from the E. coli K-12 strain A1002 is coupled to translocation of protons across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [6249272]|. , E. coli K-12 contains two membrane bound, H(2) uptake hydrogenases - |FRAME: FORMHYDROGI-CPLX "hydrogenase 1"| (Hyd1) and hydrogenase 2 (Hyd2). Hydrogenase 2 (shown in this pathway) is the major hydrogenase when cells respire with H(2) and fumarate |CITS: [3905769][3894325][3516690][8021226][DUBINI02]|. Fumarate reductase does not contribute to the generation of proton potential |CITS: [10373108]|. Hyd 2 is presumed to be an energy conserving enzyme (see |CITS: [9230919]|). H2-dependent reduction of the quinol analogs, menadione, and ubiquinone-1, in E. coli spheroplasts is coupled to a protonophore-sensitive, proton translocation with H+/2e- stoichiometry of approx. 2 |CITS: [6249272]|. Both menaquinone (shown here) and demethylmenaquinone can operate in hydrogen to fumarate respiration |CITS: [2204318][1444716][25368299]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the degradation pathways for the two dicarboxylic acid sugars |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE|. Many organisms, including the bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, can use both compounds as the sole source of carbon for growth., The initial step in the degradation of both compounds is their dehydration. Even though different enzymes, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.40| and |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.42|, are responsible for the dehydration of the two compounds, both form the same product, |FRAME: 5-KETO-4-DEOXY-D-GLUCARATE| |CITS: [9772162][10769114]|., The next step in the pathway is cleavage by |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.20| to form |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: TARTRONATE-S-ALD| |CITS: [FishMethEnz9529]|, and the reduction of the latter to |FRAME: GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.60| |CITS: [13900766]|., The final step is the phosphorylation of |FRAME: GLYCERATE| to form the glycolytic intermediate |FRAME: 2-PG|, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.165| |CITS: [1336459]|.

General Background, Heptose sugars, mostly glycero-manno-heptoses, are found in the cell surface polymers of many bacteria., They are most common in the |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) of most Gram-negative bacteria |CITS:[1794130][1618845]|, but are also found in capsules |CITS: [11373120]| and O-antigens |CITS: [10512635]| of some Gram-negatives, and in the S-layer of certain Gram-positive bacteria |CITS:[8720077][10406844][12101286]|. Glycosylation of an autotransporter adhesin protein with glycero-manno-heptose residues has also been reported |CITS: [11442838]|., D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units have been found in different anomeric configurations. The core oligosaccharide of the LPS of |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-573| contain short heptan chains composed of α-configured D-glycero-D-manno-heptose units |CITS: [9346320][9507008]|, while the O-antigen of |FRAME: TAX-703| was shown to contain β-configured residues |CITS: [10712598]|., Prior to their incorporation, the heptose residues are activated by attachment to a nucleotide. Two pathways for the activation of heptose sugars have been described - |FRAME: PWY0-1241| in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and |FRAME: PWY-6478| in |FRAME: TAX-143495|., About This Pathway, The S-layer glycoprotein of the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-143495| DSM 10155 is composed of disaccharide repeating units of |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: CPD-12339| units., The genes responsible for the biosynthesis of the activated form, |FRAME: CPD-12336|, have been identified, cloned, and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified to homogeneity and characterized in vitro |CITS: [11279237]|., The process starts with |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and intermediate of the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|, which is converted to |FRAME: D-ALPHABETA-D-HEPTOSE-7-PHOSPHATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15573| (|FRAME: G-11949|). This compound is converted to |FRAME: CPD-12335| in two steps - the addition of a phosphate group at position 1, and the removal of the phosphate at position 7 (|FRAME: G-11951|, |FRAME: G-11950|, respectively). Finally, the molecule is activated by the addition of GTP, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15576| (|FRAME: G-11952|)., GTP is the only nucleotide that was able to serve as a substrate for this enzyme |CITS: [11279237]|.

Summary: |FRAME:NAD| and its reduced and phosphorylated derivatives are essential metabolites in all organisms and are, except for protons, water and oxygen, integrated with more biochemical reactions than any other biochemical agent |CITS:[22404877]|. As major players involved in energy metabolism, electron transfer and indispensable metabolic cycles the various |FRAME:NAD| species have attracted much attention and generated significant research efforts in elucidating their specific roles in relevant catalyses. In addition, there is growing evidence that |FRAME:NAD| species also operate in signaling pathways |CITS:[19211509] [21349851]|.   , In |FRAME:TAX-4932| the interconvertibility of the various |FRAME:NAD| species is of utmost importance for maintaining the redox balance of the cells which, in turn determines growth efficiency and metabolite excretion |CITS:[1900238]|.  For example, Baker's yeast requires |FRAME:NADPH| in the mitochondria for protection against oxidative stress and the operation of several biosynthetic pathways |CITS:[12727869]|. The various pyridine nucleotides, in particular |FRAME:NADH| cannot permeate the inner membrane of mitochondrion. For that reason direct transversal exchanges of |FRAME:NAD| and reduced and/or phosphorylated derivatives from the cytosol to the mitochondria and vice versa are not possible. Moreover, yeast does not possess transhydrogenases, hence cannot directly convert |FRAME:NAD| and |FRAME:NADPH| into |FRAME:NADP| and |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[3789705]|. Consequently, to ensure the availability of the required |FRAME:NAD| metabolites in each organelle, yeast has developed independent sets of interconversion reactions that provide the supply of all |FRAME:NAD| types through various enzymatic reactions., In the mitochondria of |FRAME:TAX-4930| two main sources for the generation of |FRAME:NADPH| have been proposed. The NADH kinase encoded by the POS5 gene is considered to be the main provider of |FRAME:NADPH| in the mitochondrion by phosphorylation of |FRAME:NADH|. However, since POS5 also works as NAD kinase |CITS:[12727869] [12912900]| this reaction followed by the dehydrogenase reaction of |FRAME:MONOMER-13666|/|FRAME:MONOMER-13665| |CITS:[9675847] [9059631]| is the other source for the synthesis of |FRAME:NADPH| in |FRAME:TAX-4930| mitochondria |CITS: [19158096]|. The deletion of both the mitochondrial POS5 and cytosolic UTR1 (see |FRAME:PWY-7268|) is lethal in yeast but the loss of one of the main NADH kinases can be partially compensated |CITS:[16760478]|. The oxidation of cytosolic |FRAME:NADH| via the mitochondrial respiration chain is catalyzed by three NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductases, one internal, i.e. NDI1 |CITS:[23086143] [1900238] [1735444] [3138118]| and two external, i.e. NDE1/NDE2 |CITS:[ 9733747] [9696750] [10781551] [12032156]|. The malate-aspartate shuttle in coordination with the 2 external NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductases is also considered to contribute to the reoxidation of cytosolic |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[9696750]|.

The |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| is considered one of the three essential pathways of central metabolism. It is an alternative way of oxidizing glucose, and it produces three of the 13 precursor metabolites (a small set of compounds that can be used to produce all others): |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|, |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| |CITS: [zubay1983]|., For convenience, the pentose phosphate pathway is commonly divided into its preliminary |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative portion"|, in which |FRAME: GLC-6-P| is oxidized to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, and its subsequent |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative portion"| in which through a series of transaldolase and transketolase reactions, |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| is converted into |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| and |FRAME: GAP|., About This Pathway, Genome information suggests that the conventional pentose phosphate pathway is incomplete or lacking in several archaea. The organisms that lack a complete pentose phosphate pathway appear to possess genes usually associated with the |FRAME: PWY-1861 "RuMP pathway"|, a pathway used for formaldehyde fixation or detoxification. Thus, it has been suggested that these organisms may employ a reverse RuMP pathway for pentose synthesis |CITS: [15876568]|., One such organism is the hyperthermophilic and anaerobic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-53953|. In this organism the hps (|FRAME: EC-4.1.2.43|) and phi (|FRAME: EC-5.3.1.27|) genes are fused to a single open reading frame that encodes a bifunctional enzyme harboring both activities. The enzyme is produced constitutively even in the basence of formaldehyde, supporting the proposal that the RuMP pathway in this organism is involved in a more general metabolic activity |CITS: [15901685]|. A subsequent study of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-311400| showed that inactivation of the |FRAME: G-44608| gene prevents growth in minimal medium, but growth could be recovered by the addition of nucleosides to the medium. Since |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| is a precursor of nucleoside biosynthesis (it is converted to |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P| within the pentose phosphate pathway, and the latter is converted to |FRAME: PRPP|, which provides the ribose skeleton to nocleosides - see |FRAME: PWY-5686| for an example), the experimet supported the proposal that in |FRAME: TAX-311400| the |FRAME: G-44608| gene functions is the sole pathway leading to the production of |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| and nucleotides |CITS: [16788179]|., In conclusion, Thus the hps (EC 4.1.2.43) and phi (EC 5.3.1.27) enzyme system plays a different role in bacteria and archaea by catalyzing the forward and reverse reactions respectively |CITS: [16428816]|., It should be noted that unlike the traditional oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, this pathway does not produce any NADPH.

Summary: General Background, Ommochromes are widespread phenoxazinone pigments of invertebrates. They act as light filters in compound eyes and determine the integumental coloration of a large range of invertebrates. The two major families of natural ommochromes are the yellow-to-red ommatins and the purple ommins that contain a supplemental phenothiazine ring. Ommatins are currently the best described family of ommochromes and occur throughout invertebrates |CITS: [Figon19]|. , In the fruit fly |FRAME: TAX-7215 "Drosophila"| eye color is determined by the presence of two classes of pigments - the pteridine red drosopterins and the brown ommochromes. They are located in pteridine or ommochrome pigment granules present in cells of the ommatidia. The drosopterins are derived from |FRAME: GTP| as shown in |FRAME: PWY-7442|., |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN Xanthommatin| is the predominant pigment in arthropods and cephalopods, and is redox-active, absorbing UV-vis light to display yellow or red colors that are dependent on their local microenvironments |CITS: [30507139]|. It exists in several natural systems including butterflies, dragonflies, and cephalopods, where it gives rise to a broad spectrum of color |CITS: [6772026][Nijhout97][20224921][22778425]|. It has been suggested that in the squid |FRAME: TAX-1051067| different ratios of |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN| and its |FRAME: CPD-24276 "decarboxylated form"| combine to form a range of colors that span the UV-vis range |CITS: [27049640][27911390]|, although this claim has been disputed on the bases that the experimental absorbance spectrum of |FRAME: CPD-24276| was not different from that of |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN| in the visible region |CITS: [32574597]|., About This Pathway, Ommochromes biosynthesis in invertebrates, including insects |CITS: [Linzen74][Han07a]|, spiders |CITS: [24314324]|, planarians |CITS: [27240733]| and cephalopods |CITS: [30824708]|, starts with the catabolism of |FRAME: TRP| into |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE|. These steps are homologous to the early part of the kynurenine pathway of vertebrates (see |FRAME: PWY-6309|), though the latter part of the tryptophan catabolic pathway diverges between vertebrates and invertebrates., Ommochromes are produced within specialized intracellular organelles, called ommochromasomes, most likely after the import of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| by a dedicated ABC transporter (the White and Scarlet transporters) |CITS: [8144619][11294610][32574597]|. Two hypotheses have been proposed for the next steps:, (1) Oxidative dimerization of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| into the unstable intermediate |FRAME: CPD-24273|, followed by intramolecular cyclization, forming the ommochrome |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN|, from which other ommochromes are synthesized |CITS: [Butenandt62]|, (2) The condensation of ortho-aminophenols with |FRAME: XANTHURENATE|, which is formed from |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.7|, could form directly the |FRAME: CPD-24277| chromophore of ommatins |CITS: [Linzen74][30208047]|., The former hypothesis appears to be more likely, since the predicted unstable intermediate |FRAME: CPD-24273| has been confirmed to be generated in vitro by the oxidative condensation of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| |CITS: [Butenandt62][Iwahashi97][30532237][Williams19][Figon19]|. A more conclusive evidence was provided by the discovery of the compound in ommochrome organelles of ommatidia isolated from house flies (|FRAME: TAX-7370|) |CITS: [32574597]|., Whether the in vivo oxidative dimerization of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| is catalyzed enzymatically remains a key question. Despite an early report of |FRAME: EC-1.10.3.4| (phenoxazinone synthase, PHS) activity in purified ommochromasomes of |FRAME: TAX-7227| |CITS: [828051]|, no such enzyme has been isolated or identified in species producing ommochromes |CITS: [Figon19]|. However, this activity could in theory be catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.10.3.2|, |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.6|, and |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.7| |CITS: [15216500][19268377]|. Importantly, insects mutated for the heme peroxidase Cardinal accumulate |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| without forming ommochromes |CITS: [414739][26328757][ 28657684]|., The next steps are not well characterized. The exact nature of cyclization to form |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN| is not well understood. It is also possible that decarboxylation to form |FRAME: CPD-24276| occurs directly from |FRAME: CPD-24273|, following a rearrangement catalyzed by an unknown tautomer., The study of ommatins and ommochromes is complicated by the fact that biological ommochromes are difficult compounds to analyze by NMR spectroscopy. As of 2020, only |FRAME: XANTHOMMATIN|, the most common and best studied ommochrome, has been successfully subjected to 1H-NMR |CITS: [30507139]|. In addition, biological extracts are prone to yield artifactitious ommatins |CITS: [32574597]|.
