Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-12776 Pyrrolnitrin| is a secondary metabolite produced by a number of Gram-negative bacteria. It has antibacterial and antifungal activity. Its antifungal activity may be a mechanism for the biological control of fungal plant pathogens by bacteria that produce it (|CITS: [9721657]| and in |CITS: [9537395]|). Its biosynthesis was first described in |FRAME: TAX-587851 "Pseudomonas chlororaphis aureofaciens (previously known as Pseudomonas aureofaciens)"| |CITS: [5985273][7275838]| and the genes and enzymes involved were later determined in |FRAME: ORG-6185| |CITS: [9172332][9537395]|., About This Pathway, Although its biosynthetic pathway and the functions of the enzymes have now been elucidated, the exact reaction equations for the PrnB, PrnC and PrnD catalyzed reactions have not been specified in the literature., PrnA selectively catalyzes the chlorination of |FRAME: TRP| to form |FRAME: CPD-11751| as described by EC 1.14.14.7. PrnB catalyzes the rearrangement of the indole ring of |FRAME: CPD-11751| to a phenylpyrrole and the decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-11751| to form |FRAME: CPD-12774|. PrnC catalyzes the chlorination of |FRAME: CPD-12774| at the 3-position to form |FRAME: CPD-12775| |CITS: [9537395]|. PrnD catalyzes the oxidation of the amino group of |FRAME: CPD-12775| to a nitro group to form |FRAME: CPD-12776| |CITS: [9537395]|. In some strains of |FRAME:TAX-32008| species pyrrolnitrin biosynthesis was shown to be regulated by quorum sensing |CITS: [19220396]|.

|FRAME:CPD-14483 Glycyrrhetinate| is the aglycone of |FRAME:GLYCYRRHIZINATE|, a triterpenoid saponin that belongs to a class of natural compounds which is known for its many potent and varying bioactivities. , Glycyrrhizin is very sweet (150 times sweeter than sucrose |CITS:[Kitagawa02]|) and used worldwide as a flavoring and sweetening agent for candies and medical remedies. Besides that, a wide variety of pharmacological activities have been reported for glycyrrhizin including antiviral activities against Hepatitis C virus |CITS:[21762538]|, anti-inflammatory activity through thrombin inhibition |CITS:[9196073]|, detoxifying and protective (hepatoprotective) activities in the liver |CITS:[17979145]| as well as immunomodulary |CITS:[7814808]|, antiulcer |CITS:[11767109]| and antiallergy activities |CITS:[1496934]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-14483| has been reported to inhibit linoleic acid desaturation in soybean chloroplasts indicating a possible involvement in the stress response of plants through plant chloroplast and plant desaturase regulation |CITS:[7615067]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-14483| comprises the initial cyclization of 2,3-oxidosqualene to form β-amyrin (see for example |FRAME:PWY-5203|) followed by a series of C-11 and C-30 site specific oxidative reactions which transform β-amyrin into glycyrrhetinate. Two Cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenases have been cloned and characterized in |FRAME:TAX-74613| which can catalyze this multi-step biotransformation when coexpressed together with β-amyrin synthase in yeast. , CYP88D6 was demonstrated in vivo and in vitro to carry out single oxidation reactions specifically at C-11 of the C-ring converting |FRAME:CPD-6948| into |FRAME:CPD-13667| in two sequential reactions and also act on |FRAME:CPD-13668| forming |FRAME:CPD-13669| |CITS:[18779566]|. The other Cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenase (CYP72A154) identified from a licorice cDNA library acting on the C-30 position of the E ring was also characterized as a multifunctional enzyme that catalyzed single oxidative reactions in the |FRAME:PWY-7066| namely the three sequential oxidation steps transforming |FRAME:CPD-13667| into |FRAME:CPD-14483|. In addition, the 30-C oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-6948| to form |FRAME:CPD-13668| carried out by CYP72A154 is the committed step in a different route leading to |FRAME:CPD-13670|, representing the common node in the pathway towards |FRAME:CPD-14483|. Within this route CYP72A154 also catalyzes its last step, the biotransformation of |FRAME:CPD-13669| to |FRAME:CPD-13670| which CYP88D6 is unable to perform. While the site specific oxidative steps could be demonstrated and the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14483| was obtained in in vivo coexpression in yeast, the precise sequence of the steps requires further research and a possible participation of other, as yet unknown Cytochrome P450's cannot be ruled out |CITS:[22128119]|., The third route to |FRAME:CPD-14483| comprising steps classified as hypothetical in the pathway may also exist as an Cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenase (CYP72A63) cloned from |FRAME:TAX-3880| was not only able to carry out the C-30 oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-6948| but also produced |FRAME:CPD-14486|, an possible intermediate on route towards |FRAME:CPD-14483| |CITS:[22128119]|.

The purine degradation pathway plays an important role in nitrogen metabolism in most organisms. The final product of de novo purine biosynthesis, |FRAME:IMP|, is degraded through sequential enzymatic steps into |FRAME: URATE|, which contains a high level of nitrogen |CITS: [11891236]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6353|)., In most organisms, including some bacteria, plants, and certain animals, |FRAME: URATE| is metabolized via a common pathway, producing the stereospecific form |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as the final product |CITS: [16317038]|. Some organisms that are not able to degrade urate include humans, apes, birds and reptiles |CITS: [16462750]|., It has previously been thought that |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| is formed from |FRAME: URATE| in a single step, catalyzed by urate oxidase. However, it is now established that the process involves three different enzymes |CITS: [16462750]|. In the first step of the pathway |FRAME: URATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|. There are four analogous types of urate hydroxylase enzymes, all of which hydroxylate |FRAME: URATE| to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|. The first type, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10284| gene, was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-3847| |CITS: [16593585]|. The other three types are represented by the |FRAME: G-11762 HpxO| from |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [19260710]|, |FRAME: G-17772 HpyO| from |FRAME: TAX-339| |CITS: [23760935]|, and |FRAME: G-2243 PuuD| from |FRAME: TAX-176299| |CITS: [26349049]|., |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE| is relatively unstable, and indeed decomposes in vitro to yield allantoin. However, this spontaneous reaction is unlikely to be physiologically relevant, because spontaneous decomposition yields racemic |FRAME: ALLANTOIN|, while organisms contain mostly the |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| enantiomer., An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of the N1-C6 bond of |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|, forming |FRAME: CPD-5821|, has been discovered and isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3847| |CITS: [10567345]|. An enzyme that catalyzes the decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-5821| to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| was first discovered in mouse |CITS: [16462750]| and eventually purified from |FRAME: TAX-272620| |CITS: [20826786]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathway derives in part from the central metabolic precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from oxaloacetate, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The de novo biosynthesis of UMP appears to be one of the most ancient biochemical pathways, as it is evolutionary conserved in all species. The pathway converts |FRAME: HCO3|, |FRAME: GLN|,, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to |FRAME: UMP| (UMP), a pyrimidine nucleotide that can be subsequently converted to all other pyrimidine nucleotides., The enzyme |FRAME: UMPKI-CPLX| catalyzes the phosphorylation of UMP to form UDP. The eukaryotic enzyme also catalyzes the phosphorylation of CMP to CDP, and was thus named |FRAME: AT5G26667-MONOMER| |CITS: [15604701]|., The penultimate enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX| (NDK), catalyzes a reaction in which the terminal phosphate of a nucleoside triphosphate is transferred to a nucleoside diphosphate - in this case, the, transfer of a phosphate from the purine ATP to the pyrimidine UDP, forming UTP. The enzyme has a broad substrate specificity, and is involved in the biosynthesis of several nucleoside-triphosphates, including formation of CTP from CDP., Interconversion between thymidine and cytidine nucleotides is possible only at the level of nucleoside triphosphates, by the glutamine (or ammonia)-dependent enzyme |FRAME: CTPSYN-CPLX|.

The organism produces, |FRAME: CPD-10246|, which it exports to the medium |CITS: [15340795]|. Similarily, the aerobic marine, gammaproteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-207954| also excrete sulfoacetate when utilizing taurine as a, source of nitrogen |CITS: [18506422]|. The key enzyme is |FRAME: CPLX-7633|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10764|., The enzyme is an inducible, soluble homotetrameric enzyme, and has been purified to homogeneity from, |FRAME: TAX-207954| |CITS: [18506422]|., The product of the reaction, |FRAME: CPD-10246|, was previously believed to be formed solely, from |FRAME: CPD-10247|. It is highly ionic, and is removed from the cell by a dedicated transporter,, encoded by the safE1/safE2 genes |CITS: [18506422]|.

Summary: This superpathway shows the production of both |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: GLY|, as the biosynthesis of each these two compounds is tightly affected by the other, via the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|., Serine biosynthesis is a major metabolic pathway in many organisms. |FRAME: SER| is not only used in protein synthesis, but also as a precursor for the biosynthesis of glycine, cysteine, tryptophan, and phospholipids. In the pathway shown here, which operates in bacteria, yeast, and animals, serine is derived from |FRAME: G3P|, an intermediate of glycolysis. , |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, converts serine to glycine, transferring a methyl group to |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|, thus forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate|, the major source of one-carbon units in many organisms, making serine hydroxymethyltransferase a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of many compounds that require a one-carbon unit, such as purines, thymidine, methionine, choline and lipids.

The messenger RNAs (mRNAs) of eukaryotes from yeasts to mammals, as well as most eukaryotic viruses, possess a 5' cap structure consisting of a 7-methyl guanosine (m7G) linked via an inverted 5'5' triphosphate bridge to the initiating nucleoside of the transcript |CITS: [1194288][9275164][12154373]|., The inverted m7G structure, also known as cap0, marks transcription start sites and has multiple effects on gene expression, including enhancement of RNA stability, splicing, nucleocytoplasmic transport and translation initiation, as facilitated by interactions with nuclear and cytoplasmic cap binding proteins |CITS: [8069914][9628920][14967145][10872469][18678651]|., The cap structure is formed cotranscriptionally by the sequential action of three enzymes. The first step is the hydrolysis of the 5'-triphosphate terminus of a nascent pre-mRNA to a diphosphate, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.33| (often referred to as RNA triphosphatase). The diphosphate RNA end is capped with GMP by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.50|, to yield a GpppNpNp- structure, also known as capG, and finally capG is methylated by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.56| to yield a cap0 structure., While in some cases (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-10245|) a multifunctional polypeptide contains all three active sites, in other cases (e.g. fungi) each function is catalyzed by a different polypeptide., In many eukaryotes the small nuclear (sn) RNAs involved in splicing also receive cotranscriptional cap0. However, following the formation of cap0 they are modified further by hypermethylation of m7G, forming m2,2,7G (trimethylguanosine or TMG), a reaction catalyzed in the cytoplasm by trimethylguanosine synthase 1 (Tgs1)., In higher eukaryotes, including insects, vertebrates and their viruses, further modification of mRNAs and snRNAs 5' ends involves the 2'-O-ribose methylation of the first transcribed nucleotide, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.57| (see |FRAME: PWY-7379|). The structure that includes a cap0 and the 2'-O-ribose methylation is called cap1. In about 50% of the mRNAs the second nucleotide is also methylated at the same position by a different enzyme, forming cap2 |CITS: [21310715]|.

Summary: General Background, Most organisms have less than 45 different tRNAs despite the fact that there are 61 different amino acid codons. The reason for this is that the third base of the codon is less discriminatory for the amino acid than the other two bases. Thus, the first base of the tRNA anticodon, which pairs with the third base of the codon, is more permissive for mismatches than the other two positions. At this position, which is known as the wobble position, 'U's and 'C's may be read by a 'G' in the anticodon. Similarly, 'A's and 'G's may be read by a 'U' or 'y' (pseudouridine) in the anticodon., The nucleotide at the wobble position is often modified, and particularly uridines, which are almost invariably modified. In yeast, 11 out of 13 wobble uridine-containing tRNAs are modified in some manner. The modifications increase the efficiency of codon reading and prevent mistranslation by limiting wobbling. In particular the 2-thiolation of the uridine is required for efficient codon recognition on the ribosome., The uridine34 wobble bases of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu are universally modified, although different modifications occur in different taxa and even in different cell compartments., In |FRAME: PWY-7891 "yeast mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19983| (τm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7889 "mammalian mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19980| (cmnm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7888 "cytoplasmic tRNAs of all eukaryotes"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19978| (mcm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7892 "the bacterium E. coli"| the modification is |FRAME: 5-METHYLAMINOMETHYL-2-THIOURIDINE| (mnm5s2U) or |FRAME: 5-METHYLAMINOMETHYL-2-SELENOURIDINE| (mnm5se2U)., About This Pathway, It has been shown that the 2-thio modification of mnm5s2U in tRNALys of |FRAME: TAX-562| confers efficient ribosome binding |CITS: [10024171][11063576]|. The same modification in tRNAGlu is required for specific recognition by glutaminyl-tRNA synthetase |CITS: [8385989]|. Thus, this modification plays a critical role in RNA translation by bacteria., The thiolation of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| is catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: EG11344| gene |CITS: [12549933][16387657]|., The source of the sulfur is |FRAME: CYS|. However, a complex sulfur relay system consisting of IscS and the TusABCDE proteins is required for delivery of the sulfur atom to MnmA |CITS: [16387657]|., IscS is a general sulfur donor, obtaining a sulfur from cysteine and delivering it to sulfur-accepting proteins in various metabolic pathways. Here it transfers the sulfur to |FRAME: TusA|, which transfers it to |FRAME: TusD|. TusD, which forms a hexameric complex with TusB and TusC, transfers the sulfur to |FRAME: Sulfur-Carrier-Proteins-TusE|, which finally delivers the sulfur to the MnmA protein |CITS: [16387657]|., Independently of the thiolation, the C5 position of the uracil is modified by the action of three other proteins. The |FRAME: EG10997| and |FRAME: EG10375| complex catalyzes the formation of a 5-carboxymethylaminomethyl group in a mechanism that has not been fully characterized yet |CITS: [19591841][19767610][24293650]|. The |FRAME: G7199 MnmC| protein, which consists of two conserved domains, an N-terminal methyltransferase domain and a C-terminal FAD-dependent oxidoreductase domain, catalyzes the last two reactions. The oxidoreductase domain removes the carboxymethyl moiety in the form of |FRAME: GLYOX|, while the methyltransferase domain adds a methyl group, generating the final 5-methylaminomethyl group |CITS: [15247431][18186482]|., In some organisms a further modification replaces the sulfur with a selenium atom. The responsible enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.9.1.3|, activates the sulfur atom by attaching a geranyl moiety to it, followed by replacement with selenium phosphate. The latter reacts with a watrer molecule, resulting in hydrolysis of the phosphate group |CITS: [6345544][14594807]|.

Summary: The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-671143| has not been cultured, but its genome has been assembled from a metagenomic sequence obtained from the sediment of two canals in the Netherlands. Both metagenomic samples were dominated (70-80%) by |FRAME: TAX-671143| |CITS: [19329658]|., Both enrichment cultures were grown anoxically and performed |FRAME: CH4| oxidation coupled to the complete denitrification of |FRAME: NITRITE| to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [16612380][18721142]|. Suprisingly, the genes responsible for the aerobic oxidation of methane (see |FRAME: PWY-1641|) were expressed and active even though the enrichments grew anaerobically. In addition, some of the genes required for complete denitrification were missing. This paradoxical observation lead the researchers to look for alternative pathways that could explain the observations., One pathway that could explain the data was the reduction of |FRAME: NITRITE| to |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|, followed by an "NO dismutase" reaction that generates |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| and |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| from two molecules of |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|. This hypothesis was tested using <sup>13</sup>C-labeled methane and <sup>15</sup>N-labelled nitrite. When nitrite (but not nitrate) was added methane oxidation began and labeled N<sub>2</sub> was formed in stoichiometric amounts.  The experiment also confirmed that complete denitrification was achieved despite the lack of genes encoding N<sub>2</sub>O reductase in the genome |CITS: [20336137]|., While the first reaction is likely catalyzed by a nirS encoded nitrite reductase (the putative nirS gene of |FRAME: TAX-671143|, DAMO_2415, has 70% similarity to the nirS gene of |FRAME: TAX-266|), the identity of the proposed "NO dismutase" is not known., |FRAME: TAX-671143| cells were found to have an atypical polygonal (star-like) shape that is very different from other bacterial shapes described so far. In addition, intracytoplasmic membranes, which are common in proteobacterial methanotrophs, have not been observed |CITS: [22020652]|. The organism also contains a unique fatty acid that has not been reported elsewhere, |FRAME: CPD-18002|, which makes up to 10 % of the total fatty acid in the organism |CITS: [23042164]|., The nitrite-dependent anaerobic methane oxidation pathway is one of the few known cases where molecular oxygen is produced in a metabolic reaction. Other such cases include |FRAME: PWY-101 "photosynthesis"|, |FRAME: PWY-6529 "chlorate respiration"| and the detoxification of reactive oxygen species.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HISTAMINE Histamine| is a biologically active diamine with important roles in animals. In mammals it is involved in the immune response, gastric secretion, neurotransmission and cell growth. |FRAME: HISTAMINE Histamine| metabolism includes its biosynthesis, degradation, storage, secretion and receptor interaction. Most current anti-histamine drugs interfere with cellular receptor interaction (reviewed in |CITS: [15612036] [18377770]|). The transport and compartmentalization of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| in relevant cell types is an important area about which little is currently known |CITS: [16648665]|. In some mammalian cells, it has been suggested that histamine and polyamine metabolism may be interrelated (reviewed in |CITS: [16364195]|). See pathway |FRAME: PWY-6181|. , The enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.22|, is responsible for |FRAME: HISTAMINE| biosynthesis from |FRAME: HIS|. In humans, |FRAME: HIS| is considered to be an essential amino acid that must be obtained in the diet, because the human genome lacks |FRAME: HIS| biosynthetic enzymes |CITS: [15173430] [10867060]|. Histidine decarboxylase is of interest as a drug target |CITS: [16547811]| due to the role of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| in pathological states such as inflammatory, neurological and neuroendocrine diseases, as well as osteoporosis and some neoplasias. However, the mammalian enzyme has not yet been fully structurally characterized due to its instability in purified preparations (reviewed in |CITS: [15612036]|). Histidine decarboxylase knockout mice have been constructed and studied, giving new insights into the role of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| in physiological processes |CITS: [12763012] [12716972] [17982051]|. In |FRAME: TAX-7215|, |FRAME: HISTAMINE| is a photoreceptor transmitter and a histidine decarboxylase homolog has been demonstrated by genetic studies |CITS: [8096176]|., In both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, strains of some species have been shown to produce inducible histidine decarboxylases. These enzymes are responsible for instances of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| poisoning resulting from the toxic effects of ingesting spoiled food containing high levels of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| (in |CITS: [18756395]|). Reports of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| contamination in food, especially fish |CITS: [17220267]| and fermented food including wine |CITS: [18065614]|, make this a significant economic issue, as well as a significant health risk (in |CITS: [15964650]|). As an aid in the assay of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| in food and wine, a histamine dehydrogenase with high specificity for |FRAME: HISTAMINE| as substrate has been characterized from |FRAME:TAX-379| sp. |CITS: [15964650]|., Physiologically, histidine decarboxylase is thought to have a role in metabolic energy generation and/or pH regulation of growth. In lactobacilli synthesis and secretion of histamine counters the lowering of pH by lactic acid that is produced during growth and allows denser cell growth (|CITS: [8387991]| and in |CITS: [11243783]|). In |FRAME:TAX-1581| the histidine decarboxylase gene cluster was found to contain four genes, one of which (hdcC) encodes a putative histidine/histamine antiporter |CITS: [15817789]|., About This Pathway, In animals, |FRAME: HIS| can be taken up by membrane transporters in relevant cell types (reviewed in |CITS: [9790568] [9050235]| and converted to |FRAME: HISTAMINE| by histidine decarboxylase. During inflammatory reactions, large amounts of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| are released from effector cells (mast cells and basophils) where it is stored in intracellular granules. Mast cells and basophils contain the highest amounts of histamine and histidine decarboxylase, but other cell types also contain histidine decarboxylase and can release histamine immediately after its synthesis. The enzyme can be modulated by a variety of stimuli in vivo including allograft rejection, infection, inflammation and stimulation by lipopolysaccharide (in |CITS: [17982051]| and reviewed in |CITS: [12102747]|)., In mammals and some Gram-negative bacteria (for example |FRAME: TAX-575|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, |FRAME: TAX-582|) histidine decarboxylase is a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|-dependent enzyme |CITS: [15583342]|. However, some Gram-positive bacteria (for example |FRAME: TAX-1593|, |FRAME: TAX-1502|, |FRAME: TAX-64642|, |FRAME: TAX-54062|, |FRAME: TAX-29388|, |FRAME: TAX-1247|, |FRAME: TAX-38293|) have a histidine decarboxylase that is a pyruvoyl-containing enzyme with a different reaction mechanism |CITS: [2745463] [12010554] [17887985] [18065614] [17220267]|. The mammalian enzymes appear to undergo post-translational proteolysis to produce active forms. Reviewed in |CITS: [15612036]|.

Summary: General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: penams (e.g. penicillins), ceph-3-ems (e.g. cephalosporins, cephamycins), clavams (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), carbapenems (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9377|, thienamycins) and monolactams (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while the remaining three classes of beta-lactams are produced by bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|., Penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins are produced by different organisms from branches of a common pathway. The pathway branches at isopenicillin N to form penicillins and branches again at deacetylcephalosporin to form cephalosporins and cephamycins (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|)., The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem and clavam antibiotics see |FRAME: PWY-5737| and |FRAME: PWY-5679|) differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). The pathway for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially elucidated and the order of some known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., The antibacterial mechanism of action of β-lactam antibiotics involves inhibition of the transpeptidation reaction during bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which leads to cell lysis. This reaction is catalyzed by class A and class B penecillin binding proteins. It is specifically inhibited by penicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics via formation of a covalent complex with the active serine of the transpeptidation domain of penicillin binding proteins. This prevents crosslinking and weakens the peptidoglycan polymer (in |CITS: [12867450]|). See pathways |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5265|. Bacterial resistance to β-lactam antibiotics can involve alterations in penicillin binding proteins, reduced antibiotic permeation across the membrane, or the production of β-lactamase enzymes (in |CITS:[12195735]|). See enzymes |FRAME: EG10040-MONOMER|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13427| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13428|., About This Pathway, Cephalosporin C is a medically important antibiotic biosynthesized as an end product by the filamentous fungus |FRAME: TAX-5044 "Acremonium chrysogenum (previously known as Cephalosporium acremonium)"|. The first two reactions in the cephalosporin C biosynthesis pathway (shown in the pathway link) producing isopenicillin N are shared with penicillin and cephamycin biosynthesis. The next reaction is the first committed step in cephalosporin and cephamycin biosynthesis in which the L-α-aminoadipate side chain in isopenicillin N is isomerized to the D enantiomer, producing penicillin N. In subsequent steps the five-membered penam thiazolidine ring is oxidatively opened and expanded to a six-membered dihydrothiazine ring characteristic of ceph-3-ems. In A. chrysogenum these two reactions are catalyzed by a single enzyme. The last step involves acetylation of deacetylcephalosporin C to produce cephalosporin C. Other cephalosporins are produced by bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-1901|. Deacetylcephalosporin C is a branch point in the pathway that leads not only to cephalosporins but also to bacterial cephamycins. Reviewed in |CITS: [9729600]| and |CITS: [12749845]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Factor-420 "Factor 420"| (also known as coenzyme F420, or simply F420) is a redox-active compound well-known for its role in methanogenesis. Although playing a crucial role in methanoarchaeal metabolism, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage., F420 was first isolated as a cosubstrate involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-19258| in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1960 |CITS: [McCormick82]| (see |FRAME: EC-1.3.98.4|). It is currently known to be involved in the biosynthesis of a number of secondary metabolites |CITS: [8577249]|, the degradation of nitroaromatics |CITS: [10217752]|, and activation of nitroimidazofurans |CITS: [10879539]|. Mycobacterium and Nocardia contain an |FRAME: EC-1.1.98.2 "F420-dependent glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase"| |CITS: [8997717][8631674]|, and an F420-containing photolyase has been discovered in a number of microorganisms |CITS: [2110564]|. However, F420 is best known for its role in methanogenesis (see |FRAME:CPLX-341| and |FRAME:CPLX-323|)., The structure of factor 420 from |FRAME: TAX-145262| was elucidated by Eirich et al, who showed that it was an [N-(N-L-lactyl-γ-L-glutamyl)-L glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin] |CITS: [728375]|. That compound contained two glutamate residues, with the terminal glutamate bound through an amide bond to the γ position of the other glutamate. Subsequent work revealed variation in the polyglutamylation of F420 among different organisms, with up to a total of seven γ-linked glutamates, sometimes capped by a terminal α-linked glutamate (see |FRAME:PWY-5199|) |CITS: [12867481]|., About This Pathway, The assembly of |FRAME:CPD-10333| (the core F420 molecule with no glutamate side chains) from |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE|, |FRAME:AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| and |FRAME:TYR| is a complicated process that requires multiple steps. In one route |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-7601|. In a parallel route |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| and |FRAME:TYR| are combined to form |FRAME: CPD-7602|. The products of the two branches, |FRAME:CPD-7601| and |FRAME: CPD-7602| are combined, generating |FRAME: CPD-10333| |CITS: [11535063]|., Even though |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE| has been documented in methanogenic archaea, it is still not known how it is produced. In 2019 it was reported that in mycobacteria the precursor for F420 is |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| rather than |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE|, and it was shown that the archaeal enzyme can accept that substrate |CITS: [30952857]|. However, a later study has reported that |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE| was the best, substrate of |FRAME: TAX-2190| CofC, suggesting that the pathway may start from different precursors in mycobacteria and archaea |CITS: [31469543]|,

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 Salicylate| is a key phenolic compound biosynthesized by many plants and some microorganisms. It is a member of an important anti-inflammatory drug class used widely in human medicine. In microorganisms |FRAME: CPD-110| is a biosynthetic precursor of secondary metabolites and siderophores, and a regulator of antibiotic efflux |CITS: [15837391]|. In plants |FRAME: CPD-110| may be converted by glucosylation, esterification, or methylation to physiologically active derivatives |CITS: [11607533]|. The source of the name |FRAME: CPD-110| (salicylic acid) comes from the name of the willow tree, |FRAME:TAX-40685|, from whose bark it can be obtained., For examples of salicylate biosynthetic pathways, see |FRAME: PWY-6408|, |FRAME: PWY-6407|, |FRAME: PWY-6406|, |FRAME: PWY-981|, |FRAME: PWY-6621|, |FRAME: PWY-6624| and |FRAME: PWY-4203| |CITS: [20020317]|., In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-110| can be degraded through several pathways including oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6183|), oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-633| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6224|), direct fission of |FRAME: CPD-110| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8159|), and degradation after CoA derivative formation. |FRAME: CPD-110| is also an intermediate in |FRAME: PWY-5427|., In yeast, earlier work on |FRAME: TAX-5554| showed |FRAME: CPD-110| oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [7364712] [6539772]|. In a more recent report using |FRAME: ORG-6162| a novel pathway of |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation via |FRAME: PHENOL| was elucidated (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6636|) |CITS: [20020317]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway, which has been documented in |FRAME:TAX-70356|, |FRAME: CPD-110| is degraded to |FRAME: CPD-633| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7830|., Gentisate is then degraded further to TCA cycle intermediate as described in |FRAME: PWY-6223| |CITS: [9573207]|.

A new group of substituted α-pyrones such as |FRAME:CPD-18129|, |FRAME:CPD-18130| and their isomers |FRAME:CPD-18134| and |FRAME:CPD-18135| collectively termed arabidopyrones (APs) have been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[22923580]|. This is one more example for the diversity of specialized pathways and the multitude of specialized compounds arising therefrom which may occur across the plant kingdom or been restricted to few or even single plant species |CITS:[16469917] [22683039]|. One of the central specialized plant pathways is the phenylpropanoid pathway (see |FRAME:PWY1F-467| and |FRAME:PWY-361|) which is considered pivotal for the land colonization of plants and occurs in all tracheophytes, i.e. plants who could develop a vascular system due to the ability to biosynthesize lignin |CITS:[20642725]|. This phenylpropanoid polymer provides rigidity to cell walls and xylem elements allowing upright standing plants and a vascular system which can withstand the enormous negative pressure caused by transpiration |CITS:[11960740] [14503002]|. From the phenylpropanoid pathway numerous specialized pathways branch out from the relatively limited number of intermediates which are subjected to a combination of decorating enzymes such as oxygenases, reductases and transferases |CITS:[20035037] [Wink10] [12946402] [Seigler98]|., One of the key enzymes in the phenylpropanoid pathway is the ferulate 5-hydroxylase (F5H), a multifunctional cytochrome P450 monooxygenase which activity significantly affects the monomeric composition of lignin |CITS:[9618461]| and also influences the biosynthesis of hydroxycinnamic esters and anthocyanins |CITS:[26048881]|. The F5H is encoded in Arabidopsis thaliana by CYP84A1 and a paralog of this gene, i.e. CYP84A4 has been found to catalyze the entry and rate-limiting step towards the biosynthesis of arabidopyrones (APs), i.e. the 3-hydroxylation of |FRAME:COUMARALDEHYDE| to yield |FRAME:CPD-18120|. Isotopic labeling allowed associating the origin of the APs to |FRAME:PHE| which strongly indicates the synthesis of APs via the phenylpropanoid pathway. , The molecular function of the p-coumaraldehyde 3-hydroxylase has been demonstrated by generating T-DNA insertional mutants (Δapd1) unable to produce the APs, rescue of the Δapd1 mutants by CYP84A4 transformation and in vitro by recombinant expression of CYP84A4 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae |CITS:[22923580]|. The following step in the pathway is the extradiol ring-cleavage by a dioxygenase encoded in Arabidopsis by LigB. The reaction has been proposed to be similar to the 4,5-ring cleavage of |FRAME:L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| forming |FRAME:CPD-253|, e.g. |CITS:[22270561]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5394|). T-DNA insertional mutants (Δapd2) were shown to produce no arabidopyrones anymore whereas the overexpression of LigB in Δapd2 mutants restored the arabidopyrone production to wild-type levels. The formation of |FRAME:CPD-18129| and |FRAME:CPD-18130| result from the 4,5-ring cleavage of the proposed substrate |FRAME:CPD-18120| forming the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-18126| which is spontaneously cyclized to |FRAME:CPD-18127|. The synthesis of the isomers |FRAME:CPD-18134| and |FRAME:CPD-18135| has been proposed to proceed via 2,3-ring cleavage yielding the respective intermediate |FRAME:CPD-18131| which spontaneously cyclizes to |FRAME:CPD-18132| |CITS:[22923580]|. The subsequent steps of the pathway remain to be elucidated but have been proposed to be carried out by a glucose oxidase like protein (GOLP) and alcohol- and aldehyde dehydrogenases (ADH, ALDH) |CITS:[22923580]|.

Summary: |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN "Riboflavin"| is the precursor for the essential flavin cofactors |FRAME:FMN| and |FRAME:FAD|, which are used in a wide variety of redox reactions. Riboflavin is also known as vitamin B2, because it is an essential nutrient and can not be synthesized by mammals., The biosynthesis of one riboflavin molecule requires one molecule of |FRAME: GTP| and two molecules of, |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| as substrates., The imidazole ring of GTP is hydrolytically opened, yielding a 4, 5-diaminopyrimidine which is converted to, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| by a sequence of deamination, side chain reduction and dephosphorylation. Condensation of |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| with, |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-BUTANONE-P| obtained from |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| results in the formation of, |FRAME: DIMETHYL-D-RIBITYL-LUMAZINE|., Dismutation of the lumazine derivative yields |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN| and |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE|, which is recycled within the pathway |CITS: [10940330]|., While the archaeal riboflavin biosynthesis pathway is rather similar to the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, many of the archaeal enzyme that catalyze the pathway's reactions are quite different., The first two steps of the flavin biosynthesis pathway in the hyperthermophilic euryarchaeon |FRAME: TAX-2190|, are catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7773| and a deformylase encoded by the |FRAME:G-11702| gene., The combined outcome of these enzymes is similar to that of the bacterial and eukaryotic , |FRAME: YBL033C-MONOMER|. The product, |FRAME: DIAMINO-OH-PHOSPHORIBOSYLAMINO-PYR| is converted to, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| following the fungal route, utilizing a reductase, a deaminase and a phosphatase, in this order., Other archaeal enzymes are different as well: the archaeal |FRAME: CPLX-7776| shares no sequence similarity with, non-archaeal enzymes, while the archaeal |FRAME: MONOMER-13864| is the only such enzyme known to utilize CTP, instead of ATP. The enzyme that catalyzes the last step of the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-8283|, is a monofunctional enzyme that has no sequence similarity to the eukaryotic monofunctional enzymes or the bacterial bifunctional enzymes. The fact that two of the pathway's enzymes have not been identified yet suggests that the sequence of, the genes encoding them is also likely to be divergent from the bacterial and eukaryotic genes.

General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms., Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7027|), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., |FRAME: TAX-38881|, a green colonial microalga, is regarded as a potential source of biofuel because of its ability to produce large amounts of hydrocarbons. Depending on the strain and growth conditions, up to 75% of algal dry mass can be hydrocarbons., Different strains of |FRAME: TAX-38881| produce different hydrocarbons. Three races have been documented: |FRAME: TAX-869302| (A race) produces odd numbered (C25 to C31) n-alkadienes and trienes, |FRAME: TAX-869301| (B race) produces triterpenoid hydrocarbons known as botryococcenes (CnH2n-10, n = 30-37) of isoprenoid origin |CITS: [Chisti80]|, and the L race produces |FRAME: CPD-13313|, a C40 tetraterpene |CITS: [Metzger90]|., About This Pathway, Alkanes are produced in multiple organisms - for example, in the |FRAME: PWY-282 "production of plant cuticular waxes"| |CITS: [18251711]|, as |FRAME: PWY-7035 "insect pheromones"| |CITS: [7937826][10406089]|, in green algae |CITS: [1898004][15630516]|, in fungi |CITS: [18957585]| and in bacteria |CITS:[ 6025301][15170379]|, especially cyanobacteria, which produce mostly |FRAME: CPD-7946| and |FRAME: HEPTADECANE-CPD| |CITS:[17731762][McInnes80][12495426]|., The alkanes are typically produced from long-chain and very-long chain (20-34) fatty acids that are produced from the "standard" C16 and C18 fatty acids by specialized fatty acid synthases, known as elongases (see |FRAME: PWY-5080|). These fatty acids are converted to alkanes in three steps - activation of the fatty acid by an |FRAME: ACP "acyl-carrier-protein"| or |FRAME: CO-A|, reduction of the activated fatty acid to an aldehyde, and decarbonylation of the aldehyde, resulting in an alkane that is one carbon short of the original fatty acid |CITS: [3343228][1608940][12467640]|., Since most fatty acids have an even number of carbons (fatty acids are synthesized by the addition of two carbon units), the resulting alkanes have an odd number of carbons., |FRAME: TAX-869302| produces alkanes when grown anaerobically. The pathway leading to alkane production begins with fatty acids that are activated to a CoA derivative and reduced to aldehydes by an NADH-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-17304| |CITS: [1898004][7649295]|. The aldehydes are decarbonylated into alkanes by an |FRAME: MONOMER-17303|, a cobalt-depndent, integral membrane protein |CITS: [1608940]|. Unlike cyanobacterial decarbonylases that produce formate |CITS: [21341652]|, the decarbonylases from higher plants and green algae produce carbon monoxide |CITS: [1608940][10845712]|.

General Background, The 3',5'-methylated flavonol syringetin and its precursor myricetin has been , found throughout the plant kingdom (e.g. |CITS: [1367884]| |CITS: [10856635]| |CITS: [14690384]| |CITS: [15806302]| , but as for many other flavonoids the glycosylated derivatives occur more frequently than their aglycons , |CITS: [Wollenweber94]| |CITS: [ Williams94]|. , The occurrence of laricitrin, the 3'-monomethylated derivative of myricetin and direct precursor for syringetin , has been verified during metabolic profiling in plants |CITS: [17002441]|. That demonstrates the existence , of that compound (and its glucosides) on its own, indicating that laricitrin is not merely a transient intermediate , of the pathway as assumed earlier. The pharmaceutical importance for human health has been demonstrated for , many flavonols (for example |FRAME:PWY-5059|, |FRAME:PWY-5320|, |FRAME:PWY-5390|). Similar reports , exist with regard to myricetin and its methylated derivatives. The therapeutic potential of these compounds are , considerable, as antioxidants as well as their use as anti-inflammatory, antiartherosclerotic and antithrombotic , agents that have been revealed in related animal research (reviewed by |CITS: [9251891]|). Moreover, myricetin , was found to reduce the danger of skin cancer, indicating its usefulness as an anticarcinogen |CITS: [3128399]|. , About This Pathway, The enzymatic step(s) representing the entry towards the biosynthetic route , of syringetin are catalyzed by enzymes that form the intermediate dihydromyricetin. That is the first flavonol bearing , three hydroxyl groups on the flavonoid B-ring. Dihydromyricetin is the branch point flavonol that is central to both , the formation of syringetin and the biosynthesis of corresponding anthocyanins such as delphinidin , (see |FRAME:PWY-5153|) and derivatives thereof (e.g. petunidin, hirsutin, ternatin). The enzymes catalyzing , the formation of dihydromyrecetin are cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases that either introduce two , hydroxyl groups to dihydrokaempferol (flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylases)(e.g. |CITS: [10476065]|) or form that , compound using the successive interconnection of flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase (e.g. |CITS: [10504566]|) and , flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylase (e.g. |CITS: [10567704]|) via dihydroquercetin., The 2-oxoglutarate dependent flavonol synthase catalyzing the formation of flavonols from dihydroflavonols , (EC 1.14.11.23) have been found in several plants |CITS: [16556978]| |CITS: [12620339]| |CITS: [12782296]| , however the specific conversion of dihyromyricetin to myricetin remains to be corroborated. , The final step in the pathway, the 3'- and 5'-O-methylation forming laricitrin and syringetin, respectively , is carried out by a unique O-methyltransferase (CrOMT2) that catalyzes two consecutive methylation , steps on the same substrate. It was demonstrated that dihydromyricetin was also a suitable substrate for , this enzyme. The methylation pattern corresponds to the glycosides and anthocyanins found in |FRAME:TAX-4058| , which supports the involvement of CrOMT2 in their biosynthesis |CITS: [12482447]|.

Summary: General Background, The two acyclic homoterpenes |FRAME:CPD-8844| (DMNT) and |FRAME:CPD-8846| (TMTT) are widespread constituents of flower fragrances |CITS:[boland89],[gabler91],[donath95]|. These homoterpenes are released from the foliage of many plant species following herbivore damage |CITS:[boland92],[dicke94]|. These compounds are part of the arsenal used in plant tritrophic 'indirect defense', which uses the volatile compounds to attract predators of the herbivores and help them locate their prey so that they do less damage to the host plants |CITS:[Dicke99],[10517823],[16723271]|., It has been suggested that |FRAME:CPD-8844 DMNT| might be stored as a β-glucoside of its sesquiterpenoid precursor |FRAME:CPD-12568| and is cleaved by a β-glucosidase contained in the regurgitant of the feeding insect. |FRAME:CPD-8844 DMNT| would then be generated by an oxidative degradation as exemplified in this pathway., Synthesis of sesquiterpenes occurs in the cytosol, however, several studies have shown that the isoprene units of |FRAME:CPD-8844 DMNT| originate both from the cytosolic |FRAME:PWY-922| and the plastidic |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY| |CITS:[15796607],[16580034]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP FPP| isoprenoid precursor to this pathway is first acted on by a terpene synthase to form nerolidol. Two different enantiomers may be formed. Different plant species have been observed to contain one or both of these enantiomers (see refs in |CITS: [DONATH95]|) and plant enzymes that produce both the |FRAME:CPD-8843 R-enantiomer| |CITS: [12481088]| and the |FRAME:CPD-12568 S-enantiomer| |CITS: [10805454][10482672]| have been experimentally identified. , The next step in the pathway is an oxidative degradation. This was long hypothesized to occur through the activity of a cytochrome p450 monooxygenase, but experimental proof was lacking until an Arabidopsis p450 enzyme, |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1|, was discovered that can catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8844 DMNT| from |FRAME: CPD-12568| when expressed in yeast |CITS: [21088219]|. |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| is unlikely to perform this function in planta because |FRAME: ORG-5993| does not appear to have a nerolidol synthase. However, several potential orthologs of this enzyme in DMNT-producing species may be good candidates to test for DMNT synthase activty. For example, poplar produces DMNT |CITS: [14756770]| and has a member of the CYP82 family of enzymes, CYP82L2 with 53% amino acid identity to |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1||CITS: [21088219]|. Although |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| acted on the |FRAME:CPD-12568| and a number of other plant species, such as |FRAME: TAX-3884 "Phaseolus lunatus (lima bean)"|, exclusively act on the S-enantiomer, a broad survey of plants revealed that there are examples of species where both enantiomers can be used |CITS: [DONATH95]|. And a direct test revealed that the |FRAME:CPD-8843 R-enantiomer| can be taken up and used by |FRAME: TAX-4577 maize| to produce |FRAME:CPD-8844 DMNT| |CITS: [12481088]|., Although there is now firm evidence that a cytochrome p450 enzyme can catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8844 DMNT| the exact mechanism of enzyme action is still being investigated. For instance, it is possible that |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| may promote the direct transformation of |FRAME: CPD-12568| to |FRAME: CPD-8844 DMNT| with the concomittant release of |FRAME: CPD-8847| as depicted in this pathway diagram. However, this reaction is labeled a "hypothetical" because this has not been experimentally verified. Interestingly, the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8847| has not been detected in reactions using an analogous compound |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| when |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| is expressed in yeast (see |FRAME: PWY-6668 TMTT biosynthesis|)|CITS: [21088219]|. The authors state that |FRAME: CPD-8847| may not be detected because of its high chemical reactivity. However, it is also possible that a two-step conversion may occur that includes the formation of intermediate C-13 compound |FRAME: CPD-12901|. This compound has been detected to exist in numerous plant species such as apple and |FRAME: TAX-183823| |CITS:[20860027][20658674]|. Several researchers have examined this |FRAME: CPD-12568| to |FRAME: CPD-8844 DMNT| chemical conversion in different plants (|CITS: [DONATH95]| and see refs in |CITS: [21088219]|), but further work will be required to clarify the exact manner in which the final step of this pathway is executed., Interestingly, a second pathway for the production of |FRAME: CPD-8844| has been discovered in the roots of |FRAME: TAX-3702| - see |FRAME: PWY-6007|.

|FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is an essential component of protein and peptidoglycan. The later also contains about three molecules of D-alanine  for every L-alanine. Only about 10 percent of the total alanine synthesized flows into peptidoglycan., At least three pathways (|FRAME: ALANINE-VALINESYN-PWY|, |FRAME: ALANINE-SYN2-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY0-1021|) are known for production of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|. The contribution of |FRAME: ALANINE-VALINESYN-PWY| to alanine synthesis remains speculative because alanine auxotrophs have not yet been isolated. Because alanine, but not valine, represses |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.66|, its primary purpose is probably synthesis of L-alanine |CITS: [396446]||CITS: [7040341]|., The second pathway, based on the activity of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.2|, is assumed to provide much of the cell's L-alanine requirement., The |FRAME: PWY0-1021| pathway is mediated by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.7|. This activity is required for the synthesis of Fe-S clusters, thiamine, thionucleosides in tRNAs, biotin, lipoate, and molybdopterin |CITS: [12382038]|. However, it  probably contributes only a minor amount of the cell's L-alanine requirement, as judged by the cell's total requirement for sulfane sulfur.

Summary: |FRAME: FLUORENE|, a 3-ring polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH), is a  constituent of  fossil fuels and is a product of incomplete combustion.  It is also an EPA priority pollutant., Several bacteria, including |FRAME: ORG-5880| |CITS: [8300532]|, |FRAME: ORG-5868|, |CITS: [9055403][1444405]|, and |FRAME: ORG-6007| |CITS: [8439154]| are able, to utilize fluorene as a sole source of carbon and energy.  |FRAME: TAX-110517|, on the other hand,, cannot grow with fluorene as a sole source of carbon and energy, but can transform fluorene to |FRAME: 9FLUORENOL| by the reduced substrate specificity of its naphthalene dioxygenase |CITS: [8899998]|., Three pathways were proposed for fluorene degradation by |FRAME: ORG-5868|, two of which are, believed to be productive routes that lead to central metabolism while the third is believed to be a non-productive, route that leads to dead-end products |CITS: [9055403][1444405]|.  A similar non-productive pathway for fluorene, transformation was proposed for |FRAME: ORG-6007| |CITS: [8439154]|.  Since |FRAME: ORG-6007| is able to grow on fluorene as the sole source of carbon and energy a productive route must exist as well; however, it has yet to be elucidated., |FRAME: ORG-5880| |CITS: [8300532]| is postulated to degrade fluorene via |FRAME: 9FLUORENOL| and |FRAME: 9FLUORENONE|, the initial two products in the proposed non-productive routes of fluorene transformation in |FRAME: ORG-5868| |CITS: [9055403][1444405]| and |FRAME: ORG-6007| |CITS: [8439154]|.  No 9-fluorenol, monoxygenase activity was detected in crude cell extracts of |FRAME: ORG-5880|, so it was, postulated that the transformation is probably due to monooxygenation by a dioxygenase type system, such as, naphthalene dioxygenase |CITS: [8300532]|.  9-Fluorenol is postulated to be transformed to 9-fluorenone by a, dehydrogenase, which is induced during growth on fluorene, but not on dibenzofuran |CITS: [8300532]|.  The subsequent product, 9-fluorenone, is postulated to undergo angular dioxygenation to |FRAME: 110-DIHYDRO-110-DIHYDROXYFLUOREN-9-ONE| (DDF) |CITS: [8300532]|.  The metabolites, |FRAME: 9FLUORENOL|, |FRAME: 9FLUORENONE|, |FRAME: 110-DIHYDRO-110-DIHYDROXYFLUOREN-9-ONE| and |FRAME: PHTHALATE| were detected in assays of dibenzofuran-grown cells of |FRAME: ORG-5880| |CITS: [2612886]|.

Names: methane oxidation to methanol II // methanotrophy
Summary: Methanotrophic bacteria, or methanotrophs, are a part of a physiological group of bacteria known as methylotrophs., Methanotrophic bacteria are unique in their ability to utilize |FRAME: CH4| as a sole carbon and energy source., A defining characteristic of all methanotrophs is the use of the enzyme methane monooxygenases (MMO) to catalyze the oxidation of methane to |FRAME: METOH|. Methane monooxygenases is oxygen-dependent and requires reducing equivalents to activate the oxygen. The oxygen molecule is split during catalysis, with one atom reduced to water and the other incorporated into methane to produce methanol. Methanol is subsequently oxidized to formaldehyde, which can be assimilated to provide carbon, or further oxidized to CO2 in a reaction that generates energy., MMOs exhibit a striking lack of substrate specificity, resulting in the metabolism of a very large number of compounds including xenobiotic chemicals such as small, unactivated alkanes and halogenated hydrocarbon solvents |CITS: [78039848]|., Methanotrophs are divided into two phylogenetic groups. Type I methanotrophs include γ-Proteobacteria, of the genera |FRAME: TAX-413|, |FRAME: TAX-39773|, |FRAME: TAX-429|, |FRAME: TAX-416|, |FRAME: TAX-73778| and |FRAME: TAX-54115|. These bacteria possess bundles of intracytoplasmic membranes, contain predominantly 16-carbon, fatty acids and assimilate formaldehyde produced from the oxidation of methane by the |FRAME: PWY-1861 "ribulose monophosphate cycle"|.The type II methanotrophs contained the closely related α-Proteobacteria genera |FRAME: TAX-133| and |FRAME: TAX-425|. These organisms have intracytoplasmic membranes arranged around the periphery of the cell, contain predominantly 18-carbon fatty acids in their membranes and assimilate formaldehyde into cell carbon using the |FRAME: PWY-1622 "serine cycle"| |CITS: [7857800][8801441]|., All methanotrophs appear to express a membrane-bound MMO (known as pMMO, since it is localized in the particulate fraction of cell extracts), which contains copper and apparently uses a quinol as the electron donor. A few species of methanotrophic bacteria produce a second, soluble form of MMO (sMMO) that does not contain copper and utilizes NAD(P)H as the electron donor (see |FRAME: PWY-1641|)., The particulate MMOs are notoriously difficult to purify, partially due to the fact that the copper is loosly bound and easily dissociates from the enzyme, and partially due to solubilization issues. The enzyme was shown to be reduced directly by quinols |CITS: [7646068]|. Unlike the sMMOs, which can oxidize large aliphatic and aromatic compounds, pMMOs cannot oxidize hydrocarbons larger than butane., Differential expression of the two enzyme systems is regulated by the availability of copper ions. When the copper, to biomass ratio is low, sMMO activity is observed, whereas pMMO is expressed at high copper to biomass ratios |CITS: [Prior85]|., Even though the reaction of methane oxidation requires oxygen, the pathway has been demonstrated in a bacterium that lives under anaerobic conditions. This organism, |FRAME:TAX-671143|, generates the required oxygen as a by-product of nitrite reduction |CITS: [20336137]|.

Summary: Plant defenses against herbivores and insects range from morphological modifications to biosynthesis of toxic compounds. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids  (PA) are one such group of plant defense compounds that occur in a wide range of plants, but more so in Asteraceae and Boraginaceae. The high toxicity of Senecio species is due to high concentrations of pyrrolizidine alkaloids in the plant tissues |CITS: [HARTMAN99]|. The major product is |FRAME: CPD-8987| and the main site of biosynthesis is the roots of the plants |CITS: [15466410]|. , A gene duplication of a metabolic enzyme from primary metabolism followed by diversification and further modifications is believed to be the basis for the evolution of these compounds |CITS: [15466410]|. The underlying biosynthesis of pyrrolizidine alkaloids have been extensively studied in insect species which are known to have recruited these compounds for their own defense. They have also had to develop complex mechanisms to protect themselves from the toxicity of PAs . One of the most common methods of detoxification is by N-oxidation of the pyrrolizidine alkaloids |CITS: [20454663 ]|. A gene duplication of pyrrolizidine alkaloid N-oxygenases in adapted Lepidoptera moths is traced back to an ancestral flavin monooxygenase of unknown function |CITS: [21288541]|. Estigmene acrea is able to sequesters all known pyrrolizidine alkaloids from all major plant families known produce PAs. Insect adaptation strategies include (i) pyrrolizidine alkaloid-specific taste receptors; (ii) detoxification of pyrrolizidine alkaloids by N-oxidation, catalyzed by a specific flavin-dependent monooxygenase; (iii) transfer and maintenance of all types of pyrrolizidine N-oxides through all developmental stages |CITS: [15804574 ]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The O antigen of group D2 |FRAME: TAX-590| strains is produced by a Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway. The basic repeat unit of O antigens from D group strains contains a |FRAME: CPD-9395| dideoxysugar |CITS: [14479760][14324537][ 4380946][5327479][5326096]|. The presence of this sugar results in epitope O9 and is the basis of the early differentiation of the group. The O antigen of group D2 |FRAME: TAX-590| strains corresponds to serogroups O9 and O46. The ancestral D form is believed to be group D3. Group D1 evolved later by incorporation of a second wzy gene and subsequent inactivation of the original polymerase.Group D2 arose by recombination between groups D1 and E |CITS: [23874940]|., The first step in Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways is the addition of a sugar phosphate residue to |FRAME: CPD-9646| (Und-P) to form the undecaprenyl diphosphate-linked sugar. Most O antigens found in |FRAME: TAX-590| species start with GlcNAc or GalNAc and their biosynthesis is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). However, the Salmonella O antigens belonging to serogroups O2 (A), O4 (B), O8 (C2C3), O9 (D1), O9,46 (D2), O9,46,27 (D3), O3,10 (E1E3), and O1,3,19 (E4) form a distinct set that is characterized by having a Gal residue as the first sugar of the O unit., The enzyme responsible for the initiation of these pathways is |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.6| (WbaP, previously called RfbP |CITS: [9004408]|). The use of Gal as initial sugar appeared in |FRAME: TAX-590| after its divergence from |FRAME: TAX-561|, but the eight Gal-initiated O antigens have grown to be very important in this species |CITS: [23874940]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O-antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes. The O antigen biosynthetic gene cluster of the group D2 strain |FRAME: TAX-682796| has been cloned and sequenced multiple times |CITS: [8021222][23874940]|. Strains belonging to group D2 produce an O antigen similar to that produced by group B members, but contain a |FRAME: CPD-9395| rather than |FRAME: CPD-9394| attached to the mannose at position 3, and the mannose residue has a β configuration rather than α. In both of these changes D2 resembles subgroup E1, but has the |FRAME: CPD-9395| side branch of D1., Following the completion of the synthesis of a repeat unit, the flippase Wzx flips the full molecule to the other side of the membrane, where the Wzy polymerase transfers additional repeat units from their anchor to a single elongating molecule. The Wzz protein ensures termination of the polimerization once the correct chain length has been achieved., The polymerase of D2 strains is a |FRAME: G-80955| type that links the repeat units by an α(1,6) linkage between the galactose and the mannose residues [α-D-Gal-(1→6)-β-D-Man] |CITS: [8021222]|.

General Background, The major flavonoids found in pea (|FRAME:TAX-3888|) are glucosylated , and acylated flavonols. Kaempferol (this pathway) and quercetin (see |FRAME:PWY-7173|) appear mainly as 3-triglucoside and their p-coumaric acid ester and have been identified in different tissues indicating that each organ in pea seedlings develops his own specific flavonoid pattern |CITS: [FURUYA65]|. It appears that light influences the formation of the various flavonols, kaempferol dominating in the absence of light and both kaempferol and quercetin derivates formed , under light conditions., Although the physiological function of those flavonol glycosides in pea is not exhaustively investigated it could , be demonstrated that the compounds are somehow associated with chlorophyll content, specific leaf mass, , photosynthetic rate and stomatal frequency |CITS: [16665658]| |CITS: [16663526]|., About This Pathway, Time course experiments indicated that the formation of the flavonol 3-triglucosides , involves three different glucosyltransferases sequentially adding glucose to the flavonol aglycones |CITS: [160697]|. , It has been demonstrated that each glucosylation step is carried out by a similar yet different flavonol , glucosyltransferase distinguished by substrate specificity and physico-chemical and kinetic properties |CITS: [6462109]|. , Only flavonol 3-O-triglucosides accumulate in vivo whereas the intermediates, i.e. flavonol mono- and diglucosides have been verified in in vitro experiments |CITS: [160697]|. It has been suggested that the different Km values of the involved glucosyltransferases are responsible for this phenomena since the rate-limiting step is , located at the beginning of the pathway. The subsequent enzymes efficiently convert the intermediates to the , flavonol 3-triglucoside not allowing to pile up the intermediate mono- and diglucosides |CITS: [6462109]|. , The final enzyme activity catalyzing the acylation of flavonol 3-triglucoside has been observed in crude enzyme , extracts of pea seedlings |CITS: [145116]|. The final product (this pathway), i.e. |FRAME:CPD-8069|, constitutes one of the most abundant flavonoids characterized in |FRAME:TAX-3888| |CITS: [FURUYA65]|.

Summary: General Background, Cardiac glycosides are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies. |CITS: [28561136]|., The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Cardiac glycosides having a terminal glucose are called primary glycosides whereas those lacking such a sugar are termed secondary glycosides., There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring)., The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides have a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis- fused while rings B/C are trans- fused. The nucleus has β configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|)., While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange |CITS: [KAUTE08]|., The |FRAME: Cardenolides cardenolides| have been divided into 6 series according to their genin part, which can be |FRAME: CPD-10537|, |FRAME: CPD-22576|, |FRAME: CPD-22579|, |FRAME: CPD-22581|, |FRAME: CPD-22583|, and |FRAME: CPD-22585| (termed series A through F, respectively). , |FRAME: TAX-4163| cardenolides are valuable drugs in the medication of patients suffering from cardiac insufficiency, and are known (together with the bufadienolides) as "cardiac glycosides". The major sources of the cardiac glycosides most frequently employed in medicine are |FRAME: TAX-49450| (for digoxin and other compounds) and |FRAME: TAX-4164| (for digitoxin)., About This Pathway, Like all plant steroids, the cardenolides are derived from |FRAME: MEVALONATE|. For simplicity this pathway starts at |FRAME: PROGESTERONE|. The path from |FRAME: MEVALONATE| to |FRAME: PROGESTERONE| can be traced via the following pathways:, |FRAME: PWY-922| → |FRAME: PWY-5123| → |FRAME: PWY-5670| → |FRAME: PWY-8028| → |FRAME: PWY18C3-1| → |FRAME: PWY66-377| → |FRAME: PWY-7299|., The first two enzymes of this pathway are progesterone 5-reductases, but their action results in different configuration of the respective products. |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.278| (P5αR) |CITS: [2106876]| competes with |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.277| (P5βR) for substrates and redirects sterol precursors to the formation of the less common 5α-cardenolides |CITS: [16386278][17184799][19895417]|. The product of the latter is reduced at position 3 to |FRAME: CPD-5961| |CITS: [Gartner93]|. The next two enzymes, involved in pregnane 21-hydroxylation and pregnane 14β-hydroxylation, have not been described yet |CITS: [28561136]|. The formation of the butenolide ring system is achieved by nucleophilic attack of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| at the C-20 carbonyl of a pregane-20-one (catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-20975|), followed by spontaneous decarboxylation and dehydration |CITS: [Stuhlemmer96][Kaute08]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-17477 "Juniperonate"| is a naturally occurring methylene-interrupted polyunsaturated fatty acids., It is found in high abundance in the seeds of the conifer |FRAME: TAX-58039| (common juniper), but is also found in other conifers, flowering plants, and also in some marine invertebrates. It is present in the seeds of the conifer |FRAME: TAX-58046|, which is used in traditional Chinese medicines, and was shown to have an an antiproliferative activity |CITS: [18758077]|., Two Δ5-desaturases, |FRAME: G-12182| and |FRAME: G-12183|, were cloned and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-212809|, an angiosperm species whose seed oil contains a significant amount of |FRAME: CPD-17350|, which is incorporated mainly into the sn-2 position of triacylglycerols in the seed. The two desaturases act on acyl-CoA, rather than acyl-lipd substrates |CITS: [17384161]|., Co-expression of either enzyme with a Δ9-elongase from |FRAME: TAX-37099| resulted in the production of |FRAME: CPD-17477| |CITS: [17384161]|.

General Background, The major pathway of |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| metabolism involves its role as a precursor metabolite in the biosynthesis of the catecholamines |FRAME: DOPAMINE|, |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY66-301|). The pathway shown here is a relatively minor catabolic pathway for |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| that has been demonstrated in rat liver. It involves methylation of |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| to |FRAME: CPD-11496| and final conversion to |FRAME: CPD-11831| (vanillactate) which is excreted in urine |CITS: [14789] [28856]| . Unlike |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE|, |FRAME: CPD-11496| is not easily decarboxylated, so the equilibrium is shifted to |FRAME: CPD-11830| formation |CITS: [28856]|. |FRAME: CPD-11830| undergoes |FRAME: NADH|-dependent reduction to |FRAME: CPD-11831| (vanillactate) predominantly by aromatic α-keto acid reductase, and also by lactate dehydrogenase |CITS: [28856]|., It was also suggested that |FRAME: CPD-11830| may be oxidatively decarboxylated to |FRAME: CPD-7651| as evidenced by identification of a small amount of this compound by thin layer chromatography |CITS: [14789]|. Summary: General Background, The monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, |FRAME: BENZENE|, |FRAME: TOLUENE|, |FRAME: ETHYLBENZENE|, and the xylene isomers (|FRAME: CPD-1421|, |FRAME: META-XYLENE|, and |FRAME: CPD-1422|), collectively know as BTEX, are some of the most water-soluble constituents of gasoline and are toxic. As a consequence, BTEX compounds pose a particular threat to human health and the environment because once released into the environment, they can migrate readily wtih water, and eventually contaminate drinking water supplies. BTEX compounds have become prevalent soil and groundwater contaminants as a result of leaking underground storage tanks and improper handling and disposal of gasoline., Aromatic compounds such as BTEX are important growth substrates for microorganisms. Initially it was believed that these compounds could only be degraded under aerobic conditions, i.e. in the presence of molecular oxygen. Aerobic degradation of aromatic compounds is characterized by the use of molecular oxygen, which is used in the initial oxidative attack of the aromatic compound, and in the subsequent cleavage of the aromatic ring structure |CITS: [1368147]|. Thus, anaerobic degradation of aromatic compounds, by definition, requires a completely different strategy. BTEX compounds were initially believed to be recalcitrant to anaerobic degradation due to the resonance stability of their aromatic ring structure and their lack of any reactive functional groups. However, beginning around 1990, microbiological research began to demonstrate that particular microorganisms can anaerobically degrade such aromatic compounds. Since then several bacterial pure cultures have been isolated that can anaerobically degrade BTEX compounds., Toluene-degrading bacteria isolated thus far range phylogenetically from nitrate-reducing bacteria clustering in the |FRAME:TAX-12960|/|FRAME:TAX-33057| branch |CITS: [7537067][9023943][7710331][8590677]| of the β-subclass of proteobacteria, to two sulfate-reducing bacteria (Desulfobacula toluolica |CITS: [7686000]| and strain PRTOL1 |CITS: [8919780]|) and one ferric iron reducing bacteria (Geobacter metallireducens |CITS: [8387263]|) belonging to the δ-subclass of proteobacteria to one toluene-utilizing phototrophic bacterium (Blastochloris sulfoviridis , |CITS: [10525736]|) belonging to the α-subclass of proteobacteria. Although the pathway for anaerobic toluene degradation shown here was demonstrated in denitrifying |FRAME:TAX-12960| and |FRAME:TAX-33057| species, there is some evidence suggesting that the initial steps of this pathway are common to other phylogenetic groups., About This Pathway, This pathway for anaerobic toluene degradation was proposed based on in vitro studies conducted with two denitrifying bacteria (|FRAME:TAX-59405| |CITS: [8706665]| and |FRAME: TAX-90060| |CITS: [9006019]|). Anaerobic toluene degradation is initiated by |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.11|, a glycyl radical enzyme catalyzing a non-redox reaction in which the methyl carbon of toluene is added to the double bond of |FRAME: FUM|. The subsequent reactions transforming |FRAME: BENZYLSUCCINATE| to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| resemble those of β-oxidation of fatty acids |CITS: [HEIDER99] [10629170]|. Benzoyl-CoA is a known central intermediate in anaerobic degradation of many aromatic compounds |CITS: [9057820][HARWOOD99]|. The pathway's intermediates |FRAME: E-PHENYLITACONYL-COA|, |FRAME: CARBOXYMETHYL-HYDROXYPHENYLPROPCOA|, and |FRAME: BENZYLSUCCINYL-COA|, and the enzyme activities for the corresponding reactions, were confirmed in 2021 |CITS: [34601806]|., The initial reaction, the formation of |FRAME: BENZYLSUCCINATE| from |FRAME: TOLUENE| and |FRAME: FUM| has also been observed in sulfate-reducers |CITS: [BELLER97][RABUS98]| and in a phototrophic bacterium |CITS: [10525736]|, suggesting that this may be a general strategy for anaerobic toluene degradation by phylogenetically diverse bacteria.
