Summary: |FRAME:NAD| and its reduced and phosphorylated derivatives are essential metabolites in all organisms and are, except for protons, water and oxygen, integrated with more biochemical reactions than any other biochemical agent |CITS:[22404877]|. As major players involved in energy metabolism, electron transfer and indispensable metabolic cycles the various |FRAME:NAD| species have attracted much attention and generated significant research efforts in elucidating their specific roles in relevant catalyses. In addition, there is growing evidence that |FRAME:NAD| species also operate in signaling pathways |CITS:[19211509] [21349851]|.   , In |FRAME:TAX-4932| the interconvertibility of the various |FRAME:NAD| species is of utmost importance for maintaining the redox balance of the cells which, in turn determines growth efficiency and metabolite excretion |CITS:[1900238]|. The various pyridine nucleotides, in particular |FRAME:NADH| cannot permeate the inner membrane of mitochondrion. For that reason direct transversal exchanges of |FRAME:NAD| and reduced and/or phosphorylated derivatives from the cytosol to the mitochondria and vice versa are not possible. Moreover, yeast does not possess transhydrogenases, hence cannot directly convert |FRAME:NAD| and |FRAME:NADPH| into |FRAME:NADP| and |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[3789705]|. Consequently, to ensure the availability of the required |FRAME:NAD| metabolites in each organelle, yeast has developed independent sets of interconversion reactions that provide the supply of all |FRAME:NAD| types through various enzymatic reactions., In the cytoplasm two NAD kinases have been characterized that can phosphorylate |FRAME:NAD|. The main cytosolic NAD kinase is encoded by UTR1 |CITS:[16760478] [11425472]|. A second, less important NAD kinase for phosphorylation of |FRAME:NAD|, i.e. YEF1 has also been described and shown to compensate for the loss of UTR1 |CITS:[15978040]|. The deletion of both the mitochondrial POS5 (see |FRAME:PWY-7269|) and cytosolic UTR1 (see |FRAME:PWY-7268|) is lethal in yeast and YEF1 can only compensate when POS5 still operates. These findings support the notion that the main NADH kinases of yeast, i.e. POS5 and UTR1 can partially compensate for the loss of one's respective activity |CITS:[16760478]|. Both UTR1 and YEF1 have been shown to exhibit NADH kinase activity as well providing the cytosolic set of enzymes with the catalytic ability to phosphorylate |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[15978040] [16760478]|. , Various enzymatic reactions have been shown to account for the provision of the cytosol with |FRAME:NADPH| required for biosynthetic pathways and anti-oxidant functions. The cytosolic acetaldehyde dehydrogenase encoded by ALD6 |CITS:[9392076] [9473035]|  and the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (ZWF1) catalyzing the first step in the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| to convert |FRAME:GLC-6-P| to |FRAME:D-6-P-GLUCONO-DELTA-LACTONE| |CITS:[2269430] [12584194] [11557322]| are considered as the main suppliers of |FRAME:NADPH|. A third enzyme producing |FRAME:NADPH| in the cytoplasm is the cytosolic NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDP2) |CITS:[8068643] [15574419]|. It has been demonstrated that ZWF1 has overlapping functions with the isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDP2) and the acetaldehyde oxidoreductase (ALD6) indicating the compensation for the deficiency of |FRAME:NADPH| should one of the involved reactions fail to operate |CITS:[16179340]|., In the mitochondria of |FRAME:TAX-4930| two main sources for the generation of |FRAME:NADPH| have been proposed. The NADH kinase encoded by the POS5 gene is considered to be the main provider of |FRAME:NADPH| in the mitochondrion by phosphorylation of |FRAME:NADH|. However, since POS5 also works as NAD kinase |CITS:[12727869] [12912900]| this reaction followed by the dehydrogenase reaction of |FRAME:MONOMER-13666|/|FRAME:MONOMER-13665| |CITS:[9675847] [9059631]| is the other source for the synthesis of |FRAME:NADPH| in |FRAME:TAX-4930| mitochondria |CITS: [19158096]|. The oxidation of cytosolic |FRAME:NADH| via the mitochondrial respiration chain is catalyzed by three NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductases, one internal, i.e. NDI1 |CITS:[23086143] [1900238] [1735444] [3138118]| and two external, i.e. NDE1/NDE2 |CITS:[9733747] [9696750] [10781551] [12032156]|. The malate-aspartate shuttle in coordination with the 2 external NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductases is also considered to contribute to the reoxidation of cytosolic |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[9696750]|.

Filamentous fungi from the genus Fusarium are well known for their ability to biosynthesize a vast variety of structural diverse secondary metabolites. Amongst them is |FRAME:CPD-17957| (compare also |FRAME:PWY-7668|), a cyclic tetrapeptide which is best known for its ability to exhibit antiprotozoal activity against Apicomplexa |CITS:[8917558]|, a phylum of parasitic protozoans causing a number of diseases such as malaria (e.g. |CITS:[22276399]|) and coccidiosis, a parasitic infection of the intestinal tract (e.g. |CITS:[25201405]|). |FRAME:CPD-17957 Apicidin| and congeners such as |FRAME:CPD-17971| and |FRAME:CPD-17970| have been isolated and structurally characterized from Fusarium incarnatum (formerly Fusarium semitectum and also referred to as Fusarium pallidoroseum) |CITS:[11529764] [11856024]|. , It has been demonstrated that |FRAME:CPD-17957| acts as coccidiostats agent |CITS:[Singh96]|, inhibits the histone deacetylase (HDAC) of protozoal parasites |CITS:[8917558]| and has therefore been become a target for the development of new antimalarial drugs |CITS:[22607140] [12678732]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-17957| has shown anti-cancer activity against endometrial and ovarian cancer cells |CITS:[17203205]|, inhibited proliferation and interfered with the differentiation of the leukemia cell line HL-60 |CITS:[12490313]|, caused hemorrhage in the stomach of rats |CITS:[9872769]| and also displayed phytotoxicity on seedlings of diverse plant species |CITS:[Jin08]|., Insertional mutants of Fusarium incarnatum generated via Agrobacterium tumefaciens mediated transformation allowed the identification for a non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS), i.e. apicidin synthetase (APS1) and the biosynthetic gene cluster involved in the |FRAME:PWY-7667|. Targeted gene disruption and metabolic profiling of the resultant mutants allowed to propose a pathway and to determine the molecular function of the catalytic enzymes. The apicidin synthetase encoded by APS1 consisting of four modules with adenylation (A), thiolation (T) and condensation (C) domains for modules 2 to 4 plus an additional epimerization (E) domain for the first module was shown to incorporate four amino acids, i.e. |FRAME:L-PIPECOLATE|, |FRAME:ILE|, |FRAME:CPD-17973| and finally |FRAME:CPD-17966| into the nascent peptide molecule in that order. Although not all steps of the pathway generating the four amino acids to be forming the tetrapeptide core of |FRAME:CPD-17957| have been elucidated yet the selected deletion of genes such as APS7 encoding for the L-2-aminodecanoate 8-hydroxylase, APS9 coding for the L-2-amino-8-hydroxdecanoate dehydrogenase and APS3 encoding for the 1-piperideine 6-carboxylate reductase resulted in the accumulation of various intermediates, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17962|, |FRAME:CPD-17970| and |FRAME:CPD-17971|, respectively which strongly supported the molecular functions of those enzymes in the pathway |CITS:[20233305]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-20974 Pinoresinol| is a dilignan produced by the radical β-β' coupling of two |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL| molecules. It is produced by plants as a major component of |FRAME: Lignins lignin|, and also serves as a defense molecule. It is liberated from lignin during the degradation of dead plant material., Pinoresinol is degraded by either oxidative or reductive pathways. A reductive pathway, initiated by |FRAME: MONOMER-20459| (PinZ), has been suggested in |FRAME: TAX-627192|, although only the first steps have been characterized |CITS: [23199737]|. Oxidative pathways has been reported from white rot fungi |CITS: [Kamaya81][Iwahara82][Kamaya83]|, as well as from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1914534| |CITS: [29222099]|, as described here., |FRAME: TAX-1914534| has been isolated from composting plant material based on its ability to degrade |FRAME: CPD-8905|. The organism rapidly mineralizes the compound via an inducible pathway that ends in |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which enters central metabolism as described in |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|., The pathway is initiated by α-hydroxylation, forming |FRAME: CPD-20976|. This enzyme, which is linked to an electron-transporting system via the blue-copper protein |FRAME: Azurins azurin|, utilizes a water molecule as the oxygen source |CITS: [29222099][32198167]|., Following the hydroxylation, the pathway proceeds with an alkyl-aryl cleavage to generate the γ-lactone |FRAME: CPD-20977| and |FRAME: CPD-20978|. While both branches are eventually metabolized into |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, they take very different rounts. |FRAME: CPD-20978| is metaboilized into |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| in three steps as shen here. The other cleavage product is processed via a branched pathway, since the lactone can be either α-hydroxylated again, or hydrolyzed. However, these two parallel branches converge at |FRAME: VANILLIN|, which is oxidized to |FRAME: VANILLATE| |CITS: [29222099]|. |FRAME: VANILLATE Vanillate| is processed to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| via |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| as described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-7098| and |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY| |CITS: [32198167]|., While most of the enzymes have not been characterized yet, the gene cluster that encodes them, which occupies a 35.1 kb region on the |FRAME: TAX-1914534| chromosome, has been sequenced, and many of the genes have been flagged as potential candidates. It was also shown that the genes are induced more than 2-fold by exposure to |FRAME: CPD-20974| |CITS: [32198167]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran|, marketed under the trade name Furadan, is one of the most toxic broad-spectrum and systemic N-methyl carbamate pesticides, which is used extensively as insecticide, nematicide and acaricide for agricultural, domestic and industrial purposes. The chemical is highly toxic to mammals, birds, and honeybees, and has a moderate to high toxicity to most aquatic organisms |CITS: [32593003]|. |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran| is an endocrine disruptor and a probable reproduction/development intoxicant. It is an inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.7|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.8| |CITS: [18706518]|., |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran| has been banned in Canada and the European Union for many years. It was banned in the US in 2009 after the U.S. Supreme Court denied a counter petition by FMC and several corn grower associations., Despite its considerable toxicity, |FRAME: CPD-24209| is still used in some countries with a wide variety of field crops including potatoes, corn and soybeans. In addition, according to several journalistic investigations illegally smuggled |FRAME: CPD-24209| is used on marijuana grown illegally on public land in California, and |FRAME: CPD-24209|-contaminated marijuana appears to be the main source of marijuana consumed in states where it hasn't been legalized. In East Africa |FRAME: CPD-24209| is used by farmers to poison lions., Diverse carbofuran-degrading bacteria have been described, including members of the genera Pseudomonas, Flavobacterium, Achromobacter, Sphingomonas, Novosphingobium, and Paracoccus. However, most of these organisms are only capable of hydrolyzing |FRAME: CPD-24209| to |FRAME: CPD-24214|. Only sphingomonads are able to proceed by fully degrading |FRAME: CPD-24214| |CITS: [ 29884759]|., About This Pathway, Two types of carbofuran hydrolases, Mcd and CfdJ, have been reported. Mcd was purified from |FRAME: TAX-104199| |CITS: [ 2661544]|. Homologs of |FRAME: G-107481| were detected in phylogenetically diverse carbofuran-degrading isolates, but not in the sphingomonads |CITS: [Parekh95]|. The |FRAME: G-107480| gene, which was reported from |FRAME: TAX-1478134| |CITS: [26159535]|, is a close homolog of the cehA gene of |FRAME: TAX-168685|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.137|. It was named differently because at the time it was believed that CehA is not able to hydrolyze carbofuran. However, subsequent studies have shown that that CehA is indeed able to hydrolyze carbofuran, and that CehA and CfdJ are perfect homologs with similar substrate range. As a result, homologs isolated subsequently from |FRAME: TAX-2004404| and |FRAME: ORG-57100| were named CehA |CITS: [31759739]|., Most of the genes involved in carbofuran degradation appear to be located in the cfd operon. In |FRAME: TAX-1478134| the cluster contains 8 open reading frames allowing the organism to degrade carbofuran to |FRAME: CPD-14447| and |FRAME: CPD-14642|, as shown in |FRAME: PWY-8286|., |FRAME: TAX-2004404| and |FRAME: ORG-57100| have truncated clusters, missing some of the genes. A study of the |FRAME: G-107478| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1478134| suggested that it encodes a monooxygenase that hydroxylates carbofuran phenol at the C8 position, resulting in the opening the furan ring |CITS: [ 24931307]|. However, studies with the homologous enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-2004404| and |FRAME: ORG-57100| suggested that at least in these organisms the enzyme hydroxylates carbofuran phenol at position C4 within the benzene ring, and does not lead to the furan ring cleavage |CITS: [29884759][31759739]|. Idenitification of common intermediates in the pathway suggested the presence of the quinone form |FRAME: CPD-24540|., |FRAME: ORG-57100| is able to use carbofuran as its sole carbon and nitrogen source, suggesting that the pathway continues towards full mineralization. However, as of 2021 the rest of the pathway remains unknown.

Summary: General Background, Protein glycosylation is an important process found in all kingdoms of life. N-glycosylation is found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria. During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. In eukaryotes, the nascent proteins that are synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane where they acquire the initial carbohydrate chains on specific asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes can be divided into the following three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7919|)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (this pathway)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and use somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathway is in general similar to the eukaryotic one, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7658|)., About This Pathway, The last phase in the synthesis of complex asparagine-linked glycans (N-glycans) starts with the five mannose N-glycan |FRAME: Mannosyl5-N-Glycans|. The process in metazoa involves the action of five different N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases, which were named GlcNAc-TI through GlcNAc-TV (a sixth one, GlcNAc-TVI has been characterized from chicken)., GlcNAc-TI (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.101 "EC 2.4.1.101"|) catalyzes the addition of GlcNAc in β1-2 linkage to the Manα(1-3) terminus of the five-mannose structure. This is followed by mannosidase II (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.114 "EC 3.2.1.114"|), which removes two mannosyl residues, exposing the Manα(1-6) terminus that serves as a substrate for GlcNAc-T II (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.143 "EC 2.4.1.143"|). Addition of a second GlcNAc residue by GlcNAc-T II results in the complex N-glycan |FRAME: 2-2-N-linked-Glycan|. This structure is the precursor to a large assortment of branched complex N-glycans involving three more N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases., One of the unique features of N-glycan structures is the large number of potential branches. The branching is introduced by four enzymes: GlcNAc-III (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.144 "EC 2.4.1.144"|), GlcNAc-IV (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.145 "EC 2.4.1.145"|), GlcNAc-V (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.155 "EC 2.4.1.155"|), and a fucosyltransferase, encoded by the FUT8 gene (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.68 "EC 2.4.1.68"|)., GlcNAc-III catalyzes the transfer of a GlcNAc residue to the β-mannose via a β1,4-linkage, generating the so-called "bisecting GlcNAc" structure. Unlike other branches, bisecting residues are not elongated. In addition, the presence of a bisecting residue has a negative impact on the activities of other glycosyltransferases, including GlcNAc-IV and GlcNAc-V |CITS: [3521675][8393437]|. Mannosidase II also cannot act on bisected oligosaccharides. Thus, if GlcNAc-T III acts on the product of GlcNAc-T I before mannosidase II, the pathway is committed to the simple structures known as "hybrid structures" rather than complex branched structures (Hybrid N-glycans are defined by having only mannosyl (Man) residues on the α-Man-(1→6) arm and only N-acetylglucosaminyl (GlcNAc) residues on the α-Man-(1→3) arm |CITS: [24178944]|). Therefore, the relative abundance of GlcNAc-T III and mannosidase II in a particular tissue controls the ratio of hybrid vs. complex N-glycans., Following the creation of the branches, the non-reducing ends (except for branches created by GlcNAc-III) are galactosylated in a β1,4 linkage to form an N-acetyllactosamine unit, in a reaction catalyzed by seveal galactosyltransferases (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.38 "EC 2.4.1.38"|). On the β1,6-branch N-acetyllactosamine unit is often repeated to form a polylactosamine chain (not shown in this pathway), the formation of which is catalyzed by the sequential action of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.38 "EC 2.4.1.38"| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.149|. This polylactosamine structure acts as a high-affinity ligand for galectins |CITS: [20064370]|., The mammalian N-glycan modification process ends with sialylation of the non-reducing ends of the branched glycan by either an α2,3 linkage (|FRAME: EC-2.4.3.6 "EC 2.4.99.6"|) or an α2,6 linkage (|FRAME: EC-2.4.3.1 "EC 2.4.99.1"|).

General Background, |FRAME: CHOLINE Choline| is a quaternary ammonium compound and a fundamental metabolite for eukaryotic organisms, forming the head group of important phospholipids such as |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| |CITS: [12215503]|., Choline is also the precursor for the neurotransmitter |FRAME: ACETYLCHOLINE|, and serves as a precursor for the formation of the important osmoprotectant |FRAME: BETAINE| (see |FRAME:PWY1F-353| for an example) ., Most plants synthesize choline, since phosphatidylcholine accounts for 40 to 60% of lipids in non-plastid plant membranes |CITS: [12215503]|. Animals cannot synthesize |FRAME: CHOLINE|, which must be consumed through the diet, making it a vitamin. It is usually grouped within the B-complex vitamins. Most microbes are not able to produce choline, although many have transporters for its uptake., About This Pathway, The first step in choline biosynthesis is the direct decarboxylation of serine to ethanolamine , |CITS: [11461929]|, which is catalyzed by a serine decarboxylase unique to plants |CITS: [14634155]|. Ethanolamine is, widely recognized as the entrance compound to choline biosynthesis. , The synthesis of choline from ethanolamine may take place at three parallel pathways, where three consecutive , N-methylation steps are carried out either on free bases, phospho-bases, or phosphatidyl-bases |CITS: [11481443]|., The N-methylation of free base intermediates has been demonstrated in crude extracts of castor bean (Ricinus , communis) endosperm tissue. In this nutritive tissue the first methylation step appears to favor ethanolamine , |CITS: [PRUDHOMME92B]| over phosphoethanolamine, which was thought to be the key substrate for further metabolic , steps in the plant's choline/phosphocholine biosynthesis |CITS: [Datko88a]| |CITS: [Datko88b]|. The resulting , monomethylethanolamine (MMEta) is than converted partially to dimethylethanolamine (DMEta) or phosphorylated , to phosphomonomethylethanolamine (PMMEta). The DMEta is again partitioned between methylation to choline (Cho) , and phosphorylation to phosphodimethylethanolamine (PDMEta). Taken together, it has been demonstrated that , N-methylation in castor bean takes part on two different levels of intermediates, the free base laevel to produce choline, (Cho) and the phospho-base level to generate phosphocholine (P-Cho) |CITS: [PRUDHOMME92A]|., The metabolic fate of the end products of those two pathways is different. Free choline accumulates in a major , sequestered pool, and is more or less inaccessible for phosphatidylcholin biosynthesis. In contrast, phosphocholin is, decidedly involved in this pathway supported by a high in vitro activity of the nucleotide (CDP) pathway |CITS: [KINNEY87]| , |CITS: [Tang97]| as found in castor bean endosperm. Although the rate and direction of choline recycling still remains , to be investigated, the extractable enzyme activities acting on different intermediate levels indicated a well developed , capability of this plant to work efficiently with small, highly regulated pools.

Summary: General Background , Hydrogenases catalyze the reversible interconversion of protons, electrons and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, resulting in |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| oxidation to two protons or in the reverse direction, molecular hydrogen production by the reduction of protons., Most hydrogenases are metalloenzymes that contain iron-sulfur clusters. They have been subdivided into two main classes based on the composition of two metal atoms at their active center: |FRAME: NiFe-hydrogenases "[NiFe] hydrogenases"| and |FRAME: FeFe-hydrogenases "[FeFe] hydrogenases"|. These two classes are phylogenetically distinct. In some of the [NiFe] hydrogenases one of the Ni-bound cysteine residues is replaced by selenocysteine, and those enzymes are known as [NiFeSe] hydrogenases. While [FeFe] hydrogenases are limited to certain bacteria and a few unicellular eukaryotes, [NiFe] hydrogenases are widespread in both bacteria and archaea |CITS: [20463892]|. , [NiFe] hydrogenases are usually heterodimeric proteins, but can be associated with additional subunits.The large subunit contains a |FRAME: CPD-24862| at the catalytic site, while the smaller subunit contains 3 FeS clusters that transfer electrons from an external electron donor (such as ferredoxin or flavodoxin) to the |FRAME: CPD-24862| site for reduction of protons |CITS: [20463892]|., About This Pathway, The catalytic cofactor is strictly conserved among all [NiFe]-hydrogenases. The nickel ion is coordinated by four cysteinyl thiolates in the active site, while two of the thiolates additionally bind an iron ion. The iron site carries one CO and two, CN- ligands |CITS: [8990114][9920874]|. The ligands are proposed to maintain the low-spin Fe2+ state important for H2 activation., The synthesis and insertion of the |FRAME: CPD-24862| into the apo-enzyme are complex processes that require a number of maturation accessory proteins. In |FRAME: TAX-562| these include the products of the hypABCDEF and slyD genes. It should be noted that some of the reactions described here are a working hypothesis and have not been confirmed conclusively as of 2021., The |FRAME: HypC "HypC protein"| binds both iron and CO2 |CITS: [23851071]|. Upon contact with HypD HypC forms a HypCD complex, which catalyzes an ATP-dependent reduction of the CO2 to CO. The source of electrons required for this reduction is unknown |CITS: [31614069]|., The CN- ligands are generated by the maturation proteins HypE and HypF. HypF activates |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| using ATP, and transfers the carbamoyl group to the carboxy terminal cysteine of HypE |CITS: [12586941]|. During the carbamoyl transfer reaction, HypE and HypF form a tight stoichiometric complex |CITS: [15291820]|. HypE then catalyzes the ATP hydrolysis-dependent dehydration of the carbamate group to a cyanate group |CITS: [12586941]|. HypE forms a dimer, which binds to HypCD complexes, forming a [HypCDE]2 complex. Two cyano groups are transferred from HypE to the Fe(CO) cluster on HypCD, forming a Fe(CO)(CN)2 cluster |CITS: [15504408][23022438][23123111]|., The Fe(CO)(CN)2 cluster is transferred from the HypCDE complex to the hydrogenase large subunit in a complex process that involves three proteins - SlyD, |FRAME: HypB HypB|, and a third hydrogenase-specific protein (in |FRAME: TAX-562| HypA for hydrogenase 3 and HybF for hydrogenases 1 and 2). While the exact mechanism is not known, all three proteins were shown to bind Ni(II) ions |CITS: [15569666][16142921][19769985]|. HypB from |FRAME: TAX-562| has two Ni-binding domains and GTPase activity |CITS: [8423137]|, while orthologs from Thermococcales have a single Ni-binding domain and ATPase activity |CITS: [23399544]|. The role of SlyD is not fully understood, but it can interact with and transfer its nickel to HypB |CITS: [23708681][35099020]|. In organisms that possess a GTPase-tpye HypB, it was shown that SlyD is required for release of the Ni(II) ion from HypB, allowing it to be transferred to the Ni-chaperon HypA, which eventually transfers it to the hydrogenase |CITS: [23899293]|. HypA is thought to serve as a scaffold that docks the other nickel accessory proteins onto the hydrogenase precursor protein |CITS: [22016389]|. In organisms that have an ATPase-type HypB, it has been proposed that HypA binds Ni directly, but interaction with HypB is necessary for the relase of the bound Ni and its transfer to the hydrogenase large subunit |CITS: [32227866]|., Further processing, which involves cleavage of the hydrogenase large subunit C-terminus, results in rearrangement that forms the active cofactor |CITS: [15667279][17150961][27192667][29526754]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.1|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.1|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.2| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the last part of the eukaryotic thiamine biosynthesis pathway - the coupling of the two moieties of thiamine, the thiazole and the pyrimidine, forming |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|, and its phosphorylation to the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|., While most bacteria achieve this phosphorylation in a single step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.16| (|FRAME: G6234|) (see for example |FRAME: PWY-6893|), eukaryotes lack that enzyme and instead utilize a pathway where |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| is first dephosphorylated to |FRAME: THIAMINE|, which is then diphosphorylated to |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: THISYNARA-PWY|) |CITS: [19888457]|., In |FRAME: TAX-3702| the first step of the pathway is catalyzed by the |FRAME: AT1G22940| gene product, a multifunctional, chloroplast-localized protein capable of catalyzing several sequential steps in thiamine (vitamin B1) biosynthesis |CITS: [17174261] [16666289]|., The next step iscatalyzed by |FRAME:EC-3.1.3.100|. Despite earlier work that associated a different protein with this activity |CITS: [16666289]|, it is now accepted that the enzyme is encoded in |FRAME: TAX-3702| by the |FRAME: GQT-4007| gene |CITS: [26537753][27677881]|., The last activity of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.7.6.2|, is catalyzed in Arabidopsis by two similar cytosolic proteins, |FRAME: AT1G02880| and |FRAME: AT2G44750| |CITS: 17611796|., The subcellular compartmentalization of thiamine biosynthesis is a subject of on-going investigation. While the Arabidopsis proteins TH1, ThiC, and TH1, which catalyze the early parts of the pathway, all localize to the chloroplasts |CITS:[18048325][18332905][17174261][11575719]|, the downstream TPK1 and TPK2 enzymes are both cytosolic in Arabidopsis |CITS:[17611796]|, suggesting that intermediates in the vitamin B1 biosynthesis pathway may need to be transported out of organelles for TPP synthesis to be completed.

General Background, Organophosphate pesticides such as |FRAME: PARATHION| and |FRAME:CPD-8973| have been used extensively as insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides. These compounds, being potent cholinesterase inhibitors (see EC 3.1.1.7 and 3.1.1.8 for cholinesterases), are extremely toxic to most animals including humans (in which LD50 is 5 to 10 mg/kg), and may cause death by inducing respiratory failure., Under aerobic conditions, |FRAME: PARATHION| is activated by oxidative desulfuration to the oxygen analog |FRAME: PARAOXON| |CITS: [Spencer80]|, which has a potent anticholinesterase effect and is more toxic than the parent chemical |CITS: [8867149]|., About This Pathway, The enzymes of the aryldialkylphosphatase family (EC 3.1.8.1) generally have broad substrate specificity, and are capable of accepting many different organophosphate substrates. For more information about this pathway, please see |FRAME:PARATHION-DEGRADATION-PWY|, as the same enzymes catalyze the degradation of paraoxon., It should be mentioned that the Keasling lab has constructed a genetically engineered |FRAME: TAX-303| strain that can fully mineralize paraoxon |CITS: [17021221]|. This organism contains the |FRAME: TAX-336203| |FRAME:G-2401| gene encoding |FRAME:MONOMER-3321|, the |FRAME: ORG-5968| genes encoding the degradation of |FRAME:P-NITROPHENOL| (see |FRAME:PWY-5487|), the |FRAME: TAX-80866| |FRAME:G-9921| gene encoding |FRAME:CPLX-7319|, and a constitutively expressed phoA gene from |FRAME: TAX-287|, encoding |FRAME:ALKAPHOSPHA-CPLX|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| is the universal precursor for the synthesis of the 4'-phosphopantetheine moiety of |FRAME:CO-A| and |FRAME: ACP "acyl carrier protein"|. Only plants and microorganisms (including some eukaryotic microbes, such as |FRAME: TAX-4932|) can synthesize pantothenate de novo - animals require a dietary supplement. The enzymes of this pathway are therefore considered to be antimicrobial drug targets., About This Pathway, The starting compound for pantothenate biosynthesis, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, is derived from the |FRAME: VALSYN-PWY| pathway. The first committed step in the pathway is the transfer of a methyl group to 2-keto-isovalerate by |FRAME: 3-METHYL-2-OXOBUT-OHCH3XFER-CPLX|. The product of this reaction, |FRAME: 2-DEHYDROPANTOATE|, is subsequently reduced by |FRAME: 2-DEHYDROPANTOATE-REDUCT-MONOMER| to |FRAME: L-PANTOATE|. The final step is the ATP hydrolysis-dependent condensation of L-pantoate with |FRAME: B-ALANINE| to form |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: PANTOATE-BETA-ALANINE-LIG-CPLX|., The enzymes of this pathway are not essential for viability of |FRAME: TAX-83333| grown on media supplemented with pantothenate, due to the presence of a transporter for pantothenate, PanF |CITS: [2193919]|., This pathway in Yeast, Three out of the four reactions involved in the conversion of |FRAME:2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| to the common intermediate towards |FRAME:CO-A| biosynthesis, i.e. |FRAME:4-P-PANTOTHENATE| have been associated with enzymes in |FRAME:TAX-4932|. The second reaction in the pathway catalyzed by the 2-dehydropantoate 2-reductase in bacteria is still elusive for yeast and remains to be resolved. Utilizing genetic and biochemical approaches the functions of |FRAME:MONOMER3O-90| |CITS:[11154694] [16232925] [19266201]|, |FRAME:YIL145C-MONOMER| |CITS:[11154694] [19266201]| and |FRAME:MONOMER3O-268| |CITS:[19266201]| have been elucidated and emphasizes the general notion that the pathway sequences of |FRAME:4-P-PANTOTHENATE| and |FRAME:CO-A| biosynthesis are almost identical among the various kingdoms. , This Pathway in Plants, Feeding studies in |FRAME:TAX-3888| leaf discs support the existence of a similar biosynthesis pathway of pantothenate via pantoate: when fed with [14C]valine, the radiolabel was incorporated into α-oxoisovalerate, oxopantoate and pantoate |CITS:[jones94]|., A number of enzymes involved in pantothenate biosynthesis have been characterized from different plants, including the enzyme catalyzing the last step of the pathway: pantothenate synthetase. This enzyme catalyzes the formation of pantothenate from pantoate and β-alanine. The origin of plant β-alanine is uncertain but appears to be different from that of bacteria which synthesize it from L-aspartate. Instead plants seem to produce β-alanine from a variety of other sources, like polyamines, uracil and propionate (see |FRAME:PWY-3941|) |CITS: [RAMAN04]|.

In plants, on the other hand, oleate is produced via, |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs|, an acyl-carrier-protein bound intermediate |CITS: [4831331]| (see, |FRAME: PWY-5147|)., An NADH-dependent |FRAME:ENZRXN-15266| system has been isolated from rat liver, microsomes |CITS: [4373719]|., The desaturase is a single polypeptide that contains one atom of non-heme iron,, and utilizes molecular oxygen and electrons from |FRAME: FERROCYTOCHROME-B5| to catalyze the, insertion of a double bond into a spectrum of fatty acyl-CoA substrates in the range of 12-19 carbons,, including |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA| and |FRAME: STEAROYL-COA| |CITS: [4373719]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| (16:1Δ9) is a common unsaturated fatty acid, found in bacteria, fungi |CITS: [8294460]|, plants |CITS: [7548115]| and animals |CITS:[14321753] [6030882]|. It comprises from 10% to 65% of the seed oil of several plants., |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| can be formed directly from the saturated fatty acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| by the action of Δ9 desaturase enzymes. Such enzymes have been reported from cyanobacteria |CITS: [7929259][10937442][16689682][17385315]|, fungi |CITS: [2674136][12055292]|, higher plants |CITS: [12208502][8861937]|, , fish |CITS: [11170264]| and mammals |CITS: [16443825]|., Desaturase enzymes do not operate on a free acid substrate. Three types of desaturases are known, that act on acyl-CoA, acyl-[acp], and acyl-lipid conjugates, respectively., In many bacteria and some plants |FRAME: CPD-9245| is derived from |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs| |CITS: [9154992]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5366|). In mammals the enzyme acts only on CoA-derivatives |CITS: [16443825]|, while in some plants and cyanobacteria the desaturase acts on fatty acids embedded within the structure of lipids, as shown in this pathway |CITS: [7929259]|., About This Pathway, Four types of acyl-lipid desaturases, DesA, DesB, DesC and DesD, have been described in cyanobacteria. All of them desaturate single bonds in fatty acids that are esterified to the sn-1 position of membrane-bound glycerolipids, but differ in the location of the bonds, acting at the 12, 15, 9 and 6 positions, respectively., While all of these enzyme are specific for fatty acids bound to the sn-1 position of glycerolipids (which are invariably C18 acids), a Δ9 desaturase from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-261476| desaturates C16 fatty acids esterified on the sn-2 position of glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|., Homologs of the |FRAME:G-14791| gene that encodes the enzyme were found in |FRAME: TAX-103690|, |FRAME: TAX-264691|, |FRAME: TAX-272131|, and |FRAME: TAX-146786| |CITS: [16689682]|.

Summary: Besides acylsugars (summarized in |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-17 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (wild tomato)|) diterpenoids are the major specialized metabolites of the Solanaceae family formed in glandular trichomes of leaves, stems and flowers |CITS:[16668241] [Severson85a] [24242718] [23757397]|. The latter compound class distinguishes two major groups, i.e. the macrocyclic cembrenoids (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-7 cembratrienediol biosynthesis|) and the dicyclic labdanoids (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-18 labdenediol and sclareol biosynthesis| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-13 cis-abienol biosynthesis|) |CITS:[Severson85a] [Guo95a]|. Plant specialized tissues such as trichomes have been found to be involved in fending off pathogenic attackers by physically hampering the invasion and by excreting toxic and/or signaling compounds |CITS:[16668241] [22979959]|. , The cembratrienediols |FRAME:CPD-18857 α-cembratriene-4,6-diol| and |FRAME:CPD-18856 β-cembratriene-4,6-diol|, formerly referred to as duvatrienediols |CITS:[1255021] [16664523] [3138948]|, are main components of tobacco trichome exudates |CITS:[12569411]| and suspected to contribute to tobacco aroma and smoke flavor |CITS:[Bentley45] [Uzelac15]|. They also exhibited tumor-promoter inhibitory properties and been found to inhibit enzymes such as aldose reductase, the synthesis of fatty acid compounds such as prostaglandins |CITS:[8372141] [19490913]| and carry out a wider spectrum of biological activities acting as insect repellants |CITS:[11283597] [Wang04]|, and pheromones and toxins (reviewed in |CITS:[Wahlberg92]|, |CITS:[Tius88]|). Labdanoids such as |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol|, |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| and |FRAME:CPD-18878 labdenediol| have been reported to protect Nicotiana species from pathogens such as the fungus Colletotrichum lagenarium |CITS:[24234021]|, prevent the germination of the causative agent for blue mold in Nicotiana |CITS:[24254279]| and act as insecticide on Nicotiana tabacum plants |CITS:[24242718]|. |FRAME:CPD-10110 Sclareol| has also been demonstrated to influence growth-regulatory processes of fungal hyphae and thus prevents fungal infections on Nicotiana glutinosa leaves |CITS:[4436652]|. Moreover, labdanoids such as |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| and |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| have commercial value as precursor for compounds that increase the smoke quality during leaf curing |CITS:[Severson85a]| and are precursors for the semi-synthesis of Ambrox, an amber substance with a widespread usage in the fragrance industry |CITS:[Barrero93] [25846965]|., The biosynthetic route towards |FRAME:CPD-18857 α-cembratriene-4,6-diol| and |FRAME:CPD-18856 β-cembratriene-4,6-diol| is realized by two enzymes, i.e. cembratrienol synthase and cembratrienol hydroxylase. The partially purified protein clearly demonstrated the catalytic activities but despite efforts to further purify and separate the respective enzymes this goal could not be achieved at the time and remains to be verified |CITS:[Guo95a]|.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) can occur via two distinct routes: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway) and the |FRAME:PWY-7560 "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (MEP pathway, this pathway) |CITS: [11078528]|. In the former, IPP is synthesized from the condensation of three acetyl-CoA molecules; in the MEP pathway IPP is synthesized via the condensation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP|., For many years, the MVA pathway was considered to be the sole source of IPP in all living organisms. However, several inconsistencies led to the discovery of the MEP pathway in bacteria and plants., In plants the MVA pathway is located in the cytosol whilst the MEP pathway is found in plastids |CITS:[LICHTENTHALER97]|. The MEP pathway is present in most eubacteria, unicellular green algae, the chloroplasts of phototrophic organisms and some unicellular eukaryotes related to photosynthetic phyla, such as the Plasmodium parasites |CITS: [15473867]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP "3-Methylbut-3-en-1-yl diphosphate"| (IPP) and its isomer |FRAME: CPD-4211| (DMAPP) are the fundamental units in isoprenoid biosynthesis. Both are produced from |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| via this pathway., D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate are initially combined to yield |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| (DOXP). DOXP is then rearranged and reduced to generate the pathway's namesake compound, |FRAME: 2-C-METHYL-D-ERYTHRITOL-4-PHOSPHATE| (MEP). , Interestingly, two rather different enzymes, that share no sequence homology, are able to catalyze this reaction - the |FRAME: DXPREDISOM-CPLX "DXR"| enzymes, and the |FRAME:MONOMER-15827 "DRL"| (DXR-like) enzymes |CITS: [20660776]|., In the third reaction MEP is converted into |FRAME: 4-CYTIDINE-5-DIPHOSPHO-2-C|, which is subsequently phosphorylated at the 2 position hydroxy group, yielding, |FRAME: 2-PHOSPHO-4-CYTIDINE-5-DIPHOSPHO-2-C-MET|. This product is then converted into, |FRAME: 2C-METH-D-ERYTHRITOL-CYCLODIPHOSPHATE|. Subsequently, it is reduced to generate |FRAME: HYDROXY-METHYL-BUTENYL-DIP| |CITS: [12198182]|., This diphosphate compound is converted by a single enzyme into a 5-6:1 ratio of IPP and DMAPP in the final step. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this ratio is subsequently adjusted to 3:7 by |FRAME: IPPISOM-MONOMER|. IPP and DMAPP serve as the basic building blocks of polyisoprenoid biosynthesis. , The difference between this pathway variant and the bacterial variant described in |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| is the use of ferredoxin rather than flavodoxin as the electron donor for (|FRAME: EC-1.17.7.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.17.7.4|., This pathway, which is not present in humans, is involved in production of phosphate-containing antigens recognized by γ-δ T lymphocytes |CITS: [11675382]|.

Summary: |FRAME:MYRICETIN Myricetin| and its glycosides belong to the subclass of flavonols, which constitute one of the largest groups within the flavonoids and stand out because of the magnitude of modifications on the flavonol core |CITS:[17587669]| |CITS:[16137727]|. Glucosylation is an important and regular modification reaction in plant metabolism. The attachment of sugar molecules enables several strategies; it is protective, stabilizing and adds properties such as solubility for transport of molecules tolerance |CITS: [10973093]|. Flavonols inclusive |FRAME:MYRICETIN| and its glucosides are wide spread in the plant kingdom (e.g. |CITS:[22279376]|) and have a variety of useful pharmacological properties. |FRAME:MYRICETIN Myricetin| prevents aggregation of amyloids which cause Alzheimer's disease |CITS:[22961751]| |CITS:[22995388]| and show antiviral, antibacterial, antiprotozoal, hypoglycemic, anticancer and diuretic activity |CITS:[22279376]| |CITS:[22195992]|. Flavonol glucosides, inclusive |FRAME:MYRICETIN| glucosides, are involved in flower coloration |CITS:[22485167]|, hence playing a part in developmental processes in plants. , Myricetin 3-O-glucosyltransferases |CITS:[Fukuchi-Mitzutani11]| |CITS:[19733370]| and myricetin 3-O-glucoside 1,6-glucosyltransferases |CITS:[19561332]| |CITS:[17940060]| are the enzymes catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-14844| via |FRAME:CPD-14843|. Although the glucosyltransferases serve a broader spectrum of flavonoids and phenolics (for example see |FRAME:PWY-7137|, |FRAME:PWY-7143|) the observed strict regiospecificity of the glucosyltransferases towards their potential substrates emphasizes a strong preference of flavonoles over other flavonoids or phenolics. The occurrence and physiological role of the various flavonol gentiobiosides remains to be shown.

Hydroxycinnamate (HCA) esters are frequently found in a broad array across the plant kingdom and can form, for instance up to 20 different HCA conjugates in Secale cereale |CITS:[Strack86]|. The formation of HCA esters may proceed via three different routes, one of them includes the utilization of HCA-CoA thioesters and the other one exploits HCA-glucosides such as |FRAME:P-COUMAROYL-COA|, |FRAME:FERULOYL-COA| and |FRAME:SINAPOYL-COA| (this pathway), whereas the third route proceeds via HCA-quinate such as |FRAME:CAFFEOYLQUINATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-6673|). The pathway depicted above points out that both biosynthetic routes may occur within one plant, i.e. Cestrum elegans forming the exact same product (|FRAME: O-SINAPOYLGLUCARATE|) |CITS:[Strack88a]|. It might be reasonable to assume that the formed HCA conjugates accumulate outside the protoplast in the cell walls as HCA conjugates have not been found within mesophyll protoplasts |CITS:[Schulz86]| and are known to form aggregates with cell wall bound carbohydrates |CITS:[Harris80]|., The pathway describes the formation of HCA conjugates, i.e. |FRAME: O-SINAPOYLGLUCARATE| and |FRAME: O-SINAPOYLGLUCAROLACTONE|, using various activated sugar acids such as |FRAME:SINAPOYL-COA| and |FRAME:1-O-SINAPOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| as acyl donors. It should be noted that the enzymes of the pathway accept |FRAME:P-COUMAROYL-COA| and |FRAME:FERULOYL-COA| with a comparable turnover rate but are more specific towards their acyl-acceptors such as |FRAME:D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME:CPD-12595| which results in the observed variety of HCA conjugates in the respective plants |CITS:[Strack87a] [Strack88a]|.

Summary: The plant cuticle is a lipophilic layer that covers all above-ground epidermal surfaces of vascular plants and functions as a barrier to control the movement of gas, water and solutes, as well as protect from plant pathogens. The cuticles is composed of two main ingredients - |FRAME: Cutins cutin| and cuticular wax., |FRAME: Cutins Cutin| is a polymer comprised of |FRAME: OMEGA-HYDROXY-FATTY-ACID "ω-hydroxy fatty acids"| and their derivatives, interlinked via ester bonds and forming a polyester polymer of indeterminate size. There are two major families of cutin monomers, comprising C16 and C18 compounds. The C16 family consists mainly of |FRAME: 16-HYDROXYPALMITATE| and |FRAME: CPD-17653| and |FRAME: 1016-DIHYDROXYPALMITATE|. The C18 family consists mainly of |FRAME: 18-HYDROXYOLEATE|, |FRAME: 910-EPOXY-18-HYDROXYSTEARATE|, and |FRAME: 91018-TRIHYDROXYSTEARATE|., Cutin biosynthesis consists of sequential reactions including the activation of acyl chains to acyl-CoAs by the long-chain, acyl-CoA synthetase encoded by the |FRAME: AT1G49430| gene, hydroxylation and epoxidation catalyzed by several cytochrome P450 family members, and esterification to glycerol-3-phosphate by glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases, (GPATs) |CITS: [25053648]|, Among the enzymes characterized from this pathway, the Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT2G45970| and |FRAME: AT2G27690| are fatty acid ω-hydroxylases that display distinct substrate specificities. CYP86A8 hydroxylates palmitate and stearate, but not expoxy fatty acids |CITS: [11493698]|, while CYP94C1 metabolize the latter more effectively |CITS: [17868380]|. A CYP P450 activity detected in soybean also had preference towards fatty acid epoxides |CITS: [Blee93]|., Note that even though α,ω-Dicarboxylic acids are signatures of suberin (see |FRAME: PWY-1121|) and are generally found only in trace level in cutin, they count for more than 50% of cutin monomers in Arabidopsis.

Summary: General Background, The antibiotic |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| is an antifungal agent used as a crop protectant. The compound is produced by sveral |FRAME: TAX-1883| strains, including |FRAME: TAX-311982|, |FRAME: TAX-264445|, and |FRAME: ORG-6031| |CITS: [16151088][16632251][16725283][11456959][16680521]|. |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A Validamycin A| is a glucosylated form of the active ingredient |FRAME: CPD-9669|. The glucose attachment is critical for the intake of the drug by the fungal cells through the common oligosaccharide transport system. Once inside the cells, the compound is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-9669|, which serves as a competitive inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.28|. |FRAME: TREHALOSE Trehalose| is a common storage carbohydrate in fungi, and is hydrolyzed by trehalase to produce glucose., Commercially available validamycin usually contains ~60% |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A|, ~15% |FRAME: CPD-18790|, and other minor analogues. |FRAME: CPD-18790 "Validamycin B"| is significantly less active against fungal pathogens |CITS: [22961651]|., |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A "Validamycin A"| is a C7N aminocyclitol antibiotic and a member of a large family of sugar-derived microbial secondary metabolites. It is biosynthesized from |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, an intermediate of central metabolism derived from the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY|). In the |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| biosynthetic pathway, |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9663|. This compound is a common intermediate for other C7N aminocyclitols including the anti-diabetic drug |FRAME: CPD-17528|, the pyralomicin antibiotics, and |FRAME: CPD-17535|, an antitumor agent. Reviewed in |CITS: [17661520]|., About This Pathway, Intermediates in the |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| biosynthetic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-264445| have been identified by feeding experiments with radiolabeled compounds |CITS: [11456959] [11893070]|. In addition, the gene cluster for |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| biosynthesis has been characterized from several organisms |CITS: [16151088] [16632251] [16725283] [16680521]|. The val gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-311982| contained 27 genes, sixteen of which were structural genes. Eight of these structural genes were found to be essential for |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| biosynthesis in the heterologous host |FRAME: TAX-1200984| |CITS: [16632251]|. In |FRAME: TAX-264445| genes in the |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| biosynthetic cluster are named vld. Although several of the enzymes involved in the pathway have been characterized, a number of reactions remain uncertain., The pathway begins with cyclization of |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-9663|. Following epimerization at the C-2 position, a potentially spontaeous dehydration, and phospohrylation, |FRAME: CPD-9667| is formed, which serves as a branch point, leading to the synthesis of both the unsaturated and saturated cyclitol moieties of |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A|., An oxidoreductase encoded by the |FRAME: G-44398| gene appears to be responsible for the reduction of the double bond within the core ring, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-9668| |CITS: [18820907]|, which, following a transamination, becomes |FRAME: CPD-18788|. An as-yet unidentified enzyme reduces the oxo group of |FRAME: CPD-9667|, and following the relocation of the phosphate group, the compound is activated to a cyclitol-nucleotide by a transferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-44397| gene |CITS: [21766819]|., Another transferase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10506| (valL) gene, combines the two molecules, forming |FRAME: CPD-18789| |CITS: [21766819][22384130]|. Finally, the phosphate group is removed |CITS: [21766819]| and the compound is glycosylated to form |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| |CITS: [16632251][18563934]|., A dioxygenase that is responsible for the hydroxylation of |FRAME: VALIDAMYCIN-A| to |FRAME: CPD-18790|, encoded by |FRAME: G-44396|, has been reported |CITS: [22961651]|.

Summary: The mycobacterial cell wall is a unique structure among prokaryotes, which consists of an outer layer of mycolic acids covalently bound to peptidoglycan via an arabinogalactan layer., More specifically, the extensively cross-linked peptidoglycan is bound by a linker unit to a linear galactan (galactofuran) chain, which in turn is attached to several branched arabinan (arabinofuran) chains esterified at the other end to mycolic acids., The synthesis of the |FRAME: Arabinogalactan "arabinogalactan"| portion of the cell wall begins with the synthesis of the linker unit, which is composed of α-L-rhamnosyl-(1->3)-D-glocusaminyl-N-acetyl phosphate. The linker unit is synthesized while attached to a lipid anchor, specifically a molecule of |FRAME: CPD-11994|, starting with attachment of the glucosaminyl-N-acetate unit (provided by |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|) |CITS:[8631826]|, and followed by attachment of a rhamnosyl unit provided by |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| |CITS: [8631826][10934214]|., The next step in the process is the building of the galactofuran, which consists of alternating 5- and 6-linked |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTO-14-FURANOSE| units |CITS: [2108960]|. The galactofuranose units, which are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-12575| in two steps |CITS: [9692181]|, are added by two galactosyl transferases with different specificity., The first enzyme, |FRAME: G185E-8078-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8078|) catalyzes the addition of the first galactofuranosyl residue to the α-L-Rhap-(1->3)-α-D-GlcNAc linker unit by a (1->4) linkage, followed by the addition of a second galactofuranosyl unit by a (1->5) linkage |CITS: [16952951][18055597]|., The second enzyme, the bifunctional |FRAME: G185E-8104-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8104|), extends the galactan chain by attaching new galactofuranosyl units in alternating (1->5) and (1->6) linkages |CITS: [11304545]|., The synthesis of the galactofuran chain terminates when it reaches a length of about 30 units., Next comes the synthesis of the arabinofuran chains. Three such chains are attached to a single galactofuran chain, at positions 8, 10 and 12 |CITS: [16040600]|. These chains consist of about 23 residues each, and are rather branched |CITS: [18303028]|. The arabinofuran units are synthesized from |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) in four steps, while anchored to a |FRAME: CPD-11994| lipid |CITS:[15878857][16291675]|. They are added by several arabinofurantransferases. In the first step the galactan chain is primed with a single arabinofuranosyl residue in a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-8088|-encoded protein |CITS: [16595677]|. The chain is elongated by linear (1-->5) linkages, in a reaction catalyzed by two similar enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8090| and |FRAME: G185E-8091| |CITS:[8876238][9142129]|. The branching in the chains is introduced by (1-->3) linkages, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-6921|-encoded |FRAME: G185E-6921-MONOMER| |CITS: [18627460]|. Finally, the chains are "capped" by the addition of a (1-->2) linked residue, catalyzed by an enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8101| |CITS: [17387176]|. Terminal β-D-Araf-(1-->2)-α-D-Araf- units are attached to both positions 3 and 5 of arabinofuranosyl units at the end of branches, and form the non-reducing end of the molecule |CITS: [18303028]|., The distal ends of the arabiofuran chains are almost completely esterified with mycolic acids |CITS: [1906464]| to generate a very large macromolecular structure that is known as the mycolylarabinogalactan (mAGP) complex |CITS: [7703239]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Lower-case-i-Antigens "i antigen"| is found on membrane proteins in red blood cells and many other cell types as well as various body secretions of developing fetuses and newborn infants |CITS: [13767181][4971635]|, while the |FRAME: Upper-case-I-antigens "I antigen"| is found in all adults |CITS: [13292836]|. Most antigens are further glycosylated., (Reviewed in |CITS: [Daniels13]|).

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter (Wzk)-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The O-polysaccharides of |FRAME: TAX-210| often contains Lewis (Le) antigens, which are structures found on human epithelial and cancer cells. These structures allow the organism to evade innate and adaptive immune responses |CITS: [7591106][8675304]|. In addition to Le antigens, LPS of |FRAME: TAX-210| contains other unusual structural elements, namely homopolymeric sequences built of glucose (α-(1→6)-glucan) and D-glycero-D-manno-heptose (DD-heptan) residues |CITS: [11836945][12907691]|., |FRAME: TAX-210| LPS were found not only on the cell membrane, but also in flagellar sheaths |CITS: [8487294]|, Despite earlier work, which suggested a branched structure, it is now documented that the LPS core region of |FRAME: TAX-85962| is linear |CITS: [21903201]|. A 2017 study reported that the |FRAME: TAX-210| core-oligosaccharide domain is a short conserved hexasaccharide decorated with the O-antigen domain encompassing a conserved trisaccharide (-DD-Hep-Fuc-GlcNAc-) (known as the trio region) and variable glucan, heptan and Lewis antigens |CITS: [28306723]|., The complete O antigen thus have the following complex structure: the trio region; a glucan region consisting of a variable number of α-Glc-(1→6) residues (3 residues shown in the diagram here) capped by a single α-Glc-(1→3) residue; a heptan region consisting of a large number of α-D,D-Hep-(1→3) residues (3 residues shown in the diagram here); a region consisting of several repeats of |FRAME: CPD-8594| (2 shown here), and finally |FRAME: Antigen-Ley| |CITS: [28306723]|., The three genes that encode fucosyltransferases involved in Lewis epitope biosynthesis (|FRAME: HP_RS01865|, |FRAME: HP_RS03210|, and |FRAME: HP_RS00480|) contain poly(C) [C13 or C14] tracts that result in translational frameshifts, causing reversible inactivation of the enzymes, which leads to significant variation in the content of Lewis epitopes in the LPS |CITS: [10496917]|. This phenomenon was described as phase variation |CITS: [9423841]|., The polymerization of the O-antigen unit appears to be terminated by Lewis y-glycosylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: HP_RS00475-MONOMER| |CITS: [8652594][10632700]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Pyochelin Pyochelin| is one of the siderophores of |FRAME: TAX-287| and of some related bacterial species. It is a condensation product of |FRAME: CPD-110| and two molecules of |FRAME: CYS|. The structure of pyochelin was established as 2-(2-O-hydroxyphenyl-2-thiazolin-4-yl)-3-methylthiazolidine-4-carboxylate |CITS: [6794030]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6408|). , A different stereoisomer, |FRAME: CPD-12093|, is produced by different organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-1124983| and |FRAME: TAX-220664| |CITS: [17938167][19297329][28553520]|. Like pyochelin, enantio-pyochelin promotes growth under iron-limiting conditions and acts as an inducer of its own biosynthetic genes. |FRAME: TAX-287| is not able to utilize enantio-pyochelin, and |FRAME: TAX-380021| is not able to utilize pyochelin, indicating different transporters for the two siderophores |CITS: [17938167]|., Like many other siderophores, enantio-pyochelin is synthesized by non-ribosomal peptide synthetases. The assembly line for enantio-pyochelin consists of proteins encoded by the |FRAME: G-124732|, |FRAME: G-124731|, |FRAME: G-124733|, and |FRAME: G-124734| genes, plus an as-yet unidentified epimerase., The process starts with the |FRAME: G-124732| gene product, which activates |FRAME: CPD-110| to |FRAME: CPD-12084| and transfers it to the |FRAME: MONOMER-124733|., PhcE* is a large non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) that contains 4 domains. One of these domains is an adenylation domain that activates an |FRAME: CYS| molecule to a |FRAME: CPD-12085|. A second domain is a peptidyl-carrier protein that binds the activated cysteine. A third domain is an aryl-carrier protein. The activated salicylate is transferred from PhcD to this domain. With the help of the fourth domain (a cyclization domain) the salicylate and cysteine are combined and cyclized, forming |FRAME: Hydroxyphenyl-thiazolinyl-PchE-protegens|. Unlike the analogous PchE protein from |FRAME: TAX-287|, the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-380021| does not have an active methyltransferase-like (MTe) domain that catalyzes epimerization of the cysteine-derived stereocenter , resulting in different stereochemistry of the product |CITS: [15375116][28553520]|. , The third protein, |FRAME: MONOMER-124735|, is also a large NRPS protein and contains five domains. An adenylation domain activates a second |FRAME: CYS| molecule to |FRAME: CPD-12085|, and a peptidyl carrier protein domain binds it., At this point the PchE* protein transfers its product to PchF, and with the help of the PchF cyclization domain |FRAME: SR-Hydroxyphenyl-bis-thiazolinyl-PchF| is formed. Based on the stereochemistry of |FRAME: CPD-12093|, it is expected that at this stage an epimerase modifies the intermediate to |FRAME: SS-Hydroxyphenyl-bis-thiazolinyl-PchF|. In the next step one of the two thiazoline rings is reduced to a thiazolidine by the NADPH-dependent |FRAME: G-124734|-encoded dehydrogenase. Since a motif search indicated that PchK could have a reductase and/or epimerase function, it is possible that PchK catalyzes both the reduction and epimerization activities., The last two steps in the process are catalyzed by the remaining two domains of the |FRAME: MONOMER-124735|. A methyltransferase domain catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| to the nitrogen of the thiazolidine ring, and a thioesterase domain cleaves the final |FRAME: CPD-12093| compound from the protein |CITS: [17938167]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10198 Furaneol| was first reported as a product of the Maillard reaction |CITS: [Hodge63]|, and was later identified as a natural aroma component in |FRAME: TAX-4615| (pineapple) |CITS: [Rodin65]|, |FRAME: TAX-3747| (strawberry) |CITS: [Ohloff96]| and several other fruits, including tomato |CITS: [Buttery95]|, raspberry |CITS: [Honkanen80]|, kiwi, and mango |CITS: [Pickenhagen81]| |CITS: [Schwab97]|. The characteristic caramel flavor and mild odor of |FRAME: CPD-10198 furaneol| and its methylated derivative |FRAME: CPD-10213 mesifuran| make them the most important flavor compounds in strawberry |CITS: [12083877]|., When occurring in plants, both compounds are only found in fruits, and have not been detected in any other plant parts |CITS: [Schwab97]|. There is a correlation between the fruit ripening stage and the |FRAME: CPD-10211 furaneol| concentration |CITS: [Sanz95]|., Even though the enzyme forming furaneol appears to produce the |FRAME: CPD-20130| isomer preferentially |CITS: [12840820]|, the compound occurs in the fruits as a racematic mixture |CITS: [Bruche91]|. The quick racemization at neutral pH is a result of rapid |FRAME: CPD-10198 keto|-|FRAME: CPD-10211 enol|-tautomerism |CITS: [12840820]|. The (2R)-isomer is the principal contributor to the characteristic burnt caramel aroma |CITS: [19817418]|., About This Pathway, Incorporation of radio tracers and other experiments suggested that |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| had the highest incorporation rate into the furanone structures |CITS: [Roscher98][16233003]|. Further incorporation experiments with labeled |FRAME: FRU| suggested the transformation of the complete carbon chain of |FRAME: FRU| into |FRAME: CPD-10211 furaneol| |CITS: [Schwab98]|. Additional studies demonstrated the involvement of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.9| in the conversion of |FRAME: D-Glucose| to the furanones, suggesting that the natural precursor is |FRAME: D-Glucose|, which is metabolized to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| by glycolytic enzymes prior to the transformation into the furanones |CITS: [11368615]|. |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| is converted by an as-yet unidentified enzyme to |FRAME: CPD-10205| |CITS: [12110193]|. A study in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4956|, which also produces furaneol (see also |FRAME: PWY-7910|) reported that |FRAME: CPD-20125| is an intermediate in this conversion |CITS: [12839760]|., |FRAME: CPD-10205| is reduced by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.105| to |FRAME: CPD-10198 furaneol|. The enzyme can act on other similar substrates such as |FRAME: CPD-10206| and |FRAME: CPD-10207| |CITS: [16517758][17636940][24133645]|., Radiotracer studies showed that furaneol is further converted to its methyl ether |FRAME: CPD-10213 mesifuran|, its β-D-glucopyranoside |FRAME: CPD-10216|, and the malonylated derivative |FRAME: CPD-17454| |CITS: [Mayerl89][Roscher97][Roscher98]|. The enzymes catalyzing the methylation and glucosylation have been identified and characterized |CITS: [12220266][26993618]|. The enzyme catalyzing the malonyl transfer is unknown as of 2017.

Summary: General background, |FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291| and |FRAME:PWY-7292|) |CITS:[12697341] [14523547] [8685242]|., The degradation of the trans-unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME:CPD-15679| in |FRAME:TAX-4930| (this pathway) has been investigated by monitoring the formation of polyhydroxyalkanoates (see |FRAME:PWY-6657|). The commonly used method to study the degradation of unsaturated fatty acids in yeast such as observing clearing zones around colonies growing on media which provide those fatty acids as sole carbon source has its limits in detecting certain intermediates |CITS:[11566445]|. The formation of polymers from polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) had been originally developed for commercial purposes by producing protein-based polymers and elastomers as part of the efforts to produce renewable and biodegradable raw materials |CITS:[10209132] [9634754]|. However, it rapidly became apparent that the polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) polymerization method also represented a powerful tool to follow carbon fluxes, monitor substrate specificities, detect and engineer new metabolic routes and analyze quantity and quality of unusual fatty acid degradation intermediates in a variety of organisms |CITS:[9634754] [11679353] [10571864] [18657232]|. , About the pathway, By introducing a bacterial PHA synthase from Pseudomonads modified for yeast peroxisomal targeting which polymerizes the various 3-hydroxy-acyl-CoA species generated in the β-oxidation cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-7288|) it is now possible to determine the composition and amount of the substrates and intermediates in a range from 5 to 16 carbons in length |CITS:[16347790] [11679353]|. The degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15679| following the fatty acid activation to form the respective CoA derivative occurs in two pathways which combine auxiliary enzymes with core-enzymes of the β-oxidation cycle. Utilizing yeast mutants, i.e. Δeci1, Δsps19 and Δdci1 and evaluating the quantity and monomer composition of the synthesized PHA the pathway sequences degrading |FRAME:CPD-15679| could be determined |CITS:[15904873]|. As mentioned above the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15679| could only be monitored via PHA polymerization to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15660| as this is the detection limit of the method |CITS:[16347790]|. , Whereas the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15680| is done by one single pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-7337|) the breakdown of its trans-isomer , i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15679| is realized via two metabolic routes |CITS:[15904873]|. The first part of the two pathways is catalyzed by the β-oxidation enzymes POX1 |CITS: [2189786] [11431484]|, the multifunctional enzyme FOX2 |CITS:[1551874] [10497229] [16574148]| and the 3-keto-thiolase (POT1) |CITS:[7754706] [9402066] [7812714]| up to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15661|. At this point the pathway splits up in two directions. The reductase-dependent pathway (this pathway) converts |FRAME:CPD-15661| to |FRAME:CPD-15655| by the enzymatic action of 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase (SPS19) |CITS:[9268358] [1738316]| which represents a compound that can be further degraded utilizing Δ3-Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) |CITS:[9837886] [9813046]| and core-enzymes of the β-oxidation spiral. The other metabolic sequence is basically directed by the action of the multifunctional enzyme (MFE) trans-2-enoyl-CoA hydratase 2/3R-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FOX2) which is responsible for the naming of this pathway branch (see |FRAME:PWY-7339|).

Summary: General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , In order to avoid self-intoxication cyanogenic glucosides are stored in the vacuole. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks they come in contact with activating enzymes (specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases) that reside in the cytoplasm or apoplastic space of the cells, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN| that serves as the first line of chemical defense |CITS:[16667728][Ganjewala10]|., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME:CPD-1103 Taxiphyllin| is the (R)-enantiomer of |FRAME:CPD-1042|, which constitutes the main cyanogenic glucoside in |FRAME:TAX-4557|. It is found in a variety of plants, including bamboo. Cyanide poisoning from pickled bamboo shoots is a common phenomenon |CITS: [21972937]|., The production of different stereoisomers arising from the same precursor requires enzymes that can recognize stereospecific structures on the aglycone as well as the glycone level. The Cytochrome P-450 that catalyze the first part of the pathway has been described from Triglochin maritima (seaside arrow grass), which produces the cyanogenic glucosides |FRAME: CPD-1103| and |FRAME: CPD-14589| |CITS: [10759528]|. However, this enzyme catalyzes the same reaction as in dhurrin biosynthesis. The enzyme responsible for production of a different stereoisomer has not been reported., It had been speculated that |FRAME:CPD-1103| might be a precursor in |FRAME:CPD-14589| biosynthesis. However, feeding experiments with labeled precursors had shown that |FRAME:PWY-7088| and |FRAME:CPD-14589| biosynthesis represent two different pathways that most likely diverge at |FRAME:CPD-1074| |CITS:[17340339]| |CITS:[1194256][7012151]|. Whereas in |FRAME:TAX-55500| the general steps and enzymes of the |FRAME:PWY-7088| have been verified |CITS:[7458352][10415119][10759528][6230992]|, the series of reactions that convert |FRAME:CPD-1074| to |FRAME:CPD-14589|, which includes ring opening and rearrangements, remain unknown.
