Summary: General Background, Glycosylated microbial natural products possess a wide range of pharmaceutical properties such as anticancer, antiviral, antifungal or antibiotic. The sugar moieties often contribute significantly to the biological activities of the these compounds., |FRAME: CPD-18159 "Ravidomycin V"| and |FRAME: CPD-18160| are glycosylated antibiotics produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-691266| |CITS: [6853365]|. Both antibiotics contain a common angucyclinone-derived tetracyclic aromatic benzo[d]naptho[1,2-b]pyran-6-one core moiety, but differ in the sugar that is connected at the C-4 position through a C-C bond. |FRAME: CPD-18160 "Deacetylravidomycin V"| contains |FRAME: CPD-18163|, while |FRAME: CPD-18159| contains a 4-O-acetyl-D-ravidosamine |CITS: [Findlay81]|. The members of this class of antibiotics are also often called |FRAME: CPD-12943 "gilvocarcin"|-type anticancer agents |CITS: [12822997]|., |FRAME: CPD-18159 "Ravidomycin V"| shows a broad range of biological activities, both antibacterial and antitumor. The activity requires the presence of near-UV light at low concentration |CITS: [3729344]|. These activities primarily arise from the inhibitory effect of the compound on bacterial DNA and RNA synthesis, although the exact mechanism is not understood |CITS: [6421790]|. The compound also possesses strong cytotoxicity against human colon carcinoma cell lines |CITS: [6853365][3729344]| and was shown to act as potent inhibitor of human topoisomerase II |CITS: [8280493]|. |FRAME: CPD-18160 "Deacetylravidomycin V"| exhibits even better anticancer and antibacterial activities than |FRAME: CPD-18159| |CITS: [21264378]|., About This Pathway, The genes included in this pathway are located in a single cluster that contains 36 open reading frames, encoding the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-18159|. The cluster was identified by screening a cosmid library of the |FRAME: TAX-691266| genome using probes constructed from the gilA gene of |FRAME: TAX-35619| (encoding a polyketide synthase involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12943|) and a consensus sequence from |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.46| |CITS: [20140934]|., Transformation of the full cluster into |FRAME: TAX-457428| resulted in production of |FRAME: CPD-18173|, whose only difference from |FRAME: CPD-18160| is full saturation of the 8-sidechain |CITS: [20140934]|. In a later study all genes except for |FRAME: G-44104|) were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified and characterized biochemically |CITS: [21264378]|., Like several other modified sugar nucleotide biosynthetic pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-6942| for an example), the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13784| starts with |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is activated by |FRAME: TTP| and converted to |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps. The next two steps are less common, but also participate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15596| (see |FRAME: PWY-6953|). These enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44100| and |FRAME: G-44099| genes, catalyze isomerization and transamination, respectively, producing |FRAME: CPD-15596|. The step catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.236|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-13784|, is the first step that is unique to this pathway.

General Background, Plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-40553| family have been valued both for flavor and medicinal purposes throughout the world., The domestic Alliums (such as onion, garlic, chives and leek) contain high concentrations of organic sulfur compounds especially in their bulbs and leaves. These compounds consist mostly of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| such as |FRAME: CPD-9269|, |FRAME: CPD-9307|, and |FRAME: CPD-9277|, as well as γ-glutamyl peptides (together these compounds make up over 70% of the total sulfur in garlic |CITS: [ Lawson96]|)., These compounds, which are found in the cytoplasm, are produced constitutively. The S-alkyl cysteine S-oxides are substrates for the alliinase enzymes (|FRAME: EC-4.4.1.4|), which convert them to |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|. However, the enzymes are kept in vacuoles, and are thus sequestered from their substrates |CITS: [Lancaster81][19463015]|. Only when the tissue is injured, the alliinase enzymes are released from the vaculoes and interact with their substrates, producing |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|., |CITS: [16010345]|. Once formed, S-alkylsulfenates are very active and tend to condense spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-17425 thiosulfinates| |CITS: [21905712]|. Depending on the Allium species, and under differing conditions, the thiosulfinates can decompose to form additional sulfur constituents including diallyl, methyl allyl, and diethyl mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, and hexasulfides, vinyldithiins, and (E)- and (Z)-ajoene |CITS: [16010345]|., In some species, dedicated enzymes commonly known as "lachrymatory-factor synthases" act on the S-alkylsulfenates rapidly, before they condense, producing volatile compounds that cause the eyes of animals to tear (lachrymatory factors) - a further defense mechanism against herbivory., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-105310| (Sicilian honey lily) is an attractive ornamental bulbous plant native to Asia Minor, southern France, and Sicily. The skunky odor released when |FRAME: TAX-105310| plants are cut makes the plant resistant to herbivory by deer., |FRAME: TAX-105310| was shown to contain several |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"|, including |FRAME: CPD-17440| and |FRAME: CPD-13604|, compounds with a four-carbon side-chain that have not been reported from any other species |CITS: [20047275]|., The |FRAME: MONOMER-16811| enzyme converts |FRAME: CPD-17440| and |FRAME: CPD-13604| into |FRAME: CPD-17442| and |FRAME: CPD-13605|. While the former forms butyl thiosulfinates spontaneously, |FRAME: CPD-13605| is converted into |FRAME: CPD-13606|, a sulfine with lachrymatory properties (this is only the 4th naturally-occurring sulfine to be reported) |CITS: [20047275]|. Although the mechanism was not studied in detail, it is assumed that |FRAME: CPD-13606| is produced by a concerted action of both a C-S lyase (alliinase) and a lachrymatory-factor synthase (see |FRAME: PWY-5707|).

Summary: In the respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase II (NDH-II) and cytochrome bo oxidase the transfer of electrons from NADH to oxygen is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. NDH-II does not contribute to the generation of proton potential |CITS: [3122832], [2679883]|; cytochrome bo oxidase contributes to the PMF |CITS: [7045115], [6308657], [6093862]| (H+/e-=2) through its action as a proton pump (H+/e-=1) |CITS: [2544445]| and through a redox loop mechanism (H+/e-=1) (|CITS: [1850294]|, During glucose limited aerobic growth E. coli directs electron flux through both |FRAME: NADH-DHI-CPLX "NADH dehydrogenase I"| (NDH-I) and NDH-II |CITS: [8491720]|. Electron transport from NADH to oxygen is not affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but is significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II; similarly nitrate respiration with NADH was only slightly affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II. Summary: General Background, Calcium is a ubiquitous second messenger in eukaryotic cells that regulates a wide variety of signaling pathways, such as fertilization, gene transcription, cell division, differentiation, muscle contraction, neuronal signaling, inflammation, and programmed cell death. Many of the effects of |FRAME: CA+2| are transmitted by |FRAME: ENSG00000143933-MONOMER| and by |FRAME: HS07962-MONOMER "protein kinase C"|. , While searching for inhibitors of the |FRAME: CA+2|-messenger system, a novel indolocarbazole alkaloid was discovered from the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-83682 "Nonomuraea longicatena (at the time known as Nocardiopsis sp. K-252)"|, which exhibited an extremely potent inhibitory activity towards |FRAME: HS07962-MONOMER "protein kinase C"|. The compound was named |FRAME: CPD-11887| |CITS:[3759657]|. At the same time, three similar compounds, named |FRAME: CPD-11889|, |FRAME: CPD-11789| and |FRAME: CPD-11888|, were discovered in the related organism |FRAME: ORG-6119|. These compounds, all structurally related to |FRAME: CPD-11887|, were also strong protein kinase C inhibitors |CITS: [3759658]|. , Further analysis showed that these compounds were not specific to protein kinase C. They selectively inhibit protein kinases by competitive interaction with the ATP binding site, and are effective against a large number of different kinases |CITS: [2672462]|. Other similar compounds, including |FRAME: STAUROSPORINE| and |FRAME: CPD-11752|, have been discovered in other organisms |CITS: [12678746 ]|, and found to possess additional protperties, including inhibition of DNA topoisomerases and DNA intercalation |CITS:[11937631][15801827]|., As such, the indolcarbazole alkaloids exhibit potent neuroprotective and broad anticancer activities, and are considered lead compounds with potential therapeutic applications in the treatment of cancer and neurodegenerative disorders |CITS: [7953671][12388555][12118367][19132059][19366805]|., About This Pathway, A pathway for the biosynthesis of K-252 compounds has been proposed following the cloning of a gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-83682|, based on both experimentally determined data and computationally predicted gene functions |CITS: [19756308]|. Co-expression of these enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11577|, |FRAME: G-11578|, |FRAME: G-11579| and |FRAME: G-11580| genes, in an |FRAME:TAX-562| host was partially successful, resulting in the production of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-11786| (CPA)., |FRAME: CPD-11789| can be converted to different compounds by glycolsylation with different sugars. General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, The majority of bacteria contain ars operons that consist of three genes, arsR (transcriptional regulator), arsB (|FRAME: EC-7.3.2.7|), and arsC (arsenate reductase). In those organisms |FRAME: ARSENATE| is reduced by ArsC to |FRAME: CPD-763|, which is removed from the cell by the ArsB transporter (see |FRAME: PWY-8101| for an example)., In |FRAME: TAX-382| the ars operon includes a gene encoding an aquaglyceroporin (|FRAME: G-81183| ) in place of arsB. As a result, this organism utilizes a unique detoxification pathway wherein following the reduction of |FRAME: ARSENATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-21683| (ArsC), the neutral form of |FRAME: CPD-763|, |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, is exported through an |FRAME: MONOMER-21671| channel (aquaporin channels can only transport uncharged molecules) |CITS: [16199569]|., It should be noted that in most cells aquaglyceroporin channels facilitate uptake of |FRAME: CPD0-2040| into cells, rather than its efflux.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase I (NDH-I) and cytochrome bd oxidase the transfer of electrons from NADH to oxygen is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is thought to function as a proton pump translocating 4H+ per NADH oxidised (2e-) [H+/e- = 2] however a lower ratio of 3H+/2e- has also been proposed |CITS: [8892824], [22392981]|. Cytochrome bd oxidase translocates 1 H+/e- by means of an oriented redox loop |CITS: [1850294]|., During glucose limited aerobic growth E. coli K-12 directs electron flux through both |FRAME: NADH-DHII-MONOMER "NADH dehydrogenase II"| (NDH-II) and NDH-I |CITS: [8491720]|. Electron transport from NADH to oxygen is not affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but is significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II which suggests that NDH-II is used preferentially in aerobic respiration |CITS: [9063459]|., Cytochrome bd oxidase is expressed under oxygen-limiting conditions |CITS: [2172211], [8576043]| unlike cytochrome bo oxidase which is expressed when oxygen levels are high |CITS: [6365921]|. E. coli K-12 also contains a second bd-type cytochrome (|FRAME: APP-UBIOX-CPLX|) encoded by the appBC genes. The physiological role of cytochrome bd-II is uncertain although it is able to generate PMF via a mechanism similar to cytochrome bd-I |CITS: [21987791]|.

Summary: The pvcABCD operon of |FRAME: TAX-287| was originally reported to participate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12096| |CITS: [8704959][10383985][12354233]| and |FRAME: CPD-20764|, a fluorescent bicyclic compound that resembles the pyoverdine chromophore |CITS: [8363709]|. However, Additional research disproved these reports, and revealed that these genes are involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20762|, an isonitrile-functionalized cumarin |CITS: [18689486]|. |FRAME: CPD-20762 Paerucumarin| chelates iron, and appears to enhance the expression of iron-controlled genes by chelating iron within the |FRAME: TAX-287| extracellular environment. One of the genes positively influenced by the presence of |FRAME: CPD-20762| is pvdS, which is essential for the expression of the pyoverdine genes. Although |FRAME: CPD-20762| chelates iron, it does not function as a siderophore |CITS: [23646138][27480638]|., The first step in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20762| is the addition of the isonitrile group to |FRAME: TYR|, which is catalyzed by a tyrosine isonitrile synthase encoded by the |FRAME: G-58181| gene. Isonitrile synthases were discovered in 2005, when the |FRAME: G-58184| gene, which catalyzes a step in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20765| was identified from a soil DNA sample |CITS: [16206308]|. Despite the fact that PcvA acts on |FRAME: TYR| and IsnA acts on |FRAME: TRP|, the two enzymes possess a similar mechanism, utilizing |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| as the source of the carbon atom in the isonitrile group., The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.9|, an Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-58182| gene. The reaction involves the liberation of a water molecule, and thus results in desaturation of a C-C bond. The last reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.M1|, which introduces a second oxygen atom to the aromatic ring. This is followed by spontaeous rearrangement to form |FRAME: CPD-20762|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathway derives in part from the central metabolic precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from oxaloacetate, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here is similar to pathway |FRAME: PWY-7184| with the exception of the |FRAME: RXN-8850 "flavin-dependent thymidylate synthase reaction"| |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.148 "EC 2.1.1.148"| (catalyzed by ThyX), which substitutes for the more common |FRAME: THYMIDYLATESYN-RXN "thymidylate synthase reaction"| |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "EC 2.1.1.45"| (catalyzed by ThyA). In 2002 it was discovered that some organisms do not posses the thyA gene (named TYMS in animals), and instead have an alternate, novel |FRAME: CPLX-8096| encoded by gene thyX., Both thymidylate synthases catalyze a reductive methylation involving the transfer of the methylene group of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| to the C5-position of |FRAME: DUMP| and a two electron reduction of the methylene group to a methyl group. However, the reductive mechanisms of ThyA and ThyX are distinctly different. The ThyA reductive mechanism uses folate as both a 1-carbon donor and a source of reducing equivalents, producing |FRAME: DUMP| and |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE| as products, and does not involve a flavin coenzyme or a third substrate. Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In |FRAME: TAX-810| additional Kdo units are added by a (2->8) or (2->4) linkages (see |FRAME: PWY-6467|). The actual donor of Kdo units is its activated form, |FRAME: CMP-KDO|., Many organisms have monofunctional enzymes that catalyze one of these steps. |FRAME: TAX-562| has a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes the addition of two Kdo units with different glycosidic linkages., Kdo-containing |FRAME:CPD-22402| molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety., There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are also synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, A few bacterial phyla appear to possess menaquinones with very long prenyl side chains. Several members of the |FRAME: TAX-976| phylum, which consists of obligate anaerobes, were reported to produce |FRAME: CPD-9723| as either their main quinone (as in the case of |FRAME: TAX-28131| |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|), in combination with |FRAME: CPD-9719|, as reported for |FRAME: TAX-28111| |CITS: [6363375]|, |FRAME: TAX-817| |CITS: [6363375][7118751][7462123]|, |FRAME: TAX-28132| |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|, |FRAME: TAX-28116| |CITS: [6363375]|, |FRAME: TAX-28134| strains 5540, G9a-C2 and 7880, |FRAME: TAX-818|, and |FRAME: TAX-821| |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|, or in combination with |FRAME: CPD-9722|, as in |FRAME: TAX-28134| strains 1210 and 1221and |FRAME: TAX-839| |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|., In addition, several species that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-201174| phylum, and especially to the |FRAME: TAX-33882| genus, were reported to contain |FRAME: CPD-9723|. Some of these, such as |FRAME: TAX-144185|, contain |FRAME: CPD-9723| along with |FRAME: CPD-9719| |CITS: [Yamada76b]| . Others, including |FRAME: TAX-33884|, |FRAME: TAX-33917|, |FRAME: TAX-41986|, |FRAME: TAX-33885|, |FRAME: TAX-33918| |CITS:[7462123][7022156]|, |FRAME: TAX-69368| and |FRAME: TAX-2033| |CITS: [6775048]| contain |FRAME: CPD-9723| along with |FRAME: CPD-9722|.

Summary: Guadinomines are a family of anti-infective compounds produced by |FRAME: TAX-1238679|. |FRAME: CPD-18226 "Guadinomine B"| and |FRAME: CPD-18225| are the most potent known inhibitors of the type III secretion system of Gram-negative bacteria, with IC50 of 14 nM and 39 nM, respectively |CITS: [18503201][18503202]|., A gene cluster responsible for guadinomine biosynthesis has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1238679| |CITS: [23030602]|. The cluster contains 26 open reading frames spanning 51.2 kb. It includes a nonribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS)-like loading module and four consecutive polyketide synthase (PKS) modules and several tailoring enzymes, as well as genes required for producing some of the compounds that feed into the main pathway, including the |FRAME: GUANIDOACETIC_ACID| starter unit, the unusual |FRAME: Aminomalonyl-PCP "aminomalonyl-[acyl carrier protein]"| extender unit, and carbamoyl phosphate., Missing from the cluster are genes encoding enzyme(s) responsible for synthesis and attachment of an |FRAME: CPD-18228| dipeptide., Based on the proposed model, guadinomine biosynthesis begins with production of |FRAME: GUANIDOACETIC_ACID|, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44131| gene product. Guanidinoacetate is activated by the adenylationpeptidyl carrier protein (A-PCP) didomain of the first module of the |FRAME: CPLX-9009|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-44132| gene. The activated precursor is transferred to the ketosynthase (KS) domain of GdnE, where it undergoes condensation with a malonyl extender unit bound to the ACP domain of the same module. The ketoreductase (KR) and dehydratase (DH) domains of GdnE reduce the bound diketide to an α,β-unsaturated diketide that undergoes cyclization with the nucleophilic guanidino group., The next module, encoded by |FRAME: G-44133|, incorporates the C-7-hydroxyl group common to guadinomines. The third module, encoded by |FRAME: G-44134|, incorporates a fully reduced ketide unit. Both GdnF and GdnG have malonyl-specific AT domains., The fourth and last module, encoded by |FRAME: G-44135|, is a minimal PKS that uses the uncommon extender unit |FRAME: Aminomalonyl-PCP "aminomalonyl-[acp]"|. Incorporation of this extender unit into the polyketide backbone yields an [acp]-bound α-amino-β-oxothioester that subsequently undergoes reductive amination via tan unusual aminotransferase domain of GdnH. There are only a few examples in the literature for such a domain within a PKS, module |CITS: [23030602]|., The next step involves the addition of a |FRAME: CPD-18228| dipeptide. No genes encoding this function were found in the cluster. It is possible that the C domain of GdnH (the terminal domain) transfers the product to an as-yet unknown bimodular |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "non-ribosomal peptide synthase"| (NRPS) responsible for synthesizing the |FRAME: CPD-18228| dipeptide. In this case the NRPS would extend that intermediate by the successive addition of the two peptides, followed by release of the product by the |FRAME: G-44136| thioesterase|. However, this is still speculative., Other tailoring enzymes include a carbamoyltransferase, encoded by |FRAME: G-44137|, and a hydroxylase, encoded by |FRAME: G-44124| |CITS: [23030602]|.

Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., The sugar |FRAME: KDO| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is the first sugar added to lipid A in the majority of Gram-negative bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-1269|). In strains of |FRAME: TAX-22|, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-211586|, Kdo undergoes a modification prior to its attachment to the lipid, in which the C8 hydroxyl group is converted to a primary amine, forming |FRAME: CPD-18063| (Kdo8N) (see |FRAME: PWY-7674|) |CITS: [14499575][15013415][18619581][23413030]|., Many species, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, add two Kdo sugars with a single Kdo transferase (see |FRAME: KDOSYN-PWY|), whereas others, including members of the genera |FRAME: TAX-22| and |FRAME: TAX-724|, add a single Kdo that is then phosphorylated by a separate enzyme (see |FRAME: PWY-7675|)., About This Pathway, In members of |FRAME: TAX-22| a unifunctional transferase add a single |FRAME: CPD-18063| (Kdo8N) sugar to lipid A, followed by its phosphorylation at the 4-OH position, the same site at which the second Kdo residue is attached in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [9047308]|., Kdo-containing |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A| molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety.

Autoinducers are bacterial cell-cell communication messengers that allow bacteria to detect the density of neighboring cells. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., Many types of autoinducers exist, for example |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "N-acylhomoserine lactones"| (AHLs), |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "γ-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, |FRAME: Butenolides "γ-butenolides"|, |FRAME: Photopyrones photopyrones|, and |FRAME: Dialkylresorcinols dialkylresorcinols| (DARs). The signaling molecules bind to a dedicated receptor (e.g. LuxR, which binds AHL-type molecules), which in turn binds to the promoter/operator regions of the target genes/operons, resulting in changes in gene expression in response to the number of cells., The |FRAME: Photopyrones photopyrones| are a class of α-pyrone compounds discovered in the insect pathogen |FRAME: TAX-29488| that serve as signaling molecules that are detected at low nanomolar concentrations |CITS: [23851573]|. , While the production of photopyrones is not limited to |FRAME: TAX-29488|, not all |FRAME: TAX-29487| species produce the same photopyrones. Eight different photopyrones were isolated from |FRAME: TAX-230089|, while only three (|FRAME: CPD-28091|, |FRAME: CPD-28092| and |FRAME: CPD-28094|) are produced by |FRAME: TAX-29488|., The photopyrones were shown to be produced by a single enzyme, photopyrone synthase |CITS: [23851573]|. A mechanism for the enzyme has been described. The enzyme first covalently binds a fatty acyl ester to an active site, cysteine residue. Deprotonation of the substrate yields a nucleophile, which subsequently attacks the carbonyl carbon of a 5-methyl-3-oxohexanoyl thioester that is formed by the |FRAME: PWY-8174 "branched iso fatty acid biosynthesis pathway"|, forming a new carbon-carbon bond. After an additional deprotonation of the bound intermediate, the pyrone ring is formed and the product is released from the enzyme |CITS: [26425196]|., The two substrates might be thioesters of either acyl carrier protein or coenzyme A, depending on whether they originate from fatty acid biosynthesis or degradation, respectively. While the second substrate is always the same, variability in the first substrate results in formation of the different photopyrones that are detected in the organism |CITS: [26425196]|., In |FRAME: TAX-29488| the photopyrones are sensed by PluR, a LuxR-like receptor. PluR is most sensitive to |FRAME: CPD-28094|, which it can detect at a concentration of 3.5 nM, but can also sense the other photopyrones at higher concentrations. Upon binding of a photopyrone PluR activates expression of the adjacent pcfABCDEF operon, resulting in production of a clumping factor named PCF (Photorhabdus Clumping Factor) and intense cell clumping |CITS: [23851573]|.

Summary: This is an alternative degradation route of fatty acids with cis-double bonds on odd-number carbons, for example, |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|, that was proposed after the identification of |FRAME: EC-5.3.3.21|, from yeast |CITS: [10455114]|. The physiological role of the yeast DCI1 however remains unclear since yeast mutants with a deletion in DCI1 showed no deficiency in utilization of |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| |CITS: [10455114]|. Later, this pathway was thought to be present in Arabidopsis based on the identification of the Arabidopsis DCI1 |CITS: [16040662][17434787]|. No genetics data are available for the Arabidopsis DCI1 thus its physiological role in fatty acid degradation is still unclear., In this pathway, unsaturated fatty acids with cis-double bonds on odd-number carbons (i.e. a double bond on the 9th position in the case of oleate) are converted to cis-5-enoyl-CoA after two rounds of |FRAME: PWY-5136 "core beta oxidation cycle"|. Instead of continuing for another round of core beta-oxidation cycle which would yield cis-3-enoyl-CoA to enter |FRAME: PWY-5137|, cis-5-enoyl-CoA once being oxidized to trans-2,cis-5-dienoyl-CoA exits the core beta oxidation. It is converted to trans-3,cis-5-dienoyl-CoA by delta3,delta2-enoyl-CoA isomerase. Trans-3,cis-5-dienoyl-CoA is then converted by the di-isomerase delta3,5-delta2,4-dienoyl-CoA isomerase to trans-2,trans-4-dienoyl-CoA. The latter is further converted to trans-3-enoyl-CoA by 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase. Finally, trans-3-enoyl-CoA is converted to trans-2-enoyl-CoA to reenter core beta oxidation for complete degradation.

Summary: General Background, Tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis., Folates also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine, play a role in histidine catabolism |CITS: [11001804]|, and in plants are also involved in photorespiration, amino acid metabolism and chloroplastic protein biosynthesis |CITS: [11960743]| |CITS: [12644692]|., Folates are abundant in green leaves, and folic acid was initially isolated from a large amount (four tons) of spinach leaves. The name folate is derived from the Latin folium (leaf) |CITS: [3067148]|., Folates are modified by the addition of glutamate moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail. The polyglutamylated forms are usually preferred by the enzymes that use folates since the turnover rate of those compounds is markedly increased |CITS: [9190084][SCOTT00][KIRK94]|. In addition, in eukaryotic cells the glutamylated forms of folate facilitate the retention of the vitamin within the cell and its subcellular compartments |CITS: [1916088]|., The product of this pathway, |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydropteroylmonoglutamate, H4PteGlu1,, THF), is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. Members of the family differ in the oxidation state, of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions (see, |FRAME: PWY-2201|), and the number of conjugated glutamate residues (see |FRAME: PWY-2161|)., About This Pathway, This pathway for the de novo biosynthesis of folates is found in bacteria, fungi, and plants. , Folates are tripartite molecules and are made up of a pterin, |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| and |FRAME:GLT| moieties., The first two are synthesized from |FRAME:GTP| and |FRAME:CHORISMATE|, respectively (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6147| for the biosynthesis of the former). The consecutive action of the FolK, FolP, FolC, and FolA enzymes finally produces the final product, |FRAME: THF| |CITS: [12039964]|., In plants the pterin moiety is formed from GTP in the cytosol, which couples to pABA (synthesized in plastids) in mitochondria followed by subsequent glutamylation and reduction steps which may take place in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids |CITS: [11960743][11752472]|. The recent discovery that folylpolyglutamate synthases are present in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids with each of them encoded by a different gene in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [11752472]| points to the fact that at least parts of the pathway can be carried out independently in those compartments., In addition to the de novo pathway, many organisms also possess salvage pathways that are used, to re-synthesize tetrahydrofolate from breakdown products of folates in the cell, such as 5 or 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate., About Folates In Animals, While plants and many microorganisms can synthesize folate coenzymes by the de novo synthesis pathway, vertebrates are absolutely dependent on nutritional sources, making folate a vitamin. Food folates exist mainly as |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N 5-methyl-H4PteGlun| and |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N 10 formyl-H4PteGlun| |CITS: [405403]|., Polyglutamyl folates are hydrolyzed to folylmonoglutamates by |FRAME: HS06361-MONOMER|, and metabolized within the enterocyte into 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1. This monoglutamyl folate coenzyme is the plasma form of the vitamin |CITS: [13906633][2736319]|, and is transported to peripheral tissues where it is demethylated by the vitamin B12-dependent |FRAME:EC-2.1.1.13| to monoglutamyl tetrahydrofolate (H4PteGlu1)., Insufficient supply of the vitamin in vertebrates leads to anemia in adults, and has been shown to cause neural tube malformation in human embryos |CITS: [11744531]|. In addition, folate defficiency has been linked to a number of other birth defects, several types of cancer, dementia, affective disorders, Down's syndrom, and serious conditions affecting pregnancy outcome (for a review, see |CITS: [11001804]|).

The main biosynthetic route for |FRAME: CYS| in |FRAME: TAX-562| is from |FRAME: ACETYLSERINE| and |FRAME: HS|, as described in pathway |FRAME: CYSTSYN-PWY|. The source of sulfide is the assimilatory reduction of sulfate, as described in the pathway |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|., However, when |FRAME: S2O3| or |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE| are available, the organism is able to use a second pathway, in which |FRAME: CYS| is produced from |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE|, as described here |CITS: [22607201]|., Thiosulfate enters the cell via the |FRAME: ABC-7-CPLX|, a complex of four types of subunits plus the thiosulfate-binding protein |FRAME: EG10929 Sbp| |CITS: [2188959][2188958]|. Once inside the cell, thiosulfate can be converted to |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE| by the action of |FRAME: ACSERLYB-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME: EG10193| gene |CITS: [12640465]|. , When |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE| is available, it enters the cell via the |FRAME: G6934-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: G6934| gene. A mutant lacking the gene is unable to grow with |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE| as the sole sulfur source |CITS: [27481704]|., |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE| appears to be the subject of reductive cleavage by |FRAME: RED-GLUTAREDOXIN "glutaredoxin 1"|, forming |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: SO3|. Several purified glutaredoxins (Grx1, Grx2, and Grx3), as well as thioredoxins (Trx1 and Trx2) and glutaredoxin-like proteins (NrdH), are able to catalyze the reaction in vitro |CITS: [22607201]|. However, it has been shown that growth with |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE| as the sole sulfur source requires glutathione. Mutations in both |FRAME: EG10418| and |FRAME: EG10419|, which are essential for glutathione biosynthesis, abolish growth on |FRAME: SULFO-CYSTEINE|. Since only glutaredoxins require glutathione for their activity, it is likely that only glutaredoxins catalyze this activity in vivo |CITS: [27481704]|. The only glutaredoxin that was shown to have an affect on |FRAME: CYS| biosynthesis in vivo is |FRAME: RED-GLUTAREDOXIN Grx1| |CITS: [22607201]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-620| is a well-known human pathogen that causes diseases such as diarrhea and bacilliary dysentery (shigellosis). It is closely related to |FRAME: TAX-562|, and while was given its own genus in the 40s, sequence-based phylogeny suggests that the genus may have to be re-incorporated into |FRAME: TAX-562|., The Shigella serotypes were named B/D/F/S for variations found in the four species |FRAME: TAX-621|, |FRAME: TAX-622|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, and |FRAME: TAX-624|, respectively |CITS: [18422615]|., The structure of the O antigen repeat unit of |FRAME: ORG-57080| was reported in 2005 , as was the sequence of the gene cluster encoding its biosynthesis |CITS: [15774901]|. The cluster contains genes involved in |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| biosynthesis, five glycosyltransferase, an O antigen repeat unit flippase, and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [11598067]|., The repeat unit is very similar to that produced by |FRAME: ORG-57079| but contains an additional ribofuranose residue |CITS: [15774901]|. Inactivation of the extra glycosyltransferase gene (|FRAME: G-81106|) found in the cluster of |FRAME: ORG-57080| resulted in production of the |FRAME: CPD-24152| by the mutant, indicating that the gene encodes the enzyme responsible for the transfer of the ribosyl residue. While |FRAME: D-Ribofuranose| (D-Ribf) is present in the O antigens of several bacterial strains (such as the |FRAME: TAX-562| serogroups O5, O20, O54, O105, O114, O153, O178, O183 and O185), ribofuranose transfer reactions are not well characterized, and even though the donor in these reactions is assumed to be a nucleotide diphosphate form, as is standard in this type of reactions, this has not been verified. As of 2020 WbaM is the only enzyme catalyzing a ribosyltransfere reaction that has experimental evidence., In 2008 a Shiga toxin 1 (Stx1)-producing E. coli strain that didn't cross react with any known E. coli antisera was isolated from a patient with hemorrhagic colitis in Japan. Sequencing of its O antigen gene cluster has revelaed that it is identical to that of |FRAME: ORG-57080| |CITS: [21865424]|. The new E. coli serogroup was originally named OSB10, but later renamed O:183 |CITS: [25428893]|. As could be expected, the structure of the O antigen repeat unit was also shown to be identical between the two strains |CITS: [27301288]|.

Avenacins are triterpene glucosides which act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents conferring resistance against soil-borne pathogens and influencing the development of close neighbors |CITS:[10536024] [16995908]|. The occurrence of the phytoalexic avenacins appears to be restricted to the genus Avena which is an expression of a highly specialized defense biochemistry |CITS:[Hostettmann95]|. In general, triterpenes are valued compounds with a wide range of commercial applications and because of that in the focus of metabolic engineering. One of the major goals is to re-introduce lost traits of resistance into cultivated crops |CITS:[22639586]|., As a general rule genes in plant biochemical pathways, unlike bacterial biochemical pathways, have been regarded as unlinked. However, the avenacin biosynthesis appears to be carried out by an avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster which implies a high degree of coordination regarding avenacin synthesis, transport and sequestration, all of which must be precisely orchestrated in time and space between different cell organelles and compartments |CITS:[21876149] [15148404] [21443624] [20040536]|., |FRAME:CPD-16624 Des-methyl avenacin A-1| (this pathway) is the avenacin species found in Avena mutants such as sad9 which lack the anthranilate N-methyltransferase, hence have a deficiency in catalyzing |FRAME:CPD-402| and apparently acylate with |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| instead. |FRAME:CPD-16623 Des-acyl avenacin A| is the origin within the |FRAME:PWY-7473| which deviates towards the synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-16624|. The first reaction of the pathway is the glucosylation of |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| which yields |FRAME:CPD-12835| catalyzed by two anthranilate glucosyltransferases encoded by SAD10 (aka UGT74H5) and UGT74H6. Both glucosyltransferases accept |FRAME:CPD-402| and |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| with varying efficiency and therefore are capable of forming |FRAME:CPD-16600| (see |FRAME:PWY-7463|) and |FRAME:CPD-12835|, respectively |CITS:[23258535]|. The following step in the pathway of |FRAME:CPD-16624| biosynthesis is the acylation of |FRAME:CPD-16623| with |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| which is provided through the acyl-donor |FRAME:CPD-12835|. The catalyzing enzyme is a serine carboxypeptidase-like (SCPL) protein (SCPL1) encoded by SAD7, also a member of the avenacin genetic cluster, which can utilize both |FRAME:CPD-16600| and |FRAME:CPD-12835| as acyl-donor, in the latter case resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16624| |CITS:[19684243]|.

Summary: |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate "3-Sulfopropanediol"| (2,3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate, DHPS) is a widespread intermediate in plant and algal transformations of |FRAME: CPD-10247| from the plant sulfolipid |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL "6-sulfo-α-D-quinovosyl diacylglycerol"| |CITS: [7626014]| (see |FRAME: PWYQT-4427|). It is also recovered quantitatively during bacterial degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10247| |CITS: [14602597]|, and is secreted by all diatoms |CITS: [5085579]|., Two pathways have been described for the degradation of |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| under anaerobic conditions. The pathways involve two different glycyl radical enzymes - |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.41| (described in |FRAME: PWY-8215|) and |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.177|, which is described here., In this pathway, which has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-571|, |FRAME: CPD-12693| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-11726|. This aldehyde is further reduced to |FRAME: CPD-24088|, which is excreted out of the cell by an exporter encoded by the hpfE gene |CITS: [32571930]|.

|FRAME: CPD-23439 "Carminic acid"| is a C-glycoside natural red pigment found in some scale insects including the American cochineals (|FRAME: TAX-765876|), which are mostly sessile phloem feeders, living as parasites exclusively on cacti belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-106975| genus. Carminic acid, which is thought to serve as a defense compound against predation by ants |CITS: [17779027]|, makes up to 26% of the dry weight of adult females in this species |CITS: [25195465]|., Carminic acid has been used as colorant by the Mayans, Incas, and Aztecs. During the Spanish colonial era, the dried insect powder was exported to Europe, where it became an important commodity. By the early nineteenth century, the American cochineal was introduced and reared on its cactus host outside Central and South America. Today carminic acid is widely used as a colorant in the food, textile, cosmetic, paint, and coating industry. Peru is the main producer of carminic acid from |FRAME: TAX-765876| |CITS: [29215010]|., Carminic acid production is very labor-intensive. After harvesting and drying the adult females the pigment is extracted by boiling the dried insects in an alkaline solution and removal of the insect parts. The dye can be further purified by precipitation with alum under acidic conditions to produce a more intense red aluminum salt called carmine lake., C-glycosides like carminate can be degraded by a two enzyme system. The first enzyme oxidizes the hydroxyl moiety at position 3 of the glucose moiety to an oxo group, while the second enzyme catalyzes C-deglycosylation of the product |CITS: [32385077]|., |FRAME: ORG-57113| was isolated from a soil sample around the University of Tsukuba, Japan, based on its ability to degrade |FRAME: CPD-23439|. The enzyme catalyzing the first reaction, CarA, was partially purified, and its N-terminal amino acid sequence was determined. The sequence was used to identify the |FRAME: G-107946| gene, which was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [34583991]|. The recombinant protein was purified and found to be monomeric and to contain one molecule of FAD. The enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of the O3' position in the presence of oxygen, forming |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| |CITS: [34583991]|., CarA homologues were found in various soil bacteria, but not in intestinal bacteria. The |FRAME: G-107946| genes are located next to genes that encode C—C bond-cleaving enzymes that catalyze the second reaction. Those genes are found in intestinal bacteria as well, but instead of a |FRAME: G-107946| homologue, they are located next to |FRAME: G-107947| homologues |CITS: [34583991]|., CarA from |FRAME: ORG-57113|, and its homologues from |FRAME: TAX-1665| and |FRAME: TAX-69370| strains were active against glycosides such as |FRAME: CPD-23439|, |FRAME: CPD-25755|, and |FRAME: CPD-20048 "C6-glycosylated flavonoids"|, but had no activity against |FRAME: 8-C-glucosyl-flavone "C8-glycosylated flavonoids"| or D-glucose., The |FRAME: G-124412| and |FRAME: G-124413| genes of |FRAME: ORG-57113|, encoding |FRAME: CPLX-85444|, were found based on their similarity to the |FRAME: G-107948| and |FRAME: G-107949| genes of the |FRAME: TAX-498716|, which encode the two subunits of |FRAME: CPLX-9779| |CITS: [34728636]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in dicotyledon type I cell walls. The cross-linking between xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the three-dimensional matrix between adjacent cellulose microfibrils |CITS: [Whitney95]|., Xyloglucan has a backbone of β-1,4-linked cellotetraose units, which are substituted in C-6 by α-D-xylosyl residues at two or three of the first four glucosyl residues (but not the residue closest to the reducing end) |CITS: [8252539]|. Some of the xylosyl residues are subsequently further substituted by (1,2)-β-D-galactosyl residues at the second and/or third xylose residue and by (1,2)-α-L-fucose at the galactosyl unit of the third xylose residue |CITS:[12837954][17011813]|. , A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose and β-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, β-D-galactose and α-L-fucose |CITS:[Fry93]|., Using this terminology, most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide XXXG units as well further modified XXLG, XLXG, and XLLG units., About This Pathway, The enzyme described in this pathway has been originally isolated from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-203496|. It is an exoglucanase that recognizes and attacks the reducing end of oligoxyloglucan, releasing segments composed of two glucosyl residues (with their xylose modifications) from the main xyloglucan chain (a modified cellobiohydrolase activity). For example, when the enzyme acts on the reducing end of the oligoxyloglucan heptasaccharide |FRAME: CPD-13375 XXXG|, it produces the tetrasaccharide |FRAME: CPD-10498 XX| and the trisaccharide |FRAME: ALPHA-D-XYLOSYL-1-6-BETA-D-GLUCOS XG|., A thorough study of the substrate specificity showed that the terminal residue (site +2) must be an unbranched glucose. The glycosylation of the glucose at site +1 is not important, thus the reducing end unit that is being cleaved may be GG, XG, or LG. It is also important that the third glucose residue from the reducing end (site -1) is branched with a unmodified xylose residue |CITS: [12374797]|., An enzyme with similar properties has been characterized from the fungus |FRAME:TAX-162425| |CITS: [16214120]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine nucleotides can be catabolized through three different pathways. The best characterized is the reductive pathway (this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-6430|) in which the pyrimidine nucleotides are reduced to |FRAME:Beta-amino-acids|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. The pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms |CITS:[13428755][13416173][16655478][16656066][10656811]|. The oxidative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6426|) is only found in a few bacterial species and has not been characterized nearly as well. In it uracil is converted to |FRAME: UREA| and |FRAME: MALONATE| via |FRAME: BARBITURATE| |CITS: [12981104][14955523]|. A third pathway, known as the Rut pathway, was discovered much later in |FRAME: TAX-562| and other bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY0-1471|) |CITS: [16540542]|. That pathway starts by ring opening of the pyrimidine nucleotide, and forms |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| from uracil, with concomitant production of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|., About This Pathway, The pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms. It has been observed in various microorganisms including |FRAME: ORG-6124| |CITS: [13416173][13416174]|, |FRAME: TAX-12917| |CITS: [4986615]|, |FRAME: TAX-37762| |CITS: [3553866]|, |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [1903745]|, |FRAME: TAX-329| |CITS: [ 7710277]|, |FRAME: TAX-316| |CITS: [Xu92]|, |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [11759049]|, |FRAME: TAX-292| |CITS: [West97]|, |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS: [3926948]| and |FRAME: TAX-51101| |CITS: [12670488]|, as well as the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4934| |CITS: [10656811]| and mammalian tissues |CITS: [12981074][13428755]|., The product of the pathway, |FRAME: B-ALANINE|, is a central component of |FRAME:PANTOTHENATE| and |FRAME:GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| biosynthesis, and in mammals also functions as a neurotransmitter |CITS: [6117607]| and as a precursor for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CARNOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-401| |CITS: [3108250]|. While in bacteria |FRAME: B-ALANINE| biosynthesis usually occurs through the decarboxylation of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5155|), it is generally thought that the pyrimidine degradation pathway is the main route for the synthesis of |FRAME: B-ALANINE| in mammals |CITS: [14705962]|., Radiotracer experiments in germinating grains of |FRAME: TAX-4565| |CITS: [mazus72]|, whole plants of |FRAME: TAX-227291| |CITS: [duhaze03]| and potato tubers |CITS: [12244448]| showed that uracil is efficiently converted to |FRAME: B-ALANINE|. Mutant analyses in |FRAME: ORG-5993| further support the existence of this pathway and indicate that it might be important for helping plants to reallocate nitrogen from pyrimidines into general nitrogen metabolism |CITS: [19413687]|, The pathway proceeds in three sequential enzymatic steps. The first enzyme is |FRAME: MONOMER-15398| (EC 1.3.1.2), which catalyzes the reversible reduction of both |FRAME:URACIL| and |FRAME: THYMINE| to |FRAME: DI-H-URACIL| and |FRAME: DIHYDRO-THYMINE|, respectively (see also the |FRAME: PWY-6430| pathway). The second enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15399| (EC 3.5.2.2) performs reversible hydrolytic ring-opening of |FRAME: DI-H-URACIL| and |FRAME: DIHYDRO-THYMINE| to |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-ISOBUTYRATE|, respectively. Finally, |FRAME: MONOMER-15400| (EC 3.5.1.6) catalyzes the irreversible hydrolysis of |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-ISOBUTYRATE| to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| and |FRAME: 3-AMINO-ISOBUTYRATE|, respectively, in a reaction that produces ammonium and carbon dioxide., This pathway has special importance in humans, since it is responsible for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD0-1327|, an important anticancer drug. Patients with defects in the enzymes of this pathway show adverse response to treatment with this drug, including death |CITS: [993199]|.

Plants and pathogens interact via a complex network of recognition, signaling and response. Resistance built up as the result of an infection is part of the defense arsenal plants have at their disposal. Usually, the resistance is very specific towards the respective pathogen and can be classified as either incompatible or compatible interactions. The former interaction provides protection and avoids infection while the latter allows the pathogen to invade and spread throughout the plant |CITS:[15012275]|. Plants use signaling molecules such as |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| |CITS:[17904410]|, |FRAME:CPD-734 (-)-jasmonate| |CITS:[16039901]| or |FRAME:ETHYLENE-CMPD ethylene| |CITS:[16602950]| to communicate pathogen attacks within and between species and to trigger a corresponding defense response. Incompatible host-pathogen interactions with |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| as signaling molecule have been intensively investigated |CITS:[17904410]| while compatible host-pathogen interactions are less well understood |CITS:[12712338]|. , In general, hydroxylated benzoates such as |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| and |FRAME:CPD-633 gentisate| accrue in plants as glycoconjugates, most typically linked with molecule(s) of |FRAME:GLC β-D-glucopyranose|. In tomato |FRAME:CPD-633 gentisate| has been shown to accumulate exclusively as |FRAME:CPD-19191 gentisate 5-O-β-D-xylopyranoside| |CITS:[16321412]| which represents the chief metabolite that accumulates upon viroid infections in this species |CITS:[19866456]|. Glycosylation has been recognized as the most common biochemical modification within the class of specialized metabolites conferring beneficial properties like stabilization, better solubility, exerting control over hormones and signaling molecules and detoxifying xenobiotica |CITS:[16214386]|. It also has been proposed to play a crucial role in regulating cellular homeostasis in plants where a great number of glycosyltransferases with more or less specificity target and biochemically convert metabolites from a vast array of diverse compound classes |CITS:[15241472] [16669774]|., In a number of plants, amongst them cultivated tomato, |FRAME:CPD-633 gentisate| accumulates at a higher level than |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| when exposed to compatible infections and has been proposed to act as an facilitator in compatible interactions. Both hydroxybenzoates are then fast converted to glycosides, with |FRAME:CPD-19191 gentisate 5-O-β-D-xylopyranoside| being the major glycoconjugate found in tomato |CITS:[Belles99]|. |FRAME:CPD-633 Gentisate| itself has been reported as a very effective fungicide |CITS:[Lattanzio94]| whereas its 5-O-β-D-xyloside appears to be involved in systemic, non-necrotizing infections of tomato plants |CITS:[16331468]|. , The cDNA encoding for a gentisate 5-O-β-D-xylosyltransferase was identified in Solanum lycopersicum, cloned and recombinant expressed in Pichia pastoris. When subjected to biochemical assays the protein, i.e. gentisate 5-O-β-D-xylosyltransferase displayed very specific substrate affinities towards |FRAME:UDP-D-XYLOSE UDP-α-D-xylose| as glycoside donor and |FRAME:CPD-633 gentisate| as glycoside acceptor forming the respective |FRAME:CPD-19191 gentisate 5-O-β-D-xylopyranoside| in the process |CITS:[20729481]|. The expression profile of the respective gene (gtsatom) followed the activity pattern of the enzyme and also responded accordingly to the treatment with pathogens, e.g. the citrus exocortis viroid (CEVd) and tomato mosaic virus (ToMV). Interestingly, a similar enhancing effect for both gene expression and enzyme activity was observed when either |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| or |FRAME:CPD-633 gentisate| was exogenously administered. However, wounding, |FRAME:CPD-734 (-)-jasmonate| treatment and incompatible interactions had no effect on gene expression and enzyme activity supporting the involvement of the formed |FRAME:CPD-19191 gentisate 5-O-β-D-xylopyranoside| in compatible pathogen infections |CITS:[20729481]|.

Summary: The monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and the xylene isomers , (o-, m-, and p-), collectively know as BTEX, are some of the most water-soluble , constituents of gasoline and are toxic. As a consequence, BTEX compounds pose a particular threat to human, health and the environment because once released into the environment, they can migrate readily wtih , water, and eventually contaminate drinking water supplies. BTEX compounds have become prevalent soil, and groundwater contaminants as a result of leaking underground storage tanks, and improper handling , and disposal of gasoline., Aromatic compounds such as BTEX are important growth substrates for microorganisms. Initially, it was believed that, these compounds could only be degraded under aerobic conditions, i.e. in the presence of molecular oxygen. , Aerobic degradation of aromatic compounds is characterized by the use of molecular oxygen,, which is used in the initial oxidative attack of the aromatic compound, and in the subsequent, cleavage of the aromatic ring structure |CITS: [1368147]|. Thus, anaerobic degradation of aromatic , compounds, by definition, requires a completely different strategy. BTEX compounds were initially believed to be, recalcitrant to anaerobic degradation due to the resonance stability of their aromatic ring structure, and their lack of any reactive functional groups. However, beginning around 1990, microbiological , research began to demonstrate that particular microorganisms can anaerobically degrade such aromatic, compounds. Since then several bacterial pure cultures have been isolated that can anaerobically , degrade BTEX compounds. Toluene-degrading bacteria isolated thus far range phylogenetically from , nitrate-reducing bacteria clustering in the, |FRAME:TAX-12960|/|FRAME:TAX-33057| branch |CITS: [7537067][9023943][7710331][8590677]| of the , β-subclass of proteobacteria, to two sulfate-, reducing bacteria (Desulfobacula toluolica |CITS: [7686000]| and strain PRTOL1 |CITS: [8919780]|) and one ferric iron reducing , bacteria (Geobacter metallireducens |CITS: [8387263]|) belonging to the δ-subclass of , proteobacteria to one toluene-utilizing phototrophic bacterium (Blastochloris sulfoviridis , |CITS: [10525736]|) belonging to the α-subclass of proteobacteria. Although the pathway for , anaerobic toluene degradation shown here was demonstrated in denitrifying |FRAME:TAX-12960| and, |FRAME:TAX-33057| species, there is some evidence suggesting that the initial step of , this pathway and probably the initial steps are common to other phylogenetic groups., Anaerobic toluene degradation is initiated by a novel glycyl radical enzyme catalyzing a non-redox reaction , in which the methyl carbon of toluene is added to the double bond of fumarate. , The subsequent reactions transforming benzylsuccinate to benzoyl-CoA resemble those of , β-oxidation of fatty acids |CITS: [HEIDER99] [10629170]| . Benzoyl-CoA is a known central intermediate in anaerobic , degradation of many aromatic compounds |CITS: [9057820][HARWOOD99]|. , , This pathway for anaerobic toluene degradation was proposed based on in vitro studies conducted, with two denitrifying bacteria |FRAME:TAX-59405| |CITS: [8706665]| and |FRAME:TAX-12960| sp. strain T, |CITS: [9006019]|. Although postulated, the intermediates, 2-carboxymethyl-3-hydroxyphenylpropionyl-CoA, and benzoylsuccinyl-CoA and the enzyme activities for the corresponding reactions have yet to be detected , in cell free extracts. The initial reaction, the formation of benzylsuccinate from toluene and fumarate has , also been observed in sulfate-reducers |CITS: [BELLER97][RABUS98]|, and a phototrophic , bacterium |CITS: [10525736]| , suggesting that this may be a general strategy for anaerobically degrading , toluene in phylogenetically diverse bacteria.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of sulfated |FRAME:CPD-12557| and |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues. The |FRAME: CPD-12557| residues are substituted to varying degrees with sulfate linked to 4- and/or 6-hydroxyl positions, forming |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, and to a lesser extent the uronic acid residues may be substituted with sulfate at the 2-hydroxyl position forming |FRAME: CPD-12527|. The uronic acid residues may also be substituted with sulfate at the 3-hydroxyl positions, although this substitution is quite rare., The following names have been used to define different sulfation states:, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A "Chondroitin sulfate A"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C "Chondroitin sulfate C"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12565|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-D "Chondroitin sulfate D"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12527| and |FRAME: CPD-12565|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-E "Chondroitin sulfate E"| contains |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12526|, The term "chondroitin sulfate B" has been used in the past to refer to |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, but is not used any more., The chondroitin chains vary in size up to a hundred or more disaccharide repeating units. They are usually found attached to assorted core proteins as part of a proteoglycan complex. Chondroitin sulfate is a major component of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but is also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors., Chondroitin sulfate chains are synthesized in situ on the protein chain. They are attached to the core protein via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the "glycoaminoglycan-protein linkage region", which is formed by sequential stepwise additions of the sugar residues to specific core proteins. The synthesis of the linkage region is described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|, and the polymerization of the chondroitin chain is described in |FRAME: PWY-6566|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the later modifications of the chondroitin chain. These modifications include the sulfation of the |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME:CPD-12557| residues at different positions by a number of sulfotransferases with strict specificities. , The sulfation of |FRAME:CPD-12557| at the 4-hydroxyl position is catalyzed by three enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: HS10284|, |FRAME: HS06130| and |FRAME: HS11524| genes |CITS: [10722746][10781601][12080076]|. Another enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: HS11694|, catalyzes the sulfation at the C6 position of residues already sulfated at the C4 position |CITS: [11572857]|., The C2 position of |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues is also often sulfated in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: ENSG00000111962-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS03488| gene |CITS: [10187838]|.

Summary: In the anaerobic respiratory chain formed by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and nitrate reductase the transfer of electrons from glycerol-3-phosphate to nitrate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. Nitrate reduction in whole cells or membrane vesicles of E. coli K-12 can be coupled to the oxidation of glycerol-3-phosphate |CITS: [127786][5996]|; oxidation of glycerol-3-phosphate with nitrate as electron acceptor supports the anaerobic transport of lactose and amino acids in membrane vesicles of E. coli |CITS: [1099094]|, E. coli K-12 contains two energy conserving (H+/e- = 1) nitrate reductases. Nitrate reductase A (NRA) is the major anaerobic nitrate reductase; expression of NRA occurs in response to high levels of nitrate in the environment whereas expression of nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is not dependent on nitrate levels or anaerobiosis |CITS: [2832376][10464201]|. NRZ expression is dependent on |FRAME: RPOS-MONOMER "σS"|; NRZ may assist the cell to use nitrate efficiently under stress conditions |CITS: [10564515]|. NRZ may be important during the transition from aerobic to anaerobic conditions |CITS: [2139607]|. , E. coli also contains two glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases - an anaerobic enzyme encoded by glpABC (shown in this pathway) and an aerobic enzyme encoded by glpD. Either enzyme suffices for anaerobic growth with glycerol or glycerol-3-phosphate as the electron donor and nitrate as the terminal electron acceptor; GlpABC is required for anaerobic growth with glycerol (or glycerol-3-phosphate) and fumarate while |FRAME: AERGLYC3PDEHYDROG-MONOMER "GlpD"| is required for aerobic growth with glycerol (or glycerol-3-phosphate) (|CITS: [4945192], [127786]| and review by |CITS: [3045516]|. The ratio of GlpD to GlpABC is high when oxygen or nitrate serves as a terminal electron acceptor and low when fumarate serves this role |CITS: [4580569]|., Quinones are the obligate redox carriers during anaerobic nitrate respiration; the concentration of menaquinone increases in cells grown anaerobically with nitrate while the concentration of ubiquinone decreases (as compared with cells grown aerobically) |CITS: [195602]|. NRA can use both menaquinol (shown in this pathway) and ubiquinol as electron donors |CITS: [2204318], [1444716]|. In anaerobic growth with nitrate and glycerol-3-phosphate as electron donor the major quinone is demethylmenaquinone (DMK) |CITS: [2849923]|; an E. coli strain containing only DMK is unable to grow with nitrate as terminal reductase |CITS: [1444716]|.

Summary: The ornithine-ammonia cycle is a cyanobacterial cyclic pathway that allows for rapid remobilization of nitrogen reserves under starvation and a high rate of nitrogen assimilation and storage after the nutrient becomes available., The pathway starts with |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|, which is synthesized by |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.5|, and ends with conversion of |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME: AMMONIUM| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.3.27| (ArgZ). , In the presence of high nitrogen concentrations cyanobacteria store excess nitrogen in the form of |FRAME: Cyanophycin| polymers. When nitrogen is limiting, cyanophycin is degraded into |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: ARG| (see |FRAME: PWY-7052|). The ornithine-ammonia cycle can route access nitrogen onto |FRAME: ARG|, and upon nitrogen stravation, the pathway can quickly mobilize nitrogen by releasing |FRAME: AMMONIUM| from |FRAME: ARG| via the activity of |FRAME: EC-3.5.3.27| (ArgZ). The liberated |FRAME: AMMONIUM| can then be assimnilated into |FRAME: GLN| by |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.2| |CITS: [29632414]|., Disruption of the pathway by deletion of the |FRAME: SGL_RS17085| gene in |FRAME: TAX-1148| impaired cell growth when nitrogen availability oscillated. |CITS: [29632414]|., |FRAME: EC-3.5.3.27| is widely present among cyanobacteria exhibiting diverse morphological and physiological attributes, suggesting that the pathway may be widely distributed as well.

The metabolic versatility of |FRAME:TAX-286| strains is well illustrated by the catabolism of |FRAME: ARG|. |FRAME: TAX-287| has at least 4 different pathways for this purpose, including the arginine deiminase pathway (|FRAME:ARGDEGRAD-PWY|), the arginine succinyltransferase pathway (|FRAME:AST-PWY|), the arginine decarboxylase pathway (|FRAME:ARGDEG-III-PWY|) and the arginine:pyruvate transaminase pathway (|FRAME: PWY-5742|). |FRAME: TAX-303| has a slightly modified version of the last pathway, based on the enzyme arginine oxidase, (this pathway)., The pathway, which was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-303|, differs significantly from the other three pathways found in |FRAME:TAX-286|, and is similar to the |FRAME: ARG| degradation pathway of |FRAME: TAX-1911| (see |FRAME: ARGDEG-V-PWY|) |CITS: [5570437]|., In this pathway |FRAME:ARG | is converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-824| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-11561|. |FRAME: CPD-824| is further degraded into |FRAME: CPD-825|, |FRAME: CPD-592|, and |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-11559|, |FRAME: MONOMER-11560|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6898|, respectively |CITS: [6423769][237915]|., This pathway is probably the main |FRAME: ARG| catabolic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-303| during aerobic growth |CITS: [6423769]|.

|FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negatives is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as KDO, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A| in sequential steps, with different KDO units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In some cases a third Kdo residue is added to the second one., In |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: DODECANOATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7836| fatty acids are incorporated into the distal unit of lipid A. |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.241|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10464|, is a KDO-dependent lauroyltransferase. |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.243|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10614|, functions after laurate has been added to KDO2-lipid IVA |CITS: [8662613] [2203778] [9099672]|.
