Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14811 Diazinane-3-carboxylate| (piperazate) is a six-membered cyclic nonproteinogenic amino acid with an N-N bond within the ring that is the aza analog of the more common nonproteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: CPD-20333|. It is incorporated into a number of N-acyl hexadepsipeptide natural products of mixed nonribosomal peptide/polyketide origin, such as the kutznerides, padanamides, himastatins, and sanglifehrins, which are produced in pathways involving nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) or nonribosomal peptide synthetase/polyketide synthase (NRPS/PKS) hybrid systems. Piperazate was first identified in 1971 as a consitutent of the antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-24798 monamycin|, and was named based on the systematic name hexahydropyridazine-3-carboxylate |CITS: [Bevan71]|., X-ray structures obtained from multiple piperazate-containing compounds indicate that the piperazate rings are present as six-membered chair conformers that impose conformational constraints that rigidify the depsipeptide macrocyclic scaffolds |CITS: [16619323][17221946][19919082][20062866]|., Both |FRAME: CPD-24776| and |FRAME: CPD-24775| residues have been described from natural products, as well as 5-hydroxy-, 5-chloro-, and N(1)-6-dehydro forms |CITS: [ 21648411]|. For a list of natural products that contain piperazate rings, see |CITS: [30949650]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-24775| is produced from |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| in two enzymatic steps, via |FRAME: CPD-11571|. Both enzymes have been characterized from the kutznerides-producer |FRAME: TAX-345341|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-24775|. The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.196|, was discovered in 2012 |CITS: [22522643]|, and the second enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.1|, was discovered five years later |CITS: [28628093]|.

Summary: Coenzyme Q6 (ubiquinone, |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30|) biosynthesis in yeast (|FRAME:TAX-4932|) synthesizes a redox-active lipid involved in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and has been also demonstrated to function as an membrane antioxidant, cofactor of uncoupling proteins and functional modulator of membrane transition pores |CITS:[20494114]|. Eleven genes (COQ1-9, ARH1, YAH1) encoding for proteins directly or indirectly involved in the biosynthetic sequence of the proposed 9 reaction steps to form |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| have been identified and characterized. A characteristic feature of |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| biosynthesis is that the catalysis of the various steps is realized through an multi-subunit complex. For eight of the participating polypeptides (COQ1-3, COQ5-7, ARH1, YAH1) a enzymatic function has been established |CITS:[17482885] [10375636] [9818721]| whereas the functions of COQ4, COQ9 |CITS:[22593570]| and COQ8 |CITS:[18801050] [21944752] [22593570]| is still under investigation., The discovery that besides |FRAME:4-hydroxybenzoate| (see |FRAME:PWY3O-19|) also the 4-amino-substituted |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE|  (see |FRAME:PWY-7230|) serves as a precursor of |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| biosynthesis has extended the scope of this pathway considerably |CITS:[20534343] [20592037]|. The reason that |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| as a natural substrate of the pathway has been overlooked lies in the fact that this compound is a constitutive component of the glucose synthetic medium for yeast cultivation and has therefore never been tested as a substrate. In addition, only after the role of a novel ferredoxin/ferredoxin reductase (YHD1/ARH1) system essential for the first hydroxylation step of the pathway had been detected |CITS:[20534343]| a targeted investigation for intermediates of affected reactions became possible., The elucidation of the exact reaction sequence in the |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| biosynthesis in |FRAME:TAX-4932| is hampered by the existence of the multi-subunit complex consisting of various COQ polypeptides. Knocking-out any one of the COQ polypeptides (COQ3-COQ9) significantly decreased |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| formation and leads to the accumulation of only one early pathway intermediate (|FRAME:3-HEXAPRENYL-4-HYDROXYBENZOATE|). The utilization of COQ8 overexpressed Δcoq mutants in which the Q6 biosynthetic complex |CITS:[19002377] [17482885] [18801050]| remained functional allowed for the direct investigation of selective reaction steps clarifying the function of the corresponding COQ gene and searching for alternative analog compounds which could bypass the reaction and restore |FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30| biosynthesis |CITS:[21944752] [20534343] [22593570]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Linalools Linalool| is an acyclic monoterpene alcohol with a pleasant fragrance associated with a diverse array of plant |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. It is a primary compound in floral scent research. Both |FRAME: CPD-8996| and |FRAME: CPD-8997| enantiomeric forms occur in nature., Linalool is involved as an attractant in plant interactions with pollinators, herbivores and parasitoids |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. It has also been shown to be induced by artificial wounding and by jasmonic acid |CITS: [17440821]|. The de novo synthesis of linalool has been demonstrated in floral tissues |CITS: [17440821]|, barks and roots |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. Fungi, junipers, dicots and monocots emit linalool along with other monoterpenoids |CITS: [RAGUSO]|., Even though fungi typically do not produce monoterpenes, the de novo synthesis of linalool was demonstrate in the wine yeast strain, S. cerevisiae M522, in the absence of grape derived precursors |CITS: [15668008]|., Recently, it has been demonstrated that linalool is a potent precursor for an advanced biofuel. It can be chemically converted to 1-methyl-cyclopent-2-enol and isobutylene. Dehydration of the alcohol gives rise to methylcyclopentadiene dimers which can be converted into a high density fuel |CITS: [21488169]|., About this Pathway, This superpathway describes the production of the two linalool enantiomers |FRAME: CPD-8996| and |FRAME: CPD-8997|, which does not necessarily occur in the same organism., The C10 monoterpene |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| (GPP) is synthesized from the C5 compounds |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| and |FRAME: CPD-4211| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.1| |CITS: [11848932]|., |FRAME: CPD-8997| is produced in a single step from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| by the monomeric enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.25| (LIS), which was discovered in the plant |FRAME: TAX-36903| |CITS: [7864636]|. LIS activity is detected only in floral tissues of the plant., |FRAME: CPD-8996| is produced in a single step from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.26|, which was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-650269| (bergamot mint) |CITS: [12176064]|.

Summary: The curacins are natural products produced by marine cyanobacteria via a mixed polyketide synthase/non-ribosomal peptide synthase (PKS/NRPS) pathway. The compounds have unusual structural features, containing a cyclopropane group, a thiazoline moiety, and a terminal double bond. , |FRAME: CPD-10376 "Curacin A"|, |FRAME: CPD-10377|, and |FRAME: CPD-25505| were isolated from the marine cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-489825| at Curaçao |CITS: [Gerwick9][Yoo95]|, |FRAME: CPD-25504| was obtained from the same organism isolated at the Virgin islands |CITS: [9887531]|, and |FRAME: CPD-25506| was isolated from the Brittle Star |FRAME: TAX-1365868| harvested at Kabira Reef of Ishigaki Island, Okinawa (presumably formed by cyanobacterial symbionts) |CITS: [27684202]| (note that earlier reports refer to the producing organism as |FRAME: TAX-158786| 3L. However, that strain has been reclassified as |FRAME: TAX-489825| |CITS: [ 21724952]|)., |FRAME: CPD-10376 "Curacin A"| is a potent antiproliferative agent that inhibits the binding of colchicine to tubulin and arrests mitosis |CITS: [Gerwick9][7565634][10496976][10496976]|., |FRAME: TAX-1155739| produces several metabolites of mixed PKS/NRPS origin (including the curacins, |FRAME: CPD-10375|, |FRAME: CPD-17692|, and antillatoxin) making it challenging to identify the gene cluster encoding curacin biosynthesis.However, the cluster could be identified based on the prediction that a cycteine-specific peptidyl-carrier protein participates in the pathway. 13 open reading frames, named curA-curM, encode the pathways enzymes, which include nine PKS modules and one NRPS module that combined hold 41 catalytic domains |CITS: [15332855]|., The first enzyme in the pathway is |FRAME: MONOMER-21982|, a large polyketide synthase that contains 9 domains, including a GNAT loading domain, a halogenase domain, and three acyl-carrier domains (ACPI, ACPII, and ACPIII) that are arranged in tandem. A starter malonyl unit is loaded via the GNAT domain, decarboxylated to an acetyl unit, and then transferred to the ACPI domain. The transformation of the acetyl unit to a cyclopropane ring occurs while bound to the tandem array of ACP domains. This transformation comprises extension by a second malonyl-CoA unit, condensation with a second acetyl unit carried by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21986|, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-21987| and forming a branch at the β position, halogenation by the halogenase domain of CurA, dehydration by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21983 "CurE dehydratase"|, and eventually decarboxylation and cyclization by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21984| to form the cyclopropane moiety., At this point the intermediate is transferred to an L-cysteine that is bound to the peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domain of CurF, forming the thiazole structure. The pathway continues with a series of polyketide synthases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107734|, |FRAME: G-107735|, |FRAME: G-107736|, |FRAME: G-107737|, |FRAME: G-107738|, and |FRAME: G-107739| genes, that extend the product, introducing cis and trans double bonds and two methyl groups. Since two of these enzymes lack a dehydratase domain, two other enzymes catalyzes two dehydration events each |CITS: [27960309]|. The last enzyme in the pathway is the unusual |FRAME: MONOMER-21994|. This enzyme contains (in addition to more common domains) a sulsotransferase (ST) and a thioesterase (TE) domains. The enzyme catalyzes sulfonation of the β-hydroxyl group of the product by |FRAME: PAPS| (PAPS), followed by a hydrolysis/decarboxylation reaction that releases the product from the PKS, eliminates the sulfate, and forms the alkene terminal double bond of |FRAME: CPD-10376| |CITS: [19835378]|.

Summary: |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that is abundant in many vegetable oils,, especially safflower and sunflower oils. It is an essential dietary requirement for all mammals, since they, lack the Δ12 desaturase enzyme that produces it. , Linoleate is an ω-6 fatty acid, referring to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end, of the fatty acid., While most animals cannot produce |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, some insects are known do so,, including members of the orders |FRAME: TAX-6993|, |FRAME: TAX-7524| and |FRAME: TAX-7516|, |CITS: [Cripps86]|., The key enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-14127|, has been studied in the American, cockroach (|FRAME: TAX-6978|) |CITS: [2248971]|, and shown to prefer the CoA derivative of the fatty, acid substrate (unlike the plant enzymes, which usually perform the desaturation on fatty acids that are, incorporated into lipids (see |FRAME: PWY-5995|). The presence of the enzyme enables the cockroach, to become nuritionally independent of dietary lipid, and to synthesize eicosanoids de novo., An similar enzyme that prefers the CoA derivative was also described in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-29829|, |CITS: [8900454]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway menaquinone is synthesized from chorismate via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|. In a series of reactions, |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE| is converted to the two-ring compound |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| via several intermediates that include |FRAME: O-SUCCINYLBENZOATE|. At this point a prenyltransferase enzyme attaches a polyprenyl tail to form |FRAME: Demethylmenaquinones|, which can be converted to |FRAME: Menaquinones| by a, dedicated methylase., Demethylquinones were first discovered in |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [14214086]|. The main form was |FRAME: CPD-9732| (DMK-6), although lesser amounts of DMK-5 and DMK-7 were also detected. Additional studies found that DMK-6 is involved in respiration in |FRAME: TAX-729|, and could mediate electron transfer between NADH and succinate, similar to ubiquinone (Q). In addition, DMK-6 could act as a mediator in fumarate reduction, similar to menaquinone (MK)., Thus, in contrast to Q and MK, DMK acts equally well in succinate respiration and in fumarate reduction |CITS: [187454]|.

Summary: General Background, Most microorganisms capable of osmotic adaptation accumulate compatible solutes in response to increases in the levels of salts or sugars in the environment. |FRAME: 2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE| (MG) is a compatible solute that is very common in organisms living near or at the highest growth temperatures for life |CITS: [17061210]|. It has been detected in thermophilic bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-29549|, |FRAME: TAX-274|, |FRAME: TAX-28237| and |FRAME: TAX-49319| |CITS: [8824608][16535053][10357003]|, and in the hyperthermophilic archaea of the genera |FRAME:TAX-2260|,|FRAME:TAX-2263|, Palaeococcus, Aeropyrum, and in some strains of |FRAME:TAX-2233| |CITS:[16535556][9758772]|. Even though MG is usually found in hyperthermophilic organisms, low levels have also been identified, in red algae |CITS: [Karsten03]| and in mesophilic bacteria |CITS: [15205409]|., Physiological studies were conducted with several organisms, and showed that MG behaves like a typical solute, accumulating concomitantly with increasing levels of NaCl in the growth medium |CITS: [12220406]|. It is the primary osmolyte in many archaea, including |FRAME: TAX-2261|, |FRAME: TAX-53953|, |FRAME: TAX-2265|, |FRAME: TAX-2264|, and |FRAME: TAX-49900|, and also in the thermophilic and slightly halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29549|., In addition to protection against osmotic pressure, MG was shown to protect proteins against thermal denaturation |CITS: [16535713]|., About This Pathway, In most organisms MG is produced from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| via |FRAME: ALPHA-D-MANNOSYL-3-PHOSPHOGLYCERATE| in two steps, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13380| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13379| |CITS: [11562374]|. In the mesophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-61435| a single bifunctional enzyme was shown to catalyze both steps |CITS: [15205409]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29549| posseses a second, single step, route from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| to MG (see |FRAME: PWY-5658|).

Summary: General Background, In mammals |FRAME: TRP| is an essential amino acid that must be obtained in the diet. It is utilized in protein synthesis and in biosynthesis of the neurotransmitter |FRAME: SEROTONIN|. It is catabolized via the kynurenine pathway in most tissues. This pathway is the major catabolic route of |FRAME: TRP| in mammals, as well as an anabolic source of |FRAME: NAD|. |FRAME: TRP| is also catabolized via the serotonergic pathway in the central nervous system (CNS), producing |FRAME: SEROTONIN| and other indoleamines. Metabolites of the kynurenine pathway are involved in many biological processes. In the CNS products of both pathways have consequences for the modulation of physiology and behavior and for the pathophysiology of some diseases (in |CITS: [18282734]|, |CITS: [9291104]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16942634]| and |CITS: [15018833]|). See pathways |FRAME: PWY-5651| and its pathway links and pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|., About This Pathway, The kynurenine pathway in mammalian liver is initiated by tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase, EC 1.13.11.11. In mammalian brain and other peripheral tissues and cells the kynurenine pathway is initiated by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase EC 1.13.11.52. This is the first and rate-determining step of this pathway. In addition to the acidic metabolites shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5651|, other reactions can form the acidic, neuroactive metabolites |FRAME: KYNURENATE|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE|, |FRAME: XANTHURENATE| and |FRAME: PICOLINATE|, as shown in this pathway., |FRAME: CPD-14736| can be enzymatically converted to the neuroactive compounds |FRAME: KYNURENATE| (via transamination) or |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| (via hydrolysis). |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| can be enzymatically transaminated to |FRAME: XANTHURENATE|, possibly by the same enzyme that transaminates |FRAME: CPD-14736|. |FRAME: 2-AMINO-3-3-OXOPROP-2-ENYL-BUT-2-ENEDI| is an unstable intermediate in the kynurenine pathway that is transformed spontaneously into |FRAME: QUINOLINATE| (see linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-5653|), or enzymatically into |FRAME: 2-AMINOMUCONATE_SEMIALDEHYDE|. |FRAME: 2-AMINOMUCONATE_SEMIALDEHYDE| can undergo spontaneous cyclization to |FRAME: PICOLINATE|, or enzymatic conversion to |FRAME: 2-AMINO-MUCONATE|. |FRAME: PICOLINATE| has been identified in body fluids, including cerebrospinal fluid (in |CITS: [19141084] [9291104] [18027945]| and |CITS: [19268309]| and reviewed in |CITS: [18220779]|)., In rat brain slices, evidence has been presented that |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| may be preferentially produced by microsomal hydroxylation of |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| by unspecified hydroxylases |CITS: [2384749]|. However, mouse studies supported the formation of |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| from |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-L-KYNURENINE| in brain and from hydroxylation of |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| in peripheral tissues |CITS: [8764597] [12763538]|. Therefore, this remains to be investigated in other species and tissues (in |CITS: [9784247]|)., As noted above, metabolites of the kynurenine pathway are involved in many biological processes. Some of these metabolites are potentially toxic if their levels are increased in various disorders. The physiological functions of |FRAME: KYNURENATE|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE|, |FRAME: XANTHURENATE| and |FRAME: PICOLINATE| are under investigation (reviewed in |CITS: [18220779]|). |FRAME: XANTHURENATE| is a possible synaptic signaling molecule in brain |CITS: [18182052]|. Although |FRAME: QUINOLINATE| is neurotoxic, |FRAME: KYNURENATE| and |FRAME: PICOLINATE| are neuroprotective (in |CITS: [18032661]|). |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| may be involved in oxidative stress and neuronal damage (reviewed in |CITS: [19268309]|).

Summary: In most plants, purine nucleotides are completely degraded to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| via the ureides |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|. This degradation proceeds via the intermediates |FRAME: XANTHINE| and |FRAME: URATE|., The initial step of AMP degradation is the conversion of AMP to IMP, which is converted to xanthine in two alternative routes, via |FRAME: XANTHOSINE| or |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|. The initial step of GMP degradation is the conversion of GMP to guanosine, which is also degraded to xanthine in two ways, via |FRAME: GUANINE| or |FRAME: XANTHOSINE|., Studies in tea leaves and cultured |FRAME: TAX-4058| cells showed that guanosine deaminase activity was much higher than that of guanine deaminase |CITS: [Ashihara97]|. It indicates the degradation pathway of GMP via xanthosine is likely to be the major route. Xanthine is then converted to urate by xanthine dehydrogenase |CITS: [14726515]|.  , The product of this pathway, |FRAME: URATE|, is converted to to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as described in |FRAME: PWY-5691|., The plant pathway is very similar to that found in mammals. However, mammals do not have the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-11783| (EC 3.5.4.15) |CITS: [14725335]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6353|).

Summary: The pathways of biosynthesis of |FRAME: PHE| and |FRAME: TYRSYN| are intimately connected. The first step of both pathways is the conversion of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to |FRAME: PREPHENATE|; the third step of both is the conversion of a ketoacid to the aminoacid through transamination. The two pathways differ only in the second step of their three-step reaction sequences: In the case of |FRAME: PHE| biosynthesis a dehydratase converts |FRAME: PREPHENATE| to |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE| (a reaction that occurs slowly in the absence of enzymic acitivity); in the case of |FRAME: TYR| biosynthesis, a dehydrogenase converts |FRAME: PREPHENATE| to |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate). Also in both pathways the first two steps are catalyzed by two distinct active sites on a single protein. Thus the first step of each pathway can be catalyzed by two enzymes: those associated with both the phenylalanine-specific dehydratase and the tyrosine-specific dehydrogenase. Three enzymes, those encoded by tyrB, aspC, and ilvE, are involved in catalyzing the third step of these pathways: all three can contribute to the synthesis of |FRAME: PHE|; only TyrB and AspC contribute to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: TYR|. Reviewed in Pittard, J. and J. Yang (2008) "Biosynthesis of the Aromatic Amino Acids." Summary: General Background, Androgens are steroid hormones that stimulate or control the development and maintenance of male characteristics in vertebrates, including the activity of the accessory male sex organs and development of male secondary sex characteristics, by binding to androgen receptors. Androgens are also produced by females, and are the precursors to estrogens. Present in lower concentrations than in males, androgens contribute to libido and sexual arousal in females., Important androgens include |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| (DHT) and |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE androstenedione|. |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE Testosterone| is the major androgen in adult males, while DHT plays a crucial role in utero, triggering differentiation of the penis, scrotum and prostate. In adulthood DHT contributes to balding, prostate growth, and sebaceous gland activity., About This Pathway, The usual pathway leading to the biosynthesis of DHT in adults is shown in |FRAME: PWY66-378|. In that pathway DHT is formed from |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, which in turn is formed from |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE|., During prenatal development in mammals a different pathway operates, which bypasses the formation of these two intermediates. The pathway, which leads to early male sexual differentiation, has been named "the backdoor pathway" of androgen biosynthesis. The pathway was initially described from marsupials |CITS: [11035809]| and later reported from mouse |CITS: [15249131]| and humans |CITS: [21802064][30943210]|., This pathway may play an important role in castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) patients. Prostate cancer is dependent on androgen hormones, and androgen deprivation therapy is currently the primary treatment. However, while this clinical approach is initially effective, most cases progress to castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) over time. While CRPC is also dependent on the presence of DHT, it proliferates in the absence of testicular |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|. It seems likely that DHT is formed via the backdoor pathway in CRPC tumors |CITS: [ 21795608]|, and potentially also in healthy prostate |CITS: [18471780]|., The pathway proceeds via |FRAME: 17-ALPHA-HYDROXYPROGESTERONE|, which in adults normally participates only in formation of corticoids (see |FRAME: PWY66-381|). This compound undergoes 5α-reduction by |FRAME: HS07261|/|FRAME: HS00619| enzymes, forming |FRAME: CPD-23955|, which is converted to DHT in 4 steps |CITS: [30943210]|., The pathway is activated regardless of age and sex by even a mild increase in circulating |FRAME: 17-ALPHA-HYDROXYPROGESTERONE| levels, which can be caused by deficiency of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.16| or |FRAME: EC-1.6.2.4| |CITS: [22170725][31611378]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Monoterpenes Monoterpenoids|, the main volatile components in essential oils, have been used historically in the food, perfume and pharmaceutical industries because of their culinary, fragrance and antimicrobial properties. Commercially, menthol is one of the most valuable monoterpenes. The essential oils of the genus |FRAME:TAX-21819| (mint) occurs in the peltate glandular trichomes. The monoterpene constituents of the essential oils of mint are distinguished by the position of oxygenation on the p-menthane ring |CITS:[LAWRENCE81]|., Of the agronomically important mints, peppermint (M. piperita L.) produces almost exclusively monoterpenes bearing an oxygen function at position C-3 such as menthol (responsible for the cooling sensation of peppermint), whereas spearmint types such as native spearmint (|FRAME: TAX-29719|) and Scotch spearmint (M. gentilis var cardiaca) produce almost exclusively monoterpenes bearing an oxygen function at position C-6, typified by carvone (responsible for the typical spearmint note)., The biosynthesis of p-menthane monoterpenes in |FRAME:TAX-21819| species proceeds from geranyl pyrophosphate via the cyclic olefin limonene. Biosynthetic investigations have demonstrated that regiospecificity is established very early on the monoterpene biosynthesis pathways in which (-)-4S-limonene, the common precursor of both oxygenated series, undergoes cytochrome P450-mediated hydroxylation at C-3 to yield (-)-trans-isopiperitenol or at C-6 to afford (-)-trans-carveol. The remaining enzymatic machinery responsible for the subsequent redox transformations of isopiperitenol to menthol is present in both peppermint and spearmint species; however, carveol is a poor substrate for these reactions, with the consequence that only the dehydrogenation product, carvone, accumulates in spearmint types |CITS:[CROTEAU91]|. Typically, superior oils of peppermint contain high quantities of menthol, moderate amounts of menthone and low levels of pulegone and menthofurane (both of which are undesirable for their hepatotoxicity in humans)., In the final reductive step of the menthol biosynthesis pathway, (-)-menthone and (+)-isomenthone are reduced to (-)-menthol and (+)-neoisomenthol, respectively, by MMR and to (+)-neomenthol and (+)-isomenthol by MNR; the latter three monoterpenol isomers are minor constituents of peppermint oil.

Summary: Methylotrophic bacteria are aerobic bacteria that utilize one-carbon compounds more reduced than, formate as sources of carbon and energy, and assimilate formaldehyde as a major source of cellular, carbon |CITS [8801441]|. , Methylotrophic bacteria utilize a variety of different one-carbon compounds including methane, (see |FRAME: PWY-1641|), methanol, methylated amines, halomethanes and methylated compounds, containing sulfur. , The common product of these oxidation reactions is |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which is either, oxidized to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| via |FRAME: FORMATE|, or assimilated (see formaldehyde, assimilation and formaldehyde oxidation pathways)., Please note: This superpathway integrates several base pathways that are found in, different methylotrophic bacteria, for the purpose of displaying the different routes found in the biosphere, in a single general diagram., There may be no single organism that possesses all of these pathways., For more information about the pathways and enzymes shown in here, please see the, individual pathways that make up this superpathway.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Very early studies of corrinoids from methanogens reported the presence of cobamides with |FRAME: CPD-18497| as the lower ligand base. The cobamide was given the name ""factor III" |CITS: [Friedrich53]|. It was soon found that this new cobamide was prevalent among methanogens |CITS: [Friedrich58]|. It was also reported from "Methanobacillus omelianskii" |CITS: [14311623]|, which was later shown to be not a pure culture but rather a synergistic association of the methanogen |FRAME: TAX-2161| (which produces the cobamide) and an ethanol-oxidizing organism (organism s). The two organisms exchanged hydrogen among them, leading to the understanding of the "interspecies hydrogen transfer" phenomenon |CITS: [5602458][5058442]|. Analysis of the cobamides from |FRAME: TAX-2208| showed Co-methyl and Co-aquo derivatives of 5-hydroxybenzimidazolylcobamide |CITS: [7150319][Hollriegl83]|. Spectroscopic structure analysis of the cobamides isolated from |FRAME: TAX-79929| confirmed that it was 5'-hydroxybenzimidazolyl-cobamide |CITS: [Krautler87]|. The general observation was that the corrinoids found in methanogens are either |FRAME: Co-a-5-hydroxybenzimidazolyl-cobamides "5-hydroxybenzimidazolyl-cobamides"| or |FRAME: Co-a-adenyl-cobamide "pseudo vitamin B12"|, which contains an adenine as the lower ligand base |CITS: [Stupperich88]|., Cobamides perform a crucial role in the metabolism of methanogens. The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds all follow a similar route, where methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]| and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20849|. The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the lower ligand base is activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (CobT) by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide or a related compound to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) and the ribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), to form the cobamide., The order of events in this pathway was deduced from studies of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.405| (BzaC), which indicated that its preferred substrate is |FRAME: CPD-20841| |CITS: [32503839]|., The enzymes that operate in this pathway are the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis. Studies of the specificity of these enzymes have suggested that the nature of the lower ligand is controlled by the presence or absence of different methyltransferases that can further modify it and by the specificity of CobS |CITS: [36371846]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins Anabaenopeptins| are a family of non-ribosomally synthesized cyclic peptides produced by some cyanobacterial species. They have a well-conserved structure comprising a ring of five amino acids connected through an ureido linkage to an exocyclic sixth amino acid. Counting the exocyclic amino acid as residue 1, the 2nd residue is |FRAME: CPD-219|, and the ring is formed by cyclization of the C-terminal carboxyl of the 6th residue to the ε-amino group of the D-lysine at position 2. The ureido bridge connecting the α-amino group of |FRAME: CPD-219| to the exocyclic amino acid is a unique feature among cyanobacterial peptides., The five amino acids other than |FRAME: CPD-219| are not conserved and may consist of either proteinogenic or non-proteinogenic amino acids. A review published in 2006 listed 124 different anabaenopeptin variants |CITS: [16774586]|. Many of the anabaenopeptins have been isolated under different names such as oscillamides, lyngbyaureamides, ferintoic acids, nodulapeptins, schizopeptins and more |CITS: [Sano95][11520225]|., Anabaenopeptins have been found in an enormous variety of cyanobacteria isolated from both the aquatic and terrestrial environments, including |FRAME: TAX-1163|, |FRAME: TAX-1177|, |FRAME: TAX-1125|, |FRAME: TAX-54304|, |FRAME: TAX-28073|, and |FRAME: TAX-383614| |CITS: [Harada95][26096276][27604544]|. In general, these compounds are produced by filamentous cyanobacteria belonging to the orders |FRAME: TAX-1161| and |FRAME: TAX-1150|. The production by members of the unicellular genus |FRAME: TAX-1125| is beleived to be due to horizontal transfer of the biosynthetic gene cluster from a filamentous organism |CITS: [28261178]|., Anabaenopeptins exhibit a functional diversity that includes inhibitory activity for proteases, phosphatases, and carboxypeptidases |CITS: [ 10340607][11520225][Zafrir-Ilan10]|, and are believed to provide protection against zooplankters and crustaceans., About This Pathway, The gene cluster responsible for anabaenopeptin biosynthesis was discovered in 2005 in a |FRAME: TAX-59512| strain. The cluster comprised 5 genes (anaABCDE) encoding four non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs) and one ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter. Interestingly, even though that organism produces several different anabaenopeptins (|FRAME: CPD-26928|, |FRAME: CPD-26929|, |FRAME: CPD-26933| and |FRAME: CPD-26942|), it contains only a single cluster, indicating that some of the enzymes are promiscuous and can accept different substrates |CITS: [19706155]|. Similar clusters were soon described from multiple species, including |FRAME: TAX-46234|, |FRAME: TAX-313624|, and |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [20338518]|. A cluster from |FRAME: TAX-984208| was reported in 2017 |CITS: [28085246]|. In many organisms a gene cluster encoding |FRAME: PWY-7275| is located next to the anabaenopeptin biosynthesis cluster, and it is assumed that those enzymes produce the homo-amino acids |FRAME: CPD-15322| and |FRAME: CPD-17729| that are incorporated into many anabaenopeptins |CITS: [28085246]|., The AptA NRPS contains two adenylation and two thiolation domains, for activating and binding tof he first two amino acids, a condensation domain, and an epimerization domain for converting |FRAME: LYS| into |FRAME: CPD-219|. The AptB NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the third amino acid, respectively. The AptC NRPS contains two sets of adenylation, thiolation, and condensation, responsible for the fourth and fifth amino acids. It also contains methylation domain, for methylation of the fifth residue (often |FRAME: CPD-298|). The AptD NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the sixth amino acid, and a thioesterase domain, which is responsible for cyclization and release of the product., An unanswered question as of 2024 is the mechanism responsible for formation of the ureido bridge. A similar structure exists in |FRAME: CPD-26948|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-317|, and it has been shown that in that organism the formation of the ureido bridge is catalyzed by the SylC protein |CITS: [19968303]|. However, SylC possesses a domain with structural similarity to acetyltransferase between the A- and C-domains of the NRPSs, and no similar domain was found within the anabaenopeptins NRPSs, suggesting that a different mechanism may exist during anabaenopeptin biosynthesis |CITS: [34437393]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-26869 2-Chloro-4-nitrophenol| (2C4NP) is widely utilized as a component of the antibiotic/fungicide |FRAME: CPD-26876| |CITS: [13717477][4727830][4767981]|. It is also used in the manufacture of the pesticide |FRAME: CPD-26875| |CITS: [25279599][24477548]|. 2C4NP, which is highly toxic to humans, is a chlorinated analog of |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL|, which has been listed as a priority environmental pollutant by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency., Several pure bacterial cultures have been isolated on the basis of their ability to utilize 2C4NP as a sole carbon and energy source, leading to characterization of several different degradation pathways |CITS: [20050667][20359211][21626025][21960016][22701692]|., The first pathway that was characterized at the genetic and biochemical levels was that of |FRAME: TAX-406819|. Dechlorination occurs spontaneously following the formation of the unstable compound |FRAME: CPD-19731|. The pathway genes were found in a single operon, which is unusual.

Summary: Fumitremorgins (see |FRAME:PWY-7525| and |FRAME:PWY-7526|) are tremorgenic mycotoxins |CITS:[5122678]| which have been named after their tremor inducing effect on the central nervous system in mice |CITS:[14107473]|. These compounds represent a group of prenylated indole alkaloids which are mostly found in the genera Aspergillus and Penicillium of the fungi kingdom |CITS:[11245401] [23467716] [20024094]||. Aspergillus fumigatus, a main producer of tremorgins, is the foremost cause for fungal diseases with a high mortality rate in immunocompromised humans |CITS:[20618330] [21102391]|. Because of their considerable impact on human health, Aspergillus fumigatus has been in the focus of researchers for some time now which, amongst others, resulted in the deciphering of its genome |CITS:[16372009] [16371993]| and the elucidation of gene clusters involved in the making of fungal secondary metabolites exhibiting numerous activities of physiological importance |CITS:[16322742]|. , In spite of their food poisoning and lung disease causing properties fumitremorgins and their pathway intermediates also exhibit a variety of interesting pharmacological activities which makes them promising candidates for drug improvement and cancer treatments. Aspergillus fumigatus has been reported to produce at least 226 bioactive secondary metabolites many of which possess such novel traits |CITS:[18763205]|. , |FRAME:CPD-15262 Tryprostatin B| and |FRAME:CPD-15262| inhibit the mammalian cell-cycle progression |CITS:[8698634]| through disruption of microtubule assembly |CITS:[9677311] [11058035]| and have been demonstrated to express growth inhibitory properties in certain human cancer types such as breast, lung, and prostate cancer |CITS:[11931609]|. Special notice deserves the research done with |FRAME:CPD-15266| with respect to its inhibition of an breast cancer resistant protein (BCRP) |CITS:[10646850]| which represents an drug transporter conferring drug resistance to its host by extruding a wide variety of structurally divergent drugs across cell membranes |CITS:[16402910]|. |FRAME:CPD-15260 Fumitremorgin B| and |FRAME:CPD-15259| efficiently inhibit mammalian cell-cycle progression |CITS:[8698634] [22575049]| and have been generally classified as genotoxic |CITS:[14627292]|. , The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-15266| originates from the formation of cyclic dipeptides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15265| catalyzed by the brevianamid F synthase which synthesizes the peptide bond between |FRAME:TRP| and |FRAME:PRO| |CITS:[16755625] [Williams00]|. The formed cyclic |L-Trp-L-Pro| undergoes prenylation and the type of prenylation, i.e. 'regular' versus 'reverse' at position C-2 directs the pathway either to compound classes such as fumitremorgins and spirotryprostatins (regular prenylation) or compound classes such as brevianamides and notoamides (reverse prenylation) |CITS:[20024094] [20722388]|. The brevianamide F prenyltransferase catalyzes the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15263| from |FRAME:CPD-15265| using |FRAME:CPD-4211| |CITS:[16000710] [21105662]| and was also shown to be able to prenylate the C-3 of the indole nucleus |CITS:[23090579]| indicating the capability to produce an even wider spectrum of cyclic dipeptide intermediates., Further chemical modifications of the diketopiperazine core include the 6-hydroxylation of the indole ring of |FRAME:CPD-15263| yielding |FRAME:CPD-15264| which is then further methylated to generate |FRAME:CPD-15262|. The molecular functions of the respective enzymes, i.e. tryprostatin B 6-hydroxylase |CITS:[19226505]| and 6-hydroxytryprostatin B methytransferase |CITS:[19226505] [23649274]| have been demonstrated in direct assays as well as in functional complementation and mutant knock-outs. Finally, the formation of cyclization products, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15266| and |FRAME:CPD-15267| is realized via the formation of a C-N bond catalyzed by the first described fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme carrying out that reaction, i.e. fumitremorgin C synthase |CITS:[19226505]|. It remains to be shown whether |FRAME:CPD-15267| represents a shunt-product or a variant in the |FRAME:PWY-7525|., The wild-type of Aspergillus fumigatus appears not to have the necessary genetic make-up for |FRAME:PWY-7526| |CITS:[23109474] [16755625]| but other Aspergillus fumigatus strains |CITS:[6988091] [Horie81]| and close relatives such as Neosartorya fischeri |CITS:[3415223]| have been shown to produce |FRAME:CPD-15261|. For this reason various authors |CITS:[19763315] [21063425]| have proposed |FRAME:CPD-15259| as the final product of the pathway for Aspergillus. One of the possible reasons for finding |FRAME:CPD-15261| only in a few strains of Aspergillus fumigatus might be that the gene encoding verruculogen prenyltransferase catalyzing the last step of the pathway, is not part of the tremorgin biosynthetic cluster in Aspergillus fumigatus but is located on another chromosome |CITS:[23109474]| and may have been lost or rendered inactive in certain Aspergillus strains. , The substrate of the first committed reaction of the |FRAME:PWY-7526|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15266| has been produced previously (see |FRAME:PWY-7525| and also |FRAME:PWY-7537|) and is hydroxylated in both the C-12 and C-13 position of the indole ring by the cytochrome P450 dependent fumitremorgin C hydroxylase |CITS:[19226505]| yielding the next intermediate |FRAME:CPD-15268| of the pathway. After the C-prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-15268| by the 12α,13α-dihydroxyfumitremorgin C prenyltransferase |CITS:[18683158]| forming |FRAME:CPD-15260|, the next reaction, the formation of an endoperoxide bond between the two prenyl moieties generating the cyclic |FRAME:CPD-15259| is considered the key reaction of the pathway. The catalyzing enzyme, i.e. verruculogen synthase, is a α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase able to insert both oxygen atoms from molecular |FRAME:OXYGEN-MOLECULE| and the first one of its kind reported for fungal pathways |CITS:[19763315] [21404415]|. The last step of the pathway, as mentioned above, is catalyzed by an O-prenyltransferase generating the final product |FRAME:CPD-15261| |CITS:[23109474]|.

Summary: General Background, Phospholipids are important membrane components. Most of the phospholipids belong to the category of phosphoglycerides. The simplest phosphoglycerides, which are known as phosphatidate (or diacylglycerol phosphate), are composed of a glycerol molecule attached to two fatty acids and one phosphate group. The carboxyl group of each fatty acid is esterified to the hydroxyl groups on carbon-1 and carbon-2 of the glycerol molecule, while the phosphate group is attached to carbon-3 by an ester link. Phosphatidates are precursors for many phosphoglycerides found in animals, plants and yeast, including |FRAME: Phosphatidylinositols|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-SERINE|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE|, and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN|., As part of the synthesis of phosphoglycerides, either the phosphatidate or the modifying compound need to be activated by |FRAME:CTP|. In some cases, the modifying compound is activated, as in the case of |FRAME: CHOLINE| and, |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, which form |FRAME: CDP-CHOLINE| and |FRAME: CDP-ETHANOLAMINE|, respectively. However, in the case of other compounds, such as |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, the phosphatidate is activated first, forming |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL|, which then reacts with the modifying compound to form the, phosphoglyceride., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL| in eukaryotes and some Gram-negative bacteria (primarily the |FRAME: TAX-1236|). In this pathway the production of the intermediate |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P| is catalyzed by the membrane-bound enzyme |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3-P-ACYLTRANSFER-MONOMER|. The bacterial enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: EG10740|, can utilize either |FRAME: ACYL-ACP| or |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs| thioesters as the acyl donors, while the eukaryotic enzymes can only accept the acyl-CoA thiesters., The addition of the second acyl moiety is catalyzed by |FRAME: 1-ACYLGLYCEROL-3-P-ACYLTRANSFER-MONOMER|. The bacterial enzyme, which is universally expressed in all bacteria, is encoded by |FRAME: EG11377|. As in the case of PlsB, the bacterial enzyme can utilize either a fatty acyl-[acp] or an acyl-CoA thioester as the acyl donor, while the eukaryotic enzyme can only accept acyl-CoA thioesters., A pathway that describes the usage of fatty acyl-[acp] donors can be found at |FRAME: PWY0-1319|. It should be noted that most bacteria utilize a different route for the synthesis of |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5981|., More information can be found in |FRAME: PHOSLIPSYN2-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-19011 "Methyl tert-butyl ether"| (MTBE) is used at large scale since the 1990s as a fuel oxygenate for reducing carbon monoxide emissions in the United States and Europe. In the European Union, MTBE is the most frequently used fuel oxygenate, with a mean concentration in gasoline of 2-3% (w/w). Environmental and health concerns have led to a progressive phase-out in the US. In 2003 it was banned from use in California., This usage, coupled with high incidences of leaking underground storage tanks, has led to MTBE contamination of surface waters, groundwater, soils, and sediments |CITS: [Keller98][26616267]|. MTBE is highly soluble and persists in contaminated aquifers. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) lists MTBE as a possible carcinogen. In addition, one of its biodegradation products, |FRAME: CPD-19012| (TBA), is also a potential carcinogen., Several bacterial strains were shown to be able to degrade MTBE to a certain extent |CITS: [9035411][11722912]|. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-420662|, which was isolated from a compost biofilter at the Los Angeles Joint Water Treatment Plant, can use MTBE as its sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [10543787]|., About This Pathway, The initial reactions of MTBE degradation were studied in the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6300|, which cometabolizes MTBE when grown on |FRAME: CPD-18984|. It was found that MTBE is attacked by a monooxygenase that hydroxylates the methoxy carbon, generating the hemiacetal compound |FRAME: CPD-19043|, which is oxidized to form |FRAME: CPD-19044| (TBF). TBF is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-19012| (TBA) by an esterase, releasing |FRAME: FORMATE|. TBA is attacked again by a monooxygenase , generating the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-19013| |CITS: [12570997]|., Coversion of |FRAME: CPD-19013| to |FRAME: CPD-19014| was first demonstrated in the MTBE degrader |FRAME: ORG-6301| |CITS: [16622053]|. A gene cluster, designated the mpd cluster, was isolated from |FRAME: ORG-6301| and shown to contain genes encoding an alcohol dehydrogenase and an aldehyde dehydrogenase that catalyze this transformation |CITS: [16622053]|., In the last segment of the pathway, |FRAME: CPD-19014| is activated by coenzyme A, and the molecule is rearranged by the B12-dependent |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.64| into the common metabolite |FRAME: S-3-HYDROXYBUTANOYL-COA|. Two more reactions of central metabolism can convert this intermediate into |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [17890343]|., In most organisms the genes involved in MTBE degradation are carried on highly conserved megaplasmids that appear to be transferred between species |CITS: [17158667]|. In most organisms the genes were named mdp for MTBE degradation pathway.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: GLN| is the amino group donor for many cellular biosynthetic reactions and serves as a storage reservoir of ammonia, playing an important role in nitrogen metabolism. In eukaryotes, |FRAME: GLN| is converted to |FRAME: GLT| by glutaminase, the enzyme responsible for |FRAME: GLN| catabolism. In plants, bacteria, and archaea, |FRAME: GLN| can also be converted to |FRAME: GLT| by the reversible glutamate synthase reaction, also known as GOGAT for glutamine: α-oxoglutarate aminotransferase (see pathway |FRAME: GLUTAMINEFUM-PWY|) |CITS: [VOET04] [GOTTSCHALK1986]|., About This Pathway, Glutaminases are present in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes and play important roles in nitrogen metabolism by effecting glutamine breakdown. Many microorgansisms can grow with |FRAME: GLN| as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen. The catabolism of glutamine in mammals is initiated by mitochondrial glutaminases. Mammals typically express two forms of mitochondrial glutaminase. The liver type glutaminase is expressed only in adult liver tissue, while the kidney type glutaminase is expressed in kidney, brain, intestine, immune system cells, and in many transformed cells, as well as fetal liver cells |CITS:[11130979]|, Eukaryotic glutaminases differ in properties from those of prokaryotes. The mammalian enzyme is encoded by a single gene and expressed as a proenzyme with a mitochondrial targeting signal |CITS:[12963351]|. Upon entering the mitochondrion the protein is processed into two different forms. Upon activation by phosphate, the two subunits form a heterotetramer, composed of one large subunit and three of the smaller subnits |CITS:[2211660][7836378]|. Most prokaryotic enzymes are different, forming a regular homodimer, although a |FRAME: CPLX-7345 "phosphate-activated glutaminase"| has been characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1474| |CITS: [11786258]|., Two enzymes able to degrade |FRAME: GLN|, |FRAME: GLUTAMINA-CPLX| and |FRAME: GLUTAMINB-CPLX|, were purified from |FRAME: TAX-413997|; no mutants were identified at the time, and thus the identity of the genes encoding them has not been established. Recently, two genes encoding glutaminases with properties resembling those of glutaminase A and B have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS: [18459799]|. Reviewed in Reitzer, L., Catabolism of Amino Acids and Related Compounds,, Module 3.4.7 |CITS: [ecosal]|.

Summary: The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| from |FRAME:CPD-691| requires the attachment of an aminopropanol group to the propionate side chain of the corrin ring. Isotope studies with cultures of microorganisms that biosynthesize vitamin B12 have clearly shown that the amino group and carbon chain of this part of cobalamin are both, derived from |FRAME: THR| |CITS: [13416277]|., Initial work suggested that |FRAME: 1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| might be formed from L-threonine by sequential action of two separate enzymes, namely |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.103| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.75| |CITS: [4577583]|. These two enzymes have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-83333| and were shown to catalyze the proposed reactions in vitro |CITS: [359547]|. The second enzyme was later shown to be identical with glycerol dehydrogenase |CITS: [3920199]|., At the time, it was proposed that |FRAME: 1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| is the substrate for the |FRAME: MONOMER-13228 CbiB| enzyme, originally proposed to convert |FRAME:CPD-691| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| |CITS: [9446573]|., Suprisingly, a few years later a |FRAME: TAX-90371| mutant blocked in |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| biosynthesis was found to be not defective in either of these two enzymes. That observation lead to the discovery of an alternative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5443|). Characterization of the alternative pathway suggested that the actual substrate for the |FRAME: MONOMER-13228 CbiB| enzyme is the phosphorylated form, |FRAME: R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE|, and that the product of CbiB is |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P| |CITS: [9446573]|., If indeed |FRAME: R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE| is the substrate for |FRAME: MONOMER-13228 CbiB|, the pathway shown here requires a phosphorylation step. As such a kinase has not been found yet, it is doubtful whether this pathway is important in vivo for cobalamin biosynthesis.

Summary: All plants store carbohydrates in the form of sucrosyl oligosaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-1099| and |FRAME: CPD-170|. Sucrosyl oligosaccharides are defined as oligosaccharides synthesized by the action of a glycosyl transferase that mediates the transfer of a glycopyranosyl residue to either the glucopyranosyl or fructofuranosyl moiety of sucrose, and represent a large portion of primary oligosaccharides in plants. They are differentiated from secondary oligosaccharides which are generated by the hydrolysis of higher oligosaccharides, polysaccharides or heterosides. For review, see |CITS:[KANDLER82]|)., Members of the |FRAME: TAX-3568|, however, lack |FRAME: CPD-170| and accumulate other sucrosyl oligosaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-12462|, |FRAME: CPD-12463| and |FRAME: CPD-12464|. |FRAME: CPD-12463 Stellariose| was isolated and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-13274|, and NMR studies showed that it is a pentasaccharide, while |FRAME: CPD-12464| is a tetrasaccharide |CITS: [18855444]|. , |FRAME: CPD-12464 Mediose| is a novel tetrasaccharide isolated and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-13274|. In vitro experiments show that |FRAME: CPD-12462| and |FRAME: CPD-12464| are both synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-1099|. Experiments with partially purified extracts confirmed that the same enzyme synthesizes both |FRAME: CPD-12464| and |FRAME: CPD-12463| |CITS: [20452631]|., In vitro studies showed that the pentasaccharide |FRAME: CPD-12463| can not be synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-1099| alone, and it has been hypothesized that both |FRAME: CPD-1099| and |FRAME: CPD-12462| are required for the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12463|. This hypothesis was supported by experiments conducted with a partially purified extract |CITS: [20452631]|.

Thousands of nonsteroidal triterpenes have been identified, though functions for specific compounds, remain to be determined. Summary: Note that the quinolone compounds in this pathway and in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6661| exist in tautomeric forms (as indicated on their respective compound display pages). The forms shown on this page were suggested to be predominant in the physiological pH range (see |CITS: [20738404]|, Fig. 2). However, in some publications and databases they are shown in the non-physiological tautomeric form (reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|)., General Background, Microorganisms, plants and animals produce many types of quinolone compounds. Bacteria produce a variety of 2-alkylquinolones some of which have antimicrobial properties, or act as quorum sensing molecules (see below). Chemically synthesized quinolone antibiotics that contain a 3-carboxy group, such as |FRAME: CPD-12843|, are well known (reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|)., In bacteria, small diffusible extracellular signal transduction molecules can control a cell density-dependent process known as quorum sensing. In the opportunistic human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287| the biosynthesis of virulence factors and the generation of biofilm are under quorum sensing control. In addition to quorum sensing based on the production of acyl-homoserine lactone signal transduction molecules (see |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones| and pathway |FRAME: PWY-6157|, |FRAME: TAX-287| produces a family of 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines one of which is the |FRAME:TAX-286| quinolone signal molecule (|FRAME: CPD-12838|) (PQS) |CITS: [14739337]|. In addition to functioning as an autoinducer, PQS may also function in iron scavenging and in formation of membrane vesicles (|CITS: [18630345] [16872396] [17254955]| and in |CITS: [19788310]|). Targeting specific parts of the PQS biosynthetic pathway for the development of inhibitory compounds may lead to potential therapeutics that decrease the virulence of |FRAME: TAX-287| (in |CITS: [18083812]|). In addition, studies have suggested that the PQS precursor metabolite |FRAME: CPD-12836| (HHQ) also acts as an autoinducer. Reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]| and in |CITS: [16483840]|. , About This Pathway, The |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| utilized in this pathway may be derived from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.27|, or from |FRAME: TRP| via |FRAME: CPD-14736|, as described in |FRAME: TRPCAT-PWY|. |FRAME: TAX-287| has two different anthranilate synthases - one, encoded by the phnAB genes, is dedicated to quinolones biosynthesis. The other, encoded by the trpEG genes, is dedicated to tryptophan degradation |CITS: [17337571][18539738]|., The first step in this pathway is the activation of |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| to its |FRAME: CO-A| derivative by an anthranilate CoA ligase encoded by gene pqsA. The presence of pqsA within the pqsABCDE operon suggested its specific function in activating |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| for |FRAME:TAX-286| quinolone signal molecule (|FRAME: CPD-12838|, PQS) biosynthesis, distinguishing it from the catabolic enzyme for growth on aromatic substrates |CITS: [18083812]|., The next step involves the condensation of activated anthranilate with |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to form |FRAME: CPD-19114|, which is catalyzed by PqsD. The enzyme first binds the anthraniloyl group by transferring it from |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZOYL-COA| to an internal Cys residue, and then transfers it to |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, producing the short-lived thioester |FRAME: CPD-19113|. In the absence of PqsE this compound undergoes rapid spontaneous cyclization to form |FRAME: 4-hydroxy-2-1H-quinolone|. However, when PqsE is present, it removes the CoA moiety, forming |FRAME: CPD-19114| |CITS: [25960261]|., The pathway continues by condensation of |FRAME: CPD-19114| with |FRAME: CPD-195|, a reaction that is catalyzed by PqsB and PqsC. PqsC acquires an octanoyl group from |FRAME: CPD-196|, and attaches it to a cysteine residue (C129). Together with PqsB, the proteins catalyze the coupling of |FRAME: CPD-19114| with the octanoate group, resulting in decarboxylation and the closing of the quinoline ring |CITS: [24239007]|., The final step in PQS biosynthesis involves the product of gene pqsH, an FAD-dependent monooxygenase that hydroxylates |FRAME: CPD-12836| (HHQ) (also referred to as its tautomer |FRAME: CPD-12837|) to form PQS. Mutants in this gene do not produce 3-hydroxylated quinolones, but can produce other alkylquinolones. It is independently regulated by LasR. It has been found that HHQ can be released from cells and taken up by cells, suggesting its function as a messenger molecule (|CITS: [14739337]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|)., In |FRAME: TAX-287| the biosynthesis of PQS and other alkylquinolones involves genes of the PqsABCDE operon. Adjacent to this operon is the phnAB operon encoding a second anthranilate synthase, an alternative to trpE and trpG in this organism, that produces the |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| precursor for this pathway. Also adjacent is gene pqsR which encodes a LysR-type transcriptional regulator of both operons. Genes pqsH and pqsL are each found at separate and different locations on the chromosome and also encode enzymes that may be involved in this pathway |CITS: [2153661]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|., In |FRAME: TAX-28450|, |FRAME: TAX-57975| and |FRAME: TAX-152480|, 4-hydroxy-3-methyl-2-alkylquinolones with a functionally important methyl group at the 3-position have been identified. They are biosynthesized by a homologous hmqABCDEFG operon, the last gene encoding a putative methyltransferase |CITS: [18539738]|.

These enzymes are present in organisms of all domains, the major one being the latter., In addition, some organisms employ a tRNA-dependent transamidation mechanism for conversion of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to |FRAME: ASN| |CITS: [9789001]|., In |FRAME: TAX-562| null mutations in both |FRAME: EG10091| and |FRAME: EG10092| genes result in asparagine auxotrophy, as does a null mutation only in |FRAME: EG10092| under conditions of ammonia-limited growth. A null mutation only in |FRAME: EG10091| has no observable phenotype.

Summary: The polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|) are a group of positively charged organic polycations that are involved in any biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [3157043][4873311][1409623][2185470]|. While it is clear that polyamines are essential for normal cell growth, we still do not fully understand their specific molecular functions in vivo |CITS:[3157043]|. |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| are found in all life forms, and |FRAME:SPERMINE| is found mostly in eukaryotes., |FRAME:PUTRESCINE Putrescine| can be formed either directly from |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| by ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) (see |FRAME:PWY-46|) or indirectly from |FRAME:ARG| by arginine decarboxylase (ADC) (see |FRAME:PWY-40| and |FRAME:PWY-43|). While the ODC pathway was considered the only mammalian pathway for polyamine biosynthesis, recently the presence of the ADC pathway in mammals has been demonstrated |CITS:[11804860] [14738999]|. In higher plants the presence of both pathways has been known for some time |CITS: [11537482]|. In bacteria, both pathways are common, and are often found side by side in the same organism |CITS:[3157043]|. In the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-69014| both this pathway and pathway |FRAME:PWY-6834| may lead to the synthesis of longer chain polyamines, with the latter pathway being the main route |CITS: [20675472]|., In |FRAME:TAX-4932| the pathway is realized via the ODC pathway. |FRAME:SPERMIDINE Spermidine| is formed by |FRAME:YPR069C-MONOMER| which has been characterized through the complementation of a mutant strain (Δspe3). It has been demonstrated that |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| was absolutely necessary for such mutants to restore wild-type growth and sporulation |CITS:[9073064]|. The null mutant Δspe3 accumulates |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| which is an activator of |FRAME:CPLX3O-10520| providing the propylamine moiety necessary to form |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| |CITS:[11526206]|. The formed other product of the reaction |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE| is not only a strong competitive inhibitor for the |FRAME:CPLX3O-10520| but is poisonous for yeast when accumulating in Δspe3 mutants |CITS:[9073064]|., |FRAME:SPERMIDINE Spermidine| is formed by the addition of a propylamine moiety to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, catalyzed by an aminopropyltransferase termed |FRAME: CPLX-6907|. The source of the propylamine group is decarboxylated |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (|FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE|) which is produced by the action of the pyruvoyl-containing enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6906|. The other product of the aminopropyltransferase reaction is |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA), which is recycled back to |FRAME: MET|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Omega-3-Fatty-Acids "ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids"| are essential for proper neuronal and immune function. Deficiencies in these important fatty acids are associated with mental dysfunction, cardiovascular disorders, cancer and other diseases., Resolvins (resolution phase interaction products) are a class of lipid based anti-inflammatory mediators derived from the ω 3 fatty acids |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) and |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA). Those derived from DHA are termed the D-series resolvins |CITS: [15726828]|. These endogenous mediators have a wide distribution in leukocytes, brain and glial cells. , About this Pathway, This pathway has been elucidated by experiments performed using both human glial cells and leukocytes. The depicted pathway is tentative as the complete stereochemistry has yet to be established. , Unesterified DHA is release from phosphatidylethanolamine and converted via a lipoxygenase-type reaction to |FRAME: CPD66-80 "(17S)-hydroperoxy-DHA"|. Following the insertion of a hydroperoxy moiety at either the 4 or 7 position,which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, two intermediates are formed. These are rapidly converted to the 4,5 epoxide and 7,8 epoxide, respectively, resulting in formation of the (17S)-series resolvins |CITS: [12590139][34911767][39236243]|., This pathway, which is expressed in glial cells, plays a role in protecting the brain under ischemic conditions like stroke. Ischemia triggers the release of DHA from membrane phospholipids leading to production of the (17S)-series resolvins and inhibition of leukocytes infiltration |CITS: [15726828]|. The (17S)-series resolvins can also downregulate cytokine expression in glial cells |CITS: [12590139]|. Aspirin activates a similar pathway that produces (17R)-resolvins (see |FRAME: PWY66-395|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1281 "Coenzyme B"| is one of the many unusual cofactors present in methanogens and required for methane formation. Like |FRAME: Factor-420|, |FRAME: CPD-1281| acts as an electron carrier in the metabolism of methanogens (see |FRAME: P241-PWY|)., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| functions as a methyl carrier in methanogenesis, and |FRAME: Me-CoM| has been established as the terminal intermediate of methanogenesis from all substrates (see |FRAME:METHFORM-PWY|). In addition to its role in methanogenesis, different forms of |FRAME: CoM| have physiological roles in methanogens, and are specific enzyme substrates |CITS: [2115763]|., All catabolic processes in methanogenesis lead to the formation of a mixed disulfide bond between |FRAME: CoM| and |FRAME: CPD-1281|, by a reaction in which |FRAME: CPD-1281| reduces |FRAME: Me-CoM|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CH4| and a |FRAME:CPD-1282| |CITS: [12102556]| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|)., The process in which |FRAME:CPD-1282| is reduced back to |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| has been studied extensively. There are two different enzyme systems that are capable of reducing the |FRAME:CPD-1282|. One is a membrane-bound system, encoded by the hdrDE genes, which uses |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE| as its electron donor |CITS: [15168610]|. The other is a soluble cytoplasmic system encoded by the hdrABC genes, which can use several types of electron donors, either directly, or by forming a complex with other enzymes., About This Pathway, Heterodisulfide reductases (Hdr) of the HdrABC class are ancient enzymes that existed in the prokaryotic common ancestor. The enzymes consist of a large HdrA subunit that contains FAD and multiple [4Fe-4S] clusters, a smaller catalytic HdrB subunit, and an electron transfer HdrC subunit. Electrons enter the enzyme at HdrA, and are transferred via HdrC to the active site of HdrB., Many methanogens have two copies of HdrABC proteins. The |FRAME: G-55046|, |FRAME: G-55047|, and |FRAME: G-55048| genes are located in a single operon, while the |FRAME: G-55049|, |FRAME: G-55050| and |FRAME: G-55051| genes are fdound in two operons - the |FRAME: G-55049| gene is located in one operon that also contains a gene encoding a polyferredoxin, while |FRAME: G-55050| and |FRAME: G-55051| form an operon of their own. The hdrA2 gene is a fusion of an hdrA1 homolog and an mvhD homolog (mvhD encodes a hydrogenase electron-transfer subunit) |CITS: [19968794]|. In |FRAME: TAX-2214| transcription of hdrA1B1C1 was observed during growth on methanol and trimethylamine, but not on acetate, and thus HdrA1B1C1 is assumed to be involved only in methanogenesis from methyotrophic substrates in that species. On the other hand, the hdrA2B2C2 genes exhibited reporter activity under all conditions tested |CITS: [19968794]|., Studies with purified HdrA2B2C2 protein found that the enzyme can use reduced ferredoxin as the electron source for the reduction of the |FRAME: CPD-1282|, and it is believed that this is the role the enzyme fulfills in |FRAME: TAX-2214| during methanogenesis from acetate. However, the enzyme can also use |FRAME: Reduced-Factor-F420 "reduced coenzyme F420"| as an electron donor (and HdrA2 can catalyze on it own the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.5.7.2|). When accepting electrons from a reduced coenzyme F420, electron bifurcation occurs at the HdrA subunit, resulting in direction of the electrons towards the reduction of both ferredoxin and |FRAME: CPD-1282| |CITS: [28174314]|. The enzyme may function in its coenzyme F420 electron bifurcation mode during Fe(III)-dependent anaerobic methane oxidation |CITS: [28174314]|.

Summary: |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it accumulates at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant |CITS: [9736747]|., Many organisms are able to catabolize |FRAME: BETAINE|, using it as a sole source for both carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [6406829][3290197]|., The degradation of |FRAME: BETAINE|, as well as its potential precursor, |FRAME: CHOLINE|, has been proposed to exist as a mechanism for osmoregulation in |FRAME:TAX-382| and other organisms. When the bacteria grow at inhibitory osmolarity the enzyme activities that lead to |FRAME: BETAINE| degradation decrease, while the enzyme activities that convert |FRAME: CHOLINE| to |FRAME: BETAINE| either remain constant or increase. In this way a high concentration of |FRAME: BETAINE| can be maintained in osmotically stressed cells |CITS: [Bernard86][3290197]|., The degradation of |FRAME: BETAINE| was originally characterized in several bacterial species such as |FRAME: TAX-266834|, |FRAME: TAX-1665|, and |FRAME: TAX-1720|, and the pathway used by those organisms is described in |FRAME: PWY-3661|., Later studies discovered different enzymes and pathways in other species. The pathway described here was studied in the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [17951379]| and |FRAME: TAX-141390| |CITS: [29703733][32631860]|. Like the other pathway, degradation proceeds by the sequential removal of methyl groups, from |FRAME: BETAINE| (3 methyl groups) to |FRAME: DIMETHYL-GLYCINE| (2 methyl groups) to |FRAME: SARCOSINE| (1 methyl group) to |FRAME: GLY| (no methyl groups). However, the enzymes catalyzing the demethylation events are different., The first methyl group is removed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.251|. This enzyme is composed of two subunits - a ferredoxin reductase component that contains FAD, and a terminal oxygenase component that contains a [2Fe-2S] Rieske-type iron-sulfur cluster and a nonheme iron center., The second and third methyl groups are removed by the bifunctional |FRAME: EC-1.5.7.3|, producing |FRAME: GLY|. This enzyme contains non-covalently bound FAD and NAD(P) cofactors. Its native electron acceptor is a membrane-bound clostridial-type ferredoxin, which transfers the electrons to an electron-transfer flavoprotein (ETF) (ETF transfers electrons to the membrane quinone pool)., Many enzymes that catalyze similar functions have been shown to bind tetrahydrofolate and transfer the methyl group directly to it, forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N| and avoiding formation of the toxic |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. However, none of the demethylating enzymes of this pathway can bind folate, and their combined action results in formation of three |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| molecules., The pathway continues with |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, which catalyzes the reversible conversion of |FRAME: GLY| to |FRAME: SER|, and |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, which catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: SER| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: AMMONIUM|, fedding into basic metabolism.

Summary: Trichothecene are sequiterpenoids characterized by a varying pattern of oxygen and ester groups on a core tricyclic skeleton bearing an epoxide function which is commonly referred to as 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene (EPT) structure |CITS:[Grove07]|. More than 200 trichothecene have been identified from various genera of fungi and classified into four groups according to the substitution pattern on the basic EPT core |CITS:[Ueno80]|. In general, type A trichothecene carry either a hydroxyl group on C-8 (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18505|), an ester at C-8 (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18416| - see |FRAME:PWY-7730|) or bear no oxygen at this position (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18439| and |FRAME:CPD-18430| - this pathway). Trichothecene of type B carry a carbonyl group (keto) on that C-8 position, for instance in |FRAME:CPD-18427| (see |FRAME:PWY-7713|) and |FRAME:CPD-18421| (see |FRAME:PWY-7712|). Trichothecenes of type C have an additional epoxide function (C7/C8) on the core structure, as exemplified in |FRAME:CPD-18597| and finally type D trichothecenes possess an additional ring which has been formed by connecting the C-4 and the C-15 position (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18598|) |CITS:[22069741]|. , Sesquiterpenoids from the trichothecene compound class have been reported to interfere with protein synthesis |CITS:[4521056]|, induce apoptosis in eucaryotes and act as immunosupressors (summarized in |CITS:[23274714]|). Mainly however trichothecene are considered mycotoxins which are phytotoxic |CITS:[22295175]|, contaminate food and animal feed and have been reported to cause vomiting, skin dermatitis, and hemorrhagic lesions |CITS:[3158480]|. The type A trichothecene |FRAME:CPD-18430| has been isolated from Trichoderma arundinaceum (formerly known as Trichoderma harzianum) and found to express modest antifungal activities |CITS:[8201317]| which could be confirmed in other studies |CITS:[21642405] [6353639]|. Moreover, several species of Trichoderma have been applied as biocontrol agents across a variety of crops |CITS:[11770814] [18943537] [21998166] [22562989]| and more detailed studies are carried out to address this complex issue |CITS:[20192757]|. , The biosynthetic cluster for trichothecene biosynthesis (TRI) has been studied mostly in Fusarium species |CITS:[14998528]| where most of the genes appear to be coordinately expressed and regulated |CITS:[12080147]|. It has been demonstrated that the TRI cluster in Trichoderma species has seven orthologs of the Fusarium TRI cluster but TRI5 (trichodiene synthase) of Trichoderma, in contrast to Fusarium, was not included in the main cluster |CITS:[21642405]|. The genes TRI5 encoding for the trichodiene synthase and TRI4 coding for the trichodiene oxygenase are part of the |FRAME:PWY-7714| but have been placed in the general sequence towards |FRAME:CPD-18411| (see |FRAME:PWY-7711|) to avoid redundancy. The junction in the latter pathway is |FRAME:CPD-18383| from which the |FRAME:PWY-7714| branches out., After the spontaneous formation of |FRAME:CPD-18428| from |FRAME:CPD-18383| the subsequent reaction is catalyzed by the 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene 4-hydroxylase forming the respective |FRAME:CPD-18429|. The molecular function of the Trichoderma TRI11 encoded protein differs from the Fusarium TRI11 protein in that the former catalyzes the C-4 hydroxylation whereas the latter hydroxylates the C-15 position |CITS:[21642405 ]|. Although the molecular function of the putative trichodermol acyltransferase encoded by TRI3 remains to be demonstrated, bioinformatics analysis indicates that gene TRI3 is employed to acetylate |FRAME:CPD-18429| with |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| forming |FRAME:CPD-18439| in Trichoderma brevicompactum and acylate |FRAME:CPD-18429| with |FRAME:CPD-18440| yielding |FRAME:CPD-18430| in Trichoderma arundinaceuam. Both compounds are marker compounds of the respective species |CITS:[21642405]|.
