Summary: The pathway is found in both animals and bacteria, but serves different purposes., The Pathway in Animals, There are several degradation pathways for cysteine in mammals. The major route of cysteine degradation is most likely the oxidation of cysteine to |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| (see |FRAME:CYSTEINE-DEG-PWY|). However, cysteine can also be metabolized to pyruvate by 3-sulfinoalanine-independent pathways. These involve the cysteine desulfhydrase activity of |FRAME: CPLX-5163| (see |FRAME: LCYSDEG-PWY|), or an initial direct transamination by |FRAME:ENZRXN-13116| to form |FRAME: 3-MERCAPTO-PYRUVATE| (this pathway) |CITS: [3309559]|., Several enzymes catalyzing cysteine transamination have been isolated from mammalian tissues, but the relative or absolute importance of the various activities in vivo has not been established. While much of the activity in liver and kidney homogenates is attributable to mitochondrial |FRAME: ENZRXN-9021|, the contribution of this enzyme in vivo is unclear, since the Km for cysteine is 22 mM |CITS: [7113743]|, a value about 100-fold greater than its physiological concentration., |FRAME: 3-MERCAPTO-PYRUVATE|, the product of cysteine transamination, is efficiently converted to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: HS| by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.2|. It is probable that the |FRAME: HS| formed in vivo is ultimately converted to sulfate |CITS: [3309559]|., The Pathway in Bacteria, It has long been known that many bacteria are able to produce |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [3299028]|. However, the physiological role of H2S in nonsulfur bacteria was unknown. A recent report has now shown that production of H2S serves to defend cells from antibiotics by mitigating oxidative stress |CITS: [22096201]|., This pathway is one of two pathways for hydrogen sulfide biosynthesis. Neither of the two activities have been shown biochemically for the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzymes. The function of |FRAME: ASPAMINOTRANS-DIMER "AspC"| as a cysteine transaminase is hypothesized based on sequence similarity to mammalian enzymes. The function of |FRAME: EG11600-MONOMER "SseA"| was determined based on the mutant phenotype of an sseA null mutant, which does not produce hydrogen sulfide |CITS: [22096201]|.

Summary: General Background, ||FRAME: Opines Opines| are a large family of low molecular weight compounds. The vast majority of opines are secondary amine derivatives resulting from the reduction of the imine formed by condensation of an amino acid, either with a keto acid or a sugar. Opines from the |FRAME: CPD-308| family are formed when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| serves as the keto substrate in the condensation reaction, while those of the |FRAME: CPD-309| family are formed when |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is involved in the condensation reaction. Opines of the |FRAME: CPD-15773| and |FRAME: CPD-26410| families are formed by the condensation of an amino acid with a sugar., A small, separate class of opines is the |FRAME: Agrocinopines agrocinopines|, which are sugar-phosphodiesters (e.g., |FRAME: CPD-15774|, which is a phosphodiester of sucrose and L-arabinose)., While opines are found in marine invertebrates, fungi, higher plants and mammals, they are most commonly found in plant crown gall tumors or hairy root tumors, where they are produced by bacteria of the genera |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379|, respectively. Biosynthesis of opines in crown gall tumors is performed by enzymes encoded by genes contained in T-DNA (transfer DNA), which is part of the Ti plasmid (in Agrobacterium) or Ri plasmid (in Rhizobium). The plasmids are inserted by the bacteria into the plant genome, where they are integrated and expressed. Those opines are used by the bacteria as energy, carbon and nitrogen sources. Each strain of Agrobacterium and Rhizobium induces and catabolizes a specific set of opines, determined by the specific Ti or Ri plasmid they possess. Over 30 different opines have been described., The enzymes catalyzing the condensation of amino acids with 2-oxo acids to form opines are known as opine dehydrogenases. These enzymes are oxidoreductases that catalyze the reversible, |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP|-dependent reductive condensation reaction between an α-keto acid and the α-amino or ω-amino group of an amino acid to form imino acids (opines) and water. They have been classified into several Enzyme Commission (EC) entries depending upon their substrate specificity, as shown here. Studies have shown that opines are synthesized in plant crown gall tumors as a result of infection by |FRAME: TAX-358|, and in some marine invertebrates under hypoxic or anoxic conditions (see below) (reviewed in |CITS: [23644944][10869063][GADEG86]|)., About This Pathway, Marine invertebrates can survive under environmental hypoxic or anoxic conditions, and can undergo functional hypoxia during bursts of locomotion. Under these conditions they use anaerobic energy producing pathways. For example during environmental hypoxia they may use anaerobic glycolysis which terminates with the pyruvate-utilizing oxidoreductases L-lactate dehydrogenase (|FRAME: L-LACTATE-DEHYDROGENASE-RXN "EC 1.1.1.27"|), D-lactate dehydrogenase (|FRAME: DLACTDEHYDROGNAD-RXN "EC 1.1.1.28"|), and/or opine dehydrogenases., These enzymes allow a continuous glycolytic flux during anaerobic glycolysis that results in the production of a constant supply of |FRAME: ATP| by maintaining a low cytosolic ratio of |FRAME: NADH| to |FRAME: NAD| during anaerobiosis. The coupling of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase with lactate dehydrogenase, or an opine dehydrogenase, ensures continuous replenishment of |FRAME: NAD| by these pyruvate oxidoreductases, resulting in dehydrogenation of |FRAME: GAP| and accumulation of lactate or opines as end products (see pathways |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5481|). Thus, in marine invertebrates opine synthesis is a cytosolic fermentation pathway that maintains redox balance during the early response to hypoxia.., During prolonged environmental hypoxia another means of anaerobic energy production is |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| degradation, resulting in the production of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and the mitochondrial generation of |FRAME: SUC|, |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate), and |FRAME: ACET| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-7383|, |FRAME: PWY-7384| and |FRAME: PWY-7389|). During functional hypoxia, phosphagen breakdown can also generate |FRAME: ATP| (see |FRAME: MONOMER-18221|) (in |CITS: [18599075]| and reviewed in |CITS: [23644944][22688819][LIVINGSTO91][GADEG86]|)., In some organisms the presence of lactate could not be demonstrated during hypoxia. In these species (some members of the |FRAME: TAX-33317| and several other phyla of lower marine invertebrates such as the |FRAME: TAX-6073|, |FRAME: TAX-7586| and |FRAME: TAX-6040|) opine synthesis by |FRAME: NADH|-utilizing opine dehydrogenases functions analogously to lactate synthesis by lactate dehydrogenase., Although lysopine dehydrogenase activity (|FRAME: D-LYSOPINE-DEHYDROGENASE-RXN "EC 1.5.1.16"|) has been found in marine invertebrates, |FRAME: CPD-306| has not been identified in this group to date. Among the opine dehydrogenases of marine invertebrates, |FRAME: MONOMER-18218| from the sponge |FRAME: TAX-6062| was found to be structurally unique as compared with the mollusk/annelid type enzyme |CITS: [15914052]|. Some marine invertebrate species are known to possess multiple opine dehydrogenase activities and isoforms, but their biological role remains incompletely understood., Some marine invertebrates maintain large amino acid pools for osmotic balance which can serve as precursors for opines. Opines that accumulate in response to hypoxia are thought to either be excreted from the organism, or remain in tissues such as the body wall and be reoxidized when the organism returns to aerobic conditions. Anaerobic opine production has been suggested to be an advantage over lactate production because opines are less acidic that lactate. In addition, one amino acid is consumed per opine synthesized resulting in an osmotically neutral process (reviewed in |CITS: [23644944][22688819]|).

General Background, |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053 "Panax (ginseng)"|. They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng., Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|., Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to., The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the, minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly |CITS: [Su06]|, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes |CITS: [8923812][11748374]||., Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest., The compounds |FRAME: CPD-9249|, |FRAME: CPD-12102| and |FRAME: CPD-15444| have been shown to have anticancer activity. |FRAME: CPD-12102| inhibited tumor angiogenesis in in vitro studies |CITS: [18781130]| and has inhibitory effect on breast cancer in mice |CITS: [18999937]|. Studies have shown that ovarian cancer metastasis is inhibited by |FRAME: CPD-12102| |CITS: [18959116]|. |FRAME: CPD-15451 "Ginsenoside Rb2"| has inhibitory effects on tumor angiogenesis in mice |CITS: [7522731][8845804]|. |FRAME: CPD-12102| was recently produced as an anti-angiogenic and anti-cancer drug in China. , About This Pathway, Like other saponines, ginsenosides provide protection to the plants from fungal pathogens like trichoderma |CITS: [12946424]|. However certain fungal pathogens like |FRAME: TAX-36331| and |FRAME: TAX-29920| thrive on the ginsenosides in the roots. It appears that Panax plants and soil borne microbe have allelopathic interactions |CITS: [16242739]|. This above pathway shows the sequential deglycosylation of |FRAME: CPD-9250| to |FRAME: CPD-12100| by two ginsenosidases characterized in the fungal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-36331| |CITS: [19818460]|.

Summary: While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]| it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|. The most common mechanism for retreiving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid. In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde. Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols", or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids (fusel acids) |CITS: [15933030]|., Aromatic amino acids, such as |FRAME:TRP|, can be used as a nitrogen source, but not as a carbon source. Following the transamination of |FRAME: TRP| to |FRAME: INDOLE_PYRUVATE|, the 2-oxo acid is converted to |FRAME:INDOLE_ACETALDEHYDE| and eventually |FRAME:CPD-341|, which is excreted from the cell., The first step is performed by either of two aromatic amino acid transaminases. |FRAME: YHR137W-MONOMER| is the main catabolic enzyme, and accepts |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: PYRUVATE| or |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, but not |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, as the amino acceptor |CITS: [6763508][9491082]|., However, a reaction utilizing |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| as the amino acceptor has also been demonstrated, and is likely catalyzed by |FRAME: YGL202W-MONOMER| |CITS: [9491082]|., Once transaminated, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated by either of four decarboxylases, although recent results suggest that the main decarboxylase performing this reaction in vivo is the |FRAME:CPLX3O-71|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: YDR380W| gene |CITS: [15933030]|. The last step can be performed by any of the yeast six alcohol dehydrogenases |CITS: [12499363]|.

General Background, Sophorolipids are extracellular glycolipids secreted by several nonpathogenic yeasts including |FRAME: TAX-75736 "Starmerella bombicola (previously known as Candida bombicola ATCC 22214)"| (an ascomycete) and |FRAME: TAX-106002 "Rhodotorula bogoriensis (previously known as Candida bogoriensis ATCC 18809)"| (a basidiomycete) (in |CITS: [15218385]|, |CITS: [10843082]|). The function of this glycolipid is unknown, but glycolipids such as this are of interest for their biological activities and chemical properties. They are biosurfactants that are potentially useful in medical, cosmetic and chemical engineering applications (reviewed in |CITS: [23475585][23516968]|). Chemical derivatives of biologically produced sophorolipids have been described |CITS: [12839437]|., Sophorolipids are relatively rare. They contain the glucose disaccharide |FRAME: CPD-13242|, which has a glucosyl-β-(1-2)glucosyl linkage. |FRAME: CPD-13242 "Sophorose"| is joined to a hydroxyl group of a hydroxy fatty acid aglycone (in |CITS: [5012313]|). Analysis of the sophorolipids produced by |FRAME: TAX-106002| revealed des-, mono- and di-acetylated |FRAME: CPD-13242| moieties, with the lipid in the free acid form. The majority of the hydroxy fatty acids had a chain length of 22 carbons, with less than 10% containing 24 carbons |CITS: [15218385]|. Sophorolipids may be produced in lactonized, or free acid forms, depending on species |CITS: [20738402]|. An esterase responsible for lactonization has been reported in |FRAME: TAX-75736| |CITS: [24418522]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-75736| sophorolipids were shown to be derived from ω-hydroxy fatty acids and (ω-1)-hydroxy fatty acids, the synthesis of which is catalyzed by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases of the CYP52 family |CITS: [19054129]|, specifically CYP52M1 |CITS: [24242247]|., Gene |FRAME: G-15427| from |FRAME: TAX-75736| was identified by mutant analysis and enzyme assay as catalyzing the first glucosylation reaction in sophorolipid biosynthesis |CITS: [21073653]|. Recombinant enzyme was later produced and its activity confirmed |CITS: [24242247]|. Evidence also suggested that a second glucosyltransferase in this organism independently catalyzes the second step, which was found to be encoded by gene |FRAME: G-34480| |CITS: [21456054][21073653]|. This is in contrast to the findings of |CITS: [6213610 ]| for |FRAME: TAX-106002| which suggested a single multifunctional glucosyltransferase. In addition, a |FRAME: TAX-75736| broad-specificity glucosyltransferase encoded by gene gtf-1 that utilizes sterol or hydroxy fatty acid substrates has been cloned and characterized |CITS: [24566005]|., Earlier work on |FRAME: DIGLUCODIACETYL-DOCOSANOATE| biosynthesis:, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DIGLUCODIACETYL-DOCOSANOATE| in |FRAME: TAX-106002| was extensively studied by Light and co-workers. An in vivo time course of production of these glycolipids in relation to growth phase suggested that the diacetyl derivative is formed first and is a precursor of the mono- and unacetylated forms. This indicated removal of acetyl groups from the diacetyl form (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SOPHOROSYLOXYDOCOSANOATE-DEG-PWY|). The glycolipids disappeared from older cultures, suggesting that they were either incorporated into other molecules, or degraded |CITS: [5075510]|. Radiolabeling experiments also demonstrated that the glucosyl residues are added to |FRAME: CPD-802| after its biosynthesis |CITS: [5075510]|., Glucosyltransferase activity was demonstrated in crude extracts of |FRAME: TAX-106002| by glucose incorporation into lipid soluble form from UDP-[14C]-glucose. Two enzymes were proposed, UDP-glucose:13-hydroxydocosanoate glucosyltransferase and UDP-glucose:13-glucosyloxydocosanoate glucosyltransferase. Acetyltransferase activity was also demonstrated in crude extracts by acetate incorporation into lipid soluble form from [14C]acetyl-CoA. The diacetyl derivative was the major product formed. The effect of culture age on glucosyltransferase and acetyltransferase activities was also studied. The glucosyltransferases appeared in young cultures, with peak activity before stationary phase. They disappeared at approximately the same time, consistent with glycolipid biosynthesis. The UDP-glucose:13-glucosyloxydocosanoate glucosyltransferase activity predominated. The acetyltransferase activity maximum lagged behind the glucosyltransferase activities. Significant amounts of acetylated glycolipid did not accumulate extracellularly until after maximum acetyltransferase activity |CITS: [5012313]|., Partial purification of the two glucosyltransferases using several different steps failed to separate the two activities, which also co-migrated during discontinuous gel electrophoresis |CITS: [5012313]|. Subsequent affinity chromatography methods resulted in purification to near homogeneity without separating the activities. Further characterization of the purified material failed to provide evidence for two separate proteins, suggesting a single multifunctional protein |CITS: [6213610]|. Partial purification and characterization of acetyl-CoA-13-sophorosyloxydocosanoic acid acetyltransferase also suggested that both acetylation activities were inseparable |CITS: [1245481]|. , Micellar properties of the hydroxy acid sophorosides have been investigated |CITS: [1245481]|. Regulation of |FRAME: CPD-802| biosynthesis, and its conversion to |FRAME: DIGLUCO-DOCOSANOATE| by levels of glucose in the growth medium, relative to other nutrients, have also been studied |CITS: [422563]|.

Three bacterial isolates, |FRAME: TAX-166498|, |FRAME: TAX-76114| and, |FRAME: TAX-76115|, all of which are denitrifyers, can degrade ethylbenzene to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, in the absence of molecular oxygen., As denitrifying bacteria they use nitrate as a terminal electron acceptor and reduce it to, N<sub>2</sub>.  All three strains are closely related, and belong to the genus |FRAME: TAX-12960|, in the β-subclass of the |FRAME: TAX-1224|.  |FRAME: TAX-166498| was isolated from, an oil refinery treatment pond |CITS: [8824622]|, and strains |FRAME: TAX-76114| and, |FRAME: TAX-76115| were isolated from freshwater mud |CITS: [7710331]|., The pathway for anaerobic ethylbenzene degradation has been elucidated from studies of, |FRAME: TAX-166498| |CITS: [8824622][10482506][11443088]| and |FRAME: TAX-76114|, |CITS: [Rabus98][10941798][11479712][11294876][12420173]|., Ethylbenzene, similar to many other aromatic hydrocarbons, such as |FRAME: TOLUENE|,, is mineralized via |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| as a transient intermediate., In denitrifying bacteria, |FRAME: ETHYLBENZENE| is dehydrogenated to |FRAME: S-1-PHENYLETHANOL|,, which is subsequently oxidized to |FRAME: PHENYL|. Formation of |FRAME: S-1-PHENYLETHANOL| and, |FRAME: PHENYL| from |FRAME: ETHYLBENZENE| was demonstrated in cell suspensions and cell-free extracts, |CITS: [8824622][10482506][Rabus98]|.  The oxygen atom of the hydroxyl group of 1-phenylethanol and the keto group, of acetophenone are derived from water |CITS: [8824622]|, demonstrating the initial step is truly an anaerobic, dehydrogenation reaction and that molecular oxygen is not involved. The subsequent steps, leading from |FRAME: PHENYL| to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| are only supported by indirect experimental evidence., First, growth of |FRAME: TAX-166498| |CITS: [8824622]| and |FRAME: TAX-76114| |CITS: [10941798]| on ethylbenzene and, acetophenone depended on the presence of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, in contrast to their growth on, |FRAME: BENZOATE|, suggesting that carboxylation is involved in the mineralization of ethylbenzene and acetophenone,, but not benzoate., Second, ethylbenzene- and acetophenone-metabolizing suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-166498| cells transiently, formed and consumed an unknown compound, which exhibited a similar UV-visible, spectrum to acetophenone, suggesting that it shares some features with acetophenone. Summary: Flavonoids represent a highly diverse class of plant secondary metabolites. The basic chemical structure of flavonoids is a C15 skeleton which consists of two aromatic rings linked by a C3 chain. About 9000 compounds have been identified so far |CITS: [16137727]|. They are involved in a wide range of biological processes in higher plants such as UV protection, flower coloration, and antimicrobial activity |CITS: [11130659]|. They also have demonstrated antioxidant and anticancer properties |CITS: [12224601]| |CITS: [18645020]|., Flavones, Flavones are a class of flavonoids synthesized directly from flavanones. Flavone formation in various tissues of a wide range of higher and lower plant species is catalyzed by a flavone synthase which belongs to the plant cytochrome P450 superfamily |CITS: [18645020]|. The flavones can be classified into several subgroups based on (i) hydroxylation, (ii) O-methylation, (iii) C-methylation, (iv) isoprenylation, or (v) methylenedioxy substitutions., Most of the flavonoids, including flavones such as |FRAME:CPD-431| occur as glycosides. Glycosylation increases the chemical stability, bioavailability and bioactivity |CITS:[10973093]| of flavonoids and potentially improves their intrinsic pharmacological properties for human health |CITS:[12055336]|. The formation of |FRAME:CPD-14824| is catalyzed by a flavonoid 1,6-glucosyltransferase characterized from |FRAME:TAX-4058| which adds |FRAME:GLC| to the |FRAME:GLC| attached to the A-ring 7-O-position of |FRAME: APIGENIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCOSIDE|  yielding the corresponding gentiobioside, hence contributing yet another structural variety of apigenin glycosides as displayed in the pathway |CITS:[19561332]|.

Enteric bacteria must be able to survive extremely acidic conditions in order pass through the, stomachs of their hosts.  |FRAME:TAX-562| contains acid resistance systems in order to maintain, an internal pH of about 4.0 to 5.0 in a highly acidic environment with a pH of 2.0 to 2.5.  Acid, resistance system 3 (AR3) is the arginine-dependent acid resistance system which couples, the transport activity of an arginine:agmatine antiporter, AdiC, with arginine decarboxylase, AdiA. , AdiC functions by exchanging external arginine for internal agmatine.  Arginine is imported into, the cell through AdiC.  Within the cell arginine is decarboxylated by AdiA to agmatine, releasing, CO<sub>2</sub> and replacing it with a proton.  Agmatine is then exported through AdiC. , This effectively consumes protons within the cytoplasm, raising the pH.  An additional effect, of the acid resistance systems that may be more important for survival is a reversal of the, membrane potential such that a build-up of positive charges within the cell due to influx of protons, and increased agmatine concentrations will counteract proton influx beyond a certain limit. , ClC chloride channels provide a control mechanism to help maintain appropriate membrane, potential by mediating chloride import coupled to proton export.  AR2 is more efficient than AR3, or AR4 as a mediator of acid resistance at low pH. |CITS:[15494746],[12964244]|

Summary: Cinchona alkaloids are a group of 35 alkaloids occurring in the bark of |FRAME: TAX-43462| trees. General Background, |FRAME: Strigolactones Strigolactones| are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi., The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels |CITS: [17780042]|., Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| |CITS: [Hauck92]|, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| |CITS: [Mueler92]| and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) |CITS: [Yokota98]|., The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis |CITS: [15944687]|., The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone |CITS: [Mosse73]|., Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interaction between the fungi and the roots., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14652| is produced from the common intermediate |FRAME: CPD-14651| (see |FRAME: PWY-8606|) is a reaction catalyzed by a cytochrome P450, CYP722C, which has been characterized from cotton (|FRAME: TAX-29729|). The enzyme introduces a hydroxy group at position 18, which results in spontaneous loss of a water molecule and cyclization to form |FRAME: CPD-14652| |CITS: [32306106]|., Note that is some other plants, such as |FRAME: TAX-4081| and |FRAME: TAX-3917|, CYP722C continues to catalyze an additional oxidation reaction, generating |FRAME: CPD-28129|, which spontneously forms |FRAME: CPD-14657| (see |FRAME: PWY-8604|).

General Backround, Polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME:SPERMINE|), a group of positively charged small molecules present in virtually all living organisms, have been implicated in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [4873311][3157043][2185470][1409623]|. Although polyamines are clearly necessary for optimal cell growth, a surplus of polyamines can cause inhibition of growth and protein synthesis |CITS: [8223591]|, and thus a balance is desired between the production and breakdown of polyamines. Several metabolic pathways for the degradation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| are known., About This Pathway, This pathway is very similar to |FRAME: PUTDEG-PWY|, which was found in |FRAME: TAX-83333| and, |FRAME: TAX-548|., However, while the putrescine transaminases found in those organisms use, |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| as the amino group acceptor, the enzymes from organisms that, possess this pathway use |FRAME: PYRUVATE| as the preferred acceptor |CITS: 12081945[]|., |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, the product of the transamination, is then oxidized to, generate |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, or GABA,, which is further degraded into |FRAME: SUC| by the |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY| pathway.

Summary: Glandular trichomes found on the surface of leaves, stems and flowers are known to secrete specialized metabolites involved in the defense system of plants |CITS:[18476873]|. Ayclsugars, i.e. ayclsucroses (summarized in |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)|) and acylglucoses |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| are characteristic specialized metabolites found predominantly in the Solanaceae family |CITS:[21098679]| and may account for up to 20% of the leaf dry weight |CITS:[16664099]|., Those compounds have been shown to exhibit a broad-range of insecticidal properties |CITS:[Hawthorne92] [18807203] [Maluf10] [Leckie12]| which include interacting with phytohormones |CITS:[21068365]|, feeding behaviors of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94] [Liedl95]| and serving as food source for pest larvae, e.g. in Nicotiana plants |CITS:[Severson85]| causing a certain volatile profile that attracts the larvae predators |CITS:[21518882]|. Acylsugars have also found applications in the food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical industries where they are used as nonhazardous additives |CITS:[Hill99]|., Tetraacylsucroses (this pathway) and triacylsucroses (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-10 triacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) are the major acylsucroses accumulating in the cultivated tomato Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[22988115] [24772058]| and are dependent on the precursor flux from monoacylated (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-8 monoacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) via diacylated (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-9 diacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) intermediates. Research on these specialized metabolites of the Solanaceae family has been intensified because of the widespread occurrence throughout the family, acylsugar diversity and geographical distribution which reflects acyl pattern on the |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold |CITS:[20113441] [Leckie14]|. The latter is especially obvious in wild species of Solanum (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) |CITS:[Shapiro94] [23054567]|. One of the research focus points is the elucidation of respective acylsugar pathways which will eventually allow conferring beneficial properties (for instance stress tolerance) |CITS:[25064008]| of wild species, e.g. Solanum pennellii to cultivated Solaneceae species such as Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[Lawson97]|, potato or Petunia |CITS:[Chortyk97]|. , Investigation of overlapping regions on chromosome 1 of introgression lines of Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum pennellii enabled to identify a gene, i.e. ASAT4, formerly referred to as AT2 |CITS:[22988115]|, which encodes for an acyltransferase of the BAHD family |CITS:[16616872]|. The molecular function of the ASAT4 encoded protein could be demonstrated via virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS), RNAi transformed Solanum lycopersicum plants and functional complementation of Solanum pennelliii introgression lines lacking the ASAT4 gene. Moreover, heterologous expression of ASAT4 (AT2) in the yeast Pichia pastoris resulted in a recombinant protein which was able to utilize |FRAME:ACETYL-COA acetyl-CoA| as acyl donor forming |FRAME:CPD-19057 sucrose-2-acetyl-3-decanoyl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate| from |FRAME:CPD-19055 sucrose-3-decanoyl-4-isoveleroyl-3'-isovalerate|, |FRAME:CPD-19058 sucrose-2-acetyl-3-isobutanoyl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate| from |FRAME:CPD-19054 sucrose-3-isobutanoyl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate|, |FRAME:CPD-19050 sucrose-2-acetyl-3-lauroyl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate| from |FRAME:CPD-19047 sucrose-3-lauroyl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate| and also |FRAME:CPD-19049 sucrose-2-acetyl-3-(2-methyl)butyryl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate| from |FRAME:CPD-19048 sucrose-3-(2-methyl)butyryl-4-isovaleroyl-3'-isovalerate| |CITS:[22988115]|. The latter experiment was confirmed via an in vitro experiments with all four acyltransferases (ASAT1-4) in the assay which produced the main acylsucrose metabolites found in Solanum lycopersicum M82 when fed with various acyl-CoA's |CITS:[26715757]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-10247 Sulfoquinovose| is a major component of organo-sulfur compounds in nature |CITS: [428677]|. It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes |CITS: [15012227][17334828]|., Bacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated, and multiple degradation pathways have been described |CITS: [Liu21]|., About this pathway, The enzymes involved in this pathway were initially identified by analysis of differences in the proteomes of |FRAME: TAX-562| cultures grown with glucose vs. sulfoquinovose |CITS: [24463506]|., |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.199| catalyzes the hydrolysis of terminal non-reducing sulfoquinovoside residues in sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerides and sulfoquinovosyl glycerol, releasing the α anomer of sulfoquinovose |CITS: [26878550][30276262]|., |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.31| catalyzes the initial isomerization of |FRAME: CPD-10247| to |FRAME: CPD-16501|. |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.184| phosphorylates |FRAME: CPD-16501| to |FRAME: CPD-16502|, which is cleaved by |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.57|, to form |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: CPD-18717|. |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.373| reduces |FRAME: CPD-18717| to |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| (DHPS) in an NADH-dependent reaction. , The final products of this pathway are |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, which powers the cell via |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS|, and |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate DHPS|, which is excreted and can be further degraded by other bacteria.

|FRAME:TAX-358| is a soil organism and plant pathogen. It contains a tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid , which mediates formation of crown galls on many dicotyledonous plants. The organism is an , α-proteobacterium and a member of the family Rhizobiaceae. It metabolizes plant sugars found in the , rhizosphere, including glucose, fructose, sucrose, ribose, xylose, xylulose and lactose |CITS: [11743193]|., Bacterial formation of 3-ketoglycosides from disaccharides was first described and studied by , Bernaerts and De Ley |CITS: [13799610][13799611]|. The production of 3-ketolactose has been considered , characteristic of |FRAME:TAX-357| biovar 1 strains |CITS: [7581688]|, although |FRAME:TAX-13687| species , have also been reported to produce this compound |CITS: [Sakane95]|. 3-Ketoglycosides are useful substrates in , chemical engineering |CITS: [8180983]|. , Hexopyranoside: cytochrome c oxidoreductase (D-glucoside 3-dehydrogenase) which catalyzes the formation , of 3-ketolactose in |FRAME:TAX-358| has been purified and , characterized |CITS: [6038493]|, |CITS: [5726844]|. An enzyme hydrolyzing α-3-ketoglucosides, such as , 3-ketosucrose, has also been purified from A. tumefaciens |CITS: [5438043]|. In addition, partial purification , and characterization of two 3-ketoglucose oxidoreductase enzymes from A. tumefaciens has been , reported |CITS: [4144143]|. All three enzymes have been purified from A. tumefaciens strain , IAM 1525 |CITS: [6038493]|, |CITS: [5438043]|, |CITS: [4144143]|. , The genome sequence of |FRAME:TAX-358| C58 (biovar 1) has been determined and , analyzed |CITS: [11743193][11743194]|. Evidence was found for TCA cycle, glycolysis, and Entner-Doudoroff , pathways for carbohydrate metabolism. Many ABC transporters were identified, with 53 ABC transport systems , predicted for sugars |CITS: [11743193]|. Routes for the metabolism of sucrose, a major plant sugar, were identified as: , an α-glucosidase utilization operon, agl; an orphan α-glucosidase and a sucrose hydrolase; , and the unique periplasmic oxidation of sucrose to 3-ketosucrose, followed by transport into the cytoplasm and , cleavage to 3-ketoglucose and fructose. However, enzymes involved in 3-keto sugar metabolism were not , identified due to lack of homologs for comparison |CITS: [11743194]|., A model for sucrose metabolism by conversion to 3-ketosucrose in |FRAME:TAX-358| biotype 1 , (biovar 1) has been proposed |CITS: [9210346]|. In it, sucrose is transported into the periplasm where , 3-ketosucrose is formed by D-glucoside 3-dehydrogenase. It then enters the cytoplasm where it is hydrolyzed , by α-3-ketoglucosidase to 3-ketoglucose and fructose. The 3-ketoglucose can be converted to glucose , by 3-ketoglucose reductase. The model was based on the ability of a plasmid carrying |FRAME:TAX-357| , genes for a 3-ketoglycoside pathway for sucrose metabolism to confer a sucrose utilizing phenotype in , an |FRAME:TAX-562| sucrose negative mutant grown on sucrose. The authors stated that lactose was also converted , to its 3-ketoglycoside derivative. The plasmid also complemented an |FRAME:TAX-357| strain with a , D-glucoside 3-dehydrogenase negative mutation, restoring its ability to make 3-ketoglycosides. Although the , significance of the 3-ketosucrose pathway is unclear, the authors suggest that it may have a role in selectively , maintaining sucrose metabolism genes when the organism is in a soil, rather than plant environment. Or, it may , be part of a general mechanism for glycoside metabolism |CITS: [9210346]|. Catabolism of glucose in A. tumefaciens was found to be oxidative, involving the Entner-Doudoroff pathway , and pentose cycling reactions, as well as the TCA and glyoxylic acid cycles |CITS: [4745418]|.

Summary: General Background, The two primary bile acids biosynthesized in the human liver, |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189|, are further metabolized in the liver by conjugation to |FRAME: GLY|, or |FRAME: TAURINE| to form |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, or |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6061|). These conjugates are almost fully ionized at physiological pH and are therefore described as bile salts. Bile salts are concentrated in the gallbladder and are released into the duodenum upon stimulation by the hormone cholecystokinin. They promote digestion of dietary lipids in the small intestine and are then reabsorbed via the enterohepatic circulation., Intestinal anaerobic and facultatively anaerobic bacteria metabolize bile salts primarily by deconjugation and oxidation of hydroxyl groups. A small proportion of bile acids are not reabsorbed in the small intestine and enter the large intestine where they are metabolized to secondary bile acids such as |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7754|), or |FRAME: CPD-7235| (which is produced similarly from |FRAME: CPD-15189|). These secondary bile acids enter the bile acid pool. In some individuals they can accumulate to relatively high levels and may contribute to the pathogenesis of gastrointestinal diseases. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., Non-intestinal bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [9812981] [19683506]|, or the laboratory strain of the intestinal bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-511145|, also produce enzymes that can catalyze some of these transformations (see |FRAME: 7-ALPHA-HYDROXYSTEROID-DEH-CPLX|)., About This Pathway, Bile salts are deconjugated by bile salt hydrolases as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8135|. The benefit of deconjugation to the bacteria is the subject of a number of hypotheses., In addition, constitutively expressed hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases carry out oxidation and epimerization of hydroxyl groups at the 3, 7 and 12 positions of the bile acid steroid rings. These reactions convert (epimerize) hydroxyl groups from α to β positions via stable oxo-intermediates. Two distinct, stereospecific hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases are required for epimerization, and they may be from the same, or different species of bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-8254| and |FRAME: PWY-8256|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22651 "Roxarsone"| and |FRAME: CPD-24364 nitarsone| are aromatic arsenicals that have been used worldwide as a feed additive for farm animals (particularly poultry). Roxarsone has been used for prevention of coccidiosis, a protozoan disease caused in poultry by coccidian protozoa of the |FRAME: TAX-5800| genus, and nitarsone was used to prevent histomoniasis (blackhead disease, which is caused by the protozoan |FRAME: TAX-135588|). Both compounds have the added benefit of enhanced growth. In 2010 nearly 90% of all broiler chickens in the U.S. were estimated to be treated with roxarsone |CITS: [27735790]|. Roxarsone is excreted from chickens as a mixture of unaltered and partially metabolized species. When the chicken litter is used as a fertilizer or moved into landfills, roxarsone and its metabolites are broken down to inorganic arsenic, and the resulting inorganic |FRAME: ARSENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-763| can be taken up by crop plants or enter the groundwater |CITS: [24461427]|. In addition, the use of these compounds was found to increase inorganic and methylated arsenic species concentrations in poultry meat, resulting in a source of arsenic exposure for consumers |CITS: [22897610][23259671][23694900][26320952][27735789]|. Roxarsone and nitarsone are no longer used either in member countries of the European Union or in the United States, but are still in use as animal feed supplements in other countries |CITS: [23694900]|., About This Pathway, In 2006 it was reported that under anaerobic conditions the nitro group of |FRAME: CPD-22651| is reduced into an amino group, resulting in for mation of |FRAME: CPD-24365| in a process that is biologically catalyzed |CITS: [16719096]|., A 2007 publication described that this degradation is carried out by a bacterial isolate now known as |FRAME: TAX-350688|. The organism, which can tolerate high arsenate concentrations (>40 mM) and readily degrades |FRAME: CPD-22651| within 48 hours, formed |FRAME: CPD-24365| and |FRAME: CPD0-2040| as the main products. The enzymes involved were not characterized |CITS: [17328188][18378595]|. Similar observations were later made for the bacterial species |FRAME: TAX-399804| |CITS: [27366920]| and |FRAME: TAX-211586| |CITS: [29987384]|., More insight into this degradation process surfaced in 2019, with the discovery of the four gene operon arsREFG in the arsenic island of |FRAME: TAX-399804|. ArsE and ArsF are thioredoxin-like enzymes whose combined action results in reduction of the nitro group of |FRAME: CPD-22656|, as well as |FRAME: CPD-24364|, to an amino group. ArsG is an efflux permease that removes the resulting |FRAME: CPD-24365| and |FRAME: CPD-24366| out of the cell |CITS: [31059239]|., As of 2021, the mechanism by which these enzymes are able to reduce the nitro group remains unknown. Neither ArsE nor ArsF are related to classical nitroreductases, which are flavoenzymes that catalyze the NAD(P)H-dependent reduction of the nitro groups on nitroaromatic and nitroheterocyclic compounds and usually generate the hydroxylamino or the amino derivative as the end product. Neither of these two enzymes has a cannonical flavin binding site motif, and instead they contain the thioredoxin cannonical motif., The fate of |FRAME: CPD-24365| and |FRAME: CPD-24366| is not well characterized. It was reported that during long-term incubations under methanogenic and sulfate-reducing conditions both comounds were slowly biologically eliminated by up to 99%, forming |FRAME: CPD-763| and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: ARSENATE| |CITS: [16719096]|.

Summary: Many bacterial species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: ACETOIN| and |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols| via, |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|., In lactic acid bacteria (LAB), pyruvate (which can be formed in large amounts from citrate) is converted into either lactate, by the enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-5241| or |FRAME: CPLX-5242|, or to |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-5243| (α-ALS). , The conversion of pyruvate to lactate requires NADH, so under conditions of low NADH, the majority of the pyruvate is converted to 2-acetolactate. The relative activities of α-ALS and α-ALD in specific strains determine the fluxes and concentrations of the different intermediates in these organisms., 2-acetolactate is an unstable intermediate. In the presence of oxygen it can undergo a spontaneous decarboxylation, producing |FRAME: DIACETYL|.  Once diacetyl is formed, it can be converted to acetoin by the activity of the enzyme |FRAME: ENZRXN-8948| (also known as acetoin dehydrogenase)., Under anaerobic conditions 2-acetolactate is converted directly to acetoin by |FRAME: CPLX-5262| (α-ALD) (see |FRAME: PWY-5939|)., |FRAME: CPD-10353| is often converted to |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| by the enzyme R-acetoin reductase (see |FRAME: PWY-5951|)., There seems to be some confusion concerning the two enzyme activities acetoin reductase and, diacetyl reductase., Initially, they were reported to be catalyzed by two different enzymes |CITS: [13211662]|, and two different EC numbers were issued based on that observation (EC 1.1.1.4 and EC 1.1.1.5). However, later research indicated that at least in |FRAME:TAX-548| both activities are catalyzed by the same enzyme, for which the name diacetyl(acetoin) reductase was suggested |CITS: [5540507]|. Subsequent work supported that finding |CITS: [4350968][2040298][10647818]|. As a matter of fact, the enzyme appears to have a much wider substrate, range than orignally believed, and it has been suggested to rename it L-glycol dehydrogenase |CITS: [2040298]|., This pathway includes multiple decarboxylation reactions, generating |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., This CO<sub>2</sub> is the source of the  "eyes", or holes that certain cheeses, such as Swiss cheese, develop during maturation.

Summary: |FRAME: D-Glucose| is an extremely abundant monosaccharide that is used as an energy source in most organisms, from bacteria to humans. In humans D-glucose is the key source of energy, through aerobic respiration, but other organisms can also metabolize glucose by anaerobic respiration and fermentation., D-Glucose is also used as a precursor for the synthesis of several important substances, such as |FRAME: CELLULOSE cellulose| and |FRAME: CELLULOSE chitin|. Many organisms store glucose as an energy and carbon reserve in the form of polymers such as |FRAME: Starch| and |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|., In addition, D-glucose is often added onto certain proteins and lipids through glycosylation, which is often critical for their functioning., The form of |FRAME: D-Glucose| used in biosynthesis is the activated sugar-nucleotide form, and usually the UDP-derived form |FRAME: CPD-12575|. This common activated form of glucose participates in a variety of enzymatic reactions in the cell, including the synthesis of many polysaccharides (such as |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|, |FRAME: Starch starch|, |FRAME: CPD-3602 laminarin| and |FRAME: CELLULOSE cellulose|), disaccharides (such as |FRAME: SUCROSE| and |FRAME: TREHALOSE|) and a very large number of β-glucosides. Summary: General Background, Nitrogen is a vital building block of amino and nucleic acids, and despite its abundance in the atmosphere is a limiting nutrient in many ecosystems. This is because the dinitrogen molecule can not be used directly for biosynthesis and must be converted to the reduced form |FRAME: AMMONIA|, to become bioavailable. The process of reductive breakage of the nitrogen-nitrogen bond to form two |FRAME: AMMONIA| molecules is called nitrogen fixation, and can be performed biologically only by certain bacteria and archaea that possess the nitrogenase enzyme system (microorganisms that fix atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia are called diazotrophs). This system is is only active under anaerobic conditions as it is extremely sensitive to molecular oxygen., Filamentous cyanobacteria perform nitrogenase activity in specialized cells known as heterocysts, which possess thicker cell envelope that allows reduced oxygen permeability. The heterocysts do not perform photosynthesis, and thus these organisms physically separate oxygen evolution from nitrogenase activity, allowing the filament to perform both processes simultaneously |CITS: [16371161]|. Non-heterocystous cyanobacteria perform these functions altrernatively during light and dark periods, separate oxygen evolution from nitrogenase activity temoprally |CITS: [1620069]|. , While most of the nitrogen-fixing organisms are free living, some exist in a symbiotic relationship with plants. A well known example is |FRAME: TAX-356|, which live within the root nodules of leguminous plants., In non-oxygenic phototrophs such as the purple non-sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1061| no oxygen is produced during photosynthesis, hence they naturally foster the anaerobic conditions required by hydrogenase and nitrogenase during photosynthesis., Nitrogen fixation is accompanied by an obligatory reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|. Of the diazotrophic microbes known to possess this function, some species of |FRAME: TAX-1117| are among the best categorized |CITS: [16371161]|. , About This Pathway, The reaction in this pathway is catalyzed by a multiprotein nitrogenase complex, comprising of a dinitrogenase reductase component and a dinitrogenase component |CITS: [1529353]|. Dinitrogenase reductase transfers electrons from the external electron donor (a ferredoxin in the case of |FRAME: EC-1.18.6.1|, or a flavoprotein in the case of |FRAME: EC-1.19.6.1|) to dinitrogenase. Dinitrogenase is a metalloprotein that reduces dinitrogen in three successive two-electron reductions: nitrogen to diimine, diimine to hydrazine, and hydrazine to two molecules of ammonia and one molecule of hydrogen. , Three types of nitrogenase systems have been described based on the metal content of the second cofactor (they also differ in their protein structures). Type I contains a molybedenum and iron cofactor (|FRAME: CPD-41 "[FeMo]-cofactor"|), type II contains vanadium and iron cofactor ([FeV]-cofactor) and type III contains only iron ([FeFe]-cofactor). Different genes and gene products are associated with the different types |CITS: [11848850]|. All diazotrophic organisms sequenced to date encode an [FeMo]-nitrogenase, but some also have one or two alternative forms. , It has been reported that of the three nitrogenases, the [FeFe] nitrogenase and [FeV] nitrogenase produce more |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| than the [Mo] nitrogenase., The reduction of nitrogen to ammonia is highly endergonic and requires metabolic energy, which is provided in the form of ATP |CITS: [17903205]|. , In addition to nitrogen and protons, the nitrogenase complex can reduce |FRAME: ACETYLENE|, |FRAME: HCN|, and a number of other small molecules |CITS: [11848850]|., About hydrogen production by nitrogenase, The reduction of nitrogen to ammonia is accompanied by the reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [4344006]|. In a pure nitrogen atmosphere, more of the electrons are allocated for nitrogen reduction than for proton reduction and the reaction requires a minimum of 16 ATP molecules to reduce nitrogen to ammonia and hydrogen |CITS: [11875125]|. , |FRAME: TAX-1117| contain an uptake hydrogenase encoded by the hup (hydrogen uptake) genes. This hydrogenase reutilizes the H2 produced by the nitrogenase to reconstitute some of the ATP used during nitrogen fixation., In addition to nitrogen and protons, the nitrogenase complex can reduce |FRAME: ACETYLENE|, |FRAME: HCN|, and a number of other small molecules containing C, N or O multiple bonds |CITS: [11848850]|.

|FRAME: CPD-13832 Methymycin| is a macrolide antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-54571|. It was first reported from two strains isolated from Florence, Italy, and Oswego, New York. A patent was filed in 1952 |CITS: [Dutcher52]|, and the first publication was made in 1954 |CITS: [Donin54]|. Its absolute configuration was reported in 1970 |CITS: [5439234]|., Already in 1963 it has been shown that cultures deposited as methymycin producers also produce |FRAME: CPD-13835| |CITS: [14274878]|. When the picromycin biosynthetic pathway was elucidated after the biosynthetic gene cluster encoding its synthesis was cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-54571| |CITS: [9770448]|, it became clear that the same set of enzymes is responsible for producing both |FRAME: CPD-13832| and |FRAME: CPD-13835|. The cluster contains 18 discreet genes that can be divided into five separate loci: a polyketide synthase (PKS, pikA), a desosamine biosynthesis locus (des), a cytochrome P450 hydroxylase (pikC), a transcriptional activator (pikD), and a resistance locus (pikR)., The pikA gene locus encodes five polypeptides (|FRAME: G-17908|, |FRAME: G-17909|, |FRAME: G-17910|, |FRAME: G-17911| and |FRAME: G-17907|) that together encode a type I modular polyketide synthase. The first four polypeptides consist of a single loading module and six PKS elongation modules. While the first two polypeptides contain two elongation modules each, |FRAME: G-17910| and |FRAME: G-17911| contain only a single elongation module each |CITS: [10713461]|. The fifth polypeptide, PikAV, is a type II thioesterase. In vitro characterization of this enzyme suggests that it functions to remove aberrantly decarboxylated extender units from PKS ACP domains, preventing blockage of the PKS assembly line |CITS: [12368286]|., The picromycin PKS is unique from other known PKS systems due to its capacity to efficiently generate two distinct macrolactone products. Early termination of polyketide biosynthesis at the |FRAME: G-17910| level results in production of the 12-membered ring macrolactone |FRAME: CPD-13831|, while continued elongation through |FRAME: G-17911| results in the synthesis of the 14-membered ring macrolactone |FRAME: CPD-15995| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7421|) |CITS: [10421766][12031664][12733905]|., Both macrolactones are glycosylated at the C5 position with the deoxyamino sugar |FRAME: CPD-13780|, via the activity of the |FRAME: G-17903|-encoded glycosyltransferase, generating |FRAME: CPD-13830| and |FRAME: CPD-13834|, respectively., Following glycosylation, both compounds are either singly or doubly hydroxylated by the same |FRAME: G-17902|-encoded cytochrome P450 hydroxylase to yield several antibiotic compounds |CITS: [9873687][16825192]|. In the case of the 12-membered ring macrolide, the products are |FRAME: CPD-13832|, |FRAME: CPD-13833|, and |FRAME: CPD-15998| |CITS: [11720530]|. In the case of the 14-membered ring macrolide, the products include |FRAME: CPD-13835|, |FRAME: CPD-15997|, and |FRAME: CPD-15996| |CITS: [16724858]|., The unique substrate flexibility of the tailoring enzymes of the picromycin biosynthesis pathway make them a promising tool for the generation of novel macrolide antibiotic compounds |CITS: [19027305]|.

General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common biosynthetic pathways. Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi., Ceph-3-ems are produced by both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while clavams, carbapenems and monolactams are produced by bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|. The pathways for biosynthesis of the clavam (see |FRAME: PWY-5679|) and bicyclic carbapenem (this pathway) antibiotics differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). They are medically important due to their broad specificity and resistance to β-lactamase , enzymes. The biosynthetic pathway for the simplest carbapenem antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-9377| (not used clinically), has been elucidated, but the biosynthesis of thienamycin, a medically important carbapenem produced by |FRAME:TAX-29303|, has been proposed but not fully characterized, although the gene cluster encoding it has been cloned and sequenced. Stable derivatives of thienamycin are produced commercially by total chemical synthesis |CITS: [12725858]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-555 "Pectobacterium carotovorum (previously known as Erwinia carotovora)"| the car gene cluster encoding enzymes and regulatory proteins for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9377| has been characterized |CITS: [15659168] [8939426]| and functionally analyzed |CITS: [Li00]|. In this pathway the initial oxidation of |FRAME: PRO| to |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, or its spontaneously cyclized form |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|, by the products of genes carD and carE remains hypothetical. Along with the co-substrate |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, they are converted to |FRAME: CPD-9369|., Following epimerization and desaturation of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-9371| by carbapenem synthase, the main, product of the pathway is |FRAME: CPD-9377|. Some inactive |FRAME: CPD-9376| is also produced, possibly as an intermediate |CITS: [14677956]|, and may be desaturated to |FRAME: CPD-9377| by this enzyme, as indicated in the pathway. The enzyme products of |FRAME: G-10343|, |FRAME: G-10342| and |FRAME: G-10344| have been crystallized, their structures determined, and their novel mechanisms studied (click on the above enzymes for further descriptions). , In |CITS: [14625287]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15759042]|.

Summary: The conversion of |FRAME: PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| is a key reaction of central metabolism, which links the substrate-level phosphorylation |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| pathway (which ends with the generation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE|) to the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, which accepts the input of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. In addition, acetyl-CoA is a substrate for many biosynthetic processes., Most eukaryotes perform the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate in mitochondria using the NAD<sup>+</sup>-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| (PDH). Eukaryotes that lack mitochondria use instead the oxygen-sensitive enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.1| (PFO), which is localized either in the cytosol or in hydrogenosomes. , The mitochondrion of the photosynthetic protist |FRAME: TAX-3039| is a facultatively anaerobic organelle that produces ATP in the presence and absence of oxygen. However, unlike typical mitochondria it does not use the PDH system but the unusual oxygen-sensitive, NADP-dependent  |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.51| (PNO) for the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate |CITS:[6438078][3110154]|., Under aerobiosis, acetyl-CoA from PNO enters a modified Krebs cycle, which drives oxidative phosphorylation using O2 as the terminal electron acceptor. However, the pyruvate dehydrogenase system is indispensable for aerobic cell growth |CITS: [28463550]|., Under anaerobiosis, PNO is the key enzyme of a unique wax ester fermentation. Acetyl-CoA from PNO is used both as primer and as C2-donor for fatty acid synthesis in mitochondria, consuming the electrons that originate from glucose breakdown.The fatty acids are reduced and esterified to form waxes that are stored in the cytosol. Upon return to aerobic conditions, the waxes are utilized via β-oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation |CITS:[3919646][11319255][28463550]|.

Summary: Genetral Background, In gram-positive bacteria, the ε-amino group of L-lysine in the pentapeptide stem of peptidoglycan precursors is often replaced by amino acid chains of various lengths and compositions., During the cross-linking of the peptide stems of nascent chains of peptidoglycan these amino acids form cross bridges, between L-Lys3 of one glycan thread and D-Ala4 of another thread |CITS: [4568761]|., In enterococci, streptococci, and staphylococci, the enzymes that add the bridge amino acids are membrane-associated, and act on late peptidoglycan precursors that are already linked to the undecaprenyl-phosphate lipid carrier |CITS: [5218655]|., Two types of enzymes catalyze the addition of the cross-bridge amino acids. |FRAME: GLY| and L-amino acids are added by a special type of non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) that use charged aminoacyl tRNAs as substrates. D-amino acids, on the other hand, are added in tRNA-independent reactions |CITS: [4248526][4262567]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-1629| the cross bridge is composed of one |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| residue and one |FRAME: SER| residue. The |FRAME: G-11874| gene encoding it has been identified |CITS: [11083873]|., The enzyme that catalyzes the second step, the addition of an |FRAME: SER| residue, has not been characterized yet.

All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-2208| is one of the few methanogenic species that are capable of methylotrohpic methanogenesis, and can grow on various methyl-containing substrates such as |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME: METOH|, methylthiols and methylamines as a sole energy source., The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., Coenzyme M (CoM) is methylated during methanogenesis from monomethyamine in a reaction catalyzed by three proteins. Using monomethylamine, a 52-kDa polypeptide termed |FRAME:CPLX-7101| (MMAMT) methylates the corrinoid cofactor bound to a second polypeptide, |FRAME: MONOMER-12209| (MMCP). Methylated MMCP then serves as a substrate for |FRAME:MONOMER-12205| (MT2-A), which methylates CoM., The genes for these proteins are clustered on 6.8 kb of DNA in |FRAME: TAX-2208|. The gene encoding MMCP (|FRAME: G-9439|) is located directly upstream of the gene encoding MMAMT (|FRAME: G-9440|). The gene encoding MT2-A (|FRAME: G-9436|), which is not specific to |FRAME:METHYLAMINE|, was found 1.1 kb upstream of |FRAME: G-9439| |CITS: [9642198]|.

Summary: |FRAME:THIAMINE Thiamine| (vitamin B1) and its biological active derivate |FRAME:THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| is synthesized in prokaryotes, yeasts and plants utilizing complex pathways |CITS:[Rapala-Kozik11] [18161008]|. Besides the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| and derivatives many salvage pathways have been evolved to recycle thiamine degradation products from the endogenous and exogenous environment |CITS:[19348578] [16826377] [4591128] [3027234] [2407290]|., Thiaminase II activity has been observed in bacteria |CITS:[15709744]| and fungi, more specifically in cell free extracts of |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS:[3305065]| but its physiological role remained unresolved for a long time. In bacteria a thiamine salvage pathway has been reported in which the key enzyme thiaminase II (TenA) catalyzed the hydrolysis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| and thiamine analogs to form |FRAME:HMP|. The latter represents a precursor for the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| and its phosphorylated derivatives (see |FRAME:PWY-6899|) |CITS:[17618314] [17637774]|., |FRAME:TAX-4932| employs an enzyme, i.e. THI20p which is characterized by unique properties, i.e. the display of both |FRAME:THIAMINE| biosynthetic and degradation activities in one fusion protein. The |FRAME:THIAMINE| degrading property of thiaminase II had been demonstrated in yeast |CITS:[15967475]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7356|) but THI20p was also able to hydrolyze |FRAME:THIAMINE| analogs such as |FRAME:CPD-13578| (see |FRAME:PWY-6899|) or |FRAME:CPD-15776| and |FRAME:CPD-15777| (this pathway) |CITS:[18028398]|. , The pathway depicted above illustrates the ability of |FRAME:TAX-4932| to hydrolyze synthetic antagonists of |FRAME:THIAMINE| which are known to inhibit the growth of yeast by each of the thiamine analogs alone |CITS:[6373358]|. However, when both synthetic thiamines are applied together the production of the potential de novo |FRAME:THIAMINE| precursor |FRAME:HMP| and |FRAME:THZ| increases significantly indicating a hydrolysis of the |FRAME:THIAMINE| analogs. This was not the case when yeast mutants deficient in THI20 (Δthi20) were assayed with |FRAME:CPD-15776| and |FRAME:CPD-15777| |CITS:[18028398]| emphasizing the participation of the thiaminase II in the process as previously reported |CITS:[3305065]|.

Brassica species produce high levels of indole-sulfur phytoalexins - a family of compounds that originate from |FRAME: CPD-1863| (also known as indole glucosinolate). Different subsets of indole-sulfur phytoalexins are produced by different edible crucifers |CITS: [21681321]|. Like |FRAME: Glucosinolates glucosinolates|, indole-sulfur phytoalexins confer resistance to plant diseases and are thought to modulate human health. However, in contrast to glucosinolates, indole-sulfur phytoalexins are produced only following pathogen elicitation |CITS: [19844641]|., A key intermediate in the biosynthesis of indole-sulfur phytoalexins is |FRAME: CPD-19510|, which has antifungal and anticancer activities |CITS: [Sellam07][18026137][33552104][33562611][33792984][35884601][36829581][37683699][37762214][38807976][39846413]|. Labeling experiments demonstrated that brassinin is biosynthesized from indole glucosinolate through an isothiocyanate intermediate |CITS: [Monde94]|., The brassinin biosynthetic pathway has been partially caracterized from |FRAME: TAX-3711| (field mustard) |CITS: [28154137]|. The proposed pathway was verified when brassinin was produced by tobacco leaves coexpressing the |FRAME: TAX-3711| glucosinolate and brassinin biosynthetic genes |CITS: [28154137]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TETRACHLOROETHENE Tetrachloroethene| (also known as perchloroethene or PCE) is a common groundwater contaminant. PCE is a federally regulated toxic compound and is widely used as a solvent, making it a serious health concern. The oxidized nature of PCE makes it difficult to degrade via oxidative processes, and its chemical characteristics make it difficult to remove via standard pump-and-treat techniques. Several anaerobic microbes belonging to diverse groups, including methanogens, acetogenes, and sulfate-reducing bacteria, contain reduced transition metal cofactors, such as corrinoids, hemes and cofactor F<sub>430</sub>, which can reductively dechlorinate chloroethenes in a cometabolic process |CITS: [2403257][3223763][1526465][3426224]|., Another group of organisms, called the halorespirators, has been shown to metabolize tetrachloroethene in a process known as dehalorespiration, in which halogenated organic compounds are used as electron acceptors in an anaerobic respiratory process |CITS: [10664879]|. Halorespiration can result in the complete dechlorination of PCE and |FRAME: TRICHLOROETHENE| (TCE) to the benign end products |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9312|. In most cases different organisms specialize in different steps of this pathway. Thus far, only |FRAME: TAX-243164| has been shown to completely dechlorinate |FRAME: TETRACHLOROETHENE| to |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| through anaerobic reductive dechlorination (dehalorespiration) |CITS: [9171062]|., |FRAME: TAX-243164| achieves this utilizing only two enzymes: |FRAME: EC-1.21.99.5| (PCE-RDase), which degrades PCE to TCE, and |FRAME: EC-1.21.99.M1| (TCE-RDase), which performs all the other steps of the pathway. However, TCE-RDase has a very low activity using |FRAME: DICHLOROETHENE| and |FRAME: VINYL-CHLORIDE| (vinyl chloride, or VC) as substrates, and is apparently catalyzing these reductions as a slow, cometabolic reaction (the reaction rate in μmol/min/mg is 5.2 for TCE but only 0.036 for VC) |CITS: [11097881]|. This phenomenon poses a problem for the treatment of contaminated sites, as it results in the accumulation of |FRAME: VINYL-CHLORIDE|, which is the most toxic compound of all the chloroethenes. The problem can be alleviated by other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-311424|, which have a dedicated |FRAME: EC-1.21.99.M2|, which reduces VC and all dichloroethene (DCE) isomers at a high rate |CITS: [15294827]|., All of these enzymes are inhibited by the addition of iodoalkanes, and this inhibition is reversed by exposure to light, indicating the presence of corrinoid cofactors. In addition, most (but not all) of these enzymes have been shown to contain at least one [4Fe4S] cluster.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain. Recent, findings suggest that GABA has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well |CITS: [15003233]|. In animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: GLUTDECARBOX-RXN "glutamate decarboxylase"|., The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|. Different variants of both enzymes are known. The amino-group acceptor for the transamination can be either |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|) or |FRAME:PYRUVATE| (e.g. in the plant |FRAME: ORG-5862| |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|). Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+., The action of glutamate decarboxylase, γ-aminobutyrate aminotransferase and succinate semialdehyde, dehydrogenase, combined, defines a short pathway known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. , While there is no evidence for a special role for GABA in bacteria, the capability to degrade it exists in many strains. GABA is present in the environment as a product of plant and animal tissue decay, and many bacteria can synthesize GABA as an intermediate in the degradation of putrescine (see |FRAME: Putrescine-Degradation "putrescine degradation"|). , The first indication for a bacterial pathway for GABA degradation was found in |FRAME: TAX-294|, |CITS:[13654294][13654295]|. While some organisms, like |FRAME: TAX-294|, can grow on GABA as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, others, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, can grow on it only as a nitrogen source |CITS: [8951816][12123465]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| is a neurotransmitter inhibitor and is known to lower the blood pressure in humans |CITS: [12627188]|. The foods containing |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| or GABA receives a lot of attention due to their known human health benefits. Wheat germ, wine and chocolate are some of the food products containing |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|. Several plants synthesize GABA under stress conditions such as anaerobic conditions, low pH, low or high temperatures, darkness, and mechanical manipulation., GABA in plants provides protection against oxidative stress, and is also involved in pollen growth and development. |FRAME: TAX-4081| plants have relatively higher levels of GABA |CITS: [17955994]|, the molecular mechanism underlying GABA accumulation and catabolism is only now being revealed with several enzymes in this pathways being cloned and characterized |CITS: [18713763]|., It is currently assumed that the main GABA transaminase in plants utilizes pyruvate rather than 2-ketoglutarate. In |FRAME: TAX-3702|, only the |FRAME: AT3G22200-LER| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: PYRUVATE|-dependent transminase (GABA-TP), have been isolated. In an in vitro study, recombinant Arabidopsis GABA-TP used pyruvate and glyoxylate but not 2;-ketoglutarate as an amine acceptor |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|. The GABA contents in flowers of an Arabidopsis GABA-TP-disrupted mutant were 100-fold higher than those measured in wild-type plants |CITS: [12859897]|., Transaminase activity has also been studied in soybean seeds, rice roots, tobacco leaves, radish mature leaves, tomato leaves and potato tubers, and in all of these cases, pyruvate-dependent activities were 1.2-19 times higher than 2-ketoglutarate-dependent activities |CITS: [16658005][Reggiani88][16663565][Shelp95]|., The dehydrogenases studied from plants so far appear to prefer NAD |CITS: [18713763]|.
