Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| (phytate, phytic acid) is one of the most prevalent forms of phosphorylated inositols in the eukaryotic cell, with a total concentration of 15-100 μM |CITS:[3426614][1684044][8435066]|. It's cellular distribution is not completely known - some of it is soluble, some is "wall-papered" around membranes, while some is bound to proteins |CITS: [9838040]|. In plant seeds, large amount of phytate are complexed with cations and deposited as globular inclusions in membrane-bound storage bodies |CITS: [15700415]|., The compound has been proposed to have a number of signaling roles, including regulation of insulin exocytosis |CITS: [9114007]|, regulation of nuclear mRNA export |CITS:[10390371][10683435]|, binding of the clathrin assembly proteins AP2 and AP3 |CITS: [1849645][1371119]|, inhibition of clathrin cage assembly |CITS: [7814377][7829485]|, and inhibition of serine and threonine protein phosphatases that are thought to regulate L-type Ca2+ channels |CITS: [9334307]|., About This Pathway, Unlike the phytate biosynthetic pathways found in yeast and in Drosophila, which proceed directly from |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| by a series of successive phosphorylations (see |FRAME: PWY-6361|), the mammalian pathway uses a detour: |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is first isomerized to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| (via |FRAME: CPD-506|) |CITS: [3010126]|, and further phosphorylation proceeds from there |CITS: [15531582]|., The multiplicity of enzymes that catalyze inositol phosphate transformations and the lack of in vivo studies have made determining the pathway difficult. However, as more in vivo results became available, and as the catalytic efficiencies of the enzymes with different substrates were determined, it became clear that the main tetra-phosphate intermediate in the human pathway is |FRAME: CPD-505| |CITS: [12223481]|, supporting the pathway presented here |CITS:[2584198][15531582]|., It is still not clear whether this pathway exists in plants. One of the key enzymes, |FRAME: RXN-8730 "myo-inositol-1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate 5-phosphatase"|, has not been identified in plants. Yet, |FRAME:AT5G16760-MONOMER| that catalyzes a reaction that appears to be unique to this pathway has been found in |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [12226109]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME:D-perosamine| is a 4-aminodeoxy sugar that is found in glycoconjugates of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. An example for its use in Gram-positive bacteria is the antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-24119| of |FRAME: TAX-1902| |CITS: [5980011][5788396]|. In Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: D-perosamine| is a main constituent of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) in several genera, including |FRAME: TAX-127906| |CITS: [10880560]|, |FRAME: TAX-235|, |CITS: [3114617]| and |FRAME: TAX-83334| |CITS: [8890241]|., In |FRAME: TAX-127906| the O-antigen is a homopolymer of |FRAME: D-perosamine|, which is substituted via the amino group with a 4-carbon aliphatic acid, |FRAME: CPD-25708| (referred to in the literature as 3-deoxy-L-glycero-tetronic acid) |CITS: [8422256]|. The form of perosamine that is incorporated into the polysccharide is the activated form |FRAME: CPD-9387|, which is biosynthesized from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| in two steps., The |FRAME: MONOMER-13574| and |FRAME: CPLX-7538| enzymes that catalyze these reactions have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-127906| |CITS: [11479276]|. The |FRAME: G-10345| and |FRAME: G-10346| genes that encode the two enzymes, respectively, have been subcloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the proteins characterized., Surprisingly, the recombinant |FRAME: G-10345| gene product did not show any activity |CITS: [11479276]|. Since no similar gene is present in the perosamine biosynthesis gene cluster, it is assumed that the protein is active in its native host. The |FRAME: G-10346| gene product, on the other hand, was active upon cloning and expression in a heterologous host, and was found to catalyze the transamination of |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE| with |FRAME:GLT| to form |FRAME: CPD-9386|, as predicted |CITS: [11479276]|.

Summary: General Background, The dimeric, benzoisochromanequinone antibiotic, |FRAME: CPD1A0-6123|, is an aromatic polyketide. Polyketides have been found to possess extensive biological activities and therefore the actinorhodin pathway has undergone intensive genetic and biochemical studies for several years. The actinorhodin cluster is composed of 22 genes (SCO5071-SCO5092), which, in addition to the genes that encode catalytic enzymes, include genes that encode regulatory (SCO5082, SCO5085) and actinorhodin transport (SCO5083) proteins., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD1A0-6123 Actinorhodin| biosynthesis starts with 8 |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| molecules and the minimal PKS, composed of |FRAME: SCO5087-MONOMER| (KS), |FRAME: SCO5088-MONOMER| (CLF), and , |FRAME: SCO5089-MONOMER| (ACP) |CITS: [8248802]|. The KS and CLF components form a heterodimer |CITS: [1527048]| and create a tunnel that stabilizes the growing polyketide backbone and controls chain length |CITS: [1458809][15286722]|. , The first malonyl group is loaded onto the ACP |CITS: [1453961][16793516]| by either the ACP itself |CITS: [9479478][9862793][16285746][16793516]| or a malonyltransferase from primary metabolism in a phenomenon termed 'cross talk' |CITS: [7608065][9518007][10872449][14966533]|. Once loaded, it is decarboxylated to the starter acetyl group by the KS |CITS: [15286722]| and subsequently bound to KS via a thioester bond. Once KS is primed, a second malonyl group is transferred to the ACP and undergoes a KS-catalyzed condensation with the acetyl starter group. 6 more malonyl groups are inidividually transferred and condensed to the growing polyketide chain in the same manner |CITS: [2583128][2684656] [7814341][16793516]|. The resultant chain is attached to the ACP by a thioester bond., As the chain grows into the KS-CLF tunnel, it buckles, which is believed to initiate the first ring cyclization. Further molecular interactions complete formation of the first ring |CITS: [15286722]|., Following first ring cyclization and with the carbon chain still attached to the ACP, the C-9 keto-group is reduced to a hydroxyl group by |FRAME: SCO5086-MONOMER| |CITS: [2469622][2583128][2394677][McDaniel1993] [8248802] [Fu1994][8169211][15159580][15458634] |. Subsequently, the first ring is aromatized by |FRAME: SCO5090-MONOMER| |CITS: [McDaniel1994]| and then a second ring is formed by |FRAME: SCO5091-MONOMER| via an intramolecular aldol condensation |CITS: [McDaniel1994]|. At this stage the compound is released from ACP, as it was determined that a non-enzyme bound acid is the likely substrate for the next enzyme, |FRAME: SCO5072-MONOMER| |CITS: [15645472]|., |FRAME: SCO5072 ActVI-1| then reduces the keto-group at C-3, resulting in a chiral secondary alcohol |CITS: [7929165][10091691][10805574][15498668]|. A pyran ring is formed with the assistance of |FRAME: SCO5074-MONOMER|, followed by a spontaneous dehydration |CITS: [7929165][10091691][10805574]|. The resulting compound, |FRAME: CPD1A0-6111|, was found to be the best trigger for actinorhodin export via a 'feed-forward' mechanism. |FRAME: CPD1A0-6111|, and to a lesser extent, actinorhodin itself, eliminates the interaction between the repressor, |FRAME: SCO5082-MONOMER|, and the operon, actII-2-actII-3 (SCO5083-SCO5084), allowing transcription of the operon. actII-3 may encode an enzyme involved in the synthesis of a second actinorhodin pigment, γ-actinorhodin, while actII-2 encodes the protein that exports both actinorhodins before their intracellular levels become toxic |CITS: [8636024] [Tahlan2007]|., In the next step the double bond between C-14 and C-15 is reduced by |FRAME: SCO5073-MONOMER|, while |FRAME: SCO5075-MONOMER| assists in formation of the chemically favored isomer |CITS: [7929165][10805574]|. At this point, a two-component NADH:flavin-dependent monooxygenase system comprising the |FRAME: SCO5080| monooxygenase and , the |FRAME: SCO5092-MONOMER| NADH:flavin reductase |CITS: [15297451]| catalyzes the hydroxylation of both the C-6 and C-8 positions of |FRAME: CPD1A0-6112| |CITS: [23601640]|., The last stage, the dimerization to form |FRAME: CPD1A0-6123|, has not been characterized yet.

The glycation reaction, also known as the Maillard reaction as it was first identified by the French chemist L. Maillard, is ubiquitous in nature. The reaction involves the formation of Schiff's bases between reducing sugars (such as glucose and fructose) and biological amines such as an amino acid, which then rearrange to form stable ketoamine products, referred to as amadori compounds., |FRAME: CPD-26024| (F-Asn) is an Amadori rearrangement product that occurs naturally in substantial quantities in foods, particularly after heating |CITS: [Anet57][20837201]|. |FRAME: TAX-90371| can utilize the compound as its sole carbon and nitrogen source. F-Asn was even deemed essential for Salmonella fitness in the inflamed intestine, and reported to be the primary nutrient utilized by organism in that environment |CITS: [24967579]|., Utilization of F-Asn is enabled by the products of the fra locus - a deglycase (|FRAME: STM3601|), kinase (|FRAME: STM3600|), transporter (|FRAME: STM3599|), and asparaginase (|FRAME: STM3598|) |CITS: [28177776]|. This gene cluster is a horizontally acquired island that is not present in |FRAME: TAX-562|. Similar genes were found in only in |FRAME: TAX-544| and |FRAME: TAX-186801| |CITS: [27403719]|., FraB is considered a drug target, since mutations in the fraB gene cause a severe attenuation in mouse, models of inflammation due to the toxicity of |FRAME: CPD-26026| |CITS: [27403719]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain. Recent, findings suggest that GABA has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well |CITS: [15003233]|. In animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: GLUTDECARBOX-RXN "glutamate decarboxylase"|., The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|. Diiferent variants of both enzymes are known. The amino-group acceptor for the transamination can be either |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|) or |FRAME:PYRUVATE| (e.g. in the plant |FRAME: ORG-5862| |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|). Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+., The action of glutamate decarboxylase, γ-aminobutyrate aminotransferase and succinate semialdehyde, dehydrogenase, combined, defines a short pathway known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. , While there is no evidence for a special role for GABA in bacteria, the capabillity to degrade it exists in many strains. GABA is present in the environment as a product of plant and animal tissue decay, and many bacteria can synthesize GABA as an intermediate in the degradation of putrescine (see |FRAME: Putrescine-Degradation "putrescine degradation"|). , The first indication for a bacterial pathway for GABA degradation was found in |FRAME: TAX-294|, |CITS:[13654294][13654295]|. While some organisms, like |FRAME: TAX-294|, can grow on GABA as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, others, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, can grow on it only as a nitrogen source |CITS: [8951816][12123465]|., About This Pathway, This variant of the pathway includes a |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent 4-aminobutyrate transaminase and an NADP+-dependent dehydrogenase., This combination of enzymes has been documented in several bacteria including |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [10564790]| and |FRAME: TAX-511145| |CITS: [20174634]|. In both organisms a secod variant of the dehydrogenase exists; in |FRAME: TAX-106590| an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme, and in |FRAME: TAX-511145| an |FRAME: CPLX0-7687|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-21472 Leinamycin| (LNM) is an antitumor antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-66869| |CITS: [2925527][2621160]|. It features an unusual 1,3-dioxo-1,2-dithiolane moiety that is spiro-fused to a thiazole-containing 18-membered lactam ring, a molecular architecture that hasn't been found in any other natural product., LNM possesses potent DNA cleavage activity via an unprecedented mode of action. Upon the attack of cellular thiol agents at the 1,3-dioxo-1,2-dithiolane moiety, the compound undergoes a tandem rearrangement to form an episulfonium ion intermediate that can efficiently alkylate the N-7 position of deoxyguanosine bases of DNA |CITS: [11080040][21954957][22682923][26071634][29231931]|. This unique mode of action confers potent cytotoxicity against tumors including those resistant to clinically important anticancer drugs, making LNM a promising anticancer drug lead., Total synthesis of LNM has been accomplished |CITS: [Kanda93]|, followed by assorted chemical modifications |CITS: [9871510][10212117][Kanda03]| and generation of functional mimics |CITS: [8639657][12708847]|., About This Pathway, The gene cluster that encodes leinamycin biosynthesis was identified in 2002 |CITS: [12446651]|. The cluster spans 61.3 kb of DNA and consists of 27 genes encoding nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS), polyketide synthase (PKS), hybrid NRPS-PKS, resistance, regulatory, and tailoring enzymes, as well as some proteins whose function is still unknown., The backbone of the compound is generated by a very large non-ribosomal peptide synthase/polyketide synthase (NRPS/PKS) hybrid complex, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107645|, lnmP, |FRAME: G-107646|, |FRAME: G-107647|, and |FRAME: G-107648| genes. LnmQ and LnmP are single-domain proteins. LnmQ activates a |FRAME: D-ALANINE| molecule and transfers it to the peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domain of LnmP |CITS: [17502372]|. LnmI and LnmJ are very large PKS proteins that carry the bulk of the complex's domains. Interestingly, despite the large size of these proteins (LnmI is >466 kDa and LnmJ is >775 kDa), they lack acetyltransferase (AT) domains. The six |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| molecules that are bound by the complex are transferred by the stand alone trans-acting LnmG protein, which consists of a single AT domain |CITS: [12598647]|. The six |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| molecules form a basic backbone, which is methylated at C6 by a methyl group donated by |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| |CITS: [16562841]|, while |FRAME: D-ALANINE| and |FRAME: CYS| molecules which are bound by LnmP and LnmI, respecvively, form the thiazole moiety |CITS: [15112993]|., The |FRAME: G-107649 LnmK|, LnmL, |FRAME: G-107650 LnmM|, and |FRAME: G-107651 LnmF| proteins form a "β-hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HCS) cassette" that is responsible for the introduction of a β-ethyl branch into the C3 carbon |CITS: [19405532][21192727][23320975][33095002]|. Two unusual domains within LnmJ insert a persulfide group into the same atom |CITS: [26240335][34584078]|. Finally, the thioesterase domain of LnmJ cyclizes the nascent chain and releases the first free intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-25389|., The rest of the pathway involves tailoring enzymes that convert |FRAME: CPD-25383| to |FRAME: CPD-21472|. As of 2022, two of them, cytochromes P450s encoded by the |FRAME: G-107644| and |FRAME: G-107643| genes, were shown to catalyze hydroxylations at C-8 and C-4', respectively |CITS: [30070831]|.

General Background, |FRAME: SHIKIMATE "Shikimate"| is a common biosynthetic precursor of many compounds in microorganisms, higher plants, and animals (see |FRAME: ARO-PWY|). As such, it is an abundant compound in the biosphere, and occurs commonly in decaying pant matter |CITS: [14642355][8126417]|., In addition to its biosynthetic role, shikimate can be used by several microorganisms as a carbon and energy source. It is metabolized by two enzymatic reactions to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, a central intermediate leading to complete mineralization (see |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|)., Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of |FRAME: SHIKIMATE|. Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD-dependent enzyme while Gram-negative bacteria use a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: 1.1.99.25-RXN "EC 1.1.99.25"|) |CITS: [3044290]|. The later pathway is desribed in |FRAME: SHIKIMATEDEG-PWY|., About This Pathway, The Gram-Positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1718| grows well with shikimate as the sole carbon source |CITS: [19376919]|., This organism produces |FRAME: CPLX-7981|, an NAD-dependent enzyme capable of using either |FRAME: QUINATE| or |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| as a substrate |CITS: [19376919][18566515]|., The |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE| formed is dehydrated to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:MONOMER-15334| |CITS: [19376919]|., The |FRAME: G-11733| and |FRAME: G-11736| genes, which encode the pathway's enzymes, are present in a single operon that also includes qsuA and qsuC, which encode a quinate transporter and dehydroquinate dehydratase, respectively. The expression of the qsu genes is markedly induced during growth in the presence of either quinate or shikimate, and is regulated by the LysR-type transcriptional regulator QsuR |CITS: [19376919]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"|-containing phospholipids play an important role in the control of cellular functions within eukaryotic cells, being part of the intracellular signal transductions pathways from various regulators, including hormones, neurotransmitters, growth factors, and serum |CITS: [164246]|. When these regulators interact with their receptors in cell membranes, they induce the hydrolysis of certain |FRAME: Phosphoinositides "phosphoinositides"| to produce second messenger molecules., A particularly important reaction is the cleavage of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol 4,5-bisphosphate"|, which produces two important secondary messaengers., One of the cleavage products, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE|, mobilizes |FRAME: CA+2| ions from intracellular vesicular stores |CITS: [6605482][6146314]| while the other product, |FRAME: DIACYLGLYCEROL "1,2-diacyl-sn-glycerol"|, activates |FRAME: HS07962-MONOMER "protein kinase C"| |CITS: [438153][6232463]|, resulting in a variety of biochemical and pharmacological responses. The second messengers derived from inositol phospholipids are crucial for initiation of cellular activation, proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis., Variability in the sensitivity of individual receptors to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is a key factor that determines whether transient fluxes of |FRAME: CA+2| release are destined to remain a localized phenomenon, or instead are recruited to produce calcium waves that sweep across the cell., About This Pathway, |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols "Phosphatidylinositol"| is synthesized from |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL "CDP-diacylglycerol"| and |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| by phosphatidylinositol synthase., This compound can be phosphorylated by several kinases. In this pathway, it is converted by phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase enzymes to |FRAME: CPD-1108 "phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate"|, which is phosphorylated again by phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate 5-kinases to form |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"|. Even though it has been shown that |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| is also synthesized from |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate"| |CITS: [9367159]|, it is generally accepted that the majority of the |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| in mammalian cells comes from |FRAME: CPD-1108 "phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate"| phosphorylation |CITS: [12897244]|., The last step in this pathway, which is the most important, is catalyzed by phospholipase C enzymes. These enzymes, acting in response to receptor activation, cleave |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate"| to |FRAME: DIACYLGLYCEROL "1,2-diacylglycerol"| (DAG) and, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (IP3)., This signal transduction pathway is common to all eukaryotes, and these enzymes are found from yeast to mammals |CITS: [4301226]|. However, while yeast only have one or two isoform for each enzyme, mammals have very many isoforms (not all of which are presented here) that are expressed in different tissues and under different circumstances. The presence of so many isoforms enables the transducton of multiple signals without interference in complex networks of signaling cascades that are not yet well understood |CITS: [18341203]|., For example, humans have at least four isoforms of phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase, four isoforms of phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate 5-kinase, and eleven isoforms of phospholipase C enzymes that belong to at least six distinct classes |CITS: [11395409][12117804][17895620]|.

Avenacins are triterpene glucosides which act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents conferring resistance against soil-borne pathogens and influencing the development of close neighbors |CITS:[10536024] [16995908]|. The occurrence of the phytoalexic avenacins appears to be restricted to the genus Avena which is an expression of a highly specialized defense biochemistry |CITS:[Hostettmann95]|. In general, triterpenes are valued compounds with a wide range of commercial applications and because of that in the focus of metabolic engineering. One of the major goals is to re-introduce lost traits of resistance into cultivated crops |CITS:[22639586]|., As a general rule genes in plant biochemical pathways, unlike bacterial biochemical pathways, have been regarded as unlinked. However, the avenacin biosynthesis appears to be carried out by an avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster which implies a high degree of coordination regarding avenacin synthesis, transport and sequestration, all of which must be precisely orchestrated in time and space between different cell organelles and compartments |CITS:[21876149] [15148404] [21443624] [20040536]|., The formation of |FRAME:CPD-16600| (this pathway) as acyl-donor is critical for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-10678| (see |FRAME:PWY-7473|). It has been demonstrated that the C-21 acylation of the avenacin skeleton is pivotal for the biological activity of this antimicrobial agent |CITS:[20835386]|. , The N-methylation of |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| is the first step in the pathway. This reaction is catalyzed by the anthranilate N-methyltransferase (MT1) which is encoded by SAD9, a component of the avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster promoting |FRAME:PWY-7473| |CITS:[23532069]|. The MT1 protein demonstrated strict affinity towards |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and did not N-methylate any other anthranilate derivatives. Mutants of SAD9, i.e. sad9 were unable to produce |FRAME:CPD-402| as shown by the purple fluorescence indicative for unmethylated |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| which accumulates in sad9 mutants. Co-expression of three SAD gens, i.e. SAD9 (anthranilate N-methyltransferase), SAD10 (N-methylanthranilate glucosyltransferase) and SAD7 (des-acyl avenacin A acyltransferase) demonstrated that those SAD genes are involved in consecutive steps of the acylation of avenacin and that a loss of any of them resulted in enhanced disease susceptibility of the respective mutant |CITS:[23532069]|. The subsequent glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-402| is catalyzed by two glucosyltransferases, SAD10 (UGT74H5) and UGT74H6. SAD10 appears to be included in the avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster but UGT74H6, although catalyzing the same reaction, albeit with lower efficiency, may have other or additional biochemical functions in Avena |CITS:[23258535]|.

Together with |FRAME: YHAO-MONOMER| these two enzymes for a system that enables the organism to grow with |FRAME: CYS| as the sole nitrogen and carbon/energy source |CITS: [35377168]|. , CyuA is very oxygen-labile and functions only under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [28607157]|. Summary: |FRAME: MORPHINE Morphine| is a plant (|FRAME: TAX-3469|, opium poppy)-derived alkaloid and one of the strongest, known analgesic compounds., The presence of opiate receptors in mammalian tissue suggests that endogenous ligands must exist. Other types of evidence, such as an increased urinary morphine concentrations observed in a parkinsonian patient undergoing |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| therapy prompted suggestions for a possible biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: MORPHINE| from |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| in humans |CITS: [1545408]|., The occurrence and/or formation of the simpler alkaloid |FRAME: S-NORLAUDANOSOLINE| has been reported multiple times from human and rodent brain tissue as well as in urine |CITS: [4705752][ 4847815][3605593][8491812][10754228][14697886]|., Following the discovery of opioid peptides, evidence was obtained for the presence of small amounts of morphine, alkaloids in animals. The origin of the endogenous morphine has been a matter of controversy. Studies involving, heavy-isotope labelling experiments have suggested that human cells are capable of synthesizing endogenous morphine, |CITS:[15383669][15937106]|., The first part of the proposed pathway, up to |FRAME: S-RETICULINE|, which is described here, is different from the plant pathway (as described in |FRAME: PWY-3581|). The second part of the pathway, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5270|,, is proposed to be identical between human cells and the opium poppy., The proposed pathway starts with two molecules of |FRAME: TYR|, which have to be converted to the intermediates, |FRAME: 34-DIHYDROXYPHENYLACETALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: DOPAMINE|, respectively., Several routes can lead to the formation of these intermediates: |FRAME: TYR| can be hydroxylated to yield, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE|, which can undergo either decarboxylation to |FRAME: DOPAMINE|, or a possible deamination to |FRAME: 34-DIHYDROXYPHENYLPYRUVATE|,, which, in turn, is assumed to be decarboxylated to |FRAME: 34-DIHYDROXYPHENYLACETALDEHYDE|., In a parallel route |FRAME: TYR| can be decarboxylated to |FRAME: TYRAMINE|, which could then be converted to, |FRAME: DOPAMINE| by the action of an enzyme such as the cytochrome P450 CYP2D6, which has been reported to catalyze this reaction in human polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells |CITS: [16301642]|. However, a subsequent study reported that isolated human white blood cells (PMN and MN) do not transform tyramine by action of CYP2D6 to dopamine and fail to synthesize morphine |CITS: [16670271]|., Once both intermediates are formed, they could be enzymatically condensed to |FRAME: S-NORLAUDANOSOLINE|, which has been observed in brains and urine of different mammals as described above., In order to produce morphine, |FRAME: S-NORLAUDANOSOLINE| needs to be methylated three times to form |FRAME: S-RETICULINE|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: R-RETICULINE|, a key intermediate in morphine biosynthesis. Since the exact sequence of methylation reactions is still not known, they are shown as a single general uncharacterized reaction in this pathway., Injection of |FRAME: S-NORLAUDANOSOLINE| intraperitoneally into mice followed by analysis of urine metabolites revealed the presence of |FRAME: SALUTARIDINE|, an intermediate in the opium poppy morphine biosynthetic pathway derived from |FRAME: R-RETICULINE|. Similarly, injection of |FRAME: SALUTARIDINOL| (which is derived from |FRAME: SALUTARIDINE| in the pathway) was followed by detection of |FRAME: CPD-7710| in the urine. Finally, injection of |FRAME: CPD-7710| resulted in traces of |FRAME: MORPHINE| in the urine |CITS: [20421505]|. , It should be noted that this pathway was proposed based on heavy-isotope labelling and radiotracer experiments, and very few enzymes have been characterized so far. The human cytochrome P-450 enzymes 2D6 and |FRAME: HS08544-MONOMER 3A4| and the rat cytochrome P450 2D2 have been shown to catalyze the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.67| |CITS: [19561069][22641033]|, and the human N-methyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: HS00305| gene has been shown to act on the (R) enantiomers of some benzylisoquinolines including |FRAME: CPD-21515| |CITS: [21093406]|. This last observation suggests that the pathway may proceed via (R) enantiomers, and not (S) enantiomers as shown here.

General Background, Organosulfonate compounds are found in the environment as both natural products and xenobiotics. They are catabolized by microorganisms that utilize the carbon and sulfur moieties. The bacterial catabolism of C2 sulfonates such as |FRAME: CPD-10434|, |FRAME: TAURINE|, |FRAME: CPD-3745|, |FRAME: CPD-10431| and |FRAME: CPD-10246| has been studied (reviewed in |CITS: [12471498]|). |FRAME: CPD-10246| is a widespread natural product found in plants and algae. It is also an intracellular product of the bacterial degradation of plant |FRAME: CPD-10247| (a component of |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL|) and the bacterial degradation of |FRAME: TAURINE| (in |CITS: [20693281]|). , This Pathway, A novel pathway for |FRAME: CPD-10246| degradation has been described in |FRAME: TAX-381666 "Ralstonia eutropha H16 (previously known as Cupriavidus necator H16)"|. The organism can utilize |FRAME: CPD-10246| as a sole source of carbon and energy. This inducible, |FRAME: CPD-10246| utilization (sau) pathway is comprised of a four-gene cluster sauRSTU. Gene sauR is a putative transcriptional regulator of the putative sauSTU operon encoding an acylating dehydrogenase, a CoA ligase and a putative transporter, respectively. It was shown that the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: CPD-10246| to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| involves a |FRAME: CPD-12645| intermediate that is produced by SauT, an energy-utilizing sulfoacetate-CoA ligase, and is acted upon by SauS, an |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent acylating dehydrogenase |CITS: [20693281]|., The |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| produced in this pathway is degraded as shown in the pathway link in a pathway common to many bacteria. That pathway involves the |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|-dependent acetyltransferase and phosphate acetyltransferase products of genes xsc and pta (in |CITS: [20693281]|). Evidence suggests that the |FRAME: SO3| produced in that pathway is processed by a sulfite transporter TauE, and a sulfite dehydrogenase SorAB, both of which remain to be fully characterized |CITS: [18174144] [19933343] [17768248]| and in |CITS: [20693281]|.

|FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| is a natural product first found in wool, and is an intermediate in cysteine metabolism involved in, for example, the synthesis of |FRAME: TAURINE| in mammals |CITS: [3346220]|. The compound also serves as a precursor of the cytophagal sulfolipid |FRAME: CPD-12704| |CITS: [6330048]| and is found extracellularly in spiders' webs |CITS: [Vollrath90]|., Cysteate can serve as a sole source of carbon and energy for the aerobic growth of some bacteria |CITS: [Stapley70][15758220]|, as an electron acceptor for several sulfate-reducing bacteria |CITS: [8703197][10508097]|, as an electron donor for some nitrate-reducing bacteria |CITS: [9202468][10376831]|, and as the substrate for a fermentation in a sulfate-reducing bacterium |CITS: [Laue97]|., The nitrogen-reducing bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6160| can utilize |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| as a sole source of carbon and energy for growth, with either nitrate or molecular oxygen as terminal electron acceptor |CITS: [10376831]|., An inducible protein was found in extracts of cysteate-grown cells. The protein was purified and found to be |FRAME: CPLX-8146| (encoded by |FRAME: G-12195| and |FRAME: G-12194|), an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-367| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: HSO3| |CITS: [15758220]|., Unlike the inducible |FRAME: CPLX-8146|, the other two enzymes in this pathway are constitutive. The first reaction is the constitutive transamination of |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| to |FRAME: CPD-380|. It is still unclear whether a unique cysteate:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase is expressed, or whether the reaction is catalyzed by a protein with another function (e.g. |FRAME: ASPAMINOTRANS-RXN "aspartate transaminase, EC 2.6.1.1"|)., The second reaction is an NAD-dependent reduction of |FRAME: CPD-380| to |FRAME: CPD-367|. This enzyme is constitutive as well. At the time of publication, it was not known whether a unique 3-sulfolactate dehydrogenase exists, or a malate dehydrogenase is involved. However, since then a specific |FRAME: MONOMER-2264|, involved in |FRAME: CoM| biosynthesis, has been characterized from the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [11830598]|, and an |FRAME: MONOMER-15868 "NADP+-specific enzyme"| has been described in |FRAME: TAX-290398| |CITS: [20007648]|. Summary: General Backround, The polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|,, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|) are a group of positively charged organic polycations that are involved in many, biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating, several enzymes |CITS: [3157043][4873311][1409623][2185470]|., While it is clear that polyamines are essential for normal cell growth, we still do not fully, understand their specific molecular functions in vivo |CITS:[3157043]|., |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| are found in all life forms, and, |FRAME:SPERMINE| is found mostly in eukaryotes., |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| can be formed either directly from |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| by ornithine, decarboxylase (ODC) (see |FRAME:PWY-46|) or indirectly from |FRAME:ARG| by arginine decarboxylase, (ADC) (see |FRAME:PWY-40| and |FRAME:PWY-43|)., While the ODC pathway was considered the only mammalian pathway for polyamine biosynthesis,, recently the presence of the ADC pathway in mammals has been demonstrated |CITS:[11804860], [14738999]|. In higher plants the presence of both pathways has been known for some time, |CITS: [11537482]|., In bacteria, both pathways are common, and are often found side by side in the same organism, |CITS:[3157043]|., There are two flavors of the ADC pathway. In both cases |FRAME:ARG| is first converted to, |FRAME:AGMATHINE| by a biosynthetic arginine decarboxylase. However, in enterobacteria and, mycobacteria |FRAME:AGMATHINE| is converted directly to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| by the enzyme, |FRAME:AGMATIN-CPLX| (this pathway),, while in higher plants, |FRAME:TAX-286| spp., |FRAME:TAX-642| spp., and, lactic bacteria, |FRAME:AGMATHINE| is first hydrolyzed by |FRAME:CPLX-31| into |FRAME:CPD-597|, and |FRAME:AMMONIA|, and |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| is formed by removal of the ureido group from, |FRAME:CPD-597| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-39| (see pathway |FRAME:PWY-43|)., About This Pathway, This pathway was studied mostly in enterobacteria, but it was also found in the mycobacteria, |FRAME: TAX-1771| and |FRAME: TAX-1772| |CITS:[13192096]| and in the Gram positive bacterium, |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [9723923]|. While |FRAME: TAX-83333| possesses both an ODC and an ADC, pathways, in |FRAME: TAX-1423| this is the only |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| biosynthetic pathway., Remarkably, even though |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| is only synthesized in |FRAME: TAX-1423| via, |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, no intracellular |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| was found in this organism, |CITS:[9723923]|., It should be mentioned that in some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-83333|, this pathway can also, operate in a catabolic manner |CITS:[3897201]|, catalyzing the degradation of |FRAME:ARG|, through |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| into |FRAME:SUC| (see |FRAME:PWY0-823|)., However, the main catabolic arginine pathway in these bacteria is the succinyltransferase pathway, (|FRAME:AST-PWY|). Interestingly, unlike |FRAME: TAX-83333|, wild-type |FRAME:TAX-562| strains are unable to, use |FRAME:ARG| as a carbon source, even though they can use it as a nitrogen source |CITS:[3534538]|., |FRAME: TAX-83333| has two forms of the enzyme arginine decarboxylase: a constitutive, biosynthetic form,, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10959| gene, and an inducible catabolic form, encoded by the |FRAME:EG11501| gene., When the cataolic form is not expressed, the pathway operates only in an anabolic manner, catalyzing, the biosynthesis of |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, which is used by the bacteria either directly or as a, precursor for the biosynthesis of other polyamines (see |FRAME:POLYAMSYN-PWY|)., However, when the cells are grown in an arginine-rich medium, especially if the medium is acidic and, conditions are semi-anaerobic, the catabolic arginine decarboxylase is expressed, and the pathway, operates in a catabolic manner, feeding |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| via |FRAME:4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, and |FRAME:SUC| into the |FRAME:TCA| |CITS:[3157043]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is the second most abundant biologically produced polymer (|FRAME: CELLULOSE| is the most abundant). |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is found in the cell walls of fungi, yeast and green algae, as well as the exoskeletons of crustaceans (including planktonic types) and insects. In the marine environment |FRAME: CHITIN| is an abundant polysaccharide that is a source of carbon and nitrogen for marine organisms. Its degradation by several genera of marine chitinolytic bacteria is part of the cycling of nutrients in ocean water. In addition to ocean water, chitinase genes have been identified in bacteria from freshwater and saline lakes, estuaries, and soil. Within bacteria, the ability to degrade chitin appears to be limited to the |FRAME: TAX-1224|, |FRAME: TAX-976|, |FRAME: TAX-201174| and |FRAME: TAX-1239| (in |CITS: [17933912]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21607543]|). Some bacterial species have been shown to contain multiple chitinase genes to efficiently utilize different forms of |FRAME: CHITIN| and some of its by-products |CITS: [16535505]|., About This Pathway, This pathway is based on studies of the chitinolytic machinery of |FRAME: TAX-615|, which has been studied as a, model system for chitin degradation. The system includes four chitin-active enzymes:|FRAME: G-44748 CBP21|, a surface-active lytic polysaccharide monooxygenase that introduces chain breaks by oxidative cleavage, |FRAME: G-44749 ChiC|, an endo-acting nonprocessive chitinase; and |FRAME: G-15389 ChiA| and |FRAME: G-15390 ChiB|, two processive chitinases moving along chitin chains in opposite directions. The major product produced by the combined action of these four enzymes is |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE|, which is degraded to monomeric |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| by an |FRAME: G-15388 N-acetylhexosaminidase| (also known as chitobiase)., |FRAME: TAX-615| is an extremely efficient chitin degrader. In 1969 it was found to be the most efficient amongst 100 tested microorganisms |CITS: [4894282]|. In 1986 the chitin degradation system was resolved into five chitinolytic proteins with subunit molecular masses of 21, 36, 48, 52, and 57 kilodaltons (later known as |FRAME: G-44748 CBP21|, |FRAME: MONOMER-20053 ChiC2|, |FRAME: MONOMER-20052 ChiC1|, |FRAME: G-15390 ChiB|, and |FRAME: G-15389 ChiA|) |CITS: [16347012]|. It was later shown that C1 and C2 are two forms encoded by the same |FRAME: G-44749| gene - ChiC2 corresponds to the catalytic domain of C1, and is generated by proteolytic removal of its chitin-binding domains |CITS: [9495026][10527937][18323665]|., For many years it was known that the externally-secreted small |FRAME: G-44748 CBP21| protein binds to chitin and promotes the activity of other chitinases. However, no enzymatic activty has been associated with the protein until it was discovered that the enzyme is a monooxygenase in 2010. It binds to the least-accessible parts of the crystalline chitin molecule and catalyzes an oxygen-dependent monooxygenation reaction that breaks the chain, leaving an oxidized aldonic acid terminus at the reducing end |CITS: [20929773]|. The discovery has resulted in reclassification of the full CAZy class to which the enzyme belongs from CBM33 (chitin binding module 33) to AA10 (auxiliary activities 10)., The three chitinases of |FRAME: TAX-615| are all extracellular, and all belong to glycoside hydrolase family 18 (GH18), yet they all posses different poroperties. The ChiC chitinase is a non-processive, endo-cleaving enzyme. It binds to crystalline chitin and cleaves the β(1-4) bond between two monomers, releasing its substrate upon cleavage. ChiA and ChiB, on the other hand, are processive exo-cleaving enzymes that attack the chains formed by the other two enzymes from both ends - ChiA attacks the reducing end, while ChiB attacks the non-reducing end., The last enzyme, chitobiase, contains a catalytic domain that belongs to family GH20. This enzyme is extracellular as well, binding to the external side of the outer membrane., The endo-cleaving chitinase (ChiC) and the lytic chitin monooxygenase break down the |FRAME: CHITIN| polymer into chitodextrins of various sizes (N-acetyl-D-glucosamine oligosaccharides, GlcNAcn). These oligosaccharides are attacked by the exo-cleaving chitinases, whose main product is the disaccharide |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE|. Since ChiB is able to act on trisaccharides, that form does not accumulate |CITS: [10823940]|. However, cleavage of the products formed by the lytic monooxygenase also produces di- and tri-saccharides that contain a aldonic acid at the reducing end. When chitobiase acts on those products, liberating |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| from the non-reducing end, it forms small amounts of |FRAME: CPD-370| |CITS: [27059395]|.

Names: thiazole component of thiamine diphosphate biosynthesis III
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the |FRAME: THIAMINE|-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|. Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820 Plasmodium|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, |FRAME: THIAMINE-P "Thiamine phosphate"| is formed by the coupling of two moieties, the pyrimidine |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP| and the thiazole |FRAME: THZ-P|, which are produced by two different pathways. This pathway describes the formation of the thiazole moiety in eukaryotes., Genetic studies in |FRAME: TAX-4932| have demonstrated that |FRAME: G3O-154| is the only gene required for thiamin thiazole formation |CITS: [7941734]|. The donor of the sulfur atom was elusive for a long time. It has been shown that THI4 promotes a very unusual chemical reaction in which it supplies the sulfur through an iron-dependent transfer from an internal cysteine amino acid residue (Cys-205). The reaction converts Cys-205 to |FRAME:2-AMINOACRYLATE| and renders THI4 inactive. Hence, THI4 represents a single-turnover (suicide) enzyme |CITS:[22031445]|. Another single-turnover enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-8694| (THI5), is involved in the pyrimidine moiety formation in |FRAME:TAX-4932| (see |FRAME:PWY-7282|)., When expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, the enzyme copurified with its product (|FRAME: CPDQT-400 "adenylated thiazole"|) and two additional adenylated intermediates that shed light on its complex mechanism |CITS: [18652458]|. Similarly, in the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| the multifunctional protein |FRAME: AT5G54770| is sufficient for thiazole production. While it has been shown that NAD and |FRAME: GLY| are substrates for the enzyme, the exact source of sulfur for THI1 is still not known., The THI1 protein localizes to the chloroplasts, suggesting that this part of the pathway occurs in this organelle |CITS:[11575719][18048325][17174261][18332905]|. However, THI1 can also localize to the mitochondria |CITS:[11575719]|, and the downstream TPK1 and TPK2 enzymes are both cytosolic in Arabidopsis |CITS:[17611796]|, suggesting that intermediates in the vitamin B1 biosynthesis pathway may need to be transported out of organelles for |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| synthesis to be completed., The pathway has also been shown to function in halophilic archaea, which possess a homolog of THI4 |CITS: [25348237]|.

General Background, Acetylated anthocyanins have been identified in a wide variety of flowering plants |CITS: [Honda02]| |CITS: [Takeda86]| contributing to the coloration of flowers |CITS: [10066805][10845463][Heller94]|, UV protection and defense |CITS: [11130659]|. It has been found that anthocyanins exposed to UV irradiation are quite stable in neutral aqueous solutions supporting their biological role in blooming tissues under solar radiation. However, a change in pH or a decreasing number , of molecular associations (e.g. acylation) causes the isomerization of the usually predominant E-isomers into their Z-configured counterparts |CITS: [Yoshida03]| which may affect their further conversion in the pathway. , The color-stabilizing effect of acetylated anthocyanins has been investigated with regard to their possible usage as food colorants |CITS: [Fossen98]|. Moreover, in dye-sensitized solar cells shisonin has been used as a coating pigment that contributes to light energy harvesting |CITS: [Kumara06]|., Shisonin (this pathway), a mono-malonylated anthocyanin, has been found in high amounts in Labiatae. Together with the bi-malonylated anthocyanin salvianin (|FRAME:PWY-5268|) shisonin constitutes a major flower pigment in that genus |CITS: [11809447]|. Both anthocyanins occur predominantly in different species, i.e. shisonin in Perilla |CITS: [12590125]| and salvianin in Salvia |CITS: [Kondo89]| and share key enzymatic steps of their respective biosyntheses comprising glucosylation and aromatic and aliphatic acylation., About This Pathway, Cyanidin 3-O-β-D-glucoside represents the starting compound that is 5-O-glucosylated |CITS: [10066805]| to yield cyanidin-3,5-diglucoside. The formation of shisonin, the precursor for the aliphatic acylation with malonyl-CoA to form malonylshisonin is carried out via 3-aromatic acylation with p-coumaric acid |CITS: [Fujiwara98]| |CITS: [10845463]|. The exact biosynthetic route towards shisonin is still a matter of debate and the succession of 5-O-glucosylation and 3-O-acylation remains to be demonstrated. However, it has been experimentally verified that the involved enzymes, i.e. anthocyanin 5-O-glucosidase and anthocyanidin 3-aromatic acyltransferase, accept the various intermediates in both branches |CITS: [10066805]|., Both enzymes, the 3-aromatic acyltransferase |CITS: [Fujiwara98]| and the anthocyanin-5-O-glucoside-6'''-O-malonyltransferase |CITS: [12578391]| that produces malonylshisonin express high affinities towards both pelargonidin (see |FRAME:PWY-5268|) and cyanidin (shisonin biosynthesis) derived anthocyanidin intermediates forming the corresponding aromatic and aliphatic acylated compounds., Interestingly, metabolic profiling of two chemo-varietal forms of Perilla, a green and a red form, revealed that only the red form accumulates malonylshisonin. The occurrence of other primary and secondary metabolites had not been influenced indicating that specific genes encoding anthocyanin biosynthesis and regulatory proteins such as Myb and bHLH transcribtion factors account for the difference in anthocyanin production between those two anthocyanin-chemotypes of Perilla |CITS: [12590125]|.

Names: megalomicin A biosynthesis // megalomycin A biosynthesis
Summary: The |FRAME:Megalomicins megalomicins|, which were discovered in 1968 |CITS:[5735370][5810991]|, are a family of related macrolide antibiotics produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47868|. They are therapeutically diverse compounds that possess antiparasitic, antiviral and antibacterial properties. Like other macrolide antibiotics, they are more active against Gram-positive bacteria than against Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4390258][4996819]|., The first family member to have its structure reported was |FRAME: CPD-12966| |CITS: [5358619][5358620]|. Acyl derivatives of |FRAME: CPD-12966|, including |FRAME: CPD-14689|, |FRAME: CPD-12967|, |FRAME: CPD-14691|, and |FRAME: CPD-14690|, were soon discovered |CITS: [4795255]|., The megalomicins have the same aglycone as |FRAME: CPD-13804| and |FRAME: CPD-13951|, but include a unique deoxyamino sugar, |FRAME: CPD-14692|, at the C-6 hydroxyl., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13806| and |FRAME: CPD-14683| is described in |FRAME: PWY-7106| and |FRAME: PWY-7104|, respectively. This pathway describes the final assembly of |FRAME: CPD-12966| by two enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15351| and |FRAME: G-15348| genes., The |FRAME: G-15351| gene encodes a P450 hydroxylase that catalyzes the 12-C hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-13806|, converting it to |FRAME: CPD-13951| |CITS: [15870344]|. The |FRAME: G-15348| gene encodes a megosaminyl transferase that catalyzes the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-14692| to the hyroxyl at position 6 |CITS: [20418422]|., Several dTDP-aminosugar transferase systems require a helper protein, whose function is still not undertstood, for activity. The megDVI gene, which is located immediately upstream of |FRAME: G-15348|, encodes such a helper protein that is essential for MegDI activity |CITS [20418422]|.

|FRAME: CPD-9699 "Hypoglycin A"| and |FRAME: CPD-9700| were originally identified as bioactive compounds in the ackee plant (|FRAME: TAX-259381|) |CITS:[13144762]|. These plants produce ackee fruit, the national fruit of Jamaica. Although this fruit is safe to eat when ripe, ingestion of the unripe fruit may contribute to a suite of symptoms known as "vomiting disease" that can even cause death in extreme cases |CITS:[16099087][21324617]|. Hypoglycin A appears to be a primary causative agent; it is present in the portion of the fruit that is consumed (the arillus), but its levels drop more than 10-fold during the ripening process |CITS: [Brown92]|. When hypoglycin A is ingested by an animal, it is converted to |FRAME: CPD-20989|, which can irreversibly bind to |FRAME: FAD| and interfere with the complete β-oxidation of fatty acids by inhibiting the FAD-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenase ( |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.7|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.8|, or |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.9|) |CITS:[16099087]|., Although enzymatic activities have been detected in ackee plants for the final two steps of the hypoglycin biosynthetic pathway |CITS:[Kean80] [Kean81]|, many of the steps are hypothetical and await further characterization. Some general evidence for this pathway is provided by radiotracer studies. For instance, radio-labeled threonine can be incorporated in hypoglycin A. Radio-labeled methionine can also be incorporated, but, it is hypothesized to act as the methyl donor to 2-oxobutanoate |CITS:[Kean81]|. In addition, incorporation of radiolabeled acetate into hypoglycin A is predicted to occur through the conversion of acetate to acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA is then hypothesized to react with |FRAME:CPD-9735|. Additional enzymatic assays using ackee protein extracts suggest the presence of an enzyme capable of performing this reaction to produce |FRAME:CPD-9736|, but the precursor compound could not be isolated for in vitro assays |CITS:[Kean81]|. In general, most of the intermediates in this proposed pathway have not been isolated, and the steps in the pathway from |FRAME:CPD-9736| to |FRAME:CPD-9739| are only suggested by analogy to the leucine biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [Kean81] [13978769]|. A study in the related species, |FRAME:TAX-124994| led to the hypothesis that MCPG could also be used as a precursor for hypoglycin |CITS:[Eloff70]|, but this has not been studied in ackee plants., Production of hypoglycin A and B occurs in a number of other plants, including |FRAME:TAX-124994|, several species in the genus |FRAME: TAX-4022| including sycamore (|FRAME: TAX-4026|) |CITS: [FOWDEN73][24863395][26278545][26593855][26995161]|, and soapberry (|FRAME: TAX-23672|) |CITS: [ 27367968]|. Studying the biosynthesis of these compounds may have more widespread importance because hypoglycin A and B are part of a larger family of oligopeptide and other amino acid derivatives produced in plants. For example, γ-glutamyl peptides similar to hypoglycin B serve as precursors for a number of flavor compounds in onion, and a γ-glutamyltranspeptidase has been identified in this species |CITS:[15721943]|. There may be considerable opportunities for the identification of common compounds and similar enzymes found by simultaneous study of these related pathways.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-16741 "Paspaline"| is |FRAME: Secondary-Metabolites| produced by filamentous fungi. It has been proposed to be the first stable intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Indole-Diterpenes "indole-diterpenes"|, a diverse class that includes |FRAME: Mycotoxins "mycotoxins"| such as |FRAME: CPD-16744|. These compounds can have neurotoxic effects in mammals (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7493|). Their common structural core is comprised of a cyclic diterpene skeleton derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| and an |FRAME: INDOLE| group that is thought to be derived from the |FRAME: TRP| precursor |FRAME: INDOLE-3-GLYCEROL-P| (indole-3-glycerol phosphate). A gene cluster involved in i|FRAME: Indole-Diterpenes "indole-diterpene"| biosynthesis was identified in the |FRAME: CPD-16744| producer |FRAME: TAX-70109| and the involvement of genes paxG, paxM, paxB and paxC in |FRAME: CPD-16741| biosynthesis was demonstrated |CITS: [9618588][11169115][16494875][23949005]| and reviewed in |CITS: [18262778]|., Gene clusters containing functional orthologs of the pax genes as well as some unique genes have been identified in other fungi. They produce a variety of bioprotective indole-diterpene metabolites from |FRAME: CPD-16741| including aflatrems in |FRAME: TAX-5059| |CITS: [25087641][19801473][24038699][15528556]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7540|), terpendoles in |FRAME: TAX-124418| |CITS: [23261604]| (see |FRAME: MONOMER-18795|), lolotrems in |FRAME: TAX-73839| |CITS: [16765617]|, and lolitrems and terpendoles in |FRAME: TAX-35717| |CITS: [22750140]|., About This Pathway, Four genes have been shown to be involved in |FRAME: CPD-16741| biosynthesis paxG, paxM, paxB and paxC |CITS: [16494875][23949005]|. PaxG is a geranygeranyl diphosphate synthase that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This compound is proposed to condense with |FRAME: INDOLE-3-GLYCEROL-P| to form |FRAME: CPD-16736| in a reaction catalyzed by PaxC. The |FRAME: CPD-16736| intermediate then undergoes epoxidation and cyclization steps catalyzed by PaxM and PaxB. These steps are shown here according to |CITS: [23311903]| in which the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-16741| was reconstituted in the heterologous host |FRAME: TAX-5062|.

General Background, Xanthones are yellow pigments of phenolic origin restricted in occurrence to only a few families of higher plants and some fungi and lichens. The majority of xanthones is rarely glucosylated and has been found in basically two families of higher plants, the Clusiaceae (syn. Guttiferae) and |FRAME:TAX-21472| |CITS: [Hostettmann89][Bennett89]|. However, xanthones also appear sporadically throughout the remainder of the plant kingdom. Xanthone-C-glucosides, such as mangiferin are the exception with a much wider distribution among plants and also arising in ferns and fungi |CITS: [Hostettmann89]|., Xanthones can be classified based on their oxygenation, prenylation and glucosylation pattern. The majority of xanthones, isolated so far are of the tetraoxygenated-type which have been intensively studied in plants of the Guttiferae and, |FRAME:TAX-21472| but are reported from 12 other plant families as well |CITS: [11190384]|. The restricted biosynthesis of, xanthones and their plant-specific substitution pattern has been employed as a useful marker for systematic purposes,, i.e. comparing the phyletic order of genera within the Guttiferae |CITS: [Da Mate Rezente73]|and chemotaxonomic differentiation between plant families |CITS: [Sultanbawa80]|., Xanthones posses a number of remarkable pharmacological traits and bioactivities (summarized in |CITS: [11190384]|) and, have been used as, e.g. cardiovascular protective agents |CITS: [15179447]| and antitumor promotors |CITS: [10397461]|. Tetrahydroxylated xanthones can be induced by phytopathogens |CITS: [12391565]| and accumulate in calli and cell suspension upon treatment with plant hormones and supplements, such as naphtaleneacetic acid (NAA) in combination with kinetin |CITS: [DIAS00]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of plant xanthones originates mainly from a mixed shikimate-acetate pathway, however xanthones entirely derived from acetate have also been reported in lower plants |CITS: [11190384]| |CITS: [Hostettmann89]|. The main steps in the xanthone biosynthesis involve the condensation of shikimate and acetate moieties which constitute a benzophenone intermediate followed by a regioselective, oxidative mediated intra-molecular coupling to form the xanthone, ring |CITS: [Peters98]|., The shikimate derivatives used as entry compounds for the tetrahydroxyxanthone biosynthesis differ in relation to the, investigated plants (|FRAME:TAX-140968| vs |FRAME:TAX-172057|) |CITS: [11216850]| |CITS: [11882941]|. These plants belong to different families that seem to have developed biosynthetic variants of the tetrahydroxyxanthone synthesis which involves enzymes of diverse regioselectivity and substrate preference and leads to varying intermediates |CITS: [Peters98]| , |CITS: [9459298]|., The biosynthesis of tetrahydroxyxanthone via benzoate (this pathway) in |FRAME:TAX-140968| is achieved by the stepwise condensation of 3 malonyl-CoA and benzoyl-CoA to form an intermediate tetrahydroxybenzophenone. This pathway is different from the |FRAME:TAX-172057| variant (|FRAME:PWY-5002|) with regard to the regiospecificity and substrate usage of the involved enzymes. The benzophenone synthase prefers benzoyl-CoA |CITS: [12795704]|, which, in turn is provided by the catalytic action of a 3-hydroxybenzoate:coenzyme A ligase using benzoic acid |CITS: [12054436][9459298]|. The new intermediate, 2,4,6-trihydroxybenzophenone is further hydroxylated and converted to the , 2,3',4,6-tetrahydroxyphenone intermediate, common to both pathways., The crucial step in the biosynthetic sequence is the cyclization of the benzophenone to form a xanthone, catalyzed by xanthon synthases. While in |FRAME:TAX-172057| the xanthone synthase converts this tetrahydroxybenzophenone intermediate regioselective to 1,3,5-trihydroxyxanthone the xanthone synthase of |FRAME:TAX-140968| converts it to the , 1,3,7-trihydroxyxanthone. Therefore all xanthones and their derivatives in |FRAME:TAX-140968| are 7-oxygenated in contrast to the constituents in the |FRAME:TAX-172057| pathway which all carry a 5-hydroxy group |CITS: [Peters98]|., The last step in the biosynthesis of the tetrahydroxyxanthones is the introduction of a hydroxyl group to the C-ring of the, xanthone skeleton. This reaction is carried out by the plant-specific cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, xanthone-6-hydroxylase to form the 1,3,6,7-tetrahydroxyxanthone |CITS: [10731018]|. Further products found in |FRAME:TAX-140968| are all derivatives of either 1,3,6,7- or 1,3,5,6-tetrahydroxyxanthones |CITS: [NIELSEN79]| |CITS: [10865463]| implicating that no more hydroxylations occur in this species.

This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of adenosylcobalamin starting with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of cobamides with different lower ligand bases. By definition, the lower ligand base of cobalamin-type B12 vitamins is |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|., In this pathway |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| is tethered to the corrin ring via a structure known as the nucleotide loop, which is composed from |FRAME:R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME:DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|., Until 2007 it was believed that the last reaction in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| was the linking of |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| (a product of |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|) to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP|, in a reaction catalyzed by cobalamine synthase. However, it has been shown that the true substrate for the enzyme is |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P|, and not |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| |CITS: [17209023]|, and that the product of the reaction is actually |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P|. Thus, there is one more reaction in the pathway, the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-13213|, the enzyme initially proposed to catalyze the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| |CITS: [17209023]|., While many organisms form |FRAME: ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| from |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (see |FRAME: PWY-5509|), some cobalamin-producing Firmicutes, such as |FRAME: TAX-1637| species, do not have a homolog of the |FRAME: G-10055| gene that encodes this enzyme., In these organisms |FRAME: ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| is produced from |FRAME: ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| by a kinase that is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58236| gene. While at least some of these organisms cannot produce |FRAME: ALPHA-RIBAZOLE|, they are able to salvage it from the environment by a dedicated transporter encoded by the |FRAME: G-58237| gene |CITS: [20633228]|. A similar system has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-1462| |CITS: [27748967]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-15302 Platensimycin| (PTM) is a potent and selective inhibitor of the elongation-specific condensing enzymes of type II fatty acid biosynthesis (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.41| (FabB) and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.179| (FabF)). The compound, produced by |FRAME: TAX-58346|, was discovered in 2006 by researchers at Merck, using an antisense differential sensitivity screening focused on selective inhibitors of fatty acid biosynthesis |CITS: [16710421]|., PTM interacts specifically with the acyl-enzyme intermediate of the FabF enzyme. Crystalographic studies have shown that it binds in the malonyl subsite of FabF, with its benzoic acid ring positioned to interact with important residues of the catalytic machinery. Because of its unique mode of action, platensimycin is efficient against notorious antibiotic-resistant strains such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus, and vancomycin-resistant enterococci. PTM is not active against wild-type |FRAME: TAX-562| due to efflux mechanisms, has no antifungal activity, and has low mammalian cell toxicity (MIC is ~1000 fold higher than towards the bacterial target) |CITS: [16710421]|., A related compound, |FRAME: CPD-23571|, was identified one year later, and shown to act not only against FabB and FabF but also against |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.180| (FabH) |CITS: [17456595]|. Deletion of the ptmR1 gene, which encodes a transcriptional regulator, from the |FRAME: TAX-58346| MA7327 strain resulted in production of both compounds, with yields of 323 mg/liter and 255 mg/liter, respectively |CITS: [19164156]|., Due to its inhibition of mammalian fatty acid synthase PTM has been proposed for the treatment of diabetes and related metabolic disorders. PTM is advantagious compared with the widely used inhibitors of mammalian fatty acid synthase |FRAME: CPD-23599 C75| and |FRAME: CPD-6901| because it does not inhibit sterol synthesis |CITS: [21389266][27695056]|., In 2016 a sulfur-containing congener of |FRAME: CPD-15302|, |FRAME: CPD-23570|, was discovered and shown to retain strong antibacterial activity |CITS: [ 27134119]|. This compound was eventually shown to be a precursor in the biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [29915173]|., The utility of |FRAME: CPD-15302| as a drug is hampered by poor pharmacokinetic properties and negligible, oral bioavailability. Clinical trials have been delayed pending the development of chemical analogues with more favorable drug-like properties |CITS: [19164156][18442030][ 26942008]|., About This Pathway, Structurally, PTM is composed of two distinct moieties - a 3-amino-2,4-dihydroxybenzoate moiety and an aliphatic cage moiety, joined together by a flexible propionamide chain. Each of these moieties is synthesized in a parallel branch. Stable isotope feeding studies have shown that the benzoate moiety is derived from a C4 intermediate originating from the TCA cycle (now known to be |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which is derived from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|) and a C3 intermediate from glycolysis (now known to be |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), while the aliphatic cage moiety is derived from the |FRAME: PWY-5121 "MEP pathway"| |CITS: [18034483][Herath08]|. The unique carbon scaffold pointed toward an |FRAME: CPD1F-128| intermediate., The PTM/PTN biosynthetic gene cluster was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-58346| MA7327 and found to contain 43 open reading frames |CITS: [21825154]|., Many researchers, working on a subset of the enzymes, have pieced together the complex biosynthetic pathway. In general, the cage moiety is synthesized from |FRAME: ENT-COPALYL-DIPHOSPHATE| via |FRAME: CPD-23584| |CITS: [27966343][27490479][27599271]|. Following the creation of an epoxy bridge |CITS: [27966343][30216060]| it is α-hydroxylated at C-7 |CITS: [30735041]| and esterified with coenzyme A |CITS: [29867143]| before cyclization into the cage structure. Prior to condensation with the benzoate moiety, the cage moiety undergoes one cycle of β-oxidation, eliminating 3 carbons |CITS: [26055255]|., The benzoate moiety is generated from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS: [17003031][27599271]|. Following activation by coenzyme A it is sulfurated, forming a thiocarboxylate group. The sulfur is provided by a small sulfur-carrier protein that carries a thiocatboxylate on its C-terminal glycine |CITS: [29915173]|. The two moieties are condensed, with the product retaining the thiocarboxylate group, which is hydrolyzed non-enzymatically to form the final product |CITS: [27599271][29915173]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lignins "Lignin"| is the most abundant aromatic compound in nature, and its mineralization is an important step in the terrestrial, carbon cycle. Lignin is broken down to various biaryl and monoaryl compounds such as |FRAME: BIPHENYL|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|., Complex lignin is resistant to most bacterial enzymes, and its degradation is usually initiated by white rot fungi, which secrete extracellular degradation enzymes such as |FRAME: MONOMER-14338 "lignin peroxidase"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14335 "manganese peroxidase"|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14334 "laccase"| |CITS: [8246842]|. The resulting low-molecular-weight lignin can be further degraded and mineralized by bacteria |CITS: [1785937]|., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-303| and |FRAME: TAX-101510|, have also been shown to degrade complex lignin |CITS: [20567767]|., Many bacterial species are able to grow on many of the lower complexity compounds that are formed by the fungal peroxidases as their sole sources of carbon and energy., About This Pathway, |FRAME: VANILLIN "Vanillin"| and |FRAME: VANILLATE| are important intermediate metabolites of lignin-derived aromatic compounds., Several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-86003| |CITS: [ 9098058]| and |FRAME: TAX-101510| |CITS: [22057861]| convert |FRAME: VANILLIN| to |FRAME: VANILLATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-17594| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-15313| gene), followed by demethylation of the latter to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, catalyzed by a formaledehyde-producing monooxygenase-type |FRAME: CPLX-7630| (encoded by |FRAME: G-10746| and |FRAME: G-10747| genes). , It has been shown that in |FRAME: TAX-101510| |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "protocatechuate"| is degraded into central metabolism intermediates using the |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY "ortho cleavage pathway"| |CITS: [22057861]|., A similar pathway, which operates in |FRAME: TAX-502559|, utilizes somewhat different enzymes, and continues by the |FRAME: P184-PWY "meta cleavage pathway"| |CITS: [17928721]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7097|).

General Background, |FRAME: Strigolactones Strigolactones| are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi., The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635 "Gossypium hirsutum (cotton)"| infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels |CITS: [17780042]|., Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| |CITS: [Hauck92]|, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| |CITS: [Mueler92]| and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) |CITS: [Yokota98]|., The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis |CITS: [15944687]|., The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone |CITS: [Mosse73]|., Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interaction between the fungi and the roots., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14657 Orobanchol| is a strigolactone compound originally isolated from the root exudates of red clover (|FRAME: TAX-57577|) based on its ability to stimulate germination of |FRAME: TAX-36748| seeds |CITS: [Yokota98]|. It has been later detected in the root exudates of numerous plants, including Fabaceae, Solanaceae, a few Gymnosperm species, and rice. , The genuine structure of orobanchol was established in 2011 |CITS: [21899364]|. Based on the structure, all strigolactones have been divided into two subgroups - the orobanchol-type and strigol-type, which differ in their C-ring configuration., Orobanchol is produced from |FRAME: CPD-14651| in two routes - either directly, or via a |FRAME: CPD-28128| intermediate |CITS: [32064317][35222492]|. The direct route was shown in |FRAME: TAX-3917| (cowpea) and |FRAME: TAX-4081| (tomato) to be catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 CYP722C |CITS: [32064317]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-630526| was identified in 1954 |CITS: [13250367]| and classified into serogroup O:28 (formerly group M). The O28 epitope was originally divided into three subfactors - O28a, O28b and O28c. |FRAME: TAX-630526| has the subfactors O28a and O28c, while another O:28 strain, |FRAME: TAX-1151184|, has O28a and O28b., The structure of the O antigen repeat unit of |FRAME: TAX-630526| was reported in 2007 |CITS: [17583683]|. The structure of the O antigen of |FRAME: ORG-57089|, reported 3 years later, was found to be highly related to the |FRAME: TAX-630526| antigen |CITS: [20482625]|. On the other hand, the structure from |FRAME: TAX-1151184|, which was reported in 2011, was found to be different |CITS: [21999539]|. The similarity of the two antigens is limited to the presence of the common β-D-Gal-(1→3)-α-D-GalNAc-(1→4)-D-Qui3NAc trisaccharide fragment in the main chain. Based on these differences the Salmonella O:28 serogroup was divided into two serovars - O:28ab and O:28ac., The O antigen biosynthetic gene clusters of both |FRAME: TAX-630526| and |FRAME: ORG-57089| were sequenced and found to be highly similar |CITS: [20482625]| (the cluster from the O:28ab strain |FRAME: TAX-570935| was also sequenced and shown to be different |CITS: [20652070]|). The clusters contain 12 genes, encoding enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|, enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15598|, three glycosyltransferases, an O antigen repeat unit flippase, and an O antigen polymerase. It is believed that |FRAME: TAX-630526| and |FRAME: ORG-57089| produce the same O unit, which is flipped across the membrane and polymerized in the periplasm. Further modifications that differentiate these O antigens (glucosylation in Salmonella and O-acetylation in Escherichia) are catalyzed by prophage genes located outside the O antigen gene cluster., The qdtC gene, found in the clusters, is a rare oddity. As mentioned above, most of the genes in the enterobacteria O-antigen gene clusters are transcribed in the same direction in a region between galF and gnd. The qdtC gene, which is involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15598|, is one of two genes that are transcribed in the opposite direction (the other is the gne gene in Salmonella O:21) and was probably added to the cluster at a later stage |CITS: [23848592]|.

Flavonoids are highly diverse class of plant polyphenols (more than 9000 compounds have been identified so far |CITS: [16137727]|) that impart much of the color and flavor of fruits and vegetables. They exhibit a wide range of biological functions in higher plants such as UV protection, flower coloration, and antimicrobial activity |CITS: [11130659]|. Whewn ingested, flavonoids exhibit antioxidant and anticancer properties |CITS: [12224601]| |CITS: [18645020]|., Flavan-3-ols represent a classs of flavonoids and are the building blocks of condensed tannins. They have antioxidant properties and clinical studies have shown ant-icancer protective effects of the flavanols catechin, epicatechin, gallocatechin, and epigallocatechin |CITS: [14725861]|. It has been shown that epicatechin present in dark chocolate has the potential to promote cardiovascular health in humans., |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.3| ,converts leucoanthocyanidins to their corresponding 2,3-trans-flavan-3-ols.
