Summary: General Background, |FRAME:Pyrrolobenzodiazepines Pyrrolobenzodiazepines| are a class of natural products, produced by actinomycetes, that comprise organic heterotricyclic compounds with a skeleton consisting of a pyrrole ring ortho-fused at any position to a benzodiazepine bicyclic system. The pyrrolobenzodiazepines are sequence-selective DNA alkylating compounds with significant antitumor properties |CITS: [12678826]|., The compounds bind to the minor groove of a double-stranded DNA, where they form a bond between the electrophilic C-11 of the compound and the exocyclic N-2 of a guanine base |CITS: [7947769]|. Once bound to DNA, pyrrolobenzodiazepines have been shown to mediate a number of biological effects in cells, including DNA strand breakage |CITS: [21188379],| inhibition of DNA processing enzymes |CITS: [8367284][9054552][16942018]| or transcription factors |CITS: [11097052][18483319]| and modulation of the signalling pathways |CITS: [21708181][26756315]|. Formation of the pyrrolobenzodiazepine-DNA complex causes very little distortion of the double-helical structure of DNA and is thus less readily repaired by DNA repair proteins compared to DNA adducts with other alkylating agents |CITS: [15944449]|. , O-glycosylation at C7, as in |FRAME: CPD-18442|, significantly enhances DNA-binding affinity |CITS: [12678745]|. A loose correlation between DNA binding affinity and cytotoxicity has been shown with naturally and synthetically produced compounds |CITS: [10354403]|., |FRAME: CPD-18442 Sibiromycin|, which is produced by |FRAME: TAX-457432|, has the highest DNA binding affinity and cytotoxicity of the known pyrrolobenzodiazepines, with 50% inhibitory concentrations varying from 4 to 1.7 pM in leukemia, plasmacytoma, and ovarian cancer cell lines |CITS: [10354403]|. Despite its potency, sibiromycin is not a suitable drug because the presence of a hydroxyl group at C-9 results in cardiotoxic properties, as in the case of |FRAME: CPD-18441| |CITS: [4276468][6928034][6261786][12678745]|. |FRAME: TAX-457432| was genetically engineered to form a 9-deoxy variant with diminished cardiotoxicity |CITS: [22390171]|., The natural role of |FRAME: CPD-18442| is likely as an antibiotic, as the compound inhibits the growth of many bacterial species, including |FRAME: TAX-1405|, |FRAME: TAX-1423|, and |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [4907802][4647835][19270142]|., About This Pathway, Early experiments have shown that the metabolic precursors of the pyrrolobenzodiazepine ring of |FRAME: CPD-18442| are |FRAME: TRP| for the anthranilate moiety and |FRAME: TYR| for the hydropyrrole moiety |CITS: [Hurley80]|. The tyrosine-to-hydropyrrole transformation has been also identified in the biosynthesis of the lincosamide antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-13893|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6955| |CITS: [9531633][15355345][18817745][21919439][31710815]|., The sibiromycin biosynthetic gene cluster was identified in a cosmid library prepared from |FRAME: TAX-457432| DNA and found to contain 26 open reading frames |CITS: [19270142]|. The pathway could be divided into four segments: (1) the biosynthesis of the anthranilate moiety, ending at |FRAME: 35-Di-OH-MA-SibE-Proteins|; (2) the biosynthesis of the hydropyrrole moiety, ending at |FRAME: Dihydropyrrole-SibD|; (3) the condensation of the two moieties by SibD to form |FRAME: CPD-25731| and its conversion to the |FRAME: CPD-25719|; and (4) the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-25725| sugar, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-25724|, and its transfer to the aglycon., |FRAME: TRP| is processed to |FRAME: CPD-403| as described in |FRAME: PWY-7765| |CITS: [21612226]| (that compound also serves as a building block of the |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN actinomycin| phenoxazinone chromophore, although those organisms may use a different pathway to produce it |CITS: [20945860]|). |FRAME: CPD-403| is adenylated by the |FRAME: MONOMER-19743| and loaded on it aryl-carrier protein domain. Once bound it is 5-hydroxylated by the SibG monooxygenase. |CITS: [21612226]|., |FRAME: TYR| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-25718| by six enzymes, in a process that is very similar to that found in |FRAME: PWY-6955|. That compound is activated and loaded on the |FRAME: MONOMER-22178|. SibD then accepts the anthranilate moiety from SibE, forming the pyrrolobenzodiazepine core structure., Two more activities are required to form the final compound: oxidation of the three carbon tail by the FAD-dependent enzyme SibW |CITS: [28699733]|, and attachment of the |FRAME: CPD-25725| sugar (the biosynthesis of which is described in |FRAME: PWY-8380|) by the glycosyltransferase SibH |CITS: [19270142]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the conversion of the amino acid |FRAME: ARG| to the polyamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, its subsequent degradation to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, and finally the conversion of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC|, which is fed into the TCA cycle., |FRAME: TAX-83333| has two forms of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.19|: a constitutive biosynthetic form, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10959| gene, and an inducible catabolic form encoded by the |FRAME:EG11501| gene. When the cells are grown in an arginine-rich medium, especially if the medium is acidic and conditions are semi-anaerobic, the catabolic arginine decarboxylase is expressed, and |FRAME: ARG| is converted to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| in two steps via |FRAME: AGMATHINE|., When |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is produced by this catabolic enzyme it can be degraded further to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| and eventually |FRAME:SUC|, which is fed into the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"| |CITS:[3157043]|., There are two routes in which |FRAME: TAX-562| can degrade |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|:, In one route, which is described in |FRAME: PUTDEG-PWY|, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is transaminated with |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to generate |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, which is then oxidized to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA). GABA can be further degraded into |FRAME: SUC| as described in |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY| pathway., In a second pathway, which is described in |FRAME: PWY0-1221|, |FRAME:PUTRESCINE | is first γ-glutamylated at the expense of an ATP molecule. The resulting |FRAME: GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-PUTRESCINE| is oxidized to |FRAME:GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-GAMMA-AMINOBUTYRALDEH|, which is then dehydrogenated into |FRAME: CPD-9000|. In the last step, the γ-glutamyl group is removed by hydrolysis, generating |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| |CITS: [15590624]|., It has been suggested that the former pathway is dedicated to the degradation of intracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, while the latter is dedicated to the degradation of extracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. However, the most significant, difference between these two pathways is the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| in the latter route. One possible explanation for this is the fact that the intermediate fromed in the former pathway, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, is unstable and tends to form the cyclic form |FRAME: CPD-6124| nonenzymatically. It is possible that the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| facilitates its catabolism by preventing this cyclization |CITS: [15590624]|., The last part of this superpathway is the degradation of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC|. The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|, and is known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. Summary: General Background, Terpenes comprise a very large class of plant secondary metabolites that serves a variety of different functions in basic and specialized metabolism. The majority of these compounds are likely to operate as direct defense agents because they often exhibit toxic and deterrent effects against plant pathogens and herbivores. However, since all monoterpenes, many sesquiterpenes and a few diterpenes have high vapor pressure at ambient temperature and volatize easily, these compounds could also act at a distance from the plant, serving as attractants or deterrents for pollinators and herbivores, or as signals released after damage by herbivores to attract their predators and parasitoids. In fact, volatile monterpenes and sesquiterpenes have frequently been shown to be emitted from flowers and other aerial parts of the plant, and their release is often developmentally regulated or induced by damage |CITS: [12724546],[15310830],[14756770]|. Curiously,volatile monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes have also been reported to be synthesized and accumulated in roots and rhizomes of various plant species |CITS: [12214699]|. As a consequence of their antimicrobial and antiherbivore activity, these substances may serve as direct defenses of below-ground tissue when they accumulate., Structural Information, Monoterpenes contain a 10-carbon backbone and are all synthesized from the common precursor geranyl diphosphate by the action of various monoterpene synthases. One characteristic feature of most terpene synthases (TPSs; monoterpenes, diterpenes, sesquiterpenes) is the formation of multiple products from a single substrate |CITS: [9442047]|. Comparative sequence analyses have shown that, within the same plant genome, TPSs making different products may be more similar to each other than TPSs making the same product in different species., Commercial Uses, There is an increasing need to find sustainable and renewable liquid fuels in the face of concerns over energy security and global petroleum supply. Monoterpenes are currently being exploited to determine their feasibilty as alternative fuels. Several isoprenoid based biofuels have shown great potential so far. Of these, pinene and limonene have recently been highlighted |CITS: [22895337]|. Pinene can be dimerized to yield a high density fuel and limonene is a natural potential biofuel. 1,8-cineole can be used in an 8:1 blend with gasoline.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| is a naturally occurring dicarboxylate that can be used by some species of bacteria. It can also be formed from |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.203|, which forms |FRAME: CPD-12595| that converts spontaneously to |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| in the presence of water., Enterobacteria such as |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-548| degrade |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| by a different pathway (see |FRAME: GLUCARDEG-PWY|). Both pathways share the first enzyme, which produces |FRAME: 5-KETO-4-DEOXY-D-GLUCARATE| |CITS: [4311826]|, but differ in the latter part of the pathway., The genes and enzymes that participate in this pathways were studied in |FRAME: TAX-62977| (previously known as Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1) |CITS: [18364348]|., About This Pathway, The genes encoding enzymes for the degradation of |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE| in |FRAME: TAX-62977| were identified by mutant analysis and complementation studies. The genes were cloned and over-expressed and the recombinant gene products were characterized., Intermediates in the pathway were identified by LC/MS |CITS: [18364348]|. The genes include a D-glucarate/D-galactarate permease; two dehydratases specific for |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE|, respectively; a 5-dehydro-4-deoxy-D-gluccarate dehydratase; and a 2-oxoglutarate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (also see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6497|)., The |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate) produced in the pathway can be metabolized in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| as shown in the pathway link, or used in many other pathways.

General Background, |FRAME: Cobalamins Cobalamin|-derived cofactors are required by two important human enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.2|. The former utilizes |FRAME: CPD-9037|, while the latter requires |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|., While humans cannot synthesize these cofactors de novo, they can convert basic cobalamin forms acquired in the diet such as |FRAME: CPD-315| and |FRAME: CPD0-1256| to the forms required by the enzymes. The cobalamin compounds are present at a very low concentration in the serum (30-700 nM), and thus are escorted by different chaperones from their point of entry and until they are delivered to the target enzymes |CITS: [17163662]|. , Cobalamin compounds derived from the diet are bound immediately upon ingestion to transcobalamin-1 (haptocorrin), a salivary glycoprotein encoded by the TCN1 gene. This protein escorts cobalamin through the stomach to the duodenum, where it is released by pancreatic proteases and binds to a second glycoprotein, the gastric intrinsic factor (GIF) |CITS: [2070790][11788601]|. The GIF-B12 complex is absorbed by intestinal mucosal cells via cubilin (CUBN)-receptor mediated endocytosis at the apical side of the brushborder membranes |CITS: [10080186]|. Following absorption, GIF is degraded, and the cobalamin appears in the blood stream, where it associates with either transcobalamin-1 (TCN1) or transcobalamin-2 (TCN2) |CITS: [338237]|. The TCN1-B12 complex is thought to remain in the serum, forming a cobalamin reservoir, while the TCN2-B12 complex is imported into the lysosome by a specific transcobalamin receptor encoded by the CD320 gene |CITS: [18779389]|. Inside the lysosome CD320 is recycled, and TCN2 is degraded, releasing the cobalamin |CITS: [19665918]|. It has been suggested that the passage through the acidic lysosome aids in converting the cobalamin compounds from the "base-on" configuration to a 'base-off' form. The export of cobalamin from the lysosome is enabled by a specific transporter, encoded by the LMBD1 gene (previously known as the cblF locus) |CITS: [19136951]|., About This Pathway, The first protein that binds cobalamin in the cytoplasm as the cofactor exits the lysosome is the multifunctional enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000132763-MONOMER CblC|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS13442| gene. The N-terminal domain of MMACHC is predicted to interact with the lysosomal LMBD1 transporter, allowing passage of cobalamin into the cytoplasm. The enzyme can bind all forms of vitamin B12 that are available in the cell and catalyze reductive decyanation of |FRAME: CPD-315| and dealkylation of alkylcobalamins, forming |FRAME: CPD-1829|, which remains bound to the enzyme. , |FRAME: CPD-1829 Cob(II)alamin| serves as the common precursor for both |FRAME: CPD-9037|, which is synthesized in the cytoplasm by the enzyme that requires it, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, and |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, which is synthesized in the mitochondria, where it acts as a cofactor for |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.2|. CblD, encoded by the |FRAME: HS15658| gene, binds to CblC (but only when |FRAME: CPD-1829| is bound to it) and serves as an adaptor protein supporting the cytoplasmic cobalamin trafficking pathway. CblD is reported to be a monomer in solution |CITS: [22832074][23415655]|, and its globular C-terminal domain is sufficient for its interaction with CblC and |CITS: [23415655]|. The C-terminal domain exhibits a structural fold very similar to that found in CblC |CITS: [26364851]|., The CblC-CblD complex is believed to deliver |FRAME: CPD-1829| directly to |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, which can convert it to methylcobalamin using the help of a repair enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.16.1.8| |CITS: [18264093]|. It is believed that CblD is responsible for diverting some of the |FRAME: CPD-20917 "CblC-cob(II)alamin"| molecules to the mitochondrion, where the cobalt is transferred to |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.17| (encoded by the |FRAME: HS13779| gene) |CITS: [23415655]|., Before the adenosylation of cobalamin can take place, the cobalt has to be reduced to the |FRAME: COB-I-ALAMIN| form. However, the midpoint redox potential of the Co2+/Co1+ couple is -610 mV, which is is too low for any known cellular reductant |CITS: [4489]|. The enzyme overcomes this thermodynamic barrier by displacing the |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| lower ligand after binding the compound |CITS: [19236001][15913339]|, generating a four-coordinate |FRAME: CPD-1829| intermediate, the reduction potential of which is higher by more than 250 mV than the free form, bringing it to within physiological range |CITS: [15954777][18672897]|. The cobalt is subsequently reduced to the +1 valence by free reduced flavins or non-specific flavoproteins |CITS: [19933577]|., The enzyme forms a tightly associated trimer, but only two of the three active sites are loaded with adenosylcobalamin |CITS: [17176040]|. The enzyme employes a rotary mechanism: the binding of ATP to the third site of an enzyme with two adenosylcobalamin-occupied sites, in the presence of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, leads to the transfer of one adenosylcobalamin molecule to the mutase |CITS: [19413290]|. This direct transfer overcomes the problem of delivering a very low concentration molecule, which would be inefficient if it relied on diffusion |CITS: [15950874][18264093]|., The transfer involves another protein, encoded by the MMAA gene (meaB in bacteria), which is assumed to play a role in gating the transfer reaction and ensuring that no other cobalamin compounds are transferred |CITS: [19665918][23873214]|., Disease, Inborn errors affecting synthesis of adenosylcobalamin result in a decreased function of methylmalonyl CoA mutase and accumulation of the hydrolysis product of its substrate, |FRAME: CPD-546|, while inborn errors affecting methylcobalamin result in a decreased activity of methionine synthase and accumulation of its substrate, |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|. Defects in early steps of the pathway result in accumulation of both compounds. Methylmalonic acidemia/aciduria (MMA), the result of |FRAME: CPD-546| accumulation, is associated with episodes of life-threatening metabolic acidemia and long-term development of neurologic and renal problems. When the defficiency results from defects in the |FRAME: HS13442| gene, it is referred to as cblC type methylmalonic aciduria. Mutations in |FRAME: HS13779| cause cblB type methylmalonic aciduria, and mutations in |FRAME: HS15658| result in cblD type methylmalonic aciduria.

Summary: General Background, The two primary bile acids biosynthesized in the human liver, |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189|, are further metabolized in the liver by conjugation to |FRAME: GLY|, or |FRAME: TAURINE| to form |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, or |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6061|). These conjugates are almost fully ionized at physiological pH and are therefore described as bile salts. Bile salts are concentrated in the gallbladder and are released into the duodenum upon stimulation by the hormone cholecystokinin. They promote digestion of dietary lipids in the small intestine and are then reabsorbed via the enterohepatic circulation., Intestinal anaerobic and facultatively anaerobic bacteria metabolize bile salts primarily by deconjugation and oxidation of hydroxyl groups. A small proportion of bile acids are not reabsorbed in the small intestine and enter the large intestine where they are metabolized to secondary bile acids such as |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7754|), or |FRAME: CPD-7235| (which is produced similarly from |FRAME: CPD-15189|). These secondary bile acids enter the bile acid pool. In some individuals they can accumulate to relatively high levels and may contribute to the pathogenesis of gastrointestinal diseases. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., Non-intestinal bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [9812981] [19683506]|, or the laboratory strain of the intestinal bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-511145|, also produce enzymes that can catalyze some of these transformations (see |FRAME: 7-ALPHA-HYDROXYSTEROID-DEH-CPLX|)., About This Pathway, Bile salts are deconjugated by bile salt hydrolases as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8135|. The benefit of deconjugation to the bacteria is the subject of a number of hypotheses., In addition, constitutively expressed hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases carry out oxidation and epimerization of hydroxyl groups at the 3, 7 and 12 positions of the bile acid steroid rings. These reactions convert (epimerize) hydroxyl groups from α to β positions via stable oxo-intermediates. Two distinct, stereospecific hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases are required for epimerization, and they may be from the same, or different species of bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-8255| and |FRAME: PWY-8256|.

Names: L-valine degradation III (oxidative Stickland reaction) // L-valine fermentation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, The branched-chain amino acids serve most often as substrates for the oxidative branch of the Stickland reactions, as indicated by formation of branched-chain fatty acids shorter by one carbon compared to the original amino acids (|FRAME: LEU| is an exception, as it participates in both branches). , As described above, the amino acid is first transaminated to a 2-oxoacid, which is oxidatively decarboxylated to an acyl-CoA, shutlling the electrons to ferredoxin., Already in 1948 it was shown that cell suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-1509| and related clostridia converted |FRAME: VAL| to |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE|, |FRAME: LEU| to |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|, and |FRAME: ILE| to |FRAME: CPD-7076| |CITS: [Cohen-Bazire48]|, results that were reproduced by multiple researchers over the years |CITS: [678022]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-8184| and |FRAME: PWY-8185|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE Caffeine| is found in several plant species including coffea, tea and cacao. The contents of caffeine vary greatly from cultivar to cultivar, tissue to tissue, and from different developmental stages. One mechanism that plants use to control caffeine level is by balancing between caffeine biosynthesis and degradation. The main |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation pathway has been proposed to proceed via |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE|, which is depicted here. In addition to the main caffeine degradation pathway, minor plant species-specific degradation pathways have also been proposed. All the proposed pathways were based on radio-tracer studies (reviewed in |CITS: [18068204][14977550]|). No enzyme activity has been detected or characterized to date., About This Pathway, In this main caffeine degradation pathway, caffeine is degraded by sequential removal of the three methyl groups, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: XANTHINE|. |FRAME: XANTHINE Xanthine| is further degraded to CO2 and NH3 (see |FRAME: PWY-5044|). 14C labeled theophylline was degraded to CO2 far more rapidly than 14C labeled caffeine, indicating the first step of the pathway is the rate-limiting step |CITS: [9305805]|.

With more than 750 known natural occurring carotenoids this group of compounds has gained attention not only because of the variety in structure, function and properties benefitting human health but also due to the fact that each carotenoid appears to have individual characteristics which cannot easily be replaced by compounds of similar structures |CITS:[Britton04]|. Besides |FRAME:CPD-7847| known to prevent oxidation of lipoproteins and considered an agent in preventing atherosclerosis |CITS:[11521685]| and possessing many more traits exploited in pharmacy, aquaculture, human food and animal feed (see |FRAME:PWY-5288| and |FRAME:PWY-7636|) there are further substituted ketocarotenoids along that line, i.e. 2,2;-hydroxylated ketocarotinoids which have shown great promise as pharmaceutical drugs |CITS:[16085816]|. Considering the value of such pharmaceutics which could not or only with great difficulties and costs be produced synthetically the genetic engineering or combinatorial biosynthesis in suitable hosts for the bio-production of such rare carotinoids has great scientific and economic appeal |CITS:[21429538] [25467956] [21673887]|. , The enzyme catalyzing the formation of 2- and 2'-hydroxylated ketocarotinoids, for instance |FRAME:CPD-17662|, |FRAME:CPD-17663|, |FRAME:CPD-17665| and |FRAME:CPD-17664| is the carotenoid 2-hydroxylase encoded by crtG which is able to decorate the 2- and 2'-positions of the β-ionone-rings of |FRAME:CPD-7852| and |FRAME:CPD-7847| with the corresponding hydroxyl groups |CITS:[16085816]|. All these compounds have been identified as natural ketocarotenoids in various α-proteobacteria such as Brevundimonas |CITS:[Yokoyama96]|. However, the crtG genes from various organisms even as close as the marine proteobacteria species Brevundimonas sp. SD212 and the soil-residing Brevundimonas vesicularis DC263 encode proteins with very different substrate preferences. In spite the very high sequence similarity between the crtG of SD212 and DC263 (79% amino acid identity) crtG from SD212 encoded a carotenoid 2-hydroxylase operating on ketocarotinoids (this pathway) whereas the same enzyme from DC263 2- and 2'-hydroxylated |FRAME:CPD1F-130| forming |FRAME:CPD-15033| via |FRAME:CPD-15032| (see |FRAME:PWY-7175|) |CITS:[16781830]|. The latter substrate preference has also been observed in the cyanobacterium Thermosynechococcus elongates |CITS:[18794175]| and the proteobacteria Sphingomonas elodea |CITS:[22509387]| where the crtG is also only involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15033|.

Summary: General Background, Many terpenoids have been identified in plants and fungi. More recently, a number of bacterial cyclic terpenes have been discovered, especially in the |FRAME: TAX-201174| (for example, this pathway and pathways |FRAME: PWY-5950|, |FRAME: PWY-6915|, |FRAME: PWY-6919| and |FRAME: PWY-5887|). These compounds are formed by variations of the common cyclization mechanism of terpene synthases that utilize the universal acyclic precursors geranyl diphosphate, farnesyl diphosphate, or geranyl geranyl diphosphate., The monoterpenoid |FRAME: CPD-14016| has an earthy, musty odor similar to |FRAME: CPD-10158|. Although it has no known biological function, its presence in water can impart an unpleasant taste. In addition to many |FRAME: TAX-201174|, |FRAME: CPD-14016| is also biosynthesized by some members of the |FRAME: TAX-1117| and |FRAME: TAX-29| |CITS: [21174459][21490938][18563898][18492804]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22039990]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| was shown to be converted to |FRAME: CPD-14016| in a two-step pathway catalyzed by the products of ORFs SCO7701 and SCO7700 in |FRAME: TAX-100226|. The proteins were expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, purified and characterized. Metabolites were analyzed by GC-MS and NMR techniques. It was demonstrated that product of SCO7701 catalyzes the |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent C-methylation of |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| to produce |FRAME: CPD-14015|. The terpene synthase encoded by SCO7700 then cyclizes the latter compound to |FRAME: CPD-14016| |CITS: [18563898]|., This pathway has also been experimentally demonstrated in several other species, including |FRAME: TAX-278992|, |FRAME: TAX-455632|, |FRAME: ORG-6218| and |FRAME: TAX-405948|. However, |FRAME: TAX-227882| was reported to be naturally deficient in this pathway as a result of gene deletion and insertion events |CITS: [18492804]|.

Summary: General Background, Protein glycosylation is an important process found in all kingdoms of life. N-glycosylation is found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria. During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. In eukaryotes, the nascent proteins that are synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane where they acquire the initial carbohydrate chains on specific asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes can be divided into the following three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (this pathway)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7918|)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7426|)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and use somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathway is in general similar to the eukaryotic one, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7658|)., About This Pathway, The eukaryotic biosynthetic pathway begins with the phosphorylation of dolichol, followed by stepwise addition of sugar residues to form the product dolichyl-diphosphooligosaccharide. This pathway is of particular interest in humans, because defects in the glycosyltransferases involved lead to congenital disorders of glycosylation. The genetic analysis of this pathway in a model organism, the budding yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|, has helped to elucidate the molecular basis of these disorders (reviewed in |CITS: [11306275]|). However, the enzymes that participate in this pathway are found in all eukaryotes |CITS: [26398792]|., In |FRAME: TAX-4932|, the polyisoprenol |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichol| contains 14 to 18 isoprene units, with 15 or 16 as the predominant components (|CITS: [4580884]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [9878760]|). It is synthesized from farnesyl diphosphate produced by the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5123| and |FRAME: PWY-6129|). Dolichol can be phosphorylated de novo to dolichyl phosphate by the CTP-mediated |FRAME: YMR013C-MONOMER|, the product of gene |FRAME: YMR013C| |CITS: [2657387][1323123]|. Dolichyl phosphate can also be regenerated by other reactions (reviewed in |CITS: [9878760]|)., Dolichyl phosphate is the essential carrier lipid for glycosyl residues. Each of the glycosyl residues is added by a specific glycosyltransferase |CITS: [10336995]|, (in |CITS: [15665075][15044395]|), reviewed in |CITS: [9878760][15189166]|. The substrate specificity of these enzymes results in a highly ordered assembly of glycosyl residues |CITS: [10336995]|. In |FRAME: TAX-4932|, Alg (Asparagine-linked glycosylation) mutants of the glycosyltransferases have been isolated and the accumulated dolichyl-diphospho-glycan intermediates analyzed. On the cytosolic side of the endoplasmic reticulum, glycosyltransferase |FRAME: YBR243C| adds phospho-N-acetylglucosamine to dolichol-P; |FRAME: G3O-28| and |FRAME: G3O-29| form a complex that adds N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [16100113][16100110][15615718]|; |FRAME: YBR110W| adds the first mannose residue; |FRAME: YGL065C| adds the second and third mannose residues |CITS: [16878994]|; and |FRAME: YNL048W| adds the fourth and fifth mannose residues |CITS: [16878994]|, creating the (mannosyl)5-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2-diphosphodolichol intermediate |CITS: [11278778]|, (reviewed in |CITS: [9878760]|). There is evidence that |FRAME: YBR110W|, |FRAME: YGL065C| and |FRAME: YNL048W| are physically associated in oligomeric complexes, suggesting a possible regulatory mechanism |CITS: [15044395]|., After the fifth mannose residue is added, the dolichol-diphospho-glycan is translocated (flipped) into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum by a "flippase". It has been initially thought that the flippase is encoded by the |FRAME: G3O-28923| gene, but that has proven incorrect, and the identity of the flippase is still unknown. Mannosyltransferases in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum, |FRAME: YBL082C|, |FRAME: YNL219C|, and |FRAME: YNR030W| use dolichyl β-D-mannosyl phosphate, synthesized by the product of gene |FRAME: YPR183W|, as a sugar donor to add other mannose residues. Also in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum, dolichyl β-D-glycosyl phosphate, synthesized by |FRAME: YPL227C|, is the sugar donor to add the three glucose residues via |FRAME: YOR002W|, |FRAME: YOR067C|, and |FRAME: YGR227W| (|CITS: [15987956]| and reviewed in |CITS: [9878760]|)., Note that the seven sugars added outside the ER are nucleoside-activated, while the seven sugars added inside the lumen are derived from individually charged and flipped phosphodolichol carriers., This core lipid-linked oligosaccharide, (glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2-diphosphodolichol (|FRAME: OLIGOSACCHARIDE-DIPHOSPHODOLICHOL|), is then transferred by the |FRAME: CPLX3O-10527| (OST) to asparagine residues within the recognition sequence asparagine-x-threonine/serine (N-X-T/S) on nascent polypeptides |CITS: [9405463][11580295]|. During the transfer |FRAME: Dolichol-PP| is released in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum, where it is cleaved by a dolichyl diphosphate phosphatase to |FRAME: DOLICHOLP|. Mechanisms for recycling of this dolichyl phosphate have been proposed |CITS: [18077451]|., In higher eukaryotes, further processing of the glycosylated, nascent polypeptide by enzymatic glucose addition and removal serves as a quality control mechanism for improperly folded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, although this mechanism appears to be modified in |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [9451025]|. Final glycosylation of properly folded proteins occurs in the Golgi (reviewed in |CITS: [8472892]|). In |FRAME: TAX-4932|, expression of the alg genes may also have a role in regulation of the cell cycle (reviewed in |CITS: [9878828]|).

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, Shiga toxin (Stx)-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) are an important group of intestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli strains. STEC strains cause diarrhea, bloody diarrhea, and, because of toxemia and not dissemination, the hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). , The |FRAME: CPD-24295| has the same structure as the main chain of the branched |FRAME: CPD-24294|, whose structure was reported in 1987. The O2 antigen differs only in the presence of a side-chain |FRAME: CPD-13886| residue |CITS: [3555792]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8251|)., The the O antigen biosynthetic cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2067429| was sequenced in 2010 |CITS: [20434495][20453897]| and that of |FRAME: TAX-1963785| in 2015 |CITS: [25428893]|. When the two sequences were compared it was found that the two clusters are nearly identical |CITS: [29787897]|. Both clusters contain genes involved in |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|, genes involved in |FRAME: PWY-6953|, three glycosyltransferase genes (|FRAME: G-81166|, |FRAME: G-81168|, and |FRAME: G-81169|), and the |FRAME: G-81165| and |FRAME: G-81167| genes |CITS: [20434495][20453897]|. However, the fdtB gene of |FRAME: TAX-1963785|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.90|, contains a point mutation resulting in a single amino acid change from histidine to arginine, which inactivates the enzyme and abolishes the production of |FRAME: CPD-15596| in this strain |CITS: [29787897]|.

Unlike the other pathways of microbial toluene degradation, which involves meta cleavage of the aromatic ring, the enzymes in this degradation pathway use ortho ring cleavage |CITS: [2019564]|., The initial step in this pathway involves the hydroxylation of toluene by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.236|, to form |FRAME: CPD-108| (p-cresol) |CITS: [1885512]|. p-Cresol is subsequently converted to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| by a flavocytochrome, |FRAME: EC-1.17.9.1| |CITS: [3790500]|. |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE "4-Hydroxybenzaldehyde"| is then oxidized by an NAD+- or NADP+-dependent dehydrogenase to form |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| |CITS: [2722739]|, which is hydroxylated to form |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|. General Background, |FRAME: CARNITINE L-Carnitine| is a ubiquitously occurring trimethylammonium compound that plays several roles in metabolism. Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and the name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes, plants, and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. In eukaryotes, among other roles, it is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The physiological role of carnitine in bacteria is still unknown |CITS: [9037756]|. Bacteria are able to metabolize carnitine in multiple ways., Various bacteria utilize an L-carnitine consuming pathway that forms |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| (see |FRAME: CARNMET-PWY|). In this pathway |FRAME: CARNITINE| is used as an alternative electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [Seim80][7815937][15731894]|. |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| accumulates and is released to the environment. When the pathway occurs in gut bacteria, the released |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| is degraded by other organisms in a pathway that releases |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA) (see |FRAME: PWY-8337|)., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-469| species, degrade L-carnitine in a reaction that produces |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| directly (this pathway). These organisms can use L-carnitine as a sole carbon source, but require an alternative nitrogen source |CITS: [25440057]|. This pathway is also used by some gut bacteria, but since the enzyme responsible for this transformation, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.239|, requires oxygen, the pathway is not significant in anaerobic environments |CITS: [24591617]|. It has been estimated that the previous pathway occurs at a rate that is almost 1000-fold higher than the direct formation of TMA |CITS: [25440057]|., Other bacteria, especially |FRAME:TAX-286| species, can assimilate and utilize L-carnitine as the sole source of both carbon and nitrogen. The first catabolic step in this pathway is catalysed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.108| (see |FRAME: PWY-3602|)., In another L-carnitine degradation pathway found in acetogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1736| the compound is demethylated. The methyl group is fed to the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"| |CITS: [32571881]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8307|)., About This Pathway, In some bacterial species, carnitine is metabolized to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: MAL| by cleavage of the C4-N bond. This pathway was first demonstrated in |FRAME:TAX-615| in 1966 |CITS: [5334176]|. Subsequently it was shown that |FRAME:TAX-471| 69/V can metabolize |FRAME: CARNITINE|, |FRAME: O-Acyl-L-Carnitines "O-acyl-L-carnitines"|, and |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE|, producing |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| in stoichiometric amounts |CITS: [Kleber77][Miura83]|., |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| was metabolized only in the presence of an additional carbon source such as L-carnitine. It was shown that in cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-471| there was enzymatic cleavage of the C4-N bond of |FRAME: CARNITINE|, |FRAME: D-CARNITINE|, |FRAME: CROTONO-BETAINE|, and |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| (but not |FRAME: BETAINE| or |FRAME: CHOLINE|) |CITS: [Seim82]|. Based on the data, a mechanism involving hydroxylation was proposed, that would result in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-16618| |CITS: [Englard83]|., Ditullio et al |CITS: [8000862]| found that D,L-carnitine was cleaved by a monooxygenase, resulting in formation of trimethylamine and malic semialdehyde. The initial step was a hydroxylation at carbon 4 requiring molecular oxygen., The resulting unstable intermediate spontaneously degrades to trimethylamine and malic semialdehyde, which is convereted to malate by a dehydrogenase. The oxidation of the semialdehyde regenerates the NAD(P)H with the formation of malate, and thus only catalytic concentrations of NAD(P)H are required for converting carnitine to trimethylamine and malate |CITS: [8000862]|., This pathway was reported to occur in the human gut by gut microbiota. However, while this pathway may be responsible for some TMA formation by γ-proteobacteria in the intestine using oxygen that diffuses into the luminal content, the pathway is unlikely to be significant in the mostly anoxic luminal intestinal environment due to its oxygen requirement. Furthermore, genes encoding |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.239|, have been identified only in facultative organisms and not in the many anaerobes that form the bulk of the gut microbiota |CITS: [28506279]|., Pathways that produce |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| in the human gut are particularly important because this compound is converted into |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| (TMAO) by liver flavin-containing monooxygenases (FMOs), especially |FRAME: HS00223| (see |FRAME: PWY-8292|). TMAO promotes atherogenesis through its interaction with macrophages and lipid metabolism |CITS: [23563705][23312283][23614584]|. High serum levels of TMAO have been shown to promote formation of atherosclerotic plaques in a mouse model |CITS: [21475195]|, and serum levels of TMAO were significantly correlated with the incidence of heart attack, stroke, and death in a clinical population |CITS: [24497336]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-3421 Genistin| is involved in the conjugation circle of |FRAME:CPD-3141| which facilitates the transportation, storage and bioactivation of the isoflavone in the metabolic grid of defense in plants (see |FRAME:PWY-2345|) |CITS:[11730862]|. In addition isoflavones such as |FRAME:CPD-3421| and further glucosylated derivatives are valuable pharmaceutical constituents in human food which have been shown to induce cancer cell apoptosis |CITS:[22953905]|, are considered nonhazardous  because of their non-teratogenic nature |CITS:[22617716]|, have anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative properties |CITS:[22644850]| and are appraised overall as dietary components exerting anti-invasive and anti-metastatic activities |CITS:[22314287]|., The genistin 1,6-glucosyltransferase which glucosylates the (1->6) position of the glucose moiety of |FRAME:CPD-3421| hence forming |FRAME:CPD-14848| is characterized as a multifunctional enzyme |CITS:[19561332]|. However, the regiospecificity of the glucosylation demonstrated towards a number of phenolics indicates the preference of flavonols and isoflavones. The occurrence and physiological role of the various flavonol gentiobiosides remains to be shown.

Summary: The Calvin cycle is the major |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation pathway, found in all in green plants and many autotrophic bacteria., In this cycle, one |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecule at a time is added to the acceptor molecule |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| (RuBP) generating two molecules of |FRAME: G3P|. The |FRAME: G3P| is then passed through a cyclic series of reactions in which the acceptor molecule (RuBP) is regenerated. Out of the six carbons present in two molecules of |FRAME: G3P|, five are recycled and only one remains available for biosynthesis. Since in each turn of the cycle only one carbon atom is assimilated, the cycle must go through three turns to produce one molecule of |FRAME: G3P|, or six turns to produce one molecule of a hexose sugar., The Calvin cycle can be divided into three stages: fixation, reduction and regeneration., In the first stage the reductive carboxylation of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| (RuBP) is catalyzed by the the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX2PN3-59| (RubisCO), forming 2 molecules of |FRAME: G3P|. , In the second stage these two molecules are phosphorylated to |FRAME: DPG| and then reductively dephosphorylated to |FRAME: GAP|. The process requires reducing power, in the form of NADPH, for the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.13|. The reducing power is provided by the |FRAME: PWY-101|., In three turns of the cycle 3 molecules of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| are fixed, and 6 molecules of |FRAME: GAP| are formed. Out of these, one is diverted to biosynthetic pathways, while the other 5 are used up in the next stage., The third stage is the most complicated one. It consists of a series of rearrangements that eventually regenerate RuBP., Some of the |FRAME:GAP| molecules are converted to |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|. |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| are then condensed into |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| which is dephosphorylated to |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|. |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| is then combined with another |FRAME: GAP| molecule and cleaved into |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| (X5P) and |FRAME:ERYTHROSE-4P|. The later is combined with |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| forming |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-1-7-P2|, which is dephosphorylated to |FRAME:D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|. , |FRAME:D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| is combined with |FRAME: GAP| and is cleaved into a second |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| and a |FRAME:RIBOSE-5P| (R5P). Both of these are converted into |FRAME:RIBULOSE-5P|, which is finally phosphorylated to |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|, regenerating the key |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|-acceptor molecule., During this cycle, especially during the day, |FRAME: G3P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, or |FRAME:GAP| can be siphoned off and sent out to the cytosol via the triose phosphates transporter for |FRAME: SUCSYN-PWY|. Plants need to carefully control the carbon flux between this and competeing pathways to make sure that the Calvin cycle can proceed |CITS: [19325167]|.

Summary: General Background, Bacteria often accumulate choline, since it can easily be converted to glycine betaine, a common osmoprotectant, in bacteria |CITS: [LeRudulier84]|., Many organisms can also catabolize glycine betaine, and can thus use choline as a sole source for both carbon, and nitrogen |CITS: [3290197] [6406829]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3661|)., While the conversion of choline to glycine betaine for the purpose of accumulating the later as an osmoprotectant is, considered biosynthetic (see |FRAME:BETSYN-PWY|, |FRAME:PWY-3722|, and |FRAME:PWY1F-353|), , the conversion of choline to glycine betaine for the purpose of further catabolism should be considered as a choline, degradation pathway. Two such pathways have been demonstrated: Certain Gram-negative bacteria, such as Synrhizobium meliloti degrade choline to glycine betaine using a combination of two different, dehydrogenases (see |FRAME:CHOLINE-BETAINE-ANA-PWY|), while certain Gram-positive bacteria, as well, as certain fungi, achieve this by the activity of a single enzyme, choline oxidase (this pathway)., About This Pathway, Ikuta et al have shown that |FRAME:TAX-1665| oxidizes choline to betaine aldehyde in a reaction, coupled with H2O2 generation and oxygen consumption. Betaine aldehyde was, further oxidized to glycine betaine through two distinct oxidative reactions, involving, H2O2 generation and oxygen consumption and NAD reduction |CITS: [197073]|., It was soon found that a single enzyme, choline oxidase, catalyzes both reactions |CITS: [599154]|., When the gene encoding choline oxidase from |FRAME:TAX-1677| was cloned and expressed in E., coli, it conferred on the host enhanced resistance to osmotic stress |CITS: [1987142]|. Furthermore, when the, same gene from A. globiformis was introduced into the the cyanobacterium |FRAME:TAX-1129|, |CITS: [8555454]| and the plant Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [9263456]|, the transformed organisms, accumulated glycine betaine and aquired enhanced resistance to salt and cold stress., However, the Gram-positive bacteria from which the genes were isolated do not accumulate glycine betaine., In these organisms choline is transformed to glycine betaine for the purpose further degradation, providing carbon, and nitrogen to the cells |CITS: [1987142]|., The gene encoding the choline oxidase of A. globiformis has recently been cloned and sequenced again, , exposing multiple errors in the original sequence. The gene was cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| in high, yields, enabling its purification to high levels |CITS: [14678796]|., A similar enzyme has also been purified from a fungus, Cylindron didymum M-1 |CITS: [Tani79][3306651]|., Choline oxidase activity has been demonstrated in several fungal species, including several strains of |FRAME:TAX-5506| , and |FRAME: TAX-5506| |CITS: [Tani79]|.

Summary: Beta-carbolines are indole alkaloids derived from tryptophan. They are found in plants as well as in , animals. This group of compounds has diverse biological activities and pharmacological properties , including sedative, antitumor, antiviral, and antioxitant |CITS: [17545209],[17305548]|. Enzyme activity in converting harmol to harmine , was also detected. However it is still not clear what steps are involved in converting tryptophan to , harmalol, the first beta-carboline synthesized in this pathway |CITS: [Berlin94]|.

Summary: General Background, Plants accumulate and mobilize starch in both photosynthetic tissue (leaves) and non-photosynthetic storage tissues (such as tuber and seed endosperm). In leaves, starch is synthesized during the light period and is degraded during the dark period. In storage tissues, starch is degraded during tuber sprouting and seed germinating. Except for seed endosperm where starch degradation occurs in an acellular tissue, starch degradation generally occurs in the plastids (chloroplast of leaves and amyloplast of tubers) where starch accumulates. Isoforms of the starch degradation enzymes are also found and in many cases abundant in extra-plastidic subcellular locations in leaves and tubers. Their physiological functions are not well understood |CITS: [20192737]|., About This Pathway, This pathway represents the starch degradation route present in the endosperm of cereal crops. Many details of the pathway as well as the relative importance of the four types of enzymes that contribute to this process, namely α-amylases, β-amylases, limit dextran debranching enzymes, and α-glucosidases, are still the subject of investigation and debate |CITS: [20192737][21098673]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycolysis, which was first studied as a pathway for the utilization of glucose, is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, the other two being the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| and the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. Glycolysis is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces six of the 13 precursor metabolites that are the starting materials for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules (the six compounds are |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:G3P|, |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). Glycolysis can be found, if at least in part, in almost all organisms., Even though glycolysis is often described starting with glucose, other hexoses (e.g. fructose) can also serve as input (as its name implies - glycose is a general term for simple sugars)., Glycolysis has evolved to fulfill two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) being an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism), it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy., This switching of direction is possible because all but two of the enzymatic reactions comprising glycolysis are reversible, and the conversions catalyzed by the two exceptions are rendered functionally reversible by other enzymes (|FRAME:F16B-CPLX "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase"| and |FRAME:PEPSYNTH-CPLX|) that catalyze different irreversible reactions flowing in the opposite direction., About This Pathway, This varant of glycolysis includes two enzymes that are different from those described in other variants: |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.90|, which provides an alternative to |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.11|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.9|, which provides a bypass between |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:G3P|. These enzyme are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, but are more common in lower eukaryotes and plants., In plants, glycolysis is the predominant pathway fueling respiration (see |FRAME:PWY-5690|) because, unlike animal mitochondria, plant mitochondria rarely respire fatty acids. In plants, this pathway occurs in two different subcellular locations: the cytosol and plastids, which are the sites of |FRAME:PWY-621| and |FRAME: PWY-6724|, respectively., Whereas the plastidic glycolysis pathway is identical to the conventional microbial glycolysis (see |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY|), the cytosolic pathway (i.e. this pathway) is slightly modified. These pathways can interact with one another though the action of highly selective transporters present in the inner plastid envelope |CITS:[Emes93]|., In chloroplasts in the dark, as well as in plastids of non-photosynthetic tissues, the primary function of the glycolitic pathway is the degradation of |FRAME:Starch| to generate carbon skeletons, reductants and ATP for anabolic pathways such as that of |FRAME:PWY-4381| via |FRAME:PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|. In the cytosol, the same products are generated from the degradation of |FRAME:SUCROSE|., In the cytosol, two enzymes catalyze alternative reactions to those of the plastidic pathway: |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.90| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.9|., The former enzyme, EC 2.7.1.90, provides an alternative to |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.11|; it utilizes |FRAME:PPI| rather than ATP to convert |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| to |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE|. The plant cytosol lacks soluble inorganic alkaline pyrophosphatases and, consequently, contains higher concentrations of |FRAME:PPI| (up to 0.3 mM |CITS:[WEINER87]|). It has been proposed that the utilization of pyrophosphate rather than that of ATP in glycolysis is favored under nutritional Pi deprivation or oxygen deficiency |CITS:[DAVIES93][15012287]|., The second enzyme, EC 1.2.1.9, provides a bypass between |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:G3P|, which allows for their conversion without phosphorylation by a non-phosphorylating glyceraldehyde 3-P dehydrogenase |CITS:[15012287][16927206]|. This reaction produces |FRAME:NADPH| but not |FRAME:ATP|.

It is incorporated into skeletal muscles and appears to largely compete with |FRAME: CPD-10244| (22:6n-3) for incorporation into lipids |CITS: [17459159]|., The biosynthesis of the 4-desaturated docosanoid fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-17364| (22:5n-6) and |FRAME: CPD-10244| (22:6n-3) were believed to proceed via a complex pathway requiring repeated use of the fatty acid desaturase encoded by the |FRAME: HS05918| gene to perform Δ6 desaturation on C24 fatty acids in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by 1 round of β-oxidation in the peroxisomes (see |FRAME: PWY-7726|)., However, it has been shown that the |FRAME: HS05918| gene product can directly 4-desaturate |FRAME: CPD-17323| (22:4n-6) to |FRAME: CPD-17365| (22:5n-6) |CITS: [26065859]|. This pathway is parallel to the |FRAME: PWY-7727|, pathway which involves ω3 docosanoid fatty acids.

Summary: General Background, The major pathway for fatty acid degradation in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans is fatty acid β-oxidation. However, pathways for fatty acid α-oxidation and ω-oxidation have also been characterized in plants and animals (see MetaCyc pathways under |FRAME: Fatty-Acid-Degradation|). A mammalian peroxisomal fatty acid α-oxidation pathway for β-methyl branched (3-methyl branched) long chain fatty acids is shown here. Because the presence of a methyl group at C-3 prevents the third step of β-oxidation, it is first removed by α-oxidation, allowing the fatty acid to enter β-oxidation (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]| and in |CITS: [17956236]|)., The most well studied substrate for this pathway is |FRAME: PHYTANATE| (phytanic acid), a branched chain, saturated fatty acid comprising a C16 backbone and four methyl groups, one of which is at the C-3 position. In humans it is not synthesized, but is obtained in the diet. |FRAME: PHYTANATE| is produced from |FRAME: PHYTOL|, a breakdown product of chlorophyll. |FRAME: PHYTANATE| is synthesized by rumen bacteria in ruminants, and is also found in marine animals. In humans |FRAME: PHYTANATE| derived from the diet is converted to |FRAME: CPD-206|. Humans can also metabolize |FRAME: PHYTOL| to |FRAME: CPD-206| (reviewed in |CITS: [16799769]| and |CITS: [21683154]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY66-389|). Other 3-methyl branched physiological substrates for peroxisomal α-oxidation have been postulated, but remain incompletely characterized. However several synthetic |FRAME: PHYTANATE| analogs have been shown to be utilized (|CITS: [7692128]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20558530]|)., A deficiency of peroxisomes, or key peroxisomal metabolic pathways can give rise to several disorders including Refsum's disease. This disease can be caused by mutations in gene |FRAME: HS03003|. Such mutations result in elevated phytanate levels that have pathological consequences (reviewed in |CITS: [16799769][20558530]|)., An ortholog of 2-hydroxyphytanoyl-CoA lyase encoded by gene |FRAME: HS05516| was identified in |FRAME:TAX-6239| suggesting that this peroxisomal α-oxidation pathway may also be present in invertebrates |CITS: [10468558]|., In addition to the α-oxidation of β-methyl branched fatty acids, 2-hydroxylated straight chain (unbranched) fatty acids may also undergo peroxisomal α-oxidation (see pathway |FRAME: PWY66-388|). These even numbered, long chain or very long chain fatty acids are oxidized to odd-chain-length fatty acids. Such 2-hydroxy fatty acids are found in a subset of mammalian sphingolipids where they are present as the N-acyl chain of ceramide (reviewed in |CITS: [20026285]|). A fatty acid 2-hydroxylase encoded by gene |FRAME: HS02454| was recently identified as a catalyzing this C-2 hydroxylation (|CITS: [15337768][15863841][15644336][21708296][22517924]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17956236]|)., About This Pathway, In the first step of this fatty acid α-oxidation pathway, a β-methyl branched long chain fatty acid (e.g. |FRAME: PHYTANATE|) that is present in plasma is taken up by the liver. It is activated to its |FRAME: CO-A| (CoA) derivative in mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum or peroxisomes. The exact acyl CoA synthetase(s) involved remain unclear, but the products of genes |FRAME: HS07766| and |FRAME: HS06695| (ACSVL1) can activate |FRAME: PHYTANATE|, as shown for the rat |CITS: [8978480]| and human |CITS: [10198260]| enzymes, respectively. In the second step the fatty acyl-CoA derivative (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-206|) is hydroxylated in the peroxisome by the product of |FRAME: HS03003| to produce a 2-hydroxy-fatty-acyl-CoA (e.g. |FRAME: 2-HYDROXYPHYTANOYL-COA|) (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|)., The lyase encoded by gene |FRAME: HS05516| then cleaves the 2-hydroxy-fatty-acyl-CoA to produce a fatty aldehyde (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-14674|) that has been shortened by one carbon unit (an n-1 aldehyde), and |FRAME: FORMYL-COA| |CITS: [9276483]|. An aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizes the aldehyde to the corresponding fatty acid (e.g. |FRAME: PRISTANATE|). It has been shown that peroxisomes contain pristanal dehydrogenase activity, as do mitochondria and microsomes |CITS: [11341778]|. No gene(s) has yet been identified that encodes this aldehyde dehydrogenase, although ALDH3A2 (FALDH) has been suggested |CITS: [9662422][17510064]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|., Following production of the shortened fatty acid by α-oxidation, it is again activated to its CoA ester. It remains to be established which isoform(s) of ASCL or ACSVL catalyzes this reaction, although ACSVL1 can activate |FRAME: PRISTANATE| |CITS: [10198260]|. The |FRAME: FORMYL-COA| is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: FORMATE| which is exported from the peroxisome to the cytosol and used in folate metabolism (see pathway )|FRAME: PWY-2201|). No hydrolase has been identified for this reaction, which may occur nonenzymatically (|CITS: [9276483]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21683154][20558530]|)., The shortened fatty acyl-CoA derivative (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-14675|) produced in peroxisomes, or a fatty acyl-CoA that was taken up into peroxisomes from the cytosol, can then undergo limited peroxisomal β-oxidation (three cycles in the case of |FRAME: CPD-14675|) |CITS: [9469587]|. Three types of fatty acids are known to undergo limited peroxisomal β-oxidation: |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids|; |FRAME: 2-Me-Branched-234-Sat-FA| (eg. |FRAME: PRISTANATE|); and the bile acid synthesis intermediates |FRAME: CPD-1834| and |FRAME: CPD-1836| (reviewed in |CITS: [20558530]|). The products of peroxisomal β-oxidation are then shuttled into mitochondria and undergo further rounds of β-oxidation by either carnitine-dependent or carnitine-independent routes. These routes are tissue-dependent (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|) (see pathway |FRAME: FAO-PWY|)., The enzymes of this pathway accept both R and S isomers of the substrates. However, if an acyl-CoA substrate contains a 2R-methyl branch, it must be converted to the 2S configuration by |FRAME: HS01416-MONOMER| (|FRAME: 5.1.99.4-RXN "EC 5.1.99.4"|) encoded by gene AMACR before it can undergo peroxisomal β-oxidation. This enzyme has been proposed to convert racemic |FRAME: PRISTANATE| to its S isomer before it enters peroxisomal β-oxidation (|CITS: [10191284]| and in |CITS: [16186124]|)., The various mechanisms of peroxisomal import and export of metabolites involved in this pathway are also under investigation and include the porin encoded by PXMP2, as well as carrier proteins such as that encoded by SLC25A17 (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|)., As noted above, long chain, or very long chain fatty acids hydroxylated at the C-2 position can also enter α-oxidation |CITS: [15337768]|. After CoA esterification and cleavage by the |FRAME: HS05516| encoded lyase, the resulting aldehyde joins the common pathway |CITS: [15644336][22517924]|.

Several enzymes depend on a covalently bound |FRAME: CPD0-2654 "pyruvoyl cofactor"| for activity |CITS: [5681461][1989676]|. These enzymes catalyze either the reduction or the decarboxylation of amino acids and amino acid derivatives., Pyruvoyl-dependent reductases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.2|, |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.3|, and |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.4|, have been described mostly from Gram-positive anaerobes performing Stickland reactions, although they can be found in Gram-negative bacteria, such as the |FRAME: CPLX-9661| of |FRAME: TAX-876|. Decarboxylases, such as |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.11|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.22|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.65|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.50|, have been described in a wide range of bacteria as well as in mammals., The pyruvoyl group is thought to act analogously to a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| cofactor by first forming a Schiff base between its carbonyl residue and the amino group of the substrate and then serving as an electron sink to facilitate the reaction |CITS: [338609]|. The pyruvoyl group is essential for catalytic activity and can be inactivated by carbonyl reagents. In many cases, the eukaryotic or archaeal homologs of these enzymes utilize |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| instead of the pyruvoyl group., Pyruvoyl-containing enzymes are expressed as proenzymes (also known as zymogens or π proteins), which undergo a post-translational self-maturation/cleavage that generates two chains, β and α (by convention β is the N-terminal chain and α is the C-terminal chain). An |FRAME: CYS| residue was shown to be the precursor of the pyruvoyl group in the reductases, while an |FRAME: SER| residue is the precursor in the decarboxylases |CITS: [11422384]|., While the exact process of pyruvoyl group formation in reductases (from an |FRAME: CYS| residue) is still not understood, the process is much better understood in the case of the decarboxylases. The self-cleavage reaction occurs through nonhydrolytic serinolysis, in which the side chain hydroxyl group of the serine residue attacks the C-N bond between the serine and the amino acid preceeding it, forming an oxyoxazolidine intermediate. Breakage of the C-N bond results in formation of an ester intermediate |CITS: [9546220][11583148]|, which is resolved by β-elimination, generating the two chains. The β chain ends with a carboxylate, in which pne of the oxygens originates in the side chain hydroxyl group of the serine residue. The remainder of that residue is attached to the N-terminus of the α chain as a 2-aminoprop-2-enoyl group. The last reaction converts that group to purovoyl group, releasing ammonia |CITS: [3944098]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CARNITINE L-Carnitine| is a ubiquitously occurring trimethylammonium compound that plays several roles in metabolism. Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and the name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes, plants, and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. In eukaryotes, among other roles, it is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The physiological role of carnitine in bacteria is still unknown |CITS: [9037756]|. Bacteria are able to metabolize carnitine in multiple ways., Various bacteria utilize an L-carnitine consuming pathway that forms |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| (this pathway). In this pathway |FRAME: CARNITINE| is used as an alternative electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [Seim80][7815937][15731894]|. |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| accumulates and is released to the environment. When the pathway occurs in gut bacteria, the released |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| is degraded by other organisms in a pathway that releases |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA) (see |FRAME: PWY-8337|)., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-469| species, degrade L-carnitine in a reaction that produces |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| directly (|FRAME: PWY-3641|). These organisms can use L-carnitine as a sole carbon source, but require an alternative nitrogen source |CITS: [25440057]|. This pathway is also used by some gut bacteria, but since the enzyme responsible for this transformation, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.239|, requires oxygen, the pathway is not significant in anaerobic environments |CITS: [24591617]|. It has been estimated that the previous pathway occurs at a rate that is almost 1000-fold higher than the direct formation of TMA |CITS: [25440057]|., Other bacteria, especially |FRAME:TAX-286| species, can assimilate and utilize L-carnitine as the sole source of both carbon and nitrogen. The first catabolic step in this pathway is catalysed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.108| (see |FRAME: PWY-3602|)., In another L-carnitine degradation pathway found in acetogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1736| the compound is demethylated. The methyl group is fed to the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"| |CITS: [32571881]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8307|)., About This Pathway, Under anaerobic conditions, in the absence of exogenous electron acceptors like nitrate, nitrite, fumarate, dimethyl sulfoxide or trimethylamine-N-oxide, some organisms are able to utilize |FRAME: CARNITINE| as the terminal electron acceptor. Early studies have shown that during anaerobic growth in the presence of carbon and nitrogen sources, |FRAME:TAX-562| is able to catalyze the dehydration and reduction of |FRAME: CARNITINE| to |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| via a cyclic pathway of CoA-linked intermediates. The carbon and nitrogen skeleton of carnitine is not assimilated, suggesting carnitine is used as an electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [7815937]|., The pathway was also demonstrated to operate in several members of the gut microbiota, including |FRAME: TAX-636|, |FRAME: TAX-84112|, |FRAME: TAX-564|, and |FRAME: TAX-102862| |CITS: [30530985]|. The product pof the pathway, |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE|, is exported by CaiT, an antporter that imports |FRAME: CARNITINE| and |FRAME: CROTONO-BETAINE| and exports |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE|. In the gut, |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| is processed by |FRAME: TAX-1776384| to form |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8337|) |CITS: [30530985]|.

Summary: Background, The cellulose and hemicellulose components of lignocellulosic biomass can be converted into soluble sugars during yeast and bacterial fermentation |CITS: [19429550]|. However, the degradation of these complex carbohydrates requires chemical and enzymatic pre-treatments to open up the structure of lignocellulosic biomass, which can produce side products such as furans and phenolics which are detrimental to the microbial fermentation process |CITS: [19684179]|., |FRAME: CPD-11572| is a dehydration product of hexose sugars and is toxic to cells, causing DNA damage and inhibition of glycolysis, especially in yeast |CITS: [19684179]|. The detoxification of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural would therefore benefit the industrial production of |FRAME: ETOH| from lignocellulosic biomass. Furthermore, a byproduct of |FRAME: CPD-11572| detoxification, |FRAME: CPD-14105| (FDCA), can form the polyester polyethylene furanoate (PEF), which is comparable to the well-known polyester polyethylene terephthalate (PET), which is generated from petroleum-based |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| |CITS: [20363622]|., About this Pathway, This pathway has been initially elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-68895| based on presumptive gene functions of the hmfFGH'H operon |CITS: [20194784]|. The hmfH gene encodes an FAD-dependent oxidase that was predicted to catalyze three oxidation eventsat the beginning of the pathway, converting |FRAME: CPD-11572| to |FRAME: CPD-14105|. In addition, mutants of |FRAME: TAX-68895| with disruptions in the hmfFG genes demonstrated that hmfFG expresses an FDCA decarboxylase |CITS: [20194784]|., To verify the functionality of this pathway, the characterized encoding genes from |FRAME: TAX-68895| were expressed in a heterologous host |FRAME: TAX-303|. The resulting strain was able to use 5-hydroxymethylfurfural as the sole carbon source |CITS: [20194784]|., In a subsequent study the hmfH gene from |FRAME: TAX-887061| was characterized in detail and confirmed to catalyze three oxidation events |CITS: [24271187]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| (CoA) is a cofactor of ubiquitous occurrence in plants, bacteria, and animals needed in, a large number of enzymatic reactions central to intermediary metabolism, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids. Coenzyme A is the common acyl carrier in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells required for a multitude of reactions for both biosynthetic and degradative pathways amongst others forming derivatives that are key intermediates in energy metabolism |CITS: [16415216]|., The biosynthesis of CoA is of equal importance with regard to its recognition as a target for antibacterial drug discovery and to the association of human neurodegenerative disorder with mutations in |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.33| |CITS: [15893380]|., About This Pathway, The CoA biosynthesis precursor |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| is an intermediate in the synthesis of |FRAME: VAL| (see |FRAME: VALSYN-PWY|). This compound is converted in two steps to |FRAME: L-PANTOATE|, as shown in |FRAME: PANTO-PWY|., The latter is converted into |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| is two steps, involving a β-alanine ligase and a kinase., In most organsims the ligase acts before the kinase (|FRAME: EC-6.3.2.1| followed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.33|, as described in |FRAME: PANTO-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-3961|. However, in archaea the order is reversed, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.169| acts before |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.36|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6654|., The kinases are feedback inhibited by CoA itself, accounting for the primary regulatory mechanism of CoA biosynthesis., The addition of |FRAME: CYS| to |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE| (PPC), is followed by decarboxylation of PPC to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|. The ultimate reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.24|, which converts 4'-phosphopantetheine to CoA. All enzymes of this pathway are essential for growth., The reactions in the biosynthetic route towards CoA are identical in most organisms, although there are differences in the functionality of the involved enzymes. In plants every step is catalyzed by single monofunctional enzymes, whereas in bacteria and mammals bifunctional enzymes are often employed |CITS: [16415216]|.

Summary: This pathway is widely spread, and is found in archaea, bacteria and eukarya., When halophilic archaea grow on glucose they form |FRAME:ACET| which is excreted into the medium. This conversion is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.13| (see |FRAME: PWY-5535|). In stationary phase the cells consume the excreted acetate, in a pathway that involves its conversion back to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|. This reverse reaction is not catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7000|, but by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.1|, which forms AMP |CITS:[11409546]|., In yeasts, respiratory dissimilation of |FRAME:PYRUVATE| is initiated by its conversion into |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, which occurs either a direct reaction catalyzed by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, or via an indirect route, involving pyruvate decarboxylase, acetaldehyde dehydrogenase and acetyl-coenzyme A synthetase |CITS:[13522696][8012582]|., Acetate plays multiple roles in the metabolism of |FRAME: TAX-83333|. In the absence of other substrates acetate can serve as a total source of carbon and energy. The acs pathway (named after the |FRAME: EG11448| gene, which encodes |FRAME: ACS-MONOMER| in this organism) is an inducible pathway that plays a major role in the aerobic utilization of acetate. Mutant strains blocked in the acs pathway grow poorly on acetate. Mutants blocked in both pathways are unable to grow on acetate. Because it is a high-affinity system, the acs pathway is the major scavenger of acetate when extracellular concentrations of it are low. It also enables |FRAME:TAX-562| to utilize |FRAME:PROPIONATE|.
