Summary: General Background, One of the most striking physiological differences between the archaea and other organisms is the structure of their, membrane lipids. The most exclusive feature of archaeal phospholipids is their |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, backbone, which is an enantiomer of the |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| used by bacteria and eukaryotic organisms. It has been suggested that archaea and bacteria were differentiated by the occurrence of cells enclosed by membranes of phospholipids with |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| as a backbone, respectively |CITS: [9419225]|., Other features that are unique to archaeal phospholipids include side chains that are derivatives of isoprenoid alcohols rather than fatty acids, which are linked by ether linkages (rather than ester linkages) to the glycerophosphate backbone |CITS: [358256]|. The isoprenoids are usually modified by saturation of the double bonds - a modification that is believed to increase the ability of the lipids to survive the extreme conditions that archaea often face. Another unique feature is the occurrence of bipolar lipids with a tetraether core, which are present in significant numbers in archaeal species., In contrast to these differences, most of the polar head groups of archaeal phospholipids are similar to those found in the other kingdoms - |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CHOLINE| |CITS: [17347520]|., The major polar lipids of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-145262| are L-serine, ethanolamine, or myo-inositol-containing di- and, tetraether type phospholipids and phosphoglycolipids, and gentiobiose-containing di- and tetraether type glycolipids., Examples of non-glycosylated lipids include |FRAME: CPD-10741 "archaetidylserine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11919 "archaetidylethanolamine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11918 "archaetidylinositol"| and |FRAME: CPD-11920 "archaetidylglycerol"|., About This Pathway, The pathway leading to the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10740 "CDP-archaeol"| is described in |FRAME: PWY-6349|., CDP is replaced with |FRAME: SER| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-14511| resulting in formation of either |FRAME: CPD-10741| or |FRAME: CPD-15257| |CITS: [12562787]|. The enzyme's activity has been characterized in extracts of |FRAME: TAX-145262| cells, and a candidate gene (|FRAME: G-11080|) has been proposed, although this proposed function has not been confirmed yet |CITS: [12562787]|., A gene next to |FRAME: G-11080| is homologous to the bacteria gene that encodesl |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.65|, and thus has been identified putatively as encoding an |FRAME:MONOMER-15157|, which is believed to transform |FRAME: CPD-10741 archaetidylserine| to |FRAME: CPD-11919 archaetidylethanolamine| in this organism |CITS: [16243780]|.

Summary: Trichomonads are anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes that lack mitochondria, and instead possess hydrogenosomes, unusual organelles that are bound by double membranes, but do not contain DNA. Hydrogenosomes have been referred to as the "anaerobic equivalent of the mitochondrion". Hydrogenosomes are characterized by anaerobic pyruvate metabolim, and the use of protons as electron acceptors, producing molecular hydrogen |CITS: [4750424 ]|., In the eukaryotic unicellular organism |FRAME: TAX-5722|, the key step of |FRAME:PYRUVATE| oxidative decarboxylation, with formation of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, is catalyzed by the hydrogenosomal protein |FRAME: CPLX-7459| (PFO) and not by the ubiquitous pyruvate dehydrogenase multienzyme complex., The |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| that is formed is not degraded to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| via the |FRAME:TCA|, but is converted into |FRAME:ACET| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-13300| (ASCT), an enzyme that transfers the CoA group from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME:SUC|, producing |FRAME: SUC-COA| |CITS: [Muller88]|., The phosphorylation reaction of |FRAME:CPLX-7458| is crucial for the organisms, as it harnesses the energy liberated from the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate |CITS: [1898409]|., Several other organisms have been shown to utilize this pathway, including other hydrogenosome-containing trichomonads |CITS: [3090435]| and the anaerobic fungus |FRAME: TAX-73818| |CITS: [8257282]|.

It is the most prevalent salicylate compound in certain northern willows |CITS: [12921436]|. Studies related to this compound have been undertaken in a number of species including |FRAME: TAX-339964|, |FRAME: TAX-77065|, |FRAME: TAX-75715|, and |FRAME: TAX-3691| |CITS: [12921436][ZENK67][20177744]|. In general, a number of different phenolic glycosides, including |FRAME: CPD-13173| and |FRAME: CPD-1142| can accumulate to extremely high levels in leaves of |FRAME: TAX-3689| and |FRAME: TAX-40685| species, with exact levels of specific PGs varying based on genotype, environment, time of day, and developmental stage |CITS: [17226439][11504029][16724272][5886251]|. Interestingly, there is evidence that the creation of large amounts of these compounds may impose a metabolic cost that can negatively impact plant growth |CITS: [11504029][16411958]|, suggesting that plants must finely tune PG biosynthesis to maximize overall fitness., |FRAME: CPD-1142 Salicin| may deter herbivore attack when it is hydrolyzed by β-glucosidases to |FRAME: CPD-173| in insect guts, possibly leading to the formation of gut lesions |CITS: [12921436]|., The pathways of PG biosynthesis, including |FRAME: CPD-1142| and |FRAME: PWY-6763 salicortin| biosynthesis have been explored over many years often through the use of radioactive tracers |CITS: [16748997][ZENK67][20177744][12921436]|. Summary: General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , Under pathogen or herbivore attacks, cyanogenic glycosides are cleaved, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN|, which serves as the first line of chemical defense., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME: LINAMARIN Linamarin| and |FRAME: CPD-10277| have a broader distribution in the plant kingdom than most cyanogenic glycosides. They have been reported in five plant families, and co-exist in lotus, flax and cassava (|FRAME: TAX-3983|), the most important tropical root crop., Over-dose eating of cyanogenic glycoside-containing plants by animals and humans can be lethal. The high linamarin content in cassava hinders its direct consumption. It is thus highly desired to reduce the linamarin level possibly by metabolic engineering., Studies using seedlings indicated that linamarin is synthesized in the cotyledons and transported to the other tissues in cassava. In |FRAME:TAX-34305|, linamarin and lotaustralin are synthesized and stored in young growing tissues like seedlings, apical leaves and stems. They are not transported to other tissues. Roots and dry seeds contain no detectable cyanogenic glucosides.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-7425 Coenzyme F430| is a nickel containing tetrapyrrole cofactor, which is present in all methanogenic, bacteria. It was initially observed in 1977 by Jean LeGall in extracts of |FRAME: TAX-145262|. The name factor 430 (F430) was coined by Gunsalus and Wolfe who reported the absorbance maximum at 430 nm |CITS: [Gunsalus78]|. The compound belongs to the corphins, a class of compounds that combine structural elements of both corrins and porphyrins |CITS: [Eschenmoser86]|., In 1982 Ellefson et al showed that |FRAME:CPD-7425| is a cofactor of the enzyme methyl-coenzyme M reductase (see |FRAME: CPLX-664| and |FRAME: CPLX-668|) |CITS: [6954513]|. This enzyme catalyzes the final step of methane production in all methanogenic bacteria: the reduction of the methyl group in |FRAME: Me-CoM| to |FRAME:CH4|., F430 exists in two distinct intracellular pools: either bound to methyl-CoM reductase or free of protein in the cytosol. Early literature on F430 was confusing due to reports of heterogeneity in F430 samples that depended on the isolation and purification procedures used in different laboratories. Later work showed that F430 exists primarily in two isomeric forms. These forms differ in the relative stereochemical disposition of acid side chains at positions 12 and 13 |CITS: [3356701]|., The biosynthetic route leading to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-7425| has not been elucidated completely until 2016. It has been shown early on that it is produced from |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| (which in methanogens is synthesized from |FRAME:GLT|), through the intermediate |FRAME:DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| |CITS: [ 7212929][7428919][Jaenchen81][7842854]|. A plausible scheme for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-7425| from |FRAME:DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| has been proposed in 1987 |CITS: [3691535]|, but eventually found incorrect |CITS: [27846569]|., The pathway proceeds from |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| to |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| as in |FRAME: PWY-5194| and |FRAME: PWY-5507 "anaerobic adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis"|. However, at this step a nickel-specific chelatase catalyzes nickelochelation, followed by amidation to form |FRAME: CPD-7590|. Next, a primitive homolog of nitrogenase catalyzes a six-electron reduction and γ-lactamization reaction, followed by the final reaction, which forms the six-membered carbocyclic F ring |CITS: [27846569]|.

Summary: Oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) are among the most conserved sterol biosynthetic enzymes at the sequence level, and homologues have been detected in all species capable of sterol synthesis., There are two main types of sterols-producing OSCs based on the end product of the cyclization: |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.7|, which is found in animals, fungi, choanozoa, trypanosomatids, dinoflagellates, and some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-414|; and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.8|, which is found in higher plants, red and green algae, amoebozoa, diatoms, euglenids, heterolobosea and some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-41| (see |FRAME: PWY-8028|) |CITS: [12519197][24596261]|. A rare third type is |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.47| |CITS: [21526825]|., The reaction catalyzed by OSCs is remarkably complex |CITS: [16754609]|. The key steps in the cyclization include:, 1. Positioning of squalene 2,3-epoxide in a prefolded configuration within the active site., 2. Protonation of the epoxide group by a catalytic acid., 3. Ring formation, during which cation intermediates are stabilized by cation–π interactions with aromatic residues of the active site, followed by migration of the cation out to C20., 4. Skeletal rearrangement via hydride- and methyl-shifts (largely spontaneous) as the proton migrates back to a region of high π-electron density around the B/C rings., 5. Deprotonation by basic residues to quench the final protosteryl cation; the position of the deprotonation determines the OSC product (lanosterol versus cycloartenol)., It has been proposed that the ancestral sterol biosynthesis pathway produced cycloartenol as a final product, and that the evolution of the pathway beyond cycloartenol took place only as a result of the rising concentrations of oxygen in the atmosphere following the onset of photosynthesis |CITS: [9383366]|.

Summary: The sequence of reactions in the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway may vary.  This pathway shows one possible , variant of cholesterol biosynthesis.  This and other alternate routes exist because reduction of the , carbon 24,25 double bond on the hydrocarbon side chain of the sterol ring structure by sterol , Δ<sup>24</sup>-reductase can occur at multiple points in the pathway, giving rise to different , intermediates.  These intermediates, with or without a double bond in the hydrocarbon side chain, can serve , as substrates for the other enzymes in the pathway.  However, there is evidence that the preferred point of , carbon 24,25 double bond reduction is directly after the isomerization of zymosterol |CITS: [9291139]|, as shown , in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-341|.  In |CITS: [11519011]| and reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|., In the pathway shown here reduction of the carbon 24,25 double bond in the hydrocarbon side chain occurs in the , last reaction, converting desmosterol to cholesterol.  This pathway represents the reactions in a , frequently published order.  The isomerase reaction is followed by the Δ<sup>5</sup>-desaturase, , the Δ<sup>7</sup>-reductase (producing desmosterol) and the Δ<sup>24</sup>-reductase, , producing cholesterol (reviewed in |CITS: [11969204], [RILLING85] [Salway04]|).  This pathway variation is , evidenced by the genetic disorder desmosterolosis.  In this disorder, patients have elevated levels of desmosterol , in their plasma and tissues due to mutations in the Δ<sup>24</sup>-reductase gene |CITS: [11519011]|.  , Another variation of the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway involves reduction of the Δ<sup>24</sup> , double bond at the point of lanosterol, producing 24,25-dihydrolanosterol.  Metabolism of this compound is shown , in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-3|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SUCROSE Sucrose| is an important disaccharide in plants and plays a major role in moving carbon through the plant via the phloem from "source" tissues such as photosynthesizing leaves to "sink" tissues such as roots |CITS:[23393426]|. In the light, triose phosphate, the product of photosynthetic carbon fixation, is transported from the chloroplast into the cytoplasm where it is transformed to hexose phosphate by enzymes of the gluconeogenesis pathway. These hexoses are then used in |FRAME: SUCSYN-PWY sucrose biosynthesis|. However, as shown in this pathway, |FRAME: SUCROSE| is also produced from the |FRAME: PWY-6724 degradation of starch reserves| using |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: GLC| exported from the chloroplast |CITS:[23393426]|., About This Pathway, During |FRAME: PWY-6724 starch breakdown| in the chloroplast, |FRAME: MALTOSE| and |FRAME: GLC| are liberated through a cascade of different enzymatic reactions. |FRAME: MALTOSE| can then be transported to the cytosol via |FRAME: AT5G17520-MONOMER MEX1| while |FRAME: GLC| can be transported by |FRAME:AT5G16150-MONOMER pGlcT|. , In the cytosol, the |FRAME: MALTOSE| is used by |FRAME: AT2G40840-MONOMER DPE2| to attach glucosyl units to the poorly defined class of compounds referred to as |FRAME: Soluble-Heteroglycans Soluble HeteroGlycans| (SHG). This liberates one glucose directly, but |FRAME: AT3G46970-MONOMER PHS2| can also liberate the deposited glucose from SHG in the form of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS: [16980562][23393426][16640603]|. This can then be used in a series of reactions shared with the other |FRAME: SUCSYN-PWY sucrose biosynthesis pathway|. Namely, |FRAME: GLC-1-P| can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-12575| and then |FRAME:SUCROSE| via a |FRAME: SUCROSE-6P| intermediate. , Meanwhile, the |FRAME: GLC| derived from |FRAME: PWY-6724 starch degradation| can be converted to |FRAME: GLC-6-P| vias the activity of cytosolic hexokinase. This product can also then be funneled toward the production of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| via the activity of a |FRAME: AT5G51820-MONOMER phosphoglucomutase|. , There is another enzyme that can form sucrose - |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.13|. However, the name of this latter enzyme is misleading, since it has been shown that under most physiological conditions it catalyzes a sucrose cleavage reaction, and is thus involved in sucrose degradation |CITS: [plantbiochemistry97]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3801|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-14817 Emetine| and |FRAME: CPD-14816|, known as ipecac alkaloids, belong to monoterpenoid-isoquinoline alkaloids. They are normally found in root extracts of |FRAME: TAX-77880|, a medicinal plant native to South and Central America. Both emetine and cephaeline exhibit pharmacological activities, and are used as an emetic after poisoning, an expectorant in treating cough and asthma, and an amebicide in treating amoebic dysentery (Drugstore museum). Emetine was also shown to be apoptosis-inducing |CITS: [17912675][17671728]|, and thus a potential candidate in treating cancers., The biosynthetic pathway of emetine was proposed based on the integration of kinetic properties of the recently cloned three methyltransferases |CITS: [20061395]| and one beta-glucosidase |CITS: [18927081]|. No data is available on the in vivo role(s) of any of the cloned enzymes. The pathway starts from the condensation of dopamine and secologanin. The condensation yields two epimers, the (S)-deacetylisoipecoside and the (R)-deacetylipecoside. The (S)-epimer is further converted to ipecac alkaloids such as cephaeline and epemine (depicted here), whereas the (R)-epimer gives rise to alkaloidal glucosides such as ipecoside and alangiside |CITS: [20061395]|.

Summary: The production of |FRAME: BUTANOL| by solvent-producing |FRAME: TAX-186801| strains is well documented (see |FRAME: PWY-6583|). Starting from acetyl-CoA, the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME:THLCLOS-CPLX "thiolase/acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase"| (|FRAME:G-96|), |FRAME: CPLX-7035 "3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase"| (|FRAME:G-97|), |FRAME:CPLX-41 crotonase| (|FRAME: G-98|), |FRAME: BCDCLOS-MONOMER "butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase"| (|FRAME: G-93|), and |FRAME: MONOMER-15847 "alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase"| (|FRAME:G-12174|). Expressing these genes in |FRAME:TAX-562| resulted in successful production of |FRAME: BUTANOL| |CITS: [17942358][18060402]|., A higher-titer of |FRAME: BUTANOL| production (15-30 g/L) was achieved by replacing |FRAME: G-93| with the |FRAME:MONOMER-16778| from |FRAME: TAX-3039| (|FRAME:G-14619|), which directly utilizes NADH as the reducing equivalent, and by artificially building up NADH and acetyl-CoA as driving forces |CITS: [21398484]|. , In this synthetic pathway, the butanol pathway has been extended to support the production of |FRAME: HEXANOL-CMPD| |CITS: [21707101]|. The key additional enzyme is a |FRAME: MONOMER-16779| from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-106590| (|FRAME: G-14620|). This enzyme catalyzes the additon of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|, forming |FRAME: K-HEXANOYL-COA|. The product is then processed by the same enzymes of the butanol production pathway, namely |FRAME: G-97|, |FRAME: G-98| and |FRAME: G-14619|, resulting in |FRAME: HEXANOYL-COA|. Finally, the |FRAME: MONOMER-15847| (|FRAME: G-12174|) catalyzes the reduction steps leading to |FRAME: HEXANAL| and |FRAME: HEXANOL-CMPD|., Further improvements of the producing strain included deletion of the |FRAME: EG10031|, |FRAME: G592|, |FRAME: EG10330| and |FRAME: EG10331| genes and overexpression of the |FRAME: EG10285| gene to increase the NADH availability, and deletion of the |FRAME: EG20173| gene to increase acetyl-CoA availability. The strain produced 47 mg/L of 1-hexanol (at 48 h) under anaerobic conditions. This strain also produced 5.1 g/L of 1-butanol during the same period |CITS: [21707101]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17730| is one of the nonproteinogenic amino acid residues which form the cyclic hexapeptide skeleton of the |FRAME: Echinocandins echinocandins|. Echinocandins represent a family of fungal cyclic lipo-hexapeptides characterized by their fungicidal and fungistatic properties against ascomycetes of the genera Candida and Aspergillus, respectively |CITS:[25156669] [23463246]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17711| (see |FRAME:PWY-7650|) is closely related to the biosynthesis of its amino acid building blocks supported by the presence of two independent gene clusters involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-17711|, i.e. the echinocandin (ecd) gene cluster and the L-homotyrosine (hyt) gene cluster |CITS:[22998630]|. , Out of the six amino acid residues integrated in the hexapeptide scaffold four are nonproteinogenic and either mono-, or dihydroxylated. The nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) encoded by EcdA in Emericella rugulosa adds successively |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, |FRAME:THR|, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE|, |FRAME:CPD-17730| (this pathway), again |FRAME:THR| and finally |FRAME:CPD-17747| (see |FRAME:PWY-7648|) to the growing peptide chain |CITS:[22998630]|. , The two independent gene cluster for the |FRAME:PWY-7650| ecd and hty |CITS:[22998630]| are both involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17730|. |FRAME:CPD-17730| is the fourth amino acid to be added to the peptide chain and indispensable for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17711| as demonstrated by knock-out experiments. The gene HtyA from Emericella rugulosa, a putative 2-(4-hydroxybenzyl)-malate synthase was identified using the isopropyl-malate synthase (IPMS) from Mycobacterium and shown, when disrupted, to abolish |FRAME:CPD-17711| production. Bioinformatics analysis corroborated that also the following genes HtyD (2-(4-hydroxybenzyl)-malate isomerase), HtyC (3-(4-hydroxybenzyl)-malate dehydrogenase) and HtyB (4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-oxobutanoate transaminase) are involved in the biosynthetic sequence to yield |FRAME:CPD-17729|. However, experimental evidence for the involved enzymes remains to be provided |CITS: [22998630]|. , The last step in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17730| is the 3-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17729|. The gene cluster for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17711| (ecd) contained three predicted genes (EcdG, EcdH, EcdK) presumably participating in the oxidative tailoring of the echinocandin backbone or the amino acids forming the respective cyclolipohexapeptide scaffold. It could be shown that the EcdG encoded nonheme iron oxygenase hydroxylated the 3-position of |FRAME:CPD-17729|, hence acted as L-homotyrosine-3-hydroxylase. In addition, it could be shown that the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17730| including all the hydroxylation steps is completed before its integration into the growing lipo-peptide chain |CITS:[23451921]|. Not unexpected, the genes necessary for biosynthesizing |FRAME:CPD-17729| have also been found to be involved in the biosynthesis of a close relative of |FRAME:CPD-17711|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17738| indicating the similarities between the two biosyntheses |CITS:[ 23688303]|. Moreover, structure-activity relationship investigations of the amino acid residues in the lipo-hexapeptide backbone of |FRAME:CPD-17711| and related semisynthetic derivatives revealed that the |FRAME:CPD-17730| residue is central for the inhibition of the 1,3-β-glucan synthase |CITS:[1495015]|.

Summary: Choline is a fundamental metabolite in plants because of its contribution to the synthesis of the membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylcholine, which accounts for 40 to 60% of lipids in non-plastid plant membranes |CITS: [12215503]|. Choline is also a precursor for the formation of glycine betaine (|FRAME:PWY1F-353|) in certain plants such as spinach, where this osmoprotectant is accumulated and confers also tolerance to salinity, drought, and other environmental stresses. In addition choline has been recognized as an essential nutrient for humans |CITS: [11481443]|., The choline biosynthetic pathway enables plants to decouple choline synthesis from lipid metabolism (Kennedy pathway - FRAME: TRIGLSYN-PWY|) and provides them with the metabolic flexibility to adapt to environmental conditions where large and variable amounts of choline are beneficial for survival |CITS: [11461929]|., The first step in choline biosynthesis is the direct decarboxylation of serine to ethanolamine |CITS: [11461929]|, which is catalyzed by a serine decarboxylase unique to plants |CITS: [14634155]|. Ethanolamine is widely recognized as the entrance compound to choline biosynthesis. The synthesis of choline from ethanolamine may take place at three parallel pathways, where three consecutive N-methylation steps are carried out either on free-bases |CITS: [PRUDHOMME92A]|, phospho-bases |CITS: [10799484]|, phosphatidyl-bases |CITS: [11481443]| or a mixture of the latter |CITS: [Datko88a]| |CITS: [Datko88b]|. , The biosynthesis of choline appears to be regulated by a feedback response of phosphocholine inhibiting its own synthesis by decreasing N-methyltransferase (PEAMT) activities involved in the pathway |CITS: [10799484]|. The activity of PEAMT was considerably increased when plants were exposed to salt stress |CITS: [10799484]| |CITS: [12232019]|, which is consistent with the high demand for choline as osmoprotectant precursor in such plants., The release of choline from the different pathway levels is species-specific. Phosphocholine can either be directly dephosphorylated to release choline as observed in spinach |CITS: [12232019]| or incorporated into phosphatidylcholine with the subsequent release of choline, as in tobacco |CITS: [10806254]|.

General Background, Sialic acids are a family of polyhydroxylated α-keto acids that contain nine carbon atoms. Most sialic acids are derivatives of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, or |FRAME: CPD-21259| (KDN). |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is the most common sialic acid in mammals (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6138|), while KDN is abundant in lower vertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Their core structures can be modified at the hydroxyl groups, lactonized, or hydroxylated at the acetamido group, generating many derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-262| is a derivative of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6144|). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Sialic acids are found mainly in vertebrates and a few higher invertebrates (ascidians and echinoderms). These acidic sugars are usually the terminal sugar residue in the glycan chains of vertebrate glycoconjugates (mostly glycoproteins and glycolipids, but also proteoglycans and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors). They function in mediating cellular recognition and adhesion events for many important processes such as development, the immune and inflammatory responses, and oncogenesis. Sialic acid occurs rarely in invertebrates. Endogenous sialylation has been shown to occur in |FRAME: TAX-7215|, but details of sialic acid biosynthesis in this organism remain to be determined |CITS: [18568399]|. However, it is possible the sialic acids might be biosynthesized by other eukaryotes in a species and/or life cycle-dependent manner. In |CITS: [7841794]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Most bacteria do not biosynthesize sialic acids, but some pathogenic, or symbiotic bacteria biosynthesize sialic acids as a means of evading a host's immune system (this pathway). The sialic acid is displayed on the bacterial cell surface (in capsular polysaccharides) in order to mimic vertebrate cells. Pathogens that biosynthesize sialic acids include |FRAME: TAX-487|, |FRAME: TAX-1392869| and |FRAME: TAX-197|. In addition, the human gut symbiont |FRAME: TAX-818| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-21259| |CITS: [18804026]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Whether or not archaea contain sialic acids remains to be determined (reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|). Other sialic acid-like sugars biosynthesized by bacteria include the nonulosonic acids |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [16751642]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|) and legionaminic acid see pathway class |FRAME: CMP-Legionaminate-Biosynthesis| |CITS: [18275154]|., Protists are thought to lack the ability to biosynthesize sialic acids although more genome data are needed to confirm this. Sialic acids have been thought to be absent in plants but some studies raise the possibility |CITS: [18258224]|. Fungi appear to lack any known sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, although strain-specific, or novel pathways could exist. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Also, see |FRAME: PWY-6145|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-316275| is a Gram-negative, psychrophilic fish pathogen whose genome sequence has been determined |CITS: [19099551]|. Little is known about its mechanism of virulence. This organism contains three copies of a gene cluster that is homologous to the Escherichia coli neu gene cluster for the synthesis of capsular sialic acids (see |FRAME: PWY-6139|). In |FRAME: TAX-316275| the first copy of the gene cluster, neu1, is also likely involved in sialic acids biosynthesis. The second copy neu2, which is less homologous, is likely involved in the synthesis of alternative compounds such as legionaminate (see pathway class |FRAME: CMP-Legionaminate-Biosynthesis|). The third copy is an exact duplicate of the neu2 gene cluster |CITS: [23481098]|., Data suggest that both |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| and |FRAME: CPD-1803| (7-O-acetyl-N-acetylneuraminate) are present in this organism and that their synthesis is catalyzed by the sialic acid synthase product of gene neuB1 which is present in the neu1 gene cluster. Based on genome analysis, enzyme kinetics, and structural analysis, the putative substrate for NeuB1 is |FRAME: CPD-16880| and its product is |FRAME: CPD-1803|. In addition to |FRAME: TAX-316275|, this gene was also predicted to be present in other species including Escherichia coli and |FRAME: TAX-1311|. , A pathway for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-1803| has been proposed and is shown here. In addition to the experimentally determined NeuB1, predicted enzymes of the pathway include the O-acetyl transferase NeuD1, the hydrolyzing 2-epimerase NeuC1, and NeuA1 which activates |FRAME: CPD-1803| to a |FRAME: CMP| derivative |CITS: [23481098]|.

General Background, |FRAME: D-APIOSE| is a unique branched-chain pentose found principally in plants. It is a key component of structurally complex cell wall polysaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| (RG-II) in the cell walls of higher plants and in apigalacturonan in the cell walls of aquatic monocots, and is a building block of a large number of naturally occurring secondary metabolites., The name "apiose" is derived from the flavonoid glycoside |FRAME: 7-O-BETA-D-APIOFURANOSYL-12-BETA-D-GLU apiin|, from which it was first obtained |CITS: [Vongerichten01]|. Apiin itself is named after parsley (|FRAME: TAX-4043|), which at the time was known as Apium petroselinum |CITS: [26848180]|., About This Pathway, The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway were found by first identifying genes encoding D-apiose-specific substrate binding proteins (SBPs), since SBPs, which are components of certain types of transporters, are often clustered with catabolic genes that metabolize the compound the SBPs bind to., The pathway shown here was characterized using enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-311403|, |FRAME: TAX-396598|, |FRAME: TAX-218491|, |FRAME: TAX-558270|, |FRAME: TAX-1042878| and |FRAME: TAX-78245|.

Summary: The enzymes of the Leloir pathway (here named |FRAME: PWY-6317|) catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: D-Galactose| to the more metabolically versatile |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|. This pathway is required since galactose itself cannot be used for glycolysis directly., In most organisms five enzymes are required to catalyze this conversion: a |FRAME:EC-5.1.3.3|, a |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.6|, a |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.12|, a |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.2|, and a |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.2|., |FRAME:EC-5.1.3.3| participates by producing the galactokinase substrate |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| from its β-anomer |CITS: [8647345]|. The only product of this pathway is |FRAME: GLC-6-P|. The other product, |FRAME: CPD-12575|, is consumed by |FRAME: GALACTURIDYLYLTRANS-CPLX|, forming a cycle., The cycle requires an initial amount of |FRAME: CPD-12575|, which is produced by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.9| |CITS: [COLISALII]|.

Summary: Multiple degradation pathways lead to the metabolite |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE|., One group of such pathways is the degradation of glucuronate-containing polymers such as |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans|. These pathways contain a step for the removal of |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| residues, which are then converted to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.12| |CITS: [13794771]|., In the hyper thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2336|, the degradation of |FRAME: Pectin pectin|, which results in formation of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, also feeds into |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE|, since |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is isomerized to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-8661|, which is then epimerized to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-8660| |CITS: [22925190]|., Another |FRAME: TAX-2336| pathway that leads to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| is the degradation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| |CITS: [23441918]|., |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| is converted in three steps (dehydrogenation, dehydration, and phosphorylation) to |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, which is then cleaved by |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.14| to form the central metabolites |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP|, leading to the TCA cycle and glycolysis (the last two steps are known as the |FRAME: PWY-2221 "semi-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway"|).

Summary: General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms., Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (this pathway), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., About This Pathway, Certain microbes make olefinic long-chain hydrocarbons, generally C25 to C33, that contain a double bond near the middle of the chain. This class of compounds has been described both in Gram-positive bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1270| |CITS: [6039357][6039356]| and |FRAME: TAX-43663| |CITS: [19168653]|, and in Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-40324| |CITS: [Suen88]|. , The source of these hydrocarbons has been shown by carbon-14 labeling studies to derive from fatty acids |CITS: [5781029]|. The process by which these olefins are synthesized, which was initially described in 1929 |CITS: [16744199]|, is known as head-to-head hydrocarbon biosynthesis and involves the coupling of the head (C1) and the α-carbon (C2) of two fatty acids |CITS: [5785213][4390164]|. This type of reaction is known as a non-decarboxylative Claisen condensation |CITS: [ Claisen81]|., A set of four |FRAME: TAX-40324| genes involved in the pathway has been reported in patent applications filed by researchers from the LS9 company |CITS: [Friedman08]|, and was subsequently studied in |FRAME: TAX-1270| |CITS: [20038703]|, |FRAME: TAX-211586| |CITS: [20418444]|, and |FRAME: TAX-339| |CITS: [21266575][28029240][28223313]|., The key reaction in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.20| (OleA), which condenses C8-C16 fatty acyl groups via a non-decarboxylative Claisen condensation reaction to form a β-keto acid (3-oxo acid). However, if OleD (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.412|) is present, it catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reduction of the β-keto acid intermediate to produce a β-hydroxy acid that is significantly more stable than the β-keto acid |CITS: [21958090]|. Summary: |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is a secondary messenger molecule used in signal transduction and lipid signaling in eukaryotic cells., It mediates the biological response of a large number of hormones and neurotransmitters in target cells by regulating calcium release from intracellular stores., |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is synthesized by hydrolysis of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| (PIP2), a phospholipid that is located in the plasma membrane, by the action of phospholipase C, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6351|., Once formed, the levels of |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| are tightly regulated by two mechanisms., In the first mechanism the compound is dephosphorylated to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-BISPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [6285891][6095097]|, initiating a pathway that recycles the inositol moiety to the plasma membrane as phosphatidylinositols., In the second mechanism, it is phosphorylated by inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate 3-kinase to |FRAME: CPD-506|. This compound has been suggested to have roles in controlling calcium homeostasis, transferring calcium between intracellular stores, and/or regulating calcium entry across the plasma membrane |CITS: [1659392]|. It may also play a role in regulating cross-talk between the calcium and other signaling pathways. A |FRAME: CPD-506|-binding protein has been identified that can stimulate the GTPase activity of the ras and rap small GTP binding proteins |CITS: [7637787][9038348]|., |FRAME: CPD-506| can be cleaved to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [3010126]|, or it could be phosphorylated further to |FRAME: CPD-1107| and eventually I|FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [2550825][2548474]|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6361|., |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| links the degree and duration of receptor-dependent phospholipase C activation to the generation of |FRAME: CPD-178|, a cellular signal that regulates the ionic conductance of Cl-channels |CITS: [9660883][10383396][9838040]|.

Summary: Monoterpenoid indole alkaloids (MIAs) are a large group of plant-derived natural products with a range of pharmacological properties. A few examples include the antimalarial drug |FRAME: QUININE|, the anticancer drugs |FRAME: CPD-11776|, |FRAME: CPD-7858| and |FRAME: CPD-19894|, and the anti-hypertension drugs |FRAME: CPD-14751| and |FRAME: CPD-21281|. Terpenoid indole alkaloids are found in a number of plants belonging to the families Apocynaceae, Loganiaceae, Rubiaceae, and Nyssaceae. , The pathway(s) leading to their biosynthesis in complex. The upper branch consists of the biosynthesis of the monoterpenoids (also called iridoids or secoiridoids). It starts with the common precursor |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|, which is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9978| via |FRAME: GERANIOL| and |FRAME: CPD-7857|. |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.122|, and |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.34| catalyze a reduction and a cyclization, forming the first cyclic intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-15030|. The cytochrome P450 |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.161|, acts next, catalyzing three sequential reactions and forming |FRAME: CPD-9980|. This intermediate is glucosylated, hydroxylated, and methylated to yield |FRAME: LOGANIN|. In the last reaction of this branch |FRAME: LOGANIN| is converted to |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD| by another cytochrome P450, |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.62|., In the next part of the pathway, |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD| is condensed with |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| (formed from |FRAME: TRP|) by |FRAME: EC-3.5.99.13|, forming |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE|. This compound is a central branch point, leading to the biosynthesis of a variety of terpenoid indole alkaloids., The biosynthesis of terpenoid indole alkaloids in |FRAME: TAX-4058| displays striking intercellular locations. The so-called early-stage enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.105|, and |FRAME: EC-3.5.99.13|, are expressed specifically in the upper and lower epidermis of young leaves. The late-stage enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.20|, and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.107|, are expressed in the laticifer and idioblast cells in the leaf mesophyll |CITS: [10330473][16262708]|.

Summary: General Background, The two primary bile acids biosynthesized in the human liver, |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189|, are further metabolized in the liver by conjugation to |FRAME: GLY|, or |FRAME: TAURINE| to form |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, or |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6061|). These conjugates are almost fully ionized at physiological pH and are therefore described as bile salts. Bile salts are concentrated in the gallbladder and are released into the duodenum upon stimulation by the hormone cholecystokinin. They promote digestion of dietary lipids in the small intestine and are then reabsorbed via the enterohepatic circulation., Intestinal anaerobic and facultatively anaerobic bacteria metabolize bile salts primarily by deconjugation and oxidation of hydroxyl groups. A small proportion of bile acids are not reabsorbed in the small intestine and enter the large intestine where they are metabolized to secondary bile acids such as |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7754|), or |FRAME: CPD-7235| (which is produced similarly from |FRAME: CPD-15189|). These secondary bile acids enter the bile acid pool. In some individuals they can accumulate to relatively high levels and may contribute to the pathogenesis of gastrointestinal diseases. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., Non-intestinal bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [9812981] [19683506]|, or the laboratory strain of the intestinal bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-511145|, also produce enzymes that can catalyze some of these transformations (see |FRAME: 7-ALPHA-HYDROXYSTEROID-DEH-CPLX|)., About This Pathway, Bile salts are deconjugated by bile salt hydrolases as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8135|. The benefit of deconjugation to the bacteria is the subject of a number of hypotheses., In addition, constitutively expressed hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases carry out oxidation and epimerization of hydroxyl groups at the 3, 7 and 12 positions of the bile acid steroid rings. These reactions convert (epimerize) hydroxyl groups from α to β positions via stable oxo-intermediates. Two distinct, stereospecific hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases are required for epimerization, and they may be from the same, or different species of bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|.

|FRAME: Salmochelins Salmochelins| are C-glucosylated |FRAME: Siderophore siderophores| related to |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN| that are produced by |FRAME: TAX-590| species, uropathogenic and avian pathogenic |FRAME: TAX-562| strains, and certain |FRAME: TAX-570| strains. Mono- (MGE), di- (DGE), and triglucosylated (TGE) forms have been reported |CITS: [12655053][15259369][15598734]|., These compounds were initially reported to confer protection against |FRAME: TAX-590| when included in the diet of mice, and were named "Salmonella Resistance Factors" (SRF) or "Salmonellosis pacifarins" |CITS: [5288264][1090527]|, although today it is known that siderophores are actually virulence factors |CITS: [23959718]|. The most commonly observed salmochelin is the diglucosylated form, which is known as |FRAME: CPD-21578 "salmochelin S4"|. Macrolactone-opened derivatives have also been isolated |CITS: [15259369]|., The glucosylation has been interpreted as a bacterial evasion mechanism that prevents sequestration of the siderophore by the mammalian host's serum albumin |CITS: [6234017]| or the catecholate siderophore-binding protein siderocalin |CITS: [12453412]|., The apo siderophores are exported from the cell into the extracellular matrix by the inner membrane transporter IroC |CITS: [8996108]|, and the Fe3+-bound salmochelins are imported back into the cell by the outer membrane receptor IroN |CITS: [9515912][12655053]|. Once back inside the cell, the holo-siderophores are acted upon by |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.109| (IroD) |CITS: [12655053]|., IroD catalyzes the hydrolysis of Fe3+-bound forms of |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN|, |FRAME: CPD-21577|, |FRAME: CPD-21578| (diglucosyl-enterobactin), and |FRAME: CPD-21581|. While IroD can also hydrolyze the apo siderophores, it has higher catalytic efficiencies (kcat/Km) with the Fe3+-bound forms, suggesting that it is the ferric salmochelin esterase responsible for cytoplasmic iron release |CITS: [16076215]|. The enzyme is also very active with |FRAME: FERRIC-ENTEROBACTIN-COMPLEX|. IroD catalyzes several hydrolytic reactions, producing a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-17082| and |FRAME: CPD-21579| as the final products |CITS: [16076215]|., A second esterase, |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.107| (IroE), prefers apo siderophores as substrates, and has been proposed to hydrolyze apo enterobactins while they are being exported |CITS: [16076215]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, A few bacterial phyla appear to possess menaquinones with very long prenyl side chains. Several members of the |FRAME: TAX-838| genus, which consists of obligate anaerobes, were reported to produce |FRAME: CPD-9722|. This quinone was found in combination with either |FRAME: CPD-9723|, as reported for |FRAME: TAX-28134| strains 1210 and 1221, |FRAME: TAX-83231| strains B5 and 118B, and |FRAME:TAX-839| strain R2, or |FRAME:CPD-9721|, as in |FRAME:TAX-28134| strains VP1 8906D and HS4 and |FRAME: TAX-83231| strains NP333, 75J1, J1 and WP H61, |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|., In addition, several species that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-201174| phylum, and especially to the |FRAME: TAX-33882| genus, were reported to contain |FRAME: CPD-9722|. These organisms, which contain |FRAME: CPD-9722| along with |FRAME: CPD-9723|, include: |FRAME: TAX-33884|, |FRAME: TAX-33917|, |FRAME: TAX-41986|, |FRAME: TAX-33885|,, |FRAME: TAX-33918| |CITS:[7462123][7022156]|, |FRAME: TAX-69368| and |FRAME: TAX-2033| |CITS: [6775048]|.

Notoamides such as |FRAME:CPD-17362| and |FRAME:CPD-17361| and stephacidine (see |FRAME:PWY-7603|) belong to the family of fungal bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane indole alkaloids derived from aromatic (e.g. |FRAME:TRP|) and isoprenoid moieties (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-4211|) |CITS:[23213353]| which have been recognized for their wide range of bioactivities and intriguing reaction chemistry |CITS:[Williams00] [16322742] [20024094]|. The elucidation of the marine-derived Aspergillus sp. MF297-2 genome and the identification of the notoamide (not) gene cluster |CITS:[20722388]| significantly advanced the progress in determining the biosynthesis of integrated metabolites., , Interestingly, various Aspergillus species produce enatiomerically opposite products. For example, the marine Aspergillus sp. MF297-2 produces (-)-notoamide and (+)-stephacidine |CITS:[19281134]| whereas the terrestrial Aspergillus versicolor facilitates the opposite stereochemistry, i.e. the antipodal counterparts (+)-notoamide and (-)-stephacidine |CITS:[18389509] [21714564]|. The determination of the order and mechanism of successional steps in the |FRAME:PWY-7603| has been an joined effort of biochemistry and organic chemistry. The approach to combine biochemical assays, organic chemical reaction analysis and radioactive traced feeding experiments contributed to the confirmation of the biochemistry in early steps in the pathway and reaction chemistry of later steps, even though the corresponding enzymes of the latter remain to be identified |CITS:[21796227] [21818159] [McAfoos11]|., , The first steps of the pathway are shared reactions with the |FRAME:PWY-7603|, especially the two prenylation steps (reversed and normal) catalyzed by the deoxybrevianamide F synthase (notF) |CITS:[20722388]|, the brevianamide F reverse prenyltransferase (brePT) |CITS:[22660767]| and the 6-hydroxy-deoxybrevianamide E prenyltransferase (notC) |CITS:[20722388]| resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17357|. The latter appears to be a pivotal branch point separating |FRAME:PWY-7603| from the |FRAME:PWY-7604|. From |FRAME:CPD-17357| the pathway branches out to |FRAME:CPD-17360| , a short-lived intermediate which had been isolated from marine Aspergillus species |CITS:[19292484]| and shown to be incorporated into |FRAME:CPD-17362| and |FRAME:CPD-17361| |CITS:[22140279]|. The respective enzyme, i.e. notoamide E monooxygenase (notB) is an |FRAME:FAD| dependent monooxygenase which shows a high specificity towards its substrate |FRAME:CPD-17360| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17361| as an major and |FRAME:CPD-17362| as an minor (ratio 6:1) product. The results indicate that the reaction proceeds via a β-stereospecific epoxidation and subsequent pinacol rearrangement |CITS:[22188465]|.

Adenosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: AMP| (AMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC|, which is converted to AMP by the action of |FRAME: ASL-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6126|). Note that the free base |FRAME: ADENINE| or the ribonucleoside |FRAME: ADENOSINE| are not produced via the de novo pathway., Many organisms can also recycle adenosine nucleotides by a combination of degradation and salvage pathways. The degradation pathways are responsible for the conversion of the nucleotides to the nucleoside (|FRAME: ADENOSINE|) and free base form (|FRAME: ADENINE|), and further degradation to compounds that can be catabolized to basic building blocks (for example, see |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|)., However, both |FRAME: ADENOSINE| and |FRAME: ADENINE| can be salvaged by certain enzymes, and be converted back to nucleotide form., The enzyme |FRAME: HS08097-MONOMER| (EC 2.7.1.20) can phosphorylate |FRAME: ADENOSINE| directly to the mono-nucleotide |FRAME: AMP|. The enzyme has been described in bacteria, yeast, plants and animals |CITS: [5092557][8577746][11115893][16511094][17869216][19329636]|. , Other routes from |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: AMP| involve two steps, and are described in |FRAME: P121-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6605|., Either of these routes enables the organism to salvage the degradation products of adenosine nucleotides, and recycle them back to nucleotide form.

About Pectin, |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is one of the major components of the primary cell wall of plants. It is composed of four structurally distinct polysaccharides, namely |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl "homogalacturonan"| (HG), rhamnogalcturonan I (RG-I), rhamnogalacturonan II (RG-II) and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan "xylogalacturonan"| (XGA)., Although all four components appear to be present in all cells, their relative abundance and structural details differ among cell types and species |CITS: [17827695]|., Pectin is synthesized in Golgi vesicles. The structural complexity of pectin suggests that a large number of enzymes is involved in the process, including glycosyltransferases, methyltransferases, acetyltransferases and feruloyltransferases., Evidence indicates a role for pectin in plant growth, development, morphogenesis, defense, cell adhesion, wall structure, signaling, cell expansion, wall porosity, binding of ions, growth factors and enzymes, pollen tube growth, seed hydration, leaf abscission, and fruit development |CITS: [15377216][11554482]|., Pectin is also used in the food and cosmetic industries, and has been shown to have several positive effects on human health |CITS: [17513886]|., About Xylogalacturonan, |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan "Xylogalacturonan"| is a substituted |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl "homogalacturonan"| in which the α-1,4-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| backbone is substituted at position O-3 with a β linked |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Occasionally the xylose is further substituted at position O-4 with an additional β linked xylose. The homogalacturonan backbone is partially methylesterified at the C-6 carboxyl, and may be O-acetylated at positions O-2 or O-3. , |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan "Xylogalacturonan"| has been reported to be abundant in the reproductive tissues of many plants. Recently it was reported to be present in vegetative tissues of Arabidopsis |CITS: [17336350]|.

General Background, Thiols play several major roles in the cell; they help maintain the redox balance, keep a reduced environment, fight reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and they are involved in the detoxification of many other toxins and stress-inducing factors (see |FRAME: PWY-4061|). In most organisms, the major thiol is the tripeptide |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly, known as GSH), whose intracellular concentration ranges from 0.5-10 mM (see |FRAME: PWY-4041|)., Most of the glutathione pool is kept in its reduced form. For example, in |FRAME:TAX-562|, the ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione is 200:1 |CITS: [11544348]|. The functionality of GSH largely depends on its being in a reduced form., About This Pathway, Oxidative damage to proteins often results in the formation of mixed disulfides within the polypetides. A primary defense against this damage is mediated by the action of GSH-dependent thiol-disulfide oxidoreductases, also called thioltransferases and best known as glutaredoxins (Grx). These proteins reduce the protein disulfide groups back to their native form |CITS: [ 9571241]| (an example for these proteins is |FRAME: RED-GLUTAREDOXIN| from |FRAME:TAX-562|)., The glutaredoxins, which are oxidized during this process, are reduced back to active form with electrons that are donated by reduced GSH molecules. In this reaction, two molecules of the reduced form GSH are oxidized, condensing into the single molecule |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE|. The disulfide is reduced back into two individual GSH molecules by the action of the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.8.1.7|., Another redox cycle involving glutathione, which is found in eukaryotic organisms, is described in |FRAME: PWY-4081|.

Summary: General Background, Fagopyritols are galactosyl cyclitols found primarily in seeds of buckwheat (|FRAME:TAX-3617|). Whereas maturing embryos of many plant seeds accumulate |FRAME:CPD-1099|, |FRAME:CPD-170| and |FRAME:CPD-8065| (in addition to sucrose) as the predominant soluble sugars, maturing embryos of buckwheat seeds accumulate fagopyritols. These compounds are grouped into two main series: A and B, which differ from the positioning of the O-α-D-galactopyranosyl linkage to |FRAME:CPD-8052| [(1->3) for A series, (1->2) for B series]. The first fagopyritol of the B series is termed |FRAME:CPD-8253|. The subsequent di- and tri-galactopyranosyl-fagopyritols (B2 and B3) result from the addition of galactosyl units linked in (1->6)-O-α-D-galactopyranosyl to fagopyritol B1. Fagopyritols of the B series have been detected in several species: lupins |CITS:[LAHUTA00],[GORECKI96]|, soybean |CITS:[Schweizer81],[Schweizer78]|, chickpea |CITS:[quemener83]|, sugar beet |CITS:[SHIOMI88]| and jojoba |CITS:[ogawa97]|. Fagopyritols have attracted attention as they are structurally similar to a galactosamine derivative of D-chiro-inositol, a putative insulin mediator, and may be useful in the treatment of non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and polycystic ovary syndrome (for references, see the introduction of |CITS:[11093720]|)., Key Notes on the enzymes: Crude extracts from immature embryos harvested 20 days after pollination or from buckwheat bran prepared from mature dry seeds did not show any fagopyritol synthase activity using galactinol as galactosyl donor. The same experiments was successful in producing |FRAME:CPD-8253| using UDP-galactose instead of galactinol, suggesting that fagopyritol synthases might be homologous to galactinol synthases (GolS). Using conserved oligonucleotide sequences of GolS, two fagopyritol synthases genes (|FRAME:G-9730| and |FRAME:G-9731|) were identified from cDNA libraries of buckwheat developing seeds harvested 20-25 days after pollination. The enzymes catalyze the formation of fagopyritol A1 and B1 but not the subsequent compounds in the series |CITS:[UEDA05]|. To date, no enzymes have been identified that can catalyze the formation of fagopyritols A2, B2, A3 or B3. The enzyme(s) responsible for the linkage of additional galactosyl units has(have) not yet been identified.

Summary: General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives. These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|. |FRAME: CPD-701| is a precursor to the explosive |FRAME: CPD-9138| (TNT), which is a major product of the explosives industry. Many sites are contaminated by TNT and by mono- and dinitrotoluenes |CITS: [8245826]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|. The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two broad categories - oxidative and reductive. In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, The soil bacterium |FRAME: ORG-5918| can utilize |FRAME: CPD-701| as the sole source of nitrogen, carbon, and energy. The pathway is very similar to pathways for the degradation of related compounds (for example, see |FRAME: PWY-5637|), even though the enzymes are different., Under aerobic conditions, resting cells metabolize |FRAME: CPD-701| with concomitant release of small amounts of ammonia. Under anaerobic conditions 4-nitrotoluene is degraded up to the level of |FRAME: CPD-9147|, which accumulates, since the next step, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-13352|, requires the presence of oxygen., , The enzymes in this pathway are inducible, and are only expressed in cells grown in the presence of the substrates of the pathway, or related compounds. The upper part of the pathway was discovered and reported by Spiess et al |CITS: [9464378]|. The lower part of the pathway was investigated by He and Spain, who also verified the earlier findings, |CITS: [10877799]|., Note: the structures of the compounds in this pathway were derived from structures from a homologous pathway described in |CITS: [8002948]|, which are based on NMR analyses, and not those shown in |CITS: [10877799]|, which are simply based on the ring structures from which they are derived.

Summary: |FRAME: BLASTICIDIN-S "Blasticidin S"| is a peptidyl nucleoside antibiotic, first isolated in 1958 from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-68214| |CITS: [13525246]|. It blocks protein synthesis in eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells by binding to the P-site on the 50S ribosomal subunit |CITS: [4917792][12860128]|, and was once used on a large scale in Asia as a fungicide for the prevention of rice blast, a disease caused by the fungus |FRAME: TAX-318829| |CITS: [14157011]|., Today blasticidin S is used mostly as a selectable marker in cell-culture applications, when coupled with resistance genes - either an acetyl transferase or a deaminase |CITS: [1720391][9580709][10411941]|., Like other members of the peptidyl nucleoside family of antibiotics, blasticidin S contains an amino sugar coupled via an amide bond to an amino acid. Its structure is composed of three main parts - a cytosine base, an amino deoxyglucuronic acid, and N-methyl β-arginine., Initial incorporation experiments with labeled compounds showed that the primary precursors are cytosine, D-glucose, L-arginine and L-methionine |CITS: [Seto68]|. Several biosynthetic intermediates that were identified include |FRAME: CPD-17171| |CITS: [Prabhakaran88]|, |FRAME: CPD-17160| |CITS: [956050][Guo91a]|, |FRAME: CPD-17163| |CITS: [7649864]|, |FRAME: CPD-17168| |CITS: [Seto68a]| and |FRAME: CPD-17170| |CITS: [591457]|. An initial proposal for the pathway has been suggested based on these observations |CITS: [Prabhakaran88]|., A revision of the final steps of the pathway was proposed to account for the presence of acylated intermediates that provide a self-resistance mechanism |CITS: [Zhang00a]|. As shown in this pathway diagram, the first toxic intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-17170|, is acylated with an L-leucine amino acid. The toxicity of |FRAME: CPD-17168| is 20-fold lower than that of |FRAME: BLASTICIDIN-S| |CITS: [Zhang00a]|. The leucyl moiety is removed only at the last step, potentially by an extracellular enzyme., The identification of the blasticidin S biosynthetic gene cluster was facilitated by the discovery of two small fragments, presumably encoding a resistance gene, that were able to confer increased resistance to blasticidin S upon |FRAME: TAX-457428|. These fragments were used to identify larger cosmids that included most of the pathway genes |CITS: [9711220]|. A 20-kb cluster was subsequently cloned and expressed in S. lividans, resulting in production of |FRAME: CPD-17168| |CITS: [12964155]|. The reason for why no |FRAME: BLASTICIDIN-S| was detected in the recombinant S. lividans was clarified later, when a blasticidin S deaminase gene was discovered in that organism. Upon inactivating that gene, blasticidin S was produced |CITS: [23377931]|., Several resistance mechanisms towards |FRAME: BLASTICIDIN-S| have been reported. The producing organism |FRAME: TAX-68214| encodes a a membrane-spanning enzyme, BlsJ, thought to be a part of an ABC transporter that removes the compound out of the cell |CITS: [12964155]|. Another producer, |FRAME: TAX-1970|, was reported to produce an |FRAME: RXN-15940 acetyltransferase| that acetylates and inactivates the compound |CITS: [17158669]|. Finally, an |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.23|, has been reported from several organisms |CITS: [236272][1368770][7742811][23377931]|.

General Background, |FRAME:TAURINE| (2-aminoethanesulfonate), a natural occuring amino acid analogue of, |FRAME:B-ALANINE|, plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many, species., The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation,, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular |FRAME: CA+2| homeostasis., While plants or animals cannot degrade taurine, several species of bacteria and fungi are capable of, doing that., For example, |FRAME: ORG-5927| can grow on taurine as the sole source of carbon,, nitrogen, sulfur and energy |CITS: [113035]|., Some anaerobic bacteria can use taurine for respiration as either an electron acceptor (eg., |FRAME: ORG-5878|) or an electron donor (eg. |FRAME: TAX-56119|, |FRAME: ORG-5923|,, |FRAME: TAX-82367| NKNCYSA). Others can use it as a fermentative substrate (eg. |FRAME: ORG-5898|), |CITS: [12471498][9297467]|., The different species often utilize different pathways, resulting in conversion of taurine into different, sulfur compounds. For example, |FRAME: ORG-5927| converts taurine to, |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| |CITS: [11082195]|, which is cleaved to |FRAME: SO3|, |CITS: [11160104]|, and eventually converted to |FRAME:HS| by a sulfite reductase |CITS: [9143131]|., |FRAME: TAX-56119| |CITS: [9202468]|, |FRAME: ORG-5923| (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), and, |FRAME: TAX-82367| NKNCYSA (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), all convert taurine to, |FRAME: SULFATE| (additional products are ammonia and CO2), while, |FRAME: ORG-5898| converts taurine to thiosulfate, ammonia and acetate |CITS: [9297467]|., Taurine degradation is known to be initiated by at least three different types of reactions: transamination,, which appears to be the most widespread |CITS: [113035][5058441][5012173][629994]|, oxidation, |CITS: [5551654]|, and oxygenation |CITS: [9287300]|. In the first two cases sulfoacetaldehyde is an, intermediate, whereas in the third case taurine is converted to sulfite and aminoacetaldehyde, |CITS: [9287300]|.

Summary: General Background, Grixazone is a yellow pigment produced by |FRAME: TAX-1911| that contains a phenoxazinone chromophore. It consists of |FRAME: CPD-14874| and |FRAME: CPD-14875|, the latter having a carboxyl group in place of the aldehyde group. The grixazone biosynthesis gene cluster has been cloned from this organism and was shown to be regulated by the transcriptional activator GriR. Both A-factor (|FRAME: CPD-10135|) and |FRAME: Pi| depletion signals are transmitted to this gene cluster via the griR promoter and induce grixazone biosynthesis |CITS: [17337580][17617696][16282322][15152808]|., About This Pathway, The grixazone biosynthesis gene cluster consists of 13 genes organized into six transcriptional units griT, griSR, griR, griAB, griCDEFG, and griJIH. GriJ is an aspartokinase homolog that may catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to |FRAME: L-BETA-ASPARTYL-P|, although this has not been biochemically demonstrated. |FRAME: L-BETA-ASPARTYL-P| was proposed to be converted to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| by the aspartate semialdehyde dehydrogenase of central metabolism |CITS: [17337580]|. The functions of GriI and GriH |CITS: [17003031]|, GriC and GriD |CITS: [17617696]|, and GriE and GriF |CITS: [16282322]| have been experimentally demonstrated., GriI catalyzes an aldol condensation between |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| to form a C7 compound, probably 2-amino-4,5-dihydroxy-6-one-heptanoic acid-7-phosphate (|FRAME: CPD-14872|). GriH catalyzes the cyclization of this compound to the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-14873| |CITS: [17003031][17337580]|., GriC and GriD together were suggested to comprise an ATP- and NAD(P)-dependent carboxylic acid reductase complex that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-14873| to another key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-7367|. This reaction was suggested to occur via formation of an acyl-AMP intermediate (not shown) |CITS: [17617696]|. , The copper chaperone GriE activates GriF via transfer of |FRAME: CU+2| (not shown). GriF oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-7367| to form an o-quinone imine, two molecules of which nonenzymatically couple to form a phenoxazinone. In the presence of |FRAME: CPD-9175|, |FRAME: CPD-14874| is formed from |FRAME: CPD-7367| by GriF. Evidence suggested that the sulfhydryl group of |FRAME: CPD-9175| is nonenzymatically conjugated to the o-quinone imine, followed by dimerization with another o-quinone imine to produce |FRAME: CPD-14874| |CITS: [16282322]|., |FRAME: CPD-14874 "Grixazone A"| can be oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-14875| by an unidentified oxidase independently of the gene products of the grixazone biosynthesis gene cluster |CITS: [17337580]|., The |FRAME: G-15472| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1911| encodes an arylamine N-acetyltransferase that has been shown to acetylate 2-aminophenols. It produces |FRAME: CPD-14877| and |FRAME: CPD-14876| as shunt products. However, other acetyltransferases may also be involved in |FRAME: CPD-14876| production |CITS: [17158669]|., Among the other gri genes, griG encodes a protein similar to a benzoate transporter and was shown to be involved in exogenous |FRAME: CPD-14129| uptake |CITS: [17337580]|. Based on sequence similarities, the products of griB and griT were suggested to be a putative membrane efflux protein, and a regulator of grixazone biosynthesis, respectively |CITS: [17337580]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the biosynthesis of the amino acids |FRAME: HOMO-SER| and |FRAME: MET| from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, and the single step conversion of |FRAME: MET| to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|. The sub-pathways used for construction of this superpathway are those used by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|., |FRAME: MET| (met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids, but is also required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines., In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., In the pathway shown here, |FRAME: MET| is synthesized using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of O-acylated homoserine with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine |CITS: [3309561]|., The methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| to |FRAME: MET| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., The O-acyl group of homoserine is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast, and most Gram-positive bacteria (see |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|) and a succinyl group (as shown here) in enteric bacteria and some other Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME:TAX-303| (|CITS: [3309561][9409150][10482527]|)., Once |FRAME: MET| is formed, a single enzyme, the ATP-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.6|, can convert it to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) |CITS: [6251075]|. SAM is the principal biological methyl donor in transmethylation reactions, and is also used as a sulfur donor in transsulfuration reactions, as an aminopropyl group donor in polyamine biosynthesis, and as a cofactor of many enzymes that use radical chemistry by generating a |FRAME: CPD-15400|.

General Background, Four types of aromatic compounds degradation pathways are thought to occur in different types of bacteria: , Aerobic organisms take advantage of the availability of molecular oxygen, and use oxygenases that introduce hydroxyl groups, and cleave the aromatic ring. These pathways usually lead to a few central intermediates such as |FRAME: CATECHOL|,, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-633| (see |FRAME: PWY-6079|)., Facultative aerobes utilize two types of pathways, depending on the availability of oxygen., When oxygen is present, these organisms use the so-called "hybrid" type of aerobic metabolism for some aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: BENZOATE|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE|., These pathways use |FRAME: CO-A| to activate and form thioesters of the substrates, followed by an oxygenase/reductase step to dearomatize (but not cleave) the ring. Cleavage of the dearomatized ring does not require oxygen (see |FRAME: PWY-6077|)., Under anaerobic conditions, facultative aerobes and phototrophs use a reductive aromatic metabolism., The aromatic compounds are activated by |FRAME: CO-A| to an active intermediate that can be transformed to important, central intermediate such as |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|. Reduction of the aromatic ring of |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-883| and is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 ATP molecules (see, |FRAME: 2AMINOBENZDEG-PWY|)., Strict anaerobes utilize a completely different and not well characterized benzoyl-coenzyme A reductase that does not utilize ATP |CITS: [18378589]|., About This Pathway, The facultative aerobe |FRAME: TAX-59406| processes several aromatic compounds by aerobic pathways that belong, to the second type. In these "hybrid" pathways oxygen is used to introduce hydroxyl groups, as in the classic aerobic, pathways. However, the aromatic ring is reduced and CoA thioesters are used, as in the anaerobic route., In addition, ring cleavage also does not require oxygen., The first step in the degradation of anthranilate by this pathway is its activation to a CoA ester, which is catalyzed, by |FRAME:ENZRXN-15575|. This organism has several such enzymes, some of which induced under aerobic, conditions, and some under anaerobic conditions. The aerobic alleles are encoded by the almost identical, |FRAME: G-10942| and |FRAME: G-10941| genes |CITS:[1315272][11514509]|., The activated form |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZOYL-COA| is then converted by |FRAME: CPLX-7687| to a non-aromatic, cis-dihydrodiol, |FRAME: 2-AMINO-5-OXOCYCLOHEX-1-ENECARBOXYL-COA|., The exact nature of the subsequent ring cleavage reaction and the intermediates downstream has not been, studied yet |CITS: [2176602]|.

|FRAME:CPD-14899| is a major sterol found in green algae, including |FRAME: TAX-3055| where it accounts for roughly 45% of the total sterol content found when analyzing whole cells or isolated flagella |CITS:[GEALT81]|. Sterols are typically found in plasma membranes where they may affect membrane flexibility and fluidity. It is unclear whether sterols also play signaling roles in green algae., The primary evidence for this pathway comes from radiotracer and metabolite-based experiments demonstrating that |FRAME: TAX-3055| synthesizes |FRAME: CPD-14899| via a Δ25(27)-olefin pathway |CITS: [22591742]| distinct from the Δ24(28)-olefin pathway used for the |FRAME: PWY-6075| found in yeast and other fungi |CITS: [346585] [2654239]|. Like |FRAME: PWY-7154 "ergosterol biosynthesis"| in |FRAME: TAX-3055| and the |FRAME: PWY-2541| found in land plants, this pathway uses |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL| as the primary backbone for |FRAME:CPD-14899| biosynthesis |CITS: [20333205][22591742]| rather than the |FRAME: LANOSTEROL| intermediate used by fungi. It is also interesting to note that while the isoprenoid precusors used for |FRAME: PWY-6075| in fungi originate from the |FRAME: PWY-922|, they are exclusively derived from the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| in Chlamydomonas and other green algae |CITS: [11289606][10584331]|., To date, this Δ25(27)-olefin pathway has only been studied in |FRAME: TAX-3055|. However, there is also some evidence that members of the |FRAME:TAX-3650| family of land plants synthesize intermediate compounds in this pathway |CITS: [8934454][SEO89]|. In contrast, while there is experimental evidence that |FRAME:CPD-14899| is found in marine sponges such as |FRAME:TAX-6069| |CITS: [CIMINIELLO90]| it may be synthesized by an alternative route |CITS: [STOILOV87]|.
