Summary: General Background, Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are fatty acid that have 13 or more carbon atoms and contain more than one double bond in their backbone. Mammals require PUFAs, and most can convert certain PUFAs to other forms, but all mammals depend on certain PUFAs in their diet. Those are called essential fatty acids, and are classified as either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, depending on the distance of the last double bond from the end of the molecule., PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturated long chain fatty acids as common constituents of their lipids. They are produced by many algae, lower ukaryotes, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|. They are also produced by some marine bacteria that are adapted to cold temperatures and high pressure., |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID "Arachidonate"| (arachidonic acid) is a polyunsaturated ω-6 fatty acid with a 20-carbon chain and four cis-double bonds. It is produced de novo at high levels by mosses, by some lower eukaryotes (e.g. Euglena), and by some marine bacteria adapted to low temperatures and high pressures., About this Pathway, The most common |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| synthesis pathway is the |FRAME: PWY-6000 "6-desaturase/Δ6-elongase pathway"|, in which |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| is first desaturated by a 6-desaturase to yield |FRAME: CPD-8117|, followed by a Δ6-elongation to produce |FRAME: CPD-8120| and a |FRAME: PWY-7592 "second desaturation"| by a 5-desaturase to form |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-5353|). However, some of the organisms that produce |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| lack a 6-desaturase and utilize an alternative pathway that includes a Δ9 elongase and an 8-desaturase, as described in this pathway |CITS: [10328826]|., The Δ8 pathway has been described in the ciliated protozoan |FRAME: TAX-5908| |CITS: [5961271]|, in the soil amoebae |FRAME: TAX-5756| |CITS: [4309952]|, in euglenoid species |CITS: [14216427]| and in the microalga |FRAME: TAX-561169| |CITS: [17291553]|. Interestingly, it has also been described in rat and human testis (|CITS: [588579][459715]|, but not in healthy breast tissue or brain., See also |FRAME: PWY-7602|.

Summary: The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| from |FRAME:CPD-691| requires the attachment of an aminopropanol group to the propionate side chain of the corrin ring. Isotope studies with cultures of microorganisms that biosynthesize vitamin B12 have clearly shown that the amino group and carbon chain of this part of cobalamin are both, derived from |FRAME: THR| |CITS: [13416277]|., Initial work suggested that |FRAME: 1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| might be formed from L-threonine by sequential action of two separate enzymes, namely |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.103| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.75| |CITS: [4577583]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7378|). These two enzymes have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-83333| and were shown to catalyze the proposed reactions in vitro |CITS: [359547]|. At the time it was proposed that |FRAME: 1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| is the substrate for the |FRAME: MONOMER-13228 CbiB| enzyme, originally proposed to convert |FRAME:CPD-691| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| |CITS: [9446573]|., Suprisingly, a few years later a |FRAME: TAX-90371| mutant blocked in |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| biosynthesis was found to be not defective in either of these two enzymes. Furthermore, the researchers could demonstrate that blocking the two enzymes does not effect B12 biosynthesis in this organism |CITS: [1551838]|. The mutation responsible for the phenotype was eventually traced to |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.81| (|FRAME:G-9854|). This enzyme does not accept |FRAME:THR| as a substrate, and is specific to |FRAME:L-THREONINE-O-3-PHOSPHATE|. The authors suggested that the product of this reaction, |FRAME:R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE|, is the actual substrate for the |FRAME: MONOMER-13228 CbiB| enzyme, originally proposed to convert |FRAME:CPD-691| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| |CITS: [9446573]|., The evidence for this proposed pathway was strengthened by the discovery of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.177| (|FRAME: G-10070|) in |FRAME: TAX-90371|. This enzyme generates |FRAME:L-THREONINE-O-3-PHOSPHATE| from |FRAME:THR| |CITS: [18308727]|. Growth studies showed that pduX mutants were impaired for the synthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| de novo and from |FRAME: CPD-9083|, but not from |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| |CITS: [18308727]|., Homologs of |FRAME: G-10070| were only found in some proteobacteria, actinobacteria, and firmicutes, leaving an open question whether a different enzyme catalyzes the phosphorylation of |FRAME: THR| in other cobalamin-producing bacteria. Indeed in 2018 it was found that the the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-272943| possesses a unique L-threonine kinase, named BluE |CITS: [30098062]|, and that the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-192952| possesses a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.177| and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.81| activities |CITS: [29950091]|.

Summary: |FRAME: MET| can be catabolized by several possible pathways., One of these pathways is a single reaction in which |FRAME: MET| is simultaneously deaminated and dethiomethylated to |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11|., Methionine γ-lyase (MGL) is widely distributed in bacteria, especially in |FRAME: TAX-286| spp., and is also found in archaea |CITS: [17914603]|, fungi |CITS: [5370277][11928962][19048340]| and plants |CITS: [17030798]|. , Bacteria, archaea, plants and protozoans produce an intracellular enzyme, while fungi produce an extracellular version., Crystal structures have been reported from |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [8440][17289792]|, |FRAME: TAX-546| |CITS: [16511092]|, |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [1953661]|, and |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [17012806][18678935]|., The pathway has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS:[6742420][3309561][3657560]|, and has also been observed in |FRAME: ORG-5993|, the first such report from plants |CITS:[17030798]|., The MGL enzyme, which is not produced by mammals, has been used in cancer therapy, depriving L-methionine from cancer cells, which become methionine dependent and eventually follow apoptosis due to methionine limitation |CITS: [8242623][14585259][20146062][25250324]|., The enzyme demonstrated antitumour efficacy in a number of methionine-dependent cancer cell lines including lung cancer, colon cancer, kidney cancer, brain cancer, prostate cancer, melanoma and fibrosarcoma |CITS: [9056489][10473100][10825143] [10770644][12768189]|. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-10763 Methanopterin| is one of several modified folates that have been identified in Archaea |CITS: [6319137][2624671][1910453][1915350][8501071]| (see also |FRAME: CPD-10764|)., While common in all methanogenic archaea, some C1-oxidizing members of the domain Bacteria also contain an, |FRAME: THMPT|-related carrier, which they use in energy metabolism (see |FRAME: PWY-1723|)., Serving a similar role to the one that folates serve in bacteria and eukaryotes, |FRAME: CPD-10763| carries C1 (single, carbon) fragments between formyl and methyl oxidation levels in methanogens and several other Archaea (see, |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., Despite the similarities, there are clear differences between |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydrofolate) and |FRAME: THMPT|. In the reductive direction, ATP is consumed in the entry of carbon from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into the |FRAME: THF| pathway, but not in entry into the |FRAME: THMPT| pathway., In the oxidative direction, methyl groups are much more readily oxidized on |FRAME: THMPT| than on |FRAME: THF|., Moreover, the redox reactions on |FRAME: THMPT| are coupled to more negative reductants than the pyridine, nucleotides which are used in the |FRAME: THF| pathway |CITS: [10970772]|., The biosynthetic pathway for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10763| was initially elucidated by the use of labeled isotopes, studies and azo dye derivatives |CITS: [8639495]| and has been refined incremently ever since |CITS: [9698382][19746965][21634403][25002541]|. The identification of the enzymes that catalyze the pathway's reactions has proved very difficult, and while all of the enzymes from the early part of the pathway have been identified, most of the enzymes in the later part of the pathway are still unknown., The methyl groups at C-7 and C-9 of the pterin ring of |FRAME: CPD-10763| distinguish it from all other pterin-containing natural products. The methyltransferase that methylates these positions has been one of the enigmatic enzymes of the pathway. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-2190| has been identified, and it has been suggested that in this organism methylation occurs early in the pathway, most likely at the level of |FRAME: AMINO-OH-HYDROXYMETHYL-DIHYDROPTERIDINE| |CITS: [25002541]|. Thus, all compounds in the pathway shown here are dimethylated starting with that intermediate. However, methylation may occur at different steps of the pathway in different organisms. It has been shown that methylation can occur at |FRAME: CPD-16957| in |FRAME: TAX-187420| and |FRAME: TAX-79929| |CITS: [9565696]|.

Summary: Background, Biologically, |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (also known as ethylene) is a plant hormone that plays a role in fruit ripening and senescence, see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|. While all plants produce ethene as described in |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|, two biosynthetic pathways for ethylene production have been reported from microorganisms, see |FRAME: PWY-6853| and |FRAME: PWY-6854|. The plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-319| utilizes |FRAME: PWY-6853| to synthesize ethene as a defence mechanism during host infection. , The |FRAME: TAX-319| efe gene product |FRAME: MONOMER-16773| mediates the synthesis of ethene from the TCA cycle intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS: [1770346]|. The enzyme catalyzes two simultaneous reactions. In one reaction 2-oxoglutarate is dioxygenated to form one molecule of ethene and three molecules of carbon dioxide. In the other reaction both 2-oxoglutarate and |FRAME: ARG| are mono-oxygenated to yield |FRAME: SUC| plus |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: CPD-26627|, respectively. The latter is further transformed to |FRAME: CPD0-1470| and |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, some of which cyclizes spontaneously to form |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| |CITS: [1445291]|., |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| can be converted to |FRAME:GLT| by |FRAME:CPLX-6746|., The glutamate that is formed can be recycled back to L-arginine via the |FRAME: ARGSYNBSUB-PWY "acetyl cycle"|., |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD "Ethene"| has a diverse array of uses commercially. It is an intermediate in the production of fuel as it can be hydrated to ethanol or polymerized to gasoline. It can also be used to synthesize a variety of plastics such as polystyrene and PVC, or fabrics such as polyester. It is currently obtained from fossil fuels at an ecological cost as its production results in the emission of huge amounts of carbon dioxide |CITS: [Ungerer]|. , About this Pathway, This pathway utilizes carbon dioxide from photosynthesis to produce ethene and demonstrates a carbon neutral method of obtaining sufficient amounts for commercial use. The |FRAME: TAX-319| efe gene was previously cloned into the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| which was then able to synthesize ethene as a byproduct of glucose utilization via the TCA cycle, see |FRAME: PWY-7126| |CITS: [18640286]|. , In the current pathway, the |FRAME: TAX-319| efe gene was engineered into the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148|. The efe gene was subsequently modified to eliminate potential hotspots that could cause gene inactivation |CITS: [16233410]|. Multiple copies of the mutated efe gene were introduced into the |FRAME: TAX-1148| genome under the control of the pea plant psbA promoter |CITS: [Ungerer]|., Experimental data concluded that this synthetic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1148| was able to phototrophically produce significant amounts of ethene with no deleterious side effects on the organism |CITS: [Ungerer]|.

Summary: Despite the fact that fluorine is abundant in the earth's crust, organically bound fluorine is relatively rare in nature, owing to its low solubility and the high redox potential required for its oxidation., Only a handful of biologically synthesized carbon-fluorine bonds are known |CITS: [15209126]| . The most common natural organofluorine species is |FRAME: CPD-12709|, a toxin found in the leaves and seeds of a variety of tropical plants, often in high concentrations |CITS:[13444108][3334144]|. Other compounds include |FRAME: CPD-12714|, |FRAME: CPD-12713|, |FRAME: CPD-12712| (4-fuoro-5-O-sulphamoyladenosine), |FRAME: CPD-12710|, and |FRAME: FLUORO-CITRATE|., The extreme toxicity of |FRAME: CPD-12709| stems from its similarity to acetate. Fluoroacetate combines with coenzyme A to form |FRAME: CPD-12716|, which can substitute for acetyl CoA in the tricarboxylic acid cycle. |FRAME: CPD-12716 Fluoroacetyl-CoA| reacts with citrate synthase to produce |FRAME: FLUORO-CITRATE|, a metabolite of which then binds very tightly to aconitase, halting the cycle., Sodium fluoroacetate was introduced as a rodenticide in the US in 1946, but its extreme toxicity limits its uses. Currently, it is licensed in the US for use against coyotes, which prey on sheep and goats, and in Australia and New Zealand to kill unwanted introduced species |CITS: [17288493]|., Only a few bacterial strains have been identified with the ability to synthesize organofluorine compounds. |FRAME: TAX-67282| produces |FRAME: CPD-12712| |CITS: [13425454][1262649]|, while |FRAME: TAX-29303| and |FRAME: TAX-37326| produce both |FRAME: CPD-12709| |CITS: [11571203]| and |FRAME: CPD-12710| |CITS: [12404452][24795808]|. , Most of the current knowledge about the biosynthesis of organofluorine compounds comes from |FRAME: TAX-29303|., About This Pathway, The first fluorine-biochemistry enzyme to be identified was |FRAME: MONOMER-15922|. The enzyme, discovered in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29303|, catalyzes the fluorination of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) to form |FRAME: CPD-5923| |CITS: [11907567]|., Subsequently, the different intermediates in the pathway were detected, usually by labelled isotopes studies. , |FRAME: CPD-12708| was shown to be the precursor of both |FRAME: CPD-12709| and |FRAME: CPD-12710| |CITS: [Moss00]|, and the enzymes responsible for its conversions to those products, |FRAME: MONOMER-15926| and |FRAME: CPLX-8162|, respectively, were identified |CITS: [11571203][12404452]|. |FRAME: CPD-12706| was shown to be an intermediate |CITS: [14973623]|, and the last intermediate to be discovered was |FRAME: CPD-12707| |CITS: [17574646]|., Characterization of the gene cluster for fluorometabolite biosynthesis, which included |FRAME: G-12239| (the gene encoding |FRAME: CPLX-8161|), has revealed several additional genes, including |FRAME: G-12240|, the gene encoding the protein that catalyzes the second step in the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-15923| |CITS: [16720268]|., The only enzyme that has not been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-29303| at this point is the aldolase that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12708| from |FRAME: CPD-12707|. An in vitro assay utilizing the proteins from |FRAME: TAX-29303|, along with a fuculose aldolase from |FRAME:TAX-1902|, substituting for the missing aldolase, was successful in reconstituting the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12710| starting from the |FRAME: F-| ion |CITS: [19101471]|.

|FRAME: Urolithins Urolithins| are intestinal microbial metabolites produced from |FRAME: Ellagitannins ellagitannin|- and |FRAME: CPD-17769|-containing foods such as walnuts, strawberries, and pomegranates |CITS: [15998116]|. Many forms of urolithins exist, differing in their hydroxylation status. Most of them appear to be intermediates in the pathways that produce three final products - |FRAME: CPD-20705|, |FRAME: CPD-20711|, and |FRAME: CPD-20710|., The urolithins are absorbed much better than their precursors, and thus can contribute significantly to the beneficial properties attributed to those foods. Recent research, mostly based on in vitro testing, has shown preliminary evidence of the anti-inflammatory, anticarcinogenic, antiglycative, antioxidant, and antimicrobial effects of urolithins |CITS: [21843938][22648625][23710216][26307544][26872561][28683791][28784820]|., Since the urolithins are only produced by gut bacteria, their production in the gut depends on the bacterial population composition in a particular individual. Several metabotypes have been characterized: metabotype A poduces ony |FRAME: CPD-20705|, metabotype B produces |FRAME: CPD-20710| and |FRAME: CPD-20711| besides |FRAME: CPD-20705|, and metabotype 0 does not produce any of the final metabolites |CITS: [24976365][28347564][27158799]|., Urolithins circulate in plasma as glucuronate and sulfate conjugates, at concentrations in the range of 0.2 -20 μM. A study of the Iberian pig, which feeds on oak acorns that are very rich in ellagitannins, found that the degradation pathway started with a tetrahydroxy-urolithin through the removal of one of the lactone rings of |FRAME: CPD-17769|, and continued by sequential removal of hydroxyl groups, ending with |FRAME: CPD-20705| and |FRAME: CPD-20711|. Analysis of plasma and urine samples showed that glucuronate and sulfate conjugates of urolithin A were the main metabolites, with glucuronate and sulfate conjugates of urolithin C and B present as minor metabolites |CITS: [17990850]|. The glucuronide forms do not have the active properties of non-conjugated urolithins |CITS: [24077694]|. It has been proposed that the inactive glucuronides are reactivated by β-glucuronidases, which are present at high concentrations at inflammation and infection sites and in the microenvironments of solid tumors |CITS: [28283501]|., The bacterial species |FRAME: TAX-471189| and |FRAME: TAX-1335613| have been shown to produce |FRAME: CPD-20709| |CITS: [24744017][24909569]|, while an as-yet unclassified species, also from the |FRAME: TAX-1643826| family, was shown to produce |FRAME: CPD-20710| |CITS: [28824607]|. Unfortunately none of the enzymes involved have been studied.

|FRAME:CPD-7035 2-Phenylethanol| belongs to the main floral scent compounds found in the genus |FRAME:TAX-3764| and many other flowering plants. It has been suggested that glucosidic bound scents or aromas constitute a pool from which the volatiles can be released in a controlled manner through the action of β-glucosidases |CITS:[Ackermann89]|. |FRAME:CPD-14528 2-Phenylethyl β-D-glucopyranoside| is the most abundant glucoside found in roses |CITS:[Watanabe01]| and has been proposed to be involved as a precursor in the emission pattern of |FRAME:CPD-7035| |CITS:[Hayashi04]|., The emission pattern of various volatile scents has been reported to follow a diurnal rhythm (|CITS:[17636322]|) which in case of |FRAME:CPD-7035| was ascribed to the action of a β-glucosidase. Hayashi et al. (|CITS:[Hayashi04]|) proposed a metabolic schema which included the glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-7035| and hydrolyzing of |FRAME:CPD-14528| as well as the reversible conversion of the aglycone into |FRAME:PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5751|), hence creating the observed emission pattern of main volatile scents found in roses. Although the activity of the corresponding β-glucosidase did correlate with the emitted amount of |FRAME:CPD-7035| in roses |CITS:[Hayashi04]| no such diurnal relationship could be found for the amount of |FRAME:CPD-14528| in Trifiolium repens |CITS:[Jacobsen02]| indicating a species-dependent regimentation of scent patterns and release mechanisms., The 2-phenylethyl β-D-glucopyranoside glucosidase responsible for the cleavage of |FRAME:CPD-14528| to produce |FRAME:CPD-7035| has been partially purified from roses |CITS:[18175907]|. In addition, the existence of a glucosyltransferase |CITS:[12092844]| |CITS:[Watanabe01]| has also been demonstrated in this plant, hence complementing the pair of enzymes which may well play a role in the controlled manner of release of major volatiles in flowering plants.

|FRAME:CPD-17747| is one of the nonproteinogenic amino acid residues which form the cyclic hexapeptide skeleton of the |FRAME: Echinocandins echinocandins|. Echinocandins represent a family of fungal cyclic lipo-hexapeptides characterized by their fungicidal and fungistatic properties against ascomycetes of the genera Candida and Aspergillus, respectively |CITS:[25156669] [23463246]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17711| (see |FRAME:PWY-7650|) is closely related to the biosynthesis of its amino acid building blocks supported by the presence of two independent gene clusters involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-17711|, i.e. the echinocandin (ecd) gene cluster and the L-homotyrosine (hyt) gene cluster |CITS:[22998630]|. , Out of the six amino acid residues integrated in the hexapeptide scaffold four are nonproteinogenic and either mono-, or dihydroxylated. The nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) encoded by EcdA in Emericella rugulosa adds successively |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, |FRAME:THR|, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-L-PROLINE|, |FRAME:CPD-17730| (see |FRAME:PWY-7649|), again |FRAME:THR| and finally |FRAME:CPD-17747| (this pathway) to the growing peptide chain |CITS:[22998630]|. , Currently, it is unknown if the final hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17722| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17747| occurs before or after the release of the macrocyclized lipo-hexapeptide complex and also the catalyzing enzyme for this reaction remains to be demonstrated. However, the gene cluster for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17711| (ecd) contained three predicted genes (EcdG, EcdH, EcdK) presumably participating in the oxidative tailoring of the echinocandin backbone or its components. It could be shown that EcdK encoded for a nonheme iron oxygenase which iteratively hydroxylated the 5-position of |FRAME:LEU|, forming |FRAME:CPD-17723| and |FRAME:CPD-17724|, respectively, hence acting as a multifunctional leucine 5-hydroxylase/5-hydroxyleucine 5-hydroxylase |CITS:[23451921]|. The reduction of the spontaneously formed |FRAME:CPD-17725| to |FRAME:CPD-17722| is probably catalyzed by a NADH-dependent reductase but has not yet been isolated. Knocking-out EcdH resulted in the loss of |FRAME:CPD-17711| production indicating the crucial role |FRAME:CPD-17747| played in |FRAME:PWY-7650|. Although other leucine 5-hydroxylases have been characterized, e.g. the L-leucine 5-hydroxylase of the cyanobacterium Nostoc punctiforme |CITS:[22584432]|, the EcdH encoded enzyme is the only one so far identified catalyzing a tandem hydroxylation at the same carbon of |FRAME:LEU| |CITS:[23451921]|. In addition, the importance of the |FRAME:CPD-17747| residue for the overall activity of |FRAME:CPD-17711| and semisynthetic derivatives thereof has been demonstrated in structure-activity relationship investigations |CITS:[1495015]|.

Summary: General Background, Marine organisms, including bacteria, algae and invertebrates, contain many organobromine compounds. Over 2,200 of those, with a wide range of biological properties, have been reported by 2017. Some brominated compounds, such as |FRAME: PBDEs "polybrominated diphenyl ethers"| (PBDEs) in their hydroxylated and methoxylated forms, are found across all trophic levels in marine biota, from cyanobacteria and macroalgae to whales and seabirds. In some marine sponges within the |FRAME: TAX-190525| family PBDEs can exceed 10% of the sponge tissue by dry weight |CITS: [Unson94][Becerro04]|., In addition to hydroxylated PBDEs such as |FRAME: CPD-20585| and |FRAME: CPD-20560|, brominated compounds found in sponges include methoxylated derivatives of dihydroxylated polybrominated diphenyl ethers (di-OH-BDEs) such as |FRAME: CPD-20562| (which is likely derived from |FRAME: CPD-20563| by methylation) and polybrominated dioxins such as |FRAME: CPD-20602|, |FRAME: CPD-20604|, and |FRAME: CPD-20564|., The polybrominated dibenzo-p-dioxin |FRAME: CPD-20564| has been first reported from the marine sponge |FRAME: ORG-6352|, along with its methoxylated form, |FRAME: CPD-20565| |CITS: [12193037]|. The toxicity potential for, dibenzo-p-dioxins is very high, as they are structurally analogous to some of the most toxic anthropogenic molecules ever produced |CITS: [16445906]|., An analysis of the metagenomes of several sponges has concluded that the brominated compounds are produced exclusively by symbiotic cyanobacteria. The search, which was conducted using known γ-proteobacterial genes that are involved in bromophenol biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-7929|), identified homologous regions in several symbiotic |FRAME: TAX-190968| strains |CITS: [28319100]|., About This Pathway, It is believed that the formation of polybrominated dioxins involves condensation of two building blocks - |FRAME: CPD-20548| and |FRAME: CPD-20594| |CITS: [25061970]|. The biosynthesis of the former is described in |FRAME: PWY-7929|. In general, that pathway starts with the conversion of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-58118| gene), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-20548| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.55|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58119| gene. This unusual brominase, which resembles flavin-dependent oxygenases, catalyzes two successive brominations, the second of which also involves decarboxylation |CITS: [24974229]|., The route to |FRAME: CPD-20594| also starts with |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40|. However, the next step is believed to be a hydroxylation that forms |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|. In |FRAME: TAX-190968| this reaction may be catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 hydroxylase encoded by the |FRAME: G-58121| gene. This enzyme's activity has not been characterized on its own. However, a |FRAME: TAX-1140| strain expressing the other enzymes of the pathway but no |FRAME: G-58121| produced only PBDEs. When Bmp12 was co-expressed, the recombinant host began to produce di-OH-BDEs and polybrominated dioxins, supporting the proposed role of Bmp12 |CITS: [28319100]|. Following the hydroxylation, the same brominase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58119| gene, acts on |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, generating |FRAME: CPD-20594| |CITS: [25061970]|., The next step in the pathway involves |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-58120| gene). This enzyme from the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1353533| is known to be very promiscuous, and can catalyze the coupling of phenol rings in many different ways, producing many brominated biphenyls and diphenyl ethers (see |FRAME: PWY-7932|) |CITS: [24974229]|. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-190968| appears more limited, and when acting on |FRAME: CPD-20548| mainly forms |FRAME: CPD-20561|. However, the enzyme was shown to efficiently couple |FRAME: CPD-20548| and |FRAME: CPD-20594|, forming |FRAME: CPD-20563| and |FRAME: CPD-20591| |CITS: [28319100]|. Cyclization of the former, accompanied by the release of a bromide ion, leads to formation of |FRAME: CPD-20564|.

|FRAME: CPD-8915 Gramine| is a simple indole alkaloid. It is found in certain wild and cultivated barley lines. Accumulation of gramine in barley is subjected to both developmental and environmental control. The highest content of gramine is found in young leaves, particularly in the first leaf. Each successive leaf contains less gramine. Heat can induce the accumulation of gramine, but only if the leaves were expanding while exposed to high temperature |CITS: [ 16662926]|. In barley, gramine was reported as an antifungal defense compound and is also active against aphids |CITS: [11673626]|. Gramine was also reported toxic to Meadow voles (filed mice) |CITS: [7020159]|., Gramine is synthesized from tryptophan via |FRAME: CPD-8913| (AMI), involving two well-characterized N-methylation steps |CITS: [7141562][16664431][16930646][21074448]|. The step from trytophan to AMI, which is believed to be the rate-limiting step, is still not well characterized |CITS: [16664431]|.

Summary: Please Note: This pathway represents the biosynthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOL| molecule containing 80 carbon atoms (16 isoprenoid units) found in organisms such as the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|. The carbon chain length of dolichols varies within a range in a species, and the range varies among species |CITS: [9878760]|., General Background, Dolichyl monophosphates are polyisoprenoid glycosyl carrier lipids found in eukaryotes. They have been characterized in yeasts and in mammalian cells. They function in C- and O-mannosylation and N-glycosylation of proteins and in the biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors in the endoplasmic reticulum (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|). Bacteria also contain polyisoprenoid glycosyl carrier lipids, but they differ from dolichols in that the prokaryotic molecules are fully unsaturated polyprenols, whereas in dolichols the α-isoprene unit is saturated and the chain lengths are generally longer. The carbon chain length of |FRAME: DOLICHOL| molecules varies within a range in a species, and the range varies among species |CITS: [9878760]|. For example the yeasts |FRAME: TAX-4932| and |FRAME: TAX-4896| contain dolichols of mainly 15,16 and 16,17 isoprenoid units, respectively (in |CITS: [9514857]|). Animal cells contain a family of dolichols with 15-23 isoprenoid units. Major dolichols in rat and human contain 18,19 and 19,20 isoprenoid units, respectively (in |CITS: [3291859]|). These molecular, characteristics of polyisoprenoids are critical for recognition by enzymes involved in glycosylation pathways. Dolichols are present in human tissues in relatively large amounts, especially in liver and some endocrine organs |CITS: [1449704]|. Dolichols have also been reported in archaea |CITS: [2857171]| and characterized in plants |CITS: [18302278] [18612099]|, although the cellular details of their biosynthetic pathways in these organisms remain to be determined |CITS: [18612099] [18302278]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [11425794]| and in |CITS: [9473469]|., About This Pathway, Dolichyl monophosphate biosynthesis is initiated by microsomal, membrane-bound cis-isoprenyltransferases which elongate the polyisoprenoid chain. These enzymes add isoprenoid units from |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| to form diphosphorylated polyprenyl intermediates. In the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|, this enzyme is encoded by gene |FRAME: YBR002C|. An alternative cis-isoprenyltransferase encoded by gene |FRAME: YMR101C| is also present that is able to extend the polyisoprenoid chain length to 19-22 isoprenoid units, similar to the mammalian dolichols |CITS: [11181565]|. The initial substrates |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|i are present in the cytosol, but the polyprenyl diphosphate intermediates are hydrophobic and are thought to be embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. The biosynthesis of dolichols in rat liver peroxisomes has also been studied |CITS: [1527001]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [11425794] [9473469]|., After chain elongation, the final polyisoprenoid diphosphate intermediate is dephosphorylated to a polyprenol. Candidate phosphatases have been reported, but it is not known which one(s) function in this pathway. , The next steps of the pathways have been significantly revised by a 2024 study |CITS: [38821050]|. Previous to that study it was commonly thought that dolichol is directly produced from |FRAME: Ditrans-polycis-polyprenols polyprenol| by the enzyme SRD5A3. However, the new study has discovered that dolichol synthesis requires a three-step detour involving oxidation of the terminal alcohol group to an aldehyde. First, the polyprenol is oxidized to a |FRAME: Ditrans-polycis-polyprenals polyprenal| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.441| (DHRSX), whose gene resides on the pseudoautosomal regions of the X and Y chromosomes. It is the polyprenal that is reduced by SRD5A3 (|FRAME: EC-1.3.1.94|), forming |FRAME: Dolichals dolichal|. Finally, DHRSX catalyzes a second reaction, converting dolichal to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichol| |CITS: [38821050]|., The terminal step in this pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.108|, which phosphorylates dolichol to dolichol phosphate |CITS: [16923818][17273964]|.

The mycobacterial cell wall functions as an immunoprotective barrier against host mechanisms of recognition and killing, but also sheds lipids that activate immune responses in the human cell. Human CD1a, CD1b, and CD1c proteins bind several types of mycobacterial lipids and traffic them to the cell surface, enabling direct contact of the intracellularly derived mycobacterial lipids with T cell antigen receptors of lipid-reactive T cells. The CD1-restricted T cells express antimicrobial proteins such as γ-interferon and granulysin and have the ability to lyse mycobacteria-infected target cells., The only known microbial lipid presented by CD1c is |FRAME: CPD-18607 "β-D-mannosyl phosphomycoketide"|, an antigen with an unusual structure that was isolated originally from |FRAME: TAX-1764| |CITS: [10786796]|. This glycolipid contains a mannosyl-β-1-phosphate moiety that is identical to those found in |FRAME: ALPHA-D-MANNOSYLCHITOBIO "mannosyl-β-1-phosphodolichols"| from mammalian cells. The lipid portion, on the other hand, is composed of an unusual 4, 8, 12, 16, 20-pentamethylpentacosyl unit, which has a fully saturated backbone and is much shorter than polyunsaturated C95 polyisoprenols found in mammalian cells., The polyisoprenoid-like structure of this compound and the number of carbons (30) found in the backbone of the compound identified in |FRAME: TAX-1764| prompted the suggestion that it is biosynthesized from condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, like true polyisoprenols (maintaining the required C5 repeating unit), followed by saturation of the double bonds. However, an analysis of several Mycobacterium species identified |FRAME: CPD-18607 "β-D-mannosyl phosphomycoketides"| that contained 30, 31, 32, 33 or 34 carbons. Thus, a polyisoprenols-like biosynthesis was ruled out., An alternative model for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-18607 "β-D-mannosyl phosphomycoketides"| is by an unusual ployketide synthase (PKS) that incorporates both malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA extender units, alternatively. By binding differernt starter units, such a PKS could produce the expected products of varying chain length., Analysis of the mycobacterial genome for a gene that could encode such as enzyme suggested |FRAME: G185E-6251|. This gene, which encodes the largest open reading frame in the |FRAME: TAX-83332| genome, was previously thought to be involved in |FRAME: CPD-18612| biosynthesis |CITS: [12819062]|. However, it was shown that pks12-deficient strain was able to produce |FRAME: CPD-18612|, disproving this proposal |CITS: [15611286]|., On the other hand, |FRAME: G185E-6251|, which encodes a very large 12-domain PKS enzyme, contains two complete sets of FAS-like catalytic domains, as would be required for an enzyme that is able to incorporate both malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-Coa. Furthermore, it has been predicted that the two AT domains are specific for malonyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA, respectively |CITS: [12691745]|., To test this hypothesis, pks12 mutants were generated in three different Mycobacterium strains. Deletion of the |FRAME: G185E-6251| genes in each of the three strains completely abolished production of their respective |FRAME: CPD-18607 "β-D-mannosyl phosphomycoketide"|, as well as their ability to activate CD1c-restricted T cells |CITS: [15611286]|., Biosynthesis of the final products requires several additional steps - release of the CoA factor, phosphorylation, and attachement of the mannosyl group. The enzymes responsible for these steps have not been identified as of 2015.

General Background, |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf., Chlorophyll functions as the main light harvesting pigment in photosynthesis, capturing photons and transfering them to the reaction centers. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-18895|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, |FRAME: CPD-10335|, |FRAME: CPD-18896|, |FRAME: CPD-18897| and |FRAME: CPD-18898|)., |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLL-A "Chlorophyll a"| is found in all green plants, cyanobacteria, euglenozoa, and all photosynthetic algae. In these organisms, the pigment is found mostly in its monovinyl form (a vinyl group at C-3 and an ethyl group at C-8). However, its biosynthetic pathway involves largely divinyl intermediates (vinyl groups at both C-3 and C-8). Two different enzymes are known to catalyze the reduction of the C-8 vinyl group. This pathway describes |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.75|. The gene encoding this enzyme has been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-3702| and named |FRAME: G-9133| |CITS: [15632054]|. Homologues of the gene were initially found in the genomes of higher plants and green algae. A bacterial homolog was later found in phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1097| and named |FRAME:G-10101| |CITS: [17148453]|., The last step in the biosynthesis of chlorophyll is the esterification of a side chain. The enzyme responsible for the esterification reaction (|FRAME: EC-2.5.1.62|) prefers phytyl diphosphate, but can also use geranylgeranyl diphosphate, in which case the geranylgeranyl side-chain is subsequently reduced to a phytyl chain by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.83|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17786 Griseofulvin|, an polyketide antibiotic produced by ascomycetes such as Penicillium aethiopicum, is the first oral antifungal medication |CITS:[14433006] [4583105]| which has been widely used for treatments of dermatophytes in humans and as a drug for applications in veterinary care |CITS:[18611708]|. Although by now superseded by modern drugs such as echinocandins (see |FRAME:PWY-7650|) |FRAME:CPD-17786| is still considered an interesting drug due to its ability to intervene in mitosis |CITS:[15985553]| inducing multipolar spindles by inhibiting centrosome clustering which eventually leads to the death of tumor cell lines |CITS:[17616693]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-17786| has been shown to suppress hepatitis C virus (HCV) replication and therefore has potential in the development of novel therapies for patients diseased with HCV |CITS:[18624717]|., Penicillium aethiopicum is known to mainly produce three secondary metabolites, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17786| (this pathway), |FRAME:CPD-17868| (see |FRAME:PWY-7659|) |CITS:[20534346]| and |FRAME:CPD-17869| (see |FRAME:PWY-7660|) |CITS:[21299212]| which are also chemotaxonomic markers indicative for the fungal genus Penicillium |CITS:[Frisvad04]|. Besides their medical importance, |FRAME:CPD-17786| and congeners have been attracted researchers because of their unusual structural features such as the spirocyclic grisan ring indicating an challenging reaction mechanism. Interestingly, similar compounds with this spirocyclic scaffold have also been reported from lichens which may point to the existence of homologue genes in the respective fungal symbionts |CITS:[Peres97]|. The gene cluster responsible for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17786| has been found by bioinformatics mining (see also references |CITS:[16426969] [18559263]|) of the Penicillium aethiopicum genome through its nonreductive polyketide synthase (NR-PKS) encoded by GsfA |CITS:[20534346]|. Often polyketide synthases (PKSs) catalyze committed steps of an pathway and the respective clusters in fungi could be identified via their PKSs |CITS:[17390002] [17369821]| (for instance see |FRAME:PWY-7565| - polyketide; |FRAME:PWY-7520| - bisindole alkaloids)., The first step in |FRAME:PWY-7653| is the formation of an intermediate, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17791| via |FRAME:ACP|-bound metabolite undergoing a C8-C13 aldol condensation and a C1-C6 Claisen-type cyclization. The catalyzing enzyme, i.e. norlichexanthone synthase only forms this compound when the subsequent genes of the pathway are present. Otherwise, the same reaction resulted in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17790| under spontaneous release of water |CITS:[20534346] [23978092]|. Subsequently two methylations at the 3-hydroxy (GsfB) and 9-hydroxy group (GsfC) are carried out resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17787| |CITS:[23978092]|. The latter is substrate for the griseophenone C halogenase (GsfI) which in a flavin-dependent halogenation yields |FRAME:CPD-17789|. In the following step the phenolic coupling reaction that converts |FRAME:CPD-17789| to |FRAME:CPD-17792| is carried out by an cytochrome P450 dependent synthase (GsfF) which also can act on |FRAME:CPD-17787| to form |FRAME:CPD-17799| (see |FRAME:PWY-7655|). Another methylation step at position 5 of the already formed grisan ring is catalyzed by the griseofulvin 5-O-methyltransferase (GsfD) and produces |FRAME:CPD-17793| which, in the last step of the pathway is stereospecific reduced on the double bond between C-13 and C-12 (1,4-hydride addition) by the dehydrogriseofulvin reductase (GsfE) yielding the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17786| |CITS:[23978092]|.

Summary: General Background, Sorbitol is a hexitol, |FRAME:Sugar-alcohols| found in higher plants |CITS:[BIELESKI82]|. In Rosaceae plants, sorbitol is the main photoassimilate produced in the leaves from which it is translocated to sink tissues |CITS:[WEBB62],[BIELESKI85]|. Sorbitol synthesis shares a common hexose phosphate pool with sucrose synthesis, and it was recently shown in apple that synthesis pathways are not independent from one another |CITS:[ZHOU02]|. Indeed, |FRAME:MONOMER-11709| was shown to be inhibited by |FRAME:D-SORBITOL-6-P|, an intermediate in the biosynthesis pathway of sorbitol.

Antifungal agents such as |FRAME:CPD-17786| (see |FRAME:PWY-7653|) and |FRAME:CPD-17801| are polyketide antibiotics produced by ascomycetes |CITS:[25476923]|. |FRAME:CPD-17801 Dechlorogriseofulvin| has been found side-by-side with |FRAME:CPD-17786| in various Penicillium species such as Penicillium urticae |CITS:[5415206]|, Penicillium canescens |CITS:[17429757]| and Penicillium aethiopicum |CITS:[20534346]| but has also been reported from endophytic fungi such as Nigrospora sp. isolated from the medicinal plant Moringa oleifera |CITS:[22806033]| or an marine Nigrospora strain living on mangroves |CITS:[21512970]|. Although not as effective as |FRAME:CPD-17786| the dechlorinated metabolite, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17801| still exhibits antifungal activities |CITS:[22806033]| and has been recognized to kill cancer cell lines by apoptosis when extracted from its native fungal host |CITS:[22397996]|. , Penicillium aethiopicum is known to produce secondary metabolites such as |FRAME:CPD-17786|, |FRAME:CPD-17801|, |FRAME:CPD-17868| |CITS:[20534346]| and |FRAME:CPD-17869| |CITS:[21299212]| which are also considered chemotaxonomic markers for the fungal genus Penicillium |CITS:[Frisvad04]|. Both |FRAME:CPD-17786| and |FRAME:CPD-17801| have been attracted researchers because of their unusual structural features such as the spirocyclic grisan ring indicating an challenging reaction mechanism. Interestingly, similar compounds with this spirocyclic scaffold have also been reported from lichens which may point to the existence of homologue genes in the respective fungal symbionts |CITS:[Peres97]|. The gene cluster responsible for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17786| and its dechlorinated derivative |FRAME:CPD-17801| has been found by bioinformatics mining of the Penicillium aethiopicum genome through its nonreductive polyketide synthase (NR-PKS) encoded by GsfA |CITS:[20534346]|. , The pathway towards |FRAME:CPD-17801| branches out of the |FRAME:PWY-7653| at the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-17787|. It has been demonstrated that all enzymes involved in reactions down-streams of |FRAME:CPD-17787| can also act on corresponding non-chlorinated intermediates.The phenolic coupling reaction carried out by the grisophenone C synthase (GsfF) converts |FRAME:CPD-17787| to |FRAME:CPD-17799| the same way as shown for the chlorinated intermediate |FRAME:CPD-17789| (see |FRAME:PWY-7653|). The methylation step at position 5 of the already formed grisan ring is catalyzed by the griseofulvin 5-O-methyltransferase (GsfD) which produces |FRAME:CPD-17800|. The latter compound serves as substrate in the last step of the pathway and is stereospecific reduced on the double bond between C-13 and C-12 (1,4-hydride addition) by the dechloro-dehydrogriseofulvin reductase (GsfE) yielding the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17801| |CITS:[23978092]|.

Enzymes of pathway: MONOMER-21961 // NICONUCADENYLYLTRAN-MONOMER // NICOTINATEPRIBOSYLTRANS-MONOMER // MONOMER-21964 // MONOMER-21963 // NAD-SYNTH-CPLX // NICOTINAMID-MONOMER
Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, The deamidated NAD salvage pathway (via |FRAME: NIACINE|) is an evolutionarily ancient pathway that exists in all kingdoms of life |CITS: [19721089]|. While the main source of NAD in most mammalian cells and tissues is the amidated pathway (|FRAME: NAD-BIOSYNTHESIS-III|) |CITS: [15381699]|, the deamidated pathway is the only pathway to recycle |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| produced by NAD consuming enzymes in the majority of lower organisms |CITS: [32130883]|.

Sugar derivative metabolites such as acylsugars are specialized compounds comprised of either a glucose backbone, i.e. acylglucoses |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| or a |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold, i.e. acylsucroses which are decorated with acyl groups of varying length and structure |CITS:[18931142]|. Wild tomato species have been shown to possess a greater diversity in the acylation pattern of those sugar frameworks than cultivated tomatoes |CITS:[Shapiro94] [21098679]|. The diversity is most strikingly in Solanum habrochaites (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) |CITS:[23054567]| but also Solanum pennellii acylsucroses (this pathway) deviate remarkably from the acylation pattern observed in cultivated species of tomato., Acylsugars such as acylsucroses are produced in specialized glandular trichomes of leafes, stems and flowers and are generally confined to the Solanaceae plant family |CITS:[2652002]|. A few types of glandular trichomes, e.g. type I, IV or VI present in the Solanaceae family, have been found to be associated with the biosynthesis of acylsugars |CITS:[21098679]| which are produced and secreted onto leaf or stem surfaces |CITS:[Severson85]|. Although the role of acylsugars in those plants is incompletely researched and not well understood acylsugars have been reported to exhibit broad-spectrum insecticidal properties |CITS:[Hawthorne92] [18807203] [Maluf10] [Leckie12]| based on findings on how those compounds interact with phytohormones |CITS:[21068365]|, interfere with feeding behavior of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94] [Liedl95]| and are able to alert and lure predators of feeding pest larvae as demonstrated for Nicotiana species |CITS:[21518882]|. Acylsugars also have had limited applications in the food, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries as non-hazardous additives |CITS:[Hill99]|., The biochemistry in trichomes related to the production of specialized metabolites has been found to be highly dynamic |CITS:[22563774]| and mutants with disturbed trichome development due to silenced genes lost most of their resistance against certain herbivores |CITS:[20668059]|. The existence of plant metabolic networks producing a tremendous amount of specialized metabolites |CITS:[21275647]| is paramount for the chemical diversity that confers strength and adaptability to plant defense and communication/signaling pathways. Although the variability of acyl group appendices to the |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold in Solanum pennellii is somewhat lower than in Solanum habrochaites (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|), the former wild species displays some acylation pattern in acylsucroses not found in other tomato species so far. , All acylsucroses found in Solanum pennellii lack furanose acylation which is attributed to an ASAT3 like gene encoding a acyltransferase which instead of acylating the 3'-ring position of furanose decorates the 2-position of the pyranose moiety. Biochemical assays with purified Solanum pennellii ASAT3 encoded enzyme demonstrated the inability of this enzyme to accept diacylsucrose metabolites as substrates. Instead, monoacylated sucrose such as |FRAME:CPD-19018 sucrose-4-isovalerate| was accepted (see also |FRAME:PWY18C3-8 monoacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-9 diacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) and the ASAT3 encoded protein from Solanum pennellii was shown to use either |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA isovaleryl-CoA| or |FRAME:ISOBUTYRYL-COA isobutanoyl-CoA| as acyl donor to produce |FRAME:CPD-19120 sucrose-2,4-diisovalerate| and |FRAME:CPD-19121 sucrose-2-isobutyryl-4-isovalerate|, respectively |CITS:[25862303]|. Moreover, the in vitro assays did correspond with the in vivo identified metabolites in Solanum pennellii which were shown to be not acylated on the furanose moiety and do not have a acetyl group associated to the C-2 position of the pyranose ring |CITS:[20113441]|.

Summary: Natural essential oils contain monoterpenes as one of their major constituents. The oil accumulates , in glands found in leaves, petals and trichomes. |FRAME: GERANIOL "Geraniol"| is an acyclic monoterpene alcohol , that is found in the essential oils of |FRAME: TAX-66014| (lemon grass) |CITS: [17230350]|, |FRAME: TAX-94328| (ginger) |CITS: [11743782 ]| and |FRAME: TAX-39350| (basil) |CITS: [14657409]|. It is also emitted from flowers of many plant species with an intense rose scent. In the camphor tree (|FRAME: TAX-192326|) the leaves accumulate almost 86-98% |FRAME: GERANIOL| in their essential oil |CITS: [15680985]|. , |FRAME: GERANIOL "Geraniol"| decreases the activity of a key polyamine biosynthesis enzyme, i.e. ornithine decarboxylase which is enhanced during cancer growth. The antiproliferative properties of |FRAME: GERANIOL| are based on its inhibitory effect on polyamine metabolism |CITS: [CARNESECCHI01]|., The oxidation products of |FRAME: GERANIOL|, |FRAME: GERANIAL| and |FRAME: CPD-9762| are often found together, this mixture is also called citral which imparts the characteristic 'lemon' flavor to the oils. Citral is a valuable flavor and scent reagent used extensively in food and perfume industry |CITS: [16150417]|, |FRAME: GERANIOL Geraniol| is also the key precursor of |FRAME: CPD-7978|, citronellol and their esters., Many plant enzymes that participate in the biosynthetic pathways of oil compounds have been characterized., |FRAME: GERANIOL Geraniol| is synthesized from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| and geraniol synthase (GES), the enzyme catalyzing this conversion has been isolated from many species. The flavor and aroma of |FRAME: TAX-4081| has been modified by metabolic engineering utilizing the basil GES gene under the control of the tomato ripening specific , polygalactouronase promoter, which successfully increased the monoterpene content |CITS: [17592476]|.

Summary: General Background, verbascose and ajugose are two members of the so-called 'raffinose series' of sucrosyl oligosaccharides (also known as raffinose family oligosaccharides, RFOs). Sucrosyl oligosaccharides represent a large portion of primary oligosaccharides in plants (defined as oligosaccharides synthesized by the action of a glycosyl transferase that mediates the transfer of a glycopyranosyl residue to either the glucopyranosyl or fructofuranosyl moiety of sucrose. They are differentiated from secondary oligosaccharides which are generated by the hydrolysis of higher oligosaccharides, polysaccharides or heterosides. For review, see |CITS:[KANDLER82]|). Members of the raffinose series occur at least in traces in each plant family; it is one of the most widespread sucrosyl oligosaccharide series in flowering plants and might even be ubiquitous (see |CITS:[KANDLER82]| for review). This series comprises |FRAME:CPD-1099|, |FRAME:CPD-170|, |FRAME:CPD-8065|,|FRAME:CPD-8066| (see also |FRAME:PWY-5342|) as well as several other compounds with a higher degree of polymerization (DP; the highest is a nonasaccharide; none of these higher-DP oligosaccharides in the series have not yet been named). The sugars of this series consist of α1,6-linked chains of D-galactose attached to the 6-glucosyl position of sucrose. They are synthesized in leaves, roots and tubers. Raffinose and stachyose are the two most commonly found oligosaccharides of this series (see |FRAME:PWY-5337|). However, higher RFOs with DP are also found in certain species such as the frost-hardy |FRAME:TAX-38596|, in which both short-chain and long-chain RFOs are present and have been speculated to act as antifreeze or antisalt agents |CITS:[12232288],[12228647],[12223871],[10758476]|. The biosynthesis of higher-DP RFOs appears to occurs via two routes: one is dependent on galactinol, and requires enzymes similar to that of the |FRAME:PWY-5337| pathway, the other does not appear to require galactinol (this pathway). This latter route has been discovered recently |CITS:[12232288],[12060258]|., Enzymes of the pathway: A single enzyme has been described that can catalyze all the polymerization steps of this pathway. This enzyme, galactan:galactan galactosyltransferase, catalyzes the chain elongation of RFOs by transferring a terminal α-galactosyl residue from one RFO molecule to another instead of using galactinol as galactosyl donor |CITS:[12060258],[15034167]|.

Summary: Background, After cellulose, chitin is the most abundant natural polymer in the biological kingdom. It is present in the cell walls of fungi, the exoskeletons of arthropods and in parts of cephalopods. A nitrogen containing modified polysaccharide made up of N-acetylglucosamine units, chitin is akin to cellulose with one acetyl amine group replacing one hydroxyl group on each monomer. The degradation of chitin by yeast chitin deacetylases yields significant amounts of acetate. The reduction of acetate to ethanol has been shown to be an economically promising source of viable bioethanol |CITS: [22141374]|., About this Pathway, The yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| naturally produces all of the enzymes required to produce ethanol from chitin. Chitin deacetylases expressed during sporulation mediate the hydrolysis of the N-acetamido groups on N-acetyl-D-glucosamine residues in developing chitin chains, releasing chitosan and acetate |CITS: [9133736]|. As a result, spore walls of |FRAME: TAX-4932| contain the deacetylated form chitosan |CITS: [8367456]|., The released acetate is converted by the enzyme |FRAME: YBL015W-MONOMER| to acetyl CoA, which can proceed to the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS| in yeast glyoxysomes. Acetyl coA is condensed with glyoxylate to yield malate, which is converted to pyruvate via malate dehydrogenase |CITS: [1454530]|., Pyruvate is fermented to ethanol as described in |FRAME: PWY-5486|.

Summary: |FRAME: 14-DICHLOROBENZENE 1,4-Dichlorobenzene| is a volatile organic compound used in mothballs and some air fresheners, and a common contaminant of indoor air. It is also used against termites in soil. It has been classified as a possible carcinogen and may be related to decreased pulmonary function in adults |CITS: [18091427]|., |FRAME: 14-DICHLOROBENZENE 1,4-Dichlorobenzene| has been identified as a priority pollutant, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Chlorinated benzenes are chemically stable in nature, so biological degradation is the only process by which these compounds are eliminated |CITS: [8526500]|., Several bacterial species were reported to catabolize |FRAME: 14-DICHLOROBENZENE|, including |FRAME: ORG-6072|, |CITS: [3789724]|, an unidentified Pseudomonas species |CITS: [3606087]|, |FRAME: TAX-65067| |CITS: [1987135]|, |FRAME: ORG-6071| |CITS: [8526500]| and other not well characterized bacteria |CITS: [16962633]|., The best studied case is that of |FRAME: ORG-6071|, a bacterium that is able to utilize |FRAME: 14-DICHLOROBENZENE| as a sole source of carbon and energy. The degradation pathway in this organism begins with dioxygenation of |FRAME: 14-DICHLOROBENZENE| by a |FRAME: MONOMER-41|, followed by |FRAME: CPLX-1641|, resulting in |FRAME: 36-DICHLOROCATECHOL|. Ring opening then proceeds via a modified ortho cleavage pathway, yielding |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| which is processed to TCA cycle intermediates |CITS: [8526500]|. The intermediates of the pathway up to |FRAME: 2-CHLOROMALEYLACETATE| were isolated and identified by gas chromatography, confirming the propsed pathway |CITS: [8526500]|. In addition, individual enzyme activities have been, measured with whole cells and cell extracts |CITS: [9148781]|., Even though |FRAME: ORG-6071| can not grow with |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE| or |FRAME: CPD-10603| as the, sole carbon source, all the enzymes that participate in this pathway can also accept the respective intermediates of the, degradation of these two compound |CITS: [9148781]|. In the case of |FRAME: CPD-10603|, lack of growth results probably from failure to induce the enzymes. Growth with |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE|, on the other hand, does induce the key enzymes. The authors speculate that lack of growth with this compound may be the result of toxicity of the one of the intermediates involved |CITS: [9148781]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Cobamides Cobamides| are |FRAME: Corrinoids corrinoids| that contain upper and lower ligands. At least 16 different cobamides with structural variability in the lower ligand have been described. Some of the lower ligands found in cobamides include |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108| |CITS: [24055007]|. , The most common cobamide, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin|, contains |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| (DMB) as the lower ligand and either a methyl group or 5'-deoxyadenosyl group as the upper ligand., Different routes for the biosynthesis of cobamide lower ligands have been desctribed. It has been shown that some aerobic microorganisms synthesize |FRAME:DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| from |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN| via |FRAME:FMN| (see |FRAME: PWY-5523|)., Comparable anaerobic pathways were not known until 2015. Earlier work reported that |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| was generated from |FRAME: GLY|, |FRAME: GLN|, |FRAME: ERYTHROSE|, |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: MET| |CITS: [6812527]| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-18497| and |FRAME: CPD-18526| |CITS: [8223635]|. However, the anaerobic pathway was not well understood., A key finding occurred in 2015 when |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.23|, was discovered. This radical S-adenosylmethionine enzyme, which is similar to |FRAME: EG11585| (encoding |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.17|), catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: 5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-5-AMINOIMIDAZOLE| (AIR) to |FRAME: CPD-18497| in a single step |CITS: [26237670]|. Two versions of this enzyme were described - a monomeric enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-44253| |CITS: [26237670]|, and a heteromeric enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-44254| and |FRAME: G-44255| genes |CITS: [26246619]|., In |FRAME: TAX-1736| the genes encoding the enzyme were found in a short operon that contains the rest of the genes necessary for DMB biosynthesis, paving the way to the characterization of the pathway shown here. Cloning and expression of the full operon in |FRAME: TAX-562| supplied with external |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| afforded the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD0-1256| (see |FRAME: COBALSYN-PWY|), indicating that expression of the |FRAME: TAX-1736| bza operon is sufficient for anaerobic |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [26246619]|., The complement of bza genes present in an organism are predictive of the benzimidazole lower ligand, and thus the cobamide that it produces. For example, |FRAME: TAX-269797| contains only a bzaF gene, and thus produces |FRAME: CPD-18497| (verified biochemically); |FRAME: TAX-264732| contains bzaA, bzaB and bzaC and produces |FRAME: CPD-18321| (verified biochemically); |FRAME: TAX-760568| contains bzaA, bzaB, bzaC and bzaD and is thus produces |FRAME: CPD-18495| (predicted); and |FRAME: TAX-33952| contains all genes and produces |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| (verified biochemically) |CITS: [26246619]|., The |FRAME: G-80505| gene of |FRAME: TAX-243231| is located in an operon together with other genes involved in cobamide biosynthesis and is the only bza-type gene found in this organism |CITS: [26246619]|. Analysis of the cobamides synthesized by |FRAME: TAX-243231| confirmed the production of |FRAME: CPD-20849| as the major corrinoid species |CITS: [26246619]|.

Names: L-malate degradation I // malolactic fermentation (misleading) // (S)--malate degradation I
Summary: Most lactic acid bacteria (LAB) possess an enzyme that can decarboxylate |FRAME: MAL| to |FRAME: L-LACTATE|., The enzyme, which has been named |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.101|, has been purified from several lactic acid bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1245| |CITS: [16345941]|, |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [6833282]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1247| |CITS: [2097345]|. The active form of these proteins is either a homodimer or a homotetramer, and the enzymes contain a tightly bound NAD+ cofactor and require Mn<sup>2+</sup>., The metabolism of |FRAME: MAL| by lactic acid bacteria has considerable interest because of its relevance in winemaking. The conversion of |FRAME: MAL| to |FRAME: L-LACTATE| leads to a reduction in the acidity of wine, and provides microbiological stability by preventing the secondary growth of lactic acid bacteria after bottling |CITS: [10532386]|. The process has been named malolactic fermentation, although this name is misleading, as no fermentation actually occurs., Up to ten lactic acid bacteria species can be identified in must (freshly pressed grape juice), belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-1578|, |FRAME: TAX-1253|, |FRAME: TAX-1243| and |FRAME: TAX-46254| genera. However, after the alcoholic fermentation (carried by yeast) begins and the alcohol concentration increases, only |FRAME: TAX-46254| prevails, since it can survive at pH values below 3.5, ethanol concentrations above 10% (v/v), and moderately high |FRAME: SULFUR-DIOXIDE| levels (50 mg/l) |CITS: [Costantini09]|., Studies with |FRAME: TAX-1582|, which possesses a second pathway for |FRAME: MAL| degradation (see |FRAME: PWY-7686|), suggest that malolactic fermentation does not allow the organism to grow on |FRAME: MAL| as a carbon source, and actually competes with the second pathway that does allow that, resulting in slower growth. Thus, malolactic fermentation is optimized for raising external pH (since the reaction consumes a proton), and provides an advantage by preventing excessive acidification of the medium when cometabolized with substrates such as glucose |CITS: [23835171]|.

Names: caffeine degradation V (bacteria, via trimethylurate) // caffeine C-8 oxidation pathway // caffeine degradation V (bacteria, to trimethylurate)
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is a commercially important alkaloid produced by some plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5037| and |FRAME: PWY-5038|). |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation pathways have been reported in yeast, filamentous fungi, some plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6552| and |FRAME: PWY-6553|), bacteria and animals. Although the overall scheme of demethylation and oxidation reactions is similar, the main pathways, enzymes used, and some of the products vary. In humans |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is degraded by cytochrome P-450, N-acetyltransferase and xanthine oxidase enzymes |CITS: [15013152]|, whereas the bacterial pathways appear to involve enzymes different from these. The bacterial enzymes are of interest in bioremediation of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-containing waste from coffee and tea processing, the conversion of such waste to animal feed, the development of biodecaffination techniques, as well as their use in the development of pharmaceuticals and biofuels. Although these pathways are relatively well characterized, the demethylation enzymes have generally been unstable during purification. Work on gene cloning and recombinant enzyme purification and characterization is in progress |CITS: [22328667]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [14977550] [17009088]| and |CITS: [8919637]|., Although |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| in high concentrations is toxic to bacteria, some develop the ability to catabolize it. This includes strains of |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-507| and an unnamed strain of |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [MAZZA96]|). |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading strains have been isolated from the soil under coffee trees and in the laboratory by enrichment procedures involving |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| addition to the growth media. |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading bacteria use both N-demethylation and oxidation for |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| catabolism, as shown in this pathway and in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6538| and |FRAME: PWY-6632|. In the N-demethylating pathway, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is thought to be initially degraded by an oxidative demethylation mechanism. This mechanism involves N-demethylating monooxygenases that utilize NAD(P)H, producing dimethylxanthines, followed by monomethylxanthines and |FRAME: XANTHINE|. This mechanism has been supported by the creation of EC 1.14.13.128. |FRAME: XANTHINE| is degraded by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to |FRAME: URATE|, which is then degraded as shown in the pathway link. In these reactions the methyl groups are oxidized to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and its derivatives may also be oxidized by caffeine oxidases or dehydrogenases to their corresponding methylurate derivatives as shown in this pathway and pathway |FRAME: PWY-6632| (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550]| and |CITS: [17009088]|)., Although most studies report an oxidative demethylation mechanism for |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and its derivatives as shown here, an early study by |CITS: [1158847]| proposed a hydrolytic demethylation mechanism (not shown). It was suggested that |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| is metabolized by a demethylating enzyme capable of hydrolyzing each of the three methyl groups and converting them to |FRAME: METOH|. |FRAME: METOH| was proposed to be oxidized by dehydrogenases to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| via |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550] [17009088]|., Bacteria have not been reported to demethylate |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| to |FRAME: CPD-12479| (1,3-dimethylxanthine), a reaction found in |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading fungi and plants (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6552|). However, it has been shown that |FRAME: ORG-6144| was able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| as sole carbon and nitrogen source, in addition to |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE|. |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| were metabolized to |FRAME: XANTHINE| via N-demethylation. |FRAME: CPD-12479| and its |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-9025| derivatives were also metabolized by oxidation to methylurates although these did not appear to be further metabolized. Growth of |FRAME: ORG-6144| on either |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: CPD-12479|, or the N-demethylated metabolites of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| resulted in coexpression of enzymes involved in the N-demethylation pathways of both |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12479| |CITS: [19447909]|. More recently, enzymes degrading both |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12479| have been characterized |CITS: [22328667][20966097]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6999|)., The inducible nature of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading enzymes in |FRAME: TAX-286| strains has been demonstrated |CITS: [18720498] [7461603]|. Recent studies of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| degradation done with whole cells, or cell-free extracts include |CITS: [20495941] [19229573] [19447909] [18720498] [17554468]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17009088]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| can be oxidized directly by caffeine oxidase or caffeine dehydrogenase to |FRAME: CPD-12480|. Caffeine oxidase has been reported in |FRAME: ORG-6150| |CITS: [16647778]| and in a mixed culture consortium of |FRAME:TAX-570| and |FRAME:TAX-1827| |CITS: [9705852] [10491316]|. In the mixed culture consortium |FRAME: CPD-12480| was further metabolized to |FRAME: CPD-12485| and then to |FRAME: CPD-12484| (not shown) |CITS: [9705852]|. A novel caffeine dehydrogenase has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-765715| |CITS: [17981969]|., Subsequent work using |FRAME: TAX-765715| demonstrated the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12480| to |FRAME: CPD-16697| catalyzed by a novel NADH-dependent trimethyluric acid monooxygenase encoded by gene tmuM. The |FRAME: CPD-16697| product of TmuM was proposed to either spontaneously decomposes to racemic |FRAME: CPD-12485| through a |FRAME: CPD-16698| intermediate, or be enzymatically converted to |FRAME: CPD-16699| by a putative TmuH hydrolase and a putative TmuD decarboxylase (see below). The further metabolism of |FRAME: CPD-16699| remains to be determined |CITS: 22609920|., Based on sequence similarities, two nearby genes tmuH encoding a putative 1,3,7-trimethyl-5-hydroxyisourate hydrolase, and tmuD encoding a putative 3,6,8-trimethyl-2-oxo-4-hydroxy-4-carboxy-5-ureidoimidazoline decarboxylase were also identified. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Vitamins-B6 Vitamin B6| is a group term for |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| (PL), |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| (PN), |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| (PM) and their 5'-phosphorylated derivatives |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| (PLP), |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE-5P| (PNP) and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP), which are also referred to as vitamers. Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) is the biochemically active form, and is an essential cofactor in all living systems |CITS: [7748903]|. It plays an important role in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism and has been implicated in singlet oxygen resistance |CITS: [10687384]|. Most bacteria, archaebacteria, fungi, and plants synthesize PLP in a single reaction, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6466|, although some bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, use a longer, more complex pathway (|FRAME: PYRIDOXSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [9696782][12896974]|. Animals do not synthesize this compound, making it an essential nutrient in their diet., PLP is an essential cofactor of numerous metabolic enzymes, predominantly in amino acid metabolism. It is one of the most versatile cofactors and participates in transamination, decarboxylation, racemization, Cα-Cβ cleavage and α-β elimination reactions. In humans this vitamin has a role in numerous functions ranging from modulation of hormone function to potent antioxidant activity., About This Pathway, The reaction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX8J2-131|, a dimeric complex that includes two different subunits |CITS: [16030023]|. Summary: General Background, One of the most striking physiological differences between the archaea and other organisms is the structure of their, membrane lipids. One defining feature of archaeal phospholipids is that they are based on a backbone consisting of |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, which is an enantiomer of the |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| used by bacteria and eukaryotic organisms. It has been suggested that archaea and bacteria were differentiated by the occurrence of cells enclosed by membranes of phospholipids with |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| as a backbone, respectively |CITS: [9419225]|., Another feature unique to archaeal phospholipids is side chains that are derivatives of isoprenoid alcohols rather than fatty acids, which are linked by ether linkages (rather than ester linkages) to the glycerophosphate backbone |CITS: [358256]|. The isoprenoids are usually modified by saturation of the double bonds - a modification that is believed to increase the ability of the lipids to survive the extreme conditions that archaea often face. Yet another unique feature is the occurrence of bipolar lipids with a tetraether core, which are present in significant numbers in archaeal species., It should be noted that bacteria of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-456828| of the |FRAME: TAX-1783270 "Fibrobacteres-Chlorobi-Bacteroidetes (FCB) group superphylum"|, are able to synthseize both canonical bacterial lipids and archaeal-like ether-linked isoprenoid phospholipids |CITS: [32929208]|., In contrast to these differences, most of the polar head groups of archaeal phospholipids are similar to those found in the other kingdoms - |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CHOLINE| |CITS: [17347520]|., The major polar lipids of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-145262| are L-serine, ethanolamine, or myo-inositol-containing di- and, tetraether type phospholipids and phosphoglycolipids, and gentiobiose-containing di- and tetraether type glycolipids., Examples of non-glycosylated lipids include |FRAME: CPD-10741 "archaetidylserine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11919 "archaetidylethanolamine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11918 "archaetidylinositol"| and |FRAME: CPD-11920 "archaetidylglycerol"|., CDP-archaeol, either in its unsaturated form or its saturated form, is the common precursor of biosynthesis of all the archaeal phospholipids, analogous to |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL "CDP-diacylglycerol"| in bacteria. While most archaea produce an archaeol that contains two C20 isoprenoid chains, a few genera of archaea, all of which are hyperthermophiles or halophiles, are known to utilize diether lipids with extended C25 isoprenoid chains. The C25,C25-diether lipids isolated from |FRAME: TAX-56636| were shown to form liposomes that are characterized by low leakage even at temperatures approaching 100°C |CITS: [21295560]|., |FRAME: TAX-56636| is an absolutely aerobic, hyperthermophilic archaeon that was isolated from a costal solfataric thermal vent in Japan |CITS: [8863437]|. The polar lipids of |FRAME: TAX-56636| consist solely of |FRAME: CPD-25564 C25,25-archaeol| (2,3-bis-sesterterpanyl-sn-glycerol), with |FRAME: CPD-25563 "C25,25-archetidylglucosylinositol"| (AGI) accounting for 91%, and |FRAME: CPD-25561 "C25,25-archetidylinositol"| (AI) accounting for the remaining 9%. Membranes composed of such C25,25 diether lipids have 20% greater thickness than those composed of tetraether |FRAME: CPD-17762 "C20,20 archaeol"|-based lipids |CITS: [9989273]|., About This Pathway, The pathway leading to the synthesis of C25,C25-archaeol is similar to that of the more common C20,C20 archaeol (see |FRAME: PWY-6349|), although the enzymes have much stronger affinity for for the longer substrates. The pathway starts with the reduction of |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of glycolysis, to |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.261|. Activity of this enzyme or presence of the the genes encoding it have been detected in all archaeal species studied so far |CITS: [9973362]|., A difference between the pathways leading to C20,C20 archaeol and C25,C25-archaeol is the participation of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.81|, which produces the longer prenyl donor |FRAME: ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| by extending |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|., The pathway continues by the attachment of two molecules of |FRAME: ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| to the |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| backbone through two ether bonds at the sn-2 and -3 positions. The product of these additions is |FRAME: CPD-25554|. The enzyme have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-56636| and found to have much higher affinity to the C25 substrates |CITS: [29427665]|., This intermediate can be reduced to |FRAME: CPD-15250| (saturated archaetidate) by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.M2|. Either form of archaetidate can be activated by |FRAME: CTP| (catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.67|) to form the corresponding form of CDP-archaeol, which is modified by different enzymes (such as |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.39|) to form the final lipids., In the case of |FRAME: TAX-56636|, |FRAME: CPD-25563| accounts for 91% of the total polar lipids, and |FRAME: CPD-25561| accounts for the remaining 9% |CITS: [9989273]|. However, as of 2022 the enzyme catalyzing the glucosylation has not been identified., This pathway is analogous to the bacterial pathway of |FRAME: CDP-diacylglycerol-Biosynthesis|, from which it differs, in the use of |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, the formation of ether bonds, and the nature of the hydrocarbon, chains.
