Summary: Pterocarpans constitute a group of natural isoflavonoids, which are typically involved as phytoalexins in the defense , against pathogens of leguminous plants. In contrast to many other isoflavonoids, pterocarpans are mostly not , constitutively expressed but induced by biotic and abiotic stress. In accordance with their chemical structure , pterocarpans are subdivided into pterocarpans, 6a-hydroxypterocarpans and pterocarpens |CITS: [Dewick94]|, Formononetin is a crucial intermediate in the biosynthesis of phytoalexins, and as such the starting point for the , formation of various pterocarpans.  The recent discovery of a new 4'-O-methyltransferase |CITS: [12610212]|, , which facilitates an additional biosynthetic route to synthesize formononetin, sheds new light on the intermediary , steps of phytoalexin production in legumes., The biosynthetic route of pterocarpans leads to various compounds distinctive for certain leguminous species. , The simple pterocarpans medicarpin (alfalfa), maackiain (chickpea) and pisatin (pea) are characterized by methoxy, , methylendioxy and 6a-hydroxyl ring substitutents. On the other side there are the complex type pterocarpans, such , as phaseollins (bean) and gluceollins (soybean) bearing prenyl substituents on their furan ring structure, |CITS: [Dixon99][Tahara95]|, The biosynthesis of pterocarpans is salient by the stereo-specificity of many of the enzymes involved. Pterocarpan , synthase, the enzyme converting 2'-hydroxyisoflavanones [e.g. (-)-vestitone] to the corresponding pterocarpans , [e.g. (6aR, 11aR)-medicarpin] has been demonstrated in alfalfa to consist of in fact two enzymes, a reductase and , a dehydratase |CITS: [8071365][7805842]|. The precedent enzyme, isoflavone reductase, catalyzes the , stereo-specific formation of the 2'-hydroxyisoflavanones (6aS or 6aR configuration), which determines the , stereochemistry of the subsequent pterocarpans, e.g. (+)-maackiain in pea and (-)-maackiain in chickpea.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. Summary: General Background, The reductive tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle is a carbon dioxide fixation pathway found in some autotrophic eubacteria and archaea. It is considered to be a primordial pathway for production of starting organic molecules for biosynthesis of sugars, lipids, amino acids, pyrimidines and pyrroles |CITS: [15340153][9084754] [11540925]|., Other pathways of this type are the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|, the |FRAME: CODH-PWY|, and the |FRAME: PWY-5743|., The reductive TCA cycle is largely the oxidative, catabolic |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| in reverse. Most of the enzymes of the TCA cycle work reversibly and could catalyze both directions. Only three counteracting enzyme pairs are thought to determine the oxidative or reductive direction of the cycle. These three enzymes are |FRAME:CPLX-7013|; |FRAME:CPLX-7011|; and |FRAME:MONOMER-11860| (the names provided here are the names of the enzyme catalyzing the reductive direction) |CITS: [SCHAUDER87][SHIBA85][15028704]|. It should be noted that these enzymes may participate in other pathways (for example, |FRAME:CPLX-7011| also participates in the oxidative TCA cycle found in |FRAME: TAX-72293|). Nonetheless, the presence of these enzyme activities in autotrophically grown bacteria and archaea is considered indicative of the presence of the reductive TCA cycle., |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.1| (|FRAME:CPLX-7014|) is also a key enzyme in the cycle |CITS: [15838028]|. The cycle results in the fixation of two molecules of carbon dioxide in the production of one molecule of acetyl-CoA (in |CITS: [15838028]|, |CITS: [16269773]| and |CITS: [15028704]|)., In a few cases, the presence of both the oxidative and reductive TCA cycles has been shown in the same organism, as in |FRAME: TAX-2271| and |FRAME: TAX-2277| |CITS: [SELIG94][15028704][12610721]|., About This Pathway, A modified reductive TCA cycle has been found in |FRAME: TAX-940| |CITS:[SHIBA85]|. There are a few differences between the pathway in this organism and the pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1092|, the organism in which the pathway was initially described (see |FRAME: P23-PWY|). One key difference is in the conversion of citrate to oxaloacetate and acetyl-coA. In |FRAME: TAX-1092| this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.8|, an α4β4 complex which is a key enzyme of the pathway. In |FRAME: TAX-940| this conversion is catalyzed by two different enzymes. The first enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-7216|, catalyzes the convcersion of citrate to citryl-coA, while the second enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-7215|, catalyzes the splitting of citryl-coA into oxaloacetate and acetyl-coA |CITS: [15101982]|., A similar difference is the carboxylation of |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: THREO-DS-ISO-CITRATE|, which in |FRAME: TAX-1092| is catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-11847|., Once again, in |FRAME: TAX-940| this reaction is catalyzed by two enzymes. The first enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-7218|, catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME:OXALO-SUCCINATE|, while the second enzyme catalyzes the NAD-dependent conversion of |FRAME:OXALO-SUCCINATE| to |FRAME: THREO-DS-ISO-CITRATE| |CITS: [17076668]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFA) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes., The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in these compounds. The icosanoids are derived from the 20-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (AA; 20:4n-6), |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA; 20:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-8120| (DGLA; 20:3n-6)., Additional fatty acids are also oxygenated to yield bioactive products, including the the 18-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (LA; 18:2n-6) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (ALA; 18:3n-3) and the 22-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| (DPA; 22:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA; 22:6n-3). Strictly speaking, the derivatives of such acids should be named octadecanoids (for C18 compounds) and docosanoids (for 22 carbon compounds), though these compounds are often included in the icosanoids, making the definition broader than initially intended., In mammals icosanoids and related mediators mediate a wide array of critical biological processes such as ovulation, initiation of labor, bone metabolism, nerve growth and development, wound healing, kidney function, blood-vessel tone, blood coagulation, immune responses, and inflammation. Despite the great importance of these compounds, mammals are not able to form a double bond at either the n-3 or n-6 position of a fatty acyl chain and must rely entirely on dietary intake for PUFAs., Three main enzyme families act on PUFAs. The first one is |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.1| (the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes), which possess dual cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activities and catalyze the oxidative cyclization of PUFAs to |FRAME: CPD-24676|, |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|, or |FRAME: CPD-26009| (depending on the starting PUFA), which are subsequently converted to a variety of prostanoids and thromboxanes by cell-specific terminal synthases and isomerases., The second family is the lipoxygenases (LOX), which catalyze the stereoselective insertion of molecular oxygen into PUFA with the formation of hydroperoxy fatty acids that are subsequently reduced to the corresponding hydroxy-fatty acids. The lipoxygenases are divided into three main form depneding on the carbon at which they oxygenate |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|: |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|., The third family is cytochrome P450 monooxygenases that catalyzes the hydroxylation and/or epoxygenation of PUFAs. In addition to producing LOX-like monohydroxy fatty acids, CYP can add a hydroxyl moiety to the ω-carbons, of PUFA to form a unique class of omega-hydroxylated fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-21314|). The epoxides that are formed by these enzymes can be hydrolyzed to the corresponding dihydroxyfatty acids by |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| (sEH).

|FRAME: DIPHTHAMIDE "Diphthamide"| is a unique posttranslationally modified histidine residue found only in translation elongation factor 2 (|FRAME: Elongation-factor-2|). This factor is found in archaea and in all eukaryotes, but not in eubacteria, and is conserved from archaea to humans. The role of diphthamide is still not understood. Mutants defective in its biosynthesis are viable in yeast, but mutant mice are retarded in growth and development, and almost always die before birth |CITS:[16648478][18765564]|. A potential role of diphthamide may be to protect ribosomes fom ribosome-inactivating proteins (such as ricin), which are widely distributed in nature |CITS: [18460012]|., The conversion of |FRAME: HIS | to |FRAME: DIPHTHAMIDE "diphthamide"| is a complex process. It starts by the transfer of a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl moiety from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|. In eukaryotes four different proteins required for this step, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11954|, |FRAME: G-11955|, |FRAME: G-11956|, and |FRAME: G3O-31725| genes |CITS: [15485916]|. However, the |FRAME: G-34534| gene of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-53953| encodes a single protein that catalyzes this reaction on its own |CITS: [20559380][20931132]|., The |FRAME: G-34533| gene of |FRAME: TAX-53953| catalyzes the second step in the pathway - the triple methylation of 2-[(3S)-3-amino-3-carboxypropyl]-L-histidine to |FRAME: CPD-17004| (the eukaryotic homolog catalyzes a quadruple methylation, resulting in diphthine methyl ester, see |FRAME: PWY-7546|) |CITS: [20873788]|., The identity of the archaeal gene encoding the last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.14|, is still not known., Diphthamide serves as the target for two important bacterial toxins - the |FRAME: CPLX-8048| (DT) and the Pseudomonas |FRAME: MONOMER-15589 "endotoxin A"|. Both toxins catalyze the transfer of |FRAME: ADENOSINE_DIPHOSPHATE_RIBOSE| from NAD+ to |FRAME: DIPHTHAMIDE| on eEF-2, inactivating it and halting cellular protein synthesis, causing cell death |CITS: [15485916]|. By targeting this unique modified amino acid which does not exist in bacteria, these pathogens are able to shut down the eukaryotic protein synthesis machinery without jeopardizing their own system.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-10754 "Pseudaminic acid"| is a sialic acid-like sugar that was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [6437679]|. It belongs to a class of nonulosonic acids that are unique to microorganisms and consists of, 5,7-diacetamido-3,5,7,9-tetradeoxy-nonulosonate derivatives that can exhibit configurational differences compared, with |FRAME: CPD-10760| |CITS: [14719362]|., Sugars that belong to this class have been found in many Gram-negative bacterial species as constituents, of important cell surface glycoconjugates, such as LPS |CITS: [14719362]|, capsular polysaccharide |CITS: [11768534]|,, pili |CITS: [11342554]|, and flagella |CITS: [11461915][12791140]|. These modifications are expected to influence, pathogenesis through bacterial adhesion, invasion, and immune evasion |CITS: [16462751]|. |FRAME: CPD-10754 "Pseudaminic acid"| has been reportede only from bacterial pathogens. It is not produced or utilized by humans, nor it is present in commensal bacteria that dominate the human gut microbiome, and this its biosynthesis pathway represents an attractive target for selective inhibition., |FRAME: TAX-210|, which is known as a causative agent of gastric and duodenal ulcers, heavily modifies its flagellin with, |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [12791140]|. Flagellin glycosylation is a necessary modification allowing flagellar assembly, bacterial motility,, colonization, and as a result, virulence |CITS: [12044670][16316188]|., Several genes involved in this process have been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-197| and |FRAME: TAX-210|, and mutations, in these genes completely abolished flagellar assembly and cell motility |CITS: [12044670][12791140][16120604]| ., A six step pathway from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-10754| was ultimately proposed, for |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [16651261]|, and all six enzymes catalyzing it have been identified and characterized, although, not all of them to the same level |CITS:[10954725][16286454][16421095][16651261][16751642]|., When all of the purified enzymes were combined in a single reaction vessel, they were able to catalyze the total, conversion of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-10755|., However, since |FRAME: CPD-10755| apparently inhibits some of the earlier enzymes of the pathway, optimal, conversion was achieved when the process was divided into two reactions, the first one consisting of the first five, enzymes, and the second one consisting of |FRAME: HP0326-MONOMER| alone |CITS: [16751642]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Macrolide-Antibiotics "Macrolide antibiotics"|, such as |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycin|, |FRAME: CPD-13808|, |FRAME: CPD-13809|, and |FRAME: CPD-13810|, constitute a well-established class of antimicrobial agents used for the treatment of respiratory tract, urinary tract, skin, and soft tissue infections., As the name implies, these drugs contain a macrolide or lactone ring, which can be 14-, 15-, or 16-membered. Attached to these rings are a number of unusual 2,6-dideoxy- or 2,3(4),6-trideoxysugars, one of which is |FRAME: CPD-13780|., Desosamine is a 3-(dimethylamino)-3,4,6-trideoxyhexose found, for example, in |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycin|, |FRAME: CPD-13808|, and |FRAME: CPD-13809|., It is produced in the activated form of |FRAME: CPD-13776 "dTDP-desosamine"| in a pathway that requires six enzymes. This activated form is recognized a glycosyltransferase that transfers the desosamine moiety to the macrolide rings of the antibiotics. Desosamine is essential for the bactericidal activity of many of these antibiotics, including erythromycin and many of its derivatives., About This Pathway, While this pathway has been studied in several organisms, the final sequence of reactions as shown here has been determined from the |FRAME: CPD-12966| producer |FRAME: TAX-47868| |CITS: [16514147]|., The first two steps, namely, the attachment of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| to |FRAME: TTP| and the subsequent removal of the C-6' hydroxyl group and the oxidation of the C-4' hydroxyl group, are typical for most pathways leading to the formation of, 3,6-dideoxyhexoses or 2,3(4),6-trideoxyhexoses (see for example |FRAME: PWY-6808| and |FRAME:DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|). In |FRAME: TAX-54571| these two reactions are catalyzed by |FRAME: G-14788 DesIII| and |FRAME: G-14772 DesIV|, respectively |CITS: [14570895]|., The next two steps in the pathway, which are catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-54571| by |FRAME: G-14770 DesI| and |FRAME: G-14771 DesII|, respectively, lead to the loss of the sugar C-4' hydroxyl group and the oxidation of the C-3' hydroxyl |CITS: [17630700][19746907]|. This is followed by a PLP-dependent transamination, catalyzed by |FRAME: G-14773 DesV| |CITS: [17456741]|, and two methylations of the amino group, catalyzed by |FRAME: G-14774 DesVI| |CITS: [12119032]|., Following its synthesis, the desosamine moiety of |FRAME: CPD-13776| is transferred to different macrolide antibiotics by the action of the DesVII glycosyltransferase and its homologs |CITS: [20695498][18548476][17049185]|. In |FRAME: TAX-54571| the enzyme is involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13832|, |FRAME: CPD-13833|, |FRAME: CPD-13834|, and |FRAME: CPD-13835|.

The first purine nucleotide that is synthesized de novo is |FRAME: IMP| (IMP). IMP is converted to |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.4|, and the latter is converted to the first adenosine nucleotide, |FRAME: AMP "adenosine 5'-monophosphate"| (AMP) by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.3.2.2|., AMP is phosphorylated to ADP and subsequently to ATP. The first reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.3|. , Reactions that convert ADP to ATP are numerous and found in multiple pathways, including fueling pathways such as anaerobic respiration, TCA-cycle based aerobic respiration, fermentation, and glycolysis, and thus this conversion is not included in this pathway. A major source for this conversion is the |FRAME: CPLX490-3510 ATP synthase| complex (|FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "EC 3.6.3.14"|), which is membrane bound and utilizes the proton gradient across membranes to phosphorylate ADP. That enzyme is described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7980|., In some bacteria ADP can also be converted to the deoxy form |FRAME: DATP| (see |FRAME:PWY-7220|)., Genetic studies indicate that in bacterial systems the majority of de novo purine biosynthetic genes are unlinked but may act as a single unit of regulation controlled by the |FRAME: PC00033| |CITS:[2404765]|.

Summary: General Background, Nascent proteins synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane and acquire carbohydrate chains on specific serine, threonine, and asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., Protein O-mannosylation is an essential protein modification in fungi and animals |CITS: [12369018][15383666][15948957]|. O-mannosyl glycans were first identified in |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [5685868]| where they are frequent modifications of secreted and cell wall proteins |CITS: [15896991]|. The yeast glycans are short oligomannose chains |CITS: [9878752]| that are attached via a glycosidic bond in α anomeric configuration to the hydroxyl group of Ser or Thr residues |CITS: [391559]|. Studies with mutants have shown that protein O-mannosylation is essential for cell wall rigidity and cell integrity, and is vital for |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [8918452]|., About This Pathway, Biosynthesis of O-mannosyl glycans is initiated in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where mannose is transferred from |FRAME: CPD-171| to serine and threonine residues of protein substrates |CITS: [6347716]|. This reaction is conserved between fungi and animals and is catalyzed by a family of enzymes named protein O-mannosyltransferases (PMTs), which are integral ER membrane proteins that contain seven transmembrane domains, a cytoplasmic N-terminus, and a C-terminal catalytic domain that faces the ER lumen |CITS: [10085156]|. It has been shown in |FRAME: TAX-4932| that the PMTs act on substrate proteins during their translocation into the ER lumen |CITS: [24519942]|., Properly folded glycoproteins are transported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where the initial mannose is further elongated. The further elongation is species-specific and differs markedly between fungi and animals, and even among fungal species., In |FRAME: TAX-4932| the initial mannose residue is extended in the Golgi apparatus, first by α1,2-mannosyltransferases that form a mannotriose, and then by α1,3-mannosyltransferases, which extend the chain up to a mannopentose. Unlike the initial transferase, which uses |FRAME: CPD-171|, the Golgi enzymes utilize |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| as the mannose donor |CITS: [9878809]|., The O-glycans are further modified by the transfer of |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P| group, catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-9678|. The mannose 1-phosphate group is attached to the first mannosyl residue that is linked by α-1,2 linkage |CITS: [7559601][9813355]|.

|FRAME:CPD-17052 Gliotoxin| is the prototype compound of epipolythiodioxopiperazines (ETPs), a class of secondary metabolites produced only in fungi |CITS:[15817772] [24816491] [18272357]|. |FRAME:CPD-17052 Gliotoxin| has been reported to possess antiviral |CITS:[14254440]|, antibacterial |CITS:[9304400]|, and immunosuppressive |CITS:[7510665]| properties and caused in in vitro experiments apoptotic and necrotic cell death |CITS:[7535293]|. |FRAME:CPD-17052 Gliotoxin| is considered a virulence factor which, however, only becomes apparent in certain virulence models |CITS:[18608908] [17030582] [18199036]|. The characteristic structural feature of epipolythiodioxopiperazines (ETPs) such as |FRAME:CPD-17052| is an internal transannular disulfide bridge |CITS:[22575049]| which has been attributed to confer toxicity by conjugation with thiol-containing proteins |CITS:[7539267] [19608453]| or the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) |CITS: [2461370] [15817772] [20495914]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7533|). Thiomethylation is considered as a detoxifying mechanism employed by plants, microorganisms and animals to convert reactive thiols in less reactive thiomethyls |CITS:[7437088]|. The toxicity of |FRAME:CPD-17052| has been shown to be significantly lower when the core structure was reduced and/or S-methylated |CITS:[4670497]| indicating that the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17053| may well play a role in controlling the toxicity of |FRAME:CPD-17052|. , The discovery of the gliotoxin (gli) biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS:[15979823]| comprising of 13 genes significantly accelerated the elucidation of the respective molecular function of those genes. The reduced and oxidized forms of gliotoxin have been shown to cause cell and protein damage by forming thioconjugates with susceptible proteins |CITS:[7539267] [19608453]|. The selfprotection of Aspergillus against his own toxin has multiple facets, genes such as GliT have been reported to prevent autointoxication either by oxidation of reactive thiols |CITS:[20593880]| or GliT mediated secretion pathway for |FRAME:CPD-17052| |CITS:[20548963]|. Moreover, a recently discovered S-methyltransferase able to methylate |FRAME:CPD-17052| has been shown to render the product of this reaction, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17053| inactive, hence attenuating the toxicity of |FRAME:CPD-17052|. This compound had also been reported as an metabolite in the fungus Gliocladium deliquescens |CITS:[Kirby80]| and occurs in Aspergillus fumigatus |CITS:[25062268]| and several other fungi such as Penicillium |CITS:[Intaraudom13]| and Pseudallescheria |CITS:[16830893]|., The S-methyltransferase is encoded by TmtA which is not part of the gli biosynthetic cluster indicating its general detoxifying function in both epipolythiodioxopiperazine (ETP) producers and non-producers |CITS:[25062268]|. The reaction sequence from |FRAME:CPD-17453| (reduced form of |FRAME:CPD-17052|) has been proposed to occur in two methylation steps forming |FRAME:CPD-17455| and |FRAME:CPD-17053|, respectively |CITS:[25126990]|. In addition, the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17053| was shown to act as negative regulator mechanism for |FRAME:PWY-7533|. The intermediate of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17453| was discussed as a shared co-substrate for both the bis-thiomethyltransferase TmtA and the dithiol oxidase GliT of the |FRAME:PWY-7533|. Hence, by out-competing GliT for |FRAME:CPD-17453| TmtA potentiated its own biosynthesis and in turn reduced |FRAME:PWY-7533| |CITS:[25126990]|.

The cleavage of the s-triazine ring is an important step in the mineralization and complete removal of s-triazine compounds from the environment. Several pathways for the degradation of s-triazines (such as |FRAME: ATRAZINE|, |FRAME: CPD-7398| and |FRAME: CPD-7403|) converge at |FRAME:CYANURIC-ACID| |CITS: [6762212][6477516]|, which can be used as the sole source of nitrogen by bacteria and fungi |CITS: [Cook81]|., In |FRAME: TAX-47660|, |FRAME:CYANURIC-ACID| degradation starts with a ring-cleaving hydrolysis by |FRAME: CPLX-7082| (|FRAME: G-10314|), which forms |FRAME: CPD-21687|. The pathway continues with a second hydrolysis, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.131|, an enzyme complex encoded by the |FRAME: G-10309| and |FRAME: G-58806| genes, forming |FRAME: CPD-21688| and releasing a molecule of |FRAME: AMMONIA|. A decarboxylation reaction, catalyzed by an unknown enzyme (as of 2018) forms |FRAME: CPD-578|, which is degraded completely to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| by a third hydrolase (|FRAME: G-10288|) |CITS: [29523689]|. , Understanding of the pathway evolved over the years. A number of research papers and reviews have stated that |FRAME: CPD-809| is metabolized to |FRAME: UREA| before it is broken down to the final metabolites. A study from 2005 has shown that the actual intermediate is |FRAME: CPD-578| (allophanate), which can decarboxylate spontaneously to urea under the acidic conditions used in previous studies |CITS: [16085834]|. However, at that time |FRAME: CPD-809| was thought to be the product of ring cleavage |CITS: [11544232][12788776]|. In 2018 it was reported that the actual product is |FRAME: CPD-21687| |CITS: [29523689]|., Cook et al have shown that |FRAME: CYANURIC-ACID| degradation can proceed under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions |CITS: [3904735]|.

Summary: Background, There is an enhanced interest in the production of alternative fuels from renewable sources due to energy and environmental concerns |CITS: [18676713]|. |FRAME: CPD-7032 3-Methylbutanol|, a minor product in fungus fermentation, is a five carbon alcohol and a good candidate for a biomass derived gasoline replacement |CITS: [18676713]|. Gene targets, mutations and pathways for increased |FRAME: CPD-7032| production have been identified from experiments in yeast |CITS: [16041576]|. , |FRAME: CPD-7032| is also a precursor for isoamyl acetate synthesis |CITS: [14586577]| and for the biocatalysis of triolein to biodiesel |CITS: [15950307]|. , About this Pathway, This metabolically engineered pathway for the enhanced production of |FRAME: CPD-7032| was developed in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [18676713] [20072783]|., |FRAME: TAX-4932| produce small quantities of |FRAME: CPD-7032| under fermentative conditions at low pH, and the identification of target genes for |FRAME: CPD-7032| production were first identified in this organism |CITS: [16041576]|. |FRAME: TAX-4932| generate L-leucine via pyruvate metabolism, and |FRAME: CPD-7032| is generated via the |FRAME: PWY-5076| pathway. The gene products of bat1 and bat2, a mitochondrial branched chain amino acid transferase and cytosolic branched chain amino acid transferase respectively, convert |FRAME: LEU| to |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE|, which is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-7032| via the gene products of pdc1, 2, 5 and adh1 |CITS: [16041576]|., 2-Keto acids are intermediates in amino acid biosynthesis pathways, and can be converted to aldehydes and then to alcohols by 2-keto acid decarboxylases (KDCs) alcohol dehydrogenases (ADHs) respectively |CITS: [18172501]|. Therefore, by shunting intermediates from amino acid biosynthesis pathways to alcohol production, only two non-native steps were needed to produce |FRAME: CPD-7032| in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [18172501]|. , |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| is generated from the |FRAME: VAL| and |FRAME: LEU| biosynthetic pathways in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [18172501]|. The entire pathway from pyruvate to |FRAME: CPD-7032| was overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| to produce sufficient quantities of |FRAME: CPD-7032| |CITS: [18676713]|. As |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-7032| via a decarboxylation and reduction, this was enhanced by expression of the the genes kivd from |FRAME: TAX-1358| and adh2 from |FRAME: TAX-4932| in |FRAME: TAX-562|. The gene kivd expresses the protein |FRAME:CPLX-7431| which catalyzes the decarboxylation of |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| to |FRAME:CPD-7031|. The gene product of adh2 |FRAME: CPLX-8688|, an NAD dependent enzyme, reduces |FRAME:CPD-7031| to |FRAME: CPD-7032| and is repressed by glucose |CITS: [12499363]|., Significant |FRAME: CPD-7032| production was observed with deletions of genes tyrB, ilvE, adhE, frdBC, ldhA, pta, fnr and pflB |CITS: [18676713]|, and optimized by employing a feedback-insensitive mutant of |FRAME: 2-ISOPROPYLMALATESYN-MONOMER| (IPMS) U.S. patent 6403,3402.

General Background, Kavalactones are known for their psychoactive effects and have pharmaceutical potentials for treating anxiety, insomnia and pain |CITS: [2401104][11374340][27332705][26199594]|. The compounds are named after the Polynesian plant kava or kava-kava (|FRAME: TAX-130404|), which contains |FRAME: CPD-22603| and is often ingested for these psychoactive effects during cultural rituals |CITS: [31332312]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8103|). However, kavalactones are also produced by different plants. |FRAME: CPD-26562 5,6-Dehydrokavain"| (DK) and |FRAME: CPD-26563| (DDK) are produced by the tropical plant |FRAME: TAX-97723| (shell ginger), which is known as a traditional herbal medicine, food, and dietary supplement |CITS: [26370954]|. These two compounds significantly increased lipolysis when incubated with differentiated 3T3-L1 adipocytes and may form a new therapeutic principle for anti-obesity with lipocytes as the primary organ target rather than liver or intestinal cells |CITS: [25322285]|. Summary: General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmpspheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described below., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the peptidoglycan found in several Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1280|. This peptidoglycan is characterized by having |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of the pentapeptide, and by including a pentaglycine bridge in the crosslinks between glycan strands., Six cytoplasmic steps catalyze the formation of the |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| precursor. This precursor is attached to the memberane acceptor |FRAME:CPD-9646|, generating |FRAME: NAcMur-Peptide-Peptidoglycan|, also known as lipid I., Another transferase adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding |FRAME:NAcMur-Peptide-NAcGlc-Undecaprenols "lipid II"|, which carries the full monomer unit., The next step of the pathway describes the amidation of the |FRAME: D-GLT| at the second position of the pentapeptide. , In most of the organisms which have been examined, including |FRAME: TAX-1280|, the α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is present as an amide; i.e. the second amino acid in the peptide sequence is |FRAME: CPD-12296| |CITS: [5219821][6025572][5968582]|. Some characterization of the reaction has been carried out, although the identity of the enzyme that catalyzes it in |FRAME: TAX-1280| is still unknown |CITS: [5638594]|., Following amidation, the final lipid intermediate is transferred by an as yet unknown mechanism through the membrane., The peptidoglycan monomers are polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide crosslinks |CITS: [11320055]|. While some of these enzymes are mono-functional, the main enzymes are bifunctional proteins possessing both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activities |CITS: [9791115]|., Peptide cross-links form between different parts of the peptides depending on the organism. In |FRAME:TAX-1280| the crosslinks includes an interpeptide bridge of five glycine residues. The five glycines are added to lipid II by three enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-11836|, |FRAME: G-11837| and |FRAME: G-11839|, and are donated by charged |FRAME: Charged-GLY-tRNAs| molecules. The crosslinks are formed between the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide and the amino group at the end of the pentaglycine bridge of a second glycan chain., The crosslinking reaction is catalyzed by D-D transpeptidases, a group of enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin-binding proteins"| (PBPs), and involves the cleavage of the D-alanyl-D-alanine bond of the pentapeptides, which provides the energy to drive the reaction. As a result, the peptides in the peptidoglycan polymers are one amino acid shorter than the peptides in the monomers., About the variability of peptidoglycan peptide composition, The peptide moiety, which is bound through its N terminus to the carboxyl group of muramate and contains alternating L and D amino acids, reveals considerable variation among Gram-positive bacteria., The amino acid linked directly to muramate is usually |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, but in some cases, can be replaced by |FRAME: GLY| or |FRAME: SER| |CITS: [5777324][5965240][4385976][6029599], [5704800][5469569][6033749]|., The most common amino acid in the second position is |FRAME: D-GLT|, but in some cases (in a few, coryneform bacteria) it is hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-48| |CITS: [6072398]|. In some organisms the, α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is modified by amidation or substituted by |FRAME: GLY|, |CITS: [5965232][6064598]|, by |FRAME: GLYCINAMIDE| |CITS: [Interschick70]|, or by |FRAME: CPD0-1578|, |CITS: [4683671]|., The greatest variation occurs at position 3. The residue at this position is usually a diamino acid and is involved in cross-linking through the second amino group. , The most common residue at this position in Gram-positive bacteria is |FRAME: LYS|, as described in this pathway. , The next common residue at this position is |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is present in most Gram-negative bacteria and in some species of bacilli, clostridia, lactobacilli, corynebacteria, propionibacteria, actinomycetales, myxobacteriales, rickettsiae, and cyanobacteria |CITS: [410379][6131881]| (see |FRAME:PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY|)., Other substituitions have been documented, including |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| |CITS:[4884715][14152785][6035494][6031807]|, |FRAME:LL-DIAMINOPIMELATE| |CITS: [14024243][13882624][13525638][11945321]|, |FRAME: CPD-7690| |CITS: [5870104]|, and |FRAME: 5-HYDROXY-L-LYSINE| |CITS: [16562051]|., In some cases the diamino acid in position 3 is not involved in cross linking. In these cases the residue in position 3 can be |FRAME: N-ACETYL-L-24-DIAMINOBUTANOATE|, as in the case of |FRAME:TAX-28447| |CITS: [5704800][5119774]|, or even a monoamino acid, such as |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| |FRAME: GLT| |CITS: [4259817]| or |FRAME: HOMO-SER| |CITS: [5119774][5119774 ][5469569]|., Position 4 and 5 are almost always occupied by two D-alanine residues, which are added as a |FRAME: D-ALA-D-ALA| dipeptide. In some enterococci and lactobacilli the terminal |FRAME:D-ALANINE| is replaced by |FRAME:D-LACTATE|, |CITS: [1503450]| or |FRAME:D-SERINE| |CITS: [8852545]|, which entails resistance to the glycopeptide antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-12245|., Peptidoglycan is the only cell wall polymer common to both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria,, as well as cyanobacteria.

Summary: The arginine succinyltransferase (AST) pathway is a catabolic pathway whose purpose is the dissimilation, of the carbon skeleton of |FRAME:ARG| |CITS:[2865249][3129535]|. , The pathway was detected in many Gram-negative proteobacteria able to utilize arginine as a, sole carbon and nitrogen source, including |FRAME: TAX-287|, |FRAME: TAX-303|, |FRAME: TAX-294|,, |FRAME: TAX-300|, |FRAME: TAX-333|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, |FRAME: TAX-292|, |FRAME: TAX-648|,, |FRAME: TAX-84158|, and |FRAME: TAX-45465| |CITS:[3534538]|. , The pathway is also present in the enteric bacteria |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-90371|, and it has been, shown to account for 97% of the total arginine degradation in |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS:[9696779]|. , In most organisms the pathway coexists with other arginine dissimilation pathways, such as, the |FRAME: ARGDEG-III-PWY| and the |FRAME:ARGDEGRAD-PWY|, which provide different purposes, (e.g. polyamine production and energy generation). However, in some organisms, such as, |FRAME: TAX-292|, the arginine succinyltransferase pathway is the only arginine catabolic pathway. , In |FRAME: TAX-287| this is the major arginine utilization pathway under aerobic conditions, |CITS:[9393691]|., The enzyme arginine succinyltransferase, which catalyzes the succinylation of |FRAME:ARG|,, also catalyzes the succinylation of |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| to |FRAME:N2-SUCCINYLORNITHINE|,, which is another intermediate of this pathway. Thus, the routes for the degradation of both |FRAME:ARG|, and |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| converge at |FRAME:N2-SUCCINYLORNITHINE| |CITS:[3144259][7523119]|., The aru genes encoding all of the proteins of this pathway have been cloned from, |FRAME: TAX-287| and sequenced. They all belong to a single operon, controlled by the ArgR regulatory protein, |CITS:[9393691]|., This pathway is also the only arginine-degrading pathway found in |FRAME:TAX-562|. This pathway, which, yields 2 molecules of |FRAME: AMMONIA| and 2 of |FRAME: GLT|, can satisfy |FRAME:TAX-562|'s total nitrogen, requirement, but not its total carbon requirement. It does, however, permit other organisms, for, example |FRAME: TAX-548| to utilize |FRAME: ARG| as a total source of carbon. With the exception of the, third enzyme in the pathway, succinylornithine transaminase (encoded by astC), enzymes of this pathway, from |FRAME:TAX-562| have not been characterized beyond assaying crude extracts. Succinylornithine transaminase, gained special attention and was originally designated as argM because is can substitute for acetylornithine, transaminase (encoded by argD) in the biosynthesis of arginine. The substrates of the two enzymes differ, only in |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| being acetylated in the biosynthetic pathway and succinylated in the degradative, pathway. Reviewed in Reitzer, L. Summary: General Background, The anaerobic fermentation of purines was first observed in the organisms |FRAME: TAX-1556| and, |FRAME: TAX-1495| in 1942 |CITS:[16560499]|. , These organisms can utilize only a small number of purine derivatives including |FRAME:PURINE|,, |FRAME: CPD-9017|, |FRAME: CPD-9016|, |FRAME:HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME:GUANINE| and, |FRAME:XANTHINE| under anaerobic conditions as carbon, nitrogen, and energy sources, and are, unable to ferment any other organic compounds., The purines |FRAME:URATE|, |FRAME:GUANINE| and |FRAME:XANTHINE| are readily, decomposed by these organisms, while growth on |FRAME:HYPOXANTHINE| is appreciably, slower, and |FRAME:ADENINE| does not support growth at all |CITS:[16560499]|., The slow growth on |FRAME:HYPOXANTHINE| was explained upon the characterization of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7371| from |FRAME: TAX-1495|. Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, An early characterization of the xxxx only reported the presence of d-GalN, d-Man and l-Fuc |CITS: [ 5324647]|. General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The presence of the O7 antigen in |FRAME: TAX-1392869| strains contributes to the overall virulence of this pathogen, commonly found in extraintestinal infections in humans, and particularly in neonatal meningitis and urinary tract infections., The O7 antigen subunit of |FRAME: TAX-1072458| contains five sugars, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: MANNOSE|, |FRAME: CPD-14794| and |FRAME: L-rhamnose|., Like several other modified sugar nucleotide biosynthetic pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-6942| for an example), the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-14794| starts with |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is activated by |FRAME: TTP| and converted to |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps. These steps are also involved in the synthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| (see |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|) and many other deoxysugars. However, the last two steps of this pathway are catalyzed by unique enzymes - a transaminase (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.33 "EC 2.6.1.33"|) and an acetylase (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.209 "EC 2.3.1.209"|)., The region of the |FRAME: TAX-1072458| chromosome encoding for synthesis of the antigen has been sequenced, and the two functions were assigned to the |FRAME: G-17643| and |FRAME: G-17644| genes, respectively, based on their sequence |CITS: [10517601]|. In a subsequent study both genes were cloned, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| and purified, and their function was verified |CITS: [17905981]|.

Summary: General Background, Phospholipids are important membrane components. Most of the phospholipids belong to the category of phosphoglycerides. The simplest phosphoglycerides, which are known as phosphatidate (or diacylglycerol phosphate), are composed of a glycerol molecule attached to two fatty acids and one phosphate group. The carboxyl group of each fatty acid is esterified to the hydroxyl groups on carbon-1 and carbon-2 of the glycerol molecule, while the phosphate group is attached to carbon-3 by an ester link. Phosphatidates are precursors for many phosphoglycerides found in animals, plants and yeast, including |FRAME: Phosphatidylinositols|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-SERINE|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE|, and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN|., As part of the synthesis of phosphoglycerides, either the phosphatidate or the modifying compound need to be activated by |FRAME:CTP|. In some cases, the modifying compound is activated, as in the case of |FRAME: CHOLINE| and, |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, which form |FRAME: CDP-CHOLINE| and |FRAME: CDP-ETHANOLAMINE|, respectively. However, in the case of other compounds, such as |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, the phosphatidate is activated first, forming |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL|, which then reacts with the modifying compound to form the, phosphoglyceride., About This Pathway, In this pathway, which is the most common variant in bacteria, the intermediate |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P| is produced via |FRAME: Acyl-Phosphates| by two enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-10761| and |FRAME: G-10762| |CITS: [16949372]|. PlsX is a soluble protein that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: Acyl-Phosphates| from |FRAME: ACYL-ACP|. This activated fatty acid is then used by the membrane-bound PlsY acyltransferase to acylate the 1-position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|. The second acyltransferase, PlsC, is universally expressed in bacteria and completes the synthesis of |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE| by transferring an acyl chain from acyl-ACP or acyl-CoA to the 2-position of, |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P| |CITS: [16949372][19282621]|., Alternative routes for synthesizing |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL| are described in |FRAME: PWY-5667| and |FRAME: PWY0-1319|. More information can be found in |FRAME: PHOSLIPSYN2-PWY|.

|FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., Oxalate degradation by ruminal microbes was recognized as an important function quite early |CITS: [Talapatra48][Morris55]|., Increased dietary oxalate induces selection of oxalate-degrading ruminal bacteria and make it possible for the animal to tolerate quantities of oxalate that would otherwise be toxic or even lethal |CITS: [Allison77]|., The obligate anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-847| resides in the rumen and the large bowel of certain mammals (including man) where it degrades oxalate by a decarboxylation pathway |CITS: [3994481]|. Oxalate is first activated to |FRAME: OXALYL-COA| and then decarboxylated by |FRAME: CPLX-8223|, giving |FRAME: FORMYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. |FRAME: CPLX-8222 "Formyl-CoA transferase"| then exchanges the formyl group for an oxalyl-group on CoA, thus producing |FRAME: FORMATE| and regenerating |FRAME: OXALYL-COA|. Most of the formate that is produced is excreted from the cell by an |FRAME: MONOMER-16176|, which exchanges the formate for a molecule of oxalate that is imported into the cell., The entry of the divalent |FRAME: OXALATE| coupled to the exit of the monovalent |FRAME: FORMATE| leads to formation of an internally negative membrane potential. Because intracellular oxalate decarboxylation consumes a cytosolic proton, entry of negative charge is accompanied in stoichiometric fashion by appearance of internal hydroxyl ion. As a result, the combined activities of the vectorial antiport reaction and the scalar decarboxylation step comprise a thermodynamic proton pump. In this process, which has been named a "proton-motive metabolic cycle", |FRAME: TAX-847| establishes the proton-motive force required for the synthesis of ATP |CITS: [2708365]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-rhamnose| is a 6-deoxy-aldohexose that occurs in nature., Some fungi and bacteria posess an |FRAME: L-rhamnose| degradation pathway that involves non-phosphorylated intermediates (this pathway), analogous to the |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY|. This pathway is in contrast to the known bacterial |FRAME: L-rhamnose| degradation pathway which involves phosphorylated intermediates (see |FRAME: RHAMCAT-PWY|)., Genes encoding enzymes of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-322104 "Scheffersomyces stipitis CBS 6054 (previously known as Pichia stipitis)"|, |FRAME: TAX-284592| and |FRAME: TAX-354| have been cloned, expressed and their products functionally characterized. Phylogenetic studies of the fungal and bacterial 2-keto-3-deoxy-L-rhamnoate aldolases (L-KDR aldolases) suggested that they are unrelated evolutionarily. Their respective non-phosphorylative |FRAME: L-rhamnose| degradation pathways appear to have evolved independently and are the result of convergent evolution (in |CITS: [18505728]| and in |CITS: [19187228]|)., In |FRAME: TAX-314266|, a variation of this non-phosphorylative pathway was demonstrated in which |FRAME: DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-L-RHAMNONATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-13044|, followed by hydrolysis of this compound to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: L-LACTATE| (L-lactate) |CITS: [19187228]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6714|). , About This Pathway, The first reaction in this pathway shows the spontaneous conversion of the pyranose ring form of |FRAME: L-rhamnose| to its furanose ring form |FRAME: L-RHAMNOFURANOSE| (the α and β anomers of each form are not specified here). This reaction is shown because the reaction that follows is catalyzed by L-rhamnose 1-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.173) which specifies |FRAME: L-RHAMNOFURANOSE| as a substrate and |FRAME: L-RHAMNONO-14-LACTONE| (L-rhamnono-γ-lactone) as a product. As noted in |CITS: [4335867]|, a δ-lactone (1,5-lactone) would be produced by a pyranose ring form. Because the pyranose ring appears to be more stable than the furanose ring in aqueous solution (in |CITS: [MA98]| and reviewed in |CITS: [FRANKS87]|) this raises a question as to the actual identity of the lactone (1,4-lactone versus 1,5-lactone) produced in the dehydrogenase reaction. To date it has been identified as the 1,4-lactone |CITS: [18505728] [19187228] [18793327]|., The genes encoding enzymes of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-322104|, |FRAME: TAX-284592|, |FRAME: TAX-354| and |FRAME: TAX-95486| have been identified in homologous clusters and designated lra1, lra2, lra3 and lra4. In |FRAME: TAX-322104| (Pichia stipitis), |FRAME: TAX-284592| and |FRAME: TAX-354| they were shown to encode L-rhamnose 1-dehydrogenase, L-rhamnono-γ-lactonase, L-rhamnoate dehydratase and 2-keto-3-deoxy-L-rhamnoate aldolase functions, respectively. The products of the pathway are |FRAME: LACTALD| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| |CITS: [18505728]|. This pathway is the significant physiological origin of |FRAME: LACTALD| in fungi. In addition, a L-lactaldehyde dehydrogenase that produces |FRAME: L-LACTATE| (L-lactate) was cloned and characterized in |FRAME: TAX-322104| and |FRAME: TAX-354| (|CITS: [18505728] [19187228] [18793327]|)., In |FRAME: TAX-314266| the first three enzymatic reactions of this pathway are shared, but the last two reactions of the pathway were shown to be catalyzed by L-2-keto-3-deoxyrhamnoate 4-dehydrogenase and L-2,4-diketo-3-deoxyrhamnoate hydrolase encoded by genes lra5 and lra6, respectively. |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: L-LACTATE| are the end products of that pathway variant and |FRAME: LACTALD| was not produced |CITS: [19187228]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6714|).

The |FRAME: Tetracyclines tetracycline| antibiotics, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1948, are one of the most widely used classes of antibiotics in agriculture, aquaculture, and medicine. They have a broad antimicrobial spectrum, can be administered orally, and have a low cost. They were originally polyketide natural products of actinomycete secondary metabolism, but over the years many synthetic analogues have been introduced., Tetracycline resistance has been expanding in environmental microorganisms, human and animal commensals, and among bacterial pathogens. In the case of human pathogens, tetracycline resistance occurs almost exclusively by ribosomal protection or antibiotic efflux. Unlike the case of |FRAME: Beta-Lactams "β-lactam antibiotics"|, enzymes that can directly inactivate tetracycline antibiotics are rare., The |FRAME: G-44627| genes have been identified on transposable elements found in anaerobic bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-816 Bacteroides|. Expression of these genes in |FRAME: TAX-562| confers resistance under aerobic growth conditions to all clinically relevant tetracyclines |CITS: [6379711][3072922][2832361]|, including the recently approved, broad-spectrum analogue |FRAME: CPD-19260|, which is considered a critical last-ditch defense against multidrug-resistant pathogens |CITS: [16128584]|., Purification of the enzyme showed that TetX is a FAD-containing NADPH-dependent monooxygenase that can act on tetracycline and a broad spectrum of its analogues |CITS: [15452119]|. TetX inactivates tetracycline antibiotics by introducing a hydroxyl group at position 11a, generating extremely unstable products. Under pH higher than 1 these compounds undergo a spontaneous intramolecular cyclization and non-enzymatic breakdown to other undefined products |CITS: [15452119][21402075]|., TetX has been reported in pathogens only once |CITS: [23688520]|. While originally discovered in obligate anaerobic Bacteroides spp. (where the enzyme is inactive due to lack of oxygen), it has been subsequently identified in aerobic organisms [19187139]|. In addition, other genes with no sequence similarity to tetX appear to encode proteins with similar functionality. Such a gene, named tet37 (GenBank accession number AF540889), has been cloned from a human oral metagenome |CITS: [12654685]|, and several others have been cloned from soil metagenomes |CITS: [26097034]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE Nitric oxide| (NO) plays an important role in cell signaling in the nervous system, and is implicated in synaptic plasticity. It also participates in the immunologic response to infection. In the vasculature NO relaxes smooth muscle and inhibits platelet and leukocyte adhesion., NO is synthesized from arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), generating |FRAME:L-CITRULLINE| as a by-product. NO production is absolutely dependent on arginine availability. Arginine can be provided either by exogenous sources (via blood circulation) or by the citrulline-NO cycle. In this cycle, arginine is used by NOS forming NO and citrulline, and then regenerated from citrulline by the combined action of the enzymes |FRAME:CPLX-6641| and |FRAME:CPLX-6661|., The citrulline-NO cycle functions in many different types of cells. It has been demonstrated in endothelial cells |CITS:[2236071]|, macrophages |CITS:[1731766]|, and the peripheral nervous system, including canine enteric neurons |CITS:[8545001]|, opossum internal anal sphincter |CITS:[9098009]| and canine esophageal sphincter |CITS:[9575812]|., The different enzymes of this cycle are coregulated. Coregulation of |FRAME:CPLX-6582| and |FRAME:CPLX-6641| has been shown in activated murine macrophage-like cells |CITS:[7507106]|, in vascular smooth muscle cells |CITS:[7511585]|, in in vivo-activated rat and mouse macrophages |CITS:[8576237][10409134]|, and in rodent and human pancreatic β-cells |CITS:[7628352]|. In addition, a coinduction of |FRAME:CPLX-6582|, |FRAME:CPLX-6641| and |FRAME:CPLX-6661|, has been demonstrated PC12 cells |CITS:[11072090]|.

Background, The search for feasible petroleum substitutes from renewable resources is becoming increasingly important in the face of rising petroleum prices and increased atmospheric |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| levels |CITS: [17933911]|. |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL "Isopropanol"| is a secondary alcohol produced by microbes that can be used to partially replace gasoline |CITS: [17933911]|. It can also be used instead of methanol to esterify fats and oils to produce biodiesel. , |FRAME: TAX-1520| naturally produce |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| as a major product |CITS: [16346237]|. While |FRAME: TAX-562| have been engineered to produce acetone by the introduction of four genes from |FRAME: TAX-1488| at the same level as |FRAME: TAX-1488| |CITS: [9501448]|, isopropanol production in |FRAME: TAX-562| has not been reported., About this Pathway, The strategy for the biosynthesis of isopropanol in |FRAME: TAX-562| utilizes the pathway modeled after |FRAME: TAX-1520|, which produces |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| from |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| via |FRAME: ACETONE| |CITS: [17933911]|., The entry point to the pathway is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. |FRAME: PYRUVATE "Pyruvate"| condenses with |FRAME: CO-A| to form |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-62|. |FRAME: THLCLOS-CPLX "Acetyl-coA C-acetyltransferase"| catalyzes the condensation of two molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to one molecule of |FRAME: ACETOACETYL-COA| |CITS: [16347774]|. |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| is then transferred from |FRAME: ACETOACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: ACET| or |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| by the enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-161| or |FRAME: ACETOACETYL-COA-TRANSFER-CPLX | to form |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE| |CITS: [2719476]|. This is then converted to |FRAME: ACETONE| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| by |FRAME: CPLX-102| |CITS: [2268159]|. The final step in the pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: ACETONE| to |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8349| |CITS: [8349550]|.

Summary: General Background, Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|. The requirement for oxygen suggests that bioluminescence evolved after oxygen levels began to rise through the activities of early oxygenic phototrophic cyanobacteria. Bacterial bioluminescence has been known since 1875, when it was reported in the surface slime of a fish |CITS: [Pfluger75]|., The luminous bacteria are grouped primarily in the |FRAME: TAX-641| family and a few closely related families, and the majority of them are found in the marine environment. Depending on the species, luminous bacteria occur either free in, seawater and in sediments, or (more commonly) in association with surfaces and gut tracts of marine animals. Some of them developed highly specific mutualistic relations with their hosts and live as bioluminescent light organ symbionts of many marine fish and squid. Luminous bacteria of the Photorhabdus genus occur in terrestrial environments and as symbionts of terrestrial heterorhabditid nematodes., All of the luminous bacteria utilize the same enzymatic reaction for light production, based on the bacterial luciferase enzyme. This heterodimeric protein mediates the oxidation of |FRAME: FMNH2| and |FRAME: Long-Chain-Aldehydes| by molecular oxygen to produce blue-green light. It should be noted that bioluminescent eukaryotes employ different chemistries and luciferases that are not homologous to bacterial luciferase |CITS: [25084994]|., The lux operon, luxCDABEG, contains all of the genes necessary for light production in bacteria. The |FRAME: G-247| and |FRAME: G-248| genes encode the luciferase, |FRAME: G-44236|, |FRAME: G-44237|, and |FRAME: G-44238|, respectively, encode the reductase, synthetase, and transferase polypeptides of the multienzyme long-chain fatty acid reductase complex that synthesizes and recycles aldehyde substrate for luciferase, and |FRAME: G-44232| encodes an NAD(P)H-dependent FMN reductase. Expression of the genes is controlled by quorum sensing. |FRAME: G-11135| encodes an |FRAME: MONOMER-14564 "autoinducer synthase"|, while luxR encodes a receptor protein that interacts with the autoinducer to activate transcription of the lux operon. At low population density very little luciferase is synthesized, and consequently little light is produced, whereas at high population density, luciferase levels are induced 100-1,000-fold and light levels increase by 103-106-fold., The physiological role of bacterial bioluminescence is not clear. One theory proposes that luminescence of food particles may attract animals to feed on them, aiding the bacteria in these particles in colonizing the animal's nutrient-rich gut tract |CITS: [6358519]|. Another theory suggests that luciferase, as an oxidase, may function as a secondary respiratory chain that is active when oxygen or iron levels are too low for the cytoplasmic membrane-associated, ATP-generating electron transport system to operate. Yet another theory suggests that the function of the bacterial lux system might be to generate a halotolerant flavodoxin, with light emission an incidental consequence |CITS: [16567412 ]|., About This Pathway, The bacterial luciferase requires reduced FMN and aliphatic long-chain aldehydes (the best substrate is |FRAME: CPD-7886|). |FRAME: FMNH2| is produced by NAD(P)H-dependent FMN reductases that use either NADH, NADPH, or NAD(P)H as their electron donors (|FRAME: EC-1.5.1.42 "EC 1.5.1.42"|, |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.38 "EC 1.5.1.38"| and |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.39 "EC 1.5.1.39"|, respectively). In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-669|, all three forms are found |CITS: [6981058]|., The long-chain aldehyde is formed by a multienzyme fatty acid reductase complex that is composed of three components, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44236|, |FRAME: G-44237| and |FRAME: G-44238| genes. The components are a reductase, a transferase, and a synthetase, respectively. Since free fatty acids rarely occur in the cell, the transferase LuxD can utilize activated fatty acids (either |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs| or |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-ACPs|) and transfer the acyl groups to water, generating free fatty acids |CITS: [Meighen88]|. LuxE, the synthetase, activates the free fatty acids by adenylation and transfers the acyl group to an internal cysteine residue. The acyl group is then transferred to the LuxC reductase, which catalyzes its NADPH-dependent reduction to an aldehyde that is released from the enzyme. LuxC can also accept an acyl group from an acyl-CoA, followed by the same reduction activity as described above, and thus it has been classified in the past as a long-chain-fatty-acyl-CoA reductase |CITS: [3782102][2030669]|., Once formed, the long-chain aldehyde and |FRAME: FMNH2| serve as substrates for the bacterial luciferase, a unique flavin-dependent monooxygenase that catalyzes a light-emitting reaction. In this reaction molecular oxygen is added to |FRAME: FMNH2| bound to the enzyme, forming luciferase peroxyflavin. The peroxyflavin interacts with the aliphatic long-chain aldehyde , producing a highly fluorescent species (probably luciferase hydroxyflavin) that has been named the "fluorescent transient" (FT) |CITS: [23479819][16593462]|. The emission maximum of luciferase hydroxyflavin is near 496 nm., In many organisms a second protein is involved, which provides a spectral shift of the luminescence. In |FRAME: TAX-668|, this second protein is a 21 kDa protein called "lumazine protein" because its fluorescent ligand is |FRAME: DIMETHYL-D-RIBITYL-LUMAZINE|, which has an emission maximum at 475 nm. A protein-protein complex is formed between the luciferase and the lumazine protein, and a rapid energy transfer (faster than 109 s-1) occurs between the flavin on the luciferase and the lumazine derivative bound to the lumazine protein |CITS: [8298053][8679599]|.
