Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: PWY-5686 "de novo pathway of pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis"| produces only the uridine ribonucleotide |FRAME: UMP|. All other ribo- and deoxyribonucleotides have to be derived from that nucleotide., Neither |FRAME:UMP| nor |FRAME:UDP| can be directly converted to |FRAME:CMP| or |FRAME:CDP|, respectively. The only uridine-based nucleotide that can be converted to a cytidine-based nucleotide is the triphosphate form |FRAME:UTP|. Thus the conversion of uridine-based nucleotides to cytidine-based nucleotides involves the phosphorylation of the de novo-synthesized UMP to UTP and its conversion to CTP (see |FRAME: PWY-7176|)., Since the mono- and diphosphate forms are essential for protein and lipid glycosylation reactions (for example, in compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-606| and |FRAME: CMP-KDO|), nucleotide triphosphates need to be dephosphorylated to the mono- and diphosphate forms., There are many enzymes that catalyze phosphorylation, dephosphorylation, and amination of pyrimidine nucleotides, and these enzymes are often restricted to specific taxonomic groups. Thus, several pathway variants exist in MetaCyc to describe these transformations., About This Pathway, This pathway is predicted to occur only in eukaryotes and thermophilic bacteria and archaea, since one of its key enzymes, |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.15 "EC 3.6.1.15, nucleoside-triphosphatase"|, is not present in mesophilic bacteria (note that in this pathway display, the reactions of this enzyme are actually labeled as [EC 3.6.1.5])., This enzyme removes the terminal phosphate group from nucleoside triphosphates, generating the corresponding diphophates., Even though the enzymes |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.2|, CTP synthase, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.5|, 5′-nucleotidase, have not been studied in plants at this time, they are predicted to function in them |CITS: [16669783]|.

Diacylsucroses (this pathway) are the metabolic intermediates biosynthesized from monoacylsucroses (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-8 monoacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) and precursors on the way to the triacyl- (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-10 triacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) and tetraacyl sucroses (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-11 tetraacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) usually accumulating in the cultivated tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) |CITS:[22988115] [24772058]|. Acylsucroses (summarized in in |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)|) as well as acylglucoses |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| are produced in glandular trichomes of and confined to plants of the Solanaceae family |CITS:[2652002]|. Acylsugars have been shown to exhibit broad-spectrum insecticidal properties |CITS:[Maluf10] [Leckie12]| through interacting with phytohormones |CITS:[21068365]| and feeding behaviors of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94]|. Acylsugars also serve as first food for pest larvae causing them to emit distinctive volatiles which then attract predators of those larvae |CITS:[21518882]|. Moreover, acylsugars have commercial value as safe additives to food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical products |CITS:[Hill99]|. , The wide occurrence and diversity of acylsucrose and acylglucose compounds is a characteristic feature for the genus of Solanum |CITS:[20113441]| and has prompted the research on their basic pathways |CITS:[Leckie14]|. The high variability of acylated sucrose is particularly obvious in wild species of Solanum (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) and appears to be associated with geographical locations |CITS:[Shapiro94] [23054567]|. A useful tool to elucidate the diverse acylation on both the pyranose and furanose moieties of the |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold was the generation of ingression lines with species possessing acylsugars of unique acylation patterns |CITS:[24772058]|., The catalyzing enzymes for the versatile decoration of acylsucrose metabolites found in the Solaneceae family are BAHD acyltransferases |CITS:[16616872]|. During evolution some of the encoding genes have undergone structural changes which influence the resulting proteins to accept acyl donors of different length and process acylation on varying positions of the respective pyranose and furanose rings |CITS:[25862303]| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-10 triacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|). , A functional genomics approach was used to identify genes encoding for potential acyltransferases of the BAHD family in Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum pennellii. Metabolic profiling of RNAi silenced Solanum lycopersicum plants indicated the gene ASAT2 (Solyc04g012020) as the acyltransferase involved in the second acylation step. This has been confirmed through RNAi silenced plants, in vitro assays with heterologously expressed protein and functional complementation of introgression mutants with the ASAT2 gene which restored the metabolic profile of Solanum lycopsersicum. In summary, it could be demonstrated that the ASAT2 encoded acyltransferase readily acylated the 3-position of the pyranose moiety of |FRAME:CPD-19018 sucrose-4-isovalerate| and formed |FRAME:CPD-19023 sucrose-3-isobutanoyl-4-isovalerate| with |FRAME:ISOBUTYRYL-COA isobutanoyl-CoA|, |FRAME:CPD-19026 sucrose-3-decanoyl-4-isovalerate| with |FRAME:2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA 2-methylbutanoyl-CoA|, |FRAME:CPD-19027 sucrose-3-lauroyl-4-isovalerate| with |FRAME:CPD-10267 decanoyl-CoA| and |FRAME:CPD-19025 sucrose-3-(2-methyl)butyryl-4-isovalerate| with |FRAME: LAUROYLCOA-CPD lauroyl-CoA| |CITS:[26715757]|. , In addition, the substrate specificity of the ASAT2 enzyme has been shown to be dependent on two amino acid residues in the vicinity of the putative acyl-CoA-binding pocket, i.e. Val/Phe408 which strongly determined whether or not |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA isovaleryl-CoA| is used as acyl donor and Leu43 which governed the use of |FRAME:2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA 2-methylbutanoyl-CoA| as acyl donor |CITS:[26715757]|.

General Background, In |FRAME: TAX-9606| the skin of the underarm (axilla) is a unique niche for bacteria. It is nutrient-rich thanks to secretions of various glands that open onto the skin or into hair follicles, and hosts a unique microbial community |CITS: [18494895]|., The chemical composition of the secreted nutrients is complex. The sebaceous gland secretes esterified fatty acids and other lipids; the eccrine glands produce a dilute salt solution with lactate and other organic solutes |CITS: [Bovell15]|; and the apocrine gland secretes an odourless lipid-rich viscous secretion (only with the onset of puberty). , The malodour that is typical to the axilla is produced by metabolism carried out by the axillary microbiota, the main members of which are |FRAME: TAX-1279|, |FRAME: TAX-1912216|, |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-165779| and |FRAME: TAX-162289| |CITS: [19478181][21428987][25653852]|., Three types of compounds have been linked with the malodour - 16-androstene steroids |CITS: [8142319][23278215]|; a series of structurally-unusual medium-chain (C6-C10) acids originating from N-acylglutamine precursors |CITS: [12468539][17193210]|; and thioalcohols (also called sulfanylalkanols) |CITS: [17191898][17191839]|., The thioalcohols are particularly pungent and can be detected at extremely low concentrations. The most abundant and pungent of these thioalcohols is |FRAME: CPD-21078| (3M3SH). An odourless precursor of this compound, |FRAME: CPD-21107| (also known as 3-methyl-3-sulfanylhexan-1-ol-[Cys-Gly] conjugate, or Cys-Gly-3M3SH), is produced by the human host and secreted from the apocrine glands in the axilla, followed by processing by bacteria |CITS: [17192014]|., About This Pathway, It is still not known how |FRAME: CPD-21199| is formed. However, it has been shown that the ABC-type transporter |FRAME: HS02475| transports it into the secretory vesicles of the apocrine sweat gland, where the terminal glutamyl residue gets cleaved off by the ectoenzyme |FRAME: HS01957|, generating |FRAME: CPD-21107|. This compound ultimately gets onto the skin surface by apocrine secretion, where it is converted to 3M3SH by bacterial action on the skin surface |CITS: [ 24533866]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8302|).

General Background, Tetrathionate is a common sulfur compound, present in most soils (except for very humid regions). Since it is unstable, its occurrence suggests that it is contantly generated by the chemical or biological oxidation of thiosulfate |CITS: [Starkey50]|. The ability to respire tetrathionate is rather widespread in bacteria |CITS: [Barbosa98]|. It is found among the sulfate reducing bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-872| and |FRAME:TAX-1562| |CITS: [14908011]|, but also in various non-sulfate reducing bacteria, including several genera of the enterobacteriaceae (|FRAME:TAX-590|, |FRAME:TAX-583|, |FRAME:TAX-544| and |FRAME:TAX-635| |CITS: [16747675][Richard77][3299028]|), |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [3094300]|,, |FRAME: TAX-24| |CITS: [5726148]|, |FRAME: TAX-670| |CITS: [5784207]| and others., The ability of bacteria to respire tetrathionate is exploited in clinical diagnostics and classification |CITS: [16747675][3094300]|. In some bacteria, the product of |FRAME:CPD-14| reducion, |FRAME: S2O3|, is a dead-end metabolite. Other organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-90371|, are able to reduce thiosulfate further to |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: HS|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: TAX-90371| |FRAME:CPLX-7189| is a membrane-bound enzyme containing a |FRAME:CPD-582| cofactor |CITS: [4564717][3518717 ][10231485]|., The enzyme catalyzes the two-electron reduction of |FRAME: CPD-14| to two molecules of |FRAME: S2O3|. When all of the tetrathionate in the growth medium is fully reduced, the bacterium can utilize the thiosulfate produced as an additional electron acceptor. It is reductively cleaved to sulfite and sulfide by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7186|, which is also a membrane-bound, |FRAME:CPD-582|-binding enzyme that utilizes |FRAME:REDUCED-MENAQUINONE| as electron donor |CITS: [3108233]|. The sulfite that is produced by thiosulfate reductase is further reduced to sulfide by the cytoplasmic enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7187| |CITS: [1704886]|., Tetrathionate is the only electron acceptor that is known to support B12-dependent anaerobic growth of |FRAME: TAX-90371|, using |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| as electron and carbon source |CITS: [11274105]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins Anabaenopeptins| are a family of non-ribosomally synthesized cyclic peptides produced by some cyanobacterial species. They have a well-conserved structure comprising a ring of five amino acids connected through an ureido linkage to an exocyclic sixth amino acid. Counting the exocyclic amino acid as residue 1, the 2nd residue is |FRAME: CPD-219|, and the ring is formed by cyclization of the C-terminal carboxyl of the 6th residue to the ε-amino group of the D-lysine at position 2. The ureodi bridge connecting the α-amino group of |FRAME: CPD-219| to the exocyclic amino acid is a unique feature among cyanobacterial peptides., The five amino acids other than |FRAME: CPD-219| are not conserved and may consist of either proteinogenic or non-proteinogenic amino acids. A review published in 2006 listed 124 different anabaenopeptin variants |CITS: [16774586]|. Many of the anabaenopeptins have been isolated under different names such as oscillamides, lyngbyaureamides, ferintoic acids, nodulapeptins, schizopeptins and more |CITS: [Sano95][11520225]|., Anabaenopeptins have been found in an enormous variety of cyanobacteria isolated from both the aquatic and terrestrial environments, including |FRAME: TAX-1163|, |FRAME: TAX-1177|, |FRAME: TAX-1125|, |FRAME: TAX-54304|, |FRAME: TAX-28073|, and |FRAME: TAX-383614| |CITS: [Harada95][26096276][27604544]|. In general, these compounds are produced by filamentous cyanobacteria belonging to the orders |FRAME: TAX-1161| and |FRAME: TAX-1150|. The production by members of the unicellular genus |FRAME: TAX-1125| is beleived to be due to horizontal transfer of the biosynthetic gene cluster from a filamentous organism |CITS: [28261178]|., Anabaenopeptins exhibit a functional diversity that includes inhibitory activity for proteases, phosphatases, and carboxypeptidases |CITS: [ 10340607][11520225][Zafrir-Ilan10]|, and are believed to provide protection against zooplankters and crustaceans., About This Pathway, The gene cluster responsible for anabaenopeptin biosynthesis was discovered in 2005 in a |FRAME: TAX-59512| strain. The cluster comprised 5 genes (anaABCDE) encoding four non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs) and one ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter. Interestingly, even though that organism produces several different anabaenopeptins (|FRAME: CPD-26928|, |FRAME: CPD-26929|, |FRAME: CPD-26933| and |FRAME: CPD-26942|), it contains only a single cluster, indicating that some of the enzymes are promiscuous and can accept different substrates |CITS: [19706155]|. Similar clusters were soon described from multiple species, including |FRAME: TAX-46234|, |FRAME: TAX-313624|, and |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [20338518]|. A cluster from |FRAME: TAX-984208| was reported in 2017 |CITS: [28085246]|. In many organisms a gene cluster encoding |FRAME: PWY-7275| is located next to the anabaenopeptin biosynthesis cluster, and it is assumed that those enzymes produce the homo-amino acids |FRAME: CPD-15322| and |FRAME: CPD-17729| that are incorporated into many anabaenopeptins |CITS: [28085246]|., The AptA NRPS contains two adenylation and two thiolation domains, for activating and binding tof he first two amino acids, a condensation domain, and an epimerization domain for converting |FRAME: LYS| into |FRAME: CPD-219|. The AptB NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the third amino acid, respectively. The AptC NRPS contains two sets of adenylation, thiolation, and condensation, responsible for the fourth and fifth amino acids. It also contains methylation domain, for methylation of the fifth residue (often |FRAME: CPD-298|). The AptD NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the sixth amino acid, and a thioesterase domain, which is responsible for cyclization and release of the product., An unanswered question as of 2024 is the mechanism responsible for formation of the ureido bridge. A similar structure exists in |FRAME: CPD-26948|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-317|, and it has been shown that in that organism the formation of the ureido bridge is catalyzed by the SylC protein |CITS: [19968303]|. However, SylC possesses a domain with structural similarity to acetyltransferase between the A- and C-domains of the NRPSs, and no similar domain was found within the anabaenopeptins NRPSs, suggesting that a different mechanism may exist during anabaenopeptin biosynthesis |CITS: [34437393]|.

General Background, Chlorobenzoates are a group of compounds that occur in the environment in large amounts either because of their release, as herbicides or as products of bacterial degradation of polychlorinated biphenyls |CITS: [7217013]|., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation seems to have evolved recently as a result, of their widespread release to the environment., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-6102| was isolated based on its ability to grow with |FRAME: CPD-256| as the sole source for carbon, and energy |CITS: [2610934]|. This ability was linked to the |FRAME: CPLX-7829| that catalyzes the double, hydroxylation of 2-halobenzoates with concomitant release of halogenide and carbon dioxide, yielding |FRAME:CATECHOL|,, which is degraded further via a meta degradation pathway |CITS: [2610934]|., The enzyme has been purified and shown to catalyze the dehalogenation of several 2-halobenzoates,, including |FRAME: CPD-256|, |FRAME: 2-FLUOROBENZOATE|, |FRAME: CPD-11238| and |FRAME: CPD-11239|, |CITS: [1370284]|. The gene cluster encoding this enzyme, cbdABC, was localized on a 70-kbp conjugative plasmid, designated pBAH1 |CITS: [7530709]|.

Summary: Photosynthesis is composed of two processes, the light reactions and the dark reactions. The light reactons take place in the two photosystems - photosystem I and photosystem II, where light energy is harvested and is used to power the transfer of electrons from water, via a series of electron donors and acceptors, to the final acceptor NADP+, which is reduced to NADPH. The NADPH generated by the light reactions is used for sugar synthesis in the dark reactions., The light reactions also generate a proton motive force across the thylakoid membrane, and the proton gradient is used to synthesize ATP. , There are two general chemical reactions involved in the light reactions: water oxidation in photosystem II, and NADP reduction in photosystem I. Both of the photosystems are large multiprotein complexes contained within the thylakoid membranes of all types of plants, algae and cyanobacteria, and both photosystems capture the light by means of large antennae systems, consisting of chlorophylls and carotenoids., |FRAME: EC-1.10.3.9| (PSII) utilizes solar energy for splitting water molecules, and transfers the electrons obtained from the water molecule via an electron transfer chain that ends with |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE|., The excitation of the photosystem II reaction center (RC) via light absorption by chlorophylls in the antenna drives the transfer of a very high potential electron from the cluster of four chlorophylls bound to the D1- and D2-proteins (known as P680) to a pheophytin acceptor, resulting in a P680* radical. The radical transfers the electron to a firmly bound |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE| (PQ) called QA, which transfers it to a second, not firmly bound PQ, called QB. When QB is fully reduced and protonated to |FRAME: Plastoquinols| (PQH2) form, it diffuses from the QB-binding site into the lipid matrix of the membrane (for more information see |FRAME:CPLX490-3506|)., The path between the two photosystems is not direct. The QB plastoquinone first transfers the electrons to a third complex, |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.6| (better known as the cytochrome b6f complex), where the electrons are transferred to the protein |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin|. Finally |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin| travels to |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.12|, and delivers the electrons to one of its components, P700, which is located on the inside of the thylakoids (the lumen). Under copper deprivation conditions |FRAME: Cytochromes-C6 "cytochrome c6"| substitutes for plastocyanin. , Photosystem I (PS I) catalyzes the light driven electron transfer from |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin| or |FRAME: Cytochromes-C6 "cytochrome c6"| to |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxin|, which is on the stromal side of the membrane. As in photosystem II, photosystem I performs both light capturing and electron transfer. The light capturing is performed by the large antenna system that consists of 90 antenna chlorophylls and 22 carotenoids. The electron transport chain consists of six chlorophylls, two phylloquinones and three |FRAME:CPD-7 "[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters"|., The electron transfer chain of PS I starts with P700, a heterodimer of a |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| and a |FRAME: CPD-10334| (the C13 epimer of chlorophyll a). As in photosystem II, a high energy electron is removed from P700 after excitation by light, and that electron is transferred through the system. The role of the electron delivered from photosystem II by plastocyanin is to re-reduce P700., From P700 the electron is transferred stepwise to A (a |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| molecule), A0 (another |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| molecule), A1 (a |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| molecule) and then through three 4Fe4S clusters, named FX, FA and FB. From the terminal 4Fe4S cluster, FB, the electron is transferred to the 2Fe2S cluster of |FRAME:Ferredoxins|, which leaves photosystem I and transfers the electron to the, |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|, where NADP+ is finally reduced to NADPH. Under conditions of iron limitation, |FRAME: Flavodoxin| may replace the ferredoxin |CITS: [15977059]|., Cyanobacterial PS I can exist in both trimeric and monomeric forms. The trimeric form has been shown to be the prominent oligomeric state at low light intensity. The monomeric unit of PSI from |FRAME:TAX-32046| consists of 12 protein subunits, to which 127 cofactors are non-covalently bound. , Some components of photosystem I and photosystem II in plants are different from those in photosynthetic microbes.

Summary: |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE "1,2-Diacyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphate"|, often referred to as phosphatidate (PA), is a class of compounds consisting of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone, a (usually) saturated fatty acid bonded to carbon 1, a (usually) unsaturated fatty acid bonded to carbon 2, and a phosphate group esterified to carbon 3., PA is an intermediate in structural lipid biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PHOSLIPSYN2-PWY| and |FRAME: TRIGLSYN-PWY|), and an important second messenger. In plants, PA is rapidly and transiently generated in response to a number of biotic (pathogens) and abiotic (such as cold and salt stress) stimulates (reviewed in |CITS: [16023886]|). Using a so-called differential labeling method, it was shown that there are two pathways, the phospholipase C and diacylglycerol kinase pathway (PLC pathway), and the phospholipase D pathway (PLD pathway), that generate PA as a signaling molecule in response to environmental signals (reviewed in |CITS: [19394438]|). In the PLC pathway, phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate, derived from phosphatidylinositol, is converted to diacylglycerol which is rapidly phosphorylated to PA. In the PLD pathway, PA is directly formed from structural lipid phosphatidylcholine. The two pathways are differentially activated in response to different stimulates |CITS: [16023886]|. Once formed, PA can be further converted to diacylglycerol pyrophosphate (DGPP) by PA kinase (reviewed in |CITS: [16469533]|). This is a possible mechanism in PA attenuation. Interestingly, mammals do not seem to have PA kinase activity.

Summary: General Background, The lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are a group of Gram positive bacteria that produce lactate as the major end product of the fermentation of carbohydrates. The LAB were divided early on into two main groups, depending on their fermentation products. One group included those bacteria that convert carbohydrates essentially into lactate, while the other group included those producing, in addition, substantial quantities of volatile acids and carbon dioxide |CITS: [Orla-Jensen19]|., A few years after this initial classification was established the terms homo- and hetero-fermentative, respectively, were proposed for the two groups (see also |FRAME: ANAEROFRUCAT-PWY|) |CITS: [Kluyver24]|. It should be noted that at least some organisms (such as |FRAME: TAX-1582|) are capable of shifting from one mode of fermentation to the other depending on oxygen or nutrient availability |CITS: [108249]|., Within the group of heterofermentative lactic acid bacteria, two fermentation patterns were described |CITS: [16559863]|. When glucose is used as the carbon source, the two patterns are:, (1) the production of equimolar quanitities of lactate, ethanol, and carbon dioxide, with occasional, traces of acetate., (2) the formation of glycerol along with lactate, acetate, and carbon dioxide., The pathway described here is responsible for the first pattern., About This Pathway, Early work demonstrated that aldolase and isomerase enzymes were absent in heterolactic fermenting organisms, suggesting that the pathway does not follow the usual Embden-Meyerhof pattern of glycolysis |CITS: [14897820]|. As more research was conducted, it was realized that these organisms utilize a different pathway, which was named the phosphoketolase pathway. Many of the enzymes used in this pathway are shared with the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY|., In most heterofermentative strains sugars are transported into the cell by a non-phosphorylating sugar permease system. After entering the cell the intracellullar sugars are phosphorylated by a dedicated kinase, such as glucokinase or fructokinase |CITS: [16741753]|. In the case of glucose , the phosphorylation results in the formation of |FRAME:GLC-6-P|. The phosphorylated forms of other sugars (such as |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|) are also converted to, |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, which is channeled into the phosphoketolase pathway, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:GAP|, |FRAME:ACETYL-P|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and two equivalents of reducing power, in the form of NAD(P)H., These two equivalents of reducing power are then reoxidized via |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (derived from the acetyl-phosphate) yielding |FRAME: ETOH|. |FRAME:GAP| is processed by glycolytic enzymes to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and then |FRAME: Lactate|, generating two molecules of ATP. Since one ATP was used in the initial phosphorylation of the sugar, the net gain is only one ATP per sugar |CITS: [WHITE95]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| anaerobic respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase I (NDH-1) and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) reductase the transfer of electrons from NADH to TMAO is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [7000002]|. , By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is thought to function as a proton pump translocating 4H+ per NADH oxidised (2e-) [H+/e- = 2] however a lower ratio of 3H+/2e- has also been proposed |CITS: [8892824], [22392981]|. TMAO reductase does not contribute to proton potential and thus proton pumping by NDH-I is the only mechanism for proton motive force (PMF) generation in anaerobic NADH → TMAO respiration (see review by |CITS: [18930017]|. Menaquinone (shown here) or demethylmenaquinone serves as the redox mediator during anaerobic respiration with TMAO |CITS: [2204318], [1444716]|., In addition to the inducible TMAO reductase encoded by torCA (shown here), E. coli K-12 contains a second TMAO reductase encoded by the |FRAME: G7022| gene. TorZ has low constitutive expression and is not induced by TMAO or dimethyl sulfoxide |CITS: [11004177]|. TorAC is an inducible TMAO reductase and is expressed in both anaerobic and aerobic conditions |CITS: [17850256]|. The DMSO reductase, |FRAME: DIMESULFREDUCT-CPLX "DmsABC"|, is also able to reduce TMAO. , Many early studies on anaerobic TMAO respiration were done using E. coli K-10 |CITS: [7031034], [393699]|., Reviews: |CITS: [3904597], [16221580]|.

Summary: General Background, A rhamnolipid is |FRAME: Glycosides| exoproduct of various bacteria. The exact physiological function of these secondary metabolites remains unclear. These amphipathic molecules have detergent and surfactant properties and wetting ability. They may aid in the uptake and degradation of poorly soluble substrates, they may be involved in surface motility and bacterial biofilm development, and they may act as virulence factors and immune modulators. They may also have antimicrobial activities (reviewed in |CITS: [20336292]|). , Rhamnolipids from species of |FRAME:TAX-286| and |FRAME:TAX-32008| have been characterized. Analysis has shown that the glycone portion consists of a rhamnose or di-rhamnose moiety O-glycosidically linked to a lipid moiety (see |FRAME: Mono-Rhamnolipids| and a |FRAME: Di-Rhamnolipids| for a more detailed description). Approximately 60 different rhamnolipid congeners and homologs have been identified to date. |FRAME: TAX-287| is considered to be the primary rhamnolipid producing species. Other, non-pathogenic rhamnolipid producing species are of interest for commercial production of rhamnolipids (reviewed in |CITS: [20336292]|). Heterologous production of mono-rhamnolipids in |FRAME:TAX-562| has also been reported |CITS: [16847602]|. , About This Pathway, This pathway shows the unique rhamnolipid biosynthetic pathway. However, the presence of the |FRAME: CPLX-8167| encoded by gene rhlG in this pathway as shown in |CITS: [16160828]| has been brought into question. It is therefore not shown in this pathway., Mutant analysis showed RhlG to be necessary for rhamnolipid biosynthesis and it was suggested that it diverts acyl chains away from fatty acid biosynthesis |CITS: [9721281]| (see reaction |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-REDUCT-RXN|). However, after its purification, kinetic characterization and structural analysis it was concluded that RhlG would not be able to compete for substrate with the fatty acid biosynthetic β-ketoacyl reductase encoded in these organisms by gene fabG. RhlG was shown to be similar to, but distinct from |FRAME:TAX-562| FabG (|FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-REDUCT-MONOMER|) (EC 1.1.1.100) and was three orders of magnitude less active with acyl carrier protein thioesters than FabG. It was suggested that although RhlG is involved in the pathway for rhamnolipid biosynthesis, there may be other as yet unidentified enzymes earlier in the pathway that supply substrate to RhlG |CITS: [16624803]|., In another more recent report, |CITS: [18326581]| suggested that RhlG has no role in rhamnolipid biosynthesis. They showed that RhlA alone is necessary and sufficient to form the acyl moiety of rhamnolipid, and that flux through the fatty acid synthesis pathway would accelerate to support both rhamnolipid and fatty acid biosynthesis (see the pathway link from |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY|). It has also been determined that the stereochemistry of the chiral center of β-hydroxy acids in rhamnolipid biosynthesis is the same as that of the β-hydroxy intermediates in fatty acid biosynthesis |CITS: [18326581]|., Genes rhlA, rhlB and rhlC encode enzymes that catalyze the terminal steps of the pathway. Enzyme RhlA is involved in synthesis of |FRAME: 3-3-HAAs| (the fatty acid dimer moiety) from |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP|. As noted above, RhlA may directly utilize |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP| produced by FabG during fatty acid biosynthesis for rhamanolipid biosynthesis, eliminating the necessity for RhlG in the pathway. Enzyme RhlB is a rhamnosyltransferase predicted to be membrane-associated, that produces |FRAME: Mono-Rhamnolipids|. |FRAME: Mono-Rhamnolipids| is the substrate for the RhlC rhamnosyltransferase, a predicted inner-membrane associated enzyme, which produces |FRAME: Di-Rhamnolipids|. The mechanism of excretion of rhamnolipids into the extracellular environment is unknown. The most abundant rhamnolipids produced by |FRAME: TAX-287| contain the dimeric |FRAME: 3-3-HAAs| and the most abundant fatty acid has a chain length of C10 (in |CITS: [11359576]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20336292]| and in |CITS: [16160828]|)., The |FRAME: B-KETOACYL-ACP| conversion to |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP| step in the linked fatty acid biosynthesis pathway catalyzed by FabG also serves as a branch point for the biosynthesis of 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines and polyhydroxyalkanoates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6657|). In some organisms polyhydroxyalkanoate biosynthesis is mediated by PhaG (see |FRAME: G1G01-1499-MONOMER|) (reviewed in |CITS: [16160828]|). , In |FRAME: TAX-287| the enzymes RhlA and RhlB are encoded in a bicistronic rhlAB operon and enzyme RhlC is encoded elsewhere in the genome. In contrast, |FRAME: TAX-587753| appears to produce only mono-rhamnolipids and may lack a homolog of gene rhlC. In |FRAME:TAX-32008| species three homologous enzymes are encoded in two paralogous rhlA1B1C1 and rhlA2B2C2 gene clusters, both of which are functional. This arrangement may result in differences in timing and level of gene expression as compared with |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [20017946]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20336292]|., In |FRAME: TAX-287| the rhlAB operon is clustered with genes rhlR and rhlI which encode regulatory proteins for rhlAB that are involved in transcriptional regulation through the quorum sensing response. The operon containing rhlC is also regulated in this manner (reviewed in |CITS: [16160828]|).

Summary: General Background, All organisms living in an aerobic environment are exposed to reactive oxygen, species (ROS) that are formed through metabolic processes and various environmental stresses such as, drought, air pollutants, UV light and high light intensities, chilling temperatures and external chemicals, |CITS: [VANBREUSGEM99][11997379]|. For example, active oxygen species are produced during the, β-oxidation of fatty acids or as a result of photorespiration in photosynthetic organisms |CITS: [8819328]|., ROS such as |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| and hydroxyl radicals as well as |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|, can cause significant damage to proteins, nucleic acids and cell organelles., Most of the aerobic organisms have developed defense systems to face oxidative stress and to scavenge, oxidative radicals in the form of enzymes that can detoxify ROS, such as |FRAME: SUPEROX-DISMUTMN-ENZRXN|, (SOD) and |FRAME: HYDROPEROXIDI-ENZRXN| (CAT) |CITS: [BEYER87]|. For example, |FRAME: TAX-3702|, a member of the mustard family (oilseed plants), stores energy reserves preliminary, as lipids that undergo β-oxidation during germination. The |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| that is produced, during this metabolic process is detoxified by catalase. Another form of ROS, |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| radicals, are by-products of aerobic electron transfer chains, and are disposed of by the action of superoxide dismutase., Since ROS can be found in any compartment of the eukaryotic cell, organisms have developed small gene families, encoding for several SOD and CAT enzymes that operate in the various cell compartments |CITS: [9765550][9214587]|., About This Pathway, SODs represent the first line of defense against ROS, converting |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| radicals to, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and water. SODs are differentiated with regard to their metal cofactor. There, are iron-dependent, manganese-dependent and copper/zinc-dependent SODs, which differ not only in their metal, cofactor but also in their subcellular location. In plants, FeSODs are located in chloroplasts and are regarded the, most ancient SOD group. MnSODs are found in the mitochondrion and the peroxisome and are structurally very, similar to FeSODs. The last group, the Cu-ZnSODs operates in chloroplasts, the cytosol and even the extracellular, space. They are structurally very different from the other two SOD groups because of the different electrical properties, of copper in comparison to iron or manganese, which resulted in a major structural change in the protein |CITS: [11997379]|., To date seven SODs have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, three of them iron-dependent, three having copper as, metal cofactor and one manganese-dependent SOD |CITS: [1731963][2263641][9765550]|., It has been demonstrated that a copper-chaperone (AtCCS, At1g12520) is crucial for the activation of all three, Cu/Zn-dependent SODs in this organism. The SOD holoenzyme usually constitutes either a homodimer or a, homotetramer. However, the exact composition of the SODs in Arabidopsis is currently not known and remains, to be verified (here displayed as polypeptides)., Catalase is second in the defense line against active oxygen, converting |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|, into water and oxygen. Three genes encoding subunits of catalase and at least 6 catalase isoenzymes have, been identified in Arabidopsis so far |CITS: [12232134][9214587][8819328][8668130]|. Besides their, implication in detoxifying ROS, catalases are thought to play a role in the signal transduction pathway in plants, leading to the development of SAR (systemic aquired resistance) |CITS: [7953568]|. The functional protein of, catalase is a tetramer but the question whether it exists as homo- or heterotetramer of different subunits remains, to be investigated.

Several strains of bacteria are able to utilize |FRAME: MALONATE| as sole source of carbon and energy. The key reaction in the pathway is the decarboxylation of malonate to acetate, which is catalyzed by one of two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.88| or |FRAME: EC-7.2.4.4|. Malonate is a rather inert compound, and its decarboxylation under physiological conditions requires an activation step, in which malonate forms a thioester derivative., Malonate decarboxylase is an enzyme complex composed of three subunits, one of which is a dedicated acyl-carrier protein (acp). The acp protein is synthesized in an apo form, and is converted to its holo form by the covalent binding of the prosthetic group |FRAME: 2-5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-3-DEPHOSPHO-COA| to a serine residue. This prosthetic group is very unusual and the only other enzyme known to use it is |FRAME: ACECITLY-CPLX| (see |FRAME: P2-PWY|)., The synthesis and attachment of the prosthetic group are catalyzed by two different enzymes. The first step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.52| is the formation of an unusual α-1,2-glycosidic linkage between ATP and dephospho-CoA, forming the prosthetic group and releaing adenine |CITS: [10924139]|. In the second step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.66|, the group is transferred to the apo-[acp] protein, generating the holo-[acp] form |CITS: [11052675]|., The genes involved in the activation of malonate decarboxylase in |FRAME: TAX-573| were named |FRAME: G-10848| and |FRAME: G-10849|, respectively |CITS: [11052675]|.

General Background, Cyclopamine is a steroidal alkaloid produced by some members of the |FRAME: TAX-4677| family. it was originally discovered due to its teratogenic effect that resulted in significant craniofacial anomalies in lambs in 1957. These anomlaies included a single cenrtral malformed eye (cyclopia) |CITS: [13869306]|, which inspired the name of the compound., The sheep, which moved to higher altitudes due to draught conditions, consumed the flowers of the California corn lily (|FRAME: TAX-50242|), which were identified as the source of the teratogen. Further analysis identified |FRAME: CPD-26576| as the direct cause of the anomalies |CITS: [5919283][5950658][Keeler69][4986631][4986632]|., The teratogenic effects of cyclopamine and the related compound |FRAME: CPD-26587| are due to their specific inhibition of vertebrate cellular responses to the Hedgehog (Hh) family of secreted growth factors |CITS: [9616123][9716521]|. The compounds inhibit the Hedgehog signaling pathway by direct binding to the G protein-coupled receptor Smoothened |CITS: [12414725]|. As a result, the embryonic brain does not separate into two lobes., In addition to the teratogenic effects, cyclopamine has shown promising antineoplastic activities against several cancers in which Hedgehog signaling malfunction is implicated, including pancreatic cancer, renal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma, basal cell carcinoma, and leukemia |CITS: [10984056][12202832][19460966][21203400][22076568][23956832]|. Cyclopamine has been investigated as a treatment agent in basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, glioblastoma, and multiple myeloma |CITS: [10984056]|., A semi-synthetic analog of cyclopamine, IPI-926, has been in clinical trials for treatment of several cancers including pancreatic cancer and leukemia |CITS: [19522463][21203400]|, and two functional analogs of cyclopamine have been approved by the FDA; vismodegib in 2012, and sonidegib in 2015 |CITS: [26110074][26323341]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-26576 Cyclopamine| is currently derived solely from collection of wild |FRAME: TAX-50242|. The early part of its biosynthetic pathway has been determined by comparing RNA-seq data with the cyclopamine accumulation profile in the plant. Expression of candidate genes in Sf9 insect cells identified four enzymes that catalyze the first six steps in the pathway, producing |FRAME: CPD-26583| from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. Three of the enzymes are cytochromes P450, while the 4th one is an aminotransferase |CITS: [25939370]|. The enzymes catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-26583| to |FRAME: CPD-26576| have not been identified as of 2024., The genes involved are most highly expressed in root, bulb, and spring rhizome, and cyclopamine is highest in spring- and fall rhizome |CITS: [25939370]|.

General Background, The proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: GLY| can biosynthesized via several different pathways. The main pathway in most organisms is the production of glycine from |FRAME:SER| via |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|. Eukaryotic organisms have both a cytosolic enzyme (SHMT2) and a mitochondrial enzyme (SHMT1) (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-PWY|). The two isoforms were reported to work in opposite directions depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [9398220]|., A less well described glycine production pathway is acheived by the operation of the |FRAME: CPLX-7302| in reverse (see |FRAME: GLYCINE-SYN2-PWY|)., In a third pathway glycine is formed from |FRAME: GLYOX|, a product of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-ALA-PWY|)., And finally, glycine can also be formed from |FRAME:THR| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.48| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-THR-PWY|)., About This Pathway, This single reaction pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, is the major pathway for biosynthesis of |FRAME: GLY| in many organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-4932|. It is also the main source for one carbon units, which are stored in the form of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF|., In eukaryotes mitochondrial and cytoplasmic serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) isozymes are encoded by distinct nuclear genes (|FRAME: YBR263W| and |FRAME: YLR058C| in yeast) |CITS: [9398220]|. When yeast was grown on |FRAME: SER| as the primary one-carbon source, the cytoplasmic isozyme was the main provider of glycine and one-carbon groups for purine synthesis. When grown on |FRAME: GLY|, the mitochondrial SHMT was the predominant isozyme catalyzing the synthesis of serine from glycine and one-carbon units. However, when both serine and glycine were present, the mitochondrial SHMT made a significant contribution of one-carbon units, but not glycine, for purine synthesis |CITS: [9398220]|.

Summary: General Background, Chloroaromatic compounds occur in the environment in large amounts due to their release as herbicides or as byproducts, of industrial production., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation capabilities have evolved only recently as a response, to their widespread availability in soil and water., Many of the degradation pathways merge at the level of chlorocatechols. Often organisms that can degrade, non-chlorinated aromatic compounds (such as benzoate) can convert the chlorinated vatiants to the level of, chlorocatechols, due to enzyme promiscuity |CITS: [4836257]|. However, the enzymes that degrade catechol have, little activity with chloro-substituted compounds, and the chlorocatechols that accumulate as a result are toxic to the, bacteria. Thus, in order to be able to degrade chlorobenzoates and chlorobenzenes successfully, the bacteria must, possess specific enzymes for the degradation of chlorocatechols., About This Pathway, Several proteobacterial strains have been shown to degrade chlorocatechols, including |FRAME: CPD-9151| and, |FRAME: CPD-9152|, which are degraded via |FRAME: CPD-10608| and, |FRAME: 4-CARBOXYMETHYLENEBUT-2-EN-4-OLIDE|, respectively (see |FRAME: PWY-6089| and, |FRAME: PWY-6087|)., This |FRAME: CPD-9151| degradation pathway, which has been described in the actinobacterium |FRAME: ORG-6091|,, combines the upper portion of the proteobacterial |FRAME: CPD-9151| degradation pathway with the lower part of, the proteobacterial |FRAME: CPD-9152| degradation pathway. The two parts are connected by a unique, |FRAME: MONOMER-14666|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11225| gene |CITS:[11405892][12218013]|., The enzymes of this modified ortho cleavage pathway are only distantly related to the known proteobacterial, enzymes, whereas ClcF is distantly related to |FRAME: CPLX-7802|., The |FRAME: G-11224|, |FRAME: G-11223|, |FRAME: G-11226| and |FRAME: G-11225| are clustered in a single operon,, and encode enzymes that are optimized for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-9151|. For example, the activity of the, |FRAME: G-11224|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14665| is higher with |FRAME: CPD-9151| than with, |FRAME: CATECHOL| or |FRAME: CPD-9152| |CITS: [11405892]|. These enzymes are also able to transform, fluorinated substrates |CITS: [12957954]|., The organism also contains a second cluster of chlorocatechol degradation genes that are similar to the proteobacterial, genes. These genes encode the enzymes for catabolism of |FRAME: CPD-9152| (as described in |FRAME: PWY-6087|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:CPD-844 "Carbon disulfide"| (CS2) is a geochemically abundant trace gas with both natural and, anthropogenic sources. The gas has an atmospheric life time of 7-12 days, but the product of its oxidation, |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE|, has a half life of at least one year |CITS: [Jordan95]|., |FRAME:CPD-844 "Carbon disulfide"| has several biogenic sources totalling at least one million tons, annually. The main source of CS2 to the atmosphere are the degradation of sulfur-containing compounds in soils, manures, and decomposing plant material. Five plant species, including the |FRAME: TAX-3808| tree and valley oak (|FRAME: TAX-97700|), are known to produce CS2, which acts as a fungicide., About This Pathway, The bacterium |FRAME: ORG-5989| was shown to utilize both |FRAME:CPD-844| or |FRAME:CARBONYL-SULFIDE| as an energy source. This bacterial strain could oxidize |FRAME:CPD-844| either aerobically or anaerobically. Under anaerobic conditions sulfur was converted to |FRAME: HS|, while under aerobic conditions the sulfur was oxidized to sulfate |CITS: [Smith88]|. Since the organism was able to oxidize |FRAME:CPD-844| under anaerobic conditions, the authors speculate that the first oxidation reaction is not catalyzed by an oxygenase, and propose that a hydrolase is involved. The product of the hydrolase, |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE| (COS), is also hydrolyzed, resulting in |FRAME: HS| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., The enzyme has been studied in much more detail from the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-1071056|, which has been isolated from the fumarolic ancient sauna building at the Solfatara volcano (Naples, Italy) on a mineral, medium supplemented with |FRAME:CPD-844|. It has been shown that the enzyme evolved from an ancient |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.1 "β-carbonic anhydrase"|. However, while the monomer displays a typical β-carbonic anhydrase fold and active site, the enzyme forms an unusual hexadecameric catenane oligomer that blocks the entrance to the active site that is found in canonical β-carbonic anhydrases. Instead, the enzyme forms a 15Å-long highly hydrophobic tunnel that functions as a specificity filter, but permits the hydrophobic |FRAME:CPD-844| to reach the site |CITS: [22012399]|.

Summary: General Background, Arginase-mediated |FRAME: ARG| degradation is widely distributed in the biosphere, and is found, in all primary kingdoms |CITS: [8759304]|. The first step in this process, catalyzed by the enzyme, arginase, is the hydrolysis of |FRAME:ARG| to form |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME:UREA|., There are many variations of the arginase pathway, since the fate of the products of the arginase, reaction may be different in different organisms. , Variants of arginase-based |FRAME: ARG|-degradation pathways include |FRAME: ARGASEDEG-PWY|,, |FRAME:ARG-PRO-PWY|, and |FRAME: ARG-GLU-PWY|., About This Pathway, This variant is the "classical" arginase pathway, having the widest distribution. The pathway, is found in mammals as well as many bacteria. , In this pathway |FRAME:ARG| is converted into |FRAME:GLT| in a series of three steps;, following the initial step, catalyzed by arginase, |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| is converted to, |FRAME:L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| by |FRAME:CPLX-6747| (OAT). , |FRAME:L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| undergoes a spontaneous conversion to, |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|, which is then converted in the third step, catalyzed, by |FRAME:CPLX-6746|, to |FRAME:GLT|. , In a subsequent step glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) removes the amino group from |FRAME:GLT|,, generating |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, which is fed to the |FRAME:TCA|, (see |FRAME: GLUTAMATE-DEG1-PWY|). , Such conversion into |FRAME:GLT| is a common route for the degradation of amino acids, including, |FRAME:GLN|, |FRAME:HIS|, and, |FRAME:PRO| (see the pathways |FRAME: GLUTAMINDEG-PWY|, |FRAME: HISDEG-PWY| and, |FRAME: PROUT-PWY|)., In mammals, the enzymes catalyzing the reactions of this pathway are present in the mitochondrial matrix. , There are two isoforms of mammalian arginases - a mitochondrial form, including the humane |FRAME:CPLX-6622|,, and a cytosolic form, which includes the human |FRAME:CPLX-6621|. , The cytosolic arginases, however, are believed to be involved mostly in the urea cycle (see, |FRAME: PWY-4984|) |CITS: [6408859]|, although this notion has been questioned |CITS: [15050972]|. , Human arginases were found in many tissues, including kidney and prostate, brain,, skeletal muscle, placenta, lung, mammary gland, macrophage, uterus, testis, and gut |CITS: [9256072], [15050972]|., In prokaryotes, this pathway is used for the catabolism of |FRAME: ARG| as either a carbon or a, nitrogen source. Arginases have been detected in and characterized from several species,, including bacilii |CITS: [2029528][7540694]|, agrobacteria |CITS: [3758074][3957872]|,, cyanobacteria |CITS: [Gupta81][100070][10648527]|, |FRAME:TAX-583| spp. |CITS: [4579440]|,, |FRAME: TAX-271| |CITS: [64178]|, and mycobacteria |CITS: [13192096]|. However, in most of these, cases the fate of |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| is not known |CITS: [3534538]|. , In some cases |FRAME: ARG| can can be utilized by the organism as both carbon and nitrogen source,, while in others it is used only as a nitrogen source. In addition, some organisms possess the enzyme, urease, which converts the urea formed by arginase into |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| and, |FRAME: AMMONIA|, a favorite nitrogen source., In some strains, such as |FRAME: TAX-1402|, the pathway is subject to strong catabolite repression during growth, on glucose |CITS: [5674049]|. In some strains, the pathway is also subject to nitrogen catabolite, repression. Such regulation is species specific and is not universal |CITS: [6124533]|., Although this pathway was not originally believed to act in plants, later studies provided evidence for its existence |CITS: [18419821][18621980]|. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-3349| (Scots pine), this pathway appears to be required to provide the glutamate that is needed for glutamine biosynthesis during the early stages of seed germination |CITS: [18621980]|. However, further work will be required to determine if this is the only pathway that operates in plants, or whether additional pathways such as |FRAME: ARG-PRO-PWY| can also contribute to arginine degradation |CITS: [18419821][9576796]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "Hapalindole-type alkaloids"| are a group of hybrid isoprenoid-indole alkaloids produced solely by members of Subsection V of the cyanobacteria, such as the |FRAME: TAX-1190| and |FRAME: TAX-162985| species. These compounds often have antibacterial, antimycotic, or antialgal activities., Since the initial isolation of |FRAME: CPD-20793| in 1984 |CITS: [Moore84]|, more than 80 members of this family have been isolated |CITS: [Moore87][Smitka92][Park92][Stratmann94][17315959][19371071]|. All of these compounds have an isonitrile- or isothiocyanate-containing indole alkaloid skeleton, with a cyclized isoprene unit. The major classes of the hapalindole-type molecules are the |FRAME: Hapalindoles hapalindoles|, the |FRAME: Fischerindoles fischerindoles|, the |FRAME: Welwitindolinones welwitindolinones|, and the |FRAME: Ambiguines ambiguines|, which differ in their core structure., |FRAME: CPD-20800 "Hapalindole H"| was shown to induce apoptosis in prostate cancer cells, acting as an inhibitor of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) |CITS: [29848677]|., About This Pathway, The first biosynthetic pathway for a hapalindole-type alkaloid was reported for |FRAME: CPD-20794|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-230521|, which was the only axenic cyanobacterial hapalindole-type-molecule producer available at the time. The genome of the organism was sequenced, and searches for putative genes encoding isonitrile synthase and prenyltransferase have identified a cluster of 32 protein-coding genes involved in ambiguine biosynthesis. This discovery was made by two different labs, which named the genes in the cluster amb and fam, respectively |CITS: [24180436][26629885]|., In addition to genes unique to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "hapalindole-type alkaloids"|, the cluster contains homologs of the trpA-E genes, which are responsible for |FRAME: TRP| biosynthesis, as well as five dedicated genes for |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, |FRAME: CPD-4211|, and |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| biosynthesis., The first committed step in the pathway is the addition of an isonitrile function to |FRAME: TRP|, which is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-230521| by two paralougous enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-58189| and |FRAME: G-58190| genes. Both genes are homologous to the |FRAME: G-58184| gene, which has been shown to encode an |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.25| |CITS: [16206308]|. The enzyme is known to use |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-20766| |CITS: [16217820]|. The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.11|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58188| gene. This enzyme catalyzes an Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent monooxygenation at C-3 of the substrate, followed by decarboxylation and dehydration to form a cis C-C double bond |CITS: [24180436][28212039]|. The third enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.146|, catalyzes geranylation of the intermediate, forming the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-20795| |CITS: [26629885]|., This intermediate is the last common intermediate in the synthesis of the different hapalindole-type alkaloids, as the next step is catalyzed by different cyclases that form different core structures while acting on it., The gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-230521| includes four genes that encode such cyclases - |FRAME: G-124535|, |FRAME: G-58195|, |FRAME: G-58194|, and |FRAME: G-58192|. This family of cyclases, which was named Stig cyclases, catalyzes a three step process including a Cope rearrangement, 6-exo-trig cyclization and electrophilic aromatic substitution. The transformation catalyzed by a specific cyclase or cyclase heteromeric complex determines the four chiral centers and three types of ring systems of the different potential products |CITS: [26629885][35520811]|., A key reaction in this pathway, the formation of |FRAME: CPD-20791|, is catalyzed only by a heteromeric complex of |FRAME: G-58192| and |FRAME: G-124535| (or their orthologs) |CITS: [28626997][32052896]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-7959| and |FRAME: PWY-7958|.

Summary: General Background, Four types of aromatic compounds degradation pathways are thought to occur in different types of bacteria: , Aerobic organisms take advantage of the availability of molecular oxygen, and use oxygenases that introduce hydroxyl groups, and cleave the aromatic ring. These pathways usually lead to a few central intermediates such as |FRAME: CATECHOL|,, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-633| (see |FRAME: PWY-6079|)., Facultative aerobes utilize two types of pathways, depending on the availability of oxygen., When oxygen is present, these organisms use the so-called "hybrid" type of aerobic metabolism for some aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: BENZOATE|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE|., These pathways use |FRAME: CO-A| to activate and form thioesters of the substrates, followed by an oxygenase/reductase step to dearomatize (but not cleave) the ring. Cleavage of the dearomatized ring does not require oxygen (see |FRAME: PWY-6077|)., Under anaerobic conditions, facultative aerobes and phototrophs use a reductive aromatic metabolism., The aromatic compounds are activated by |FRAME: CO-A| to an active intermediate that can be transformed to important, central intermediate such as |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|. Reduction of the aromatic ring of |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-883| and is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 ATP molecules (see, |FRAME: 2AMINOBENZDEG-PWY|)., Strict anaerobes utilize a completely different and not well characterized benzoyl-coenzyme A reductase that does not utilize ATP |CITS: [18378589]|., About This Pathway, In this aerobic pathway |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| is converted |FRAME:CATECHOL| in a single step, catalyzed, by the |FRAME: CPLX-4662| complex., These enzymes vary among different organisms. In |FRAME: TAX-292| it is a three-component Rieske-type [2Fe-2S], dioxygenase composed of a reductase, a ferredoxin, and a two-subunit oxygenase |CITS: [13129960]|., In |FRAME: TAX-62977|, |FRAME: TAX-208964|, and P. putida P111 the enzyme is a two, component complex |CITS: [11114907]|., |FRAME:CATECHOL "Catechol"| can be degraded in multiple routes under aerobic conditions. See |FRAME: PWY-5415|, and |FRAME: PWY-5417| for more details.

General Background, |FRAME: Strigolactones Strigolactones| are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi., The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels |CITS: [17780042]|., Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| |CITS: [Hauck92]|, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| |CITS: [Mueler92]| and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) |CITS: [Yokota98]|., The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis |CITS: [15944687]|., The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone |CITS: [Mosse73]|., Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interaction between the fungi and the roots., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14655 Strigol| was the first identified strigolactones, isolated in 1966 from |FRAME: TAX-3635| (cotton) as a germination stimulant for root parasitic weeds |CITS: [17780042]|. It was subsequently found to exist widely in |FRAME: TAX-4169| hosts such as maize (|FRAME: TAX-4577|), sorghum (|FRAME: TAX-4558|), and proso millet (|FRAME: TAX-4540|) |CITS: [Siame93]|. , An enzyme that produces strigol was described only in 2023 |CITS: [37292030]|. The enzyme was characterized from peach (|FRAME: TAX-3760|) and very close homologs of it are found in all |FRAME: TAX-3754| species (peaches, apricots, plums, and almonds)

Summary: General Background, Benzoxazinoids were identified in the early 1960s as secondary metabolites of the grasses (including the major agricultural crops maize (|FRAME: TAX-4577|), wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|), and rye (|FRAME: TAX-4550|)) that function as natural pesticides and exhibit allelopathic properties |CITS:[BARNES87][10804466]|. Benzoxazinoids are synthesized in two subfamilies of the |FRAME: TAX-4479| and sporadically in single species of the dicots |CITS: [19577780]|. They play an important role in defense against pests such as insects, pathogenic fungi and bacteria |CITS:[niemeyer88]|. The most common benzoxazinoids are |FRAME: CPD-6365| and |FRAME: CPD-6366|., Since the aglycone benzoxazinoids (see |FRAME:PWY-4161|) are autotoxic, they are stored in glucosylated forms that have reduced chemical reactivity |CITS: [10804466]|. The glucosides are stored in the vacuoles |CITS:[12239364]|., This allows the plants to store the toxic compounds in anticipation of pathogen attacks, prompting the suggestion to name these compounds "phytoanticipins". , About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-22324| and |FRAME: CPD-22325| are two 8-O-methylated benzoxazinoid glucosides produced in maize. They are derived from another benzoxazinoid glucoside, |FRAME: CPD-6562|, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-22323|. Benzoxazinoids serve as anti-herbivore defense compounds in grasses, and the 8-O-methylated compounds produced by this pathway appear to target phloem-feeding insects specifically, as they were found to affect the reproductive rate of aphids but not the chewing insect pests such as the armyworm |CIT: 27317675|.

Summary: RNA modification is a post-transcriptional process by which certain nucleotides are altered after their initial incorporation into an RNA chain., The most heavily modified class of RNA molecules is the tRNA - an average of 11%, 14%, and 17% of the tRNA residues are modified in |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-4932|, and mammalian cytoplasm, respectively |CITS: [9399820]|. These modifications expand the chemical and functional diversity of tRNA, and enhance its structural stability |CITS: [3304135]|., In some bacterial genomes, about 1% of the coding genes are devoted to tRNA modification |CITS: [3304135]|., One of the most common modifications of tRNA bases is methylation. Methylation is known to help control tRNA folding, to ensure decoding specificity during translation of the genetic code, and to enhance aminoacylation by certain tRNA synthetases. In the great majority of cases, the methyl group is derived from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), linking tRNA modifications to the intermediary metabolism of this cofactor., SAM-dependent methyltransferases have been divided into five structural classes (I-V) based on their active-site, folds |CITS: [12826405]|. The vast majority of the known enzymes that catalyze tRNA nucleotide base methylation belong to class I, with the remainder belonging to class IV., Class I enzymes feature the ancient Rossmann-fold, consisting largely of a parallel β-sheet with α-helical crossovers. A final β strand is oriented in an anti-parallel direction relative to the others. Class IV enzymes, also known as the SPOUT family of RNA methyltransferases |CITS: [11763972]|, have a structural core made up of six parallel β-strands, with the final three folded into a rare protein subdomain known as a deep trefoil knot. Another characteristic feature of the class IV structure is that the active site is assembled at the interface of a homodimer, in which both monomers contribute to the cofactor binding |CITS: [12773376][14583191]|., Methylation of a specific tRNA nucleotide base is sequence-dependent and varies greatly from species to species for different amino acid acceptors, and even among the three domains of life for the same amino acid acceptor |CITS: [19944101]|.

General Background, Inorganic reduced sulfur compounds serve as electron donors in many phototrophic and chemotrophic bacteria |CITS: [9328649]|. Sulfide oxidation plays an important role in the global sulfur cycle by reoxidizing the sulfide produced by sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic habitats., Phototrophic purple and green sulfur-oxidizing bacteria use the sulfur compounds as electron donors for reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation during photolithotrophic growth., Light energy is used to transfer electrons from the sulfur compounds to levels found in highly reducing electron carriers such as |FRAME:Ferredoxins| and |FRAME:NADP| |CITS: [2663079]|. Similarly, non-sulfur purple bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1061| and cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-54310| are also able to use sulfide as the electron source for anoxygenic photosynthesis., The purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| carries out the complete eight-electron oxidation of sulfide and thiosulfate to sulfate. The process involves the formation of sulfur globules as obligate intermediates |CITS: [9695921]|. The globules are intracellular and extracytoplasmic |CITS: [9560425]|, and the sulfur in them occurs in the molecular structure of sulfur chains |CITS: [11782519]|, enclosed by a protein envelope |CITS: [7575095]|. In the process of further oxidation, the sulfur in the globules may be reduced inside the bacteria back to sulfide, which is then oxidized by a second sulfide-oxidizing, system., About This Pathway, At this point it is still not completely clear which enzymatic systems are responsible for sulfide oxidation at particular stages of the pathway. Clearly, there are several such systems, and it is likely that different organisms employ different systems to achieve this goal., One possibility is that the sulfide oxidation reaction is catalyzed by a sulfide dehydrogenase that shuttles electrons from sulfide to a cytochrome c. One such enzyme that has been characterized from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-1049|, |FRAME: ORG-5987|, and |FRAME: TAX-1092|, is |FRAME:CPLX-7131|. This enzyme has been shown to catalyze the conversion of sulfide to elemental sulfur or polysulfide with a variety of small, soluble c-type cytochromes as electron acceptors in vitro |CITS: [4357558][222744][6301383]|., The sulfide dehydrogenases from most purple photosynthetic bacteria are soluble periplasmic heterodimeric enzymes, consisting of a flavoprotein subunit and a heme subunit. A different form has been isolated from the alkaliphilic chemolithoautotrophic sulfur-oxidizing bacterium strain AL3 and from the purple phototrophic sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1054|. That second form is membrane-bound and monomeric, consisting of a single heme c554-containing subunit |CITS: [9613590][10809687]|., In |FRAME: ORG-5987|, |FRAME: CPLX-7132| is assumed to be the main sulfide oxidizing system, |CITS: [9094227]|. Somewhat surprisingly, disruption of the genes encoding the enzyme in, |FRAME: TAX-1049| did not have any significant effect on the sulfide oxidizing abillity of this organism, |CITS: [9639604]|. It has been suggested that in this organism the enzyme may be involved in a high, affinity sulfide oxidation system, which functions only only under conditions of very low sulfide, concentrations., An alternative sulfide-oxidizing pathway that is more likely to function in periplasmic sulfide oxidation in, |FRAME: TAX-1049|, as well as several other organisms, consists of the enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-12314|, which mediates the transfer of electrons from sulfide directly into the, quinone pool. That system is described in |FRAME:P222-PWY|., Steudel suggested a mechanism for the formation of sulfur globules from sulfide, which is mediated, by an initial enzyme-catalyzed oxidation step and a series of subsequent spontaneous chemical, reactions |CITS: [Steudel96]|., The first step is the formation of HS* radicals by a single electron oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-846|., At pH 7, the HS* radical dissociates to a proton and a S* radical, which dimerizes to, S2-2. The disulfide is then spontaneously oxidized by more S* radicals,, leading to larger and larger polysulfides. When the polysulfide reaches the length of 6, 7 or 8, it, spontaneously cyclizes to form the homocyclic sulfur molecules S6, S7, and S8, that, are found in extracts of sulfur containing |FRAME: TAX-1049| cells |CITS: [Steudel90]|., Both |FRAME:CPLX-7131| and |FRAME: MONOMER-12314| are theoretically capable of generating, such radicals, via the production of semiquinones.

Acidithiobacilli are prominent bacteria that catalyse the oxidation of inorganic sulfur compounds under, acidic conditions (pH 1 to 3) and ambient temperatures. |FRAME: TAX-920| is an important member, of this family, which obtains energy via the oxidation of iron as well as sulfur, and is often found in pyrite, deposits. , |FRAME: TAX-920| is an important industrial microorganism, involved in bioleaching of copper ores and, the biooxidation of gold-containing ores |CITS: [Rawlings2001]|. The organism can oxidize sulfur compounds, under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, using either molecular oxygen or |FRAME: FE+3| ions, as electron acceptors, respectively |CITS: [FEMSMicroLett41-1]|., Extracellular elemental sulfur most likely enters the periplasmic space by binding to thiol groups of, special outer-membrane proteins and being transported as persulfide sulfur |CITS: [12855721]|., The thiol-bearing membrane proteins have not been identified conclusively, but candidates include a, sulfide-binding protein isolated from |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [Sugio91]| as well as several outer-membrane, proteins which have been associated with sulfur oxidation in this organism, |CITS: [Buonfiglio93][10406099][8824625]|., In all cases of elemental sulfur oxidation, an activation reaction is assumed to take place prior to, oxidation, because elemental sulfur, which consists of stable polysulfane rings (such as S6, S7 or S8), forms orthorhombic crystals that are not soluble in water |CITS: [Steudel00]|., Many studies of sulfur oxidation by acidophilic bacteria showed that the first step of the pathway depends, on low-molecular-mass thiols, such as glutathione (GSH), for activity |CITS:[Suzuki66][4968764]|. , Similar GSH-dependent activity has also been detected in |FRAME: TAX-28034| |CITS: [15029700]|., In an earlier work Sugio et al reported the purification of a |FRAME:CPLX-921| from |FRAME: TAX-920|., The presence of |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| in the reaction buffer was absolutely essential, |CITS: [3667519]|., The authors later reported that elemental sulfur was reduced by |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| to, |FRAME: HS|, and that |FRAME: HS| was the actual substrate for the enzyme. Based on these finding,, the authors suggested that |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| is one of the substrates of the enzyme, |CITS: [BBA973-250]|. Other works also reported that sulfur was enzymatically converted to |FRAME: HS|, prior to further oxidation |CITS: [FEMSMicroLett58-189]|., However, in a later study by Rohwerder and Sand |CITS: [12855721]| it was shown that cell-free systems, from several members of the Acidithiobacillus and Acidiphilium spp., including |FRAME: TAX-920|, oxidized, elemental sulfur only via |FRAME: CPD-11281| (GSSH), a non-enzymic reaction product, from glutathione (GSH) and elemental sulfur., Thus, while GSH (and possibly other cellular thiols) plays a crucial role in elemental, sulfur activation, it is not consumed during the enzymic sulfane sulfur oxidation., The enzyme that oxidizes the sulfur, the periplasmic |FRAME:CPLX-7137|, cannot accept sulfur or sulfide,, but is specific for the sulfane sulfur of monoorganylpolysulfanes (RSnH, where n>1),, and predominantly persulfides (where n=2), which is oxidized to sulfite in the presence of molecular, oxygen and water., Organic persulfides such as |FRAME: CPD-11281| could not be replaced by other, sulfane-sulfur-containing compounds (thiosulfate, polythionates, bisorganylpolysulfanes or, monoarylthiosulfonates) as sulfur donor., The product of the sulfur dioxygenase activity was shown to be |FRAME:SO3|, which, is subsequently oxidized to |FRAME:SULFATE| by a |FRAME: CPLX-922|., Most of the sulfite:acceptor oxidoreductases that were isolated from other organisms were shown, to use c-type cytochromes as electron acceptors |CITS: [5142118][deJong2000]|, and such an, enzyme was also isolated from |FRAME: TAX-920| (see |FRAME:CPLX-7140|) |CITS: [Nakamura95]|., However, Sugio et al isolated from |FRAME: TAX-920| an enzyme that utilizes only |FRAME: FE+3| as an, electron accpetor |CITS: [3345075]|., It is possible that this organism has two systems for the oxidation of sulfur: one that utilizes a, cytochrome c, and one that utilizes |FRAME: FE+3| ions., For a discussion of an |FRAME: FE+3|-independent sulfur oxidation system, see |FRAME:SULFUROX-PWY|., For a discussion of sulfide oxidation in this strain, see |FRAME:PWY-5285|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-18984 Propane|, along with |FRAME: CPD-9312|, |FRAME: CPD-18985|, and |FRAME: CPD-9285|, is a gaseous n-alkane. The main sources for gaseous n-alkanes in the atmosphere are natural oil seepage and oil spills., A number of microorganisms have been isolated for their ability to use gaseous n-alkanes as a sole carbon source, including some |FRAME: TAX-286| strains |CITS: [Takahashi80]| and many strains belonging to the order |FRAME: TAX-2037|, such as those of the genera |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, and |FRAME: TAX-1847| |CITS: [7958761][11679317]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-235467| is capable of aerobic growth on |FRAME: CPD-18984|, but no other gaseous alkanes, as the sole source of carbon (it can also utilize n-alkanes with C13 to C22 carbon chains) |CITS: [17071761]|. The pathway starts with the oxidation of propane to |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| by an NADH-dependent monooxygenase that belong to the family of dinuclear-iron oxygenases, followed by conversion to |FRAME: ACETONE| by three distinct NAD-dependent secondary alcohol dehydrogenases |CITS: [14645271]|., Acetone is oxidized to |FRAME: METHYL-ACETATE| by a novel Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase (BVMO) encoded by the |FRAME: G-44522| gene, and the latter is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: METOH| by a dedicated esterase (the |FRAME: G-44523| gene product) |CITS: [17071761]|.
