Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN "Adenosylcobalamin"| (also known as vitamin B12 or coenzyme B12) was discovered in the 1920s after Minot and Murphy reported that they could cure the symptoms of pernicious anaemia by feeding patients with crude liver extract |CITS: [Minot26]| (they received the Nobel prize in 1934 for this discovery)., The unknown factor has been isolated and subsequently crystallized in 1948 |CITS:[Lester48][Rickes48]|, and was given the name vitamin B12 and, as it was shown to contain a cobalt ion, |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamin| (although this term is used to describe a family of related compounds) |CITS: [12195810]|., Cobalamins are some of the most structurally complex small molecules made in Nature. They contain a contracted porphinoid ring with a cobalt ion ligated at its center and further held in place by a lower axial base (|FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|) and a methyl or adenosyl group that function as an upper axial ligand. Their biosynthesis is similarly complex, and requires more than thirty genes. Cobalamin biosynthesis is confined to only some bacteria and archaea |CITS: [11935176]|., Two main pathways are known for |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthesis - an aerobic pathway (see |FRAME:P381-PWY|) and an anaerobic pathway (this pathway). The main differences between these pathways are the timing of the |FRAME: CO+2| ion insertion and the ring-contraction mechanism (for more about ring contraction, see |CITS: [16592942]|). |FRAME: CO+2| is inserted early on in the anaerobic pathway, and rather late in the aerobic pathway., The two different routes then merge at |FRAME: CPD-689|, and the latter part of the pathway is identical, or at least very similar., About This Pathway, The best characterized anaerobic pathway is the one from |FRAME: TAX-90371|, although much of the early work was performed with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1752| and much of the more recent work was done with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1404|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| starts with the biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole intermediate |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of several important compounds such as |FRAME: Hemes heme| and |FRAME: Chlorophylls chlorophyl|. |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III "Uroporphyrinogen-III"| is converted to a corrin ring by a complex process that involves (among other things) the attachment of eight methyl groups, all derived from |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM)., During the process the ring contracts via bonding of carbons C-1 and C-19, eliminating carbon C-20 from the ring. This contraction process converts the ring from a porphyrin ring to a corrin ring. Both the C-20 carbon and the added C-20 methyl group are lost in the form of |FRAME: ACETALD|., The intermediates formed prior to the formation of the corrin ring are called precorrins. The precorrins are numbered corresponding to the number of methyl groups that have been already introduced. If two different intermediates have the same number of methyl groups, they are also labeled by A or B (as in |FRAME:CPD-675|). If there is still some uncertainty about an intermediate, it is given a temporary designation of X or Y., There is indeed some uncertainty about the path from |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| to |FRAME: CPD-9040|. Early work, performed mostly with |FRAME: TAX-28901|, suggested that this transition may be catalyzed in two steps - the insertion of cobalt into |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-10021|, followed by methylation by |FRAME: G-10057|. However, information gathered from multiple studies, most recently with the aerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1404| that posseses a complete anaerobic pathway, suggests that this conversion may proceed through the oxidized factor intermediates, which is favored for the ease of cobalt insertion. Thus, |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| is first oxidized to |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| by |FRAME: STM3477|. Cobalt in then inserted (either by |FRAME: G-10021| or |FRAME: G-11338|), followed by methylation to |FRAME: COBALT-FACTOR-III| and reduction to |FRAME: CPD-9040| |CITS: [12408752][17567575][16042604][12917443][12686546][23155054]|., The first intermediate with a corrin ring is |FRAME:CPD-9049|. However, this intermediate still needs to be modified extensively. Successive amidation reactions transfer amide groups from two |FRAME: GLN| molecules to the carboxy groups a and c, resulting in |FRAME:CPD-689|. The |FRAME: CO+2| ion is then reduced to |FRAME: CO+1|, and the molecule is adenosylated to form |FRAME:CPD-690|. Additional amidation of the carboxyl groups b, d, e and g generates |FRAME:CPD-691|., At this point the lower ligand base is synthesized and tethered to the corrin ring via a structure known as the nucleotide loop, which is composed of some form of |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL| and |FRAME:DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|., More information about the biosynthesis of these side chains is provided at |FRAME:PWY-5443| and |FRAME:PWY-5523|., There is some uncertainty about the order in which some of the final reactions of the pathway occur. Depending on the order of the reactions, different intermediates may form. A 2002 study concluded that |FRAME:R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE| is formed and added to |FRAME:CPD-691|, forming |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P|, which is then phosphorylated by GTP to form |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| |CITS: [12195810]|. A study of |FRAME: TAX-90371| suggests that |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P|, which is formed from |FRAME:DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, is then added, forming |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P| |CITS: [17209023]|. The last reaction in the pathway is the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|., A study of the anaerobic biosynthesis of the benzimidazole lower ligand, which focused on |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.405| (BzaC), concluded that activation of the lower ligand to |FRAME: CPD-20830|, followed by hydrolysis of the phosphate group, precedes its methylation |CITS: [32503839][36371846]|., Adenosylcobalamin Biosynthesis in Archaea, It is well documented that some archaea require and synthesize cobamides. For example, methanogens contain extraordinarily high concentrations of cobamides, in the form of |FRAME: COBALT-FACTOR-III| and Pseudo B12, which are required for methanogenesis from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: METOH| |CITS: [16672609][16835730][17142327]| (for a review see |CITS: [2115763]|)., Other archaea, such as the halophile |FRAME: TAX-64091| |CITS: [12486068]|, the sulfur metabolizing |FRAME: TAX-2283| |CITS: [3416881]| and the thermophile |FRAME: TAX-1525| |CITS: [17211893]|, also require cobamides. Comparative genomics studies find cobalamin biosynthetic genes in many archaea |CITS: [12869542]|. However, at this point the actual pathways employed by archaea are not well understood.

Summary: Many aromatic compounds are converted by bacteria and fungi to catechol and protocatechuate. Catechol and protocatechuate are then degraded by common ortho, or meta cleavage pathways. Examples of protocatechuate precursors are 4-hydroxymandelate, quinate, and shikimate (as shown in this pathway, and in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: QUINATEDEG-PWY|, and |FRAME: SHIKIMATEDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|., It has been demonstrated that the first five enzymes of the mandelate degradation pathway also degrade 4-hydroxymandelate in |FRAME:TAX-303| |CITS: [5929747]|, and |FRAME:TAX-294| |CITS: [13096484]|. The mandelate degradation pathway and its enzymes are shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-1501|. Compounds effective as inducers of these enzymes include |FRAME: CPD-121|, |FRAME: CPD-122|, |FRAME: PHENYLGLYOXYLATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-105| |CITS: [5929747]|., In reactions analogous to those of the mandelate pathway, p-hydroxybenzoate, rather than benzoate, is formed. In the second reaction, the identity of the electron acceptor is not known, but it may be a ubiquinone |CITS: [14604988]|. p-Hydroxybenzoate is hydroxylated to protocatechuate. In P. putida and P. fluorescens, protocatechuate is metabolized to intermediates of central metabolism by the ortho cleavage pathways (|CITS: [4380381]|, and in |CITS: [13096484]|). This is shown in the pathway link above.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest., Plants and algae are exposed to rapidly changing light conditions and light intensities. Illumination with high light intensities has the potential to overexcite the photosynthetic pigments and the electron transport chain and induce the production of toxic reactive oxygen species. Many photoprotection mechanisms exist to prevent this problem. One of the most important protection mechanisms is the dissipation of excessive excitation energy as heat in the light-harvesting complexes of the photosystems. This process requires a structural change of the photosynthetic antenna complexes that are normally optimized for efficient light-harvesting. Enhanced heat dissipation in the antenna systems is achieved by a strong quenching of the chlorophyll a fluorescence, and has been termed non-photochemical quenching, or NPQ |CITS: [24854581]|., About This Pathway, The most important photoprotection mechanism in algae that belong to the classes |FRAME: TAX-33849| (diatoms), |FRAME: TAX-2825|, |FRAME: TAX-2833| and |FRAME: TAX-2864| is the diadinoxanthin (Ddx) cycle, which is the functional equivalent of the |FRAME: PWY-5945 "violaxanthin cycle"| which operates in green plants and many other photosynthetic organisms |CITS: [Stransky70]|. When cells are illuminated with high light intensity the cycle converts the epoxide-containing carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-20680| to |FRAME: CPD-20693|, which quenches chlorophyll fluorescence, effectively conversting PS II from a light-harvesting state to a heat dissipating state. Low light stimulates the back reaction, in which the de-epoxidized |FRAME: CPD-20693| is epoxidized to |FRAME: CPD-20680|, restoring light-harvesting functionality |CITS: [24310118 ][18397307]|., Like the better characterized |FRAME: EC-1.23.5.1|, diadinoxanthin de-epoxidase (DDE) is a water-soluble lumenal protein that undergoes a conformational change when pH drops due to the light-driven proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane during photosynthesis. The change in enzyme conformation is accompanied by the functional binding of the enzyme to the thylakoid membrane, where the substrate |FRAME: CPD-20680| is located |CITS: [Jakob01][15751979][Grouneva06][19604599]|., Much less in known about the other enzyme of the cycle, diatoxanthin epoxidase (DEP). The enzyme is located at the stromal side of the thylakoid membrane, possibly with a membrane spanning domain to sense the luminal pH |CITS: [18682837]|. It requires NADPH and O2 as cosubstrates. DEP is strongly regulated by the proton gradient (the optimal pH is 7.0), making it virtually inactive once the transmembrane ΔpH gradient has been established. In the absence of the proton gradient the epoxidation reaches extremely high rates, more than 20 times higher than the epoxidation rates by |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.21| observed in higher plants |CITS: [Goss06][24854581]|.

General Background, Acylated amino acids function as important components of the cellular membrane in some bacteria. The best characterized and most widespread amino acid lipids are the |FRAME: ORNITHINE-LIPIDS "ornithine lipids"|, which are found in the membranes of many Gram-negative bacteria and in some Gram-positive bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-6818|). However, not much is known about the function of these non-phosphorus lipids. It has been shown that ornithine lipids are important for growth during acid and temperature stress in |FRAME: TAX-398| |CITS: [21205018]|, and depletion of the lipids results in an increase in the speed of crown gall tumor formation in plants infected with |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [ 22958119]|., Biosynthesis is initiated by the N-acylation of the amino acid by a 3-hydroxy fatty acid, followed by subsequent O-acylation of the acylated molecule, resulting in a diacylated amino acid lipid., About This Pathway, The monoacylated glycine species |FRAME: CPD-21035| was originally identified from Bacteroides. This compound has hemolytic activity and the ability to solubilize cholesterol micelles. The compound is formed by the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-58278| gene, originally identified in metagenomic sequences and later characterized from |FRAME: TAX-821| |CITS: [26283367][29038461]|., A subsequent study of the gene from |FRAME: TAX-821| and |FRAME: TAX-818| showed that it is located in an operon together with a second gene, |FRAME: G-80449|, which encodes the second enzyme of the pathway, an O-acyltransferase that forms the diacylated compound |CITS: [30367006]|.

General Background, There is little known about the occurence of |FRAME: D-Gulose| and D-gulosides in nature. |FRAME: D-Gulose| was found in the EPS of |FRAME: TAX-155892| |CITS: [1885545]| and in an extracellular matrix glycoprotein of |FRAME: TAX-3067| |CITS: [1544415]|. |FRAME: CPD-15624| was discovered as a sugar moiety in the antibiotic |FRAME: Bleomycins bleomycin| |CITS: [4645953]|; 6-deoxy-D-gulose was found in the O-antigen of |FRAME: TAX-630| |CITS: [9004221]|; 6-deoxy-3-C-methyl-gulose occurs in the LPS of |FRAME: TAX-777| |CITS: [3996391]|., About This Pathway, Three enzymes encoded in the ycj gene cluster of E. coli were investigated; their combinded catalytic activities were demonstrated to convert a D-guloside to a D-glucoside |CITS: [30742415]|., The NAD+-dependent |FRAME: G6651-MONOMER| YcjQ converts a D-guloside to a 3-dehydro-D-guloside. The |FRAME: G6652-MONOMER| YcjR converts the 3-dehydro-D-guloside to a 3-dehydro-D-glucoside, which can subsequently be reduced to a D-glucoside by the |FRAME: G6653-MONOMER| YcjS. For the conversion of |FRAME: CPD0-2667| to |FRAME: CPD0-2668|, a mixture of YcjQ, YcjR and YcjS has a calculated equilibrium constant of 9.0. The specific physiological substrates for the enzymes in this pathway are so far unknown.

Some secondary metabolites that belong to the |FRAME: Ansatrienins ansatrienins| family, such as |FRAME: CPD-21971| |CITS: [7161184]| and |FRAME: CPD-21973| |CITS: [3840155][2991181]|, contain a unique |FRAME: CPD-575| moiety linked via a D-alanine residue to the macrocyclic lactam ring. An unsubstituted cyclohexane ring at the terminus of a carbon chain is also found in |FRAME: CPD-18764| |CITS: [Kakunima79]| and |FRAME: CPD-22120| |CITS: [2753809][2793587]|. All of these compounds are produced by |FRAME: TAX-1883| strains. In addition, unsubstituted cyclohexane ring has been shown to be biosynthesized and utilized as a starter unit for fatty acid biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-405212| and related bacteria |CITS: [Moore93]|., Studies with |FRAME: TAX-42684| and |FRAME: TAX-405212| using labeled |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| have shown that the |FRAME: CPD-575| moiety is derived from |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| in a pathway that involves a series of dehydration and double-bond reduction steps |CITS: [Casati87][3598593][Moore93a][Moore93][8201312]|. Most of the steps in this process occur with the carboxylic acid activated as a coenzyme A thioester |CITS: [Reynolds91][Moore93][8201312]|., Assays performed with cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-42684| have suggested that the last two steps of the pathway are the isomerization of the double bond in |FRAME: CPD-22109| to form |FRAME: CPD-533|, followed by a reduction of the final double bond |CITS: [Reynolds91][1577668]|. The enzyme catalyzing the last reduction, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.120|, was purified from |FRAME: TAX-42684| |CITS: [1597409]| and the |FRAME: G-63041| gene encoding it was identified |CITS: [8955309]|. Assays of the recombinant enzyme showed that it could catalyze three different reduction steps in the pathway. This was followed by the purification of a |FRAME: TAX-42684| enzyme capable of catalyzing the isomerization reaction |CITS: [10858310]|., The partial sequencing of the ansatrienin biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-42684| was accomplished using the sequence information of the |FRAME: G-63041| gene, and revealed a total of five genes (ansJ, ansK, ansL, |FRAME: G-63041|, and ansM) that encode enzymes proposed to be involved in |FRAME: CPD-577| biosynthesis (the |FRAME: G-63046| gene that encodes the isomerase is loacted outside the cluster) |CITS: [10103039]|., The ansJ and ansK genes were proposed to encode |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.M27|, and |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.M35|, respectively, based on their sequence |CITS: [10103039]|. These two genes are fused into a single |FRAME: G-63043| gene in |FRAME: TAX-67297| |CITS: [ 21948600]|. The ansM gene appears to encode an NADPH-dependent oxidoreductase similar to to various 2,4 dienoyl CoA reductases, and was thus assigned the function of |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.M23| |CITS: [10103039][10973220]|. The role of AnsL was less clear based on its sequence, but it has been proposed to catalyze the activity of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.M28| |CITS: [10973220]|., To test whether these 5 genes can indeed encode the complete conversion of |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| to |FRAME: CPD-577|, they were cloned into a plasmid and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-33903| and |FRAME: TAX-1916|. Expression in these strains resulted in production of significant amounts of ω-cyclohexyl fatty acids (as high as 49% of total fatty acids). In addition, the recombinant |FRAME: TAX-33903| produced |FRAME: CPD-22128|, a commercial antiparasitic |FRAME: Avermectins avermectin| analog that contains a cyclohexyl moiety |CITS: [10973220]|.

Summary: General Background, Sphingolipids are ubiquitous components of eukaryotic cells. They are composed of a long-chain base (amino alcohol), an amide linked fatty acyl chain, and a polar head. The predominant long-chain bases in plants are C18 amino alcohols, with sphinganine, 4-hydroxysphinganine, and 4-hydroxy-8-sphingenine being the prevalent long-chain bases. Whilst, the prevalent long-chain bases of many mammalian sphingolipids, sphingosine (4-sphingenine), is found only in trace amounts in plants. The predominant fatty acyl chains in plants are alpha-hydroxy fatty acids, with saturated C22 to C26 hydroxy fatty acyl chains, especially 2-hydroxylignoceric acid, are the most common ones., Ceramide (without a polar head group), glucosylceramide, and derivatives of inositolphosphorylceramide are the predominant plant sphingolipids. Sphingomyelin, which has phosphocholine as the polar head group and is the major phosphosphingolipid in animals, has not been detected in plants. On the other hand, yeast contains exclusively inositolphosphorylceramides., About This Pathway, The defining step in the de novo biosynthesis of ceramides is the pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-dependent condensation of |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA| with |FRAME: SER| catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-305 "serine palmitoyltransferase"| |CITS: [9363775]|. The resultant |FRAME: DEHYDROSPHINGANINE| is immediately reduced to |FRAME: CPD-13612| in an NADPH dependent reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: HS04306-MONOMER|. |FRAME: MONOMER66-34367 "Dihydroceramide synthase"| catalyzes the acylation of sphinganine to yield |FRAME: CPD3DJ-82|, followed by a desaturation at the 4,5 position to form |FRAME: Ceramides| |CITS: [9312549]|. The pathway occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum., |FRAME: Sphingomyelins Sphingomyelin| is a type of |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS sphingolipid| found in animal cell membranes, especially in the membranous myelin sheath that surrounds some nerve cell axons. It usually consists of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and |FRAME: Ceramides|. , Sphingomyelin is found in all tissues and lipoproteins; for example, it accounts for ~5% of the lipid phosphate in liver and 25% in pancreas |CITS: [2187537]|. Sphingomyelin has a function in signal transduction |CITS: [8086039]|. , Sphingomyelin is highly enriched in the plasma membrane of cells, and was considered to be found largely in the exoplasmic leaflet of the cell membrane. However, there is some evidence that there may also be a sphingomyelin pool in the inner leaflet of the membrane |CITS: [2187537]|. Moreover, neutral sphingomyelinase-2, an enzyme that breaks down sphingomyelin into ceramide, has been found to localize exclusively to the inner leaflet, further suggesting that there may be sphingomyelin present there., Sphingomyelin can accumulate in a rare hereditary disease called Niemann-Pick Disease. The disease is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme sphingomyelinase, rsulting in accumulation of sphingomyelin in the spleen, liver, lungs, bone marrow, and the brain, causing irreversible neurological damage.

Plant specialized tissues such as trichomes have been found to be involved in fending off pathogenic attackers by physically hampering the invasion and by excreting toxic and/or signaling compounds |CITS:[16668241] [22979959]|. This has been observed in about 30% of vascular plants which use glandular trichomes for production and exudation of specialized volatile and non-volatile substances |CITS:[23235331]|. In this way, trichomes form a first line of defense and have also become a target for molecular engineering and farming of natural products |CITS:[Wagner01]|. Glandular trichomes are considered an important but non-essential tissue. Nevertheless, studies on cell division pattern and structural specificities of trichomes during developmental stages of leaves reveal the importance of this epidermal structures for production and timely release of special metabolites and their contribution to herbivore resistance |CITS:[Bergau15]|., Together with sucrose esters (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)|), |FRAME:CPD-18857 α-cembratriene-4,6-diol| and |FRAME:CPD-18856 β-cembratriene-4,6-diol|, formerly referred to as duvatrienediols |CITS:[1255021] [16664523] [3138948]|, are the main components of tobacco trichome exudates |CITS:[12569411]| and suspected to contribute to tobacco aroma and smoke flavor |CITS:[Bentley45] [Uzelac15]|. The two positional cembratriene-4,6-diol isomers have been attributed with tumor-promoter inhibitory properties and have also been found to inhibit enzymes such as aldose reductase, the synthesis of fatty acid compounds such as prostaglandins |CITS:[8372141] [19490913]| and reported to exhibit a wider spectrum of biological activities acting as insect repellants |CITS:[11283597] [Wang04]|, pheromones and toxins (reviewed in |CITS:[Wahlberg92]|, |CITS:[Tius88]|)., Using labeled precursors, the involvement of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP geranylgeranyl diphosphate| (see |FRAME:PWY-5120 geranylgeranyl diphosphate biosynthesis|, |FRAME:PWY-5122 geranyl diphosphate biosynthesis|) produced via the |FRAME:PWY-5760 β-alanine biosynthesis IV| (|CITS:[15012203]|) in the |FRAME:PWY18C3-7 cembratrienediol biosynthesis| has been shown previously |CITS:[Crombie88] [Guo95]|. Terpenoids are considered highly interactive compounds to enable communication of plants with their environment. The important role of terpenoids in the life cycle of Solanaceae is underlined, for instance, by the presence of 44 terpene synthases in the genome of Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[21813655]|. This has initiated efforts to engineer terpenoids in plants to increase terpenoid production and to gain insights in the underlying pathways |CITS:[26603654]|. Moreover, investigation of different types of glandular trichomes (short and tall) in Nicotiana tabacum have revealed varying roles of such structures in biochemical syntheses highlighting the complex issue of form, function, location and specialized metabolism |CITS:[24865179]|. , The biosynthetic route towards |FRAME:CPD-18857 α-cembratriene-4,6-diol| and |FRAME:CPD-18856 β-cembratriene-4,6-diol| is realized by two enzymes, i.e. cembratrienol synthase and cembratrienol hydroxylase. The cembratrienol synthase in Nicotiana tabacum (CYC-1) identified from a cDNA library |CITS:[11283597]| is able to catalyze the formation of both positional isomers |FRAME:CPD-18854 α-cembratriene-ol| and |FRAME:CPD-18855 β-cembratriene-ol| from |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP geranylgeranyl diphosphate| |CITS:[12569411]|. The same molecular function has been established for three cembratrienol synthases (CBTS-2a, CBTS-2b, CBTS-3) isolated from Nicotiana sylvestris utilizing the CYC-1 gene from Nicotiana tabacum |CITS:[20495852]|. The subsequent 6-hydroxylation of both |FRAME:CPD-18854 α-cembratriene-ol| and |FRAME:CPD-18855 β-cembratriene-ol| to form the respective |FRAME:CPD-18857 α-cembratriene-4,6-diol| and |FRAME:CPD-18856 β-cembratriene-4,6-diol| is catalyzed by the cembratrienol 6-hydroxylase which has been elucidated by a combination of antisense suppression and co-suppression of the gene (CYP71D16) in transformed Nicotiana tabacum plants |CITS:[12569411] [11283597]|. In addition, the promoters of both cembratrienol synthases |CITS:[20495852]| and cembratrienol 6-hydroxylase |CITS:[12177128]| were identified and demonstrated to direct the tissue-specific expression in the glandular trichomes of Nicotiana tabacum.

Summary: Purine nucleotides participate in many aspects of cellular metabolism including the structure of DNA and RNA, serving as enzyme cofactors, functioning in cellular signaling, acting as phosphate group donors, and generating cellular energy. Maintenance of the proper balance of intracellular pools of these nucleotides is critical to normal function. This occurs through a combination of de novo biosynthesis and salvage pathways for pre-existing purine bases, nucleosides and nucleotides., The de novo biosynthetic pathway for purine nucleotides is highly conserved among organisms, but its regulation and the organization of the genes encoding the enzymes vary. This fourteen step pathway contains ten steps that branch at |FRAME: IMP| to form |FRAME: AMP| and |FRAME: GMP|, each in two steps. Regulation of the pathway has been well studied in microbes such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME:TAX-1423| and |FRAME:TAX-4932|, but little is known about its regulation in higher eukaryotes (metazoa, and plants |CITS: [8938402]|). The pathway appears to vary in archaea |CITS: [9150241]|. Some organisms, such as the mycoplasmas, do not biosynthesize purine and pyrimidine bases de novo and must rely on salvage pathways |CITS: [11737647]|., In bacterial systems genetic studies indicate that the majority of de novo purine biosynthetic genes are unlinked but may act as a single unit of regulation controlled by the |FRAME: PC00033| protein. In |FRAME:TAX-562| the 14 reactions involved in the de novo synthesis of AMP and GMP are catalyzed by 12 known genes. These genes occur mostly as unlinked single units or as small functional operons carrying two or, at the most, three structural genes each. The |FRAME: EG10800| gene encodes the repressor controlling the synthesis of all of these enzymes. Sequences similar to the protected region (PUR box) in purF are present in the regulatory regions of purMN. The expression of |FRAME: EG10800| was shown to be autoregulated, probably through blocking of transcription elongation by binding of PurR to the two PUR boxes. So far, six genes/operons have been reported to contain PUR box-like sequences., The purine biosynthetic pathway is controlled by feedback regulation of activity as well as at the level of transcription, |CITS:[2404765]|., Reactions that convert ADP to ATP are found in multiple pathways, including fueling pathways such as anaerobic respiration, TCA-aerobic respiration, fermentation, and glycolysis, and are thus not included in this pathway.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22925 Spectinomycin| is an aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-68270| and related species. It has a unique tricyclic structure in which a single sugar component, |FRAME: CPD-27051|, is linked to a diaminocyclitol moiety (|FRAME: CPD-27044|) by β-glycosidic and hemiketal bonds., |FRAME: CPD-22925 Spectinomycin| possesses a broad spectrum of activities against many Gram-positive as well as Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4274968]|. It binds to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, inhibiting the binding of the elongation factor G and interrupting protein synthesis. It possesses a particularly potent activity against |FRAME: TAX-485|, and is used (as its dihydrochloride pentahydrate) to treat gonorrhea in cases where the organism has acquired resistance to penicillin |CITS: [14461632]|., Spectinomycin was discovered in 1961 under the name actinospectacin |CITS: [13767811][13711223][13761690][13867836]| and later sold under the trade name Trobicin (among others). It is included in the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines., About This Pathway, Early studies have shown that the |FRAME: CPD-27044| moiety of spectinomycin comes from D-glucose via |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| while the remainder of the molecule is derived directly from glucose |CITS: [Mitscher71]|., A DNA fragment from |FRAME: TAX-55404| containing most of the genes involved in spectinomycin biosynthesis was deposited in Genbank in 1999 |CITS: [9245803]|. A 45 kb region containing most of the gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-68270| was reported in 2000 |CITS: [10650224]|, and the full cluster was sequenced subsequently |CITS: [Sohn01][Jo03][18663525]|. Expression of the cluster in |FRAME: TAX-54571| enabled spectinomycin production |CITS: [24503209]|. Based on the similarity of the genes to characterized enzymes, a pathway has been proposed |CITS: [Jo03][18663525][18355231]|., While the earlier part of the pathway has been studied in some detail, not much is known about the finals steps, which lead to the formation of the central dioxane ring. Careful analysis of the activity of the radical SAM-dependent enzyme SpeY (found to be a |FRAME: MONOMER-124596|), has led to a significant modification of the latter part of the pathway |CITS: [35622017]|., Please note that the exact asignment of some of the enzymes, particulalry those of |FRAME: G-124592 SpeH| and |FRAME: G-124591 SpeI|, is speculative.

|FRAME: CPD-20677 Flexixanthin| is a monocyclic carotenoid that possesses one oxygenated β-ionone ring analogous to that of |FRAME: CPD-11473| and one hydroxylated aliphatic end group as found in |FRAME: CPD-11464|. It was characterizede from several strains of |FRAME: TAX-992 flexibacteria| back in the 60s |CITS: [5973663]|., The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-356796| was isolated from a marine sponge, |FRAME: TAX-163232|, which was collected at the coastal area in Numazu, Japan. The bacterium formed orange colonies, suggesting the presence of carotenoids. Analysis of the carotenoid content of the organism showed |FRAME: CPD-20677| as the main carotenoid, along with the minor products |FRAME: CPD1F-114|, |FRAME: CPD-12611|, and |FRAME: CPD-20674| |CITS: [16625353]|., Since |FRAME: CPD-20677| is a ketocarotenoid, it was assumed that the organism would have |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.63|. To find the gene encoding the ketolase, a DNA library of the bacterium was transformed into a |FRAME: CPD1F-129|-producing strain of |FRAME: TAX-562|. Since the enzyme converts |FRAME: CPD1F-129| into |FRAME: CPD-7850| and |FRAME: CPD-7851|, colonies that contain it change their color from yellow to orange. Analysis of orange colonies confirmed the presence of the |FRAME: G-58163| gene, encoing a ketolase. Screening of a cosmid library identified a 22-kb region that contained the |FRAME: G-58163| gene along with six other genes, including crtI (encoding |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.31|, crtB (encoding |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.32|), and |FRAME: G-58164| (encoding |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.19|) |CITS: [16625353]|., Based on the observed intermediates and the presence of the |FRAME: G-58163| and |FRAME: G-58164| genes, a pathway has been proposed for the biosynthesis |FRAME: CPD-20677|. The pathway predicts the presence of additional genes, namely crtC (|FRAME: EC-4.2.1.131|), crtD (|FRAME: EC-1.3.99.27|), and crtZ (|FRAME: EC-1.14.15.24|). However, these genes have not been identified yet. Analysis of the 15-kb region downstream of the seven-gene cluster showed that the missing genes are not located there |CITS: [16625353]|.

|FRAME:CPD-18416 T-2 toxin| is the predominant trichothecene generated in Fusarium sporotrichioides. |FRAME:CPD-18416 T-2 toxin| is a type A trichothecene such as |FRAME:CPD-18439| and |FRAME:CPD-18430| (see |FRAME:PWY-7714|) and differs from the type B trichothecenes primarily produced in Fusarium graminearum, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18421| (see |FRAME:PWY-7712|) and |FRAME:CPD-18427| (see |FRAME:PWY-7713|) in bearing a hydroxyl instead of an carbonyl function on C-8 of the trichothecene core structure. A large number of trichothecenes have been identified from various genera of fungi and classified into four groups (type A to D) according to the substitution pattern on the basic 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene (EPT) core |CITS:[Ueno80] [Betina89] [Alexander09] [22069741] [Grove07]|., Chemically trichothecene belong in the compound class of sequiterpenoids and have been associated with a number of biological activities in a variety of organisms. Trichothecene are mycotoxins which display phytotoxic activities |CITS:[22295175]|, are the origin of contaminated food and animal feed, and have been reported to cause vomiting, skin dermatitis, and hemorrhagic lesions |CITS:[3158480] [8246841]|. In general, it has been established that a bigger number and more intricate side groups increase the toxicity of trichothecenes |CITS:[4827835]|. The mycotoxin |FRAME:CPD-18416| in particular may act as immunosuppressor |CITS:[8923234]|, has been found to elicit neurochemical injuries |CITS:[3764907]|, is highly cytotoxic |CITS:[2918501]|, and has multiple effects in cellular systems such as inhibition of DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis, cell division and destruction of red blood cells (summarized in |CITS:[2200582]|). The higher phytotoxicity of C-4 hydroxylated metabolites, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18416| compared to its acetylated precursor, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18415| has been confirmed in an Chlamydomonas reinhardtii test system |CITS:[11122517]|. The increased toxicity of the C-4 hydroxylated vs C-4 acylated compound has also found to be the case in an mice test system |CITS:[4699224]|. In addition, trichothecene have also been found to induce and/or increase virulence in wheat head scab, also referred to as Fusarium ear blight, causing significant losses in major cereals like wheat and oats |CITS:[Desjardins96] [Proctor02]|. Many studies have been carried out to elucidate the harmful effects of trichothecenes and to investigate the underlying pathways in order to counteract the significant losses caused by Fusarium pathogens worldwide |CITS:[18791024] [19385728] [5816375] [15762554] [25680507]| which threaten the existence of farms and whole rural communities |CITS:[18944567]|., The |FRAME:PWY-7730| emerges from the core reactions of the |FRAME:PWY-7711| at the branch point compound |FRAME:CPD-18411| which splits up trichothecenes towards |FRAME:CPD-18421| and eventually |FRAME:CPD-18427| and |FRAME:CPD-18416|. The genes encoding for proteins involved in the biosynthetic sequence towards |FRAME:CPD-18416| are organized in the gene clusters (TRI) known to operate in this pathway |CITS:[14998528] [12650935] [12080147]|. Similar to the reaction steps which connect the |FRAME:PWY-7712| with the |FRAME:PWY-7713| the TRI13 encoded protein from Fusarium sporotrichioides catalyzes the C-4 hydroxylation of an precursor, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18411| to form |FRAME:CPD-18412| |CITS:[12135578]| which is substrate for the trichothecene 4-acetyltransferase (TRI7) from the same species which yields |FRAME:CPD-18413| |CITS:[11352533]|. This intermediate is also a branch off compound towards the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-18427|. The following C-8 hydroxylation is carried out by the trichothecene 8-hydroxylase (TRI1) which has been shown by disruption of the gene, heterologous expression of TRI1 in the non-trichothecene producing Fusarium verticillioides and functional complementation of Δtri1 mutants of Fusarium sporotrichioides |CITS:[12620849] [16604118]|. The utilization of the unusual acyl donor |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA| and the attachment of |FRAME:ISOVALERATE| to |FRAME:CPD-18414| generating |FRAME:CPD-18415| is catalyzed by the trichothecene 8-acyltransferase (TRI16) |CITS:[14690377] [14532047]|. However, the synthesis of the acyl donor |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA| remains to be shown. The final step in the pathway yielding |FRAME:CPD-18416| is carried out by the TRI8 encoded 3-acetyl T-2 toxin C-3 esterase |CITS:[12039755]|.

|FRAME: CPD-8097 Esculetin| is a coumarin compound that has a strong antioxidant activity. It exhibits a vast array of biological activities, such as the inhibition of free radical generation, inflammatory markers, influencing of glycemic index, and abnormal functioning of genes in cancer and hepatic failures |CITS: [36293500]|., Esculetin may form nonenzymatically from |FRAME: CAFFEATE| |CITS: [13806518]|. |FRAME: CAFFEATE Caffeate| exists in cis and trans forms, although the trans form is the predominant naturally occurring form. Solutions of |FRAME: CPD-676| and its derivatives (e.g.,|FRAME: CAFFEOYLQUINATE|) are unstable in sunlight and ultraviolet light, and when exposed, are partially converted to the cis form. |FRAME: CPD-8098| in turn is partially converted to the lactone, |FRAME: CPD-8097| |CITS: [4781486][Hartley75][Borges89]|., Nevertheless, enzymatic catalysis has been observed. The biosynthesis pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-8097| in plants is still largely unclear. Genetic and biochemical evidence in Arabidopsis supports that coumarins derived from CoA-derivatives rather than free acids as previously thought |CITS: [18547395]|. A 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase (|FRAME: MONOMER-18295|) was shown to catalyze the hydroxylation of |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA| in a recombinant bacterium, generating |FRAME: CPD-18078| |CITS: [25927349]|., The hydroxylation is followed by trans-cis isomerization of the side chain, and subsequent lactonization to close the ring and yield |FRAME: CPD-8097|. The mechanism of the E-Z isomerization step in the biosynthesis of coumarins varies between genera or even species, for being either light-dependent photoisomerization or light-independent enzyme catalyzed isomerization |CITS: [19004461]|.

General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons across a membrane., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons on one side of a membrane, or produce them on the other side of the membrane, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Several NAD molecules are reduced to NADH in the glycolytic and TCA cycles. These energy-rich molecules have a pair of electrons with high transfer potential. The free energy liberated during transfer of those electrons can be used for synthesizing ATP. The aerobic respiration pathway shown here parallels the transport of electrons resulting from the oxidation of NADH with the creation of a proton gradient and accompanying membrane potential, leading to the synthesis of ATP |CITS: [Dey97]|. This electron transfer is performed in plants and animals, as well as some bacteria, by a series of four large electron carriers complexes also known as complex I-IV (electron transport chain or respiratory chain), present in the inner mitochondrial membrane. These complexes facilitate the passage of electrons from lower to higher redox potentials., Of those complexes, complex I accepts NADH and complex II accepts the TCA cycle intermediate succinate. The flow of electrons resulting from these oxidations causes protons to be pumped from the matrix side to the intermembrane space. This flow generates a proton-motive force composed of a pH gradient and a membrane potential. Those protons flow back into the matrix through various routes. Particularly, protons flow back through the ATP-synthesizing complex embedded in the mitochondrial membrane or bacterial inner membrane, leading to the synthesis of ATP., In contrast to the mitochondrial respiration in mammals and plants (this pathway), the oxidative phosphorylation in |FRAME: TAX-4932| via the respiration chain occurs without complex I. Instead Baker's yeast employs three NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductases (type II - one internal, two external) which catalyze the reoxidation of cytosolic |FRAME:NADH| to provide |FRAME:NAD| (see |FRAME:PWY-7279|) |CITS:[23086143] [1900238] [9733747] [9696750]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the pyrimidine ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, mono- or diphosphorylated forms of pyrimidine nucleotides activate other molecules, as in |FRAME: CMP-KDO|, |FRAME: CPD-12575|, and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., The de novo biosynthetic pathways of pyrimidine nucleotides consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. Salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides, and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways to form other nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|).However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level. These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The de novo pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthetic pathway converts |FRAME: HCO3|, |FRAME: GLN|,, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to |FRAME: UMP| (uridine 5'-monophosphate), a pyrimidine nucleotide that can be subsequently converted to all other pyrimidine nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7176|)., The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.5|, forms |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|, which is not only an intermediate of pyrimidine synthesis but also a precursor for the synthesis of amino acids such as |FRAME: ARG|, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: CANAVANINE|. The pathway continues with the condensation of |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| with |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to form |FRAME: CARBAMYUL-L-ASPARTATE| |CITS: [8041358]|. The products is cyclized to, |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE|, the first intermediate that contains a pyrimidine ring., The next step, the oxidation of |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| to |FRAME: OROTATE| is carried out by different enzymes in different organisms. In general, Gram-positive bacteria and fungi contain class 1 enzymes, which are cytosolic, include |FRAME: FMN| cofators, and use |FRAME: FUM| or NAD(P)+ as electron acceptors (|FRAME: EC-1.3.98.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.14|, or |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.15|). Gram-negative bacteria and eukaryotes possess class 2 enzymes, which are membrane bound and use |FRAME: Quinones| as electron acceptor (|FRAME: EC-1.3.5.2 "EC 1.3.5.2"|) |CITS: [Jensen98]|., The final two steps, the condensation of |FRAME: OROTATE| with PRPP forming |FRAME: OROTIDINE-5-PHOSPHATE|, (OMP) followed by the decarboylation of OMP to UMP, are carried out by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.10|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.23|. The last step is considered the rate-limiting step of the overall de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [7579161]|., The de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides appears to be one of the most ancient biochemical pathways, as it is evolutionary conserved in all species. Although the enzymatic steps in this pathway are conserved throughout all organisms (with the exception of the oxidation of |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| to |FRAME: OROTATE|), some differences in the enzymes do exist. For example, in plants and bacteria the three steps leading from |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| to |FRAME: OROTATE| are catalyzed by three different proteins, while in mammals they are catalyzed by the single multifunctional |FRAME: CPLX-6703| |CITS: [8619816]|., Similarly, the last two steps of the pathway are carried out by a bi-functional enzyme (|FRAME: AT3G54470-MONOMER|) in plants and animals |CITS: [2876681][7579161][9878395]| whereas bacteria express two separate proteins for that purpose., About The Pathway in |FRAME: TAX-4932| , In |FRAME: TAX-4932|, the first two steps of pyrimidine biosynthesis are catalyzed by the |FRAME: YJL130C| protein. This enzyme is controlled by feedback inhibition and repression |CITS: [5651325]|. The enzymes that follow later in the pathway are induced in a sequential way by the intermediary products and are insensitive to pyrimidine repression. When the pool of |FRAME: UTP| is limited, the pathway is activated and intermediary products are accumulated. The accumulation of |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| induces the transcription of the |FRAME: YLR420W|, |FRAME: YKL216W| and |FRAME: YEL021W| genes in a process mediated by the PPR1 protein |CITS: [24189721][6278253]|.

Summary: |FRAME: DIHYDROPTERIN-CH2OH-PP| (6-hydroxymethyl-dihydropterin diphosphate) is the pterin precursor for the biosynthesis of several important cofactors, including |FRAME:THF tetrahydrofolate|, |FRAME: CPD-10763| and |FRAME: CPD-10764|. The compound is always synthesized from GTP, but the enzymes involve may differ among organisms., The malaria parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833| synthesizes folate. The pathway appears crucial, as disrupting folate synthesis by gene deletion is lethal in |FRAME: TAX-5833| even when folate is supplied |CITS: [14982635]|. Thus folate metabolism in this organism is the target of several antimalarial agents. , |FRAME: TAX-5833| possesses most of the enzymes that are known to participate in the pathway of folate biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-6147|), with the exception of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.25|. No gene homologous to genes known to encode the enzyme are present in the |FRAME: TAX-5833| genome, and no such activity could be demonstrated in cell extracts. Thus, the exact folate biosynthetic pathway in the organism was unknown., The mystery was solved in 2008, when it was found that a homolog of |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.12|, which is known to participate in |FRAME: PWY-5663 "tetrahydrobioterin biosynthesis"|, is a bifunctional enzyme that also catalyzes a novel activity of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.60|, effectively bypassing the steps catalyzed by both |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.67| and |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.25|., Thus, when acting on |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3|, the enzyme produces a mixture of two products - |FRAME: AMINO-OH-HYDROXYMETHYL-DIHYDROPTERIDINE| and |FRAME: 6-PYRUVOYL-5678-TETRAHYDROPTERIN|, leading to the biosynthesis of both folate and tetrahydrobioterin, respectively |CITS: [18093090]|., Bioinformatic analysis suggests that this pathway variant is not limiteed to plasmodium, and is likely to be present in the |FRAME: TAX-33634| - a large group that includes oomycetes, various microalgae and brown algae |CITS: [18805734]|. In addition, the pathway is present in many groups of bacteria that are known to lack |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.25|, including the |FRAME: TAX-1239|, |FRAME: TAX-57723|, |FRAME: TAX-200795|, |FRAME: TAX-203682|, and |FRAME: TAX-203691| |CITS: [19395485]|.

Summary: General Background, The mycobacterial cell envelope contains an usually rich variety of complex free lipids and glycolipids associated with the, mycolic acid layer of the cell wall. These lipids and glycolipids are located in the membrane outer leaflet. Together with the membrane inner leaflet, which is based on mycolic acids, they form the asymmetric lipid bilayer that constitutes the characteristic mycobacterial outer membrane., All strains of |FRAME: TAX-1773| examined to date synthesize |FRAME: CPD-18612 "dimycocerosyl phthiocerols"| (DIMs), but only few of them produce the structurally related |FRAME: PGL "dimycocerosyl triglycosyl phenolphthiocerols"| (PGLs). Despite that, many sera from tuberculous patients contain antibodies specifically recognizing the major PGL of the Canetti subspecies, |FRAME: CPD-18579|., The reason for the existence of the antibodies is that the strains that do not produce PGLs produce smaller molecules that contain a similar glycosylated aromatic moiety as that of |FRAME: CPD-18579|. Two such compounds have been described from |FRAME: TAX-83332|, which does not produce PGLs: |FRAME: CPD-18617|, which contains only one modifed rhamnosyl residue, and |FRAME: CPD-18619|, which contains the full tri-glycosylated moiety as PGL-tb |CITS: [12138124]|., Since these compounds lack the long hydrocarbon chain found in PGLs, they are released into the culture medium instead of being attached to the hydrophobic mycobacterial cell surface. It is not known whether these compounds serve any purpose for the bacteria, or whether they are produced only as an artifact due to the mutation in the |FRAME: G-15015| gene encoding the PKS15/1 synthase, which prevents these bacteria from forming the phenolphthiocerol backbone |CITS: [12138124]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate 4-Hydroxybenzoate|, a common precursor for HBAD and PGL, is formed from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40| |CITS: [16210318]|. Three glycosyltranferases and four methyltransferases are involved in the formation of the glycosyl moiety of |FRAME: CPD-18619| |CITS: [15292272][15292265][23536839]|., In |FRAME: TAX-1765| mutations in the |FRAME: G185E-7212| ortholog, which encodes the glycosyltransferase that transfers the second rhamnose residue, as well as in genes that encode enzymes involved the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13118|, prevent the transfer of the second and third glycosides, and production ends at |FRAME: CPD-18617| |CITS: [18390543]|., Both |FRAME: CPD-18617| and |FRAME: CPD-18619| bear an additional methoxyl group in proximity to the carbonyl, group, indicating the existence of a methyltransferase that acts on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|. However, the identity of this enzyme has not been described.

Summary: The isoflavonoid glycosides in legumes have conserved patterns of glycosylations, the more abundant monosaccharides , are usually β-glucopyranosides and the fewer dissacharides are also of the β-glucopyranosides type. , There are some uncommon sugars reported, among them β-apiofuranose which is found invariably linked to C-4' of the isoflavone aglycone and also appears as a terminal sugar on various disaccharides |CITS: [VEITCH06]|. , The biosynthesis of legume isoflavonoid glycosides is poorly understood. A few isoflavonoid-specific , glucotransferases have been cloned providing some insight into the mechanism of isoflavonoid production , in legumes. Most of the plant glucosidases belong to the glucosyl hydrolase family (GH1). The 3 dimensional , structure of these enzymes reveal a common α-/β- barrel |CITS: [16814564]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-298683|, an isoflavonoid β-glucosidase has been isolated and cloned |CITS: [17998137]|. , This enzyme hydrolyzes the natural substrates |FRAME: CPD-9710| and |FRAME: CPD-9716| |CITS: [16098548]| by cleaving off only dissacharides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-9004| and not monosaccharides.

The genus Fusarium comprises filamentous fungi which are worldwide distributed and known to produce a wide variety of structural diverse secondary metabolites. Amongst them are many plant-pathogenic species such as Fusarium fujikuroi infamously known as the causing agent of the 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease induced through unbalanced production of gibberellins (see also |FRAME:PWY-5047|), which leads to substantial losses of crops in rice-growing countries all over the world |CITS:[19560174]|. Fusarium species also produce a broad variety of mycotoxins, however many of those secondary metabolites in fungi are cryptic or silent and cannot be reproduced under laboratory conditions |CITS:[24958266]|. The deciphering of the Fusarium fujikuroi genome not only revealed detailed insights into the gibberellin biosynthesis restricted to Fusarium fujikuroi but also allowed the identification of biosynthetic gene clusters which are uniquely found only in this species |CITS:[23825955]|. , The gene encoding a non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS), i.e. AFS1 is one of them and shown to belong to a biosynthetic gene cluster involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17958| |CITS:[24195442]|. Although chemically related to |FRAME:CPD-17957| (see |FRAME:PWY-7667|) and biosynthetically produced in a similar way the biogenesis of |FRAME:CPD-17958| differs in various aspects resulting in an distinctive product which is only produced in Fusarium fujikuroi. The analysis of the APF1 region revealed the presence of 11 genes forming the |FRAME:CPD-17958| biosynthetic gene cluster (apf) of which 5 genes were shown to be essential for the pathway and assigned molecular functions through targeted gene disruption and chemical profiling of the respective mutants |CITS:[25058475]|. In contrast to the similar gene cluster in Fusarium incarnatum producing |FRAME:CPD-17957| |CITS:[20233305]| the gene cluster in Fusarium fujikuroi (this pathway) does not possess APS10 and has an opposite orientation for the APS2/APS3 genes encoding for an transcription factor and the L-piperideine 6-carboxylate reductase, respectively. , The apicidin F synthetase (AFP1) possess four NRPS modules consisting of adenylation (A), thiolation (T) and condensation (C) domains for modules 2 to 4 plus an additional epimerization (E) domain for the first module which also indicated the order of the activated amino acids to be incorporated into the nascent peptide molecule, i.e. |FRAME:L-PIPECOLATE|, |FRAME:PHE|, |FRAME:CPD-17973| and finally |FRAME:CPD-17965|. Similar to the |FRAME:PWY-7667| the genes APF3 encoding for the L-piperideine 6-carboxylate reductase, APF6 coding for the N-hydroxy-L-tryptophan O-methyltransferase and APF9 encoding for the L-2-amino-8-hydroxyoctanoate monooxygenase were selectively disrupted and accumulating intermediates such as |FRAME:CPD-17961| (APF3) and |FRAME:CPD-17959| (APF9) pointed out the molecular functions of the enzymes in that pathway |CITS:[25058475]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-535 "Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate"| is a potent allosteric regulator with dual simultaneous functions. It is an activator of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.11| and an inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.11|, the key rate-limiting enzymes of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, respectively |CITS: [1657152][8393580][7574501]|. In plants |FRAME: CPD-535| is a key regulator of primary carbohydrate metabolism in photosynthetic tissues |CITS: [10899575]|., An increased concentration of intracellular |FRAME: CPD-535| increases glycolytic flux, while at low concentrations of the metabolite, there is a net increase in gluconeogenic flux |CITS: [12379646]|. The latter metabolite is diverted into the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY| resulting in the generation of |FRAME: NADPH| required for |FRAME: PWY-4081| and |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY| and production of |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, an important anti-oxidant.

|FRAME:CPD-17359 Stephacidin A| and notoamides (see |FRAME:PWY-7604|) belong to the family of fungal indole alkaloids derived from aromatic (e.g. |FRAME:TRP|) and isoprenoid moieties (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-4211|) which have been recognized for their wide range of bioactivities and intriguing reaction chemistry |CITS:[Williams00] [16322742] [20024094]|. Besides |FRAME:CPD-17359| (this pathway), an anticancer agent against various human cell tumor cell lines |CITS:[12465964]| the biosynthesis of other members of this indole alkaloid family such as the insect repellent |FRAME:CPD-15265| and tremorgenic mycotoxin |FRAME:CPD-15266| (see |FRAME:PWY-7525|) have been explored in the effort to detect novel bioactive metabolites |CITS:[23213353]|. The elucidation of the marine-derived Aspergillus sp. MF297-2 genome and the identification of the notoamide (not) gene cluster |CITS:[20722388]| significantly advanced the progress in determining the biosynthesis of integrated metabolites. , Interestingly, various Aspergillus species produce enatiomerically opposite products. For example, the marine Aspergillus sp. MF297-2 produces (-)-notoamide and (+)-stephacidine |CITS:[19281134]| whereas the terrestrial Aspergillus versicolor facilitates the opposite stereochemistry, i.e. the antipodal counterparts (+)-notoamide and (-)-stephacidine |CITS:[18389509] [21714564]|. The determination of the order and mechanism of successional steps in the |FRAME:PWY-7603| has been an joined effort of biochemistry and organic chemistry. The approach to combine biochemical assays, organic chemical reaction analysis and radioactive traced feeding experiments contributed to the confirmation of the biochemistry in early steps in the pathway and reaction chemistry of later steps, even though the corresponding enzymes of the latter remain to be identified |CITS:[21796227] [21818159] [McAfoos11]|. , Descending from |FRAME:CPD-15265| (see |FRAME:PWY-7525|) the first committed step in the pathway is the reversed prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-15265| at the C-2 position of the indole ring to form |FRAME:CPD-15273| catalyzed by the deoxybrevianamide F synthase (notF) of Aspergillus sp. MF297-2 |CITS:[20722388]|. Accordingly, the respective enzyme characterized from Aspergillus versicolor, i.e. brevianamide F reverse prenyltransferase (brePT) executes the same reaction in the terrestrial species |CITS:[22660767]|. Prenylation steps are considered key reactions in pathways producing hybrid natural products. In addition, new prenyltransferases with novel functionalities discovered along the way significantly expand our knowledge about the complexity and order in the biosynthetic grid of such compounds |CITS:[19149573]|. The second prenylation step of the pathway is carried out by the 6-hydroxy-deoxybrevianamide E prenyltransferase (notC) which catalyzes the normal prenylation of specifically |FRAME:CPD-17356| at the C-7 position of the indole ring to form |FRAME:CPD-17357| |CITS:[20722388]|. Bioinformatic analysis indicates that the generation of the precursor |FRAME:CPD-17356| for notC is probably carried out by one of the two not genes (notG, notH) predicted to function as P450 dependent monooxygenases |CITS:[20722388]|. For this and the remaining steps of the pathway bioconversions have been observed but the corresponding enzymes remain to be characterized |CITS:[19292484] [21504234] [23249380]|.

Summary: The capsular polysaccharide (CPS) plays an integral role in |FRAME: TAX-1313| virulence. Strains that are deficient in CPS production are avirulent |CITS: [11349040]|., Over 90 different serotypes of |FRAME: TAX-1313| have been defined, based on their CPS |CITS: [16532061]|. |FRAME: TAX-170187| belongs to serotype 4 and uses the a Wzy-dependent pathway (the predominant mechanism for CPS synthesis in Gram-positive bacteria.) for the synthesis of its CPS. In this type of pathway the capsule repeat unit is synthesized in the cytoplasm on a membrane lipid acceptor (undecaprenyl phosphate) by multiple glycosyltransferases. The completed repeat unit is transferred across the cytoplasmic membrane by the Wzx floppase and polymerized on the external side of the membrane by the Wzy polymerase. The Wzy-dependent pathway is not limited to CPS, and is also used in the synthesis of O-antigens and many exopolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The pathway starts with the linking of the first monosaccharide unit, UDP-GalNAc, to the lipid carrier undecarprenyl by the initiating transferase |FRAME: SP_RS01710 WciI|. The glycosyl transferases |FRAME: SP_RS01715 WciJ|, |FRAME: SP_RS01720 WciK|,and |FRAME: SP_RS01725 WciL| add the monosaccharides |FRAME: CPD-26549|, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-mannosamine| and |FRAME: D-galactopyranose|, respectively. The repeat unit is terminated by pyruvoylation, catalyed by |FRAME: SP_RS01735 WciM|. The |FRAME: SP_RS01740-MONOMER "floppase Wzx"| flips the complete repeat unit to the cell surface, where multiple repeat units are linked by the |FRAME: SP_RS01730-MONOMER| forming a long polysaccharide. In serotype 4 the polymerase links the polysaccharides between the Gal and GalNAc monosaccharides, leaving pyruvate as a side chain |CITS: [16532061]|., The mature polysaccharide is then linked to the |FRAME: NACMUR| residue of cell wall peptidoglycan by the same proteins that attach teichoic acids to peptidoglycan. The main enzyme catalyzing the attachment is the Wzg protein, but in its absence  the attachment can be catalyzed by LytR |CITS: [22432711]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN Dimethylsulfoniopropionate| (DMSP) is an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS:[12124622][17068264]|., DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|., Two main routes are known for DMSP degradation. In the first route DMSP is cleaved to |FRAME: CPD-7670| (forming |FRAME: ACRYLATE| or |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6046| and |FRAME: PWY-6056|, respectively), while in the second route DMSP is a demethylated to form |FRAME: CPD-7672| (MTPA) (see |FRAME: PWY-6052|), which is processed in different ways in different organisms., About This Pathway, In this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-7672| is demethylated further, forming |FRAME: CPD-7673|, |CITS:[16347732][16348607]|. The second methylation was observed with anoxic slurries of coastal, marine sediments |CITS: [16347732]|. |FRAME: CPD-7673| is a major organic sulfur compound, in the pore water of these sediments |CITS: [Kiene88]|., The |FRAME: ORG-6055|, an aerobic methylotrophic marine bacterium that was isolated from an, intertidal mud sample, was able to demethylate both DMSP and |FRAME: CPD-7672| to, |FRAME: CPD-7673| quantitatively |CITS: [7811100]|., The enzyme(s) responsible for the methylation reactions were not identified.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12857 "L,L-di-myo-inositol 1,3'-phosphate"| (also known as di-myo-inositol phosphate, or DIP) is the most widespread organic solute in microorganisms adapted to hot environments. It was first identified in |FRAME: TAX-2262|, in which it is the dominant counterion of K+, which ranges from 500 to 600 mM |CITS:[1633880]|. Since then it has been detected in many archael species |CITS: [16349412][12586398][9758772][16957243][8824608][16535556]| and some thermophilic bacteria |CITS: [17510735]|. So far DIP has not been encountered in organisms with optimal growth temperatures below 60°C, and is thus believed to play a role in the thermoprotection of cellular components |CITS: [17526717]|., The pathway leading to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12857| has been described. The pathway consists of four steps - formation of |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P|, activation to |FRAME: CPD-12855|, combining the latter with |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| to yield |FRAME: CPD-12856| (DIPP), and the dephosphorylation to the final product |CITS: [17028285]|., In many organisms the enzymes that catalyze the two key steps, activation to |FRAME: CPD-12855|, and formation of |FRAME: CPD-12856|, are fused into a single gene, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-56636|, |FRAME: TAX-2336|, and |FRAME: TAX-54248|, have individual genes and gene products |CITS: [17526717][17360515]|. The |FRAME: G-12326| gene, encoding the |FRAME: MONOMER-16017|, was identified in the |FRAME: TAX-2234| genome and characterized. The DIPPS domain of that enzyme showed some plasticity in regard to the alcohol-activated donor, and could also accept |FRAME: CPD-606| instead of CDP-inositol, leading to production of phosphorylated |FRAME: CPD-541| |CITS: [17526717]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD0-1308 Glyphosate| is a broad-spectrum systemic herbicide used to kill weeds. It was initially patented and sold by the Monsanto Company in the 1970s under the tradename Roundup, and has become the most used herbicide in the world |CITS: [21668647]|., Glyphosate's mode of action is to inhibit the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.19|, which catalyzes the transfer of the enolpyruvyl moiety of |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: SHIKIMATE-5P| to form |FRAME: 3-ENOLPYRUVYL-SHIKIMATE-5P|. This is a key reaction in the |FRAME: ARO-PWY "shikimate pathway"|, leading to synthesis of aromatic amino acids via |FRAME: CHORISMATE| in plants, fungi, bacteria, and apicomplexan parasites |CITS: [7396959]|., While little degradation of glyphosate has been reported in plants (most likely due to contaminating microbes), glyphosate degradation in soils is extensive and rapid |CITS: [Torstensson85]|. A number of pure cultures of bacteria have been identified that degrade glyphosate |CITS: [16346357][Talbot84][2430939][16346999][2442160][3804975][2439330][16347356][Hallas88][3997803][3223761][16347639][Quinn88][Lerbs90][2339877][16348512]|., Three degradation pathways have been described so far, two of which involve production of |FRAME: CPD0-1074| (AMPA) |CITS: [16347639][Monsanto95]|, a phosphonate that can be metabolized by a wide variety of microorganisms |CITS: [14088788][14302415][618850][Daughton79][Daughton79a][453832][3804975]|. The third pathway (this pathway) is catalyzed by the C-P lyase complex, and results in formation of |FRAME: SARCOSINE| and the transfer of the phosphonate phosphorus to the ribose moiety of ATP, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD0-2463|, which can be processed to |FRAME: Pi|., About This Pathway, Phosphonate compounds are imported into bacterial cells by an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transport system consisting of a periplasmic binding protein for phosphonates (encoded by |FRAME: EG10714| in |FRAME: TAX-562|), an ATP-binding polypeptide (|FRAME: EG10713|), and a membrane-spanning transporter polypeptide (|FRAME: EG11283 phnE|). Once inside the cell, the compounds are processed by the C-P lyase enzyme system, which includes 10 different polypeptides (using |FRAME: TAX-562| nomenclature, they are encoded by the genes |FRAME: EG10716|, |FRAME: EG10717|, |FRAME: EG10718|, |FRAME: EG10719|, |FRAME: EG10720|, |FRAME: EG10721|, |FRAME: EG10722|, |FRAME: EG10723|, |FRAME: EG10724|, and |FRAME: EG10725|) |CITS: [24600043]|. Four or five of the proteins form a complex. While the exact stoichiometry is not known yet, the complex contains at least PhnG4PhnH2PhnI2PhnJ2PhnK |CITS: [21705661]|. , The combined action of four enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.37|, |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.63|, |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.55|, transfer the phosphonate phosphorus to a ribose that originates from ATP, generating |FRAME: RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE|. Since the activity of the C-P lyase complex disappears when the integrity of the cytoplasmic membrane is violated, its activity is detected by the appearance of |FRAME: SARCOSINE|, which is a side product of |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|., Many organisms possess more than one C-P lyase system. For example, two such systems exist in Arthrobacter sp. GLP-1, one for |FRAME: CPD0-1068| and the other for glyphosate |CITS: [1368477]|., Several microbial species or strains have been shown to be able to utilize glyphosate via this pathway, utilizing it as a source of inorganic phosphate. They include |FRAME: TAX-439375|, isolated from glyphosate-contaminated, soil |CITS: [21789492]|, |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [9882650]|, |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [3804975]|, |FRAME: TAX-28450| |CITS: [7574593]|, and several species of cyanobacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-103690| |CITS: [18263622]|.

Summary: |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE 5-Oxo-L-proline| (also known as L-pyroglutamate) is formed via the spontaneous cyclization of the central metabolites |FRAME: GLN| |CITS: [13994204]|, |FRAME: GLT| |CITS: [11472943]|, and |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE-5-P| |CITS: [Orlowski71]|. Under physiological conditions |FRAME: GLN| cyclizes to |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| at the rate of 10% per day |CITS: [13994204]|., The cyclization is not limited to free amino acids. N-terminal glutaminyl and glutamyl residues of polypeptides can also spontaneously cyclize to |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| residues. The former transformation is also enzymically catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.5| |CITS: [ 18979624][20868223]|. Once formed, the abberant residue is removed from the peptide by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.3|, yielding free |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| |CITS: [1353026]|., |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| is also formed by additional routes. One such route is from |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.3.2.7| |CITS: [23070364]|. In eukaryotic organisms it is also formed by |FRAME: EC-4.3.2.9| as part of the |FRAME: PWY-4041| |CITS: [5781001]|. , Accumulation of |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| is deleterious to the organism. Its reported effects include growth inhibition in prokaryotes and plants |CITS: [Perdotti94][11472943]| and interference with energy production, lipid synthesis, and antioxidant defenses in mammalian brain |CITS: [11885778][17238006]|. Human inborn errors of glutathione metabolism that lead to |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| buildup result in metabolic acidosis, hemolytic anemia, neurological problems, and massive urinary excretion of |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| |CITS: [17397529][ 27477828]|., An ATP-dependent enzyme that hydrolyzes |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| to |FRAME: GLT|, |FRAME: EC-3.5.2.9|, has been known for a while, as it functions in the |FRAME: PWY-4041|. Until recently, the enzyme, which is encoded by the |FRAME: HS11319| gene, was thought to be a eukaryotic enzyme exclusively |CITS: [14993790]|. However, in 2017 a widespread prokaryotic enzyme that catalyzes the same reaction was discovered |CITS: [28830929]|. The trimeric enzyme is encoded by the |FRAME: G6382|, |FRAME: G6380|, and |FRAME: G6381| genes. Inactivation of any of these genes in |FRAME: TAX-1423| slowed growth and caused |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| accumulation in the cells.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-22651 "Roxarsone"| is an aromatic arsenical that was first synthesized in 1923. It has been used commercially since 1944 for prevention of coccidiosis in chickens and other farm animals. In 2010 nearly 90% of all broiler chickens in the U.S. were estimated to be treated with roxarsone |CITS: [27735790]|. Roxarsone is excreted from chickens as a mixture of unaltered and partially metabolized species. When the chicken litter is used as a fertilizer or moved into landfills, roxarsone and its metabolites are broken down to inorganic arsenic, and the resulting inorganic |FRAME: ARSENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-763| can be taken up by crop plants or enter the groundwater. In the U.S roxarsone production ceased in 2011. However, it is still produced and used in other countries., An enzyme that catalyzes the cleavage of the C-As bond of |FRAME: CPD-22656|, releasing |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, was described in 2014 from |FRAME: TAX-1501233|. The gene encoding the enzyme, |FRAME: G-80527|, was reported earlier from arsenic resistance operons, although its function has not been known at the time |CITS: [24821808]|. , The enzyme is a nonheme iron-dependent dioxygenase that cleaves the carbon-arsenic bond. The gene was cloned, and when expressed in an arsenic-hypersensitive strain of |FRAME: TAX-562| conferred |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|-demethylating activity and |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| resistance on its host. Purified recombinant ArsI catalyzes Fe<sup>2+</sup>-dependent |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| demethylation as well as cleavage of the C-As bond in several aromatic arsenicals, including |FRAME: CPD-22656|, |FRAME: CPD-24364| and |FRAME: CPD-22663| |CITS: [24821808]|., Once |FRAME: CPD0-2040| is released, it is converted spontaneously to |FRAME: CPD-763| at the cell's neutral pH, and can be exported out of the cell by |FRAME: EC-7.3.2.7|, or by a |FRAME: CPLX-7| such as |FRAME: EG12236| of |FRAME: TAX-562|., ArsI homologs are widely distributed in prokaryotes, including cyanobacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, and Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [24821808]|

The pathway depicted here is believed of less significance in planta. The formation of hydroxycinnamic acids, at least ferulic acid and sinapic acid has been demonstrated not to occur via the free phenylpropanoid acids (this pathway) but via the metabolic sequence described in the ferulate amd sinapate biosynthesis (|FRAME:PWY-5168|). However, the existence of this pathway cannot entirely ruled out since mutants defective in the key enzyme presumably generating ferulic acid and sinapic acid |CITS: [14729911]| still possess small amounts of corresponding hydroxycinnamic acid esters. , The free phenylpropanoid acid biosynthesis pathway generates simple hydroxycinnamic acids, containing the haracteristic C6C3 phenylpropane skeleton, as found in cinnamic acids (cinnamic acid, caffeic acid, sinapic acid) and their descendants in the lignin biosynthetic route, coumaryl alcohol, coniferyl alcohol, and sinapyl alcohol. Moreover, the phenylpropanoid pathway is the origin of more complex secondary compounds such as flavonoids, isoflavonoids and stilbenes, formed by condensation with phenylpropanoids and malonyl coenzyme A |CITS: [Dixon02]|., More compound classes derived from phenylpropanoids include sinapate esters, condendsed tannins, anthocyanins, coumarins, and benzoic acids. Some phenylpropanoids such as lignins, hydroxycinnamic acids and flavonoids are ubiquitous distributed in higher plants whereas other classes, like the isoflavonoids and stilbenes have a more restricted distribution within the plant kingdom. , The functions of phenylpropanoid vary as much as their structural composition. Phenylpropanoids serve as pigments, phytoalexins, phytoanticipins, UV protectants and signal molecules between plant and microbes, they can polymerize and fulfill functions of cell wall stability, provide structures for evapotranspiration (lignin) and protect plants against loss of water (cutin, suberin) |CITS: [Hahlbrock89]|., It has been argued for a long time that the enzymes of the phenylpropanoid pathway are organized in one or more enzyme complexes. Phenylpropanoid metabolism is largly unique to plants, and although quite complex one of the best-studied pathways in plants. There is now evidence for the coordinated expression of genes and enzymes, channeling intermediates into a controlled metabolic flux which triggers the subsequent pathways in a concerted manner |CITS: [15725058]|., Dixon's group |CITS: [15472080]| could demonstrate the existence of a multi-enzyme complex for the coordinated action of phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) and cinnamate-4-hydroxylase (C4H) controlling the flux of intermediates in the phenylpropanoid biosynthesis.
