Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Vernolates Vernolate| (vernolic acid) is an unusual fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain that contains a cis double bond at position 9 and an epoxy group at positions 12-13. This unusual fatty acid is found in high concentration (from 60 up to 75%) in seed oils of several |FRAME: TAX-4210| genera, including |FRAME: TAX-13695 Stokesia|, |FRAME: TAX-13753|, and |FRAME: TAX-13464| |CITS: [Gunstone54][7033990]|, as well as certain |FRAME: TAX-3977| species such as |FRAME: TAX-54672| |CITS: [Kleiman65]| and |FRAME: TAX-1441922| |CITS: [Spitzer96]|. Small amount of |FRAME: Vernolates| and related epoxy fatty acids are also found in |FRAME: TAX-4498| (white oat) |CITS: [18707115][Doehlert10]|., Epoxy fatty acids are valuable products and are widely used as plastisizers. The ability of the epoxy group to crosslink makes vernolate-containing oils useful in adhesives and coating materials such as paint |CITS: [Perdue86]|. It can also be used as a precursor of monomeric components of nylon-11 and nylon-12 |CITS: [Ayorinde89][Ayorinde97]|., Several types of enzymes have been reported to catalyze the synthesis of |FRAME: Vernolates| from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|., In |FRAME: TAX-72611| a fatty acid desaturase-like enzyme is responsible for the epoxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-6014|) |CITS: [9572738]|. , In the plant |FRAME: TAX-54672| two different enzymes have been described - a peroxygenase that can epoxidize free |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| to generate |FRAME: Vernolates| |CITS: [8267615][21784965]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6917|), and a cytochrome P450 enzyme (this pathway)., About This Pathway, The cytochrome P450 has been reported to act on |FRAME: Linoleoyl-groups "linoleate bound to phosphatidylcholine"| |CITS: [8489257]| as well as on free |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| |CITS: [8267615]|. A cDNA encoding the enzyme, CYP726A1, was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-54672| and heterologously expressed in yeast, confirming its proposed activity |CITS: [11842164]|. Its epoxygenase activity was demonstrated in an in vitro enzyme assay with the labeled substrate sn-1-palmitoyl-sn-2-[1[14C]linoleoyl-phosphatidylcholine. The epoxygenase activity was also demonstrated in an in vivo assay of the transgenic yeast cells when the growth medium was supplied with either |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| or |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| |CITS: [11842164]|.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme. Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones. The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length. However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain length. Quinones that contain a chain of 6 isoprenyl units are not common in bacteria, although they are quite common in yeast. Among the bacteria whose primary quinone contains a 6-isoprenyl chain are members of the Gram-negative genera |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [8674971]|, |FRAME: TAX-1016| and |FRAME: TAX-872|, as well as some members of the Gram-positive genus |FRAME:TAX-1279|. For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length distribution in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|.  , In |FRAME: TAX-4932| the initial addition of two isoprenyl units to form |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-710|, encoded by |FRAME: YJL167W|. An additional unit is added by |FRAME: YPL069C-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: YPL069C|), resulting in formation of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. The last enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-7572| (encoded by |FRAME: YBR003W|), which adds additional isoprenoid units to a maximal length of 6 units. When yeast COQ1 mutants are complemented with homologs from other organisms, ubiquinone biosynthesis is restored, but the tail lenghth of the quinone depends on the source of the enzyme |CITS: [9324242]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-8212|), and the synthase-dependent pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-8204|) |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-562| strains that express the O:1 antigen cause extraintestinal infections in humans |CITS: [4133095][ 49468][330559][334154][6208464]|. A study of over 60 E. coli O:1 strains revealed the existence of three LPS types, which were named |FRAME:CPD-24176 O:1A|, |FRAME: CPD-23791 O1B|, and |FRAME: CPD-24175 O1C| |CITS: [2426197]|. The |FRAME: CPD-24176 "O:1A antigen"| has a different composition, substituting a galactose residue with a mannose residue |CITS: [Jann92]|. The other two antigens only differ in the linkage of one of the rhamnose units |CITS: [1281148]|. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-23791 "Escherichia coli serotype O:1B O antigen repeat unit"|., The sequence of the O antigen biosynthetic cluster of an O:1B strain (|FRAME: ORG-57087|) was reported in 2010 |CITS: [20434495]|. The cluster contains 10 genes, encoding enzymes involved in |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| biosynthesis, an |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.14|, three glycosyltransferases, an O antigen repeat unit flippase and an O antigen polymerase., A 2014 study has shown that the O:42 serogroup of Salmonella produces an indentical O repeat unit to the Escherichia coli O:1B serogroup members, and that the gene clusters of the two organisms are very similar |CITS: [23848592]|., Since the O unit contains five sugar residues (and the first sugar is attached by a house keeping gene), one would have expected four glycosyltransferase genes in the cluster, but only three are present. It is assumed that the |FRAME: G-81132| gene encodes a rhamnosyltransferase that catalyzes two successive addtions of rhamnose residues in α-(1→2) linkage |CITS: [23848592]|.

General Background, Cell-cell communication in bacteria is accomplished through the exchange of extracellular signalling molecules called autoinducers. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., Autoinducer systems depend on two main components - the autoinducer and its receptor, which also functions as an autoinducer-dependent transcriptional regulator that binds DNA immediately upstream of the genes that are controlled., Autoinducer systems have been implicated in regulation of various systems. For example, |FRAME: G-11135|/luxR of |FRAME: TAX-668| regulate bioluminescence, luxM/luxN of |FRAME: TAX-669| regulate bioluminescence and polyhydroxybutyrate biosynthesis, |FRAME: G-11138|/lasR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates virulence factors, |FRAME: G-11136|/rhlR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates rhamnolipid synthesis as well as virulence factors, and |FRAME: G-11137|/TraR of |FRAME: TAX-358| regulates plasmid conjugal transfer |CITS: [8905097]|., Several types of autoinducers are known. Gram-negative bacteria typically use |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "acyl-homoserine lactones"|, known as type AI-1, as their autoinducers. The first autoinducer to be discovered was |FRAME: CPD-10780|, an AI-1 type compound from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [7236614]|. Many variants of AI-1 type inducers exist, differing from each other in the composition of the acyl moiety. In some cases, one organism may produce multiple types of acyl homoserine lactone type autoinducers, each produced by a dedicated synthase., A few examples are |FRAME: CPD-10781| from |FRAME: TAX-669|, |FRAME: CPD-10782| from |FRAME: TAX-358|,, |FRAME: CPD-10783| and |FRAME: CPD-10784| from |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: CPD-10780| and, |FRAME: CPD-10785| from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [8905097]|., Another very common family of autoinducers include compounds produced from |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|, which was first described from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-669|, in which it is used to control luciferase expression |CITS:[7984107][9990077]|. AI-2 type compounds are produced by a remarkably wide variety of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, leading to the proposal that AI-2 is a 'universal' signal that functions in interspecies cell-to-cell communication |CITS: [11544353][18803868]|., About This Pathway, The precursor of AI-2, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|, is synthesized by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7755|, in a reaction that is also a step in the |FRAME: PWY-6151| pathway (SAM cycle). The enzyme converts |FRAME: CPD-564| to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| in a reaction that also produces |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|. Within the SAM cycle, the main product of the enzyme is the former compound. However, in organisms that produce an AI-2 autoinducer, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE| is of major importance as it appears to be the last enzyme-generated precursor for AI-2, and is converted to the functional autoinducer in a series of chemical modifications without the help of any known enzyme., The exact nature of the chemical transformations depends on the species. In most pathogenic bacteria that form AI-2 the spontaneous transformations include cyclyzation to |FRAME: CPD-10773| and hydration to the final autoinducer |FRAME: CPD-10774|. This form of the autoinducer, which was first characterized from |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS: [15350213]|, turned out to be different from the form that was initially described from |FRAME: TAX-669| (see below). It is recognized by the |FRAME:YNEA-MONOMER| periplasmic binding protein, which is a part of a dedicated ABC transporter |CITS: [15350213]|., |FRAME: TAX-135623| form a different form of the autoinducer. In those organisms, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE| appears to form a different stereoisomer, namely |FRAME: CPD-10775|, which hydrates to |FRAME: CPD-10776| and forms a complex with a borate ion to form |FRAME: CPD-10777| |CITS: [11823863][18803868]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6154|). The mechanism that controls which stereoisomer is formed is still not understood.

Summary: General Background, Inorganic reduced sulfur compounds serve as electron donors in many phototrophic and chemotrophic bacteria |CITS: [9328649]|. Sulfide oxidation plays an important role in the global sulfur cycle by reoxidizing the sulfide produced by sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic habitats., Phototrophic purple and green sulfur-oxidizing bacteria use the sulfur compounds as electron donors for reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation during photolithotrophic growth. Light energy is used to transfer electrons from the sulfur compounds to levels found in highly reducing electron carriers such as |FRAME:Ferredoxins| and |FRAME:NADP| |CITS: [2663079]|. Similarly, non-sulfur purple bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1061| and cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-54310| are also able to use sulfide as the electron source for anoxygenic photosynthesis., The purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| carries out the complete eight-electron oxidation of sulfide to sulfate. The process involves the formation of sulfur globules as obligate intermediates |CITS: [9695921]|. Since the initial sulfide oxidation system is periplasmic, the globules are deposited in the periplasm |CITS: [9560425]|. The sulfur in the globules occurs as sulfur chains |CITS: [11782519]| enclosed by a protein envelope |CITS: [7575095]| (see |FRAME: P222-PWY|). , In the process of further oxidation, the sulfur in the globules is reduced inside the bacterial cell to a thiol form, which is transported into the cytoplasm and oxidized by a cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation system. , There may be several oxidation systems, employed by different organisms. , About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-1049| the initial oxidation of sulfide to sulfur is most likely performed by a periplasmic |FRAME: EC-1.8.5.4|, which mediates the transfer of electrons from sulfide directly into the quinone pool (this enzyme is described in the pathway |FRAME:P222-PWY|). This process generates the sulfur globules mentioned above. The sulfur in the globules is then reduced again to either |FRAME: CPD-846| or perthiols, which enter the cytoplasm, and the sulfur is transferred to an L-cysteine residue of the |FRAME: Rhd|, forming a perthiol. The sulfur is then transferred first to an L-cysteine residue in a second carrier protein, |FRAME: TusA TusA|, and then to an L-cysteine residue in the |FRAME: DsrE-Protein "DsrE sulfur-carrier protein"|, a part of the |FRAME:CPLX-8192 "DsrEFH complex|. DsrE in turn transfers the sulfur to the |FRAME: CPLX-8190 "DsrC protein"| |CITS: [24648525]|., DsrC has two active L-cysteine residues. The residue located closer to the C-terminal receives the sulfur atom in the form of a perthiol |CITS: [18952098][22815818]|. The |FRAME: CPLX-8189| (or potentially the DsrK component) oxidzes the molecule, forming |FRAME: DsrC-trisulfides| |CITS: [20952577]|. At this point, a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME:CPLX-9518| oxidizes the sulfur using 3 water molecules, releasing the sulfur in the form of |FRAME: SO3| |CITS: [9695921]|., It should be noted that |FRAME:CPLX-7133|, the enzyme that oxidizes the sulfur, is also present in sulfite reducing bacteria, where it functions in the opposite direction (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|) |CITS: [18826437]|. Sulfur oxidation activity of sulfite reductase was first suggested by Peck et al in 1974 |CITS: [4526215]|, and was investigated in |FRAME: TAX-1049| by Schedel et al, who concluded that the physiological role of the enzyme in this organism is "at all probablity the oxidation of sulfide and/or elemental sulfur to sulfite" |CITS: [Schedel79]|., A later study showed that a sulfite-reductase-defective |FRAME: TAX-1049| mutant, while able to oxidize sulfide to sulfur with specific rates comparable to those of the wild-type, was unable to oxidize the intracellularly stored sulfur, confirming a role of the enzyme in the later stages of the process |CITS: [9695921]|., A similar enzyme has also been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-36861| |CITS: [486494]|.

Summary: General Background, The catecholamines |FRAME: DOPAMINE|, |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| (norepinephrine), and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| (epinephrine) function as neurotransmitters and hormones. They have important physiological regulatory roles and are involved in the development of many diseases. Their biosynthesis from |FRAME: TYR| is shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-301|. Overall, approximately half of the |FRAME: DOPAMINE| produced in the body is not converted to |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and is degraded to inactive metabolites (in |CITS: [9360553]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY6666-2|). Although the degradation of endogenous catecholamines has been well studied, many inaccuracies based on early studies still remain in the literature. For example, |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| degradation has been depicted as a series of reactions, including oxidative deamination, that form |FRAME: CPD-11879|, followed by O-methylation to form |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE|. However, updated pathways are shown in |CITS: [15317907]| and here., Catecholamines are biosynthesized in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells, including the central nervous system, sympathetic nerves, adrenal medulla, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys. They have previously been considered to be metabolized after their release from cells. They are now believed to be largely metabolized in the cells in which they are biosynthesized. In addition, intracellular catecholamines stored in vesicles were believed to be released extracellularly only upon stimulation. It is now thought that vesicular catecholamines are in a dynamic equilibrium with the cytoplasm. Outward leakage from vesicles is countered by active transport back into vesicles by monoamine transporters. The small amount of catecholamines remaining in the cytoplasm are a major source of metabolites. Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|., The metabolism of the transient (and toxic) aldehyde intermediates of catecholamine metabolism |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPHENYLGLYCOLALDEHYDE| (this pathway) and |FRAME: 34-DIHYDROXYPHENYLACETALDEHYDE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY6666-2|) is dependent upon the presence (in |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE|) or absence (in |FRAME: DOPAMINE|) of the β-hydroxyl group. Its absence in |FRAME: DOPAMINE| and |FRAME: 34-DIHYDROXYPHENYLACETALDEHYDE| favors oxidation by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Its presence in |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE|, |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPHENYLGLYCOLALDEHYDE| favors reduction by aldehyde reductase, or aldose reductase. Thus, |FRAME: DOPAMINE| is preferentially converted to an acid metabolite, and |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| are preferentially converted to an alcohol metabolite. Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|., About This Pathway, The major route of |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE| production from |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| is currently believed to involve initial oxidative deamination to the unstable aldehyde intermediate |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPHENYLGLYCOLALDEHYDE| and reduction to |FRAME: CPD-11878| by aldehyde reductase (alcohol dehydrogenase) |CITS: [3466164]| (or aldose reductase as stated in |CITS: [15317907]|). These reactions occur mainly in neuronal tissue, whereas the O-methylation of |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: CPD-11878| occurs in extraneuronal tissues. |FRAME: CPD-11878| is O-methylated to |FRAME: CPD-11497| and this alcohol is dehydrogenated to the unstable aldehyde intermediate |FRAME: CPD-11876| which is then dehydrogenated to |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE|, the major end product of |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| degradation. Alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase play the major role in |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE| production in liver. |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE| is excreted in urine. Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907] [12649306]|., An alternative route following the oxidative deamination of |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| to |FRAME: 34-DIHYDROXYPHENYLACETALDEHYDE| is its dehydrogenation to |FRAME: CPD-11879|, which was believed for many years to be the main route. It is now considered by |CITS: [15317907]| to be quantitatively insignificant under normal conditions and |FRAME: CPD-11878| is the main product (see above). Consequently, the O-methylation of |FRAME: CPD-11879| to |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE| is no longer considered to be the main source of |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE|. Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|., Two minor routes that contribute to |FRAME: VANILLYL_MANDELATE| production are via the O-methylation of |FRAME: NOREPINEPHRINE| and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| to |FRAME: CPD-11875| and |FRAME: CPD-11877|, respectively. These compounds are oxidatively deaminated to the unstable aldehyde intermediate |FRAME: CPD-11876| |CITS: [3996536]|. This compound may also be reduced to |FRAME: CPD-11497| in a minor reverse reaction. Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|., In addition to the above pathways, the sulfates of |FRAME: CPD-11875|, |FRAME: CPD-11877| and |FRAME: CPD-11497| can be formed by |FRAME: CPLX6666-1| (EC 2.8.2.1) in cells that contain this activity. Glucuronides of these compounds may also be formed and are either excreted in bile, or they may enter the circulation and be excreted in urine (reviewed in |CITS: [12649306]|) (not shown).

Summary: Chlorobenzenes are used in the production of pesticides, dyes, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, rubbers, plastics,, and electric goods |CITS: [11472925]|. Their occurrence in the environment is widespread and they are, found in the atmosphere |CITS: [10864157]|, water |CITS: [3314709][16157172]|, soil |CITS: [17988797][2695324]|,, sediments |CITS: [15694470]|, vegetables |CITS:[16002141]|, and animals |CITS: [15325147]|., Chlorobenzenes are of great concern because of their toxicity, persistence and accumulation in the food chain,, and many of them have been declared, priority pollutants, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)., An important chlrobenzene compound, |FRAME: O-DICHLOROBENZENE|, is degraded via |FRAME: CPD-10626|., This catechol is degraded to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| in a modified ortho cleavage pathway., A few bacterial species were reported to be able to utilize |FRAME: O-DICHLOROBENZENE| as the sole source of carbon., These include an unidentified Pseudomonas sp. |CITS: [3281582]|, |FRAME: TAX-65067| |CITS: [1987135]|,, |FRAME: TAX-393999| |CITS: [11526005]| and |FRAME: TAX-1288| |CITS: [Ziagova07]|., The |FRAME: TAX-65067| enzymes catalyzing this pathway have been studied and characterized |CITS: [2013566], [10390818]|.

It has been said that no biological compound functions in as many different types of biological reactions as |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (known as SAM or AdoMet). It is probably second only to ATP in the variety of reactions for which it serves as a cofactor. SAM is found in all living organisms, and fulfils three important roles:, *  In transmethylation, SAM is the principal biological methyl donor., *  In transsulfuration, the sulfur atom of the SAM is converted via a series of enzymatic steps to cysteine, a precursor of taurine and glutathione, a major cellular anti-oxidant., *  In polyamine biosynthesis, SAM is the donor of aminopropyl groups., The structure of SAM was first elucidated by Cantoni in 1951 |CITS: [Cantoni51]|. The key to SAM's activity lies in the presence of the high energy sulfonium ion, which activates each of the attached carbons toward nucleophilic attack. In most cases, SAM reacts by transfer of the S-methyl group to a long list of possible acceptors in transmethylation reactions., SAM is synthesized in the cytosol of every cell from |FRAME: MET| and |FRAME: ATP|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.6|. In animals, up to half of the daily intake of |FRAME: MET| is converted to SAM., In this unusual reaction, the adenosyl moiety of ATP is transferred to methionine, forming a sulfonium ion which is a high energy reagent that can easily transfer its methyl group to a large variety of acceptor substrates including nucleic acids, proteins, phospholipids, biologic amines, and a long list of small molecules |CITS: [Lu00]|.

|FRAME: CPD0-1192 "Poly-β-1,6-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine"| (PNAG) is an exopolysaccharide that is a key component of the biofilm matrix of many pathogenic bacteria |CITS: [15090514][15601723][18359807][29684093]|., PNAG is formed in |FRAME: TAX-562| by |FRAME: CPLX0-7994| (PgaCD), which forms the polymer from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| precursors |CITS: [15090514]| and transports it across the inner membrane., Once in the priplasm, PNAG is partially deacetylated and hydrolyzed by |FRAME: G6530-MONOMER PgaB|, an outer membrane lipoprotein. PgaB also interacts with the outer membrane porin |FRAME: G6531-MONOMER PgaA|, promoting the export of deacetylated PNAG across the outer membrane |CITS: [26957546]|., Formation of PNAG is regulated by the second messenger |FRAME: C-DI-GMP| (c-di-GMP) |CITS: [19460094]|. c-di-GMP stimulates PgaC-PgaD interaction and complex stability. c-di-GMP binds to PgaCD with high affinity, increasing the enzyme's velocity but not its affinity for substrate. c-di-GMP is an allosteric activator and stimulates the glycosyltransferase activity of PgaCD approximately 20-fold in vitro |CITS: [23202856]|. The binding of c-di-GMP to PgaCD increases in the presence of UDP-GlcNAc |CITS: [23202856]|, pgaC and pgaD mutants show reduced biofilm formation and do not accumulate PNAG in a crsA background compared to wild-type |CITS: [15090514], [18359807]|. PgaC contains 4 predicted trans-membrane domains plus 2 membrane-associated domains; PgaD contains 2 predicted trans-membrane domains. PgaC also contains 2 catalytic domains predicted to be in the cytoplasm. The N and C-termini of both proteins are predicted to be in the cytoplasm |CITS: [15090514], [23202856]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7079 Sakuranetin| is a phenylpropanoid-derived flavonoid phytoalexin that belongs to a biosynthetic diverse group of compounds involved in the self-defense system of rice against fungal attacks. Other phytoalexins of importance in rice are diterpenes such as |FRAME:CPD-7092|, |FRAME:CPD-7093| and |FRAME:CPD-7094| |CITS: [15388982]| (see |FRAME:PWY-2981|). Sakuranetin possesses antifungal activity against |FRAME: TAX-318829|, the agent of blast, a fungal rice disease causing yield losses up to 50% worldwide. This activity is significantly higher than that of its direct precursor naringenin |CITS: [KODAMA92]|., Sakuranetin is a highly inducible compound being formed after UV-irradiation |CITS: [KODAMA92][12596847]|, methionine application and wounding |CITS: [10803956]|, jasmonic acid, CuCl2 and the phytotoxin |FRAME:CPD-7081|, |CITS: [10975503]|, treatment with (-)-enantiomers of jasmonate-amino acid-conjugates, e.g. |FRAME: CPD-11235| |CITS: [9013895]| and after fungal infection |CITS: [12596847]| |CITS: [15907692]|. However, sakuranetin is not restricted to rice and has also been found in other plants executing a similar function as a phytoalexin |CITS: [12943774]|. , About This Pathway, Sakuranetin is synthesized by |FRAME: MONOMER-11973| from |FRAME: NARINGENIN-CMPD| using S-adenosyl-L-methionine as methyl group donor. The 7-O-methylation is responsible for the toxicity againt the fungus since naringenin itself does not exhibit significant anti-fungal activities |CITS: [KODAMA92]|. It has been demonstrated that introducing a methyl group to the 7-O-position of the flavonoid A-ring of potential phytoalexins such as |FRAME:CPD-7096| considerably increased their fungicidal activity |CITS: [8987602]|., The naringenin 7-O-methyltransferase (NOMT) catalyzing the formation of sakuranetin has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-4530| and characterized with regard to physical properties and kinetic parameters |CITS: [8651913][10814825][22895058]|. Besides naringenin other flavanones such as luteolin and apigenin (see |FRAME:PWY-5060|) were accepted as substrates with comparable turnover rates but isoflavanones, dihydroflavonols and phenylpropanoid acids, such as caffeic acid, were not |CITS: [10814825]|., The degradation of sakuranetin has been far less investigated. The metabolism of sakuranetin by the filamentous fungi |FRAME: TAX-4853| yielded both naringenin and its 4'-sulfate derivative, suggesting that the fungus is able to demethylate the 7-O-position of the flavanone A ring followed by sulfation of the 4'-position in ring B |CITS: [12576658]|.

Pine species growing in the Western USA emit volatiles such as |FRAME: CPD-13614| (previously referred to as MBO, for 2-methyl-3-buten-2-ol ). This five carbon alcohol is released in large enough quantities that affect the ozone layer and impact global warming |CITS: [11469599]|., The biosynthesis of MBO has been studied mostly due to its effect on the immediate atmosphere. It has been demonstrated that MBO is primarily formed from |FRAME: CPD-4211| (DMAPP) that is generated via the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"|. The enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-4211| to MBO, |FRAME: MONOMER-16830|, has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-268869| |CITS: [21504898]|. The enzyme also produces small amounts of |FRAME: CPD-9436|. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that the enzyme belongs to the class of gymnosperm monoterpene synthases (TPS-d1) |CITS: [21504898]|.

Summary: This pathway for the anaerobic biosynthesis of the unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-17910| branches from the pathway leading to saturated fatty acids at |FRAME: Beta-hydroxydecanoyl-ACPs|. , Only bacteria can produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically, and thus the key enzymes of this pathway (particularly |FRAME: EG10273 FabA|) have been targeted for development of new antibacterial agents |CITS: [22188524][23174186]|., The pathway was originally characterized in the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|. In that organism, two dehydratases, |FRAME: EG10273 FabA| and |FRAME: EG11284 FabZ|, function for the most part interchangeably in converting |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP "(3R)-3-hydroxyacyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| of various chain lengths, saturated or unsaturated, to the corresponding |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-ACP "trans-2-enoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| forms. However, |FRAME: EG10273 FabA| alone has the unique ability of converting some of the trans form |FRAME: Trans-D2-decenoyl-ACPs "(2E)-dec-2-enoyl-[acp]"| produced to the cis form |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"|., While the trans form can be reduced and elongated leading to saturated fatty acids, the cis-form cannot be reduced. Instead it serves directly as a substrate for the condensing enzyme, |FRAME: EG10274 FabB|, producing a product that can be acted on by the regular fatty acid elongation enzymes, resulting in an unsaturated acid with a chain lengthened by two carbon atoms. As might be predicted, mutant strains unable to produce active FabA are unable to make unsaturated fatty acids, but make a normal complement of saturated fatty acids., It should be noted that only α- and γ-proteobacteria have the fabA and fabB genes. Other bacterial species that produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically possess alternative enzymes, such as |FRAME: EF_RS01435| and |FRAME: EF_RS01430| in |FRAME: TAX-1351| |CITS: [15194690]| and |FRAME: G-44020| in |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [12237320]|., Repeated cycling of these four elongation reactions eventually lead to the unsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247| that are incorporated into various lipids (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6282| and |FRAME: PWY-5973|).

Names: enediyne-induced DNA damage // DNA cleavage by NCS // DNA cleavage by neocarzinostatin
Summary: |FRAME: Enediyne-Antibiotics "Enediyne antibiotics"| are bacterial natural products characterized by either a nine- or ten-membered ring containing a conjugated system of two carbon-carbon triple bonds separated by a carbon-carbon double bond. Most of the enediyne antibiotics are protected within the producing organism by a dedicated protein to which they bind non-covalently. Following delivery to a target organism, the enediyne-containing molecule, known as the chromophore, is released from the protective protein |CITS: [19747549]|. The chromophore intercalates into the target cell's DNA within the minor groove of the DNA double helix |CITS: [6456758][ 2523731]|. The antibiotic is activated either by reducing compounds or by a spontaneous process, leading to cycloaromatization of the enediyne and formation of a 1,4-benzenoid diradical. The diradical is perfectly positioned to strip hydrogen atoms from the sugar phosphate backbone of adjacent strands of DNA, generating a radical deoxyribose sugar., Three main attack sites (C5', C4', and C1') have been characterized. In each case the deoxyribose radical reacts with an oxygen molecule, forming a hydroperoxide radical. Reduction of the compound results in release of a water molecule , leaving an unstable hydroxy compound that decomposes, resulting in a break in the DNA backbone. The different radicals that are formed (depending on the attack site) resolve into different final products, but all lead to DNA strand breaks (as well as abasic sites)., The |FRAME: Enediyne-Antibiotics "enediyne antibiotics"| are extremely potent. Some of them, such as the |FRAME: CPD-27409|, the |FRAME: Calicheamicins calicheamicins|, and the |FRAME: Esperamicins esperamicins|, are among the most potent cytotoxic molecules known. In order to demonstrate the chemistry of the DNA strand breaking process we have selected one such drug, |FRAME: CPD-16912 neocarzinostatin| (NCS). This pathway shows the transformations that produce the diradical and its interaction with the DNA substrate, as summarized by |CITS: [8667354]|. The mechanism by which the |FRAME: CPD-16912| exerts its DNA-damaging properties was first suggested in 1987 |CITS: [Myers87]|. The reductive conditions at the target result in the binding of a thiol molecule, causing reduction of the epoxide and triggering a Bergman cyclization that forms a benzyne radical |CITS: [2957284]|. It has been shown that at least 80% of the DNA cleavage caused by NCS leads to the 5'-aldehyde of A and T residues selectively, indicating the NCS attacks the C-5' position preferentially |CITS: [6227335]|. The other 20% result from hydrogen atom abstraction at C-4' |CITS: [Saito89]| and C-1' |CITS: [Kappen90]|., Like other enediyne antibiotics, NCS, which is secreted by |FRAME: TAX-1897| |CITS: [14326086]|, consists of two components - a |FRAME: CPD-16912 chromophore| |CITS: [Edo85]| and a 113 amino acid protein, named neocarzinostatin |CITS: [8369747]|, to which the chromophore is tightly and non-covalently bound |CITS: [1834636]|., The DNA-cleaving activity of NCS made it a drug of interest for cancer treatment. Data from early clinical trials conducted in Japan suggested that neocarzinostatin had activity in the treatment of patients with acute leukemia |CITS: [144198][143343]| and in the therapy of selected solid tumors including carcinoma of the stomach, colon, bladder, and pancreas |CITS: [130432][141012][6444585]|. However early phase I clinical trials were not promising, due to NCS's severe toxicity and bone marrow suppression |CITS: [151899][159119]|.

Summary: The phenylpropanoid biosynthesis (see |FRAME:PWY1F-467|, |FRAME:PWY-361|) generates a multitude of compounds involved in structural integrity, plant defense and interactions with the biotic and abiotic environment |CITS:[20035037]|. It is also the gateway to a number of phenylpropanoid derivatives, for instance flavonoids which fulfill important roles in the reproduction and survival of plants. The model plant Arabidopsis thaliana represents the most thoroughly researched plant in terms of elucidating the biosynthetic routes, enzymes, encoding genes and regulatory aspects of the diverse compound classes originating from the basic phenylpropanoids |CITS:[Fraser11] [Saito13]|. Descendants of this compounds, e.g. simple anthocyanins are often further modified by sequential hydroxylation, methylation, glucosylation and acylation which often results in complex anthocyanin structures such as the main anthocyanin found in Arabidopsis, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16540| |CITS:[11830144]|. Such modifications are discussed as metabolic events which may alter light-absorption properties, stabilize pigments, effect water solubility, lower enzymatic degradation and enhance their bioavailability in diet |CITS:[Tanaka06] [Strack94]|., The pathway depicted above describes the biosynthetic route of this compound also referred to as A11 according to the classification of |CITS:[15807784]|. Although the various steps leading to A11 have been enzymatically characterized and the reaction sequence is supported by experimental data certain modifications may still occur in a different order, for instance the xylosylation |CITS:[21899608]| or early acylation |CITS:[17425720]| of |FRAME:CPD1F-766| which is illustrated by the fork in the pathway which eventually merges into the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16536|. Nevertheless, in general the biosynthetic route to A11 is thought to proceed in a defined order rather than in a network of reactions |CITS:[17425720]|., Oftentimes enzymes catalyzing modification steps in secondary metabolism are characterized by broad substrate specificity and may not be identifiable through sequence homology which requires variegated approaches including transcriptomics and metabolomics analyses |CITS:[17425720] [15807784] [17292360] [15908604]|. The xylosylation at C-2" and the coumaryolation at C-6" appear to be the first modifications of |FRAME:CPD1F-766| because |FRAME:CPD-7138| is not a suitable acceptor for the corresponding cyanidin 2"-xylosyltransferase |CITS:[21899608]| and cyanidin 6"-coumaroyltransferase |CITS:[17425720]|. Following the 5-O-glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-16536| |CITS:[15807784]| malonysation of the 5-Oglucose moiety is next because the cyanidin 5-O-glucoside 6"-O-malonyltransferase (5MaT) does not accept more advanced modified cyanide where the coumaroyl group has been further glucosylated |CITS:[17292360]|. In vivo experiments with Arabidopsis mutants with a knocked out serine carboxypeptidase-like (SCPL) enzyme that catalyzes sinapoylation indicate that this is the second to last step in the A11 formation |CITS:[17600138]| which biosynthesis is finalized by an acylglucose dependent anthocyanin glucosyltransferase |CITS:[23298714]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-354| is the activated sugar nucleotide form of |FRAME: CPD-15587|, an unusual sugar that has been identified as a constituent of only a few microbial polysaccharides. In rare cases extracellular polysaccharides are found that consist of only |FRAME: CPD-15587|. This has been described in |FRAME: TAX-41899| strain DSM 6535 |CITS: [9203339]|, and |FRAME: TAX-714|. The latter is a nonmotile, Gram-negative bacterium that has been implicated in the etiology and pathogenesis of localized juvenile periodontitis, adult periodontitis, and severenonoral human infections |CITS: [12444986]|., |FRAME: CPD-354| is synthesized from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| in two steps. In the first step a water molecule is removed by |FRAME: CPLX-7273|, generating |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE|, which is reduced in the second step by |FRAME: MONOMER-12852|, producing |FRAME: CPD-354|., A gene cluster associated with the biosynthesis of this polysaccharide (also known as serotype a-specific antigen) was cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-714| SUNYaB 75 (serotype a) |CITS: [11118626]|., The genes encoding these enzymes have been subcloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the proteins were purified and shown to catalyze the reactions in vitro. The nature of the product was verified by reversed-phase, HPLC |CITS: [12444986]|.

The cpk gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-100226| encodes the enzymes that are involved in the biosynthesis of the unusual polyketide alkaloid |FRAME: CPD-19921|., For some time the gene cluster was considered cryptic, as its product was unknown. It was reported in 2010 that the cluster results in production of a yellow pigment and is associated with antimicrobial activity. The pigment production depended on the medium composition and did not occur in the presence of glucose |CITS: [20447997][20924201]|. Structural characterization of that yellow pigment was not performed at the time, and it is now thought that it is different from the one described here (it is most likely a glutamate adduct of an intermediate in the pathway, which has been named coelimycin P2)., Further progress in understanding the role of the cpk gene cluster was obtained by generating a strain missing this cluster and comparing its metabolite profiles to a similar strain that contained the cluster. It was found that the product of the clustrer is a yellow pigment that contains an extremely unusual 1,5-oxathiocan-2-one ring system. The compound was named |FRAME: CPD-19921| |CITS: [Gomez-Escribano12]|., The pathway starts with a type I polyketide synthase (PKS) composed of three sububnits, encoded by the |FRAME: SCO6275|, |FRAME: SCO6274|, and |FRAME: SCO6273| genes. While a part of the PKS-encoding genes was discovered in the 1990s |CITS: [8020754][9418255]|, most of the gene cluster was discovered only when the full |FRAME: TAX-100226| genome was sequenced. Together the three subunits comprise six modules that contain a total of 28 domains. Analysis of the module and domain organization suggests that the enzyme forms a δ-hydroxy thioester, attached to the acyl carrier protein domain within the final module, from six molecules of malonyl-CoA and five equivalents of NADPH |CITS: [17009021]|. Instead of a typical thioesterase, a thioester reductase domain at the C-terminus of the last module catalyzes the NADH-dependent reductive cleavage of the product, releasing the unsaturated hydroxyaldehyde |FRAME: CPD-19920| |CITS: [Awodi17]|. However, a type II thioesterase encoded by scoT is absolutely required for the functionality of the PKS, as it removes acyl residues blocking the extension module |CITS: [24660171]|., The product of the PKS is modified by up to ten tailoring reactions to form |FRAME: CPD-19921|. The enzymes involved have not been characterized biochemically, and their function is proposed only based on their sequence. However, isotope labeling experiments suppor the proposed pathway diagram. Addition of |FRAME: CPD-9175|, which results in the opening of the two epoxy rings, has been shown using deuterium-labeled substrate. Incorporation of molecular oxygen into the keto group of 1,5-oxathiocan-2-one ring was demonstrated using 18O2., The cluster is believed to be regulated by the γ-butyrolactone |FRAME: CPD-19918|, as a pair of γ-butyrolactone related genes, scbR and |FRAME: SCO6266|, are located next to cpk cluster |CITS: [15813737]|.

Summary: |FRAME: MORPHINE "Morphine"| is an alkaloid found only in opium poppy (|FRAME: TAX-3469|) and related species (e.g., |FRAME: TAX-215229|). Opium alkaloids, including morphine, are known to act as chemical defense compounds to protect opium poppy against various herbivores., In response to stress, the capsules of opium poppies immediately metabolize morphine to dimeric morphine species, called |FRAME: CPD-12315| and |FRAME: CPD-12316|. These compounds bind to the cell wall polysaccharide pectins, resulting in cross-linking pectins to each other through bismorphine bridges and leading to resistance against hydrolysis by pectinase |CITS:[11498543][12880320]|., Morphine is an extremely potent opiate analgesic psychoactive drug in mammals, due to its strong binding to the opioid receptors, a group of G-protein coupled receptors. Morphine and its precursor |FRAME: CODEINE| are used extensively in medicine to relieve severe or agonizing pain and suffering. Although pharmaceutical synthesis of these compounds has been successful for many years, a commercially feasible total chemical synthesis of morphine has not been achieved, and these compounds are still extracted from the plants. That fact has stimulated recent interests in dissecting the biosynthetic pathway, and the possible development of a combined chemical and enzymatic synthesis alternative., The pathway was best studied in |FRAME: TAX-3469|. The accumulation of morphine in the poppy occurs in laticifer cells, but many of the pathway enzymes and their corresponding gene transcripts are localized in several cell types., The biosynthesis of morphine and related alkaloids in opium poppy occurs via a multistep pathway beginning with the amino acid |FRAME: TYR|. |FRAME: TYR| is converted to |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| in 7 steps (see |FRAME: PWY-3581|). |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| is then converted to its stereomer |FRAME: R-RETICULINE|, a unique case among the many benzylisoquinone pathways that are known. The conversion occurs via a |FRAME: 12-DEHYDRORETICULINIUM| intermediate, and is catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-19543 "reticuline epimerase"|, a fusion protein between a cytochrome P450 (CYP) and an aldo-keto reductase (AKR) |CITS: [26113639][26147354]|., |FRAME: R-RETICULINE| is converted to |FRAME: 7-O-ACETYLSALUTARIDINOL| in three steps. Although an enzyme for the conversion from |FRAME: 7-O-ACETYLSALUTARIDINOL| to |FRAME: CPD-7710| has been reported |CITS: [Fisinger07]|, |FRAME: CPD-7710| can also be formed spontaneously. At this point there is a potential split in the pathway - depending on the order in which enzymes act, the pathway can proceed either via |FRAME: CODEINONE| and |FRAME: CODEINE|, or via |FRAME: CPD-7713| and |FRAME: MORPHINONE|. Kinetic analysis of the enzymes suggests that the |FRAME: CODEINONE| route is active in vivo |CITS: [20228795]|., , All enzymes characterized for this pathway show high substrate specificities and stereo-selectivities. In addition, all four oxidoreductases of this pathway are strictly NADPH-dependent, and NADH cannot take its place. , The last two enzymes of the pathway to be discovered were |FRAME: MONOMER-15552| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15553|, both members of the Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase family |CITS: [20228795]|., The full pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-7710|, including the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| precursor, was engineered in yeast in 2015, utilizing 21 enzyme activities from plants, mammals, bacteria, and yeast itself |CITS: [26272907]|. A later report established production of |FRAME: CPD-7710| by stepwise culture of four engineered |FRAME: TAX-562| strains, affording a yield 300-fold higher than that obtained in the yeast host |CITS: [26847395]|., The biosynthetic morphine pathway, that was believed to be restricted to certain members of poppies |CITS: [facchini2005]|, has been reported from human neuroblastoma cells |CITS: [15937106]|. Injection of |FRAME: S-NORLAUDANOSOLINE| intraperitoneally into mice followed by analysis of urine metabolites revealed the presence of |FRAME: SALUTARIDINE|. Similarly, injection of |FRAME: SALUTARIDINOL| led to detection of |FRAME: CPD-7710| in the urine, and injection of |FRAME: CPD-7710| resulted in traces of |FRAME: MORPHINE| in the urine |CITS: [20421505]|. However, this claim is still controversial. The earlier part of the pathway, leading to production of |FRAME: S-RETICULINE|, appears to be different in humans (see |FRAME: PWY-6133|).

Avenacins are triterpene glucosides which act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents conferring resistance against soil-borne pathogens and influencing the development of close neighbors |CITS:[10536024] [16995908]|. The occurrence of the phytoalexic avenacins appears to be restricted to the genus Avena which is an expression of a highly specialized defense biochemistry |CITS:[Hostettmann95]|. In general, triterpenes are valued compounds with a wide range of commercial applications and because of that in the focus of metabolic engineering. One of the major goals is to re-introduce lost traits of resistance into cultivated crops |CITS:[22639586]|., As a general rule genes in plant biochemical pathways, unlike bacterial biochemical pathways, have been regarded as unlinked. However, the avenacin biosynthesis appears to be carried out by an avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster which implies a high degree of coordination regarding avenacin synthesis, transport and sequestration, all of which must be precisely orchestrated in time and space between different cell organelles and compartments |CITS:[21876149] [15148404] [21443624] [20040536]|., |FRAME:CPD-16599 Avenacin A-2| (this pathway) is another major form of avenacins found in the roots of the genus Avena which also harbors |FRAME:CPD-10678| (see |FRAME:PWY-7473|) and |FRAME:CPD-16597| and |FRAME:CPD-16598| |CITS:[Crombie86a]|. In contrast to the |FRAME:CPD-402| acylated |FRAME:CPD-10678| the triterpenoid saponin |FRAME:CPD-16599| is acylated with |FRAME:BENZOATE|. The decisive step in the pathway of |FRAME:CPD-16599| biosynthesis is the acylation of |FRAME:CPD-16623| with |FRAME:BENZOATE| which is provided through the acyl-donor |FRAME:CPD-12630| (see |FRAME:PWY-7468|). The catalyzing enzyme is a serine carboxypeptidase-like (SCPL) protein (SCPL1) encoded by SAD7, also a member of the avenacin genetic cluster, which can utilize |FRAME:CPD-16600| (see |FRAME:PWY-7473|), |FRAME:CPD-12835| (see |FRAME:PWY-7475|) and |FRAME:CPD-12630| (this pathway) as acyl-donor, in the latter case resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16599| |CITS:[19684243]|.

Summary: De novo synthesis of cobamides requires a great deal of genetic information, which is only found in some prokaryotes., Many bacterial species do not have the full genetic information required for de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, but can synthesize cobalamin when supplied with |FRAME: COBINAMIDE|, a stable cobalt-corrinoid hexaamide form that is not a true intermediate of the de novo pathway |CITS: [14351147][8770581]|., In order to process |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, it has to be converted into a real intermediate of the pathway. |FRAME: RiPPs "Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides"| (RiPPs), also known as ribosomal natural products, are a diverse class of natural products of ribosomal origin. RiPPs are produced by a variety of organisms, including prokaryotes, eukaryotes, and archaea, and possess a wide range of biological functions., In this pathway, characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-629265|, the product is not a RiPP but the modified amino acid |FRAME: CPD-25469|, whose function in the organism is still not known. However, the compound is produced in an unusual pathway, in which a RiPP is used as a scaffold for its synthesis., The pathway starts with the ribosomally-synthesized peptide TglA (WP_007252214), which contains 50 amino acids, ending with an alanyl residue. The process starts with a |FRAME: MONOMER-21965|, which adds a cycsteine residue to the C-terminus of the peptide through ATP and amino acyl-tRNA. The process continues with oxidative rearrangement, carboxymethylation, and proteolysis, to produce the unusual metabolite |FRAME: CPD-25469|, restoring TglA to its original state |CITS: [31320540]|., The authors point out that the pathway enables each TglA peptide to participate in many rounds, producing mutiple |FRAME: CPD-25469| molecules. If the cysteine residue was encoded in tglA and added by the ribosome, then each ribosomally produced peptide would be able to generate only a single |FRAME: CPD-25469| product |CITS: [31320540]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Kanamycins Kanamycins| are a group of |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1967|. The compounds were discovered in 1957 by researchers in the National Institute of Health of Tokyo, Japan |CITS: [13513509][13595489]|. Due to their wide range of activity, especially against severe staphylococcal and mycobacterial infections, these antibiotics gained almost immediate acceptance, and the most common form, |FRAME: CPD-4821|, was produced commercially within a year of its discovery |CITS: [13566481]|., Kanamycins interact with the 30S subunit of the prokaryotic ribosome, inducing substantial amounts of mistranslation and indirectly inhibiting translocation during protein synthesis, resulting in death |CITS: [391568][9662506]|. Kanamycins are currently used to treat a wide variety of infections., Kanamycins share several biosynthetic intermediates with other aminoglycosides, including the core moiety |FRAME: CPD-10151| and the pseudodisaccharides |FRAME: CPD-14126|, |FRAME: CPD-14125| and |FRAME: CPD-14137|., While the main product produced by |FRAME: TAX-1967| is |FRAME: CPD-4821|, additional products are also produced, including |FRAME: CPD-4822|, |FRAME: CPD-4823| |CITS: [13563334][13587408]|, |FRAME: CPD-14138| |CITS: [Adams96]| and |FRAME: CPD-4824| |CITS: [Chang80]|., About This Pathway, The first part of the pathway is common to several aminoglycoside antibiotics, and was described mostly from studies of |FRAME: CPD-14140 butirosin| and |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin| production. In this common route a unique aminocyclitol, |FRAME: CPD-10151|, is biosynthesized from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| in four steps by three crucial enzymes, |FRAME: MONOMER-17187|, |FRAME: MONOMER-17185| and |FRAME: MONOMER-17186| (the aminotransferase catalyzes two steps) |CITS: [16506694][19362652]|. , After the formation of |FRAME: CPD-10151| the kanamycin pathway splits into two branches due to the promiscuity of the next enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-17218|, which can utilize two glycosyl donors - |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12575|. When the former is used, the product is |FRAME: CPD-14126|, which is deacetylated by a dedicated enzyme to form |FRAME: CPD-14125|. When |FRAME: CPD-12575| is used, the product is |FRAME: CPD-14127|. Since |FRAME: MONOMER-17218| prefers |FRAME: CPD-12575|, the latter branch has much higher flux than the former., In the last part of the pathway, multiple forms of kanamycin are formed from |FRAME: CPD-14125| and |FRAME: CPD-14127|. When the |FRAME: G-15009|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17222|, which uses the modified amino sugar |FRAME: CPD-10223| as its preferred glycosyl donor (see |FRAME: PWY-5978|), acts directly on |FRAME: CPD-14125| or |FRAME: CPD-14127|, it forms |FRAME: CPD-4823| and |FRAME: CPD-4824|, respectively. However, this direct reaction is rare. Most of the molecules of |FRAME: CPD-14125| or |FRAME: CPD-14127| are modified by the |FRAME: G-15007|/|FRAME: G-15008| oxidase/aminotransferase system, producing |FRAME: CPD-14137| and |FRAME: CPD-14128|, respectively. When |FRAME: G-15009| acts on these compounds using |FRAME: CPD-10223|, the prducts are |FRAME: CPD-4822| and |FRAME: CPD-4821|, respectively. Two additional enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-15974| and |FRAME: G-15975|, convert |FRAME: CPD-4822| to |FRAME: CPD-4821|, the main product of this pathway |CITS: [22374809]|., In addition, |FRAME: G-15009| can also use |FRAME: CPD-12575| as a glycosyl donor, producing |FRAME: CPD-14139| and |FRAME: CPD-14138|, respectively. Since the activity with |FRAME: CPD-10223| is much higher, the main product of the pathway is |FRAME: CPD-4821| |CITS: [21983602]|.

Summary: A bewildering number of post-transcriptional modifications are introduced into cellular RNAs by different enzymes |CITS: [12581659]|. The most abundant post-transcriptional nucleobase modification in cellular RNAs is the isomerization of, |FRAME:URIDINE| to |FRAME: CPD-497|, which is carried out by the enzyme pseudouridine synthase in a reaction that does not require any cofactors. In pseudouridine uracil is bound to the to ribose through C5 rather than through N1 as is the case for uridine. The synthase severs the normal glycosidic C-N bond of uridine, flips the uracil moiety along its N3-C6 axis, and forms a glycosidic C-C bond with C5. Pseudouridine is one of few molecules that have a glycosidic C-C bond., Pseudouridine synthases belong to four different families, which are represented in |FRAME:TAX-562| by the |FRAME: EG10454|, |FRAME: EG11177|, |FRAME: EG12609| and |FRAME: EG12044|. The only sequence element that is absolutely conserved among the four families of enzymes is a catalytic aspartic acid |CITS: [9425056][11720289][10428788]|., Pseudouridylation is found in organisms from all kingdoms. Mammalian rRNA contains about 100 pseudouridines per ribosome, and tRNAs contain an average of 3 - 4 pseudouridines. While many eukaryotes possess the ability to degrade pseudouridine, mammals appear to have lost this ability, and pseudouridine is excreted in their urine., Pseudouridine has been shown to serve as a source of uracil for a strain of |FRAME:TAX-562| that is deficient in pyrimidine synthesis |CITS: [4882030]|. It was shown that pseudouridine was first phosphorylated by a kinase to |FRAME: PSEUDOURIDINE-5-P| |CITS: [4334133]|, followed by hydrolysis to |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P| and |FRAME: URACIL| |CITS: [4912525]|., The genes encoding these two enzymes have been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-364106|, a uropathogenic, strain |CITS: [18591240]|. The genes were cloned, and the enzymes were purified and characterized,, conforming the proposed function., Similar genes were found in the genomes of many bacteria and almost all eukaryotes |CITS: [18591240]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD1F-114 "All-trans-lycopene"| is a bright red carotenoid pigment and phytochemical found in many photosynthetic organisms, as well as some non-photosynthetic organisms. Its name is derived from the name of the tomato plant, |FRAME: TAX-4081|, in which it is found in large amounts., |FRAME: CPD1F-114 "All-trans-lycopene"| is an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of many carotenoids, which are responsible for pigmentation, photosynthesis, and photo-protection in plants, algae, and other organisms., The first committed step of carotenoid biosynthesis is the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12321|. Two molecules of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (GGPP) are condensed to give |FRAME: CPD-464|, followed by rearrangement of the cyclopropylcarbinyl intermediate to |FRAME: CPD-12321|. This conversion is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.32|., Different strategies exist among different organisms for the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12321| to |FRAME: CPD1F-114|. In fungi and most non-oxygenic bacteria the pathway proceeds via exclusively all-trans isomers (see |FRAME: PWY-5942|). In oxygenic phototrophs such as plants, algae and cyanobacteria, as well as green sulfur bacteria, the pathway proceeeds via different cis isomers, and the final conversion to all-trans occurs at the very end of the pathway, where |FRAME: CPD-7496| is converted to |FRAME: CPD1F-114| (this pathway)., It should be noted that exceptions do occur - for example, the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-251221| utilizes the bacterial pathway |CITS: [15811329]|., About This Pathway, In oxygenic phototrophs such as plants, algae and cyanobacteria, as well as in green sulfur bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-12321| undergoes a series of four desaturation reactions leading to the formation of |FRAME:CPD1F-114| via |FRAME: CPD-7535|, |FRAME: CPD-7526| and |FRAME: CPD-7496|. To catalyze this transformation, plants and cyanobacteria require two phylogenetically related desaturases [|FRAME: EC-1.3.5.5| (PDS, crtP) and |FRAME: EC-1.3.5.6| (ZDS, crtQ)] and two isomerases [|FRAME: EC-5.2.1.12| (Z-ISO) and |FRAME: EC-5.2.1.13| (CRTISO, crtH)]., The first desaturase, |FRAME: CPLX1F-15| (|FRAME: AT4G14210|), removes two hydrogens and introduces trans double bonds at 11 and 11', along with a cis bond at the 9 and 9' double bond positions, producing |FRAME: CPD-7535| which is isomerized at the 15-cis double bond to |FRAME: CPD-7526| by |FRAME: AT1G10830-MONOMER| (|FRAME: AT1G10830|). The isomerization can occur spontaneously in light, but not in the dark., The second desaturase, |FRAME: CPLX1F-19| (|FRAME: AT3G04870|), removes two hydrogens from |FRAME: CPD-7526|, introducing cis double bonds at the 7 and 7' positions, leading to formation of conjugated cis double bonds at 7,9 and 7', 9'. Finally, the second isomerase, |FRAME: MONOMER-12167| (|FRAME: G-9408|), isomerizes the cis double bonds at 7,9 and 7', 9', producing |FRAME: CPD1F-114| |CITS: [18948076][20335404]|. The accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-7496| in tangerine tomato mutants |CITS: [15557094]|, as well as the biochemical activities tested for CRTISO and ZDS support the existence of this branch of the pathway |CITS: [15557094][18948076]|., It should also be noted that there is no evidence for a Z-ISO gene in the genome of green sulfur bacteria. It is possible that this reaction occurs in these organisms strictly by photoisomerization |CITS: [20335404]|., Plants use oxidized plastoquinones as electron acceptors in the desaturation sequence.

Summary: Note: this pathway describes a process that involves both the cytoplasmic membrane and the outer membrane. Due to current limitations in the pathway layout algorithm, the pathway is displayed using only a single membrane. Read the following text to get more information about the localization of the different components., General Background, Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. In the environment, iron is mostly found in two different oxidation states: II and III. Fe(II) is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions, while Fe(III) is favored at high pH and oxic conditions. In oxic environments iron forms various oxide and hydroxide compounds; iron(II,III) oxides (such as magnetite, Fe3O4) and iron(III) oxides (such as hematite, Fe2O3) are most common. Under anoxic conditions the soluble |FRAME: FE+2| species is the most common., In certain environments Fe(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands., Oxidation of ferrous iron (Fe(II)) by microbes is an important component of the iron geochemical cycle. Bacterial iron oxidation is well documented under anaerobic conditions (see for example |FRAME: PWY-8554|), or under aerobic, acidic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6692|). Even though iron is oxidized spontaneously and rapidly in the presence of oxygen, many bacterial species have been found to oxidize Fe(II) at neutral pH |CITS: [20565252][32071158][33328652]|., About This Pathway, A genomic analysis of bacteria that oxidize Fe(II) at neutral pH has identified several genes that are similar to those used by |FRAME: TAX-920| for iron oxidation, including a distant homolog of |FRAME: MONOMER-16162 Cyc2|, the iron-oxidizing outer membrane single-heme cytochrome c. While not the only iron-oxidizing system found in neurophilic bacteria, the Cyc2 system is the most common and is found in nearly all well-characterized neutrophilic iron-oxidizing bacteria like the |FRAME: TAX-90627| and |FRAME: TAX-580370| |CITS: [37882557]|., Cyc2 proteins have a unique fused cytochrome-porin structure. The porin domain, which is very divergent, consists of multiple transmembrane segments that form a pore in the outer membrane |CITS: [34311573]|. The N-terminal cytochrome c region binds a single heme and is highly conserved |CITS: [26092463]|., |FRAME: TAX-314344| is one of the dominant biomineralizing organisms associated with Fe-rich hydrothermal ecosystems in the ocean |CITS: [12039770][19397679]|. It is a microaerophilic, chemolithoautotrophic iron-oxidizing bacterium that is known for its ability to biomineralize iron in the form of extracellular twisted filaments |CITS: [17668050][21107443]|. It oxidizes iron at circum-neutral pH and in the presence of oxygen, in direct competition with the chemical oxidation that takes place under these condtions. The organism has a Cyc2 protein that was shown to oxidized Fe(II) following purification., While Cyc2 of |FRAME: TAX-920| transfers its electrons to |FRAME: Rusticyanins rusticyanin|, no such protein exists in |FRAME: TAX-314344|. It has been proposed that the enzyme transfers the electrons directly to CycA1, a cytochrome c4 that is encoded by the organism |CITS: [34311573]|, though this hypothesis has not been verified. In any case, the periplasmic electron acceptor(s) deliver the electrons to |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.8| (cytochrome bc1), which is located in the cytoplasmic membrane, where the electrons are used to reduce the quinone pool. The reduced quinols then shuttle the electrons for reduction of oxygen or NAD(P).

Summary: The initial steps of glucose degradation can involve phosphorylative or non-phosphorylative (oxidative) reactions (see MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-2221|, |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS|, |FRAME: P341-PWY|, and |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY|). Another route of glucose oxidation is found in some species of bacteria such as |FRAME:TAX-286|, |FRAME:TAX-551|, |FRAME:TAX-434|, |FRAME:TAX-441|, and |FRAME:TAX-613| in which D-glucose is oxidized to D-gluconate and ketogluconates such as 2-dehydro-D-gluconate (2-ketogluconate), 5-keto-D-gluconate, and 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate., These ketogluconates, or their phosphorylated forms, then enter central metabolism (in |CITS: [9352901]|). Both the phosphorylative and oxidative pathways converge at 6-phospho-D-gluconate, a branch point at which further metabolism can be directed through several central metabolic pathways (see below) (in |CITS: [4154932]|). Other organisms, such as |FRAME:TAX-106590| H16, cannot degrade glucose, but can utilize 2-dehydro-D-gluconate for growth |CITS: [4212460]|. There is also evidence that 2-dehydro-D-gluconate, other ketogluconates, and gluconate may be metabolized by |FRAME:TAX-562| (see MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: KETOGLUCONMET-PWY| and |FRAME: GLUCONSUPER-PWY|)., This pathway shows the degradation of glucose through the periplasmic glucose catabolites gluconate and 2-dehydro-D-gluconate (2-ketogluconate) in several pseudomonads. Depending upon conditions, in aerobically grown |FRAME:TAX-287| extracellular glucose can be catabolized by either the physphorylative pathway, or the oxidative pathway |CITS: [6404887]|. In the oxidative pathway, glucose is oxidized to gluconate and 2-dehydro-D-gluconate in the periplasm by membrand-bound, cytochrome-linked dehydrogenases. The conversion of D-glucono-1,5-lactone to gluconate can occur spontaneously in solution, or be catalyzed by a lactonase, although information on which mechanism is operative in the periplasm of these organisms was not found. At neutral and alkaline pH, lactone hydrolysis to gluconate is favored, while at low pH the lactone is more stable |CITS: [11790736]|. 2-Dehydro-D-gluconate (2-ketogluconate) is thought to be actively transported into the cell where it is degraded by the reactions indicated here. A putative 2-ketogluconate utilization operon (kgu) has been identified in this organism |CITS: [10931350]|. Under anaerobic or low oxygen conditions, |FRAME:ORG-5927| uses the phosphorylative pathway |CITS: [6404887]|., In |FRAME:TAX-294| metabolic flux analysis suggested that most extracellular glucose is converted to gluconate and 2-dehydro-D-gluconate (2-ketogluconate). These oxidized metabolites are transported into the cell and degraded. Some glucose is also be taken up directly and catabolized by the phosphorylative pathway. The oxidized metabolites were produced during the first growth phase, and degraded in later phases. In contrast, a similar analysis of P. putida KT2440 suggested that the predominant route was through direct glucose uptake (|CITS: [15716428]|. |FRAME:TAX-303| strain C5V86 has been shown to catabolize glucose by the phosphorylative pathway only, whereas strain KT2442 used both the oxidative pathway shown here, and the phosphorylative pathway |CITS: [16734795]|. , The use of central metabolic pathways for further degradation of glucose catabolites also varies among bacterial species and their growth conditions. For example, in the well studied |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME:TAX-1423|, catabolism is primarily via the Embden Meyerhof Parnus pathway (|FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS|), with the latter organism lacking the Entner Doudoroff pathway (|FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|). In both organisms, the pentose phosphate pathway (|FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|) is also used to a lesser extent. In Pseudomonas fluorescens, Psuedomonas putida, |FRAME:TAX-358|, |FRAME:TAX-382|, Rhodobacter sphaeroides, |FRAME:TAX-542| and |FRAME:TAX-34007|, the Entner Doudoroff pathway is the primary route of glucose catabolism, and the penotse phosphate pathway functions biosynthetically |CITS: [15716428]|.

Summary: The phenylpropanoids are a large family of compounds, mostly found in plants, that are synthesized from |FRAME: PHE| and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: TYR|. The pathway that starts from |FRAME: PHE| forms |FRAME: COUMARATE| as a main intermediate. The name "phenylpropanoid" is derived from this compound, which consists of an aromatic phenyl group and a propene tail. Further processing results in the biosynthesis of many types of compounds, including |FRAME: Lignols monolignols| (precursors to |FRAME: Lignins lignin| and lignocellulose), |FRAME: Flavonoids flavonoids|, |FRAME: Coumarins coumarins|, |FRAME: Stilbenoids stilbenoids|, and phenolic acids., Phenylpropanoids are found throughout the plant kingdom, where they serve as essential components of a number of structural polymers, provide protection from ultraviolet light, defend against herbivores and pathogens, and also mediate plant-pollinator interactions as floral pigments and scent compounds., |FRAME: Lignins Lignin| is a three dimensional polymer of phenylpropanoid alcohols (monolignols). Lignin is always associated with cell wall |FRAME: CELLULOSE| and |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|, and provides mechanical rigidity to plant-supporting and plant-conducting tissues. , There are three monolignols, |FRAME: COUMARYL-ALCOHOL|, |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL|, and |FRAME: SINAPYL-ALCOHOL|. The relative amounts of these monolignols found in lignin show plant specificity. Gymnosperm lignins contain mainly coniferyl alcohol, angiosperm lignins contain both coniferyl alcohol and sinapyl alcohol, whereas all three types of monolignols are found within lignins of grasses. , The transport of monolignols to the cell wall and their lignification to lignin is poorly understood. These events possibly involve glucosylation. Lignification is possibly catalyzed by peroxidase. In the past decade, the lignin biosynthesis pathway has been redrawn several times based on new genetic and biochemical evidences. The pathway depicted here only illustrates the major routes to lignin monomers.

General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Organophosphonates| are organic compounds containing C-PO(OH)2 or C-PO(OR)2 groups (where R can be either an alkyl or an aryl group). Phosphonates are quite common among different organisms, including both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. They occur primarily as components of phosphonolipids (|FRAME: CPD-1106| is a common phosphonate constituent of phospholipids, analogous to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE|). In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics., Many bacterial species can utilize organophosphonates as the sole source of phosphorous |CITS: [16245012]|. Breaking the C-P bond, which is much more stable than the C-O-P phosphoester bonds of phosphates, requires special enzymes |CITS: [7765831]|., The utilization of |FRAME: CPD0-1068|, the most common organophosphonate, has been studied in detail and several different pathways have been described., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here enables the degradation of |FRAME: CPD0-1068| in the absence of a C-P lyase. The genes encoding the two enzymes of this pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.71| and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.89|, are very similar to the genes that encode |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.46| and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.78|, which are involved in |FRAME: PWY-7447 "2-aminoethylphosphonate degradation"|, and initially their true function was not known |CITS: [19788654]|. However, by cloning the genes and production of recombinant proteins it was shown that |FRAME: G-80427| encodes an enzyme that is specific for hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD0-1068|, and that the |FRAME: G-80428| gene product oxidatively converts |FRAME: CPD-11729| into |FRAME: FORMATE| and phosphate |CITS: [30810303]|.
