Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SO3 Sulfite| plays a key role in oxidative sulfur metabolism. It is derived from multiple sources: First, sulfite is the main intermediate in the oxidation of sulfur compounds to |FRAME: SULFATE| |CITS: [11557133]|., In purple sulfur bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1049|, the oxidation of |FRAME: HS| and |FRAME:S2O3| results in formation of intracellular sulfur globules, which are oxidized to sulfite by the Dsr system (see |FRAME: PWY-6676|)., A second source for sulfite is the desulfonation of organic compounds by enzymes like |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15| (Xsc) (see |FRAME: PWY-1281|)., A third source of sulfite is extracellular sulfite retrieved from the environment. Free sulfite in the periplasm (which most likely exists as bisulfite) is bound to the |FRAME: SoxY-Protein "SoxYZ"| protein complex in the form of |FRAME: SoxY-Systeine-Sulfinate|. The binding acts to shield components of the periplasm from chemical reactions with sulfite, and may also be required for delivering the sulfite to a transporter that exports it into the cytoplasm for oxidation |CITS: [24030319]|., , Some microorganisms (such as |FRAME: TAX-60136| species) can use sulfite as their sole electron source |CITS: [Sorokin95][10319472 ]|. , Enzymes that catalyze the direct oxidation of sulfite to sulfate are molybdenum hydroxylases, and belong to the sulfite oxidase family, which includes both sulfite-oxidizing enzymes and plant assimilatory nitrate reductases (such as the |FRAME: CPLX-7196| of |FRAME: ORG-5993|). The best characterized members of this family are sulfite oxidases, from avian and mammalian sources. However, these enzymes differ from the bacterial enzymes in that they can use oxygen as an electron acceptor (see |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.1|)., Some sulfite oxidizing enzymes are located in the periplasm. The best characterized enzyme from this group is |FRAME: EC-1.8.2.1| (SOR) from |FRAME: TAX-921|, which contains a molybdopyranopterin cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-5276|). Another well-characterized periplasmic enzyme is the |FRAME:CPLX-882| (such as that from |FRAME: TAX-82367|). It has been shown that this system can oxidize sulfite independently from the presence of the |FRAME:CPLX-7150| component (a molybdohemoprotein), but it is not clear whether the Sox system functions in vivo as a sulfite-oxidizing enzyme |CITS:[10940005][Lu84][11425697]|)., Other enzyme systems that oxidize sulfite are located in the cytoplasm. Two general mechanisms for sulfite oxidation in the cytoplasm have been described: a direct oxidation by a membrane-bound iron-sulfur molybdoprotein (|FRAME: EC-1.8.5.6|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7457|), and an indirect, AMP-dependent oxidation via the intermediate |FRAME:APS| (APS) (see |FRAME:PWY-5279| and |FRAME:PWY-5278|) |CITS: [11557133]|. The direct oxidation route is much more prevalent, but the two mechanisms are present simultaneously in many organisms, including β and γ proteobacteria (|FRAME: TAX-931|, |FRAME: TAX-1049|, |FRAME: TAX-36861|, |FRAME: TAX-1021|), green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1091|), Gram-positive bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-28034|) and even archaea (|FRAME: TAX-2283|) |CITS: [11557133]|., About This Pathway, Two variations are known for the non-direct sulfite oxidation pathway. Both variations share the same first step, the AMP-dependent oxidation of sulfite to |FRAME:APS|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.8.99.2|. The pathways differ in the second step. In one variation (depicted here) the AMP moiety of APS is transferred to |FRAME:PPI| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4|, generating sulfate and ATP, while in the other variation the AMP-moiety is transfered to phosphate by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.5| (APAT), generating sulfate and ADP (see |FRAME:PWY-5279|)., The APS pathways can operate in both directions (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|), and were discovered originally in sulfate-reducing organisms |CITS: [14484819]|. When operating in sulfite oxidation mode, they result in substrate level, phosphorylation, and may provide the bacteria with energy |CITS: [4972376]|., The oxidation of sulfite by the indirect pathway occurs in the cytoplasm. The first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-7168|, has been described as either a soluble enzyme, or a membrane bound enzyme. The other enzymes are soluble |CITS: [11557133]|. Even though the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7165| has only been isolated mostly from sulfate-reducers, this pathway has been demonstrated in several sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [10939523]|, |FRAME: TAX-1092|, |FRAME: TAX-1058|, |FRAME: TAX-931|, and |FRAME: TAX-36861|, (|CITS: [11685375][9308173][11557133]| and references therein).

|FRAME: DIGLUCO-DOCOSANOATE Sophorosyloxydocosanoate| is an extracellular glycolipid secreted by several yeasts including the ascomycete |FRAME: TAX-75736 "Starmerella bombicola (previously known as Candida bombicola)"| and the basidiomycete |FRAME: TAX-106002 "Rhodotorula bogoriensis (previously known as Candida bogoriensis ATCC 18809)"| |CITS: [15218385]||CITS: [10843082]|. The function of this glycolipid is unknown, but glycolipids such as this are of interest for their biological activities and chemical properties. They are potentially useful in medical, cosmetic and chemical engineering applications. Chemical derivatives of biologically produced sophorolipids have been described |CITS: [12839437]|., Sophorolipids are relatively rare. They contain the glucose disaccharide |FRAME: CPD-13242|, which has a , glucosyl-β-(1,2)glucosyl linkage. |FRAME: CPD-13242| is joined to a hydroxyl group of a hydroxy fatty acid aglycone (in |CITS: [5012313]|). Analysis of the sophorolipids produced by |FRAME: TAX-106002| revealed des-, mono- and di-acetylated |FRAME: CPD-13242| moieties, with the lipid in the free acid form. The majority of the hydroxy fatty acids had a chain length of 22 carbons, with <10% containing 24 carbons |CITS: [15218385]|. , The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DIGLUCODIACETYL-DOCOSANOATE| in |FRAME: TAX-106002| has been extensively studied by Light and co-workers (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SOPHOROSYLOXYDOCOSANOATE-SYN-PWY|). They characterized three glycolipids produced by |FRAME: TAX-106002| cells as the diacetyl, monoacetyl and unacetylated forms of |FRAME: DIGLUCO-DOCOSANOATE|. An in vivo time course of production of these glycolipids in relation to growth phase suggested that the diacetyl derivative is formed first and is a precursor of the mono- and unacetylated forms. This indicated removal of acetyl groups from the diacetyl form. The glycolipids disappeared from older cultures, suggesting that they were either incorporated into other molecules, or degraded |CITS: [5075510]|. , A catabolic acetylesterase having 13-sophorysyloxydocosanoate 6',6''-diacetate acetylhydrolase (acetylesterase) activity was purified from |FRAME: TAX-106002| cell extracts and partially characterized. Although it had the required activity in vitro, its broad substrate specificity makes conclusions about its in vivo role uncertain. It may also participate in other reactions |CITS: [1245482]|.

Summary: General Background, The pyridine nucleotides coenzymes NAD and NADP are omnipresent in all living organisms and are involved in a vast amount of reactions with an enormous variety of corresponding enzymes (>17% of all classified enzymes)., The majority of these enzymes exhibit absolute stereospecificity, and use the coenzymes as acceptors for a hydride ion (H-) or an equivalent thereof originating from the reaction substrate. In most cases there is a specific interaction between the enzyme and the coenzyme, causing a change in the coenzyme stereochemistry. Based on this fact the pyridine nucleotide coenzymes are sometimes referred to as "cosubstrates" |CITS: [3157549]|., The dynamics and regulative aspects of both phosphorylation and desphosphorylation of NAD and NADH are not well understood. Whereas the importance of e.g. NAD(H) and NADP(H) is obvious through their close involvement in energy metabolism and reductive biosynthesis, their interconversion and the role of some of the participating enzymes requires further research., About This Pathway, NAD kinases are found in all organisms indicating a crucial role for this enzyme. The enzymes have been discussed in the context of maintaining a physiological balance of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated in mitochondria |CITS: [15247403]|, where significant changes in the NADP+/NAD+ ratio are observed upon oxidative stress |CITS: [11337409]|., On the other side a novel NADH kinase has been identified in |FRAME:TAX-3701| which is not associated with mitochondria and related metabolic processes. This NADH kinase has been discussed in connection with an increased metabolic flexibility of nicotinamide metabolism by uncoupling NADP+ synthesis from the redox status of the corresponding pool. However, further research is required to precisely describe its physiological role in the cell |CITS: [15347288]|., The interconversion of NAD+ to NAD(H) can be performed by two enzymes that are included in this pathway, the |FRAME: MONOMER-11877| (E.C. 1.6.1.1) where another pyridine nucleotide redox carrier is the acceptor of the hydride ion |CITS: [10548498]|, and the |FRAME: CPLX-5263| (E.C. 1.6.5.3), (also referred to as complex I), which couples oxidation of NAD(H) to the reduction of ubiquinone (and vice versa) |CITS: [12837548]|., The hydrolysis of NADP and NADPH in plants is carried out by corresponding phosphatases in dependence on the plant developmental stages and metabolic requirements. The |FRAME: MONOMER-11869| activity correlates with the dormancy state of |FRAME: TAX-4498| caryopses being involved in the maintenance of steady ratios of NADP and NADPH during seed imbibition, in spite of likewise increased NAD kinase activities |CITS: [10944152]|., While all of the processes and reactions mentioned so far are universal, the last two enzymes in this pathway have been described only in certain eukaryotic organisms. |FRAME: CPLX-7016| has been described only in green plants and several yeast species |CITS: [15347288][642063][ 642066]|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-11870| was described only in |FRAME: TAX-4577| |CITS: [16658848]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE Naphthalene| is the simplest fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, and is abundant in soils., Several bacterial species are able to grow on naphthalene as the sole cource of carbon and energy |CITS:[4423716][10433976][10620687]|. At least two pathways for naphthalene degradation exist - an aerobic pathway and an anaerobic pathway., The anaerobic degradation of naphthalene was demonstrated with an enrichment of a sulfate-reducing culture obtained from a former coal gasification site and named N47 |CITS: [Safinowski04]|. The culture included a dominant Deltaproteobacterium and a minor Spirochaete. The genome of the dominant member was sequenced and annotated |CITS: [21176053]| and all relevant enzymes were eventually shown to belong to it |CITS: [21221530]|., Studies on anaerobic naphthalene degradation have shown that the first intermediate is |FRAME: CPD-15898| |CITS: [9471963][10877763][18811643]|. The enzymatic decarboxylation of naphthalene has been demonstrated in crude cell extracts of the sulfate-reducing |FRAME: TAX-700510 "enrichment culture N47"| |CITS: [22564331]|. The enzyme has not been purified, but candidate genes that encode it have been suggested based on their sequence |CITS: [21221530]|. Since no equivalent reaction that could carboxylate hydrocarbons without an energy input is known in chemistry or biochemistry, the reaction, if proven, would constitute a novel type of carboxylation., A candidate gene for encoding the next enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-19097|, has also been identified and shown to be expressed in the presence of naphthalene |CITS: [21221530]|. The next two enzymes, both members of the "old yellow enzyme" family, have been identified and characterized, and shown to convert |FRAME: CPD-15896| to |FRAME: CPD-15897| in two steps, via |FRAME: CPD-17487| |CITS: [23646996][25424741]|., As of 2015, the rest of the pathway is unknown, although it is documented that  the |FRAME: TAX-700510| completely mineralizes naphthalene to CO<sub>2</sub>| |CITS: [11207761][11097910][18811643]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Jasmonates Jasmonates| (JA) are an important class of compounds, related to |FRAME:CPD-734|, found throughout the plant kingdom as well as in fungi |CITS:[17513307]|. They participate in a number of biological processes including resistance to herbivores and some pathogens, protection against ozone, senescence, and reproductive development (reviewed in |CITS:[19025383][17513307]|)., Many different jasmonate precursors and jasmonate derivatives have biological activity, including |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Amino-Acid-Conjugates "jasmonoyl-amino acid conjugates"|. Different species may have a different array of JA-amino acid conjugates, and the biological activity of each compound may differ between species. For example, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"| (JA-Ile) has been shown to have biological activity in a number of different plants, including |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS:[15258265][18247047]|, |FRAME:TAX-49451| |CITS:[17273867][17085687]|, |FRAME: TAX-384659| |CITS:[18812165]|, |FRAME: TAX-4513| (barley) |CITS:[9315685]|, |FRAME: TAX-4081| (tomato) |CITS:[18458331]|, |FRAME: TAX-4530| (rice) |CITS:[ 9013895]|, and others., In |FRAME: TAX-3702|, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmoonyl-L-isoleucine"| promotes the interaction between the COI1 protein (Coronatine-insensitive protein 1) and the TIFY10A (JAZ1) repressor protein. In this manner, JA-Ile is believed to help destabilize the JAZ1 repressor and thereby promote JA-responsive transcription |CITS:[17637677]|. COI1 and JAZ1 homologs have been found in other plants, such as tomato, where they also bind in a JA-Ile-dependent manner |CITS:[18458331]|, indicating that JA-Ile might have a similar function in other plant species. However, this is not a universal phenomenon. For example, a treatment of 100 uM JA-Ile fails to stimulate JA-responsive emissions of volatile sesquiterpenes in |FRAME: TAX-467333|, a weed commonly found in Japan |CITS:[TAMOGAMI07]|. Other differences in biological activity have been observed across species for many other conjugates including |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-ACCs "jasmonoyl-1-aminocyclopropane-1 carboxylate"| (JA-ACC), |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Leucines "jasmonoyl-L-leucine"| (JA-leucine), and |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Valines "jasmoonyl-L-valine"| (JA-valine). , Jasmonates are found in nature in two isomeric forms, which can have very different biological effects. For example, the biologically active form of |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"| is |FRAME: CPD-11259|, while |FRAME: CPD-11232| does not promote JAZ1/COI1 binding in vitro |CITS: [19349968]|. Initial studies actually suggested that |FRAME: CPD-11232| was a biologically active phytohormone |CITS: [SEMBDER93][17291501]|, but it is now believed that this was due to impure preparations that contained small amounts of |FRAME: CPD-11259|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-49451|, jasmonate signaling is an important part of the response to herbivory |CITS:[17513307]|. The level of JA as well as |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"|, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Leucines "jasmonoyl-L-leucine"|, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Valines "jasmonoyl-L-valine"|, and |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Glutamines "jasmonoyl-L-glutamine"| all rise in response to wounding and treatment with oral secretions from the herbivorous tobacco hornworm |FRAME:TAX-7130|. On the other hand, JA-Trp, JA-Met, and |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-ACCs "jasmonoyl-1-aminocyclopropane-1 carboxylate"| have not been detected in this species |CITS:[17513307]|. |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"| is involved in herbivore resistance |CITS:[17085687]|, but |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Valines "jasmonoyl-L-valine"| and |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Leucines "jasmonoyl-L-leucine"| do not appear to stimulate herbivore defense responses |CITS:[18065562]|. It is unclear whether these are storage forms of JA or catabolic intermediates., Another important phytohormone, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA), can be conjugated with several amino acids, as shown in |FRAME:PWY-6219|. Some of these compounds, such as |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP|, are targeted for further breakdown (|CITS:[9733548]| while others, such as, |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ALA|, may serve as storage forms. A family of amidohydrolases can release free, active IAA from some of these "storage" IAA conjugates |CITS:[7792259][10072397]|. To date, no corresponding JA-amidohydrolases were identified in plants, although an enzyme that can catalyze this activity has been detected in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-45133| |CITS:[9141491]|. Further work will be required to determine the metabolic and functional fate of the "inactive" JA-amino acid conjugates identified in |FRAME: TAX-49451|., Two enzymes that catalyze the conjugation of JA with amino acids, encoded by |FRAME: G-11278| and |FRAME: G-11279|, have been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-49451|. Reduced levels of their transcripts lead to lower levels of JA-Ile, JA-Leu, and JA-Val, suggesting that the in vivo synthesis of these compounds requires these enzymes. JA-Gln levels are not affected in these mutants, indicating that at least one other enzyme capable of generating jasmonyl-amino acid conjugates exists in this species |CITS:[17273867][17085687]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis, (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|),, and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is, highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for, a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes, that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase, enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal, dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, Methylglyoxal dehydrogenases catalyze the direct oxidation of methylglyoxal to pyruvate., The first enzyme that was shown to catalyze this reaction was partially purified from sheep liver, |CITS: [4383524]|. That enzyme was able to utilize both NAD and NADP, and was not specific, for methylglyoxal. However, later work suggested that this enzyme might have been a mixture of two, different enzymes - one specific for NAD and the other for NADP. Such two enzymes were purified, from goat liver, and were shown to be of exactly the same size - 42 kDa |CITS: [7107625]|., An NADP-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-12918| specific for methylglyoxal was also purified from rat, liver |CITS: [20958]|. That enzyme had absolutely no activity with NAD, and requiredan amine with a, vicinal hydroxyl group for activity.

|FRAME: LACTALD| is one of two products resulting from degradation of the two methylpentoses |FRAME: L-fucoses| and |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, which are metabolized by an analogous series of reactions., Anaerobically, |FRAME: LACTALD| is converted into |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| by a reversible reaction catalyzed by, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.77|. |FRAME:TAX-562| excretes L-1,2-propanediol into the medium, possibly by facilitated diffusion |CITS: [2644239]|., Currently two unrelated genes are known to encode such enzymes in different organisms. In |FRAME:TAX-562| the enzyme is encoded by |FRAME: EG10351| gene |CITS: [6421801]| (known as rhaO in other organisms |CITS: [18848625]|), in |FRAME: TAX-99287| it is encoded by the |FRAME: STM4044| gene |CITS: [24391637]|.

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., The purpose of arsenic methylation in eukaryotes is controversial, since methylated As(III) species are more toxic than non-methylated As(III). If the gene arose before the atmosphere became oxidizing, then the products would have remained trivalent. In such a case, the enzyme would activate inorganic arsenic into more toxic methylated species. One interpretation is that those products could be used by the cells (following their secretion) as powerful antibiotics in a competitive environment., About This Pathway, Detoxification of inorganic arsenate often involves methylation. Methylation of arsenic compounds has been documented in many organisms, including bacteria, fungi, green plants, and higher organisms (for a detailed list of organisms and the corresponding arsenic species, see |CITS: [Cullen89]|). The process is so common that in certain environments methylated arsenic species become the dominant form of arsenic |CITS: [Anderson91]|. Because of the overwhelming diversity of methylated arsenic species that have been observed, and the scarcity of biochemical data, this pathway is limited to the methylation of inorganic arsenic in mammals., Arsenic detoxification in most mammals involves alternative steps of reduction and oxidative methylation. The end metabolites are |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINATE|, and |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINOUS-ACID|, which are less reactive than arsenate and arsenite, and are excreted in the urine., The pathway starts with the reduction of arsenate to arsenite. Even though arsenite is more toxic than arsenate, this transformation is essential, since only arsenite can be methylated. The reduction of arsenate to arsenite has been reported to occur in two routes: In the first route arsenate can be conjugated to ribose by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6181| (PNP), which accepts arsenate as an alternative substrate to its normal substrate, phosphate. The ribose-1-arsenate thus formed is converted to arsenite in the presence of |FRAME: CPD-296|, in a process that has not been fully characterized yet |CITS: [12018991]|., A second route was reported to be the direct reduction by liver arsenate reductase |CITS: [10649963]|. Several reports have linked this activity to the |FRAME: CPLX-8377| (|FRAME: HS03433|) |CITS: [15470234][15788720][15788719][16322075]|. However, the discovery of a different activity of GAPDH with arsenate (see |FRAME: PWY1YI0-1|) casts doubt on the original interpretation, and until further information becomes available, this route will not be included in this pathway., A key enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.137|, which catalyzes the methylation of As(III). The gene encoding this enzyme was initially identified in rat |CITS: [11790780]|, and subsequently in other mammals, including humans |CITS: [15808521]|. |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE Glutathione|, the major thiol in most organisms, is present at millimolar concentrations and reacts readily with AS(III) compounds to form the glutathione complexes inside cells |CITS: [7841340]|. The triglutathione complex is believed to be the substrate for |FRAME: HS01822-MONOMER| |CITS: [15526190]|. The methyltransferase binds As(III) in a series of three thiol transfer reactions from |FRAME: CPD-22658|. Once bound to the enzyme, As(III) undergoes methylation events. Most of the substrate remains bound to the enzyme after the first methylation, with only a small fraction being released as |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, and is released after the second methylation as |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINOUS-ACID|. An even smaller fraction proceeds to a third methylation event and is released as |FRAME: CPD-22659|, which is a volatile compound, and is found in much smaller amounts in urine., During the reaction the arsenic atom changes valencies between (III) and (V) several times, being oxidized during methylation, and reduced back to (III) valency with electrons derived from thioredoxin. In the presence of oxygen the released products |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| and |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINOUS-ACID| can be oxidized nonenzymatically to |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE| and |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINATE|, respectively |CITS: [25325836]|. Analysis of urine samples found that methylated pentavalent arsenic species are the major arsenic species, followed by only a minor amount of trivalent methylated arsenic species., If no oxidation takes place, the trivalent methylated species can react again with glutathione, forming |FRAME: CPD-24323| and |FRAME: CPD-24324|, which can serve as an alternative substrates for the methyltransferase. , It is interesting to note that some mammals, including certain primates, do not methylate arsenite |CITS: [10328340]|., In chimpanzees the most likely cause is a deletion within the AS3MT gene |CITS: [15808521]|.

It is an effective insect repellent, plant species emit 2-(Decahydro-4a-methyl-1-methylenenaphthalen-7-yl)-propan-2-ol which deter pests., |FRAME: CPD-11430| is a potent inhibitor of presynaptic omega-agatoxin IVA-sensitive (P/Q-type) Ca(2+) channel. Summary: |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN (Indole-3-yl)acetate| (IAA) is an abundant form of the potent phytohormone auxin. It affects many aspects of plant growth and development and also participates in responses to biotic and abiotic stimuli |CITS: [15749753] [18541211]|. IAA can be conjugated to a number of small molecules, including sugars and amino acids and it can be modified with additional functional groups, including a methyl group. All of these additions, including methylation, can affect the biological activity and biochemical properties of this important hormone |CITS: [15749753]|. , The biological relevance of |FRAME: CPD-10546| (MeIAA) is still under investigation. Some experiments suggest that MeIAA is an inactive form of IAA, although the addition of a methyl group to IAA, which converts it from an acid to a nonpolar compound, should enable it to cross membranes more easily |CITS:[18467465]|. Thus endogenous MeIAA, like methyl salicylate |CITS:[17916738]|, may be a transport form of the hormone that is moved from its site of production to a site of auxin activity and then transformed into active IAA by |FRAME: AT3G10870-MONOMER| |CITS:[18467465]|., Several studies have shown that the exogenous application of MeIAA can cause auxin-like phenotypic changes in plants, and, in some cases, the phenotypes are even stronger than when IAA is applied directly |CITS:[16169896][17926040]|. Therefore, if MeIAA is inactive, this suggests that plants must have adequate levels of MeIAA methylesterase activity to convert exogenously applied MeIAA to IAA. , MeIAA is difficult to detect in plants |CITS:[16169896][18467465]|. It accumulates at very low levels in Arabidopsis |CITS:[18367217]|, but it has been observed in a number of plant species (catalogued in KNApSAcK). In addition, the phenotypic effects caused by changes the levels of |FRAME: AT5G55250| or |FRAME: AT3G10870| activity in plants argue that this pathway is important for normal plant growth and development |CITS:[16169896][18467465]|. , Additional work will be needed to clarify the biological role of MeIAA and to identify the taxonomic distribution of this pathway that can reversibly methylate an important regulator of plant growth, development, and environmental response., Please note: Neither MeIAA nor MeIAA methylesterase activity have been experimentally verified in |FRAME:TAX-3694| or |FRAME:TAX-3330|, even though both have active IAA methyltransferases |CITS: [17499822][19369216]|. However, it seems likely that the reverse reaction occurs. Notably, |FRAME:TAX-3694| and other |FRAME:TAX-3328| species do have predicted proteins with high similarity to the MeIAA methylesterase from Arabidopsis.

Summary: General Background, The two primary bile acids biosynthesized in the human liver, |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189|, are further metabolized in the liver by conjugation to |FRAME: GLY|, or |FRAME: TAURINE| to form |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, or |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6061|). These conjugates are almost fully ionized at physiological pH and are therefore described as bile salts. Bile salts are concentrated in the gallbladder and are released into the duodenum upon stimulation by the hormone cholecystokinin. They promote digestion of dietary lipids in the small intestine and are then reabsorbed via the enterohepatic circulation., Intestinal anaerobic and facultatively anaerobic bacteria metabolize bile salts primarily by deconjugation and oxidation of hydroxyl groups. A small proportion of bile acids are not reabsorbed in the small intestine and enter the large intestine where they are metabolized to secondary bile acids such as |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7754|), or |FRAME: CPD-7235| (which is produced similarly from |FRAME: CPD-15189|). These secondary bile acids enter the bile acid pool. In some individuals they can accumulate to relatively high levels and may contribute to the pathogenesis of gastrointestinal diseases. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., Non-intestinal bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [9812981] [19683506]|, or the laboratory strain of the intestinal bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-511145|, also produce enzymes that can catalyze some of these transformations (see |FRAME: 7-ALPHA-HYDROXYSTEROID-DEH-CPLX|)., About This Pathway, Bile salts are deconjugated by bile salt hydrolases as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8135|. The benefit of deconjugation to the bacteria is the subject of a number of hypotheses., In addition, constitutively expressed hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases carry out oxidation and epimerization of hydroxyl groups at the 3, 7 and 12 positions of the bile acid steroid rings. These reactions convert (epimerize) hydroxyl groups from α to β positions via stable oxo-intermediates. Two distinct, stereospecific hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases are required for epimerization, and they may be from the same, or different species of bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|., see also |FRAME: PWY-8255| and |FRAME: PWY-8254|.

Summary: General Background, Kavalactones are known for their psychoactive effects. The Polynesian plant |FRAME: TAX-130404|, also known as kava, contains kavalactones and is often ingested for its psychoactive effects by local natives. Kava roots are known to contain up to 15% of kavalacatones by dry weight. |FRAME: TAX-130404| derived enzymes have been experimentally examined, and hypothesized to generate 12 kavalactone compounds |CITS: [31332312]|. This cocktail includes the six most present compounds, |FRAME: CPD-22603|, dihidrokavain, methysticin, dihidromethysticin, yangonin, and desmethoxyyangonin. |FRAME: CPD-22603 "Kavain"| has been demonstrated to bind to γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors, which can lead to intensified activity and possibly contribute to the calming effects experienced by kava ingestion |CITS: [27332705]|. Unlike other compounds that elicit sedative effects in humans, there is currently no strong indication that individuals can overdose on kavalactones. Therefore, kavalactones have garnered international interest from the medical and recreational drug communities |CITS: [31332312]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of kavalactones usually begins when a 4-coumarate-coenzyme A ligase catalyzes the production of |FRAME: 3-Aryl-Acryloyl-CoAs| from |FRAME: Phenylpropanoids|. The final kavalactone product is primarily determined by which acyl-CoA reactant is used as the substrate. A styrylpyrone synthase then catalyzes the production of a 4-hydroxy-styrylpyrone from |FRAME: 3-Aryl-Acryloyl-CoAs|, which is then dehydrated at the C5-C6 double bond to generate a 5,6-dihydro-4-hydroxy-styrylpyrone by a styrylpyrone reductase. Then, a styrylpyrone O-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group to the C4 hydroxyl group, resulting in a kavalactone. Other major kavalactones are generated when the reactants skip dehydrogenation at the C5-C6 double bond and are directly methylated at the C4 hydroxyl group |CITS: [31332312]|.

Polyketides are known to form the largest group of secondary metabolites in Fusarium species and a number of polyketide synthases (PKSs) involved in the biosynthesis of such polyketide-derived metabolites have been identified in the genomes of various species from this genus |CITS:[16278459]|. Amongst them are also polyketide synthases (PKSs) or non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) unique to the species, for instance PKS19 and NRPS31 biosynthesizing apicidin-like compounds in Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[23825955]|. Such PKSs in fungi are often associated with respective biosynthetic gene clusters |CITS:[16322742]| and are able to give rise to a remarkable structural diversity of the produced compounds |CITS:[21102597] [Tkacz00]|., The polyketide pigment |FRAME:CPD-18207| has been first described from Fusarium lycopersici and named lycopersin at that time |CITS:[18120664]|. The polyketide origin of |FRAME:CPD-18207| and |FRAME:CPD-18212| had been suggested but the proposed starter unit, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-47| has been later shown not to be applicable |CITS:[5168485]|. Most of the pigments found in the genus Fusarium are colored naphtoquinones |CITS:[16240659]|. Although the physiological roles of fungal pigments are not well explored they are generally associated with protection against irradiation and virulence (summarized in |CITS:[11837241]|) and found to be preferably formed in response to stress as defense metabolites |CITS:[16240659] [24036343]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-18207| has been demonstrated to exhibit antioomycete activity against Phytophthora infestans |CITS:[17927749]|, nematicidal activity against the pine wood nematode Bursaphelenchus xylophilus |CITS:[Kwon07]|, antiprotozoal activity against Leishmania brasiliensis |CITS:[5497222]| and antibacterial activity |CITS:[24183988]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-18207| has expressed anticancer activity against human lung and pancreatic cell lines |CITS:[17286429]|, shown to have neuroprotective effects on damaged neurons caused by oxidative stress |CITS:[24848007]|, regarded as tool for disease control in certain crops |CITS:[12846324]| and proven to induce senescence through cell vacuolization |CITS:[5168483]|. , |FRAME:CPD-18207 Bikaverin| and its congenial partner |FRAME:CPD-18180| (see |FRAME:PWY-7689|) form the red pigments in Fusarium which contribute to the color of the fungal fruiting body, i.e. the perithecium, but are mutually exclusive as they are formed under different pH conditions |CITS:[Studt14]|. The gene cluster responsible for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18207| has not only been found in Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[19400779]| but has also been identified in rare strains of the fungus Botrytis cinerea |CITS:[23308280]|. It appears that the control of the |FRAME:CPD-18207| is negatively controlled by regulatory proteins of the velvet complex in the former species |CITS:[20572938]| whereas the latter species has been reported to be positively controlled by velvet |CITS:[23308280]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-18207| is realized by an gene cluster (bik) consisting of 6 genes (bik1 to bik6) of which only the first three (bik1 to bik3) are biosynthetically involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-18207|. , The initiating step of the |FRAME:PWY-7692| is catalyzed by the polyketide synthase bik1 which produces the first detectable and stable intermediate of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-18208| |CITS:[19400779]|. The molecular function of the bik1 encoded protein as pre-bikaverin synthase was demonstrated by gene deletion (Δbik1) which completely abolished the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18207| |CITS:[12409099]|, the restoration of the |FRAME:CPD-18207| production by adding back bik1 to the Δbik1 mutant |CITS:[19400779]| and biochemical assays of the heterologously expressed and purified pre-bikaverin synthase (bik1) which showed in vitro the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18208| from nine |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| starter units |CITS:[17696354]| and also appears as the first intermediate in vivo in double mutants (Δbik2bik3) which had bik1 overexpressed |CITS:[19400779]|. The decoration of |FRAME:CPD-18208| via hydroxylation (C-6 and C-7) and O-methylation (C-3 and C-8) is carried out by the FAD-dependent monooxygenase encoded by bik2 and the bikaverin O-methyltransferase encoded by bik3. Both functions have been shown through single gene deletion but biochemical assays to confirm the various reactions remain to be carried out. In addition, the order of the oxygenation and methylation steps is not resolved and awaits further exploration |CITS:[19400779]|., The regulation and expression of the genes bik1, bik2 and bik3 is complex and depends on various conditions, i.e. low nitrogen levels and an pH below 5.0 |CITS:[12409099] [19400779] [Giordano99]| but appears to be independent of the nitrogen regulatory protein AreA (see also |CITS:[19047398]|) and differently regulated by the pH-response transcription factor PacC |CITS:[19400779]|. In addition, the expression of bik1 is also time-dependent which pattern only coincides with the time-dependent expression pattern of the other biosynthetic genes in the cluster, i.e. bik2 and bik3 |CITS:[19400779]|.

The degradative pathway of |FRAME:TOLUENE| in |FRAME: ORG-5948| consists of two parts:, an upper pathway that converts toluene and xylene to their carboxylic acid derivatives, (this pathway, and see also |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5428|),, and a lower pathway that converts the (substituted) benzoic acids to Krebs cycle intermediates, (see |FRAME: PWY-5430|)., In the upper pathway, the methyl side chain of toluene is subjected to several progressive oxidations, to carboxylic acid, followed by an oxygenative cleavage of the aromatic ring., The upper pathway is induced by toluene, xylenes, and their alcohol derivatives. The , lower pathway is induced by benzoic acids, or by upper pathway substrates |CITS: [1176436]|., In |FRAME: ORG-5948|, the TOL plasmid pWW0 encodes all the enzymes responsible for the degradation, of toluene and xylene. The genes encoding these enzymes are organized into two operons,, the upper operon, which contains the first three enzymes in the pathway, and the meta operon,, which contains the genes responsible for the degradation of benzoates and toluates., In addition, some strains have integrated very similar genes in their chromosomes, where they have, aquired little mutation. For example, strains TW3 and 4NT have been shown to , express similar but chromosomally-encoded enzymes which catalyze the same pathway, |CITS: [8357257][8245826][9555884]|.

General Background, Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum)., The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids., Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|)., While the majority of bile acids (up to 97%) are reabsorbed in the ileum and return to the liver, the remaining 3% enter the large intestine, where they are modified by gut bacteria. The main modifications are C24-amide hydrolysis and 7α-dehydroxylation, which form the secondary bile acids |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| (see |FRAME: PWY-7754|). However, many additional transformations occur. Although |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| are the most abundant secondary bile acids, ~50 different secondary bile acids have been detected in human feces |CITS: [6631236]|., The most abundant bile acids in the healthy human gut after |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| are |FRAME: CPD-18796| and |FRAME: CPD-18797| (at about 50 μM). Iso-bile acids differ from bile acids in the configuration of their 3-hydroxy group (β instead of α). While the biological activities of iso-bile acids are not well understood, they have less detergent activity and are less toxic to bacteria |CITS: [26192599]|., About This Pathway, Early studies have shown that the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-84112| and |FRAME: TAX-1502| convert primary and secondary bile acids into their 3β isomers through 3-oxo intermediates |CITS: [4581568][6947718][6271056][2866156]|. The enzyme that converts the 3α-OH group into an oxo group was called 3α-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase |CITS: [201289][39496]|, while the enzyme that converts the oxo group to a 3β-OH group was named 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase |CITS: [Edenharder89]|. Both enzymes were dependent on nicotinamide cofactors, and enzymes depending on both NAD(H) and NADP(H) were described from different species. This pathway describes the NADP(H)-dependent enzymes, NAD(H)-dependent enzymes are described in |FRAME: PWY-7755|., Gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry analysis showed that the prominent gut bacterium |FRAME: TAX-411470| is also capable of synthesizing several iso-bile acids |CITS: [26192599]|., The genes encoding the relevant enzymes in |FRAME: TAX-411470| were found by searching for genes similar to those encoding |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.395| |CITS: [7766153][10698778][19464381]|. Six putative genes were identified, cloned with an N-terminal His6 tag, and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [26192599]|. Assays performed with cell lysates of the recombinant hosts identified one candidate bile acid 3α-dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-44400|) and one candidate bile acid 3β-dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-44402|). These enzymes were purified to homogeneity, and their activity was verified in vitro. Both enzymes preferred NADP(H) over NAD(H) |CITS: [26192599]|.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) can occur via two distinct routes: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway, such as this pathway) and the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (MEP pathway). In the former, IPP is synthesized from the condensation of three acetyl-CoA molecules; in contrast, in the MEP pathway IPP is synthesized via the condensation of pyruvate and D-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate., For many years, the MVA pathway was considered to be the sole source of IPP in all living organisms, until several inconsistencies led to the discovery of the MEP pathway in bacteria and plants. The MEP pathway is present in most eubacteria, in unicellular green algae, in the chloroplasts of phototrophic organisms and in some unicellular eukaryotes related to photosynthetic phyla, such as the Plasmodium parasites. , The mevalonate pathway is found in animals, fungi, the cytoplasm of phototrophic organisms, archaea, and some, eubacteria. A considerable variability exists among archaea, and at least four different variants of the MVA pathway have been described from that kingdom. The |FRAME: PWY-922 "eukaryotic variant"| is rare in archaea, but occurs in members of the order |FRAME: TAX-2281|, such as |FRAME: TAX-2287| |CITS: [23378249]|. While most archaea posses a variant now known as the |FRAME: PWY-8125 "archaeal pathway"| |CITS: [30224495]|, a |FRAME: PWY-6174 "third variant"| has been described from halophilic archaea such as |FRAME: TAX-2246| |CITS: [24375100]| (that pathway was also found in the eubacterium |FRAME: TAX-120962| |CITS: [24327557]|), and a |FRAME: PWY-7524 "fourth variant"| has been described from archaea of the order |FRAME: TAX-2301| |CITS: [24755225][25636853]|., About This Pathway, Early work with the methanogen |FRAME: TAX-2190| suggested that the archaeal mevalonate pathway is somewhat different from the eukaryotic/bacterial pathway. Initially it was not realized that multiple variants of the pathway exist among different archaeal taxonomic clades, leading to some confusion regarding the nature of the pathway in different archaeons., While earlier work has characterized a number of the involved enzymes |CITS: [10497066][16621811][21908638]|, the exact nature of this pathway (now known as the "archaeal" pathway) was established only in 2018, with the discovery of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.182| and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.126| |CITS: [30224495]|., This study established that the vast majority of archaeons possess this pathway, which involves the unique intermediate |FRAME: CPD-22924|., All mevalonate pathway variants that have been described share the first three reactions, leading from |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: MEVALONATE|. The next step, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.36|, is found in all organisms but the |FRAME: TAX-2301|. However, the path from |FRAME: CPD-499| to |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| varies greatly among the different variants.

Summary: |FRAME:TAX-2261| is a strict anaerobic archaeon, capable of utilizing pyruvate, sugars and complex , organic compounds as carbon and energy sources. It is a facultative sulfur-reducing species that is able to grow , in the absence of sulfur by fermentation of peptides, carbohydrates, and pyruvate. P. furiosus employs a , modified glycolytic pathway for the catabolism of sugars, as shown in the pathway link. There are two ADP-dependent , kinases, a glucokinase and a phosphofructokinase, and a tungsten-containing , |FRAME:MONOMER-11816| (GAPOR). GAPOR converts glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate , into 3-phosphoglycerate in a single reaction. The main products of sugar fermentation are acetate, alanine, carbon , dioxide, and hydrogen. |CITS: [11133967] [9783166] [Kengen96] [10762259] [9119024] [8530474] , [8830684] [7721730]|, Hydrogen is thought to be produced in the reactions involving GAPOR and pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase , via coupled reactions with ferredoxin:NADP oxidoreductase and ferredoxin-dependent hydrogenase. However, the , precise mechanism is not known. It has been postulated that the ferredoxin-dependent hydrogenase reaction , generates oxidized ferredoxin for reuse by these enzymes. However, under conditions of high hydrogen pressure, , hydrogenase activity is inhibited and alanine may be produced as a fermentation end product. Under these , conditions, oxidation of reduced ferredoxin produced by GAPOR has been postulated to occur via ferredoxin:NADP , oxidoreductase activity coupled with glutamate dehydrogenase and alanine aminotransferase reactions , (in |CITS: [11133967]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16233230]|)., A similar pathway leading from pyruvate to acetate has also been described in the human parasite, |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [13076]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10534 Ursodeoxycholate| (UDCA) is a bile acid that makes up a small percentage (< 5%) of the biliary pool in most healthy mammals. In most mammals it is a secondary bile acid, produced from primary bile acids by the action of intestinal bacteria. It is an important ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine, and has verified therapeutic benefits for the treatment of several ailments including cholestatic liver disease |CITS: [74722][7372061][7051912][16530513][17185355]| and colon cancer |CITS: [7923119][12839936][14747693]|., The name is derived from the Latin "ursus", which means bear, because it was originally discovered from the bile of the Polar bear (under the name ursocholeinsaure) |CITS: [Hammarsten01][Hammarsten02]|. Twenty-five years later, the compound was crystallized from a commercial preparation of bile of the Black bear, found to be an isomer of |FRAME: CPD-15189|, and named ursodeoxycholic acid |CITS: [Shoda27]|., Bears and the nutria (|FRAME: TAX-10157|) are the only mammals in which UDCA is a dominant primary biliary bile acid, being formed by hepatic enzymes |CITS: [Tammar70][Haslewood78][Hagey92]|. In all other species it appears to be a secondary bile acid, produced by bacteria from primary bile acids |CITS: [8263415]|., Even though UDCA is chemically synthesized by multiple companies, several countries in East Asia, including China, South Korea, Laos, Vietnam, and Myanmar, still use "bile bears" - bears that are kept in captivity and used for harvesting their bile by surgery. Bear farming is extremely inhumane and many bears die of illness such as chronic infections and liver cancer. Despite being illegal in some of these countries, bear bile farming still exists in all of those countries and is a significant problem |CITS: [15066772][19138420]|., In most mammals UDCA is a secondary bile acid, produced from primary bile acids by bacterial members of the gut microbiome. The bile acids are imported into the bacterium, converted, and then putatively exported |CITS: [8955384]|. In humans UDCA is a minor component of bile acids, making up about 5% of the biliary pool in healthy individuals., About This Pathway, The epimerization of |FRAME: CPD-15189| into |FRAME: CPD-10534| proceeds via a 7-oxo intermediate, and is catalyzed by two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.159|, and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.201|., |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.159| has been isolated and characterized from many organisms |CITS: [2007545][1856160][8050999][14756531][16307764][22198717][28193327]|. These enzymes usually exhibit robust activity., Unlike the former, only few examples of bioconversion with |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.201| have been reported in the literature. The human intestinal bacterium |FRAME: TAX-74426| was reported to catalyze the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-22298| to |FRAME: CPD-22299| |CITS: [16232971][16232975]|. An NADP+-dependent enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-29369| |CITS: [22198717]| was used in two different processes for the production of UDCA |CITS: [Bovara96][21526768]|. Another NADP+-dependent enzyme was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-74426|, but showed a significantly lower specific activity |CITS: [21181147]|. A third NADP+-dependent enzyme was isolated from |FRAME: ORG-6269| |CITS: [23729502]|, and an NAD+-dependent enzyme has been reported from |FRAME: TAX-40324|, although no sequence is available for it |CITS: [16307764]|. In many cases the purified enzymes catalyzed reactions that were either reversible |CITS: [7119570][3480890][21181147]| or favored in the oxidative direction |CITS: [6572075]| (and in |CITS: [23729502]|). In order to increase the activity and stability of these enzyme, protein engineering studies were carried out |CITS: [Hummel16][28116898]|., A promising candidate for the production of UDCA is the enzyme from |FRAME: ORG-6269|, a bacterium that was isolated from human feces and showed a growth-dependent conversion of |FRAME: CPD-17275| to |FRAME: CPD-10534|, with the reverse reaction undetectable. A |FRAME: MONOMER-19021| known to catalyze such a reaction was cloned, overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| and characterized. It was shown to strongly favor the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-17275| to |FRAME: CPD-10534| |CITS: [23729502]|., |FRAME: TAX-33038| is a core member of the human gut microbiome and its ability to produce the beneficial secondary bile acid |FRAME: CPD-10534| suggests an important role in host health |CITS: [15159320][20203603][23729502]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN actinomycins| are a family of bicyclic chromopeptide lactones with strong antineoplastic activity that are produced by various streptomycete strains |CITS: [16588723][18910692][ 24543239]|. The first actinomycin was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1890| in 1940, and was the first antibiotic obtained in pure form from an actinomycete |CITS: [Waksman40]|. |FRAME: ACTINOMYCIN-D "Actinomycin D"| was the first antibiotic shown to have anti-cancer activity |CITS: [13112124][4130354]|, and was approved as an anticancer drug in 1964, making it one of the oldest anticancer drugs. Actinomycin D inhibits transcription by binding DNA at the transcription initiation complex and preventing elongation of RNA chain by RNA polymerase |CITS: [ 2410919]|., A common feature of all actinomycins is the chromophoric moiety |FRAME: CPD-18447|, which is a unique phenoxazinone dicarboxylic acid to which two pentapeptide lactone rings are attached with amide linkages |CITS: [15395378][13505348][13790233]|., The precursor of |FRAME: CPD-18447| is |FRAME: CPD-403| (4-MHA), but actinocyn is not derived directly from it. Rather, phenoxazinone formation takes place by oxidative condensation of preformed |FRAME: CPD-18437 "4-MHA pentapeptide lactones"| |CITS: [6203903 ]|, a process that is believed to be catalyzed by phenoxazinone synthase (|FRAME: EC-1.10.3.4|) |CITS: [13440935][16584173]|., |FRAME: CPD-403 "3-Hydroxy-4-methyl-anthranilate"| is derived from |FRAME: TRP| as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7717|. It is subsequently adenylated by a non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) encoded by the |FRAME: G-44214| gene and transferred to a dedicated carrier protein, encoded by |FRAME: G-44211| |CITS: [10212227]|. From AcmD the compound is transferred to the different modules of two non-ribosomal peptide synthases encoded by |FRAME: G-44213| and |FRAME: G-44212|, where it is condensed with |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: GLY| and a second |FRAME: VAL|. The product is N-methylated twice using |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as the methyl donor, once at the glycine residue, generating |FRAME: SARCOSINE|, and once at the second valine residue, resulting in |FRAME: CPD0-1059|. Upon removal of the product from the NRPS, the N-methy-L-valine residue is condensed with the L-threonine residue, forming a cyclized pentapetide lactone., The question how are the peptide lactones dimerized is still an open one. The enzyme shown here, |FRAME: MONOMER-19511|, was first described in 1961 from |FRAME: TAX-1890| |CITS: [13784113]|. The enzyme was subsequently purified to homogeneity |CITS: [7305384]|, and analyses of the purified protein showed that it could catalyze the dimerization of |FRAME: CPD-403| (4-MHA) in vitro and that it displays little selectivity between this compound and 4-MHA peptides |CITS: [4180726][4118295]|., However, the gene was only identified in |FRAME: TAX-1890|, and repeated attempts to identify it in other actinomycin producers have been unsuccessful. When the |FRAME: G-44215| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1890| was disrupted and the resulting mutant was analyzed |CITS: [10770769]|, it was found that despite the absence of detectable PHS activity the mutant produced slightly more actinomycin than did the wild-type parent strain, suggesting that PhsA is not required for actinomycin biosynthesis. Sequence analysis suggests that role of PhsA in |FRAME: TAX-1890| may be involved in the process of pigmentation during spore formation |CITS: [10770769][19268377]|., The enzyme is currently shown in the pathway for |FRAME: PWY-7718| since it can catalyze the reaction in vitro and since no other enzyme is known to catalyze it. Yet, in most likelyhood the enzyme does not participate in the pathway in vivo.

Summary: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and potato (Solanum tuberosum) are staple vegetable crops which constitute a large part of the daily diet worldwide. Besides being a source for starch (energy), protein, fiber and vitamins, potato and tomato also contain specialized (secondary) metabolites with adverse nutritive properties |CITS:[17090106]|. Steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-17696| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-3|) and derivatives thereof are typically found in the Solanaceae family |CITS:[Ripperger98]| and considered antinutritional compounds |CITS:[23788733]|, which cannot completely be removed from food |CITS:[17090106]|. In certain concentrations or consumed by susceptible persons steroidal glycoalkaloids may be even toxic, causing digestive problems and hamper the absorption of nutrients |CITS:[22069686] [25556315]|. , On the other side, steroidal alkaloids have been reported to serve as phytoanticipins and provide a protective shield against pathogens of all kinds including bacteria and fungi and are even effective against animals and other plants |CITS:[Guntner97] [18944982] [18624637] [Hoagland09]|. Some fungal and bacterial pathogens have developed a detoxifying response towards steroidal glycoalkaloids by attacking the |FRAME:CPD-18735| moiety of |FRAME:CPD-17696|, a modification which may reduce the toxicity for the attackers (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-5 |) |CITS:[18944982] [10477313]|. In addition, tomato steroidal alkaloids such as the aglycon |FRAME:CPD-18644|, the glycosylated |FRAME:CPD-17696| and other Solanaceae glycoalkaloids have been proven to possess many beneficial traits for humans and exhibit anticarcinogenic, cardioprotective and immunostimulating properties (summarized in |CITS:[24079774] [25821990]|). , It has long been proposed and shown in feeding experiments that both steroidal alkaloids and non-nitrogenous steroidal saponins |CITS:[11783842] [21333312] [25217510]| may include |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| as intermediate metabolite (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-1|) |CITS:[Heftmann67] [Ronchetti75]| (summarized in |CITS:[Eich08]|). A positive correlation between sterols (|FRAME:CHOLESTEROL|) and glycoalkaloid biosynthesis has been observed in transgenic potato plants overexpressing essential enzymes involved in sterol biosynthesis, which strongly supports the view of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| serving as a branch point metabolite towards steroidal glycoalkaloids |CITS:[12692338]|. Glycosyltransferases and cytochrome P450 dependent oxygenases are known as enzymes central to the modification of specialized metabolites such as steroidal glycoalkaloids and terpenoid saponins |CITS:[10973093] [25951908]|. , The 10 genes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-13080| (this pathway) and further to |FRAME:CPD-17696| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-3|) in Solanum lycopersicum are mostly organized in gene clusters on chromosome 7 (6 genes) and chromosome 12 (2 genes) |CITS:[23788733]|. The first conversion of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| to |FRAME:CPD-14702| is part of a more complex reaction and has been shown to be possibly catalyzed by an cytochrome P450 dependent oxygenase named GAME7 (Glycoalkaloid metabolism = GAME) |CITS:[Umemoto12]| but detailed genetic and biochemical experiments are still outstanding. , The two cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases catalyzing the C-22 and C-26-hydroxylation have been characterized in Solanum tuberosum by downregulating the responsive genes (PGA2 and 1) and confirming the respective hydroxylation steps using recombinant expressed and purified PGA2, i.e. cholesterol 22-hydroxylase and PGA1. i.e. 22-hydroxycholesterol 26-hydroxylase |CITS:[27307258]|. Those steps in the pathway have also been elucidated by virus induced gene silencing (VIGS), transgenic plants and metabolic profiling as well as in vitro assays with purified recombinant enzymes. GAME8 silenced tomato plants accumulated |FRAME:CPD-14702| indicating that the encoded protein acts as 22-hydroxycholesterol 26-hydroxylase (cytochrome P450) and catalyzes the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18643| which is subsequently converted via a number of hitherto unknown reactions to |FRAME:CPD-18646|. One of the elucidated reactions immediately following the 22,26-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| is the hydroxylation of the 16α-position catalyzed by a steroid 16α-hydroxylase, which has been characterized from both Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum tuberosum |CITS:[28754839]|. , All the involved reactions are not yet completely understood but the participation of GAME 11 and GAME6 encoded proteins has been made plausible in respective mutants |CITS:[23788733]|. The cytochrome P450 dependent GAME4 encoded protein then oxidizes |FRAME:CPD-18646| to |FRAME:CPD-18645| which could be demonstrated in plants with either the silenced or the overexpressed GAME4 gene and concomitant metabolite profiling |CITS:[23788733]|. The |FRAME:CPD-18646| is also a possible metabolite from which pathway(s) towards steroidal saponins such as |FRAME:CPD-18759| branches out. , The reaction mechanism of the following transamination of |FRAME:CPD-18645| to form |FRAME:CPD-18644| catalyzed by the GAME12 encoded furostanol 26-aldehyde transaminase |CITS:[23788733]| has been confirmed by feeding experiments of stable isotope labeled compounds |CITS:[23473422]|. The reaction that generates |FRAME:CPD-13080| has not yet been elucidated but the subsequent series of glycosylations adding the |FRAME:CPD-18735| to |FRAME:CPD-17697| could be experimentally verified (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-3|). It appears that the recently described GAME25 extends the biosynthetic sequence beyond the formation of |FRAME:CPD-13080| towards |FRAME:CPD-22270|. GAME25 belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family and has been demonstrated to exhibit dual activities, one as 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and the other as Δ5,4 isomerase. The GAME25 catalyzed reaction is however just one out of three reactions that convert unsaturated steroidal alkaloids (SG) towards saturated SGs. While the remaining two reductase reactions remain to be elucidated, the blocking of the GAME25 is already sufficient to redirect the formation of saturated SGAs towards the unsaturated SGAs. However, some of the cultivated species such as potato and eggplant have lost the ability to form saturated SGAs such as |FRAME:CPD-22270|. Although the GAME25 encoded protein still works in potato, the remaining reactions might not, which prevents the formation of saturated SGAs in cultivated potato, an ability that wild species still possess |CITS:[29784829]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD1F-135 Neoxanthin| is an allenic xanthophyll recognized as the last product of carotenoid synthesis in green plants |CITS: [11029576 ]|., Neoxanthin is believed to play two key roles:, i) it is a part of the light-harvesting complex (LHC), ii) it is a precursor to the plant growth hormone |FRAME: CPD-693 "abscisic acid"| (ABA) |CITS: [11094161]|., Loss of neoxanthin in parasitic plants like Cuscuta, and its impact on LHC, is under investigations |CITS: [ 14610095]|., |FRAME: MONOMER-16625 "Neoxanthin synthase"| catalyzes the conversion of the di-epoxidated precursor |FRAME: CPD1F-133| into |FRAME: CPD1F-135|. The enzyme has been isolated from land plants such as |FRAME: TAX-4113 "Solanum tuberosum (potato)"| and |FRAME: TAX-4081 Solanum lycopersicum (tomato)"| |CITS: [ 11029576]| and several Chromalveolate algae such as the diatom |FRAME: TAX-2850| |CITS: [32181334]|.

Summary: Chlorobenzenes are used in the production of pesticides, dyes, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, rubbers, plastics,, and electric goods |CITS: [11472925]|. Their occurrence in the environment is widespread and they are, found in the atmosphere |CITS: [10864157]|, water |CITS: [3314709][16157172]|, soil |CITS: [17988797][2695324]|,, sediments |CITS: [15694470]|, vegetables |CITS:[16002141]|, and animals |CITS: [15325147]|., Chlorobenzenes are of great concern because of their toxicity, persistence and accumulation in the food chain,, and many of them have been declared, priority pollutants, by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)., Two important chlrobenzene compounds, |FRAME: CPD-9009| and |FRAME: CPD-10603|, are degraded via, |FRAME: 35-DICHLOROCATECHOL|. This catechol is subsequently degraded to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| in a modified, ortho cleavage pathway, as described in this pathway., Several bacterial species were reported to possess the pathway, including, |FRAME:TAX-264198| |CITS:[14676989]|, |FRAME:TAX-393999| |CITS:[11526005]|, |FRAME:TAX-65741| |CITS:[Schwien88]|,, |FRAME: TAX-244562| |CITS: [12089027]|, |FRAME: TAX-69003| |CITS: [8779585]|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| |CITS:[11572451]|,, |FRAME:TAX-140098| |CITS: [11368916]| and |FRAME: ORG-6081| |CITS: [16030237]|., The enzymes catalyzing this pathway have been studied and characterized from several organisms |CITS:[Schwien88], [2013566]|. They are usually encoded by transmissible plasmids, such as the pJP4 plasmid of |FRAME: TAX-264198|, or the pB13 plasmid of |FRAME: TAX-65741|., The catechol is attacked by a |FRAME: MONOMER-14417| that opens the ring, generating |FRAME: CPD-10632|., |FRAME: CPLX-7702| catalyzes a reaction that combines isomerization to a lactone with the loss of one of the chlorine, atoms. In |FRAME:TAX-65741| the lacton that is produced is in the trans form, and is isomerized to a cis, form by a |FRAME: MONOMER-14432|. It is not clear if this occurs in other organisms as well |CITS: [Schwien88]|., The lactone is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: 2-CHLOROMALEYLACETATE| by a hydrolase. Finally, ther last enzyme, of the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-7708|, catalyzes two successive reductions, during which the second chlorine atom is, lost. Summary: The 2-keto acid |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is a common intermediate in the degradation of organic acids. For example, both |FRAME: THR| and |FRAME: MET| are catabolized  into |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| (see |FRAME:THREOCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: METHIONINE-DEG1-PWY|)., |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be further metabolized to at least three possible products: |FRAME: 2-Aminobutyrate|,, |FRAME:CPD-3564|, or by oxidative decarboxylation, |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|., The oxidative decarboxylation of 2-keto acids such as |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to their acyl coenzyme A (acyl-CoA) derivatives is a key reaction of intermediary metabolism in virtually all organisms and is catalyzed by two types of |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| (TPP)-containing enzymes., Most aerobic organisms contain large, multienzyme complexes which function as 2-keto acid dehydrogenases. These contain |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| and |FRAME: FLAVIN| as prosthetic groups, use |FRAME: NAD| as an electron acceptor, and have been extensively studied (see |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-5046| and |FRAME: PWY-5084|). Apparently, no such dehydrogenase is specific for |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|. Rather, both |FRAME:PYRUVDEHYD-PWY| and |FRAME:PWY-5046| are able to accept it as a substrate |CITS: [3718468]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5130|)., In contrast, anaerobic organisms, as well as some aerobic archaea, utilize a different enzyme family, 2-keto acid oxidoreductases, to carry out the same reaction. Unlike the dehydrogenases, these enzymes contain iron-sulfur (FeS) clusters, lack both |FRAME: FLAVIN| and |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID|, and use redox proteins such as ferredoxin or flavodoxin as electron acceptors. Once again, there does not appear to be a |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|-specific enzyme., The most common 2-keto acid oxidoreductases are the |FRAME: PYRUFLAVREDUCT-RXN "pyruvate oxidoreductases"| (PORs). These enzymes have been purified from a variety of microorganisms and can be classified into four groups based on their subunit compositions (for example see |FRAME: CPLX-62| from |FRAME: TAX-1488|)., 2-keto acid oxidoreductase which are able to utilize substrates other than pyruvate are less common. These include |FRAME: 1.2.7.8-RXN "indolepyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase"| (IOR), which preferentially use the transaminated forms of aromatic amino acids as substrates, |FRAME: 1.2.7.7-RXN "2-ketoisovalerate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase"| (VOR), which prefers the transaminated forms of branched-chain amino acids, and |FRAME: 2-OXOGLUTARATE-SYNTHASE-RXN "2-oxoglutarate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase"| (KGOR), which accepts mostly |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|  as substrate |CITS: [8830683]|., However, several 2-keto acid oxidoreductases, including the |FRAME:CPLX-7029| from |FRAME: TAX-273063|, have been shown to accept a broad range of substrates, including |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| |CITS: [8902625][8620891]|.

Summary: Members of the |FRAME: TAX-29465| genus belong to the |FRAME: TAX-909932| class. Even though the negativicutes are genetically part of the Gram-positive |FRAME: TAX-1239| phylum, they have a peculiar cell wall with a lipopolysaccharide outer membrane that stains Gram-negative., |FRAME: TAX-29466| is a strict anaerobe found in the gut and oral cavity. It is not able to utilize sugars, and instead ferments organic acid produced as by-products by carbohydrate-processing organisms. Its main carbon and energy source is |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, which it ferments to |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: PROPIONATE|, as well as small amount of hydrogen gas., The pathway starts with |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.27| that works in the opposite direction to that usually found in fermenting bacteria, producing |FRAME: PYRUVATE| from |FRAME: L-LACTATE|. The pathway splits at this point - |FRAME: PYRUVATE| could be targeted to |FRAME: ACET| production via the action of |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.54| (see |FRAME: PWY-5485|), or it could be carboxylated to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| by |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|, leading to production of |FRAME: PROPIONATE|., Unlike the propanoate-forming fermentation pathway found in propionic acid bacteria (see |FRAME: P108-PWY|), the pathway found in |FRAME: TAX-29466| does not involve the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|. Summary: General Background, Verbascose and ajugose are two members of the so-called 'raffinose series' of sucrosyl oligosaccharides (also known as raffinose family oligosaccharides, RFOs). Members of the raffinose series occur at least in traces in each plant family; it is one of the most widespread sucrosyl oligosaccharide series in flowering plants and might even be ubiquitous (see |CITS:[KANDLER82]| for review). This series comprises |FRAME:CPD-1099|, |FRAME:CPD-170|, |FRAME:CPD-8065|,|FRAME:CPD-8066| as well as several other compounds with a higher degree of polymerization (DP; the highest is a nonasaccharide; none of these higher-DP oligosaccharides in the series have not yet been named). The sugars of this series consist of α1,6-linked chains of D-galactose attached to the 6-glucosyl position of sucrose. They are synthesized in leaves, roots and tubers. Raffinose and stachyose are the two most commonly found oligosaccharides of this series (see |FRAME:PWY-5337|). However, higher RFOs with DP are also found in certain species such as the frost-hardy |FRAME:TAX-38596|, in which both short-chain and long-chain RFOs are present and have been speculated to act as antifreeze or antisalt agents |CITS:[12232288],[12228647],[12223871],[10758476]|. This enzyme, galactinol:raffinose galactosyltransferase, catalyzes the chain elongation of RFOs by transferring the α-galactosyl residue of galactinol to RFO molecules. The enzyme appears to be primarily a stachyose synthase catalyzing the galactosylation of raffinose into stachyose. However, it was shown to also use stachyose and verbascose as substrates.
