These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, Methane is produced in large quanitities from coal beds. The global reserves of coal methane in 2014 were estimated at 50 trillion m3, which is equal to 11% of conventional natural gas resources. Isotope-based studies suggest that 40% of coal bed methane produced in the United States is of microbial origin |CITS: [Strapoc11]|. Methanogenesis from coal tends to occur in immature coal rather than in mature coal |CITS: [Jones08]|., Coal is an extremely complex material derived from lignin monolignols, which are often substituted with hydroxyl, methoxy, and carboxyl groups. Methoxy groups are particularly abundant in immature coal raising the possibility of methanogenesis from methoxy groups. The possibility of methoxylated aromatic compounds serving as substrates for methylotrophic methanogens was studied in 2016, revealing that strains of |FRAME: TAX-660064| do indeed possess the potential of using such compounds for methanogenesis. The organisms were tested with 40 commercially available methoxylated aromatic compounds and could use used 35 of them |CITS: [27738170]|., A 2021 study uncovered the genes and enzymes involved in the novel methanogenesis pathway. An extensive genome analysis of |FRAME: TAX-660064| identified an operon encoding a putative methyltransferase complex of unknown specificity that has previously been overlooked. The operon includes a corrinoid protein (|FRAME: BP07_RS03260|), three methyltransferases (|FRAME: BP07_RS03240|, |FRAME: BP07_RS03255|, and |FRAME: BP07_RS03250|) and a corrinoid activator protein (mtoD), and is distantly related to known methanogen methyltransferase components., The corrinoid protein MtoC, as well as the MtoB1/2 methyltransferases were much more similar to the MtvC corrinoid protein and |FRAME: G-107542 "MtvB methyltransferase"| of the homoacetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1525|, which are involved in demethylation of methoxylated aromatic compounds |CITS: [11344134][18631365]|, suggesting that the archaeal operon was acquired through horizontal gene transfer from Bacteria |CITS: [34145392]|., Like in other methanogenesis pathways the methyl group is transferred from the substrates to a corrinoid methyl-carrier protein (MtoC). The organisms have two methyltransferases capable of catalyzing the transfer, with specificities towards different substrates, enabling a wider substrate range. Unlike other methanogenesis pathways from methylated substrates, the methyl group is not transferred from the corinoid protein directly to |FRAME: CoM|, but is transferred first to |FRAME: THMPT|, from which it is transferred to CoM., Similar gene clusters encoding demethoxylation systems were found in a number of non-methanogenic archaea, such as members of the phyla Bathyarchaeota, Lokiarchaeota, Korarchaeota, Helarchaeota, Verstraetearchaeota and Nezhaarchaeota, suggesting that methoxydotrophic growth might play an underestimated role in the global carbon cycle. The ability to grow with methoxylated aromatic compounds was demonstrated for |FRAME: TAX-2234| (see |FRAME: PWY-8305|) |CITS: [34145392]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-9436 Isoprene| is a volatile compound produced by many plants. The yearly production of isoprene emissions by vegetation is around 600 million tons (with half of it coming from tropical broadleaf trees), making it about a third of all hydrocarbons released into the atmosphere, and on the same scale as the global emission of |FRAME: CH4| |CITS: [Guenther06]|. Isoprene plays an important role in atmospheric chemistry, being involved in the generation of |FRAME: CPD-19034| and |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| |CITS: [1317061]|., Microbial degradation appears to provide a significant sink for atmospheric isoprene. It has been shown that bacteria consume isoprene even when present at trace concentrations |CITS: [16349477]|. Like the case of all other alkenes (see |FRAME: PWY-7776| and |FRAME: PWY-5534|), the degradation of isoprene starts with a monooxygenase that oxidizes it to an epoxide |CITS: [van-Ginkel87]|., Epoxides contain an oxirane ring that makes them highly reactive electrophilic molecules, and are thus quite toxic to the cells. Depending on the organism, the epoxides are processed in several ways. Some organisms use glutathione and an enzyme such as |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.34|, to attack and open the oxirane ring |CITS: [10715003]|. Other organisms have been shown to use the unusual cofactor |FRAME:CoM| |CITS: [10411892]|, yet others use epoxide hydrolases |CITS: [25576605]|. The products of these reactions are then catabolized to central metabolites |CITS: [11352719]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-103808| was isolated from freshwater sediment for its capability to use |FRAME: CPD-9436| as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [9687433]|. Following the initial attack on isoprene by a monooxygenase enzyme, the organism employs a dedicated glutatione S-transferase to conjugate the epoxide product with |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, forming |FRAME: CPD-19029| |CITS: [9687433][10094686]|. The alcohol function of the conjugate is then sequentially oxidized by an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase, first to an aldehyde, and then a carboxylate |CITS: [10094686]|.

Summary: General background, C-type cytochromes (cytC) are electron-transfer proteins that have one or more |FRAME: HEME_C| groups. They are characterized by the covalent attachment of the heme to the polypeptide chain via two (or rarely one) thioether bonds formed between thiol groups of cysteine residues and vinyl groups of a |FRAME: PROTOHEME| molecule. The two cysteine residues almost always occur in the amino-acid sequence CXXCH |CITS: [10647174]|., C-type cytochromes possess a wide range of properties and function in a large number of different redox processes. In general, the differences in c-type cytochromes among bacteria are much larger than those among animal species. The use of the term term "c-type cytochromes" was introduced to distinguish this family of diverse proteins from the well-characterized mitochondrial protein, which is often referred to as "cytochrome c"., Bacterial c-type cytochromes function in the electron transport chains of bacteria with many different types of energy metabolism, including phototrophs, methylotrophs, denitrifiers, sulfate reducers and the nitrogen-fixers. , The biogenesis of c-type cytochromes involves covalent attachment of |FRAME: PROTOHEME| to two cysteines at a conserved CXXCH sequence in the apocytochrome. The histidine residue acts as an axial ligand to the heme iron., Three unique cytochrome c assembly pathways, known as systems I, II, and III, have been described. This pathway describes system I, which is found in archaea, α-proteobacteria, γ-proteobacteria, some β- and some δ-proteobacteria, Deinococci, plant mitochondria, and in mitochondria from some protozoa (such as |FRAME: TAX-5884|, |FRAME: TAX-48482| and |FRAME: TAX-5890|) |CITS: [19721088]|., About This Pathway, System I is the most complex pathway for c-type cytochrome biogenesis. Components of this system were discovered in the late 1980s and early 1990s, mostly in the α-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-1060| |CITS: [2536664][1310666][8384715][8752349]|, |FRAME: TAX-265 Paracoccus| |CITS: [7746152][9220005][9043133][10589712]|, and |FRAME: TAX-379| |CITS: [1850420][7715601]|. However, due to the complexity of the process, some of the transformations are still being studied 30 years later |CITS: [28634234]|., It is easier to describe system I as two different processes: the first one is the formation and release of a complex of oxidized (Fe3+-containing) heme bound to the CcmE protein, while the second one describes the reduction (potentially by membrane quinols) of the heme and its attachment to the apo-cytochrome protein., Process 1: This part of the pathway is catalyzed by the CcmABCDE proteins. |FRAME: EG12057 CcmC| is a membrane protein with 6 transmembrane domains and a periplasmic WWD domain, which binds heme. Reduced heme, which is produced in the cytosol by |FRAME: EC-4.98.1.1|, crosses the membrane, presumably via CcmC, and binds to the WWD domain, concomitant with binding of |FRAME: EG12055 CcmE|, forming a heme/CcmC/CcmD/CcmE complex. It has been shown that CcmC is sufficient to bring heme to CcmE |CITS: [9560218][10339610]|. This is followed by a spontaneous covalent attachment of the 2-vinyl group of the heme molecule to a histidine residue of CcmE |CITS: [9712585][15465823][15771504][16373344][17142277]|. The binding process also involves the oxidation of the heme's iron to Fe3+., The next step involves the binding of the |FRAME: EG12059 CcmA| and |FRAME: EG12058 CcmB| proteins to the complex, prompting ATP hydrolysis and release the heme-CcmE complex (holoCcmE) |CITS: [16824107][17419738]|. CcmA and CcmB are very similar to the ATP-binding and membrane protein of ABC (ATP-binding cassette)-type transporters, respectively, prompting earlier suggestions that they are involved in heme transport. However, it is now accepted that their role is the release of holoCcmE rather than heme transport |CITS: [19721088]|. During the release the heme axial ligands switch from the histidine residues in CcmC to a tyrosine residue in CcmE, suggesting major conformational movements following CcmAB binding, which is typical for ABC-type transporters., Process 2: The roles of holocytochrome c synthase include reducing both the heme molecule (from Fe3+ to Fe2+) and the cysteine residues of the apo-cytochrome, followed by ligation of the two. The complex consists of |FRAME: EG12052 CcmH|, which is involved in the reduction of the cysteine residues of the apocytochrome, and |FRAME: EG12054 CcmF|, which is responsible for reduction of the heme molecule and its attachement to one of the reduced cysteines of the apocytochrome., Like protoheme, the apo-cytochrome is synthesized in the cytosol and needs to be exported into the periplasm (the transport is conducted via the |FRAME: SEC-SECRETION-CPLX|). Once in the periplasm, the polypeptide is exposed to the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.15|, which oxidizes its active thiols forming a disulfide bridge., Once liberated from the complex, holoCcmE is free to interact with |FRAME: EG12054-MONOMER CcmF|. CcmF contains a WWD domain in its periplasmic region (two conserved histidine residues, His173 and His303, flanking a tryptophan rich region) that binds the heme delivered by holoCcmE |CITS: [24397552]|. In addition. CcmF contains another heme molecule, a β-heme bound non-covalently via His261 and His491, which reside in the transmembrane region. The β-heme can be reduced by ubiquinol-1 and dimethylquinone, suggesting that its physiological role may be to pass the electrons from the membrane quinol pool to the Fe3+-containing heme of holoCcmE, reducing it to the Fe2+ valency |CITS: [19629033][22066495]|., Two thiol:disulfide oxidoreductases, encoded by the |FRAME: EG12053| and |FRAME: EG12052| genes, have been known for many years to be involved in c-type cytochrome biogenesis. However, specifying the exact reactions catalyzed by the two enzymes has proved challenging. A study of CcmG in 2001 has found that a mutation in |FRAME: EG12053| cannot be compensated by a second mutation in the disulfide-bond-forming proteins |FRAME: EG11297 DsbA| and |FRAME: EG11393 DsbB|, or by chemical reductants. The oxidized form of CcmG accumulated in |FRAME: EG12054| and |FRAME: EG12052| mutants, suggesting that CcmG functions later than CcmF and CcmH in cytochrome c assembly. The authors proposed three alternative models to explain their observation, with the preferred one including a disulfide formation between CcmG and CcmH |CITS: [11256948]|., A much later study from 2017 has found that CcmG is best suited to reduce directly and efficiently the disulfide bond of apocytochrome c (CcmH could also carry out this task, but slower than CcmG). In addition, CcmG could rapidly resolve a mixed disulfide between CcmH and apocytochrome c. The authors concluded that the most likely scenario is that CcmG is the enzyme that initially reduces apocytochrome c. One of the reduced cysteine residues then attacks Cys-45 of oxidized CcmH, yielding a CcmH(Cys-45)--(Cys-34) apocytochrome c mixed disulfide (as has been suggested in the 2001 study), leaving Cys-37 of apocytochrome c available to form a thioether bond with the vinyl-4 of heme, which is still attached to CcmE. This mixed disulfide bond is then be resolved by reduced CcmG, initially forming a CcmG-(Cys-75)--(Cys-45)-CcmH mixed disulfide, which is resolved when the second cysteine residue of CcmG attacks Cys-75, yielding an oxidized CcmG, which is reduced back to its active state by |FRAME: EG12178 DsbD|., According to this model, the {apocytochrome c]-Cys-37–heme vinyl-4 thioester bond is formed first, while the second thioether bond (between Cys-34 of apocytochrome c and the heme vinyl-2) is formed later, only upon resolution of the CcmE-heme-apocytochrome c complex intermediate. By forming only a single heme-thiol bond initially, the mechanism ensures stereo-specificity during cytochrome c maturation |CITS: [28634234]|.

Names: icosapentaenoate biosynthesis I (lower eukaryotes) // eicosapentaenoate biosynthesis I (lower eukaryotes)
Summary: General Background, Polyunsaturated |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "long-chain fatty acids"| (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear., These compounds are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturatedare very long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. , Polyunsaturated very long chain fatty acids are also found in mammals. In humans |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| are precursors of the regulatory molecules eicosanoids, which are involved in many cellular functions including vascular permeability, inflammation, regulation of immune system, blood clotting, neurotransmission and cholesterol metabolism., |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Eicosapentaenoate| (EPA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains five cis double bonds, one of which is located at the third carbon from the omega end, which makes it an omega-3 fatty acid. EPA is produced by microalgae and is common in fish who eat the algae, although the fish can not produce it. It is also produced by mosses and ferns, but is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. EPA is also produced by some marine bacteria, mostly those adapted to low temperatures and high pressures, via a completely different pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7050|) |CITS: [10220156]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| in the moss |FRAME: TAX-3218| starts with |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (see |FRAME: PWY-5997| for the first part) and involves sequential Δ6 desaturation, elongation, and a Δ5 desaturation., An acyl-lipid 6-desaturase was identified and cloned in |FRAME: TAX-3218| |CITS: [9744093]|, as were a Δ6-acyl-CoA elongase |CITS: [12164806]| and an acyl-lipid 5-desaturase |CITS: [16728405]|. The Δ5 and Δ6 desaturases are front-loading desatrurases, meaning that they introduce the new double bonds based on the distance from the carboxyl end of the fatty acid. Unlike mamalian Δ5 and Δ6 desaturases, which act on acyl-coAs, the enzymes from lower plants, fungi, worms and algae prefer to act on fatty acids that are incorporated at the sn-2 position of glycerolipids |CITS: [12835316]|. The elongase, on the other hand, acts on coenzyme A-linked substrates. Thus, following the Δ6 desaturation the fatty acids have to be transferred from a lipid to CoA for elongation, after which they are transferred back to a lipid for the Δ5 desaturation |CITS: [12835316]|.

Glycolate is an indirect product of the Calvin cycle, resulting from the hydrolysis of phosphoglycolate, a product of the oxidation of ribulose 1,5 bisphosphate (see |FRAME: PWY-181|). Glycolate can be metabolized by both anaerobic and aerobic heterotrophic bacteria. The Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-214819| is capable of fermenting glycolate in pure culture in the absence of external electron acceptors |CITS: [12658332]|., |FRAME: TAX-214819| is capable of growth on either glycolate or fumarate, resulting in the production of acetate, succinate, and CO<sub>2</sub> as the end-products |CITS: [12658332]|. Other anaerobic bacteria have been isolated which are capable of growth on glycolate, but they couple the oxidation  of glycolate with the reduction of external electron acceptors, such as sulfate (e.g., the sulfate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-51195|), O<sub>2</sub> (e.g., the homoacetogenic bacterium |FRAME:TAX-1525|), and protons (e.g., the syntophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-51197|), which produced hydrogen in the process |CITS: [12658332]|., |FRAME: TAX-214819| does not form H<sub>2</sub> during growth on glycolate, and is able to grow in pure culture without syntrophic H<sub>2</sub> transfer |CITS: [12658332]|. The enzymes involved in glycolate metabolism by |FRAME: TAX-214819|  have yet to be identified as of April 2003 |CITS: [12658332]|.

Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|). Analogs for these pathways are also found in the metabolism of deoxyhexoses such as |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-fucoses| (see |FRAME: PWY-6714| and |FRAME: PWY-8318|)., About This Pathway, The earlier steps of this pathway have been characterized from multiple bacterial species, as they are common to all three routes of the third type of pathways. The last two steps, which are specific for this route, were characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-863372| |CITS: [30655589]|.

Summary: Some strains of |FRAME: TAX-287| can grow with |FRAME: LYS| as the sole source of carbon and energy. Growth rate is usually slow, but mutants that are able to grow at a high speed spontaneously occur., The pathway employed by these organisms differs from those reported previously in other species of Pseudomonas (see |FRAME: PWY-5280| and |FRAME: PWY-5283|)., The early steps in this pathway are identical to those described in |FRAME: PWY0-461|: |FRAME: LYS| is decarboxylated to |FRAME: CADAVERINE|, which is converted to |FRAME: CPD-12763|, |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE|, |FRAME: CPD-280|, and |FRAME: GLUTARATE|. However, in this pathway the latter is activated to |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA|, leading to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, thus providing carbon and energy to the bacteria |CITS: [405455]|. In |FRAME: PWY0-461| |FRAME: GLUTARATE| is converted to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, and thus in that pathway lysine can only serve as nitrogen source., The enzymatic activities associated with this pathway were characterized from cell extracts of cells grown on L-lysine  |CITS: [405455]|. In addition, the identity of genes that encode a few of the enzymes has been discovered using computational analysis, and their function was verified biochemically |CITS: [17388807]|., Studies with mutants unable to grow on L-lysine supported the existence of more than one catabolic pathway for L-lysine in |FRAME: TAX-287|. All the pathways converge at |FRAME: GLUTARATE|, which is catabolyzed to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [405455]|., This pathway was also demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-294| |CITS: [405455]| and |FRAME: TAX-176299| |CITS: [33154364]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN Cardiolipin| is an anionic membrane phospholipid. Along with |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol|, the anionic lipids are important for the biogenesis and function of membranes. Cardiolipin is present in the plasma membrane of bacteria and in the mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes., A main difference exists between bacterial and eukaryotic cardiolipin biosynthesis; In bacteria cardiolipin is formed by the condensation of two molecules of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol|, while in eukaryotes it is formed from one molecule of |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL CDP-diacylglycerol|  and one molecule of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol|., In all eukaryotes, cardiolipin biosynthesis occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane |CITS: [15811335]|. In mung bean mitochondria, the |FRAME: MONOMER-12278| activity is much higher than the |FRAME: MONOMER-12277| activity, resulting in a quick turn over of phosphatidylglycerolphosphate to phosphatidylglycerol |CITS: [12232283]|. In fact, phosphatidylglycerolphosphate is not detected in mitochondrial membranes of mung beans., It is noteworthy that, in addition to being synthesized in mitochondria, phosphatidylglycerol may also be imported from the endoplasmic reticulum to serve as the cardiolipin precursor |CITS: [12609031]|., The reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-12277| is the rate-limiting step of cardiolipin biosynthesis.

Names: rotenoid biosynthesis I // rotenone and amorphigenin biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Rotenoid compounds are a class of plant secondary metabolites that derive from isoflavones. They are commonly found in leguminous species, but also occur in other families, such as the Iridiceae (see refs in |CITS: [11711058]|). These compounds play a role in plant interactions with insects |CITS: [Birch85]|. But, they have also been extracted for use by humans. Rotenone, perhaps the most commonly known member of the family, has a long history of use as a fish poison |CITS: [Leonard39]|, and it is also the major bioactive component of a commerically available insecticide |CITS: [16332203]|. Rotenone is also used in scientific experiments due to its ability to interfere with the electron transport chain |CITS: [4295606]| and it can also interfere with tubulin self-assembly |CITS: [568944]|. Other studies suggest that rotenone can promote Parkinson's Disease |CITS: [18155613]|. However, several rotenoids also have medicinal qualities. For example, amorphigenin |CITS: [8350086]|, |FRAME: CPD-12163|, and alpha-toxicarol |CITS: [14765285], [17125241]| seem to have anti-tumor effects., About This Pathway, Rotenone and amorphigenin are two closely related rotenoid compounds that have been studied in Derris elliptica and |FRAME: TAX-48131|, though they can be produced by other species |CITS: [11711058], [17125241], [14733510]|. An extensive series of radiotracer studies have elucidated the primary steps in the synthesis of rotenone and amorphigenin as they progress through the early stages of the isoflavone synthesis, and then undergo rotenoid-specific prenylation and cyclization steps. The biosynthesis of the common precursor to several rotenoids is depicted in |FRAME: PWY-6427|, whereas the specific steps required to produce several rotenoids identified in |FRAME: TAX-48131| are shown here. Several other rotenoid compounds can be generated through modifications of rotenone, amorphigenin, or their precursors |CITS: [11711058]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain. Recent, findings suggest that GABA has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well |CITS: [15003233]|. In animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: GLUTDECARBOX-RXN "glutamate decarboxylase"|., The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|. Diiferent variants of both enzymes are known. The amino-group acceptor for the transamination can be either |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|) or |FRAME:PYRUVATE| (e.g. in the plant |FRAME: ORG-5862| |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|). Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+., The action of glutamate decarboxylase, γ-aminobutyrate aminotransferase and succinate semialdehyde, dehydrogenase, combined, defines a short pathway known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. , While there is no evidence for a special role for GABA in bacteria, the capabillity to degrade it exists in many strains. GABA is present in the environment as a product of plant and animal tissue decay, and many bacteria can synthesize GABA as an intermediate in the degradation of putrescine (see |FRAME: Putrescine-Degradation "putrescine degradation"|). , The first indication for a bacterial pathway for GABA degradation was found in |FRAME: TAX-294|, |CITS:[13654294][13654295]|. While some organisms, like |FRAME: TAX-294|, can grow on GABA as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, others, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, can grow on it only as a nitrogen source |CITS: [8951816][12123465]|., About This Pathway, This variant of the pathway includes a |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent 4-aminobutyrate transaminase and an NAD(P)+-dependent dehydrogenase., This combination of enzymes has been documented in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-381666| |CITS: [19648235]| and in Baker's yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [3888627]|. Another study of |FRAME: TAX-106590| (Ralstonia eutropha) showed that the bacterium posseses two different dehydrogenases - an NAD(P)-specific one, and an NADP-specific one |CITS: [10564790]|., In |FRAME: TAX-4932| GABA plays an important role in nitrogen utilization and oxidative stress tolerance |CITS: [11031268][3888627]|. GABA accumulates in |FRAME: TAX-4932| either through permease-mediated uptake (by Uga4p,, Put4p, and Gap1p), or by intracellular production via |FRAME:GLT| degradation, catalyzed by the |FRAME: YMR250W-MONOMER| Gad1p |CITS: [11031268][3888627]| (see |FRAME: PWY0-1305|)., The presence of GABA causes an increase in expression of the genes |FRAME: YGR019W| and |FRAME: YBR006W|, which encode the enzymes responsible for degrading GABA into |FRAME: SUC| |CITS:[3888627]|., This GABA-induced upregulation is mediated by the transcriptional activators Uga3p and Uga35p/Dal81p |CITS:[2653828]|. These transcription factors bind to upstream activation sites in the promoters of GABA-regulated genes known as the UAS-GABA |CITS:[12235130][2653828]|., The level of |FRAME: YBR006W| transcript is also upregulated under conditions of oxidative stress |CITS:[11031268]|. |FRAME: TAX-4932| cells in which GABA degradation is blocked are more sensitive to oxidative stress and can no longer grow on GABA as their sole nitrogen source |CITS:[11031268][3888627]|., An alternative route for GABA catabolism in |FRAME: TAX-4932| has been proposed |CITS: [19411412]|. that pathway involves the reduction of succinate-semialdehyde into |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE| and its polymerization to form poly-(3-hydroxybutyric acid-co-4-hydroxybutyric acid).

Summary: Background, During fermentative growth, formate is produced via |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.54| (pyruvate formate lyase, PFL) from pyruvate. The physiological function of the |FRAME: FHLMULTI-CPLX "formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex"| reaction is to prevent acidification of the cytoplasm by converting formate to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| and the FHL complex can effectively function at a pH lower than 7.0. Recently, a potential second |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolving hydrogenase Hyd-4 encoded by the hyf operon was identified in |FRAME:TAX-562|. This system has been designated FHL-2 and is driven by the F0F1-ATPase and is composed of Hyd4 and FdhH. Hydrogen production via the Hyd-3 and Fdh-H-dependent pathway versus the Hyd-4, Fdh-H and F0F1-ATPase-dependent pathway has been shown to be pH dependent |CITS: [11959127]|. , About this Pathway, |FRAME: FORMATEDEHYDROGH-MONOMER "Formate dehydrogenase H"| (FDH) and |FRAME: HYDROG3-CPLX| together form the membrane |FRAME: FHLMULTI-CPLX| (FHL-1) of |FRAME: TAX-562|. It oxidizes endogenously produced formate to produce carbon dioxide and passes the generated electrons to |FRAME: PROTON| to evolve |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [2187144]| |CITS: [1625581]|. , Formate dehydrogenase H, a FdhF encoded selenopolypeptide, catalyzes the oxidation of formate generating |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and transferring the electrons to hydrogenase 3, which is the first part of the reaction |CITS: [13449036]|. Hydrogenase 3 is encoded by the hyc operon which has eight ORFs, hycA, hycB, hycC, hycD, hycE, hycF, hycG and hycH |CITS: [21261819]| |CITS: [1812811]|. A model has been proposed that demonstrates how FdhF tranfers electrons to the catalytic subunit HycE of hydrogenase 3 via HycB, HycF and HycG subunits. HycB and HycF are both [4Fe-4S] ferredoxin type electron transport proteins, while HycE and HycG have homology to NADH ubiquinone oxidoreductase (NUO) subunits of mitochondria and chloroplasts |CITS: [2187144]|. The model demonstrates electron transfer from FdhF to HycB to HycF to HycG to HycE, with HycC and HycD acting as membrane anchoring proteins |CITS: [1625581]|. , The product of hycH is required for the conversion of a precursor form of HycE into the mature form but is not part of the functional FHL complex |CITS: [1625581]|. , HycA is a FHL repressor protein encoded by hycA, which represses the hyc operon |CITS: [11931558]|, and its deletion results in increased FDH-H and hydrogenase activity |CITS: [1625581]|. The fhlA gene encodes the FHL activator protein FhlA which also controls the transcription of the FHL complex |CITS: [16269707]|. FhlA promotes the transcription of the fdhF, hyc and hyp operons |CITS: [10848985]| |CITS: [2280686]|. It might be possible to control FHL activity and the hydrogen production rate by manipulating fhlA and hycA |CITS: [16269707]|., The biosynthesis of the FHL complex is controlled by the concentration of formate in the cell |CITS: [16269707]||CITS: [1779767]|. Selenium and molybdenum are necessary at the active site of FDH-H, and nickel is necessary at the active site of Hyd-3 |CITS: [9036855]| |CITS: [1482271]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additinal reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, It has been well documented that some strains catalyze a Stickland reaction by which |FRAME: GLY| is oxidized by the |FRAME: GLYCLEAV-PWY "glycine-cleavage system"| and is reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.2| (as shown in this pathway). In both branches energy is conserved by substrate level phosphorylation |CITS: [7747933]|. Other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1731|, combine the reduction of glycine with the oxidation of other amino acids such as alanine or valine |CITS: [Schneeberger99]|. , The glycine reductase system catalyzes the reductive deamination of |FRAME: GLY|, forming |FRAME: ACETYL-P|. The enzyme contains three main components, called protein A, B and C |CITS: [4734725]|. Protein A, a monomeric 17 kDa selenocysteine-containing protein, is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58757 grdA| gene |CITS: [1825826]|; protein B is composed of three polypeptides - a 47 kDa selenocysteine-containing protein encoded by |FRAME: G-58760| |CITS: [8529640]| and two proteins of 25 and 22 kDa, which are the cleavage products of a 48 kDa proprotein encoded by |FRAME: G-58761| |CITS: [10091582][11422384]|; and protein C consists of two polypeptides (54 and 40 kDa) encoded by the |FRAME: G-58758| and |FRAME: G-58759| genes, respectively |CITS: [11271425][11737196]|., While glycine reductase has been found mostly in species of Clostridium, it has also been observed in Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [11797052]|.

Summary: tRNAs contain extensive post-transcriptional modifications. The most frequently modified nucleotide is in the wobble position, i.e. the 5' nucleotide of the anticodon which decodes the third codon postion. For example, the cmo5U modification allows |FRAME: EG30052 "tRNALeuUAG"| to read the CUU codon |CITS: [16236318]|. , The cmo5U modification was shown to be derived from the 5-hydroxyuridine (ho5U34) percursor |CITS: [418384]|. Two enzymes responsible for generating this initial modification have been identified; |FRAME: G7118-MONOMER| appears to utilize prephenate, while |FRAME: EG11116-MONOMER| utilizes molecular oxygen |CITS: [31253794]|. The precise reactions catalyzed by these enzymes are still unknown., The donor molecule for the carboxymethyl group is carboxy-S-adenosyl-L-methionine (Cx-SAM), which is synthesized from S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) by |FRAME: CPLX0-8010|. The reaction utilizes prephenate as the carboxyl donor |CITS: [23676670]|. A link between chorismate biosynthesis and cmo5U modification of tRNA was discovered many years ago. tRNA from a transposon insertion mutant in |FRAME: EG10076 "aroD"| as well as mutants in other genes of the |FRAME: ARO-PWY| pathway were found to lack this modification |CITS: [6160251][2104604]|., |FRAME: G7021-MONOMER| then catalyzes the transfer of the carboxymethyl group from carboxy-S-adenosyl-L-methionine (Cx-SAM) to ho5U34 in tRNA |CITS: [23676670]|. Finally, |FRAME: EG12167-MONOMER| transfers the methyl group from SAM to ho5U34, generating cmo5U34 |CITS: [26681692]|., An additional modification, 2'-O-methylation, which affects only a minor fraction of 5-methoxycarbonylmethoxy-modified U34 of |FRAME: serT-tRNA|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX0-7421| (|FRAME: EG11888|) |CITS: [26681692]|. , Review: |CITS: [22905870]|

Flavonoids have been researched in much detail because of their impact on UV-protection, defense and resistance and hormone interactions in plants |CITS: [11960739]| (see also |FRAME:PWY-5321|). In general, polyphenolic glucosides constitute a very heterogenic group with about 6500 identified compounds in plants |CITS:[11130659]| |CITS:[Harborne99]|. With an annual production of about 44 million tons per year (1999) onions are next to tomatoes the most cultivated horticulture vegetable |CITS:[12410539]|. , The benefits of onions for humans are manifold and reach from flavor, color and taste of food to health issues |CITS:[17484375]| |CITS:[12410539]| |CITS:[17997520]|. The glucosylation pattern of |FRAME:CPD-520| has been found to be important for absorption and utilization of this dietary flavonol |CITS:[9802557]|. The bioavailability of quercetin glucosides in onions for the dietary benefit of humans was much better than that of quercetin glycosides, e,g, quercetin-3-O-rutinoside (|FRAME:RUTIN|) |CITS:[Olthof00]| |CITS:[9414116]|. The uptake and consumption of |FRAME:CPD-520| originating from onion quercetin glucosides improved about 3 times compared to |FRAME:RUTIN| and to the same ratio regarding the bioavailability of quercetin glucosides from apples. The increased antioxidant capacity of blood plasma caused by the accumulation of |FRAME:CPD-520| also improved its anticarcinogenic defense forces |CITS:[ 9103273]|., , There are about 20 flavonols found in onion species |CITS:[Beesk10]|. The main flavonol glucosides present in onions (|FRAME:TAX-4679|) are the monoglucoside |FRAME:CPD-11685| (OMG) and the diglucoside |FRAME:CPD-14753| (QDG) which account for 85% |CITS:[Rhodes96]| |CITS:[Price97]| |CITS:[Tsushida95]| to 90% |CITS:[Bonaccorsi08]| of total flavonoids and up to 97% of total quercetin |CITS:[20492220]| in onion. However, the amount of quercetin glucosides can differ significantly between the various cultivars |CITS:[Caridi07]|. Red and yellow cultivars have been shown to possess very high concentrations of quercetin glucosides in contrast to white onion cultivares where only traces of the flavonols can be found. Nevertheless, quercetin glucosyltransferases were also found to be active in white cultivars of onions |CITS:[Tsushida96]|. Likewise, the concentration of the quercetin glucosides within the onion bulb varied considerably. Quercetin glucosides (QMG and QDG) were present in high amounts in the inner (QDG) and middle parts (QMG) of the onion bulb whereas |FRAME:CPD-520| and QMG dominated in the outer scale |CITS: [Beesk10]|. , These results coincide with the finding of the activities of regiospecific quercetin glucosyltransferases activities reported in onions |CITS:[Tsushida96]| where the glucosyltransferase activity was found higher in the inner than in the outer scales. The outer peel of the onion contains the highest amount of |FRAME:CPD-520| |CITS:[Bilyk84]| which, among other phenolics, contributes to the antifungal properties of the desiccated tissue that makes the onion more resistant towards pathogens |CITS:[Walker55]|. , The cloned quercetin glucosyltransferases UGT73G1 and UGT73J1 from onion expressed activities towards a broader (UGT73G1) and a narrower (UGT73J1) substrate spectrum. UGT73G1 was regiospecific towards the positions C-3 (C-ring), C-7 (A-ring) and C-4' (B-ring) forming in vitro 3 monoglucosides (|FRAME:CPD-11685|, |FRAME:CPD1F-437|, |FRAME:CPD-8006|) and two diglucosides (|FRAME:CPD-14753|, |FRAME:CPD-8033|) when |FRAME:CPD-520| was provided as substrate. When incubated with |FRAME:CPD1F-437| two diglucosides were produced, |FRAME:CPD-14753| (major product) and |FRAME:CPD-8033| (minor product) indicating that |FRAME:CPD1F-437| is the major intermediate for the biosynthesis of both diglucosides in vitro |CITS:[14568073]|. UGT73J1 only regiospecifically glucosylated the C-7 position of the A ring of an isoflavone (|FRAME:CPD-3141|) and |FRAME:CPD1F-437| forming the diglucoside |FRAME:CPD-8033| |CITS:[14568073]|. Hence, both flavonol glucosyltransferases produced the known spectra of flavonols occurring in onions |CITS:[Tsushida95]|.

Names: thiocyanate degradation I // thiocyanate metabolism // thiocyanate utilization // cyanate pathway
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HSCN Thiocyanate| is a major constituent of waste water from coal gasification factories. |FRAME: CPD-13584 Cyanide|, a by-product of coal gasification, is converted to thiocyanate by the addition of sulfur because thiocyanate is less toxic than cyanide. The resulting thiocyanate is then treated by activated sludge, where it is degraded by microorganisms |CITS: [1577754]|. Thiocyanate is also produced as a result of plant decomposition by the hydrolysis of cellular |FRAME: Glucosinolates glucosinolates| (thioglucosides) by glucosidase |CITS:[9573140]|., Microorganisms are known to use thiocyanate as a source of nitrogen, sulfur, carbon, energy, or some combination thereof. Some strains of the autotrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-931| |CITS: [7545513]|, as well as the sulfur-oxidizing alkaliphilic bacteria of the genus |FRAME:TAX-106633| |CITS: [11157213]| were shown to use thiocyanate as the sole source of carbon and energy. On the other hand, some organisms, including soil bacteria |CITS: [8000536]|, alkaliphiles belonging to the γ subdivision of |FRAME:TAX-1224| in the group |FRAME:TAX-2745| |CITS: [11157213]|, and the methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-47958| |CITS: [9446686]| can use thiocyanate only as a nitrogen source and require alternative carbon and energy sources., These observations suggest that two distinct pathways are involved in microbial thiocyanate degradation. In one pathway, which is known as the "cyanate pathway", thiocyanate is hydrolyzed by cleavage of the CS bond to form |FRAME: CPD-69| and a sulfur compound (this pathway) |CITS: [Youatt54][8000536][7698442][32094184]|. In the other pathway (named the "carbonyl sulfide pathway") thiocyanate is hydrolyzed by cleavage of the nitrile bond (triple N-C) forming |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE|, which is subsequenstly hydrolyzed to sulfide and carbon dioxide |CITS: [1577754][9573140]| (see |FRAME: PWY-743|)., About This Pathway, Early studies of the "cyanate pathway" were conducted with the autotroph |FRAME: TAX-931| |CITS: [Youatt54]| and with an uncharacterized Gram-negative heterotrophic soil bacterium that was named isolate 26B |CITS: [8000536]|., |FRAME: TAX-931| degrades thiocyanate to sulfate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. Thiocyanate degradation by washed suspensions of thiocyanate-grown cells produced sulfide, and although and although no cyanate production was observed, the authors proposed the presence of cyanase |CITS: [Youatt54]|., Similarly, studies of thiocyanate degradation by the Gram-negative heterotrophic soil bacterium isolate 26B suggested that it performs an initial hydrolysis of thiocyanate to cyanate and sulfide |CITS: [8000536]|. Cyanate was proposed to be further hydrolyzed to ammonia and carbon dioxide. The sulfide was oxidized to tetrathionate via thiosulfate |CITS: [8000536]|. Further oxidation of tetrathionate was not observed |CITS: [8000536]|., In a study of alkaliphilic bacteria able to utilize thiocyanate, Sorokin et al found that large amounts of cyanate accumulated in the media during utilization of thiocyanate, supporting the presence of a "cyanate pathway", this time in pure cultures of thiocyanate-degrading bacteria |CITS: [11157213 ]|. Similar results were obtained with strains of obligate chemolithoautotrophic sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-243063|) that were isolated from soda-lake sediments by enrichment culture with thiocyanate and nitrate |CITS: [15256585]|., The first enzyme responsible for cleaving the CS bond in |FRAME: HSCN| was isolated only in 2020 from the haloalkaliphilic sulfur-oxidizing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-713585|. The enzyme was shown to possess a cluster of three copper ions located at the corners of a near-isosceles triangle, and to catalyze a direct conversion of thiocyanate to cyanate and elemental sulfur, using a C-type cytochrome as the electron acceptor |CITS: [32094184]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-15537| is one of the sugars that are found in the |FRAME: CPD-24118|. The first dedicated step in its biosynthesis is the conversion of |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-9387|, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.102|. |FRAME: CPD-9387| is then acetylated by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.227|. In |FRAME: TAX-83334| these two enzymes are encoded by the |FRAME: G-81068| and |FRAME: G-81067| genes, which are located in O antigen biosynthetic cluster |CITS: [9673232]|., Both genes were cloned from |FRAME: TAX-83334| and overexpressed, and the recombinant proteins were purified and characterized |CITS: [17888872][18201574]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Linalools Linalool| (3,7-dimethyl-1,6-octadien-3-ol) is an acyclic monoterpene alcohol with a pleasant fragrance associated with a diverse array of plants |CITS: [7522061][RAGUSO]|. It is found in lavender, bergamot, jasmine, basil, rosemary, sage, star-anise, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, coriander, cardamom, ginger, black pepper and mandarin, and is one of the three terpene compounds principally responsible for Muscat aroma., Linalool is a primary compound in floral scent research. Both |FRAME: CPD-8996| and |FRAME: CPD-8997| enantiomeric forms occur in nature., Linalool is involved as an attractant in plant interactions with pollinators, herbivores and parasitoids |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. It has also been shown to be induced by artificial wounding and by jasmonic acid |CITS: [17440821]|. The de novo synthesis of linalool has been demonstrated in floral tissues |CITS: [17440821]|, barks and roots |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. Junipers, dicots and monocots emit linalool along with other monoterpenoids |CITS: [RAGUSO]|., Even though fungi typically do not produce monoterpenes, the de novo synthesis of linalool was demonstrate in some fungi, including the wine yeast strain, Saccharomyces cerevisiae M522, in the absence of grape derived precursors |CITS: [15668008]|., Recently, it has been demonstrated that linalool is a potent precursor for an advanced biofuel. It can be chemically converted to 1-methyl-cyclopent-2-enol and isobutylene. Dehydration of the alcohol gives rise to methylcyclopentadiene dimers which can be converted into a high density fuel |CITS: [21488169]|., About This Pathway, The C10 monoterpene |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| (GPP) is synthesized from the C5 compounds |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| and |FRAME: CPD-4211| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.1| |CITS: [11848932]|., |FRAME: CPD-8996| is produced in a single step from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.26|. The enzyme was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-650269| (bergamot mint), which produces an essential oil in which |FRAME: CPD-8996| and its acetate ester are the only components |CITS: [12176064]|. Other well-documented plants producing |FRAME: CPD-8996| include |FRAME: TAX-39329| (lavender) |CITS: [17662687]|, the traditional Chinese medical herb |FRAME: TAX-35608| |CITS: [10562427]|, and |FRAME: TAX-4081| (tomato) |CITS: [17440821]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| is a non-standard amino acid that is not normally incorporated into proteins during protein synthesis. Citrulline was first isolated from |FRAME:TAX-3653| (watermelon) in 1914 |CITS: [Koga14]|. It was re-isolated in 1930, at which time its chemical formula was determined and it was named (after the Latin name of the watermelon) |CITS: [Wada30]|., Citrulline is generated as an intermediate in a metabolic pathway called the |FRAME: PWY-4984 "urea cycle"|, in which |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| is converted to |FRAME: ARG| and vice versa. The urea cycle was the first metabolic cycle ever discovered |CITS: [Krebs32]|. It was originally reported to be present in all mammals, plants, and many insects |CITS: [697760]|, but eventually documented in many other organisms, including birds |CITS:[4217066]|, invertebrates |CITS:[14465664][5869779]|, insects |CITS: [697760][5791517]|, plants |CITS: [13741005] [13958361]|, yeast |CITS:[11946245]|, fungi |CITS:[4996649]|, and even microorganisms |CITS:[5593971][5709377]|., Citruline is also formed during the production of nitric oxide by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.39|., Citrulline metabolism falls into two categories: free citrulline and citrullinated proteins. For more information about free citrulline, see |FRAME: PWY-5004|., About This Pathway, Although citrulline cannot be incorporated into proteins during protein synthesis, some proteins contain citrulline residues |CITS: [14493344]|. These proteins are modified post-translationally, by the conversion of arginine residues to citrulline., This reaction is performed by members of the peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) family (EC 3.5.3.15). Five isotypes of PAD, numbered I to V, have been identifed to date, only four of which (I, II, III and V) are present in humans. The fact that this protein is present in various tissues and is active on many proteins suggests it may have an important biological role. This role is still not well understood., In addition to the eukaryotic PADs, a single prokaryotic PAD has been discovered in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-837|. This enzyme is not evolutionarily related to the eukaryotic enzymes, and is different in many aspects, even though it catalyzes the same reaction |CITS: [10377098][11504612]|., The best known cases of citrullinated proteins include the proteins that are involved in epidermal keratinization (trichohyalin, keratin and filaggrin) |CITS: [9129218][11069618][12392711]|, and the basic myelin protein, which makes up to 35% of the proteic component of the central nervous system |CITS: [2466844][11858705]|. Less well documented cases include citrullination of B23 nucleophosmin and some histones in leukocyte nuclei |CITS: [10488123][11798170]| and PAD I activity in decidual cells of the female genital system |CITS: [7593250]|., Insufficiencies in protein citrullination occurs in some autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis or multiple sclerosis |CITS: [16082501]|. In particular, several experimental results suggest that the immune response to citrulline could play a significant role in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis inflammation |CITS: [15290721]| .

Summary: |FRAME:PHE Phenylalanine| is one of the three proteinogenic aromatic amino acids that are produced only in plants and microorganisms. It is a central metabolite, and plants direct up to 30% of the carbon flux from photosynthesis towards its biosynthesis |CITS:[22554242]|. Moreover, |FRAME:PHE| is precursor of a plethora of secondary metabolites involved in plant defense (e.g. flavonoids |CITS:[11743081][22404468]|), signaling and protection (e.g. isoflavonoids |CITS:[12644640][20921162]|), reproduction (e.g. phenylpropanoids and volatiles |CITS:[20035037]|) and general plant fitness (e.g. vitamin E,  plastoquinone, and suberin). , The biosynthesis of |FRAME:PHE| has been known to comprise two major pathways, a plant pathway via |FRAME:CPD-659|, which has been claimed to occur exclusively in plastids (|FRAME: PWY-3462|) and the microbial pathway via |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE| (|FRAME: PHESYN|)., The phenylpyruvate route has been confirmed in many microorganisms, including |FRAME: TAX-562| and yeast, and the two routes have been reported co-exist in many microorganisms. However, compelling evidence suggests that many plants employ only the arogenate route |CITS: [3985619][3463961]|. So far the evidence for the phenylpyruvate route in plants is lacking, as |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.51|, has never been detected in any plant (for a conflicting view, see |FRAME: PWY-7432|). , |FRAME: CPD-659| is the branch-point and the immediate precursor for the synthesis of both |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: PHE|. |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.91|, is the key enzyme channeling |FRAME: CPD-659| towards |FRAME: PHE| synthesis |CITS: [3124763]|. Its activity is strongly feedback inhibited by the latter.

|FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of |FRAME: CPD-12557|(β1,3)|FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to each other by a β(1,4) linkage. It is usually found attached to proteins as part of a proteoglycan.Chondroitin sulfate is a major component of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but is also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors., Degradation of |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| within the animal is part of many processes. For example, such degradation increases the permeability of connective tissues and decreases the viscosity of body fluids. Although some of the enzymes involved are circulated in the plasma, the general process of chondroitin sulfate degradation generally takes place in the lysosome. Chondroitin degradation promoted by bacterial of other enzymes is also involved in bacterial pathogenesis and the spread of toxins and venoms. The process starts with hydrolysis of the large |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| polymer to small segments, which is catalyzed by a family of enzymes known as hyaluronidases. One of these enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: HS02883|, is a dedicated chondroitinase. Others, encoded by |FRAME: HS03763| and |FRAME: HS02884|, have higher affinity towards |FRAME: Hyaluronan|, but also degrade chondroitin sulfate at a lower rate., Depending on the enzyme, the large chondroitin sulfate polymers are degraded into smaller oligosaccharides, often hexa- and tetrasaccharides, and eventually into disaccharides. Since the sugars in the chondroitin sulfate molecule are sulfated, dedicated enzymes, such as the |FRAME: HS03665-MONOMER| and |FRAME: HS06790-MONOMER| remove the sulfate groups, resulting in regular disaccharide molecules that can be degraded further into basic building blocks.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-145262| is a thermophilic methanogenic archaeon. The organism is an autotrophic anaerobe and can grow on a gas mixture of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as its carbon and energy sources, respectively. This organism does not possess the Calvin cycle nor a full reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle. Instead, it fixes |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| via several alternative routes., The first, and main route, is the |FRAME: CODH-PWY|. The product of this pathway, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, is a central intermediate in this organism and is used for all subsequent biosynthetic pathways |CITS:[Fuchs80a][Jansen82]|., An additional |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecule is incorporated by the |FRAME: CPLX-7744| complex, which converts, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|., |FRAME: PYRUVATE "Pyruvate"| can be processed in multiple ways. It can be converted to |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, enabling amino acid biosythesis. It could be carboxylated to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| by |FRAME: CPLX-7747|, enabling the capture of a third |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecule |CITS: [9478969]| (|FRAME: CPLX-7747| accepts only |FRAME: HCO3| molecules, but |FRAME: TAX-187420| possesses a |FRAME: CPLX-7750|, enzyme, which can convert |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| into |FRAME: HCO3|). Finally, |FRAME: PYRUVATE| could also be converted to |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| (PEP)., PEP can be processed in two ways: it can lead to a gluconeogenesis pathway that ends at |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, |CITS:[Fuchs80a]|, or it could be carboxylated to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|,  enabling the capture of a fourth, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecule. This carboxylation reaction is performed by |FRAME: CPLX-7743| |CITS: [15262949]|., |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID "Oxaloacetate"| can be pocessed in two ways as well. It can lead into an incomplete reductive TCA cycle that ends at |FRAME: GLT|, or it could be processed directly to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| |CITS:[Fuchs80a]|., Most of the enzymes catalyzing these pathways have not been identified or characterized from |FRAME: TAX-145262|. The pathways were predicted using stable isotope labeling and NMR spectroscopy experiments |CITS: [Jansen82][3782122]|.

Summary: Acute inflammation is a beneficial response to injury and infection that involves neutrophils, eosinophils, and M1-polarized macrophages, which produce bioactive molecules such as leukotrienes and prostaglandins. If successful, this response leads to clearance of invading organisms, tissue repair, and regeneration. The pro-inflammatory response eventually transitions to the pro-resolution phase of inflammation, during which M2-polarized macrophages produce potent molecules collectively known as |FRAME: SPMs "specialized pro-resolving mediators"| (SPMs). The SPMs include |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, which are derived from either |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) or |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA), and the DHA-derived |FRAME: protectins protectins| and |FRAME: Maresins maresins|., In 2014 a new type of pro-resolving and tissue-regenerative compounds was found, consisting of sulfido-conjugates of resolvins and protectins. The conjugates appeared to contain either glutathione, cycteinylglycine, or cysteine |CITS: [25324525][25713027]|. A subsequent study from 2019 also identified similar conjugates of maresins |CITS: [31589826]|. The sulfido-conjugates stimulated human macrophage bacterial phagocytosis, phagolysosomal acidification, and efferocytosis., The pathway starts with |FRAME: CPD-10244 DHA|, which is acted upon by either |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, or |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|, generating |FRAME: CPD-25487| or |FRAME: CPD66-80|, respectively. These enzymes catalyze the insertion of molecular oxygen into polyunsaturated fatty acids, forming hydroperoxides. They can also catalyze an additional step - the conversion of the hydroperoxide product to an epoxide intermediate |CITS: [3012557]|., In the case of |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, the enzyme carries out both steps, ending with |FRAME: CPD-25480|. This compound can be processed in two ways - it could be conjugated with glutathione, as shown here, or it could be hydrolyzed to form the maresins., In the case of |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|, the pathway encounters a branch point. If the enzyme proceeds to catalyze the second reaction, it forms |FRAME: CPD-25482|. As in the case described above, this compound could be hydrolized to form |FRAME: CPD-24703|, or it could be conjugation to glutathione as shown here., However, after the lipoxygenase catalyzes the first reaction, a peroxidase can reduce the product to |FRAME: CPD-17450|. In this case, the product can be processed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, forming |FRAME: CPD66-79|. This compound could then be hydrolyzed into D-series resolvins (see |FRAME: PWY66-397|), or it could be conjugated to glutathione as shown here., In all cases, the glutathione-conjugates can be processed further, first by |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.2|, forming cysteinylglycyl-conjugates, and then by |FRAME: EC-3.4.13.19|, forming cysteinyl-conjugates |CITS: [25713027][31589826]|.

Summary: General Background, Benzoate is derived from the phenylpropanoid biosynthesis pathway. A subset of the benzoate-derived compounds, such as |FRAME:CPD-12217|, |FRAME:CPD-6443| |FRAME:CPD-6441|, are volatile and are often important constituents of floral scents |CITS: [15286288][12884048][12226525][12361714]|. In addition, salicylic acid (SA) and methylsalicylate (MeSA) contribute significantly to plant defense signaling |CITS:[19400653]| and benzoate-derived secondary metabolites, such as xanthones |CITS: [20156171][19384730]|, may also help to protect plants from attack |CITS: [16600669]|., An important step in the creation of these volatile compounds is the shortening of the 3-carbon side-chain present on trans-cinnamic acid. At least three different biosynthetic routes for volatile benzenoid biosynthesis have been proposed and there is evidence that a subset of the different pathways may operate in individual species. For example, |FRAME:TAX-4102| has at least two pathways present (|FRAME: PWY-6443 "beta-oxidative, CoA-dependent"| and |FRAME: PWY-6444 "non-beta-oxidative, non-CoA-dependent|), whereas cucumber (|FRAME:TAX-3659|) and |FRAME:TAX-49451| seem to lack the "non-oxidative" variant |CITS: [11219576]|. Meanwhile, this pathway, a hybrid between the other two, exists in |FRAME: TAX-140968|. , A greater understanding of the metabolic pathways involved in benzenoid biosynthesis may contribute to genetic engineering efforts aimed at altering floral scents |CITS: [17234289]|, modifying SA-based defense responses, or changing the levels of other secondary defense metabolites and pigment compounds, such as xanthones |CITS: [11882941]|, that derive from this pathway., About This Pathway, In this benzoate biosynthesis variant, the removal of the 2-carbon unit from the side chain is accomplished by adding a water across the double bond in |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA| and then removing |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. Thus, this pathway is CoA-dependent but does not involve the other enzymatic steps associated with β-oxidation |CITS: [11882941]|. Although all enzymatic activities associated with all of the steps in this pathway have been observed experimentally in |FRAME: TAX-140968|, none of the genes encoding the enzymes have been cloned to date |CITS: [11882941]|., The activity of several enzymes in this pathway appears to be up-regulated by methyl jasmonate and precedes a rise in the production of xanthones, a class of secondary metabolites made in |FRAME: TAX-140968| |CITS: [11882941]|.

Summary: General Background, In fungi the metabolic intermediate |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| (propionyl-CoA) is generated during the degradation of |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate), odd-chain fatty acids, and some amino acids (for example see pathways |FRAME: PWY0-42|, |FRAME: PWY-7288| and |FRAME: VALDEG-PWY|). |FRAME: PROPIONATE "Propanoate"| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| are toxic at high concentrations and catabolic pathways found in all domains of life prevent their accumulation. Although fungi generally use the |FRAME: PWY0-42| to catabolize |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, |FRAME: TAX-237561| was found to utilize a modified β-oxidation pathway for |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| catabolism. In contrast, a complete peroxisomal β-oxidation cycle would shorten |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| by two carbon atoms, producing |FRAME: FORMYL-COA| |CITS: [24497638]|., |FRAME: TAX-5476| can exist in humans as a harmless commensal in healthy individuals, or it can become an opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised individuals. It is likely to use host-derived fatty acids and amino acids as nutrients in addition to glucose, making catabolism of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| of probable importance for proliferation within the host |CITS: [24497638][21538235]|., This pathway has also been suggested to occur in other fungi |CITS: [MIYAKOSHIS87]|, plants |CITS: [17580301]|, insects |CITS: [2647392]|, and bacteria |CITS: [19494695]| (also see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6373|)., About This Pathway, The pathway was elucidated using a combination of growth, proteomic, genetic, and metabolite analyses, as well as recombinant protein production and enzyme characterization in the case of Hpd1p. , In contrast to |FRAME: TAX-4932|, |FRAME: TAX-5476| can utilize |FRAME: PROPIONATE| (propionate) as a sole carbon source in the absence of glucose, although a prolonged adaptation phase is required and growth is slow. Evidence suggests that |FRAME: TAX-5476| does not degrade |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| (propionyl-CoA) via either the the |FRAME: PWY0-42| or the |FRAME: PROPIONMET-PWY| pathway, but utilizes a modified β-oxidation pathway. Evidence for this pathway included a gene deletion analysis which confirmed the essential contributions of enzymes Fox2p, Ehd3p, Hpd1p, and Ald6p to the pathway |CITS: [24497638]|., In the first reaction of fungal peroxisomal β-oxidation |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| is oxidized to |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA| (acrylyl-CoA) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7288|). Pox1-3p was identified as a likely candidate to catalyze this reaction based on proteomic analysis of |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: ACET| grown cells, although other isozymes could also be involved. The POX1-3 gene is annotated as a putative |FRAME: FAD|-binding acyl-CoA oxidase/dehydrogenase. Due to its peroxisomal location in members of the |FRAME: TAX-4891| |CITS: [18795352]|, the oxidase reaction is shown in this pathway., |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA "Acryloyl-CoA"| is then hydrated to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONYL-COA| (3-hydroxypropionyl-CoA), likely by Fox2p, the only peroxisomal bifunctional enoyl-CoA hydratase/hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase found in |FRAME: TAX-5476|. Gene deletion experiments showed that none of the three 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolases found in this organism were essential for |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| degradation., In the next proposed step, |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONYL-COA| exits the peroxisomal β-oxidation pathway and enters the mitochondrion where hydrolysis of the |FRAME: CO-A| thioester produces the key intermediate |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| (3-hydroxypropionate). Mutant analysis suggested that mitochondrial Ehd3p performs |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONYL-COA| hydrolysis., The |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| is then converted to |FRAME: MALONATE-S-ALD| by the product of mitochondrial orf19.5565 which was named HPD1. Its protein product Hpd1p was recombinantly expressed, purified and characterized., |FRAME: MALONATE-S-ALD "Malonate semialdehyde"| then undergoes oxidation and esterification to produce |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which enters the fungal TCA cycle as indicated in the pathway link. An aldehyde dehydrogenase encoded by ALD6 was proposed to have the malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase (acylating) activity. Another enzyme encoded by ALD5 might contribute to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| degradation, but is not essential., Using a murine sepsis model, the HPD1 mutant was shown to have attenuated virulence, suggesting that during infection |FRAME: TAX-5476| utilizes host compounds to generate |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [24497638]|.

Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxinitriles. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks, cyanogenic glycosides are cleaved releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN|, which serves as the first line of chemical defense., |FRAME: CPD-1125 "(R)-Amygdalin"| is a phenylalanine-derived cyanogenic diglucoside. It accumulates in seeds of rosaceous stone fruits such as bitter almonds, apricots, cherries, peaches and plums, and is responsible for the bitterness in the seeds., Because of the high amounts of amygdalin in seeds, it was suggested that it may serve as storage forms for reduced nitrogen. Studies have shown that upon seed germination, amygdalin is metabolized to form hydrogen cyanide, which is detoxified into the amino acids asparagine and aspartate to provide nitrogen and carbonyl compounds for the developing seedlings |CITS: [16652959][12232341]|., The same process also occurs in the intestine of mammals that ingest cyanogenic glycosides in their food, largely due to the hydrolytic activity of the intestinal microbiota. It has been shown that strains of |FRAME: TAX-1590| and |FRAME: TAX-60520| are able to use |FRAME: CPD-1125| as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [25421573]|.

Summary: This pathway, which describes a novel route for CO<sub>2</sub> fixation, was proposed in 2012 |CITS: [22200662]| and confirmed in 2020 from two different organisms. It is considered the 7th CO<sub>2</sub> fixation pathway |CITS: [32170009][33037220]|., In the first case, the pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-332101|, an organism known to possess the linear |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"|. The genomic cluster encoding that pathway's genes in this organism also includes genes encoding |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, which alerted the researchers to the possibility that the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and a glycine synthase pathway (the glycine cleavage system operating in the reverse direction) are functionally interconnected in this organism to fix CO<sub>2</sub>. <sup>13</sup>C-label metabolite-tracing experimental data validated the synthesis of |FRAME: GLY| from CO<sub>2</sub> and transcriptional studies confirmed that the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway and the glycine reductive pathway coexist in |FRAME: TAX-332101|. However, the organism was not grown fully autotrophically, as the growth medium contained yeast extract |CITS: [32170009]|., In the second case, the pathway was demonstrated in the chemolithoautotrophic sulfate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-876|. That organism was shown to fix CO<sub>2</sub> via the reductive glycine pathway while growing fully autotrophically with hydrogen and sulfate as energy substrates. The reductive glycine pathway was found to be the sole carbon fixation pathway in this organism |CITS: [33037220]|., The first 4 steps of the pathway are identical to the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. CO<sub>2</sub> is reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.17.2.3 "EC 1.17.2.3, formate dehydrogenase"|, to |FRAME: FORMATE|, which is transferred to tetrahydrofolate and reduced further to form |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate"|. However, in the next step |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, condenses the single carbon from 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate with ammonium and a second CO<sub>2</sub> molecule to generate |FRAME: GLY|, which is reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.21.4.2|, to |FRAME: ACETYL-P|. |FRAME: ACETYL-P "Acetyl phosphate"| can be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| either directly, via |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.8|, or indirectly, via the combined activity of |FRAME: EC-2.7.2.1| and |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.1| (ACS). The high up-regulation of ACS in |FRAME: TAX-876| grown under autotrophic conditions, and the accumulation of acetate in the growth medium, indicated that the indirect route is the major pathway of acetyl-CoA biosynthesis in that organism |CITS: [33037220]|. In the last step of the pathway acetyl-CoA is condensed with a third CO<sub>2</sub> molecule to form |FRAME: PYRUVATE|., It should be noted that assimilation of glycine into the central metabolism could proceed via two main routes: either by conversion to |FRAME: ACETYL-P|, as shown here, or by conversion to |FRAME: SER| via |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1| (as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1608|). In both organisms only the enzymes involved in the first route were upregulated during autotrophic growth, suggesting that it is the main route for glycine incorporation for autotrophic CO<sub>2</sub> fixation. It is thought that organisms that utilize a glycine reductive pathway via the serine route use the pathway as a sink for excess reducing power |CITS: [500560][Fuchs86][22536150]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE| is an industrial chemical and an environmental pollutant in wastewater |CITS: [18557616][22780451][21134717]|. It may have deleterious effects on human health |CITS: [10341738]|. A bacterial strain R4 identified as |FRAME: TAX-37930| was isolated by enrichment culture from an activated sludge sample from a |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE|-containing wastewater treatment pool. This strain could efficiently grow on |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE|, |FRAME: DIETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: ETHANAMINE| as sole source of carbon and nitrogen, producing |FRAME: AMMONIA| as one of the end products. This suggested complete mineralization. Both whole cells of this organism in liquid culture and whole cells immobilized on alginate gel were shown to degrade these compounds, demonstrating potential utility in bioremediation |CITS: [21134717]|., About This Pathway, Metabolites produced during |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE| degradation were identified by mass spectrometry. These included |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE|, |FRAME: DIETHYLAMINE|, |FRAME: ETHANAMINE|, |FRAME: CPD-14564|, and |FRAME: CPD-14565|. Both |FRAME: DIETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: ETHANAMINE| were degraded more rapidly than |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE|. However |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| could not be degraded under these conditions. High concentrations of |FRAME: SULFATE|, |FRAME: AMMONIUM|, and some metal ions inhibited the degradation., Cell-free extracts of cells grown in |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE| showed triethylamine, diethylamine, and ethylamine monooxygenase activity and the pathway shown here was proposed. |FRAME: TRIETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: DIETHYLAMINE| were suggested to be degraded similarly, producing |FRAME: ETHANAMINE|, which was proposed to be degraded to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: ACETALD|, followed by complete mineralization |CITS: [21134717]|.
