Summary: Several aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: TOLUENE|, |FRAME:4-TOLUENESULFONATE|,, |FRAME: 4-TOLUENECARBOXYLATE||FRAME: CPD-8815|, and |FRAME: CPD-10664|, are degraded aerobically, by bacteria into the common intermediate |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL|, which is degraded further by modified, meta- or ortho-cleavage pathways., This ortho-cleavage pathway of |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL| has been demonstrated in full or in part, in several organsims, including the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5554|, that can degrade |FRAME: CPD-108| |CITS: [4040904]|,, and several bacterial species., In this pathway, the aromatic ring of |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL| is opened by |FRAME: MONOMER-14435|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-10656|, which is closed to a lactone ring structure by |FRAME: MONOMER-14436|., Since direct degradation of a 4-substituted lactone results in the formation of dead-end metabolites, this lactone is, rearranged to |FRAME: CPD-10824| by the action of |FRAME: CPLX-7800|, a unique enzyme dedicated to this task., Degradation proceeds in an analogous manner to the usual ortho cleavage pathway, with methylated intermediates,, resulting in formation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CPD-9407| |CITS: [4040904]|. , The enzymes catalyzing the last steps of the pathway have not been purified from organisms that metabolize, |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL|, and the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-9407| has not been well characterized., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-264198| is known to possess three distinct ortho-cleavage pathways, one of which, is adapted for the degradation of |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL| |CITS:[Pieper85][9461415]|. The pathway has been studied, in this organism up to |FRAME: CPD-10825|., This pathway is most likely present also in |FRAME: TAX-395598|, an organism that can utilize |FRAME: CPD-8815| and, |FRAME: CPD-10664| as growth substrates. The degradation pathway for those compounds start with hydroxylation, into |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL|. The enzymatic transformations up to |FRAME: CPD-10823| have been, characterized in this organism |CITS: [17172348]|., A similar pathway has been described in a strain of the actinomycete |FRAME:TAX-1829|. However, that organism, lacks |FRAME: CPLX-7801|, and instead activates |FRAME: CPD-10824| to a CoA derivative which is processed, further |CITS: [9852013 ]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Ceramides Ceramides| belong to a diverse class of lipids called sphingolipids that have important biological properties and control many aspects of cellular metabolism |CITS: [22248339]|. They are composed of |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| linked to |FRAME: Fatty-Acids| via an amide bond. Ceramides make up a large percentage of the cell membrane and are the major lipid constituent of lamellar sheets in the intercellular spaces of the stratum corneum |CITS: [12553851]|. These lamellar sheets provide the barrier property of the epidermis. , Besides having structural properties, ceramides can act as a second messengers in the sphingomyelin cycle |CITS: [8106344]|, and also play a role in cell aging, apoptosis and differentiation |CITS: [10652518]|. There are three major pathways for ceramide generation. This pathway describes de novo biosynthesis., About this Pathway, The defining step in the de novo biosynthesis of ceramides is the pyridoxal-5'-phosphate-dependent condensation of |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA| with |FRAME: SER| catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-305 "serine palmitoyltransferase"| |CITS: [9363775]|. The resultant |FRAME: DEHYDROSPHINGANINE| is immediately reduced to |FRAME: CPD-13612| in an NADPH dependent reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: HS04306-MONOMER|. |FRAME: MONOMER66-34367 "Dihydroceramide synthase"| catalyzes the acylation of sphinganine to yield |FRAME: CPD3DJ-82|, followed by a desaturation at the 4,5 position to form |FRAME: Ceramides| |CITS: [9312549]|. , The last two steps of the pathway were decided by the discovery of the fungal secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-13181| |CITS: [8850625]|. Fumonisin B1 is a potent inhibitor of the N-acylation of sphingoid bases and blocks the pathway at the |FRAME: MONOMER66-34367 "dihydroceramide synthase"| step. This clarified that the latter part of the pathway proceeds first by acylation and then desaturation instead of vice versa |CITS: [1860857]|. The pathway occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum.

General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway: , Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes have been involved in a variety of biological processes: inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Dehydroabietic acid (DHA), an abietane-type DRA, is one of the principal resin acids |CITS:[17082986],[11269960]|. DHA has one of the highest index of cytotoxicity among all the resin acids |CITS:[7887603]|. This compound has also been shown to have some gastroprotective properties in mice |CITS:[16125407]|. These properties are shared by |FRAME:CPD-8722| and |FRAME:CPD-8724|, as well as a methyl ester |CITS:[16125407]|. In trout (|FRAME:TAX-8022|) hepatocytes, DHA causes a reduction in cellular ATP content and a concomitant enhancement of glycolytic activity of the cells in a dose-dependent manner |CITS:[12413793]|. The formation of this acid involves the formation of the abietane skeleton via cyclization of the diterpenoid precursor |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This cyclization occurs presumably via the formation of the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-4750| and is followed by the oxidation to |FRAME:CPD-8721| and the stepwise oxidation of the C18 methyl group of the derived olefin |FRAME:CPD-8725|. Several levopimaradiene/abietadiene synthases have been identified, which can produce a variety of olefins such as |FRAME:--ABIETADIENE|, |FRAME:CPD-8695| or |FRAME:CPD-8697| |CITS:[8798524],[15310829],[16497345]|. The mechanism of oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-8721| to |FRAME:CPD-8725| resembles that of the oxidation of |FRAME:CPD1F-128| to |FRAME:CPD1F-132| and that |FRAME:CPD1F-132| to |FRAME:CPD1F-95| (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|) in which a single multifunctional enzyme (ent-kaurene oxidase) catalyze the consecutive oxidation steps. No single enzyme has been found to date that could catalyze all three conversion steps from |FRAME:CPD-8721| to |FRAME:CPD-8725|, however, one enzyme from |FRAME:TAX-3352| (loblolly pine) could catalyze the oxidation steps from |FRAME:CPD-8722| to |FRAME:CPD-8725| |CITS:[15911762]|. This same enzyme was additionally shown to be involved in the formation of other diterpene resin acids (such as |FRAME:CPD-8729|, |FRAME:CPD-8694| and |FRAME:CPD-8712|) |CITS:[15911762]|. To date, however, no enzyme catalyzing the first step of oxidation of dehydroabietadiene to |FRAME:CPD-8722| has been identified.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39|, commonly referred to as ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase or RubisCO, is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both the carboxylation and oxygenation of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| (RuBP). The carboxylation process is generally known as CO2 fixation (see |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|) whereas the oxygenation process is known as photorespiration (this pathway)., The two substrates (CO2 and O2) are competitive with regard to RubisCO, so that an increase in CO2 concentration inhibits oxygenation and vice versa |CITS:[Bowyer97]|. An important factor influencing the rate of oxygenation is temperature, as photorespiration is enhanced by high temperature. The reasons for this are twofold: (i) as temperatures increase the solubility of CO2 diminishes more rapidly than that of O2 and (ii) the specificity factor (Ω) of RubisCO (which represents a measure of the relative specificity for CO2) decreases with increasing temperatures between 7°C and 35°C., While the carboxylation reaction results in two molecules of |FRAME:G3P|, which are processed in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|, the oxygenation reaction forms one molecule of |FRAME:G3P| and one molecule of |FRAME:CPD-67| (2PG). The latter cannot be used in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY| and, instead, is salvaged in the photorespiration pathway. , While photorespiration is essential for the viability of all organisms that perform oxygenic photosynthesis, including cyanobacteria and C3 plants, at ambient CO2 conditions |CITS: [18957552][26994478]|, the photorespiratory cycle results in carbon, nitrogen and energy losses, and, unlike true respiration, does not produce ATP or reducing power. As a matter of fact, despite its name photorespiration does not involve neither light nor respiration., About This Pathway, The main features of the photorespiration pathway include: (i) the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-67| into |FRAME: GLY|; (ii) the processing of two glycines into |FRAME: SER|, CO2 and ammonia; and (iii) the conversion of |FRAME: SER| into |FRAME: G3P|, which is directed towards CO2 fixation via the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|., The first step of the pathway involves the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:CPD-67|, which not only recycles phosphate but also prevents accumulation of this compound, which is a potent inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.1|. The next step is the oxidation of |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| to |FRAME:GLYOX|. This step is catalyzed by different enzymes in plants and some algae (see |FRAME: PWY-181|) and in chlorophytes and cyanobacteria (this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-8363|)., Glyoxylate is converted into |FRAME:GLY| by two different enzymes: |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45| and |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.4|. One of the glycine molecues is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, to CO2, ammonia, and a single carbon that is transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate|. The methylene group is then transferred to the second glycine molecule by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, forming |FRAME: SER|. , The serine molecue feeds back into |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, closing a cycle. The main carbon molecule produced by this cycle is |FRAME:OH-PYR|, which is reduced into |FRAME:GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.29|. The pathway ends with the phosphorylation of glycerate to |FRAME:G3P|, which re-enters the Calvin cycle. The phosphorylation is performed by different enzymes in cyanobacteria vs. other photosynthetic organisms., The outcome of photorespiration in photosynthetic cells is loss of carbon via CO2 release, as well as loss of energy, yet the pathway is essential at atmospheric concentrations of CO2. The biological function of photorespiration is not clear. One possibility is that photorespiration is necessary under conditions of high light intensity and low CO2 concentration to dissipate excess ATP and NADPH from the photosynthesis light reactions, and prevent damage to the photosynthetic apparatus |CITS: [11299007]|. Another explanation is that the pathway is necessary for the assimilation of nitrate |CITS: [15272076]|., There are two main differences between this pathway variant, which exists in cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1148|, and the pathway variant in plants:, 1. In plants and some algae |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| is exported to the cytoplasm, where it is oxidized in the peroxisomes to |FRAME:GLYOX| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.15|. In chlorophytes and cyanobacteria glycolate is oxidized to glyoxylate by |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.14| |CITS: [18957552]|., 2. Unlike plants that encode a type II glycerate kinase, which produces |FRAME: G3P|, |FRAME: TAX-1148| encodes a class I glycerate kinase that produces |FRAME: 2-PG| and thus requires a mutase to convert the product to a form that can enter the Calvin cycle |CITS: [18675808]|.

Summary: In |FRAME: TAX-4081| cotyledons, the major intermediates of phenylpropanoid metabolism are chlorogenic acid and |FRAME: 2-O-CAFFEOYLGLUCARATE|. In quantitative analysis these two compounds appear to be in a precursor-product relation. Protein extracts of tomato cotyledons were able to catalyze the formation of caffeoylglucaric acid when chlorogenic acid was supplied as the acyl donor |CITS: [16665274]|. Glucaric acid is the oxidation product of glucose and |FRAME: 2-O-CAFFEOYLGLUCARATE| is the acylated product., The biosynthesis of the hydrocinnamic acid esters has for long been thought be similar to the caffeic acid ester, the chlorogenic acid. Alternate routes of enzymic synthesis are being pursued such as the possibility of chlorogenic acid acting as an acyl donor molecule for caffeoyltransferases |CITS: [16667263]|. , Leaves of |FRAME: TAX-4081| plants accumulate caffeate esters with quinate, glucarate and galactarate. These esters are formed by the action of three enzymes; caffeate CoA ligase, caffeoyl-CoA quinate caffeoyltransferase and chlorogenate-glucarate caffeoyltransferase as shown in the above pathway |CITS: [20880851]|.

RNA modification is a post-transcriptional process by which certain nucleotides are altered after their initial incorporation into an RNA chain., The most heavily modified class of RNA molecules is the tRNA - an average of 11%, 14%, and 17% of the tRNA residues are modified in |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-4932|, and mammalian cytoplasm, respectively |CITS: [9399820]|. These modifications expand the chemical and functional diversity of tRNA, and enhance its structural stability |CITS: [3304135]|., In some bacterial genomes, about 1% of the coding genes are devoted to tRNA modification |CITS: [3304135]|., Position 34 (the anticodon first letter, or the wobble position) or position 37 (the position next to the anticodon) frequently contains highly modified nucleosides. The wobble modifications at position 34 are important for precise decoding mediated by the codon-anticodon interaction. The so called "hypermodified" nucleosides at position 37 function in translational reading-frame maintenance. These are usually modified purine nucleosides with large molecular weight. Their high hydrophobicity enhances the codon-anticodon interaction, and their modifications prevent the formation of an incorrect Watson-Crick base pair with the codon's first letter. Some of these hypermodified nucleosides, known as wye bases, contain a tricyclic structure. The most complex wye base identified thus far is |FRAME: CPD-15385| (yW)., |FRAME: CPD-15385 Wybutosine| is found only at position 37 of eukaryotic |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|, and is generated from guanine |CITS: [4586620]| in 5 steps. The whole set of genes responsible for its biosynthesis has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [16642040]|. , The first reaction, catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G3O-31120| gene, is not specific for |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|, as the anticodon sequence is not critical for the tRNA recognition by this enzyme |CITS: [3556165][15248782]|. However, all subsequent steps are specific for |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|., The second reaction, the formation of a tricyclic structure, is catalyzed by the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G3O-34098| gene. The enzyme contains two domains - a radical Ado-Met domaint hat contains iron-sulfur clusters, and a flavodoxin domain that donates an electron to the iron-sulfur clusters |CITS: [16642040]|., The latter part of the pathway is responsible for the addition of an α-amino-α-carboxypropyl side chain at carbon C-7. It consists of several steps catalyzed by |FRAME: G3O-32610|, |FRAME: G3O-30560| and |FRAME: YOL141W|, and was reconstituted in vitro |CITS: [16642040]|. Plants contain a large fusion protein that includes TYW3, the C-terminal domain of TYW4 and TYW2 |CITS: [16642040]|., It should be noted that while |FRAME: CPD-15385| has been found only in eukaryotic |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|, two of the intermediates in this pathway, namely |FRAME: CPD-15399| and |FRAME: CPD-15401|, have also been found as the final products in tRNA of several Archaea that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-28890| phylum |CITS: [20382657]|. Thus, the existence of the α-amino-α-carboxypropyl side chain is not specific to eukaryotes, but the |FRAME: YOL141W| enzyme, and its product |FRAME: CPD-15385|, are.

Summary: This pathway describes autotrophic production of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| from two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules. The pathway was originally documented in homoacetogenic |FRAME: TAX-186801| |CITS: [Jansen82]| (see |FRAME: CODH-PWY|). In that pathway the methyl carbon of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| is derived from CO<sub>2</sub> via the reductions of the tetrahydrofolate route, while the carbonyl group is obtained via reduction of a second CO<sub>2</sub> via CO., In methanogens, a modified pathway exists, where the methyl group of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| is derived from CO<sub>2</sub> via the tetrahydromethanopterin route, which is also a part of the of methanogenic pathway (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., The evidence for the existence of this pathway in methanogens derives from three observations:, 1. No other known autotrophic pathways exist in these organisms |CITS: [914779][101522][718369][3667534]|., 2. Isotopic labeling of whole cells show that acetate or acetyl-CoA is the first product of CO<sub>2</sub> fixation |CITS: [Fuchs80a][Ruehlemann85]|., 3. The enzymatic activities associated with this pathway were detected in cell extracts |CITS: [711675][7287757][6840273][3102234]|., The pathway starts like the methanogenic pathway with activation of one molecule of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| by the unique cofactor |FRAME:Methanofurans methanofuran|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:Formyl-methanofurans|. The formyl group is then transferred to another cofactor, |FRAME:THMPT|. A succession of transformations, catalyzed by |FRAME:CPLX-601|, |FRAME:CPLX-622|, and finally |FRAME:CPLX-641|, which depends on the methanogenic cofactor |FRAME:Factor-420|, results in the formation of |FRAME:METHYL-THMPT|., This last compound serves as the branch point between methanogenesis and acyl-CoA biosynthesis. During methanogenesis, it serves its methyl group to |FRAME: CoM| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.4|. However, during acetyl-CoA biosynthesis it transfers the methyl group to a corrinoid protein that forms a part of acetyl-CoA synthase. This transfer is likely catalyzed by a homolog of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.258|. This methyl group then reacts with the CO formed  by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.4|, producing |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|., |FRAME:ACETYL-COA Acetyl-CoA| is used as the precursor of carbohydrate synthesis, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6142|., It should be noted that the non-methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2234| also utilizes this pathway, but converts the formed acetyl-CoA to acetate in a reaction that produces ATP. Acetate is the sole product produced by that organism in the absence of sulfate |CITS:[11790732][17350930][17564616][26068860]|.

Summary: General Background, Creatine is a naturally occurring amino acid that is used to store and supply energy to muscle cells in vertebrates., The name creatine is derived from the Greek kreas (flesh). , The enzyme creatine kinase adds a phosphate to creatine (see |FRAME: CREATINE-KINASE-RXN|), generating, |FRAME: CREATINE-P|. The energy stored in the creatine-phosphate bond can be reused when creatine phosphate, reacts with ADP to regenerate ATP. , In fast-twitch skeletal muscles, a large pool of creatine-phosphate is available for immediate regeneration of ATP, hydrolyzed during short periods of intense work. Because of the high cytosolic creatine kinase activity in these, muscles, the creatine kinase reaction remains in a near-equilibrium state, keeping ADP and ATP almost constant,, and buffering the cytosolic phosphorylation potential that is crucial for proper functioning of cellular ATPases, |CITS: [10893433]|. , Creatine is found in the blood, brain, and muscle of many organisms. , Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate in muscle, and is usually produced at a fairly constant rate, by the body in a nonenzymatic process. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, and is mainly filtered by the kidney and, excreted in the urine. , Both creatine and creatinine can be used by microorganisms as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [Tsuru77]|., At least three different routes by which different microbes degrade creatinine have been discovered, |CITS: [10893433]|., About This Pathway, This pathway for creatinine degradation has been demonstrated in various strains of |FRAME:TAX-507|,|FRAME:TAX-1663|,, Flavobacterium,|FRAME:TAX-1269|,|FRAME:TAX-286|, and |FRAME:TAX-41273| |CITS: [8590669][9734055][Kim86][9563845], [shimizu86]|. This pathway has been studied extensively in |FRAME: TAX-243975| and |FRAME: TAX-68999|. , The first step is the hydrolysis of creatinine back to creatine, which is performed by the enzyme creatininase, (also known as creatinine amidohydrolase). Summary: General Background, |FRAME:ACET Acetate| production from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| can occur via several distinct pathways, which are found in different organisms., Many bacterial and archaeal species produce acetate from acetyl CoA via a two-step pathway in which |FRAME:ACETYL-P| occurs as an intermediate (see |FRAME:PWY0-1312|) |CITS: [21941]|. The second reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME:EC-2.7.2.1|, results in the generation of ATP from ADP., In most archaea |CITS: [8830684]|, some eubacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-971| |CITS: [Michel90]| and |FRAME: TAX-1108| |CITS: [24164217]|), and amitochondriate protists (such as |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [13076]| and |FRAME: TAX-5741| |CITS: [8557109]|) acetate is produced from acetyl CoA in a single step via the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.2.1.13|. In this process, the formation of acetate from acetyl CoA concomitantly produces ATP from ADP (see |FRAME:PWY-5535|)., A third pathway was described from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-316277|, where acetate is produced from acetyl CoA in a single step via the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.2.1.1|. Unlike in the previous pathway, ATP is produced from AMP (see |FRAME:PWY-8328|)., A fourth variant (|FRAME:PWY-5536|) is found in a diverse group of organisms, which includes some bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-33011| |CITS: [33931420]|), the hydrogenosome-containing trichomonads (such as |FRAME: TAX-56690| and |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [3090435]|), some anaerobic fungi (such as |FRAME: TAX-73818| |CITS: [8257282]|), the parasitic helminth |FRAME: TAX-6192| |CITS: [681067][421954][8885873]| and the trypanosomatides |CITS: [9501211][15326192]|. These organisms produce acetate from acetyl CoA by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.18| (ASCT), an enzyme that transfers the CoA group from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME:SUC|, producing |FRAME: SUC-COA|. |FRAME: SUC-COA| is restored to |FRAME:SUC| by |FRAME:CPLX-7458|, a TCA cycle enzyme that generates ATP from ADP., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-316277| is a model syntrophic bacterium that, when grown with hydrogen- or formate-consuming microorganisms, degrades key intermediates of anaerobic decomposition to acetate. The main source for energy conservation by the organism is ATP formation coupled to acetate production., While most bacterial species utilize the |FRAME: PWY0-1312| pathway, the |FRAME: TAX-316277| genome does not encode the required enzymes. Instead, the organism uses |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.1|. This enzyme usually operates in the opposite direction, converting acetate to acetyl-CoA at the expense of ATP (see |FRAME: PWY0-1313|). However, high diphosphate levels and a high AMP-to-ATP ratio (~6) in |FRAME: TAX-316277| cells support the operation of the enzyme in the acetate-forming direction |CITS: [27531911]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-8046| is a methylated cyclitol that plays an important role in osmoregulation and osmoprotection. It has been found in bacteria, fungi, algae and plants. Summary: General Backround, The polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|) are a group of positively charged organic polycations that are involved in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [4873311][3157043][2185470][1409623]|., While it is clear that polyamines are essential for normal cell growth, we still do not fully understand their specific molecular functions in vivo |CITS:[3157043]|. |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| are found in all life forms, and |FRAME:SPERMINE| is found mostly in eukaryotes., |FRAME:PUTRESCINE Putrescine| can be formed either directly from |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| by ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) (see |FRAME:PWY-46|) or indirectly from |FRAME:ARG| by arginine decarboxylase (ADC) (see |FRAME:PWY-40| and |FRAME:PWY-43|). While the ODC pathway was considered the only mammalian pathway for polyamine biosynthesis, recently the presence of the ADC pathway in mammals has been demonstrated |CITS:[11804860][14738999]|. In higher plants the presence of both pathways has been known for some time |CITS: [11537482]|., In bacteria, both pathways are common, and are often found side by side in the same organism |CITS:[3157043]|., About This Pathway, In the ODC pathway |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| is generated in a single reaction from |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| by the enzyme ornithine decarboxylase. |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| can be decarboxylated into |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| for two purposes - either anabolically, for the generation of |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| as a polyamine on its own, or as a precursor of |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, or catabolically, as a carbon and nitrogen source. Catabolic |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| degradation is illustrated in the pathway |FRAME:ORNDEG-PWY|., Enteric bacteria possess two forms of ornithine decarboxylase, a biosynthetic (or constitutive) form (for example, |FRAME:ORNDECARBOX-BIO-CPLX|), apparently present in all strains of |FRAME:TAX-562|, and a biodegradative (or inducible) form (for example, |FRAME:ORNDECARBOXDEG-CPLX|), which is present in only some strains of |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [3157043] [1939141]|. Other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-287| appear to have only a single |FRAME:CPLX-25|, which is regulated in a complex manner to ensure proper expression for both polyamine biosynthesis and catabolism., Biosynthetic ornithine decarboxylase is inhibited by both |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and is activated by |FRAME: GTP| and other nucleotides |CITS: [4370496]|. A synthetic compound, |FRAME:DIFLUOROMETHYLORNITHINE|, is a very potent mechanism-based (suicide) irreversible inhibitor of most ornithine decarboxylases, which has attracted much attention |CITS:[6421528]|. Interestingly, the |FRAME: TAX-83333| enzyme is completely immune to this inhibitor |CITS:[6800359]|., The formation of |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| by the catalytic action of |FRAME:YKL184W-MONOMER| in |FRAME:TAX-4932| has been determined utilizing null mutants of the encoding gene (Δspe1) which are unable to grow but can be rescued by addition of polyamines to the growth medium |CITS:[7929015] [7492339]|. The regulation of the |FRAME:YKL184W-MONOMER| activity in yeast has been proposed to occur via an antizyme-like mechanism which controls the degradation of the enzyme |CITS:[11535806]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Phosphonates| are quite abundant in nature, primarily as components of phosphonolipids, where |FRAME: CPD-1106| is analogous to ethanolamine phosphate as the constituent of phospholipids. In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics |CITS: [7765831]|. Phosphonates contain a direct carbon-phosphorus (C-P) bond in place of the more familiar carbon-oxygen-phosphorus bond, which makes their degradation challenging., Bacteria have evolved many different mechanisms for cleaving the carbon-phosphorus bond. Enzymes that have been described include the following:, 1. |FRAME: EG10719-MONOMER "Carbon-phosphorus lyase"|, a widespread but poorly characterized enzyme. See |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|., 2. Hydrolytic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.1| (phosphonatase, see |FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY|), |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.2| (shown in pathway |FRAME: P483-PWY|)., 3. Dioxygenases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.78|, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7447|., Data suggest that additional pathways for phosphonate degradation may exist (in |CITS: [21543322]|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1106| is the most common naturally occurring phosphonate. Many organisms, particularly phytoplankton, use it as a substitute for |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| for the synthesis of phosphonolipids. The pathway shown here was discovered by screening marine-derived metagenomic DNA for genes that can restore the ability of a Δ|FRAME: EG10724| mutant of |FRAME: TAX-562| to grow in the presence of |FRAME: CPD-1106| as the sole source of phosphate |CITS: [19788654]|., In this pathway the product of the |FRAME: G-17966| gene hydroxylates |FRAME: CPD-1106| to |FRAME: CPD-16526|, which is then oxidatively cleaved by the |FRAME: G-17967| gene product to form |FRAME: GLY| and |FRAME: Pi| |CITS: [22564006]|.

Summary: The glandular trichomes found on |FRAME: TAX-4081| plants are regions for active biosynthesis of secondary metabolites. Several types of monoterpernes have been isolated from tomato trichomes. The biosynthetic machinery underlying their production has been studied and a number of genes and enzymes have been characterized. Two genes the |FRAME: G-11834| and |FRAME: G-11833| are located on chromosome 8. In this pathway, the authors of a new study report that in tomato trichomes, the precursor to monoterpenes is |FRAME: CPD-461| and not |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| which is a predominant route in a large number of plants |CITS: [19487664]|. , In this pathway, the formation of cyclic monoterpenes from the precursor |FRAME: CPD-461| that occurs in the glandular trichomes of tomato is depicted. The preference for |FRAME: CPD-461| over GPP has been shown. The |FRAME: G-11834|-encoded enzyme ionizes |FRAME: CPD-461| to form the cyclic intermediate |FRAME: CPD-12228| which remains bound to the enzyme |CITS: [7436420]|. It is from this cyclic intermediate that all other cyclic products of NPHS are formed. Only cyclic monoterpenes are found in the trichomes. Non cyclic terpenes like myrcene, linalool are formed by the transformation of the linalyl cation acted on by the terpene synthases that prefer |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| as precursor molecule |CITS: [19487664]|., In some earlier research on salvia plants, it had been observed that cell extracts were able to convert |FRAME: CPD-461| to several monoterpenes although no enzyme was purified until now |CITS: [CROTEAU76]|. With this new biosynthetic information, the dynamic nature of terpene synthases is more clearly elucidated and the previously held view that they are of monophyletic origin is now reexamined. They appear to be belong to at least two distinct families and new functions have evolved |CITS: [19487664]|

Summary: The purine degradation pathway plays an important role in nitrogen metabolism in most organisms. The final product of de novo purine biosynthesis, |FRAME:IMP|, is degraded through sequential enzymatic steps into |FRAME: URATE|, which contains a high level of nitrogen |CITS: [11891236]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5044|)., In most organisms, including some bacteria, plants, and certain animals, |FRAME: URATE| is metabolized via a common pathway, producing the stereospecific form |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as the final product |CITS: [16317038]|. Some organisms that are not able to degrade urate include humans, apes, birds and reptiles |CITS: [16462750]|., It has previously been thought that |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| is formed from |FRAME: URATE| in a single step, catalyzed by urate oxidase. However, it is now established that the process involves three different enzymes |CITS: [16462750]|. In the first step of the pathway |FRAME: URATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|. There are four analogous types of urate hydroxylase enzymes, all of which hydroxylate |FRAME: URATE| to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|. The first type, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10284| gene, was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-3847| |CITS: [16593585]|. The other three types are represented by |FRAME: G-11762 HpxO| from |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [19260710]|, |FRAME: G-17772 HpyO| from |FRAME: TAX-339| |CITS: [23760935]|, and |FRAME: G-2243 PuuD| from |FRAME: TAX-176299| |CITS: [26349049]|., |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE| is relatively unstable, and indeed decomposes in vitro to yield allantoin. However, this spontaneous reaction is unlikely to be physiologically relevant, because spontaneous decomposition yields racemic |FRAME: ALLANTOIN|, while organisms contain mostly the |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| enantiomer., An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of the N1-C6 bond of |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|, forming |FRAME: CPD-5821|, has been discovered and isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3847| |CITS: [10567345]|. An enzyme that catalyzes the decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-5821| to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| was first discovered in mouse |CITS: [16462750]| and later purified from |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [20167108][20511299]|, |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [17567580]| and |FRAME: TAX-272620| |CITS: [20826786]|., This pathway is part of various metaboilc processes, including both degradative pathways, such as the degradation of purines to glyoxylate and urea or ammonia, and biosynthetic pathways, such as the plant biosynthesis of ureides, which is part of the mechanism used by tropical legumes to trasport the nitrogen fixed by their bacterial symbionts in the root nodules to the rest of the plant (see |FRAME: URSIN-PWY|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, This variant is the predominant mechanism by which mammalian cells synthesize phosphatidylcholine. The pathway was first described by Eugene Kennedy in 1956, and is known, together with the parallel |FRAME: PWY4FS-6 "phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis"| pathway, as the Kennedy Pathway |CITS: [13366993]|., The pathway depends on choline kinase and on the availability of |FRAME: CHOLINE|. Animals obtain |FRAME: CHOLINE|, an essential nutrient, primarily from the diet. They can also produce |FRAME: CHOLINE| by conversion of phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine followed by catabolism of phosphatidylcholine to |FRAME: CHOLINE| (see pathway |FRAME: LIPASYN-PWY|) (reviewed in |CITS: [18204095]|)., The yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| also utilizes the pathway shown here, although the methylation pathway shown in |FRAME: PWY-6825| is its primary pathway. When yeast use the pathway shown here, they obtain choline either by active transport of exogenous choline or by turnover of phosphatidylcholine (reviewed in |CITS: [16246068][17010666]|)., It is generally accepted that plants produce phosphatidylcholine via a mixed CDP-choline and methylation pathway (see pathway |FRAME: PWY4FS-5|) |CITS: [15147879]|. Choline kinase activity has been reported from a number of plants such as |FRAME: TAX-3701| |CITS: [15147879]|, soybean |CITS: [8934624]| and castor bean |CITS: [2925673]|. In |FRAME: TAX-3701|, this pathway is significant when the plants are under salt stress |CITS: [2925673]|. , In addition, this pathway has been identified in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-158|, in which |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| makes up to 30% of the total membrane phospholipids |CITS: [4436256][14756787]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (also known as geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, or GGPP) is a crucial compound involved in the biosynthesis of a variety of terpenes and terpenoids, including central compounds such as ubiquinones and menaquinones., In plants, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of essentail compounds such as chlorophylls, carotenoids, tocopherols, plastoquinones, and gibberellins |CITS:[12427975]|, as well as a variety of secondary metabolites. In addition, GGPP is also used in posttranslational modifications of proteins (geranylgeranylation) which is important for membrane adhesion as well as the function of some proteins |CITS:[11500541][16183844]|., GGPP is synthesized from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| either by dedicated enzymes, such as the |FRAME: YPL069C-MONOMER| of |FRAME: TAX-4932|, or by the action of polyprenyl transferases such as the |FRAME: MONOMER-13766| from |FRAME: TAX-1061| or |FRAME: CPLX0-7426| from |FRAME: TAX-83333|. It should be noted that the building blocks for |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| are synthesized in different organisms by different pathways. While most eukaryotes and some bacteria use the |FRAME: PWY-922|, most bacteria, as well as green algae utilize the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (as described in the two superpathways |FRAME: PWY-5910| and |FRAME: PWY-5121|)., In plants, GGPP is synthesized using both routes - in the cytosol using the |FRAME: PWY-922|, and in the plastids using the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|., This superpathway describes the production of GGPP via the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY|., In plants, plastidic GGPP is a central metabolite, involved in the biosythesis of a variety of compounds, (see list given above).

Summary: General Background, Marine organisms, including bacteria, algae and invertebrates, contain many organobromine compounds. Over 2,200 of those, with a wide range of biological properties, have been reported by 2017. Some brominated compounds, such as |FRAME: PBDEs "polybrominated diphenyl ethers"| (PBDEs) in their hydroxylated and methoxylated forms, are found across all trophic levels in marine biota, from cyanobacteria and macroalgae to whales and seabirds. In some marine sponges within the |FRAME: TAX-190525| family PBDEs can exceed 10% of the sponge tissue by dry weight |CITS: [Unson94][Becerro04]|., In addition to hydroxylated PBDEs such as |FRAME: CPD-20585| and |FRAME: CPD-20560|, brominated compounds found in sponges include methoxylated derivatives of dihydroxylated polybrominated diphenyl ethers (di-OH-BDEs) such as |FRAME: CPD-20562| (which is likely derived from |FRAME: CPD-20563| by methylation) and polybrominated dibenzo-p-dioxins such as |FRAME: CPD-20602|, |FRAME: CPD-20604|, and |FRAME: CPD-20564|., The biosynthesis of di-OH-BDEs and dibenzo-p-dioxins requires an additional hydroxylation step compared with the synthesis of PBDEs. The hydroxylation appears to happen early in the pathway, converting |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| |CITS: [25061970]|. This proposal is supported by the fact that rates OH-BDEs hydroxylation are very low |CITS: [21439595]|, and that bromocatechols bromoresorcinols have been isolated from marine sources |CITS: [7494145]|. Further support was provided by experiments that showed that |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.55| can act on |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| as well as |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, producing |FRAME: CPD-20594| |CITS: [25061970]|., About This Pathway, It is believed that the formation of polybrominated dioxins involves condensation of two building blocks - |FRAME: CPD-20548| and |FRAME: CPD-20594| |CITS: [25061970]|. The biosynthesis of the former is described in |FRAME: PWY-7929|. In general, that pathway starts with the conversion of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-58116| gene), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-20548| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.55|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58115| gene. This unusual brominase, which resembles flavin-dependent oxygenases, catalyzes two successive brominations, the second of which also involves decarboxylation |CITS: [24974229]|., The route to |FRAME: CPD-20594| also starts with |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40|. However, the next step is believed to be a hydroxylation that forms |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|. In |FRAME: TAX-717774| this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.2|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58114| gene. Following the hydroxylation, the same brominase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58115| gene, acts on |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, generating |FRAME: CPD-20594| |CITS: [25061970]|., The next step in the pathway involves |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-58117| gene). This enzyme is known to be very promiscuous, and can catalyze the coupling of phenol rings in many different ways, producing many brominated biphenyls and diphenyl ethers (see |FRAME: PWY-7932|) |CITS: [24974229]|. Assays performed with the purified enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-717774| showed that it can also couple brominated catechols. When acting on |FRAME: CPD-20594|, the enzyme formed 4 different isomers of dihydroxylated polybrominated diphenyl ethers, as well as two dibenzo-p-dioxins - |FRAME: CPD-20600| and |FRAME: CPD-20599| |CITS: [25061970]|., When |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| was supplied to an |FRAME: TAX-562| host co-expressing the |FRAME: G-58114|, |FRAME: G-58115|, and |FRAME: G-58117| genes of |FRAME: TAX-717774|, the recombinant host produced bromophenols, bromocatechols, mono- and dihydroxylated dibenzo-p-dioxins, mono- and di-OH-BDEs, and biphenyls, representing all structural classes of naturally detected polybrominated natural products of marine sponges |CITS: [25061970]|.

General Background, Chlorotoluenes are important intermediates in many chemical processes, and are still produced in large amounts., Due to their chemical stability and recalcitrance to degradation they tend to accumulate in the environment., Only a few bacterial strains that can mineralize chlorinated toluenes are known, and only a few of those can degrade, dichlorotoluenes. One of these organisms is |FRAME: TAX-393999|, a strain that is known to mineralize a broad spectrum, of chloro-substituted benzenes, as well as |FRAME: CPD-10654|, |FRAME: CPD-7697|, |FRAME: CPD-10836|,, |FRAME: CPD-10837| and |FRAME: CPD-10838| |CITS: [16348484]|. , The key to the metabolic versatility of |FRAME: TAX-393999| is the presence of two enzymes - a broad-substrate-spectrum, |FRAME: CPLX-7696|, known as TecA, and a similarly broad spectrum |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, known as TecB., Together these two enzymes catalyze the initial steps in the metabolism of all of these compounds, converting, them to modified catechols. The modified catechols are then processed by modified ortho-cleavage pathways, that utilize enzymes specilized in the degradation of chloro-substituted aromatic compounds., About This Pathway, The degradation of the different chlorinated toluenes by |FRAME: TAX-393999| utilizes the same enzymes,, although the pathways follow different routes |CITS: [12218011]|., |FRAME: CPD-10837| is initially activated by dioxygenation, catalyzed by the broad spectrum |FRAME: CPLX-7696|,, followed by rearomatization catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14401|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-10855|., In addition, since the dioxygenase also has monooxygenase activity with this compound, a small fraction (20%) of, |FRAME: CPD-10837| is converted by this activity to |FRAME: CPD-10858|. However, further processing of the alcohol, results in the dead-end metabolite |FRAME: CPD-10860|., Ring opening of the catechol proceeds via a modified ortho cleavage pathway, employing |FRAME: CPLX-7713|., The product of this reaction, |FRAME: CPD-10853|, is subject to both 1,4- and 3,6-cycloisomerization by, |FRAME: CPLX-7712|. However, the product of the 1,4 cycloisomerization,|FRAME: CPD-10861|,, is not degraded further, and is thus converted back to the muconate form by the reversible |FRAME: CPLX-7712|, reaction., The other product (generated by 3,6-cycloisomerization), |FRAME: CPD-10848| (generated in two steps - , a lactonization to |FRAME: CPD-10851| followed by dehalogenation), is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-10846|, by |FRAME: MONOMER-14658| |CITS: [12218011]|., The intermediates of the proposed pathway were isolated and identified by HPLC and NMR analyses. In addition,, the individual enzymes were completely or partially purified, and their activities confirmed |CITS: [12218011]|., The end product of this pathway is assumed to be further degraded to TCA cycle intermediates by a modified, |FRAME: PWY-2361| pathway that has not been characterized in this organism |CITS: [12218011]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13955 Mithramycin| is an |FRAME: Aureolic-Acids "aureolic acid"|-type antibiotic produced by several Streptomyces species, such as |FRAME: TAX-41951|. It possesses antibiotic activity against Gram-positive but not Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [9150235]|., Mithramycin can also be used as an anticancer agent. In the presence of Mg2+ cation it forms a dimeric molecule that interacts with GC-rich DNA regions in a non-intercalative manner |CITS: [1828228]|. It has been used in the treatment of testicular cancer |CITS:[14224214][7700186]|, Paget's disease of bone |CITS: [12846580]|, and other bone growth disorders, and has been used to manage hypercalcemia in patients with malignancy-associated bone lesions. It is also researched as a treatment for pancreatic cancer |CITS: [21447740][21673052]|., Mithramycin inhibits the growth of cancer cells by cross-linking GC-rich DNA regions, thereby shutting down transcription factors (Sp1 or Sp3)-dependent pathways towards proto-oncogenes |CITS:[21543616][22545098]|, such as the |FRAME:ENSG00000136997-MONOMER| |CITS: [1827033]|, the |FRAME: ENSG00000134982-MONOMER| |CITS: [16150893]|, and the |FRAME: HS02256-MONOMER| |CITS: [12846580]|., Due to its gastrointestinal, hepatic, renal, and bone marrow toxicity, which cause nausea, vomiting, and bleeding, the clinical use of mithramycin is limited |CITS: [11853433]|, but there is much interest in developing mithramycin analogues with advantageous properties |CITS: [11853433][12022840][12733914][21067184]|., Mithramycin is an aromatic polyketide containing a three-ring chromophoric aglycone derived from the condensation of one |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and nine |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| molecules, which is modified by a trisaccharidal chain [D-olivosyl-(3→1)-D-oliosyl-(3→1)-D-mycarosyl] and a disaccharidal chain [D-olivosyl-(3→1)-D-olivosyl], attached at the 2 and 6 positions of the aglycone, respectively., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13955| has been studied intensively. The process starts with a type II polyketide synthase (PKS) mediated condensation of multiple acyl-CoA units |CITS: [8807845]|. The polyketide skeleton undergoes several modifications |CITS: [Rohr99][16856198]| leading to the formation of the first isolable tetracyclic intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-14360|, which is 4-O-methylated to give the aglycone, |FRAME: CPD-13965| |CITS: [10652287]|., The aglycone is glycosylated by a total of 5 modified sugars - three |FRAME: D-Olivose|, one |FRAME: CPD-13963| and one |FRAME: CPD-13964| (for the synthesis of these unusual sugars, please see |FRAME: PWY-6973|). Three saccharides are first attached sequentially to the 2 position by the glucosyl transferases |FRAME: G-15163| and |FRAME: G-15162| |CITS: [10660060]|, followed by two additional saccharides that are attached sequentially to position 6 by |FRAME: G-15164| and |FRAME: G-15165| |CITS: [15712316]|. At about the same time the aglycone is C-methylated at position 9 |CITS: [10652287]|. The fully glycosylated, 9-methylated intermediate is named |FRAME: CPD-14352|., The final steps in mithramycin biosynthesis include an oxidative cleavage of the fourth ring, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-15166| oxygenase |CITS: [9889148][12813091]|, followed by spontaneous decarboxylation and reduction of the 4'-keto group, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-15167| ketoreductase |CITS: [12733914]|.

General Background, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate 4-Hydroxybenzoate| (p-hydroxybenzoate) is widespread in plants. It is one of the major cell wall-bound phenolic acids that play a major role in plant defense against pathogens. It has also been identified as an important dietary anti-oxidant. In addition, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-9| and several plant secondary metabolites, such as |FRAME: CPD-9322|. , There are at least two biosynthetic routes leading to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| that have been proposed in plants: 1) the β-oxidation route that converts |FRAME: COUMARATE| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| via |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| (|FRAME: PWY-6435|); and 2) the non-β oxidative pathway that converts |FRAME: COUMARATE| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| via |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| (|FRAME: PWY-6431|)., In plants, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| has an origin from |FRAME: PHE|, where |FRAME: COUMARATE| is an intermediate |CITS: [17658659][Yazaki91][12232327]|. In the β-oxidation pathway, the side-chain shortening is analogous to |FRAME: PWY-5136| via CoA esters. In the non-oxidative pathway, the side-chain shortening is achieved through a lyase reaction that does not require CoA as a cofactor. , About This Pathway, The existence of the non-beta oxidation pathway has been reported in a number of plant species including, but not limited to, |FRAME:TAX-34254| and |FRAME:TAX-4039|. In carrot, the accumulation of p-hydroxybenzoate in hairy root culture was dramatically increased by methyl jasmonate (MeJA) treatment. The enzymatic activities of the first and last enzymes of the biosynthetic pathway, phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) and 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde dehydrogenase (HBD) were coordinately increased by MeJA treatment |CITS: [17658659]|.

Summary: The major constituent of |FRAME: TAX-48386| essential oil is |FRAME: CPD-1084|. Like most mint oils, the |FRAME: TAX-48386| oils accumulate in the glandular trichomes. The formation of |FRAME: CPD-1084| involves three steps: cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| to form |FRAME: CPD-4886|, hydroxylation of C7 position and oxidation to the aldehyde. This is similar to the production of |FRAME: CPD-263| in peppermint |CITS: [20079506]|. , |FRAME: CPD-4886| and its derivatives menthol, carvone, |FRAME: CPD-10051|, |FRAME: CPD-261|, and |FRAME: CPD-1084| have been used in anti cancer drug trials. The mechanism by which they are effective as anticancer drugs is by disrupting isoprenylation of members of the Ras family of G proteins. Among these monoterpenoids |FRAME: CPD-1084| was found to be more toxic than the others in a chemotherapeutic drug trial |CITS: [12488578]|. |FRAME: CPD-261| in low doses in believed to have prophylactic potential in the treatment of breast cancer., Note that |FRAME:MONOMER-15423|, the cytochrome P450 hydroxylase that catalyzes the second step in this pathway, also catalyzes the formation of two additional products from |FRAME: CPD-4886|: |FRAME: CPD-263| and |FRAME: CPD-10051| |CITS: [14599518]|.

General Background, Kavalactones are known for their psychoactive effects. The Polynesian plant |FRAME: TAX-130404| is often ingested for these psychoactive effects during cultural rituals. |FRAME: CPD-22603| is one of the six most abundant compounds found in |FRAME: TAX-130404| roots |CITS: [31332312]|, About This Pathway, |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA "Cinnamoyl-CoA"| has ketone groups added to it to form a polyketide chain, which is then cyclized to form a styrylpyrone, |FRAME: CPD-22601|. |FRAME: CPD-22601| has the double bond found between the C5 and C6 carbon reduced to a sinlge bond, producing |FRAME: CPD-22602|. The hydroxyl group attached to the C4 carbon is methylated, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-22603| |CITS: [31332312]|.

Oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) are among the most conserved sterol bosynthetic enzymes at the sequence level, and homologues have been detected in all species capable of sterol synthesis., There are two main types of sterols-producing OSCs based on the end product of the cyclization: |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.7|, which is found in animals, fungi, choanozoa, trypanosomatids, dinoflagellates, and some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-414|; and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.8|, which is found in higher plants, red and green algae, amoebozoa, diatoms, euglenids, heterolobosea and some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-41| (see |FRAME: PWY-8028|) |CITS: [12519197][24596261]|. A rare third type is |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.47| |CITS: [21526825]|., |FRAME: CPD-13879 Parkeol| is rare |FRAME: LANOSTEROL| isomer. It has been detected in several plant species such as the shea tree |FRAME: TAX-292385  | |CITS: [Akihisa10]| and olives (|FRAME: TAX-4146|) |CITS: [17393211]|. Parkeol has also been detected in sea cucumbers |CITS: [Kerr95]|, and is produced by dome bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-114| |CITS: [14660793]|., While parkeol has not been detected in rice, a recombinant rice enzyme expressed in yeast was found to catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-13879| with no side products |CITS: [21526825]|.

Summary: Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are fatty acid that have 13 or more carbon atoms and contain more than one double bond in their backbone. The PUFAs that have 2 or more cis double bonds separated from each other by a single methylene group generally belong to the essential fatty acids which are all either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, meaning that there will be a double bond at carbon 3 or 6, respectively, from the end of the molecule., PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturated long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. They are produced in many algae, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|., |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID "Arachidonate"| (arachidonic acid) is a polyunsaturated ω-6 fatty acid with a 20-carbon chain and four cis-double bonds. It is produced de novo at high levels by mosses, by some lower eukaryotes (e.g. Euglena), and by some marine bacteria adapted to low temperatures and high pressures., About this Pathway, Most mammals have desaturase and elongase enzymes that enable the synthesis of highly polyunsaturated fatty acids from simpler ones, but lack the enzymes necessary for producing the simpler fatty acids (some carnivores, such as cats, are not able to desaturate simpler fatty acids, and must obtain all polyunsaturated fatty acids in their diet |CITS: [1186900]|)., In order to produce |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|, mammals must obtain |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| in their diet. Once introduced and activated into its |FRAME: CPD-18| form, linoleate can be desaturated to |FRAME: GAMMA-LINOLENOYL-COA| by a 6-desaturase (see |FRAME: PWY-6000|)., |FRAME: GAMMA-LINOLENOYL-COA| is then extended by two carbons to form |FRAME: CPD-14407| by an elongase system dedicated for the extension of polyunsaturated fatty acids. The elongase complex is composed of four proteins, each catalyzing one of the four required steps (for more information about fatty acid elongation, see |FRAME: PWY-7036|)., The identity of most of the elongase components is not known. One exception is the enzyme that catalyzes the first step, which is also the rate limiting. This step is catalyzed by a member of the ELOVL (elongation of very long-chain fatty acids) family, and in the case of |FRAME: GAMMA-LINOLENOYL-COA|, by |FRAME: HS00335|., The elongation is followed by a desaturation at the C5 position, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.44|., Desaturation reactions in animals require oxygen, and are catalyzed by a microsomal membrane-bound three-component enzyme complex that includes |FRAME: ENSG00000166347-MONOMER|, an |FRAME: HS02015-MONOMER|, and the fatty acid desaturase. In many cases, as for the human |FRAME: HS07617-MONOMER|, the desaturases are fusion products composed of an N-terminal cytochrome b5-like domain and a C-terminal multiple membrane-spanning desaturase portion, and thus the enzyme complex does not require an additional free cytochrome b5 |CITS: [10860662]|.

|FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., |FRAME: EC-1.2.3.4|, an enzyme that catalyzes the oxidative cleavage of oxalate to carbon dioxide with reduction of dioxygen to hydrogen peroxide, is widespread in cereal plants |CITS: [12049198][10861243][8509360]|. The enzyme has also been described in bacteria |CITS: [Koyama88]| and fungi |CITS: [16000768]|, although it does not appear to be common in these organisms., Germin is a |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| generating enzyme found in several plant species, including barley (|FRAME: TAX-4513|) and wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|), and some fungi. Germin's synthesis coincides with the onset of growth in germinating wheat embryos (hence the name). The enzyme serves as a marker of embryonic development in germinating wheat grains, The enzyme has been shown to be an |FRAME: CPLX-8224| |CITS: [8044704] [8509360]| that is involved in the defense against biotic and abiotic stress in plants |CITS: [12049198]|. Enzyme activity is detected in barley seedling roots during development and in the leaves of mature plants in response to powdery-mildew infection |CITS: [12228419]|. , The exact nature of the elevated resistance to pathogens is still not clear, but several hypotheses exist |CITS: [12049198]|:, (1) generation of microcidal concentrations of hydrogen peroxide, (2) elicitation of hypersensitive cell death at lower concentrations of hydrogen peroxide, (3) formation of effective barriers against predator penetration by the hydrogen-peroxide-mediated lignification of cell walls, (4) destruction of oxalate, which is an inhibitor of the hypersensitive response, a strategy employed byubiquitous predator organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-5180|, which secretes high concentrations of oxalate as a toxin., The fight against chestnut blight, The pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-5116|, native to East Asia and South East Asia, was introduced into Europe and North America in the early 1900s. The fungus has killed an estimated four billion American chestnut (|FRAME: TAX-134033|) trees in the United States through 2013, threatening to completely anihilate the American chestnut. The fungus enters through wounds on susceptible trees and grows in and beneath the bark, producing several toxic compounds, the most notable of which is |FRAME: OXALATE|. The acid lowers the pH of the infected tissue to 2.8, killing the cells., A fully resistant tree was developed by 2013 by a team from SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry, who introduced the OxO gene from wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|) |CITS: [8509360]| into the American chestnut genome |CITS: [23543108]|. Unfortunately, government approval for releasing the blight resistant tree (code named Darling 58) to the wild has not been obtained as of 2022. The team hopes that the regulatory process will complete by fall of 2023.

General Background, The inorganic sulfur compound |FRAME: S2O3| contains two sulfur atoms: a sulfone-sulfur (oxidation state +V), and a sulfane-sulfur (oxidation state -I). At low pH thiosulfate decomposes spontaneously to |FRAME: SO3| and elemental sulfur, |CITS: [4552952]|. At neutral pH the compound is relatively stable, but several types of bacteria can catalyze its disproportionation in a process in which thiosulfate serves as both an electron donor and an electron acceptor. , Several types of enzymes have been described that are able to catalyze the disproportionation of thiosulfate. These enzymes have been differentiated based on the nature of the electron donor: some enzymes require thiols for this purpose, some utilize cytochrome c3, which receives the electrons from molecular hydrogen via a hydrogenase, some accept the electrons from the quinone pool, and some have only been active in vitro when coupled to cyanide. These four classes of enzymes are described in the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5277|, |FRAME:PWY-5352|, |FRAME: PWY-7813|, and |FRAME:PWY-5350|, respectively., About This Pathway, Non thiol-dependent dissimilatory thiosulfate reduction is found in two unrelated groups of bacteria. One group consists of the sulfate reducing bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-872| and |FRAME:TAX-1562| (described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-5352|), while the other includes several genera of the enterobacteriaceae - |FRAME:TAX-590|, |FRAME:TAX-583 Proteus|, |FRAME:TAX-544|, |FRAME:TAX-82978| and |FRAME:TAX-635 Edwardsiella| |CITS: [3299028]| (described in this pathway)., |FRAME:TAX-544|,|FRAME:TAX-583 Proteus|, and |FRAME:TAX-590| are the major |FRAME: HS|-producing genera of the Enterobacteriaceae. Reports of |FRAME: HS| production by |FRAME:TAX-583 Proteus| and |FRAME:TAX-590| spp. go back into the clinical literature of the 19th century. This dissimilatory pathway is independent of biosynthetic sulfur assimilation |CITS: [3299028]|., In |FRAME: TAX-90371| thiosulfate reduction is mediated by a quinone-dependent membrane-bound system, the essential components of which are encoded by the phs (production of hydrogen sulfide) locus |CITS: [3108233][7751291][7737516]|. Sequence analysis of this locus identified three genes that encode the structural components of a molybdopterin-containing oxidoreductase |CITS: [7751291]|. Operons encoding orthologs of these proteins are found in the genomes of all enteric bacteria that respire thiosulfate |CITS: [22081391]|., The reduction of thiosulfate by menaquinol is highly endergonic under standard conditions, and the reaction is driven by the proton motive force (PMF) across the cytoplasmic membrane. Although thiosulfate reduction requires energy, the overall electron transfer pathway, assuming NADH and/or fermentation products (including hydrogen) are the electron donors for thiosulfate respiration, would result in overall PMF generation |CITS: [22081391]|. In addition, the pathway helps the cell with the removal of excess NADH. In the case of |FRAME: TAX-90371| (but not all sulfide-producing enteric bacteria), the sulfite that is generated in the pathway can be further reduced to sulfide by |FRAME: CPLX-7187|, encoded by the asr locus, consuming three molecules of NADH in the process |CITS: [2163396][1704886]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN "Indole-3-acetate"| (IAA) is a well-known phytohormone. Several biosynthetic routes have been reported in higher plants (see |FRAME: PWY-581|). In one such route, |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD|, which is formed from |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETALDOXIME| by |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.3|, or from |FRAME: CPD-1863| by the combined action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147 "EC 3.2.1.147, myrosinase"| and |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5|, is converted to IAA by the plant's |FRAME: CPLX-1525| enzymes (|FRAME: EC-3.5.5.1 "EC 3.5.5.1"|)., Several plant-associated bacteria and fungi also have the ability to produce IAA, which they use to force plants to produce compounds that provide the bacteria with carbon, nitrogen, and energy sources. The production of plant hormones such as IAA and cytokinin seems to be essential for the virulence of these bacteria., The microbial conversion of |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD| to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| can proceed by two enzymatic pathways |CITS: [1368882]|. The other route is described in |FRAME: PWY-5026|., About This Pathway, This pathway was discovered in the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-358| and in several strains belonging to the leguminous bacteria family |FRAME: TAX-82115|. This route from |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD| to IAA involves two steps., |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.84|, catalyzes the hydration of |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD| to an amide form, |FRAME: CPD-237|, which is then converted to IAA and ammonia by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.4| |CITS: [11607511]|., |FRAME: TAX-358| was shown to posses a second IAA biosynthetic pathway, encoded by the |FRAME: G-5923| and |FRAME: G-5922| genes present on the Ti plasmid (see |FRAME:PWY-3161|). The |FRAME: G-5922| gene product, |FRAME: MONOMER-7862|, catalyzes the same reaction as the amidase. Those enzymes, however, are not expressed in the bacterium. Rather, the genes are transferred into the plant tissue, where they are integrated into the plant's genome and expressed., The |FRAME: TAX-358| |FRAME: CPLX-6913| has been purified and characterized. The amidase has not been purified. However, based on the cases of nitrile hydratase/amidases systems from other organisms, the two genes are expected to reside in a single operon |CITS: [1368882][11607511]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation, and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|. Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria, and certain archaea and fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. The biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail in bacteria. Sequencing analysis and some experimental evidence suggests that the steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, derived from a |FRAME: CPD-205|-like structure. The biotin biosynthetic pathway in bacteria can be divided into two portions. In the first, several routes are known to exist for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-558| or |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs pimeloyl-[acp]|. These routes are described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-6519|, |FRAME: PWY-7147|, and |FRAME: PWY-6578|. In the second portion of the pathway, the pimeloyl intermediates are converted to biotin. The most prevalent pathway constitutes of reactions catalyzed by four enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: EG10121|, |FRAME: EG10117|, |FRAME: EG10120| and |FRAME: EG10118| genes (see |FRAME: PWY0-1507|)., In most halophilic archaea, as well as some cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1148|, the |FRAME: EG10117| gene is missing. Instead, these organisms possess a different gene, which has been named |FRAME: SGL_RS13315|. The gene encodes a rather complicated enzyme that catalyzes multiple reactions, although it is capable of catalyzing only a single turnover, making it a suicide enzyme. BioU forms a conjugate with |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| and catalyzes a reduction, followed by carboxylation of the ε-amino group of Lys124 and successive oxidative cleavage of the conjugate to release |FRAME: CPD1ZN3-1|. During this process the lysine residue serves as an amino donor and is converted to 2-amino-6-oxohexanoate, resulting in inactivation of the enzyme |CITS: [32042199]|. Given that the amount of biotin required for cell growth is quite low, a process based on a single turnover may be sufficient to supply the necessary limited amount., The product of BioU, |FRAME: CPD1ZN3-1|, is an intermediate that is formed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.3.3| (bioD) in other organisms, and can be used directly by BioD, which catalyzes the first ring closure, forming |FRAME: DETHIOBIOTIN| |CITS: [4921568]|., The ultimate step in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.6| (|FRAME: EG10118|). This enzyme inserts a sulfur atom between C6 and C9 of dethiobiotin in a |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent reaction. It has not been possible to reconstitute a catalytic reaction of this enzyme in vitro, and there was some uncertainty regarding the reaction mechanism, cofactor requirements, and the source of the sulfur atom |CITS: [15850974]|. However, it is now accepted that a |FRAME: CPD-6| of the enzyme is the source of the sulfur atom. Consistent with its proposed role as the sulfur donor, degradation of the [2Fe-2S] cluster |CITS: [14967042]| as well as exchange of sulfur atoms between the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] clusters is observed during turnover of the enzyme |CITS: [16533066]|., The distribution of BioU is limited to haloarchaea and cyanobacteria. While it is widely present in haloarchaea, it is only sparsely found in cyanobacteria, suggesting that the gene was horizontally transferred from haloarchaea to cyanobacteria |CITS: [32042199]|.
