Summary: The ABH histo-blood antigen system, The ABH histo-blood group system (sometimes referred to as the ABO system) was originally defined in terms of the antigenic substances occurring in red blood cells |CITS: [Landsteiner00][Landsteiner40]|. However, the same antigens also occur in various mucous bodily fluids (such as saliva and milk), and thus the system is referred to as a histo-blood group system |CITS: [16747710][Morgan44]|., The ABH and the related Lewis blood group determinants are formed from |FRAME: Blood-Group-Antigen-Precursor "precursor disaccharides"| that decorate glycosphingolipids or protein glycans by concerted actions of several glycosyltransferases., There are differences between the ABH antigens found in red blood cells (RBCs) and those found in bodily fluids. The ABH-antigens in the RBC membrane are N-linked to glycoproteins and sphingolipids |CITS: [6799656]|, while those in fluids are O-linked to glycoproteins by O-glycosidic linkage to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues of the peptide chains |CITS: [Wu88a]|. In addition, in red blood cells both glycoproteins and glycosphingolipids contain only the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 precursor"| |CITS: [729592]| while in the fluids both |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1"| and |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2"| precursors are used |CITS: [6156588]| (see also |FRAME: PWY-7832|)., A key reaction in this pathway is the formation of |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen| on the surface of the cell by fucosylation of the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 precursor"| at the 2 position. The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction in red blood cells is encoded by the |FRAME: HS10855| gene, also known as the H gene. In secretions and on epithelial cells, a parallel reaction is catalyzed by the product of a different gene, |FRAME: HS11104| (also known as the Se gene). , Additional glycosyltransferases can modify the H type 2 structure. The |FRAME: HS10887 "A-glycosyltransferase"| and |FRAME: G-54960 "B-glycosyltransferase"| of the ABO system, which are encoded by different alleles of the same gene, add either an N-acetylgalactosamine or a galactose in an α(1,3) linkage, forming |FRAME: Type-2-A-antigen| and |FRAME: Type-2-B-antigen|, respectively., A number of α(1,3)fucosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249|, |FRAME: HS07593|, |FRAME: HS05379|, |FRAME: HS08124|, |FRAME: HS11506|, and |FRAME: HS10520| genes, can add a fucose residue to the non-terminal sugar of the precursor disaccharide, generating the assorted Lewis antigens shown here., The Lewis antigen system, The Lewis blood group antigens, discovered in 1946, are biosynthetically and structurally related carbohydrate structures used as markers of cell differentiation and embryonic development, based on fucosylation carried by a number of fucosyltransferases. The system is named after Mrs. H. D. G. Lewis, in whose serum the first member of the family was discovered |CITS: [20995492]|. However, the presence of the Lewis antigens is not limited to erytrocytes, and they are found in different tissues and organs., One of these fucosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249| gene, is bifunctional and can fucosylate both the 3 and 4 positions of the penultimate sugar in the precursor disaccharide. The gene, also known as the Lewis gene, has a dominant allele (which was named Le) and a recessive non-functional allele (known as le). The α(1,4)-fucosyltransferase activity is only relevant when the substrates are derived from the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharide"|, as that position is already occupied in the type 2 disaccharide., The first Lewis antigens to be discovered were the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| antigens, which are produced from |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor disaccharides"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7832|). However, the α(1,3) fucosylation of the N-acetylglucosaminyl residue of |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| leads to formation of several related antigens known as the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| (also known as SSEA-1, for stage-specific embryonic antigen 1), |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y epitope"|, and the |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x epitope"|., The |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"|, also known as stage-specific embryonic antigen-1 (SSEA-1) or CD15 |CITS: [281705]|, is expressed on several glycolipids, glycoproteins, and proteoglycans of the nervous system and has been implicated in cell-cell recognition, neurite outgrowth, and neuronal migration during development. It appears to be involved in regulating neural stem cells via the Notch signaling pathway |CITS: [22645129]|., When the five human α-1,3-fucosyltransferases known at the time were tested for their ability to form this antigen, it was found that |FRAME: HS08124| was by far the most active, although |FRAME: HS10249|, |FRAME: HS07593|, |FRAME: HS05379| and |FRAME: HS11506| could also catalyze at reduced rates |CITS: [9266844]|. When |FRAME: HS10520| was discovered a few years later, it was shown that it too can catalyze this activity |CITS: [10386598]|. In fact, in mice |FRAME: HS10520| is the main contributor to the production of the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"| epitope |CITS: [16973732]|., The |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y epitope"| (Ley) is a difucosylated oligosaccharide derived from |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 precursor disaccharides"| carried by glycoconjugates on the cell surface. Ley is expressed predominately during embryogenesis, and expression on adult tissue is restricted to granulocytes and epithelial surfaces |CITS: [11037972]|, where it acts as a ligand for lectin-like proteins |CITS: [18711002][22101897]|. However, Ley is overexpressed in the majority of carcinomas, including breast, ovary, pancreas, prostate, colon, and non-small cell lung cancers, and has been correlated to the pathological staging and prognosis |CITS: [2537068][7714977][8621218][9824007][21512109]|. In these cases, Ley occurs either at the plasma membrane as a glycolipid or linked to surface receptors |CITS: [2436750][14871842]|., Ley was shown to play an important role in promoting cell proliferation, tumorigenecity and adhesion |CITS: [21152298][18205178]|, and several clinical trials were conducted using Ley monoclonal antibodies for targeted immunotherapy of tumors |CITS: [1327079][8577771][8640770][10829049][10861456][16963623][17545534][17909358][19825951][26026738]|., The human pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| is known to express the Ley antigen in its lipopolysaccharide, mimicking human cell surface glycoconjugates |CITS: [8890213][10096092][11237846][11741906]|., Another important member of the Lewis system is the |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl Lewis X epitope"| (SLeX). In adults, SLeX is expressed principally on the surfaces of granulocytic cells. It plays an important role during early steps of inflammatory response as a ligand of E-selectin (the product of the SELE gene, also known as endothelial leucocyte adhesion molecules, ELAM-1) and P-Selectin, resulting in the attachment and rolling of leucocytes to blood endothelial cells |CITS: [2210723][7591266]|. A sulfated version, |FRAME: 6-Sulfo-sLex-Antigen "6-sulfo-sialyl-Lewis x antigen"| serves as the ligand for the third group of selectin, known as L-selectins |CITS: [9722682][16380447]|. The antigen is also highly expressed in tumor tissue, where it plays a role in adhesion between tumor cells and blood endothelial cells in tumor metastases |CITS: [6386148][12029441][1699667][1701275]|., The SLeX antigen is synthesized from |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| by the action of two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.4.3.6| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.152| |CITS: [1339443]|. When the five human α-1,3-fucosyltransferases known at the time were tested for their ability to catalyze the latter activity, it was found that |FRAME: HS08124|, |FRAME: HS05379| and |FRAME: HS10249| were able to catalyze it at an appreciable rate (|FRAME: HS11506| could also catalyze the activity, but at a much reduced rate) |CITS: [9266844]|. |FRAME: HS10520| cannot catalyze this activity |CITS: [10386598]|., The SLeX antigen is also a substrate for sulfotransferases that convert it to |FRAME: 6-Sulfo-sLex-Antigen|, which serves as the ligand for L-selectin |CITS: [9556613]|., ABH and Lewis epitopes in Helicobacter pylori, The human pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| synthesizes fucosylated oligosaccharides (see |FRAME: PWY-7833|). Most strains are able to synthesize type 2-based blood group antigens such as |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen "H type 2"|, |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y"| |CITS: [9398905][8890213]|, some can synthesize |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x"| |CITS: [10632700]|, and a small population also expresses the type 1 based blood group antigens |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "H type 1"| |CITS: [23828675]|, |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a|, and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| |CITS: [9565568][10992504][18436591][22160312]|. Several roles have been proposed for the presence of these antigen in the bacterium, including mucosal adhesion, immune evasion, permiting the bacteria to escape from the host immune respons, and autoantibody induction |CITS: [18279843]|.

Agarwood is the dark resinous heartwood of evergreen trees |FRAME: TAX-223751| and |FRAME: TAX-223756| which grow in Southeast Asia. Agarwood finds use in medicine and as a fragrant incense. However, the rapid destruction of the habitats where these tree species grow as well as the relentless exploitation of resin from young branches has reduced the availability of this important resource. , The resin of these agarwood trees is rich in sesquiterpenoids. The resin is produced as response to an infection by a mold fungus. The incense is prepared from the fragrant compounds which are chromone derivatives of phenylethyl |CITS: [15938144]|, |CITS: [11911212]|. It has a pleasant aroma that does not have any similar analogues, given its cultural importance in Southeast Asia with mentions of agarwood in ancient texts, it is constantly under demand. The agarwood oil contains benzylacetone or or alpha-gurjunene and (+)-calarene. Inhalation of agarwood oil vapors induced sedation in mice |CITS: [18404340]|. Extracts from agarwood leaves acts as a laxative in mice |CITS: [18256503]|, |CITS: [20699592 ]|., Biotechnological approaches to find alternative means of production of the useful compounds in agarwood are underway. The known medicinal uses are as a digestive, anti-emetic and sedative. The main sesquiterpenoids in the resin are a-guaiene, a-humulene, and d-guaiene among numerous other sesquiterpenoids |CITS: [16464597]|. The above pathway detailing the metabolic steps leading to the formation of one of the sesquiterpenoids in agarwood, namely |FRAME: CPD-12888| has been elucidated from cell cultures of |FRAME: TAX-223751| |CITS: [20959422]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is an important and ubiquitous structural component of eukaryotic cell, membranes. Many bacterial species possess the capability to metabolize cholesterol and can survive on cholesterol as a single carbon source. The exact taxonomy of some species or genera recognized to catabolize cholesterol has changed over time. Two of the strains that were studied extensively, Nocardia restrictus ATCC 14887 and |FRAME:TAX-1702| ATCC 21387, are now classified as strains of |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [874450][12843070]|. In general, the mycolate-containing nocardioform actinomycetes, which include the genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus| and |FRAME: TAX-2060|, have all been shown to catabolize cholesterol and plant sterols |CITS: [19843168]|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1883| have also been shown to decompose different steroids, including cholesterol |CITS: [Arima69]|. There have also been some reports of Proteobacteria that can degrade cholesterol |CITS: [4628510][9572974][18039763]|., Prior to their degradation, sterols are actively transported into the actinobacterial cells by the Mce4 steroid transporter |CITS: [18955493]|., The microbial degradation of cholesterol is challenging because of its complex chemical structure, low solubility in water, low number of functional groups and the presence of four alicyclic rings and two quaternary carbon atoms. A preliminary aerobic cholesterol degradation pathway has been proposed based on metabolites of cholesterol that have been identified in several actinomycete strains |CITS: [17345852]|, and has been greatly updated with new information obtained by several groups. In general, the steroid is sequentially oxidized and dehydrogenated forming several molecules of acetate and propioniate that can feed the citric acid cycle and generate ATP, or feed biosynthetic pathways such as lipid biosynthesis |CITS: [Murohisa93]|., Cholesterol-regulated genes are usually located in gene clusters that are induced by cholesterol. In |FRAME: TAX-101510|, for example, the cluster contains 82 genes, whose proposed functions mostly fit the predicted pathway |CITS: [17264217]|., About This Pathway, Generally, microbial degradation of cholesterol starts with oxidation of the cholesterol 3β-hydroxyl moiety and isomerization of the structure from Δ5 into Δ4. This transformation is catalyzed by either |FRAME: MONOMER-16891| or |FRAME: G185E-5271-MONOMER|, depending on the species, and results in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-323|., Following the initial reaction, the cholesterol degradation pathway involves two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. While it becomes clear that different organisms perform these processes in different order, the order in specific organisms is still not well known. It has been suggested that the side chain is eliminated first in |FRAME: TAX-101510|, while in |FRAME:TAX-1773| the two processes may occur simultaneously |CITS: [21987574]|. The pathway depicted here follows a route where the side chain is degraded completely before the steroid rings are opened., Side-chain degradation starts with |FRAME: RHA1_RO04679 Cyp125|, a P450 cytochrome that catalyzes the C-26 hydroxylation of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and subsequently oxidizes the hydroxylation product to |FRAME: CPD-13689| via an aldehyde intermediate |CITS: [19843222]|. Degradation proceeds via two cycles of a β-oxidative type process. The first step is activation of the molecule by forming a coenzyme A ester, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-14719|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-16899| |CITS: [21602385]|. The first β-oxidation cycle removes a |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety, while the second cycle removes |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. The exact identity of the enzymes involves in these two cycles is not known with certainty, but they are thought to include |FRAME: G185E-4366| (|FRAME: G185E-4366-MONOMER|), |FRAME: G185E-5233| (|FRAME: G185E-5233-MONOMER|), |FRAME: G185E-7779| (|FRAME: G185E-7779-MONOMER "3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase"|), and |FRAME: G185E-7823| (|FRAME: G185E-7823-MONOMER|) |CITS: [Griffin11]|., The degradation of the side chain is completed by the removal of a second |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety in a process that involves three enzymes, which have been studied in |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [Thomas11]|. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenation of the 2'-propanoate side chain, followed by enoyl-CoA hydration, produce a quaternary alcohol, which then undergoes a retroaldol C1-C2' cleavage reaction catalyzed by a third enzyme, producing |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| and liberating another |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| molecule |CITS: [Thomas11]|. Homologous genes are found in the chromosomes of other cholesterol-degrading organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-685727|., For a description of the second part of the pathway, please see |FRAME: PWY-6944|., For the complete degradation of cholesterol by Rhodococci, please see |FRAME: PWY-6928|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-259| (p-aminophenol) is a metabolite of compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-7669| (paracetamol) and azo dyes |CITS: [10422231][18968869]| that has been shown to be toxic to mammalian cells |CITS: [7556113]|. |FRAME: TAX-221273| is able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-259| as a sole source of carbon, nitrogen and energy. It was shown to degrade |FRAME: CPD-259| by a pathway that differs from the degradation pathway for |FRAME: ANILINE| and C-4 substituted anilines that produces catechols |CITS: [12957929]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6533|)., In addition, it was later shown that this organism produces two enzymes, a Fe-containing superoxide dismutase (see |FRAME: MONOMER-17536|) and a 2-hydroxy-1,4-benzoquinone reductase (see |FRAME: CPLX-8522|) that prevent auto-oxidation of the labile intermediate |FRAME: CPD-8130| to |FRAME: HYDROXYBENZOQUINONE|. The reductase was proposed to have a direct role in the pathway as indicated by the reaction link. The superoxide dismutase was proposed to have an indirect role |CITS: [20480210]|. |FRAME: CPD-259| has also been shown to be degraded by |FRAME:TAX-286| sp. strain ST1 although the pathway was not determined |CITS: [11995823]|., About This Pathway, Pathway metabolites |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE|, |FRAME: CPD-8130| and |FRAME: CPD-294| were identified by GC-MS. The two initial degradation reactions were postulated, but have not been characterized. They presumably involve a deamination and two hydroxylations of the benzene ring to produce |FRAME: CPD-8130|. The possibility of lyase cleavage in the initial step was acknowledged, although a direct conversion of |FRAME: CPD-259| to |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| was proposed. The elimination of |FRAME: AMMONIA| was also demonstrated. The enzymes in the pathway responsible for |FRAME: CPD-259|, |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| and |FRAME: CPD-8130| metabolism were shown to be induced in cells grown on |FRAME: CPD-259| |CITS: [12957929]|. The |FRAME: MONOMER-17532| that converts |FRAME: CPD-8130| to |FRAME: CPD-294| was purified from cell extracts and characterized |CITS: [12957929]|.

Summary: The clinically used antibiotic |FRAME: CPD0-1113| is produced naturally by some species of |FRAME:TAX-1883|. |FRAME: TAX-317| has also been reported to produce this compound |CITS: [3759643]|, but studies suggest that only the first and last steps are shared between the |FRAME: TAX-1883| and the |FRAME: TAX-286| pathways |CITS: [22615277]|. , This antibiotic is a phosphonate, one of several natural products that contain a carbon-phosphorous bond. The |FRAME: CPD0-1113| biosynthetic gene cluster has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-43759| |CITS: [7500951][10681332]| and |FRAME: TAX-1906| |CITS: [17113999]|. The pathway was originally suggested to include four steps, but has been revised to include five reaction steps |CITS: [17220970]| and eventually seven steps |CITS: [28678474]|., The first three reactions in the pathway are not unique and are also found in the biosynthesis of other phosphonate compounds. The decarboxylation reaction by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.82|, drives the initial mutase reaction in the direction of the pathway. The product of the first three reactions, |FRAME: CPD-9466|, is a biosynthetic intermediate for other phosphonates, such as |FRAME: CPD-10013| and |FRAME: CPD-11749|, which are both antibiotics and herbicides |CITS: [9127192] [17632514]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6322|)., The fourth reaction, catalyzed by the N-terminal domain of |FRAME: G-10413 Fom1|, is unique to this pathway. The cytidylation is apparently required before |FRAME: G-10416 Fom3|, a radical SAM enzyme, can methylate its substrate. Following the methylation, the cytidylate is removed, leaving |FRAME: CPD-9465|., The last reaction involves an oxidative cyclization of |FRAME: CPD-9465| to form the epoxide. It is an unusual epoxidation in which the secondary hydroxyl oxygen of |FRAME: CPD-9465| is retained in the product., The |FRAME: CPD0-1113| molecule contains an oxirane ring that is reactive with enzyme nucleophiles. The target , of this antibiotic is the enzyme |FRAME: UDPNACETYLGLUCOSAMENOLPYRTRANS-MONOMER| the product of , gene |FRAME: EG11358| which catalyzes the first committed step in bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan biosynthesis , (see |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [8075065]|. In |CITS: [17927218] [16981707] [17113999] [16015285] [16511089]| and |CITS: [7500951]|., Some bacteria have developed mechanisms of resistance to |FRAME: CPD0-1113|, for example see |FRAME: CPLX-8947|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylic acid"| (salicylate; SA) is an aromatic compound commonly found throughout the plant kingdom that is also found in some bacteria., In plants |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| affects numerous biological and physiological processes, including plant defense (via the systematic acquired resistance system |CITS: [15283665][12873532]|), allelopathy, flowering, and stomatal movement |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|. Given its important signaling role, plants often chemically modify |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| by attaching glycosyl, methyl, or other groups to |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| to alters its activity, volatility, or other properties |CITS [PIERPOINT94][SCHULZ93]|. In particular, |FRAME: CPD-12628| (SAG) is believed to be more water-soluble than |FRAME: CPD-110 SA|, thus enabling it enter the vacuole more easily via an ABC transporter or a H+-antiporter |CITS: [15032822][15871031]|. This process may serve to prevent plants from being over-exposed to active SA and/or may enable the storage of this important signaling compound |CITS: [18248508]|. Notably, in some species, enzymes that perform this glucosylation are up-regulated as levels of |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| rise |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|., About This Pathway, A number of plant species have been shown to perform the first step in this pathway and to catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12628 SAG|, such as |FRAME: TAX-4097 "Nicotiana tabacum (tobacco)"| |CITS: [15871031]| and |FRAME: TAX-4530 "Oryza sativa (rice)"| |CITS: [12228500]|, but it is unclear whether they also hydroxylate this compound to form |FRAME: CPD-12663| (DHB2G), as seen in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [18248508]|. However |FRAME: CPD-12663 DHB2G| has been identified as a naturally occurring compound in other species, such as Cotoneaster orbicularis |CITS: [10746883]|.

|FRAME: Gellan Gellan| is a water-soluble polysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-179878|. The repeating unit of the polymer is the tetrasaccharide [β-D-Glc(1→4)-βD-GlcA(1→4)-β-D-Glc(1→4)-α-L-Rha(1→3)]., Gellan is primarily used in microbiological cultures as a gelling agent, alternative to agar. It is also used as a food additive, as a thickener, emulsifier, and stabilizer., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-84635| is known to assimilate two kinds of heteropolysaccharides, |FRAME: Gellan| and |FRAME: Xanthan|. The organism breaks down the polymers by the action of gellan and xanthan lyases, respectively, and produces unsaturated saccharides as the first degradation products., |FRAME: MONOMER-16405 "Gellan lyase"| is a 140 kDa extracellular enzyme that is produced constitutively. The enzyme acts on gellan exolytically and releases a tetrasaccharide of glucuronyl-glucosyl-rhamnosyl-glucose with unsaturated glucuronic acid at the non-reducing terminal |CITS: [9056228]|., The |FRAME: G-12559|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-16269| acts on the tetrasaccharide, releasing the |FRAME: CPD-13122| residue from the non-reducing end of the terasaccharide. Since it can also act on unsaturated chondroitin and hyaluronate disaccharides produced by chondroitin and hyaluronate lyases, respectively, it is likely to play specific and ubiquitous roles in the degradation of oligosaccharides with unsaturated uronic acid at the nonreducing terminal produced by polysaccharide lyases |CITS: [10441389]|.

General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, The thermoacidophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2283| produces |FRAME: S2O3| as one of the products of the initial step of the elemental sulfur oxidation pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7147| (see |FRAME: PWY-5304|). Thiosulfate is then oxidized by the membrane-bound cytoplasmically oriented |FRAME:CPLX-7152| (TQO) with quinone as electron acceptor, producing |FRAME:CPD-14|., The conversion of |FRAME: S2O3| to |FRAME:CPD-14| is not limited to |FRAME: TAX-2283| and is typical to acidophilic sulfur-oxidizing archaea, including those that do not possess a TQO enzyme, such as members of the |FRAME: TAX-41980| genus |CITS: [25122768]|. Thiosulfate is also generated in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [12855721][15178473]|., A study of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-1006006| has shown that the |FRAME: CPD-14| that is formed reacts with a |FRAME: DsrE3A|, forming S-thiosulfonate modifications on two different L-cysteine residues. The thiosulfonates are then transferred to an L-cysteine residue of |FRAME:TusA| |CITS: [25122768]|. While the exact path of further oxidation is still not known, it is well known that the gene cluster hdrC1B1A1orf2hdrC2B2 is present in a wide array of chemotrophic and phototrophic sulfur oxidizers that do not contain the Dsr pathway. The cluster encodes a possible, heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr)-like complex, similar to |FRAME: EC-1.8.98.1| of methanogenic archaea, which catalyze the reduction of the |FRAME: CPD-1282|, formed in the last step of methanogenesis. The Hdr-like complex in sulfur oxidizers is predicted to have a completely different function and to be involved in a process functionally replacing the Dsr system, releasing |FRAME: SO3| from |FRAME: TusA-L-cysteine-S-thiosulfonates "[TusA]-L-cysteine-S-thiosulfonate"| |CITS: [19703284][24662917][25913822]|. In addition, genetic evidence suggests that a liponamide-binding protein may take an active part in the reaction catalyzed by the Hdr-like proteins |CITS: [25122768]|.

Summary: General Background, Benzoxazinoids were identified in the early 1960s as secondary metabolites of the grasses (including the major agricultural crops maize (|FRAME: TAX-4577|), wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|), and rye (|FRAME: TAX-4550|)) that function as natural pesticides and exhibit allelopathic properties |CITS:[BARNES87][10804466]|. Benzoxazinoids are synthesized in two subfamilies of the |FRAME: TAX-4479| and sporadically in single species of the dicots |CITS: [19577780]|. They play an important role in defense against pests such as insects, pathogenic fungi and bacteria |CITS:[niemeyer88]|. The most common benzoxazinoids are |FRAME: CPD-6365| and |FRAME: CPD-6366|., Since the aglycone benzoxazinoids (see |FRAME:PWY-4161|) are autotoxic, they are stored in glucosylated forms that have reduced chemical reactivity |CITS: [10804466]|. The glucosides are stored in the vacuoles |CITS:[12239364]|., This allows the plants to store the toxic compounds in anticipation of pathogen attacks, prompting the suggestion to name these compounds "phytoanticipins". , About This Pathway, The synthesis of benzoxazinoids starts with the cleavage of |FRAME: INDOLE-3-GLYCEROL-P "indole-3-glycerol phosphate"| (an intermediate in tryptophan biosynthesis) to form |FRAME: INDOLE|. Indole is a volatile compound and can be used, in conjunction with several terpenoids, to form cocktails of volatile products that are used in parasitic defense |CITS:[11556781]|. However, indole can be directed to the pathway described here, where is it converted into benzoxazinoids by a series of cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenases. In successive reactions catalyzed by |FRAME: G-7861|, |FRAME: G-7862|, |FRAME: G-7863| and |FRAME: G-7864| four oxygen atoms are introduced into the indole moiety, producing |FRAME: CPD-6365|, which is glucosylated by the enzymes |FRAME: G-8201| and |FRAME: G-8202|, forming |FRAME: CPD-13811|., While |FRAME: CPD-6365| is the main benzoxazinoid in some plants, including barley, in other plants, such as maize, |FRAME: CPD-13811| is further converted to |FRAME: CPD-6562| by a two-step hydroxylation/methylation at position C7, catalyzed by |FRAME: G-7822| and |FRAME: G-14794|, respectively |CITS:[18192444]|., |FRAME: CPD-6562| has been reported to be further methylated into |FRAME: CPD-6561| |CITS:[12359519]|. |FRAME: CPD-6561| is relatively lipophilic amongst benzoxazinoid glucosides, a property that may affect its absorption by pathogens at the site of interaction |CITS:[12359519]|. Action of β-glucosidases on |FRAME: CPD-6561| releases HDMBOA, which is highly unstable and degrades quickly into MBOA, an important allelochemical |CITS:[9647804][15504434]|. A number of defense reaction elicitors (chitin and chitosan fragments, heavy metal ions such as copper and jasmonic acid) have been shown to lead to the production of HDMBOA-glucoside in wheat, maize and Job's Tears plants |CITS:[11314951][12359519]|., The proteins catalyzing the many steps of this pathway have been found in maize to be encoded by a cluster of genes on chromosome 4 (Bx1 to Bx8). Most of those genes have been confirmed to be involved in this pathway by mutant analysis as well as heterologous expression of the genes in yeast |CITS:[9235894]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD Ethene| (also known as ethylene) is known in plants, fungi and bacteria. In plants, ethene is an important hormone that regulates plant growth and development. It is well-known as a fruit-ripening hormone and is biologically active in trace amounts. Ethene also plays a general role as a growth inhibitor in promoting leaf and flower senescence and abscission., All plants produce ethene from |FRAME: MET| as described in the pathway |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|. In addition, two alternative ethene biosynthetic pathways have been reported from microorganisms. Most microorganisms produce only trace amounts of ethene via the |FRAME: CPD-479| (KMBA) pathway |CITS: [Kazuhiro92]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6854|). In that pathway ethene is produced non-enzymatically by hydroxyl radicals that are produced from molecular oxygen by an |FRAME: MONOMER-16774| |CITS: [3541827][2792734][Ogawa90]|. The second microbial pathway, which is described here, is found mostly in members of the |FRAME: TAX-136849|. In this pathway ethene is formed enzymatically from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|., Being the simplest unsaturated organic molecule, ethene is the building block for synthetic polymers including plastics such as polyethylene. Large amounts of ethene are currently produced in a chemical process from fossil fuels. Ethene has the highest annual global production of all synthetic organic molecules. , About This Pathway, A novel ethene-forming enzyme that forms ethene from 2-ketoglutarate was purified in 1989 from |FRAME: TAX-36651| IFO 9372, the green mold of citrus fruit that is known to produce large quantities of ethene |CITS: [Fukuda89]|. The substrate and cofactor specificities of the enzyme, which was named simply "ethylene-forming enzyme", were highly specific for 2-oxoglutarate and L-arginine, respectively., An enzyme with a very similar activity, although a different amino acid sequence, has been described from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-319| |CITS:[Goto87][Nagahama91][Nagahama91b][1445291]|. The enzyme is plasmid-encoded, and has been eventually detected in many strains of |FRAME: TAX-317| |CITS:[1445325][7952184]|. The enzyme catalyzes a very complex reaction, or more accurately, two simultaneous reactions followed by yet a third reaction. In the main reaction 2-oxoglutarate is dioxygenated to form one molecule of ethene and three molecules of carbon dioxide. In a second reaction both 2-oxoglutarate and |FRAME: ARG| are mono-oxygenated simultaneously to yield |FRAME: SUC| plus |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: CPD-26627|, respectively. The latter is further transformed in a third reaction to |FRAME: CPD0-1470| and |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, some of which cyclizes spontaneously to |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|. The overall reaction can be described as, |FRAME: RXN-12535|, The main product of the enzyme is |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|. The purpose of the in vivo production of |FRAME: SUC| is not clear. It has been suggested that this reaction supresses the ethene-forming reaction via the decomposition of |FRAME: ARG|., One of the final products, |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, can be converted to |FRAME: GLT| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.88|. The glutamate that is formed can be recycled back to L-arginine via the |FRAME: ARGSYNBSUB-PWY "acetyl cycle"|, thus feeding back into the succinate-forming reaction of the |FRAME: MONOMER-16773 "ethene-forming enzyme"|., The |FRAME: G-14615| gene, which encodes the ethene-forming enzyme, has been cloned and expressed successfully in many organisms including |FRAME: TAX-511693| |CITS: [Dong07]|, |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [18640286]|, |FRAME: TAX-5547| |CITS: [18575855]|, |FRAME: TAX-1140| |CITS: [16233410]| and in |FRAME: TAX-160488| |CITS: [ 20399645]|., The organism |FRAME: TAX-36651| is unique in that it is able to produce ethene via both this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-6854|, depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [16660102]|.

Summary: The β-glucoside |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE| is the major breakdown product of |FRAME: CHITIN|, the second most abundant biopolymer after cellulose. |FRAME:TAX-562| is capable of using N,N'-diacetylchitobiose as the sole source of carbon |CITS: [9405618]|. , Chitobiose is imported and concurrently phosphorylated to |FRAME: DIACETYLCHITOBIOSE-6-PHOSPHATE| (GlcNAc6P-GlcNAc) by the |FRAME: CPLX-155 chitobiose PTS transporter|. Recent evidence suggests that this is followed by deacetylation of the phosphorylated N-acetylglucosamine moiety at the nonreducing end of GlcNAc6P-GlcNAc by |FRAME: EG12198-MONOMER|. |FRAME: CPD0-2705| (GlcN6P-GlcNAc) is subsequently hydrolyzed by the glycosyl hydrolase |FRAME: EG10144-MONOMER| to |FRAME: D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| (GlcN6P) and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) |CITS: [33794535]|. |FRAME: TAX-1772| is able to grow with the polyol |FRAME: CPD-6995| as its sole carbon source, but only with a very long lag time of almost 60 hours |CITS: [26560079]|., The catabolic pathway for this tetritol was studied in this organism in combination with the pathways for the degradation of the related tetritols |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-12825|. The enzymes that participate in all three pathways were found to reside in three clusters, with some of the enzymes participating in more than one pathway., The degradation of |FRAME: CPD-6995| begins with its oxidation to |FRAME: ERYTHRULOSE|, which is catalyzed by a promiscuous dehydrogenase that catalyzes the oxidation of many tetritols and pentitols, including |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL| l and |FRAME: CPD-6995|. |FRAME: ERYTHRULOSE| is phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.209|, and the phosphorylated product is converted by an epimerase and an isomerase to |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, a member of central metabolism that contributes directly to the pentose phosphate pathway.

Summary: General Background, Manganese is the second most abundant transition metal found in the Earth's crust. In the environment, manganese is mostly found in three different oxidation states: II, III, and IV. Mn(II), primarily occurring as the soluble |FRAME: MN+2| species, is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions. Mn(III) and Mn(IV), which are commonly found in the form of various oxides and oxyhydroxides, are favored at high pH and oxic conditions (although in certain environments Mn(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands |CITS: [17008530]|). Mn(III) also occurs as a transient intermediate in the oxidation of Mn(II) to Mn(IV) oxides |CITS: [15800042]|., Mn oxides are highly reactive. They mediate redox reactions with organic and inorganic compounds (see for example |CITS: [31466008][34157973]|) and sequester a variety of metals, thus controlling the distribution and availability of many trace elements and influencing several elemental biogeochemical cycles. As the strongest environmentally relevant oxidant after oxygen, they serve as electron acceptors for anaerobic respiration by Mn-reducing organisms |CITS: [Tebo04]|. , Microorganisms, especially bacteria but also fungi, are known to catalyze the oxidation of Mn(II) and the formation of Mn(III) and Mn(IV) oxide minerals. The majority of naturally occurring environmental Mn oxides are believed to be derived either directly from biogenic Mn(II) oxidation processes or from the subsequent alteration of biogenic oxides |CITS: [Tebo04]|. , Despite the great importance of microbial Mn(II) oxidation, many aspects of the physiology and biochemistry of this process remain obscure |CITS: [16054815]|., Biochemical studies have shown the involvement of two types of enzymes in Mn oxidation - a peroxidase (described in |FRAME: PWY-6591|) and a multicopper oxidase (described in |FRAME: PWY-6592|). At least one organism, |FRAME: TAX-76869|, contains both types of enzymes |CITS: [27084014]|., About This Pathway, Several studies have shown a direct correlation between Mn-oxidation and multicopper oxidase enzymes., The strongest case is clearly that of marine Mn-oxidizing Bacilii. The metabolically dormant spores of several strains of marine Bacilii oxidize Mn(II) via a Mn(II)-oxidizing enzyme located in the exosporium, the outermost layer of the spore coat |CITS:[11823231][12420165]|. A cluster of seven genes, designated the mnx genes, is required for Mn oxidation by the spores of |FRAME: TAX-161544| |CITS: [8655549]|. One of these genes, |FRAME: G-12161|, encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-15835 "multicopper oxidase"|., Mn(II) oxidation by the spores proceeds through a Mn(III) intermediate, and MnxG is required for both the oxidation of Mn(II) to Mn(III) and of Mn(III) to Mn(IV) |CITS: [15800042]|. The presence of mnxG was confirmed in multiple species of Mn-oxidizing Bacilli |CITS: [ 16672456]|. MnxG proteins have been purified from both |FRAME: TAX-161544| and |FRAME: TAX-161537| and were shown to directly catalyze biogenic Mn oxide formation |CITS: [18165363]|., |FRAME: TAX-89| is a sheath-forming β-proteobacterium that is characterized by the precipitation of iron and, manganese oxides on its sheath. The strain |FRAME: TAX-89| SS1 lost its ability to form a structured sheath upon subcultivation in the laboratory. Since it retained its manganese-oxidizing ability, it excretes the manganese-oxidizing protein into the medium during growth |CITS: [16346750][3818545]|, The Mn2+-oxidizing protein has been concentrated from the supernatant |CITS: [3818545]|, and a small amount of it was purified and used to generate an antibody that was used for the identification of the gene that encodes the protein, |FRAME: G-12162|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CARNITINE L-Carnitine| is a ubiquitously occurring trimethylammonium compound that plays several roles in metabolism. Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and the name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes, plants, and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. In eukaryotes, among other roles, it is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The physiological role of carnitine in bacteria is still unknown |CITS: [9037756]|. Bacteria are able to metabolize carnitine in multiple ways., Various bacteria utilize an L-carnitine consuming pathway that forms |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| (see |FRAME: CARNMET-PWY|). In this pathway |FRAME: CARNITINE| is used as an alternative electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [Seim80][7815937][15731894]|. |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| accumulates and is released to the environment. When the pathway occurs in gut bacteria, the released |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| is degraded by other organisms in a pathway that releases |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA) (see |FRAME: PWY-8337|)., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-469| species, degrade L-carnitine in a reaction that produces |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| directly (|FRAME: PWY-3641|). These organisms can use L-carnitine as a sole carbon source, but require an alternative nitrogen source |CITS: [25440057]|. This pathway is also used by some gut bacteria, but since the enzyme responsible for this transformation, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.239|, requires oxygen, the pathway is not significant in anaerobic environments |CITS: [24591617]|. It has been estimated that the previous pathway occurs at a rate that is almost 1000-fold higher than the direct formation of TMA |CITS: [25440057]|., Other bacteria, especially |FRAME:TAX-286| species, can assimilate and utilize L-carnitine as the sole source of both carbon and nitrogen (this pathway). The first catabolic step in this pathway is catalysed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.108|., In another L-carnitine degradation pathway found in acetogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1736| the compound is demethylated. The methyl group is fed to the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"| |CITS: [32571881]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8307|)., About This Pathway, There have been numerous reports in the literature of bacteria that are able to grow on |FRAME: CARNITINE| as the sole source of both carbon and nitrogen. The key enzyme that confers this ability is |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.108|, which converts |FRAME: CARNITINE| to |FRAME: 3-DE-H-CARNITINE|. The enzyme has been isolated from numerous organisms, including |FRAME:ORG-5927| |CITS: [4302217]|, |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [3058208]|, |FRAME:TAX-357| sp. |CITS: [8645721]|, |FRAME:TAX-343| |CITS: [Mori88]| and |FRAME:TAX-507| sp., It took many years to decipher the latter part of the pathway. Earlier reports found that |FRAME: 3-DE-H-CARNITINE| is broken down to |FRAME: BETAINE|, though the exact steps were not clear |CITS:[14296565][Lindstedt67][5438040]|. A 2009 study has identified two gene clusters in |FRAME: TAX-287| that appeared involved in the pathway, and characterized some of the genes, although the crucial components (|FRAME: G1FZ6-5512| and |FRAME: G1FZ6-5514|) were not characterized at the time, and the proposed pathway turned out to be incorrect |CITS: [19406895]|. The final clarification of the pathway was provided only in 2014, with the proper characterization of these two enzymes |CITS: [24240508]|. The pathway's enzymes were subsequently characterized also from |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [30670548]|., There is indication that at least some of the bacteria mentioned above can also grow on |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| as the sole carbon and nitrogen source. The enzyme that converts |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| to |FRAME: CARNITINE|, |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.1|, has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-29440| |CITS: [861203]|, as well as from bovine and human sources |CITS: [6497835]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3621|).

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-8212|), and the synthase-dependent pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-8204|) |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-6234| has been reported as a shigatoxigenic Escherichia coli (STEC). In a study of STEC strains in England |FRAME: ORG-6234| was one of 12 strains isolated from medical cases. That serotype (O52:H25) was resistant to ampicillin, kanamycin, streptomycin, sulfathiazole, tetracylines and trimethoprim |CITS: [12010174]|. The O52:H45 serotype infects sheep, but is able to infect humans that consume contaminated meat |CITS: [24849211]|. It has also been isolated from yaks that suffer outbreaks of fatal hemorrhagic diarrhea |CITS: [28546830]|., As of 2021, there is still much that is not known about the O:52 antigen and the enzymes that generate it., The |FRAME: CPD-24311| consists of β-D-fucofuranosyl-(1→3)-β-6-deoxy-D-manno-heptose disaccharides connected by a β(1→3) linkage |CITS: [15231783]|. Both of these sugars are rare in O antigens. The gene cluster encoding the biosynthesis of this O antigen was sequenced and found to contain genes encoding enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of these two sugars, as well as four additional glycosyltransferases and the two components of an ABC transporter, indicating that this antigen is one of few that are synthesized by the ABC transporter-dependent pathway |CITS: [15231783]|., In this type of pathway the O antigen is synthesized while attached to the 55-carbon polyisoprenoid lipid |FRAME: CPD-9646|, which serves as a membrane anchor, and the first repeat unit is separated from the anchor by a short core region. While the structure of the |FRAME: CPD-24311| is well documented, the structure of the core region is not known. Sugar composition analysis of the polysaccharide revealed small amounts of glucosamine, glucose and galactose, suggesting that these sugars may be present in the core region. However, the only enzyme that could potentially be involved in the synthesis of the core region, a putative galactosyltransferase named orf16 present in the O antigen gene cluster, was deemed non-functional since inactivation of that reading frame did not interfere with production of the O antigen |CITS: [15231783]|. In the diagrams shown here no core region is shown except for the |FRAME: CPD-12541| that is transferred to |FRAME: CPD-9646| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). WecA is part of the machinery for |FRAME: ECASYN-PWY "biosynthesis of the enterobacterial common antigen glycan"|, and the wecA gene is not located in the O-polysaccharide locus |CITS: [6183115][7514591]|., Polymerization of the repeat unit is catalyzed by two enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107415| and |FRAME: G-107416| genes. However, it is still not known which sugar is added by which gene product. In this pathway diagram we have randomly assigned |FRAME: G-107415| to encode the β-(1,3)-6-deoxy-D-manno-heptosyltransferase and |FRAME: G-107416| to encode the β-(1,3)-fucofuranosyltransferase, but these assignments may be incorrect., The polymerization of O antigens produced by the ABC-transporter type pathways is terminated by some sort of modification of a terminal residue. During the composition analysis a small amount of 6-deoxy-3-O-methylhexose was observed. Methylation analysis identified minor amounts of terminal 6-deoxy-3-O-methylhexofuranose, and the authors suggested that the termination signal is methylation of a terminal fucofuranose residue. Supporting this hypothesis, the remaining glycosyltransferase gene in the cluster, |FRAME: G-107417|, encodes a bifunctional glycosyltransferase/methyltranferase enzyme. Since the glycosyltransferase domain of the enzyme belongs to the GT2 family of inverting transferases, we show the terminal residue in α configuration. It is not known if this terminal residue is connected to a fucofuranose residue as shown, or to a heptose residue.

General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Corrinoid-requiring enzymes isolated from the anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1525| have been shown to utilze |FRAME: CPD-20847| as a cofactor |CITS: [4699238][8449924]|. This cobamid contains |FRAME: CPD-18321| as its lower ligand |CITS: [5880685][5880686]|. Early studies have shown that this compound is derived from |FRAME: CPD-18497| |CITS: [1175633]|. It is now known to be an intermediate in the anaerobic biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, and is converted into the latter by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.M10| (|FRAME: G-44259|) and |FRAME: MONOMER-19558| (|FRAME: G-44260|). Organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD-20848| as their major cobamide lack these two enzymes |CITS: [27417261]|. For example, the bza operon of |FRAME: TAX-1525| contains only the bzaA, bzaB, and bzaC genes, along with |FRAME: G-58211|. Expression of this operon in |FRAME: TAX-562| deleted for |FRAME: EG10584| and |FRAME: EG12151| resulted in production of 5-methoxybenzimidazolyl cobamide |CITS: [26246619]|., This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20847|. The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the lower ligand base is activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (CobT) by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide or a related compound to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) and the ribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), to form the cobamide., The order of events in this pathway was deduced from studies of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.405| (BzaC), which indicated that its preferred substrate is |FRAME: CPD-20841| |CITS: [32503839]|., The enzymes that operate in this pathway are the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis. Studies of the specificity of these enzymes have suggested that the nature of the lower ligand is controlled by the presence or absence of different methyltransferases that can further modify it and by the specificity of CobS |CITS: [36371846]|.

Summary: Several Actinobacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1911|, |FRAME: TAX-67377|, |FRAME: TAX-1704| and |FRAME: TAX-1665| can utilize |FRAME: ARG| as the sole source for carbon and nitrogen utilizing a pathway that involves the intermediate |FRAME:4-GUANIDO-BUTYRAMIDE| |CITS: [Thoai62b][Thoai62a][Yorifuji89][7766193]|. The same pathway was also observed in the eukaryotic parasite |FRAME: TAX-5661| |CITS: [3600696]|., In this pathway |FRAME: ARG| is degraded via |FRAME:4-GUANIDO-BUTYRAMIDE|, |FRAME: CPD-592|, and |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, which is eventually degraded via |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD| into |FRAME: SUC|, and fed into the |FRAME: TCA| (see the pathway |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY|) |CITS: [13373855][5936244]|., |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: UREA| are produced during this process, providing the direct nitrogen source for the organism (urea can be used after it is split by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6897| into |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|)., The enzymes involved, |FRAME: EC-1.13.12.1|, |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.4|, and |FRAME: EC-3.5.3.7|, were shown to be induced by |FRAME: ARG| added to the culture medium., A commercial process has been developed to produce |FRAME: CPLX-85406| from |FRAME: TAX-1911| in 20 and 200 liter tank fermentors |CITS: [Delcambe65]|., There is also evidence that this pathway can occur in citrus trees (|FRAME: TAX-55188|) |CITS: [Kato86]|, and the intermediate compounds have been found in several other plant species |CITS: [Kato86a]|., In some |FRAME: TAX-1883| species the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-592| serves as a starter unit for the biosynthesis of several guanidine-containing polyketide products , such as |FRAME: CPD-25992| and desulfoclethramycin |CITS: [24218293]|.

Summary: The ripe cones of the hop plant (|FRAME:TAX-3486|) are covered with glandular hairs containing a mixture of essential oil and |FRAME: BITTER-ACIDS "bitter acids"|. In addition to having a major effect on the final aroma and taste of beer, these compounds also have antimicrobial, antifungal and antifeedant activities |CITS:[mizobuchi85a]|., The bitter acids that are synthesized by hop plants fall into two types: the |FRAME: ALPHA-ACIDS "α acids"|, which contain two prenyl side chains, and the |FRAME: BETA-ACIDS "β acids"|, which contain three such chains. The former group is of particular importance for the brewing industry as they are transformed during the brewing process into |FRAME: Iso-Alpha-Bitter-Acids "iso-α bitter acids"|, such as |FRAME:CPD-7116| and |FRAME:CPD-7115|, which contribute to the bitter taste of beer |CITS:[15953717]|., The pathway described here shows the parallel biosynthesis of three types of α and β acids. These acids differ from each other in the structure of a side chain that is contributed early in the process in the form of a branched fatty acyl-CoA molecule, derived from the degradation of branched-chain fatty acids., The first commited step of the pathway, leading to the formation of a 2-acyl-phloroglucinol derivative, is catalyzed by the chalcone synthase-like enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.156|. The next steps consist of prenylations catalyzed by two different prenyltransferases |CITS: [22166201][25564559]|. The prenyl moieties are provided by |FRAME: CPD-4211| that predominantly originates from the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"|, although a small fraction has been shown to derive from the |FRAME:PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| |CITS:[10406953]|. Following an initial prenylation at position 4 by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.136|, a second prenylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.137|, adds a second prenyl side chain at position 6. If the same enzyme adds a third prenyl chain at position 6, a β bitter acid is formed. If, instead, a monooxygenation occurs, an α acid is formed. Since the identity of the oxygenase is not known yet, this last step of the pathway is not well understood.

|FRAME: TAX-3039|, a unicellular phytoflagellate, can accumulate a large amount of medium-chain wax esters under anaerobic growth conditions. The wax esters are formed from fatty acids by the action of two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.108| (FAR) and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.75| (WS or WSD)., The substrates for the fatty acyl-CoA reductase are fatty acyl-CoAs formed by a dedicated system in the mitochondria, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8568|. Those fatty acyl-CoAs range from C<sub>10</sub> to C<sub>17</sub>, but the predominant one is |FRAME: CPD-7836| |CITS: [Inui83]|., The formation of fatty alcohols and wax esters takes place in the microsome. Earlier work reported that FAR from |FRAME: TAX-3039| can use 14:0, 16:0 and 18:0 fatty acyl-CoAs as substrates. It was also reported that, unlike several other similar enzymes from other organisms, which utilize NADPH as a cosubstrate, the |FRAME: TAX-3039| enzyme requires NADH |CITS: [4313936][4634163]|., The gene encoding FAR was identified in 2010, along with the gene encoding a wax ester synthase (WS1), based on their similarity to the genes from |FRAME: TAX-3999| (jojoba) |CITS: [20195781]|., Several years later a second gene encoding wax ester synthase, named WS2, was found in the |FRAME: TAX-3039| genome (UniPrort ID A0A1E1GJF8). In addition, six genes encoding putative bifunctional wax ester synthase/diacylglycerol acyltransferase were found in the genome, and two of them, WSD2 and WSD5, were shown to predominantly function as wax ester synthases that participate in wax ester biosynthesis. Despite the sequence-based prediction, those proteins did not demonstrate any diacylglycerol acyltransferase activity |CITS: [29044218]|.

Summary: Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman's net, with each cell of the mesh defined by two segments of parallel, glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks, which allow the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|. These peptide crosslinks are usually composed of two pentapeptides, each attached in one end to one of the glycan segment and extending towards (but not reaching) the other one. The two pentapeptides can form a crosslink with each other in more than one way., The composition and structure of peptidoglycan varies among different bacterial species, but in general consists of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues. The pentapeptide is bound through its N terminus to the carboxyl group of muramate., The pentapeptide is formed through the action of soluble enzymes that couple ATP-hydrolysis to the ligation of the amino acid monomers. This ATP-dependent coupling of amino acid monomers and elongating peptides by soluble enzymes is very unusual, as oligopeptides are usually formed either by ribosomes or by |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "nonribosomal peptide synthases"|. A similar mechanism is also found in the |FRAME: GLUTATHIONESYN-PWY "biosynthesis of glutathione"|., The pentapeptide, which contains alternating L and D amino acids, reveals considerable variation among species, with the greatest variation found in the third position. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: UDP-NAcMur-Peptides "UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-pentapeptide"| found in most of the Gram-negative organisms and some Gram-positive organisms, which contains |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in the third position., Review: |CITS: [18266853]|

Summary: Over 200 non-protein amino acids are present in plants. Many occur in free forms while some are detected in , peptide conjugates. Many have toxic properties. The role of non-protein amino acids in plants has been proposed to , include serving as defense compounds against predators, as storage forms of carbon and nitrogen, and as , detoxification products |CITS: [wallsgrove95]|. , Willardiine is a non-protein amino acid naturally found in Acacia willardiana, Mimosa asperata, and pea , (Pisum sativum). It exists as either a free amino acid, a γ-glutamylpeptide or a tripeptide. Isowillardiine, , a willardiine isoform, is only detectable from the genus Pisum. The biosynthesis of these two uracilylalanines may , contribute to the plant mechanisms of uracil detoxification. The occurrence of enzyme activities synthesizing , willardiine and isowillardiine was demonstrated in pea, Lathyrus odoratus, Albizia julibrissin, Leucaena leucocephala , and Fagus crenata |CITS: [murakoshi78]|. The enzyme activities could not be detected in Citrullus vulgaris or , Lupinus luteus even though analogous reactions for the synthesis of β-pyrazol-1-ylalanine have been , reported in those species.  Studies of a partially purified enzyme from pea suggest that a single monomeric enzyme , is responsible for the synthesis of both willardiine and isowillardiine |CITS: [Ahmmad84]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, The fish pathogen |FRAME: TAX-55601| is the causative agent of vibriosis, a highly fatal haemorrhagic septicemia affecting marine and freshwater fish species throughout the world. The main serovars implicated in disease are |FRAME: TAX-42323| and |FRAME: TAX-105260|., Two different siderophore-mediated systems have been described in these serotypes. Most pathogenic strains of |FRAME: TAX-42323 "serovar O1"| produce the siderophore |FRAME: CPD-9990|. On the other hand, all |FRAME: TAX-105260 "serovar O2"| strains tested so far as well as some plasmidless |FRAME: TAX-42323 "serovar O1"| strains produce a different siderophore, named |FRAME: CPD-21007| |CITS: [Soengas06][17159203][18451049][18005167]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7987|)., |FRAME: CPD-9990 Anguibactin| was originally identified as an essential virulence factor of |FRAME: TAX-42323| |CITS: [7366725]|. The structure of the compound was described in 1989, showing that it contains both a catecholate and a hydroxamate iron-chelating functional groups |CITS: [Jalal89]|., The majority of genes involved in |FRAME: CPD-9990| biosynthesis and transport are encoded on the 65-kb pJM1 plasmid |CITS: [13129954]|. A full set of the |FRAME: CPD-9990| biosynthesis genes has been found on the chromosome of |FRAME: TAX-669| |CITS: [23660776]|., The pathway starts with the formation of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| as described in |FRAME: PWY-5901|. |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE 2,3-Dihydroxybenzoate| is then activated by the adenylation domain of |FRAME: G-58261 AngE|, which transfers it to the aryl-carrier domain of the AngB protein, a homologue of the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10260 "EntB aryl-carrier protein"|. In a parallel route |FRAME: CYS| is activated by |FRAME: G-58260 AngR| and transferred to the peptidyl-carrier domain of the AngM protein., In the next step, the |FRAME: G-58262 AngN| protein's Cy2 domain catalyzes the transfer of the 2,3-dihydroxybenzoyl moiety from AngB to the L-cysteinyl group attached to AngM, followed by a cyclodehydration of the product catalyzed by the Cy1 domain of |FRAME: G-58262 AngN|, forming a |FRAME: DHB-thiazolinyl-PCP "2,3-dihydroxybenzoylthiazolinyl group"| still attached to AngM., In another branch of the pathway, the histidine decarboxylase AngH and histamine N-monooxygenase |FRAME: G-58263 AngU| convert |FRAME: HIS| to |FRAME: CPD-21001|. The last enzymatic activity in this pathway is the transfer |FRAME: CPD-21001| to |FRAME: DHB-thiazolinyl-PCP "2,3-dihydroxybenzoylthiazolinyl-[AngM]"|, forming |FRAME: CPD-9990|, which is released from the prtoein. This final transfer can be catalyzed by the C domain of AngM, by one of the Cy domains of AngN, or by a nucleophilic attack by hydroxylamine |CITS: [23660776]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-25616 "Leporin A"| is an N-methoxy pyridone alkaloid that was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-41062| in 1991 |CITS: [Tepaske91]|. |FRAME: CPD-25616 "Leporin A"| showed activity against the corn earworm |FRAME: TAX-7113| and moderate antibacterial activity against |FRAME: TAX-1423|. Its relative stereostructure was solved and verified in a racemic total synthesis in 1996 |CITS: [11667120]|. A demethylated version of |FRAME: CPD-25616|, which was named |FRAME: CPD-25617|, was isolated from an unidentified fungal species in 2003. It was later observed |FRAME: TAX-5059| and |FRAME: TAX-266817| |CITS: [24983640][26051490][26525642][35370209]|. |FRAME: CPD-25617 "Leporin B"| was found to induce the |FRAME: HS08399-MONOMER| gene (|FRAME: HS08399|) |CITS: [12668006]|, and was later reported to have cytotoxicity against three human tumor cell lines and antibacterial activity against |FRAME: TAX-5476| and |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [ 26525642]|., The gene cluster that encodes the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-25617| was identified in |FRAME: TAX-5059| in 2015 and named cluster 23 |CITS: [26051490]|. Transcription of the cluster was shown to be controlled by the LepE transcription factor. A mutant lacking the lepE gene produced an orange-red pigment that was found to be a complex of trimeric leporin B and iron in zero valent form, raising the possibility that the natural role of leporin B is as a siderophore |CITS: [26051490]|. A similar phenomenon was shown for another fungal 2-pyridone alkaloid, |FRAME: CPD-17122| |CITS: [34903054]|., In order to decipher the reactions of this pathway, different combination of genes from the leporin B biosynthetic gene cluster were heterologously reconstituted in |FRAME: TAX-162425| |CITS: [28902839]|. It was found that the combined action of the |FRAME: G-107845 "LepA polyketide synthase/non-ribosomal peptide synthase"| (PKS/NRPS), the |FRAME: G-107843 "LepG trans-enoyl reductase"|, and the |FRAME: G-107847 "LepH ring-expansion oxidase"| (a cytochrome P-450) is responsible for fusion of phenylalanine with a hexaketide and the subsequent release of the stable tetramic acid precursor, |FRAME: CPD-25620|. This compound is reduced into |FRAME: CPD-25619| by the |FRAME: G-107846 "LepF dehydrogenase"| |CITS: [28902839]|., The next step involves a very complex reaction catalyzed by SAM-dependent enzyme LepI |CITS: [28902839]|. This reaction involves stereoselective dehydration, bifurcating intramolecular Diels-Alder/hetero-Diels-Alder reactions via an ambimodal transition state, and a [3,3]-sigmatropic retro-Claisen rearrangement |CITS: [28902839]|. The final reaction in the pathway is catalyzed by a second cytochrome P-450, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107844| gene, which introduces a hydroxyl group at the ring nitrogen to form |FRAME: CPD-25617| |CITS: [28902839]|.

|FRAME: CPD-11725 "Homotaurine"| is a natural product in red algae and an analogue of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA)., It can be used by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-381666| as a sole source of nitrogen, which is assimilated into cell material., The organosulfonate part of the molecule was excreted into the medium in the form of |FRAME: CPD-11727| |CITS: [19648235]|., The first reaction was shown to be catalyzed by an inducible |FRAME: CPLX-7897 "homotaurine:2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase"|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-11726|. A second Inducible enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15033 "NAD(P)+-dependent 3-sulfopropanal dehydrogenase"|, converted the later into |FRAME: CPD-11727|. Both enzymes have been purified, and were shown to be identical to the enzymes responsible for the metabolism of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (see |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY|)., The product of this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-11727|, is transported out of the cell via the broad substrate range sulfite exporter TauE, which is associated with sulfur, rather than GABA, metabolism |CITS: [19648235]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in dicotyledon type I cell walls. The cross-linking between xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the three-dimensional matrix between adjacent cellulose microfibrils |CITS: [Whitney95]|., Xyloglucan has a backbone of β-1,4-linked cellotetraose units, which are substituted in C-6 by α-D-xylosyl residues at two or three of the first four glucosyl residues (but not the residue closest to the reducing end) |CITS: [8252539]|. Some of the xylosyl residues are subsequently further substituted by (1,2)-β-D-galactosyl residues at the second and/or third xylose residue and by (1,2)-α-L-fucose at the galactosyl unit of the third xylose residue |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. , A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose and β-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, β-D-galactose and α-L-fucose |CITS:[Fry93]|., Using this terminology, most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide XXXG units as well further modified XXLG, XLXG, and XLLG units., About This Pathway, Some organisms have xyloglucan-specific exo-β-1,4-glucanases (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.120|) that cleave the , (1→4)-β-D-glucosidic links in oligoxyloglucans so as to remove successive |FRAME: CPD0-1202| (α-D-xylosyl-(1→6)-Beta;-D-glucose) disaccharides from the non-reducing chain ends., Such enzymes have been characterized from the fungi |FRAME: TAX-51453| and |FRAME: TAX-85845| |CITS: [15541296]|., The action of |FRAME: MONOMER-16611| releases the galactosyl residues, converting all of these oligosaccharides to |FRAME: CPD-13375|. This heptasaccharide can be hydrolyzed further by |FRAME: CPLX-8293| to |FRAME: CPD0-1202| and |FRAME: GLC| |CITS: [4019436]|.

Summary: Pterocarpan phytoalexins are antimicrobial compounds in leguminous plants formed upon pathogenic attacks and similar biotic stress-related events. |FRAME: Medicarpin Medicarpin|, first isolated from heartwood of the tropical tree |FRAME: TAX-149635| |CITS: [Harper65]|, is a major pterocarpan phytoalexin. It has been reported from many legumes, including alfalfa (|FRAME: TAX-3879|) |CITS: [Smith71][8071365]|, red clover (|FRAME: TAX-57577|) |CITS: [Higgins72]|, broad bean (|FRAME: TAX-3906|) |CITS: [Hargreaves76]|, all members of the |FRAME: TAX-78532| genus |CITS: [Ingham76]|, and the model legume |FRAME: TAX-3880| |CITS: [15605242]|. |FRAME: Medicarpin Medicarpin| is found in both a (-) and a (+) conformations. While |FRAME: CPD-3402| appears to be the most common form, |FRAME: CPD-20031| has been reported from several plants such as |FRAME: TAX-3897| and |FRAME: TAX-77268| |CITS: [Vanetten83][Martinez-Sotres12]|., The biosynthetic route of |FRAME: CPD-3402| starts with |FRAME: FORMONONETIN|, a 4'-methoxylated isoflavone, which is also the origin for the pterocarpans |FRAME: CPD-3631| in chickpea and |FRAME: CPD-3944| in pea. All pterocarpans are easily induced and show time- and tissue-specific expression patterns |CITS: [7866024]| |CITS: [Daniel90]|., Malonate glucosides of pterocarpans frequently accumulate constitutively in below-ground organs of legumes, indicating that under certain physiological circumstances a metabolic link exists between isoflavone conjugation reactions and pterocarpan synthesis |CITS: [Daniel90][Weidemann91][Barz92]|., In leguminous plants pterocarpans have been found with different stereochemical orientation. Chick pea and alfalfa accumulate only (-)- or (6aR,11aR)-pterocarpans, whereas peanuts accumulate pterocarpans of the opposite stereochemistry (+)- (6aS, 11aS). Some legumes (e.g. the scholar tree, Sophora japonica) build up an racemic mixture of both (-)- and (+)-pterocarpans. The stereochemistry of this phytoalexins can be crucial since it has been found that pathogens cannot break down the opposite enantiomer of the pterocarpans usually found in their target plants |CITS: [VanEtten83]|., A study of the last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.139|, from |FRAME: TAX-46348| has shown that the stereochemistry of the final product is determined by the chiral center at C-3. A (3R) configuration results in production of a (-) pterocarpan, while a (3S) configuration produces a (+)-pterocarpan. However, it is still not known at what step the conformation of the C-3 carbon is modified and by which enzyme |CITS: [28394400]|.

Ornithine is an amino acid derivative, usually derived from arginine. Its production is shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: ARGASEDEG-PWY|, |FRAME: ARGDEGRAD-PWY|, |FRAME: ARG-PRO-PWY|, |FRAME: ARG-GLU-PWY|, |FRAME: GLYCGREAT-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-4981|, |FRAME: PWY-4984|, |FRAME: ARGSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|, |FRAME: GLUTORN-PWY|, and |FRAME: CITRULBIO-PWY|., Species of the anaerobic clostridia can interconvert arginine, ornithine and proline using Stickland reactions. In |FRAME:TAX-1509| ornithine can be produced from arginine by the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6344| |CITS: [195930]|. However, the organism also possesses |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.12|, which produces proline directly from ornithine, as shown above. It continues as shown in |FRAME: PWY-8186|, using ornithine as an electron acceptor, ultimately reducing it to |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| |CITS: [10220161][4373469][3534538]|). Further degradation of 5-aminopentanoate has not been described in this organism., Ornithine cyclodeaminase is also found in aerobic soil bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-358| and |FRAME:TAX-303|, where is is involved in proline biosynthesis (|CITS: [3129535][15518536][2644238]|). In |FRAME:TAX-303| ornithine is formed from arginine via the |FRAME: ARGDEGRAD-PWY "arginine deaminase pathway"| |CITS: [237904] [3968036]|. |FRAME:TAX-358| uses the arginase pathways to form ornithine, as indicated by the pathway links above. In those organisms proline can be degraded as described in |FRAME: PROUT-PWY|.
