Summary: Plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-40553| family have been valued both for flavor and medicinal purposes throughout the world., The domestic Alliums (such as onion, garlic, chives and leek) contain high concentrations of organic sulfur compounds especially in their bulbs and leaves. These compounds consist mostly of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| such as |FRAME: CPD-9269|, |FRAME: CPD-9307|, and |FRAME: CPD-9277|, as well as γ-glutamyl peptides (together these compounds make up over 70% of the total sulfur in garlic |CITS: [ Lawson96]|)., These compounds, which are found in the cytoplasm, are produced constitutively. The S-alkyl cysteine S-oxides are substrates for the alliinase enzymes (|FRAME: EC-4.4.1.4|), which convert them to |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|. However, the enzymes are kept in vacuoles, and are thus sequestered from their substrates |CITS: [Lancaster81][19463015]|. Only when the tissue is injured, the alliinase enzymes are released from the vaculoes and interact with their substrates, producing |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|., |CITS: [16010345]|. Once formed, S-alkylsulfenates are very active and tend to condense spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-17425 thiosulfinates| |CITS: [21905712]|. Depending on the Allium species, and under differing conditions, the thiosulfinates can decompose to form additional sulfur constituents including diallyl, methyl allyl, and diethyl mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, and hexasulfides, vinyldithiins, and (E)- and (Z)-ajoene |CITS: [16010345]|., In some species, dedicated enzymes commonly known as "lachrymatory-factor synthases" act on the S-alkylsulfenates rapidly, before they condense, producing volatile compounds that cause the eyes of animals to tear (lachrymatory factors) - a further defense mechanism against herbivory.

|FRAME: Heme-d1 "Heme d1"| is only made by denitrifying bacteria with a cytochrome nitrite reductase cd1 (|FRAME: G-250|) for which |FRAME: Heme-d1| acts as an essential cofactor, tailored to meet the mechanistic requirements of the reaction., Bacteria that produce NirS always contain (downstream of the |FRAME: G-250| gene) a set of contiguous genes necessary for |FRAME: Heme-d1| synthesis |CITS: [7588711]|. The operon contains the nirECFDLGHJ genes (in |FRAME: TAX-265 Paracoccus| species nirD and nirL are fused into a single gene), and is transcribed in the presence of |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| |CITS: [15667289]|., Although the operon was thought to encode all the enzymes for |FRAME: Heme-d1| biogenesis, initially only the function of NirE has been unambiguously determined, as an S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet)-dependent uroporphyrinogen methyltransferase, producing |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| |CITS: [19754882][19796169]|., To elucidate the complete pathway, the D-L, G, H, J, and F genes of |FRAME: TAX-82367| were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| and cell-free extracts of strains overproducing either individual proteins or combinations of them were incubated with |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| and their products analyzed |CITS: [21969545]|., It was found that |FRAME: TAX-562| cell lysate overexpressing NirD (where the C-terminal NirL encoding sequence was removed) or NirH could catalyze a single decarboxylation reaction of siroheme. However, all four proteins were required for the total conversion of siroheme to didecarboxysiroheme.

Summary: |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| is a key substrate in glycoprotein formation., In eukaryotes, |FRAME:MANNOSE| is a key monosaccharide for the glycosylation of proteins and lipids., Mannose-containing glycoconjugates, such as protein N- and C-glycans, some, O-glycans, glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) protein membrane anchors, and some glycolipids,, have a variety of important functions. These functions include the promotion of correct folding, solubility,, stability and intracellular sorting of proteins, promoting the enzymatic, hormonal or receptor activity of, many proteins, and the formation of cell surface glycocalyces, extracellular matrices and protective cell, walls. In addition, glycoproteins are known to play major roles in cell-cell interactions, (see |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|) |CITS: [11447107]|., |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| is the critical metabolite of the mannose activation pathway for, glycoconjugate synthesis in eukaryotes, as it is utilized directly or indirectly as a mannose donor for all, mannosylation reactions., In addition, |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| is a precursor for the biosynthesis of several important, compounds, including |FRAME: CPD-13118| (see |FRAME: PWY-66|), |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-882|), |FRAME: 2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE|, (see |FRAME: PWY-5656|) and |FRAME: CPD-353| (see |FRAME: GDPRHAMSYN-PWY|)., The crucial role of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| is supported by the finding that deletion of certain genes, in this pathway are lethal in |FRAME: TAX-4932| and |FRAME: TAX-5476| |CITS:[9195935][10844699], [3288631][3053713]|.

Summary: General Background, Pterocarpans constitute a group of natural isoflavonoids, which are typically involved as , phytoalexins in the defense against pathogens of leguminous plants. In contrast to many other isoflavonoids, pterocarpans , are mostly not constitutively expressed but induced by biotic and abiotic stress |CITS: [Dewick94]|., Daidzein is a crucial intermediate in the biosynthesis of phytoalexins, and as such the branching point for the formation , of various complex pterocarpans, such as phaseollin and glyceollin. The biosynthetic route of pterocarpans leads to , various compounds distinctive for certain leguminous species. The simple pterocarpans medicarpin (alfalfa), maackiain (chickpea) , and pisatin (pea) are characterized by methoxy, methylendioxy and 6a-hydroxyl ring substitutents. On the other side , there are the complex type pterocarpans, such as phaseollins (bean) and gluceollins (soybean) bearing prenyl substituents , on their furan ring structure |CITS: [Dixon99]| |CITS: [Tahara95]|., About This Pathway, Glyceollins are the main phytoalexins found in soybean (|FRAME:TAX-3847|). Consistent , with most of the isoflavonoid derived phytoalexins, glyceollins are induced in response to plant pathogens |CITS: [10888516]| , |CITS: [6540173]| and related stress |CITS: [12590114]|. , The initial enzymatic steps of the glyceollin biosynthesis parallel the biosynthesis of medicarpin and maackiain. In contrast , to those simple pterocarpans the complex prenylated pterocarpans (phaseollin, glyceollin) derive from the 5-deoxyisoflavone , daidzein but do not involve a methoxylation step during their biosynthesis. , Glycinol, the final compound in this part of the glyceollin pathway, is stereospecifically hydroxylated at the 6a position , resulting in the (-) or (6aS,11aS)-3,6a,9-configuration of this compound |CITS: [6540173]|. The remaining enzymatic , reactions maintain this configuration as demonstrated for other pathways that involve a pterocarpan-6a-hydroxylase , in their biosynthesis (e.g. pisatin) |CITS: [2505672]|. The final enzymatic steps in glyceollin biosynthesis include the introduction , of dimethylallyl groups to (-)-glycinol leading to two prenylated precursors (glyceollidin I and II) with the subsequent , cyclization of those intermediates producing the three glyceollins (I - III) identified in soybean. These steps closely resemble , the final biosynthetic sequence reported for phaseollin accumulation in bean |CITS: [Biggs87]|. , Cytochrome P450 dependent enzymes are highly involved in the glyceollin biosynthesis, catalyzing five out of fourteen , enzymatic steps |CITS: [Heller94]|. Prenylation of pterocarpans, and isoflavonoids in general, lead to more complex , structures, improve solubility and have been reported to increase their antifungal and antifeedant activity |CITS: [Tahara95]|. , Plants, involving the phytoalexin glyceollin in their defense repertoire, can obviously distinguish between different kinds , of stress. Simple wounding of plant tissues was not sufficient to increase glyceollin production, whereas elicitation with , fungal pathogens resulted in a fast and specific glyceollin accumulation |CITS: [Zahringer78]| |CITS: [Leube83]|. , However, it has been shown that such a response is triggered by a complex cascade of events and depends on many , different factors including the age of tissues, light and the generation of an "elicitation competency" in the responding , cells |CITS: [Abbasi01]|. , Phaseollin, one of the major phytoalexins in bean (|FRAME:TAX-3885|), also belongs to the complex types of , pterocarpans. The biosynthesis of phaseollin parallels the biosynthesis of gluceollins, the prenylated pterocarpans in soybean , (|FRAME:TAX-3847|). The limited distribution of prenyltransferases has resulted in a smaller number of plants being , able to synthesize complex isoflavonoids. The prenylated pterocarpans are even restrictively distributed throughout the , legumes |CITS: [Tahara95]|. Phaseollin was the first antifungal isoflavonoid identified from bean and is believed to play , an important role in host plant defense. , It has been confirmed that prenylation occurred after the basic skeleton of pterocarpans (or other classes of isoflavonoids) , has been constructed |CITS: [Dewick82]|. As most of the enzymes involved in phytoalexin biosynthesis the prenyltransferase , activity was significantly increased by biotic and abiotic elicitors (yeast extract, CuCl2 treatment) |CITS: [Biggs87]|.

Afrormosin conjugates are one of the major constitutive secondary metabolites in cell suspension cultures of |FRAME: TAX-3879 Medicago sativa (alfalfa)"| |CITS: [16667691]| and |FRAME: TAX-3880| (barrel medic) |CITS: [17156801]|., Afrormosin has also been identified in other leguminous plants, such as |FRAME: TAX-158323|, where it appears to show antioxidative benefits |CITS: [Shirataki97]|, Feeding experiments with [3H1] formonetin in |FRAME: TAX-3880| suggest the production of, labeled versions of all of the compounds shown in this diagram, but the exact position of the glucose attachment was not confirmed in these experiments.|CITS: [18055588]|. Similarly, there is evidence for the generation of these compounds based on L-[U-14C]-phenylalanine labeling experiments in |FRAME: TAX-3879| |CITS: [16667691]|. Little is known about the exact nature of these biochemical transformations and neither the glucose donor, nor any other co-factors have been identified. It is also unclear whether the conjugated forms of these compounds can be released into the free form of afrormosin. However, there is evidence that the increase in afrormosin levels observed in |FRAME: TAX-3880| following MeJA elicitation is achieved, in part, from a decrease in afrormosin glycoside levels, suggesting the presence of, a glucoside cleavage reaction |CITS: [18055588]|., Although high levels of these compounds may be present in the absence of an external stimulus, their levels may also change to varying degrees in response to different signals. It should be noted that differences can be observed between the responses of the two |FRAME:TAX-3877| species as well |CITS: [16667691][18055588]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "Fatty acids"| are carboxylic acids with a long unbranched aliphatic tail., Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID| (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids., Fatty acids are often classified into four groups by their lengths:, |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of fewer than six carbons., |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 6-12 carbons., |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 13-21 carbons., |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 22 carbons or longer., Very-long-chain fatty acids are components of eukaryotic cells and are involved in many different physiological functions in different organisms. They are abundant in some tissues, for example as constituents of myelin in the brain or of storage triacylglycerols in plant seeds, and are components of plant cuticular waxes |CITS: [14581464]| (see |FRAME: PWY-282|), of sphingolipids |CITS: [16730802]|, and of the lipid barrier of the skin. They are also involved in the pathways for protein trafficking and for the synthesis of the glycosylphostphatidylinositol (GPI) lipid anchor |CITS: [16980694]|., About This Pathway, VLCFAs are synthesized in eukaryotes in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound enzyme complex known as the elongase |CITS: [10907783]|. This complex catalyzes the sequential additions of C2 moieties from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to preformed C18 acyl groups derived from the de novo fatty acid biosynthesis pathway. Each elongation cycle is composed of 4 reactions: condensation of |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs| and |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to form |FRAME: 3-KETOACYL-COA|, reduction to, |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYACYL-COA|, dehydration to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA|, and a final reduction to yield a chain-elongated fatty acyl-CoA |CITS: [16950653][16564093]|., While the reactions catalyzed by the elongase are similar to those of de novo fatty acid biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5994| and |FRAME: PWY-5971|), there are several differences between the elongase complex and the fatty acid synthase (FAS) complex. In animals and yeast all of the functions of FAS are present in either one (mammals) or two (yeast) large multidomain subunits (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628 "human fatty acid synthase"| and |FRAME: CPLX-7627 "yeast fatty acid synthase"|). The elongase, on the other hand, is composed of four enzymes that catalyze independent reactions, similarly to the bacterial/plants FAS systems. In addition, the elongase always utilizes |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| as the C2 donor unit, while FAS uses either malonyl-CoA (in yeast and animals) or |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"| in bacteria and plants. , The elongase accepts long-chain fatty acids [usually |FRAME: PALMITATE| (C16) or |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| (C18)] made by the cytosolic fatty acid synthase complex, and produces |FRAME: ARACHIDIC_ACID| (C20), |FRAME: DOCOSANOATE| (C22), |FRAME: TETRACOSANOATE| (C24), |FRAME: CPD-7832| (26) or even longer acids. , The four enzymes that form the elongase complex are |FRAME: YCR034W-MONOMER| or condensing enzyme |CITS: [11341960]|, |FRAME: MONOMER3O-79|, |FRAME: MONOMER3O-85| and |FRAME: G3O-29445-MONOMER|., While only one enzyme catalyzes each of the last three reactions of the cycle (respectively), the first step (the condensation of the 2 carbons from malonyl-CoA to the nascent acyl-CoA) is catalyzed by several different enzymes that differ from each other in their preference towards substrates with different lengths and degrees of desaturation., These enzymes, which are also the rate-limiting step in the cycle, thus determine the length of the final acyl-CoA produced by the complex they participate in |CITS: [11113186]|., In yeast the |FRAME: YCR034W| and |FRAME: G3O-14| genes encode condensing enzymes that participate in the elongase complex. In mammals there are seven distinct "elongase for very long fatty acids" (ELOVL) subtypes. The human enzymes are encoded by the |FRAME: HS00873|, |FRAME: ENSG00000096256|, |FRAME: HS04346|, |FRAME: HS04216|, |FRAME: HS00335|, |FRAME: HS10142|, and |FRAME: HS09036| genes |CITS: [16564093]|.

General Background, Most microorganisms capable of osmotic adaptation accumulate compatible solutes in response to, increases in the levels of salts or sugars in the environment., |FRAME: CPD-9190| (glucosylglycerate, GG) is a rather rare compatible solute that was first identified in the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-32049 "Synechococcus sp. PCC 7002 (referred to as Agmenellum quadruplicatum in the text"|) |CITS: [Kollman79]|. Following that initial discovery, GG was observed in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-39664| strain FDF-1 |CITS: [16348748][16348748]|, and in several bacteria, including a salt-sensitive mutant of the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-2746| |CITS: [10473374]|,, in the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [15528516]|, and in the thermophilic and slightly halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-309805|, that belongs to the Aquificae class |CITS: [17189358]|., The role of GG as a compatible solute during osmotic stress has not been verified in most of these organisms, but has been demonstrated unequivocally in |FRAME: TAX-556| under nitrogen limiting conditions. When nitrogen concentration is high the organism synthesizes mostly other, nitrogen-containing compatible solutes (|FRAME:GLT| and |FRAME:GLN|). It has been suggested that GG may also accumulate in the other organisms during salt stress only under, nitrogen-limiting conditions |CITS: [15528516]|., Two pathways are known for the biosynthesis pf GG, a two-step pathway (described in |FRAME: PWY-5662|) and a single-step pathway, which is described here., About This Pathway, The single-step pathway for the synthesis of glucosylglycerate was proposed based on the activity of the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8213| (Ggs), which was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-309805| |CITS: [17369297]|., The |FRAME: G-12442| gene that encodes the enzyme was found as part of the operon that also contains the |FRAME: G-10189| and |FRAME: G-10190| genes, which encode the enzymes involved in the two-step pathway of glucosylglycerate biosynthesis. The |FRAME: G-12442| gene was expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant product catalyzed the synthesis of GG in one step from |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| and |FRAME: GLYCERATE| |CITS: [17369297]|.

Summary: Magnetotactic bacteria produce crystals of |FRAME: CPD-27483| (FeIIFeIII2O4) or |FRAME: CPD-27485| (FeIIFeIII2S4) that enable them to sense the earth's magnetic field., The crystals are located in a dedicated organelle called the magnetosome, and are embedded in a lipid vesicle. The alignment of magnetosomes inside the cell acts like a compass needle, orienting the bacteria passively in geomagnetic fields, a phenomenon known as magnetotaxis. It is thought that magnetotaxis helps magnetotactic bacteria perform more efficient chemotaxis and aerotaxis in the water column, as their swimming behavior is restricted to one dimension instead of a three dimensional run and tumble movement |CITS: [9251816]|., The genes encoding proteins involved in the formation of the magnetosome are located in the magnetosome genetic island |CITS: [11571158][16237001][16423350]|. These genes encode the formation of the vesicles, their alignment in the cell, their loading with iron, and the biomineralization into magnetite or greigite |CITS: [18537832][9575557][27620945][32053597]|., Since the available iron inside the cell is FeII, but magenetite and greigite also involve FeIII, iron must be oxidized prior to formation of the minerals. Magnetic and structural studies have found that there are two steps in the biomineralization process of magnetite: in the first step Fe is accumulated in the form of |FRAME: CPD-27482|, and in the second magnetite is rapidly biomineralized from ferrihydrite |CITS: [23530668][23980143]|., A search for potential redox proteins within the magnetosome genetic island has led to the identification of four genes that encode products containing at least two tandem c-type cytochrome motifs CX2CH (which were named magnetochrome domains): MamE, MamP, MamT and MamX |CITS: [ 23176475]|. Deletion mutants of mamE and mamP show defects in the biocrystallization process |CITS: [20212111][22043287]|., MamP is a diheme c-type cytochrome. The soluble part of |FRAME: G-124850| from |FRAME: TAX-451514| (residues 26-260) was cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant protein was purified and crystallized. The protein is dimeric, and can form tetramers, depending on the pH. It contains an unusual PDZ domain. While this type of domain is usually used for interaction with other proteins, the PDZ domain of MamP is self-plugged, fused to the two magnetochrome domains |CITS: [24097349]|.

In addition to be a major constituent of proteins, proline also acts as an osmotic protectant in bacteria, plants and animals that are under osmotic stress. In Arabidopsis, proline can account for up to 20% of the free amino acid pool after salt stress |CITS: [8022935]|., There are two alternative routes in proline biosynthesis in higher plants: the ornithine pathway (this pathway) and the glutamate pathway (|FRAME: PROSYN-PWY|). Both ornithine and glutamate are precursors of proline biosynthesis in microorganisms, plants and mammals., Many research activities have been devoted to understand the relative contributions of the two alternative pathways to the increased proline accumulations under stress. Measurement of free proline content and gene expression and enzyme activity levels from salt-stress treated plants |CITS: [9576796]| showed that in young Arabidopsis plants, both the ornithine and the glutamate pathways contribute to the increase of proline level during osmotic stress, whereas, in adult plants, only the glutamate pathway plays an important role in proline accumulation. The decreased ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) and increased pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthetase (P5CS) transcripts level in salt-stressed month bean plants suggested that the glutamate pathway is the major contributor in proline accumulation upon osmotic stress |CITS: [8103048]|. The same study also found that the glutamate pathway is upregulated under nitrogen limitation, whereas, the ornithine pathway is prominent under high nitrogen input. Studies of transcripts level of P5CS and OAT and their correlations with the free proline content in Medicago, however, suggested that both the ornithine and the glutamate pathways contribute to the osmotic stress-induced proline accumulation |CITS: [15032841]|., Abscisic acid (ABA) and salt stress stimulate proline biosynthesis in plants |CITS: [12602867]|. On the other hand, phospholipase D (PLD) was shown a negative regulator of proline biosynthesis in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [14742440]|.

Summary: The production of |FRAME: ACETONE| and |FRAME: BUTANOL| by means of solvent-producing strains of Clostridium spp. was one of the first large-scale industrial fermentation processes to be developed, and during the first part of the 20th century it ranked second in importance only to ethanol fermentation. Advances in the chemical synthesis of these solvents, together with low oil prices, led to the decline of this commercial fermentation |CITS: [7576767]|., The Gram-positive, obligately anaerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1488| is one of the few organisms known to produce |FRAME: BUTANOL| as a major fermentation product. In continuous culture, |FRAME: TAX-1488| can be maintained in three different stable metabolic states |CITS: [Girbal95]|: acidogenic (production of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID|) when grown at neutral pH on glucose, solventogenic (production of |FRAME: ACETONE|, |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH|) when grown at low pH on glucose, and alcohologenic (formation of |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH| but not |FRAME: ACETONE|) when grown at neutral pH under conditions of high NAD(P)H availability. Despite numerous physiological studies, it is still unclear how the metabolic switch from acid to solvent production is regulated at the molecular level |CITS: [10191392]|., Once this metabolic transition has been initiated, most of the excreted acids are taken up and converted into solvents, Up to the onset of solventogenesis, |FRAME: TAX-1488| produces |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (see |FRAME: CENTFERM-PWY|). The pathways leading to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| and |FRAME: BUTANOL| production share most of the early steps (up to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|), and differ only in the last two steps., The pathway from |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is a major carbon metabolism channel and in |FRAME: TAX-1488| contains the branch points to solventogenesis and acidogenesis, which are the three key intermediates |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA |, and |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|., Butanol production involves the conversion of |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| to |FRAME: BUTANAL|, and of the latter to |FRAME: BUTANOL|. These conversions are catalyzed by several dehydrogenases. It is still not completely clear how the different dehydrogenases relate to the reactions and the growth conditions., |FRAME: TAX-272562| posseses two multifunctional aldehyde/alcohol dehydrogenases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-101| and |FRAME: G-12174| genes, both present on the pSOL1 megaplasmid |CITS: [8300540][9286999]|. It has been shown that |FRAME: G-101| is expressed only under solventogenic conditions, while |FRAME: G-12174| is expressed under alcohologenic conditions |CITS: [11790753]|. Both enzymes can catalyze the two conversions required to produce butanol., In addition, |FRAME: TAX-272562| posseses two other NADH-dependent butanol dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-181 BDH I| and |FRAME: CPLX-201 BDH II|), encoded by the |FRAME: G-91| and |FRAME: G-92| genes. These enzymes can catalyze only the conversion of |FRAME: BUTANAL| to |FRAME: BUTANOL| |CITS: [2673038][1385386]|. It has been shown that |FRAME: CPLX-181 BDH I| (|FRAME:G-91|) is expressed only during the transition to alcohologenic conditions, while |FRAME: CPLX-201 BDH II| is expressed throughout butanol formation., In |FRAME: TAX-169679| an |FRAME: BDHNADPHCLOS-MONOMER| has been described |CITS: [16347579][2673928]|.

Summary: The mycobacterial cell wall is a unique structure among prokaryotes, which consists of an outer layer of mycolic acids covalently bound to peptidoglycan via an arabinogalactan layer., More specifically, the extensively cross-linked peptidoglycan is bound by a linker unit to a linear galactan (galactofuran) chain, which in turn is attached to several branched arabinan (arabinofuran) chains esterified at the other end to mycolic acids., The synthesis of the |FRAME: Arabinogalactan "arabinogalactan"| portion of the cell wall begins with the synthesis of the linker unit, which is composed of α-L-rhamnosyl-(1->3)-D-glocusaminyl-N-acetyl phosphate. The linker unit is synthesized while attached to a lipid anchor, specifically a molecule of |FRAME: CPD-11994|, starting with attachment of the glucosaminyl-N-acetate unit (provided by |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|) |CITS:[8631826]|, and followed by attachment of a rhamnosyl unit provided by |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| |CITS: [8631826][10934214]|., The next step in the process is the building of the galactofuran, which consists of alternating 5- and 6-linked |FRAME: CPD0-2485| units |CITS: [2108960]|. The galactofuranose units, which are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-12575| in two steps |CITS: [9692181]|, are added by two galactosyl transferases with different specificity., The first enzyme, |FRAME: G185E-8078-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8078|) catalyzes the addition of the first galactofuranosyl residue to the α-L-Rhap-(1->3)-α-D-GlcNAc linker unit by a (1->4) linkage, followed by the addition of a second galactofuranosyl unit by a (1->5) linkage |CITS: [16952951][18055597]|., The second enzyme, the bifunctional |FRAME: G185E-8104-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8104|), extends the galactan chain by attaching new galactofuranosyl units in alternating (1->5) and (1->6) linkages |CITS: [11304545]|., The synthesis of the galactofuran chain terminates when it reaches a length of about 30 units., Next comes the synthesis of the arabinofuran chains. Most sources report that three such chains are attached to a single galactofuran chain, at positions 8, 10 and 12 (as shown here) |CITS: [16040600]|, although it was more recently proposed that only two arabinan units are attached per galactan chain |CITS: [21555513]|. These chains consist of 21 residues each, and are rather branched |CITS: [18303028][26488279]|. The arabinofuran units are synthesized from |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) in four steps, while anchored to a |FRAME: CPD-11994| lipid |CITS:[15878857][16291675]|. They are added by several arabinofuranosyltransferases. In the first step the galactan chain is primed with a single arabinofuranosyl residue in a reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-8088|-encoded protein |CITS: [16595677]|. The chain is elongated by linear (1-->5) linkages by two similar enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8090| and |FRAME: G185E-8091| |CITS:[8876238][9142129]|. The branching in the chains is introduced by (1-->3) linkages, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-6921|-encoded |FRAME: G185E-6921-MONOMER| |CITS: [18627460]|. Finally, the chains are "capped" by the addition of a (1-->2) linked residue, catalyzed by an enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G185E-8101| |CITS: [17387176]|. The terminal β-D-Araf-(1-->2) residues are attached to the arabinofuranosyl units at both the 3 and 5 branches and form the non-reducing end of the molecule |CITS: [18303028]|., The distal ends of the arabiofuran chains are almost completely esterified with mycolic acids |CITS: [1906464]| to generate a very large macromolecular structure that is known as the mycolylarabinogalactan (mAGP) complex |CITS: [7703239]|. The mycolic acids are attched to both the terminal β-D-Araf and the penultimate α-D-Araf residues. The mycolyl units were shown to cluster in groups of four and occupy only about two-thirds of the available attachment sites |CITS: [1906464]|.

Summary: General Background, Sinapoylesters (sinapoylmalate, sinapoylcholine) have been found predominantly in the , Brassicaceae family, where those esters are among the major soluble phenylpropanoid metabolites to be accumulated , |CITS: [8972602]|. While the function of sinapoylcholine as such is not yet elucidated, sinapoylmalate has been found , to act as an UV-B protectant in vegetative plant tissues |CITS: [11080303]|., It has been established that each of the sinapoyl esters are produced and utilized at different times in the course of , the plant's development. During the germination of the seeds the formation of sinapoylglucose and sinapoylcholine , prevails, which is reflected by the fact that most crucifer seeds are especially rich of sinapoylcholine (sinapine) , |CITS: [8382030]|. The sinapine esterase hydrolyzes sinapine producing sinapate and choline which has been proposed , to be needed for the biosynthesis of phosphatidylcholine (|FRAME:PWY-3561|) in the growing seedlings |CITS: [Strack81]|. , In this development stage the seedlings use the released sinapate to produce sinapoylmalate via the intermediate , sinapoylglucose |CITS: [8972602]| to increase UV-B tolerance. Sinapoylmalate is not produced under light limiting , conditions, implicating that a light factor may be required for the final assembly of the compound |CITS: [9880351]|. , This finding fits in the role and timed appearance of sinapoylmalate. Indeed , dark-grown seedlings contain considerably , less sinapoylmalate and accumulate another sinapate ester, 1,2-disinapoylglucose instead. This has been discussed as , a 'disproportionation' reaction to channel 1-sinapoylglucose towards diverse metabolic products in response to , developmental circumstances |CITS: [Strack84]|., It has been shown that the biosynthesis and deposition of sinapate esters takes place in the vacuole, whereas the , energy rich compound sinapoylglucose is probably formed in the cytosol |CITS: [Strack85]|. Sinapoylmalate has also , been found to be accumulated in the adaxial surface of the leaves, suggesting the possibility of a transportation step , between biosynthesis and accumulation of sinapate esters |CITS: [9880351]|., Special information: The sinapate ester pathway is governed by five enzymes, which appear to be transcriptional , regulated in response to seed and seedling development. It has been proposed that the transcriptional control of the , glucosyltransferase and sinapoyltransferases link sinapate to the sinapate ester pathway in a coordinated manner , |CITS: [15053762]|. However, how the sinapate ester pathway is actually regulated is still a matter of debate. Based on , results with a mutant line of Arabidopsis thaliana with enhanced expression of the gene encoding cinnamate 4-hydroxylase , (C4H) coinciding with a increased production of sinapate esters, the C4H was proposed to be the rate-limiting step of this pathway , |CITS: [11080161]|. This enzyme catalyzes the first step in the phenylpropanoid acid biosynthetic sequence leading to , sinapic acid, the direct precursor for the sinapate esters. This sequence is also involved in the biosynthesis of syringyl , lignin, where the ferulate-5-hydroxylase (F5H) catalyzing the final step to sinapate, is considered as a rate-limiting step , |CITS: [0009618461]|. Consequently, this enzyme was proposed to be regulatory for the sinapate ester biosynthesis as , well. However, Ruegger and coworkers |CITS: [9880351]| could demonstrate that, while F5H is regulatory involved in , the making of syringyl lignin its role in sinapate ester biosynthesis is different. The results of this work point out either a , more upstream transcriptional regulation excluding the phenylpropanoid acid pathway or a regulation which may be , posttranscriptional in nature. , Sinapoylesters are considered as antinutritive compounds |CITS: [Naczk98]|, contributing to bitter taste, forming complexes , with proteins during oil refining, and overall diminishing the value of seeds for human purposes. Special attention within this , area is given to the prime model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, where the pathway has already been investigated , on the molecular level |CITS: [15053762]|.

Summary: During the middle ages a common plague in Europe was caused by the consumption of rye bread. Symptoms varied in different parts of Europe -  convulsions and deep-seated mental problems were called 'St Anthony's fire', while the affliction of blackening of limbs and gangrene was called the 'holy fire'. , The cause for the disease was eventually traced to infection by certain species of fungi. The fungi infect rye and other grasses, where they produce ergot alkaloids (also known as mycotoxins) that cause the disease, now known as ergotism., Ergotism is also one of the explanations that have been offered for the phenomenon of mental affliction that spread among young girls in New England in 1692. These afflictions were blamed on bewitchment, resulting in imprisonment of over 150 people and execution of 20 following the infamous Salem witch trials |CITS: [769159]|., Ergot alkaloids are a complex family of indole derivatives with diverse structures and biological activities. They are produced by endophytic fungi of the families |FRAME: TAX-34397|, |FRAME: TAX-28568| and |FRAME: TAX-34384| and are believed to increase the resistance of the hosts towards attacks by other organisms., Some of these compounds and their semi-synthetic derivatives are important drugs in modern medicine, such as |FRAME: CPD-12363| and |FRAME: CPD-14462|, which are used for the treatment of migraines., The early part of the pathway of ergot alkaloids biosynthesis is common to all three families and ends with |FRAME: CPD-14459|, as described here. This important branch point is converted to different products within the different fungal families. The |FRAME: TAX-34397| produce ergoamides and ergoppeptines (see |FRAME: PWY-6495|), the |FRAME: TAX-28568| produce clavin-type alkaloids (see |FRAME: PWY-7059|). The nature of the products formed by the |FRAME: TAX-34384| is still not known |CITS: [22403186]|., Several lines of evidence have shown that the pathway starts with the condensation of |FRAME: TRP| with |FRAME: CPD-4211| produced by the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"|. The product |FRAME: N-METHYLTRYPTOPHAN| is then modified via |FRAME: CPD-12352| and |FRAME: CPD-12356| to |FRAME: CPD-14459|. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12352| to |FRAME: CPD-12356| has not been fully characterized yet, although it is known that the |FRAME: G-15217| gene and its homologs are involved.

Anthocyanin biosynthesis is a crucial biochemical process involved in the flower development of many angiosperms. Flavonoid pigments provide the means to attract pollinators through bright colors |CITS:[Harborne66]| and/or certain color patterns |CITS:[11511673]| |CITS:[Eisner02]|. Research over the last decades on anthocyanin biosynthesis has led to the discovery of many genes involved in the pathway. Advanced gene technologies enabled molecular breeding of flower colors in many commercially valuable ornamental species such as carnation resulting in novel and intriguing colors and hues |CITS:[Yonekura-Sakakibara09]|., Anthocyanins are most often decorated with glucose or other sugar moieties at the 3-position (A-ring) and the 5- and 7-position of the C-ring. Among the most prominent anthocyanins in |FRAME:TAX-3570| (carnation) are cyclic 3,5-malyl anthocyanins (|FRAME:CPD-15294|, |FRAME:CPD-15295|) |CITS:[11140528]|. However, the 5-O-glucosylation had not yet been elucidated. Likewise in |FRAME:TAX-46246| the main anthocyanin, i.e. cyanodelphin, a tetra p-hydroxybenzoated anthocyanin |CITS:[Kondo91]| is glucosylated at both 3 and 7 position but the 7-O-glucosylation remained unresolved as well |CITS:[Davies09]|. The monocotyledone |FRAME:TAX-51501|, a popular ornamental plant because of the blue and white flower colors which also is frequently used as a traditional medicine in South Africa has become the object of major studies regarding relevant pharmacological properties |CITS:[18343601] [15907963]|. The two main anthocyanins are 3,7-glucosylated delphinidin coumaroyl glucoside linked to a variety of kaempferol glycosides |CITS:[10724183]|. , Despite the taxonomic distance between the species mentioned above, i.e. the dicotyledones carnation (Caryophyllacea) and delphinium (|FRAME:TAX-3440|) and the monocotyledone |FRAME:TAX-51426| (|FRAME:TAX-4668|) all species have glucosyltransferases that realize either the 5-O- or 7-O-glucosylation. Instead of the usual sugar donor |FRAME: CPD-12575| the glucosyltransferases utilize acyl-glucoses such as the benzoyl-glucose derivatives |FRAME:CPD-15006|, |FRAME:CPD-15283| and |FRAME:CPD-15281| and the hydroxycinnamoyl-glucose derivatives |FRAME:CPD-15281| and |FRAME:1-O-SINAPOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| as glucose donors |CITS:[20971893] [22048706] [22673029]|. The acyl-glucose dependent glucosyltransferases (AAGTs) belong in the glycosyl hydroxylase (GH) 1 family and show significant amino acid sequence identities across the taxonomic range indicating that the AAGTs evolved before the divergence of monocots and dicots. The AAGTs very position specifically (either A5 - AA5GT or A7 - AA7GT) glucosylate anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides such as |FRAME:CPD1F-766| (see |FRAME:PWY-7256|), |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-3-GLUCOSIDE-CMPD| (see |FRAME:PWY-7259|) and |FRAME:CPD-7117| (this pathway). According to the structural properties, the AAGTs belong to the glycosyl hydroxylases, however their β-glucosidase activity is only 4 - 6% of the corresponding glucosyltransferase activity emphasizing a novel enzymatic property probably developed over the course of evolution of their host species |CITS:[20971893] [22048706] [22673029]|. Various genes in Arabidopsis thaliana have also been identified as candidates for acyl-dependent anthocyanin 5 and 7 glucosyltransferases but their molecular function remains to be shown experimentally |CITS:[Miyahara11]|.

It is similar to |FRAME: TYR|, but its side chain is extended by one carbon., This compound is integrated into some of the active peptides produced by cyanobacteria, including many |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins anabaenopeptins|, protease inhibitor depsipeptides produced by some cyanobacteria including |FRAME: TAX-46234| |CITS: [20338518]|., A pathway leading to the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15322| and |FRAME: CPD-17729| has been reported from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [23354699]|. The enzymes that paprticipate in the pathway include an aminotransferase whose identity has not been studied that catalyzes the first and last steps, and three enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-16016|, |FRAME: G-16018| and |FRAME: G-16017| genes. These three enzymes catalyze a biochemical transformation that is homologous to the process of |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| convertsion to |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| during |FRAME: LEUSYN-PWY|., An |FRAME:TAX-562| strain harboring hphABCD-expressing plasmids was able to produce |FRAME: CPD-15322| from |FRAME: PHE| |CITS: [23354699]|. While not proven experimentally, it is expected that the same enzyme can also produce |FRAME: CPD-17729| from |FRAME: TYR|, since the gene cluster encoing the enzymes is found in many bacteria that produce |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins anabaenopeptins| that contain |FRAME: CPD-17729|, and is located next to the anabaenopeptin biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS: [34437393]|.

Summary: General Background, This pathway and the linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-7028| depict parts of the pathway for the N-linked glycosylation of certain protein |FRAME: ASN| residues in |FRAME: TAX-197|., An analogous pathway leading to O-linked glycosylation of certain |FRAME: SER| residues in proteins such as pilin has been described in |FRAME: TAX-482| species (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7037|). The pgl genes in these organisms produce glycans with variable structures |CITS: [21542610][21606362]|. Protein O-linked glycosylation has been also described in |FRAME: TAX-287| strains |CITS: [16740931][17085575]|, |FRAME: TAX-817| |CITS: [21115495]|, and possibly other genera |CITS: [22391990]|, although the pathways have not been shown., Until the mid-1970s, protein glycosylation was thought to occur only in eukaryotes. However, prokaryotic N-linked and O-linked protein glycosylation was later found in a restricted set of archaea and bacteria, including pathogens and commensals. The prokaryotic glycans can include both common and rare monosaccharides (reviewed in |CITS: [18694827][9076508]|). The biological role of protein glycosylation in prokaryotes is not yet fully elucidated, but it is thought to be involved in host interactions such as adherence and pathogenicity (|CITS: [19681908]|, in |CITS: [22389484]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [12687605][14659687][20948550][20371512]|). Prokaryotic protein glycosylation may also enhance protein stability |CITS: [19154179]|., Eukaryotic N-linked glycosylation has been extensively studied in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|). Archaeal N-linked glycosylation was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-2242| |CITS: [1270419][4455689]|. Bacterial N-linked glycosylation was discovered in the Gram-negative |FRAME: TAX-197| (|CITS: [10361304]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [15738950][12781527]|). The overall process of protein N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes, archaea and bacteria is similar and results in the attachment of certain oligosaccharides to an |FRAME: ASN| residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein in a β-glycosylamide linkage (see |FRAME: Protein-heptasaccharide-L-asn|). The similarities and differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic N-linked glycosylation have been reviewed |CITS: [16510493][21506607]|., In archaea, protein glycosylation is more widespread than in bacteria although its function remains unclear. A wider variety of monosaccharide subunits are found in the protein-linked glycans of archaea than in those of bacteria or eukaryotes. In archaea, glycosylation has been identified on S-layer (surface-layer) proteins, flagellins, pilins, and membrane-bound proteins. Similar to eukaryotes, in archaea the N-linked oligosaccharide is synthesized on |FRAME: DOLICHOLP| carrier. Archaeal proteins can also contain O-linked glycans. Although pathways for archaeal protein N-linked glycosylation have been proposed, many details are lacking and all proposed pathways are still working models. Pathways for archaeal protein O-linked glycosylation remain undefined (reviewed in |CITS: [18694827][20371512][20976295][21506607]|). , About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-197| is a pathogen of the human gut mucosa that is associated with gastroenteritis (reviewed in |CITS: [9025274]|). The pgl gene cluster in this organism was identified as being involved in protein N-linked glycosylation |CITS: [10361304]|. It was shown that the pgl gene cluster could be functionally transferred from |FRAME: TAX-197| to |FRAME:TAX-562| resulting in glycosylation of two periplasmic proteins with a heptasaccharide |CITS: [12459590]|. Expression of the genes in this cluster in |FRAME:TAX-562| followed by mutational analysis and structural analysis of the glycans produced suggested the functional roles of the genes |CITS: [15752194]|. Subsequent biochemical analyses confirmed their functions in the pathway |CITS: [16356848][16186480]|., An N-linked heptasaccharide was found to be present on multiple glycoproteins in |FRAME: TAX-197|. Its structure was determined by MS and NMR analysis of glycopeptides to be GalNAc-α1,4-GalNAc-α1,4-[Glc-β1,3-]GalNAc-α1,4-GalNAc-α1,4-GalNAc-α1,3-Bac-β1,N-Asn. Bac represents N,N'-diacetylbacillosamine, an unusual sugar derivative found in some bacteria |CITS: [12186869][19154179]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17717023]|., During its biosynthesis, this heptasaccharide was found to be attached to the membrane-anchored lipid |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| in an α1 linkage (GalNAc-α1,4-GalNAc-α1,4-(Glcβ1,3)-GalNAc-α1,4-GalNAc-α1,4-GalNAc-α1,3-Bac-α1-PP-Und) |CITS: [16201778]|. |FRAME: CPD-9647| (bactoprenol) is a polyisoprene that contains 11 isoprene units, with the α-isoprene unit unsaturated. This compound is also involved in peptidoglycan biosynthesis (see pathway |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY|). In eukaryotes the analogous lipid is |FRAME: DOLICHOL|. Reviewed in |CITS: [22093697]|., Data suggested that the periplasm is the site of protein glycosylation by oligosaccharyltransferase PglB |CITS: [15574802]|. It was shown that the heptasaccharide is added to over 65 proteins in the periplasm and membrane. PglB can also cleave oligosaccharides from their lipid anchor to produce free oligosaccharides in the periplasm. Possible functions of free oligosaccharides have been proposed, including protection from osmotic stress (|CITS: [19706478]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21178500]|., The heptasaccharide was found to be conserved in strains of |FRAME: TAX-197| and |FRAME: TAX-195| |CITS: [12186869][12716884 ]|. In a study of nine |FRAME: TAX-194| species, the |FRAME: TAX-195| pgl gene cluster appeared to be closely related to that of |FRAME: TAX-197|, while that of |FRAME: TAX-201| was similar but less related. More significant differences were found in the pgl gene clusters of |FRAME: TAX-194| species more distantly related to |FRAME: TAX-197|. In vitro evidence suggested that other |FRAME: TAX-194| species can produce a range of structurally different N-linked glycans. Differences included penta-, hexa- and heptasaccharides, branching sugars, and monosaccharide content |CITS: [22389484][20847188]|. Biosynthesis of a novel N-linked pentasaccharide has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-552535| |CITS: [20581208]|., The roles of the Pgl enzymes in this pathway were biochemically validated in vitro using using chemically synthesized N,N'-diacetylbacillosaminyl-diphospho-undecaprenol and purified enzymes. The sequential enzymatic steps in this pathway were reconstituted and enzymatic function at the membrane surface was shown |CITS: [16186480]|. The in vitro synthesis of the complete lipid-linked heptasaccharide has been demonstrated |CITS: [17087520]|., The pathway is initiated by enzymes PglF, PglE and PglD which transform |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-14248| as shown in the pathway link. The N,N'-diacetylbacillosamine residue later becomes the carbohydrate-peptide linking monosaccharide. As shown in this pathway, enzymes PglA, PglC, PglH, PglI and PglJ are glycosyltransferases that assemble the heptasaccharide on the membrane-bound lipid anchor |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE|. PglH was shown to be a processive polymerase that adds three N-acetyl-D-galactosamine residues |CITS: [19159314]|. In analogy with the eukaryotic system, a flippase encoded by pglK translocates the final lipid-linked heptasaccahride across the bacterial inner membrane into the periplasm (not shown) |CITS: [16498400]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21506607]|., The protein glycosylation reaction is thought to occur at the periplasmic face of the bacterial inner membrane, catalyzed by bacterial oligosaccharyltransferase PglB |CITS: [12459590]|. PglB transfers the heptasaccharide "en bloc" from its lipid-linked carrier and covalently attaches it to an |FRAME: ASN| residue of the target protein within the consensus sequence (sequon) D/E-Y-N-X-S/T (where Y and X are not proline) (|CITS: [16619027][17439157][15574802]| and reviewed in |CITS: [18694827]|) (see the reaction link at the end of the pathway)., The periplasmic PglB oligosaccharyltransferase and the enzymes shown in this pathway are of interest as potential targets for antibacterial drug and vaccinie therapy (|CITS: [15703289]| reviewed in |CITS: [16510493]|). This bacterial pathway may also potentially be used to engineer homogeneous eukaryotic N-linked glycoproteins for therapeutic use (|CITS: [20190762][21131519]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21506607]|).

General Background, Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The lipid A component of pathogenic bacteria is detected by the host serum LPS-binding protein (LBP), which is dependent on two cofactors: cluster of differentiation 14 (CD14) and myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD2). The lipid A/LBP complex is subsequently recognized by the opsonic receptor CD14, forming a triple complex that activates Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). TLR4 activation triggers a signalling cascade, leading to the production of cytokines and clotting factors and the secretion of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) and other stimulatory molecules |CITS: [10963608]|. CAMP binds to negatively charged structural motifs such as the phosphate groups on lipid A, leading to cell lysis and death |CITS: [19601838]|. If the immune response is too strong sepsis and septic shock can occur, leading to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome and death |CITS: [12857774]|., In many bacterial species lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor lipid IVA. , Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. , About This Pathway, The innate immune system of vertebrate hosts produces positively charged peptides known as cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) that bind to bacteria through charged surface features, forming pores and thereby disrupting membrane integrity., In order to survive the CAMP response many Gram-negative bacteria utilize lipid A modifications. Bacteria accomplish this via several strategies, including adding positively charged moieties, such as phosphoethanolamine or L-4-aminoarabinose to the outer leaflet, removing phosphate groups from the lipid A backbone, or changing the acylation pattern., Compared with other enterobacterial lipid As, the lipid A of |FRAME: TAX-210| activates TLR4 in a much weaker form, displaying a 1000-fold lower endotoxicity compared with lipid A from |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [Yamaoka08]|. Several modifications result in this weak TLR4 elicitation: the major form of |FRAME: TAX-210| lipid A is acylated by four rather than six fatty acids, contains only a single Kdo residue, lacks the usual 4'-phosphate group, and has a phosphoethanolamine (PEtN) moiety replacing the 1-position phosphate group |CITS: [1903201][26646009]|.

Summary: The major lignans accumulating in suspension cultures of certain Linum species |CITS:[Fuss03] [Kuhlmann02]| and Podophyllum organs |CITS:[2890742]| are glucosides of |FRAME:CPD-8962|, |FRAME:CPD-8959| and similar structured lignans |CITS:[3760883]|. The formation of the lignan glucosides, stowed safely away in the vacuole, is necessary to prevent deterioration of the cells producing the cytotoxic |FRAME:CPD-8962| and |FRAME:CPD-8959| |CITS:[3174856] [7783142]|. |FRAME:CPD-8959 Podophyllotoxin| and its derivatives are aryltetralin-type lignans which gained great significance due to their use in cancer chemotherapy as antiviral and antineoplastic drugs |CITS:[10872202]|. Serving as precursors for semi-synthetic derivatives, |FRAME:CPD-8959| has been utilized to synthesize |FRAME:CPD-16754| and |FRAME:CPD-16755| which are exploited in the treatment of malignant ailments |CITS:[9615861]|. The observed cytotoxicity of |FRAME:CPD-8959| and semi-synthetic derivatives is based on their inhibitory effect on the assembly of microtubules |CITS:[9615861]| which has also been observed in plant roots |CITS:[Oliva02]|. , The formation of the respective 7-O-glucopyranosides of |FRAME:CPD-8959| and |FRAME:CPD-8962| (see |FRAME:PWY-5479|) |CITS:[17449073]| is the last step in the biosynthetic route |CITS:[Kuhlmann02]| of those aryltetralin lignans. The 7-O-glucosylation is catalyzed by a rather regio-specific glucosyltransferase which converts the naturally occurring |FRAME:CPD-8959|, |FRAME:CPD-8962| and |FRAME:CPD-16749| to the respective |FRAME:CPD-16746|, |FRAME:CPD-16747| and |FRAME:CPD-16748| |CITS:[17870138]| which reside in the vacuole. When the cells integrity is damaged due to feeding damage or pest attacks the less toxic lignan glucosides are hydrolyzed by specific lignan β-glucosidases which cause the release of the considerably more toxic aglycons |CITS:[11270736]|. Such lignan specific glucosidases have been characterized for the hydrolyzation of |FRAME:CPD-16746| in Podophyllum peltatum |CITS:[12637023]| and the deglucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-16747| in Linum flavum |CITS:[3174856]|.

Summary: Many bacterial species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| via, |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|., In lactic acid bacteria (LAB), pyruvate (which can be formed in large amounts from citrate) is converted, into either lactate, by the enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-5241| or |FRAME: CPLX-5242|, or to, |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-5243| (also known as α-acetolactate, synthase, or α-ALS). , The conversion of pyruvate to lactate requires NADH.  So, under conditions of low NADH, the majority, of the pyruvate is converted to 2-acetolactate., 2-acetolactate is an unstable intermediate.  Under anaerobic conditions it is converted to acetoin by a, decarboxylation step catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-5262|. However, in the presence of oxygen it can undergo a spontaneous decarboxylation, producing |FRAME: DIACETYL| (see |FRAME: PWY-5938|)., The relative activities of |FRAME:CPLX-5243| and |FRAME: CPLX-5262| in specific strains determine the fluxes and, concentrations of the different intermediates in these organisms., |FRAME: CPD-10353| is often converted to |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| by the enzyme R-acetoin reductase (see |FRAME: PWY-5951|)., This pathway includes two decarboxylation reactions, generating |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. This CO<sub>2</sub> is the source of the  "eyes", or holes that certain cheeses, such as Swiss cheese, develop during maturation.

Summary: General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the, synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives., These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere, |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms,, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation, pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|., The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two, broad categories - oxidative and reductive., In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or, di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and, |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is, released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, Several bacterial strains are capable of utilizing |FRAME: CPD-704| as the sole source of carbon and, energy., The degradation of |FRAME: CPD-704| was first demonstrated for a |FRAME: TAX-80866| strain, |CITS: [1527502]|. This process proceeds through partial reduction of the nitro group prior to its release, as ammonia., The first enzyme of this pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-2123|, catalyzes the transformation of, |FRAME: CPD-704| to |FRAME: CPD-705|. The hydroxylamino group is subsequently, removed from the aromatic ring as |FRAME:AMMONIA| through the action of a, |FRAME: MONOMER-2124| with the concomitant formation of |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|., This reductive pathway for 4-nitrobenzoate degradation has also been shown in |FRAME: TAX-329|, |CITS: [8534095]| and in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-303| which degrade |FRAME: CPD-701|, |CITS: [8245826][8357257]|., The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway, |FRAME: G-1462| and |FRAME: G-1463|, have been, cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: ORG-5960| and from |FRAME: TAX-329|.

General Background, |FRAME: Carrageenans Carrageenans| and |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-2763 "Rhodophyta (red algae)"|, mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera. They are laid out in the cell wall at a high density and can constitute up to 50% of the algae dry mass., The basic units of |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenans| are repeats of alternating β -1,3 linked D-galactose and α-1,4- linked D-galactose units, which are often substituted by sulfate. Carrageenans are classified according to the, number and the position of sulfated ester |CITS: [1367970]|. , In |FRAME: Carrageenoses carrageenoses| the α-1,4- linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6 - anhydro bridge. These bridges, which form a double helix during aggregation, are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds. Despite this distinction, carrageenoses are often referred to as carrageenans., The three most industrially exploited carrageenans, namely, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan|, are distinguished by the presence of one, two or three ester-sulfate groups per repeating disaccharide unit respectively., |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| is sulfated at position 2 of the β -1,3 linked D-galactose units and positions 2 and 6 of the α-1,4- linked galactose units. Some carrabiose units of the λ-carrageenan from |FRAME: TAX-2765380| are substituted with four sulfate groups (D2S,6S-G2S,4S) |CITS: [16716278]|., Since λ-carrageenans do not feature 3,6-anhydro-bridges, they do not make physical gels., About This Pathway, Carrageenans constitute a crucial carbon source for a number of marine bacteria. These organisms, which belong mainly to the classes Gammaproteobacteria, Flavobacteria and Sphingobacteria, degrade the cell walls of marine red algae, by secreting specific glycoside hydrolases known as carrageenases., The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-227| is the first organism reported to degrade |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| |CITS: [ 4727801]|. The |FRAME: MONOMER-16657| from |FRAME: TAX-227| has been purified and the |FRAME: G-14515| gene that encodes it has been cloned. Nucleotide sequence suggested that it is the first described member of a new family of glycoside hydrolases, distinct from hydrolases of other types of carrageenans |CITS: [17269933]|.

Summary: The mycobacterial cell envelope contains an usually rich variety of complex free lipids and glycolipids associated with the, mycolic acid layer of the cell wall. These lipids and glycolipids are located in the membrane outer leaflet. Together with the membrane inner leaflet, which is based on mycolic acids, they form the asymmetric lipid bilayer that constitutes the characteristic mycobacterial outer membrane., One group of these glycolipids is phthiocerol dimycocerosates (DIMs or PDIMs). A closely realted group consists of glycosylated phenolphthiocerol dimycocerosates (PGL) (see |FRAME: PWY-7743|)., Both PDIMs and PGLs play important roles in host-pathogen interaction and/or virulence in various mycobacterial pathogens |CITS: [10573420][11081637][15019737][15343336][15942899][18700620][18764820][18443098][19622047][19197369][20844580][21375593]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Opines Opines| are a large family of low molecular weight compounds. The vast majority of opines are secondary amine derivatives resulting from the reduction of the imine formed by condensation of an amino acid, either with a keto acid or a sugar. Opines from the |FRAME: CPD-308| family are formed when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| serves as the keto substrate in the condensation reaction, while those of the |FRAME: CPD-309| family are formed when |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is involved in the condensation reaction. Opines of the |FRAME: CPD-15773| and |FRAME: CPD-26410| families are formed by the condensation of an amino acid with a sugar., A small, separate class of opines is the |FRAME: Agrocinopines agrocinopines|, which are sugar-phosphodiesters (e.g., |FRAME: CPD-15774|, which is a phosphodiester of sucrose and L-arabinose)., While opines are found in marine invertebrates, fungi, higher plants and mammals, they are most commonly found in plant crown gall tumors or hairy root tumors, where they are produced by bacteria of the genera |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379|, respectively. Biosynthesis of opines in crown gall tumors is performed by enzymes encoded by genes contained in T-DNA (transfer DNA), which is part of the Ti plasmid (in Agrobacterium) or Ri plasmid (in Rhizobium). The plasmids are inserted by the bacteria into the plant genome, where they are integrated and expressed. Those opines are used by the bacteria as energy, carbon and nitrogen sources. Each strain of Agrobacterium and Rhizobium induces and catabolizes a specific set of opines, determined by the specific Ti or Ri plasmid they possess. Over 30 different opines have been described., The enzymes catalyzing the condensation of amino acids with 2-oxo acids to form opines are known as opine dehydrogenases. These enzymes are oxidoreductases that catalyze the reversible, |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP|-dependent reductive condensation reaction between an α-keto acid and the α-amino or ω-amino group of an amino acid to form imino acids (opines) and water. They have been classified into several Enzyme Commission (EC) entries depending upon their substrate specificity. Studies have shown that opines are synthesized in plant crown gall tumors as a result of infection by |FRAME: TAX-358|, and in some marine invertebrates under hypoxic or anoxic conditions (reviewed in |CITS: [23644944][10869063][GADEG86]|)., About This Pathway, Opine dehydrogenases are cytosolic oxidoreductases that catalyze the reversible, |FRAME: NADH-P-OR-NOP|-dependent reductive condensation reaction between an α-keto acid and the α-amino or ω-amino group of an amino acid to form imino acids (referred to as opines) and water. They have been characterized from some soil bacteria and marine invertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7351|). , In |FRAME: TAX-357| species opine dehydrogenases are encoded on Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmids which are involved in plant crown gall tumor formation. Portions of Ti plasmid DNA are transferred to a susceptible host plant cell and become integrated into its nuclear genome. Expression of these bacterial genes in the resulting plant tumor cell directs the synthesis and secretion of opines. The opines that are synthesized vary among bacterial strains. |FRAME: TAX-358| genes |FRAME: G-15382| and |FRAME: G-17722| encode enzymes that direct the synthesis of several opines (reviewed in |CITS: [10869063]|). The opines produced and secreted by the plant crown gall tumor can subsequently be used by the infecting bacteria as a carbon or nitrogen source during host colonization. They are taken up by the bacteria via permeases and degraded by opine-specific enzymes (see pathways |FRAME: OCTOPINEDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: NOPALINEDEG-PWY|)., Genes encoding the enzyme described here are located on the on Ti plasmids pTi15955 and pTiAch5. The enzyme, characterized from |FRAME: TAX-190386|, catalyzes a reductive condensation between |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ARG| or |FRAME: LYS| to form |FRAME: CPD-309| or |FRAME: CPD-306|, respectively., Octopine synthase (octopine dehydrogenase) was also purified from a culture of crown gall tumor tissue from |FRAME: TAX-4097|. A radiotracer study showed that it stereospecifically removes the pro-S hydrogen atom of the dihydronicotinamide ring of |FRAME: NADH| with transfer of label to the solvent and to the product |FRAME: CPD-309|. This was also demonstrated for |FRAME: MONOMER-17683| from |FRAME: TAX-6579| |CITS: [7096344][4354812]|., Purified recombinant enzyme expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| was found to also found catalyze the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15781| that can act as a source of sulfur for |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [22486934]|.

Names: cytidylyl molybdenum cofactor sulfurylation // sulfo-cytidylyl molybdopterin cofactor biosynthesis // MCD sulfulylation
Summary: General Background, The transition element molybdenum (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. This molybdenum cofactor (MoCo) consists of a unique tricyclic pterin compound (molybdopterin) containing a Mo-binding and coordinating dithiolene group. MoCo binds to diverse apoproteins and confers activity to the resulting holoproteins ubiquitously involved in essential redox reactions in the global C-, N-, and S-cycles |CITS: [11848841]| |CITS: [16307306]|., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of MoCo has been investigated in detail in bacteria, e.g. |CITS: [1587808][8514783][8514782][7836363][14761975]|., About This Pathway, Many enzymes depend on the sulfo-form of molybdenum cofactor (MoCo). The so called maturation of MoCo involves the addition of sulfur to the Mo center, replacing an oxo group. In eukaryotes this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.9| (e.g. the plant ABA3) |CITS: [11553608][15561708]|. However, prokaryotes do not have such an enzyme. In prokaryotes MoCo first binds to a chaperone (such as XdhC) before it is sulfurylated by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.7|. Many of the prokaryotic molybdoenzymes have a specific chaperone |CITS: [23201473]|. The chaperones interact with the desulfurase, so that MoCo is sulfurated while it is still bound to the chaperone and before the insertion into the target protein. Binding to the chaperone stabilizes the sulfurated form of MoCo. Once sulfurylated, the chaperone transfer the cofactor to its target protein |CITS: [17649978]|., The crystal structures of several molybdoenzymes revealed that MoCo is deeply buried inside the proteins, at the end of a funnel-shaped passage giving access only to the substrate |CITS: [9242907]|. The insertion step is believed to be catalyzed by the chaperones. It has been suggested that at least some of the target proteins exist in a different structure prior to the cofator insertion, facilitating the insertion. Once the cofactor is transferred to the apo-protein, the final folding is induced, resulting in the active form of the enzyme |CITS: [8522945][19519768]|,, The sulfurylated cytidylyl molybdenum cofactor shown here is the form of the cofactor that is present in all members of the xanthine oxidase (XO) family of enzymes |CITS: [11848841][24467397]|. The best studied example is |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.4| from |FRAME: TAX-1061|. Both a dedicated chaperone (|FRAME: G-80798|) and a specific L-cysteine desulfurase (|FRAME: G-80799|) have been characterized for the maturation of that enzyme |CITS: [16597619][17649978]|, Another example is the |FRAME: CPLX0-7805 "aldehyde oxidoreductase PaoABC"| of |FRAME: TAX-562|, which was shown to bind the sulfurated form of MCD |CITS: [19368556]| via the action of the |FRAME: CPLX0-8110| (|FRAME: G6154|) |CITS: [23201473]|., See |CITS: [32239579]| for a review.

Summary: Avenacins are triterpene glucosides which act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents conferring resistance against soil-borne pathogens and influencing the development of close neighbors |CITS:[10536024] [16995908]|. There are four avenacins known, the ones acylated with |FRAME:CPD-402| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7463|), i.e. |FRAME:CPD-10678| and |FRAME:CPD-16597| and the ones acylated with |FRAME:BENZOATE| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7468|), i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16599| and |FRAME:CPD-16598|, all of them exclusively found only in roots |CITS:[Crombie86a]|; more specifically in the vacuoles of the root epidermal cells |CITS:[18203919]|. The occurrence of the phytoalexic avenacins appears to be restricted to the genus Avena which is an expression of a highly specialized defense biochemistry |CITS:[Hostettmann95]|. , |FRAME:CPD-10678 Avenacin A-1| (see |FRAME:PWY-7473|) is the most abundant avenacin found in Avena. As a general rule genes in plant biochemical pathways, unlike bacterial biochemical pathways, have been regarded as unlinked. However, the avenacin biosynthesis appears to be carried out by an avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster which implies a high degree of coordination regarding avenacin synthesis, transport and sequestration, all of which must be precisely orchestrated in time and space between different cell organelles and compartments |CITS:[21876149] [15148404] [21443624] [20040536]|. , The first committed step into the |FRAME:CPD-10678| biosynthesis is the cyclization of |FRAME:EPOXYSQUALENE| to form |FRAME:CPD-6948| catalyzed by the Avena oxidosqualene cyclase encoded by SAD1 (saponin-deficient = SAD) |CITS:[11606766]|. The following step(s) of hydroxylation and epoxidation of |FRAME:CPD-6948| to yield the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-16622| via two possible routes is carried out by a cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase (CYP51H10) encoded by SAD2 |CITS:[17124172] [22687421] [23940321]|. The enzymes and the exact position within the avenacin biosynthetic sequence of the glycosylation steps of |FRAME:CPD-10678| are mostly unknown. However, two genes SAD3 and SAD4 have been identified which are able to glucosylate |FRAME:CPD-16625| and add the 1->4 linked |FRAME:GLC|. Mutants deficient in SAD3 and 4 form incompletely glucosylted avenacins (|FRAME:CPD-16626|) which causes a phenotype of stunted roots with a decreased number of root hairs. While SAD3 is a member of the avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster SAD4 is unlinked and might have other biochemical functions in Avena |CITS:[18203919]|. The correct and complete glucosylation of the avenacin skeleton is very important for its biological activity as phytoalexin. It has been shown that incomplete glucosylated avenacins are less toxic, hence less efficient in warding off microbial attacks |CITS:[7824933]| and fungi which possess the ability to de-glucosylate avenacins are more successful to invade Avena plants |CITS:[Osbourn91]|., The last step in the direct pathway of |FRAME:CPD-10678| biosynthesis is the acylation of |FRAME:CPD-16623| with |FRAME:CPD-402| which is provided through the acyl-donor |FRAME:CPD-16600|. |FRAME:CPD-16623 Des-acyl avenacin A| is the cross point that leads to |FRAME:CPD-16599| and |FRAME:CPD-16624|. The enzyme is a serine carboxypeptidase-like (SCPL) protein (SCPL1) encoded by SAD7, also a member of the avenacin genetic cluster, which catalyzes the final conversion of |FRAME:CPD-16623| to |FRAME:CPD-10678| |CITS:[19684243]|. , |FRAME:CPD-16624 Des-methyl avenacin A-1| (see |FRAME:PWY-7475|) is the avenacin species found in Avena mutants such as sad9 which lack the anthranilate N-methyltransferase, hence have a deficiency in catalyzing |FRAME:CPD-402| and apparently acylate with |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| instead |CITS:[19684243]|. |FRAME:CPD-16599 Avenacin A-2| (see |FRAME:PWY-7474|) is another major form of avenacins found in the roots of the genus Avena |CITS:[Crombie86a]|. In contrast to the |FRAME:CPD-402| acylated |FRAME:CPD-10678|, the triterpenoid saponin |FRAME:CPD-16599| is acylated with |FRAME:BENZOATE|., All avenacin species are finalized by the acylation through either |FRAME:CPD-16600| or |FRAME:CPD-12630| serving as acyl-donors. In the pathway of the former (see |FRAME:PWY-7463|) the decisive step is the N-methylation of |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| catalyzed by the anthranilate N-methyltransferase (MT1) encoded by SAD9 |CITS:[23532069]|. The subsequent glucosylation in this pathway as well as the formation of |FRAME:CPD-12630| (see |FRAME:PWY-7468|) is catalyzed by two glucosyltransferases, SAD10 (UGT74H5) and UGT74H6. SAD10 appears to be included in the avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster but UGT74H6, although catalyzing the same reaction, albeit with lower efficiency, may have other or additional biochemical functions in Avena |CITS:[23258535]|. The formation of the acyl-donors |FRAME:CPD-16600| and |FRAME:CPD-12630| is critical for the biosynthesis of the various avenacins. It has been demonstrated that the C-21 acylation of the avenacin skeleton is pivotal for the biological activity of this antimicrobial agent |CITS:[20835386]|.

Summary: |FRAME: XYLITOL Xylitol| is a naturally occurring pentitol sugar alcohol. It is found in low concentrations in the fibers of many fruits and vegetables, and can be extracted from various berries, oats, and mushrooms, as well as fibrous material such as corn husks, sugar cane bagasse and birch |CITS: [16242318]|. , Xylitol is roughly as sweet as sucrose, and is used as a diabetic sweetener. Since it is symmetrical, there are no D or L forms of xylitol., |FRAME: XYLITOL Xylitol|, like |FRAME: L-ARABITOL|, is rather rare in nature, compared with the much more abundant pentitols |FRAME: RIBITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-355|., Pentitols and other neutral polyols can be taken up by bacteria and oxidized by a polyol dehydrogenase to the corresponding keto sugar. The keto sugar is then phosphorylated and metabolized in the pentose phosphate or glycolytic pathways. Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1582| |CITS: [118163]| and |FRAME: TAX-33945| |CITS: [12467497]|, transport polyols into the cell using a phosphotransferase system. The polyol phosphates are oxidized by polyol phosphate dehydrogenases (in |CITS: [12467497]|). , Several species of enteric bacteria have been shown to have naturally occurring xylitol degradation pathways. These include |FRAME: TAX-582|, |FRAME:TAX-588| ATCC 25827, |FRAME:TAX-615| ATCC 13880, and |FRAME:TAX-551| sp. strain 4D2P. P. stuartii utilized xylitol as a sole carbon and energy source, S. marcescens could utilize both xylitol and ribitol as sole carbon and energy source, and the |FRAME:TAX-551| strain could utilize xylitol, ribitol, and D-arabitol as sole carbon and energy source. However, the |FRAME:TAX-551| species oxidized xylitol at the C-4 position to produce |FRAME: L-XYLULOSE|. Inducible NAD-dependent pentitol dehydrogenases were demonstrated in pentitol grown cells.
