Summary: The jadomycins are a unique family of |FRAME: Angucyclins angucycline|-derived antibiotics with a unique oxazolone ring formed through non-enzymatic condensation of a polyketide-derived intermediate with amino acids |CITS: [Ayer91]|. Jadomycins are produced by |FRAME: TAX-953739| under stress conditions such as heat shock, phage infection, and particularly ethanol treatment |CITS:[8514643] [7764672]|., |FRAME: CPD-12934 "Jadomycin B"| is the major product in |FRAME: TAX-953739|, and its structure includes the deoxysugar |FRAME: CPD-11914| |CITS: [11932454]|. It is bioactive against Gram-positive (including the methicillin-resistant |FRAME:TAX-1280|) and Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [19075054]|, and against yeast |CITS: [8514643]|. It is also a promising anti cancer drug that was shown to inhibit the activity of Aurora-B kinase, blocking the phosphorylation of histone H3 and inducing apoptosis in tumor cells |CITS: [18723485]|., The jad gene cluster was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-953739| in the early 1990s, and the biosynthetic pathway has been studied, although some steps have still not been completely characterized., The pathway begins with the synthesis of the polyketide core. The |FRAME: G-12385|, |FRAME: G-12386| and |FRAME: G-12387| genes are believed to encode the minimal polyketide synthase (PKS) core of two β-ketoacyl synthase units (KSα and KSβ) and an acyl-carrier protein (ACP), respectively. This enzyme complex builds on the starter unit |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by the repetitive addition of 9 two-carbon units (via an enzyme-bound form of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|), and ends catalysis when the polyketide backbone has reached its proper size |CITS: [7881555][9224566]|., Following the formation of the polyketide backbone several additional "tailoring" enzymes act on the product to modify it. The first free intermediate in the pathway is a compound known as |FRAME: CPD-12949| |CITS: [Kulowski99]|. The formation of this compound requires the activity of three enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12388|, |FRAME: G-12389| and |FRAME: G-12390| genes, which encode a |FRAME: MONOMER-16083|, a |FRAME: MONOMER-16082|, and a |FRAME: MONOMER-16084|, respectively. The JadD cyclase is beleved to catalyze the formation of the first ring, while JadI is probably responsible for formation of the other three rings. , It has been shown that JadD can not catalyze the reaction unless the substrate has been reduced by the JadE reductase, |CITS: [9224566]|. However, the exact reaction catalyzed by each enzyme has not been reported, and the literature usually refers to |FRAME: CPLX-8206| as a single entity |CITS: [9224566][Kulowski99]|., The key step of the jadomycin biosynthesis is the oxidative opening of the 5,6-bond of the angucyclinone intermediate, which likely leads to the formation of an aldehyde that can easily react with the amino acid isoleucine, thereby forming an aldimine., This step is catalyzed by three oxygenases (encoded by |FRAME: G-12391|, |FRAME: G-12393| and |FRAME: G-12392|) that are involved in a multistep oxygenation cascade that leads to the oxidative ring cleavage |CITS: [15817470][15776503][20422670]|., The incorporation of |FRAME:ILE| produces |FRAME: CPD-12938|. The addition of the amino acid is most likely, nonenzymatic - the product has been shown to be a mixture of 5-diastereomers, supporting a nonenzymatic reaction, and when other amino acids are provided in excess, they are incorporated into the jadomycin skeleton |CITS: [15070349]|., Taking advvantage of this nonenzymatic step, analogues have been produced using various natural and nonnatural amino acids, extending the reservoir of potentially active therapeutic agents |CITS:[15070349][15713404][16185863][19075054]|., The last step in the pathway is believed to be the attachemnt of an |FRAME: CPD-11914| residue. This 2,6 dideoxysugar is synthesized from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by six enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7657|), all of which are encoded by genes in the jad cluster, and is attached to |FRAME: CPD-12938| by |FRAME: MONOMER-16089|, encoded by |FRAME: G-12395| |CITS: [11932454][17047829]|.

Summary: Industrially important yeasts such as |FRAME: TAX-94006| and |FRAME: TAX-5482| are capable of taking up and utilizing alkanes and long chain fatty acids as sole carbon sources for growth. Alkanes and long chain fatty acids are first metabolized through ω-oxidation. The methyl group at the end of the molecule (the ω carbon) is oxidized to a hydroxyl group, then to an oxo group, and finally to a carboxyl group. The long chain dicarboxylates derived from ω-oxidation then enter the β-oxidation pathway for further degradation., In alkane-utilizing yeasts the CYP52 subfamily of cytochrome P450s and their corresponding NADPH cytochrome P450 reductases form the monooxygenase system that catalyzes the ω-oxidation steps in the utilization of alkanes and fatty acids |CITS: [14532053]|. In |FRAME: TAX-94006| and |FRAME: TAX-5482| the oxidation of the ω-hydroxy group of the intermediate ω-alcohol, or ω-hydroxy fatty acid is catalyzed by an alcohol oxidase |CITS: [16046182]|. This differs from what is known of ω oxidation in other species including animals and certain alkane-, or fatty acid-, utilizing bacteria. In those organisms, the conversion is catalyzed by an alcohol dehydrogenase., The finding of the potential |FRAME: TAX-3701| homolog of the yeast alcohol oxidase suggests that plants may also operate such an ω oxidation pathway. Confirmation of the hypothesis awaits the functional characterization of the homolog and the identification of other enzymes involved in the pathway. The role of the pathway in plants is probably in wax biosynthesis, rather than in fatty acid degradation |CITS: [10660617]|.

Summary: |FRAME:RUTIN Rutin| is one of the flavonols especially appreciated for its high nutritional value. However, |FRAME:RUTIN| is rarely found in food plants for humans. In plants, |FRAME:RUTIN| is proposed to function as UV screen |CITS:[11849980]| and to participate in the chemical defense of plants to pathogens and herbivores |CITS:[Levin76]|., The distribution of |FRAME:RUTIN| in seeds and leaves of buckwheat and |FRAME:RUTIN| degrading enzymes has shown no direct physiological relationship. |FRAME:RUTIN Rutin| has been found mostly in the embryo (developing cotyledons) of seeds |CITS:[Suzuki02b]| |CITS:[Suzuki07]| and the upper epidermis of leaves |CITS:[Zhanaeva98]| whereas the |FRAME:RUTIN| degrading enzymes are located in the testa of the seeds |CITS:[Suzuki02b]| |CITS:[Suzuki07]| and the lower epidermis of leaves |CITS:[Zhanaeva98]|. In addition, differences in the distribution of |FRAME:RUTIN|, |FRAME:CPD-520| and corresponding degrading enzyme activities in common buckwheat (|FRAME:TAX-3617|) and tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tartaricum) may point to specific physiological roles in those species |CITS:[Suzuki07]|. , The degrading enzymes of |FRAME:RUTIN| in buckwheat have been reported under different names, i.e. rhamnodiastase-like enzyme |CITS:[Bourbouze74]|, |FRAME:RUTIN| degrading enzymes (RDE) |CITS:[Yasuda94]|, flavonol-3-glucosidase (f3g) |CITS:[Suzuki02b]| and flavonol 3-O-β-heterodisaccharide glycosidase (FHG) |CITS:[12943757]|. Summary: Germacrenes are the bitter sesquiterpene olefins produced by a number of plants representing compounds that , possess antifeedant, antimicrobial and insecticidal properties and also function as insect pheromones , |CITS: [Rostelien00]|. There are 4 known types of germacrenes, |FRAME: CPD-8743|, |FRAME: CPD-8744|, |FRAME: CPD-8745|, |FRAME: CPD-8746|, which are unstable due to their susceptibility to proton-induced cyclization towards , α-selinene and β-selinene |CITS: [9701594]|. , Most of these compounds can exist as enantiomers. |FRAME: CPD-8743 Germacrene A| is postulated to be an , intermediate bound to sesquiterpene cyclase(s) involved in the biosynthesis of patchoulol, aristolochene, capsidiol and , vetispiradiene. Insect response studies show that |FRAME: CPD-8746| targets insect neurons in a highly selective way and significantly stands out amongst a host of similar compounds |CITS: [Rostelien00]|., Germacrene synthases, the specific sesquiterpene synthases that cyclize |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| , into germacrenes have been isolated from a number of plants including, |FRAME: TAX-59297| , |CITS: [12127586]|, |FRAME: TAX-4081| |CITS: [9482865]|, |FRAME: ORG-6001| |CITS: [12031443]| and others. , The enantiomer-specific synthases produce different enantiomeric products |CITS: [16839518]|. The , biosynthesis of these compounds involves stereoselective oxidative enzymes that might be useful as , catalysts in organic syntheses |CITS: [9701594]|. Active site modification and mutagenesis studies , show that subtle changes in the active site residues are necessary for carrying out the synthesis of , enantiomeric germacrenes. On the other side it has been demonstrated that the Mg2+-binding motif of the sesquiterpene synthases might not be as stringent as previously thought as the aspartate at position 303 can either be replaced by asparagine or might even be lacking as found for the germacrene D synthase (Sc11) of |FRAME:TAX-59297|  |CITS: [12127586]|.

General Background, The three aromatic amino acids, |FRAME: TRP|, |FRAME: TYR|, and |FRAME: PHE|, derived from the common precursor, |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, are constituents of proteins, and precursors of many plant secondary metabolites., , Two steps are required for conversion of |FRAME: PREPHENATE| to |FRAME: TYR|: a dehydrogenation/decarboxylation, and a transamination., Two possible routes for this conversion are known. In the route described in |FRAME: TYRSYN| the, decarboxylation occurs first, resulting in the intermediate |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, followed by, a transamination to |FRAME: TYR|. In the second route, described here, transamination occurs first, resulting in formation of, |FRAME: CPD-659|, which is subsequently decarboxylated to |FRAME: TYR|., While the first route has been confirmed in many microorganisms, including E.coli and yeast,, some other bacteria, including cyanobacteria, as well as many plants, employ the arogenate route |CITS: [4206476][3298985]|., The two routes have been reported to co-exist in many microorganisms. In addition, the, |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| route cannot be completely ruled out for plants based on these facts:, 1) early studies detected prephenate dehydrogenase activity in mung bean shoots |CITS: [4379953]|., 2) the Arabidopsis arogenate dehydrogenase TyrAAT2 presents a weak prephenate dehydrogenase , activity |CITS: [12354106]|, even though the high Km for prephenate and low specific activity of prephenate , dehydrogenase reaction indicates the reaction is unlikely physiologically significant., Two types of arogenate dehydrogenase are known, that utilze either NADP+ or NAD+. These two types, are described by the pathways |FRAME: PWY-3461| and |FRAME: PWY-6120|, respectively., About This Pathway, The two key reactions in this pathway are catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-8101| and, |FRAME: AT5G34930-MONOMER|, respectively., Arogenate is the branch-point and the immediate precursor for the synthesis of both tyrosine and phenylalanine., Arogenate dehydrogenase is the key enzyme channeling arogenate towards tyrosine synthesis. Its activity is, strongly feedback inhibited by tyrosine., The Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT5G34930-MONOMER| |CITS:[12354106]|, as well as the enzyme from the cyanobacterium, |FRAME: TAX-1148| |CITS: [15171683]|, are strictly NADP-dependent (see |FRAME: PWY-3461|)., The enzymes from maize |CITS:[Byng1981]| and the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1866|, |CITS:[2590341]| are strictly NAD-dependent.

|FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate "Dermatan sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of repeating disaccharide units of variable composition. Dermatan sulfate is expressed in many mammalian tissues and is the predominant glycan present in the extracellular matrix of skin. Dermatan and dermatan sulfate proteoglycans have also been implicated in cardiovascular disease, tumorigenesis, infection, wound repair, and fibrosis |CITS: [12213784]|. The most common disaccharide unit in dermatan sulfate is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12515| and |FRAME:CPD-12557|, which are often sulfated to |FRAME: CPD-12518|, |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|., Within cells, dermatan sulfate is degraded in two steps. An initial endohydrolysis is followed by the sequential action of lysosomal exoenzymes to reduce the resulting oligosaccharides to monosaccharides and inorganic sulfate. The first step is catalyzed by a class of human enzymes known as hyaluronidases. This family of enzymes is known to degrade |FRAME: Hyaluronan| as well as |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| by cleaving internal β-linked (1,4)-glycosidic bonds |CITS: [8528065]|. The products of this cleavage vary in size, but fragments of hexa- or tetrasaccharides are often observed. , Following partial catabolism by endoenzymes, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| is degraded from the non-reducing terminus by the sequential action of highly specific lysosomal exoenzymes. These lysosomal exoenzymes include |FRAME: CPLX-8129 "N-acetyl-β-D-galactosaminidases"| (several forms exist, composed of different combinations of the products of the |FRAME: HS06726| and |FRAME: HS00629| genes), which remove terminal |FRAME: CPD-12557| residues |CITS: [8663217]|, and |FRAME: HS05096-MONOMER|, which remove terminal |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues |CITS: [30407]|., A crucial step in the process is the removal of inorganic sulfate from |FRAME: CPD-12518| residues, which is necessary to enable exit out of the lysosome. The enzyme that catalyzes this step is the |FRAME: CPLX-8124| ((EC 3.1.6.13, encoded by |FRAME: HS00286|). This enzyme removes the C2-sulfate ester bond of non-reducing terminal |FRAME: CPD-12518| residues only |CITS: [8424762]|. The combined action of these enzyme acts to reduce |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| and similar oligosaccharides to monosaccharides, which exit the lysosome and recycled by the cell |CITS: [12213784]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Pyochelin "Pyochelin"| is a siderophore produced by the Gram-negative pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-287|. It is also made by some related bacterial species during iron starvation |CITS: [6794030]| as well as some Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1930| |CITS: [21757492]|. A stereoisomer of pyochelin, named |FRAME: CPD-12093|, is produced by |FRAME: TAX-294| |CITS: [17938167][19297329]|., The siderophore chelates iron in the extracellular medium and transports it into the cells via a specific outer membrane transporter, encoded by the fptA gene |CITS: [15388952][16499928]|., Like many other siderophores, pyochelin is synthesized by non-ribosomal peptide synthetases. The assembly line for pyochelin consists of four proteins, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11713|, |FRAME: G-11714|, |FRAME: G-11715| and |FRAME: G-11716| genes. These four proteins form a complex that together includes 11 different domains |CITS:[10555976][11467965]|., The net reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-7976| is:, |FRAME: RXN-11114|, The process starts with the |FRAME: G-11713| gene product, which activates |FRAME: CPD-110| to |FRAME: CPD-12084| and transfers it to |FRAME: MONOMER-15302|., |FRAME: MONOMER-15302| is a large non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) that contains 4 domains. One of these domain is an adenylation domain that activates an |FRAME: CYS| molecule to a |FRAME: CPD-12085|. A second domain is a peptidyl-carrier protein that binds the activated cysteine. A third domain is an aryl-carrier protein. The activated salicylate is transferred from PhcD to this domain. With the help of the fourth domain (a cyclization domain) the salicylate and cysteine are combined and cyclized, forming |FRAME:hydroxyphenyl-thiazolinyl-PchE| |CITS: [10555976]|., The third protein, |FRAME: MONOMER-15303|, is also a large NRPS protein and contains five domains. An adenylation domain activates a second |FRAME: CYS| molecule to |FRAME: CPD-12085|, and a peptidyl carrier protein domain binds it., At this point the PchE protein transfers its product to PchF, and with the help of the PchF cyclization domain |FRAME: RR-Hydroxyphenyl-bis-thiazolinyl-PchF| is formed |CITS: [10555976]|. One of the two thiazoline rings is then reduced to a thiazolidine by the fourth member of the |FRAME: CPLX-7976| - the NADPH-dependent |FRAME: G-11716|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15304| |CITS: [11467965]|., The last two steps in the process are catalyzed by the remaining two domains of the |FRAME: MONOMER-15303| protein. A methyltransferasec domain catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| to the nitrogen of the thiazolidine ring, and a thioesterase domain cleaves the final |FRAME: Pyochelin| compound from the protein |CITS: [11467965]|., All four components have been cloned, expressed in heterologous host and purified, and the purified proteins were used for |FRAME: Pyochelin| synthesis in vitro |CITS: [11467965]|., Another enzyme, the product of the pchC gene, is also involved in pyochelin biosynthesis. This enzymes plays a role in removing wrongly charged molecules from the peptidyl carrier protein domains of |FRAME: MONOMER-15302| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15303| |CITS: [15375116]|.

Summary: General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway:, Many monoterpene synthases can produce a single product but often will produce a variety of monoterpenes of which a few are produced preferentially |CITS:[12176064],[16684230],[15310829],[10562434]| (for additional information concerning monoterpenes, see |FRAME:PWY-3041|). Conifer monoterpenes produce mainly acyclic and cyclic olefins as product, which is consistent with the measured constituents of turpentine, in which oxygenated monoterpenes only represent trace components. The volatile monoterpene constituents of conifer oleoresin is involved in a variety of roles in bark boring bettle (the most destructive agent of conferous forests worldwide |CITS:[berryman72]|) chemical ecology: host recognition and selection; pheromone signaling and tritrophic level interactions (interactions between the tree, beetle and parasitoids; for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). Resin monoterpenes are toxic to the bark beetles; however, they provide the insect with olfactory cues that it uses to locate its target host. Many bark beetles use monoterpene volatiles to synthesize aggregation pheromones (produced by pioneer-beetle to attract other insects to initiate aggregation and colonization). The pheromones |FRAME:CPD-8832|, |FRAME:CPD-8833|, |FRAME:CPD-8834| and |FRAME:CPD-8835| are derived from |FRAME:CPD-8754|, |FRAME:CPD-4892| and |FRAME:CPD-4888| |CITS:[11337413]|. The function of these hormones as aggregation or aggregation inhibition pheromones is dependent on the species and potentially their geographical location. Several enzymes have been identified from different coniferous species which can produce monoterpenes in a variety of mixtures in vitro.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13430 "6-Anhydro-α-L-galactopyranose"| (AHG) is the major monomeric sugar component of the polysaccharides found in red macroalgae, such as |FRAME: Agaroses agarose| and |FRAME: Porphyrans porphyran|. Since AHG is not catabolized by ordinary fermentative microorganisms, it hampers the utilization of red macroalgae as renewable biomass for biofuel and chemical production. However, some marine bacteria are abe to completely degrade AHG and utilize it as a source of carbon and energy., The pathway shown here has been initially characterized from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1116375| |CITS: [25156229]|. The pathway begins with the oxidation of the aldehyde group by |FRAME: MONOMER-18902| to form |FRAME: CPD-17129|, leaving the 3,6-anhydro ring intact. In the original study it was reported that |FRAME: CPD-17129| is isomerized directly to |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GALACTONATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-18903|, in which the configurations of the hydroxyl groups are rearranged and the 3,6-anhydro ring is cleaved |CITS: [25156229]|. However, it was later shown that the actual product of this enzyme is |FRAME: CPD-12349|, which needs to be isomerized to |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| via |FRAME: CPD-343| |CITS: [Lee14]|. , The downstream part of the pathway is common with the |FRAME: GALACTCAT-PWY "D-galactonate degradation"| pathway. |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GALACTONATE "2-Dehydro-3-deoxy-D-galactonate"| is phosphorylated to |FRAME: DEHYDRO-DEOXY-GALACTONATE-PHOSPHATE|, which is then split in a single step into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP|, both members of central metabolism.

|FRAME: CPD-6401| (GASH) is one of several glutathione-related compounds that are found in prokaryotes, |CITS: [11544359]|., The compound is produced at milimolar levels by the purple photosynthetic bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1049|, and |FRAME: TAX-1048| |CITS: [8755912]|. , A GASH-dependent peroxidase has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1048|. The enzyme belongs to the, peroxiredoxin family, even though other members of the family are thioredoxin-dependent., Since this enzyme is capable of reducing hydrogen peroxide, and since |FRAME: TAX-1048|, while an anaerobic, organism, is capable of surviving under microaerobic conditions, it was suggested that |FRAME: CPD-6401|, mediated peroxide detoxification represents an early adaptation for fighting oxidative stress |CITS: [11399772]|., During the reduction of peroxide, GASH forms a disulfide, similar to |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE|., However, GASH is maintained in a reduced state by a dedicated |FRAME: CPLX-6061| (GAR), which converts, it back to the reduced form, utilizing NADH |CITS: [11399772]|., When grown on |FRAME: HS| as a hydrogen donor, most of the GASH is converted to a perthiol form (GASSH),, suggesting that it may be involved in sulfide metabolism in the organism, perhaps assiting the import of sufide into, the cell, where it forms sulfur globules |CITS: [9695921][8755912]|., Another amide derivative of glutathione is glutathionylspermidine (see |FRAME: PWY-4121|).

General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on single carbon (C1) compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. , While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 "Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| (see |FRAME: PWY-5506|)., The key enzyme in the oxidation of methanol in methylotrophic bacteria is methanol dehydrogenase (MDH). Different bacterial strains use different types of MDH. Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria have a periplasmic |FRAME: CPLX-3264| that contain a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ) cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-1701|). Thermophilic methylotrophic Bacili such as |FRAME: TAX-1471| use an |FRAME: CPLX-8059| (see |FRAME: PWY-6510|), while Gram-positive bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1814|, |FRAME: TAX-1777| MB19, |FRAME: TAX-1829| LMD 89.129 and |FRAME: TAX-1833| DSM 1069 possess nicotinoprotein methanol dehydrogenases with a bound NAD(P) cofactor that use an unknown electron acceptor for reduction of their bound cofactor and can use the artificial electron acceptor |FRAME: CPD-12424| in vitro |CITS:[1995642][8385013][8449887]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6509|)., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branch point, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (see |FRAME:P185-PWY|), or a dissimilatory pathway that provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|)., About This Pathway, All thermotolerant methanol-utilizing Bacillus spp. studied to date oxidize methanol by an |FRAME: CPLX-8059|. These enzymes, which are composed of ten identical subunits, oxidize primary C1-C4 alcohols and 1,3-propanediol and also catalyzes the NADH-dependent reduction of the corresponding aldehydes., Each subunit contains a tightly, but non-covalently, bound NAD(H) molecule, in addition to 1 |FRAME: ZN+2| and 1-2 |FRAME: MG+2| ions. The NAD(H) cofactor is oxidized and reduced by formaldehyde and methanol, respectively, while it remains bound to the enzyme. In addition, the enzyme utilizes exogeneous NAD for reduction of the bound cofactor. Thus, NAD plays two different roles in the reaction, with the bound NAD cofactor acting as primary electron acceptor and the NAD coenzyme being responsible for reoxidation of the reduced cofactor |CITS: [ 9119008]|., A 50,000 kDa activator protein is responsible for the oxidative reactivation of the reduced NADH cofactor of the enzyme |CITS: [1995643]|.

Summary: Vitamin B6 is a group term for |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| (PL), |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| (PN), |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| (PM) and their 5'-phosphorylated derivatives |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| (PLP), |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE-5P| (PNP) and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP) which are also referred to as vitamers. Plants, fungi and bacteria possess the biosynthetic capability to produce vitamin B6 via a de novo PLP biosynthesis |CITS:[17822383]| however auxotrophic organisms such as mammalians require the external uptake of the non-phosphorylated vitamers which are then being converted to PLP in the intracellular vitamin B6 salvage pathway |CITS:[15483325]|. |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate| is considered the active form of vitamin B6 and is involved as essential cofactor in amino acid biosynthetic pathways |CITS:[7840669]| |CITS:[11402193]| |CITS:[11344332]| and a diversity of other enzymatic reactions |CITS:[17512961]| |CITS:[19145213]|. , In plants, PLP is known as cofactor of various key enzymes which play a role in ethylene biosynthesis |CITS:[10557240]|, chlorophyll and tetrapyrrole synthesis |CITS:[12767809]|, de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis |CITS:[11171191]| and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS:[6778873]|. Moreover, vitamers have been shown to have antioxidant properties impeding the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and are considered to be involved in stress response pathways |CITS:[10687384]| |CITS:[17227548]| |CITS:[19903353]| |CITS:[19145213]|. , The vitamin B6 salvage pathway for plants is very similar to the bacterial variant (see |FRAME:PLPSAL-PWY|). Three enzymes from plants catalyzing main reactions in the salvage pathway have been characterized so far. The non-phophorylated vitamers PL, PN, and PM are phosphorylated to PLP, PNP, and PMP through pyridoxal kinase(s). So far the phosphorylation of |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| to |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| has been demonstrated in wheat and |FRAME:TAX-3701|. Although not tested as substrates in these experiments it is expected that the pyridoxal kinase works likewise with |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| |CITS:[12244454]| |CITS:[15499907]|. The reverse reactions catalyzed by phosphatases have been suggested based on homologues of microbial and animal genes that exist in plant genomes but no enzymes have been reported yet. The formed phosphorylated vitamers, i.e. |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE-5P| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| are converted to |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE| by the catalytic action of pyridoxine/pyrimidine 5'-phosphate oxidases |CITS:[17224143]| |CITS:[7138019]|. In addition, a pyridoxal reductase from |FRAME:TAX-3701| has been purified that catalyzes the NADPH-dependent reduction of |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| to |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| |CITS:[21533842]|. Hence, it appears that plants, with the vitamin B6 salvage pathway, maintain pools of the various vitamers and possess the ability to generate and recycle non-phosphorylated and phosphorylated forms which upon demand generate the active vitamin B6 |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|.

Hydroxycinnamic acids, such as |FRAME: COUMARATE|, |FRAME: CPD-676|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, and |FRAME: SINAPATE|, are the most abundant class of phenolic acids in fruits, vegetables, and cereal grains and are toxic for bacteria., In |FRAME: TAX-1590| two metabolic pathways exist for the detoxification of hydroxycinnamates. The most efficient pathway comprises the successive action of decarboxylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.102|, followed by reduction, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.ba| |CITS: [10919793]|. In this pathway, |FRAME: COUMARATE|, |FRAME: CPD-676|, and |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, are decarboxylated to their corresponding vinyl derivatives (|FRAME: CPD-1075|, |FRAME: CPD-22699|, and |FRAME: CPD-1072|, respectively) |CITS: [9143125][Cavin97][18416556]|, which are subsequently reduced to the ethyl derivatives (|FRAME: CPD-10596|, |FRAME: CPD-28241|, and |FRAME: CPD-10601|) |CITS: [24068507]|., The ethylphenols that are produced by this pathway are strong odorants. They have very low perception thresholds, and have a major impact on the aroma of wine, beer, and cider. Winemakers consider their presence in wine to be a key concern |CITS: [Suarez06]|. On the other hand, these compounds are considered the most important flavor components of fermented soy sauce |CITS: [3526828]|., A second route for hydroxycinnamic acids detoxification involves the direct reduction of hydroxycinnamic acids to their corresponding phenylpropionic substituted acids, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.az| |CITS: [Rodriguez08][29776925]|.

Summary: General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway:, Compared to monoterpenes, fewer sesquiterpene synthases from conifers have been identified and studied to date. Generally, the longer chain of |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| compared to that of |FRAME:GERANYL-PP|, and the additional double bond, allows for a greater diversity of products being formed by those enzymes. Two coniferous enzymes |FRAME:ENZRXN-13510| and |FRAME:ENZRXN-13583| from Grand Fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) produces each in excess of 30 different sesquiterpenes olefins. In contrast, |FRAME:MONOMER-12817| catalyzes only the synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-8738| |CITS:[9618485]|. Importantly, this compound has been shown to be converted by methyl-jasmonate-induced suspension cell cultures of Grand Fir into |FRAME:CPD-8836|, a sesquiterpene derivative structurally similar to the insect |FRAME:CPD-8838| |CITS:[9618485]|, and can disrupt insect reproduction and/or larval development |CITS:[11337413]|.

The guanidyl moiety is a component of importantl metabolites such as the amino acid |FRAME: ARG|, the energy carrier |FRAME: CREATINE|, and the nucleobase |FRAME: GUANINE|. Free guanidine (shown here in its protonated form |FRAME: CPD0-1470|, which is major form present at cellular pH) was first discovered as a thermal decomposition product of guanine |CITS: [Strecker61]|. Guanidine is formed during the degradation of multiple compounds, such as |FRAME: CANAVANINE| |CITS: [13271411]| and |FRAME: CPD-27994| |CITS: [33741630]|., The bacterial degradation of guanidine has been studied for many years |CITS: [Iwanoff31][Mitchell85][3440154]|. In 2017 it was found that many bacteria employ guanidine-binding riboswitches (subtype 1 ykkC RNAs) to regulate genes encoding proteins that overcome guanidine's toxicity. In many organisms a cassete of genes controlled by the guanidine riboswitch encodes a guanidine transporter as well as a set of enzymes that convert guanidine to ammonia and CO<sub>2</sub> |CITS: [27989440]|. One of the enzymes, |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.26|, was previously interpreted to be a urea carboxylase. However, more detailed characterization of the enzyme has shown that activity is ~40-fold higher with guanidine than with urea. The product of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-28002|, is extremely unstable, and is quickly hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-578| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.140| |CITS: [32786413]|. Finally, |FRAME: CPD-578| is hydrol;yzed further by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.54|, producing ammonia and CO<sub>2</sub> |CITS: [32786413]|.

Summary: |FRAME: GDGTs "Glycerol dialkyl glycerol tetraether lipids"| (GDGTs) are a class of membrane lipids synthesized by archaea and some bacteria., The first GDGTs to be reported were |FRAME: Isoprenoid-GDGTs "isoprenoid GDGTs"| produced by extremophilic archaea cultures (they are now known to be synthesized by many archaeal classes) |CITS: [De-Rosa77]|. Most of these lipids contain (up to 8) cyclopentane rings present within the carbon skeleton structure |CITS: [Schouten13]|, and in the case of |FRAME: CPD-25326|, also a cyclohexane ring |CITS: [12364548][20033067]|. The prevalence of cyclic moieties within GDGTs was shown to increase as a function of temperature. This, combined with the fact that GDGTs can be preserved in the environment for hundreds of millions of years, lead to development of the TEX<sub>86</sub> system, which uses their relative concentration in sediments as a paleothermometer |CITS: [Schouten0][Kim08a]|., Various polar headgroups can be attached to the glycerol and calditol backbones and yield either monopolar or bipolar tetraether lipids. Archaeal bipolar tetraether lipids are either glycolipids or phosphoglycolipids., Because GDGTs have two hydrophilic head groups, they form a lipid monolayer in the cell membrane instead of a bilayer, making GDGT-producing archaea exceptional among all clades of life |CITS: [Schouten13]|. , The enzyme responsible for formation of GDGTs is |FRAME: EC-1.21.98.5|. The reaction catalyzed by the enzyme is challenging since it necessitates the coupling of two completely inert sp<sup>3</sup>-hybridized carbon centers. The enzyme is a radical SAM enzyme that contains three [Fe<sub>4</sub>S<sub>4</sub>] clusters and one mononuclear rubredoxin-like iron ion, each found in a separate domain. It forms a |FRAME: CPD-15400| and utilizes it to activate its substrate. The reaction involves an intermediate bond between the substrate carbon and a sulfur of one of the [Fe<sub>4</sub>S<sub>4</sub>] clusters |CITS: [35882349]|., The enzyme acts specifically on fully saturated substrates, following the action of |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.11|. When forming GDGTs, the reaction proceeds via an intermediate in which only one intramolecular C-C bond has been formed (this intermediate has been named GTGT for glycerol trialkyl glycerol tetraether |CITS: [35318330]|)., Tetraether lipid synthases have been described from |FRAME: TAX-2190|, |FRAME: TAX-2214| and |FRAME: TAX-42879| |CITS: [35882349][35318330]|.

General Background, |FRAME: MET "Methionine"| is an essential amino acid in mammals. It is not biosynthesized and must be obtained in the diet. Methionine, or its metabolites, participate in fundamental processes such as protein synthesis, S-adenosylmethionine-dependent transmethylations, polyamine formation, cysteine biosynthesis, and homocysteine biosynthesis which is necessary for folate and choline metabolism (reviewed in |CITS: [15539209]|). Its major routes of metabolism in mammalian liver involve transmethylation and transsulfuration pathways. In the transmethylation pathway methionine is converted to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, a compound that participates in most biological methylation reactions. , S-adenosylmethionine is demethylated to S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is reversibly hydrolyzed to homocysteine and adenosine, see |FRAME: METHIONINE-DEG1-PWY|. High levels of homocysteine are toxic, and further metabolism of homocysteine is required. Methylation of homocysteine regenerates methionine. , About this Pathway, |FRAME: HOMO-CYS "Homocysteine"| is a branch point between methionine degradative and biosynthetic pathways. The conservation of homocysteine completes a "methionine cycle" (reviewed in |CITS: [3309559], [15539209], [15189131]|). Hyperhomocysteinemia in humans has been associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular, disease |CITS: [11453979]|., In humans and rodents approximately half of the homocysteine formed condenses with |FRAME: SER| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE| via the transsulfuration pathway |FRAME: HOMOCYSDEGR-PWY| |CITS: [6746658]|. The remainder is remethylated to methionine via three salvage reactions. As shown here, one involves |FRAME: HS04076-MONOMER|, which uses |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF| as the methyl donor |CITS: [9013615]|. A second reaction involves |FRAME: CPLX66-334|, which uses |FRAME: BETAINE| as the methyl donor |CITS: [8798461]|. The third reaction involves |FRAME: CPLX66-333| which uses |FRAME: CPD-397| as the methyl donor |CITS: [18230605]|.

Summary: General Background, The naphtoquinones |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| and |FRAME:CPD-12831| are both designated as vitamin K1. The former acts as electron transfer cofactor (known as A1) of photosystem I (PS I) in higher plants and cyanobacteria. It is very similar to |FRAME: Menaquinones| (vitamin K2), a naphthoquinone which is common in non-photosynthetic microbes, in which it serves in anaerobic electron transport systems |CITS:[8626063]|. The only difference between phyloquinone and menaquinone is in the polyprenyl tail. Menaquinones contain 1-14 isoprene units, while phyloquinone contains a phytyl side chain of 4 units |CITS: [15686525]|., |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE Phylloquinone| was given the name vitamin K by Dam in 1935, |CITS: [Dam35]| and was first isolated in 1939 from alfalfa |CITS: [805522]|., It has been found that phylloquinone is not absolutely required for efficient electron transfer in PS I, |CITS: [10722690]|. In |FRAME:TAX-1148| benzoquinones such as plastoquinone-9, which usually act as secondary electron acceptors in PS II |CITS: [11470786][15681848]|, can efficiently replace phylloquinone in the A1-site of PS I as a one-electron cofactor. However, as shown in an |FRAME:TAX-3701| mutant the deficiency of phylloquinone causes distortions in the thylakoid structure of chloroplasts, may abolish PS I, and affects the functionality of PS II |CITS: [15686525]|., The biosynthesis of phylloquinone was studied in detail in the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148| and the genes encoding enzymes of this pathway were identified by comparison with genes encoding enzymes of the menaquinone biosynthetic pathway in |FRAME:TAX-562| (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|) |CITS: [8626063]|. With the isolation and functional confirmation of the homolog genes in |FRAME:TAX-1142| encoding for phytyl transferase, 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate, synthase |CITS: [10722690]|, 2-phytyl-1,4-naphthoquinone methyltransferase |CITS: [11772039]|, SHCHC synthase, and o-succinylbenzoic acid-CoA synthase |CITS: [JOHNSON03]| most of the enzymatic steps of the phylloquinone bisoynthesis have been determined and proven to be highly identical with those in the menaquinone biosynthesis., About This Pathway, The enzymatic steps involved in the biosynthesis of phylloquinone in cyanobacteria and plants are similar to the biosynthetic route leading to the microbial complement menaquinone., The discernible step between phylloquinone and menaquinone biosynthesis is the prenylation step. |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.130| catalyzes the attachment of a C-20 phytyl side chain leading to |FRAME:CPD-6947| |CITS: [15686525]|, whereas microbial DHNA prenyltransferases attache a multiprenyl side chain, forming demethylmenaquinones. , It has been demonstrated that the final step of the pathway, a transmethylation reaction to form |FRAME:CPD-12831|, depends on the oxidation state of the penultimate substrate. Only this reduced (quinol) substrate is able to accept the electrons from the electrophilic |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| for the transmethylation. This led to the discovery that one more reaction was inserted in between |FRAME:CPD-6947| and the final product |FRAME:CPD-12831|. This reaction is catalyzed by type II NAD(P)H dehydrogenases in both Arabidopsis thaliana and the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 encoded by NDC1 and ndbB, respectively (now classified as |FRAME: EC-1.6.5.12|). Mutants lacking this enzyme accumulate |FRAME: CPD-6947| |CITS:[26023160]|. , This indicates that the pathway intermediates prior to this step are in the quinone form, since they require reduction by |FRAME: EC-1.6.5.12|. Thus |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE|, or an earlier intermediate, must be oxidized to a qunone form such as |FRAME: CPD-18334| by an unknown process prior to the phytyl chain attachment., In general, the intermediates of the |FRAME:PWY-5027| including in-feeding pathways such as |FRAME:PWY-5837| are depicted in their dihydroxy conformation, for example see |FRAME:DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| and |FRAME:CPD-9925|, although the latter has been shown to be used in vitro in its diketo form |CITS:[19321747]|. However, the study on the dehydrogenases of Arabidopsis and Synechocystis provide evidence that |FRAME:CPD-6947| and probably any other preceding intermediates occur in their diketo instead of the dihydroxy form |CITS:[Basset15]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7670 Dimethylsulfide| (DMS) is a major contributor to the total sulfur emissions to the atmosphere from land and the ocean., In marine, estuarine, and salt marsh systems, the main source of DMS is the degradation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. Other sources for DMS include the reduction of |FRAME: DMSO| and the degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids (this pathway)., |FRAME: CPD-7670 "Dimethyl sulfide"|, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere, and is considered the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: CPD-3746|, which attract water and promote cloud formation and thus influence the climate |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, up to 90% of the DMS in the ocean is degraded biologically |CITS: [Kiene90]|., About This Pathway, Microbial DMSP-independent pathways generating DMS that are not limited to marine environments have been described |CITS: [1971234]|. Varied anoxic environments, including freshwater lake sediments |CITS: [16345275][16535751]|, salt marsh sediments |CITS: [16347461]|, cyanobacterial mats |CITS: [413485]| and peat bogs |CITS: [16535080]|, have been shown to produce DMS at high levels. It has been suggested that the production of DMS in these environments occurrs through microbial methylation of |FRAME: CPD-7671|, which can be generated either by |FRAME: HS| methylation, or by |FRAME: MET| catabolism., The ability to generate |FRAME: CPD-7671| from |FRAME: HS| and/or |FRAME: MET| also occurs under oxic conditions, and is common in heterotrophic bacteria from many diverse environments |CITS: [3662509]|. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-882211|, which was isolated from Antarctic marine sediments, produces DMS from either |FRAME: MET| or |FRAME: CPD-7671| under oxic conditions. The organism does not synthesize or catabolize DMSP, and thus was assumed to possess a novel DMS-production pathway |CITS: [25807229]|. The organism was shown to produce DMS from |FRAME: MET| by the action of two enzymes - the well characterized |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11|, and a novel |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.334|., The novel enzyme was shown to be present in a wide range of bacterial taxa, and is particularly common in species of the actinobacterial genera |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia|, |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus| and |FRAME: TAX-1763|, in Rhizobiales members including the N2-fixing genera |FRAME: TAX-68287| and |FRAME: TAX-374|, and in N2-fixing cyanobacteria including |FRAME: TAX-43988|, |FRAME: TAX-1152| and |FRAME: TAX-1120752| species. The enzyme also exists, although less frequently, in some |FRAME: TAX-203682|, |FRAME: TAX-117743|, |FRAME: TAX-203691 Spirochaetes|, |FRAME: TAX-74201| and |FRAME: TAX-28211|, |FRAME: TAX-28216|, |FRAME: TAX-1236| and |FRAME: TAX-29547|. Analysis of metagenomes from terrestrial and marine environments suggests that the enzyme is much more abundant in terrestrial environments. Despite its predicted prevalence, the role of the pathway is unclear |CITS: [25807229]|.

Summary: General Background, Monoterpenoid indole alkaloids (MIAs) are a very large class of terpenoid indole alkaloids synthesized by the Apocynaceae, Loganiaceae, and Rubiaceae plant families. Almost all of the 2000 known members are derived from |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE|, which is biosynthesized from |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD|., Though more than 42 skeletons have been described, they can be classified according to their carbon skeleton and biogenetic branch points into five major subgroups - the Aspidosperma, Ajmalan, Corynanthe, Iboga, and Quinoline alkaloids., |FRAME: CPD-14751 Ajmaline|, the prototype compound for the Ajmalan skeleton, is a natural plant product produced by most species of the genus |FRAME: TAX-4059| as well as by |FRAME: TAX-4058| that is used as an anti-arrhythmic drug |CITS: [ 7350760]|. It was discovered in the roots of the Indian medicinal plant |FRAME: TAX-4060| in 1931 by S. Siddiqui |CITS: [Siddiqui31]|, who named it after his mentor Hakim Ajmal Khan |CITS: [Akhtar96]|., The elemental composition of ajmaline was reported already in 1932 |CITS: [VanItallie32]|, but the structure, which is very complex, was reported much later |CITS: [18131506][Chatterjee51]|. It harbors a six ring system with a total of nine chiral carbon atoms. Total chemical synthesis of ajmaline has not been exploited commercially, and it is extracted from Rauvolfia roots. A semisynthetic propyl derivative called |FRAME: CPD-21574| was developed that induces similar effects |CITS: [10944783]|., About This Pathway, Most steps of the ajmaline biosynthesis pathway have been delineated. The pathway leading to production of |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| is described in |FRAME: PWY-5290|, and the pathway from |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| to |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| is described in |FRAME: PWY-8519|., The first dedicated step of the ajmaline pathway is the cyclization of |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| to |FRAME: POLYNEURIDINE-ALDEHYDE| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.81| |CITS: [29942076]|., In the next step |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.78|, hydrolyzes a methanol group. The hydrolysis results in an unstable carboxylate, and the carboxylic acid decarboxylates spontaneously, forming the Sarpagan skeleton compound |FRAME: 16-EPIVELLOSIMINE|. This compound is a branch point, as it also leads to the biosynthesis of the side product |FRAME: CPD-4243|., The pathway towards |FRAME: CPD-14751| continues with |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.160|, an enzyme that forms the first compound with an Ajmalan structure - |FRAME: VINORINE|. Following hydroxylation by the cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.104|, |FRAME: CPD-21572| is formed, followed by spontaneous epimerization to |FRAME: VOMILENINE| |CITS: [28654178]|. This is a major branch point, as three different direct products are known to derive from it - |FRAME: 12-DIHYDROVOMILENINE| |CITS: [11937349]|, |FRAME: RAUCAFFRICINE| |CITS: [10234858]|, and |FRAME: CPDMETA-13651| |CITS: [Falkenhagen95]|. The first product leads to the formation of |FRAME: 17-O-ACETYLNORAJMALINE|, which can be converted into |FRAME: CPD-14751| by deacetylation and methylation., Rauvolfia plants accumulate |FRAME: CPD-14751| as a major alkaloid, whereas cell suspension cultures of Rauvolfia mainly accumulate the glucoalkaloid |FRAME: RAUCAFFRICINE|. However, raucaffricine can be redirected to ajmaline by the action of a highly specific glucosidase, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.125| |CITS: [Schubel86][10975500]|.

As |FRAME: TAX-562| lacks a glycine transaminase, glycine needs to be converted to |FRAME: SER|. This is achieved by the combined activities of |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| (GCV), cleaving one |FRAME: GLY| molecule to |FRAME: AMMONIUM|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, and |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate|, and |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, which subsequently condenses the latter with a second |FRAME: GLY| molecule to form |FRAME: SER|. It is used as the main carbon pathway by several microorganisms, including |FRAME: TAX-33033| growing with glycine |CITS: [14456783]|, and various methylotrophic bacteria growing on one-carbon compounds |CITS: [13651189][4929654]|. Summary: Natural rubber is an important raw material in an enormous number of products. The backbone of natural rubber comprises a (cis)-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans-isoprene units at the ω-terminus, formed by the sequential condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) units in cis configuration onto a short all-trans prenyl diphosphate. It is very similar in structure to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichols|, but the chain length is much longer (C>1500)., Natural rubber is produced from latex - a material that makes up the cytoplasmic content of the latecifers or latex vessels of |FRAME: TAX-3981| (the Brazilian rubber tree) |CITS: [17545224]|. Although over 2000 plant species capable of producing rubber have been identified, only a few synthesize the high molecular weight rubber that is required for the production of high quality rubber products, and natural rubber is currently produced commercially only from |FRAME: TAX-3981|., Despite the enormous amounts of rubber waste materials that are released into the environment, complete degradation in nature is still rare, and rubber wastes usually remain in the envireonment for a very long time. There have been reports of microorganisms that can attack from many ecosystems with moderate physical parameters (temperature, pH, and salinity) |CITS: [16535106][9170260][10742254][15638519][22142727][23863290][Chia14]|. Three types of rubber-cleaving enzymes have been characterized so far. One is the rubber oxygenase |FRAME: G-55185 RoxA|, which was first isolated from |FRAME: TAX-230757| and so far found only in Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [16348100][15574940][15870336][23934498]|; the second is the latex clearing protein (|FRAME: G-55186 Lcp|), which has been reported so far only from Gram-positive Actinobacteria |CITS: [15638519][16672480][24928880][27215318]|; and the third one is |FRAME: G-55188 RoxB| from |FRAME: TAX-230757|, which has sequence similarity to RoxA, but produces the same products as Lcp |CITS: [28500046]|., RoxA is a c-type diheme dioxygenase that cleaves |FRAME: cis-14-isoprene| from its end into |FRAME: CPD-20487|, a C15 compound with a terminal keto and aldehyde groups (this pathway). Lcp is a b-type cytochrome and cleaves rubber to several products of different sizes (C20-C35 and higher) via an endo-type mechanism |CITS: [24907333][25819959]|. RoxB is also a c-type diheme dioxygenase, but catalyzes an endo-type reaction, producing the same products as Lcp (see |FRAME: PWY-7925|)., Despite their differences, all three enzymes are dioxygenases that catalyze an oxidative cleavage of the cis double bonds in the polymer backbone, generating carbonyl and aldehyde end groups.

Summary: |FRAME: GFP "Green fluorescent proteins"| (GFPs) are proteins that exhibit bright green fluorescence when exposed to light in the blue to ultraviolet range. GFPs form a part of the bioluminesence systems of many marine organisms, and the first such protein, from the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100|, was described already in 1962 |CITS: [13911999]|., Some other species, including non-bioluminesent species, encode homologs of GFP. Many |FRAME: TAX-6101| species exhibit bright fluorescent colors, and while the most common color is green, other colors are also found |CITS: [Catala59][Mazel95]|. The fluorescence in these species is assumed to provide protection from strong solar radiation |CITS: [Kawaguti44]|. A different function has been proposed for organisms living in deeper habitats - the conversion of blue light into a longer wavelength that is more suitable for photosynthesis by the algal endosymbionts |CITS: [28313957]|., In a 1999 study genes encoding remote homologs of the |FRAME: G-55175| gene of |FRAME: TAX-6100| were cloned from six non-bioluminescent reef corals and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified. Despite a low overall identity with GFP (26-30%), all of the proteins fluoresced, and two of them (from |FRAME: TAX-105401| and |FRAME: TAX-86599| species) were found to fluoresce at the yellow and red wavelengths, respectively |CITS: [10504696]|. It is now recognized that the family of GFP-like proteins includes |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent proteins"| (GFP), |FRAME: PWY-8514 "red fluorescent proteins"| (RFP), |FRAME: YFP-Chromophore "yellow fluorescent proteins"| (YFP), |FRAME: CFP-Chromophore "cyan fluorescent proteins"| (CFP) and |FRAME: BCP-Chromophore "purple-blue non-fluorescent chromoproteins"| (CP) |CITS: [18648549]|., All of these proteins share the same β-can fold first observed in GFP, but most are not associated with bioluminescence. While the fluorophores of previously-described GFPs are formed autocatalitically from the three amino acids Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly, later identified proteins have significant variability in the first position, containing Gln, Lys, His, or Asn |CITS: [10504696][12271129]|., ZsYellow (originally named zFP538) is a yellow fluorescent protein described in the 1999 study a |FRAME: TAX-105401| sp. coral |CITS: [10504696]|. Even though the protein shares only 28% sequence homology with the |FRAME: TAX-6100| |FRAME: MONOMER-20291| (GFP), the ZsYellow protein forms a similar very stable three-dimensional β-can barrel structure. The Ser-Tyr-Gly motif of GFP is replaced with a Lys-Tyr-Gly motif, and crystal structures and mass spectrometric studies suggested that that the mature protein contains a |FRAME: CPD-27122 "three ring chromophore"| vs the |FRAME: GFP "two ring chromophore"| found in GFP |CITS: [15096045][15628861]|. It has been proposed that the chromophore is produced by a transimination reaction, in which the α-carbon of a proposed acylimine intermediate is attacked by the terminal amino group of the lysine residue. The lysine residue undergoes cyclization, and the protein backbone is broken at the Cα-N bond of the Lys residue, releasing the N-terminal part of the protein as an amide. A double bond is formed between the α-carbon and the nitrogen, resulting in a tetrahydropyridine ring |CITS: [17886433]|., Similar to other fluorescent proteins isolated from reef corals, ZsYellow exhibits a marked tendency to form tetramers when expressed in vivo |CITS: [17886433]|. The chromophore has been synthesized chemically |CITS: [19610669]|.

|FRAME: CPD-13804 "Erythromycin A"| is a macrolide antibiotic with an antimicrobial spectrum similar to or slightly wider than that of penicillin. The antibiotic was isolated in 1952 from |FRAME: TAX-1836| by scientists from the Lilly research laboratories |CITS:[McGuire52]|. It was given the trade name "Ilotycin", but the name erythromycin was introduced the same year in an editorial announcing this antibiotic |CITS: [12984186]|, Erythromycin A is used in clinical medicine against infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria. It is also used for many pulmonary infections such as Legionnaire's disease and as an alternative for patients allergic to penicillins |CITS: [11851474]|., Erythromycin contains a 14-membered lactone ring with ten asymmetric centers (the aglycon is called |FRAME: CPD-13947|) and two sugars (|FRAME: CPD-13969| and |FRAME: CPD-13780|). The structure was elucidated in 1957 |CITS: [Wiley57]|, and the absolute stereochemistry was assigned by X-ray crystallography in 1965 |CITS: [14295195]|., The first part of the biosynthesis of erythromycin, up to the first compound with antibiotic activity, |FRAME: CPD-13806|, is described in |FRAME: PWY-7106|. Two additional steps are required to generate the most active compound, |FRAME: CPD-13804| - an oxygenation |CITS: [8416893]| and a methylation |CITS: [2185226]|, catalyzed by enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-14865| and |FRAME: G-14864|, respectively. Depending on the order in which these two enzymes act, two other active intermediates are formed - |FRAME: CPD-13805| and |FRAME: CPD-13951|.

General Background, The thyroid hormones |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| (T4) and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| (T3) are essential for normal vertebrate metabolism, growth and development. These |FRAME: CPD-387|-containing molecules are biosynthesized in the thyroid gland, the function of which is to concentrate environmentally scarce |FRAME: CPD-387| in order to make it available for thyroid hormone biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-387| insufficiency in the diet remains a public health problem in some parts of the world (reviewed in |CITS: [19196800]|). Various human disorders of thyroid metabolism are characterized by hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, goiter, and cretinism (a syndrome resulting from hypothyroidism during development (in |CITS: [VOET04]|). These phenotypes have many possible causes including mutations in receptors, transporters, proteins involved in the pathway and its regulation, developmental defects, inflamation, autoimmune reactions, drug side effects, diet, or deficiency of other hormones. Also see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6260| and |FRAME: PWY-6261|., The specialized biosynthesis of thyroid hormones in the follicles of the thyroid gland has been described and illustrated in the |CITS: [19196800]| review. The follicles are lined with a single layer of thyroid epithelial cells (thyrocytes). The lumen of the follicles is filled with a colloid composed mainly of the protein |FRAME: Thyroglobulins thyroglobulin|. Thyroid hormones are derived from tyrosyl resides in this large glycoprotein, by a unique mechanism. |FRAME: CPD-387| is taken up by thyrocytes at the basolateral membrane via the sodium-iodide symporter NIS (TC# 2.A.21.5.1), with energy for the sodium gradient generated by the sodium-potassium ATPase (EC 3.6.3.9) (TC# 3.A.3.1.1). |FRAME: CPD-387| efflux through the apical membrane of the thyrocyte into the follicular lumen is mediated in part by the pendrin anion transporter (Na+-independent) (TC# 2.A.53.2.4). Upon reaching the cell-colloid interface in the follicular lumen, |FRAME: CPD-387| is oxidized and incorporated into tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin (organification) as described below (reviewed in |CITS: [19196800]|). Studies suggest that specific tyrosyl residues in thyroglobulin are involved (reviewed in |CITS: [10403182]|). , About This Pathway, The organification reaction that incorporates |FRAME: CPD-387| into tyrosyl residues of |FRAME: Thyroglobulins thyroglobulin| is catalyzed by thyroid peroxidase in the presence of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. The generation of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| is mediated by the calcium-dependent NADPH dual oxidase type 2 (DUOX2) (EC 1.6.3.1). Thyroid peroxidase-catalyzed |FRAME: CPD-387| incorporation forms |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-3-iodotyrosines| and |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-3-5-diiodotyrosines|. This enzyme also catalyzes the coupling of |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-3-iodotyrosines| and |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-3-5-diiodotyrosines| to form |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-triiodothyronines| (T3), or the coupling of two |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-3-5-diiodotyrosines| residues to form |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| (T4) (note - click on this reaction in to see the correct stoichiometry) (in |CITS: [19196800]|). The coupling reaction results in the production of a |FRAME: Thyroglobulin-aminoacrylates| (thyroglobulin-dehydroalanine) derivative of thyroglobulin after release of the thyroid hormone outer ring from the thyroglobulin polypeptide. This aminoacrylate residue then becomes hydrated to a |FRAME: SER| residue |CITS: [7021557]|. Thyroid peroxidase has been identified and characterized as a major autoantigen in autoimmune thyroid disease |CITS: [16959834]|., Release of |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| or |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| occurs by initial proteolysis in the lumen to solubilize the colloidal, cross-linked thyroglobulin. Further lumenal proteolysis can liberate |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| |CITS: [12782676]|. After pinocytosis of the partially degraded thyroglobulin into the thyrocyte, it is further proteolytically digested by lysosomal proteases, liberating |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE|. Proteases involved in these processes include the cathepsins. Studies of cathepsin-deficient mice suggested that |FRAME: MONOMER-14810|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14811| and |FRAME: MONOMER-14812| have a role in proteolytic release of |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| and |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| from thyroglobulin in vivo. A sequence of proteolytic events leading to thyroglobulin degradation was proposed |CITS: [12782676]|. In vitro studies of purified human thyroid |FRAME: HS04183-MONOMER| degradation of rabbit thyroglobulin identified its cleavage specificities. This enzyme was previously shown to be important in this process |CITS: [1939080]|., Hormone secretion into the bloodstream occurs through the basolateral membrane of the thyrocyte. This secretion step remains uncharacterized. Released mono- and diiodotyrosine molecules remain in the thyrocyte and are deiodinated by iodotyrosine dehalogenase. The released |FRAME: CPD-387| can be exported into the lumen and reused (in |CITS: [19196800]| and reviewed in |CITS: [11396699]|). In blood, thyroid hormones are transported in complex with thyroxine-binding globulin, prealbumin and albumin, and are taken up by target cells (in |CITS: [VOET04]|)., This biosynthetic pathway is regulated by complex positive and negative regulatory mechanisms involving the hypothalmus-pituitary-thyroid axis and production of hypothalmic thyrotropin releasing hormone, pituitary thyroid stimulating hormone and nuclear thyroid hormone receptors (reviewed in |CITS: [19179434]|). After biosynthesis, the biological activity of the |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| or |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| products of this pathway is mainly regulated in tissues by the selenoenzyme iodothyronine deiodinases, and thyroid hormone transporters (in |CITS: [17062880]|). See pathways |FRAME: PWY-6260| and |FRAME: PWY-6261|., Another type of deiodinase, iodotyrosine deiodinase, catalyzes a reductive deiodination of |FRAME: CPD-12288| and |FRAME: DIIODO-L-TYROSINE| residues that are also released from thyroglobulin by proteolyis. Its function is to salvage iodide from these molecules. The crystal structure of a soluble domain of this membrane-bound flavoprotein has been solved |CITS: [19436071]|.

Names: spermine and spermidine degradation I // polyamine degradation I
Summary: General Background, Polyamines such as |FRAME: SPERMINE| and |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| are required for normal cellular, function through their interaction with cellular macromolecules. They are critical regulators of cell growth,, differentiation and death. Their metabolism is complex and many mechanisms regulate their levels to maintain, polyamine homeostasis, including transcriptional, translational and post-translational regulation. Polyamine, research has been of particular interest in the development of drugs to treat parasitic infections and, cancer. Polyamines are found in all forms of life with the exception of the Methanobacteriales and Halobacteriales, orders of archaea., In eukaryotic cells, the three polyamines |FRAME: SPERMINE|, |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| and, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| are biosynthesized from |FRAME: ARG| (via |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE|) and, |FRAME: MET| (see pathways |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and, |FRAME: PWY-46|). Their degradation has been described as a retroconversion (or counter-conversion) of the, biosynthetic process. Reviewed in |CITS: [13678416]| and |CITS: [16756494]|. Also see |FRAME: PWY-0|., About This Pathway, In mammalian cells, the main mechanism for |FRAME: SPERMINE| and |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| degradation, involves the use of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to convert them to N1-acetylated derivatives, in the cytosol (a rate-limiting, or regulatory step) controlled by the inducible enzyme spermidine/spermine, N1-acetyltransferase. This is followed by oxidation of the N1-acetylated, derivatives in perosxisomes by a peroxisomal polyamine oxidase that has a preference for acetylated, substrates. In addition, a cytosolic spermine oxidase degrades |FRAME: SPERMINE| to, |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|. The |FRAME: CPD-6082| formed in this reaction is an intermediate, in |FRAME: B-ALANINE| biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3981| and |FRAME: PWY-5760|). The metabolic, fate of |FRAME: CPD-10687| is unclear, although it may be metabolized within peroxisomes by aldehyde and, alcohol dehydrogenases and may give rise to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| via EC 3.5.1.21, (reviewed in |CITS: [15221502]|). Hydrogen peroxide may be degraded by peroxisomal catalase., In addition to their retroconversion to |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| or |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, the, N1-acetylated derivatives are also be exported from normal cells into the extracellular, environment, as is |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. However, they are found in high concentration inside cancer cells,, which links altered polyamine metabolism with carcinogenesis. This is an active field of research. The direct, conversion of |FRAME: SPERMINE| to |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| without acetylation, via spermine oxidase, is a, more recent discovery and its significance to polyamine metabolism is under investigation. Reviewed, in |CITS: [13678416] [16756494]| and |CITS: [17371265]|.

Summary: Arsenic, the 20th most common element in the earth's crust, is distributed widely in the environment in bioalkylated forms, such as the organophosphonates. |FRAME: CPD-762 Arsonoacetate| is a synthetic, organic compound containing a single arsenic atom. Arsonoacetate is commonly found in agricultural applications, and is used in animal feed additives and herbicides. , An unidentified Gram-negative bacterium, strain ASV2, was isolated from activated sludge and found to be capable of utilizing |FRAME: CPD-762| as a sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [7711909]|. Isolate ASV2 was shown to be Gram-negative, motile, non-fermentative, and weakly-oxidase and catalase-positive. It most resembles |FRAME: TAX-293|, but differs in that ASV2 can not assimilate malate and propionate and is unable to grow at 37°C. Besides arsonoacetate, strain ASV2 was capable of utilizing acetate and sulfoacetate, but was unable to grow on phosphonoacetate, malonate, or glyoxylate., Bacterial strain ASV2 liberates |FRAME: CPD0-2040| (AsIII), suggesting that it degrades |FRAME: CPD-762| by cleavage of the C-As bond. Since As(III) is 100 to 200 times more toxic than As(V), it is further detoxified by oxidation to |FRAME: ARSENATE|, presumably by arsenite oxidase. Arsenate is then likely to be exported from the cells., It should be noted that while C-As bond cleavage has been demonstrated for As(III) compounds (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.M19|), it has not been described for As(V) compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-762|., C-As bond cleavage could not be detected in vitro using extracts from from arsonoacetate-grown cells, but was shown to be inducible by arsonoacetate in resting-cell suspensions. ASV2 was also able to efficiently cleave the C-As bond of the arsonoacetate analogue arsonochloroacetate, even though it was unable to utilize this compound as a carbon source |CITS: [7711909]|., There has been no attempt to idetify the enzyme(s) involved, and there has been no follow up on this report, casting some doubt on the accuracy of the cleavage reaction described here.

Summary: General Background, In many bacteria |FRAME: Glycogens "glycogen"| is the primary carbon and energy storage compound. Evidence suggests that it may play a role in the long-term survival of the cell., In |FRAME: TAX-562| glycogen is stored in granules in the cytosol |CITS: [16816199]|. It is biosynthesized in a highly regulated manner when carbon is plentiful but other nutrients are limiting (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCOGENSYNTH-PWY|). The glycogen is broken down and utilized when carbon sources become limiting |CITS: [21421758][22750467]|., |FRAME: Glycogens "Glycogen"|, |FRAME: Starch|, or |FRAME: Pullulans| are too large to be imported into the cell, and bacteria that do not have extracellualr enzymes that can break it outside the cell are not able to grow on exogenous polymers, although they are able to grow on smaller linear α-1,4-linked |FRAME: Maltodextrins "maltodextrins"| ranging in size from maltose up to about 20 glucose units in length (in Mayer and Boos |CITS: [ecosal]|)., About This Pathway, During endogenous glycogen degradation, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.1| (encoded by |FRAME: EG10380|) progressively releases |FRAME: GLC-1-P| from the non-reducing ends of linear α-(1,4)-glycan chains, but is not able to break bonds that are close to α(1,6)-branch linkages, leaving tails of 4 α-1,4-linked residues next to branching points. The highly-branched, short-chained product formed by exhaustive hydrolysis by |FRAME: GLYCOPHOSPHORYL-CPLX| has been named |FRAME: CPD0-971|, since it is the limit of what this enzyme is able to achieve on its own., This pathway is defined by the next enzyme, a type of debranching enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: EG10381| gene, which is unique to bacteria. This enzyme can remove α-1,6-linked branches that are up to four glucosyl residues in length, to produce a debranched limit dextrin (also called a debranched glycogen phosphorylase limit dextrin) and shorter |FRAME: MALTOTETRAOSE| molecules |CITS: [15687211][16816199]|. Note that this enzyme is different from the debranching system composed of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.25| and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.33|, which releases monosaccharides (see |FRAME: PWY-5941|)., Maltodextrin phosphorylase, encoded by |FRAME: EG10560|, phosphorylytically cleaves glucosyl residues from the nonreducing end of the resulting maltodextrins producing α-D-glucose-1-phosphate and a shortened maltodextrin. Maltotetraose is the smallest acceptable substrate, and thus the ultimate product of MalP is maltotriose, an endogenous inducer of the maltose system (see below) |CITS: [16816199][16321936]|., Further breakdown of the maltodextrin intermediates, |FRAME: MALTOTRIOSE| and |FRAME: MALTOSE|, involves the products of the maltose utilization genes |FRAME: EG10565| and |FRAME: EG10561|. In |FRAME: TAX-562| the expression of these genes, as well as |FRAME: EG10560|, is activated by |FRAME: MALTOTRIOSE| |CITS: [16321936][16816199][19028900]|., Maltodextrin glucosidase, encoded by |FRAME: EG10565|, can cleave an α-D-glucose residue from maltotriose, producing maltose |CITS: [16816199][19028900]|., Amylomaltase, encoded by |FRAME: EG10561|, is a 4-α-glucanotransferase that is essential for maltose degradation in |FRAME: TAX-562|. Amylomaltase preferentially removes glucose from the reducing ends of maltose and small maltodextrins, transferring the enzyme-bound dextrinyl residue to the nonreducing ends of other maltodextrins, thereby forming longer maltodextrins (in |CITS: [21421758]|). Radiotracer experiments in |FRAME:TAX-4577| showed that maize shoots can convert, spermidine and spermine to β-alanine and its biosynthesis intermediate 1,3-diaminopropane, |CITS:[Terano78]|. General Background, The |FRAME: Tetracyclines tetracycline| antibiotics, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1948 |CITS: [18112227]|, are one of the most widely used classes of antibiotics in agriculture, aquaculture, and medicine. They have a broad antimicrobial spectrum, can be administered orally, and have a low cost. Following widespread use, tetracycline resistance mechanisms emerged and continue to create a need for new derivatives that are active against resistant bacterial strains. Semisynthesis has led to second and third generation tetracycline derivatives with enhanced antibiotic activity and pharmacological properties., The original tetracyclines are natural polyketides produced by actinomycete bacteria. They are characterized by their tetracyclic ring structure, a richly substituted A ring, and a heavily oxidized periphery that includes a C11, C12, and C11a keto-enol configuration, which let them bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit, interfering with the binding of aminoacylated tRNA to the A-site of the 30S subunit and halting protein synthesis |CITS: [11163189][11381101]|., |FRAME: CPD-19258 7-Chlorotetracycline|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-1894|, was the first tetracycline compound to be discovered |CITS: [18112227]|. Early knowledge about the pathway was obtained through a series of blocked mutants and substrate feeding experiments, revealing the nature of several key intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-19273| and |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE| |CITS: [McCormick62][McCormick63a][McCormick63b][14289339][5641578]|. Later work using 13C-labeled acetate revealed the polyketide origin of the tetracycline backbone, and supported the idea of |FRAME: CPD-17870| as the origin of the C-2 amide |CITS: [Thomas83a][Thomas83b]|., In 1989 it was shown that all of the genes required for |FRAME: CPD-19255| synthesis were located within a a single DNA segment on the |FRAME: TAX-1927| chromosome |CITS: [2914874]|. This was followed by the complete sequencing of the gene clusters encoding |FRAME: CPD-19258| |CITS: [Ryan99]| and |FRAME: CPD-19255| biosynthesis |CITS: [8163168][Hunter02][16597959]|., Following the sequencing, the function of all of the involved genes has been shown through either direct isolation and characterization, genetic knockouts |CITS: [10551844][16148009]|, or expression in other Streptomyces strains |CITS: [16597959][17125237][17631493][17625867][18422316]|., About This Pathway, The first steps of tetracycline biosynthesis, up to |FRAME: CPD-19273|, are described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7811|., The combined action of the next four enzymes result in production of |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE|. These enzymes include the |FRAME: G-44638| and |FRAME: G-44639| monooxygenases, |FRAME: G-44640| aminotransferase, and |FRAME: G-44641| methyltransferase |CITS: [18422316]|. Two additional enzymes, a monooxygenase encoded by |FRAME: G-44642| and an F420-dependent dehydrogenase encoded by |FRAME: G-44643|, afford the production of |FRAME: CPD0-1414| |CITS: [23621493]|., The production of |FRAME: CPD-19258| involves one additional enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.49|. Older work has found that inactivation of the 6-hydroxylase in |FRAME: TAX-1894| NRRL3203 resulted in accumulation of 6-demethylanhydrochlortetracycline, leading to the suggestion that the chlorinase may act earlier in the pathway, and thus several of the later steps in the pathway would involve chlorinated substrates |CITS: [7612997]|. However, later work has found that when the chlorinase is inactivated, |FRAME: TAX-1894| produces pure |FRAME: CPD0-1414| at high yield, suggesting that the chlorinase is likely to be the last acting enzyme in the pathway |CITS: [23800859]|.
