Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., IAA (indole-3-acetic acid), one of the most common active forms of the phytohormone auxin, is often, present in conjugated forms. Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. Meanwhile, conjugated forms of auxin play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., About This Pathway, Several steps in the inactivation pathway in |FRAME: TAX-3702| have been proposed based on in vivo feeding experiments performed with plants during vegetative growth. The low IAA concentrations (0.5 uM) used in the initial, feeding experiments are near the endogenous level |CITS: [9733548]|. At 0.5 uM most of the fed IAA enters the |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETIC-ACID| branch. The final compound in this branch was originally identified as |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETYL-HEXOSE| |CITS: [9733548]|. Subsequent analyses demonstrate the existence of |FRAME: CPD-9592| in untreated |FRAME: TAX-3702| seedlings |CITS: [17548096]|. Feeding studies with radiolabeled |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETIC-ACID| confirmed that this compound can be glucosylated in vivo, and no other hexoses were found to be attached |CITS: [17548096]|. Interestingly, radiolabeled |FRAME: CPD-9567| can also be incorporated into |FRAME: CPD-9592|, but there is evidence that the radiolabeled IAA-glucose can be deglucosylated to radiolabeled IAA in these experiements, and can then proceed down the normal |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETIC-ACID| branch of the pathway. A radiolabeled glucose moeity will be required to ascertain if |FRAME: CPD-9567| can be directly oxidized in |FRAME: TAX-3702|., At higher auxin concentrations (5 uM), there is a marked induction of the |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| branch indicating differential regulation of the pathway at different auxin levels |CITS: [9733548]|. Further oxidation of |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| is only detected when very high levels of IAA are fed to the plants |CITS: [9733548]|. No enzyme or gene information is available for the pathway.

The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among , different organisms. , There are at least four alternative routes have been reported in plants. Two additional routes were , reported in animals |CITS: [438165]| and bacteria |CITS: [10858449]| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6825| and |FRAME: PWY-6826|)., 1) The Kennedy pathway (|FRAME: PWY3O-450|) depends on choline kinase and on the availability of , choline. , 2) The second pathway (|FRAME: PWY4FS-2|) depends on three consecutive N-methylation steps that , are carried out on phospho-bases, phosphoethanolamine, phospho-N-methylethanolamine, and , phospho-N-dimethylethanolamine. , 3) The third pathway (|FRAME: PWY4FS-3|) depends on an initial N-methylation with phospho-base , phosphoethanolamine, and followed by two downstream N-methylations on phosphatidyl-bases, , phosphatidyl-N-methylethanolamine and phosphatidyl-N-dimethylethanolamine. In plants, , phosphatidyl-N-methylethanolamine is believed to be derived from CDP-methylethanolamine, whereas , in animals, it is a direct methylation product from phosphatidylethanolamine. , 4) The fourth pathway (|FRAME: PWY4FS-4|) depends on two N-methylations with phospho-base , phosphoethanolamine and phospho-N-methylethanolamine, followed by a downstream N-methylation , on phosphatidyl-base phosphatidyl-N-dimethylethanolamine.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MET| (Met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in protein biosynthesis, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines. In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., Some bacteria can synthesize methionine using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE| with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine (|FRAME: HOMOSER-METSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [3309561]|. Plants use a modification of this pathway, where |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, instead of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting homoserine to cystathionine (this pathway)., Other bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi, can use a different route in which they directly assimilate inorganic sulfur by a sulfhydrylation (see |FRAME:HSERMETANA-PWY|). In that route |FRAME: HS|, the final product of microbial sulfate reduction (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) reacts with O-acetylated homoserine, with replacement of the acetyl group by sulfide to form |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is once again methylated to methionine (see |FRAME: PWY-5344|)., Most methanogenic archaea utilize yet a different pathway. While these organisms also use |FRAME: HS| as the sulfur source, the other precursor for |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| production is |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, produced from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7977|)., Methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., About This Pathway, In plants the nitrogen and carbon skeleton of methionine comes from |FRAME: HOMO-SER|, the sulfur atom from |FRAME: CYS|, and the methyl group from folate. , Methionine biosynthesis in plants differs from that in microorganisms, as |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, rather than |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting |FRAME: HOMO-SER| to |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. , Plants also have additional enzymes (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.10|) that can methylate |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| to |FRAME: MET|, using |FRAME: CPD-397| and |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as the methyl donors. However, those enzymes participate in the |FRAME: PWY-5441| rather than in in vivo methionine biosynthesis |CITS: [11309147]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran|, marketed under the trade name Furadan, is one of the most toxic broad-spectrum and systemic N-methyl carbamate pesticides, which is used extensively as insecticide, nematicide and acaricide for agricultural, domestic and industrial purposes. The chemical is highly toxic to mammals, birds, and honeybees, and has a moderate to high toxicity to most aquatic organisms |CITS: [32593003]|. |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran| is an endocrine disruptor and a probable reproduction/development intoxicant. It is an inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.7|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.8| |CITS: [18706518]|., |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran| has been banned in Canada and the European Union for many years. It was banned in the US in 2009 after the U.S. Supreme Court denied a counter petition by FMC and several corn grower associations., Despite its considerable toxicity, |FRAME: CPD-24209| is still used in some countries with a wide variety of field crops including potatoes, corn and soybeans. In addition, according to several journalistic investigations illegally smuggled |FRAME: CPD-24209| is used on marijuana grown illegally on public land in California, and |FRAME: CPD-24209|-contaminated marijuana appears to be the main source of marijuana consumed in states where it hasn't been legalized. In East Africa |FRAME: CPD-24209| is used by farmers to poison lions., Diverse carbofuran-degrading bacteria have been described, including members of the genera Pseudomonas, Flavobacterium, Achromobacter, Sphingomonas, Novosphingobium, and Paracoccus. However, most of these organisms are only capable of hydrolyzing |FRAME: CPD-24209| to |FRAME: CPD-24214|. Only sphingomonads are able to proceed by fully degrading |FRAME: CPD-24214| |CITS: [ 29884759]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8286|)., About This Pathway, Two types of carbofuran hydrolases, Mcd and CfdJ, have been reported. Mcd was originally purified from |FRAME: TAX-104199| |CITS: [ 2661544]|. It is a Mn2+-dependent metallohydrolase with carboxylesterase and phosphotriesterase activity |CITS: [2661544][19770008]|). The enzyme displays a tandem organization of two metallohydrolase domains with the β-lactamase fold (Pfam PF00144) and forms a homodimer. It cleaves |FRAME: CPD-24209| into |FRAME: CPD-24214| and |FRAME: CPD-22706|, which then dissociates into |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [Karns91]|., Homologs of |FRAME: G-107481| were detected in phylogenetically diverse carbofuran-degrading isolates including Achromobacter, Rhodococcus and Pseudomonas |CITS: [7504430][Parekh96][11102695]|, but not in the sphingomonads |CITS: [22534290]|.

|FRAME: CPD-10158 "Geosmin"| is the substrate that gives fresh moist soil its typical "earthy" smell., When present in water, wine or fish, it conveyes an undesirable muddy flavor., The human taste buds are very sensitive to geosmin, and can detect a concentration as small as 0.7, ppb (parts per billion). Geosmin was first isolated from actinomycetes |CITS: [Gerber65]|., Geosmin is produced by a number of microorganisms, including most Streptomyces strains, |CITS: [7227551]| and several species of cyanobacteria |CITS:[6820045][1814277][11314247][15237639]|,, myxobacteria |CITS: [15960521]|, fungi |CITS:[3150540][16096689]| and liverworts |CITS: [SPORLE91]|., It has been suggested that the distinctive smell of geosmin enables camels to find water in the desert., In return, the animals aid the bacteria by spreading their spores |CITS: [Simons03]|., As is the case of many other secondary metabolites, geosmin is synthesized from, |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| (FPP)., In |FRAME: TAX-1902| a single enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-14022|, catalyzes all steps required., It is a bifunctional enzyme, with its N-terminal domain responsible for converting, |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| to |FRAME: CPD-10159|, and the C-terminal domain catalyzing the, transformation of |FRAME: CPD-10159| to |FRAME: CPD-10158|, in a process that generates, acetone |CITS: [16787064][17873868][18095691]|. Both steps require |FRAME: MG+2|.

Summary: Vitamin K-dependent proteins are modified by carboxylation of clusters of glutamate residues to carboxylated glutamate as they transit through the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [12475254]|. The modified proteins are diverse in both structure and function and are found in many cell and tissue types, including several proteins of the blood-clotting system. The carboxylation is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.90| (|FRAME: HS03897|), an enzyme that uses various vitamin-K hydroquinones, including menaquinol, as co-substrates that are epoxidated during the reaction, generating |FRAME: 23-EPOXY-23-DIHYDRO-2-METHYL-14-NAPHTHOQ|. This posttranslational protein modification is the only firmly established biochemical function of vitamin K in animals |CITS: [1749935][17073445][17935315]|., The epoxidated forms of the vitamin can be recycled back to the native quinone form by |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.4|. The enzyme has a significant effect on blood clotting, and its deficiency in mice causes early postnatal lethality due to severe bleeding |CITS: [19492146]|. The activity has been identified in the early 1970s |CITS: [4155625][646989]|, but the |FRAME: HS15548| gene that encodes the enzyme was discovered only in 2004 |CITS: [14765194][14765195]|. The enzyme is an integral membrane protein, located in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane |CITS: [15716279]|. Its activity is strongly inhibited by the coumarin derivative |FRAME: CPD-20636|, which led to the use of this compound as the therapy of choice for the long-term treatment and prevention of thromboembolic events |CITS: [4555434][3310547]|. Another naturally occurring and highly potent inhibitor of the enzyme is |FRAME: CPD-21309|, derived from |FRAME: TAX-54829| (giant fennel), which is more than  20 times more potent an inhibitor than warfarin |CITS: [17275317]|., The last activity in the cycle is that of vitamin K reductase, which reduces the quinone form to the quinol form, the only one accepted by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.90|. The reductase also needs to act on newly introduced molecules of vitamin K, since vitamin K is present in foods in its stable oxidized quinone form. The identity of the reductase is still the subject of ongoing research. Two routes have been reported - the so called "physiological" route, a disulfhydryl-dependent reductase that is sensitive to |FRAME: CPD-20636|, and an NAD(P)H-dependent reductase that is less sensitive to |FRAME: CPD-20636| |CITS: [3098238][3593198]|. Current candidates include |FRAME: HS15548|, which has been demonstrated to have a weak reductase activity |CITS: [17164330]|, the paralogous |FRAME: G66-30969| |CITS: [21367861]|, and the NAD(P)H:quinone dehydrogenase |FRAME: HS01604| |CITS: [6799508]|.

In |FRAME:TAX-562| the disaccharide lactose is degraded by hydrolysis of the β-1,4 glycosidic bond by , β-galactosidase, producing β-D-glucose and β-D-galactose. The enzyme can also catalyze , conversion of lactose to allolactose (β-D-galactopyranosyl-(1-6)-D-glucopyranose) by transglycosylation, , and can hydrolyze allolactose (in |CITS: [6767683]|). Allolactose is the physiological inducer of this pathway. , Further metabolism of glucose and galactose inside the cell is thought to proceed by their initial transport out of the , cell, followed by reentry. It has been shown that when lactose is added to a growing culture of |FRAME:TAX-562|, , galactose, glucose and allolactose reach high levels inside the cells and are rapidly effluxed into the medium , |CITS: [6767683]|. It has also been shown that an |FRAME:TAX-562| mutant defective in the uptake of glucose and , galactose grew poorly with lactose as a sole carbon source. Additional transport rate and radiotracer studies , supported the efflux mechanism |CITS: [6426769]|. No |FRAME:TAX-562| genes specifically involved in sugar efflux during , lactose metabolism have been conclusively identified. However, SetA and SetB, members of the SET , (sugar efflux transporter) family may have a role |CITS: [10438463] [10209755]|., It has been suggested that as glucose reenters the cell it could be phosphorylated to glucose-1-phosphate by the , phosphoenolpyruvate-phosphotransferase system (in |CITS: [6767683]|). Glucose-1-phosphate could then be , converted to glucose-6-phosphate by phosphoglucomutase and enter glycolysis. Galactose could reenter the cell , by facilitated diffusion (in |CITS: [6767683]|), or active transport systems galP, or mgl , (Lin in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|). Galactose can also be converted to glucose-1-phosphate , (Fraenkel in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|). (See EcoCyc pathways: glucose and glucose-1-phosphate degradation; , galactose degradation I; and superpathway of glycolysis and Entner-Doudoroff). , The E. coli lacZ gene coding for β-galactosidase is the first of three structural genes of the historically , significant lac operon. The study of this operon provided the primary basis for the original operon concept , |CITS: [13718526]|. Lactose and other galactosides are transported into the cell by lactose permease, the product of , the second structural gene of the operon |CITS: [12893935]|. The third structural gene codes for galactoside , acetyltransferase (thiogalactoside transacetylase). The proposed function of this enzyme is acetylation of potentially , toxic pyranosides that are exported from the cell, thereby preventing their reentry |CITS: [11937062]|. A review of , biochemical studies of the three lac enzymes by Zabin and Fowler can be found in |CITS: [Operon78]|., |FRAME:TAX-382| is a soil bacterium that exists either free-living, or in a symbiotic nitrogen-fixing relationship , in root nodules of leguminous plants such as alfalfa (|FRAME:TAX-3879|) (in |CITS: [11481430]|). R. meliloti , requires large amounts of metabolic energy for nitrogen fixation and can utilize many compounds as carbon sources, , including α-galactosides and β-galactosides |CITS: [12218025]| and reviewed in |CITS: [3904617]|. , Nomenclature note: |FRAME:TAX-382| is also known as |FRAME:TAX-382| (|CITS: [9922248]| and , URL cited in |CITS: [11474104]|). , In |FRAME:TAX-382| Rm2011 (a derivative of SU47), two distinct β-galactosidase activities are present, , one that is inducible, and another that is constitutive at a low level |CITS: [409467]| . The inducible , β-galactosidase activity is necessary for growth on lactose, as mutants lacking the inducible enzyme cannot , use lactose as a sole carbon source. The lactose utilization locus is located on the megaplasmid pRmeSU47b, , one of the two megaplasmids present in R. meliloti. There is evidence to suggest that succinate also , plays a role in regulating |FRAME:TAX-379| lactose utilization. Summary: Folates are required in a variety of reactions (known as one-carbon metabolism) in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic tissues, where they act as carriers of one-carbon units in various oxidation states. These one-carbon units are utilized in the biosynthesis of various cellular components, including glycine, methionine, formylmethionine, thymidylate, pantothenate and purine nucleotides., During folate biosynthesis (as described in |FRAME:FOLSYN-PWY|) the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.12|, adds a glutamate residue to |FRAME: 7-8-DIHYDROPTEROATE|, resulting in |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE|, also known as H<sub>2</sub>PteGlu<sub>1</sub>. This molecule in turn is reduced by |FRAME:EC-1.5.1.3| (FolA) to |FRAME: THF| (H<sub>4</sub>PteGlu<sub>1</sub>, or THF), which can be converted to several other folate molecules |CITS: [11501996]|., However, most folate molecules are further modified in cells by successive additions of glutamate residues, forming folate polyglutamates (or folylpoly-γ-glutamates). Most of the glutamates are added by γ-carboxy-linked polyglutamylation via an amide linkage to the γ-carboxylate group of the folate or folate derivative. Since these isopeptide bonds are not the normal amide bonds they are not hydrolyzed by peptidases or proteases that are specific for  α-carboxyl-linked peptide  bonds., The addition of glutamyl residues probably occurs after the reduction of newly synthesized dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate and its conversion to other tetrahydrofolate derivatives., The glutamylation of folate residues serves several goals: it prevents the efflux of folates out of the cell, it increases the binding of folate cofactors to the enzymes of folate interconversion and biosynthesis, and in mammals, it allows the accumulation of folates in the mitochondria, which is required for glycine synthesis |CITS: [10598551]|., Folylpolyglutamates are generally better substrates for folate-dependent enzymes than their monoglutamyl counterparts. Km values decrease with increasing oligo-γ-glutamyl chain length |CITS: [2688305]|. At least in one case, the vitamin B<sub>12</sub>-independent methionine synthetase, there is an absolute requirement for the polyglutamate cofactor |CITS: [2985605]|., In addition, many folate enzymes are multifunctional and channel one-carbon units between reactions without achieving equilibrium with the cell medium. Therefore, the conjugated oligo-γ-glutamyl chain can potentially regulate the reaction rates, and allows channeling of the substrate between enzymes in a way which controls biosynthetic pathways |CITS: [2688305]|., Folylpoly-γ-glutamate synthetase (FPGS), the enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of folates to polyglutamates, has been purified from several organisms, including |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [2985605]|. It is a MgATP-dependent enzyme present in all cells. FPGS forms a complex with MgATP, a folate derivative, and glutamate, in an ordered manner whereby the three substrates are added sequentially |CITS: [11501996]|. In |FRAME:TAX-562|, FPGS is a bi-functional enzyme, which also catalyzes the addition of glutamate to 7,8-dihydropteroate, generating 7,8,-dihydrofolate (dihydrofolate synthetase, (E.C# 6.3.2.12)., In exponentially growing cells of |FRAME:TAX-562| folylpoly-γ- glutamates have short glutamate chain lengths: mono- and triglutamate derivatives are most abundant, with tetra-, penta- and hexaglutamate derivatives also present (in order of decreasing abundance). However, in stationary phase, cells contain longer-chain-length folypolyglutamates, with the predominant chain length containing six or seven  glutamyl residues. These longer chains are generated by a second enzyme, which adds glutamate moieties in α-linkage to tetrahydropteroyl- triglutamates |CITS: [3536926]|. However, this enzyme has not been purified, nor has the gene encoding it been identified. , Both folylpolyglutamate synthetases can accept several different folate derivatives as substrates. It seems that the preferred substrate for the addition of a second glutamate residue is 10-formyl-THF (10-formyl-H<sub>4</sub>PteGlu<sub>1</sub>), while the preferred substrate for the addition of a third glutamate residue is the glutamated form of 5,10-methylene-THF (5,10-methylene-H<sub>4</sub>PteGlu<sub>2</sub>).

Summary: Fatty acids constitute a major component of plant membranes in the form of glycerolipids, mainly phosphoglycerolipids and glycosylglycerolipids. The majority of them have C16 or C18 carbon chains and are attached to the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of the glycerol backbone. In Arabidopsis, the major fatty acids are C16:0, C16:1, C16:2, C16:3, C18:1, C18:2, and C18:3. Unsaturated fatty acids are significant to membrane functions such as photosynthesis and cold tolerance. C16:3 and C18:3 together make up more than 90% of the fatty acid content of monogalactosyldiacylglycerol (MGDG), a , major glycosylglycerolipid of leaf chloroplast membranes |CITS: [arabidopsis94]|.   , C18:1 is desaturated from C18:0 in the form of stearoyl-ACP (|FRAME: PWY-5147|) and is subsequently incorporated into glycerolipids. The rest of the unsaturated fatty acids, C16:1, C16:2, C16:3, C18:2 and C18:3, on the other hand, are desaturated from C16:0 or C18:1 after C16:0 and C18:1 are incorporated into glycerolipids. These latter desaturation processes are catalyzed by membrane-bound fatty acid desaturases, and occur in chloroplasts and ER. Fatty acid desaturation is best studied in Arabidopsis using desaturase mutants. , The desaturation of phosphatidylglycerol occurs in the chloroplast, and the desaturation of phosphatidylcholine occurs in the ER. Note that desaturation occurs on both sn-1 and sn-2 acyl chains, and that the order of the desaturation steps on one chain versus the other is not known. Here, all the possible steps are presented.

General Background, Lignans are a group of dimeric and/or oligomeric plant natural compounds of phenylpropanoid origin. They represent a structurally highly diverse compound class that is characterized by a 8,8'-linkage found in the C6-C3 dimers of coniferyl alcohol or other cinnamoyl alcohols although other interunit linkages (e.g. 8-5', 8-O-4) may also occur |CITS: [Lewis99]| |CITS: [FUSS03]|., Lignans and lignins are biosynthesized in two major branches which descend from the phenylpropanoid pathway. During the conquest of land this pathway has been substantially advanced with consequences for derivative biosyntheses such as for lignins/lignans, hydrolyzable and condensed tannins and flavonoids |CITS: [STAFFORD00]|. Lignans are widespread among the plant kingdom but have not been found in aquatic plants such as algae indicating their crucial contribution to adaptation and fitness of terrestrial plants |CITS: [AYRES90][11423139]|. The structural biopolymers lignins and lignans accomplish different tasks in plants, lignins are involved in structural support and lignans have been attributed to protection and defense as their primary physiological functions. Taken together lignins and lignans count for about 30% of carbon in vascular plants |CITS: [Lewis99]|. , Beside their recognized functions as defense compounds in plants some lignans have attracted the attention of scientists because of their application in medicine and human health |CITS: [MACRAE84]|. Lignans possess most effective health protective and curative properties and have been employed as antioxidants |CITS: [14995053]|, anti-carcinogenic agents |CITS: [10800470]| |CITS: [16311631]| and phytoestrogens |CITS: [15377220]|., Lignans can be subdivided into several structural subfamilies. The matairesinol pathway is an excellent example for a pathway that not only contains several types of lignans but also gives rise to other lignan subfamilies. (+)-pinoresinol (a furofuran) is sequentially converted to (+)-lariciresinol (a benzylaryltetrahydrofuran), (-)-secoisolariciresinol (a dibenzylbutane) and (-)-matairesinol (a dibenzylbutyrolactone) which is an intermediate in the biosynthetic route towards podophyllotoxin (an aryltetrahydronaphthalene) (compare |FRAME:PWY-5479|)., About This Pathway, The pathway begins with the formation of |FRAME: CPD-18761| from |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL|. Whether |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.7|, or |FRAME: EC-1.10.3.2|, function in the oxidation of monolignols to radicals has been under active evaluation for many years |CITS: [13657039][17812228][Sterjiades93][9914531]|. Both peroxidases and laccases were shown to catalyze the oxidation of |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL| to a radical in vitro |CITS: [16027971][25626739]|. , The next step involves the stereo-specific coupling of two phenoxy radicals to form dimers. Most lignans are optically active as a result of specific regio- and stereo specificity in the coupling process. Interestingly, the proteins responsible for the linkages are not enzymes. These proteins, which were named 'dirigent proteins' (DP) serve only to bind and orientate the coniferyl alcohol-derived free radicals |CITS: [10859176][16023845][8994027]|. It could be demonstrated that dirigent proteins form a multigene family in plants |CITS: [12359517]|, and their function is not limited to the formation of lignans but also includes other biosyntheses of various phenolics employing corresponding radicals., The next step in the pathway is catalyzed by two distinct enzyme classes of pinoresinol/lariciresinol reductases (PLR). These bifunctional enzymes are stereospecific and catalyze the enantioselective reduction of either (+)-pinoresinol and (+)-lariciresinol towards (-)-secoisolaricinol (as discovered in Forsythia) |CITS: [8910615]| or (-)-pinoresinol and (-)-lariciresinol, forming (+)-secoisolaricinol, as demonstrated in western red cedar |CITS: [9872995]|., Similar enantiospecific enzymes have also been found in different species of the same genus |CITS: [15949826]|., Another bifunctional enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.331| (SDH) affords the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8912| |CITS: [2037574]| via a stable lactol intermediate |CITS: [11278426]|.

Summary: There are several degradation pathways for cysteine in mammals., The major route of cysteine degradation most likely starts by the oxidation of cysteine to, |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE|., The conversion of |FRAME: CYS| to |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| (L-cysteine sulfinic acid) forms, a branch point., In one route, |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| is transaminated by |FRAME:ENZRXN-9021| to, |FRAME: 3-SULFINYL-PYRUVATE|, which spontaneously degrades to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and, |FRAME:SO3|, as shown here |CITS: [13314623]|. Sulfite is oxidized by |FRAME:CPLX-7169| to, |FRAME: SULFATE|, which is excreted in the urine |CITS: [7491943]|, and pyruvate is converted by, |FRAME:PYRUVDEHYD-PWY| to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, which enters the |FRAME: TCA|., A second route involves the decarboxylation of |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| to form, |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE|, which is further oxidized to |FRAME:TAURINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5331|)., Taurine is used in the synthesis of bile salts., In addition, cysteine can also be metabolized to pyruvate by 3-sulfinoalanine-independent pathways., These involve the cysteine desulfhydrase activity of |FRAME: CPLX-5163|, (see |FRAME: LCYSDEG-PWY|), or an initial direct transamination by |FRAME:ENZRXN-13116|, to form |FRAME: 3-MERCAPTO-PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5329|) |CITS: [3309559]|., The relative use of these two pathways shows species and tissue specificity (reviewed in, |CITS: [3309559]|). In vitro studies of freshly isolated rat renal cortical tubules |CITS: [2111378]|,, and freshly isolated rat enterocytes |CITS: [2621485]|, showed that these cell types predominantly used, this 3-sulfinoalanine transmination pathway to pyruvate, rather than the decarboxylation pathway, to taurine. Substantial amounts of |FRAME:MONOMER-8844| and |FRAME:CPLX-5342| activities, were demonstrated in rat renal cortical tubules |CITS: [2111378]|. 3-Sulfinoalanine-independent, pathways, particularly cleavage by |FRAME:CPLX-5163|, also had significant roles in these, cell types. However, in freshly isolated rat hepatocytes, the 3-sulfinoalanine-independent pathways,, particularly the pathway involving cleavage by |FRAME: CPLX-5163|, had a predominant role., The hepatocytes also used the 3-sulfinoalanine decarboxylation pathway to taurine, to a lesser, extent |CITS: [3117038]|.

Summary: In prokaryotes and eukaryotes the four-carbon amino acid |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is converted to the corresponding keto acid |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| by transamination using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| as acceptor of the amino group. The reaction is reversible and can also biosynthesize aspartate (see pathway |FRAME: ASPARTATESYN-PWY|)., |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID Oxaloacetate| is a |FRAME: TCA "|tricarboxylic acid cycle"| intermediate. It can also be , converted by phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase to phosphoenolpyruvate for use in gluconeogenesis (see pathway |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY|). Aspartate is therefore a link between amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism., In addition, aspartate is a precursor for the biosynthesis of many other compounds including lysine, threonine, methionine and NAD+ (see |FRAME: PWY0-781| and |FRAME: ASPARTATESYN-PWY|). , There are several other routes for aspartate degradation. In mammals and most land vertebrates, aspartate can be degraded by entering the urea cycle at the point of citrulline, and is ultimately converted to fumarate (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-4984|). In another eukaryotic route, aspartate is degraded to malate as part of the reversible malate-aspartate shuttle found in liver, heart and kidney. This is one of several shuttle mechanisms used to transfer electrons from cytosolic NADH produced by glycolysis into the mitochondrion, because NADH itself cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane (see pathway |FRAME: MALATE-ASPARTATE-SHUTTLE-PWY|). In prokaryotes, aspartate can be degraded to fumarate by |FRAME: ASPARTASE-CPLX| (see pathway |FRAME: GLUTDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [Voet04] [Gottschalk1986][Salway04]|.

Summary: This Pathway in Bacteria, |FRAME: GLYCEROL Glycerol| uptake in bacteria is mediated by the glycerol diffusion facilitator, an integral membrane protein catalyzing the rapid equilibration of concentration gradients of glycerol across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8436953]|. Intracellular glycerol is converted to |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.30|, which uses ATP as phosphoryl donor. |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P "Glycerol-3-P"| is not a substrate of the glycerol diffusion facilitator and thus remains in the cell, where it is further metabolized. As a result, the driving force for the uptake of glycerol is generated by the phosphorylation of glycerol by glycerol kinase |CITS: [9162046]|. , While |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| can not leave the cytoplasm, it can be imported into the cell by the GlpT transporter, a member of the major facilitator superfamily, that couples the import of glycerol-3-P into the cytoplasm to the export of inorganic phosphates from the cytoplasm to the periplasm |CITS: [3522583][12893936]|. , |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P "glycerol 3-phosphate| can be further metabolized to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| by a number of different enzymes. This pathway described |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.3| , which transfers the electrons to the quinone pool., This Pathway in Yeast, Under aerobic conditions |FRAME: TAX-4932| is able to utilize glycerol as a sole carbon and energy source. Glycerol degradation is a two-step process that involves translocation. The first step, glycerol phosphorylation, occurs in the cytosol. The product, glycerol-3-phosphate, enters the mitochondrion where it is converted to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS:[191434]|. |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| is then returned to the cytosol, where it enters into either glycolysis or gluconeogenesis., The genes encoding the enzymes catalyzing glycerol catabolism are regulated by the carbon source. Gene expression is repressed in the presence of fermentable carbon sources such as glucose, and upregulated by non-fermentable carbon sources such as glycerol or ethanol |CITS:[191434][10536147][11142398]|., This Pathway in Plants, In higher plants, the primary seed storage reserve is triacylglycerol. During seed germination, triacylglycerol is broken , down to fatty acids and glycerol. Fatty acids are converted to sucrose via glyoxylate cycle to support seedling growth. , Radio tracer experiments have also demonstrated that glycerol can be converted to sucrose as well. The contribution , of carbon stored as glycerol is relatively small, being estimated of 5% of the total carbon. Two possible routes of , glycerol catabolism have been proposed. In the first pathway, glycerol is phosphorylated to glycerol-3-phosphate by , glycerol kinase, and then converted to dihydroxyacetone phosphate by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. In the , second pathway, glycerol is coverted to dihydroxyacetone by NAD-dependent glycerol dehydrogenase, and then , phosphorylated to dihydroxyacetone phosphate by dihydroxyacetone kinase. The assertion of the first pathway, not , the second pathway, in plants is supported by the following evidence: glycerol kinase and glycerol-3-phosphate , dehydrogenase activities are detected in germinating seeds, whereas NAD-dependent glycerol dehydrogenase activity , is not; the highest expression of the glycerol kinase and the FAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase , genes are detected during seed germination; the glycerol kinase mutant, gli1, of Arabidopsis is disrupted in glycerol , catabolism and accumulates glycerol. It is worth noting that, in addition to the mitochondrial FAD-dependent , glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, plants also have cytosolic and plastidial NAD-dependent , glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase that can convert glycerol-3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate. But , the NAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase is unlikely to be involved in glycerol degradation since the , equilibrium constant favors the synthesis of glycerol-3-phosphate. The product of glycerol degradation, , dihydroxyacetone phosphate, can be converted to sugars via gluconeogenesis.

The formation of disulfide bonds is crucial for the folding and maturation of the extracellular domains of both membrane and secreted proteins in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. The decrease in chain entropy that accompanies disulfide bond formation disfavors the unfolded form and helps stabilize the tertiary structure of the protein., In eukaryotic organisms the formation of disulfide bonds occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum. In that system disulfides are generated de novo within |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.2| |CITS: [9659913][9659914]|, and are transferred via |FRAME: EC-5.3.4.1|, to the substrate proteins by a dithiol-disulfide exchange reactions |CITS: [10549279]|., In Gram-negative bacteria disulfides are introduced in periplasmic proteins by the DsbA-DsbB system, which is described here. Electrons from reduced substrate proteins in the periplasm flow through this pathway via a series of inter and intra-molecular thiol-disulfide exchange reactions before being passed to the membrane quinones and ultimately to the terminal acceptors of aerobic and anaerobic respiration., |FRAME: DISULFOXRED-MONOMER "DsbA"| is a small periplasmic protein with a single redox-active disulfide bond; disulfide bonded DsbA is a strong oxidant and undergoes disulfide exchange with the reduced cysteine residues of numerous substrate proteins. To restore it's activity, reduced DsbA is then reoxidized by the inner membrane protein thiol:quinol oxidoreductase, |FRAME: DSBBPROT-MONOMER "DsbB"|. DsbB contains two redox active disulfides which are involved in the transfer of electrons from reduced DsbA to ubiquinone (under aerobic conditions) or menaquinone (under anaerobic conditions); the mechanism of DsbB mediated electron transfer remains an area of active research., Periplasmic proteins which contain more than two cysteines may be misoxidized by the DsbA-DsbB system; the correction of non-native disulfides relies on the action of periplasmic disulfide isomerases |FRAME: DSBC-CPLX "DsbC"| and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: DSBG-CPLX "DsbG"| (see |FRAME: PWY0-1600|). , Disulfide bond formation and isomerization in E. coli has been reviewed by |CITS: [15546661][16446111][19567379]| , Selected related reviews: |CITS: [12524212][18406599][19634988]|

Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFA) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes., The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in these compounds. The icosanoids are derived from the 20-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (AA; 20:4n-6), |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA; 20:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-8120| (DGLA; 20:3n-6)., Additional fatty acids are also oxygenated to yield bioactive products, including the the 18-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (LA; 18:2n-6) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (ALA; 18:3n-3) and the 22-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| (DPA; 22:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA; 22:6n-3). Strictly speaking, the derivatives of such acids should be named octadecanoids (for C18 compounds) and docosanoids (for 22 carbon compounds), though these compounds are often included in the icosanoids, making the definition broader than initially intended., In mammals icosanoids and related mediators mediate a wide array of critical biological processes such as ovulation, initiation of labor, bone metabolism, nerve growth and development, wound healing, kidney function, blood-vessel tone, blood coagulation, immune responses, and inflammation. Despite the great importance of these compounds, mammals are not able to form a double bond at either the n-3 or n-6 position of a fatty acyl chain and must rely entirely on dietary intake for PUFAs |CITS: [25486530]|., Three main enzyme families act on PUFAs. The first one is |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.1| (the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes), which possess dual cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activities and catalyze the oxidative cyclization of PUFAs to |FRAME: CPD-24676|, |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|, or |FRAME: CPD-26009| (depending on the starting PUFA), which are subsequently converted to a variety of prostanoids and thromboxanes by cell-specific terminal synthases and isomerases., The second family is the lipoxygenases (LOX), which catalyze the stereoselective insertion of molecular oxygen into PUFA with the formation of hydroperoxy fatty acids that are subsequently reduced to the corresponding hydroxy-fatty acids. The lipoxygenases are divided into three main form depneding on the carbon at which they oxygenate |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|: |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|., The third family is cytochrome P450 monooxygenases that catalyzes the hydroxylation and/or epoxygenation of PUFAs. In addition to producing LOX-like monohydroxy fatty acids, CYP can add a hydroxyl moiety to the ω-carbons, of PUFA to form a unique class of omega-hydroxylated fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-21314|). The epoxides that are formed by these enzymes can be hydrolyzed to the corresponding dihydroxyfatty acids by |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| (sEH).

Summary: General Background, Androgens are steroid hormones that stimulate or control the development and maintenance of male characteristics in vertebrates, including the activity of the accessory male sex organs and development of male secondary sex characteristics, by binding to androgen receptors. Androgens are also produced by females, and are the precursors to estrogens. Present in lower concentrations than in males, androgens contribute to libido and sexual arousal in females., Important androgens include |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| (DHT) and |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE androstenedione|. |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE Testosterone| is the major androgen in adult males, while DHT plays a crucial role in utero, causing differentiation of the penis, scrotum and prostate. In adulthood DHT contributes to balding, prostate growth, and sebaceous gland activity., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the conversion of the inactive C21 steroid hormone precursor |FRAME: PREGNENOLONE| to the androgens |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE androstenedione|, |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| and |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| (DHT). Unlike androstenedione and testosterone, which can be converted into estrogens via the |FRAME: PWY66-380| pathway, |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| can not be converted to estrogens and is the only committed androgen. It is also the most potent activator of the androgen nuclear hormone receptor., Androgens are synthesized in testes, ovaries, placenta and other tissues and are required for normal sexual development in males and females. Mutations in all of the genes in this pathway result in varying degrees of sexual and genital malformation.

Names: thiosulfate oxidation IV (incomplete Sox system, sulfur-depositing)
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: S2O3 Thiosulfate| is a relatively stable environmentally abundant sulfur compound of intermediate oxidation state. Several pathways of thiosulfate oxidation are known. The two best understood pathways are the direct oxidation of thiosulfate to sulfate, catalyzed by the |FRAME:CPLX-882|, and the indirect oxidation of thiosulfate through polythionate intermediates, the main of which is |FRAME:CPD-14| (see |FRAME:THIOSULFOX-PWY|)., Two versions of the direct oxidation pathway are known. A number of facultatively chemo- or photolithotrophic organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-82367| or |FRAME: TAX-35806|, which possess the SoxCD proteins, oxidize a single molecule of thiosulfate to two molecules of sulfate (see |FRAME: PWY-5296|). Organisms that lack the SoxCD proteins utilize a different route, in which one molecule of thiosulfate is converted into only one molecule of sulfate while the other sulfur atom is added to inorganic sulfur globules that are deposited either in the periplasmic space or outside the cells (this pathway)., About This Pathway, Many organisms, including the phototrophic green and purple sulfur bacteria, as well as free-living and symbiotic chemotrophic sulfur oxidizers like |FRAME: TAX-1021| or |FRAME: TAX-1030|, oxidize thiosulfate in a pathway that invovles the intermediate deposition of sulfur either inside (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-1021|, |FRAME: TAX-1046|) or outside (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-191412|, |FRAME: TAX-72276|) of the cells. These organisms utilize a version of the Sox protein complex that lacks the SoxCD proteins., The pathway has been studied in detail in the model sulfur oxidizer |FRAME: TAX-1049|. The sox genes of |FRAME: TAX-1049| are located in two loci. Gene inactivation and complementation experiments showed that these proteins are indispensable for thiosulfate oxidation to sulfate |CITS: [16995898]|. Purified enzymes were used for an in vitro reconstituted Sox system., The first two reactions in this cycle are common with the pathway of |FRAME: TAX-82367| - the first step is the |FRAME: CPLX-8196|-mediated binding of thiosulfate to a cysteine residue of |FRAME: SoxY-Protein "a SoxY protein"|. When thiosulfate binds, a |FRAME: SoxY-Thiocysteine-Sulfate| is formed, which is then hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16064|, liberating a sulfate, and forming a |FRAME: SoxY-S-Thiocysteine|., At this point the pathways divert. In the absence of a SoxCD complex, the sulfane moiety of the original thiosulfate molecule, which is bound to the SoxY protein, is transferred to form sulfur globules in a reaction that restores SoxY to its original condition |CITS: [16995898][19303410]|. This process occurs via an unresolved mechanism, though a candidate for a sulfurtransferase that transfers the sulfane sulfur to the globules has been suggested - the rhodanese-like protein encoded by the |FRAME: G-12375| gene |CITS: [19303410]|., The overall reaction of thiosulfate oxidation by this pathway is:, |FRAME: S2O3| + |FRAME: Intracellular-Sulfur|(n) + |FRAME:WATER| = |FRAME:SULFATE| + |FRAME: Intracellular-Sulfur|(n+1) + 2|FRAME:E-| + 3|FRAME:PROTON|, In some organisms the truncated Sox system combines with cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation systems such as the |FRAME: PWY-6675 "rDsr system"| or the |FRAME: PWY-8573 "sHdr system"|, enabling complete oxidation to sulfate. In those organisms the remaining sulfur does not end in sulfur globules, but is exported from the periplasm to the cytoplasm for further oxidation. The exact manner in which the sulfur is transferred to the cytoplasm is still not clear, although the transporter SoxT (such as UniProt D8JT34 from |FRAME: TAX-53399|) appears to be involved |CITS: [36367491]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Phytobilins Phytobilins| are tetrapyrrole molecules that are synthesized by plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Major classes of phytobilins are:, 1. |FRAME: Phycobilins Phycobilins|, which are the chromophores of |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins| |CITS: [16663825]| and some algal phytochromes |CITS: [8616213]|, 2. |FRAME: Phytochromobilins Phytochromobilins|, which are the chromophores of higher plants |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| |CITS: [1634523][7744741]|., |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins Phycobiliproteins| are light-harvesting accessory pigments of cyanobacteria, red algae and cryptophytes, and |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| are photoreversible light signal-transducing pigments of plants, some algae, and some cyanobacteria., One of the major phycobiliproteins in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: Phycoerythrins phycoerythrin|, which is also found in the chloroplasts of red algae, glaucophytes and some cryptomonads. One of the chromophores which are always attached to phycoerythrin is |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins phycoerythrobilin|, a red light absorbing pigment that belongs to the |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|. It is found in |FRAME: TAX-1117| and in the chloroplasts of |FRAME: TAX-2763 rhodophytes|, |FRAME: TAX-38254 glaucocystophytes|, and some |FRAME: TAX-3027 cryptomonads|., |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins Phycoerythrobiln| is covalently linked to both subunits of |FRAME: Phycoerythrins phycoerythrin| by a thioether bond to conserved cysteine resudues at position 84. In addition, in some Rhodophytes and oceanic cyanobacteria, phycoerythrobilin also functions as the chromophore of another phycobiliprotein, |FRAME: R-Phycocyanins R-Phycocyanin|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathways for the production of the four cyanobacterial |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-3702| pathway for |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| biosynthesis, have been elucidated. These five chromophores share a common precursor, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, which is the product of heme macrocycle cleavage by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18| |CITS: [9744099]|. |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is subsequently reduced by one of several possible ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases., In most cyanobacteria |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| is converted to |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN| in two steps, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13950| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13952|, encoded by the genes |FRAME: G-10652| and |FRAME: G-10653|, respectively |CITS: [11283349]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5915|)., This pathway describes an alternative route that occurs in |FRAME: TAX-1218| cyanobacteria infected by phages that carry phycobilisome pigment biosynthesis genes., In contrast to other cyanobacteria, |FRAME: TAX-1218| is characterized by divinyl-chlorophyll containing light-harvesting complexes and the lack of phycobilisomes. Curiously, despite the lack of phycobilisomes, all sequenced genomes of |FRAME: TAX-1218| possess genes that encode enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of open-chain tetrapyrrole molecules |CITS: [17439544]|. It has also been shown that the products of these genes are assembled into proteins |CITS: [ 20724022]|., Even more interestingly, some Prochlorococcus cyanophages, which often harbor photosynthesis-related genes |CITS: [15256601]| that yield proteins during host infection |CITS: [16222247]|, also carry homologs of phycobilisome pigment biosynthesis genes |CITS: [18356052]|., The |FRAME: TAX-268746| possesses homologs of |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.20| (|FRAME: G-43731|), |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.2| (|FRAME: G-43733|), and ferredoxin (petF), while the |FRAME: TAX-268747| carries an |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.5| (|FRAME: G-43736|) homolog. All genes were shown to encode fully functioning proteins that mostly resemble the activity of the cyanobacterial enzymes. One exception is the phage pebA homolog (|FRAME: G-10659|), which encodes an enzyme that catalyzes a single reaction for which uninfected host cells require two consecutive enzymes, |FRAME: G-10652| and |FRAME: G-10653| |CITS: [18356052]|., It has been shown that the genes encoded by |FRAME: TAX-268746 P-SSM2| (petF and ho1) are transcribed during infection, suggesting that they can improve phage fitness. While PcyA and Ho1 occur in both cyanobacteria and their phages, pebS is exclusive to phages |CITS: [18356052]|., Like in other phycoblilin biosynthesis pathways, the product of the pathway is the Z-isomer, |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN|, which is converted to its E-isomer either spontaneously or by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|., Curiously, a family of genes (which were named pcyX) similar to |FRAME: G-43736| but encoding an enzyme with the same activity as |FRAME: G-10659 PebS| was found in marine pelagiphages that infect α-proteobacteria, along with genes encoding heme oxygenase. The presence of these genes in pelagiphages suggests a role of phycobilins in anoxygenic phototrophs. Despite the fact that they catalyze the same reaction, the PebS and PcyX proteins share only 9% amino acid identity |CITS: [26950653]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Estrogens Estrogens| are steroid hormones synthesized in the ovaries, breasts, adipose and other tissues that are critical for sexual development and function. They can also act as inducers of tumour growth in estrogen dependent cancerous tissues and as such are targets for widely used anti-cancer therapies, such as |FRAME: CPD-4541| and aromatase inhibitors. Estrogen levels at baseline and when increased during pregnancy correlate with breast cancer risk, so enzymes in this pathway are targets of existing or potential cancer therapies., The main estrogens in humans are |FRAME: ESTRONE|, |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRIOL|, which differ in the number of hydroxyl groups (one for |FRAME: ESTRONE|, two for |FRAME: CPD-352| and three for |FRAME: ESTRIOL|). |FRAME: CPD-352| is about 10 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRONE| and about 80 times as potent as |FRAME: ESTRIOL| in its estrogenic effect., |FRAME: CPD-352| is the predominant estrogen in non-pregenant women during their reproductive years in terms of serum levels. |FRAME: ESTRONE Estrone| is the predominant circulating estrogen in women during menopause and |FRAME: ESTRIOL| is the predominant circulating estrogen during pregnancy., In premenapausal women 17β-estradiol is produced by the granulosa cells of the ovaries by the aromatization of |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| (via |FRAME: ESTRONE|) as described here., |FRAME: CPD-352| is also present in males at roughly the same concentration as in postmenopausal women. However, It is produced as an active metabolic product of testosterone (see |FRAME: PWY-7306|)., The key enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: HS06413| (aromatase), which is required for all estrogen production. This enzyme, which acts an a monooxygenase to make the first carbon ring aromatic, is the target of the aromatase inhibitors which are given to post-menopausal breast cancer patients., |FRAME: CPD-4541 Tamoxifen| is an estrogen analog that must be metabolized into its active form by cyp2D6 and cyp3A4. Polymorphisms have been identified at the CYP2D6 locus that result in differing levels of conversion to active 4-hydroxy tamoxifen and endoxifen (N-demethyl-4-hydroxytamoxifen) and consequently differing effectiveness of tamoxifen treatment. Tamoxifen metabolites act by binding to and inhibiting the nuclear hormone estrogen receptors. Additional,  non-canonical estrogen receptors are not inhibited by these hormone analogs and are thought to mediate the increased risk of endometrial cancer among patients using tamoxifen and related therapies.

Summary: General Background, Phylloquinone (vitamin K1, 2-methyl-3-phytyl-1,4-naphthoquinone) acts as the electron , transfer cofactor A1 of photosystem I (PS I) in higher plants and cyanobacteria. In non-photosynthetic, microbes the very similar compound |FRAME: Menaquinones| plays an, essential role in several anaerobic electron transport systems |CITS: [8626063]|., The chemical structure of menaquinone (vitamin K2) exhibits a partly unsaturated side chain consisting, most often 7 prenyl units, whereas phylloquinone consists of a mostly saturated phytyl side chain of, 4 units |CITS: [15686525]|., The biosynthesis of phylloquinone was studied in detail in the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148| and, the genes encoding enzymes of this pathway were identified by comparison with genes encoding, enzymes of the menaquinone biosynthetic pathway in |FRAME:TAX-562|, (see |FRAME:MENAQUINONESYN-PWY|) |CITS: [8626063]|. With the isolation and functional, confirmation of the homolog genes in |FRAME:TAX-1142| encoding for |FRAME: SGL_RS09385-MONOMER|,, |FRAME: MONOMER-13896| |CITS: [10722690]|, |FRAME: SGL_RS03195-MONOMER|, |CITS:[11772039]|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13897| and |FRAME: MONOMER-11678| |CITS: [JOHNSON03]|,, most of the enzymatic steps of the phylloquinone bisoynthesis have been determined and proven to be highly, identical with those in the menaquinone biosynthesis., The biosynthesis of certain components of the multienzyme complex PS I (such as phylloquinone), in cyanobacteria and plants have been found to follow analogous routes, including corresponding, enzymatic activities |CITS: [HEIDE82]| |CITS: [KOLKMANN87][SIMANTIRAS89][SIMANTIRAS91]|,, reflecting the phylogenetic origin of PS I in photosynthetic microbes. , About This Pathway, The enzymatic steps involved in the biosynthesis of phylloquinone in cyanobacteria and plants are almost, identical to the biosynthetic route leading to the microbial complement menaquinone., The discernible step between phylloquinone and menaquinone biosynthesis is the prenylation of, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| (DHNA)., The DHNA phytyltransferase catalyzes the attachment of a C-20 phytyl side chain leading to, |FRAME:CPD-6947| |CITS: [15686525]|, whereas microbial DHNA prenyltransferases attache a, multiprenyl side chain, forming demethylmenaquinones. The length of the side chain varies among, different species., It has been found that phylloquinone is not absolutely required for efficient electron transfer in PS I, |CITS: [10722690]|. At least in |FRAME: TAX-1148|, benzoquinones such as, |FRAME:PLASTOQUINONE-9|, which usually act as secondary electron acceptors in PS II, |CITS: [11470786][15681848]|, can efficiently replace phylloquinone in the A1-site of PS I as a, one-electron cofactor. However, as shown in both |FRAME:TAX-3701| and |FRAME: TAX-1148| mutants,, the deficiency of phylloquinone causes distortions in the thylakoid structure of chloroplasts,, decreases the content of PS I, and affects the functionality of PS II |CITS: [15686525]|., It has been demonstrated that the final step of the pathway, a transmethylation reaction to form |FRAME:CPD-12831|, depends on the oxidation state of the penultimate substrate. This led to the discovery that one more reaction was inserted in between |FRAME:CPD-6947| and the final product |FRAME:CPD-12831|. This reaction was catalyzed by type II NAD(P)H dehydrogenases in both Arabidopsis thaliana and the cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 encoded by NDC1 and ndbB, respectively, which resulted in the formation of the reduced |FRAME:CPD-12830| |CITS:[26023160]|. Only this reduced (quinol) substrate was able to accept the electrons from the electrophilic |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| for the subsequent transmethylation step of the |FRAME:PWY-5027| to yield |FRAME:CPD-12831| |CITS:[26023160]|. In general, the intermediates of the |FRAME:PWY-5027| including in-feeding pathways such as |FRAME:PWY-5837| are depicted in their dihydroxy conformation, for example see |FRAME:DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| and |FRAME:CPD-9925|, although the latter has been shown to be used in vitro in its diketo form |CITS:[19321747]|. However, the study on the dehydrogenases of Arabidopsis and Synechocystis provide evidence that |FRAME:CPD-6947| and probably any other preceding intermediates occur in their diketo instead of the dihydroxy form |CITS:[Basset15]|.

General Background, Aryl carotenoids that contain φ-type rings were first discovered in the Japanese sea sponge |FRAME: TAX-6062|, which at the time was known as Reniera japonica |CITS: [Yamaguchi57]| (in retrospect they were most likely produced by bacterial endosymbionts of the sponge). Thus the first compounds to be defined from that organism were named |FRAME: CPD-20646| (φ,χ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi57a]| and |FRAME: CPD-20624| (φ,φ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi58][Yamaguchi59]|. Aryl carotenoids were subsequently identified in most non-oxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (green and purple sulfur bacteria) as well as some non-photosynthetic species of the |FRAME: TAX-1763| and |FRAME: TAX-1883| genera |CITS: [5711189][5781524][Schmidt70][4635689]|. , In green sulfur bacteria (GSB) the carotenoids are found in chlorosomes. These obligately anaerobic photoautotrophs can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph (up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight |CITS: [Overmann92]|) due to their chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. The chlorosome consists of mostly |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"|, or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| that self-aggregate into large oligomers, but also contains up to 10% carotenoids., The main carotenoid produced by GSB species with |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| or |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| as the primary antenna component is the monocyclic |FRAME: CPD-20625| (see |FRAME: PWY-7939|), while the main carotenoids produced by brown-colored green sulfur bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-274537|), which contain |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| as their primary antenna bacteriochlorophyl are the dicyclic |FRAME: CPD-20626| and |FRAME: CPD-20624| (see |FRAME: PWY-7941|), as well as small quantities of |FRAME: CPD-20627| and |FRAME: CPD-20629| (see |FRAME: PWY-7940|) |CITS: [15115301][18676669]|., About This Pathway, Brown-colored GSB that synthesize |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| as their main antenna bacteriochlorophyll and that generally grow at greater depths in stratified lakes primarily make the dicyclic carotenoids |FRAME: CPD-20624| and/or |FRAME: CPD-20626|, as well as small quantities of |FRAME: CPD-20627| and |FRAME: CPD-20629| |CITS: [15115301]|. |FRAME: CPD-20624 Isorenieratene| is also produced by actinobacteria, but via a different pathway that does not produce |FRAME: CPD-20625| as an intermediate (see |FRAME: PWY-7938|)., Earlier steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20624| are described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-6475| and |FRAME: PWY-7939|. This pathway only describes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-20625| to |FRAME: CPD-20624|, which requires two activities: |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.M8| (CruB), which forms |FRAME: CPD-20626|, and |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.39| (CrtU)., CruB is a paralog of CruA, an enzyme that is more widespread and is found in all GSB as well as in cyanobacteria |CITS: [17606904]|. Despite their similarity, the two enzymes are very different in their activities. CruA acts on |FRAME: CPD1F-114| as a β-monocyclase, while CruB adds a second β ring to compounds that already have one ring. While CruB can act on |FRAME: CPD1F-126| (which contains a β ring at one end), its relevant activity in this pathway is with |FRAME: CPD-20625|, in which the ring has been modified into an aromatic φ ring |CITS: [18676669]|., The second activity in this pathway is the conversion of the β ring that was added by CruB into a second aromatic φ ring. This activity believed to be catalyzed by CrtU. However, as of 2017 no CrtU enzyme has been characterized from an |FRAME: CPD-20624|-producing GSB.

In addtion to their major role as precursors of DNA and RNA synthesis, nucleotides play various additional roles, such as signal transmitters, molecular switches, coenzymes and carriers of energy. for example, the pyrimidine ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are utilized to form active intermediates in the biosynthesis of phospholipids and polysaccharides, respectively., Nucleotides are susceptible to various chemical modifications caused by endogenous reactive molecules such as reactive oxygen species, chemicals and ionizing irradiation. The incoporation of modified deoxynucleotides into DNA is hazardous and often leads to cell death., Nucleoside triphosphate diphosphatases (NTPases) are enzymes that hydrolyze the α-β phosphodiester bond of nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs). The hydrolysis of this bond, often followed by hydrolysis of the released diphosphate, is a highly exergonic reaction that is often used in cell metabolism to ensure irreversibility of a particular reaction or a pathway. The action of NTPases is often used for the removal of non-canonical nucleotide triphosphates to prevent their incorporation into DNA or RNA or the degradation of a damaged nucleotide |CITS: [15740738]|., This collection of reactions includes three cases that are dedicated to the hydrolysis of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates., The deoxynucleotide |FRAME: DUTP| is not a building block of DNA, and its incorporation in DNA is hazardous. The enzyme |FRAME: DUTP-PYROP-CPLX "dUTP diphosphatase"| (dUTPase) catalyzes the hydrolysis of dUTP to dUMP and diphosphate, acting to ensure chromosomal integrity by reducing the effective ratio of dUTP/dTTP |CITS: [8646528]|., The enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8631 "dCTP diphosphatase"| has the highest activity with modified dCTP molecules such as |FRAME: CPD0-1344| and |FRAME: CPD-1094| |CITS: [19220460]|. It has been suggested that despite its activity with dCTP, its in vivo substrates are modified analogs, and its role is the prevention of the incorporation of these analongs into DNA |CITS: [19220460]|., The enzyme |FRAME: G6954-MONOMER|, encoded in |FRAME: TAX-83333| by the |FRAME: G6954| gene, shows high specificity for hydrolysis of oxidized pyrimidine (deoxy)nucleoside triphosphates and is therefore expected to function in DNA damage avoidance |CITS: [11053429][11676470]|. Its preferred substrate appears to be |FRAME: 5-HYDROXY-CTP| |CITS: [12509230]|. A nudG deletion strain exhibits a 2-3-fold elevated rate of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|-induced mutations |CITS: [14750949]|.

Summary: General Background, The clinically used antibiotic |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| is an aminoglycoside antibiotic that inhibits translation (|CITS: [4875806]| and discussed in |CITS: [11863397]|). It binds to the sugar-phosphate backbone of the bacterial 16S rRNA of the 30S ribosomal subunit in four different regions, thereby affecting initial selection and proofreading steps of translation (reviewed in |CITS: [19362651]|). |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| and some other aminoglycoside antibiotics are derived in part from specific modifications of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| in their respective biosynthetic pathways (reviewed in |CITS: [19362651] [17390001]|). Other species of |FRAME: TAX-1883| produce structurally related aminoglycoside antibiotics such as 5'-hydroxystreptomycin (|FRAME: TAX-1907|) and bluensomycin (|FRAME: TAX-1912|) (reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|). However, biochemical details of aminoglycoside biosynthetic pathways are still lacking and the pathways remain incompletely analyzed (reviewed in |CITS: [19362651]|). The genes encoding the biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| have been studied in Actinomycetes for over two decades, but many of their encoded functions remain only computationally predicted (in |CITS: [1377151]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|). Earlier genetic and biochemical work in the field elucidated many of the enzymatic reactions involved in |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| biosynthesis (in |CITS: [1698764]|. , About This Pathway, The complete biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| remains to be experimentally characterized. A pathway has been postulated based on both experimentally determined and computationally predicted gene functions in the |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN|-producing |FRAME: TAX-1911| and the 5'-hydroxystreptomycin-producing |FRAME: TAX-1907| (reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|). Experimentally supported portions of the |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1911| are shown here, as indicated., The pathway ultimately originates from |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, a compound of primary metabolism (as shown here and in the |FRAME: PWY-2301| pathway link) |CITS: [6049494]|. Three branches lead to the biosynthesis of the three activated intermediates |FRAME: STREPTIDINE-6-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME: DTDP-L-DIHYDROSTREPTOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-10137|, that form the monomeric functional units of |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN|., In one branch, oxidation and transamination of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| produces |FRAME: CPD-1105|. Phosphorylation and amidination produce |FRAME: CPD-7167|. Additional uncharacterized, or incompletely characterized phosphatase, dehydrogenase, transaminase, phosphotransferase and amidination steps (via the products of genes stsB, stsA and |FRAME: G-10702| or strB2) produce the |FRAME: STREPTIDINE-6-PHOSPHATE| moiety (reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|)., Another branch, beginning with the |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY| pathway link, indicates the biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|. Genes strD strE strM and strL for the production of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1911| and |FRAME: TAX-1907|. Their products have activities similar to the products of |FRAME:TAX-562| genes |FRAME: EG11978|, |FRAME: EG12412|, |FRAME: EG11979| and |FRAME: EG12411|, respectively (reviewed in |CITS: [19362651]|). In |FRAME: TAX-1907| they appear to be involved in |FRAME: DTDP-L-DIHYDROSTREPTOSE| biosynthesis (in |CITS: [17390001]| and in |CITS: [9990325]|)., However, the conversion of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| to |FRAME: DTDP-L-DIHYDROSTREPTOSE| has not yet been characterized although putative orfs within the gene cluster are candidates for a dTDP-dihydrostreptose synthase (in |CITS: [17390001]| and in |CITS: [9990325]|). Earlier work (|CITS: [109125] [238519]|) demonstrated a |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent dTDP-dihydrostreptose synthase activity in |FRAME: TAX-1911|. Their proposed sequence of reactions involved EC 4.2.1.46 and EC 5.1.3.13 as in pathway |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY| and a NADPH-dependent dTDP-dihydrostreptose synthase activity converting |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: DTDP-L-DIHYDROSTREPTOSE| |CITS: [109125]|. This is in contrast to the reduction of |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|, in pathway |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|. Later work described in |CITS: [19362651]| found no evidence for a dTDP-L-dihydrostreptose synthase with properties similar to a dTDP-L-rhamnose synthase in |FRAME: TAX-1911|. Thus, the conversion(s) involved in |FRAME: DTDP-L-DIHYDROSTREPTOSE| biosynthesis from |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| remains uncharacterized, as indicated by the triple arrow in this pathway. , As shown in the third branch, biosynthesis of the third, |FRAME: CPD-10137| moiety is poorly characterized and multiple reactions follow |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE| to produce |FRAME: CPD-10137|. However, many orfs within the |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| biosynthetic cluster have predicted functions that could effect these conversions and candidate genes have been proposed (reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|). The product of gene strN was suggested to be a phosphoglucomutase, EC 5.4.2.2. However gene strQ encoding an alpha-D-glucose-1-phosphate cytidylyltransferase (CDP-D-glucose synthase) in S. glaucescens has not yet been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1911|, leaving the possibility that a different nucleoside diphosphate could be used by this organism (|CITS: [9990325]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|)., Two condensation reactions produce |FRAME: DIHYDROSTREPTOMYCIN-6-PHOSPHATE| and a dehydrogenation reaction produces |FRAME: CPD-529|. The antibiotic |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| is produced by the product of gene strK, an extracellular phosphatase. Intracellular |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| is toxic to the organism and can be inactivated by phosphorylation via the product of gene strA as shown in this pathway (|FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN-6-KINASE-RXN|) and discussed below (reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|., The pathway is regulated by |FRAME: CPD-10135| (A-factor). This compound acts as a microbial hormone that creates a regulatory cascade leading to expression of StrR, a regulatory transcription factor that upregulates the |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| biosynthetic genes |CITS: [16077104]|. Expression of the kinase product of gene strA is also induced, which phosphorylates any intracellular |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN|, providing |FRAME: TAX-1911| with self-resistance to the antibiotic (see above). An extracellular phosphatase, the product of gene strK, dephosphorylates |FRAME: STREPTIDINE-6-PHOSPHATE| to biologically active |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN|. A cell wall channel with a binding site for |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| has been identified |CITS: [11532134]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17390001]|.

|FRAME: ECTOINE Ectoine| is a natural compound found in high concentrations in some halophilic microorganisms. It is a compatible solute, helping the organisms survive extreme osmotic stress by acting as an osmolyte. Along with |FRAME: BETAINE|, it is one of the two predominant compatible solutes in halophilic bacteria |CITS: [16176595]|., Ectoine was discovered in the halophilic γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1052| (at the time identified only as a species of |FRAME: TAX-1051|, hence the name ectoine) |CITS: [3838936]|, but is now known to be synthesized by a wide range of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. |FRAME: ECTOINE Ectoine| has commercial uses as an enzyme stabilizer and as a cell protectant in skin and health care applications, and is produced in an industrial process using the halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2746| as a producer strain., Ectoine is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, the central intermediate in the synthesis of amino acids belonging to the aspartate family. The process involves three enzymatic steps. First, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| is transaminated to |FRAME: CPD-470| using glutamate as amino group donor by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.76|. Next, an acetyl group is added by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.178|, resulting in |FRAME: N-ACETYL-L-24-DIAMINOBUTANOATE|. Finally, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.108|, catalyzes the hydrolytic cyclization of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-L-24-DIAMINOBUTANOATE|, leading to the formation of |FRAME: ECTOINE| |CITS: [Peters90][9924816]|.

Summary: The Entner-Doudoroff pathway provides cells with an alternative to glycolysis for fermenting sugars. Using this pathway, the cells can maximize the production of reducing power at the expense of ATP production |CITS: [12981024]|., The |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway"| converts |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| to |FRAME: CPD-2961| in two steps. Instead of proceeding to the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative branch"| of that pathway, which forms several metabolite precursors, the Entner-Duodoroff pathway provides a shunt that returns |FRAME: CPD-2961| to glycolysis via the intermediate |FRAME: GAP|. , This pathway is important to |FRAME:TAX-562| because it enables the organism to metabolize sugar acids, which are significant nutrients in both of its habitats, intestinal and aquatic. Strains that are mutationally blocked in this pathway are unable to grow on gluconate, glucuronate, or galacturonate and are also unable to colonize the mouse intestine |CITS: [8751891]|. The uronic acids feed into the pathway's intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, so the dependence of their metabolism on an intact Entner-Doudoroff pathway is clear |CITS: [9657988]|. The dependence of gluconate's metabolism on an intact Entner-Doudoroff pathway is less obvious because it is also metabolized via the pentose phosphate pathway., Enzymes of the Entner-Doudoroff pathway are induced by growth on gluconate, glucuronate, or methyl-β-D-glucuronide; phosphate or carbon limitation |CITS: [15659677]|.
