Summary: The homeostasis of glycerophospholipids constitutes an indispensable element for buildup, maintenance and component dynamics of cell membranes in all organisms. The many different phospholipid molecular species found in yeast basically vary in their composition of fatty acids esterified to the sn-1 and sn-2 position of a phosphorylated |FRAME:GLYCEROL| and a head group which can either be a |FRAME:CHOLINE|, |FRAME:ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME:MYO-INOSITOL| or the one phospholipid without a head group, i.e. phosphatidate (for example |FRAME:CPD-8291|) |CITS:[14321173] [22345606]|. After the de novo synthesis of phospholipids in the Kennedy pathway (see |FRAME:TRIGLSYN-PWY|, |FRAME:PWY3O-450|) glycerophospholipids can be degraded (see |FRAME:LIPAS-PWY|) and remodeled (this pathway; see also |FRAME:PWY-7409| and |FRAME:PWY-7417|). The latter has been proposed by William E.M. Lands |CITS:[14413818]| who describes in the eponymous 'Lands cycle' a de-acylation-re-acylation process of phospholipids typically characterized by saturated acyl chains at the sn-1 and unsaturated acyl chains at the sn-2 position |CITS:[7871882]|., This remodeling process starts with the de-acylation at the sn-2 position of phospholipids catalyzed by phospholipases (e.g. phospholipase A2) generating the corresponding lyso-phospholipids. The resulting lyso-phospholipids represent the substrates for acyl-CoA dependent lyso-phospholipid acyltransferases or phospholipid transacylases which can re-acylate the sn-2 position. Generally, the Lands cycle constitutes an exchange of fatty acids at the sn-2 position which is an substantial factor in the maintenance of the homeostasis of phospholipids |CITS:[17010666]|. This de- and re-acylation process translates into many physiological functions, for example increasing membrane fluidity through a higher percentage of unsaturated acyl chains, re-esterification of exogenous lyso-phospholipids |CITS:[17726007]|, buffering excess toxic fatty acids |CITS:[22090344] [19608739]| and maintenance of the intrinsic membrane curvature necessary to preserve membrane integrity |CITS:[16339082] [31173]|., Phosphatidate (PA) is a central metabolite for the biosynthesis of major phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphatidylinositol (PI) because they are synthesized through the metabolization of PA via the CDP-diacylglycerol pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5667|) |CITS:[20332534]|. It is not unexpected therefore that many of the lyso-phospholipid acyltransferases accept lyso-phosphatidate, e.g. |FRAME:L-1-LYSOPHOSPHATIDATE| as substrate and re-esterify it to the corresponding phosphatidate molecular species, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-8268| with varying efficiency. Besides the triacylglycerol lipases TGL4p |CITS:[16135509] [16267052] [20332534]| and TGL5p |CITS:[16135509] [20016004]| which also demonstrated oleoyl-CoA:lysophosphatidate acyltransferase (LPAT) activity the major LPATs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae are SLC1p |CITS:[8408076] [1767529]| and LOA1p |CITS:[22090344]| which have both a dual location at the endoplasmatic reticulum and lipid droplets in the yeast cell. The reverse reaction, i.e. deacylation of phosphatidate by a phospholipase A2 activity as shown for TGL4p is possible but remains to be shown.

General Background, Betaxanthins represent a subclass of betalains, the nitrogen-containing , compounds that replace the anthocyanins in the order of Caryophyllales and some higher fungi |CITS: [12620337]| , |CITS: [16212790]|. These pigments are biosynthesized by the condensation of betalamic acid (|FRAME:PWY-5394|) , and amino acids/amines forming a Schiff-base that causes the yellow to orange colors (λ max 470-486 nm) , |CITS: [Christinet04]|., About This Pathway, The first enzymatic step in the pathway is the decarboxylation of the , aromatic amino acid DOPA to form the corresponding amine, dopamine. An enzyme,, |FRAME: MONOMER-8382| (TYDC), capable of, catalyzing this reaction has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3469|, |CITS: [7929401]| |CITS: [12242361]| and its molecular , function has been confirmed by heterologous expression in |FRAME:TAX-562|. But, no comparable enzyme, has been characterized within the |FRAME:TAX-3568| to date., The second step of the pathway represents another example of the spontaneous condensation of , an amine (compare |FRAME:PWY-5426|), i.e. dopamine with betalamic acid forming miraxanthin V that has , been described in the literature |CITS: [12620337]| |CITS: [11261575]| |CITS: [15231409]|.

General Background, Four types of aromatic compounds degradation pathways are thought to occur in different types of bacteria: , Aerobic organisms take advantage of the availability of molecular oxygen, and use oxygenases that introduce hydroxyl groups, and cleave the aromatic ring. These pathways usually lead to a few central intermediates such as |FRAME: CATECHOL|,, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-633| (see |FRAME: PWY-6079|)., Facultative aerobes utilize two types of pathways, depending on the availability of oxygen., When oxygen is present, these organisms use the so-called "hybrid" type of aerobic metabolism for some aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: BENZOATE|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE|., These pathways use |FRAME: CO-A| to activate and form thioesters of the substrates, followed by an oxygenase/reductase step to dearomatize (but not cleave) the ring. Cleavage of the dearomatized ring does not require oxygen (see |FRAME: PWY-6077|)., Under anaerobic conditions, facultative aerobes and phototrophs use a reductive aromatic metabolism., The aromatic compounds are activated by |FRAME: CO-A| to an active intermediate that can be transformed to important, central intermediate such as |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|. Reduction of the aromatic ring of |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-883| and is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 ATP molecules (see, |FRAME: 2AMINOBENZDEG-PWY|)., Strict anaerobes utilize a completely different and not well characterized benzoyl-coenzyme A reductase that does not utilize ATP |CITS: [18378589]|., About This Pathway, Under anaerobic conditions, aromatic compounds have to be dearomatized by means other than oxygenases., A common mechanism involves their activation by |FRAME: CO-A| to an activated intermediate that can be, transformed to the important central intermediate, |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|., Transformation of |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| is accomplished in two steps,, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14350| and by |FRAME: AMBENCOATHAUERA-MONOMER|., Cells of |FRAME: TAX-59406| grown anaerobically with |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| had three different CoA ligases, for aromatic compounds, which were named E1, E2 and E3 |CITS: [1885526]|. The first one is |FRAME: CPLX-924|,, an enzyme that prefers |FRAME: BENZOATE| as a substrate, although it is active with |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE|., The two other enzymes preferred the later substrate. However, only one of them, |FRAME: MONOMER-14350|, is, highly expressed. The third enzyme (|FRAME: MONOMER-931|) appears to be active mostly under aerobic, conditions, but apparently is not completely repressed under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [1885526]|., For similar pathways leading to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, see |FRAME: PHENOLDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-81|., The product |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| enters the central anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway (see, |FRAME: CENTBENZCOA-PWY|) |CITS: [9683649][1592816]|.

General Background, Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|. Bioluminescence is particularly predominant in the marine environment, in members of planktonic bacteria and protozoa, many invertebrates, and vertebrates with specialized light producing organs that harbor symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-7723|). The requirement for oxygen suggests that bioluminescence evolved after oxygen levels began to rise through the activities of early oxygenic phototrophic cyanobacteria., Many coelenterates and ctenophores, such as the sea pansy |FRAME: TAX-6134|, the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6099|, the hydroid |FRAME: TAX-32569|, and the ctenophore |FRAME: TAX-27922|, are bioluminescent. The luciferin in these organisms is |FRAME: Coelenterazines coelenterazine|, an imidazopyrazinone derivative that is also found in distantly related types of luminous organisms such as squids, shrimps, fishes, and some chaetognaths |CITS: [Shimomura80][Campbell90][20972255]|, as well as in many nonluminous organisms |CITS: [9336010]|. The biosynthetic origin of coelenterazine is not known. However, it has been shown that the hydromedusa |FRAME: TAX-6100| is not able to synthesize it, and is dependent on a dietary supply of this luciferin for bioluminescence |CITS: [11572972]|. The only report of de novo biosynthesis of coelenterazine is from the bioluminescent shrimp |FRAME: TAX-576189| |CITS: [Thomson95]|., Even though many different types of organisms use |FRAME: RENILLA-LUCIFERIN coelenterazine| as the luciferin, the enzymes employed are not the same. For example, the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100| uses the Ca2+-regulated photoprotein aequorin (as shown here), while the sea pansy |FRAME: TAX-6134| uses a luciferase (see |FRAME: PWY-7914|)., About This Pathway, Unlike the parallel system in cnidaria, it could be shown that the jellyfish bioluminescence system does not involve dedicated coelenterazine-binding protein and a luciferase. The key enzyme in the jellyfish system is the single protein |FRAME: Aequorins aequorin|, also known as Ca2+-regulated photoprotein. The enzyme was first purified in 1962 from |FRAME: TAX-2747904|. The purification involved the painstaking collection and processing of more than 10,000 jellyfish, and resulted in 5 mg of purified protein |CITS: [Shimomura62][13911999][7654844]|., One of the peculiarities of this system was the fact that it appeared to generate light without the need for oxygen. This phenomenon was reported as early as 1810 |CITS: [Macartney10]| and was reproducible |CITS: [Harvey26]|. It was suggested that the oxygen may be stably bound within the photogenic granules, a theory that was later verified |CITS: [Harvey38]|., The name aequorin refers not to the gene product, which is named aopaequorin, but rather to the non-covalent complex formed by apoaequorin and a |FRAME: CPD-20222 hydroperoxide of coelenterazine"|. This complex is formed by binding of the coelenterazine chromophore, followed by its peroxidation with molecular oxygen. In the absence of calcium ions, this complex is stable, explaining why oxygen is not needed for the downstream light-emitting step. When calcium ions become available, they bind to three calcium-binding sites, triggering the aequorin luminescence reaction. During the reaction, a change in the conformation of aequorin takes place, leading to cyclization of the peroxide into a dioxetanone structure, which collapses, releasing a CO2 molecule. The spontaneous breakdown of the dioxetanone releases the energy (about 60 kcal/mole) that is necessary to generate an |FRAME: CPD-20235 "excited state of coelentramide|. In vitro this decarboxylation is accompanied by the emission of blue light, while in vivo the energy is transferred to excite |FRAME: GFP "a green fluorescent protein"| by Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) |CITS: [4151620]|., During the luminescence reaction aequorin is converted into a |FRAME: Excited-blue-fluorescent-proteins "blue fluorescent protein"| (BFP), a dissociable complex of Ca2+-bound apoaequorin and coelenteramide. It has been shown that BFP has the activity of luciferase and can catalyze the oxidation of coelenterazine to coelenteramide on its own |CITS: [15527769][16545379][19549504]|. Upon dissociation of BFP, apoaequorin is restored, and can be reconstituted into active aequorin in the presence of coelenterazine and oxygen., Both of the jellyfish proteins that participate in this pathway, aequorin and GFP, have become important tools for molecular biology. Aequorin provides a highly sensitive and rapid assay for intracellular calcium, while GFP is a uniquely valuable reporter of gene expression. The scientists Roger Y. Tsien, Osamu Shimomura, and Martin Chalfie were awarded the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery and development of GFP.

Summary: Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which form insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms. As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., Amino acid conjugates of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| make up a major class of siderophores, including |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN|, |FRAME: CPD-9984| and |FRAME: CPD-9983|. In fact, the latter was the first siderophore to be chemically identified |CITS: [Ito58]|. |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| is synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE| and |FRAME: DIHYDRO-DIOH-BENZOATE|.

Names: L-tyrosine degradation V (reductive Stickland reaction) // L-tyrosine fermentation // L-tyrosine reductive fermentation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additinal reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, It has been well documented that aromatic amino acids can serve as electron acceptors in the reductive branch of the Stickland reaction. The final products of the fermentation of |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR|, and |FRAME: TRP|, which are |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE|, |FRAME: PHLORETATE|, and |FRAME: INDOLE-PROPIONATE|, respectively, have been observed to accumulate in cultures fed with the respective amino acid |CITS: [16746719] [Boezi59][1275638][Li14][29168502]|. The best studied aromatic amino acid fermentation pathway is the |FRAME: PWY-8014 "one for L-phenylalanine"|, but it is now known that all three aromatic amino acids are fermented by the same enzymes in parallel pathways |CITS: [Li14][29168502]|., A study from 1976 found that cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1509| and |FRAME: TAX-1491| that were fed with |FRAME: TYR| accumulated |FRAME: PHLORETATE| as the final fermentation product |CITS: [1275638]|. The pathway was shown to involve transamination of the aromatic amino acid to a 2-oxoacid, reduction to a 2R-hydroxyacid, dehydration to an enoate, and finally reduction of the double bond to form the 3-propanoate derivative |CITS: [7353645][7084457]|., The dehydration step is the most energetically-demanding step in the pathway, owing to the poor acidity of the β-hydrogen. The reaction requires activation of the substrate by coenzyme A, followed by a dehydration reaction that involves the formation of a highly reactive ketyl radical that helps to acidify the β-hydrogen |CITS: [18337824]|., The reduction of the 2-oxoacid and the enoate intermediates are catalyzed by dehydrogenases whose combined action consume the reducing equivalents produced by the amino acid oxidation branch of the Stickland reaction |CITS: [6354130]|. The enoate reductase has been assumed to be encoded by the fldZ gene, but in 2017 it has been shown that the reductase is an ETF-dependent dehydrogenase, the product of the |FRAME: G-58752| gene |CITS: [29168502]|.

Summary: General Background, Chlorobenzoates are a group of compounds that occur in the environment in large amounts either because of their release, as herbicides or as products of bacterial degradation of polychlorinated biphenyls |CITS: [7217013]|., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation seems to have evolved recently as a result, of their widespread release to the environment., About This Pathway, The first bacterium that was isolated based on its ability to grow with |FRAME: CPD-3486| as the sole carbon source, was |FRAME:TAX-65741 "Pseudomonas knackmussii (then called Pseudomonas sp. strain B13)"| |CITS: [4852581]|., That study showed that |FRAME: CPD-3486| was attacked by a dioxygenase forming two isomers,, |FRAME: CPD-10618| and |FRAME: CPD-10619|, which were reduced by a dehydrogenase to |FRAME: CPD-9151|, and |FRAME: CPD-9152|, respectively |CITS:[4852581][3025183]|., The chlorinated catechols were degraded in a modified ortho cleavage pathways via |FRAME: CPD-294| to, |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which was degraded further to TCA cycle intermediates., Organisms that are capable of converting benzoate to catechol (see |FRAME: PWY-2503|) are often able to convert, chlorobenzoates to chlorocatechols due to the promiscuity of the enzymes |CITS: [4836257]|. However, the enzymes that, continue the degradation of the catechols have little activity with chloro-substituted compounds, and the chlorocatechols that, accumulate as a result are toxic to the bacteria. Thus, in order to be able to degrade chlorobenzoates efficiently, the, bacteria must possess specific enzymes for the degradation of chlorocatechols., Later work found that most of the genes encoding chloroaromatic-specific enzymes were present on plasmids., However, at least in some organisms, including |FRAME:TAX-65741| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, the genes encoding, the enzymes responsible for converting chlorobenzoate to chlorocatechols are the same ones involved in, benzoate degradation, and are chromosomaly encoded. |FRAME: ORG-6075|, which is, a strain of |FRAME: TAX-264198| that has been cured of the pJP4 plasmid, was still able to, convert |FRAME: CPD-3486| to chlorocatechols |CITS: [2981813][3025183]|.

Summary: Phenols and methyl-substituted phenols can be used by a number of different bacterial and fungal strains, including |FRAME: TAX-79676|, which grows efficiently with phenol, cresols, or |FRAME: CPD-10888| as, the sole carbon and energy source., The most common first step in the aerobic degradation of phenols is hydroxylation to a catechol., In |FRAME: TAX-79676| this reaction is catalyzed by a multicomponent |FRAME: CPLX-7253|, encoded by six, different gene that are located on pVI150, an IncP-2 megaplasmid |CITS: [1732207][7765834]|. , These genes are clustered along with 9 other genes that are involved in the catabolism of the catechol to TCA, cycle intermediates via a meta-cleavage pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5420|)., Similar operons were found not only on plasmids but also in the chromosomes of some phenol-degrading bacteria, such as |FRAME: ORG-5955| |CITS: [7828892]| and |FRAME: TAX-471| |CITS: [12732969]|, as well as fungi such as, |FRAME: TAX-5554| |CITS: [17425111]|.

General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , In order to avoid self-intoxication cyanogenic glucosides are stored in the vacuole. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks they come in contact with activating enzymes (specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases) that reside in the cytoplasm or apoplastic space of the cells, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN| that serves as the first line of chemical defense |CITS:[16667728][Ganjewala10]|., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, The formation of the cyanogenic glucoside |FRAME:CPD-14593| is catalyzed by a glucosyltransferase that also catalyzes the glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-14590| to yield |FRAME:CPD-1103|. Although the occurrence of the |FRAME:CPD-14593| precursor, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14592|, has not been verified yet, its efficient incorporation into |FRAME:CPD-14589| in |FRAME:TAX-55501| and |FRAME: TAX-619227| plants has been demonstrated |CITS:[Jaroszewski81][Dewick 84]|. |FRAME:CPD-14592| was also the only other substrate accepted by the |FRAME:CPD-1103|-specific glucosyltransferase characterized from |FRAME:TAX-55501| |CITS: [6230992]||.

General Background, Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|. The requirement for oxygen suggests that bioluminescence evolved after oxygen levels began to rise through the activities of early oxygenic phototrophic cyanobacteria., The fireflies (|FRAME: TAX-7049|) are a large family of bioluminescent beetles that contain over 100 genera and 2,000 species |CITS: [McDermott64]|. Of these 100 genera, only a few species have been studied, mostly members of the North American |FRAME: TAX-7053| and |FRAME: TAX-41715| genera and the Asian |FRAME: TAX-39202| and |FRAME: TAX-7050| genera., Bioluminescence in fireflies is generated by a chemical reaction that occurs in organs called lanterns that contain specialized cells known as photocytes. The lanterns are situated in the sixth and seventh ventral segments, and are lined with a rows of cells filled with uric acid crystals that reflect the light produced by the photocytes |CITS: [11746215][22242133]|. The reaction, which is catalyzed by a luciferase enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.13.12.7|) in the presence of molecular oxygen, ATP, and Mg2+ |CITS: [775940][8805542]|, consists of three steps; |FRAME: PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN| reacts with ATP at the luciferase active site and is converted into |FRAME: CPD-20210|. The adenylate is then oxygenated, forming an excited state |FRAME: OXIDIZED-PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN|. Finally, the excited state oxyluciferin returns to its ground state by the emission of a visible photon |CITS: [272645][18264582][19722653][23244350]|. The luciferase has been shown to be localized in the peroxisomes of the photocytes |CITS: [3554235][3480287]|., The first studies of bioluminescence in fireflies were carried out in 1885 by Raphael Dubois, who coined the terms "luciferin" and "luciferase". Dubois documented the requirement for oxygen; the requirement for ATP was observed much later |CITS: [16588763]|. The luciferase enzyme was purified and crystallized as early as 1956 |CITS: [13315363]|, and the structure of the firefly luciferin was obtained soon after, using 15,000 fireflies to produce 9 mg of the compound |CITS: [13479120][White61][White63]|. At that time it was discovered that light is only produced with one of the two enantiomers of firefly luciferin, |FRAME: PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN| |CITS: [13749882]|., A second activity of the firefly luciferase is that of acyl-CoA ligase. It was initially observed that the enzyme acts as a CoA-ligase on |FRAME: CPD-20212|, a byproduct of the bioluminescence process |CITS: [5339507][13535634]|. Much later it has been discovered that the enzyme catalyzes different activities depending whether it acts on the D- or L-enantiomer of its substrate. In both cases the enzyme catalyzes the initial adenylation. However, in the case of |FRAME: CPD-20206|, the enzyme proceeds to form |FRAME: CPD-20207|, while in the case of |FRAME: PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN| the enzyme proceeds to catalyze a monooxygenase reaction, resulting in bioluminescence |CITS: [15850783]|. The former reaction is believed to play an important role in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN|, which is described below., About This Pathway, It should be noted that the biosynthesis of the firefly luciferin is still not firmly established. This pathway shows the currently accepted model, although not all steps have been confirmed., Early studies of the biosynthesis of the firefly luciferin concluded that the precursors were |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| and two |FRAME: CYS| molecules |CITS: [McCapra75][Okada76][McCapra76]|. These finding were confirmed recently in a study that also suggested that |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| is formed from |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| |CITS: [24391868][27098929]|. Because |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| is toxic to living organisms, its concentration in the beetles is 10-fold lower than that of |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE|, yet its incorporation efficiency into firefly luciferin was higher, suggesting that it may be the preferred substrate. As free |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE| is not detected in beetles, it is likely stored as the non-toxic glucoside |FRAME: HYDROQUINONE-O-BETA-D-GLUCOPYRANOSIDE| and released by the digestive enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.21| |CITS: [24391868]|., The condensation of |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| with two |FRAME: CYS| molecules, either spontaneously or catalyzed by unknown enzymes, results in production of |FRAME: CPD-20206|, which is not a substrate for bioluminescence. Many theories have been proposed regarding its conversion into the D-enantiomer. The most plausible ones involve its well-documented activation to |FRAME: CPD-20207|, which is catalyzed by the luciferase, followed by epimerization by an unknown enzyme and hydrolysis to form |FRAME: CPD-20206| |CITS: [15850783][16979628]|., The last part of the pathway regards the recycling of the luciferase's product, |FRAME: OXIDIZED-PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN|, back to the substrate |FRAME: PHOTINUS-LUCIFERIN|. Oxyluciferin has been reported to be recycled into |FRAME: CPD-20205| by a dedicated enzyme that was named luciferin regenerating enzyme (LRE) |CITS: [11457857][12234677][Emamzadeh10][25665080]|. This compound combines with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: CPD-20206|, which is converted to the D-form via the CoA derivatives as described above. The formation of |FRAME: CPD-20206| from |FRAME: CPD-20205| and |FRAME: CYS| can occur spontaneously |CITS: [Okada74][14981641]|, and it is still not known whether this process is catalyzed by an enzyme.

Summary: Once the ribonucleoside |FRAME: GDP| is formed (see |FRAME: PWY-7221|), it can be reduced to the deoxy form |FRAME: DGDP| by the enzyme ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase., This enzyme can only accept ribonucleoside diphosphates, and are inacative with the mono- or triphosphate forms., dGDP is phosphorylated to the DNA precursor |FRAME: DGTP| by the broad-substrate range |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX|., This pathway is universal, and is found in archaea, bacteria, plants, fungi and animals.

Anthocyanins are a group of vacuolar pigments which contribute in plants to color and color pattern in flowers which are not only an attractant for pollinators but also an important traits in ornamental plants |CITS:[Heller94]|. The unstable aglycone anthocyanins are stabilized by 3-O-glucosylation, forming anthocyanidin 3-O-β-D-glucosides which are prerequisite for further decoration of the anthocyanidin skeleton via glycosylation, acylation and methylation. Such modifications significantly determine stability, bioavailability and various pharmacological activities of the particular anthocyanidins (summarized in |CITS:[24792223]|).The latter comprise the potential of anthocyanins to promote health issues such as prevention of obesity, strengthening the cardiovascular system and exhibiting anti-inflammatory and anti-cancer effects |CITS:[17015246]|. , Anthocyanidins may occur as sambubioside, i.e. diglucosides which contain a xylose attached to the 2''-O-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of anthocyanidins. Such anthocyanidin sambubiosides and acylated derivatives thereof have been found in a number of plants from different families such as Rosaceae (Rubus occidentalis) |CITS:[Dossett11]| , Brassicaceae (Lobularia maritima - |CITS:[Tatsuzawa10]|; Matthiola incana - |CITS:[Seyffert60] [8722092] [7766384]|; Lunaria annua, Cheiranthus cheiri - |CITS:[16777160]|; Raphanus sativus - |CITS:[11985855]|), Adoxaceae (Sambucus canadensis) |CITS:[1367876] [7766167]| and Theaceae (Camellia reticulata) |CITS:[18037731]|. In addition to that, anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubiosides have been found in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[21899608]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7450|) which are part of an bigger pathway towards the main anthocyanidin found in this plant, i.e. Arabidopsis anthocyanidin 11 |CITS:[11830144]|., The two reaction steps towards anthocyandin 3-O-sambubioside 5-O-glucoside have been investigated in detail in petals of various genetic lines of Matthiola incana. It could be shown that the formation of the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides is a prerequisite for the xylolysation taking place at the 2''-O-position of the glucose attached to the 3-position at the C-ring of the anthocyanidin skeleton. The latter reaction is catalyzed by an anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside 2''-O-xylosyltransferase which is very specific for |FRAME:UDP-D-XYLOSE| as sugar donor and 3-O-glucosylated and acylated anthocyanidins as substrates |CITS:[Teusch86a]|. Moreover, the enzymes activity coincides with the accumulation pattern of the formed anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubiosides at the developmental stage 4 of the petals (petals unrolled but not yet unfolded - |CITS:[Dangelmeyr83]|). , The second pathway reaction is the 5-O-glucosylation at the A-ring of the anthocyanidin sambubioside molecule catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubioside 5-O-glucosyltransferase with a high preference for |FRAME:CPD-12575| as sugar donor and anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubioside and acylated derivatives thereof as substrates |CITS:[Teusch86]|. The finding that acylated anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides are even better substrates for the anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubioside 5-O-glucosyltransferase than anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubioside may indicate that acylation precedes 5-O-glucosylation |CITS:[Teusch86] [Teusch87]| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7679|). Both enzymes can operate on pelargonidin-, cyanidin-, and delphinidin 3-O-glucosides and 3--O-sambubiosides, respectively, however only pelargonidin- and cyanidin sambubiosides have been found in Matthiola incana |CITS: [Seyffert60]|.

General background, In contrast to mammals where peroxisomal and mitochondrial pathways of oxidative fatty acid degradation exist the fatty acid β-oxidation in |FRAME:TAX-4932| is exclusively carried out in peroxisomes. Fatty acid β-oxidation is a crucial component in a process that supplies energy to the cell for maintenance and growth and as such has been thoroughly investigated for a long time |CITS:[8685242]|., |FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (this pathway). The β-oxidation of fatty acids is a straightforward process which requires the participation of three enzymes, i.e. acyl-CoA oxidase (POX1), the multifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase (FOX2) and the thiolase (POT1). At the end of the process stands a saturated fatty acid shortened by 2 carbon units (|FRAME:ACETYL-COA|) which is further metabolized in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-5690|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291|, |FRAME:PWY-7292| and |FRAME:PWY-7307|). , Besides the location and certain biochemical differences β-oxidation of fatty acids in |FRAME:TAX-4932| is distinguished by the stereo-specificity of their multifunctional enzyme/protein (MFE/P) from other organisms. While yeast exclusively employs the enzyme catalyzing the (3R)-hydroxyacyl-CoA variety, plants have a pronounced S stereo-specificity (see |FRAME:PWY-5136|) and animals can both utilize S- and R-stereo-specific compounds (see |FRAME:PWY66-391|) |CITS:[17028011]|. It has been proposed that the evolutionary development of the 3R-variant of the yeast pathway was the result of the overall function rather than the compound stereo-specificity as the chirality of the intermediates could be changed in yeast by replacing yeast MFE with rat peroxisomal MFE which had no influence on the growth of yeast on |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD| |CITS:[7499202]|., About this pathway, Prior to the process of breaking down saturated fatty acids in the peroxisomal β-oxidation cycle, fatty acids of varying length need to be transported from the cytoplasm across the peroxisomal membrane and activated by acyl-CoA synthetases/ligases. The process of how fatty acids are taken up has been a matter of debate for some time and various models from passive diffusion to vectorial acylation and a combination of both have been proposed (reviewed in |CITS:[12697341]|. Experimental evidence point out a close relationship between fatty acid transporter proteins such as the bifunctional FAT1 (long chain fatty acid transport and very long chain fatty acid activation) |CITS:[12052836] [12601005]|, peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthases/ligases (FAA1-4) |CITS:[8206942] [7962057] [8027063]| and ABC transporter proteins such as PXA1 and 2 |CITS:[8670886]|. A current model proposes that acyl-CoA's are hydrolyzed before transported across the peroxisomal membrane, re-esterified after the entry into the peroxisomes by acyl-CoA synthases (e.g. FAA2 and possibly FAT1) in concord with the PXA1/2 complex which delivers the acyl-group from the cytoplasm to the peroxisomal matrix |CITS:[22493507]|., The first enzymatic conversion of the β-oxidation cycle is catalyzed by the fatty acyl-CoA oxidase (POX1) and regarded as the rate-limiting step of the pathway |CITS:[2189786] [11431484]|. All of the enzymes involved in the peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation are inducible by fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD|) which also causes increased proliferation of the peroxisomal compartment |CITS:[5325972] [3332968]|. This dual event is under the control of the transcription factors PIP2-OAF1 |CITS:[8662598] [8670793]| which have been shown to bind to the upstream activation sequence (UAS1) of the oleate response element (ORE1) responsible for activating POX1 and other fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes |CITS:[8993556]|. The regulation of those enzymes also involves the transcription factor ADR1 which has been shown to act indirectly through influencing the transcription of PIP2-OAF1 |CITS:[11431484]|., The multifunctional protein type 2 (FOX2) catalyzing a hydratase and dehydrogenase reaction was shown to have a pronounced stereo-specificity towards the 3R-isomer of the hydroxyacyl-CoA |CITS:[1551874]|. The enzyme possesses two dehydrogenase domains, one responsible for catalyzing medium- and long-chain fatty acyl-CoA's whereas the second dehydrogenase domain preferred short-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters. Both dehydrogenase activities have been shown necessary for yeast growth when fatty acids were the only source of carbon |CITS:[10497229] [16574148]|., The last step in the pathway is carried out by the 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (POT1) which catalyzes the thiolytic cleavage to yield a C2-shortened acyl-CoA and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| |CITS:[7754706]|. Interestingly, the 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase had also been demonstrated to exhibit antifungal activities, hence the enzyme represents an natural anti-fungicide occurring in yeast peroxisomes |CITS:[19470242]|.

|FRAME: CPD-27993 Metformin|, sold under the brand name Glucophage, among others, is the main first-line medication for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, particularly in people who are overweight. It has been categorized as one of the top pharmaceuticals present in the environment |CITS: [36107956]|. Exposure to the drug or to its direct metabolite |FRAME: CPD-27994| exhibits adverse effects on aquatic life |CITS: [26752244][30594717][ 33332093]|. It has also been shown to bioaccumulate in plants, including many edible plants |CITS: [22712757]|., An enzyme that hydrolyzes |FRAME: CPD-27993| to |FRAME: CPD-27994| and |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE| has been identified from |FRAME: TAX-2979870|, an organism capable of growing on |FRAME: CPD-27993| as a sole source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy. |FRAME: CPD-27994 Guanylurea| is a dead-end product that is excreted to the environment and is degraded further by other organisms, as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8592|. |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE Dimethylamine| is degraded further by |FRAME: TAX-2979870| as described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6965|, supporting its growth |CITS: [36624085]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycosylation is one of the major types of post-translational modification of proteins, and is an essential process in all eukaryotes. Protein glycosylation is known to be involved in cellular targeting and secretion, and helps to regulate enzymatic activity, confer enhanced stability and solubility to secreted proteins, and affect the functionality of proteins in the immune system. In addition, glycoproteins participate in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions., The two major types of protein glycosylation are known as N-linked and O-linked glycosylation. O-linked oligosaccharides are variously attached to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues in the target proteins. Most commonly O-glycosylation begins with the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-3604| to the free hydroxyl group of the amino acid, although O-linkages to fucose, glucose, mannose, xylose and other sugars are known., About This Pathway, Mucin-type O-glycosylation, consisting of glycans attached via O-linked |FRAME: CPD-3604| to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues, is one of the most abundant forms of protein glycosylation in animals., Initiation of glycosylation occurs in the Golgi, after the target proteins have been completely folded. Initiation is followed by the action of numerous very specific glycosyltransferases, resulting in the extension of |FRAME: CPD-3604| into numerous different O-glycan structures |CITS: [17988798][18695988]|. Eight different core structures of |FRAME: Mucin-type-glycans "mucin-type O-glycans"| have been described, many with the same monosaccharide residues in different linkages. The most abundant core structures in humans are |FRAME: Core1 "core 1"| and |FRAME: Core2 "core 2"|. |FRAME: Core1 "Core 1"| glycans are small glycans that are often terminated with |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE "sialic acid"| by |FRAME: EC-2.4.3.4|, whereas |FRAME: Core2 "core 2"| glycans have the potential to be elaborated into larger glycans |CITS: [19919547]|., Protein glycosylation pathways are usually controlled by the genes that encode the enzymes responsible for the initiation of glycosylation. In mucin-type O-glycosylation, there is a great abundance of such genes (up to 20 homologous genes) encoding |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.41| (only a single representative of these genes is shown in this MetaCyc pathway). These genes are differentially expressed over tissue and developmental phase, enabling complex and strict regulation |CITS: [22183981]|. In addition, many have clear specificities for the sites of attachment, thus determining the density and site occupancy of the mucin-type O-glycosylation |CITS: [8922959][12634319]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Megalomicins megalomicins|, which were discovered in 1968 |CITS:[5735370][5810991]|, are a family of related macrolide antibiotics produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47868|. They are therapeutically diverse compounds that possess antiparasitic, antiviral and antibacterial properties |CITS: [8631986][9296385][9434722][9756774], |. Like other macrolide antibiotics, they are more active against Gram-positive bacteria than against Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4390258][4996819]|., The first family member to have its structure reported was |FRAME: CPD-12966| |CITS: [5358619][5358620]|.  Acyl derivatives of |FRAME: CPD-12966|, including |FRAME: CPD-14689|, |FRAME: CPD-12967|, |FRAME: CPD-14691|, and |FRAME: CPD-14690|, were soon discovered |CITS: [4795255]|., The megalomicins have the same aglycone as |FRAME: CPD-13804| and |FRAME: CPD-13951|, but include a unique deoxyamino sugar, |FRAME: CPD-14692|, at the C-6 hydroxyl., A partial sequence of the megalomicin biosynthesis gene cluster, which appeared to contain the complete pathway for megosamine biosynthesis, has been reported in 2000 |CITS: [10972798]|. The putative L-megosamine biosynthetic enzymes were validated by transfer of the complete pathway, along with the glycosyltransferase that attaches L-megosamine to the aglycone, to an |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycin|-producing strain of |FRAME: TAX-1836| and demonstration of the production of megalomicin |CITS: [10972798]|. The sequencing of the cluster was completed in 2005, and many of the genes were used for production of |FRAME: CPD-13951| in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [15870344]|., While the roles of the different enzymes were confirmed, the exact order of transformations required further work, which was performed in 2010 |CITS: [20418422]|. Mass spectrometric identification of the intermediates produced from different sets of genes expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| clarified the order of events and showed that the production of |FRAME: CPD-14683| from |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| requires five enzymes |CITS: [20418422]|.

General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: penams (e.g. penicillins), ceph-3-ems (e.g. cephalosporins, cephamycins), clavams (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), carbapenems (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9377|, thienamycins) and monolactams (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while the remaining three classes of beta-lactams are produced by bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|., Penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins are produced by different organisms from branches of a common pathway. The pathway branches at isopenicillin N to form penicillins and branches again at deacetylcephalosporin to form cephalosporins and cephamycins (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|)., The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem and clavam antibiotics see |FRAME: PWY-5737| and |FRAME: PWY-5679|) differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). The pathway for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially elucidated and the order of some known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., The antibacterial mechanism of action of β-lactam antibiotics involves inhibition of the transpeptidation reaction during bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which leads to cell lysis. This reaction is catalyzed by class A and class B penecillin binding proteins. It is specifically inhibited by penicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics via formation of a covalent complex with the active serine of the transpeptidation domain of penicillin binding proteins. This prevents crosslinking and weakens the peptidoglycan polymer (in |CITS: [12867450]|). See pathways |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5265|. Bacterial resistance to β-lactam antibiotics can involve alterations in penicillin binding proteins, reduced antibiotic permeation across the membrane, or the production of β-lactamase enzymes (in |CITS:[12195735]|). See enzymes |FRAME: EG10040-MONOMER|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13427| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13428|., About This Pathway, Penicillins are medically important antibiotics biosynthesized as end products by certain filamentous fungi, including |FRAME: TAX-5076| and |FRAME: TAX-162425|. Three enzymes catalyze penicillin biosynthesis, encoded by clustered genes acvA (pcbAB), ipnA (pcbC) and aatA (penDE). Penicillin biosynthesis genes are regulated by a complex network that includes pH, carbon source, amino acids and nitrogen. Reviewed in |CITS: [15719552]| |CITS: [10422579]| and |CITS: [9729600]|., 2-Aminoadipate (a non-proteinogenic amino acid) is one of the three precursor amino acids in the fungal penicillin and cephalosporin biosynthetic pathways. In |FRAME:TAX-5076|, the formation of 2-aminoadipate can occur via lysine biosynthesis |CITS: [14766586]|, or catabolism |CITS: [8031073]|. The pool of penicillin biosynthetic precursors 2-aminoadipate, cysteine and valine is sequestered in vacuoles, along with the vacuolar membrane-associated ACV synthase. However, isopenicillin N synthase is cytosolic. Reviewed in |CITS: [10714900]| and |CITS: [9729600]|., In the first reaction of the pathway the three L-amino acids condense to form the tripeptide δ-(L-α-aminoadipyl)-L-cysteinyl-D-valine (ACV). This reaction is catalyzed by ACV synthetase, a nonribosomal peptide synthetase which also epimerizes L-valine to D-valine. The second reaction involves oxidative ring closure catalyzed by isopenicillin-N synthase leading to the formation of isopenicillin N. Isopenicillin N has weak antibiotic activity and is the first bioactive intermediate in the pathway. In the third step, the hydrophilic L-α-aminoadipate side chain is exchanged for a a hydrophobic acyl group, catalyzed by isopenicillin-N N-acyltransferase. In naturally occurring penicillins DF, F and K the side chains are hexanoate, Δ3-hexanoate, or octanoate, respectively. Semi-synthetic penicillins G and V are produced by adding phenylacetate or phenoxyacetate, respectively, to the culture medium. Reviewed in |CITS: [12749845]| and |CITS: [9729600]|.

General Background, Pinosylvin (3,5-dihydroxystilbene) is found predominantly as a constituent in the heartwood , of trees but is also formed in response to biotic stress in young tree seedlings, thus considered as a phytoalexin. Unlike , other related hydroxystilbenes such as resveratrol (|FRAME:PWY-84|) pinosylvin lacks a hydroxyl group in ring B and , originates by condensation of 3 malonyl-CoA and cinnamoyl-CoA instead of p-coumaroyl-CoA |CITS: [10080690]|., Beside pinosylvin (PS), pinosylvin monomethylether (PSM) is another major stilbene that has been found in heartwood , of trees being considered as constitutive protectant preventing the decay of wood by microorganisms |CITS: [HART81]| , |CITS: [Kindl85]|. Both compounds are rapidly induced upon biotic stress, e.g. caused by the fungus |FRAME:TAX-40559| , the pathogen of the gray-mold rot |CITS: [1451785]| or abiotic stress such as exposure to ozone |CITS: [11027734]| , or UV |CITS: [GEHLERT90]|. It has been demonstrated that pinosylvin and its monomethylether is much more effective , to prevent the growth of most wood-rotting fungi than the also tested resveratrol |CITS: [14714142]|., The enzyme, stilbene synthase (STS), catalyzing the formation of pinosylvin belongs to the plant specific polyketide , synthases (PKS) and is closely related to the chalcone synthase(s) (CHS) |CITS: [2033084]| |CITS: [8083886]|. Stilbene , synthases (STS) are homodimeric, plant-specific polyketide synthases occurring in widely unrelated plants. Stilbene , synthases function as unimodular PKS's with a single active site and each subunit of the protein is able to synthesize , the end products but with lower efficiency and product specificity |CITS: [7713888]| |CITS: [11880657]|., Stilbene synthases have been found to represent a small multigene family in plants where the several members are , differentially expressed in response to exogenous stimuli. This applies even to the most primitive vascular plant, i.e. , |FRAME:TAX-3240| |CITS: [11762173]| which contain a family of four CHS/STS synthases. The most receptive , element to stress seems to correspond to only one sort of stilbene synthase |CITS: [1451785]| |CITS: [10080690]| in , pine seedlings indicating a functional ranking among the STS's responsible for pinosylvin formation in heartwood and , upon stress. , About This Pathway, The stilbene synthase specific for the catalyzation of pinosylvin not only accepts cinnamoyl-CoA , but also its dihydro-isomer phenylpropionyl-CoA (dihydrocinnamoyl-CoA) forming dihydropinosylvin. However, this kind , of reaction does not require a different enzyme (dihydropinosylvin synthase) as previously thought |CITS: [1536925]| but , merely reflects the broader substrate acceptance of the pinosylvin-forming stilbene synthases |CITS: [1426272]| where , some members of this family express a higher affinity towards phenylpropionyl-CoA than others. The product specificity , and enzyme activity of different STS's can be influenced by a single amino acid exchange in the protein sequence , |CITS: [7698342]|., The other enzyme of the pathway, pinosylvin methyltransferase (PMT) has been purified and sequenced |CITS: [CHIRON98]|. , The PMT like the STS is induced in the sapwood, phloem, and needles of conifers as a response to wounding, fungal , attack |CITS: [11027734]| or chemical stress such as ozone or sulphur dioxide |CITS: [ROSEMANN91]| with pinosylvin , and pinosylvin monomethylester accumulating in those tissues. The experimental data so far indicate a transcriptional , induction of ozone-induced stilbene biosynthesis where the sequence of polyketide synthesis (pinosylvin) and O-methylation , (pinosylvin monomethylether) is triggered upon stress |CITS: [11202436]|. As for the STS's the pinosylvin methyltransferase , (PMS) represents a small multigene family in pine species where various members might be differentially regulated upon , environmental signals |CITS: [11027734]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The 6-deoxy sugar |FRAME: CPD-15695| is present in the O-antigens of many Gram-negative bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-287| serotypes O6 and O10 and |FRAME: TAX-29449|. It is synthesized as the activated form |FRAME: CPD-15647| from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|. The O6 serotype is the most prevalent serotype among all clinical |FRAME: TAX-287| isolates |CITS: [8722547]|., The wbp gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-287| serotype O6 has been studied |CITS: [10627048]|. The cluster includes, among others, four biosynthetic genes - |FRAME: G-17654|, |FRAME: G-10027|, |FRAME: G-17660| and |FRAME: G-17659|. While the first two participate in |FRAME: PWY-7336|, the latter two are responsible for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15647|., The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.135| (encoded by |FRAME: G-17659|) catalyzes a dehydration reaction in which the hydroxyl group at C6 is lost, and the hydroxy group at position C4 is oxidized to a keto group. This enzyme maintains the stereo configuration at carbon C5 [unlike |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.115|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-17655| gene in different serotypes of |FRAME: TAX-287|, which catalyzes a similar reaction that also includes inversion of the C5 bond]. The product, |FRAME: CPD-13847|, can be a substrate for two similar enzymes that reduce the C4 keto group, resulting in different stereo configurations. |FRAME: G-17660 WbpV| generates |FRAME: CPD-15647|, while |FRAME: G-17661 WbpK| generates |FRAME: CPD-15648| (see |FRAME: PWY-7333|).

The essential oils from fruits of bitter fennel (|FRAME: TAX-2849586|) have been used since antiquity as medicines against digestive disorders and as a flavoring agent in the food and perfumery industries |CITS: [GROSS02]|., The volatiles found in glands and trichomes of fennel are several types of phenylpropenes that act as pollinating attractants. They also accumulate in vegetative tissues where they act in plant defense. The phenylpropenes differ from each other in the moieties attached to the phenyl ring and in the position of the double bond in the propenyl side chain |CITS: [18987218]|. The major components of the bitter fennel essential oils are |FRAME: CPD-6484| (estragole) and |FRAME: CPD-9930|, which differ only in the position of the double bond on the propenyl chain., |FRAME: CPD-9930 t-Anethole| is also found in other plants like |FRAME: TAX-39350| (basil) and |FRAME: TAX-124778| (star anise). The  precursors of these molecules are phenylpropanoids derived from the |FRAME:PWY-361| pathway.

Summary: Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Recently an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate, which proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-10477|, has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|. Initial analysis of sequenced genomes suggested that the pathway might be present in a variety of organisms |CITS: [19557031]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6262|). However, further analysis revealed that the newly discovered pathway is not identical among all of these organisms. A related, yet different route, has been described in |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-197| |CITS: [21489995]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7371|)., This route is similar to the |FRAME: PWY-6262 "futalosine pathway"|, but proceeds via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-13324| rather than |FRAME: CPD-10477|. The two pathways differ from each other only by the enzymes that form and hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-13324| and |FRAME: CPD-10477|, respectively. , This short pathway describes the condensation of two components - |FRAME: CPD-11420|, whose production is described in the pathways of |FRAME: 14-Dihydroxy-6-Naphthoate-Biosynthesis|; and |FRAME: TRANS-POLYISOPRENYL-PP|, whose length varies among different taxa, and is determined by the specificity of the polyprenyl diphosphate synthase., This particular pathway describes the step in organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-210| that possess |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.83|, and thus produce |FRAME: ALL-TRANS-HEXAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE|, leading to production of |FRAME: PWY-5853| |CITS: [8674971]|., The genes that participate in this conversion have been identified in several organisms on the basis of sequence similarity and clustering with known menaquinone biosynthetic genes. It has been predicted that MqnP catalyzes the prenylation reaction; MqnL and MqnM work together to catalyze the decarboxylation, and MenG catalyzes the methylation reaction to yield menaquinone. However, the order of these reactions is not yet known |CITS: [30447488]|.

Names: terminal olefins biosynthesis II // 1-alkenes biosynthesis II
Summary: General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms., Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7027|), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., |FRAME: 1-Alkenes 1-Alkenes| are acyclic hydrocarbons with a single carbon-carbon double bond at the very end of the molecule. Terminal olefins are similar, but may contain additional double bonds throughout the molecule. They are natural products that have important industrial applications as both fuels and chemicals. 1-Alkenes have been reported to occur in both prokaryotes eukaryotes, and are produced by several mechanisms. One such mechanism is the decarbonylation of unsaturated fatty aldehydes |CITS:[17731762][Tornabene82][3343228][Ladygina06]|. However, in some cases the alkenes are synthesized by decarboxylation of free fatty acids. Examples are |FRAME: CPD-14227| in beetles of the genus |FRAME: TAX-7069| |CITS: [Goergen90][Villaverde07]|, |FRAME: CPD-14223| and related higher unsaturated polyenes in plants such as |FRAME: TAX-4222| |CITS: [2583180][3816783]|, and C23-C33 dienes and trienes in the green microalga |FRAME: TAX-869302|., About This Pathway, The locations of double bonds and the stereochemistry of the n-alkadienes produced by the green algae |FRAME: TAX-869302| resemble that of |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|, suggesting that oleate is the direct precursor of the n-alkadienes. Oleate is first extended by successive addition of C2 units derived from malonyl Co-A. Once the appropriate chain length is attained, the compound is decarboxylated and released from the complex. This system that has been named the elongation-decarboxylation mechanism |CITS: [Templier84]|. , An isomerization system in |FRAME: TAX-38881| converts |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| to |FRAME: CPD-14260|, resulting in production of both cis and trans dienes |CITS: [Yong86][12405558]|., The cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-32049| produces several terminal olefins |CITS: [17731762]|, the major ones being |FRAME: CPD-14220| and |FRAME: CPD-14252|, although |FRAME: CPD-14229| and an unspecified form of octadecadiene are also formed |CITS: [21531827]|. These terminal olefins are produced from fatty-acyl-[acp] molecules that are one carbon shorter than the olefins in the same elongation-decarboxylation process that has been described in |FRAME: TAX-38881|., In |FRAME: TAX-32049| this transformation is catalyzed by a single large polyketide synthase (PKS) that is encoded by the |FRAME: G-15088| gene |CITS: [21531827]|. The synthase, which includes eight domains, catalyzes the transfer of the activated fatty acyl from a free carrier protein to an internal acyl-carrier protein module. Once loaded, a central extension module adds two carbons from malonyl-coenzyme A to the acyl-substrate (the third carbon is released as a CO2 molecule) and reduces the β-keto group to a β-hydroxyl. The β-hydroxyl group is activated via sulfation, and subsequently dehydrated, decarboxylated, and finally cleaved off as a terminal olefin |CITS: [21531827]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins Anabaenopeptins| are a family of non-ribosomally synthesized cyclic peptides produced by some cyanobacterial species. They have a well-conserved structure comprising a ring of five amino acids connected through an ureido linkage to an exocyclic sixth amino acid. Counting the exocyclic amino acid as residue 1, the 2nd residue is |FRAME: CPD-219|, and the ring is formed by cyclization of the C-terminal carboxyl of the 6th residue to the ε-amino group of the D-lysine at position 2. The ureido bridge connecting the α-amino group of |FRAME: CPD-219| to the exocyclic amino acid is a unique feature among cyanobacterial peptides., The five amino acids other than |FRAME: CPD-219| are not conserved and may consist of either proteinogenic or non-proteinogenic amino acids. A review published in 2006 listed 124 different anabaenopeptin variants |CITS: [16774586]|. Many of the anabaenopeptins have been isolated under different names such as oscillamides, lyngbyaureamides, ferintoic acids, nodulapeptins, schizopeptins and more |CITS: [Sano95][11520225]|., Anabaenopeptins have been found in an enormous variety of cyanobacteria isolated from both the aquatic and terrestrial environments, including |FRAME: TAX-1163|, |FRAME: TAX-1177|, |FRAME: TAX-1125|, |FRAME: TAX-54304|, |FRAME: TAX-28073|, and |FRAME: TAX-383614| |CITS: [Harada95][26096276][27604544]|. In general, these compounds are produced by filamentous cyanobacteria belonging to the orders |FRAME: TAX-1161| and |FRAME: TAX-1150|. The production by members of the unicellular genus |FRAME: TAX-1125| is beleived to be due to horizontal transfer of the biosynthetic gene cluster from a filamentous organism |CITS: [28261178]|., Anabaenopeptins exhibit a functional diversity that includes inhibitory activity for proteases, phosphatases, and carboxypeptidases |CITS: [ 10340607][11520225][Zafrir-Ilan10]|, and are believed to provide protection against zooplankters and crustaceans., About This Pathway, The gene cluster responsible for anabaenopeptin biosynthesis was discovered in 2005 in a |FRAME: TAX-59512| strain. The cluster comprised 5 genes (anaABCDE) encoding four non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs) and one ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter. Interestingly, even though that organism produces several different anabaenopeptins (|FRAME: CPD-26928|, |FRAME: CPD-26929|, |FRAME: CPD-26933| and |FRAME: CPD-26942|), it contains only a single cluster, indicating that some of the enzymes are promiscuous and can accept different substrates |CITS: [19706155]|. Similar clusters were soon described from multiple species, including |FRAME: TAX-46234|, |FRAME: TAX-313624|, and |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [20338518]|. A cluster from |FRAME: TAX-984208| was reported in 2017 |CITS: [28085246]|. In many organisms a gene cluster encoding |FRAME: PWY-7275| is located next to the anabaenopeptin biosynthesis cluster, and it is assumed that those enzymes produce the homo-amino acids |FRAME: CPD-15322| and |FRAME: CPD-17729| that are incorporated into many anabaenopeptins |CITS: [28085246]|., The AptA NRPS contains two adenylation and two thiolation domains, for activating and binding tof he first two amino acids, a condensation domain, and an epimerization domain for converting |FRAME: LYS| into |FRAME: CPD-219|. The AptB NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the third amino acid, respectively. The AptC NRPS contains two sets of adenylation, thiolation, and condensation, responsible for the fourth and fifth amino acids. It also contains methylation domain, for methylation of the fifth residue (often |FRAME: CPD-298|). The AptD NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the sixth amino acid, and a thioesterase domain, which is responsible for cyclization and release of the product., An unanswered question as of 2024 is the mechanism responsible for formation of the ureido bridge. A similar structure exists in |FRAME: CPD-26948|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-317|, and it has been shown that in that organism the formation of the ureido bridge is catalyzed by the SylC protein |CITS: [19968303]|. However, SylC possesses a domain with structural similarity to acetyltransferase between the A- and C-domains of the NRPSs, and no similar domain was found within the anabaenopeptins NRPSs, suggesting that a different mechanism may exist during anabaenopeptin biosynthesis |CITS: [34437393]|.

Summary: General Background, Chlorobenzoates are a group of compounds that occur in the environment in large amounts either because of their release, as herbicides or as products of bacterial degradation of polychlorinated biphenyls |CITS: [7217013]|., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation seems to have evolved recently as a result, of their widespread release to the environment., |FRAME: CPD-615| is not known to be a natural product but is introduced into the environment through its use as a, precursor in the synthesis of dye stuffs, pigments and pharmaceuticals. It is also produced as a by-product in the, microbial breakdown of certain herbicides and of the ubiquitous pollutants, polychlorinated biphenyls (introduced into, the environment through their former use in plastics, carbon paper, cooling systems and transformers) |CITS: [7765837]|, About This Pathway, Several strains of |FRAME: CPD-615| degrading bacteria, belonging to the genera |FRAME: TAX-507| |CITS: [3579283]|,, |FRAME: TAX-286| |CITS: [6873881]|, |FRAME: TAX-1716| |CITS: [1884993]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1663|, |CITS: [16346660][3223988][16347854][2036004]| have been isolated from |FRAME: CPD-615|, enrichment cultures of soil or sludge samples., All of these organisms appear to have a similar degradation pathway, which starts with a three-step conversion of, |FRAME: CPD-615| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|. The later is converted to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|,, which is degraded via an ortho-cleavage pathway to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: SUC-COA|, (see |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|) |CITS: [7765837]|.

Summary: Many organisms possess enzymes for the transformation of |FRAME: UREA| into |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. This conversion can occur in two distinct routes, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.5|, and |FRAME:EC-6.3.4.6|, respectively., The nickel-enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.5| (urea amidohydrolase) catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea to yield |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: CARBAMATE|, which spontaneously hydrolyzes to form |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and a second molecule of |FRAME: AMMONIA|, in a reaction that consumes two protons. Ureases have been described in plants, fungi, and bacteria, and have been extensively characterized. The enzyme is nickel dependent, and a number of accessory proteins are necessary for formation of the active enzyme |CITS:[12896998][17205208]|., The enzyme is particularly important for the human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-210|, which uses |FRAME: AMMONIA| production by urease for raising the pH in its microenvironment, as well as for controlling the pH homeostasis within the cell |CITS: [17464061]|. In that organism, urease accounts for 1015% of the total protein content of the cell |CITS: [9155571]|., The other route of urea conversion, catalyzed by |FRAME:ENZRXN3O-319|, has been reported for yeast, algae |CITS: [5679987][4556303][6753831]| and some bacteria |CITS: [15090492]|. It is described in |FRAME: PWY-5703|., Urea hydrolysis by ureolytic bacteria is used in technological applications for the precipitation of carbonates, as the pathway results in an alkaline environment, and the CO<sub>2</sub> product dissolves in the water, producing carbonate, which in the presence of calcium ions precipitates as calcium carbonate |CITS: [24194735]|. Organisms reported to precipitate calcium carbonate due to urea hydrolysis include |FRAME: TAX-1474|, |FRAME: TAX-1245|, |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: TAX-29573|, |FRAME: TAX-42566|, |FRAME: TAX-34|, as well as unidentified species of |FRAME: TAX-286|, |FRAME: TAX-34072|, and |FRAME: TAX-1269| |CITS: [Rivadeneyra91][8661675][Ferris96][Stocks-Fischer99][Tiano99][Fujita00][Rodriguez-Navarro03][19712429]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylic acid"| (salicylate; SA) is an aromatic compound commonly found throughout the plant kingdom that is also found in some bacteria., In plants |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| affects numerous biological and physiological processes, including plant defense (via the systematic acquired resistance system |CITS: [15283665][12873532]|), allelopathy, flowering, and stomatal movement |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|. Given its important signaling role, plants often chemically modify |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| by attaching glycosyl, methyl, or other groups to |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| to alters its activity, volatility, or other properties |CITS [PIERPOINT94][SCHULZ93]|. The formation of |FRAME: CPD-12665| is believed to be a detoxification response by plants to prevent the over-accumulation of toxic levels of |FRAME: CPD-110 SA|. Several physiological problems can result from excess |FRAME: CPD-110 SA|. For instance, in |FRAME: TAX-3617| high levels of |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| diminish the level of H+-efflux and thus completely eliminate potassium uptake in the roots |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-12665| has been identified as an |FRAME: CPD-110 SA|-metabolite in several species to date, including |FRAME: TAX-3617|, Cassia absus, Picnomon acarna, and boron-deprived |FRAME: TAX-4232|. Early work on the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12665| in |FRAME: TAX-3617| identified the proper ordering of the intermediates in the pathway and suggested that the reactions were likely catalyzed by an NADH-dependent monooxygenase and a gentisic acid β-D-glucosyltransferase. These enzymes may act cooperatively based on the observation that |FRAME: CPD-633| was never found alone but was always accompanied by |FRAME: CPD-12665|. Enzymatic assays performed using protein extracts from |FRAME: TAX-3617| indicated that the glucosyltransferase activity was |FRAME: CPD-110 SA|-inducible, and that its specific activity reached a level of 48.8 pKat in extracts generated following 14 hrs of incubation |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|. Unfortunately, neither enzyme from this species was cloned. However, an Arabidopsis glucosyltransferase capable of acting on |FRAME: CPD-633| was identified through an in vitro assay. It acts on several other compounds in vitro, so it is unclear whether this does promote the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12665| in planta, however, this compound has been found in Arabidopsis plants with a mutation in |FRAME: AT2G43820-MONOMER UGT74F2|. |FRAME: CPD-12665| may not be a standard SA-metabolite in Arabidopsis, but, it appears that when the two other SA-glucosylation pathways (|FRAME: PWY-6621 I| and |FRAME: PWY-6624 III|) are blocked, Arabidopsis enzymes can detoxify |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| through this alternative route |CITS: [18248508]|., Interestingly, although radiotracer studies indicate that this pathway does occur in plants |CITS: [18248508][SCHULZ93]|, no plant enzyme catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-110| to |FRAME: CPD-633| has been identified yet, despite the fact that bacterial enymzes that carry out his reaction have been characterized |CITS: [9573207]|.

General Background, Quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) are produced by many plants, bacteria and marine algae in response to abiotic stresses such as drought, salinity and hypoxia. Most members of the highly stress-tolerant plant family Plumbaginaceae accumulate β-alanine betaine as osmoprotectant. Its potential role in plant tolerance to salinity and hypoxia makes it an interesting target for metabolic engineering. The utilization of another QAC: |FRAME:BETAINE|, was attempted which failed to achieve the expected stress-tolerance in transgenic plants due to the limited availability of the substrate choline required for glycine betaine synthesis. Unlike glycine betaine, β-alanine does not require choline or oxygen for its biosynthesis, and has therefore been suggested to be a better osmoprotectant under saline and hypoxic conditions |CITS:[hanson00],[rathina00]|., Enzymes: The β-alanine betaine biosynthesis pathway in |FRAME:TAX-227291| requires three rounds of N-methylation, each of which is performed by the same N-methyltransferase encoded by the BANMT1 gene. The enzyme converts each methyl acceptor (β-alanine, N-methyl-β-alanine and N,N-dimethyl-β-alanine) with similar catalytic efficiency |CITS:[11457974]|.

Other bacteria,, including |FRAME:TAX-562| K-12, can utilize |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, the most common form of sialic acid, as a sole source of carbon |CITS: [3902799][9864311]|. , Production of the enzymes involved in |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| degradation is induced by growth on, sialic acid as the sole source of carbon, which is due to transcriptional regulation by the repressor NanR, |CITS: [12897000]|. |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-mannosamine| is only metabolized slowly by |FRAME:TAX-562| K-12, which, may be due to low expression of an N-acetylmannosamine transporter and the, |FRAME: NANE-MONOMER| in the absence of the inducer |CITS: [9864311]|. , Reviews: |CITS: [15007099]|; C. Mayer and W. Boos, Hexose/Pentose and Hexitol/Pentitol Metabolism,, EcoSal Module 3.4.1 |CITS: [ecosal]|, Among other bacteria shown to have this pathway is the Gram-positive anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-1502|. The |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| then enters glycolysis (see pathways |FRAME: GLCMANNANAUT-PWY| and |FRAME: P441-PWY|). The nanA-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-18990| from strain A99 has been characterized |CITS: [11432751][9511987]|, and the nanE-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-8940| from strain 13 has been characterized and its crystal structure determined |CITS: [25320079]|.
