Summary: The glyoxylate cycle is a sequence of anaplerotic reactions (reactions that form metabolic intermediates for biosynthesis) that enables an organism to use substrates that enter central carbon metabolism at the level of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| as the sole carbon source. Such substrates include fatty acids, alcohols, and esters (often the products of fermentation),, as well as waxes, alkenes, and methylated compounds. The pathway does not occur in vertebrates, but it is found in plants and certain bacteria, fungi, and invertebrates., The pathway is essentially a modified version of the |FRAME:TCA| that bypasses those steps in the cycle that lead to a loss of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Acetyl-CoA enters the cycle at two steps, but no carbon escapes it in the form of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|., The glyoxylate cycle uses a two-step bypass. One key enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-1402| (EC 4.1.3.1), converts |FRAME: THREO-DS-ISO-CITRATE| to form |FRAME: SUC| and |FRAME: GLYOX|. A second key enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-1403| (EC 2.3.3.9), condenses glyoxylate and a second molecule of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to form |FRAME:MAL|. The subsequent oxidation of malate regenerates the initial acetyl-CoA acceptor molecule of the TCA cycle, |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|. Thus, the |FRAME: SUC| that was formed by |FRAME:CPLX-1402| (EC 4.1.3.1) can be withdrawn from the cycle and used for cell carbon biosynthesis., The pathway was originally discovered in bacteria |CITS: [13430766]|, but later was found to operate in some eukaryotic organisms as well. In plants the cycle is invovled in the metabolism of storage oils during germination of seeds |CITS:[Brownleade97]|. The cycle also operates in developing eggs of nematodes, where it converts triacylglycerols to carbohydrates |CITS: [627278]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| the pathway is active when growth on 2 carbon compounds requires conservation of 4 carbon TCA intermediates. Two acetyl-CoA are taken up per turn.  The glyoxylate cycle is repressed during growth on glucose and induced by growth on acetate |CITS: [2512996][6378912][6389540][6329757]|., It should be noted that some organisms possess alternative pathways that convert |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to 4 carbon biosynthetic intermediates, such as the |FRAME: PWY-5741| and the |FRAME: PWY-6728|.

Summary: A significant amount of the fatty acids synthesized in animals by the cytosolic enzyme complex fatty acid synthase (FAS) or taken up by the diet are further elongated into |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "very long chain fatty acids"| (VLCFAs), which are at least 22 carbons in length. VLCFAs are also important in plants, where they are the main constituents of hydrophobic polymers (such as cuticular waxes, seed oils and membrane sphingolipids) that prevent dessication at the leaf surface and provide stability to pollen grains |CITS: [15277688]|., VLCFAs are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum by sequential addition of C2 moieties from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to preformed C18 acyl groups derived from the de novo fatty acid biosynthesis pathway. Each elongation cycle is composed of 4 reactions, similar to de novo fatty acid biosynthesis. The cycle includes the condensation of |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs| and |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to form |FRAME: 3-KETOACYL-COA|, reduction to, |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYACYL-COA|, dehydration to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA|, and a final reduction to yield a chain-elongated fatty acyl-CoA |CITS:[16564093]|., Unlike in de novo fatty acid biosynthesis, |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| rather than |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| is used in the condensing reaction. The elongation cycle is catalyzed by a membrane-bound enzyme complex, the elongase |CITS: [10907783]|, which is composed of four enzymes, |FRAME: AT4G34520-MONOMER| or condensing enzyme |CITS: [11341960]|, 3-ketoacyl-CoA reductase, |FRAME: AT5G10480-MONOMER| and |FRAME: AT3G55360-MONOMER| |CITS: [15829606]|., Substrate and tissue specificity of VLCFAs elongation is determined by the condensing enzyme, which catalyzes the rate-limiting reaction. Both saturated and unsaturated fatty acids are elongated via this pathway. While both NADPH and NADH were shown to be an effective reducing power for the two reduction steps, in many cases NADPH is the 'preferred' reductant (reviewed in |CITS: [8190743]| and |CITS: [16564093]|)., For a pathway that specifies the intermediates involved, please see |FRAME: PWY-7036|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.1|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.1|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.2| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., Thiamine biosynthesis is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| (see |FRAME: PWY-6893|)., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the last part of the thiamine biosynthesis pathway - the coupling of the two moieties of thiamin, forming |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|, and its phosphorylation to the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. , Although it is not absolutely clear at this time, it is possible that the key enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: THIE-MONOMER|, acts in vivo on different substrates in different organisms [see |FRAME: PWY-6893|]. This pathway describes the process as understood in |FRAME: TAX-511145|.

Summary: Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the first segment, up to the intermediate lipid IV<sub>A</sub>., In many bacterial species, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., This pathway includes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A|. Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. One exception is |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.54|, which is known to be catalyzed by three completely different types of enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: EG12666| |CITS: [12000770]|, |FRAME: G-55034| |CITS: [20608695]|, and |FRAME: G-55035| |CITS: [27006461]| genes., There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

General Background, Nascent proteins synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane and acquire carbohydrate chains on specific serine, threonine, and asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., In higher eukaryotes, the majority of protein O-glycosylation is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.41|, which adds |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine| to the side chain of specific serine and threonine residues, mainly in mucin-type glycoproteins (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-7433| and |FRAME: PWY-7435|). However, alternative O-glycosylation modifications exist, and one of those is protein O-mannosylation, which is an essential protein modification in fungi and animals |CITS: [12369018][15383666][15948957]|., Protein O-mannosylation is less frequent in metazoa than it is in fungi, where the majority of secreted and cell wall proteins are substantially O-mannosylated (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7921|). In mammals, O-mannosyl glycans were isolated from chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and total glycopeptides from brain tissue |CITS: [39937][2941416][3663149][9083013]|, on α-dystroglycan originating from nerve and muscular tissues |CITS: [8999917][9838223][9726975]|, and on neuron-specific receptor protein-tyrosine phosphatase β |CITS: [18838383]|., The vast majority of mammalian O-mannosyl glycans includes variations of the tetrasaccharide α-NeuAc-(2→3)-β-Gal-(1→4)-β-GlcNAc-(1→2)-α-Man-1-Ser/Thr, often with fucose attached to GlcNAc by an α-1,3 linkage. In general, structures of mammalian O-mannosyl glycans are classified into three types: |FRAME: GlcNAc-b2-O-D-mannosyl-Protein "core M1"|, βGlcNAc(1→2)Man; |FRAME: GlcNAc-b2-GlcNAc-b6-O-D-mannosyl-Protein "core M2"|, βGlcNAc(1→2)[βGlcNAc(1→6)]Man; and |FRAME: bGalNAc-13-bGlucNAc-14-Man-R "core M3"|, βGalNAc(1→3)βGlcNAc(1→4)Man |CITS: [8999917][14617637][20044576]|., About This Pathway, In humans, α-dystroglycan links the extracellular matrix with the cytoskeleton. The protein is extensively modified by sugar chains, including an unusual O-linked glycan. The phosphorylated O-mannosyl trisaccharide |FRAME: bGalNAc-13-bGlucNAc-14-Man6P-R "βGalNAc(1→3)βGlcNAc(1→4)(phospho-6)Man"| whose biosynthesis is described here is required for dystroglycan to bind laminin-G domain-containing extracellular proteins with high affinity in muscle and brain., The biosynthesis of this structure is initiated in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where mannose is transferred from |FRAME: CPD-171| to serine and threonine residues of dystroglycan |CITS: [6347716]|. This reaction is conserved between fungi and animals and is catalyzed by a family of enzymes named protein O-mannosyltransferases (PMTs), which are integral ER membrane proteins that contain seven transmembrane domains, a cytoplasmic N-terminus, and a C-terminal catalytic domain that faces the ER lumen |CITS: [10085156]|. It has been shown in |FRAME: TAX-4932| that the PMTs act on substrate proteins during their translocation into the ER lumen |CITS: [24519942]|., Properly folded glycoproteins are transported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where the initial mannose is further elongated into a trisaccharide by the actions of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.312| (POMGNT2) and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.313| (B3GALNT2). The elongation is followed by phosphorylation of the mannose at the position by an atypical kinase, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.183| (POMK) |CITS: [23929950]|., Defects in dystroglycan glycosylation lead to congenital disorders, termed dystroglycanopathies. Notable is Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), a severe muscular dystrophy with malformations of the eyes and brain, associated with defective binding of α-dystroglycan to its ligands, such as laminin. Other mutations result in Fukuyama CMD, Muscle-Eye-Brain disease (MEB), and certain types of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy |CITS: [2140558]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-6252| and |FRAME: TAX-6253| are parasitic intestinal helminths whose metabolism is predominantly anaerobic |CITS: [14774531]|. The organisms ferment glucose to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and a mixture of products. The major product (about 20%) is |FRAME: CPD-7076| |CITS: [14907729]|., Saz and Weil have found that the precursors for |FRAME: CPD-7076| in |FRAME: TAX-6252| are |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: PROPIONATE| |CITS: [14442156]|, which are produced by the fermentation of either glucose or lactate |CITS: [13673003][14442156]|. The enzymatic steps involved in this process have not been characterized in detail, but the authors suggested that the pathway consists of the steps illustrated in here, which are based on the labeling patterns observed in the study, and on the presence of |FRAME: CPD-7077| in |FRAME:TAX-6251| tissues |CITS: [13061475]|., The authors suggest that it is likely that this sequence of reactions requires the coenzyme A derivatives, similar, to the formation of |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| from |FRAME: ACET| (see |FRAME: CENTFERM-PWY|)., In subsequent work Saz and Weil also showed that two molecules of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| may be condensed to form |FRAME: CPD-15866| in a similar series of reactions |CITS: [14497735]|. A putative acyl-CoA transferase produces the free fatty acids. Both |FRAME: CPD-7076| and |FRAME: CPD-15866|, along with |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: SUC| are excreted (|CITS: [2736251]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22688819]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7384|)., Unfortunately, most of the enzymes of this pathway have not been purified yet from |FRAME:TAX-6251|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Pectin Pectin| is an important component of the plant cell wall. Pectin contains polygalacturonan as a linear component and |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| (RG-I) and |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan type II"| (RG-II) as branched chains |CITS: [16660529][9067088]|. , The back bone of |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| consists of repeating α-(1,2)-|FRAME:L-rhamnose|-α-(1,4)-|FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| disaccharide units. About half of the Rha residues are substituted with side chains of various neutral oligosaccharides such as arabinans, galactans, and arabinogalactans |CITS: [16661590 ]|. RG-II contains a polygalacturonan backbone and a complex of approximately 30 monosaccharides, including rare sugars such as apiose and aceric acid as a side chain |CITS: [8798473]|., Many plant-pathogenic fungi and bacteria produce enzymes responsible for plant cell wall degradation. The degradation pathway for the polygalacturonan region in pectin has been extensively characterized in plant-pathogenic microbes such as |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [8905080]| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species |CITS: [11729262]|. A large number of polygalacturonan-degrading enzymes (i.e., pectin lyase, pectate lyase, and polygalacturonase) have also been identified from many fungi and bacteria. However, studies of the microbial degradation system for the RG region in pectin have been limited., About This Pathway, Prior to its degradation, the acetyl groups that decorate RG-I need to be removed. This deacetylation is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16189| |CITS: [7592973]|., Once deacetylated, the |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| backbone is cleaved to smaller fragments by two extracellular enzymes that cleave in an endo fashion, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.171|, and |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.23|. The |FRAME: G-12556| and |FRAME: G-12673| genes encoding these enzymes in |FRAME: TAX-5053| have been cloned and expressed in a fungal system |CITS: [7961884]| and both enzymes have been characterized |CITS: [8720076]|. The hydrolase generates oligosaccharides with intact rhamnose or galacturonate moieties at the ends, while the lyase generates unsaturated galacturonate residues at the non-reducing end., Further degradation of the backbone is provided by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.174| |CITS: [7972516]| and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.173| |CITS: [9576784]|, which remove rhamnose and galacturonate residues, respectively, from the non-reducing end of the oligosaccharides., The galactan side chain is degraded by multiple enzymes, including exo-β-1,4-galactanase and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.23|, which remove terminal galactose residues from the non-reducing end, and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.89|, which cleaves in the middle of the galactan chain. The arabinan chains, which contain α(1→5)-L-arabinofuranose chains with α(1→3) branches and some α(1,2) residues, are degraded by endo-α-(1,5)-arabinofuranosidases and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.55|, which cleaves the (1,2) and (1,3) linkages.

General Background, Chlorophyll degradation, corresponding to the loss of green color, is an integral part of leaf senescence and fruit ripening |CITS:[16113212],[15012204],[10767575],[12675736]|. Chlorophyll degradation may follow one of two routes, likely depending on the physiogical context in which it occurs. This pathway, |FRAME: PWY-6927|, begins in the chloroplast and may be the primary route for chlorophyll degradation in senescing leaves in |FRAME: ORG-5993| and other species, such as broccoli (|FRAME: TAX-3712|) |CITS: [19304936][20727617]|. Meanwhile, the |FRAME: PWY-5098| pathway may be cytosolic and may operate during fruit senescence and in response to pathogens and wounding |CITS: [15598807][18633118]|., Both of these pathways appear to lead to the production of a colourless, blue-fluorescing intermediate (|FRAME: CPD-7064| or pFCC) via the formation of a red chlorophyll catabolite (RCC). Following export of pFCC from the chloroplast, the final steps of chlorophyll catabolism are species-specific and involve a diversity of modifications of pFCC before the catabolites are finally stored in the vacuole in the form of |FRAME:NCCS|, or NCCs |CITS:[15012204],[16448336]|. NCCs share a common tetrapyrrolic skeleton with an oxygenolytically opened porphyrin macrocycle |CITS:[KRAEUTER03]|, with peripheral, species-specific modification at several side chains within different NCCs. The final conversion of modified FCCs to NCCs is a non-enzymatic reaction catalyzed by the acidic vacuolar pH., About This Pathway, In this route of chlorophyll degradation, the magnesium is removed from chlorophyll a prior to the dephytylation step. The first enzyme in this pathway has not been discovered to date, but the |FRAME: AT5G13800-MONOMER pheophyinase| (PPH) enzyme catalyzing the second reaction in |FRAME: ORG-5993| has been identified and characterized |CITS: [19304936]|. Evidence for this alternative route was collected after it was observed that the two chlorophyllases that catalyze the first step of the |FRAME: PWY-5098| variant pathway are not required for chlorophyll breakdown during leaf senescence in |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [17996203]|. It was also noted that PPH transcript levels are upregulated in senescing Arabidopsis leaves |CITS: [19304936]|., The next two steps, which are shared by both variant pathways, are decisive in the loss of green colour. The ring-opening of, and production of the first identifiable colourless product pFCC from pheophorbide a requires two proteins from gerontoplasts membranes and stroma. Opening of the ring through oxygenolysis of pheophorbide a is catalyzed by the membrane-localized, nonheme iron-containing monooxygenase, pheophorbide a oxygenase (PaO) which yields red bilin RCC. This compound is channeled to RCCR which further reduces it to form pFCC. Both enzymes use reduced ferredoxin as immediate electron donor |CITS:[15012204]|.

Names: Fe(II) oxidation III (neutrophilic environment, MtoA/B system)
Summary: Note: this pathway describes a process that involves both the cytoplasmic membrane and the outer membrane. Due to current limitations in the pathway layout algorithm, the pathway is displayed using only a single membrane. Read the following text to get more information about the localization of the different components., General Background, Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. In the environment, iron is mostly found in two different oxidation states: II and III. Fe(II) is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions, while Fe(III) is favored at high pH and oxic conditions. In oxic environments iron forms various oxide and hydroxide compounds; iron(II,III) oxides (such as magnetite, Fe3O4) and iron(III) oxides (such as hematite, Fe2O3) are most common. Under anoxic conditions the soluble |FRAME: FE+2| species is the most common. In certain environments Fe(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands., Oxidation of ferrous iron (Fe(II)) by microbes is an important component of the iron geochemical cycle. Bacterial iron oxidation is well documented under anaerobic conditions (see for example |FRAME: PWY-8554|), or under aerobic, acidic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6692|). Even though iron is oxidized spontaneously and rapidly in the presence of oxygen, many bacterial species have been found to oxidize Fe(II) at neutral pH |CITS: [20565252][32071158][33328652]|., About This Pathway, One organism that oxidizes iron under neutral pH is |FRAME: TAX-580332|. This Gram-negative bacterium can grow on FeCO3 or FeS at oxic-anoxic interfaces, where oxygen concentrations are low, and small amounts of iron(II) diffuse from the anoxic region into the oxic region, so that both oxygen and iron(II) co-occur |CITS: [9406396][17668050]|. Like other iron(II)-oxidizing bacteria, the organism oxidizes Fe(II) extracellularly, to avoid accumulation of Fe(III) oxides inside the cells. To accomplish this, the bacteria need an electron transfer chain that can transfer electrons from the extracellular surface, where iron is oxidized, through the outer membrane, and into the plasma membrane, where the electrons can be delivered to the pool of quinones and be forwarded to assorted terminal acceptors., The iron oxidation system of |FRAME: TAX-580332| consists of at least three proteins that are encoded by a single operon. The |FRAME: G-124839| and |FRAME: G-124840| genes are homologs of the |FRAME: G-124824| and |FRAME: G-124838| genes of |FRAME: TAX-395960|, which participate in iron(III) oxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-8554|), while the |FRAME: G-124841| gene encodes a c-type cytochrome homologous to the |FRAME: G-55066 SymA| protein of |FRAME: TAX-211586|, which is involved in iron(III) reduction (see |FRAME: PWY-8553|)., Like PioA, the decaheme c-type cytochrome MtoA is an iron-oxidizing protein that interacts directly with the iron at the extracellular surface. MtoB forms a large pore in the outer membrane, though which MtoA can reach the periplasm, where it delivers the electrons. The authors proposed that MtoA delivers the electrons to periplasmic proteins that have yet to be identified, which in turn deliver them to the |FRAME: MONOMER-124842|, a cytoplasmic membrane-bound tetraheme c-type cytochrome that functions as a major quinol dehydrogenase. Once the electrons reduce the quinone pool of the cytoplasmic membrane, they can be used to reduce oxygen or NADP+ |CITS: [22347878]|.

So far no biological activities have been associated with |FRAME:CPD-17074| but the core of this compound, the γ-hydroxybutenolide moiety, is a structural element of agents expressing a variety of bioactivities |CITS:[22795900] [Parker13]|. , The evaluation of nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS) in Aspergillus nidulans revealed the existence of 13 NPRS's |CITS:[18804170]| but only one of them, i.e. TdiA encoding for the didemethylasterriquinone D synthetase involved in |FRAME:PWY-7520| |CITS:[ 16426969] [17704773]| has been associated with the production of secondary metabolites. The gene named micA which encoded for the microperfuranone synthetase was identified in Aspergillus nidulans and recombinant expressed in Aspergillus niger which is known not to produce |FRAME:CPD-17074| |CITS:[19756540]|. It could be shown that micA does not belong to a biosynthetic gene cluster but was a stand-alone NRPS which thioesterase (TE) domain, after iteratively loading two |FRAME:PHENYL-PYRUVATE|, is responsible for hydrolysis, decarboxylation and keto-enol tautermization which generates and releases |FRAME:CPD-17074| |CITS:[22627757]|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important cofactors in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, Sirtuins (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.286|) are a family of NAD+-dependent protein deacetylases that are found in all domains of life. In multicellular organisms, sirtuins deacetylate histones and transcription factors that regulate stress, metabolism, and survival pathways. In yeast, sirtuins regulate gene silencing by histone deacetylation and via formation of |FRAME: CPD-14762|., The byproduct of this reaction is |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE|. This pathway described the salvage of |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| back to NAD+, in a pathway known as the PNC V cycles.

Vetter et al. (|CITS: [23586652]|) have now shown that these enzymes in fact synthesize kanosamine via a novel pathway.  In an NAD-dependent reaction, |FRAME: BSU10530-MONOMER glucose-6-phosphate 3-dehydrogenase| dehydrogenates |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate D-glucose-6-phosphate| at the 3 postion to form |FRAME: 3-oxo-D-glucose-6-phosphate 3-oxo-D-glucose-6-phosphate|.  |FRAME: BSU10550-MONOMER 3-oxo-glucose-6-phosphate:glutamate aminotransferase| subsequently transfers the amine group of L-glutamate to this keto group, forming |FRAME: CPD-10225 kanosamine-6-phosphate|, and |FRAME: BSU10540-MONOMER kanosamine-6-phosphate phosphatase| hydrolyzes the 6-phosphate group to produce |FRAME: CPD-10224 kanosamine|.

Summary: General Background, Inorganic reduced sulfur compounds serve as electron donors in many phototrophic and chemotrophic bacteria |CITS: [9328649]|. Sulfide oxidation plays an important role in the global sulfur cycle by reoxidizing the sulfide produced by sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic habitats., Phototrophic purple and green sulfur-oxidizing bacteria use the sulfur compounds as electron donors for reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation during photolithotrophic growth. Light energy is used to transfer electrons from the sulfur compounds to levels found in highly reducing electron carriers such as |FRAME:Ferredoxins| and |FRAME:NADP| |CITS: [2663079]|. Similarly, non-sulfur purple bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1061| and cyanobacteria such as, |FRAME: TAX-54310| are also able to use sulfide as the electron source for anoxygenic photosynthesis., The purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| carries out the complete eight-electron oxidation of sulfide to sulfate. The process involves the formation of sulfur globules as obligate intermediates |CITS: [9695921]|. The globules are intracellular and extracytoplasmic |CITS: [9560425]|, and the sulfur in them occurs in the molecular structure of sulfur chains |CITS: [11782519]|, enclosed by a protein envelope |CITS: [7575095]|. In the process of further oxidation, the sulfur in the globules is reduced inside the bacteria back to sulfide, which is then oxidized by a second sulfide-oxidizing system., At this point it is still not completely clear which enzymatic systems are responsible for sulfide oxidation at particular stages of the pathway. Clearly, there are several such systems, and it is likely that different organisms employ different systems to achieve this goal., About This Pathway, The most important mechanism in |FRAME: TAX-1049| for the initial sulfide oxidation appears to be the transfer of electrons from sulfide directly into the quinone pool, mediated by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-12314|. , Sulfide-quinone oxidoreductase activity was readily detected in crude extracts of |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [9639604]|, and the enzymes have been purified from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-1061| and |FRAME: TAX-54310| |CITS: [9092526][8119908]|. The gene encoding the enzyme was found in many other organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-24|, |FRAME: TAX-266|, and |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [10852862]|. Interestingly, the gene has not been found in the |FRAME: TAX-1049| genome, suggesting it may be considerably different from known sequences., Steudel suggested a mechanism for the formation of sulfur globules from sulfide, which is mediated by an initial enzyme-catalyzed oxidation step and a series of subsequent spontaneous chemical reactions |CITS: [Steudel96]|., The first step is the formation of HS* radicals by a single electron oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-846|. At pH 7, the HS* radical dissociates to a proton and a S* radical, which dimerizes to S2-2. The disulfide is then spontaneously oxidized by more S* radicals, leading to larger and larger polysulfides., Both |FRAME: MONOMER-12314| and |FRAME:CPLX-7131| (discussed in |FRAME: PWY-5274|) are theoretically capable of generating such radicals, via production of semiquinones., Steudel also suggested that when the polysulfide reaches the length of 6, 7 or 8, it spontaneously cyclizes to form homocyclic sulfur molecules S6, S7, and S8, that he found in extracts of sulfur containing |FRAME: TAX-1049| cells |CITS: [Steudel90]|. It should be mentioned, though, that other authors claim that no cyclic sulfur is found in |FRAME: TAX-1049|,, and that this organism is completely unable to metabolize sulfur rings |CITS: [17379736]|.

Summary: Diazo-containing natural products have been reported from soil and marine bacteria. They were first isolated in the 1950s, and include simple compounds such as |FRAME: L-AZASERINE| and |FRAME: CPD-24753|, as well as more complex compounds such as diazobenzoquinones, diazonaphthoquinones, and the diazofluorene-based |FRAME: Kinamycins kinamycins| and |FRAME: Lomaiviticins lomaiviticins| |CITS: [21589994]|. Many of the simpler compounds consist of modified α-amino acids and have antitumour properties, leading to considerable interest in these compounds. , The diazo group (=N+=N-) is an important functional group and has been used for over 100 years in organic synthesis., The pathway was elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-66881|, which produces the ortho-diazoquinone |FRAME: CPD-24753|. Identification of the gene cluster involved in |FRAME: CPD-24753| biosynthesis was followed by generation of mutants defective in individual genes of the cluster. Mutations in two of the genes, |FRAME: G-107505| and |FRAME: G-107504|, resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-23564|, a physiological intermediate of cremeomycin that lacks the diazo function |CITS: [26689788]|., The two genes were cloned and expressed recombinantly, and it was found that CreE can oxidize |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| using NADPH as a reducing agent, forming |FRAME: CPD-24752|. The enzyme consume 3 equivalents of NADPH to produce one equivalent of |FRAME: CPD-24752|, indicating that it catalyzes three iterative oxidations, via |FRAME: CPD-13364| and |FRAME: CPD-24765|. CreD was shown to catalyze a β-elimination reaction on |FRAME: CPD-24752|, releasing |FRAME: NITRITE| and forming |FRAME: FUM| as a side product. CreD accepts |FRAME: CPD-24752| as a substrate only when it is directly delivered by CreE immediately after its synthesis |CITS: [26689788]|.

General Background, |FRAME: SO3 Sulfite| plays a key role in oxidative sulfur metabolism. It is derived from multiple sources: First, sulfite is the main intermediate in the oxidation of sulfur compounds to |FRAME: SULFATE| |CITS: [11557133]|., In purple sulfur bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1049|, the oxidation of |FRAME: HS| and |FRAME:S2O3| results in formation of intracellular sulfur globules, which are oxidized to sulfite by the Dsr system (see |FRAME: PWY-6676|)., A second source for sulfite is the desulfonation of organic compounds by enzymes like |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15| (Xsc) (see |FRAME: PWY-1281|)., A third source of sulfite is extracellular sulfite retrieved from the environment. Free sulfite in the periplasm (which most likely exists as bisulfite) is bound to the |FRAME: SoxY-Protein "SoxYZ"| protein complex in the form of |FRAME: SoxY-Systeine-Sulfinate|. The binding acts to shield components of the periplasm from chemical reactions with sulfite, and may also be required for delivering the sulfite to a transporter that exports it into the cytoplasm for oxidation |CITS: [24030319]|., Some microorganisms (such as |FRAME: TAX-60136| species) can use sulfite as their sole electron source |CITS: [Sorokin95][10319472 ]|. , Enzymes that catalyze the direct oxidation of sulfite to sulfate are molybdenum hydroxylases, and belong to the sulfite oxidase family, which includes both sulfite-oxidizing enzymes and plant assimilatory nitrate reductases (such as the |FRAME: CPLX-7196| of |FRAME: ORG-5993|). The best characterized members of this family are sulfite oxidases, from avian and mammalian sources. However, these enzymes differ from the bacterial enzymes in that they can use oxygen as an electron acceptor (see |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.1|)., Some sulfite oxidizing enzymes are located in the periplasm. The best characterized enzyme from this group is |FRAME: EC-1.8.2.1| (SOR) from |FRAME: TAX-921|, which contains a molybdopyranopterin cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-5276|). Another well-characterized periplasmic enzyme is the |FRAME:CPLX-882| (such as that from |FRAME: TAX-82367|). It has been shown that this system can oxidize sulfite independently from the presence of the |FRAME:CPLX-7150| component (a molybdohemoprotein), but it is not clear whether the Sox system functions in vivo as a sulfite-oxidizing enzyme |CITS:[10940005][Lu84][11425697]|)., Other enzyme systems that oxidize sulfite are located in the cytoplasm. Two general mechanisms for sulfite oxidation in the cytoplasm have been described: a direct oxidation by a membrane-bound iron-sulfur molybdoprotein (|FRAME: EC-1.8.5.6|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7457|), and an indirect, AMP-dependent oxidation via the intermediate |FRAME:APS| (APS) (see |FRAME:PWY-5279| and |FRAME:PWY-5278|) |CITS: [11557133]|. The direct oxidation route is much more prevalent, but the two mechanisms are present simultaneously in many organisms, including β and γ proteobacteria (|FRAME: TAX-931|, |FRAME: TAX-1049|, |FRAME: TAX-36861|, |FRAME: TAX-1021|), green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1091|), Gram-positive bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-28034|) and even archaea (|FRAME: TAX-2283|) |CITS: [11557133]|., About This Pathway, Two variations are known for the non-direct sulfite oxidation pathway. Both variations share the same first step, the AMP-dependent oxidation of sulfite to |FRAME:APS|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.8.99.2|. The pathways differ in the second step. In one variation the AMP moiety of APS is transferred to |FRAME:PPI| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4|, generating sulfate and ATP (see |FRAME:PWY-5278|), while in the other variation the AMP-moiety is transfered to phosphate by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.5| (APAT), generating sulfate and ADP (depicted here)., The APS pathways can operate in both directions (see |FRAME: DISSULFRED-PWY|), and were discovered originally in sulfate-reducing organisms |CITS: [14484819]|. When operating in sulfite oxidation mode, they result in substrate level, phosphorylation, and may provide the bacteria with energy |CITS: [4972376]|., The oxidation of sulfite by the indirect pathways occurs in the cytoplasm. The first enzyme of both pathways, |FRAME: CPLX-7168|, has been described as either a soluble enzyme, or a membrane bound enzyme. The other enzymes are soluble |CITS: [11557133]|. This pathway has been demonstrated in several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-1058|, |CITS: [2855979]|, |FRAME: TAX-931| and |FRAME: TAX-36861| |CITS: [10636864]|. However, all of these organisms also contain the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7165|, suggesting the two variations of indirect sulfite oxidation co-exist in these organisms.

Summary: Flavonol 3-glucosides esterified with hydroxycinnamic acids have been found very effective compounds in screening out ultraviolet-B radiation (280-320 nm). In |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles the most abundant UV-B protective pigments are mono- and diacylated flavonol 3-glucoside which are esterified with |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| on the 3" and 6"-position of the glucose molecule |CITS:[Schnitzler96]| |CITS:[Fischbach99]|. Although |FRAME:CPD1F-90| acylglucosides dominate both |FRAME:CPD-8004|- and |FRAME:CPD-520| acylglucosides are major UV-screening pigments found in pine needles |CITS:[Schnitzler96]|. , The soluble and cell-wall bound flavonol acylglucosides, e.g. derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-520| (this pathway) are accumulating in the epidermal layer of the needles, hence efficiently shielding and protecting the mesophyll cells from UV-B radiation |CITS:[Schnitzler96]|. Based on data obtained from UV experiments on |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles it appears that the soluble flavonol glucosides are first generated within the cell and then transported to the cell wall where the acylation with |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| and association with cell wall components takes place |CITS:[16898012]|. UV-B radiation induces the formation of diacylated flavonol glucosides. |FRAME:CPD-14984 Quercetin 3-O-(3",6"-O-di-p-coumaroyl)-glucoside| was strongly induced in pine cotyledons after exposure to UV-B radiation |CITS:[Jungblut95]| whereas the content of hydroxycinnamic acids remained unchanged |CITS[Schnitzler96]|. The biosynthesis of acylated flavonol glucosides appears to occur in a seasonal fashion. The soluble flavonol glucosides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-453|, |FRAME:CPD-14969| and |FRAME:CPD1F-437| peak in June at the beginning of needle development and act at this time as the prominent UV-screening pigments. In July the more effective diacylated flavonol glucosides, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-14982| are formed and resume the role of UV-protective pigments (see also |FRAME:PWY-7168|, |FRAME:PWY-7171|) |CITS:[Fischbach99]|. , Three hydroxycinnamoyl transferases (HCT) have been identified and characterized in cell extracts of |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles. The HCT's catalyze the addition of |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| in a position-specific manner and have been characterized as 3"-, 4"- and 6"-HCT's |CITS:[15752358]|. The 6"-HCT was inducible by UV-B radiation and present in the first year needle's development whereas the 3"-HCT was constitutively expressed and showed high values throughout a 2 year period of needle development |CITS:[16898012]|. The 4"-acylation was an unexpected activity as 4"-acylated compounds have not yet been identified in Pinus species. However, similar flavonol acylglucoside with the 4"-pattern have been found in broadleaf species such as oak |CITS:[Romussi83]| indicating the potential occurrence of minor flavonol acylglucoside in other species as well. The sequence of acylation has been determined as 3" followed by 6". The 3"-position of pine flavonol acylglucosides is invariably acylated with |FRAME:COUMARATE| whereas the 6"-position can be acylated with either |FRAME:COUMARATE| or |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| |CITS:[15752358]|.

Attachment of the threonylcarbamoyl moiety to the A37 nucleotide of tRNAs is catalyzed by a heteromultimeric enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.234| |CITS: [25578970]|.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn this variant of the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules and reduces one molecule of |FRAME: NAD|, one of |FRAME: NADP|, and two |FRAME: Quinones quinones| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinols|, respectively., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, Acetic acid bacteria are Gram-negative acidophilic α-proteobacteria that oxidize ethanol to acetate. These bacteria are highly resistant to high levels of both of these membrane-permeable compounds. The citric acid cycle of these organisms has been shown to converts acetate to CO2., Studies of the the vinegar producing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-435| have shown that instead of the |FRAME: SUCCCOASYN| enzyme, which catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: SUC-COA| to |FRAME: SUC| in most bacteria, this organism possesses a |FRAME: CPLX-8672|, an enzyme that links acetate metabolism with the TCA cycle |CITS: [18502856]|. The enzyme couples the conversion of |FRAME: SUC-COA| to |FRAME: SUC| to the conversion of acetate to acetyl-CoA, and thus simultaneously reduces the acetate concentration and reduces the metabolic demand for free |FRAME: CO-A|. The enzyme is essential for survival in high acetate concentrations |CITS: [2156811]|. Another enzyme of the TCA cycle, |FRAME: CPLX-8671|, has also been found to be essential for acetate resistance |CITS: [2156811]|., A 2017 study has reported the presence of the pathway in diverse bacterial groups, including microbial symbionts of animals such as humans and insects |CITS: [28452983]|.

Summary: General Background, Manganese is the second most abundant transition metal found in the Earth's crust. In the environment, manganese is mostly found in three different oxidation states: II, III, and IV. Mn(II), primarily occurring as the soluble |FRAME: MN+2| species, is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions. Mn(III) and Mn(IV), which are commonly found in the form of various oxides and oxyhydroxides, are favored at high pH and oxic conditions (although in certain environments Mn(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands |CITS: [17008530]|). Mn(III) also occurs as a transient intermediate in the oxidation of Mn(II) to Mn(IV) oxides |CITS: [15800042]|., Mn oxides are highly reactive. They mediate redox reactions with organic and inorganic compounds (see for example |CITS: [31466008][34157973]|) and sequester a variety of metals, thus controlling the distribution and availability of many trace elements and influencing several elemental biogeochemical cycles. As the strongest environmentally relevant oxidant after oxygen, they serve as electron acceptors for anaerobic respiration by Mn-reducing organisms |CITS: [Tebo04]|., Microbial Mn reduction has been reported numerous times from marine, freshwater, and terrestrial environments |CITS: [Mann46][Bromfield76][Davidson82][16346865][3013837][Ehrilch87][24193963][9758801][24266405][36463988][39021633]|. Microbes that couple growth to the reduction of manganese oxides play an important role in the biogeochemistry of certain anaerobic environments, such as the zone between the region of oxygen removal and the region of sulfate reduction in marine sediments, or between the regions of oxygen depletion and CO2 reduction in freshwater sediments |CITS: [17815852]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-211586| is one of the first organisms studied for this ability. It was isolated from the anaerobic sediments of Oneida Lake, New York, which are located only a few milimeters below an oxic layer |CITS: [Dean81] [17815852]|. MR-1 can use a wide variety of terminal electron acceptors for anaerobic respiration, including certain insoluble manganese and iron oxides. Initial studies have shown that rates of Mn reduction by MR-1 were optimal at pH 6 to 7 - a pH at which no abiotic reduction of Mn oxides takes place |CITS: [17815852]|., Studies that describe mutants of MR-1 that are deficient in particular electron transport components have demonstrated that menaquinone |CITS: [Myers93]| and a 21-kDa tetraheme c-type cytochrome (|FRAME: MONOMER-20175 CymA|) localized to the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [9023196][10613864]| are both required for the reduction of Mn(IV) and Fe(III). However, those two proteins are believed to be common intermediates in electron transport chains that subsequently branch to different terminal reductases., On the other hand, mutatants in genes encoding the outer membrane cytochromes |FRAME: G-124823 OmcA| and |FRAME: G-124821 MtrC| (then known as OmcB) displayed normal growth on most substrates, but were 45 and 75% slower than MR-1, respectively, at reducing MnO2 oxides |CITS: [11133454]|. The two proteins were shown to interact and form a complex |CITS: [16788180]|. Both proteins were found to also be important for the reduction of iron, and in recent years were studied mostly in that respect |CITS: [17468239][32978123]|., The direct electron donor to these the outer membrane cytochromes is still not known.

Summary:
General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7670 Dimethylsulfide| (DMS) is a major contributor to the total sulfur emissions to the atmosphere from land and the ocean., In marine, estuarine, and salt marsh systems, the main source of DMS is the degradation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|. There are two main routes for DMSP degradation, leading to formation of either |FRAME: CPD-7670| or |FRAME: CPD-7672|. Other sources for DMS include the reduction of |FRAME: DMSO|, the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-7671|, and the degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids., DMS, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere, and is considered the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: CPD-3746|, which attract water and promote cloud formation and thus influence the climate |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, up to 90% of the DMS in the ocean is degraded biologically |CITS: [Kiene90]|., DMS is toxic, and attempts to isolate in pure culture DMS-degrading organisms that can use it as the sole carbon and energy source have been often unsuccessful due to this toxicity. However, several organisms capable of degerading DMS have been isolated over the years. Aerobic bacterial DMS oxidation has been demonstrated in organisms from a few taxonomic domains, including Thiobacillus sp. strain MS1 |CITS: [Sivela80]|, |FRAME: ORG-5989| |CITS: [Kanagawa82], [Kanagawa86][2930168][Tanji89][Gould92]|, |FRAME: ORG-6053| |CITS: [1872604][8285684]|, |FRAME: ORG-6050| |CITS: [Debont81]|, |FRAME: ORG-6052| |CITS:[3767349][Suylen86][Suylen87][Smith88a]| and |FRAME:TAX-392484| |CITS:[16535680][17322322]|.
, Anaerobic degradation of DMS has been documented by methanogens |CITS: [11073950]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5258|) and by sulfate-reducing bacteria |CITS: [8074524]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.131|, was described as the key enzyme in DMS metabolism in many organisms, including |FRAME: ORG-6050| |CITS: [Debont81]|, |FRAME: ORG-6052| |CITS: [3767349]|, |FRAME: ORG-6053| |CITS: [1872604]|, and several strains of |FRAME: TAX-121290| |CITS: [10896224]|. This enzyme produces |FRAME: CPD-7671| and |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. Since many of these organisms are methylotrophs, a fraction of the latter is channeled to the |FRAME: PWY-1622 "serine pathway"| for incorporation into the cell carbon, while the |FRAME: CPD-7671| is oxidized further by |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.4|, to |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [Debont81][29064480]|. The sulfide is oxidized to sulfate, and the unassimilated portion of the formaldehyde is fully oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., Dissimilatory dimethyl-sulfide monooxygenase has been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-121290| and found to be an FMN-dependent monooxygenase. The enzyme consists of two subunit - a |FRAME: MONOMER-16507|, and an |FRAME: MONOMER-16508| |CITS: [21216999]|.

Summary: General Background, Tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis., Folates also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine, play a role in histidine catabolism |CITS: [11001804]|, and in plants are also involved in photorespiration, amino acid metabolism and chloroplastic protein biosynthesis |CITS: [11960743]| |CITS: [12644692]|., Folates are abundant in green leaves, and folic acid was initially isolated from a large amount (four tons) of spinach leaves. The name folate is derived from the Latin folium (leaf) |CITS: [3067148]|., Folates are modified by the addition of glutamate moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail. The polyglutamylated forms are usually preferred by the enzymes that use folates since the turnover rate of those compounds is markedly increased |CITS: [9190084][SCOTT00][KIRK94]|. In addition, in eukaryotic cells the glutamylated forms of folate facilitate the retention of the vitamin within the cell and its subcellular compartments |CITS: [1916088]|., The product of this pathway, |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydropteroylmonoglutamate, H4PteGlu1,, THF), is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. Members of the family differ in the oxidation state, of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions (see, |FRAME: PWY-2201|), and the number of conjugated glutamate residues (see |FRAME: PWY-2161|)., About This Pathway, This pathway for the de novo biosynthesis of folates is found in bacteria, fungi, and plants., Folates are tripartite molecules and are made up of a pterin, |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| and |FRAME:GLT| moieties., The first two are synthesized from |FRAME:GTP| and |FRAME:CHORISMATE|, respectively., The first committed step catalyzed by |FRAME: FOLE-CPLX| converts GTP into |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3|., The triphosphate motif is removed by a still unknown process, and the resulting, |FRAME: DIHYDRO-NEO-PTERIN| is converted to |FRAME: AMINO-OH-HYDROXYMETHYL-DIHYDROPTERIDINE|, by |FRAME: CPLX0-3936| (FolB). The consecutive action of the FolK, FolP, FolC, and FolA enzymes finally produces the final product, |FRAME: THF| |CITS: [12039964]|., In plants the pterin moiety is formed from GTP in the cytosol, which couples to pABA (synthesized in plastids) in mitochondria followed by subsequent glutamylation and reduction steps which may take place in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids |CITS: [11960743][11752472]|., The recent discovery that folylpolyglutamate synthases are present in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids with each, of them encoded by a different gene in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [11752472]| points to the fact that at least, parts of the pathway can be carried out independently in those compartments., In addition to the de novo pathway, many organisms also possess a salvage pathway that is used, to re-synthesize tetrahydrofolate from breakdown products of folates in the cell, such as 5 or 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate., About Folates In Animals, While plants and many microorganisms can synthesize folate coenzymes by the de novo synthesis pathway, vertebrates are absolutely dependent on nutritional sources, making folate a vitamin., Food folates exist mainly as |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (N5-methyl-H4PteGlun) and |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (N10-formyl-H4PteGlun) |CITS: [405403]|., Polyglutamyl folates are hydrolyzed to folylmonoglutamates by |FRAME: HS06361-MONOMER|, and metabolized within the enterocyte into 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1. This monoglutamyl folate coenzyme is the plasma form of the vitamin |CITS: [13906633][2736319]|, and is transported to peripheral tissues where it is demethylated by the vitamin B12-dependent |FRAME:ENZRXN-5465| to monoglutamyl tetrahydrofolate (H4PteGlu1)., Insufficient supply of the vitamin in vertebrates leads to anemia in adults, and has been shown to cause neural tube malformation in human embryos |CITS: [11744531]|. In addition, folate defficiency has been linked to a number of other birth defects, several types of cancer, dementia, affective disorders, Down's syndrom, and serious conditions affecting pregnancy outcome (for a review, see |CITS: [11001804]|).

General Background, Some Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria form capsules, which are coats of slime that surround the exterior of the cell and are attached to it. Capsules are usually composed of polysaccharides that are synthesized intracellularly and secreted. Capsules aid bacterial survival under certain environmental conditions. Bacterial polysaccharide synthesis and secretion is mediated by three pathways, the Wzy-dependent pathway, the synthase-dependent pathway and the ABC transporter-dependent pathway. , The capsular polysaccharide of the human Gram-positive pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1313| is an important virulence factor that enables it to evade destruction by phagocytic cells in the bloodstream. It is anchored to the peptidoglycan cell wall. Variations in structure of the capsular polysaccharide in this organism result in its division into 90 different serotypes. This variation may affect not only phagocytosis, but also response to complement, antigenicity and clearance. The capsular polysaccharide is composed of repeating oligosaccharide units of two to eight monosaccharides. It is a major immunogen and is the basis of pneumococcal vaccines., In |FRAME: TAX-1313| capsular polysaccharide is biosynthesized by the Wzy-dependent pathway in 88 of the 90 serotypes. The remaining two serotypes utilize the synthase-dependent pathway. The biochemical structures of 54 capsular polysaccharides are known. The capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis genes are located at a chromosomal site known as the cps (capsular polysaccharide synthesis) locus. The sequences of cps genes in the 90 serotypes are known and bioinformatic analysis has predicted their function. However, biochemical confirmation of many of these predicted gene functions is needed. In |CITS: [20729354 ] [17766420 ] [17766424] [16532061]| and reviewed in |CITS: [8531887]|., During capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-1313| the monosaccharide units are transferred from their nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) derivatives. Among the 54 known capsular polysaccharide structures, the biosynthetic genes for 14 of their NDP-monosaccharide precursors have been found in the cps locus. Biosynthetic pathways for five of of these precursors have remained putative, including NDP-D-mannitol, NDP-D-arabinitol, NDP-ribofuranose, CDP-glycerol and NDP-2-glycerol. However, the latter pathway utilizing |FRAME: CPD-12670| has now been elucidated (see below) (in |CITS: [20729354]|)., About This Pathway, A biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-12670| involved in capsular polysaccharide antigen biosynthesis has been proposed for |FRAME: TAX-216600| (also designated as strain G1934 in |CITS: [20729354]|). The pathway was based on the identification and characterization of gene function using biochemical and molecular biological methods. Genes gtp1, gtp2 and gtp3 encode enzymes of the pathway. These genes have also been identified in serotypes 15B, 15C, 15F, 23A, 23B, 28A and 28F. The compound |FRAME: CPD-536| is rare in bacteria, but has been found in serotyes 15A and 23F. This pathway provides a source of enzymes for the production of |FRAME: CPD-12670|, an uncommon sugar derivative (in |CITS: [20729354]|)., The Gtp1 enzyme can use either |FRAME: DIHYDROXYACETONE| or |FRAME: CPD0-1551| (its enantiomer specificity was not reported), so this pathway may start with either compound. These two compounds are intermediates of glycerolipid metabolism (in |CITS: [20729354]|).

Summary: Gluconeogenesis is the generation of glucose from non-sugar carbon substrates such as |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, and glucogenic amino acids (primarily |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and |FRAME: GLN|). The process is essentially the reversal of the |FRAME:GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| pathway. However, two glycolytic enzymes catalyze irreversible reactions. In order to enable the pathway to flow in the direction of glucose production, these reactions are catalyzed by other enzymes (|FRAME:EC-3.1.3.11| and |FRAME:EC-2.7.9.2|) in the opposite direction., Enzymes of the gluconeogenic pathway are widely distributed in archaea, bacteria, fungi, plants and animals, and are often considered to be central to the origins of metabolism |CITS: [15803666]|. Note that this pathway describes gluconeogenesis in plants and microorganisms, the mammalian pathway is described at |FRAME: PWY66-399|., Bacteria use gluconeogenesis to synthesize glucose from non-sugar C2 or C3 compounds or the intermediates of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle when there sufficient amounts of hexose are not available to them |CITS: [9168612][11815613][16109965][20439709]|., In photosynthetic organisms, the product of photosynthetic carbon fixation (|FRAME: GAP|) is transported from the chloroplast into the cytoplasm, where it is transformed to hexose phosphate via gluconeogenesis. In plants, these hexose phosphates are used to synthesize sucrose, as documented in |FRAME: PWY-7347| |CITS: [Sung88]|.

Names: protein SAMPylation and SAMP-mediated thiolation // small archaeal modifier protein transformation
Summary: Archaea have a mechanism of protein post-translational modification, termed SAMPylation, that shares many biochemical features with the ubiquitination system of eukaryotes. The archaeal equivalents of ubiquitin have been named Small Archaeal Modifier Proteins (SAMPs). Like ubiquitin, these proteins possess a β-grasp fold and carboxy-terminal diglycine motif, and as in ubiquitination, the C-terminal carboxylate forms an isopeptide bond with the ε-amino group of lysine residues on target proteins |CITS: [20054389]|. The C-terminal glycine of SAMP2 can form a bond with a lysine residue of another SAMP2 molecule, forming poly-SAMP chains, as in the case of polyubiquitination., The key enzyme in SAMPylation is the |FRAME: CPLX-9231|, encoded by |FRAME: G-55126|. Most archaea encode only a single such enzyme in their genomes. The sequence of UbaA shows strong similarities to the sequences of |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10154| and |FRAME: EG11587|, as well as to yeast UBA4 and its mammalian ortholog |FRAME: HS04742|. Unlike the cascade of E1/E2/E3 enzymes found in eukaryotes (see |FRAME: PWY-7511|), it appears that the single E1 enzyme of archaea is responsible for the full SAMPylation process - activating SAMPs by adenylation of their C-terminal glycine,  transferring them to an internal cysteine residue, and eventually transferring them to the lysine residues of the target protein |CITS: [ 23140889]|., In addition to their role in SAMPylation, SAMP proteins are also involved in sulfur transfer. Following the initial adenylation of the terminal glycine, the AMP group can be replaced with a sulfur atom, forming a C-terminal thiocarboxylate, which then serves as a sulfur donor for several processes that include thiolation of certain tRNAs and biosynthesis of certain sulfur-containing molecules such as |FRAME: CPD-4|. It has been shown that in the halophile |FRAME: TAX-2246| SAMP1 is involved in |FRAME: CPD-4| biosynthesis, while SAMP2 is involved in the thiolation of tRNA |CITS: [21368171]|. Some residues of the E1 enzyme have been shown to be essential for the sulfur transfer reaction, although the exact mechanism is still not known |CITS: [27459543]|.

Summary: General Background, It is well known that |FRAME:TAX-562| can use glucose as a sole source of carbon and energy. The D isomer of glucose is widely found in nature and |FRAME: Glucopyranose| is predominant in aqueous solution |CITS: [FRANKS87]|. Exogenous |FRAME: Glucopyranose| enters the cell through outer membrane porins and is then actively transported into the cell via the inner membrane phosphotransferase system (PTS) which transforms it into |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| as it crosses the cell membrane. |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| is also produced biosynthetically during gluconeogenesis. |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| is one of the basic precursor metabolites for biosynthetic pathways. It is also a substrate for the central degradative pathways glycolysis and the pentose phosphate cycle., |FRAME:TAX-562| can also grow on exogenously supplied glucose-1-phosphate (minimal medium containing glucose 1-phosphate) as sole carbon source |CITS: [1648777]|. Endogenous |FRAME: GLC-1-P| is an intermediate in the metabolism of |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen| and |FRAME: D-Galactose|. It is a building block for the sugar nucleotide |FRAME: CPD-12575|, which is used in some biosynthetic pathways. Reviewed by Mayer, C. and W. Boos in |CITS: [ecosal]| (see below)., About This Pathway, Substrates |FRAME: Glucopyranose| and |FRAME: GLC-1-P| may be derived from exogenous sources, or endogenously produced, as indicated by the input pathway links. In general, the ability to utilize sugars and their modes of utilization are strain-dependent in |FRAME:TAX-562|., Exogenous |FRAME: GLC| uptake via the PTS curbs the utilization of other exogenous sugars, which is known as the glucose effect. This effect is lost if |FRAME: GLC| becomes limiting. Under these conditions |FRAME: GLC| can also enter the cell without phosphorylation, via outer membrane porins and the Mgl ABC transporter (not shown)., Endogenous |FRAME: GLC| can be produced by pathways for the degradation of glucose-containing disaccharides such as |FRAME: MALTOSE| (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY|) |FRAME: TREHALOSE|, |FRAME: Alpha-lactose| and |FRAME: MELIBIOSE|, as shown in the pathway links. In contrast to exogenous |FRAME: GLC| which is phosphorylated by the PTS, endogenous |FRAME: GLC| is phosphorylated by glucokinase before entering central metabolism, as shown in the pathway links (in |CITS: [9023215]|). More recently, a role for glucokinase and glucose in a complex regulatory mechanism for maltose utilization involving Glk, MalT, Mlc and PtsG has been proposed |CITS: [19028900]|., It is possible that high levels of |FRAME: GLC| could accumulate inside the cell under certain conditions. It has been shown that the maltose acetyltransferase product of gene maa efficiently acetylates both maltose and |FRAME: GLC| (not shown). Evidence suggests that acetylation could be a detoxification mechanism in which acetylated |FRAME: GLC| diffuses from the cell |CITS: [7012137] [1856235]|. , There is evidence that |FRAME: GLC| can be oxidized to |FRAME: GLC-D-LACTONE| (glucono-δ-lactone) by inner membrane glucose dehydrogenase. However, the fate of the |FRAME: GLC-D-LACTONE| remains unclear. It has been reported that membrane vesicles from glucose-grown |FRAME:TAX-562| oxidized glucose to gluconate in the presence of |FRAME: PQQ|, a cofactor for glucose dehydrogenase |CITS: [3926746]|. A gluconolactonase (EC 3.1.1.17) has been partially characterized in |FRAME:TAX-562|, but its |FRAME: GLUCONATE| product was not specifically identified |CITS: [4625870]| and no gene encoding this enzyme has been identified. |FRAME: GLUCONATE| can be degraded by a glucose utilization pathway that was described early |CITS: [14882337]|, as shown in the pathway link. In addition, more recent work suggested possible excretion of |FRAME: GLUCONATE| although this compound was not specifically identified |CITS: [20215780]|., |FRAME: GLC-1-P| is reversibly converted by phosphoglucomutase to |FRAME: ALPHA-GLC-6-P|. |FRAME: GLC-1-P| is used in glycogen biosynthesis (see |FRAME: GLYCOGENSYNTH-PWY|) and is produced during glycogen degradation (see |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY|). |FRAME: ALPHA-GLC-6-P| may spontaneously convert to |FRAME: GLC-6-P| in the physiological pH range |CITS: [14275652]|. In addition, a glucose-6-phosphate 1-epimerase had been identified in |FRAME:TAX-562| ATCC 9637 that could catalyze this production of |FRAME: GLC-6-P|., Several phosphatases may catalyze the production of |FRAME: D-Glucose| (anomeric form unspecified) from |FRAME: GLC-1-P|. The product of gene agp is a periplasmic enzyme that scavenges glucose and allows |FRAME:TAX-562| to grow with glucose-1-phosphate as sole carbon source |CITS: [1648777]| and in |CITS: [12782623]|., Reviewed in Mayer, C. and W. Boos (2005) "Hexose/Pentose and Hexitol/Pentitol Metabolism." EcoSal module 3.4.1 |CITS: [ecosal]|.

Summary: General Background, The main input of |FRAME: P-NITROPHENOL| (PNP) into the environment is the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-8973| or |FRAME: PARATHION|, which are commonly used as pesticides in agriculture (see |FRAME:PARATHION-DEGRADATION-PWY |)., PNP is also found in industrial wastes since it is a precursor not only of of pesticides such as carbofuran, nitrofen, methyl parathion and parathion, but also of certain pharmaceuticals, plasticizers, azo dyes, explosives etc. In addition, diesel fuel and gasoline exhaust also contain PNP |CITS: [Tremp93]|. Because of the widespread nature of p-nitrophenol and other nitrophenols, they are considered as major pollutants by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA)., Several bacterial species have the ability to degrade p-nitrophenol. These include Nocardia |CITS:[8250573]|, Arthrobacter |CITS: [8085840]|, |FRAME: TAX-46429| and |FRAME: TAX-262099| |CITS: [Leung97]|, Flavobacterium |CITS: [Raymond71]|, |FRAME: TAX-292| |CITS: [8702398]|, |FRAME: TAX-1421| |CITS: [9647818]|, |FRAME: ORG-6211| |CITS: [15262926]|, Pseudomonas |CITS: [8005]| and |FRAME: TAX-475| |CITS: [16348446]|., In general, aerobic degradation of PNP by Gram-negative bacteria is initiated by formation of |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| (this pathway), while the first intermediate of PNP degradation by Gram-positive bacteria is 4-nitrocatechol (see |FRAME: PWY-5488|) |CITS: [16329872]|. Exceptions, however, do occur. For example, |FRAME: TAX-336938| is a Gram-negative organism that degrades PNP via 4-nitrocatechol |CITS: [17043828]|, and the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-633150| possesses both pathways |CITS: [22380602]|., About This Pathway, The degradation pathway of PNP has been characterized in a |FRAME: TAX-475| strain isolated from activated sludge. In the initial reaction the nitro group of PNP is removed by a |FRAME: MONOMER-13030|, and the resulting |FRAME: P-BENZOQUINONE| is converted to |FRAME:HYDROQUINONE| by |FRAME:MONOMER-13026| before ring cleavage by, |FRAME:MONOMER-13028|. The resulting intermediate, |FRAME:4-HYDROXYMUCONIC-SEMIALDEHYDE| is converted to |FRAME:CPD-294| via |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which is channeled to central metabolism., The genes encoding these enzymes were initially cloned from |FRAME: ORG-5968| and |FRAME: ORG-5947| |CITS: [Zylstra00]|. However, these sequences were not made public, and no functional characterization of the genes was published. Later works have isolated the genes from several other organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-165468| |CITS: [19218392]|, |FRAME: TAX-690235| |CITS: [20049512]| and |FRAME: ORG-6172| |CITS: [20466541]|. These genes were sequenced and analyzed, and the encoded proteins were characterized., Using green fluorescent protein (GFP) labeling, researchers were able to show that the |FRAME:TAX-475| strain can degrade PNP efficiently at concentration as high as 1.4 mM |CITS: [9675864]|, survive in a PNP-spiked soil for more than four weeks |CITS: [10525179]|, and is protected by encapsulation in alginate |CITS: [10670767]|. , Genetically engineered strain of |FRAME:TAX-475| and |FRAME: ORG-5947|, expressing a surface-expressed organophosphorus hydrolase, were able to break down simultaneously PNP and other organophosphorus pesticides, including methyl parathion, parathion, and paraoxon |CITS: [11745159][15932242]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-575 Cyclohexane-1-carboxylate| is formed by oxidative microbial degradation of n-alkylcycloparaffins and anaerobic degradation of benzoate. It also occurs in nature as a functional group in more complex compounds (e.g. polyketide antibiotics from Streptomyces species). Several pathways for its degradation, both aerobic and anaerobic, have been described., An aerobic pathway has been described during the 70s from several organisms |CITS: [4584719][4831062][Blakley74][1202160][207665]|. The pathway has been referred to as the "aromatization pathway", as it involves full aromatization of the ring prior to cleavage. The pathway is initiated by a hydroxylase that generates |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYCYCLOHEXANECARBOXYLATE|, which, following dehydrogenation to form |FRAME: 4-OXOCYCLOHEXANECARBOXYLATE|, is aromatized to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| and subsequently degraded via established protocatechuate metabolism (see |FRAME: P184-PWY|)., The enzyme activities involved in the pathway have been described in the early work, though at the time none of the enzymes has been purified. |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.226|, was purified in 1988, |CITS: [3292236]| |FRAME: EC-1.17.3.5|, in 1993 |CITS: [8281951]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.2|, in 2005 |CITS: [Iwaki 05]|. A 2021 study identified the gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-322009| that encodes the pathway's enzymes. The authors used the information to clone, purify, and characterize the remaining enzymes |CITS: [34583900]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CARNITINE L-Carnitine| is a ubiquitously occurring trimethylammonium compound that plays several roles in metabolism. Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and the name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes, plants, and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. In eukaryotes, among other roles, it is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The physiological role of carnitine in bacteria is still unknown |CITS: [9037756]|. Bacteria are able to metabolize carnitine in multiple ways., Various bacteria utilize an L-carnitine consuming pathway that forms |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| (see |FRAME: CARNMET-PWY|). In this pathway |FRAME: CARNITINE| is used as an alternative electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [Seim80][7815937][15731894]|. |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| accumulates and is released to the environment. When the pathway occurs in gut bacteria, the released |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| is degraded by other organisms in a pathway that releases |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA) (see |FRAME: PWY-8337|)., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-469| species, degrade L-carnitine in a reaction that produces |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| directly (|FRAME: PWY-3641|). These organisms can use L-carnitine as a sole carbon source, but require an alternative nitrogen source |CITS: [25440057]|. This pathway is also used by some gut bacteria, but since the enzyme responsible for this transformation, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.239|, requires oxygen, the pathway is not significant in anaerobic environments |CITS: [24591617]|. It has been estimated that the previous pathway occurs at a rate that is almost 1000-fold higher than the direct formation of TMA |CITS: [25440057]|., Other bacteria, especially |FRAME:TAX-286| species, can assimilate and utilize L-carnitine as the sole source of both carbon and nitrogen. The first catabolic step in this pathway is catalysed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.108| (see |FRAME: PWY-3602|)., In another L-carnitine degradation pathway (this pathway) found in acetogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1736| the compound is demethylated. The methyl group is fed to the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"| |CITS: [32571881]|., About This Pathway, In the mammalian gut, L-carnitine, which is abundant in foodstuff, is primarily dehydrated and reduced to γ-butyrobetaine, which is then converted to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA). TMA is transported in the bloodstream to the liver where it is converted into |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| (TMAO), a compound correlated with the incidence of heart attack, stroke, and death., The acetogenic gut bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1736| degrades L-carnitine in a pathway that does not lead to TMA production. In this pathway L-carnitine is demethylated, producing |FRAME: CPD-24803|, which is not degraded further. The demethylation is calayzed by a system of three proteins - |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.383| (MtcB), |FRAME: MtqC-corrinoid-proteins| (MtqC), and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.389| (MtqA), all of which are highly enriched in cells grown on L-carnitine. The methyl group of carnitine ends up transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N 5-methyltetrahydroholate|, which is processed to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by enzymes of the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood–Ljungdahl pathway"| |CITS: [32571881]|., |FRAME: TAX-1736| strains are known to utilize a number of quaternary amines in addition to |FRAME: CARNITINE|, including |FRAME: BETAINE|, |FRAME: CHOLINE| |CITS: [16345842]|, and |FRAME: CPD-821| |CITS: [31341018]|., The MtqC corrinoid protein is able to be methylated by additional enzymes that transfer the methyl group from other substrates, as has been documented for |FRAME: CPD-821| |CITS: [31341018]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8109|).
