Summary: General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various, insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are, believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness, of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans, was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose, |CITS: [12065209]|. , In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits, of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosil α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus, nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, , including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects, and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein). , In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity,, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation, and no internal hydrogen bond formation. , The combination of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms, trehalose can be used as an external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute, (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a, structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|., In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as, a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|., The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood, |CITS: [11081789]|., About This Pathway, Trehalose has been identified as the exclusive compatible solute in the hyperthermophilic archaeon, |FRAME: TAX-2271|, The |FRAME: G-10766| gene was identified based on its similarity to trehalose related genes from other, organisms. The gene has been cloned, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| and the recombinant gene product was, purified and analyzed for its activity |CITS: [18483808]|., The enzyme catalyzes a reaction similar to that catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-10765|-encoded, |FRAME: CPLX-7634| of |FRAME: TAX-2265| and |FRAME: TAX-53953||CITS: [15364950][15737605]|, (see |FRAME: PWY-5983|). However, the |FRAME: TAX-2271| enzyme is different in two ways: its, prefered substrate is UDP-glucose (rather than ADP-glucose), and the reaction it catalyzes is, unidirectional., Phylogenetic analyses, comparative gene context analyses as well as available biochemical studies, indicate that the unidirectional TreT pathway is present as pathway for trehalose synthesis in several, Archaea and few, selected Bacteria |CITS: [18483808]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, A limited number of species of Gram-negative bacteria, all in the family |FRAME: TAX-543|, utilize unusual sugars, derivatives of 3,6-dideoxyhexose, as |FRAME: O-Antigens| of their lipopolysaccharides. These sugars are the dominant antigenic determinants in the membranes of these organisms., Out of the eight possible stereoisomers of 3,6-dideoxyhexoses, only five have been identified in nature. These are |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: CPD-9396|, |FRAME: CPD-9388|, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: CPD-9395|. All five 3,6-dideoxyhexoses have been found in different serovars of |FRAME: TAX-633|, while other genera possess only some of them. For example, |FRAME: TAX-90371| group B contains |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: TAX-295319| contains ||FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: TAX-90370| contains |FRAME: CPD-9395| |CITS: [8071227]|., These sugars are synthesized via a complex series of enzymatic reactions starting, in most cases, from |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE|, derived from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| (for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9391|, see |FRAME: PWY-5740|)., In a reaction catalyzed by the NAD+-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7584|, |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-658|, which is then converted to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1078| in two consecutive enzymatic reactions, mediated by two components of the |FRAME: CPLX-7585| enzyme complex. The first component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13781| (E1), a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP)-linked iron-sulfur-containing catalyst, while the second, component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13782| (E3), a [2Fe-2S]-containing flavoprotein., The product of this complex, |FRAME: CPD-1078|, is the parent to four different 3,6-dideoxyhexoses. To see the different fates of |FRAME: CPD-1078|, please see |FRAME: PWY-5823|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation |CITS: [8490246]|. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces., Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| |CITS: [25969757]|., Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage., |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| |CITS: [10320813]|., About globo-series glycosphingolipids, Originally, the name "globoside" was used as a generic name for the mucolipids present on human erythrocytes |CITS: [Yamakawa52]|. Later it was used for mucolipids possessing hexosamines as the only nitrogen-containing sugars. A structural analysis of the main component of the mucolipids identifed it as |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINYL-13-D-GALACT globotetraosylceramide| |CITS: [14002302][14002301]| and today the term globoside is a synonym for that compound., Globosides were reported from other tissues beside erythrocytes, including the brain |CITS: [14148094]|, kidney |CITS: [14135465]|, and adrenal gland |CITS: [5416888][3349045]|. Accumulation of large amounts of globosides was tied to Tay-Sachs disease |CITS: [14148094][5688464][5651108]|, and a powerful animal hapten (a small molecule that elicits an immune response only when attached to a large carrier such as a protein) was reported to be a globoside (it is known as |FRAME: FORSSMAN-HAPTEN|) |CITS: [4994225][4363681][4823436]|., The |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"| of glycosphingolipids includes compounds related to globoside that contain the core structure GalNAcβ(1,3)Galα(1,4)Galβ(1,4)Glcβ-Cer. In healthy adult humans, globo-series glycosphingolipids are the major red-cell glycolipids |CITS: [8031119]|, but also occur in kidney |CITS: [9673272]| and on various stem cells |CITS: [21161592]|. The main forms found are |FRAME: Globotriosylceramides globotriosylceramide| and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINYL-13-D-GALACT globotretraosylceramide|, which were named the Pk and P histo-blood group antigens, respectively |CITS: [7010611]|. The latter was shown to be the preferred binding receptor for uropathogenic Escherichia coli |CITS: [9860857]|., In addition, high concentrations of globosides are correlated with certain tumors. The adhesion of human embryonal carcinoma cells was found to be dependent on globoside-mediated carbohydrate-carbohydrate interaction |CITS: [9446552]|. |FRAME: Globotriosylceramides Globotriosylceramide| and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINYL-13-D-GALACT globotretraosylceramide| are the major glycolipid components of fibroblasts in scirrhous gastric carcinoma tissues |CITS: [9548444]|., The variety of globoside compounds keeps increasing. A mannose-containing globoside was isolated from spermatozoa of fresh-water bivalves |CITS: [845129][591501]|. The |FRAME: SSEA3| antigen (SSEA stands for stage-specific embryonic antigen), along with its sialylated and fucosylated forms |FRAME: SSEA4| and |FRAME: Globo-H| |CITS: [2874662][6141938]|, are found exclusively on the cell surface of many cancers, including breast cancer and breast cancer stem cells |CITS: [18685093][18689688][24550271]|. |FRAME: SSEA3| has been named a significant marker for breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs), which are rare cells with the ability of self-renewal and tumor initiation., However, |FRAME: SSEA3| was detected not only in cancer cells. It has been reported from bovine, rat, and normal adult human brain, as well as bovine myelin |CITS: [7595524]|, and |FRAME: SSEA4| was detected in cord blood-derived mesenchymal stem cells |CITS: [21149348]|., The enzyme that forms the core structure that defines the globo series, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.79|, was identified in 1979 from chicken brain |CITS: [4632917]|. A second enzyme that forms the |FRAME: FORSSMAN-HAPTEN| from the core structure was described shortly after |CITS: [4823436][4433547]|. The identities of the enzymes that are responsible for the formation of |FRAME: SSEA3|, |FRAME: SSEA4| and |FRAME: Globo-H| were discovered later |CITS: [10837462][12716912][18685093]|.

Summary: This universal L-proline biosynthesis pathway is found in organisms ranging from bacteria to |FRAME: TAX-9606|, although, the input to the pathway, |FRAME:GLT|, is formed by different means in different organisms., For example, in mammals, L-glutamate is formed in the mitochondrial matrix by an NAD(P)<sup>+</sup>-dependent, glutamate dehydrogenase (EC 1.4.1.3) and transported to the cytoplasm, where the rest of the reactions occur,, while in bacteria glutamate is formed by a NADP+-dependent enzyme (EC 1.4.1.4)., The first two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.7.2.11| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.41|, catalyze the formation of |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, which rearranges spontaneously to form |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|. In higher plants these two reactions are catalyzed by a single bi-functional enzyme in a single , reaction |CITS: [1384052]|. |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:PRO| in a single step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.2|., In addition to being a major constituent of proteins, proline also acts as an osmotic protectant in bacteria, plants and , animals that are under osmotic stress. Abscisic acid (ABA) and salt stress stimulate proline biosynthesis in plants |CITS: [12602867]|. In Arabidopsis, proline can account for up to 20% of the free amino acid pool after salt stress |CITS: [8022935]|. In young Arabidopsis plants, both the ornithine (|FRAME: PWY-3341|) and the glutamate pathways contribute to the increase of proline level during osmotic stress, whereas in adult plants only the glutamate pathway plays an important role in proline accumulation |CITS: [9576796]| . The glutamate pathway was also shown to be the major contributor in proline accumulation upon osmotic stress in salt-stressed month bean plants |CITS: [8103048]|. In Medicago, on the other hand, both the ornithine and the glutamate pathways contribute to the osmotic stress-induced proline accumulation |CITS: [15032841]|.

Summary: During the middle ages a common plague in Europe was caused by the consumption of rye bread. Symptoms varied in different parts of Europe -  convulsions and deep-seated mental problems were called 'St Anthony's fire', while the affliction of blackening of limbs and gangrene was called the 'holy fire'. , The cause for the disease was eventually traced to infection by certain species of fungi. The fungi infect rye and other grasses, where they produce ergot alkaloids (also known as mycotoxins) that cause the disease, now known as ergotism., Ergotism is also one of the explanations that have been offered for the phenomenon of mental affliction that spread among young girls in New England in 1692. These afflictions were blamed on bewitchment, resulting in imprisonment of over 150 people and execution of 20 following the infamous Salem witch trials |CITS: [769159]|., Ergot alkaloids are a complex family of indole derivatives with diverse structures and biological activities. They are toxins, produced by fungi of the families |FRAME: TAX-34397|, |FRAME: TAX-28568| and |FRAME: TAX-34384|., Some of these compounds and their semi-synthetic derivatives are important drugs in modern medicine, such as |FRAME: CPD-12363| and dihydroergotamine, which are used for the treatment of migraines., The early part of the pathway of ergot alkaloids biosynthesis is common to all three families and ends with |FRAME: CPD-14459|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6493|. This important branch point is converted to different products within the different fungal families. The |FRAME: TAX-34397| produce ergoamides and ergoppeptines (as seen here), whereas the |FRAME: TAX-28568| produce clavin-type alkaloids (see |FRAME: PWY-7059|). The nature of the products formed by the |FRAME: TAX-34384| is still not known |CITS: [22403186]|.

Summary: General Background, The prodiginines are a family of red-pigmented antibiotics produced by various actinomycetes and other eubacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-615|. Members of this family include |FRAME: CPD-17025| and its cyclic derivatives |FRAME: CPD-23498| and |FRAME: CPD1A0-6177|, as well as the cometabolites |FRAME: CPD-23499| and |FRAME: CPD-23500|., The prodiginines display a broad range of biological activities. Their cytotoxicity may arise from their ability to bind to DNA and cause double-strand cleavage in the presence of molecular oxygen and copper(II) ions |CITS: [1674696][Melvin00]|. |FRAME: CPD-23501|, a synthetic analogue of |FRAME: CPD-23498| and |FRAME: CPD1A0-6177| also known as GX15-070, is an experimental drug for the treatment of various types of cancer., |FRAME: CPD1A0-6177 "Streptorubin B"| is a red pigmented antibiotic of the prodiginines family that is produced by some actinomycetes. The first description of the compound was made in 1975 |CITS: [1092639]|. The structure assigned to it at that time was incorrect, but the authors corrected the mistake three years later |CITS: [Gerber78]|. The compound was isolated in 1985 from |FRAME: TAX-1902| but was assigned the original, incorrect structure |CITS: [3972724]|. It was isolated from a different strain in 1988, with the authors reporting the correct structure and proposing that all previous isolations are of the same compound |CITS: [2010358]|., The controversy surrounding the structure was reignited in 2005, when once again the compound was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1902| and assigned the incorrect structure |CITS: [15798986]|. However, a careful study performed in 2008 conclusively determined the structure as shown here |CITS: [18291318]|., The structure is rather complex, since transannular strain within the pyrrolophane substructure causes restricted rotation that gives rise to diastereomeric atropisomers. The major atropisomer (88% of the total product) was shown to be the anti form with 7'S configuration |CITS: [21166415]|., About This Pathway, The red gene cluster consists of 23 genes and forms 4 transcription units. It includes two pathway-specific transcriptional regulators, RedD and RedZ., Biosynthetic studies of the prodiginines revealed the formation of the two key intermediates: |FRAME: CPD-17013| (MBC) and |FRAME: CPD-17026| (UP) |CITS: [11514230]|. Labeling studies have demonstrated that MBC is derived from |FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: MET|, and acetate or malonate |CITS: [Wasserman73][Wasserman74][Gerber78]|. The redXWONMI gene products are involved in MBC biosynthesis |CITS: [17003872]|., The redRPQLK gene products, along with the fatty acid biosynthesis enzymes, are involved in the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-17026| (UP) component |CITS: [18291318]|. Condensation of MBC and UP results in |FRAME: CPD-17025| |CITS: [18401500]|, which is cyclized to form |FRAME: CPD1A0-6177| |CITS: [21505498]|.

Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and protein modification, where fatty acyl moieties of proteins modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II. The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|). The pathway catalyzed by the type I systems is available at |FRAME: PWY-5994|., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|. Unlike the type I system that accepts |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of the two-carbon units, the type II systems accept only |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|., About This Pathway, Many Gram-positive organisms, such as the bacilli, staphylococci, and streptomycetes, produce odd- and even-carbon-number branched-chain fatty acids. Branched-chain fatty acids display a lower melting point temperature than their straight-chain equivalents, and their presence in the membrane is expected to increase its fluidity, similar to the effect of unsaturation |CITS: [26300876]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| 95% of the total fatty acids are branched |CITS: [4392505][1886522]|. The most common fatty acids are |FRAME: CPD-9917| (34%), |FRAME: CPD-19657| (24%), |FRAME: CPD-18175| (13%), |FRAME: CPD-23515| (12%), |FRAME: CPD-23509| (9%), and |FRAME: CPD-19660| (4%) |CITS: [28825491]|., The substrate specificity of the FabH condensing enzyme is the determining factor in the biosynthesis of branched-chain fatty acids by type II fatty acid synthases. In organisms that produce non-branched fatty acids such as |FRAME: TAX-562| FabH is specific for |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as the starter molecule. In contrast, the FabH enzymes from organisms that produce branched-chain fatty acids, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, utilize branched-chain acyl-CoA primers much more efficiently than |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (for |FRAME: TAX-1423| the ratio is 100:1) |CITS: [1886522]|. The rest of the enzymes that form the fatty acid synthase system do not have a significant degree of selectivity for either branched-chain or straight-chain fatty acids |CITS: [10629181]|., The most common starter molecules for branched-chain fatty acids are derived from the branched-chain amino acids |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: VAL|, and |FRAME: ILE|. An aminotransferase converts these acids to the α-keto acids |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE|, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, and |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE|, respectively. A specialized α-keto acid dehydrogenase, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25|, is critical for generating the branched-chain acyl-CoA primers for the FabH enzymes (|FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA|, |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, and |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|, respectively) |CITS: [ 3142877]|., The type of primer used determines the type of the branched-chain fatty acid formed. |FRAME: Anteiso-fatty-acids "Anteiso-fatty acids"|, which are derived from |FRAME: ILE|, have an odd number of carbons and are characterized by a methyl-substituent located on the antepenultimate carbon of the carboxyalkyl chain. Anteiso-fatty acids are the most prominent fatty acids of cell membranes of some bacteria, especially of the genus Bacillus. The most relevant anteiso-fatty acids in food and bacteria are |FRAME: CPD-9917| and |FRAME: CPD-23509| |CITS: [28129363]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, In this pathway menaquinone is synthesized from chorismate via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|. In a series of reactions, |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE| is converted to the two-ring compound |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| via several intermediates that include |FRAME: O-SUCCINYLBENZOATE|. At this point a prenyltransferase enzyme attaches a polyprenyl tail to form |FRAME: Demethylmenaquinones|, which can be converted to |FRAME: Menaquinones| by a, dedicated methylase., The first |FRAME: CPD-9733| (DMK-9) was detected in |FRAME: TAX-1351| in 1963 |CITS: [14086754]|. The chemical structure was reported by the same authors two years later |CITS: [14321383]|. This finding was later corroborated by a study of the distribution of isoprenoid quinones in Streptococci of the serological groups D and N |CITS: [118232]|., DMK-9 was initially reported to be the only quinone in |FRAME: TAX-1351|, but it was later shown that DMK-8 is also present |CITS: [11722738]|., Some of the |FRAME: TAX-1351| genes encoding enzymes of this pathway have been identifed and knocked out. The corresponding mutants were not able to synthesize DMK-8 and DMK-9 |CITS: [11722738]|.

Rice (Oryza sativa) is capable of producing a broad scope of about 15 different types of antimicrobial compounds in response to pathogenic attacks, for instance by the rice blast fungus |FRAME:TAX-318829| |CITS:[16956633] [20615111]|. Apart from the flavanone |FRAME:CPD-7079| (see |FRAME:PWY-5116|) all other phytoalexins formed in rice are diterpenoids such as momilactones (this pathway), phytocassanes (see |FRAME:PWY-7484|), oryzalide (see |FRAME:PWY-7481|) and oryzalexine (see |FRAME:PWY-7478|, |FRAME:PWY-7489|, |FRAME:CPD-16616|). The latter belong to the labdane-related diterpenoids which basic formation is realized by bicyclyzation of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| catalyzed by copalyl/labdadienyl diphosphate synthases (CPS) |CITS:[15341631] [15542489]|. The further cyclization/rearrangement of the resulting |FRAME:CPD-8719| or |FRAME:ENT-COPALYL-DIPHOSPHATE| are carried out by proteins of the kaurene synthase like (KSL) type (see |FRAME:PWY-2981|) |CITS:[17141283]| to form the various olefins which give rise to the above mentioned diterpenoid phytoalexin subclasses., In contrast to microbes where gene clusters of co-regulated genes referred to as operons are a common feature in their genetic makeup |CITS:[18216259]| higher plants are rather known for the disparate distribution of unlinked genes in their genomes |CITS:[19662496]|. However, the discovery of physically linked groups of genes which are functionally connected and coregulated are an emerging theme in plant metabolism |CITS:[20921179]|. So far only a few of those gene clusters have been reported such as for the biosynthesis of benzoxazinoids in maize (see |FRAME:PWY-6949|), the triterpenoids avenacins in oat (see |FRAME:PWY-7473|, |FRAME:PWY-7474|) and thalianol in Arabidopsis (see |FRAME:PWY-5992|) and the various diterpenoid phytoalexin classes in rice (this pathway, |FRAME:PWY-7478|, |FRAME:PWY-7481|, |FRAME:PWY-7484|) which originate from biosynthetic gene clusters on chromosome 2 and 4 |CITS:[19662496]|. , According to their function as defense compounds against pathogen attacks the momilactones biosynthesis is inducible by various chemical and environmental factors such as the elicitors chitin oligosaccharide |CITS:[19635799]|, |FRAME:CHOLATE| |CITS:[18045629]| and UV |CITS:[17498837]| and is also triggered by the plant hormone |FRAME:CPD-734| |CITS:[12226190]|. Besides their role as phytoalexins |FRAME:CPD-7092| and |FRAME:CPD-16731| have been recognized as allelochemicals |CITS:[15077625]| involved in fending off the invasion of neighboring plants such as Lepidium sativum (cress) and Lactuca sativa (lettuce) |CITS:[12809715] [12081533]|, Echinochloa crus-galli (barnyardgrass) |CITS:[21758010]| and Alisma plantago-aquatica (mad-dog weed, common water plantain) |CITS:[Mennan12]|. , Momilactones have first been discovered in rice, characterized as growth inhibitors and structural elucidated |CITS:[Kato73] [Cartwright81]| and are one of the few natural diterpenoid phytoalexins for which a total synthesis in the laboratory has been achieved |CITS:[12126415]|. Although all of the diterpenoid phytoalexis observed in rice seem rather specific and appear to be restricted to the plant family Poaceae exceptions occur which indicate a broader distribution of these compounds within the realm of plants. Besides in rice |FRAME:CPD-7092| and |FRAME:CPD-16731| have been reported in the bryophytes, i.e. the moss Hypnum plumaeforme |CITS:[18071239]| where they are secreted in the environment proposed to act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents to ensure pure and healthy colonies of the moss |CITS:[19820317]|. The occurrence of both mamilactones in the taxonomically distant moss has been discussed as a convergent or parallel evolution event reinforcing the defense system of the respective plants |CITS:[21620514]|. As observed in rice |FRAME:CPD-734| also induces the biosynthesis of momilactones in Hypnum plumaeforme indicating that the formation of momilactones relates to biotic and abiotic stressors to which the moss might be exposed |CITS:[19232772]|. , The |FRAME:PWY-7477| pathway and its reaction sequence is only partially known. The function of the cytochrome P450 dependend syn-pimaradiene oxidase (CYP99A3) catalyzing the formation of the momilactone intermediate |FRAME:CPD-13923| has been determined, its encoding gene identified and the biochemistry of the reaction characterized. The observed transformation on C19 from a methyl to a carboxylic acid is one of the structural features of |FRAME:CPD-7092| |CITS:[21175892]| and the enzyme has been shown to be part of the momilactone biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS:[17872948]|. In order to complete the eponymous 19,6-γ-lactone ring of |FRAME:CPD-7092| the C6β-position must be hydroxylated which has been demonstrated with a multifunctional cytochrome P450 dependent 6-hydroxylase which utilized |FRAME:CPD-4754| yielding |FRAME:CPD-16670| |CITS:[22215681]|. However, it remains to be corroborated if this enzyme is involved at all and if so at what point of the biosynthetic sequence the 6β-hydroxylation occurs. The last step of the |FRAME:CPD-7092| formation is realized by the |FRAME:MONOMER-13863| which catalyzes the ketonization of the hydroxyl group at C3 |CITS:[17872948]|.

Summary: General Background, Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight |CITS: [Overmann92]|., Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10-30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics., The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C31 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-132-methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates |CITS: [16245042]|., Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported., In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-82 and C-121 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-82 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. , |FRAME: CPD-9092 "Bacteriochlorophyll c"| is more efficient than |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| at limiting red and near-infrared light intensities. Thus the latter is more commonly found in shallow lakes, while the former is found at deeper water., About This Pathway, The pathways leading to |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| diverge from that for |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| and |FRAME: CPD-9067| after |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| is formed., The pathway starts with the removal of the C-132-methylcarboxyl moiety, forming |FRAME: CPD-18841| |CITS: [21550979]|., Two radical-SAM (S-adenosyl-lmethionine) oxidative methyltransferases, |FRAME: G-44408 BchR| and |FRAME: G-44409 BchQ|, add methyl groups to the C-121 ethyl and C-82 methyl carbons, respectively |CITS: [17586634]|. The latter can add a second methyl group at the same position. These four different forms (non-methylated, mono-methylated, di-methylated and tri-methylated) serve as substrates to the hydratases BchV (most of them can also serve as substrate for BchF, a homologous enzyme that is primarily involved in |FRAME: PWY-5526|). These enzymes hydrate the C-31 carbon, converting the vinyl group to the 1-hydroxyethyl group that is necessary for the aggregation of the chlorophyll molecules inside the chlorosomes. The hydroxyl group produces a chiral center. Experiments looking at the stereo-specificity of the two enzymes were inconclusive, as different results were obtained in vivo and in vitro. However, it was shown that in the absence of BshF the bacteria produced higher ratios of (S) epimers to (R) epimers |CITS: [26331578]|., At this point the pathways for |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| and |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| diverge. The only difference between the two is the presence of a methyl group at the C20 methine bridge position in the former. Thus, the next step in |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| biosynthesis is C20 methylation, which is catalyzed by a methyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-44417| gene |CITS: [15090495]|., Interestingly, a copy of the |FRAME: G-44417| gene was found in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1098| that produces only |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"|. However, the gene contained a frameshift mutation that inactivated it. A spontaneous mutant of this strain that produces |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| has a second frameshift mutation that restores the correct reading frame |CITS: [15090495]|. It has been suggested that activation/inactivation of the gene may be an adaptation mechanism for changing environments |CITS: [15292118]|., The last step in the pathway is the attachment of the farnesyl tail, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44411 "BchK synthase"|, which is specific for bacteriochlorophyll c, d and e |CITS: [12029054]|.

Names: farnesylcysteine salvage pathway // farnesylcysteine detoxification pathway // (E,E)-farnesyl diphosphate biosynthesis II // all trans-farnesyl diphosphate biosynthesis II // farnesylcysteine from farnesylated protein salvage pathway
Summary: Protein prenylation is an important regulatory modification that can often affect the ability of proteins to interact with membranes or other proteins. Through a series of successive reactions, prenylated proteins typically end up with a C-terminal cysteine residue bearing a farnesylcysteine or geranylgeranylcysteine methyl ester. Therefore, during the process of prenylated protein degradation, |FRAME: CPD-12581| or |FRAME: CPD-20307| are typically released |CITS: [17425716][19969520]|. The pathway depicted here shows a way that these isoprenylcysteine compounds can be recycled for further use in the cell while preventing the accumulation of potentially dangerous substances. For instance, free |FRAME: CPD-12581| can cause problems for cells by acting as a competitive inhibitor of regulatory isoprenylcysteine methyltransferases (ICMTs) that modify prenylated proteins |CITS: [19969520]|. And, |FRAME: 2-TRANS6-TRANS-FARNESOL| can be toxic at high levels |CITS: [10938345]|. Meanwhile, |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is an important compound used for protein prenylation, sterol biosynthesis, and sesquiterpene biosynthesis |CITS: [10557276]|., Although this pathway has been hypothesized to occur in |FRAME: ORG-5993| and other important enzymatic activities associated with the pathway have been detected in |FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-4120|, there is no direct evidence for all of the enzymes present in the pathway in any one species. It is also unclear what other species this pathway is likely to exist in. Given the widespread occurence of prenylated proteins and biosynthetic pathways that utilize |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| in the plant kingdom, numerous plant species may use this pathway. However, there are alternative mechanisms for metabolizing |FRAME: CPD-12581| and farnesylcysteine methyl esters that depend on the activity of flavin-dependent monooxygenases or cysteine Β-lyases shown to exist in pigs and rats |CITS:[8199308] [2318851]| which may also exist in some plants. Yeast also certainly generate farnesylated proteins |CITS: [1917931]|, but the fate of |FRAME: CPD-12581| and farnesylcysteine methyl esters in fungi is unknown. Currently, there is no evidence for the existence of this pathway in prokaryotes., Interestingly, blocks in early steps in this pathway can affect biological processes that depend on protein prenylation. For instance, |FRAME: CPD-693 abscisic acid (ABA)|-mediated signaling in |FRAME: ORG-5993| involves the targeted methylation of the farnesylcysteine residue on prenylated proteins via isoprenylcysteine methyltransferases (ICMTs). Normal ABA signaling is disrupted when mutants with lowered farnesylcysteine lyase activity have elevated levels of free |FRAME: CPD-12581| that acts as a competitive inhibitor of ICMTs |CITS: [17425716][19969520]|.

General Background, The thiol-containing compound |FRAME: CPD0-1262| is used in several different technologies. A strain of |FRAME: TAX-34073| isolated aerobically from soil was found to utilize |FRAME: CPD0-1262| as a sole source of carbon and sulfur. The unique, key enzyme in the pathway was found to be mercaptosuccinate dioxygenase, a homolog of the cysteine dioxygenases that are found in a variety of organisms |CITS: [25228698]|. , About This Pathway, In an update |CITS: [25228698]| of the previously proposed mercaptosuccinate degradation pathway |CITS: [21075928]| in |FRAME: TAX-1246301|, |FRAME: CPD0-1262| is converted to the highly unstable intermediate |FRAME: CPD-17260|, which spontaneously hydrolyzes to |FRAME: SUC| and |FRAME: SO3|. The toxic |FRAME: SO3| is putatively converted to |FRAME: SULFATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.8.2.1|. |FRAME: SUC "Succinate"| enters central metabolism |CITS: [25228698]|.

tRNAs are the molecular adapters that carry amino acids and enable the synthesis of proteins based on mRNAs transcribed from protein-coding genes. The active form of tRNA is generated by a combination of nuclease-based processing, the modification of select nucleosides, and finally charging with an amino acid via the |FRAME: TRNA-CHARGING-PWY|., The processing of tRNA in |FRAME: TAX-2157| and |FRAME: TAX-2759| involves the splicing of introns by a mechanism that involves protein enzymes (unlike mRNA splicing, which is RNA catalyzed). While there are some examples of tRNA intron splicing in prokaryotes, that process occurs via the so called "primitive" autocatalytic mechanism and does not involve dedicated enzymes., Much of the knowledge about tRNA intron splicing comes from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|, in which 25% (59) of tRNA genes contain introns |CITS: [15684411]|. In humans, only 6% of tRNA genes contain introns |CITS: [9023104]|. All eukaryotic tRNA introns are 14-60 nucleotides in length and interrupt the anticodon loop one nucleotide 3' to the anticodon., Splicing of the introns from the precursor tRNA is accomplished in metazoa through the action of a site-specific endonuclease and a specialized ligase. The tRNA splicing endonuclease, a complex of four different subunits, cleaves pre-tRNA at the 5' and 3' splice sites to release the intron. The products of this cleavage are an intron and two tRNA half-molecules, one bearing a 2',3' cyclic phosphate terminus and the other bearing a 5'-OH terminus |CITS: [6186398]|. |FRAME: EC-6.5.1.8| (|FRAME: HS02006|), which is not found in yeast or plants, joins the two tRNA halves to mature-sized tRNAs in a single step. This ligase differs from the "classic" ligases, which join strands with 5'-phosphate to strands with 3'-hydroxyl |CITS: [26385509]|. RTCB is part of the |FRAME: CPLX-9136|, which includes several other subunits, some of which have been shown to be involved in activation of the catalytic component RTCB |CITS: [24870230]|., The pathway found in yeast is described in |FRAME: PWY-6689|.

Summary: |FRAME: Poly-Gamma-Glutamylcysteine-Glycines Phytochelatins| are oligomers of glutathione that function as metal chelators and are vital for heavy metal detoxification by organisms |CITS: [19224399]|. They are widely distributed among living organisms including fungi, algae, nematodes and higher plants. , Phytochelatins are formed by the action of the enzyme phytochelatin synthase |CITS: [21369921]|. The enzyme mechanism has been studied in detail and it appears that the substrate is glutathione molecules with blocked thiol groups. Increase in the amount of heavy metals leads to glutathione being blocked, which in turn results in increased phytochelatin synthase activity in the cells |CITS: [19067014][19017114 ]|. In higher plants the phytochelatins are transported to the vacuoles for the sequestering of metal ions away from proteins in the cytosol.

Note: click on the More Detail button at the top of the page to see the enzymes involved in this pathway., General Background, |FRAME: CPD-11406 Thyronamine| and its iodinated derivatives are a novel class of signaling molecules that are distinct from thyronines in their lack of the carboxylate group of the β-alanine side chain. Their physiological roles and their biosynthetic pathways are incompletely understood. They may be synthesized de novo, or they may be derived from iodothyronines, possibly by decarboxylation catalyzed by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (in |CITS: [18279024] [16131336] [15146179] [18339710]|). Only |FRAME: CPD-11405| and |FRAME: CPD-11406| have been identified in vivo |CITS: [15146179]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19016324]| and |CITS: [20880963]|. Using a reliable and sensitive monoclonal antibody-based immunoassay for monitoring |FRAME: CPD-11405| levels in human serum, patient studies suggested that it is mainly produced in extrathyroidal tissues |CITS: [21490071]|., It has been shown in vitro that the entire series of iodothyronamines, like iodothyronines, are substrates for the three types of vertebrate iodothyronine deiodinases, Dio1, Dio2 and Dio3. This supports a role for these deiodinases in |FRAME: CPD-11406| biosynthesis |CITS: [18339710]|. Also see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6260| and |FRAME: PWY-6261|., About This Pathway, In this pathway only |FRAME: CPD-11405| and |FRAME: CPD-11406| have been identified in vivo. Their functional roles as well as the potential roles of the other metabolites shown remain to be completely elucidated. Using a novel liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry based method, |FRAME: CPD-11406| and its iodinated derivatives were identified and quantitated |CITS: [18339710]|. They were also shown in assays to be isozyme-specific substrates for the three types of deiodinase isozymes. The isozymes used in this study were derived from human cell lines (Dio1, Dio2 or Dio3), or mouse liver membrane preparations (Dio1) |CITS: [18339710]|., Dio1 in the human HepG2 cell line lysate and Dio2 in the human MSTO-211H cell line lysate deiodinated |FRAME: CPD-13022| and |FRAME: CPD-13020| at the phenolic (outer) ring. Dio3 in the human ECC-1 cell line lysate deiodinated thyronamines containing iodine atoms in the tyrosyl (inner) ring., None of the enzymes in this study catalyzed the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13023| to |FRAME: CPD-13021|, |FRAME: CPD-13021| to |FRAME: CPD-13019|, or |FRAME: CPD-13016| to |FRAME: CPD-11406|. It was suggested that species-specific factors may modulate the substrate specificity of deiodinase isozymes in different species |CITS: [18339710] [18821722]|. In this study, Dio1 preparations from human HepG2 cells and mouse liver membrane preparations showed some differences in substrate specificity. Overall, these data also suggested a deiodinase-catalyzed route for |FRAME: CPD-11405| and |FRAME: CPD-11406| biosynthesis |CITS: [18339710]|.

Summary: General Background, Antibiotics are secondary metabolites, a diverse group of chemicals that are produced by a few common biosynthetic pathways. Naturally occurring β-lactam antibiotics contain the β-lactam ring and are classified into five groups according to their chemical structure: penams (e.g. penicillins), ceph-3-ems (e.g. cephalosporins, cephamycins), clavams (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9261|), carbapenems (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-9377|, thienamycins) and monolactams (e.g. nocardicins, monobactams). Penams are only produced by filamentous fungi. Ceph-3-ems are produced by both filamentous fungi and bacteria, while the remaining three classes of beta-lactams are produced by bacteria. Reviewed in |CITS: [16322742]| and |CITS: [9729600]|., Penicillins, cephalosporins and cephamycins are produced by different organisms from branches of a common pathway. The pathway branches at isopenicillin N to form penicillins and branches again at deacetylcephalosporin to form cephalosporins and cephamycins (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|)., The pathways for biosynthesis of the bicyclic carbapenem and clavam antibiotics see |FRAME: PWY-5737| and |FRAME: PWY-5679|) differ from the classic β-lactam pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5634|). The pathway for nocardicin A biosynthesis is also different, but it has only been partially elucidated and the order of some known reactions is unclear. However, some of the enzymes of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and characterized (see enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13594| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13595|)., The antibacterial mechanism of action of β-lactam antibiotics involves inhibition of the transpeptidation reaction during bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis, which leads to cell lysis. This reaction is catalyzed by class A and class B penecillin binding proteins. It is specifically inhibited by penicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics via formation of a covalent complex with the active serine of the transpeptidation domain of penicillin binding proteins. This prevents crosslinking and weakens the peptidoglycan polymer (in |CITS: [12867450]|). See pathways |FRAME: PEPTIDOGLYCANSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5265|. Bacterial resistance to β-lactam antibiotics can involve alterations in penicillin binding proteins, reduced antibiotic permeation across the membrane, or the production of β-lactamase enzymes (in |CITS:[12195735]|). See enzymes |FRAME: EG10040-MONOMER|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13427| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13428|., About This Pathway, The antibiotic cephamycin C is produced by bacteria. Its biosynthesis is less well characterized than that of penicillins and cephalosporins, but has been studied in |FRAME:TAX-1901|. The first two reactions in the cephamycin C pathway (shown in the pathway link) producing isopenicillin N are shared with penicillin and cephalosporin biosynthesis. The next reaction is the first committed step in cephalosporin and cephamycin biosynthesis in which the L-α-aminoadipate side chain in isopenicillin N is isomerized to the D enantiomer, producing penicillin N. In subsequent steps the penam thiazolidine ring is oxidatively opened and expanded to a six-membered dihydrothiazine ring characteristic of ceph-3-ems. Deacetylcephalosporin C is a branch point in the pathway that leads to the biosynthesis of both cephamycin C and cephalosporins., Three reactions lead to the conversion of deacetylcephalosporin C to cephamycin C. As shown in the literature, in the first reaction the C-3' hydroxyl group of deacetylcephalosporin C is carbamoylated by deacetylcephalosporin C-carbamoyltransferase. Then the C-7 position undergoes hydroxylation, followed by methylation of the hydroxylated intermediate to form cephamycin C (7-methoxycephalosporin C). However, it has been noted that the sequential order of the carbamoylation and methoxylation reactions has not been firmly established, nor has the nature of the cofactors used in the last two reactions (in |CITS: [16527306]|). Evidence suggests that a two-protein system composed of the products of genes cmcI (P7) and cmcJ (P8) is involved in both of these reactions in |FRAME: TAX-1913 "Amycolatopsis lactamdurans (previously known as Nocardia lactamdurans)"| |CITS: [7721717]|. The x-ray structure of CmcI from S. clavuligerus suggests that it is a S-adenosylmethionine utilizing methyltransferase |CITS: [16527306]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [9729600]| and |CITS: [12749845]|.

Summary: This arginine catabolic pathway has been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-287| by Mercenier et al, |CITS:[6768836]|. , The pathway is essentially identical to an anabolic pathway that is used by higher plants, and many, bacteria, for the biosynthesis of putrescine (see  |FRAME:PWY-43| |CITS:[Smith64][12435743]|. , However, there are indications that in |FRAME: TAX-287| the pathway also operates in a catabolic form,, where the putrescine formed from arginine is degraded further to provide the bacteria with carbon and nitrogen. , When grown on arginine as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, the activity of |FRAME:CPLX-13|, increased significantly, and the addition of |FRAME:AGMATHINE| and |FRAME:CPD-597|, increased the synthesis of |FRAME:CPLX-31| and |FRAME:CPLX-39|.  In addition, adding succinate,, citrate, glutamine, or ammonia to the medium led to the repression of these enzymes, indicating that the, pathway is regulated by both carbon catabolite repression as well as nitrogen catabolite repression, |CITS:[6768836]|., While there are several reports supporting the function of this pathway as a catabolic arginine, degradation pathway |CITS:[6423933][11673419][12634339]|, it is clear that the main catabolic arginine, pathway in Pseudomonads is the succinyltransferase pathway (see, |FRAME:AST-PWY|).  In addition, unlike the case in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, where there are two varieties, of arginine decarboxylase, a biosynthetic variety and a degradative variety, there is no indication for the, presence of a homolog of the degradative form in |FRAME: TAX-287|.  Thus, there is still some debate, whether this is a true arginine degradation pathway. , However, it is agreed that at least the last two steps of the pathway are used for catabolic, |FRAME:AGMATHINE| degradation |CITS:[12634339]|., It should be noted that while this pathway has been studied mostly in |FRAME: TAX-287|, it was also, observed in |FRAME: TAX-648| |CITS:[6303241]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium Selenium| is an essential micronutrient for animals and humans but has not yet been proven to be an essential micronutrient for land plants |CITS: [11683552][16307305]|. There is evidence, however, of Chlamydomonas proteins that contains a |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| residue suggesting that algal species might also require |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [17105189][12110581]|. The health requirement of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for humans and animals can be met by crops and forage plants that contain selenocompounds. |FRAME: TAX-4232| among the oilseed crops was shown to be a good source for this micronutrient |CITS: [15012198]|. In addition, there is evidence that certain seleno-compounds, including |FRAME: CPD-12024|, have anti-carcinogenic properties |CITS: [21213327][14748935]|. , Despite its importance as a micronutrient, higher concentrations of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| are toxic to humans, other animals, and plants largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064][12753978][16661781]|. , In general, plants take up both |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE| from soil. A series of |FRAME: PWY-6932 reduction steps| converts |FRAME: SELENATE| to |FRAME: SE-2| / |FRAME: CPD-678| and this is assimilated into the seleno-amino acids |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19309459]|., In Se accumulator plants, these seleno-amino acids may be modified to create organic seleno-compounds for storage. Seasonal weeds like |FRAME: TAX-3575| and |FRAME: TAX-83445| along with perennial weeds like |FRAME: TAX-41550| employ this strategy and accumulate high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [19800657]|. Se accumulation can help to protect plants against attacks by prairie dogs, insects, and fungi (see refs in |CITS: [21628258]|)., Other plants, like |FRAME: ORG-5993| generate seleno-compounds as well, but rather than storing them, they transform them into less toxic volatile compounds, such as |FRAME: CPD-12006| (DMDSe) that can then be released from the plants |CITS: [10759525]|. This process is also called phytovolatilization |CITS: [19656903]|. , While these strategies directly benefit the plants that employ them, they can also be put to use for the phytoremediation of seleniferous soils that contain dangerously high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium|. Numerous insights into endogenous seleno-compound metabolism in plants have been gained through efforts to engineer plants that show improved selenium phytoremediation abilities |CITS: [15005814][19800657][19893365][17445958][10759525]|., About this pathway, To reduce the risk of misincorporating |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| into proteins, this compound can be methylated to form the non-coding seleno-amino acid |FRAME: CPD-12024|. Some Se hyperaccumulating plants may contain very high levels of this compound., In addition Se-non-accumulators and accumulators may also further metabolize |FRAME: CPD-12024| to produce the volatile |FRAME: CPD-12006|. For example, this compound, and not |FRAME: CPD-12005| appears to be the only seleno-volatile compound produced by the hyperaccumulator |FRAME: TAX-20406| whereas both are made by |FRAME:TAX-3707| |CITS: [14671009]|., The exact steps involved in this pathway have not been elucidated. It is possible that a series of reactions involving first a |FRAME: CPD-13774| intermediate and then a methaneseleniol intermediate are required, similar to the enzymatic steps observed for dimethyldisulfide biosynthesis |CITS: [16307305]|., It is also possible that some of the |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| can be shunted toward |FRAME: CPD-12005| production if enzymes such as the bacterial thiopurine methyltransferase are found to occur in plants |CITS:[12003960] [16307305]|., |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE Selenocysteine| may also be used to form |FRAME: CPD-13788| as this compound has been seen to accumulate in Arabidopsis over-expressing a selenocysteine methyltransferase enzyme and natively, in the hyperaccumulator |FRAME: TAX-20406| |CITS: [NIGAM69A][5370015][16307305]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:ACET Acetate| production from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| can occur via several distinct pathways, which are found in different organisms., Many bacterial and archaeal species produce acetate from acetyl CoA via a two-step pathway in which |FRAME:ACETYL-P| occurs as an intermediate (see |FRAME:PWY0-1312|) |CITS: [21941]|. The second reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME:EC-2.7.2.1|, results in the generation of ATP from ADP., In most archaea |CITS: [8830684]|, some eubacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-971| |CITS: [Michel90]| and |FRAME: TAX-1108| |CITS: [24164217]|), and amitochondriate protists (such as |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [13076]| and |FRAME: TAX-5741| |CITS: [8557109]|) acetate is produced from acetyl CoA in a single step via the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.2.1.13|. In this process, the formation of acetate from acetyl CoA concomitantly produces ATP from ADP (see |FRAME:PWY-5535|)., A third pathway was described from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-316277|, where acetate is produced from acetyl CoA in a single step via the enzyme |FRAME:EC-6.2.1.1|. Unlike in the previous pathway, ATP is produced from AMP (see |FRAME:PWY-8328|)., A fourth variant (|FRAME:PWY-5536|) is found in a diverse group of organisms, which includes some bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-33011| |CITS: [33931420]|), the hydrogenosome-containing trichomonads (such as |FRAME: TAX-56690| and |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [3090435]|), some anaerobic fungi (such as |FRAME: TAX-73818| |CITS: [8257282]|), the parasitic helminth |FRAME: TAX-6192| |CITS: [681067][421954][8885873]| and the trypanosomatides |CITS: [9501211][15326192]|. These organisms produce acetate from acetyl CoA by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.18| (ASCT), an enzyme that transfers the CoA group from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME:SUC|, producing |FRAME: SUC-COA|. |FRAME: SUC-COA| is restored to |FRAME:SUC| by |FRAME:CPLX-7458|, a TCA cycle enzyme that generates ATP from ADP., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-5691|, one of the causative agents of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), alternates during its life cycle between the bloodstream of its mammalian host and the blood-feeding tsetse fly, |FRAME: TAX-7393|., The parasite exhibits different cellular morphology during its life cycle. In the mammalian bloodstream it exhibits a long, slender morphology, while in the insect host it exhibits a stubby morphology known as procyclic cells. Profound differences exist in the metabolism of the two life cycle phases., In the procyclic stage the mitochondrion is directly involved in the degradation of substrates, in contrast to the situation in the long slender bloodstream stage. |FRAME: PYRUVATE Pyruvate| enters the mitochondrion and is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|, into |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| (see |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|). The acetyl-CoA is not degraded to carbon dioxide via the |FRAME:TCA|, but is converted into |FRAME:ACET| |CITS: [15326192]|., This reaction is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.18| (ASCT), an enzyme that transfers the CoA group from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME:SUC|, producing |FRAME: SUC-COA|., Several other organisms have been shown to catalyze this reaction, including the hydrogenosome-containing trichomonads (such as |FRAME: TAX-56690| and |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [3090435]|), some anaerobic fungi (such as |FRAME: TAX-73818||CITS: [8257282]|), the parasitic helminth |FRAME: TAX-6192| |CITS: [681067][421954][8885873]|, and the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-33011|. Phylogenetic analysis suggests it occurs in other bacterial species that belong to 5 different phyla (Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Proteobacteria) |CITS: [33931420]|. , A knockout mutant of |FRAME: TAX-5691| depleted for ASCT showed a reduced acetate production, supporting the role of this enzyme in acetate production. However, ASCT mutants still excrete acetate from glucose metabolism, implying that ASCT is not the only acetate-producing pathway in this parasite |CITS: [15326192]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, Carotenes are oxygenated in various ways (hydroxylation, epoxydation, de-epoxidation) to form xanthophylls, which comprise most of the carotenoid pigments in the thylakoid membranes. Hydroxylations play an important role in the oxygenation of carotenes and are catalyzed by hydroxylases acting specifically onto β or ε rings., |FRAME: CPD1F-130| is one of the most common carotenoid alcohols found in nature. It is the pigment that gives corn, saffron, and many other plants their characteristic color. Zeaxanthin breaks down to form |FRAME: CPD-8668| and |FRAME: CPD-8669|, which are responsible for the taste and aroma of saffron. Mono- and di-glucosylated forms of zeaxanthin are found in some strains of |FRAME: TAX-53335|, namely |FRAME: TAX-549| and |FRAME: TAX-553| |CITS: [1946693][2254247]|.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|.|., The TCA cycle is so named because the first step in the pathway is the condensation of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT citrate|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The cycle is also known as the citric acid cycle, the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle and the Krebs cycle, named after the scientists who first described it., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA acetyl-CoA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET acetate| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE pyruvate|, which is generated by |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., One turn of the cycle in eukaryotes produces 3 molecules of |FRAME: NADH NADH|, one molecule of |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol| and 2 molecules of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE CO2|., The reduced molecules of NADH and quinol serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation. As electrons flow throught the electron transport chain to a terminal acceptor, protons are pumped across the inner mitochondrial membrane generating a proton motive force (PMF). When the protons return to the mitochondrial matrix, they power ATP synthase which phosphorylates ADP to ATP. The total energy gained from the catabolism of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation is about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., About This Pathway, There are several differences between the mammalian TCA cycle, which is described here, and the TCA cycles that occur in prokaryotes (the most common of which is described in |FRAME:TCA TCA cycle I (prokaryotic)|., One difference concerns isocitrate dehydrogenase. The mammalian |FRAME: CPLX66-11 "isocitrate dehydrogenase"| (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.41 "EC 1.1.1.41"|) uses NAD+ as a cofactor, as opposed to the prokaryotic NADP+-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.42 "EC 1.1.1.42"|). Mammals do possess an NADP+-dependent isozyme, but it is used in glutamate biosynthesis and does not participate in the TCA cycle |CITS: [2198251]|., Another difference concerns the conversion of |FRAME: MAL (S)-malate| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID oxaloacetate|. This step is catalyzed in mammals by an NAD+-dependent |FRAME: HS07366-MONOMER "malate dehydrogenase"| (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37 "EC 1.1.1.37"|). In some prokaryotic organisms this step of the cycle is catalyzed by an NADP+-dependent |FRAME: EG12069-MONOMER malate:quinone oxidoreductase| (|FRAME: EC-1.1.5.4 "EC 1.1.5.4"|)., The last difference regards the conversion of |FRAME: SUC-COA| to |FRAME: SUC|. While the prokaryotic pathway, as well as the pathway that operates in plants and fungi (see |FRAME: PWY-5690|), utilize only an ATP-dependent enzyme to catalyze this interconversion, the mammalian TCA cycle utilizes two isoforms, |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.5| and |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.4|. The level of utilization of each isoform is tissue-dependent |CITS: [15234968]|. It is believed that the ATP-forming enzyme is used for oxidatve phosphorylation, while the GTP-forming enzyme directs its product towards anabolic reactions |CITS: [15234968]|. This is the only difference between the mammalian pathway and the one found in plants and fungi., Flux through the cycle is regulated on many different levels. Although |FRAME: CPLX66-272 pyruvate dehydrogenase complex| is not a component of the cycle, it plays a pivotal role in determining TCA cycle flux |CITS: [Salway]|. |FRAME: CPLX-7863 "Citrate synthase"|, |FRAME: CPLX66-11 isocitrate dehydrogenase (NAD)| and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 2-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex| are other major regulators of the cycle. At the protein modification level, lysine acetylation of enzymes controls cycle activity |CITS: [20167786]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Cardiac-Glycosides "Cardiac glycosides"| are plant-made compounds (mostly by members of the |FRAME: TAX-4163| genus, or Foxgloves) that have beneficial effects over patients with cardiac failure. The treatment of congestive heart failure (dropsy), among other ailments like tuberculosis, by the use of Foxglove is mentioned in writings as early as 1250 A. D., when the Welsh Physicians of Myddva collected foxglove as one of their many herbs and included it in their remedies |CITS: [28561136]|. As of 2019, the Digitalis cardenolides do not play a major role in the cardiovascular drug market. However, their use in the treatment of other diseases, such as cancer or viral infections, may make them commercially important again |CITS: [28561136]|., The cardiac glycosides are composed of two structural features: a sugar moiety that may contain one or more saccharides, and a steroid aglycone. Most cardiac glycosides have a terminal glucose, and are stored in the vacuole. They have been named primary glycosides. Compounds lacking the terminal glucose are called secondary glycosides and are located in the cytoplasm., There are two classes of cardiac glycosides differing by the group attached at the 17-position of the aglycone: the |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolides"|, which have a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring (but-2-en-4-olide ring) and the |FRAME: Bufadienolide-Glycosides bufadienolides|, which have a six membered doubly unsaturated lactone ring (penta-2,4-dien-5-olide ring)., The steroid nucleus of the cardiac glycosides has a unique configuration: rings A/B and C/D are cis- fused while rings B/C are trans- fused. The nucleus has β configured hydroxyls at the positions C-3 and C-14, and many compounds have additional hydroxyl groups at positions 12 and 16. The sugars found in the glycoside moiety range from common hexoses and pentoses (such as |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-Xylose|) to very uncommon sugars, some of which have only been found in cardiac glycosides (e.g. |FRAME: D-quinovopyranose|, |FRAME: CPD-22597|, |FRAME: D-Digitoxose|, |FRAME: CPD-22572|, |FRAME: D-Olivose|, and |FRAME: D-Fucoses|)., While the mechanism whereby cardiac glycosides cause a positive inotropic effect and electrophysiologic changes of the hurt is still not completely clear, the most widely accepted mechanism involves the ability of cardiac glycosides to inhibit the membrane bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump responsible for Na+/K+ exchange |CITS: [KAUTE08]|., The |FRAME: Cardenolides cardenolides| have been divided into 6 series according to their genin part, which can be |FRAME: CPD-10537|, |FRAME: CPD-22576|, |FRAME: CPD-22579|, |FRAME: CPD-22581|, |FRAME: CPD-22583|, and |FRAME: CPD-22585| (termed series A through F, respectively). , |FRAME: TAX-4163| cardenolides are valuable drugs in the medication of patients suffering from cardiac insufficiency, and are known (together with the bufadienolides) as "cardiac glycosides". The major sources of the cardiac glycosides most frequently employed in medicine are |FRAME: TAX-49450| (for digoxin and other compounds) and |FRAME: TAX-4164| (for digitoxin)., About This Pathway, Once the steroid aglycone has been formed (as described for |FRAME: CPD-10537| in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6032|), the sugar moiety is attached by one or more glycosyltransferases. The sugar side chain can contain up to five carbohydrate units, but the most common cardiac glycosides have a tetrasaccharide moiety, where the terminal sugar is D-glucose., The pathway includes several branches, that depend on the nature of the first sufgar added. This pathway diagram includes |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CPD0-1898|, |FRAME: CPD-10544|, and |FRAME: CPD-22609|, but other sugars do participate., In addition to the assorted glucsyltransferases, severalmodifying enzymes are involved in the biosynthesis of the cardenolide glucosides. The main modifying enzymes are |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.M45|, and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.M87|. The activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.M47|, is believed to occur earlier in the pathway, at the level of the genins.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "Protocatechuate"| is one of the key intermediate metabolites in the microbial degradation of various aromatic compounds, including phthalates, hydroxybenzoates, and lignin-derived aromatic compounds such as |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|., The key step in these degradation pathways, the fission of the protocatechuate aromatic ring, can be catalyzed by one of the three distinct dioxygenases |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, |FRAME: CPLX-2721| and |FRAME: CPLX-7915|., The fission products, and thus the degradation pathways, depend on the type of dioxygenase employed. The three pathways are described in |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6336|, respectively., About This Pathway, Some soil pseudomonads catalyze the breakdown of |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| using the meta-cleavage pathway |CITS: [Gottschalk-1986]|. |FRAME: CPLX-2701 "Protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase"|, the key enzyme of this pathway, was first described in 1957 |CITS: [13445676]| and subsequently purified and characterized from several organisms |CITS:[5683506][5487881][6317682][2997190][2280721]|. The genes encoding the enzyme were first cloned from |FRAME: TAX-502559|, an organism that is able to grow on a wide variety of dimeric lignin compounds with guaiacyl moieties, which are converted into protocatechuate by the actions of lignin degradation enzymes |CITS: [2185230]|., Upon the discovery of |FRAME: CPD-184| as an intermediate of the pathway |CITS: [528534]| and the characterization of another pathway enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-3467| |CITS: [6841353]|, a pathway scheme was suggested |CITS:[7142106][6841354]|., The enzymes catalyzing the steps of the pathway have been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-47882| |CITS: [26671][528534][6841353][3985968 ][2229032]| and |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [7142106 ][5076765]|., Clusters containing the full complement of genes involved in this pathway were found in several organisms |CITS: [9864312][11495993][15277747]|., A slight modification of the pathway was prompted by a study of gallate degradation by |FRAME: TAX-160488|, a process that shares the later steps of this pathway.
