Summary: General Background, Aflatoxins are highly toxic and carcinogenic crop contaminants that create major economic and public health problems worldwide. Much research has been focused on identifying compounds that inhibit aflatoxin biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-4592 "Aflatoxin B1"| is metabolized by mammalian liver cytochrome P450 enzymes to a mutagenic epoxide that covalently binds to DNA. Its genotoxic mechanism of action has been studied in yeast |CITS: [8968101] [9771940]|. The species |FRAME: TAX-5062| and |FRAME:TAX-41058| that are used in food fermentation are unable to produce aflatoxins |CITS: [17665189]|., The mycotoxins |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of the B-group and G-group aflatoxins, which constitute the major groups of naturally occurring aflatoxins. The production of aflatoxins by some strains of several |FRAME:TAX-5052| species has been extensively studied. However many species, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425|, produce only |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| as a final product (in |CITS: [18486503]|). |FRAME: TAX-5067| produces both B- and G-group aflatoxins from |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587|, while |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces only B-group aflatoxins. The biological role of these mycotoxins in fungi remains unclear (in |CITS: [17620135] [18246345]| and, reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|)., Most of the aflatoxin biosynthetic genes are clustered in Aspergilli and are positively regulated by the aflR gene (in |CITS: [17620135] [16448506] [16108793] [15094053] [7618880] [16535712]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]| and |CITS: [15006741]|). The enzyme reactions and biosynthetic intermediates in the aflatoxin biosynthetic pathway have been reviewed in detail, but are nt completely understood as of 2020 |CITS: [15022028]|. See MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5954|, |FRAME: PWY-5955|, |FRAME: PWY-5959|, |FRAME: PWY-5960| and |FRAME: PWY-5961|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-10175 "Versicolorin B"| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and the B- and G-group aflatoxins. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10175| to |FRAME: CPD-10176| involves a desaturation of the tetrahydrobisfuran ring of |FRAME: CPD-10175| to the dihydrobisfuran ring of |FRAME: CPD-10176| |CITS: [Yabe1991]|, which persists in |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and aflatoxins B1 and G1. The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10176| to |FRAME: 6-DEMETHYLSTERIGMATOCYSTIN| has not been completely characterized. The genes |FRAME: G-80800| (ordB), |FRAME: G-80803| (hypA), |FRAME: G-80802| (ver-1) and |FRAME: G-80801| (verA) are believed to be involved |CITS: [16461654] [16332900] [15771506] [8953728] [1339261]|. The subsequent |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent methylation of |FRAME: 6-DEMETHYLSTERIGMATOCYSTIN| to , |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| has been better characterized |CITS: [10543813] [16349476] [2802602]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|)., The pathway shown here was derived by MetaCyc curator and is mostly hypothetical. It is based on results obtained from biochemical characterization of the |FRAME: G-80802| gene product in 2015. The enzyme, which was purified and analyzed in vitro, produced |FRAME: CPD-23462|, indicating that it has a different activity from the one predicted earlier, and challenging the previously proposed pathway |CITS: [ 26266881]|., The pathway proposed here continues from this product, integrating the available information about the three other enzymes known to be involved - the |FRAME: G-80801 "cytochrome P-450 AflN"|, which was predicted to catalyze an epoxidation reaction |CITS: [15771506]|, the |FRAME: G-80800 "AflX oxidoreductase"|, which was predicted to catalyze the epoxide ring-opening step |CITS: [16461654]|, and the |FRAME: G-80803 AflY oxidase|, which was predicted to catalyze a Bayer-Villiger type oxidation |CITS: [16332900]|., Supporting the proposed pathway, the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-23464| shown here has been observed in extracts of an |FRAME: G-80803|, but not |FRAME: G-80802|, knockout cultures |CITS: [16332900]|.

General Background, Yellow color of flowers is mainly conferred due to the presence of carotenoids. , However, in some species such as |FRAME:TAX-101596| or |FRAME:TAX-4151| chalcones and/or , aurones are the only source of yellow coloration |CITS: [Brouillard94]|. Dahlia has been found to accumulate , preferably 6'-deoxychalcones such as isoliquiritigenin and butein and their 4'-glucosides contributing to the , yellow flower color |CITS: [13498771]| |CITS: [HARBORNE90]| which is more or less accentuated in dependence , on the presence of co-pigments, largely glucosides of apigenin, luteolin and anthocyanin |CITS: [Heller94]|. , The 4'-glucosides of butein and isoliquiritigenin are stable compounds which mainly contribute to the flower , coloration. Further decoration of the chalcones such as methylation and malonylation occur but the catalyzing , enzymes have not yet been identified |CITS: [HARBORNE90]|. 6'-deoxychalcones are fairly stable substrates , for the subsequent glucosylation. In contrast, 6'-hydroxychalcone such as naringenin chalcone has not been , reported to serve as a major substrate for glucosylation. This has been ascribed to the activity of chalcone isomerase, which immediately converts the chalcone to the corresponding flavanone, i.e. naringenin |CITS: [STICH94]|., The 6'-deoxychalcone are the entrance compounds for the 5-deoxy series of flavonoids giving rise to isoflavonoids , (|FRAME:PWY-2002|) such as glyceollin, medicarpin, maackiain and pisatin. The 6'-deoxychalcone butein is , also a branchpoint leading to the biosynthetically related aurones (|FRAME:PWY-1901|) such as the 4-deoxyaurone , sulfuretin |CITS: [11418122]| which has been found to co-act with the 6'-deoxychalcones and their glucoside , derivatives in the coloration of flowers |CITS: [HALBWIRTH97]|. , About This Pathway, Butein is formed by the catalytic action of a Cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase , tentatively named chalcone 3-hydroxylase (CH3H) |CITS: [WIMMER98]|. The formation of butein has also , been observed when caffeoyl-CoA was added to an enzyme assay employing chalcone synthase and chalcone , (polyketide) reductase in vitro suggesting that a co-action between those enzymes may also contribute , to the biosynthesis of butein |CITS: [Welle88]| |CITS: [2500065]|. However, the high substrate specificity of , a 4'-glucosyltransferase for butein but not for its immediate precursor isoliquiritigenin seems to be more indicative , for the existence of a separate hydroxylating enzyme |CITS: [HALBWIRTH97]|., Butein is further metabolized at the 4'-O-position adding glucose which stabilizes the chalcone and deepens , the yellow hue. The respective chalcone 4'-glucosyltransferase has been identified in |FRAME:TAX-101596| , |CITS: [STICH94]| and |FRAME:TAX-13449| |CITS: [HALBWIRTH97]|. Both enzymes also glucosylate , flavanones such as naringenin, eriodictyol and the flavones apigenin and luteolin at the 7-O-position of the A-ring , (corresponds to the 4'-position of the chalcon A-ring) but did not accept chalcones of the 6'-hydroxy-type , (naringenin chalcone, eridodictyol chalcone). The enzyme isolated from |FRAME:TAX-13449| was also , able to efficiently glucosylate the aurone sulfuretin at the corresponding 6-position of the aurone A-ring.

Summary: Toluene is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic compounds can be degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus |FRAME:TAX-286| and closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward bioremediation of environmental pollutants by metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|). Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various species that involve different initial monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these pathways converge in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-111| |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound is a substrate for ring cleavage enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission pathway, resulting in the formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and pathways |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-2-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-DIOL-PWY|)., Toluene degradation in |FRAME: TAX-329 "Ralstonia pickettii (previously known as Pseudomonas pickettii and Burkholderia pickettii)"| is controlled by a chromosomal regulon |CITS: [10671442]|. The initial hydroxylation reactions are catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-6542|, followed by meta cleavage of the benzene ring by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, and subsequent degradation via the meta cleavage pathway |CITS: [8206853]|., There is disagreement in the literature over the hydroxylation reactions of the first enzyme of this pathway. Initial reports suggested that the first hydroxylation is at the meta position yielding |FRAME: CPD-112| as an intermediate, and the second yields |FRAME: CPD-111| |CITS: [8206853]|. However, later work suggested that toluene 3-monooxygenase is predominantly a para cleaving enzyme, and its initial products were shown in that study to be 90% |FRAME: CPD-108|, and only 10% |FRAME: CPD-112|. |FRAME: CPD-108| was further hydroxylated to |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL| |CITS: [15126473]|. Although further metabolism of 4-methylcatechol was not studied in that report, it has been shown to be a substrate of catechol 2,3-dioxygenase in |FRAME: TAX-329| |CITS: [1856161]|., Ring fission of |FRAME: 4-METHYLCATECHOL|, catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, produces |FRAME: CPD-8781|. This compound is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-22385|, or its tautomeric dienol form (this tautomerization occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|). A second hydrolysis, catalyzed by TbuJ afford |FRAME: CPD-13722|, which is cleaved by the aldolase TbuK into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: CPD-665| |CITS: [1856161]|., The final products of the pathway are |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which enters central metabolism, and |FRAME: CPD-665|, which may be converted by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.87| to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, which can be converted into the central metabolite |FRAME: SUC-COA| as described in |FRAME: PROPIONMET-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD Ethene| (also known as ethylene)is known in plants, fungi and bacteria. In plants, ethene is an important hormone that regulates plant growth and development. It is well-known as a fruit-ripening hormone and is biologically active in trace amounts. Ethene also plays a general role as a growth inhibitor in promoting leaf and flower senescence and abscission., All plants produce ethene from |FRAME: MET| as described in the pathway |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|). In addition, two alternative ethene biosynthetic pathways have been reported from microorganisms., Most microorganisms produce only trace amounts of ethene via the |FRAME: CPD-479| (KMBA) pathway, which is described here |CITS: [Kazuhiro92]|. In this route ethene is produced non-enzymatically by hydroxyl radicals that are produced from molecular oxygen by an |FRAME: MONOMER-16774| |CITS: [3541827][2792734][Ogawa90]|. In the second microbial pathway, which is found mostly in members of the |FRAME: TAX-136849|, ethene is formed enzymatically from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6853|)., Being the simplest unsaturated organic molecule, ethene is the building block for synthetic polymers including plastics such as polyethylene. Large amounts of ethylene are currently produced in a chemical process from fossil fuels. It is the organic compound that has the highest annual global production. , About This Pathway, The production of ethene from methionine by some microbial organisms has been observed already in the 1960s. Enzymatic systems for conversion of methionine analogues to ethene were first reported by |CITS: [6032971][4963359]|. It was subsequently showed that horseradish peroxidase could catalyze the conversion of either |FRAME: CPD-7036| or |FRAME: CPD-479| to ethene |CITS: [6066254]|. An enzyme that facilitates this conversion has been reported from |FRAME: ORG-6186| and described to require oxygen and pyridoxal phosphate |CITS: [16080]|. The enzyme has been subsequently studied in greater detail, and described as a soluble enzyme that requires NAD(P)H, |FRAME: FE+3| chelated to EDTA, and oxygen. The products of the reaction included not only ethene, but also |FRAME: CPD-7671| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [3541827]|., The enzyme has been purified from the fungus |FRAME: ORG-6187| and described as an |FRAME: MONOMER-16774| |CITS: [2792734]|. The enzyme produces ferrous iron, which reacts chemically with molecular oxygen, forming |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| radicals. This radical is converted to hydrogen peroxide by |FRAME: SUPEROX-DISMUT-RXN "EC 1.15.1.1, superoxide dismutase"|. Hydrogen peroxide also reacts with ferrous iron via the |FRAME: RXN-12540 "Fenton reaction"|, producing a |FRAME: CPD-12377|. Finally, the hydroxyl radical reacts with |FRAME: CPD-479|, generating |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| along with |FRAME: CPD-7671| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [ 6258481][2792734]|., It should be noted that the production of ethene in most microbes depends only upon the presence of the specific transaminase that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: CPD-479| from |FRAME: MET|, because enzymes that, can catalyze the production of |FRAME: CPD-12377| are present in all microorganisms |CITS: [Ogawa90]|., The organism |FRAME: TAX-36651| is unique in that it is able to produce ethene via both this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-6853|, depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [16660102]|.

Summary: Theobromine is the immediate precursor of caffeine biosynthesis in caffeine accumulating plants such as coffee and tea plants. However theobromine plants accumulate theobromine instead of caffeine as the predominant purine alkaloid. The major route of theobromine biosynthesis |FRAME: PWY-5039| is similar to the major pathway of caffeine biosynthesis |FRAME: PWY-5037|, except that conversion of theobromine to caffeine is very slow or blocked in these plants. In addition to the major route, theobromine can also be derived from xanthine, although the majority of the xanthine pool is readily degraded to CO2 via purine degradation. No enzyme information is available.

Sophoraflavanone G (SFG), also called kushenin (in traditional Chinese medicinal recipes) is a volatile plant defense compound that exists in the root bark of Sophora flavescens. SFG is a branched prenyl (lavandulyl)-conjugated flavanone, characteristic to the Sophora genus. It is anti-bacteria, especially against antibiotic-resistant bacteria and thus is a promising candidate for the treatment of deadly bacteria infections |CITS: [19288534][17137127]|. , SFG is synthesized from the common flavanone naringenin. The unusual, branched prenyl adduct is added by two prenylation steps using dimethylallyl diphosphate as the sole prenyl donor |CITS: [18218974][14551337]|. A 2'-hydroxylation reaction, in between the prenylation reactions, is necessary for the action of the second prenylation enzyme |CITS: [14551337]|.

Summary: |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE Phenylacetate| is a major intermediate in bacterial degradation of many aromatic compounds |CITS: [11260461]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Vitamins-B6 "Vitamin B6"| is an important cofactor of many enzymes. While the active form of the vitamin is |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, it occurs in several forms within organisms. There are three free forms, |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE|, |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| (|FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| is the form given as vitamin B6 supplement) and three phosphorylated forms (|FRAME:PYRIDOXINE-5P|, |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|), all of which can be interconverted. Two different but related degradation pathways have been described (|FRAME: PWY-5499| and |FRAME: PWY-8384|) |CITS: [ 21004555][13610871][Burg70]|., About This Pathway, In the pathway shown here, which was originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-60694|, |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| are converted to |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL|, and the latter is degraded to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, |FRAME:AMMONIA|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| in seven enzymatic steps |CITS: [13806048]|., While all of the involved enzymes have been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-60694| |CITS: [14004227][14339645][5769992][4306030][4306031][5769993][6348042][3972793][3771565][3533936]|, none of genes encoding the enzymes were identified. In 2002 the gene encoding |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.12|, has been identified from |FRAME: TAX-69367| |CITS: [12092811]|. Significant progress in gene identification occurred when the genome of |FRAME: TAX-381| was sequenced in 2000 and the pyridoxine 4-oxidase gene was identified in it, suggesting that this bacterium was capable of degrading vitamin B6 |CITS: [15135526]|. This led to the discovery of the other catabolic genes |CITS: [16226926][17270714][16824480][17868768][18216065][18476725][18635903]|. Crystal structures have been determined for some of the enzymes |CITS: [17973403][17989071][19317437][20099871]|., |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD "Succinate semialdehyde"| can be converted to |FRAME:SUC| and channeled into the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| by either |FRAME:EC-1.2.1.24|, or |FRAME:EC-1.2.1.16|, although these enzymes have not been characterized yet from any of the organisms listed above.

Summary: General Background, The phytyl chain is an essential component in the structure of diverse prenyllipids such as chlorophylls, tocopherols and phylloquinone |CITS:[9492312]|. The phytyl chain allows for the insertion of those compounds into the hydrophobic core of membranes such as the plastid membrane of chloroplasts and etioplasts. To date, two pathways of prenylation have been described:, a) The first pathway concerns the prenylation of chlorophyllide a with |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (GGPP) to form |FRAME: CPD-7005|, which is subsequently converted through several successive steps of reduction to form |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| (see |FRAME:PWY-5064|)., b) In the second pathway (this pathway) free |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| is converted to |FRAME: PHYTYL-PYROPHOSPHATE|, which is then prenylated to |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| to form |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|. , The former route was detected in plant etioplasts |CITS:[7408876]|, whilst the second was reported in chloroplasts, where the biosynthesis of tocopherol |CITS:[7447462]| and phylloquinone |CITS:[7274213]| also utilizes preformed |FRAME: PHYTYL-PYROPHOSPHATE|. , Enzyme Information:, In Arabidopsis thaliana a multifunctional enzyme was shown to be able to catalyze the multiple reduction steps in both routes: |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| to |FRAME: PHYTYL-PYROPHOSPHATE| as well as |FRAME: CPD-7005| to |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| |CITS:[9492312]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, Carotenoids with cyclic ends are integral constituents of plants, algae and cyanobacteria photosynthetic, reaction centers |CITS:[GOODWIN80],[YOUNG93]|. |FRAME: CPD1F-119 Lutein| is a xanthophyll carotenoid abundant in green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale, but also found in other organisms. Lutein is used as an antioxidant and for blue light absorption. In some fruits and flowers, such as marigolds lutein is covalently bound to one or more fatty acids., In animals lutein is found in egg yolks, fats and the corpus luteum (endocrine structure in mammals, involved in the production of the progestogens during pregnancy). It is also found in a concentrated area of the macula, a small area of the retina responsible for central vision., Lutein is produced from |FRAME: CPD1F-115| in three steps via |FRAME: CPD1F-118| and |FRAME: CPD-5661|.

|FRAME: L-THREONATE| is a four-carbon acid sugar that can be used by some bacteria as the sole carbon source., This pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: L-THREONATE| was found by a bioinformatic analysis of genes clustered with an L-threonate-binding protein (SBP), which is a part of a TRAP (tripartite ATP-independent permease) transporter for the compound |CITS: [25540822]|., Following import into the cell, |FRAME: L-THREONATE| is dehydrogenated at the C2 position, forming |FRAME: CPD-19882|. The dehydrogenase, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.411|, can use both NAD+ and NADP+, but prefers the former. The product is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-19884| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.35|, followed by phosphrylation to |FRAME: CPD-19880| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.217|., The kinase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55079| gene, is one of the first members of a large family of enzymes, known as DUF (domain of unknown function) 1537, to which a function has been assigned |CITS: [27402745]|., Following phosphorylation, the compound is decarboxylated by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.104|, yielding the central metabolite |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS: [27402745]|.

Summary: The |FRAME:Megalomicins megalomicins|, which were discovered in 1968 |CITS:[5735370][5810991]|, are a family of related macrolide antibiotics produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47868|. They are therapeutically diverse compounds that possess antiparasitic, antiviral and antibacterial properties. Like other macrolide antibiotics, they are more active against Gram-positive bacteria than against Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4390258][4996819]|., The first family member to have its structure reported was |FRAME: CPD-12966| |CITS: [5358619][5358620]|.  Acyl derivatives of |FRAME: CPD-12966|, including |FRAME: CPD-14689|, |FRAME: CPD-12967|, |FRAME: CPD-14691|, and |FRAME: CPD-14690|, were soon discovered |CITS: [4795255]|., The megalomicins have the same aglycone as |FRAME: CPD-13804| and |FRAME: CPD-13951|, but include a unique deoxyamino sugar, |FRAME: CPD-14692|, at the C-6 hydroxyl., The biosynthesis of megalomicin is complex, and has thus been divided into multiple pathways. The synthesis of the aglycone is described in |FRAME: PWY-7106| . The synthesis of the three modified sugars has been described in |FRAME: PWY-6976|, |FRAME: PWY-6942|, and |FRAME: CPD-14683|, and the final assembly of |FRAME: CPD-12966| is described in |FRAME: PWY-7109|. Please refer to those pathways for more information.

General Background, |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan "β-(1,4)-D-Mannans"| are one of the major constituents of the hemicellulose present in the cell walls and tissues of higher plants. Enzymes that degrade |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan "β-(1,4)-D-mannans"| include endo-1,4-β-mannanases and α-galactosidases. Short |FRAME: Short-Mannan "β-(1,4)-D-mannooligosaccharides"| are further degraded by exo-β-mannosidases which catalyze the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-12601| at the nonreducing end (in |CITS: [21539815]| and reviewed in |CITS: [18385995]|., Mannan degradation begins in the extracellular space where the |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan "mannan"| backbone is hydrolyzed to by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.78|. In some species galactomannan side chains are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.22| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8834|) and the |FRAME: Short-Mannan "mannooligosaccharides"| may be further hydrolyzed by exo-cleaving |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.25| which catalyze the hydrolysis of the nonreducing end of β-D-mannosides (in |CITS: [24217874]|)., About This Pathway, This pathway has been proposed for several anaerobic bacteria, but it may also occur in aerobic bacteria |CITS: [23093406]|. |FRAME: TAX-272559| is an obligate anaerobe that inhabits the human gut. Its genome was found to contain an operon encoding putative |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan "mannan"| metabolizing enzymes. The genes were designated by locus tags BF0771 (gene |FRAME: G-17993|), |FRAME: G-18005|, BF0773 and BF0774 (gene |FRAME: G-17997|). They encode a novel |FRAME: CPD-13746|-forming exo-mannanase, a novel mannosylglucose phosphorylase, a putative mannobiose and/or sugar H+ (Na+) symporter, and a cellobiose/mannobiose 2-epimerase, respectively |CITS: [21539815][24217874]|. This operon was also conserved in the genomes of other |FRAME: TAX-816| species, as well as species of |FRAME: TAX-375288|, |FRAME: TAX-237| and |FRAME: TAX-10| |CITS: [21539815]|., In |FRAME: TAX-272559| the products of genes |FRAME: G-17993|, |FRAME: G-18005| and |FRAME: G-17997| have been characterized |CITS: [24217874][21539815][19202279]|. The |FRAME: G-17993| gene product was cloned, expressed, partially purified, and characterized as a novel mannobiose-forming exo-mannanase. It was originally designated as |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.78| but analysis revealed that it utilizes both |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan "mannans"| and |FRAME: Short-Mannan "mannooligosaccharides"|, generating |FRAME: CPD-13746| as the major end product. It recognizes the nonreducing terminal |FRAME: CPD-13746| units in |FRAME: 1-4-Mannan "mannans"|, making it a typical exo-acting, |FRAME: CPD-13746|-forming enzyme |CITS: [24217874]|., |FRAME: ORG-6253| was shown to contain multiple mannanase genes, the enzyme products of which are capable of producing |FRAME: CPD-13746| and |FRAME: Short-Mannan "mannooligosaccharides"|. Several of these genes have been annotated as |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.78|. The |FRAME: CPD-13746| and |FRAME: Short-Mannan "mannooligosaccharide"| products are transported into the cell via a putative mannobiose and/or sugar H+ (Na+) symporter encoded by gene Rumal_0598 |CITS: [23093406]|., In both organisms intracellular |FRAME: CPD-13746| is epimerized by |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.11| to |FRAME: CPD-14017| via enzymes encoded by gene |FRAME: G-17997| in |FRAME: TAX-272559| and Rumal_0019 in |FRAME: ORG-6253|. This compound then undergoes phosphorolytic cleavage via |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.281| in both organisms. , However, in |FRAME: ORG-6253| the |FRAME: Short-Mannan "mannooligosaccharides"| can also undergo phosphorolytic cleavage by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.319| encoded by gene |FRAME: G-18007|. Based on its substrate preference, |FRAME: Short-Mannan "mannooligosaccharide"| degradation is thought to be its physiological role |CITS: [23093406]|., The phosphorolytic cleavage products are converted to glycolytic intermediates. Genes encoding putative |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.8| and |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.8| have been identified in the |FRAME: TAX-272559|, |FRAME: ORG-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-697329| genomes |CITS: [21539815][23093406][24217874]|.

General Background, Sialic acids are nine-carbon keto sugars that mediate a variety of cell-cell and cell-molecule interactions in eukaryotes and can be utilized by pathogens to evade the host immune response. Some bacteria can release and transport |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| (the most common form of sialic acid) from host cells and utilize it as a source of carbon and nitrogen for growth. In many bacteria the genes for |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| utilization are arranged in an operon that includes genes encoding a negative regulator NanR, a transporter NanT, a lyase NanA, a kinase NanK, and a 2-epimerase NanE (in |CITS: [19304853]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1324|)., About This Pathway, The Gram-negative human gut commensal and opportunistic pathogen |FRAME: TAX-817| can utilize |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| as the main source of carbon and energy for growth in minimal medium via a variant pathway for |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| degradation and |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-mannosamine| utilization. An ortholog of the |FRAME: G7676|-encoded kinase is not found in its genome., This variant pathway involves a three-gene operon nanLET that is regulated by a NanR repressor. A lyase encoded by nanL cleaves |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| to |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-mannosamine|. A nanE-encoded 2-epimerase, which does not require a phosphorylated substrate, produces |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine|. In members of the |FRAME: TAX-816| genus NanE is structurally more similar to the mammalian renin-binding protein than to other members of the bacterial NanE family. |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| is then phosphorylated to |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| by the |FRAME: MONOMER-19002| product of gene rokA. The latter compound is further metabolized through the common amino sugar utilization and glycolytic pathways as shown in the pathway link |CITS: [19304853]|.

Names: indole-3-acetate inactivation II // IAA inactivation II // indole-3-acetic acid inactivation II
Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms. A common mechanism involves non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., IAA (indole-3-acetic acid), one of the most common active forms of the phytohormone auxin, is often, present in conjugated forms. Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. Meanwhile, conjugated forms of auxin play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., About This Pathway, The degradation pathway in hybrid aspen as depicted here is based solely on in vivo shoot feeding experiments |CITS: [12232425]|. No enzyme or gene information is currently available. The end product in the pathway, |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETIC-ACID|, may be subjected to further hydroxylation. The position of the hydroxyl group is not identified.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22158 "Apratoxin A"| is a secondary metabolite isolated from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-207920| in shallow coral reef environments surrounding the islands of Guam, Palau |CITS: [11389621][11937357]| and Papua New Guinea |CITS: [18444683]|., The compound is composed of a polyketide section fused with a modified pentapeptide to form a cyclic lipopeptide that possesses a unique tertiary butyl group at one terminus. It exhibited potent cytotoxicity to cancer cells grown on solid agar media as well as in vivo anticancer effects in a mouse model |CITS: [11389621][20512792]|. The mechanism of cytotoxic action involves the reversible inhibition of a secretory pathway for several cancer-associated receptors through interference with their co-translational translocation |CITS: [19403701]|., About This Pathway, The gene cluster encoding apratoxin A biosynthesis has been identified, and a biosynthetic pathway has been proposed |CITS: [21533272]|. The gene cluster, which extends to ~58 kb, consists of 12 genes encoding 2 polyketide synthases, 4 nonribosomal peptide synthases, and additional enzymes. The loading domain of the pathway is unique, resulting in generation of a t-butyl function, which ends up in the final product. Similarly, the offloading and cyclization of the linear apratoxin A intermediate appears to be catalyzed by a novel mechanism that does not involve a thioesterase |CITS: [21533272]|.

Names: benzoate biosynthesis II (CoA-independent, non-β-oxidative) // benzoate biosynthesis (non-oxidative) // benzoic acid biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Benzoic acid, derived from phenylalanine, is a precuror to several important benzenoid compounds, including floral scent constituents, such as |FRAME:CPD-12217|, |FRAME:CPD-6443| |FRAME:CPD-6441| |CITS:[15286288][12884048][12226525][12361714]|; the defense signaling compounds salicylic acid (SA) and its derivatives |CITS:[19400653][19820324]|, and a number of pharmacologically active compounds, such as taxol |CITS: [11095755 ]| (rev in |CITS: [16600669]|). An important step in the creation of benzoic acid is the cleavage of two carbon atoms from the 3-carbon side-chain present on trans-cinnamic acid. At least three different chain-shortening routes have been proposed in plants |CITS: [15286288]| and there is evidence that a subset of the different pathways may operate in individual species, and may differentially contribute to benzoic acid biosynthesis within each species. For example, |FRAME:TAX-4102| has at least two pathways present (this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-6443|), whereas cucumber (|FRAME:TAX-3659|) and |FRAME:TAX-49451| seem to lack this variant |CITS: [11219576]| and |FRAME:TAX-140968| relies on a third pathway (|FRAME: PWY-6446|) that incorporates elements of the other two variants. , A greater understanding of the metabolic pathways involved in benzoic acid biosynthesis may contribute to genetic engineering efforts aimed at altering floral scents, modifying SA-based defense responses, and increasing the production of pharmaceutically important compounds |CITS: [17234289][17511599]|., Although benzoate biosynthesis has been primarily studied in plants, there is evidence that |FRAME: TAX-115828| bacteria make |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| using the early steps in the |FRAME: PWY-6443| pathway |CITS: [12502351]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway, the chain shortening is accomplished through the removal of an acetate in the third reaction giving rise to |FRAME: BENZALDEHYDE|. Although this compound does not function as an intermediate in the |FRAME: PWY-6443| pathway, the characterization of benzaldehyde dehydrogenases in snapdragon and Arabidopsis indicate that benzoic acid can be generated from this precursor in a subset of plant species |CITS:[19292760][19297586]|., PAL, the enzyme catalyzing the first step in this reaction is subject to regulation in many plant species and thus controls the flux through many secondary metabolic biosynthetic pathways. More specific regulation may be achieved in this pathway through fine-tuned expression of downstream enzymes. For example, transcript levels of the snapdragon |FRAME: CPLX-8012| are highest in the parts of the flower that produce scent (the upper and lower petal lobes) and they also show developmental and diurnal changes that are correlated with the production of methylbenzoate and benzoic acid respectively |CITS: [19292760]|. On the other hand |FRAME: AT1G04580-MONOMER| transcripts seem to be expressed predominantly in developing seeds in Arabdopsis |CITS: [19297586]|., Despite years of study, little is known about the subcellular localization of various components of the benzoic acid biosynthesis pathways. The finding that the snapdragon |FRAME: CPLX-8012| localizes to the mitochondria |CITS: [19292760]| while the Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT1G04580-MONOMER| lacks any discernable targeting signal and thus likely resides in the cytosol |CITS: [19297586]| may further complicate efforts to study the compartmentalization of this pathway.

General Background, Xanthones are yellow pigments of phenolic origin restricted in occurrence to only a few families of higher plants and some fungi and lichens. The majority of xanthones is rarely glucosylated and has been found in basically two families of higher plants, the Clusiaceae (syn. Guttiferae) and |FRAME:TAX-21472| |CITS: [HOSTETTMANN89][BENNETT89]|. However, xanthones also appear sporadically throughout the remainder of the plant kingdom. Xanthone-C-glucosides such as mangiferin are the exception with a much wider distribution among plants and also arising in ferns and fungi |CITS: [HOSTETTMANN89]|., Xanthones can be classified based on their oxygenation, prenylation and glucosylation pattern. The majority of xanthones isolated so far are of the tetraoxygenated-type which have been intensively studied in plants of the Guttiferae and |FRAME:TAX-21472| but are reported from 12 other plant families as well |CITS: [11190384]|. The restricted biosynthesis of xanthones and their plant-specific substitution pattern has been employed as a useful marker for systematic purposes, i.e. comparing the phyletic order of genera within the Guttiferae |CITS: [DAMATEREZENTE73]| and hemotaxonomic , differentiation between plant families |CITS: [SULTANBAWA80]|., Xanthones posses a number of remarkable pharmacological traits and bioactivities (summarized in |CITS: [11190384]|) and have been used as, e.g. cardiovascular protective agents |CITS: [15179447]| and antitumor promotors |CITS: [10397461]|. tetrahydroxylated xanthones can be induced by phytopathogens |CITS: [12391565]| and accumulate in calli and cell suspension upon treatment with plant hormones and supplements, such as naphtaleneacetic acid (NAA) in combination with kinetin |CITS: [Dias00]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of plant xanthones originates mainly from a mixed shikimate-acetate pathway, however xanthones entirely derived from acetate have also been reported in lower plants |CITS: [11190384]| |CITS: [HOSTETTMANN89]|. The main steps in the xanthone biosynthesis involve the condensation of shikimate and acetate moieties which constitute a benzophenone intermediate followed by a regioselective, oxidative mediated intra-molecular coupling to form the xanthone , ring |CITS: [PETERS98]|., The shikimate derivatives used as entry compounds for the tetrahydroxyxanthone biosynthesis differ in relation to the investigated plants (|FRAME:TAX-140968| vs |FRAME:TAX-172057|) |CITS: [11216850]| |CITS: [11882941]|. These plants , belong to different families that seem to have developed biosynthetic variants of the tetrahydroxyxanthone synthesis which involves enzymes of diverse regioselectivity and substrate preference and leads to varying intermediates |CITS: [PETERS98][9459298]|., The biosynthesis of tetrahydroxyxanthone via 3-hydroxybenzoate (this pathway) in |FRAME:TAX-172057| is obtained by the stepwise condensation of 3 malonyl-CoA and 3-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA to form an intermediate tetrahydroxybenzophenone. The crucial step in this biosynthesis is the cyclization of the benzophenone to form a xanthone, catalyzed by xanthon synthases. In |FRAME:TAX-172057| the xanthone synthase converts the tetrahydroxybenzophenone intermediate regioselective to 1,3,5-trihydroxyxanthone. Therefore all xanthones and their derivatives in |FRAME:TAX-172057| are 5-oxygenated in contrast to the constituents in the |FRAME:TAX-140968| pathway (|FRAME:PWY-5001|) which all carry a 7-hydroxy group |CITS: [PETERS98]|., The last step in the biosynthesis of the tetrahydroxyxanthones is the introduction of a hydroxyl group to the C-ring of the xanthone skeleton. This reaction is carried out by the plant-specific Cytochrome P450-dependend monooxygenase, xanthone-6-hydroxylase, to form 1,3,5,6-tetrahydroxyxanthone |CITS: [10731018]|. Cell cultures of |FRAME:TAX-172057| furthermore accumulate 3,5,6,7,8-pentamethoxy-1-O-primeverosyl-xanthone |CITS: [BEERHUES94]| as the main xanthone which implies two additional hydroxylation steps of the corresponding tetrahydroxyxanthone not yet described in the literature., Another representative of the |FRAME:TAX-21472|, chirayta (Swertia chirata), again hydroxylates 1,3,5-trihydroxyxanthone in the 8-position of the C-ring resulting in the major xanthone of this species 1,3,5,8-tetrahydroxyxanthone |CITS: [12846828]|. However, the enzyme and corresponding reaction involved remains to be characterized.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of several important metabolites involves the consumption of |FRAME: MET| through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), in a reaction that releases |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA). , These metabilites include polyamines (see |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME:BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-1303|), |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|), and bacterial auto-inducers (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration is tightly regulated. Several pathways that recycle MTA back to |FRAME: MET| have been described., The pathway shown here, also known as the universal methionine salvage pathway, is present with some variations in almost all eukaryotes and some bacteria |CITS: [19946895]|. It has been partially characterized from a number of organisms, including bacteria |CITS:[8227039][7852397][8694776][9880484][11371200]|, plants |CITS: [Baur72][Murr75][Kushad83][Miyazaki87]|, yeast |CITS: [3906034]|, protozoal parasites |CITS: [8585735][ 11443076]| and rat |CITS: [7007366][7068632][7852397]|. The pathway was best studied in the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-573|., A limiting factor to the distribution of this pathway is that it contains an oxygen-requiring step (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|), and is thus present only in aerobic organisms. Alternative pathways exist in anaerobic organisms and are described in |FRAME: PWY-7174| and |FRAME: PWY-8132|., While most of the pathway is conserved among the different organisms that possess it, several variants exist that differ in the initial steps of the pathway, between |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) and |FRAME: CPD-1063| (MTRP). These variants, describing bacteria and plants, higher eukaryotes, and protozoa, are described by several pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|. The metabolic differences in the early steps of the methionine salvage pathway are being exploited for developing new drugs targeted against pathogenic microorganisms that utilize the MTA nucleosidase-MTR kinase pathway |CITS: [2854458][2153115][1929327]|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here depicts the formation of MTA by the production of |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|, although MTA is also formed during the biosynthesis of other compounds, such polyamines (as described in |FRAME: PWY-7528|) and phytosiderophores (as described in |FRAME: PWY-5912|)., The pathway was discovered in plants by Baur and Yang |CITS:[baur72]| while studying |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY "ethylene biosynthesis"| in apple fruit tissue. They noticed that although initial methionine quantities were only sufficient for the production of ethylene for a few hours, ethylene was being produced for months. Since no volatile sulfur was detected, they had concluded that the methionine pool had to be replenished during ethylene production., Indeed, the pathway plays an important role in plants by preventing the depletion of methionine pools during times of ethylene production. When |FRAME: CPD-68| is siphoned off to produce ethylene, the methylthio group of |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) is recycled to methionine via this pathway. , Unlike in higher eukaryotes, where the recycling of MTA to methionine starts with phosphorolytic cleavage by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.28| to yield |FRAME: CPD-444|, in most bacteria and plants this conversion is achieved by the action of two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.16| and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.100|, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-560| |CITS: [8694776][10574451]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6754|)., Once |FRAME: CPD-444| is formed, it is recycled back to L-methionine in 6 steps, comprising an isomerase, a dehydratase, an enolase, a phosphatase, an oxygenase, and a transaminase. The last enzyme, a glutamine-dependent transaminase, produces the byproduct |FRAME: 2-KETO-GLUTARAMATE|, which is believed to be toxic. Thus an additional enzyme, an ω-amidase that converts the latter to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, is also considered a part of the pathway |CITS: [24837359]|., A note about |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|, The reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|, can occur non-enzymatically in the presence of air. It is yet unknown whether the non-enzymatic reaction occurs in vivo |CITS: [7852397]|., If the enzyme that usually catalyzes this reaction binds a Ni2+ instead of Fe2+, it catalyzes a different reaction (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.53|), forming a shunt of the methionine salvage pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5389|) |CITS:[7852397] [9880484][11371200]|. While the purpose of this shunt is yet unknown, it has been suggested that it may provide a mechanism for regulating |FRAME: MET| levels in vivo |CITS: [11371200]|.

Names: ultra-long-chain fatty acid biosynthesis // hexatriacontanoate biosynthesis // ULCFA biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "Fatty acids"| are carboxylic acids with a long unbranched aliphatic tail., Even though fatty acids derived from natural fats and oils are usually at least 8 carbon atoms long, carboxylic acids as short as |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID| (4 carbon atoms) are considered to be fatty acids., Fatty acids are often classified into four groups by their lengths:, |FRAME: Short-chain-fatty-acids "Short-chain fatty acids"| (SCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of fewer than six carbons., |FRAME: Medium-chain-fatty-acids "Medium-chain fatty acids"| (MCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 6-12 carbons., |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "Long-chain fatty acids"| (LCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 13-21 carbons., |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "Very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFA) are fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 22 carbons or longer., More recently the term "|FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "ultra-long-chain fatty acids"|" has been introduced for fatty acids with aliphatic tails of 28 carbons or longer |CITS: [1378993][20156336][23826266][23954553][24753812][27257090]|., Ultra-long-chain fatty acids (ULCFA) are common in |FRAME: Linoleate-Acylceramides acylceramides|, which are epidermis-specific ceramide species that are very important for skin barrier formation. They consist of |FRAME: Ceramides| ester linked to |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|. The typical chain-length of the fatty acid within the ceramide moiety is C28–C36, making acylceramides one of the most hydrophobic lipids in mammalian bodies |CITS: [28248318]|., Acylceramides are also important as precursors of protein-bound ceramides, which connect lipid lamellae and corneocytes |CITS: [20937905]|., About This Pathway, The synthesis of ULCFAs has not been characterized well. It is assumed that they are formed by the same machinery that produces VLCFAs, which is located in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) |CITS: [1378993]|. The elongation process is catalyzed by a membrane-bound enzyme complex known as the elongase |CITS: [10907783]|. This complex catalyzes the sequential additions of C2 moieties from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to preformed C18 acyl groups derived from the de novo fatty acid biosynthesis pathway. Each elongation cycle is composed of 4 reactions: condensation of |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs| and |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to form |FRAME: 3-KETOACYL-COA|, reduction to, |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYACYL-COA|, dehydration to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA|, and a final reduction to yield a chain-elongated fatty acyl-CoA |CITS: [16564093][16950653]|., While the reactions catalyzed by the elongase are similar to those of de novo fatty acid biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5994| and |FRAME: PWY-5971|), there are several differences between the elongase complex and the fatty acid synthase (FAS) complex. In animals and yeast all of the functions of FAS are present in either one (mammals) or two (yeast) large multidomain subunits (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628 "human fatty acid synthase"| and |FRAME: CPLX-7627 "yeast fatty acid synthase"|). The elongase, on the other hand, is composed of four enzymes that catalyze independent reactions, similarly to the bacterial/plants FAS systems. In addition, the elongase always utilizes |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| as the C2 donor unit, while FAS uses either malonyl-CoA (in yeast and animals) or |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"| in bacteria and plants. , The elongase accepts long-chain fatty acids [usually |FRAME: PALMITATE| (C16) or |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| (C18)] made by the cytosolic fatty acid synthase complex, and produces |FRAME: ARACHIDIC_ACID| (C20), |FRAME: DOCOSANOATE| (C22), |FRAME: TETRACOSANOATE| (C24), |FRAME: CPD-7832| (26) or even longer acids. , The four enzymes that form the elongase complex are |FRAME: YCR034W-MONOMER| or condensing enzyme |CITS: [11341960]|, |FRAME: MONOMER3O-79|, |FRAME: MONOMER3O-85| and |FRAME: G3O-29445-MONOMER|., While only one enzyme catalyzes each of the last three reactions of the cycle (respectively), the first step (the condensation of the 2 carbons from malonyl-CoA to the nascent acyl-CoA) is catalyzed by several different enzymes that differ from each other in their preference towards substrates with different lengths and degrees of desaturation., These enzymes, which are also the rate-limiting step in the cycle, thus determine the length of the final acyl-CoA produced by the complex they participate in |CITS: [11113186]|., In yeast the |FRAME: YCR034W| and |FRAME: G3O-14| genes encode condensing enzymes that participate in the elongase complex. In mammals there are seven distinct "elongase for very long fatty acids" (ELOVL) subtypes. The human enzymes are encoded by the |FRAME: HS00873|, |FRAME: ENSG00000096256|, |FRAME: HS04346|, |FRAME: HS04216|, |FRAME: HS00335|, |FRAME: HS10142|, and |FRAME: HS09036| genes. |FRAME: HS00873| and |FRAME: HS04216| seem to be the crucial elongases to generate ULC-FAs with 26 or more carbon atoms |CITS: [17311087][22100072][23689133]|. Mice deficient in one of these elongases have a disturbed barrier function and die neonatally from an increased transepidermal water loss. |FRAME: HS00873| appears to be involved in producing C26 fatty acyl CoAs, while |FRAME: HS04216| is responsible for elongation up to C36 products |CITS: [12584204][26056268][28248300]|.

Names: trans,octa-cis decaprenyl phosphate biosynthesis // mono-trans,poly-cis decaprenyl phosphate biosynthesis
Summary: The most common prenol and polyprenol structures are confined to four main groups - all-E-prenols; di-E, poly-Z-prenols; tri-E, poly-Z-prenols; and all-Z-prenols. Most bacteria typically contain a single predominant polyprenol composed of 11 isoprene units with the di-E, poly-Z configuration, known as |FRAME: CPD-9646|., However, mycobacteria contain an unusual prenol that does not fit any of these groups. In these bacteria, the common form of poly-prenol has the configuration of one ω, one E, and eight Z-isoprene units, known as |FRAME: CPD-11984| |CITS: [8083238]|., |FRAME: CPD-11984 "Mono-trans, poly-cis-decaprenyl diphosphate"| plays a central role in the biosynthesis of essential mycobacterial cell wall components, such as the mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex and lipoarabinomannan, serving as a membrane anchor. This compound is unique to mycobacteria |CITS: [11555614]|., The first two reactions in this pathway are universal, and found in most organisms, including those that produce |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| (see |FRAME: PWY-5123|). A key reaction is the production of |FRAME: CPD-9444|, which is catalyzed by the membrane bound |FRAME: G185E-5248-MONOMER| (EC reaction |FRAME:2.5.1.68-RXN "2.5.1.68"|)., The enzyme has been purified to near homogeneity from |FRAME: TAX-83332| and characterized |CITS: [11152452]|., The purified enzyme catalyzed the addition of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| to either |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| or |FRAME: CPD-461|, yielding |FRAME: CPD-9444| and |FRAME: CPD-11293|, respectively., It should be noted that mycobacteria also have a cytosolic enzyme that produces |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| (|FRAME: FPPSYN-RXN "EC 2.5.1.10"|). This enzyme may be involved in mycobacterial sterol biosynthesis |CITS: [9804188]|., The second key enzyme is the |FRAME: G185E-6587|-encoded |FRAME: G185E-6587-MONOMER|, which successively adds seven isoprene units to |FRAME: CPD-9444| in the cis configuration, releasing |FRAME: CPD-11984| |CITS: [10816587]|. This enzyme has also been purified and characterized |CITS: [15516568]|. While it could accept many different substrates, the highest catalytic efficiency was found with |FRAME: CPD-9444|, suggesting that this is the natural substrate in vivo. It is the first bacterial Z-prenyl diphosphate synthase that preferentially utilizes an allylic diphosphate primer having the α-isoprene unit in the Z configuration |CITS: [15516568]|.

General Background, Gibberellins (GAs) are plant hormones that regulate growth and influence various developmental processes, including stem elongation, germination, dormancy, flowering, sex expression, enzyme induction, and leaf and fruit senescence., All known gibberellins are diterpenoid acids that are synthesized by the terpenoid pathway in plastids and then modified in the endoplasmic reticulum and cytosol until they reach their biologically-active form (see |FRAME: PWY-5052|). The gibberellins are named GA1 through GAn in order of discovery., All gibberellins have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD1F-128| represents the first committed step in the biosynthesis of gibberellins. As diterpenoids, gibberellins are synthesized from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (GGPP), which is also an essential precursor in the biosynthesis of several isoprenoids necessary for plant growth and development such as carotenoids, prenyl quinines, and chlorophylls, as well as the formation of geranygeranylated proteins., |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.29|, catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP), which originates in plants from the plastidic |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY|), with |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| (FPP) to give GGPP. Cyclization of the linear GGPP to the tetracyclic |FRAME: CPD1F-128| occurs in two steps; GGPP is converted to the bicyclic compound |FRAME: ENT-COPALYL-DIPHOSPHATE| by |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.13| (CPS), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD1F-128| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.19| (KS)., In the fungi |FRAME:TAX-5127| and |FRAME:TAX-55067| spp. CPS and KS activities reside in the same protein, albeit in separate catalytic sites |CITS:[9268298][10644675][10803977]|. In plants, however, theh activities are carried by two separate enzymes. In |FRAME:TAX-3701| these enzymes have been shown to be localized in plastids. CPS transcripts are present in much lower quantities than those of KS transcripts, indicating that CPS may act as a bottle-neck regulator, functioning as a branch point in terpenoid biosynthesis and committing to the synthesis of ent-kaurenoids and gibberellins |CITS:[Sponsel04]|.

Summary: |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| is one of the building blocks of DNA and is released when cells die and their DNA degrades. It is released from 2'-deoxyribonucleosides by the action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.M2| |CITS: [468819][2026165]|., Some organisms are able to metabolize |FRAME: 2-DEOXYRIBOSE| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.229| (|FRAME: G-63084|), which phosphorylates it to |FRAME: DEOXY-RIBOSE-5P| |CITS: [13563487][13641245][4867740][13563487]|. , A specific aldolase, |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.4|, splits |FRAME: DEOXY-RIBOSE-5P|, yielding |FRAME: GAP|, which enters central metabolism through the glycolytic pathway, and |FRAME: ACETALD|, which must be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| before it can enter central metabolism via the TCA cycle.

Summary: Evidence from tracer studies in tea indicates that an alternative caffeine biosynthesis pathway via paraxanthine exists in addition to the major pathway|FRAME: PWY-5037|. Partially purification and subsequent characterization of a tea N-methyltransferase showed that 7-methylxanthine is metabolized to theobromine as well as paraxanthine. However its conversion to theobromine is at a 10-fold faster rate than its conversion to paraxanthine. Because of this preferential, conversion of 7-methylxansine to theobromine, the depicted caffeine biosynthesis via paraxanthine is a minor route |CITS: [Kato96]|.  Caffeine synthases characterized from both tea and coffee showed effective conversion of paraxanthine to caffeine |CITS: [10984041][10364410][12746542][12527364]|.

Summary: General Background, Cyanobacterial lipids consist of glycerolipids with a C18 fatty acid esterified at position sn-1 and a C16 fatty acid esterified at position sn-2 |CITS: [Sato82]|., The cyanobacteria have been classified into four groups according to the distribution of the fatty acids in their glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|. , Strains in Group 1 are characterized by the presence of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (|FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9245|) at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively., Strains in Group 2 contain the tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| at the sn-1 position and the mono-unsaturated C16 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-9245| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 3 have a different tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid (|FRAME: CPD-8117|) at the sn-1 position and the saturated C16 acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 4 are similar to strains in Group 3 except that they have, in addition, the tri-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| and the tetra-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: CPD-12653| at the sn-1 position., |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID Linoleate|, whose production is described here, is not found in cyanobacterial lipids. Rather, it is transformed by further desaturation to either |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.36|) or |FRAME: CPD-8117| (by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.46|)., |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID Linoleate| is an ω-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid, the 6 referring to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid., It is also produced by plants and is abundant in many vegetable oils, especially safflower and sunflower oils. It is an essential dietary requirement for all mammals, that lack the Δ12 desaturase that produces it. A few animals are able to synthesize |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6001|., About This Pathway, In cyanobacteria |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is formed bound to an acyl-carrier protein, part of the fatty acid synthase complex. Stearate is transfered to the sn-1 position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.15| |CITS: [16039611]|., As described above, glycerolipids from all cyanobacteria contain unsturated C18 fatty acids in the sn-1 position, but differ in the degree and nature of unsaturation. The desaturation occurs only after |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| has been incorporated into the glycerol backbone, and is catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes known as acyl-lipid desaturases., The first desaturation occurs at position 9, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS15040|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS15040-MONOMER| |CITS: [7929259]|. This is followed by desaturation at position 12, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.45| (encoded by |FRAME: SGL_RS10130|), producing |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| |CITS: [2118597]|.

General Background, Both alkyl and alk-1-enyl phospholipids appear to serve as important structurally-stable lipid components of membranes, since the ether linkage can impede the hydrolysis of the acyl moiety by phospholipases |CITS: [Snyder85]|. |FRAME: Plasmalogens Plasmalogens| are a unique class of membrane glycerophospholipids that contain a fatty alcohol with a vinyl-ether bond at the sn-1 position, and an ester-linked fatty acids at the sn-2 position of the glycerol backbone. They are widely distributed in anaerobic bacteria and animals. In humans and other mammals they represent up to 20% of the total phospholipid mass (between 1/2 and 2/3 of the ethanolamine phospholipids in humans are plasmalogens |CITS: [11275267]|). , The earliest report of alkylglycerols was made in 1909, from lipids isolated from starfish |CITS: [16742127]|. The name plasmalogen was coined in 1924 by Feulgen and Voit to describe an unknown compound that produced an aldehyde (which they called "plasmal") that they observed in plasma after acid treatment |CITS: [Feulgen24]|. It took nearly 40 years to establish the exact structure of the plasmalogens |CITS: [13416288][13499384][13576152][Marinetti59][Warner63]|., While plasmalogens are widely found in anaerobic bacteria, invertebrates, and vertebrates, they are absent from aerobic bacteria (an exception are myxobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-34|) and most fungi and plants. This distribution suggests that they appeared, disappeared, and then reappeared during evolution, an explanation that is supported by major differences in their biosynthesis between anaerobic bacteria and animals |CITS: [22627108]|., About This Pathway, In animals plasmalogen biosynthesis begins with |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| (DHAP), and the characteristic vinyl ether is formed by the oxygen-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.77| (see |FRAME: PWY-7782|). Feeding studies have suggested that the anaerobic pathway in bacteria does not start with DHAP |CITS: [5417192]|, and pulse labeling studies suggested that anaerobic bacteria may directly convert a diacyl precursor to a plasmalogen product |CITS: [28617934]|. , The key enzyme in the anaerobic pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-9692|, was discovered in 2021 in the anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-1502|. The enzyme, which belongs to the BCR/HAD family, initiates the reduction of the ester bond using an ATP-driven electron transfer to create a ketyl intermediate. The reaction proceeds via protonation, a subsequent one-electron reduction, a second protonation, and dehydration |CITS: [33350306]|., Homologs of the |FRAME: G-107624| and |FRAME: G-107623| genes that encode the enzyme were found in a wide variety of obligate and facultative anaerobes. Among the microbial phyla most typical for the human gut microbiome, organisms that contained the genes partially corresponded to Gram staining - 53% of the Gram-positive Firmicutes and 44% of the Actinobacteria were classified as plasmalogen-positive, while only ~15% of Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria contained homologous genes |CITS: [33350306]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the glycolysis pathway with the Entner-Doudoroff pathway., |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS Glycolysis| is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, and is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces many key precursor metabolites that are essential for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules. Due to its importance, glycolysis can be found in almost all organisms., Glycolysis fulfills two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) it can produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules by running in the reverse direction., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy. The glycolysis pathway used in this superpathway is the well characterized glycolysis pathway of the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| growing with |FRAME: D-Glucose| as a source of carbon and energy (glucose is phosphorylated by the phosphotransferase system that import it into the cell, and thus the pathway starts with |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|)., When the cells need reducing power more than they need ATP, they can maximize reducing power production by using an alternative pathway for metabolizing glucose - the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|. The |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative branch"| of that pathway converts the glucose to the sugar acid |FRAME: CPD-2961| by the action of two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.49| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.31|., The pentose phosphate pathway can proceed via its |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative branch"| to form multiple precursor metabolites. However, when this is not necessary, the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"| functions as a short shunt that returns |FRAME: CPD-2961| to glycolysis by converting it to the glycolytic intermediate |FRAME: GAP| and the glycolysis end-product |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. The Entner-Doudoroff pathway consists of the two enzymes |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.12| and |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.14| |CITS: [12981024]|.

Names: cytochrome c biogenesis (system II type) // cytochrome c biogenesis
Summary: General background, C-type cytochromes (cytC) are electron-transfer proteins that have one or more |FRAME: HEME_C| groups. They are characterized by the covalent attachment of the heme to the polypeptide chain via two (or rarely one) thioether bonds formed between thiol groups of cysteine residues and vinyl groups of a |FRAME: PROTOHEME| molecule. The two cysteine residues almost always occur in the amino-acid sequence CXXCH |CITS: [10647174]|., C-type cytochromes possess a wide range of properties and function in a large number of different redox processes. In general, the differences in c-type cytochromes among bacteria are much larger than those among animal species. The use of the term term "c-type cytochromes" was introduced to distinguish this family of diverse proteins from the well-characterized mitochondrial protein, which is often referred to as "cytochrome c"., Bacterial c-type cytochromes function in the electron transport chains of bacteria with many different types of energy metabolism, including phototrophs, methylotrophs, denitrifiers, sulfate reducers and the nitrogen-fixers. , The biogenesis of c-type cytochromes involves covalent attachment of |FRAME: PROTOHEME| to two cysteines at a conserved CXXCH sequence in the apocytochrome. The histidine residue acts as an axial ligand to the heme iron., Three unique cytochrome c assembly pathways, known as systems I, II, and III, have ben described. , About This Pathway, The first indication for the existence of the system II pathway was the discovery that the ccsA gene (named for cytochrome c synthesis) in chloroplasts contains a WWD domain (a tryptophan-rich domain that is known to maintain a heme molecule in the reduced state by two external histidines) that is different from that found in the bacterial CcmF genes of system I |CITS: [1310666]|. The gene was later shown to be required for cytochrome f biosynthesis (cytochrome f, a part of the cytochrome b6f complex, is analogous to cytochrome c1 of the bc1 complex and contains the CXXCH motif), and led to the discovery of the rest of the involved genes |CITS: [8617725][ 9395519][9504916]|. Analogous genes were discovered in the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [9068642][9226261][10844653]| and the β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [11069671][11881892][15937156]|., The system is now known to operate in a wide range of organisms, including chloroplasts, Gram-positive bacteria, cyanobacteria, most β-proteobacteria, some δ-proteobacteria, and all ε-proteobacteria |CITS: [19721088]|., In organisms that utilize system II the apocytochrome polypeptide, upon translocation from the cytosol, is exposed to the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.15|, which forms a disulfide bridge between the two cysteines in the CXXCH motif. This bridge must be reduced before the heme molecule can be attached to the polypeptide. System II uses reducing equivalents from inside the cell (likely thioredoxin) to reduce the cysteine residues. Dedicated thioredoxin-related proteins called ResA (in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) and CcsX (in |FRAME: TAX-520|) can reduce the cysteines directly |CITS: [11069671][12637552][15667290]|. These proteins are kept in their reduced active form by the DsbD protein, or by the similar, smaller protein CcdA |CITS: [9068642][9226261][11844773]|., The other components of system II are the CcsA and CcsB proteins, which form a tight complex with the activity of |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.17|. In a few bacterial species (such as |FRAME: TAX-209|, |FRAME: TAX-816|, and |FRAME: TAX-843|) the two proteins are fused into one large ORF called CcsBA. The two proteins are membrane-bound. CcsA, which has either eight or six transmembrane domains |CITS: [9560218][12427766][17706591]|, contains the WWD domain that binds the heme molecule, as well as conserved histidine residues that are believed to help keep the heme iron in its reduced form. The reduced heme molecule moves from the cytosol through CcsA until it reaches the WWD domain, where it is liganded in place. CcsB has four transmembrane domains, with the third and fourth separated by a large periplasmic domain that includes the apocytochrome c CXXCH recognition function. CcsB thus recruits the apocytochrome polypeptide and presents it to the heme bound to CcsA |CITS: [30563894]|.

The |FRAME: Gaburedins gaburedins| are a family of γ-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas whose biosynthesis is encoded by a silent gene cluster in the |FRAME: TAX-54571| genome. The cluster, which consists of the three genes |FRAME: G-124751|, |FRAME: G-124752|, and gbnC, is located adjacent to a putative regulatory, system homologous to the the mmfR-mmfLHP-mmyR cluster of |FRAME: TAX-100226|. The products of the mmfLHP genes are the |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, which act as inducers of |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production in |FRAME: TAX-100226|, while MmfR and MmyR are ArpA-like transcriptional repressors, which repress |FRAME: CPD-27200 methylenomycin| production |CITS: [18988741]|., Based on the sequence homology, it was hypothesized that the gbnABC genes encode a natural product(s), whose production is controlled by a regulatory system encoded by the mmfR-mmfLHP-mmyR genes homologs. The gbn cluster contains highly conserved DNA sequences, which were predicted to be binding motifs for the transcriptional repressor GbnR, the mmyR homolog. To test this hypothesis, the gbnR gene was knocked out. Indeed, the mutant produced six new metabolites, the products of the gbnABC genes, which were named gaburedin A-F. The compounds structures were shown to be γ-aminobutanoate (GABA)-derived ureas, containing an amino acid linked by a ureido bridge |CITS: [Sidda14]|., The |FRAME: G-124751| gene encodes a putative pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent amino acid decarboxylase, and was proposed to decarboxylate |FRAME: GLT| to give |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA). The |FRAME: G-124752| gene encodes a putative ATP-dependent enzyme belonging to the acyl-CoA synthetase superfamily, and was proposed to adenylate either the carboxyl or the carbamoyl group of |FRAME: CPD-27332|, which forms by the spontaneous carboxylation of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|. The carbamoyl adenylate, which is shown here, can react with the appropriate amino acids either directly, or via a cyclical anhydride form, to form the gaburedins. Deletion of |FRAME: G-124752| in the gbnR mutant abolished gaburedin production |CITS: [Sidda14]|., GbnA and GbnB are the only enzymes that appear to be necessary for formation of the gaburedins. GbnC is a membrane protein that contains an EamA domain, which is found in some transporters. It has been proposed to export either the gaburedins or a pathway intermediate, which could react with amino acids in the extracellular milieu to form the gaburedins |CITS: [Sidda14]|., Attempts to express the gaburedin biosynthesis enzymes in |FRAME: TAX-562| have failed |CITS: [Sidda15]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, |FRAME:TAX-1511| can grow on |FRAME: ARG| by converting it to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE|, which is processed via both the oxidative and reductive branches of the Stickland reaction. The oxidation branch leads to production of acetyl-CoA and generates ATP, while producing 4 reducing equivalents. The reductive branch utilizes these reducing equivalents by production of |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| via proline |CITS: [10220161] [Brock97]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8187|)., Following the conversion of |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE|, the oxidation route begins with racemization of |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| to |FRAME: CPD-217|, followed by migration of the amino group from C5 to C4 to form 2.4-diaminopentanoate |CITS: [11577113]|. This compound is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-299| and ammonia. CoA-mediated thiolytic cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-299| produces |FRAME: D-ALANINE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which leads to ATP production via acetyl phosphate.
