Summary: General Background, The superpathway of anthocyanin biosynthesis that originates from delphinidin 3-O-glucoside comprises the formation of compounds such as ternatin C5, anthocyanidin sophoroside and gentiodelphin. Those anthocyanins are usually very stable pigments contributing to a wide variation of flower colors in different species., Ternatins are a group of 15 polyacetylated delphinidin glucosides that confer blue color to the petals of butterfly pea (|FRAME:TAX-43366|). The general structure of ternatins consists of malonylated delphinidin 3,3',5'-triglucosides having 3',5'-side chains with alternating D-glucose and p-coumaric acid units of varying lengths |CITS: [8991946][12482461]|., Antocyanidins often occur as sophoroside, i.e. a diglucoside that consists of glucose attached to the 2''-O-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of anthocyanidins. The anthocyanidin that confers the bright blue color to |FRAME:TAX-35883| (a member of the Convolvulacea) is a sophoroside that forms a complex with several caffeoyl residues, known as |FRAME:CPD-7841| (WBA). Reddish-brown flowers of dusky mutants of |FRAME:TAX-35883| contain |FRAME:CPD-7840| (HBA) representing the most favorite flower hue for Japanese floriculturists |CITS: [15842621]|. , Gentiodelphin, i.e. delphinidin 3-O-glucosyl-5-O-caffeoylglucoside-3'-O-caffeoylglucoside found in the genus Gentiana is a unusual stable anthocyanin conferring deep blue flower colors to this species |CITS: [Goto82]|. The stability of this compound has been proposed as an effect of the intramolecular stacking of acyl residues attached to the opposite sides of the A and B-ring sandwiching the corresponding anthocyanidin |CITS: [Yoshida91]|., About This Pathway, Ternatin C5: The simplest ternatin is ternatin C5 that is the starting point for the formation of the most complex ternatin, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-7865| and its intermediates. The characteristic glucosylation pattern of ternatins, the 3,3',5'-triglucosylated delphinidin is formed by the catalytic activity of 3' and 5'-position specific glucosyltransferases |CITS: [Kazuma04]| thought to be involved in the early biosynthetic pathway of ternatins following the 6''-O-malonysation of the delphinidin 3-O-glucoside., Anthocyanin sophoroside: The crucial step in the formation of anthocyanidin sophoroside as , precursors for HBA and WBA in Ipomoea is catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside 2-O''-glucosyltransferase (3GGT). , The enzyme adds glucose to anthocyanidin 3-glucosides at the 2''-O-position of the glucose moiety forming the corresponding sophorosides. Although the enzyme accepts all three major anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside, anthocyanidin 3,5-diglucoside are not suitable substrates for the 3GGT |CITS: [15842621]|., Gentiodelphin: The first committed step in the gentiodelphin biosynthesis is the 5-O-glucosylation , of delphinidin 3-O-glucoside. The next steps that further decorate delphinidin 3,5-glucoside with caffeic acid and glucose are proposed to constitute a metabolic grid in the biosynthetic route towards gentiodelphin. Both possible routes, i.e. 3'-O-glucosylation followed by the aromatic 5-O-acylation or vice versa are displayed and thought to be present in Gentiana |CITS: [9881162][12857844]|. The glucosyltransferases involved in the biosynthesis of gentiodelphin are highly position specific and follow a defined order which is the 3-O-glucosylation followed by the 5-O-glucosylation and the subsequent 3'-O-glucosylation of the delphinidin backbone |CITS: [12857844]|. The 5-aromatic acyltransferase |CITS: [9363752][9881162]| can only acylate the 5-O-glucoside but not the 3, 7 or 3' positions of anthocyanins.

A similar enzyme was also reported from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-5476|, but that enzyme was NADP+-specific |CITS: [1903434]|.,  A thermostable L-lysine 6-dehydrogenase has also been purified from the moderately thermophilic, |FRAME: TAX-1422|, and the gene encoding it was cloned, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant enzyme purified |CITS: [14766574]|., In both organisms |FRAME: CPD-7682| has been identified as the reaction product. Summary: General Background, Anthocyanins are water-soluble, secondary plant products that constitute a , major subgroup (about 15 to 20%) of flavonoids |CITS: [Andersen06]|. Almost all vascular plants possess , basic anthocyanins such as pelargonidin-3-O-glucoside and cyaniding-3-O-glucoside (this pathway) responsible , for the red to magenta coloration of flowers and fruits and delphinidin-3-O-glucoside (|FRAME:PWY-5153|) , introducing blue tones to the floral organs of plants |CITS: [11130659]|., Anthocyanins play important roles as pigments of flowers and fruits in numerous plants across the plant , kingdom to attract insects for pollination and act as protectants against UV-B irradiation |CITS: [14561507]|. , They also exhibit anti-oxidant activities and therefore may serve as potential anticancer |CITS: [16084717]| , and anti-arteriosclerosis compounds in human health |CITS: [15282635]| |CITS: [12828368]| |CITS: [11960739]|. , Anthocyanines constitute biological active metabolites that also modulate inter-species relationships being , intimately connected with the co-existence of plants with, e.g. insects, mammals, and birds |CITS: [11820759]|., About This Pathway, Enzymes: The crucial step in this pathway is the oxidation of leucoanthocyanidins to generate respective , cyanidins. Despite of intensive research over the last years (e.g. |CITS: [14552794]| |CITS: [16106293]|) this enzymatic , step is still not completely understood and requires further study. Anthocyanidin synthase (ANS), a 2-oxoglutarate , iron-dependent oxygenase, catalyzes the penultimate step in the biosynthesis of the anthocyanin class of , flavonoids |CITS: [11796114]|. Anthocyanidin synthase catalyzes the in vitro conversion of leucoanthocyanidins , to dihydroflavonol and flavonol intermediates (cis- and trans-isoforms) and to a minor degree , anthocyanidins |CITS: [Turnbull00]|. Moreover, the cyanidin synthase of the gymnosperm Ginkgo biloba (ANS/FLS) has been shown to have bifunctional properties and can also act as flavonol synthase (see |FRAME:PWY-3101|), hence catalyzing key reactions in more than one pathway |CITS:[18779661]|. , The formation of colored anthocyanidins such as pelargonidin and cyanidin from colorless leucoanthocyanidins , (leucopelargonidin, leucocyanidin) was detected by the ANS-catalyzed reaction in the presence of ferrous ion, , 2-oxoglutarate and ascorbate, being followed by acidification with HCI |CITS: [10074715]|. It has been shown , that recombinant ANSs from several model plant species, snapdragon, petunia, torenia, and maize, catalyze , the formation of anthocyanidins in vitro through a 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxidation of corresponding , leucoanthocyanidins |CITS: [11316805]|. Assuming that the site of initial oxidation is the same for anthocyanidin , and dihydroflavonol formation, evidence is presented for initial oxidation at the C-3 position of the flavonoid C-ring , and for two bifurcating steps during catalysis by anthocyanidin synthase |CITS: [12240335]|., It is assumed that the anthocyanidin synthase proceeds via stereospecific hydroxylation at the C-3 atom of the , leucocyanidins which furthermore spontaneously dehydrate and finally form stable isomers, i.e. anthocyanidin , pseudobase (3-flaven-2,3-diol) |CITS: [DAVIES06]|. , The other enzyme of the pathway, UDPG: flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferase (3-UGT) is considered as a final , enzyme necessary for producing the earliest stable anthocyanin molecules in plant cells |CITS: [KITAMURA06]|. , Glucosylation is one of the most prominent modifications of compounds involved in plant secondary metabolism , and often represents final steps within a pathway |CITS: [15647808]|. Flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferases catalyzing , red to magenta colored anthocyanins have been identified in many plant genera such as Arabidopsis |CITS: [15807784]| , and Gentiana |CITS: [8819318]|., Regulation: The flavonoid biosynthetic pathway belongs to one of the most intensely studied areas of , plant secondary metabolism |CITS: [11743081]| and provides probably the best-investigated regulatory system , in plants |CITS: [15860424]| |CITS: [QUATTROCCHIO06]|. It has long been suggested that enzymes involved in , the phenylpropanoid and flavonoid pathweay form multienzyme complexes that channel substrates towards required , metabolic routes and entail a complex regulation |CITS: [STAFFORD74]| |CITS: [3970546]|., Anthocyanin and proanthocyanin biosynthesis is basically regulated by transcription factors with MYB or , helix-loop-helix (HLH) domains and a WD40 protein. Those proteins are able to mutually interact in response to , the demand of the plant resulting in the activation of corresponding structural pigmentation genes |CITS: [16464150]| , |CITS: [15882656]| |CITS: [12586894]|. Little is known so far what regulates the regulators, but light and plant , hormones have been established to be central to the expression of anthocyanin biosynthetic genes |CITS: [16464150]|., Transport: Anthocyanins are known to be accumulated in vacuoles where the acidic environment finally , causes the alteration from colorless to colored pigments. A growing body of evidence specifies that flavonoid , synthesis takes place in the cytoplasm indicating that a transport step is involved in the overall biosynthesis scheme , |CITS: [KITAMURA06]| |CITS: [16464150]|., Genes encoding glutathione S-transferases (GST's) linked to the sequestration of anthocyanins into the tonoplast , have been found in Petunia (AN9) |CITS: [10938372]|, carnation |CITS: [12789508]| and Arabidopsis (TT19) |CITS: [14675436]|. , Besides transporters that bind to certain anthocyanins and carry them to the vacuole special intravacuolar bodies, , i.e. anthocyanic vacuolar inclusions (AVIs) have been found to be involved in the transport and/or accumulation of anthocyanins. , They appear to serve as anthocyanin traps concentrating the pigments (preferentially anthocyanidin 3,5-diglycosides) , to a proteinaceous matrix |CITS: [11117881]|.

With over 50.000 identified structures terpenoids represent one of the largest and most diverse compound classes of specialized metabolites across all domains of life. The molecular skeleton of terpenoids is formed by cyclization of oligoprenyl diphosphates which is catalyzed by a formidable number of terpene synthases/cyclases being able to synthesize compounds with various chiral centers, which in turn results in a multitude of structural arrangements and bioactivities |CITS:[16895335] [22907771] [Cane99] [24858310]|. , Fungi contribute a growing number of novel natural metabolites which are of significant interest in terms of unique structures and biological potential |CITS:[25122538] [Singh15]|. However, many of the natural products observed in fungi are not synthesized under conditions in the laboratory and their biosynthetic genes reside in silent gene clusters which require new technologies and approaches to be activated and deciphered |CITS:[Wawrzyn15]|. Genome mining and traversing the fungal metabolom has resulted in the detection and elucidation of many new pathways which otherwise would remain untapped |CITS:[21826184]|. , Fungi are especially well suited for the production of terpenoids which span all classes of sesqui-, di-, sester-, and triterpenoids |CITS:[25171145]|. The biosynthesis of the diterpenoid |FRAME:CPD-18470| and its methylated derivative |FRAME:CPD-18471| has been discovered by genome mining utilizing a chimeric cyclase |FRAME:MONOMER-14878| (see |FRAME:PWY-6659|) |CITS:[17360612]|. Not only could the respective homolog of a chimeric terpenoid synthase involved in the |FRAME:PWY-7721| of Diaporthe amygdali been identified but also the putative biosynthetic cluster adjoining the |FRAME:MONOMER-19520| (PS). The terpene cyclase-like protein encoded by the gene PS was shown to consist of two domains, the terpene cyclase domain at the N-terminus and the prenyltransferase domain at the C-terminus. It could be demonstrated that the cyclase portion of the phomopsene synthase formed |FRAME:CPD-18470| from |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| whereas the prenyltransferase part of the phomopsene synthase catalyzed the formation of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| from |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| indicating the multiple functions this enzyme exhibits in this pathway |CITS:[19161275]|.

Summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., The best characterized wall teichoic acids are those from |FRAME: TAX-224308| and |FRAME: TAX-655816|, in which the polymeric units are |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY "glycerol phosphate"| and |FRAME: PWY-7815 "ribitol phosphate"|, respectively |CITS: [13684313]|. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 1-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. The anomeric phosphate of the linkage unit is covalently attached to peptidoglycan (PG) via a phosphodiester bond to the C6 hydroxyl of N-acetylmuramate., It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: PWY-7819 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]|. , Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, Even though the main form of wall teichoic acids in |FRAME: TAX-224308 "Bacillus subtilis 168"| is a poly(glycerol phosphate) polymer (also known as the |FRAME: CPD-75 "major teichoic acid"| of this strain), the organism also produces another type of wall teichoic acid, which has been named the |FRAME: CPD-19345 "minor teichoic acid"| |CITS: [4198356]|. This polymer is composed of poly(3-O-β-D-glucopyranosyl-N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]| and is linked to the peptidoglycan moiety by a linkage unit identical to that found in the major teichoic acid, consisting of sn-glycerophospho-4-O-N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine, which during biosynthesis is hooked on a diphospho-ditrans,octacis-undecaprenol membrane anchor |CITS: [16735734]|., The synthesis of the minor teichoic acid does not appear to be essential for cell growth, and its only known function is to serve as adsorption site for bacteriophages |FRAME: TAX-10736| and ρ11 |CITS: [1906927]|., The biosynthetic process can be divided into the following main steps: first, the linkage unit is synthesized, attached to a lipid carrier. Next, the polymeric chain is added by alternate addition of glucosyl and N-acetyl-D-galactosamine 1 phosphate. The polymer is then transported through the membrane to the outer cell wall and transferred from its lipid carrier to peptidoglycan. A more detailed description follows:, The first step is the attachment of an N-acetyl-glocasamine molecule to the lipid carrier |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P|, by the action of the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35530-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35530| gene |CITS: [12101296]|. The N-acetyl-glucosamine has to be activated, in the form of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (for more information on the acivation of this donor molecule see the pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|)., Next, an activated |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| unit is added by the enzyme |FRAME: BSU35750-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35750| gene, to generate an N-acetyl-mannosaminyl-β-(1->4)-N-acetyl-glucosamine disaccharide, attached to the lipid., UDP-N-acetyl-mannosamine is synthesized from UDP-N-acetyl-glocasamine by |FRAME: BSU35660-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35660| gene |CITS: [1906927][12107153]|. The last step in the synthesis of the linkage unit is the addition of one glycerol phosphate unit, which is performed by a dedicated |FRAME: BSU35760-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: BSU35760|. The glycerol-phosphate unit has to be activated as well, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-606|, which is generated from glycerol-3-phosphate by |FRAME: CPLX-5322|, the product of the |FRAME: BSU35740| gene., Once the linkage unit is ready, a transferase encoded by |FRAME: BSU35680| adds the first N-acetyl-D-galactosamine 1 phosphate. This is followed by alternate additions of glucosyl and N-acetyl-D-galactosamine 1 phosphate residues catalyzed by |FRAME: BSU35690 GgaA| and |FRAME: BSU35680 GgaB|, respectively |CITS: [16735734]|., The completed polymer is then exported (flipped) to the external side of the cytoplasmic membrane by the teichoic acid ABC transporter, which is encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35710| and |FRAME: BSU35700| genes. This is followed by the transfer of the teichoic acid including its linkage unit to C-6 of a MurNAc residue of a growing peptidoglycan chain, which is catalyzed by any of three members of the LCP (LytR-CpsA-Psr) protein family (|FRAME: BSU35840|, |FRAME: BSU35650|, and |FRAME: BSU35520|), releasing the undecaprenyl anchor |CITS:[21964069]|., Many of the enzymes involved in this pathway are common to the the biosynthesis of the major teichoic acid (see |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY|)|. The only two enzymes that are specific for this pathway are the transferases encoded by the |FRAME: BSU35690| and |FRAME: BSU35680| genes, which reside in an operon that is located between the tagF and gtaB loci |CITS: [1906927]|.

Summary: The application of natural |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|-fixing pathways for converting |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into value-added multicarbon products has been limited in chemistry and biotechnology due to several limitations. Firstly, natural |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation has developed to generate biomass and not a dedicated product. Secondly, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|-fixing enzymes and pathways are notoriously inefficient. For example, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39| (RubisCO), which is responsible for carbon fixation in the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|, is a slow catalyst that has a strong side reaction with oxygen, resulting in |FRAME: PWY-181 photorespiration|, a process that leads to a loss of up to 30% of the light energy that is absorbed by the photosystem., The synthetic pathway described here, which includes enzymes from eight different organisms (the mammal |FRAME: TAX-9606|, the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1534|, |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-408|, |FRAME: TAX-1061|, and |FRAME: TAX-1063|, and the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-338192|) aims to provide an alternative to natural pathways |CITS: [27856910]|., The pathway converts |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into the organic molecule |FRAME: MAL| at a rate of 5 nmoles per minute per milligram protein. Two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules are fixed per cycle by an enoyl-CoA carboxylase that can act on two different intermediates (|FRAME: CROTONYL-COA| and |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA|). Two of the enzymes, |FRAME: CPLX-9177| and |FRAME: CPLX-9180|, have been engineered to modify their natural properties., Operation of the pathway in vitro requires a few accessory enzyme that are not shown in the pathway diagram, including |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.6|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.24|, |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.9|, |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.9| and |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.1| |CITS: [27856910]|.

General Background, In mammals |FRAME: TRP| is an essential amino acid that must be obtained in the diet. It is utilized in protein synthesis and in biosynthesis of the neurotransmitter |FRAME: SEROTONIN|. It is catabolized via the kynurenine pathway in most tissues. This pathway is the major catabolic route of |FRAME: TRP| in mammals, as well as an anabolic source of |FRAME: NAD|. |FRAME: TRP| is also catabolized via the serotonergic pathway in the central nervous system (CNS), producing |FRAME: SEROTONIN| and other indoleamines. Metabolites of the kynurenine pathway are involved in many biological processes. In the CNS products of both pathways have consequences for the modulation of physiology and behavior and for the pathophysiology of some diseases (in |CITS: [18282734]|, |CITS: [9291104]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16942634]| and |CITS: [15018833]|). See pathways |FRAME: PWY-5651| and its pathway links and pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|., About This Pathway, The trace amine |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| is produced in the brain and possibly other tissues by the decarboxylation of |FRAME: TRP|. |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| is believed to function as a neurotransmitter or neuromodulator in the CNS of mammals (in |CITS: [12538805]|). It is catabolized by monoamine oxidase A catalyzed oxidation to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETALDEHYDE|. This aldehyde can then be oxidized to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| by an undetermined isoform of aldehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.3), or reduced to |FRAME: CPD-341| (tryptophol) by aldehyde reductase in the presence of |FRAME: NADPH| (|CITS: [12538805] [4146452]| and in |CITS: [8098507]|). It was previously suggested that the cytochrome P450 isozyme CYP2D6 mediates the oxidative deamination of |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE|, but later work showed that monoamine oxidase A was responsible for this activity |CITS: [12538805]|. An additional metabolite of |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| has been identified as (4R)-2-(3-indolylmethyl)-1,3-thiazolidine-4-carboxylate, a condensation product of |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETALDEHYDE| and free |FRAME: CYS| present in brain tissue. Its formation in vitro is spontaneous and its bioligical function is unknown |CITS: [3689382] [3373215]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [8098507]|.

|FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it accumulates at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant |CITS: [9736747]|., |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| can serve as carbon, nitrogen, and energy source for many microbes that utilize an aerobic degradation pathway |CITS: [3290197][6406829]|. However, only a few organisms are able to catabolize |FRAME: BETAINE| anaerobically. These are the methanogenic archaea |CITS: [24162571]|, the sulfate-reducing bacteria |CITS: [Heijthuijsen89]| and the acetogenic bacteria |CITS: [16345842][Eichler84]|. These organisms have in common the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, also known as the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway (WLP) that metabolizes C1 compounds such as methyl groups (see |FRAME: PWY-7784| and |FRAME: CODH-PWY|) |CITS: [18378591][21740227][25383604]|., The strict anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-138119| can grow on |FRAME: BETAINE| when an exogenous electron acceptor such as fumarate or nitrate is provided. When grown with nitrate as the electron acceptor, |FRAME: BETAINE| was converted to |FRAME: DIMETHYL-GLYCINE|, along with production of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. These findings suggest that |FRAME: TAX-138119| is capable of methylotrophic growth in which only one methyl group of |FRAME: BETAINE| is removed and subsequently oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to provide reducing equivalents for anaerobic respiration |CITS: [25313086]|., The two enzymes and one methyl-carrier corrinoid protein that participate in this pathway have been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-138119|. |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.376|, the adjacently encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-21033|, and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.378|, form a three-component system for the methylation of tetrahydrofolate with |FRAME: BETAINE|. Glycine betaine—corrinoid protein Co-methyltransferase is similar to members of the trimethylamine methyltransferase family, but unlike most members of that family, it does not contain an |FRAME: CPD-3321| residue. , The product of this methyltransfer system, |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N 5-methyltetrahydrofolate|, is processed via the enzymes of the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"|, enabling the organism to generate reducing equivalents, which could be passed to the electron transport chain for reduction of the anaerobic electron acceptor, and form an ATP molecule for each molecule of |FRAME: BETAINE| consumed |CITS: [25313086]|. The same pathway has been described from the acetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-33952| |CITS: [30136352]|.

Summary: Photosynthesis is composed of two processes, the light reactions and the dark reactions. The light reactons take place in the two photosystems - photosystem I and photosystem II, where light energy is harvested and is used to power the transfer of electrons from water, via a series of electron donors and acceptors, to the final acceptor NADP+, which is reduced to NADPH. The NADPH generated by the light reactions is used for sugar synthesis in the dark reactions., The light reactions also generate a proton motive force across the thylakoid membrane, and the proton gradient is used to synthesize ATP. , There are two general chemical reactions involved in the light reactions: water oxidation in photosystem II, and NADP reduction in photosystem I. Both of the photosystems are large multiprotein complexes contained within the thylakoid membranes of all types of plants, algae and cyanobacteria, and both photosystems capture the light by means of large antennae systems, consisting of chlorophylls and carotenoids., |FRAME: EC-1.10.3.9| (PSII) utilizes solar energy for splitting water molecules, and transfers the electrons obtained from the water molecule via an electron transfer chain that ends with |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE|., The excitation of the photosystem II reaction center (RC) via light absorption by chlorophylls in the antenna drives the transfer of a very high potential electron from the cluster of four chlorophylls bound to the D1- and D2-proteins (known as P680) to a pheophytin acceptor, resulting in a P680* radical. The radical transfers the electron to a firmly bound |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE| (PQ) called QA, which transfers it to a second, not firmly bound PQ, called QB. When QB is fully reduced and protonated to |FRAME: Plastoquinols| (PQH2) form, it diffuses from the QB-binding site into the lipid matrix of the membrane (for more information see |FRAME:CPLX490-3506|)., The path between the two photosystems is not direct. The QB plastoquinone first transfers the electrons to a third complex, |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.6| (better known as the cytochrome b6f complex), where the electrons are transferred to the protein |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin|. Finally |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin| travels to |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.12|, and delivers the electrons to one of its components, P700, which is located on the inside of the thylakoids (the lumen). Under copper deprivation conditions |FRAME: Cytochromes-C6 "cytochrome c6"| substitutes for plastocyanin. , Photosystem I (PS I) catalyzes the light driven electron transfer from |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin| or |FRAME: Cytochromes-C6 "cytochrome c6"| to |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxin|, which is on the stromal side of the membrane. As in photosystem II, photosystem I performs both light capturing and electron transfer. The light capturing is performed by the large antenna system that consists of 90 antenna chlorophylls and 22 carotenoids. The electron transport chain consists of six chlorophylls, two phylloquinones and three |FRAME:CPD-7 "[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters"|., The electron transfer chain of PS I starts with P700, a heterodimer of a |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| and a |FRAME: CPD-10334| (the C13 epimer of chlorophyll a). As in photosystem II, a high energy electron is removed from P700 after excitation by light, and that electron is transferred through the system. The role of the electron delivered from photosystem II by plastocyanin is to re-reduce P700., From P700 the electron is transferred stepwise to A (a |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| molecule), A0 (another |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| molecule), A1 (a |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| molecule) and then through three 4Fe4S clusters, named FX, FA and FB. From the terminal 4Fe4S cluster, FB, the electron is transferred to the 2Fe2S cluster of |FRAME:Ferredoxins|, which leaves photosystem I and transfers the electron to the, |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|, where NADP+ is finally reduced to NADPH. Under conditions of iron limitation, |FRAME: Flavodoxin| may replace the ferredoxin |CITS: [15977059]|., Cyanobacterial PS I can exist in both trimeric and monomeric forms. The trimeric form has been shown to be the prominent oligomeric state at low light intensity. The monomeric unit of PSI from |FRAME:TAX-32046| consists of 12 protein subunits, to which 127 cofactors are non-covalently bound. , Some components of photosystem I and photosystem II in plants are different from those in photosynthetic microbes.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Omega-3-Fatty-Acids "ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids"| are known to be essential for proper neuronal and immune function. Deficiencies in these important fatty acids are associated with mental dysfunction, cardiovascular disorders, cancer and other diseases., Resolvins (resolution phase interaction products) are a class of anti-inflammatory mediators derived from the ω 3 fatty acids |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) and |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA). Those derived from EPA are termed the E-series resolvins |CITS: [15726828]|. These endogenous mediators have been found in leukocytes, brain and glial cells. They function to halt leukocyte recruitment to sites of inflammation and facilitate resolution of the inflammatory process., |FRAME: CPD-524 "Aspirin"| has well known anti-inflammatory and antipyretic functions. It also has an anti-clotting function through the inhibition of thromboxane synthesis, and is often prescribed long-term at low doses, to help prevent heart attacks, strokes, and blood clot formation in high risk patients. Aspirin may also prevent the occurrence of certain types of cancer. |FRAME: CPD-524 "Aspirin"| exerts its actions by the inhibition of both |FRAME: HS01815| (COX1) and |FRAME: HS01115| (COX2), causing a direct negative effect on prostaglandin synthesis. It irreversibly acetylates COX-2, which loses the ability to generate prostaglandin intermediates. However, the acetylated COX-2 retains its oxygenase activity, which results in the production of anti-inflammatory mediators like resolvins. The administration of aspirin during inflammation results in the production of the (18R)-series resolvins from EPA |CITS: [16757471]|., EPA-derived resolvins E1 and E2 can also be formed by microbial cytochrome P450 monooxygenase independent of |FRAME: CPD-524| |CITS: [16112645]|., About this Pathway, Aspirin mediated acetylation of COX-2 triggers the synthesis of resolvins E1 and E2 from eicosapentaenoate |CITS: [15753205]|. Following the introduction of an 18R hydroxy group by COX2, forming |FRAME: CPD66-68| (18-HEPE) , |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34| introduces a hydroperoxy group at position 5, followed by epoxidation, which eads to the downstream production of resolvins E1 and E2 |CITS: [17114001]|. The enzyme |FRAME: HS03372-MONOMER| catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-22264| to |FRAME: CPD66-57| |CITS: [21206090]|., Resolvin E1 inhibits leukocyte transendothelial migration and IL-2 production |CITS: [15753205]|. Resolvin E1 can prevent the development of inflammatory bowel disease in a mouse model, and may play a protective role in a number of disorders that involve inflammation |CITS: [15890784]|. Resolvin E2 is produced in neutrophils and can inhibit neutrophil transmigration in vivo |CITS: [17114001]|. The actions of resolvins are mediated by G-protein coupled receptors |CITS: [22450811]|.

Summary: Coagulation, also known as clotting, is the process by which blood changes from a liquid to a gel, forming a blood clot. Coagulation begins almost instantly after an injury to the endothelium lining a blood vessel. The key protein responsible for blood clotting is |FRAME: CPLX66-1741|. Fibrin (also called coagulation factor Ia) is a fibrous, non-globular protein that polymerizes to form (together with platelets) a hemostatic plug or clot over a wound site., |FRAME: CPLX66-1741 Firbrin| is produced in a non-active form called |FRAME: CPLX66-1740 fibrinogen| and must be converted into the active fibrin form by cleavage catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-1723| (coagulation factor IIa). The platelets that form the platelet plug at a wound site have thrombin receptors on their surfaces that bind serum thrombin molecules, which then convert soluble fibrinogen in the serum into fibrin. Fibrin forms long strands of tough insoluble protein that are bound to the platelets. |FRAME: CPLX66-1743 "Coagulation factor XIIIa"| cross-links the fibrin molecules to form a hardened mesh atop the platelet plug., There are two regulatory cascades that control the activation of fibrinogen to fibrin. The one described here, which is the primary pathway, used to be known as the extrinsic pathway but is now referred to as the tissue factor pathway., |FRAME: ENSG00000117525-MONOMER "Tissue factor"| (coagulation factor III) is a glycoprotein present on the outside of blood vessels, and is normally not exposed to the bloodstream. Upon vessel injury TF is exposed to the blood, where it interacts with |FRAME: HS00709-MONOMER|, resulting in the latter being cleaved by different proteases (|FRAME: CPLX-8138|, |FRAME: CPLX66-1727|, |FRAME: CPLX66-1725|, or |FRAME: CPLX66-1723|) into two chains that associate via a disulfide bond to form the dimeric active form |FRAME: MONOMER66-44307|. This form of activation is common for most of the enzymes involved in this cascade., The active |FRAME: CPLX66-1737| cleaves an Arg-|-Ile bond in |FRAME: CPLX-8137| to form the active |FRAME: CPLX-8138|. It can also convert |FRAME: CPLX66-1724| to |FRAME: CPLX66-1725|., Once activated, |FRAME: CPLX-8138| associates with |FRAME: CPLX66-1733| to form a complex known as the |FRAME: CPLX66-1734|. The complex assembles on negatively charged phospholipid membranes in the presence of calcium ions and catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: HS11470-MONOMER| (coagulation factor II) to the active |FRAME: CPLX66-1723| (coagulation factor IIa), an active serine protease |CITS: [12379114][12163491][12056907]|. The activity of |FRAME: CPLX-8138| is inhibited by |FRAME: ENSG00000003436-MONOMER|, which forms a complex with the activated factor Xa. This complex also inhibits the activity of the |FRAME: CPLX66-1737|., |FRAME: CPLX66-1723 Thrombin|, which cleaves bonds after Arg and Lys, converts |FRAME: CPLX66-584 fibrinogen| to |FRAME: CPLX66-1741|, resulting in formation of fibrin blood clots., However, it also activates numerous participants in the blood clotting cascade, including factors V, VII, VIII, XI, and XIII. Thrombin also forms a complex with |FRAME: ENSG00000178726-MONOMER| that activates protein C to protein Ca. Once evolved, protein Ca cleaves |FRAME: G66-30677-MONOMER| and |FRAME: MONOMER66-42680| and thereby reduces the amount of thrombin generated., Once |FRAME: CPLX66-1729| is activated by thrombin, it catalyzes the activation of |FRAME: CPLX66-1724|, which then forms a complex with the activated |FRAME: CPLX66-1732| (also activated by thrombin). The complex, known as the |FRAME: CPLX66-1735 "tenase complex"| catalyzes activation of |FRAME: CPLX-8137| to |FRAME: CPLX-8138|, restoring levels of the latter and ensuring that the cycle continues., The clots formed by |FRAME: CPLX66-1741| molecules are stabilzed by the action of the glutaminase |FRAME: CPLX66-1743|, which forms isopeptide bonds between various glutamine and lysine residues of the fibrin molecules.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-11420| from chorismate in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-7374|). Recently an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate (|FRAME: PWY-7371|) has been identified in some bacteria |CITS: [18801996]|., This pathway describes the last reaction in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12115| in organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD-11420|. The pathway describes the combining of the two precursors - |FRAME: OCTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: CPD-11420|, a process that has not been fully characterized yet., The genes that participate in this conversion have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1902| on the basis of sequence similarity and clustering with known menaquinone biosynthetic genes. It has been predicted that MqnP (SCO4491) catalyzes the prenylation reaction; MqnL (SCO4490) and MqnM (SCO4492) work together to catalyze the decarboxylation, and MenG (SCO4556) catalyzes the methylation reaction to yield menaquinone. However, the order of these reactions is not yet known |CITS: [30447488]|.

Summary: General Background, The ability to reduce sulfur using |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| or organic substrates as electron donors is widespread among thermophiles. It is mostly found in hyperthermophilic archea living in volcanic habitats, and in mesophilic and thermophilic bacteria living in anoxic marine or brackish sediments, fresh water sediments, bovine rumen, hot water pools from solfataric fields, and volcanic hot springs |CITS: [FEMSMicRev22-353]|., Some methanogens, especially the thermophilic and hyperthermophilic members of the genera |FRAME:TAX-2319|,|FRAME:TAX-2160|,|FRAME:TAX-2179|, and |FRAME:TAX-2184| are also able to reduce elemental sulfur to |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [Stetter83]|., Elemental sulfur is not a good substrate for enzymatic reactions because its solubility in water is very low (5 μg/L at 25 °) |CITS: [Boulegue78]|. One mechanism that solves the problem is the conversion of the sulfur ring to a more soluble sulfur intemediate (sometimes referred to as activated sulfur) prior to reduction |CITS:[16346781][Zoephel88][Schauder93]|. This mechanism has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-844|, in which the soluble compound has, been shown to be |FRAME: Polysulfides| |CITS: [Klimmek91]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5364|)., A second possibility is the physical attachment of the microbes to the elemental sulfur, resulting in a direct conversion of sulfur to sulfide. Such physical attachment has been shown to be important during aerobic sulfur oxidation by |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS:[16349107][16535613]|. In addition, a recently purified |FRAME: CPLX-7193| from the acidophilic hyperthermophile |FRAME: TAX-2283| was shown to oxidize elemental sulfur in vitro without the need for |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [12949162]|. Since polysulfides are unstable at low pH, it is possible that |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| is the actual substrate for acidophilic organisms. With the exception of a few organisms, it is still not clear which of these two possible mechanisms is used by the different sulfur reducers., About This Pathway, The hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2261| uses different carbohydrates as a carbon source and produces acetate, CO2, and H2 as end products. In the presence of elemental sulfur the organism produces |FRAME: HS| at the expense of the produced H2., The enzyme responsible for this activity was purified to homogeneity and termed NAD(P)H elemental sulfur oxidoreductase (NSR). The enzyme is a cytoplasmic homodimeric flavoprotein that contains FAD |CITS: [17449625]|. It utilizes NADPH, which is presumed to be reduced by a ferredoxin-oxidizing membrane-bound oxidoreductase (MBX)., Expression of the |FRAME: G-16044| gene, which encodes the enzyme, is up-regulated up to seven-fold within 10 min of |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| addition. The 13-gene region that encodes the MBX enzyme is upregulated >16-fold under these conditions., When induced, MBX is proposed to replace the ferredoxin-oxidizing, H2-evolving membrane-bound hydrogenase |FRAME: CPLX-8266 MBH"|, which is down-regulated >12-fold under the same conditions |CITS: [17449625]|., While a mutant lacking MBX produced little, if any, sulfide, a mutant lacking the |FRAME: G-16044| gene produced comparable amounts of sulfide to the wild type, suggesting that two sulfide dehydrogenase isoenzymes provide a compensatory NADPH-dependent sulfur reduction system |CITS: [21965560]|.

Summary: De novo synthesis of cobamides requires a great deal of genetic information, which is only found in some prokaryotes., Many bacterial species do not have the full genetic information required for de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, but can synthesize cobalamin when supplied with |FRAME: COBINAMIDE|, a stable cobamide that is not a true intermediate of the de novo pathway |CITS: [14351147][8770581]|., In order to process |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, it has to be converted into a real intermediate of the pathway. In most bacteria this is done by the attachment of the upper ligand 5'-deoxyadenosine to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE|, followed by phosphorylation to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P|, an intermediate of the de novo biosynthetic pathway (see |FRAME: COBALSYN-PWY|)., Archaebacteria utilze a different salvage pathway, where |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| is first converted to |FRAME: CPD-691| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.90| (CbiZ). |FRAME: CPD-691 " Adenosylcobyrate"| is then converted to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P| by the action of |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.10| (CbiB) |CITS: [14990804]|., Archaea possess several enzymes that are non-orthologous replacements for the bacterial genes. For example, the archaeal |FRAME: G-11341| catalyzes the same reaction as the bacterial |FRAME: G-10054| |CITS: [16547066]|, and the archaeal |FRAME: G-11343| replaces the bacterial |FRAME: G-502| and |FRAME: G-10056| |CITS: [12486068]|., Some archaea carry the |FRAME: G-11342| gene, which encodes a fusion of the genes |FRAME: G-11339| and |FRAME: G-11341| |CITS: [16740929]|., There are many bacterial species that carry the genes of the archaeal salvage pathway. It is believed that the origin of the genes is archaeal, and that the bacterial genes were acquired by horizontal gene transfer |CITS: [18808385]|

Summary: General Background, This superpathway illustrates the metabolic steps of the rosmarinic acid biosynthesis. , Rosmarinic acid (RA) is an ester of caffeic acid and 3,4-dihydrophenyllactic acid and is widely spread in species of the , |FRAME:TAX-4136| and |FRAME:TAX-21571| |CITS: [12482446]| but also occurs in lower plants such as ferns and hornworts , |CITS: [TAKEDA90]| |CITS: [12721853]|. Beside rosmarinic acid its 3'-O-β-glucoside (|FRAME:CPD-7018|) has been , identified in the hornwort |FRAME:TAX-41834| |CITS: [16133208]| accumulating up to 1% of the cell dry weight. , Other rosmarinic acid derivatives of biological importance are lithospermic acid, a conjugate of rosmarinic acid and , caffeic acid, and lithospermic acid B a dimer of rosmarinic acid |CITS: [12482446]|., The biosynthesis of rosmarinic acid has been extensively studied for two reasons. Rosmarinic acid has been shown to , be a useful compound with regard to medicine virtue and as food additive. In addition, RA is considered as a preformed, , constitutively accumulated compound involved in the defense against microbes |CITS: [SZABO99]|. The other reason , was the challenge to unravel the interesting biosynthesis consisting of two parallel biosynthetic pathways that have to be , regulated in a coordinated manner |CITS: [11943155]|. , About This Pathway, RA biosynthesis has been first investigated in Mentha arvense and |FRAME:TAX-34256| , |CITS: [5484678]| confirming the involvement of two parallel pathways for the making of rosmarinic acid. The metabolic origin , for the formation of the two crucial compounds coumaroyl-CoA and 4-hydroxyphenyllactate was identified as L-phenylalanine , and L-tyrosine, respectively. The most experimental support for the RA biosynthesis has been obtained from species of the , |FRAME:TAX-4136| family (|FRAME:TAX-4142|,|FRAME:TAX-89630|) elucidating the detailed enzymatic steps resulting in , the formation of RA (|FRAME:PWY-5048|) |CITS: [Petersen93]| |CITS: [12482446]|., Coumaroyl-CoA is one of the essential components being used for the assembly of rosmarinic acid. It is derived from , L-phenylalanine in three well characterized enzymatic steps in plants catalyzed by L-phenylalanine-ammonia-lyase (PAL), , cinnamic acid 4-hydroxylase (C4H) and 4-coumaric acid-CoA ligase (4CL) (compare |FRAME:PWY1F-467|). , The other metabolic branch contributing to the biosynthesis of RA originates from L-tyrosine resulting in the formation of , 4-hydroxyphenyllactate (4HPL). The two moieties of the parallel pathways are connected by rosmarinic acid synthase (RAS) , catalyzing a transesterification reaction |CITS: [PETERSEN88]| |CITS: [PETERSEN91]|. The RAS accepted caffeoyl-CoA and , 3,4-dihydroxyphenyllactic acid (DHPL) resulting in the formation of rosmarinic acid. It should be noted that only the , R(+)-stereoisomer of 3,4-dihydroxyphenyllactic acid is accepted by the RAS. On the other side 4-coumaroyl-CoA and either , DHPL or its monohydroxylated isomer, 4-hydroxyphenyllactic acid (pHPL) was converted to their corresponding , coumaroyl-hydroxyphenyllactates. , The enzymatic capability of RAS and the precedent enzyme hydroxypuruvate reductase |CITS: [HAUSLER91]| |CITS: [15284489]| , to accept different substrates (mono- or dihydroxylated forms of phenyllactates/phenylacetates) prompted the proposition , for a potential second biosynthetic route for RA (|FRAME:PWY-5049|). The enzyme catalyzing the entry step into this , potential pathway is tyrosine hydroxylase (EC 1.14.16.2) and has been purified from |FRAME:TAX-3583| |CITS: [YAMAMOTO01]|. , The formation of L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) can also be accomplished by the action of polyphenol oxidases (EC 1.10.3.1) , (e.g. |CITS: [7948897]|). , It is not known precisely at what stage or order in the rosmarinic acid biosynthesis the two hydroxygroups in the 3- and 3'-position , of the phenolic rings of 4-coumaroyl-4'-hydroxyphenyllactate are introduced. These two last steps are catalyzed by two separate , cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases introducing hydroxyl groups to the 3- and 3'-position of 4-coumaroyl-4'-hydroxyphenyllactate , |CITS: [PETERSEN97]| |CITS: [11943155]|. Whereas the 3-hydroxylation of this hydroxycinnamic acid ester has been established , the 3'-hydroxylation has yet to be fully characterized.

Summary: The indoleamine |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is a vertebrate hormone secreted by the pineal gland.  It is involved in regulation of circadian and seasonal rhythms.  |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| also has immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties.  In addition to the pineal gland it is synthesized in many vertebrate cells and tissues (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|).  It is ubiquitously present in cells and body fluids due to its amphiphilic properties that allow it to cross membranes.  Mitochondria have the highest intracellular concentration of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| |CITS: [15981996]|.  Its functional groups allow both specific receptor binding and a role in oxidation chemistry.  |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also found in invertebrates |CITS: [12662344]|, protozoa |CITS: [12899443]|, plants |CITS: [11485009]|, fungi |CITS: [12662344]| and bacteria |CITS: [9181522]| although its function in many cases remains incompletely defined.  |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also used as a human dietary supplement.  In vertebrates, endogenous or ingested |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is catabolized several ways in different tissues (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6398| |FRAME: PWY-6399| and |FRAME: PWY-6400|).  Reviewed in |CITS: [16219483] [18344019]|., The enzymatic pathways of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| degradation are shown in this superpathway.  Melatonin can also be degraded by nonenzymatic pathways involving melatonin radical species, reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, or ultraviolet B radiation.  It can also be degraded by nonenzymatic reactions involving oxoferryl hemoglobin, or hemin.  These nonenzymatic reactions are not shown here, but are shown in |CITS: [18344019] [18155917] [17198536] [16793870]|., The pathway of degradation of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| by deacetylation to |FRAME: CPD-12018| has been demonstrated in the non-mammalian vertebrate eye, pineal gland, brain and skin |CITS: [7530349] [1782560] [2492661] [8812361]|.  It has also been shown in mammalian skin |CITS: [16217127] [15677341]|.  Deacetylation is also a minor pathway in mammalian liver (in |CITS: [8436983]|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Phthiocerols Phthiocerol|-based lipids and glycolipids have been found in the outer layer of the cell envelope of a small number of slow-growing |FRAME: TAX-1762|, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-33894|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1777|, |FRAME: TAX-1769| and |FRAME: TAX-1809| |CITS: [3149973]|., Phthiocerols comprise a linear carbohydrate molecule to which one methoxyl group, one methyl group, and two secondary hydroxyl groups are attached. Two types of phthiocerols have been described. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-A "phthiocerol A"| the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 3 and 4, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 9 and 11. In |FRAME: Phthiocerol-B "phthiocerol B"| a methyl group is missing from the beginning of the molecule, and thus the methoxyl and methyl groups are attached at positions 2 and 3, respectively, and the hydroxyl groups are at positions 8 and 10. , The phthiocerol molecules have a range of 28 to 34 carbon atoms in the main chain, indicating a promiscuity of the enzymes involved in their biosynthesis. Longer molecules have additional carbon atoms added at the ω end of the molecule. In most organisms the two hydroxyl groups are esterified by |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"|. In |FRAME: TAX-1781| and |FRAME: TAX-1809|, however, they are esterified by |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"| |CITS: [3149973][3113946]|., About This Pathway, Phthiocerols biosynthesis starts with the adenylation-based activation of long-chain fatty acids (catalyzed by |FRAME: G-44327 FadD26|) |CITS: [20553505]|, followed by their transfer to |FRAME: CPLX-9045|, a large polyketide synthase (PKS) complex encoded by the ppsA-ppsE genes. |FRAME: G-44327 FadD26| appears to be able to accept fatty acids within a certain size range (probably C20-C24), and the length of the final phthiocerol product is determined by the length of the fatty acid that is used as the starter molecule., The |FRAME: CPLX-9045| PKS complex extends the fatty acid by the addition of three |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and two |FRAME: METHYL-MALONYL-COA| units, producing an intermediate (|FRAME: Phthiodiolenone-A phthiodiolenone|) that contains an oxo group instead of the methoxyl group found in phthiocerols |CITS: [9201977][15749014]|. Because the PpsD protein is missing a required enoyl reductase domain, the product also contains a double bond between the C4 and C5 carbons. This bond is reduced by the product of the |FRAME: G185E-7207| gene |CITS: [17468241]|. The pathway is completed by reduction of the oxo group to a hydroxyl group, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-7205| gene product |CITS: [15995190]|, and its methylation to form the methoxyl group, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G185E-7206| gene product |CITS: [15292265]|., Many organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-1769|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, and |FRAME: TAX-78331|, also produce a related product, |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerols|, in which a phenol group is added at the ω end of the molecule |CITS: [3113946]|. The synthesis of phthiocerols and phenolphthiocerols converges at |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.292|, which can load a different starter unit, |FRAME: CPD-18623| |CITS: [9201977][20553505]|. The synthesis of phenolphthiocerols is described in |FRAME: PWY-7742|.

General Background, Most organisms have less than 45 different tRNAs despite the fact that there are 61 different amino acid codons. The reason for this is that the third base of the codon is less discriminatory for the amino acid than the other two bases. Thus, the first base of the tRNA anticodon, which pairs with the third base of the codon, is more permissive for mismatches than the other two positions. At this position, which is known as the wobble position, 'U's and 'C's may be read by a 'G' in the anticodon. Similarly, 'A's and 'G's may be read by a 'U' or 'y' (pseudouridine) in the anticodon., The nucleotide at the wobble position is often modified, and particularly uridines, which are almost invariably modified. In yeast, 11 out of 13 wobble uridine-containing tRNAs are modified in some manner. The modifications increase the efficiency of codon reading and prevent mistranslation by limiting wobbling. In particular the 2-thiolation of the uridine is required for efficient codon recognition on the ribosome., The uridine34 wobble bases of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu are universally modified, although different modifications occur in different taxa and even in different cell compartments., In |FRAME: PWY-7891 "yeast mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19983| (τm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7889 "mammalian mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19980| (cmnm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7888 "cytoplasmic tRNAs of all eukaryotes"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19978| (mcm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7892 "the bacterium E. coli"| the modification is |FRAME: 5-METHYLAMINOMETHYL-2-THIOURIDINE| (mnm5s2U)., About This Pathay, The process starts with formation of |FRAME: CPD-19984| (cmnm5U) by |FRAME: CPLX3O-10528|, a complex of the proteins encoded by the |FRAME: G3O-32728| and |FRAME: G3O-30709| genes |CITS: [15509579][17706197]|. The subsequent thiolation is catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G3O-29458| (MTO2) gene |CITS: [15509579]|. A mutation in |FRAME: G3O-29458| impairs the thiolation of these tRNAs and resulted in a marked decrease in the steady-state levels of some mitochondrial mRNA including CYTB, COX1, COX2, COX3, and ATP6 |CITS: [17706197]|., In |FRAME: G3O-29458|/|FRAME: G3O-32728|, |FRAME: G3O-29458|/|FRAME: G3O-30709|, and |FRAME: G3O-29458|/|FRAME: G3O-30709|/|FRAME: G3O-32728| double- and triple-mutant strains no detectable levels of nine tRNAs including tRNALys, tRNAGlu, and tRNAGln were detected. The mutants also exhibited extremely low levels of COX1 and CYTB mRNA and 15S and 21S rRNA as well as the complete loss of mitochondrial protein synthesis. The complete loss of modifications at U34 of tRNAs lead to the complete loss of mitochondrial translation |CITS: [20004207]|., The sulfur used for the 2-thiolation originates from |FRAME: CYS|, and is delivered to |FRAME: G3O-29458| via a short relay chain that includes the L-cysteine desulfurase |FRAME: G3O-29283| and the sulfurtransferase |FRAME: YOR251C| |CITS: [19151091]|.

Summary: General Background, Many bacteria are able to respire in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative electron acceptors. Due to the low redox potential of the nitrate/nitrite pair, nitrate is one of the preferred alternative electron acceptors. Bacterial anaerobic nitrate respiration can proceed along two different pathways. One pathway is the denitrification process, in which nitrate is sequentially reduced through nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and finally to dinitrogen (see |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY|). In the second pathway, nitrate is first reduced to nitrite and the latter is subsequently converted in a six-electron reduction step to ammonia, which is secreted from the cell., This six-electron reduction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: NRFMULTI-CPLX|, a periplasmic complex made of several proteins. The catalytic subunit of this complex is |FRAME: CYTOCHROMEC552-MONOMER|, a hexaheme c-type cytochrome encoded by the |FRAME: EG11781| gene |CITS: [7309757][3002798][2833168]|., The dissimilatory nitrite reductases are different from the assimilatory nitrite reductases in several ways, including their induction by nitrate under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [4405508]| and the fact that they are not suppressed by the presence of ammonium |CITS: [5726295]|., Four classes of nitrate reductases are known - a eukaryotic class, and three prokaryotic classes. The eukaryotic nitrate reductases are found in plants, algae and fungi, and are involved in assimilation of nitrate. They are composed of two identical subunits, and contain a |FRAME: CPD-15870| and an |FRAME:FAD| prosthetic group. In general, plant enzymes prefer NADH as the electron donor (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.1"|) and fungal enzymes prefer NADPH (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.3"|), although some enzymes were reported, to accept either of these compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPORNOPH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.2"|) |CITS: [14209328]|., Example for eukaryotic enzymes include the |FRAME: CPLX-7198| from |FRAME: TAX-3702| and the, |FRAME: CPLX-7498| from |FRAME: TAX-5141|. , Prokaryotic nitrate reductases are divided into three classes, including a class of assimilatory enzymes and two classes of respiratory enzymes. All of them include a |FRAME: CPD-582| cofactor, but differ in their substructures, cellular location, and cofactor requirement. Variabillity among enzymes is also found within the classes. Assimilatory prokaryotic nitrate reductases (NAS) are involved in the assimilation of nitrogen from nitrate for incorporation into protein. Despite their, relatedness, these enzymes vary in their substructures and cofactors. For example, |FRAME: CPLX-7499| from |FRAME:TAX-290336| is a heterodimer that utilizes NAD(P)H, while |FRAME: MONOMER-13441| from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1140| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13440| from the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-354| are monomeric and utilize ferredoxin (|FRAME: 1.7.7.2-RXN "E.C. 1.7.7.2"|) and flavodoxin, respectively., Respiratory nitrate reductases use nitrate as the electron acceptor of an anaerobic respiratory chain which, usually starts with the quinone pool (|FRAME: RXN0-6369 "EC 1.7.99.4"|)., One of these classes (NAR) consists of membrane-bound enzymes that are composed of three different subunits. These enzymes, which include |FRAME: CPLX-7502| from |FRAME: TAX-316| and the |FRAME:TAX-83333| enzymes |FRAME:NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX| and |FRAME:NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX|, are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane, with the active site facing the cytoplasm., The second class of bacterial respiratory nitrate reductases (NAP) consists of periplasmic enzymes, which are usually heterodimers, although monomeric forms have been reported. Examples for enzymes belonging to this class include |FRAME:NAP-CPLX| from |FRAME:TAX-83333| (|FRAME: RXN0-6369 "EC 1.7.99.4"|) and |FRAME:CPLX-7500| from |FRAME: TAX-668| (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-CYTOCHROME-RXN "EC 1.9.6.1"|)., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME:TAX-562| anaerobic respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase and nitrate reductase the transfer of electrons from NADH to nitrate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force (H+/e- = 3) across the cytoplasmic membrane (|CITS: [4385809], [5996] [776172]| and see |CITS: [9230919]|)., E. coli K-12 contains two NADH dehydrogenases - energy conserving NDH-I (shown in this pathway) and NDH-II which does not contribute to the proton gradient; both enzymes appear to be involved in anaerobic nitrate respiration |CITS: [7565112], [9063459]|. By analogy to the related enzyme from mitochondria, NDH-I is thought to function as a proton pump translocating 4H+ per NADH oxidised (2e-) [H+/e- = 2] however a lower ratio of 3H+/2e- has also been proposed |CITS: [8892824], [22392981]|. Nitrate induces the expression of the nuo operon (encoding NDH-I) in a NarL dependent manner |CITS: [7565112]|, E. coli K-12 also contains two energy conserving (H+/e- = 1) nitrate reductases. Expression of nitrate reductase A (NRA) occurs in response to high levels of nitrate in the environment whereas expression of nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is not dependent on nitrate levels or anaerobiosis (|CITS: [10464201]| and see |CITS: [7747940]|)., Quinones are the obligate redox carriers during anaerobic nitrate respiration; the concentration of menaquinone increases in cells grown anaerobically with nitrate while the concentration of ubiquinone decreases (as compared with cells grown aerobically) |CITS: [195602]|. Nitrate reductase A can use both menaquinol (shown in this pathway) and ubiquinol as electron donors |CITS: [2204318], [1444716]|. In anaerobic growth with nitrate the major quinone is demethylmenaquinone (DMK) |CITS: [2849923]|; an E. coli strain containing only demethylmenaquinone is unable to grow with nitrate as terminal reductase |CITS: [1444716]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Rhodoquinones Rhodoquinone| (RQ) is a modified ubiquinone, where the methoxyl group in position 3 is replaced by an amino group. The compound was originally isolated from |FRAME:TAX-1085| |CITS:[Glover62][14293762][14285535]|, where is it used for the reduction of fumarate to succinate under anaerobic conditions. The rhodoquinone/rhodoquinol standard redox potential is substantially lower than that of ubiquinone/ubiquinol/UQH2 (-63 vs. +110 mV). The lower redox potential drives the succinate dehydrogenase complex (complex II) in reverse to function as a fumarate reductase., Rhodoquinone is not limited to prokaryotes. It was soon discovered that some eukaryotic parasites such as the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6252| |CITS: [5796154][811785]|, as well as parasitic helminths |CITS:[4795616]| also contain rhodoquinone, which is essential for fumarate reduction under anaerobic conditions |CITS:[2843227]|. Later it was shown that rhodoquinone is present in all eukaryotes that reduce fumarate during anoxia, including freshwater snails, mussels, lugworms, and oysters |CITS: [8537365]|. More recently, rhodoquinone has been detected in mitochondria purified from certain mouse and human tissues |CITS: [39909039]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Rhodoquinones Rhodoquinone| (RQ) is a required cofactor for anaerobic respiration in |FRAME: TAX-1085|. In prokaryotes, but not in most eulkaryotes, it is produced from |FRAME: Ubiquinones ubiquinone| (UQ) |CITS: [19933361]|., A single |FRAME: TAX-1085| gene, |FRAME: G-124906| gene, was found to be necessary for R biosynthesis |CITS: [22194448]|. An attempt to identify additional genes essential for RQ biosynthesis (other than those required for ubiquinone synthesis) were not successful |CITS: [31112563]|. Expression of the gene in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-4932| showed that the gene is sufficient for RQ biosynthesis |CITS: [31121262]|., The gene is extremely rare. It is sparingly distributed among only seven different orders of the alphaproteobacteria, betaproteobacteria, and gammaproteobacteria classes of bacteria. the gene was also transferred by multiple independent lateral gene transfer events to a few eukaryotes that produce RQ, such as |FRAME: TAX-3039| and the protist |FRAME: TAX-1277256| |CITS: [29697049]|. , The RquA protein shares sequence and predicted secondary structure similarities with class I S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases. However, despite the resemblance to methyltransferases, RquA uses SAM as the amino group donor. The enzyme catalyzes a complex reaction, the exact mechanism of which is not known as of 2025. However, it has been shown that during the reaction the enzyme forms RQ, |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA), methanol, bicarbonate, and an aldehyde hydrate (potentially |FRAME: CPD-27752|) |CITS: [36697674]|.

Summary: General Background, Most flavonoid glycosides are O-glycosides, in which the sugar is linked to the flavonoid skeleton by an oxygen atom. In C-glycossylated flavonoids the anomeric carbon of the sugar is directly bound to an aromatic ring carbon through a C-C bond |CITS: [17404902][16305533]|. Unlike the O-glycosidic bonds, C-glycosidic bonds are resistant to acid hydrolysis and glycosidase cleavage, and thus exhibit different properties from other glycosides |CITS: [Talhi12][26462718]|., C-glycosylated compounds occur in many plants, including species of bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms |CITS: [Talhi12]|. In addition, C-glycosides of flavonoids have been found in many plants. For example, citrus plants contain a large amount of C-glycosylflavonoids in their fruits and leaves, including both mono- and di-C-glucosides |CITS: [Manthey00][11397442][17960080]|. C-glycosylated flavonoids are known to have medicinal properties, including antioxidant, antitumor, hepatoprotective, antidiabetic, and anti-inflammatory activities, indicating the potential health benefits of these compounds |CITS: [26462718]|., About This Pathway, The enzymes that form the C-C bond of C-glycosylated compounds are known as C-glycosyltransferases (CGTs). Several CGT genes were identified from citrus trees, including |FRAME: TAX-85681| (clementine), |FRAME: TAX-481547|, |FRAME: TAX-76966| (Kumquat), |FRAME: TAX-2711| (navel orange), |FRAME: TAX-37690| (trifoliate orange), and |FRAME: TAX-55188| (satsuma mandarin). The enzymes were more than 95% identical to each other, and 48% and 44% identical to the enzymes from rice and buckwheat, respectively |CITS: [28370711]|., The genes from |FRAME: TAX-76966| and |FRAME: TAX-55188| were recombinantly expressed and purified and their activity was studied in detail. Both enzymes could act on the open-circular form of the flavanone |FRAME: CPD-15074|. While the product of this glycosylation can undergo dehydration to form |FRAME: VITEXIN| and |FRAME: ISOVITEXIN| (probably due to the activity of an uncharacterized enzyme), it could also be C-glucosylated again. The second glycosylation also requires the open circular form of the substrate, as the enzyme does not act on |FRAME: VITEXIN| and |FRAME: ISOVITEXIN|. The product of this second glucosylation can also undergo dehydration, forming |FRAME: CPD-20014|. The results indicate that the citrus CGT is able to catalyze both the first C-glucosylation and the successive second C-glucosylation of flavonoids |CITS: [28370711]|., In addition to its activity against the open circular forms of 2-hydroxyflavanones such as |FRAME: CPD-15074| and |FRAME: CPD-15080|, the enzyme was also active against flavonoids having 2',4',6'-trihydroxyacetophenone-like structures such as |FRAME: PHLORETIN|, |FRAME: CPD-6881|, |FRAME: CPD-19213|, |FRAME: CPD-20022|, and |FRAME: CPD-20021|, although with |FRAME: CPD-19213|, |FRAME: CPD-20022|, and |FRAME: CPD-20021| the enzyme formed only mono-C-glucosides. UDP-xylose could be used as an alternative sugar donor |CITS: [28370711]|., The enzyme did not act on compounds without the 2',4',6'-trihydroxyacetophenone structure, such as |FRAME: NARINGENIN-CMPD|, |FRAME: CPD-431|, |FRAME: CPD-520|, |FRAME: CPD-3041|, |FRAME: CPD-6542|, and |FRAME: CPD-242| |CITS: [28370711]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees |CITS: [Pingman57]|). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. Free arabinose is formed during the degradation of complex polymers, as in |FRAME: PWY-6790|, |FRAME: PWY-8006|, and |FRAME: PWY-6813|., This variant of L-arabinose degradation ends with |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, a |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| intermediate. The pathway was first described from |FRAME: TAX-304| in 1956 by Weimberg and Doudoroff (though the later steps have not been characterizerd at the time) |CITS: [13271422]|, and is known as the Weimberg pathway. The pathway was later described from other organisms, such as |FRAME:TAX-192|, |FRAME:TAX-964| and |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [762018] [6798025][2768202]|. Organisms that possess this pathway can grow on L-arabinose as a sole carbon source. , The key step that defines the this pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.43|, converting |FRAME: CPD-1134| to |FRAME: CPD-654| |CITS: [16950779]|. This is followed by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.26|, which forms |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, a TCA cycle intermediate., Similar oxidative pathways exist for the degradation of |FRAME: D-Xylose| (see |FRAME: PWY-6760|) and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE| (|FRAME: PWY-5519|).
