Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is the second most abundant biologically produced polymer (|FRAME: CELLULOSE| is the most abundant). |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is found in the cell walls of fungi, yeast and green algae, as well as the exoskeletons of crustaceans (including planktonic types) and insects. In the marine environment |FRAME: CHITIN| is an abundant polysaccharide that is a source of carbon and nitrogen for marine organisms. Its degradation by several genera of marine chitinolytic bacteria is part of the cycling of nutrients in ocean water In addition to ocean water, chitinase genes have been identified in bacteria from freshwater and saline lakes, estuaries, and soil. The ability to degrade chitin appears to be limited to the Proteobacteria, Bactriodetes, Actinobacteria and Firmicutes (in |CITS: [17933912]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21607543]|). Some bacterial species have been shown to contain multiple chitinase genes to efficiently utilize different forms of |FRAME: CHITIN| and some of its by-products |CITS: [16535505]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CHITIN| catabolic pathway has been studied in species of the genus |FRAME: TAX-662| |CITS: [1761533][11850417][17933912][19553519]|. The proposed pathway shown here for |FRAME: TAX-666| and |FRAME: TAX-29494| involves a core set of genes that appear to be conserved in members of the family |FRAME: TAX-641|. The predicted gene functions are based on a combination of biochemical evidence in |FRAME: TAX-662| species, microarray expression data, experimental evidence, and bioinformatic predictions |CITS: [17933912]|. Overall, |FRAME: CHITIN| utilization is a highly complex process that has been divided into several stages (sensing, attachment, extracellular degradation, uptake and catabolism) and involves many genes |CITS: [14699052][14983042]|., The overall pathway spans the extracellular space, periplasm, and cytosol. This pathway shows the reactions that can occur in the cytosol, as proposed and summarized in |CITS: [17933912]|. The reactions occurring in the extracellular space and periplasm are described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6902| as indicated by the pathway link. Transport of compounds from the periplasm into the cytosol is also indicated here. Click on the PTS transport links for transport figures., As described in the summary for pathway |FRAME: PWY-6902|, partially deacetylated chitooligosaccharides such as GlcNAc-GlcN (|FRAME: CPD-12274|) may also be deacetylated in the extracellular space or periplasm to form (GlcN)2 (|FRAME: CPD-13545|). This compound can undergo PTS transport from the periplasm into the cytosol with concomitant phosphorylation to |FRAME: CPD-15993| as shown in the transport reaction link |CITS: [17933912][14983042]|., In the cytosol |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE| is ultimately converted into two molecules of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| via the combined action of |FRAME: MONOMER-16878| which produces |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-1-P| and |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| |CITS: [10913116]|; N-acetylglucosamine -1-phosphate mutase which produces |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| |CITS: [14699052][17933912]|; and an ATP-dependent kinase specific for |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| (EC 2.7.1.59, |FRAME: MONOMER-16883|) |CITS: [1761533]|. The |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| generated by these enzymes, or by PTSGlcNAc transport, is ultimately converted into |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| via the combined action of |FRAME: CPLX-8363| |CITS: [8987551][9301118]| and |FRAME: MONOMER-16884| |CITS: [14983042][1761533]|. |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| enters central metabolism., After chitobiase cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-15993| which produces |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| and |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| |CITS: [14983042][17933912]|, and phosphorylation of the |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.8| |CITS: [11850417]|, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| enters the final reaction in the pathway |CITS: [17933912]|., Overall, |FRAME: CHITIN| is degraded to monomers which are channeled into central metabolism as |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: AMMONIUM|) (|CITS: [17933912]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21607543]|)., The regulation of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| catabolism in |FRAME: TAX-666| is also relevant to its pathogenic mechanism in humans due to the presence of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| residues in glycosaminoglycans, glycoproteins and glycolipids. This regulation appears to be more complex than originally thought |CITS: [21488982]|. In a transcriptional regulation study, analysis of microarray expression data suggested the involvement of two gene clusters. In addition to the gene cluster encoding β-N-acetylglucosaminidase, the N-acetylglucosamine-specific transporter, N-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate deacetylase and glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase, which is under negative control by the |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| specific repressor nagC, a second gene cluster is also involved in coordinate regulation, which is under positive control by nagC |CITS: [21488982]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Acetan Acetan| is an acidic heteropolysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-28448 "Gluconacetobacter xylinus (previously known as Acetobacter xylinum)"| that consists of a cellulose backbone with side-chains attached to alternate glucose units. , The polymer is composed of repeating units of a heptasaccharide with the following structure: α-L-rhamnose-(1->6)-β-D-glucose-(1->6)-α-D-glucose-(1->4)-β-D-glucuronate-(1->2)-α-D-mannose-(1->3)-β-D-glucose-(1->4)-β-D-glucose. These repeating units are attached to each other via β(1->4) links between the terminal two glucose units, forming a cellulose backbone with alternating pentasaccharide branches |CITS: [8370027][7780996]|., The biosynthetic pathway by which acetan is produced involves several steps: , (1) assembly of heptasaccharide subunits attached to an inner-membrane polyprenol phosphate carrier, (2) addition of acetyl groups, (3) polymerization of the heptasaccharide repeating units and secretion out of the cell., The genes that encode the enzymes of this pathway are located in a cluster, which was identified and isolated using PCR amplification of a conserved region of UDP-glycosyl transferase enzymes from other organisms |CITS: [7727341]|. The initial work identified three genes - |FRAME: G-12297|, |FRAME: G-12299|, and manB - a gene that encodes a bifunctional phosphomannose isomerase/GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase. Further work identified several additional genes, including |FRAME: G-12299|, |FRAME: G-12301|, |FRAME: G-12300| and |FRAME: G-12302|. Gene-disrupted mutants were prepared for almost all genes, and the activity of their products was identified |CITS: [8935665][8988363][10411277][12150936]|., The final assembly of the polymer involves the translocation of the mature heptasaccharide unit from the cytoplasm to the periplasm, polymerization and export via the outer membrane. Two genes proposed to be involved in this process are aceD and aceE |CITS: [8988363]|.

Malonyl glucosides have been frequently overlooked due to their lability and inadequate isolation procedures. Numerous, N-and O-malonyl conjugates have been reported in different plant species, including isoflavones, isoflavanones and , isoflavonoids but also xenobiotics, D-amino acids and the ethylene precursor 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid., The latter are considered to be detoxification products |CITS: [6497385]|, whereas the former may serve as pools for , the release of free aglycons. Released isoflavones can be either incorporated into the biosynthetic pathway of phytoalexins , or act as phytoanticipins |CITS: [11730862]|., The finding that isoflavone conjugates are sometimes constitutively present in considerable amounts in legumes |CITS: [Graham91]|,, support such a possible role as preformed toxins (phytoanticipins). , Glucosides and malonyl glucosides of isoflavones, such as biochanin A and formononetin and further metabolic derivatives , (e.g. cicerin, medicarpin) are exclusively located in the vacuole |CITS: [Mackenbrock92]| and it has been speculated, that acylation , of these compounds could precede and facilitate their transport through the tonoplast |CITS: [6639051]|.

Seed oils of a few plant species are enriched in conjugated fatty aids, which are fatty acids containing conjugated or non-methylene-interrupted double bonds. Because conjugated double bonds have high rates of oxidation, seed oils rich in conjugated double bonds are used commercially as drying agents in paints and varnishes., The conjugated double bonds are introduced by "conjugases", divergent forms of |FRAME: AT3G12120| (|FRAME: EC-1.14.19.22|). Conjugases act on fatty acids bound to phosphatidylcholine as substrates, as has been shown for FAD2 enzymes, and modify an existing double bond to produce the conjugated double bonds with or without introducing a new double bond., |FRAME: CPD-8229 Punicate| ((9Z,11E,13Z)-octadeca-9,11,13-trienoate) is a conjugated form of |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (18:3Δcis9,cis12,cis15). It accounts for 40% (w/w) and 80% of the total seed oil in |FRAME: TAX-3677| and |FRAME: TAX-22663|, respectively. |FRAME: CPD-8229 Punicate| is derived from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| by a fatty, acid conjugase that converts a cis Δ12 double bond into a conjugated trans-cis double bond pair.

Summary: The primary nitrogen assimilation routes in photosynthetic eukaryotes and prokaryotes are nitrogen fixation, nitrate assimilation, and ammonia assimilation. Ammonia is liberated by photorespiration, protein and amino acid metabolism, and the breakdown of nitrogen transport compounds. The rate of ammonia generation during photorespiration is about 10 times the rate of nitrate assimilation., The ammonia released from photorespiration is immediately re-assimilated via the ammonia assimilation cycle. The net result of this cycle is the conversion of one molecule of ammonia to one molecule of glutamate at the expense of one ATP molecule., The pathway includes two steps catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-4585 "glutamine synthetase"| (GS) and |FRAME: MONOMER-7421 "glutamate synthase"| (also known as glutamine oxoglutarate aminotansferase or GOGAT), and thus is often referred to as the GS/GOGAT pathway. Two types of GOGAT are known in photosynthetic organisms - NADH-dependent, and ferredoxin-dependent. NADH-GOGAT is found in the nucleus of vascular plants, fungi, and diatoms (see |FRAME: PWY-6963|). The ferredoxin-dependent enzyme is only found in Cyanobacteria and photosynthetic eukaryotes (this pathway). , An NADPH-dependent version of GOGAT is found in non-photosynthetic bacteria and archaea (see |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY|).

Summary: Hydrogen dependent reduction of trimethyamine N-oxide (TMAO) has been described in E. coli K-10 |CITS: [363703]| and in the K-12 derived sub-strain AN387 |CITS: [2204318]|. , E. coli K-12 contains two membrane bound, H(2) uptake hydrogenases - |FRAME: FORMHYDROGI-CPLX "hydrogenase 1"| (Hyd1) and hydrogenase 2 (Hyd 2). Hydrogenase 2 (shown in this pathway) is a standard O2 sensitive hydrogenase and is the major hydrogenase during anaerobic respiration with hydrogen and fumarate |CITS: [3905769] [11506918]| while Hyd 1 is an O2 tolerant hydrogenase whose physiological function is not yet clearly defined (see for example |CITS: [24715724][23260654]|., E. coli K-12 also contains two TMAO reductases: the inducible enzyme encoded by torCA (shown in this pathway), and a second TMAO reductase encoded by the |FRAME: G7022| gene, which has low constitutive expression and is not induced by TMAO or dimethyl sulfoxide |CITS: [11004177]|. , TMAO reductase does not contribute to proton potential (see review by |CITS: [18930017]|). Hyd 2 is presumed to be an energy conserving enzyme (see |CITS: [9230919]|). Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| is synthesized by C-2 epimerisation of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.14|), The pathway was first established as part of the synthesis of the enterobacterial common antigen (ECA), which contains the modified sugar |FRAME: CPD-15664| (see |FRAME: ECASYN-PWY|), but the gene was subsequently identified in the polysaccharide biosynthesis gene clusters of other bacteria, such as the Vi cluster of |FRAME: ORG-6239| and the capsule biosynthesis cluster of |FRAME: TAX-1280|., Originally named |FRAME: EG11451|, the recommended name for the gene is now mnaA |CITS: [14670712]|., The structure of MnmA has been described, and reveals a surprising structural homology with glycogen phosphorylase |CITS: [11106477]|. The MnaB protein from |FRAME: TAX-1280| (known as Cap5O) has been biochemically characterized |CITS: [11159986]|.

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxin. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenate enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the E. coli |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX "Pst"| systems. Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, while prokaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump, multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, continue by methylating the arsenite to several methylated forms that are excreted from the organism in the urine (see |FRAME: PWY-4202|)., About This Pathway, Most microorganisms are able to detoxify arsenic species by pumping them out of the cell. This cytoplasmic detoxification system involves the arsC-encoded cytoplasmic arsenate reductase, which reduces arsenate to arsenite, and an efficient arsenite efflux pump consisting of a two-component ATPase complex. The arsA gene product is a soluble ATPase subunit, while the arsB product is an integral membrane protein. Arsenite is the preferred substrate of ArsB, as well as an activator of ArsA ATPase activity. In many cases arsB and arsC are found in an operon without an arsA gene |CITS: [12165430]|., ArsC cytoplasmic arsenate reductases are found widely in microbes, and are found in almost all organisms with a genome larger than 2 Mb |CITS: [15691908]|. There are three different clades of ArsC proteins in bacteria, which share no sequence similarity. The first clade includes the glutathione-glutaredoxin-coupled enzymes, and is found in many Gram-negative bacteria, as well as carried on many plasmids. The second clade consists of glutathione-only dependent enzymes, and is found only in yeast, while the third clade consists of thioredoxin-dependent enzymes, and is found in Gram-positive bacteria, as well as many Gram-negative proteobacteria. In addition, archaea also possess ArsC reductases. The archaeal genes are closest to those of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [15691908]|.

Summary: Fluorinated organic compounds have widespread applications as pesticides, herbicides, pharmaceuticals, flame-retardants, refrigerants and foam-blowing agents, and are consequently accumulating in the environment, However, only a handful of biologically synthesized carbon-fluorine bonds are known |CITS: [15209126]|. The most common natural organofluorine species is |FRAME: CPD-12709|, a toxin found in the leaves and seeds of a variety of tropical plants, often in high concentrations |CITS:[13444108][3334144][10843319][17966275]|., The extreme toxicity of |FRAME: CPD-12709| stems from its similarity to acetate. Fluoroacetate combines with coenzyme A to form |FRAME: CPD-12716|, which can substitute for acetyl CoA in the tricarboxylic acid cycle. |FRAME: CPD-12716 Fluoroacetyl-CoA| reacts with citrate synthase to produce |FRAME: FLUORO-CITRATE|, a metabolite of which then binds very tightly to aconitase, halting the cycle., Sodium fluoroacetate was introduced as a rodenticide in the US in 1946, but its extreme toxicity limits its uses. Currently, it is licensed in the US for use against coyotes, which prey on sheep and goats, and in Australia and New Zealand to kill unwanted introduced species |CITS: [17288493]|. , Microbial fluoroacetate degradation is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8166|, the only known enzyme that can specifically hydrolyze the carbon-fluorine bond. The enzyme was first described from a Pseudomonas sp. in 1965 |CITS: [5928195]|, and since then has been described in multiple bacterial strains and a fungus |CITS: [Walker81][9812982][Kurihara03][19218394]|. The enzyme has been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-118147| (now |FRAME: TAX-80866|) |CITS: [9812982]| and |FRAME: ORG-6164| |CITS: [18807226]|. , The dissociation energy of the C-F bond of aliphatic fluoro compounds is among the highest found in natural products. This is achieved by a nucleophilic attack of an aspartate residue on the α-carbon of the substrate, leading to the formation of an ester intermediate, which is subsequently hydrolyzed by the nucleophilic attack of a water molecule on the carbonyl carbon atom. The cleavage of the strong C-F bond is greatly facilitated by the hydrogen-bonding interactions between the leaving fluorine atom and three amino acid residues (a histidine, a tryptophan, and a tyrosine). The hydrolysis of the ester intermediate is initiated by a proton transfer from the water molecule to a histidine and by the simultaneous nucleophilic attack of the water molecule |CITS: [9812982][19551770]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. Their diphosphates, form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, for use in biosynthesis. The, pathway for de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotides is derived from the pathway for, |FRAME: PWY0-162| as shown above in the pathway links. In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage, pathways re-utilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can, enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleoside triphosphate products of these pathways are incorporated into DNA (|FRAME: DCTP| and, |FRAME: TTP|) and RNA (|FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways are, necessary in order to supply the cell with nucleoside triphosphates for stable RNA and DNA synthesis when, precursors are limiting. These biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate, and reducing power. In |FRAME:TAX-562| they are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene, expression level in order to conserve resources under different growth conditions., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathways derive in part from the central metabolic, precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. Oxaloacetate from the |FRAME: TCA|, gives rise to the aspartate family of amino acids and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is a precursor of both pyrimidine, ribonucleotides and nicotinamide coenzymes (see |FRAME: ASPARTATESYN-PWY|). The overall pathway begins, with the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| from bicarbonate, phosphate from ATP and nitrogen from, glutamine. This compound then condenses with |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to, form |FRAME: CARBAMYUL-L-ASPARTATE| as shown in pathways |FRAME: PWY0-162| and |FRAME: PWY-5686|. , The overall pathway branches at |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|, which is an intermediate in |FRAME: ARG|, biosynthesis (see |FRAME: ARGSYN-PWY|). The activated intermediate |FRAME: PRPP| is derived from, |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P| and is a precursor in the de novo and salvage pathways for pyrimidine and purine, nucleotides, as well as in biosynthetic pathways for nucleotide coenzymes, |FRAME: HIS| and |FRAME: TRP|, (see |FRAME: PRPP-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY0-662|)., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here illustrates the point at which the pyrimidine ribonucleotides |FRAME: CDP|, |FRAME: CTP|,, |FRAME: UDP| and |FRAME: UTP| are converted to their corresponding deoxyribonucleotides and the, DNA-specific thymine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate |FRAME: TTP| is formed. Deoxyribonucleotides are, synthesized by reduction of ribonucleotides, which is regulated by the rate-limiting enzyme ribonucleotide reductase, that carries out reduction at the C2' position. This enzyme has a central role in DNA replication and repair. , In |FRAME:TAX-562| this ribo- to deoxyribo- conversion is catalyzed by aerobic ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase, or, anaerobic ribonucleoside triphosphate reductase. Electrons for these reductions are derived, from |FRAME: NADPH| and are transferred via |FRAME: Red-Thioredoxin|, |FRAME: Red-Glutaredoxins|,, or |FRAME: Reduced-flavodoxins|., The ribonucleotide reductase product of genes |FRAME: EG10660| and |FRAME: EG10661| functions aerobically, and under microaerophilic conditions. A normally cryptic enzyme encoded by genes |FRAME: EG20257|, and |FRAME: EG12381| cannot support aerobic, or microaerophilic growth in a nrdAB deletion mutant. , However, it supports aerobic growth in such a mutant when genes nrdHIEF are overexpressed on a, plasmid |CITS: [16771665]|. It has been speculated that this additional aerobic enzyme may enhance, ribonucleotide reductase activity under conditions of oxidative stress. The anaerobic enzyme is encoded by, gene |FRAME: EG11417| which functions in a multienzyme complex with the products of genes |FRAME: G812|, and |FRAME: EG10628|. Pathways for the reduction of these reductase enzymes have also been studied, |CITS: [16771665]|., The major pathway for the aerobic, de novo formation of the intermediate |FRAME: DUMP|, the immediate, precursor of thymine-containing nucleotides, is via phosphorylation of |FRAME: DCDP|, to |FRAME: DCTP| and deamination of |FRAME: DCTP| to |FRAME: DUTP| which is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: DUMP|. , This pathway supplies 70-80% of total |FRAME: DUMP| |CITS: [17651436]|. Most of the remainder is presumed to, be formed from |FRAME: DUDP|, as shown. In |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: EG11418|, |FRAME: EG10219| mutants, an, alternate de novo deoxycytidine pathway to |FRAME: DUMP| is used that relies on salvage enzymes, |CITS: [17827303]|. Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of, |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by, |FRAME: THYMIDYLATESYN-CPLX|. Two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is, catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: DTMPKI-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the product, of gene |FRAME: EG10650| which also catalyzes two preceding reactions., Review: Neuhard J. and R.A. Summary: General Background, Phospholipids are important membrane components. Most of the phospholipids belong to the category of phosphoglycerides. The simplest phosphoglycerides, which are known as phosphatidate (or diacylglycerol phosphate), are composed of a glycerol molecule attached to two fatty acids and one phosphate group. The carboxyl group of each fatty acid is esterified to the hydroxyl groups on carbon-1 and carbon-2 of the glycerol molecule, while the phosphate group is attached to carbon-3 by an ester link. Phosphatidates are precursors for many phosphoglycerides found in animals, plants and yeast, including |FRAME: Phosphatidylinositols|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-SERINE|, |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE|, and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN|., As part of the synthesis of phosphoglycerides, either the phosphatidate or the modifying compound need to be activated by |FRAME:CTP|. In some cases, the modifying compound is activated, as in the case of |FRAME: CHOLINE| and |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, which form |FRAME: CDP-CHOLINE| and |FRAME: CDP-ETHANOLAMINE|, respectively. However, in the case of other compounds, such as |FRAME: SER| and |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, the phosphatidate is activated first, forming |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL|, which then reacts with the modifying compound to form the phosphoglyceride., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL| in some Gram-negative bacteria (primarily the |FRAME: TAX-1236|) as well as the chloroplasts of green plants. In this pathway the production of the intermediate |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P| is catalyzed by a type of the membrane-bound enzyme |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3-P-ACYLTRANSFER-MONOMER| that uses |FRAME: ACYL-ACP| as the acyl donor., Bacteria enzymes that can utilze |FRAME: ACYL-ACP| are found only in some Gram-negative bacteria., They are encoded by the |FRAME: EG10740| gene, and can also utilize |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-CoAs| thioesters. The plasitidic enzyme can use only |FRAME: ACYL-ACP| |CITS: [9370311]|., The addition of the second acyl moiety is catalyzed by |FRAME: 1-ACYLGLYCEROL-3-P-ACYLTRANSFER-MONOMER|. The bacterial enzyme, which is universally expressed in all bacteria, is encoded by |FRAME: EG11377|., As in the case of PlsB, it can utilize either a fatty acyl-[acp] or an acyl-CoA thioester as the acyl donor., A pathway that describes the usage of acyl-CoA donors can be found at |FRAME: PWY-5667|., It should be noted that most bacteria utilize a different route for the synthesis of |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5981|., More information can be found in |FRAME: PHOSLIPSYN2-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| (phytate, phytic acid) is one of the most prevalent forms of phosphorylated inositols in the eukaryotic cell, with a total concentration of 15-100 μM |CITS:[3426614][1684044][8435066]|. It's cellular distribution is not completely known - some of it is soluble, some is "wall-papered" around membranes, while some is bound to proteins |CITS: [9838040]|. In plant seeds, large amount of phytate are complexed with cations and deposited as globular inclusions in membrane-bound storage bodies |CITS: [15700415]|., The compound has been proposed to have a number of signaling roles, including regulation of insulin exocytosis |CITS: [9114007]|, regulation of nuclear mRNA export |CITS:[10390371][10683435]|, binding of the clathrin assembly proteins AP2 and AP3 |CITS: [1849645][1371119]|, inhibition of clathrin cage assembly |CITS: [7814377][7829485]|, and inhibition of serine and threonine protein phosphatases that are thought to regulate L-type Ca2+ channels |CITS: [9334307]|., Phytate in Plants, In plant cells phytate serves as a storage form of myo-inositol, phosphate and mineral nutrients for utilization during seed germination and seedling growth. It is deposited within single-membrane storage organelles referred to as protein bodies and is usually present as mixed complexes with different cations, including |FRAME: K+|, |FRAME: MG+2|, |FRAME: CA+2|, |FRAME: FE+2|, and |FRAME: ZN+2|, known as phytin |CITS:[11590064][8744268]|., Although phytin only makes up about 1% of the seed weight, it may contain up to 80% of the total seed phosphorus |CITS:[15700415]|. Phytate is also present in other plant tissues and organs such as pollen, roots, tuber and turions in smaller quantities |CITS:[14568069]|. , About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge about |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| biosynthesis concerns lipid-dependent pathways, where the inositol phosphate precursor originates from a phospholipid, as described in pathways |FRAME: PWY-6361| and |FRAME: PWY-6362|. However, information exists that suggests that certain organisms synthesize this compound from |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| or |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| that do not originate from phospholipids., To date such pathways have only been reported in two organisms - the aquatic monocotyledonous plant |FRAME: TAX-29656| |CITS:[8660287]| (described here), and the slime mold |FRAME:TAX-44689|, which utilizes different intermediates |CITS: [2198472]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6372|)., The sequence of conversions from |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| to |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| in |FRAME: TAX-29656| has been illucidated only by the use of radiolabeled compounds and no enzymes have been characterized from this organism. However, the pathway is also believed to exist in maize, and several maize enzymes have been characterized |CITS:[15237968][12586875][15918884]|., These include |FRAME: MONOMER-10801| (MIPS) |CITS:[15237968]|, which produces |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-10821| |CITS:[15918884]|, which which produces |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| from |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|., The rest of the enzymes of this pathway have not been characterized in great detail as yet. While a |FRAME:MONOMER-10868| that phosphorylates |FRAME: CPD-178| has been detected in maize, the exact nature of the kinase activity of this enzyme is not yet known as the reaction product have not been characterized |CITS:[12586875]|.

Summary: General Background, Marine organisms, including bacteria, algae and invertebrates, produce many organobromine compounds. Over 2,200 of those, with a wide range of biological properties have been reported by 2017. Some brominated compounds, such as |FRAME: PBDEs "polybrominated diphenyl ethers"| (BDEs) in their hydroxylated and methoxylated forms, are found across all trophic levels in marine biota, from cyanobacteria and macroalgae to whales and seabirds. In some marine sponges within the |FRAME: TAX-190525| family BDEs can exceed 10% of the sponge tissue by dry weight |CITS: [Unson94][Becerro04]|., Other compounds, such as the brominated biphenyl |FRAME: CPD-20552|, the brominated bipyrrole |FRAME: CPD-20553|, and the hybrid |FRAME: CPD-20554|, have been shown to be synthesized by several species of |FRAME: TAX-53246|, a marine γ-proteobacterial genus often associated with eukaryotic hosts |CITS: [4380876][Andersen74][12543647]|., To find the genes encoding the biosynthesis of brominated compounds, the genomes of two |FRAME: TAX-53246| species, |FRAME: TAX-1315281| and |FRAME: TAX-1353533|, were sequenced, and the genomes were searched for homologs of two genes known to be involved in the formation of chlorinated pyrroles - |FRAME: G-55300| and |FRAME: G-55299| (based on the assumption that a similar mechanism may operate in the formation of chlorinated and brominated pyrroles). The search led to the identification of a brominated marine pyrroles/phenols (bmp) biosynthetic gene cluster in both bacteria |CITS: [24974229]|., Cloning of the bmp1-8 genes and their expression in |FRAME: TAX-562| led to production of many typical brominated compounds, including brominated phenols, pyrroles, biphenyls, bipyrroles and hydbrid phenyl-pyrrole molecules. By expressing the bmp cluster with individual gene deletions it was possible to delinetate the function of the individual enzymes, and to show that the cluster encodes all of the enzymes that are necessary for production of brominated phenols, brominated pyrroles, and their derivatives |CITS: [24974229]|., About This Pathway, The bromopyrrole and bromophenol biosynthetic modules function independently, and not all organisms have both. A detailed discussion of each module is provided in |FRAME: PWY-7931| and |FRAME: PWY-7929|, respectively., In organisms that possess |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18|, the products of both of those pathway can be coupled, forming a large assortment of polybrominated biphenyls and biphenyl esters, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7932| |CITS: [24974229]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the pyrimidine ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, mono- or diphosphorylated forms of pyrimidine nucleotides activate other molecules, as in |FRAME: CMP-KDO|, |FRAME: CPD-12575|, and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., The de novo biosynthetic pathways of pyrimidine nucleotides consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. Salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides, and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways to form other nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|).However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level. These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The de novo pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthetic pathway converts |FRAME: HCO3|, |FRAME: GLN|,, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to |FRAME: UMP| (uridine 5'-monophosphate), a pyrimidine nucleotide that can be subsequently converted to all other pyrimidine nucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7176|)., The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.5|, forms |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|, which is not only an intermediate of pyrimidine synthesis but also a precursor for the synthesis of amino acids such as |FRAME: ARG|, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: CANAVANINE|. The pathway continues with the condensation of |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| with |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to form |FRAME: CARBAMYUL-L-ASPARTATE| |CITS: [8041358]|. The products is cyclized to, |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE|, the first intermediate that contains a pyrimidine ring., The next step, the oxidation of |FRAME: DI-H-OROTATE| to |FRAME: OROTATE| is carried out by different enzymes in different organisms. In general, Gram-positive bacteria and fungi contain class 1 enzymes, which are cytosolic, include |FRAME: FMN| cofators, and use |FRAME: FUM| or NAD(P)+ as electron acceptors (|FRAME: EC-1.3.98.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.14|, or |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.15|). Gram-negative bacteria and eukaryotes possess class 2 enzymes, which are membrane bound and use |FRAME: Quinones| as electron acceptor (|FRAME: EC-1.3.5.2 "EC 1.3.5.2"|) |CITS: [Jensen98]|., The final two steps, the condensation of |FRAME: OROTATE| with PRPP forming |FRAME: OROTIDINE-5-PHOSPHATE|, (OMP) followed by the decarboylation of OMP to UMP, are carried out by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.10|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.23|. The last step is considered the rate-limiting step of the overall de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [7579161]|., The de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides appears to be one of the most ancient biochemical pathways, as it is evolutionary conserved in all species., About This Pathway In |FRAME: TAX-1423|, A 10.5-kilobase segment of the |FRAME: TAX-1423| chromosomal DNA containing the entire pyrimidine biosynthetic gene cluster was cloned, expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and shown to complement multiple mutants including |FRAME: EG10805|, |FRAME: EG10806|, |FRAME: EG10807|, |FRAME: EG10808|, and |FRAME: EG10809| mutants. The gene order in the fragment was reported to be pyrBCADFE |CITS: [3106333]|., In a subsequent study a somewhat larger 12.5-kilobase segment was cloned and sequenced, and shown to encode the six enzymes of de novo pyrimidine nucleotide biosynthesis as well as two open reading frames of unknown function |CITS: [1709162]|. The genes are transcribed in one large polycistronic message, in the order ORF1, |FRAME: BSU15490|, |FRAME: BSU15500|, |FRAME: BSU15510|, |FRAME: BSU15520|, ORF2, |FRAME: BSU15540|, |FRAME: BSU15550|, |FRAME: BSU15560|. This is very different from the situation in |FRAME: TAX-562|, where the pyr genes are scattered around the chromosome and are not coordinately regulated., The ORF 1 region was later shown to contain a 151-nucleotide (nt) untranslated leader; pyrR, encoding a 20-kDa protein; and pyrP, encoding a 46-kDa protein. PyrR is a regulator that binds to a conserved sequence in the pyr mRNA and disrupts the antiterminator, permitting terminator hairpin formation and promoting transcription termination. PyrP is a probable integral membrane uracil permease |CITS: [8206849]|. ORF2 was shown to be |FRAME: BSU15530|, encoding the electron transfer subunit of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase |CITS: [10545205]|.

General Background, The biosynthesis of several important metabolites involves the consumption of |FRAME: MET| through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), in a reaction that releases |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA). , These metabilites include polyamines (see |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME:BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-1303|), |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|), and bacterial auto-inducers (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration is tightly regulated. Several pathways that recycle MTA back to |FRAME: MET| have been described., A pathway known as the universal methionine salvage pathway (|FRAME: PWY-4361|) is present with some variations in almost all eukaryotes and some bacteria |CITS: [19946895]|. However, a limiting factor to the distribution of that pathway is that it contains an oxygen-requiring step (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|), and is thus present only in aerobic organisms. Alternative pathways exist in anaerobic organisms and are described here and in |FRAME: PWY-7174|., About This Pathway, An exclusively anaerobic methionine salvage pathway that couples |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| metabolism to |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| formation was characterized in the phototrophic bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1085| and |FRAME: TAX-1076|. These organisms also possess the |FRAME: PWY-7174 "MTA-isoprenoid shunt"| pathway, which functions under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions., The pathway was shown to include the activities of |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.28| (MtnP) (described in |FRAME: PWY-6756|), |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.23| (MtnA), and |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.62| (Ald2), which form |FRAME: CPD-23221| as an intermediate. The authors also noticed fast conversion of the latter to |FRAME: CPD-7677|, and could demonstrate a 1:1 conversion of |FRAME: CPD-7677| to |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|, although they did not identify the responsible enzyme, or the identity of the other product |CITS: [29133429]|. However, it could be shown that the unknown product is later converted to |FRAME: CPD-7671|, which is then used to restore |FRAME: MET| via the activity of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.49| |CITS: [31950558]|.

However, some bacteria that produc e the compound, like |FRAME: TAX-562|, do not have a phenylalanine hydroxylase gene, and the purpose of the production of |FRAME: CPD0-2101| in these organisms is still not well understood., In fact, |FRAME: CPD0-2101 5,6,7,8-Tetrahydromonapterin| is the major tetrahydropterin in |FRAME:TAX-562|, though the organism does not produce any enzyme that requires it |CITS: [11934271]|. Summary: General Background, Rotenoid compounds are a class of plant secondary metabolites that derive from isoflavones., They are commonly found in leguminous species, but also occur in other families, such as, the Iridiceae (see refs in |CITS: [11711058]|). These compounds play a role in plant, interactions with insects |CITS: [Birch85]|. But, they have also been extracted for use, by humans. Several rotenoids also have medicinal qualities. For example, deguelin |CITS:[19861542][18575727][18089792]|, tephrosin |CITS:[20056314][17158054]| and, rotenolone |CITS: [15043430] [9520374]| seem to have anti-cancer effects. Other rotenoids have important commercial applications. Rotenone, perhaps the most commonly known member of the family,, has a long history of use as a fish poison |CITS: [Leonard39]|, and it is also the major, bioactive component of a commerically available insecticide |CITS: [16332203]|. Rotenone, is also used in scientific experiments due to its ability to interfere with the, electron transport chain |CITS: [4295606]| and it can also interfere with tubulin, self-assembly |CITS: [568944]|. Although rotenone also has anti-cancer effects, |CITS:[19442964][19777565]|, some studies suggest that rotenone can promote Parkinson's Disease |CITS: [18155613]|., About This Pathway, Radiotracer studies indicate that |FRAME:PHE| is a precursor of deguelin and roteneone in |FRAME: TAX-1157238| |CITS: [CROMBIE92]|. The specific details of the biosynthetic steps between |FRAME:PHE| and |FRAME: CPD-9534| have not been worked out in this species, but, it seems plausible that |FRAME: CPD-9534| is produced in the manner identified in two other leguminous species as depicted in the |FRAME: PWY-6427| pathway. Interestingly, experiments performed with cell cultures grown under heteotrophic and photomixotrophic culture conditions caused differential accumulation of the four compounds shown in this pathway. This finding could have implications for industrial production of these bioactive substances |CITS: []|[LAMBERT93]|.

Summary: Allelochemicals are chemicals produced by one plant species that inhibit the growth of another.  The allelopathy of |FRAME: TAX-4558| (sorghum) was first observed from reduced growth of other crop species when grown in rotation with sorghum. One of the allelochemicals synthesized by |FRAME: TAX-4558| is |FRAME: CPD-10259|, which is produced by root hairs |CITS: [22283312][17178719]|. It accounts for between 40% and 90% of the exudate material (w/w) in various accessions. The remaining exudate consists primarily of |FRAME: CPD-12348| and sorgoleone congeners differing in the length or degree of saturation of the aliphatic side chain and in the substitution pattern of the quinone ring |CITS: [11714356][14664512][12542343][19357432]|., Labeling studies suggested the involvement of a polyketide synthase in forming the quinone head of sorgoleone and attaching the fatty acid tail |CITS: [12771136]|. The enzyme catalyzing this condensation reaction, |FRAME: MONOMER-15595|, has been characterized |CITS: [20348430]|. The sorgoleone fatty acid tail has an unusual terminal double bond introduced by a dedicated desaturase |CITS: [17178719]|. The reduced form of sorgoleone, dihydrosogoleone, is rapidly oxidized to the highly phytotoxic sorgoleone upon exudation into the soil.

About lipoate, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| is a sulfur-containing cofactor found in many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms. It is utilized by several enzymes involved in oxidative metabolism, including the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, the |FRAME: PWY-5084| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, the |FRAME: PWY-5046| |CITS: [2188967]|, and the |FRAME: GLYCLEAV-PWY| |CITS: [1655709][8444795]|., Each of these enzyme complexes is composed of multiple copies of three enzymes: a substrate-specific, decarboxylase-dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), specific for each type of complex, and a dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3), a flavoprotein, that is a common component of these multienzyme complexes., E1 catalyzes both the decarboxylation of the α-keto acid and the subsequent reductive, acylation of the lipoyl moiety, which is covalently bound to E2. E2 catalyzes, the acyl transfer step, and E3 catalyzes the reoxidation of the dihydrolipoyl moiety with NAD, as the ultimate electron acceptor |CITS: [2188967]|., The lipoate cofactor is bound to the E2 by an amide linkage between its carboxylate moiety, and a specific lysine residue in the enzyme |CITS: [8444795]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.20| (LplA, LplB or LplJ, depending on strain) attaches pre-existing lipoate that has been imported from outside the cell to an E2 enzyme, thus catalyzing a salvage pathway |CITS: [8002607]|. , The pathway has been shown to occur in archaea |CITS: [19520844]|, bacteria |CITS: [8206909][8002607]| and animals |CITS: [10103005][11382754]|., It is generally believed that mammals primarily rely on salvaged |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID|. Even though the genes encoding LipA and LipB have been identified in mammalian genomes, and it has been shown that mammalian cells are capable of synthesizing |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| in mitochondria |CITS: [11389890]|, their significance is not fully understood., The ligation of salvaged |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| in mammals is performed by a single enzyme, LplA (lipoate protein ligase A), which catalyzes both the activation of |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| to a |FRAME: LIPOYL-AMP| intermediate, and the ligation of the later to the E2 subunits, as described here |CITS: [10103005][11382754]|. A similar enzyme has been characterized in bacteria |CITS: [8206909][8002607]|., In most Archaea the enzyme that catalyzes these reactions is a heterodimer, composed of proteins encoded by |FRAME: G-12044| and |FRAME: G-12043| genes |CITS: [19520844]|. LplB is required for |FRAME: LIPOYL-AMP| formation but is not required for transfer of the lipoyl moiety of lipoyl-adenylate to acceptor proteins |CITS: [19520844]|., For the de novo synthesis of lipoate from |FRAME: CPD-195| or |FRAME: Octanoyl-ACPs "octanoyl-[acp]"|, see |FRAME: PWY0-501| and |FRAME:PWY0-1275|.

General Background, Iron is an essential micronutrient for most microorganisms. It is a cofactor required for growth and metabolism. However, it is present in the environment as relatively insoluble ferric oxyhydroxide complexes that are not readily bioavailable. Siderophores are high-affinity ferric iron (|FRAME: FE+3|) chelators secreted by microorganisms as a means to access this iron. Bacterial pathogens also utilize siderophores to scavenge tightly bound iron from their hosts. Secreted siderophores solubilize and bind ferric iron. The ferric iron-siderophore complex binds to cell surface receptors and is actively transported into the cell (in |CITS: [19482931]| and in |CITS: [19182782]|). In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., There are two general pathways for siderophore biosynthesis. One is the nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) dependent pathway that is based on the well characterized NRPS multienzyme superfamily. The other is the NRPS-independent pathway, referred to as the NIS pathway. The NIS pathway utilizes a novel superfamily of NIS synthetases that are only beginning to be characterized. Unlike NRPS pathways, NIS pathways involve individual enzymes and free intermediates. NIS synthetases catalyze the condensation of carboxylic acids with amines and alcohols. NIS synthetases are divided into three subfamilies A, B and C based on their carboxylic acid substrate specificities. Type A utilizes |FRAME: CIT|, type B utilizes |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate) and type C utilizes monoamide or monoester derivatives of |FRAME: CIT|, or a monohydroxamate derivative of |FRAME: SUC| (in |CITS: [19182782]|)., Genes encoding NIS synthetases have been identified in over 40 species of bacteria. These genes are associated with the production of at least eight distinct siderophores (in |CITS: [19482931]|). In addition to the biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-9986| |CITS: [19482931]| (this pathway), the biosynthetic pathways for the siderophores |FRAME: CPD-12589| and |FRAME: CPD-12590| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| have recently been elucidated |CITS: [19775248] [19400778] [19138128]|., About This Pathway, This pathway is a proposed NIS (NRPS-independent) pathway for biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9986|, a siderophore secreted by the plant pathogens |FRAME: TAX-205918| and |FRAME: TAX-198628 "Dickeya dadantii strain 3937 (also named Erwinia chrysanthemi strain 3937 or Pectobacterium chrysanthemi strain 3937"| |CITS: [15612933] [18997340] [19182782]|). These two organisms are evolutionarily and pathologically distinct from each other. |FRAME: CPD-9986| has a role as a virulence factor in these organisms (in |CITS: [19182782]|). This pathway has been studied in both |FRAME: TAX-205918| |CITS: [19482931]| and |FRAME: TAX-198628| |CITS: [15612933] [19182782]|., |FRAME: TAX-198628| synthesizes the siderophores |FRAME: CPD-12582| and |FRAME: CPD-9986| in response to iron limitation. In |FRAME: TAX-198628| the genes involved in |FRAME: CPD-9986| biosynthesis have been identified |CITS: [15612933]|. Biochemical analysis suggested that the product of the AcsD catalyzed reaction is |FRAME: CPD-12576| |CITS: [19182782]|. However, the roles of AcsE, AcsC and AcsA in |FRAME: TAX-198628| remain to be experimentally characterized. The putative |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|-dependent decarboxylase product of AcsE could catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12577|. AcsC was proposed to catalyze the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12578|. AcsA was proposed to catalyze the successive addition of two |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate) moieties to produce |FRAME: CPD-9986| (in |CITS: [19482931]| in |CITS: [19182782]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15719346]|). It has been shown that the |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate) moieties of |FRAME: CPD-9986| cyclize in neutral aqueous solution to form pyrrolidine rings |CITS: [10928541]| and in |CITS: [19482931]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-205918| mutant analysis showed that this organism produces both |FRAME: CPD-9986| and |FRAME: Pyoverdines|) siderophores under iron-limited conditions. Recombinant NIS synthetases AcsA, AcsC and AcsD from |FRAME: TAX-205918| were expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, purified and kinetically characterized. A minimal |FRAME: CPD-9986| synthetase was reconstituted in vitro using these three proteins. Active |FRAME: CPD-9986| analogs could also be produced using this in vitro system |CITS: [19482931]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-18984 Propane|, along with |FRAME: CPD-9312|, |FRAME: CPD-18985|, and |FRAME: CPD-9285|, is a gaseous n-alkane. The main sources for gaseous n-alkanes in the atmosphere are natural oil seepage and oil spills., A number of microorganisms have been isolated for their ability to use gaseous n-alkanes as a sole carbon source, including some |FRAME: TAX-286| strains |CITS: [Takahashi80]| and many strains belonging to the order |FRAME: TAX-2037|, such as those of the genera |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, and |FRAME: TAX-1847| |CITS: [7958761][11679317]|., The bacteria |FRAME: ORG-6296| and |FRAME: TAX-246196| can grow on |FRAME: CPD-18984| as their sole carbon and energy source. The pathway employed by these organisms is similar to the pathway that has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-235467| (see |FRAME: PWY-7774|). However, while in that pathway |FRAME: METHYL-ACETATE| is produced from |FRAME: ACETONE|, in this pathway |FRAME: ACETOL| is produced. The enzyme that produces acetol from acetone is the same enzyme that acts on propane, a a dinuclear-iron oxygenase that includes large and small subunits of an oxygenase component, a reductase component, and a coupling protein. Interestingly, the same enzyme acts on both |FRAME: CPD-18984| and |FRAME: ACETONE| in this pathway |CITS: [26293913]|, and also has the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.M33| |CITS: [ 21183637]|.

General Background, Coumarins are widespread among plants and found in especially high concentrations , and structural variations in members of the carrot family |CITS: [Seigler98]|. Coumarin is not a dead end , product of a metabolic pathway but has been demonstrated to be readily metabolized either as the free , |CITS: [13673026]| or the corresponding glucosylated compound |CITS: [13753452]|., When administered to excised clover shoots, coumarin was rapidly converted to melilotyl glucoside, melilotic , acid and two other unidentified products. In contrast, o-coumaric acid was not formed during that experiment , indicating that the formation of free melilotic acid as the main product of this metabolic pathway proceeds , via a hydrogenated intermediate of coumarin |CITS: [13673026]|., About This Pathway, The formation of melilotic acid from coumarin has been proposed to occur in , two steps. The first step involves the hydrogenation of coumarin yielding dihydrocoumarin. This reaction is , very slow and appears to be the rate-limiting step of this pathway |CITS: [14458747]|. However, a corresponding , enzyme has not yet been described and remains to be characterized. , At a much faster rate dihydrocoumarin is been converted to melilotic acid by dihydrocoumarin hydrolase, an , enzyme that has been identified in roots and shoots of |FRAME:TAX-47082|. Because of that rapid conversion , dihydrocoumarin does not accumulate in those plants. Although the enzyme accepts also other substrates , such as 7-hydroxydihydrocoumarin and homogentisic acid lactone, dihydrocoumarin represents the only natural , occurring substrate found in plants |CITS: [14458747]|., The activity of dihydrocoumarin hydrolase (synonym: dihydrocoumarin lactonase) has only been demonstrated , in plants that actively synthesize coumarin (compare |FRAME:PWY-5176|). For that reason it has been , proposed that the enzyme is limited to those species. White sweet clover (|FRAME:TAX-47082|) and , yellow sweet clover (|FRAME:TAX-47083|) had been shown to possess the highest enzyme activity , among the set of plants tested |CITS: [14458747]|.

|FRAME: CPD-24774 Streptozotocin| is a glucosamine-nitrosourea antibiotic produced by the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-285532|. Being a strong alkylating agent, it is toxic to cells by causing damage to the DNA. The compound was discovered by scientists at the drug company Upjohn in 1959 |CITS: [13841501]|., In the mid-1960s streptozotocin was found to be selectively toxic to the β cells of the pancreatic islets, which normally regulate blood glucose levels by producing insulin |CITS: [4170654][4176152][4921840]|. Streptozotocin is similar enough to glucose to be transported into the cell by the glucose transport protein |FRAME: HS08885| (though it is not recognized by the other glucose transporters). Its high toxicity towards β cells is caused by the high levels of |FRAME: HS08885| transporters found in those cells., Upjohn filed for FDA approval of streptozotocin as a treatment for pancreatic islet cell cancer in November 1976, and approval was granted in July 1982. The drug was subsequently marketed as Zanosar. The patent has eventually expired, and today many generic formulations are available., The gene cluster responsible for production of |FRAME: CPD-24774| in |FRAME: TAX-285532| was discovered in 2019. The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-9653| (|FRAME: G-107511|), an enzyme that catalyzes a complex reaction, consisting of two N-hydroxylations and an oxidative rearrangement, forming |FRAME: CPD-24772|, which includes the N-nitrosourea pharmacophore., The products of three other genes in the cluster, the sznH, sznJ, and sznK, are predicted to catalyze the transfer of the N-nitrosourea group of |FRAME: CPD-24773| to the D-glucosamine scaffold to form |FRAME: CPD-24774|, though as of 2021 these enzymes have not been studied., Gene clusters encoding |FRAME: G-107511| homologs are widely distributed among bacteria, including soil and rhizosphere Burkholderia and Paraburkholderia strains, the plant symbiont Frankia, and the human pathogen Legionella pneumophila, suggesting that diverse bacteria are able to produce N-nitroso-containing compounds |CITS: [30728519]|.

Summary: The gram-positive, soil residing bacterial genus Streptomyces comprises more than 550 species |CITS:[9103655]| and represents the most abundant source for bioactive agents applied in human medicine |CITS:[23471619]|. Species of Streptomyces are known to produce a high variety of secondary metabolites, many of them being utilized as antibiotics and agents involved in immunosuppression and anticancer treatments (reviewed in |CITS:[12970466]|. To improve fitness and adaptability, Streptomyces bacteria produce a number of specialized products involved in protection against biological competitors and damaging environmental stress. Amongst them are protective pigments such as melanins and dimeric, aromatic polyketides (this pathway). The biflaviolins produced in the pathway have been discussed to prevent deleterious effects of UV radiation which may compromise the genetic integrity of the organism |CITS:[12028378] [16291687]|., The first step in the pathway is catalyzed by a novel type III polyketide synthase (PKS) (rppA) which has been first cloned and characterized from Streptomyces griseus |CITS:[12139488]|. The polyketide synthase rppA from Streptomyces griseus and other Streptomyces species such as Streptomyces peucetius |CITS:[18612244]| and Streptomyces coelicolor |CITS:[12905073]| catalyzed the sequential decarboxylative condensation, cyclization and aromatization of 5 molecules of |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| to produce |FRAME:TETRAHYD-CPD| which is considered a key intermediate in bacterial pigment biosynthesis. The type III polyketide synthase was regarded earlier as a sole plant enzyme but has been shown to be wider distributed and more diverse in structure and functional mechanism than thought before |CITS:[12714063] [11196653]|. The subsequent reactions carried out by enzymes which modify the PKS catalyzed intermediate are thought to confer the desired biological properties to the polyketide compounds |CITS:[10066498]|. , The next step in the pathway forming |FRAME:CPD-10679| has been shown to occur either spontaneously or enzymatically catalyzed by a novel quinone-forming monooxygenase encoded by MomA in Streptomyces antibioticus. The 1,3,6,8-tetrahydroxynaphthalene (THN) monooxygenase catalyzed this reaction without any reduced nicotinamide cofactors or flavin but required redox-active transition metal ions |CITS:[15701630]|. MomA also catalyzed the NADH-dependent monooxygenase reaction beyond |FRAME:CPD-10679| forming |FRAME:CPD-16816| in the process but required the participation of an unknown proteinaceous factor contained in cell lysates of Streptomyces lividans which remains to be identified |CITS:[15701630]|. The last reactions in the pathway forming the 3,3'- and 3,8'-dimers of |FRAME:CPD-10679| are carried out by two homologous biflaviolin synthases identified in Streptomyces coelicolor. Both biflaviolin synthases CYP158A1 |CITS:[17614370]| and CYP158A2 |CITS:[15659395]| catalyze the same reaction but exhibit a different molar ratio of the two products, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-10680| and |FRAME:CPD-10681| which is probably due to the different structural organization of the active sites in both enzymes. Replaced amino residues and different orientation of amino residues in each of the active sites results in a different catalytic regio-specificity which mechanism is still under investigation |CITS:[17614370] [22203090]|.

General Background, The proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: GLY| can biosynthesized via several different pathways. The main pathway in most organisms is the production of glycine from |FRAME:SER| via |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|. Eukaryotic organisms have both a cytosolic enzyme (SHMT2) and a mitochondrial enzyme (SHMT1) (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-PWY|). The two isoforms were reported to work in opposite directions depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [9398220]|., A less well described glycine production pathway is acheived by the operation of the |FRAME: CPLX-7302| in reverse (see |FRAME: GLYCINE-SYN2-PWY|)., In a third pathway glycine is formed from |FRAME: GLYOX|, a product of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-ALA-PWY|)., And finally, glycine can also be formed from |FRAME:THR| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.48| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-THR-PWY|)., About This Pathway, In this pathway |FRAME: GLY| is formed from |FRAME: GLYOX| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44|., In the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| this is one of three different enzymes used for glycine synthesis. The enzyme is active in yeast only during growth on non-fermentable carbon sources and enables the organism to grow on ethanol as sole carbon source, by alleviating the need for glycolytic intermediates as the precursors for |FRAME: GLY| |CITS: [14745783]|., The pathway was also shown to operates in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-198252|, arguably the most abundant bacterium on earth. |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE Glycolate| is commonly formed by phytoplankton as a result of |FRAME: PWY-181 photorespiration|. Glycolate is oxidized to glyoxylate by |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.15 "glycolate oxidase"|. When glycine is avaliable, glyoxylate is converted to malate and directed to the TCA cycle. However, when glycine levels are low, glyoxylate is converted to glycine via |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| |CITS: [18337719][23096402]|., Genes encoding |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| are widely distributed and have been documented in archaea, bacteria and eukaryota.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22712 "Ochratoxin A"| (OTA) is a natural, toxic, secondary metabolite produced by several fungal species, of the genera |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| |CITS: [15752329]|. OTA spreads widely in many crops, particularly in areas with a hot and humid climate |CITS: [19426279]|. In particular, |FRAME: TAX-60171| is mainly responsible for OTA contamination of cereal-based products, |FRAME: TAX-229535| is responsible for contamination of some dry-cured foods, |FRAME: TAX-40380|, |FRAME: TAX-40993|, |FRAME: TAX-357447|, and |FRAME: TAX-306088| are responsible for contamination of coffee, cocoa, spices, and dried fruits, and |FRAME: TAX-40993|, and, to a lesser extent, |FRAME: TAX-5061| aggregate species, are responsible for contamination of grapes, grape juice, dried vine fruits, must, and wine., OTA is one of the most dangerous mycotoxins for humans and animals, causing nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, carcinogenicity, and teratogenicity. It has also been classified as a class 2B human carcinogen by the International Agency for research on Cancer (IARC) |CITS: [17195275][24448208][26506387][24874522][27384585]|., About This Pathway, OTA biosynthesis begins with a polyketide synthase (OtaA) that utilizes an |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| starter unit and four |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender units to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-22718| |CITS: [16156116][18955151][23334095][24699234]|. This intermediate is hydroxylated twice by the cytochrome P-450 monooxygenase OtaC, forming |FRAME: CPD-22717| (OTβ) |CITS: [16517184][24426165][26256718]|. OTβ is condensed with |FRAME: PHE| by a nonribosomal peptide synthase (OtaB), forming |FRAME: CPD-22715| |CITS: [22983973]|. Finally, a reductive halogenase (OtaD) adds a chlorine atom, forming |FRAME: CPD-22712| |CITS: [27422838]|.
