Summary: The pungency of chili or hot peppers comes from phenolic alkaloids called |FRAME: Capsaicinoids capsaicinoids|. These compounds are exclusively produced in fruits of plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-4071| genus. A quarter of the world population consumes hot peppers in some form daily |CITS: [16938870]|. Structurally capsaicinoids consist of a common aromatic moiety, |FRAME: CPD-9327|, modified by a short chain fatty acid that may have variable length and different degrees of saturation |CITS: [Curry99]|. , The accumulation of |FRAME: Capsaicinoids capsaicinoids| is strictly correlated with developmental stages of the fruit and usually spans the ripening stages after fruit size increase has ceased |CITS: [SUKRASNO93]|. The capsaicinoids are localized in the epidermal cells of the fruit placenta |CITS: [12810854]|. Pungency differs considerably in species ranging from very hot to sweet peppers and has a positive correlation with the level of capsaicinoids biosynthetic gene expression |CITS: [12810854]|., |FRAME: CAPSAICIN Capsaicin| and |FRAME: CPD-9185| are the most common types. Other naturally occurring capsaicinoids include |FRAME: CPD-9182|, |FRAME: CPD-9333|, |FRAME: CPD-9331|, |FRAME: CPD-9181|, and |FRAME: CPD-9330|, which differ in the fatty acid chain length (n=7-10) and the presence and/or position of a double bond |CITS: [Curry99]|., The pathway leading to capsaicin formation has two distinct arms, one that contributes the fatty acid moiety, usually formed via CoA derivatives of an amino acid like valine and the other is an aromatic component that is derived from the |FRAME: PWY-361| |CITS: [Sukrasno93]|. The initial steps of |FRAME: PWY-361| is similar to ones in other plants that give rise to a number of metabolic intermediates, but the steps from |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| to |FRAME: CPD-9327| production is unique to |FRAME: TAX-4071|., Vanilloid receptor (VR1) is responsible for the perception of these compounds; birds the main dispersal agent of |FRAME: TAX-4071| seeds lack a functional VR1. In humans, the VR1 is involved in the pain sensing pathways |CITS: [10764638]| and capsaicins have been used as analgesics and are an effective treatment against nerve pain and arthritis |CITS: [11387594]|.

General Background, Kievitone is a complex prenylated isoflavanol and together with the pterocarpan phaseollin , (|FRAME:PWY-3042|) one of the major phytoalexins present in the subtribe Phaseolinae of the legume family , |CITS: [Ingham90]| |CITS: [WOODWARD82]| |CITS: [Woodward79]|. Kievitone is strongly induced upon wounding and, elicitors |CITS: [3996394]| |CITS: [WHITEHEAD82]| |CITS: [ONeill83]| and under the influence of abscisic acid as , demonstrated in light-grown cotyledons of Phaseolus vulgaris |CITS: [BROOKS85]|., It has been observed that kievitone accumulation upon stress precedes the increase of phaseollin accompanied by rapid , transient increases of enzyme activities involved in both pathways |CITS: [WHITEHEAD82]| |CITS: [3996394]| indicating , a very specific induction of enzymes associated with the production of phytoalexins. , The isoflavone 2,3-dehydrokievitone has been found frequently in annual (|FRAME:TAX-3883| spec. - |CITS: [WOODWARD79A]| , |CITS: [ONeill83]|) and perennial plants (Erythrina sacleuxii - |CITS: [11140607]|). The occurrence of 2,3- dehydrokievitone , has been discussed as evidence for an alternative route leading to kievitone |CITS: [WOODWARD79A]| |CITS: [ONeill83]|, where the order of prenylation and reduction is reversed (both routes are displayed in this pathway)., Prenylated isoflavones such as wighteone and luteone along with the prenylated isoflavanone kievitone are more active , against pathogens then their non-prenylated analogues (dalbergioidin, genistein, 2'-hydroxygenistein). It has been , proposed that the greater lipid-solubility of the prenylated compounds may improve their efficiency |CITS: [ONeill83]|., Kievitone can be degraded to kievitone hydrate by the fungus |FRAME:TAX-169388| (|FRAME:KIEVITONE-HYDRATASE-RXN|). , The gene encoding kievitone hydratase has been isolated |CITS: [7655061]|. The enzyme catalyzes the hydration of , the isopentenyl side chain which reduces the pathogenic toxicity of kievitone |CITS: [VANETTEN89]|., About This Pathway, The prenyltransferase reaction seems to be the pathway-specific and determinative step, for the formation of the end-products kievitone and phaseollin, respectively. Cultivars of |FRAME:TAX-3885| being , resistant and susceptible to the |FRAME:TAX-290576| fungus both accumulate phaseollin whereas , kievitone is only built up in the resistant variety |CITS: [Durango02]|. , There is evidence that substrate-specific prenyltransferases are involved in kievitone and phaseollin biosynthesis , |CITS: [Woodward80]|. The enzyme catalyzing the prenylation of (-)-3,9-dihydroxypterocarpan (DHP) to phaseollidin is , specific for the 10-position of DHP and does not prenylate isoflavanone |CITS: [Biggs87]| whereas the monprenylation , of isoflavones such as genistein and their 2'-hydroxy derivative has been reported in |FRAME:TAX-3870| |CITS: [Schroeder79]|.

General Background, Astaxanthin (3,3'-dihydroxy-4,4'-diketo-β,β-carotene) is the red ketocarotenoid. This pigment gives the orange-red color to the flesh of wild salmon and other fish |CITS:[9491309]|. The pigment is ingested by the animals through their feed and accumulates in their skin, muscle, exoskeleton and gonads. In the aquatic environment, astaxanthin (AX) is produced by microalgae which are consumed by zooplankton, insects or crustaceans, to be finally ingested by fish. Farmed fish and crustaceans which do not have access to the natural sources of AX have their feed supplemented with synthetic AX. Incidentally, |FRAME:CPD-7851|, an intermediate ketocarotenoid in the biosynthesis AX, is also used as a synthetic supplement for the pigmentation of farmed fish although AX is usually preferred to canthaxanthin due its higher color intensity achieved at similar concentration |CITS:[Storebakken92]|; AX is also thought to be deposited in the muscles more efficiently (probably the result of a better absorption through the digestive tract) although this observation might be species-dependent |CITS:[torrisen89],[10554206],[buttle01]|. In addition to its relevance as a pigment, AX has many other important functions particularly in fish reproduction. Indeed, this compound was shown to be involved in acceleration of sexual maturity, increase in fertilization and egg survival, as well as a better embryo development of fish |CITS:[putnam91]|. That being said, AX is mostly known for its antioxidant properties, which have been reported to surpass even those of |FRAME:CPD1F-129| or |FRAME:ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| |CITS:[miki91]|. These properties have led to the initiation of a number of pre-clinical trials aiming to test the effectiveness of AX as an anticancer drug, its prevention of cardiovascular drugs or as a booster of the immune system (for more information, please see the recent review by |CITS:[16431409]|). The biosynthesis of astaxanthin mainly occurs in a number of bacteria (e.g. |FRAME:TAX-188916| and |FRAME:TAX-44155|), fungi (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-264483|) and in a few unicellular algae (e.g. |FRAME:TAX-44745|) |CITS:[goodwin80],[16001255],[16431409]|. In plants, astaxanthin is mostly only found in the |FRAME:TAX-46984| sp. where it is found to accumulate in the flowers; very few other plants produce this compound. Astaxanthin presents three stereochemical isomers: two enantiomers (|FRAME:CPD-7847| and |FRAME:CPD-7957|) and a meso form (|FRAME:CPD-7958|). The 3S,3'S form is the most abundant in nature. Synthetic astaxanthin consists of a racemic mixture of all three forms. Finally, astaxanthin can be found associated to a variety of other compounds: sterified in one or both of the hydroxyl groups with fatty acids (e.g. palmitic, oleic, estearic or linoleic), bound to proteins (carotenoproteins), or lipoproteins (carotenolipoproteins)., About This Pathway, The pathway leading to astaxanthin is |FRAME:TAX-46984| sp. appears to be similar to that observed in other species (see |FRAME:PWY-5288|). Recent study of the enzymes catalyzing the formation of the C4 keto groups has however shown to function according to a mechanism different from that of the carotene 4-ketolases described for other organisms |CITS:[8764486],[7750556],[9523693],[7733978],[7592436]|. Indeed, whereas microbial enzymes appears to catalyze the reaction following a simple one-step mechanism marked by an absence of release of catalytic intermediates, the |FRAME:TAX-46984| enzymes Keto1 and Keto2 appear to be bifunctional enzymes with 4-hydroxylase and 3,4-desaturase activities. It had been previously postulated that the formation of the C4-keto group occurred via the oxidation of 4-hydroxyls, based on the observation that carotenoids with 4-hydroxy-β-rings were found in large quantities in yellow-petalled |FRAME:TAX-46984| flowers unable to produce ketocartenoids |CITS:[czygan69]|. Instead, it would appear that the dual activity of |FRAME:TAX-46984| 'Keto' enzymes (4-hydroxylase/3,4-desaturase) leads to the formation of enol tautomers which spontaneously rearrange to form a more stable keto tautomer form (for example, the enol tautomer |FRAME:CPD-7854|, reaches equilibrium with the keto tautomer |FRAME:CPD-7851|). To date, the activities of the |FRAME:TAX-46984| Keto enzymes have only been assessed for the conversion of |FRAME:CPD1F-129| to |FRAME:CPD-7851| |CITS:[15659105]|. It is however postulated that, in |FRAME:TAX-46984| sp., all reaction leading to the formation of the C4-keto group of ketocarotenoids in the |FRAME:PWY-5288| pathway will be similar to that of canthaxanthin presented in this pathway. A number of other compounds with a single C4-keto groups (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-7860| and |FRAME:CPD-7861|) also appear to be produced |CITS:[15659105]|., Important note: Although the 3,4-didehydro- and 4-hydroxy-β-ring intermediates are detected when the |FRAME:TAX-46984| genes are expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, none of these compounds have been detected in the flowers of |FRAME:TAX-46984| (or any other plants). The authors of the study have therefore postulated that the bacterial system might provide a suboptimal comparison system for the events occuring in |FRAME:TAX-46984| chromoplasts. They postulated that these intermediates might be the result of an aberrant or premature release from the |FRAME:TAX-46984| enzymes and might, under normal in vivo conditions be short-lived intermediates |CITS:[15659105]|.

Names: L-glutamate biosynthesis IV // L-glutamate biosynthesis from L-glutamine
Summary: Yeast cells contain 3 pathways for the synthesis of glutamate.  Two pathways are mediated by two isoforms of glutamate dehydrogenase, encoded by GDH1 and GDH3 |CITS: [2989290]||CITS: [9287019]|.  The third pathway is driven by the combined activities of glutamine synthetase and glutamate synthase, encoded by GLN1 and GLT1, respectively |CITS: [2570348]||CITS: [8923741]|.  Gln1p catalyzes amination of glutamate to form glutamine; Glt1p then transfers the amide group of glutamine to 2-oxoglutarate, generating two molecules of glutamate.  Glutamate synthase, also referred to as GOGAT, is a trimer of three Glt1p subunits.  Expression of the GLT1 gene is modulated by glutamate-mediated repression and by Gln3p/Gcn4p-mediated activation, depending upon the availability of nitrogen and glutamate in the medium.  In amino acid starvation conditions, GLT1 expression is activated to a moderate degree by Gcn4p |CITS: [9657994]|.

General Background, Saffron is is commonly considered the most expensive spice on Earth. It consists of the dried red stigmas of |FRAME: TAX-82528|, a perennial, sterile, vegetatively propagated small plant from the |FRAME: TAX-26339| family. The high price is a result of the labor-intensive collection of the stigmas - 1 kg of dry saffron requires the manual harvest of stigmas from around 110,000170,000 flowers., Saffron is characterized by its color, bitter taste and fragrance. All three attributes are due in large part to products of the degradation of the carotenoid |FRAME:CPD1F-130|. |FRAME:CPD-8668 Picrocrocin|, a compound produced from |FRAME:CPD1F-130| in two enzyme-catalyzed steps, is largely responsible for the bitter taste of saffron., |FRAME:CPD-8669 Safranal|, a volatile compound that is produced non-enzymatically from |FRAME: CPD-8668| by the action of heat, is the main constituent of its aroma. It is present in saffron crocus stigmas only in the range of 0.1-0.6% |CITS: [27979282]|. Safranal is an effective anticonvulsant in animal models, shown to act as an agonist at GABAA receptors |CITS: [16253437][16707256]|. It also exhibits high antioxidant and free radical scavenging activity |CITS: [16317646][16401389]|, and demonstrated cytotoxicity towards cancer cells in vitro |CITS: [8620447][11788779][15582266]|., |FRAME:CPD-8669 Safranal| was also shown to have antidepressant properties in animals and pilot studies in humans |CITS: [Hosseinzadeh04][15341662]|. It is considered to be a suitable candidate for the management of anxiety, depression, neuropsychiatric disorders, as well as the long-term effects of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection such as fatigue, dyspnoea, cognitive problems, sleep abnormalities, and deterioration in the quality of life |CITS: [34007917][Qadir21][Mentis21]|., Traditional drying methods have been optimized to preserve saffron's volatile aroma (for review see |CITS:[16939346]|)., The color is mainly due to a number of carotenoid glycosides derived from |FRAME:CPD-8662|, an insoluble aglycone compound, which, through sequential glucosylation, is converted to the soluble |FRAME:CPD-8666| (see |FRAME:PWY-5398|)., Enzymes of the pathway:, The first reaction in this pathway, the cleavage of |FRAME:CPD1F-130|, was initially attributed to an enzyme from the CCD1 (carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 1) family that was named |FRAME: MONOMER-12426 "zeaxanthin cleavage dioxygenase"| (ZCD). That enzyme was shown, when heterologously expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, to specifically catalyze the conversion of zeaxanthin into |FRAME: CPD-21154| |CITS:[12509521]|. However, later work has suggested that ZCD is a truncated form of a plastoglobule-localized CCD4 enzyme, devoid of cleavage activity, and that the full-length form cleaves |FRAME: CPD1F-129| at the 9,10 and/or the 9',10' positions, yielding |FRAME: CPD-7204| |CITS: [18611853]|., A later study that identified all CCDs expressed during saffron stigma development has indeed concluded that ZCD was not able to cleave |FRAME:CPD1F-130|. Instead, that study reported the finding of a different enzyme, the first member of a new carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase, which was named |FRAME: G-43705|, that catalyzed the reaction |CITS: [25097262]|.

Glandular trichomes of various types are covering leaves, stems and flowers of many higher plants |CITS:[16668241]|. Besides providing plants with the means to regulate temperature and light, glandular trichomes have often been found to exude specialized compounds synthesized for the defense against herbivores |CITS:[2652002] [Severson85]|. In the Solanaceae family the prevailing compounds secreted are acylsugars (summarized in |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-17 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (wild tomato)|) and diterpenoids (this pathway) |CITS:[Severson85a] [24242718] [23757397]|. The latter compound class can be classified into two groups, i.e. the macrocyclic cembrenoids (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-7 cembratrienediol biosynthesis|) and the dicyclic labdanoids (see also |FRAME:PWY18C3-18 labdenediol and sclareol biosynthesis|) |CITS:[Severson85a]|. , Trichome exudates such as the labdanoid |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| and other diterpenes have been reported to protect Nicotiana species from pathogens such as the fungus Colletotrichum lagenarium |CITS:[24234021]|, prevent the germination of the causative agent for blue mold in Nicotiana, i.e. the oomycete Peronospora tabacina |CITS:[24254279]| and act as insecticide on Nicotiana tabacum plants |CITS:[24242718]|. However, |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| has also been identified in various other plants than Nicotiana such as conifers |CITS:[Gray64] [DeSimon01] [21299139]| and the Asteraceae species Smallanthus sonchifolius |CITS:[Miyazawa08]|. The labdanoid |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| also has commercial value in the tobacco industry because it serves as precursor for compounds that increase the smoke quality during leaf curing |CITS:[Severson85a]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| has been used as raw material in the semi-synthesis of Ambrox, an amber substance with a widespread usage in the fragrance industry |CITS:[Barrero93] [25846965]|. In addition, the structural similarity of |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| to |FRAME:CPD-19175 WAF-1|, a diterpene from Nicotiana tabacum activating a wound-induced protein kinase |CITS:[12671083]| is interesting in terms of synthesizing bioactive compounds. , The formation of |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| has been shown to proceed via two enzymatic reactions. The first reaction is the conversion of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP geranylgeranyl diphosphate| to |FRAME:CPD-12745 copal-8-ol-diphosphate| catalyzed by the copal-8-ol diphosphate synthase (CPS2) in Nicotiana tabacum |CITS:[22672125]|. In the subsequent reaction |FRAME:CPD-12745 copal-8-ol-diphosphate| is used by the cis-abienol synthase (ABS) of Nicotiana tabacum to form the final product |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| |CITS:[22672125]|. Both CPS2 and ABS were shown to be highly and specifically expressed in trichomes using GFP (green fluorescence protein) fusion constructs |CITS:[22672125]|., The identification of the catalyzing enzymes was possible through the availability of the genome of tobacco |CITS:[24807620]| and previous results, which localized the control of |FRAME:CPD-14803 cis-abienol| production to the locus Abl |CITS:[20014852]|. Earlier investigations of cell free extracts obtained from trichome-heavy tissues of Nicotiana tabacum already indicated the respective enzymatic activities which however could not be separated at the time |CITS:[8311442]|.

General Background, There are two main sources for |FRAME: ACETONE| production in organisms: the decarboxylation of |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE| (EC 4.1.1.4) and the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL| (EC 1.1.1.80)., Acetoacetate decarboxylation is the major source of acetone in mammals, and arises from either ketogenesis or amino acid degradation |CITS: [12726989]|. Acetoacetate decarboxylation may happen either enzymatically or non-enzymatically. The enzyme responsible for this reaction, |FRAME:CPLX-102|, was first identified in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1488|. However, the existence of this enzymatic activity in mammals, including rat and humans has been documented |CITS: [4624981][963888]| (see |FRAME: PWY66-367|)., The conversion of isopropanol to acetone is catalyzed by the class I isozymes of the hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase family |CITS: [4358273][12726989]|. Over the years, differences in the activity of enzymes from different sources have been noted |CITS: [6389978]|. For example, horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase could not react with isopropanol |CITS: [Theorell51]|., About This Pathway, Once |FRAME: ACETONE| is formed, it can be metabolized in several pathways. One of these pathways involve its conversion to |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| in two consecutive steps via |FRAME: ACETOL| as intermediate., |FRAME: HS05414-MONOMER "Cytochrome P450 2E1"| is one of the most conserved xenobiotic metabolizing P450s in mammals |CITS: [15579107]| and its substrates include acetone and ethanol, which are also two of its prominent inducers. This protein, which is localized to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, is also induced by the diabetic state and by starvation. When acting on acetone, the enzyme produces |FRAME: ACETOL|., The conversion of actetol to |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| in mammalian systems is catalyzed by |FRAME: HS01502-MONOMER| |CITS: [1537826]|. In mammals |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| is metabolized in the liver to L-lactate |CITS: [1537826]|.

Summary: The strictly anaerobic, thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1515| is the microorganism with the fastest documented growth rate on the recalcitrant substrate crystalline |FRAME: CELLULOSE| |CITS: [12209002]|. Unlike fungal cellulases,  |FRAME: TAX-1515| is able to completely solubilize crystalline forms of cellulose such as cotton and |FRAME: CPD-13204| |CITS: [16346009]|. The organism achieves this remarkable ability by forming very large extracellular multi-enzyme complexes, known as cellulosomes. The complex has a diameter of 18 nm and a mass in excess of 2000 kDa |CITS: [10390637]|. Similar complexes are formed by related Clostridia (such as |FRAME: TAX-1488|, |FRAME: TAX-1521|, |FRAME: TAX-1493|, |FRAME: TAX-1499| and |FRAME: TAX-29362|) and other anaerobic cellulose-degrading bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-35830|, |FRAME: TAX-35825| and |FRAME: TAX-1264| |CITS: [19107866]|., Although these bacteria cannot readily utilize carbohydrates other than cellodextrins |CITS: [15755956]|, the cellulosome contains not just endo- and exo-cellulases but also a number of hemicellulolytic enzymes, including xylanases, non-glucanolytic polysaccharide hydrolases and lyases, feruloyl esterases etc. The function of the non-cellulolytic enzymes is presumably the unwrapping of the cellulose crystals from the covering matrix of |FRAME: Lignins lignin|, |FRAME: Pectin pectin| and |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|., The cellulosome is a modular complex. The center of the complex consists of a central non-catalytic protein known as the |FRAME: MONOMER-16412 scaffoldin| (CipA), which binds up to nine catalytic subunits |CITS: [Wu88]|. The attachment of each catalytic subunit is mediated by the interaction of its type I dockerin domain with one of the nine type I cohesin domains of CipA |CITS: [7568112]|., CipA is, in turn, bound to the cell surface by the interaction of its type II dockerin domain with the type II cohesin domain of one of three S-layer anchor proteins, |FRAME: MONOMER-16407 SdbA|, |FRAME: MONOMER-16410 Orf2p|, or |FRAME: MONOMER-16411 OlpB| |CITS: [10049808 ]|., Each of these anchor proteins contains a C-terminal S-layer homology module that mediates attachment to the bacterial cell surface, and a different number of type II cohesin modules capable of binding CipA molecules. Thus different anchoring scaffoldins form cellulosome complexes of differing sizes. The smallest one, |FRAME: MONOMER-16407|, contains one cohesin domain, and thus binds one CipA molecule along with the nine catalytic units bound to it. The medium size |FRAME: MONOMER-16410| contains two cohesin domains and thus binds two CipA molecules and forms complexes with 18 catalytic units. The most abundant anchor protein is |FRAME: MONOMER-16411|, which contains seven cohesin domains and forms complexes of up to 63 catalytic units., In addition to nine type I cohesin domains and a type II dockerin domain, the CipA scaffoldin also contains a type III cellulose-binding module for attachment of the complex to cellulose |CITS: [8316083]|. Many of the catalytic units also contain carbohydrate-binding domains with differing specificities., The exact composition of the cellulosomes depend on growth rate and the nature of substrates available. A 2007 experiment that compared the protein components of cellulosomes formed under conditions of growth on either |FRAME: CELLOBIOSE| or |FRAME: CPD-13204| found significant differences |CITS: [17644599]|. Over 70 proteins that possess type I dockerin modules have been identified in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-203119| |CITS: [19758121]|.

Summary: General Background, Six pathways are now recognized in bacteria, most algae, fungi and higher plants for the biosynthesis of lysine. They are divided into two groups - the diaminopimelate (DAP) pathways, and the |FRAME:CPD-468| pathways., In the pathways that belong to the DAP group, lysine is produced from aspartate (along with methionine, threonine and isoleucine). All of the DAP group pathways share the upper segments, which include the four steps required for conversion of L-aspartate to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|. They also share the last step, which is the conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (D,L-DAP, or meso-DAP) to lysine., However, these pathways differ in the routes leading from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|. The four variations include:, (I) the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|), which involves succinylated intermediates. In this route |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is coverted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in four enzymatic steps., (II) the acetylase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2941|), which involves acetylated intermediates. This route also involves four enzymatic steps for the conversion of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|., (III) the dehydrogenase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2942|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in a single enzymatic step. , (IV) the diaminopimelate-aminotransferase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5097|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in two steps., In addition to lysine, all of the pathways in this group also produce |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is an important metabolite on its own (for example, as a constituent of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan)., The two other pathways belong to the |FRAME: CPD-468| group. They are found in organisms that have no requirement for |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, as it is not a component of their cell walls. These pathways also share the first segments, leading to the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-468| (α-aminoadipate)., However, in yeast and fungi, as well as |FRAME: TAX-3038|, the pathway continues with the key enzyme |FRAME: YBR115C-MONOMER|, leading to the intermediate |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see |FRAME: LYSINE-AMINOAD-PWY|), while in prokaryotes the pathway continues in a path similar to bacterial arginine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., Most of the bacteria that have been investigated in detail appear to utilize only one of these pathways |CITS: [1906065]|. A few exceptions include |FRAME: TAX-44252|, in which variants (II) and (III) seem to coexist |CITS: [BARTLETT85]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, in which variant (I) and (III) coexist |CITS: [1906065]|., Lysine is one of the 10 essential amino acids that mammals are unable to synthesize, and must therefore acquire in their diets. , About This Pathway, The acetylase variant of the lysine biosynthesis pathway is found mostly in the Gram-positive bacilli |CITS: [bartlett85]|., In this pathway, an acetate moiety is added to tetrahydridipicolinate, followed by an amino group, , to form N-acetyl-L,L-DAP., The acetate is then removed, and an epimerase converts the resulting L,L-DAP, to meso-DAP. , In spore-forming Gram-positive organisms, this pathway has yet an additional role, forming dipicolinate. , Dipicolinate is a small molecule that accumulates to high concentrations in bacterial endospores., It is synthesized in a single reaction from dihydrodipicolinate, by dipicolinate synthase., This pathway has been experimentally verified in many Bacilli, including B. cereus, B. circulans, B. laterosporus,, B. licheniformis, B. macerans, B. megaterium, B. mycoides, B. pumilus, B. subtilis, S. pasteurii, S. globispora, G., stearothermophilus, P. polymyxa and V. pantothenticus |CITS: [5411754][chatterjee82][bartlett85]|.

Lotaustralin is a plant cyanogenic glycoside, β-glycosides of α-hydroxinitriles. Under , pathogen or herbivore attacks, cyanogenic glycosides are cleaved by plant beta-glucosidases to , release the toxic hydrogen cyanide which serves as the first line of chemical defense. Bioactivation of , lotaustraline, is best characterized in lotus where lotaustralin is the major cyanogenic glycosides , accumulated in the leaves. , This pathway is analogous to |FRAME: PWY-3121| and |FRAME: PWY-5976|. Two homologous , genes encoding beta-glucosidases responsible for lotaustralin degradation in the leaves have been , cloned from Lotus japonicus. The alpha-hydroxynitrilase catalyzing the second reaction has not been , characterized in this plant.

General Background, |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) is a side product in the biosynthesis of several important compounds., An important case is polyamine synthesis, where |FRAME: MET| is consumed through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) in a reaction that releases MTA (see the pathway |FRAME:POLYAMINSYN3-PWY|). MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration needs to be tightly regulated., Another example is found in the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287|, where MTA is a by product in the synthesis of the autoinducer compounds |FRAME: CPD-10783| and |FRAME: CPD-10784| (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., To ensure that the pathways that produce MTA as a byproduct are not blocked, the organism must remove this compound. The most common way of achieving it is through the |FRAME: PWY-4361 "methionine salvage"| pathway, in which MTA is recycled through a series of reactions back to AMP and |FRAME: MET|., While the methionine salvage pathway is widely conserved, its initial steps, converting MTA to |FRAME:CPD-444|, differ among microorganisms and plants (such as the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [8694776]| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [12022921]|), protozoans (such as |FRAME: TAX-5741| and |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [2854458]|) and mammalian cells. The different routes employed by these organisms are described in the different pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|., About This Pathway, Eukaryotes, some archaea, and about 30% of bacteria possess the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-1163| (|FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE-PHOSPHORYLASE-RXN "EC 2.4.2.28"|), which converts |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| into |FRAME: CPD-444| in a single step |CITS: [29133429]|., The enzyme draws special interest since it has been shown that all normal tissues (and cell lines established from normal tissues) show clearly detectable MTAPase activity, while a large number of cell lines derived from malignancies and primary tumors completely lacks the phosphorylase activity |CITS: [6785752]|. This may make it possible to administer drug therapies that would only affect tumor cells |CITS: [8687427]|.

Summary: The major site for fatty acid β-oxidation in animal cells is the mitochondrion, although partial β-oxidation has also been shown to occur in peroxisomes (see pathway |FRAME: PWY66-391|) (reviewed in |CITS: [20558530][21683154]|). In plant cells, on the other hand, the major sites are the peroxisome and glyoxysome (a specialized peroxisome found only in germinating seeds). The mitochondrion is also active, but is most likely responsible only for degradation of branched-chain fatty acids., Another major difference lies in the structure of the enzymes. In animal mitochondria, after initial metabolism of long chain acyl-CoAs by membrane-bound enzymes, medium and short chain acyl-CoAs are metabolized in the matrix by separate soluble enzymes. In contrast, plant and animal peroxisomes and plant glyoxysomes contain multifunctional proteins (MFPs) that catalyze multiple steps of the pathway. Plant MFPs appear to have S stereospecificity, whereas the fungal counterparts are R stereospecific (see |FRAME:PWY-7288|). Mammals contain two distinct MFPs, one with S and the other with R stereospecificity (reviewed in |CITS: [17434787][17028011][20558530][20195903]|)., The main biochemical difference between the animal mitochondrial and bacterial β-oxidation pathway (see |FRAME: FAO-PWY|) and the plant and animal peroxisomal counterpart lies in the first step, which converts |FRAME: ACYL-COA| to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA|. In bacteria or animal mitochondria, this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: ACYLCOADEHYDROG-MONOMER|. The electrons removed by the oxidation pass through the respiratory chain to oxygen, generating water as the final product. In plant and animal peroxisomes, this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7064|. The electrons pass directly to oxygen and produce |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|, which is immediately cleaved by peroxisomal catalases. , It is still debated whether fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoAs prior to or after their transport into peroxisomes. Two peroxisomal acyl-CoA synthetases have been recently identified and characterized from |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [12366803]|. Both enzymes are able to activate the full spectrum of fatty acids naturally found in the seed, and both genes are strongly induced during seed germination. These observations suggest that the two peroxisomal enzymes are involved in the fatty acid β-oxidation pathway. Reviewed in |CITS: [11755682]|.

Nicotine is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME:TAX-4097| , and N. rustica) |CITS: [SCHMELTZ77]|. Nicotine in tobacco leaves and in plant-derived preparations is , mostly in the (S)-nicotine isomeric form |CITS: [ARMSTRONG98]|. However, tobacco smoke contains up to 10% , (R)-nicotine, probably because of racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine is the addictive , compound in tobacco |CITS: [8301571]| and is a commonly used psychoactive drug. It enters the body by systemic , absorption through cigarette smoking, oral snuff, pipe tobacco, cigars and chewing tobacco use , |CITS: [6705448], [10224986]|. It can also enter in purified form as a medication. , Nicotine has complex physiological effects |CITS: [3054551]|. In cigarette smoke nicotine is carried into the body , on particulate matter. It is rapidly absorbed in the small airways and alveoli of the lung |CITS: [11712903]|. In this , neutral pH environment, it is un-ionized, soluble, and can be transferred across cell membranes and into the , blood. It moves into the pulmonary venous circulation, to the left ventricle of the heart, and into the systemic arterial , circulation |CITS: [8646831], [10482401]|. It travels to the brain within seconds where it binds to nicotinic , cholinergic receptors and activates the dopaminergic reward system |CITS: [10336551]| (and reviewed , in |CITS: [8725403]|). Other forms of nicotine (such as nicotine gum, transdermal patch, inhaler, lozenges and , sublingual tablets) are usually buffered at alkaline pH and quickly traverse cell membranes, but most reach the , blood and brain more slowly. They are less likely to cause addiction because of the delayed reward of nicotine effects , |CITS: [3391001], [8245272]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|. , In humans, the primary site of nicotine metabolism is the liver. There is little evidence in the literature for any , extrahepatic metabolism, despite the presence of isoforms of nicotine metabolizing enzymes in other tissues , (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine and its metabolites are excreted in urine, where they have been , analyzed and quantitated |CITS: [8301571], [1352209], [12376133], [2249376]|. These data showed considerable , interindividual variability in the amount of each metabolite produced |CITS: [7955812], [8301571], [1352209]|., Cotinine is the primary metabolite of nicotine and is found in the urine of smokers |CITS: [13872096], [12376133], , [1352209], [8301571], [2249376]|. In studies of nicotine metabolism in smokers, it has been estimated that 70% of , a nicotine dose is metabolized to cotinine |CITS: [8301571]|. Cotinine reaches high levels in the blood and has a long , half-life |CITS: [9209247]|. The cotinine metabolite trans-3'-hydroxycotinine is the most abundant metabolite , in urine |CITS: [8301571]|. Glucuronide conjugation is a significant route of nicotine metabolism, with nicotine, , cotinine and trans-3'-hydroxycotinine glucuronides accounting for up to 30% of total metabolites recovered , in urine |CITS: [1352209]|., cotinine -> trans-3'-hydroxycotinine , Trans-3'-hydroxycotinine has been found in the urine of smokers , |CITS: [3557628], [2249376], [13872096], [12376133], [1352209], [8301571]| as has its glucuronide conjugate , |CITS: [12376133], [1352209], [8301571]|. Trans-3'-hydroxycotinine and its glucuronide conjugate are the , main nicotine metabolites in the urine of smokers |CITS: [8301571]|. These metabolites account for 40-60% of a , nicotine dose |CITS: [1352209], [8301571], [10548320]|. The reaction is stereoselective for the trans isomer , of 3'-hydroxycotinine |CITS: [2362266], [2075752]|, although the cis isomer has been detected in smokers' , urine |CITS: [2075752]|. The most abundant metabolite in the urine of smokers is trans-3'-hydroxycotinine , |CITS: [3557628], [8301571]|. , In a human subject given oral cotinine, it was established that humans excrete hydroxycotinine in urine. Crystalline , cotinine, hydroxycotinine and 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-N-methylbutanamide were recovered |CITS: [13872096]|. , Hydroxycotinine was also chemically synthesized by these authors |CITS: [MCKENNIS63]|. More recently, the , chemical synthesis of trans-3'-hydroxycotinine from cotinine was reported and metabolic formation was , found to be stereoselective for the trans isomer |CITS: [2362266]|. The degree of glucuronide conjugation , in urine was found to vary between individuals |CITS: [1352209], [8301571]|, as was the percent of cotinine , converted to 3'-hydroxycotinine |CITS: [8301571]|. , Trans-3'-hydroxycotinine glucuronide was identified in the urine of smokers and nonsmokers after one , dose of intravenous 14C-nicotine. Smokers eliminated nicotine and cotinine more rapidly than , nonsmokers who were given these compounds, probably because of inductive effects of smoking on metabolism of , xenobiotics in the liver |CITS: [2249376]|. The 3'-hydroxycotinine glucuronide conjugate is found in urine as an , O-glucuronide |CITS: [8123688]|. Human liver microsomes were found to catalyze N-glucuronidation of , nicotine and cotinine, as well as N- and O-glucuronidation of trans-3'-hydroxycotinine. However, only the , O-glucuronide was found in urine. The authors concluded that the same enzyme(s) probably catalyze , N-glucuronidation of all three compounds and a different enzyme catalyzes O-glucuronidation |CITS: [14680362]|., cotinine -> 5'-hydroxycotinine , The 5'-hydroxycotinine pathway is considered a minor pathway in humans. The main source of urinary , 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate and 4-hydroxy-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate is 2'-hydroxylation of , nicotine |CITS: [11050152]|. The amount of 5'-hydroxycotinine in smokers' urine is <4% of levels of , 3'-hydroxycotinine |CITS: [8012160]|. When oral cotinine was given to a human and urinary metabolites were , analyzed, 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-N-methylbutanamide was identified and its structure determined |CITS: [13872096]|, , although the structure was subsequently corrected in another publication |CITS: [MCKENNIS62]|. Conversion of , 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-N-methylbutanamide to 3-pyridylacetate in humans is largely hypothetical , (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). In a human subject given oral cotinine followed by urine analysis, the , conversion of cotinine to 3-pyridylacetate was shown |CITS: [14257634]|. 3-Pyridylacetate was chemically , identified as a metabolite of cotinine, but the intermediate pyridyl acids were not identified. Therefore, these , reactions remain hypothetical., cotinine -> cotinine N-oxide, Cotinine N-oxide has been isolated and quantitated from urine of smokers and found to be a minor metabolite of , nicotine |CITS: [3443673]|. Cotinine N-oxide is formed from 2-5% of nicotine and metabolites in smokers' urine , |CITS: [1352209], [8301571], [12376133]|. Cotinine N-oxide was identified in the urine of smokers and nonsmokers , after one dose of intravenous 14C-nicotine |CITS: [2249376]|. More recently, liquid chromatography , tandem mass spectroscopy was used to simultaneously identify and quantitate nicotine and 8 metabolites in , smokers' urine. Nicotine-N'-oxide, cotinine-N-oxide and norcotinine represented about 10% of nicotine , metabolites in urine |CITS: [12376133]|. Unlike nicotine N'-oxide, cotinine N-oxide is formed by cytochrome P450 , enzymes (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). , cotinine -> cotinine methonium ion, This reaction involves biological methylation of the pyridine ring of cotinine. Cotinine methonium ion was isolated , and identified from human urine after cotinine administration to a single human subject |CITS: [13932077]|. , cotinine -> cotinine glucuronide, Cotinine glucuronide has been identified in the urine of smokers |CITS: [1643259], [12376133], [8123688], [1352209], , [8301571]|. It was synthesized and characterized as (S)-(-)-cotinine N-glucuronide, establishing its identity , |CITS: [1643259]|. Cotinine glucuronide has been directly determined in the urine of smokers (versus indirect , assay using β-glucuronidase treatment of urine and assay of cotinine release). Interindividual differences were , seen in the production of cotinine glucuronide |CITS: [8123688]|. , cotinine -> norcotinine , Norcotinine (demethylcotinine) has been identified in the urine of smokers |CITS: [1352209], [12376133]|. In , smokers and nonsmokers who were given a single intravenous dose of 14C-nicotine, demethylcotinine , (norcotinine) was identified in urine |CITS: [2249376]|. Norcotinine constitutes about 1% of total nicotine and , metabolites in smokers urine |CITS: [1352209]|. There are two pathways for its formation: oxidative metabolism of , nornicotine, and demethylation of cotinine. Both pathways have been demonstrated in animals. The conversion , of nicotine to nornicotine and then to norcotinine has been shown in rabbit liver |CITS: [14166990]|. Dog studies , showed the conversion of nicotine to cotinine to hydroxycotinine and norcotinine |CITS: [14004224]|. , N'-hydroxymethylnorcotinine was first detected in vitro in hamster liver microsomes after incubation with , cotinine. The compound has been synthesized and characterized |CITS: [8079500]|. It was speculated to be an , intermediate, although contradictory results have been reported |CITS: [10409404]|. Therefore, it is a hypothetical , intermediate in humans. Norcotinine can be further metabolized by rat liver microsomes to , 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanamide. This compound can be converted to 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate , (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|. Small amounts of 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanamide have been reported in , the urine of smokers (Jacob, Yu and Benowitz unpublished, in review |CITS: [15734728]|. It has been shown , that human cytochrome P450 2A6 is involved in the formation of norcotinine, 5'-hydroxycotinine, and , trans-3'-hydroxycotinine from cotinine |CITS: [10409404]|., Evidence for conversion of 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanoate to 3-pyridylacetate in humans is largely hypothetical. , In a human subject given oral cotinine followed by urine analysis, the conversion of cotinine to 3-pyridylacetate was , shown |CITS: [14257634]|. 3-Pyridylacetate was chemically identified as a metabolite of cotinine, but the , intermediate pyridyl acids were not identified. The metabolism of norcotinine to pyridyl acids (via oxidation of the , pyrrolidone ring) was shown in the rat and dog, but the authors suggested that this is not , necessarily applicable to humans |CITS: [14257634]|. Therefore, these reactions remain hypothetical.

Summary: General Background, Chlorophyll degradation, corresponding to the loss of green color, is an integral part of leaf senescence and fruit ripening |CITS:[16113212],[15012204],[10767575],[12675736][ 16669755]|. Chlorophyll degradation in land plants may follow one of two routes, likely depending on the physiogical context in which it occurs. This pathway, |FRAME: PWY-5098| may be cytosolic and may operate during fruit senescence and in response to pathogens and wounding |CITS: [15598807][18633118]|. Meanwhile, |FRAME: PWY-6927|, begins in the chloroplast and may be the primary route for chlorophyll degradation in senescing leaves in |FRAME: ORG-5993| and other species, such as broccoli (|FRAME: TAX-3712|) |CITS: [19304936][20727617]|. Evidence for the existence of that alternative pathway was collected after it was observed that two Arabidopsis chlorophyllases (CLH1 and CLH2) are not required for chlorophyll breakdown during leaf senescence |CITS: [17996203]|., Both of these pathways appear to lead to the production of a colourless, blue-fluorescing intermediate (|FRAME: CPD-7064| or pFCC) via the formation of a red chlorophyll catabolite (RCC). The final steps of chlorophyll catabolism are species-specific and involve a diversity of modifications of pFCC before the catabolites are finally stored in the vacuole in the form of |FRAME:NCCS|, or NCCs |CITS:[15012204],[16448336]|. NCCs share a common tetrapyrrolic skeleton with an oxygenolytically opened porphyrin macrocycle |CITS:[KRAEUTER03]|, with peripheral, species-specific modification at several side chains within different NCCs. The final conversion of modified FCCs to NCCs is a non-enzymatic reaction catalyzed by the acidic vacuolar pH., About This Pathway, One of the first step in this route of chlorophyll degradation is dephytylation, or removal of the phytol moiety of the compound. A substantial portion of this phytol remains esterified with fatty acids |CITS:[PATTERSON93]| and with acetic acid |CITS:[BORTLIK90]|, whilst the rest is photooxidatively converted into various isoprenoid compounds |CITS:[RONTANI96]|. This step is catalyzed by chlorophyllases which have been described in several plants species (for review see |CITS:[16448336]|) and acts primarily on chlorophyll a., The second enzyme of the pathway, Mg dechelatase, remains elusive. This enzyme catalyzes the release of Mg2+ from chlorophyllide a in exchange from two protons to form pheophorbide a. Since the purification of the protein has been unsuccessful and has led to the detection of a low-molecular-weight compound rather than a protein, the removal of Mg2+ from chlorophyllide a has been postulated to be performed by a 'Mg-dechelating substance', or MCS. It is uncertain whether MCS represents an active cofactor of Mg-dechelatase. The structure of either Mg-dechelatase or MCS remains to be determined |CITS:[16448336]|., The next two steps are decisive in the loss of green colour. The ring-opening of, and production of the first identifiable colourless product pFCC from pheophorbide a requires two proteins from gerontoplasts membranes and stroma. Opening of the ring through oxygenolysis of pheophorbide a is catalyzed by the membrane-localized, nonheme iron-containing monooxygenase, pheophorbide a oxygenase (PaO) which yields red bilin RCC. This compound is channeled to RCCR which further reduces it to form pFCC. Both enzymes use reduced ferredoxin as immediate electron donor |CITS:[15012204]|.

Summary: Fatty acid biosynthesis in plants mainly occurs in plastids, although mitochondria are also capable to , synthesize fatty acids |CITS: [14660674]|. The active sites for fatty acid biosynthesis are photosynthetic , leaf mesophyll cells, seeds, and oil-accumulating fruits. In plants, the initial condensation of an , acetyl group and a malonyl group to give rise to acetoacetyl-ACP is carried out by the condensing , enzyme isoform KAS III. The enzyme specifically uses the substrates acetyl-CoA and malonyl-ACP. , There is no evidence for the existence, or physiological significance if exists, of a bacterial version of , the initial condensation reaction, which utilizes acetyl-ACP and , malonyl-ACP |CITS:[plantbiochemistry97],[12624762]|. Acetoacetyl-ACP (a beta-ketoacyl-ACP) then , enters the elongation cycle, composed of four reactions. One cycle extends the chain length of an , acyl-ACP by two carbon units using malonyl-ACP as the carbon donor. The condensing enzyme , isoforms KASI and KASII are responsible for elongation steps from C4 to C16, and from C16 to C18, , respectively. Unlike their bacterial counterparts, plants KAS I and KAS II do not accept unsaturated , acyl-ACP substrates.  , In most plants, the primary products of the fatty acid elongation cycle are 16:0-ACP and 18:0-ACP. The , first double bond is then introduced to 18:0-ACP by delta9 18:0-ACP desaturase, which is ubiquitous , to all plants. Additional double bonds are inserted to oleate and palmitate after they are incorporated , into lipids (|FRAME: PWY-782|, |FRAME: PWY-762|). Plants also contain very , long-chain fatty acids (chain length larger than 18). The additional chain elongation occurs via the , very long chain fatty acid biosynthesis pathway (|FRAME: PWY-5080|) located in the ER. Free fatty acids are , released from acyl-ACPs and are exported out of plastids.

Names: sterculate biosynthesis // cyclopropane and cyclopropene fatty acid biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Cyclopropane fatty acids (CPA-FAs), unusual fatty acids containing three-carbon cyclic rings, are found in both bacteria and plants |CITS: [9409147]|. One striking difference between the bacteria CPA-FAs and the plant CPA-FAs is that the bacteria CPA-FAs are normally esterified at the sn-2 position of phosphatidylethanolamine, whereas the plant CPA-FAs are preferentially esterified at the sn-1 position of phosphatidylcholine. In plants most CPA-FAs are desaturated to cyclopropene fatty acids (CPE-FAs). CPA-FAs and CPE-FAs are distributed across several plant orders, including certain gymnosperms, |FRAME: TAX-41938|, and |FRAME: TAX-41937| |CITS: [21612656]|., Plant CPE-FAs may function as anti-fungal agents. Feeding animals with CPE-FA-containing oilseeds, such as cotton seed meal, causes physiological disorders due to the fact that CPE-FAs are strong inhibitors of fatty acid desaturases in animals. There is an interest in both reducing the CPE-FAs contents in feeding oilseeds and increasing the CPE-FAs contents for industrial oleochemical applications., About This Pathway, Our knowledge of the plant pathway of cyclopropane and cyclopropene biosynthesis mainly came from studies of |FRAME: TAX-195802|, a tropical tree whose seed oil contains 65-78% CPE-FAs, mainly sterculic acids. , The key enzyme in the pathway is |FRAME: MONOMER-11215|, an enzyme that converts the double bond of |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| to a cyclopropane group. The enzyme does not act of free acids, but on oleate groups incorporated into phosphatidylcholine. In vivo labeling experiments and in vitro enzyme assays indicate that S-adenosylmethionine is the methylene donor for the synthesis of |FRAME: DIHYDROSTERCULIC-ACID| from |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|., The synthesized |FRAME: DIHYDROSTERCULIC-ACID| was only detected in phosphatidylcholine (predominantly on the sn-1 position), not in other phospholipids. EST profile of the |FRAME: TAX-195802| |FRAME: MONOMER-11215| indicates a correlation of gene expression and high seed stercuate content., |FRAME: DIHYDROSTERCULIC-ACID Dihydrosterculate| is further desaturated to |FRAME: STERCULATE| by the enzyme cyclopropane desaturase, which has not been characterized to date. It is interesting to note that even though |FRAME: DIHYDROSTERCULIC-ACID| is predominantly esterified at the sn-1 position, |FRAME: STERCULATE| is equally distributed on sn-1 and sn-2 positions of phosphatidylcholine, suggesting that the |FRAME: DIHYDROSTERCULIC-ACID| synthesized at the sn-1 position may be removed from the lipid before further desaturation, followed by reincorporation into the sn-2 position.

Names: alliin metabolism // allium thiosulfinates metabolism // garlic thiosulfinate metabolism
Summary: General Background, Plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-40553| family have been valued both for flavor and medicinal purposes throughout the world., The domestic Alliums (such as onion, garlic, chives and leek) contain high concentrations of organic sulfur compounds especially in their bulbs and leaves. These compounds consist mostly of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| such as |FRAME: CPD-9269|, |FRAME: CPD-9307|, and |FRAME: CPD-9277|, as well as γ-glutamyl peptides (together these compounds make up over 70% of the total sulfur in garlic |CITS: [ Lawson96]|)., These compounds, which are found in the cytoplasm, are produced constitutively. The S-alkyl cysteine S-oxides are substrates for the alliinase enzymes (|FRAME: EC-4.4.1.4|), which convert them to |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|. However, the enzymes are kept in vacuoles, and are thus sequestered from their substrates |CITS: [Lancaster81][19463015]|. Only when the tissue is injured, the alliinase enzymes are released from the vaculoes and interact with their substrates, producing |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|., |CITS: [16010345]|. Once formed, S-alkylsulfenates are very active and tend to condense spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-17425 thiosulfinates| |CITS: [21905712]|. Depending on the Allium species, and under differing conditions, the thiosulfinates can decompose to form additional sulfur constituents including diallyl, methyl allyl, and diethyl mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, and hexasulfides, vinyldithiins, and (E)- and (Z)-ajoene |CITS: [16010345]|., In some species, dedicated enzymes commonly known as "lachrymatory-factor synthases" act on the S-alkylsulfenates rapidly, before they condense, producing volatile compounds that cause the eyes of animals to tear (lachrymatory factors) - a further defense mechanism against herbivory., About This Pathway, In garlic the predominant |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxide"| is |FRAME: CPD-9269|, with lower concentrations of |FRAME: CPD-9307| and |FRAME: CPD-9277| and trace amounts of |FRAME: CPD-9278|. |FRAME: CPD-9269 Alliin| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-9298|, presumably by the action of an |FRAME: MONOMER-13526| |CITS: [Oshumi93]|. The path of synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9298| is still speculative. An early research paper reported that γ-glutamyl peptides are not the immediate precursors for its synthesis |CITS: [Edwards94]|. However, later work has suggested two possible routes that may coexist - one from serine and allyl thiol, and the other (which is shown here) from γ glutamyl peptides. Radiolabeled |FRAME: VAL| has been shown to give rise to to radiolabeled |FRAME: CPD-13859| |CITS: [Granroth70]|, and thus L-valine degradation is a potential source for the side group of the S-alk(en)yl-L-cysteine S-oxides |CITS: [15234988][15652575]|., In garlic allinase and its substrate are contained within a specific tissue, the bundle sheath cells of the clove |CITS: [Ellmore94]|. They are separated from each other by compartmentalization in the vacuole (alliinase) and cell cytoplasm (alliin) |CITS: [17174334]|. Once the tissue is injured, allinase is released and rapidly converts |FRAME: CPD-9269| to |FRAME: CPD-9273|, which then condenses with a variety of other S-alkylsulfenates, forming |FRAME: CPD-9275| and other assorted thiosulfinate compounds spontaneously., |FRAME: CPD-9269 Alliin| is odorless, and the characteristic pungent odor of garlic is produced only when the tissue is crushed and the thiosulfinates are formed |CITS: [1385120]|. , |FRAME: CPD-9275 Allicin| is a defense molecule with a broad range of biological activities. It is physiologically active in microbial, plant and mammalian cells, due to its ability to participate in redox-reactions with thiol groups in glutathione and proteins |CITS: [25153873]|. In a dose-dependent manner allicin can inhibit the proliferation of both bacteria and fungi, and even kill cells, including antibiotic-resistant strains like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) |CITS: [25153873]|. |FRAME: CPD-9275 Allicin| is also a parent compound of a number of other sulfur-containing compounds such as thiosulfinates, allyl sulfides, dithiines and ajoenes.

Summary: |FRAME:SIROHEME Siroheme| is the prosthetic group of assimilatory sulfite and nitrite reductases, found in many prokaryotes, and in the dissimilatory sulfite reductases of sulfate-reducing bacteria., While isolating siroheme from enzymes or whole cells of |FRAME:TAX-872| species, it was discovered that the main product after metal removal and esterification was not the octamethyl ester derivative of sirohydrochlorin, but a monoamide, heptamethyl ester derivative. In the purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049|, which oxidizes sulfide and thiosulfate, the prosthetic group of |FRAME: EC-1.8.1.22| (DsrAB) was also identified as siroamide |CITS: [16907720]|. A gene that is present in the same operon of the |FRAME:G-9511| and |FRAME:G-9512|, genes, |FRAME:G-9534|, is homologous to the |FRAME:G-487|  gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.11| (see |FRAME:P381-PWY|), and is predicted to encode a |FRAME: CPLX-7144| that catalyzes glutamine-dependent amidation of |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| |CITS: [16907720]|.

Summary: General Background, Sulfur is an essential nutrient for all life forms. Plants, fungi, and many bacteria reduce inorganic |FRAME: SULFATE| to sulfide to cover their need for the element. Before the sulfur can be assimilated into biosynthetic pathways it needs to be reduced to |FRAME:HS|. Pathways catalyzing the reduction of sulfate to sulfide for the purpose of incorporation into newly synthesized molecules are called pathways of assimilatory sulfate reduction. In addition, certain organisms can use sulfate as an alternative electron acceptor in the absence of oxygen. Pathways of sulfate reduction for the purpose of energy production are called pathways of dissimilatory sulfate reduction., Sulfate can not be reduced to sulfide in a single step, and is first reduced to |FRAME: SO3|. However, two electrons required to reduce of sulfate to sulfite have a standard redox potential (E0') of -516 mV, which is too high for physiological electron carriers |CITS: [860983]|. The problem is solved by the activation of the sulfate by phosphorylation, forming a mixed anhydride between phosphate and sulfate as in |FRAME:APS| (APS) or |FRAME:PAPS| (PAPS). This linkage lowers the potential of the electrons to E0' = -60 mV, which is easilly covered by thiols or pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [14627706]|., In plants, as well as in certain bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [10939523]|), |FRAME:APS APS| is reduced directly to sulfite. In enteric bacteria, cyanobacteria, and yeast, on the other hand, |FRAME:APS APS| is further phophorylated to |FRAME:PAPS PAPS|, and only the latter is reduced to sulfite (see |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) |CITS: [11940598]|., About This Pathway, Even though this pathway was intially described in plants, it has been shown to exist in some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [10939523]|., As described above, the initial step of sulfate reduction is its activation to |FRAME: APS| (APS). This phosphorylation is performed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.4| (often known as ATP sulfurylase). It should be noted that in some sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1049|, there are two two such enzymes - an |FRAME: CPLX-8836| and a |FRAME: CPLX-8194|. Only the latter is relevant for this pathway., Two types of enzymes are known to catalyze the second step - the direct reduction of APS to sulfite - |FRAME:EC-1.8.4.9| and |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.10|. This pathway describes organisms that posses the former. The latter enzyme is described in |FRAME: PWY-6683|., Once formed, sulfite can reduced to sulfide by the action of multiple enzymes. While most bacteria utilze NADPH as an electron donor (|FRAME: EC-1.8.7.2|), the plant sulfite reductases, as well as the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-1049|, use ferredoxin for this purpose (|FRAME: EC-1.8.7.1|)., In bacteria and plants, sulfide is finally incorporated into |FRAME: ACETYLSERINE| by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.47| yielding |FRAME: CYS|, and later into |FRAME: MET|, which are the two major sulfur-containing precursor compounds (see |FRAME: CYSTSYN-PWY|)., Earlier literature, describing work mostly performed with the alga |FRAME: ORG-6016|, describes a different sulfate reduction pathway in plants, involving thiol-bound sulfite intermediates |CITS: [16655178][16655893][16656806][4788946][398767]|. However, the purification and characterization of |FRAME:CPLX-7175| from |FRAME: TAX-4472| revealed that the only product of the enzyme is indeed free sulfite, and that the thiol-bound intermediates were most likely artefacts due to the presence of oxidized thiols in the reaction media |CITS: [10625629]|., Regulation of the pathway in plants , Sulfate assimilation in plants is regulated by several factors., (i) Developmental stage: the highest activities of sulfate assimilation enzymes are found in growing tissues including young leaves and root tips where there is a high demand for cysteine and metionine for protein biosynthesis., (ii) Availability of reductants: two of the enzymes in this pathway, APS reductase and sulfite reductase, require reductants (glutathione and ferredoxin, respectively) to remain active. In addition, the availability of reductants is related to the availability of light, the ultimate electron source in photosynthetic tissues. In leaves, the activity of sulfite reductase was shown to be directly linked to circadian phasing., (iii) Sulfur availability: gene expression of sulfate assimilation enzymes was induced by sulfur deficiency conditions |CITS: [9380766]|., (iv) Stress: gene expression was also found to be induced by exposing plants to heavy metals and oxidative stress |CITS: [9380766]|., More information is available in |CITS: [leustek02]| and |CITS:[16307301]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Gentamycins Gentamicins| are a family of |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| produced by Gram-positive bacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-1873| genus. They were discovered in 1963 by a group of scientists at the Schering Corporation |CITS: [14274893]|., Gentamicins are particularly active against Gram-negative bacteria, and are bactericidal. They act by binding the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, interrupting protein synthesis. Despite their high antibacterial activity, intravenous use is limited by their ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. However, they are used commonly as a topical treatment to skin infections. The most common form of gentamycin is the |FRAME: GENTAMICIN-C "C complex"|, which consists of a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-14213|, |FRAME: CPD-14216|, |FRAME: CPD-14211|, |FRAME: CPD-14212| and |FRAME: CPD-15231|., While the name can be written as both gentamicin and gentamycin, the former is more common, to emphasize the biological origin of the antibiotics., About This Pathway, The Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1877| produces several related compounds of the gentamicin family. The main products are |FRAME: CPD-14213|, |FRAME: CPD-14216|, |FRAME: CPD-14211| and |FRAME: CPD-14212|, but the organism produces a number of minor products including |FRAME: CPD-14206|, |FRAME: CPD-14217|, |FRAME: CPD-14218|, |FRAME: CPD-14214|, and |FRAME: CPD-14209| |CITS:[5050712][1259389]|., The first gentamicin-specific intermediate is |FRAME: CPD-14207|, produced from |FRAME: CPD-14125| by the |FRAME: G-15082|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17295| |CITS: [18550838]| (for synthesis of paromamine, please see the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7014|)., In the next segment of the pathway, four enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124790|, |FRAME: G-124791|, |FRAME: G-124794|, and |FRAME: G-15084| genes, |FRAME: CPD-14207| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-14214| |CITS: [25641167]|., |FRAME: CPD-14214 "Gentamycin X2"| is a branch point. One branch continues directly with the action of the |FRAME: G-124792 "GenQ oxidase"| and |FRAME: G-124793 "GenB1 aminotransferase"|. The combined action of the oxidase and the aminotransferase converts the 6-hydroxyl group of the hexosamine sugar to an amino group |CITS: [24746560]|., The second branch proceeds via the action of the |FRAME: G-15083 "radical SAM-dependent methyltransferase GntK"|, which converts |FRAME: CPD-14214| to |FRAME: CPD-14209| (G-418) |CITS: [18533111][23149679]|. This is followed by the action of the GenQ oxidase and either |FRAME: G-124793 "GenB1 aminotransferase"| or |FRAME: MONOMER-124796 GenB2|, a different aminotransferase that adds the amino group at the same location but in a different stereo configuration. The combination of the two branches and the two different aminotransferases results in formation of three intermediates: |FRAME: CPD-14215|, |FRAME: CPD-14210|, and |FRAME: CPD-27389| |CITS: [24746560][26083124]|., A short route branching from |FRAME: CPD-14215|, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-124799| and |FRAME: G-124800| genes, has been shown to produce the minor component |FRAME: CPD-14217| |CITS: [34765440]|. Presumably the same enzymes, acting on |FRAME: CPD-14210|, form |FRAME: CPD-14218|., The biiosynthesis of the C complex components proceeds with a C-3',4'-dideoxygenation process. This process is carried out by the |FRAME: MONOMER-17935| (GenP) and the PLP-dependent enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-124796| and |FRAME: G-124797| genes. Following 3'-phosphorylation by GenP, GenB3 acts on the phosphorylated products, catalyzing the removal of the C-3'-phosphate group as well as the 3' and 4' hydroxyl groups, forming 3',4'-dideoxy-4',5'-ene-6'-oxo products. Depending on the starting compound, GenB3 produces |FRAME: CPD-15230| or |FRAME: CPD-27392|. Different combinations of reactions catalyzed by GenB1, GenB2, and GenB4 then produce |FRAME: CPD-14216|, |FRAME: CPD-27400|, |FRAME: CPD-27398|, |FRAME: CPD-14211|, and |FRAME: CPD-14212| |CITS: [23339967][32156271][33750386]|. Finally, a methyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124798| gene produces |FRAME: CPD-14213| and |FRAME: CPD-15231| |CITS: [29358400]|.

Summary: General background, Maintenance of genomic and transcriptomic integrity is a vital goal of all organisms. Cells are often subjected to reactive oxygen species (ROS), such as |FRAME: CPD-12377|, that arise due to oxidative stress, ionizing radiation, and certain aspects of normal cellular metabolism. For human pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-1773| the problem is particularly significant, since they are exposed to reactive oxygen species generated within the host macrophages., ROS can modify nucletide bases and cause problems during DNA replication and RNA transcription. This damage can occur on free nucleotides or in the context of DNA or RNA macromolecules. Organisms have evolved several strategies for combating the damage that can be caused by oxidative stress, including this pathway that is involved in eliminating a source of potentially mutagenic nucleotides before they can be used for DNA replication or mRNA transcription |CITS: [Rogacheva08]|., Oxidation of the free nucleotides |FRAME: GTP| and |FRAME: DGTP| can occur spontaneously in cells when a hydroxyl radical attacks the C8 position of the purine base |FRAME: GUANINE| |CITS: [16863995]|. If |FRAME: 8-Oxo-dGTP| is incorporated into DNA it can pair with a C or an A and lead to G:C ->T:A or A:T -> C:G transversions, respectively, although the A:T to C:G transversion seems to be more common in vivo (|CITS: [1309939] [Rogacheva08]|). Similarly, an |FRAME: CPD-12366| can be incorrectly incorporated opposite an adenosine residue during RNA transcription |CITS: [17804481]|. Oxidized (d)GTP is a major source of genetic lesions. In animals errors caused by the failure of this detoxification pathway may be linked to cancer and other DNA-damage related diseases |CITS: [1309939][17804481][Rogacheva08]|., To prevent these errors, Nudix hydrolase-type enzymes act to remove one or two phophate groups from the oxidized nucelotides, rendering them incompetent for incorporation into DNA or RNA |CITS: [Rogacheva08]|. It is important to note that there is evidence from humans that |FRAME: CPD-12365| cannot be re-phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.8| |CITS: [7819228]|. Both bacteria and eukaryotes show marked increases in DNA and RNA errors when this pathway is blocked., About this pathway, The detoxification of the oxidized guanine nucleotides is carried out by members of the Nudix family of hydrolases. In many organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-562|, yeast, Arabidopsis plants, and humans, the oxidized nucleotides are dephosphorylated to nucleoside monophosphates in a single step, catalyzed by the Nudix hydrolase |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.55| (see |FRAME: PWY-6502|)., The human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1773| does not have a homolog of |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.55|. Instead, this organism was shown to possess two related enzymes, both of which are Nudix hydrolases, each catalyzing the removal of one phospho group |CITS: [23463507]|., The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.69|, is highly specific for |FRAME: CPD-12366| and |FRAME: 8-Oxo-dGTP|, and removes only one phosphate group from its substrates. The products of this enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-13853| and |FRAME: CPD-14101|, can be converted back to 8-oxo-dGTP and 8-oxo-GTP (for example by |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.6|), and thus still pose danger to the cell and must be hydrolyzed further. This is achieved by the |FRAME: G185E-5891| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.58| |CITS: [23463507]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium Selenium| is an essential micronutrient for animals and humans but has not yet been proven to be an essential micronutrient for land plants |CITS: [11683552][16307305]|. There is evidence, however, of Chlamydomonas proteins that contains a |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| residue suggesting that algal species might also require |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [17105189][12110581]|. The health requirement of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for humans and animals can be met by crops and forage plants that contain selenocompounds. |FRAME: TAX-4232| among the oilseed crops was shown to be a good source for this micronutrient |CITS: [15012198]|. Despite its importance as a micronutrient, higher concentrations of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| are toxic to humans, other animals, and plants largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064][12753978][16661781]|., In general, plants take up both |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE| from soil. A series of reduction steps converts |FRAME: SELENATE| to |FRAME: SE-2| / |FRAME: CPD-678| and this is assimilated into the seleno-amino acids |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19309459]|., About This Pathway, In many plant species the metabolism of selenium appears to mirror the metabolism of sulfur and often uses the same enzymes. Therefore, although this pathway has not been completely elucidated in plants, it has been built based on the comparable |FRAME: SULFMETII-PWY reductive sulfur assimilation pathway| found in plants |CITS: [16307305]|., As in the sulfur reduction pathway, the ATP sulfurylase enzyme appears to catalyze the first step in selenium reduction. This claim is supported by the finding that overexpression of an Arabiopsis ATP sulfurylase promotes selenate reduction |CITS: [9880353][15941393]|., The second step in the pathway is still being investigated. There is evidence for non-enzymatic conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13713| to selenite in vitro |CITS: [328009]|, but selenite reductase activity has been observed in planta and has been measured in a number of selenium hyperaccumulators |CITS: [15941393]|., The latter part of the pathway is believed to differ from the parallel sulfur pathway. To date, there is no evidence that a sulfite reductase enzyme is needed to catalyze the transformation of |FRAME: SELENITE| to |FRAME: CPD-678| in plants. Rather, evidence collected using pea chloroplasts suggests that this reaction can proceed non-enzymatically and uses both glutathione and NADPH as reducing agents |CITS: [JABLONSKI82]|. Expected intermediates are |FRAME: CPD-13909| and |FRAME: CPD-13909|., Analyses of the overall reduction of selenate to organic selenium suggest that the first step of selenate reduction is rate-limiting |CITS: [9701603]|. , This pathway is believed to occur in the choloroplast |CITS: [12753978]|.
