Summary: General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (beetles and fungal pathogens). Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids)., The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also forming a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|., The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|. Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir |FRAME: TAX-46611| oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes have been involved in a variety of biological processes: inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Naturally occurring resin acids are liberated from wood during pulping and are toxic to fish and microorganisms |CITS:[7887603]|.

Names: reactive oxygen species degradation // removal of superoxide radicals
Summary: General Background, All organisms living in an aerobic environment are exposed to reactive oxygen species (ROS) that are formed through metabolic processes and various environmental stresses |CITS: [11997379]|. ROS are unstable and extremely reactive, the chemical reactivity induces lipid peroxidation and protein oxidation/degradation |CITS: [10638941]|. The effect of ROS on cell fate depends on the level at which they are present., There are three main types of ROS: |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| arises from the mitochondrial respiratory chain and is constitutively present in cells; |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| arises from dismutation of |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| (by way of |FRAME: EC-1.15.1.1|) or the action of oxidase enzymes; and highly reactive |FRAME: CPD-12377| produced from the decomposition of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|, modifies purine and pyrimidine bases and cause DNA strand breaks |CITS: [24511533]|. , ROS levels in moderation have a normal physiological role in health, controlling inflammatory and immune responses and participating in signal transduction. However, unbalanced levels of ROS are related to many disorders, including cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer's disease, pulmonary diseases, diabetes, aging and cancer. , Most aerobic organisms have developed defense systems to scavenge oxidative radicals and combat oxidative stress, in the form of enzymes that can detoxify ROS. Since ROS can be found in any compartment of the eukaryotic cell, organisms have developed small gene families encoding specific enzymes that operate in the various cell compartments |CITS: [9765550][9214587]|., About this Pathway, The superoxide dismutases (SODs) represent the first line of defense against ROS, converting |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE| radicals to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and water |CITS: [2853161]|. SODs are differentiated with regard to their metal cofactor. There are manganese-dependent and copper/zinc-dependent SODs, which differ not only in their metal cofactor but also in their subcellular location. Human |FRAME: CPLX66-541| is found in the mitochondrion and is structurally very similar to bacterial FeSODs. , In mammals the |FRAME: CPLX66-540| operates in the cytosol and the |FRAME: CPLX66-542| operates outside the cell. Both are structurally different from |FRAME: CPLX66-541| because of the different electrical properties of copper in comparison to manganese, which results in a major structural change in the protein |CITS: [11997379]|. , Hydrogen peroxide can be converted to water and/or oxygen by the glutathione peroxidases or by catalase |CITS: [10666617]|. In mammals catalases are found in the peroxisome., Hydrogen peroxide can also spontaneously form |FRAME: CPD-12377|. Due to its extremely short life time the hydroxyl radical cannot be eliminated by an enzymatic reaction and reacts with many types of biomolecules (see for example pathway |FRAME: PWY-6502| which describes the repair of nucleotide damage caused by hydroxyl radicals). The radical can be neutralized by interaction with antioxidants such as |FRAME: ASCORBATE|.

Names: methylglyoxal degradation VIII // glyoxalase pathway // methylglyoxal catabolism
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|), and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, This pathway for methylglyoxal degradation has been characterized from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|. This pathway is based on a glyoxalase system in which |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| is first condensed with |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| to give |FRAME: S-LACTOYL-GLUTATHIONE| by the action of glyoxalase I (|FRAME: YML004C|) |CITS: [8824231]|, followed by hydrolysis of the glutathione thiolester to |FRAME: D-LACTATE| and |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| by glyoxalase II (|FRAME: YDR272W| and |FRAME: YOR040W|) |CITS: [9261170]|., The |FRAME: YDR272W| gene is expressed when the yeast cells are grown on either glucose or glycerol and the active Glo2p protein is localized in the cytoplasm. The |FRAME: YOR040W| gene is only active during growth on glycerol and the active Glo4p is localized in the mitochondrial matrix |CITS: [9261170]|. , Deletion of either |FRAME: YML004C| or |FRAME: YDR272W| and |FRAME: YOR040W| results in increased sensitivity to exogenous methylglyoxal |CITS: [8824231]||CITS: [9261170]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lignins "Lignin"| is the most abundant aromatic compound in nature, and its mineralization is an important step in the terrestrial carbon cycle. Lignin is composed of various intermolecular linkages between phenylpropanes,, including guaiacyl, syringyl, and p-hydroxyphenyl, and contains biphenyl nuclei |CITS: [10347082]|., Lignin degrading organisms brake down the complex polymer to various biaryl and monoaryl compounds such as |FRAME: BIPHENYL|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|., Complex lignin is resistant to bacterial enzymes. Its degradation is initiated by white rot fungi, which secrete extracellular degradation enzymes such as |FRAME: MONOMER-14338 "lignin peroxidase"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14335 "manganese peroxidase"|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14334 "laccase"| |CITS: [8246842]|. The resulting low-molecular-weight lignin can be further degraded and mineralized by bacteria |CITS: [1785937]|., |FRAME: TAX-502559| is a Gram-negative bacterium that was isolated from a kraft pulp effluent based on its ability to grow on the lignin-derived biphenyl compound |FRAME: CPD-11859| (DDVA). It can utilize many lignin degradation products possessing guaiacyl (4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl) and syringyl (4-hydroxy-3,5-dimethoxyphenyl) moieties, which it degrades to |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|, respectively. These compounds are then completely mineralized, as described in the |FRAME: PWY-6338| and |FRAME: PWY-6339| pathways., About This Pathway, Since lignin is so complex, the study of its degradation usually focuses on the degradation of lignin model compounds that represent the different types of bonds found within the lignin molecule. One of the most important of those is |FRAME: Guaiacylglycerol-guaiacyl-ether| (GGE), a molecule that contains a β-O-4 substructure, arylglycerol-β-, aryl ether, which is very abundant in lignin (approximately 50% of the mass)., Complicating the degradation of these compounds is the fact that arylglycerol-β-aryl ether structures in lignin often comprise two asymmetric carbons, and thus consist of two diastereomers, erythro and threo isomers, each of which is a combination of two enantiomers. For example, GGE consists of |FRAME: CPD-11867|, |FRAME: CPD-11868|, |FRAME: CPD-11869| and |FRAME: CPD-11870|., This pathway describes the degradation of the four GGE enantiomers by |FRAME: TAX-502559|. Prior to the cleavage of the ether bond the compounds have to be oxidized by dedicated alcohol dehydrogenases. The organism has multiple such enzymes (|FRAME: G-11562|, |FRAME: G-11564| and |FRAME: G-11563|) with differing enantioselectivity |CITS: [7764263][19542348]|., Following oxidation, the compounds are activated and cleaved by the enantioselective glutathione-S-transferase/β-etherase enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-11566| and |FRAME: G-11565| |CITS: [12618439]|, liberating |FRAME: CPD-400| and a steroisomer of α-glutathionyl-β-hydroxypropiovanillone., The glutathione moiety is cleaved by glutathione lyases such as the enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-11567|, generating |FRAME: CPD-11873|, a non-stereoactive molecule |CITS: [12618439]|., |FRAME: CPD-11873| is degraded into |FRAME: VANILLIN| or |FRAME: VANILLATE| in a process that hasn't been defined yet, and those are degraded to central metabolism intermediates as described in |FRAME: PWY-6338|., Several other organisms are known to catalyze the degradation of GGE, although the exact pathway is not known in such detail. They include the bacteria |FRAME: ORG-6112| |CITS: [3839140]| and |FRAME: ORG-6113| |CITS: [3841290]|, and the fungus |FRAME: TAX-2822231| |CITS: [16345527]|.

Summary: |FRAME: ANILINE "Aniline"| and its derivatives are important chemicals with major use in the production of antioxidants, dyes, rubbers, pharmaceuticals, and herbicides. These compounds are frequently found in industrial effluents and surface water due to their disposal, and cause a series of environmental problems |CITS: [ 4074935]|., They have been identified as potential carcinogens |CITS: [13536376]| and were found to possess the ability to prevent oxygen uptake in the blood and damage the spleen |CITS: [19931273]|., Aniline can be completely mineralized by certain bacteria |CITS: [6613168][2589921][16347847]|. The degradation pathway starts with conversion of aniline to |FRAME: CATECHOL|, which is then mineralized to TCA intermediates by standard pathways. , The genes encoding the proteins involved in the process have been characterized from several organisms, including |FRAME: ORG-6140| |CITS: [8990291]|, |FRAME: TAX-278934| |CITS: [9025282]|, |FRAME: TAX-70412| |CITS: [14646193]|, |FRAME: ORG-6141| |CITS: [15618615]|, |FRAME: ORG-6142| |CITS: [16207925]|, and |FRAME: TAX-173681| |CITS: [18763567]|. In all cases there appears to be a similar pattern: five genes are necessary for the conversion of |FRAME: ANILINE| to |FRAME: CATECHOL|. The genes encode a dioxygenase (a large and small subunits of an oxygenase component and a ferredoxin-reductase component) |CITS: [8990291]|, an enzyme similar to |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.2| (glutamine synthetase), and a gene resembling |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.2| |CITS: [8990291][14646193]|. , While the expression of all five genes from |FRAME: TAX-70412| in |FRAME:TAX-562| resulted in the conversion of anilin to catechol, expression of only the genes encoding the dioxygenase did not result in aniline transformation |CITS: [14646193]|. These results indicated that the substrate of the dioxygenase may not be aniline, but the pathway remained unknown at that time., A breakthrough was achieved by characterization of the |FRAME: G-12079| gene (encoding the enzyme similar to glutamine synthetase) from |FRAME: TAX-278934| |CITS: [23893114]|. This organism, which is capable of using aniline as the sole carbon and energy source, carries the five genes, along with other genes involved in aniline degradation, on the pYA1 plasmid |CITS: [9025282][Takeo98]|. The gene was cloned and the enzyme was purified and shown to catalyze the ATP-dependent ligation of |FRAME: GLT| to |FRAME: ANILINE| in a reaction similar to that catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.2| |CITS: [23893114]|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-15475|, can be either oxygenated by the |FRAME: CPLX-8085|, or could be hydrolyzed back to |FRAME: ANILINE| by the product of the glutaminase-like gene (|FRAME: G-12080|), possibly to ensure that its concentration does not rise to a toxic level. , The dioxygenase has been shown to accept only |FRAME: CPD-15475|, and not |FRAME: ANILINE|. However, since the enzyme has not been investigated thoroughly yet, the exact nature of its immediate product as well as the later steps in the pathway are not known. The pathway shown here is a hypothesis taken from |CITS: [23893114]|., An anaerobic aniline degradation pathway that proceeds by carboxylation of aniline in the para position has also been described |CITS: [2589921]|.

General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the, synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives., These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere, |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms,, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation, pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|., The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two, broad categories - oxidative and reductive., In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or, di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and, |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is, released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9132| (DNT) is the major contaminant resulting from the manufacture of, |FRAME: CPD-9138| (TNT), and is a common precursor for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9139|,, which is used in the production of polyurethane foam., |FRAME: CPD-9132| is highly toxic, and contamination occurs in both waterways and soils.,, DNT is listed as a priority pollutant by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Several 2,4-DNT-degrading strains have been isolated, and all of those apparently utilize the same, oxidative degradation pathway that yields nitrite, pyruvate, and propionyl-CoA |CITS: [12107140]|., The process is initiated by a dioxygenase attack that removes the first nitrite group, and produces, |FRAME: CPD-9134| (MNC). Subsequent oxidation of MNC by a monooxygenase results in the removal, of the second nitrite, and further enzymatic reactions lead to ring fission |CITS: [8449889]|., Genetic characterization of the 2,4-DNT degradation pathway has been carried out in the strains, |FRAME: ORG-5883| and |FRAME: TAX-233098|. , In these strains, the degradative genes are organized into an upper pathway and a lower pathway, and are located in plasmids pJS311 and pJS1, respectively |CITS: [10795678][8449889]|., The upper pathway includes the genes |FRAME: G-10145|, |FRAME: G-10146|, |FRAME: G-10147|,, |FRAME: G-10148| and |FRAME: G-10149|, encoding |FRAME: CPLX-7471| and, |FRAME: MONOMER-13337|, the enzymes responsible for hydroxylation of the aromatic ring and, elimination of nitro substituents., The resulting compound, |FRAME: CPD-9135|, is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9136|, by a non-specific reductase, for which no gene has been isolated so far |CITS: [12107140]|., The lower pathway operon, encoding a |FRAME: CPLX-7473|, a coenzyme A (CoA)-dependent, methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (dntE), and a bifunctional isomerase/hydrolase (dntG),, is responsible for extradiol fission of the aromatic ring, catalyzing the production of , |FRAME: CPD-9137| (DMOHA) and subsequent degradation of this, compound to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, |CITS: [9922262][10795678][12107140]|., Cloning of the |FRAME: TAX-233098| genes encoding the 2,4-dinitrotoluene degradation pathway enzymes, into |FRAME: TAX-294| ATCC 17400 resulted in the ability of this organism to utilize 2,4-DNT as the sole, source for carbon, nitrogen, and energy at levels equivalent to those of |FRAME: TAX-233098| |CITS: [16332883]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 Salicylate| is a key phenolic compound biosynthesized by many plants and some microorganisms. It is a member of an important anti-inflammatory drug class used widely in human medicine. In microorganisms |FRAME: CPD-110| is a biosynthetic precursor of secondary metabolites and siderophores, and a regulator of antibiotic efflux |CITS: [15837391]|. In plants |FRAME: CPD-110| may be converted by glucosylation, esterification, or methylation to physiologically active derivatives |CITS: [11607533]|. The source of the name |FRAME: CPD-110| (salicylic acid) comes from the name of the willow tree, |FRAME:TAX-40685|, from whose bark it can be obtained., For examples of salicylate biosynthetic pathways, see |FRAME: PWY-6408|, |FRAME: PWY-6407|, |FRAME: PWY-6406|, |FRAME: PWY-981|, |FRAME: PWY-6621|, |FRAME: PWY-6624| and |FRAME: PWY-4203| |CITS: [20020317]|., In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-110| can be degraded through several pathways including oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6183|), oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-633| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6224|), direct fission of |FRAME: CPD-110| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8159|), and degradation after CoA derivative formation. |FRAME: CPD-110| is also an intermediate in |FRAME: PWY-5427|., In yeast, earlier work on |FRAME: TAX-5554| showed |FRAME: CPD-110| oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [7364712] [6539772]|. In a more recent report using |FRAME: ORG-6162| a novel pathway of |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation via |FRAME: PHENOL| was elucidated (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6636|) |CITS: [20020317]|., About This Pathway, A novel pathway for |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation has been demonstrated in the yeast |FRAME: ORG-6162| in which |FRAME: CPD-110| is initially decarboxylated to |FRAME: PHENOL| and then oxidized to |FRAME: CATECHOL| as shown in the pathway link. |FRAME: CATECHOL Catechol| is further degraded via |FRAME: CIS-CIS-MUCONATE| as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5417|. |FRAME: PHENOL Phenol| is the key intermediate that distinguishes this pathway |CITS: [20020317]|. , This pathway was shown to be induced upon growth of the organism with |FRAME: CPD-110|. |FRAME: PHENOL| was detected as a metabolite in the culture broth. When metabolites of either |FRAME: CPD-110| or |FRAME: PHENOL| from resting cells or cell-free extracts were analyzed by TLC and/or HPLC this pathway was suggested. A more detailed characterization of the enzymes involved remains to be performed |CITS: [20020317]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Fenchol Fenchol| is a monoterpenoid and an isomer of |FRAME: Borneol|. It was originally isolated from fennel (German: Fenchel), hence its name |CITS: [35011331]|. Fenchol is produced by many other plant species including Aster |CITS: [Matasyoh06]| ginger |CITS: [33301679]|, the medicinal plants |FRAME: TAX-41650| |CITS: [33250655]|, |FRAME: TAX-2862117| |CITS: [32924270]|, and |FRAME: TAX-260142| |CITS: [32415726]|, the tree |FRAME: TAX-34316| |CITS: [30887609]|, and many others., Two diastereoisomers exist, endo-fenchol (also known as α-fenchol) and exo-fenchol (also known as β-fenchol), with each present in two configurations of the hydroxyl group |CITS: [30225485]|., Enzymes producing |FRAME: CPD-685| have been characterized from fennel and basil |CITS: [2919880][15516500]|., β-Fenchol has been reported from multiple species, including |FRAME: TAX-992795| |CITS: [9225614]|, |FRAME: TAX-205367| |CITS: [17612552]|, |FRAME: ORG-57129| |CITS: [21366065]|, |FRAME: TAX-39352| |CITS: [23553824]|, and |FRAME: TAX-34316| |CITS: [30887609]|. In most cases the authors did not specify whether it is the (-) or (+) enantiomer. The enzyme producing β-fenchol has not been described., Fenchol is used extensively in perfumery as a fragrance of soaps, shampoos, and other toiletries and detergents |CITS: [18640185]|., The naturally occurring enantiomer |FRAME: CPD-685| is one of the compounds that give basil its characteristic scent |CITS: [15516500]|. Several studies have established the mechanism by which the precursor |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| (GPP) is converted into |FRAME: CPD-685|. |FRAME: CPD-14089| is an intermediate in the reaction |CITS: [7436420][7436421][4055764][3170591][15516500]|.

|FRAME: CPD-18833 "Bisphenol A"| (BPA) is a widely used plasticizer (3.2 million metric tons were produced globally in 2003). It is used for the production of engineering plastics (e.g., polycarbonate/epoxy resins), food cans (i.e., lacquer coatings), and dental composites/sealants |CITS: [17114111]|. Releases of BPA to the environment exceed 1 million pounds per year |CITS: [EPA-BPA]|., BPA is an estrogen and androgen receptor agonist and has negative effects on aquatic life at concentrations measured in the environment |CITS: [11478243][16818258][22481365]|. Humans are exposed primarily through food packaging manufactured using BPA, although those products account for less than 5 percent of the total use of BPA |CITS: [EPA-BPA]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1301087|, which was isolated from activated sludge, is capable of degrading BPA down to to 5 ng/L |CITS: [23455956]|. The pathway involved in BPA degradation has not been studied much as of 2015. A study of the pathway in |FRAME: TAX-1301087| focused on the identification of pathway intermediates and proteins that are upregulated during growth on BPA |CITS: [26390302]|. The study has found only one intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-18836|, which is likely the product of the first step of the pathway, and 43 upregulated proteins., Among the upregulated proteins were those known to be involved in protocatechuatre degradation, indicating that protocatechuate is likely an intermediate in BPA degradation. The pathway shown here was proposed based on these findings. As of late 2015, a biochemical confirmation still awaits.

Fucose is a hexose deoxy sugar. It received its name from the brown algae genus |FRAME: TAX-3011|, from which it was first decribed. The alga was named because of its dark redish color, as one of the meanings of the Latin word fucus is "red paint"., Fucose is a common sugar, found in N-linked glycans on the mammalian, insect and plant cell surface, in many bacterial glycans, and in other biomolecules. Most of the fucose found in biology is in the |FRAME: L-fucoses "L conformation"|, and the use of |FRAME: D-Fucoses| is rather rare (for example in some |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolide glycosides"|)., |FRAME: L-fucoses| can be used by some organisms as a total source of carbon and energy. It has been shown to be metabolized via three separate pathways - |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-8444|, and |FRAME: PWY-8318|., An early step in this pathway is the isomerization of |FRAME: CPD-10329| to |FRAME: L-FUCULOSE|, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.25|. Since this enzyme is specific for the α anomer of fucopyranose, β anomers are converted to the α form by |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.29| (this maturotation process also occurs spontaneously, but the enzyme greatly accelerates the conversion)., A kinase phosphorylates |FRAME: L-FUCULOSE| to |FRAME: FUCULOSE-1P|, which is cleaved by a specific aldolase, into |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| (an intermediate of glycolysis, which thereby enters central, metabolism), and |FRAME: LACTALD|., The enzymes of this pathway can be used for degradation of |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE| to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|; see |FRAME: DARABCATK12-PWY|. |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, also a methylpentose, is metabolized by different enzymes, but in an analogous series of reactions (see |FRAME: RHAMCAT-PWY|). , Two pathways can be used for degradation of |FRAME: LACTALD|. Aerobically, it is converted via |FRAME: L-LACTATE| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, also an intermediate of glycolysis. Anaerobically, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.77| converts |FRAME: LACTALD| into |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL|., An overview of fucose and rhamnose degradation is shown in the |FRAME: FUC-RHAMCAT-PWY|.

Summary: De novo biosynthesis of purines starts with the synthesis of |FRAME: IMP|, which can be converted to all, other purines., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME:IMP| is synthesized from |FRAME: 5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-5-AMINOIMIDAZOLE| in 6 steps (see |FRAME: PWY-6123|). In eukaryotes the pathway consists of only 5 steps. The difference is in the first two steps, which are replaced in eukaryotes with a single reaction., The first 3 steps of this pathway are catalyzed in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| by individual enzymes, while the last two steps are catalyzed by a single multifunctional enzyme. |FRAME: TAX-4932| possesses two isozymes of the multifunctional enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: YLR028C| and |FRAME: YMR120C| genes. While these isozymes are indistinguishable with respect to activity, cellular location and subunit structure, they do differ in expression levels, and Ade17 is the major isozyme, accounting for approximately 90% activity|CITS: [10877846] [9143321]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:TAURINE Taurine| (2-aminoethanesulfonate), a natural occuring amino acid analogue of |FRAME:B-ALANINE|, plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many species., The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular |FRAME: CA+2| homeostasis. While plants or animals cannot degrade taurine, several species of bacteria and fungi are capable of doing that. For example, |FRAME: ORG-5927| can grow on taurine as the sole source of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and energy |CITS: [113035]|., Some anaerobic bacteria can use taurine for respiration as either an electron acceptor (eg. |FRAME: ORG-5878|) or an electron donor (eg. |FRAME: TAX-56119|, |FRAME: ORG-5923|, |FRAME: TAX-82367| NKNCYSA). Others can use it as a fermentative substrate (eg. |FRAME: ORG-5898|) |CITS: [12471498][9297467]|., The different species often utilize different pathways, resulting in conversion of taurine into different sulfur compounds. For example, |FRAME: ORG-5927| converts taurine to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| |CITS: [11082195]|, which is cleaved to |FRAME: SO3| |CITS: [11160104]|, and eventually converted to |FRAME:HS| by a sulfite reductase |CITS: [9143131]|., |FRAME: TAX-56119| |CITS: [9202468]|, |FRAME: ORG-5923| (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), and |FRAME: TAX-82367| NKNCYSA (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), all convert taurine to |FRAME: SULFATE| (additional products are ammonia and CO2), while |FRAME: ORG-5898| converts taurine to thiosulfate, ammonia and acetate |CITS: [9297467]|., Taurine degradation is known to be initiated by at least three different types of reactions: transamination, which appears to be the most widespread |CITS: [113035][5058441][5012173][629994]|, oxidation |CITS: [5551654]|, and oxygenation |CITS: [9287300]|. In the first two cases sulfoacetaldehyde is an intermediate, whereas in the third case taurine is converted to sulfite and aminoacetaldehyde |CITS: [9287300]|., About This Pathway, Two aminotransferases involved in taurine dissimilation have been described, |FRAME:MONOMER-3663| in |FRAME: ORG-5927| and |FRAME: ORG-5878| (this pathway) |CITS: [113035][11082195]| and |FRAME:MONOMER-2966| in |FRAME: ORG-5857| (see |FRAME:TAURINEDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [5058441][5012173][629994]|., Cook and Denger |CITS: [12471498]| speculated that the physiological role of |FRAME:MONOMER-2966| in |FRAME: ORG-5857| is the transamination of |FRAME:B-ALANINE| rather than taurine, since the enzyme is induced by former but not the later., |FRAME:MONOMER-3663| transfers the amino group from taurine to |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|. |FRAME:CPLX-7180| (EC 1.4.1.1) catalyzes the oxidative deamination of alanine to pyruvate, regenerating the amino-group acceptor pyruvate, and releasing ammonium (see |FRAME:PWY1-2|). |FRAME:CPLX-7180| from |FRAME: ORG-5878| has been purified and characterized |CITS: [11041346]|., It should be noted that the taurine:pyruvate aminotransferase has been found in both aerobic (|FRAME: ORG-5927|) and unaerobic (|FRAME: ORG-5878|) organisms.

Names: NADH to hydrogen peroxide electron transfer
Summary: This pathway depicts an anaerobic respiratory chain that couples NADH oxidation in the cytoplasm to the reduction of H2O2 in the periplasm., E. coli K-12 contains a periplasmic cytochrome c peroxidase (CCP) that enables it to respire using H2O2 as an anaerobic terminal electron acceptor and support growth in environments where H2O2 is produced and oxygen levels are diminished |CITS: [28696311]|. CCP derives electrons directly from the quinone pool - menaquinol is shown here as the electron donor; a mutant strain which is unable to synthesize menaquinone shows a significant reduction in H2O2 scavenging during anaerobic growth in LB medium, whilst a strain lacking both ubiquinone and menaquinone is essentially devoid of this activity |CITS: [28696311]|. The H+/e- ratio of CCP is not known., This pathway depicts oxidation of NADH by the proton translocating enzyme, NADH dehydrogenase I (NDH-I), which is used preferentially over NDH-II during anaerobic respiration with fumarate and DMSO (see |CITS: [9063459][9230919]|) however its participation in a pathway of anaerobic respiration with H2O2 has not been confirmed.

Names: Fe(II) oxidation IV (phototrophic, PioA/B system) // photoferrotrophy // phototrophic iron oxidation
Summary: Note: this pathway describes a process that involves both the cytoplasmic membrane and the outer membrane. Due to current limitations in the pathway layout algorithm, the pathway is displayed using only a single membrane. Read the following text to get more information about the localization of the different components., General Background, Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. In the environment, iron is mostly found in two different oxidation states: II and III. Fe(II) is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions, while Fe(III) is favored at high pH and oxic conditions. In oxic environments iron forms various oxide and hydroxide compounds; iron(II,III) oxides (such as magnetite, Fe3O4) and iron(III) oxides (such as hematite, Fe2O3) are most common. Under anoxic conditions the soluble |FRAME: FE+2| species is the most common. In certain environments Fe(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands., Oxidation of ferrous iron (Fe(II)) by microbes is an important component of the iron geochemical cycle. Bacterial iron oxidation is well documented under anaerobic conditions (see for example |FRAME: PWY-8554|), or under aerobic, acidic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6692|). Even though iron is oxidized spontaneously and rapidly in the presence of oxygen, many bacterial species have been found to oxidize Fe(II) at neutral pH |CITS: [20565252][32071158][33328652]|., About This Pathway, Members of the purple and green bacteria perform a process known as phototrophic Fe(II) oxidation or photoferrotrophy, in which electrons obtained from oxidation of extracellular iron are used in anoxygenic photosynthetic carbon fixation. , Purple phototrophic bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1076| perform anoxygenic photosynthesis where, following photon absorption by bacteriochlorophyll and carotenoid pigments in dedicated light harvesting (LH) complexes, excitation energy is passed to the special pair bacteriochlorophylls in the reaction center (RC). Subsequently, a cyclic electron flow between the RC, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c generates a transmembrane proton gradient that is used to power ATP synthesis. More specifically, electrons are transferred from NADH to the membrane quinone pool by complex 1. Cytochrome bc1 complex III) transfers the electrons from the membrane quinol pool to cytochrome c2, generating proton-motive force. Cytochrome c2 delivers the electrons to the RC, which cycles them back to the quinone pool at the expense of absorbed photons. The final output of the system is the generated proton motive force, which is used to generate ATP |CITS: [18197174]|. The purple bacteria use reverse electron flow to endergonically reduce NADP+ to NADPH by quinols., The |FRAME: G-124824| gene of the purple bacterium |FRAME: TAX-395960| encodes a decaheme c-type cytochrome that is homologous to the |FRAME: MONOMER-124821| of |FRAME: TAX-211586|. The gene is located in an operon together with the |FRAME: G-124838| gene, which encodes an outer membrane porin, homologous to |FRAME: G-124822| of |FRAME: TAX-211586|, and |FRAME: G-124837|, which encodes a high potential iron-sulfur protein (HiPIP). Deletion of the pio operon results in loss of Fe(II) oxidation activity |CITS: [17189359]|., The operon is transcribed and translated only during anaerobic growth under photoferrotrophic conditions |CITS: [21166894]|., PioA and PioB were shown to form a complex allowing extracellular electron uptake across the outer membrane from both soluble iron and poised electrodes. Unlike the |FRAME: TAX-22| iron reduction system, which includes the MtrC extracellular protein that reacts with the metal (see |FRAME: PWY-8553|), the PioAB outer-membrane porin—cytochrome complex does not include an extracellular component |CITS: [31690680]|. The complex transfers electrons from iron outside of the cell to the PioC HIPIP |CITS: [37375288]|. PioC has a midpoint potential of 450 mV, suggesting that it transfers electrons from iron to the photosystem reaction center and does not participate in cyclic electron flow (a role fulfilled cytochrome c2) |CITS: [ 24317397]|

Summary: The enzymatic detoxification of phytoalexins, small antimicrobial metabolites produced by plants in response to pathogenic attacks, is one strategy of pathogenic organisms to counteract the defense of plants which usually comes along with increased virulence of the attacking microorganism (see also |FRAME:PWY-7615|) |CITS:[20214490] [VanEtten95]|. |FRAME:CPLX-8970 Kievitone hydratase| was the first phytoalexin detoxifying enzyme purified and characterized from an pathogenic fungus |CITS:[Kuhn79] [Cleveland83]| and found to confer pathogenicity to wild-type isolates of Fusarium and its telemorphic form Nectria |CITS:[Smith82]|. Studies on variants of Fusarium solani f. sp. phaseoli, the causative agent of foot rot in Phaseolus vulgaris (French or garden bean) |CITS:[Clarkson78]|, clearly demonstrated a connection between kievitone hydratase activity and virulence. Moreover, this enzyme not only detoxified the plant isoflavone phytoalexin |FRAME:KIEVITONE-CPD| but also played a role in the establishment of the fungus in the host's infected tissues |CITS:[Smith84]|. , The |FRAME:CPLX-8970| of Fusarium solani f. sp. phaseoli had been characterized from elicited tissues of Phaseolus vulgaris, where it is secreted and catalyzes the hydration of |FRAME:KIEVITONE-CPD| to the less toxic |FRAME:CPD-34| |CITS:[Kuhn79] [Cleveland83]|. The activity of the |FRAME:CPLX-8970| can be boosted up to threefold by its substrate |FRAME:KIEVITONE-CPD| but the most effective inducer was |FRAME:BIOCHANIN-A| |CITS:[1366757]|. The activity of |FRAME:CPLX-8970| co-eluted with |FRAME:CPLX-8969| which hydrated the pterocarpane |FRAME:CPD-4885| (see |FRAME:PWY-7615|) but the activities could be separated on non-denaturating polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and shown to be different enzymes |CITS:[1521768]|. The gene (khs) was identified in Fusarium, heterologously expressed in two ascomycetous fungi Emericella nidulans and Neurospora crassa and shown to encode the |FRAME:CPLX-8970|. In addition, all highly pathogenic Fusarium lines to Phaseolus vulgaris possess the khs gene encoding for the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-8970| which confirms the connection between |FRAME:CPLX-8970| activity and virulence |CITS:[7655061]|.

General Background, Polyunsaturated long- and very-long-chain fatty acids (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear. While PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants and are not synthesized by animals, they are also produced by a narrow group of predominately marine γ-proteobacteria, which includes (among others) species of the |FRAME: TAX-22|, |FRAME: TAX-657|, |FRAME: TAX-58050|, |FRAME: TAX-28228| and |FRAME: TAX-662| genera |CITS: [4197274][Johns77][16347037][16535638][11777566][12594015]|. Since these organisms are associated with growth in low temperatures and often high pressure, it has been suggested that PUFA synthesis by these organisms is an important adaptation for countering the effects of elevated hydrostatic pressure and low temperature on membrane fluidity or phase. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that in strains that have been analysed, PUFA synthesis is temperature-dependent and, for deep-sea isolates, pressure-dependent |CITS: [10671446]|., |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID "Arachidonate"| (arachidonic acid) is a polyunsaturated ω-6 fatty acid with a 20-carbon chain and four cis-double bonds. It is produced de novo at high levels by mosses, by some lower eukaryotes (e.g. Euglena), and by some marine bacteria adapted to low temperatures and high pressures. The pathways used by moss and bacteria are completely different. In the aerobic pathway, used in mosses, saturated fatty acids synthesized by fatty acid synthase are desaturated and elongated to PUFAs in many enzymatic reactions, some of which oxygen-requiring. In the anaerobic pathway utilized by bacteria, PUFAs are anaerobically synthesized from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by PUFA synthases., About this Pathway, Even though the exact mechanism of the bacterial PUFA synthases has not been defined, it is well documented that these complexes are encoded by four or five genes |CITS: [9274025][11104010]|, which have been designated pfaEABCD |CITS: [12055309]|. The genetic structure of the PUFA biosynthetic genes consists of a four-gene operon that includes pfaABCD, while pfaE, which encodes the phosphopantetheinyl transferase required for catalytic activation of acyl carrier protein domains, may be found elsewhere in the genome |CITS: [21105981]|., PUFA synthases capable of synthesizing |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) were found in several marine bacteria including |FRAME: TAX-314092| |CITS: [11452122][8729138]| and |FRAME: TAX-298386| |CITS: [12055309]|. A synthase responsible for synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) was identified in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-90736| |CITS: [16988784]|, and a synthase capable of producing |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| was identified in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-365033| |CITS: [25263707]|., |FRAME: TAX-365033|, which was isolated from a marine sponge and algae collected from the southern coastline of Thailand, produces large amounts of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|, which consist of 30-40% of its total fatty acids. A gene cluster encoding a PUFA synthase responsible for |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| production was identified in the organism and its activity confirmed |CITS: [25263707]|.

|FRAME: FRUCTOSELYSINE| is formed by the non-enzymatic reaction of glucose with the ε-amine of lysine, followed by a spontaneous isomerization of the sugar, referred to as an Amadori rearrangement |CITS: [2675036]|. Similarly, |FRAME: CPD-21707| is formed by the non-enzymatic reaction of fructose with the ε-amine of lysine, followed by a spontaneous isomerization of the sugar, referred to as Heyns rearrangement |CITS: [2537288]|., The utilization of these compounds differs between |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-90371|. The former uses genes of the frl operon, phosphorylating fructoselysine with cytosolic |FRAME: G7726-MONOMER| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY0-521|). The latter uses genes of the gfrABCDEF operon, phosphorylating the compounds via a phosphotransferase system (PTS). Orthologs of gfrABCDEF have been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-1352| |CITS: [26100043][16153181]|. Expression of the Salmonella gfr operon is dependent on the alternative sigma factor RpoN as well as the RpoN-dependent transcriptional activator GfrR |CITS: [26100043]|. , Genes gfrABCD encode the mannose-type |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|-dependent sugar PTS components EIIA-D (see |FRAME: CPLX1QP9-157|). This system transports exogenous fructoselysine and glucoselysine, phosphorylating them at position C-6 during translocation across the cell membrane. Genes |FRAME: STM14_RS23785| and |FRAME: STM14_RS23790| encode deglycases that cleave these phosphorylated products |CITS: [16153181][26100043]|. GfrE cleaves |FRAME: CPD-21708| (glucoselysine 6-phosphate) to produce fructose-6-phosphate and L-lysine. GfrF cleaves |FRAME: FRUCTOSELYSINE-6-PHOSPHATE| (fructoselysine 6-phosphate) to produce glucose 6-phosphate and L-lysine. These genes allow Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium to utilize fructoselysine and glucoselysine as carbon and nitrogen sources. Although Salmonella can utilize endogenous L-lysine derived from fructoselysine or glucoselysine as a sole nitrogen source for growth, it cannot utilize exogenous L-lysine |CITS: [26100043]|., The substrate fructoselysine is a fructosamine found in plant matter. It is formed during the Maillard reaction, the initial steps of which involve spontaneous Schiff base formation between the ε-amino group of |FRAME: LYS| and the carbonyl group of the reducing sugar |FRAME: CPD-15374|, followed by an Amadori rearrangement which leads to a 1-amino-2-keto sugar derivative. Glucoselysine is similarly formed from reaction between the ε-amino group of L-lysine and fructose, with spontaneous isomerization of the sugar known as the Heyns rearrangement. Such spontaneous Amadori and Heyns rearrangement products may be encountered by enteric bacteria in the gut of the host (|CITS: [26100043][16153181]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21347729]|)., Genes gfrF and gfrE are required for growth with fructoselysine and glucoselysine, respectively. Using a coupled enzyme assay, purified recombinant |FRAME: STM14_RS23790-MONOMER "GfrF"| was shown to have fructoselysine 6-phosphate deglycase activity |CITS: [26100043]|., ΔgfrAB and ΔgfrR mutants lose the ability to grow in minimal medium with either fructoselysine or glucoselysine as the sole carbon or nitrogen source. A ΔgfrE mutant did not grow in minimal medium with glucoselysine as the sole carbon or nitrogen source, but grew normally in minimal medium with fructoselysine as the sole carbon and nitrogen source. A ΔgfrF mutant did not grow in minimal medium with fructoselysine as the sole carbon or nitrogen source, but grew normally in minimal medium with glucoselysine as the sole carbon and nitrogen source. These data suggest that GfrE is the deglycase for glucoselysine and GfrF is the deglycase for fructoselysine. Deletion mutants of rpoN and PTS system component ptsH did not grow in minimal medium with fructoselysine or glucoselysine as sole carbon source |CITS: [26100043]|.

Plaunotol is the bioactive compound responsible for the medicinal properties found in |FRAME: TAX-431156|, a Thai medicinal plant. |FRAME: CPD-11423| is an acyclic diterpene alcohol which is formed from four isoprenoid units. |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| molecules are condensed by the enzyme Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate synthase (GGPPS). This reaction results in the formation of the product geranylgeranyldiphosphate (GGPP) |CITS: [19782428]|. This is followed by a two step monodephosphorylation of GGPP to form geranylgeraniol |CITS: [16445953]|. The final step is catalyzed by GGOH 18-hydroxylase to form |FRAME: CPD-11423|., |FRAME: CPD-11423| shows broad spectrum inhibition of acute gastric and duodenal ulcers |CITS: [15855831]|. It also helps the healing of the chronic gastric ulcers by reducing the size of ulcers, reduced secretion of gastric juice, acid and pepsin, reviewed here |CITS: [18845620]|. It also significantly helps the regeneration of mucosa. Several papers report the positive effects of |FRAME: CPD-11423| on colon cancer |CITS: [15746576]|, |CITS: [17691055]|, |CITS: [18805546]|. , The purification of |FRAME: CPD-11423| is a patented procedure, the elucidation of the biosynthesis of this compound is underway and the above pathway shows the last few steps. A few of the enzymes in the precursor |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| has also been isolated, cloned and characterized |CITS: [18451506]|. Expression studies on these enzymes have shown their localization to be leaf and twig specific and absent in roots. Some of the enzyme sequences show the presence of chloroplast targeting sequences |CITS: [19782428]|.

Over 200 non-protein amino acids are present in plants. Many occur in free forms while some are detected in , peptide conjugates. Many have toxic properties. The role of non-protein amino acids in plants has been proposed to , include serving as defense compounds against predators, as storage forms of carbon and nitrogen, and as , detoxification products. Lathyrine is a non-protein amino acid. It occurs in various Lathyrus species. It may serve as , a nitrogen storage form. Lathyrine constitutes more than 2% of the dry weight of Lathyrus tingitanus seeds. It may , also serve as a plant uracil detoxification mechanism.|CITS: [wallsgrove95]| , The pyrimidine ring of lathyrine is originated from uracil. Unlike other N-heterocyclic β-substituted alanines, such , as pyrazol-1-ylalanine, mimosine, willardiine and isowillardiine, the alanyl moiety of lathyrine is derived from serine, , not acetyl-serine.  Lathyrine synthase is a novel enzyme which catalyzes the last step of lathyrine biosynthesis, a , decarboxylation reaction occurring simultaneously with the introduction of the alanine side chain to the pyrimidine ring. , The enzyme is biotin-dependent which is unusual for a decarboxylation enzyme, as biotin is usually involved in , carboxylation. Like other N-heterocyclic β-substituted alanines, lathyrine can be synthesized in a non-enzymic , pyridoxal-metal ion system. Either Al3+ or Ga3+ can be effective ions.|CITS: [brown94]|

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Peptidoglycans Peptidoglycan|, the bacterial bag-shaped envelope, is best described as a fisherman net. The net is made of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads consisting of alternating |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) and |FRAME: CPD-19950| (MurNAc) sugars, which are held together by small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., Gram-negative bacteria recycle a very large proportion of the peptidoglycan polymer during normal growth in a process termed cell wall recycling. For example, the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| recycles about half of its cell wall within one generation |CITS: [18535144][23163477]|., During this process anhydromuropeptides (mainly |FRAME: CPD0-1080|), which are steadily released during growth by lytic transglycosylases and endopeptidases, are imported back into the cytoplasm by the |FRAME: EG12183|-encoded |FRAME: AMPG-MONOMER|., Once inside the cytoplasm, the anhydromuropeptides are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.28| (|FRAME: EG10041|), |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.52| (|FRAME: G6567|) and |FRAME: EC-3.4.17.13| (|FRAME: G6621|), yielding |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: CPD0-882|, |FRAME: L-ALA-GAMMA-D-GLU-DAP| and |FRAME: D-ALANINE| |CITS: [ 3891732]|., |FRAME: CPD0-882| is phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.170| (|FRAME: G6880|). In many organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: CPD0-881| is then converted into |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.126| (|FRAME: G7263|) (see |FRAME: PWY0-1261|). However, many Gram-negative bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-286| species, lack a MurQ ortholog. These organisms utilize an alternative recycling pathway, which is described here., About This Pathway, The pathway in these organisms continues by the action of a phosphatase, encoded by the |FRAME: G1G01-1865| gene, which produces |FRAME: NACMUR| |CITS: [28351914]|. |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.221|, encoded by the |FRAME: G1G01-442| gene, phosphorylates the compound at position 1, generating |FRAME: CPD0-1643|. The last enzyme that is unique to this pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.99| (|FRAME: G1G01-443|), replaces the phosphate with a UDP moiety, generating |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYLMURAMATE|, which is fed back into murein biosynthesis |CITS: [23831760]|., Since this pathway bypasses the requirement to produce |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYLMURAMATE| by the action of MurA/MuB, its presence confers resistance to the antibiotic |FRAME: CPD0-1113|, which blocks MurA (|FRAME: EC-2.5.1.7|) |CITS: [24819062]|., The tripeptide |FRAME: L-ALA-GAMMA-D-GLU-DAP|, which is generated by |FRAME: EC-3.4.17.13|, can be degraded further, as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1546|. However, the vast majority of these peptides are recycled by muropeptide ligase (|FRAME: EG12440|). This enzyme is a dedicated recycling enzyme that attaches the recovered Ala-Glu-DAP tripeptide to |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYLMURAMATE|, thereby substituting three amino acid ligases of the peptidoglycan de novo biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [8808921]|.

Summary: The two enantiomers of |FRAME: Limonenes "limonene"| are the most-abundant monocyclic monoterpenes in nature., |FRAME: CPD-4886| (L-limonene) is found in a variety of trees and herbs such as Mentha spp., while |FRAME: CPD-8785| (D-limonene) is the major component of peel oil from oranges and lemons, and the essential oil of caraway., The natural functions of limonene are thought to include prevention of dehydration and inhibition of microbial (especially fungal) growth |CITS: [12743755]|. , The first biodegradation study of |FRAME: CPD-8785| was conducted at the Indian National Chemical Laboratory in Poona in the 1960s. The researchers isolated |FRAME: TAX-432615|, a strain able to grow with D-limonene as the sole carbon and energy source. Characterizartion of compounds isolated from the induced strain lead to the suggestion that limonene is attacked at several positions, and that a major pathway in this strain probably starts with hydroxylation at the 7-position yielding |FRAME: Perillyl-Alcohols| |CITS: [4227571]|. The authors suggested that subsequent oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-12443|, hydration of the 6-10 double bond to form |FRAME: CPD-12444|, and eventual degradation via a pathway analogous to regular beta-oxidation, results in complete degradation., They have also characterized unpurified forms of |FRAME: MONOMER-15685| |CITS:[4289759][4234666]| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15686| |CITS:[6076233]| from this organism., More recently, a number of similar Pseudomonas strains have been reported. A "Pseudomonas incognita" strain was shown to convert D-limonene to perillate |CITS: [612543]| and a strain of |FRAME: TAX-28095| was shown to accumulate |FRAME: CPD-12443| when grown on D-limonene |CITS: [Cadwallader89]|. , The |FRAME: CPD-1001|-degrading strain |FRAME: TAX-644631| was also reported to degrade D-limonene to perillate |CITS: [Speelmans98]|, and it was later suggested that the responsible enzymes are those that convert |FRAME: CPD-1001| to |FRAME: CPD-1004| (see |FRAME: PWY-741|) |CITS: [11499915]|. A recombinant |FRAME:TAX-562| strain that carried the genes of the cym pathway of |FRAME: TAX-351746| indeed converted limonene to perillate |FRAME: TAX-644631|., The pathway is not limited to Pseudomonads. Several studies has documented to conversion of D-limonene to |FRAME: Perillyl-Alcohols| and |FRAME: CPD-1084| by Bacillus strains |CITS: [Chang94][Chang95][10849845]|.

Summary: Fatty acid biosynthesis in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-208964| is initiated by the β-ketoacyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] synthase |FRAME: G-15300 FabY| that catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"|, producing |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs "acetoacetyl-[acp]"|, which can be elongated into longer fatty acids via the |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY "fatty acid elongation cycle"| |CITS: [22753059]|., |FRAME: G-15300|-mutants are defficient in fatty acid biosynthesis. However, this phenotype can be suppressed by supplementation of the growth media with exogenous fatty acids with chain lengths of eight or more carbons |CITS: [22753057]|. Upon transport into the cell the fatty acids form acyl-CoA thioesters, which are catabolized by the β-oxidation cycle., Studies showed that when |FRAME: CPD-196| is formed, it can be shunted into the fatty acid elongation cycle by a dedicated enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15305| gene |CITS: [22753057]|. This enzyme, which has a storng preference for |FRAME: CPD-196| (although |FRAME: CPD-10267| is also used at a lower rate), condenses the acyl-CoA thioester with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP malonyl-[acp]|, forming |FRAME: 3-oxo-decanoyl-ACPs "3-oxo-decanoyl-[acp]"|, an intermediate of the fatty acid elongation cycle, thus by-passing the limitation imposed by lack of initiation, and enabling fatty acid biosynthesis., The presence of this shunt may curtail the efficacy of inhibitors targeting the |FRAME: G-15300 FabY| initiator.

Summary: |FRAME: 1R2S-EPHEDRINE "Ephedrine"| and |FRAME: CPD-9954 pseudoephedrine| are plant-specific aromatic amines synthesized by some members of the |FRAME: TAX-3387| genus (known as "Ma Huang" in Chinese medicine). |FRAME: 1R2S-EPHEDRINE "Ephedrine"| was first isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3389| in 1885 by Nagayoshi Nagai., The compounds are sympathomimetic in humans - they interact with the adrenergic receptor system, part of the sympathetic nervous system, resulting in an increase in the release of the neurotransmitters |FRAME: DOPAMINE| and |FRAME: SEROTONIN|. Ephedrine alkaloids are used in traditional Chinese medicine for the treatment of asthma, and are commonly used as stimulants, appetite suppressants, and decongestants. Ephedrine is listed as an essential medicine by the World Health Organization for the prevention of low blood pressure induced by spinal anesthesia., Early work on the ephedrine biosynthesis pathway, using radio tracer experiments, showed efficient incorporations of |FRAME: BENZOATE|, |FRAME: BENZALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: CPD-674| into the α-carbon atom of the side chain, and concluded that a C6-C1 unit related to |FRAME: BENZALDEHYDE| or |FRAME: BENZOATE| generates the benzylic fragment of the carbon skeleton of the Ephedra alkaloids, ruling out the hypothesis that a C6-C2 unit is derived directly from the aminophenylpropanoid system of phenylalanine |CITS: [Yamasaki73]|. A later radio tracer study has concluded that |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is the precursor of the aliphatic C2 carbon of the side chain |CITS: [Grue-sorensen88][Grue-sorensen89]|. Additional work by the authors showed that it is |FRAME: BENZOATE| rather than |FRAME: BENZALDEHYDE| that contributes the C6-C1 unit |CITS: [Grue-sorensen94]|. These studies also identified |FRAME: CPD-9949| and |FRAME: CPD-9950| as intermediates, even though these compounds have not been previously detected in or isolated from any Ephedra species |CITS: [Grue-sorensen94]|. The existence of both compounds was confirmed later in |FRAME: TAX-33152| using GC-MS analysis |CITS: [20417943]|., Based on the proposed pathway, the first step in the ephedrine alkaloid biosynthesis is the deamination of |FRAME: PHE| by |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.24|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-674|, is converted into |FRAME: BENZOATE| or |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| by β-oxidation, a process that results in branching off from the common phenylpropanoid pathway. These C6-C1 units react with |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, the donor of the C2 unit, forming |FRAME: CPD-9949|, which is the first intermediate with the basic C6-C3 skeleton of ephedrine alkaloids., In the latter part of the pathway |FRAME: CPD-9949| is transaminated to |FRAME: CPD-9950|, which is reduced in a stereoselective manner to either (1S,2S)- or (1R,2S)-form isomers. N-methylation forms |FRAME: 1R2S-EPHEDRINE "ephedrine"| and |FRAME: CPD-9954 pseudoephedrine|, respectively |CITS: [Grue-sorensen94]|., At the time the pathway was proposed none of the pathway's enzymes were characterized, and by 2020 only two of them have been isolated. The first enzyme is |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.24| |CITS: [19043198]|, and the second is |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.M76| |CITS: [29929980]|, both studied from |FRAME: TAX-33152|. In addition, the activities of two stereo-specific (S)-cathinone reductases were demonstrated in cell extracts |CITS: [20417943]|., It should be noted that the N-methyltransferase demonstrated the highest activity with |FRAME: CPD-9950|, raising the possibility that N-methylation may occur earlier in the pathway than previously proposed |CITS: [29929980]|.

Summary: Biologically, |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (commonly known as ethylene) is a plant hormone that plays a role in fruit ripening and senescence, see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|. While all plants produce ethylene as described in |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|, two biosynthetic pathways for ethene production have been reported from microorganisms, see |FRAME: PWY-6853| and |FRAME: PWY-6854|. The plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-319| utilizes |FRAME: PWY-6853| to synthesize ethene as a defence mechanism during host infection., The |FRAME: TAX-319| efe gene product |FRAME: MONOMER-16773| mediates the synthesis of ethene from the TCA cycle intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS: [1770346]|. The enzyme catalyzes two simultaneous reactions. In one reaction 2-oxoglutarate is dioxygenated to form one molecule of ethene and three molecules of carbon dioxide. In the other reaction both 2-oxoglutarate and |FRAME: ARG| are mono-oxygenated to yield |FRAME: SUC| plus |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: CPD-26627|, respectively. The latter is further transformed to |FRAME: CPD0-1470| and |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE|, some of which cyclizes spontaneously to form |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| |CITS: [1445291]|., |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| can be converted to |FRAME:GLT| by |FRAME:CPLX-6746|., The glutamate that is formed can be recycled back to L-arginine via the |FRAME: ARGSYNBSUB-PWY "acetyl cycle"|., |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD "Ethene"| has a diverse array of uses commercially. It is an intermediate in the production of fuel as it can be hydrated to ethanol or polymerized to gasoline. It can also be used to synthesize a variety of plastics such as polystyrene and PVC, or fabrics such as polyester. It is currently obtained from fossil fuels at an ecological cost as its production results in the emission of huge amounts of carbon dioxide |CITS: [Ungerer]|. , About this Pathway, The |FRAME: TAX-319| efe gene was introduced into the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|. |FRAME: TAX-4932|, which is not a natural ethene producing organism, was able to synthesize ethene from 2-oxoglutarate with the inserted efe gene, using glucose as the carbon source. , The substitution of L-glutamate as a nitrogen source enhanced the synthesis of ethene, as L-glutamate can be converted to the precursor 2-oxoglutarate in a single reaction catalyzed by glutamate dehydrogenase. 2-Oxoglutarate is otherwise supplied to the pathway by the workings of the |FRAME: PWY-5690|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SO3 Sulfite| plays a key role in oxidative sulfur metabolism. It is derived from multiple sources: First, sulfite is the main intermediate in the oxidation of sulfur compounds to |FRAME: SULFATE| |CITS: [11557133]|., In purple sulfur bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1049|, the oxidation of |FRAME: HS| and |FRAME:S2O3| results in formation of intracellular sulfur globules, which are oxidized to sulfite by the Dsr system (see |FRAME: PWY-6676|)., A second source for sulfite is the desulfonation of organic compounds by enzymes like |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15| (Xsc) (see |FRAME: PWY-1281|)., A third source of sulfite is extracellular sulfite retrieved from the environment. Free sulfite in the periplasm (which most likely exists as bisulfite) is bound to the |FRAME: SoxY-Protein "SoxYZ"| protein complex in the form of |FRAME: SoxY-Systeine-Sulfinate|. The binding acts to shield components of the periplasm from chemical reactions with sulfite, and may also be required for delivering the sulfite to a transporter that exports it into the cytoplasm for oxidation |CITS: [24030319]|., , Some microorganisms (such as |FRAME: TAX-60136| species) can use sulfite as their sole electron source |CITS: [Sorokin95][10319472 ]|. , Enzymes that catalyze the direct oxidation of sulfite to sulfate are molybdenum hydroxylases, and belong to the sulfite oxidase family, which includes both sulfite-oxidizing enzymes and plant assimilatory nitrate reductases (such as the |FRAME: CPLX-7196| of |FRAME: ORG-5993|). The best characterized members of this family are sulfite oxidases, from avian and mammalian sources. However, these enzymes differ from the bacterial enzymes in that they can use oxygen as an electron acceptor (see |FRAME: EC-1.8.3.1|)., Some sulfite oxidizing enzymes are located in the periplasm. The best characterized enzyme from this group is |FRAME: EC-1.8.2.1| (SOR) from |FRAME: TAX-921|, which contains a molybdopyranopterin cofactor (this pathway). Another well-characterized periplasmic enzyme is the |FRAME:CPLX-882| (such as that from |FRAME: TAX-82367|). It has been shown that this system can oxidize sulfite independently from the presence of the |FRAME:CPLX-7150| component (a molybdohemoprotein), but it is not clear whether the Sox system functions in vivo as a sulfite-oxidizing enzyme |CITS:[10940005][Lu84][11425697]|)., Other enzyme systems that oxidize sulfite are located in the cytoplasm. Two general mechanisms for sulfite oxidation in the cytoplasm have been described: a direct oxidation by a membrane-bound iron-sulfur molybdoprotein (|FRAME: EC-1.8.5.6|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7457|), and an indirect, AMP-dependent oxidation via the intermediate |FRAME:APS| (APS) (see |FRAME:PWY-5279| and |FRAME:PWY-5278|) |CITS: [11557133]|. The direct oxidation route is much more prevalent, but the two mechanisms are present simultaneously in many organisms, including β and γ proteobacteria (|FRAME: TAX-931|, |FRAME: TAX-1049|, |FRAME: TAX-36861|, |FRAME: TAX-1021|), green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1091|), Gram-positive bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-28034|) and even archaea (|FRAME: TAX-2283|) |CITS: [11557133]|., While many organisms possess only the direct mechanism, the only examples for organisms that possess only the non-direct mechanism are found in the bacterial endosymbionts of invertebrates |CITS: [Nelson95]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CPLX-7139 "SorAB protein"| from the α-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-921| is the best characterized periplasmic sulfite:acceptor oxidoreductase. It is a heterodimer, with a large subunit that binds a molybdopyranopterin cofactor and a smaller monoheme cytochrome c subunit |CITS: [10788424]|., During catalysis electrons are transferred to the single heme c552 located on the smaller subunit, and passed to a cytochrome c550 which is believed to be the enzyme's natural electron acceptor |CITS: [Yamanaka81]|. The enzyme exhibits a Ping Pong mechanism (similarly to eukaryotic SORs), and is non-competitively inhibited by sulfate. A structure revealed that the short distance between the two redox centers in the protein complex allows for rapid electron transfer via tunnelling. A potential site of electron transfer to an external acceptor cytochrome c was identified on the SorB subunit |CITS: [15863498]|.

Summary: General Background, Arginine biosynthesis is notable for its complexity and variability at the genetic level, and by its connection with several other pathways, such as pyrimidine and polyamine biosynthesis, and certain degradative pathways. The initial steps of the arginine biosynthetic pathways proceed via N-acetylated intermediates. The presumed reason for this is that the acetylation prevents the spontaneous cyclization of glutamate derivatives, which leads to proline biosynthesis, thus keeping the two pathways separate |CITS: [12633501]|. A variation of the pathway found in some archaebacteria and hyperthermophilic bacteria utilizes a dedicated carrier protein to protect the intermediates instead of acetylation., Several alternative arginine biosynthetic pathways have evolved in bacteria:, In |FRAME:ARGSYN-PWY|, which is not very common, the key intermediate |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG) is formed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1|. A second key intermediate downstream, |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE|, is hydrolyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.16|, releasing acetate, and forming the arginine precursor |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|., In |FRAME:ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|), which is found in most of the prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbes investigated up to now, the two reactions mentioned above are linked: the acetyl group which is removed from |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is recycled onto glutamate, regenerating |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG)., This recycling is performed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35|. This pathway is considered more evolved, since the overall reaction is energetically more favorable |CITS: [3534538]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-5154| is found in several eubacteria. While in the two pathways mentioned above |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is deacetylate to |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, which is subsequntly transcarbamoylated to form |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|, in this variant |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is not deacetylated. Instead, it is, transcarbamoylated directly by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.9|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-7224|. The enzyme |FRAME:ACETYLORNDEACET-CPLX| can accept |FRAME: CPD-7224| as a substrate, and deacetylates it into |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| |CITS: [16585758]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-7400|, which has been described in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2285|, involves early intermediates that are protected not by acetylation but by a carrier protein (the LysW |FRAME: LysW|), which participates in the biosynthesis of both |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: LEU| in these organsims |CITS: [23434852]|., About This Pathway, The linear pathway of arginine biosynthesis has been described in several organisms including the Enterobacteriaceae |CITS: [3534538]|, the |FRAME:TAX-641| |CITS: [10692366]|, and the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME:TAX-34| |CITS: [ 9829957]|. The pathway in these organisms starts with the acetylation of the amino moiety of |FRAME: GLT| catalyzed by ArgA, ArgJ or both, yielding |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG)., Some archaeal species, such as |FRAME: TAX-2284|, which are known to produce |FRAME: ARG|, do not have either ArgA and ArgJ orthologs. Instead, these organisms use the |FRAME: G-17812|-encoded ligase to bind |FRAME: GLT| to a dedicated |FRAME: LysW "carrier protein"| encoded by the lysW gene. The carrier protein, as well as the next 4 enzymes in the pathway, are bifunctional and participate in both |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: LEU| biosynthesis in these organisms (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., The C-terminal part of the carrier protein is acidic and is easily recognized by the subsequent enzymes, all of which have a basic environment around their active sites. In this way the subsequent transformations leading to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| occur while the amino acid is attached to LysW |CITS: [19620981]|. Once formed, the ornithine is removed from the carrier protein by a dedicated enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-17816| gene |CITS: [23434852]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-1590| is a lactic acid bacterium that produces |FRAME: D-LACTATE| and |FRAME: L-LACTATE| using stereospecific NAD-dependent lactate dehydrogenases - |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.28| (|FRAME: G-6662|) and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.27| (ldhL), respectively. This organism incorporates |FRAME: D-LACTATE| as the last residue of the muramoyl-pentadepsipeptide peptidoglycan precursor, leading to resistance to high concentrations of |FRAME: CPD-12245| (see |FRAME: PWY-6454|)., A |FRAME: TAX-1590| mutant defective in |FRAME: G-6662| still produces both lactate isomers, indicating the existence of a different route for production of |FRAME: D-LACTATE| |CITS: [8808932]|. The second route was found to be the enzyme |FRAME: EC-5.1.2.1|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-44202| gene |CITS: [16166538]|., The enzyme contains a unique nickel-containing cofactor - |FRAME: CPD-18436|, which is tethered to a lysine residue and forms a tridentate pincer complex that coordinates nickel through one metal-carbon and two metal-sulfur bonds, with His200 as another ligand |CITS: [26138974]|., The biosynthesis of this cofactor requires three proteins: LarB, LarC, and LarE. LarB carboxylates and hydrolyzes the NAD precursor |FRAME: DEAMIDO-NAD|, producing |FRAME: CPD-20508|. LarE inserts two sulfur atoms into this compound, forming |FRAME: CPD-20518|. The source of the sulfur atoms is an L-cysteine residue within LarE. The transfer of the sulfur to the substrate converts the cysteine residue to hydroalanine, effectively inactivating the enzyme. Since two sulfur-insertion cycles are required, with each cycle inactivating the enzyme, two different LarE molecules participate and are inactivated for each cofactor molecule produced. Finally, LarC inserts the nickel ion to form the mature cofactor |CITS: [27114550]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, Strains of |FRAME: TAX-562| possessing the O:117 antigen produces the Shiga toxin Stx1 and have been implicated in diarrhea, septicemia, neuroinvasiveness and hemolyticuremic syndrome |CITS: [2513199][2004811][8460339][15804665][25375900][29318066][ 29781799]|., The structure of the repeat unit of O antigens isolated from |FRAME: TAX-2067430| was reported in 2000 |CITS: [10782292]|. It is very similar to the |FRAME: CPD-24102|, differing only in the substitution of D-glucose for N-acetyl-D-glucosamine |CITS: [19040662]|., The O antigen gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2067430| was cloned and sequenced in 2007. The cluster contains 12 genes, encoding enzymes necessary for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|, four glycosyltransferases, an O antigen repeat unit flippase and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [17452091]|. That study, which named the glycosyltransferase genes wbeA through wbeD, did not propose a specific function for each glycosyl transferase gene., In 2009 the gene cluster was sequenced again, along with the cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2162915|. The two clusters were found to be very similar, sharing 98.6% overall DNA identity. In this study the authors renamed the glycosyltransferase genes wclW through wclZ |CITS: [19040662]|. , The product of the |FRAME: G-81051| gene shares 31-35% identities to many rhamnosyltransferases and was proposed to encode the glycosyltransferase that forms the α-L-Rha-(1→4)-α-D-Glc linkage |CITS: [19040662]|. The product of the |FRAME: G-81050| gene shares 45% identity to |FRAME: G-27214 WbwC| of |FRAME: TAX-2072453|, which is a galactosyltransferase responsible for the β-D-Gal-(1→3)-β-D-GalNAc linkage in its O antigen. As the same linkage is present in the antigens of O107 and O117 strains, the same function was assigned to |FRAME: G-81050| |CITS: [19040662]|., The function of the other two glycosyltransferases remained unknown until 2012, when it was shown that the genes named wclY encode a GlcNAc-transferase and a glucosyltransferase in |FRAME: TAX-2162915| and |FRAME: TAX-2067430|, respectively, even though they differ by only three residues |CITS: [Wang12]|. That left the last gene, |FRAME: G-81052|, as the only candidate for encoding the β-(1,3)-GalNAc-transferase., As in all other Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways, the Wzx flippase flips the completed O-unit across the inner membrane from the cytoplasm to the periplasm, where the O-units are linked together by the Wzy polymerase. In the case of the |FRAME: CPD-24108|, the repeat units are linked in an α(1,4) linkage.

C50 carotenoids are only produced by several restricted groups of actinobacteria (including species belonging to the bacterial genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-37914|, and |FRAME: TAX-1269|) and extremely halophilic archaea. The C50 β-cyclic carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-20665| and its glucoside |FRAME: CPD-20664| have been documented in several species of actinobacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-2035| and |FRAME: TAX-370437| |CITS: [5485033][17008032]|., Analysis of the carotenoids produced by |FRAME: TAX-2035| identified four pathway intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-18006| (described in that paper as C.p.482), |FRAME: CPD-18008| (C.p.496), |FRAME: CPD-20666|, and |FRAME: CPD-20665| (C.p.450), although no pathway was proposed at the time |CITS: [5485033]|., The genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-20664| production were identified 37 years later in |FRAME: TAX-370437| by complementation of an |FRAME: TAX-562| strain producing |FRAME: CPD1F-114| with a Dietzia genomic DNA library and searching for colonies with altered color |CITS: [17008032]|., Only two genes were found to be responsible for the conversion of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to |FRAME: CPD-20665| - |FRAME: G-58156| and |FRAME: G-58157|. The former is similar to the |FRAME: G18NG-10184| gene of |FRAME: TAX-196627|, which encodes one of the subunits of the heterodomeric |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.M9|. The latter contains two domains - one is similar to the |FRAME: G18NG-10183| gene, which encodes the second subunit of |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.M9|, while the other appears to be an ortholog of the |FRAME: G-58155| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.149|. Thus the |FRAME: G-58157| gene is a fusion of two genes, and encodes a bifunctional protein with a C50 carotenoid β-cyclase domain and a lycopene elongase domain. When the two genes were expressed in the lycopene-producing |FRAME: TAX-562| strain, the cells produced |FRAME: CPD-20665| almost exclusively |CITS: [17008032]|., A gene downstream of the carotenoid biosynthetic gene cluster is highly similar (40% amino acid identity, 60% amino acid similarity) to the |FRAME: G18NG-10193| gene of |FRAME: TAX-196627|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.M35| |CITS: [17008032]|.

Alanine is an essential component of protein (as |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|) and peptidoglycan (as a roughly 3:1 mix of |FRAME: D-ALANINE| and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|). Only about a tenth of total alanine synthesized is incorporated into peptidoglycan., At least three pathways (|FRAME: ALANINE-VALINESYN-PWY|, |FRAME: ALANINE-SYN2-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY0-1021|) are known for production of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|. This pathway is carried out in a single step by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.7|, in a reaction that is critical for generation of iron-sulfur clusters, thiouridine groups in tRNAs, and a number of other sulfur-and selenium-containing proteins. Although this pathway does generate alanine, a major role in generating the cellular supply of alanine has not been demonstrated.

Glycolipids based on the disaccharide |FRAME: TREHALOSE| have been identified in members of the |FRAME: TAX-85007|, including the |FRAME: TAX-1762| and the |FRAME: TAX-85025|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
