At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, In several strains, including the respiratory pathogens |FRAME: ORG-6217| |CITS: [19282284]| and |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [11526328]|, and the periodontal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-837| |CITS: [24852504]|, the O antigen contains the modified sugar |FRAME: CPD-14608| [UDP-ManNAc(3NAc)A ]., In the case of |FRAME: TAX-208964| (and other serotype O5 strains of |FRAME:ORG-5927|), the organism possesses two types of O-antigens, which were named the A-band and the B-band. Summary: General Background, The common |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| pathway, used by most organisms for the catabolism of glucose and related sugars, can be regarded as both an energy-producing catabolic pathway and an anabolic pathway, producing |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which can be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|. While |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| can be fed to the TCA cycle for further energy production, it is also used as a biosynthestic precursor for many types of biomolecules (e.g. fatty acids). However, glycolysis is unable to produce 5-carbon sugars such as |FRAME: D-Ribose|, which are essential for the biosynthesis of DNA and RNA, neither can it form the 4-carbon sugar |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, a precursor of aromatic amino acids and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, or the 7-carbon sugar |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, a precursor for |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|., The |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| is an alternative way of oxidizing glucose that is targeted at anabolic reactions. The pathway fulfills two anabolic roles: it produces NADPH, making it a major source of reducing equivalents for biosynthetic reactions, and it produces C4, C5, and C7 sugars |CITS: [13129245][13174590][14790817][14285485]|., About This Pathway, The pentose phosphate pathway is an important member of central metabolism, as it supplies three of the 13 precursor metabolites (compounds needed for the biosyntheses): |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|, |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|. For convenience, the pentose phosphate pathway is commonly divided into its preliminary |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative portion"| and the subsequent |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative portion"|., The unidirectional oxidative branch fulfills two roles of the pathway - it produces a pentose sugar (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|) from the hexose |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, and it produces two equivalents of NADPH in the process., The non-oxidative branch of composed of a series of rearrangements catalyzed by an isomerase, an epimerase, a transketolase, and a transaldolase, involving a C3 compound (|FRAME: GAP|), a C4 compound (|FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|), C5 compounds (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|), a C6 compound (|FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|), and a C7 compound (|FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|). Unlike the oxidative branch, the non-oxidative branch is fully reversible, allowing for different molecules to enter the pathway at different stages and be transformed to any other intermediate in this branch. No energy or reducing power is produced by the non-oxidative branch - it's sole purpose is carbon rearrangements. It should be noted that due to its reversibility, the non-oxidative branch also participates in the catabolism of pentoses (see |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|)., In prokaryotes and animals the pentose phosphate pathway takes place in the cytosol, the same location as glycolysis. In plants, the oxidative part of the pathway also takes place in plastids |CITS: [Foster93]|.

The different sub-classes of ansamycins differ mainly in their aromatic moiety, which can include a naphthalene ring, a naphthoquinone ring, a benzene ring or or a benzoquinone ring |CITS: [4148590]|., The naphthalenic ansamycin |FRAME: Streptovaricins streptovaricins|, chemically related to the |FRAME: Rifamycins rifamycins|, are highly effective antibacterial agents with a broad antibacterial spectrum against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, particularly against mycobacteria including |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [13441565][237470]|. In addition, many of the compounds are efficient antivirals, inhibiting RNA-dependent DNA synthesis (reverse transcription), The |FRAME: Streptovaricins streptovaricins| were first discovered from |FRAME: TAX-68270| in 1957 |CITS: [13411413]|, and the first chemical structures, for |FRAME: CPD-21849| and |FRAME: CPD-21851|, were determined 11 years later |CITS: [4384966]|. S012 |CITS: [Zhang17]|., About This Pathway, The earlier steps of of ansamycins biosynthesis follow a common root. A type I modular polyketide synthase (PKS) initiates the polyketide chain with a |FRAME: CPD-10231| starter unit |CITS: [1672686]|, followed by multiple steps of chain elongation with various extender units on subsequent modules of the PKS |CITS: [Milavetz73]|. Summary: The |FRAME: s-Triazines| herbicide |FRAME: ATRAZINE| is a widely used that is persistant in the soil., It is prone to ground and surface water contamination. Some countries such as Germany, Italy,, Norway and Sweden have banned its use because of its widespread presence in water |CITS: [16162227]|., A range of soil bacteria, including both Gram-negative and Gram-positive strains can degrade atrazine,, utilizing it as a nitrogen and carbon source., In this aerobic pathway, which has been studied in most detail in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47660|,, atrazine is catabolized in three enzymatic steps to |FRAME: CYANURIC-ACID|, which can be further, metabolized by ring cleavage to carbon dioxide and ammonia. The first enzyme, encoded by, either |FRAME: G-124| or |FRAME: G-10313|, converts |FRAME: ATRAZINE| to, |FRAME: HYDROXYATRAZINE|. While some organisms possess all of the required enzymes, other communities degrade, atrazine by a community-appraoch, where different organisms have some of the enzymes, and the, intermediates in the pathway are passed between the organisms |CITS: [16329946]|., The genes encoding the pathway shown here were named either atz or trz, depending on, the organism. Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The presence of the O:7 antigen in E. coli K1 strains contributes to the virulence of the organisms, which are commonly found in extraintestinal infections in humans, especially neonatal meningitis and urinary tract infections |CITS: [6198283]|., The structure of the O:7 antigen was elucidated in 1984 |CITS: [6370430]|. The O antigen biosynthetic cluster was sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-1072458| and found to contain fourteen open reading frames, which encode enzymes that produce the precusors |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|, |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|, and |FRAME: CPD-14793|, as well as four glycotransferases, a flippase, and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [7677991][7559340][10517601]|., The activity of the floppase and polymerase was confirmed using transposon mutants |CITS: [10517601]|. The activity of the |FRAME: G-81008|-encoded galactosyltransferase was confirmed by a biochemical assay |CITS: [15625181]|.

Summary: General Background, Nascent proteins synthesized by membrane-bound ribosomes are translocated across the ER membrane and acquire carbohydrate chains on specific serine, threonine, and asparagine residues. These glycoproteins then proceed through the Golgi complex where their oligosaccharides are modified further., In higher eukaryotes, the majority of protein O-glycosylation is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.41|, which adds |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine| to the side chain of specific serine and threonine residues, mainly in mucin-type glycoproteins (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-7433| and |FRAME: PWY-7435|). However, alternative O-glycosylation modifications exist, and one of those is protein O-mannosylation, which is an essential protein modification in fungi and animals |CITS: [12369018][15383666][15948957]|., Protein O-mannosylation is less frequent in metazoa than it is in fungi, where the majority of secreted and cell wall proteins are substantially O-mannosylated (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7921|). In mammals, O-mannosyl glycans were isolated from chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and total glycopeptides from brain tissue |CITS: [39937][2941416][3663149][9083013]|, on α-dystroglycan originating from nerve and muscular tissues |CITS: [8999917][9838223][9726975]|, and on neuron-specific receptor protein-tyrosine phosphatase β |CITS: [18838383]|., The vast majority of mammalian O-mannosyl glycans includes variations of the tetrasaccharide α-NeuAc-(2→3)-β-Gal-(1→4)-β-GlcNAc-(1→2)-α-Man-1-Ser/Thr, often with fucose attached to GlcNAc by an α-1,3 linkage. In general, structures of mammalian O-mannosyl glycans are classified into three types: |FRAME: GlcNAc-b2-O-D-mannosyl-Protein "core M1"|, βGlcNAc(1→2)Man; |FRAME: GlcNAc-b2-GlcNAc-b6-O-D-mannosyl-Protein "core M2"|, βGlcNAc(1→2)[βGlcNAc(1→6)]Man; and |FRAME: bGalNAc-13-bGlucNAc-14-Man-R "core M3"|, βGalNAc(1→3)βGlcNAc(1→4)Man |CITS: [8999917][14617637][20044576]|., About This Pathway, Biosynthesis of O-mannosyl glycans is initiated in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where mannose is transferred from |FRAME: CPD-171| to serine and threonine residues of protein substrates |CITS: [6347716]|. This reaction is conserved between fungi and animals and is catalyzed by a family of enzymes named protein O-mannosyltransferases (PMTs), which are integral ER membrane proteins that contain seven transmembrane domains, a cytoplasmic N-terminus, and a C-terminal catalytic domain that faces the ER lumen |CITS: [10085156]|. It has been shown in |FRAME: TAX-4932| that the PMTs act on substrate proteins during their translocation into the ER lumen |CITS: [24519942]|., Properly folded glycoproteins are transported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where the initial mannose is further elongated. This elongation is species-specific and differs markedly between fungi and animals, and even among fungal species and different animals (e.g. insects)., The elongation of O-mannosyl glycans in mammals is only partially understood. The transfer of GlcNAc to mannose in the 2-OH position is catalyzed by |FRAME: ENSG00000085998-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS01515|) |CITS: [11181560][11742540]|, while |FRAME: HS15606-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS15606|) links GlcNAc to mannose in the 6-OH position in vitro |CITS: [14617637]|. The addition of GlcNAc in β1,2 linkage by |FRAME: HS01515| is required before |FRAME: HS15606| can add GlcNAc, strongly suggesting that the latter is responsible for the formation of 2,6-branched structures in brain O-mannosyl glycans |CITS: [14617637]|.

Summary: General Background, The main CO2 fixation enzyme in plants, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39 "EC 4.1.1.39, ribulose-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase"| (RuBisCO), has both carboxylase (photosynthetic CO2 fixation) and oxygenase (photorespiration) activities. The carboxylase activity is favored at high CO2/O2 ratio, whereas the oxygenase activity predominates at a decreased CO2/O2 ratio., At the time when RuBisCO first evolved, atmospheric CO2 concentration was very high and thus the enzyme's carboxylase activity was favored. However, later in evolution, atmospheric O2 concentration began to rise and RuBisCO's oxygenase activity increased at the expense of the carboxylase activity. In temperate climates and under moderate light levels, when the stomata are fully open, diffusion from the atmosphere is fully sufficient to ensure an ample supply of CO2 and C3 photosynthesis is rather efficient. However, in hot climates and under high light levels, the plants need to close their stomata to avoid water loss, restricting the ability of the CO2 to diffuse. Under these conditions the CO2 levels can go down to the point where photorespiration becomes a serious problem, reducing photosynthesis by more than 40%. The C4 system, which is found only in plants growing in conditions that require closure of the stomata, has evolved to address this problem., C4 plants have evolved to respond to lowered CO2 levels. The C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle starts with carbon fixation in the mesophyll cells by a combination of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.1 "EC 4.2.1.1, carbonic anhydrase"|, which converts the gasous CO2 to soluble |FRAME: HCO3|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31|, which incorporates the latter, forming the C4 acid |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|. Oxaloacetate or a derivative thereof (|FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|) is then transported from the mesophyll cells to bundle sheath cells. Once inside the bundle sheath cells, CO2 is released from the C4 acids, generating a micro-environment with a much higher concentration of CO2, suitable for an efficient carboxylation by RuBisCO., Three variations of the C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle have been described in plants, namely the |FRAME: PWY-241 "NADP-ME"| (NADP-malic enzyme), |FRAME: PWY-7115 "NAD-ME"| (NAD-malic enzyme), or |FRAME: PWY-7117 PEPCK| (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) types. The NADP-ME variant does not involve L-aspartate and utilizes an NADP-dependent malic enzyme to releases CO2 from |FRAME: MAL|. The NAD-ME variant does involve L-aspartate and utilizes an NAD-dependent malic enzyme. The PEPCK variant contains an additional route for CO2 release by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49|, which usually operates to supplement the NADP-ME variant., However, some research suggests that different C4 decarboxylation pathways may cooccur in plants that were previously considered to belong to exclusively one C4 photosynthetic type |CITS:[24609651]|. For instance, |FRAME: TAX-4577| has been shown to use both |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| for the generation of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[Chapman81]|. In addition, it has been demonstrated that maize leaves require the activity of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1| to maintain an efficient flow-rate. Moreover, the |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49 "phosphoenol carboxykinase"| (PEPCK), considered the hallmark of the PEPCK pathway, is also active in maize and shown to support |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE|-driven photosynthesis |CITS:[22186372]|. Similar results have been reported from the NADP-ME type plant |FRAME: TAX-4224|, which also utilizes both |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| equally and demonstrates aspartate aminotransferase activity |CITS:[Meister96]|. In general, current discussion of the C4 photosynthetic pathway types moves in a direction favoring the existence of only two subtypes, i.e. NADP-ME and NAD-ME, both of which may contain a supplementary PEPCK cycle |CITS:[24609651]|., About This Pathway, C4 photosynthesis basically represents a |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| concentrating mechanism (CCM) which independently originated more than 60 times in plants indicating the evolutionary drive to optimize photosynthetic |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation as a tool to keep pace with an ever-changing environment |CITS:[21631531]|. This MetaCyc pathway describes the PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) variant. Note that the pathway spans two cell types, mesophyll and bundle sheath., The roles and sub-cellular locations of different carbonic anhydrase (CA) isozymes in plants are various and are metabolically integrated in a rather complex manner regardless of the seemingly simple reaction they catalyze, i.e. the reversible hydration of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:HCO3| |CITS: [Moroney01][Badger03]|. In C3 plants the main function of CA's is to increase |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| concentration in micro-compartments, creating a more efficient environment for carbon fixation by RuBisCO in the chloroplast. They also have non-photosynthetic functions as in lipid biosynthesis and as antioxidants |CITS:[24146374]|. In C4 plants β-carbonic anhydrases operating in the cytoplasm of mesophyll cells are considered essential for the operation of the C4 photosynthetic carbon assimilation cycle by providing the substrate of PEP-carboxylase (|FRAME:HCO3|) , which incorporates it into |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| |CITS:[16666063]|. Corresponding β-carbonic anhydrases (|FRAME: G-43870| in |FRAME: TAX-4577| |CITS:[20933433][Burnell97]| and |FRAME: G-43871| in |FRAME: TAX-4224| |CITS:[17496111]|) are part of a small CA family where only one member is directly involved in the first reaction of C4 photosynthesis |CITS:[23414801] [Burnell90]|. However, it appears that even those β-carbonic anhydrases have only a limited role in C4 photosynthesis under current climate conditions and are more essential when C4 plants are stressed by high temperature and drought |CITS:[24706552]|., The initial CO2 fixation occurs in the mesophyll cells in the form of |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|. Aspartate enters the bundle sheath cells and is converted to back to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|. Inside the bundle sheathe cells CO2 is released from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.49| (PEPCK)., Not all the oxaloacetate formed in the mesophyll cells by carbon fixation is converted to aspartate. A fraction of it is converted to |FRAME: MAL|, which enters the bundle sheath cells and releases its CO2 by a malic enzyme, similar to the |FRAME: PWY-7115 "NAD-ME C4 pathway"|. The major reason for this route in PEPCK-plants is to generate NADH in the bundle sheath cells |CITS: [20188622]|. NADH is necessary for ATP production, which is required to drive the PEPCK reaction.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium Selenium| is an essential micronutrient for animals and humans but has not yet been proven to be an essential micronutrient for land plants |CITS: [11683552][16307305]|. There is evidence, however, of Chlamydomonas proteins that contains a |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| residue suggesting that algal species might also require |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [17105189][12110581]|. The health requirement of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for humans and animals can be met by crops and forage plants that contain selenocompounds. |FRAME: TAX-4232| among the oilseed crops was shown to be a good source for this micronutrient |CITS: [15012198]|. In addition, there is evidence that certain seleno-compounds, including |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE|, have anti-carcinogenic properties |CITS: [14748935]|. , Despite its importance as a micronutrient, higher concentrations of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| are toxic to humans, other animals, and plants largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064][12753978][16661781]|. , In general, plants take up both |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE| from soil. A series of |FRAME: PWY-6932 reduction steps| converts |FRAME: SELENATE| to |FRAME: SE-2| / |FRAME: CPD-678| and this is assimilated into the seleno-amino acids |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19309459]|., In Se accumulator plants, these seleno-amino acids may be modified to create organic seleno-compounds for storage. Seasonal weeds like |FRAME: TAX-3575| and |FRAME: TAX-83445| along with perennial weeds like |FRAME: TAX-41550| employ this strategy and accumulate high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [19800657]|. Se accumulation can help to protect plants against attacks by prairie dogs, insects, and fungi (see refs in |CITS: [21628258]|)., Other plants, like |FRAME: ORG-5993| generate seleno-compounds as well, but rather than storing them, they transform them into less toxic volatile compounds, such as |FRAME: CPD-12005| (DMSe) that can then be released from the plants |CITS: [10759525]|. This process is also called phytovolatilization |CITS: [19656903]|. , While these strategies directly benefit the plants that employ them, they can also be put to use for the phytoremediation of seleniferous soils that contain dangerously high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium|. Numerous insights into endogenous seleno-compound metabolism in plants have been gained through efforts to engineer plants that show improved selenium phytoremediation abilities |CITS: [15005814][19800657][19893365][17445958][10759525]|., About This Pathway, To reduce the risk of misincorporating |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| into proteins, this compound can be methylated to form the non-coding seleno-amino acid |FRAME: CPD-12025|. Some Se hyperaccumulating plants may sequester this compound., Both Se-non-accumulators and accumulators may also further metabolize |FRAME: CPD-12025| to produce the volatile |FRAME: CPD-12005|. This could occur in at least two manners. Many plants, such as Arabidopsis, may simply break down |FRAME: CPD-12025| in a |FRAME: PWY-6931 one-step process| that could be based on chemical decomposition or enzyme catalysis |CITS: [12376649]|., However, as depicted in this pathway, halophytic species likely produce |FRAME: CPD-12005| through a four-step process that mimics their |FRAME: PWY-6055 dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) biosynthesis pathway|. In |FRAME:TAX-3707| the intermediate compound |FRAME: CPD-13770| serves as an excellent precursor for |FRAME: CPD-12005| production |CITS: [10759525]|. Moreover, there is evidence that |FRAME:TAX-29706| produces |FRAME: CPD-13770| when grown in the presence of elevated levels of selenate, providing further support for this biosynthetic route in planta |CITS: [ANSEDE99]|. The |FRAME:TAX-15853| enzymes shown to function in |FRAME: PWY-6055 DMSP biosynthesis| |CITS: [10889264]| may perform analogous functions in DMSeP production.

Summary: General Background, Sialic acids are a family of polyhydroxylated α-keto acids that contain nine carbon atoms. Most sialic acids are derivatives of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, or |FRAME: CPD-21259| (KDN). |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is the most common sialic acid in mammals (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6138|), while KDN is abundant in lower vertebrates (this pathway). Their core structures can be modified at the hydroxyl groups, lactonized, or hydroxylated at the acetamido group, generating many derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-262| is a derivative of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6144|). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Sialic acids are found mainly in vertebrates and a few higher invertebrates (ascidians and echinoderms). These acidic sugars are usually the terminal sugar residue in the glycan chains of vertebrate glycoconjugates (mostly glycoproteins and glycolipids, but also proteoglycans and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors). They function in mediating cellular recognition and adhesion events for many important processes such as development, the immune and inflammatory responses, and oncogenesis. Sialic acid occurs rarely in invertebrates. Endogenous sialylation has been shown to occur in |FRAME: TAX-7215|, but details of sialic acid biosynthesis in this organism remain to be determined |CITS: [18568399]|. However, it is possible the sialic acids might be biosynthesized by other eukaryotes in a species and/or life cycle-dependent manner. In |CITS: [7841794]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Most bacteria do not biosynthesize sialic acids, but some pathogenic and symbiotic bacteria biosynthesize sialic acids as a means of evading a host's immune system (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6139|). The sialic acid is displayed on the bacterial cell surface (in capsular polysaccharides) in order to mimic mammalian cells. Pathogens that biosynthesize sialic acids include |FRAME: TAX-487|, |FRAME: TAX-1392869| and |FRAME: TAX-197|. In addition, the human gut symbiont |FRAME: TAX-818| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-21259| |CITS: [18804026]| (this pathway). Whether or not archaea contain sialic acids remains to be determined. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Other sialic acid-like sugars biosynthesized by bacteria include the nonulosonic acids |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [16751642]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|) and legionaminic acid |CITS: [18275154]|., Protists are thought to lack the ability to biosynthesize sialic acids although more genome data are needed to confirm, this. Sialic acids have been thought to be absent in plants but some studies raise the possibility |CITS: [18258224]|. Fungi appear to lack any known sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, although strain-specific, or novel pathways could exist. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Also see |FRAME: PWY-6145|., About This Pathway, The natural occurrence of the deaminated sialic acid |FRAME: CPD-21259| (deaminated |FRAME: CPD-10760|) was discovered in 1986 (|CITS: [3745155]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16897172]|). It is abundant in extracellular glycoconjugates of lower vertebrates such as fish and amphibians and has been well studied in |FRAME: TAX-8022| (rainbow trout)., |FRAME: CPD-21259| has also been found in mammalian cells and tissues, but in two to three orders of magnitude lower amounts, and mostly as free monosaccharide. Studies with a monoclonal antibody that recognizes |FRAME: CPD-21259|-containing sequences in glycoproteins have shown immunoreactive protein in mammalian tissues, but the presence of |FRAME: CPD-21259| was not confirmed by chemical analysis. In addition, it has been reported that in vitro, human recombinant |FRAME: HS01818-MONOMER| expressed in insect cells can utilize either |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-MANNOSAMINE-6P| or |FRAME: MANNOSE-6P| to synthesize |FRAME: N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE-9P|, or |FRAME: CPD-10735|, respectively. However, it had a much higher efficiency for production of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE-9P| |CITS: [10749855]|. Mutagenesis studies showed that the human |FRAME: CPD-10735| synthase activity can be eliminated by a single point mutation |CITS: [16503877]|. In contrast, the mouse |FRAME: MONOMER-14514| cannot use |FRAME: MANNOSE-6P| as substrate. The human CMP-sialic acid synthase shows a broad substrate specificity that includes |FRAME: CPD-21259|. It appears that further work is needed to confirm the biosynthesis and significance of |FRAME: CPD-10737| in mammals. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-21259| has been reported to occur in the bacterial capsular polysaccharides of the human pathogen Klebsiella ozaenae serotype K4, the human intestinal symbiont |FRAME: TAX-226186| |CITS: [18804026]| the plant symbiont |FRAME:TAX-380| strain SVQ293, and the cell wall polymers of the plant pathogen Streptomyces sp. MB-8. It appears to have a role in the bacterial-host interaction. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., The biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-21259| is hypothesized to be similar to that of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| biosynthesis in eukaryotes (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6138|). No evidence for direct conversion of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| to |FRAME: CPD-21259| has been reported. General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-6366|, the first organism that was found to use |FRAME: BETAINE| as a methanogenic substrate, was isolated in 2015. The organism can use |FRAME: BETAINE| as the sole carbon source, with approximately 0.75:1 stoichiometry of methane produced to |FRAME: BETAINE| consumed |CITS: [25319587]|., The pathway for methanogenesis from |FRAME: BETAINE| follows a similar route to those of other methylated amines. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., The three components were identified and isolated from |FRAME: ORG-6366|, and activity was demonstrated for each. A major difference between the MT1 invovled in this pathway and similar enzymes involved in methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds is that this enzyme does not contain the unusual amino acid |FRAME: CPD-3321| |CITS: [25313086][Creighbaum19]|., It is well documented that the Co(I)/Co(II) transformation has a very low redox potential (it is -525 mV in the cobalamin binding domain of methionine synthase |CITS: [9398303]|). These low redox potentials make the corrinoid cofactor subject to adventitious oxidation to the Co(II) state, which renders the proteins inactive |CITS: [19043046]|. The glycine betaine corrinoid protein appears to be particularly vulnerable, as reconstitution of the pathway in vitro required including a 4th enzyme that reduces a corrinoid protein with a cob(II)alamin cofactor back to the active cob(I)alamin state |CITS: [Creighbaum19]|.

The other known route for this conversion is the two-step GSH-dependent pathway catalyzed by glyoxalase I and II, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-5386|., In |FRAME: TAX-562| the activity was attributed to enzymes that function as protein/nucleic acids deglycases. Summary: The enterobacterial common antigen (ECA) is an outer membrane glycolipid shared by all members of the |FRAME: TAX-543| and is restricted to this family. A notable exception is |FRAME: TAX-556|, which does not produce ECA |CITS: [3078744]|., ECA was discovered in 1962 in antisera against |FRAME: TAX-2100498|, and originally named "Kunin antigen" |CITS: [Kunin62]|. It is located in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane, and is a glycophospholipid built up by an aminosugar heteropolymer linked to an L-glycerophosphatidyl residue., The carbohydrate portion consists of trisaccharide repeat units of |FRAME: CPD-12541|, |FRAME: CPD-23559| and |FRAME: CPD-15611| |CITS: [658050][Lugowski83]|. These repeating units are concatenated into longer linear heteropolysaccharide chains |CITS: [2166030]|, and each polysaccharide chain is covalently linked to diacylglycerolphosphate via a glycosidic linkage between the potential reducing terminal GlcNAc residue and the phosphate residue of the aglycone |CITS: [9592122]|. The phosphoglyceride aglycone anchors the ECA chains to the outer membrane |CITS: [6154038][7021535]|. The number of repeats units in each chain varies within the organism and among organisms. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-83333| the chains range from 1 to 14 repeat units |CITS: [10515954]|., The ECA trisaccharide repeat unit is assembled on the cytosolic face of the cytoplasmic membrane as an undecaprenyldiphosphate-linked intermediate (lipid III). However, the Wzy-catalyzed polymerization of repeat units to form linear polysaccharide chains occurs on the periplasmic face of the membrane. This requires the translocation of lipid III to the periplasmic face of the membrane, which is mediated by a flippase encoded by the wzxE gene |CITS: [7698674]|., Polymerization is followed by the transfer of polysaccharide chains from the lipid carrier to either an as yet unidentified acceptor to yield phosphoglyceride-linked chains or to the core region of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|. ECA linked to phosphoglycerides is known as |FRAME: CPD-21605 ECA<sub>PG</sub>| and ECA linked to the core region of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides| is known as |FRAME: CPD0-2294 ECA<sub>LPS</sub>| |CITS: [352696][3078744]|.  Both of those forms are translocated, by different mechanisms, to the outer membrane.  A third form is |FRAME: CPD0-2646 ECA<sub>CYC</sub>|, a cyclic water-soluble polymer that contains only ECA trisaccharide repeat units and is found in the periplasm |CITS: [6498860][8039177][11297429][12618464]|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (this pathway), while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, As a general rule, most prokaryotes utilize the aspartate de novo pathway, in which the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| |CITS: [11153263]|, while in eukaryotes, the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| |CITS: [12062417]| (|FRAME: NADSYN-PWY|)., In aerobic bacteria the first reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.16|, utilizes oxygen as the electron acceptor (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|). However, it has been shown for the |FRAME: TAX-562| enzyme that it can use fumarate as an alternative electron acceptor under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [8706750]|. Indeed, homologs of the |FRAME: TAX-562| L-aspartate oxidase are found in strictly anaerobic organisms such as the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-53953| and the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-837| |CITS: [12215812]|.

Summary: General Background, The antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-15417|, |FRAME: CPD-15421|, and |FRAME: CPD-15504| target the bacterial DNA gyrase, to which they bind with KD of 10-8 to 10-10 M |CITS: [8231802]|. The three antibiotics, which are produced by different microorganisms, share several characteristics., All three antibiotics contain a 7-hydroxy-2-aminocoumarin core. The phenolic 7-hydroxyl group of the bicyclic aminocoumarin scaffold is attached to an L-noviosyl sugar moiety, while the 2-amino group is ligated to a prenylated, hydroxybenzoate unit (in |FRAME: CPD-15417| and |FRAME: CPD-15421|) or to a methylpyrroledicarboxylic acid that links two aminocoumarin moieties (in |FRAME: CPD-15504|). The noviosyl sugar is then methylated at the 4'-OH position and acylated at the 3'-OH position to produce the mature, active antibiotic., The pharmacophore of these antibiotics is the decorated noviosyl sugar, which is presented by the planar aminocoumarin to the ATP binding site of the GyrB subunit of gyrase to interdict DNA replication |CITS: [8635474][9144789]|., About This Pathway, The pathway can be divided into 4 parts: synthesis of the aminocoumarin core, the noviose sugar, and the prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit, and the final assembly and decoration of the final product., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15417| and |FRAME: CPD-15421| is identical through much of the pathway, up to formation of |FRAME: CPD-15416|. While in |FRAME: PWY-7287| this intermediate is methylated by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.284|, during |FRAME: CPD-15421| formation it is chlorinated at that position by |FRAME: MONOMER-18096| |CITS: [12670542]|., In addition, while the last reaction in |FRAME: PWY-7287| is the addition of a carbamoyl moiety to the penultimate intermediate, the comparable intermediate in |FRAME: PWY-8368| is modified by the attachment of a |FRAME: PYRROLE-2-CARBOXYLATE| moiety, followed by methylation of the pyrrole ring., The complete biosynthetic gene cluster for clorobiocin has been cloned and sequenced from the natural producer, |FRAME: TAX-285450|. The cluster was orifginally reported to contain of 27 open reading frames |CITS: [12480894]|, though later analysis reveal the presence of two more frames |CITS: [16276503]|., Pathways leading to the formation of several of the precursors for |FRAME: PWY-8368| can be accessed via the pathway links., A route that is unique to |FRAME: PWY-8368| is the formation of |FRAME: PYRROLE-2-CARBOXYLATE|. This route starts with |FRAME: G-107832 CloN3|, |FRAME: G-107831 CloN4| and |FRAME: G-107837 CloN5|, which are responsible for converting the amino acid |FRAME: PRO| to |FRAME: PYRROLE-2-CARBOXYLATE|. CloN4 activates the amino acid to its adenylate form and transfers it to the peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domain of CloN5. CloN3 then catalyzes the reduction of the proline ring, forming a pyrrole ring |CITS: [15723521]|., The pathway continues with the activities of |FRAME: G-107836 CloN1|, |FRAME: G-107835 CloN2| and |FRAME: G-107833 CloN7|. CloN2 catalyzes the transfer of the pyrrole-2-carboxyl moiety from CloN5 to another prolyl-carrier protein, CloN1, while CloN7 catalyzes the transfer of this moiety from CloN1 to the noviose sugar moiety in |FRAME: CPD-15419| |CITS: [12904558][16276503][16834331]|., The last transformation of this pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-107834 CloN6|, a radical SAM methylcobalamin-dependent methylase that transfers a methyl group to position 5 of the pyrrole ring |CITS: [12898629]|. Initially it was thought that this reaction occurs after the transfer reaction catalyzed by CloN7. However, a later experiment has concluded that the methylation and transfer reactions occur simultaneously, and that CloN7 requires the presence of CloN6 for full catalytic effciency in vivo, potentially due to the formation of a ternary CloN1/CloN6/CloN7 complex |CITS: [17308937]|. The two reactions are shown as taking place successively in this pathway diagram to illustrate the two chemical transformations that take place.

The proportion of unsaturated fatty acids is known to increase in |FRAME:TAX-562| with lower growth temperature, a phenomenon found in most organisms that provides a mechanism for adjusting the lipid phase transition of the membrane phospholipids to differing temperatures., This control is achieved via |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| (|FRAME: EG12606|) - the only enzyme that can catalyze further elongation of |FRAME: CPD-9245| to |FRAME: CPD-9247|. It has been shown that |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| is more active at low temperatures (relative to the overall rate of fatty acid synthesis) than at high temperatures |CITS: [7002930]|. Pregnenolone is synthesized in the mitochondrial inner membrane and is the biosynthetic precursor of all steroid hormones--androgens, estrogens, mineralo-and gluco-corticoids. Cholesterol is released from lipid droplets or endosomes and transported to the mitochondria by carrier proteins. The rate limiting step for steroid hormone synthesis is the transport of cholesterol from the outer to inner mitochondrial membrane by the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR)|CITS: [16973755]|. StAR functions at the outer mitochondrial membrane to bind and release cholesterol during a pH mediated molten globule confirmational change |CITS: [10377400]|. The cytosolic carrier proteins, StARD4, -5 and -6, contain a StAR-related lipid binding domain and exhibit tissue specific expression patterns |CITS: [12724317]|. The conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone is catalyzed in three distinct reactions by a single cytochrome p450 enzyme |FRAME: HS06719|.

Summary: Oxygen deprivation is a primary stress in plants subjected to flooding. Under low oxygen tensions, plants modify several aspects of their metabolism, in particular by shifting from respiratory to fermentative energy production |CITS:[RICARD94],[VARTAPETIAN97]|., Increased activity of the ethanol fermentation pathway from pyruvate allows reoxidation of NADH produced in glycolysis, thus enabling the plant to generate ATP independent of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS:[11787018]|., Anaerobic treatment of maize seedling was shown to drastically alter the profile of total protein synthesis. In an anaerobic environment 20 proteins, which account for more than 70% of the total translation, are selectively synthesized |CITS:[7418006]|. Most of the anaerobic proteins identified were found to be enzymes of glycolysis or sugar-phosphate metabolism: sucrose synthase, aldolase, pyruvate decarboxylase, enolase, glucose-6-phosphate isomerase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, alcohol dehydrogenase |CITS:[12509333]|. Under anaerobic conditions, sucrose is mobilized from several other pathways to enter glycolysis via its conversion to glucose and fructose. Whereas in an aerobic environment pyruvate, the end-product of glycolysis, is metabolized into acetyl-CoA and carbon dioxide, under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is metabolized to form either lactate or ethanol., Evidence suggests that the reduction of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase is a minor pathway in plants. Indeed, the lowering of pH concomitant with lactate accumulation is likely to switch off lactate production whilst activating pyruvate decarboxylase involved in the conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde, in turn metabolized to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase |CITS:[DEY97]|.

Summary: Flavonoids are a class of plant secondary metabolites widely distributed in the plant kingdom. Over 10,000 flavonoids have been , described in the literature |CITS: [17587669]|. They display important functions as attractants for pollinators,  protective agents , against UV light and various pathogens,  antibiotics, and  signal molecules involved in symbiosis with Rhizobia. Apart from their biological functions, they are also known for their antioxidant and anticancer and other bioactivities in humans. , Flavonoids are usually found as water-soluble glycosides. However, the occurrence of methoxylated, acylated or sulfated derivatives , of flavonoids have also been reported in plants. The presence of over 80 different flavonoids sulfates has been reported from various plant species , |CITS: [Barron88]|.  , Enzymatic sulfonation of flavonoids is catalyzed by a family of sulfotransferases (STs) that transfer the sulfonate group of , |FRAME:PAPS | to the hydroxyl group of a flavonoid to produce a sulfate flavonoid ester.

Pisatin is the major phytoalexin in pea (|FRAME:TAX-3888|) |CITS: [Banks82]|. Unlike the other major pterocarpans in legumes pisatin possesses a (+) or (S) stereochemistry, which is opposite to even the intermediates found in the biosynthetic route of pisatin., The question of how the final stereochemistry of pisatin is accomplished is still not known, and accordingly, two potential pathways are shown in this diagram. It has been shown that (+) and/or (-)-pisatin can be produced in pea if provided with a maackiain enantiomer of the same stereochemistry |CITS: [Banks82a]| |CITS: [Banks83]|., The penultimate intermediate in maackiain biosynthesis of pea, |FRAME: CPD-3630|, has been shown to have a (-) or (R) stereochemistry, introduced by the isoflavone reductase |CITS: [8037464]|. It has also been demonstrated that the last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.270| (HMKMT) prefers the (+)-enantiomer over the (-)-enantiomer of 6a-hydroxymaackiain |CITS: [9349277]|. Thus, the change in stereochemistry during the synthesis of pisatin must occur between the production of |FRAME: CPD-3630| and (|FRAME: CPD-3942|., The detection and partial characterization of an new enzyme presumably involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-3944|, |FRAME: MONOMER-19164|, indicates another path towards |FRAME:CPD-3944| than the previously proposed isomerization of |FRAME:CPD-3631| to |FRAME:CPD-4462|. It has been previously demonstrated that the sophorol reductase catalyzed the reduction of |FRAME:CPD-3630| and exclusively produced |FRAME:CPD-14741| and not its trans-enantiomer |CITS:[16504226]|. Only the former cis-enantiomer was shown to be accepted by the isoflavene synthase (IFSV) catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17616| from |FRAME:CPD-14741| via a dehydratase-like mechanism |CITS:[24332213]|. This enzymatic reaction was only detected in the |FRAME:CPD-3944|-producing |FRAME: TAX-3888|, and does not appear to operate in other legumes such as alfalfa, chickpea and bean, which produce (-)-phytoalexins. Therefore it has been discussed that the reaction catalyzed by IFVS is a branching point towards |FRAME:PWY-2467|, although the step(s) forming (+)-enantiomeric intermediates still remain to be elucidated |CITS:[24332213]|.

Summary: |FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., Numerous filamentous fungi, including the food biotechnology fungus |FRAME: TAX-5061|, the opportunistic human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-746128|, the phytopathogenic fungi |FRAME: TAX-40559| and |FRAME: TAX-5180|, as well as many brown-rot and white-rot basidiomycetes, are able to efficiently produce large quantities of oxalate  |CITS: [3132096][10500844]|. It is known that oxalate secretion is associated with fungal pathogenesis |CITS: [3132096][11810498][15502012][15962786]|. In the wood-rotting fungus |FRAME: TAX-2870670| oxalate is formed as the product of glucose metabolism via oxaloacetate |CITS: [11553780]|. , There are three potential routes for production of oxalate in fungi: oxidation of glyoxylate (|FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-OXIDASE-RXN "EC 1.2.3.5"|) |CITS: [6712607]|, oxidation of glycolaldehyde |CITS: [7947743]|, and hydrolysis of oxaloacetate (|FRAME: OXALOACETASE-RXN "EC 3.7.1.1"|) |CITS: [179820]|. However, the results of studies of <sup>14</sup>CO<sub>2</sub> incorporation into the metabolite pools of |FRAME: TAX-5061| indicated that oxalate is derived from oxaloacetate |CITS: [3132096]|. Thus, while oxalate is generated through several different biochemical pathways in fungi, oxaloacetate acetylhydrolase-catalyzed hydrolytic cleavage of oxaloacetate is believed to be an especially important route |CITS: [3132096]|., The enzymatic formation of |FRAME: OXALATE| and |FRAME: ACET| from |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| has been first reported in 1956, from the mold |FRAME: TAX-5061| |CITS: [Hayaishi56]|. That enzyme was not purified at the time, but it was shown that it required manganese. In subsequent studies the enzyme was partially purified |CITS: [179820]| and a mutant was obtained |CITS: [8590475]|. The |FRAME: G-12485| gene encoding the enzyme has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-5061| and cloned from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-40559| |CITS: [17244616]|., While the enzyme is most common in fungi, its activity has been described in some plants, especially those of the genus |FRAME: TAX-4034| |CITS:[16749035][16656975][16342929][16395587]|. The petal death protein from the flowering plant |FRAME: TAX-3570| has been purified and shown to possess oxaloacetate acetylhydrolase activity in addition to 2-alkylmalate CC bond lyase activity |CITS: [16342930]|.

|FRAME: PQQ "Pyrroloquinoline quinone"| (PQQ) is a cofactor of quinoprotein dehydrogenases that function in the periplasm of Gram-negative bacteria (for example, |FRAME: CPLX-3264| and |FRAME: MONOMER-12743|)., PQQ, which was originally named methoxatin, was first isolated from the glucose dehydrogenase of |FRAME: TAX-470| |CITS: [14257587]| and the methanol dehydrogenase of of |FRAME:TAX-286| sp. M27 |CITS: [6049934]|. Its structure was subsequently elucidated by x-ray crystallography |CITS: [471057]|. PQQ has a high midpoint redox potential in the range of +90 mV (at pH 7). All PQQ-containing enzymes are likely to have PQQ complexed with a divalent metal ion in, their active sites |CITS: [9572874][11761326]|., PQQ was the first cofactor to be found in the ortho-quinone cofactor family, which also includes |FRAME: CPD-12145| (TTQ), |FRAME: TOPAQUINONE| (TPQ), |FRAME: CPD-12143| (LTQ) and the |FRAME: CPD-12146|. PQQ is unique in being the only member of this family that it is not biosynthesized directly on the polypeptide chain of the enzyme it is associated with. Instead, PQQ is synthesized independently of its site of action, from a precursor peptide known as |FRAME: PqqA-Proteins "PqqA"|. The pathway has not been completely characterized, and some of the steps presented here are still pending biochemical confirmation., All PqqA peptides include the sequence motif -E-X-X-X-Y-, that is, an |FRAME: GLT| and an |FRAME: TYR| separated by three amino acid residues. Before the first enzyme of the pathway can act, the precursor peptide PqqA must be recognized and bound by PqqD |CITS: [25817994]|, a peptide chaperone that presents it to the first tailoring enzyme, a radical SAM enzyme encoded by the |FRAME:G-11753| gene. PqqE catalyzes the formation of a C-C bond between the C9 atom of the L-glutamate and the C9a atom of the L-tyrosine residues. It has been suggested that the product of the pqqB gene may encode a hydroxylase involved in the oxidation of the tyrosine of PqqA prior to its cross-linking with glutamate |CITS: [22324760]|., The next step involves the cleavage of the structure from the PqqA peptide, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: MONOMER-15351|, encoded by the |FRAME:G-11754| gene |CITS: [27231346]|. The cleaved product goes through a series of rearrangements, and is oxidized by an as-yet unidentified oxygenase, yielding |FRAME: CPD-7244|. The last step of the pathway is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-11755|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-7987|. This reaction involves ring cyclization and eight-electron oxidation, utilizes three oxygen molecules, and produces |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| |CITS: [15148379]|., The final product needs to be transported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm before it is released from PqqC, since free PQQ can react with oxygen to generate deleterious free radicals. The enzymes that are responsible for these processes have not been pin-pointed yet. However, a set of six genes that is sufficient for PQQ biosynthesis has been identified |CITS: [19902179]|. In addition to the |FRAME: G-11752|, |FRAME: G-11753|, |FRAME: G-11754|, and |FRAME: G-11755| genes, the cluster also includes pqqB and pqqD, which are believed to encode an uncharacterized oxidase and the protein responsible for exporting PQQ/PqqC to the periplasm |CITS: [7665488][18371220]|., The crystal structure of PqqB was reported. It contains a metallo-hydrolase/oxidoreductase fold and a putative PQQ binding site near a zinc atom |CITS: [18371220]|. The tertiary structure of PqqD was determined from the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-339| at a resolution of 1.66 Å |CITS: [19475705]|. The structure suggests that PqqD can possibly bind PQQ and serve as a PQQ carrier.

Summary: General Background, Glycogen is a highly branched glucose polymer that serves as a form of energy storage in animals and fungi. It resembles plant-produced |FRAME: Starch starch| and is sometimes called "animal starch"., Glycogen is formed of small chains of 8 to 12 glucose molecules linked together by α (1->4) bonds. These small chains, also known as |FRAME: Maltodextrins maltodextrins|, are in turn linked together by α (1->6) bonds. The α-1,4 linkages make up approximately 95% of the total molecule. The α-1,6 branches accounts for 7-10% of the linkages and are evenly distributed within the glycogen particle., Since each chain (with the exception of the outer unbranched chains) supports two branches, glycogen particles grow spherically by adding tiers (a tier corresponds to the spherical space separating two consecutive branches from all chains located at similar distance from the center of the particle)., Mathematical modelling predicts a maximal value for the particle size above which further growth is impossible as there would not be sufficient space for interaction of the chains with the catalytic sites of glycogen metabolism enzymes. This generates a particle consisting of 12 tiers corresponding to a 42 nm maximal diameter including 55 000 glucose residues. 36% of this total number rests in the outer (unbranched) shell and is thus readily accessible to glycogen catabolism without debranching |CITS: [12179957]|., Although glycogen and starch are two distinct physical states of the same type of storage polysaccharide, starch is solid semi-crystalline while glycogen particles are entirely hydrosoluble |CITS: [21220783]|., Glucose is polymerized within the polysaccharides thanks to its activation in the form of a nucleotide-sugar through the action of NDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase. All eukaryotes known synthesize glycogen from |FRAME: CPD-12575| while all Gram-negative glycogen accumulating bacteria use |FRAME:ADP-D-GLUCOSE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5067| and |FRAME:GLYCOGENSYNTH-PWY|)., About This Pathway, In mammals glycogen is synthesized and stored primarily in liver and muscle cells |CITS: [8354390][9023518]|., Glycogen metabolism is a major component of whole-body glucose metabolism, and defective glycogen storage is associated with several diseases, including type 2 diabetes., The precursor for glycogen synthesis in mammals is |FRAME: CPD-12575|, which is produced from, |FRAME:GLC-1-P| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6973|., Initiation of glycogen biosynthesis in mammals is mediated by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.186|. This unusual enzyme catalyzes two reactions: first, it catalyzes its own glucosylation, transferring one glucose unit from UDP-glucose to a tyrosine residue (Tyr194). Next it catalyzes the transfer of additional glucose units to the first one by α-1,4-glucosidic linkages, forming a glycogen primer |CITS:[15238248][12051921]|. , The mammalian |FRAME:CPLX-6975|, which is a homotetramer of 85 kDa subunits, attaches to the glucosylated glycogenin complex, and catalyzes the transfer of the glucose moiety of additional |FRAME: CPD-12575| molecules by α-1,4-glucosidic linkage, extending the glycogen chain further. , During this elongation process, branched α-1,6-glucosidic linkages are formed by the |FRAME: HS03772-MONOMER|, which cuts groups of ~6 glucose units from the end of the chains, and reattaches them by α-1,6-linkages, forming branched points., This process continues, forming a complex termed proglycogen, which is about 400 kDa. At this point, a different glycogen synthase, with a lower affinity for |FRAME: CPD-12575|, replaces the previous synthase, and along with the branching enzyme, catalyzes the synthesis of a final macroglycogen polymer, which is about 10,000 kDa |CITS: [7672505]|.

There are several alternative pathways for the degradation of trehalose., Depending on the organism, trehalose may enter the cell either through a permease, in which case it remains, unmodified, or it may be transported by a phosphotransferase system (PTS), resulting in the phoshorylated, trehalose-6-phosphate form., Degradation then proceeds by different mechanisms: , Unmodified trehalose may be degraded by a hydrolyzing trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|), or it may be split, by the action of a trehalose phosphorylase (see|FRAME: PWY-2722| and |FRAME: PWY-2723|)., Likewise, trehalose-6-phosphate may be either hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase, (see |FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) or it could be attacked by a trehalose-6-phosphate phosphorylase, (see |FRAME: PWY-2721|). , Trehalose degradation utilizing a trehalose-6-phosphate is found in many bacteria. It was studied extensively, in the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562| (under conditions of low osmolarity). However, it has also been, demonstrated in some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-78057| and |FRAME:TAX-1423|, |CITS: [4369400][7651129]|., While |FRAME:TAX-562| only synthesizes trehalose under conditions of high osmolarity, it can degrade the sugar under, conditions of both low and high osmolarity. In fact, |FRAME:TAX-562| can grow with trehalose as the sole carbon, source. Different pathways are employed under different osmolarity conditions., Since no trehalose biosynthesis is happening in low osmolarity conditions, the only source of trehalose is external, supply. Trehalose is imported into the cell by a PTS system for trehalose, which is composed of the, EIIAGlc of the glucose-PTS, and a trehalose-specific EIITre, encoded by the, treB gene. Trehalose is phosphorylated during the transport and enters the cytoplasm as, trehalose-6-phosphate., The resulting trehalose-6-phosphate is then hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase, which is encoded by, the treC gene, yielding glucose and glucose-6-phosphate. The free glucose is phosphorylated further by, glucokinase into a second molecule of glucose-6-phosphate, and both glucose-6-phosphate moieties enter, glycolysis |CITS: [7608078][8083158]|.

|FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE Terephthalate| (TPA) is a commodity chemical, used principally as a precursor to the polyester |FRAME: CPD-19188| (PET), used to make clothing and plastic bottles. TPA is manufactured by oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-1422|. , |FRAME: CPD-19188 "Polyethylene terephthalate"| (PET) is the most common thermoplastic polymer resin of the polyester family and is used in fibers for clothing, containers for liquids and foods, thermoforming for manufacturing, and in combination with glass fiber for engineering resins. In the context of textile applications, PET is referred to by its common name, polyester., Degradation of PET is limited to a few fungal and bacterial species. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1547922|, which fully degrades PET, utilizes the enzymes |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.101|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.102|, to convert the polymer into |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOL| |CITS: [26965627]|. The bacterium |FRAME: ORG-5891| forms |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| as an intermediate of |FRAME: 4TOLCARBDEG-PWY| |CITS: [9006050]|. In both cases terephthalate, which has a very low toxicity (LD50 on the order of grams/kg |CITS: [Sheehan00]|), is degraded further into |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, as shown in this pathway., |FRAME: TAX-364029|, which can utilize |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| as its sole source of carbon and energy, contains two |FRAME: TEREPHTHALATE| degradation gene clusters. Each cluster contains six open reading frames, including genes encoding the three subunits of |FRAME: EC-1.14.12.15|, and a gene that encodes |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.53| |CITS: [16517628]|.

Over 200 non-protein amino acids are present in plants. Many occur in free forms while some are detected in , peptide conjugates. Many have toxic properties. The role of non-protein amino acids in plants has been proposed to , include serving as defense compounds against predators, as storage forms of carbon and nitrogen, and as , detoxification products |CITS: [Wallsgrove95]|. , β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine is a non-protein amino acid first isolated from water melon and later found in several , other species of Cucurbitaceae. It makes up about 0.1% of the total dry weight of water melon seeds which suggest , its role of a storage form of carbon and nitrogen. Given the toxicity of pyrazole and 1,3-diaminopropane, and the , less toxicity of β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine, it is suggested that the biosynthesis pathway of , β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine serves as one of the detoxification mechanisms in cucurbit plants |CITS: [Brown90]|., β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine is synthesized from pyrazole and O-acetyl-serine, catalyzed by , β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine synthase. The enzyme is reported to be same enzyme of cysteine synthase in water , melon |CITS: [8280125]|. As far as concerning the origin of the pyrazole moiety of β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine, it was before , implicated that 1,3-diaminopropane is the precursor of pyrazole. A partially purified enzyme, tentatively named , pyrazole synthase here in MetaCyc, otherwise was not named, from cucumber which was demonstrated to , convert 1,3-diaminopropane to pyrazole via 2-pyrazoline confirmed the previous hypothesis |CITS: [Brown90]|. The enzyme is the , first to be described, from any biological source, catalyzes the covalent linking of two organic N-atoms.      , Preliminary results suggested 1,3-diaminopropane was derived from spermidine in cucumber. Studies in other , non-cucurbit plant species also indicated that 1,3-diaminopropane arises from spermidine and spermine and that , 1,3-diaminopropane is also metabolized to β-alanine |CITS: [Brown90]|. , The supply of pyrazole is the limiting factor of β-pyrazole-1-ylalanine synthesis |CITS: [Frisch67]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additinal reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, It has been well documented that aromatic amino acids can serve as electron acceptors in the reductive branch of the Stickland reaction. The final products of the fermentation of |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR|, and |FRAME: TRP|, which are |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE|, |FRAME: PHLORETATE|, and |FRAME: INDOLE-PROPIONATE|, respectively, have been observed to accumulate in cultures fed with the respective amino acid |CITS: [16746719] [Boezi59][1275638][Li14][29168502]|., There is a special interest in the pathway leading to production of |FRAME: INDOLE-PROPIONATE|, since the compound has been shown to prevent oxidative stress and death of primary neurons and neuroblastoma cells exposed to the amyloid β-protein in the form of amyloid fibrils, one of the most prominent neuropathologic features of Alzheimer's disease |CITS: [10419516]|., The pathway was studied mostly with the degradation of |FRAME: PHE|. However, it has been shown that the same enzymes catalyze the degradation of all three aromatic amino acids |CITS: [Li14][29168502]|. In this pathway the aromatic amino acid is converted to its 3-propanoate derivative via transamination to a 2-oxoacid, reduction to a 2R-hydroxyacid, dehydration to an enoate, and finally reduction of the double bond to form the 3-propanoate derivative |CITS: [7353645][7084457]|., The dehydration step is the most energetically-demanding step in the pathway, owing to the poor acidity of the β-hydrogen. The reaction requires activation of the substrate by coenzyme A, followed by a dehydration reaction that involves the formation of a highly reactive ketyl radical that helps to acidify the β-hydrogen |CITS: [18337824]|., The reduction of the 2-oxoacid and the enoate intermediates are catalyzed by dehydrogenases whose combined action consume the reducing equivalents produced by the amino acid oxidation branch of the Stickland reaction |CITS: [6354130]|. The enoate reductase has been assumed to be encoded by the fldZ gene, but in 2017 it has been shown that the reductase is an ETF-dependent dehydrogenase, the product of the |FRAME: G-58752| gene |CITS: [29168502]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13619 Pentalenolactone| is a widely occurring sesquiterpenoid antibiotic produced by some |FRAME: TAX-1883| strains. It was first reported under the name PA 132 in 1957 |CITS: [13425447]|, and subsequently isolated from more than 30 species |CITS: [5808206][5500064]|., |FRAME: CPD-13619 Pentalenolactone| is a specific irreversible inhibitor of the glycolytic enzyme NAD-dependent glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH, |FRAME: GAPOXNPHOSPHN-RXN "EC 1.2.1.12"|) |CITS:[361434][7034785][3736593]|. During the phase of pentalenolactone production, the bacteria express a pentalenolactone-insensitive isoform of GAPDH |CITS:[6822480][2592349][8599535]|., The compound exerts its antibiotic action against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria as well as fungi and protozoa, by a reaction of the electrophilic epoxylactone moiety with the active-site cysteine of GAPDH |CITS:[2930199][8286343][8204587]|. Four molecules of the antibiotic bind to each homotetramer of the enzyme., Pentalenolactone is also a potent and specific antiviral agent, inhibiting the replication of DNA viruses, such as the, causal agent of herpes simplex HSV-1 and HSV-2 |CITS: [4044412]|, and can inhibit vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation |CITS: [11137857]|., About This Pathway, Large (13 kb) biosynthetic gene clusters that were sequenced from several of the |FRAME: CPD-13619|-producing organisms were shown to encode all of the enzymes that are required for synthesis. The gene clusters were named differently in different organisms - pen and ptl in different strains of |FRAME: TAX-1905|, and pnt in |FRAME: TAX-29301|. A related cluster in |FRAME: TAX-33903| is believed to encode the biosynthesis of a related compound, |FRAME: CPDMETA-13642| (see |FRAME: PWY-6919|) |CITS: [19485417]|., The committed step in the biosynthesis of pentalenolactone is the cyclization of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| to the triquinane sesquiterpene |FRAME: CPD-1763|, a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16834| |CITS: [Cane84]|., The next three steps in the pathway are believed to be catalyzed by the same P450 monooxygenase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-14672| (penI, |FRAME: G-14659|) gene, producing |FRAME: CPD-13616|, |FRAME: CPD-13617|, and |FRAME: CPD-13618| in three successive oxygenation steps. An |FRAME: FE+2|,|FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent dioxygenase, encoded by |FRAME: G-14674| (penH, |FRAME: G-14661|) hydroxylates the latter to |FRAME: CPD-13620|., The next step is catalyzed by an NAD+-dependent hydrogenase (|FRAME: G-14673|, pntF, |FRAME: G-14666|), which oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-13620| to the corresponding ketone, |FRAME: CPD-13625|. , So far |FRAME: G-14672|, |FRAME: G-14661| and |FRAME: G-14666| were characterized only in the non |FRAME: CPD-13619|-producer |FRAME: TAX-33903| |CITS: [17017767][16704250][17178094]|., The late steps in the pathway are catalyzed by three additional enzymes. A flavin-dependent monooxygenase, encoded by |FRAME: G-14669|, catalyzes a Baeyer-Villiger reaction, producing |FRAME: CPD-13621|. |FRAME: G-14670 PenD|, another |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, |FRAME: FE+2|-dependent dioxygenase, oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-13621| to either |FRAME: CPD-13632| or |FRAME: CPD-13622|, and can also catalyze the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-13632| to |FRAME: CPD-13622| |CITS: [21250661]|.
