Summary: In dark anoxic environments, where light and inorganic electron acceptors such as oxygen, nitrate, iron, manganese, and sulfate are absent, organic matter is degraded to methane in a process that requires at least four physiologically different microbial groups. The primary fermenting bacteria hydrolyze polymers to monomers and further ferment these monomers to reduced compounds such as alcohols, short-chain fatty acids, organic acids, certain aromatics, hydrogen and CO2. The secondary fermenting bacteria (also called proton-reducing syntrophic bacteria) oxidize these products to acetate, hydrogen and CO2. The two remaining groups, aceticlastic methanogens and hydrogenotrophic methanogens, convert the acetate and the hydrogen and CO2, respectively, into methane |CITS: [9184013]|., The second group, which oxidizes reduced compounds, faces a thermodynamically unfavorable transformation. The oxidation reactions proceed only if hydrogen partial pressure is kept low by coupling with hydrogen-consuming methanogenesis. The process is known as interspecies hydrogen transfer |CITS: [16478444]|. Some examples of such syntrophic reactions include a butanoate and propanoate oxidizers |CITS: [Kamagata05][26771931]|. In addition, several bacteria can oxidize acetate syntrophically when hydrogenotrophic and/or formate-utilizing methanogens are present |CITS: [Zinder84][16347518][Schnurer94][8863449][10939667][30990997][32480003]|. The process is particularly common in environments with high ammonia concentrations, which inhibit aceticlastic methanogens |CITS: [17399981][23835276]|., Syntrophic acetate oxidation was predicted by Barker already in 1936 |CITS: [Barker36]|. The first demonstration of the process was reported in 1984 |CITS: [Zinder84]|, and the responsible organism, which was named strain AOR (for acetate-oxidizing "reversibacter") was isolated in 1988 |CITS: [16347518]|. Unfortunately the strain is no longer available. A second syntrophic acetate-oxidizing bacterium, |FRAME: TAX-45497| (then called Clostridium ultunense strain BS), which could oxidize acetate in the presence of the hydrogenotrophic methanogen |FRAME: TAX-86622|, was reported in 1996 |CITS: [8863449]|. Four more such such organisms, |FRAME: TAX-1089553|, |FRAME: TAX-416591|, |FRAME: TAX-499207|, and |FRAME: TAX-499229|, were reported in 2000, 2002, 2010 and 2011, respectively |CITS: [10939667][12148651][20546311][21498020]|. Pure culture and enzymatic studies affiliated most of these organisms| to the physiological group of acetogens, which produce acetate as the main end product using the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "reductive Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"| when growing heterotrophically., Studies of some of the organisms suggested that they utilize a pathway which is essentially the reverse of the reductive Wood-Ljungdahl pathway when performing acetate oxidation. In this oxidative pathway, theoretically 1 mol of acetate is oxidized to produce 2 moles of CO2 and 8 reducing equivalents (some in the form of molecular hydrogen). However, |FRAME: TAX-45497| and |FRAME: TAX-416591| lack important key genes of the pathway and must use an alternative pathway for acetate oxidation |CITS: [12148651][29690652]|., While it is not known with certainty how the bacteria derive energy from the pathway, candidate reactions include the oxidation of CO and of formate. A genomic analysis of |FRAME: TAX-499229| has shown that it lacks formate dehydrogenase, suggesting that the oxidative pathway can occur in that organism only if formate is removed. The authors suggested possible formation of an electrochemical gradient by putative |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2 "electron-bifurcating Rnf complex"| and |FRAME: FeFe-hydrogenases "[Fe-Fe] hydrogenases"| |CITS: [25811859]|.

General Background, |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL Erythritol| is produced by microorganisms as an osmoprotectant, and occurs naturally in small quantities in mushrooms, fruits such as pears, grapes, and watermelons, and in fermented foods. , Erythritol is a four-carbon polyol that is used a natural sweetener in the food and pharmaceutical industries. It exhibits about 70% of the relative sweetness of sucrose, and was approved as low calorie sweetener by the FDA in 2001. The majority of erythritol (ca. 90%) is not metabolized in the human body and is excreted into urine within 48 h after oral intake, resulting in an extremely low energy value (0.2 - 0.4 kcal/g) |CITS: [28954540]|., Erythritol is produced on an industrial scale through the fermentation of sugars by some yeasts, such as |FRAME: TAX-64607| sp., |CITS: [28954540]|. As of 2018, the world production of erythritol was about 60000 ton/year |CITS: [32095676]|., About This Pathway, Yeast produce |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL| as an osmoprotectant. |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL Erythritol| is biosynthesized from |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, derived from the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|. The pathway consists of the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| to |FRAME: ERYTHROSE| followeed by reduction to |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL| at the expense of NAD(P)H |CITS: [20529366]|., The pathway is used commercially for the production of |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL|. The isolation of |FRAME: TAX-203381| in 1988 (then called Aureobasidium sp. SN-124A) |CITS: [Wako88]|, followed by the development of a mutant with enhanced production |CITS: [Ishizuka89]| lead to the industrial production of erythritol in Japan in 1990. In contrast to ethanol, erythritol hardly suppresses the growth of yeasts, and a high concentration of erythritol (>200 g/L) can be obtained in a batch fermenter |CITS: [19169680]|., Erythrose reductase has been identified and described in a few erythritol-producing yeasts including: Torula sp. |CITS: [12200310]|, |FRAME: TAX-203381| |CITS: [Tokuoka92][23294575]|, |FRAME: TAX-5490| |CITS: [12839736][20529366]|, and |FRAME: TAX-4952| |CITS: [28693571]|., Using stable isotope tracing it has been shown that human erythrocytes are capable of erythritol synthesis from glucose via the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [28484010]|. Both the mammalian alcohol dehydrogenase 1 (ADH1) and sorbitol dehydrogenase (SORD) reduce |FRAME: ERYTHROSE| to |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL| using NADPH |CITS: [31511322]|.

Summary: |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD Oleate| (oleic acid) is the first unsaturated fatty acid that is generated from the saturated, fatty acids produced by the fatty acid synthase. It makes up 55-80% of olive oil (although the free acid may consist only 0.5-2.5%) and 15-20% of grape seed oil and sea buckthorn oil., Oleate synthesis occurs with membrane-bound systems. The desaturase enzymes that produce oleate have been isolated from fungi, yeast, and mammalian liver and found to be specific for |FRAME: STEAROYL-COA|. In plants, on the other hand, oleate is produced via |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs|, an acyl-carrier-protein bound intermediate |CITS: [4831331]|., In most plants, the primary products of fatty acid biosynthesis (|FRAME: PWY-5971|) are |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"| (16:0-ACP) and |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| (18:0-ACP). The enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7072|, which is ubiquitous in plants, introduces the first double bond in |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| while still bound to the ACP protein., The oleate product can either be utilized within the plastid for lipid assembly and further desaturation, or exported to allow further desaturation in the endoplasmic reticulum, as well as incorporation into lipids., The fatty acids that are exported out of the chloroplast are first cleaved from ACP by thioesterases, followed by activation to fatty acyl-CoAs by an outer envelope |FRAME: AT1G77590| activity. Once activated to acyl-CoAs, they are exported to the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [14973169]|., The incorporation into lipids occurs via the |FRAME: TRIGLSYN-PWY "Kennedy pathway"| or via alternative, acyl-CoA-independent enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.158| (PDAT) |CITS: [10829075]| or |FRAME: MONOMER-16590| (DGTA) activities |CITS: [Stobart97]| (see also |FRAME: PWY-782| and |FRAME: PWY-762|)., Other desaturases that insert double bonds in positions other than the δ9 position of 18:0-ACP, have been reported. However, |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is the only fatty acid that is desaturated in its ACP-bound form. All other desaturation reactions occur only after the fatty acid has been attached to a glycerolipid backbone. Unusual unsaturated fatty acids are mostly found in seed storage lipids.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ILE| is almost always synthesized from |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|. In the most, common pathway, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is generated from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| via, |FRAME: THR| (see |FRAME:PWY-3001|)., The key enzyme in that pathway is |FRAME:THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10493| gene., In addition to the standard pathway, microorganisms have developed several alternative pathways for, |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis. |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be synthesized from |FRAME: GLT| via |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| (this pathway) |CITS: [4550817]|, from |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5101|) |CITS: [4607875][4808901][15292141]|, and from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| by carboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-5104|) |CITS: [5800441][1212197][Eikmanns83a]|)., In addition, there are several reports that under anaerobic conditions some anaerobic bacteria can carboxylate, |FRAME: CPD-7076| to |FRAME: ILE| via |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5108|) |CITS: [5813342][6726176][6440485]|., About This Pathway, This pathway was first described in 1962 by Abramsky et al, who observed that in |FRAME: TAX-566546|, |FRAME:L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| was exclusively converted to |FRAME: ILE| |CITS: [13859068]|., The authors suggested a pathway in which |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| is transaminated to, |FRAME: METHYLOXALO-ACETATE| (based on earlier reports by |CITS: [13766613]|), followed by decarboxylation, to |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|, which is then used for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ILE| in the, "conventional" manner. The proposed pathway was substantiated by a second paper published, by the same group |CITS: [14342322]|. However, the biological significance of this pathway was not clear,, as it was not known whether |FRAME:L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| occurs naturally in |FRAME: TAX-566546|., In 1972 Phillips et al have demonstrated that a different strain of |FRAME:TAX-562| (|FRAME: ORG-5900|, ATCC 8739), was able to synthesize |FRAME: ILE| from |FRAME: GLT|. The authors were able to demonstrate activity, in crude extracts of several enzymes, including the key enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7027|, which converts |FRAME:GLT|, to |FRAME:L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE|, as well as |FRAME: MONOMER-11907| |CITS: [4550817]|., Please note that the last 4 steps in this pathway are identical to the "common" |FRAME: ILE| biosynthetic pathway., For information about |FRAME: TAX-83333| enzymes catalyzing these steps, see the pathway |FRAME:PWY-3001|.

Triacylglycerol (TAG) metabolism in yeast is realized by a number of anabolic and catabolic pathways which include the esterification and re-esterification of the various intermediates such a mono- and diacylglycerols. The enzymes involved in the metabolism of acylglycerols and glycerolipids in Saccharomyces cerevisiae have been shown to be associated with membranous organelles, particularly the endoplasmatic reticulum and lipid droplets and shown to be conserved between yeast and mammals |CITS:[22345606]|. The conversion of monoacylglycerols to diacylglycerols or other precursors for glycerophospholipids may utilize different paths and contribute significantly to the regulation of triacylglycerol homeostasis during the different developmental phases of growth in yeast |CITS:[20231294]|. Although it has been shown that the biosynthesis of storage lipids such as steryl esters and triacylglycerol (TAG) is non-essential in yeast it may positively influence the long term survival under certain stress conditions such as nitrogen starvation |CITS:[11741946]|., The pathway depicted here exemplifies the various metabolic possibilities monoacylglycerols have in the biochemical scheme of TAG and phospholipid catabolic and anabolic processes. The only monoacylglycerol lipase in yeast, i.e. YUJ3p was shown to accept both |FRAME:CPD-11690| and |FRAME:CPD0-1812| as substrates indicating that the spontaneous racemization of the sn-2 to the sn-1 (or sn-3) position (see |FRAME:LIPAS-PWY|) is not a necessity for enzymatic activity |CITS:[10515935] [20554061]|. The buildup of diacylglycerols from monoacylglycerols has been demonstrated by the bifunctional acyl-CoA: acylglycerol acyltransferase (DGA1). While DGA1p is the only acyl-CoA dependent diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) in TAG formation |CITS:[11751830]| the enzyme also acts as acyl-CoA dependent monoacylglycerol acyltransferase (MGAT) |CITS:[20554061]|. In addition, the acyl-CoA independent phospholipid: diacylglycerol acyltransferase (PDAT) in yeast encoded by LRO1 |CITS:[10829075]| had been reported to utilize monoacylglycerols as well, hence may be involved in the formation of DAG as an gateway compound to the biosynthesis of phosphoglycerides |CITS:[18037386]|. Finally, the CTP dependent diacylglycerol kinase encoded by DGK1 |CITS:[18458076]| is suspected to convert monoacylglycerols into lysophospholipids which may be discharged into phosphatidate and phospholipid metabolic pathways (see for example |FRAME:PWY-7411|, |FRAME:PWY-7417|) |CITS:[20554061]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CHORISMATE Chorismate| is an intermediate in the synthesis of three amino acids: |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. In addition it is a precursor of folic acid, ubiquinone, menaquinone, and enterochelin |CITS:[4200844][BSUB225]|. |FRAME: CHORISMATE Chorismate| is synthesized from |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE|, which can be synthesized in different pathways in different organisms., In this pathway, which describes |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| biosynthesis in bacteria,  it is synthesized from the common central metabolism intermediate |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| in two steps. The pathway describes the first part of the shikimate pathway (see |FRAME: ARO-PWY|), and is found in prokaryotes (mostly bacteria) and several eukaryotes, including ascomycete fungi, apicomplexans, plants and algae |CITS: [16963634]|., In |FRAME: TAX-562|, the first reaction in the pathway is catalyzed by three separate enzymes, each of which is subject to feedback inhibition by one of the three amino acids that are synthesized from chorismate - |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|.  , The enzyme subject to regulation by tryptophan (encoded by |FRAME: EG10080|) cannot be inhibited more than 60 percent, ensuring that sufficient enzymatic activity is present to permit synthesis of the other four metabolites synthesized from chorismate even in the presence of all three amino acids |CITS: [Pittard04]|.

Summary: The strictly anaerobic, thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1515| is the microorganism with the fastest documented growth rate on the recalcitrant substrate crystalline |FRAME: CELLULOSE| |CITS: [12209002]|. Unlike fungal cellulases,  |FRAME: TAX-1515| is able to completely solubilize crystalline forms of cellulose such as cotton and |FRAME: CPD-13204| |CITS: [16346009]|. The organism achieves this remarkable ability by forming very large extracellular multi-enzyme complexes, known as cellulosomes. The complex has a diameter of 18 nm and a mass in excess of 2000 kDa |CITS: [10390637]|. , Similar complexes are formed by related Clostridia (such as |FRAME: TAX-1488|, |FRAME: TAX-1521|, |FRAME: TAX-1493|, |FRAME: TAX-1499| and |FRAME: TAX-29362|) and other anaerobic cellulose-degrading bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-35830|, |FRAME: TAX-35825| and |FRAME: TAX-1264| |CITS: [19107866]|. Although these bacteria cannot readily utilize carbohydrates other than cellodextrins |CITS: [15755956]|, the cellulosome contains not just endo- and exo-cellulases but also a number of hemicellulolytic enzymes, including xylanases, non-glucanolytic polysaccharide hydrolases and lyases, feruloyl esterases etc. The function of the non-cellulolytic enzymes is presumably the unwrapping of the cellulose crystals from the covering matrix of |FRAME: Lignins lignin|, |FRAME: Pectin pectin| and |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|., The cellulosome is a modular complex. The center of the complex consists of a central non-catalytic protein known as the |FRAME: MONOMER-16412 scaffoldin| (CipA), which binds up to nine catalytic subunits |CITS: [Wu88]|. The attachment of each catalytic subunit is mediated by the interaction of its type I dockerin domain with one of the nine type I cohesin domains of CipA |CITS: [7568112]|. CipA is, in turn, bound to the cell surface by the interaction of its type II dockerin domain with the type II cohesin domain of one of three S-layer anchor proteins, |FRAME: MONOMER-16407 SdbA|, |FRAME: MONOMER-16410 Orf2p|, or |FRAME: MONOMER-16411 OlpB| |CITS: [10049808 ]|.Each of these anchor proteins contains a C-terminal S-layer homology module that mediates attachment to the bacterial cell surface, and a different number of type II cohesin modules capable of binding CipA molecules. Thus different anchoring scaffoldins form cellulosome complexes of differing sizes. The smallest one, |FRAME: MONOMER-16407|, contains one cohesin domain, and thus binds one CipA molecule along with the nine catalytic units bound to it. , The medium size |FRAME: MONOMER-16410| contains two cohesin domains and thus binds two CipA molecules and forms complexes with 18 catalytic units. The most abundant anchor protein is |FRAME: MONOMER-16411|, which contains seven cohesin domains and forms complexes of up to 63 catalytic units. In addition to nine type I cohesin domains and a type II dockerin domain, the CipA scaffoldin also contains a type III cellulose-binding module for attachment of the complex to cellulose |CITS: [8316083]|. Many of the catalytic units also contain carbohydrate-binding domains with differing specificities.The exact composition of the cellulosomes depend on growth rate and the nature of substrates available. A 2007 experiment that compared the protein components of cellulosomes formed under conditions of growth on either |FRAME: CELLOBIOSE| or |FRAME: CPD-13204| found significant differences |CITS: [17644599]|. Over 70 proteins that possess type I dockerin modules have been identified in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-203119| |CITS: [19758121]|.

Summary: General Background, The mycotoxin |FRAME: CPD-10167| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the mycotoxin |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN|. |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of the B-group and G-group aflatoxins, which constitute the major groups of naturally occurring aflatoxins. The production of aflatoxins by some strains of several |FRAME:TAX-5052| species has been extensively studied. However many species, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425 "Emericella nidulans (previously known as Aspergullus nidulans)"|, produce only |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| as a final product (in |CITS: [18486503]|). |FRAME: TAX-5067| produces both B- and G-group aflatoxins from |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587|, while |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces only B-group aflatoxins. The biological role of these mycotoxins in fungi remains unclear (in |CITS: [17620135] [18246345]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|). , Aflatoxins are highly toxic and carcinogenic crop contaminants that create major economic and public health problems worldwide. Much research has been focused on identifying compounds that inhibit aflatoxin biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-4592| is metabolized by mammalian liver cytochrome P450 enzymes to a mutagenic epoxide that covalently binds to DNA. Its genotoxic mechanism of action has been studied in yeast |CITS: [8968101] [9771940]|. Other species, such as |FRAME: TAX-5062| and |FRAME:TAX-41058|, are unable to produce aflatoxins and are used in food fermentation |CITS: [17665189]|., Most of the aflatoxin biosynthetic genes are clustered in Aspergilli and are positively regulated by gene aflR (in |CITS: [17620135] [16448506] [16108793] [15094053] [7618880] [16535712]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]| and |CITS: [15006741]|). The enzyme reactions and biosynthetic intermediates in the aflatoxin biosynthetic pathway have been reviewed in detail |CITS: [15022028]|. See MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5955|, |FRAME: PWY-5956|, |FRAME: PWY-5959|, |FRAME: PWY-5960| and |FRAME: PWY-5961|., About This Pathway, The mycotoxin |FRAME: CPD-10167| has been shown exert its toxic effect by uncoupling mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [6712217]|. Although its biosynthesis as part of the biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN|, |FRAME: CPD-4592|, |FRAME: CPD-10177|, |FRAME: CPD-10178|, and |FRAME: CPD-10179| has been well studied, the initial reactions that produce the first isolable intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-12588|, remained incompletely characterized. This has recently changed with the detailed characterization of the nonreducing iterative polyketide synthase, |FRAME: MONOMER-17895| encoded by gene aflC (pksA) |CITS: [22452347]|., PksA utilizes a |FRAME: HEXANOATE| starter unit that is produced by a novel type I fatty acid synthase (hexanoate synthase) distinct from that of primary metabolism. This hexanoate synthase is encoded by genes aflA (fas-2, hexB) and aflB (fas-1, hexA). It utilizes |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to produce |FRAME: HEXANOATE| for the polyketide synthase reactions that follow |CITS: [TOWNSEND84]|. , Earlier studies suggested that the fatty acid synthase and the polyketide synthase form a multienzyme complex that utilizes |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and |FRAME: NADPH| to produce |FRAME: CPD-10162| |CITS: [8807876] [16256699] [12323372]|. The product of the fatty acid synthase reaction was thought to be a free |FRAME: HEXANOYL-COA| intermediate (in |CITS: [15022028]|). However later studies suggested that the hexanoyl unit may be transferred directly from the fatty acid synthase to the polyketide synthase by transthioesterification and not released as a free intermediate |CITS: [17071746] [18403714]|., The polyketide synthase adds seven malonyl-derived units to the hexanoyl starter unit to ultimately form the polyketide backbone. It also mediates cyclization and release of |FRAME: CPD-12588|. |FRAME: CPD-12588 "Norsolorinate anthrone"| is then oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-10162| (|CITS: [17071746] [18403714]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028][15006741][21079635]|)., The |FRAME: MONOMER-15818| product of gene hypC in |FRAME: TAX-5067| oxidizes |FRAME: CPD-12588| to |FRAME: CPD-10162|. This monooxygenase was found to be similar to the anthrone oxidases of bacteria. A putative catalytic mechanism was proposed. However, this anthrone oxidase did not appear to be essential because ΔhypC mutants produced aflatoxins and accumulated |FRAME: CPD-10162|, suggesting that an alternative nonenzymatic route for |FRAME: CPD-12588| oxidation may also occur |CITS: [20348292]|., |FRAME: CPD-10162 "Norsolorinate"| is considered the first stable, isolable, pigmented precursor of |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and the aflatoxins. It is formed by the stereospecific norsolorinate reductase that determines the course of the subsequent reactions shown. Following hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-10163|, two stereoisomers are produced and both are converted to |FRAME: CPD-10166|. There is disagreement in the literature as to whether averufanin is an intermediate in this series of reactions. A cyclase converts |FRAME: CPD-10166| to |FRAME: CPD-10167| (reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|).

Summary: Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., The initial stage of dental caries requires the fermentation of sugars to acid in dental plaque. Caries formation in the presence of readily fermentable carbohydrates, such as sucrose, has led to the use of sugar substitutes, such as the sugar alcohols (hexitols) |FRAME: SORBITOL|, which is added to sugar-free gums and lozenges, and |FRAME: MANNITOL|, which is used as a sweetener in "breath-freshening" candies., Sorbitol and mannitol are  found naturally in some fruits and berries (see |FRAME:PWY-5054| and |FRAME: PWY-3881|). In addition, sorbitol is used in medicines and tooth paste, and mannitol is used as a sweetener for people with diabetes. , Initial studies indicated that sugar alcohols have a low or no cariogenicity. More recently, however, the frequent use of sugar alcohol-containing products has been shown to result in increased levels of sugar alcohols utilizing bacteria |CITS:[4145128][6592773]|., Several oral strains of |FRAME: TAX-1301| can ferment sugar alcohols. The only mechanism found to date for the transport of sorbitol and mannitol into the cell is by dedicated phosphoenolpyruvate:sugar phosphotransferase systems (PTS), which phosphorylate sorbitol and mannitol to |FRAME: D-SORBITOL-6-P| and |FRAME:MANNITOL-1P|, respectively, during the transport |CITS: [1945499][1896926][10639465][10878121]|. The intracellular sugar phosphates are then oxidized by |FRAME: SORB6PDEHYDROG-CPLX| and |FRAME:MONOMER-13098|, respectively, to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| that enters glycolysis., The final product of glycolysis, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, can then be metabolized in different routes, leading to the formation of |FRAME:L-LACTATE|, |FRAME:FORMATE|, |FRAME:ETOH| and |FRAME:ACET|, depending on the conditions. In the presence of excess glucose the main fermentation product is |FRAME:L-LACTATE|, but under glucose limitation only |FRAME:FORMATE|, |FRAME:ETOH| and |FRAME:ACET| are formed |CITS: [4531871][1176435]|., The pathway is regulated by catabolite repression through multiple regulation points. When glucose is present, PTS-mediated sugar alcohol transport and phosphorylation are inhibited |CITS: [6401708]|. Another major point of regulation is the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7363|, which in many strains requires |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| for activity |CITS: [1176435][6840832]|. When glucose concentration is low, there is not enough |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| to activate |FRAME:CPLX-7363|, and pyruvate is routed towards the production of |FRAME:FORMATE|, |FRAME:ETOH| and |FRAME:ACET|. In other strains |FRAME:CPLX-7358| depends on |FRAME:GLC-6-P| |CITS: [240810][7054143]|.

Summary: Phytohormones such as |FRAME:CPD-693| (ABA) are instrumental in plant growth and developmental processes and adaptive responses to alterations of endogenous conditions and environmental stimuli. For instance, |FRAME:CPD-693| controls seed dormancy and germination |CITS:[Nambara10]|, regulates enzyme activities in fatty acid accumulation |CITS:[18823922]|, triggers signaling pathways |CITS:[21976481]|, affects the onset of ripening |CITS:[Owen09]|, and adjusts to various stresses such as dehydration |CITS:[Andrade08]| and cold |CITS:[22669585] [22304971]|. Of utmost importance for controlling all those activities is the homeostasis of |FRAME:CPD-693| which is maintained by a fine-tuned network of anabolic and catabolic processes |CITS:[16669782] [15862093] [Cutler09]|. , The central anabolic sequence generating |FRAME:CPD-693| is the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-693| (see |FRAME:PWY-695|) whereas several routes exist that can degrade |FRAME:CPD-693|. The major catabolic pathway for |FRAME:CPD-693| has been considered to be the 8'-hydroxylation pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5271| which generates the inactive ABA-derivatives |FRAME:CPD-7725| and |FRAME:CPD-7726| |CITS:[15862093]|. In addition, the 7'-hydroxylated, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17688| (see |FRAME:PWY-7642| and 9'-hydroxylated metabolites (this pathway) also produce inactive ABA-derivatives. In contrast to the former catabolic pathways which irreversibly remove active ABA from the equilibrium of the cell, the |FRAME:PWY-5272| pathway retains a metabolite, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-7727| which can be readily converted back to |FRAME:CPD-693| |CITS:[Schwartz10] [Zaharia05]|., The |FRAME:PWY-7640| pathway produces the spontaneously cyclized |FRAME:CPD-7729| from |FRAME:CPD-7728| |CITS:[14671016]|, the former being an ABA derivative which has been found in a varieties of plants such as Nicotiana tabacum |CITS:[19782241]|, Hordeum vulgare |CITS:[22669585]| , Brassica napus |CITS:[18823922]| , Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[21976481]| and also in fruits of Citrus sinensis and Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[14671016]|. It has been demonstrated that the genes encoding for abscisic acid 8'-hydroxylases (|FRAME:AT4G19230|, |FRAME:AT2G29090|, |FRAME:AT5G45340|, |FRAME:AT3G19270|) are also able to catalyze the 9'-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-693| as a side-reaction indicating another flexibility in the regulation of the cellular concentration of |FRAME:CPD-693| |CITS:[21414645]|.

Summary: Ergot alkaloids are a complex family of indole derivatives with diverse structures and biological activities. They are toxins, produced by some fungi from the families |FRAME: TAX-34397|, |FRAME: TAX-28568| and |FRAME: TAX-34384|., Some of these compounds and their semi-synthetic derivatives are important drugs in modern medicine, such as |FRAME: CPD-12363| and |FRAME: CPD-14462|, which are used for the treatment of migraines. |FRAME: CPD-12363 Ergotamine| , along with |FRAME: CPD-14457|, have also been used for a very long time as uterine contracting agents following childbirth., |FRAME: CPD-12363 Ergotamine| is the major alkaloid produced by |FRAME: TAX-5111| and related species., The early part of the pathway is common to all three families and ends with |FRAME: CPD-14459| (see |FRAME: PWY-6493|). This compound is an important branching point, and is converted to different products within the different fungal families. Within the |FRAME: TAX-34397|, such as |FRAME: TAX-40602|, an enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-15215| converts |FRAME: CPD-14459| to |FRAME: CPD-12357| |CITS: [21494745]|, which is then converted to assorted amides and peptides of |FRAME: CPD-12364|, known as ergoamides and ergopeptines, respectively., The potent synthetic hallucinogen |FRAME: CPD-14458| (LSD) is a diethylamide of this intermediate., A biosynthetic gene cluster involved in ergot alkaloids biosynthesis has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-5111|. While not all steps have been associated with an enzyme, the |FRAME: G-11992| gene was shown to encode a cytochrome P-450 enzyme that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12359| from |FRAME: CPD-12358|, while |FRAME: G-11999| and |FRAME: G-15216| encode two non-ribosomal peptide synthases that form the subunits of a very large complex that catalyzes the addition of a tripeptide tail to the lysergic moiety |CITS: [19672909]|. The last step in the pathway is a hydroxylation by a dioxygenase that results in formation of the final product |CITS: [24361048]|.

Summary: General Background, At the time of this review, over 130 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity. Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana. GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and GA4 enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed. It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis., Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). During active growth, the plant will maintain gibberellin homeostasis by metabolizing most gibberellins by rapid hydroxylation to inactive conjugates. Active |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed in the disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen produces large amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Inactive conjugates might be stored or translocated via the phloem and xylem before their release (activation) at the proper time and in the proper tissue., About This Pathway, The irreversible deactivation of GAs is achieved by 2β-hydroxylation of the active form. This reaction is performed by dioxygenases known as gibberellin 2-oxidases (GA 2-oxidases) which are essential for effective regulation of GA concentration in planta. In some tissues such as the cotyledons and the testae of some developing seeds, 2β-hydroxylation is pushed further to form a ketone, hence giving rise to compounds known as 'GA-catabolites'. These catabolites appear as dicarboxylic acids with an open lactone ring. It has however been postulated that this open form might be artefactual and the result of the analytical procedure. Study of recombinant GA 2-oxidases expressed in E .coli showed that ketone formation is relatively inefficient and only occurs when the enzymes is present at high concentrations |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|. Deactivation of gibberellins by 2β-hydroxylation is not observed in |FRAME:TAX-5127|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

While |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| (18:1Δ9) is the most commonly found mono-unsaturated fatty acid, in plant oils, a number of other mono-unsaturated fatty acid species naturally accumulate in some plants. |FRAME: CPD-8477 "Petroselinate"| ((6Z)-octadec-6-enoate) is the principal fatty acid of the seed oil of most |FRAME: TAX-4037| (Umbelliferae) and |FRAME: TAX-4286| species, such as |FRAME: TAX-4039| (carrot) and |FRAME: TAX-4047| (coriander). , Unlike the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-14393| ((6Z)-hexadec-6-enoate|) which is derived from |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs palmitoyl-[acp]| in a single step catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.26| (see |FRAME: PWY-5362|), the biosynthesis |FRAME: CPD-8477| involves both desaturation and elongation steps., Curiously, evidence suggests that |FRAME: CPD-8477| is formed using acyl-carrier protein-bound intermediates, and not fatty acids bound to a glycerolipid or coenzyme A |CITS: [11669576]|., Several steps are required, including a 4-desaturase, a 3-oxoacyl synthase and others. The enzymes appear to be specialized for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-8477|, and were found specifically expressed in the coriander seed endosperm |CITS: [11669576]|.

|FRAME:GLUTATHIONE Glutathione| represents an ubiquitous thiol-containing tripeptide which occurs in almost all eukaryotes |CITS:[3657565]|. It is regarded as an important cell redox buffer, has been shown to play pivotal roles in iron metabolism, is involved in detoxification processes of endogenous toxins and xenobiotics, and provides resistance against heavy metals and oxidative stress (summarized in |CITS:[12702279][12809732]|. In addition, |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| is a valuable cell resource for sulfur and nitrogen |CITS:[6137189]| and integrated in the complex network of protein regulation via S-glutathionylation |CITS:[24396728]|., The maintenance of |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| homeostasis in the cell is critical in terms of protection against a wide range of stress factors and the normal function of numerous cell processes. Consequently, biosynthesis and degradation of |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| which is summarized in the |FRAME:PWY-4041| is tightly regulated |CITS:[22170048]|. However, it appears that in Saccharomyces cerevisiae this cycle is truncated and several enzymes of the |FRAME:PWY-4041| do not operate in Saccharomyces |CITS:[Jaspers85]|. Only the vacuolar γ-glutamyl transpeptidase encoded by ECM38 had been characterized and found to be able to degrade |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE|, and had been consequently considered to be the main player in the catabolic part of |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| metabolism |CITS:[6102906][6143574][11672438]|. , However, a new pathway operating in the cytosol and coined DUG (Defective in Utilization of Glutathione) (this pathway) was identified |CITS:[17179087][12620619]| and appears to be the only pathway involved in |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| homeostasis by degrading |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| in Saccharomyces |CITS:[22170048]| but also in Candida |CITS:[21994941]|. Three genes, i.e. DUG1, DUG2 and DUG3 encode for the set of reactions which convert |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| into |FRAME:CYS| progressively releasing |FRAME:GLT| and |FRAME:GLY|. The first enzyme, i.e. glutathione hydrolase is interesting with regard to the interactions taking place between the two involved enzymes - DUG2p and DUG3p. DUG2p belongs to the M20A family of metallopeptidases and does not exhibit any catalytic activity. However, it serves as an scaffolding enzyme binding DUG3p, an enzyme with an functional glutamine amidotransferase II domain (N-terminal hydrolase enzyme family) and building an degradosomal complex (DUG2p-DUG3p)2 which only in this form is able to degrade |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| yielding |FRAME:CYS-GLY| under release of |FRAME:GLT| |CITS:[17179087] [22277648]|. The subsequent reaction, the cleavage of |FRAME:CYS-GLY| forming |FRAME:CYS| and |FRAME:GLY| is catalyzed by the CYS-GLY metallopeptidase encoded by DUG1 |CITS:[17179087][19346245]|. Whereas the DUG2-DUG3 genes are transcriptional regulated and dependent on the availability of sulfur, DUG1 is constitutively expressed and independent of sulfur supply. Overall, biochemical and genetic evidence confirms the involvement of the DUG pathway in the cellular homeostasis of |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| and sulfur |CITS:[22277648]|.

Summary: General Background, The anaerobic fermentation of purines was first observed in the organisms |FRAME: TAX-1556| and, |FRAME: TAX-1495| in 1942 |CITS:[16560499]|. , These organisms can utilize only a small number of purine derivatives including |FRAME:PURINE|,, |FRAME: CPD-9017|, |FRAME: CPD-9016|, |FRAME:HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME:GUANINE| and, |FRAME:XANTHINE| under anaerobic conditions as carbon, nitrogen, and energy sources, and are, unable to ferment any other organic compounds., The purines |FRAME:URATE|, |FRAME:GUANINE| and |FRAME:XANTHINE| are readily, decomposed by these organisms, while growth on |FRAME:HYPOXANTHINE| is appreciably, slower, and |FRAME:ADENINE| does not support growth at all |CITS:[16560499]|., The slow growth on |FRAME:HYPOXANTHINE| was explained upon the characterization of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7371| from |FRAME: TAX-1495|. The enzyme was shown to catalyze not only the, reversible conversion of |FRAME: URATE| to |FRAME: XANTHINE|, but also the oxidation of most other, substrates, sometimes requiring multiple steps, eventually converging at |FRAME: XANTHINE|., While the enzyme is able to oxidize hypoxanthine to xanthine, this reaction proceeded very slowly, |CITS: [13278325]|., The products of this fermentation were identified as |FRAME: AMMONIA|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, and |FRAME: ACET|. Early studies using tracer experiments revealed that |FRAME: GLY|,, |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: SER| were intermediates of the pathway |CITS: [Barker41], [16589398][13278324][13366899]|., Work by Rabinowitz and coworkers helped discover many of the intermediates of this pathway., The intermediates |FRAME:4-AMINO-5-IMIDAZOLE_CARBOXYLATE| and |FRAME:CPD-54| were, discovered first |CITS: [13278326]|, followed by |FRAME:5-UREIDO-4-IMIDAZOLE_CARBOXYLATE|, |CITS: [13278327]| and |FRAME:N-FORMIMINO-GLYCINE| |CITS: [13367024]|., The next step of the pathway is the transfer of a formimino group from |FRAME:N-FORMIMINO-GLYCINE|, to the single-carbon carrier |FRAME:THF|, generating |FRAME: GLY| and |FRAME:CPD-671|., The discovery of this step eventually lead Rabinowitz to focus on folate metabolism, where he made, significant contributions., Deciphering the later steps of the pathway was more complex., Formate is generated via the intermediates |FRAME: 5-10-METHENYL-THF| and |FRAME:10-FORMYL-THF|,, by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13125| (EC 4.3.1.4), |FRAME:MONOMER-13130| (EC 3.5.4.9), and |FRAME:CPLX-7369| (EC 6.3.4.3) |CITS: [13907490]|., Formate is then converted to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| by an |FRAME:CPLX-7375|. See below, for discussion of other branches., About This Pathway, Rresearch conducted about two decades after the intial characterization of the pathway has shown that, several branches of this pathway are modified when the cells are supplied with selenium, due to the, activation of certain |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE|-containing enzymes., While in the original pathway (|FRAME:PWY-5497|) purines are oxidized largely via |FRAME: URATE|, by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7371|, in selenium-supplemented cells a second enzyme, the, |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE|-containing |FRAME:CPLX-7376|, oxidizes purines directly to, |FRAME: XANTHINE| |CITS: [10860985]|., A second major change is the activation of the selenium-dependent |FRAME:CPLX-7378|,, an enzyme complex that reduces |FRAME: GLY| directly to |FRAME: ACETYL-P|, bypassing , many of the steps that are required when selenium is not available |CITS: [6833177][762072]|., Initially it was believed that |FRAME:CPLX-7378| produces |FRAME:ACET| directly, but more research, showed that the actual product is |FRAME: ACETYL-P|, which is converted to |FRAME:ACET|, by |FRAME:MONOMER-13133| in a step that provides most of the energy that these organisms, generate from purine fermentation |CITS: [Arkowitz89]|.

Summary: General Background, Vitamin B12 (also known as adenosylcobalamin or |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|) was discovered in the 1920s after Minot and Murphy reported that they could cure the symptoms of pernicious anaemia by feeding patients with crude liver extract |CITS: [Minot26]| (they received the Nobel prize in 1934 for this discovery)., The unknown factor has been isolated and subsequently crystallized in 1948 |CITS:[Lester48][Rickes48]|, and was given the name vitamin B12 and, as it was shown to contain a cobalt ion, cobalamin |CITS: [12195810]|., Vitamin B12 is one of the most structurally complex small molecules made in Nature. It contains a contracted porphinoid ring with a cobalt ion ligated at its center and further held in place by a lower axial base (a dimethylbenzimidazole) and an upper methyl or adenosyl group. Its biosynthesis is similarly complex, and requires more than thirty genes. It's biosynthesis is confined to only some bacteria and archaea |CITS: [11935176]|., Two main pathways are known for |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthesis - an aerobic pathway (see |FRAME:P381-PWY|) and an anaerobic pathway (this pathway). The main differences between these pathways are the timing of the |FRAME: CO+2| ion insertion and the ring-contraction mechanism (for more about ring contraction, see |CITS: [16592942]|). |FRAME: CO+2| is inserted early on in the anaerobic pathway, and rather late in the aerobic pathway., The two different routes then merge at |FRAME: CPD-689|, and the latter part of the pathway is identical, or at least very similar., About This Pathway, The best characterized anaerobic pathway is the one from |FRAME: TAX-90371|, although much of the early work was performed with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1752| and much of the more recent work was done with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1404|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| starts with the biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole intermediate |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of several important compounds such as |FRAME: Hemes heme| and |FRAME: Chlorophylls chlorophyl|. |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III "Uroporphyrinogen-III"| is converted to a corrin ring by a complex process that involves (among other things) the attachment of eight methyl groups, all derived from |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM)., During the process the ring contracts via bonding of carbons C-1 and C-19, eliminating carbon C-20 from the ring. This contraction process converts the ring from a porphyrin ring to a corrin ring. Both the C-20 carbon and the added C-20 methyl group are lost in the form of |FRAME: ACETALD|., The intermediates formed prior to the formation of the corrin ring are called precorrins. The precorrins are numbered corresponding to the number of methyl groups that have been already introduced. If two different intermediates have the same number of methyl groups, they are also labeled by A or B (as in |FRAME:CPD-675|). If there is still some uncertainty about an intermediate, it is given a temporary designation of X or Y., There is indeed some uncertainty about the path from |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| to |FRAME: CPD-9040|. Early work, performed mostly with |FRAME: TAX-28901|, suggested that this transition may be catalyzed in two steps - the insertion of cobalt into |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-10021|, followed by methylation by |FRAME: G-10057|. However, information gathered from multiple studies, most recently with the aerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1404| that posseses a complete anaerobic pathway, suggests that this conversion may proceed through the oxidized factor intermediates, which is favored for the ease of cobalt insertion. Thus, |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| is first oxidized to |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| by |FRAME: STM3477|. Cobalt in then inserted (either by |FRAME: G-10021| or |FRAME: G-11338|), followed by methylation to |FRAME: COBALT-FACTOR-III| and reduction to |FRAME: CPD-9040| |CITS: [12408752][17567575][16042604][12917443][12686546][23155054]|., The first intermediate with a corrin ring is |FRAME:CPD-9049|. However, this intermediate still needs to be modified extensively. Successive amidation reactions transfer amide groups from two |FRAME: GLN| molecules to the carboxy groups a and c, resulting in |FRAME:CPD-689| - the point where the early-insertion and late-insertion pathways combine. , Additional steps in the pathway of cobalamin biosynthesis are described in |FRAME: PWY-5509| and |FRAME: PWY-5507|.

Summary: Please note: This pathway does not represent a single organism. Rather, it is a superpathway, assembled from pathways found in a variety of organisms. Its purpose is to provide an overview, of the diversity of ways that microorganisms can degrade |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| and their precursors or derivatives., Degradation of the pectin metabolite |FRAME: CPD-37|:, In |FRAME: TAX-198628 "Dickeya dadantii 3937 (previously known as Erwinia chrysanthemi strain 3937)"| the main pathway for degradation of the polygalacturonate component of pectin involves production of the monomer |FRAME: CPD-37|. It is degraded intracellularly by isomerization to |FRAME: CPD-343| followed by reduction to the common metabolite |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE|. |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| is phosphorylated and then cleaved by an aldolase encoded by gene kdgA which produces the central metabolites |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. In |FRAME:TAX-562| the aldolase encoded by gene eda is involved in the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|. However, in |FRAME: TAX-556| this enzyme does not appear to be involved in |FRAME: GLUCONATE| catabolism and no product of the edd gene that encodes the |FRAME: PGLUCONDEHYDRAT-MONOMER| of the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY| could be detected in various species of |FRAME:TAX-551|. These observations question the existence of the Entner-Doudoroff pathway in these organisms (|CITS: [8145647]| and reviewed in |CITS: [8905080]|). See subpathway |FRAME: PWY-6507|., |FRAME: Beta-D-Glucuronides|, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation in |FRAME:TAX-562|:, In |FRAME:TAX-562| K-12, degradation of |FRAME: Beta-D-Glucuronides| begins with hydrolysis to yield |FRAME: GLUCURONATE|. This compound is isomerized to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| and reduced to |FRAME: D-MANNONATE|. Analogous reactions occur in |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation, forming |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| and |FRAME: D-ALTRONATE|. Dehydration of |FRAME: D-MANNONATE| and |FRAME: D-ALTRONATE| yields the common metabolite |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE|. The product of gene kdgK phosphorylates it to yield |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, which enters central metabolism via the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|. See subpathways |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|., Oxidative |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation in bacteria:, In the oxidative pathway for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| and |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| degradation found in some bacteria, these compounds are oxidized by an inducible uronate dehydrogenase |CITS: [19060141]|. This conversion may occur via a 1.4-lactone |CITS: [19921179] [2471]|. The lactone is thought to spontaneously hydrolyze (in |CITS: [19897761] [2471] [19921179]|). It is not known if the lactone form can be utilized directly by the following enzyme, or if cleavage to the linear acid form is required. The pathway proceeds to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate) formation, which can be metabolized in the |FRAME: TCA|, or used in many other pathways. Reviewed in |CITS: [19159926]|. In |FRAME: TAX-62977 "Acinetobacter sp. ADP1 (previously known as Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1)"| genes encoding enzymes for the degradation of |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE| have been identified. Compound intermediates in the pathway were also identified |CITS: [18364348]|. See subpathways |FRAME: PWY-6501|, |FRAME: PWY-6486|, |FRAME: PWY-6499| and |FRAME: PWY-6497|., |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE| degradation in |FRAME:TAX-562|:, |FRAME:TAX-562| can use both |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE| as the sole source of carbon for growth. The initial step in their degradation is dehydration to |FRAME: 5-KETO-4-DEOXY-D-GLUCARATE|. The subsequent steps include cleavage of this compound into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: TARTRONATE-S-ALD|, reduction of |FRAME: TARTRONATE-S-ALD| to |FRAME: GLYCERATE|, and its phosphorylation to form |FRAME: 2-PG|. See subpathways |FRAME: GLUCARDEG-PWY| and |FRAME: GALACTARDEG-PWY|., Reductive |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation in fungi:, In this pathway the degradation of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| occurs via L-compounds |CITS: [18768163]|. The first step is reductive. In |FRAME: TAX-5061| a reversible reaction catalyzed by a reductase that can utilize |FRAME: NADH| or |FRAME: NADPH| converts |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| to |FRAME: CPD0-1083|. This reductase is the product of gene GAAA in |FRAME: TAX-5061|, with an ortholog GAR2 in |FRAME: TAX-51453|. It is co-expressed in |FRAME: TAX-5061| along with GAAB encoding a L-galactonate dehydratase, and GAAC and GAAD encoding the putative aldolase and L-glyceraldehyde reductase, respectively. These genes are evolutionarily conserved in pectin-degrading filamentous fungi |CITS: [18768163]|. However, a previously identified enzyme encoded by GAR1 in |FRAME: TAX-51453| that only uses |FRAME: NADPH| may also participate this pathway |CITS: [16101307]|. It showed no nucleotide sequence similarity with GAAA |CITS: [18768163]|. The second step is a dehydration, followed by a reversible aldolase splitting of |FRAME: CPD-12349| to produce |FRAME: L-GLYCERALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is utilized in many pathways. |FRAME: L-GLYCERALDEHYDE| is reduced to |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, which can be catabolized as indicated in the pathway link |CITS: [2033381]|. In |FRAME: TAX-51453| the product of gene gld1 was shown to catalyze this reaction and was |FRAME: NADPH|-specific making it a likely candidate for this pathway. Reviewed in |CITS: [19159926]|. See subpathway |FRAME: PWY-6491|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine "N-acetyl-D-galactosamine"| (GalNAc, Aga) and |FRAME: GALACTOSAMINE| (GalN, Gam) are amino sugars that are found in cellular structures of both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. For example GalNAc is a component of the major cell surface carbohydrates of |FRAME: TAX-197| |CITS: [15509570]|, and GalN is a component of the lipopolysaccharide of |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [21999536]|. GalNAc is found in the carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes |CITS: [18694827]|. It is also found in eukaryotic glycosaminoglycans (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6572|, |FRAME: PWY-6573| and |FRAME: PWY-6576|)., Some proteobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| B and C strains and |FRAME:TAX-562| EC3132 can utilize GalNAc or GalN as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [10931310]|. Species of |FRAME: TAX-22| can grow on GalNAc as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [20836887]|. Utilization is controlled by the AgaR regulon. Other proteobacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, strains of |FRAME: TAX-573| and |FRAME: TAX-571|, and |FRAME: TAX-99287| cannot utilize these compounds |CITS: [10931310][20836887][22711537]|., About This Pathway, This pathway represents GalNAc utilization in the aquatic |FRAME: TAX-22| species shown here. The reactions catalyzed by the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-94122| define a unique route of GalNAc degradation that was both computationally predicted and experimentally validated. Strains |FRAME: TAX-94122|, |FRAME: TAX-60480|, |FRAME: TAX-60481| and |FRAME: TAX-326297| were shown to grow on GalNAc as a sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [20836887]|. Enzymes AgaK, AgaA, and AgaS from |FRAME: TAX-94122| were expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, purified, and characterized. The segment of the pathway that utilizes these three enzymes was also reconstructed in vitro |CITS: [22711537]|., Bioinformatic analyses have shown that different proteobacteria utilize different phosphorylation routes to produce |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| or |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE|, while some of the downstream reactions may be shared |CITS: [22711537][20836887]|. As indicated at the beginning of the pathway, in |FRAME: TAX-22| species GalNAc enters the cell via a predicted outer membrane porin (OMP) and a predicted inner membrane permease encoded by agaP and is then phosphorylated by the product of agaK. In contrast, in GalNAc and GalN utilizing |FRAME:TAX-562| strains, two specific PTS systems are respectively used to transport these compounds into the cell with concomitant phosphorylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7395|) |CITS: [22711537]|., In |FRAME: TAX-22| species, after phosphorylation of GalNAc by the novel kinase product of agaK, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| is deacetylated to |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| by the novel deacetylase AgaA-II which is non-orthologous to |FRAME:TAX-562| AgaA. The deaminase/isomerase product of AgaS then converts |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: L-TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE|. The kinase product of agaZ is predicted to convert |FRAME: L-TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: TAGATOSE-1-6-DIPHOSPHATE|. The latter compound was proposed to be cleaved to glycolytic intermediates by the non-committed class II fructose-bisphosphate aldolase present in |FRAME: TAX-22| species |CITS: [22711537]|., Conserved gene agaS was found in all proteobacterial genomes examined by |CITS: [22711537]|. In the |FRAME:TAX-562| C strain |FRAME: TAX-481805| the function of gene agaS was experimentally validated by mutant analysis to be the main D-galactosamine-6-phosphate isomerase in the the GalNAc utilization pathway in that organism |CITS: [22711537]|.

Summary: Chloroaromatic compounds occur in the environment in large amounts due to their release as herbicides or as byproducts, of industrial production., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation capabilities have evolved only recently as a response, to their widespread availability in soil and water., Many of the degradation pathways merge at the level of chlorocatechols.Often organisms that can degrade, non-chlorinated aromatic compounds (such as benzoate) can convert the chlorinated vatiants to the level of, chlorocatechols, due to enzyme promiscuity |CITS: [4836257]|. However, the enzymes that degrade catechol have, little activity with chloro-substituted compounds, and the chlorocatechols that accumulate as a result are toxic to the, bacteria. Thus, in order to be able to degrade chlorobenzoates and chlorobenzenes successfully, the bacteria must, possess specific enzymes for the degradation of chlorocatechols., The first bacterium that was isolated based on its ability to grow with |FRAME: CPD-3486| as the sole carbon source, was |FRAME:TAX-65741 "Pseudomonas knackmussii (then called Pseudomonas sp. strain B13)"| |CITS: [4852581]|., That study showed that |FRAME: CPD-3486| was converted by two enzymes to a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-9151|, and |FRAME: CPD-9152| |CITS:[4852581][3025183]|., The chlorinated catechols were degraded in a modified ortho cleavage pathways via |FRAME: CPD-294| to, |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which was degraded further to TCA cycle intermediates., This pathway for |FRAME: CPD-9152| degradation starts with a dioxygenase attack, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-279|., The "regular" catechol 1,2 dioxygenases have little activity with chlorocatechol. Instead, chlorocatechols, are substrates to specialized enzymes that evolved for this purpose, known as "type II" enzymes., The next enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7704|, catalyzes a single reaction that converts the chloromuconate directly to, |FRAME: 4-CARBOXYMETHYLENEBUT-2-EN-4-OLIDE| |CITS: [11443090]|. The reaction includes the removal of the, chloride residue., Two last steps, catalyzed by a hydrolase and a reductase, generate the common intermediate |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|., Most of the genes encoding chlorocatechol catabolism enzymes are present on plasmids. Examples include the two, tdf operons on the |FRAME: TAX-264198| plasmid pJP4 |CITS: [2981813]|, the clc operon on the, |FRAME: TAX-65741| plasmid pB13 (pWR1) |CITS: [7217013]|, and the tcb operon on the |FRAME: TAX-65067|, plasmid pP51 |CITS: [1987135]|., In bacteria that lack |FRAME: CPLX-7704| formation of |FRAME: CPD-9152| leads to accute toxicity. Apparently, |FRAME: CPD-279| can be converted by the regular, chromosomally-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-2843| to the, toxic antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-10640| via the following reactions:, |FRAME:RXN-9892| |FRAME:RXN-9869|, Accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-10640| leads to cell death |CITS: [7493952]|.

Summary: |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN| is the precursor for the essential flavin cofactors |FRAME:FMN| and |FRAME:FAD|, which are, used in a wide variety of redox reactions. Riboflavin is also known as vitamin B2, because it is an essential nutrient, and can not be synthesized by mammals., The biosynthesis of one riboflavin molecule requires one molecule of |FRAME: GTP| and two molecules of, |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| as substrates., The imidazole ring of GTP is hydrolytically opened, yielding a 4, 5-diaminopyrimidine which is converted to, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| by a sequence of deamination, side chain reduction, and dephosphorylation. Condensation of |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| with, |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-BUTANONE-P| obtained from |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| results in the formation of, |FRAME: DIMETHYL-D-RIBITYL-LUMAZINE|., Dismutation of the lumazine derivative yields |FRAME: RIBOFLAVIN| and, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE|, which is recycled in the pathway |CITS: [10940330]|., The fungal riboflavin biosynthesis pathway and its enzymes are well understood, with the exception of, the enzyme catalyzing the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: CPD-1086|. This enzyme has not been isolated, and it has, been suggested that the reaction may be catalyzed by a phosphatase of broad substrate specificity., Unlike the bacterial enzymes, many of which are bifunctional and catalyze more than one reaction in the pathway, all, of the yeast enzymes are monofunctional, each catalyzing a single pathway reaction., Different variations of the pathway are found in the different kingdoms of life., A main difference between the fungal and bacterial/plant pathways (see |FRAME: RIBOSYN2-PWY|) is in the order in which two of the enzymes act. Two enzymatic steps are required to convert |FRAME: DIAMINO-OH-PHOSPHORIBOSYLAMINO-PYR| to |FRAME: CPD-1086| - a demaination and a reduction., In bacteria and plants, the deaminase acts first, followed by the reductase (although both steps are catalyzed by a single, bifunctional enzyme in some organisms), while in fungi the reductase acts first, followed by the deaminase., The archaeal pathway also differs in several steps (see |FRAME: PWY-6167|).

The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones γ-butyrolactones|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "γ-butenolides"| as chemical signalling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation |CITS: [2268871]|. At least 60% of Streptomyces species appear to produce γ-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011), only a small number of which have been identified |CITS: [21090718]|., In many cases these signaling molecule control production of specific products. For example, |FRAME: CPD-10135 A-factor| induces production of the antibiotic |FRAME: STREPTOMYCIN| and the yellow pigment |FRAME: CPD-14874 grixazone| in |FRAME: TAX-1911|., Another family of signaling molecules, produced by |FRAME: TAX-100226|, are the |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"| (MMFs), which induce the production of the antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-27200| and |FRAME: CPD-27334| |CITS: [18988741]|., Biosynthesis of the MMFs begins in the same manner as that of γ-butyrolactones, with the condensation of |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: B-KETOACYL-ACP|, forming |FRAME: CPD-19941|, which loses a water molecule spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-19943|, which possesses the bunenolide structure. The enxt reaction, which is still conserved among multiple pathways, is the dephosphorylation of the product, forming |FRAME: 3-Acyl-4-hydroxymethyl-5H-furan-2-one|., The final step in the pathway is proposed to be catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G-124755| gene, which is similar to flavin-dependent oxidoreductases. It has been proposed that the enzyme catalyzes conversion of the 2-acyl-3-hydro, xymethylbutenolides, which are formed by |FRAME: MONOMER-124756| (|FRAME: G-124754 MmfP|) to the methylenomycin furan structure |CITS: [33146163]|.

Summary: The terphenylquinones are among the most prominent mushroom natural products. In some mushrooms their biosynthesis is elicited by cell wall damage caused by microbial lytic enzymes, suggesting a defensive role, which is supported by the fact that these compounds inhibit bacterial motility and modulate biofilms |CITS: [27699944][30496678][34081381]|. In the case of the cobalt crust mushroom (|FRAME: TAX-40462|), production of these compounds was found to be triggered by exposure to light, as part of the morphogenesis associated with production of fruiting bodies |CITS: [36094086]|., The most important representatives of terphenylquinones are |FRAME: CPD-27553| and |FRAME: CPD-14619| |CITS: [Stahlschmidt77][Thorner78]|. These two compounds are synthesized in similar pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7518|), in which an aromatic amino acid (|FRAME: PHE| or |FRAME: TYR|, respectively) is deaminated and the resulting 2-oxo acid undergoes symmetric dimerization by a non-ribosomal peptide synthase-like enzyme, forming the quinone. These enzyme consist of three domains - an adenylation (A) domain, a thiolation (T, or ACP) domain, and a thioesterase (TE) domain. Despite the similarity, the polyporic acid synthases and the atromentin synthases belong to distinct phylogenetic groups and evolved in parallel processes |CITS: [37400920]|.

General Background, Disproportionation is a process in which a reactant is both oxidized and reduced in the same chemical reaction, forming two separate products. The disproportionation of |FRAME: S2O3|, an important step in sulfur transformation in aquatic systems, was discovered in 1987 |CITS: [Bak87]|. Thiosulfate-disproportionating bacteria are numerically significant, and have been detected in high numbers in several environments, including freshwater, mud, and marine sediments (see |FRAME:PWY-5277|)., Several microorganisms have also been shown to grow by the disproportionation of elemental sulfur |CITS: [16348835]|., This observation was initially surprising, because under standard conditions the reaction is endergonic with G'° = 40.9 kJ. However, the removal of sulfide, which occurs in the presence of sulfide scavengers such as oxidized metals (for example iron and manganese oxides) makes the process energetically favorable |CITS: [15028874]|., About This Pathway, Sulfur disproportionation was initially discovered under anaerobic conditions |CITS:[16348835][9435068]|. This disproportionation reaction takes place in the absence of oxygen or |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [Bothe-Trebst]|. A second variation, which is aerobic, has also been documented (see |FRAME:PWY-5302|)., Several organisms have been reported to disproportionate elemental sulfur anaerobically, including |FRAME: TAX-115852|, |CITS:[4209228]|, |FRAME: TAX-894| |CITS: [16349323]|, |FRAME: TAX-53321| |CITS: [Janssen96]|, and |FRAME: TAX-65555| |CITS:[9435068]|. |FRAME: TAX-65555| is a marine bacterium that can grow by the disproportionation of thiosulfate, sulfite, or elemental sulfur |CITS:[9435068][12889609]|. The enzyme(s) that catalyzes the disproportionation reaction have not been characterized yet.

Summary: All the eukaryotic N-linked glycans are based on the common core pentasaccharide, |FRAME: CPD-5162 Man33GlcNAc2|. Further processing in the golgi results in several N-linked glycan classes, one of which is the high-mannose N-linked glycans (HMNG), which contain unsubstituted terminal mannose sugars. These glycans typically contain between five and nine mannose residues attached to the chitobiose (GlcNAc2) core (see pathways |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS| and |FRAME: PWY-7919|)., HMNG is a viable food source for the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-818|, a dominant member of the human large bowel microbiota. Transcriptional studies have identified three polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs) in the |FRAME: TAX-818| genome. While PULs often have genes that are required for the degradation of more than one type of polysaccharide, the PUL3 cluster is dedicated to the degradation of HMNG |CITS: [25567280]|., The degradation of HMNG occurs in two locations. In the first stage an extracellular |FRAME: MONOMER-124366| (GH18), encoded by the |FRAME: G-124364| gene, releases the glycan from the protein that carries it, leaving only one GlcNAc saccharide attached to the protein., The liberated glycan is attracted to the bacterium's outer membrane by interactions between mannose residues and the membrane-bound mannose-binding protein encoded by the BT_3791 gene. The reducing end of the GlcNAc residue interacts with a homolog of SusD encoded by the BT_3789 gene (SusD is a starch-binding protein that participates in starch degradation), guiding the glycan into a SusC-like (C) porin, which transports it into the periplasm. Genes encoding SusD-like and SusC-like proteins are present in all three PULs |CITS: [25567280]|., Once inside the periplasm, the oligosaccharides are degraded by the cummulative action of three enzymes. The |FRAME: G-124365| and |FRAME: G-124366| genes encode an |FRAME: MONOMER-124367| and an |FRAME: MONOMER-124368|, respectively (both GH92), whose combined action leaves an α-(1,6) manno-trisaccharide attached to a GlcNAc residue at the reducing end. An |FRAME: MONOMER-124369| encoded by the |FRAME: G-124367| gene (also GH92), which requires that its substrate contains a GlcNAc residue at the reducing end, removes the mannosyl residue from the non-reducing end, leaving a trisaccharide. The trisaccharide is degraded to completion by uncharacterized enzymes that are not encoded by HMNG-PUL |CITS: [25567280]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, Shiga toxin (Stx)-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) are an important group of intestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli strains. STEC strains cause diarrhea, bloody diarrhea, and, because of toxemia and not dissemination, the hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). , |FRAME: TAX-2067429| is a STEC strain isolated from patients with diarrhea. However, it is also known to be associated frequently with urinary tract infections and is also considered a uropathogenic (UPEC) strain., The organism possesses virulence loci of both the STEC and UPEC groups, and phylogenetic studies have suggested that it is a transitional pathogen in the process of morphing between the STEC group to the ExPEC (extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli) group (which inludes UPEC strains) |CITS: [24413188]|., The structure of the |FRAME: CPD-24292| was reported in 1987 and shown to contain five sugar residues: three L-Rha residues, a D-GlcNAc residue and a D-Fuc3NAc residue |CITS: [3555792]|. The sequence of its O antigen biosynthetic cluster was reported in 2010. The cluster contains genes involved in |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|, genes involved in |FRAME: PWY-6953|, three glycosyltransferase genes (|FRAME: G-81166|, |FRAME: G-81168|, and |FRAME: G-81169|), and the |FRAME: G-81165| and |FRAME: G-81167| genes. The gene cluster also contains genes that encode for transposases and a sulfatase that is unlikely to be involved in the O antigen biosynthesis process |CITS: [20434495][20453897]|. Specific functions were assigned to the glycosyltransferases in a later work |CITS: [29787897]|., The |FRAME: CPD-24295| is nearly identical to that of |FRAME: TAX-2067429|, differing only in the lack of the |FRAME: CPD-13886| side chain, due to a mutation in |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.90| |CITS: [29787897]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8252|).

Summary: General Background, L-Asparagine is hydrolyzed to L-aspartate and ammonia by the enzyme asparaginase |CITS: [VOET04]|. The enzyme has been characterized from diverse sources, including bacteria, archaea |CITS: [15735339]|, fungi |CITS: [8026756] [7772845] [2080924]|, ciliates |CITS: [8012291]| and plants |CITS: [SODEK80]|. It has also been characterized from the liver and serum of guinea pigs |CITS: [8590375]|., The enzyme has anti-tumor activity and purified L-asparaginase from |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-556| have been used clinically to treat lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphosarcoma (in |CITS: [15951039]|). The enzyme from some species contains glutaminase activity, believed to cause clinical side-effects. Enzyme preparations from species with decreased glutaminase activity, such as |FRAME: TAX-554 "Pectobacterium carotovorum (previously known as Erwinia carotovora)"| have been characterized as potential therapeutics |CITS: [15951039]|., Asparagine Degradation in Plants, Asparagine is the first amino acid discovered in plants, where it is the major nitrogen transport and storage compound. Asparagine is metabolized in plants in two routes, either via asparaginase (this pathway|) or via asparagine aminotransferase (see |FRAME: PWY-4002|). Studies in pea suggested that the predominant route differs in different tissues. The asparaginase pathway predominates in seeds, whereas the aminotransferase pathway predominates in leaves |CITS: [Ireland81]|., In the asparaginase pathway, as depicted here, asparagine is deaminated to release aspartate and ammonia. The liberated ammonia is reassimilated and utilized for synthesis of all nitrogen containing compounds of the cell and in particular the amino acids. There is no evidence that aspartate is metabolized further in plants.
