Summary: General Background, Methylated amines are ubiquitous in the environment, especially in the marine ecosystem. They are produced by the degradation of proteins and of quartenary amines such as |FRAME: BETAINE|, |FRAME: DL-CARNITINE carnitine|, |FRAME: CHOLINE|, and |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|, which are common osmolytes of many marine organisms., |FRAME: METHYLAMINE Methylamine| can be converted to |FRAME: CH4| by methanogenic archaea via methanogenesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5247|). In addition, some microorganisms are able to use it as the sole source for carbon, nitrogen and energy. , Bacteria that possess the enzyme methylamine dehydrogenase (|FRAME: RXN-2841 "EC 1.4.9.1"|), can oxidize |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and ammonia is a single reaction (see |FRAME: PWY-6967|). MMA-degrading bacteria that lack that enzyme can achieve the same outcome by a pathway that proceeds via two unusual amino acids - |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-404|, as described here. , The microbial oxidation of methylated amines is an important component of environmental cycling of carbon and nitrogen, as well as an essential step in preventing formation of methane, the second most important greenhouse gas, following carbon dioxide |CITS: [19943898]|., About This Pathway, The intermediates of this pathway were discovered in the 1960s and a preliminary pathway has been proposed |CITS: [5905132]|. The original pathway involved two key enzymes, |FRAME: MONOMER-17025| (EC 2.1.1.21) and |FRAME: MONOMER-17027| (EC 1.5.99.5). The first enzyme was believed to convert methylamine into |FRAME: CPD-404| |CITS: [5905132][5562354]| and the second to cleave the latter to formaldehyde and glutamate |CITS:[4399353][5028076]|. In a parallel route, an enzyme that converts methylamine into |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| (|FRAME: CPLX-8403|, EC 6.3.4.12) has also been reported |CITS: [5800436]|. The relation between these two branches has not been clear. A potential solution has been proposed in a much later study involving the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-199596|, according to which the actual in vivo substrate of EC 2.1.1.21 is |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| rather than methylamine |CITS: [20472738]|. This proposal is supported by the observation that |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-404|, as determined by radiotracer work in |FRAME: TAX-83| |CITS: [940497]|. Based on this proposal, all three enzymes form a linear route, with methylamine first converted to |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: CPD-404| and oxidized to formaldehyde and glutamate |CITS: [20472738]|., The methyl groups are released in this pathway in the form of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which can be assimilated via the |FRAME: PWY-1622 "serine pathway"| or |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation "oxidized to CO2"|. The nitrogen is released in the form of ammonia and can be assimilated via the |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY "GS/GOGAT pathway"|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in cell walls of dicotyledon type I and non-graminaceous monocotyledons plants. It also exists in some seeds of trees growing in the tropical zone., Xyloglucan interacts with cellulose microfibrils via hydrogen bonds to form a structural network that is assumed to play a key role in cell wall integrity. Cross-linking between the xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the resulting three-dimensional matrix |CITS: [Whitney95]|., Xyloglucan has a backbone of β-1,4-linked glucose residues, most of which are substituted in C-6 by α-D-xylosyl residues |CITS: [8252539]|. Some of the xylosyl residues are further substituted by (1,2)-β-D-galactosyl residues, and some of the galactosyl residues are capped by (1,2)-α-L-fucose |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. , A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose and β-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, β-D-galactose and α-L-fucose |CITS:[Fry93]|., Fucosyl residues are typically absent from seed xyloglucans but present on the xyloglucans in the vegatative portions of the same plant |CITS: [Mishra09]|., Most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide XXXG units. The average molecular weight of xyloglucan is more than 50 000 |CITS: [Mishra09]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of xyloglucan is still not well understood. It is well established that xyloglucan is assembled within Golgi stacks and transported in Golgi-derived vesicles to the cell wall., The glucan synthase that is involved in xyloglucan synthesis is likely encoded by |FRAME: AT3G28180| gene, characterized from Nasturtium and Arabidopsis |CITS: [17488821]|., Three xyloglucan 6-xylosyltransferase enzymes that catalyze the transfer of xylose from |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| onto β(1,4)-linked glucan chains have been reported from |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [12032363][16982611][18557833]|. Two of the enzymes (|FRAME: AT3G62720| and |FRAME: AT4G02500|) were shown to preferentially add one xylose to unsubstituted glucans at the second position from the non-reducing end. When using |FRAME: CPD-13238| (GGGGGG), the preferred substrate, the enzymes produced mostly GGXGGG, with GGXXGG also formed after long incubations with a high substrate ratio |CITS: [16982611]|. While the activity of the third enzyme, |FRAME: AT1G74380|, has not been well characterized, it has been shown that a mutant lacking it shows a reduced xyloglucan content |CITS: [18557833]|., A xyloglucan galactosyltransferase (|FRAME: AT2G20370|) that attaches an α-L-D-galactose residue specifically to the third xylose residue within the XXXG core structure has been reported from Arabidopsis |CITS: [12837954]|. Other galactosyltransferases may be necessary for galactosylation of other opsitions |CITS: [15020758]|., Finally, the Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT2G03220-MONOMER| (|FRAME: AT2G03220|) that attaches an α-L-fucose residue to the third xylose residue within the XXXG core structure has been identified and characterized |CITS: [11854459]|.

The degradation of carbohydrates from agricultural byproducts is a massive ecological and industrial management issue. Disaccharide degradation pathways involve the breakdown of the two monosaccharide units. Some examples include the |FRAME: SUCROSEUTIL2-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY0-1301|, |FRAME: PWY0-1182|, |FRAME: LACTOSEUTIL-PWY| and |FRAME: MALTOSECAT-PWY| pathways. , Some microbes possess specialized disaccharide phophorylases that catalyze the transfer of a glycosyl moiety to a phosphate when a disaccharide is the donor substrate. Several disaccharide phosphorylases that catalyze the conversion of sucrose, trehalose, cellobiose etc have been extensively characterized. , |FRAME: CPD-10703 Laminaribiose| is a dissaccharide found in many agricultural plants. This pathway describes its phosphorolytic degradation by one such enzyme characterized from the unicellular flagellate protist |FRAME: TAX-3039| |CITS: [5504634]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium Selenium| is an essential micronutrient for animals and humans but has not yet been proven to be an essential micronutrient for land plants |CITS: [11683552][16307305]|. There is evidence, however, of Chlamydomonas proteins that contains a |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| residue suggesting that algal species might also require |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [17105189][12110581]|. The health requirement of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for humans and animals can be met by crops and forage plants that contain selenocompounds. |FRAME: TAX-4232| among the oilseed crops was shown to be a good source for this micronutrient |CITS: [15012198]|. In addition, there is evidence that certain seleno-compounds, including |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE|, have anti-carcinogenic properties |CITS: [14748935]|. , Despite its importance as a micronutrient, higher concentrations of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| are toxic to humans, other animals, and plants largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064][12753978][16661781]|. , In general, plants take up both |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE| from soil. A series of |FRAME: PWY-6932 reduction steps| converts |FRAME: SELENATE| to |FRAME: SE-2| / |FRAME: CPD-678| and this is assimilated into the seleno-amino acids |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19309459]|., In Se accumulator plants, these seleno-amino acids may be modified to create organic seleno-compounds for storage. Seasonal weeds like |FRAME: TAX-3575| and |FRAME: TAX-83445| along with perennial weeds like |FRAME: TAX-41550| employ this strategy and accumulate high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [19800657]|. Se accumulation can help to protect plants against attacks by prairie dogs, insects, and fungi (see refs in |CITS: [21628258]|)., Other plants, like |FRAME: ORG-5993| generate seleno-compounds as well, but rather than storing them, they transform them into less toxic volatile compounds, such as |FRAME: CPD-12005| (DMSe) that can then be released from the plants |CITS: [10759525]|. This process is also called phytovolatilization |CITS: [19656903]|. , While these strategies directly benefit the plants that employ them, they can also be put to use for the phytoremediation of seleniferous soils that contain dangerously high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium|. Numerous insights into endogenous seleno-compound metabolism in plants have been gained through efforts to engineer plants that show improved selenium phytoremediation abilities |CITS: [15005814][19800657][19893365][17445958][10759525]|., About This Pathway, In many plant species the metabolism of selenium appears to mirror the metabolism of sulfur and often uses the same enzymes. Therefore, although this pathway has not been completely elucidated in plants, it has been built based on the comparable sulfur-based pathways, such as the |FRAME: SULFMETII-PWY reductive sulfur assimilation pathway| found in plants |CITS: [16307305]|., As in the sulfur reduction pathway, the ATP sulfurylase enzyme appears to catalyze the first step in selenium reduction. This claim is supported by the finding that overexpression of an Arabiopsis ATP sulfurylase promotes selenate reduction |CITS: [9880353][15941393]|., The second step in the pathway is still being investigated. There is evidence for non-enzymatic conversion of to selenite in vitro |CITS: [328009]|, but selenite reductase activity has been observed in planta and has been measured in a number of selenium hyperaccumulators |CITS: [15941393]|., To date, there is no evidence that a sulfite reductase enzyme is needed to catalyze the third reaction in the pathway in plants. Rather, evidence collected using pea chloroplasts suggests that this reaction can proceed non-enzymatically and uses both glutathione and NADPH as reducing agents |CITS: [JABLONSKI82]|. , Analyses of the overall reduction of selenate to organic selenium suggest that the first step of selenate reduction is rate-limiting |CITS: [9701603]|. , This portion of the pathway is believed to occur in the choloroplast |CITS: [12753978]|., Similar to the selenate reduction portion of the pathway, selenocysteine formation likely parallels the cysteine biosynthetic pathway in plants, and may use many of the same enzymes.The first step in cysteine biosynthesis involes a serine acetyltransferase (SAT). While there is definite evidence of enzymes capable of producing O-acetyl-L-serine in Arabidopsis and many other plant species, these enzymes have not yet been explicitly linked to selenium metabolism in planta. In fact, when SAT activity is compared across different |FRAME:TAX-20400| species that accumulate vastly different levels of selenium, no correlation is detected |CITS: [15941393]|. Selenocysteine formation is likely to be catalyzed by O-acetyl-L-serine (thiol) lyase (OAS-TL) enzymes and selenocysteine production in the presence of O-acteyl-serine has been measured in a number of plants including including |FRAME:TAX-3888| (pea), clover, and several Astralagus species |CITS: [NG78]|. This activity could be competitively inhibited by sulfur, and conversely, cysteine biosynthesis could be competetively inhibited by selenium, arguing that these reactions are catalyzed by the same enzymes |CITS: [NG78]|. Direct evidence for OAS-TL-based production of selenocysteine has only been demonstrated in the bacteria |FRAME:TAX-266| to date |CITS: [14692]|, but it is likely that plant OAS-TLs catalyze this reaction, too., |FRAME: CPD-13717| production probably depends on the activity of the cystathionine synthase enzymes that play a comparable role in sulfate metabolism. Over-expression of an Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT3G01120| enzyme in |FRAME:TAX-3707| appears to increase flux through this pathway and leads to higher levels of volatile selenium compound production |CITS: [14618405]|., Evidence for activity of the next enzyme in the pathway, β-(seleno)cystathionine lyase can be detected in plant extracts from several species including selenium non-accumulators, such as spinach (see |FRAME: MONOMER-16912| ), pea and Se accumulators, such as |FRAME:TAX-20406|. As seen for many other enzymes in this pathway, it is active with both the sulfur and selenium analogs |CITS: [MCCLUSKEY86]|., The final step toward selenomethionine biosynthesis could be catalyzed by at least three different types of enzymes if the proteins involved in |FRAME: PWY-702| also participate in selenomethionine (Se-Met) metabolism. For instance, E.coli has both cobalamin-dependent (2.1.1.13) and cobalamin-independent enzymes (|FRAME: RXN-12730 2.1.1.14|) that can catalyze the formation of Se-Met |CITS: [11078203]|. No cobalamin-independent candidates have been found in Arabidopsis. On the other hand, it does have three cobalamin-independent methionine synthases (see |FRAME: RXN-12730 2.1.14|) which could also potentially accept selenohomocysteine, but their role in seleno-amino acid biosynthesis has not yet been tested |CITS: [15024005]|. , Both seleno-amino acids, |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE|, can be misincorporated during protein synthesis. To prevent this, selenium accumulating or hyperaccumulating plants typically transform them into non-coding seleno-amino acids, such as Se-methylselenocysteine or other related compounds. Non-accumulating plants employ a different strategy and further metabolize these seleno-amino acids into the production of volatile compounds that can be released into the atmosphere |CITS: [16307305]|. Several different routes for seleno-amino acid detoxification are incorporated into this superpathway and it is unlikely that any one species employs all of them. In particular, within the plant kingdom, |FRAME: PWY-6935| via |FRAME: CPD-13770| production, may be limited to halophytic species., Two sub-pathways describe alternative routes that Se-non-accumulating and accumulating plants may use to further metabolize |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| to produce the volatile |FRAME: CPD-12005|. In the hyperaccumulator |FRAME:TAX-15853| species, this may occur in a |FRAME: PWY-6935 four-step process| that involves the formation of the intermediate compound |FRAME: CPD-13720|. The |FRAME:TAX-15853| enzymes shown to function in |FRAME: PWY-6055 DMSP biosynthesis| |CITS: [10889264]| may perform analogous functions in DMSeP production. However, this intermediate is not likely produced in Arabidopsis and many other plants. Therefore, a one-step variant has been proposed. Formation of |FRAME: CPD-12005| may be catalyzed by a putative methylmethionine / Se-methyl-Se-methionine hydrolase in Arabidopsis thaliana and other plants, but no such enzyme has been identified or characterized yet, particularly with respect to seleno-compound metabolism |CITS: [12376649]|. It is also possible that this reaction may happen spontaneously through chemical decomposition, but this would be expected to occur very slowly at physiological pH., Roots may be the primary site of |FRAME: CPD-12005| production (see citations in |CITS: [9701603]|)., Only one sub-pathway describing the further metabolism of |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| has been suggested so far, and it lacks some important details concerning the final steps of |FRAME: CPD-12006| production. It is possible that a series of reactions involving first a |FRAME: CPD-13774| intermediate and then a methaneseleniol intermediate are required, similar to the enzymatic steps observed for dimethyldisulfide biosynthesis |CITS: [16307305]|., It is also possible that some of the |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| can be shunted toward |FRAME: CPD-12005| production if enzymes such as the bacterial thiopurine methyltransferase are found to occur in plants |CITS:[12003960] [16307305]|., |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE Selenocysteine| may also be used to form |FRAME: CPD-13788| as this compound has been seen to accumulate in Arabidopsis over-expressing a selenocysteine methyltransferase enzyme and natively, in the hyperaccumulator |FRAME: TAX-20406| |CITS: [NIGAM69A][5370015][16307305]|.

Summary: An enzyme system has been demonstrated in the leaves of |FRAME: TAX-69904|, a common hedge plant in India, that converts |FRAME: INDOLE| to |FRAME: CPD-16173| |CITS: [14170321]|. While the enzymes associated with this degradation pathway have not been purified, a crude extract of soluble enzymes from the leaves was able to catalyze this transformation in vitro. The compounds |FRAME: CPD-248| and |FRAME: CPD-16172| were identified as intermediates., Even though the enzyme(s) involved have not been purified or characterized specifically, it has been shown that the conversion required 3 atoms of oxygen for each molecule of |FRAME: INDOLE| that was oxidized. It has also been shown that the enzyme(s) is both FAD- and Cu2+-dependent |CITS: [14170321]|., A similar enzyme system was later documented in |FRAME: TAX-4577|. The system, which was very similar to the one previosuly reported in having FAD and Cu2+ dependency and similar intermediates, was reported to form both |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: CPD-16173| |CITS: [697856]|., A third system was soon reported from the plant |FRAME: TAX-389181|. This enzyme, which was also FAD- and Cu2+-dependent, produced only |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| |CITS: [Divakar79]|., Finally, a second enzyme has been described from |FRAME: TAX-69904| that produced |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE|. Unlike the three enzymes described earlier, this enzyme did not contain FAD or Cu2+ |CITS: [16662784]|., Unfortunately none of these enzyme systems were studied in sufficient detail to suggest an accurate mechanism, or even a credible pathway. While the pathway shown here suggests the production of |FRAME: FORMATE|, this hypothetical intermediate has never been detected., In |FRAME: TAX-69904| |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| was shown to be further degraded into |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL| |CITS: [Nair64]|. The final fate of this degradation route is unclear. Some reports suggested conversion to catechol |CITS: [Nair64]|, others suggested formation of |FRAME: CPD-16175| |CITS: [5966524]| or |FRAME: ISOPHENOXAZINE| |CITS:[14170322][4166439]|. There has been little progress in the field in subsequent years.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-11967 "Putrebactin"| is a cyclic dihydroxamate siderophore that was discovered in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-399804|. This siderophore is a cyclic dimer of |FRAME: CPD-11964|, and is similar to the siderophores |FRAME: CPD-11970| and |FRAME: CPD-11968|, which are produced by unrelated bacteria |CITS: [Ledyard97]|., Sequence analysis revealed that the genomes of several |FRAME: TAX-22| species, including |FRAME: TAX-24|, |FRAME: TAX-60480| and |FRAME: TAX-60481|, contain a cluster of five genes that are involved in the biosynthesis and utilization of |FRAME: CPD-11967| |CITS: [18630910]|. The |FRAME: G-11642|, |FRAME: G-11641| and |FRAME: G-11640| genes are homologous to the |FRAME: G-11638|, |FRAME: SCO2784| and |FRAME: SCO2785| genes which direct the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-3764| and |FRAME: CPD-11957| in |FRAME: TAX-1883| species (see |FRAME: PWY-6375|), as well as the |FRAME: G-11643|, |FRAME: G-11644| and |FRAME: G-11646| genes that direct the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-11968| in |FRAME: TAX-517| species (see |FRAME: PWY-6379|). These three genes were proposed to catalyze the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-11967| |CITS: [18630910]|., In addition, the cluster contains the putA and putB genes, which encode an outer-membrane ferric-siderophore transporter and a cytoplasmic ferric-siderophore reductase, which catalyzes the reductive removal of iron from ferric-putrebactin., Based on sequence analysis, the |FRAME: G-11642| and |FRAME: G-11641| genes were proposed to encode a |FRAME: MONOMER-15212| and a |FRAME: MONOMER-15211|, respectively. Combined, these two enzymes can convert |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| to |FRAME: CPD-11964|. The function of |FRAME: G-55136| has been confirmed by cloning the gene from |FRAME: TAX-211586| |CITS: [27541336]|., The |FRAME: G-11640| gene product, |FRAME: CPLX-7950|, then catalyzes both the condensation of two |FRAME: CPD-11964| molecules into the free intermediate |FRAME: CPD-11965|, and the cyclization of the later to the final product |FRAME: CPD-11967| |CITS: [18630910]|., The |FRAME: G-11640| genes of |FRAME: TAX-60480| and |FRAME: TAX-60481| were cloned, and the purified proteins were able to catalyze the predicted reactions in vitro |CITS: [18630910]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD0-1099 "Colanic acid"|, also known as the M antigen, is an extracellular polysaccharide found in |FRAME: TAX-543|. It is a polyanionic heteropolysaccharide containing a repeat unit with |FRAME: D-Glucose|, |FRAME: L-fucoses|, |FRAME: D-Galactose|, and |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| sugars that are nonstoichiometrically decorated with O-acetyl and pyruvate side chains |CITS: [4902806 ][4941627]|. The sugars need to be activated in the form of nucleotide sugars (|FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CPD-13118|, |FRAME: CPD-14553| and |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE|, respectively) prior to their assembly |CITS: [8759852] [8763957]|., The |FRAME: CPD0-1099| polysaccharide repeat is assembled on the membrane lipid |FRAME: CPD-9650| by a series of glycosyl transferases on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane, after which the single repeat is flipped to the periplasmic side and polymerized by the Wzy-dependent pathway (reviewed in |CITS: [12045108]| and |CITS: [16756484]|)., Subsequently, the polymer is believed to be cleaved from the |FRAME: CPD-9650| anchor, transported across the periplasm, and excreted into the extracellular space, although this process is not well understood., |FRAME: CPD0-1099 "Colanic acid"| biosynthesis has been linked to a cluster of 19 genes, which were named wca |CITS:[8759852][8763957]|. This gene cluster is tightly regulated by a complex signal transduction cascade governed by the rcs (regulator of capsule synthesis) phosphorelay system |CITS: [3888955][16153174]|.

General Background, N-glucosylnicotinate is a compound derived from nicotinic acid and considered , as a storage compound that feeds back into the |FRAME:PWY-5381|. Nicotinate has been regarded as an , important branch point between primary and secondary metabolism as it is precursor and degradation product , of the pyridine nucleotide coenzymes NAD and NADP as well as a building block for secondary metabolits, e.g. , the pyridine alkaloid trigonelline (|FRAME:PWY-5110|) |CITS: [UPMEIER88A]| |CITS: [WAGNER85]| |CITS: [Dewick97]| , |CITS: [Seigler98]|., N-glycosyl conjugates of nicotinic acid have not been the focus of research and were identified so far , only in a few families such as the Asteridae and Rosidae |CITS: [WILLEKE79]| although a broader occurrence , may be expected due to their connections to the more ubiquitous present pyridine nucleotide cycle in plants., About This Pathway, The enzyme catalyzing the glucosylation of nicotinic acid to form N-glucosylnicotinate , is UDPG:nicotinate N-glucosyltransferase. The activity of this enzyme has been found and characterized , in parsley (|FRAME:TAX-4043|) and shows very narrow substrate specificity towards nicotinate. , For activity the tertiary nitrogen atom and a functional group in position 3 of the pyridine ring appears to be vital , |CITS: [Upmeier88]|. , The enzyme executes complete free reversibility of the reaction |CITS: [Upmeier88]|, something which is only , found in a few cases with regard to UDPG glucosyltransferases, e.g. |CITS: [1124927]|. That highlights the , high group-potential of N-glucosylnicotinate and points to a possible regulatory function of the catalyzing , enzyme as it links to the metabolism of nicotinate., The product of this reaction, i.e. N-glucosylnicotinate is discussed as a true storage compound for the , recycling of NAD. The steady production during the growth cycle, the short half-life time of this compound (24 hrs) , and the reversibility of the reaction supports this view in contrast to another nicotinate derivative (trigonelline) , which demethylation appears to proceed too slowly to meet the demand for nicotinate in the recycling procedure , |CITS: [Upmeier88]| |CITS: [UPMEIER88A]|.

Summary: |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain, and has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well [Bouche04]. In both animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.15|., In yeast, glutamate degradation by this pathway and expression of its genes have been shown to be important for oxidative stress tolerance. Conditions of oxidative stress elevate the transcript levels of |FRAME: YMR250W| and |FRAME: YBR006W| |CITS: [11031268]|. |FRAME: YGR019W| and |FRAME: YBR006W| expression is also upregulated in the presence of GABA which is mediated by the transcriptional activators Uga3p and Uga35p/Dal81p |CITS: [3888627][2653828]|. These transcription factors bind to upstream activation sites in the promoters of GABA-regulated genes known as the UAS-GABA |CITS: [12235130][2653838]|. Regulation of Gad1p is suggested to be linked to calcium levels as the protein is able to bind calmodulin |CITS:[11031268]|.,  , |FRAME: TAX-4932| cells in which this pathway is blocked are more sensitive to oxidative stress and can no longer grow on GABA as their sole nitrogen source |CITS: [11031268][3888627]|., In enteric bacteria that must be able to survive extremely acidic conditions that pathway functions as an acid resistance system. This glutamate-dependent acid resistance system couples the transport activity of a glutamate:4-aminobutyrate antiporter, GadC, with glutamate decarboxylase, GadA/GadB. GadA or GadB is sufficient for survival at pH 2.5, but both GadA and GadB are required for survival at pH 2.0. GadC functions by exchanging external glutamate for internal 4-aminobutyrate. Glutamate is imported into the cell through GadC. Within the cell glutamate is decarboxylated by GadA/GadB to 4-aminobutyrate, releasing CO2 and replacing it with a proton. 4-aminobutyrate is then exported through GadC. This effectively consumes protons within the cytoplasm, raising the pH.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: PWY-7024 "3-hydroxypropionate cycle"| is one of few |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation pathways that are known. The pathway was discovered in the green nonsulfur phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1108| |CITS: [Holo89][8354269]|, and seems to be limited to organisms that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-1106| phylum |CITS: [17635550]|, one of the five major lineages of phototrophic bacteria., A related pathway operates in some acidophilic archaebacteria of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-28889|, such as |FRAME: TAX-41673|, |FRAME: TAX-47303| and |FRAME: TAX-43687| (see |FRAME: PWY-5789|)., The pathway is composed of two cycles that operate simultaneously. The two cycles, which are described individually in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-5743| and |FRAME: PWY-5744|) share their first half, but separate at |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|. Each turn of the first cycle (which is depicted by the outside circle in this pathway diagram) results in the net fixation of two molecules of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| (in the form of |FRAME: HCO3|) into one molecule of |FRAME:GLYOX|. The glyoxylate, which is an unconventional carbon source, is combined with propanoyl-coA via the second cycle and is eventually converted into |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, a central carbon precursor., Detailed description of the pathway, The pathway starts with |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| carboxylation to |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, catalyzed by |FRAME: ENZRXN-14489|. Under autotrophic growth conditions |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| is reduced with NADPH by |FRAME: CPLX-7550| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE|, a characteristic intermediate of this pathway., 3-Hydroxypropionate is reductively converted to |FRAME: SUC-COA| in a process in which |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| is carboxylated, fixing another molecule of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Succinyl-CoA, which has been thus formed from one |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and two |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, is used to regenerate the initial CO2 acceptor molecule |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, and |FRAME:GLYOX| is released., |FRAME:GLYOX Glyoxylate| is combined with |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| forming |FRAME: CPD-9409|, which is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-9408|. A dedicated enzyme catalyzes an unusual reaarangement which transfers the CoA moiety to the C4 carbon, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-14205|. The latter is hydrated to form |FRAME: CPD-627|, which is cleaved by a lyase to form |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|., The acetyl-CoA that is formed by the lyase is condensed with a |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecule forming |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, which is processed to regenerate |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, completing the cycle. Thus the net output of the glyoxylate assimilation cycle is pyruvate, a common central metabolism carbon source |CITS: [11929869]|., Several of the enzymes of this pathway are multifunctional. |FRAME: MALONYL-COA "Malonyl-CoA"| is reduced to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| in two steps by the bifunctional enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7551| |CITS: [11948153]|, while |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| is converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| in a single step by a remarkable single trifunctional enzyme, a natural fusion protein that integrates a CoA ligase, an enoyl-CoA hydratase, and an enoyl-CoA reductase |CITS: [11821399]|. Some of the enzymes also participate in the |FRAME: PWY-5744| cycle, which converts the |FRAME:GLYOX| formed by this pathway into |FRAME:PYRUVATE|. These enzymes catalyze the reactions in different direction in the two cycles. In some cases, as in the case of |FRAME: CPLX-7549|, they accept a different substrate when catalyzing the reaction in the opposite direction |CITS: [12374834]|., The genes encoding several of the enzymes that participate in this pathway were identified by their sequence when the |FRAME: TAX-1108| genome was sequenced |CITS: [21714912]|. These enzymes still await purification and characterization at the biochemical level.

Summary: The structure of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL| (PG) was determined in 1958 from lipid isolates of the single-cell photosynthetic organism Scenedesmus |CITS: [13510267]|. Its structure is analogous to phosphatidylinositol (PI), but with a glyceryl moiety replacing the inosityl moiety of PI. , Within a decade it has been found in higher plants |CITS: [Benson61]|, Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [4868364][4295332]| and mammals |CITS: [5660098]|. It was later discovered in the archaeon Haloferax volcanii, indicating that it is produced by all three domains of life. The biosynthetic pathway was elucidated in the early 60s |CITS: [14033231]|, and a laboratory synthesis was completed a few years later |CITS: [5916374]|., The abundance of PG is relatively low compared with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in prokaryotes or with either PE or phosphatidylcholine (PC) in eukaryotes |CITS: [18216768][20671299][21172818]|. It is typically more concentrated in plant systems than in animals, forming 1.5-4·5% of the lipid fraction |CITS: [23532185][3592680]|, Since its discovery, biochemical research into PG has been dominated by its roles in the surfactant of lung tissue (PG is the second largest lipid constituent of lung surfactant in almost all mammals), chloroplast membranes (PG is the only phospholipid found in chloroplast thylakoids) and in both bacterial and mammalian systems., In plants PG biosynthesis can occur at three subcellular locations - chloroplast, mitochondrion and ER. In the plastid (see |FRAME: PWY4FS-7|), phosphatidylglycerol is assembled de novo from the newly synthesized fatty acids, and acyl-ACPs are the acyl donors |CITS: [16774646]|. In the non-plastidic pathway (depicted here) acyl-CoA are used as the acyl-donor |CITS: [Moore82]|.

Summary: Pericarp browning of fruits has serious commercial implications for storage and transport. One of the reasons for fruit browning is the catalytic oxidation of phenolic substrates by polyphenoloxidase (PPO). Polyphenol oxidases catalyze two distinct reactions: the hydroxylation of monophenols to ortho-dihydroxyphenols (|FRAME: EC-1.14.18.1|), and the dehydrogenation of the roducts to |FRAME: Orthoquinones "ortho-quinones"| (|FRAME: EC-1.10.3.1|). The products of the latter reaction are strong electrophiles that autoxidize, forming |FRAME: MELANIN|, and are also capable of covalently modifying and crosslinking a variety of cellular nucleophiles. The formation of quinone adducts, usually brown or black, is the primary effect of PPO leading to fruit browning |CITS: [7678763]|., Some PPO endogenous substrates that have been identified in the pericarp tissues include |FRAME: Flavan-3-ols "flavan-3-ols"| and their dimers in lychee and longan, |FRAME: PA-N proanthocyanidins|, |FRAME: CPD-1961|, and |FRAME: CPD-12447| in apple, |FRAME: DOPAMINE| in banana, and |FRAME: CPD-7630| and proanthocyanidin A2 in rambutan |CITS: [20722899 ]|., This pathway shows the formation of a typical ortho-quinone, |FRAME: CPD-385|, by the action of catechol oxidases on catechol, which has been observed in potato tubers |CITS: [7678763]| and fruits of tomato plants |CITS: [8098228]|. In tomato the PPOs belong to a gene family of seven members. They fall into three structural classes and all are located on chromosome 8. The PPOs encode copper-binding sites typical of bacterial and fungal PPOs |CITS: [8098228]|. , Full characterization of the activity of PPO could lead to finding ways of delaying or preventing browning.

|FRAME: GLUTARATE Glutarate| is a five carbon platform chemical produced during the catabolism of L-lysine. It is commonly degradaded after activation to |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA|, as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-5177|. However, in some organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-160488| it can be degraded via an alternative pathway that involves |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.64| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.M4|., The first enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G1G01-3088| gene, is a non-heme Fe<sup>2+</sup>/2-oxoglutarate dependent dioxygenase that is specific for |FRAME: GLUTARATE|. The second enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G1G01-3089| gene, is a FAD-dependent oxidase |CITS: [29844506]|., Competitive fitness assays suggest that the pathway described here has a competitive advantage over the glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenation pathway during glutarate degradation |CITS: [29844506]|., Phylogenetic analysis revealed that homologs of |FRAME: G1G01-3088 CsiD| are only found in bacteria, while homologs of |FRAME: G1G01-3089 LhgO| are also widespread in eukaryotic microorganisms, animals, and plants |CITS: [29844506]|.

Summary: The meta-cleavage pathway of catechol is one of the major pathways for the degradation of, aromatic compounds. Its importance has been well demonstrated in bacteria of many, genera, including species of Azotobacter, Ralstonia and numerous species of, Pseudomonas. , The most comprehensively studied meta-cleavage pathway is that of the TOL plasmid pWWO,, which encodes a toluene degradation pathway in |FRAME: TAX-303|., The genes are located in an operon that encodes the enzymes for conversion of benzoate to catechol,, and catechol to the cenrtal metabolites pyruvate and acetaldehyde |CITS: [2183008]|., |FRAME: CATECHOL "Catechol"| itself is an intermediate in the degradation of many different aromatic compounds., In addition to |FRAME:BENZOATE|, including toluate, |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE|, |FRAME:CPD-110|, and |FRAME: PHENOL|, and substituted catechols are intermediates in the catabolism of methylated and chlorinated derivatives, of these compounds., In this pathway, the aromatic ring of |FRAME:CATECHOL| is cleaved by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-2841|, adjacent to the two catechol hydroxyls., The product of this cleavage, |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD|, can be metabolized in two routes. In the variant described in this pathway, it is hydrolyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-12763|, generating the important intermediate |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| in a single step., In the second variant (see |FRAME:PWY-5420|), |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD| is dehydrogenated by |FRAME:CPLX-7245| to the enol-form of 4-oxalocrotonate, which is then isomerized by |FRAME:CPLX-7237| to the keto-form, and decarboxylated by |FRAME:CPLX-7239|. The later is in a tight complex with the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7240|. It's product, |FRAME:CPD-6761|, is an unstable tautomer of |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE|. This product is transferred to |FRAME: CPLX-7240| within the complex., Thus, the two variants, which separated at |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD|, join again at, |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| (or its tautomer |FRAME:CPD-6761|)., The hydrolase-based variant is the preferred route for 3-substituted catechols, while the dehydrogenase-based route is the preferred route for non-substituted and 4-substituted catechols |CITS: [7890778]|., |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| is metabolized to pyruvate and acetaldehyde (and eventually, acetyl-coA) by successive action of the enzymes |FRAME:CPLX-7240|, |FRAME:MONOMER-12778| and |FRAME:MONOMER-12780|. The last two enzymes form a |FRAME: CPLX-7250| complex, which facilitates the transfer of the toxic acetaldehyde intermediate between them |CITS: [8419288]|.

General Background, Sulfate-reducing bacteria belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-872| use oxidized sulfur compounds as their terminal electron, acceptors. Many Desulfovibrio species can use |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as a sole source of electrons and energy under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [623496]|. The hydrogen oxidation is thought to take place on the periplasmic, side of the inner membrane, and the electrons are transferred to the membrane bound electron transfer chain, resulting the creation of a proton motive force., Alternatively, these organisms can produce hydrogen when growing fermentatively on a suitable carbon source (such as lactate and pyruvate) in the absence of sulfate as an electron acceptor. The oxidation of these compounds occurs in the cytoplasm., It has also been demonstrated that hydrogen is successively produced and consumed during the degradation of organic compounds even in the presence of sulfate |CITS: [7462143][Tsuji80]|. , The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-878| possesses four types of hydrogenases - a periplasmic [NiFe] hydrogenase |CITS: [2154378][2227457]|, a cytoplasmic |FRAME: CPLX-7203| |CITS: [7751270]|, a periplasmic [Fe] hydrogenase |CITS: [16887623]|, and a fourth, uncharacterized hydrogenase |CITS: [11790758]|., When studying soluble cell extracts of the organism, a 10-fold induction of NADP reduction was observed when |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| was present, but no H2-dependent NAD reduction ever occurred. The genes encoding the four subunits of the cytoplasmic NADP-dependent dehydrogenase have been cloned |CITS: [ 7751270]|., An NADP-dependent [NiFe]-hydrogenase has also been characterized from the cytoplasm of the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-69014|. This enzyme was also composed of four subunits, and had an optimum temperature of 95 °C |CITS: [12591889]|.

Summary: The epiphyte |FRAME: TAX-321| strain 22d/93 (Pss22d) produces the rare amino acid |FRAME: CPD-12429| as an antibiotic against the related species |FRAME: TAX-318|, a plant pathogen that is responsible for bacterial blight of soybean, a leaf spot disease of great economic impact |CITS: [18655083]|. |FRAME: CPD-12429| is also found as part of the antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-17158|, which is produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1295550| |CITS: [24907335]|, and |FRAME: CPD-17167|, which is produced by |FRAME: TAX-1522108|., |FRAME: CPD-12429 "3-Methylarginine"| is produced from arginine in three steps, via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-824| and |FRAME: CPD-12430|., The genes that are involved in this pathway, |FRAME: G-12010|, |FRAME: G-12011| and mrsC, are present in a single cluster. The first two genes encode enzymes involved in its biosynthesis, and the third gene encodes a transporter. When the cluster was cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, the recombinant host was able to produce and secrete |FRAME: CPD-12429| |CITS: [20190091]|., The first step, the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-824|, is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-12010|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15641| |CITS: [20190091]|. The gene has been cloned as a His-tag fusion, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| and purified to homogeneity. The recombinant enzyme was highly selective and catalyzed a fast methylation of its substrate using |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as the methyl donor |CITS: [20190091]|. The second gene, |FRAME: G-12011|, has been identified as a |FRAME: MONOMER-15642| based on its sequence, although the enzyme has not been purified yet.

Acetyl-CoA is a central metabolite that plays important roles in many aspects of metabolism. In plants, like in animals, mitochondrial acetyl-CoA feeds into the TCA cycle for the generation of energy and reducing power. In the plastid, acetyl-CoA serves as a substrate for de novo fatty acid biosynthesis. In the plant cell cytosol, acetyl-CoA (its derivative malonyl-CoA to be precise) is a precursor for the synthesis of very long chain fatty acids and many secondary metabolites including flavonoids and terpenoids. The distinct pools of acetyl-CoA are generated via different biosynthetic routes in plants., The mitochondrial and plastid acetyl-CoA pools are derived from pyruvate by pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (see pathway |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|), whereas the cytosolic pool is derived from |FRAME: CIT| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.8|., Besides plants, the pathway for acetyl-CoA biosynthesis from cirate, illustrated here, also occurs in vertebrates. In vertebrates, de novo fatty acid biosynthesis and cholesterol genesis are cytosolic processes. The acetyl-CoA synthesized from citrate in the cytosol feeds into these processes.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [Shellhammer90][15012185][11706201]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.15|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.4|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|. Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria and certain fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. While the biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail only in bacteria, ongoing success in sequencing whole genomes from other organisms has provided evidence that the general steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Despite the importance and prevalance of biotin, its detailed biosynthetic pathway remained enigmatic for over 70 years. Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, and is derived from |FRAME: CPD-205|. The early steps of the pathway, which are described here, are limited to the synthesis of the precursor pimelate moiety. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described in |FRAME: PWY0-1507|., Gram-positive bacteria are believed to generate |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| de novo from acyl-[acp] molecules (see |FRAME: PWY-7147|). However, some also use a salvage pathway in which externally provided |FRAME:CPD-205| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-558| by the |FRAME: G-10705| gene product. |FRAME: CPD-558 Pimelyl-CoA| is an alternative substrate for the |FRAME: G-10706| gene product, |FRAME: CPLX8J2-214|, which catalyzes the first step in the assembly of the bicyclic rings of biotin |CITS:[12658511]|. |FRAME: BSU30240| homologs have been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-1404|, |FRAME: TAX-1421| and |FRAME: TAX-300| |CITS: [IZUMI74][1445232][10359666]|., The importance of this pathway is still unclear, since the origin of the external |FRAME: CPD-205| is not obvious. Pimelate is not part of central metabolism and is not abundant in the environment. The only other known source for |FRAME: CPD-558| is benzene degradation by |FRAME: TAX-1076| (see |FRAME: P321-PWY|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-183 "Gallate"|, gallate esters, and compounds structurally related to them are widely distributed in nature. Plant lignin and tannins are major sources of these compounds, which are degraded by soil microorganisms as part of the terrestrial carbon cycle (in |CITS: [15262932]|)., Fission of the benzene nucleus of gallate and its esters is catalyzed by bacterial dioxygenases. Several distinct pathways of aerobic aromatic catabolixm can be initiated by these dioxygenases, and their distribution among bacteria is complex |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|. Examples of these oxidative pathways are MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|, |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-II-PWY|, |FRAME: P184-PWY|, , |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY-2504|. An anaerobic pathway for gallate degradation is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P3-PWY|., Cell suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-285| grown with |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| contain induced |FRAME: CPLX-2701|. This enzyme cleaves the benzene nucleus of |FRAME: CPD-721| by meta fission to produce |FRAME: CPD-184| and |FRAME: METOH|. , Methanol was shown to be eliminated by the cells during pyrone formation, and a mechanism for this reaction was proposed. The |FRAME: CPD-184| product of the dioxygenase is then degraded by |FRAME: MONOMER-3463|. The product can spontaneously or enzymatically form the enol tautomer, |FRAME: CPD-185|. Hydration forms |FRAME: 4-OH-4-ACETYL-2-OXOGLUTARATE|. Finally, an aldolase cleaves this compound to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which enter central metabolism |CITS: [7142106]|. , The hydrolase, hydratase, and aldolase also function in the |FRAME: P184-PWY "protocatechuate meta cleavage pathway"|, and are enzymes central to aromatic compound degradation |CITS: [11495993]|., In |FRAME: TAX-502559| a dedicated |FRAME: MONOMER-15115| has been found (the product of the |FRAME: G-11550| gene). This enzyme catalyzes a similar ring fission reaction to the one catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7916| |CITS: [15262932]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9138 2,4,6-Trinitrotoluene"| (TNT), a nitroaromatic explosive, is a highly persistent organic pollutant introduced into the environment from the industries involved in the manufacture, packaging, use and decommissioning of explosives. It is a primary target for remediation because of its toxicity (as a class-C carcinogen) and the global extent of environmental contamination., Phytoremidiation is emerging as a viable alternative strategy to the current methods of TNT clean-up. With their extensive root systems, plants have a remarkable ability to extract compounds from their surroundings. Several studies have investigated the tolerance of plants to TNT and the active uptake of TNT by plant roots. A study with the aquatic plant |FRAME: TAX-208873| (Eurasian Watermilfoil) has shown that it can transforms TNT. Rapid disappearance of TNT from the plant culture media was followed by the appearance of aminodinitrotoluenes (ADNT), with lower levels of  hydroxylaminodinitrotoluene (HADNT) and diaminonitrotoluenes (DANT). However, these products accounted for less than 20% of the transformed TNT. The unaccounted for mass of TNT and/or transformation products was not detectable in the plant culture media nor was it extractable from the plant matrix |CITS: [Pavlostathis98]|., A later study with |FRAME: TAX-3702| has demonstrated the reductive transformation of TNT to hydroxylaminodinitrotoluene (HADNT), and then aminodinitrotoluene (ADNT), followed by glucosylation |CITS: [18702669]|.

General Background, Polyacylated anthocyanins are widespread among flowering plants |CITS: [HONDA02]| as exemplified by |FRAME: CPD-7142| (this pathway) |CITS: [KONDO89]| and |FRAME: CPD-7708| (|FRAME:PWY-5284|) |CITS: [TAKEDA86]|, which are found in Labiatae and by |FRAME:CPD-7700| |CITS: [NAKAYAMA97]|, which has been detected in the Asteraceae., The varying flower coloration of |FRAME: TAX-21880| has been investigated and found to be dependent on the distribution of anthocyanins, or more precisely of the backbone compounds that formed those anthocyanins. Red to pink-coloured flowers contain pelargonidin derived anthocyanins whereas blue and violet flowers are composed of delphinidin and cyanidin building blocks, respectively |CITS: [11809447]|., |FRAME: CPD-7142 Salvianin|, the predominant anthocyanin causing the scarlet flower coloration of |FRAME: TAX-180675| has two malonyl groups linked to the 4" and 6"-hydroxyl groups of the 5-glucosyl moiety |CITS: [11809447]| |CITS: [KONDO89]|. , Its biosynthesis represents a species-specific variety of the decoration of pelargonin (compare |FRAME:PWY-5139|) that involves glucosylation and aromatic and aliphatic acylation to increase stability, solubility and color variation of the chromophoric anthocyanins |CITS: [10066805]| |CITS: [10845463]| |CITS: [Heller94]|., About This Pathway, Pelargonidin 3-O-β-D-glucoside represents the starting compound that is stepwise converted into bisdemalonylsalvianin, the precursor for the aliphatic acylation with malonyl-CoA. Those reactions involve 5-O-glucosylation |CITS: [10066805]| and 3-aromatic acylation with caffeic acid |CITS: [Fujiwara98]| |CITS: [10845463]| which may proceed via two parallel pathway branches. The exact metabolic succession is not known and possibly will depend on the species involved., Bisdemalonylsalvianin is further malonylated twice on its 5-O-glucosidic moiety which is carried out by two different regio-specific malonyltransferases |CITS: [11598135]| |CITS: [15165190]|. Both acyltransferases belong to the BAHD group |CITS: [16616872]| that constitutes a large family of acyl CoA-utilizing enzymes of high catalytic versatility which often includes numerous homologs of unknown biochemical functions |CITS: [10712525]|. Although acetyltransferases show low similarities with each other they possess highly conserved sequences indicating the evolvement from a common ancestral gene |CITS: [9681034]|., The reaction mechanism of the first enzyme, i.e. malonyl-CoA: anthocyanin 5-O-glucoside-6'''-O-malonyltransferase (Ss5MaT1) producing monodemalonylsalvianin has been studied in detail revealing a ternary complex mechanism where both substrates and the enzyme must form a complex before catalysis can take place |CITS: [12578391]|., The second malonylation forming salvianin is catalyzed by malonyl CoA: anthocyanin 5-O-glucoside-4'''-O-malonyltransferase (Ss5MaT2), an enzyme that despite its close substrate similarity evolved from a different branch of the BAHD family |CITS: [15165190]|. This enzyme is more related to acetyl-CoA:benzylalcohol acetyltransferase (BEAT) and , thus differs from Ss5MaT1 associated with the anthocyanin acyltransferase (AAT) family.

Although |FRAME: Sphingomyelins "sphingomyelin"| is an important component of the plasma membranes of mammalian cells, |FRAME: TAX-7215 "Drosophila"| lacks |FRAME: Sphingomyelins "sphingomyelin"| and instead produces the analog |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS "sphingolipid"|, |FRAME: Ceramides-PE "ceramide phosphoethanolamine"| (CPE)., In mammals |FRAME: Sphingomyelins "sphingomyelin"| is produced by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.27| (ceramide:phosphatidylcholine cholinephosphotransferase), which catalyzes the transfer of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| from |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| onto |FRAME: Ceramides|, producing |FRAME: Sphingomyelins| and |FRAME: DIACYLGLYCEROL|. In |FRAME: TAX-7215 "Drosophila"| CPE is produced by |FRAME: MONOMER-18328| which catalyzes the transfer of |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE "phosphoethanolamine"| from |FRAME: CDP-ETHANOLAMINE| onto |FRAME: Ceramides|, producing CPE and |FRAME: CMP| |CITS: [23449981]|., In addition to |FRAME: TAX-6656 "arthropods"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-18328| has homologs among members of the |FRAME: TAX-6073| and |FRAME: TAX-6447|, but not in most other animal phyla. It represents a new branch within the CDP-alcohol phosphotransferase superfamily |CITS: [23449981]|., The mammalian sphingomyelin synthase occurs in two isoforms SMS1 and SMS2 as well as a closely related enzyme SMSr. Mammalian cells also produce small amounts of CPE via the bifunctional SMS2 and the monofunctional SMSr, both of which are located in the endoplasmic reticulum. |FRAME: TAX-7215 "Drosophila"| contains a homolog of SMSr with CPE synthase activity, but it is not responsible for the bulk of CPE production in |FRAME: TAX-7215 "Drosophila"| S2 cells |CITS: [19506037][23449981]|.

Summary: The |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)| summarizes the formation of acylsucroses with varying acyl pattern on both the pyranose and furanose moieties of |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose|. The various acylations occur along the biosynthetic route from monoacylated (|FRAME:PWY18C3-8 monoacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) to diacylated (|FRAME:PWY18C3-9 diacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|), triacylated (|FRAME:PWY18C3-10 triacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) and tetraacylated (|FRAME:PWY18C3-11 tetraacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) metabolites, the latter two representing the main acylsucroses accumulating in the cultivated tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) |CITS:[22988115] [24772058]|. In general acylsugars such as acylglucose |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| and acylsucrose metabolites (this pathway) are produced in glandular trichomes of and confined to plants of the Solanaceae family |CITS:[2652002]|. The interest in those pathways lies in the wide occurrence and diversity of acylsucrose and acylglucose compounds which are typifying compounds for the genus Solanum |CITS:[20113441]|. The high variability of acylated sucrose is particularly obvious in wild species of Solanum (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) and appears to be associated with geographical locations |CITS:[Shapiro94] [23054567]|., The availability of an increasing number of genomes from tomato species, e.g. the stress-tolerant Solanum pennellii |CITS:[25064008]| also opens paths to confer desired properties of wild species, e.g. Solanum pennellii to cultivated Solanaceae species such as Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[Lawson97]|, potato or Petunia |CITS:[Chortyk97]|. Acylsugars have been shown to exhibit a broad-range of insecticidal properties |CITS:[Hawthorne92] [18807203] [Maluf10] [Leckie12]| which include interacting with phytohormones |CITS:[21068365]|, feeding behaviors of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94] [Liedl95]| and serving as food source for pest larvae, e.g. in Nicotiana plants |CITS:[Severson85]| causing a specific volatile profile that attracts the larvae predators |CITS:[21518882]|. Those compounds have also found applications in the food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical industries where they are used as nonhazardous additives |CITS:[Hill99]|., The catalyzing enzymes for the versatile decoration of acylsucrose metabolites found in the Solaneceae family are BAHD acyltransferases |CITS:[16616872]| which have undergone structural changes resulting in genetic variations which accept and process various acyl groups of varying length as suitable substrates at specific ring positions |CITS:[25862303]|. The formation of monoacylated sucrose metabolites is the first step in the biosynthetic path towards tri- and tetraacyl sucroses. Metabolic profiling of RNAi silenced Solanum lycopersicum plants indicated the gene ASAT1 (Solyc12g006330) as the acyltransferase involved in the first acylation step because no acylsucrose intermediates usually decorated with up to four acyl-groups have been detected in those RNAi silenced plants |CITS:[26715757]|. It was shown that ASAT1 of Solanum lycopersicum and its ortholog in Solanum pennellii was able to monoacylate |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| at the 4-position of the pyranose ring with a number of acyl-CoA's |CITS:[26715757]|. The subsequent step, acylating the 3-position of the pyranose moiety of |FRAME:CPD-19018 sucrose-4-isovalerate| was carried out by an acyltransferase which is encoded by the gene ASAT2 (Solyc04g012020). In addition, the substrate specificity of the ASAT2 enzyme has been shown to be dependent on two amino acid residues in the vicinity of the putative acyl-CoA-binding pocket, i.e. Val/Phe408 which strongly determined whether or not |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA isovaleryl-CoA| is used as acyl donor and Leu43 which governed the use of |FRAME:2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA 2-methylbutanoyl-CoA| as acyl donor |CITS:[26715757]|., A forward genetic screen of the cultivated Solanum lycopersicum M82 and introgression lines of Solanum lycopersicum M82 and Solanum pennellii LA0716 allowed to identify the acyltransferase (ASAT3) which is able to decorate the backbone of |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| at the 3'-position of the furanose moiety |CITS:[25862303]|. The last acylation, which results in the formation of tetraacylsucroses has been elucidated by investigating overlapping regions on chromosome 1 of introgression lines of Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum pennellii which allowed the identification of the catalyzing acyltransferase encoded by the gene ASAT4, formerly referred to as AT2 |CITS:[22988115]|. The molecular function of the ASAT4 encoded protein could be demonstrated via virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS), RNAi transformed Solanum lycopersicum plants and functional complementation of Solanum pennelliii introgression lines lacking the ASAT4 gene. Moreover, heterologous expression of ASAT4 (AT2) in the yeast Pichia pastoris resulted in a recombinant protein which was able to utilize |FRAME:ACETYL-COA acetyl-CoA| as acyl donor generating the tetraacylsucrose metabolites characteristically been found in the cultivated tomato Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[22988115] [26715757]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is an important and ubiquitous structural component of eukaryotic cell, membranes. Many bacterial species possess the capability to metabolize cholesterol and can survive on cholesterol as a single carbon source. The exact taxonomy of some species or genera recognized to catabolize cholesterol has changed over time. Two of the strains that were studied extensively, Nocardia restrictus ATCC 14887 and |FRAME:TAX-1702| ATCC 21387, are now classified as strains of |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [874450][12843070]|. In general, the mycolate-containing nocardioform actinomycetes, which include the genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus| and |FRAME: TAX-2060|, have all been shown to catabolize cholesterol and plant sterols |CITS: [19843168]|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1883| have also been shown to decompose different steroids, including cholesterol |CITS: [Arima69]|. There have also been some reports of Proteobacteria that can degrade cholesterol |CITS: [4628510][9572974][18039763]|., Prior to their degradation, sterols are actively transported into the actinobacterial cells by the Mce4 steroid transporter |CITS: [18955493]|., The microbial degradation of cholesterol is challenging because of its complex chemical structure, low solubility in water, low number of functional groups and the presence of four alicyclic rings and two quaternary carbon atoms. A preliminary aerobic cholesterol degradation pathway has been proposed based on metabolites of cholesterol that have been identified in several actinomycete strains |CITS: [17345852]|, and has been greatly updated with new information obtained by several groups. In general, the steroid is sequentially oxidized and dehydrogenated forming several molecules of acetate and propioniate that can feed the citric acid cycle and generate ATP, or feed biosynthetic pathways such as lipid biosynthesis |CITS: [Murohisa93]|., Cholesterol-regulated genes are usually located in gene clusters that are induced by cholesterol. In |FRAME: TAX-101510|, for example, the cluster contains 82 genes, whose proposed functions mostly fit the predicted pathway |CITS: [17264217]|., About This Pathway, Generally, microbial degradation of cholesterol starts with oxidation of the cholesterol 3β-hydroxyl moiety and isomerization of the structure from Δ5 into Δ4. This transformation is catalyzed by either |FRAME: MONOMER-16891| or |FRAME: G185E-5271-MONOMER|, depending on the species, and results in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-323|., Following the initial reaction, the cholesterol degradation pathway involves two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. While it becomes clear that different organisms perform these processes in different order, the order in specific organisms is still not well known. It has been suggested that the side chain is eliminated first in |FRAME: TAX-101510|, while in |FRAME:TAX-1773| the two processes may occur simultaneously |CITS: [21987574]|. The pathway depicted here follows a route where the side chain is degraded completely before the steroid rings are opened., Side-chain degradation starts with either |FRAME: RHA1_RO04679 Cyp125| or |FRAME: G185E-7795 Cyp142|, P450 cytochromes that catalyze the C-26/C-27 hydroxylation of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and subsequently oxidize the hydroxylation product to a carboxylate via an aldehyde intermediate |CITS: [19843222]|. The two enzyme oxidize different carbon atoms and thus the products they produce have different stereo conformation |CITS: [20843794]|. Degradation proceeds via two cycles of a β-oxidative type process. The first step is activation of the molecule by forming a coenzyme A ester, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-14719|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-16899| |CITS: [21602385]|. The first β-oxidation cycle removes a |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety, while the second cycle removes |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. The exact identity of many of the enzymes involved in these two cycles has been reported |CITS: [Griffin11][Wipperman14][Yang15]|. Since a key enzyme in this step, |FRAME: CPLX-8814|, is specific for the (25S) diastereomers, a racemase needs to convert the products of Cyp142 degradation from (25R) to (25S) before their degradation can proceed., The degradation of the side chain is completed by the removal of a second |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| moiety in a process that involves three enzymes, all of which encoded by genes in the intracellular growth (igr) operon |CITS: [Thomas11]|. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenation of the 2'-propanoate side chain, followed by enoyl-CoA hydration, produce a quaternary alcohol, which then undergoes a retroaldol C1-C2' cleavage reaction catalyzed by a third enzyme, producing |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| and liberating another |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| molecule |CITS: [Thomas11][25203216][Yang15]|., For a description of the second part of the pathway, please see |FRAME: PWY-6944|., For the complete degradation of cholesterol by Mycobacteria, please see |FRAME: PWY-6946|.

|FRAME:CPD-16684 Secoisolariciresinol diglucoside| is an lignan glucoside mainly found in flax (Linum usutatissimum) or more specifically in flax seeds |CITS:[19779640]|. This lignan diglucoside is associated with numerous health benefits for humans due to its influence on hormone balance, antioxidant activity and effects on the activity of certain enzymes involved in lipid and glucose metabolism |CITS:[20003621]|. It is also a precursor to diversified lignans, e.g. the phytoestrogen enterolactol |CITS:[24429845]|. , Glucosylation represents one of the key modifications in the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites and is often catalyzed by UDP-glucose dependent glucosyltransferases (UGT's) |CITS:[21443631]| which belong to the family 1 of the superfamily of glycosyltransferases |CITS:[16415215]|. The genome of flax appears to host about 137 UGT's |CITS:[22568875]| but only comparably few have been characterized and their molecular function confirmed (see |FRAME:PWY-7491|, |CITS:[17870138]|; |FRAME:PWY-7139|, |CITS:[18248594] [19561332]|)., The |FRAME:CPD-16684| differs from other lignan di-, and triglucosides, for instance |FRAME:CPD-14839| and |FRAME:CPD-14841| (see |FRAME:PWY-7139|) in structure and biosynthetic genesis. Whereas the sesaminol di- and triglucoside originate from |FRAME:CPD-8905| (see |FRAME:PWY-5466|) via |FRAME:CPD-8922| (see |FRAME:PWY-5469|), |FRAME:CPD-16684| stems from the (-) enatiomer, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-8906| of the |FRAME:PWY-5466| pathway. Lignans show a high diversity |CITS:[Umezawa03]|, their biosynthesis is often enantiomer-specific |CITS:[15949826] [20514607]| and even differ between the various organs of a plant |CITS:[12162547]|. The formation of |FRAME:CPD-16684| is realized by the consecutive glucosylation via |FRAME:CPD-16683| which is catalyzed in flax by the (+)-secoisolariciresinol glucosyltransferase |CITS:[24678929]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-27292 Lydicamycin| is an antibiotic originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-47763| in 1991. It is characterized by an unprecedented modified pyrrolidine ring and is active against several Gram-positive bacteria including MRSA |CITS: [2026553][2026554]|. Lydicamycin was also reported to have a strong anti-oomycete activity, showing equal or better EC50 values than the commercialized drug metalaxyl |CITS: [38383306]|., In 2002 the compound was isolated, along with several congeners (|FRAME: CPD-27293|, |FRAME: CPD-27296|, |FRAME: CPD-27294|, and |FRAME: CPD-27295|) from a deep sea bacterium that was named Streptomyces sp. TP-A0598 |CITS: [12523820]| (the organism was later renamed |FRAME: TAX-1546107| |CITS: [32155704]|). Genome sequencing of this organism revealed the gene cluster that encodes lydicamycin biosynthesis, and a biosynthetic pathway was proposed |CITS: [26380643]|., About This Pathway, The lydicamycin biosynthetic gene cluster contains seventeen polyketide synthase (PKS) modules organized into eight enzymes, as well as one non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS). The cluster also includes genes encoding the biosynthesis of a |FRAME: CPD-592| starter unit., The authors proposed that the pathway starts with the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.25| (attributed to |FRAME: G-124713|), which forms |FRAME: CPD-824|, followed by an acyl-CoA ligase encoded by |FRAME: G-124714|, which forms |FRAME: CPD-25991| |CITS: [26380643]|. They based this hypothesis on a previously proposed similar scenario for the biosynthesis of the antifungal agent ECO-02301 |CITS: [15844935]|. However, both scenarios appear to be incorrect, as they do not account for the loss of a carbon in the transition from |FRAME: CPD-824| to |FRAME: CPD-25991|. A 2013 paper reported on a common pathway for the formation of |FRAME: CPD-25991| as a starter unit for polyketide synthases, which is applicable for lydicamycin biosynthesis. According to that proposed pathway, |FRAME: ARG| is converted to |FRAME: 4-GUANIDO-BUTYRAMIDE| by |FRAME: EC-1.13.12.1|, which accounts for the loss of a carbon. That compound is converted to |FRAME: CPD-592| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.4|, and that product serves as the substrate for the acyl-CoA ligase |CITS: [24218293]|. Supporting this mechanism in |FRAME: PWY-8532|, a BLAST analysis of the |FRAME: G-124713| gene identifies its product as an L-arginine 2-monooxygenase rather than L-argfinine oxidase (72% identity to |FRAME: CPLX-85406| from |FRAME: TAX-1911|), and the gene next to it, |FRAME: G-124716|, encodes an amidase (MetaCyc curator observation)., After the 4-guanidinobutanoyl starter is loaded onto an acyl-carrier protein domain of the first PKS, the polyketide chain is extended by eight PKSs using eleven |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and six |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| extender units. A |FRAME: GLY| molecule, loaded by the NRPS enzyme, is added to the polyketide terminus. Following release from the PKS, the molecule undergoes several modifications, resulting in the formation of an octalin and a tetramic acid ring. It is not known if any of these modifications involve enzymes. The last reaction of the pathway involves a cytochrome P450 that hydroxylates the octalin carbon at C-8, forming |FRAME: CPD-27292| |CITS: [26380643]|., The proposed pathway has not been validated by biochemical experiments.
