Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PHE| is an essential amino acid in humans and must be obtained in the diet. The major pathway of mammalian |FRAME: PHE| degradation is via hydroxylation to |FRAME: TYR| in the liver, followed by complete oxidation of |FRAME: TYR| (see pathway |FRAME: PHENYLALANINE-DEG1-PWY| and associated pathway link). However, a minor pathway of |FRAME: PHE| side chain degradation by transamination or decarboxylation also occurs (this pathway). Metabolites formed in this alternative pathway include |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: CPD-7999|, |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE|, |FRAME: CPD-11495| (o-hydroxyphenylacetate), |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-1097| or |FRAME: CPD-11715|, which can be identified in urine. In individuals with hyperphenylalaninemia, such as phenylketonuria patients, these minor metabolites are increased in urine (in |CITS: [18566668] [15149604] [12771361] [17467347]| and |CITS: [10077654]|)., About This Pathway, The enzyme involved in transamination of |FRAME: PHE| to |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE| was hypothesized to be mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferase (EC 2.6.1.1). This was supported by later work that showed a narrow substrate specificity for human tyrosine aminotransfrase (EC 2.6.1.5), making this enzyme an unlikely candidate |CITS: [16640556]|. |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE| may be oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-11495|, or reduced to |FRAME: CPD-7999|. Note that pathway diagrams in the literature also suggest that |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE| can be metabolized to |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| (in |CITS: [18566668]| and in |CITS: [10077654]|) (not shown) although the reaction, or route, was not given. A microbial route for this conversion is shown in |FRAME: ANAPHENOXI-PWY|., The enzyme involved in the decarboxylation of |FRAME: PHE| is aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (in |CITS: [1729407]|). The decarboxylation product |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE| (β-phenylethylamine) is a trace amine in the mammalian central nervous system and is hypothesized to function as a neuromodulator, enhancing dopaminergic transmission. It is metabolized by mitochondrial monoamine oxidase B to |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE|. This compound is dehydrogenated to |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (EC 1.2.1.3) and possibly also by aldehyde oxidase (EC 1.2.3.1) and xanthine oxidase (1.2.3.2). |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| may subsequently be activated and conjugated to amino acids (see below) |CITS: [11134050] [15230339] [15569272] [8605195] [6181210] [11797065] [2193105] [4748552]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15228583]|., An enzymatic activity in extracts from human and bovine liver mitochondria that catalyzed the activation of |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| to its |FRAME: CO-A| derivative was characterized early |CITS: [13491597]|. It is now known that many endogenous and xenobiotic substrates are metabolized in liver and kidney mitochondria via the formation of acyl-CoA derivatives in reactions catalyzed by ATP-dependent acid-CoA ligases (AMP-forming) (EC 6.2.1.1 through EC 6.2.1.3) (note that EC 6.2.1.30 is a microbial enzyme). The mitochondrial medium-chain CoA ligase EC 6.2.1.2 is associated with metabolism via amino acid conjugates (reviewed in |CITS: [9784915]| and |CITS: [19035562]|) and is a candidate enzyme for this pathway. Different forms of this enzyme have been purified and characterized from human and bovine sources, although species differences may exist as to which ligases function in a given reaction (in |CITS: [12616642]|). Two of these enzymes from human liver mitochondria, HXM-A and HXM-B, have been purified and characterized and were shown in vitro to have phenylacetate-CoA ligase activity, although highest activity was found with |FRAME: BENZOATE| and |FRAME: HEXANOATE|, respectively |CITS: [10434065] [12616642]|., Amino acid conjugation of phenylacetyl-CoA with |FRAME: GLN| or |FRAME: GLY| is catalyzed by mitochondrial arylacetyl acyl-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase of liver and kidney. The |FRAME: CPD-1097| conjugate has been shown to occur in humans and monkeys, whose enzyme is |FRAME: GLN|-specific. In other mammals the |FRAME: CPD-11715| conjugate is predominantly formed (|CITS: [13491597] [457678] [931988]| in |CITS: [9664233]|, in |CITS: [1956990]| and in |CITS: [6857245]|)., Although not shown here, it should also be noted that |FRAME: CPD-11495| may also be formed from the biogenic amine |FRAME: CPD-11758| and has been identified in aqueous humor of the human eye |CITS: [1727423]|. |FRAME: CPD-11758| is formed by decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-11757|, which is formed from |FRAME: PHE| by oxygen radicals under conditions of oxidative stress |CITS: [16298866] [8509373]| . Normal |FRAME: TYR| (p-tyrosine) can be similarly decarboxylated to |FRAME: TYRAMINE| which is found in tissues and urine |CITS: [1997791] [6131938] [5914747]| and further oxidative metabolism of |FRAME: TYRAMINE| has also been shown |CITS: [6830619] [518681]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15228583]|.

General Background, Most organisms have less than 45 different tRNAs despite the fact that there are 61 different amino acid codons. The reason for this is that the third base of the codon is less discriminatory for the amino acid than the other two bases. Thus, the first base of the tRNA anticodon, which pairs with the third base of the codon, is more permissive for mismatches than the other two positions. At this position, which is known as the wobble position, 'U's and 'C's may be read by a 'G' in the anticodon. Similarly, 'A's and 'G's may be read by a 'U' or 'y' (pseudouridine) in the anticodon., The nucleotide at the wobble position is often modified, and particularly uridines, which are almost invariably modified. In yeast, 11 out of 13 wobble uridine-containing tRNAs are modified in some manner. The modifications increase the efficiency of codon reading and prevent mistranslation by limiting wobbling. In particular the 2-thiolation of the uridine is required for efficient codon recognition on the ribosome., The uridine34 wobble bases of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu are universally modified, although different modifications occur in different taxa and even in different cell compartments., In |FRAME: PWY-7891 "yeast mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19983| (τm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7889 "mammalian mitochondria"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19980| (cmnm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7888 "cytoplasmic tRNAs of all eukaryotes"| the modification is |FRAME: CPD-19978| (mcm5s2U)., In |FRAME: PWY-7892 "the bacterium E. coli"| the modification is |FRAME: 5-METHYLAMINOMETHYL-2-THIOURIDINE| (mnm5s2U)., About This Pathay, The process starts with formation of the 5-taurinomethyl group of the uracil ring (τm5U) by the |FRAME: CPLX-9233|, which is composed of |FRAME: HS05977| and |FRAME: HS05366| |CITS: [12011058][12370316]|., The subsequent thiolation is catalyzed by the |FRAME: ENSG00000100416-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS02078| (MTO2) gene |CITS: [15944150][17706197]|. The sulfur used for the thiolation originates from |FRAME: CYS|, and is delivered to |FRAME: HS02078| by a short sulfur relay chain that includes the L-cysteine desulfurase |FRAME: HS01304| and the sulfurtransferase |FRAME: HS05177| (TUM1) |CITS: [19151091][25336638]|., Mutations in the genes involved in this pathway lead to the diseases MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy and ragged-red fiber) and MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy and lactic acidosis with stroke-like episodes) as a result of decoding disorders. In addition, mutations in the genes of this pathway modulate the phenotypic expression of the deafness-associated mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA mutations |CITS: [16826519]|.

Sandalwood is grown in India, Australia and China, the scented wood and oil are prized for their fragrances and use in cosmetics and medicinal use |CITS: [17045624]|. The oil is produced by the heartwood and the oil components have been isolated and characterized in |FRAME: TAX-35974|, S. spicatum and the chinese sandal. In addtion to the santanols it is composed of sesquiterpenoids mainly the |FRAME: CPD-11377| and the |FRAME: --beta-santalene| and a host of other terpenes in minor and varying quantities |CITS: [ADAMS75]|. Four structural classes of sesquiterpenoids have been isolated and found as co-occuring sesquiterpenes; |FRAME: CPD-11377|, |FRAME: --beta-santalene| and bergamotene; and b-curcumene; b-bisabolene and a-bisabolol and along with four unidentified sesquiterpenes |CITS: [17045624]|. The lack common structural intermediate between these compounds is said to indicate the possibility of 4 different classes of sesquiterpene cyclases to be present in sandal wood trees. , The glandular trichomes of wild tomato |FRAME: TAX-62890| are the sites of biosynthesis of several class II sesquiterpene olefins. The Sst2 locus on chromosome 8 is responsible for these enzymes. Two candidate genes identified from this region are, zFPS encoding a protein with homology to Z-isoprenyl pyrophosphate synthases and SBS encoding for Santalene and Bergamotene Synthase |CITS: [19155349]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, A group of 6-deoxyhexoses, including |FRAME: CPD-13559|, |FRAME: CPD-15612|, |FRAME: CPD-13829|, |FRAME: CPD-9388|, |FRAME: CPD0-1107| and |FRAME: CPD-15615| are used as components of the O-anigen repeating units in lipopolysaccharides of certain Gram-negative bacteria and of the S-layer of some Gram-positive bacteria., All of these modified sugar residues are synthesized in a GDP nucleotide-activated form from |FRAME: GLC-6-P| via |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. , Mannose is produced in its 6-phosphate form by the isomerization of |FRAME:GLC-6-P| via |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| This is achieved by the action of the ubiquitous |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.9|, which also participates in glycolysis, and the more specific |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.8| |CITS: [1846611]|. In order to produce the activated mannose donor |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| the 6-phosphate is first reconstructed as a 1-phosphate form, followed by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.13| |CITS:[GaoIntJMassSpec05] [8922954]|., Before |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| can be converted to the other sugars, it loses the the hydroxyl group connected to carbon 6 by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.47|, producing |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE| |CITS: [14739333]|. This compound is the substrate for several different enzymes, including dehydrogenases, aminotransferases, and dehydratases, resulting in the production of the different modified 6-deoxysugars shown in this pathway.

Summary: The |FRAME: Furaquinocins furaquinocins| are a family of polyketide-isoprenoid hybrid compounds produced by |FRAME: TAX-285219| |CITS: [Funayama89][2324009][2032947]| and related species |CITS: [21610713][Tistechok22]|. They show a wide range of biological effects including in vitro cytotoxicity against HeLa S3 and B16 melanoma cells, antihypertensive activity, and inhibition of platelet aggregation and coagulation., The |FRAME: Furaquinocins furaquinocins| belong to the polyketide subclass of the |FRAME: CPD-17353 meroterpenoids|, which includes compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-26296|, |FRAME: CPD-26297|, and |FRAME: CPD-26298|, all of which are produced by |FRAME: TAX-1883| strains. These meroterpenoids share a skeleton derived from |FRAME: TETRAHYD-CPD tetrahydroxynaphthalene|, with an attached 10-carbon geranyl group., The furaquinocin biosynthetic genes of |FRAME: TAX-285219| were found at regions both upstream and downstream of a mevalonate biosynthetic gene cluster (this organism has two mevalonate biosynthetic gene clusters). When two DNA fragments containing the upstream and the downstream regions were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1916| TK23, the host produced |FRAME: CPD-16660| |CITS: [16452404]|., |FRAME: TETRAHYD-CPD Tetrahydroxynaphthalene| (THN) is produced from 5 molecules of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| by the polyketide synthase |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.233|. The THN skeleton is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-10679|. This reaction was originally proposed to occur spontaneously in the presence of oxygen, but was later shown to be catalyzed by a monooxygenase |CITS: [15701630]|., |FRAME: CPD-10679 Flaviolin| is modified by two methylations, forming |FRAME: CPD-16658|. It should be noted that the order in which these two methyltransferases act is not known. For the pathway shown here we randomly selected the O-methyltransferase to act first., The product of the two methylations, |FRAME: CPD-16658|, serves as the substrate for |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.124|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124369| gene |CITS: [20937800]|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-16659|, is converted into |FRAME: CPD-16661| by a cyclase whose identity is not known as of 2022. Finally, |FRAME: CPD-16661| is converted into |FRAME: CPD-16660| and further into |FRAME: CPD-26292| by successive hydroxylations catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 encoded by the |FRAME: G-124372| gene |CITS: [16452404]|.

Summary: The first to isolate a Bifidobacterium was Tissier of the Pasteur Institute in France, who in 1899 isolated an organism from a breast-fed infant |CITS: [Tissier00]|. He named the organism |FRAME:TAX-1681|, describing the branching morphology of the bacteria (bifidus in Latin means forked or split into two parts). In the 1960s Bifidobacterium was accepted as an independent genus, and today more than 30 species are documented |CITS: [15539925]|. Bifidobacteria are accepted as important probiotic components of the human intestinal microflora, and are used in health-promoting foods |CITS: [15916644][16167966]|., The Bifidobacteria use a unique pathway of hexose catabolism, which produces primarily acetate and lactate. This fermentation pathway, which is known as the "Bifidobacterium shunt" or the "fructose-6-phosphate pathway" yields 3 mols of acetate and 2 mols of lactate for 2 mols of glucose, with production of 5 mols of ATP |CITS:[6020562][6048259][4236541][9430608]|. The key enzyme in the pathway is |FRAME:CPLX-7204|, which catalyzes two important steps: splitting |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| into |FRAME:ERYTHROSE-4P| and |FRAME:ACETYL-P|, and splitting |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| into |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:ACETYL-P|. This enzyme has often been used as a tool in the identification of Bifidobacteria |CITS: [11298932]|, even though such enzymes have been found in other organisms., Acetylphosphate, which is formed in both phosphoketolase-catalyzed steps, is converted to |FRAME: ACET|. |FRAME:ERYTHROSE-4P| is processed along with a second |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| molecule by enzymes of the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY| to |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|. This compound is then split in the second reaction catalyzed by phosphoketolase to |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:ACETYL-P|. |FRAME:GAP| is processed via the glycolytic Embden-Meyerhof pathway to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME:L-LACTATE|.

Summary: General Background, The pathway described here - the NAD-dependent oxidation of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, is found in different types of organisms., One type of organisms that employ this reaction are the hydrogen bacteria. These organisms are able to use |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as a sole source of electrons and reducing power under aerobic conditions. They are facultative lithotrophs, and are able to reduce |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| via the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|., Most of the hydrogen bacteria possess only a membrane-bound enzyme that transfers the electrons from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| to the respiratory electron transfer chain (see |FRAME: P283-PWY|), but some of them, possess a soluble hydrogenase, which is able to transfer the electrons directly to NAD, as described here. , Many, though not all, cyanobacteria also possess an NAD-dependent hydrogenase, known as a "|FRAME: CPLX-8066|". The enzyme catalyzes both hydrogen formation and hydrogen uptake, depending on the circumstances. Hydrogen uptake (oxidation) is common in nitrogen-fixing cells, where the hydrogenase consumes the hydrogen produced by the |FRAME: CPLX-525| |CITS: [12034472]|., About This Pathway, Only a few aerobic |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|-oxidizing bacteria contain a soluble hydrogenase, which is different from the more common membrane-bound hydrogenases by being able to directly reduce NAD., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-106590| possesses both membrane-bound and soluble hydrogenases, while a few species, including |FRAME: TAX-32002|, |FRAME: TAX-72557|, |FRAME: TAX-2074| and |FRAME: TAX-37919| possess only soluble enzymes., Factor specific hydrogenases, such as the soluble NAD-dependent hydrogenases (but also |FRAME: CPLX-7202|, EC 1.12.98.1, and the phenazine-dependent |FRAME:CPLX-7104|, EC 1.12.98.3, which are found in methanogens) contain one or two extra subunits in addition to the dimeric moiety |CITS: [2128802]|., Accordingly, the soluble enzyme of |FRAME: TAX-106590| is made up of two heterodimers, a |FRAME: CPLX-862| (|FRAME: G-314| and |FRAME: G-315|) and a |FRAME:CPLX-861| (|FRAME: G-313| and |FRAME: G-312|), the latter being an NADH oxidoreductase |CITS: [9495738]|., Gene clusters that contain the four genes encoding the NAD-dependent hydrogenase (|FRAME: G-315|, |FRAME: G-314|, |FRAME: G-313| and |FRAME: G-312|) have also been identified in the genomes of many cyanobacteria |CITS: [ 7588754]|. However, in cyanobacteria, a fifth subunit, |FRAME: SGL_RS09760-MONOMER|, is part of this bidirectional hydrogenase |CITS: [12034472]|. , |FRAME: TAX-106590| is capable of growing autotrophically in the absence of the soluble hydrogenase, although it does so at a slower rate. This indicates that the membrane-bound hydrogenase can take over, but also that the reverse-electron flow required for production of reducing equivalents by the membrane-bound enzyme is a growth-limiting step |CITS: [8257102]|. Similarly, the introduction of the genes encoding the soluble enzyme into the organism |FRAME: TAX-12917|, which naturally contains only a membrane-bound hydrogenase, resulted in an increased growth rate |CITS: [2188945]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: STAUROSPORINE "Staurosporine"| was isolated in 1977 (under the name AM-2282) from a culture of |FRAME: TAX-65499 "Lentzea albida (then known as Streptomyces stauroporeus AM-2282)"| that was collected from a soil sample in Japan |CITS: [863788]|. , Staurosporine and related natural indolocarbazole compounds have been isolated from actinomycetes, myxomycetes (slime molds) and cyanobacteria. They have also been found in some marine invertebrates such as sponges, tunicates, bryozoans and mollusks, where they may be synthesized by symbiotic bacteria |CITS: [17119643]|. For a list of strains shown to produce indolocarbazole compounds see |CITS: [17119643]|., In 1986 it was shown to be nanomolar inhibitor of protein kinases |CITS: [3457562]|. During the 1990s protein kinases became the second most important drug target after G-protein-coupled receptors, and |FRAME: STAUROSPORINE| became the focus of much research. |FRAME: CPD-11911| (UCN-01) showed antitumor activity in mouse tumor models, and entered clinical studies |CITS: [1893379]|. Staurosporine-related structures have been derivatized and developed into selective inhibitors of pharmacologically interesting targets |CITS: [19132059]|., About This Pathway, The first enzyme in staurosporine biosynthesis to be identified was the one catalyzing the very last step (|FRAME: MONOMER-15145|). A |FRAME: TAX-28044| mutant defective in this enzyme has been reported in 1995 |CITS: [7775266]|, and the enzyme was idendified in 1998 |CITS: [9727395]|. The complete staurosporine biosynthetic gene cluster was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-171258| based on homology with genes invovled in |FRAME: PWY-6324|, and a fragment including all the required genes was heterologously expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1916|, resulting in staurosporine production |CITS: [12617516]|. Similarly, the full cluster was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-28044| and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1888| |CITS: [16164546]|., Following sequencing of the full cluster, single-gene disruption mutants were generated and functions were proposed for the sta genes based on the mutant phenotypes and their similarity to genes involved in |FRAME: PWY-6324| |CITS: [12617516][15625109][16164546]|., |FRAME: MONOMER-15152| |FRAME: G-11591|) initiates synthesis by coverting |FRAME: TRP| to the imine form of indole-3-pyruvate (|FRAME: CPD-11890|)., |FRAME: MONOMER-15151| (|FRAME: G-11590|) then catalyzes the coupling of two IPA imines to yield |FRAME: CPD-11786| |CITS: [Asamizu06]|. Formation of the indolocarbazole core of staurosporine is catalyzed by the action of two enzymes: |FRAME: G-11588| converts |FRAME: CPD-11786| into three indolocarbazole compounds, |FRAME: CPD-11789|, |FRAME: CPD-11788| and |FRAME: CPD-11787|, by intramolecular C-C bond formation and oxidative decarboxylation, while the presence of StaC is required to ensure that the main product is |FRAME: CPD-11789| |CITS: [16967980]|., The next step is the glycosylation of the molecule, which is catalyzed by two enzymes. |FRAME: MONOMER-15148| (|FRAME: G-11587|) catalyzes N-glycosidic bond formation between N-13 and C-6' of the nucleotide sugar |FRAME: CPD-11909|. |FRAME: MONOMER-15147| (|FRAME: G-11586|) then catalyzes an additional C-N bond formation between N-12 and C-5' |CITS: [16195595]|. Combined these two enzymes convert |FRAME: CPD-11789| to |FRAME: CPD-11905| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-11906| and |FRAME: CPD-11910|., The final steps in the pathway are two methylation reactions. |FRAME: G-11585| catalyzes N-methylation of |FRAME: CPD-11905| and |FRAME: G-11584| catalyzes O-methylation, which results in the formation of staurosporine.

Strains of the ascomycetes |FRAME: TAX-5547 "Hypocrea rufa (previously known as Trichoderma viride)"| and |FRAME: TAX-5544 "Hypocrea lixii (previously known as Trichoderma harzianum)"| have been shown to degrade |FRAME: LYS| via |FRAME: CPLX-7156|. Unlike most L-amino acid oxidases, this enzyme is highly specific for L-lysine. However, its enzymatic properties and amino acid composition differ among these organisms. The enzyme is useful for the determination of L-lysine, and has also been reported to have anti-tumor activity |CITS: [6101334][Webere] [12460113]|. , The product of the reaction, |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE| (6-amino-2-oxohexanoate), can spontaneously decarboxylate to |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| in the presence of the reaction product, hydrogen peroxide. Further metabolism of |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| in |FRAME: TAX-5543| has not been reported. Further metabolism of this compound by other fungi is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: LYSDEGII-PWY|. , |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE| can also be spontaneously converted in solution to its cyclic form |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE|. This has been demonstrated in vitro in the presence of catalase, which splits hydrogen peroxide |CITS: [6101334][Webere] |. Further metabolism of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE| in |FRAME: TAX-5543| has not been reported. However, conversion of this compound to pipecolate by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-303| is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5283|.

|FRAME:TAX-573| metabolizes L-sorbose to D-fructose-6-phosphate, which then enters glycolysis. L-Sorbose is transported into the cell, phosphorylated, and then converted to D-fructose-6-phosphate by two soluble enzymes |CITS: [6361004]|.

|FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFA) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes., The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in these compounds. The icosanoids are derived from the 20-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (AA; 20:4n-6), |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA; 20:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-8120| (DGLA; 20:3n-6)., Additional fatty acids are also oxygenated to yield bioactive products, including the the 18-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (LA; 18:2n-6) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (ALA; 18:3n-3) and the 22-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| (DPA; 22:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA; 22:6n-3). Strictly speaking, the derivatives of such acids should be named octadecanoids (for C18 compounds) and docosanoids (for 22 carbon compounds), though these compounds are often included in the icosanoids, making the definition broader than initially intended., In mammals icosanoids and related mediators mediate a wide array of critical biological processes such as ovulation, initiation of labor, bone metabolism, nerve growth and development, wound healing, kidney function, blood-vessel tone, blood coagulation, immune responses, and inflammation. Despite the great importance of these compounds, mammals are not able to form a double bond at either the n-3 or n-6 position of a fatty acyl chain and must rely entirely on dietary intake for PUFAs |CITS: [25486530]|., Three main enzyme families act on PUFAs. The first one is |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.1| (the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes), which possess dual cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activities and catalyze the oxidative cyclization of PUFAs to |FRAME: CPD-24676|, |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|, or |FRAME: CPD-26009| (depending on the starting PUFA), which are subsequently converted to a variety of prostanoids and thromboxanes by cell-specific terminal synthases and isomerases., The second family is the lipoxygenases (LOX), which catalyze the stereoselective insertion of molecular oxygen into PUFA with the formation of hydroperoxy fatty acids that are subsequently reduced to the corresponding hydroxy-fatty acids. The lipoxygenases are divided into three main form depneding on the carbon at which they oxygenate |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|: |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|., The third family is cytochrome P450 monooxygenases that catalyzes the hydroxylation and/or epoxygenation of PUFAs. In addition to producing LOX-like monohydroxy fatty acids, CYP can add a hydroxyl moiety to the ω-carbons, of PUFA to form a unique class of omega-hydroxylated fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-21314|). The epoxides that are formed by these enzymes can be hydrolyzed to the corresponding dihydroxyfatty acids by |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| (sEH).

General Background, |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf., Chlorophyll functions as the main light harvesting pigment in photosynthesis, capturing photons and transfering them to the reaction centers. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-18895|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, |FRAME: CPD-10335|, |FRAME: CPD-18896|, |FRAME: CPD-18897| and |FRAME: CPD-18898|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A "Chlorophyll a"| and |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B| (Chlb) are esterified by a phytol side chain. The esterification of the side chain is the last step in the chlorophyll biosynthesis pathway., It has been shown that the enzyme that is responsible for the esterification, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.62|, can attach either a phytol chain (see |FRAME: PWY-5086|) or a geranylgeriol side chain (in both cases a diphosphate form is used by the enzyme). In the latter case, the geranylgeraniol side chain is reduced after the esterification by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.83|, producing a phytyl side chain in three steps |CITS:[9492312]|.

|FRAME: CPD-19877| is a four-carbon acid sugar that can be used by some bacteria as the sole carbon source., This pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-19877| was found by a bioinformatic analysis of genes clustered with a D-erythronate-binding protein (SBP), which is a part of a TRAP (tripartite ATP-independent permease) transporter for the compound |CITS: [25540822]|., Following import into the cell, |FRAME: CPD-19877| is dehydrogenated at the C2 position, forming |FRAME: CPD-19883|. The dehydrogenase, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.410|, can use both NAD+ and NADP+, but prefers the former. The product is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-363| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.35|, followed by phosphrylation to |FRAME: CPD-19881| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.217|., The kinase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55079| gene, is one of the first members of a large family of enzymes, known as DUF (domain of unknown function) 1537, to which a function has been assigned |CITS: [27402745]|., Following phosphorylation, the compound is decarboxylated by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.104|, yielding the central metabolite |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS: [27402745]|.

Summary: Higher plants display different mechanisms of iron absorption. Dicots and non-grass monocots extrude both protons and reducing substances from the roots and increase ferric reductase activity in the root plasma membrane in response to Fe deficiency. Fe(III) in the environment is thus reduced to the soluble Fe(II) form, which is then transported into the plant. This response is referred to as Strategy I (see |FRAME: PWY-5934|)., The graminaceous monocots respond to iron defficiency by secreting phytosiderophores, in a response known as Strategy II. Fe(III) in the rhizosphere binds to the siderophores and is absorbed as Fe(III)-siderophore complex into the root plasma membrane |CITS: [15781441]|. The uptake is said to be facilitated by a putative transporter for the ferric-phytosiderophore complex, not necessitating prior reduction., One such siderophore is |FRAME: CPD-7227|, which has been shown to promote growth by orchestrating iron uptake processes, both under low and high pH conditions |CITS: [9565671][10069850][25393516]|. This compound has been shown to play an important role in many species including |FRAME: TAX-4530|, |FRAME: TAX-4577|, |FRAME: TAX-4565|, and |FRAME: TAX-4513| (although in the latter it is converted to |FRAME: CPD-7231| and some modified forms |CITS: [11346963]|) ( (see |FRAME: PWY-5925|)., The biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-7227| has been determined. |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) is synthesized from |FRAME: MET| by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.6|. Subsequently, three molecules of SAM are combined to form one molecule of |FRAME: CPD-463| by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.43| (NAS). The product is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-7228| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.80| (NAAT), and |FRAME: CPD-7227| is synthesized by the subsequent action of |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.285| (DMAS). A further series of hydroxylation steps produces related phytosiderophores from deoxymugineic acid |CITS: [Mori87][Shojima89][16667646][12231828]|., The pathway is thought to take place in root tissue in vesicles derived from rough endoplasmic reticulum. These vesicles remain swollen until the onset of phytosiderophore secretion, and become shrunken by the end of secretion |CITS: [Mori87]|. Secretion takes place in the morning in a distinct diurnal rhythm |CITS: [Takagi84]|. It has been suggested that the pathway acts in association with the |FRAME: PWY-7270 "methionine recycling pathway"| that occurs in the roots |CITS: [7622460]|., Rice is one of the most important crop species in the world, and its low tolerance to Fe deficiency in calcareous and marginal soils restricts the world food supply. As the genes and corresponding enzymes involved in |FRAME: CPD-7227| biosynthesis have been isolated and characterized |CITS: [9952442][10557244][11169192][16926158][18034312]|, metabolic engineering of these enzymes in Fe-deficient crops is a desired goal in agricultural biotechnology.  , It should be noted that alternative systems exist for the aquizition of Fe. In a rice mutant with a defective |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.43| (NAAT) enzyme, which was unable to form |FRAME: CPD-7227|, the expression of a number of genes involved in Fe(II) acquisition was grealy increased, resulting in actually higher Fe accumulation |CITS: [17951455]|.

Names: tetrahydrofolate biosynthesis II // folic acid biosynthesis II // folate biosynthesis II // THF biosynthesis II
Summary: General Background, Tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis., Folates also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine, play a role in histidine catabolism |CITS: [11001804]|, and in plants are also involved in photorespiration, amino acid metabolism and chloroplastic protein biosynthesis |CITS: [11960743]| |CITS: [12644692]|., Folates are abundant in green leaves, and folic acid was initially isolated from a large amount (four tons) of spinach leaves. The name folate is derived from the Latin folium (leaf) |CITS: [3067148]|., Folates are modified by the addition of glutamate moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail. The polyglutamylated forms are usually preferred by the enzymes that use folates since the turnover rate of those compounds is markedly increased |CITS: [9190084][SCOTT00][KIRK94]|. In addition, in eukaryotic cells the glutamylated forms of folate facilitate the retention of the vitamin within the cell and its subcellular compartments |CITS: [1916088]|., The product of this pathway, |FRAME: THF| (tetrahydropteroylmonoglutamate, H4PteGlu1,, THF), is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. Members of the family differ in the oxidation state, of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions (see, |FRAME: PWY-2201|), and the number of conjugated glutamate residues (see |FRAME: PWY-2161|)., About This Pathway, Folates are tripartite molecules and are made up of a pterin, |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| and |FRAME:GLT| moieties., The first two are synthesized from |FRAME:GTP| and |FRAME:CHORISMATE|, respectively. In this pathway variant the folP protein catalyzes two subsequent reactions, forming |FRAME: CPD-9020|. It is assumed that the FolC protein then acts on the latter, converting it to |FRAME: THF|, and continues to add additional glutamate residues, as described in |FRAME: PWY-2161| |CITS: [15554970][17416665]|., This pathway for the de novo biosynthesis of folates is found in bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-210| that have a bifunctional FolP protein and do not have homologs of the FolA and FolM proteins. Unlike the more common variant, this pathway does not include the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.3|., The organisms in which this pathway variant is found appear to encode |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.148| (ThyX) instead of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45| (ThyA). Unlike ThyA, which produces |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATE-GLU-N|, ThyX forms |FRAME: THF-GLU-N|, and thus organisms that possess it do not need |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.3|, to resore the product to tetrahydrofolate.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms. As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, One of the first siderophores to be identified was |FRAME: AEROBACTIN|, originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-548|,, which at the time was named |FRAME:TAX-548| |CITS: [4313071]|. , |FRAME: AEROBACTIN| is a dihydroxamate comprising 2 mol |FRAME: CPD-961| and 1 mol of |FRAME: CIT|. , |FRAME: AEROBACTIN Aerobactin| was found in several enterobacterial strains, including |FRAME: TAX-548|,, |FRAME: TAX-573|, |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: TAX-90371|, multiple |FRAME: TAX-620| strains, and multiple, |FRAME: TAX-629| strains., Even though the biosynthesis of |FRAME: AEROBACTIN| was first investigated in |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [Appanna84]|, most of our knowledge comes from a similar system that was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-83333|. Both systems are encoded by plasmid-borne genes; in the case of |FRAME: TAX-548| plasmid pSMN1 |CITS: [6330037][3053646]| and in the case of |FRAME: TAX-83333| plasmid pColV-K30 |CITS: [6456229]|., While most of the |FRAME: AEROBACTIN| biosynthesis systems are plasmid borne, a few organisms have these genes in their chromosomes |CITS:[6237061][11418557]|., The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway are located in a single operon along with one gene encoding a ferric-aerobactin transporter |CITS: [6090318]|.

Summary: General Background, The predominant circulating pyrimidine in many species, including humans is |FRAME: URIDINE| |CITS: [8155674][16769123]|., In mammals |FRAME: URIDINE Uridine| is produced de novo in the liver and kidney, and is circulated to other organs, where it serves as an important precursor of pyrimidine salvage pathways |CITS: [35970][6323418][3966913][8650301][11782482]|. Its plasma level is strictly maintained at 3-5 μM, a concentration higher than that of other nucleosides |CITS: [7877593]|., Cells maintain uridine concentration by balancing its input, salvage, and catabolism. The main enzyme responsible for uridine catabolism is |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "uridine phosphorylase"|., About This Pathway, The enzyme |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "uridine phosphorylase"| (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.3 "EC 2.4.2.3"|), which is found in archaea, bacteria and animals but is absent from fungi and plants, breaks down |FRAME: URIDINE| to the free base |FRAME: URACIL| and to |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P|. The resulting |FRAME: URACIL| can be degraded in multiple routes. This superpathway includes the so-called "reductive pathway", in which pyrimidine nucleobases are reduced to |FRAME:Beta-amino-acids|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. The reductive pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms |CITS:[13428755][13416173][16655478][16656066][10656811]|., In mammals, the breakdown of |FRAME: URACIL| to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| is considered to be restricted to the liver (see |FRAME: PWY-3982|) |CITS: [13535735][10354618][16098809]|, while |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P| is converted into |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP), which is used in the salvage synthesis of purine nucleotides |CITS: [6277907][7546322]|., Since |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "uridine phosphorylase"| is not capable of cleaving |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, this nucleoside must be deaminated to uridine before it can be processed by this pathway., Catabolic nucleoside degradation is also found in bacteria. Many species are able to degrade uridine to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| |CITS: [12670488]|. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| can use both naturally occurring pyrimidine ribonucleosides (|FRAME: CYTIDINE| and |FRAME: URIDINE|) as total sources of carbon and energy. While some strains, such as |FRAME: TAX-37762|, are able to utilize the pathway described here, the well-studied |FRAME: TAX-83333| strain is not able to degrade uracil to |FRAME: B-ALANINE|, and instead utilizes a |FRAME: PWY0-1471 "uracil degradation pathway"| encoded by genes in the rut operon |CITS: [16540542]|.

Summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., LTAs have been grouped into different types (type I through V) based on their chemical structures. Type I LTA is found in a large range of Firmicutes. It has an unbranched 1-3 linked glycerol phosphate (GroP) backbone, and is usually linked to the bacterial membrane via a glycolipid anchor. The hydroxyl groups at the C-2 position of the GroP repeating units are modified with D-alanyl or glycosyl groups to varying degrees. It should be noted that not all type I LTAs are glycosylated, and variations in the type of sugar exist. For example, some |FRAME: TAX-1386 Bacillus| strains lack glycosyl groups, some contain |FRAME: CPD-12541|, and some contain |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| |CITS: [3733670][2914853]|. The LTA of all |FRAME: TAX-1639| strains investigated to date is glycosylated with |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| |CITS: [6415040][3093460]|, and the LTA of |FRAME: TAX-1280| strain H is glycosylated with |FRAME: CPD-12541| |CITS: [6268617]|., LTAs can be very abundant. In |FRAME: TAX-1280| every ninth lipid on the outer leaflet of the membrane is an LTA molecule, and the average length is 25 GroP units |CITS: [6697992]|. Although the exact role of LTA is unknown, mutants display significant growth and physiological defects. Teichoic acids are proposed to serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, The first step in the biosynthesis of type I LTA is the synthesis of glycolipid anchor. The predominant glycolipids contain a disaccharide attached to diacylglycerol. The composition of the disaccharide varies - it is |FRAME: diacyl-3-O-glucl-1-6-gluc-sn-glycerol "β-glucosyl(1→6)-β-glucosyl(1→3)-DAG"| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [7935161][9720862]|, and α-galactosyl(1→2)-α-glucosyl(1→3)-DAG in |FRAME: TAX-1639| |CITS: [3093460]|., The glycolipid anchor is produced in the cytoplasm of the cell by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.315|, a processive enzyme that transfers glucose to diacylglycerol (DAG), using UDP-glucose as its substrate |CITS: [9720862][10848996][11344159][17209021]|. After its assembly the glycolipid anchor is moved to the outside of the membrane, presumably by the flippase LtaA |CITS: [17209021]|. Glycolipids anchors containing mono-, tri-, or tetrasaccharides are also used as LTA anchors, and they can be further substituted with acyl chains or fatty acids |CITS: [24819367]|., Once the anchor is on the extrernal side of the membrane, a primase adds a GroP unit derived from the head group of the membrane lipid |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol| (PG) to the the glycolipid anchor. This is followed by the repeated addition of GroP subunits by a polymerase until the full length is attained. While in |FRAME: TAX-1639| two differrent enzymes (LtaP and LtaS) catalyze the priming and polymerization reactions |CITS: [19682249]|, in |FRAME: TAX-1280| and |FRAME: TAX-1392| a single enzyme is responsible for both activities |CITS: [17483484][22685279]|., The requirement for PG is significant - it has been shown that the PG pool is turned over more than twice per generation time to support LTA synthesis |CITS: [6697992]|. For each PG molecule that is hydrolyzed to extend the LTA chain by one repeating unit, one molecule of DAG is produced. DAG then reenters the cell, where it is either used for the synthesis of glycolipids or recycled back to PG. The recycling process, which is included in this pathway diagram, includes four steps: DAG is first converted to phosphatidate by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.107| |CITS: [17535816]|, followed by the successive actions of |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.41|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.5|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.27|., The last parts of the pathway include glycosylation and D-alanylation. The incorporation of glycosyl residues into type I LTA involves three steps and two separate glycosyltransferases and proceeds through the formation of a sugar-linked monophosphoryl undecaprenol intermediate |CITS: [7130126][ 3360021]|. First a cytoplasmic glycosyltransferase uses a nucleotide-activated sugar to form the sugar-P-lipid intermediate. The intermediate is then transported across the membrane to the external side with the aid of a dedicated lipid flippase, and finally a second glycosyltransferase with an, extracellular catalytic domain links the sugar onto LTA. It has been suggested that the two glycosyltransferases resemble |FRAME: G7167| and |FRAME: G7170| of |FRAME: TAX-562|, respectively., As of 2016, only one such enzyme (the cytoplasmic glycosyltransferase) has been identified, by searching for |FRAME: G7167| homologs in |FRAME: TAX-1639| |CITS: [27185829]|., The remaining modification, D-alanylation, is only partially understood. This process is carried by a complex system encoded by the dlt operon |CITS: [10085071]|. More information about this process is provided in the summary notes for |FRAME: MONOMER-19990|.

Summary: General Background, Inorganic reduced sulfur compounds serve as electron donors in many phototrophic and chemotrophic bacteria |CITS: [9328649]|. Sulfide oxidation plays an important role in the global sulfur cycle by reoxidizing the sulfide produced by sulfate-reducing bacteria in anoxic habitats., Phototrophic purple and green sulfur-oxidizing bacteria use the sulfur compounds as electron donors for reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation during photolithotrophic growth. Light energy is used to transfer electrons from the sulfur compounds to levels found in highly reducing electron carriers such as |FRAME:Ferredoxins| and |FRAME:NADP| |CITS: [2663079]|. Similarly, non-sulfur purple bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1061| and cyanobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-54310| are also able to use sulfide as the electron source for anoxygenic photosynthesis., The purple sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1049| carries out the complete eight-electron oxidation of sulfide to sulfate. The process involves the formation of sulfur globules as obligate intermediates |CITS: [9695921]|. Since the initial sulfide oxidation system is periplasmic, the globules are deposited in the periplasm |CITS: [9560425]|. The sulfur in the globules occurs as sulfur chains |CITS: [11782519]| enclosed by a protein envelope |CITS: [7575095]| (see |FRAME: P222-PWY|). , In the process of further oxidation, the sulfur in the globules is reduced inside the bacterial cell to a thiol form, which is transported into the cytoplasm and oxidized by a cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation system. , At this point the cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation pathway is still not completely understood. In addition, there are several oxidation systems, and different organisms employ different systems to achieve this goal. , About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-1049| the initial oxidation of sulfide to sulfur is most likely performed by a periplasmic |FRAME: MONOMER-12314|, which mediates the transfer of electrons from sulfide directly into the quinone pool (this enzyme is described in the pathway |FRAME:P222-PWY|). This process generates the sulfur globules mentioned above. The sulfur in the globules is then reduced again to either |FRAME: CPD-846| or perthiols, which enter the cytoplasm, where they are oxidized to sulfite by the |FRAME:CPLX-7133| |CITS: [9695921]|. While the exact details of the process are still unknown, some of the key players have been identified., According to the latest model, the protein that donates the sulfur substrate to the |FRAME:CPLX-7133| is |FRAME: CPLX-8190 "DsrC protein"|. DsrC carries a sulfur atom on a cystein residue in the form of a perthiol. The source of the sulfur atom is still not clear, but may be DsrL |CITS: [18656485]| or the |FRAME:CPLX-8192 "DsrEFH complex| |CITS: [18952098]|. As the sulfur is transferred to the dissimilatory sulfite reductase an intramolecular disulfide is formed in DsrC, which is subsequently restored to its active form by the |FRAME: MONOMER-16043| subunit of the |FRAME: CPLX-8189| |CITS: [20952577]|., The |FRAME:CPLX-7133| is the enzyme that is responsible for sulfite reduction in sulfate reducing bacteria (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|). However, in sulfur-oxidizing bacteria the enzyme works in the reverse direction |CITS: [18826437]|. Reversed activity of sulfite reductase was first suggested by Peck et al in 1974 |CITS: [4526215]|, and, was investigated in |FRAME: TAX-1049| by Schedel et al, who concluded that the physiological role of the enzyme in this organism is "at all probablity the oxidation of sulfide and/or elemental sulfur to sulfite" |CITS: [Schedel79]|., A later study showed that a sulfite-reductase-defective |FRAME: TAX-1049| mutant, while able to oxidize sulfide to sulfur with specific rates comparable to those of the wild-type, was unable to oxidize the intracellularly stored sulfur, confirming a role of the enzyme in the later stages of the process |CITS: [9695921]|., The sulfite that is formed by |FRAME:CPLX-7133| can be oxidized to sulfate in several routes. The main system in |FRAME: TAX-1049| is the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8835| (see |FRAME: PWY-7457|). An alternative route, which appears to be less important, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8193| and |FRAME: CPLX-8194| |CITS:[trueper82][9004500][11685375]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1061| is a purple, nonsulfur facultative phototrophic alphaproteobacterium that can grow as an aerobic heterotroph in the dark, and shifts to anaerobic phototrophic growth in the light. The organism uses UQ-10 as its, sole quinone source for both growth modes., A study of the hydroxylases involved in ubiquinone biosynthesis in this organism uncovered a new type of enzyme - the |FRAME: G-124913|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-124918|. This enzyme acts early in the pathway, catalyzing both the decarboxylation and the hydroxylation of position C1 of |FRAME: CPD-9864| (which becomes position C4 in ubiquinone). Due to this activity, the order of hydroxylations that take place in this pathway is C4 → C2 → C3, diverging from the canonical pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-8535|), where the order is C2 → C4 → C3 |CITS: [37716914]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLINE Choline| is a quaternary ammonium compound and a fundamental metabolite for eukaryotic organisms, forming the head group of important phospholipids such as |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| |CITS: [12215503]|., Choline is also the precursor for the neurotransmitter |FRAME: ACETYLCHOLINE|, and serves as a precursor for the formation of the important osmoprotectant |FRAME: BETAINE| (see |FRAME:PWY1F-353| for an example) ., Most plants synthesize choline, since phosphatidylcholine accounts for 40 to 60% of lipids in non-plastid plant membranes |CITS: [12215503]|. Animals cannot synthesize |FRAME: CHOLINE|, which must be consumed through the diet, making it a vitamin. It is usually grouped within the B-complex vitamins. Most microbes are not able to produce choline, although many have transporters for its uptake., About This Pathway, The first step in choline biosynthesis is the direct decarboxylation of serine to ethanolamine , |CITS: [11461929]|, which is catalyzed by a serine decarboxylase unique to plants |CITS: [14634155]|. Ethanolamine is, widely recognized as the entrance compound to choline biosynthesis. , The synthesis of choline from ethanolamine may take place at three parallel pathways, where three consecutive N-methylation , steps are carried out either on free bases, phospho-bases, or phosphatidyl-bases |CITS: [11481443]|. Although choline , biosynthesis accommodates different pathways in plants, most of them share the enzymatic step forming phosphoethanolamine , |CITS: [DATKO88A]| |CITS: [DATKO88B]|. The N-methylation, catalyzed by the phosphoethanolamine N-methyltransferase , (PEAMT), is considered to be the committing step exerting a major control over flux throughout the pathway. It has been , demonstrated that the PEAMT of spinach catalyzes all three N-methylations necessary to yield phosphocholine. The , confirmed intermediates of this pathway have been determined as monomethyl- and dimethylphosphoethanolamine , |CITS: [10799484]|. However, Weretilnyk and coworkers |CITS: [12228655]| argued that the N-methylation of those , three steps may be exercised by two different enzymes as they found a different behavior of the enzyme(s) in response , to different light settings. , The pathway displayed (methylation pathway) represents the main biosynthetic route as found in the chenopods family. , The N-methylation may also occur species-specific on the free-base level |CITS: [PRUDHOMME92A]|or the phosphatidyl-base , level as shown for soybean |CITS: [DATKO88A]|, castor bean |CITS: [TANG97]| and barley |CITS: [HITZ81]|. Consequently, it , has been assumed that the reactions embedded in the nucleotide and methylation pathways may be two characteristics, of one overall phosphoaminoalcohol pathway for the formation of phosphatidylcholine |CITS: [KINNEY93]| in plants., The further metabolic fate of phosphocholine is also species-specific. Phosphocholine can either be directly dephosphorylated , to release choline as observed in spinach |CITS: [12232019]| or incorporated into phosphatidylcholine with the subsequent , release of choline, as in tobacco |CITS: [10806254]|. It has also been suggested that the hydrolization of sinapine yielding , sinapic acid and cholin (|FRAME:PWY-3301|) may contribute to the content of free choline in plants |CITS: [Strack81]|., The biosynthesis of choline appears to be regulated by a feedback response of phosphocholine inhibiting its own , synthesis by decreasing N-methyltransferase (PEAMT) activities involved in the pathway |CITS: [10799484]|. Pre-growth , of carrot and soybean suspension cells as well as |FRAME:TAX-89585| in choline enriched culture medium , caused a significant decrease of methylated derivatives of phosphoethanolamine |CITS: [MUDD89A]| |CITS: [MUDD89B]|. , In contrast, the activity of PEAMT was considerably increased when plants were exposed to salt stress |CITS: [10799484]|, |CITS: [12232019]|, which is consistent with the high demand for choline as osmoprotectant precursor in such plants.

Summary: Iron deficiency effects all aspects of plant development, including photosynthesis, respiration, and growth processes. Though abundant in soil, iron is frequently found in the form of insoluble oxides and oxyhydroxides, and is not available for direct uptake., Plants have evolved several tightly regulated strategies to absorb iron. Chelation of |FRAME: FE+3| by |FRAME: Phytosiderophores phytosiderophores"| secreted from the plant roots is one such strategy |CITS: [17449639]|. , Under low Fe conditions the enzyme |FRAME: AT5G49740-MONOMER| is induced and reduces the chelated , |FRAME: FE+3| to |FRAME: FE+2|, which is taken into the plant by Fe-regulated transporters in the roots |CITS: [GUERINOT07]|., This process is widespread in non graminaceous plants.

Summary: General Background, Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. In the environment, iron is mostly found in two different oxidation states: II and III. Fe(II) is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions, while Fe(III) is favored at high pH and oxic conditions. In oxic environments iron forms various oxide and hydroxide compounds; iron(II,III) oxides (such as magnetite, Fe3O4) and iron(III) oxides (such as hematite, Fe2O3) are most common. Under anoxic conditions the soluble |FRAME: FE+2| species is the most common., In certain environments Fe(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands., Oxidation of ferrous iron (Fe(II)) by microbes is an important component of the iron geochemical cycle. Bacterial iron oxidation is well documented under anaerobic conditions (see for example |FRAME: PWY-8554|), or under aerobic, acidic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6692|). Even though iron is oxidized spontaneously and rapidly in the presence of oxygen, many bacterial species have been found to oxidize Fe(II) at neutral pH |CITS: [20565252][32071158][33328652]|., About This Pathway, At low pH the chemical oxidation of iron is greatly reduced, a phenomenon that is utilized by organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-920 |, an obligate chemolithotroph that lives at extremely low pH. The sole energy-producing processes that it uses for growth and cell maintenance involve oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds and/or Fe(II) under acidic conditions, using molecular oxygen as oxidant |CITS: [14897836][5972649]|. |FRAME: TAX-920 | is the main bacterium used in the industrial extraction of copper and uranium from ores, using the microbial leaching technique., Fe(II) is oxidized by |FRAME: MONOMER-16162| (encoded by |FRAME: G-12463|), which transfers the electrons to the blue copper protein |FRAME: MONOMER-16161| |CITS: [8049223]|. Cyc2 has a redox potential of 560 mV, the highest measured for a cytochrome c. , Rusticyanin (680 mV) functions as a split point in the pathway, as it can transfer the electrons to two different periplasmic diheme cytochromes c4: |FRAME: MONOMER-16160| shuttles them to the inner-membrane located |FRAME: CPLX-8217|, while |FRAME: MONOMER-18880| shuttles the electrons to the similarly located |FRAME: CPLX-8219|. This phenomenon is known as electron bifurcation., In this manner the electrons that are derived from Fe(II) are directed towards one of two competing pathways., The downhill pathway directs the electrons towards an |FRAME: CPLX-8217| (|FRAME: CYTOCHROME-C-OXIDASE-RXN "EC 1.9.3.1"|) that uses the electrons to reduce oxygen to water. This reaction is coupled to pumping of protons from the cytoplasm to the acidic periplasm, maintaining a strong proton motive force. The proteins that are involved in the downhill pathway are encoded by genes present on a single operon, and form a large |FRAME: CPLX-8218| that spans the outer membrane, the periplasm, and the inner membrane |CITS: [18632666]|., The uphill pathway shuttles the electrons toward a |FRAME: CPLX-8219| (|FRAME: EC-7.1.1.8|) that utilizes the proton motive force that exists between the acidic periplasm and the much more basic cytoplasm to drive the reduction of ubiquinone, forcing this pathway to operate in the reverse direction to that observed in most organisms. Ubiquinol transfers its electrons to an NADH-quinone oxidoreductase (|FRAME: NADH-DEHYDROG-A-RXN "EC 7.1.1.2"|, NADH dehydrogenase complex), which also utilizes the proton motive force to reduce NAD(P)+ to NAD(P)H), required for biosynthesis and carbon fixation.

Note: click on the More Detail button at the top of the page to see the enzymes involved in this pathway., General Background, The thyroid hormones |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| (T4) and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| (T3) are essential for normal vertebrate metabolism, growth and development. These |FRAME: CPD-387|-containing molecules are biosynthesized in the thyroid gland, the function of which is to concentrate environmentally scarce |FRAME: CPD-387| in order to make it available for thyroid hormone biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-387| insufficiency in the diet remains a public health problem in some parts of the world (reviewed in |CITS: [19196800]|). Various human disorders of thyroid metabolism are characterized by hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, goiter, and cretinism (a syndrome resulting from hypothyroidism during development (in |CITS: [VOET04]|). These phenotypes have many possible causes including mutations in receptors, transporters, proteins involved in the pathway and its regulation, developmental defects, inflammation, autoimmune reactions, drug side effects, diet, or deficiency of other hormones. Also see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6241| and |FRAME: PWY-6261|., About This Pathway, The thyroid hormones |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| are regulated at many levels. An important aspect of their regulation is enzymatic activation and inactivation. Three different types of deiodinases are primarily responsible for these processes. They are selenoenzymes that contain selenocysteine as a key active site residue. Type I deiodinase can catalyze both 5'-deiodination and 5-deiodination of a variety of iodothyronines and their derivatives. Type II deiodinase efficiently catalyzes 5'-deiodination of |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| to |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE|, an activating reaction. This reaction contributes to systemic and serum |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| levels. Although |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| is the major secreted product of the thyroid gland, |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| is the major bioactive hormone and most circulating |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| is generated by type II deiodinase in peripheral tissues (in |CITS: [8070342]|). Type III deiodinase produces inactive or less active metabolites by catalyzing the 5-deiodination of |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| to |FRAME: CPD-10813| (reverse triiodothyronine), and the 5-deiodination of triiodothyronine to |FRAME: CPD-11395|. Although the roles of these enzymes in some physiological situations have been determined, their roles in others remain unclear. Reviewed in |CITS: [19179439]|., The reactions shown in this pathway are derived from the work of |CITS: [18821722] [18339710]| in which a novel liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry method was developed to identify and quantitate both new and previously known thyronine and thyronamine substrates of deiodinase isozymes. A liquid-liquid extraction procedure allowed isolation of the metabolites from deiodinase reaction mixtures. An HPLC protocol allowed their identification. The deiodinase reaction mixtures utilized either human cell line lysates as sources of the type I, II and III deiodinase isozymes (Dio1, Dio2 and Dio3), or mouse liver membrane fractions as a source of Dio1. The work not only verified previously described deiodination reactions, but two new reactions were also identified: the human Dio2 catalyzed deiodination of the phenolic ring of |FRAME: CPD-13008| and the human Dio3 catalyzed deiodination of the tyrosyl ring of |FRAME: CPD-13009| |CITS: [18821722]|., Also in this work, a weak 5'-deiodination reaction was observed for the human HepG2 Dio1-catalyzed conversion of |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| to |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE|. A weak 3'-deiodination reaction was observed for the mouse liver Dio1-catalyzed conversion of |FRAME: CPD-11395| to |FRAME: CPD-13009| as well as faint 5-deiodinations of |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| to |FRAME: CPD-11395|, and |FRAME: CPD-11396| to |FRAME: CPD-13009|., None of the isozymes catalyzed the conversion of |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| to |FRAME: CPD-11396|, or the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13010| to |FRAME: CPD-11428|. It was suggested that species-specific factors may modulate the substrate specificity of deiodinase isozymes in different species |CITS: [18821722]|. Earlier work in this field has been reviewed in |CITS: [18279024]| and |CITS: [11898402]|., Human polymorphisms in the genes encoding the deiodinases have been described, although no inactivating mutations have been reported. Phenotypes of mice with targeted deletions of the deiodinase genes have been studied (reviewed in |CITS: [17062880]|)., The three deiodinase isozymes catalyze not only the sequential, reductive deiodination of iodinated thyronines as shown in this pathway, but also of iodinated thyronamines as shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-6688|., In addition to deoidinases, other routes of metabolism of thyroid hormones have been described and the metabolically active metabolites have been identified (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6261|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes, ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8 Ubiquinone 8| (Q-8) is a common form of ubiquinone among bacteria. Most of the Gram-negative facultative anaerobes, such as the enterobacteria, produce Q-8. The best studied ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway is that of |FRAME: TAX-83333|, which produces a |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8|. The first committed step of the pathway is the conversion of chorismate to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| (4HB) by |FRAME: CHORPYRLY-MONOMER|. Following condensation of 4HB with a polyprenyl diphosphate, the aromatic ring of 4HB is modified by a total of seven reactions - one decarboxylation, three hydroxylation, and three methylation reactions., The best characterized UQ biosynthetic pathway takes place under aerobic conditions and involves three oxygen-dependent hydroxylations, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6708|. However, already in 1978 it has been reported that |FRAME: TAX-562| can synthesize UQ under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [365223]|. The presence of an oxygen-independent UQ biosynthetic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-562| was confirmed forty years later |CITS: [31289180]|. In the anaerobic pathway the three oxygen-dependent hydroxylases are replaced by a heterodimeric complex encoded by the |FRAME: G7652| and |FRAME: G7653| genes |CITS: [31289180]|, which catalyzes |FRAME: PREPHENATE|-dependent hydroxylations |CITS: [38507448]|. Both UbiU and UbiV bind a [4Fe-4S] cluster essential for activity. The pathway also involves the product of the |FRAME: G7651| gene, an SCP2 lipid-binding domain that serves as an accessory factor |CITS: [31289180]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-3055| uses several fermentative pathways, some common to plants and some common to soil microbes, to metabolize pyruvate. The transcript levels, protein levels, and/or activities of many of the enzymes in the pathway, including the Fe hydrogenase, |FRAME: G-12758|, are induced in response to anerobic or other special conditions |CITS: [17291820][16452484][22353371][21219510]|., Pyruvate can be metabolized to acetyl-CoA via pyruvate ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFR1), producing acetyl-CoA, reduced ferredoxin and CO<sub>2</sub>.  The reduced PFR1 can then be used by the Fe-hydrogenases |FRAME: G-12758| and HYDA2 to produce hydrogen. However, the hydrogenases must first be properly assembled and activated by the |FRAME: G-15454| and |FRAME: G-15455| proteins |CITS: [15082711]|., Alternatively, pyruvate can be the substrate of an enzyme that is common to bacteria but rare to eukaryotes, , pyruvate formate lyase (PFL1) that produces acetyl-CoA and formate. A PFL- activating enzyme, |FRAME: G-15456| has also been discovered in the Chlamydomonas genome and its expression has been confirmed at the transcript level |CITS: [16452484]|., Pyruvate may also be decarboxylated by the pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC3) resulting in the production of acetaldehyde and CO<sub>2</sub>.  Under hypoxic conditions, NADH is reoxidized by ADH1, a bifunctional enzyme that has both alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase activity. Oxidation of NADH may also be catalyzed by a putative D-lactate dehydrogenase (LDH1). , The conversion of acetyl-CoA to acetate and CoA via sequential action of acetate kinase (ACK1,ACK2) and phosphotransactylase (PAT1,PAT2) results in the production of ATP. ACK1/PAT2 are believed to act in the chloroplast while  ACK2/PAT2 are believed to act in the mitochondria |CITS: [20190198]|. This series of reactions demonstrates another branch of the pathway that is more typically associated with prokaryotic than with eukaryotic species |CITS: [16452484]|.
