Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, Inorganic arsenic enters the cell in the form of |FRAME: ARSENATE| and |FRAME: CPD0-2040|. Since there are no known export systems for |FRAME: ARSENATE|, cells reduce it to |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, which is either exported from the cell or methylated. The reduction of |FRAME: ARSENATE| to |FRAME: CPD0-2040| is described in several other pathways, classified under |FRAME: Arsenate-Detoxification|., Methylation of arsenic compounds has been documented in many organisms, including bacteria, fungi, green plants, and higher organisms (for a detailed list of organisms and the corresponding arsenic species, see |CITS: [Cullen89]|). The process is so common that in certain environments methylated arsenic species become the dominant form of arsenic |CITS: [Anderson91]|. The pathway shown here is limited to the methylation of inorganic arsenic., The key enzyme in the methylation pathway is |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.137|. The enzyme was initially identified in mammals |CITS: [11790780][15808521]|. |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE Glutathione|, the major thiol in most organisms, is present at millimolar concentrations and reacts readily with ASIII compounds to form glutathione complexes inside cells |CITS: [7841340]|. In organisms that do not produce glutathione ASIII compound believe to form complexes with other thiol compounds such as |FRAME: CoM|., The arsenic-thiol complex is believed to be the substrate for the methyltransferase, which binds AsIII in a series of three thiol transfer reactions |CITS: [15526190]|. Once bound to the enzyme, AsIII undergoes one to three methylation events. Most of the substrate remains bound to the enzyme after the first methylation, with only a small fraction being released as |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, and is released after the second methylation as |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINOUS-ACID|. An even smaller fraction proceeds to a third methylation event and is released as |FRAME: CPD-22659|, which is a volatile compound., During the reaction the arsenic atom changes valencies between (III) and (V) several times, being oxidized during methylation and reduced back to (III) valency with electrons derived from thioredoxin. In the presence of oxygen the released products |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| and |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINOUS-ACID| can be oxidized nonenzymatically to |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE| and |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINATE|, respectively |CITS: [25325836]|. Otherwise, these compounds can react again with glutathione, forming |FRAME: CPD-24323| and |FRAME: CPD-24324|, which can serve as an alternative substrates for the methyltransferase., The methylation process forms three products - |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLARSINOUS-ACID|, and |FRAME: CPD-22659|. The latter is a volatile compound, and as such as less toxic. However, both the monomethylated and dimethylate forms of AsIII are highly toxic. When exposed to oxygen, they are oxidized to the much less toxic pentavalent forms. However, the mechanisms for exporting the compounds out of the cell have not been studied yet, with the exception of |FRAME: G-80528 ArsP|, which can export |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|. However, it appears that ArsP is used by bacteria to detoxify the compounds generated by other organisms and is thus not included in this pathway.

Summary: The purine degradation pathway plays an important role in nitrogen metabolism in most organisms. The final product of de novo purine biosynthesis, |FRAME:IMP|, is degraded through sequential enzymatic steps into |FRAME: URATE|, which contains a high level of nitrogen |CITS: [11891236]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5044|)., In most organisms, including some bacteria, plants, and certain animals, |FRAME: URATE| is metabolized via a common pathway, producing the stereospecific form |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as the final product |CITS: [16317038]|. Some organisms that are not able to degrade urate include humans, apes, birds and reptiles |CITS: [16462750]|., It has previously been thought that |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| is formed from |FRAME: URATE| in a single step, catalyzed by urate oxidase. However, it is now established that the process involves three different enzymes |CITS: [16462750]|. In the first step of the pathway |FRAME: URATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|. The oxidation can be carried out by two distinct enzymes: eukaryotes and some bacteria use |FRAME: EC-1.7.3.3|, as described in this pathway variant |CITS: [Modric92][Kahn97]|, while some prokaryotes possess |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.113|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7394| |CITS: [23760935]|., |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE| is relatively unstable, and indeed decomposes in vitro to yield allantoin. However, this spontaneous reaction is unlikely to be physiologically relevant, because spontaneous decomposition yields racemic |FRAME: ALLANTOIN|, while organisms contain mostly the |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| enantiomer., An enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of the N1-C6 bond of |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYISOURATE|, forming |FRAME: CPD-5821|, has been discovered and isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3847| |CITS: [10567345]|. An enzyme that catalyzes the decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-5821| to |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| was first discovered in mouse |CITS: [16462750]| and later purified from |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [20167108][20511299]|, |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [17567580]| and |FRAME: TAX-272620| |CITS: [20826786]|., This pathway is part of various metaboilc processes, including both degradative pathways, such as the degradation of purines to glyoxylate and urea or ammonia, and biosynthetic pathways, such as the plant biosynthesis of ureides, which is part of the mechanism used by tropical legumes to trasport the nitrogen fixed by their bacterial symbionts in the root nodules to the rest of the plant (see |FRAME: URSIN-PWY|).

Summary: General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on single carbon (C1) compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. , While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| (see |FRAME: PWY-5506|)., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branch point, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (see |FRAME:P185-PWY|), or a dissimilatory pathway that provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|)., About This Pathway, Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria are aerobic bacteria that utilize one-carbon compounds more reduced than formate as sources of carbon and energy, and assimilate formaldehyde as a major source of cellular carbon |CITS [8801441]|. , Methylotrophic bacteria utilize a variety of different one-carbon compounds including methane (see |FRAME: PWY-1641|), methanol, methylated amines, halomethanes and methylated compounds containing sulfur. , Methylamine is oxidized by several species of methylotrophic bacteria by a methylamine dehydrogenase (MADH). , With the exception of the genus |FRAME:TAX-16|, which uses a c type cytochrome as an electron acceptor, , MADHs use blue copper proteins (usually amicyanins) as electron acceptors, which are encoded by a gene located in the same operon that encodes the subunits of the MADH itself |CITS [8021187]|., The product of this reaction, formaldehyde, is transported into the cytosol, where it is either oxidized to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, or assimilated (see formaldehyde assimilation and formaldehyde oxidation pathways).

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., About This Pathway, Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. IAA is often present in conjugated forms. Conjugated forms of auxin play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., IAA-amino acid conjugates have been identified and studied in many species, including |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [15749753]|, cucumber (|FRAME: TAX-3659|) |CITS: [16664134]|, Scots pine (|FRAME:TAX-3349|) |CITS: [11154354]|, and, rice (|FRAME: TAX-4530|) |CITS: [17628621] [15849417]|, and an |FRAME: CPD-9567| conjugate has been detected in rice |CITS: [17628621]|. These is also now evidence for an oxidized form of |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| that can be linked to one or two glucose molecules via the nitrogen of the indole portion of IAA. These compounds were identified in green pericarp discs of tomato (|FRAME: TAX-4081|)., Tracer studies using radioactively labeled-IAA indicated that green pericarp discs of tomato generate an IAA-glucose compound, with an unknown site of glucose attachment (reaction not shown) |CITS: [16653145]|. IAA-glucose may act as an auxin reservoir since the ester bond is easily hydrolyzed in this tissue to release free IAA. On the other hand, |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP|, also generated by the pericarp discs, appears to be a nonhydrolyzable IAA conjugate destined for further modification and degradation |CITS: [16653145][Ostin95]|, but the biological activities of these downstream metabolites have not been tested., Further work will be required to determine whether the hypothetical reactions proposed in this pathway occur in vivo and to ascertain the functional importance of this pathway in tomato and other plant species.

The Entner-Doudoroff pathway, in combination with the |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway"|, provides cells with an alternative to glycolysis for fermenting sugars. Using this pathway, the cells can maximize the production of reducing power at the expense of ATP production |CITS: [12981024]|., The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway converts |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| to |FRAME: CPD-2961| in two steps. Instead of proceeding to the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative branch"| of that pathway, which forms several metabolite precursors, the Entner-Duodoroff pathway provides a shunt that returns |FRAME: CPD-2961| to glycolysis via the intermediate |FRAME: GAP|. , This pathway is important to |FRAME:TAX-562| because it enables the organism to metabolize sugar acids, which are significant nutrients in both of its habitats, intestinal and aquatic. Strains that are mutationally blocked in this pathway are unable to grow on gluconate, glucuronate, or galacturonate and are also unable to colonize the mouse intestine |CITS: [8751891]|. The uronic acids feed into the pathway's sole intermediate, |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, so the dependence of their metabolism on an intact Entner-Doudoroff pathway is clear |CITS: [9657988]|. The dependence of gluconate's metabolism on an intact Entner-Doudoroff pathway is less obvious because it is also metabolized via the pentose phosphate pathway., Enzymes of the Entner-Doudoroff pathway are induced by growth on gluconate, glucuronate, or methyl-β-D-glucuronide; phosphate or carbon limitation |CITS: [15659677]|.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, This pathway covers the anaerobic oxidation of |FRAME: Me-CoM| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. It should be noted that most of the enzymes in this pathway catalyze reversible reactions, and operate in different directions in the two branchs of the pathway., One of the differences between the methanogens and other methylotrophic bacteria is that the methanogens often have modified versions of the |FRAME: THMPT| cofactor and its derivatives. Some organisms produce only |FRAME: THMPT| (see |FRAME: PWY2OBG-1|). Some methanogens that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-94695| and |FRAME: TAX-2182| orders form |FRAME: CPD-8|, which is generated from |FRAME: THMPT| by the addition of a glutamate residue |CITS: [6698019]| (this pathway). Members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-2195| contain |FRAME: CPD-24457 tatiopterin|, which is different from |FRAME: CPD-8| in having an additional aspartate in the side chain of the molecule, and in not having the 7-methyl group in the pterin moiety |CITS: [2105296]|.

The catecholamines dopamine, noradrenaline (norepinephrine), and adrenaline (epinephrine) function as , neurotransmitters and hormones. They have important physiological regulatory roles and are involved in the , development of many diseases. Their biosynthesis is shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-301|. Although the , degradation of endogenous catecholamines has been well studied, many inaccuracies based on early studies , still remain in the literature. For example, noradrenaline degradation has been depicted as a series of reactions, , including oxidative deamination, that form 3,4-dihydroxymandelate, followed by O-methylation to form , vanillylmandelate. However, different and updated pathways are shown in |CITS: [15317907]| and here. , Catecholamines are biosynthesized in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells, including the central nervous , system, sympathetic nerves, adrenal medulla, gastrointestinal tract, and kidneys. They have previously been , considered to be metabolized after their release from cells. They are now believed to be largely metabolized in , the cells in which they are biosynthesized. In addition, intracellular catecholamines stored in vesicles were , believed to be released extracellularly only upon stimulation. It is now thought that vesicular catecholamines , are in a dynamic equilibrium with the cytoplasm. Outward leakage from vesicles is countered by active transport , back into vesicles by monoamine transporters. The small amount of catecholamines remaining in the cytoplasm , are a major source of metabolites. Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|. , The metabolism of the transient (and toxic) aldehyde intermediate 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetalcehyde by a , dehydrogenase is dependent upon the presence (in noradrenaline and adrenaline) or absence (in dopamine) , of the β-hydroxyl group. Its absence in dopamine and 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetaldehyde favors oxidation , by aldehyde dehydrogenase. Its presence on noradrenaline, adrenaline and 3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycolaldehyde , favors reduction by aldehyde reductase or aldose reductase. Thus, dopamine is preferentially converted to an , acid metabolite, and noradrenaline and adrenaline are preferentially converted to an alcohol metabolite. , Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|., Overall, approximately half of the dopamine produced in the body is not converted to noradrenaline and is , degraded to inactive metabolites (in |CITS: [9360553]|) (see |FRAME: PWY66-301|). The proportion varies , as to site, with the brain being a minor source of dopamine metabolites. Dopamine and all of its metabolites are , produced in mesenteric organs (gastrointestinal tract, spleen and pancreas). The major end products of , dopamine metabolism, homovanillate, 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate, and dopamine sulfate are excreted in urine. , Free dopamine is also excreted in urine in significant amounts and is thought to be formed from , dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) that is removed from circulation by the kidneys (in |CITS: [9360553]|)., The conversion of 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetaldehyde to 3.4-dihydroxyphenylacetate by NAD-dependent aldehyde , dehydrogenase has been shown in rat liver |CITS: [7034733]|. The O-methylation of , 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate to form homovanillate is suggested by the use of this substrate by the rat enzyme , |CITS: [13575440]|, and the identification of these metabolites in human plasma |CITS: [9360553]|. , 3-Methoxytyramine can potentially be deaminated and oxidized to homovanillate. Most , homovanillate is produced in peripheral tissues, with only about 12% produced in brain. Dopamine and its , metabolites 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate and 3-methoxytyramine can also be conjugated to their respective , sulfates in the gastrointestinal tract, an important route for metabolism of dietary biogenic amines and peripherally , produced dopamine. These sulfates are excreted in the urine |CITS: [9360553] [10404831]|. , Reviewed in |CITS: [15317907]|.

It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes |CITS: [15012227][17334828]|., Bacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated, and multiple degradation pathways have been described |CITS: [Liu21]|., About this pathway, The first |FRAME: CPD-10247| degradation pathway was characterized in |FRAME: TAX-562| (see |FRAME: PWY-7446|). In addition to the five enzymes that participate in this pathway, the cluster also contains other genes that are likely to be involved in SQ utilization |CITS: [26195800]|., Homologous putative SQ-degradation gene clusters were found in other γ-proteobacteria as well as in β- and, α-proteobacteria, including organisms from the genera Vibrio, Aeromonas, Enterobacteria, Burkholderia, Janthinobacterium, Herbaspirillum, Rhizobium, Ensifer, Microvirga, Salinarimonas, and Acidocella |CITS: [26195800]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "Fatty acids"| are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and fatty acyl moieties of proteins that modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II., Type I systems are found in lower eukaryotes and animals, while type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. Thus both systems operate in animals - the type I system in the cytosol, (see |FRAME: PWY-5994|), and the type II system in the mitochondria (this pathway)., The main difference between the two systems is that type I systems consist of one (in the case of animals) or two (in the case of fungi) large multifunctional gene products that form a single complex that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while in type II systems the different reactions are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., About This Pathway, The contribution of the mitochondrial pathway counts for only a few percentage of the overall cellular fatty acid biosynthesis, as the bulk of endogenously derived fatty acids is synthesized in the cytosol by the type I fatty acid synthase system |CITS: [9187370]|. The mitochondrial pathway is believed to provide the octanoyl group that is required for the endogenous synthesis of |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID|. Additionally there is putative evidence suggesting its involvement in remodeling of cardiolipins |CITS: [1397269][8595652]|., The mitochondrial FAS pathway is indespensible, as demonstrated by the observation that the inactivation of any FAS II gene in yeast results in the loss of mitochondrially encoded cytochromes and ultimately in a respiratory-deficient phenotype., The pathway starts with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"|, whose production is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY66-429|. The malonyl moiety is attached to the |FRAME: ENSG00000004779-MONOMER|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: HS00112| gene. The four steps of the iterative fatty acid biosynthesis process - malonyltransfer, reduction of the oxo group to a 3R hydroxy group, dehydration, which forms a trans double bond, and reduction of this bond, are carried out by the |FRAME: CPLX66-554| (a heterotetramer encoded by a |FRAME: HS03575| and |FRAME: HS07256| genes), a |FRAME: G66-33210-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: G66-33210|), a |FRAME: CPLX66-553| (encoded by |FRAME: HS04010|), and a |FRAME: HS07707-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: HS07707|)., While all enzymes have been shown to act with substrates having chain lengths up to 16 carbon atoms, the physiological relevance of products longer than octanoate (used as a precursor for |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| biosynthesis), however, is not clear. Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, Rhizobactin 1021 is a siderohpore isolated from the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6005|, an endosymbiont of the plant |FRAME: TAX-3879|, under conditions of iron stress |CITS: [Persmark93]|., A DNA cluster that contains all of the genes necessary for the regulation, biosynthesis, and transport of |FRAME: CPD-1021| by transposon mutagenesis |CITS: [8416915]|. The cluster was located on the pSyma megaplasmid., Specific mutations in different genes in this cluster identified which of the genes were involved in biosynthesis of the siderophore, and which were involved in transport or regulation |CITS: [11274118]|. Six biosyntesis gene, which form an operon, were identified and named rhbABCDEF (for rhizobactin 1021 biosynthesis). Transcription of the genes was iron-dependent, and controlled by the RirA iron response regulator |CITS: [15899411]|., The first two genes, |FRAME: G-11911| and |FRAME: G-11912|, are homologous to the |FRAME: G-18| and |FRAME: G-9| genes of |FRAME: TAX-469| species, respectively, which catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: CPD-313| in that organism., The other four genes, |FRAME: G-11915|, |FRAME: G-11914|, |FRAME: G-11913| and |FRAME: G-11916|, are homologous to the |FRAME: G-9031|, |FRAME: G-9027|, |FRAME: G-9026|, and |FRAME: G-9028|, respectively, whose products catalyze the production of the |FRAME: AEROBACTIN| siderophore by by many Gram-negative bacteria (see |FRAME: AEROBACTINSYN-PWY|). Considering the structural similarity of |FRAME: CPD-1021| to |FRAME: AEROBACTIN|, the most likely scenario for |FRAME: CPD-1021| biosynthesis is a similar paythway that utilizes |FRAME: CPD-313| rather than |FRAME:LYS| as a starting point |CITS: [11274118]|., Unlike |FRAME: AEROBACTIN|, the mature |FRAME: CPD-1021| siderophore contains a lipid moiety that gives the siderophore its amphiphilic properties. The enzyme that is responsible for the attachment of this lipid moiety has not been identified conclusively yet.

Summary: Chlorogenic acids (CGAs) are a group of soluble phenolic compounds that are produced by a variety of plants, including |FRAME: TAX-49390 "Coffea canephora (robusta coffee)"|., CGAs include esters formed between certain hydroxycinnamic acids and quinate or its derivative shikimate. For example, they are known to be involved in the protection of plants from abiotic stresses such as UV damage |CITS:[Burchard00]| and in increased resistance to bacterial infections |CITS: [15107863]|., Biosynthesis of 5-CQA can be catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme, CYP98A36. Another enzyme, CYP98A35, is able to metabolize both |FRAME: 4-COUMAROYLQUINATE "4-coumaroyl quinate"| and |FRAME: CPD-412| with the same efficiency. , CGA biosynthesis and accumulation occurred mainly in the shoot tip and in the phloem of the vascular bundles. The biosynthetic activity of chlorogenic acids was clearly reduced in ripening and ripe seeds, especially in |FRAME: TAX-49390| |CITS: [18069248]|.

Summary: Rhizoctinins are phosphonate-containing di- or tripeptide antibiotics formed by the gram-positive bacterium |FRAME:TAX-703612| which specifically exhibit anti-fungal activities. Organo-phosphonates are widely used for the development of new drugs in human medicine, basic components in cosmetics and detergents, as fertilizer and herbizides in agriculture and efficient catalysts in chemical research (reviewed in |CITS:[24271089]|. The biosynthetic pathways of phosphonate-derived antibiotics often display complex sequences and stand out because of unusual reaction chemistry and enzymology |CITS:[23870698]|., , So far four rhizocticins have been determined, i.e. the dipeptide |FRAME:CPD-16791| and the tripeptides |FRAME:CPD-16792|, |FRAME:CPD-16812| and |FRAME:CPD-16813| which vary in the second amino acid attached to the C-terminal of |FRAME:ARG| of |FRAME:CPD-16791|. The elucidated structure of rhizocticins reveals the non-proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME:CPD-16790| (L-APPA) as major component of rhizocticins |CITS:[Rapp88]|. When rhizocticins enter fungal cells via a special oligopeptide transport system |CITS:[2110446]| host specific peptidases cleave the peptide bonds and release |FRAME:CPD-16790| which is a potent inhibitor of threonine synthase |CITS:[8042902]| hence compromising protein synthesis and developmental processes in the host organism. |FRAME:CPD-16790 L-APPA| inhibits an enzyme not present in mammals and therefore is a promising agent for the development of analogs with target-specific activities in humans., The biosynthesis of rhizocticin A and B (this pathway) in |FRAME:TAX-703612| is executed through a gene cluster (rhi) which has been confirmed by heterologous expression of the rhi cluster in the non-rhizocticin producing strain 168 of Bacillus subtilis resulting in the production of |FRAME:CPD-16792| |CITS:[20142038]|. The existence of biosynthetic gene clusters in microbes is a common feature and has also been reported for the biosynthesis of the phosphonate-derived antibiotics |FRAME:CPD0-1113| (see |FRAME:PWY-5757|), |FRAME:CPD-10013| (see |FRAME:PWY-6322|) and |FRAME:CPD-15961| (see |FRAME:PWY-7419|) |CITS:[23034226]|. The depicted pathway of |FRAME:PWY-7510| is only supported in some portions and requires further research to substantiate the reaction sequence for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16792| and other rhizoctocins. , The first two steps in the pathway, i.e. the formation of the common intermediate |FRAME:CPD-551| from |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| via |FRAME:CPD-235| is shared by most known phosphonate antibiotics pathways |CITS:[19489722]| and catalyzed by the phosphoenolpyruvate phosphomutase (rhiH) and 3-phosphonopyruvate decarboxylase (rhiEF) in |FRAME:TAX-703612|. The latter is interesting because of the existence of two subunits encoded by two different genes, i.e. rhiE and rhiF of the enzyme |CITS:[20142038]|. The next step is a unusual aldolase reaction where the catalyzing enzyme (rhiG) uses |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| instead of the typical |FRAME:PYRUVATE| to yield |FRAME:CPD-16788| from |FRAME:CPD-551|. The formed |FRAME:CPD-16788| is spontaneously converted to its trans-isomer which indicates the necessity for a not yet identified dehydratase forming the cis-isomer as found in the structure of |FRAME:CPD-16793| |CITS:[20142038]|. The putative dehydratase and also the L-α-amino acid transaminase encoded by rhiJ may act on various levels and compounds as indicated in the pathway but the exact substrate specificity for those enzymes remains to be shown. The attachment of the L-amino acid |FRAME:ARG| to |FRAME:CPD-16790| which forms |FRAME:CPD-16791| and the further ligation of |FRAME:VAL| to the C-terminal of |FRAME:ARG| of |FRAME:CPD-16791| to yield |FRAME:CPD-16792| is potentially carried out by corresponding L-α-amino acid ligases encoded by rhiM (dipeptide formation) |CITS:[19352016]| and rhiC (oligopeptide formation) |CITS:[20057135]|, respectively . However, the exact substrate specificity remains to be validated because of the unavailability of the respective intermediates at the time |CITS:[ 20142038]|.

Summary: General Background, Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The lipid A component of pathogenic bacteria is detected by the host serum LPS-binding protein (LBP), which is dependent on two cofactors: cluster of differentiation 14 (CD14) and myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD2). The lipid A/LBP complex is subsequently recognized by the opsonic receptor CD14, forming a triple complex that activates Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). TLR4 activation triggers a signalling cascade, leading to the production of cytokines and clotting factors and the secretion of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) and other stimulatory molecules |CITS: [10963608]|. CAMP binds to negatively charged structural motifs such as the phosphate groups on lipid A, leading to cell lysis and death |CITS: [19601838]|. If the immune response is too strong sepsis and septic shock can occur, leading to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome and death |CITS: [12857774]|., In many bacterial species lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor lipid IVA. , Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. , About This Pathway, Compared with other enterobacterial lipid As, the lipid A of |FRAME: TAX-210| activates TLR4 in a much weaker form, displaying a 1000-fold lower endotoxicity compared with lipid A from |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [Yamaoka08]|. Several modifications result in this weak TLR4 elicitation: the major form of |FRAME: TAX-210| lipid A is acylated by four rather than six fatty acids, contains only a single Kdo residue, lacks the usual 4'-phosphate group, and has a phosphoethanolamine (PEtN) moiety replacing the 1-position phosphate group |CITS: [ 21903201]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8816 "γ-Resorcylate"| and |FRAME: CPD-623| occur in nature as secondary metabolites in plants and fungi |CITS: [18427109][19795855]|. , A bacterial strain that could use |FRAME: CPD-623| as the sole source of carbon (|FRAME: ORG-5953|) was originally isolated by enrichment culture in 1976. While the pathway's intermediates are shared within all of these organisms, variability occurs in the enzymes that catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-623| to |FRAME: CPD-8130|. In |FRAME: TAX-267998| the reaction is catalyzed by a two-component FADH2-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.27|), in |FRAME: TAX-1718| it is catalyzed by a single-component NADPH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.219|), and in |FRAME: TAX-101510| it is catalyzed by a single-component NADH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.220|)., About This Pathway, The industrial value of |FRAME: CPD-8816|, which is an important intermediate in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, and agricultural chemicals |CITS: [14858847][4801686]|, and the fact that the reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.103|, is reversible, resulted in interest in this enzyme, which in vivo functions in the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-8816|. While several such enzymes have been characterized prior to 2015, none has been described from a Gram-positive bacterium., |FRAME: TAX-101510| is a Gram-positive bacterium, originally isolated from |FRAME: BETA-HCH|-contaminated soil |CITS: [16535122]|, that is able to grow on |FRAME: CPD-8816| as its sole carbon and energy source., The gene cluster encoding |FRAME: CPD-8816| catabolism was identified by screening the genome using the sequence of the |FRAME: G-44491| gene of |FRAME: TAX-267998|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.103|. The orthologous gene, |FRAME: G-44499|, was found in a cluster that contained several additional genes - |FRAME: G-44492|, |FRAME: G-44493|, and |FRAME: G-44494|, which form a transcription unit with |FRAME: G-44499|, as well as a transporter and a hydrolase which form their own transcription unit, and a transcriptional regulator, which represses transcription of both units in the absence of |FRAME: CPD-8816| |CITS: [26319878]|., The |FRAME: G-44499|, |FRAME: G-44492|, |FRAME: G-44493|, and |FRAME: G-44494| genes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and their function characterized. The pathway is very similar to that characterized from the Gram-negative |FRAME: TAX-267998|, with one exception. The enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-44492| is a novel NADH-dependent single component hydroxylase, which differs from other enzymes known to catalyze the transformation of |FRAME: CPD-623| to |FRAME: CPD-8130| |CITS: [26319878]|.

Summary: Alkaloids are nitrogen-containing natural plant products, some of which are believed to function as plant defense compounds. |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| is a branch-point intermediate in the biosynthesis of many benzylisoquinoline alkaloids including those in pharmaceutical usage such as |FRAME: CODEINE|, |FRAME: MORPHINE|, |FRAME: BERBERINE| and |FRAME: SANGUINARINE|. Benzylisoquinoline alkaloids are restricted to several families including the |FRAME: TAX-3465| and the |FRAME: TAX-3440|. They often accumulate in the latex of the plant. , The first committed step in |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| biosynthesis is the condensation of |FRAME: DOPAMINE| and |FRAME: HYDRPHENYLAC-CPD|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.99.14|, which introduces the cyclic nitrogen ring structure. This enzyme is stereoselective and establishes the stereochemical (S)- configuration of the compounds in the rest of the pathway., |FRAME: DOPAMINE Dopamine| is derived from |FRAME: TYR| via either |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| or |FRAME: TYRAMINE|. It was once hypothesized that |FRAME: TYRAMINE| could also be a precursor of |FRAME: HYDRPHENYLAC-CPD|. However, in |FRAME: TAX-3469| |FRAME: TYRAMINE| is always incorporated into the isoquinol-ring system of |FRAME: S-NORCOCLAURINE|, but not into the benzyl-moiety, suggesting that |FRAME: TYRAMINE| is not a precursor of |FRAME: HYDRPHENYLAC-CPD| |CITS: [Dewick97]|., The condensation step is followed by three methylation reactions and a hydroxylation reaction, forming |FRAME: S-RETICULINE|.

CysO is both adenylated and sulfurylated by a bifunctional |FRAME: G185E-7476-MONOMER| encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7476| gene, resulting in |FRAME: Thiocarboxylated-CysO| |CITS: [16104727]|., |FRAME: CYS| is formed tethered to the CysO protein by a |FRAME: G185E-5515-MONOMER "cysteine synthase"| encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-5515| gene, which catalyzes the addition of |FRAME: 3-P-SERINE| (an intermediate of the |FRAME: SERSYN-PWY| pathway) to the thiocarboxylate at the carboxy terminus of the CysO, generating |FRAME: CysO-S-Cysteine| conjugate |CITS: [18799456][18842002]|., The last step of this pathway is catalyzed by a |FRAME: G185E-5513-MONOMER| (encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-5513| gene), which hydrolyzes the CysO-cysteine conjugate to release |FRAME: CYS| and regenerate CysO |CITS: [16104727]|.

Summary: Back in 1977 it was discovered that the genome of |FRAME: TAX-260586| does not contain |FRAME: ADENINE| bases. Analysis of the genomes of several of those phages confirmed that they too contain Z instead of adenine |CITS: [33926954]|., Interestingly, the Z base was identified in a carbonaceous meteorite and was proposed as a nucleobase that could have been available at the time life evolved on earth |CITS: [21836052]|.

TtuD transfers the sulfur to a |FRAME: TtuB-Sulfur-carrier-proteins "TtuB protein"|, a small sulfur-carrier protein that is similar to |FRAME: G1 ThiS| and |FRAME: EG11597 MoaD| |CITS: [16547008]|. Following the activation of the carboxylate group of the terminal glycine to a carboxy-adenylate form, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.M15| (TtuC), the protein accepts the sulfur atom from TtuD, forming a C-terminal thiocarboxylate |CITS: [19037260][27878988]|., Finally, another enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.15| (TtuA) transfers the sulfur to the uracil at position 54 of the tRNA |CITS:[16547008][19037260][23444054]|.

Nicotinate (niacin, vitamin B3, 3-pyridinecarboxylate) is a pyridine ring-containing compound. Microorganisms have multiple ways of degrading pyridine and its derivatives, and degradation of these compounds is relevant to both biological and industrial processes. The degradation of nicotinate by both aerobic and anaerobic organisms involves the initial formation of 6-hydroxynicotinate, but the pathways diverge after that. Among aerobic , organisms, the pathways in |FRAME:TAX-286| and |FRAME:TAX-86668| are shown in MetaCyc pathways , |FRAME: PWY-722|, and |FRAME: PWY-5033|, respectively. An anaerobic pathway for nicotinate degradation in |FRAME: TAX-1528 "Eubacterium barkeri (previously knowns as Clostridium barkeri)"| is shown here (|CITS: [4553843]| and reviewed in |CITS: [8840783], [3550408], [4075828]|). This anaerobic fermentation pathway results in the formation of equimolar amounts of propionate, acetate, carbon dioxide and ammonia |CITS: [4553843]|. The acetate and carbon dioxide are thought to be derived from pyruvate |CITS: [4332128]|, as indicated by the pathway link., The first reaction is ring hydroxylation, resulting in the formation of 6-hydroxynicotinate (sometimes shown in its 6-oxo tautomeric form) |CITS: [3550408], [4553843]|. The next reaction is ring reduction. The following three reactions have been elucidated by the discovery of two chiral intermediates and three enzymes |CITS: [16894175]|. These investigators also cloned the entire gene cluster encoding the nicotinate fermentation enzymes in Eubacterium barkeri. The enamidase is a bifunctional hydrolase that produces the chiral 2-formylglutarate and ammonia. This compound is then reduced to the chiral (S)-2-hydroxymethylglutarate. There is evidence that degradation of pyruvate via a ferredoxin-linked process, with acetyl-CoA and acetyl phosphate intermediates, results in ATP generation and the formation of acetate and carbon dioxide |CITS: [4332128], [6489933]|. Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Tetracyclines tetracycline| antibiotics, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1948 |CITS: [18112227]|, are one of the most widely used classes of antibiotics in agriculture, aquaculture, and medicine. They have a broad antimicrobial spectrum, can be administered orally, and have a low cost. Following widespread use, tetracycline resistance mechanisms emerged and continue to create a need for new derivatives that are active against resistant bacterial strains. Semisynthesis has led to second and third generation tetracycline derivatives with enhanced antibiotic activity and pharmacological properties., The original tetracyclines are natural polyketides produced by actinomycete bacteria. They are characterized by their tetracyclic ring structure, a richly substituted A ring, and a heavily oxidized periphery that includes a C11, C12, and C11a keto-enol configuration, which let them bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit, interfering with the binding of aminoacylated tRNA to the A-site of the 30S subunit and halting protein synthesis |CITS: [11163189][11381101]|., |FRAME: CPD-19255 Oxytetracycline|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-1927|, was the second tetracycline compound to be discovered |CITS: [15400447]|, and its biosynthesis is the best studied among the tetracyclines. Early knowledge about the pathway was obtained through a series of blocked mutants and substrate feeding experiments, revealing the nature of several key intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-19273| and |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE| |CITS: [McCormick62][McCormick63a][McCormick63b][14289339][5641578]|. Later work using 13C-labeled acetate revealed the polyketide origin of the tetracycline backbone, and supported the idea of |FRAME: CPD-17870| as the origin of the C-2 amide |CITS: [Thomas83a][Thomas83b]|., In 1989 it was shown that all of the genes required for |FRAME: CPD-19255| synthesis were located within a a single DNA segment on the |FRAME: TAX-1927| chromosome |CITS: [2914874]|. This was followed by the complete sequencing of the gene clusters encoding |FRAME: CPD-19258| |CITS: [Ryan99]| and |FRAME: CPD-19255| biosynthesis |CITS: [8163168][Hunter02][16597959]|., Following the sequencing, the function of all of the involved genes has been shown through either direct isolation and characterization, genetic knockouts |CITS: [10551844][16148009]|, or expression in other Streptomyces strains |CITS: [16597959][17125237][17631493][17625867][18422316]|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the upper part of the tetracyclines biosynthetic pathway, which is common to all tetracyclines., The first steps of tetracycline biosynthesis are catalyzed by a minimal polyketide synthase (PKS). Initiation involves an amide-containing starter unit (either |FRAME: CPD-17870|, as shown here, or malonamyl-ACP) |CITS: [Thomas83b][10551844][16148009]|. Following the initiation, the PKS catalyzes the iterative condensation of 8 malonyl-CoA molecules to yield the poly-β-ketone backbone of tetracycline. Throughout the proccess, the nascent chain is attached to the |FRAME: OxyC "OxyC acyl-carrier protein"|. The oxygen attached to the C-9 carbon of the nonaketide is then reduced by a dehydrogenase., Two cyclases/dehydratases, encoded by |FRAME: G-44634| and |FRAME: G-44635|, bring about the formation of |FRAME: CPD-19275|, the first intermediate that contains the four rings |CITS: [17631493]|. The biochemical basis of the A ring cyclization is not well understood. While some data indicates that it may happen spontaneously |CITS: [17631493]|, it may also be catalyzed by the product of |FRAME: G-44637| |CITS: [16597959]|., A methyltransferase encoded by |FRAME: G-44636| adds a methyl group at position 6, generating |FRAME: CPD-19273|. This compound can be modified into different types of tetracycline compounds depending on the bacterial strain (e.g. |FRAME: CPD0-1414|, |FRAME: CPD-19255|, |FRAME: CPD-19258|, or the anticancer natural product |FRAME: CPD-19287| |CITS: [1577661][23024027]|).

|FRAME: TRICHLOROETHENE Trichloroethylene| (TCE) is one of the most common industrial pollutants. It has been used widely as degreaser, drycleaning agent and as anesthetic. Phytoremidiation has been studied as an alternative and effective way to remove TCE. Several plants have been shown to be capable of taking up and metabolizing TCE |CITS: [9703485][17969684][17940038]|., In mammals, TCE is metabolized via two pathways: the oxidative pathway mediated by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (primarily |FRAME: HS05414-MONOMER|), and the glutathione conjugation pathway catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.18|. The oxidative pathway is the predominant one, resulting in metabolites such as |FRAME: CPD-9673|, |FRAME: CPD-9675|, and |FRAME: CPD-9674|, which are known to be dechlorinated to |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [10807551]|., The same three metabolites, |FRAME: CPD-9673|, |FRAME: CPD-9675|, and |FRAME: CPD-9674|, were also found in plants exposed to TCE, both in controlled exposures and in field conditions |CITS: [Newman97][Doucette98][Newman99][Orchard00]|., It has also been shown, a long time ago, that tomato and gourd plants take up |FRAME: CPD-9673| and metabolize it to |FRAME: CPD-9676| |CITS: [Miller41]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (ascorbic acid, vitamin C) is a reducing agent and antioxidant biosynthesized by plants, eukaryotic algae, some bacteria and many, but not all vertebrates.|FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it. These species rely on mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries. Reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|., In photosynthesizing plants and eukaryotic algae |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has roles in metabolism, electron transport, the cell cycle and responses to pathogens and abiotic stress. When coupled with its redox system, the ascorbate/glutathione cycle, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| can effectively regulate cellular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| levels (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-2261|) |CITS: [18460785]|. Interestingly, |FRAME: TAX-1117| do not possess any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis, and minimize photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases, suggesting that the use of ascorbate evolved after the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote |CITS: [23109712][25768426]|., |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is the most abundant water-soluble redox compound in photosynthesizing plants and eukaryotic algae. In plants it is biosynthesized mainly by the L-galactose pathway (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-882|), although other plant pathways have also been proposed (see pathways |FRAME: PWY4FS-11|, |FRAME: PWY4FS-12| and |FRAME: PWY4FS-13|). In addition, a pathway based on uronic acid intermediates has been proposed in higher plants, but a key enzyme, aldonolactonase, has not been identified (in |CITS: [18782759]|). However, there is evidence for a unique |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis pathway based on uronic acid intermediates in the photosynthetic, unicellular eukaryote |FRAME: ORG-6122|, in which aldonolactonase has been identified (|CITS: [18782759]| and in |CITS: [17090924]|) (this pathway)., About This Pathway, An early report provided evidence for a major |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis pathway based on uronic acid intermediates in the photosynthetic, unicellular eukaryote |FRAME: ORG-6122|, based on feeding and isotope dilution experiments, and enzyme assays |CITS: [118242]|. In later work the gene encoding the key enzyme aldonolactonase was cloned, expressed and its product characterized. The role of this enzyme in the pathway was demonstrated by silencing the expression of aldonolactonase using RNA interference. It was concluded that this is the major pathway for |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis in |FRAME: ORG-6122|. However, more work in needed to determine its role in other eukaryotic photosynthetic algae and in higher plants |CITS: [18782759]|. The pathway is shown here along with enzymes participating in the pathway that have been characterized |CITS: [18782759] [17090924] [SHIGEOKA79]|., In addition, evidence for a minor, alternative pathway for |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis via |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| -> |FRAME: L-GULONATE| -> |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| was also found in |FRAME: ORG-6122| |CITS: [118242]| (not shown). However, the flux through this pathway is much lower than the pathway shown here (|CITS: [18782759]| and in |CITS: [17090924]|). It is likely that the pathway shown here is an effective route for maintenance of cellular |FRAME: ASCORBATE| levels in this organism (in |CITS: [18782759]|). Reviewed in |CITS: [18460785]|., The dehydrogenase that catalyzes the final step in |FRAME: ORG-6122| differs from the analogous plant (EC 1.3.2.3) and animal (EC 1.1.3.8) enzymes in substrate specificity and electron acceptor |CITS: [SHIGEOKA79]|.

In plants and algae nitrate is an important source of nitrogen. Nitrate assimilation begins with the uptake of nitrate from the soil by the root. Root epidermal and cortical cells are the first to actively transport nitrate into their cytosols. Nitrate then crosses the endodermis of the root and is released into the xylem. After long distance transport up the xylem, nitrate is again actively transported into the cells of the leaf. Once in the cell, nitrate can be stored in the vacuole (due to toxicity) or reduced to nitrite by the enzyme nitrate reductase (NR)., Four classes of nitrate reductases are known - a eukaryotic class, and three prokaryotic classes. The eukaryotic nitrate reductases are found in plants, algae and fungi, and are involved in assimilation of nitrate. They are composed of two identical subunits, and contain a |FRAME: CPD-15870| and an |FRAME:FAD| prosthetic group. In general, plant enzymes prefer NADH as the electron donor (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.1"|) and fungal enzymes prefer NADPH (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.3"|), although some enzymes were reported, to accept either of these compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE-REDUCTASE-NADPORNOPH-RXN "E.C. 1.7.1.2"|) |CITS: [14209328]|., Example for eukaryotic enzymes include the |FRAME: CPLX-7198| from |FRAME: TAX-3702| and the, |FRAME: CPLX-7498| from |FRAME: TAX-5141|. , Nitrite is transported into the chloroplast, where it is reduced to ammonia by nitrite reductase (NiR). The final step of the pathway is the incorporation of ammonia into glutamine by glutamine synthetase |CITS: [ARABIDOPSIS94]|.

Summary: Triterpene saponins, a class of secondary metabolites found primarily in dicotyledonous plants, |CITS: [12475612]| (but also produced in some lower marine animals |CITS: [Riguera97]|),, help plants to defend themselves against a variety of biotic threats, including microbes, insects, and, other plants |CITS: [12475612]|, (see refs in: |CITS: [17141815]|). They also impact the, palatability and digestibility of plants to specific animals, including grazing ruminants, |CITS: [10552705], [8726748]|. In addition, many saponins have pharmaceutical benefits such, as anticancer |CITS: [17317337]|, hepatoprotective |CITS: [12951488]|,, hemolytic |CITS: [10985074]|, anti-viral |CITS: [10919372]|, or other medicinal, properties (see refs in |CITS: [15743451]|). , |FRAME:TAX-3880|, a model legume, produces over 30 different saponins. Methyl jasmonate (MeJA),, a hormone involved in plant biotic stress responses, induces saponin accumulation in |FRAME:TAX-3880|, cell suspension cultures |CITS: [12492844]|. This suggests a protective role for these compounds. Some, attempts have been made to test the role of Medicago saponins in plant defense |CITS: [17610116]|, and medical applications |CITS: [17006971]| and to determine the structure-activity relationships, of the bioactive substances |CITS: [17006971], [16619355]|. , All triterpene saponins made in plants, originate from |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE|, but a series of different oxidations,, glycosylations, and other modifications lead to the production of a great number of different, compounds. Most plants only produce a subset of the total array of triterpene saponins, but multiple, species may synthesize the same compound. At least five different aglycone sapogenins derived from |FRAME:CPD-6948|,, namely medicagenic acid, soyasapogenol B, soyasapogenol E, hederagenin, and, bayogenin undergo various glycosylations to produce the triterpene saponins found, in |FRAME:TAX-3880| |CITS: [11830145]|. Although an enzyme |FRAME:MONOMER-12196| responsible, for beta-amyrin synthesis has been characterized in M. truncatula, |CITS: [12492844]|,, many of the downstream steps in sapogenin and saponin formation are poorly understood., However, two glycosyltransferases, UGT73K1 and UGT71G1 responsible for the glucosylation of some, of the aglycone saponins have been isolated based on transcript and metabolite profiling. In vitro, assays were used to characterize their biochemical activities, but, unfortunately, the exact location, of the glucosylation on the substrate could often not be determined using mass spectrometry., In addition, some unexpected compounds serve as good substrates for UGT71G1 in vitro., Therefore, additional factors, such as changes in transcript expression levels and saponin abundance, in response to MeJA have to be considered to make hypotheses about the in vivo substrate, preferences and regiospecificity of UGT73K1 and UGT71G1 |CITS: [15743451]|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, Even though NAD molecules are not consumed during oxidation reactions, they have a relatively short half-life. For example, in |FRAME:TAX-562| the NAD+ half-life is 90 minutes. Once enzymatically degraded, the pyrimidine moiety of the molecule can be recouped via the NAD salvage cycles. This pathway is used for two purposes: it recycles the internally degraded NAD product |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE| (also known as nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN), and it is used for the assimilation of exogenous NAD+., Since the NAD+ molecule is highly polar, it has to be hydrolyzed before it can be transported across the cytoplasmic membrane for final uptake. It does seem to be able to penetrate the external membrane, though, as the enzymes that break it down are found in the periplasm |CITS: [2841298]|. NAD+ is first hydrolyzed by NAD pyrophosphatase into NMN , which can be hydrolyzed further to nicotinamide by NMN nucleosidase. Both enzymes are periplasmic. Both NMN and nicotinamide can be transported across the inner membrane into the cytoplasm. Once there, nicotinamide is converted via nicotinate to nicotinate nucleotide, at which point the pathway merges with the de novo biosynthesis pathway, and continues to NAD via deamido-NAD., There are several flavors of the salvage pathway found in different organisms, and even within the same organism. The one described above contains 4 reaction steps, and is often referred to as the PNC IV pathway, for Pyridine Nucleotide Cycling. However, there are also a five-step cycle and a six-step cycle, termed PNC V and VI, respectively |CITS: [220211][6445894]|., In the PNC IV cycle, the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.42| converts NMN (which can be transported across the inner membrane in Enterobacteria) directly to nicotinate nucleotide, bypassing the enzymes nicotinamidase (PncA) and nicotine phosphoribosyl transferase (PncB), which are members of the PNC VI cycle (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSAL-PWY|)., PNC IV is the major intracellular recycling pathway in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [7021549]|, while PNC VI is the major cycle of |FRAME:TAX-90371| |CITS: [6445894]| and yeast |CITS:[12062417][11884393]|.

General Background, |FRAME: SER| biosynthesis is a major metabolic pathway in many organisms. Its end product, |FRAME: SER|, is not only used in protein synthesis, but also as a precursor for the biosynthesis of glycine, cysteine, tryptophan, and phospholipids. In addition, it directly or indirectly serves as a source of one-carbon units for the biosynthesis of various compounds., Three different |FRAME: SER| biosynthetic pathways operate in plants. The best studied pathway occurs in relation to |FRAME: PWY-181 photorespiration|, where serine is formed from two molecules of |FRAME: GLY|. Another pathway, which operates in plastids and forms |FRAME: 3-P-HYDROXYPYRUVATE| as an intermediate, is described in |FRAME: SERSYN-PWY|. The third pathway, described here, is initiated in the cytosol and involves a |FRAME: GLYCERATE| intermediate., About This Pathway, The glycerate–serine pathway is initiated in the cytosol by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.38| (PGA phosphatase). This enzyme, which has been described in 1971 |CITS: [10970181]|, has not been studied since and the gene encoding it is not known yet. The enzyme has a broad specificity, but |FRAME: G3P| is its preferred substrate. It is confined to the cytosol and is active at low pH (optimum pH 5.9). Its activity was found high in a C4 plant (sorghum), where serine, formation via the photorespiratory pathway is very limited due to a low or absent photorespiration. So far PGA phosphatase has only been reported from plants., The second step of the pathway is catalyzed by isoforms of glycerate dehydrogenase/hydroxypyruvate reductases (HPRs). Three isoforms of hydroxypyruvate reductase have been described in plants - a peroxisomal form (|FRAME: AT1G68010|) |CITS: [9177031]|, a cytosolic form (|FRAME: AT1G79870|) |CITS: [3548703][3281657][16667010][2039466][18952776]|, and a plastidal form (|FRAME: AT1G12550|) |CITS: [16666441][21205613]|. While the cytosolic isoform is the most relevant to this cytosolic pathway, it is not impossible that the pathway occurs under certain conditions also in the peroxisome or plastid |CITS: [29593770]|., Enzymes catalyzing the last step of the pathway, aminotransferases that form |FRAME: SER| from |FRAME: OH-PYR|, exist in the peroxisome, cytosol and plastid |CITS: [21205613]|. The reaction can proceed with either |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.51|) or |FRAME: GLY| (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|) as the amino group donor. The Arabidopsis enzyme |FRAME: AGT1|, which is classified as |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.14|, can transaminate |FRAME: OH-PYR| using |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: ASN|, |FRAME: GLY| and other amino acids |CITS: [23098902]|., While the first enzyme of the pathway has so far been described only from plants, the later steps of the pathway, resulting in the production of |FRAME: SER| from |FRAME: GLYCERATE|, have been described from animals |CITS: [13385257]| and bacteria |CITS: [4315933]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Sphingomyelins Sphingomyelin| is a type of |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS sphingolipid| found in animal cell membranes, especially in the membranous myelin sheath that surrounds some nerve cell axons. Sphingomyelin has a function in signal transduction |CITS: [8086039]|. , Sphingomyelin is highly enriched in the plasma membrane of cells, and was considered to be found largely in the exoplasmic leaflet of the cell membrane. However, there is some evidence that there may also be a sphingomyelin pool in the inner leaflet of the membrane |CITS: [2187537]|. Moreover, neutral sphingomyelinase-2, an enzyme that breaks down sphingomyelin into ceramide, has been found to localize exclusively to the inner leaflet, further suggesting that there may be sphingomyelin present there., Sphingomyelin can accumulate in a rare hereditary disease called Niemann-Pick Disease. The disease is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme sphingomyelinase, rsulting in accumulation of sphingomyelin in the spleen, liver, lungs, bone marrow, and the brain, causing irreversible neurological damage.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8| (Q-8) is a common form of ubiquinone among bacteria. Most of the Gram-negative facultative anaerobes, such as the enterobacteria, produce Q-8 (in addition to |FRAME: CPD-9728| and |FRAME: DEMETHYLMENAQUINONE|). Q-8 has been documented in several strains of |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [13673033]|,, |FRAME: TAX-546|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, |FRAME: TAX-554|, |FRAME: TAX-584|, |FRAME: TAX-585| |CITS: [4886765]| and |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [Bezborodov69]|, as well as in the non-eneterobacteria |FRAME: TAX-644|, |FRAME: TAX-648| |CITS: [4886765]| and |FRAME: TAX-51367| |CITS: [Collins81]|. It is also common in aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-354| |CITS:[13673033] [4288128]|, |FRAME: TAX-353| |CITS: [13869492]|, |FRAME: TAX-107673| |CITS: [Denis75]|, |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [4351160]|, |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [Yamada68]|, and various, |FRAME: TAX-338| strains |CITS: [Ikemoto80]|. Q-8 was also found to be the major quinone in an unidentified strain of the gliding bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1021| |CITS: [Carr67]| and in some phototrophic bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1049|, |CITS:[14240125]|, |FRAME:TAX-1053|, |FRAME: TAX-28068| |CITS: [Carr65][5727384]|, and a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1081| |CITS: [5727384]|. Q-8 is often found as a secondary quinone in |FRAME: TAX-286| strains |CITS: [4886765]|., The best studied ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway is that of |FRAME: TAX-83333|, which produces a |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8|. The first committed step of the pathway is the conversion of chorismate to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, by |FRAME: CHORPYRLY-MONOMER|. The enzyme retains and is efficiently inhibited by the product of the reaction, 4-hydroxybenzoate, which may present a control mechanism for the ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway or a mechanism for delivery of 4-hydroxybenzoate to the membrane |CITS: [11455603][11825618]|., The second step in the pathway is the transfer of the polyisoprenoid tail onto |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| by the membrane-bound |FRAME: 4OHBENZOATE-OCTAPRENYLTRANSFER-MONOMER|. This is followed by the, decarboxylation of the ring structure by |FRAME: CPLX0-301| to form |FRAME: 2-OCTAPRENYLPHENOL|. Under anaerobic conditions, this compound accumulates in the membrane and is not converted into ubiquinone. Further steps in the pathway require the presence of dioxygen |CITS: [361395]|., Following is the alternating introduction of three hydroxyl- and three methyl groups. With the exception of the methyltransferase that catalyzes both of the O-methyltransferase reactions, UbiG, none of the enzymes have been studied biochemically and their substrate and cofactor requirements are still unknown., The enzymes of this pathway may form a membrane-associated complex |CITS: [393264]|. UbiX shows a genetic interaction with UbiG, suggesting a possible physical interaction within a complex |CITS: [16923914]|., For the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8| in yeast, see |FRAME: PWY-5870|.
