Summary: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) and turmeric (Curcuma longa) both belong to the ginger family (Zingiberaceae). They accumulate bioactive compounds in their rhizomes, gingerols in ginger and |FRAME: PWY-6432 "curcuminoids"| in turmeric |CITS: [16890967]|. , Gingerols such as |FRAME: CPD-13494|, |FRAME: CPD-13645| and |FRAME: CPD-13646| are known to have enormous human health beneficial effects, most notably anticancer. Gingerol biosynthesis is thus a highly desired target for bioengineering. While the biosynthetic pathway of gingerols in plants is not fully understood |CITS: [16890967][20836122]|, a combinatorial pathway was successfully constructed and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [20836122]|. The system was composed of: , 1) A short chain fatty acid CoA ligase from rice that efficiently converted octanoate, supplied in the medium, to octanoyl-CoA. , 2) A portion of the beta oxidation pathway from yeast that included Pox1p (acyl-CoA oxidase) and Fox2p (bifunctional with 2-enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3S-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activities). This beta oxidation system converted octanoyl-CoA to 3-oxooctanoyl-CoA. The yeast enzymes were chosen because the bi-functionality of Fox2p meant that only two enzymes were needed instead of three. 3-oxoacyl-CoA thiolase was not over-expressed in this system so that over-produced 3-oxooctanoyl-CoA was not further metabolized via the rest of beta oxidation pathway.  , 3) A 4-coumarate CoA ligase from Lithospermum erythrorhizon that converted 4-coumarate to 4-coumaroyl-CoA. , 4) A curcuminoid synthase (CUS) from rice that can effectively condense 4-coumaroyl-CoA with 3-oxooctanoyl-CoA to form 4-coumaroylhexanoylmethane, an analog of |FRAME: CPD-13645| and |FRAME: CPD-13494|. , The physiological role of the rice CUS in rice plants is unclear. Rice does not produce gingerols nor curcuminoids. Although several CUS have been identified from the curcuminoid-producing plant Curcuma longa |CITS: [19622354][19258320]|, it is not clear whether they have the same enzyme activity as the rice CUS in forming gingerol analogs. Gingerol synthase has not yet been identified in ginger |CITS: [16890967]|.   , The highest yield of 4-coumaroylhexanoylmethane in the |FRAME:TAX-562| expression system was 84 mg/L.

Selenium is an essential trace element that is crucial for the normal development of bacteria and animals. High concentrations of selenium are however toxic, largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064]|. In humans the safety threshold between acute selenium poisoning (>400 μg/day) and selenium deficiency (<40 μg/day) is very narrow. , The natural forms of selenium include |FRAME: SELENATE| [Se(VI)], |FRAME: SELENITE| [Se(IV)], |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| [Se(0)], and |FRAME: SE-2| [Se(-II)]. Selenite is the most toxic, while elemental selenium is insoluble and is generally considered to be non-toxic |CITS: [25631289]|. However, selenium rarely occurs in its elemental state in nature. , Elemental selenium can be formed by certain organisms, usually by reduction of the oxidized forms |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE|. Some bacterial species are known to form selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) that consist of elemental selenium coated by a mixture of proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates |CITS: [26801915][32854560][35398797]|., |FRAME: TAX-1423| is able to reduce selenite and produce SeNPs under aerobic conditions. A study aimed to identify |FRAME: TAX-1423| enzymes involved in |FRAME: SELENITE| reduction found three enzymes that catalyze the reduction of selenite to |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| in vivo - |FRAME: BSU03210-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: BSU03210|), |FRAME: BSU03910-MONOMER| (encoded by |FRAME: BSU03910|), and |FRAME: CPLX8J2-20|, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU33430| and |FRAME: BSU33440| genes. The three enzymes were purified, and in vitro assays confirmed that they could catalyse the reduction of Se(IV) under optimal conditions using NADPH as a cofactor |CITS: [35398797]|.

Names: fatty acid biosynthesis initiation (type I) // fatty acid biosynthesis initiation (animals and fungi, cytoplasm)
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "Fatty acids"| are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and fatty acyl moieties of proteins that modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II., Type I systems are found in lower eukaryotes and animals, while type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. Thus both systems operate in animals - the type I system in the cytosol, (see |FRAME: PWY-5994|), and the type II system in the mitochondria (this pathway)., The main difference between the two systems is that type I systems consist of one (in the case of animals) or two (in the case of fungi) large multifunctional gene products that form a single complex that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while in type II systems the different reactions are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., Fatty acid biosynthesis starts with an initiation sequence that produces |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs|, an activated molecule that is used for subsequent elongation reactions, which ultimately produce the final fatty acid products. This pathway describes the initiation sequence that occurs in the cytoplasm., About This Pathway, The first committed and rate-limiting step in de novo fatty acid biosynthesis is the carboxylation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, which is catalyzed by the cytosolic isoform of |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.2|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS05598| gene. The enzyme is a dimeric, multifunctional enzyme composed of four distinct domains; a biotin carboxylase (BC) domain, a biotin carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) domain, the ACC central region, and a carboxyltransferase (CT) domain., The rest of the fungal/animal fatty acid biosynthesis pathway is catalyzed by the type I fatty acid synthase (FAS). The process is initiated by the sequential transfer of a primer substrate, usually an acetyl moiety, from CoA thioester form (|FRAME: ACETYL-COA|), first to the nucleophilic serine residue of the acyltransferase domain, then to the phosphopantetheine thiol of the acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain, and finally to the active site cysteine residue of the β-ketoacyl synthase domain. , In the next step the chain extender substrate, a malonyl moiety, is transferred from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| via the nucleophilic serine residue of the acyltransferase domain to the phosphopantetheine thiol. Formation of a new C-C bond, by condensation of the acetyl and malonyl moieties, is coupled with an energetically favorable decarboxylation., The condensation product, |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE|, marks the end of the fatty acid biosynthesis initiation process. This intermediate is then extended by several cycles catalyzed by FAS, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5994|.

|FRAME:ORG-6143| can utilize |FRAME: CPD-7035| as its sole carbon source by degrading it to |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| via |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE|. |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE Phenylacetate| is degraded further to TCA cycle intermediates as described in |FRAME: PWY0-321| |CITS: [18177365]|., The genes that are involved in |FRAME: CPD-7035| degradation are located in |FRAME:ORG-6143| in a single operon. The pathway involves the participation of two different two-component signal-transducing systems (PedS1R1 and PedS2R2), a periplasmic binding protein (PedG), two quinoprotein alcohol dehydrogenases (|FRAME: G-80791 PedE| and |FRAME: G-80792 PedH|), a c-type cytochrome (PedF), an aldehyde dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-80790 PedI|), a pentapeptide repeat protein (PedD), and an ABC efflux system (PedABC) |CITS: [18177365]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-6534|.

|FRAME: CPD-17024 Pyoluteorin| is a compound with antimicrobial and antifungal activities. It was first isolated in the late 1950s from cultures of the |FRAME: TAX-287| strains T359 and IFO 3455, but later found in many other strains of Pseudomonads |CITS: [Takeda58][10094695][21392918][22761817]|. |FRAME: CPD-17024 Pyoluteorin| is toxic, against Oomycetes |CITS: [Howell80]| certain bacteria and fungi |CITS: [Takeda58]| and, at high concentrations, exhibits phytotoxicity against certain plants |CITS: [Maurhofer92]|. As the compound controls a wide range of pests, including epiphytes and weeds, it has the potential to be used as a new biological pesticide |CITS: [21141897]|., |FRAME: CPD-17024 Pyoluteorin| is a hybrid polyketide-nonribosomal peptide molecule that carries two chlorine atoms on a pyrrole moiety attached to a resorcinol ring. A biosynthetic cluster that contains ten genes (pltLABCDEFGMR) is responsible for its production in |FRAME: TAX-220664| |CITS: [10094695]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-17024| occurs while the substrate is attached to the dedicated peptidyl-carrier protein PltL. The pathway begins when an |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.53|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55298| gene, activates |FRAME: PRO| and attaches it as a thioester on the phosphopantetheinyl arm of |FRAME: Holo-PltL PltL|. Tandem four-electron oxidation of the attached prolyl residue, which is catalyzed by the flavoprotein |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.14| (PltE) yields a pyrrolyl 2-carboxylate residue |CITS: [11880032]|. This is followed by double chlorination by the FAD-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.56| (PltA) |CITS: [16162666]|. At this point the intermediate is transferred to the polyketide synthases PltB and PltC, which add three |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| molecules. Finally, the thioesterase PltG releases the compound and triggers a cyclization that is accompanied by the release of water molecules, generating the |FRAME: CPD-623| ring of the final |FRAME: CPD-17024| molecule |CITS: [19844639]|.

|FRAME:CPD-14529 Phenylethyl acetate| has been found in a number of plants and belongs to the major group of volatile esters which define scent in flowering plants |CITS:[Knudsen93]| |CITS:[Jacobsen02]|. The many volatiles that determine the composition of scent in plants are biosynthesized by a relatively small number of enzymes |CITS:[15326281]| which belong to basically three gene families: O-methyltransferases, acyltransferases and terpene synthases |CITS:[15862098]|., Acetyltransferases generally express activities towards a broader substrate spectrum; the ones which specifically acetylate |FRAME:CPD-7035| have been identified in the genus |FRAME:TAX-3764| |CITS:[12692346]|, |FRAME:TAX-4101| |CITS:[16525891]| and |FRAME:TAX-3655| |CITS:[Shan12]|. However, to determine their role with certainty in vivo is difficult and often remains to be elucidated. It has been proposed that the specificity of acetyltransferases may be dependent on the availability of substrates and that the preferred substrates ascertained in vitro may not be consistent with the in vivo 'natural' substrate of the acetyltransferase |CITS:[16525891]|., The corresponding esterases which would convert |FRAME:CPD-14529| back to |FRAME:CPD-7035| still remain to be determined. However, enzymes expressing activities towards similar compounds like 1-phenylethyl acetate |CITS:[Vandenberghe13]| or phenyl acetate |CITS:[13058402]| in plants and microorganisms |CITS:[16845703]| have already been reported.

Names: misacylated tRNA editing // mischarged tRNA editing
Summary: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (AARS) join amino acids with their cognate tRNAs in high fidelity reactions that define the genetic code. There are many tRNAs, most of which are specific for a particular amino acid, and in general, a dedicated AARS exists for each tRNA-amino acid pair., The AARS starts the reaction by activating the amino acid to an adenylate form, using ATP. The aminoacyl-adenylate, intermediate is initially held noncovalently in the active site, and subsequently the amino acyl group is transferred  to the 2' or 3' hydroxyl group of the terminal ribose of the tRNA, with liberation of AMP., Based on the active site structure, AARSs are grouped into two independently evolved classes |CITS: [2203971]|. Class I and II enzymes attach amino acyl groups to the 2'- and 3'-OH groups, respectively |CITS: [1103137][319826]|. However, in solution the 2'- or 3'-linked amino acids spontaneously transacylate to the neighboring OH at high rates, resulting in a mixture of 2'- and 3'-linked AA-tRNA isomers irrespective of the type of AARS involved |CITS: [Griffin66]|., While some AARSs are highly specific already in the activation reaction, others are less accurate. Ten of the 24 AARS families cannot achieve the tolerable level of fidelity in protein biosynthesis (estimated to be 1 in 3300) |CITS: [4643706]| in the synthetic reactions alone |CITS: [23852030]|. For example, class I isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS) activates |FRAME: VAL| only 200-fold less efficiently than its cognate amino acid cognate |FRAME: ILE| |CITS: [321008]|. Class I valyl- and leucyl-tRNA synthetases (ValRS and LeuRS), as well as a number of class II AARS, also efficiently activate noncognate amino acids and transfer them to tRNA |CITS: [182209][3534789][19379069]|., In order to overcome these errors the AARSs possessing reduced amino acid discrimination in the synthetic reactions developed hydrolytic proofreading activities. Two types of correction mechanisms are known: In pre-transfer editing, the AARS hydrolyzes the noncognate amino acid adenylate prior to transfer to the tRNA, while in post-transfer editing a misacylated tRNA is hydrolyzed after a noncognate amino acid is transferred to it., Pre-transfer editing resides within the synthetic active site, as shown for IleRS |CITS: [20498377]|, while post-transfer editing requires a dedicated editing domain. In Class I IleRS, ValRS, and LeuRS this domain is called CP1 (connective polypeptide 1) |CITS: [8900273][15775966][17474713]|. This domain acts on most noncognate amino acids, and selectivity has evolved against the cognate amino acid, which is discriminated against and thus not hydrolyzed |CITS: [35357484]|. The editing domains of class II enzymes are not conserved and show significant diversity.

Names: methoxylated aromatic compound degradation I // bacterial methoxydotrophic metabolism
Summary: Methoxylated aromatic compounds are important components of lignin and are found in significant amounts in the environment. Acetogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-33952|, |FRAME: TAX-82116|, and |FRAME: TAX-1525|, are able to grow on such compounds |CITS: [Bache81]|. These organisms do not metabolize the aromatic ring itself but use the O-methyl group as a one-carbon growth substrate. |FRAME: TAX-1525| can metabolize at least 20 different methoxylated aromatics |CITS: [1930235]|., It is well documented that there are different aromatic compound demethoxylation systems that differ in their substrate range. For example, two different systems have been described from |FRAME: TAX-82116|, one that can demethoxylate |FRAME: VANILLATE| |CITS: [9654069][9826201]|, and the other acting on |FRAME: CPD-24802|, but not on |FRAME: VANILLATE| |CITS: [11409548][15968525]|., The aromatic compound demethoxylation systems were shown to require |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| as the methyl acceptor |CITS: [7727373][Messmer96][9238105][9654069]|. In 2001 a vanillate-degrading demethoxylation system from |FRAME: TAX-1525| was characterized and found to include three components: the MtvB methyltransferase transfers the methyl group from the methoxylated substrate to a dedicated methyl-carrier corrinoid protein, MtvC; and a second methyltransferase, MtvA, then transfers the methyl group to |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|. The rest of the pathway utilizes enzymes of the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood-Ljungdahl pathway"| - the methyl group is first transferred to the |FRAME: Corrinoid-Fe-S-Proteins "corrinoid iron-sulfur protein"|, which serves as one of the substrates of |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.M5|. That enzyme uses electrons donated by ferredoxin to combine the methyl group with CO2, forming |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [11344134]|., When the |FRAME: TAX-1525| genome was sequenced in 2008 it was found to contain at least two operons encoding two sets of the demethoxylation sysytem enzymes. The two mtvA genes are nearly identical, as are the mtvC genes,but the mtvB genes are only eighty percent identical. Having multiple and different MtvB proteins results in an increased substrate range of the demethoxylation system. Additional homologous genes were found in the genome, which may encode additional such systems |CITS: [18631365]|.

Names: saponin biosynthesis II // oleanolate glucuronide triterpene saponin biosynthesis // oleanolate glucuronide biosynthesis // triterpene saponin biosynthesis II
Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9459 Oleanolate|, a common triterpene derived from |FRAME: CPD-6948|, can be found in its free form in plants, but is also subject to glycosylation. Oleanolate and its derivatives have been detected in at least 120 species of plants and exhibit numerous biological activities that can contribute to plant defense and human health. Anti-ulcer |CITS: [9543723]|, anti-nociceptive |CITS: [1974618]|, anti-tumor |CITS: [4828716]|, anti-viral |CITS: [2991440]| and other beneficial activities have all been attributed to oleanolic triterpene saponins., During oleanolate glycosylation, sugar moieties are typically attached to the C-3 hydroxyl group or the C-28 on the carboxyl group of oleanolate |CITS: [Szakiel05]|. Oleanolate derivatives can be separated into two major classes, glucosides and glucuronides, based on the nature of the initial glycosylation they undergo. The first step in oleanolate glucoside synthesis occurs when glucose is added to the C-3 hydroxyl group. Subsequent addition of glucose and/or galactose residues at the C-3 or C-28 positions leads to the formation of at least seven additional glucosides in |FRAME:TAX-41496| (marigold), but the biochemical steps involved have not been well characterized. Meanwhile, oleanolate glucuronides arise from the addition of a glucuronic acid to the C-3 hydroxyl group, catalyzed by oleanolate UDP glucuronosyltransferase. Further glucosylations on oleanolate 3-beta-D-glucuronoside generate at least five additional glucuronides in marigold |CITS: [Wojciechowski75], [Szakiel05]|., Oleanolate glucuronides share some properties that distinguish them from their glucoside counterparts. For example, in feeding experiments, the rate of glucoside biosynthesis exceeds the rate of glucuronide biosynthesis |CITS: [Szyja83]| and the rates of glucuronide and glucoside biosynthesis are differentially affected by light, and the hormones auxin and cytokinin |CITS: [Szakiel03]|. In addition, oleanolate glucuronides can be passively and irreversibly transported into vacuoles, whereas oleanolate glucoside transport into vacuoles is active and reversible |CITS: [Szakiel02]|. Thus, oleanolate glucuronides appear to behave more like traditional secondary metabolites in this respect. And, although each compound may have unique biological activities, in general, glucuronides tend to have lower allelopathic, but higher antifungal and wormicidal activity than the oleanolate glucosides. These classes of compounds also have different patterns of distribution within the plants that may be linked to their different biological functions |CITS: [Szakiel05]|. , Despite the prevalence of these compounds in the plant kingdom, much remains to be discovered about their biosynthesis. Currently, little is known about the reactions that occur to transform |FRAME: CPD-6948| into oleanolate, but a hypothetical reduction series of beta-amyrin to erythrodiol to oleanolic aldehyde to oleanolate was proposed in Machaerium incorruptible |CITS: [Alves66]|. Downstream of oleanolate, the synthesis of glycosylated derivatives has been studied in the medicinal and ornamental plant marigold |CITS: [Wojciechowski75], [Szakiel05]|. Immediately, downstream of oleanolate, the enzyme responsible for the first committed step in oleanolate glucuronide biosynthesis, oleanolate UDP glucuronosyltransferase, has been partially purified and characterized in the microsomal fraction of, marigold seedling extracts |CITS: [Wojciechowski75]|. The downstream enzymes that add additional galactose and glucose residues have not been well-characterized, but a series of feeding experiments have led to a proposed biosynthetic pathway for these oleanolate saponins. There is some evidence that the biosynthesis of these compounds occurs in several parts of the cell. For instance, the enzyme(s) responsible for the addition of UDP-glucose to the C28 carboxyl residue in oleanolate and its derivatives appear to reside in the cytoplasm based on subcellular fractionation results |CITS: [Wojciechowski75]|. Meanwhile, the addition of galactose and/or glucose residues to the glucuronic acid may be performed in the Golgi complex |CITS: [Wojciechowski75]|. Though the enzyme(s) responsible for these glycosylations have not been isolated, the reactions do appear to proceed in a somewhat fixed order; feeding experiments suggest that the glucose cannot be attached to the glucuronic acid prior to galactose addition |CITS: [Wojciechowski75]|. , Oleanolate glucuronide synthesis can occur in the leaf, roots, and in suspension cultures, though some later glycosylation reactions are organ-specific |CITS: [Szakiel05]|, and this process appears to go on throughout the life cycle of the plant |CITS: [Szakiel02]|.

General Background, N-linked glycosylation is an important process found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria., During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. It has been shown that the glycosylation is essential for the proper folding of some eukaryotic proteins., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes consists of three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (this pathway)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7426|)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and use somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathway is in general similar to the eukaryotic one, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7658|)., About This Pathway, Processing of the N-linked oligosaccharides begins immediately following the transfer of the tetradecasaccharide from its dolichol-bound form to nascent proteins. The first step in the processing is the removal of the terminal α-1,2-linked glucose, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.106| (α-glucosidase I) |CITS: [9363442][11971867]|. , This is followed by the removal of the two α-1,3-linked glucose residues, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.207| (α-glucosidase II) |CITS: [8910335][16373354]|. It has been shown that trimming of the glucose residues is identical in |FRAME: TAX-4932| and in mammalian cells. The removal of glucosyl residues is probably concomitant with completion of both glycosylation and folding of the target protein |CITS: [7881169]|., Following the removal of the three glucosyl residues, α-mannosidases remove some or all of the α-1,2-linked mannose residues. In |FRAME: TAX-4932| only one specific α-mannosidase has been found. The enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: YJR131W| gene, primarily trims a single α-1,2-linked mannose residue from Man9GlcNAc2 to produce Man8GlcNAc2, but at high enzyme concentrations it further trims the carbohydrates to Man5GlcNAc2 |CITS: [12090241]|., In mammalian cells more enzymes exist. The different mannosidases, which are expressed in different tissues, have slightly different affinities to different intermediates. They trim the mannoses in a different order (Tremblay and Herscovics, 2000), but end up producing the same Man5GlcNAc2 heptasaccharide |CITS: [8054711][9878780][10915796]|., Following the removal of glucose and mannose residues, Golgi glycosyltransferases add different sugars in a species- and cell-specific manner, leading to production of complex glycans. One such route is described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7426|., It should be mentioned that misfolded glycoproteins are handled in the ER mostly by the cytoplasmic |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.52| (|FRAME: YPL096W|), resulting in free N-glycans. A cytosol/vacuole α-mannosidase, |FRAME: YGL156W| (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.24 "EC 3.2.1.24"|) then trims these free glycans, eventually forming the trisaccharide |FRAME: CPD-20274|, which is not catabolized further |CITS: [26264652]|.

General Background, The common |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| pathway, used by most organisms for the catabolism of glucose and related sugars, can be regarded as both an energy-producing catabolic pathway and an anabolic pathway, producing |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which can be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|. While |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| can be fed to the TCA cycle for further energy production, it is also used as a biosynthestic precursor for many types of biomolecules (e.g. fatty acids). However, glycolysis is unable to produce 5-carbon sugars such as D-ribose, which are essential for the biosynthesis of DNA and RNA, neither can it form the 4-carbon sugar |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, a precursor of aromatic amino acids and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, or the 7-carbon sugar |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, a precursor for |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|., The |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| is an alternative way of oxidizing glucose that is targeted at anabolic reactions. The pathway fulfills two anabolic roles: it produces NADPH, making it a major source of reducing equivalents for biosynthetic reactions, and it produces C4, C5, and C7 sugars |CITS: [14790817][13129245][13174590][14285485]|., About This Pathway, The pentose phosphate pathway is an important member of central metabolism, as it supplies three of the 13 precursor metabolites (compounds needed for the biosyntheses): |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|, |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|. For convenience, the pentose phosphate pathway is commonly divided into its preliminary |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative portion"| and the subsequent |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative portion"|., The unidirectional oxidative branch fulfills two roles of the pathway - it produces a pentose sugar (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|) from the hexose |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, and it produces two equivalents of NADPH in the process., The non-oxidative branch of composed of a series of rearrangements catalyzed by an isomerase, an epimerase, a transketolase, and a transaldolase (see below), involving a C3 compound (|FRAME: GAP|), a C4 compound (|FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|), C5 compounds (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|), a C6 compound (|FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|), and a C7 compound (|FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|). Unlike the oxidative branch, the non-oxidative branch is fully reversible, allowing for different molecules to enter the pathway at different stages and be transformed to any other intermediate in this branch. No energy or reducing power is produced by the non-oxidative branch - it's sole purpose is carbon rearrangements. It should be noted that due to its reversibility, the non-oxidative branch also participates in the catabolism of pentoses (see |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|)., The genomes of most cellulolytic clostridia do not contain genes annotated as |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.2|. Yet, these organisms operate a pentose phosphate pathway for the assimilation of pentose sugars or for the generation of C5 precursors during growth on other (non-C5) substrates. In these organisms the role of the transaldolase has been taken by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.90| that acts on |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, forming |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-1-7-P2|, which is cleaved by fructose-bisphosphate aldolase into |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|. The enzymes from these organisms have been shown to have similar affinities for |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P| and the canonical substrate |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| |CITS: [31871051]|., This pathway variant is common among the cellulolytic clostridia. It is still unknown how widespread the pathway is outside this clade. However, the pathway was shown to operate in the eukaryotic amoebozoan |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [6180735]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: FeS-Centers "Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters"| are cofators of |FRAME: FeS-Proteins "iron-sulfur proteins"| and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein., Several cluster types have been described, including |FRAME: CPD-6|, |FRAME: CPD-23|, |FRAME: 3FE-4S| and |FRAME: CPD-7|. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as |FRAME: CPD0-1098|, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular |FRAME: CPD-6| are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons., Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxins|. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. , In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, Fe-S clusters are also known to participate in, the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes, and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression |CITS: [16466637]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of Fe-S clusters in a living cell is a highly evolved process, requiring the assistance of complex assemblies of proteins. At present, three different biogenesis systems have been identified. The ISC (iron-sulfur cluster) system, which is present in α-, β-, and γ-proteobacteria as well as in mitochondria of eukaryotes, the SUF (sulfur mobilization) system, which is found in a wide range of bacteria (including cyanobacteria), archaea, and plastids of plants, and the NIF (nitrogen fixation) system, which is used in the synthesis of nitrogenase, but also occurs in nondiazotrophic ε-proteobacteria., It should be noted that the mitochondrial ISC system comprises more proteins than in bacteria, but the underlying mechanistic principles are analogous. This pathway is modeled after the bacterial ISC system., All three systems have in common two key proteins - |FRAME: L-Cysteine-Desulfurases| (|FRAME: G7325 IscS|/|FRAME: HS01304|, |FRAME: G6906 SufS| or NifS) and |FRAME: Iron-Sulfur-Cluster-Scaffold-Proteins "a scaffold protein"| (|FRAME: G7324 IscU|, SufU or NifU)., Cysteine desulfurase is a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent enzyme that converts the amino-acid |FRAME: CYS| to |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, liberating a sulfur atom that is covalently bound as a persulfide at a conserved Cys residue of the enzyme., The scaffold protein, which also contains Cys residues, serves as a platform for the assembly of Fe-S clusters. The scaffold protein exists in equilibrium between two conformational states: a more structured state (S) and a partially disordered state (D) |CITS: [12909018][14688265][19492851]|. , The process begins when the cysteine desulfurase binds to the scaffold protein in its disordered state |CITS: [22203963]|. Sulfur atoms are transferred by the desulfurase from L-cysteine to the cysteine side chains of the scaffold protein, forming persulfides |CITS: [11577100]|., The process continues with the addition of two iron atoms, and the iron and sulfur atoms rearrange to form a [2Fe2S] cluster. The newly-formed cluster stabilizes the scaffold protein, transforming it to its structured state |CITS: [23333622]|. The process of iron addition is not well understood. The protein frataxin (|FRAME: EG11653 CyaY| in bacteria, |FRAME: G3O-29519| in yeast, FXN in humans) is essential for the process, and may act as a metallochaperone, but its weak iron binding activity and other observations suggest that its main role may be to maintain iron homeostasis under oxidative stress |CITS: [20956517][19932164][20522547]|. Another candidate for iron delivery is |FRAME: EG12132|, which has a strong binding activity for mononuclear iron, and has been shown to provide iron to the scaffold protein |FRAME: G7324 IscU| in the presence of |FRAME: G7325 IscS| and L-cysteine |CITS: [14720122][15828873][16877383]|., The next steps involve chaperone proteins. The first one, also known as a |FRAME: FeS-Cluster-Co-Chaperones co-chaperone| (|FRAME: EG12131 HscB| in |FRAME:TAX-562|) binds to the scaffold protein, causing the cysteine desulfurase to fall off. The co-chaperone-scaffold protein complex then binds to another |FRAME: FeS-Cluster-Chaperones chaperone| (|FRAME: EG12130 HscA|), which is an ATPase with a bound ATP molecule., At this point the complex is ready to transfer its [2Fe2S] cluster to a receipient. When a suitable acceptor protein approaches the complex one or two of its thiol groups attack the cluster iron atoms, liberating one or two of the scaffold protein cluster ligands and leading to a conformational change in the co-chaperone that activates the ATPase activity of the main chaperone. Cleavage of the bound ATP leads to an additional conformational change that results in a fundumental change |CITS: [11053447][15485839]|. A binding site on the ligand binding domain of the chaperone protein opens up and binds the scaffold protein in its disordered state. The conversion of the scaffold protein to its disordered state releases both the Fe-S cluster, which moves to the acceptor protein, and the co-chaperone. , The last step shown in the pathway is the exchange of the bound ADP for ATP, which restores the chaperone to its active state and releases the scaffold protein, both of which become ready to take part in the next cycle |CITS: [23333622]|., About [4Fe-4S] clusters biosynthesis, While less is known about the synthesis of [4Fe-4S] clusters, it seems that they are formed on the same scaffold proteins that are used for [2Fe-2S] clusters synthesis. These proteins are dimeric, and since a [2Fe-2S] cluster is formed within a single subunit, a dimeric scaffold protein can form two such clusters. Some evidence suggests that [4Fe-4S] clusters are formed at the subunit interface, involving two electron reductive coupling of the two adjacent [2Fe-2S] clusters |CITS: [19021507]|., The |FRAME: G7748 NfuA| protein has been proposed to be an intermediate [4Fe-4S] cluster carrier or chaperone for clusters assembled on |FRAME: G7324 IscU| |CITS: [18339629]| or act as a scaffold protein itself in some species |CITS: [15031412][15361144]|. The presence of |FRAME: EG12130| and |FRAME: EG12131| had no effect on the rate of [4Fe-4S] cluster transfer from |FRAME: G7324| to apo aconitase, suggesting different conformations for the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] cluster-bound forms of |FRAME: G7324 IscU|, with only the former having the ability to interact productively with |FRAME: EG12130 HscA| |CITS: [17506526]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Rhodoquinones Rhodoquinone| (RQ) is a modified ubiquinone, where the methoxyl group in position 3 is replaced by an amino group. The compound was originally isolated from |FRAME:TAX-1085| |CITS:[Glover62][14293762][14285535]|, where is it used for the reduction of fumarate to succinate under anaerobic conditions. The rhodoquinone/rhodoquinol standard redox potential is substantially lower than that of ubiquinone/ubiquinol/UQH2 (-63 vs. +110 mV). The lower redox potential drives the succinate dehydrogenase complex (complex II) in reverse to function as a fumarate reductase., Rhodoquinone is not limited to prokaryotes. It was soon discovered that some eukaryotic parasites such as the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-6253| and |FRAME: TAX-6252| |CITS: [5796154][811785]|, as well as parasitic helminths |CITS:[4795616]| also contain rhodoquinone, which is essential for fumarate reduction under anaerobic conditions |CITS:[2843227]|. Later it was shown that rhodoquinone is present in all eukaryotes that reduce fumarate during anoxia, including freshwater snails, mussels, lugworms, and oysters |CITS: [8537365]|. More recently, rhodoquinone has been detected in mitochondria purified from certain mouse and human tissues |CITS: [39909039]|., About This Pathway, In most parasitic helminths, there is a major shift in quinone composition as they move from aerobic to anaerobic environments. The first clue for the rhodoquinone biosynthetic pathway in animals came with the observation that |FRAME: TAX-6239| mutants that lack a functional |FRAME: PWY-5651 "kynureninase pathway"| are unable to synthesize RQ |CITS: [31232688][31177094]|. This observation led to the hypothesis that |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE|, which is formed by the kynurenine pathway, may be prenylated in a reaction catalyzed by COQ2. Once prenylated, the benzoquinone ring could be modified by methyltransferases and hydroxylases that are involved in UQ biosynthesis, forming RQ. such a pathway would be similar to UQ biosynthesis from |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE|, which has been described from yeast (see |FRAME: PWY-7230|)., The mechanism by which COQ2 switches from acting on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| (leading to UQ biosynthesis) to acting on |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| (leading to RQ biosynthesis) was clarified in 2020, when it was found to be alternative spicing of the gene. Helminths, and other animals that produce RQ, synthesize two coq-2 splice forms, coq-2a and coq-2e, and the coq-2e-specific exon is only found in species that synthesize RQ. These organisms switch from COQ-2a to COQ-2e when they transit into anaerobic environments |CITS: [32744503]|., No such splicing regulation was found for other enzymes that are required for both RQ and UQ synthesis downstream of COQ-2, suggesting that they are more promiscuous than COQ-2 and act on both RQ and UQ precursors |CITS: [32744503]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Cobamides that contains |FRAME: CPD-18320| were originally isolated from a culture of |FRAME: TAX-1744| grown with added 5-methylbenzimidazole |CITS: [Bernhauer54]|, and later observed in sewage sludge |CITS: [Friedrich58][Friedrich58a]|. A later study confirmed the ability of a pure culture of |FRAME: TAX-1744| to produce them |CITS: [3728985]|. Another study reported that this was the main type of cobamides formed by the sulfate-reducing bacteria |FRAME: TAX-2296| and |FRAME: TAX-894| and the archaea |FRAME: TAX-2234| and |FRAME: TAX-2303| |CITS: [3416881]|. In addition, 5-methylbenzimidazole-containing cobamides were reported to be the main cobamides of the methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2223| |CITS: [Kohler88]|., This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20846|. The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the lower ligand base is activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (CobT) by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide or a related compound to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphoribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) to form the cobamide. The enzymes that operate in this pathway are the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis. Studies of the specificity of these enzymes have suggested that the nature of the lower ligand is controlled by metabolic factors rather by the specificity of the enzymes involved |CITS: [11441022]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, Postweaning diarrhea and edema disease are two of the most prevalent porcine diseases worldwide. |FRAME: TAX-562| strains causing these diseases in pigs is limited to a few O serogroups, including O8, O45, O138, O139, O141, O147, O149, and O157. The enterotoxigenic |FRAME: ORG-57092| is a predominant cause of neonatal and post-weaning diarrhea in pig worldwide, causing major losses to the swine industry |CITS: [17449692][21864997][28119370]|., The structure of the O antigen produced by this strain was reported in 1988, and found to consist of a trisaccharide repeat unit that is linked by a β(1→3) linkage. The repeat unit contains a pyruvoyl group substituting positions 4 and 6 of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine |CITS: [3046745]|, an uncommon modification in E. coli O antigens (the only other known example is strain O112ac |CITS: [31778182]|). An identical O antigen is also produced by |FRAME: ORG-57093| |CITS: [16088333][18422615]|., The first sequence of the O:149 antigen biosynthetic cluster was deposited in GenBank in 2005 (accession number DQ091854). The O-antigen gene cluster of |FRAME: ORG-57093| was reported in the same year and found to have the same genes and organization |CITS: [16088333]|. A second O:149 sequence was deposited in 2007 (accession number DQ868764) |CITS: [17449692]|., The cluster contains nine genes, four of which encode enzymes involved in |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| biosynthesis, two encoding glycosyl transferases, one encoding pyruvoyltransferase, and two genes encoding an O antigen repeat unit flippase and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [16088333][19733452]|.

Summary: Malaria is the most widespread and severe tropical disease, causing more than one million deaths each year., In humans malaria is caused by four species of the |FRAME: TAX-5820 Plasmodium| genus, |FRAME: TAX-5833|, |FRAME: TAX-5855|, |FRAME: TAX-36330|, and |FRAME: TAX-5858|., |FRAME: TAX-5833| is the most lethal species and together with |FRAME: TAX-5855| accounts for more than 95% of all malaria cases., The malaria parasite spends much of its life cycle inside the erythrocyte. During that time the parasite degrades most of the host cell hemoglobin |CITS: [8257787]|. Hemoglobin degradation is essential to the survival of the parasite, as it possess a limited capacity for de novo synthesis of amino acids |CITS: [4987071]|., The amino acids derived from hemoglobin degradation are incorporated into parasite proteins or utilized for energy, metabolism. In addition, it has been suggested that removal of hemoglobin through degradation provides space in the red blood cell for the growing parasite and prevents premature erythrocyte lysis., Heme degradation is carried out in a specialized organelle, the food vacuole. The vacuole is acidic, with pH around 5.2. Several vacuole-located proteases are responsible for the process, which is carried out in a semi-ordered fashion |CITS: [8163662]|., The process starts with an attack on the native hemoglobin. Enzymes capable of such attack include the aspartic proteases |FRAME: MONOMER-15375| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15374|, which cleave the alpha chain of hemoglobin, breaking the structure and releasing the heme |CITS: [11782538][2007860]|. In addition, it has been suggested that the cysteine proteases |FRAME: MONOMER-15378| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15380| are also able to attack native hemoglobin., The next step in the degradation process is carried out by the aspartic protease |FRAME: MONOMER-15376|, a |FRAME: MONOMER-15377|, and three falcipain proteins - |FRAME: MONOMER-15378|, |FRAME: MONOMER-15379| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15380|, resulting in peptides thatare larger than 20 amino acids in length |CITS: [15070727][16337629][11716777]|. These in turn are degraded by |FRAME: MONOMER-15381|, a zinc metalloprotease that breaks these peptides to smaller ones, around 5-8 amino acid in length |CITS: [10542284]|. The final step within the food vacuole is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15382|, an enzyme that produces dipeptides |CITS: [15304495]|. These can be exported to the cytoplasm, where they are process into individual amino acids and incorporated into proteins., To date, resistance has emerged to all classes of antimalarial drugs, and new drugs are desparately needed |CITS: [19526594][19877309]|. Some of the proteases that are involved in this pathway are prime targets for new drugs |CITS: [19526594]|., The massive degradation of hemoglobin generates a large amount of heme, which is toxic to the parasite. The released heme is detoxified by the parasite by conversion to a cyclic dimer, |FRAME: CPD-11680|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7894| |CITS: [18437218]|. The dimers crystallize spontaneously generating |FRAME: CPD-11679| (also known as insoluble malaria pigment).

Summary: Background, The cellulose and hemicellulose components of lignocellulosic biomass can be converted into soluble sugars during yeast and bacterial fermentation |CITS: [19429550]|. However, the degradation of these complex carbohydrates requires chemical and enzymatic pre-treatments to open up the structure of lignocellulosic biomass, which can produce side products such as furans and phenolics which are detrimental to the microbial fermentation process |CITS: [19684179]|. |FRAME: CPD0-2357 "Furfural"| is a toxic byproduct of pentose sugar metabolism and is toxic to cells, causing DNA damage and inhibition of glycolysis, especially in yeast |CITS: [19684179]|. The detoxification of furfural would therefore benefit the industrial production of |FRAME: ETOH| from lignocellulosic biomass. Many microorganisms have evolved mechanisms to metabolize furfural to less toxic compounds and a furfural degradation pathway was first described in |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [4318274]|., About this Pathway, This pathway was elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-68895| based on presumptive gene functions of the hmfABCDE operon |CITS: [20194784]|. This gene cluster has corresponding enzyme activities with those of the |FRAME: TAX-303| furoic acid degradation pathway |CITS: [20194784]|., In hmfD mutants of |FRAME: TAX-68895|, grown in the presence of furfural, there was an accumulation of 2-furoic acid, and a lack of ATP dependent CoA ligation, indicating that this gene may code for the acyl-CoA synthetase which produces 2-furoyl-CoA from 2-furoic acid in |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [20194784]|. A Mo-dependent 2-furoyl-CoA dehydrogenase converts 2-furoyl-CoA to 5-hydroxy-2-furoyl-CoA in |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [20194784]||CITS: [4655411]|. The |FRAME: TAX-68895| hmfABC gene products are similar to the three subunits of the Mo-dependent dehydrogenases. Further experiments revealed that the hmfE gene codes for a protein that has 2-oxoglutaratoyl-CoA thioesterase activity, one of the last steps in the furfural degradation pathway. No enzyme has yet been specified for the lactone hydrolysis and this along with the keto-enol tautomerizations probably occur spontaneously |CITS: [20194784]|.

General Background, Most pathogenic bacteria have an absolute requirement for iron, which is scarce within their host environment. In vertebrates the majority of the iron is found in the form of heme. Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. In general, the bacteria express outer membrane proteins that bind heme compounds, extract heme from them, and transport the heme into the cell, where it is degraded to release the iron |CITS: [1425573][7783623][9157245]|. The most common heme-degradation systems utilize heme oxygenase enzymes that degrade heme to yield iron, carbon monoxide, and biliverdin., Several forms of bacterial heme oxygenases are known, and they are described in the various heme degradation pathways in MetaCyc. The enzymes consume three molecules of oxygen and a total of seven electron equivalents to break the tetrapyrrole ring and liberate the iron. However, while some enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), others produce different unusual isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| (|FRAME: PWY-7844|), |FRAME: CPD-18928| (|FRAME: PWY-7843|), |FRAME: CPD-19710| (|FRAME: PWY-7846|), |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| (|FRAME: PWY-7847|) and |FRAME: CPD-19716| and |FRAME: CPD-19715| (|FRAME: PWY-7848|)., About This Pathway, The bacterial pathogen |FRAME: TAX-83334| possesses at least two different enzymes that are involved in heme degradation. One enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44457| gene, is described in |FRAME: PWY-7843|, and, like all other previously described heme-degrading enzymes, requires molecular oxygen., The second enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-54977| gene, is |FRAME: Radical-AdoMet-Enzymes| that can catalyze heme degradation under anaerobic conditions. It uses radical chemistry to catalyze methyl transfer and rearrangement of the porphyrin ring of heme, resulting in the liberation of iron. The gene is similar to the |FRAME: EG11836| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-1.3.98.3|, a radical SAM enzyme that is iinvolved in the anaerobic biosynthesis of heme, The enzyme contains |FRAME: CPD-7|, and uses flavodoxin as its electron donor. The reaction requires two SAM molecules. The first is used to generate a |FRAME: CPD-15400|, which abstracts a hydrogen atom from the methyl group of the second SAM molecule. The newly formed methylene radical attacks the substrate, causing a rearrangement of the porphyrin ring that results in the liberation of iron |CITS: [27791000]|., The product of ChuW, |FRAME: CPD-19710|, is reduced by a |FRAME: CPLX-9193|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55033| gene |CITS: [28045510]|. The fate of the resulting anaerubin products is still not known.

Polyamines (such as spermidine) and thiols (such as glutathione) are found in millimolar concentrations in, most living organisms. Polyamines have a variety of roles, including charge neutralization and complexation, of the anionic phosphodiester backbone of DNA. Thiols also have many roles, including detoxification of, xenobiotics and reactive oxygen species, maintaining the redox balance in the cell, and serving as cofactors, for many enzymatic reactions (see |FRAME: PWY-4041|)., Several organisms are able to conjugate the two together, by forming an amide link between spermidine and, glutathione, resulting in either of the two forms N1-glutathionylspermidine, or, N8-glutathionylspermidine., This compound was first discovered in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [Dubin59]|, but was not characterized in regard, to its physiological role. Later it was shown that the compound is present in the pathogenetic protozoa, |FRAME:TAX-5690| and Leishmania |CITS: [3883489]|. In these parasites, a second glutathione molecule, is added to glutathionylspermidine, forming trypanothione, which in these organisms provides the functional roles, of glutathione (see |FRAME: TRYPANOSYN-PWY|)., The conjugation of glutathione and spermidine to glutathionylspermidine can be catalyzed by either of two enzymes., In |FRAME:TAX-562| the only enzyme that can catalyze the reaction is glutathionylspermidine synthetase., However, it has been shown that in Trypanosomes both glutathionylspermidine synthetase and trypanothione, synthetase can catalyze the reaction. The second enzyme also catalyzes the conversion of glutathionylspermidine, to trypanothione., Glutathionylspermidine can be recycled back to spermidine and glutathione by an amidase activity, (|FRAME: GSPAMID-RXN|) which both of these enzymes possess |CITS: [8999955]|., Another amide derivative of glutathione is |FRAME: CPD-6401| (see |FRAME: PWY-4181|).

Summary: General background, The source of the chromophore in the visual system is |FRAME: CPD-13524|, derived from the blood circulation (see |FRAME: PWY-6857| for its synthesis). The compound is taken up from the choroid blood vessels into the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, a monolayer of epithelial cells adjacent to the outer segments of photoreceptors. In the RPE |FRAME: CPD-13524| is converted in several steps to |FRAME: CPD-881|, which is then introduced into the photoreceptors, where it combines with |FRAME: Aporhodopsins opsin| to form the visual pigments., Following photoactivation of the pigment, the chromophore is released as |FRAME:RETINAL|, which is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-13524| and then removed from the bleached photoreceptors and transported back to the RPE, where it enters the cycle again. Since the supply of new |FRAME: CPD-13524| from blood vessels is rather slow, the cycle is driven primarily by the recycled photolytic |FRAME: CPD-13524| released from the bleached photoreceptors., This process is known as the visual cycle, and it provides |FRAME: CPD-881| for pigment regeneration in both rods and cones., About This Pathway, When |FRAME: CPD-13524| arrives in the blood, it is bound as |FRAME:RPB-Retinol| complex. Upon entering the RPE cells, retinol dissociates from the |FRAME: ENSG00000138207-MONOMER| (which remains outside the cells) and binds instead to the |FRAME: ENSG00000114115-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS03740|), which diffuses from the apical processes to the RPE cell body. Once there, it is esterified to |FRAME: All-trans-Retinyl-Esters "all-trans retinyl ester"| by the enzyme |FRAME: HS04474-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS04474|). The ester is then hydrolyzed and isomerized into |FRAME: CPD-882| in a single reaction catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000116745-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS04044|). , Bound to another protein called |FRAME: ENSG00000140522-MONOMER "cellular retinaldehyde binding protein"| (|FRAME: HS06733|), |FRAME: CPD-882| is oxidized into |FRAME: CPD-881| by |FRAME: CPLX-8338| (|FRAME: HS06003|). Still bound to RLBP, |FRAME: CPD-881| diffuses to the apical processes of RPE cells, which are close to the photoreceptors outer segments. At the apical processes |FRAME: CPD-881| exits the RPE to the extracellular interphotoreceptor matrix (IPM), possibly facilitated by RLBP and other proteins. Binding with another carrier protein, |FRAME: ENSG00000107618-MONOMER| (IRBP), |FRAME: CPD-881| is transferred back to the photoreceptor outer segment, where it recombines with |FRAME: Aporhodopsins "apo-opsin"| to regenerate the visual pigment., Photon absorption by |FRAME: CPD-881| converts it to the all-trans form, which is a strong agonist for opsin. The photoisomerization of the retinoid induces a series of rapid conformational changes of the pigment molecule that convert it to the physiologically active state (|FRAME: Metarhodopsins-II "Meta II"|) within ~1 milisecond. Meta II is the form of rhodopsin that activates the visual G-protein, transducin, triggering a second messenger cascade. Meta II decays to an inactive form, Meta III, and following the hydrolysis of the Schiff-base bond dissociates into free opsin and |FRAME: RETINAL|. This decay takes minutes in rods but only seconds in cones. The released |FRAME: RETINAL| is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-13524| by several NADPH-dependent retinol dehydrogenases, and |FRAME: CPD-13524| is transferred from the photoreceptors to the apical processes of the RPE cells in a process facilitated by the |FRAME: ENSG00000107618-MONOMER| (IRBP). In the RPE, |FRAME: CPD-13524| binds to the |FRAME: HS03740 "Cellular Retinol Binding Protein"| and re-enters the cycle.

Developing primary leaves of Secale cereale show a very distinct compartmentation and tissue specificity of flavonoids |CITS:[Strack82]|. Luteolin glucuronide such as |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONIDE| and |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| accumulate only in the photosynthetically active mesophyll of the primary leaves of this plant |CITS: [Schulz85]|. It appears that a connection exists between organogenesis, i.e. the primary leaf development and tissue specific distribution and metabolism of flavonoids |CITS:[Schulz86] [Schulz88a]|. Following the biosynthesis of luteolin triglucuronides (see |FRAME:PWY-7444|) the final product |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| of this pathway is transported to the extracellular space where it is subjected to degradation |CITS:[24177970]|. , The activity of the enzymes so far identified and involved in the biodegradation of |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2|, i.e. luteolin triglucuronide β-glucuronidase and various luteolin glucuronides specific peroxidases increase steadily during primary leaf development and peak at around day 7. That coincides with a drastic drop in the biosynthetic activities of the anabolic luteolin glucuronide glucuronosyltransferases |CITS:[Schulz88]|. , The first reaction of the pathway is catalyzed by a luteolin glucuronides specific β-glucuronidase which deglucuronidates |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONOSYL-1-2| to yield |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-DIGLUCURONIDE| |CITS:[Schulz87]|. The latter but not the former is substrate for three luteolin diglucuronide β-peroxidases (rPOXN1-N3) which specifically attack with varying efficiency luteolin glucuronide with free 3'(5')/4'-OH groups |CITS:[17266998]|. The resulting products of this reaction have not yet been characterized and remain to be identified. Although |FRAME:5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE| is also accepted by peroxidases |CITS:[11182292]| it seems unlikely to be a substrate in vivo as this flavone aglycon is found in the nonaqueous phase and not in the apoplastic space of the cell |CITS:[17266998]|. The luteolin glucuronide specific β-glucuronidase also catalyze the deglucuronidation of |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCURONIDE| to form |FRAME:5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE| |CITS:[Schulz87]| which is a activity also been observed in animals |CITS:[11216484]|. However, the rye luteolin glucuronide β-glucuronidase seems unable to cleave the bond between the two |FRAME:CPD-12521| of |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-DIGLUCURONIDE|, which constitutes a step in the pathway which remains to be elucidated |CITS:[Schulz87]|.

Summary: Molybdenum-containing nitrogenases (classified as either |FRAME: EC-1.18.6.1 "EC 1.18.6.1"| or |FRAME: EC-1.19.6.1 "EC 1.19.6.1"| based on their electron donors), present in a diverse group of bacteria and archaea, are the major contributing enzymes to biological nitrogen fixation. The active site of these enzymes contains an |FRAME: CPD-41 "iron-molybdenum cofactor"| (FeMo cofactor, M-cluster) that consists of 7Fe, 9S, 1Mo, one carbide(4-) atom, and a homocitrate decoration. The core of this cofactor can be viewed as a complex bridged metal assembly consisting of a [4Fe-3S] cluster linked to a [Mo-3Fe-3S] cluster by three sulfides and a central carbon., The cofactor is completely encopassed by the α subunit () of the nitrogenase component of the enzyme |CITS: [25989647]|., The biosynthesis of the FeMo cofactor is arguably one of the most complicated processes in bioinorganic chemistry., FeMo cofactor assembly begins with the formation of |FRAME: CPD-6 "[2Fe-2S]"| and |FRAME: CPD-7 "[4Fe-4S]"| clusters, which are synthesized by the combined actions of NifS, a cysteine desulfurase, and NifU, a scaffolding protein. NifS and NifU are homologs of |FRAME: G7325| and |FRAME: G7324|, respectively, which have analogous roles in general FeS cluster assembly (see |FRAME: PWY-7250|)., Two |FRAME: CPD-7 "[4Fe-4S] clusters"| are bound to the radical SAM enzyme |FRAME: NifB NifB|, forming a structure known as the K-cluster |CITS: [21551100]|. Following the transfer of these [4Fe-4S] clusters to NifB, radical SAM chemistry is used to create a FeMo cofactor precursor cluster that has six to eight iron atoms, nine sulfur atoms, and one central carbon, known as the |FRAME: CPD-18407|. NifB uses two molecules of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| - one generates a |FRAME: CPD-15400| that activates the substrate by abstracting a hydrogen atom from it, while the methyl group of the other one serves as the source for the carbide atom |CITS: [21551100][23019640][23019652]|. The 9th sulfur atom is derived from |FRAME: SO3| |CITS: [29662207][34635813]|., This carbon-containing |FRAME: CPD-18407| is transferred to the |FRAME: NifEN "NifEN scaffold protein"|, which is structurally similar to the MoFe protein component (NifDK) of the nitrogenase |CITS: [17050696][16423898][21212358]|. The |FRAME: CPD-18407| then undergoes a maturation process, during which molybedum and a homocitrate molecule are added. It appears that Mo and homocitrate are not incorporated stepwise into the NifEN-associated precursor, but are delivered simultaneously |CITS: [20221547]|. The maturation process requires the presence of |FRAME: G-44199 NifH|, the reductase component of the nitrogenase complex, as well as ATP. The direct source of molybdenum is the |FRAME: G-44193 NifQ| protein, which carries it in a dedicated iron-sulfur-molybdenum cofactor |CITS: [18697927][19514721]|. The homocitrate molecule is generated by |FRAME: G-44194 NifV| |CITS: [9294461][20221547]|., Once the maturation process is complete, the cofactor is transferred from NifEN to the |FRAME: CPLX-9019 NifDK| heterotetrameric complex component of |FRAME: CPLX-9021 nitrogenase|.

Summary: General Background, Stachyose and raffinose are two members of the so-called 'raffinose series' of sucrosyl oligosaccharides (also known as raffinose family oligosaccharides, RFOs). Sucrosyl oligosaccharides represent a large portion of primary oligosaccharides in plants (defined as oligosaccharides synthesized by the action of a glycosyl transferase that mediates the transfer of a glycopyranosyl residue to either the glucopyranosyl or fructofuranosyl moiety of sucrose). They are differentiated from secondary oligosaccharides which are generated by the hydrolysis of higher oligosaccharides, polysaccharides or heterosides. For review, see |CITS:[KANDLER82]|). Members of the raffinose series occur at least in traces in each plant family; it is one of the most widespread sucrosyl oligosaccharide series in flowering plants and might even be ubiquitous (see |CITS:[KANDLER82]| for review). This series comprises |FRAME:CPD-1099|, |FRAME:CPD-170|, |FRAME:CPD-8065|,|FRAME:CPD-8066| (see also |FRAME:PWY-5342|) as well as several other compounds with a higher degree of polymerization (DP; the highest is a nonasaccharide; none of these higher-DP oligosaccharides in the series have not yet been named). The sugars of this series consist of α1,6-linked chains of D-galactose attached to the 6-glucosyl position of sucrose. They are synthesized in leaves, roots and tubers. Raffinose is usually found in all parts of the plants including seeds, unless another sucrosyl oligosaccharide series prevails. Stachyose is often the main oligosaccharide in storage organs although variations occur between species. Functionally, these soluble carbohydrates are used for carbon transport and storage by the plant, although they have also been reported as possibly acting as protective agents during maturation of drying seeds |CITS:[HORBOWICZ94]| and during cold stress |CITS:[12223781],[11115899]|. Sugars of this series have long been considered as undesirable non-digestible factors that promote flatulence. Recently, however, it has been suggested that they might have beneficial effects on the gut microflora |CITS:[TORTUERO97]|. Moreover, they have been suggested for non-food applications (organ preservation) |CITS:[11308150]|., Enzymes of the pathway: The first step of the biosynthesis starts with the formation of the unusual galactosyl donor |FRAME:CPD-458|. The enzyme allowing the formation of this compound is galactinol synthase, which catalyzes the transfer of a galactosyl residue from UDP-galactose onto myo-inositol [UDP-galactose:myo-inositol (1-α-D) galactosyltransferase]. Several enzymes with this activity have been characterized and purified. The only known function of galactinol is in the biosynthesis of RFOs; it has therefore been postulated that galactinol synthase might be the committed and regulatory step for the synthesis of these compounds. The following step consists in the transfer of galactosyl units from galactinol to sucrose to form raffinose, the first RFO of the series. The enzyme catalyzing this reaction is known as raffinose synthase (galactinol:sucrose 6-galactosyltransferase). Stachyose is formed by the additional incorporation of a galactosyl unit to raffinose by a stachyose synthase (galactinol:raffinose 6-galactosyltransferase).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14125 Paromamine| is a common moiety of several |FRAME: Aminoglycoside-Antibiotics "aminoglycoside antibiotics"| including |FRAME: CPD-14177|, |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin|, |FRAME: Lividomycins lividomycin| and certain forms of |FRAME: Kanamycins kanamycin|., Paromomycin was originally described as a minor form of neomycin, and was named neomycin D |CITS: [5459627]|. It was later shown to be an intermediate in the neomycin biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [6698890]|., About This Pathway, The first part of the pathway is common (with a slight difference, see |FRAME: PWY-7022|) to several aminoglycoside antibiotics, and was described mostly from studies of |FRAME: CPD-14140 butirosin| and |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin| production. A unique aminocyclitol, |FRAME: CPD-10151|, is biosynthesized from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| in four steps by three crucial enzymes, |FRAME: MONOMER-17187|, |FRAME: MONOMER-17185| and |FRAME: MONOMER-17186| (the aminotransferase catalyzes two steps) |CITS: [16506694][19362652]|. , After the formation of |FRAME: CPD-10151| the pathway continues with glycosylation. The enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-17218| utilizes |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to form |FRAME: CPD-14126|. The acetate moiety is then removed by a dedicated deacetylase to form |FRAME: CPD-14125|.

|FRAME: CPD-18103 Carnosic acid| is a natural benzenediol abietane diterpene synthesized by some members of the |FRAME: TAX-4136| family. Due to its strong antioxidant |CITS: [14582962][22957812]|, anti-inflammatory |CITS: [18508031][22511203]| and anticancer |CITS: [23531917][23614740]| properties it is of high importance for the food and cosmetic industry, and may also have pharmaceutical applications. It is currently used as a preservative or antioxidant in food and nonfood products such as toothpaste, mouthwash and chewing gum., The biosynthesis of all phenolic diterpenes starts with two successive cyclization events |CITS: [19905026]|. The initial cyclization converts the common diterpene precursor |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (GGDP) to one of the various stereoisomers of copalyl diphosphate. This in turn is a substrate for a second diterpene synthase that forms a specific polycyclic compound. The formation of the parent skeleton is often followed by cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases that catalyze secondary transformations., Both |FRAME: TAX-268906| and |FRAME: TAX-39367| (rosmary) are known to be rich in |FRAME: CPD-18103|. The |FRAME: G-44071| and |FRAME: G-44072| genes of |FRAME: TAX-39367|, which encode |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.12| and |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.131|, respectively, were identified based on their similarity to genes from |FRAME: TAX-226208| |CITS: [24569175]|. It has been shown that |FRAME: CPD-14312| can be converted non-enzymatically to |FRAME: CPD-8721|, although it is possible that this transformation is catalyzed by an as-yet unknown enzyme in plantae |CITS: [24108414]|., The next step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.175|, a cytochrome P-450 monooxygenase that converts |FRAME: CPD-8721| to |FRAME: CPD-16534|. Several forms have been characterized, including CYP76AH1 from |FRAME: TAX-226208| |CITS: [23812755]| and CYP76AH4 from |FRAME: TAX-39367| |CITS: [24108414]|. Orthologous genes for all three enzymes have also been identified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-268906| |CITS: [26020634]|., The final steps, leading from |FRAME: CPD-16534| to |FRAME: CPD-18103|, are catalyzed by two additional cytochrome P-450 enzymes. Summary: Many bacterial and yeast species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: ACETOIN|., While the principal function of pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC) is to convert pyruvate into acetaldehyde, it is well documented that a small fraction of the pyruvate is converted to acetoin, as a by-product from the hydroxyethyl-thiamin diphosphate reaction intermediate., As a matter of fact, acetoin production is thought to be an adjunct of acetadehyde production by all enzymes capable of decarboxylating pyruvate |CITS: [Juni61]|. Acetoin production by pyruvate decarboxylase from wheat was first reported in 1952 by Singer and Pensky |CITS: [Singer52]| and verified in later work |CITS: [Crout86]|., It is also well documented that the enzyme can catalyze an aldol type condensation reaction between two molecules of acetaldehyde to form acetoin |CITS:[4754749][6383467][8257682][8536715]|. In this reaction the active acetaldehyde intermediate bound to the enzyme is condensed with a second acetaldehyde to form acetoin. This reaction is often called the carboligase activity |CITS: [11029594]|., Acetoin is often fermented further to 2,3-butanediol by the enzyme acetoin(diacetyl) reductase (see pathways under |FRAME:Butanediol-Biosynthesis|).

Summary: Human Milk Oligosaccharides (HMOs) are abundant carbohydrates fundamental to infant health and development. They account for 11-17% of the milk (dry weight) |CITS: [8441573][11236733]| and are known to improve infant immediate and long-term health and development |CITS: [26375354]|., HMOs impact the infants immune system, protect the infant from intestinal and immunological disorders |CITS: [25047751]|, shape the infants gut microbiome |CITS: [22513036][30247646]|, and may aid in proper brain development and cognition |CITS: [26375354]|., HMOs are unconjugated glycans consisting of 3-20 total monosaccharides composed of only 5 building blocks: D-galactose, D-glucose, N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, L-fucose, and N-acetyl-neuraminate. , More than a hundred different oligosaccharides have been characterized from human milk. Every woman produces a distinct profile of different HMOs at different concentrations that can change over the course of lactation |CITS: [26375354]|., About The Pathway, All of the HMOs contain a |FRAME: CPD-15972| core at their reducing end, which can be elongated by the addition of β1-3- or β1-6-linked |FRAME: BETA-D-GAL-1-3-D-GLCNAC| or |FRAME: BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSAMINE|. Elongation with |FRAME: BETA-D-GAL-1-3-D-GLCNAC| terminates the chain, whereas |FRAME: BETA-D-GALACTOSYL-ETCETERA-GLUCOSAMINE| can be further extended by the addition of one of the two disaccharides. Linear structures without branches are designated as para-HMO, while branched structures, resulting from β1-6 linkages, are designated as iso-HMOs. Lactose, as well as the elongated oligosaccharide chaina, can be fucosylated in α1-2, α1-3 or α1-4 linkage and/or sialylated in α2-3 or α2-6 linkages., Similar to the concept of blood groups, breast milk has been assigned into four groups based the activity of two genes: |FRAME: HS11104 (also known as Se)|, which encodes an α1-2-fucosyltransferase, and |FRAME: HS10249| (also known as Le), which encodes an α1-3/4-fucosyltransferase. The 4 groups were named , Le-positive Secretors (Se+Le+), Le-negative Secretors (Se+Le-), Le-positive non-Secretors (Se-Le+) and Le-negative non-Secretors (Se-Le-) |CITS: [2246720][1490103][9511984][11787693][20522272]|. It should be noted that the classification of individual milk samples into these four groups is an oversimplification, not taking into account contribution of other fucosyltransferases |CITS: [16011458]|., 16 HMOs usually make up more that 95% of the total HMOs in milk. The pathway shown here shows the biosynthesis of most of the major forms. The enzymes have been assigned in a study that integrated expression data for the HMOs and transcripts |CITS: [35508452]|.
