Summary: Background, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| is a linear polysaccharide found in all animal tissues. It occurs as a proteoglycan in which two or three heparan sulfate chains are attached to cell surface or extracellular matrix proteins, known as "core proteins". |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| binds to diverse protein ligands (known as heparin-binding proteins) and regulates a wide variety of biological activities, including developmental processes, cell adhesion and motility, angiogenesis, blood coagulation and tumour metastasis., The molecule is built of |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| chains attached to specific serine residues in a core protein. The chains are composed of a simple sugar backbone that is modified to different degrees depending on the cellular conditions. The backbone is built of several types of disaccharide building units with different sulfation patterns and can accomodate over 1,000,000 different sequences built up of up to 200 disaccharide units |CITS: [11102866]|., The disaccharide building units are composed of a hexose sugar and a uronic acid. The most common repeating unit, which makes up around 50% of the total disaccharide units in heparan sulfate, is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12541|. In other units |FRAME: CPD-12521| may be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12515| or its sulfated form |FRAME: CPD-12518|, and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| may be sulfated to |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: CPD-12533|, |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-3-N-disulfate| or |FRAME:Heparan-Glc-N-3-6-trisulfate|., |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| chains comprise three different types of domains: S-domains that contain contiguous N-sulfated residues, unmodified N-acetyl-rich regions, and mixed transition zones between the S-domains and the unmodified segments. Only the S-domains have binding capacities for growth factors and other proteins |CITS: [11489926]|. The structure of |FRAME: HEPARIN| is very similar, but its chains are not organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains |CITS: [15047699]|., The synthesis of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| takes place in the Golgi apparatus, with the exception of the first reaction, the attachemnt of xylose to the core protein, which takes place within the endoplasmic reticulum., About This Pathway, The synthesis of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| begins with the formation of a tetrasaccharide linkage region on the core protein, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|. Once the linkage region is synthesized, a key reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME: HS08719| and |FRAME: HS00333|, adds an |FRAME: CPD-12541| residue to the linkage region tetrasaccharide. This addition is a molecular switch that prevents the synthesis of |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| or |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| on the linkage region., The chain is then elongated by the |FRAME: CPLX-8112|, a bifunctional protein composed of |FRAME: HS00012| and |FRAME: HS07726| units, that can add both |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12541| in an alternating manner to the nascent chain. Once the basic backbone is synthesized, many enzymes alter the structure., A key enzyme is the bifunctional |FRAME: HS01001-MONOMER "heparan sulfate N-deacetylase/N-sulfotransferase"| (4 isoforms are encoded by |FRAME: HS01001|, |FRAME: HS09410|, |FRAME: HS09011| and |FRAME: HS06527|). The enzyme removes the acetyl groups from |FRAME: Heparan-NAc-Glc| residues in what would become S-regions, and sulfates the free NH2 groups, resulting in |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-D-GlcNS|., |FRAME: HS11947-MONOMER "Heparosan-N-sulfate-glucuronate 5-epimerase"| (|FRAME: HS11947|) converts |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues to |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues. |FRAME: ENSG00000153936-MONOMER "[Heparan sulfate]-uronosyl-2-O-sulfotransferase 1"| (|FRAME: HS07933|), which interacts with |FRAME: HS11947|, transfers a sulfate group to the C2 position of the |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues., Finally, a set of 3-O-sulfotransferases and 6-O-sulfotransferases act on the |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-D-GlcNS| residues, resulting in formation of the bi-sulfated forms |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-3-N-disulfate|, |FRAME: Heparan-GlcN-6-N-bisulfate| and the triple-sulfated |FRAME: Heparan-Glc-N-3-6-trisulfate| residues.

A group of structurally-related nitrophenyl pyrones has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-66431|, |FRAME: TAX-68270|, |FRAME: TAX-173858|, |FRAME: TAX-1911|, and |FRAME: TAX-1806334|. Five compounds have been characterized: |FRAME: CPD-13144| |CITS: [Hirata54a][Hirata61]|, |FRAME: CPD-21805| |CITS: [17551211]|, |FRAME: CPD-21806| (also known as neoaureothin) |CITS: [Kakinuma76][17763486]|, |FRAME: CPD-21803| (also known as griseulin) |CITS: [Koyama69][Nair93]|, and |FRAME: CPD-21800| (also known as deoxyaureothin) |CITS: [Ishibashi95]|., |FRAME: CPD-21806 Spectinabilin| is produced by |FRAME: TAX-68270| and |FRAME: TAX-67339|. It differs from |FRAME: CPD-13144| only in the length of its polyketide backbone, and has shown some activity against Rauscher Leukemia Virus (RLV) reverse transcriptase |CITS: [Kakinuma76]|., The gene cluster encoding the enzymes of spectinabilin biosynthesis was found in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-67339| using the |FRAME: TAX-66431| gene that encodes |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.38| as a probe |CITS: [17763486]|. In general, the cluster's genes are very similar to those involved in |FRAME: CPD-13144| biosynthesis., The compound's backbone is assembled by a type I polyketide synthase (PKS) that uses the unusual starter unit |FRAME: CPD-704|, which is produced from |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| (originally derived from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|) by a 6-electron oxidation reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.68| |CITS: [15038705][20798054]|., The PKS is encoded by four genes (|FRAME: G-58860|, |FRAME: G-58861|, |FRAME: G-58862|, and |FRAME: G-58863|) and comprises 6 modules that total 28 domains |CITS: [14700630]|. Following the addition of 6 |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| and one |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender units the backbone is released from the PKS in a reaction that forms a pyrone ring. The PKS is somewhat unusual since the first domain is used twice in an iterative fashion, so that the six PKS modules catalyze seven rounds of elongation and reduction |CITS: [17763486][20094652]|., The pathway is completed by two more reactions - the formation of a methoxy group by the methyltransferase |FRAME: G-58865 NorI|, and the formation of the five-membered heterocycle by the multifunctional cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: G-58866 NorH| |CITS: [17763486]|., A short-chain analogue named |FRAME: CPD-21838|, which is also found in |FRAME: TAX-67339|, is generated from |FRAME: CPD-21806| through "polyene splicing", a light-induced rearrangement cascade with loss of |FRAME: CPD-21839| |CITS: [Mueller06]|., Integration of the gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-68270| into the genome of |FRAME: TAX-1916| resulted in |FRAME: CPD-21806| production, confirming the proposed functions of the different genes |CITS: [20094652]|.

The metabolic profile of the wild tomato |FRAME:TAX-62890| reveals a number of polymethylated myricetins such as |FRAME:CPD-14943|, |FRAME:CPD-14944| and |FRAME:CPD-14945|. In contrast to the pathways |FRAME:PWY-7150| and |FRAME:PWY-7151| which accumulate polymethylated flavonol glucosides wild tomato species store polymethylated non-glucosylated flavonols instead. The polymethylated myricetins are stored in the two main types of trichomes, i.e. the 1/4 type secreting glands and the storage type gland 6 |CITS:[21343428]|. These gland types have been recently revisited and investigated in a comparative functional genomics approach. It has been found that the former secretory glands classified as type 1 and 4 represent in fact the same type but at different developmental stages. All tomato species who possess secretory glands have either type 1 or 4 or 1/4 which only are distinguished by their stalk length |CITS:[21098679]|. , Three different methyltransferases have been identified and characterized from |FRAME:TAX-62890| and |FRAME:TAX-4081| |CITS:[21343428]| |CITS:[22711283]|. The three myricetin ortho-methyltransferases (MOMT's) have been isolated, cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. In order to determine the function of the three enzymes in the depicted pathway their substrate specificity was ascertained in in vitro assays. The purified enzymes designated as MOMT1, MOMT2 and MOMT3 exhibited strong position-specificity. MOMT1 (|FRAME:TAX-62890|) specifically methylated either the 3'-position or, when already methylated, the 5'-position of |FRAME:MYRICETIN| and |FRAME:CPD-520| and partly methylated derivatives thereof but did not accept |FRAME:CPD1F-90| as substrate. MOMT2 (|FRAME:TAX-62890|) was designated as 7/4'-methyltransferase which accepted all three flavonols (|FRAME:MYRICETIN|, |FRAME:CPD-520|, |FRAME:CPD1F-90|) and their partially methylated derivatives |CITS:[21343428]|. MOMT3 (|FRAME:TAX-62890| and |FRAME:TAX-4081|) finally was assigned as 3-methyltransferase responsible for the catalysis of the first committed step in the pathway |CITS:[22711283]|. All three methyltransferases were only expressed in trichomes, with a higher expression in the secretory glands (type 1/4) than in the storage gland (type 6). , Deduced from the obtained catalytic data the methylation sequence of the pathway was projected to be 3-, 7- (A-ring) followed by 3'-, 5'- and finally 4'-methylation of the C-ring. However, more research is needed to confirm the proposed methylation sequence as several partially methylated myricetins were not available as substrates. In some of those cases |FRAME:CPD-520| and |FRAME:CPD1F-90| methyl derivatives (see |FRAME:PWY-7161| and |FRAME:PWY-7163|, respectively) were useful as substitutes to better estimate the likely substrate specificity for the MOMT's in the polymethylated myricetin biosynthesis (this pathway). The pathway shown here reflects the broad methylation capacity of the involved MOMT's projected onto the production of a number of not-accumulating potential precursors and probable interconnections rather than the exact methylation succession which remains to be verified. , The function of the polymethylated myricetins in tomato species remains to be resolved but it is likely that they play a similar role than other flavonoids in plants, i.e. UV-protection, chemical defense, pigmentation, part of signaling interactions, radical-scavenging and antioxidant activity |CITS:[16388461]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Fructans are a class of highly water-soluble polysaccharides consisting of linear or branched |FRAME:FRU| chains attached to |FRAME: SUCROSE| by β-2,1or β-2,6-linkage. They are used by plants or microorganisms as a form of carbon and energy storage, similarly to starch., There are 3 types of fructans:, 1. |FRAME: Inulin Inulin| - linear fructans generally linked by β(2->1) glycosidic bonds, 2. |FRAME: Levan Levan| - linear fructans generally linked by β(2->6) glycosidic bonds, 3. |FRAME: Graminans Graminan| - branched fructans linked by both β(2->1) and β(2->6) glycosidic bonds., This |FRAME: Inulin inulin| degradation pathway involves three enzymatic steps: in the first step the large fructan chain is attacked by |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.18|, an enzyme that cleaves difructose units from one end of the molecular chain. The difructose units that are liberated contain a new anhydride linkage, in the form of α-D-fructofuranose-β-D-fructofuranose 2',1:2,3'-dianhydride (|FRAME: DFA-III|) |CITS: [Uchiyama73][1148257][17192265][28824157]|., In the second step the difructose anhydride is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.178|, forming the disaccharide |FRAME: INULOBIOSE| |CITS: [1225919][NEUBAUER00][16233453][26555784]|. Finally, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.26|, hydrolyzes inulobiose to two molecules of |FRAME: Fructofuranose|., In |FRAME: TAX-85085| a single enzyme is able to catalyze the two first reactions of the pathway |CITS: [Shuhuai18]|., About |FRAME: DFA-III| (DFA III): Di-D-fructose dianhydrides (DFAs) are expected to be novel food additives or sweeteners because of their physiological functions |CITS: [10945246]|. DFA III, whose structure was first determined in 1940 |CITS: [McDonald40]|, has been extensively investigated due to its promising properties and functions. It has low degradability and Maillard reactivity |CITS: [Kikuchi04]|, and was shown to promote the absorption of minerals such as calcium and iron in rats. In humans it was reported to enhance absorption of calcium |CITS: [15170103][17341829]|. Industrial interest in production of DFA III as a low-calories sugar substitute has been increasing |CITS: [19269589][21874274]|.

Enzymes of pathway: CPLX-9129 // HS08982-MONOMER // HS03371-MONOMER // CPLX-9127 // CPLX-9128 // ENSG00000121579-MONOMER
Summary: General Background, Protein substrates of the |FRAME: Ubiquitins ubiquitin| (Ub) system, which controls the levels of many intracellular proteins, are conjugated to ubiquitin through the action of |FRAME: E3-independent-Ubiquitin-carrier-E2 "E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes"| or |FRAME: E3-ubiquitin-carrier-proteins "E3 ubiquitin transferases"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7511|). , |FRAME: E3-ubiquitin-carrier-proteins "E3 ubiquitin transferases"| recognize their substrates by specific degradation signals, known as degrons |CITS: [11017125][14744430][15688063][15950869]|. Once recognized, the protein substrate is ubiquitylated and degraded by the 26S proteasome |CITS: [9476896][15571806]|., One class of degrons, called N-degrons, is the substrate's N-terminal residue. Certain residues (named "destabilizing residues") are recognized by the ubiquitin system and mark the protein for degradation. The set of destabilizing residues in a given cell type yields a rule, called the N-end rule, which relates the in vivo half-life of a protein to the identity of its N-terminal residue |CITS: [3018930]|., The original (classical) N-end rule pathway (now called the |FRAME: PWY-7799 "Arg/N-end rule pathway"|) targets certain unmodified destabilizing N-terminal-residues for degradation by recognition with the UBR1/UBR2 E3 ubiquitin transferase. A different branch of the N-end rule pathway, which is called the Ac/N-end rule pathway, recognizes certain N-terminal amino acids that have been acetylated on their Nα atom. This degron, named the ACN-degron, is recognized by a different ubiquitin transferase, named |FRAME: HS14096| (mammals) or |FRAME: G3O-31303-MONOMER DOA10| (yeast) |CITS: [20110468]|., About This Pathway, Owing to the design of the genetic code, nascent eukaryotic proteins contain N-terminal |FRAME: MET|., |FRAME: EC-3.4.11.18|, cleaves off the N-terminal L-Met if the residue at position 2 has a small enough side chain, resulting in N-terminal |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: CYS|, |FRAME: GLY|, or |FRAME: PRO| |CITS: [16963780]|. Initiator L-Met removal occurs in approximately two-thirds of cellular proteins |CITS: [25450248]|., Retained N-terminal |FRAME: MET| that is followed by "acetylation-permissive" residues is usually acetylated at the Nα position |CITS: [12507466][19420222][19885390]|. Two main acetyltransferase complexes act on such Met residues: |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.254|, acts when the amino acid in the second position is |FRAME: GLT|, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: ASN| or |FRAME: GLN| |CITS: [18570629]|. A different complex, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.256|, acts when the amino acid in the second position is a bulky hydrophobic residue, such as |FRAME: LYS|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TRP| or |FRAME: TYR| |CITS: [12890471]|., Similarly, with the near-exception of Gly and Pro, the newly exposed N-terminal Ala, Val, Ser, Thr, and Cys that were produced by the action of methionyl aminopeptidase are also acetylated, by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.255|. N-terminal acetylation, which is irreversible, is extremely common, and occurs in 80-90% and 50-70% of cytosolic human and yeast proteins, respectively |CITS: [22814378]|., Even though N-terminal acetylation has been largely regarded as a metabolic stabilizer that protects proteins or peptides from destruction |CITS: [1207150]|, and can block the Nt-ubiquitylation-mediated degradation as well as the |FRAME: PWY-7799 "Arg/N-end rule pathway"|, it also creates a specific degron that is targeted by the Ac/N-end rule pathway. The N-acetylated Met, Ala, Val, Ser, Thr, and Cys act as ACN-degrons, and are targeted by the |FRAME: ENSG00000145495-MONOMER| |CITS: [20110468][21633985]|., The Ac/N-end rule pathway is involved a in variety of cellular functions, including protein quality and subunit stoichiometry control |CITS: [20110468][23603116][24698805]|, blood pressure regulation via G-protein signaling |CITS: [25766235]|, and immune responses to pathogens in plants |CITS: [25966763]|. The topic has been recently reviewed |CITS: [26883906]|.

Anandamide, a member of the endocannabinoid class of signaling lipids, is the amide of ethanolamine and , arachidonate. It is part of the endocannabinoid system, a neural signaling pathway consisting of endogenous , cannabinoids (endocannabinoids), cannabinoid receptors, and the enzymes that biosynthesize and degrade , endocannabinoids. Studies suggest that the function of the endocannabinoid system is related to pain modulation, , the immune system, neuroprotection, and addiction. Models have been proposed for endocannabinoid regulation , of endogenous reward mechanisms in the brain. , Anandamide is biosynthesized in the membrane from the phospholipid precursor , N-arachidonoylphosphatidylethanolamine. Calcium activated phospholipase D releases it into the synapse. , Anandamide is thought to interact with the G-protein coupled CB1 cannabinoid receptor in the central nervous , system. Activation of CB1 receptors by enodcannabinoids (or by exogenous cannabinoids) suppresses , neurotransmission. Its action at the CB1 receptor is terminated by a comnbination of transport (by an as yet , unidentified mechanism), followed by hydrolysis by fatty acid amino hydrolase (FAAH). , This enzyme has been studied as a potential therapeutic target and inhibitors of its activity have been developed. , FAAH knockout mice have been produced that show CB1-dependent behavioral responses |CITS: [11470906]|. , A single nucleotide polymorphism in the human gene encoding FAAH has been found to be strongly associated , with drug and alcohol abuse |CITS: [12060782]|. This polymorphism results in an enzyme with increased sensitivity , to proteolysis. The arachidonate product of the enzyme can be oxidized as shown by the pathway link, or it can be , converted to biologically active eicosanoids (prostaglandins, prostacyclins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and , lipoxins). Ethanolamine can be used in the biosynthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine, as shown by the pathway , link. In |CITS: [16314570] [12459591]| and reviewed , in |CITS: [16402900] [12843414] [15936806]|.

|FRAME: CPD-13052 Sangivamycin| is |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines| antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1927|., Sangivamycin has been initially isolated from an unidentified species of Streptomyces and was at that time referred, to as BA-90912 |CITS: [14275003]|. It possess cytotoxicity against cancer cells, but produces no toxicity in humans at maximally tolerated doses |CITS: [4318252][4823899][11295049][17371872][17956898]|. The compound was shown to be incorporated in RNA |CITS: [5651645][7059368]| and inhibit its synthesis |CITS: [7362643][7295353]|. It is also a potent inhibitor of protein kinases |CITS: [7290086][3338987][2921215]|., The structure has been reported in 1968 |CITS: [5634627][5748694]|. The X-ray crystal structure has been determined |CITS: [2365059]|. , |FRAME: CPD-13052 Sangivamycin| is generated from |FRAME: CPD-13056| in a single step, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8239|. The enzyme has been purified and found to contain three different types of subunits. The |FRAME: MONOMER-16221| subunit is homologous the the α subunit of known nitrile hydratases, while the |FRAME: MONOMER-16223| and |FRAME: MONOMER-16222| subunits are homologous to the N- and C-terminal halves of the β subunits of those enzymes. Sequence analysis of ToyJ suggests that it contains a non-corrinoid cobalt |CITS: [18721750]|.

Summary: |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL Ergosterol| is a major constituent of the fungal plasma membrane |CITS:[Paltauf][8561481]|., In other organisms the plasma membranes contain other types of sterols, such as |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| in mammals., |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| share most of their biosythesis pathway, up to, |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL|. From this intermediate different paths lead to synthesis of different sterols in different organisms., The pathway from |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL| to |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|, which is described here, is fungal-specific, although, not all fungi possess it. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4754| plasma membranes lack ergosterol |CITS:[12531182]|., The pathway has been best studied in |FRAME: TAX-4932|, in which most steps are not essential for viability, |CITS:[8277826][9294256]|., The pathway consists of five enzymatic steps, catalyzed by enzymes encoded by the |FRAME:YML008C|,, |FRAME:YMR202W|, |FRAME: YLR056W|, |FRAME: YMR015C| and |FRAME: YGL012W|, not necessarily in this order., To learn about the full pathway for the biosynthesis of ergosterol, see |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL-SYN-PWY|.

Summary: |FRAME: Cyanophycin Cyanophycin| is an amino acid polymer that is found in most cyanobacteria. It is a high-molecular weight copolymer, composed of an |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| backbone and |FRAME: ARG| side groups, with typical size of 25-100 kDa. The arginine moieties are linked to the β-carboxyl group of each aspartate by their α-amino group., |FRAME: Cyanophycin Cyanophycin| serves as a temporary nitrogen reserve and accumulates during the transition from the exponential- to the stationary-growth phase and disappears when balanced growth resumes. It is largely insoluble under physiological conditions and is accumulated in the form of granules in the cytoplasm during phosphate or sulfur starvation, generally in the early and mid-stationary phase |CITS: [16591901]|. Even though cyanophycin is considered largely exclusive for cyanobacteria, it is also found in a few heterotrophic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-62977| |CITS: [11976746][15289556]|., When the bacteria need the nitrogen stored in |FRAME: Cyanophycin|, the dipeptidase |FRAME: EC-3.4.15.6| (CphB) catalyzes the specific hydrolysis of the polymer to produce |FRAME: CPD-14415| dipeptides |CITS: [10429200]|, which are hydrolyzed further by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.5|, producing |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: ARG| |CITS: [24550502]|. , Some cyanobacteria grow as chains of cells (filaments) that, under nitrogen deprivation, contain two cell types: vegetative cells that fix CO2 through oxygenic photosynthesis and heterocysts that fix N2. The heterocysts are surrounded by a thick wall that protects the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase from the oxygen produced during photosynthesis. The heterocysts provide the vegetative cells with fixed nitrogen, and the vegetative cells provide the heterocysts with reduced carbon, mainly in the form of sucrose, through intercellular molecular transfer |CITS: [25784700]|. The fixed nitrogen is stored in the heterocysts in the form of |FRAME: Cyanophycin|. When the bacteria require nitrogen, cyanophycin is cleaved to dipeptides within the heterocysts, and the dipeptides are transferred to the adjacent vegetative cells, where they are cleaved into individual amino acids |CITS: [30636068]|., Cyanophycin is synthesized from arginine and aspartate in an ATP-dependent reaction catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-8481| (CphA). The enzyme contains two catalytic domains - one for the addition of aspartate, and the other for the addition of arginine (the two reactions are assigned two different EC numbers) |CITS: [15952894][17390395]|. , Several cyanobacterial cyanophycin synthases have been purified and characterized, including those from |FRAME: TAX-113355| |CITS: [11319097]|, |FRAME: TAX-240292| (ATCC29413) |CITS: [9652408]|, |FRAME: TAX-83377| |CITS: [11772614]| and |FRAME: TAX-197221| |CITS: [9652408]|., It was thought that most cyanophycin synthases require a primer (low-molecular mass cyanophycin). In the case of |FRAME: TAX-240292|, (β-Asp-Arg)3 could be used as a primer in vitro |CITS: [10951215]|. However, the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-197221| did not require any primer |CITS: [9652408]|. It is still unknown how the primer is synthesized in organisms that require it.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-19635 Valproate| (valproic acid; VPA) is widely used as a major drug in the treatment of epilepsy and in the control of several types of seizures. The compound was first synthesized in 1882 |CITS: [Burton82]| but its anticonvulsant activity was discovered serendipitously, in an assay in which it was used as a control |CITS: [Meunier63]|., The mechanism of the antiepileptic action of VPA is complex and not well-defined |CITS: [12269861]|. It involves regional changes in the concentration of the neurotransmitter |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) in the brain |CITS: [1975331][12269862][14624230]|, and VPA may have a direct effect on the potassium channels of the neuronal membrane., Upon ingestion, VPA is absorbed quickly, with the majority of the molecules (>90%) bound to plasma proteins, mainly albumin. As with any xenobiotic, only the free fraction of VPA will cross membranes and enter the cell. The therapeutic concentration of VPA in plasma for most patients ranges from 40 to 100 μg/ml, which results in brain concentration of 6-27 μg/g., The compound is known to have hepatic side effects that can be severe. They may arise from interference of |FRAME: CPD-19635| metabolites with the mitochondrial β-oxidation pathway |CITS: [12475192 ]|. Another hypothesis is that |FRAME: CPD-23630| inhibits the hepatic carnitine palmitoyl-transferase I (CPT IA) enzyme |CITS: [19854160]|., About This Pathway, Valproate is almost entirely metabolized by the liver, and less than 3% of it is excreted unchanged into the urine. Multiple metabolic pathways are involved in VPA biotransformation, giving rise to more than 50 known metabolites |CITS: [Abbott99]|. VPA is a 2-branched fatty acid, and as such one of its main degradation routes is the fatty acid β-oxidation pathway, which takes place primarily in mitochondria. It has been estimated that about 40% of VPA are degraded using this route |CITS: [18392741]|., Indication for the presence of this pathway were provided by detection of its intermediates in many studies |CITS: [788806][Kuhara78][104869][6798485][6795343][6801254][6325140][3122428]|. Direct proof of VPA β-oxidation was obtained through in vitro studies using isolated rat liver mitochondria |CITS: [1680661][1988037]|. Some stereochemical aspects of the reactions were elucidated using 13C-labeled analogues of VPA |CITS: [Shirley93]|., Following entry into the mitochondria, the first step of the pathway is the activation of VPA to its CoA thioester |CITS: [ 6407400]|. Even though it has not been proven, the major candidate for this reaction is the medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetase (EC 6.2.1.2). The activated compound then goes through the regular cycles of β-oxidation, with each cycle involving four consecutive reactions catalyzed by separate enzymes., The first reaction is the conversion of valproyl-CoA to |FRAME: CPD-23631|, which has been shown to be mediated by |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.5|, using the enzyme purified from rat liver mitochondria |CITS: [ 2112956]|. The second step is catalyzed by the mitochondrial enoyl-CoA hydratase (|FRAME: HS05132|), which has been shown to act on branched substrates. The third step could be demonstrated using solubilized rat liver mitochondria (RLM) or a mitochondrial membrane fraction in the presence of NAD. However, the identity of the enzyme is still not known |CITS: [18392741]|. , The final reaction of the β-oxidation cycle of straight-chain fatty acids consists of the thiolytic cleavage of 3-oxoacyl-CoA derivatives, releasing |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. In the case of this pathway, the cleavage releases |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|. At the end of the first cycle, the product is |FRAME: PENTANOYLCOA-CPD|, which can go through a second β-oxidation cycle, producing a second molecule of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [11879205]|. However, the identity of the thiolase is also unknown.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13969| is a 3-methylated, 2,6-dideoxysugar that is attached to the aglycones of several marolide antibiotics, including |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycin|, which is produced by |FRAME: TAX-1836| (see |FRAME: PWY-6975|), |FRAME: CPD-12966|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-47868|, and |FRAME: TYLOSIN|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-1906|., Several mutants affected in the biosynthesis of l-mycarose were isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1836| and the phenotype was named EryB. Seven eryB genes have been subsequently cloned and sequenced. While all of these genes are located within the erythromycin gene cluster, they are not clustered, but are dispersed in two sets, at both sides of the very large erythromycin polyketide synthase genes., The first two steps in the biosynthesis of all deoxysugars (included in this pathway) are the activation of |FRAME: GLC-1-P| into |FRAME: DTDP-D-GLUCOSE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-17088| (EC 2.7.7.24), followed by dehydration at C-4 and C-6 by a |FRAME:CPLX-8417| (EC 4.2.1.46). These two genes are not specific for L-mycarose, and are not located within the erythromycin gene cluster |CITS: [10399362]|., Six enzymes specific for L-mycarose biosynthesis have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-1836|, five of which participate in this pathway (the sixth one attaches the deoxysugar to the macrolide aglycone). While the general roles of the enzymes were proposed based on their sequences, the exact order of action has not been clear. Some authors suggested that the epimerase EryBVII acts early in the pathway, on |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| |CITS: [9613575][15609849]|, while others proposed that it acts later, following 2-deoxygenation |CITS: [9353926]|. The exact sequence of reactions was determined much later, by heterologous expression of the genes from the |FRAME: CPD-12966| producer |FRAME: TAX-47868| in |FRAME:TAX-562| and mass spectrometric analysis of the dTDP-sugar intermediates produced from operons containing different sets of the genes |CITS: [1092798][15870344]|. The pathway was also studied in the |FRAME: TYLOSIN| producer |FRAME: TAX-1906| |CITS:[Chen99a][11180386][15984840]|.

General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms. In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central intermediate., It has been suggested that the formaldehyde concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph would rise to 100mM in less than 1 minute if formaldehyde consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by unrelated or distantly related genes., About This Pathway, Different variations of this pathway are known - one utilizes the cofactor |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| (H4F), while the other uses the "archaea-like" cofactor |FRAME: THMPT| (H4MPT)., The reaction of formaldehyde with |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| is spontaneous |CITS: [5954363][14645276]|, but the condensation of formaldehyde with |FRAME: THMPT| is catalyzed by an enzyme (|FRAME: EC-4.2.1.147|)., It has been shown that in some well-studied methylotrophs such as |FRAME: TAX-272630| the different variants of the pathway run in opposite directions and serve very different physiological roles. The |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|-based pathway is a major biosynthetic pathway (|FRAME: PWY-1722|), while the |FRAME: THMPT|-based pathway is used mostly for the generation of reducing power (|FRAME: PWY-1723|)., However, a |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|-based formaldehyde oxidation pathway has been reported in the facultative methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-1471| |CITS: [26303953]|. During methylotrophic growth the organism produces large amounts of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| that must be processed. The presence of a linear formaldehyde oxidation pathway that includes formaldehyde dehydrogenase and formate dehydrogenase in |FRAME: TAX-1471| has been reported already in 2002, although the nature of the cofactor involved was not known at the time |CITS: [12368456]|. Surprisingly, bioinformatic analysis of the genome suggested that the pathway uses the |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| cofactor |CITS: [22610424]|. Experiments using 13C labeled formaldehyde have confirmed that exposure to fomaldehyde results in the appearance of |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "formyltetrahydrofolate|. THF usually carries several glutamate residues, with the exact numbers depending on the species. In the case of |FRAME: TAX-1471|, only |FRAME: CPD-1301| and |FRAME: CPD-12995| versions of |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| are used in formaldehyde oxidation |CITS: [26303953]|., Including this pathway, four different formaldehyde-metabolizing pathways operate in |FRAME: TAX-1471|: one assimilatory pathway (|FRAME: PWY-1861|) and three dissimilatory pathways - |FRAME: RUMP-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-7909|, and |FRAME: PWY-7908| |CITS: [26303953]|.

Names: dihydroconiferyl alcohol biosynthesis // dihydroconiferyl aldehyde biosynthesis
Summary: Lignins are a complex phenolic polymers involved in providing mechanical strength to cell wall, defense, and water transport in terrestrial vascular plants. They are mainly derived from three hydroxycinnamyl alcohol precursors namely p-coumaryl, coniferyl and sinapyl alcohols. In addition, presence of low levels of cinnamaldehydes and benzaldehydes has been reported in isolated lignins.  Although dihydroconiferyl alcohol and its glucosides have been reported in the plant tissues, their participation in the normal lignin biosynthetic pathway has not been demonstrated yet. However, effective incorporation of dihydroconiferyl alcohol monomers into lignin has been  reported in a loblolly pine mutant defective for cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase activity, which converts coniferaldehyde to coniferyl alcohol, the primary lignin precursor in pines.|CITS: [9211851]|.

|FRAME: GFP "Green fluorescent proteins"| (GFPs) are proteins that exhibit bright green fluorescence when exposed to light in the blue to ultraviolet range. GFPs form a part of the bioluminesence systems of many marine organisms, and the first such protein, from the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100|, was described already in 1962 |CITS: [13911999]|., Some other species, including non-bioluminesent species, encode homologs of GFP. It is now recognized that the family of GFP-like proteins includes |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent proteins"| (GFP), |FRAME: PWY-8514 "red fluorescent proteins"| (RFP), |FRAME: YFP-Chromophore "yellow fluorescent proteins"| (YFP), |FRAME: CFP-Chromophore "cyan fluorescent proteins"| (CFP) and |FRAME: BCP-Chromophore "purple-blue non-fluorescent chromoproteins"| (CP) |CITS: [18648549]|., All of these proteins share the same β-can fold first observed in GFP, but most are not associated with bioluminescence. While the chromophores of the first-described GFPs are formed autocatalitically from the three amino acids Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly, later identified proteins have significant variability in the first position, containing Gln, Lys, or Asn |CITS: [10504696]|., The non-fluorescent or low-fluorescence chromoproteins of the anthozoan chromoprotein family have vivid visible pigmentation due to their high molar extinction coefficients in the visible spectrum. Blue chromoproteins result in the striking blue color of some anemones and corals., The anthozoan chromoproteins were first isolated in 1995 |CITS: [29244570]| and were found to have a similar structure to the fluorescent proteins of the GFP family. Like GFP, chromoprotein monomers have a β-barrel structure that contains a chromophore, which is constructed autocatalytically from an Xaa-Tyr-Gly motif encoded within the protein. Also similar to the GFP proteins, they form dimers or tetramers. Following folding of the protein, the three chromophore-forming residues cyclize to form an imidazolinone ring system that is then oxidized by molecular oxygen in a rate-limiting process that is essential for full chromophore maturation and color development |CITS: [35503208]|., The chromophore of the blue chromoprotein is very similar to that of the |FRAME: RFP-Chromophore "red fluorescent protein DsRed"|. The main difference is that the blue chromoprotein chromophore adopts a trans noncoplanar conformation of the Cα2-Cβ2 bond, while the bond in fluorescent proteins is in a cis conformation |CITS: [11682051][16135569][17028187][24888769][26218063][30836182]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis, (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|),, and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is, highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for, a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes, that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase, enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal, dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, In this pathway, which has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-4932|, methylglyoxal is reduced to the, L form of lactaldehyde by the enzyme methylglyoxal reductase., |FRAME: LACTALD| is then reduced to |FRAME:L-LACTATE| which is finally converted to, |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and joins the pool of central metobolites |CITS: [2663129]|., Methylglyoxal reductases have been characterized in bacteria |CITS: [SaikusaAgBioChem51-1893]|, and fungi |CITS:[3896793][3276516]|. Some of the enzymes are NADP-linked, while others, are NAD-linked., Two variants of this pathway have been entered in MetaCyc to reflect the different biochemistry, of the last enzyme, L-lactate dehydrogenase. The |FRAME: TAX-83333| enzyme encoded by gene |FRAME: EG11963| uses an unidentified electron acceptor (see |FRAME:PWY-5459|), while the |FRAME: TAX-4932| enzyme uses an |FRAME: Cytochromes-C-Oxidized| (see |FRAME:PWY-5458|)., |FRAME:MGLDLCTANA-PWY| is a similar pathway based on methylglyoxal reductases that are specific, for the D form of lactaldehyde.

Enzymes of pathway: G3O-30552-MONOMER // CPX-1672 // CPX-1839 // YBR015C-MONOMER // YJL186W-MONOMER // YER001W-MONOMER // G3O-31694-MONOMER // CPLX-9678
Summary: General Background, N-linked glycosylation is an important process found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria., During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to an asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein. It has been shown that the glycosylation is essential for the proper folding of some eukaryotic proteins., N-linked glycosylation in eukaryotes consists of three stages:, (i): the initial synthesis of |FRAME: DOLICHOLP "dolichol phosphate"|-linked precursor tetradecasaccharides [(glucosyl)3(mannosyl)9-(N-acetylglucosaminyl)2] and their transfer from the dolichol phosphate anchor to newly synthesized polypeptides, where they are attached to the asparagine residues in Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. This process occurs on the luminal face of the ER (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., (ii): the trimming of these high-mannose structures by α-glucosidases and α-mannosidases, which occurs in the ER and Golgi complex (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7918|)., (iii): the synthesis of branched oligosaccharide chains, carried out by Golgi glycosyltransferases (several pathways exist, including this one)., The structure of the tetradecasaccharide precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor, although other protists are konwn to differ in the composition of the precursor |CITS: [6088086][DELACANAL][15665075]|. The pathway for the biosynthesis of the precursor is highly conserved, even though later processing and elongation steps differ among different organisms., About This Pathway, Following the removal of the three glucosyl residues and several mannosyl residues from the |FRAME: CPD-18077 tetradecasaccharide|, the N-glycosylated proteins in the yeast ER are in the form of |FRAME: Man8GlcNAc2-protein-A123B13| |CITS: [12090241]|., Upon transfer of the proteins from the ER to the cis-Golgi, the core N-linked glycans receive an α-1,6-linked mannose by the transferase |FRAME: G3O-30552| |CITS: [1628616][8253757]|. The next phase of processing splits into two different pathways. In one pathway, which applies to proteins targeted for retention in cellular organelles, the newly added α-1,6 mannosyl residue is extended by only two additional mannosyl residues (see |FRAME: PWY-8322|). In the second pathway, which applies to proteins destined to the cell wall and some periplasmic proteins (this pathway), the newly added α-1,6 mannosyl residue is extended by the |FRAME: CPX-1672| complex by at least 10 α-1,6-linked mannose residues, forming an initial mannan backbone |CITS: [9430634]|. This backbone is extended further with α-1,6-linked mannose residues by the |FRAME: CPX-1839| complex, which adds up to 50 additional residues |CITS: [9430634][10037752][10635561]|. Additional mannosyltransferases (|FRAME: YBR015C|, |FRAME: YJL186W| and |FRAME: YER001W|) add branches consisting of two α-1,2- and a terminal α-1,3-linked mannosyl residues |CITS: [9756928][9878809]|. One additional modification is the addition of phosphomannose to some of the middle mannosyl residues in the side-chains, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G3O-31961| and |FRAME: YPL053C| proteins, and possibly by |FRAME: G3O-31694| |CITS: [9218445][9878815][28101612]|, resulting in the final |FRAME: Branched-alpha-1-6-mannans "mannan polymer"|., The proteins modified by this pathway, which are known as mannoproteins, carry up to 200 mannose residues on each of their N-linked glycans |CITS: [8472892]|. Following the completion of mannosylation, the mannoproteins leave the trans-Golgi in vesicles that fuse with the membrane, releasing their content to the extracellular space. Outside the cell the mannoproteins either associate with or are transglycosylated into β-glucan to form the outer layer of the fungal cell wall |CITS: [9211929]|. The mannan polymer component of the outermost layer of the fungal cell wall can make up to 40% of the cell dry weight |CITS: [6991499][8253757][17397128]|. It is thought to shield the cell from digestive enzymes and neutralizing antibodies, to contribute to cell wall integrity, and to serve as ligand for cell-cell associations such as flocculation and host cell attachment during invasive growth. It also determines the wall's porosity and thereby regulates leakage of proteins from the periplasmic space and entrance of macromolecules from the environment.

General Background, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is a reducing acidic sugar that often forms a hexapyranose ring structure. It is common in carbohydrate chains of proteoglycans and is part of mucous animal secretions (such as saliva), cell glycocalyx and intercellular matrix. The hexapyranosic form |FRAME: CPD-12521| is found in the glycosaminoglycans |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates|, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: Hyaluronan|., In animals D-glucuronate is degraded as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5525|. Bacteria degrade |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by three different pathways: the isomerase pathway, which is found in enterobacteria (see |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY|), an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-17141| (this pathway), and an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8390|)., About This Pathway, Both oxidative pathways begin with the oxidation of |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by the inducible |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.203| to |FRAME: CPD-12595| |CITS: [19060141][19921179]|. The lactone was initially thought to hydrolyze only by a spontaneous reaction |CITS: [2471][19897761]|. Later |FRAME: EC-5.4.1.4| was found, an enzyme that converts |FRAME: CPD-17138| to the 1,4-lactone, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6486|. Though that enzyme was not tested for its activity with |FRAME: CPD-12595|, enzymatic conversion of that compound is likely. , A 2012 study of the degradation pathway in |FRAME: TAX-176299| described a dedicated enzyme that is responsible for isomerization of |FRAME: CPD-17141| to a linear form |CITS: [22493433]|., With the help of two additional enzymes, a dehydratase and a dehydrogenase, the pathway proceeds to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, which can be metabolized in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, or used in many other pathways.

|FRAME: CPD-27195 "Sclerate"| (Scleric acid) is a novel microbial natural product whose biosynthesis is encoded by |FRAME: TAX-1957|. However, the genes that are involved in its biosynthesis are silenced under normal growth by a cassette of five regulatory genes (a similar cassette has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-100226|, where it controls the biosynthesis of methylenomycin |CITS: [18988741]|). , The gene cluster includes two adjacent and divergent operons. When expressed in heterologous hosts (|FRAME: TAX-457425| and |FRAME: TAX-1902| M1152) no new metabolites were produced. However, when one of the regulatory genes, sclM4, was inactivated, the heterologous hosts accumulated a major metabolite that was identified as |FRAME: CPD-27195| |CITS: [30746093]|., |FRAME: CPD-27195 "Sclerate"| showed moderate antibacterial activity against |FRAME: TAX-1773| and inhibitory activity on the cancer-associated metabolic enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.1| (NNMT) |CITS: [30746093]|., |FRAME: CPD-27195 "Sclerate"| comprises of a central glycolate moiety to which a benzoate is attached on one side and |FRAME: PRO| is attached on the other. Since the products of the sclQ1-4 genes show high homology to the QncN, QncL and QncM proteins from |FRAME: TAX-1957|, which have been shown to direct the biosynthesis and attachment of a glycolate unit to a non-ribosomal peptide synthase |CITS: [22586110]|, it was proposed that SclQ1-4 provide a similar function. SclQ1 is an acyl-carrier protein; SclQ2 is homologous to the thiamine diphosphate binding domain of transketolase enzymes; SclQ3 is similar to other domains of transketolases; and SclQ4 has a lipoyl attachment domain and an acyltransferase catalytic domain. Based on the similarity to QncN, QncL and QncM it has been proposed that SclQ2, SclQ3 and SclQ4 catalyze a transketolase-like reaction, splitting a ketose phosphate from the primary metabolism (such as |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|) and forming a glycolate molecule, which is transferred first to the thiamine diphosphate cofactor of SclQ2, then to the lipoyl cofactor of SclQ4, and eventually to the acyl-carrier protein SclQ1 |CITS: [30746093]|. This type of system has been termed transketolase/acyl-carrier protein system, or Kase-ACP system |CITS: [22586110]|., SclN is a non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NPRS) that contains three domains - a condensation (C) domain, an activation (A) domain, and a peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domain. It is proposed that the enzyme activates and binds |FRAME: PRO|, then condenses it with the glycolate moiety transferred from SclQ1. The product is removed from the NRPS by a thioesterase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124663| gene. While it is not known how |FRAME: BENZOATE| is produced, it is assumed that it is activated by adeylation and ligated to |FRAME: CPD-27197| by the SclG ligase |CITS: [30746093]|.

Names: NAD salvage pathway IV (from nicotinamide riboside) // nicotinamide riboside salvage pathway // nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide salvage
Enzymes of pathway: CPLX-7559 // YGR010W-MONOMER // CPLX66-380 // HS08173-MONOMER // CPLX66-381 // MONOMER-8322 // MONOMER3O-4139 // CPLX0-7975
Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine, dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell., Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions., Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these, compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where, NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the, reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one, proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in, the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional, regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects, longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent, deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems;, the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway., In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from aspartate, (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with, tryptophan (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, In this salvage pathway |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE| is converted to |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE| and subsequently to |FRAME: NAD|, in reactions catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.22|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.1| |CITS: [15137942]|., While the presence of this pathway has been suggested to occur in several bacteral species, including |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-272131|, |FRAME:TAX-1358|, |FRAME:TAX-727|, |FRAME: TAX-730|, |FRAME: TAX-714|, and |FRAME:TAX-747| |CITS: [12446641]|, it is of particular importance to |FRAME:TAX-727| and other so-called "V-factor-dependent" members of the |FRAME:TAX-745| family. These organisms lack the enzymes necessary for the de novo synthesis of NAD, as well as most of the enzymes for the more common NAD salvage pathway, and therefore require exogenous NAD supply in the form of one of the V-factor compounds (which include NADP, NAD, NMN, and NR). However, only the non-phosphorylated V factor, NR, can be transported across the inner membrane into the cytoplasm, where it can be converted back to NAD and NADP |CITS: [12446641]|. Thus this pathway is critical for these organisms |CITS: [1694467]|. For additional information about V-factor-dependent bacteria, look at the pathway |FRAME: NAD-BIOSYNTHESIS-III|., The enzymes of this pathway are also present in |FRAME:TAX-543| and in eukaryotic organisms, and the pathway has been reported to be utilzed by yeast and mammals in addition to de novo NAD biosynthesis and other salvage pathways (such as (|FRAME: PYRIDNUCSAL-PWY|) |CITS: [14907738][10464228][12446641][15137942]|, The identity of the bacterial NR transporter has not been confirmed experimentally, but it is suggested that it is encoded by the pnuC gene, although earlier work with the PnuC protein of |FRAME:TAX-28901| serovar Typhimurium suggested that it encodes the transport of NMN |CITS: [6216244][11395461]|.

Names: adipate biosynthesis // reverse adipate degradation pathway // RADP
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ADIPATE Adipate| is a dicaboxylic acid that is present in the juice of sugar beet and sugar cane, though the biosynthetic pathway in these plants is still unknown. Adipate has also been identified as a metabolic intermediate in the biodegradation pathways of cyclic alkanes, cyclic alcohols, and long chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acids |CITS: [3136163][12021788][22824738]|., Adipate is used in the chemical manufacturing industry, mostly for the production of nylon. Adipate monomers are condensed with hexamethylene diamine, forming |FRAME: Nylon-6|, the most common form of nylon. Other uses for adipate include the production of polyurethane, formation of plasticizers and lubricant components, and as a flavorant and gelling aid in the food industry. Most of the adipate in commercial processes is produced from petrochemicals, specifically by oxidation of KA oil (|FRAME: CYCLOHEXANOL| and |FRAME: CYCLOHEXANONE|) catalyzed by nitric acid |CITS: [11529791]|., About This Pathway, Organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-5076| have the ability to naturally degrade adipate using a degradation pathway that resembles fatty acid β-oxidation |CITS: [Thykaer2002]|. The first step in that pathway is the ATP-dependent activation of adipate with CoA, and the rest of the pathway proceeds via CoA-derivatives, ending with the central metaboiltes acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA., A patent application in 2011 has described an engineered pathway, which was termed the "reverse adipate degradation pathway", in which the same enzymes involved in adipate degradation could catalyze its production. It was calculated that the pathway could transform glucose into adipate and CO2 under anaerobic conditions with a 92% molar yield |CITS: [Burgard11]|. In 2014 the pathway was tested successfully by cloning enzymes from multiple organisms and expressing them in |FRAME: TAX-562|, though the yield was rather low, at 0.7mg adipate per liter |CITS: [24895214]|., In 2015 the pathway was unexprectedly found to function in the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-57106| |CITS: [26189483]|. |FRAME: ORG-57106| is an engineered strain constructed to produce |FRAME: PROPANOL|. The native celR gene (encoding |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.4|) was replaced by the |FRAME: G-12174| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1488|, which encodes a bifunctional |FRAME: MONOMER-15847| |CITS: [21757023][26227414]|. When grown on glucose (5 g/L) the organism was found to produce 0.18 g/L adipate |CITS: [26189483]|., The five enzymes involved in the pathway were identified. While all enzymes are native, expression of the |FRAME: G-107676| gene in the B6 strain was significantly higher than in the wild type strain. The authors concluded that low transcription of the gene is the limiting step for significant adipate production in the |FRAME: TAX-2021| wild type |CITS: [26189483]|., In later work the pathway was reconstructed in |FRAME: TAX-562| by cloning all of the |FRAME: TAX-2021| genes. This work confirmed that the step catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-107676| gene product is the rate-limiting step of the pathway. Overexpression of the gene, combined with deletion of the succinate-CoA ligase gene to promote accumulation of succinyl-CoA, resulted in production of 68.0 g/L adipate |CITS: [29625225]|.

Summary: |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD Ethylene| is an important plant hormone that regulates growth and development. It is well-known as a fruit-ripening hormone and is biologically active in trace amounts. Ethylene also plays a general role as a growth inhibitor in promoting leaf and flower senescence and abscission. |FRAME:HCN Hydrogen cyanide| is formed in plants in stoichiometrically equal amounts to ethylene as a byproduct of ethylene biosynthesis (see |FRAME:ETHYL-PWY|) |CITS:[16593463]| |CITS:[Grossmann03]|. , Cyanide is toxic to all living cells and requires rapid detoxification in the plant tissues |CITS: [3073064]| |CITS: [12422245]|. Furthermore, as a defense mechanism, cyanide is also released from cyanogenic glucosides, i.e. cyanogenesis, by cyanogenic plants (see for example |FRAME:PWY-7089|, |FRAME:PWY-7093|). Cyanide is detoxified to |FRAME:CPD-603|, a non-protein amino acid which is wide-spread in higher plants and is neurotoxic to many animals. In most plants, |FRAME:CPD-603| can be further metabolized to |FRAME:ASN| and |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| (this pathway) |CITS:[11060302]|., There is also evidence that |FRAME:HCN| plays a regulatory (maybe signaling) function in physiological processes (|CITS:[Siegien06]|, e.g. seed germination (|CITS:[Bogatek99]|  |CITS:[18448476]| |CITS:[Gniazdowska10]|), nitrate assimilation (|CITS:[Solomonson90]|) or in plant responses to stress and other environmental factors (|CITS:[Grossmann96]| |CITS:[21075959]|)., Since the early 1960s, studies have shown that C-14 labeled hydrocyanic acid can be incorporated to |FRAME:ASN| in the seedlings of an array of plants, including sorghum, barley, pea, flax, and soybean |CITS: [4798760]|. Enzymes that catalyze the two sequential reactions, β-cyanoalanine synthase and β-cyanoalanine hydrolase have been isolated and their enzyme activities have been confirmed in |FRAME:TAX-3701| and other higher plants |CITS: [4627358][11060302][1055433][10845460][10889265] [16786295]|. , A temporal and spatial association exists between ethylene synthesis and cyanide detoxifying activity (this pathway) indicating a semi-quantitative relationship between ACC oxidase and β-cyanoalanine synthase, the two key enzymes of the respective pathways |CITS: [3073064]|.

Anthocyanin biosynthesis is a crucial biochemical process involved in the flower development of many angiosperms. Flavonoid pigments provide the means to attract pollinators through bright colors |CITS:[Harborne66]| and/or certain color patterns |CITS:[11511673]| |CITS:[Eisner02]|. Research over the last decades on anthocyanin biosynthesis has led to the discovery of many genes involved in the pathway. Advanced gene technologies enabled molecular breeding of flower colors in many commercially valuable ornamental species such as carnation resulting in novel and intriguing colors and hues |CITS:[Yonekura-Sakakibara09]|., Anthocyanins are most often decorated with glucose or other sugar moieties at the 3-position (A-ring) and the 5- and 7-position of the C-ring. Among the most prominent anthocyanins in |FRAME:TAX-3570| (carnation) are cyclic 3,5-malyl anthocyanins (|FRAME:CPD-15294|, |FRAME:CPD-15295|) |CITS:[11140528]|. However, the 5-O-glucosylation had not yet been elucidated. Likewise in |FRAME:TAX-46246| the main anthocyanin, i.e. cyanodelphin, a tetra p-hydroxybenzoated anthocyanin |CITS:[Kondo91]| is glucosylated at both 3 and 7 position but the 7-O-glucosylation remained unresolved as well |CITS:[Davies09]|. The monocotyledone |FRAME:TAX-51501|, a popular ornamental plant because of the blue and white flower colors which also is frequently used as a traditional medicine in South Africa has become the object of major studies regarding relevant pharmacological properties |CITS:[18343601] [15907963]|. The two main anthocyanins are 3,7-glucosylated delphinidin coumaroyl glucoside linked to a variety of kaempferol glycosides |CITS:[10724183]|. , Despite the taxonomic distance between the species mentioned above, i.e. the dicotyledones carnation (Caryophyllacea) and delphinium (|FRAME:TAX-3440|) and the monocotyledone |FRAME:TAX-51426| (|FRAME:TAX-4668|) all species have glucosyltransferases that realize either the 5-O- or 7-O-glucosylation. Instead of the usual sugar donor |FRAME: CPD-12575| the glucosyltransferases utilize acyl-glucoses such as the benzoyl-glucose derivatives |FRAME:CPD-15006|, |FRAME:CPD-15283| and |FRAME:CPD-15281| and the hydroxycinnamoyl-glucose derivatives |FRAME:CPD-15281| and |FRAME:1-O-SINAPOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| as glucose donors |CITS:[20971893] [22048706] [22673029]|. The acyl-glucose dependent glucosyltransferases (AAGTs) belong in the glycosyl hydroxylase (GH) 1 family and show significant amino acid sequence identities across the taxonomic range indicating that the AAGTs evolved before the divergence of monocots and dicots. The AAGTs very position specifically (either A5 - AA5GT or A7 - AA7GT) glucosylate anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides such as |FRAME:CPD1F-766| (this pathway), |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-3-GLUCOSIDE-CMPD| (see |FRAME:PWY-7259|) and |FRAME:CPD-7117| (see |FRAME:PWY-7260|). According to the structural properties, the AAGTs belong to the glycosyl hydroxylases, however their β-glucosidase activity is only 4 - 6% of the corresponding glucosyltransferase activity emphasizing a novel enzymatic property probably developed over the course of evolution of their host species |CITS:[20971893] [22048706] [22673029]|. Various genes in Arabidopsis thaliana have also been identified as candidates for acyl-dependent anthocyanin 5 and 7 glucosyltransferases but their molecular function remains to be shown experimentally |CITS:[Miyahara11]|.

Names: bis(guanylyl molybdenum cofactor) biosynthesis // bisMGD biosynthesis // bis-MPT guanine dinucleotide cofactor biosynthesis
Summary: The transition element molybdenum (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. There are several molybdenum cofactors, including |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT), |FRAME: CPD-582| (MGD), |FRAME: CPD-23445|, or others |CITS: [1587808]|., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of molybdenum cofactors have been investigated in detail in bacteria |CITS: [7836363][8514783][8514782][1587808][14761975]| and plants |CITS: [16669776][16784786][12147719][16234918][9421926]|. All of the cofactors are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT)., The MPT structure is conserved in all organisms and it has been demonstrated that its biosynthesis is preserved in bacteria and plants alike., It is produced from |FRAME: GTP| via |FRAME: PRECURSOR-Z| in two steps catalyzed by |FRAME: AT1G01290-MONOMER| and |FRAME: CPLX-7191| |CITS: [7890743]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6823|). The variability of the molybdenum cofactors found in bacteria is achieved by the attachment of GMP, AMP, IMP, or CMP to the phosphate group of MPT., One of the molybdenum cofactors produced by bacteria is |FRAME: CPD-15873|. This form includes two MPT units coordinated at one molybdenum atom, as well as two GMPs bound to the terminal phosphate group of the MPTs. The enzyme responsible for the production of this cofactor is |FRAME: EG11829-MONOMER MobA|, an enzyme that is also responsible for producing |FRAME: CPD-582| (see |FRAME: PWY-5964|)., This dual functionality enzyme is able to form the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-15874|, followed by nucleotide attachment and release of the final |FRAME: CPD-15873| product |CITS: [24003231]|., This cofactor is known to be required by several enzymes, including |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.3| |CITS: [18522945]|, |FRAME: EC-1.17.5.3| |CITS: [11884747]|, |FRAME: EC-1.8.5.3| |CITS: [21357619]| and |FRAME: EC-1.7.5.1 |CITS: [12910261]|., Studies with |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.3| (TorA) of |FRAME: TAX-562| have shown that the presence of the GMP nucleotides is crucial for the insertion of the cofactor into the apo enzyme |CITS: [35566344]|.

Summary: General Background, Plant growth and development requires macro and micronutrients, some of which are available only from external sources like the soil in which they grow. Phosphorous is one such essential macronutrient, it is usually absorbed and utilized by the plants in the form of |FRAME: Pi| (also known as inorganic phosphate, or Pi) |CITS: [18713395]|. Many soils are deficient in |FRAME: Pi|, leading to |FRAME: Pi| starvation for plants growing in them. Plants develop several strategies to overcome |FRAME: Pi| limitation, including morphological, biochemical and physiological responses to enhance the acquisition of this vital macronutrient. These combined responses enhance the chances of plants to survive the prospects of |FRAME: Pi| starvation. Due to continous leaching, ancient soils are known to become limited in the availability of |FRAME: Pi|. , Once absorbed, the |FRAME: Pi| is utilized inside the cells at optimum cellular concentration for the various developmental and biochemical processes. Phosphate acquisition is a complicated process and has various modified routes. The |FRAME: Pi| homeostasis is maintained by acquisition, limited consumption and effective recycling, when the supply and demand is not equitable. The molecular basis for these strategies is being studied in a number of species |CITS: [19168668]|. The Gulf Ryegrass is an ideal model plant as it hyperaccumulates |FRAME: Pi| utilizing multiple acquisition and mobilization systems under varying |FRAME: Pi| regimes |CITS: [1882180]|. In some plants the chief enzymes that partcipate in the transport and recycling of |FRAME: Pi| are developmentally regulated |CITS: [12021284]|. , About This Pathway, The Purple Acid Phosphatases (PAP's) are said to play a role in |FRAME: Pi| salvaging when cells are depleted or starved of |FRAME: Pi| and under oxidative stress. Thus PAP's are crucial for the cellular metabolism and energy transduction processes. , PAP's have also been isolated from mammalian and fungal sources, although the physiological function of these enzymes has yet to be established |CITS: [10510276]|. Genes encoding such enzymes are also present in some bacteria, including cyanobacteria, but their role is not clear. It has been suggested that they prevent damage caused by generated by invaded host cells (mycobacteria) or by the light-harvesting complex (cyanobacteria) |CITS: [11024303]|. However, the enzyme of |FRAME: TAX-216591| is induced by lack of phosphate and excreted from the cell, suggesting it may be involved in phosphate acquisition |CITS: [19376213]|., The PAP enzymes may exist in two forms: the inactive purple form, where the redox-active iron is in the ferric state, and the active pink form, where the iron is reduced to the ferrous state.The PAP's are expressed in a tissue specific manner and often exist as isozymes |CITS: [16244908][15375722 ]|. The isozymes exhibit variation in molecular structure, substrate specficity and localization., Some PAP's, such as |FRAME: MONOMER-15162| from |FRAME: TAX-4081|, are multifunctional enzymes that have both a purple acid phosphatase and an alkaline peroxidase function. These enzymes are hypothesized to function in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) |CITS: [12473124]|. The phosphatase and oxygen radical-generating activities of PAP's are functionally independent, similar to those of mammalian PAP |CITS: [11890682]|.

Names: polybrominated biphenyls and diphenyl ethers biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Marine organisms, including bacteria, algae and invertebrates, produce many organobromine compounds. Over 2,200 of those, with a wide range of biological properties have been reported by 2017. Some brominated compounds, such as |FRAME: PBDEs "polybrominated diphenyl ethers"| (BDEs) in their hydroxylated and methoxylated forms, are found across all trophic levels in marine biota, from cyanobacteria and macroalgae to whales and seabirds. In some marine sponges within the |FRAME: TAX-190525| family BDEs can exceed 10% of the sponge tissue by dry weight |CITS: [Unson94][Becerro04]|., Other compounds, such as the brominated biphenyl |FRAME: CPD-20552|, the brominated bipyrrole |FRAME: CPD-20553|, and the hybrid |FRAME: CPD-20554|, have been shown to be synthesized by several species of |FRAME: TAX-53246|, a marine γ-proteobacterial genus often associated with eukaryotic hosts |CITS: [4380876][Andersen74][12543647]|., To find the genes encoding the biosynthesis of brominated compounds, the genomes of two |FRAME: TAX-53246| species, |FRAME: TAX-1315281| and |FRAME: TAX-1353533|, were sequenced, and the genomes were searched for homologs of two genes known to be involved in the formation of chlorinated pyrroles - |FRAME: G-55300| and |FRAME: G-55299| (based on the assumption that a similar mechanism may operate in the formation of chlorinated and brominated pyrroles). The search led to the identification of a brominated marine pyrroles/phenols (bmp) biosynthetic gene cluster in both bacteria |CITS: [24974229]|., Cloning of the bmp1-8 genes and their expression in |FRAME: TAX-562| led to production of many typical brominated compounds, including brominated phenols, pyrroles, biphenyls, bipyrroles and hydbrid phenyl-pyrrole molecules. By expressing the bmp cluster with individual gene deletions it was possible to delinetate the function of the individual enzymes, and to show that the cluster encodes all of the enzymes that are necessary for production of brominated phenols, brominated pyrroles, and their derivatives |CITS: [24974229]|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the coupling of polybrominated phenols and pyrroles to form assorted biphenyls and diphenyl ethers, and requires only one enzyme - |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-55297| gene). This cytochrome P450 enzyme can act on either |FRAME: CPD-20548| or |FRAME: CPD-20566| and form a large assortment of coupled molecules. In the lab, the enzyme was also shown to act on |FRAME: CPD-20551|, although the relevance of this activity inn vivo is not known yet., The bromopyrrole and bromophenol biosynthetic modules function independently, and not all organisms have both. Thus, the exact products formed by this pathway will depend on the starting compounds produced by the individual organism |CITS: [24974229]|.
