Summary: The pathway of |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis from |FRAME: THR| is a five-step pathway that shares several steps with the pathway of |FRAME: VAL| biosynthesis. These entwined pathways are part of the |FRAME:BRANCHED-CHAIN-AA-SYN-PWY|, that generates not only |FRAME: ILE| and |FRAME: VAL|, but also |FRAME: LEU|., As a consequence of having several of its component enzymes involved in the synthesis of three different amino acids, the pathway of isoleucine biosynthesis is subject to regulation by all three amino acids. The first enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX|, is downregulated by isoleucine and leucine, but is upregulated by valine. The following pathway step, catalyzed by |FRAME: ACETOLACTSYNI-CPLX| (AHAS I) and |FRAME: ACETOLACTSYNIII-CPLX| (AHAS III), is inhibited by all three amino acids. This apparent paradox of valine stimulation of step one followed by valine inhibition of step two is a product of the preference of AHAS III for processing of the isoleucine precursor |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| rather than the valine precursor |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. When valine is abundant in the cell, both AHAS, enzymes are inhibited, blocking valine production and potentially disrupting isoleucine synthesis as well. However, the stimulation of |FRAME: THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX| generates a substantial pool of |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|. Combined with the high affinity of AHAS III for this compound, this allows the isoleucine synthesis to continue despite inhibition caused by the parallel valine synthesis pathway., Enteric bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-511145| and |FRAME: TAX-90371| have been shown to possess two types of threonine dehydratases - a catabolic enzyme, which is induced by threonine (see |FRAME: THREDEHYDCAT-CPLX|), and a consistitutively-produced biosynthetic enzyme (|FRAME: THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX|) |CITS: [13405870]|. Both enzymes convert threonine to |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, but differ in their regulation and expression., Biosynthetic threonine dehydratases were also described in several soil bacteria |CITS: [16743051]|. A survey of 75 soil isolates capable of growth on L-threonine revealed a group of three organisms that possessed substantial L-threonine dehydratase activity, to the exclusion of any other threonine-catabolyzing enzyme |CITS: [5076220]|.  The group consisted of |FRAME:ORG-5895| and two |FRAME:TAX-1696| isolates. The enzyme from |FRAME:ORG-5895| was partially purified, and was found to be of the biosynthetic type on the criteria that its formation was consitutive, it was susceptible to inhibition by |FRAME:ILE|, |FRAME:VAL| protected against denaturation and was a positive effector and antagonist of isoleucine, and neither AMP nor ADP acted as effectors |CITS: [16743051]|. Interestingly, even though the enzyme was of the biosynthetic type, the researchers found that much of the threonine in these organisms was converted to |FRAME:PROPIONATE| in a catabolic pathway identical to that described in |FRAME:PWY-5437|. Thus, the biosynthetic enzyme was recruited to a catabolic pathway., A biosynthetic threonine dehydratase was also reported in |FRAME:TAX-615| |CITS: [355220]|.

General Background, Glycosylation is one of the major types of post-translational modification of proteins, and is an essential process in all eukaryotes. Protein glycosylation is known to be involved in cellular targeting and secretion, and helps to regulate enzymatic activity, confer enhanced stability and solubility to secreted proteins, and affect the functionality of proteins in the immune system. In addition, glycoproteins participate in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions., The two major types of protein glycosylation are known as N-linked and O-linked glycosylation. O-linked oligosaccharides are variously attached to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues in the target proteins. Most commonly O-glycosylation begins with the attachment of |FRAME: CPD-3604| to the free hydroxyl group of the amino acid, although O-linkages to fucose, glucose, mannose, xylose and other sugars are known., About This Pathway, Mucin-type O-glycosylation, consisting of glycans attached via O-linked |FRAME: CPD-3604| to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues, is one of the most abundant forms of protein glycosylation in animals., Initiation of glycosylation occurs in the Golgi, after the target proteins have been completely folded. Initiation is followed by the action of numerous very specific glycosyltransferases, resulting in the extension of |FRAME: CPD-3604| into numerous different O-glycan structures |CITS: [17988798][18695988]|. Eight different core structures of |FRAME: Mucin-type-glycans "mucin-type O-glycans"| have been described, many with the same monosaccharide residues in different linkages. The most abundant core structures in humans are |FRAME: Core1 "core 1"| and |FRAME: Core2 "core 2"|, and the enzymes catalyzing their formation have been well-characterized |CITS: [19919547]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7433|). |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-13-N-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINY "Core 3"| and |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-16-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINYL- "core 4"| structures are restricted in their occurrence to mucins from specialized tissues such as colon and salivary glands from several species, including humans, pig and rat |CITS: [3160388][4008490]|., Protein glycosylation pathways are usually controlled by the genes that encode the enzymes responsible for the initiation of glycosylation. In mucin-type O-glycosylation, there is a great abundance of such genes (up to 20 homologous genes) encoding |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.41| (only a single representative of these genes is shown in this MetaCyc pathway). These genes are differentially expressed over tissue and developmental phase, enabling complex and strict regulation |CITS: [22183981]|. In addition, many have clear specificities for the sites of attachment, thus determining the density and site occupancy of the mucin-type O-glycosylation |CITS: [8922959][12634319]|., The enzymes involved in synthesis of |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-13-N-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINY "core 3"| and |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINYL-16-ETCETERA-GALACTOSAMINYL- "core 4"| are less studied. The enzymatic activities, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.147| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.148|, have been documented in colon mucosa from several mammals, including pig, rat and human |CITS:[6226356] [3160388][7655172]|. However, these two enzymes have not been purified, and the genes encoding them have not been identified as of 2014.

|FRAME: Porphyrans Porphyran| is a sulfated carbohydrate extracted from the cell wall of red seaweeds belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-2784| |CITS: [Anderson65]|. Unlike |FRAME: Agaroses agarose| and |FRAME: Carrageenans carrageenan|, porphyran is not utilized as ingredient for its gelling or texturizing properties. However, it is one of the most consumed algal polysaccharides because it is the main component of edible |FRAME: TAX-2788| and |FRAME: TAX-2785|, both of which are extensively used in the preparation of sushi |CITS: [Correc11]|., The backbone of porphyran is composed of about 30% of |FRAME: Agaroses agarose| repeating units (1,3-linked β-D-galactopyranose followed by 1,4-linked 3,6-anhydro-α-L-galactopyranose), with the remaining residues being 3-linked β-D-galactopyranose and 4-linked α-L-galactopyranose-6-sulfate. The 4-linked α-L-galactopyranose-6-sulfate residues can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-13430| by the enzyme |FRAME: 2.5.1.5-RXN "galactose-6-sulfurylase, EC 2.5.1.5"|., In addition, the galactan backboned is decorated by methyl-ether groups at the C6 position of the 3-linked β-D-galactopyranose residues. As other sulfated galactans, porphyran may have some potential pharmacological applications |CITS: [18796647]|, based on, for example, its hypolipidemic |CITS: [19202270]| and anti-allergic properties |CITS: [16244430]|., |FRAME: Porphyrans Porphyran| can be degraded by several enzymes. The agarose portion of the backbone can be digested by α- and β-agarases (such as |FRAME: MONOMER-16651| and |FRAME: CPLX-8301|) while the rest of the backbone is cleaved by dedicated porphyranase enzymes (such as |FRAME: MONOMER-16647| and |FRAME: MONOMER-16646|), which cleave the (1→4) linkages between β-D-galactopyranose and α-L-galactopyranose-6-sulfate, forming mostly the disaccharide α-L-galactopyranose-6-sulfate-(1→3)-β-D-galactose |CITS: [20376150]|., are known to degrade it very slowly |CITS: [5386190]|.

General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on single carbon (C1) compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. , While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 "Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| (see |FRAME: PWY-5506|)., The key enzyme in the oxidation of methanol in methylotrophic bacteria is methanol dehydrogenase (MDH). Different bacterial strains use different types of MDH. Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria have a periplasmic |FRAME: EC-1.1.2.7| that contain a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ) cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-1701|). Thermophilic methylotrophic Bacili such as |FRAME: TAX-1471| use an NAD-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.244| (see |FRAME: PWY-6510|), while Gram-positive bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1814|, |FRAME: TAX-1777| MB19, |FRAME: TAX-1829| LMD 89.129 and |FRAME: TAX-1833| DSM 1069 possess |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.37| with a bound NAD(P) cofactor that use an unknown electron acceptor for reduction of their bound cofactor and can use the artificial electron acceptor |FRAME: CPD-12424| in vitro |CITS:[1995642][8385013][8449887]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6509|)., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branch point, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (see |FRAME:P185-PWY|), or a dissimilatory pathway that provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|)., About This Pathway, Gram-positive bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1814|, |FRAME: TAX-1777| MB19, |FRAME: TAX-1829| LMD 89.129 and |FRAME: TAX-1833| DSM 1069 possess |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.37|, an enzyme that uses the artificial electron acceptor |FRAME: CPD-12424| in vitro and can accept ethanol as a substrate. The native electron acceptor for this enzyme is still not known |CITS:[1995642][8385013][8449887]|., The enzymes are decameric proteins and possess a tightly but noncovalently bound NADP(H) cofactor. They also contain |FRAME: ZN+2| and |FRAME: MG+2| ions |CITS: [8449887]|. The |FRAME: MG+2| ions are essential for binding of the NADP(H) cofactor |CITS: [12351635]|. The bound NADP(H) act as a cofactor and becomes reduced when the enzyme oxidizes primary alcohols to the respective aldehydes. NAD can not act as an electron acceptor, and while the natural acceptor is not known, it is possible that it is a part of the electron transfer chain., The purified enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-1471| strain JC1 oxidize ethanol and formaldehyde as well as methanol, and also has the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.2.98.1| |CITS: [19875438]|., Studies of methanol utilization in |FRAME: TAX-1772| suggest that expression of methanol oxidoreductase (Mno) is reduced so that methanol oxidation happens at a lower rate and the formaldehyde thus generated can be dissimilated by Mno itself. The organism also possesses a dedicated |FRAME: CPLX-5781|, encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-6476| gene. However, that enzyme appears to be required only when there is an overload of formaldehyde |CITS: [29891642]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Much later an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate, which proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-10477|, has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|. Initial analysis of sequenced genomes suggested that the pathway might be present in a variety of organisms |CITS: [19557031]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6262|). Further analysis revealed that the newly discovered pathway may not be identical among all of these organisms. It appears that in some organisms |FRAME: CPD-13324| is converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-10484| (as shown here), while in others this transformation occurrs via |FRAME: CPD-10477| (see |FRAME: PWY-7374|)., In both pathway |FRAME: CHORISMATE| is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-16467| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-16550| (|FRAME: G-12801|), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-13324| in a complex reaction catalyzed by a radical Ado-Met enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-17947| |CITS: [24083939]|. In this pathway the latter is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16549 MqnB| to form |FRAME: CPD-10484|, a common intermedaite to both pathways |CITS: [21489995]|., The rest of the pathway is identical in both pathway variants. The last intermediate shown here is |FRAME: CPD-11420|. It is still not known how this intermediate is coenverted to menaquinone.

Summary: General Background, The mycobacterial cell envelope contains an usually rich variety of complex free lipids and glycolipids associated with the, mycolic acid layer of the cell wall. These lipids and glycolipids are located in the membrane outer leaflet. Together with the membrane inner leaflet, which is based on mycolic acids, they form the asymmetric lipid bilayer that constitutes the characteristic mycobacterial outer membrane., |FRAME: PGL "Phenolic glycolipids"| (PGLs) are found in a limited group of pathogenic mycobacteria including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1765|, |FRAME: TAX-33894|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1768|, |FRAME: TAX-1777|, |FRAME: TAX-1769| and |FRAME: TAX-1809| |CITS: [3149973][16115688]|. PGLs, as well as the related |FRAME: CPD-18612 PDIMs|, play important roles in host-pathogen interaction and/or virulence in various mycobacterial pathogens |CITS: [10573420][11081637][15019737][15343336][15942899][18700620][18764820][18443098][19622047][19197369][20844580][21375593]|., PGLs are composed of a mixture of long chain β-diols esterified by multimethyl-branched |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"| or |FRAME: Phthioceranic-Acids "phthioceranic acids"|. The long chain β-diol is terminated by a glycosylated aromatic nucleus. The sugar moiety consists of 1 to 4 sugar residues, depending on the mycobacterial species, and most are O-methylated deoxysugars |CITS: [16115688]|., The major variant of PGL produced by |FRAME: TAX-1773|, named |FRAME: CPD-18579 PGL-tb|, is glycosylated by the triglycoside 2,3,4-tri-O-methyl-α-L-fucopyranosyl-(1→3)-α-L-rhamnopyranosyl-(1→3)-2-O-methyl-α-L-rhamnopyranose. |FRAME: TAX-1773| also secretes a smaller molecule that contain the same glycosylated phenolic moiety, known as |FRAME: CPD-18619 p-HBAD-II| (see |FRAME: PWY-7745|)., Other well-characterized PGL molecules include |FRAME: CPD-18679| from |FRAME: TAX-1765| and |FRAME: CPD-18692| from |FRAME: TAX-1769|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the triglycosylated PGL described from the Canettii strains of |FRAME: TAX-1773|. Note that that the |FRAME: TAX-83332| strain does not produce PGL due to a natural mutation in the |FRAME: G-15015| gene, whose product is essential for |FRAME: PWY-7742|. However, the rest of the enzymes that participate in this pathway do exist in this strain, and were used for the study and characterization of their activities, as the |FRAME: TAX-83332| is the the neotype and best studied strain of the species M. tuberculosis species. Thus, the vast majority of the enzymes that appear in this pathway are from the H37Rv strain., The PGL molecule could be regarded as consisting of three main parts - a |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerols| skeleton, two esterified |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "mycocerosic acids"|, and a sugar moiety., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerols| is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7742|., |FRAME: Mycocerosic-Acids "Mycocerosic acids"| are polymethyl-branched fatty acids that are unique to the cell wall of pathogenic mycobacteria |CITS: [1527058]|. They are produced by extending a C18 - C20 straight chain fatty acyl-CoAs using methylmalonyl-CoA instead of malonyl-CoA as the extender unit, resulting in a tri- or tetra-methyl branched segment at the carboxy terminal end |CITS: [6402506]|., The elongation process is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.111|, a homodimeric multifunctional enzyme |CITS: [3880746]|. The enzyme does not contain a thioesterase domain and the mechanism of chain-termination remains somewhat obscure |CITS: [9159514]|, although the thioesterase encoded by the |FRAME: G-44345| gene may be responsible for the release of the product from the synthase |CITS: [15668773][21375593]|., Following their release from the synthase, the free acids are activated by adenylation, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.49| (FadD28) |CITS: [9525903][21771578]|. The activated acids are then loaded onto the |FRAME: G-44341 PapA5| transferase, which catalyzes their esterification to the two hydroxyl groups in |FRAME: Phthiocerols phthiocerols|, or, as shown in this pathway, |FRAME: Phenolphthiocerols phenolphthiocerols|, forming |FRAME: CPD-18669| |CITS: [15070765][22361940][26271001]|., The last part of the pathway involves the species-specific glycosylation process. In |FRAME: TAX-1773 | glycosylation requires three glycosyltranferases and four methyltransferases |CITS: [15292272][15292265][23536839]|., In |FRAME: TAX-1765| mutations in the |FRAME: G185E-7212| ortholog, which encodes the glycosyltransferase that transfers the second rhamnose residue, as well as in genes that encode enzymes involved the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13118|, prevent the transfer of the second and third glycosides, and production ends at |FRAME: CPD-18679|. Similar mutations have also been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1806|, |FRAME: TAX-194542|, and some strains of |FRAME: TAX-33894| |CITS: [18390543]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-23316 Succinoglycan| (initially known as EPS I) is an acidic exopolysaccharide that is produced by the nitrogen-fixing plant symbiont |FRAME: TAX-382| and is required for the invasion of plant root nodules by the bacterium. , The repeating unit of the succinoglycan polymer is composed of a backbone of one galactose and three glucose residues, a side chain of four glucose residues, and succinyl-, acetyl- and pyruvoyl modifications of certain glucosyl residues. The functions of the individual enzymes in this pathway have largely been determined by the precursors produced in the respective mutants., It is assumed that the repeating unit, once assembled, is translocated from the cytoplasm to the periplasm, where it is polymerized into the mature polysaccharide, followed by exportation through the outer membrane |CITS: [27255488]|. , The proteins encoded by the exoPQT genes catalyze the polymerization of the succinoglycan repeating units and polymer secretion (Glucksmann et al., 1993). ExoP of |FRAME: TAX-382| is an autophosphorylating protein tyrosine kinase catalyzing the formation of dimers of octasaccharide units of succinoglycan |CITS: [19888830]|. ExoQ protein (like the Wzy polymerases) is needed for high-molecular weight succinoglycan biosynthesis, and ExoT (like the Wzx flippases) is involved in low-molecular-weight succinoglycan production |CITS: [9811825]|.

Summary: General Background, One of the most striking physiological differences between the archaea and other organisms is the structure of their, membrane lipids. One defining feature of archaeal phospholipids is that they are based on a backbone consisting of |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, which is an enantiomer of the |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| used by bacteria and eukaryotic organisms. It has been suggested that archaea and bacteria were differentiated by the occurrence of cells enclosed by membranes of phospholipids with |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| as a backbone, respectively |CITS: [9419225]|., Another feature unique to archaeal phospholipids is side chains that are derivatives of isoprenoid alcohols rather than fatty acids, which are linked by ether linkages (rather than ester linkages) to the glycerophosphate backbone |CITS: [358256]|. The isoprenoids are usually modified by saturation of the double bonds - a modification that is believed to increase the ability of the lipids to survive the extreme conditions that archaea often face. Yet another unique feature is the occurrence of bipolar lipids with a tetraether core, which are present in significant numbers in archaeal species., It should be noted that bacteria of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-456828| of the |FRAME: TAX-1783270 "Fibrobacteres-Chlorobi-Bacteroidetes (FCB) group superphylum"|, are able to synthseize both canonical bacterial lipids and archaeal-like ether-linked isoprenoid phospholipids |CITS: [32929208]|., In contrast to these differences, most of the polar head groups of archaeal phospholipids are similar to those found in the other kingdoms - |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CHOLINE| |CITS: [17347520]|., The major polar lipids of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-145262| are L-serine, ethanolamine, or myo-inositol-containing di- and, tetraether type phospholipids and phosphoglycolipids, and gentiobiose-containing di- and tetraether type glycolipids., Examples of non-glycosylated lipids include |FRAME: CPD-10741 "archaetidylserine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11919 "archaetidylethanolamine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11918 "archaetidylinositol"| and |FRAME: CPD-11920 "archaetidylglycerol"|., About This Pathway, CDP-archaeol, either in its |FRAME: CPD-10740 "unsaturated form"| or its |FRAME: CPD-15253 "saturated form"|, is expected to be the common precursor of biosynthesis of all the archaeal phospholipids, analogous to |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL "CDP-diacylglycerol"| in bacteria., The pathway leading to the synthesis of CDP-archaeol has been partially characterized in the organisms |FRAME: TAX-145262| and |FRAME: TAX-145263|. The four enzymes catalyzing the steps leading to CDP-archaeol have been studied in vitro and are well characterized |CITS: [8586635][8408023][10960477][12562787]|. A large part of this pathway (up to |FRAME: BIS-GERANYLGERANYLGLYCEROL-PHOSPHATE|) has been reconstructed in |FRAME:TAX-562| using cloned genes from |FRAME: TAX-2234| |CITS: [19558961]|., The pathway starts with the reduction of |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of glycolysis,, to |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.261| (G-1-P dehydrogenase). Activity of this enzyme or presence of the the genes encoding it have been detected in all archaeal species studied so far |CITS: [9973362]|., In the next two steps, two molecules of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| are bound to the, |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| backbone through two ether bonds at the sn-2 and -3 positions., The product of these additions is |FRAME: BIS-GERANYLGERANYLGLYCEROL-PHOSPHATE| (unsaturated archaetidate). This intermediate can be reduced to |FRAME: CPD-15250| (saturated archaetidate) by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-17978|., Either form of archaetidate can be activated by |FRAME: CTP| (catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14510|) to form the corresponding form of CDP-archaeol, which is modified by different enzymes to form the final lipids, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6350| and |FRAME: PWY-6141|., This pathway is analogous to the bacterial pathway of |FRAME: CDP-diacylglycerol-Biosynthesis|, from which it differs, in the use of |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, the formation of ether bonds, and the nature of the hydrocarbon, chains.

Summary: |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2| (previously EC 3.6.3.14) is an enzyme that uses the free energy derived from the transmembrane proton gradient to catalyze the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate., Several types of ATP synthases are known. The F-type is a large enzyme found in mitochondria, chloroplasts and bacteria. The enzyme comprises two subcomplexes - a membrane sector (Fo) and a cytoplasmic-compartment sector (F1). Functionally, ATP synthase may be considered tripartite, consisting of a rotor, a rotor stalk or stator, and three catalytic sites where ATP synthesis or hydrolysis occurs |CITS: [11997128][17662937]|. , The enzyme is a rotary molecular nanomotor that couples the mechanical force of subunit rotation to the synthesis or hydrolysis of ATP at the enzyme's catalytic sites. Proton movement across the membrane, which is driven by the H+ electrochemical potential gradient, generates subunit rotation that drives ATP synthesis by forcing sequential conformational changes at each of the three catalytic sites. The rotor rotates by consecutive 120° angles, and performs parts of the ATP synthesis reaction during rotation. , The V-type (in vacuoles and clathrin-coated vesicles) and bacterial P-type (plasma) enzymes have a similar structure but, under physiological conditions, operate in the opposite direction, utilizing energy from ATP hydrolysis to pump protons or other ions across the membrane |CITS: [10600677][ 21179061]|., In facultative organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-562| the enzyme can change its direction according to the growth mode. While the enzyme operates as an ATP synthase during aerobic respiration, it functions in the reverse direction during fermentation, catalyzing the hydrolysis of ATP to generate the electrochemical proton gradient needed for other membrane functions |CITS: [14985119]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1281 "Coenzyme B"| is one of the many unusual cofactors present in methanogens and required for methane formation. Like |FRAME: Factor-420|, |FRAME: CPD-1281| acts as an electron carrier in the metabolism of methanogens (see |FRAME: P241-PWY|)., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| functions as a methyl carrier in methanogenesis, and |FRAME: Me-CoM| has been established as the terminal intermediate of methanogenesis from all substrates (see |FRAME:METHFORM-PWY|). In addition to its role in methanogenesis, different forms of |FRAME: CoM| have physiological roles in methanogens, and are specific enzyme substrates |CITS: [2115763]|., All catabolic processes in methanogenesis lead to the formation of a mixed disulfide bond between |FRAME: CoM| and |FRAME: CPD-1281|, by a reaction in which |FRAME: CPD-1281| reduces |FRAME: Me-CoM|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CH4| and a |FRAME:CPD-1282| |CITS: [12102556]| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|)., The process in which |FRAME:CPD-1282| is reduced back to |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| has been studied extensively. There are two different enzyme systems that are capable of reducing the |FRAME:CPD-1282|. One is a membrane-bound system, encoded by the hdrDE genes, which uses |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE| as its electron donor |CITS: [15168610]|. The other is a soluble cytoplasmic system encoded by the hdrABC genes, which can use several types of electron donors, either directly, or by forming a complex with other enzymes., About This Pathway, The HdrDE system is found only in the |FRAME: TAX-94695|, which have the unusual ability (among methanogens) to synthesize cytochromes. The |FRAME: G-390|-encoded subunit contains the active site and two [4Fe-4S] clusters, while the |FRAME: G-389|-encoded subunit is |FRAME: Cytochromes-B| |CITS: [9665708][19968794]|., The direct electron donor to the HdrDE system is |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE|, a quinone-like compound found inside the membrane. It is obtained by the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-7323| using electrons derived from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, either directly, or via |FRAME: Reduced-Factor-F420|. The direct route involves |FRAME: EC-1.12.98.3|, which transfers electrons from |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| to |FRAME: CPD-7323|. The indirect route involves |FRAME: EC-1.5.98.3|, a membrane bound protein complex that transfers two electrons from |FRAME: Reduced-Factor-F420|, which has been reduced at the expense of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| by |FRAME: EC-1.12.98.1|, to |FRAME: CPD-7323|., Using |FRAME: DIHYDROMETHANOPHENAZINE|, |FRAME: EC-1.8.98.1| (HdrDE) catalyzes the reduction of |FRAME:CPD-1282| (using two protons in the process) to |FRAME: CoM| and |FRAME: CPD-1281| |CITS: [10471795]|. The HdrDE-mediated electron transfer results in consumption of protons in the cytoplasm and generation of proton motive force, which is used for ATP generation |CITS:[11034998]|.

Tungsten (W) and molybdenum (Mo) have equal atomic and ionic radii and similar electronegativity, and initially it was believed that tungsten only acts as an antagonist of molybdoenzymes. The first indications that tungsten might have a positive biological role were in the 1970s, when it was reported that tungstate stimulated the growth of certain acetate- and methane-producing microorganisms |CITS: [4147651][4154039][1132514][324989]|. However, the first naturally occurring tungstoenzyme was purified only in 1983, from the acetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1525| |CITS: [6822536]|. Another tungsten enzyme was purified from the same organism in 1989 |CITS: [2550230]|. In addition, tungsten-dependent enzyme was purified from the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2261| |CITS: [2538471][2164004]|. Following this discovery, numerous tungsten-dependent enzymes were isolated from hyperthermophilic archaea, leading to the idea that W enzymes are more ancient than the Mo enzymes. Unlike the enzymes previously isolated from bacterila species, which could use either tungsten or molybdenum, many of the archaeal enzymes are specific for tungsten. In fact, some of these organisms do not have any molybdoenzymes |CITS: [ 8550411]|., Tungsten-containing enzymes are now known from a variety of organisms, including acetogens, methanogens, hyperthermophiles, acetylene-utilizing anaerobes, sulfate-reducing anaerobes, and some aerobic, methylotrophic organisms |CITS: [Girio92][7592321][7592385]|. However, unlike Mo-enzyme, W-enzymes have not been detected in eukaryotes. The tungsten enzymes fall into two families, exemplified by aldehyde:ferredoxin reductase (AOR family) and the formate dehydrogenases (FDH), respectively |CITS: [11952415]|., Study of "true W-enzymes", mainly isolated from hyperthermophilic archaea, showed that the tungsten is bound to a 6-substituted pterin (molybdopterin), similarly to molybdenum in Mo-enzymes. A main feature of tungsten coordination in the active site of W-enzymes is that the cofactor contains two molecules of molybdopterin, which are coordinated by four sulfur ligands |CITS: [9861725]|. It has been stated that all members of the AOR family contain the non-nucleotide form |FRAME: CPD-22998|, whereas the FDH type enzymes appear to contain |FRAME: CPD-21374| |CITS: [11848842][10447686]|., This pathway describes the addition of guanylyl mucleotides to |FRAME: CPD-22998| to form |FRAME: CPD-21374|. While the latter has been observed in FDH-type W-enzymes, the enzyme that catalyzes this reaction has not been biochemically characterized as of 2020. However, the |FRAME: G-80652 MobA| protein, which is present in several hyperthermophilic archaeons that do not possess Mo-enzymes, is homologous to bacterial proteins that catalyze the guanylylation of |FRAME: CPD-15870| to form |FRAME: CPD-15873| (|FRAME: EC-2.7.7.77|), and was thus proposed to catalyze the homologous reaction in the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-21374| |CITS: [18154309]|.

|FRAME: CPLX0-3104| is a serine protease complex responsible for the ATP-dependent degradation of a number of proteins |CITS: [3049606]|. |FRAME: EG10156-MONOMER "ClpA"| functions as an ATP-dependent chaperone component and |FRAME: EG10158-MONOMER "ClpP"| as the serine protease component., In general, proteases recognize their substrates by specific degradation signals, known as degrons. One of the degrons that are recognized by ClpAP is the identity of the amino-terminal residue of the protein, known as N-degron. Certain residues (named "destabilizing residues") are recognized by the protease complex and mark the protein for degradation. The set of destabilizing residues in a given cell type yields a rule, called the N-end rule, which relates the in vivo half-life of a protein to the identity of its N-terminal residue |CITS: [3018930][1962196]|., ClpAP rapidly degrades proteins whose N-terminal amino acid is |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|, all of which are considered primary N-terminal destabilizing residues (Ndp) |CITS: [1962196]|. Although ClpAP alone can recognize N-end rule motifs, binding of the adaptor protein |FRAME: G6463-MONOMER "ClpS"| specifically enhances their turnover |CITS: [16467841]|. ClpS is the bacterial N-recognin, and binds to the Ndp residues Leu, Phe, Trp, or Tyr |CITS: [16467841]|. ClpS also binds to the ClpA subunits of ClpAP and thereby functions as an adaptor in mediating the processive degradation of N-end rule substrates by ClpAP., The ClpS-ClpAP complex recognizes an N-end motif using both a free alpha-amino group and the identity of the N-terminal residue. The identity of adjacent residues can also affect recognition, and the distance between the N-end residue and the folded portion of a protein is critical |CITS: [18550545]|., In organisms that possess |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.6|, |FRAME:ARG| and |FRAME: LYS| are considered secondary N-terminal destabilizing residues (Nds). When these amino acids are present at the N-terminus, they are recognized by |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.6| (encoded by the |FRAME: EG11112| gene), which attaches an |FRAME: LEU| residue to them, transforming the N-terminus to an Ndp |CITS: [4894363]|. In vitro, the enzyme can also transfer |FRAME: PHE|, but this activity does not appear to be important in vivo |CITS: [8331068]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Phosphonates| are quite abundant in nature, primarily as components of phosphonolipids, where |FRAME: CPD-1106| is analogous to ethanolamine phosphate as the constituent of phospholipids. In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics |CITS: [7765831]|. Phosphonates contain a direct carbon-phosphorus (C-P) bond in place of the more familiar carbon-oxygen-phosphorus bond, which makes their degradation challenging., Bacteria have evolved many different mechanisms for cleaving the carbon-phosphorus bond. Enzymes that have been described include the following:, 1. |FRAME: EG10719-MONOMER "Carbon-phosphorus lyase"|, a widespread but poorly characterized enzyme. See |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|., 2. Hydrolytic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.1| (phosphonatase, see |FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY|), |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.2| (shown in pathway |FRAME: P483-PWY|)., 3. Dioxygenases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.78|, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7447|., Data suggest that additional pathways for phosphonate degradation may exist (in |CITS: [21543322]|). , About This Pathway, The pathway for |FRAME: CPD-1106| degradation shown here has been experimentally studied in the Gram-negative, symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-266834| |CITS: [21543322]|, although homologous gene clusters encoding the enzymes of this pathway have been found in other bacterial genomes |CITS: [21543322][21366328]|. Although |FRAME: TAX-266834| can also degrade |FRAME: CPD-1106| via the carbon-phosphorus lyase pathway encoded by genes phnFGHIJKL (|CITS: [9882650][11481431]|), it was found to lack genes for the phosphonatase pathway (|FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY|) and evidence suggested the novel pathway shown here (in |CITS: [21543322]|)., The pathway was proposed based on identification of a putative gene cluster encoding enzymes for |FRAME: CPD-1106| degradation, deletion studies of the phn genes in this organism, and biochemical studies of recombinant PhnY and PhnA |CITS: [21543322]|., |FRAME: CPD-1106| was hypothesized to be transported into the cell by either a putative phosphate transporter (locus tag SM_b21536), or an ABC transporter (SM_b21540-43). |FRAME: CPD-1106| was proposed to be transaminated to |FRAME: CPD-551| by PHnW (SM_b21537), followed by oxidation of this compound to |FRAME: CPD-764| by phosphonoacetaldehyde dehydrogenase PhnY (SM_b21539), and hydrolysis of the carbon-phosphorus bond to |FRAME: ACET| and inorganic |FRAME: Pi| by phosphonoacetate hydrolase PhnA (SM_b21538) as shown in the pathway link |CITS: [21543322]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-20103 Rhizobitoxine| is a compound known to be synthesized by the legume symbiont |FRAME: TAX-29448| |CITS: [Owens72]| and the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-28092| |CITS: [Mitchell86]|., |FRAME: CPD-20103 Rhizobitoxine| inhibits |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.13|, which is involved in |FRAME: PWY-702 "methionine biosynthesis"| |CITS: [4872846][Xiong96]| and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.14|, which participates in |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY "ethylene production"| |CITS: [9925628]|, resulting in foliar chlorosis of soybeans, and was thus considered a plant toxin |CITS: [Johnson59][16656176][Xiong96]|. However, a beneficial role for rhizobitoxine has also been revealed. Rhizobitoxine production by |FRAME: TAX-29448| was shown to enhance nodulation and competitiveness in |FRAME: TAX-90550| (siratro), and |FRAME: TAX-157791| (mung beans) |CITS: [Duodu99][10831453]|. This effect is achieved via the inhibition of ethylene production |CITS: [16516430]|. Thus, at least for some plants, rhizobitoxine is a nodulation enhancer rather than a phytotoxin., About This Pathway, The use of transposon mutagenesis of |FRAME: TAX-29448| revelaed the presence of a gene, which was named |FRAME: G-55155|, that is essential for |FRAME: CPD-20103| production |CITS: [1317377]|. Sequence analysis suggested that the N-terminal region of RtxA resembles aminotransferases, while the C-terminal portion is similar to |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.49|., A mutant with a Tn5 insertion in a part of the |FRAME: G-55155| gene corresponding to the N-terminal part of the protein stopped producing |FRAME: CPD-9382|, a proposed precursor of |FRAME: CPD-20103|, suggesting that the N-terminal domain of RtxA catalyzes an aminotransferase activity during serinol production |CITS: [1317377][11679318]|. A similar activity, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.M7|, has been described in |FRAME: TAX-4547| (sugarcane) |CITS: [16660234]|., Interestingly, transposon insertion in the C-terminal potion of the gene abolished production of |FRAME: CPD-20104| and |FRAME: CPD-20103|, but did not affect |FRAME: CPD-9382| production. Based on the similarity of the C-terminal domain to |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.49|, which catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: CPD-667| with an alcohol, it has been proposed that the C-terminal domain of RtxA catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: CPD-667| with |FRAME: CPD-9382|. Supporting this conclusion, addition of of various compounds that participate in the methionine biosynthetic pathway (along with |FRAME: CPD-667|) resulted in a dramatic increase in |FRAME: CPD-20104| production |CITS: [11679318]|., The |FRAME: G-55156| gene, which is present downstream of the |FRAME: G-55155| gene, is highly homologous to a |FRAME: TAX-317| enzyme that has been annotated as a fatty acid desaturase based on its homology to characterized desaturases |CITS: [9353942]|. Supporting this function, RtxC includes the copper-binding signature and eight histidine residues conserved in membrane-bound desaturases |CITS: [11679318]|., Since rhizobitoxine possesses a double bond between C-3 and C-4, it has been proposed that RtxC catalyzes the desaturation of this position. A mutant with a Tn5 insertion in the |FRAME: G-55156| gene produced |FRAME: CPD-9382| and |FRAME: CPD-20104|, but not |FRAME: CPD-20103|, supporting its role in the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-20104| to |FRAME: CPD-20103| by catalyzing a desaturation reaction |CITS: [11679318][14711685]|., The rtx gene cluster contains four more genes, named rtxDEFG. While these genes are not essential for |FRAME: CPD-20103| biosynthesis, rtxDEG mutants produce less of the compound. Introduction of the full operon into |FRAME: TAX-358|, combined with supply of the precursor |FRAME: CPD-667|, resulted in production of rhizobitoxine in culture |CITS: [17227467]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NICOTINE Nicotine| is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-4093|) |CITS: [Schmeltz77]|, where it functions as a defense compound. In the plant tissue nicotine is mostly present in the |FRAME: NICOTINE| isomeric form |CITS: [Armstrong98]|, although tobacco smoke contains up to 10% of |FRAME: R-NICOTINE|, probably due to racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|)., Nicotine is composed of a pyridine ring joined with an N-methylpyrrolidine ring. The pyridine ring is derived from an intermediate in NAD biosynthesis, most likely |FRAME: NIACINE| |CITS: [Dawson56]|. The pyrrolidine ring is derived from |FRAME: CPD-7994|, a common intermediate for the tropane alkaloids that is derived from |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| |CITS: [Leete67]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5315|)., Somewhat surprisingly, the condensation of the two rings to form nicotine is largely uncharacterized at this time. A pathway has been proposed based on several observations, for example, that a hydrogen is lost from C-6 of nicotinate when it is incorporated into nicotine, while all the other hydrogens remain intact |CITS: [Friesen90]|. However, the individual steps in the pathway have not been characterized, and no enzymes have been purified. A generic "nicotine synthase" activity was detected in a crude enzyme preparation from |FRAME: TAX-4097| supplemented with |FRAME: NIACINE| and N-methyl-delta1-pyrrolinium chloride |CITS: [Friesen90]|., Once formed, nicotine may be demethylated to |FRAME: CPD-2748| by a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. Nornicotine formation in tobacco is undesired because it serves as a precursor of the carcinogen N'-nitrosonornicotine during the curing and processing of tobacco |CITS: [16192354]|.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) can occur via two distinct routes: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway) and the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (MEP pathway, this pathway) |CITS: [11078528]|. In the former, IPP is synthesized from the condensation of three acetyl-CoA molecules; in the MEP pathway IPP is synthesized via the condensation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP|., For many years, the MVA pathway was considered to be the sole source of IPP in all living organisms. However, several inconsistencies led to the discovery of the MEP pathway in bacteria and plants., In plants the MVA pathway is located in the cytosol whilst the MEP pathway is found in plastids |CITS:[LICHTENTHALER97]|. The MEP pathway is present in most eubacteria, unicellular green algae, the chloroplasts of phototrophic organisms and some unicellular eukaryotes related to photosynthetic phyla, such as the Plasmodium parasites |CITS: [15473867]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP "3-Methylbut-3-en-1-yl diphosphate"| (IPP) and its isomer |FRAME: CPD-4211| (DMAPP) are the fundamental units in isoprenoid biosynthesis. Both are produced from |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| via this pathway., D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate are initially combined to yield |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| (DOXP). DOXP is then rearranged and reduced to generate the pathway's namesake compound, |FRAME: 2-C-METHYL-D-ERYTHRITOL-4-PHOSPHATE| (MEP). , Interestingly, two rather different enzymes, that share no sequence homology, are able to catalyze this reaction - the |FRAME: DXPREDISOM-CPLX "DXR"| enzymes, and the |FRAME:MONOMER-15827 "DRL"| (DXR-like) enzymes |CITS: [20660776]|., In the third reaction MEP is converted into |FRAME: 4-CYTIDINE-5-DIPHOSPHO-2-C|, which is subsequently phosphorylated at the 2 position hydroxy group, yielding, |FRAME: 2-PHOSPHO-4-CYTIDINE-5-DIPHOSPHO-2-C-MET|. This product is then converted into, |FRAME: 2C-METH-D-ERYTHRITOL-CYCLODIPHOSPHATE|. Subsequently, it is reduced to generate |FRAME: HYDROXY-METHYL-BUTENYL-DIP| |CITS: [12198182]|., This diphosphate compound is converted by a single enzyme into a 5-6:1 ratio of IPP and DMAPP in the final step. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this ratio is subsequently adjusted to 3:7 by |FRAME: IPPISOM-MONOMER|. IPP and DMAPP serve as the basic building blocks of polyisoprenoid biosynthesis. , The difference between this pathway variant and the variant described in |FRAME: PWY-7560| is the conversion of |FRAME: HYDROXY-METHYL-BUTENYL-DIP| to |FRAME: 2C-METH-D-ERYTHRITOL-CYCLODIPHOSPHATE|. In this variant, that enzyme utilizes flavodoxin as the electron donor (|FRAME: EC-1.17.7.3|), while in the other variant the enzyme utilizes ferredoxin (|FRAME: EC-1.17.7.1|)., This pathway, which is not present in humans, is involved in production of phosphate-containing antigens recognized by γ-δ T lymphocytes |CITS: [11675382]|.

Diterpenoids are a large class of more than 10,000 known compounds, with diverse physiological and biological functions. Plants typically harbor a widely conserved subset of diterpenoids with diverse roles in chemical ecology and plant, adaptation., Two groups of terpenoids, the diterpenoid |FRAME: Kauralexins kauralexins| and the sesquiterpenoid |FRAME: Zealexins zealexins|, are well described from maize (although their biosynthesis is not well understood). These compounds participate in defense against pathogenic fungi, both above and below-ground. The kauralexins also function as insect feeding deterrents, and accumulate in response to salt and drought stress. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of a different branch of diterpenoids known as dolabralexins, Dolabralexins biosynthesis is induced by oxidative stress and elicitation with the fungal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-117187| and |FRAME: TAX-5518|. |FRAME: CPD-21266 "15,16-Epoxydolabrene"| significantly inhibited the growth of both pathogens in vitro, while |FRAME: CPD-21268| inhibition was limited to |FRAME: TAX-117187| |CITS: [29475898]|., The core compound of this branch, |FRAME: CPD-21265|, is formed from the common precursor |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| by the action of two diterpene synthases - |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.13| (|FRAME: G-14667|) and |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.196| (|FRAME: G-58304|). This compound is then converted into |FRAME: CPD-21266| and its hydroxylated form |FRAME: CPD-21267| by the cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.159| (|FRAME: G-58305|). Hydrolysis of the epoxy group of |FRAME: CPD-21267| leads to formation of a tri-hydroxylated form, which accumulates as the dominant dolabralexin pathway metabolite. It is not known whether |FRAME: CPD-21268| is formed via an enzymatic or spontaneous hydrolysis |CITS: [29475898]|., The production of dolabralexin is inducible. Increased transcript levels of all three genes was observed upon exposure to CuSO4, with |FRAME: G-14667| showing the most significant up-regulation of ~400-fold. Similarly, accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-21265|, |FRAME: CPD-21266|, and |FRAME: CPD-21268| was induced significantly by inoculation with live Fusarium spores.

|FRAME:CPD-17992 Equisetin| is a hybrid compound with a polyketide moiety condensed with amino acids and cyclized to generate 3-acyl pyrrolidinediones |CITS:[17707105]|, also referred to as tetramic acids |CITS:[18334299] [Royles95]|. Other examples for tetramic acid derived secondary metabolites are |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-7555|) |CITS:[108598]| and |FRAME:CPD-16924| (see |FRAME:PWY-7535|) |CITS:[10381407]|. |FRAME:CPD-17992 Equisetin| was first isolated and characterized as antibiotic compound from Fusarium equiseti |CITS:[15825417]|. It has since attracted much attention due to its ability to inhibit the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) integrase, responsible for infecting human DNA |CITS:[10335400]|. The HIV-I integrase inhibition of |FRAME:CPD-17992| isolated from Fusarium heterosporum also included the inhibition of preintegration complexes involved in the integration reactions |CITS:[Singh98]|. The unique pharmacological properties of |FRAME:CPD-17992| prompted efforts to achieve the total synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17992| |CITS:[15632969]|. The anti-HIV I integrase activity of |FRAME:CPD-17992| was decisive for the development of the first licensed HIV integrase inhibitor, i.e. raltegravir which turned out to be an effective and safe drug for HIV patients including pregnant women and co-infected patients |CITS:[25931236]|., It is noteworthy to mention that both |FRAME:CPD-17992| and its immediate precursor |FRAME:CPD-17993| have been labeled not mutagenic which allows to further develop such compounds as therapeutic agents |CITS:[Alad09]|. |FRAME:CPD-17992 Equisetin| has been shown to exhibit activity against several gram-positive bacteria and one gram-negative bacteria (Neisseria perflava) but not against other gram-negative bacterial species |CITS:[541270]|. For the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-17993| phytotoxicity of the compound which affects root and shoot growth has been reported |CITS:[12620323]| as well as a significant activity against the gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus subtilis causing infections of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract of humans, respectively |CITS:[12132686]|., The interaction of polyketide synthases (PKS) and non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS) in the biosynthesis of fungal hybrid secondary metabolites are well documented |CITS:[18804170]|. The importance of iterative type I polyketide synthases (IPKSs) which belong to the highly reducing PKSs (HR-PKSs) |CITS:[22938194]| and are composed of various enzymatically active domains including an enoylreductase (ER) domain (within the PKS or as an stand-alone protein) |CITS:[22733743]| for the formation of a wide array of polyketide moieties has been demonstrated and shown to significantly contribute to the vast structural diversity of secondary compounds produced by fungal PKS-NRPS hybrids |CITS:[23225733]|. The metabolic potential of the genus Fusarium for producing such compounds has been revealed through comparative analysis of 10 different Fusarium species which led to the identification of 52 PKS and 52 NRPS orthology groups of which most remain to be explored |CITS:[25543026]|. , Sequencing the genome of Fusarium heterosporum ATCC 74349 and searching the genome for polyketide synthase (PKS) and polyketide synthase (PKS)-non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) hybrids with homology to the |FRAME:CPLX-8893| (see |FRAME:PWY-7535| resulted in the identification of the PKS-NRPS gene eqxS and the biosynthetic gene cluster for the |FRAME:PWY-7669|. The formation of the polyketide moiety most probably arrives through the condensation of 8 |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| and the subsequent multiple methylation of the nascent polyketide by the C-methyltransferase (MT) domain of the PKS |CITS:[Schmidt15]|. Targeted knocking out of genes in the cluster and metabolic profiling of the resultant mutants allowed to outline the |FRAME:PWY-7669| as displayed above. The deletion of the PKS-NRPS equisetin synthetase (eqxS) resulted in the complete disappearance of |FRAME:CPD-17992| which was also true when eqxC encoding for the trans-enoyl reductase (ER) was disrupted. In addition, pyrophosphate exchange assays carried out with the heterologously expressed and purified adenylation (A) domain of the NRPS pointed out the strong preference of |FRAME:SER| which is a component of the structure of |FRAME:CPD-17992| and thus further supported the molecular role of the eqxS encoded PKS-NRPS in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17992| |CITS:[23614392]|. , The release and cyclization mechanism of the ACP-product has been shown to occur via a Dieckmann condensation/cyclization catalyzed by the C-terminal reductive (R) domain of the NRPS which is a Dieckmann cyclase and not a reductase |CITS:[18652469]| and produces the intermediate of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-24550| |CITS:[23614392]|. , Another enzyme, the Diels-Alderase Eqx3 is involved in endo-selective Diels-Alder cycloaddition to form the decalin ring of |FRAME: CPD-17992| from the PKS product |FRAME: CPD-24550| |CITS: [23614392]|. The enzyme was also shown to control the stereochemistry of the decalin component of the related |FRAME:CPD-17998| |CITS:[25770422]|., The molecular function of the trichosetin N-methyltransferase encoded by eqxD forming the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17992|, was demonstrated in the ΔeqxD mutant which accumulated the desmethyl derivative of |FRAME:CPD-17992|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17993| |CITS:[23614392]|.

Summary: General Background, Flavanone glycosides such as the sugar derivatives of naringenin (this pathway) and hesperitin (|FRAME:PWY-5105|) are the dominant group of flavonoids found in the genus |FRAME:TAX-2706| |CITS: [10552686][16428836]| but are rather minor constituents in the closely related genus Fortunella |CITS: [11397442]|. The content of flavanone glycosides and their corresponding aglycones undergoes significant changes upon the attack of the phytopathogen Phytophthora citrophthora, the agent for the brown rot lesion in citrus fruits. It was discussed that these compounds participate in the defense mechanism of |FRAME:TAX-2706| species and may act as fungicides |CITS: [15053528]|. The 2"-O-rhamnoside of naringenin, i.e. naringin has been investigated with respect to its ability to scavenge oxygen free radicals involved in the oxidation of hemoglobin |CITS: [12967034]|, lowering the plasma total cholesterol level |CITS: [14738906]| and blocking the cytotoxity and apoptosis of cytosine arabinoside (Ara-C), a chemotherapeutical drug used for acute leukemia |CITS: [15135655]|., The sugar substitution of flavanone glycosides primarily determines the taste of citrus fruits. The bitterness of certain citrus species such as grapefruit (|FRAME:TAX-37656|), bitter orange (|FRAME:TAX-43166|) and pummelo (|FRAME:TAX-37334|) is caused by flavanone neohesperidosides, e.g. naringin. Flavanone rutinoside, e.g. narirutin are tasteless and occur predominantly in sweet citrus fruits such as orange (|FRAME:TAX-2711|) and mandarin (Citrus reticulata) |CITS: [15361143]|. The chemical reason for bitter or tasteless is how L-rhamnose is attached to the flavanone 7-O-glucosides. The bitter neohesperidoside consists of a rhamnose attached via the C-2 hydroxyl group of glucose (1-2 binding) whereas the tasteless rutinoside have the L-rhamnose attached to the C-6 hydroxyl group of the glucose moiety (1-6 binding) |CITS: [13715944]| |CITS: [HOROWITZ69]|. Interestingly, the seminatural produced dihydrochalcones of flavanones, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-7067| and |FRAME:CPD-7069| (NHDC) are up to 1.500 times sweeter than sucrose making them a desired low-calories sweetener and flavor enhancer |CITS: [16332119][HOROWITZ69]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with the formation of prunin, i.e. naringenin 7-O-glucoside. The enzyme catalyzing the 7-O-glucosylation has been purified from various plants such as |FRAME:TAX-43166| |CITS: [LEWINSOHN89A]|, |FRAME:TAX-37334| |CITS: [LEWINSOHN89B]|, |FRAME:TAX-37656| |CITS: [2171434]| |CITS: [MCINTOSH90]| and |FRAME:TAX-4102| |CITS: [10626374]|. However, prunin does not accumulate to a significant amount |CITS: [10552686]| , |CITS: [16428836]| and is often found in immature fruits |CITS: [12900888]| |CITS: [BERHOW89]|. Prunin appears to be further metabolized rather fast forming the diglycosylated flavanones naringin and narirutin |CITS: [LEWINSOHN86]|., The attachment of L-rhamnose to the various positions of the glucosyl moiety is carried out by position specific flavanone 7-O-glucoside rhamnosyltransferases producing the diglycosyl flavanoids that can accumulate up to 75% of dry weight |CITS: [12232031]|. L-rhamnose is transferred in plants either via the sugar donor dTDP-rhamnose (|FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|) as reported for mung beans |CITS: [13864834]| or via the most certainly more general sugar donor UDP-rhamnose (|FRAME:PWY-3261|) |CITS: [1898019]| |CITS: [1939145]| |CITS: [LEWINSOHN89B]|. Although the formation of narirutin catalyzed by the UDP-rhamnose:flavanone-7-O-glucoside-6"-O-rhamnosyltransferase has been demonstrated |CITS: [LEWINSOHN89B]| its molecular characterization still requires further research. In contrast, the UDP-rhamnose:flavanone-7-O-glucoside-2"-O-rhamnosyltransferase has been purified to homogeneity |CITS: [1939145]| and the gene encoding the enzyme isolated and functionally characterized |CITS: [15361143]|.

Summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., The best characterized wall teichoic acids are those from |FRAME: TAX-224308| and |FRAME: TAX-655816|, in which the polymeric units are |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY "glycerol phosphate"| and |FRAME: PWY-7815 "ribitol phosphate"|, respectively |CITS: [13684313]|. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 1-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. The anomeric phosphate of the linkage unit is covalently attached to peptidoglycan (PG) via a phosphodiester bond to the C6 hydroxyl of N-acetylmuramate., It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: PWY-7819 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]|. , Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, The main form of the wall teichoic acids in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| and |FRAME: TAX-1280| is a poly(ribitol phosphate) polymer. This polymer of |FRAME: TAX-1280| is composed of about 30-50 repeating units, and is linked to the peptidoglycan moiety by the highly conserved linkage unit (in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| there is a single glycerol phosphate residue in the linkage unit, while in |FRAME: TAX-1280| there are two). The repeating ribitol phosphate units are decorated by monosacharides (|FRAME: GLC| in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| in |FRAME: TAX-1280|) and |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residues., The biosynthetic process can be divided into several main steps: first, the linkage unit is synthesized, attached to an undecaprenol lipid carrier. Next, the polymeric chain is added, one unit at a time, and is decorated with monosaccharides. The polymer is subsequently translocated across the cytoplasmic membrane by an ABC transporter, D-alanylated, and ultimately cross-linked to the cell wall peptidoglycan, upon which the liberated undecaoprenyl carrier is recycled. A more detailed description follows:, The first step is the attachment of an |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| molecule to the lipid carrier |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33 "EC 2.7.8.33"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44679| gene |CITS: [14758355]|. The |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| has to be activated, in the form of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (for more information on the acivation of this donor molecule see the pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|)., Next, an activated |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| unit is added by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.187 "EC 2.4.1.187"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44684| gene, to generate an N-acetyl-mannosaminyl-β-(1->4)-N-acetyl-glucosamine disaccharide, attached to the lipid |CITS: [18215769]|., UDP-N-acetyl-mannosamine is synthesized from UDP-N-acetyl-glocasamine by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.187 "EC 2.4.1.187, UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44682| gene |CITS: [27144276]|. The last step in the synthesis of the linkage unit is the addition of two glycerol-phosphate units, which is performed by two different enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-44683| and |FRAME: G-44677|, respectively |CITS: [18215769]|. The glycerol-phosphate units have to be activated as well, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-606|, which is generated from |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.39|, the product of the |FRAME: G-44685| gene |CITS: [12637027]|., Once the linkage unit is ready, |FRAME: MONOMER-19978|, encoded by |FRAME: G-44678|, adds multiple |FRAME: CPD-372| units |CITS: [16595020]|. |FRAME: CPD-372| is formed from |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| by the action of the products of the |FRAME: G-44686| and |FRAME: G-44687| genes |CITS: [15362865]|., The ribitol molecules are glycosylated at the C-2 hydroxyl groups with |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, which is attached in two differenent anomeric configurations by two different glycosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44681| and |FRAME: G-44680| genes |CITS: [20185825][23027967]|., Following glycosylation, the lipid-anchored polymer is exported via the membrane to the external side by a dedicated ABC-type transporter encoded by the |FRAME: G-44688| and |FRAME: G-44689| genes |CITS: [21280653]|. At that location the polymer is modified further by D-alanylation of the ribitol units at the C-4 hydroxyl groups, which is carried by a complex system encoded by the dlt operon |CITS: [10085071]|. , Finally, the complete teichoic acid is hooked through its linkage unit on the C-6 of a MurNAc residue of a growing peptidoglycan chain in a transfer reaction catalyzed by any of three members of the LCP (LytR-CpsA-Psr) protein family, releasing the undecaprenyl anchor |CITS:[23935043]|., The tar genes that encode the pathway's enzymes are located in a 50 kbp region of the chromosome |CITS: [11882717]|. Mutations that disrupt the biosynthesis of wall teichoic acids in |FRAME: TAX-1280| result in a morphological change of the cell from rod shape to a sphere shape, and were initially known as rod mutations. The mutants are compromised and can grow only under a narrow range of conditions, they manifest increased sensitivity to temperature and certain buffer components, and tend to aggregate in culture. Mutants lacking both LTA and WTA are non-viable |CITS: [19229300]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.109|) are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, The first step of this pathway involves the conversion of |FRAME: GLT| to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via an oxidative deamination reaction. The 2-oxo acid is subsequently reduced to |FRAME: R-2-HYDROXYGLUTARATE| in a reaction that consumes one reducing equivalent. The product is activated to its CoA ester and dehydrated to |FRAME: GLUTACONYL-COA|. This is followed by decarboxylation that forms |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA| |CITS: [Lengeler99]|., |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA Crotonyl-CoA| is reduced to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| at the expense of a second reducing equivalent. The latter can be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, leading to formation of |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| and ATP (via |FRAME: PWY0-1312|)., This pathway is found in organisms living in anoxic niches within humans and animals, including members of the genera |FRAME:TAX-904|, |FRAME:TAX-1485|, |FRAME:TAX-848| and |FRAME: TAX-1257|. Another major pathway by which glutamate can be fermented is the methylaspartate pathway, which is used by several |FRAME:TAX-1485| and enterobacteria spp. That pathway also produces butanoate, but in addition produces |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| (see |FRAME:GLUDEG-II-PWY|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-14834 Noscapine| is an isoquinoline alkaloid found in the opium poppy (|FRAME: TAX-3469|). It has been used as a cough suppressant and was found to have antitumor activity due to its tubulin-binding and apoptosis-inducing effects in tumor cells |CITS: [19149691]|. Unlike many other clinically used alkaloids from the morphinan subclass of isoquinoline alkaloids, for example |FRAME: CODEINE|, noscapine is not pain-killing and is also not addictive., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-14834| involves 11 enzymatic reactions, which convert the 1-benzylisoquinoline backbone of |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| to the phthalide isoquinoline scaffold. Many of the genes encoding the pathway's enzymes are located in a complex ten-gene cluster spanning a 220 kb chromosome region |CITS: [22653730]|., The pathway starts with formation of a methylene bridge in |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| to generates the protoberberine |FRAME: S-SCOULERINE|, which is functionalized via 9-O-methylation |CITS: [22535422]|, closure of a methylenedioxy bridge on the isoquinoline moiety |CITS: [24316226]|, N-methylation producing a quaternary intermediate |CITS: [17389594]|, three hydroxylations at C1 |CITS: [24324259]|, C8 and C13 |CITS: [25485687]|, 4'-O-methylation |CITS: [27378283][29723437]|, and 13-O-acetylation |CITS: [25485687]|. The acetylation protects the 13-hydroxyl position from precocious hemiacetal formation, ensuring that the seco-berbine scaffold does not undergo rearrangement to the phthalide isoquinoline backbone until the acetyl ester is hydrolyzed by the |FRAME: G-15445| carboxylesterase towards the end of the pathway. Dehydrogenation completes the pathway via the formation of a lactone from the hemiacetal |CITS: [24708518]|.
