Summary: General Background, Flavones such as apigenin and luteolin represent one of the most abundant and important , subclasses of the 9000 flavonoids described so far |CITS: [10652133]|. Flavones belong to the most widespread compounds , in plants and have been found in all major land-plant lineages. , The biosynthesis of flavones has been studied intensively because of their contribution to unique physiological and , developmental processes in plants. Luteolin has a defined role as a signalling molecule involved in the induction and , expression of nodulation genes |CITS: [3738520]|. Flavones in general have been demonstrated to be significantly , involved in the evolvement of the preferred attractant for bee pollinators, i.e. blue flower colours which are restricted to the , higher developed angiosperm plant families |CITS: [11130659]|. In addition, flavones possess antioxidative activity , |CITS: [11516175]| frequently employed in the prevention of cancer and coronary heart disease |CITS: [16137727]|. , About This Pathway, The oxidation of flavanones to flavones is catalyzed by flavone synthases introducing a , double bound between the C atoms 2 and 3 of the C-ring. Interestingly, the biosynthesis of flavone is carried out by two , completely different flavone synthases, i.e. flavone synthase I (EC 1.14.11.22) and flavone synthase II. , While flavone synthase II (FNS II), a membrane bound cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase is found in many , plant families the soluble dioxygenase flavone synthase I (FNS I) has only been isolated from members of the Apiacea , family to date |CITS: [2221917]|. FNS I belongs to the family of 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases which are involved , in many different metabolic processes of plants, bacteria, fungi and animals |CITS: [11516175]|. Among the five , 2-oxoglutarate-dependent enzymes involved in flavonoid biosynthesis (compare |FRAME:PWY-3101|) FNS I is considered , highly pathway specific because of its distinct substrate specificity |CITS: [12782296]|., The flavone synthases I and II catalyze the 2,3-desaturation of the flavanone in one step, i.e. the formation of apigenin , from naringnin and luteollin from eriodictyol, respectively (this pathway). Although it had been suggested that FSN I may , catalyze a sequential C3 hydroxylation and dehydration a vicinal desaturation without the release of a free intermediate , was experimentally verified |CITS: [12782296]|. The formation of the dihydroxylated B-ring compound luteolin requires an , additional hydroxylation step carried out by the cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase flavonoid 3'(β)-hydroxylase , |CITS: [11773526]| |CITS: [UEYAMA02]|. The two possible routes leading to luteolin (via eridictyol or apigenin) are displayed , in this pathway.

|FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| is the common biogenetic intermediate for all monoterpenoid indole alkaloids |CITS: [28827772]|. This pathway describes its biosynthesis, starting from the earlier intermediate |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE|. The pathway leading to production of |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| is described in |FRAME: PWY-5290|., This pathway starts with |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.105|, which removes the glucose moiety from |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE| |CITS: [11985599]|, resulting in an active product (|FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE-AGLYCONE|) that spontaneously isomerizes to a number of products, including |FRAME: CPD-21552| and |FRAME: 421-DEHYDROGEISSOSCHIZINE| |CITS: [29511102]|. The latter is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.36| into |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE|., The activity of |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.36|, has been reported from |FRAME: TAX-4058| cell extracts already in 1979. Under NADPH regenerating conditions, |FRAME: 421-DEHYDROGEISSOSCHIZINE| was transformed to |FRAME: GEISSOSCHIZINE| |CITS: [Rueffer79]|. Later a partially purified enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-4058| was shown to catalyze the reverse reaction |CITS: [Pfitzner82]|. The |FRAME: G-58792| gene encoding the enzyme was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-4058| in 2017 |CITS: [28827772]|.

General Background, Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum)., The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids., Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|)., While the majority of bile acids (up to 97%) are reabsorbed in the ileum and return to the liver, the remaining 3% enter the large intestine, where they are modified by gut bacteria. The main modifications are C24-amide hydrolysis and 7α-dehydroxylation, which form the secondary bile acids |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| (see |FRAME: PWY-7754|). However, many additional transformations occur. Although |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| are the most abundant secondary bile acids, ~50 different secondary bile acids have been detected in human feces |CITS: [6631236]|., The most abundant bile acids in the healthy human gut after |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| are |FRAME: CPD-18796| and |FRAME: CPD-18797| (at about 50 μM). Iso-bile acids differ from bile acids in the configuration of their 3-hydroxy group (β instead of α). While the biological activities of iso-bile acids are not well understood, they have less detergent activity and are less toxic to bacteria |CITS: [26192599]|., About This Pathway, Early studies have shown that the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-84112| and |FRAME: TAX-1502| convert primary and secondary bile acids into their 3β isomers through 3-oxo intermediates |CITS: [4581568][6947718][6271056][2866156]|. The enzyme that converts the 3α-OH group into an oxo group was called 3α-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase |CITS: [201289][39496]|, while the enzyme that converts the oxo group to a 3β-OH group was named 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase |CITS: [Edenharder89]|. Both enzymes were dependent on nicotinamide cofactors, and enzymes depending on both NAD(H) and NADP(H) were described from different species. This pathway describes the NAD(H)-dependent enzymes, NADP(H)-dependent enzymes are described in |FRAME: PWY-7756|., The genes encoding these enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-84112| were found by searching for genes similar to those encoding |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.395| |CITS: [7766153][10698778][19464381]|. 11 putative genes were identified, cloned with an N-terminal His6 tag, and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [26192599]|. Assays performed with cell lysates of the recombinant hosts identified one candidate bile acid 3α-dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-44401|) and two candidate bile acid 3β-dehydrogenases (|FRAME: G-44403| and Elen_1325). These enzymes were purified to homogeneity, and their activity was verified. All three enzyme were specific for NAD(H).

Names: Salmonella enterica serotype O:3,10 O antigen biosynthesis // group E Salmonella O antigen biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The O antigen of group E |FRAME: TAX-590| strains corresponds to serogroups O3 and O10. Group E was initially subdivided into groups E1, E2, E3 and E4, based on serology. However, the repeat unit in all of these strains is synthesized by enzymes encoded by identical gene clusters. The E2 and E3 variants of the E1 structure are due to presence of bacteriophages, and correspond to the O15 and O34 epitopes, respectively. In these strains the repeat units are connected by a β(1→6) linkage instead of an α linkage, due to a bacteriophage-encoded polymerase. The bacteriophage also suppresses the native polymerase. In E3 strains there is also an additional glucose residue attached to the galactose residue by β(1→4) linkage by a bacteriophage-encoded enzyme |CITS: [14253440][4970574][4970573][17825342][19091116]|. In E4 strains a glucose residue is added to the galactose residue by a α(1→6) linkage by an uncharacterized locus named oafC, generating serogroup O19 |CITS: [23874940]|. All of these antigens are produced by a Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O-antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., The first step in Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways is the addition of a sugar phosphate residue to |FRAME: CPD-9646| (Und-P) to form the undecaprenyl diphosphate-linked sugar. Most O antigens found in |FRAME: TAX-590| species start with GlcNAc or GalNAc and their biosynthesis is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). However, the Salmonella O antigens belonging to serogroups O2 (A), O4 (B), O8 (C2C3), O9 (D1), O9,46 (D2), O9,46,27 (D3), O3,10 (E1E3), and O1,3,19 (E4) form a distinct set that is characterized by having a Gal residue as the first sugar of the O unit., The enzyme responsible for the initiation of these pathways is |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.6| (WbaP, previously called RfbP |CITS: [9004408]|). The use of Gal as initial sugar appeared in |FRAME: TAX-590| after its divergence from |FRAME: TAX-561|, but the eight Gal-initiated O antigens have grown to be very important in this species |CITS: [23874940]|., The repeat unit of E strains does not contain a dideoxyhexose side chain. In addition, the α-mannosyl transferase gene wbaU that is found in B strains is replaced by a β-specific 1-mannosyl transferase gene, which was named |FRAME: G-80930| |CITS: [Zhao98][10520265]|., Following the completion of the synthesis of a repeat unit, the flippase Wzx flips the full molecule to the other side of the membrane, where the Wzy polymerase transfers additional repeat units from their anchor to a single elongating molecule. The Wzz protein ensures termination of the polimerization once the correct chain length has been achieved., |FRAME: TAX-590| strains belonging to group E1 contain a WzyE-type polymerase that links the repeat units by an α(1,6) linkage between the galactose and the mannose residues [α-D-Gal-(1→6)-β-D-Man] |CITS: [23874940]|. This enzyme is not related to the WzyB-type polymerase found in B2 and D3 strains, which also forms an α(1,6) linkage.

Summary: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) and potato (Solanum tuberosum) are staple vegetable crops which constitute a large part of the daily diet worldwide. Besides being a source for starch (energy), protein, fiber and vitamins, potato and tomato also contain specialized (secondary) metabolites with adverse nutritive properties |CITS:[17090106]|. Steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-17696| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-3|) and derivatives thereof are typically found in the Solanaceae family |CITS:[Ripperger98]| and considered antinutritional compounds |CITS:[23788733]| which cannot completely be removed from food |CITS:[17090106]|. In certain concentrations or consumed by susceptible persons steroidal glycoalkaloids may be even toxic, causing digestive problems and hamper the absorption of nutrients |CITS:[22069686] [25556315]|. |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-Tomatine| and derivatives have been found to disrupt the integrity of membranes causing the leakage of electrolytes and subsequent depolarization of membrane potential |CITS:[Steel88] [1390841]|., On the other side, steroidal alkaloids have been reported to serve as phytoanticipins and provide a protective shield against pathogens of all kinds including bacteria and fungi and are even effective against animals and other plants |CITS:[Guntner97] [18944982] [18624637] [Hoagland09]|. Some fungal and bacterial pathogens have developed a detoxifying response towards steroidal glycoalkaloids by attacking the |FRAME:CPD-18735| moiety of |FRAME:CPD-17696|, a modification which may reduce the toxicity for the attackers (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-5 |) |CITS:[18944982] [10477313]|. In addition, tomato steroidal alkaloids such as the aglycon |FRAME:CPD-18644|, the glycosylated |FRAME:CPD-17696| and other Solanaceae glycoalkaloids have been proven to possess many beneficial traits for humans and exhibit anticarcinogenic, cardioprotective and immunostimulating properties (summarized in |CITS:[24079774] [25821990]|). |FRAME:CPD-13080 Solasodine| and its glucosylated derivative |FRAME:CPD-13081| may also act as phytoalexins and are increasingly formed when plants are attacked by pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum. The mode of action in such cases is the inhibition of hyphae formation in the fungus |CITS:[23229144]|. The many facets of steroidal glycoalkaloids and respective aglycones with respect to their antimicrobial, anticancer, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory properties have been addressed in various reviews |CITS:[21401040]|., More than 120 steroidal glycoalkaloids have been observed in various organs of tomato and potato |CITS:[18266924] [19053181] [18441227] [23941899] [20113441]|. Whereas |FRAME:CPD-9214| and |FRAME:CPD-9211| are the principal glycoalkaloids found in Solanum tuberosum (see |FRAME:PWY-5666|), |FRAME:CPD-17696| (this pathway) is the major steroidal glycoalkaloid in green tissues (leaves and fruits) of Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[15053555]|. The tomato pathway(s) that, with the onset of fruit maturation, lead to further decorated steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-18747| are largely unknown but a number of derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-17696| have been identified by metabolic profiling |CITS:[23788733] [19415927]|., |FRAME:CPD-13080 Solasodine| is the main steroidal alkaloid aglycone in Solanum melongena from which the steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-13081|, |FRAME:CPD-18738| and others are formed in unripe fruits |CITS:[DeWaal60] [Bajaj79]|. Together with the steroidal saponins (melongosides), which are derivatives of e.g. |FRAME:CPD-15437| and accumulate in the roots |CITS:[Kintia85a] [Kintia85b]|, they form the bulk of steroidal glycosides found in this plant. Solanum melongena is able to synthesize both steroidal saponins and glycoalkaloids and has therefore been a suitable subject for studying the respective pathways |CITS:[Heftmann83] [Tschesche80]|. In comparison to the high variety and number of steroidal saponins in plants the glycoalkaloids show less diversity and are scarcer in nature |CITS:[Hostettmann95]| which make the Solaneceae the best resource for this type of steroidal glycosides as shown in analyses of various Solanum tuberosum cultivars |CITS:[18616273]| and other members of the Solaneceae family |CITS:[17265223]|., The 10 genes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17696| (see also |FRAME:PWY18C3-2|) in Solanum lycopersicum are mostly organized in gene clusters on chromosome 7 (6 genes) and chromosome 12 (2 genes) |CITS:[23788733]|. The first conversion of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| to |FRAME:CPD-14702| is part of a more complex reaction and has been shown to be possibly catalyzed by an cytochrome P450 dependent oxygenase named GAME7 (Glycoalkaloid metabolism = GAME) |CITS:[Umemoto12]| but detailed genetic and biochemical experiments are still outstanding. The two cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases catalyzing the C-22 and C-26-hydroxylation have been characterized in Solanum tuberosum by downregulating the responsive genes (PGA2 and 1) and confirming the respective hydroxylation steps using recombinant expressed and purified PGA2, i.e. cholesterol 22-hydroxylase and PGA1. i.e. 22-hydroxycholesterol 26-hydroxylase |CITS:[27307258]|. One of the elucidated reactions immediately following the 22,26-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| is the hydroxylation of the 16α-position catalyzed by a steroid 16α-hydroxylase, which has been characterized from both Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum tuberosum |CITS:[28754839]|. Those steps in the pathway have also have been elucidated by virus induced gene silencing (VIGS), transgenic plants and metabolic profiling as well as in vitro assays with purified recombinant enzymes |CITS:[23788733] [23473422]|. , The reaction that generates |FRAME:CPD-17697| from |FRAME:CPD-22267| has not yet been elucidated but the subsequent series of glycosylations adding the |FRAME:CPD-18735| to |FRAME:CPD-17697| could be experimentally verified. It appears that the recently described GAME25 extends the biosynthetic sequence beyond the formation of |FRAME:CPD-13080| towards |FRAME:CPD-22270| in |FRAME:PWY18C3-2|, and clarified the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-22267| to |FRAME:CPD-17697| in the |FRAME:PWY18C3-3|. GAME25 belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family and has been demonstrated to exhibit dual activities, one as 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and the other as Δ5,4 isomerase. The GAME25 catalyzed reaction is however just one out of three reactions that convert unsaturated steroidal alkaloids (SG) towards saturated SGs. While the remaining two reductase reactions remain to be elucidated, the blocking of the GAME25 is already sufficient to redirect the formation of saturated SGAs towards the unsaturated SGAs. However, many of the cultivated species such as potato and eggplant do not produce saturated SGAs because, in spite of functioning GAME25 genes the remaining two conversions towards saturated SGAs might have been lost during domestication |CITS:[29784829]|., The GAME1 encoded tomatidine 3-O-galactosyltransferase |CITS:[23788733] [22180624] [Zimowski98]| first adds |FRAME:ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| which is followed by two glucosylations carried out by the GAME17 and GAME18 encoded tomatine galactoside glucosyltransferase and γ-tomatine glucosyltransferase, respectively |CITS:[23788733]|. The last step in the pathway that generates the final product |FRAME:CPD-17696| is catalyzed by the GAME2 encoded β1-tomatine xylosyltransferase |CITS:[23788733]|., The glycosylation of |FRAME:CPD-13080| is carried out by glycosyltransferases from a variety of plant species. Bioinformatics and genetic analyses allowed to document specific domains in glycosyltransferases and sterol glycosyltransferases in particular which makes the identification of newly detected enzymes and their possible molecular function significantly more efficient |CITS:[10521532] [12538870]|. |FRAME:CPD-13080 Solasodine| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-2|) is glycosylated in various species of the Solaneceae family. A solasodine 3-O-glucosyltransferase has been observed in protein extracts from leaves of eggplant (Solanum melongena) seedlings |CITS:[Paczkowski94]|. In addition, the solasodine 3-O-glycosyltransferase encoded by GT4A from Solanum aculeatissimum has been cloned, recombinant expressed and functionally characterized |CITS:[15821879] [17204296]|. The galactosylation of |FRAME:CPD-13080| to form |FRAME:CPD-18738| has been observed in Solanum lycopersicum where the GAME1 codes for a tomatidine 3-O-galactosyltransferase but shows comparable activities towards |FRAME:CPD-13080| |CITS:[Zimowski98]|. Moreover, the glycosyltransferase of Solanum tuberosum (SGT1) was much more active with |FRAME:CPD-14553| than with |FRAME:CPD-12575| hence acting as galactosyltransferase rather than glucosyltransferase |CITS:[McCue05] [17204296]|.

|FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN "Riboflavin"| is the precursor for the essential flavin cofactors |FRAME:FMN| and |FRAME:FAD|, which are used in a wide variety of redox reactions. Most archaea, bacteria, fungi and plants are able to produce |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN| de novo (see |FRAME: RIBOSYN2-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-6167|, and |FRAME: PWY-6168|). However, some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1351|, |FRAME: TAX-1639|, and |FRAME: TAX-1314| |CITS: [12136096]|, as well as all mammals, are not able to produce it. These organisms depend on acquiring |FRAME:RIBOFLAVIN| by transport reactions or by nutrition, but are able to cnovert it to |FRAME:FMN| and |FRAME:FAD|. Because mammals are not able to produce riboflavin, it is known as vitamin B2., In most bacteria and plants these two reactions are carried out by a single multifunctional enzyme (type I FADS) that is unrelated to the mammalian enzymes, making the bacterial enzyme a potential target for a new class of antibiotics |CITS: [12142426]|. Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1639|, possess a type II enzyme that can only catalyze the phosphorylation of FMN to FAD |CITS: [31132361]|., In fungi and animals these enzymatic activities are carried out by two enzymes encoded by distinct genes that are often tightly associated. The mammalian |FRAME: HS05938-MONOMER| is located in the cytosol, while the |FRAME: HS08520-MONOMER| exists in two isoforms - a shorter cytosolic isoform that associates with |FRAME: HS05938-MONOMER| |CITS: [3034893]|, and a longer mitochondrial isoform |CITS: [16643857][20060505]|. Both isoforms exhibit FAD synthetase activity.

Summary: Methanotrophic bacteria oxidize |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: METOH| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which can be assimilated to form intermediates of the central metabolic pathways. These intermediate compounds are subsequently used for biosynthesis |CITS:[353476][6768606][2110811]|. , There are two known pathways that are used by methanotrophic bacteria for the assimilation of formaldehyde: the serine pathway (this pathway) and the |FRAME: PWY-1861 "RuMP cycle"| |CITS: [8801441]|., In the first reaction of the serine pathway, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which is carried by |FRAME: THF-GLU-N THF| in the form of |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate|, is transferred to |FRAME: GLY| to form |FRAME: SER|. The reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1| (SHMT). Two such enzymes, one for assimilation of formaldehyde and one for biosynthesis of glycine from serine, are known in |FRAME: TAX-272630| and |FRAME: TAX-410| |CITS: [241747]|., In the next step |FRAME: SER| is transaminated with |FRAME: GLYOX| as the amino group acceptor by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, to produce |FRAME: OH-PYR| and |FRAME: GLY| (the glycine can be recycled and serve as a substrate for serine hydroxymethyltransferase). |FRAME: OH-PYR Hydroxypyruvate| is reduced to |FRAME: GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.81|, followed by phosphorylation by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.165| to produce |FRAME: 2-PG|., At this point there is a split in the pathway. Some of the |FRAME: 2-PG| is converted by |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.11| to |FRAME: G3P|, which is an intermediate of the central metabolic pathways, and is used for biosynthesis, while the rest of the |FRAME: 2-PG| is converted by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.11| to |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|., |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31|, then catalyzes the fixation of carbon dioxide, conveting |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which is reduced to |FRAME: MAL| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37|. |FRAME: CPD-208 "Malyl coenzyme A"| is formed in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.9| and is cleaved by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.24| into |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: GLYOX|., When the last two enzymes (EC 6.2.1.9 and EC 4.1.3.24), as well as EC 1.1.1.81 and EC 2.7.1.165, are found in methylotrophs, they indicate the presence of the serine pathway |CITS: [6768606][1515161][8092853]|., The fate of the |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| depends on wheher the organism possesses the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.1|, which is a key enzyme of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|. If the enzyme is present, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| is converted to glyoxylate by the glyoxylate cycle. However, if the enzyme is missing, as is the case in |FRAME: TAX-272630|, it is converted by the |FRAME: PWY-5741| |CITS: [ 22105076]|. In both cases the resulting |FRAME: GLYOX| can serve as substrate for |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, regenerating glycine and closing the circle., The net balance of this cycle is the fixation of two mols of |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and 1 mol of CO<SUB>2</SUB> into 1 mol of |FRAME: G3P|, which is used for biosynthesis, at the expense of 3 mols ATP and the oxidation of 3 mols of NAD(P)H. This does not include the reduction/oxidation of NAD(P)H and/or |FRAME: Etf "electron-transfer flavoprotein"| that occur in the segments of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS| or |FRAME: PWY-5741|., Please note that reaction of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, appears twice in the diagram, (once for the reaction |FRAME: SER| to |FRAME: OH-PYR|, and once for the reaction |FRAME: GLYOX| to |FRAME: GLY|) even though in reality the two reactions are coupled.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-1488| is a Gram-positive anaerobe of commercial importance, capable of fermenting a variety of sugars to solvents and acids. During acidogenesis |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| are produced, while solventogenesis yields |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ACETONE|, and |FRAME: BUTANOL|. The production of acetone, and butanol by |FRAME: TAX-1488| was a thriving industrial process, but lost its importance since the fermentation could no longer compete economically with the chemical synthesis of solvents from petroleum., In continuous culture, |FRAME: TAX-1488| can be maintained in three different stable metabolic states |CITS: [Girbal95]|: acidogenic - production of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| when grown at neutral pH on glucose (see |FRAME: PWY-6590|), solventogenic - production of |FRAME: ACETONE|, |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH| when grown at low pH on glucose (|FRAME: PWY-6594|), and alcohologenic - formation of |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH| but not |FRAME: ACETONE| when grown at neutral pH under conditions of high NAD(P)H availability. Despite numerous physiological studies, it is still unclear how the metabolic switch from acid to solvent production is regulated at the molecular level |CITS: [10191392]|. Once this metabolic transition has been initiated, most of the excreted acids are taken up and converted into solvents, The pathway from |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is a major carbon metabolism channel and in |FRAME: TAX-1488| contains the branch points to solventogenesis and acidogenesis. , The three key intermediates are |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA |, and |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|. |FRAME:ACETYL-COA Acetyl-CoA| is a branching point for the production of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: ETOH|.  |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA Acetoacetyl-CoA| is the branching point for |FRAME: ACETONE| production, and |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is the branching point for |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| and |FRAME: BUTANOL| production., For more information about the pathways leading to fermentation of individual compounds, please look at the respective sub-pathways - |FRAME: PWY-6587|, |FRAME: P142-PWY|, |FRAME: CENTFERM-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-6583| and |FRAME: PWY-6588|.

Names: 9-lipoxygenase and 9-allene oxide synthase pathway // 9-LOX and 9-AOS pathway
Summary: Lipoxygenases (LOX) are ubiquitous enzymes in eukaryotes. Depending on the positional specificities, they are further classified as 9-LOX and 13-LOX, converting poly unsaturated fatty acids to 9-hydroperoxides and 13-hydroperoxides, respectively.  In plants, most reported LOXs are 13-LOXs, which are important in the biosynthesis of plant hormone |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "jasmonic acid"|., Interestingly, potato has strong 9-lipoxygenase (9-LOX) activity. The preferred substrates for these enzymes are |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, and the resulting products are the hydroperoxides |FRAME: CPD-8677| and |FRAME: CPD-8678|, respectively., The major metabolic products from these hydroperoxides are divinyl ethers and epoxy alcohols, obtained via the activities of |FRAME: PWY-5406| (DES) and epoxy alcohol synthase (EAS), respectively. Divinyl ethers and epoxy alcohols are potato defense compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-5406|)., In addition to DES and EAS, a |FRAME: MONOMER-12729| (9-AOS) activity has been reported. To date, 9-AOS has only been detected in a few plants including tomato, barley and potato. The limited tissue distribution of 9-AOS suggested a specialized function in plant development control, rather than ubiquitous defensive roles as DES and EAS. It was shown that the |FRAME: CPD-8683| produced from |FRAME: CPD-8677| in |FRAME: TAX-89585| and |FRAME: TAX-35883| functions as a component of a flower-inducing factor.

The marine cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1155739| (previously Lyngbya majuscula), harvested in Jamaica, produces a rich array of biologically active secondary metabolites. One of these compounds, named |FRAME: CPD-17689|, acts as a blocker of the voltage-gated sodium channel |CITS: [15217615]|., The gene cluster encoding the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-17689| has been identified, and the genes responsible for synthesizing the terminal alkyne function of the compound were found in a three genes operon, named jamABC., The operon encodes a fatty-acyl:acyl-carrier protein ligase (|FRAME: G-43925|), a desaturase (|FRAME: G-43926|), and an acyl-carrier protein (jamC). A very similar three-genes cassette in the same organism (camABC) encodes a similar function in the biosynthesis of a different compound that contains a terminal alkyne function, |FRAME: CPD-17692| |CITS: [9584405]|., In vitro characterization of the three proteins showed that JamA can activate |FRAME: CPD-17686| with ATP and load it onto the acyl-carrier protein JamC. The activated fatty acid is then modified by the desaturase JamB to form a terminal alkyne moiety, before priming the polyketide synthase enzyme that produces the skeleton of |FRAME: CPD-17689|. Promiscuity of both JamA and jamB regarding unsaturation of their substrate suggests that it is likely that JamB also generates the first double bond in |FRAME: Hexanoyl-ACPs "hexanoyl-JamC| |CITS: [25531891]|.

General Background, 2-Hydroxyphenylthiazolines are a family of iron-chelating nonribosomal peptide natural products that act as siderophores. Many such compounds have been reported from various Gram-negative bacteria. However, transcriptional analyses of the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-54571| identified a putative 2-hydroxyphenylthiazoline biosynthetic gene cluster. When the cluster was expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1902|, the host organism produced three main products, which were identified as |FRAME: Thiazostatin thiazostatin|, |FRAME: Watasemycin watasemycin|, and a novel isomer of |FRAME: Pyochelin| containing a C-methylated thiazolidine that was named |FRAME: CPD-27017|. Minor additional products included |FRAME: CPD-27016|, |FRAME: CPD-27018| and |FRAME: CPD-27019| |CITS: [28553520]|., The |FRAME: Thiazostatin thiazostatins| were originally identified in Japan in 1988 from the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-68276| during a search for novel antioxidative compounds. Two different strcutures were described, differing in their stereochemistry. They were reported to have no antimicrobial activity, but they inhibited erythtrocyte hemolysis caused by |FRAME: CPD-27309| (AAPH) |CITS: [2808141]|., |FRAME: CPD-27012 "Watasemycin A"| and |FRAME: CPD-27015| are antibiotics isolated in 2002 from the marine bacterium Streptomyces sp. TP-A0597 in Toyama Bay, Japan. They are very similar to |FRAME: CPD-27013| and |FRAME: CPD-27014|, respectively, possessing a methyl group at the 5'-position instead of a hydrogen atom. The compounds were found to possess antibiotic activity against a wide range of organisms, including the Gram-positive bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1280| and |FRAME: TAX-1423|, the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-584|, and the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5207| |CITS: [12014439]|., |FRAME: CPD-27016 Aerugine| has been described as a byproduct of siderophores such as |FRAME: Pyochelin| and |FRAME: CPD-9991|, produced by a non-enzymatic hydrolysis of a pathway intermediate |CITS: [28553520][33577297]|., Aerugine was first reported in 1987 from |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [Zunnundzhanov87]|. In 2003 the compound was isolated from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-294| and reportedf to be active against the fungal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-5465| and |FRAME: TAX-4784| |CITS: [12676678]|. A 2006 study has identified aerugine in the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1906|. That study confirmed the activity against fungal pathogens and reported that the compound completely inhibited conidial germination of |FRAME: TAX-474922| and inhibited encysted zoospore germination of |FRAME: TAX-4792| |CITS: [Apichaisataienchote06]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with the formation of |FRAME: CPD-110| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| as described in |FRAME: PWY-6406| |CITS: [11222588]|. |FRAME: CPD-110 Salicylate| is then activated by the adenylation domain of |FRAME: G-124735|, which binds it at its aryl-carrier domain. The much larger, four-domain |FRAME: MONOMER-124738| activates an |FRAME: CYS| molecule and transfers it to its peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domain (Sven0512 contains a fifth domain, similar to a methyltransferase, which is not active). A cyclization (Cy) domain then transfers the salicyl moiety from Sven0510 to the L-cysteinyl group, forming a 2-hydroxyphenylthiazolinyl thioester that remains attached to Sven0512. A different five-domain NRPS, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124737| gene, activates and binds a second |FRAME: CYS| molecule, then transfers the salicylthiazoline group from Sven0512, forming a salicyl-thiazolil-thiazoline structure, which it then methylates. This is followed by reduction of the double bond in the second thiazoline ring, catalyzed by a dehydrogenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124738| gene |CITS: [28553520]|., At the point the intermediate can be processed in two different ways: a hydrolysis y the thiesterase (TE) domain of Sven0517 releases the novel siderophore |FRAME: Pyochelin|. Alternatively, the methyltransferase domain of Sven0517 can catalyze a second reaction, this time methylating a nitrogen atom, forming |FRAME: Thiazostatin|, which is then released by the TE domain |CITS: [28553520]|., Following the release of |FRAME: Thiazostatin| it can be methylated by a type B radical SAM enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-124730| gene, forming |FRAME: Watasemycin| |CITS: [28553520]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: RETINOATE "All-trans retinoic acid"|, one of the forms of vitamin A, is a metabolite of |FRAME: CPD-13524| that mediates the functions of vitamin A required for growth and development, and is required in all chordate animals., During early embryonic development, retinoic acid generated in a specific region of the embryo helps determine position along the embryonic anterior/posterior axis by serving as an intercellular signaling molecule that guides development of the posterior portion of the embryo |CITS: [18805086]|. It acts through Hox genes, which ultimately control anterior/posterior patterning in early developmental stages |CITS: [17495912]|., In the adult, the normal growth and differentiation of the epidermis require an adequate supply of |FRAME: RETINOATE|, which is responsible for most of the activity of vitamin A, save visual pigment effects which require |FRAME: RETINAL| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6861|), and some cell metabolism effects that may require |FRAME: CPD-13524|., Retinoic acid controls the expression of retinoid-responsive genes via interactions of the retinoic acid/nuclear receptor complexes at specific DNA sequences in their control regions. , About This Pathway, In non-ocular tissues |FRAME: RETINOATE| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-13524|, which arrives to the tissues via blood, bound to |FRAME: Retinol-Binding-Proteins|. Upon entering the cell retinol dissociates from this carrier protein, which remains outside the cell, and immediately binds to the intercellular |FRAME: ENSG00000114115-MONOMER|., |FRAME: RETINOATE "All-trans-retinoate| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-13524| in two sequential oxidation steps, via |FRAME: RETINAL|. Once formed, it cannot be reduced back to retinol., Several retinol dehydrogenase (RDH) enzymes, members of the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) gene superfamily, catalyze the first and rate-limiting step that generates |FRAME: RETINAL| |CITS: [21138835]|. Several observations suggest that the reaction is catalyzed while the substrate is bound to the |FRAME: ENSG00000114115-MONOMER| (holo-CRBP1). These SDR enzymes display NADP or NAD cofactor preference and a substrate preference (all-trans- or cis-retinol substrates) |CITS: [12226107]|. Mutations in different enzymes result in distinct phenotypes, suggesting that each of them fulfills a specific function that cannot be supported by the others., Once |FRAME: RETINAL| is generated, it is subsequently oxidized to form |FRAME: RETINOATE|. This activity is known to be mediated by the three members of the RALDH family, |FRAME: HS09183|, |FRAME: HS05232|, and |FRAME: HS00013| |CITS: [9106168]|. As with the RDH enzymes, mutations in different retinal dehydrogenases result in distinct phenotypes, suggesting that each of them fulfills a distinct role |CITS: [21621639]|.

|FRAME: ITACONATE| is an unsaturated acid with conjugated double bonds and two carboxyl groups. The acid was discovered in 1837 |CITS: [Baup37]|, and was named |FRAME: ITACONATE| as an anagram of |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE|, from which it was first derived by Crasso in 1840 |CITS: [Turner41]|., Because of its unique structure and characteristics, itaconate and its ester are useful materials for the bioindustry. It is used for the synthesis of fiber, resin, plastic, rubber, paints, surfactant, ion-exchange resins and lubricant |CITS: [17451943]|., Many microorganisms are able to grow on |FRAME: ITACONATE| as their sole source of carbon |CITS:[14056350][16561921]|. In addition, |FRAME: ITACONATE| is oxidized in liver mitochondria in a pathway that involves activation to |FRAME: CPD-1137| followed by hydration and cleavage to yield |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE| |CITS: [13502348][13783048]|., |FRAME: ORG-5967| was shown to employ a pathway that is very similar to that found in liver mitochondria |CITS: [4284209]|. When cell-free extracts were incubated with |FRAME: ITACONATE|, |FRAME:MG+2|, ions, |FRAME:CO-A| and ATP, |FRAME:PYRUVATE| was formed. The amount of pyruvate formed was proportional to the quantities of |FRAME:CO-A| added. Synthetic |FRAME: CPD-1137| could replace |FRAME: ITACONATE| , |FRAME:CO-A| and ATP, suggesting that |FRAME: ITACONATE| is first activated to |FRAME: CPD-1137|. , In addition, washed suspensions of |FRAME: ORG-5967| grown on |FRAME: ITACONATE| readily oxidized |FRAME: S-CITRAMALATE|, whereas washed suspensions of the organism grown on |FRAME:SUC| did not. Further studies established that in the presence of |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: ITACONATE| |FRAME: CPD-627| is formed as an intermediate in the pathway. A similar conculsion was arrived in an earlier study with |FRAME: TAX-294| |CITS: [14056350]|., The three enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13628|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13629| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13630| were partially purifed, and shown to catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: ITACONATE| to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| in vitro. The first enzyme was also able to accept |FRAME: S-CITRAMALATE| as substrate, enabling the organism to grow on |FRAME: S-CITRAMALATE|. All of these enzymes were induced by growth on |FRAME: ITACONATE|, |FRAME: S-CITRAMALATE| or |FRAME: CPD-2461|., A fourth enzyme, |FRAME:ENZRXN-14521|, was isolated and shown to form |FRAME: CPD-1137| from |FRAME: ITACONATE|. This enzyme was shown to be identical to |FRAME: MONOMER-13627|, and was not inducible |CITS: [4284209]|., An identical pathway was also reported in a |FRAME:TAX-1269| sp. |CITS: [14342240]|.

|FRAME: TAX-168697| is an obligate marine bacterium that is known to produce the ansamycin antibiotic |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B|. The organism also produces the bicyclic polyketides |FRAME: CPD-21939| and |FRAME: CPD-21940|, both of which inhibit the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.17|, a key enzyme in polyamine biosynthesis that is required for cell proliferation, and is thus a drug target for cancer treatment |CITS: [17253854]|. In addition, the organism produces |FRAME: CPD-21937|, which was shown to inhibit the growth of a human lung adenocarcinoma cell line with an IC(50) value of 3 μg/ml and also showed antimicrobial activity |CITS: [19662086]|., The rifamycin biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-168697| is very similar to that found in the well-studied rifamycin-producer |FRAME: TAX-33910|, suggesting horizontal gene transfer |CITS: [19474814]|. However, there are several differences between the clusters in the two organisms. One such difference regards genes encoding cytochrome P-450 enzymes. |FRAME: TAX-33910| has two such genes that similar to each other, named rif-13 and |FRAME: G-58871|. A study from 2005 suggested that rif-13 does not participate in |FRAME: PWY-5984| and that |FRAME: G-58871| encodes an enzyme that catalyzes the transformation of |FRAME: CPD-10243| to |FRAME: CPD-10239| - a complex reaction in which the enzyme attacks the substrate 4 times, catalyzing two oxygenation reactions and two reductions, accompanied by the release of one CO2 molecule |CITS: [16079331]|., |FRAME: TAX-168697| possesses only one similar gene, |FRAME: G-63008|, that is 79% and 71% identical (at the amino acid level) to rif-13 and |FRAME: G-58871|, respectively. A thorough study of the gene's product has revealed that it is a cytochrome P-450 enzyme with multiple activities. The enzyme acts on |FRAME: CPD-10242| and can convert it to |FRAME: CPD-10239|, leading to |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B| production. However, it can also form |FRAME: CPD-21938|, which leads to production of |FRAME: CPD-21939| and |FRAME: CPD-21940|. The authors suggested that the timing of the decarboxylation reaction determines which reaction is carried out |CITS: [20726561]|., The presence of |FRAME: CPD-21938| has been confirmed several years later |CITS: [27232659]|. Once produced, it is assumed to be decarboxylated to |FRAME: CPD-21937|, followed by removal of the aromatic portion of the molecule to form |FRAME: CPD-21939|. It is not known whether the last step is acheived by a simple hydrolysis or by dehydrogenation. , It is speculated that |FRAME: CPD-21940| is formed in a similar manner from |FRAME: CPD-21943|, a compound that has been reported from |FRAME: TAX-33910| |CITS: [ 7319929]|.

Names: ubiquinol-6 biosynthesis (late decarboxylation) // Q-6 biosynthesis // ubiquinone-6 biosynthesis (eukaryotic) // ubiquinol-6 biosynthesis from 4-hydroxybenzoate (eukaryotic)
Summary: General Background, Ubiquinone (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., Coenzyme Q6 (|FRAME:UBIQUINOL-30|) can also be biosynthesized via |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| which has been demonstrated for |FRAME: TAX-4932| (see |FRAME:PWY-7230|) |CITS:[20534343][20592037]|. The reason that |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| was overlooked for 40 years as a precursor for coenzyme Q6 biosynthesis is twofold. The determination of the exact function and involvement of essential genes in coenzyme Q6 biosynthesis such as |FRAME:G3O-34137-MONOMER| and |FRAME:YDR376W-MONOMER| was only possible after the systematic repression of their expressions became possible |CITS:[20534343]|. The other more simple reason is that |FRAME:P-AMINO-BENZOATE| is a constitutive component of glucose synthetic medium and has therefore never been considered to be tested as a potential precursor |CITS:[20534338]|., About This Pathway, The main ubiquinone in |FRAME: TAX-4932| and other |FRAME: TAX-4891| species is |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-6| |CITS: [13673033][13835567]|. RNA modification is a post-transcriptional process by which certain nucleotides are altered after their initial incorporation into an RNA chain., The most heavily modified class of RNA molecules is the tRNA - an average of 11%, 14%, and 17% of the tRNA residues are modified in |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-4932|, and mammalian cytoplasm, respectively |CITS: [9399820]|. These modifications expand the chemical and functional diversity of tRNA, and enhance its structural stability |CITS: [3304135]|., In some bacterial genomes, about 1% of the coding genes are devoted to tRNA modification |CITS: [3304135]|., Position 34 (the anticodon first letter, or the wobble position) or position 37 (the position next to the anticodon) frequently contains highly modified nucleosides. The wobble modifications at position 34 are important for precise decoding mediated by the codon-anticodon interaction. The so called "hypermodified" nucleosides at position 37 function in translational reading-frame maintenance. These are usually modified purine nucleosides with large molecular weight. Their high hydrophobicity enhances the codon-anticodon interaction, and their modifications prevent the formation of an incorrect Watson-Crick base pair with the codon's first letter. Some of these hypermodified nucleosides, known as wye bases, contain a tricyclic structure., |FRAME: CPD-15388 Isowyosine| (imG2) and |FRAME: CPD-15389| (mimG) are relatively simple wye bases that contain a methyl group at C7, instead of the α-amino-α-carboxypropyl side chain found in eukaryotes and some uryarchaeota. Both derivatives were unambiguously identified in several Crenarchaeota such as |FRAME: TAX-273057|, |FRAME: TAX-2285|, |FRAME: TAX-12915| and |FRAME: TAX-2286|. In the latter, the dimethylated form |FRAME: CPD-15389| was found to be more abundant than the monomethylated intermediate |FRAME: CPD-15388|., A phylogenetic analysis of archaeal homologs of the five yeast enzymes involved in |FRAME: PWY-7283| suggested a potential pathway for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15388| and |FRAME: CPD-15389| and candidate genes that encode the required enzymes |CITS: [17881823]|. Purification and biochemical characterization of the |FRAME: G-16040| and |FRAME: G-16041| demonstrated that both enzymes can catalyze the first step of the pathway, but the former can also catalyze the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-15386| to |FRAME: CPD-15388| |CITS: [17881823]|., The second step is catalyzed by homologs of the yeast |FRAME: G3O-34098|, |FRAME: Radical-AdoMet-Enzymes| that contains multiple iron-sulfur centers. Unlike the eukaryotic enzymes, the archaeal enzymes do not have a flavodoxin domain (which usually serves in electron transfer to the iron-sulfur cluster). Thus, it is likely that another enzyme serves as the elctron donor to the |FRAME: G-16042| enzymes |CITS: [17881823]|., The last step of the pathway is predicted to be catalyzed by products of the taw3 genes, which are homologs of the yeast |FRAME: G3O-30560| gene. It has been proposed that the archaeal Taw3 proteins can methylate |FRAME: CPD-15399|, |FRAME: CPD-15386| and |FRAME: CPD-15388| at the N4 position (unlike the yeast enzyme, which can methylate only |FRAME: CPD-15399|) |CITS: [20386657]|. If this is true, the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-15386| would produce |FRAME: CPD-15387|, a documented modification in archaeal tRNAs. It is not known whether each of the two taw3 genes found in |FRAME: TAX-29292| can catalyze all activities, or perhaps each gene is specific for one or two substrates. The enzymes have not been characterized biochemically as for June 2013.

Summary: |FRAME: Collagens Collagen| is a group of naturally occurring animal proteins. They are the main component of connective tissue of animals and the most abundant protein in mammals, making up about 25% to 35% of the whole-body protein content., The unique mechanical properties of the collagen fibers stem from the fact that each molecule of collagen is a rigid, fully extended compound rope of three helically entwined polypeptide chains. The triple helix is resistant to most proteolytic enzymes and, in fibrous form, is stable at body temperature. Additional stabilization is achieved by covalent cross-linkages between neighboring molecules in their fibrous array. At least 28 different types of collagen have been identified and described. However, all collagen molecules contain three domains. Only the central domain, which is rich in glycine and proline, form the triple helix |CITS: [164327]|., The collagen protein is translated in a form known as the pre-propeptide, which contains a signal peptide that targets it to the endoplasmic reticulum. Removal of the signal peptide from the N-terminus generates the propeptide, which then goes through several post-translational processing steps that are described in this pathway., The first modification is the hydroxylation of many of the |FRAME: PRO| and |FRAME: LYS| residues, which aids the cross-linking of the alpha chains. Three different enzymes catalyze the hydroxylations - |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.2|, |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.4|, and |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.7|., Hydroxylated lysine (but not proline) residues are then glycosylated with glucose and galactose monomers by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.66| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.50|, respectively. Once these modifications have taken place, three of the hydroxylated and glycosylated propeptides twist into a triple helix, forming procollagen, which is packaged into a transfer vesicle and sent to the Golgi apparatus, where it is packaged and secreted by exocytosis., Once outside the cell, two membrane bound enzymes, |FRAME: EC-3.4.24.14| and |FRAME: EC-3.4.24.19|, remove the N-terminal and C-terminal loose ends that are left in the procollagen molecule, respectively, generating a molecule known as tropocollagen. The final step in the collagen synthesis pathway is the oxidation of lysines and hydroxylysines in the tropocollagen, producing aldehyde groups, by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.13|. The aldehyde groups undergo covalent bonding between tropocollagen molecules, forming a collagen fibril., Prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase require vitamin C as a cofactor. When not enough vitamin C is available, the lack of hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues causes a looser triple helix that causes impaired wound healing, deformed bones, and abnormal bleeding, among other symptoms, leading to the disease known as scurvy., Mutations in the genes described here often result in significant phenotypes. Mutations in |FRAME: HS01440| lead to the connective tissue disorder Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type VI |CITS: [1345174][8449506]|, and mutations in the PLOD2 gene lead to the Bruck syndrome |CITS: [12881513]|. A deficiency in the |FRAME: HS04122| gene causes a severe form of osteogenesis imperfecta |CITS: [17630507][20363744]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|). An analog for these pathways is also found in the metabolism of the deoxyhexose |FRAME: L-rhamnose| (see |FRAME: PWY-6713|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, The pentose |FRAME: D-Xylose| (also known as wood sugar) is a major monosaccharide component of |FRAME: Xylans xylan|, a polysaccharide found in the hemicellulose of plant cell walls. It can be degraded by some microorganisms via a number of different pathways., This pathway, which belongs to route I of the third type of pentose degradation pathways, was first described from an unidentified Pseudomonas strain |CITS: [4423285]|. The defining step of this pathway is catalyzed by an aldolase (|FRAME: EC-4.1.2.28|) that produces |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| |CITS: [4423285][7154955][7154961]|., The pathway was later observed in the archaeal species |FRAME: TAX-2287| and |FRAME: TAX-2285|, which can utilize the pentoses |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| as carbon sources |CITS: [20736170]|. In these organisms the pathway was shown to proceed via |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: GLYOX| to form |FRAME: MAL|, a TCA cycle intermediate., The |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: D-Xylose| degradation pathways of these organisms share several promiscious enzymes - |FRAME: CPLX-3781|, |FRAME: CPLX-8707|, and |FRAME: CPLX-3801| (KDG aldolase), which also participate in the |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-2221| pathways |CITS: [20736170]|. Together these enzymes catalyze the degradation of the two pentoses to |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|., The enzymes that catalyze the latter steps of the pathway, which combined catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: GLYOX|, were also identified. The latter compound is a substrate for |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.9|, feeding into the TCA cycle |CITS: [20736170][21612976]|., The lactonase reaction shown in this pathway is hypothetical in hyperthormophiles. Although two |FRAME: TAX-2287| genes have been identified as lactonases, they are not differentially expressed under conditions of D-xylose degradation. It has been postulated that there may be no need for a lactonase in hyperthermophiles since spontaneous lactone hydrolysis at 80 °C may be rapid enough to not be rate-limiting |CITS: [16849334]|., Halophilic archaea possess a different |FRAME: D-Xylose| degradation pathway that belongs to route II, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-6760|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylate"| is an aromatic compound that is is common throughout the plant kingdom and is also found in some bacteria. Salicylate is an important phytohormone, mediating both local and systemic defense responses in plants. It induces flowering and is involved in resistance against pathogen infection through the systematic acquired resistance mechanism |CITS: [12873532][15283665]|., Two pathways have been described for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-110| in plants. In Arabidopsis, the major part of |FRAME: CPD-110| is derived from |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, as is the case in bacteria. However, whereas bacteria employ an |FRAME: EC-4.2.99.21| to catalyze the turnover of isochorismate to pyruvate and salicylate (see |FRAME: PWY-6406|), plants do not contain an ortholog of that enzyme. Instead, plants utilize the product of the |FRAME: AT5G13320| gene, which catalyzes ATP- and Mg<sup>2+</sup>-dependent conjugation of |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE| with |FRAME: GLT|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-24912|, is unstable, and could decompose spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-110|. However, this decomposition was found to be catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: AT5G67160| gene. Together, |FRAME: AT5G13320| and |FRAME: AT5G67160| form a two-step metabolic pathway to produce |FRAME: CPD-110| from |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE| |CITS: [31760159]|., The minor plant pathway for |FRAME: CPD-110|, which is derived from |FRAME: PHE|, is described in |FRAME: PWY-981|.

While this compound has not yet been isolated from Arabidopsis or any other plants, the iridals produced by members of the |FRAME: TAX-26339| are believed to arise through the formation of a marneral or marneral-like intermediate  |CITS: [Marner92]|., A later study discovered the cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: AT5G42590|, which catalyzes the hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-10285| to |FRAME: CPD-21325| |CITS: [23570231][28734978]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14 Tetrathionate| is a common sulfur compound, present in most soils (except for very humid regions). Since it is unstable, its occurrence suggests that it is constantly generated by the chemical or biological oxidation of thiosulfate |CITS: [Starkey50]|. It is also known to be can be produced in the vertebrate intestinal mucosa from the oxidation of thiosulfate by reactive oxygen species during inflammation |CITS: [20864996]|., The ability to respire tetrathionate is rather widespread in bacteria |CITS: [Barbosa98]|. It is found among the sulfate reducing bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-872| and |FRAME:TAX-1562| |CITS: [14908011]|, but also in various non-sulfate reducing bacteria, including several genera of the enterobacteriaceae (|FRAME:TAX-590|, |FRAME:TAX-583|, |FRAME:TAX-544| and |FRAME:TAX-635| |CITS: [16747675][Richard77][3299028]|), |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [3094300]|, |FRAME: TAX-24| |CITS: [5726148]|, |FRAME: TAX-670| |CITS: [5784207]| and others. The ability of bacteria to respire tetrathionate is exploited in clinical diagnostics and classification |CITS: [16747675][3094300]|., About This Pathway, In most of the organisms in which |FRAME: CPD-14| reduction has been characterized, it is catalyzed by a membrane bound electron transport system consisting of dehydrogenases, electron carrier(s), and a tetrathionate reductase |CITS: [860983][435281]|., In |FRAME: TAX-90371| |FRAME:CPLX-7189| is a membrane-bound enzyme containing a |FRAME: CPD-582| cofactor |CITS: [4564717][3518717 ]|. The enzyme catalyzes the two-electron reduction of tetrathionate to two molecules of |FRAME: S2O3|, which is reduced further to |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: HS| (see |FRAME:PWY-5360|)., Tetrathionate is the only electron acceptor that is known to support B12-dependent anaerobic growth of |FRAME: TAX-90371|, using |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| as electron and carbon source |CITS: [11274105]|., In |FRAME: TAX-584| tetrathionate reductase is a dual-function enzyme that can catalyze the reduction of both tetrathionate and thiosulfate |CITS: [4599885]|. That enzyme is also a membrane-bound molybdoprotein |CITS: [387443]|., In 2004 a novel |FRAME: MONOMER-18518| has been purified and crystalized from |FRAME: TAX-70863|. This enzyme contains eight covalently attached heme groups. One of the hemes, which is presumed to be the active site for tetrathionate reduction, is attached by an unusual ligation to the ε-amino group of a lysine residue |CITS: [15361860]|., A third type of tetrathionate reductase was reported in 2013 from the microaerophilic mucosal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-197| . This enzyme is bifunctional and can also catalyze |FRAME: EC-1.8.2.2| |CITS: [23421726]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| is used as a pro-drug for the neurotransmitter |FRAME: DOPAMINE| in the therapy of central nervous system disorders such as Parkinson's disease because |FRAME: DOPAMINE| cannot cross the blood-brain barrier., To be effective, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| needs to cross the barrier before it is metabolized into compounds that cannot cross it. One such transformation is decarboxylation to |FRAME: DOPAMINE| in peripheral tissues by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.28|. In addition, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| can be methylated to |FRAME: CPD-11496| by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.6|. To decrease these conversions, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| is administered in combination with inhibitors of these enzymes (reviewed in |CITS: [17894650] [19231266][19407449]|)., However, the decarboxlation of |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| to |FRAME: DOPAMINE| still takes place in the gut of some individuals due to bacterial activity. |FRAME: DOPAMINE Dopamine| is then dehydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-22700|, rendering the treatment much less effective |CITS: [4926994]|., About This Pathway, The enzymes that catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| to |FRAME: CPD-22700| do not occur in the same organism, and thus this is a chimeric pathway, that typically does not occur in a single organism., The first enzymatic activity, L-dopa decarboxylation, was shown to be the result of promiscuity by the PLP-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.25|. Such promiscuous enzymes were found mostly (but not exclusively) in members of the |FRAME: TAX-1350| genus |CITS: [31196984]|., The second activity, |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.M7|, was found only in strains of |FRAME: TAX-84112|. Even among those strains that carry this molybdenum-dependent enzyme, many have a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) that prevents the enzyme from acting on |FRAME: DOPAMINE| |CITS: [31196984]|., Drugs that target the human |FRAME: CPLX-7890| (mostly |FRAME: CPD-11550|) do not inhibit the bacterial |FRAME: MONOMER-21044|, explaining the low efficiency of treatments in patients with certaim gut flora populations. However, a compound that inhibits this activity, |FRAME: CPD-22701|, was found to increase |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE| bioavailability in mice and to inhibit the activity in Parkinson's patient microbiotas making it a candidate drug to use in combination therapies |CITS: [31196984]|.

Summary: Triacylglycerol (TAG) is the major lipid reserve in plants and animals. The assembly of TAG occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Four consecutive reactions are catalyzed by ER membrane bound enzymes. The two intermediates, phosphatidate and 1,2-diacylglycerol, are also substrates for the synthesis of membrane lipids glycosylglycerides and phosphoglycerides. Thus, the last step in the pathway, catalyzed by diacylglycerol acyltransferase, is the only dedicated step in triacylglycerol synthesis., The traditional Kennedy pathway does not include the reaction (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.158|, PDAT) where phospholipid is utilized as the acyl donor in TAG formation. The role of the PDAT route in TAG biosynthesis was clearly shown in yeast |CITS: [10829075]|. PDAT activity in plants was demonstrated in a few oil seed plants including caster bean |CITS: [10829075]|. The caster bean seeds have a high content of ricinoleat in the seed oil. Ricinoleat and other unusual fatty acids are modified from acyl groups linked to phospholipids, and transferred to TAG afterwards. PDAT was proposed playing an important role in the last step. However, the contribution of PDAT to TAG biosynthesis in other plants is not clear. Overexpressing or knockout of the Arabidopsis PDAT had no effect on TAG biosynthesis |CITS: [15247387][15907694]|. , The well-coordinated regulation of lipid homeostasis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is exemplified by the cooperation of two enzymes operating through catabolic and anabolic steps of triacylglycerol (TAG) metabolism. The formation of diacylglycerol, a precursor for TAG and phospholipid biosynthesis, is catalyzed both by the triacylglycerol lipase TGL4 |CITS:[16135509]| and phosphatidate phosphatase PAH1 |CITS:[2542283]|, the former catalyzing the degradation of TAG and the latter forming DAG by dephosphorylation of phosphatidate (PA). Both enzymes are controlled in their activity by Cdk1/Cdc28-dependent phosphorylation, with TGL4 being phosphorylated (activated) and PAH1 being phosphorylated (deactivated) at different times in the cell cycle |CITS:[19150427]|. The interaction of two enzymes involved in different metabolic events of TAG metabolism which are controlled by the same cyclin-dependent kinase ensures a steady and regulated flow of precursors for membrane phospholipid synthesis highlighting the importance of TAG homeostasis in the critical phase of cell growth in yeast |CITS:[22910056]|., A third route forming TAG may also exist. Diacylglycerol transacylase activity was detected in plant |CITS: [Stobart97]| as well as in animal |CITS: [8473321]|. It catalyzes the formation of one molecule TAG and one molecule monoacylglycerol from two molecules of diacylglycerol., The constitution of different species of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids at the sn-1, sn-2, and sn-3 positions of the glycerol backbone varies among different plants, and is determined by substrate specificities of the three acyltransferases involved in this pathway. The composition of distinct fatty acids in TAG determines the quality and property of lipids of different plants, and also contributes to cold temperature sensitivity of different plants.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| is an amino acid, but it is not a component of proteins nor is it coded for by DNA. In mammals, it plays a role in the |FRAME: PWY-4984| for the disposal of ammonia where it is synthesized from |FRAME: ARG| by |FRAME: CPLX-6621|. It is also a precursor of |FRAME: ARG| synthesis in the |FRAME: PWY-4984| and |FRAME: PWY-4983|., The initial steps of ornithine biosynthesis in lower organisms proceeds either via N acetylated intermediates or the use of a dedicated carrier protein to protect the intermediates. This is presumed to prevent the spontaneous cyclization of glutamate derivatives, which leads to proline biosynthesis |CITS: [12633501]|. Indeed in mammals, |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| can spontaneously cyclize to |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|, an intermediate in |FRAME: PROSYN-PWY|. In lower organisms that lack the |FRAME: PWY-4983| and |FRAME: PWY-4984|, ornithine participates in the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: ARG|., About this Pathway, This pathway describes the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| in the mitochondria. |FRAME: GLT| is formed from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| within the mitochondrial matrix by the mitochondrial glutamate dehydrogenases, as described in |FRAME: GLUTAMATE-SYN2-PWY| |CITS: [8207021]|. |FRAME: GLT| is then converted to |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| by mitochondrial |FRAME: HS00730-MONOMER| |CITS: [8761662]|. , The conversion of |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| occurs within the mitochondrial lumen by |FRAME: CPLX-6747| |CITS: [2507357]|. At this point, |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| can enter either |FRAME: PWY-4983| or |FRAME: PWY-4984| to synthesize |FRAME: ARG|.
