Summary: General Background, During senescence chlorophyll is degraded by chlorophyllase. This results in the release of large amounts of chlorophyllide and phytol. Although the degradation pathway of chlorophyllide (see |FRAME:PWY-5098|) has been the subject of a number of studies, the fate of phytol is not so clear. It has been shown that chlorophyll degradation is linked to |FRAME:PWY-1422| during senescence, prompting the hypothesis that phytol released from chlorophyll might be channeled into tocopherol synthesis via a salvage pathway |CITS:[Rise89],[Peisker89]|. Feeding experiments of |FRAME:TAX-3701| seedlings with radioactive phytol have indeed shown that, besides chlorophyll, free phytol is incorporated into tocopherol and a variety of undefined lipid esters |CITS:[16306049]|. Moreover, although it is unlikely that large amounts of phytol released from chlorophyll degradation be incorporated into phylloquinone, this compound was nevertheless identified as a product of phytol recycling along with the other lipid esters |CITS:[16306049]|., Enzymatic steps: Although both enzyme activities required for this pathway (phytol kinase and phytyl-P kinase activities) have been detected in plants, only the enzymes catalyzing the phytol kinase reaction has been isolated: a mutant involved in tocopherol biosynthesis in |FRAME:TAX-3701| (vte5-1) has been shown to be affected in phytyl-P formation. The gene affected by the mutation was subsequently shown to encode a protein with phytol kinase activity when heterologously expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|.

General Background, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound derived from |FRAME: CPD-195|, that contains a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide. Lipoic acid is an essential prosthetic group of four mitochondrial enzymes involved in oxidative decarboxylation, the |FRAME: CPLX66-42|, the |FRAME: CPLX-7050|, the |FRAME: CPLX66-272| and the |FRAME: CPLX66-539| |CITS: [22152680]|., Each of these enzyme complexes are composed of multiple copies of three enzymes: a substrate-specific decarboxylase-dehydrogenase E1, a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase E2 specific for each type of complex, and a |FRAME: CPLX-7868| E3. Lipoate is bound via an amide bond to the ε-amino group of a strictly conserved lysine of the respective E2 subunits. The E3 subunit binding protein of the |FRAME: CPLX66-272|, which resembles the E2 subunit, is also lipoylated. Similarly, lipoate acts as a prosthetic group of the |FRAME: PROTEIN-LIPOYLLYSINE "H protein"| of the |FRAME: CPLX66-539| |CITS: [8444795]|., E1 catalyzes a reaction in which the substrate is attached to the lipoate cofactor and decarboxylated. During this reaction, the lipoate cofactor is reduced to dihydriolipoate. E2 then catalyzes an acyl transfer step, in which the product of the reaction is released. Finally, E3 catalyzes the oxidation of the dihydrolipoyl cofactor back to lipoyl form, with |FRAME: NAD| being the ultimate electron acceptor |CITS: [2188967]|., Lipoate is a universally conserved cofactor across all kingdoms of life. In mammals lipoate is biosynthesized de novo in the mitochondrial matrix from octanoyl-acyl carrier protein (octanoyl-ACP) which is produced during fatty acid biosynthesis., About This Pathway, The synthesis of lipoate occurs in the mitochondrion. Initially, the starting substrate octanoyl-ACP is synthesized by mitochondrial |FRAME: CPLX-7628| in a series of reactions |CITS: [22152680]|. Lipoate synthesis begins with the transfer of the octanoyl moiety of an octanoyl-ACP to a conserved lysine residue of a lipoyl carrier protein, such as the H protein of the glycine cleavage complex (see pathway |FRAME: GLYCLEAV-PWY|). This reaction is catalyzed by the octanoyltransferase product of human gene |FRAME: G66-33937| (homologs LIP2 in yeast and LipB in Escherichia coli). , The octanoyl moiety is then sulfurated at carbons 6 and 8 by the |FRAME: HS04528-MONOMER| product of human gene |FRAME: HS04528| (homologs LIP5 in yeast, and LipA in E. coli). It catalyzes the conversion of the octanoyl side chain to an active lipoyl, generating a fully active lipoylated domain. The enzyme contains iron-sulfur clusters and human iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis genes GLRX5, ISCA2, IBA57, NFU1 and BOLA3 are associated with defects in lipoate biosynthesis (reviewed in |CITS: [24777537][27586888]|). The reaction mechanism of this radical SAM superfamily enzyme has been studied in the E. coli homolog (see |FRAME: EG11306-MONOMER "LipA"|)., While mammalian cells are capable of synthesizing |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| in mitochondria, this pathway has not been completely elucidated in humans. It is generally believed that humans require some exogenous lipoate as a dietary supplement and rely on |FRAME: PWY0-522| to meet lipoate requirements |CITS: [11389890]|., Human mutant studies suggest that the lipoyl moiety of lipoyl-H protein is transferred to conserved lysine residues in other lipoylated proteins such as the 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes via the lipoate protein ligase product of gene |FRAME: HS07153| (homolog LIP3 in yeast) |CITS: [24256811][23960015][19570983][28757203]|.

Sandalwood is grown in India, Australia and China, the scented wood and oil are prized for their fragrances and use in cosmetics and medicinal use |CITS: [17045624]|. The oil is produced by the heartwood and the oil components have been isolated and characterized in |FRAME: TAX-35974|, |FRAME: TAX-453088| and the Chinese sandal. In addition to the santanols it is composed of sesquiterpenoids mainly the |FRAME: CPD-11377| and the |FRAME: --beta-santalene| and a host of other terpenes in minor and varying quantities |CITS: [ADAMS75]|. Four structural classes of sesquiterpenoids have been isolated and found as co-occuring sesquiterpenes; |FRAME: CPD-11377|, |FRAME: --beta-santalene| and bergamotene; and β-curcumene; β-bisabolene and α-bisabolol and along with four unidentified sesquiterpenes |CITS: [17045624]|. The lack of a common structural intermediate between these compounds is said to indicate the possibility of four different classes of sesquiterpene cyclases to be present in sandal wood trees. , The study by |CITS: [21454632]| was designed to isolate the various enzymes responsible for the biosynthesis of santalene and other terpenes that are responsible for the typical fragrance of sandalwood oil. Molecular analysis led to the isolation and cloning of three terpene synthases from three divergent species of sandalwood; |FRAME: TAX-35974|, |FRAME: TAX-293154| and |FRAME: TAX-453088|. The genes named SaSSy, SauSSy, and SspiSSy encoded enzymes that catalyzed the formation of α-, β-, epi-β-santalene, and α-exo-bergamotene from (E,E)-farnesyl diphosphate (E,E-FPP) shown here in this pathway |CITS: [21454632]|. The enzymes catalyzed the formation of the products by converting the substrate (E,E)-farnesyl diphosphate (E,E-FPP). The santalene synthases that catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-11293| is shown here |FRAME: PWY-6254|.

Simple hydroxylated and methoxylated coumarins are widely distributed in plants as well as in microorganisms and animals. Contrary to that the more complex coumarins (e.g. bicoumarins) are often highly specific for certain plant families with only limited knowledge about their metabolic scope or physiological functions |CITS:[Hussain12]|. Among the estimated 1000 natural occurring coumarins so far only a minority could be linked to metabolic activities in plants such as growth and development processes |CITS:[Downum92]|, or acting as peroxyl radical scavengers |CITS:[12480941]| and defense agents |CITS:[Seigler98]|. , |FRAME:CPD-14427 Daphnetin| (7,8-dihydroxycoumarin), the aglycone of daphnin, has been first isolated and characterized in |FRAME:TAX-23110| |CITS:[Bohm61]| and later on shown to be present in other plant families as well (e.g. |CITS:[Lin-gen82]|). Daphnetin has been reported to undergo a variety of metabolic modifications. Besides position specific glycosylation in ring position 3 (|CITS:[18487633]|), 4 (|CITS:[Fleuriet80]|), 7 (|CITS:[Ibrahim80]|) and 8 (|CITS:[Sato69]| (|CITS:[Sato71]|) daphnetin was also the exclusive substrate for a O-methyltransferase forming 7-hydroxy-8-methoxycoumarin (hydrangetin) (|CITS:[12480941]|). Interestingly, daphnetin had also been reported as a protein kinase inhibitor (|CITS:[10403826]|). The fact that its methoxylation modulated the kinase inhibition and as a result influenced cold acclimation and photosystem II excitation pressure in rye (|CITS:[12480941]|) has been discussed as a hormone-like signaling event (|CITS:[Bourgaud06]|) which has not been reported for coumarins before.

General Background, Chloroacetamide herbicides are a class of efficient pre-emergence herbicides that are widely used for controlling annual grass and broadleaf weeds in cotton, corn, soybean, and other crops. The major function of these herbicides is to inhibit the synthesis of protein, lipid, and lignin of weeds |CITS: [Couderchet98]|., The most frequently used chloroacetamide herbicides are |FRAME: CPD-18948|, |FRAME: CPD-18949|, |FRAME: CPD-18950|, |FRAME: CPD-18951|, and |FRAME: CPD-18941|. They are persistent chemicals, and have been frequently detected in a wide range of the environment, such as soil, plants, and ground and surface waters |CITS: [11080329][18502469]|., The yearly production of |FRAME: CPD-18941| alone reaches 107 kg |CITS: [12688489]|. It is a highly stable and persistent, with a typical field half-life of 18-19 days. Butachlor is known to exert genotoxic effects on amphibians and to induce apoptosis in mammalian cells |CITS: [10687284][16222508]|, and is toxic to earthworms in soil |CITS: [Muthukaruppan05]|. Although photooxidation and chemical hydrolysis slowly degrade butachlor in the environment, most of its degradation occurs via microbial metabolism. Many bacterial strains are able to degrade butachlor, including Sphingomonas sp. |CITS: [Chen13]|, Paracoccus sp. |CITS: [21417467]|, Pseudomonas sp. |CITS: [Wang08]|, Catellibacterium caeni sp. |CITS: [Zheng12]|, Rhodococcus sp. |CITS: [23186529]|, Acinetobacter sp. |CITS: [22618300]|, Mycobacterium sp. |CITS: [23617893]|, and Sphingobium sp. |CITS: [23617893][24075675]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1622086|, which can use |FRAME: CPD-18941| as its sole carbon source, was isolated from activated sludge obtained from a pesticide manufacturer in the Zhejiang province in China. When grown at a butachlor concentration of 100 mg/L, the organism completely mineralized more than 90% of it within 7 days. HPLC-ESI-MS/MS analysis identified three of the metabolites that accumulated during the degradation as |FRAME: CPD-18943|, |FRAME: CPD-18945|, and |FRAME: CPD-18946| |CITS: [26368393]|. The organism mineralized |FRAME: CPD-18946| completely, although the later part of the pathway has not been studied in it., The later part of the pathway has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-911638|, in which the upper part of the pathway differs (|FRAME: CPD-18941| is first degraded to |FRAME: CPD-18948|, which is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-18945| by N-dealkylation) |CITS: [21417467]| and in Sphingobium sp. J7B |CITS: [23617893]|. It was shown that |FRAME: CPD-18946| is converted to |FRAME: ANILINE|, which is deaminated/hydroxylated to |FRAME: CATECHOL| as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6533|., In |FRAME: TAX-911638| catechol is degraded further via |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.1| (see |FRAME: CATECHOL-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|) |CITS: [21417467]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22719 Colibactin| is a genotoxic compound synthesized by some extraintestinal pathogenic and human gut commensal enterobacterial strains |CITS: [25657191][28987619]|. Colibactin belongs to the cyclomodulins - bacterial toxins that interfere with the eukaryotic cell cycle. It induces DNA double-strand breaks, DNA cross-linking, chromosome aberrations, and cell cycle arrest in the G2/M phase |CITS: [16902142][20534522]|. Colibactin-producing |FRAME: TAX-562| are over-represented in colorectal cancer (CRC) |CITS: [22903521][23457644][23846483][28833079]| and have been shown to increase the number of tumors in various CRC mouse models |CITS: [22903521][24334760][24658599][28416491]|., |FRAME: CPD-22719 Colibactin| is a complex molecule produced by polyketide synthases (PKS), non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPS), hybrid enzymes (PKS-NRPS), and a number of tailoring enzymes, all of which are encoded on a 54-kb genomic island that was originally designated pks and later clb. The clb island was initially identified in |FRAME: TAX-714962| isolated from neonatal bacterial meningitis |CITS: [16902142]|. Epidemiological studies have shown that while the clb island is mostly found in |FRAME: TAX-562| strains of the B2 phylogenetic group, it is also present in some other |FRAME: TAX-91347|, including |FRAME: TAX-573|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, and |FRAME: TAX-545| |CITS: [18945841][19720753][24852749][28233784]|., |FRAME: CPD-22719 Colibactin| contains two cyclopropane war-heads that are extremely reactive. Its high reactivity along with the fact that it is produced in very small amounts made it impossible to isolate the molecule in its native form for over a decade. Its exact structure was elucidated only in 2019 |CITS: [31395743]|., About This Pathway, As mentioned above, the clb gene cluster, which encodes |FRAME: CPD-22719|, was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-714962| in 2006. Deletion of the entire island resulted in a non-cytopathic mutant, and conversely, |FRAME: TAX-316385| carrying a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) containing the complete island triggered megalocytosis and proliferation arrest in transiently infected eukaryotic cells |CITS: [16902142]|., |FRAME: CPD-22719 Colibactin| biosynthesis is initiated by the |FRAME: G-80584 "non-ribosomal peptide synthetase ClbN"| and |FRAME: G-80585 "hybrid non-ribosomal peptide synthetase/polyketide synthase ClbB"| NRPS enzymes. ClbN uses |FRAME: ASN| and |FRAME: TETRADECANOYL-COA| to generate N-myristoyl-D-Asn, a prodrug motif, which is accepted by ClbB. ClbB adds |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and then incorporates a |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender unit into the nascent chain |CITS: [23406518]|., Synthesis continues with the NRPS-PKS assembly line ClbCHIJ, which adds two units of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, and |FRAME: GLY|. The use of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as an extender unit is very unusual. Following its incorporation |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| is cleaved off, resulting in generation of a cyclopropane ring, which is crucial for colibactin-induced DNA alkylation |CITS: [27025153]|. ClbH and ClbI are essential for cyclopropane formation |CITS: [28805802][28240912]|., Following the addition of |FRAME: GLY| by |FRAME: G-80587 ClbJ| the pathway branches. Some of the molecules are cleaved from ClbJ by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21075 "ClbQ thioesterase"| |CITS: [27547923][31395743]| and attached to the |FRAME: MONOMER-21076 "ClbL amidase"| |CITS: [31251062]|. The rest of the molecules are extended further by the NRPS module of ClbJ, which adds an |FRAME: CYS| and cyclizes it to a thiazoline ring, then transferred to the |FRAME: G-80588 "ClbK hybrid non-ribosomal peptide synthetase/polyketide synthase"|, which performs several tasks: it oxidizes the thiazoline to a thiazole ring, it adds an unusual |FRAME: AMINOMALONATE| extender unit, and it adds a second |FRAME: CYS| residue, which is also cyclized and oxidized to form a thiazole ring. The product is then transferred to the |FRAME: G-80595 "ClbO polyketide synthase"|, which adds a second aminomalonyl unit |CITS: [26890481][28805802]|. The aminomalonyl groups are generated from |FRAME: SER| by the ClbDEF enzymes, and are transferred to ClbK and ClbO by the |FRAME: G-80597 "ClbG carrier protein"| |CITS: [26191546][26890481]|., At this point the |FRAME: MONOMER-21076|, which is attached to the molecule that was cleaved off ClbJ by ClbQ (see above), catalyzes the formation of an amide bond between the molecule it carries and the product carried by ClbO, joining the products of the two pathway branches together, and forming the prodrug |FRAME: CPD-22722|, which is a free molecule |CITS: [31251062][31395743]|., Finally, the prodrug is exported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21080| |CITS: [27571755][27939886]|, where it is cleaved by the |FRAME: G-80596 "ClbP peptidase"|, which removes the two N-myristoyl-D-Asn side chains |CITS: [21795676][23041299][23406518]|. The cleavage product loses four water molecules spontaneously, resulting in formation of |FRAME: CPD-22721|. The formation of the active |FRAME: CPD-22719| molecule requires a further oxidation, which either occurrs spontaneously or is catalyzed by an as-yet unknown enzyme, and a spontaneous hydrolytic deamination |CITS: [31395743]|., |FRAME: CPD-22719 Colibactin| producers are able to protect themselves from the presence of small amounts of the toxin in the cytoplasm by producing a |FRAME: MONOMER-21081|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80599| gene |CITS: [26560421][29112397]|.

The |FRAME: Lanthipeptides lanthipeptides| are a family of |FRAME: RiPPs "ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides"| (RiPPs) that is characterized by the presence of multiple |FRAME: CPD-3736| (Lan) and |FRAME: CPD-25467| (MeLan) residues. These residues are formed during the cyclization of these compounds, which is catalyzed by lanthipeptide synthases. These enzymes catalyze dehydration of Ser/Thr residues, followed by intramolecular addition of the thiol group of a Cys residue to the dehydro amino acids, which results in the formation of the thioether crosslinks of (methyl)lanthionine |CITS: [17506681]|. Members of the lanthipeptides that have antimicrobial activity are known as lantibiotics., Five classes of lanthipeptides have been defined, based on the type of lanthipeptide synthase involved. The venezuelins are a family of class IV |FRAME: Lanthipeptides lanthipeptides| that were first inferred from the discovery of a cryptic lanthibiotic gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-54571| |CITS: [20351769]|. Non-silent gene clusters encoding venezuelins were later reported from multiple strains of |FRAME: TAX-42684| and |FRAME: TAX-68223| |CITS: [25888176][26437689]|, and an |FRAME: TAX-562|-based heterologous production system has been established |CITS: [29633842]|., The biosynthesis of class IV lanthipeptides involves a single three-domain enzyme (LanL) consisting of an N-terminal lyase, a central kinase and a C-terminal cyclase domains. Dehydration of Ser/Thr residues is achieved through ATP-dependent phosphorylation of the hydroxyl groups, followed by elimination of the phosphate group |CITS: [31243957]|. The cyclase domain of class IV enzymes is similar to the stand-alone LanC cyclase of class I enzymes, which contains conserved Zn<sup>2+</sup> binding sites |CITS: [34490957]|.

General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic formaldehyde is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms. In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central intermediate., It has been suggested that the formaldehyde concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph would rise to 100mM in less than 1 minute if formaldehyde consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by unrelated or distantly related genes., About This Pathway, This pathway, like |FRAME: PWY-1722|, is carried out by enzymes that utilize either the cofactor |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| (H4F), or the "archaea-like" cofactor |FRAME: THMPT| (H4MPT). In the methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-272630|, formaldehyde that enters the cytoplasm condenses with one of the two pterin cofactors, |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| or |FRAME: THMPT|, and forms the respective methylene derivative. The reaction of formaledehyde with |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| is spontaneous |CITS: [5954363][14645276]|, but the condensation of formaldehyde with |FRAME: THMPT| is catalyzed by an enzyme., While the methylene derivatives of both |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| and |FRAME: THMPT| are processed by somewhat similar pathways, it has been shown that these pathways have different physiological roles. The |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| pathway is a major biosynthetic pathway, while the |FRAME: THMPT| pathway is used mostly for the generation of reducing power and ATP., |FRAME: METHYLENETETRAHYDROMETHANOPTERIN| is oxidized into |FRAME:METHENYLTETRAHYDROMETHANOPTERIN|, |FRAME:FORMYL-THMPT|, and eventually |FRAME:FORMATE| by the pathway listed above. Formate can then be oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| through the action of multiple formate dehdrogenases (see |FRAME: PWY-1881|), or be fed through the H4F pathway and converted to |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF|, which would then enter the serine pathway for assimilation (|FRAME: PWY-1622|) |CITS: [10848995][ 11889483][14645276][10215859][12123819][9765566]|., This pathway is also present in the free-living bacterium |FRAME: TAX-266265|, which is not a methylotroph. Upon growth on choline, the oxidation of which results in the formation of formaldehyde, |FRAME: TAX-266265| cells expressed enzymes of three different formaldehyde oxidation pathways, including the H4MPT pathway |CITS: [15028703]|.

Summary: |FRAME: LEU| is one of the three main branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), along with |FRAME: ILE|, and |FRAME:VAL|., The catabolic pathways of the BCAAs can be divided into two sequential series of reactions, referred to, as the common pathway and the distal pathway., The common pathway includes the enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-6941|, |FRAME: CPLX8J2-279|, and, |FRAME: CPLX-6942|. These three enzymes catalyze the conversion of all three BCAAs to their, respective acyl-CoA derivatives, (|FRAME:METHACRYLYL-COA|, |FRAME:3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA|, and |FRAME: CPD-1083|, for |FRAME:VAL|, |FRAME:LEU|, and |FRAME:ILE|, respectively), though the intermediates formed, by these enzymes are different for the different amino acids., The distal parts of the pathways are completely different for the three BCAAs, and comprise enzymes, specific for each amino acid |CITS: [773366]|., This Leucine degradation pathway is wide spread, and is found in microorganisms, higher plants, and, animals, including mammals., The catabolism of |FRAME: LEU| begins with its transamination to |FRAME:2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE|,, followed by oxidative decarboxylation to |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA|., |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA| then undergoes a four-step process, involving, dehydrogenation to |FRAME:3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA|, carboxylation to, |FRAME:TRANS-3-METHYL-GLUTACONYL-COA|, hydration to, |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA|, and finally a thioester hydrolysis, forming |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:3-KETOBUTYRATE| |CITS: [4150714]|., Leucine degradation is different from the degradation of the other branched-chain amino acids, in that it, includes a carboxylation step. The |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixing enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|,, requires a biotin cofactor., In adipocytes, unlike other tissues, leucine is a significant precursor for fatty acid and sterol, biosynthesis, especially in the presence of glucose |CITS: [13892210]|. Furthermore, leucine apparently, serves as a source of nitrogen for synthesis of |FRAME: GLN| and, to lesser extents, |FRAME: GLT|, and |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, which are released by adipocytes |CITS: [6773935]| and can serve as, substrates for gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney |CITS: [6304077]|., It should be mentioned that alternative leucine degradation pathways exist. In one such pathway, , documented in |FRAME: TAX-1509|, leucine is degraded to |FRAME:ISOBUTYRATE| and, |FRAME: ACET| via |FRAME:CPD-2041| (see |FRAME:PWY-5075|). Additional pathways which are currently not characterized very well include the conversion, of leucine to |FRAME: ACETONE| by members of the |FRAME:TAX-662| family |CITS: [10601206]|, and the, catabolism of leucine to branched-chain fatty acids in |FRAME: TAX-1288| |CITS: [15078537]|., A portion of this leucine degradation pathway also participates in the final phase of the acyclic terpene utilization pathway, beginning at |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA| as shown in the pathway link from |FRAME: PWY-6672|. The acyclic terpene utilization pathway includes pathways |FRAME: PWY-6670|, |FRAME: PWY-6672| and this pathway, with its associated pathway link to |FRAME: ACETOACETATE-DEG-PWY|. In species of |FRAME:TAX-286| the enzymes of |FRAME: LEU|/|FRAME: ISOVALERATE| utilization are encoded in the liuRABCDE gene cluster (reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]|).

General Background, |FRAME: Lignins "Lignin"| is the most abundant aromatic compound in nature, and its mineralization is an important step in the terrestrial carbon cycle. Lignin is composed of various intermolecular linkages between phenylpropanes,, including guaiacyl, syringyl, and p-hydroxyphenyl, and contains biphenyl nuclei |CITS: [10347082]|., Lignin degrading organisms brake down the complex polymer to various biaryl and monoaryl compounds such as |FRAME: BIPHENYL|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|., Complex lignin is resistant to bacterial enzymes. Its degradation is initiated by white rot fungi, which secrete extracellular degradation enzymes such as |FRAME: MONOMER-14338 "lignin peroxidase"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14335 "manganese peroxidase"|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14334 "laccase"| |CITS: [8246842]|. The resulting low-molecular-weight lignin can be further degraded and mineralized by bacteria |CITS: [1785937]|., |FRAME: TAX-502559| is a Gram-negative bacterium that was isolated from a kraft pulp effluent based on its ability to grow on the lignin-derived biphenyl compound |FRAME: CPD-11859| (DDVA). It can utilize many lignin degradation products possessing guaiacyl (4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl) and syringyl (4-hydroxy-3,5-dimethoxyphenyl) moieties, which it degrades to |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|, respectively. These compounds are then completely mineralized, as described in the |FRAME: PWY-6338| and |FRAME: PWY-6339| pathways., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-11859| (DDVA) is a lignin-related biphenyl compound. It's degradation pathway by |FRAME: TAX-502559| starts with demethylation to a diol compound, |FRAME: CPD-11860| (OH-DDVA), catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G-11558| gene |CITS: [10788391]|, followed by a meta-ring cleavage catalyzed by a dioxygenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-11559| gene |CITS: [9647824]|., The product of this cleavage is then hydrolyzed by the |FRAME: G-11560| gene product, yielding |FRAME: CPD-11853| and |FRAME: CPD-11863| |CITS: [10347082]|., |FRAME: CPD-11853| is decarboxylated to |FRAME: VANILLATE| by one of two decarboxylases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11557| and |FRAME: G-11561| genes |CITS: [12200294][16151081]|., |FRAME: VANILLATE "Vanillate"| is converted to protocatechuate and degraded to central metabolism intermediates as described in |FRAME: PWY-6338| |CITS: [9501423][2185230]|.

Hot red pepper |FRAME: TAX-4072| is widely used as a spicy seasoning and in medicinal materials , worldwide. The pungency of the fruits of red pepper is caused by a lipophilic alkaloid |FRAME: CAPSAICIN| , and its analogs, termed capsaicinoids |CITS: [18190936]|. The fundamental structure of capsaicinoids is , that of an acid amide of |FRAME: CPD-9327| with a fatty acid. Numerous reports on the chemical, , biological, and physiological properties of capsaicinoids have been published; in particular, studies on the , use of capsaicinoids as a medicinal target have increased tremendously since the cloning of a, |FRAME: CAPSAICIN| receptor from mammalian sensory nerves |CITS: [9349813 ]|., A novel compound group named capsinoids as an ingredient of the fruits of a non-pungent cultivar of , |FRAME: TAX-4072|, 'CH-19 Sweet' |CITS: [KOBATA98]| has been reported. The basic structure of , capsinoids comprises an ester of vanillyl alcohol with a fatty acid, and the chemical structure of , capsiate (3) the major component of capsinoid is similar to capsaicin. Interestingly, it was found that the , TRPV1 agonist potential of capsiate was comparable to that of capsaicin despite its pungency being , considerably lower than that of capsaicin |CITS: [Lida03]|.

Summary: General Background, The ripe cones of the hop (|FRAME:TAX-3486|) plant are covered with glandular hairs containing a mixture of essential oil and |FRAME: BITTER-ACIDS "bitter acids"|. These compounds are commercially important. In addition to their great importantce for the beer brewing industry, having a major effect on the final aroma and taste of beer, they also have antimicrobial, antifungal and antifeedant activities |CITS:[mizobuchi85a]|., The bitter acids that are synthesized by the hop fall into two types: the |FRAME: ALPHA-ACIDS "α acids"|, which contain two prenyl side chains, and the |FRAME: BETA-ACIDS "β acids"|, which contain three such chains. The former group is of particular importance for the brewing industry as they are transformed during the brewing process into |FRAME: Iso-Alpha-Bitter-Acids "iso-α bitter acids"|, such as |FRAME:CPD-7116| and |FRAME:CPD-7115|, which contribute to the bitter taste of beer |CITS:[15953717]|., About This Pathway, The pathway described here shows the biosynthesis of the α acid |FRAME: CPD-19791| and the β acid |FRAME: CPD-19790|. The first commited step of the pathway, leading to the formation of the 2-acyl-phloroglucinol derivative |FRAME: CPD-19784|, is catalyzed by the chalcone synthase-like enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.156|, using |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA| as the starter molecule. The |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA| was shown to be derived from |FRAME: CPD-7076| by |FRAME: MONOMER-20125|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55018| gene |CITS: [23300257]|., The next steps consist of prenylations catalyzed by two different prenyltransferases |CITS: [22166201][25564559]|. The prenyl moieties are provided by |FRAME: CPD-4211| that predominantly originates from the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY|, although a small fraction has been shown to derive from the |FRAME:PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| |CITS:[10406953]|. Following an initial prenylation at position 4 by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.136|, a second prenylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.137|, adds a second prenyl side chain at position 6. If the same enzyme adds a third prenyl chain at position 6, |FRAME: CPD-19790| is formed. If, instead, a monooxygenation occurs, |FRAME: CPD-19791| is formed. Since the identity of the oxygenase is not known yet, this last step of the pathway is not well understood.

One of the early steps in the biosynthesis of coenzyme F420 in |FRAME: TAX-2190| requires |FRAME: DL-Phospholactate|, which is formed by the phosphorylation of |FRAME: L-LACTATE|., Grochowski et al |CITS: [16585745]| showed that |FRAME: L-LACTATE| is formed in |FRAME: TAX-2190| by the NAD(+)-dependent oxidation of |FRAME:LACTALD| by the |FRAME: G-9416| gene product, |FRAME:CPLX-7093|., The |FRAME:LACTALD|, in turn, was found to be generated by two routes; either by the |FRAME: Factor-420|-dependent reduction of |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL|, which is performed enzymatically by |FRAME: MONOMER-14613| |CITS: [18363381]|, or by the aldol cleavage of |FRAME:FUCULOSE-1P|, catalyzed by |FRAME:CPLX-7092|, the |FRAME: G-9415| gene product |CITS: [16585745]|., |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL Methylglyoxal| is readily formed from |FRAME:GAP| by cell extracts of |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [16585745]|. It has been shown that |FRAME: GAP| is unstable above 60°C and is decpomposed to |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [2021650]|. Most likely, |FRAME:GAP| is first converted to |FRAME:CPD-10807| by |FRAME: CPLX-7765| (this activity was proven using labeled isotope studies), and the latter spontaneously decomposes to |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [17014089]|.

Summary: Background, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl "Homogalacturonan"| (HGA) is a polysaccharide consisting of α-1,4-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units. HGA accounts for up to 60% of the |FRAME: Pectin pectin| found in primary cell walls of all plants. Many of the carboxyl groups of HGA in pectin are methyl-esterified at position 6. The regions of pectin with an HGA backbone are called "smooth" regions, as opposed to the "hairy" regions, which consist of a |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan| or |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| backbones., Degradation of HGA occurs under two rather different situations. In the first one, indigenous plant enzymes disassemble the polymer as part of normal growth and development. In the second, fungi and bacteria degrade the polymer, either as a part of pathogenic attack, or simply as part of the degradation of dead plant matter. Even though pectin is degraded for very different purposes in these two different scenarioes, the plant, fungal, and bacterial enbzymes involved are rather similar., The enzymes that cleave the main chain can be conceptually divided into hydrolases and lyases. While hydrolases release either monomers or oligomers of D-glucuronate, lyases cleave the backbone by β-elimination, resulting in the formation of a Δ4,5-unsaturated non-reducing end. Either type of enzyme can be endo-cleaving (attacking at random positions in the middle of the chain) or exo-cleaving enzyme (attacking either at, or close to, one of the ends of the molecule). Most exo-cleaving enzymes are specific for the non-reducing end., Degradation by plant enzymes, The pectin network is systematically disassembled during many stages of plant development, especially those that require cell separation including fruit ripening, organ abscission, pod and anther dehiscence, and pollen grain maturation. Two key enzymes in the homogalacturonan disassembling process are |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.11|, and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.15|. The pectinesterase removes the methyl groups in the form of |FRAME: METOH|, preparing de-esterified domains of homogalacturonan |CITS: [8018878][11943159][12033812]|. The de-esterified domains are suitable substrates for the endo-polygalacturonase |CITS: [6489331][1392611][8208850][7972500][8029352]| and other pectinolytic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.67| |CITS: [8433375]|. These de-esterified domains can also be cross-linked with calcium, resulting in gel formation that contributes to intercellular adhesion., Pectate lyases have also been documented in plants |CITS: [19144526]|. Plant genomes contain a large number of genes that encode pectate lyase-like proteins (26 such genes are present in the Arabidopsis genome), although they haven't been biochemically characterized yet |CITS: [17447910][12324535]|., Degradation by fungi and bacteria, Fungal and bacterial enzymes involved in HGA degradation include |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.11|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.2|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.9|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.10|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.15|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.67|, and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.82|. Many organisms have many different paralogs of a particular enzyme, each somewhat different in its preferences and serving a somewhat different role (for example, |FRAME: TAX-5061| has seven different variants of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.15|). The combined action of these many enzymes result in an efficient degradation process., Some of the enzymes require that the backbone has little or no methyl-esterification (e.g. |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.2|), while others require methyl-esterification for activity (e.g. |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.10|). Pectinesterases that remove the methyl groups have been purified from both fungi |CITS: [1937044][8920970][10677368]| and bacteria |CITS: [2837615][8370537][10872083]|. A pectin molecule that has been de-esterified is called |FRAME: PECTATE|., Two types of endo-lyases that act on HGA are |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.10|, which prefers substrates with a high degree of methylesterification, and |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.2|, which prefers those with a low degree of esterification. A clearer distinction between these two enzyme regards their dependence on Ca2+ ions: while pectate lyases have an absolute requirement for Ca2+, pectin lyases do not require it |CITS: [9195887]|. Six pectin lyase genes and one pectate lyase gene have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-5061| |CITS: [2535502][7788717][11112543]|. Another type of lyase, reported only from bacteria, is |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.9|, which cleaves an unsaturated disaccharide from the non-reducing end |CITS: [14188174][10049400][10383957]|. Yet another lyase, |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.27|, described from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5060|, cleaves an unsaturated monosaccharide from the non-reducing end of methyl-esterified susbstrates |CITS: [25610636]|., The main hydrolases that act on the HGA backbone are |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.15|, which cleaves randomly within the pectin smooth region, forming shorter oligosaccharides |CITS: [2535502][2331322][10675564]|, and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.67|, an exo-polygalacturonase that removes monosaccharides from the non-reducing ends of these oligosaccharides |CITS:[Hata84][24414660][Beldman96][8856078]|. Another hydrolase, reported so far only from bacteria, is |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.82|, which cleaves disaccharides off the non-reducing end |CITS: [5661621][2168372]|., No less than seven endopolygalacturonases have been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-5061|. These enzymes differ in their specific activity (varying from 25 to 4,000 U/mg), sensitivity to methylation of the substrate |CITS: [10092840][10601263][10642523][10675564]|, and mode of action. Endopolygalacturonases I, A, C, and D show processive behavior |CITS: [10092840][10642523][10675564]|, whereas the other three enzymes (endopolygalacturonases II, B, and E) work via a single-attack mechanism |CITS: [10092840][10642523][10675564]|., All of the endo- and exo-polygalacturonases hydrolyze the substrate via an inverting mechanism and belong to the GH28 glycoside hydrolase family |CITS: [8605979]|.

Summary: Microorganisms such as |FRAME: TAX-546| or |FRAME: TAX-573| are able to grow anaerobically on |FRAME: GLYCEROL| as the sole carbon and energy source. In the absence of an external oxidant, glycerol is fermented by a dismutation process involving two pathways., Through one pathway, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-573 "Klebsiella pneumoniae 1033 (previously known as Aerobacter aerogenes 1033)"|, glycerol is dehydrogenated by an NAD+-linked |FRAME: CPLX-3681| (E.C. 1.1.1.6) to |FRAME: DIHYDROXYACETONE|, which is then phosphorylated and funneled to glycolysis by |FRAME: CPLX-3605| |CITS: [13438878]|. , Through the other pathway, originally discovered in Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 8724, glycerol is dehydrated by the coenzyme B12-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-3702| (E.C. 4.2.1.30) to form |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL|, which is reduced to the major fermentation product |FRAME: CPD-347| (PDO) by the NADH-linked |FRAME: CPLX-3663|, thereby regenerating the NAD+ which is used by |FRAME: CPLX-3681|. |FRAME: CPD-347| is not metabolized further, and is excreted by the cells into the medium., The four enzymes that participate in these two pathways are encoded by the dha regulon, the expression of which is induced when dihydroxyacetone or glycerol are present. , Some other species utilize the same pathways, although the regulation may be different. For example, |FRAME: TAX-1580| and |FRAME: TAX-1581| express glycerol dehydratase and 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase during cofermentation of glycerol and other carbon sources, such as glucose, fructose, ribose and lactate |CITS: [1622279]|. These strains cannot grow on glycerol alone, and the dha regulon does not require glycerol for induction., PDO has become a commercially important chemical, due to the recent development of a new polyester called poly(propylene terephtalate), with unique properties for the fiber industry. The |FRAME:TAX-570| enzymes glycerol dehydratase and 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase are used in engineered strains of |FRAME:TAX-562| for the commercial production of PDO.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD0-1308 Glyphosate| is a broad-spectrum systemic herbicide used to kill weeds. It was initially patented and sold by the Monsanto Company in the 1970s under the tradename Roundup, and has become the most used herbicide in the world |CITS: [21668647]|., Glyphosate's mode of action is to inhibit the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.19|, which catalyzes the transfer of the enolpyruvyl moiety of |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: SHIKIMATE-5P| to form |FRAME: 3-ENOLPYRUVYL-SHIKIMATE-5P|. This is a key reaction in the |FRAME: ARO-PWY "shikimate pathway"|, leading to synthesis of aromatic amino acids via |FRAME: CHORISMATE| in plants, fungi, bacteria, and apicomplexan parasites |CITS: [7396959]|., While little degradation of glyphosate has been reported in plants (most likely due to contaminating microbes), glyphosate degradation in soils is extensive and rapid |CITS: [Torstensson85]|. Three degradation pathways have been described so far, two of which involve production of |FRAME: CPD0-1074| (AMPA) |CITS: [16347639][Monsanto95]|, a phosphonate that can be metabolized by a wide variety of microorganisms |CITS: [14088788][14302415][618850][Daughton79][Daughton79a][453832][3804975]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7805|). , A number of pure cultures of bacteria have been identified that degrade glyphosate by one of the known routes |CITS: [16346357][Talbot84][2430939][16346999][2442160][3804975][2439330][16347356][Hallas88][3997803][3223761][16347639][Quinn88][Lerbs90][2339877][16348512]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-694258| was isolated by scientists from the Monsanto company from a |FRAME: CPD0-1308| waste stream treatment facility based on its ability to degrade |FRAME: CPD0-1308| and use it as a phosphorus source |CITS: [Monsanto95]|. The organism was found to produce a FAD-containing |FRAME: MONOMER-19919| that catalyzes the cleavage of the carbon-nitrogen bond of |FRAME: CPD0-1308|, yielding |FRAME: CPD0-1074| (AMPA) and |FRAME: GLYOX| without production of hydrogen peroxide. The activity of the enzyme was quite low due to a very high (27 mM) Km for |FRAME: CPD0-1308|. A mutated form exhibited a substantially higher kinetic efficiency |CITS: [Monsanto95]|., Another strain of |FRAME: TAX-528| shown to use |FRAME: EC-1.5.3.23|, is |FRAME: ORG-6332|, isolated from soils contaminated with glyphosate |CITS: [21789492]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MET| (Met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in protein biosynthesis, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines. In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., Some bacteria can synthesize methionine using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE| with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine (see |FRAME: HOMOSER-METSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [3309561]|. Plants use a modification of this pathway, where |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, instead of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting homoserine to cystathionine (see |FRAME: PWY-702|)., Other bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi, can use a different route in which they directly assimilate inorganic sulfur by a sulfhydrylation (this pathway). In this route |FRAME: HS|, the final product of microbial sulfate reduction (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) reacts with O-acetylated homoserine, with replacement of the acetyl group by sulfide to form |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is once again methylated to methionine (see |FRAME: PWY-5344|)., Most methanogenic archaea utilize yet a different pathway. While these organisms also use |FRAME: HS| as the sulfur source, the other precursor for |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| production is |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, produced from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7977|)., Methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., About This Pathway, Organisms for which there is evidence for the existence of a direct sulfhydrylation pathway for methionine biosynthesis include |FRAME:TAX-4932| (reviewed in |CITS: [9409150]|), the spirochete |FRAME: TAX-29508| |CITS: [9440513], [12951250]|, |FRAME:TAX-1423| |CITS: [11832514]|, |FRAME:TAX-92706| |CITS: [7096282], [7275950]|, |FRAME:TAX-1718|, |CITS: [11844756]|, |FRAME:TAX-287| |CITS: [10482527]|, and |FRAME:TAX-303| |CITS: [10482527]|. In these organisms, there is also evidence for the transsulfuration pathway, and the use of one pathway may predominate over the other., In |FRAME:TAX-562| and other enteric bacteria only the transsulfuration pathway is used (Greene, R.C. in |CITS: [COLISAL]| pp. 542-560). , The presence of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.49|, is considered indicative of the presence of a direct sulfhydrylation pathway., Note that all bacterial methionine biosynthetic pathways involve acylated homoserine. However, the O-acyl group is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast, and most Gram-positive bacteria (see |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|) but a succinyl group in enteric bacteria and some other Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-287| and |FRAME:TAX-303| (this pathway) (|CITS: [10482527][3309561][9409150]|).

|FRAME:CPD-14703 Furcatin| (|CITS:[Hase82]|), is the β-D-apiofuranosyl-(1->6)-β-glucoside of |FRAME:CPD-6483| (p-allylphenol) which has been found in |FRAME:TAX-237940|. |FRAME:CPD-6483 Chavicol| associates with various sugar moieties, thus forming species-specific phenolic heterosides such as chavicol rutinoside (Cerasus lusitanica - |FRAME:TAX-3745|), the xylopyranosyl glucopyranoside myaginin (Lespedeza thunbergii - |FRAME:TAX-3803|) and chavicol β-D-glucoside (Cedronella canariensis - |FRAME:TAX-4136|) |CITS:[Coen95]|. , The release of the volatile |FRAME:CPD-6483| (this pathway) is probably a defense reaction against predators for which several facts are indicative. First of all |FRAME:CPD-6483| has been shown to possess fungicide, insect-deterring, larva growth-inhibiting, and nematocide activity |CITS:[12481100]| |CITS:[Dube89]| |CITS:[Evans84]|. In this respect |FRAME:CPD-6483| and its methylester |FRAME:CPD-6484| as well as other volatile cinnamoic esters (see |FRAME:PWY-4201|) are part of the versatile defense mechanisms plants have developed over time. The separated location of |FRAME:CPD-14703| (probably vacuole) and its diglucoside glucosidase (furcatin hydrolase) (chloroplast) is another cue for a predator deferring defense as both compounds can only come into contact and react with each other when plant tissues are disrupted (see cyanogenesis, e.g. |FRAME:PWY-7089|)., Furcatin hydrolase is a unique diglucoside-specific glucosidase (|CITS:[14579595]|) which hydrolyzes substrates under retention of stereochemistry and only cuts the β-glycosidic bond between the aglycon and disaccharide but not inter-glycosidic bonds |CITS:[14976214]| |CITS:[13717574]|. FH expressed his highest activity toward the native substrate |FRAME:CPD-14703| in |FRAME:TAX-4204| and only furthermore cleaves disaccharides composed of two different monosaccharides from the aglycone, e.g. |FRAME:6-O-BETA-D-XYLOPYRANOSYL| (β-primeverose) and |FRAME:VICIANOSE| but not disaccharides made up by monosaccharides of the same type such as |FRAME:CPD-3605| |CITS:[17998137]|. Furcatin hydrolase is among the two out of four diglucoside glucosidases which have been cloned and sequence analyzed which provided a better understanding of the cleavage mechanism on a molecular level |CITS:[18667453]|.

|FRAME: GALACTITOL Galactitol| is one of the three abundant naturally-occuring hexitols (the others are |FRAME: SORBITOL| and |FRAME: MANNITOL|), which are produced by many plants of genera such as |FRAME: TAX-90353|, |FRAME: TAX-1501480|, |FRAME: TAX-52724|, and |FRAME: TAX-4163|. , |FRAME: CPD-12811| is a much rarer sugar alcohol. It was originally isolated from brown algae of the order |FRAME: TAX-3009| |CITS: [11557070]|. Various organisms, including fungi, yeast, and bacteria, can probably synthesize D-altritol, but the pathways leading to its production are still uncharacterized |CITS: [MUNIRUZZAMAN9][Sasahara98][16716921][18175917]|., A pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-12811| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| has been characterized from the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-176299|. The pathway was discovered based on the proximity of the genes encoding its enzymes to a gene encoding a solute-binding protein that reacted with both |FRAME: CPD-12811| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|. Transcript levels for all four genes were up-regulated several thousand-fold when the organism was grown on |FRAME: CPD-12811| or |FRAME: GALACTITOL| compared with |FRAME: D-Glucose| |CITS: [26472925]|., All four enzymes were produced recombinantly and purified, and their activity was demonstrated in vitro. In addition, knock-outs mutants of each of the two dehydrogenases abolished growth on the respective substrate |CITS: [26472925]|., Orthologous genes encoding the pathway's enzymes have been observed in plant pathogens, plant-associated bacteria, or soil-dwelling bacteria belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-357|, |FRAME: TAX-379|, and |FRAME: TAX-68287| genera |CITS: [26472925]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-20340 Ophthalmate| is a tripeptide analog of |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| in which the |FRAME: CYS| group is replaced by |FRAME: CPD0-1942|. It was first discovered during the study of peptides present in calf lens, and was named based on its presence in that tissue |CITS: [Waley56][13471529]|. The exact structure was reported in 1958 |CITS: [13522597]|., The similarity in the structures of |FRAME: CPD-20340| and |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| prompted the suggestion that the two share the same biosynthetic pathway. Indeed, incubation of |FRAME: GLT|, |FRAME: CPD0-1942|, and |FRAME: GLY| in the presence of ATP and lens extract resulted in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20340|. The authors noted that this process consisted of two enzymatic reactions, and that at least one of the enzymes also participated in |FRAME: GLUTATHIONESYN-PWY| |CITS: [13572330]|. In a different study of the bovine lens, radioactivity from labeled L-glutamate was found in ophthalmate, supporting the proposed pathway |CITS: [4772629]|. While both |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| and |FRAME: CPD-20340| are produced by the enzymes, production of the former is usually much more significant. A study with rabbit lens found that the rate of glutathione formation under normal conditions was more than 40 fold higher than that of ophthalmate |CITS: [5927446]|., In addition to |FRAME: GLT|, the second input of the pathway is |FRAME: CPD0-1942|. This compound has been shown to be produced from |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| by a number of aminotransferases, such as |FRAME: CPLX66-371| |CITS: [27827456]|. |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is produced by many enzymes, but the main source is belived to be |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.1|, which is involved in |FRAME: CYS| production |CITS: [27827456]|., Later studies have shown that production of |FRAME: CPD-20340| is not limited to the lens. Studies with mouse have shown synthesis taking place in the liver and the kidney |CITS: [637852]|. |FRAME: CPD-20340 Ophthalmate| was also detected in liver and brain of higher animals |CITS: [6721150]|. More recent work has shown that |FRAME: CPD-20340| production is not limited to mammals. It was first discovered that both |FRAME: CPD-20340| and |FRAME: CPD0-2056| form and accumulate in the model cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148| that has been stressed by glucose |CITS: [26713511]|. It was later announced that both compounds are produced in all plants |CITS: [29413907]|., Since conjugation with glutathione is one of the main pathways for the detoxification of reactive metabolites in the liver, depletion of glutathione concentration is a sign of oxidative stress. However, glutathione concentration is difficult to measure directly due to its instability. As the first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.2|, is inhibited by glutathione, |FRAME: CPD-20340| production is expected to be reversibly correlated to glutathione concentration and thus the serum concentration of |FRAME: CPD-20340| has been suggested as a sensitive indicator of hepatic |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| depletion and oxidative stress |CITS: [16608839]|. Later work suggested that ophthalmate concentration on its own is not a reliable marker since additional information about the |FRAME: MET| status of the system is needed in order to relate it uniquely to the intracellular glutathione concentration.  However, when ophthalmate concentration is measured simultaneously with |FRAME: 5-OXOPROLINE| concentration, a direct inference of the glutathione concentration can be made |CITS: [21888969][23632663]|., An |FRAME: TAX-562| ΔyggS mutant, which accumulates large amounts of |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| and |FRAME: CPD0-1942|, has been found to produce large amounts of |FRAME: CPD-20340| |CITS: [27426274]|. Further modifications, which included overexpressing gshA and gshB, modifying GshA to avoid inhibition by GSH, and eliminating the catabolic enzyme γ-glutamyltranspeptidase, which can catabolize |FRAME: CPD-20340|, resulted in a strain that produces 277 μmol ophthalmate per liter in 24 h |CITS: [29352090]|.

Cyanobacteria are able to live in waters of differing salt concentrations due to several mechanisms for salt adaptation. One of those is the production of osmoprotective compounds, also known as compatible solutes., The first osmoprotective compound reported from a marine cyanobacterium, |FRAME: CPD-16855|, was identified in the cyanobacterium Synechococcus sp. strain N100 in 1980 |CITS: [17815155]| and subsequently observed in many other strains |CITS: [Erdmann83][Reed86][Stal87]|. The compound is absent in unstressed cells and is synthesized immediately after a salt shock to an intracellular concentration which corresponds to the strength of the stress |CITS: [Hagemann87][Erdmann92]|., A correlation exists between the salt tolerance limit and the nature of the main osmolyte. Poorly halotolerant strains accumulate |FRAME: SUCROSE| and |FRAME: TREHALOSE|, moderately halophilic strains accumulate |FRAME: CPD-16855|, and strains exhibiting the highest salt tolerance synthesize betaines (see |FRAME: Betaine-Biosynthesis|) |CITS: [Reed86]|., The moderately halotolerant cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148| accumulates |FRAME: CPD-16855| as its main compatible solute |CITS: [Reed85]|. The osmolyte is produced mainly by de novo synthesis from photosynthetically fixed CO2 with only a small fraction synthesized from stored glycogen |CITS: [Mackay87]|. , |FRAME: CPD-16855| is synthesized from |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by the action of two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.213|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.69| |CITS: [Hagemann94][9045835][9733686]|. Analysis of different mutants showed that the |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| is formed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.94|, and not by phosphorylation of |FRAME: GLYCEROL|., |FRAME: CPD-16855| that leaks from the cellular cytoplasm to the extracellular space may be imported back into the cell by the GgtABCD system |CITS: [9006025][11081796]|. Upon transition from a high-salt to a low-salt environment, osmoprotective compounds, are no longer needed, and |FRAME: CPD-16855| is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.M9| |CITS: [27621728]|.

|FRAME:NAD| and its reduced and phosphorylated derivatives are essential metabolites in all organisms and are, except for protons, water and oxygen, integrated with more biochemical reactions than any other biochemical agent |CITS:[22404877]|. As major players involved in energy metabolism, electron transfer and indispensable metabolic cycles the various |FRAME:NAD| species have attracted much attention and generated significant research efforts in elucidating their specific roles in relevant catalyses. In addition, there is growing evidence that |FRAME:NAD| species also operate in signaling pathways |CITS:[19211509] [21349851]|.   , In |FRAME:TAX-4932| the interconvertibility of the various |FRAME:NAD| species is of utmost importance for maintaining the redox balance of the cells which, in turn determines growth efficiency and metabolite excretion |CITS:[1900238]|. The various pyridine nucleotides, in particular |FRAME:NADH| cannot permeate the inner membrane of mitochondrion. For that reason direct transversal exchanges of |FRAME:NAD| and reduced and/or phosphorylated derivatives from the cytosol to the mitochondria and vice versa are not possible. Moreover, yeast does not possess transhydrogenases, hence cannot directly convert |FRAME:NAD| and |FRAME:NADPH| into |FRAME:NADP| and |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[3789705]|. Consequently, to ensure the availability of the required |FRAME:NAD| metabolites in each organelle, yeast has developed independent sets of interconversion reactions that provide the supply of all |FRAME:NAD| types through various enzymatic reactions., In the cytoplasm two NAD kinases have been characterized that can phosphorylate |FRAME:NAD|. The main cytosolic NAD kinase is encoded by UTR1 |CITS:[15978040] [11425472]|. A second, less important NAD kinase for phosphorylation of |FRAME:NAD|, i.e. YEF1 has also been described and shown to compensate for the loss of UTR1 |CITS:[15978040]|. The deletion of both the mitochondrial POS5 (see |FRAME:PWY-7269|) and cytosolic UTR1 is lethal in yeast and YEF1 can only compensate when POS5 still operates. These findings support the notion that the main NADH kinases of yeast, i.e. POS5 and UTR1 can partially compensate for the loss of one's respective activity |CITS:[16760478]|. Both UTR1 and YEF1 have been shown to exhibit NADH kinase activity as well providing the cytosolic set of enzymes with the catalytic ability to phosphorylate |FRAME:NADH| |CITS:[15978040] [16760478]|. , Various enzymatic reactions have been shown to account for the provision of the cytosol with |FRAME:NADPH| required for biosynthetic pathways and anti-oxidant functions. The cytosolic acetaldehyde dehydrogenase encoded by ALD6 |CITS:[9392076] [9473035]|  and the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (ZWF1) catalyzing the first step in the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| to convert |FRAME:GLC-6-P| to |FRAME:D-6-P-GLUCONO-DELTA-LACTONE| |CITS:[2269430] [12584194] [11557322]| are considered as the main suppliers of |FRAME:NADPH|. A third enzyme producing |FRAME:NADPH| in the cytoplasm is the cytosolic NADP-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDP2) |CITS:[8068643] [15574419]|. It has been demonstrated that ZWF1 has overlapping functions with the isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDP2) and the acetaldehyde oxidoreductase (ALD6) indicating the compensation for the deficiency of |FRAME:NADPH| should one of the involved reactions fail to operate |CITS:[16179340]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase I (NDH-1) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), reductase the transfer of electrons from NADH to DMSO is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane., Two electrons are transferred from the NADH oxidation site to the DMSO reduction site by a menaquinone pool. The number of protons pumped across the membrane by NDH-1 is currently unknown |CITS: [12600193]| however the H+/e- ratio for NDH-1 is at least 1.5 |CITS: [8892824]|. DMSO reductase does not catalyse vectorial proton translocation however the reduction of the DMSO and many other amine-N-oxides and methyl-sulfoxides, including trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), contributes two protons to the proton-motive force. , DMSO reductase is functionally similar to the TMAO reductases but genetically distinct |CITS: [2832366]|. This enzyme functions under anaerobic conditions and in the absence of nitrate (a preferred electron acceptor) |CITS: [2544558]|. DMSO is the preferred substrate for this enzyme |CITS: [3280546]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, Carotenoids with cyclic ends are integral constituents of plants, algae and cyanobacteria photosynthetic, reaction centers |CITS:[GOODWIN80],[YOUNG93]|. An important branch-point in the biosynthesis of carotenoids lies in the cyclization of the linear, pink |FRAME:CPD1F-114| into carotenes with all-β-, all-ε- or mixed β and ε rings. The cyclization reactions are catalyzed by lycopene β- or ε-cyclases. These cyclases all share a conserved amino acid sequence signature and bind dinucleotides such as FAD and NADP |CITS:[8837512]|, but otherwise share little resemblance., A single cyclization reaction by |FRAME: MONOMER-12151| results in the formation of |FRAME: CPD1F-115|. A second cyclization is performed by |FRAME: MONOMER-12154|, generating |FRAME: CPD1F-118|. A second cyclization by |FRAME: MONOMER-12151| is unlikely, as the ε-cyclase does not seem to be able to add a second ε ring to the monocyclic |FRAME: CPD1F-115| |CITS:[8837512]|., It has been postulated that the regulation of ε-cyclase, possibly through control of gene expression, determines xanthophylls composition in leaves and other plant tissues, since its products (δ-carotene) is destined to the α-carotene branch |CITS:[10205893]|.

Summary: Coenzyme B Background, |FRAME: CPD-1281 "Coenzyme B"| is one of the many unusual cofactors that are present in methanogens and required for methane formation. Like |FRAME:Factor-420|, |FRAME: CPD-1281| acts an an electron carrier. All catabolic processes in methanogenesis require |FRAME: CPD-1281| for the reduction of the methylated form of |FRAME: CoM| (|FRAME: Me-CoM|) to |FRAME:CH4|, which is the terminal step of methanogenesis (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [12102556]|. The |FRAME: CPD-1282| is produced along with |FRAME: CH4| during this step and subsequently acts as a terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic respiration (see |FRAME:PWY-5207 |) |CITS: [12102556]|., The structure of |FRAME: CPD-1281| was determined as N-7-mercaptoheptanoyl)threonine phosphate |CITS: [3086878]| and confirmed by chemical synthesis |CITS: [3100513]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1281| is composed from two moieties - |FRAME: CPD-349| and |FRAME: THR|. The |FRAME: CPD-349| moiety is synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-337|, which is produced from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| by repeated cycles of α-ketoacid chain elongation. This cycle occurs three times, increasing the number of methylenes from two in |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to three in |FRAME: 2K-ADIPATE|, four in |FRAME: CPD-291|, and finally five in |FRAME: CPD-337| |CITS: [White89][2495771][9665716]|., The series of reactions in α-ketoacid chain elongation involves three basic reactions: a condensation between an α-ketodiacid and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to form a citrate homolog, isomerization of the citrate homolog to an isocitrate homolog, and oxidative decarboxylation of the isocitrate homolog to an α-ketodiacid containing an additional methylene group |CITS: [9665716]|. These reactions are analogous to the reactions catalyzed by citrate synthase, aconitase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase in the |FRAME:TCA| and the reactions catalyzed by (R)-homocitrate synthase, homoaconitase and (-)-threo-isohomocitrate dehydrogenase in |FRAME: PWY-3081| |CITS: [9665716]|., The pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-349| was postulated based on measuring the incorporation of 3H and 13C labeled precursors by growing cells of methanogens using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry |CITS: [White89][2495771][2514799]|. The reactions converting |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: CPD-337| were also demonstrated in cell free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-2210| |CITS: [9665716]|., The product of the α-ketoacid chain elongation process, |FRAME: CPD-337|, is converted to a thiol by decarboxylation and sulfonation in an analogous fashion to the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-380| to |FRAME: CoM|, |CITS: [White89]|. The thiol form, |FRAME: CPD-349|, is then coupled to threonine, forming |FRAME: CPD-359|, which is phosphorylated to form |FRAME: CPD-1281| |CITS: [8003472]|., The protein product of the |FRAME: TAX-2190| |FRAME: G-1382| gene was overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-83333| and demonstrated to catalyze the condensation of |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, |FRAME: 2K-ADIPATE| and |FRAME: CPD-291| with |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, forming |FRAME: HOMO-CIT|, |FRAME: CPD-152| and |FRAME: CPD-301|, respectively |CITS: [9665716]|., The |FRAME: TAX-2190| |FRAME: G-1383| and |FRAME: G-1385| genes were cloned and overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and shown to encode the large and small subunits of a |FRAME: CPLX-7737|, respectively. Unlike the bacterial aconitase, which is involved in lysine biosynthesis, this enzyme catalyzes both the dehydration and hydration reactions of the pathway. The enzyme is rather specific, and does not accept the compounds used in lysine biosynthesis |CITS: [18765671]|., The |FRAME: G-1384| gene from |FRAME: TAX-2190| was cloned and overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and it's product was found to catalyze the NAD-dependent decarboxylation of the three products of the aconitase, namely |FRAME: HOMO-I-CIT|, |FRAME: CPD-285|, and |FRAME: CPD-336|., The last four enzymes of this pathway have not been characterized yet.

General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified., The hydrolysis of glucosinolates by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147|, leads to the production of isothiocyanates, which have a wide variety of pharmacological activities, including antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and anti-tumor properties. For example, the 4-methylsulfinylbutyl glucosinolate |FRAME: CPDQT-280| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-19494|, which is a major inducer of phase II detoxification enzymes that are important in chemoprotection from carcinogens |CITS: [9294217]|. The enzyme, which is found in glucosinolate-producing plants, is often inactivated during cooking., About This Pathway, Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-550|, |FRAME: TAX-316435|, |FRAME: TAX-684738|, and |FRAME: TAX-1590| KW30, were found to catalyze degradation of the glucosinolates |FRAME: CPDQT-280| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLSULFINYLPROPYL-GLUCOSINOLATE|. Differences were reported between the Enterobacteriaceae and the lactic acid bacteria, with the former converting these glucosinolates to |FRAME: CPDQT-281| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLTHIOPROPYL-GLUCOSINOLATE|, respectively, and the latter converting them into nitriles and further unidentified metabolites. The authors suggested that the Enterobacteriacea may utilize only |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.13|, while the lactic acid bacteria utilize |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) |CITS: [23461529]|., A 2025 study that studied glucosinolate degradation by |FRAME: TAX-1590| has concluded that |FRAME: CPDQT-281| was degraded via three distinct pathways. The authors identified a myrosinase, encoded by the |FRAME: LP_RS12660| gene. The enzyme had been previously characterized biochemically as |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.86| |CITS: [36454042]|. However, purified recombinant enzyme was shown to possess myrosinase activity, converting |FRAME: CPDQT-280| to |FRAME: CPD-19506|, which loses a sulfate group spontaneouly and rearranges to form the isothiocyanate |FRAME: CPD-19494| (a process known as Lossen rearrangement) |CITS: [40062683]|., In agreement with a proposal originally made in |CITS: [23461529]|, the authors suggested that |FRAME: CPD-19494| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-28110| by |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.13| (MsrA) - |FRAME: TAX-1590| possesses three genes encoding such enzymes. Summary: Cytotoxic benzophenanthridine alkaloids are accumulated in certain species of |FRAME: TAX-3465| in response to pathogenic attack and, therefore, function as phytoalexins. |FRAME: TAX-3467| California poppy  root cultures produce a variety of benzophenanthridine alkaloids, such as |FRAME: SANGUINARINE|, chelirubine and |FRAME: CPD-7848|, with potent biological activity |CITS: [12602874]|. The accumulation of benzophenanthridine alkaloids and the enzyme activity during diseased states emphasizes the integral role of the berberine bridge enzyme in the plant response to pathogens |CITS: [1946465 ]|. Several studies involving the introduction of sense and antisense construct of genes of benzophenanthridine alkaloid metabolism have helped in getting a clearer picture and thereby improve approaches to metabolic engineering of benzophenanthridine alkaloid pathways |CITS: [11842172]|.

Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, In this pathway, the pyrimidine nucleoside |FRAME: CYTIDINE| is first hydrolyzed to the nucleobase |FRAME: CYTOSINE| by removal of the ribose sugar by the enzyme |FRAME: YDR400W-MONOMER "ribonucleoside nucleosidase"| (|FRAME: EC-3.2.2.3 "EC 3.2.2.3"|). Cytosine is then deaminated by |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.1 "cytosine deaminase (EC 3.5.4.1)"| to the pyrimidine base |FRAME: URACIL| |CITS: [10024464][10469156]|., The resulting uracil base can be salvaged to form a pyrimidine nucleotide (see |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7193|). Alternatively, uracil can be degraded to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| by releasing NH3 and CO2 in a three step reductive pathway (|FRAME: PWY-3982|). β-Alanine is a precursor of pentothenate and coenzyme A., The overall metabolic outcome of this pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: CYTIDINE| to |FRAME: URACIL|, can also be achieved by a different pathway, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6556|., Mammals and plants do not have either of the enzymes of this pathway, and thus can not salvage cytosine by this route. Instead they utilize a nucleoside kinase-based pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7183|). Plants can also salvage pyrimidine nucleosides via the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6556|.
