Summary: General Background, Chloroaromatic compounds occur in the environment in large amounts due to their release as herbicides or as byproducts, of industrial production., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation capabilities have evolved only recently as a response, to their widespread availability in soil and water., Many of the degradation pathways merge at the level of chlorocatechols. Often organisms that can degrade, non-chlorinated aromatic compounds (such as benzoate) can convert the chlorinated vatiants to the level of, chlorocatechols, due to enzyme promiscuity |CITS: [4836257]|. However, the enzymes that degrade catechol have, little activity with chloro-substituted compounds, and the chlorocatechols that accumulate as a result are toxic to the, bacteria. Thus, in order to be able to degrade chlorobenzoates and chlorobenzenes successfully, the bacteria must, possess specific enzymes for the degradation of chlorocatechols., About This Pathway, The more common route for |FRAME: CPD-9151| degradation involves ortho cleavage, performed by, |FRAME: MONOMER-14417|., Usually, meta cleavage of chlorinated catechols by 2,3-dioxygenases results in an inactivation of the enzyme., This inactivation is most likely caused by the strong chelating activity of |FRAME: CPD-9151|, which removes, the |FRAME: FE+2| cofactor of the enzyme |CITS: [7259155]|, or by suicide inactivation of the enzyme due to the, formation of a reactive intermediate or product, such as an acylchloride |CITS: [16346490]|., Surprisingly, the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6096| is able to grow on |FRAME: CHLOROBENZENE| as the sole source, for carbon, nitrogen and energy. The bacterium degrades chlorobenzene via |FRAME: CPD-9151| using a, meta-cleavage pathway |CITS: [9226262]|., The key enzyme of the pathway is a unique |FRAME: CPLX-7823| that is not sensitive to inhibition by acylchlorides., This enzyme has been purified and characterized, and remarkably, its activity with |FRAME: CPD-9151| is 95% of the, activity with |FRAME: CATECHOL|., The product of the enzyme is believed to be |FRAME: CPD-11210|, an acylchloride that spontaneously eliminates, the chloride, forming |FRAME: CPD-13339| |CITS: [9440519]|. The later can be converted using the regular, meta-cleavage enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-7237| and |FRAME: CPLX-7822| to |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|,, which is degraded to central metabolism intermediates (see |FRAME: PWY-5162|)., the pathway has been demonstrated in several other strains that are able to metabolize |FRAME: CPD-9151|,, including |FRAME: TAX-231957|, |FRAME: ORG-6097| and |FRAME: ORG-6098| |CITS: [15340793]|. All of these, organisms possess genes very similar to |FRAME: G-11254|.

Triterpene compounds are plant secondary, metabolites that are often involved in plant, defense and, may also have beneficial effects when, ingested by humans. They arise from numerous, different, cyclizations of 2,3-oxidosqualene catalyzed by, various oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs), |CITS:[16581287][ 17446857][10536024]|., Attempts to determine the functional specificity of, members of the OSC family of enzymes in, Arabidopsis led to the discovery that BARS1, produces, baruol, when expressed in yeast, or examined, in vitro |CITS:[17705488]|., This compound has not yet been, isolated from Arabidopsis, but it has been, found in a specimen of the |FRAME: ORG-6046| tree,, collected in Panama |CITS: [Nunez04]|. , The identification of baruol in Arabidopsis should help to, confirm the presence of this biosynthetic pathway and further characterization of BARS1 should, clarify its biological importance. , This enzyme also produces 22 minor triterpenes, with quite different structures when it is, analyzed in a heterologous system, |CITS:[17705488]|. So, further work will also, help to elucidate whether these products, are generated in Arabidopsis and, if so,, what role they play in plant survival.

General Background, Creatine is a naturally occurring amino acid that is used to store and supply energy to muscle cells in vertebrates., The name creatine is derived from the Greek kreas (flesh)., The enzyme creatine kinase adds a phosphate to creatine (see |FRAME: CREATINE-KINASE-RXN|), generating, |FRAME: CREATINE-P|. The energy stored in the creatine-phosphate bond can be reused when creatine phosphate, reacts with ADP to regenerate ATP. , In fast-twitch skeletal muscles, a large pool of creatine-phosphate is available for immediate regeneration of ATP, hydrolyzed during short periods of intense work. Because of the high cytosolic creatine kinase activity in these, muscles, the creatine kinase reaction remains in a near-equilibrium state, keeping ADP and ATP almost constant,, and buffering the cytosolic phosphorylation potential that is crucial for proper functioning of cellular ATPases, |CITS: [10893433]|., Creatine is found in the blood, brain, and muscle of many organisms. , Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate in muscle, and is usually produced at a fairly constant rate, by the body in a nonenzymatic process. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, and is mainly filtered by the kidney and, excreted in the urine., Both creatine and creatinine can be used by microorganisms as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [Tsuru77]|., At least three different routes by which different microbes degrade creatinine have been discovered, |CITS: [10893433]|., About This Pathway, This pathway of creatinine degradation has not been characterized as well as the other ones. As a matter of fact,, it is described in only one publication., In this pathway, which was detected in |FRAME: TAX-316|, creatinine is degraded into |FRAME: CPD-593| and, |FRAME: ACET| |CITS: [5652018]|., Under aerobic conditions, 85 % of the creatinine added to the bacterial suspension was converted quantitatively, to methylguanidine and acetate (in a 1:1 ratio), and only a few percents of urea and ammonia were formed., However, under unaerobic conditions only 50% of the creatinine was converted. About 50% of this proportion was, converted to methylguanidine and acetate, while the rest was converted to urea., The active enzyme was not isolated or characterized., Even though the second enzyme in the pathway (|FRAME: MONOMER-11026|) has not been documented in, |FRAME: TAX-316|, it is included in this pathway to suggest a possible route for the methylguanidine formed, during the first step (as suggested in |CITS: [10893433]|., This enzyme hydrolyzes methylguanidine to urea and methylamine, and was discovered in an unidentified, |FRAME:TAX-507| species (N-42), which was isolated from soil |CITS: [7353662]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-19988 Ethionamide| is an antibiotic used to treat active multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. It was discovered in 1956, and the first clinical trials were started by Brouet in France already in 1957. It was approved for medical use in the United States in 1965, and is currently used with other antituberculosis agents as part of a second-line regimen for active tuberculosis., |FRAME: CPD-19988 Ethionamide| is a prodrug, and requires metabolism by a bacterial enzyme before having a bactericidal effect. It has been known since 2000 that it is activated in situ by a Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase of |FRAME: TAX-1773| encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-8152| gene |CITS: [10869356][10944230]|. The final product of three rounds of oxygenation by EthA is |FRAME: CPD-19991|, an active compound that binds NAD+ to form an adduct. Following hydrolysis of an imino group, the final product inhibits the |FRAME: CPLX-8831| (encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-5668| gene) |CITS: [8284673][11823459]|., InhA is a component of the FAS II system of |FRAME: TAX-1773|, catalyzing the enoyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] reductase step in the elongation cycle. The enzyme acts on very long and unsaturated fatty acids before they are modified and incorporated into mycolic acids. Disruption of the enzyme results in disruption in mycolic acid biosynthesis |CITS: [1416831]|., More recently additional |FRAME: TAX-83332| enzymes capable of activating |FRAME: CPD-19988| have been discovered. The |FRAME: G185E-7345| gene encodes a second Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenase that has a very similar activity to that of EthA |CITS: [27321573]|. A third enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-4192| gene, appears to catalyze similar activation |CITS: [28302858]|., The prodrug |FRAME: ISONIAZIDE| is activated in a very different manner by |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.21| (KatG), but its activated product also acts on InhA |CITS: [10508348][9417034]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-21372 γ-Hexachlorocyclohexane|, better known as γ-lindane, is a halogenated organic insecticide which has been used worldwide. Due to its toxicity and long persistence in soil, its use has been banned in most countries. However, many contaminated sites still remain throughout the world., Some organisms are able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-21372, | as a sole source of carbon and energy through aerobic degradation. The degradation pathway has been studied in detail in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-332055 "Sphingobium japonicum (at the time described as Sphingomonas paucimobilis UT26)"| |CITS: [10542173] [Chemosphere9-1719][7854251]|., Through the "upstream" portion of the pathway |FRAME: CPD-21372, | is transformed to |FRAME: 25-DICHLOROHYDROQUINONE| through sequential reactions catalyzed by the products of |FRAME: G-257|, |FRAME: G-258|, and |FRAME: G-259|., |FRAME: 25-DICHLOROHYDROQUINONE| is further metabolized via the "downstream" portion of the pathway, through, reactions catalyzed by the products of |FRAME: G-260|, |FRAME: G-261|, |FRAME: G-11202|, LinGH, and LinJ to |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which are metabolized in the |FRAME: TCA|. The last two reactions are described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-2361|., In addition to these catalytic enzymes, a putative ABC-type transporter system encoded by linKLMN is also essential for |FRAME: BETA-HCH| utilization by |FRAME: TAX-332055| |CITS: [17634937]|., Two dead-end metabolites can be formed from intermediates of this pathway by spontaneous reactions, |FRAME: 124-TCB| and |FRAME: 25-DICHLOROPHENOL|.

Phospholipids are the major structural components of biological membranes in plants, animals, and , yeasts. In plants, phospholipids predominate extra-chloroplast membranes including the plasma , membrane, mitochondria membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, and microsomal membrane, with , phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine being the major constituents. Phospholipids are , mostly synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. Once synthesized, they are transported to , other phospholipid containing membranes., At least three different pathways contribute to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE| in plants:, The decarboxylation pathway (|FRAME: PWY-5669|), the |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| transfer pathway (|FRAME: PWY4FS-6|), and the base (head group) exchange pathway (|FRAME: PWY-6273|)., The phosphoethanolamine transfer pathway is believed to be the major pathway in plants.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Coumarins Coumarins| are a major group of plant natural products derived from the phenylpropanoid pathway. At least 1000 natural occurring coumarins, among them about 300 simple coumarins, have been found in many families of higher plants |CITS: [BERENBAUM91]|., Coumarins and their derivatives are used in many therapeutic applications including anti-bacterial agents, anti-inflammation, central nervous system stimulants, and anti-coagulants. Synthetic derivatives of 4-hydroxycoumarin such as warfarin, phenprocoumon, and acenocoumarol are among the most widely prescribed anticoagulant pharmaceuticals for the prevention and treatment of thrombosis and embolism. In addition, coumarins may have therapeutic roles in the treatment of cancers and AIDS |CITS: [15579072][17497014][16570501][18991629]|., About This Pathway, This pathway provides the de novo biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-562| of the simple coumarins |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN|, |FRAME: CPD-8186|, and |FRAME: CPD-8097| by connecting the coumarin formation reactions with the bacterial primary metabolism., In plants coumarins are derived from |FRAME: PHE| (see |FRAME: PWY1F-467|). In that pathway, |FRAME: COUMARATE| is formed from |FRAME: PHE| in two steps, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.25| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.91|, which is a cytochorme P-450 hydroxylase. Since the functional expression of plant P-450 enzymes is always difficult in bacterial systems due to their requirement for anchorage on endoplasmic reticulum and redox partners, this engineered pathway (described in |CITS: [21320631]|) starts with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.23|, which converts |FRAME: TYR| to |FRAME: COUMARATE| in a single step. The enzyme that was selected for this pathway is from the red yeast |FRAME: TAX-5535|, since it has a high activity with L-tyrosine |CITS: [17204442]|., The addition of the plant enzymes |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12| and |FRAME: MONOMER-18295| enable the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-8186| |CITS: [22168819]|., The synthesis of |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN| and |FRAME: CPD-8097| involves a second challenge regarding the formation of the intermediate |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA|. In plants, |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA| is produced from |FRAME: COUMARATE| by two enzymes, one of which, |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.96|, is another P-450 enzyme (see |FRAME: PWY-361|). To bypass that enzyme, this pathway utilizes the bacterial enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.9| (encoded in |FRAME: TAX-566546| by the |FRAME: G-2001| gene) that can catalyze the hydroxylation of |FRAME: COUMARATE| to |FRAME: CPD-676| |CITS: [22475509]|, which is converted to |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA| by the plant enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12|., Once |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA| is formed, |FRAME: CPD-8097| can be produced by including the plant enzyme |FRAME: AT3G13610-MONOMER| |CITS: [25927349]|, and |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN| is produced by adding the plant enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.104| |CITS: [18547395]|., It should be notes that the final conversion in each case involves a trans-cis isomerization followed by a subsequent lactonization to close the side chain. The exact mechanism is unknown, and while no enzyme has been identified, the reaction is likely to proceed spontaneously |CITS: [Hartley75][Borges89]|.

Summary: General Background, Pterocarpans constitute a group of natural isoflavonoids, which are typically involved as , phytoalexins in the defense against pathogens of leguminous plants. In contrast to many other isoflavonoids, pterocarpans , are mostly not constitutively expressed but induced by biotic and abiotic stress |CITS: [Dewick94]|., Formononetin is a crucial intermediate in the biosynthesis of phytoalexins, and as such the starting point for the formation , of various pterocarpans. The recent discovery of a new 4'-O-methyltransferase |CITS: [12610212]|, which facilitates an , additional biosynthetic route to synthesize formononetin, sheds new light on the intermediary steps of phytoalexin production in legumes., The biosynthetic route of pterocarpans leads to various compounds distinctive for certain leguminous species. The simple , pterocarpans medicarpin (alfalfa), maackiain (chickpea) and pisatin (pea) are characterized by methoxy, methylendioxy , and 6a-hydroxyl ring substitutents. On the other side there are the complex type pterocarpans, such as phaseollins (bean) , and gluceollins (soybean) bearing prenyl substituents on their furan ring structure |CITS: [Dixon99]| |CITS: [Tahara95]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of pterocarpans is salient by the stereo-specificity of many of the enzymes , involved. Pterocarpan synthase, the enzyme converting 2'-hydroxyisoflavanones [e.g. (-)-vestitone] to the corresponding, pterocarpans [e.g. (6aR, 11aR)-medicarpin] has been demonstrated in alfalfa to consist of in fact two enzymes, a reductase and a dehydratase |CITS: [8071365]| |CITS: [7805842]|. The precedent enzyme, isoflavone reductase, catalyzes the stereo-specific formation of the 2'-hydroxyisoflavanones (6aS or 6aR configuration), which determines the stereochemistry of the subsequent pterocarpans, e.g. (+)-maackiain in pea and (-)-maackiain in chickpea., Pterocarpan phytoalexins are antimicrobial compounds in leguminous plants formed upon pathogenic attacks and similar , biotic stress-related events. Maackiain is together with medicarpin the main pterocarpan phytoalexin in chickpea and occurs there exclusively in a (-)-(6aR,11aR)-configuration |CITS: [8071365]|. Maackiain was allocated within the two subtribes Diocleinae and Erythrininae to 12 species representing 4 genera |CITS: [Ingham90]|., The biosynthetic route of maackiain starts with formononetin, a 4'-methoxylated isoflavone, which is also the origin for , the pterocarpans medicarpin in chickpea and pisatin in pea. The biosynthetic route differs in essentially two additional steps, one introducing a hydroxyl group to the 3'-position of the isoflavone B-ring |CITS: [Dewick78]| followed by another one forming the methylendioxy bridge of maackiain |CITS: [Clemens96]|., The question of how the final stereochemistry is applied to the various pterocarpans is still under discussion. In leguminous plants pterocarpans have been found with different stereochemical orientation. Chick pea and alfalfa accumulate only (-)- or (6aR,11aR)-pterocarpans, whereas peanuts accumulate pterocarpans of the opposite stereochemistry (+)- (6aS, 11aS). The stereochemistry of this phytoalexins can be crucial since it has been found that pathogens cannot break down the opposite enantiomer of the pterocarpans usually found in their target plants |CITS: [VanEtten83]|., There are two possibilities to introduce stereo-specificity to pterocarpans, one is that the reduction of the first chiral , center (6a), catalyzed by the isoflavanone reductase, determines the final stereochemistry of the pterocarpans. It has , been argued that once this center is fixed the second chiral center (11a) cannot invert the stereochemistry which would , cause undue ring strain |CITS: [7805842]|. This would require isoflavone reductase(s) catalyzing two different stereospecific reactions. , The other possibility is that the stereochemistry alters after the first reduction. The isoflavones isolated to date possess only one configuration, which is the (-)- or (6aR,11aR). It is not clear yet how this configuration is converted into the opposite form such as in plants like pea and peanut, where the (+)-pterocarpans accumulate. It has been suggested that a special epimerase exists in this plants, which carries out the epimerization on the stage of either the isoflavanones or pterocarpanes |CITS: [Dixon95]|. However the existence of such an enzyme remains to be shown |CITS: [8071365]| |CITS: [7805842]| |CITS: [7625843]|., The detection and partial characterization of an new enzyme presumably involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-3944|, i.e. isoflavene synthase indicates another path towards |FRAME:CPD-3944| than the proposed isomerization of |FRAME:CPD-3631| to |FRAME:CPD-4462|. It has been previously demonstrated that the sophorol reductase catalyzed the reduction of |FRAME:CPD-3630| and exclusively produced |FRAME:CPD-14741| and not its trans-enantiomer |CITS:[16504226]|. Only the former cis-enantiomer was shown to be accepted by the isoflavene synthase (IFSV) catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17616| from |FRAME:CPD-14741| via dehydrogenation |CITS:[24332213]|. This enzymatic reaction is only present in Pisum sativum known for producing the phytoalexin |FRAME:CPD-3944| and does not operate in other legumes such as alfalfa, chickpea and bean which produce (-)-phytoalexins. Therefore it has been discussed that the reaction catalyzed by IFVS is a branching point towards |FRAME:PWY-2467| although the step(s) forming (+)-enantiomeric intermediates still remain to be elucidated |CITS:[24332213]|.

The degradation of |FRAME:CPD-12724|, a main flavone found in the genus |FRAME:TAX-4139|, is part of a novel and rapid detoxification process of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| generated in oxidative bursts. Oxidative bursts are caused by mechanical damage or pathogen attacks and constitute a first response in plant defense |CITS:[12232215]|. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are known to inhibit spore germination of fungal pathogens |CITS:[Peng92]| and are generally recognized for lowering pathogen viability |CITS:[Keppler89]|. However, if not maintained at a non-lethal level |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| may cause irreparable oxidative damage to its host. Except for the hypersensitive response, which causes the death of host cells and creates a barrier against pathogens |CITS:[2152793]|, plants need to keep a low level of ROS through the enzymatic action of peroxidases and catalases |CITS:[20870416]|. , The first step in the pathway is the deglucuronidation of |FRAME:CPD-12725| to |FRAME:CPD-12724| catalyzed by the baicalin β-D-glucuronidase (baicalinase) (see |FRAME:PWY-7212|) |CITS:[Morimoto95]|, |CITS:[8593473]|, |CITS: [10858442]| |CITS:[Zhang05]|. This reaction produces |FRAME:CPD-12724| which is an potent antifungal and antiviral agent. In addition |FRAME:CPD-12724| is, besides |FRAME:5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE|, also the only substrate for anionic cell-wall associated peroxidases which catalyze its oxidation to |FRAME:CPD-15172|. Three |FRAME:CPD-12724| specific peroxidases have been cloned and characterized to date |CITS:[9575222]| |CITS:[10473572]|. , Peroxidase 1 is special in a sense that, upon stress, it not only acts as an enzyme but also as an structural protein that covalently cross-links with lignincellulose and in doing so reinforces the stability of the cell wall. In the presence of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| peroxidase 1 becomes insoluble, hence, acts like defense-related structural proteins (extensins and proline-rich proteins) |CITS:[2643477]|. This reaction is catalyzed by peroxidase itself and efficiently consummates |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. The other two |FRAME:CPD-12724| specific peroxidases (peroxidase 2 and 3) remain soluble upon stress, hence act not as structural proteins but also efficiently detoxify |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. The pathway is activated in a short time after exposure to stress. It was proposed that the constitutive presence of the peroxidases and the substrates, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-12724| allow for such a rapid response as the peroxidases are not up-regulated under stress |CITS:[10473572]|.

Heliocides (HHs) and methylated heliocides (HBs) are terpenoids, related to gossypol. They are found , co-existing with gossypol in the foliar glands in cotton |CITS: [Bell78]|.  Heliocides have been shown to protect , cotton from insects. Among the heliocides, HH1 is most toxic to the tobacco budworm. Its stereo isomer , HH4 is least toxic, indicating that stereochemistry is a big factor in determining toxicity. The methyl , ethers of heliocides are less toxic to insects. , Heliocides are formed by the condensation of hemigossypolone with monoterpenes, either myrcene or , beta-ocimene (in |FRAME: PWY-3041|), as shown by in vitro chemical synthesis |CITS: [stipanovic78a], [stipanovic78b]|. , No other experimental data supports the pathway.

General Background, A limited number of species of Gram-negative bacteria, all in the family |FRAME: TAX-543|, utilize unusual sugars, derivatives of 3,6-dideoxyhexose, as |FRAME: O-Antigens| of their lipopolysaccharides. These sugars are the dominant antigenic determinants in the membranes of these organisms., Out of the eight possible stereoisomers of 3,6-dideoxyhexoses, only five have been identified in nature. These are |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: CPD-9396|, |FRAME: CPD-9388|, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: CPD-9395|. All five 3,6-dideoxyhexoses have been found in different serovars of |FRAME: TAX-633|, while other genera possess only some of them. For example, |FRAME: TAX-90371| group B contains |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: TAX-295319| contains, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: TAX-90370| contains |FRAME: CPD-9395| |CITS: [8071227]|., These sugars are synthesized via a complex series of enzymatic reactions starting, in most cases, from |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE|, derived from |FRAME: GLC-1-P|. In a reaction catalyzed by the NAD+-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7584|, |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-658|, which is then converted to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1078| in two consecutive enzymatic reactions, mediated by two components of the |FRAME: CPLX-7585| enzyme complex. The first component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13781| (E1), a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP)-linked iron-sulfur-containing catalyst, while the second component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13782| (E3), a [2Fe-2S]-containing flavoprotein., The product of this complex, |FRAME: CPD-1078|, is the parent to four different 3,6-dideoxyhexoses., About This Pathway, The O-antigen of organisms that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-28901| Group B is composed of a repeat unit of four sugars - mannosyl-rhamnosyl-galactosyl-abequose. The last sugar, |FRAME: CPD-9394|, is a dideoxyhexose that confers the O4 antigenic epitope specificity, characteristic of the organisms in this group., Abequose is synthesized from its precursor, |FRAME: CPD-1078|, by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-13793|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10523| gene. During catalysis, the enzyme transfers two hydrogen atoms from NAD(P)H to the keto group on carbon 4 of its substrate, reducing it to the galactose conformation. The corresponding enzyme from group A strains, |FRAME: CPLX-7587|, catalyzes a similar reaction, but the end product assumes the glucose isomeric form |CITS: [2793832]|.

Summary: Hydroxynitrile glucosides are glucosylated compounds that contain nitrile groups |CIT: 18539303|. They may be classified as α-, β-, or γ-hydroxynitrile glucosides depending on the position of the glucosylated carbon relative to the nitrile group. The α-hydroxynitrile glucosides are cyanogenic and serve as anti-herbivory defense compounds; hydrolysis, as occurs when tissue is digested, will result in the release of the nitrile group as |FRAME: HCN|, which is toxic to animals. The β- and γ-hydroxynitriles are produced via a similar mechanism but are not cyanogenic, and their function in the plant is not known., The leucine-derived hydroxynitrile glucosides found in barley (|FRAME: TAX-4513|) are the α-hydroxynitrile |FRAME: CPD-22477|, the β-hydroxynitrile |FRAME: CPD-22484|, and the γ-hydroxynitriles |FRAME: CPD-22481|, |FRAME: CPD-22483|, and |FRAME: CPD-22486|. They are thought to be formed via a branching pathway from |FRAME: LEU| via a mechanism similar to that of |FRAME: PWY-861| |CIT: [12114561][27337134]|. Multifunctional cytochrome P450 enzymes perform the N-monooxygenation, elimination, decarboxylation, and isomerization steps to produce the common intermediate |FRAME: CPD-22475|, which is then transformed to the hydroxynitrile aglycones via monooxygenation and dehydration of various carbons by the cytochromes. A pair of glucosyltransfetases then attach the glucose to the appropriate hydroxyl group.

Seed oils of a few plant species are enriched in conjugated fatty acids (fatty acids containing conjugated or non-methylene-interrupted double bonds). These conjugated double bonds are introduced by divergent forms of the |FRAME: AT3G12120| desaturase that have been named "conjugases"., The conjugases modify an existing double bond to produce the two conjugated double bonds flanking the position of the original bond. This process is sometimes accompanied by the introduction of a new double bond., The substrates for conjugases, just like those of the desaturases, are fatty acids bound to glycerolipids such as phosphatidylcholine. Because conjugated double bonds have high rates of oxidation, seed oils rich in conjugated double bonds are used commercially as drying agents in paints and varnishes., |FRAME: CPD-8231 α-Eleostearate| (18:3Δ9cis,11trans,13trans) is a conjugated fatty acid that accounts for 80% (w/w) of tung oil (the seed oil of the tung tree, |FRAME: TAX-73154|). It is derived from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (18:2Δ9cis,12cis) by a, fatty acid conjugase that converts the 12Z double bond into a conjugated 11E-13E double bond system |CITS: [10536026][12481086]|.

Summary: General Background, Thiols play a major role in the detoxification of stress-inducing factors such as reactive oxygen species, free radicals, peroxides, lipid peroxides, and heavy metals. In mammals, the major thiol is the tripeptide |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly, known as GSH). Toxins are conjugated to GSH in the liver by a dedicated enzyme, resulting in a |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "cysteine-toxin conjugate"|. The conjugate is acetylated in the kidney to form |FRAME: Mercapturates|, and is then excreted |CITS: [8145281]| (see |FRAME: PWY-4061|)., In addition to oxidative stress management, low molecular weight thiols have been found to be involved in critical cellular processes including DNA synthesis and formaldehyde reduction |CITS: [Patel98]|., Gluathione is the major thiol not only in eukaryotic organisms but also in Gram negative bacteria and in the majority of Gram positive bacteria. Pathogenic bacteria live in a particularly hostile environment, in which the host deliberately generates toxins, including reactive oxygen species, to destroy the invading organism, thus thiols are particularly important for the survival of these organisms. , Despite the ubiquity of GSH, it is not universal. In many organisms, including some eukaryotes, other thiols have taken its role. Some of these thiols are |FRAME: CoM|, |FRAME: TRYPANOTHIONE|, |FRAME: Ergothioneine|, |FRAME: CPD1G-2| and |FRAME: CPD-17028|., About This Pathway, The synthesis of GSH from its three amino acid precursors L-glutamate, L-cysteine and glycine takes place in the cytosol. GSH is synthesized in all mammalian cells, many plants, and most Gram negative bacteria. In mammals, the liver is a major site of biosynthesis., GSH is synthesized in a two-step reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.2| and |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.3|, requiring a total of two moles of ATP per mole of GSH. This ATP-dependent coupling of amino acid monomers and elongating peptides by soluble enzymes is very unusual, as oligopeptides are usually formed either by ribosomes or by |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "nonribosomal peptide synthases"|. A similar mechanism is also found in the |FRAME: Acetylmuramoyl-Pentapeptide-Biosynthesis "formation of the bacterial cell wall pentapeptide"|., The first step in glutathione biosynthesis is controlled by negative feedback from its end product, GSH. However, feedback inhibition can be partially prevented by an excess of glutamate that blocks the regulatory site on the enzyme, |CITS: [6151157][6137189]|. When GSH is consumed and feedback inhibition is lost, the availability of cysteine as a, precursor can become the limiting factor |CITS: [9755286]|., In plants , Glutathione acts in plants as an antioxidant that counteracts reactive oxygen species thus reducing oxidative stress |CITS: [NOCTOR98]|. as in animals, it is a major player in detoxifying xenobiotics |CITS: [16665956]| by forming less reactive or storage conjugates catalyzed by GHS S-transferases |CITS: [15012285]|. Glutathione has also been reported to detoxify air pollutants such as ozone and sulfur dioxide in palnts |CITS: [16668420]|., GHS appears to be an important storage form of reduced sulfur in plants, regulating inter-organ sulfur allocation. Its biosynthesis seems to be coupled with the sulfate assimilation pathway (see |FRAME:SULFMETII-PWY|) |CITS: [12481075]|. As a precursor for |FRAME: Poly-Gamma-Glutamylcysteine-Glycines phytochelatin|, the principal metal-binding agent in plants, glutathione is considered a vital component for the detoxification of heavy metals |CITS: [GRILL85]| |CITS: [16594069][11402187]|., The biosynthesis of glutathione is universally catalyzed in all organisms by two enzymes, glutamate-cysteine ligase, |CITS: [May94][15180996]| regarded as the rate-limiting step of the pathway |CITS: [1112810]| and glutathione synthetase |CITS: [8612643][8914526][15302873]|., The regulation of the plant enzymes is unlike that reported from other eukaryotes. For the glutamate-cysteine ligase a conformational change has been observed as means to modify enzyme activities in response to redox conditions. That differs from mammalian enzymes that regulate activity through a regulatory subunit of the enzyme |CITS: [15180996]|.

General Background, A broad variety of volatile ester compounds have been found to constitute components , of complex cocktails in numerous plants emitted to serve in both reproductive and vegetative processes. More , than 1.000 low-molecular-weight organic compounds have been identified to date |CITS: [15326281]|, most of , them components of floral scents. The flower volatiles function as pollinator attractants but may also be involved , in defense mechanism, such as airborne signals to attract natural predators of herbivores |CITS: [12732318]|, to, directly repel herbivores |CITS: [Gershenzon91]| or to activate defense-related genes in neighboring plants or , healthy tissue in infected plants |CITS: [Shulaev97]|. , Methylbenzoate, methylsalicylate, benzylbenzoate and benzylacetate are found and investigated in floral scents of , |FRAME:TAX-36903| and Arabidopsis thaliana. Together with cinnamoic esters, terpenoids, fatty acid , derivatives, C5-branched compounds, and various nitrogen and sulfur containing compounds |CITS: [15326281]| , benzenoid esters form the core of physiologically active volatiles in plants. Certain volatiles such as methylsalicylate , and methyl jasmonate (|FRAME:PWY-735|) are also thought to be involved in cell-to-cell signaling |CITS: [Shulaev97]|., , Special information: The acetyl CoA:acetyl alcohol acetyltransferase (BEAT) catalyzes the formation of , benzylacetate in |FRAME:TAX-36903| which represents 20 to 40% of the total scent output of this plant. Two , other major volatiles benzylbenzoate and methylsalicylate account for 5% each of the scent |CITS: [9489012]|. , In Arabidopsis thaliana the emission of methylsalicylate and methylbenzoate has been observed as a , response to biotic and abiotic stress. The enzyme(s) catalyzing those reactions SAMT (salicylic acid , methyltransferase) and BAMT (benzoic acid methyltransferase) - together with the THeobromine , synthase termed as SABATH family - represent a structural related group with no significant sequence , similarity to other methyltransferases |CITS: [DAURIA03]|. The Arabidopsis thaliana gene AtBSMT1 and , its ortholog in |FRAME:TAX-59689| (AlBSMT1) can use both substrates (salicylic acid, benzoic acid) but , express different substrate affinities |CITS: [14617060]|., Benzoyl-coenzyme A (CoA):benzyl alcohol benzoyl transferase (BEBT) identified from |FRAME:TAX-36903| , catalyzes the formation of benzylbenzoate (a major volatile) with a broader substrate specificity towards other , alcohols and acetyl CoAs. Interestingly, the most similar protein to BEBT found in Arabidopsis does not accept , benzoyl CoA but catalyzes the formation of cis-3-hexen-1-yl acetate, another green-leaf volatile using acetyl CoA , as substrate |CITS: [12226525]|.

|FRAME: TRYPANOTHIONE Trypanothione| is a unique thiol apparently present only in the trypanosomatids (order |FRAME: TAX-5653|). Trypanothione is synthesized in two steps from a thiol (glutathione) and a polyamine (spermidine) via an N1- or N8-glutathionylspermidine intermediate., Trypanosomatids lack both the typical catalase and peroxidase hemoproteins, which function in oxidant defense in other organisms |CITS: [3622780]|, and the glutathione peroxidase-glutathione reductase enzymes which are prevalent in other eukaryotes |CITS: [3990705]|., Instead, a considerable portion of their glutathione is conjugated with spermidine |CITS: [3807945]|, and they possess a sytem that converts glutathionylspermidine to trypanothione and vice versa, which seems analogous to the glutathione peroxidase-glutathione reductase system. Thus, trypanothione appears to be an essential redox intermediate and important antioxidant in trypanosomatids, filling the roles that are filled by glutathione in other organisms |CITS: [9677355][7775463]|.

Names: Escherichia coli serotype O:9 O antigen biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The O-polysaccharides of |FRAME: TAX-1010796|, |FRAME: TAX-1010797|, and |FRAME: ORG-6346| form a family of related structures comprising linear homopolymers of mannopyranose. Their biosynthetic pathways are considered prototypes for the ABC transporter-dependent pathway., In all three serotypes the O-antigen is composed of an |FRAME: CPD-12541| residue that serves to link the polysaccharide to its |FRAME: CPD-9646| membrane anchor during its biosynthesis |CITS: [6183115]|, a short adapter region comprising three mannose residues connected in α(1→3) linkages, and a long repeat unit domain, which consists of many repeats of a serotype-specific repeat unit. The chain is terminated by either a methyl phosphate or a methyl group that is recognized by the ABC transporter., The first 4 residues are identical among the three serotypes, and are synthesized by identical enzymes (WecA, WbdC, and WbdB). The repeat unit differs among the serotypes, and is synthesized by serotype-specific multifunctional WbdA enzymes. Chain termination is catalyzed by WbdD proteins. WbdDO8 is a membrane-associated methyltransferase, whereas WbdDO9/O9a is a bifunctional kinase/methyltransferase., The O-polysaccharide of |FRAME: TAX-1010797| is identical to that of |FRAME: ORG-6347| |CITS: [4778906][786626]|. The genetic locus encoding the involved enzymes was sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-1010797| in 1995 |CITS: [7536735]|. , The pathway begins with the transfer of |FRAME: CPD-12541| to the 55-carbon polyisoprenoid lipid acceptor |FRAME: CPD-9646|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). WecA is part of the machinery for |FRAME: ECASYN-PWY "biosynthesis of the enterobacterial common antigen glycan"|, and the wecA gene is not located in the O-polysaccharide locus |CITS: [6183115][7514591]|., |FRAME: ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINYLDIPHOSPHO-UNDECAPRE| is committed to the polysaccharide biosynthesis by the action of WbdC and WbdB, two GDP-mannose-dependent mannosyltransferases that transfer one and two α-(1,3)-linked mannose residues, respectively, forming the trimannosyl adapter region |CITS: [22875852]|. These enzymes and the resulting structure are conserved in E. coli serotypes O8, O9, and O9a |CITS: [22475157]|., The adapter domain is then extended by a serotype-specific multidomain polymerizing mannosyltransferase (WbdA) |CITS: [22475157][22989876]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1010797| the repeat unit consists of [→3)-α-D-Man-(1→3)-α-D-Man-(1→2)-α-D-Man-(1→2)-α-D-Man-(1→2)-α-D-Man-(1→] trisaccharides |CITS: [786626]|, The polymerase, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-81161| gene, is a large (91.4 kDa) multidomain, multifunctional enzyme that contains two glycosyltransferase domains that possess an EX7E motif found in other retaining glycosyltransferases. The enzyme is responsible and sufficient for extending the repeat unit of the |FRAME: CPD-24283|. Since the number of glycosyltransferase domains is correlated with the number of different linkage types catalyzed by the enzyme, it is thought that each domain catalyzes formation of a different linkage |CITS: [22989876]|., When the antigen has reached the correct length, the extension process is terminated by 3-O-phosphorylation of the terminal mannose residue, followed by methylation, which is carried out by the bifunctional |FRAME: G-81162| enzyme |CITS: [15184370]|. Wbd also recuits the WbaA polymerase, and the methylation is required for the export of the mature O antigen from the cytoplam to the priplasm by the |FRAME: CPLX-9621| |CITS: [15980069]|.

|FRAME: Fructans Fructans| are a class of highly water-soluble polysaccharides consisting of linear or branched |FRAME:FRU| chains attached to |FRAME: SUCROSE| by β-2,1or β-2,6-linkage., There are 3 types of fructans:, 1. |FRAME: Inulin| - linear fructans generally linked by β(2->1) glycosidic bonds, 2. |FRAME: Levan| - linear fructans generally linked by β(2->6) glycosidic bonds, 3. |FRAME: Graminans| - branched fructans linked by both β(2->1) and β(2->6) glycosidic bonds., The fructosyl units may be linked to the sucrose base unit either to the fructose moiety, or to the glucose moiety by a β 2->6 bond. In the latter case, the resulting molecule name is marked by a 6<sub>G</sub>, as in |FRAME: NEOKESTOSE 6<sub>G</sub>-kestotriose|., Fructans are synthesized from sucrose by a restricted number of plant species and many microorganisms, which include Archaea, fungi and a wide range of bacteria. , Plants synthesize fructans in the vacuole by the concerted action of various fructosyltransferases, each with its own preferredl donor and acceptor substrates. Fructans are among the few abundant storage carbohydrates in plants and are accumulated in roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves, and seeds. In addition to their function as storage carbohydrates, fructans may have functions involved in drought and cold tolerance., The degradation of fructans in plants is catalyzed by fructan 1-exohydrolase, which hydrolyzes the β-2,1-linkages  and /or fructan 6-exohydrolase, which hydrolyzes the β-2,6-linkages. The released fructose re-enters cell metabolism in the cytosol.

Summary: General Background, Aryl carotenoids that contain φ-type rings were first discovered in the Japanese sea sponge |FRAME: TAX-6062|, which at the time was known as Reniera japonica |CITS: [Yamaguchi57]| (in retrospect they were most likely produced by bacterial endosymbionts of the sponge). Thus the first compounds to be defined from that organism were named |FRAME: CPD-20646| (φ,χ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi57a]| and |FRAME: CPD-20624| (φ,φ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi58][Yamaguchi59]|. Aryl carotenoids were subsequently identified in most non-oxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (green and purple sulfur bacteria) as well as some non-photosynthetic species of the |FRAME: TAX-1763| and |FRAME: TAX-1883| genera |CITS: [5711189][5781524][Schmidt70][4635689]|. , About This Pathway, The typical product of carotenoid biosynthesis in several carotenogenic |FRAME: TAX-1883| species, such as |FRAME: TAX-68237|, |FRAME: TAX-53450|, |FRAME: TAX-1916| and |FRAME: TAX-1902|, is the rare carotene |FRAME: CPD-20624| |CITS: [10395965]|., Strain JA3933 of |FRAME: TAX-1911| is a non-carotenogenic bacterium. However, a full set of genes for carotenoid biosynthesis is present in the organism. When the genes were cloned without a terminator region and expressed in a different non-carotenogenic strain, the host produced |FRAME: CPD-20624| |CITS: [2254247]|., The conversion of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to |FRAME: CPD-20624| requires only two genes. |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.19|, which is encoded by a CrtY-type cyclase in actinobacteria, introduces β-type rings at both ends of the carotenoid. A dedicated desaturase, |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.39|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58128| gene, converts these rings to aromatic φ-type rings |CITS: [10395965]|.

General Background, Carotenoids with cyclic ends are integral constituents of plants, algae and cyanobacteria photosynthetic reaction centers |CITS:[GOODWIN80],[YOUNG93]|. A wide variety of organisms produce carotenoid glycosides, which act as natural surfactants, stabilize membranes, and possibly contribute to regulating the permeability of membranes to oxygen |CITS: [16149733]|., The glycosylated carotenoids of |FRAME: TAX-1117| differ from ones found in other organisms in that glycosylation characteristically occurs on the C-2'-hydroxyl group rather than that at the C-1' position of the ψ end of either |FRAME: CPD-11449| or |FRAME: CPD-11451| molecules, forming |FRAME: CPD-11452| or |FRAME: CPD-11455|, respectively., Myxoxanthophyll compounds have so far been found only in |FRAME: TAX-1117|, where thery were shown to be required for normal cell wall structure and thylakoid organization |CITS: [16199557]|., About This Pathway, Myxoxanthophyll compounds are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD1F-114|, the acyclic precursor of all carotenoids in cyanobacteria. The first reaction in this pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14923|, encoded by |FRAME: G-11373|. This gene is found in a wide variety of carotenoid-synthesizing bacteria that do not have the crtC gene |CITS: [19304845]|. The enzyme adds a hydroxyl group to the C-1' carbon, a committed step towards the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-11450|., The next step is assumed to be catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-11376|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14926|, forming |FRAME: CPD-11446| |CITS: [17606904]|. , The next step is still uncertain, but involves the addition of a second hydroxyl group at the C-2' position (providing an anchor for the subsequent attachment of the sugar). Additional processing involves hydroxylation of the ring by the |FRAME: G-11375|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14925|, and the final attachment of a fucose sugar at the C-2' position by |FRAME: MONOMER-14924|. This enzyme is encoded by |FRAME: G-11374|, a gene that often forms a bicistronic operon with |FRAME: G-11373| |CITS: [19304845]|.

Summary: General Background, The broad definition of a |FRAME: Lipoproteins lipoprotein| is a protein to which lipids are bound. Many enzymes, transporters, structural proteins, antigens, adhesins, and toxins are lipoproteins, including the high-density (HDL) and low-density (LDL) lipoproteins that carry fats in the blood stream., The lipoprotein known as |FRAME: EG10544-MONOMER| (Lpp) is considered the most abundant protein in |FRAME: TAX-562| and accounts for more than 40% of the peptidoglycan on a weight basis. It is necessary for the stabilization and integrity of the bacterial cell envelope and is thought to physically tether the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan layer |CITS:[4899922][4565677][4578317]|., Membrane-attached lipoproteins of Gram-negative bacteria and Mycobacteria are tethered to the membrane by an N-acyl-(S-diacylglyceryl)-cysteine anchor that is variably acylated depending on the genus. In many Gram-positive bacteria certain variations exist (see below)., About This Pathway, In bacteria all lipoproteins are initially translated as precursors (|FRAME: Prolipoproteins prolipoproteins|) containing an N-terminal signal peptide that contains a conserved lipobox motif sequence preceding a cysteine residue. The signal peptide is inserted into the inner membrane, serving as a membrane anchor for the protein |CITS: [12876315][19367716]|. Once transported to the outer face of the membrane, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.145| (Lgt) attaches a diacylglycerol moiety from a phospholipid donor by a thioether bond to the cysteine residue. At this point the protein is attached to the membrane by three anchors - the two fatty acids of the diacylglycerol molecule and the signal peptide |CITS: [8051048]|., In most organisms |FRAME: EC-3.4.23.36| (Lsp) then cleaves the leader peptide, leaving the cysteine as the N-terminal amino acid of the protein |CITS: [7040395]|. Some variations exist - for example, in |FRAME: TAX-2115| the peptide is cleaved two amino acids away from the cysteine (towards the N-terminus) |CITS: [22303020]|., In most Gram-negative bacteria biosynthesis is completed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.269| (Lnt), which transfers a fatty acid from a membrane phospholipid to form an amide linkage with the N-terminus of the cysteine residue, generating a triacylated molecule. All three acyl moieties are inserted into the membrane, providing three membrane anchors for the lipoprotein |CITS: [2032623]|. Some Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-953| lack this modification |CITS: [19458089]|., More variety is found in some low GC Gram-positive bacteria. Three new forms have been observed - a |FRAME: Peptidyl-Form-Lipoprotein-N-terminus "peptidyl form"| (which results from the alternative cleaving by Lsp, with two amino acids present before the lipid-modified cysteine residue), an |FRAME: N-Acetyl-Lipoprotein "N-acetyl form"|, and an N-acylated monoacyl-glyceryl form known as the |FRAME: Lyso-Form-Lipoprotein-Cysteine "lyso-form"| |CITS: [22135097][22303020][28320885]|., The latter part of the pathway is known as the Lol pathway, and is concerned with the translocation of some of the lipoproteins from the inner membrane to the outer membrane. The |FRAME: ABC-62-CPLX| (LolCDE), which is localized in the inner membrane, catalyzes the ATP-dependent transfer of the lipoprotein to the chaperone LolA |CITS: [7628437][10783239]|. Lipoproteins that have an Asp residue at position + 2 are not recognized by LolCDE, and thus remain in the inner membrane |CITS: [12032293]|., Following the loading of a lipoprotein LolA travels to the outer membrane, where it transfers its cargo to the LolB protein, which is attached to the outer membrane |CITS: [ 9384574]|. The Lol pathway ends with the transfer of the lipoprotein from LolB to the outer membrane. Incorporation into the inner leaflet of the outer membrane is the final localization step for most lipoproteins, though a few undergo further sorting |CITS: [27871940]|. Cross-talk between lipoprotein and lipopolysaccharide trafficking pathways may be responsible for targeting a subset of surface-exposed lipoproteins to the outer membrane |CITS: [40348743]|.

Summary: Sterols such as cholesterol are important structural components of eukaryotic cell membranes. It is also a precursor of steroid hormones and bile acids. The impact of cholesterol and its regulation on human health is well known. Its role in arteriosclerosis, and drug therapy for this process, has been extensively studied (reviewed in |CITS: [10441607]|). Nobel prizes in Physiology or Medicine were awarded to Konrad Bloch in 1963 and to M. S. Brown and J. L. Goldstein in 1985 for their work on the metabolism and regulation of cholesterol. Several interesting historical reviews detail the discovery of cholesterol and work leading to the elucidation of its structure and function |CITS: [5319508][1519268][11111073]|., The first nine reactions of cholesterol biosynthesis are described in the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"|. Mevalonate is the precursor of isoprenoids, which are involved in the biosynthesis of many classes of compounds in addition to cholesterol. As shown in the mevalonate pathway, the cholesterol molecule is formed from acetate units (reviewed in |CITS: [RILLING85], [5319508]|). The acetate units are joined in a series of reactions to form farnesyl pyrophosphate, a branch point for the biosynthesis of other isoprenoid compounds such as ubiquinone, dolichol, and farnesylated proteins (see |FRAME: PWY-5123|). The mevalonate pathway is highly regulated, as reviewed in |CITS: [1967820]|. HMG-CoA reductase from the mevalonate pathway is the rate-determining enzyme for the entire pathway from acetate to cholesterol. This enzyme is the target for the well-known cholesterol-lowering statin drugs (reviewed in |CITS: [10441607]|)., Farnesyl-diphosphate farnesyltransferase (squalene synthase) is the first specific enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. It catalyzes a 2-step reaction involving a "head-to-head" condensation of two molecules of farnesyl pyrophosphate to form presqualene pyrophosphate |CITS: [HCRILLING][ALTMANLJ][COREYEJ]|. Presqualene pyrophosphate is then reduced to squalene. Details of the enzymatic reaction mechanism, which involves carbocation intermediates, have been described |CITS: [12137537]|. The importance of squalene synthase has been demonstrated in squalene synthase knockout mice, which results in embryonic lethality and retardation of development |CITS: [10521476]|. Squalene epoxidase (monooxygenase) catalyzes oxygen-dependent epoxidation of squalene |CITS: [5438357]|. Oxidosqualene cyclase (lanosterol synthase) catalyzes its remarkable cyclization, in a single reaction, to form lanosterol |CITS: [6027261]|. This cyclization mechanism was proposed by several researchers, but the correct structure was determined by R. B. Woodward and K. Bloch |CITS: [WOODWARD53]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [5319508]|., The enzymology of the multistep conversion of lanosterol to cholesterol was largely determined in rat liver by J. L. Gaylor and coworkers (reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|). The human pathway is therefore inferred from this work. The order of some of the reactions in this pathway may vary. The pathway shown here represents the reactions in a frequently published order, updated as follows. The last three reactions, as illustrated in two reviews (|CITS: [11969204] [RILLING85]|), have more recently been reordered as shown here (|CITS: [9291139]|, in |CITS: [11519011]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|). Previously, the isomerase reaction was followed by the Δ5-desaturase, the Δ7-reductase (producing |FRAME: DESMOSTEROL-CPD|) and the Δ24-reductase, producing cholesterol (as shown by clicking on the pathway link above that leads to pathway |FRAME: PWY66-4|) (reviewed in |CITS: [11969204], [RILLING85]|, in |CITS: [Salway04]|). In the pathway shown here, the isomerase reaction is followed by the Δ24-reductase, the Δ5-desaturase and the Δ7-reductase, producing cholesterol. Desmosterol is not shown. This reordering is based on substrate specificity studies of the Δ24 reductase |CITS: [9291139]|. However, the Δ24 double bond reduction can also occur at other times, using other intermediates as substrates |CITS: [9291139]|. This is evidenced by the genetic disorder desmosterolosis. In this disorder, patients have elevated levels of desmosterol in their plasma and tissues due to mutations in the Δ24-reductase gene |CITS: [11519011]|. Another route involves reduction of the Δ24 double bond at the point of lanosterol and leads to the production of |FRAME: CPD-8606|. Metabolism of this compound is shown by clicking on the pathway link above that leads to pathway |FRAME: PWY66-3|., The lanosterol-to-cholesterol conversion involves the oxidative removal of three methyl groups, reduction of double bonds, and migration of the lanosterol double bond to a new position in cholesterol (in |CITS: [3997841]| and reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|). Unlike the mostly cytosolic reactions of the mevalonate pathway, the reactions shown here are catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes (reviewed in |CITS: [11969204], [RILLING85]|). In rat liver, they have been localized in the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [3597431]|. Solubilization and characterization of these enzymes had to be achieved before this segment of the pathway could be determined, as reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|. Human genes have been identified for all the enzymes in this pathway and human disorders of cholesterol metabolism have been associated with genetic defects in most of these enzymes. Mouse models also exist for several of these human disorders (|CITS: [12829805]| and reviewed in |CITS: [12668600]|). , In the pathway shown here, the first of the three methyl groups, the 14α methyl group, is removed from lanosterol by a cytochrome P450 isozyme |CITS: [6208195]|. The reaction proceeds through alcohol and aldehyde intermediates |CITS: [3514778]|. This is followed by decarbonylation with formate release, and Δ14 double bond formation. Details of this reaction mechanism have been published and involve formation of a formyl ester intermediate (not shown), suggesting a Bayer-Villiger reaction mechanism (|CITS: [2007571]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [11969204]|). The resulting Δ14 double bond of the conjugated diene is then reduced by an NADPH-dependent reductase |CITS: [6444198]|., Another multienzyme complex, C4 methyl sterol oxidase, removes the second (4α) and third (4β) methyl groups in a sequential oxidative series of reactions that include carboxylic acid intermediates |CITS: [4394229], [4398294], [4383278], [4394228]|. This enzyme is not a cytochrome P450. It utilizes cytochrome b5 as an electron carrier |CITS: [3949790], [7228857]|. The first of the two decarboxylation reactions is accompanied by epimerization of the 4β methyl group to the 4α position |CITS: [4401584]|. Thus, after subsequent reduction, the remaining methyl group is in the 4α orientation for further stereospecific oxidation by this enzyme (|CITS: [240818], [SHARPLESSKB]| and in reviews |CITS: [11969204], [RILLING85], [6810750]|)., Following decarboxylation, a 3-ketosteroid intermediate is formed and is reduced by 3-ketosteroid reductase |CITS: [4387005], [6946726]|. The final demethylated intermediate then undergoes isomerization of the Δ8(9) double bond, which moves to the Δ7(8) position of the sterol B-ring |CITS: [4404598], [2422166]|. The Δ24-reductase then catalyzes reduction of the side chain double bond |CITS: [9291139]|. The Δ5-desaturase is a multienzyme system utilizing cytochrome b5 as an electron carrier. It catalyzes formation of the Δ5 double bond to form 7-dehydro-cholesterol (|CITS: [3949790], [3997841]|, and in |CITS: [10651635]|). The terminal enzyme of the pathway reduces the Δ7 double bond to form cholesterol |CITS: [LEEJN]|., Acknowledgment: We thank Drs. Anne Venturelli and Ripudaman Malhotra, SRI International, for their help in providing chemical names for many of the intermediates shown in this pathway.

General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on single carbon (C1) compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. , While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 "Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| (see |FRAME: PWY-5506|)., The key enzyme in the oxidation of methanol in methylotrophic bacteria is methanol dehydrogenase (MDH). Different bacterial strains use different types of MDH. Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria have a periplasmic |FRAME: CPLX-3264| that contain a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ) cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-1701|). Thermophilic methylotrophic Bacili such as |FRAME: TAX-1471| use an |FRAME: CPLX-8059| (see |FRAME: PWY-6510|), while Gram-positive bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1814|, |FRAME: TAX-1777| MB19, |FRAME: TAX-1829| LMD 89.129 and |FRAME: TAX-1833| DSM 1069 possess nicotinoprotein methanol dehydrogenases with a bound NAD(P) cofactor that use an unknown electron acceptor for reduction of their bound cofactor and can use the artificial electron acceptor |FRAME: CPD-12424| in vitro |CITS:[1995642][8385013][8449887]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6509|)., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branch point, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (see |FRAME:P185-PWY|), or a dissimilatory pathway that provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|)., About This Pathway, In fungi |FRAME:METOH| is oxidized to |FRAME:FORMALDEHYDE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7392| (AOD) in a reaction that produces two very reactive compounds, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. To avoid damage to the cell, alcohol oxidase is compartmentalized in peroxisomes, together with |FRAME: ENZRXN-14009|, an enzyme that decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen., Compartmentalization of the enzymes that produce and decompose hydrogen peroxide in the peroxisome is an efficient way to prevent diffusion of this hazardous compound into the cytoplasm., In methanol-grown cells |FRAME:CPLX-7392| is extremely abundant, up to 70% of total cellular proteins. At these high concentration the protein forms crystalloids, which are responsible for the cubic shape, characteristic of peroxisomes. The |FRAME: ENZRXN-14009| is located mostly at the periphery, forming a barrier that prevents leakage of hydrogen peroxide out of the organelle |CITS: [17023065]|., The other toxic product, formaldehyde, is shuttled into either of two pathways. Formaldehyde can react with |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| in a reaction catalyzed by another peroxisomal enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-7394|, entering an assimilatory pathway in which three molecules of formaldehyde are condensed into a single molecule of |FRAME:GAP|, which is used for biosynthesis of cell building blocks., However, when not enough |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| is available, formaldehyde diffuses into the cytosol, where it enters a dissimilatory pathway in which it is oxidized to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, generating energy.

|FRAME:CPD-16767 Parthenolide| and hydroxylated derivatives thereof are the main sesquiterpene lactones found in Tanacetum parthenium (feverfew), a medicinal plant with a long history in traditional and folk medicine |CITS:[22096324]|. Sesquiterpene lactones constitute a class of the terpenoids with more than 4000 compounds, many of them known to display various anti-flammatory and anticancer activities |CITS:[22797176]|. Feverfew has been used in folk medicine as treatment against fever, migraine, infertility, asthma and all kinds of allergies |CITS:[22096324]|. In modern medicine |FRAME:CPD-16766|, the principal sesquiterpene lactone in feverfew, is valued because of its promise as anticancer and anti-inflammatory drug. It has been shown in experiments that |FRAME:CPD-16766| efficiently inhibits NF-κB, a transcription factor which triggers the inflammatory response and is involved in general immune reactions as activator of various anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9013864] [22797176]|. , The highest amounts of |FRAME:CPD-16766| are found in flowers of Tanacetum parthenium and it has been shown that its biosynthesis varies and is influenced by genetical, developmental and spatial factors |CITS:[Majdi13]|. The sequiterpene lactone |FRAME:CPD-9410| is considered as the immediate precursor for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16766|. Indeed, all genes and respective enzymes required for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-16766| via |FRAME:CPD-9410| have been identified and characterized in feverfew. The three enzymes involved in the |FRAME:CPD-9410| biosynthetic pathway, i.e. |FRAME:MONOMER-18664|, |FRAME:MONOMER-18665| and |FRAME:MONOMER-18666| have been shown to function in glandular trichomes of Tanacetum parthenium (see |FRAME:PWY-6540|) forming the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-9410| |CITS:[21620424] [24704560]|. The substrate specificity and molecular function of the enzymes have been demonstrated in vitro and though transient heterologous expressed genes in the host plant Nicotiana benthamiana |CITS:[21858047]|. , The Cytochrome P450 dependent |FRAME:MONOMER-18667| catalyzing the epoxidation of the C4-C5 double bond in |FRAME:CPD-9410| and forming |FRAME:CPD-16766| has also been identified in feverfew and its catalytic activity determined. In addition, another Cytochrome P450 dependent oxygenase responsible for the 3β-hydroxylation of both |FRAME:CPD-9410| and |FRAME:CPD-16766|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16771| and |FRAME:CPD-16767| was characterized |CITS:[24704560]|. The existence of the pathway was also demonstrated in Nicotiana benthamiana plants transiently expressing all four genes identified for |FRAME:CPD-16766| biosynthesis. However, |FRAME:CPD-16766| in this system was fast converted to conjugates such as |FRAME:CPD-16773| and |FRAME:CPD-16772|. Interestingly, these conjugates were quite efficient against colon cancer cells and so were the 3β-hydroxy derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-9410| and |FRAME:CPD-16766|. Although not as efficient as |FRAME:CPD-16766| the respective conjugates and 3β-derivatives had a better water solubility which would improve the physico-chemical properties of a potential drug |CITS:[24704560]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Dapdiamides dapdiamides| were discovered by constructing a genomic DNA library from |FRAME: TAX-549| and screening it against the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-552| |CITS: [20041689]|., This family of antibiotics consists of fumaramoyl and epoxysuccinamoyl dipeptides, and was named for the presence of |FRAME: 23-Diaminopropanoate| (DAP) and two amide linkages in the antibiotics scaffold |CITS: [20041689]|., The compounds are similar in structure to synthetic |FRAME: CPD0-1236| dipeptides, which show broad spectrum activity by targeting bacterial and fungal |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.16|, the enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the formation of the essential cell-wall building block |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| |CITS: [2111163][1901701]|., The compounds are likely cleaved intracellularly to generate acyl-DAP warheads that interact with the enzyme. The fumaramoyl-DAP warheads which would be derived from |FRAME: CPD-18311|, |FRAME: CPD-17539|, |FRAME: CPD-17540|, |FRAME: CPD-17541| and |FRAME: CPD-17542| provide a conjugated eneamide system that is likely attacked by the thiolate side chain of the active site Cys in the glutaminase domain of the enzyme, leading to alkylation of that residue, preventing the formation of ammonium essential of enzyme activity |CITS: [2111163]|. The epoxysuccinamoyl moiety in |FRAME: CPD-18309|, |FRAME: CPD-18310|, and |FRAME: CPD-17543| could function as a similar inactivating electrophile for the catalytic Cys residue |CITS: [19807062]|., About This Pathway, The gene cluster encoding dapdiamides biosynthesis was identified and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-549| |CITS: [20041689]|, and a pathway has been proposed |CITS: [19807062][20945916]|. The first pathway-specific enzyme, |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.46| (encoded by |FRAME: G-44180|) ligates |FRAME: FUM| to the N3 position of |FRAME: L-23-DIAMINOPROPANOATE|. Amidation by an uncharacterized enzyme presumably encoded by |FRAME: G-44182| produces a key intermediate in the pathway, |FRAME: CPD-18312|., Three of the antibiotics, |FRAME: CPD-17539|, |FRAME: CPD-17540|, and |FRAME: CPD-17541|, are produced from this intermediate by the action of |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.47| (encoded by |FRAME: G-44181|), by ligation with the amino acids |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: ILE| and |FRAME: LEU|, respectively |CITS: [19807062]|., Production of epoxylated dapdiamides requires the participation of additional enzymes. So far the only such compound whose biosynthesis has been clarified is |FRAME: CPD-18309| (previously known as CB-25-I). To produce this compound, the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-18312| is bound to the |FRAME: MONOMER-19478|, which activates it by adenylation and then attaches it to a peptidyl-carrier domain. Once bound, the compound is epoxidated by |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.M2|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44184| gene. The epoxidated product is then released by the action of a dedicated thioesterase (|FRAME: G-44185|) and ligated to |FRAME: VAL| by |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.47| |CITS: [20945916]|.

Nitrification, the oxidation of |FRAME: AMMONIA| to |FRAME: NITRATE| by microorganisms, is a key process in the global nitrogen cycle, resulting in nitrogen loss from ecosystems, eutrophication of surface and ground waters, and the production of atmospherically active trace gases. For many years it has been thought that no one organism is capable of carrying out the whole process, with ammonia oxidizers limited to the conversion of ammonia to |FRAME: NITRITE| and nitrite oxidizers confined to the oxidation of nitrite to nitrate. However, that paradigm has been proven unfounded with the isolation of organisms capable of the full oxidation of ammonia to nirtate |CITS: [26610024][26610025]|., Four genera of nitrite-oxidizing bacteria have been isolated, which include |FRAME: TAX-911|, |FRAME: TAX-1234 Nitrospira|, |FRAME: TAX-35796| and |FRAME: TAX-35800| |CITS: [Winogradsky92][Watson71][Watson86]|., The facultative chemolithotroph |FRAME: TAX-911| is considered the dominant nitrite oxidizer in freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems, and four species are known: |FRAME: TAX-913|, |FRAME: TAX-912|, |FRAME: TAX-29421| and |FRAME: TAX-93980|., The other three genera are obligate lithoautotrophs, and have been isolated mostly from marine environments, although |FRAME: TAX-42253| is a fresh water organism, isolated from a coroded iron pipe., |FRAME: TAX-1234| is the dominant nitrite oxidizing genus in sewage sludge, aquaria, and bioreactors |CITS: [9687471] , [9726900]|. Several of the obligate lithoautotrophs, including |FRAME: TAX-42253|, have been shown to utilize nitrite as an energy source by the oxidation of nitrite under oxic conditions |CITS: [7646315]|. , The key enzyme of nitrite oxidation is nitrite oxidoreductase (NOR), which catalyzes the conversion of nitrite to nitrate in all of the nitrite oxidizers. The enzyme is an iron-sulfur molybdoprotein, and nitrite is transformed at the molybdenum center by a two electron transfer, generating nitrate and molybdenum (IV). Under anaerobic conditions the enzyme is a nitrate reductase, catalyzing the reverse reaction |CITS: [MEINCKE92]|., The electrons that are released from the nitrite oxidoreductase complex are subsequently transferred to cytochrome c oxidase through several forms of cytochrome c550 |CITS: [2856189]|. Both soluble and membrane-bound class IA/B cytochrome c-550 proteins were purified and shown to be electron donors for theoxidase |CITS: [6291614][8392510]|.

Summary: General Background, Polyketide (exclusive of fatty acids) represent a large group of natural products, i.e. secondary metabolites that are widespread in fungi, bacteria and plants |CITS: [BIRCH68]| |CITS: [SCHRODER99]| |CITS: [12946402]|. Polyketides are often involved as intermediates in the formation of a vast variety of secondary metabolites with mixed biosynthetic origin. Polyketide such as chalcone and 6'-deoxychalcone are precursors in the biosynthesis of thousands of biologically important compounds functioning as pigments, anti-pathogens (phytoalexins), UV protectants, signals for the interaction with microorganisms and mediators of fertility |CITS: [10426943]| |CITS: [SCHRODER97]|., The entry enzymes of the biosynthesis of polyketides in plants are the polyketide synthases producing the general backbone of compounds who give rise to a large array of natural products representing an amazing degree of structural diversity. The chalcone synthase (CHS) and stilbene synthase (STS) are the most well-known plant polyketide synthases, however there exists a growing superfamily of related proteins referred to as CHS/STS-type proteins |CITS: [SCHRODER99]|. Depending on the specific polyketide synthase involved very diverse compound classes evolve such as chalcones (|FRAME: PWY1F-FLAVSYN|), stilbenes |CITS: [10426943]|, stilbenecarboxylates |CITS: [12620338]|, benzalacetone |CITS: [12226219]|, pyrone |CITS: [ECKERMANN98]|, C-methylated chalcone |CITS: [SHEN00]| and acridone alkaloids |CITS: [8148006]| |CITS: [7727746]|., The formation of polyketides resembles the biosynthesis of fatty acids but is different in various aspects. In contrast to fatty acid synthases (FAS) plant polyketide synthases (PKS) are relatively small homodimeric enzymes, which do not use , the acyl carrier protein (ACP) as activating agent but utilize acyl-CoA esters directly as substrates |CITS: [SHEN00][BIRCH68]|. Although the synthesis of chalcone usually does not involve modifications by other proteins the chalcone , derivatives reduced at a specific position in the synthesized aromatic ring are frequently found in plants increasing the , structural variability of derivatives |CITS: [SCHRODER97]|. , About This Pathway, The polyketide synthase (PKS) involved in the biosynthesis of aloesone represents a novel type of PKS. The enzyme uses acetyl-CoA as the starter unit and catalyzes six successive condensations steps using malonyl-CoA as the extender unit, forming the aromatic heptaketide aloesone. , The aloesone synthase isolated from rhubarb (|FRAME:TAX-137221|) belongs to the CHS superfamily (PKS type III). It is a plant-specific, unique enzyme taking up a central function in the biosynthesis of chromones |CITS: [15044020]|.

|FRAME: CPD-16569 Kojibiose| is a diglucoside that was initially characterized from koji extract [an extract produced from rice by the application of |FRAME: TAX-5062| (koji in Japanese) spores, an early step in the production of the Japanese liquor Sho-chu] |CITS: [Aso53]|, and later from hydrol (a light brown syrupy liquor from the manufacture of dextrose) |CITS: [13483572]|, honey |CITS: [13666886]| and dextrans |CITS: [13768213]|. Kojibiose is also found as a constituent of polysaccharides and the sugar chains of glycoproteins |CITS: [4149796]|. It can be produced from glucose by caramelization |CITS: [Sugisawa66]|., The structure, initially thought to be 3-O-α-D-glucopyranosyl-D-glucose, was shown to be 2-O-α-D-glucopyranosyl-D-glucose |CITS: [13483572]|. Crystalization was achieved in 1961 |CITS: [13787188]|., The key enzyme in the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-16569| is |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.230|, which was originally characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29323| ATCC35047 |CITS: [CHAEN99]|. This enzyme is a, phosphorylase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of kojibiose in the presence of an inorganic phosphate to form D-glucose and |FRAME: CPD-448|. The enzyme can accept additional substrates, but can act only on an α-1,2 glycosidic bond |CITS: [12681912]|. The gene encoding it was identified in 2004 |CITS: [16233673]|., A kojibiose catabolic gene cluster was reported from the hyperthrmophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-1183377| |CITS: [24391053]|. The cluster encodes |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.230| and |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.6|, that together hydrolyze |FRAME: CPD-16569| into |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, which can be used as a substrate in glycolysis.

A variety of non-proteinogenic amino acids are often found to be building blocks of nonribosomal peptides and hybrid polyketide skeletons contributing to bioactivities and expanding the chemical diversity of secondary metabolites |CITS:[23729217]|. One such compound, |FRAME:CPD-15319|, has been found to be involved in the biosynthesis of the two tetramate diasteromers |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285| (see |FRAME:PWY-7702|). , |FRAME:CPD-15319 "4-Hydroxy-4-methyl-L-glutamate"| has also been known for some time to accumulate in plants |CITS:[Grobbelaar55]|. A pathway originating from |FRAME:PYRUVATE| via |FRAME:CPD-187| towards |FRAME:CPD-15319| in |FRAME: TAX-3818| (peanut) had been proposed |CITS:[13932909]|. Both |FRAME:CPD-187| and |FRAME:CPD-15319| are neurotoxic and have been shown to paralyze the neuromuscular junction in the flight motor system of |FRAME: TAX-13632| (Green bottle fly) |CITS:[Hart78]|., The first committed step, i.e. the formation of |FRAME:CPD-187|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.17|. Isotope exchange assays in peanut indicated that the reaction may occur in vivo |CITS:[13932909]|. However, this activity could not be demonstrated in vitro, as the purified peanut aldolase only catalyzed the reaction in the reverse direction, forming two molecules of |FRAME:PYRUVATE| from |FRAME:CPD-187| |CITS:[13976791]|., A similar result was observed with the purified aldolase from the ascomycete fungus |FRAME: TAX-95324|, which is known to form |FRAME:CPD-15319| as part of the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285|. When the |FRAME: G-44173| gene, which encodes the aldolase, was expressed via the |FRAME: TAX-42747| expression platform (see |CITS:[25436464]|), it only catalyzed the reaction in the reverse direction. However, when expressed in vivo in combination with the the |FRAME: G-44171| gene and |FRAME: G-44172| gene which encode other pathway enzymes, |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285| were formed (see |FRAME:PWY-7702|), indicating that tasA does catalyze the forward reaction in vivo., In addition, supplemental administered |FRAME:CPD-187| restored |FRAME:CPD-18284| and |FRAME:CPD-18285| production in experiments without the aldolase, indicating that TasA indeed catalyzes the formation of |FRAME:CPD-187|. The gene cluster for |FRAME:PWY-7701| also contains a gene encoding an aminotransferase (tasG). However, it is still not known at what step in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-15319| the aminotransferase acts |CITS:[25885659]|.
