Summary: General Background, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is a reducing acidic sugar that often forms a hexapyranose ring structure. It is common in carbohydrate chains of proteoglycans and is part of mucous animal secretions (such as saliva), cell glycocalyx and intercellular matrix. The hexapyranosic form |FRAME: CPD-12521| is found in the glycosaminoglycans |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates|, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: Hyaluronan|., In animals D-glucuronate is degraded as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-5525|. Bacteria degrade |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by three different pathways: the isomerase pathway, which is found in enterobacteria (see |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY|), an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-17141| (see |FRAME: PWY-6501|), and an oxidative pathway that proceeds via |FRAME: D-GLUCARATE| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, Enteric bacteria such as |FRAME:TAX-562| can use |FRAME: Beta-D-Glucuronides "β-D-glucuronosides"| and the hexuronates |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| and |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| and as the sole sources of carbon for growth. β-D-glucuronosides are detoxification products that are excreted into the mammalian gut in the bile. |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is found in animal mucus and at low levels in plant tissues. The enzymes of this pathway were first described in a series of publications by Ashwell et al |CITS: [13584413][13794771][14401695][13831814][13813474]|., The initial step in the degradation of β-glucuronosides is hydrolysis by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.31| to yield |FRAME: GLUCURONATE|, which is subsequently isomerized to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.12|, an enzyme also carries out the analogous function in the |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY| pathway., |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| undergoes an NADH-dependent reduction to |FRAME: D-MANNONATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.57|, and a dehydration catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.8| yields |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE|., At this point, the |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY| pathways converge, and a common enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.45|, phosphorylates |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| to yield, |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, which enters central metabolism via the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|., Review: Mandrand-Berthelot, M.-A., Condemine, G., and Hugouvieux-Cotte-Pattat, N., EcoSal Module 3.4.2, |CITS: [ecosal]|

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7172 "Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol"| (THC) is the main psychoactive substance found in the cannabis plant. In 1988 it was found that the pharmacological actions of THC result from its binding to two receptors - the cannabinoid receptors CB1, located mainly in the central nervous system, and CB2, mainly present in cells of the immune system. Both receptors belong to the superfamily of membrane-bound G-protein-coupled receptors |CITS: [9336020]|., As THC is not a naturally occurring substance in the mammalian body, the existence of a specific receptor for THC implied that there should be endogenous molecules for these existing receptors (endocanabinoids). The first such molecule, |FRAME: CPD-7598| (N-arachidonoyl ethanolamine), was isolated by the Israeli scientist Raphael Mechoulam in 1992 |CITS: [1470919]|. Since then four more endocanabinoids have been reported - |FRAME: CPD-12600|, |FRAME: CPD-22217| (noladin ether), |FRAME: CPD-22218|, and |FRAME: CPD-22219| |CITS: [17227440]|., Binding of endocannabinoids (or cannabinoids) to cannabinoid receptors results in a decrease in the intracellular level of |FRAME: CAMP| and activation of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.24|, through the coupled Gi/o proteins. In addition, the activation of cannabinoid receptors modulates ion channels through Gi/o proteins, leading to the activation of A-type and inward-rectifyier potassium channels and the inhibition of N-type and P/Q-type calcium channels |CITS: [19126434]|., |FRAME: CPD-12600 2-Arachidonoylglycerol| (2-AG) is synthesized in mammals and is an endogenous agonist of the cannabinoid receptors, especially of CB1, for which it acts as a full agonist |CITS:[7605349][7575630][9285589][9915812][11588122]|., |FRAME: CPD-12600| is present at relatively high levels in the central nervous system |CITS: [9650580]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-12600 2-Arachidonoylglycerol| is biosynthesized in multiple pathways, all of which start from sn-2 arachidonate-containing glycerophospholipids, which are abundant in cell membranes |CITS: [16678907]|., The main precursor for 2-AG is |FRAME: 1-Acyl-2-Arachidonoyl-Glycerols "2-arachidonoyl-diacylglycerol"|, which is deacylated by |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.116| (|FRAME: HS05911|) to yield 2-AG. The main precursors for 2-arachidonoyl-diacylglycerol are inositol phospholipids with 2-arachidonoyl group such as 2-arachidonoyl-phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: HS11935-MONOMER| to form 2-arachidonoyl-diacylglycerol. However, 2-arachidonoyl-diacylglycerol is also formed by hydrolysis of glycerophospholipids other than inositol phospholipids, such as |FRAME: 1-Acyl-2-Arachidonoyl-Glycerol-P| and |FRAME: 2-arachidonoyl-PC| |CITS: [10217292][15044630][15749716]|. In addition, a rapid enzymatic conversion of |FRAME: CPD-22226| to |FRAME: CPD-12600| was observed in brain homogenates |CITS: [12051682]|., Humans have two isozymes of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.116|, |FRAME: HS05911| and |FRAME: HS09093|, both of which have been cloned in 2003 |CITS: [14610053]|. However, only in |FRAME: HS05911|-deficient mice the retrograde suppression of synaptic transmission is lost with concomitant decreases in 2-AG levels of brain and spinal cord |CITS: [20147530][20159446][21807615]|, and thus |FRAME: HS05911| is believed to be the main biosynthetic enzyme of 2-AG in the central nervous system., A second route from |FRAME: 2-Arachidonoyl-Phosphatidylinositols| to |FRAME: CPD-12600| that does not involve |FRAME: HS05911| has been documented. In this route, the sn-1 acyl group of |FRAME: 2-Arachidonoyl-Phosphatidylinositols| (usually stearate) is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.118| (|FRAME: HS02103|), forming |FRAME: CPD-22224|, which is then coverted to |FRAME: CPD-12600| by |FRAME: HS11935-MONOMER| |CITS: [20359546]|.

General Background, |FRAME:ALLANTOIN "Allantoin"| is a common product of purine degradation. Allantoin is rich in nitrogen, and many organisms are able to degrade and recycle it., Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1458|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, do so under aerobic conditions, while others such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: ORG-5985| and |FRAME: TAX-587| do so only anaerobically., Allantoin degradation is not limited to bacteria. Ureide-transporting plants convert fixed nitrogen in their, roots to |FRAME:ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|, which are then transported to upper parts, of the plant, where they are degraded to release the nitrogen. In addition, some fungi and animals also, degrade allantoin., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-64|, comprises the hydrolysis of the internal amide bond of |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN|, forming |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| |CITS: [786256]|. This enzyme turned out to be common to all organisms that can degrade allantoin, and is the first step in all allantoin degradation pathways., |FRAME: ALLANTOATE "Allantoate"| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1091| via one of two routes. In the first route the nitrogen is liberated in a single step in the form of |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: ALLANTOICASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.4"|), while in the other route it is liberated in the form of |FRAME: AMMONIA| in two steps, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD0-2298| (starting with |FRAME: ALLANTOATE-DEIMINASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.9"|)., The next step in the pathway is the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-1091| to |FRAME: GLYOX|. Similarly, this conversion can proceed with the liberation of either |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-LYASE-RXN "EC 4.3.2.3"|) or |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-HYDROLASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.19"|)., Several combinations of these routes have been documented. Some organisms possess pathways that produce solely |FRAME: UREA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5694|), some produce only |FRAME: AMMONIA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5692|), and some produce both (see |FRAME: PWY-5705|). In addition, some anaerobic organisms can degrade allantoin to |FRAME: CPD-389| instead of |FRAME: GLYOX| (see |FRAME: PWY0-41|)., About This Pathway, Several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-4932| and some bacteria, can utilize |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| as a sole nitrogen source by degrading it to |FRAME:UREA|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: GLYOX|. , In this pathway, |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-1091| by |FRAME: G6285-MONOMER|, and , |FRAME: CPD-1091| is converted to |FRAME: GLYOX| and |FRAME: UREA| by |FRAME: G6275-MONOMER|. |FRAME: GLYOX| then enters general metabolism, where it is converted by the successive action of three enzymes to |FRAME: G3P| (see |FRAME: GLYCOLATEMET-PWY|). The nitrogen, which is liberated in the form of two |FRAME:UREA| molecules, may be subsequently converted to |FRAME:AMMONIA| by |FRAME: CPLX-6897| or |FRAME: YBR208C-MONOMER| (see |FRAME:Urea-Degradation|) |CITS:[13211565][13260270][4960174][5942430][4979099][104142][385448]|., For more information about the yeast pathway, please see |FRAME: ALLANTOINDEG-PWY|.

Summary: The |FRAME: PWY-5743| is one of few |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| fixation pathways that are known. The pathway was discovered in the green nonsulfur phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1108| |CITS: [Holo89][8354269]|, and seems to be limited to organisms that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-1106| phylum |CITS: [17635550]|, one of the five major lineages of phototrophic bacteria. A similar, yet different pathway operates in some acidophilic archaebacteria of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-28889|, such as |FRAME: TAX-41673|, |FRAME: TAX-47303| and |FRAME: TAX-43687| |CITS: [12610721]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5789|)., Each turn of the |FRAME: PWY-5743| results in the net fixation of two molecules of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| (in the form of |FRAME: HCO3|) into one molecule of |FRAME:GLYOX|. Glyoxylate is an unconventional cell carbon precursor, and requires special enzymes for assimilation. The cyclical pathway that is responsible for glyoxylate assimilation was proposed in 2002 |CITS: [11929869]|, and is now considered an integral part of the |FRAME: PWY-5743|  |CITS: [17635550]|., |FRAME:GLYOX Glyoxylate| is combined with |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| forming |FRAME: CPD-9409|, which is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-9408|. A dedicated enzyme catalyzes an unusual rearrangement which transfers the CoA moiety to the C4 carbon, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-14205|. The latter is hydrated to form |FRAME: CPD-627|, which is cleaved by a lyase to form |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|., The acetyl-CoA that is formed by the lyase is condensed with a |FRAME: HCO3| molecule forming |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, which is processed to regenerate |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, completing the cycle. Thus the net output of the cycle is pyruvate, a common central metabolism carbon source |CITS: [11929869]|., Several steps remained unclear after the initial discovery of the pathway. These steps were defined in 2009 with the purification and characterization of the enzymes catalyzing them. It was shown that all the genes coding for the enzymes required for the glyoxylate assimilation route (plus the |FRAME: G-10370| and |FRAME: G-10371| genes, which encode the subunits of |FRAME:CPLX-7546|) were clustered together in the genome |CITS: [19955419]|.

About this Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CORTISOL| from |FRAME: PROGESTERONE|. Progesterone is produced from |FRAME: PREGNENOLONE| as described in |FRAME: PWY-7299| |CITS: [7673125]|., The conversion of progesterone to 17-α-hydroxyprogesterone is catalyzed by CYP17A1, a member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily of heme containing membrane associated enzymes |CITS: [3487786]|. These monooxygenases utilize NADPH for the reduction of molecular oxygen via a membrane bound microsomal electron transfer system. CYP17A1 localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and catalyzes multiple reactions critical for biosynthesis of adrenal and gonadal steroid hormones., CYP21A2 another cytochrome P450 superfamily member, localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and faces the cytoplasm, where it catalyzes the conversion of 17α-hydroxyprogesterone to11-deoxycortisol |CITS: [3487786]|. CYP21A2 is expressed only in the adrenal cortex., Another member of the cytochrome P450 superfamily, CYP11B2, localizes to the mitochondrial inner membrane and catalyzes the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to aldosterone |CITS: [1741400]|.

Summary: Like hydroxycinnamic acid serotonin amides (|FRAME: PWY-5473|), hydroxycinnamic acid tyramine amides belong to the , larger group of N-hydroxycinnamic acid amides (HCAAs). HCAAs are synthesized by the condensation , of hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA thioesters and aromatic amines. The hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA thioesters , include cinnamoyl-CoA, p-coumaroyl-CoA, caffeoyl-CoA, feruloyl-CoA and sinapoyl-CoA. The aromatic , amines include tyramine, octopamine, tryptamine, serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline. , The biosynthesis of HCAAs of tyramine is catalyzed by tyramine N-hydroxycinnamoyltransferase (THT). , Hydroxycinnamic acid tyramine amides are wide-spread in higher plants. They are frequently found , insoluble constituents of the cell wall. Incorporation of hydroxycinnamic acid tyramine amides into cell , wall is believed to enhance the efficiency of cell all to act as a barrier against pathogens by increasing , the rigidity and decreasing the digestibility of the cell wall. In agreement with their proposed roles, the , potato THT activity was shown increase upon pathogen (P. infestans) infection, and also increase in , wounded tuber |CITS: [9933628]|.

There are many types of biological 1,3-β-D-glucans - for example |FRAME: Callose|, |FRAME: Chrysolaminarin|, |FRAME: Curdlan|, |FRAME: CPD-3602|, |FRAME: Paramylon|, and |FRAME: Zymosan|, to name a few., The basic structure of these polymers is a linear chain of β-D-glucose residues, connected by 1,3 linkages. Some of the polymers contain only 1,3 linkages, while others have some additional 1,4 or 1,6 linkages., While the different polymers, which are formed by different organisms, vary in their characteristics, they are all formed by the same type of enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.34|, which transfers a glucose molecule from |FRAME: CPD-12575| to the C3 position of a nascent polymer.

Mammals, plants, and select bacterial species are known to oxidize |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| (NO) using nitric oxide synthases. NO function in Gram-positive organisms is diverse and varies across species |CITS: [19375324]|. Nitric oxide protects bacterial cells from reactive oxygen species by transiently suppressing the enzymatic reduction of free cysteine that fuels the Fenton reaction and by directly reactivating catalase |CITS: [16172391]|. It has been shown that NO renders the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1280| less sensitive to antibiotics |CITS: [19745150]|., Unlike the eukaryotic enzymes (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.39|), which consist of linked oxygenase and reductase domains, the bacterial enzyme consists of only an oxygenase domain, and thus requires an external electron donor |CITS: [11856757]|. Two flavodoxins, encoded by the ykuN and ykuP genes, were shown to act as efficient electron donors in |FRAME: TAX-1423|, and it was suggested that YkuN is the physiological redox partner |CITS: [17127770]|. The native flavodoxin reductase (|FRAME: EC-1.19.1.1|) responsible for reducing YkuN at the expense of NADPH in |FRAME: TAX-1423| is a promiscuous ferredoxin/flavodoxin reductase encoded by the yumC gene |CITS: [25194416]|.

Summary: Anthocyanins can be divided in two groups, the common 3-hydroxyanthocyanins which bear a hydroxyl group at the 3-position of the C-ring and the rare 3-deoxyanthocyanidins which are lacking this hydroxyl group. 3-Deoxyanthocyanidins are found mostly in mosses and ferns and have been reported in higher plants especially in the New World angiosperm families |FRAME:TAX-26122| and |FRAME:TAX-24079| |CITS:[Harborne66]| and some members of the |FRAME:TAX-4479| such as maize, sorghum and sugarcane |CITS:[Styles75]|. In the highly developed |FRAME:TAX-26122| species the 3-deoxyanthocyanidins are mostly involved in providing orange-red to scarlet flower colors which have been discussed as attractants for bird pollinators |CITS:[Harborne66]|. In addition, they are known to be induced as phytoalexins in response to pathogenic attacks in apple and sorghum |CITS:[12667486]|., The occurrence of the 3-deoxyanthocyanidins |FRAME:CPD-7096| and |FRAME:CPD-11945| (this pathway) has been reported from petals of |FRAME:TAX-189007| |CITS:[Stich88]| |CITS:[Winefield05]| and silk tissue of maize |CITS:[Halbwirth03]|. Both 3-deoxyanthocyanidins are precursors to the corresponding 5-O-glucosides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15272| (see |FRAME:PWY-7253|) and |FRAME:CPD-15269| (this pathway) |CITS:[Swinny00]| and the polymerized phlobaphenes in maize |CITS:[11402179]|., The first committed step of the pathway is the reduction of the respective flavanones forming flavan 4-ols. The structures of the flavan 4-ols have been questioned and a retrodihydrochalcone structure (|FRAME:CPD-15275|) proposed instead |CITS:[Khalil12]|. However, further research is needed to address this question in more detail. |FRAME:CPD-6994 Eriodictyol| is the flavanone that starts the |FRAME:PWY-7252|. The flavanone 4-reductase catalyzing this reaction has been purified and characterized from |FRAME:TAX-48789| |CITS:[Stich88]| |CITS:[Winefield05]| and maize |CITS:[Halbwirth03]|. It could be demonstrated that the enzyme had a dual activity as it also accepted dihydroflavonols, hence acted as dihydroflavonol 4-reductase (DFR)/flavanone 4-reductase (FNR). The formation of 3-deoxyanthocyanins is influenced by the activity of the flavonoid 3-hydroxylase (F3H), an enzyme involved in the formation of 3-hydroxyanthocyanins, which also competes for the available flavanones. Is the F3H inhibited, e.g in |FRAME:CPD-15293| treated |FRAME:TAX-3749| |CITS:[12667486]| or naturally absent or suppressed in certain genotypes |CITS:[Halbwirth03]| the flavanone 4-reductase directs the substrate flow towards the 3-deoxyanthocyanin biosynthesis as no flavan-3,4-diols are available for the dihydroflavonol 4-reductase to act on. , The specific anthocyanidin synthase activity which converts the flavanones (here |FRAME:CPD-11941|) to the 3-deoxyanthocyanidins, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-11945| has been shown to be expressed in petals of |FRAME:TAX-48789| |CITS:[Winefield05]| but has not yet been purified and characterized. The final step in the pathway is the formation of the 5-O-glucosides which is catalyzed by the 3-deoxyanthocyanin 5-Oglucosyltransferase. This enzyme has been identified and biochemically characterized in petals of |FRAME:TAX-189007| and shown to be very specific for the 3-deoxyanthocyanidins |FRAME:CPD-11945| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-7096| because it did not accept any other flavonoid substrates (flavonols, flavones, flavanones, 3-hydroxyanthocyanidins) |CITS:[20458497]|. It has been classified as an UGT88 enzyme, a phylogenetic clade which involves |FRAME:MONOMER-12113| (see |FRAME:PWY-5160|) |CITS:[15944692]| and |FRAME:MONOMER-12697| (see |FRAME:PWY-1901|) |CITS:[16832053]|.

General Background, |FRAME: TAURINE Taurine| is a sulfonated amino acid. The name comes from Taurus (Latin for bull), as it was first isolated from ox bile. It is found in high abundance in the tissues of many animals (especially sea animals) and, in lesser abundance, in plants, fungi, and some bacterial species., Taurine plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many species. The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis., Taurine is produced from |FRAME: CYS| in multiple pathways. Two pathways have been described in mammals: the "cysteinesulfinate pathway" (see |FRAME: PWY-5331|), which proceeds via |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| and |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| |CITS: [4297098]|, and the "cysteamine pathway" (see |FRAME: PWY-7850|), which proceeds via |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE|, |FRAME: CPD-239|, and |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| |CITS: [Cavallini76][Scandurra78]|. A third pathway that involves |FRAME: SO3| (see |FRAME: PWY-8359|) has been described from Sauropsida |CITS: [32601391]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.51|, a key member of the coenzyme A biosynthesis pathway, produces |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE|. It has been shown that this compound can be subject to a hydrolysis/decarboxylation reaction that produces |FRAME: CPD-239| |CITS: [Cavallini76]|. This compound is then converted to |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.19| |CITS: [17581819]|., |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE "Hypotaurine"| exists in low concentrations in liver and brain of adult mammals, and at least 90% of it is readily oxidized to |FRAME: TAURINE| |CITS: [Osman97]|. The evidence for an enzyme that is responsible for this conversion was controversial for 55 years |CITS: [13979247][5408877][4713187][7295801][4059226]| until it was shown in 2020 that the reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: G-80650|, one of the isozymes of |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.8| |CITS: [32156684]|.

Summary: General Background, Cell-cell communication in bacteria is accomplished through the exchange of extracellular signalling molecules called autoinducers. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., Autoinducer systems depend on two main components - the autoinducer and its receptor, which also functions as an autoinducer-dependent transcriptional regulator that binds DNA immediately upstream of the genes that are controlled., Autoinducer systems have been implicated in regulation of various systems. For example, |FRAME: G-11135|/luxR of |FRAME: TAX-668| regulate bioluminescence, luxM/luxN of |FRAME: TAX-669| regulate bioluminescence and polyhydroxybutyrate biosynthesis, |FRAME: G-11138|/lasR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates virulence factors, |FRAME: G-11136|/rhlR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates rhamnolipid synthesis as well as virulence factors, and |FRAME: G-11137|/TraR of |FRAME: TAX-358| regulates plasmid conjugal transfer |CITS: [8905097]|., Several types of autoinducers are known. Gram-negative bacteria typically use |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "acyl-homoserine lactones"|, known as type AI-1, as their autoinducers. The first autoinducer to be discovered was |FRAME: CPD-10780|, an AI-1 type compound from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [7236614]|. Many variants of AI-1 type inducers exist, differing from each other in the composition of the acyl moiety. In some cases, one organism may produce multiple types of acyl homoserine lactone type autoinducers, each produced by a dedicated synthase., A few examples are |FRAME: CPD-10781| from |FRAME: TAX-669|, |FRAME: CPD-10782| from |FRAME: TAX-358|,, |FRAME: CPD-10783| and |FRAME: CPD-10784| from |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: CPD-10780| and, |FRAME: CPD-10785| from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [8905097]|., Another very common family of autoinducers include compounds produced from |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|, which was first described from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-669|, in which it is used to control luciferase expression |CITS:[7984107][9990077]|. AI-2 type compounds are produced by a remarkably wide variety of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, leading to the proposal that AI-2 is a 'universal' signal that functions in interspecies cell-to-cell communication |CITS: [11544353][18803868]|., About This Pathway, The precursor of AI-2, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|, is synthesized by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7755|, in a reaction that is also a step in the |FRAME: PWY-6151| pathway (SAM cycle). The enzyme converts |FRAME: CPD-564| to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| in a reaction that also produces |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE|. Within the SAM cycle, the main product of the enzyme is the former compound. However, in organisms that produce an AI-2 autoinducer, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE| is of major importance as it appears to be the last enzyme-generated precursor for AI-2, and is converted to the functional autoinducer in a series of chemical modifications without the help of any known enzyme., The exact nature of the chemical transformations depends on the species., In |FRAME: TAX-135623| the spontaneous transformations include cyclyzation to |FRAME: CPD-10775|, hydration, to |FRAME: CPD-10776|, and finally, in the presence of free borate ions, complexation with the later to form the, active autoinducer, |FRAME: CPD-10777| |CITS: [11823863][18803868]|., This particular form of the autoinducer appears to be unique to |FRAME: TAX-135623|, which detect it using, dedicated AI-2 receptors encoded by the luxP and luxQ genes |CITS:[7984107][16451172]|., Other bacteria that produce AI-2 utilize a different form of the autoinducer., In those organisms |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE| appears to form a different stereoisomer,, namely |FRAME: CPD-10773|, which does not complex borate |CITS: [15350213]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6153|)., The mechanism that controls which stereoisomer is formed is still not understood.

General Background, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that contains a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide., Lipoate is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme systems involved in oxidative metabolism, including |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| |CITS: [2188967]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| |CITS: [1655709][8444795]|., Each of these enzyme complexes is composed of multiple copies of three enzymes: a substrate-specific, decarboxylase-dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), specific for each type of complex, and a dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3). , The (E2) proteins have a dedicated lipoyl domain. In order for the complex to be active, lipoate must be attached to the lipoyl domain by an amide linkage between its carboxylate moiety and a specific lysine residue in the enzyme |CITS: [8444795]|.., E1 catalyzes a reaction in which the substrate is attached to the lipoate cofactor and decarboxylated. During this reaction, the lipoate cofactor is reduced to dihydriolipoate., E2 then catalyzes an acyl transfer step, in which the product of the reaction is released. Finally, E3 catalyzes the oxidation of the dihydrolipoyl cofactor back to lipoyl form, with NAD being the ultimate electron acceptor |CITS: [2188967]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of lipoate is unusual, and shares the same mechanism as the biosynthesis of biotin., The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain, and is then converted to lipoate., In |FRAME: TAX-562| the pathway consists of two steps - first enzyme in the pathway, encoded by either |FRAME: EG11796| or |FRAME: EG11591|, transfers either free octanoate or the octanoate moiety from an |FRAME: Octanoyl-ACPs "octanoate-[acp]"| molecule, respectively, to a specific lysyl residue in any of the lipoate-dependent enzymes, while another enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: EG11306|, converts the bound octanoate to lipoate (see |FRAME: PWY0-501| and |FRAME: PWY0-1275|)., In |FRAME: TAX-1423| the pathway is somewhat more complex. The first enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: BSU24530|, can transfer the octanoate from |FRAME: Octanoyl-ACPs "octanoyl-[acp]"| only to the H protein of the glycine cleavage system. It is then converted to dihydrolipoyl by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8| (LipA). A third enzyme, an amidotransferase encoded by |FRAME:G-14913|, is required to complete the transfer of the dihydrolipoyl moiety from the |FRAME: DIHYDROLIPOYL-GCVH "lipoylated GcvH protein"| to the E2 components of the other 2-oxo acid dehydrogenases |CITS: [21338421][31066113][38624243]|.

Summary: This pathway for the anaerobic biosynthesis of the unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-17910| branches from the pathway leading to saturated fatty acids at |FRAME: Decanoyl-ACPs|. , Only bacteria can produce unsaturated fatty acids anaerobically. During normal fatty acid biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-562| two dehydratases, |FRAME: EG10273 FabA| and |FRAME: EG11284 FabZ|, function for the most part interchangeably in converting |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP "(3R)-3-hydroxyacyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| of various chain lengths, saturated or unsaturated, to the corresponding |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-ACP "trans-2-enoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| forms. However |FRAME: EG10273 FabA| alone has the unique ability of converting some of the trans form |FRAME: Trans-D2-decenoyl-ACPs "(2E)-dec-2-enoyl-[acp]"| produced to the cis form |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acyl-carrier protein]"| (see |FRAME: PWY0-862|)., While the trans form can be reduced and elongated leading to saturated fatty acids, the cis form cannot be reduced. Instead it serves directly as a substrate for the condensing enzyme, |FRAME: EG10274 FabB|, producing a product that can be acted on by the regular fatty acid elongation enzymes, resulting in an unsaturated acid with a chain lengthened by two carbon atoms., Even though only α- and γ-proteobacteria have the fabA and fabB genes, other bacterial species use the same pathway for the anaerobic production of unsaturatd fatty acids by employing alternative enzymes, such as |FRAME: EF_RS01435| and |FRAME: EF_RS01430| in |FRAME: TAX-1351| |CITS: [15194690]| and |FRAME: G-44020| in |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [12237320]|., However, |FRAME: TAX-210| possesses a different enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: HP0773| gene, which allows it to start the pathway directly from |FRAME: Decanoyl-ACPs decanoyl-[acp]|. This bifunctional enzyme catalyzes the difficult dehydrogenation of the substrate using molecular oxygen as the electron donor, introducing a trans double bond at carbon 2 of the substrate (similar to |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.6|). It then proceeds to catalyze an isomerization reaction identical to the one catalyzed by FabA (|FRAME: EC-5.3.3.14|) |CITS: [27866909]|., |FRAME: HP0558 FabF| is required for the elongation of |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs "(3Z)-dec-3-enoyl-[acp]"| to allow this intermediate entry into the fatty acid synthesis cycle. Once elongated, the product is subject to repeated fatty acid elongation cycles that lead to the unsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247|, which are incorporated into various lipids (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6282| and |FRAME: PWY-5973|).

Summary: General Background, Aurachin alkaloids were originally isolated from the myxobacterium |FRAME: TAX-675526| in the 1980s |CITS: [3106289]|. They are potent inhibitors of mitochondrial respiration through blockage of NADH oxidation, presumably because of their significant structural similarity to |FRAME: Menaquinones menaquinone| |CITS: [7827023][20335999]|. |FRAME: CPD-7733 "Aurachin C"| is a particularly effective inhibitor of the two terminal oxidases of |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: CYT-O-UBIOX-CPLX "cytochromes bo"| and |FRAME: CYT-D-UBIOX-CPLX "cytochrome bd"|, whereas |FRAME: CPD-15909| displays a selectivity for inhibition of cytochrome bd |CITS: [7827023]|. , Beside |FRAME: TAX-40|, only one other producer species has been discovered - the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6248|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-15906| |CITS: [19168983]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7405|)., |FRAME: TAX-675526| produces four major forms of aurachins (|FRAME: CPD-15911|, |FRAME: CPD-15910|, |FRAME: CPD-7733| and |FRAME: CPD-15909|) in varying ratios at different phases of growth. |FRAME: CPD-15910 "Aurachin B"| and |FRAME: CPD-15909| are minor components throughout the different growth phases, |FRAME: CPD-7733| is formed dominantly in the exponential growth phase, and |FRAME: CPD-15911| is largely, present at the stationary phase., A gene cluster involved in aurachin biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-675526| was discovered by generating a transposon mutant impacted in aurachin synthesis |CITS: [17335090]|. The cluster contained several of the genes involved, including |FRAME: G-17841| (encoding a prenyltransferase) and |FRAME: G-17843|, |FRAME: G-17844|, |FRAME: G-17845| and |FRAME: G-17846|, which encode components of a type II polyketide synthase complex. Later work identified additional genes located in two other locations in the chromosome |CITS: [21979787]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with the activation of |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| to |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZOYL-COA| |CITS: [21770425]|. |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE Anthranilate| is formed from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|. It has been shown that |FRAME: TAX-675526| possesses two copies of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.54|, a key enzyme in chorismate biosynthesis, one of which is dedicated for aurachin biosynthesis |CITS: [10896221]|., The activated |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZOYL-COA| is transferred to the acyl/aryl-carrier protein of a |FRAME: CPLX-8785 "polyketide synthase complex"|. The complex adds two |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| moieties, generating |FRAME: CPD-15907| |CITS: [17335090]|, which is prenylated to form the first aurachin, |FRAME: CPD-15909| |CITS: [21671333]|. The quinoline ring nitrogen is hydroxylated by a Reiske [2Fe-2S] oxygenase, forming |FRAME: CPD-7733| |CITS: [21979787]|., Formation of the two other aurachins involves an unusual migration of the C-3 farnesyl group to the C-4 position. A mechanistic scheme for the rearrangement reaction, as illustrated in this pathway, has been proposed |CITS: [21979787]| and later revised |CITS: [22907798]|. According to this proposal the rearrangement involves two oxygenation steps, each consisting of epoxidation followed by a reduction.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (often refferred to as simply linolenate) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid (18:3) that is an important constituent of plant membranes. It is also known as an ω-3 fatty acid, referring to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid. Seed oils are the richest sources of |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, especially those of rapeseed (canola), soybeans, walnuts, flaxseed (Linseed), perilla, chia and hemp. It is also common in the lipids that are found in thylakoid membranes in the green leaves of broadleaf plants, and in cyanobacteria and alga |CITS:[4621688][414660]|. |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| is an essential fatty acid for animals, and is considered an essential dietary requirement for all mammals., About This Pathway, In all plant tissues, the major glycerolipids are first synthesized using only palmityl (16:0) and oleoyl (18:1) acyl groups, the products of the plastidic saturated fatty acid synthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5971|, |FRAME: PWY-5989| and |FRAME: PWY-5147|). Subsequent desaturation of the fatty acids to the highly unsaturated forms typical of the membranes of plant cells is carried while they are already attached to lipids., Most of the oleoyl-[acp] is released from the [acp]-moiety and exported from the plastid to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and is converted to |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA| in the process by the plastidic |FRAME: AT1G77590-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-5147|). The |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA| is incorporated into lipids, forming |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE|, |FRAME: Diacylglycerides|, and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5995|)., Further desaturation of the oleoyl groups to linoleoyl groups in the ER occurrs while incorporated into lipids. The first step, which produces |FRAME: Linoleoyl-groups|, is catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-1903|, encoded by the |FRAME: AT3G12120| gene. The second step, which produces |FRAME: Alpha-linolenoyl-groups|, is catalyzed by the |FRAME: AT2G29980|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-1903|., A smaller portion of the oleoyl-[acp] molecules can be incorporated into |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE diacylglycerol| and |FRAME: Diacylglycerides| within the chloroplast. In this case, the desaturation to |FRAME: Linoleoyl-groups| occurs by a plastidic desaturase, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-10795| gene, and further desaturation into |FRAME: Alpha-linolenoyl-groups| is catalyzed by two plastidic desaturases, encoded by the |FRAME: AT3G11170| and |FRAME: AT5G05580| genes |CITS:[12232435][11814526]|.

General Background, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate 4-Hydroxybenzoate| (p-hydroxybenzoate) is widespread in plants. It is one of the major cell wall-bound phenolic acids that play a major role in plant defense against pathogens. It has also been identified as an important dietary anti-oxidant. In addition, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-9| and several plant secondary metabolites, such as |FRAME: CPD-9322|. , There are at least two biosynthetic routes leading to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| that have been proposed in plants: 1) the β-oxidation route that converts |FRAME: COUMARATE| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| via |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| (|FRAME: PWY-6435|); and 2) the non-β oxidative pathway that converts |FRAME: COUMARATE| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| via |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| (|FRAME: PWY-6431|)., In plants, |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| has an origin from |FRAME: PHE|, where |FRAME: COUMARATE| is an intermediate |CITS: [17658659][Yazaki91][12232327]|. In the β-oxidation pathway, the side-chain shortening is analogous to |FRAME: PWY-5136| via CoA esters. In the non-oxidative pathway, the side-chain shortening is achieved through a lyase reaction that does not require CoA as a cofactor. , About This Pathway, The existence of the beta-oxidation route has been reported in |FRAME: TAX-34254| |CITS: [12232327]|. Enzyme-dependent conversion of 4-coumarate to 4-hydroxybenzoate was detected in cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-34254| cell cultures. The assays contained CoA, ascorbate and NAD. Under the particular assay conditions, Loscher and Heide demonstrated that 4-coumaroyl-CoA was the activated intermediate and that 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde was not an intermediate. The authors proposed that the main pathway for 4-hydroxybenzoate biosynthesis from 4-coumarate proceeded via 4-coumaroyl-CoA. In this route, 4-coumaroyl-CoA is cleaved, presumably after oxidation (analogous to fatty acid beta oxidation), in a thioclastic reaction to give rise to 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. Contrary evidence from another independent study conducted in |FRAME:TAX-34254| |CITS: [Yazaki91]|, suggested that a non-beta oxidative route also exists (see |FRAME: PWY-6431|)., Although the experiments conducted by Loscher and Heide demonstrated the enzyme-dependent conversion of 4-coumaroyl-CoA to 4-hydroxybenzoate, the individual enzyme activities responsible for the sequential reactions converting 4-coumaroyl-CoA to 4-hydroxybenzoate were not specified in the study. Nonetheless, the enzymes involved appeared soluble, suggesting a cytosolic location of the pathway.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-Tomatine| is an preformed steroidal glycoalkaloid produced as a potent antimicrobial agent in tomato (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-3 α-tomatine biosynthesis|) |CITS:[5661492] [12239364] [Schonbeck76]| and a member of the vast and diverse class of saponins |CITS:[3308321] [11783842] [25951908]|. The glycoalkaloid |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| has been reported to reach concentrations up to 1 mmol |CITS:[Roddick74]|, which is high enough to inhibit the growth of most pathogenic fungi and bacteria |CITS:[18944982]| through membranolytic effects |CITS:[1390841]|. , Fungal and bacterial pathogens known to infect tomato produce a secretory enzyme, i.e. tomatinase which is able to break down |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| into less harmful metabolites for the pathogens |CITS:[10477313]|. In addition, there are reports indicating that degradation products of |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| may also interfere with induced plant defense responses |CITS:[11106022] [12192413]|. The infections of crops mediated by pathogens and the course of the respective diseases have been monitored for a long time. For instance, the fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici, the originator of the vascular wilt of tomato |CITS:[20569392]|, is omnipresent across the globe and responsible for severe crop losses each year |CITS:[Booth71]|., This pathway summarizes the catalytic actions from six fungal and two bacterial pathogens that cause the breakdown of the tomato glycoalkaloid |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine|. This compound consists of the aglycone |FRAME:CPD-17697 tomatidine| which has been stepwise glycosylated to add the |FRAME:CPD-18735 lycotetraose| side chain (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-3 α-tomatine biosynthesis|). The degradation of |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| is carried out by glycosidases, generally referred to as α-tomatinases. The α-tomatinases of the various tomato pathogenic species operate in different modes, i.e. they attack diverse sides of the attached |FRAME:CPD-18735 lycotetraose|. , The α-tomatinases of the fungi Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici |CITS:[10517025] [9237400] [8633858] [Ford77] [18624637] [15280013]|, Fusarium solani |CITS:[Lairini98]| and Passalora fulva |CITS:[23209441] [23448507]| as well as the α-tomatinases of the bacteria Clavibacter michiganensis sp. michiganensis |CITS:[16255248]| and Streptomyces scabiei |CITS:[18835993]| remove the |FRAME:CPD-18735 lycotetraose| from |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17697 tomatidine| by attacking the β-1,3-linkage of the tetraose moiety. The fungus Septoria lycopersici employs a β2-tomatinase, which cleaves |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| by attacking the 1-2 bond between the two |FRAME:GLC β-D-glucopyranose| molecules of the |FRAME:CPD-18735 lycotetraose| moiety forming |FRAME:CPD-18763 β2-tomatine| in the process |CITS:[8664505] [8664504] [15213407] [11106022]|. Yet another fungus, i.e. Botrytis cinera attacks the other terminal glycosidic residue of |FRAME:CPD-18735 lycotetraose| cleaving off |FRAME: CPD-25028 α-D-xylopyranose| and therefore producing |FRAME:CPD-18639 β1-tomatine| from |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| |CITS:[Quidde98] [23704180]|. The highest variability has been demonstrated for the fungus Alternaria solani, causing stem canker on tomatoes |CITS:[Gilchrist75]|, which successively releases single sugar residues, beginning with the terminal residues, |FRAME: CPD-25028 α-D-xylopyranose|, 2 molecules of |FRAME:GLC β-D-glucopyranose| and finally |FRAME:GALACTOSE β-D-galactose| from the |FRAME:CPD-18735 lycotetraose| chain. However, the question whether one enzyme (α-tomatinase with multiple hydrolase activities) catalyzed all the reactions or various glycosidases were involved in the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| remains to be answered |CITS:[Schlosser77] [Oka06]|., Often |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| induces the activity of α-tomatinases indicating a connection between pathogenicity and secreted α-tomatinase of the pathogen. On the other side, most pathogens did not display a changed pathogenicity when α-tomatinase-null mutants had been generated which points to an more complex infection process than the activation of an |FRAME:CPD-17696 α-tomatine| degrading enzyme alone and requires further research |CITS:[20447279] [18944982] [10477313]|.

Summary: Sucrose is a disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose joined by an α(1,2) glycosidic linkage. It is present in the tissues of higher plants and is the most abundant disaccharide in the biosphere. Sucrose biosynthesis in plants is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SUCSYN-PWY|. Some bacteria can use sucrose as a carbon source. Sucrose can be transported into the cell and hydrolyzed as shown in this pathway, or it may be hydrolyzed extracellularly and converted to polymers by secreted enzymes. These polymers function in pathogenicity, or serve as an energy source when other nutrients are depleted (in |CITS: [8550467] [8423155]|., In general, bacteria transport sucrose and other carbohydrates into the cell using specific membrane transport proteins, and catabolize them using highly regulated mechanisms in order to conserve cellular energy. Mesophilic bacteria transport carbohydrates into the cell by various mechanisms, including cation or proton-coupled transporters, ATP-dependent binding cassette (ABC) transporters, and the phosphoenolpyruvate:glycose phosphotransferase system (PTS). Archaea and thermophilic bacteria lack the PTS and use ABC transporters to transport carbohydrates |CITS: [11902154]| in |CITS: [15670594]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]|., In the organisms listed above for this pathway, genes for sucrose catabolism are organized into catabolic operons which form regulons. These genes are only expressed when sucrose is present and other preferred carbon sources are depleted. Regulation occurs at the transcriptional level and via carbon catabolite repression. Reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]|., Among the enteric bacteria, the ability to use sucrose as a sole carbon source is a highly variable phenotype. Most strains of |FRAME:TAX-573| can utilize sucrose. However, very few strains of |FRAME:TAX-590| spp and few strains of |FRAME:TAX-562|, can utilize sucrose, although mobile genetic elements such as the conjugative plasmid pUR400 of |FRAME:TAX-90371| (in |CITS: [8423155]|) and transposon CTnscr94 |CITS: [9079891]| can confer this ability upon them. Interestingly, |FRAME:TAX-562| K12 cannot utilize sucrose, but wild-type |FRAME:TAX-562| strain EC3132 contains chromosomal genes for sucrose metabolism, including a non-PTS permease, a sucrose hydrolase, and a fructokinase, that are organized into two operons, the csc regulon. However, this organism grows unusually slowly at a low concentration of sucrose. It has been speculated that the csc genes were acquired by horizontal gene transfer and their expression is not yet optimal in the new host |CITS: [12218016]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]|. , In this pathway, extracellular sucrose enters the periplasm of gram negative bacteria via porin channels in the outer membrane, and is then transported through the inner (cell) membrane. In gram positive bacteria, sucrose enters through the permeable cell wall, which in some species has been shown to contain porin channels |CITS: [12896997]|, and is then transported through the cell membrane. , This pathway involves the cell membrane-associated PTS that brings about both sugar transport and phosphorylation, resulting in an intracellular pool of phosphorylated sugar. The PTS is composed of general energy-coupling proteins (EI and HPr) that catalyze the transfer of a phosphoryl group for all PTS sugars, and sugar-specific protein(s) (EII). EI catalyzes the transfer of the phosphoryl group from phosphoenolpyruvate (a glycolytic intermediate) to a histidine residue in HPr, as shown in the linked reaction at the top of the pathway (EC 2.7.3.9). The sugar-specific EII catalyzes transfer of this phosphoryl group from HPr to the translocated sugar to yield the 6-phospho derivative of the sugar, as shown in this pathway (click on EC 2.7.1.69 to see a graphical representation of the EII sucrose transport reaction). Reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]| and |CITS: [2197982]|., The sugar-specific permeases contain domains (EIIA, EIIB and EIIC) that may be associated with a single polypeptide, a complex of two polypeptides, or a complex of three polypeptides, depending on the organism (Reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]| and |CITS: [2197982]|). Subsequent hydrolysis of the phosphorylated disaccharide in the cytosol is catalyzed by sugar specific enzymes, such as sucrose hydrolase. The product β-D-glucose-6-phosphate enters glycolysis, and D-fructose-6-phosphate is a glycolytic intermediate, and indicated by the pathway links., Other organisms use non-PTS sugar permeases to transport sucrose into the cell. The unmodified sucrose then undergoes phosphorolysis to fructose and glucose-1-phosphate (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5384| (Reviewed in |CITS: [15660210]|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that serves as a universally conserved cofactor across all kingdoms of life. The functional group of lipoate is a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide., The enzyme complexes that require lipoate have a dedicated lipoyl domain, and during lipoate de novo biosynthesis lipoate is actually produced on this domain. A precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain, and is then converted to lipoate. Enzymes known to require lipate include |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|, |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25|, and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190|. Much more recently a different lipoate-binding protein (LbpA) was found to be an essential component of a sulfur/thiosulfate oxidation pathway found in some bacteria and archaea (known as the heterodisulfide reductase (Hdr)-like pathway, or sHdr pathway) |CITS: [30004385]|., About This Pathway, Multiple enzymes can generate an octanoyl moiety on a lipoyl domain protein, either by transfering it from octanoyl-[acp] or octanyl-CoA, or by ligating free octanoate. However, only one enzyme was known to convert the octanoyl moiety to a lipoyl group - |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.8|, a radical-SAM enzyme that utilizes one of its own iron-sulfur clusters as the source of the two sulfur atoms that it inserts successively into the protein-bound octanoyl moiety. This notion changed in 2018 when a |FRAME: G-124922|-|FRAME: G-124920|-lipT-|FRAME: G-124921| gene cluster was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-396595|, with similar genes detected in other organisms that possess the sHdr pathway. At the time it was noted that the lipS1 and lipS2 genes (then named RadSAM1 and RadSAM2) encode radical SAM domain proteins, and that the |FRAME: G-124920| gene encodes an enzyme similar to LplA-type lipoate ligases. While a purified sLpl(AB) enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-396595| was not able to lipoylate lipoyl-domain proteins from E. coli, it was fully active with LbpA proteins from that organism |CITS: [30004385]|., Further characterization of the LipS1 and LipS2 proteins from the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-311400| confirmed that they catalyze the conversion of an octanoyl group (attached to a synthetic peptide) to a lipoyl group, in two steps - LipS2 transfers a sulfur to the C8 position of octanoate, followed by LipS1, which transfers the second sulfur atol to position C6. Both proteins carry a single {fe4-S4] cluster, which is essential for activity |CITS: [32978128]|., Even though most of these organisms that use the sHdr pathway for sulfur oxidation utilize a LipS1-LipS2 system to generate the lipoyl group on their LbpA proteins (74.3% of sHdr-containing bacteria and of 88.6% sHdr-containing archaea encode lipS1/S2 genes) |CITS: [37368881]|, the reverse is not true. Only 42% and 8% of LipS1/S2-containing bacteria and archaea, respectively, have the sHdr pathway., Even though the LipS1/S2-type of lipoyl synthase is less common than the LipA-type lipoate synthase, it is remarkably widespread. In bacteria, but not in archaea, it often co-occurs with LipA |CITS: [37368881]|.

Summary: General Background, Folates are tripartite molecules comprising pterin, p-aminobenzoate (pABA), and glutamate moieties. In natural folates the pterin ring exists in the dihydro or tetrahydro state. Folate usually has a gamma-linked polyglutamyl tail of up to eight residues attached to the first glutamate., Folate often serve as carriers of a one-carbon unit. The carbon (in methyl or formyl form) is either attached to N-5 of the pterin moiety, attached to N-10 of the pABA moiety, or bridged in between these two (as in 5,10-methenyl or methylene-THF). 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolates are involved in tetrahydrofolate, purine and formate synthesis |CITS: [7868604][17645794]|. , About This Pathway, The formation of the formyl and methyl derivatives of tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) directly involved in or representing sidesteps of the biosynthesis of this vital cofactor is displayed in this pathway. Conversion of 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate occurs either directly through hydrolysis or via 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate in several steps |CITS: [7868604] [17645794]|.

General Backround, Polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|), a group of positively charged small molecules present in virtually all living organisms, have been implicated in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [4873311][3157043][2185470][1409623]|. Although polyamines are clearly necessary for optimal cell growth, a surplus of polyamines can cause inhibition of growth and protein synthesis |CITS: [8223591]|, and thus a balance is desired, between the production and breakdown of polyamines., Several metabolic pathways for the degradation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| are known., About This Pathway, This pathway was initially documented for |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS:[35512]| and later observed in |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS: [3897201][3510672]|. In it |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is transaminated with |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to generate |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, which is then oxidized to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, or GABA. GABA can be further degraded into |FRAME: SUC| by the |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY| pathway., In |FRAME: TAX-548|, it was observed that the two enzymes of this pathway are induced by both the input (|FRAME: PUTRESCINE|) and the output (|FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|) of the pathway, an unusual observation |CITS:[35512]|., This is one of two known pathways for |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| degradation in |FRAME:TAX-562|, whereby |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is converted to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| via |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1221|).

Summary: Penicillium chrysogenum is a well-known producer of the antibiotic |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| and a valuable source of bioactive metabolites for medicinal research and pharmaceutical industry |CITS:[22865068] [23662444]|. Secondary metabolites of the diketopiperazine (DKP) alkaloid class |CITS:[Martins07] [23955505]| produced by the fungal genus Penicillium in pathways such as |FRAME:PWY-7605|, |FRAME:PWY-7607| (this pathway) and |FRAME:PWY-7608| (summarized in |FRAME:PWY-7609|) have been found as contaminants on food crops |CITS:[16348301]| and classified as potentially health-threatening for the known neurotoxicity of, for instance, |FRAME:CPD-17381| |CITS:[16345552] [613945]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-17391| has been reported to induce cell apoptosis and arrests the cell cycle in human HL-60 cell lines |CITS:[20186171]| which is of considerable interest for applied science in medicine and pharmacy. , |FRAME:CPD-17391 Meleagrin| and intermediates of the pathway were isolated from both deep ocean sediment-derived Penicillium species |CITS:[20186171]| as well as from wheat grain infesting Penicillium species (P. chrysogenum, P. commune, P. fellutanum, P. roquefortiii and others) |CITS:[14520967]|. Interestingly, |FRAME:CPD-17391| and intermediates were also biosynthesized from Penicillium chrysogenum and Penicillium expansum strains in a near zero-gravity environment as demonstrated on board the Mir space station |CITS:[12526198]|. The occurrence of intermediates of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17392|, |FRAME:CPD-17389| and |FRAME:CPD-17390| has been verified in various Penicillium species |CITS:[14520967]| which indicates a possible role of the respective pathways for competitive fitness of the invading fungus and outlines probable biosynthetic routes towards |FRAME:CPD-17391| |CITS:[16195849]| . , The sequencing of the Penicillium chrysogenum genome |CITS:[18820685]| provided the platform for in-depth bioinformatics analysis, molecular biology and biochemical approaches which allowed the elucidation of the |FRAME:PWY-7607| (this pathway) and closely related pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-7605|, |FRAME:PWY-7608|). It has been shown that the biosynthetic gene cluster (roq) is responsible for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17391| and descendants of this pathway. Bioinformatics studies revealed the structure of the roq cluster consisting of 7 genes and corresponding putative functions based on sequence homology with characterized enzymes |CITS:[22118684]|. , |FRAME:CPD-17381 Roquefortine C| appears to present a branching point in the pathway leading either towards |FRAME:CPD-17389| or |FRAME:CPD-17392|. The latter has been found as a new intermediate in a route towards |FRAME:CPD-17390| which includes the also novel intermediate |FRAME:CPD-17395| whereas the existence of |FRAME:CPD-17389| has been questioned |CITS:[24225953]|. The catalysis of both steps has been ascribed to roqM, an enzyme encoding a cytochrome P450 monoxygenase. The roquefortine monooxygenase encoded by roqM carries out multiple reactions of the pathway, i.e. the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-17381| into |FRAME:CPD-17389| |CITS:[23776469]|, the monooxygenation of |FRAME:CPD-17381| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17392| and the subsequent oxidation generating |FRAME:CPD-17395| from |FRAME:CPD-17392| |CITS:[24225953]|. The remaining oxidation reactions are catalyzed by roqO, another cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase realizing the reaction steps from |FRAME:CPD-17389| to |FRAME:CPD-17390| and |FRAME:CPD-17395| to |FRAME:CPD-17390|, respectively |CITS:[23776469] [24225953]|. The last step of the pathway, the O-methylation of |FRAME:CPD-17390| to gain the final product in the reaction sequence, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17391| is catalyzed by the roquefortine/glandicoline O- methyltransferase encoded by roqN which is also active in the |FRAME:PWY-7608| |CITS:[22118684] [23776469] [24225953]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-26023 "Corallopyronin A"| is an antibiotic produced by strains of |FRAME: TAX-184914|, a gliding and fruiting body-forming myxobacterium |CITS: [2581926]|. It acts as a noncompetitive inhibitor of the bacterial |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.6| by binding to the RpoB switch region, interfering with RNA synthesis |CITS: [18957204][18946472]|. The stereochemistry of the compound, as well as a proposed biosynthetic pathway, were published in 2010 |CITS: [20503218]|., Corallopyronin A is active against many Gram-positive pathogens, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, but is most promising against infections in which intracellular bacteria are involved |CITS: [22586066][33284808][36094073]|. As of 2022 the development of |FRAME: CPD-26023| has not progressed past pre-clinical testing |CITS: [35730490]|, mainly due to the non-scalable production by its natural producer. However, a heterologous expression system resulting in >100-fold higher production has been developed |CITS: [29030273][31340171]|. Another issue has been the poor solubility of the compound, but that too has been addressed by the development of solubility and stability enhanced oral formulations |CITS: [33217948]|., About This Pathway, Feeding experiments showed that the core structure of corallopyronin A is produced by a mixed PKS/NRPS biosynthetic, machinery. Studies with 13C-labelled SAM indicated that two of the methyl groups are produced not via the action of a methyltransferase, but rather via the mechanism of a β-branching cassette, the so called "HMGS-like cassette". Degenerate PCR primers designed for conserved regions of the corresponding domains were used to generate hybridization probes that were screened against a genomic cosmid library of |FRAME: TAX-184914|. The combined sequence from three cosmids (65 kbp) contained the full corallopyronin A biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS: [20503218]|., The gene cluster consists of 16 open reading frames that encode one hybrid PKS/NRPS (|FRAME: G-124380|), three PKS enzymes (|FRAME: G-124382|, |FRAME: G-124383|, and |FRAME: G-124384|), a trans-acyltransferase/enoyl reductase (|FRAME: G-124388|), a free-standing ketosynthase (|FRAME: G-124381|), a β-branching cassette (corC-|FRAME: G-124379|), an O-methyltransferase (|FRAME: G-124375|), a thioesterase (|FRAME: G-124385|) , a free-standing dehydratase (|FRAME: G-124385|) and a cytochrome P-450 (|FRAME: G-124387|). Of the 16 ORFs, 15 could be assigned to specific steps in the pathway. The last one (corP) is thought to protect the host from the effect of the antibiotic., The biosynthetic pathway starts with two parallel routes: the "western" part of the compound is produced by the |FRAME: CPLX-85438| and |FRAME: CPLX-85439|, while the "eastern" part of the molecule is produced by |FRAME: CPLX-85440| and |FRAME: CPLX-85441|. Since none of the synthases contain an acyltransferase domain, both chains are dependent on the CorA aceyltransferase, which provides this function in trans., One of the unusual features of this pathway is the use of the unique starter unit |FRAME: CPD-26309| by the CorI polyketide synthase |CITS: [24277032]|. The CorK synthase can use either acetyl-CoA (as shown here, which leads to production of |FRAME: CPD-26023|, or propanoyl-CoA, leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-26314| |CITS: [2581926]|., The two chains are connected by the |FRAME: G-124381 "free-standing ketosynthase CorB"|, which catalyzes a Claisen-type condensation, transferring the western chain onto the eastern one. A thioesterase encoded by |FRAME: G-124385| cleaves the product from the PKS, promoting keto-enol tautomerism of the carbonyl group at C-6 that results in formation of the pyrone ring. Finally, hydroxylation of C-24, catalyzed by a cytochrome P-450 encoded by the |FRAME: G-124387| gene forms |FRAME: CPD-26023| |CITS: [20503218]|., In 2017 a heterologous production platform allowing expression of the antibiotic in |FRAME: TAX-34| was reported |CITS: [29030273]|. A subsequent study improved the yield by ooverexpressing CorO, and utilized the platform to correct a mis-assigned function of CorN |CITS: [31340171]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: LYS "Lysine"| is an essential amino acid and its catabolism is unique among the common amino acids in that it proceeds via two distinct major pathways, the |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY66-425|, both of which converge into a common degradative pathway |CITS: [24043460]|. The α-amino group of lysine undergoes conversion to an α-keto group in this pathway, while the ε-amino group of lysine undergoes conversion to an aldehyde group in |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY| pathway., The |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY| is the predominant lysine catabolic pathway in the developing brain and extracerebral tissue, while the |FRAME: PWY66-425| occurs mostly in adult brain. The |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY| pathway is predominantly mitochondrial, and this pathway localizes to the peroxisome and cytosol., About this Pathway, The first step in this pathway is the conversion of the α-amino group of |FRAME: LYS| to an α-keto group to form |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE|. The mammalian enzyme that catalyzes this reaction has not yet been defined and there is debate as to whether it is an oxidase reaction |CITS: [10485319]| or a transaminase reaction |CITS: [24043460]|. In some bacterial species this conversion is catalyzed in two steps by specific lysine racemase and D-lysine oxidase (see |FRAME: PWY-5283|). In rats the peroxisomal |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.3|, catalyzes the conversion |FRAME: CPD-219| to pipecolate |CITS: [14235341]|. , Lysine was traditionally regarded to be inert to mammalian aminotransferases |CITS: [4293394]|. However, it has been demonstrated that in the presence of high levels of |FRAME: GLT| as found in the brain, the transamination of of L-lysine can occur, with the α-amino group being transferred to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or another α-keto acid |CITS: [24043460]|. Mouse |FRAME: CPLX66-375| has some transaminase activity towards lysine with |FRAME: GLYOX| as an amino group acceptor |CITS: [19029248]|., |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE| is in equilibrium with its cyclic ketimine form |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE|. This essentially renders the reverse formation of lysine by a transamination reaction unfavorable. Cytosolic |FRAME: CPLX66-517| has ketimine reductase activity and catalyzes the reduction of the imine bond in |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE| using either NADH or NADPH as cofactor, to yield |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| |CITS: [21332720]|. The |FRAME: HS11411-MONOMER| catalyzes the dehydrogenation of |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| to |FRAME: CPD-7682| |CITS: [10642506]|., The reverse reaction, |FRAME: CPD-7682| to |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-6781| |CITS: [24431009]|. |FRAME: CPD-7682| is in spontaneous equilibrium with its open aldehyde form |FRAME: ALLYSINE|. This explains why mutations in the ALDH7A1 gene leading to loss of |FRAME: CPLX66-394|, result in accumulation and excretion of |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| in patients. The downstream reactions from |FRAME: ALLYSINE| for this pathway and |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY| are identical.

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here describes the arsenate detoxification system encoded by the arsRDABC operon located on the R773 plasmid of |FRAME: TAX-562|, and similar systems |CITS: [3021763] [2408017]|., This cytoplasmic detoxification system involves an arsC-encoded cytoplasmic arsenate reductase, which reduces |FRAME: ARSENATE| to |FRAME: CPD-763|, an arsenite chaperone (ArsD), and an efficient arsenite efflux pump consisting of a two-component ATPase complex., It should be noted that |FRAME: TAX-562| also has a chromosomal operon that consists of three genes named arsR, arsB, and arsC based on their strong homology to the plasmid-borne genes (no |FRAME: G-107433| or G-81184) |CITS: [7721697][7860609]|. The pathway |FRAME: PWY-4621-1|) describes the chromosomal-encoded arsenate detoxification process, which is less efficient than the plasmid-encoded one., The |FRAME: G-107421| gene from the R773 plasmid encodes an enzyme that catalyzes the reduction of arsenate to arsenite using glutathione and glutaredoxin as electron donors and has been classified as |FRAME: EC-1.20.4.1|. ArsC cytoplasmic arsenate reductases are found widely in microbes |CITS: [15691908]|. Even though they were all named ArsC, they belong to several different clades, some of which share no sequence similarity, indicating parallel evolution |CITS: [15691908]|., The reaction catalyzed by this type of reductases involves sequential action of three different thiolate nucleophiles that function as a redox cascade |CITS: [16905151]|. All three glutaredoxins in E. coli can participate in the arsenate reductase reaction, but glutaredoxin 2 appears the most effective |CITS: [10593884]|. Crystal structures of ArsC have been solved |CITS: [11709171][15295115]|, and residues involved in arsenate binding and transition-state stabilization were identified |CITS: [14592722][15295115]|., The arsenite that is formed by ArsC appears to form a complex with glutathione. Arsenite is transferred from the complex to the |FRAME: CPLX-9632|, which in turn transfers it to the ArsA component of the ATP-driven |FRAME: CPLX-9631 "ArsAB arsenite efflux transporter"| |CITS: [17030823][20361763]|., The arsA gene product is a soluble ATPase subunit, while the arsB product is an integral membrane protein. Even though these two proteins form a complex in |FRAME: TAX-562| that carry the R773 plasmid, in many organisms arsB and arsC are found in an operon without an arsA gene, and in such cases ArsB acts a transporter that is energized by the proton gradient across the membrane, with no requirement for an ArsA component |CITS: [12165430]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Hemes Heme| (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. In addition to its role in oxidative metabolism, heme also functions as a regulatory molecule in transcription, translation, protein targeting, protein stability, and cellular differentiation., Heme is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. Even though it is biosynthesized as |FRAME: Heme-b|, different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., About This Pathway, Until recently it has been accepted that Gram-positive bacteria utilize the same aerobic heme biosynthesis pathway as Gram-negative bacteria, which proceeds via protoporphyrin (see |FRAME: HEME-BIOSYNTHESIS-II|). However, in 2014 it was reported that these organisms utilize a different pathway. In this pathway, |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| is oxidized to |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRIN_III|, and, following the insertion of ferrous iron, the the Fe-coproporphyrin (|FRAME: CPD-17070|) undergoes an oxidative decarboxylation to generate |FRAME: PROTOHEME|. The pathway is the most ancient heme synthesis pathway in the Eubacteria |CITS: [25646457]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "Lipopolysaccharides"| (LPS) are a major outer membrane component of Gram-negative bacteria. Unlike the Gram-positives, which have a thick |FRAME: Peptidoglycans "peptidoglycan"| layer, the Gram-negatives have a single layer of peptidoglycan between the inner and, outer lipid bilayer membranes, but their surface is covered with lipopolysaccharides. The presence of LPS in the outer membrane confers stability to the bacterial membrane, protection against bacteriophages and the action of certain antibiotics, as well as protection against the host defence mechanism during infections., LPS is composed of a lipid moiety (lipid A) that anchors the molecule in the outer membrane, and a polysaccharide moiety that extends out of the cell wall. The polysaccharide moiety is further divided into the core, which is an oligosaccharide consisting of an inner and outer region, and a distal repeating unit known as O-antigen. , The O-specific chain is the part of the LPS that shows the largest variation between species and the part that evokes a specific immune response. Some bacteria do not produce an O-antigen at all (the LPS of these organisms is called rough-type, because these bacteria produce colonies with rough edges when growing on agar plates)., All O-antigens are attached to the core and consist of repeated oligosaccharide units., |FRAME:TAX-562| K12 produces an O-antigen composed of four sugars: glucose, N-acetylglucosamine, galactose and rhamnose.  , This pathway depicts the synthesis of three of these sugars. UDP-galactose is transformed from its pyranose form to its furanose form. dTTP glucose-1-phosphate is derivatized to dTDP-rhamnose. Fructose-6-phosphate gains an amino group,, incorporates an acetate moiety and then acquires a nucleoside diphosphate resulting in UDP-N-acetyl-D-glucosamine., During formation of the repeat unit, the nucleoside diphosphates are removed., The repeat unit is polymerized and attached to the outer core. Formation and polymerization of the O-antigen repeat unit is not shown here |CITS: [7517391] [7512872] [ColiSalII]|.

Summary: General Background, N-linked glycosylation is an important process found in eukaryotes and archaea, and very rarely in bacteria., During this process certain oligosaccharides are attached to asparagine residue in the polypeptide chain of the target protein, which are located in sequons (Asn-X-Ser or Asn-X-Thr). It has been shown that the glycosylation is essential for the proper folding of some proteins., In eukaryotes, most N-linked oligosaccharides derive from a branched 14-residue sugar (tetradecasaccharide) attached to a |FRAME: DOLICHOLP dolichol phosphate|. The structure of this precursor is common to most eukaryotes - animals, plants, most fungi, and even the protist |FRAME:TAX-3039| use this tetradecasaccharide precursor |CITS: [6088086][DeLaCanal][15665075]| (see |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|)., While archaea use different oligosaccharides and somewhat different dolichol carriers, the archaeal pathways are in general similar to the eukaryotic ones, and there is even sequence similarity between some of the eukaryotic, bacterial and arachaeal glycosyltransferases involved in the process |CITS: [9878760]|., About This Pathway, The N-glycosylation pathway described here has been described from the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2246|, and operates to assemble and attach a pentasaccharide to select |FRAME: ASN| residues of target proteins, including the S-layer glycoprotein and archaellins., The glycosylation of Asn-13 of the S-layer glycoprotein, which is the sole component of the (S)-layer surrounding the cells, has been studied in particular during the characterization of the pathway., The S-layer glycoprotein contains seven putative N-glycosylation sites (Asn-Xaa-Ser/Thr sequence motifs, where Xaa is any residue but proline) |CITS: [2123862]|. Several types of glycans have been reported to be attached to some of these glycosylation sites. Early studies reported the presence of linear strings of glucose residues, as well as a second glycan containing glucose, galactose and idose subunits |CITS: [1569073]|. However, more recent analysis tools have shown the presence of a pentasaccharide at Asn-13, the final structure of which was reported only in 2016. The pentasaccharide is composed of a D-glucose, two hexuronic acids (glucuronate and galacturonate, a 4-O-methylated glucuronate, and a final mannose |CITS: [17996897][20149102][20487296][21091511][23086206][26863921]|. , A series of Agl (archaeal glycosylation) proteins has been shown to participate in the assembly and attachment of the oligosaccharide. Some of the genes were identified on the basis of the homology of their protein products with eukaryotic and bacterial N-glycosylation enzymes |CITS: [16762024]|, and additional genes were later identified on the basis of their genomic proximities to the first set of agl genes |CITS: [19251857]|. With the exception of |FRAME: G-44001|, all the agl genes are clustered into a single gene island., Four glycosyltransferase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-43994| |CITS: [20802039]|, |FRAME: G-43995| |CITS: [18631242]|, |FRAME: G-43996| |CITS: [18631242]| and |FRAME: G-43997| |CITS: [18310347]| genes, sequentially transfer the first four residues to an |FRAME: CPD-17858| or |FRAME: CPD-17895| carrier attached to the plasma membrane and facing the cytoplasm |CITS: [21091511]|. An epimerase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58173| gene, must convert the third residue from glucuronate to galacturonate before the 4th residue can be added. A methyltransferase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-43998| gene, methylates the 4th residue |CITS: [20149102][24236216]|., A fifth glycosyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-44001| gene transfers a mannose residue to a second dolichol phosphate carrier |CITS: [17996897]|., Once a tetrasaccharide chain is assembled, the lipid-charged glycans are translocated across the membrane by an unknown mechanism to the extracellular space, where the tetrasaccharide is transferred to a protein receptor by the archeal dolichyl-monophosphooligosaccharide--protein glycotransferase enzyme (unlike the eukaryotic complex, the archaeal enzyme comprises only one type of subunit, encoded by the |FRAME: G-43999| gene) |CITS: [17996897]|. The final step is the transfer of the mannose residue from its carrier to the tetrasaccharide by a mannosyltransferase encoded by |FRAME: G-44000|, forming the final pentapeptide |CITS: [23086206]|.
