Summary: General Background, The neurotransmitter and neuromodulator |FRAME: SEROTONIN| has important roles in the mammalian central nervous system including learning, memory and development. Imbalance of |FRAME: SEROTONIN| levels is associated with a variety of neurological disorders. Although the central nervous system has been the focus of |FRAME: SEROTONIN| research, only a small percentage of total body |FRAME: SEROTONIN| is produced and stored in serotonergic neurons of the central nervous system, where it is released into synapses. Approximately 95% of the |FRAME: SEROTONIN| in humans originates in the enteric nervous system, where it is produced and stored in enterochromaffin cells of the gastrointestinal tract. Upon release it is taken up by platelets and stored in dense granules (in |CITS: [17877637]| and |CITS: [18651566]|). |FRAME: SEROTONIN| in peripheral tissues has important roles in the regulation of many physiological processes. Additionally, a serotonergic system in mammalian skin for the biosyntheis and metabolism of |FRAME: SEROTONIN|, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-SEROTONIN| and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| has also been studied |CITS: [12899690] [14678785]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [18651566] [19264685]| and |CITS: [15677341]|. See pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-7885| is primarily responsible for the oxidative deamination of |FRAME: SEROTONIN| to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYINDOLE_ACETALDEHYDE| although |FRAME: CPLX-33| can function in its absence (in |CITS: [16537538]|). Circulating |FRAME: SEROTONIN| is mostly derived from peripheral tissues and is primarily metabolized in the liver to |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYINDOLE_ACETATE|, which is excreted in the urine. The minor metabolite |FRAME: CPD-11671| is more hydrophobic and is first sulfated, or glucuronidated before urinary excretion (|CITS: [7752817]| and in |CITS: [12231396]|). Low levels of |FRAME: CPD-11665|, produced by phenol (aryl) sulfotransferase (EC 2.8.2.1), have been identified in both the central and enteric nervous systems |CITS: [17877637] [3459671]| and isoforms SULT1A1, SULT1A3 and SULT1C#2 have been shown to sulfate |FRAME: SEROTONIN| |CITS: [17908235]|. |FRAME: CPD-11670| is a condensation product of |FRAME: 5-HYDROXYINDOLE_ACETALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: CYS| that has been shown to form in the central and enteric nervous systems, but does not accumulate presumably due to the action of |FRAME: CPLX66-81| (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2, EC 1.2.1.3) |CITS: [16537538]|. In addition, 7-hydroxylated serotonin may be formed as a result of cellular oxidative stress and subsequently sulfated |CITS: [17908235]| (not shown).

Summary: General Background, The indoleamine |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is a vertebrate hormone secreted by the pineal gland. It is involved in regulation of circadian and seasonal rhythms. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| also has immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. In addition to the pineal gland it is synthesized in many vertebrate cells and tissues (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|). It is ubiquitously present in cells and body fluids due to its amphiphilic properties that allow it to cross membranes. Mitochondria have the highest intracellular concentration of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| |CITS: [15981996]|. Its functional groups allow both specific receptor binding and a role in oxidation chemistry. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also found in invertebrates |CITS: [12662344]|, protozoa |CITS: [12899443]|, plants |CITS: [11485009]|, fungi |CITS: [12662344]| and bacteria |CITS: [9181522]| although its function in many cases remains incompletely defined. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also used as a human dietary supplement. In vertebrates, endogenous or ingested |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is catabolized several ways in different tissues (see below and pathways |FRAME: PWY-6399| and |FRAME: PWY-6400|). Reviewed in |CITS: [16219483] [18344019]|., The enzymatic pathways of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| degradation are shown in this pathway and pathways |FRAME: PWY-6399| and |FRAME: PWY-6400|. Melatonin can also be degraded by nonenzymatic pathways involving melatonin radical species, reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, or ultraviolet B radiation. It can also be degraded by nonenzymatic reactions involving oxoferryl hemoglobin, or hemin. These nonenzymatic reactions are not shown here, but are shown in |CITS: [18344019] [18155917] [17198536] [16793870]|., About This Pathway, The main pathway for degradation of circulating, pineal-derived |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| in humans is via 6-hydroxylation, catalyzed by some isoforms of cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver, or in extrahepatic tissues |CITS: [15616152]|. This compound is then sulfated and excreted in urine (in |CITS: [16793870]|). Some cytochrome P450 enzymes can also catalyze the O-demethylation of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| to |FRAME: N-ACETYL-SEROTONIN| (N-acetyl-5-hydroxytryptamine) which is either sulfated, or glucuronidated, and excreted in urine |CITS: [15616152]|. However this latter pathway is quantitatively more minor than the 6-hydroxylation route. |FRAME: CPD-12014| can also be generated by nonenzymatic means, via reactive oxygen species or reactive nitrogen species (see above, not shown). Both microsomal and mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolize |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| by these two routes |CITS: [18717775]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [18344019] [17198536]|.

Summary: |FRAME: DIHYDROPTERIN-CH2OH-PP| (6-hydroxymethyl-dihydropterin diphosphate) is the pterin precursor for the biosynthesis of several important cofactors, including |FRAME:THF|, |FRAME: CPD-10763| and |FRAME: CPD-10764|., The compound is always synthesized from GTP, but the enzymes involve may differ among organisms., The archaeal pathway differs somewhat from the pathway found in bacteria and eukarya (see |FRAME: PWY-6147|)., The first step of the pathway is catalyzed by the archaeal |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.39|. Unlike the analogous |FRAME: FOLE-CPLX| enzymes found in bacteria, where the product is |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3|, the product of the archaeal enzyme, characterized from |FRAME: TAX-2190|, is |FRAME: CPD-10812| |CITS: [17497938]|. This cyclic phosphate compound is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.56|, which forms a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-13344| and |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P| |CITS: [19746965]|., The phosphate group of these two compounds is then removed by an as-yet unidentified enzyme. Triacyglycerols (TAG) from vegetable oils are a major source of essential fatty acids in human diet, namely polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) linoleate (18:2) and linolenate (18:3). In oilseeds, TAG is synthesized via the |FRAME: TRIGLSYN-PWY "Kennedy pathway"|, where the precursor diacylglycerol (DAG) is de novo synthesized from glycerol-3-phosphate. In addition to the Kennedy pathway, there are several other |FRAME: PWY-6804 "paths"| supplying DAG for TAG biosynthesis during seed development in plants |CITS: [19329563]|. They involve a reverse activity of CDP-choline:1,2-diacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferas, and/or a novel enzyme phosphatidylcholine:diacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase. Since further desaturation of 18:1 to form 18:2 and 18:3 occurs mainly in phosphatidylcholine (PC), these alternative paths can provide PC-derived DAG species which are enriched in PUFA for TAG synthesis. Further more, an acyl editing (acyl exchange) mechanism also exists that can further enrich PUFA in oilseed TAG |CITS: [19329563]|. , Acyl exchange between acyl-CoA and PC has been detected in a number of plant species including microsomal preparations of developing safflower cotyledons |CITS: [6497849]| and developing soybean embryos |CITS: [19329563]|. Further experiments are required to reveal whether a reverse activity of acyl-CoA:lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase (LPCAT, 2.3.1.23) or a phospholipase A (3.1.1.4, 3.1.1.32), or both are involved in acyl-CoA and lysophosphatidylcholine generation |CITS: [19329563]|.  In either case, PC-derived acyl-CoAs, which are rich in PUFA, can feed into the Kennedy pathway for TAG synthesis. Lysophosphatidylcholines can be converted back to PC to replenish the PC pool by the forward reaction of 2.3.1.23. In addition, in the forward reaction de novo synthesized acyl-CoAs can be incorporated into PC.

Summary: General Background, Lipoxins belong to the eicosanoid family, have a distinct conjugated tetraene structure and are generated from |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| during inflammation. They consist of two distinct isomers, |FRAME: CPD66-51| (LXA4) and |FRAME: CPD66-56| (LXB4). These lipid derived mediators play an important role in modulating the inflammatory response. |FRAME: CPD66-51 "Lipoxin A4"| (LXA4) dampens the immune response by inhibiting leukocyte chemotaxis, transmigration and adhesion |CITS: [8326019]||CITS: [2548801]|. It also promotes the resolution phase of inflammation by enhancing phagocytosis of apoptotic leukocytes by macrophages |CITS: [10657608]|. These activities are brought about through the G protein-coupled receptor ALX |CITS: [16968948]|., About this Pathway, There are two routes of lipoxin biosynthesis in humans. One pathway occurs during platelet-leukocyte interactions. When platelet-leukocyte adhesion occurs, leukocyte 5-lipoxygenase converts |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| to |FRAME: CPD-8892| (LTA4) |CITS: [16968948]|. The released LTA4 is then transformed by adherent platelets to LXA4 and LXB4 via the LX synthase activity of 12-lipoxygenase |CITS: [1381961]|. In addition to the lipoxygenase-initiated biosynthesis of lipoxins, a novel aspirin-triggered route involving COX-2 is also present, see |FRAME: PWY66-393|. The biosynthesis of lipoxins leads to a concommitant reduction in leukotriene formation., Another biosynthetic route occurs at mucosal surfaces where |FRAME: HS08621-MONOMER| catalyzes the conversion of arachidonate to 15S-hydroxyleicosatetraenoic acid (15S-HETE) |CITS: [9112289]|. 15S-HETE is taken up by leukocytes and converted to lipoxins. Alveolar macrophages can also synthesize lipoxins via this route |CITS: [8376607]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Factor-420 "Factor 420"| (also known as coenzyme F420, or simply F420) is a redox-active compound well-known for its role in methanogenesis. Although playing a crucial role in methanoarchaeal metabolism, factor 420 has also been found in various eubacteria of the actinobacteria class, such as Streptomyces, Rhodococcus, Nocardioides, and Mycobacterium, where it assists in the synthesis of antibiotics like tetracycline and lincomycin. In addition, a modified form of the cofactor is also used by cyanobacteria in the repair of DNA damage., F420 was first isolated as a cosubstrate involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-19258| in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1960 |CITS: [McCormick82]| (see |FRAME: EC-1.3.98.4|). It is currently known to be involved in the biosynthesis of a number of secondary metabolites |CITS: [8577249]|, the degradation of nitroaromatics |CITS: [10217752]|, and activation of nitroimidazofurans |CITS: [10879539]|. Mycobacterium and Nocardia contain an |FRAME: EC-1.1.98.2 "F420-dependent glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase"| |CITS: [8997717][8631674]|, and an F420-containing photolyase has been discovered in a number of microorganisms |CITS: [2110564]|. However, F420 is best known for its role in methanogenesis (see |FRAME:CPLX-341| and |FRAME:CPLX-323|)., The structure of factor 420 from |FRAME: TAX-145262| was elucidated by Eirich et al, who showed that it was an [N-(N-L-lactyl-γ-L-glutamyl)-L glutamic acid phosphodiester of 7,8-didemethyl-8-hydroxy-5-deazariboflavin] |CITS: [728375]|. That compound contained two glutamate residues, with the terminal glutamate bound through an amide bond to the γ position of the other glutamate. Subsequent work revealed variation in the polyglutamylation of F420 among different organisms, with up to a total of seven γ-linked glutamates, sometimes capped by a terminal α-linked glutamate (see |FRAME:PWY-5199|) |CITS: [12867481]|., Prior to 2019 the pathway was studied only in archaebacteria, and reported to start with |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE|. However, in 2019 it was reported that in mycobacteria the pathway starts with |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| |CITS: [30952857]|. Even though it was suggested at the time that this could apply to all prokaryotes, a later study reported that |FRAME: S-PHOSPHOLACTATE| is a better substrate for the |FRAME: TAX-2190| enzyme than |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, indicating that the pathways may differ among archaea and mycobacteria., The assembly of |FRAME:CPD-10333| (the core F420 molecule with no glutamate side chains) in mycobacteria from |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, |FRAME:AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| and |FRAME:TYR| is a complicated process that requires five steps. In one route |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-22326|. In a parallel route |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| and |FRAME:TYR| are combined to form |FRAME: CPD-7602|. The products of the two branches, |FRAME:CPD-22326| and |FRAME: CPD-7602| are combined, generating |FRAME: CPD-22327|, which is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-10333| |CITS: [30952857]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons across a membrane., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons on one side of a membrane, or produce them on the other side of the membrane, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Several NAD molecules are reduced to NADH in the glycolytic and TCA cycles. These energy-rich molecules have a pair of electrons with high transfer potential. The transfer of the electrons is performed by a series of four large electron carriers complexes also known as complex I-IV (electron transport chain or respiratory chain), present in the inner mitochondrial membrane of plants and mammals (see |FRAME:PWY-3781|). In general, the oxidation of |FRAME:NADH| results in an electron flow and causes protons to be pumped from the matrix side to the intermembrane space. As a result a proton-motive force (PMF) composed of a pH gradient and a membrane potential is generated. This PMF causes protons to flow back through the ATP-synthesizing complex of the energized mitochondrial membrane synthesizing |FRAME:ATP| in the process. |CITS: [DEY97]|., In contrast to the aerobic respiration of plants and animals (see |FRAME:PWY-3781|) |FRAME:TAX-4932| has no complex I and realizes the oxidation of |FRAME:NADH| and the resulting electron flow into the mitochiondrial electron chain via three NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductases (NDI1, NDE1, NDE2) |CITS:[16706641] [11798023] [12961751]|. The internal NAD:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (NDI1) of the inner mitochondrial membrane facing the matrix side in concert with the two external NAD:ubiquinone oxidoreductases (NDE1, NDE2) |CITS:[9733747] [9696750] [10781551] [12032156]| of the inner mitochondrial membrane facing the intermembrane space is involved in the re-oxidation of cytosolic |FRAME:NADH|. From those three ubiquinone reductases the yeast NDI1 enzyme is the functional equivalent of complex I and represents the key entry point into the respiratory chain |CITS:[23086143] [1900238] [1735444] [3138118]|., The succinate dehydrogenase (SDH - complex II) is an enzyme that consists of 4 subunits which catalyze the sequential electron transport via the oxidation of |FRAME:SUC| to |FRAME:FUM| and reversible redox reactions coupled to a ubiquinone/ubiquinol pair into the transpiration chain. Two of the subunits (SDH1,SDH2) form a catalytic dimer containing the active site, bound FAD and three iron-sulfur clusters whereas the two other subunits (SDH3, SDH4) are integral membrane proteins which provide anchor and channel for complex II and constitute the ubiquinone reduction site |CITS:[13445213] [11803020]|. , Complex III of the respiratory chain, also referred to as cytochrome b-c1 complex, mediates the electron transfer from ubiquinol to cytochrome c. The ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase of |FRAME:TAX-4930| consists of 13 subunits, 2 core and 5 lower molecular weight proteins and represents one of the so-called supercomplexes of the respiratory chain |CITS:[11798023] [22564912]|. The multi-subunit complex of the ubiquinol-cytochrome c oxidoreductase couples the electron transfer to the translocation of protons across the membrane, hence, contributing substantially to the creation of the proton motive force which drives the |FRAME:ATP| formation of the oxidative phosphorylation |CITS:[18501197] [18038116]|. , Cytochrome c oxidase is on the receiving end of the electrons transferred from complex III. In |FRAME:TAX-4930| as in mammalian the cytochrome c oxidase is, under aerobic conditions, the terminal oxidase in the respiratory chain that catalyzes the transfer of the electrons to oxygen to form water. Again, the transfer of the electrons is connected to the transport of protons across the membrane adding to the PMF building up on the mitochondrial membrane |CITS:[21925484] [7851399]|. Cytochrome c oxidase of |FRAME:TAX-4932| has been shown to be composed of 11 subunits forming a transmembrane multi-subunit enzyme that acts as a electron vehicle between complex III and complex IV |CITS:[2164355] [1665335]|. In yeast cytochrome c can also be reduced by the lactate-cytochrome c oxidoreductase (CYB2) localized in the mitochondrial intermembrane space, however, possible functional implementations for a role in the respiratory chain remain to be determined |CITS:[6290489]|.

Summary: An Arabidopsis cytochrome P450, CYP77A4, was shown to catalyze expoxidation of free fatty acids, the first one of its kind characterized in plants |CITS: [19120447]|. The epoxides can be further metabolized by epoxide hydrolases and fatty acid hydroxylases to diols and poly-hydroxy fatty acids. Some of the derived metabolites are cutin monomers, i.e. 18-hydroxy-9,10-epoxystearate (see |FRAME: PWY-321|), some others have antifungal properties possibly involved in plant defense, i.e. 12,13,17-trihydroxyoctadeca-9-enoate |CITS: [Hou2000]|.

General Background, Betaxanthins represent a subclass of betalains, the nitrogen-containing compounds , that replace the anthocyanins in the order of Caryophyllales and some higher fungi |CITS: [12620337]| |CITS: [16212790]|. , These pigments are biosynthesized by the condensation of betalamic acid (|FRAME:PWY-5394|) and amino acids/amines , forming a Schiff-base that causes the yellow to orange colors (λ max 470-486 nm) , |CITS: [Christinet04]|., About This Pathway, It has been demonstrated that the conjugation of a broad variety of amino acids , (see |FRAME:PWY-5404|) and amino acid derivatives (e.g. 3-methoxytyramine - this pathway) with betalamic acid , results in the corresponding betaxanthins |CITS: [TREZZINI91]|. This condensation is the decisive step in the , biosynthesis of betaxanthins and has been established as a non-enzymatic reaction |CITS: [10198080]|. , The only exception of this general reaction pattern is the formation of vulgaxanthin II, the condensation product of , glutamate and betalamic acid |CITS: [HEMPEL97]|. Despite the feeding of glutamate vulgaxanthin II is only produced , in traces, instead the biosynthesis of vulgaxanthin I (glutamine as amino acid moiety) is favored. This finding has , been explained with the high metabolism of glutamate in other pathways and the suitability of the amino acid as , reaction partner, which however does not contradict the spontaneous condensation itself |CITS: [15231409]|., The first enzymatic step in the pathway is the decarboxylation of aromatic amino acids such, as tyrosine or DOPA , to form the corresponding amines tyramine and dopamine, respectively. An enzyme,, |FRAME: MONOMER-8382| (TYDC), capable of, catalyzing this reaction has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3469|, |CITS: [7929401]| |CITS: [12242361]| and its molecular , function has been confirmed by heterologous expression in |FRAME:TAX-562|. But, no comparable enzyme, has been characterized within the |FRAME:TAX-3568| to date. The catechol methyltransferase forming 3-methoxytyramine has , not yet been identified in plants and the crucial step finalizing the formation of the individual, betaxanthin occurs spontaneously as described above.

Summary: |FRAME: MET| (met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in proteins, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines., In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., This superpathway describes the biosynthesis of the amino acid |FRAME: MET| via the transsulfuration pathway., |FRAME:HOMO-SER| is biosynthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which is synthesized from |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|, a TCA cycle intermediate. Homoserine is then activated through esterification to form the O-succinyl ester. In the next step, the enzyme |FRAME:O-SUCCHOMOSERLYASE-ENZRXN| catalyzes a transsulfuration of |FRAME:O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE| with |FRAME:CYS| forming |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE|,, which is then cleaved to |FRAME:HOMO-CYS| and methylated to |FRAME: MET| |CITS: [3309561]|. The methylation can be catalyzed by either a cobalamin-independent enzyme or a cobalamin-dependent enzyme, depending upon the species and growth conditions |CITS: [12948640][9409150]|., The other route of microbial methionine biosynthesis involves the use of inorganic sulfur via sulfhydrylation of |FRAME:CPD-667| with |FRAME: HS|, forming |FRAME:HOMO-CYS| which is methylated to |FRAME: MET| (see |FRAME:PWY-5345|)., The O-acyl group of homoserine is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast and most Gram positive bacteria, or a succinyl group in enteric bacteria, as well as |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS:[10482527][3309561][9409150]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: QUINATE| is a naturally occuring compound found in decaying plant matter |CITS: [8126417]|., Quinate is one of several aromatic compounds that can be metabolized by microorganisms to the, central intermediate |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| that can be further metabolized via the β-ketoadipate pathway to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA |CITS: [Tresguerres70][14586099]|. Bacteria capable of using quinate as a sole carbon source were observed as early as 1911 |CITS: [Beijerinck11]|, Quinate degradation was initially studied in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [16589471]|, and later in other fungi (such as |FRAME: TAX-162425| |CITS: [3916726]|) and bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-62977| (at the time reported as |FRAME: TAX-471|) |CITS: [7592351][8002591]|, |FRAME: TAX-442| |CITS: [14586099]| and |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [18566515]|.| Many of these organisms can grow on quinate as a sole carbon and energy source, and the pathway is inducible by growth on either |FRAME: QUINATE|, |FRAME: SHIKIMATE|, or |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|., Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the main difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of |FRAME: QUINATE|. Filamentous fungi and Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: QUINATE-5-DEHYDROGENASE-RXN "EC 1.1.1.24"|), while Gram-negative bacteria use a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: 1.1.99.25-RXN "EC 1.1.99.25"|) |CITS: [3044290]|. The former pathway is desribed in |FRAME: PWY-6416|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-62977| and |FRAME: TAX-442|, |FRAME: MONOMER-28| is a membrane-associated enzyme that uses |FRAME: PQQ| as an electron acceptor. It is bifunctional , and can use either |FRAME: QUINATE| or |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| as a substrate |CITS: [14586098][15598527]|., The |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| formed by this enzyme is dehydrated to |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE|. This enzymatic reaction is also a part of the biosynthetic pathway known as the shikimate pathway, which forms chorismate (see |FRAME: ARO-PWY| and |FRAME: ALL-CHORISMATE-PWY|). Two different types of 3-dehydroquinate dehydratase enzymes are known. The type I enzymes (encoded by genes similar to |FRAME: EG10076|) have been found to participate only in the biosynthetic pathways. Type II enzymes, on the other hand, have been found to take part in either the biosynthetic pathway or in the catabolic pathways |CITS: [1554351]|., Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1814|, possess a single type II enzyme that participates in both the catabolic and the biosynthetic pathways |CITS: [1479361]|., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-442| the biosynthetic enzyme is cytoplasmic, while the |FRAME: MONOMER-0 "catabolic enzyme"| is located in the periplasm |CITS: [18540103]|., |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE| is subjected to a second dehydration reaction, forming |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-37|. The |FRAME: G-36| gene encoding this enzyme was found following the |FRAME: G-32| gene (which encodes |FRAME: MONOMER-33|) within a single operon |CITS: [7592351]|. The gene is not common, and has only been found in members of the |FRAME: TAX-469| genus and potentially a few strains of |FRAME: TAX-303|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lignins "Lignin"| is the most abundant aromatic compound in nature, and its mineralization is an important step in the terrestrial carbon cycle. Lignin is broken down to various biaryl and monoaryl compounds such as |FRAME: BIPHENYL|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|., Complex lignin is resistant to bacterial enzymes. Its degradation is initiated by white rot fungi, which secrete extracellular degradation enzymes such as |FRAME: MONOMER-14338 "lignin peroxidase"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14335 "manganese peroxidase"|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14334 "laccase"| |CITS: [8246842]|. The resulting low-molecular-weight lignin can be further degraded and mineralized by bacteria |CITS: [1785937]|., |FRAME: TAX-502559| is able to grow on many of these compounds as the sole sources of carbon and energy. It degrades lignin-derived compounds possessing guaiacyl (4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl) and syringyl (4-hydroxy-3,5-dimethoxyphenyl) moieties to |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|, respectively, and is able to completely mineralize these two compounds as described in the |FRAME: PWY-6338| and |FRAME: PWY-6339| pathways., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-8486 "Syringate"| degradation begins with its conversion to |FRAME: CPD-721| by the tetrahydrofolate-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-15114| (encoded by |FRAME: G-11549|) |CITS: [15090517]|., |FRAME: CPD-721| can be degraded further via three different routes that converge back at |FRAME: CPD-12849|., The main route, via |FRAME: CPD-183| , is catalyzed by two enzymes - a second tetrahydrofolate-dependent demethylase, |FRAME: MONOMER-15113| (|FRAME: G-11548|), and |FRAME: CPLX-7918| (|FRAME: G-11555|) |CITS: [16030198]|., The other two routes are the result of direct dioxygenation of |FRAME: CPD-721|. This reaction is carried out by two dioxygenases - |FRAME: CPLX-7916| (|FRAME: G-11551| and |FRAME: G-11552|) and |FRAME: MONOMER-15115| (|FRAME: G-11550|), both of which produce a mixture of two different products - |FRAME: CPD-184| (PDC) and |FRAME: CPD-11853| (CHMOD) |CITS: [17645527]|., The first product is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-3467| (|FRAME: G-2546|) to |FRAME: 4-OXALOMESACONATE|, which is tautomerized into |FRAME: CPD-12849| |CITS: [9864312][21219457]|. The second product is converted to |FRAME: CPD-12849| by the combined action of |FRAME: MONOMER-21875| (DesC) and |FRAME: MONOMER-21876| (DesD) |CITS: [30217841]|., |FRAME: CPD-12849| is degraded into TCA cycle intermediates by the action of two additional enzymes - |FRAME: CPLX-2864| (|FRAME: G-2547|) and |FRAME:CPLX-2865| (|FRAME: G-2549|) |CITS: [11092855][12486039]|.

Summary: About 20% of the |FRAME: MET| pool is used as a building block of proteins. The rest is converted to, |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), the major methyl donor in the cell., When SAM donates its methyl group, it is converted to |FRAME: ADENOSYL-HOMO-CYS|. This molecule can be, recycled back to SAM via the S-adenosyl-L-methionine cycle, also known as the activated methyl cycle (AMC)., There are two main variations of this pathway, one found mostly in prokaryotes, while the other is found predominantly, but not exclusively, in eukaryotes (for example, it operates in |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [18815415]|. The main difference between the variants is the processing of |FRAME: ADENOSYL-HOMO-CYS| (SAH), the immediate product of the methylation reactions., In the first pathway (described in |FRAME: PWY-6151|) SAH is first hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-564| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.9|, followed by conversion to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.21|. In the second pathway, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-5041|, SAH is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| in a single step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.13.2.1|., The cycle continues with the methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| to |FRAME: MET| using a methyl group from a methylated folate. In some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-9606|, this reaction is catalyzed by a |FRAME: HOMOCYSMETB12-MONOMER| (EC 2.1.1.13). In other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, the reaction is catalyzed by a |FRAME: G18NG-10711-MONOMER| (EC 2.1.1.14). Yet some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, have both enzymes, as described in the pathway |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|. In |FRAME: TAX-562| the reaction catalyzed by the B12-dependent enzyme is more than 100-fold faster than the reaction catalyzed by the B12-independent isoenzyme |CITS: [15215334]|., Finally, the cycle is completed with the regeneration of SAM by |FRAME: CPLX-7754|., About |FRAME: CPLX-5161|: While the reaction catalyzed by this enzyme is reversible, the equilibrium favors the synthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYL-HOMO-CYS|. Thus the removal of the hydrolysis product |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is critical for the continuous operation of the cycle. This is achieved by the efficient conversion of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| to |FRAME: MET| via |FRAME: AT5G17920-MONOMER|.

Summary: |FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053| (ginseng). They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng., Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|., Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to., The pharmacological activities of various ginsenosides include cardio-protective, immuno-modulatory, anti-fatigue, antitumour and hepato-protective effects |CITS: [Yue05]|. Ginsenosides are produced in the roots of |FRAME: TAX-4054| |CITS: [LUO05]|, and various types of ginsenosides accumulate as the plant ages |CITS: [15356323]|., The different ginsenoside backbones are synthesized by different forms of cyclization of |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE|, catalyzed by specific enzymes |CITS: [15356323]|. The triterpene backbones then undergo various modifications, such as oxidation, substitution, and glycosylation to give the characteristic ginsenosides., The chemical synthesis of ginsenosides has not been feasible. Recent discoveries of the enzymes involved lead the way to biosynthesis using recombinant technology |CITS: [26032089]|.

Genetral Background, In gram-positive bacteria, the ε-amino group of L-lysine in the pentapeptide stem of peptidoglycan precursors is often replaced by amino acid chains of various lengths and compositions., During the cross-linking of the peptide stems of nascent chains of peptidoglycan these amino acids form cross bridges, between L-Lys3 of one glycan thread and D-Ala4 of another thread |CITS: [4568761]|., In enterococci, streptococci, and staphylococci, the enzymes that add the bridge amino acids are membrane-associated, and act on late peptidoglycan precursors that are already linked to the undecaprenyl-phosphate lipid carrier |CITS: [5218655]|., Two types of enzymes catalyze the addition of the cross-bridge amino acids. |FRAME: GLY| and L-amino acids are added by a special type of non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) that use charged aminoacyl tRNAs as substrates. D-amino acids, on the other hand, are added in tRNA-independent reactions |CITS: [4248526][4262567]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME:TAX-1280| the crosslinks includes an interpeptide bridge of five |FRAME:GLY| residues. The five glycines are added to lipid II by three enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-11836|, |FRAME: G-11837| and |FRAME: G-11839|, and are donated by charged |FRAME: Charged-GLY-tRNAs| molecules |CITS: [15228543]|. , The first enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-11836|, catalyzes the transfer of |FRAME: GLY| from a charged |FRAME: Charged-GLY-tRNAs| to |FRAME: CPD-7695| (lipid II), attaching it to the ε position of the |FRAME: LYS| at position 3 of the pentapeptide. , The second enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-11837|, catalyzes the sequential transfer of two |FRAME: GLY| moieties from charged |FRAME: Charged-GLY-tRNAs|, attaching them to the glycine that was previously attached by |FRAME: MONOMER-15452 "FemX"|. The last enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-11839|, catalyzes the transfer of the last two |FRAME: GLY| moieties., FemA and FemB are very similar, but FemA adds only glycine residues 2 and 3, whereas FemB transfers glycine residues 4 and 5 exclusively |CITS: [9393725]|., The crosslinks are formed between the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide and the amino group at the end of the pentaglycine bridge of a second glycan chain.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (vitamin C, ascorbic acid) is a reducing agent and water-soluble antioxidant. It can be biosynthesized by plants (see |FRAME: PWY-882|), some bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-5521|) and many, but not all, vertebrates (see |FRAME: PWY3DJ-35471|). It is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries (reviewed in |CITS:[17222174]|)., |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it (some fish and birds, bats and guinea pigs). These species rely on mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin. It is taken up in the intestine, transported in plasma and delivered to tissues. It has roles in collagen biosynthesis, as an antioxidant, as a cofactor in reactions catalyzed by some metal-dependent mono- and dioxygenases, and may be involved in cell signaling reactions and transcription factor activation. A deficiency of ascorbate leads to the disorder scurvy (reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|., About This Pathway, The anionic form of L-ascorbic acid, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, is predominantly present at physiological pH |CITS: [SHASKUS84]|. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is actively transported into cells via the |FRAME: NA+|-dependent cotransporters SVCT1 and SVCT2 (not shown) and used as an antioxidant. It reduces various oxidized substrates and produces the oxidized product |FRAME: CPD-318| and a reduced substrate. This is represented in this pathway by the general reaction |FRAME: RXN-10981|. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is also used as an enzyme cofactor for |FRAME: CU+2|-dependent monooxygenases (such as EC 1.14.17.3 and EC 1.14.17.1) and |FRAME: FE+2|-dependent dioxygenases (such as EC 1.13.11.27 and EC 1.14.11.1) which leads to its one-electron oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-318| (semidehydroascorbate) (reviewed in |CITS: [17222174] [11028916]|). Two molecules of |FRAME: CPD-318| spontaneously form one molecule of |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| and one molecule of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| in a disproportionation reaction, as shown in this pathway (|FRAME: RXN-3523|) |CITS: [11020669]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|. , Several enzyme systems described below can reduce |FRAME: CPD-318| and |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| back to |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. The mechanisms used appear to depend upon the cell type, with the erythrocyte being well-studied |CITS: [11687303]|. |FRAME: CPD-318| is considered to be the quantitatively most important oxidation product of |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. Cellular compartments involved in ascorbate recycling include the cytosol (this pathway), secretory vesicles, the mitochondrion and the extracellular space. Membrane transporters and membrane electron transfer systems are also involved (as discussed below). Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|., Reduction of cytosolic |FRAME: CPD-318| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| in a one-electron step may involve the participation of either of two enzymes that have |FRAME: CPD-318| reductase activity: NADH cytochrome b5 reductase EC 1.6.2.2 (of the mitochondrial outer membrane), or |FRAME: CPLX-7940| EC 1.8.1.9. Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|., Intracellular |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| is formed by either spontaneous disproportionation of |FRAME: CPD-318|, or by its facilitative transport into the cell. Transport occurs via glucose transporters, driven by intracellular reduction of |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|., Intracellular reduction of |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| in a two-electron step can be catalyzed by five different enzymes that have |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent, or |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|-dependent |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| reductase activity: |FRAME: HS04268-MONOMER| (glutaredoxin) EC 1.8.5.1, |FRAME: CPLX-7941| EC 5.3.4.1, |FRAME: CPLX-6081| (omega class glutathione transferase) EC 2.5.1.18, |FRAME: MONOMER-14305| EC 1.1.1.213, or |FRAME: CPLX-7940| EC 1.8.1.9. |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE| can also be reduced by spontaneous reaction with |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| presumably via adduct formation (not shown in this pathway), but this is thought to be slow at physiological concentrations of |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|., In the lumen of secretory vesicles, trans-membrane electron transfer systems (not shown in this pathway) can reduce |FRAME: CPD-318| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. In the lumen of neuroendocrine secretory vesicles reduction of vesicular |FRAME: CPD-318| uses electrons from cytosolic |FRAME: ASCORBATE| and a cytochrome b561-mediated trans-membrane electron transfer system that is thermodynamically driven by a pH gradient and membrane potential created by a proton-translocating membrane ATPase. Reduction of |FRAME: CPD-318| produced by peptidylglycine monooxygenase (EC 1.14.17.3), or |FRAME: CPLX66-141| (EC 1.14.17.1) can occur in this manner. Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174] [16301310]|., In the extracellular space, trans-membrane electron transfer systems (not shown in this pathway) can also reduce |FRAME: CPD-318| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. Intracellular |FRAME: ASCORBATE| donates electrons to extracellular |FRAME: CPD-318| via an as yet unidentified membrane redox system. Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174] [16301310]|. Mitochondria have also been shown to take up and recycle |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [11368176] [18198400]|., The catabolism of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has been described for bacteria (see pathway |FRAME: PWY0-301|), but it remains poorly defined in mammals (reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|).

Summary: |FRAME: LEU Leucine| biosynthesis involves a five-step conversion process starting with the valine precursor |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|., In |FRAME: TAX-562| both the first enzyme in the pathway (LeuA) and the terminal one (TyrB) are suppressed by leucine. TyrB is subject to inhibition by the pathway's starting compound, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, and by one of its off-pathway products, |FRAME: TYR|. One consequence of this inhibition by |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| is that in the absence of IlvE activity, mutations in earlier steps in the pathway cannot be compensated for by any alternate method of introducing |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| for conversion to |FRAME: LEU|., In |FRAME: TAX-562| almost all of the genes coding for enzymes in this pathway are controlled by attenuation. Attenuation in operon |FRAME: TU00179| is effected by a leader region containing four leucines and a transcriptional terminator |CITS: [6171647][6195343]|. ilvE is a component of operon |FRAME: TU524|, that has an attenuation region containing codons for isoleucine, leucine, and valine, as well as a termination site |CITS: [6154938][2007556]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: GLY Glycine|, biosynthesized from glycolytic intermediates via |FRAME: SER| (using |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, or |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| in reverse direction), is converted to |FRAME: CREATINE| by amidino group transfer from |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: GLY| to form |FRAME: GUANIDOACETIC_ACID|, followed by methyl group transfer from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: GUANIDOACETIC_ACID|. |FRAME: CREATINE Creatine| is then phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.3.2|, to create a pool of |FRAME: CREATINE-P| (phosphocreatine, phosphoryl-creatine), as shown in the pathway link. The |FRAME: CREATINE-P| pool stores energy for the replenishment of |FRAME: ATP| during periods of high energy demand. Phosphagen kinase systems such as this are found in the tissues of most vertebrates (reviewed in |CITS: [5071177][10893433]|). Although this pathway does not occur naturally in lower eukaryotes, |FRAME:TAX-4932| has been metabolically engineered to produce intracellular creatine using human |FRAME: EC-2.1.4.1| and rat |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.2|. Co-expression of chicken creatine kinase created a phosphagen kinase system in this organism |CITS: [12036963]|., In mammals, the main route of |FRAME: CREATINE| biosynthesis involves |FRAME: GUANIDOACETIC_ACID| formation in the kidney. It is transported into the blood and methylated to |FRAME: CREATINE| in the liver. It is again transported in the blood and taken up and concentrated in tissues that contain high creatine kinase activity, such as muscle and nerve tissue. Uptake occurs via a specific, Na+-dependent creatine transporter system |CITS: [3422462] [18652074] [14977199]|. However, both of the enzymes involved in this pathway have been detected in other tissues, and the relative contribution of other tissues to total creatine biosynthesis, as well as the significance of inter-tissue transport, remains to be defined. Species differences in tissue distribution of these enzymes have also been reported. Reviewed in |CITS: [10893433]|., In vivo, |FRAME: CREATINE| can undergo spontaneous, irreversible, nonenzymatic cyclization to |FRAME: CREATININE|, which is excreted in urine. In vitro however, this reaction is reversible in a pH and temperature-dependent manner. Reviewed in |CITS: [10893433]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-4682| catalyzes the rate-limiting step. This enzyme is regulated by , competitive inhibition of its product, |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| |CITS: [7378422]|, as well as regulation at the pre-translational level (reviewed in |CITS: [10893433]|). The pathway is significant not only for its importance in energy production, but also human disorders of creatine metabolism result from mutations in the genes encoding arginine:glycine amidinotransferase (AGAT) |CITS: [11555793]|, guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) |CITS: [8651275]| and the creatine transporter (SLC6A8) |CITS: [11326334]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for O antigen synthesis are often present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The lipid A-core oligosaccharide and the O-antigens are synthesized in the cytoplasm, exported to the periplasm, and combined by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS00350-MONOMER|, forming lipopolysaccharides (LPS) attached to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane. The LPS are then transferred from the inner membrane to the outer membrane and through it, remaining attached to outer leaflet of the outer membrane., The Lpt system responsible for transporting lipopolysaccharides from the inner membrane to the outer membrane has been characterized from multiple bacterial species. It usually consists of six or seven Lpt proteins - LptA through LptF. Together these proteins form a transenvelope bridge that transports LPS from the inner membrane, across the periplasm to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane., In |FRAME: TAX-1125722| only three orthologs are found - |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS06310|, |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS00115|, and |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS00035|. As the system hasn't been studied, it is not known whether the missing members are encoded by divergent genes, or whether a different system operates in this organism.

Summary: Free |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| and its derivatives are toxic to plants even at low concentrations |CITS:[ORDIN57]|. This has been shown to be due to the inhibition of glucose incorporation into cellulose, which in turn results in an inhibition of elongation and growth., The molecular basis of galactose toxicity is unclear. Feeding inhibitory concentrations of external galactose to intact roots is linked to an increase in |FRAME: GALACTOSE-1P| but a decrease of |FRAME: CPD-14553|. It was shown that galactose-1-phosphate can act as a competitive inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.9|, thereby inhibiting the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12575|, a precursor of |FRAME: CELLULOSE cellulose| biosynthesis (note that it was subsequently argued that the concentration of galactose-1-phosphate used in the experiment is unlikely to be physiological |CITS:[9225860]|., Other studies using galactose-resistant cell lines proposed that |FRAME: CPD-14553| is the main toxic metabolite (resistant lines were characterized by increased levels of |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.2|) |CITS:[MARETZKI78]|. Irrespective of the exact mode of toxicity, plants must exercise a tight control over the levels of free galactose and its phosphorylated derivatives. Although galactose degradation is often understood to occur via the transfer of the UDP moiety of |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: GALACTOSE-1P| to form |FRAME: CPD-14553| (Leloir pathway, see |FRAME: PWY-6317|), the degradation of galactose has also been shown to occur in plants via the conversion of |FRAME: GALACTOSE-1P| to |FRAME: CPD-14553| by an uridyltransferase, using UTP as uridine diphosphate source. The uridylation of |FRAME: GALACTOSE-1P| is followed by the epimerization of |FRAME: CPD-14553| into |FRAME: CPD-12575|, which is thought to play a central role as 'branch point' metabolite (formation of glucose-1-phosphate for energy needs, synthesis of transportable sucrose, or cell-wall synthesis in developing seedlings).

Guanosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: GMP| (GMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| (XMP) , which is converted to GMP by the action of, |FRAME: GMP-SYN-CPLX|, an enzyme that can use either glutamine or ammonia as substrate (see |FRAME: PWY-6125|). Note that the free base |FRAME: GUANINE| or the ribonucleoside |FRAME: GUANOSINE| are not produced via the de novo pathway., Many organisms can also recycle guanosine nucleotides by a combination of degradation and salvage pathways. The degradation pathway is responsible for the degradation of the nucleotides to the nucleoside |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and the base |FRAME: GUANINE|, which can be further degraded via |FRAME: XANTHINE| and |FRAME: URATE|, and eventually catabolized to basic building blocks (see |FRAME: PWY-6595|)., However, both |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: GUANINE| can be salvaged by certain enzymes, and be converted back to nucleotide form., The enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-322| (EC 2.7.1.73), which has been studied in |FRAME:TAX-562|, can phosphorylate |FRAME: GUANOSINE| directly to the mono-nucleotide |FRAME: GMP|. Even though genes encoding this enzyme have been identified only in bacteria and archaea |CITS: [10879466]|, this activity has also been reported for artichoke, |FRAME: TAX-4233| |CITS: [Combes89]|., Other routes from |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME: GMP| are described in |FRAME: PWY-6620| and |FRAME: PWY-6599|., Either of these routes enables the organism to salvage the degradation products of guanosine nucleotides, and recycle them back to nucleotide form.

The siderophores |FRAME:CPD0-2241| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-17185| (see |FRAME:PWY-7571|) are microbial low molecular weight iron chelators employed for mobilization and storage of this metal which are formed under conditions of iron stress |CITS:[6455965] [17804665]|. Due to its insolubility at neutral pH the bioavailability of iron is rather restricted |CITS:[9444771]| but |FRAME:CPD0-2241| with its three hydroxamic acid groups in the side chains has been shown to efficiently capture and realize the transmembrane transport of the ferric ions |CITS:[5580666]|. |FRAME: TAX-5270|, the pathogen causing corn smut disease |CITS:[19400641]|, is able to produce both siderophores |CITS:[2531844]| and has been used as model organism to study the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17185| and |FRAME:CPD0-2241| and their proposed contribution to the virulence of the fungi |CITS:[12759789] [18680426]|., In contrast to the very similar |FRAME:CPD-17185| which comprises 2 molecules |FRAME:SER| and 1 molecule |FRAME:GLY|, |FRAME:CPD0-2241| utilizes 3 molecules |FRAME:GLY| and requires a different |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| precursor which is not only hydroxylated at N5 but also acylated at this position |CITS:[5058697]|. While the formation of |FRAME:CPD-11571| by the L-ornithine 5-monooxygenase encoded by Sid1 |CITS:[8430103] [2523381]| is a shared step for both |FRAME:CPD-17185| and |FRAME:CPD0-2241| pathways the formation of |FRAME:CPD-12101| marks the branch in the pathway where |FRAME:PWY-7577| deviates from |FRAME:PWY-7571| |CITS:[5058697]|., The following and final reaction of the pathway, the formation of |FRAME:CPD0-2241|, is catalyzed by the ferrichrome synthetase, a nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS), encoded by Sid2 and located in the ferrichrome biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS:[11395469]|. The genetic structure of Sid2 revealed the existence of three iterated modules of which only two may be involved in the iterative binding and processing of the amino acid |FRAME:GLY| and |FRAME:CPD-12101| finally releasing |FRAME:CPD0-2241|. The third module of the might be involved in hydroxylation and acylation processes which however remain to be shown in further experiments. The proposal for the existence of an multienzyme/multidomain complex had come from investigations on the ferrichrome synthetase from Aspergillus quadricinctus where the synthetase activity could be separated from the transacylation activity generating |FRAME:CPD-12101| of the apparently same enzyme |CITS:[7213752] [1986785]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17869 Tryptoquialanine| belongs to a group of mycotoxins with tremorgenic properties interfering with the central nervous system (CNS) of vertebrates |CITS:[Cole81]|. Tremorgenic compounds are classified into three different categories which reflect structural features, i.e. indole-diterpenoids (for example |FRAME:CPD-17202| see |FRAME:PWY-7572|), prenylated indolediketopiperazines (for example |FRAME:CPD-15261| - see |FRAME:PWY-7526| and |FRAME:CPD-15266| - see |FRAME:PWY-7525|), and quinazoline-containing indole alkaloids, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-17869| (this pathway) |CITS:[3912307]|. The latter compound, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17869| has been found in both Penicillium and Aspergillus species |CITS:[1133368] [12381117] [Frisvad04]|. The exact mode of action of tremorgens still remains to be elucidated but it has been shown that tremorgenic indole alkaloids inhibit high-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels which may interfere with neurotransmitter release on neuronal synapses |CITS:[7514038]|., |FRAME:CPD-17869 Tryptoquialanine| is characterized by an acylated quinazoline ring which, through a 5-membered spirolactone ring, is connected to a 6-5-5 imidazoindolone ring. The multicyclic ring scaffolds which form the skeleton of such complex compounds are usually assembled by non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) and post assembly tailoring enzymes modifying the nascent molecule |CITS:[17653357] [23659680]|. Utilizing the adenylation (A) domain of the two-modular non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NPRS) encoded by AnaPS from Neosartorya fischeri as probe (see |FRAME:PWY-7532|), which also served to identify the fumiquinazoline F synthetase from Aspergillus fumigatus in the |FRAME:PWY-7542| |CITS:[21899262]|, allowed the identification of the NPRS encoded by TqaA and localization and boundaries of the gene cluster (tqa) involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17869| |CITS:[21299212]|. , The NRPS encoded by TqaA was investigated in more detail using recombinant purified protein and shown to be suffice for catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16968|, a shared intermediate of both |FRAME:PWY-7542| and |FRAME:PWY-7660| (this pathway) |CITS:[22902615]|. The following reactions, i.e. the stereospecific C-3'-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-16968| by the TqaH encoded fumiquinazoline F monooxygenase and stereospecific incorporation of |FRAME:CPD-17880| by TqaB, a one module NRPS, determined the stereochemistry at C-2' (product |FRAME:CPD-17884|) which is opposite to the product observed in |FRAME:PWY-7542|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16970| |CITS:[21591693]|. The remaining steps of the pathways and respective genes and catalyzing enzymes, i.e. the 15-dimethyl-2-epi-fumiquinazoline A oxidase (TqaG), the TqaI encoded deoxynortryptoquialanone lactonohydrolase (a step which also may occur spontaneously), the deoxynortryptoquialanone monooxygenase encoded by TqaE, the tryptoquialanone dehydrogenase (TqaC) and the TqaD encoded tryptoquialanol O-acetyltransferase have been determined by consecutive knocking out genes and metabolic profiling of the resulting mutants |CITS:[21299212]|.

General Background, |FRAME: TAURINE Taurine| is a sulfonated amino acid. The name comes from Taurus (Latin for bull), as it was first isolated from ox bile. It is found in high abundance in the tissues of many animals (especially sea animals) and, in lesser abundance, in plants, fungi, and some bacterial species., Taurine plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many species. The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis. The roles of taurine on other organisms is less well studied, but it is known to be important in bile acid conjugation in sauropsids (only taurine conjugates are found in chicken bile) |CITS: [7306052]|., Taurine is produced from |FRAME: CYS| in multiple pathways. Two pathways have been described in mammals: the "cysteinesulfinate pathway" (see |FRAME: PWY-5331|), which proceeds via |FRAME: 3-SULFINOALANINE| and |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| |CITS: [4297098]|, and the "cysteamine pathway" (see |FRAME: PWY-7850|), which proceeds via |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE|, |FRAME: CPD-239|, and |FRAME: HYPOTAURINE| |CITS: [Cavallini76][Scandurra78]|. A third pathway that involves |FRAME: SO3| (see |FRAME: PWY-8359|) has been described from Sauropsida |CITS: [32601391]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: TAX-8457| (Reptilia), which include turtles, lizards, snakes, crocodiles, and birds, utilize a a unique taurine biosynthetic pathway in the egg during embryo development. This pathway involves |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.10|, an enzyme that converts |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: SO3| into |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| and |FRAME: HS|. |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| is converted to taurine by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.122|, while the hydrogen sulfide is recycled back into cysteine by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.22| |CITS: [32601391]|., Since the sulfur input into the pathway is the oxidized form |FRAME: SO3|, the pathway enables the formation of taurine and derived sulfonated amino acids at no cost of reduced sulfur, which is required for the formation of other metabolites and is a limited resource in the egg |CITS: [32601391]|. In addition, the pathway does not require molecular oxygen, a limiting factor in reptilian eggs |CITS: [Ackerman80][7335987]|.

General Background, |FRAME: QUINATE| is a naturally occuring compound found in decaying plant matter |CITS: [8126417]|., Quinate is one of several aromatic compounds that can be metabolized by microorganisms to the, central intermediate |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| that can be further metabolized via the β-ketoadipate pathway to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA |CITS: [Tresguerres70][14586099]|. Bacteria capable of using quinate as a sole carbon source were observed as early as 1911 |CITS: [Beijerinck11]|, Quinate degradation was initially studied in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [16589471]|, and later in other fungi (such as |FRAME: TAX-162425| |CITS: [3916726]|) and bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-62977| (at the time reported as |FRAME: TAX-471|) |CITS: [7592351][8002591]|, |FRAME: TAX-442| |CITS: [14586099]| and |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [18566515]|.| Many of these organisms can grow on quinate as a sole carbon and energy source, and the pathway is inducible by growth on either |FRAME: QUINATE|, |FRAME: SHIKIMATE|, or |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|., Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the main difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of |FRAME: QUINATE|. Filamentous fungi and Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: QUINATE-5-DEHYDROGENASE-RXN "EC 1.1.1.24"|), while Gram-negative bacteria use a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: 1.1.99.25-RXN "EC 1.1.99.25"|) |CITS: [3044290]|. The later pathway is desribed in |FRAME: QUINATEDEG-PWY|., About This Pathway, Quinate degradation was first studied in filamentous fungi such as |FRAME: TAX-5141| and |FRAME: TAX-162425|. The fungal pathway starts with conversion of |FRAME: QUINATE| to |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| by an NAD-dependent |FRAME:CPLX-7981| (EC 1.1.1.24). The genes involved in the fungal pathway (qa genes in |FRAME: TAX-5141|, qut genes in |FRAME: TAX-162425| ) were shown to be present in a single cluster, and are induced by growth on either |FRAME: QUINATE| or shikimate |CITS: [6458044][8670107][8126417]|. The clusters include a gene encoding a permease that enables |FRAME: QUINATE| to enter the organism |CITS: [2835177]|., An NAD-dependent enzyme is also present in certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-1718| |CITS: [19376919]|. As in the fungi, the |FRAME: G-11733| gene, which encodes the |FRAME:TAX-1718| enzyme, is located in a gene cluster that also contains the genes encoding the rest of the pathway's enzymes. The cluster, which is under the control of the QsuR regulator, is induced by growth on |FRAME: QUINATE| shikimate |CITS: [19376919]|.

Summary: General Background, Until fairly recently the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| in plants was poorly understood and only a few enzymes involved in this pathway had been characterized |CITS:[25217510]|. |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is present in plants at much lower concentrations than in animals (i.e. 1-2% of the total sterols) but can accumulate to significant higher levels in Solanaceae |CITS:[Whitaker88] [Whitaker91] [Japelt11]|. The more prominent sterols in plants, which have been investigated in more detail, are the phytosterols (C24-alkylsterols) |CITS:[Piironen00]| (see |FRAME:PWY-2541|). , Following the discovery of the plant |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.72| (|FRAME: G18C3-13|) in 2014 |CITS: [25217510]|, the entire set of cholesterogenesis genes in |FRAME: TAX-4081| and |FRAME: TAX-4100| were identified in 2016, leading to the entire reaction sequence required for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| in plants, as shown in |FRAME: PWY18C3-1| |CITS:[28005066] [26876023]|. It was found that the enzymes of this pathway are often promiscuous and are active in related pathways such as |FRAME:PWY-2541|. This is exemplified by the C4-demethylation complex formed by sterol methyl oxidases (SMO's), 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/C4-decarboxylase (3βHSD), and 3-oxosteroid reductase (SDR) |CITS:[8031136] [21902244] [21147141]|. The SMO proteins appear to specific for particular substrates, but 3βHSD and SDR are promiscuous. These enzymes form a multi-enzyme complexes in which the specificity of the SMO component determines in what pathway those enzyme complexes operate |CITS:[28005066] [26876023]|., The |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| biosynthetic pathway is the gateway to various steroids and vitamins, e.g. |FRAME:VITAMIN_D3| (see |FRAME:PWY-6076|) |CITS:[23717318]|. Metabolic intermediates such as |FRAME:CYCLOARTENOL| and |FRAME:DESMOSTEROL-CPD| are branching points that either give way to plant C-24 alkylsterols (see |FRAME:PWY-2541|) or |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL|. The flux into different pathways depends on the activity of basically two enzymes competing for those substrates, i.e. the sterol C-24 methyltransferase 1, which steers the flux of carbon towards C-24 alkylsterols and in doing so lowers |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| biosynthesis |CITS:[10852933] [12226510] [12692338]|, and the sterol side chain reductase (SSR2), which has been shown to form respective precursor and |FRAME:CHOLESTEROL| by reducing the side chain of |FRAME:CYCLOARTENOL| and |FRAME:DESMOSTEROL-CPD| |CITS:[25217510]|., About This Pathway, Analysis of sterol metabolites in the red alga |FRAME: TAX-2769| using mass spectrometry did not find evidence for |FRAME: CYCLOEUCALENOL|, |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|, |FRAME: CPD-22095|, and |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL|. On the other hand detected sterols included |FRAME: CPD-23705| |CITS: [Tasende00]|, |FRAME: DESMOSTEROL-CPD|, |FRAME: CPD-4161|, |FRAME: CPD-4162|, and |FRAME: CPD-4143| |CITS: [32058961]|., In order to explain the production of the observed sterols, and the lack of those not observed, a 2020 study suggested that red algae may use a different cholesterol biosynthesis variant, in which |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.72| the (|FRAME: G18C3-13| homolog) acts towards the end of the pathway, resulting in production of intermediates that contain a double bond at position 24. The last such compound is |FRAME: DESMOSTEROL-CPD|, which can be converted to |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.72|, or to |FRAME: CPD-706|, leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-4161|, |FRAME: CPD-4162|, and |FRAME: CPD-4143| |CITS: [32058961]|., While candidate genes encoding the pathway's enzymes have been identified computationally, no biochemichal proof has been provided so far for the proposed reactions.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamien-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, The active form of thiamine is |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. The non-phosphorylated form |FRAME: THIAMINE| is not produced as an intermediate in the de novo biosynthetic route in bacteria, but is found in the environment as a degradation product., Many microbes possess transporters that allow them to import thiamine |CITS: [16291685]|, as well as salvage pathways that regenerate the active form. One such pathway, which is described here, consists of the direct conversion of |FRAME: THIAMINE| to |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [15150256]|. This single-step thiamine salvage pathway was originally thought to occur only in eukaryotes, but the discovery of the enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-1423| revealed that it is also used by bacteria.

General Background, Chlorophyll degradation, corresponding to the loss of green color, is an integral part of leaf senescence and fruit ripening |CITS:[16113212],[15012204],[10767575],[12675736][ 16669755]| in land plants. In those species, chlorophyll degradation may follow one of two routes, likely depending on the physiogical context in which it occurs. In |FRAME: PWY-5098|, |FRAME: CPD-7061| is broken down to |FRAME: CPD-10296| via a two-step reaction |FRAME: 3.1.1.82-RXN 3.1.1.82| catalyzed by an enzyme known as phenophorbidase |CITS: [16228561]|. , In contrast, green algae use the same initial reactions to break down |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, but a distinct type of enzyme, called pheophorbide demethoxycarbonylase (PDC), catalyzes the breakdown of |FRAME: CPD-7061| |CITS: [16228561]|., About This Pathway, One of the first step in this route of chlorophyll degradation is dephytylation, or removal of the phytol moiety of the compound. This step is catalyzed by chlorophyllases which have been described in several plants species (for review see |CITS:[16448336]|) and acts primarily on chlorophyll a., The second enzyme of the pathway, Mg dechelatase, remains elusive. This enzyme catalyzes the release of Mg2+ from chlorophyllide a in exchange from two protons to form pheophorbide a. Since the purification of the protein has been unsuccessful and has led to the detection of a low-molecular-weight compound rather than a protein, the removal of Mg2+ from chlorophyllide a has been postulated to be performed by a 'Mg-dechelating substance', or MCS. It is uncertain whether MCS represents an active cofactor of Mg-dechelatase. The structure of either Mg-dechelatase or MCS remains to be determined |CITS:[16448336]|., The final step in this pathway is catalyzed by a class of enzymes only detected in algae to date. The exact product(s) of the pheophorbide demethoxycarbonylase (PDC) enzyme have not been identified, but there is experimental evidence of PDC activity in |FRAME: TAX-3055| |CITS: [16228561]|.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, reduces a total of four molecules of either |FRAME: NAD|, |FRAME: NADP|, or |FRAME: Quinones quinone| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively, and phosphorylates one molecule of GDP to GTP., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that transport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, In obligate autotrophs exogenously furnished organic compounds make a very small contribution to cellular carbon |CITS: [4963789]|. In a study conducted with obligate autotrophic |FRAME: TAX-919| strains, as well as several species of |FRAME: TAX-1117|, acetate, which was the most readily incorporated compound of those studied, contributed only about 10% of newly synthesized cellular carbon., The carbon from pyruvate, acetate, and glutamate provided exogenously was incorporated into restricted groups of cellular amino acids. In addition, the enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| or |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.71| are missing from the obligate autotrophs that were studied, and activities of malic enzyme and succinate dehydrogenase had extremely low levels., The authors concluded that the tricarboxylic acid cycle in these organisms is blocked at the level of |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| oxidation |CITS: [4963789]|. A later study showed that while most cyanobacteria do posses the enzymes required for a full TCA cycle (see |FRAME: P105-PWY|), cyanobacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-1218| and marine |FRAME: TAX-1129| genera lack |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.71|, and thus are likely to operate the pathway described here |CITS: [22174252]|., A more recent analysis of |FRAME: TAX-1140| concluded that the organism likely possesses the branched, non-complete TCA cycle, which the authors termed "the TCA pathway". The three enzymes comprising one branch of the pathway - |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.2|, and |FRAME: EC-1.3.5.1|, were found to be non-essential under both light and dark conditions |CITS: [27911809]|. , The pathway appears not to be energy-related. Rather, it's main role is to produce |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| that is directed towards biosynthesis.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, A group of 6-deoxyhexoses, including |FRAME: CPD-3604|, |FRAME: CPD-15665|, |FRAME: CPD-15674|, |FRAME: CPD-13462|, |FRAME: CPD-15664|, |FRAME: CPD-15695|, |FRAME: CPD-15696|, |FRAME: CPD-15698|, |FRAME: CPD-15671|, |FRAME: CPD-15672|, |FRAME: CPD-15682| and |FRAME: CPD-15681|, are used as components for the assembly of the O-anigens of certain Gram-negative bacteria. Some of these compounds are also used by some Gram-positive bacteria for construction of their S-layer., All of these modified sugar residues are synthesized in a UDP nucleotide-activated form from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| |CITS:[14670712][19710102]|. This super-pathway brings together the different routes that lead to the synthesis of these modified sugars. Note that this is a chimeric pathway - no single organism is known to synthesize all of these compounds.
