It was also found to be the, the major endogenous osmolyte of several of strains of rhizobia that nodulate Acacia trees |CITS: [17298361]|., The genome of |FRAME: TAX-176299| contains two genes that are very similar to those that encode, |FRAME: MONOMER-11709| and |FRAME: CPLX-1542|, the key enzymes for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: SUCROSE|., A study of these genes, |FRAME: G-11036| and |FRAME: G-11037|, revealed that they encode two proteins that, synthesize |FRAME: CPD-10684|., The genes are arranged in an operon structure, and their transcription is up-regulated by NaCl |CITS: [17728402]|., The first enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-14460|, catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| and, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, resulting in formation of |FRAME: CPD-10683|, and the second enzyme,, |FRAME: MONOMER-14461|, hydrolizes the product to form |FRAME: CPD-10684|., The pathway is analogous to that of |FRAME: SUCSYN-PWY|., Close homologs of these genes have so far been found only in |FRAME: TAX-187304|, indicating that the distribution, of this pathway may be narrow. However, homologs of the sucrose biosynthetic genes are found in about one of six, bacterial genomes and also in some archaeal genomes, suggesting that synthesis of similar disccharides, may be widespread |CITS: [17728402]|.

|FRAME: Prokaryotic-ubiquitin-like-proteins "Prokaryotic Ubiquitin-like Protein"| (Pup) is a functional analog of |FRAME: Ubiquitins ubiquitin|, described from members of the |FRAME: TAX-1762|., Pup essentially serves the same function as |FRAME: Ubiquitins ubiquitin|. It attaches to specific lysine residues of substrate proteins by forming isopeptide bonds. The conjugated proteins are recognized by the Mycobacterium proteasomal ATPase (Mpa), which delivers them to the 20S proteasome, coupling ATP hydrolysis with proteasomal degradation., Before it could be conjugated to its target proteins Pup needs to be activated by the deamidation of its C-terminal |FRAME: GLN| to |FRAME: GLT|. The enzyme that catalyzes the activation, |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.119|, is encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-6318| gene |CITS: [19448618]|. Interestingly, the enzyme also catalyzes |FRAME: EC-3.4.99.M1| (DPUP) activity, removing conjugated Pup from target proteins, and is thus involved in the recycling of Pup |CITS: [20705495]|., Once activated, Pup is covalently attached to substrate proteins, thereby targeting them for proteasomal degradation, in a process that is commonly known as "Pupylation". The attachment involves forming a bond between an ε-amino group of a lysine residue of the target protein and the γ-carboxylate of the C-terminal glutamate of Pup. The enzyme catalyzing the attachment, |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.19|, is encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-6303| gene |CITS: [14671303]|, which was named for "proteasome accessory factor A" |CITS: [17082771]|., Two proteasome substrates that are subject to Pupylation are |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.39| and |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.11|., In a |FRAME: G185E-6303| mutant pupylated proteins were absent and substrates accumulated, clearly connecting pupylation with degradation |CITS: [18832610]|.

In this pathway each turn of the cycle captures two molecules of |FRAME: HCO3|, but the carbons, are not exported as |FRAME:GLYOX|. Rather, they are converted directly to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by a route that is similar to that used by |FRAME: TAX-186801| for fermentation of |FRAME:SUC| (see |FRAME: PWY-5677|)., As in the conventional |FRAME: PWY-5743|, the pathway starts with |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| carboxylation to |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, catalyzed by |FRAME: ENZRXN-14489|. Under autotrophic growth conditions |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| is reduced with NADPH by |FRAME: CPLX-7550| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE|, which is reductively converted to |FRAME: SUC-COA| in a process in which |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| is carboxylated, fixing another molecule of |FRAME: HCO3|. However, from |FRAME: SUC-COA| and on the two pathways are completely divergent., The |FRAME: PWY-5789| progresses via the intermediates |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD|, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-BUTYRATE|, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-BUTYRYL-COA|, |FRAME: CROTONYL-COA|, |FRAME: 4-HYDROXY-BUTYRYL-COA|, and, |FRAME: ACETOACETYL-COA|. The latter is split into two molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, one of which is used to replenish the the cycle, while the other is removed for cell material biosynthesis., Interestingly, even the identical part of the pathway is catalyzed by enzymes that appear not to be phylogenetically related to the homologous enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-1108|, indicating convergent evolution |CITS: [18079388]|.

|FRAME: BENZENE-NO2 Nitrobenzene| is frequently released in the effluent from explosives manufacture as well as in the manufacture of organic chemicals and plastics. It is the primary starting material for the manufacture of |FRAME: ANILINE|, a compound used in the production of polyurethane |CITS: [8368838]|. The pollution potential of |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| is very large, and it is listed among the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency priority pollutants |CITS: [Callahan79]|., |FRAME: TAX-301| JS45, an isolate from soil and groundwater contaminated with nitrobenzene, is able to use nitrobenzene as the sole source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy. Analysis of cell-free extracts suggested of an initial partial reduction to |FRAME: HYDROXYAMINOBENZENE|, which undergoes a rearrangement to |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL|, followed by meta ring cleavage |CITS: [8368838]|. Additional work focused on the purification and characterization of all of the key enzymes in the pathway, including |FRAME: MONOMER-13319| |CITS: [7601851]|, |FRAME: CPLX-7467| |CITS: [8892823]|, |FRAME: CPLX-7465| |CITS: [9573204]|, |FRAME: CPLX-7466| |CITS: [9721300]| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13322| |CITS: [10877793]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6210|)., This pathway has also been described in |FRAME: ORG-5945| |CITS:[10049867]|. The portion of the pathway downstream from |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL| is identical to the |FRAME: PWY-6210| pathway of |FRAME: TAX-874293| |CITS: [9169437][9683650][11081795][15914928]|., A different pathway for the degeradation of |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| is described in |FRAME: PWY-5640|.

Summary: Pterocarpan phytoalexins are antimicrobial compounds in leguminous plants formed upon pathogenic attacks and similar biotic stress-related events. A systematic investigation within the tribe |FRAME:TAX-163735| (subfamily |FRAME:TAX-3814|) showed that pterocarpans are the most common compounds isolated from those plants., |FRAME: Maackiain Maackiain| is a common pterocarpan that has been detected in many legumes. Within the two subtribes Diocleinae and Erythrininae it was found in 12 species representing 4 genera |CITS: [Ingham90]|. Maackiain was originally discovered in the |FRAME: TAX-37501| tree, which is named after its discoverer, the 19th-century Siberian explorer Karlovich Maack. Maackiain can be found in both a (-) and a (+) conformations. In chickpea, where it is a major pterocarpan phytoalexin together with medicarpin, it occurs exclusively in the (-) [(6aR,11aR)} conformation |CITS: [8071365]|., The biosynthetic route of maackiain starts with formononetin, a 4'-methoxylated isoflavone, which is also the origin for the pterocarpans medicarpin in chickpea and pisatin in pea. The biosynthetic route differs in essentially two additional steps, one introducing a hydroxylgroup to the 3'-position of the isoflavone B-ring |CITS: [Dewick78]| followed by another one forming the methylenedioxy bridge of maackiain |CITS: [Clemens96]|., Frequently, malonate glucosides of pterocarpans are accumulated constitutively in below-ground organs of legumes (see |FRAME:PWY-2701|), indicating that under certain physiological circumstances a metabolic link between isoflavone conjugation reactions and pterocarpan synthesis exists |CITS: [Daniel90]| |CITS: [Weidemann91]| |CITS: [Barz92]|. Parts of the |FRAME:CPD-3631| biosynthetic route is also shared by other pathways, for instance |FRAME:PWY-7633|, which also requires the 3'-hydroxylation of |FRAME:FORMONONETIN| to form the aglycone in the |FRAME:CPD-17611| biosynthetic pathway |CITS:[17253088]|., In leguminous plants pterocarpans have been found with different stereochemical orientation. Chick pea and alfalfa accumulate only (-)- or (6aR,11aR)-pterocarpans, whereas peanuts accumulate pterocarpans of the opposite stereochemistry (+)- (6aS, 11aS). Some legumes (e.g. the scholar tree, Sophora japonica) build up an racemic mixture of both (-)- and (+)-pterocarpans. The stereochemistry of this phytoalexins can be crucial since it has been found that pathogens cannot break down the opposite enantiomer of the pterocarpans usually found in their target plants |CITS: [VanEtten83]|., A study of the last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.139|, from |FRAME: TAX-46348| has shown that the stereochemistry of the final product is determined by the chiral center at C-3. A (3R) configuration results in production of a (-) pterocarpan, while a (3S) configuration produces a (+)-pterocarpan. However, it is still not known at what step the conformation of the C-3 carbon is modified and by which enzyme |CITS: [28394400]|.

Summary: General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on single carbon (C1) compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. , While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 "Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| (see |FRAME: PWY-5506|)., The key enzyme in the oxidation of methanol in methylotrophic bacteria is methanol dehydrogenase (MDH). Different bacterial strains use different types of MDH. Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria have a periplasmic |FRAME: CPLX-3264| that contain a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ) cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-1701|). Thermophilic methylotrophic Bacili such as |FRAME: TAX-1471| use an |FRAME: CPLX-8059| (see |FRAME: PWY-6510|), while Gram-positive bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1814|, |FRAME: TAX-1777| MB19, |FRAME: TAX-1829| LMD 89.129 and |FRAME: TAX-1833| DSM 1069 possess nicotinoprotein methanol dehydrogenases with a bound NAD(P) cofactor that use an unknown electron acceptor for reduction of their bound cofactor and can use the artificial electron acceptor |FRAME: CPD-12424| in vitro |CITS:[1995642][8385013][8449887]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6509|)., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branch point, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (see |FRAME:P185-PWY|), or a dissimilatory pathway that provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|)., About This Pathway, Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria are aerobic bacteria that utilize one-carbon compounds more reduced than formate as sources of carbon and energy, and assimilate formaldehyde as a major source of cellular carbon |CITS [8801441]|. , Methylotrophic bacteria utilize a variety of different one-carbon compounds including methane (see |FRAME: PWY-1641|), methanol, methylated amines, halomethanes and methylated compounds containing sulfur. , The common product of these oxidation reactions is formaldehyde, which is either oxidized to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, or assimilated (see formaldehyde assimilation and formaldehyde oxidation pathways)., Methanol from both endogenous (methane oxidation) or exogenous sources is oxidized to formaldehyde by a periplasmic methanol dehydrogenase (MDH) in Gram-negative methylotrophs |CITS [3020939]|. Electrons are transferred from MDH to an atypical cytochrome cL, which in turn is oxidized by a typical class I cytochrome c (cH). The two cytochromes are periplasmic as well., The product of this reaction, formaldehyde, is transported into the cytosol, where is processed further. Depending on the organism and the growth conditions, formaldehyde can be either oxidized or assimilated.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Several pathways of thiosulfate oxidation are known. The two best understood pathways are the oxidation of thiosulfate directly to sulfate, catalyzed by the |FRAME:CPLX-882| (see |FRAME:PWY-5296|), and the oxidation of thiosulfate, to |FRAME:CPD-14| (this pathway), which in some organisms may be degraded further to sulfate (see |FRAME: PWY-6327|)., Oxidation to tetrathionate is the most common thiosulfate oxidation pathway. It is found in obligate chemolithotrophs, such as |FRAME: TAX-929|, |FRAME: TAX-920|, and |FRAME: TAX-930| |CITS: [26665]|, in facultative species such as |FRAME: TAX-76588|, |FRAME: TAX-47959|, and even in some obligate heterotrophs |CITS: [10508936]|., The enzyme catalyzing this reaction, |FRAME:CPLX-7172|, has been partially purified from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [5687645]|, |FRAME: TAX-931| |CITS: [5438323]|, and |FRAME: TAX-929| |CITS: [Lu88]|., More recently, the enzyme has been completely purified from |FRAME: ORG-5987| |CITS: [9082913]| and |FRAME: TAX-930| |CITS: [11272812]|. Despite the fact that enzymes from different organisms catalyze the same reaction, only a few structural features are shared by the enzymes that have been characterized., Certain sulfur-oxidizing organisms can utilize a wide range of polythionates in addition to tetrathionate. For example, |FRAME: TAX-929| uses the enzyme |FRAME: TRITHIOHYDRO-MONOMER| to oxidize |FRAME: CPD-552| to thiosulfate, which is then oxidized to sulfate |CITS:[JGM134-865][JGM134-877]|.

Summary: General Background, Sialic acids are a family of polyhydroxylated α-keto acids that contain nine carbon atoms. Most sialic acids, are derivatives of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| or |FRAME: CPD-21259| (KDN). , |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is the most common sialic acid in mammals (this pathway), while KDN is, abundant in lower vertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Their core structures can be modified at the, hydroxyl groups, lactonized, or hydroxylated at the acetamido group, generating many, derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-262| is a derivative of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| (see, pathway |FRAME: PWY-6144|). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Sialic acids are found mainly in vertebrates and a few higher invertebrates (ascidians and echinoderms). These, acidic sugars are usually the terminal sugar residue in the glycan chains of vertebrate glycoconjugates (mostly, glycoproteins and glycolipids, but also proteoglycans and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors). They function in, mediating cellular recognition and adhesion events for many important processes such as development, the immune, and inflammatory responses, and oncogenesis. Sialic acid occurs rarely in invertebrates. Endogenous sialylation, has been shown to occur in |FRAME: TAX-7215|, but details of sialic acid biosynthesis in this organism remain to, be determined |CITS: [18568399]|. However, it is possible the sialic acids might be biosynthesized by other, eukaryotes in a species and/or life cycle-dependent manner. In |CITS: [7841794]| and reviewed in, |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Most bacteria do not biosynthesize sialic acids, but some pathogenic, or symbiotic bacteria biosynthesize sialic, acids as a means of evading a host's immune system (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6139|). The sialic acid is, displayed on the bacterial cell surface (in capsular polysaccharides) in order to mimic mammalian cells. Pathogens, that biosynthesize sialic acids include |FRAME: TAX-487|, |FRAME: TAX-1392869| and |FRAME: TAX-197|. In, addition, the human gut symbiont |FRAME: TAX-818| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-21259|, |CITS: [18804026]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Whether or not archaea contain sialic acids remains to be, determined. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Other sialic acid-like sugars biosynthesized by bacteria include the nonulosonic acids |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [16751642]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|) and legionaminic acid |CITS: [18275154]|., Protists are thought to lack the ability to biosynthesize sialic acids although more genome data are needed to confirm, this. Sialic acids have been thought to be absent in plants but some studies raise the possibility, |CITS: [18258224]|. Fungi appear to lack any known sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, although strain-specific, or, novel pathways could exist. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Also, see |FRAME: PWY-6145|., About This Pathway, In both animals (this pathway) and bacteria (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6139|), |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| biosynthesis begins with the conversion of, |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE|. This reaction, involves both an inversion of stereochemistry at C-2 of the sugar moiety and hydrolysis of the glycosidic phosphate, bond. In animals |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE| is then phosphorylated to its 6-phosphate derivative. , Condensation with |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| then forms |FRAME: N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE-9P|, a, distinctive biosynthetic step. After dephosphorylation to |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, |FRAME: CTP| is, used to generate the activated form of sialic acid, |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE|. This step is in, contrast to activation of other vertebrate monosaccharides, the activated forms of which use |FRAME: URIDINE| or, |FRAME: GUANINE| dinucleotides. The |FRAME: CMP|-activated form is the sialic acid donor for glycoconjugates. , In contrast, in the bacterial pathway |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE| is not phosphorylated, but is, converted to |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| directly by condensation with, |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|. This is followed by formation of the activated form, |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE|. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and, |CITS: [11841250]|., In animal cells, |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is biosynthesized in the cytosol. However, its |FRAME: CMP|, derivative, |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE|, is formed in the nucleus, enters the cytosol and is then, transported into the golgi apparatus by a golgi CMP-sialic acid transporter, |CITS: [18713811] [16923816] [8755516]|. In the golgi lumen |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| serves, as a sialic acid donor for sialyltransferases in the formation of glycoconjugates. For examples of sialyltransferases, see EC 2.4.99.1 through EC 2.4.99.11. |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| can also be hydroxylated to, |FRAME: CPD-262| by the |FRAME: CPLX-7746| and transferred to glycoconjugates (as shown in the pathway link). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172]| and |CITS: [18568399]|., In mammals the first two reactions are catalyzed by a bifunctinal enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting steps in, sialic acid biosynthesis. The supply of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is regulated through feedback, inhibition by |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| |CITS: [9305887]|. Reviewed in, |CITS: [15888312] [16897172]| and |CITS: [18568399]|.

|FRAME: CPD-16430| is a component of the octasaccharide antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-16431|, a member of the orthosomycin family of antibiotics produced by some bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-47853|. Everninomicin possesses potent Gram-positive antibiotic activity, including broad-spectrum efficacy against multidrug resistant enterococci and |FRAME: TAX-1280|. , In addition to everninomicin, |FRAME: CPD-16430| is also present in the polyketide |FRAME: CPD-16432|, and is structurally related to D-kijanose from the spirotetronate polyketide antibiotic kijanimycin., |FRAME: CPD-16430| is a nitrosugar. Studies have shown that the sugar is synthesized in its activated form, |FRAME: CPD-16419|, from |FRAME: CPD-15746|, a sugar known to decorate other antibiotics, such as |FRAME: CPD-14693| |CITS: [12874381]|., The pathway starts with an 4-O-methylation of |FRAME: CPD-15746| by an as-yet unidentified enzyme, forming |FRAME: CPD-16433| |CITS: [20866105]|. Some organisms produce phospholipids in which the fatty acyl chains contain cyclopropane rings. These rings are formed by enzymes that use a methyl group from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| to convert a double bond of an unsaturated fatty acyl chain within a lipid to a cyclopropane group., In most organisms the cyclopropane groups are cis-configured and are formed by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.79|, which acts only on cis double bonds. The |FRAME: MYCOLIC-ACIDS "mycolic acids"| of mycobacteria often contain additional trans-configured cyclopropane groups that are formed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.M101| |CITS: [16741578]|., The physiological role of cyclopropane-containing fatty acyl chains (CFA) is to stabilize the membranes by increased ordering of the chains without sacrificing membrane fluidity. This can decrease the proton permeability of phospholipid bilayers, helping the bacteria survive acid shock |CITS: [9310851][18562182][25804677]|. In addition, the cyclopropane rings provide more rigid kinks in the lipid acyl chain compared to the double bonds and thus reduce the packing density of the membrane and enhance the membrane fluidity at low temperatures |CITS: [36790194]|. trans-configured CFA in mycolic acids were reported to be correlated with the persistence of the pathogen and to modulate the innate immune response of the host |CITS: [15710652]|., |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.79| (CFA synthase) is one of the few enzymes known to act on the nonpolar portion of phospholipids dispersed in a vesicle. The enzyme acts on a double bond of a phospholipid unsaturated fatty acid residue that is located 9-11 carbon atoms from the glycerol backbone of the molecule |CITS: [380648][7024727][1445840][9409147][9882672]|., CFA synthase from |FRAME: TAX-562| exhibits activity toward phosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylethanolamine, cardiolipin, and phosphatidylcholine |CITS: [380648]|.

In a different attempt to verify the genes' function, they were introduced to a |FRAME: TAX-1916| strain that expressed a modified version of the eryA gene of |FRAME: TAX-1836|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.94|. This transformant normally produces 2-desmethyl-6-deoxyerythronolide B, but when provided with the asm genes, it produced a compound identified as 2-desmethyl-2-methoxy-6-deoxyerythronolide B, confirming the proposed function of the asm13—17 genes |CITS: [11996558]|., Further proof was obtained in 2006, when the |FRAME: G-44139|, |FRAME: G-44140|, and |FRAME: G-44141| of |FRAME: TAX-1396| were shown to catalyze the production of |FRAME: 2-Hydroxymalonyl-ACP| during |FRAME: PWY-7694| |CITS: [16983083]|. These genes are orthologous to |FRAME: G-107663|, |FRAME: G-107665|, and |FRAME: G-107666|, respectively, and catalyze identical reactions.

Summary: General Background, Cellular dTTP levels need to be tightly controlled for efficient DNA replication in the cell nucleus and mitochondria |CITS: [9148948]|. An imbalance of cellular dTTP results in the incorporation of uracil into DNA which can cause instability in the nuclear genome and mitochondrial dysfunction |CITS: [21876188]|. The nucleus has been shown to possess both a salvage (|FRAME: PWY-7199|) and a de novo (|FRAME: PWY-7184|) pathway for dTTP synthesis via dTMP. The salvage pathway also occurs in the mitchondria |CITS: [14519855]|. However, dTTP requirements for mitochondrial DNA replication cannot be sustained by the salvage pathway alone. Studies to elucidate how mitochondria maintained their dTTP levels led to the discovery of a novel de novo dTMP biosynthetic pathway unique to mitochondria |CITS: [21876188]|., About this Pathway, Two of the enzymes in this pathway, |FRAME: HS11096-MONOMER| and |FRAME: HS00049-MONOMER| (SHMT2) were known to be localized to the mitochondria in mammalian cells. The third enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000178700-MONOMER| was initially considered to be a pseudogene |CITS: [3341383]|. It was later revealed as a fully functional isozyme of |FRAME: CPLX66-351|, unique to mitochondria |CITS: [21876188]|., Folates like tetrahydrofolate and tetrahydrofolate glutamate are essential cofactors for the pathway. They mediate the one carbon transfers necessary for the synthesis of dTMP. They are also required for purines, methionine and glycine biosynthesis |CITS: [14519855]|. Folate deficiency is associated with increased uracil misincorporation into DNA |CITS: [9096386]|.

The enzyme is highly conserved among different microorganisms, but its genetic organization and control of expression are highly divergent |CITS: [10715000]|., |FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to utilize proline as a sole nitrogen source. |FRAME: PRO| is catabolized within the mitochondrial matrix. Since both enzymes are encoded in the nucleus and synthesized in the cytoplasm, they are imported into the mitochondria before they become active |CITS: [387737] [6358862]|., |FRAME: PRO| can serve as a total source of carbon and energy or of nitrogen for |FRAME:TAX-562|. In the two steps (both of which are catalyzed by a product of putA) shown here, proline is converted to |FRAME: GLT|, which is further degraded to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, an intermediate of the |FRAME: TCA|. Curiously, |FRAME: GLT|, the product of |FRAME: PRO| degradation, cannot itself serve as a total source of carbon and energy for |FRAME:TAX-562| because |FRAME: GLT| transport supplies exogenous |FRAME: GLT| at an inadequate rate. , The pathway is shown here in three steps because |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| is an intermediate between |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| and |FRAME: GLT|. The hydrolysis of |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME: L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| occurs spontaneously., In addition to serving as a building block of proteins, |FRAME: PRO| acts as an osmotic protectant. Consistent with this role, high osmolarity inhibits |FRAME: PRO| degradation.

General Background, The p-hydroxycinnamates |FRAME: COUMARATE| (p-coumarate), |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| and |FRAME: CAFFEATE| are phenylpropanoid compounds produced by green plants (see pathways |FRAME: PWY1F-467| and |FRAME: PWY-2181|). These compounds are degraded by soil bacteria. An aerobic pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| has been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-502559| |CITS: [12200295]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6343|). More recently, an anaerobic pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: COUMARATE| has been proposed for the phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-258594| as shown here |CITS: [22328668][18156135]|., About This Pathway, The enzymes CouB and CouA were were shown to be capable of degrading the p-hydroxycinnamates |FRAME: COUMARATE|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| and |FRAME: CAFFEATE| via |FRAME: CO-A| esterification of their side chains, followed by side chain cleavage to generate the corresponding benzaldehydes. CouB is a predicted |FRAME: CO-A| ligase and CouA is a predicted enoyl-CoA hydratase/aldolase. Although these reactions are known to operate in aerobic bacteria, these two enzymes could be induced when |FRAME: TAX-258594| was grown anaerobically with |FRAME: COUMARATE| as a carbon source |CITS: [18156135][22328668]|., Analysis of CouA and CouB deletion mutants suggested that these enzymes are responsible for anaerobic growth of |FRAME: TAX-258594| on |FRAME: COUMARATE|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| and |FRAME: CAFFEATE| |CITS: [22328668]|. The intermediate |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE| was proposed to be degraded to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| by one of the known aldehyde dehydrogenases in this organism. This compound was found to be excreted, and then taken up by the cells and converted to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|. The latter compound is degraded by the central anaerobic pathway of aromatic ring catabolism as shown in the pathway link to |FRAME: CENTBENZCOA-PWY| (in |CITS: [22328668]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19258534]|)., Biochemical evidence was also presented for regulation of the couAB operon by a |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA|-responsive transcription factor encoded by couR, which was identified as a member of the MarR family of transcriptional regulators |CITS: [22328668]|., This organism is also known to grow under anaerobic, phototrophic conditions using |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| as a carbon source. A |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|-utilizing CoA ligase (distinct from anaerobic |FRAME: BENZOATE|-specific CoA ligase encoded by badA |CITS: [3350788][7592432]|) was purified from cells grown on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| and characterized. Its encoding gene hbaA was cloned and sequenced. A mutant that disrupted this gene was unable to grow anaerobically on |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| |CITS: [8300518]|. The |FRAME: CPD-201| product of this enzyme is dehydroxylated to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, which is the starting compound for a central pathway of anaerobic aromatic ring compound degradation, as shown in the pathway link (in |CITS: [9006014]|).

Octopine and nopaline are opines derived from arginine. They are biosynthesized in the cells of plant crown gall , tumors. These tumors are caused by infection with the plant pathogen |FRAME:TAX-358|. The , enzymes for both the biosynthesis and degradation/utilization of opines are encoded by the tumor-inducing Ti , plasmids found in A. tumefaciens. This host-pathogen interaction has an interesting mechanism. , A. tumefaciens infects wounded plants in response to chemical signals released by plant cells. Infection , by this organism involves products of the vir genes encoded by a Ti plasmid. These gene products cause , the transfer of oncogenic fragments of DNA (T-DNA) from the Ti plasmid into the nucleus of host plant cells, where , they become integrated into the host genome. , In plant cells, the T-DNA onc genes express plant hormones that cause neoplastic growth. Genes , encoding opine synthases (ops genes such as ocs encoding octopine synthase and nos , encoding nopaline synthase) are also expressed and direct the biosynthesis of opines (|FRAME: 1.5.1.11-RXN "EC 1.5.1.11"| and |FRAME: 1.5.1.19-RXN "1.5.1.19"| reactions in the reverse direction). These synthases are soluble, NAD(P)H-dependent , dehydrogenases |CITS: [8045881]| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-7351|). Opines produced in the plant tumor cells are secreted into the environment, enter the bacteria via opine permeases, and induce their catabolism by opine-specific enzymes. Opines therefore provide a source of carbon, nitrogen and energy for A. tumefaciens inside the plant tumor cells (in |CITS: [16195384], [9791116], [9244272]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [10869063]|)., The proteins required for uptake and catabolism of octopine and nopaline are organized into operons in , the occ region of an octopine-type Ti plasmid, or the noc region of a nopaline-type Ti , plasmid |CITS: [11877409], [9791116], [8288543]|. The enzymatic degradation of octopine to arginine and pyruvate , by octopine oxidase is shown here. Octopine oxidase is a membrane-bound opine oxidase that does not require, an added cofactor when assayed in crude preparations. However, it was postulated by sequence analysis to , require a cofactor such as FAD, FMN, or NAD(P)H. Therefore, the electron acceptor(s) for this reaction remains , to be identified in this organism |CITS: [8045881]|. Clicking on the pathway link shows the conversion of arginine to , proline and then glutamate in A. tumefaciens |CITS: [8045881], [8981973], [8606160]|. A similar degradation , of nopaline to arginine and α-ketoglutarate by nopaline oxidase in this organism is shown in MetaCyc , pathway |FRAME: NOPALINEDEG-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, Xanthones are yellow pigments of phenolic origin restricted in occurrence to only a few , families of higher plants and some fungi and lichens. The majority of xanthones is rarely glucosylated and has been , found in basically two families of higher plants, the Clusiaceae (syn. Guttiferae) and |FRAME:TAX-21472|, |CITS: [Hostettmann89]| |CITS: [Bennett89]|. , Xanthones can be classified based on their oxygenation, prenylation and glucosylation pattern. The majority of xanthones , isolated so far are of the tetraoxygenated-type which have been intensively studied in plants of the Guttiferae and , |FRAME:TAX-21472| |CITS: [11190384]|. , Xanthones posses a number of remarkable pharmacological traits and bioactivities (summarized in |CITS: [11190384]|) and , have been used as, e.g. cardiovascular protective agents |CITS: [15179447]| and antitumor promotors |CITS: [10397461]|. , Tetrahydroxylated xanthones can be induced by phytopathogens |CITS: [12391565]| and accumulate in calli and cell , suspension upon treatment with plant hormones and supplements, such as naphtaleneacetic acid (NAA) in combination , with kinetin |CITS: [Dias00]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of plant xanthones originates mainly from a mixed shikimate-acetate , pathway, however xanthones entirely derived from acetate have also been reported in lower plants |CITS: [11190384]| , |CITS: [Hostettmann89]|. The main steps in the xanthone biosynthesis involve the condensation of shikimate and acetate , moieties which constitute a benzophenone intermediate followed by a regioselective, oxidative mediated intra-molecular , coupling to form the xanthone ring |CITS: [Peters98]|., The shikimate derivatives used as entry compounds for the tetrahydroxyxanthone biosynthesis differ in relation to the , investigated plants (|FRAME:TAX-140968| vs |FRAME:TAX-172057|) |CITS: [11216850]| |CITS: [11882941]|. , These plants belong to different families that seem to have developed biosynthetic variants of the tetrahydroxyxanthone , synthesis which involves enzymes of diverse regioselectivity and substrate preference and leads to varying intermediates , |CITS: [Peters98]| |CITS: [9459298]|., The biosynthesis of tetrahydroxyxanthone via 3-hydroxybenzoate in |FRAME:TAX-172057| is obtained by the , stepwise condensation of 3 malonyl-CoA and 3-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA to form an intermediate tetrahydroxybenzophenone. , The biosynthesis of tetrahydroxyxanthone via benzoate in |FRAME:TAX-140968| is different from the Centaurium , erythraea variant (|FRAME:PWY-5002|) with regard to the regiospecificity and substrate usage of the involved , enzymes. The benzophenone synthase prefers benzoyl-CoA |CITS: [12795704]|, which in turn is provided by the , catalytic action of a 3-hydroxybenzoate:coenzyme A ligase using benzoic acid |CITS: [12054436]| |CITS: [9459298]|. , The new intermediate, 2,4,6-trihydroxybenzophenone is further hydroxylated and converted to the 2,3',4,6-tetrahydroxyphenone , intermediate, common to both pathways., The crucial step in this biosynthesis is the cyclization of the benzophenone to a xanthone, catalyzed by xanthon synthases. , While in |FRAME:TAX-172057| the xanthone synthase converts this tetrahydroxybenzophenone intermediate , regioselective to 1,3,5-trihydroxyxanthone the xanthone synthase of |FRAME:TAX-140968| converts it to the , 1,3,7-trihydroxyxanthone. , The last step in the biosynthesis of the tetrahydroxyxanthones is the introduction of a hydroxyl group to the C-ring of , the xanthone skeleton. This reaction is carried out by the plant-specific Cytochrome P450-dependend monooxygenase , xanthone-6-hydroxylase to form 1,3,5,6-tetrahydroxyxanthone in |FRAME:TAX-172057| and 1,3,6,7-tetrahydroxyxanthone , in |FRAME:TAX-140968| |CITS: [10731018]|. , Another representative of the |FRAME:TAX-21472|, chirayta (Swertia chirata), again hydroxylates 1,3,5-trihydroxyxanthone , in the 8-position of the C-ring resulting in the major xanthone of this species 1,3,5,8-tetrahydroxyxanthone |CITS: [12846828]|. , However, the enzyme and corresponding reaction involved remains to be characterized.

Summary: General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agent, and are believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans, was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose |CITS: [12065209]|. In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosyl α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein). , In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation and no internal hydrogen bond formation. The combination of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms trehalose can be used as external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|. In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|. The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood |CITS: [11081789]|., In insects, trehalose is produced from fat body glycogen and is released into the hemolymph (insect blood) where it is used in growth, development and response to environmental stress. In many insects, trehalose serves as an extracellular source of sugar via the action of trehalase, an enzyme widely distributed in insect tissues (as shown in the pathway link) (reviewed in |CITS: [KRAMER05][19725772]|)., About This Pathway, The enzymes for the biosynthesis of trehalose in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, trehalose-6-phosphate synthase and trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase, are encoded by the genes otsA and otsB. These genes are similar to the yeast genes TPS1 and TPS2. However, in |FRAME: TAX-4932| the two enzymes are combined into a single complex, called the trehalose synthase complex, which also includes the regulatory subunits TSL1 and TPS3 |CITS: [8045430][9837904]| (note that some authors use TPS3 as a redundant name for TSL1, while others use TPS3 for a different regulatory subunit)., Under conditions of elevated osmotic strength, |FRAME:TAX-562| can regulate the osmotic strength of the cytoplasm by accumulating K+ ions and several compatible solutes. The preferred osmoprotectant of |FRAME:TAX-562| is glycine betaine. However, its synthesis relies on an external supply of proline, betaines, or choline. When these compounds are not available, a cell can achieve a moderate level of osmotic tolerance by accumulation of glutamate and trehalose |CITS: [1825082]|., |FRAME:TAX-562| synthesizes and accumulates trehalose when exposed to osmotic stress |CITS: [2883950]| and low temperatures |CITS: [12105274]|. It is synthesized from UDP-glucose and glucose-6-phosphate via trehalose-6-phosphate, by the action of two enzymes, trehalose-6-phosphate synthase and trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase. The accumulation of trehalose is regulated on two levels: the synthesis of trehalose-6-phosphate synthase is induced by osmotic stress, and the synthase itself is activated by potassium glutamate |CITS: [1825082]|., Expression of both genes encoding the two enzymes, otsA and otsB, is osmotically regulated. Transcription from these genes increases during osmotic stress |CITS: [3131312]| and cold shock |CITS: [12105274]| and when the cells enter stationary phase |CITS: [1744047]|, and requires the stress sigma factor RpoS |CITS: [1744047][1310094]|., Under osmotic stress, |FRAME:TAX-562| overproduces trehalose, some of which is excreted to the periplasmic space. Once there, it is degraded by the periplasmic trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|). This process was named "a futile cycle for controlling the cytoplasmic level of trehalose" |CITS: [1825082]|., It should be mentioned that unusual trehalose-6-phosphate synthases have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-1772| and |FRAME: TAX-1773|. These enzymes are capable of utilizing all five nucleoside diphosphate glucose derivatives (ADP-D-glucose, CDP-D-glucose, GDP-D-glucose, TDP-D-glucose and UDP-D-glucose) as glucosyl donors |CITS: [Lapp71][8842710][12473104]|.

Summary: The aerobic degradation of |FRAME: TRP| by eukaryotes, often referred to as the kynurenine pathway, is the major route of, L-tryptophan degradation in mammals (see |FRAME: TRYPTOPHAN-DEGRADATION-1|)., The enzymology of the kynurenine pathway in humans and in yeasts has been largely elucidated over the last 20 years,, and the genes for most of the enzymes have been identified., In contrast, a lot less is known about the aerobic degradation of L-tryptophan in bacteria. It was shown, early on that certain unidentified Pseudomonads could oxidize tryptophan to catechol through kynurenine and, anthranilate |CITS: [14897807]|. In some species of Pseudomonadaceae and Bacillaceae the oxidative degradation, of exogenous L-tryptophan was implicated as a sole source of carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [803956][4316270][4628622]|., |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.11| activity has been described in some bacteria |CITS: [6431906]|, but no corresponding genes have been identified until 2003. The fact that some bacteria can degrade kynurenine further suggested the presence of two additional enzymes, |FRAME:MONOMER-7524| and |FRAME:CPLX-4521|. Based on sequence similarity to eukaryotic genes, the gene encoding |FRAME: EC-3.7.1.3|, was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-294| |CITS: [9264543]|, and the corresponding enzyme was characterized in detail |CITS: [9628740]|. Later, similarity to eukaryotic sequences revealed the bacterial gene encoding |FRAME: CPLX-4621| in several bacteria |CITS: [14592712]|. Finally, chromosomal gene clustering analysis revealed the presence of the third gene, encoding |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.9|, in an operon including the other two genes |CITS: [14592712]|., This functional prediction was experimentally verified by cloning, expression and enzymatic characterization of recombinant kynurenine formamidase orthologs from |FRAME: TAX-1396|, |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: TAX-266264|. In addition, functional expression in |FRAME:TAX-562| of the |FRAME: TAX-266264| putative kynBAU operon encoding all three genes confirmed the function of this operon |CITS: [14592712]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenem| antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-26780| was discovered in the 1970s from the soil actinomycete |FRAME: TAX-29303| |CITS: [761989]|. The |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenems| are a class of β-lactam antibiotics with broad antibacterial spectra and resistance to most classes of β-lactamases, making them an important class of antibiotics for the treatment of infectious diseases in humans. Carbapenems are distinct from other classes of β-lactams such as |FRAME: PENICILLIN pencillins| and |FRAME: Cephalosporins cephalosporins|, in which a sulfur occupies the C-1 position in the bicyclic nucleus., The simplest carbapenem is |FRAME: CPD-9377|, whose biosynthesis is described in |FRAME: PWY-5737|. The biosynthesis of more complex carbapenems, which are derived from |FRAME: CPD-9371| (an intermediate in that pathway), is less well understood., The thienamycin gene cluster was reported in 2003 |CITS: [12725858]|. The cluster consists of 22 ORFs, only two of which have apparent homologs in the nine-gene cluster for |FRAME: CPD-9377|. A biosynthetic pathway was proposed in 2011 based on mutational analysis |CITS: [21263049]|, though many of the conclusions of that study have been disputed by later discoveries., A 2008 study reported the functional assignment of four of the pathway genes that are involved in processing of the acyl group attached to the C-2 position of |FRAME: CPD-26780| |CITS: [18678912]|. The products of the |FRAME: G-124518| and |FRAME: G-124519| genes were found to catalyze reactions that hydrolyze |FRAME: CO-A| to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| and |FRAME: CPD-511|, respectively. The |FRAME: G-124520| gene product was found to hydrolyze the pantothenyl tail, leaving the shorter cystamine tail found in |FRAME: CPD-26780|, and the |FRAME: G-124521| gene product was found to be an acetyltranferase that acetylates the cystamine tail, forming |FRAME: CPD-26790|., In 2015 the |FRAME: G-124517| gene was shown to encode a radical SAM methyltransferase that catalyzes two consecutive methylations at the C-6 position, forming an ethyl group |CITS: [26240322]|. Another radical SAM, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124516| gene, was shown in 2022 to catalyze the key reaction condensing |FRAME: CPD-511| and |FRAME: CPD-9371| to form |FRAME: CPD-26777| |CITS: [35969793]|., As of 2024, the enzyme responsible for the desaturation of the core ring is still not known. In addition, it should be noted that the exact order in which the enzymes act is not known. A different order than the one shown here would result in formation of different intermediates., In addition, gene inactivations have indicated that several other genes - thnN, thnO, and thnP, are, absolutely necessary for the biosynthesis of thienamycin. On the other hand, thienamycin production was still observed, in |FRAME: G-124518| and |FRAME: G-124520| disruption mutants, suggesting that these genes are not required for, thienamycin biosynthesis |CITS: [21263049]|.

|FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| is a monosaccharide that is formed directly from starch or glycogen through the activity of |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.13|, during which its carbonyl group does not undergo hemiacetal bonding. The pathway for its production has been named |FRAME: PWY-7662 "the anhydrofructose pathway"|. It has been suggested that the pathway operates only when the organism is subjected to biotic and abiotic stresses |CITS: [16822618]|., |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| has been found in fungi, red algae, Escherichia coli C600 and rat liver tissue |CITS: [Baute91][9022716][10036159][9880813]|. It acts as an antioxidant |CITS: [11842320]|, an antibiotic |CITS: [22977551]|, and a precursor of several other antibiotics |CITS: [10446355]|., This pathway describes a catabolic route for |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| that has been described in several |FRAME: TAX-356| bacteria., About this Pathway, The key enzyme in this pathway is the NAD(P)H-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-16296|, which catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-9446|. The latter compound is presumably converted to |FRAME: MANNOSE| through a C1 oxygenation catalyzed by a P450 oxygenase enzyme |CITS: [16461673]|., The catabolism of D-mannose in Rhizobia proceeds by a two step conversion to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| via |FRAME: MANNOSE-6P| |CITS: [6286588]|., |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| is likely to be converted to |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| via |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.9|, as it has been shown that a gpi mutant of |FRAME: TAX-382| is not able to grow on D-mannose |CITS: [762017]|., |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| is fed to the oxidative branch of |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "the pentose phosphate"| pathway, forming |FRAME: CPD-2961|, which enters the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"| |CITS: [762017][3904617]|.

Summary: Adenosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: AMP| (AMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| , which is converted to AMP by the action of, |FRAME: ASL-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6126|). Note that the free base |FRAME: ADENINE| or the ribonucleoside |FRAME: ADENOSINE| are not produced via the de novo pathway., Many organisms can also recycle adenosine nucleotides by a combination of degradation and salvage pathways. The degradation pathways are responsible for the conversion of the nucleotides to the nucleoside (|FRAME: ADENOSINE|) and free base form (|FRAME: ADENINE|), and further degradation to compounds that can be catabolized to basic building blocks (for example, see |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|)., However, both |FRAME: ADENOSINE| and |FRAME: ADENINE| can be salvaged by certain enzymes, and be converted back to nucleotide form., The enzyme |FRAME: DEOD-CPLX "purine phosphorylase (DeoD)"| (EC 2.4.2.1) cleaves |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: ADENINE| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P|, while a second enzyme, such as |FRAME: ADENPRIBOSYLTRAN-CPLX|, can utilize |FRAME: PRPP| to convert the free base to the mononucleotide |FRAME: AMP|., Another route from |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: AMP| is acheived in a single step by the enzyme |FRAME: HS08097-MONOMER| (EC 2.7.1.20). The enzyme has been described in bacteria, yeast, plants and animals |CITS: [5092557][8577746][11115893][16511094][17869216][19329636]|.

Summary: General Background, Cannabinoids are terpenophenolics found in Indian hemp |FRAME: TAX-3483|. They accumulate in considerable amounts in glandular trichomes of hemp. Several compounds of this class have been the subject of extensive studies due to their psychotomimetic effects in humans, in preparations such as marijuana and hashish. Amongst the reported effects of the drugs are: changes in mood and perception, increased appetite and tachycardia. The compound responsible for these activities is |FRAME:CPD-7172| (THC). In addition to its psychoactivity, THC has been shown to act as an analgesic, appetite stimulant and antiemetic (for review, see |CITS:[PAGE06]|). Many cannabinoids are devoid of psychoactivity but sometimes possess notable pharmacological properties. For example, |FRAME:CPD-7173| (CBD), a cannabinoid present in high amount in low-THC hemp varieties, has anti-convulsive, anti-inflammatory, anti-anxiety and antinausea properties., About This Pathway, Most cannabinoids are derived from the condensation product of |FRAME:CPD-7165| with |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|., Olivetolate is synthesized from |FRAME: HEXANOYL-COA| by two enzymes - the polyketide synthase |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.206|, which condenses hexanoyl-CoA with three molecules of malonyl-CoA to yield a tetraketide, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.26| |CITS: [15120113][19454282][22802619]|., In the next step |FRAME:CPD-7165| is prenylated with |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|. A hemp enzyme (|FRAME:MONOMER-12031|) has been identified that can perform this reaction. The product of the reaction is the central branch-point intermediate |FRAME:CPD-7166| (CBGA). The enzyme can also use |FRAME: CPD-461|, but it prefers GPP. Several enzymes can catalyze the cyclization of CBGA, each forming a different cannabinoid cyclization product. Each of these enzymes was shown to be able to use |FRAME:CPD-7175| instead of CBGA, leading to the same cyclization product as CBGA |CITS:[9862135][8663284]|. The last step (decarboxylation) of this pathway occurs spontaneously in a non-enzymatic reaction during storage or smoking but is also found in vivo |CITS:[6115009][11043660]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN Dimethylsulfoniopropionate| (DMSP) is an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS:[12124622][17068264]|., DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|., Two main routes are known for DMSP degradation. In the first route DMSP is cleaved to |FRAME: CPD-7670| (forming |FRAME: ACRYLATE| or |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6046| and |FRAME: PWY-6056|, respectively), while in the second route DMSP is a demethylated to form |FRAME: CPD-7672| (MTPA) (see |FRAME: PWY-6052|), which is processed in different ways in different organisms., About This Pathway, This pathway describes a degradative pathway for |FRAME: CPD-7672| carried out by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-246200|. In this pathway, three enzymes related to fatty acid β-oxidation process |FRAME: CPD-7672| by its activation to |FRAME: CPD-13546|, reduction to |FRAME: CPD-13547|, and finally a decarboxylating hydrolysis to |FRAME: CPD-7671|, |FRAME: ACETALD|, and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [21562561]|., The cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-7672| with production of |FRAME: CPD-7671| has been known for a while, and reported in several organisms including the |FRAME: ORG-6057| |CITS: [16348607]|, |FRAME: ORG-6058| |CITS: [Diaz96]|, and |FRAME: TAX-28108| |CITS: [Ledyard93]|, although the details fo the pathway were not well understood, and the enzymes involved have not been characterized in any of these organisms., A study by Gonzalez reported 5 marine strains that were able to degrade DMSP by demthylation to MTPA, followed by cleavage to methanethiol and acrylate |CITS: [10473380]|. DMSP and methanethiol were used by these organisms as a source of sulfur for the biosynthesis of methionine and protein-sulfur |CITS: [10508088]|. An alternative proposal suggested that MMPA is catabolized in a mechanism similar to β-oxidation of fatty acids., The actual pathway was discovered only in 2011, by examination of CoA-containing intermediates produced by |FRAME: TAX-246200|, which revealed the presence of |FRAME: CPD-13546| |CITS: [21562561]|. The enzyme producing the compound was isolated, and the |FRAME: G-14624| gene encoding it identified. It was then shown that |FRAME: CPD-13546| was converted to |FRAME: CPD-13547| by crude cell extracts, and that the latter is processed to |FRAME: CPD-7671| and free CoA. The enzyme catalyzing the release of |FRAME: CPD-7671| was purified and the gene encoding it, |FRAME: G-14626|, was identified. Next to |FRAME: G-14626| was another gene, |FRAME: G-14625|, which was shown to encode the enzyme responsible for the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-13546| to |FRAME: CPD-13547|., Finally, upon purification of the |FRAME: G-14626| gene product, it was shown that the reaction produces not only |FRAME: CPD-7671| but also |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [21562561]|., Analysis of marine metagenomic data indicates that the pathway is widespread among bacterioplankton in the ocean surface waters, making it one of the most important known routes for acquisition of reduced carbon and sulphur by, surface ocean heterotrophs |CITS: [21562561]|.

Summary: Tropane alkaloids are found mostly in plants that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-4070| family. They include the medicinal alkaloids |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE| and |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE| that act on mammalian nervous systems. The alkaloids have very complex structures. The commercial natural sources of the alkaloids are plants in the genera of |FRAME: TAX-195735|, |FRAME: TAX-221161|, and |FRAME: TAX-4074|., The pathway has been studied in detail, and currently all of the enzymes involved have been discovered., There are two tropinone reductases, which catalyze the stereo-specific reduction of tropinone and give rise to separate alkaloid groups, encoded by |FRAME: G-10563| and |FRAME: G-10566| |CITS: [16653065]|. The medicinal alkaloids |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE| and |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE| are derived from |FRAME: TROPINE|, the product of tropinone reductase I (|FRAME: G-10563|), while the calystegines, a family of non-medicinal nortropane alkaloids, are derived from |FRAME: PSEUDOTROPINE|, the product of tropinone reductase II (|FRAME: G-10566|) (see |FRAME: PWY-5318|)., |FRAME: TROPINE Tropine| condenses with the phenylalanine-derived |FRAME: CPD-24928| to form |FRAME: CPD-7996| |CITS: [ 31705812]|, which is converted to |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE|, and subsequently to |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE| via |FRAME: CPD-2202|.  , Enzymes catalyzing different steps of scopolamine biosynthesis, specifically, the tropinone reductase and hyoscyamine 6-hydroxylase, were detected in different cell compartments and cell types, suggesting that the pathway intermediates are transported, crossing different compartments and cell types |CITS: [10635114]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Surfactins Surfactins| are a family of bacterial cyclic lipopeptide antibiotics. They are composed of a heptapeptide attached to a β-hydroxy fatty acid chain with which it forms a lactone ring structure. They were discovered in 1969 from cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [Kakinuma69]|, but since then were found to be produced by multiple species of Bacillus |CITS: [36833349]|, Paenibacillus |CITS: [36828452]|, and Pseudomonas |CITS: [39549338]|, as well as some fungi |CITS: [31522524][37603063]|., The cononical sequence of the peptide is L-Glu(1)-L-Leu(2)-D-Leu(3)-L-Val(4)-L-Asp(5)-D-Leu(6)-L-Leu(7) (|FRAME: CPD-26914|). However, while the amino acid composition always follows the pattern LLDLLDL, there is considerable variability due to the promiscuity of the polyketide synthases that form the peptide chain. In addition, the fatty acid side chain can range from C9 to C19, with C14 and C15 being the main variants, and can be either linear or branched. The different variations were categorized into four subclasses: surfactins, lichenysins, pumilacidins and esperins |CITS: [32695084][Sarubbo22]|., Surfactin is among the most effective biosurfactants, and can reduce the surface tension of water from 72 to 27 mN/m at a concentration as low as 0.005% |CITS: [ 8054476]|., About This Pathway, The organization of the biosynthetic gene cluster of surfactin in |FRAME: TAX-1423| was studied by several different labs. It comprises four genes, encoding three large modular nonribosomal peptide synthetases (SrfAA, SrfAB, and SrfAC) and a thiesterase (SrfAD) |CITS: [2848009][8355609][8441623][8142480][15366943]|. Curiously, the comS gene, which encodes a regulator required for competence, is located within the srfAB gene and it is co-expressed with the srfA operon |CITS: [7752896]|., SrfAA thioesterifies |FRAME: GLT| and two |FRAME: LEU| residues (the second Leu residue converted to D stereo configuration). It also contains a special N-terminal condensation domain that is responsible for the acylation reaction |CITS: [20797616]|. SrfAB incorporates |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: VAL|, and |FRAME: LEU| as thioesters (again, the Leu residue converted to D stereo configuration), and SrfAC is a one-module enzyme that contributes the C-terminal |FRAME: LEU| residue. SrfAC also contains a thioesterase domain that releases the heptapeptide chain from the polyketide synthase and catalyzes its cyclization., SrfAD is a second thioesterase that participates in the early stages of surfactin biosynthesis, promoting the hydrolysis of fatty acyl-CoA molecules that serve as the acyl donors for surfactin |CITS: [15366943]|.

In the absence of an external oxidant, glycerol is fermented by a dismutation process involving two pathways (see |FRAME: GOLPDLCAT-PWY|)., Through one of the pathways, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-573 "Klebsiella pneumoniae 1033 (previously known as Aerobacter aerogenes 1033)"|, glycerol is dehydrogenated by an NAD+-linked |FRAME: CPLX-3681| (E.C. 1.1.1.6) to |FRAME: DIHYDROXYACETONE|, which is then phosphorylated and funneled to glycolysis by |FRAME: CPLX-3605| |CITS:[13108864][13438878]|. This pathway is also found in |FRAME: TAX-284812| |CITS: [9804990]|.

Both compounds are eventually converted to |FRAME: GLUCONATE|., The metabolism of |FRAME: 25-DIDEHYDRO-D-GLUCONATE| was studied mostly due to the fact that one of the intermediates, |FRAME: CPD-13059|, is the precursor for the commercial biosynthesis of |FRAME: ASCORBATE "vitamin C"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7165|).,  A mutant (GB44) that produces |FRAME: CPD-13059| but not |FRAME: CPD-377| has been obtained |CITS: [Sonoyama87]|., Studies with cell-free extracts of |FRAME: ORG-6226| suggested that multiple NADPH-dependent enzymes catalyze the following conversions:, |FRAME: 25-DIDEHYDRO-D-GLUCONATE| to |FRAME: CPD-377|, |FRAME: 25-DIDEHYDRO-D-GLUCONATE| to |FRAME: CPD-13059|, |FRAME: CPD-377| to |FRAME: GLUCONATE|, |FRAME: CPD-13059| to |FRAME: L-IDONATE|, |FRAME: L-IDONATE| to |FRAME: 5-DEHYDROGLUCONATE|, |FRAME: 5-DEHYDROGLUCONATE| to |FRAME: L-IDONATE|, |FRAME: 5-DEHYDROGLUCONATE| to |FRAME: GLUCONATE|, |FRAME: GLUCONATE| to |FRAME: CPD-377|, The authors concluded that in |FRAME: ORG-6226| two |FRAME: 25-DIDEHYDRO-D-GLUCONATE| degradative pathways leading to |FRAME: GLUCONATE| operate simultaneously |CITS: [Sonoyama87]|., |FRAME:TAX-562| contains ketogluconate reductase genes, so it is likely that pathways exist for the metabolism of ketogluconate |CITS: [10427017] [9811658]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycolysis, which was first studied as a pathway for the utilization of glucose, is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, the other two being the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| and the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. In organisms that possess a glycolysis pathway, it is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces six of the 13 precursor metabolites that are the starting materials for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules (the six compounds are |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:G3P|, |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). While not universal, glycolysis is very common., Even though glycolysis is often described starting with glucose, other hexoses (e.g. fructose) can also serve as input (as its name implies - glycose is a general term for simple sugars)., Glycolysis has evolved to fulfill two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) being an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism), it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy., This switching of direction is possible because all but two of the enzymatic reactions comprising glycolysis are reversible, and the conversions catalyzed by the two exceptions are rendered functionally reversible by other enzymes (|FRAME:F16B-CPLX "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase"| and |FRAME:PEPSYNTH-CPLX|) that catalyze different irreversible reactions flowing in the opposite direction., About This Pathway, This pathway diagram describes the well characterized glycolysis pathway of the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| growing with |FRAME: D-Glucose| as a source of carbon and energy. Glucose enters the cell via a phosphotransferase system (|FRAME: EC-2.7.1.199|), and the first intracellular species, therefore, is |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|., While |FRAME:TAX-562| does constitutively produce |FRAME:EC-2.7.1.2| (the intracellular enzyme that converts glucose to glucose-6-phosphate), it is not needed for the utilization of glucose |CITS: [9023215]|., Other substrates may enter glycolysis at different stages. For example, the sugars and sugar alcohols |FRAME: D-Allose|, |FRAME:SORBOSE|, |FRAME:MANNITOL|, |FRAME:SORBITOL|, |FRAME:MANNOSE| and |FRAME:SUCROSE|, which are processed into |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, enter the pathway at that stage (see |FRAME: PWY-5484|). , For reviews, please see: Romeo, T. and J. L. Snoep, |CITS: [EcoSal]| module 3.5.1.; Fraenkel, D. G. |CITS: [colisalII]| p. 189-198.

Summary: Pathogenic Bacillus species, such as |FRAME: TAX-1396|, |FRAME: TAX-1392|, and |FRAME: TAX-1428|, produce an exopolysaccharide during the late stage of stationary growth phase. The polysaccharide, named pzX, is composed of an unusual |FRAME: CPD-26909 "three amino-sugar sequence repeat"| of [-3)XylNAc4OAc(α1→3)GlcNAcA4OAc(α1→3)XylNAc(α1→]n |CITS: [27402849]|., |FRAME: CPD-26910|, the third sugar of the trisaccharide repeat unit, is produced in the form of |FRAME: CPD-26905| from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| via |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-2-AMINO-D-GLUCURONATE|. The enzymes catalyzing formation of this nucleotide sugar have been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-1396| |CITS: [20529859]|. The first sugar of the repeat unit is a 4-O-acetylated version of that sugar. However, the acetyltransferase responsible for this modification has not been identified as of 2024, and it is not known whether acetylation takes place on the nucleotide sugar level, or following incorporation into the polymer.

Polyamines are polycationic hydrocarbon molecules with multiple amino groups. They include the diamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, the triamines |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (sym-norspermidine) and |FRAME: CPD-1821| (homospermidine), and the tetraamine |FRAME: SPERMINE| (in |CITS: [20194510]| and in |CITS: [19196710]|)., Polyamines are found in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes and are necessary for normal cellular physiology. In prokaryotic cells, most polyamines are bound to phosphate groups of RNA, even though they can also bind to DNA, free nucleotides, and phospholipids |CITS: [10814501]|. Polyamines may enhance protein synthesis by causing conformational changes of some mRNAs; they are scavengers of free radicals and thus reduce oxidative damage of macromolecules; the positive charge of polyamines provides a mechanism for acid resistance; they contibute to osmotic tolerance |CITS: [14612248]|; and are involved in a cold acclimation response |CITS: [21421344][37878710]|., |FRAME: SPERMIDINE Spermidine| is the dominant polyamine in the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148|; only trace amounts of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME: SPERMINE| have been observed in the organism |CITS: [20680281]|. However, the pathway leading to spermidine biosynthesis in Synechocystis was discovered only in 2023 |CITS: [37878710]|. The pathway was shown to proceed via a previously unknown metabolite, |FRAME: CPD2PN3-12|, which is produced by reductive condensation of |FRAME: AGMATHINE| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|. The product is then decarboxylated into |FRAME: CPD-13489|, which is hydrolyzed to produce |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| and urea., The pathway's genes are widespread among Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidetes, and particularly in delta- and epsilonproteobacteria (it appears to be the predominant pathway for spermidine biosynthesis in the latter). Even though the pathway was discovered in a cyanobacterium, orthologs of |FRAME: SGL_RS07180| (encoding |FRAME: SGL_RS07180-MONOMER|) were detected in only 10 of the 184 cyanobacterial species |CITS: [37878710]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1773| and other pathogenic mycobacterial species produce a capsular layer outside the bacterial wall and plasma membrane that is thought to be involved in immune evasion and virulence |CITS: [13630872][13711244]|. The capsular layer is composed of |FRAME: GlgE-Glycogen "GlgE-glycogen"| (also known as α-glucan) (80-90%) and arabinomannan (10-20%) polysaccharides, proteins of the ESX-1 secretion system, and small amounts of lipid |CITS: [20221442]|. The |FRAME: GlgE-Glycogen "GlgE-glycogen"| structure resembles classical |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|, consisting of relatively short chains of α (1->4)-linked glucose molecules, which are connected to each other in a branching pattern by α (1->6) bonds |CITS: [8297342][10656114][21341078]|. However, the polymer differs from classical glycogen in several aspects. The chains are shorter, consisting of 7 sugars vs 11. In addition, the branching pattern is different - while there are more α-1,6 branches than in glycogen (14% vs 9%), fewer branches come off each branch (1.2-1.6 vs 1.8-1.9 in glycogen) |CITS: [27221142]|., About This Pathway, The main carbon source of |FRAME: TAX-1773| within its natural human host is largely fatty acids rather than sugars. The fatty acids are broken down to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| via β-oxidation pathways, and the |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| is converted to |FRAME: MAL| via the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|. In order to produce the sugars that are necessary for glycogen biosynthesis, the bacteria need to convert the |FRAME: MAL| to |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| via |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis|., Glucose 6-phosphate feeds into GlgE-glycogen biosynthesis in mycobacteria via two routes, both of which proceed via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-13997|., In one of the routes |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| is first combined with |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| to form |FRAME: TREHALOSE-6P| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: G-4501 OtsA| |CITS: [Lapp71][8842710][12473104]|, and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: G-4502 OtsB|, forming |FRAME: TREHALOSE| |CITS: [4327508][12417583]|. Two more steps, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-4523| and |FRAME: G185E-4244| genes, which form a complex, convert |FRAME: TREHALOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-13997| |CITS: [15511231][20507595][23601637][23901909]|., In the second route |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| is converted by phosphoglucomutase into |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is then combined with |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| to form |FRAME: CPD-13997|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: G185E-5382 GlgM|, which was previously (but incorrectly) thought to be a GlgA glycogen synthase |CITS: [27513637]|. The preferred route to |FRAME: CPD-13997| depends on the species and the growth conditions |CITS: [27513637]|., Note that both of these routes require |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE|, which is produced from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.27| (|FRAME: G185E-5383 GlgC|) |CITS: [18808383][25277548]|. In general, |FRAME:ADP-D-GLUCOSE| is devoted to the synthesis of glycogen in bacteria (with the exception of the synthesis of the osmoprotectant |FRAME: CPD-16855 glucosylglycerol| in cyanobacteria) and its synthesis defines the first committed step of glycogen synthesis., Once |FRAME: CPD-13997| is formed, it feeds |FRAME: EC-2.4.99.16| (|FRAME: G185E-5506 GlgE|), an enzyme that extend 1,4-α-glucan chains by adding disaccharide units |CITS: [20305657]|. Finally, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.18| (|FRAME: G185E-5505 GlgB|) catalyzes the cleavage of an α-(1,4)-glucosidic linkage in the α-glucan and the subsequent transfer of the cleaved oligosaccharide to form a new α-(1,6)-branch, generating the branched GlgE-glycogen structure |CITS: [17005418]|., A unique feature of this pathway is the fact that the building block used for synthesizing the polymer is a phosphorylated form, |FRAME: CPD-13997|. In all other known glycogen biosynthetic pathways the building blocks are nucleotide-activated sugars - eukaryotes use |FRAME: CPD-12575|, while bacteria with the classical |FRAME: EG10377 "GlgA polymerase"| use |FRAME:ADP-D-GLUCOSE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5067| and |FRAME:GLYCOGENSYNTH-PWY|)., Studies have shown that the GlgE pathway produces both the intracellular and capsular GlgE-glycogen found in |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [27513637]|. By contrast, the GlgE pathway in streptomycetes generates only intracellular GlgE-glycogen |CITS: [27121970]|. The GlgE pathway genes are present in 14% of sequenced bacterial genomes |CITS: [21474533]|, while the classical bacterial glycogen biosynthetic gene glgA is present in ~20% |CITS: [27513637]|., A related pathway is the hydrolysis of glycogen to form |FRAME: TREHALOSE|, which is catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-4323|, |FRAME: G-4321|, and |FRAME: G-4322| genes (see |FRAME: PWY-2661|).

Summary: The catabolism of fatty acids proceeds via several routes, which depend on the length of the acids, whether the number of carbons is odd or even, and whether they are saturated or unsaturated. This pathway represents the "core" cycle of β-oxidation, a mechanism that removes two carbon atoms with each turn of the cycle. This pathway plays an important role in bacteria and eukaryotes |CITS: [627552][1998729][20195903][ 32310462]|, and has been demonstrated in certain archaea |CITS: [24818264][30948713]|., Saturated fatty acids that are routed into this core pathway are processed until only two or three carbons remain. When even-numbered fatty acids are broken down, the final product is the two-carbon compound |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which is a basic intermediate of central metabolism, and can be routed into the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| for complete catabolism or routed into the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS| to be used for biosynthesis., When odd number fatty acids are broken down, the final product of the pathway is the three-carbon compound |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, which in |FRAME:TAX-562| is carboxylated to |FRAME: Methylmalonyl-CoA| and converted to |FRAME: SUC-COA| (see |FRAME: PROPIONMET-PWY|). , Unsaturated fatty acids with cis double bonds located at odd-numbered carbon atoms enter the main pathway after a modification (see |FRAME: PWY-5137|). When cis double bonds are located at even-numbered carbon atoms (such as in |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|), the acids are modified by a different route (see |FRAME: PWY-5138|)., Although enzymes of the pathway handle both short and long chain fatty acids, it is the long chain compounds that induce the enzymes of the pathway |CITS: [6271734]|. , The pathway under anaerobic conditions, In the facultative anaerobic bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562| the pathway can proceed under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [12535077]|. The enzymatic steps are identical, and the main difference is that the product of the pathway, acetyl-CoA, is oxidized using fumarate as the terminal electron acceptor |CITS: [15213221]|. However, a different set of enzymes is active under anaerobic conditions. In the anaerobic pathway FadI, FadJ, and FadK serve functions parallel to those of FadA, FadB, and FadD in the aerobic pathway |CITS: [12535077]|. In contrast to the aerobic pathway, octanoate and decanoate can serve as substrates for the anaerobic fatty acid oxidation pathway |CITS: [12535077]|. , The |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS| is necessary under both anaerobic and aerobic conditions of fatty acid oxidation to provide the carbon and energy for cell growth |CITS: [12535077]|.
