Summary: General Background, A family of 19-membered macrocyclic lactam antibiotics, which were named maytansinoids, was isolated from the Ethiopian shrub |FRAME: TAX-1696185| in 1975. Members of this family, such as |FRAME: CPD-25407|, were found to possess extremely potent cytotoxicity against various tumor cells |CITS: [1241159][628025][367597][3834790][20937594]|., Shortly after that discovery highly related compounds were discovered in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-42198| |CITS: [593392]|. These new compounds, which were named |FRAME: Ansamitocins ansamitocins|, differed structurally from the maytansinoids only by carrying simpler acyl groups at C-3, and the two names (maytansinoids and ansamitocin) are now used interchangeably. Related compounds were later observed in moss species |CITS: [3204376][2298279]|. Structurally, the compounds belong to the |FRAME: Ansamycins ansamycin| family of polyketide macrolactams, which are defined by consisting of an aromatic moiety bridged at nonadjacent positions by an aliphatic chain |CITS: [4148590]|., The bacterial-derived ansamitocins were found to have the same activity against tumor cells as the plant compounds |CITS: [6245801][7380728]|. This activity is a result of the compounds' affinity towards |FRAME: Beta-tubulins β-tubulin| in eukaryotic cells, which inhibits microtubule assembly and chromosome segregation during the interphase and mitotic phase and causes cell apoptosis |CITS: [24124473]|. The identified |FRAME: CPD-25407|-binding site was shown to be distinct from that of |FRAME: CPD-7858| |CITS: [25114240]|. In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-25396| was shown to bind to the cell division protein FtsZ |CITS: [32365857]|., A derivative of |FRAME: CPD-25407|, named |FRAME: CPD-25409|, is used in several antibody-drug conjugates. One of those, trastuzumab emtansine, sold under the brand name Kadcyla, is currently used for treatment of HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer in some patients., About This Pathway, Like many other ansamycins, the biosynthesis of ansamitocin starts with the unusual polyketide starter unit, |FRAME: CPD-10231| (AHBA). Taking advantage of this fact, the ansamitocin biosynthetic gene cluster was identified using the |FRAME: G-10753| gene of |FRAME: TAX-33910|, which participates in |FRAME: PWY-5979|. Two clusters separated by 30 kb were identified, with one cluster containing most of the ansamitocin biosynthetic genes, and the other cluster carrying only four of the seven genes required for AHBA formation |CITS: [12060743]|., Following the synthesis of the starter unit, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-5979|, biosynthesis continues with a very large |FRAME: CPLX-9704| (PKS) consisting of 4 polyketide synthase proteins encoded by the |FRAME: G-107659|-|FRAME: G-107662| genes. The PKS loads the |FRAME: CPD-10231| starting unit and extends it by accepting extender units from three molecules of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, three molecules of |FRAME: Methylmalonyl-CoA|, and one molecule of the unusual extender unit |FRAME: CPD-25408|, which is synthesized on a dedicated acyl-carrier protein |CITS: [11996558]|., Following the formation of the polyketide skeleton, the nascent chain is terminated, cyclyzed, and released from the PKS complex as the first free intermeidate, |FRAME: CPD-21936|. Biosynthesis proceeds by multiple tailoring enzymes that include a halogenase |CITS: [14624546]|, an Omethyltransferase |CITS: [14624546]|, a carbamoyltransferase |CITS: [22195559]|, an acyltransferase |CITS: [12047169]|, and an epoxidase |CITS: [14624546]|, forming |FRAME: N-demethylansamitocins|. That compound can be either N-methylated to form |FRAME: Ansamitocins| |CITS: [21681880]|, or glycosylated to form |FRAME: Ansamitocinosides| |CITS: [18721757]|. An ansamitocinoside with a carbamoylated glucosyl moiety has also been observed |CITS: [22195559]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:CPD-844 "Carbon disulfide"| (CS2) is a geochemically abundant trace gas with both natural and, anthropogenic sources. The gas has an atmospheric life time of 7-12 days, but the product of its oxidation, |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE|, has a half life of at least one year |CITS: [Jordan95]|. , |FRAME:CPD-844 "Carbon disulfide"| has several biogenic sources, totalling at least one million tonnes annually., The main inputs of CS2 to the atmosphere are from the degradation of sulfur-containing compounds in soils, manures, and decomposing plant material. Five plant species, including the |FRAME:TAX-3808| tree and valley oak (|FRAME: TAX-97700|), are known to produce CS2, which acts as a fungicide., CS2 is widely used as an industrial solvent and is also used as a fumigant in agriculture, and most human, exposure to CS2 occurs occupationally in the viscoserayon and rubber industries. In addition to industrial and agricultural exposure, therapeutic agents such as diethyldithiocarbamates (DDCs) and |FRAME: DISULFIRAM| (antabuse) are a potential source for direct human exposure to CS2. These drugs rapidly break down in the body to CS2, which can target vital organs such as the heart, brain, and liver |CITS: [9077576][9625138]|., Exposure to CS2 has been associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, ischemic heart disease mortality, and adverse effects on the nervous system including parkinsonism and peripheral neuropathy |CITS: [ 9339488][16503300]|. Occupational exposure has also been associated with multiple reproductive effects |CITS: [6429901][8721625][10627660]|., In rats CS2 has been shown to produce hepatic necrosis, but only if the animals were previously exposed to compounds that are known to induce liver cytochrome P450 enzymes, such as CYP1A1, CYP2B1, CYP2E1, and CYP3A2 |CITS: [237636][3760457][24082506]|. The reason is that CS2 is a suicide substrate of these enzymes, which oxidize it to reactive sulfur atoms before becoming inactivated. The reactive sulfur atoms are, at least in part, responsible for the toxicity |CITS: [Dalvi09]|., About This Pathway, Several labs have shown that CS2 is a substrate for multiple microsomal cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases |CITS: [4150011][DeMatteis74][4152175][237636][Catignani75]|. Preliminary induction of various CYP enzymes results in much higher CS2 degrading activity. CYP enzymes that have been implicated in this transformation include CYP2B1, which was induced by |FRAME: CPD-20313| and |FRAME: CPD-20498| |CITS: [237636][14732219][24082506]|, CYP2E1, which was induced by |FRAME: ETOH| |CITS: [3760457]|, and CYP1A1 and CYP3A2, which were induced by |FRAME: CPD-20498| |CITS: [24082506]|., The rest of the pathway was investigated in isolated rat hepatocytes and liver microsomes |CITS: [3814176]|. Initially it was assumed that CS2 is converted directly to |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE|, which has been documented to be decarboxylated by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.1| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [6775392][PROTOSCHILL-KREBS96]|. However, treatment with |FRAME: CPD0-1626|, an inhibitor of carbonic anhydrase, did not inhibit the metabolism of CS2 to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, indicating the existence of an alternative route., Experiments with stable and radioactive isotopes as well as the use of several inhibitors suggested that CS2 is oxygenated to an unstable intermediate, most likely |FRAME: CPD-20499|. This intermediate reacts with water to form |FRAME:CPD-8042| (the hydrated form of COS) and a reactive sulfur species. In intact hepatocytes, |FRAME:CPD-8042| is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: HS| in a reaction that does not involve carbonic anhydrase. However, |FRAME: CPD-8042| and |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE| exist in equilibrium, and unmetabolized |FRAME:CPD-8042| can be dehydrated to |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE|, which is decarboxylated by carbonic anhydrase |CITS: [6775392]|., While some of the reactive sulfur species that is formed by the spontaneous decomposition of |FRAME: CPD-20499| may bind to the cytochromes, making CS2 a suicide substrate, the majority is metabolized to more stable non-volatile sulfur compounds by unknown mechanisms. The second sulfur atom, which is released in the form of |FRAME: HS|, which is rapidly metabolized by rat liver first to |FRAME: S2O3| (by |FRAME: HS06393-MONOMER|) and subsequently to |FRAME: SULFATE|, the ultimate product of CS2 degradation |CITS: [3814176]|.

Fructans are a class of highly water-soluble polysaccharides consisting of linear or branched |FRAME:FRU| chains attached to |FRAME: SUCROSE| by β-2,1or β-2,6-linkage. They are produced extracellularly by many bacteria growing on sucrose, and they also represent a major nonstructural carbohydrate in many plant species, including major crop plants such as wheat and barley. In plants, fructans accumulate in roots, tubers, bulbs, stems, leaves, and seeds. In addition to their function as storage carbohydrates, fructans may have functions involved in drought and cold tolerance,, and osmoregulation., The principal fructans formed by bacteria are called levans, and are composed of long β 2->6-linked chains of fructosyl units attached to the 6-fructosyl position of sucrose. They are synthesized by the enzyme levansucrase (EC 2.4.1.10), which cleaves sucrose, releases glucose, and attaches the remaining fructosyl residue initially to another molecule of sucrose and then to the growing fructan chain., Plant fructans, in contrast, have more varied structures, and their biosynthesis is not well understood. They are synthesized from sucrose in the vacuole, where their initial synthesis requires a sucrose:sucrose fructosyltransferase. The oligofructans are then served as the acceptor in fructosyl transferring during the synthesis of fructan polymers. Synthesis of the linear polymerfructans (G-F-Fn or Fm-F-G-F-Fn) requires a fructan: fructan fructosyltransferase. Synthesis of branched fructans requires a sucrose:fructan fructosyltransferase.

The pathway of synthesis of threonine from homoserine is a two-step pathway that converts homoserine, to threonine by way of a phosphorylated intermediate., The final product of this pathway, threonine, serves as a structural constituent of proteins and feeds into the, biosynthetic pathway for isoleucine. The enzymes carrying out both steps in this pathway are regulated, at the gene level by threonine- and isoleucine-dependent attenuation, as part of attenuation control, of an operon that also includes a gene coding for an enzyme in the upstream pathway of homoserine, biosynthesis.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|). Analogs of these pathways are also found in the metabolism of deoxyhexoses such as |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-fucoses| (see |FRAME: RHAMCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|). The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]|.
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|). The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimnberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]|.
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, This D-arabinose degradation pathway, characterized from |FRAME: TAX-37762|, belongs to the first type of pathways mentioned above. The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-5901|, which also participates in the degradation of L-fucose |CITS: [4359656]|. The pathway continues with the |FRAME: RIBITOLUTIL-PWY| pathway enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.47| yielding |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, which is fed to the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [7961494]|., The related organism |FRAME: TAX-83333| does not possess any of the pathways described above. Rather, that organism degrades D-arabinose using the enzymes of the |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY| pathway (see |FRAME: DARABCATK12-PWY|).

General Background, Almost all vascular plants possess basic, water soluble anthocyanins such as delphinidin-3-O-glucoside (this pathway) responsible for the blue coloration of flowers and fruits and/or pelargonidin-3-O-glucoside and cyaniding-3-O-glucoside (|FRAME:PWY-5125|) generating red to magenta colors in the floral organs of plants |CITS: [11130659]|., Anthocyanins play important roles as pigments of flowers and fruits in numerous plants across the plant kingdom to attract insects for pollination and seed dispersion and act as protectants against UV-B irradiation |CITS: [14561507]|. They also exhibit anti-oxidant activities and therefore may serve as potential anticancer |CITS: [16084717]| and anti-arteriosclerosis compounds in human health |CITS: [15282635]| |CITS: [12828368]| |CITS: [11960739]|. Anthocyanines constitute biological active metabolites that also modulate inter-species relationships being intimately connected with the co-existence of plants with, e.g. insects, mammals, and birds |CITS: [11820759]|., About This Pathway, As described for the biosynthesis of pelargonidin- (see |FRAME:PWY-7267| and cyanidin-derived (see |FRAME:PWY-5125|) anthocyanins delphinidin-based pigments are built up in a series of two enzymes, the anthocyanidin synthase (ANS - synonym leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase - LDOX) converting leucodelphinidin to delphinidin and the UDPG: flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferase (3-UGT) producing the first stable anthocyanin of this pathway, i.e. delphinidin 3-O-glucoside |CITS: [Kitamura06]| (for a more comprehensive comment see - |FRAME:PWY-5125|)., The anthocyanidin synthase has been proposed to be a component of a macromolecular complex located at the endoplasmatic reticulum. In dependence on the enzymes involved in the complex (e.g. flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylase) and their metabolic order the ANS is involved in the production of delphinidin-derived pigments as found in bilberry |CITS: [12376640]| and recombinant petunia ANS expressed with 3-UGT in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [11316805]|. However, specific data addressing this reaction with regard to kinetic parameter and substrate specificity remain to be reported., The flavonoid 3-O-glucosyltransferases involved in this pathway have been found to cover a broader spectrum of anthocyanidins with a somewhat higher affinity towards delphinidin in |FRAME:TAX-29760| |CITS: [9535914]| and |FRAME:TAX-55190| |CITS: [8819318]| representing species containing delphinidin-derived anthocyanins.

Summary: Isoprenoids are among the most diverse and widely distributed natural compounds. They include both, essential products (sterols, quinones, prenylated proteins, chlorophylls) and secondary metabolites, (plant terpenoids and hormones) |CITS: [15024605]|., In this pathway |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| and multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain of nine units, known as, |FRAME: CPD-21340| or solanesyl diphosphate., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME: TAX-1061| enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-13766|., Isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme. Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., On the other hand, the enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., Quinones with nine isoprenyl units in the side chains are very common. They are the predominant form of plastoquinones, found in green plants and cyanobacteria, and are the major quinones in some large Gram-negative and Gram-positive genera, including the Pseudomonads and the Streptococci., For a review detailing the distribution of polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|., Nine-isoprenyl quinones are also found in many animals, including the rat.

Summary: The rumen holotrich protozoon |FRAME: TAX-40806| produces |FRAME:ACET|, |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID|, |FRAME:Lactate|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| by the fermentation of various soluble sugars |CITS: [10343]|., Like some other anaerobic protozoal species, |FRAME: TAX-40806| lacks mitochondria, and instead possesses a unique organelle called the hydrogenosome |CITS: [6803778 ]|. Like mitochondria, the hydrogenosomes are surrounded by double membranes, but unlike mitochondria they contain no DNA., As in other anaerobic eukaryotes that contain hydrogenosomes, such as |FRAME: TAX-5722|, the key step of |FRAME:PYRUVATE| oxidative decarboxylation, along with formation of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-40806| by the hydrogenosomal protein |FRAME: MONOMER-13306| (also known as pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase) and not by the ubiquitous pyruvate dehydrogenase multienzyme complex., However, the following step of the pathway, in which |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| is converted into |FRAME:ACET|, is catalyzed in a route that is very unusual among eukaryotes, and involves the intermediate |FRAME: ACETYL-P| |CITS: [6293462]|. These two reactions are catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-13305| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13304|., |FRAME: TAX-40806| also produces butyrate from acetyl-CoA |CITS: [3924032]|. The corresponding enzymes have been detected: acetyl-CoA:acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase, 3-hydroxybutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase, hydroxyacyl-CoA hydrolyase,, 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA reductase, phosphate butyryltransferase, and butyrate kinase, which catalyzes the energy conserving step. Butyrate production happens in the cytosol. since Acetyl-CoA is produced in the hydrogenosome, it is probably exported into the cytosol |CITS: [Muller88]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: s-Triazines| herbicide |FRAME: ATRAZINE| is a widely used that is persistant in the soil., It is prone to ground and surface water contamination. Some countries such as Germany, Italy,, Norway and Sweden have banned its use because of its widespread presence in water |CITS: [16162227]|., A range of soil bacteria, including both Gram-negative and Gram-positive strains can degrade atrazine,, utilizing it as a nitrogen and carbon source., This pathway of |FRAME: s-Triazines| degradation was studied in detail in the bacterium, |FRAME: TAX-134561|., In this organism sequential hydrolytic reactions convert |FRAME: ATRAZINE| to, |FRAME: HYDROXYATRAZINE| and then to the end product |FRAME: CPD-807|. Oxygen was not, required for atrazine degradation by either whole cells or cell extracts., The |FRAME: CPLX-7533| from |FRAME: TAX-134561| was isolated and purified. The enzyme was able, to convert a range of chlorine or methylthio-substituted herbicides to the corresponding hydroxy, derivatives |CITS: [10919761]|. The second enzyme in this pathway has not been identified, but, |FRAME: ISOPROPYLAMINE|, the putative product of the second hydrolytic reaction, supported growth, of this organism as the sole carbon and nitrogen source., A similar |FRAME:TAX-1839| strain that possesses the same pathway was isolated and described, by Smith et al |CITS: [16329946]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10290| is an antibiotic that is biosynthesized by |FRAME: CPLX-7650|, a bacterial,, non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS). Bacterial strains that produce |FRAME: CPD-10290| have undergone, taxonomic reclassification since the original strain, named |FRAME:ORG-6045| var. G.B., was isolated in, 1942. |FRAME: TAX-47500| is a reclassification of |FRAME:ORG-6045| var. G.B, which also referred to in the, literature as |FRAME:ORG-5879| ATCC 9999 and |FRAME:ORG-5879| DSM 2895 |CITS: [17720841] [8863420]|. The, literature also refers to a |FRAME: CPD-10290| producing strain named |FRAME: ORG-6045|, |CITS: [6049476] [5354026] [2691508] [7822255] [9348091]|. |FRAME:ORG-6045| Migula 1900 (ATCC number, 8246) is listed as a separate taxon, |FRAME: TAX-1393| |CITS: [8863420]|. , Chemically, this antibiotic is a cyclic, cationic, amphipathic, decapeptide. Its backbone is a double-stranded,, antiparallel β-sheet connected by type II β-turns at the ends. |FRAME: CPD-10290| interacts with, cell membranes causing deformation, probable pore formation, and cell lysis, although details of its mechanism, of action are still being investigated |CITS: [18621820]|. It is active against many Gram-positive and Gram-negative, bacteria, as well as fungi. However, it also causes hemolysis of mammalian erythrocytes and is therefore used, only as a topical antibiotic. There is interest in developing antimicrobial analogs of |FRAME: CPD-10290| that, are less hemolytic |CITS: [17181140] [15686540]|., Early work on |FRAME: CPD-10290| biosynthesis established that an enzyme system was responsible for, |FRAME: CPD-10290| biosynthesis and that enzyme-bound intermediates were involved. Five different amino, acids |FRAME: CPD-216|, |FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME: LEU| each, occur twice in the cyclic decapeptide |CITS: [5506580] [11947433] [4297916] [6049476]|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-7650| is encoded by genes |FRAME: G-10798| (encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-14128|) and, |FRAME: G-10799| (encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-14129|). These gene products are large, multidomain, polypeptides (reviewed in |CITS: [15487945]| and in |CITS: [16895337]|). |FRAME: MONOMER-14128| comprises, module 1, which contains three domains: an adenylation domain, a thiolation domain and an epimerization, domain. The thiolation domain is referred to in the literature as the T, holo-[acyl-carrier protein], ACP,, peptidyl-carrier protein, or PCP domain (the latter two names are used in the case of non-ribosomal peptide, synthetases). This domain is created, from an apo form that is posttranslationally modified by phosphopantetheinyltransferase-catalyzed, covalent attachment of |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| (derived from |FRAME: CO-A|) to a conserved serine residue, (in |CITS:[16895337]| |CITS:[8939709]|)., As described in |CITS: [16195555]|, the adenylation domain of |FRAME: MONOMER-14128| binds |FRAME: PHE|,, activates it by adenylation using |FRAME: ATP| and forms the intermediate |FRAME: PHE| bound through a, thioester linkage to the peptidyl carrier protein domain (PCP domain). The epimerization domain epimerizes |FRAME: PHE|, to |FRAME: CPD-216| resulting in a D-phenylalanine-bound holo-[acyl-carrier protein] as shown in the first (combined), reaction here. This epimerization (racemization) is described by |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.11| (|FRAME: 5.1.1.11-RXN|), |CITS: [5354026]|., The polypeptide chain is then extended by |FRAME: MONOMER-14129|. This multimodular polypeptide contains, modules 2-5. These modules each contain adenylation, condensation and thiolation domains, with module 5, also containing a thioesterase domain. To extend the polypeptide chain, the adenylation domain of module 2, binds and activates |FRAME: PRO| and the condensation domain catalyzes peptide bond formation, with |FRAME: CPD-216| (see |CITS: [16195555] [17254948]| and for illustrations). |FRAME: VAL|,, |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME: LEU| are similarly joined via adenylation, condensation and thiolation, domains in modules 3, 4 and 5 to form a pentapeptide intermediate. General Background, |FRAME: Zealexins Zealexins| are a class of nonvolatile sesquiterpenoid defense compounds found in maize. They are produced in response to a wide variety of biotic threats, including |FRAME:TAX-5518| and other fungi as well as |FRAME: TAX-29057|. Jasmonic acid and ethylene can also work synergistically to promote zealexin production. Zealexins can also be detected in the scutella of 23 diverse maize inbred lines suggesting that these compounds are broadly or universally expressed among all maize varieties |CITS: [21690302]|. , Importantly, at physiologically relevant concentrations, |FRAME: CPD-13573| and |FRAME: CPD-13571| exhibit anti-fungal activity against a number of species, with |FRAME: CPD-13573| acting against a larger number of tested species. |FRAME: CPD-13570 Zealexin A2| does not show evidence of anti-fungal activity against the tested species, while the anti-fungal properties of |FRAME: CPD-13572| remain to be investigated |CITS: [21690302]|., About This Pathway, Although many of the compounds in this pathway have been identified experimentally, notably zealexin A1, A2, A3, and B1 |CITS: [21690302]| the overall pathway scheme is proposed largely based on the sequence of enzymatic activities observed in other terpenoid biosynthetic routes, such as |FRAME: PWY-6575| |CITS: [12127586]|., Several lines of evidence suggest that zealexin production depends on the activity of TERPENE SYNTHASE6 (TPS6) and TPS11 (not shown, Genbank: EU716166, UniProt Q1EG72) |CITS: [18524777]|, including the increased level of TPS6 and TPS11 transcripts that accumulate prior to zealexin accumulation |CITS: [21690302]|. TPS4 (from B73; Genbank: AY518310, UniProt Q6JD73) and TPS5 (from Delprim; Genbank:AY518313, UniProt Q6JD70 also catalyze the production of β-bisabolene |CITS: [ 15075399]| and may feed into the zealexin biosynthetic pathway. It is notable that TPS4 transcript levels rise in juvenile sheath tissue in response to herbivory |CITS: [15075399]|., The next set of three reactions are likely catalyzed by a cytochrome p450 enzyme and the predicted NADPH cofactor and oxygen input have been included on that basis. This series of alcohol to aldehyde to carboxylic acid transformations depicted to lead to the production of |FRAME: CPD-13573| have been observed for several other p450 enzymes that act in plant secondary metabolism, such as those that participate in |FRAME:PWY-6540|. A hydroxylase would be required for the production of zealixins A2 and A3, whereas a desaturase could catalyze the production of zealexin B1 from A1. Identification of all of these enzymes will lead to a better understanding of this overall pathway and its role in maize defense against fungi, herbivory, and other biotic threats.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12475 "Carbazole"| is an aromatic heterocyclic compound that has a tricyclic structure, consisting of two six-membered benzene ring fused on either side of a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring., Carbazole-based alkaloids are found in many plants |CITS: [1937313][12602038][18499945]|., Carbazole is also derived from coal tar and shale oil and possesses mutagenic and toxic activities |CITS: [15437323][12020596][ 11890938]|., Several bacterial strains capable of degrading carbazole under aerobic conditions have been reported. Most of these organisms belong to the |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-13687| genera, although strains that belong to other genera have been described |CITS: [9244273][9636667][10540744][12036072][12442306][12685705][12834291][16896599]|. Some of the organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-135214|, were shown to use carbazole as the sole source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy., The degradation of carbazole starts with dioxygenation that leads to breakage of the central ring. The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction, |FRAME: CPLX-8092 "carbazole 1,9a-dioxygenase"|, attacks at the 1 and 9a positions, opening the five carbon ring and resulting in the formation of a highly unstable hemiaminal, which after spontaneous cleavage and rearomatization gives rise to |FRAME: CPD-12476| |CITS: [20368802]|., An extradiol dioxygenase then attacks the hydroxylated ring of this intermediate at the meta position, breaking it and generating |FRAME: CPD-12502|, a compound that contains only a single aromatic ring. A hydrolase cleaves this compound, resulting in |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: CPD-6761| (the later is degraded by the common |FRAME: PWY-5162| pathway to TCA cycle intermediates). |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE "Anthranilate"| is converted to |FRAME: CATECHOL| by |FRAME: CPLX-4643| (see |FRAME: PWY-6079|), in a reaction that liberates the nitrogen in the form of ammonia., |FRAME: CATECHOL "Catechol"| could be degraded into TCA cycle intermediates in one of several possible routes (see |FRAME:Catechol-Degradation|).

These are |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: CPD-9396|, |FRAME: CPD-9388|,, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: CPD-9395|. All five 3,6-dideoxyhexoses have been found in different, serovars of |FRAME: TAX-633|, while other genera possess only some of them. For example,, |FRAME: TAX-90371| group B contains |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: TAX-295319| contains, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: TAX-90370| contains |FRAME: CPD-9395| |CITS: [8071227]|., These sugars are synthesized via a complex series of enzymatic reactions starting, in most cases,, from |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE|, derived from |FRAME: GLC-1-P|., In a reaction catalyzed by the NAD+-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7584|, |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE|, is converted to |FRAME: CPD-658|, which is then converted to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1078|, in two consecutive enzymatic reactions, mediated by two components of the |FRAME: CPLX-7585|, enzyme complex. Summary: |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate "3-Sulfopropanediol"| (2,3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate, DHPS) is a widespread intermediate in plant and algal transformations of |FRAME: CPD-10247| from the plant sulfolipid |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL "6-sulfo-α-D-quinovosyl diacylglycerol"| |CITS: [7626014]| (see |FRAME: PWYQT-4427|). It is also recovered quantitatively during bacterial degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10247| |CITS: [14602597]|, and is secreted by all diatoms |CITS: [5085579]|., Two pathways have been described for the degradation of |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| under anaerobic conditions. The pathways involve two different glycyl radical enzymes - |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.41|, which is described here, and |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.177| (described in |FRAME: PWY-8214|). , Under anaerobic conditions, degradation of DHPS by sulfate- and sulfite-reducing bacteria (SSRB) results in conversion of the sulfonate sulfur to |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [30546350]|. In the human gut fermentation of dietary |FRAME: CPD-10247|, which is abundant in fruits and vegetables, leads to formation of DHPS, and generation of |FRAME: HS| by SSRB can lead  to diseases such as inflammation and colorectal cancer., A pathway that leads from |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| to sulfide was established with the characterization of |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.41|, from |FRAME: TAX-35833|. This glycyl radical enzyme, which is very similar to |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.38| |CITS: [30962433]|, catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: 2-3-dihydroxypropane-1-sulfonate| to |FRAME: ACETOL| and |FRAME: SO3|. The released sulfite is used as a terminal electron acceptor in respiration, resulting in production of |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [32571930]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Hyaluronan Hyaluronan| is an anionic, nonsulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| distributed widely throughout connective, epithelial, and neural tissues, including the vitreous humor of the eye, the aorta, blood, brain, liver and skin |CITS: [354500]|. It is produced by almost all members of the animal kingdom as well as by certain members of streptococci |CITS: [9260563]|. Hyaluronan can be very large, with its molecular weight often reaching the millions. It forms a strikingly viscous solution and functions primarily as a joint lubricant and shock absorber, although it is also thought to be involved in cell proliferation, migration and differentiation., Hyaluronan is composed of repeating disaccharide unit of [|FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (β1,4) |FRAME: CPD-12521|] (|FRAME: HYALURONATE|) linked by β 1,3 linkages. , Though classified as a glycosaminoglycan, it differs from other members of this family. While all other glycosaminoglycans are synthesized by resident Golgi enzymes and covalently attached to core proteins, hyaluronan is synthesized at the inner face of the plasma membrane as a free linear polymer without any protein core. In addition, it is the only glycosaminoglycan that is not sulfated |CITS: [17408700]|., About This Pathway, Like other glycosaminoglycans, |FRAME: Hyaluronan| can be degraded by some bacteria. In particular, pathogenic bacteria often use the abiity to degrade hyaluronan in order to penetrate the physical defenses of the host. Hyaluronan is an important component of connective tissues, and its degradation directly contributes to bacterial invasion by allowing greater access to, or migration between, the host tissues |CITS: [8112843]|., A large number of streptococci are known to degrade hyaluronan, and some (incuding |FRAME: TAX-1313|, |FRAME: TAX-1313| and |FRAME: TAX-1314|) have been shown to be able to grow on hyalruonan as the sole carbon source |CITS: [16368955][22311922][22428019]|., The degradation pathway starts with the depolymerization of hyaluronan to unsaturated disaccharides by the action of |FRAME: MONOMER-19222|, an endolyase that catalyzes the degradation of hyaluronan, chondroitin and chondroitin sulfates. The lyase acts by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disacchrides |CITS: [13223778][1564436]|., The next step in the pathway is catalyzed by unsaturated glucuronyl hydrolase (UGL), which degrades the unsaturated disaccharides to constituent monosaccharides - an unsaturated form of the uronic acid, and a hexosamine., The unsaturated uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-13122|, is degraded to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP| as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6507|., The genes encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-19222| and |FRAME: MONOMER-16268|, as well as a phosphotransferase system for glycosaminoglycans, are assembled into a cluster in the genome of pathogenic bacteria such as streptococci and clostridia. Transcription of the cluster is induced in the presence of hyaluronan |CITS: [19416976]|. Furthermore, the disruption of the UGL genetic in |FRAME: TAX-1313| has been demonstrated to reduce the bacterial attachment to host cells and the ability to cause infectious diseases |CITS: [22311922]|.

Summary: General Background, Arginine biosynthesis is notable for its complexity and variability at the genetic level, and by its connection with several other pathways, such as pyrimidine and polyamine biosynthesis, and certain degradative pathways. The initial steps of the arginine biosynthetic pathways proceed via N-acetylated intermediates. The presumed reason for this is that the acetylation prevents the spontaneous cyclization of glutamate derivatives, which leads to proline biosynthesis, thus keeping the two pathways separate |CITS: [12633501]|. A variation of the pathway found in some archaebacteria and hyperthermophilic bacteria utilizes a dedicated carrier protein to protect the intermediates instead of acetylation., Several alternative arginine biosynthetic pathways have evolved in bacteria:, In |FRAME:ARGSYN-PWY|, which is not very common, the key intermediate |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG) is formed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1|. A second key intermediate downstream, |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE|, is hydrolyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.16|, releasing acetate, and forming the arginine precursor |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|., In |FRAME:ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|), which is found in most of the prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbes investigated up to now, the two reactions mentioned above are linked: the acetyl group which is removed from |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is recycled onto glutamate, regenerating |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG)., This recycling is performed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35|. This pathway is considered more evolved, since the overall reaction is energetically more favorable |CITS: [3534538]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-5154| is found in several eubacteria. While in the two pathways mentioned above |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is deacetylate to |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, which is subsequntly transcarbamoylated to form |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|, in this variant |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is not deacetylated. Instead, it is, transcarbamoylated directly by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.9|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-7224|. The enzyme |FRAME:ACETYLORNDEACET-CPLX| can accept |FRAME: CPD-7224| as a substrate, and deacetylates it into |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| |CITS: [16585758]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-7400|, which has been described in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2285|, involves early intermediates that are protected not by acetylation but by a carrier protein (the LysW |FRAME: LysW|), which participates in the biosynthesis of both |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: LEU| in these organsims |CITS: [23434852]|., About This Pathway, The cyclic pathway for arginine biosynthesis has been demonstrated in many organisms, including the prokaryotes |FRAME:TAX-186817|, pseudomonads, cyanobacteria, photosynthetic bacteria and archaea, as well as eukaryotic organisms such as |FRAME:TAX-4932|, |FRAME:TAX-5140| sp., and |FRAME:TAX-3052| sp., Organisms that employ this pathway possess the the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35| (argJ, ARG7). This enzyme catalyzes the transfer of the acetyl group from |FRAME: N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| to |FRAME: GLT|, generating |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU| (NAG). Since the latter is the substrate for another enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.7.2.8| (encoded by argB), which catalyzes a previous step, this reaction effectively converts the otherwise linear pathway to a cyclical pathway |CITS: [JGM138-125][8025667]|., While most of the |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU| in these organisms is generated by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35|, some of it is still generated by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1| (encoded by argA), which fulfils an anaplerotic (replenishment of pathway intermediates) role to replenish |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU| that is lost due to degradation or cell division |CITS: [12633501]|., Some bacteria, such as Bacillus sp. |CITS: [8473852 ]|, |FRAME: TAX-485| |CITS: [1339419]|, |FRAME:TAX-2337| |CITS: [10931207]| as well as the yeast |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS: [9428669]|, have a bifunctional enzyme that has the activities of both |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35|, and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1|. In these organisms, both |FRAME: N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| can be used as acetyl donors for formation of |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU|. However, these organisms still possess separate |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1| (NAGS) enzymes (argA, ARG2) genes. The biological role of duplicate NAGS activity in these organisms remains to be elucidated |CITS: [12633501]|., Additional yeast-specific info from the |FRAME:TAX-4932| Genome Database:, The first five steps of arginine biosynthesis in S. cerevisiae take place in the mitochondrion, |CITS: [11553611][Hinnebusch]|. This part of the pathway is known as the acetylated derivatives cycle because the, acetyl group that is added to L-glutamate in the first step of the pathway is recycled via N-acetylglutamate, generated in the fifth step., The enzymes that catalyze the second and third steps are encoded by a single gene (ARG5,6) that is translated, into a pre-protein which is imported into mitochondria and cleaved there to yield two enzymes, N-acetylglutamate, kinase and N-acetylglutamyl-phosphate reductase |CITS: [1649049]|., These enzymes form a complex with each other and with N-acetylglutamate synthase, the first enzyme in the, pathway, which may have implications for regulation of their activity |CITS: [11553611]|., The mitochondrial steps of the arginine biosynthesis pathway result in the formation of ornithine, which is exported, to the cytoplasm by the transporter Ort1p |CITS: [8798783]|. In the cytoplasm, L-ornithine is converted to, L-arginine in three reactions mediated by ornithine carbamoyltransferase, arginosuccinate synthase, and, argininosuccinate lyase. Transcription of genes of the arginine biosynthetic pathway, as well as of other amino, acid biosynthetic pathways, is activated by the transcription factor Gcn4p under conditions of amino acid, starvation |CITS: [11390663][Hinnebusch]|. Transcription of ARG1, ARG3, ARG5,6, and ARG8 is also, repressed in the presence of arginine by the ArgR/Mcm1p complex, which consists of Arg80p, Arg81p, Arg82p,, and Mcm1p |CITS: [14563547]|. The transcriptional activator Gcn4p interacts with subunits of the ArgR/Mcm1p, repressor, allowing for fine-tuning of transcriptional control in response to arginine availability |CITS: [15289616]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Calystegines calystegines| are polyhydroxylated |FRAME: Nortropane-Alkaloids "nortropane alkaloids"| that have been found in various solanaceous plants, including common food plants such as potatoes and eggplants. Their biological activity and potential toxicity are associated with their capacity to inhibit glycosidases and block carbohydrate metabolism, inducing lysosomal storage toxicity |CITS: [32626111]|. Some species, such as |FRAME: TAX-4079|, produce both calystegines and |FRAME: Tropane-Alkaloids "tropane alkaloids"|, while other species, such as potato, accumulate only calystegines., An early common intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-9779|, is part of the biosynthesis of both tropane alkaloids and nortropane alkaloids, including the calystegines (other examples include |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE|, |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE|, and |FRAME: CPD-9776| |CITS: [32745157][33908526]|. The compound was shown to be the product of spontaneous condensation between |FRAME: CPD-9778| and |FRAME: CPD-7994|. The former is produced by a type III polyketide synthase (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.333|) |CITS: [30538251]|, while the latter is produced by a common pathway that has been studied in the early 90s (see |FRAME: PWY-5315|) |CITS: [MCLAUCHLAN93][16653064][8038607][17283012]|., A cytochrome P450 enzyme belonging to the CYP82 subfamily (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.194|), discovered in |FRAME: TAX-33113| (Deadly Nightshade), was shown to catalyze the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-9779|, forming |FRAME: CPD-27772|, which spontaneously decarboxylates to |FRAME: TROPINONE| |CITS: [30538251]|., Two tropinone reductases, which catalyze the stereo-specific reduction of |FRAME: TROPINONE|, give rise to separate alkaloid groups. |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.206|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10563| give rise to the tropane alkaloids, while |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.236|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10566|, gives rise to the nortropane alkaloids |CITS: [16653065]|., The enzyme catalyzing the esterification of |FRAME: PSEUDOTROPINE| with |FRAME: CPD-1083| (tigloyl-CoA) to form |FRAME: CPD-27778|, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.186|, was reported alsready in 1991 |CITS: [1959620]|, though the gene encoding it was discovered only in 2024. That enzyme is a BAHD acyltransferase |CITS: [38684703]|., The next steps of the pathway were characterized in 2022, when two other cytochromes P450 were shown to be involved in the pathway. One of these enzymes, |FRAME: G-124944|, catalyzes oxidative N-demethylation in the early reaction steps during the biosynthesis of all discovered N-demethylated modified tropane alkaloids with norpseudotropine cores, releasing |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. While the exact substrate of the enzyme was not determined, it was established that it contains an acyl chain with at least three carbon atoms, and a tigloyl moiety was abundant among detected intermediates and products. |FRAME: G-124944| was also found to catalyze ring-hydroxylation at the carbon atom adjacent to the esterified carbon atom at the 3-position of tigloyl norpseudotropine. The other enzyme, |FRAME: G-124945|, was shown to hydroxylate a different position of the ring |CITS: [35780230]|., As of 2025, the enzymes catalyzing the remaining reactions of this pathway, presumably a hydroxylation and a hydrolysis, remain unknown.

Summary: |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate "Dermatan sulfate"| is a sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| composed of alternating units of sulfated |FRAME: CPD-3604| and |FRAME: CPD-12515| (and some |FRAME: CPD-12521|) residues. The |FRAME: CPD-3604| residues are substituted to varying degrees with sulfate linked to 4- and/or 6-hydroxyl positions, forming |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, and the uronic acid residues may be substituted with sulfate at the 2-hydroxyl position forming |FRAME: CPD-12527| or |FRAME:CPD-12518|., The uronic acid residues may also be substituted with sulfate at the 3-hydroxyl positions, although this substitution is quite rare., The dermatan chains vary in size up to a hundred or more disaccharide repeating units. They are usually found attached to assorted core proteins as part of a proteoglycan complex. Dermatan sulfate is a major component of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but is also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors., The dermatan chains are synthesized in situ on the protein chain. They are attached to the core protein via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the "glycoaminoglycan-protein linkage region", which is formed by sequential stepwise additions of the sugar residues to specific core proteins. The synthesis of the linkage region is described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|., The linkage region may be extended into mutiple kinds of glycosaminoglycans. However, the addition of an |FRAME: CPD-3604| residue prevents the formation of |FRAME: HEPARIN| or |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and commits the molecule to become chondroitin or dermatan. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase. Humans have two isoforms of this enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: HS07428| and |FRAME:HS10013| genes |CITS: [11788602][12716890][12433924]|., Once the linkage region has been formed and committed, the polymerzation of the chondroitin/dermatan chain proceeds by the alternate addition of |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-3604| from activated precursors to the non-reducing end of the elongating chain. The addition of both residues is catalyzed by the bifunctional chondroitin sulfate synthases., Humans possess three isoforms of this bifunctional enzyme (|FRAME: HS13400|, |FRAME: HS13103| and |FRAME: HS11959|), plus an additional enzyme that can catalyze only the addition of |FRAME: CPD-12521| (|FRAME: HS12080|) |CITS:[11514575][12907687][12145278]|. It has been suggested that chondroitin polymerization is achieved by multiple combinations of the different enzymes and that each combination may play a unique role in the biosynthesis of chondroitin or dermatan sulfate |CITS:[17253960][18316376]|., Up to this point in the pathway dermatan and chondroitin share the same biosynthesis pathway and enzymes. The difference in their synthetic routes begin only at the later stages of synthesis. A key reaction in the conversion of the chondroitin/dermatan precursor chain to a dermatan sulfate chain is the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues to |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: HS03472-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS03472| gene |CITS: [16505484]|., The rest of the modifications consist of sulfation reactions. The enzyme |FRAME: ENSG00000169105-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS09883| gene, is a sulfotransferase that appears to be specific for sulfating the C4 position of |FRAME: CPD-3604| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues, and is thus dermatan-specific. Although a similar enzyme specific for 6-sulfation of dermatan has not been found, it has been suggested that such an enzyme exists, as the enzymes that sulfate chondroitin at the 6 position of |FRAME: CPD-3604| do not have high activity when that residue is linked to |FRAME: CPD-12515| |CITS: [9883891]|., On the other hand, the enzyme that catalyzes the 6-sulfation of |FRAME: CPD-3604| residues that are already sulfated at the C4 position is the same one that catalyzes the reaction with |FRAME:CHONDROITIN-4-SULFATE|, encoded by |FRAME: HS11694| |CITS: [11572857]|., Similarly, the enzyme that catalyzes the sulfation of the C2 position of |FRAME:DERMATAN-L-IDURONATE| is the enzyme that catalyzes a similar reaction with |FRAME: Chondroitin-D-glucuronates| residues, |FRAME: ENSG00000111962-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS03488|) |CITS: [10187838]|., The very first reaction in this pathway, the addition of a xylose molecule to a serine residue of the core protein, is performed at the endoplasmic reticulum. The rest of the pathway occurs at the Golgi apparatus.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, A group of |FRAME: TAX-562| O serogroups (O:17, O:44, O:73, O:77 and O:106) and the |FRAME: TAX-28901| serogroup O:6,14 share a common four-sugar backbone O-subunit structure, and possess almost identical O-antigen gene clusters. While some Salmonella strains such as |FRAME: TAX-28901| O:6,14 strains, and |FRAME: TAX-562| O:77 strains |CITS: [11448680]|, do not have any substitutions, the other O antigens in this group differ by the addition of one or two glucose side branches at various positions of the backbone. However, the O antigen gene clusters for all members of the group encode only the proteins required for biosynthesis of the common four-sugar backbone, and the enzymes for the substitutions are believed to be encoded by prophages |CITS: [17600060]| (see |FRAME: RXN-22050 "O:6,14 O antigen ManII α-(1,3)-glucosyltransferase"|, |FRAME: RXN-22068 "O:6,14 O antigen ManIII α-(1,4)-glucosyltransferase| and |FRAME: RXN-22051 "O:6,14 O antigen GlcNAc α-(1,6)-glucosyltransferase"|). , The basic |FRAME: CPD-23771| is composed of one GlcNAc residue and three mannosyl residues. The gene cluster that encodes its biosynthesis has been cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-2024273|, |FRAME: TAX-1160739| and |FRAME: TAX-562| O:77 and found to contain only two genes encoding mannosyltransferases (|FRAME: G-80970| and |FRAME: G-80971|). The |FRAME: G-80971| gene shares 52% identity with a putative glycosyltransferase involved in |FRAME: TAX-217992| O antigen assembly, and since the β-D-Man-(1→3)-D-GlcNAc linkage is the only linkage present in both E. coli O:77 and O:6 O antigens, that gene has been proposed to encode the transferase for the β-D-Man-(1→3)-D-GlcNAc linkage. That left the |FRAME: G-80970| gene product to catalyze the other mannosyltransfer reactions |CITS: [17600060]|., Since the repeat unit has two adjacent α-D-Man-(1→2)-D-Man linkages, and since all the sequenced gene clusters have one fewer transferase gene than linkages,it has been proposed that WbaC catalyzes the formation of both alpha;-D-Man-(1→2)-D-Man linkages |CITS: [17600060]|.

General Background, A widespread group of phenolics in plants termed coumarins constitute lactones of phenylpropanoids with a 2H-benzopyran-2-one nucleus |CITS: [BROWN86]| |CITS: [Seigler98]|. At least 1000 natural occurring coumarins, among them about 300 simple coumarins have been found in many families of higher plants |CITS: [BERENBAUM91]| with an especially high number of structural variations encountered in the |FRAME:TAX-4037| |CITS: [Seigler98]|. The biosynthesis of the simplest member described in this pathway, i.e. |FRAME:COUMARIN| represents both the specific compound and serves as an eponym of the entire compound class. , Coumarin belongs to the most common coumarins in plants. The numerous pharmacological and physiological effects of coumarin and its more complex derivatives such as the furanocoumarins and prenylated coumarins have drawn significant interest of researchers across different scientific areas. Coumarins are known to exhibit anti-inflammatory as well as antioxidant activities and often serve as model compounds for synthetic drugs |CITS: [15579073]| |CITS: [16472213]|. Moreover, extensive research into their pharmacological and therapeutic properties for many years has resulted in the acknowledgment of their therapeutic role in the treatment of cancer |CITS: [15579072]|., About This Pathway, In contrast to most of the coumarins, which are biosynthesized through 4-coumaric acid and umbelliferone, the formation of coumarin occurs via 2-coumaric acid |CITS: [4153528]|. In general phenylalanine and trans-cinnamic acid are considered the precursor for the coumarin biosynthesis but Stoker |CITS: [13917373]| also reported the formation of coumarin from cis-cinnamic acid. Although free coumarin is found in small amounts in plants their β-glucoside(s) is the predominant accumulating compound. The corresponding glucosyltransferase has been partially purified from and characterized in |FRAME:TAX-47082| |CITS: [KLEINHOFS67]| |CITS: [16661155]|. Interestingly, the formed trans-2-coumarate β-D-glucoside was not accepted as substrate for the subsequent β-glucosidase reaction. The enzyme only catalyzed the cis-isomer, i.e. coumarinic acid β-D-glucoside , (also referred to as bound coumarin - |CITS: [14458750]|) forming coumarinate |CITS: [13753452]|., The way the isomerization occurs is not entirely resolved. While there is strong evidence that the trans-cis isomerization occurs spontaneously by means of UV-light |CITS: [5921806]| |CITS: [16656000]| the existence of a light-induced isomerase enzyme system has not been ruled out. Stoker |CITS: [5836500]| presented evidence for the involvement of an isomerase system in this process and found that plants kept in daylight or in the dark did not significantly differ with regard to the amount of coumarin. The last step of the pathway is the spontaneous lactonization of coumarinate forming coumarin., The typical 'hay' smell of coumarin is only found when plants are injured. It has been established that the glucosylated coumarins accumulate in the vacuole while the β-glucosidase is located to the extraplasmatic space |CITS: [16662108]|. Hence, the physical contact of the enzyme and its substrate (coumarin glucosides) only occurs after the breakup of the cell and its organelles. Coumarin itself is not a dead end product but is rather readily further metabolized |CITS: [13673026]|.

Summary: Many metabolic processes, including respiration, photosynthetic electron transport and oxidation of glycolate in photorespiration, generate reactive oxygen species such as singleton oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. , For example, the univalent reduction of dioxygen in illuminated chloroplasts produces superoxide anion radicals, which are disproportionate to hydrogen peroxide and dioxygen by the superoxide dismutase enzyme, contained in the stroma, and lumen. These highly reactive compounds can damage membrane lipids and certain enzymes and thus interrupt cell function., The ascorbate-glutathione cycle performs the scavenging of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. In this cycle, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| and |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| transfer reducing power from NADPH to hydrogen peroxide, reducing it to water. , The reduction of hydrogen peroxide is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-5127|, in a reaction that generates |FRAME: CPD-318|, a radical that can be reduced to ascorbate by |FRAME: MONOMER-5129|. If not reduced rapidly, monodehydroascorbate is disproportionated into |FRAME: ASCORBATE| and |FRAME: L-DEHYDRO-ASCORBATE|, and the latter is reduced back to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-5132| using |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| as the reducing agent. The oxidized glutathione is reduced by |FRAME: MONOMER-5145| using NADPH (see |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY|)., The ascorbate-glutathione cycle presents in at least four different subcellular locations including the cytosol, chloroplast, mitochondrion and peroxisome. Studies of the Arabidopsis enzymes of the pathway show that the same set of enzymes, including |FRAME: MONOMER-5127|, |FRAME: MONOMER-5129| and |FRAME: MONOMER-5145|, are dual targeted to chloroplast and mitochondrion |CITS: [12954611]|. Ascorbate peroxidase is in fact the major peroxidase in spinach leaves., A similar scavenging system appears to operate in several species of cyanobacteria and Euglena.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9718 "Menaquinone-7"| (MK-7) is by far the most common quinone in Gram-positive bacteria. It has been shown to be the major form of quinone in dozens of species, including many |FRAME: TAX-1386| species, as well as |FRAME: TAX-1562|, |FRAME: TAX-2755|, |FRAME: TAX-1637|, and |FRAME: TAX-1279| (see |CITS: [7022156]| for an exhaustive list)., The best studied menaquinone biosynthetic pathway outside of |FRAME: TAX-83333| (which makes |FRAME: CPD-9728|) is that of |FRAME: TAX-1423|, which makes MK-7 |CITS: [6780515][3131309] [1629163][8169214][8566759][10194342]|., Even though MK-7 is most prevalent in Gram-positive bacteria, it has been documented in other organisms as well. It has been shown to be the major quinone in several members of the |FRAME: TAX-68336|, including |FRAME: TAX-115852| (along with |FRAME: CPD-9611|) |CITS: [5782248]|, |FRAME: TAX-997| |CITS: [4216336]|, and |FRAME: TAX-28132| |CITS: [5411759]|., MK-7 also occurs as a minor quinone in several Gram-negative species, including |FRAME: TAX-51367| (which belongs to the |FRAME: TAX-1236|) |CITS: [Collins81]|, |FRAME: TAX-33| (which belongs to the |FRAME: TAX-28221|) |CITS: [5782248]|, and |FRAME: TAX-274| and |FRAME: TAX-271|, which belong to the |FRAME: TAX-1297| phylum |CITS: [7462123][7022156]|., In Green sulfur bacteria MK-7 is present in their photosystem I-type reaction centers |CITS: [11687219]|., In addition, MK-7 was found to be the major quinone of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2303|, |CITS: [4344918]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|., The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.2|, |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.4|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|., Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria, some archaea, and certain fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. While the biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail only in bacteria, ongoing success in sequencing whole genomes from other organisms has provided evidence that the general steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Despite the importance and prevalance of biotin, its detailed biosynthetic pathway remained enigmatic for over 70 years. The first complete pathway for biotin synthesis was suggested for its synthesis in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [20693992]|., Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, derived from a |FRAME: CPD-205|-like structure. The early steps of the pathway, which are described here, describe the synthesis of the precursor of the pimelate moiety in Gram negative bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|. the pathway is also present in some archaebacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-497727| |CITS: [30218044]|. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described in |FRAME: PWY0-1507|., The origins of the carbon atoms of biotin synthesized via this pathway were studied in |FRAME: TAX-562| using 13C NMR analysis of products labeled in vivo |CITS: [8125118][Indrajit94]|. The C3, C5 and C7 carbons are derived from carbon C1 of acetate, while the C2, C4 and C6 carbons are derived from carbon C2 of acetate. The C1 carbon originates from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. This labeling pattern indicated that the pimeloyl moiety of biotin is formed by head-to-tail condensation of three acetate units, similar to the synthesis of fatty acids |CITS: [Indrajit94]|. As the biotin C1 and C7 atoms show different labeling patterns, free pimelic acid (a symmetrical molecule) could not be an intermediate, and thus it has been assumed that |FRAME: CPD-558| is the precursor |CITS: [Webb07]|., The elucidation of the pathway proved difficult, mostly since only two genes, |FRAME: EG10119| and |FRAME: EG10122|, were implicated in the synthesis of the pimeloyl moiety |CITS: [4563978][8830257][4877129]|. Based on these finding there have been several suggestions that enzymes of the fatty acid biosynthesis pathway are involved, although none of these suggestions could explain the full process |CITS: [13930373][Indrajit94]|. An inclusive model was finally suggested in 2010 |CITS: [20693992]|. Based on this model, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.197| (|FRAME: EG10119 "BioC"|) converts the free carboxyl group of a |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| thioester to its methyl ester by transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|. The newly acquired methyl group mimics the methyl ends of normal fatty acyl chains, and enables the esterified |FRAME: CPD-12454| to enter the fatty acid synthetic pathway., Two iterations of the fatty acid elongation cycle (see |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY|) produce |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACP-methyl-esters "pimeloyl-[acp] methyl ester"|. The introduction of the methyl ester early in the pathway disguises the biotin synthetic intermediates so that they become substrates for the fatty acid synthetic pathway. When the synthesis of the pimeloyl moiety is complete and disguise is no longer needed, the methyl group is removed to free the carboxyl group that will eventually be used to attach biotin to its target metabolic enzymes. The removal of the methyl group is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.85|, giving |FRAME: Pimeloyl-ACPs "pimeloyl-[acp]"|. A remarkable diversity was found in the enzymes catalyzing this step, with different, non-related genes found in different organisms, including |FRAME: EG10122 BioH| from |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [20693992]|, |FRAME: G-17965| from |FRAME: TAX-401614| |CITS: [23152908]|, |FRAME: G-15494| from |FRAME: TAX-93059| |CITS: [23152908]|, |FRAME: G-15495| from |FRAME: TAX-71421| |CITS: [24313380]|, and |FRAME: HP0287| from |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [26868423]|. A remote but functional analogue was also found in archaea |CITS: [30218044]|., The [acp] protein is then removed in a complex reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EG10121 "BioF"|, forming |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE|, the first intermediate in biotin ring assembly. An in vitro system that uses dialyzed cell extracts was used in combination with several mutant strains and purified proteins to verify the proposed pathway |CITS: [20693992]|.

Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide or nucleoside forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, Degradation of nucleotides and nucleosides involves the conversion of pentose sugars to three-carbon precursor molecules. In most bacteria this could be achieved via the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway"|, however many archaea do not possess that pathway., Some arachaeal species degrade nucleosides to central carbon metabolism precursors by the pentose bisphosphate pathway, which involves type III RubisCO and other unique enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-5532|). However, multiple genomes from halophilic archaea do not harbor Rubisco enzymes, though they possess |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.29|, another enzyme involved in that pathway. These organisms were found to possess a different nucleoside degradation pathway|CITS: [36434094]|., The pathway proceeds via |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|, but involves unique enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.239| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.109|, converting the nucleoside |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOL|. While the former feeds into primary metabolism, the fate of the latter is still unknown |CITS: [36434094]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins Anabaenopeptins| are a family of non-ribosomally synthesized cyclic peptides produced by some cyanobacterial species. They have a well-conserved structure comprising a ring of five amino acids connected through an ureido linkage to an exocyclic sixth amino acid. Counting the exocyclic amino acid as residue 1, the 2nd residue is |FRAME: CPD-219|, and the ring is formed by cyclization of the C-terminal carboxyl of the 6th residue to the ε-amino group of the D-lysine at position 2. The ureodi bridge connecting the α-amino group of |FRAME: CPD-219| to the exocyclic amino acid is a unique feature among cyanobacterial peptides., The five amino acids other than |FRAME: CPD-219| are not conserved and may consist of either proteinogenic or non-proteinogenic amino acids. A review published in 2006 listed 124 different anabaenopeptin variants |CITS: [16774586]|. Many of the anabaenopeptins have been isolated under different names such as oscillamides, lyngbyaureamides, ferintoic acids, nodulapeptins, schizopeptins and more |CITS: [Sano95][11520225]|., Anabaenopeptins have been found in an enormous variety of cyanobacteria isolated from both the aquatic and terrestrial environments, including |FRAME: TAX-1163|, |FRAME: TAX-1177|, |FRAME: TAX-1125|, |FRAME: TAX-54304|, |FRAME: TAX-28073|, and |FRAME: TAX-383614| |CITS: [Harada95][26096276][27604544]|. In general, these compounds are produced by filamentous cyanobacteria belonging to the orders |FRAME: TAX-1161| and |FRAME: TAX-1150|. The production by members of the unicellular genus |FRAME: TAX-1125| is beleived to be due to horizontal transfer of the biosynthetic gene cluster from a filamentous organism |CITS: [28261178]|., Anabaenopeptins exhibit a functional diversity that includes inhibitory activity for proteases, phosphatases, and carboxypeptidases |CITS: [ 10340607][11520225][Zafrir-Ilan10]|, and are believed to provide protection against zooplankters and crustaceans., About This Pathway, The gene cluster responsible for anabaenopeptin biosynthesis was discovered in 2005 in a |FRAME: TAX-59512| strain. The cluster comprised 5 genes (anaABCDE) encoding four non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs) and one ATP-Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter. Interestingly, even though that organism produces several different anabaenopeptins (|FRAME: CPD-26928|, |FRAME: CPD-26929|, |FRAME: CPD-26933| and |FRAME: CPD-26942|), it contains only a single cluster, indicating that some of the enzymes are promiscuous and can accept different substrates |CITS: [19706155]|. Similar clusters were soon described from multiple species, including |FRAME: TAX-46234|, |FRAME: TAX-313624|, and |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [20338518]|. A cluster from |FRAME: TAX-984208| was reported in 2017 |CITS: [28085246]|. In many organisms a gene cluster encoding |FRAME: PWY-7275| is located next to the anabaenopeptin biosynthesis cluster, and it is assumed that those enzymes produce the homo-amino acids |FRAME: CPD-15322| and |FRAME: CPD-17729| that are incorporated into many anabaenopeptins |CITS: [28085246]|., The AptA NRPS contains two adenylation and two thiolation domains, for activating and binding tof he first two amino acids, a condensation domain, and an epimerization domain for converting |FRAME: LYS| into |FRAME: CPD-219|. The AptB NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the third amino acid, respectively. The AptC NRPS contains two sets of adenylation, thiolation, and condensation, responsible for the fourth and fifth amino acids. It also contains methylation domain, for methylation of the fifth residue (often |FRAME: CPD-298|). The AptD NRPS contains single adenylation, thiolation, and condensation domains, responsible for activation, binding, and condensation of the sixth amino acid, and a thioesterase domain, which is responsible for cyclization and release of the product., An unanswered question as of 2024 is the mechanism responsible for formation of the ureido bridge. A similar structure exists in |FRAME: CPD-26948|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-317|, and it has been shown that in that organism the formation of the ureido bridge is catalyzed by the SylC protein |CITS: [19968303]|. However, SylC possesses a domain with structural similarity to acetyltransferase between the A- and C-domains of the NRPSs, and no similar domain was found within the anabaenopeptins NRPSs, suggesting that a different mechanism may exist during anabaenopeptin biosynthesis |CITS: [34437393]|.
