Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn this variant of the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules and reduces one molecules of |FRAME: NADP|, two molecules of |FRAME: Quinones quinone|, and two ferredoxins to |FRAME: NADPH|, |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, and reduced ferredoxins, respectively., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, There has been considerable debate over whether |FRAME: TAX-210| has a complete oxidative citric acid cycle as shown here or a branched modified form of a citric acid cycle, similar to that of |FRAME:TAX-562| under anaerobic conditions. Since the original genomic sequence of |FRAME: TAX-210| lacked open reading frames (ORFs) for three of the typical citric acid cycle enzymes, |FRAME: TAX-210| initially was believed to contain a noncyclic branched pathway whereby one branch operates in an oxidative direction converting oxaloacetate to α-ketoglutarate via citrate and isocitrate, while the other operates in a reductive direction converting oxaloacetate to succinate via malate and fumarate |CITS: [10091606][10477311][10477312]|. , However, it was later discovered that the organism contains alternative enzymes for the three missing citric acid cycle enzymes, suggesting that it may have a complete citric acid cycle after all. Biochemical studies demonstrated that |FRAME: TAX-210| has a ferredoxin-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3| instead of the NAD+-dependent 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase |CITS: [9495749]| , |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.5| instead of succinyl-CoA synthetase |CITS: [9495749]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.4| instead of an NAD+-dependent malate dehydrogenase |CITS: [10809701]|., There is still some debate over whether the fumarate reductase of |FRAME: TAX-210| can operate as a succinate dehydrogenase as proposed in this pathway. Although several authors detected succinate dehydrogenase activity in biochemical assays |CITS: [7781988][10809701]|, and the enzyme has been shown to function in vitro using benzyl viologen as the electron donor |CITS: [9434188]|, Pitson et al. detected no such activity |CITS: [10091606]|.

Summary: General Background, Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The lipid A component of pathogenic bacteria is detected by the host serum LPS-binding protein (LBP), which is dependent on two cofactors: cluster of differentiation 14 (CD14) and myeloid differentiation factor 2 (MD2). The lipid A/LBP complex is subsequently recognized by the opsonic receptor CD14, forming a triple complex that activates Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). TLR4 activation triggers a signalling cascade, leading to the production of cytokines and clotting factors and the secretion of cathelicidin antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) and other stimulatory molecules |CITS: [10963608]|. CAMP binds to negatively charged structural motifs such as the phosphate groups on lipid A, leading to cell lysis and death |CITS: [19601838]|. If the immune response is too strong sepsis and septic shock can occur, leading to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome and death |CITS: [12857774]|., In many bacterial species lipid A consists of two glucosamine units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor lipid IVA. , Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. , About This Pathway, Compared with other enterobacterial lipid As, the lipid A of |FRAME: TAX-210| activates TLR4 in a much weaker form, displaying a 1000-fold lower endotoxicity compared with lipid A from |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [Yamaoka08]|. Several modifications result in this weak TLR4 elicitation: the major form of |FRAME: TAX-210| lipid A is acylated by four rather than six fatty acids, contains only a single Kdo residue, lacks the usual 4'-phosphate group, and has a phosphoethanolamine (PEtN) moiety replacing the 1-position phosphate group |CITS: [ 21903201]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates, formed by certain planst from any one of eight amino acids, namely, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, methionine, tyrosine and tryptophan. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified |CITS: [18458837]|. Much of, the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine. , Glucosinolates are found prominently in the order |FRAME: TAX-3700|, which includes cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, broccoli, and the model plant Arabidopsis, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are hydrolyzed by the plant to compounds that are toxic to herbivores, and play an important role in plant defense. The hydrolysis of is catalyzed by |FRAME: AT5G26000-MONOMER "myrosinases"| (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147|), enzymes that are physically segregated from glucosinolates within the intact plant in specialized myrosin cells, and are brought into contact by tissue damage |CITS: [Bones96]|., The products of the myrosinase reaction are unstable |FRAME: THIOHYDROXIMATE-O-SULFATES "thiohydroximate-O-sulfates"| that decompose to different types of products, including nitriles, isothiocyanates, thiocyanates, oxazolidine-2-thiones, and epithionitriles. The type of product(s) that form depends on the the chemical nature of the side chain of the parent glucosinolate and the presence of different enzymes. Folowing the hydrolysis of the glucose moiety, glucosinolates with aliphatic side chains generally decompose spontaneously to yield isothiocyanates at a neutral pH, and in the absence of other enzymes (as in some Capparales species), isothiocynates are the only breakdown products |CITS: [11752388]|. However, acidic pH or the presence of |FRAME:FE+2| ions favors the production of nitriles |CITS: [Gil80]|., In some plants additional proteins are involved in glucosinolate hydrolysis. The presence of |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5 "nitrile-specifier proteins (NSPs, EC 4.8.1.5)"| results in conversion of thiohydroximate-O-sulfates to bioactive nitriles. The presence of |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.6 "epithiospecifier proteins (ESPs, EC 4.8.1.6)"| results in conversion to either nitriles or epithionitriles, depending on the substrate |CITS: [11752388]|. If the parent glucosinolate possessed a terminal alkene group, epithionitriles are formed (by transfer of the sulfur atom from the basic glucosinolate backbone to the terminal alkene residue of the side chain), whereas other glucosinolates are converted to simple nitriles |CITS: [Daxenbichler68][4130022][MacLeod85][11752388][15845404]|. In one documented case the presence of |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.7 "thiocyanate-forming proteins (TFPs, EC 4.8.1.7)"| results in formation of thiocyanates., Conversion of glucosinolates to isothiocyanates has also been observed in bacterial members of the gut microbiota |CITS: [34444909]|. The first isolation of bacterial myrosinase was made already in 1974 |CITS: [Tani74]|. In 2016 two more bacterial myrosinases were isolated, one of which was reported to belong to the glycohydrolase 3 (GH3) family |CITS: [26820976][El-Shora16]|., Several genes encoding the bacterial myrosinase enzymes have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-818|, although their exact function is still not completely known |CITS: [32084341]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Pectin "Pectin"| is a structural heteropolysaccharide consisting of a complex set of polysaccharides that is present in most primary cell walls and is particularly abundant in the non-woody parts of terrestrial plants. It s involved in crosslinking cellulose and hemicellulose fibers, which provides rigidity to the cell wall., The characteristic structure of pectin is a linear chain of α-(1-4)-linked |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that forms the pectin-backbone, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|., Different components of pectin have different substitutions and additions. A common type is |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan I"| (RG-I), which makes up 20-35% of pectin. In RG-I some of the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units in the backbone are replaced by (1-2)-linked |FRAME: L-rhamnose|, to which side chains of various neutral sugars branch off, mostly |FRAME: D-Galactose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028|. Another common type is |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II), which makes up about 10% of pectin. RG-II is based on a backbone of 8-9 galacturonate units, which are decorated by four side chains consisting of 12 different types of sugars in more than 20 different linkages. RG-II usually forms dimeric structures via the formation of crosslinks by a 1:2 borate diol ester between apiosyl residues in one of the side chains., Other types of pectin include chains of |FRAME: Apiogalacturonans apiogalacturonan|, |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl homogalacturonan|, and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan|. There is currently no consensus as to how the pectic polysaccharides are linked to each other, or to other polymers, in the wall. However, it is thought that the different peptides are covalently linked to each other via their backbones, forming a large linear structure with many side branches |CITS: [11423143][12162553][Coenen07]|., In nature, around 80% of the carboxyl groups of the galacturonate units are esterified with |FRAME: METOH|. Some plants, including sugar beet, potatoes and pears, contain pectins with acetylated galacturonate in addition to methyl esters. Partially esterified pectins are often refered to as pectinate, and if the degree of esterification is below 5%, as, |FRAME: PECTATE|., Phytopathogenic and saprophytic bacteria and fungi produce variety of extracellular and intracellular enzymes that de-esterify and depolymerize pectin and its derivatives. In pectinolytic bacteria the initial steps of pectin degradation to |FRAME: PECTATE pectate| and oligogalacturonides involve the action of extracellularly secreted pectin methylesterases, pectin acetylesterases, pectin lyases, pectate hydrolases and pectate lyases. Pectate degrading hydrolases and lyases are not always extracellular and are also found in the cytoplasm and periplasm., Pectinolytic enzymes vary among species and strains. Pectin-degrading enzymes are used in the food, fiber and animal feed industries. The development of inhibitors of enzymes that degrade pectin and its derivatives is of interest as a possible way to prevent crop spoilage, although none have been reported as of 2010 |CITS: [19618506][8905080][18535148]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: G-15956| gene of |FRAME: TAX-2336| encodes an intracellular pectinolytic enzyme that belongs to family 28 of the glycoside hydrolases. The enzyme removes |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| units from the non-reducing end of polygalacturonate, and shows increasing activity on oligosaccharides with an increasing degree of polymerization., The enzyme is specific for saturated oligogalacturonate and is unable to degrade unsaturated substrates, such as those produced by the |FRAME: G-15955| gene product. The enzyme is also unable to accept methyl-esterified substrates |CITS: [16262687]|., The |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| that is released is isomerized to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| by the hexuronate isomerase encoded by the |FRAME: G-15952| gene (which can also isomerize |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE|) |CITS: [23441918]|., |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| is epimerized to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-8660|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15945| gene |CITS: [22925190]|., |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| is then metabolized to central metabolism intermediates, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7242| |CITS: [22925190]|.

Summary: General Background, Benzoxazinoids were identified in the early 1960s as secondary metabolites of the grasses (including the major agricultural crops maize (|FRAME: TAX-4577|), wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|), and rye (|FRAME: TAX-4550|)) that function as a natural defense against a wide range of pests, including insects, pathogenic fungi and bacteria |CITS:[niemeyer88]|. The benzoxazinoids also exhibit allelopathic properties |CITS:[Barnes87][10804466]|. Benzoxazinoids are synthesized in two subfamilies of the |FRAME: TAX-4479| and sporadically in single species of the dicots |CITS: [19577780]|. The most common benzoxazinoids are |FRAME: CPD-6365| and |FRAME: CPD-6366|., Since the aglycone benzoxazinoids are autotoxic, they are stored in glucosylated forms that have reduced chemical reactivity |CITS: [10804466]|. The glucosides are stored in the vacuoles |CITS:[12239364]|. This allows the plants to store the toxic compounds in anticipation of pathogen attacks, prompting the suggestion to name these compounds "phytoanticipins". , About This Pathway, The synthesis of benzoxazinoids starts with the cleavage of |FRAME: INDOLE-3-GLYCEROL-P "indole-3-glycerol phosphate"| (an intermediate in tryptophan biosynthesis) to form |FRAME: INDOLE|. Indole is a volatile compound and can be used, in conjunction with several terpenoids, to form cocktails of volatile products that are used in parasitic defense |CITS:[11556781]|. However, indole can be directed to the pathway described here, where is it converted into benzoxazinoids by a series of cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenases. In successive reactions catalyzed by |FRAME: G-7861|, |FRAME: G-7862|, |FRAME: G-7863| and |FRAME: G-7864| four oxygen atoms are introduced into the indole moiety, producing |FRAME: CPD-6365|, which is glucosylated by the enzymes |FRAME: G-8201| and |FRAME: G-8202|, forming |FRAME: CPD-13811|., |FRAME: CPD-6365| is the main benzoxazinoid in barley., Some plants, like maize, continue by modifying |FRAME: CPD-13811| into |FRAME: CPD-6562|. This is described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6950|.

General Background, The antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-9962| was first isolated from a |FRAME:TAX-1883| species from the species group, |FRAME: TAX-1886|, cluster 1. This compound had an earthy, camphor-like odor and was described as an, α,β-unsaturated sesquiterpene ketone with a zizaene skeleton. It showed antimicrobial activity, against |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [8195043]|. It biosynthetic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-100226| has, been determined |CITS: [18234666] [16669656]|. This pathway is also likely to occur in |FRAME: TAX-33903| based, on the existence of a transcriptionally coupled, two-gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-33903| encoding enzymes having, 76% amino acid sequence identity with those of |FRAME: TAX-1902|. In addition, epi-isozizaene synthase activity, was demonstrated for the corresponding |FRAME: TAX-33903| gene product (in |CITS: [18234666]|)., About This Pathway, In this pathway |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is cyclized in a |FRAME: MG+2|-dependent reaction, to form the novel sesquiterpene metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9959| |CITS: [16669656] [18234666]|. This is followed by, a two-step allylic oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-9959| to form the 5-keto derivative |FRAME: CPD-9962| via an epimeric, mixture of |FRAME: CPD-9960| and |FRAME: CPD-9961| intermediates. All four compounds were detected in, extracts of |FRAME: TAX-100226| by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry |CITS: [18234666]|. , This two-step oxidation of an allylic methylene to a conjugated ketone by a single cytochrome P450 enzyme is, less common than the three-step oxidation of methyl groups to carboxylic acids catalyzed by other single, cytochrome P450 enzymes (in |CITS: [18234666]|).

|FRAME: DIPHTHAMIDE "Diphthamide"| is a unique posttranslationally modified histidine residue found only in translation elongation factor 2 (|FRAME: Elongation-factor-2|). This factor is found in archaea and in all eukaryotes, but not in eubacteria, and is conserved from archaea to humans. The role of diphthamide is still not understood. Mutant defective in its biosynthesis are viable in yeast, but mutant mice are retarded in growth and development, and almost always die before birth |CITS:[16648478][18765564]|. A potential role of diphthamide may be to protect ribosomes fom ribosome-inactivating proteins (such as ricin), which are widely distributed in nature |CITS: [18460012]|., The conversion of |FRAME: HIS | to |FRAME: CPD-17005| is a complex process. It starts by the transfer of a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl moiety from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|. Four different genes of |FRAME: TAX-4932| have been shown to be required for this step in eukaryotes. Three of these genes, |FRAME: G-11954|, |FRAME: G-11955| and |FRAME: G-11956|, are believed to form a |FRAME: CPLX-8046| complex |CITS: [8406038][15485916]|. The fourth gene, |FRAME: G3O-31725|, is similar to DnaJ-type chaperones, and is assumed to be responsible for the proper folding of one or more of the other DPH proteins |CITS: [15485916]|., The next step, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-11958|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15582|, is the transfer of four methyl groups, donated by four molecules of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, to form a |FRAME: Diphthine-methyl-ester-EF2 "diphtine methyl ester residue"| |CITS: [1508200][24739148]|. This is followed by the action of |FRAME: G-34532|, a methylesterase that removes the methyl group connected to the oxygen, leaving a |FRAME: DIPHTINE diphtine| residue |CITS: [24739148]|., The last step is the amidation of |FRAME: DIPHTINE "diphtine"| to |FRAME: DIPHTHAMIDE "diphthamide"|, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-15503|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17855| |CITS: [23169644]|., Diphthamide serves as the target for two important bacterial toxins - the |FRAME: CPLX-8048| (DT) and the Pseudomonas |FRAME: MONOMER-15589 "endotoxin A"|. Both toxins catalyze the transfer of |FRAME: ADENOSINE_DIPHOSPHATE_RIBOSE| from NAD+ to |FRAME: DIPHTHAMIDE| on eEF-2, inactivating it and halting cellular protein synthesis, causing cell death |CITS: [15485916]|. By targeting this unique modified amino acid which does not exist in bacteria, these pathogens are able to shut down the eukaryotic protein synthesis machinery without jeopardizing their own system.

The labdane diterpenoids |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| and |FRAME:CPD-18878 labdenediol| (this pathway) exemplify dicyclic compounds which together with the macrocyclic cembrenoids (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-7 cembratrienediol biosynthesis|) represent one of the two prevailing specialized metabolite groups of the nightshade family |CITS:[Severson85a] [24242718] [23757397]|. The first occurrence of |FRAME:CPD-18878 labdenediol| was reported for Nicotiana tabacum |CITS:[Colledge75]| and Nicotiana glutinosa |CITS:[Severson91]|. But both compounds have also been found outside the Solaneceae plant family, for instance in Pinus pinea |CITS:[DeSimon01]|. As all the other major diterpenoids both |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| and |FRAME:CPD-18878 labdenediol| are produced in glandular trichomes which cover leaves, stems and flowers of many higher plants |CITS:[16668241]|. Trichomes are epidermal outgrows and fulfill in plants a number of functions such as the regulation of evaporation, temperature and light. , Various types of trichomes found in the Solanaceae family have taken over specific functions in producing specialized metabolites involved in the plants defense system |CITS:[2652002] [Severson85]| and are characterized by a high dynamic of biochemical processes |CITS:[21275647] [22563774]|. Labdanoids formed in trichomes reportedly protect Nicotiana species from pathogens such as the fungus Colletotrichum lagenarium |CITS:[24234021]|, prevent the germination of the causative agent for blue mold in Nicotiana, i.e. the oomycete Peronospora tabacina |CITS:[24254279]| and act as insecticide on Nicotiana tabacum plants |CITS:[24242718]|. |FRAME:CPD-10110 Sclareol| has also been demonstrated to influence growth-regulatory processes of fungal hyphae and thus prevents fungal infections on Nicotiana glutinosa leaves |CITS:[4436652]|. Furthermore, labdanoids such as |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| have commercial value as precursor for compounds that increase the smoke quality during leaf curing |CITS:[Severson85a]| and raw material in the semi-synthesis of Ambrox |CITS:[25846965] [23113661]|, an amber substance with a widespread usage in the fragrance industry |CITS:[Barrero93] [25846965]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| has been first described and investigated in glandular trichomes of Salvia sclarea in which the pathway, associated enzymes, genes and secretion have been elucidated |CITS:[22959531] [23133579] [22834731] [20595348]|. In cell free extracts of Nicotiana glutinosa the enzymatic activities to convert |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP geranylgeranyl diphosphate| into both |FRAME:CPD-18878 labdenediol| and |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| using radioactive labeled |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP geranylgeranyl diphosphate| have been observed. The partially purified protein clearly demonstrated the catalytic activities but despite efforts to further purify and separate the respective enzymes this goal could not be achieved at the time |CITS:[Guo95a]|. It remains to be shown whether or not one or more similar proteins are involved in the formation of the two reaction products and if the characterized protein(s) catalyze both reactions from |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP geranylgeranyl diphosphate| to |FRAME:CPD-18878 labdenediol| or |FRAME:CPD-10110 sclareol| via the supposed intermediate |FRAME:CPD-12745 copal-8-ol-diphosphate| |CITS:[Guo95a]|.

General information on carotenoids: , |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Although biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD1F-114| have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated, details of all of the enzyme reactions involved in these pathways remain to be determined (as in |CITS: [20802040] [17008032] [11511870] [11432736]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., General information on lettuce carotenoids: , Carotenoids with cyclic ends are integral constituents of plants, algae and cyanobacteria photosynthetic reaction , centers |CITS:[GOODWIN80] [YOUNG93]|. In addition to α- and β-rings, plants also contain carotenoids with ε-rings. Carotenoids with one β- and one ε-ring are relatively common and include lutein, one of the predominant carotenoid in the light-harvesting antenna of most green plants. Carotenoids with two ε-rings, on the other hand, are not commonly found in plants and algae other than in trace amounts. Members of the |FRAME:TAX-4210| family, such as lettuce, present an exception. In those species, the two ε-ringed carotenoid lactucaxanthin has , been detected in the light-harvesting complex of photosystem II where it can represent between 20 to 30% of the total thylakoid carotenoids |CITS:[PHILLIP95]| and has therefore been postulated to play an important role in light-harvesting. A lycopene ε-cyclase responsible for the addition of a ε-ring at both ends of lycopene has been cloned from |FRAME:TAX-4236| |CITS:[11226339]|.

Summary: De novo biosynthesis of purines starts with the synthesis of |FRAME: IMP|, which can be converted to all, other purines., In bacteria and archaea |FRAME:IMP| is synthesized from |FRAME: 5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-5-AMINOIMIDAZOLE| in 6 steps, while in eukarya the first two steps are replaced by a single reaction (see |FRAME: PWY-6124|)., The first 4 steps of the bacterial pathway are catalyzed by individual enzymes, and the last two steps are catalyzed by a single multifunctional enzyme, |FRAME: AICARTRANSIMPCYCLO-CPLX|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: EG10795| gene., In archaea the last two steps are catalyzes by two different enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7234|)., Genetic studies indicate that in bacterial systems the majority of de novo purine biosynthetic genes are unlinked, but may act as a single unit of regulation controlled by the `purR' repressor protein.

Summary: |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids Glycosphingolipids| are a family of complex lipids composed of |FRAME: Ceramides| and mono- or oligosaccharide moieties that play an important role in various cellular functions including recognition, cell adhesion, proliferation and differentiation |CITS: [8490246]|. The lipid portion is embedded in the outer plasma membrane leaflet and the sugar chains extended to the outer environment, acting as an antigen. Together with |FRAME: Glycoproteins glycoproteins| and |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans glycosaminoglycans|, the glycosphingolipids contribute to the glycocalyx that covers eukaryotic cell surfaces., Glycoshphingolipids have been classified into the following 12 series based on their structure: |FRAME: Arthro-Series-GSLs arthro|, |FRAME: Gala-Series-GSLs gala|, |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs ganglio|, |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs globo|, |FRAME: Isoglobo-Series-GSLs isoglobo|, |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs lacto|, |FRAME: Muco-Series-GSLs muco|, |FRAME: Mollu-Series-GSLs mollu|, |FRAME: Neogala-Series-GSLs neogala|, |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs neolacto|, |FRAME: Schisto-Series-GSLs schisto| and |FRAME: Spirometo-Series-GSLs spirometo| |CITS: [25969757]|., Glycosphingolipids are synthesized by the sequential addition of sugar residues to ceramide by glycosyltransferases that are specific to each glycosidic linkage., |FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| |CITS: [10320813]|., This rather large superpathway integrates the biosynthetic pathways for several series of gglycosphingolipids. To read information pertaining to the different classes of glycosphingolipids and their biosynthesis, please click on the individual pathways (listed below) that make up this superpathway.

Summary: General Background, The uronic acid |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is an aldose sugar containing a carboxyl group. It is the main monomeric constituent of |FRAME: Pectin pectin|, a heteropolymer present in the cell walls of dicotyledonous plants. In pectin the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| monomers are in the α-pyranose form connected through a 1,4 linkage to form long chains. |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl "Homogalacturonan"| is the simplest form of pectin. Other forms are |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan-I"|, |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-1081|, |FRAME: PWY-1061|, and |FRAME: PWY-5980|). In natural pectin the majority of the carboxyl groups of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| are methylated. Some plants also contain acetylated galacturonate residues. Non-esterified carboxyl groups may be linked through divalent cations such as |FRAME: MG+2| or |FRAME: CA+2|, causing pectin to form a gel., |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is an important carbon source for microorganisms that catabolize plant material. Bacterial pathways for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation have been described. |FRAME:TAX-562| uses the isomerase pathway (see |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|). |FRAME: TAX-358| and |FRAME: TAX-80866| use an oxidative pathway (this pathway). Other bacteria use a different variant of the oxidative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-8391|). A different pathway for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation has been described for eukaryotic filamentous fungi. That pathway is evolutionarily conserved in the fungal subphylum |FRAME:TAX-147538|, which includes |FRAME: TAX-5061|, |FRAME: TAX-162425| and |FRAME: TAX-51453| |CITS: [18768163][19159926]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6491|)., About This Pathway, In this pathway |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is oxidized by an inducible dehydrogenase to |FRAME: CPD-17138| |CITS: [2471][19921179]|. Some papers suggested that the lactone spontaneously hydrolyzes to |FRAME: D-GALACTARATE| (meso-galactarate, mucate) |CITS: [2471][19060141][19897761]|). However, this was questioned based on the observation that the lactone hydrolysis is slow at slightly basic pH and it may be relatively stable under physiological conditions |CITS: [19921179]|., Later studis conducted with |FRAME: TAX-176299| showed that two dedicated enzymes, |FRAME: EC-5.4.1.4| and |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.27|, are responsible for isomerization of |FRAME: CPD-17138|, through |FRAME: CPD-16522|, to a linear form |CITS: [22493433][24450804]|., With the help of two additional enzymes, a decarboxylating dehydratase and a dehydrogenase, the pathway proceeds to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, which can be metabolized in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, or used in many other pathways.

Summary: This pathway produces the polyamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. This metabolite like other polyamines is cationic and may be involved in interactions with proteins, DNA and RNA molecules. It particpates in the developmental and physiological functions as well as in aiding regulatory processes. In plants polyamines are also known to be stress molecules |CITS: [16531054]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| in plants occurs via either the ornithine decarboxylase or arginine decarboxylase route, sometimes by both, unlike |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| biosynthesis in microbes, where either one of these routes are exclusively followed. The pathway depicted here is one where the two routes are connected in plants. In tobacco, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is a precursor of nicotine which is a powerful anti-herbivore toxin. Nicotine is induced by wounding or by elicitation by methyljasmonate treatment. The enzymes of this pathway are recruited during stress and characterized by high transcript accumulation during the stress periods |CITS: [15322128]|., Polyamines also accumulate in plant organs as conjugates of hydrocinnamate, formed by an amide bond. Summary: Aldoximes are intermediates in the biosynthesis of biologically active compounds such as indoleacetic acid, cyanogenic glucosides, and glucosinolates in plants., The enzymatic dehydration of aldoximes forms nitriles, which are then degraded by the organisms. Various soil microorganisms have been identified that can use nitriles as a source of carbon and/or nitrogen for growth |CITS: [10469129]| . The distribution of |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDOXIME|- and |FRAME: EPYRIDALDOX|-degrading ability was examined and found in bacteria, actinomyces, fungi, and some yeasts |CITS: [10831401]|. These microorganisms typically convert nitriles into carboxylic acids using either a combination of nitrile hydratase and amidase or a nitrilase |CITS: [10831401]|., These organisms are interesting for two reasons - their aldoxime dehydratases offer an alternative method for nitrile synthesis, while their nitrile degading capabilities may help in treatment of nitriile pollution. Nitrile compounds are often discharged into the environment in industrial waste water and agricultural chemicals. , |FRAME: ORG-5982| is capable of utilizing |FRAME: EPYRIDALDOX| as a nitrogen source |CITS:[9683644][10469129]|. The organism catalyzes the stoichiometic dehydration of |FRAME: EPYRIDALDOX| to form |FRAME: 3-CYANOPYRIDINE| via a novel aldoxime dehydration activity.  3-cyanopyridine is then convered to |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| by a nitrile hydratase, which is subsequently processed by an amidase to form |FRAME: NIACINE|.

Many organisms possess enzymes for the transformation of |FRAME: UREA| into |FRAME: AMMONIA|, and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. This conversion can occur in two distinct routes, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.5| and |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.6|, respectively., Urease catalyzes the ATP-independent cleavage of the amide bonds of urea, forming |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| in a single step. Ureases have been described in plants, fungi, and bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-5704|)., Urea carboxylases (also known as urea amidolyases) catalyze the ATP-dependent carboxylation of |FRAME: UREA| to |FRAME: CPD-578| (allophanate). Urea carboxylases have been known for quite a while in yeast and algae |CITS: [5679987][4556303][6753831]|. Although they have been reported more recenty from bacteria, the native substrate of the bacterial enzymes appears to be guanidine rather than urea |CITS: [15090492][27989440][32786413]|. True urea carboxylases are usually present in organisms that lack a urease., The urea carboxylase reaction is followed by the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-578| to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [4571226]|. While in yeast a single bifunctional enzyme (resulting from gene fusion)  catalyzes both reactions |CITS: [6105114][6124544][1802034]|, in algae they are catalyzed by two separate enzymes, |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.6|, and |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.54| |CITS: [5568176]|.

Summary: General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , In order to avoid self-intoxication cyanogenic glucosides are stored in the vacuole. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks they come in contact with activating enzymes (specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases) that reside in the cytoplasm or apoplastic space of the cells, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN| that serves as the first line of chemical defense |CITS:[16667728][Ganjewala10]|., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME: LINAMARIN Linamarin| and |FRAME: CPD-10277| have a broader distribution in the plant kingdom than most cyanogenic glycosides. They have been reported in five plant families, and co-exist in lotus, flax and cassava (|FRAME: TAX-3983|), the most important tropical root crop., In |FRAME: TAX-34305|, |FRAME: CPD-10277| and |FRAME: LINAMARIN| are synthesized and stored in young growing tissues like seedlings, apical leaves and stems. They are not transported to other tissues. Roots and dry seeds contain no detectable cyanogenic glucosides. However in cassava, both cyanogenic glucosides are found in all parts of the plant.

Summary: Throughout evolution, bioluminescence has been reinvented many times; some 30 different independent systems are still extant. The responsible enzymes are unrelated in bacteria, unicellular algae, coelenterates, beetles, fishes, and other organisms, although all systems involve exergonic reactions of molecular oxygen with different substrates (luciferins) and enzymes (luciferases), resulting in photons of visible light |CITS: [9891783]|. Bioluminescence is particularly predominant in the marine environment, in members of planktonic bacteria and protozoa, many invertebrates, and vertebrates with specialized light producing organs that harbor symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-7723|). The requirement for oxygen suggests that bioluminescence evolved after oxygen levels began to rise through the activities of early oxygenic phototrophic cyanobacteria., Luminous dinoflagellates are the main eukaryotic protists capable of light production and are responsible for much of the bioluminescence in ocean surface waters |CITS: [Tett71]|. The organisms emit blue-light flashes (max 475 nm) after mechanical or electrical stimulation., Dinoflagellate bioluminescence is proposed to act as defense against predation |CITS: [Marcinko13]|. It has been shown that the bioluminescence intensity is correlated with lower grazing by copepods |CITS: [Esaias72][White79][Buskey83]|, potentially due to attracting higher level predators |CITS: [Mesinger92][Abrahams93]|., The light is produced in the scintillons, specialized organelles that project from the cytoplasm into the acidic vacuole |CITS: [4341991][2442172]|. The scintillons contain |FRAME: EC-1.13.12.18| |CITS: [9256416][15665092]|, its tetrapyrrole substrate |FRAME: CPD-13067| |CITS: [Nakamura89]|, and in most species an additional protein, the luciferin-binding protein (LBP) |CITS: [2745419][Nicolas91][8398076]|., The luciferase is only active at slightly acidic pH, while LBP binds luciferin only at neutral to alkaline pH |CITS: [5545485]|. In the absence of physical stimulation the pH in the scintillon is sufficiently high to allow LBP to bind and protect luciferin, while maintaining an inactive luciferase. Upon mechanical stimulation, voltage-gated channels in the scintillon membrane open, allowing protons from the acidic vacuole to enter, lowering the pH inside the scintillons. While the mechanism is not completely understood, it involves a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) and calcium ions |CITS: [12200401][17322118]|. Upon acidification of the scintillon, the luciferin is released by LBP and becomes available for the activated luciferase, resulting in an instant reaction and a flash of light |CITS: [5672004][4501583]|., |FRAME: CPD-13067 Luciferin| has been fully characterized from |FRAME: TAX-2972|, and shown to be a linear tetrapyrrole with similarity to |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|. The molecule exhibits a characteristic blue fluorescence (475 nm) when irradiated with UV light. A study with amino acid tracers has confirmed the intracellular production of luciferin in |FRAME: TAX-2972| |CITS: [Wu03]|. It has been suggested that luciferin is a product of chlorophyll degradation by means of photooxidation |CITS: [11668566]|, but there are some indications that may not be the case: luciferin only appears in |FRAME: TAX-160621| at the onset of the dark-phase, at which time no sun light is available for photooxidation |CITS: [14766208]|. In addition, bioluminescence persisted in the heterotrophic dinoflagellate |FRAME: TAX-281609| after after being cultured for one year on rice flour, at which point no chlorophyl was produced |CITS: [27041627]|., Most dinoflagellates luciferases contain three homologous domains, each of which is active on its own |CITS: [9256416]|. Crystal structure of the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-160621| has shown that luciferin's access to the pocket that contains the active site is restricted at neutral pH by a three-helix bundle. Protonation of four intramolecularly conserved histidines that are present at the N-terminal region of each domain |CITS: [11327847]| alters the conformation of the bundle and enables entry of luciferin to an enlarged pocket |CITS: [15665092]|.

In addition to common polyamines, thermophiles (from both bacteria and archaea) contain additional types of unusual polyamines as major polyamines. One type consists of long linear polyamines such as |FRAME: CPD-13491| and |FRAME: CPD-22711|, and the other consists of branched polyamines such as |FRAME: CPD-16925|], |FRAME: CPD-13493|, and |FRAME: CPD-17107|. Long-chain and branched-chain polyamines were shown to effectively stabilize DNA and RNA, respectively |CITS: [15673283]|., The tertiary and quaternary branched polyamines |FRAME: CPD-16925| and |FRAME: CPD-17107| were first reported to be major polyamines in three |FRAME: TAX-2263| species - |FRAME: TAX-2264|, |FRAME: TAX-2265| and |FRAME: TAX-49900|, and two |FRAME: TAX-2260| species - |FRAME: TAX-2261| and |FRAME: TAX-2262| |CITS: [7968661]|., Thermophilic bacteria and archaea produce |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| from agmatine in a unique polyamine biosynthetic pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6834|). An enzyme that catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: CPD-16925| and |FRAME: CPD-17107| from |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| (BpsA) has been identified in the sulfur-reducing hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-311400| |CITS: [24610711]|. BpsA orthologs were found only in thermophiles, both in archaea and bacteria, and are absent from mesophiles |CITS: [24610711]|.

Summary: General Background, Organosulfonate compounds are found in the environment as both natural products and xenobiotics. They are catabolized by microorganisms that utilize the carbon and sulfur moieties. Aliphatic C3 sulfonates are widespread natural products found in the environment and are derived from microbial, plant and animal sources. The bacterial catabolism of C3 sulfonates such as |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| (racemic sulfolactate), |FRAME: CPD-380|, and |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| has been studied. The work has focused on the catabolism of the carbon moiety, the fate of the sulfonate group, and the transport systems necessary for organosulfonates to cross the cell membrane. Bioinformatics analyses have shown a diversity in pathways of sulfonate degradation in bacteria from both marine and terrestrial environments (in |CITS: [20007648]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16341843]|)., To date, three desulfonation pathways have been proposed for the degradation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| including:, (1) |FRAME: PWY-6616|: direct desulfonation of |FRAME: CPD-367| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-8144|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12191| and |FRAME: G-12192| genes. |FRAME: CPD-11799| is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-367| via |FRAME: CPD-380| by two dehydrogenases of opposite stereochemistry, encoded by |FRAME: G-12189| and |FRAME: G-12190|., (2) |FRAME: PWY-6637|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), followed by decarboxylation of sulfopyruvate to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by the |FRAME: CPLX-8153| encoded by the |FRAME: G-12226| and |FRAME: G-12227| genes, desulfonation to acetyl phosphate by |FRAME: G-12229|, and conversion of acetyl phosphate to acetyl-CoA., (3) |FRAME: PWY-6638|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), |FRAME: G-12230| gene., In all of these pathways the |FRAME: HSO3| or |FRAME: SO3| produced by the desulfonation reaction is proposed to be transported through the cell membrane and oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| by a periplasmic enzyme, possibly the product of genes sorAB in some organisms |CITS: [19581363][20150239] [16341843]|., In each of these pathways a different enzymatic desulfonation mechanism is used., In |FRAME: PWY-6616| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: CPD-367| by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.24| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8146| from |FRAME: ORG-6160| and |FRAME: CPLX-8144| from |FRAME: TAX-290398| for examples |CITS: [15758220]|., In |FRAME: PWY-6637| desulfonation occurs via |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.15|. See |FRAME: CPLX-8147| from |FRAME: TAX-246200| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15910| from |FRAME: TAX-89187| for examples |CITS: [19581363][16302849]|., About This Pathway, The marine γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-290398| grows aerobically with |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| as the sole source of carbon and energy. This compound was used quantitatively with stoichiometric release of the sulfonate moiety as |FRAME: SULFATE|. Thus, both enantiomers (|FRAME: CPD-367| and |FRAME: CPD-11799|) were oxidized. Genes encoding the pathway enzymes, a putative regulator and a putative transporter were located in a cluster |CITS: [20007648]|., The pathway is inducible although its regulation has not yet been elucidated. The |FRAME: HSO3| (sulfite) produced by SuyAB was proposed to be exported from the cell although the nature of the putative cytoplasmic membrane export system and a putative periplasmic sulfite dehydrogenase remains unknown. Summary: General Background, This pathway describes the formation of the formyl and methyl derivatives of tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) |CITS: [9190084][10785666]|. Folates are involved in a wide range of key metabolic functions in plants |CITS: [11960743][12644692]|, mediating fluxes through C1-pathways with a high demand for methylated compounds such as secondary metabolites |CITS: [11337394]|., Plants prefer the polyglutamylated forms of folates (compare |FRAME:PWY-2161|, |FRAME:PWY-2161B|) since the turnover rate of those compounds is markedly increased |CITS: [9190084][Scott00]| and meets the high demands for folates as observed in plants |CITS: [11960743]|. In addition the polyglutamylated forms of folate facilitate the retention of the vitamin within the cell and its subcellular compartments |CITS: [1916088]|. The plant enzymes involved in this pathway, although essentially catalyzing the same steps, have been found to differ in many regards from their bacterial counterparts |CITS: [9190084][14745019][15500462]|., Folates are tripartite molecules and are made up of pterin, p-aminobenzoate (PABA) and glutamate moieties. The one-carbon units are either attached to the N-5 of the pterin moietie, to the N-10 of the PABA moiety or are brigded in between those two (as in 5,10-methenyl or methylene-THF) |CITS: [Basset05]|., The different forms of folates are easily converted into each other through a tight network of reactions (|FRAME:PWY-2201|). Most of the enzymes have been identified in plants but some of them, such as the formyltetrahydrofolate deformylase, presumably involved in the mutual conversion of tetrahydrofolate and its 10-formyl derivative, remain to be demonstrated., Among the folates |FRAME:N5-Formyl-THF-Glu-N "N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| is the most enigmatic. Even though |FRAME:N5-Formyl-THF-Glu-N "N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| is the only folate derivative that does not serve as a cofactor in C1 metabolism, it is the most common and stable form of folates found in plants |CITS: [8480361]|. Moreover, |FRAME:N5-Formyl-THF-Glu-N "N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| is known to inhibit most of the folate-dependent enzymes at physiological concentrations. The biological role of this compound is still poorly understood, although it has been proposed to participate in the regulation of essential biosynthetic steps such as the formation of serine during photorespiration |CITS: [15888445][12207015]|. , The complete set of folate enzymes is only present in mitochondria. However, the recent discovery that folylpolyglutamate synthases are present in cytosol, mitochondria and plastids with each of them encoded by a different gene in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [11752472]| points to the fact that at least parts of the pathway can be carried out independently in those compartments. Interestingly, the enzyme hydrolyzing the polyglutamylated folates (γ-glutamyl hydrolase) has been found to be an extracellular enzyme in plants |CITS: [8912628]|., Further understanding of the transport and conversions of folates and their derivatives within the different cell compartments, and their regulation, is required before attempting to genetically engineer this pathway.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-183 "Gallate"| and structurally related compounds are widely distributed in nature. Plant lignin and tannins are major sources of these compounds, which are degraded by soil microorganisms as part of the terrestrial carbon cycle. , Gallate is also used industrially in inks and paints, and gallate esters are used as food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical antioxidants. Gallate and its derivatives are also of interest in drug development (reviewed in |CITS: [12769668]|. , Gallate and related compounds contain a benzene nucleus and at least 2 phenolic hydroxyl groups. Under aerobic conditions the benzene ring is cleaved by varioius dioxygenases. The benzene nucleus can be cleaved by ortho or meta fission enzymes, leading to different degradation pathways. Several distinct pathways of aerobic aromatic catabolism can be initiated by these dioxygenases, and their distribution among bacteria is complex |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|. Examples of these oxidative pathways are shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|, |FRAME: METHYLGALLATE-DEGRADATION-PWY|, , |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY-2504|., An anaerobic pathway for gallate degradation is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P3-PWY|., About This Pathway, Fluorescent pseudomonads such as |FRAME: TAX-303| can cleave gallate using the inducible ortho fission enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-2721|. However, the product |FRAME: CPD-184| (PDC) is usually not degraded further due to the lack of an enzyme that can process PDC. A strain that contains a |FRAME: MONOMER-10723| enzyme was isolated from soil by selection for growth on PDC as the sole carbon source, and named |FRAME: ORG-5956|., Extracts of cells grown with PDC contained the hydrolase and high levels of gallate dioxygenase, but demonstrated only low activity against protocatechuate. Cells adapted to gallate expressed the hydrolase while cells adapted to protocatechuate did not. Thin layer chromatography of derivatized catabolites produced by cells grown with PDC revealed 4-carboxy-2-oxo-3-hexenedioate, pyruvate, and oxaloacetate. The time of the appearance of these compounds was used to propose the catabolic pathway |CITS: [7142106]|. , In this pathway, the lactone, 2-pyrone-4,6-dicarboxylate, is hydrolyzed to the open chain keto form of the ring fission product. The enol tautomer, |FRAME: CPD-185|, can form spontaneously or enzymatically |CITS: [Nogales10]|. Hydration by a hydratase forms 4-carboxy-4-hydroxy-2-oxoadipate. This is cleaved to pyruvate and oxaloacetate by the aldolase. These 2 metabolites enter central metabolism, as indicated by the pathway link. These results demonstrated that |FRAME: ORG-5956| can use enzymes of the meta fission pathway to degrade gallate |CITS: [7142106][4342601]|., It should be noted that a second route of gallate degradation exists in |FRAME: TAX-303|, which involves a highly specific |FRAME: CPLX-7918 "gallate dioxygenases"| (see |FRAME: GALLATE-DEGRADATION-II-PWY|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Summary: General Background, Isoflavonoids comprise a large group of secondary metabolites involved in plant-pathogen , and plant-animal chemical warfare. These compounds are also involved in establishing the symbiotic relationship between , legumes and rhizobial bacteria. Isoflavonoids are restrictive distributed in the plant kingdom, being mostly biosynthesized , in plants of the subfamily |FRAME:TAX-3814| of the |FRAME:TAX-3803|. , Much of the interest in these secondary metabolites is based upon the finding that isoflavones and related compounds , can act as estrogens in humans. Consequently, those compounds have now been termed phytoestrogens. In view of their , perceived chemopreventive activities against hormone-dependent cancers, cardiovascular disease, and postmenopausal , ailments, isoflavonoids are considered as major targets for metabolic engineering., Isoflavones represent the largest group of natural isoflavonoids, with some 364 known aglycones reported |CITS: [Dewick94]|. , Their synthesis from flavanones is catalyzed by isoflavone synthase, a cytochrome P450 - dependent monooxygenase. , Isoflavones (daidzein, genistein) are common precursor in the biosynthesis of antimicrobial phytoalexins (de novo synthesis) , and phytoanticipins (pre-formed infectional inhibitors) in legumes. They also play a major role in establishing the symbiotic , relationship between the plant and rhizobial bacteria as chemoattractants for the bacteria and inducers of nod gene expression., About This Pathway, Wighteone and luteone are complex prenylated isoflavones frequently found within the tribe , Phaseolae of the legume family |CITS: [Ingham90]|. Their isomers isowighteone and lupiwighteone as well as , phaseoluteone have also been isolated from various legume plants |CITS: [Woodward79]| |CITS: [Stobiecki99]|. Monoprenylated , isoflavones are both involved in defense mechanisms against pathogens |CITS: [Abe87]| and nod gene induction |CITS: [Gagnon98]|., Prenylated isoflavones such as wighteone and luteone along with the prenylated isoflavanone kievitone have been observed , to be more active against pathogens then their non-prenylated analogues (dalbergioidin, genistein, 2'-hydroxygenistein). , The hydroxylation of genistein is carried out by the isoflavone-2'-hydroxylase (I2'H). However, the enzyme(s) isolated from , different species have demonstrated various substrate preferences. While I2'H does not hydroxylate genistein in chickpea , |CITS: [Hinderer87]| |CITS: [Clemens93]| the 2'-hydroxylation is carried out in soybean |CITS: [3956488]| and licorice , |CITS: [9790908]|. The intermediate 2'-hydroxygenistein is a branch point leading to the biosynthesis of prenylated isoflavanones , such as dalbergioidin and kievitone., Kievitone is a complex prenylated isoflavanol and together with the pterocarpan phaseollin (|FRAME:PWY-3042|) one , of the major phytoalexins present in the subtribe Phaseolinae of the legume family |CITS: [Ingham90]| |CITS: [Woodward82]| , |CITS: [Woodward79]|. Kievitone is strongly induced upon wounding and elicitors |CITS: [3996394]| |CITS: [Whitehead82]| , |CITS: [ONeill83]| and under the influence of abscisic acid as demonstrated in light-grown cotyledons of |FRAME:TAX-3885| , |CITS: [Brooks85]|., The isoflavone 2,3-dehydrokievitone has been found frequently in annual (|FRAME:TAX-3883| spec. - |CITS: [Woodward79a]| , |CITS: [ONeill83]| and perennial plants (Erythrina sacleuxii - |CITS: [11140607]|). The occurrence of 2,3- dehydrokievitone , has been discussed as evidence for an alternative route leading to kievitone |CITS: [Woodward79a]| |CITS: [ONeill83]| , where the order of prenylation and reduction is reversed (both routes are displayed in the pathway)., The prenyltransferase reaction seems to be the pathway-specific and determinative step for the formation of the , end-products kievitone and phaseollin, respectively. There is evidence that substrate-specific prenyltransferases are involved , in kievitone and phaseollin biosynthesis |CITS: [Woodward80]|. The enzyme catalyzing the prenylation of (-)-3,9-dihydroxypterocarpan , (DHP) to phaseollidin is specific for the 10-position of DHP and does not prenylate isoflavanone |CITS: [Biggs87]| whereas , the monprenylation of isoflavones such as genistein and their 2'-hydroxy derivative has been reported in |FRAME:TAX-3870| , |CITS: [Schroeder79]|.

Summary: General Background, Cell-to-cell communication in bacteria is accomplished through the exchange of extracellular signaling molecules called autoinducers. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., One of the paradigms of quorum sensing is that the signaling molecule accumulates in the extracellular medium. However, at least in the case of the common |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE| (AI-2), it has been shown that some bacteria can take it up and degrade it. The role of this process in the context of its natural multi-organism habitat is not fully understood yet., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: DIHYDROXYPENTANEDIONE| degradation pathway has been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-562|. The expression of transmembrane transporter proteins and degradation enzymes is regulated by the presence of AI-2. After uptake, AI-2 kinase phosphorylates AI-2 to |FRAME: CPD-10551|. This product then undergoes isomerization to |FRAME: CPD0-2467|, followed by transfer of an acetyl group to coenzyme A and release of |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|., Notably, both end products are intermediates in central carbon metabolism. In fact, |FRAME: TAX-562| can utilize AI-2 as the sole source of carbon and energy, although very poorly compared to carbon sources such as glucose and ribose. This may be due to an imbalance in the CoA/acetyl-CoA ratio that is created by the final reaction of the pathway |CITS: [25225400]|., Review: |CITS: [22712853]|.

The degradation of the main quercetin glucosides occurring in |FRAME:TAX-4679|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14753| and |FRAME:CPD-11685| to generate |FRAME:CPD-520| is catalyzed by specific quercetin glucoside glucosidases |CITS:[Tsushida96]|. The distribution of quercetin glucosides within the onion bulb differs significantly, with |FRAME:CPD-520| being most abundant in the outer peel and |FRAME:CPD-14753| and |FRAME:CPD-11685| occurring mostly in the middle and inner parts of the bulb |CITS: [Beesk10]|., Tsushika and colleagues (1996) observed the highest glucosidase activities in the outer scales of the onion with a gradual decrease of glucosidase activity towards the inner scales. The activities of the glucosyltransferases (see |FRAME:PWY-7129|) were reversed, with the highest glucosyltransferase activities found in the inner and middle parts and the lowest activity in the outer parts |CITS:[Tsushida96]|. Hence, the liberation of |FRAME:CPD-520| was the highest in the outer scale and the dry, outer peel contributing to the antifungal properties of the peel, which in turn protects the fleshy part of the onion |CITS:[Bilyk84]| |CITS:[Walker55]|. When infected by |FRAME:TAX-5507|, onions are able to undergo fast changes in flavonoid levels to respond to the pathogenic attack. |FRAME:CPD-14753 Quercetin-3,4'-O-diglucoside| and |FRAME:CPD-11685| are hydrolyzed and release |FRAME:CPD-520| to probably act as compound with antipathogenic activity |CITS:[Lee12]|., The quercetin glucosides |FRAME:CPD-14753| and |FRAME:CPD-11685| are relatively stable and naturally resist to a certain degree degradation through curing, cooking and storage |CITS:[20099844]|. The flavonol portion before and after heating had not changed much in either ratio of |FRAME:CPD-11685| (QMD) and |FRAME:CPD-14753| (QDG) nor total content |CITS:[Lombard05]| although some initial loss was observed |CITS:[21244009]| and storage duration and conditions (temperature) contributed to the stability of the flavonol glucosides |CITS:[Price97a]|. These results indicate the necessity for enzymes, i.e. quercetin glucosidases to be involved in the efficient degradation of the respective mono- and diglucosides involved in defense of plants. However, more research is needed to describe the participating enzymes in more molecular and catalytic details beyond their partial characterization done so far |CITS:[Tsushida96]|.

Summary: |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of both |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL|, a major constituent of the, fungal plasma membrane |CITS:[Paltauf][8561481]|, and |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|, the homologous component in, mammalian membranes., |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| share most of their biosynthetic pathway, with differences only, in the part of the pathway that is downstream of |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL|., In the first part of this pathway, starting at |FRAME: LANOSTEROL|, a sequence of two enzymatic reactions, involving, |FRAME:YHR007C-MONOMER|, and |FRAME:YNL280C-MONOMER|, converts, this tetracyclic triterpenoid to the sterol intermediate |FRAME: 44-DIMETHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL|., In the second part of the pathway, a set of three enzymes removes two methyl groups from the A ring of, |FRAME: 44-DIMETHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL|, resulting in formation of |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL|., The demethylation sequence starts with |FRAME:YGR060W-MONOMER|. This enzyme acts in three steps - it first adds a, hydroxyl group to the methyl carbon, converting it to a hydroxylmethyl group. It continues by oxidation of the hydroxyl moiety, resulting in a formyl group, and ends with the addition of a second hydroxyl group, generating a carboxyl group., This carboxyl is then removed by the second enzyme, |FRAME: YGL001C-MONOMER|. In the process of decarboxylation,, a hydroxyl group attached to another carbon of the sterol ring is oxidized to a keto group, and in order to complete this cycle,, the third enzyme, |FRAME: YLR100W-MONOMER|, restores it back to the initial hydroxyl group., When the first cycle is complete, |FRAME: 44-DIMETHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL| has been converted to, |FRAME: 4-METHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL|, which is the substrate for a second round of activity. When the second, cycle is complete, |FRAME: 4-METHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL| has been converted to |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL|., This pathway has been the subject of intensive investigation as a target of antifungal drugs |CITS: [11815273]|., |FRAME: YHR007C-MONOMER|, a member of the cytochrome P450 family encoded by the |FRAME: YHR007C| gene,, is the major target of azole antifungal drugs |CITS: [14638499]|.

General Background, |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O "Trimethylamine N-oxide"| (TMAO) is an important constituent of fish muscle and body fluids. It is believed to promote atherogenesis through its interaction with macrophages and lipid metabolism |CITS: [21475195][23563705][23312283][23614584]|., In deep-living marine animals TMAO acts as a piezolyte - it stabilizes intracellular proteins and cell structure for their survival under the high hydrostatic pressure of the deep ocean |CITS: [12443924]|. It is believed that fish cannot survive without TMAO at a depth greater than 5 km |CITS: [24591588]|., In bacteria the compound serves several roles: it is used as a nitrogen source by the SAR11 clade and the marine |FRAME: TAX-2433| clade of α-proteobacteria |CITS: [28304370]|, it is used as an electron acceptor by some γ-proteobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-22| and |FRAME: TAX-662| under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [9813127][11234928]|, and it is accumulated by some deep sea bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-480520| as a mechanism to cope with the high pressure |CITS: [33771875]|, as described in this pathway., In carnivourous mammals, ingestion of |FRAME: CARNITINE|, which is common in red meat, results in its degradation by gut microbiota to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.239| (see |FRAME: PWY-3641|). |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE Trimethylamine| is converted into TMAO by liver flavin-containing monooxygenases (FMOs), especially |FRAME: HS00223|. TMAO promotes atherogenesis through its interaction with macrophages and lipid metabolism |CITS: [23563705][23312283][23614584]|. High serum levels of TMAO have been shown to promote formation of atherosclerotic plaques in a mouse model |CITS: [21475195]|, and serum levels of TMAO were significantly correlated with the incidence of heart attack, stroke, and death in a clinical population |CITS: [24497336]|., About This Pathway, The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-480520| cannot grow with either |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA) or TMAO as its nitrogen source. However, the organism imports TMA into the cell, followed by its oxidation to TMAO, to be used as a piezolyte |CITS: [33771875]|., The organism possesses a |FRAME: MONOMER-21746| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-107494| gene) and an |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.148| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-107495| gene). The monooxygenase is adapted to both cold temperatures and high-pressure adapted |CITS: [33771875]|. , TmaT-like and Tmm-like sequences extensively exist in marine metagenomes, and have been found in sequenced genomes of marine members of the Bacteroidetes |CITS: [33771875]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-20771 Rhabduscin| is an isocyanide- and aminoglycosyl-functionalized tyrosine derivative synthesized by the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-628| and |FRAME: TAX-29488|, which are symbionts of the nematodes |FRAME: TAX-34507| and |FRAME: TAX-37861|, respectively. The nematodes infect insect larvae when they are in their infective juvenile-stage and regurgitate the bacteria to initiate insect pathogenesis. Once inside the host's circulatory system, the bacteria  produce an assortment of small molecules and proteins that overcome the insects innate immune system, eventually killing it. |FRAME: CPD-20771 Rhabduscin| is a potent nanomolar-level inhibitor of the insect |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.1| (also known as phenoloxidase) |CITS: [20022247]|, the enzyme that produces melanin (the hard black polymer insects generate to seal off microbial pathogens) as a critical innate immune response to invading pathogens |CITS: [21051882]|., Production of active compounds is enhanced by the uptake of |FRAME: PRO|, an abundant amino acid in insect hemolymph, and |FRAME: CPD-20771| production is enhanced by over an order of magnitude in |FRAME: PRO|-induced cultures of |FRAME: TAX-628| |CITS: [20022247]|., The three genes that encode the enzymes described in this pathway reside in a single operon. They were discovered by searching the |FRAME: TAX-406817| genome for genes homologous to |FRAME: G-58184|, a gene isolated from an environmental sample that was found to encode |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.25| |CITS: [16206308]|. In addition to this gene, the operon contains |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.10| and a glycosyl transferase. Cloning and expression of the three genes in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in |FRAME: CPD-20771| production  |CITS: [20022247]|.

|FRAME:CPD-17703 Coniferyl alcohol 9-methyl ether| is an compound rarely found in nature and its function in plants is subject to ongoing investigation. Allylic phenylpropanoid methyl ethers are not as frequently found as their phenolic methyl ester complements but seem to occur throughout the plant kingdom (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-26628| from |FRAME: TAX-1764351| |CITS:[11076549]|)., Several Linum species, amongst them |FRAME: TAX-407264| and |FRAME: TAX-407263| accumulate |FRAME:CPD-17703| and have been investigated in connection to the biosynthesis of aryltetralin lignans (for instance see |FRAME:PWY-5466|) |CITS:[Kuhlmann02]|. In addition, very closely related compounds with an allylic 9-methyl ether have been found in essential oils of plants from the Rutaceae family |CITS:[Campbell82]|. , Methylation is a very common reaction in furnishing secondary metabolites in plants and has been thoroughly researched resulting in a plethora of enzymatic, genetic and bioinformatic data and a sophisticated system of nomenclature and classification |CITS:[Ibrahim87] [9484457] [D'Auria03]|. The function of methylation is multifaceted (summarized in |CITS:[15130560] [16766004]|) and comprises for instance the production of volatile compounds (pollinator attraction or predator defenses) |CITS:[16469917]| and the formation of monolignols which are building blocks for lignins (see |FRAME:PWY-361|) and lignans (e.g. |FRAME:PWY-5466|) |CITS:[21889043] [Dewick02]|. , Amongst the latter is |FRAME:CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL| which is also the substrate for the coniferyl alcohol 9-methyltransferase (CA9OMT) |CITS:[Schneider11] [17333502]|. This enzyme differs from other plant small molecule O-methyltransferases (SMOMTs) in various ways. X-ray diffraction with the crystallized enzyme with and without binding of its substrate and co-substrate revealed the lack of a conserved catalytic histidine in the active site. In addition, the orientation of the substrate is flipped by 180 degrees in the binding cavity. , The enzyme has very distinctive requirements for its natural substrates such as the length of the side-chain, the location of double bonds within the side-chain, and the pattern of hydroxylation and methoxylation of the phenolic ring. It also exhibits a different binding order: unlike other methyltransferases, which first bind the |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| cosubstrate, CA9OMT first binds |FRAME:CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL|, which in turn improves the affinity for the binding of |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| by up to 222 times |CITS:[23633600]|.

|FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN "Cardiolipin"| is an anionic membrane phospholipid.  In |FRAME:TAX-562|, it is one of only three major lipids present in the membrane.  The anionic lipids are important for the biogenesis and function of membranes.  Cardiolipin is present in the plasma membrane of bacteria and in the mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes., A new route for cardiolipin biosynthesis has been discovered recently, involving the condensation of one molecule of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL| and one molecule of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE| with the concomitant release of ethanolamine.  This reaction is catalyzed by the newly discovered cardiolipin synthase 3 |CITS: [22988102]|.
