Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is an important and ubiquitous structural component of eukaryotic cell, membranes. Many bacterial species possess the capability to metabolize cholesterol and can survive on cholesterol as a single carbon source. The exact taxonomy of some species or genera recognized to catabolize cholesterol has changed over time. Two of the strains that were studied extensively, Nocardia restrictus ATCC 14887 and |FRAME:TAX-1702| ATCC 21387, are now classified as strains of |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [874450][12843070]|. In general, the mycolate-containing nocardioform actinomycetes, which include the genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus| and |FRAME: TAX-2060|, have all been shown to catabolize cholesterol and plant sterols |CITS: [19843168]|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1883| have been shown to decompose different steroids, including cholesterol |CITS: [Arima69]|, and some Proteobacteria were reported as being capable to degrade cholesterol |CITS: [4628510][9572974][18039763]|., The microbial degradation of cholesterol is challenging because of its complex chemical structure, low solubility in water, low number of functional groups and the presence of four alicyclic rings and two quaternary carbon atoms. A preliminary aerobic cholesterol degradation pathway has been proposed early on based on metabolites of cholesterol that have been identified in several actinomycete strains |CITS: [17345852]|, and has been largely resolved. In general, the steroid is sequentially oxidized and dehydrogenated forming several molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: SUC-COA| that can feed the citric acid cycle and generate ATP, or feed biosynthetic pathways such as lipid biosynthesis |CITS: [Murohisa93]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6945| and |FRAME: PWY-6946|)., The anaerobic degradation of cholesterol was studied later and not all the enzymes involved have been characterized. However, significant work was conducted with the β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-157592|, leading to the pathway shown here., About This Pathway, The Gram-negative β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-157592|, which is capable of using either nitrate or oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, was reported to mineralize cholesterol to carbon dioxide under anoxic conditions |CITS: [9094222][12892131]|. Several studies have uncovered most of the steps of the pathway, which employs a composite repertoire of more than 40 genes, some known from the aerobic degradation pathway and some unique genes that are required to circumvent oxygenase-dependent reactions., Cholesterol is imported through the outer membrane via a putative FadL-like transport system, which is induced by neutral sterols. Once in the periplasm, cholesterol is attacked by the AcmA |FRAME: MONOMER-21198|, which is similar to enzymes involved in the aerobic pathway, followed by C25-hydroxylation |CITS: [17307741][18039763]|. While the C-25 hydroxylation is catalyzed by an oxygenase in the aerobic pathway, it is catalyzed by a molybdopterin-containing steroid dehydrogenase during anaerobic degradation |CITS: [22942275]|. |FRAME: TAX-157592| has multiple variants of this enzyme, which are used for C25-hydroxylations of steroids with different isoprenoid side chains |CITS: [22942275][28940833]|., Periplasmic metabolism of cholesterol ends with |FRAME: CPD-19067|, which is transported into the cytoplasm, where the rest of the degradation occurrs |CITS: [25418128]|., The cholesterol degradation pathway involves two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. Side chain degradation in both the aerobic and anaerobic pathways leads to |FRAME: CPD-13704|. However, in the anaerobic pathway this process depends on aldolytic C-C bond cleavages that involve acyl-CoA synthetases/dehydrogenases specific for the respective 26-, 24- and 22-oic acids/-oyl-CoAs and promiscuous enoyl-, CoA hydratases, aldolases and aldehyde dehydrogenases |CITS: [28940833][29374035]|., Degradation of the A and B rings of the sterol core is different between the aerobic and anaerobic pathways, and depends on unique enzymes in anaerobic steroid degraders. Following the hydrolytic cleavage of the A ring, the process again involves CoA-ester intermediates. However, the degradation of the remaining C and D rings is highly similar in aerobic and anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [28940833]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Phosphoinositides "Phosphoinositides"| play a key role in signal transduction in the eukaryotic cell, transmitting signals from the cell surface to modulate intracellular processes., The 3-phosphoinositides, which contain the monophosphate |FRAME: CPD-177 "phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate"|, the bisphosphate |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH "phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate"| and the trisphosphate |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE "phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate"|, are particularly important in signaling cascades that influence a wide variety of cellular functions. These compounds are.generated by the action of several phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases (PI 3-kinases), as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6352|., The levels of specific phosphoinositide pools are regulated by intricate networks of enzymes and proteins that govern the rates of phosphoinositide synthesis, transport, and degradation., |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL-345-TRIPHOSPHATE "Phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate"| is a transient plasma membrane signal, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by a 5-phosphatase reaction to |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH "phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate"| or by a 3-phosphatase reaction to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"|., The 5-phosphatase reaction is catalyzed by several inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases that belong to groups type II (|FRAME: HS05898|, |FRAME: HS08354|, |FRAME: HS01279|, |FRAME: HS04546|, |FRAME: HS05626|, |FRAME: HS12255|), type III (|FRAME: HS09233|, |FRAME: HS09849|) and type IV (|FRAME: HS09270|)., The 3-phosphatase reaction is catayzed by |FRAME: HS10404-MONOMER| |CITS:[8399352][12018404]|. The importance of this reaction is made clear by the fact that mutations in this gene are found in a high percentage of human tumors, and particularly in glioblastoma, melanoma, and prostate and endometrial carcinomas |CITS:[12543774][12379854][12209607][12203792][12203362][12119278][12085208]|., The bisphosphate products can also be degraded. , |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH "Phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate"|, an important second messenger on its own, is considered a more sustained signal, and lasts for up to 60 min before being hydrolyzed to form |FRAME: CPD-177| by the inositol polyphosphate 4-phosphatases (|FRAME: HS00551| and |FRAME: HS03227|) |CITS: [9417038][12101241]|. It can also be hydrolyzed by |FRAME: HS10404| to form |FRAME: CPD-1108|., |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| is hydrolyzed, by either 4-phosphatases (|FRAME: HS14553| and |FRAME: HS15363|) or the same 5-phosphatases listed above, resulting in |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA| or |FRAME: CPD-1108|, respectively., Finally, each of the monophosphates has been shown to be degraded by a specific enzyme, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols|, which is recycled back to the membrane.

, A few years later two similar compounds, |FRAME: CPD-27187| and |FRAME: CPD-27188|, were isolated from |FRAME: ORG-57120|. Those compounds, which differ from |FRAME: CPD-27175| by an isoleucyl and an isoleucyl/methylphenylalanyl modifications, respectively, are potent competitive inhibitors of isoleucyl tRNA synthetase |CITS: [10866217][10866218]|., The biosynthetic gene cluster encoding the biosynthesis of these compounds was identified in |FRAME: ORG-57120| and named sbz. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-Fucopyranoses| is an important monosaccharide found in a diverse array of organisms. It is a carbohydrate component of bacterial lipopolysaccharides, mammalian and plant glycoproteins (such as the human antigenic glycoproteins or glycolipids of erythrocyte membranes) and various plant cell wall polysaccharides. It is found in xyloglucans and rhamnogalacturonans I and II. Fucosylation is performed by fucosyltransferases which require the activated form |FRAME: CPD-13118| (GDP-Fuc) as the donor substrate., The formation of |FRAME: CPD-13118| occurs via two routes: a) a de novo synthesis route from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| (this pathway), and b) a salvage pathway leading to the formation of UDP-Fuc from free |FRAME: L-Fucopyranoses| (|FRAME:PWY-6|). , Key Notes on the Enzymes:, The de novo synthesis of GDP-Fuc from GDP-D-mannose (GDP-Man) comprises three catalytic steps: a 4,6-dehydration, a 3,5-epimerization, and a 4-reduction. The first reaction step is catalyzed by |FRAME: GDPMANDEHYDRA-CPLX|, which involved the formation of the intermediate |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE|. In |FRAME: TAX-3702|, the |FRAME: AT3G51160| encodes a protein which was shown to possess this catalytic activity. In bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-562|), fungi (|FRAME: TAX-64518|), plants (|FRAME: TAX-3702|) and humans, the second and third reactions steps have been shown to be catalyzed by a single bifunctional polypeptide: |FRAME: CPLX0-3881| |CITS:[12881408][9525924][8910301][20035716]|. The coexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana |FRAME: AT3G51160| and |FRAME: AT1G73250| (encoding for |FRAME: AT1G73250-MONOMER|) genes in yeast cells led to the production of GDP-Fuc from GDP-Man |CITS:[12881408]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1045010| is the most notorious isolate of Shiga toxin-producing |FRAME: TAX-562|. Memebrs of this serotype have been responsible for the majority of E. coli outbreaks during the past several decades |CITS: [22610457]|. The |FRAME: TAX-83334| strain in particularly has gained international attention, as it is responsible for a major proportion of cases with hemolytic-uremic syndrome |CITS: [1765120][9125570][9457432][11142505][11211220][15036541][17020797]|., The structure of the |FRAME: CPD-24118| was reported in 1986 |CITS: [3008786]|, and the sequence of the O antigen biosynthetic cluster was published in 1998 |CITS: [9673232]|. The cluster contains 12 genes comprising five sugar biosynthetic pathway genes, four transferase genes, the O unit floppase gene, and the O antigen polymerase gene., Starting with |FRAME: CPD-15430|, assembly of the |FRAME: CPD-23724| requires three glycosyltransferases. Even though the genes encoding them, |FRAME: WBDN|, |FRAME: WBDO|, and |FRAME: WBDP|, were identified in the O antigen biosynthetic cluster, the exact function of each gene was not known at the time., Later work has identified |FRAME: WBDN| as a β-(1,3)-glucosyltransferase |CITS: [22556057]|, and the functions of the remaining two genes were identified in 2016 |CITS: [27336706]|. Using |FRAME: CPD-23907| as substrate, the authors showed that only |FRAME: WBDO WbdO| was able to generate a trisaccharide-PP-Und, indicating that it is the α-(1,4)-fucosyltranferase |CITS: [27336706]|. Using a similar technique, the authors could show that incubation of purified |FRAME: WBDP WbdP| with the trisaccharide-PP-Und and |FRAME: CPD-15537| resulted in formation of the |FRAME: CPD-23724| |CITS: [27336706]|., Nearly identical O antigen is produced by members of the Salmonella enterica O:30 serogroup (previously known as group N). The O antigens in these strains are modified by enzymes beleived to be encoded by prophages following polymerization. In serovar Landau (which has not been classified by NCBI as of 2020) about 50% of the glucose residues are acetylated at position O-6 |CITS: [Bundle86] |(see |FRAME: CPD-23912|), while in |FRAME: TAX-260677| and |FRAME: TAX-2564476| the GalNAc residue is modified by β-(1→4) glucosyation |CITS: [3815404]| (see |FRAME: CPD-23914|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest., Plants and algae are exposed to rapidly changing light conditions and light intensities. Illumination with high light intensities has the potential to overexcite the photosynthetic pigments and the electron transport chain and induce the production of toxic reactive oxygen species. Many photoprotection mechanisms exist to prevent this problem. One of the most important protection mechanisms is the dissipation of excessive excitation energy as heat in the light-harvesting complexes of the photosystems. This process requires a structural change of the photosynthetic antenna complexes that are normally optimized for efficient light-harvesting. Enhanced heat dissipation in the antenna systems is achieved by a strong quenching of the chlorophyll a fluorescence, and has been termed non-photochemical quenching, or NPQ |CITS: [24854581]|., About This Pathway, One of the important factors for the induction of NPQ in higher plants is the operation of the |FRAME: CPD1F-133|, |FRAME: CPD1F-131|, |FRAME: CPD1F-130| (VAZ) cycle. In the forward reaction of the cycle, which takes place under illumination with high light intensities, the di-epoxy xanthophyll |FRAME: CPD1F-133| is de-epoxidized to the epoxy-free xanthophyll |FRAME: CPD1F-130| via |FRAME: CPD1F-131|, which contains one epoxy group. In the reverse reaction, which occurs in low light condition, |FRAME: CPD1F-130| is re-epoxidized to |FRAME: CPD1F-133|., Note that the direction in which the pathway is presented (with |FRAME: CPD1F-130| at the top) reflects the order in which these compounds are synthesized. However, the VAZ cycle is described as starting with |FRAME: CPD1F-133|, so that the "forward reaction" goes from the bottom up, while the "reverse reaction" proceeds from the top down. , The forward reaction is carried out by |FRAME: EC-1.23.5.1|. The enzyme has a low pH optimum of 5.2 and requires the reduced form of ascorbate as cosubstrate. Prior to activation the enzyme is localized in the thylakoid lumen in an inactive form. After the drop of the lumenal pH to a value of around 5, due to the light-driven electron transport and the build-up of the transmembrane proton gradient, the enzyme forms an active dimer, and binds to the thylakoid membrane., The reverse reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.21|. The enzyme is located at the stromal side of the thylakoid membrane and has a broad pH optimum. It is usually active at neutral or slightly basic pH values that are typical for the chloroplast stroma. It is active both during darkness and illumination, but since its rate slower by a factor of 10 than the respective de-epoxidation rate, its activity during periods of high light illumination does not inhibit the fast accumulation of |FRAME: CPD1F-130|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD1F-114 "All-trans-lycopene"| is a bright red carotenoid pigment and phytochemical found in many photosynthetic organisms, as well as some non-photosynthetic organisms. Its name is derived from the name of the tomato plant, |FRAME: TAX-4081|, in which it is found in large amounts., |FRAME: CPD1F-114 "All-trans-lycopene"| is an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of many carotenoids, which are responsible for pigmentation, photosynthesis, and photo-protection in plants, algae, and other organisms., The first committed step of carotenoid biosynthesis is the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12321|. Two molecules of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (GGPP) are condensed to give |FRAME: CPD-464|, followed by rearrangement of the cyclopropylcarbinyl intermediate to |FRAME: CPD-12321|. This conversion is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.32|., Different strategies exist among different organisms for the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12321| to |FRAME: CPD1F-114|. In fungi and most non-oxygenic bacteria the pathway proceeds via exclusively all-trans isomers (this pathway). In oxygenic phototrophs such as plants, algae and cyanobacteria, as well as green sulfur bacteria, the pathway proceeeds via different cis isomers, and the final conversion to all-trans occurs at the very end of the pathway, where |FRAME: CPD-7496| is converted to |FRAME: CPD1F-114| (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|)., It should be noted that exceptions do occur - for example, the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-251221| utilizes the former pathway |CITS: [15811329]|., About This Pathway, Two types of enzymes have been described in bacteria that produce |FRAME: CPD1F-114| via the first pathway. In many organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-553| and |FRAME: TAX-28068|, a single FAD-containing enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.31| (|FRAME: MONOMER-15564 "CrtI"|), catalyzes the initial isomerization and the four subsequent desaturation reactions necessary to convert |FRAME: CPD-12321| to |FRAME: CPD1F-114|, via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-7408|, |FRAME: CPD1F-98| and |FRAME: NEUROSPORENE|. In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-34|, on the other hand, two enzymes are required for this process. The first one, |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.29| (|FRAME: G-12649 CrtIa|), catalyzes the initial isomerization and the first two desaturation steps, while the second one, |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.26| (|FRAME: MONOMER-16371 CrtIb|), catalyzes the two desaturation steps from |FRAME: CPD1F-98| to |FRAME: CPD1F-114|., Yet another enzyme, the fungal |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.30|, can catalye five desaturation reactions, generating |FRAME: CPD-12932|., It should be noted that the name CrtI is used to describe two different enzymes. In some bacteria the product of crtI gene is |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.28|, an enzyme that catalyzes three successive desaturation reactions, beginning with the colorless carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-12321| and producing the colored carotenoid |FRAME: NEUROSPORENE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6287|), while in other bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-28068|, the crtI gene encodes |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.31|, an enzyme that catalyzes four desaturation steps, producing |FRAME: CPD1F-114| (this pathway). , CrtI catalyzed desaturation steps extend a chain of conjugated double bonds, the chromophore, which gives carotenoids their yellow to red color. In general, carotenoid desaturases appear to have been structurally and functionally conserved during evolution (in |CITS: [11673627]| in |CITS: [2144293]| and reviewed in |CITS: [18535920]|)., This pathway has been documented in several organisms including the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-553| and |FRAME: TAX-28068| |CITS: [9914519][11673627]| and the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [11017770]|.

Taxusin (taxa-4(20),11(12)-dien-5α,9α,10β,13α-tetraol tetraacetate) is a taxoid that has been found in the heartwood of Yew (|FRAME:TAX-25629| L.) |CITS:[DellaCasaDeMarcano69]| but is believed to be a dead-end metabolite which is not involved in taxol biosynthesis |CITS:[Floss95]|. , Nevertheless, it has been employed as surrogate substrate because of the unavailability of the metabolic intermediates downstream the taxol biosynthetic route. This approach of applying a presumed structural analog of the natural, but still unidentified substrate(s) and using it for the functional screening of Cytochrome P450 clones has been employed by the group of Rodney Croteau (Washington State University, Pullman, USA) resulting in the discovery of 2 new Cytochrome P450-dependent oxygenases which hydroxylate the 2-position of the B-ring and the 7-position of the C-ring |CITS:[Croteau06]| |CITS:[15217605]|. Although the natural substrates for the 2α- and 7β-hydroxylases are still unknown the very specific ring position hydroxylations will contribute to the establishment of the hydroxylation sequence of the taxane core and to identify the natural substrates midway of the extended taxol biosynthesis. , Applied together, both Cytochrome P450 oxygenases carry out a sequential hydroxylation on taxusin yielding  2α7β-dihydroxyltaxusin. That is of metabolic importance as those hydroxylations mirroring the 2α- and 7β-hydroxylations in the fully functionalized taxol molecule |CITS:[15178487]| |CITS:[15157877]|. Although the 7β-hydroxylation is not considered of importance for the antimitotic activity of the taxoids this group is highly reactive and has been used in the development of 'second generation' taxoid drugs |CITS:[11741476]|. On the other hand the 2α-hydroxyl of the B-ring attached to a benzoyl moiety is thought to be essential for the binding to tubulin and subsequent inhibition of cell proliferation |CITS:[15178487]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ECDYSONE "Ecdysone"| and its derivative |FRAME: CPD-276| are ecdysteroid hormones that control embryonic and larval development, molting (moulting, ecdysis) and metamorphosis in members of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-6656|. |FRAME: CPD-276 "20-Hydroxyecdysone"| is considered to be the major active molting hormone in insects. Ecdysteroid is a generic name for a class of multifunctional, polyhydroxylated steroid hormones that are also found in plants and fungi. Ecdysteroids have potential practical uses in humans and other mammals, including use as pharmacological agents (reviewed in |CITS: [22687472][20837145][19669094][19771554][15844229][11729094]|). In insects, juvenile hormone is also essential for growth and development (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6575| |FRAME: PWY-6650|)., The biosynthesis, storage, hormonal regulation, secretion, and metabolism of ecdysteroids have been studied in insects and crustaceans (also see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7321|). Although the pathway for |FRAME: ECDYSONE| and |FRAME: CPD-276| biosynthesis in the molting glands of insects and decapod crustaceans is similar, the crustacean molting gland (Y-organ) synthesizes a greater variety of ecdysteroids. For example, |FRAME: CPD-15705| and 3-dehydro-25-deoxyecdysone produced in the Y-organ can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-15707| in peripheral tissues (not shown).. These crustacean ecdysteroids have been identified by radiotracer studies and can potentially be produced by the action of the same enzymes in different sequences, depending on species and life cycle stage |CITS: [10797325][BOCKINGD93][6523542]|. The pathway depicted here is found in both insects and decapod crustaceans and can vary among species as shown, as a result of the sequence of enzyme action (see below) (reviewed in |CITS: [20837145][18222403][15026169]|)., The molting process in arthropods is regulated by ecdysteroid hormones acting via nuclear receptors (transcription factors). The insect ecdysone nuclear receptor is a target for nonsteroidal ecdysteroid agonists that disrupt molting and can be used as safe pesticides. The ecdysteroid receptor is also used in research as a gene switch tool (reviewed in |CITS: [22017307][19771554][18680437][19669094][19796154]|)., About This Pathway, In arthropods, which cannot synthesize |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| de novo, ecdysteroids are thought to be synthesized either from dietary |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|, or from plant phytosterols in the case of plant-eating arthropods (in |CITS: [21277979][16949568]|). In insects ecdysteroids are synthesized in the prothoracic gland during postembryonic development and in the ovary or male accessory gland in adults |CITS: [23383307]|. |FRAME: ECDYSONE "Ecdysone"| is secreted into the hemolymph and converted to |FRAME: CPD-276| in the peripheral tissues. In decapod crustaceans |FRAME: ECDYSONE| and several other ecdysteroids are synthesized in the molting gland (Y-organ) of the cephalothorax. |FRAME: ECDYSONE "Ecdysone"| is secreted into the peripheral tissues where it is converted to |FRAME: CPD-276| (reviewed in |CITS: [22687472][20837145][15026169][11729094]|)., The Halloween genes encode the cytochrome P450 monooxygenases responsible for |FRAME: ECDYSONE| and |FRAME: CPD-276| biosynthesis. They were first identified in embryonic lethal mutants of |FRAME: TAX-7227| that are deficient in |FRAME: ECDYSONE| and exhibit morphogenetic abnormalities. Orhologs of the Halloween genes are present in other arthropods (|CITS: [19802900][18298845][17628274]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22687472][20837145][18222403][16399407]|). None of the crustacean enzymes encoded by orthologs of the Halloween genes have been biochemically characterized (reviewed in |CITS: [20837145]|)., In insects the initial conversion of |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| to |FRAME: CPD-15500| (also called 5β-diketol) is still referred to as the "black box" because no stable intermediate has been identified and these steps remain uncharacterized. However In crustaceans the existence of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-15501| (Δ4-diketol) produced by the black box reactions was suggested in studies of the molting gland (Y-organ) of the crab |FRAME: TAX-6759|. This putative intermediate is converted to |FRAME: CPD-15500| (5β-diketol) by a 5β-reductase |CITS: [8973547]|. Note that the |FRAME: CPD-15501| (Δ4-diketol) intermediate has not been demonstrated in insects (in |CITS: [16949568]|)., In some insects such as |FRAME: TAX-7227| the putative |FRAME: CPD-15500| (5β-diketol) may be reduced by a 3-dehydroecdysteroid 3β-reductase to |FRAME: CPD-15499| (3β,5β-ketodiol). This compound tthen undergoes the cytochrome P450 monooxygenase-catalyzed hydroxylation reactions to produce |FRAME: ECDYSONE| in the prothoracic gland. However in other insects such as |FRAME: TAX-7130|, |FRAME: CPD-15500| (5β-diketol) may directly undergo the hydroxylation reactions to produce |FRAME: CPD-331| in the prothoracic gland. In some insects such as |FRAME: TAX-7109| and crustaceans such as |FRAME: TAX-28379| both branches of the pathway have been shown in the molting gland |CITS: [BOCKINGD93][8973658]|. In the peripheral tissues |FRAME: CPD-331| may be converted to |FRAME: ECDYSONE| by a 3-dehydroecdysone 3β-reductase (|CITS: [21125567][16503480]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15026169]|)., The black box reactions have been hypothesized to contain the rate-limiting step in |FRAME: ECDYSONE| biosynthesis. There is evidence that the products of Halloween genes spo (spook, CYP307A1), spok (spookier, CYP307A2 which is a paralog of spo), and spot (spookiest, CYP307B1) are involved in the black box reactions |CITS: [23383307][16949568][16188237]|. In addition, gene nm-g (non-molting-glossy in |FRAME: TAX-7091|) or its ortholog sro (shroud in |FRAME: TAX-7227|), are short chain dehydrogenase/reductase family members that are also involved in the black box reactions |CITS: [20501590]|. However the exact functions of the black box enzymes remain unclear., The products of genes phm (phantom, CYP306A1) dib (disembodied, CYP302A1) and sad (shadow, CYP315A1) sequentially convert the |FRAME: CPD-15499| (3β,5β-ketodiol) to |FRAME: CPD-15498| (3β,5β-ketotriol), |FRAME: CPD-15497|, and |FRAME: ECDYSONE| |CITS: [16503480][16164612][15350618][15197185][12177427][10976044]|. The product of gene shd (shade, CYP314A1) mediates the conversion of |FRAME: ECDYSONE| to |FRAME: CPD-276| (|CITS: [22465741][18226571][16473459][14610274]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15026169]|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| is a branch point metabolite leading to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Menaquinones , menaquinone| (vitamin K2, in bacteria), |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1 in plants), and many plant pigments, including some two-ring naphthoquinones (such as |FRAME: CPD-9608| and |FRAME: HYDROXYNAPHTHOQUINONE|) and the three-ring anthraquinones (such as |FRAME: ALIZARIN| and |FRAME: CPD-9759|). These pigments are mostly found in |FRAME: TAX-24966|, where at least some of them are phytoalexins involved in plant defense. Many of these pigments were used as dyes since the early human history., The benzenoid ring (or A ring) of 1,4-dihydroxy-2-naphthoate is derived from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, derived via the shikimate pathway. The quinone ring (or B ring) is formed by addition of |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|., About This Pathway, The first step of the pathway, conversion of chorismate to isochorismate, is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.4.4.2| (MenF). Addition of the succinic semialdehyde moiety of 2-oxoglutarate to isochorismate, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.9| (MenD), results in the formation of the unstable compound |FRAME: CPD-9924 "SEPHCHC"|. A pyruvoyl group is subsequently eliminated by |FRAME: EC-4.2.99.20| (MenH), resulting in the prearomatic compound |FRAME: CPD-9923 "SHCHC"|. It has been shown that |FRAME: CPD-9924 "SEPHCHC"| also undergoes a spontaneous isomerization to |FRAME: CPD-26609 "iso-SEPHCHC"|, though it is still not known whether this isomer is also an acceptable substrate for MenH |CITS: [35901288]|., Dehydration of |FRAME: CPD-9924 "SEPHCHC"| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.113| (MenC) results in the benzenoid aromatic compound |FRAME: O-SUCCINYLBENZOATE|. In a reaction that requires ATP hydrolysis, |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.26| (MenE) generates |FRAME: CPD-6972|. A dehydration reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.36| (MenB) results in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-9925| (DHNA-CoA). The final reaction, hydrolysis of DHNA-CoA to form |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.2.28| (MenI) |CITS: [23564174]|.

|FRAME: Xylans Xylan| is a general name given for polysaccharides composed of xylose residues., The most common form of xylan is |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan|, which is found in the cell walls of plants and some algae, where it is the major constitutent of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|., |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan " (1→4)-β-D-xylan"| is a polymer of |FRAME: BETA-D-XYLOSE| residues connected by (1→4) links. Pure xylan, consisting of only xylopyranosyl residues, is rare. Most forms of |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan| are decorated with other types of sugars, in the form of |FRAME: Arabinoxylan arabinoxylan|, |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans glucuronoxylan|, |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans glucuronoarabinoxylan| or |FRAME: Arabinoglucuronoxylans arabinoglucuronoxylan|., In woody species the reducing end of the xylan molecule is capped with a unique tetrasaccharide consisting of β-D-Xylp-(1→3)-α-L-Rhap-(1→2)-α-D-GalpA-(1→4)-D-Xylp |CITS:[Johansson77][Andersson83]|., Our current understanding of the biosynthesis of xylan is rather minimal. A number of genes from Arabidopsis, poplar and some other plants have been shown to be associated with xylan biosynthesis., In the Arabidopsis genome, four glycosyltransferases of the GT43 family, IRX9/I9H and IRX14/I14H, have been shown to be required for the normal elongation of xylan backbone |CITS: [17944810][17322407][20595206][17938130][20424005][20335400]|. It has been shown that the poplar GT43A/B/E genes are functional orthologs of the Arabidopsis IRX9, and that the GT43C/D genes are functional orthologs of IRX14 |CITS: [21596688]|., The Arabidopsis thaliana FRA8/F8H and PARVUS genes |CITS: [16272433][19224953][17991630]|, as well as the orthologous poplar GT47C and GT8E/F genes |CITS: [16887843][19789274][19395414]| and the GT8D gene |CITS: [21596688]| are involvedl in the biosynthesis of the xylan reducing end sequence.

|FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans Arabinogalactan| and |FRAME: Lipoarabinomannans lipoarabinomannan| are major cell wall polysaccharides of mycobacteria. Both polymers contain arabinan chains that are formed by arabinofuranosetransferases that utilize |FRAME: CPD-14550| (decaprenylphosphoryl-D-Araf) as the arabinofuranose (Araf) donor., Decaprenylphosphoryl-D-Araf is derived from |FRAME: PRPP| (pRpp) in a pathway that requires 4 enzymes. The pathway starts with |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.45|, which transfers pRpp to a |FRAME: CPD-11994| molecule to form |FRAME: CPD-12039|. The pathway proceeds by dephosphorylation and oxidation of the hydroxyl group at the 2 position of the ribose, forming |FRAME: CPD-12041|. Finally, a reductase reduces the molecule to |FRAME: CPD-14550| |CITS: [16291675]|.

|FRAME: CPD-10247 Sulfoquinovose| is a major component of organo-sulfur compounds in nature |CITS: [428677]|. It is synthesized by higher plants, mosses, ferns, algae and most photosynthetic bacteria and serves as the polar headgroup of the sulfolipid in photosynthetic membranes |CITS: [15012227][17334828]|., Bacteria that are able to utilize sulfoquinovose as their sole source of carbon and energy for growth have been isolated, and multiple degradation pathways have been described |CITS: [Liu21]|., About this pathway, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.199|, hydrolyzes terminal non-reducing α-sulfoquinovoside residues in |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL "α-sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerides"| and |FRAME: CPD-19111 "α-sulfoquinovosyl glycerol"|. The gene encoding it, |FRAME: EG11843|, has been found in association with all three sulfoglycolytic pathways that were reported first. It was thus employed to search for novel sulfoglycolytic pathways., A search for genes clustered in the neighborhood of this gene identified several Sequence Similarity Networks (SSNs) that were different from the three pathways known at the time. These SSNs were found to be associated with three additional sulfoglycolytic pathways |CITS: [Liu21]|., This pathway, found in Gram-positive bacteria, is analogous to the |FRAME: PWY-7446 "sulfo-EMP pathway"| in Gram-negative bacteria. However, the enzymes involved are distantly related to those of the Gram-negative bacteria, and belong to distinct enzyme families. In addition, the enzymes catalyzing the production and export of the final product, |FRAME: CPD-11799|, resemble the enzymes characterized from |FRAME: ORG-57071| (|FRAME: PWY-8213|).

General Background, Chlorobenzoates are a group of compounds that occur in the environment in large amounts either because of their release, as herbicides or as products of bacterial degradation of polychlorinated biphenyls |CITS: [7217013]|., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation seems to have evolved recently as a result, of their widespread release to the environment., About This Pathway, Many chlorobenzoate-degrading bacterial strains utilize a pathway that starts with |FRAME: CPLX-7698|,, which leads to the formation of chlorocatechols (see |FRAME: PWY-6088|)., |FRAME: TAX-285| utilizes a different pathway for |FRAME: CPD-3486| degradation, in which the key enzyme is, |FRAME: CPLX-7827|., This enzyme incorporates a dioxygen molecule into the 3,4 or 4,5 positions of of the |FRAME: CPD-3486| ring, resulting in, formation of |FRAME: CPD-11221| or |FRAME: CPD-11220|, respectively |CITS: [8285670]|., The dioxygenase has not been purified, but the genes encoding it, |FRAME: G-11259| and |FRAME: G-11260|, have, been cloned and expressed, and its proposed activity has been confirmed |CITS: [8285670]|., The next pathway enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-14758|, is encoded by the |FRAME: G-11261| gene, which is, present in the same operon. This enzyme has different activities with the two respective pathway intermediates., In the case of |FRAME: CPD-11221|, the chlorine atom is removed during catalysis, resulting in, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|., In the case of |FRAME: CPD-11220|, the chlorine atom is not removed, and thus the product is |FRAME: CPD-11222|, |CITS: [9322760]|. , Both compounds are metabolized further as described in |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|., The first enzyme of that pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, can accept |FRAME: CPD-11222|, in which case a chlorinated, intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-11223|, is formed and remains bound to the enzyme. A spontaeous reaction, results in the removal of the chlorine, and formation of |FRAME: CPD-184|, an intermediate in the protocatechuate, degradation pathway |CITS: [3988709]|.

Summary: |FRAME: BENZENE Benzene| is a highly toxic industrial compound with a broad range of industrial uses. It is one of the top 20 production volume chemicals in the United States, with an annual production of almost 9 million metric tons. In addition to being a component of petroleum-based fuels, benzene is often used as a raw material for the manufacture of other chemicals, rubbers, lubricants, dyes, detergents, drugs, and pesticides. Benzene is among the most prevalent organic contaminants in groundwater and is a major concern due to its toxicity and relatively high solubility |CITS: [12558180]|., Many soil bacteria are able to catabolize benzene under aerobic conditions. The aerobic pathway starts with a dihydroxylation reaction that is is carried out by ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase enzymes that incorporate both atoms of molecular oxygen |CITS: [8344526]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5450|). However, when soils and sediments are contaminated with benzene, extensive anaerobic zones frequently develop due to stimulation of the indigenous aerobic microbial population. Anaerobic benzene degradation has been demonstrated under nitrate-reducing |CITS: [9925578]|, Fe(III)-reducing |CITS: [8022480][16535218]|, sulfate-reducing |CITS: [16534979]|, and methanogenic |CITS: [9572976]| conditions., The pathways for anaerobic benzene degradation have been notoriously difficult to study, although it could be shown that at least two such pathways exist: in one pathway benzene is carboxylated to |FRAME: BENZOATE| |CITS: [11683870][21742914]| (this pathway), while in the other benzene is hydroxylated to |FRAME: PHENOL| |CITS: [16347109]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8375|)., In 2010 a study of an anaerobic iron-reducing enrichment culture has identified two genes that may encode a benzene carboxylaseand the enzyme that forms its cofactor (which then mamed abcAD) based on the increased expression of these proteins in benzene-grown but not in phenol- or benzoate-grown cultures. AbcA is similar to |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.98| (UbiD), while AbcD is similar to |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.129| (UbiX), which produces the |FRAME: CPD-18260| cofactor that is required by the carboxylase |CITS: [20545743]|. These enzymes have not been studied any further., In the following year it was shown that in the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-54261| genes encoding benzoate degradation are highly induce during growth of benzene, while phenol degradation genes were not |CITS: [21742914]|. The |FRAME: TAX-54261| genome contains two genes similar to abcA described in the 2010 paper. One of the two genes, |FRAME: G-107873|, had increased transcript abundance in benzene- versus acetate- or benzoate-grown cells |CITS: [21742914]|. That enzyme too has not been studied any further., A 2018 study that looked at genes induced by anaerobic growth on benzene in a benzene-degrading nitrate-reducing microbial consortium has found highly transcribed genes with high similarity (>96% at the amino acid level) and gene synteny to the abcAD genes described in 2010. Once again, the authors stated that |FRAME: G-107875| gene encodes a benzene carboxylase. Furthernmore, they claimed that the high level of transcripts indicates that benzene carboxylation to benzoate is the main initial benzene degradation pathway in that culture |CITS: [29540736]|. As of 2022, no biochemical data exists for any of these enzymes.

Names: L-leucine degradation IV (reductive Stickland reaction) // L-leucine fermentation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additinal reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, The strictly anaerobic pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1496|, which lives in the human gut, is able to thrive from fermentation of |FRAME: LEU|. It metabolizes L-leucine via two different paths: oxidation to |FRAME: ISOVALERATE| and CO2 (see |FRAME: PWY-8185|), and reducion to |FRAME: CPD-17493|, thus avoiding the need for a terminal electron acceptor |CITS: [6805929]|., As described above, both branches start with the oxidation of |FRAME: LEU| to |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| (the reversal of a biosynthetic reaction that leads to L-leucine production)., Reduction of the latter by NADH leads to |FRAME: CPD-17492|, which is converted to the thiol ester by CoA transfer to yield |FRAME: CPD-11652|. This reaction is catalyzed by a CoA transferase and uses |FRAME: CPD-17494| as the donor, and is thus coupled to the last reaction in the pathway - the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-17494| to |FRAME: CPD-17493| |CITS: [16957230]|., |FRAME: CPD-11652| is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-18023| in a reaction that is chemically difficult because the β-hydrogen to be eliminated as a proton is not acidic. The acidification of this hydrogen requires radical chemistry mediated by two enzymes, a dehydratase (a heterodimer consisting of HadB and HadC subunits) and an ATP- and ferredoxin-dependent activator, also called archerase (HadI) |CITS: [15654892][18337824][21366233][22827463]|., An enoyl-CoA reductase enzyme, which has not been characterized yet, catalyzes the reduction of |FRAME: CPD-18023| to |FRAME: CPD-17494|, which then feeds into the CoA transferase mentioned above, completing the cycle and releasing |FRAME: CPD-17493|. The use of a transferase rather than the esterification with Coenzyme A followed by hydrolysis makes the pathway more efficient by saving ATP molecules.

Summary: General Background, Most organisms have less than 45 different tRNAs despite the fact that there are 61 different amino acid codons. The reason for this is that the third base of the codon is less discriminatory for the amino acid than the other two bases. Thus, the first base of the tRNA anticodon, which pairs with the third base of the codon, is more permissive for mismatches than the other two positions. At this position, which is known as the wobble position, 'U's and 'C's may be read by a 'G' in the anticodon. Similarly, 'A's and 'G's may be read by a 'U' or 'y' (pseudouridine) in the anticodon., The nucleotide at the wobble position is often modified, and particularly uridines, which are almost invariably modified. In yeast, 11 out of 13 wobble uridine-containing tRNAs are modified in some manner. The modifications increase the efficiency of codon reading and prevent mistranslation by limiting wobbling. In particular the 2-thiolation of the uridine is required for efficient codon recognition on the ribosome., The uridine34 wobble bases of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu are universally modified, although different modifications occur in different taxa and even in different cell compartments. The different modifications of uridine 34 are sometimes referred to as xm5U, and include nm5(s2U), mnm5(s2)U, cmnm5(s2)U, and cmnm5Um]. It has been shown that the 2-thio modification of mnm5s2U in tRNALys of |FRAME: TAX-562| confers efficient ribosome binding |CITS: [10024171][11063576]|. The same modification in tRNAGlu is required for specific recognition by glutaminyl-tRNA synthetase |CITS: [8385989]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1423| has been shown to produce similar xm5s2U34 modifications to |FRAME: TAX-562|, though several differences exist between the two organisms in the thiolation enzymes |CITS: [30249152][32629984]|., The thiolation of tRNAGln, tRNALys and tRNAGlu in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-1423 | is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.13|. The source of the sulfur is |FRAME: CYS|. However, in |FRAME: TAX-562| a complex sulfur relay system consisting of IscS and the TusABCDE proteins is required for delivery of the sulfur atom to that enzyme |CITS: [16387657]|, while |FRAME: TAX-1423| uses only one relay enzyme, |FRAME: BSU27510 IscSA| (previously known as YrvO) |CITS: [25825430][28327539]|., Independently of the thiolation, the C5 position of the uracil is modified by three enzymatic reaction. In |FRAME: TAX-562| the first reaction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: EG10997| and |FRAME: EG10375| complex, which forms of a 5-carboxymethylaminomethyl group |CITS: [19591841][19767610][24293650]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| the |FRAME: BSU41020| and |FRAME: BSU41010| genes are orthologous to the |FRAME: TAX-562| genes., The second and third reactions are catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-562| by the |FRAME: G7199 MnmC| protein, which consists of two conserved domains, an N-terminal methyltransferase domain and a C-terminal FAD-dependent oxidoreductase domain |CITS: [15247431][18186482]|. However, no MnmC ortholog is present in |FRAME: TAX-1423|, and it is believed that another (currently unknown) enzyme catalyzing the same activitiesy must be present |CITS: [30249152][32629984]|.

General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway: , Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes have been involved in a variety of biological processes: inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Palustric acid, an abietane-type DRA, is one of the principal resin acids |CITS:[17082986],[11269960]|. Palustric acid has one of the highest index of cytotoxicity among all the resin acids |CITS:[7887603]|. This compound, along |FRAME:CPD-8694| has also been shown to be very effective as an inducer of germination of ectomycorrhizal fungi spores |CITS:[Fries88]|. The formation of this acid involves the formation of the abietane skeleton via cyclization of the diterpenoid precursor |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This cyclization occurs via the formation of the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-4750| and is followed by the stepwise oxidation of the C18 methyl group of the derived olefin |FRAME:CPD-8697|. Several levopimaradiene/abietadiene synthases have been identified, which, in addition to |FRAME:--ABIETADIENE| and |FRAME:CPD-8695|, can produce a variety of other olefins including |FRAME:CPD-8697| |CITS:[8798524],[15310829],[16497345]|. The mechanism of oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-8697| to |FRAME:CPD-8717| is thought to resembles that of the oxidation of |FRAME:CPD1F-128| to |FRAME:CPD1F-132| and that |FRAME:CPD1F-132| to |FRAME:CPD1F-95| (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|) in which a single multifunctional enzyme (ent-kaurene oxidase) catalyze the consecutive oxidation steps. An enzyme catalyzing those steps remains to be identified.

There are two main pigments in plants conferring red and violet colors to flowers, i.e. anthocyanins (for instance see |FRAME:PWY-5313| and betalains (see |FRAME:PWY-5405|) which replace anthocyanins in the order Caryophyllales |CITS:[23395307]|. Anthocyanins are a group of vacuolar pigments which provide flower colors as attractant for pollinators and represent the single most important feature in ornamental plants |CITS:[Heller94] [25964787] [25015943]|. Detailed knowledge about the biosynthesis and modification of anthocyanins is one of the keys for creating true blue flower colors in roses and chrysanthemum which is currently one of the most ambitious breeding goals in horticulture |CITS:[19554240] [21903230]|. In addition, acylated anthocyanidin glucoside and -sambubioside exhibit light-resistance, are able to scavenge radicals |CITS:[12951524]| and are valued food colorants with antioxidant and chemoprotective properties |CITS:[Giusti03]|., Glucosylation at the 3-O-position of the aglycon anthocyanins stabilizes the resulting anthocyanidin glucosides which are the prerequisite precursors for further decoration of the anthocyanidin skeleton via glycosylation, acylation and methylation (summarized in |CITS:[24792223]|). Anthocyanidins may occur as sambubioside, i.e. diglucosides which contain a xylose attached to the 2''-O-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of anthocyanidins (see |FRAME:PWY-7678|) and acylated derivatives thereof. Such acylated anthocyanidin glucosides and sambubiosides have been found in many plant families, most notably in the Brassicaceae, e.g. Matthiola incana |CITS:[Seyffert60] [8722092] [7766384] [Tatsuzawa12]|, Heliophila coronopifolia |CITS:[21903230]|, and Orychophragmus violaceus |CITS:[16023157]|. Acylated anthocyanidin glucosides also occur in Perilla frutescens (Lamiaceae) |CITS:[Fujiwara98] [10845463]| as intermediates in the |FRAME:PWY-5284| and |FRAME:PWY-5139|. In the pathway |FRAME:PWY-7450|, acylated anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides and 3-O-sambubiosides are involved in the biosynthetic sequence towards the major anthocyanin in Arabidopsis, i.e. A11 |CITS:[11830144] [17425720]|. , The anthocyanidin glucoside 6''-O-acyltransferase identified in petals of various genetic lines of Matthiola incana catalyzed the transfer of either |FRAME:COUMARATE| or |FRAME:CPD-676| from the corresponding acyl-CoA donors to the 6''-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of either |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-3-GLUCOSIDE-CMPD| or |FRAME:CPD1F-766| , forming |FRAME:CPD-7384|, |FRAME:CPD-7383| and |FRAME:CPD-16541| and |FRAME:CPD-18098|, respectively. In addition and with comparable efficiency anthocyanidin 3-O-sambubioside, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18091| and |FRAME:CPD-16535| were accepted as substrates yielding |FRAME:CPD-18099|, |FRAME:CPD-18100| and |FRAME:CPD-16536| and |FRAME:CPD-18097|, respectively |CITS:[Teusch87]|. The acyltransferase activity coincided with the accumulation pattern of the acylated anthocyanidine glucosides |CITS:[Teusch87]| and reached its maximum between stage 4 (petals unrolled but not unfolded) and stage 5 (petals open) |CITS:[Dangelmeyr83]|.

Names: gentisate degradation II // 2,5-dihydroxybenzoate degradation II // gentisate degradation direct hydrolysis route
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-633 Gentisate| and substituted gentisates serve as key intermediates in the aerobic pathways for the, metabolism of a large number of aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYBENZOATE| |CITS: [1427003], [2256782]|, substituted phenols |CITS: [907340][6995451]|, |FRAME: CPD-110| |CITS:[Ohmoto91][8645313]|,, |FRAME: CPD-11248| |CITS: [9696766]|, and |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE| |CITS: [9573207][1622263][2988437]|., Two pathway variants are known for the degradation of gentisate. Both pathways start with the ring-cleavage oxidation of gentisate to yield |FRAME: CPD-1070|. However, in one pathway variant (the isomerization route) maleylpyruvate is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-277|, with the subsequent hydrolysis to |FRAME: FUM| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6223|), while in the other variant (the direct hydrolysis route) maleylpyruvate is hydrolyzed directly to |FRAME: MALEATE| and pyruvate |CITS: [5704827]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-5928| (strain P25X) is a soil bacterium that was isolated from the Hull river mud and is capable of degrading |FRAME: CPD-16609|, |FRAME: CPD-16608| and |FRAME: CPD-112| via gentisate., The organism synthesizes two isofunctional gentisate 1,2-dioxygenases (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.4 "EC 1.13.11.4"|), which catalyze the ring cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-633|, forming |FRAME: CPD-1070| |CITS: [14413308]|. One of the enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-18034| gene, is constitutive |CITS: [12909360]|, while the other, encoded by the |FRAME: G-18033| gene, is inducible |CITS: [17720458]|. , Once formed, |FRAME: CPD-1070| is hydrolyzed directly into |FRAME: MALEATE| and pyruvate by |FRAME: CPLX-7831|, encoded by |FRAME: G-18032| |CITS: [7400101][23204427]|. |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.31|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124347| and |FRAME: G-124348| genes, convert |FRAME: MALEATE| to |FRAME: CPD-660| |CITS: [26070679]|., Surprisingly it was found that |FRAME: ORG-5928| lacks the last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.83|, and is thus required to utilize the other isomerization route, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6223|. An hbzG mutant, which does not produce |FRAME: EC-5.2.1.4| and thus cannot use that pathway variant, was not able to grow with |FRAME: CPD-633| as its carbon source. Introduction of the |FRAME: G6986| from |FRAME: TAX-562|, which encodes D-malate dehydrogenase, into the mutant enabled it to utilize the direct hydrolysis pathway, and restored growth on |FRAME: CPD-633| |CITS: [26070679]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chaxamycins Chaxamycins| are polyketide antibiotics of the |FRAME: Ansamycins ansamycin| class that are produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1437453|. The bacterium, which was isolated from the Chaxa Lagoon in the Atacama desert (the oldest and driest desert on Earth) was selected for chemical investigation on the basis of a genome-mining PCR-based experiment targeting the gene encoding |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.144|, a common step in the biosynthesis of ansamycins |CITS: [21553813][24604690]|., Four compounds were identified - |FRAME: CPD-21890|, |FRAME: CPD-21891|, |FRAME: CPD-21892| and |FRAME: CPD-21889|. |FRAME: CPD-21889 "Chaxamycin D"| displays a highly selective antimicrobial activity against |FRAME: TAX-1280| ATCC 25923 and a panel of methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA) strains, while |FRAME: CPD-21890| inhibits the intrinsic ATPase activity of the human Hsp90 protein, which is involved in cancer proliferation |CITS: [21553813]|., The chaxamycins differ from other naphthalenic ansamycins, such as the |FRAME: Rifamycins rifamycins|, |FRAME: Naphthomycins naphthomycin|, |FRAME: CPD-21886|, and |FRAME: CPD-21895|, in lacking a methyl group at the olefinic C-16 next to the amide bond present in all of these molecules., About This Pathway, The chaxamycin biosynthetic gene cluster, which spans about 80 kb, was identified based on similarity to the rifamycin biosynthetic gene cluster. Consequently gene names and predicted functions were assigned based on those defined in the rifamycin gene cluster |CITS: [26092459]|. , The earlier steps of of ansamycins biosynthesis follow a common root. A type I modular polyketide synthase (PKS) initiates the polyketide chain with a |FRAME: CPD-10231| starter unit |CITS: [1672686]|, followed by multiple steps of chain elongation with various extender units on subsequent modules of the PKS |CITS: [Milavetz73]|. The extended chain is then released from the PKS and cyclized by an amide synthase. A more detailed description of these steps is provided in |FRAME: PWY-5984|. The enzymes involed in this part of the pathway, the |FRAME: CPLX-9385| (which includes the |FRAME: G-62998|-|FRAME: G-63003| gene products), |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.M73| (|FRAME: G-62999|), and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.M74| (|FRAME: G-63004|), are very similar to the |FRAME: TAX-33910| enzymes that participate in |FRAME: PWY-5984| |CITS: [26092459]|., The second part of the pathway comprises tailoring enzymes that alter the product by various modifications, including hydroxylation, methylation, acetylation, and redox reactions. As of 2019, not of the genes encoding the tailoring enzymes have been identified., A single clone carrying the full chaxamycin biosynthesis cluster was integrated into the genome of |FRAME: TAX-1902|. The recombinant host successfully produced all four chaxamycins |CITS: [26092459]|.

Names: 4-aminobenzoate biosynthesis II // pABA biosynthesis II // p-aminobenzoate biosynthesis II
Summary: |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE "4-Aminobenzoate"| is an important metabolic intermediate, leading to the biosynthesis of various products such as |FRAME: All-Folates folates|, |FRAME: Ubiquinones ubiquinone| (in eukaryotes), and various bacterial antibiotics (e.g.. |FRAME: Candicidins|)., In this pathway, which was described from |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| is produced from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| in two steps. In the first step |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.123|, an enzyme that is significantly different from the enzyme described from |FRAME: TAX-562| (see |FRAME: PWY-6543|), synthesizes |FRAME: 4-AMINO-4-DEOXYCHORISMATE| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| and two molecules of |FRAME: GLN|. The enzyme is composed from two subunits, PabA and PabB (in some organisms they are fused together into a bifunctional protein). PabA functions as a glutaminase, but only when in complex with PabB. PabB is an aminodeoxychorismate synthase that utilizes chorismate and ammonia (derived from glutamine hydrolysis by PabA) as substrates. During the reaction one ammonia molecule, produced from glutamine, is added at position C-2 of chorismate, resulting in loss of the hydroxyl group at position C-4. This intermediate is then attacked by a second ammonia molecule, resulting in release of the product 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate |CITS: [15770625][16605270]|., A common feature of enzymes that utilize the |FRAME: TAX-1423| mechanism is substitution of Lys with Ala in the active site. Similar enzymes were found not only among the bacilii, but also in |FRAME: TAX-1117| and in Gram-negative proteobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-40324| and |FRAME: TAX-2371| |CITS: [19275258]|., In the second step of the pathway |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.38| (PabC), forms the final product. The reaction involves the elimination of pyruvate from 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate with concomitant aromatization of the cyclohexadiene ring. The enzyme is classified as an α,β-lyase of the fold-type IV family, and requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate for activity |CITS: [11011151]|.

Ergot alkaloids are a complex family of indole derivatives with diverse structures and biological activities. They are toxins, produced by some fungi from the families |FRAME: TAX-34397|, |FRAME: TAX-28568| and |FRAME: TAX-34384|., Some of these compounds and their semi-synthetic derivatives are important drugs in modern medicine, such as |FRAME: CPD-12363| and |FRAME: CPD-14462|, which are used for the treatment of migraines. |FRAME: CPD-12363 Ergotamine|, along with |FRAME: CPD-14457|, have also been used for a very long time as uterine contracting agents following childbirth., The early part of the pathway is common to all three families and ends with |FRAME: CPD-14459| (see |FRAME: PWY-6493|). This compound is an important branching point, and is converted to different products within the different fungal families. Within the |FRAME: TAX-28568|, such as |FRAME: TAX-746128|, |FRAME: CPD-14459| is converted by two enzymes into |FRAME: CPD-14464| |CITS: [20526482]|, which is then converted to assorted clavins., |FRAME: CPD-14469 "Fumigaclavine C"| is an indole alkaloid produced by |FRAME: TAX-746128|, an endophytic fungus that lives within the leaves of |FRAME: TAX-28909| |CITS: [350117][15522437]|. This alkaloid has been found to be a vasorelaxant in experiments, making it a potential therapeutic candidate for protection against cardiovascular disease |CITS: [16557450]|. It has also been reported to inhibit the production of |FRAME: active-TNF "tumor necrosis factor α"| |CITS:[15231043] [21762706]|., Although no nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NPRS) has been reported for the fumigaclavine biosynthetic gene cluster it appears that two NPRS's have significant impact on the pathway. Knocking-out those NPRS's, encoded by PesL and Pes1, results in the complete elimination of the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-14469| indicating the essential role of PesL and Pes1 for this pathway. At the same time an increase of fumitremorgins (see |FRAME:PWY-7525|) is observed in Aspergilllus fumigatus as well as an increased sensitivity towards |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and antifungal drugs such as amphotericin B |CITS:[22344643]|. The NPRS encoded by Pes1 has already be shown to play a role in the resistance against |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|-mediated oxidative stress |CITS:[16759234]| and PesL has been suggested to be involved in fungal peptidyl alkaloid pathways |CITS:[20225828]| and shown to increase the virulence of Aspergillus as demonstrated in an Galleria mellonella (Greater Wax Moth) infection model. The involvement of PesL and Pes1 in the |FRAME:PWY-7059| has been suggested for the last step of the ergot biosynthesis in Aspergillus, i.e. the formation of |FRAME:CPD-14469| but the exact molecular function remains to be shown. The results indicate the possibility of coordinated cross-talks between various gene clusters of related secondary metabolites |CITS:[22344643]|.

Names: flavonol acylglucoside biosynthesis II - isorhamnetin derivatives
Summary: Flavonol 3-glucosides esterified with hydroxycinnamic acids have been found very effective compounds in screening out ultraviolet-B radiation (280-320 nm). In |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles the most abundant UV-B protective pigments are mono- and diacylated flavonol 3-glucoside which are esterified with |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| on the 3" and 6"-position of the glucose molecule |CITS:[Schnitzler96]| |CITS:[Fischbach99]|. Although |FRAME:CPD1F-90| acylglucosides dominate both |FRAME:CPD-8004|- and |FRAME:CPD-520| acylglucosides are major UV-screening pigments found in pine needles |CITS:[Schnitzler96]|. , The soluble and cell-wall bound flavonol acylglucosides, e.g. derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-8004| (this pathway) are accumulating in the epidermal layer of the needles, hence efficiently shielding and protecting the mesophyll cells from UV-B radiation |CITS:[Schnitzler96]|. Based on data obtained from UV experiments on |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles it appears that the soluble flavonol glucosides are first generated within the cell and then transported to the cell wall where the acylation with |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| and association with cell wall components takes place |CITS:[16898012]|. UV-B radiation induces the formation of diacylated flavonol glucosides. Flavonol acylglucosides were strongly induced after exposure to UV-B radiation |CITS:[Jungblut95]| whereas the content of hydroxycinnamic acids remained unchanged |CITS[Schnitzler96]|. The biosynthesis of acylated flavonol glucosides appears to occur in a seasonal fashion. The soluble flavonol glucosides, i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-453|, |FRAME:CPD-14969| and |FRAME:CPD1F-437| peak in June at the beginning of needle development and act at this time as the prominent UV-screening pigments. In July the more effective diacylated flavonol glucosides, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-14982| are formed and resume the role of UV-protective pigments (see also |FRAME:PWY-7168|, |FRAME:PWY-7172|) |CITS:[Fischbach99]|. , Three hydroxycinnamoyl transferases (HCT) have been identified and characterized in cell extracts of |FRAME:TAX-3349| needles. The HCT's catalyze the addition of |FRAME:COUMARATE| and |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| in a position-specific manner and have been characterized as 3"-, 4"- and 6"-HCT's |CITS:[15752358]|. The 6"-HCT was inducible by UV-B radiation and present in the first year needle's development whereas the 3"-HCT was constitutively expressed and showed high values throughout a 2 year period of needle development |CITS:[16898012]|. The 4"-acylation was an unexpected activity as 4"-acylated compounds have not yet been identified in Pinus species. However, similar flavonol acylglucoside with the 4"-pattern have been found in broadleaf species such as oak |CITS:[Romussi83]| indicating the potential occurrence of minor flavonol acylglucoside in other species as well. The sequence of acylation has been determined as 3" followed by 6". The 3"-position of pine flavonol acylglucosides is invariably acylated with |FRAME:COUMARATE| whereas the 6"-position can be acylated with either |FRAME:COUMARATE| or |FRAME:FERULIC-ACID| |CITS:[15752358]|.

|FRAME: BENZENE Benzene| is a highly toxic industrial compound with a broad range of industrial uses. It is one of the top 20 production volume chemicals in the United States, with an annual production of almost 9 million metric tons. In addition to being a component of petroleum-based fuels, benzene is often used as a raw material for the manufacture of other chemicals, rubbers, lubricants, dyes, detergents, drugs, and pesticides. Benzene is among the most prevalent organic contaminants in groundwater and is a major concern due to its toxicity and relatively high solubility |CITS: [12558180]|., Many soil bacteria are able to catabolize benzene under aerobic conditions. The aerobic pathway starts with a dihydroxylation reaction that is is carried out by ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase enzymes that incorporate both atoms of molecular oxygen |CITS: [8344526]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5450|). However, when soils and sediments are contaminated with benzene, extensive anaerobic zones frequently develop due to stimulation of the indigenous aerobic microbial population. Anaerobic benzene degradation has been demonstrated under nitrate-reducing |CITS: [9925578]|, Fe(III)-reducing |CITS: [8022480][16535218]|, sulfate-reducing |CITS: [16534979]|, and methanogenic |CITS: [9572976]| conditions., The pathways for anaerobic benzene degradation have been notoriously difficult to study, although it could be shown that at least two such pathways exist: in one pathway benzene is carboxylated to |FRAME: BENZOATE| |CITS: [11683870][21742914]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8376|), while in the other benzene is hydroxylated to |FRAME: PHENOL| |CITS: [16347109]| (this pathway). The observation of anaerobic benzene degradation by |FRAME: TAX-28232| |CITS: [23001648]|, for which a genetic manipulation system is available, has made it possible to evaluate the pathways for benzene metabolism with targeted gene deletions |CITS: [24096430]|., Studies using H<sub>2</sub><sup>18</sup>O have shown that water is the source of the hydroxyl group in phenol produced in |FRAME: TAX-28232| cultures grown with benzene. In addition, deletion of genes that are known to participate in phenol degradation blocked growth on benzene |CITS: [24096430]|., A study in which whole-genome gene transcript abundance was compared between cells metabolizing benzene and cells metabolizing phenol has identified two genes whose deletion abolished growth with benzene, but not phenol, suggesting those genes encode a benzene hydroxylase |CITS: [24904558]|. However, as of 2022 the enzyme has not been purified and studied at the biochemical level.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-29430| is an opportunistic human pathogen that causes septicemia, pneumonia, meningitis, skin and wound infections, and urinary tract infections |CITS: [8964033]|. When grown under conditions of iron depletion, |FRAME: TAX-29430| produces the citrate-based dihydroxamate siderophore |FRAME: CPD-21021| |CITS: [8148619]|. |FRAME: CPD-21021 Acinetoferrin| is very similar in chemical structure to |FRAME: CPD-1021|, a siderophore produced by |FRAME: ORG-6005| |CITS: [Persmark93]|., The genes encoding acinetoferrin biosynthesis are located in a single 8-gene operon, together with genes encoding its transport. Transcription of the operon is iron-regulated by a Fur box located in the promoter region of the first gene, |FRAME: G-58276|. Four genes, |FRAME: G-58276| through |FRAME: G-58275|, encode the four enzymes that are required to transform |FRAME: CPD-313| and |FRAME: CPD0-2108| to |FRAME: CPD-21021|. The genes involved in |FRAME: CPD-313| are not included in the operon |CITS: [23378574]|., biosynthesis.

|FRAME: CPD-5583 Aspartam|e is a low-calorie sweetener used extensively worldwide in a wide variety of foods and beverages. Even though aspartame's calorie content per gram is similar to that of sucrose (~4 calories per gram), its sweetening intensity is approximately 200 times that of sucrose, and thus it is used in much smaller quantities., Aspartame is a methyl ester of the dipeptide L-aspartyl-L-phenylalanine, which occurs widely in fruits, vegetables, nuts, and dairy products. , The breakdown of aspartame occurs in both the gastrointestinal lumen and the inside intestinal mucosal cells and is catalyzed by esterases and peptidases, forming |FRAME: METOH|, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, and |FRAME: PHE|. None of the intact, unhydrolyzed aspartame reaches the bloodstream |CITS: [4200872][2890728][8141778][12180494]|., Incubation of aspartame with human or pig intestinal microvillar membranes demonstrated that several peptidases catalyzed its hydrolysis into |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: CPD-26467|, followed by further hydrolysis by esterases into |FRAME: PHE| and |FRAME: METOH|. The main peptidase implicated was |FRAME: EC-3.4.11.7| (aminopeptidase A), which, in addition to its main function, also catalyzes release of N-terminal aspartate from peptides |CITS: [8141778]|., A purified preparation of |FRAME: EC-3.4.11.16| (aminopeptidase W) also hydrolyzed aspartame, but with a significantly higher Km (4.96 mM).

Summary: General Background, Cyanobacterial lipids consist of glycerolipids with a C18 fatty acid esterified at position sn-1 and a C16 fatty acid esterified at position sn-2 |CITS: [Sato82]|., The cyanobacteria have been classified into four groups according to the distribution of the fatty acids in their glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|. , Strains in Group 1 are characterized by the presence of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (|FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9245|) at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively., Strains in Group 2 contain the tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| at the sn-1 position and the mono-unsaturated C16 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-9245| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 3 have a different tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid (|FRAME: CPD-8117|) at the sn-1 position and the saturated C16 acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 4 are similar to strains in Group 3 except that they have, in addition, the tri-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| and the tetra-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: CPD-12653| at the sn-1 position., About This Pathway, In cyanobacteria |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is formed bound to an acyl-carrier protein, part of the fatty acid synthase complex. Stearate is transfered to the sn-1 position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.15| |CITS: [16039611]|., As described above, glycerolipids from all cyanobacteria contain unsturated C18 fatty acids in the sn-1 position, but differ in the degree and nature of unsaturation. The desaturation occurs only after |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| has been incorporated into the glycerol backbone, and is catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes known as acyl-lipid desaturases., The first desaturation occurs at position 9, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS15040|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS15040-MONOMER| |CITS: [7929259]|. This is followed by desaturation at position 12, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10130|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS10130-MONOMER| |CITS: [2118597]|. The third desaturation occurs at position 6, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-10796|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-14125| |CITS: [16328883]|. Lastly, an |FRAME: SGL_RS10825-MONOMER| encoded by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10825| gene introduces a fourth desaturation at carbon 15, generating |FRAME: CPD-12653|.

Glycerol dissimilation in |FRAME: TAX-83333| is usually initiated by the ATP-dependent |FRAME: GLYCEROL-KIN-CPLX|, which phosphorylates glycerol to |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|; see |FRAME: PWY-4261|. However, upon inactivation of the kinase, it may be replaced by the |FRAME: EG11904| |FRAME: NAD|-linked |FRAME: GLYCDEH-CPLX| |CITS: [197059]|. , E. coli is able to utilize dihydroxyacetone as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [6368745]|. However, wild-type expression of gldA appears to be insufficient to enable growth on glycerol in the absence of GlpK |CITS: [197059]|.
