Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-rhamnose| is a component of the plant cell wall pectic polysaccharides |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| and |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan type II"| and is also present in diverse secondary metabolites including anthocyanins, flavonoids and triterpenoids., Rhamnosyl transferases have been shown to utilize |FRAME: UDP-L-RHAMNOSE| as the donor substrate |CITS: [1939145 ] [15020741]|, although in mung bean (|FRAME: TAX-157791|), both |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| and |FRAME: UDP-L-RHAMNOSE| were reported to act as sugar donors for the rhamnosylation of flavonoids |CITS: [13864832 ]| (see |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|). In general UDP-D-glucose is used in plants rather than dTDP-D-glucose as a precursor in the de novo synthesis of L-rhamnose., L-Rhamnose residues have also been reported to be present in fungal glycoproteins, exopolysaccharides, and the cell wall, although their physiological role remains to be fully elucidated |CITS: [22102281][19496815][12423948]|. Genes encoding a UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase, and a bifunctional UDP-L-rhamnose synthase with 3,5-epimerase/-4-reductase activities have been identified in the fungal plant pathogens |FRAME: TAX-318829| (referred to in |CITS: [22102281]| as "Magnaporthe grisea (Magnaporthe oryzae)") and |FRAME: TAX-40559| |CITS: [22102281]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: TAX-3702| genome contains three similar genes that were named |FRAME: AT1G78570|, |FRAME: AT1G53500| and |FRAME: AT3G14790|. All three genes encode trifunctional proteins that catalyze the three reactions that are required to convert |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: UDP-L-RHAMNOSE|: UDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase; UDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-D-glucose 3,5-epimerase; and UDP-4-dehydro-L-rhamnose 4-reductase., Functional domain analysis showed that the N-terminal region of these proteins is responsible for the first activity, while the C-terminal region carries out the two following activities. Mutations in |FRAME: AT1G53500| resulted in mucilage defects in seeds, due to defficiency of rhamnogalactan., All three genes were expressed in protease-deficient |FRAME: TAX-4932| yeast cells, and assays performed with the cytoplasmic fraction of the recombinant yeast cells have shown that all three enzymes are trifunctional and catalyze all three functions |CITS: [17190829]|.

Cubebenes are sesquiterpenes which have been isolated from a large number of flowering plants and they are commercially important as flavor ingredients in cosmetics and food products. During the history of the isolation and chemical synthesis of cubebenes there has been a confusing nomenclature, until it was finally resolved to be the same compound, namely Ylangene, copaene and cubebenes were classified as cubebenes |CITS: [VELDHUIS67]|. The terpene synthase catalyzing betacubebene has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3402|, shown in the above pathway. |FRAME: TAX-3402| is an ancient evergreen tree and is cultivated for horticultural purposes as well as for the large number of natural products it produces |CITS: [18467455]|. Studies have also shown that the structural diversity of terpenes in Magnolia may be due to the diversity of terpene synthase (TPS) genes, which in turn diverged either due to loss of introns from an ancestor TPS gene or by gain of introns of progenate TPS genes |CITS: [18467455]|

|FRAME: Arabinans "L-arabinan"| is a common |FRAME: Hemicelluloses hemicellulosic| component of the cell wall of higher plants. It is a branched polysaccharide with a backbone of α-(1,5)-linked arabinofuranosyl residues with α-(1,2)- and α-(1,3)-linked arabinofuranosyl side chains. It is usually associated with pectic substrates, and pectins with attached arabinans can be isolated from many fruits and vegetables such as apples, sugar beet, apricots, carrots, cabbage, onion and pears., Various phytopathogenic and saprophytic microorganisms are known to produce these activities |CITS: [Karimi89]|. Among the best studied organisms in respect to arabinan degradation are the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1423| and the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5061|., The degradation of L-arabinan involves two main enzymatic activities - |FRAME: MONOMER-16541 "arabinan endo-1,5-α-L-arabinanase"| (|FRAME: 3.2.1.99-RXN "EC 3.2.1.99"|) and |FRAME: MONOMER-16540| (|FRAME: 3.2.1.55-RXN "EC 3.2.1.55"|), which act in synergy |CITS: [Kaji84][Whitaker84][Beldman97]|. Arabinofuranosidases remove arabiofuranose residues from the non-reducing terminus. These enzymes attack and removes arabinose side chains, allowing the arabinanases to attack the glycosidic bonds of the arabinan backbone. , The arabinanases cleave the exposed backbone at random locations , producing shorter oligosaccharide chains (in the range of 2-5 residues), which in turn are attacked by the arabinofuranosidases, resulting in complete degradation to arabinose monomers.In |FRAME: TAX-1423| two arabinofuranosidases have been described - |FRAME: BSU28510-MONOMER| specializes in removing the side chains, while |FRAME: BSU28720-MONOMER| specializes in degradation of the linear fragments generated by the arabinases |CITS: [18757805]|.

Cyanogenic plants, such as |FRAME: TAX-47247 "Lotus corniculatus (birdsfoot trefoil)"| and |FRAME: TAX-4558|, produce cyanogenic glucosides such as |FRAME: LINAMARIN|, |FRAME: CPD-10277| and |FRAME: CPD-1042| (see |FRAME: CYANOGENIC-GLUCOSIDE-SYN "cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis pathways"|). Upon injury or infection the plants release |FRAME: HCN| from these glucosides as a defense mechanism |CITS: [Myers78]|., Some fungi, such as |FRAME: TAX-183477| (a leaf-spotting pathogen of |FRAME: TAX-47247|) and |FRAME: TAX-1682391| (a pathogen of sorghum), are able to infect the plants due to their tolerance towards cyanide |CITS: [Fry71][Fry71a][Fry75]|., When exposed to cyanide, the fungi produce |FRAME: CPLX-8578|, an enzyme that converts cyanide to |FRAME: FORMAMIDE| |CITS: [5065258]|. The enzyme, which is inducible and produced only after exposure to cyanide, appears to be common in pathogenic fungi of cyanogenic plants |CITS: [Fry77]|., The second step in the pathway is believed to consist of the hydration of |FRAME: FORMAMIDE| to form |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: FORMATE| by formamidase. While this enzyme has been documented in many organisms, including fungi (e.g. |FRAME: CPLX-8579| from |FRAME: TAX-121759|) it has not been studied in pathogens of cyanogenic plants.

Summary: General Background, Vitamin A is the name given to a family of related compounds from the |FRAME: Retinoids retinoid| group, including all-trans forms such as |FRAME: CPD-13524|, |FRAME: RETINAL| and |FRAME: RETINOATE|, cis forms such as |FRAME: CPD-882|, |FRAME: CPD-881|, |FRAME: CPD-13549| and |FRAME: CPD-13548|, and |FRAME: Retinyl-Esters "retinyl esters"| such as |FRAME: CHOCOLA_A|. Structurally, all retinoids possess a β-ionone ring and a polyunsaturated side chain, with either an alcohol, aldehyde, a carboxylic acid group or an ester group. The side chain is composed of two isoprenoid units, with a series of conjugated double bonds which may exist in trans- or cis-configuration., Vitamin A compounds have many important and diverse functions throughout the body including roles in vision, regulation of cell proliferation and differentiation, growth of bone tissue, immune function, and activation of tumor suppressor genes., Animals can not synthesize vitamin A de novo and require a dietary supplement. Carnivorous vertebrate animals can obtain it directly from dietary meat, in the form of retinyl-esters. Vegetarian animals produce retinal from one of four carotenoids: |FRAME: CPD1F-129|, |FRAME: CPD-7409|, |FRAME: CPD1F-118|, and |FRAME: CPD1F-126|, which they must obtain from plants or other photosynthetic organisms |CITS: [18979213]|., |FRAME: CPD-881| is a polyene chromophore, and when bound to |FRAME:Opsins opsin| proteins it forms the chemical basis of animal vision (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6861|). Some microorganisms utilize a similar system in which various cis forms of retinal bound to proteins called type 1 rhodopsins allow them to convert light into metabolic energy., |FRAME: RETINOATE "All-trans retinoate"| is the vitamin A form that mediates the functions required for growth and development., During early embryonic development, retinoate generated in a specific region of the embryo helps determine position along the embryonic anterior/posterior axis by serving as an intercellular signaling molecule that guides development of the posterior portion of the embryo |CITS: [18805086]|. It acts through Hox genes, which ultimately control anterior/posterior patterning in early developmental stages |CITS: [17495912]|., In the adult, retinoate is responsible for most of the activity of vitamin A (see |FRAME: PWY-6872|)., Retinoid-Binding Proteins, Due to the insolubility of retinoids, they are bound within the cell (or plasma) to specialized binding proteins. The sequestration of retinoids inside high-affinity binding-proteins increases their solubility, protects them from unfettered metabolism, and facilitates their transportation within the body, while still allowing access to the enzymes that metabolize them (e.g. the formation of retinyl esters) |CITS:[7683727][9932510]|., Several retinoid-binding proteins exist. The cellular-retinol binding proteins (encoded by |FRAME: HS03740| and |FRAME: HS03739|) bind free retinol within the cell, and continue to bind it even after it has been oxidized to retinal. |FRAME: HS03739| is expressed only in the small intestine, where it is involved in binding the retinol freshly obtained from dietary input. |FRAME: HS03740| is the main retinoid-binding protein in other cells, and also serves an a sensor for retinol availability, modulating activity of several retinol-metabolizing enzymes., The |FRAME:ENSG00000107618-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: HS03012|, shuttles retinoids between the pigment epithelium and the visual pigments in the photoreceptor cells of the retina., The |FRAME: ENSG00000138207-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS06474|) delivers retinol form liver storage to the peripheral tissues. The |FRAME: ENSG00000140522-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS06733|) binds different forms of retinal and is essential for the proper function of both rod and cone photoreceptors., Initial Synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13524|, There are two dietary inputs of retinoids. Ingested retinyl-esters are broken in the intestine into |FRAME: CPD-13524|, which is immediately bound to |FRAME: Cellular-Retinol-Binding-Proteins|. Ingested carotenoids are processed by |FRAME: CPLX-8340| into |FRAME: RETINAL|, which is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-13524| by several dehydrogenases and processed in the same way., Storage, After binding to |FRAME: Cellular-Retinol-Binding-Proteins|, |FRAME: CPD-13524| is esterified by |FRAME: HS04474-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS04474|) with long chain fatty acids, primarily |FRAME: PALMITATE|, to form |FRAME: Retinyl-Esters "retinyl esters"| that are incorporated into the hydrophobic core of chylomicrons (large lipoprotein particles that transport dietary lipids from the intestines to other locations in the body). The chylomicrons are secreted into the lymph and ultimately enter the blood via the thoracic and other lymphatic ducts. Chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver and the retinyl esters are stored. When needed, these esters are hydrolyzed to regenerate the retinol., Regeneration, When the concentration of retinoids falls, the |FRAME: Retinyl-Esters "retinyl esters"| in the liver are hydrolyzed by neutral and acid retinyl ester hydrolases, such as |FRAME: HS11616-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS11616|), releasing |FRAME: CPD-13524| |CITS: [15767260]|. The retinol is transferred to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), where it binds to |FRAME:ENSG00000138207-MONOMER| (|FRAME:HS06474|) and is secreted into the circulation as |FRAME:RPB-Retinol| complex., Utilization, |FRAME: CPD-13524 "All-trans-retinol"| is utilized mostly for production of |FRAME: CPD-881| and |FRAME:RETINOATE|. These processes are described in |FRAME: PWY-6861| and |FRAME: PWY-6872| pathways.

Nicotine is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME:TAX-4097| and |FRAME:TAX-4093|) |CITS: [SCHMELTZ77]|. Nicotine in tobacco leaves and in plant-derived preparations is mostly in the (S)-nicotine isomeric form |CITS: [ARMSTRONG98]|. However, tobacco smoke contains up to 10% (R)-nicotine, probably due to racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine is the addictive compound in tobacco |CITS: [8301571]| and is a commonly used psychoactive drug. It enters the body by systemic absorption through cigarette smoking, oral snuff, pipe tobacco, cigars and chewing tobacco use |CITS: [6705448][10224986]|. It can also enter in purified form as a medication. , Nicotine has complex physiological effects |CITS: [3054551]|. In cigarette smoke nicotine is carried into the body on particulate matter. It is rapidly absorbed in the small airways and alveoli of the lung |CITS: [11712903]|. In this neutral pH environment, it is un-ionized, soluble, and can be transferred across cell membranes and into the blood. It moves into the pulmonary venous circulation, to the left ventricle of the heart, and into the systemic arterial circulation |CITS: [8646831], [10482401]|. It travels to the brain within seconds where it binds to nicotinic cholinergic receptors and activates the dopaminergic reward system |CITS: [10336551]| (and reviewed in |CITS: [8725403]|). Other forms of nicotine (such as nicotine gum, transdermal patch, inhaler, lozenges, and sublingual tablets) are usually buffered at alkaline pH and quickly traverse cell membranes, but most reach the blood and brain more slowly. They are less likely to cause addiction due to the delayed reward of nicotine effects |CITS: [3391001][8245272]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|., In humans, the primary site of nicotine metabolism is the liver. There is little evidence in the literature for any extrahepatic metabolism, despite the presence of isoforms of nicotine metabolizing enzymes in other tissues (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine and its metabolites are excreted in urine, where they have been analyzed and quantitated |CITS: [8301571][1352209][12376133][2249376]|. These data showed considerable interindividual variability in the amount of each metabolite produced |CITS: [7955812][8301571][1352209]|., Cotinine is the primary metabolite of nicotine and is found in the urine of smokers |CITS: [13872096][12376133][1352209] [8301571][2249376]|. In studies of nicotine metabolism in smokers, it has been estimated that 70% of a nicotine dose is metabolized to cotinine |CITS: [8301571]|. It reaches high levels in the blood and has a long half-life |CITS: [9209247]|. The cotinine metabolite trans-3'-hydroxycotinine is the most abundant metabolite in urine |CITS: [8301571]|. Glucuronide conjugation is a significant route of nicotine metabolism, with nicotine, cotinine and trans-3'-hydroxycotinine glucuronides accounting for up to 30% of total metabolites recovered in urine |CITS: [1352209]| ., nicotine -> cotinine, The nicotine-to-cotinine conversion involves oxidation of the pyrrolidine ring (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). Cotinine is the main metabolite of nicotine in most mammals. The nicotine-to-cotinine conversion was studied in 20 smokers. The authors characterized the disposition kinetics of nicotine and cotinine using deuterium-labeled analogs of these compounds. On average, 72% of nicotine was converted to cotinine and a range of 55-92% indicated individual variations. Nicotine is rapidly metabolized and cotinine is slowly metabolized, but clearances were significantly correlated. The authors suggested that the same enzyme is involved in metabolism of both |CITS: [7955812]|., The presence of the intermediate, nicotine-Δ1'(5')-iminium ion, as a discrete entity in this reaction has been demonstrated |CITS: [4144545]|. In a rabbit liver microsomal preparation containing nicotine, an NADPH generating system, and potassium cyanide, the formation of 5'-cyanonicotine was shown. It was postulated that 5'-cyanonicotine was produced by reaction of nicotine-Δ1'(5')-iminium ion with cyanide. The involvement of a mixed-function oxidase was suggested by NADPH as the preferred cofactor, the requirement for O2, and inhibition of the reaction by carbon monoxide. A detailed study of the mechanism of iminium ion formation from (S)-nicotine was done using both human liver and rabbit liver microsomal preparations |CITS: [3806608]|. The authors suggested that species differences in degree of stereoselectivity could reflect species differences in isozyme composition. The synthesis and structure of crystalline iminium salt has been described and it was shown that nicotine-Δ1'(5')-iminium ion is in equilibrium with 5'-hydroxynicotine |CITS: [BRANDANGE79][3806608]|. The iminium ion is also an alkylating agent, and may have a role in the pharmacology of nicotine |CITS: [6896399]|., More recently, formation of the iminium ion has been described as hydroxylation of nicotine at the 5' position, with nicotine-Δ1'(5')-iminium ion in equilibrium with 5'-hydroxynicotine, an unstable intermediate |CITS: [11050152]|. The reaction is catalyzed by cytochrome P450 2A6, but isoforms 2B6 and 2D6 may contribute. Thus 5'-hydroxynicotine may be the aldehyde oxidase substrate to form cotinine., nicotine -> nicotine 1'-N-oxide , Oxidation of the pyrrolidine ring can also form nicotine 1'-N-oxide, a primary metabolite (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine 1'-N-oxide is found in the urine of smokers |CITS: [2249376][12376133][1352209][8301571]|. In animals, both the cis and trans stereoisomers are formed. In humans, the enzyme dimethylaniline monooxygenase (flavin-containing monooxygenase 3) (FMO 3) (formerly FMO II) selectively forms the trans isomer. In human liver microsomal preparations, the formation of nicotine 1'-N-oxide is NADPH dependent |CITS: [1446003]|. Nicotine 1'-N-oxide is not further metabolized, although evidence has been presented for reduction of this compound back to nicotine in the gut |CITS: [4394772]|., nicotine -> nicotine isomethonium ion, The formation of nicotine isomethonium ion involves nonoxidative methylation of pyridine nitrogen (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). This pathway was first reported in dogs given (S)-nicotine |CITS: [13932077]|. Animal models and human liver homogenates showed that S-adenosyl-L-methionine is the source of the methyl group. In human liver the (R)-isomer of nicotine is methylated more rapidly than the (S)-isomer, but both enantiomers were methylated |CITS: [2897456]|. Small amounts of nicotine isomethonium ion have been detected in the urine of smokers |CITS: [3557628]|. Reported pharmacologic activity of this quaternary N-methylated nicotine metabolite warrants further study |CITS: [1593921]|., nicotine -> nicotine glucuronide, The formation of nicotine glucuronide involves nonoxidative glucuronidation. This results in an N-quaternary glucuronide (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine glucuronide is found in the urine of smokers |CITS: [12376133][1352209][8301571]|. In smokers' urine, nicotine, cotinine and trans-3'-hydroxycotinine glucuronide conjugates constituted 25-30% of total metabolites, and individual variability in degree of glucuronide conjugation was noted |CITS: [1352209][8301571]|., nicotine -> nornicotine, Nicotine can undergo oxidative N-demethylation to nornicotine (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nornicotine is found in the urine of smokers |CITS: [2249376], [8301571]|. Although nornicotine is a naturally occurring minor alkaloid in tobacco, the majority of nornicotine excreted in urine by smokers is derived from nicotine metabolism |CITS: [8301571]|. In rabbit liver microsomes, an N'-methylene-iminium ion intermediate has been shown by formation of the N-(cyanomethyl)nornicotine adduct. The authors suggested that this intermediate is a product of the microsomal mixed function oxidase system. They proposed a mechanism involving oxidation of nicotine to N-(hydroxymethyl)nornicotine, ionization to nicotine-N-methyleniminium ion, and cyanide reaction to form the cyano adduct |CITS: [423207]|. , The oxidative conversion of nornicotine to norcotinine in humans has been cited as unpublished data by Jacob, Yu and Benowitz in a review |CITS: [15734728]|. Animal studies have presented qualitative evidence for this reaction |CITS: [14004224], [14166990]|., The conversion of norcotinine to 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanamide has been shown in rat liver microsomes |CITS: [9512938]|, and in humans the reaction is suggested by the presence of small amounts of 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanamide in the urine of smokers. This compound exists in equilibrium with 5'-hydroxynorcotinine (Jacob, Yu and Benowitz, unpublished, in a review |CITS: [15734728]|. The reactions converting 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)-butanamide to 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate, with subsequent conversion to 3-pyridylacetate, remain hypothetical in humans (reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|. 3-Pyridylacetate has beendetected in human urine after oral cotinine administration |CITS: [14257634]|., nicotine -> 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate and 4-hydroxy-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate, Nicotine can also be metabolized via a 2'-hydroxylation reaction producing 2'-hydroxynicotine as an intermediate in the cytochrome P450 2A6 catalyzed conversion of nicotine to 4-(methylamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone. 2'-Hydroxynicotine spontaneously yields nicotine-Δ1'(2')-iminium ion, which is in equilibrium with 4-(methylamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone |CITS: [11050152]| (and reviewed in |CITS: [15734728]|). About 10% of nicotine and metabolites is excreted as 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate (keto acid) and 4-hydroxy-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate (hydroxy acid) in the urine of smokers |CITS: [10548320,], [10027795]|. These compounds also arise from metabolism of cotinine |CITS: [14257634]|. The final product, 3-pyridylacetate, was detected in human urine after oral cotinine administration |CITS: [14257634]|. , It has been shown that during nicotine metabolism in humans, 85% of the keto acid formed is converted to hydroxy , acid. In rats, only 1% is converted, demonstrating a significant species difference. The hydroxy acid, 4-hydroxy-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate, can be in equiliburium with the lactone 5'-(3-pyridyl)-tetrahydrofuran-2-one |CITS: [11050152]|. In human smokers and smokers wearing a nicotine patch, urine analysis showed that formation of keto acid and hydroxy acid is quantitatively significant, and established this as a pathway of nicotine metabolism in humans. It was suggested that carbonyl reductase activity converts the keto acid to the hydroxy acid |CITS: [10027795]|., In smokers, or people on nicotine replacement therapy, about 10% of a nicotine dose is excreted in urine as 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate and 4-hydroxy-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate. It was established that the main source of urinary keto and hydroxy acids in humans is via 2'-hydroxylation of nicotine. The cotinine 5'-hydroxylation pathway is minor compared to the nicotine pathway for these compounds. In in vitro studies, when nicotine was added to human liver microsomes containing cofactors, the nicotine-to-keto acid pathway was shown, with 4-(methylamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone (aminoketone) conversion to the keto acid 4-oxo-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate through a possible keto aldehyde intermediate |CITS: [11050152]|. Hyopthetical intermediates in the conversion of 4-hydroxy-4-(3-pyridyl)butanoate to 3-pyridylacetate have been proposed |CITS: [14257634]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFAs) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes. The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in the |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived compounds (though the term is often used to include metabolites of 18- and 22-carbon PUFAs). , This pathway describes how the C<sub>22</sub> PUFA |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) is liberated from common glycerophopholipids and sterols in the cell, and how it is converted to some of the more common C<sub>22</sub> icosanoids.

Suberin is a polymeric plant cell wall constituent mainly found in the epidermal tissues of underground plant parts. Suberin consists of two domains, a polyaromatic and a polyaliphatic domain. The polyaromatics are predominately located within the primary cell wall, and the polyaliphatics are located between the primary cell wall and the plasmalemma. The two domains are supposed to be cross-linked. , Esterification of the different aliphatic monomers to the aromatic components and glycerol may be an important means of achieving the cross-linking that is required to form a protective hydrophobic polymeric matrix |CITS: [19846769]|.

Summary: General Background, Bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are unique and complex glycolipids that provide characteristic components of the outer monolayer of the outer membranes of gram-negative bacteria. Wild type LPS is composed of a hydrophobic domain lipid A (or endotoxin), a phosphorylated "core" oligosaccharide (core OS) and a distal O-specific polysaccharide (or O-antigen). Strains of |FRAME:TAX-562| K-12 normally do not make O-antigen, unless a mutation in the O-antigen operon is corrected |CITS: [7517391]|. O antigens are not needed for growth in the laboratory, but they protect bacteria from antibiotics and complement-mediated lysis. The lipid A and Kdo domains of LPS are required for growth |CITS: [17362200][12045108]|. , The lipid A (endotoxin) domain of LPS is a unique, glucosamine-based saccharolipid that serves as the hydrophobic anchor of LPS. It is the bioactive component of the molecule that is associated with gram-negative septic shock |CITS: [15052329]|. There are approximately 106 lipid A residues in an E. coli cell |CITS: [17362200]|. Lipid A of E. coli consists of a β (1'->6)-linked D-glucosamine disaccharide that carries four (R)-3-hydroxytetradecanoyl groups in positions 2, 3, 2', and 3' and two phosphoryl residues in positions 1 and 4'. The hydroxy fatty acids at positions 2' and 3' are acylated at their 3-hydroxyl groups by dodecanoic acid and tetradecanoic acid, respectively |CITS: [3317748]|. Given their conserved architecture, most types of lipid A molecules are detected at picomolar levels by TLR4 (toll-like receptor 4) of the innate immune system present on macrophages and endothelial cells of animals |CITS: [12045108]|., The core oligosaccharides are conceptually divided into two regions: the inner core (lipid A proximal) and the outer core. The inner core is highly conserved. It comprises three 3-deoxy-D-manno-oct-2-ulosonic acid (Kdo) and L-glycero-D-manno-heptose (Hep) residues and it is often phosphorylated. Structural diversity in the core oligosaccharide is limited by the constraints imposed by its essential role in outer membrane stability |CITS: [12935355][9791168]|. E. coli mutants that lack the heptose region of the inner core display the "deep rough" phenotype characterized by changes in both the structure and the composition of the outer membrane leading to its instability |CITS: [385128]|. Deep rough mutants of E. coli activate expression of colanic acid exopolysaccharide, lose expression of pili and flagella and secrete a form of hemolysin with reduced hemolytic activity |CITS: [1348243]|. The outer core comprises a tri-hexose backbone modified with varying side-branch substitutions of hexose and acetamidohexose residues. The outer core region provides an attachment site for O antigen |CITS: [9791168]|. Mutations that eliminate synthesis of the outer core result in increased susceptibility to some hydrophobic compounds due to an indirect effect on core phosphorylation |CITS: [2168379]|., About This Pathway, E. coli lipid A is synthesized on the cytoplasmic surface of the inner membrane by a conserved pathway of nine constitutive enzymes. The first reaction of lipid A biosynthesis is the acylation of the sugar nucleotide UDP-GlcNAc by LpxA. Deacetylation of the product, UDP-3-O-(acyl)-GlcNAc by the zinc metalloenzyme LpxC is the committed reaction of the pathway. LpxC is an excellent target for the design of novel, gram-negative specific antibiotics. Following deacetylation, a second beta-hydroxymyristate moiety is incorporated by LpxD to generate UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine. UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine is cleaved at its pyrophosphate bond by the highly selective pyrophosphatase LpxH to form 2,3-diacylglucosamine-1-phosphate (lipid X). A beta,1'-6 linked disaccharide is then generated by the condensation of another molecule of UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine with lipid X by LpxB. A specific kinase, LpxK next phosphorylates the 4' position of the disaccharide to form lipid IVA. The kinase product, lipid IVA, is of great interest because it possesses some of the properties of endotoxins |CITS: [12045108]|., E. coli LPS contains two Kdo residues that are transferred to lipid IVA by a bifunctional enzyme, encoded by waaA. The chromosomal waa region (formerly rfa) contains the major core-oligosaccharide assembly operons, and E. coli K-12 provided the first waa region sequenced in its entirety |CITS: [12935355]|. The last steps of E. coli lipid A biosynthesis involve the addition of lauroyl and myristoyl residues to the distal glucosamine unit (generating acyloxyacyl moieties by LpxL and LpxM respectively. The completed lipid A-Kdo2 serves as the acceptor on which the core oligosaccharide and lipo-oligosaccharide chains are assembled. , The lipid A-core portion (known as rough LPS (R-LPS)) is synthesized by a conserved pathway. The mechanism involves sequential glycosyl transfer from nucleotide sugar precursors with a co-coordinated complex of membrane-associated glycosyltransferases (Waa proteins) acting at the cytoplasmic surface of the inner membrane (IM). The modification of the core region of E. coli LPS requires the action of three enzymes, viz. WaaP (an LPS kinase), WaaY (an enzyme required for a second phosphorylation) and WaaQ (a transferase that adds the side-branch heptose). The WaaP enzyme is the most important of these activities since the modifications must proceed in the strict order WaaPQY. Mutants lacking WaaP activity exhibit the deep rough phenotype and are avirulent. Mutant LPSs lacking the outer core (waaG) are phosphorylated inefficiently by WaaP |CITS: [10986272]|. Conversely, the loss of phosphorylation results in a decreased efficiency of core extension, leading to more truncated cores than seen in the wild type. , The lipid A-core is then flipped to the outer surface of the inner membrane by the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter, MsbA. An additional integral membrane protein, YhjD, has recently been implicated in LPS export across the IM. The smallest LPS derivative that supports viability in E. coli is lipid IVA. However, it requires mutations in either MsbA or YhjD, to suppress the normally lethal consequence of an incomplete lipid A |CITS: [18480051]|. Recent studies with deletion mutants implicate the periplasmic protein LptA, the cytosolic protein LptB, and the IM proteins LptC, LptF, and LptG in the subsequent transport of nascent LPS to the outer membrane (OM), where the LptD/LptE complex flips LPS to the outer surface |CITS: [18768814]|., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [17362200][15052329][12935355][12045108][9791168][9157235][8330896][2663021][3317748][2446369]|.

General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and protein modification, where fatty acyl moieties of proteins modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II. The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|). The pathway catalyzed by the type I systems is available at |FRAME: PWY-5994|., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|. Unlike the type I system that accepts |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of the two-carbon units, the type II systems accept only |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|., About This Pathway, Many Gram-positive organisms, such as the bacilli, staphylococci, and streptomycetes, produce odd- and even-carbon-number branched-chain fatty acids. Branched-chain fatty acids display a lower melting point temperature than their straight-chain equivalents, and their presence in the membrane is expected to increase its fluidity, similar to the effect of unsaturation |CITS: [26300876]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| 95% of the total fatty acids are branched |CITS: [4392505][1886522]|. The most common fatty acids are |FRAME: CPD-9917| (34%), |FRAME: CPD-19657| (24%), |FRAME: CPD-18175| (13%), |FRAME: CPD-23515| (12%), |FRAME: CPD-23509| (9%), and |FRAME: CPD-19660| (4%) |CITS: [28825491]|., In many organisms (the best studies case is |FRAME: TAX-1423|) the synthesis of branched-chain fatty acids is enabled by altered substrate specificity of the FabH condensing enzyme. In organisms that produce non-branched fatty acids such as |FRAME: TAX-562| FabH is specific for |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as the starter molecule. In contrast, the FabH enzyme of |FRAME: TAX-1423| utilizes branched-chain acyl-CoA primers much more efficiently than |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (for |FRAME: TAX-1423| the ratio is 100:1) |CITS: [1886522]|. The rest of the enzymes that form the fatty acid synthase system do not have a significant degree of selectivity for either branched-chain or straight-chain fatty acids |CITS: [10629181]|. The pathway studied in |FRAME: TAX-1423| is described in |FRAME: PWY-8174|., A different strategy for synthesizing branched-chain fatty acids has been discovered in an eDNA (environmental DNA) clone that was isolated from creek bed mud/sediment in Wellsboro, PA and expressed in multiple hosts., The eDNA contained an operon consisting of the |FRAME: G-124666| and |FRAME: G-124667| genes. NasB is a complex enzyme whose purpose is to divert branched-chain 2-oxo acids to production of branched-chain N-acyl amino acids by producing a branched 3-oxoacyl-[acp] molecules. NasB accepts branched fatty acids such as |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| (the most common product of |FRAME: LEU| degradation), catalyzes a decarboxylative transfer to a |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| cofactor, transfers the remaining unit to a lipoyl cofactor, and finally transfers it to a malonyl-[acp] acceptor (in a transfer that involves a second decarboxylation event). The products, such as |FRAME: 5-Methyl-3-Oxohexanoyl-ACP|, are then be extended by the fatty acid synthase II system to form long-chain fatty-acyl-acp] molecules |CITS: [21714057]|., The second gene of the operon, |FRAME: G-124666|, encodes an |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.327|, which attaches the long branched-chain fatty acyl-acp] molecules produced by NasB to aromatic fatty acids, forming |FRAME: N-ACYL-L-AMINO-ACID "N-acylated aromatic amino acids"| |CITS: [21714057]|.

Summary: Adenosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: AMP| (AMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| , which is converted to AMP by the action of, |FRAME: ASL-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6126|). The degradation pathways are responsible for the conversion of the nucleotides to the nucleoside (|FRAME: ADENOSINE|) and free base form (|FRAME: ADENINE|), and further degradation to compounds that can be catabolized to basic building blocks (for example, see |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|)., The distinction between nucleoside degradation and recycling is not always straight forward., This pathway shares several steps with the pathway |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|. However, this salvage pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENINE| (which is often transported into the organism) and ends with |FRAME: IMP|, leading to biosynthesis of nucleotides, while the degradation pathway starts with the nucleotide form (|FRAME: AMP|) and ends with |FRAME: URATE|, which in most organisms is degraded further., A key enzyme in this pathway is adenosine deaminase, which converts |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: INOSINE|. Summary: General Background, ||FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| (CoA) is a ubiquitous compound found in archaea, bacteria, plants, and animals. It is a common acyl carrier in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and is required for a multitude of reactions for both biosynthetic and degradative pathways, including the oxidation of fatty acids, carbohydrates, and amino acids |CITS: [16415216]|., The biosynthesis of CoA occurs via different pathways in archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes, and thus enzymes specific for the bacterial pathway are targets for antibacterial drug discovery., The eukaryotic pathway has received particular attention since mutations in |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.33|, lead to a neurodegenerative disorder |CITS: [15893380]|., About This Pathway, The first compound in this pathway, |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE|, is produced by phosphorylation of |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|, as described in |FRAME: PANTO-PWY|. Only microorganisms and plants (including some eukaryotic microbes, such as |FRAME: TAX-4932|) can synthesize |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| de novo - animals must obtain it in their diet, giving it the name vitamin B5., The first step in this pathway is the ligation of |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| with |FRAME: CYS|. Eukaryotic organisms utilize an ATP dependent enzyme - |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.51|. This is the only difference between the eukaryotic pathway and the prokaryotic pathway (see |FRAME: COA-PWY|), since prokaryotes utilize a CTP-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-6.3.2.5|)., The pathway continues by decarboxylation to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.36|. The next step consists of the transfer of an adenyly group from ATP to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|, forming |FRAME: DEPHOSPHO-COA|. The ultimate reaction is a phosphorylation catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.24|, producing |FRAME: CO-A|. All of the enzymes of this pathway are essential., Several differences exist in the functionality of the enzymes of this pathway among different organisms. In plants every step is catalyzed by single monofunctional enzymes, whereas in bacteria and mammals bifunctional enzymes are often employed |CITS: [16415216]|.

General Background, Phosphonates are compounds that contain a carbon-phosphorus bond which provides chemical and biochemical stability. Phosphonates are synthesized as secondary metabolites by a variety of prokaryotes and lower eukaryotes and are part of the global phosphorus cycle (in |CITS: [16981709][19191873]|). |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE Phosphoenolpyruvate| is the key precursor of phosphonate biosynthesis (in |CITS: [Bowman88]|). Formation of the carbon-phosphorus bond in phosphonates is catalyzed by the key enzyme |FRAME: EC-5.4.2.9|, as shown here and also for the biosynthesis of other phosphonates, such as |FRAME: PWY-5757|, |FRAME: PWY-6322| (bialaphos biosynthesis) and |FRAME: PWY-6682|., |FRAME: CPD-1106| (ciliatine) is the most common naturally occurring phosphonate. It is synthesized in both prokaryotes, where it is used for tailoring cell surfaces, and eukaryotes (including fungi |CITS: [1009132]|, metazoa |CITS: [19732869][2584202][12941637]|, and protozoa |CITS: [4967076][4622267][3132161][12672809]|), where it is a incorporated into cellular lipids, glycolipids and proteins by covalent linkage., In the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-817| |FRAME: CPD-1106| serves as a functional group of Polysaccharide B in the capsular polysaccharide complex, which is the major virulence factor for abscess formation in human hosts |CITS: [12904299]|., |FRAME: CPD-1106| can be degraded by soil bacteria (see pathways |FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6832|)., About This Pathway, This pathway was first described in the free-living, ciliated protozan |FRAME: TAX-5908| |CITS: [4622267][3132161]|. In the first reaction |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: CPD-235| are reversibly interconverted by a mutase that forms the carbon-phosphorus bond in |FRAME: CPD-235| |CITS: [3138545][Bowman88]|. Although the reaction equilibrium strongly favors |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| formation, studies have suggested that the phosphomutase and the α-ketodecarboxylase reaction that follows are coupled and |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| is shuttled from one active site to the other |CITS: [Bowman88]|. The third reaction represents an amination of |FRAME: CPD-551| as suggested by |CITS: [4622267][3132161]|.

The siderophores |FRAME:CPD-17185| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD0-2241| (see |FRAME:PWY-7577|) are microbial low molecular weight iron chelators employed for mobilization and storage of this metal which are formed under conditions of reduced iron bioavailability |CITS:[6455965] [17804665]|. Ustilago maydis, the pathogen causing corn smut disease |CITS:[19400641]|, is able to produce both siderophores |CITS:[2531844]| and has been used as model organism to study the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17185| and |FRAME:CPD0-2241| and their proposed contribution to the virulence of the fungi |CITS:[12759789] [18680426]|. Transport of siderophores with regard to substrate specificity |CITS:[10802175]| and virulence in Ustilago maydis |CITS:[17138696]| appear to be closely associated with signal cascades required for the development of pathogeny including siderophores recognition by specific outer cell surface receptors formed in the presence of siderophores of the hydroxamate type, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-17185| |CITS:[16484199]|., The deciphering of the Ustilago maydis genome |CITS:[17080091]| has considerably furthered the elucidation of siderophores and related biosynthetic pathways in this organism |CITS:[18585066]| and provided the means for investigating siderophores formation and associated enzymes in closely related fungal species |CITS:[16019163] [16502473] [19055762]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17185| requires the involvement of two precursors, |FRAME:TRANS-3-METHYL-GLUTACONYL-COA| and |FRAME:CPD-11571|. The former is generated through the consecutive action of two enzymes, hydroxymethyl glutaryl-CoA synthase encoded by Hcs1 forming |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA| from |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA hydratase encoded by Fer4 catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-3-METHYL-GLUTARYL-COA| into |FRAME:TRANS-3-METHYL-GLUTACONYL-COA| |CITS:[20070524]|. While HCS1 is a stand-alone gene Fer4 is part of a biogenetic cluster involved in |FRAME:PWY-7571| |CITS:[17138696]|. The latter, |FRAME:CPD-11571|, is formed by the L-ornithine 5-monooxygenase encoded by Sid1 regarded as the first committed step of the pathway. The Sid1 encoded enzyme catalyzed the N-oxygenation of |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| to form |FRAME:CPD-11571| |CITS:[8430103] [2523381]|. The final two steps in |FRAME:PWY-7571| are carried out by the N-hydroxyornithine acylase (Fer5) fusing the Fer4 product |FRAME:TRANS-3-METHYL-GLUTACONYL-COA| with the Sid1 product |FRAME:CPD-11571| and yielding |FRAME:CPD-17186| and the ferrichrome A syntetase encoded by Fer3, a nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) converting |FRAME:CPD-17186|, |FRAME:SER| and |FRAME:GLY| into the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-17185| |CITS:[20070524] [16502473]|. Both Fer5 and Fer3 are members of the biogenetic cluster involved in |FRAME:PWY-7571| |CITS:[17138696]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: D-APIOSE| is a unique branched-chain pentose found principally in plants. It is a key component of structurally complex cell wall polysaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| (RG-II) in the cell walls of higher plants and in apigalacturonan in the cell walls of aquatic monocots, and is a building block of a large number of naturally occurring secondary metabolites., The name "apiose" is derived from the flavonoid glycoside |FRAME: 7-O-BETA-D-APIOFURANOSYL-12-BETA-D-GLU apiin|, from which it was first obtained |CITS: [Vongerichten01]|. Apiin itself is named after parsley (|FRAME: TAX-4043|), which at the time was known as Apium petroselinum |CITS: [26848180]|., About This Pathway, The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway were found by first identifying genes encoding D-apiose-specific substrate binding proteins (SBPs), since SBPs, which are components of certain types of transporters, are often clustered with catabolic genes that metabolize the compound the SBPs bind to., The pathway starts with an aldose/ketose isomerase that catalyzes isomerization of |FRAME: D-APIOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-22554|, and continues with the phosphorylation of the latter to |FRAME: CPD-22555|., |FRAME: CPD-22555| is a substrate for a heterodimeric transketolase that generates the central metabolism intermediates |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS: [29867142]|., The identified genes were cloned from either |FRAME: TAX-218491| or |FRAME: TAX-339671|, since a complete set of pathway enzymes could not be successfully purified from either organism, and the genes were recombinantly expressed and characterized. In addition, inactivation of the genes in |FRAME: TAX-554| abolished D-apiose catabolism |CITS: [29867142]|., As of 2018, the pathway's genes were found in the genomes of 860 bacterial species, incuding members of the human gut microbiota and soil microbiomes |CITS: [29867142]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, A few bacterial phyla appear to possess menaquinones with very long prenyl side chains. Several oral strains of the |FRAME: TAX-838| genus, which consists of obligate anaerobes, were reported to produce |FRAME: CPD-9721|. This quinone was found in combination with |FRAME: CPD-9722| in |FRAME:TAX-28134| strains VP1 8906D and HS4 and in |FRAME: TAX-83231| strains NP333, 75J1, J1 and WP H61 |CITS: [6102980][6363375]|., In addition, several species that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-33882| genus were reported to contain |FRAME: CPD-9721| as a minor component. These organisms, which contain |FRAME: CPD-9723| and |FRAME: CPD-9722| as their major quinones, include |FRAME: TAX-33885|, |FRAME: TAX-33918| |CITS:[7462123][7022156]|, |FRAME: TAX-69368| and |FRAME: TAX-2033| |CITS: [6775048]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-17509| is an analogue of |FRAME: GLN| that acts as an irreversible inactivator of enzymes that contain a glutaminase domain. Inactivation of |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.16|, which is involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, disrupts cell wall peptidoglycan assembly and leads to cell death |CITS: [3527630]|., |FRAME: CPD-17509| is produced by some |FRAME: TAX-1386 Bacillus| species and functions as a Trojan Horse antibiotic |CITS: [15393423]|. Once inside the victim's cell, |FRAME: CPD-17509| is liberated by the action of peptidases and attacks the host., A gene cluster responsible for bacilysin production has been identified |CITS: [15609023 ]|. The cluster consists of seven genes. BacABGF are four enzymes that act in tandem with an unidentified epoxidase to divert some of the flux of |FRAME: PREPHENATE| away from production of |FRAME: PHE| and |FRAME: TYR| into a five-step pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-17531| |CITS: [3121591][20052993][22483065][22765234][23317005]|., The exact pathway is still not fully understood. On one hand, it is known that the epoxidation occurs on an (E) isomer. On the other hand, stereochemical considerations suggest that a (Z) isomer is converted into |FRAME: CPD-17531|. Two possible routes are included in the pathway shown here - a direct tranformation of |FRAME: CPD-17551| to |FRAME: CPD-17536|, catalyzed by |FRAME: BSU37680|, and an indirect route via |FRAME: CPD-17552|, which also involves |FRAME: BSU37730| |CITS: [23317005]|. Once formed, |FRAME: CPD-17531| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-17509| by BacC and ligated to |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| by BacD, forming the final product, |FRAME: CPD-17508| |CITS: [23317005]|., The last gene in the cluster, bacE, is proposed to encode a dipeptide permease that plays a role in host resistance, pumping bacilysin from the intracellular to the extracellular environment |CITS: [15609023 ]|.

General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-28068 "Rubrivivax gelatinosus (previously known as Rhodocyclus gelatinosus and Rhodopseudomonas gelatinosa)"|, a member of the β-proteobacteria class, is a photosynthetic non-sulfur purple bacterium that produces both |FRAME: CPD-12615| and |FRAME: CPD-11468| from the common precursor |FRAME: NEUROSPORENE| (as indicated by the pathway link). These two acyclic, methylated carotenoids are accessory pigments in the light-harvesting and reaction-center complexes in these bacteria. Both carotenoids may be ketolated during aerobic growth of these organisms (in |CITS: [19136077]|). In contrast, in the photosynthetic non-sulfur purple bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1085|, an α-proteobacterium, only the |FRAME: CPD-12615| pathway is present. In the non-sulfur purple bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1061| and |FRAME: TAX-1063|, only the |FRAME: PWY-6286| pathway is present (in |CITS: [12664193]|). In |FRAME: TAX-1085|, analysis of carotenoids produced by a rhodopin 3,4-desaturase deletion mutant demonstrated the broad substrate specificity of modification enzymes in the |FRAME: CPD-12615| pathway and the potential for branching |CITS: [9636041]|. Similar studies in |FRAME: TAX-28068| confirmed these findings |CITS: [12664193]|., The |FRAME: CPD-12615| pathway proceeds from |FRAME: NEUROSPORENE| via |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to |FRAME: CPD-12615| and its keto-derivatives utilizing enzymes encoded by genes crtI (a desaturase), crtC (a hydratase), crtD (a 3,4-desaturase), crtF (an O-methyltransferase) and crtA (a monooxygenase). In |FRAME: TAX-28068| the products of genes crtC, crtD, crtF and crtA participate in both the |FRAME: CPD-12615|, and |FRAME: CPD-11468| and |FRAME: CPD-11466| biosynthesis pathways. The overall linear pathway is shown here although it has been noted that the order of modification of the pathway intermediates may give rise to other branches that also ultimately lead to |FRAME: CPD-12615| |CITS: [10880364]|.

Summary: General Background, Carbon tetrachloride (CT) is a toxic and carcinogenic compound which is used primarily as a chemical intermediate in the production of the refrigerants, |FRAME: CPD-8224| and |FRAME:CPD-8223|. Freon 11 and 12 are also used as solvents, in plastic and resin production, as foam blowing agents, and previously as aerosol propellants. CT has also been used as a grain fumigant, but this use was banned by EPA in 1985. In 2000 alone the United States exported approximately 32 billion lbs worldwide of CT |CITS: [ROC11]|. Improper disposal of CT resulted in widespread contamination of soils and groundwater., Fully halogenated compounds such as CT are resistant to aerobic degradation, and are relatively stable under aerobic conditions. However, under anaerobic conditions CT can be degraded by bacterial enzymes or compounds in several different pathways. Carbon tetrachloride degradation has been documented in many environments, including methanogenic |CITS: [Egli90]|, acetogenic |CITS: [3145712][Egli90]|, sulfate reducing |CITS: [3145712][Egli90]|, iron reducing |CITS: [8285682][7926693]|, and nitrate reducing |CITS: [6859850]| conditions., In all of these cases, CT appears to be co-metabolized, that is, the reaction is a fortuitous modification of the substrate by enzymes or cofactors that normally catalyze other reactions. The bacteria derive no benefit from co-metabolic reactions., About This Pathway, In many cases a mechanism of hydrogenolytic reductive dechlorination has been observed, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-843|, |FRAME:CPD-681|, |FRAME:CPD-845| and |FRAME:CH4|. As not all organisms can carry the reactions all the way to |FRAME:CH4|, in some cases the pathway ends at an earlier intermediate. All of these transformations appear to be non specific co-metabolic reactions, catalyzed by various tetrapyrrole-containing molecules. There have been reports of the reactions being catalazed by corrinoids |CITS:[Wood68][Krone89]|, porphyrins |CITS: [4039602][8285682]|, and |FRAME:CPD-7425 "coenzyme F430"| |CITS: [2559772]|., In liver microsomes, as well as in |FRAME: TAX-303|, a cytochrome P450 has been shown to catalyze the conversion of CT to |FRAME:CPD-843| |CITS: [Ruf84][4039602]|. In |FRAME: TAX-70863| c-type cytochromes have been implicated in the reaction |CITS: [8285682]|. Corrinoids have been shown to catalyze the reaction in many homoacetogens, methanogens and sulfate reducers |CITS: [3145712][Egli90][Krone89]|. The fact that all of these bacteria possess the |FRAME:CODH-PWY| suggests that the responsible enzyme may be the |FRAME:CPLX-1|, which catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE| to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| in these organisms |CITS: [3145712]|., The reactions are believed to proceed through the formation of a |FRAME:CPD-8214|, which temporarily binds to the metal cofactor. Thus, the first step is the single electron transfer from the transition metal to CT, with the concomitant release of a chloride anion, resulting in a formation of a |FRAME:CPD-8214|, as depicted in equation 1:, eq. 1 |FRAME:RXN-8401|, A second electron transfer generates |FRAME:CPD-843|, as in equation 2:, eq. 2 |FRAME:RXN-8402|, These two reactions are summed in equation 3, which is the form included in this pathway:, eq. 3 |FRAME:R525-RXN|

General Background, At the time of this review, over 130 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity. Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana. GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). , Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Given the important roles that GAs play in plant growth and development, several levels of regulation are used to carefully control the level and types of bioactive GAs present in various tissues. Direct chemical modifications to gibberellins including oxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-102|) methylation (|FRAME: PWY-6477|), and epoxidation (this pathway) may be used to reduce the levels of bioactive GAs., About This Pathway, Gibberellin epoxidation is believed to inactivate bioactive GAs and their precursors |CITS: [16399803]|. The existence of this pathway is supported by the identification of an enzyme from rice, |FRAME: LOC_OS05G0482400-MONOMER "CYP714D1"|, that can catalyze GA epoxidation in vitro |CITS: [16399803]|. In addition, there is also evidence that the transcript expression pattern of a putative 16α, 17 gibberellin epoxidase in Lolium temulentum may be correlated with a selective reduction in the level of active GA1 and GA4 just below the shoot apex in this species |CITS: [19825541]|. Although the epoxy forms of GA have not been detected in rice plants to date, their putative dihydroxy derivatives, such as, |FRAME: CPD-12355|, have been found in a number of plant species, including rice, |FRAME:TAX-3888|, |FRAME:TAX-3870|, |FRAME:TAX-3750| (see refs in |CITS: [16399803]|) and Lolium temulentum |CITS: [19825541]|. Although these dihydroxy compounds can be produced spontaneously in vitro by exposure to acids such as acetic acid during the compound analysis process |CITS: [16399803]|, it is likely that they are also produced in vivo through the activity of an epoxy-hydrolase or other enzyme., Although gibberellins are produced by a number of fungi (for example, see |FRAME: PWY-5047|) and bacteria, there is no evidence to date of GA epoxide formation in these species, and it may be unlikely to occur in organisms where GA does not play a role as an endogenous signaling molecule that needs to be selectively inactivated |CITS: [19560174]|., It is interesting to note that |FRAME: LOC_OS05G0482400-MONOMER "CYP714D1"| -mediated epoxidation can occur in vitro both on the biologically active |FRAME: CPD1F-137| as well as the |FRAME: CPD1F-95| precursor compound that is produced very early in the GA biosynthetic pathway. This indicates that epoxidation may be used to inactivate specific GAs that are involved in particular processes, or it may be used to more globally shut down GA signaling by acting on upstream compounds. Work in additional plant species will be required to gain a better understanding of the specificity and functional role of GA epoxidation in GA metabolism. Given the important role that the |FRAME: LOC_OS05G0482400-MONOMER "CYP714D1/EUI"| GA epoxidase plays in regulating internode elongation and facilitating hybrid rice production (see refs in |CITS: [16399803]|) this mechanism of GA regulation is likely to be subject to further study.

Summary: General Background, Caffeine is found in several plant species including coffea, tea and cacao. The contents of caffeine vary greatly from cultivar to cultivar, tissue to tissue, and from different developmental stages. One mechanism that plants use to control caffeine level is by balancing between caffeine biosynthesis and degradation. The main caffeine degradation pathway has been proposed to proceed via theophylline and 3-methylxanthine involving three sequential de-methylation steps (|FRAME: PWY-6552|), and caffeine is eventually degraded to CO2 and NH3. In addition, minor species-specific degradation pathways have also been proposed. All the proposed pathways were based on radio-tracer studies (reviewed in |CITS: [18068204][14977550]|). No enzyme activity has been detected or characterized to date. , About This Pathway, In several tea and coffea species, caffeine is degraded to liberine (O(2),1,9-trimethylurate), a pathway involves an initial oxidation reaction followed by several methyltransfer reactions.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8117| (GLA) is a polyunsaturated (18:3) ω-6 fatty acid (the 6 refers to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid). It is synthesized from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| by Δ6 desaturase enzymes. Unlike its precursor, GLA is not an essential fatty acid for animals, since almost all animals possess a Δ6 desaturase enzyme., GLA is of major importance in animal cells, being the precursor for the synthesis of several Δ6-desaturated fatty acids, such as |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5353|)., Δ6-desaturated fatty acids have roles in the maintenance of membrane structure and function, in the regulation of cholesterol synthesis and transport, in the prevention of water loss from the skin, and as precursors of eicosanoids, including prostaglandins and leucotrienes |CITS: [1334266]|., It has been documented that certain organisms, including some plants |CITS:[11170598][16718484]|, filamentous fungi |CITS:[11112411][10570972]| and cyanobacteria |CITS: [8389613][16328883]| can produce substantial portions of |FRAME: CPD-8117|., In the plant kingdom, |FRAME: CPD-8117| is only found in a few higher plants (including black currants, evening primrose, borage and hemp), and is usually found exclusively in the seeds., About This Pathway, In all plant tissues, the major glycerolipids are first synthesized using only palmitoyl (16:0) and oleoyl (18:1) acyl groups, the products of the plastidic saturated fatty acid synthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5971|, |FRAME: PWY-5989| and |FRAME: PWY-5147|). Subsequent desaturation of the fatty acids to the highly unsaturated forms typical of the membranes of plant cells is carried while they are already attached to lipids., Most of the oleoyl-[acp] is released from the [acp]-moiety and exported from the plastid to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and is converted to |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA| in the process by the plastidic |FRAME: AT1G77590-MONOMER|. The |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA| is incorporated into lipids, forming |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE|, |FRAME: Diacylglycerides|, and |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|., Further desaturation of the oleoyl groups to linoleoyl groups in the ER occurrs while incorporated into lipids. The first step, which produces |FRAME: Linoleoyl-groups|, is catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-1903|, encoded by the |FRAME: AT3G12120| gene. In order to produce a |FRAME: Gamma-linolenoyl-groups|, a second desaturation step is catalyzed by, |FRAME: MONOMER-12524|., The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-13363| has been cloned and expressed in tobacco |CITS: [9108131]|. The desaturase domain of this enzyme is preceeded at the N terminus by a sequence that is related to a cytochrome b5, the electron donor for other ER-located fatty acid desaturases |CITS: [9108131]|., Co-expression of the Δ6 desaturase from |FRAME: TAX-13363| and the |FRAME: CPLX-1903| from |FRAME: ORG-5993| in soybean resulted in high accumuolation of |FRAME: CPD-12653| |CITS: [16718484]|.

Summary: General Background, Flavanone glycosides such as the sugar derivatives of hesperetin and naringenin (see |FRAME:PWY-5094|) are the dominant group of flavonoids found in the genus |FRAME:TAX-2706| |CITS: [ROUSEFF87][10552686][16428836]|. The content of flavanone glycosides and their corresponding aglycones undergoes significant changes upon the attack of the phytopathogen Phytophthora citrophthora, the agent for the brown rot lesion in citrus fruits. It was discussed that these compounds participate in the defense mechanism of |FRAME:TAX-2706| species and may act as fungicides |CITS: [15053528]|., The 6"-O-rhamnoside of hesperitin, i.e. |FRAME: CPD-7075| has been investigated with respect to its wide range of pharmacological properties and is regarded as important constituent of the human diet |CITS: [11746857]|. Both hesperitin and its glycoside hesperidin possess significant antioxidant and radical-scavenging properties |CITS: [16101151][15453641]|. Flavanoides have been employed to investigate their impact on the reduction of lipid peroxidation. It has been demonstrated that e.g. flavanone aglycones such as hesperitin and naringenin have a better potential in their antiperoxidative action than the corresponding glycosides, i.e. hesperidin and naringin |CITS: [3355718]|., About This Pathway, Although hesperitin is a major compound found in the plant family |FRAME:TAX-23513| (genus |FRAME:TAX-2706|) and is also present in Asteracea |CITS: [2610472]| and |FRAME:TAX-3803| |CITS: [10389270]|, its biosynthesis is still unknown. The position specific 3'-O-methyltransferase forming |FRAME:CPD-7071| has been purified |CITS: [16412485]| but the isolation and characterization of the equivalent 4'-O-methyltransferase, assuming that hesperitin derives from eriodictyol, is still lacking., The pathway starts with the formation of hesperitin-7-O-glucoside. The enzyme catalyzing the 7-O-glucosylation of flavanones has been purified from various plants with focus on the formation of naringenin glycosides. However, the isolated enzymes frequently express a comparable turnover rate towards hesperitin, as found in |FRAME:TAX-37334| , |CITS: [Lewinsohn89b]|, |FRAME:TAX-37656| |CITS: [2171434]| |CITS: [McIntosh90]| and |FRAME:TAX-4102| |CITS: [10626374]|. In contrast to that the 7-O-glucosyltransferase investigated in |FRAME:TAX-2708| |CITS: [BERHOW95]| , specifically glucosylates hesperitin but did not accept naringenin as a substrate., The attachment of L-rhamnose to the various positions of the glucosyl moiety is carried out by position specific flavanone 7-O-glucoside rhamnosyltransferases producing the diglycosyl flavanoids that can accumulate up to 75% of dry weight |CITS: [12232031]|. Summary: Methanesulfonate is a very stable strong acid and a key intermediate in the biogeochemical cycling, of sulfur. It is formed in megatonne quantities in the atmosphere from the chemical oxidation of, atmospheric |FRAME: CPD-7670|. Depending on the geographical latitude, 25-70% of the flux of, dimethylsulfide is oxidized to methanesulfonate, which is deposited on the Earth by rain and snow,, and by dry deposition |CITS: [10591843]|., Methanesulfonate is remarkably stable, yet it is used by diverse aerobic bacteria as a source of sulfur for, growth., This has been demonstrated for Klebsiella sp., Comamonas acidovorans, Rhodococcus sp.,, |FRAME:TAX-1423|, Enterobacter aerogenes, Serratia marcescens, |FRAME:TAX-562| and fluorescent, pseudomonads |CITS: [Seitz93][8436944][8293962][Chih-Ching95][9782504][9990724][10369899]|., So far no anaerobe has been shown to utilize methanesulfonate., In addition, some bacteria can use methanesulfonate as a carbon and energy substrate to, support growth. Since desulfonation of methanesulfonate can lead initially only to methanol or, formaldehyde, only methylotrophic bacteria (or yeasts) are likely to be able to, use methanesulfonate in this way. Some methylotrophs that are known to grow on methanesulfonate, include the genera |FRAME: TAX-50055| and |FRAME: TAX-50056|, and some strains of, |FRAME: TAX-81| and |FRAME: TAX-407|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1035|, have been reported to utilize methanesulfonate |CITS: [15643932]|., When methanesulfonate is used a a carbon source, the formaldehyde that is formed is channeled into, two pathways: some of it is assimilated through the serine cycle (see |FRAME: PWY-1622|), while the, rest is oxidized to carbon dioxide to provide NADH and energy (see the pathways under, |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation|)., Methanesulfonate oxidation is initiated by cleavage of the C-S bond, which is catalyzed by, |FRAME: CPLX-7666|, an three-component enzyme complex that includes a hydroxylase, a reductase,, and a ferredoxin |CITS: [10094704]|., Such enzymes were reported in |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [10049377]|, |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |CITS: [9782504]|, and well characterized from |FRAME: TAX-50058| |CITS: [8932698]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Melleolides melleolides| are a large family of aryl ester secondary metabolites produced by species of the basidiomycete genus |FRAME: TAX-47424|, which are composed of an |FRAME: CPD-47| moiety esterified to a tricyclic sesquiterpene (|FRAME: CPD-14796|) alcohol |CITS: [Midland82][Donnelly82]|. Both |FRAME: CPD-47| and protoilludane derivatives have been described from numerous other organisms |CITS: [11281843][12714063][19666480]|, but these two elements are combined into a single entity only in the melleolides, which are not found outside the |FRAME: TAX-47424|. , Various melleolides have been shown to inhibit microbial growth |CITS: [Arnone86][10805573]| and display phytotoxicity |CITS: [1418682]|. The antifungal activity has been linked to the position of the double bond within the sesquiterpene moiety |CITS: [24906293]|. Melleolides have also been reported to have cytotoxic effects on human cancer cell lines by decreasing DNA synthesis |CITS: [21376582]|., About This Pathway, Biosynthesis of the sesquiterpene protoilludene moiety is achieved by cyclization of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, catalyzed, by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.135|, and results in the tricyclic |FRAME: CPD-14796| backbone |CITS: [21148562]|. Since the protoilludene moiety in most melleolides contain a double bond between carbon 2 and 3, modifying enzymes must shif the bond before the protoilludene moiety can be attached to |FRAME: CPD-47|., It has been shown in |FRAME: TAX-47429| that |FRAME: CPD-47| is biosynthesized by a seven-domain polyketide synthase whose terminal thioesterase domain also catalyzes the coupling of |FRAME: CPD-47| to a modified protoilludene-based alcohols |CITS: [23993460]|. Modifications of the basic structure include hydroxylation at various positions of the sesquiterpene, oxidation of the primary alcohol at C-1 to an aldehyde or carboxy group, shift or reduction of the cyclohexene double bond, methyl ether formation at O-5', and chlorination at C-6'. However, with the exception of the halogenases responsible for the chlorination (|CITS: [26655762]|), the identity of the modifying enzymes are still not known (as of 2017)., The numerous modifications result in excess of 60 melleolide analogs, making the melleolides one of the most diverse groups of fungal natural products |CITS: [Misiek12]|.
