Summary: The occurrence of 7-polyacylated anthocyanins as the main pigments inducing blue color(s) in flowers has been reported from various plant families |CITS:[19554240]|. Many of them are delphinidin derivatives which have been found in the Campanulaceae family, for instance |FRAME:CPD-16561| (this pathway) |CITS:[Kondo90] [7763601]|, |FRAME:CPD-16594| |CITS:[7763601] [Justesen97]| and |FRAME:CPD-16596| |CITS:[Saito71] [Goto83]| but also in the Asteracea family where |FRAME:CPD-16595| dominates |CITS:[Goto84]| and the Goodeniaceae family with |FRAME:CPD-16605| as the principal blue flower pigment |CITS:[17174991]|. The formation and color depth of the blue hues depend on the developmental stage of the sepals during anthesis |CITS:[12353624]| or the genetic constitution of the plants |CITS:[Justesen97]| which in turn reflects the activation and specificities of the involved enzymes., The formation of |FRAME:CPD-7145| from |FRAME:CPD-7117| |CITS:[Kamsteeg80]| is considered the first committed step in the |FRAME:CPD-16561| biosynthesis followed by the crucial step of the 7-O-glucosylation of the delphinidin 3-rutinoside to yield |FRAME:CPD-16558| |CITS:[20971893] [22673029]|. The anthocyanin 3,7-diglucosides are also the initial point for the biosynthesis of pigments other than delphinidin derivatives (see |FRAME:PWY-7464|). , The noteworthiness of this pathway is the utilization of one acyl-glucose donor, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15283| by both glucosyltransferases and acetyltransferases which further furnish the delphinidin 7-O-side chain. The donor provides both glucosyl- and p-hydroxybenzoyl groups and in doing so serves as a zwitter donor in the |FRAME:PWY-7458| |CITS:[24179131]|. The two acylation steps in the pathway, i.e. the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-16558| to |FRAME:CPD-16559| and |FRAME:CPD-16560| to |FRAME:CPD-16561| have been demonstrated in crude extracts from sepals of Delphinium grandiflorum. Although the cDNA (SCPL2) for the acyl-glucose dependent anthocyanin glucoside(s) acyltransferase was obtained the expression in an recombinant organism failed but its molecular function could be confirmed in vivo in white Delphinium varieties where the gene was absent |CITS:[24179131]|. Two cDNA's encoding for the acyl-glucose dependent anthocyanin 7-O-(6-O-(p-hydroxybenzoyl)-glucoside) glucosyltransferase catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-16559| to |FRAME:CPD-16560| were also isolated, expressed in E. coli and biochemically identified. Both, glucosyltransferase and acyltransferase were localized to the vacuole which coincides with the localization of |FRAME:CPD-16561| |CITS:[24179131]| and the occurrence of other enzymes of the pathway |CITS:[20971893] [22673029]|.

Summary: General Background, The avenanthramides are a group of N-cinnamoylanthranilic acids comprising |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: CPD-674| linked by an amide bond |CITS: [Collins88]|. The avenanthramides were first identified as phytoalexins in oat leaves infected by the pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-27344| |CITS: [Tani81]|, but were later found at significant levels in oat grains |CITS: [Collins89][21598950]|. They were also detected in white cabbage butterfly (|FRAME: TAX-7116|) eggs |CITS: [7964796]| and in fungus-infected carnation (|FRAME: TAX-3570|) |CITS: [Chu13]|., More than 25 different types of avenanthramides have been detected in oat grains, differing by the various substituted groups on the two main components. The three most abundant ones comprise |FRAME: CPD-23407| conjugated with |FRAME: COUMARATE| (|FRAME: CPD-23404|), |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| (|FRAME: CPD-23405|), or |FRAME: CPD-676| (|FRAME: CPD-23406|) |CITS: [Collins89]|., Avenanthramides were shown to have anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-itch, anti-irritant, and antiatherogenic activities |CITS: [17373175][21417395]|. They are currently used commercially for skin, hair, baby, and sun care products., About This Pathway, The first key enzyme in the biosynthesis of the avenanthramides to be studied was |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.302| (HHT), an anthranilate acyl-CoA dependent acyltransferase that is homologous to |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.133| |CITS: [Ishihara97][14714871][16616872][26053460]|. The acyl donors used by HHT are diverged from the phenylpropanoid pathway and their biosynthesis is predicted to require |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12| |CITS: [4364250][Hahlbrock89][12242399]|., A 2019 study has provided additional information about the pathway |CITS: [31394723]|. The authors cloned the genes encoding |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12|, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.302|, and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.104|, and used the purified proteins to verify the predicted activities., According to the proposed pathway, |FRAME: COUMARATE| is initially derived from |FRAME: PHE| by the combined action of |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.24| (PAL) and |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.91| (C4'H). It is activated into its CoA thioester by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12| (4CL), and the product is condensed by HHT with |FRAME: CPD-23407| to form |FRAME: CPD-23404|., In a parallel branch, |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-412| or |FRAME: 4-COUMAROYLQUINATE| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.133| (HCT), followed by hydroxylation by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.96|, a cytochrome P450 enzyme (CYP98). A thioesterase reaction catalyzed by HCT can then release |FRAME: CAFFEOYL-COA|, which is condensed by HHT with |FRAME: CPD-23407| to form |FRAME: CPD-23406|., Finally, |FRAME: CPD-23406| can be methylated into |FRAME: CPD-23405| by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.104| |CITS: [31394723]|.

Summary: General Background, Methylated amines are ubiquitous in the environment, especially in the marine ecosystem. They are produced by the degradation of proteins and of quartenary amines such as |FRAME: BETAINE|, |FRAME: DL-CARNITINE carnitine|, |FRAME: CHOLINE|, and |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|, which are common osmolytes of many marine organisms., The most methylated form, |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA), can be converted to |FRAME: CH4| by methanogenic archaea via methanogenesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5250|). In addition, some microorganisms are able to use TMA as the sole source for carbon, nitrogen and energy. TMA is first converted in several steps to |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| (MMA), which can be oxidized further by multiple mechanisms, depending on the bacteria., Bacteria that possess the enzyme methylamine dehydrogenase (|FRAME: RXN-2841 "EC 1.4.9.1"|), can oxidize |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and ammonia is a single reaction (see |FRAME: PWY-1701|). MMA-degrading bacteria that lack that enzyme can achieve the same outcome by a pathway that proceeds via two unusual amino acids - |FRAME: N5-METHYLGLUTAMINE| and |FRAME: CPD-404|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6965|., The microbial oxidation of methylated amines is an important component of environmental cycling of carbon and nitrogen, as well as an essential step in preventing formation of methane, the second most important greenhouse gas, following carbon dioxide |CITS: [19943898]|., About This Pathway, The catabolism of |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| under aerobic conditions has been well documented for many years, although not well-characterized |CITS: [11946146]|. It has been shown that TMAO in the Sargasso Sea is predominantly oxidized by bacterioplankton as an energy source |CITS: [21886845]| and that the marine, methylotrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-383631| can oxidize TMAO to CO2 to generate energy |CITS: [21981742]|., A monooxygenase that can oxygenate TMA to TMAO (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.148|) has been described already in the early 70s |CITS: [4404764]|. A gene encoding that enzyme was found many years later in the TMA-degrading soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-199596| |CITS: [22006322]|. Similarly, the next enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.32|, was also described in the early 70s |CITS: [11946146][5116524]|, but the gene encoding the enzyme was identified only in 2014, in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-246200| |CITS: [24550299]|. This enzyme catalyzes the nonoxidative, non-hydrolytic cleavage of |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| (TMAO) to |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, the latter used as a carbon or energy source, depending on the organism., The next enzyme in the pathway is |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.238|, which converts |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE| to |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| |CITS: [22006322][28304370]|. Finally, |FRAME: METHYLAMINE| can be converted to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and ammonia via different pathways, depending on the organism (see |FRAME: PWY-6967| and |FRAME: PWY-6965|)., The low abundance of the genes encoding |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.238| in marine metagenomes suggests that this enzyme may be a metabolic bottleneck in the marine methylated amines degradation pathway |CITS: [28304370]|.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1280| is natural inhabitant of the skin and mucous membranes of mammals, able to cause disease in humans ranging from mild wound infections to more serious ailments including septic shock, endocarditis, and osteomyletis., |FRAME: TAX-1280| is known to produce four siderophores: |FRAME: CPD-12589| |CITS: [2139423]|, |FRAME: CPD-12590| |CITS: [8400765]|, |FRAME: CPD-21048| |CITS: [14688077]|, and |FRAME: CPD-21049| |CITS: [9125585]|., A gene cluster that contains the genes necessary for production of |FRAME: CPD-12589| has been identified. The cluster contains an operon of four genes. One of the genes (|FRAME: G-58279|) encodes a PLP-dependent amino acid racemase, another encodes a transporter, and the other two genes, |FRAME: G-58280| and |FRAME: G-58281|, encode nonribosomal peptide synthase-independent (NIS) synthases. The cluster also contains a ferric uptake regulator (Fur) box upstream of the divergent promoters for the sfnaA and |FRAME: G-58281| genes and is located adjacent to a cluster coding for iron complex transporters |CITS: [19138128]|., Cloning and expressing the full operon in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in production of |FRAME: CPD-12589|, confirming that the cluster encodes its biosynthesis. In addition, both NIS synthases were purified and shown to catalyze the assigned activities in vitro |CITS: [19138128]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-25639 "Mannosylerythritol lipids"| (MELs) are amphiphilic glycolipids that display high surface activity and act as biodetergents (biosurfactants). The compounds are produced by yeast strains that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-5269| and |FRAME: TAX-63261| genera. They show excellent surface-active properties and versatile biochemical actions. The compounds were first described in 1956 from an |FRAME: TAX-5269| species |CITS: [13276861]|. However, the most common MEL producing species are members of the |FRAME: TAX-63261| genus, such as |FRAME: TAX-84753|, |FRAME: TAX-84754|, |FRAME: TAX-84752|, and |FRAME: TAX-203536| |CITS: [25723622]|., The lipids are acylated at positions O-2' and O-3' by a range of fatty acyl residues. In |FRAME: TAX-5270| the fatty acid at O-2' ranges from C2 to C6, while that at O-3' ranges from C12 to C16. In addition, MELs differ in their acetylation status. Four general types are produced differing in the acetylation of positions O-4' and O-6'. Mel-D has no acetylation, MEL-B is acetylated only at the O-6' position, MEL-C is acetylated only at the O-4' position, and MEL-A, which is the most prevalent form, is acetylated at both positions |CITS: [Kitamoto90a][Kitamoto90][10570818][17898510]|. , The biological function of MELs is still unknown, but they are of growing biotechnological interest as a sustainable alternative for chemical surfactants |CITS: [18585066][22901730]|., About This Pathway, The first gene involved in |FRAME: CPD-25639 "mannosylerythritol lipids"| (MELs) biosynthesis to be discovered was the |FRAME: G-107850| gene of |FRAME: TAX-5270|, which encodes the first enzyme of the pathway. Knocking out the gene completely abolished MEL production. |CITS: [15932999]|., A subsequent experiment that looked at |FRAME: TAX-5270| genes that were induced upon nitrogen limitation (conditions that favor MEL production) found four genes located immediately adjacent to |FRAME: G-107850| that are induced more than 2.5-fold upon nitrogen limitation. These genes were found to encode the enzyme for the rest of the pathway, as well as a major facilitator protein (Mmf1) that is involved in the export of MEL glycolipids |CITS: [16885300]|., The pathway spans several compartments. The |FRAME: G-107850| glycosyltransferase is linked to vacuoles, the |FRAME: G-107851| and |FRAME: G-107852| acyltransferases are located in the peroxisome, and the |FRAME: G-107849| acetyltransferase was detected at the plasma membrane, requiring the intermediates of MEL biosynthesis to travel between different compartments |CITS: [24835306]|.

Lacinilene C is a cotton terpenoid derived from cadinene, which is also a precursor for |FRAME: PWY-5773|. , 8-hydroxylation of cadinene leads to gossypol, whereas 7-hydroxylation leads to lacinilene. , 7-hydroxylated cadinanes, such as 2,7-dihydroxycadalene and lacinilene C, are phytoalexins induced , to accumulate in the foliar tissues after bacteria attack. Inhalation of lacinilene C 7-methyl ether from , cotton processing dust was thought to be the cause of chronic respiration distress seen in some fiber , mill workers.  , The occurrence of the lacinilenes in an optically active form indicates that they are formed enzymatically , in vivo. They can also be formed non-enzymatically by in vitro auto-oxidation of 2,7-dihydroxycadalene |CITS: [Stipanovic81]|.

General Background, Aryl carotenoids that contain φ-type rings were first discovered in the Japanese sea sponge |FRAME: TAX-6062|, which at the time was known as Reniera japonica |CITS: [Yamaguchi57]| (in retrospect they were most likely produced by bacterial endosymbionts of the sponge). Thus the first compounds to be defined from that organism were named |FRAME: CPD-20646| (φ,χ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi57a]| and |FRAME: CPD-20624| (φ,φ-carotene) |CITS: [Yamaguchi58][Yamaguchi59]|. Aryl carotenoids were subsequently identified in most non-oxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (green and purple sulfur bacteria) as well as some non-photosynthetic species of the |FRAME: TAX-1763| and |FRAME: TAX-1883| genera |CITS: [5711189][5781524][Schmidt70][4635689]|. , In green sulfur bacteria (GSB) the carotenoids are found in chlorosomes. These obligately anaerobic photoautotrophs can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph (up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight |CITS: [Overmann92]|) due to their chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. The chlorosome consists of mostly |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"|, or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| that self-aggregate into large oligomers, but also contains up to 10% carotenoids., The main carotenoid produced by GSB species with |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| or |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| as the primary antenna component is the monocyclic |FRAME: CPD-20625|, while the main carotenoids produced by brown-colored green sulfur bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-274537|), which contain |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| as their primary antenna bacteriochlorophyl are the dicyclic |FRAME: CPD-20626| and |FRAME: CPD-20624|, as well as small quantities of |FRAME: CPD-20627| and |FRAME: CPD-20629| |CITS: [15115301][18676669]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7940|)., About This Pathway, Carotenoids bearing sugars and acylated sugars have been found in many bacteria and occur in a wide range of phyla in both photosynthetic and nonphotosynthetic species. The sugar is typically glucose, although mannose |CITS: [4635697]| and fucose |CITS: [11479383][15317766][15695449]| have also been reported. The sugar is linked to a hydroxyl group on the carotenoid backbone, and may be acylated by an acyl chain of 1 to 20 carbons |CITS: [16149733]|., The green sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1097| produces a small amount of |FRAME: CPD-20629|, which is found in the cytoplasmic membrane rather than associated with the chlorosomes |CITS: [9297463][Takaichi99]|. This compound is derived from |FRAME: CPD-20625| in three steps., In the first step |FRAME: CPD-20625| is hydroxylated by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.131| (crtC) |CITS: [15292122]|. This is followed by glucosyltransfer, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.M32| (cruD), and finally acylation by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.M48| |CITS: [16923888]|., It is unlikely that |FRAME: CPD-20629| is involved in light harvesting and the conversion of light energy to chemical energy, since glycosylated and acylated carotenoids are widespread among both photosynthetic and nonphotosynthetic bacteria. It has been proposed that these compounds serve other structural or protective functions in the membrane, such as absorbing and dissipating the energy from reactive oxygen species, UV light, or chlorophyll triplet states. The acyl group likely anchors such molecules within the membrane, and could also provide structural interactions with particular membrane proteins.

Summary: General Background, Leucoanthocyanidins such as leucopelargonidin and leucocyanidin are colorless , intermediates in the biosynthetic course to build up the corresponding colored anthocyanins (|FRAME:PWY-5125|) , |CITS: [12828368]|. Leucoanthocyanidins are compounds at a branch-point embedded in that metabolic sequence. , They either can be oxidized to form anthocyanins or can be reduced to serve as precursors for catechins and , proanthocyanins (|FRAME:PWY-641|) |CITS: [12435592]| |CITS: [15720617]|. As such leucoanthocyanidins , represent an important regulatory point to feed a range of flavonoid subclasses of diverse biological properties , |CITS: [11402179]|., Flavonoids are extensively modified by a number of reactions such as hydroxylation, methylation, glycosylation , and acylation. The hydroxylation of the flavonoid B-ring at the 3',4' or 5' position leads to a variety of flavonoids , contributing to different colors of flowers and seeds |CITS: [11287230]|. The monohydroxylated leucopelargonidin , and the dihydroxylated leucocyanidin give rise to anthocyanins adding red/pink colors to a broad variety of plants, , including Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [10504566]| |CITS: [10536025]|., About This Pathway, Leucopelargonidin and leucocyanidin derive from dihydrokaempferol and dihydroquercetin, , respectively which, in turn are either formed by a Fe2+/oxoglutarate-dependent hydroxylation of , naringenin to generate dihydrokaempferol and eriodictyol to make dihydroquercetin |CITS: [8223617]| |CITS: [8685272]| , or a cytochrome P450-dependent monooxygenase (flavonoid 3'hydroxylase) which hydroxylates dihydrokaempferol , to form dihydroquercetin |CITS: [11030432]|., The discernible step in the biosynthetic route towards leucoanthocyanidins is the stereospecific reduction of 2R,3R)-dihydroflavonols carried out by dihydroflavonol 4-reductase. The enzyme exhibits a pronounced substrate specificity which determines a visible pattern of anthocyanins, catechins and proanthocyanidins indicative for certain species |CITS: [12435592]|. The reduction of |FRAME:DIHYDROKAEMPFEROL-CMPD| and |FRAME:CPD-474| to form the respective leucoanthocyanins is considered the rate-limiting step in the pathway |CITS:[22363429]|. However, the dihyfroflavonol 4-reductase (DFR) catalyzed reaction is at an branch-point for both anthocyanin and condensed tannins biosynthesis (compare |FRAME:PWY-641|). The finding that isoenzymes of DFR within the same species, e.g. Ginkgo biloba |CITS:[23991027]|, Populus trichocarpa |CITS:[22363429]| and Populus tremuloides |CITS:[12472686]| are rather involved in condensed tannins synthesis than in anthocyanin accumulation indicates a functional shift of the enzyme that supports the systemic herbivore response in wooden species |CITS:[12472686]|. , The lack of the B-ring modifying enzyme flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylase catalyzing the formation of 3',4',5'-pentahydroxylated , compounds and derivatives thereof (e.g. dihydromyricetin) in Arabidopsis |CITS: [10536025]| prevents the , biosynthesis of the glucosylated anthocyanidins delphinidin, petunidin and malvidin, contributing to the blue/violet , colors in plants (compare |FRAME:PWY-5152|).

Summary: General Background, General Background, Both alkyl and alk-1-enyl phospholipids appear to serve as important structurally-stable lipid components of membranes, since the ether linkage can impede the hydrolysis of the acyl moiety by phospholipases |CITS: [Snyder85]|. |FRAME: Plasmalogens Plasmalogens| are a unique class of membrane glycerophospholipids that contain a fatty alcohol with a vinyl-ether bond at the sn-1 position, and an ester-linked fatty acids at the sn-2 position of the glycerol backbone. They are widely distributed in anaerobic bacteria and animals. In humans and other mammals they represent up to 20% of the total phospholipid mass (between 1/2 and 2/3 of the ethanolamine phospholipids in humans are plasmalogens |CITS: [11275267]|). , The earliest report of alkylglycerols was made in 1909, from lipids isolated from starfish |CITS: [16742127]|. The name plasmalogen was coined in 1924 by Feulgen and Voit to describe an unknown compound that produced an aldehyde (which they called "plasmal") that they observed in plasma after acid treatment |CITS: [Feulgen24]|. It took nearly 40 years to establish the exact structure of the plasmalogens |CITS: [13416288][13499384][13576152][Marinetti59][Warner63]|., While plasmalogens are widely found in anaerobic bacteria, invertebrates, and vertebrates, they are absent from aerobic bacteria (an exception are myxobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-34|) and most fungi and plants. This distribution suggests that they appeared, disappeared, and then reappeared during evolution, an explanation that is supported by major differences in their biosynthesis between anaerobic bacteria and animals |CITS: [22627108]|., In mammals, the sn-1 position is typically derived from C16:0, C18:0, or C18:1 fatty alcohols while the sn-2 position is most commonly occupied by the polyunsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| or |FRAME: CPD-10244|. The most common head groups present in mammalian plasmalogens are ethanolamine (designated |FRAME: Alkyl-enyl-acyl-gly-P-EtOH-amines plasmenylethalomines|) or choline (designated |FRAME: PLASMENYLCHOLINE plasmenylcholines|), although inositol, serine and threonine have been observed., About This Pathway, Ether lipids are synthesized in a common pathway that begins in the peroxisome and continues in the endoplasmic reticulum. The first two enzymes of the pathway, glyceronephosphate O-acyltransferase (|FRAME: HS04068|) and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase (|FRAME: HS00389|), are associated with the luminal side of the peroxisome membrane. The two proteins form a complex, with two AGPS and one GNPAT molecules |CITS: [10215861]|., The product of these two enzymes, |FRAME: 1-ALKYL-GLYCERONE-3-PHOSPHATE|, is reduced to |FRAME: 1-Alkyl-sn-glycerol-3-phosphates| by an acyl/alkyl-DHAP reductase located in both peroxisomal and ER membranes |CITS: [4390729][9295290]|., The rest of the pathway, which is similar to the the pathway of diacyl glycerophosphate biosynthesis, takes place in the ER. First, an acyl group is placed at the sn-2 position by an alkyl/acyl-GPA acyltransferase and the phosphate group is removed by phosphatidate phosphatase, to form |FRAME: 1-Alkyl-2-acyl-glycerol|., |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.1|, in the presence of |FRAME: CDP-ETHANOLAMINE|, forms |FRAME: 1-Alkyl-2-acyl-glycerol-P-Etn|, while |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.2|, in the presence of |FRAME: CDP-CHOLINE|, forms |FRAME: Plasmanylcholine|., The next step is dehydrogenation of the 1,2 bond of the alkyl group in |FRAME: 1-Alkyl-2-acyl-glycerol-P-Etn| by the microsomal cytochrome b5-dependent plasmenylethanolamine desaturase, forming the vinyl ether bond and generating |FRAME: Alkyl-enyl-acyl-gly-P-EtOH-amines|. Since the desaturase is not active on |FRAME: Plasmanylcholine|, the only route to form |FRAME: PLASMENYLCHOLINE| is the two step replacement of the phosphoethanolamine head group of |FRAME: Alkyl-enyl-acyl-gly-P-EtOH-amines| by a phosphocholine group |CITS: [9795186]|.

Summary: |FRAME: THR| is an indispensable amino acid. It is degraded by a complex network of pathways, and regulatory signals |CITS: [9871012]|., Two of the major routes for the degradation of L-threonine are known to occur both in mammals and in microorganisms., In the first route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREDEHYDCAT-CPLX| (EC 4.3.1.19) to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, which is rapidly and irreversibly converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5437|). A biosynthetic version of this enzyme has also been reported in certain anaerobic bacteria (see |FRAME:ILEUSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [13405870]|., In the second route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.103| to form |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT|, which is mainly cleaved by |FRAME: AKBLIG-CPLX|, forming glycine and acetyl-CoA (see |FRAME:THREONINE-DEG2-PWY|). In the absence of the latter activity |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT| is spontaneously converted to |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|, which is further metabolized into |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| (see |FRAME: THRDLCTCAT-PWY|) or into |FRAME: R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE|, a precursor of vitamin B12 (see |FRAME:PWY-5443|)., A third route has been demonstrated in several bacteria and fungi. This route is based on the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7266| (EC 4.1.2.5), which cleaves threonine directly into |FRAME:GLY| and |FRAME:ACETALD| (see |FRAME:PWY-5436|).

Summary: General Background, Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., At the time of this review, 136 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity. Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana. GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and GA4 enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed. It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). Active |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed in the disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen is used in industry for its ability to produce large amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Incidentally, GA3 is only a minor GA in most plant species., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of GA3 in |FRAME:TAX-5127| occurs through successive oxidation steps via GA14. Unlike what is seen in plants (see |FRAME:PWY-5036|), the main route of production of GA14 occurs via GA14-aldehyde rather than GA12, which only represents a minor route of GA14 synthesis in |FRAME: TAX-5506| |CITS:[11320210]|. Following the production of GA14 the gibberellin 20-oxidase encoded by gene |FRAME:G-9093|, catalyzes the removal of C-20, thereby forming the C19-skeleton in GA4. This protein (GfGA20OX) differs from its plant counterpart in that it is a P450 monooxygenase rather than a dioxygenase. Distinctly from the plant GA 20-oxidases, GfGA20OX does not appear to accumulate the alcohol and aldehyde intermediates observed with dioxygenases, indicating that in the case of the |FRAME: TAX-5506| enzyme, the intermediates may not be released from the enzyme active site and are instead efficiently sequentially metabolized to form GA4 |CITS:[11943776]|. The following two steps are catalyzed by a gibberellin 1,2-desaturase and a gibberellin 13-hydroxylase to produce GA7 and finally GA3, respectively. The main (but not only) electron donor for the monooxygenases of this pathway in Gibberellla is the NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase CPR-Gf |CITS:[15037621]|.

Summary: In mammals, |FRAME: CYS| is synthesized from |FRAME: MET|, an essential amino acid that must be provided in food |CITS: [3309559]|. More accurately, the cysteine sulfur is derived from methionine whereas the carbon and nitrogen of cysteine are derived from |FRAME: SER| |CITS: [3309559]|., L-Methionine is converted to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| by the actions of |FRAME: CPLX-5142| (EC 2.5.1.6), various S-adenosylmethionine methyltransferases, (EC 2.1.1.-) and |FRAME: CPLX-5161| (EC 3.3.1.1)., |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| occupies a branch point in methionine metabolism. In both the rat and human about half of the, homocysteine formed is irreversibily converted by transsulfuration to |FRAME: CYS|, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|, and |FRAME: AMMONIA| as desribed in this pathway, whereas the remainder is remethylated to |FRAME: MET| |CITS: [4593752][1128236]|., |FRAME: CPLX-5162| (EC 4.2.1.22) is a PLP-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| and |FRAME: SER| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Finally, |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE| is converted to |FRAME: CYS| by |FRAME: CPLX-5163| (EC 4.4.1.1).

Autoinducers are bacterial cell-cell communication messengers that allow bacteria to detect the density of neighboring cells. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., Many types of autoinducers exist, for example |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "N-acylhomoserine lactones"| (AHLs), |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "γ-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, |FRAME: Butenolides "γ-butenolides"|, |FRAME: Photopyrones photopyrones|, and |FRAME: Dialkylresorcinols dialkylresorcinols| (DARs). The signaling molecules bind to a dedicated receptor (e.g. LuxR, which binds AHL-type molecules), which in turn binds to the promoter/operator regions of the target genes/operons, resulting in changes in gene expression in response to the number of cells., The |FRAME: Dialkylresorcinols dialkylresorcinols| (DARs) were identified in the insect and human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-171440|. The DAR molecules are recongnized by the PauR receptor, which is similar to LuxR. PauR has been shown to control the transcription of the pcf operon, the expression of which results in cell clumping |CITS: [25550519]|., DARs and their biochemical precursors |FRAME: Cyclohexanediones cyclohexanediones| (CHDs) are synthesized by enzymes encoded by the darABC operon. Many bacterial species possess DarABC homologs, several of which pathogenic to animals, plants or humans (for example, various Neisseria strains). The specific subset of DARs and CHDs produced by an organism depends on the precursors used by the DarB enzyme, which are derived from two fatty acids.

|FRAME: CPD-4841 Dipicolinate| is a small polar molecule that accumulates to high concentrations in bacterial endospores (up to 25% of spore core dry weight) |CITS: [13058860]|, and is thought to play a role in spore heat resistance, or the maintenance of heat resistance |CITS: [13622720]|., The biosynthetic pathway has been studied in |FRAME: TAX-1423| and shown to largely overlap with early stages of |FRAME: LYS| biosynthesis. The pathway starts with DapG, one of several isozymes of |FRAME: EC-2.7.2.4|, found in |FRAME: TAX-1423|. The next enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.11|, produces |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|., Synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-4841| by extracts of sporulating cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1404| provided with |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| and pyruvate has been reported already in 1966, although the identity of the enzymes involved was not known at the time |CITS: [4958818]|. , A mutant defficient in dipicolinate biosynthesis, named dpa-1, has been characterized and its phenotype suggested that the mutation is located in a dipicolinate synthase enzyme |CITS: [108357]|. A 1981 paper placed the mutation at a locus that was named spoVF |CITS: [Piggot81]|. The spoVF locus of |FRAME: TAX-1423| was cloned and sequenced and found to comprise two coordinately regulated genes, which were named |FRAME: G-5066| and |FRAME: G-5067|. When the genes were expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562| the recombinant host produced |FRAME: CPD-4841| |CITS:[8345520]|., At the time the |FRAME: CPLX-4381| was described (1993), it was thought that the DapA enzyme, which participates in |FRAME: LYS| biosynthesis, produces |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDRODIPICOLINATE| from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| |CITS:[8345520]|, and this was believed to be the substrate for dipicolinate synthase. However, in 2010 it was found that DapA produces |FRAME: CPD-14443| rather than |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDRODIPICOLINATE| |CITS: [20503968]|. Thus it appeared that the true substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-4381| was not |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDRODIPICOLINATE| as originally presumed., The later part of the pathway was studied in 2018, and it was found that |FRAME: CPLX-4381| acts directly on the product of DapA, |FRAME: CPD-14443|. It was also confirmed that that |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.8| (DapB) and its product |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| are not involved in |FRAME: CPD-4841| production |CITS: [29792931]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD0-1112| is a deoxysugar that functions as a building block of the glycan component of the lipopolysaccharide present in ECA, the enterobacterial common antigen, and of the O-antigens of many bacterial species |CITS: [11114506][14670712]|. |FRAME: L-rhamnose| is also a component of the plant cell wall pectic polysaccharides |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan type I"| and |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan type II"| and is present in diverse plant secondary metabolites including anthocyanins, flavonoids and triterpenoids. |FRAME: L-rhamnose| has also been observed in archaebacteria. For example, it is the terminal saccharide of the tetrasaccharide attached to the surface (S)-layer glycoprotein Asn-498 of the halophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2246| |CITS: [22029420][24194539][24831810]|., Some bacteria such as the actinomycete |FRAME: TAX-60894| also utilize |FRAME: CPD0-1112| as a component of secondary metabolites (see |FRAME: PWY-7100| for an example) |CITS: [11544225 ]| |CITS: [19126547]|., Like most deoxysugars, |FRAME: CPD0-1112| is synthesized in the activated form of a nucleotide sugar - |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE|. However, at least in some plants, such as mung bean (|FRAME: TAX-157791|), both |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| and |FRAME: UDP-L-RHAMNOSE| act as sugar donors for the rhamnosylation of flavonoids |CITS: [13864832 ]|., Biosynthesis starts with |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is activated by |FRAME: TTP| and converted to |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| in two steps. The first enzyme of the pathway, RmlA (RfbA) (|FRAME: EC-2.7.7.24 "EC 2.7.7.24"|), catalyzes the transfer of a thymidylmonophosphate nucleotide to |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS: [11053865]|. The second enzyme, RmlB (|FRAME: EC-4.2.1.46 "EC 4.2.1.46"|), catalyzes the oxidation of the C4 hydroxyl group of the sugar, followed by dehydration |CITS: [10666612][11243820]|. These two steps are common in the synthesis of many modified sugars used for O-antigen synthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-7317|)., |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| is then converted to |FRAME:DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-MANNOSE| by the action of  RmlC (|FRAME: EC-5.1.3.13 "EC 5.1.3.13"|) |CITS: [10089454][10802738]|. In most organisms this enzyme only participates in |FRAME: CPD0-1112| production, although in some streptomyces species it also participates in synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15496| (see |FRAME: PWY-7301|) |CITS: [15752721]|., The final enzyme of this pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.133|, reduces the carbon at the 4th position, resulting in |FRAME: CPD0-1112| |CITS: [10666586]|., The pathway is ubiquitous and highly conserved in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. It is also found in plants, fungi, and lower eukaryotes |CITS: [27009306]|. The last two enzymatic activities (epimerase and reductase) are performed in plants by one bifunctional enzyme, NRS/ER |CITS: [15020741]|.

Summary: |FRAME: ACETALD "Acetaldehyde"| is released by plants into the atmosphere after a wide variety of stresses. Acetaldehyde is a potent antibiotic and its emission from damaged tissue may help prevent infections |CITS: [12381119]| and activate the expression of plant defense genes |CITS: [ADEGE98]|. Enhanced acetaldehyde emissions have been observed following mechanical wounding, desiccation, freezethaw events, herbivore attack, ozone fumigation, high light, high temperature, and many other biotic and abiotic stresses., Since acetaldehyde is reactive in the atmosphere, its emisions is of interest to atmospheric chemists, who are not able to account for large amounts of biogenic |FRAME: ACETALD| |CITS: [19538397]|., Two models that explain the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ACETALD| have been proposed. According to the model depicted here, which is related to light-dark transition, acetaldehyde is produced as a correction for imbalance in the cytosolic and mitochondrial |FRAME: PYRUVATE| concentrations. This pathway premises on the hypothesis that the |FRAME: ACETALD| is synthesized in the leaf itself by the action of tissue localized |FRAME: MONOMER-15096|, which is usually present in the leaf veins and petioles |CITS: [19698964]|.

Summary: Please note: This pathway does not represent a single organism. Rather, it is a super-pathway, assembled from many pathways found in a variety of organisms, whose purpose is to provide an overview, of the metabolic capabilities of the ecosystem, pertaining to degradation of taurine., |FRAME: TAURINE "Taurine"| (2-aminoethanesulfonate), a natural occuring amino acid analogue of |FRAME: B-ALANINE|, plays several important roles in mammals and is essential to newborns of many species., The main functions of taurine in mammals include bile acid conjugation, detoxification, osmoregulation,, membrane stabilization, and regulation of intracellular |FRAME: CA+2| homeostasis. While plants or animals cannot degrade taurine, several species of bacteria and fungi are capable of doing that. For example,, |FRAME: ORG-5927| can grow on taurine as the sole source of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and energy |CITS: [113035]|. , Some anaerobic bacteria can use taurine for respiration as either an electron acceptor (eg. |FRAME: ORG-5878|) or an electron donor (eg. |FRAME:TAX-75697| NKNTAU, |FRAME: ORG-5923|, and |FRAME:TAX-82367| NKNCYSA). Others can use it as a fermentative substrate (eg. |FRAME: ORG-5898|) |CITS: [12471498][9297467]|., The different species often utilize different pathways, resulting in conversion of taurine into different sulfur compounds. For example: |FRAME: ORG-5878| converts taurine to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| |CITS: [11082195]|, which is cleaved to |FRAME: SO3| |CITS: [11160104]|, and eventually converted to sulfide by a sulfite reductase |CITS: [9143131]|. , A. defragrans NKNTAU |CITS: [9202468]|, |FRAME: ORG-5923| (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), and, P. pantotrophus NKNCYSA (as reported in |CITS: [12471498]|), all convert taurine to sulfate (additional products are ammonia and CO2), while |FRAME: ORG-5898| converts taurine to thiosulfate, ammonia and acetate |CITS: [9297467]|., Taurine degradation is known to be initiated by at least three different types of reactions: transamination, which, appears to be the most widespread |CITS: [113035][5058441][5012173][629994]|, oxidation |CITS: [5551654]|,, and oxygenation |CITS: [9287300]|. In the first two cases sulfoacetaldehyde is an intermediate, whereas in the third, case taurine is converted to sulfite and |FRAME: CPD-1772| |CITS: [9287300]|., Two aminotransferases involved in taurine dissimilation have been described, |FRAME: CPLX-2561| in |FRAME: ORG-5927| and |FRAME: ORG-5878| |CITS: [113035][11082195]| and |FRAME: MONOMER-2966| in |FRAME:ORG-5857| |CITS: [5058441][5012173][629994]|. Cook and Denger |CITS: [12471498]| speculated that the physiological role of taurine:α-ketoglutarate aminotransferase in |FRAME:ORG-5857| is for transamination of |FRAME: B-ALANINE| and not taurine, since the enzyme is induced by β-alanine and not taurine. , |FRAME: CPLX-2561 "Taurine:pyruvate aminotransferase"| transfers the amino group from taurine to |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|. |FRAME: CPLX-7180 "Alanine dehydrogenase"| (EC 1.4.1.1) catalyzes the oxidative deamination of alanine to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, regenerating the amino-group acceptor pyruvate, and releasing ammonium. Alanine dehydrogenase from |FRAME: ORG-5878| was purified and characterized |CITS: [11041346]|., It should be noted that the taurine:pyruvate aminotransferase has been found in both aerobic (|FRAME: ORG-5927|) and unaerobic (|FRAME: ORG-5878|) organisms.

Summary: Some non-enteric bacteria, such as the soil bacteria |FRAME:TAX-354|, |FRAME: TAX-382 "Sinorhizobium meliloti (previously known as Rhizobium meliloti)"|, |FRAME: TAX-304 "Pelomonas saccharophila (previously known as Pseudomonas saccharophila)"| and |FRAME:TAX-294|, degrade D-galactose via the De Ley-Doudoroff pathway. The initial reactions of this pathway convert D-galactose to D-galactonate, as shown in the pathway link to MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GALDEG-PWY|. In the pathway shown here, D-galactonate is further degraded to D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate by dehydration, phosphorylation, and aldol cleavage., Direct utilization of D-galactonate via the pathway shown here has been shown to occur in nonpathogenic mycobacteria, |FRAME: TAX-83333|, and archaea |CITS: [7287628][211976][15474024]|. Nonpathogenic mycobacteria such as |FRAME: ORG-5916| grown on galactonate showed galactonate dehydratase, 2-dehydro 3-deoxygalactokinase (2-keto-3-deoxy-galactonate kinase), and 2-oxo-3-deoxygalactonate 6-phosphate aldolase (6-phospho-2-keto-3-deoxy-galactonate aldolase) activities in cell-free extracts |CITS: [7287628]|., D-galactonate can serve as the sole source of carbon and energy for |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [324806]|. The initial step in the degradation of D-galactonate is dehydration to 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-galactonate by |FRAME: GALACTONATE-DEHYDRATASE-MONOMER|. Subsequent phosphorylation by |FRAME: DEHYDDEOXGALACTKIN-MONOMER| and aldol cleavage by |FRAME: DEHYDDEOXPHOSGALACT-ALDOL-MONOMER| produce pyruvate and, D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, which enter central metabolism. Reviewed in Mandrand-Berthelot, M.-A., Condemine G., and Hugouvieux-Cotte-Pattat, N., EcoSal Module 3.4.2 |CITS: [ecosal]|.

General Background, The antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-15417|, |FRAME: CPD-15421|, and |FRAME: CPD-15504| (known as the aminocoumarin antibiotics) bind type II topoisomerases, including DNA gyrase, with an extremely high affinity, with equilibrium dissociation constants in the 10 nM range |CITS: [8231802]|. They compete with ATP for binding to the B subunit of DNA gyrase and thus inhibit the ATP-dependent DNA supercoiling catalysed by gyrase., The three antibiotics, which are produced by different microorganisms (|FRAME: TAX-2893586|, |FRAME: TAX-149682| and |FRAME: TAX-68264|, respectively), share several characteristics., All three contain a 7-hydroxy-2-aminocoumarin core (ring B). The phenolic 7-hydroxyl group of the bicyclic aminocoumarin scaffold is attached to an |FRAME: CPD-15426| sugar moiety (ring C), while the 2-amino group is ligated to a prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit (in |FRAME: CPD-15417| and |FRAME: CPD-15421|) or to a methylpyrroledicarboxylic acid that links two aminocoumarin moieties (in |FRAME: CPD-15504|) (ring A). The noviosyl sugar is then methylated at the 4-OH position and acylated at the 3-OH position to produce the mature, active antibiotic. |FRAME: CPD-15421 Clorobiocin| and |FRAME: CPD-15504| are both decorated at the 3 position of ring C by a 5-methylpyrrole-2-carboxyl moiety, whereas the corresponding modification in |FRAME: CPD-15417| is a carbamoyl group |CITS: [16868863]|., , The pharmacophore of these antibiotics is the decorated noviosyl sugar, which is presented by the planar aminocoumarin to the ATP binding site of the GyrB subunit of gyrase to interdict DNA replication |CITS: [8635474][9144789]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-15417 Novobiocin| is known to be produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2893586 Streptomyces caeruleus (previously known as Streptomyces spheroides and Streptomyces niveus)"|., The novobiocin biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2893586| NCIB 11891 was identified by using a dNDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase gene fragments as probes, and cloned in its entirety |CITS: [10770754]|. Sequencing of the region revealed the presence of 23 putative open reading frames, including a novobiocin-resistant gyrB gene. Inactivation of the |FRAME: G-16080| gene (encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-18087|) abolished novobiocin production. A part of the cluster was cloned into |FRAME: TAX-457428|, and the transformed strain was shown to produce |FRAME: CPD-15415| |CITS: [10770754]|., The pathway can be divided into 4 parts: the synthesis of the aminocoumarin core, the noviose sugar, and the prenylated hydroxybenzoate unit, and the final decoration of the assembled product., The aminocoumarin core is synthesized from |FRAME: TYR|, which has to be bound to the |FRAME: MONOMER-18084| (see |FRAME: PWY-7304|). That protein contains two domains - an adenylation (A) domain and a thiolation (T) domain, similat to initiation modules in nonribosomal peptide synthetase assembly lines. The A domain activates |FRAME: TYR| to tyrosine-AMP and then covalently tethers the aminoacyl moiety to the thiol of a phosphopantetheine prosthetic group in the T domain |CITS: [11325587]|. All subsequent modifications leading to formation of the aminocoumarin core occur on this covalently tethered entity., The enzyme-bound tyrosine is first hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-15492| and then oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-15507| |CITS: [16171397]|. A 2-hydroxylation is believed to take place as the next step, although the enzyme that introduces this 2-hydroxy group is still unknown. A final lactonization results in the release of the aminocoumarin core from the NovH protein., In a parallel route the prenylated 4-hydroxybenzoate moiety |FRAME: CPD-15423| is formed from |FRAME: PREPHENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-4211| by the action of three enzymes |CITS: [19557032][12777382]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7303|). This compound is then transferred to the aminocoumarin core by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-18056| (|FRAME: G-16051|) |CITS:[10801869]|, followed by methylation to |FRAME: CPD-15415|, catalyzed by a methyltransferase encoded by |FRAME: G-16050| |CITS: [16274243]|., The third route comprises five enzymes that form |FRAME: CPD-15496| from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS: [15752721]|. The sugar is then attached to |FRAME: CPD-15415| by |FRAME: MONOMER-18054| (|FRAME: G-16049|) |CITS: [12680772]| (|FRAME: PWY-7301|)., The final portion of the pathway consists of methylation and carbamoylation of positions 4 and 3 (respectively) of the demethylnoviosyl sugar, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-16048| and |FRAME: G-16047| genes, resulting in the final product |FRAME: CPD-15417| |CITS: [14694473]|.

|FRAME: CPD-19461 "Cyclobis-(1→6)-α-nigerosyl"| is a cyclic glucotetraose with alternate α(1→6)- and α(1→3)-glucosidic linkages, produced by several bacterial species during the degradation of complex glycans., The compound was first described from |FRAME: TAX-1245|, in which it was formed by the hydrolysis of |FRAME: Alternans alternan| |CITS: [8001579][8001580]|. It was later reported that in |FRAME: TAX-1459| it is synthesized from |FRAME: MALTOTETRAOSE| |CITS: [12400677][12092816]|. Similar enzymes were reported from a Bacillus sp. |CITS: [14553982]| and an |FRAME: TAX-1665| strain |CITS: [15618624]|., |FRAME: CPD-19461 "Cyclobis-(1→6)-α-nigerosyl"| is produced extracellularly during the degradation of complex glycans such as starch by the combined action of two enzymes. The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.24|, transfers α-(1→6)-glucosyl groups to the nonreducing terminal glucose unit of α-(1→4)-glucans, producing α-isomaltosyl-α-(1→4)-glucans. , The second enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.387| (IMT), acts on the products, catalyzing the α-(1→3) transfer of the α-isomaltosyl moiety of one substrate to another, resulting in α-isomaltosyl-(1→3)-α-isomaltosyl-α-(1→4)-glucans formation. In addition, IMT catalyzes the intramolecular cyclization of the product, eventually generating |FRAME: CPD-19461| |CITS:[12092816][14553982]|., Once formed, the cyclic tetrasaccharide is imported into the cell, where it is degraded |CITS: [27302067]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7828|).

General Background, Polythioesters (PTEs) are microbially-synthesized, non-biodegradable polymers containing sulfur in the thioester linkages of the backbone |CITS: [15762657]|. They accumulate as hydrophobic inclusions in the cytoplasm of bacterial cells, similarly to |FRAME: Polyhydroxyalkanoates "polyhydroxyalkanoic acids"| (PHAs) |CITS: [15468206]|., PHAs and PTEs are industrially and scientifically interesting materials because they possess some unique characteristics regarding their biodegradability, microstructure, thermal behaviour and diverse mechanical properties, and because many of them can be produced from nonpetrochemical resources, PTE heteropolymers were first detected in |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [11160796]|. That organism naturally accumulates PHAs at levels of up to more than 90% of the cell dry matter. When given |FRAME: CPD-7673|, |FRAME: CPD-16592|, |FRAME: CPD-16591|, |FRAME: CPD-16587| or |FRAME: CPD-16586| (in addition to a second compound that serves as a carbon and energy source) its unspecific |FRAME: CPLX-7357| produces various PTE heteropolymers., While PTE polymers are structural analogs of common cell metabolites, only few bacteria are able to degrade them |CITS: [16738107][19001372]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-16586 "3,3'-Dithiodipropionate"| (DTDP) is an organic disulfide and a precursor for the synthesis of polythioesters (PTEs) in bacteria |CITS: [12725926]|. |FRAME: TAX-1247726| is a β proteobacterium that was isolated due to its ability to utilize |FRAME: CPD-16586| as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [16738107]|. , A pathway for the degradation of DTDP in this organism was constructed based on the characterization of multiple transposon mutants that lost the ability to grow with DTDP as the sole source of carbon and energy. It has been shown that the first step in the pathway is the reductive cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-16586| into two molecules |FRAME: CPD-7673|, an apparently side activity of |FRAME: EC-1.8.1.4|, the E3 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase multi-enzyme complex of this bacterium |CITS: [20833784]|., |FRAME: CPD-7673 "3-Mercaptopropionate"| is oxygenated to |FRAME: CPD-16584| by a nonheme Fe2+-dependent dioxygenase homologous to |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.20| |CITS: [18456849]|. |FRAME: CPD-16584| is activated by coenzyme A in a secondary activity catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8842|, a TCA cycle enzyme |CITS: [21515777]|. In the last step of this pathway, a dedicated sulfinase enzyme cleaves |FRAME: CPD-16582| to the common metabolic intermediate |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, liberating the sulfur as |FRAME: SO3| |CITS:[23354747]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Tetracyclines tetracycline| antibiotics, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1948 |CITS: [18112227]|, are one of the most widely used classes of antibiotics in agriculture, aquaculture, and medicine. They have a broad antimicrobial spectrum, can be administered orally, and have a low cost. Following widespread use, tetracycline resistance mechanisms emerged and continue to create a need for new derivatives that are active against resistant bacterial strains. Semisynthesis has led to second and third generation tetracycline derivatives with enhanced antibiotic activity and pharmacological properties., The original tetracyclines are natural polyketides produced by actinomycete bacteria. They are characterized by their tetracyclic ring structure, a richly substituted A ring, and a heavily oxidized periphery that includes a C11, C12, and C11a keto-enol configuration, which let them bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit, interfering with the binding of aminoacylated tRNA to the A-site of the 30S subunit and halting protein synthesis |CITS: [11163189][11381101]|., |FRAME: CPD-19255 Oxytetracycline|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-1927|, was the second tetracycline compound to be discovered |CITS: [15400447]|, and its biosynthesis is the best studied among the tetracyclines. Early knowledge about the pathway was obtained through a series of blocked mutants and substrate feeding experiments, revealing the nature of several key intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-19273| and |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE| |CITS: [McCormick62][McCormick63a][McCormick63b][14289339][5641578]|. Later work using 13C-labeled acetate revealed the polyketide origin of the tetracycline backbone, and supported the idea of |FRAME: CPD-17870| as the origin of the C-2 amide |CITS: [Thomas83a][Thomas83b]|., In 1989 it was shown that all of the genes required for |FRAME: CPD-19255| synthesis were located within a a single DNA segment on the |FRAME: TAX-1927| chromosome |CITS: [2914874]|. This was followed by the complete sequencing of the gene clusters encoding |FRAME: CPD-19258| |CITS: [Ryan99]| and |FRAME: CPD-19255| biosynthesis |CITS: [8163168][Hunter02][16597959]|., Following the sequencing, the function of all of the involved genes has been shown through either direct isolation and characterization, genetic knockouts |CITS: [10551844][16148009]|, or expression in other Streptomyces strains |CITS: [16597959][17125237][17631493][17625867][18422316]|., About This Pathway, The first steps of tetracycline biosynthesis are catalyzed by a minimal polyketide synthase (PKS). Initiation involves an amide-containing starter unit (either |FRAME: CPD-17870|, as shown here, or malonamyl-ACP) |CITS: [Thomas83b][10551844][16148009]|. Following the initiation, the PKS catalyzes the iterative condensation of 8 malonyl-CoA molecules to yield the poly-β-ketone backbone of tetracycline. Throughout the proccess, the nascent chain is attached to the |FRAME: OxyC "OxyC acyl-carrier protein"|. The oxygen attached to the C-9 carbon of the nonaketide is then reduced by a dehydrogenase., Two cyclases/dehydratases, encoded by |FRAME: G-44634| and |FRAME: G-44635|, bring about the formation of |FRAME: CPD-19275|, the first intermediate that contains the four rings |CITS: [17631493]|. The biochemical basis of the A ring cyclization is not well understood. While some data indicates that it may happen spontaneously |CITS: [17631493]|, it may also be catalyzed by the product of |FRAME: G-44637| |CITS: [16597959]|., A set of five genes encode the enzymes that are involved in the next set of modifications, generating |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE|. They include the |FRAME: G-44636| and |FRAME: G-44641| methyltransferases, |FRAME: G-44638| and |FRAME: G-44639| monooxygenases, and |FRAME: G-44640| aminotransferase |CITS: [18422316]|., The last two enzymes in the pathway are a monooxygenase encoded by |FRAME: G-44642| and an F420-dependent dehydrogenase encoded by |FRAME: G-44643|. OxyS catalyzes two successive monooxygenation reactions. First it catalyzes the stereospecific hydroxylation of |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE| at C6. If the released product is captured by OxyR, it is reduced to |FRAME: CPD0-1414|. However, if the released product is recaptured by OxyS, it performs an additional hydroxylation at C5, producing |FRAME: CPD-19268|, which, following the action of OxyR, becomes |FRAME: CPD-19255| |CITS: [23621493]|.

General Background, Amaranthin belongs to and is the eponym for a major subgroup of betacyanins , (see |FRAME:PWY-5399|) that have mostly been identified in the amaranth family. Only betacyanins contain , a glucose moiety that may be further furnished with other molecules such as malonylate and hydroxycinnamic , acids. Amaranthin (betanidin 5-O-β-glucuronosylglucoside) is a derivative of cyclo-DOPA-5-O-glucoside, , an intermediate of the betacyanin biosynthesis that has glucuronic acid attached to the glucose moiety |CITS: [12620337]| , |CITS: [16247652]|., About This Pathway, The observed diversity of betacyanin structures is due to the frequently observed , acylation and glucosylation of the aglycone betanidin or its precursor cyclo-DOPA. The 5-O-glucosylation , of cyclo-DOPA is carried out by UDPG:cyclo-DOPA 5-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS: [15695438]| which , constitutes the immediate precursor for the biosynthesis of amaranthin., The glucosylated cyclo-DOPA is further metabolized by a rather specific UDP-glucuronic acid: cyclo-DOPA 5-glucoside glucuronosyltransferase , that adds glucuronic acid to the structure thus forming amaranthin. The enzyme has been shown not to , accept betanidin glucoside indicating that the glucuronic acid is indeed introduced to the cyclo-DOPA-5-O-glucoside , and before the condensation with betalamic acid takes place |CITS: [16247652]|., The last step in this biosynthesis concerns the further configuration with hydroxylcinnamic acids that leads , to the respective compounds celosianin I (4-coumaroylamaranthin) and/or celosianin II (feruloylamaranthin). , This enzyme, i.e. 1-O-hydroxycinnamoyl-β-glucose: amaranthin O-hydroxycinnamoyl transferase , has been found specific for amaranthin and did not catalyze betanidin or its 6-O-glucoside gomphrenin I , indicating the importance of the overall structure and glucuronic acid for that reaction |CITS: [Bokern92]|.

Summary: General Background, Neomycins are a family of broad-spectrum highly toxic antibiotics produced by |FRAME: TAX-1906|. They were discovered in 1949 by Waksman and Lechevalier (Waksman later received the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physiology and medicine) |CITS: [17782716]|., Neomycin usually exists as a complex composed of two stereoisomers, |FRAME: CPD-14142| and |FRAME: CPD-14141|, which are the two active components. A third component, |FRAME: CPD-14137 "neomycin A"|, which is a degradation product, is present in small quantities., Neomycin was originally used as a treatment for tuberculosis, but serious side effects soon became apparent, including ototoxicity |CITS: [8170691]|, which sometimes developed to complete loss of hearing, and nephrotoxicity. Thus systemic use of neomycin is limited, and the most common mode of use is via topical application |CITS: [6224608]|., About This Pathway, The early parts of the neomycin biosynthesis are similar to those of related antibiotics - for discussion please see the pathways |FRAME: PWY-7014| and |FRAME: PWY-7015|. The enzymes that are unique to neomycin biosynthesis are those catalyzing the last five steps, starting with |FRAME: CPD-14143|. , The |FRAME: G-15047|-encoded glycosyltransferase adds an acetyl-glucosaminyl moiety, resulting in the four-ring structure of neomycin. The acetate residue is removed by a dual-function deacetylase (encoded by |FRAME: G-15045|), and the C-6''' position of the the glucosamine moiety is aminated by the successive action of an oxidase (|FRAME:G-15024|) and an aminotransferase (|FRAME: G-15025|), resulting in |FRAME: CPD-14141|., The last step described here is the epimerization reaction at C-5''' of |FRAME: CPD-14141| to |FRAME: CPD-14142|. However, at this time neither the timing of the epimerization nor the identity of the responsible enzyme are known.

Summary: Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. It is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles. It is biosynthesized as protoheme, but different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., The main difference between this protoheme biosynthetic pathway and the one shown at |FRAME: HEME-BIOSYNTHESIS-II| is the presence of the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.98.3|, which catalyzes the transition from |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN| without the need for molecular oxygen. In addition, |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.4|, which under aerobic conditions catalyzes the oxidation of |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN| to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| using molecular oxygen, is replaced under anaerobic conditions with |FRAME: EC-1.3.5.3|, which uses a quinone instead of molecular oxygen., |FRAME: EC-1.3.98.3|, is found in many bacteria, but does not appear to be present in archaea or eukarya (the only reference for its presence in a eukaryote is in the organism |FRAME: TAX-5911|, but this finding is based on sequence analysis alone, and has not been verified biochemically)., Important branch points within this pathway lead to biosynthesis of other important compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|), |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|), heme D biosynthesis, and bacteriochlorophyll (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|)., This topic has been reviewed in |CITS: [13680202], [12177321], [16093570]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis, (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|),, and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is, highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for, a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes, that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase, enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal, dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, This pathway is different from the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5459| and |FRAME:PWY-5458| in that, |FRAME:CPD-358| and |FRAME:D-LACTATE| are involved, rather than the L-specific isomers., Methylglyoxal reductase enzymes that are specific for the D-form of lactaldehyde have been purified from, rat liver |CITS: [14323585]| and goat liver |CITS: [6386056]|. Both enzymes were specific for NADH, (although the goat liver enzyme would accept NADPH, resulting in lower activity)., The rat enzyme was isolated as catalyzing the reverse reaction (the oxidation of D-lactaldehyde, to methylglyoxal), but that reaction was shown to be reversible., While the rest of this pathway has not been characterized well, the presence of the enzymes required, to metabolize |FRAME:CPD-358| to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| via |FRAME:D-LACTATE| in mammalian, cells is well documented |CITS: [12616643][11955284]|. Some literature suggests that |FRAME:CPD-8891|, is also a product of |FRAME:CPD-358| metabolism |CITS: [14203169]|.

Summary: Fluorescent pseudomonads such as |FRAME: TAX-303| can catabolize |FRAME: LYS| and other amino acids as a sole carbon and nitrogen source, giving them the ability to grow in the rhizosphere of plants where amino acids are part of the root exudates. These soil bacteria are believed to promote the growth and health of crop plants (in |CITS: [16237033] [15150230] [11679348]|., |FRAME: TAX-303| can catabolize |FRAME: LYS| via the |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| (δ-aminovalerate) pathway to |FRAME: GLUTARATE|. In this pathway, L-lysine is transported into the cell by basic amino acid transport systems |CITS: [5019949]|. It is oxidatively decarboxylated to |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANAMIDE| (δ-aminovaleramide), which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| (δ-aminovalerate) and ammonia. The conversion of 5-aminopentanoate to glutarate involves gene products of the davDT operon (in |CITS: [16237033]|). , Activation of glutarate to |FRAME: GLUTARYL-COA| by an as yet uncharacterized reaction(s) and further metabolism of glutaryl-CoA to carbon dioxide and acetyl-CoA have been demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-294| (in |CITS: [14257627]|)., Some |FRAME: TAX-303| strains also catabolize |FRAME: CPD-219| via a separate, pipecolate pathway (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5283|). This pathway involves a lysine racemase that converts L-lysine to D-lysine, which is then converted to cyclic, six-carbon intermediates |CITS: [5128165]| and in |CITS: [15561717] [16237033 ] [914858]|. It is also known as the α-aminoadipate (AMA) pathway, and some of the enzymes, as well as a transporter, may be encoded on the OCT plasmid |CITS: [8234494]| and in |CITS: [16237033]|. The cyclic intermediate substrates Δ1-piperideine-2-carboxylate and Δ1-piperideine-6-carboxylate exist in equilibrium with their open chain forms, α-keto-ε-aminoadipate and α-aminoadipate δ-semialdehyde (also named 2-aminoadipate-6-semialdehyde), respectively |CITS: [1909881] [4285660] [Rodwell71]|., L-lysine catabolism in |FRAME:TAX-286| varies as to species and strain. |FRAME: TAX-287| does not use the δ-aminovalerate pathway. It was proposed to catabolizes L-lysine via decarboxylation to |FRAME: CADAVERINE| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY0-461|) (in |CITS: [16237033]|).

|FRAME: RICININE "Ricinine"| is a cyano-pyridone alkaloid produced by some plants. It was first identified in the leaves and the pericarp of the fruits of the toxic plant castor bean (|FRAME: TAX-3988|) |CITS:[14916779][14365610][1041877]| (hence the name), but it is also produced by other plants including |FRAME: TAX-316701| |CITS: [22708684]|, |FRAME: TAX-454931|, |FRAME: TAX-13216|, |FRAME: TAX-4097| and other plant species belonging to the Solanaceae family |CITS: [Bullangpoti11]|., In low doses ricinine acts as a central nervous system stimulant, and in higher doses it is lethal. The therapeutic index of ricinine is of the order of 200 |CITS:[14165547][10418776][10764909]|., |FRAME: RICININE "Ricinine"| should not be confused with |FRAME: CPLX-8883|, a toxic protein that is also produced by |FRAME: TAX-3988|, and is found in the seeds., Degradation of ricinine in the living plant has been known for a long time |CITS: [16657095]|. Experiments in castor bean plants have shown that ricinine concentration decreases in the leaves upon aging when grown in nitrogen depleted soil. Despite the fact that the degradation of ricinine in the plant has been under investigation for several decades, it is still not well understood. Ricinine is rapidly utilized by castor cotyledons grown in the dark and degradation of ricinine in cell-free system of young castor plants has been demonstrated |CITS: [5829600]|. However, no enzymes have been isolated., This pathway describes the bacterial hydrolysis of ricinine, as described in several bacterial strains of Pseudomonads |CITS: [16658229][5792659]|.

Summary: General Background, Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxystilbene) is the major polyphenol produced in a restricted number , of plant genera with |FRAME:TAX-3603|, |FRAME:TAX-3817| and Pinus as the prime representatives where it is formed as a general response to biotic and abiotic stress |CITS: [KINDL85]| |CITS: [SCHRODER90]| |CITS: [COMMUN03]|. Resveratrol has been recognized as a stilbene-type phytoalexin |CITS: [8421520]| |CITS: [9127691]| and represents a parent compound of a family of molecules such as glucosides (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-6958|) |CITS: [12697026]|, methylated derivatives (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-6959|) |CITS: [LANGCAKE79]| and oligomers (|FRAME:CPD-6961|, |FRAME:CPD-6960|) |CITS: [10552833]| with some of them expressing a higher fungicide toxicity than resveratrol itself. , The enzyme, stilbene synthase (STS), catalyzing the formation of either resveratrol from p-coumaryl-CoA and/or pinosylvin , (|FRAME:PWY-5045|) from cinnamoyl-CoA belongs to the plant specific polyketide synthases and is closely related to the , chalcone synthase(s) (CHS) |CITS: [2033084]| |CITS: [8083886]|. However, and although both enzymes use the same , condensation mechanism up to the tetraketide intermediate the ring closure is different leading to resveratrol via a aldol-type cyclization and decarboxylation (STS) and to naringenin chalcone by means of a Claisen-type cyclization (CHS) |CITS: [11432743]|., While chalcone synthase is present in most higher plants stilbene synthase has a much more restricted distribution in the , plant kingdom. It has been demonstrated that CHS and STS share a high similarity on the DNA and protein level |CITS: [2450022]| and that the enzyme(s) activity and specificity can be altered by just a few changes on the nucleotide level |CITS: [2200709]| |CITS: [2033084]| |CITS: [1400374]| |CITS: [8083886]|. In general, although polyketide synthases (PKSs) from flowering plants are very similar in their genetic structure they differ in their substrate specificity, the number of condensation cycles and ring closure mechanism when releasing the products |CITS:[18068110]|. , Stilbenes have been shown to possess a number of attributes that makes them a desirable compound class for genetic , engineering. The introduction of stilbene synthase to plant species devoid of this enzymes leads to the formation of resveratrol |CITS: [2103451]| and its 3-O-glucosid (piceid) |CITS: [KOBAYASHI00]| |CITS: [8421520]|, at the same time diminishing the content of the antinutritive sinapate esters in |FRAME:TAX-3708| |CITS: [16160820]| (|FRAME:PWY-3301|) or enhancing the tolerance against the grapevine mold Botrytis cinera |CITS: [11432907]|. The often observed glucosylation of resveratrol has been discussed as protective measure to prevent molecules from enzymic oxidation and therefore extending the half-life of these compounds in the cell |CITS: [12697026]|. The increase or introduction of resveratrol and its derivatives in plants is highly beneficial for the human diet since stilbenes have been demonstrated to have cardioprotective effects and anticancer properties |CITS: [15517885]| |CITS: [9127691]|., About This Pathway, Resveratrol is synthesized from p-coumaroyl-CoA and 3 molecules of malonyl-CoA. The enzyme stilbene (or resveratrol) synthase is not very specific and can also accept other CoA esters, aliphatic as well as aromatic ones as primers for poylyketide synthesis including substrates not being present in plants |CITS: [12620343]| |CITS: [11432743]|. It is therefore considered as one of the major generators of carbon skeleton diversity in natural products |CITS: [Schroder99]|., A common observation for this type of reactions is the occurrence of derailment products such as bis-noryangonin and , p-coumaroyltriacetic acid lactone. The formation of bis-noryangonin has been detected in most stilbene synthase catalyzed reactions |CITS: [12620343]| |CITS: [11432743]| and has been described as an artificial bye-product of the chalcone/stilbene synthase reaction after the addition of 2 malonyl-CoA |CITS: [1155951]|. However, the enzyme responsible for the catalysis of bisnoryangonin, i.e. styrylpyrone synthase has been partially purified from |FRAME:TAX-3258| and demonstrated to be different from chalcone oder stilbene synthase. The enzyme also accepts with lower efficiency caffeoyl-CoA which leads to the formation of hispidin (|FRAME:CPD-6989|) representing another styrylpyrone detected in this more primitive gametophyte |CITS: [BECKERT97]|., The formation of p-coumaroyltriacetic acid lactone is catalyzed by a novel enzyme distinct from stilbene synthase , |CITS: [10469148]|. The enzyme converts p-coumaryl-CoA and 3 molecules of malonyl-CoA to a novel pyrone, a linear , tetraketide which has been elongated but not cyclized, i.e. p-coumaroyltriacetate. The final cyclization to p-coumaryltriacetic acid lactone occurs spontaneously. , The polyketide type III synthase (PKS III) from Polygonum cuspidatum represents yet another type in this superfamily. In contrast to almost all PKS III proteins which have 1 intron in their gene structure |CITS:[Schroder97]|, the PKS III encoded by PKS2 from Polygonum has 3 introns. Moreover, the highly conserved |FRAME:PHE| 'gatekeeper' residues Phe215 and Phe265 in the active site of PKS IIIs were replaced by |FRAME:LEU| and |FRAME:CYS| in PKS2. Interestingly, the PKS2 encoded protein shows a different substrate specificity in dependence on the pH conditions, at physiological normal pH (6.5-8.5) the recombinant enzyme acted as p-coumaryltriacetic lactone synthase (CTAS) forming predominantly |FRAME:CPD-6954| and |FRAME:CPD-6955| (this pathway). In contrast to that, at a higher pH of 9.0-9.5, the PKS2 mainly catalyzed the formation of |FRAME:CPD-8636|| after only one round of condensation, hence acting as benzalacetone synthase (BAS) (see |FRAME:PWY-5393|) |CITS:[18998157]|.
