Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFA) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes., The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in these compounds. The icosanoids are derived from the 20-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (AA; 20:4n-6), |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| (EPA; 20:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-8120| (DGLA; 20:3n-6)., Additional fatty acids are also oxygenated to yield bioactive products, including the the 18-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| (LA; 18:2n-6) and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| (ALA; 18:3n-3) and the 22-carbon PUFAs |FRAME: CPD-13792 docosapentaenoate| (DPA; 22:5n-3) and |FRAME: CPD-10244 docosahexaenoate| (DHA; 22:6n-3). Strictly speaking, the derivatives of such acids should be named octadecanoids (for C18 compounds) and docosanoids (for 22 carbon compounds), though these compounds are often included in the icosanoids, making the definition broader than initially intended., In mammals icosanoids and related mediators mediate a wide array of critical biological processes such as ovulation, initiation of labor, bone metabolism, nerve growth and development, wound healing, kidney function, blood-vessel tone, blood coagulation, immune responses, and inflammation. Despite the great importance of these compounds, mammals are not able to form a double bond at either the n-3 or n-6 position of a fatty acyl chain and must rely entirely on dietary intake for PUFAs |CITS: [25486530]|., Three main enzyme families act on PUFAs. The first one is |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.1| (the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes), which possess dual cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activities and catalyze the oxidative cyclization of PUFAs to |FRAME: CPD-24676|, |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|, or |FRAME: CPD-26009| (depending on the starting PUFA), which are subsequently converted to a variety of prostanoids and thromboxanes by cell-specific terminal synthases and isomerases., The second family is the lipoxygenases (LOX), which catalyze the stereoselective insertion of molecular oxygen into PUFA with the formation of hydroperoxy fatty acids that are subsequently reduced to the corresponding hydroxy-fatty acids. The lipoxygenases are divided into three main form depneding on the carbon at which they oxygenate |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|: |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31|, and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|., The third family is cytochrome P450 monooxygenases that catalyzes the hydroxylation and/or epoxygenation of PUFAs. In addition to producing LOX-like monohydroxy fatty acids, CYP can add a hydroxyl moiety to the ω-carbons, of PUFA to form a unique class of omega-hydroxylated fatty acids (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-21314|). The epoxides that are formed by these enzymes can be hydrolyzed to the corresponding dihydroxyfatty acids by |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.10| (sEH).

General Background, Dicarboxylic acids such as |FRAME: ADIPATE| (C6), |FRAME: CPD0-1264| (C8), and |FRAME: CPD-3623| (C10) are not common in nature. |FRAME: ADIPATE Adipate| has only been described as a biosynthetic product of sugar beet and sugar cane (the biosynthetic pathway in these plants is still unknown) but is produced as a metabolic intermediate in the biodegradation pathways of cyclic alkanes, cyclic alcohols, and long chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acids |CITS: [3136163][12021788][22824738]|., Dicarboxylic acids, and particularly adipate, are used in the chemical manufacturing industry, mostly for the production of nylon. Adipate monomers are condensed with hexamethylene diamine, forming |FRAME: Nylon-6|, the most common form of nylon. Other uses for adipate include the production of polyurethane, formation of plasticizers and lubricant components, and as a flavorant and gelling aid in the food industry. Most of the adipate in commercial processes is produced from petrochemicals, specifically by oxidation of KA oil (|FRAME: CYCLOHEXANOL| and |FRAME: CYCLOHEXANONE|) catalyzed by nitric acid |CITS: [11529791]|., About This Pathway, Several bacterial strains have been shown to degrade dicarboxylic acids via a β-oxidation pathway |CITS: [11571189][15758219]|. A gene cluster responsible for the degradation of dicarboxylic acids was found in |FRAME: TAX-62977| and named dca for dicarboxylic acid utilization |CITS: [11571189]|. Studies with |FRAME: TAX-381666|, which can grow with |FRAME: ADIPATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1264|, and |FRAME: CPD-3623| as its sole carbon source, have also shown that some of the enzymes that participate in |FRAME: ADIPATE| degradation are different from those that participate in the β-oxidation of fatty acids in this organism |CITS: [34731045]|., |FRAME: TAX-381666| has a particularly large number of homologous genes encoding β-oxidation enzymes. The operon, which was unfortunately named pca (the pca operon in other organisms was named for protocatechuate utilization) contains the genes |FRAME: G-107723|, |FRAME: G-107719|, and |FRAME: G-107720|, which encode |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.174|, and |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.5|. Summary: |FRAME:CPD-14536 Geodin| and its precursors (|FRAME:CPD-14537|, |FRAME:SULOCHRIN|, |FRAME:QUESTIN| and |FRAME:CPD-8215|) have been frequently isolated from various fungi |CITS: [4207788][16320762]| but are probably not limited to fungi. |FRAME:CPD-8512 Emodin| and other anthraquinoids are widely spread in nature and occur in Fungi imperfecti (Deuteromycota), Basidiomycetes, lichens and higher plants |CITS:[Thompson71]|. , |FRAME:CPD-14536 Geodin| has been reported to enhance fibrinolytic activity |CITS:[10819297]| and to stimulate, together with |FRAME:CPD-14537| and |FRAME:SULOCHRIN|, the uptake of glucose by fat cells |CITS:[16320762]|., Starting with |FRAME: CPD-8215|, the first step in the pathway is O-methylation to |FRAME:QUESTIN|, followed by the cleavage of the anthraquinone ring to form |FRAME:DESMETHYLSULOCHRIN| |CITS: [1444712][3182756]|., Following methylation by an as-yet uncharacterized enzyme, the next step is two chlorination reactions, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-21294| |CITS: [24009710]|. Summary: |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it accumulates at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant |CITS: [9736747]|., Many organisms are able to catabolize |FRAME: BETAINE|, using it as a sole source for both carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [6406829][3290197]|., The degradation of |FRAME: BETAINE|, as well as its potential precursor, |FRAME: CHOLINE|, has been proposed to exist as a mechanism for osmoregulation in |FRAME:TAX-382| and other organisms. When the bacteria grow at inhibitory osmolarity the enzyme activities that lead to |FRAME: BETAINE| degradation decrease, while the enzyme activities that convert |FRAME: CHOLINE| to |FRAME: BETAINE| either remain constant or increase. In this way a high concentration of |FRAME: BETAINE| can be maintained in osmotically stressed cells |CITS: [Bernard86][3290197]|., The degradation of |FRAME: BETAINE| via this pathway proceeds by sequential demethylation |CITS: [Bernard86][3290197]|. The first methyl group is removed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.5|, producing |FRAME: DIMETHYL-GLYCINE| (DMG)., The second methyl group is removed by |FRAME: EC-1.5.3.10|, forming N-methylglycine, or |FRAME: SARCOSINE|, and the third methyl is removed by |FRAME: EC-1.5.3.1| (or in some organisms, |FRAME: EC-1.5.8.3|), producing |FRAME: GLY|., Dimethylglycine oxidase and sarcosine oxidase are bifunctional enzymes that can bind |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| (THF). In the presence of THF the enzymes transfer the single carbon unit to THF, forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N| and thus avoiding the formation of toxic |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, which is formed in the absence of |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|. Glycine and methylenetetrahydrofolate are the substrates of the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, which removes the single carbon unit from methylenetetrahydrofolate and transfers it to glycine, producing |FRAME: SER|. In some cases the gene encoding the serine hydroxymethyltransferase is adjacent to the genes encoding the sarcosine oxidase subunits |CITS: [ 9185627]|., Much work has been done with sarcosine oxidase from |FRAME:TAX-1716| sp. P-1 |CITS: [7692961][7543100][8611516][11330998]|, but similar enzymes from other organisms have also been characterized |CITS: [11422368]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: D-fucofuranose| is an uncommon sugar found in the surface polysaccharides of several bacterial species, including the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen| of |FRAME: ORG-6234| |CITS: [11269402][12681915][15231783]|. It is also a sugar moiety of |FRAME: CPD-12943|, the most important member of a group of anticancer drugs known as benzo[d]naphtho[1,2-b]pyran-6-one C-glycosides, which are produced by a variety of streptomycetes |CITS: [3624074][12822997][15453748]|., |FRAME: D-fucofuranose| is produced in |FRAME: ORG-6234| from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| in four steps, encoded by the four genes |FRAME: G-17639|, r|FRAME: G-17640|, |FRAME: G-17637| and|FRAME: G-17638|, which are located in its O antigen gene cluster |CITS: [15231783]|. RmlA and RmlB participate in the biosynthesis of many modified sugars and have been well characterized in many bacteria. Fcf1 and Fcf2, on the other hand, are specific for D-fucofuranose biosynthesis., The |FRAME: G-17640|, |FRAME: G-17637| and |FRAME: G-17638| genes were cloned from |FRAME: ORG-6234| as His6-tagged constructs and overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-511693|. The recombinant proteins were purified and characterized, and analysis of the products produced in vitro confirmed the pathway that is described here |CITS: [19019146]|.

Summary: The enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.1.9| catalyzes the oxidation of |FRAME: FORMATE| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. In many organisms this is a detoxification mechanism to remove |FRAME: FORMATE|., In methylotrophic organisms this is the terminal enzymatic step in the metabolic conversion of C1 compounds to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Formate dehydrogenase (FDH) activity has been detected in most methylotrophs, and several FDHs have been purified from them. , Many organisms contain multiple FDHs. For example, |FRAME: TAX-272630| possesses three different FDHs. None of these is essential for growth on |FRAME: METOH| in this organism, since |FRAME: FORMATE| can also be used for biosynthesis through the reversible tetrahydrofolate pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-1722|) and the serine cycle. However, a triple mutant, lacking any FDH activity, is not able to grow on |FRAME: FORMATE|, confirming that |FRAME: FORMATE| oxidation to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| is the necessary energy-generating step during growth on |FRAME: FORMATE| |CITS: [14679220]|., An |FRAME: CPLX-1241| also exists (|FRAME: EC-1.17.1.10|). It is not found in methylotrophs, and usually catalyzes the, reaction in the opposite direction, forming |FRAME: FORMATE| from |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|.

Summary: General Background, Phosphonates and phosphinates are natural products that are of interest as enzyme inhibitors due to their stability and ability to mimic carboxylates and/or phosphate esters. These latter compounds are found in a variety of metabolic reactions. Phosphonates (see |FRAME: Organophosphonates|) contain a single carbon-phosphorus bond, whereas phosphinates (see |FRAME: Phosphinates|) contain either two carbon-phosphorus bonds, or one carbon-phosphorus bond and one hydrogen-phosphorus bond (reviewed in |CITS: [23870698]|)., Pathways for the biosynthesis of several phosphonates and phosphinates have been elucidated including those for the antibiotics |FRAME: CPD0-1113| and |FRAME: CPD-12974|, and the herbicide |FRAME: CPD-10013| (bialaphos) (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5757|, |FRAME: PWY-6682| and |FRAME: PWY-6322|). Several of the initial steps for the biosynthesis of the potential antimalarial and anti-tuberculosis agent |FRAME: CPD-15961| were studied in |FRAME: TAX-359131| by |CITS: [18721747]| and later steps in the biosynthesis of this compound and its hydroxylated derivative |FRAME: CPD-15962| were elucidated by |CITS: [20142041]| as shown here. These two compounds were originally described by |CITS: [6768704][6768705]|., |FRAME: CPD-15961| and the related phosphonate |FRAME: CPD0-441| both inhibit |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.267| in the nonmevalonate pathway of isoprenoid biosynthesis (see |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|). This pathway is utilized by some bacteria, plants and protists including the malarial parasite |FRAME: TAX-5833|. The pathway is not present in mammals. The presence of gene dxrB encoding this enzyme near the |FRAME: CPD-15961| gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-359131| may be related to self-resistance (|CITS: [18721747]| and reviewed in |CITS: [23870698]|., About This Pathway, In initial studies the |FRAME: CPD-15961| biosynthetic gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-359131| was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1916|. The production of |FRAME: CPD-15961| was confirmed and the products of genes frbD and frbC were purified and characterized. In subsequent work the |FRAME: CPD-15961| biosynthetic pathway was reconstituted in E. coli and the late steps were verified by whole cell feeding experiments and assay of purified enzymes |CITS: [20142041]|., The first reaction of this pathway is shared among all known phosphonate biosynthetic pathways. It involves the reversible interconversion of |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: CPD-235| by phosphoenolpyruvate mutase. Although the isomerization equilibrium greatly favors |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| formation, subsequent reactions drive the pathway forward., In other known phosphonate biosynthetic pathways the second step involves an irreversible decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-235| to |FRAME: CPD-551|. However the |FRAME: CPD-15961| biosynthetic gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-359131| does not contain a homolog of such a decarboxylase. Instead, FrbC, which is a homolog of homocitrate synthase, catalyzes the addition of an acetate anion equivalent to the ketone group of |FRAME: CPD-235| in an essentially irreversible reaction. |FRAME: CPD-235 "3-Phosphonopyruvate"| is a structural analog of |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| (|CITS: [20142041]| and reviewed in |CITS: [23870698]|)., The next two reactions involve the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-15963| to |FRAME: CPD-15965|, an analog of |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|. Three putative ORFs frbA, frbB and frbE were suggested to participate in these reactions and are related to genes encoding |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| enzymes. FrbA is a homolog of aconitate hydratase, and FrbB and FrbE are both homologs of isocitrate dehydrogenase. An as yet unidentified enzyme would transaminate |FRAME: CPD-15965| to |FRAME: CPD-12608|. An analogous series of reactions occurs in the |FRAME: PWY-6322| pathway in which |FRAME: 3-HYDROHYDROXYPHOSPHORYLPYRUVATE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-10011| |CITS: [18721747][20142041]|., The enzymes of the remainder of the pathway have been cloned, heterologously expressed and characterized |CITS: [20142041]|. FrbH is a bifunctional enzyme. Its nucleotide transferase domain ligates |FRAME: CMP| to the phosphonate group and the |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|-binding domain facilitates decarboxylation. FrbG catalyzes a flavin-dependent N-hydroxylation. FrbF catalyzes N-acetylation in the presence of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. The |FRAME: CMP| group can be released by FrbI (or other nucleotide hydrolases). Finally, FrbJ can oxidatively decarboxylate |FRAME: CPD-15961| to form another antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-15962|. It was noted that FrbI and FrbJ are not essential for heterologous production of |FRAME: CPD-15961| in E. coli |CITS: [20142041]|.

|FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|). The β-oxidation of saturated fatty acids is a straightforward process which requires the participation of three enzymes, i.e. acyl-CoA oxidase (POX1), the multifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase (FOX2) and the thiolase (POT1). At the end of the process stands a saturated fatty acid shortened by 2 carbon units (|FRAME:ACETYL-COA|) which is further metabolized in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-5690|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291| and |FRAME:PWY-7307|). , By employing auxiliary enzymes in addition to the classic enzymes of fatty acid β-oxidation in peroxisomes of |FRAME:TAX-4932| alternative processing routes are provided for unsaturated fatty acids which would otherwise form an metabolic block in the β-oxidative break-down |CITS:[10709656]|. The intermediate |FRAME:CPD0-1162| can take different metabolic directions (compare |FRAME:PWY-7291|), one of which is forming |FRAME:CPD0-1158| (this pathway) which is catalyzed by Δ3,Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) |CITS:[9837886] [9813046]|. |FRAME:CPD0-1158| represents a compound which cannot be metabolized via β-oxidation and must be chemically modified for further degradation |CITS:[19830908]|. Two possible metabolic directions have been described in the literature for mammalians (reductase-dependent) |CITS:[8300563] [9417087]| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7307|) and |FRAME:TAX-562| (thioesterase-dependent) |CITS:[14707139]| as minor pathways. However, analogous enzymes have also been detected in yeast which indicates the probable existence of those pathways which may contribute to the degradation of |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD| in addition to the main isomerase-dependent pathway (|FRAME:PWY-7288|). , The thioesterase-dependent pathway (this pathway) requires the catalytic activity of additionally auxiliary enzymes, i.e. Δ3,Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) and acyl-CoA thioesterase (TES1). The yeast enzyme encoded by TES1 has been shown to catalyze the cleavage of |FRAME:CO-A| from |FRAME:CPD0-1158| to yield |FRAME:CPD0-1159| which overcomes the metabolic blockage of the β-oxidation recalcitrant and inhibiting |FRAME:CPD0-1158| |CITS:[10092594] [19830908]|.

Summary: In the aerobic respiratory chain formed by glycerol-3-phosphate (G-3-P) dehydrogenase and cytochrome bo oxidase the transfer of electrons from glycerol-3-phosphate to oxygen is coupled to the generation of a proton motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. Purified G-3-P dehydrogenase supports the active accumulation of proline into reconstituted membrane vesicles |CITS: [340460]|. The H+/e- ratio for GlpD is not known but it is not expected to operate as a proton pump |CITS: [9230919]|; cytochrome bo oxidase has a H+/e- ratio of 2 |CITS: [2544445]|.

Summary: General Background, C-glycosides are widespread in the plant kingdom and have been shown to occur in at least 20 families of angiosperms |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. Moreover, they have also been found in insects and microbes |CITS:[17404902]| and are attributed to a broad range of biological activities. They act as antioxidants |CITS:[Ramarathnam89]| |CITS:[1824129]|, show antimicrobial activity |CITS:[16651765]|, facilitate mycorrhizal symbioses |CITS:[12026171]|, screen and protect from UV |CITS:[Les90]| and are valuable agents in preventing lipoprotein oxidation |CITS:[Kim2005]| and cancer development |CITS:[11172671]| in humans. , C-glycosideflavonoids represent the largest group of C-glycosides and are especially dominant in cereals such as maize, wheat and rice |CITS:[17404902]| |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. The special attachment of the aglycone directly to the C1 of the pyranose ring of a sugar confers high structural stability to the C-glycosides which even withstand acidic treatment., |FRAME: CPD-9588 Maysin| is a C-glucosyl flavone that was first detected in corn silk in 1979 |CITS: [Waiss79]|. Silks are the elongated stigmas of the female flower that grow underneath the corn husk and wrap corn ears. The compound was found to provide natural resistance against larvae of the corn earworm (|FRAME: TAX-7113|), a major pest of corn |CITS: [Waiss79][Elliger80][Wiseman92]|., |FRAME: CPD-9588 Maysin| is also UV-absorbing, and maize crops growing at high-altitudes were found to accumulate it, as well as |FRAME: CPD-9587|, in silks and leaves in response to increased UVB radiation levels |CITS: [Casati05]| , About This Pathway, Early efforts involving quantitative trait locus mapping (QTL) identified specific genomic regions responsible for regulating the accumulation of maysin. A region in the short arm of chromosome 1 that harbors the pericarp color1 (P1) locus accounted for more than half of the phenotypic variance |CITS: [11607699]|. Chemical analysis of various mutants indicated that |FRAME: 5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE|, |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN|, and |FRAME: CPD-9587| are intermediates in the pathway |CITS: [15220389]|. This suggested the need for two enzymatic steps to convert |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN| to |FRAME: CPD-9588|: incorporation of rhamnose, and dehydration of rhamnosylisoorientin into maysin. The authors proposed that these enzymes correspond to the salmon silks loci. The original salmon silks mutant was identified at a Nebraska fair in 1909, and has been corrolated with two loci, sm1 (on the long arm of chromosome 6) and sm2, on the long arm of chromosome 2 |CITS: [Anderson21][15220389]|., A 2016 study has identified and cloned the |FRAME: G-107636| and |FRAME: G-10478| genes, purified and biochemically characterized the enzymes, and completed our understanding of the maysin biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [27221383]|.

Summary: In the molluscan eye, the visual cells possess two kinds of photopigment systems. One is the |FRAME: Rhodopsins rhodopsin| system, which is localized in the outer segment of the visual cell (in the rhabdomal microvilli), and the other is the |FRAME: Retinochromes retinochrome| system, which is associated with the inner segment of the visual cells (mainly in the myeloid bodies)., The two photopigments are different from each other in the stereoisomeric form of their retinal chromophores; |FRAME: CPD-881| is bound to active rhodopsin, while |FRAME: RETINAL| is bound to active retinochrome. Upon absorption of a photon, the chromophores change to the other form, along with a conformational change in the proteins. Thus, |FRAME: Metarhodopsins-II metarhodopsin| (the form of rhodopsin generated by photon absorpsion) contains |FRAME: RETINAL| while |FRAME: Metaretinochromes metaretinochrome| contains |FRAME: CPD-881|. The function of retinochrome is believed to be the regeneration of |FRAME: CPD-881|, from |FRAME: RETINAL| produced by the rhodopsin photoreaction |CITS: [2626821][1541344]|., The molluscan retina lacks structures similar to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) found in the vertebrate retina (see |FRAME: PWY-6861|), and the mechanisms necessary for maintaining the photoreceptive function of the retina are contained within the visual cells. Since the rhodopsin in the rhabdomal microvilli is located too far away from the retinochrome in the myeloid bodies for them to come directly into contact, the retinal cofactor is transferred between the two systems by |FRAME: Retinaldehyde-binding-proteins| |CITS: [2626821]|., Most of our knowledge of the molluscan visual cycle comes from studies of the Japanese squid |FRAME: TAX-6637|. Both the |FRAME: MONOMER-17359| |CITS: [6036171][4512007][235007][7098865][7098918][2226795][8243675]| and the |FRAME: MONOMER-17360| |CITS: [3660660][2626821][1541344][8106428]| from this organism have been studied in detail. However, the enzyme were also reported from octopi, marine gastropods and other molluscs |CITS:[235007][8345366][11298362]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Phlegmacins Phlegmacins| are homodimeric dihydroanthracenone natural products featuring two |FRAME: CPD-27521| monomers unsymmetrically conjugated by 7,10'-coupling.Two atropisomers (A1 and B1) are produced by mushrooms such as |FRAME: TAX-36062| |CITS: [Steglich72]|, while the A2 and B2 atropisomers have been described from the tropical shrub |FRAME: TAX-948718| |CITS: [Takahashi77]|. This class of compounds was named after the mushroom subgenus |FRAME: TAX-2339270| |CITS: [4405264]|., In addition, phlegmacins were also reported from the ascomycetes |FRAME: ORG-57126| |CITS: [Wang14]| and |FRAME: ORG-57125| |CITS: [28457127]|. A 2022 study has identified the biosynthetic gene cluster of phlegmacins in, |FRAME: ORG-57125| |CITS: [35274920]|., Phlegmacin compounds possess a broad range of biological activities, including enzyme inhibitor |CITS: [28457127]|, antimalarial |CITS: [Gill03]|, anticancer |CITS: [Beattie11]|, and antibacterial |CITS: [23534483 ]|., About This Pathway, The mushroom |FRAME: TAX-36062| produces two atropisomers of |FRAME: Phlegmacins|, which possess a broad range of biological activities, including antifeedant, antimalarial, anticancer, and antibacterial |CITS: [4405264]|., The phlegmacin biosynthesis cluster of |FRAME: TAX-36062| contains genes encoding a polyketide synthase (PKS1) that produces |FRAME: CPD-23475| (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.336|), a methyltransferase that catalyzes methylation of |FRAME: CPD-23475| to its 6-O-methyl ether |FRAME: CPD-27521| (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.404|), and a phenol-coupling peroxidase that couples two molecules of |FRAME: CPD-27521| to form |FRAME: Phlegmacins| (|FRAME: EC-1.11.2.7|) |CITS: [38963262]|., In addition to PKS1 |FRAME: TAX-36062| was found to encode another non-reducing iterative type I polyketide synthase, PKS4, that is also able to catalyze the production of |FRAME: CPD-23475|. Unlike PKS1, PKS4 has both hepta- and octaketide synthase activity, and also produces the bicyclic heptaketide |FRAME: CPD-27853| (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.335|) |CITS: [35218274]|.

Summary: This superpathway starts with the initiation of fatty acids biosynthesis by generating |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs| from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME: HCO3| and |FRAME: ACP| protein. The product, acetoacetyl-[acp], feeds into the pathway of fatty acids elongation, which involves repetition of the same four enzymatic reactions. Each repetition constitutes one turn of a cycle that lengthens the chain of an acyl-[acp] molecule by two carbons. The products of multiple turns of this cycle are drawn off to become components of fatty acid-containing compounds such as phospholipids, lipid A, and lipoproteins. Such products include the saturated fatty acids |FRAME: DODECANOATE|, |FRAME: CPD-7836|, and |FRAME: PALMITATE| |CITS: [16561982]|., E. coli also contains unsaturated fatty acids, namely |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247|. These are formed by a pathway that branches off at the level of the 10-carbon intermediate |CITS: [14527277] [8246839]|. Once the 10-carbon unsaturated acyl-[acp] is formed, it is elongated by the same cycle., Of the four reactions involved in the cycle of fatty-acid elongation, two are catalyzed by more that one enzyme. These , function preferentially on substrates of different chain length. They also act differentially on saturated and unsaturated , substrates |CITS: [8910376]|. The first reaction in the sequence, the condensation reaction, is catalyzed by , three enzymes, FabB, FabF, and FabH. FabH initiates fatty-acid synthesis: it uses only acetyl-ACP as a substrate , (see Pathway: |FRAME: PWY-4381|) |CITS: [14523010]|. Only FabB catalyzes the extension of |FRAME: Cis-delta-3-decenoyl-ACPs| to |FRAME: Palmitoleoyl-ACPs|, and only FabF can catalyze the elongation of the later to |FRAME: CPD-9247| |CITS: [11566998]|. The activity of FabF and hence the fraction of fatty acids that are , unsaturated is modultated by temperature |CITS: [16561982]|. Thus the distribution of the flow of synthesis that proceeds to saturated , vs. unsaturated fatty acids is determined by the activities of FabA, FabB and growth temperature |CITS: [8910376]|.

Summary: General Background, Osmoprotectants or compatible solutes are small organic molecules with neutral charge and low toxicity that act as osmolytes and help organisms survive extreme osmotic stress. Most microorganisms capable of osmotic adaptation accumulate compatible solutes in response to increases in the levels of salts or sugars in the environment., |FRAME: CPD-9190| (GG) is a rather rare compatible solute that was first identified in the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-32049 "Synechococcus sp. PCC 7002 (referred to as Agmenellum quadruplicatum in the text)"| |CITS: [Kollman79]|. Following that initial discovery, GG was observed in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-39664| strain FDF-1 |CITS: [16348748][16348748]|, and in several bacteria, including a salt-sensitive mutant of the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-2746| |CITS: [10473374]|, in the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [15528516]|, and in the thermophilic and slightly halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-309805|, that belongs to the Aquificae class |CITS: [17189358]|., The role of GG as a compatible solute during osmotic stress has not been verified in most of these organisms, but has been demonstrated unequivocally in |FRAME: TAX-556| under nitrogen limiting conditions. When nitrogen concentration is high the organism synthesizes mostly other, nitrogen-containing compatible solutes (|FRAME:GLT| and |FRAME:GLN|). It has been suggested that GG may also accumulate in the other organisms during salt stress only under, nitrogen-limiting conditions |CITS: [15528516]|., Two pathways are known for the biosynthesis pf GG, a two-step pathway which is described here, and a single-step pathway described in |FRAME: PWY-6685|., About This Pathway, The two-step pathway for the synthesis of GG has been investigated in |FRAME: TAX-29291|, and found to be very similar to the pathway for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: 2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE|, a related compatible solute found in thermophilic organisms (see |FRAME: PWY-5656|) |CITS: [16428406]|. Both compounds are synthesized in two steps. In GG biosynthesis |FRAME: GDP-D-GLUCOSE| and |FRAME: G3P| are condensed by |FRAME: CPLX-7487|, forming, |FRAME: CPD-9189|, which is subsequently dephosphorylated to GG by |FRAME: MONOMER-13395|., Despite their similar functions, the enzymes catalyzing the first steps in the pathways for |FRAME: 2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE| and |FRAME: CPD-9190| share no sequence homology, and are specific for their respective substrate. On the other hand, the enzymes catalyzing the second steps of the pathways can accept both, |FRAME: ALPHA-D-MANNOSYL-3-PHOSPHOGLYCERATE| and |FRAME: CPD-9189|, indicating that these phosphatases recognize a common determinant in these substrates, probably the glycerylphosphate moiety.

General Background, Tungsten (W) and molybdenum (Mo) have equal atomic and ionic radii and similar electronegativity, and initially it was believed that tungsten only acts as an antagonist of molybdoenzymes. The first indications that tungsten might have a positive biological role were in the 1970s, when it was reported that tungstate stimulated the growth of certain acetate- and methane-producing microorganisms |CITS: [4147651][4154039][1132514][324989]|. However, the first naturally occurring tungstoenzyme was purified only in 1983, from the acetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1525| |CITS: [6822536]|. Another tungsten enzyme was purified from the same organism in 1989 |CITS: [2550230]|. In addition, a tungsten-dependent enzyme was purified from the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2261| |CITS: [2538471][2164004]|. Following this discovery, numerous tungsten-dependent enzymes were isolated from hyperthermophilic archaea, leading to the idea that W enzymes are more ancient than the Mo enzymes. Unlike the enzymes previously isolated from bacterial species, which could use either tungsten or molybdenum, many of the archaeal enzymes are specific for tungsten. In fact, some of these organisms do not have any molybdoenzymes |CITS: [ 8550411]|., Tungsten-containing enzymes are now known from a variety of organisms, including acetogens, methanogens, hyperthermophiles, acetylene-utilizing anaerobes, sulfate-reducing anaerobes, and some aerobic, methylotrophic organisms |CITS: [Girio92][7592321][7592385]|. However, unlike Mo-enzyme, W-enzymes have not been detected in eukaryotes. The tungsten enzymes fall into two families, exemplified by aldehyde:ferredoxin reductase (AOR family) and the formate dehydrogenases (FDH), respectively |CITS: [11952415]|., Study of "true W-enzymes", mainly isolated from hyperthermophilic archaea, showed that the tungsten is bound to a 6-substituted pterin (molybdopterin), similarly to molybdenum in Mo-enzymes. A main feature of tungsten coordination in the active site of W-enzymes is that the cofactor contains two molecules of molybdopterin, which are coordinated by four sulfur ligands |CITS: [9861725]|. It has been stated that all members of the AOR family contain the non-nucleotide form |FRAME: CPD-22998|, whereas the FDH type enzymes appear to contain the |FRAME: CPD-21374| |CITS: [11848842][10447686]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT) structure is produced from |FRAME: GTP| via |FRAME: PRECURSOR-Z| in three steps catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.22|, |FRAME: EC-4.6.1.17|, and |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.12| (see |FRAME: PWY-6823|)., In order to produce the |FRAME: CPD-22998|, |FRAME: CPD-4| is activated by ATP in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.75| |CITS: [18154309][24465852]|, followed by insertion of tunsten, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.10.1.M2|. The latter has not been studied as of 2020. However, homologs of the bacterial |FRAME: EG10153| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.10.1.1|, exist in W-enzyme-forming hyperthermophilic archaea such as |FRAME: TAX-2261|., Complementation of an |FRAME: TAX-562| Δ|FRAME: EG10153| mutant with the |FRAME: TAX-2261| |FRAME: G-80653| gene (coexpressed with the |FRAME: G-80654| gene) supported low activity of the |FRAME: CPD-15873|-requiring |FRAME: EC-1.9.6.1| (10.1% of the wild type activity). In addition, purified His-tagged MoeA2 protein also supported partial complementation in an in vitro assay of an |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.3|. , The low levels of complementation could be in part the result of conducting the assays at 37 °C, as required for the |FRAME: TAX-562| enzymes, which is well below the optimum temperature of 95 °C seen for most |FRAME: TAX-2261| enzymes. However, the authors interpreted the results as a demonstration that |FRAME: TAX-2261| |FRAME: G-80653| likely functions as a |FRAME: EG10153| homolog in tungsten cofactor synthesis in |FRAME: TAX-2261| |CITS: [Malotky03]|.

Anthocyanin biosynthesis is a crucial biochemical process involved in the flower development of many angiosperms. Flavonoid pigments provide the means to attract pollinators through bright colors |CITS:[Harborne66]| and/or certain color patterns |CITS:[11511673]| |CITS:[Eisner02]|. Research over the last decades on anthocyanin biosynthesis has led to the discovery of many genes involved in the pathway. Advanced gene technologies enabled molecular breeding of flower colors in many commercially valuable ornamental species such as carnation resulting in novel and intriguing colors and hues |CITS:[Yonekura-Sakakibara09]|., Anthocyanins are most often decorated with glucose or other sugar moieties at the 3-position (A-ring) and the 5- and 7-position of the C-ring. Among the most prominent anthocyanins in |FRAME:TAX-3570| (carnation) are cyclic 3,5-malyl anthocyanins (|FRAME:CPD-15294|, |FRAME:CPD-15295|) |CITS:[11140528]|. However, the 5-O-glucosylation had not yet been elucidated. Likewise in |FRAME:TAX-46246| the main anthocyanin, i.e. cyanodelphin, a tetra p-hydroxybenzoated anthocyanin |CITS:[Kondo91]| is glucosylated at both 3 and 7 position but the 7-O-glucosylation remained unresolved as well |CITS:[Davies09]|. The monocotyledone |FRAME:TAX-51501|, a popular ornamental plant because of the blue and white flower colors which also is frequently used as a traditional medicine in South Africa has become the object of major studies regarding relevant pharmacological properties |CITS:[18343601] [15907963]|. The two main anthocyanins are 3,7-glucosylated delphinidin coumaroyl glucoside linked to a variety of kaempferol glycosides |CITS:[10724183]|. , Despite the taxonomic distance between the species mentioned above, i.e. the dicotyledones carnation (Caryophyllacea) and delphinium (|FRAME:TAX-3440|) and the monocotyledone |FRAME:TAX-51426| (|FRAME:TAX-4668|) all species have glucosyltransferases that realize either the 5-O- or 7-O-glucosylation. Instead of the usual sugar donor |FRAME: CPD-12575| the glucosyltransferases utilize acyl-glucoses such as the benzoyl-glucose derivatives |FRAME:CPD-15006|, |FRAME:CPD-15283| and |FRAME:CPD-15281| and the hydroxycinnamoyl-glucose derivatives |FRAME:CPD-15281| and |FRAME:1-O-SINAPOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| as glucose donors |CITS:[20971893] [22048706] [22673029]|. The acyl-glucose dependent glucosyltransferases (AAGTs) belong in the glycosyl hydroxylase (GH) 1 family and show significant amino acid sequence identities across the taxonomic range indicating that the AAGTs evolved before the divergence of monocots and dicots. The AAGTs very position specifically (either A5 - AA5GT or A7 - AA7GT) glucosylate anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides such as |FRAME:CPD1F-766| (see |FRAME:PWY-7256|), |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-3-GLUCOSIDE-CMPD| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-7117| (see |FRAME:PWY-7260|). According to the structural properties, the AAGTs belong to the glycosyl hydroxylases, however their β-glucosidase activity is only 4 - 6% of the corresponding glucosyltransferase activity emphasizing a novel enzymatic property probably developed over the course of evolution of their host species |CITS:[20971893] [22048706] [22673029]|. Various genes in Arabidopsis thaliana have also been identified as candidates for acyl-dependent anthocyanin 5 and 7 glucosyltransferases but their molecular function remains to be shown experimentally |CITS:[Miyahara11]|.

Names: L-cysteine biosynthesis II (tRNA-dependent) // L-cysteinyl-tRNA<sup>cys</sup> biosynthesis via tRNA modification
Summary: Analysis of archaeal genomes has generally failed to show the presence of genes encoding any of the established, enzymes in the known eukaryotic and bacterial pathways for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|., The pathway for the biosynthesis of these amino acids in the extreme thermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2190|, has been studied using a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry stable isotope dilution method, and |FRAME: 3-P-SERINE| (Sep) was shown to be an important intermediate |CITS: [14642812]|. An archaeal Sep biosynthetic pathway was characterized and proven to provide a sufficient amount of Sep for serine, cystathionine and cysteine formation |CITS: [17071763]|., Biochemical studies and genetic analysis revealed that the organisms that miss these genes employ a tRNA-dependent pathway for providing |FRAME: Charged-CYS-tRNAs| for ribosomal translation as well as free cysteine biosynthesis |CITS: [15790858]|., This process couples protein synthesis with cysteine production and is mostly observed in a large subset of, the Euryarchaeota |CITS: [16380427]|., The tRNA-dependent pathway consists of two steps. In the first step the uncharged |FRAME: CYS-tRNAs| is aminoacylated with |FRAME: 3-P-SERINE| (Sep) by |FRAME: CPLX-7886| (SepRS), forming |FRAME: L-SEP-tRNACys|. , A second enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7887|, subsequently transforms the Sep moiety to tRNA-bound cysteine. The two enzymes were shown to form a stable binary complex that promotes conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: L-SEP-tRNACys| to |FRAME: Charged-CYS-tRNAs| and sequesters the intermediate from binding to elongation factor EF-1alpha or infiltrating into the ribosome |CITS: [18425141]|., While sulfide was shown to be a sufficient sulfur donor in vitro, the nature of the sulfur donor in vivo has not been investigated yet |CITS: [18252769]|., In many species, this indirect pathway coexists with the direct charging of |FRAME: CYS-tRNAs| with |FRAME:CYS|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: CYSS-MONOMER| (CysRS) |CITS: [16380427]|. It has been shown that in such organisms CysRS is not essential for viability |CITS: [11717392]|.

Names: ergosterol biosynthesis II // ergosterol biosynthesis II (Chlamydomonas) // ergosterol biosynthesis II (green algae)
Summary: |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL Ergosterol| is a major sterol found in green algae, including |FRAME: TAX-3055|, where it accounts for roughly 55% of the total sterol content found when analyzing whole cells or isolated flagella |CITS:[GEALT81]|. |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL Ergosterol| is typically found in plasma membranes where it may affect membrane flexibility and fluidity. It is unclear whether sterols also play signaling roles in green algae., The primary evidence for this pathway comes from radiotracer and metabolite-based experiments demonstrating that |FRAME: TAX-3055| synthesizes ergosterol via a Δ<sup>25(27)</sup>-olefin pathway |CITS: [22591742]| distinct from the Δ<sup>24(28)</sup>-olefin pathway found in yeast and other fungi |CITS: [346585] [2654239]|. Another notable difference between this pathway and the |FRAME: PWY-6075| pathway typically found in fungi is the use of |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL| rather than |FRAME: LANOSTEROL| as the primary backbone for |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| biosynthesis |CITS: [20333205][22591742]|. It is also interesting to note that while the isoprenoid precusors used for |FRAME: PWY-6075| in fungi originate from the |FRAME: PWY-922|, they are exclusively derived from the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| in Chlamydomonas and other green algae |CITS: [10584331][11289606]|., While this Δ<sup>25(27)</sup>-olefin pathway has only been studied in |FRAME: TAX-3055| to date, there is experimental evidence for some of the intermediate compounds existing in phylogenetically distinct members of the |FRAME: TAX-3041|, such as |FRAME: TAX-3111| |CITS: [NORTON91]|, indicating that this biosynthetic pathway may be present in other green algal species.

Names: steviol glucoside biosynthesis (rebaudioside A biosynthesis) // Stevia biosynthesis
Summary: Stevia leaf extract is a non-nutritive sweetener derived from the plant |FRAME: TAX-55670|, which contains multiple sweet-tasting compounds called steviol glycosides. The Stevia leaf extract is increasingly used worldwide as natural, low-calorie sweetener that substitutes for sucrose to counteract growing incidence of obesity and diabetes. The two main steviol glycosides are |FRAME:CPD-14504| and |FRAME:CPD-14506|. The former is about 300 times sweeter than sucrose |CITS:[18556105][Lemus-Mondaca12]|. Unlike alternative sweeteners such as |FRAME: CPD-5581|, |FRAME:CPD-14504| and |FRAME:CPD-14506| are thermostable, making them suitable for use in cooked foods |CITS:[ Lemus-Mondaca12]|., Stevia leaves were used by indigenous people in South America as both a food sweetener and medicine. Stevia became more popular following its introduction in Japan in the 1970s. It was initially banned from use as a sweetener in many countries including the United States, Europe, Australia, Canada, and other countries, due to gaps in required safety information. In 1995 tt was permitted for use in the US only as a dietary supplement. Following the establishment of safety, metabolism, and clinical data |CITS:[18556105][19427890]|, purified steviol glycosides were approved for the use as sweetener by the FDA and many other national food safety authorities starting in 2008. Approval in the European Union and Canada followed in 2011 and 2012, respectively. Stevia leaf extract compounds are specifically approved for diabetes patients |CITS:[22492420][18555575][14561506]|. , Steviol glucosides have also been reported to be effective in various in vitro anticancer tests acting as chemopreventive agents for chemical carcinogenesis |CITS:[19131254]| and offer therapeutic benefits through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory actions |CITS:[19000919]|. The steviol glucosides have been found to be efficient scavengers of reactive oxygen species (ROS) indicating their involvement in the antioxidant defense strategy of plants to thwart oxidative stress |CITS:[21043580]|. , All the compounds formed in this pathway are derivatives of |FRAME: CPD-14501| (see |FRAME:PWY-7070|), and are degraded by gut bacteria back into steviol following ingestion. Steviol itself is completely resistant to bacterial degradation |CITS: [14558786]|., All the compounds shown here have been detected in varying amounts in |FRAME: TAX-55670| |CITS:[21417451][20102764][Rajasekaran08]|. Three out of four UDP glucosyltransferases involved in the steviol glucoside biosynthesis have been isolated from EST collections and shown to regio-selectively glucosylate multiple steps in the pathway |CITS:[15610349][16667943][7646064]|. Recombinant UTG85C2 glucosylated the C-13 hydroxyl group catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-14501| to |FRAME:CPD-14502| |CITS:[15610349]| and was also capable of acting in tandem with an endogenous |FRAME:TAX-3701| enzyme to glucosylate |FRAME:CPD-14508|, forming |FRAME:CPD-14505| |CITS:[16786291]|. UTG74G1 acted on the C-19-hydroxyl of the C-4 carboxyl group, catalyzing the formation of the corresponding glucosyl esters. UTG74G1 exhibited multiple glucosylation activities towards |FRAME:CPD-14501|, forming |FRAME:CPD-14508| and |FRAME:CPD-14502| (resulting in |FRAME:CPD-14505| synthesis) and toward |FRAME:CPD-14503|, producing |FRAME:CPD-14504| |CITS:[15610349]|. , The last characterized UTG, UTG76G1, was shown to transfer glucose to the C-2' and C-3' of the 13-O-glucose and catalyzed the glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-14503| forming |FRAME:CPD-14507|, and |FRAME:CPD-14504| resulting in the production of |FRAME:CPD-14506|. The remaining fourth, and so far unidentified UGT is thought to be involved in the glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-14502| producing |FRAME:CPD-14503| and glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-14505|, which would form |FRAME:CPD-14504| |CITS:[15610349]|., The main route from |FRAME:CPD-14501| towards |FRAME:CPD-14506| based on the existing biochemical data has been proposed to be |FRAME:CPD-14501| to |FRAME:CPD-14502|, |FRAME:CPD-14503|, |FRAME:CPD-14504| and finally |FRAME:CPD-14506|. |FRAME:CPD-14503 Steviobioside| seems to be an common intermediate of two routes leading to |FRAME:CPD-14506|, one via |FRAME:CPD-14504| and the other having |FRAME:CPD-14507| as intermediate |CITS:[15610349]|. Based on the correlation of transcripts and steviol glucoside accumulation the entry reaction catalyzed by UTG85C2 has been proposed to be the rate-limiting step of the pathway |CITS:[21477883]|.

Names: polyhydroxydecanoate biosynthesis // medium chain length polyhydroxyalkanoate biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Polyhydroxyalkanoates Polyhydroxyalkanoates| (PHAs) are a class of bacterial storage compounds that accumulate inside cells in the form of inclusion bodies (granules) when carbon sources are plentyful. PHAs may accumulate to levels of up to 90% of cellular dry weight and can provide the bacterium with a source of carbon and energy during periods of nutritional deprivation. These polyesters are of industrial interest due to their biodegradability to water-soluble products, and their ability to be synthesized from renewable resources (in |CITS: [18706425]| and in |CITS: [11457823]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19270094]|). There is evidence that archaea may also synthesize PHAs (in |CITS: [19648370]|)., PHAs are generally classified as short-chain-length (monomers contain 3-5 carbon atoms) or medium-chain-length (monomers contain 6-14 carbon atoms) (in |CITS: [11425728] [19925642]|). The chain length may vary depending on organism and culture conditions. Many 3-hydroxyacids have been identified as constituents of PHA polymers and the theoretical number of copolymers is high. |FRAME: Poly-Hydroxybutyrate Poly-3-hydroxybutanoate| (PHB) is the most abundant storage compound in bacteria (see pathway |FRAME: PWY1-3|). PHB and its copolymer with |FRAME: CPD-12765| have been commercialized. Considerable progress has also been made in elucidating the molecular architecture of intracellular PHA granules and identifying them as complex subcellular organelles (in |CITS: [16511073]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19270094]|)., Enzymes that degrade PHAs can be of two types, those that are secreted and act extracellularly, or those that act intracellularly. They may be specific for either short-chain-length PHAs (|FRAME: EC-3.1.1.75|) or medium-chain-length PHAs (|FRAME: EC-3.1.1.76|) and catalyze their hydrolysis to monomeric or oligomeric hydroxyalkanoates (see |FRAME: MONOMER-15977|, |FRAME: CPLX-8171| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15978|). Intracellular enzymes degrade PHAs for direct utilization, while extracellularly secreted enzymes may act on PHAs that are released from dead bacterial cells (in |CITS: [16511073]| and in |CITS: [18706425]|)., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of medium-chain-length polyhydroxyalkanoates (monomers contain 6-14 carbon atoms) has been extensively studied in members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-286|. The biosynthesis of a polymer with monomers containing 10 carbon atoms is shown here, based on the substrate preference of the PhaC1 enzyme in |FRAME: ORG-6169| |CITS: [19925642]|. In some pseudomonads the PhaG transacylase mediates the production of |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| from |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP|, establishing a metabolic link between de novo fatty acid biosynthesis and PHA biosynthesis |CITS: [11425728] [9727022] [10788390] [10713430]|. As shown in the pathway link |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP| can be produced during fatty acid de novo biosynthesis. |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| produced during fatty acid β-oxidation can also be an input to the pathway in some organisms such as |FRAME: ORG-6169| |CITS: [19267463]| as shown in the pathway link. The |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP| is a substrate for RhlA in |FRAME: PWY-6648| as shown in the pathway link, while the |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| is a substrate for medium-chain-length polyhydroxyalkanoate synthases., The key enzyme in this pathway is the granule-associated PHA polymerase (PHA synthase). These enzymes have been identified in many bacterial genomes. They catalyze the stereoselective, covalent linkage of |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| thioesters in a transesterification reaction with concomitant release of |FRAME: CO-A| (in |CITS: [19925642]|). All PHA polymerases share a conserved active site |FRAME: CYS| residue to which the growing polymer is attached. This residue along with conserved |FRAME: HIS| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| residues constitute a putative catalytic triad, similar to esterases. The mechanism of PHA polymerase initiation, elongation and termination of the polymer has not yet been elucidated and no structural data are available. However, evidence suggests that these enzymes may dimerize when substrate is provided, with one subunit attached to the growing polymer chain and the other binding a new substrate molecule (reviewed in |CITS: [19275166] [19270094]| and in detail in |CITS: [17263145]|)., Four classes of synthases have been identified based on subunit composition and substrate specificity. Class I synthases use short-chain-length PHAs (see |FRAME: CPLX-7357|) and class II synthases use medium-chain-length PHAs (see |FRAME: MONOMER-16001|). Both class I and II consist of one type of subunit (PhaC) of 60-70 kDa. Class III and class IV synthases consist of two types of subunits (PhaC PhaE) or (PhaC PhaR) and prefer short-chain-length PHAs (in |CITS: [19925642]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19270094]|)., Studies have suggested that simultaneous accumulation and degradation of polyhydroxyalkanoates occurs, generating a potential futile cycle. An acyl-CoA synthetase associated with PHA granules has been identified that may convert PHA degradation products back into |FRAME: CO-A| thioesters. Other granule-associated structural and regulatory proteins may also be involved. Possible regulatory mechanisms have been proposed and data suggested that in |FRAME: ORG-6169| PHA metabolism is likely to be controlled by the ratios of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: CO-A|, and |FRAME: NADH| to |FRAME: NAD| which also regulate fatty acid oxidation |CITS: [19267463]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential micronutrient for most microorganisms. It is a cofactor required for growth and metabolism. However, it is present in the environment as relatively insoluble ferric oxyhydroxide complexes that are not readily bioavailable. Siderophores are high-affinity ferric iron (|FRAME: FE+3|) chelators secreted by microorganisms as a means to access this iron. Bacterial pathogens also utilize siderophores to scavenge tightly bound iron from their hosts. Secreted siderophores solubilize and bind ferric iron. The ferric iron-siderophore complex binds to cell surface receptors and is actively transported into the cell (in |CITS: [19482931]| and in |CITS: [19182782]|). In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: G1I0R-2609| gene of |FRAME: TAX-1280| is similar to plant NAS genes, which encode |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.43|. That enzyme is the key enzyme in the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-7231| family of |FRAME: Phytosiderophores phytosiderophores|, catalyzing the trimerization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| to form one molecule of |FRAME: CPD-463|. Even though CntL and NAS share only 12% sequence identity, structure prediction programs detected a structural homology of CntL with eukaryotic NAS and archaeal NAS-like enzymes, prompting a further study of CntL's activity |CITS: [27230378]|., The |FRAME: G1I0R-2609| gene, together with the |FRAME: G1I0R-2610| and |FRAME: G1I0R-2608| genes, with which it forms an operon, were found to encode enzymes that catalyze the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-21428|, a metallophore involved in the acquisition of nickel, copper, and cobalt |CITS: [27230378]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-21428| starts with |FRAME: HIS|, which is epimerized to |FRAME: CPD-12151| by |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.24|, encoded by the |FRAME: G1I0R-2610| gene. Next, a 2-aminobutanoyl moiety is transferred from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.152| (cntL). Summary: General Information: This superpathway links the conversion of fatty acids to carbohydrates. The conversion via glyoxylate cycle has been studied primarily in oil seed plants such as castor bean, peanut, sunflower, oilseed rape and the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana where lipids rather than carbohydrates are the major seed storage reserve. In this process fatty acids are converted to soluble carbohydrates, normally sucrose, which is subsequently translocated from lipid storage cells such as seed endosperm to growing seedlings. In some oilseed plants, such as Arabidopsis, which store lipids mainly in cotyledons of embryo instead of in endosperms, the conversion of lipids to sucrose for translocation is less significant. Some evidence suggests that stored lipids are involved in respiration by filling in the TCA cycle with intermediate products of the glyoxylate cycle |CITS:[11173291]|., At the onset of seed germination, lipids are broken down to fatty acids in the lipid bodies. The derived fatty acids then enter the glyoxysomes, which are specialized form of peroxisomes only present temporarily during seed germination. Within the glyoxysomes, fatty acids are broken down to Acetyl-CoA through |FRAME: PWY-5136 "fatty acid β-oxidation II (core pathway)"|. Acetyl-CoA then enters the |FRAME:GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|. The net result of the glyoxylate cycle is the conversion of two molecules of acetyl-CoA to one succinate molecule. Succinate is believed to diffuse out of the glyoxysome and is converted to malate in the mitochondrion by sharing some same reactions of the TCA cycle. In the cytosol, malate is further converted to oxaloacetate and enters the |FRAME:GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis| pathway to produce glucose and ultimately sucrose.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-28446| can ferment |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| via both the reductive and oxidative branches of the Stickland reasction. Both branches result in ATP synthesis |CITS: [ABB12-165]|. Both pathways begin with transamination of |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| by |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLT|. |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| is regenerated by NAD-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7238|, producing one equivalent of NADH., In the oxidative route |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.1|, in a reaction that reduces ferredoxin. Acetyl-CoA can then be used to generate ATP via |FRAME: ACETYL-P| and |FRAME: ACET|, as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1312|., The reductive branch of |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is described in |FRAME: PWY-8188|.

It is incorporated into skeletal muscles and appears to largely compete with |FRAME: CPD-10244| (22:6n-3) for incorporation into lipids |CITS: [17459159]|., The biosynthesis of the 4-desaturated docosanoid fatty acids |FRAME: CPD-17364| (22:5n-6) and  |FRAME: CPD-10244| (22:6n-3) is believed to proceed via a complex pathway requiring repeated use of the fatty acid desaturase encoded by the |FRAME: HS05918| gene to perform Δ6 desaturation on C24 fatty acids in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by 1 round of β-oxidation in the peroxisomes |CITS: [19202133]|., It should be noted that it has been reported that the |FRAME: HS05918| gene product can directly 4-desaturate |FRAME: CPD-17323| (22:4n-6) to |FRAME: CPD-17365| (22:5n-6) |CITS: [26065859]|, potentially resulting in a much shorter pathway similar to the one operating in lower eukaryotes (see |FRAME: PWY-7728|).

Names: vitamin K degradation // 4-menaquinone degradation // phylloquinone degradation
Summary: In contrast to other fat-soluble vitamins, dietary vitamin K is rapidly lost to the body resulting in comparatively low tissue stores. Plasma concentrations of |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| in healthy fasting people are of the order of only 0.5 nM. Tissue reserves are low as well - the median total liver pool of |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| measured in British adults was estimated at about 20 nmol. Menaquinone concnetration is higher, up to 200-300 nmol |CITS: [8785182]|. While the majority of vitamin K reserves in the liver comprise long chain forms (|FRAME: CPD-9718| through to |FRAME: CPD-9721|), extrahepatic tissues contain mainly |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| and/or |FRAME: CPD-9726|, which is formed from |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7998|) |CITS: [7947656][8785182][8632229]|., The main reason for the low concentration of vitamin K is that much of it is rapidly catabolized |CITS: [4617407]|. Both |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| and |FRAME: CPD-9726| are substrates for the cytochromes P-450 encoded by the |FRAME: HS02675| and CYP4F11 genes  |CITS: [19297519][23505319][24138531]|. The former was shown to catalyze three sequential hydroxylations, forming the hydroxy-, oxo-, and carboxy-forms of the quinones. The hydroxy form could also be metabolized to the carboxylate by microsomal NAD+-dependent alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases. Following the hydroxylation, the polyisoprenoid side chain is shortened to two major carboxylic acid aglycones with 7- and 5-carbon side chains, respectively. This process is assumed to be similar to fatty acid β-oxidation, with the substrates in their coenzyme A ester forms, although this has not been demonstrated., The final products, |FRAME: CPD-21315| and |FRAME: CPD-21316|, are excreted in bile and urine, mainly as glucuronides |CITS: [4617407][7306367][18841274]|.

General Background, In Gram-positive bacteria, the ε-amino group of L-lysine in the |FRAME: CPD-15384 "pentapeptide"| stem of peptidoglycan precursors is often replaced by amino acid chains of various lengths and compositions., During the cross-linking of the peptide stems of nascent chains of peptidoglycan these amino acids form cross bridges, between L-Lys3 of one glycan thread and D-Ala4 of another thread |CITS: [4568761]|., In enterococci, streptococci, and staphylococci, the enzymes that add the bridge amino acids are membrane-associated, and act on late peptidoglycan precursors that are already linked to the undecaprenyl-phosphate lipid carrier |CITS: [5218655]|., Two types of enzymes catalyze the addition of the cross-bridge amino acids. |FRAME: GLY| and L-amino acids are added by a special type of non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) that use charged aminoacyl tRNAs as substrates. D-amino acids, on the other hand, are added in tRNA-independent reactions |CITS: [4248526][4262567]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-1351| and |FRAME: TAX-1313| the bridge consists of two |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| residues (in |FRAME: TAX-1313| the first |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is sometimes substituted by |FRAME: SER|)., The two residues are added by two distinct enzymes. The genes encoding the enzymes are located in an operon, and have been named |FRAME: EF_RS12605| and |FRAME: EF_RS10265| in |FRAME: TAX-1351| |CITS: [12324463]| and murM and murN in |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [10759563]|., Inactivation of the operon in penicillin-resistant strains of |FRAME: TAX-1313| resulted in elimination of branched-structured muropeptides from the cell wall, complete loss of penicillin resistance, and an increased susceptibility to |FRAME: CPD0-1113|, |FRAME: CPD-2482|, |FRAME: CPD-12245|, and |FRAME: CPD-12301| |CITS:[10867238][11830670]|., When the |FRAME: EF_RS10265| gene was deleted from the |FRAME: TAX-1351| chromosome, the organism lost the ability to produce heptapeptide-type molecules. Somewhat unexpectedly the lack of complete side chains did nor interfere with efficient cross-linking. However, sensitivity to the antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-12294| grew 8-fold |CITS: [12324463]|.

Names: succinate to cytochrome bo oxidase electron transfer
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| aerobic respiratory chain formed by succinate dehydrogenase and cytochrome bo oxidase the transfer of electrons from succinate to cytochrome bo oxidase is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force (pmf) across the cytoplasmic membrane. Succinate dehydrogenase does not contribute to the generation of proton potential (see |CITS: [18930017]|); cytochrome bo oxidase contributes to the PMF |CITS: [7045115], [6308657], [6093862]| (H+/e-=2) through its action as a proton pump (H+/e-=1) |CITS: [2544445]| and through a redox loop mechanism (H+/e-=1) (|CITS: [1850294]| , Cytochrome bo oxidase is expressed when levels of oxygen are high |CITS: [6365921]| unlike the cytochrome bd oxidase which is expressed under oxygen-limiting conditions |CITS: [389237]|. The expression of succinate dehydrogenase is maximal during aerobic growth; repression under anaerobiosis is mediated by the global regulators ArcA and Fnr (reviewed in |CITS: [7855430]|). Electron transport from succinate to oxygen is dependent on the presence of ubiquinone (Q8) |CITS: [195602]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-3607 L-Glucose| does not occur naturally in higher organisms, and its production has been reported only rarely in microbes |CITS: [16233412]|. Several publications claimed that since it cannot be phosphorylated by hexokinase or glucokinase, it cannot be used as an energy source. However, there have been a few reports of bacterial |FRAME: CPD-3607| degradation., A paper from 1979 reported the discovery of an enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-28094| that could oxidize L-glucose in the presence of NAD+ |CITS: [40609]|. The enzyme, which was named D-threo-aldose dehydrogenase, could also oxidize L-xylose, D-arabinose and L-fucose., A more thorough study was conducted with |FRAME: TAX-1197861|, a soil bacterium isolated after enrichment with L-glucose |CITS: [23038265]|. The L-glucose degradation pathway in this organism could be divided into two parts. The first part includes only the first reaction, the oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-3607| to |FRAME: CPD-14804|. This reaction was catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-17722|, an enzyme that has a much higher (more than 10-fold) activity with |FRAME: CPD-8050| than with |FRAME: CPD-3607| and is encoded by a gene located in an inositol degradation cluster. Even though the main function of the enzyme is inositol degradation, it is clearly responsible also for L-glucose degradation, since inactivation of the gene abolished growth with L-glucose. Despite the high Km (59.7 mM) the enzyme maintained a reasonable activity with |FRAME: CPD-3607| (Kcat = 1040 min-1). The product of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-14804|, spontaneously hydrolyzes to |FRAME: CPD-14805|., The second part of the pathway is carried out by a group of enzymes that appear to be optimized for |FRAME: CPD-14805| degradation. The genes encoding these enzymes are located in a single cluster, and the enzymes appear to be specific for the intermediates generated from the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-14805|. The next two intermediates, |FRAME: CPD-14806| and |FRAME: CPD-14807|, rarely occur in nature and are only derived from the similarly rare |FRAME: CPD-14805|. The first intermediate that is not unique to this pathway is |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GALACTONATE|, which is also generated by the degradation of the much more common |FRAME: D-GALACTONATE| (see |FRAME: GALACTCAT-PWY|). |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GALACTONATE| is produced by the |FRAME: MONOMER-17725| enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15413| gene, and is degraded by the action of two more enzymes to the central metabolism intermediates |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GAP| |CITS: [23038265]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Tetracyclines tetracycline| antibiotics, originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1894| in 1948 |CITS: [18112227]|, are one of the most widely used classes of antibiotics in agriculture, aquaculture, and medicine. They have a broad antimicrobial spectrum, can be administered orally, and have a low cost. Following widespread use, tetracycline resistance mechanisms emerged and continue to create a need for new derivatives that are active against resistant bacterial strains. Semisynthesis has led to second and third generation tetracycline derivatives with enhanced antibiotic activity and pharmacological properties., The original tetracyclines are natural polyketides produced by actinomycete bacteria. They are characterized by their tetracyclic ring structure, a richly substituted A ring, and a heavily oxidized periphery that includes a C11, C12, and C11a keto-enol configuration, which let them bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit, interfering with the binding of aminoacylated tRNA to the A-site of the 30S subunit and halting protein synthesis |CITS: [11163189][11381101]|., |FRAME: CPD-19255 Oxytetracycline|, produced by |FRAME: TAX-1927|, was the second tetracycline compound to be discovered |CITS: [15400447]|, and its biosynthesis is the best studied among the tetracyclines. Early knowledge about the pathway was obtained through a series of blocked mutants and substrate feeding experiments, revealing the nature of several key intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-19273| and |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE| |CITS: [McCormick62][McCormick63a][McCormick63b][14289339][5641578]|. Later work using 13C-labeled acetate revealed the polyketide origin of the tetracycline backbone, and supported the idea of |FRAME: CPD-17870| as the origin of the C-2 amide |CITS: [Thomas83a][Thomas83b]|., In 1989 it was shown that all of the genes required for |FRAME: CPD-19255| synthesis were located within a a single DNA segment on the |FRAME: TAX-1927| chromosome |CITS: [2914874]|. This was followed by the complete sequencing of the gene clusters encoding |FRAME: CPD-19258| |CITS: [Ryan99]| and |FRAME: CPD-19255| biosynthesis |CITS: [8163168][Hunter02][16597959]|., Following the sequencing, the function of all of the involved genes has been shown through either direct isolation and characterization, genetic knockouts |CITS: [10551844][16148009]|, or expression in other Streptomyces strains |CITS: [16597959][17125237][17631493][17625867][18422316]|., About This Pathway, The first steps of tetracycline biosynthesis, up to |FRAME: CPD-19273|, are described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7811|., A set of four genes encode the enzymes that are involved in the next set of modifications, generating |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE|. They include the |FRAME: G-44638| and |FRAME: G-44639| monooxygenases, |FRAME: G-44640| aminotransferase, and |FRAME: G-44641| methyltransferase |CITS: [18422316]|., The last two enzymes in the pathway are a monooxygenase encoded by |FRAME: G-44642| and an F420-dependent dehydrogenase encoded by |FRAME: G-44643|. OxyS catalyzes two successive monooxygenation reactions. First it catalyzes the stereospecific hydroxylation of |FRAME: ANHYDROTETRACYCLINE| at C6. If the released product is captured by OxyR, it is reduced to |FRAME: CPD0-1414|. However, if the released product is recaptured by OxyS, it performs an additional hydroxylation at C5, producing |FRAME: CPD-19268|, which, following the action of OxyR, becomes |FRAME: CPD-19255| |CITS: [23621493]|.
