Summary: The first report about the occurrence of A-ring 6-substituted flavonols as characteristic traits for certain members of the daisy family (|FRAME:TAX-4210|) reaches back to 1941 when the structure of |FRAME:CPD-14907| extracted from Marigold (|FRAME:TAX-55843|) was published |CITS:[Rao41]|. Since then all compounds depicted in the pathway have been identified in various composites and their chemical structure elucidated |CITS:[Nair95]| |CITS:[15508135]| |CITS:[17654539]| |CITS:[Xu11]|., The flavonols of this pathway have a number of physiological properties which are of medicinal and nutraceutical importance. Flavonols extracted from |FRAME:TAX-13707| exhibited strong antibacterial activities |CITS:[Kiranmai12]| and |FRAME:CPD-14909| showed strong scavenging properties, inhibited lipoxygenases |CITS:[17708435]| and was also reported together with |FRAME:CPD-14907| to be a very effective antioxidant and stress inhibitor |CITS:[20336001]|. |FRAME:CPD-14866 Quercetagetin| and |FRAME:CPD-14907| influenced strongly the aldose reductase operating in the lens systems of rats indicating their potential for clinical applications |CITS:[1843126]|. It has also been pointed out that |FRAME:TAX-13707| and other composite possess nutraceutical and medicinal values that have been long recognized and employed in daily life |CITS:[Mlcek11]|. , Most interesting is the role these flavonols play in the reproductive biology of their native host plants. The so called 'yellow flavonols' which are typical for members of the |FRAME:TAX-4210| and |FRAME:TAX-3803| families |CITS:[Mishio06]| not only contribute the yellow color but also provide a pigmentation pattern which is known as honey guides. The physiological role of the honey guides is to provide a signpost system for directing insects towards the reproductive organs of a flower |CITS:[11511673]|. The yellow flavonols namely |FRAME:CPD-14866|, |FRAME:CPD-14909| and |FRAME:CPD-14911| are able to absorb UV and are mostly accumulating in the basal part of the petals |CITS:[5050486]|. For the human eye the petals are uniformly yellow but for the UV sensitive insects like honeybees this special distribution pattern of the yellow flavonols is received as an UV reflecting area (apical part of the petals) and a UV absorbing area (basal part of the petals) hence forming two concentric dichromatic circles, the so-called bull's eye. This bull's eye effect helps the insects in long-distance orientation and guide within the flower after landing |CITS:[Daumer58]| |CITS:[Eisner02]|. , The sequence of the pathway steps has been elucidated through kinetic data and substrate preferences obtained from in vitro experiments with crude enzymes from |FRAME:TAX-13707| and |FRAME:TAX-48209| species |CITS:[Halbwirth04]| |CITS:[19477473]|. According to the reported results the preferred route is from |FRAME:P-COUMAROYL-COA| via |FRAME:NARINGENIN-CMPD| and/or |FRAME:CPD-6994| (see |FRAME:PWY1F-FLAVSYN|) towards |FRAME:CPD-520| (see |FRAME:PWY-3101|). |FRAME:CPD-520 Quercetin| is the start compound that is hydroxylated in the 6-position of the A-ring which confers the yellow color to the flavonols and represents the first committed step of the pathway |CITS:[Halbwirth04]| |CITS:[19477473]|. The formed |FRAME:CPD-14866| undergoes various O-methylations (6 and 7-position) and O-glucosylations (3 and 7 position) to finally yield |FRAME:CPD-14911| |CITS:[19477473]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL Cholesterol| is an important and ubiquitous structural component of eukaryotic cell, membranes. Many bacterial species possess the capability to metabolize cholesterol and can survive on cholesterol as a single carbon source. The exact taxonomy of some species or genera recognized to catabolize cholesterol has changed over time. Two of the strains that were studied extensively, Nocardia restrictus ATCC 14887 and |FRAME:TAX-1702| ATCC 21387, are now classified as strains of |FRAME: TAX-43767| |CITS: [874450][12843070]|. In general, the mycolate-containing nocardioform actinomycetes, which include the genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus| and |FRAME: TAX-2060|, have all been shown to catabolize cholesterol and plant sterols |CITS: [19843168]|. In addition, several strains of |FRAME: TAX-1883| have been shown to decompose different steroids, including cholesterol |CITS: [Arima69]|, and some Proteobacteria were reported as being capable to degrade cholesterol |CITS: [4628510][9572974][18039763]|., The microbial degradation of cholesterol is challenging because of its complex chemical structure, low solubility in water, low number of functional groups and the presence of four alicyclic rings and two quaternary carbon atoms. A preliminary aerobic cholesterol degradation pathway has been proposed early on based on metabolites of cholesterol that have been identified in several actinomycete strains |CITS: [17345852]|, and has been largely resolved. In general, the steroid is sequentially oxidized and dehydrogenated forming several molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: SUC-COA| that can feed the citric acid cycle and generate ATP, or feed biosynthetic pathways such as lipid biosynthesis |CITS: [Murohisa93]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6945| and |FRAME: PWY-6946|)., The anaerobic degradation of cholesterol was studied later and not all the enzymes involved .have been characterized. However, significant work was conducted with the β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-157592|, leading to the pathway shown here., About This Pathway, The Gram-negative β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-157592|, which is capable of using either nitrate or oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, was reported to mineralize cholesterol to carbon dioxide under anoxic conditions |CITS: [9094222][12892131]|. Several studies have uncovered most of the steps of the pathway, which employs a composite repertoire of more than 40 genes, some known from the aerobic degradation pathway and some unique genes that are required to circumvent oxygenase-dependent reactions., Cholesterol is imported through the outer membrane via a putative FadL-like transport system, which is induced by neutral sterols. Once in the periplasm, cholesterol is attacked by the AcmA |FRAME: MONOMER-21198|, which is similar to enzymes involved in the aerobic pathway, followed by C25-hydroxylation |CITS: [17307741][18039763]|. While the C-25 hydroxylation is catalyzed by an oxygenase in the aerobic pathway, it is catalyzed by a molybdopterin-containing steroid dehydrogenase during anaerobic degradation |CITS: [22942275]|. |FRAME: TAX-157592| has multiple variants of this enzyme, which are used for C25-hydroxylations of steroids with different isoprenoid side chains |CITS: [22942275][28940833]|., Periplasmic metabolism of cholesterol ends with |FRAME: CPD-19067|, which is transported into the cytoplasm, where the rest of the degradation occurrs |CITS: [25418128]|., The cholesterol degradation pathway involves two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. Side chain degradation in both the aerobic and anaerobic pathways leads to |FRAME: CPD-13704|. However, in the anaerobic pathway this process depends on aldolytic C-C bond cleavages that involve acyl-CoA synthetases/dehydrogenases specific for the respective 26-, 24- and 22-oic acids/-oyl-CoAs and promiscuous enoyl-, CoA hydratases, aldolases and aldehyde dehydrogenases |CITS: [28940833][29374035]|., Degradation of the A and B rings of the sterol core is different between the aerobic and anaerobic pathways, and depends on unique enzymes in anaerobic steroid degraders. Following the hydrolytic cleavage of the A ring, the process again involves CoA-ester intermediates. However, the degradation of the remaining C and D rings is highly similar in aerobic and anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [28940833]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN "Indole-3-acetate"| (IAA) is a well-known phytohormone. Several biosynthetic routes have been reported in higher plants (see |FRAME: PWY-581|). In one such route, |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD|, which is formed from |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETALDOXIME| by |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.3|, or from |FRAME: CPD-1863| by the combined action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147 "EC 3.2.1.147, myrosinase"| and |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5|, is converted to IAA by the plant's |FRAME: CPLX-1525| enzymes (|FRAME: EC-3.5.5.1 "EC 3.5.5.1"|)., Several plant-associated bacteria and fungi also have the ability to produce IAA, which they use to force plants to produce compounds that provide the bacteria with carbon, nitrogen, and energy sources. The production of plant hormones such as IAA and cytokinin seems to be essential for the virulence of these bacteria., The microbial conversion of |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD| to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| can proceed by two enzymatic pathways |CITS: [1368882]|. The other route is described in |FRAME: PWY-5025|., About This Pathway, In this pathway a nitrilase catalyzes the direct conversion of |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD| into IAA and ammonia. This pathway has been found in several virulent fungal species such as |FRAME: TAX-5012|, |FRAME: TAX-5011| and |FRAME: TAX-48692|, which cause hyperplastic diseases in plants such as cherry, peach, and plum, respectively |CITS: [Yamada90]|. A nitrilase that is specific to arylacetonitriles, including |FRAME: INDOLEYL-CPD|, was also isolated from, the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-511| |CITS: [8419930]|., For a review of bacterial nitrilases, see |CITS: [Kobayashi94]|.

Summary: Tryptophanase (tryptophan indole-lyase; EC 4.1.99.1) is a catabolic enzyme that catalyzes the reversible conversion of tryptophan to indole, pyruvate, and ammonia, in an α,β-elimination reaction. It is one of most studied pyridoxal 5 phosphate (PLP)-requiring multifunctional enzymes, and at high substrate concentrations it can perform additional α,β-elimination, as well as β-replacement reactions. Tryptophanase can also catalyze the synthesis of tryptophan |CITS: [4556453]|, either from indole, ammonia and pyruvate, or from indole and serine or cysteine |CITS: [14171448][42371]|., The catalytic cycle of tryptophanase consists of the following steps: (1) association of the amino acid substrate with the enzyme to form the Michaelis complex; (2) formation of an external aldimine (transaldimination); (3) quinonoid formation by, R-proton abstraction from the external aldimine; (4) tautomerization of the indolyl group; (5) elimination of indole and formation of the aminoacrylate Schiff base intermediate; (6) restoration of the internal aldimine (transaldimination); (7) release of |FRAME: 2-AMINOACRYLATE| (aminoacrylate)., Once released, the enamine form |FRAME: 2-AMINOACRYLATE| spontaneously tautomerizes to form the imine form |FRAME: CPD-16015|, which is spontaneously hydrolyzed to to pyruvate and ammonia |CITS: [236639][Phillips89][9485457]|., Most studies of bacterial tryptophanases have focused on the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme. In 1969, DeMoss and Moser demonstrated that tryptophanase is common in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [5781572]|. Since then, tryptophanases have been isolated from several organisms, including |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [4551942]|, |FRAME:TAX-44250| |CITS: [4959960]|, |FRAME: TAX-587| |CITS: [1148216]|, |FRAME: ORG-5991| |CITS: [42371]|, |FRAME:TAX-585| |CITS: [1400314]|, |FRAME:TAX-2734| |CITS: [1368766]| and |FRAME:TAX-548| |CITS: [7510326]|., Tryptophanase enzymes isolated from different sources tend to have a similar molecular weight, subunit structure, and PLP content, but they show differences in amino acid composition and antigenic properties  |CITS: [1400314]|., A commercial use of tryptophenase is found in the manufacturing of the indigo dye. A bacterial system has been introduced in which |FRAME:TAX-562| has been engineered to express tryptophanase and naphtalene (di)oxygenase, breaking down tryptophan to indole, and converting indole to indoxyl, which subsequently oxidizes spontaneously to generate indigo |CITS: [6353574][7763440]|.

General Background, A limited number of species of Gram-negative bacteria, all in the family |FRAME: TAX-543|, utilize unusual sugars, derivatives of 3,6-dideoxyhexose, as |FRAME: O-Antigens| of their lipopolysaccharides. These sugars are the dominant antigenic determinants in the membranes of these organisms., Out of the eight possible stereoisomers of 3,6-dideoxyhexoses, only five have been identified in nature. These are |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: CPD-9396|, |FRAME: CPD-9388|, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: CPD-9395|. All five 3,6-dideoxyhexoses have been found in different serovars of |FRAME: TAX-633|, while other genera possess only some of them. For example, |FRAME: TAX-90371| group B contains |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: TAX-295319| contains |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: TAX-90370| contains |FRAME: CPD-9395| |CITS: [8071227]|., These sugars are synthesized via a complex series of enzymatic reactions starting, in most cases, from |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE|, derived from |FRAME: GLC-1-P|. In a reaction catalyzed by the NAD+-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7584|, |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-658|, which is then converted to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1078| in two consecutive enzymatic reactions, mediated by two components of the |FRAME: CPLX-7585| enzyme complex. The first component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13781| (E1), a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP)-linked iron-sulfur-containing catalyst, while the second component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13782| (E3), a [2Fe-2S]-containing flavoprotein., The product of this complex, |FRAME: CPD-1078|, is the parent to four different 3,6-dideoxyhexoses., About This Pathway, The O-antigen of members of the |FRAME: TAX-28901| Group D is composed of a repeat unit of four sugars - mannosyl-rhamnosyl-galactosyl-tyvelose. The last sugar, |FRAME: CPD-9395|, is a dideoxyhexose that confers the O9 antigenic epitope specificity, characteristic of this group., |FRAME: CPD-9698| is synthesized from |FRAME: CDP-36-DIDEOXY-D-MANNOSE| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-13795|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10525| gene. The gene from |FRAME: TAX-90370|, a member of this group, has been cloned and sequenced, and expressed in minicells |CITS: [2793833]|., The presence of the gene on a plasmid conferred on members of the |FRAME: TAX-28901| groups A and B the ability to synthesize tyvelose, confirming the proposed function for this gene.

General Background, Heptose sugars, mostly glycero-manno-heptoses, are found in the cell surface polymers of many bacteria. Prior to their incorporation, the heptose residues are activated by attachment to a nucleotide (see pathways |FRAME: PWY0-1241| and |FRAME: PWY-6478|). These activated heptoses can be uniquely modified by enzymes before incorporation into the polymers. In bacterial pathogens heptose derivatives such as 6-deoxyheptoses that are not found in mammals can play an important role in virulence, as demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-633| |CITS: [18284593]|. Heptose modifying enzymes are therefore of interest as potential drug targets |CITS: [19610666][18284593]|., The modified heptose |FRAME: CPD-17411| is found in the |FRAME: O-Antigens "O-antigen"| of |FRAME: ORG-6272|. The O-antigen along with core oligosaccharide and |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"| comprise |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides "lipopolysaccharide"| (LPS), a major component of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. LPS is one of several virulence factors in |FRAME: TAX-633|. It has been shown that 6-deoxy-D-manno-heptose affects the barrier function of LPS and the overall virulence of |FRAME: ORG-6272| |CITS: [18284593]|., About This Pathway, DmhA along with its corresponding reductase DmhB catalyze the formation of 6-deoxyheptose, a modified heptose present in the O-antigen of |FRAME: ORG-6272|. In this pathway both DmhA and DmhB utilize and release sugars that are in the D-manno configuration. Unlike |FRAME: PWY-7610| in |FRAME: TAX-197|, no epimerization steps are involved |CITS: [19610666][23689373]|., Both dmhA and dmhB mutants were analyzed for the composition and structure of their LPS and the virulence-related properties of these mutants and their complemented counterparts were assessed in vitro |CITS: [18284593]|. Recombinant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli, purified and biochemically characterized |CITS: [19610666]|.

Summary: |FRAME:TAX-562| can use |FRAME: Beta-D-Glucuronides "β-D-glucuronosides"| and the hexuronates |FRAME: GLUCURONATE|, |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| and |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| as the sole sources of carbon for growth. The degradation pathways for these compounds were first described in a series of publications by Ashwell et al |CITS: [13584413][13794771][14401695][13831814][13813474]|., β-D-glucuronosides are detoxification products that are excreted into the mammalian gut in the bile. |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is found in animal mucus and at low levels in plant tissues. |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is the main monomeric constituent of |FRAME: Pectin pectin|, a heteropolymer present in the cell walls of dicotyledonous plants, and is very common in plant tissue., The initial step in the degradation of β-glucuronosides is hydrolysis by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.31| to yield |FRAME: GLUCURONATE|, which is subsequently isomerized to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.12|., |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| undergoes an NADH-dependent reduction to |FRAME: D-MANNONATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.57|, and a dehydration catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.8| yields |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE|., In a parallel pathway, |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is isomerized to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.12|, the same enzyme that catalyses the analogous function in the |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY| pathway. |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| undergoes an NADH-dependent reduction to |FRAME: D-ALTRONATE| by, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.58|, and a subsequent dehydration reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.7| generates |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE|., At this point, the |FRAME: GLUCUROCAT-PWY "D-glucurunate degradation"| and |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY "D-galacturonate degradation"| pathways converge, and a common enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.45|, phosphorylates |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| to yield |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-DEOXY-6-P-GLUCONATE|, which enters central metabolism via the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "Protocatechuate"| is one of the key intermediate metabolites in the microbial degradation of various aromatic compounds, including phthalates, hydroxybenzoates, and lignin-derived aromatic compounds such as |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|., The key step in these degradation pathways, the fission of the protocatechuate aromatic ring, can be catalyzed by one of the three distinct dioxygenases |FRAME: CPLX-2701|, |FRAME: CPLX-2721| and |FRAME: CPLX-7915|., The fission products, and thus the degradation pathways, depend on the type of dioxygenase employed. The three pathways are described in |FRAME: P184-PWY|, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6336|, respectively., About This Pathway, The pathway that starts with |FRAME: CPLX-2721| is part of a pathway known as the |FRAME: PWY-5431 "3-oxoadipate pathway"| (or β-ketoadipate pathway). It is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi |CITS: [8905091]|, although the pathway organization and regulation varies among species |CITS: [8905091]|. , The β-ketoadipate pathway is comprised of two parallel branches, one branch converts |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| and the other converts |FRAME: CATECHOL| to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|. |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| is then converted to |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which are processed by the TCA cycle., A variety of aromatic compounds, such as 4-hydroxybenzoate and benzoate, are shuttled into the respective protocatechuate and catechol branches of the β-ketoadipate pathway., In |FRAME: TAX-303|, all of the enzymes involved in protocatechuate degradation via the β-ketoadipate pathway are inducible |CITS: [5916393]|. , Protocatechuate dioxygenase is induced by protocatechuate (as reported in |CITS: [8905091]|, , and the remaining five enzymes, 3-carboxymuconate cycloisomerase, 4-carboxymuconolactone, decarboxylase, β-ketoadipate enol-lactone hydrolase, β-ketoadipate:succinyl-CoA transferase, and, β-ketoadipyl CoA thiolase are induced by β-ketoadipate |CITS: [5916393][8905091]|. , The genes that encode for the synthesis of the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of the protocatechuate , branch of the β-ketoadipate pathway in P. putida are clustered into four distinct groups , (as reported in |CITS: [7961399]|): pcaHG |CITS: [8407791]|, , pcaBDC |CITS: [1390752]|, pcaIJ |CITS: [8376330]|, and pcaRKF |CITS: [761399]|. In , |FRAME:TAX-471| the genes are arranged in gene cluster pcaIJFBDKCHG that is induced by, protocatechuate (as reported in |CITS: [7961399]|).

Summary: At least 9 pathways exist for the degradation of lysine in mammals, plants, bacteria and fungi. The initial products of lysine degradation in these pathways include: L-saccharopine in mammals and plants; β-L-lysine, 5-aminovaleramide, N6-hydroxylysine, cadaverine, and α-aminoadipate-δ-semialdehyde in bacteria; and α-aminoadipate-δ-semialdehyde, D-lysine, N6-acetyl-L-lysine, and 6-amino-2-oxocaproic acid in yeasts and fungi (reviewed in |CITS: [10714900]|). See MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY0-461| to cadaverine, and |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY| via L-saccharopine. , In the fungal pathway shown here, lysine is degraded to glutarate via acetylation of the 6-amino group to the initial product N6-acetyl-L-lysine. This is followed by transamination, oxidative decarboxylation, deacetylation, transamination with loss of the second amino group, and oxidation to glutarate. Glutarate may be metabolized to other carboxylic acids (see below)., Evidence for this pathway was obtained for the fungus |FRAME: TAX-1541393| |CITS: [131119]|. When variously radiolabeled lysine preparations were added to cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-1541393|, N6-acetyl-L-lysine was formed. Acetyl-CoA was required and acetyl-phosphate was not utilized. Another experiment using DL-{4,5-3H}lysine showed 5-acetamidovalerate as the major product. If radiolabeled N6-acetyl-L-lysine was used with added α-ketoglutarate, and pyridoxal phosphate, radiolabeled 2-keto-6-acetamidocaproate was produced. α-Ketoglutarate was preferred over pyruvate, and there was little or no dependence on pyridoxal phosphate. If thiamine pyrophosphate and NAD were added to a similar reaction, virtually all of the label was in 5-acetamidovalerate. If labeled 5-acetamidovalerate was used, labeled 5-aminovalerate (5-aminopentanoate) was identified. In addition, whole cell cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1541393| incubated with labeled 5-acetamidovalerate accumulated radiolabeled glutarate. Whole cell cultures incubated with radiolabeled glutarate produced a mixture of tricarboxylic acid cycle acids and other carboxylic acids |CITS: [131119]|. , Evidence for this pathway was also obtained in other yeasts and fungi |CITS: [131119]|. In whole cell cultures, formation of the initial product, N6-acetyl-L-lysine, was demonstrated in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5141| 33933, and the yeasts |FRAME:TAX-4932| and |FRAME: TAX-907340 "Cyberlindnera saturnus (previously known as Hansenula saturnus or Williopsis saturnus) ATCC 2579"|. In these experiments, whole cell cultures of |FRAME: TAX-1541393|, N. crassa, S. cerevisiae and C. saturnus incubated with radiolabeled L-lysine all produced labeled N6-acetyl-L-lysine. Whole cell cultures of N. crassa 33933 and S. cerevisiae incubated with DL-[4,5-3H]lysine were shown to accumulate radiolabeled 5-acetamidovalerate. When N. crassa strains 33933 and 15069, and S. cerevisiae were incubated with DL-[2-14C]lysine, DL-[6-14C]lysine, or DL-[4,5-3H]lysine, radiolabeled 5-aminovalerate (5-aminopentanoate) was shown to accumulate. Species differences in the results, depending upon the radiolabel used, may be attributable to the presence of a racemase and a deacylase in |FRAME: TAX-1541393|. These experiments provided evidence for a generalized pathway of lysine degradation in yeasts and fungi |CITS: [131119]|. , Evidence for this acetylation pathway of lysine degradation has also been found in |FRAME:TAX-4952| (gene LYC1, the structural gene for lysine N6-acetyltransferase) |CITS: [8082161], [15229592]|; |FRAME:TAX-5479| (lysine N6 acetyltransferase characterization |CITS: [SCHMIDTH]|, and N6-acetyllysine aminotransferase characterization |CITS: [1285645]|); and |FRAME:TAX-5482| (evidence for lysine N6 acetyltransferase, N6-acetyllysine aminotransferase, and 5-aminovalerate aminotransferase activities) |CITS: [1682209]|. Earlier evidence for the pathway in Hansenula saturnus has also been described |CITS: [14251331]|. The S. cerevisiae lysine N6-acetyltransferase has been purified and characterized |CITS: [8257283]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-24748 Alazopeptin|, a tripeptide consisting of one |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and two |FRAME: CPD0-1627| residues, was reported from |FRAME: TAX-66896| back in 1956 |CITS: [13425456][5883414]|. The peptide, which was subsequently isolated from several other actinobacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-58347|), was shown to have anticancer and antitrypanosomal activities |CITS: [4205875][19168977]|., |FRAME: CPD0-1627 "6-Diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine"| (DON) was described in the same year from an unidentified Streptomyces species isolated from Peruvian soil, and reported to be an tumor-inhibitory antibiotic |CITS: [24544086]|. DON ended up being the best-studied broadly active |FRAME: GLN| antagonist that inhibits many enzymes that act on |FRAME: GLN|, including |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.2|. The compound was tested as a chemotherapeutic agent in several clinical studies |CITS: [26425550][27489275][27560860][28759224][28454342]|, but was never approved due to its toxicity |CITS: [30181331]|. It is gaining attention again because of the recognition of the importance of glutaminolysis in cancer cells |CITS: [30181331][31699883]|., About This Pathway, The complete biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: CPD-24748|, including the production of |FRAME: CPD0-1627| from |FRAME: LYS|, has been reported |CITS: [33624374]|., To identify the gene cluster the researchers started with known sequences of the enzymes involved in production of |FRAME: NITRITE| from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which have been characterized previously in a study of |FRAME: PWY-8296| |CITS: [26689788][30120394]|. Matching genes were found in both |FRAME: TAX-58347| and |FRAME: TAX-66896|, leading to the discovery of the full cluster. In |FRAME: TAX-58347| all the genes are clustered at a single locus, while in |FRAME: TAX-66896| the genes are divided into two clusters, with the azpE, azpD, and azpR genes located away from the main azp cluster., To characterize the enzymes, each of the |FRAME: TAX-66896| genes was inactivated separately, and the resulting changes in metabolites were measured. It was found that the ligation of two |FRAME: CPD0-1627 DON| molecules is performed by a mechanism that resembles non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs), requiring the participation of a dedicated carrier protein, encoded by the azpF gene. It was also found that the loading of DON onto the carrier protein requires that it is N-acetylated. Thus the process includes three steps - acetylation, loading, and deacetylation, which are catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-107499|, |FRAME: G-107500|, and |FRAME: G-107501| genes, respectively., Once loaded on the carrier protein, DON can be ligated to a second DON molecule by |FRAME: G-107502 AzpM|. |FRAME: CPD-24748 Alazopeptin| biosynthesis is completed by |FRAME: G-107503 AzpA|, which adds an |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| residue |CITS: [33624374]|.

Summary: General Background, 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes convert 2-oxo acids to the corresponding acyl-CoA derivatives and produce NADH and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an irreversible reaction., Five members of this family are known at present, including the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| (PDHC - this pathway), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| (OGDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| (BCDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| (GDHC), and the |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190| (ADHC). They all function at strategic points in (usually aerobic) catabolic pathways and are subject to stringent control |CITS: [9655933]|., With the exception of GDHC, the 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes share a common structure. They consist of three main components, namely a 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3)., In Gram-positive bacteria and mitochondria, the E1 component is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, while in Gram-negative bacteria it is made of a single type of subunit., In all cases described so far, many copies of each subunit assemble to form the full complex. For example, the |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| comprises 24, 24, and 12 units of the E1, E2, and E3 components, respectively., The core of the complex is made of either 24 (Gram-negative bacteria) or 60 (mitochondria) E2 units, which contain the lipoyl active site in the form of lipoylated L-lysine residues, as well as binding sites for the other two subunits. E1, which contains a |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| cofactor, catalyzes the binding of the 2-oxo acid to the lipoyl group of E2, which then transfers an acyl group (the nature of the acyl group depends on the particular enzyme) to |FRAME: CO-A|, forming an acyl-CoA. During this transfer, the lipoyl group is reduced to dihydrolipoyl. E3 then transfers the protons to NAD, forming NADH and restoring the dihydrolipoyllysine group back to lipoyllysine., Cryoelectron microscopy of PDHC from |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS:[12411477]| and ox kidney |CITS: [11752427]| has revealed that the E2 inner core is surrounded by an outer shell of E1 and E3 components, with the lipoyl domains confined to the annular space between them where they must make successive journeys between the three types of active sites (E1-E3), which are physically far apart |CITS: [12795594]|., About This Pathway, In the pathway illustrated here, |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, a key reaction of central metabolism, which links the substrate-level phosphorylation pathway |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| (which ends with the generation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE|) to the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, which accepts the input of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|., The |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX|, which in |FRAME:TAX-562| consists of 24 E1 subunits, 24 E2 subunits, and 12 E3 subunits, catalyzes three reactions that constitute a cycle. The three reactions can be summarized by the reaction, |FRAME:PYRUVDEH-RXN|., During aerobic growth of |FRAME:TAX-562| the cycle is an essential source of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to feed the |FRAME: TCA| and thereby to satisfy the cellular requirements for the precursor metabolites it forms. Mutant strains defective in the complex require an exogenous source of |FRAME: ACET| during aerobic growth, but not under anaerobic conditions,since during anaerobic growth pyruvate formate lyase generates |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| from |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. Mutant strains lacking pyruvate formate lyase have the reverse phenotype |CITS: [ecosal]|., In some strains of |FRAME: TAX-2104| the multienzyme complex reaction is part of an alternate path from phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate |CITS: [8948633] [9439886][3141576]|., Plants have two forms of pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, one in the plastid and the other in the mitochondrion. The two complexes have distinct physiological roles. The plastid pyruvate dehydrogenase complex provides the main acetyl-CoA source for de novo fatty acid biosynthesis (|FRAME:PWY-4381|). The mitochondrial complex provides acetyl-CoA , for the |FRAME: TCA| cycle and NADH for oxidative phosphorylation. Both complexes are feedback inhibited by acetyl-CoA and NADH. However the two complexes differ in other aspects of enzyme characteristics. The mitochondrial complex but not the plastid one is regulated by phosphorylation. The plastid complex requires higher Mg2+ concentration and more alkaline pH for maximal enzyme activity |CITS: [12631264]|.

Summary: General Background, The yellow color of carnations (|FRAME:TAX-3570|) has been attributed , to the occurrence of chalcone 2'-O-glucoside identified as main flavonoid in petals of this plant , |CITS: [7437010]|. The variation in content of this chalcone glucoside, accumulating in vacuoles, may be , responsible for the various yellow hues observed in Dianthus |CITS: [YOSHIDA04]|., Glucosylated chalcones are not unusual compounds identified in plants and have been reported across the , plant kingdom such as in the Acanthaceae (Andrographis echioides |CITS: [11355769]|, Aristolochiaceae , (Asarum canadense |CITS: [11140534]|, Verbenaceae (Clerodendron phlomidis |CITS: [ 7766006]| , and Caesalpiniaceae (Guibourtia tessmanii |CITS: [12150803]|. However, the biological function of most , of those glucosides is unknown and remains to be determined., About This Pathway, Although the chalcone 2'-O-glucoside has been determined to be crucial , for the yellow flower coloration in carnations the corresponding enzyme activity, i.e. chalcone 2'-O-glucosyltransferase , has only recently been reported |CITS: [Ogata04]|. The chalcone 2'-O-glucosyltransferase acts on , naringenin chalcone that is synthesized from the condensation of p-coumaryl-CoA and malonyl-CoAs by chalcone , synthase (compare |FRAME:PWY1F-FLAVSYN|)., However, the two enzymes (DicGT4, DicGT5) among 18 putative glucosyltransferases cloned from , |FRAME:TAX-3570| and being identified to express in vitro chalcone 2'-O-glucosyltransferase , activity have broader substrate specificity and are also expressed in Dianthus lines that lack the chalcone 2'-O-glucosides. , Their in vivo function is therefore not unambiguously determined and specific for this compound and , remains to be further investigated |CITS: [Ogata04]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CELLULOSE Cellulose| is the most common organic compound on earth. It is a polysaccharide consisting of a linear chain of several hundred to over ten thousand β(1→4) linked D-glucose units, and is the structural component of the primary cell wall of green plants, many forms of algae and the oomycetes., Though chemically simple, cellulose is physically complex with both crystalline and amorphous regions, and a number of, different enzymes are required for its efficient hydrolysis., The enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose by cellulolytic fungi involves three major types of cellulases (endoglucanases, exoglucanases and β-glucosidases) working in synergy. Endoglucanases (|FRAME: RXN-2043 "EC 3.2.1.4"|) randomly cleave the β-1,4 glycosidic linkages of cellulose fibers, generating shorter, more accessible fragments commonly referred to as |FRAME: Cellodextrins cellodextrins|; Exoglucanases (such as cellobiohydrolases, |FRAME: 3.2.1.91-RXN EC 3.2.1.91"|) attack the chain ends of the cellodextrins to release the constitutive unit of cellulose, |FRAME: CELLOBIOSE| (a dimer of glucose linked by a β-1,4 glycosidic bond); and β-glucosidases (|FRAME: 3.2.1.21-RXN "EC 3.2.1 21"|) hydrolyse cellobiose into two molecules of glucose., Unlike anaerobic cellulolytic bacteria, which produce large complexes of cellulolytic enzymes that are attached to the cell surface (see |FRAME: PWY-6784|), the fungal enzymes do not form complexes, and do not attach to the cells, although, some of the enzymes have been shown to cooperate and act in synergy |CITS: [8540419]|., One of the most efficient and best characterized cellulolytic fungus is the brown rot fungus |FRAME: TAX-51453|. High level of secretion and diversity of the produced enzymes promotes wide application of enzyme preparations from |FRAME: TAX-51453| in different fields of biotechnology, including the bioconversion of renewable plant raw stock to fuel and other useful products; wine production and brewing, as an additive to farm livestock fodder; in textile industry, for improving quality of cotton and linen artcles; and in biobleaching of cellulose pulp in paper production.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-2072453| is an enterohemorrhagic, |FRAME: CPLX-8880 "Shiga toxin"|-producing strain that is the causative agent of outbreaks of bloody diarrhea and hemolytic-uremic syndrome with significant mortality in humans. A massive outbreak of foodborne illness caused by |FRAME: TAX-2072453| in Germany in 2011 resulted in more than 3000 people infected and more than 50 deaths |CITS: [21752971][21727641]|., The organism synthesizes an O antigen with a tetrasaccharide repeating unit structure of |FRAME: CPD-23827 ", [-4-α-D-Gal(1-4)-α-Neu5,7,9Ac3(2-3)-β-D-Gal(1-3)-βD-GalNAc(1-]n"| |CITS: [1291048]|. It is one of the few |FRAME: TAX-562| O antigens containing sialic acid (The only E. coli O antigens known to contain sialic acid residues are found in serotypes |FRAME: CPD-24056 O24|, |FRAME: CPD-24064 O56|, |FRAME: CPD-23827 O104|, |FRAME: CPD-23816 O145|, and |FRAME: CPD-24061 O171|). Sialic acid is an important component of glycoconjugates in animal tissues, and is thought to contribute to pathogenicity by mimicking the host tissue component., The O antigen biosynthetic cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2072453| was sequenced in 2001 and found to contain 9 genes. Four of the genes are involved in the synthesis of the CMP-sialic acid precursor and sialate O-acetylation, three encode glycosyltransferases, and the remaining two encode an O antigen repeat unit flippase (Wzx) and and O antigen polymerase (Wzy) |CITS: [11404020]|., All three glycosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80995|, |FRAME: G-80996|, and |FRAME: G-27214| genes, have been purified and characterized |CITS: [26391208][29063990][24957618]|.

This pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: L-GULONATE| was discovered by studying a chromosomal region of |FRAME: TAX-141390| that contained genes encoding enzymes known to participate in |FRAME: PWY-7242| as well as an uncharacterized alcohol dehydrogenase., Since it is known that |FRAME: TAX-141390| degrades |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| by an alternative pathway that proceeds via conversion to |FRAME: CPD-12595| and not |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6501|), it was suspected that the uncharacterized dehydrogenase allows another acid sugar to be utilized as a carbon source., After an initial effort to purify the protein from |FRAME: TAX-141390| has failed, a homologous gene from |FRAME: TAX-2746| was used instead to produce a purified recombinant enzyme. The purified enzyme was screened for oxidation activity using a library of 72 acid sugars, and the highest activity was found with |FRAME: L-GULONATE| |CITS: [25145794]|., It should be noted that a similar pathway for L-gulonate degradation was suggested in 1980 for |FRAME: TAX-83333|, but the gene or enzyme responsible for oxidation of |FRAME: L-GULONATE| to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE| was not identified at that time |CITS: [6993236]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39|, commonly referred to as ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase or RubisCO, is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both the carboxylation and oxygenation of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| (RuBP). The carboxylation process is generally known as CO2 fixation (see |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|) whereas the oxygenation process is known as photorespiration (this pathway)., The two substrates (CO2 and O2) are competitive with regard to RubisCO, so that an increase in CO2 concentration inhibits oxygenation and vice versa |CITS:[Bowyer97]|. An important factor influencing the rate of oxygenation is temperature, as photorespiration is enhanced by high temperature. The reasons for this are twofold: (i) as temperatures increase the solubility of CO2 diminishes more rapidly than that of O2 and (ii) the specificity factor (Ω) of RubisCO (which represents a measure of the relative specificity for CO2) decreases with increasing temperatures between 7°C and 35°C., While the carboxylation reaction results in two molecules of |FRAME:G3P|, which are processed in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|, the oxygenation reaction forms one molecule of |FRAME:G3P| and one molecule of |FRAME:CPD-67| (2PG). The latter cannot be used in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY| and, instead, is salvaged in the photorespiration pathway. , While photorespiration is essential for the viability of all organisms that perform oxygenic photosynthesis, including cyanobacteria and C3 plants, at ambient CO2 conditions |CITS: [18957552][26994478]|, the photorespiratory cycle results in carbon, nitrogen and energy losses, and, unlike true respiration, does not produce ATP or reducing power. As a matter of fact, despite its name photorespiration does not involve neither light nor respiration., About This Pathway, The main features of the photorespiration pathway include: (i) the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-67| into |FRAME: GLY|; (ii) the processing of two glycines into |FRAME: SER|, CO2 and ammonia; and (iii) the conversion of |FRAME: SER| into |FRAME: G3P|, which is directed towards CO2 fixation via the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|., The first step of the pathway involves the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:CPD-67|, which not only recycles phosphate but also prevents accumulation of this compound, which is a potent inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.1|. The next step is the oxidation of |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| to |FRAME:GLYOX|. This step is catalyzed by different enzymes in plants and some algae (see |FRAME: PWY-181|) and in chlorophytes and cyanobacteria (this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-8362|)., Glyoxylate is converted into |FRAME:GLY| by two different enzymes: |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45| and |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.4|. One of the glycine molecues is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, to CO2, ammonia, and a single carbon that is transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate|. The methylene group is then transferred to the second glycine molecule by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, forming |FRAME: SER|. , The serine molecue feeds back into |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, closing a cycle. The main carbon molecule produced by this cycle is |FRAME:OH-PYR|, which is reduced into |FRAME:GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.29|. The pathway ends with the phosphorylation of glycerate to |FRAME:G3P|, which re-enters the Calvin cycle. The phosphorylation is performed by different enzymes in cyanobacteria vs. other photosynthetic organisms., The outcome of photorespiration in photosynthetic cells is loss of carbon via CO2 release, as well as loss of energy, yet the pathway is essential at atmospheric concentrations of CO2. The biological function of photorespiration is not clear. One possibility is that photorespiration is necessary under conditions of high light intensity and low CO2 concentration to dissipate excess ATP and NADPH from the photosynthesis light reactions, and prevent damage to the photosynthetic apparatus |CITS: [11299007]|. Another explanation is that the pathway is necessary for the assimilation of nitrate |CITS: [15272076]|., The only difference between this pathway variant, which exists in chlorophytes such as |FRAME: TAX-3055|, and the pathway variant in plants is that in plants and some algae |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| is exported to the cytoplasm, where it is oxidized in the peroxisomes to |FRAME:GLYOX| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.15|. In chlorophytes (and cyanobacteria) glycolate is oxidized to glyoxylate by |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.14| |CITS: [18957552]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-25183 "Rosmarinic acid"| (RA) is an ester of |FRAME: CAFFEATE| and |FRAME: CPD-6982|. It is widely spread in species of the |FRAME: TAX-4136| and |FRAME: TAX-21571| |CITS: [12482446]| and also occurs in some lower plants such as ferns and hornworts |CITS: [TAKEDA90]| |CITS: [12721853]|. It was first isolated in 1958 from rosemary (|FRAME: TAX-39367|), which is the source of its name. The 3'-O-β-glucoside of RA (|FRAME:CPD-7018|) has been identified in the hornwort |FRAME: TAX-41834| |CITS: [16133208]|, where it accumulates up to 1% of the cell dry weight. Other rosmarinic acid derivatives of biological importance are |FRAME: CPD-26619 "lithospermic acid"|, a conjugate of rosmarinic acid and caffeic acid, and |FRAME: CPD-26620 "lithospermic acid B", which is a dimer of rosmarinic acid |CITS: [12482446]|., Rosmarinic acid is used in foods or beverages as a flavoring, in cosmetics, and as a dietary supplement. Its biosynthesis has been studied extensively |CITS: [11943155]|., RA biosynthesis was first investigated in |FRAME: TAX-34256| |CITS: [5484678]| confirming the involvement of two parallel pathways for the making of rosmarinic acid. The metabolic origin for the formation of the two crucial compounds coumaroyl-CoA and 4-hydroxyphenyllactate were identified as L-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine respectively. Further research led to the clarification of the biosynthetic route in |FRAME: TAX-4142| |CITS: [Petersen93]| |CITS: [12482446]|. , About This Pathway, The most experimental support for the RA biosynthesis has been obtained from species of the |FRAME: TAX-4136| family elucidating the detailed enzymatic steps resulting in the formation of RA (|FRAME:PWY-5048|). However, several enzymes of this pathway possess the ability to convert different substrates with comparable efficiency indicating that the production of rosmarinic acid may also be accomplished via a pathway variant (this pathway)., Two crucial steps in the RA biosynthetic route comprise the reduction of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to 4-hydroxyphenyllactate (hydroxyphenylpyruvate reductase - |CITS: [15284489]|) and the subsequent connection of this RA intermediate with coumaroyl-CoA in a transesterification reaction catalyzed by rosmarinic acid synthase |CITS: [Petersen88]|. In addition to their usual monohydroxylated substrates, both enzymes convert readily the corresponding dihydroxylated substrates to 3,4-dihydroxyphenyllactic acid (DHPL) |CITS: [Hausler91]| |CITS: [15284489]| and rosmarinic acid |CITS: [Petersen91]| respectively., The enzyme catalyzing the entry step into this potential pathway is tyrosine hydroxylase (EC 1.14.16.2) and has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-3583| |CITS: [YAMAMOTO01]|. The formation of L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) can also be accomplished by the action of polyphenol oxidases (EC 1.10.3.1) (e.g. |CITS: [7948897]|). The following reaction (transamination to 3,4-dihydroxypyruvate) has been found to be occurring in animals and bacteria but remains to be validated for plants. It is not known precisely at what stage in the rosmarinic acid biosynthesis the two hydroxygroups in the 3- and 3'-position of the phenolic rings are introduced. At present the depicted pathway can not be ruled out but it is more likely that the major biogenesis of RA proceeds via the pathway described in |FRAME:PWY-5048|.

Summary: RNA modification is a post-transcriptional process by which certain nucleotides are altered after their initial incorporation into an RNA chain., The most heavily modified class of RNA molecules is the tRNA - an average of 11%, 14%, and 17% of the tRNA residues are modified in |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-4932|, and mammalian cytoplasm, respectively |CITS: [9399820]|. These modifications expand the chemical and functional diversity of tRNA, and enhance its structural stability |CITS: [3304135]|., In some bacterial genomes, about 1% of the coding genes are devoted to tRNA modification |CITS: [3304135]|., Position 34 (the anticodon first letter, or the wobble position) or position 37 (the position next to the anticodon) frequently contains highly modified nucleosides. The wobble modifications at position 34 are important for precise decoding mediated by the codon-anticodon interaction. The so called "hypermodified" nucleosides at position 37 function in translational reading-frame maintenance. These are usually modified purine nucleosides with large molecular weight. Their high hydrophobicity enhances the codon-anticodon interaction, and their modifications prevent the formation of an incorrect Watson-Crick base pair with the codon's first letter. Some of these hypermodified nucleosides, known as wye bases, contain a tricyclic structure. The most complex wye base identified thus far is |FRAME: CPD-15385| (yW), which is found only at position 37 of eukaryotic |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|, and is generated from guanine |CITS: [4586620]| in 5 steps, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7283|. , While |FRAME: CPD-15385| has been found only in eukaryotic |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|, two of the intermediates in the pathway leading to its synthesis, namely |FRAME: CPD-15399| (yW-86) and |FRAME: CPD-15401| (yW-72), have also been found as the final products in tRNA of several Archaea that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-28890| phylum |CITS: [20382657]|. , The first reaction in the pathway leading to their synthesis, the methylation of guanine at position 37 of tRNA, is catalyzed by trm5 gene products. These proteins are not specific for |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|, as the anticodon sequence is not critical for their tRNA recognition |CITS: [3556165][15248782]| (all subsequent steps in the pathway are specific for |FRAME: PHE-tRNAs|)., Many archaea contain two and even three homologs of the yeast |FRAME: G3O-31120| gene, which were named |FRAME: G-16040|, |FRAME: G-16041| and trm5c. The two genes from |FRAME: TAX-29292| have been cloned and studied, and were shown to differ by the fact that |FRAME: G-16040| is bifunctional and can catalyze additional methylations leading to formation of different wye bases (see |FRAME: PWY-7285|) |CITS: [20382657]|., The second step is catalyzed by homologs of the yeast |FRAME: G3O-34098|, |FRAME: Radical-AdoMet-Enzymes| that contains multiple iron-sulfur centers. Unlike the eukaryotic enzymes, the archaeal enzymes do not have a flavodoxin domain (which usually serves in electron transfer to the iron-sulfur cluster). Thus, it is likely that another enzyme serves as the elctron donor to the |FRAME: G-16042| enzymes |CITS: [17881823]|., The latter part of the pathway is responsible for the addition of an α-amino-α-carboxypropyl side chain at carbon C-7. It consists of two steps catalyzed by |FRAME: G-16043| and taw3 genes. While the |FRAME: G-16043| genes from |FRAME: TAX-53953| and |FRAME: TAX-2190| were cloned and characterized |CITS: [19717466]|, no archaeal taw3 genes, which are homologs of the yeast |FRAME: G3O-30560| gene, have been studied to date (June 2013). It has been proposed that the archaeal Taw3 proteins can methylate |FRAME: CPD-15399|, |FRAME: CPD-15386| and |FRAME: CPD-15388| at the N4 position (unlike the yeast enzyme, which can methylate only |FRAME: CPD-15399|) |CITS: [20382657]|. It is not known whether each of the two taw3 genes found in |FRAME: TAX-29292| can catalyze all activities, or perhaps each gene is specific for one or two substrates.

General Background, Sphingolipids are ubiquitous cell components present in eukaryotes and bacteria. A sphingolipid molecule is typically composed of a long-chain base (LCB, also known as sphingoid base), an amide linked fatty acyl chain, and a polar head. Ceramides (without a polar head group), glycosylceramides, and glycosylinositolphosphoceramides (GIPCs) are the predominant plant sphingolipids. Sphingomyelin, with phosphocholine as the polar head group, is the major sphingolipid in animals. Yeast contains predominantly inositolphosphoceramides (reviewed in |CITS: [Lynch04], [20028469]|., Some physiological roles of sphingolipids have been determined. Ceramides have been well known as inducers of programmed cell death in animal cells, and the same role was evidenced in plants (reviewed in |CITS: [20028469]|). In plants, GIPCs are involved in maintaining Golgi and ER integrity, in symbiosis, and function as GPI anchors for proteins (reviewed in |CITS: [20028469]|). Glycosylsphingolipids play roles in increasing plasma membrane stability, reducing ion permeability and pathogenesis. They were also implicated in chilling and freezing tolerance, as well as drought tolerance in plants (reviewed in |CITS: [20028469]|). Free LCBs (sphingoids) and phosphorylated LCBs (LCB-Ps, sphingoid 1-phosphates) were implicated as mediators of cellular responses. Like ceramides, LCBs were shown to promote programmed cell death in mammalian and plant cells. LCB-Ps were shown to be signaling intermediates in various cellular responses such as proliferation, differentiation, and cytoskeleton organization (reviewed in |CITS: [20028469]|). , About This Pathway, Ceramides are degraded by ceramidases. Ceramidases hydrolyze the N-acyl linkage between the long chain bases and the fatty acyl moieties. Ceramidases have been well characterized from human, yeast and a number of other organisms. The only characterized plant ceramidase is a rice ceramidase which however did not act with any of the predominant plant ceramides in vitro |CITS: [18547394]|. Expressing the rice ceramidase in a yeast mutant increased the yeast endogenous phytoceramide level, which indicated a reverse ceramidase activity of the rice enzyme. The in planta role of this plant ceramidase is unclear. Free long chain bases liberated from ceramides are further degraded into corresponding aldehydes and a phosphorylethanolamine via the intermediate long chain base 1-phosphates.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, A group of 6-deoxyhexoses, including |FRAME: CPD0-1112|, |FRAME: CPD-15609|, |FRAME: Fucopyranoses|, |FRAME: D-fucofuranose|, |FRAME: CPD-13886|, |FRAME: CPD-15611|, |FRAME: CPD-14794| and |FRAME: CPD-15598|, are used as components for the assembly of the O-anigens of certain Gram-negative bacteria. The same compounds are also used by some Gram-positive bacteria for construction of their S-layer., These modified sugar residues are synthesized in a dTDP nucleotide-activated form from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS:[17941826][19019146]|. The first biosynthetic pathway in this group that was biochemically characterized was |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY|. That pathway includes four reaction steps catalysed by the RmlABCD proteins., As more of the pathways were discovered, it was found that in all cases the biosynthetic pathways start with the same two steps:, The first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.24|, catalyzes the transfer of a thymidylmonophosphate nucleotide to |FRAME: GLC-1-P| |CITS: [11053865]|. The second enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.46|, catalyzes the oxidation of the C4 hydroxyl group of the sugar, followed by dehydration |CITS: [10666612][11243820]|. These two steps lead to formation of |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE|, the branching point for the different dTDP-sugars., Each of the sugars is synthesized by two or three transformation of |FRAME: DTDP-DEOH-DEOXY-GLUCOSE| (with the exception of |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, which is synthesized in a single step). These transformations are varied and can include epimerization, reduction, dehydrogenation, transamination, and acetylation.

Summary: |FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFAs) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes. The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in the |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived compounds (though the term is often used to include metabolites of 18- and 22-carbon PUFAs). , This pathway describes the liberation of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| from one of the most common glycerophopholipids in the cell, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine|, and its conversion to some of the more common icosanoids.

3-methylquinoline is commonly found in shale oil, aquifers affected by fossil fuel processing activities, in landfills contaminated by azaarene waste, and near creosote wood preservation plants. This compound is a known carcinogen, and its discharge poses a serious health threat and is an environmental concern., Relatively little information is available about the metabolism of methylquinolines, as compared with the well studied quinoline catabolism pathway. Strains of |FRAME:TAX-287| have been identified which hydroxylate 6-, 7-, and 8-methylquinoline, and |FRAME:TAX-1831| CH5, |FRAME:TAX-306| strain MPQ, an |FRAME:TAX-507| and an |FRAME:TAX-1663| strain have been isolated which degrade 2-methylquinoline. A bacterial strain, Comamonas testosteroni 63, was isolated from activated sludge, and is able to utilize 3-methylquinoline as a sole source of carbon, nitrogen and energy. The first step of the reaction involves the hydroxylation of 3-methylquinoline to form 3-methyl-2-oxo-1,2-dihydroquinoline via an oxidoreductase. Subsequently, a dioxygenation at the benzene ring by a dioxygenase results in the formation of 5,6-dihydrodiol-3-methyl-2-oxo-1,2-dihydroquinoline., 2,5,6-Trihydroxy-3-methylpyridine probably enters the maleamate pathway for further degradation |CITS: [8489738][7556204]|.

Summary: The eut operon, characterized from enteric bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-28901|, encodes enzymes required for the catabolism of |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| and its use as a carbon, nitrogen, and energy source |CITS: [1090845][784902][6374020][7868611]|., In these organisms the pathway occur within the lumen of a bacterial microcompartment (MPC) known as the eut metabolosome, a capsid-like shell composed of multiple proteins that is analogous to the carboxysome of cyanobacteria |CITS: [16585748]|. A similar compartment is used by these organsisms for the catabolism of |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| (see |FRAME: PWY-7013|). The metabolosome serves several functions - it protects the cells from the toxicity of the acetaldehyde intermediate |CITS: [16291677]|; it prevent carbon loss from volatilization of acetaldehyde |CITS: [16585748]|; and it makes it easier to recycle cofactors used in ethanolamine catabolism |CITS: [23585538]|. The eut operon, whose expression is induced by the presence of ethanolamine and |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, encodes all functions needed for the assembly and function of the metabolosome, as well as the enzymes of the3 pathway |CITS: [10464203][23920494]|. Full eut operons have been found in Enterobacteriaceae, Firmicutes, Nocardioides sp., and |FRAME: TAX-851|. It should be noted that many other organisms contain a much shorter operon that often includes only the genes encoding the first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.7| |CITS: [19783625]|., In the intestine, |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| is derived from |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE phosphatidylethanolamine|, a major component of eukaryotic membranes |CITS: [4888138][6304089]|. Use of |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| as a carbon or nitrogen source requires |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, which serves as the cofactor of |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.7| and a coinducer (with ethanolamine) of the eut operon transcription. While |FRAME: TAX-562|, which is not capable of producing |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| de novo, requires an external source of the cofactor, |FRAME: TAX-28901| can produce it under anaerobic conditions. It has been shown that one of the genes of the |FRAME: TAX-28901| operon, eutT, encodes |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.17| |CITS: [15516577]|., The operon also includes the eutE gene, which is assumed to encode |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.10|, and |FRAME: G7288|, which encodes the next enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.8| |CITS: [14996820]|.

Summary: In the mid 1990s more than 70 dead bald eagles (|FRAME: TAX-52644|) were found near the DeGray Lake in Arkansas. During the mortality events, sick eagles were observed overflying perches or colliding with rock walls. The reason was diagnosed as vacuolar myelinopathy, a neurological disease |CITS: [9823589]|., The cause of the disease was discovered only in 2021: it was |FRAME: CPD-27926|, a neurotoxin produced by the freshwater cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1550245|, which was found growing on aquatic vegetation, primarily the invasive species |FRAME: TAX-51024|. The toxin has a unique structure of a pentabrominated biindole nitrile, and appears to be produced in large amounts only in the presence of elevated bromide concentration, which is made available to the cyanobacterium by the senesce of |FRAME: TAX-51024|. H. verticillata leaves were shown to contain 500- to 1000-fold more bromide than the surrounding water |CITS: [33766860]|., The biosynthetic gene cluster encoding |FRAME: CPD-27926| biosynthesis was identified, and found to contain six genes, two of which encode putative halogenases. At the time the |FRAME: G-125007| gene product was purified and shown to act as a |FRAME: MONOMER-125009| |CITS: [33766860]|., In the following year the five enzymes that participate in the pathway were produced recombinantly, and their activity was characterized in vitro . |FRAME: CPD-27926 Aetokthonotoxin| is produced from two molecules of |FRAME: TRP| and its biosynthesis involves two halogenases (|FRAME: G-125007| and |FRAME: G-125009|), a tryptophenase-like enzyme (|FRAME: G-125010|), an unusual nitrile synthase (|FRAME: G-125008|) and a cytochrome P450 (|FRAME: G-125011|) |CITS: [ 35142504]|.

Some aerobic marine microorganisms produce |FRAME: CPD0-1068|. It has been estimated that ~16% of marine microbes are capable of phosphonate biosynthesis, whereas 0.6% have the capacity to synthesize |FRAME: CPD0-1068|. The key enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.73|, has been identified in both the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-338192| |CITS: [22936780]| and the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-198252| |CITS: [29217579]|, both of which are among the most abundant organisms in the sea., The archaeon |FRAME: TAX-338192| is believed to incorporate the compound into exopolysaccharides, similar to the |FRAME: CPD-9466|- and |FRAME: CPD-1106|-modified polymers found in many bacteria and lower eukaryotes |CITS: [22936780]|., Due to the activity of |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|, |FRAME: CPD0-1068| is a source of methane in the upper, aerobic ocean, where phosphorus-starved microbes catabolize it for its phosphorus, resulting in vast sections of the aerobic ocean that are supersaturated with methane |CITS: [Karl08][22936780]|.

Summary: |FRAME: THIAZOL-YL-INDOLE Camalexin| is the main phytoalexin in |FRAME: TAX-3702|. It is involved in plant defense and has cancer-preventive properties. The accumulation of camalexin is induced by an attack by a variety of microorganisms including bacteria, fungi and oomycetes. , Camalexin was previously proposed to be derived from indole-3-carboxaldehyde, independent of tryptophan. However, genetic evidence showed that camalexin is derived from tryptophan via |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETALDOXIME|, a branch point metabolite that also leads to the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolites glucosinolates (|FRAME: PWY-601|). Double-mutants of |FRAME: AT4G39950| and |FRAME: AT2G22330| were devoid of camalexin |CITS: [15148388]|. Indole-3-acetaldoxime is consequently converted to indole-3-acetonitrile (IAN) by |FRAME: AT2G30770| and CYP71A12 |CITS: [17573535][25953104]|. , Early in vivo feeding experiments suggested that the thiazole ring of camalexin is derived from cysteine |CITS: [9046593]|. However, it was later shown that the source of sulfur is glutathione |CITS: [21712415]|. Following the formation of the conjugate by |FRAME: AT1G02930| |CITS: [21239642]|, the γ-glutamyl residue of glutathione is removed by the cytosolic peptidases |FRAME: AT4G30530| and |FRAME: GQT-2803|. The glycine residue is assumed to be removed by an as-yet uncharacterized carboxypeptidase |CITS: [21712415]|., The last steps of camalexin biosynthesis are catalyzed by |FRAME: AT3G26830|, a multifunctional enzyme that forms |FRAME: INDOLE-CARBOXY-HYDRO-THIAZOLE| (DHCA) |CITS: [19567706]| and converts it to camalexin. CYP71B15 is the only known cytochrome P450 in plants that catalyzes both decarboxylation and introduction of a C-C double bond |CITS: [16766671]|. During the conversion of one molecule |FRAME: CPD-12636| to DHCA, one molecule of cyanide is released. In planta accumulation of cyanide may shut down the CYP P450 catalyzed camalexin biosynthesis process and thus cyanide is possibly detoxified via the cyanide detoxification pathway (|FRAME: ASPSYNII-PWY|). , The biosynthetic pathway is induced coordinately, and induction is trictly localized to the site of pathogen infection |CITS: [17073786]|.

Summary: General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmospheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5265|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the peptidoglycan found in Gram-positive Enterococci , including |FRAME: TAX-1352| and |FRAME: TAX-1354|. The peptidoglycan of these organisms is characterized by having |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of the pentapeptide, and by including a |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| bridge in the crosslinks between glycan strands., Six cytoplasmic steps catalyze the formation of the |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| precursor. This precursor is attached to the memberane acceptor |FRAME:CPD-9646|, generating |FRAME: NAcMur-Peptide-Peptidoglycan|, also known as lipid I., Another transferase adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding lipid II, which carries the full monomer unit, |FRAME:NAcMur-Peptide-NAcGlc-Undecaprenols |., The next step of the pathway describes the amidation of the |FRAME: D-GLT| at the second position of the pentapeptide. , In most of the organisms which have been examined, including |FRAME: TAX-1352|, the α-carboxyl group of |FRAME: D-GLT| is present as an amide; i.e. the second amino acid in the peptide sequence is |FRAME: CPD-12296| |CITS: [5219821][6025572][5968582]|. Some characterization of the reaction has been carried out, although the identity of the enzyme that catalyzes it in |FRAME: TAX-1352| is still unknown |CITS: [5638594]|., Following amidation, the final lipid intermediate is transferred by an as yet unknown mechanism through the membrane., The peptidoglycan monomers are polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide crosslinks |CITS: [11320055]|. While some of these enzymes are mono-functional, the main enzymes are bifunctional proteins possessing both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activities |CITS: [9791115]|., Peptide cross-links form between different parts of the peptides depending on the organism. In |FRAME: TAX-1352| the crosslinks includes an interpeptide bridge of a single |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| residue (see |FRAME: PWY-6461|). |FRAME: CPD-302| is added to lipid II by a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15487| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-11868| gene) |CITS: [16510449]| and is subsequently amidated to |FRAME: CPD-3633| by the |FRAME: G-11898|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-15525|. The crosslinks are formed between the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide and the amino group of the |FRAME: CPD-3633| of a peptide in a second glycan chain., The crosslinking reaction is catalyzed by D-D transpeptidases, a group of enzymes that belong to the |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin-binding proteins"| (PBPs), and involves the cleavage of the D-alanyl-D-alanine bond of the pentapeptides, which provides the energy to drive the reaction. As a result, the peptides in the peptidoglycan polymers are one amino acid shorter than the peptides in the monomers. These crosslinking enzymes are the target of β-lactam antibiotics., Penicillin Resistance, Some Enterococci, including |FRAME: TAX-1352|, are intrinsically resistant to moderate levels of |FRAME: CPD-9195|, with MICs typically ranging from 1 to 16 μg/ml., Studies performed with |FRAME: TAX-1354| showed that one such enzyme in particular, |FRAME: MONOMER-15537|, is responsible for the resistance in this strain. This enzyme, which has a a low-affinity towards penicillin, can substitute the functions of the other PBPs which become inactive in the presence of the antibiotic., While the |FRAME: G-11910| gene is located on a plasmid in |FRAME: TAX-1354|, it is chromosomally located in |FRAME: TAX-1352|, and is considered to be intrinsic to the species, although it can be treansferred among strains by chromosome-to-chromosome transfer |CITS: [16304165]|., Recently, an increase in ampicillin resistance has been observed in clinical |FRAME: TAX-1352| isolates. , Studies showed that increased resistance results from two mechanisms - over-production of |FRAME: MONOMER-15537| (expression of the enzyme is controlled by a regulator that is encoded upstream by the psr gene), and mutation of the enzyme to become less sensitive to the antibiotics |CITS: [7811006][9158761][8759860]|., A 2001 study reported that |FRAME: G-11910| is responsible for intrinsic resistance only to moderate levels of ampicillin, and by itself cannot confer high-level resistance |CITS: [11502534]|. However, this conclusion has been disputed |CITS: [18676222]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Pacidamycins pacidamycins| are a family of uridyl-peptide antibiotics. The first 7 compounds (pacidamycin 1-7) were discovered in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-116188| isolated from a soil sample collected at Offenburg, Germany. When discovered, the compounds were reported to exhibit highly specific activity only against |FRAME: TAX-287|, though a high level of resistance developed quite quickly |CITS: [2498263]|. Analysis of their structures has shown that the pacidamycins are composed of a pseudopeptide backbone (which contains 2S,3S-diaminobutanoate) linked by a unique exocyclic enamide to an atypical 3'-deoxyuridine nucleoside. They differ mostly in their terminal amino acid residues |CITS: [2498264]|. Additional pacidamycins (D, 4N and 5T) were reported in 2000 from a different strain |CITS: [11217807]|., The pacidamycins were reported to inhibit |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.13| (mraY) |CITS: [10557368][16789873]|. Dihydropacidamycins, produced synthetically by hydrogenation of the C(4') exocyclic olefin, were reported to have antimicrobial activity similar to that of the natural products, while being effective against additional Gram-negative pathogens |CITS: [11456620][12951115]|., About This Pathway, The pacidamycin gene cluster was identified twice (independently) in 2010 |CITS: [20665770][20826445]|. The cluster consists of several highly dissociated non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) domains and modules, which many of the proteins consisting of only a single domain. An initial pathway has been proposed at the time |CITS: [20826445]|, and has been revised within a year to reflect additional information about the participating enzymes |CITS: [21417270]|., A set of nine enzymes was shown to be sufficient for assembly of tetrapeptide pacidamycins such as |FRAME: CPD-27221| |CITS: [21417270]|. The enzyme required for addition of the fifth amino acid, PacB, was identified shortly after |CITS: [21746899]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8528|). Another study from the same year unveiled how the dehydroaminonucleoside component |FRAME: CPD-27224| is formed from |FRAME: URIDINE| by three enzymes |CITS: [21861518]|., The formation of last remaining component, |FRAME: CPD-27226|, from |FRAME: THR| was discovered only in 2024, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8526| |CITS: [38456538]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-21056 Toxoflavin| is a yellow pigmented toxin containing a 7-azapteridine core. It was originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-28095| as a contributor (along with |FRAME: CPD-21066|) to a food poisoning in Java in the 1930s |CITS: [vanVeen34][vanVeen34a][vanDamme60]|. In addition to its toxicity towards mammals, toxoflavin exhibits antibiotic activity against a variety of bacteria and fungi |CITS: [8500202]| and phytotoxicity against a broad range of monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants. Toxoflavin is produced by the plant pathogens |FRAME: TAX-337| and |FRAME: TAX-28095| (and some other bacterial strains), where it functions as a key virulence factor leading to bacterial panicle blight of rice seedlings and bacterial wilt of numerous plant species |CITS: [Jeong03][Nandakumar09][20731786][26077901]|., Toxoflavin is toxic only under aerobic conditions. It has been proposed to act as an active electron carrier between NADH and oxygen, producing toxic hydrogen peroxide and bypassing the cytochrome system |CITS: [14462713]|., About This Pathway, The toxoflavin biosynthetic gene cluster has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-337| by the use of transposon mutagenesis |CITS: [Suzuki04a]|. In addition to a biosynthetic operon that contains the toxA-E genes, the cluster also contains genes involved in resistance and export of toxoflavin., The early part of the toxoflavin pathway is identical to that of flavin biosynthesis (see |FRAME: RIBOSYN2-PWY|). The toxB gene encodes |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.25|, homologous to |FRAME: EG11331 RibA| of |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [Suzuki04a]|, and toxE is a homolog of the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG11321 RibD|, a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.26|, and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.193| |CITS: [26077901]|, Following dephosphorylation, |FRAME: AMINO-RIBOSYLAMINO-1H-3H-PYR-DIONE| is proposed to be converted to |FRAME: CPD-21063| through an unknown mechanism by ToxD and/or ToxC |CITS: [26077901]|. The last two steps in the pathway are catalyzed by a bifunctional methyltransferase encoded by toxA |CITS: [27070241]|.
