Summary: |FRAME: GLYCOL "Ethylene glycol"| has many applications commercially. It is used in antifreeze solutions and for the chemical synthesis of glyoxal, |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: GLYOX|. |FRAME: GLYOX "Glyoxylate"| is a building block for a variety of molecules of industrial interest. , While |FRAME:TAX-562| encodes the enzymes shown in this pathway by which it can degrade ethylene glycol to |FRAME: GLYOX| and subsequently 3-phosphoglycerate which can enter central metabolism through glycolysis, wild type cannot metabolize this alcohol at a sufficient rate to support growth. However, certain mutant strains with altered patterns of gene expression, can grow on ethylene glycol as a total source of carbon and energy. Some strains of |FRAME: TAX-303| may also express all or part of this pathway and are hence able to metabolize ethylene glycol to glyoxylate or further |CITS: [23023748]|.

General Background, Creatine is a naturally occurring amino acid that is used to store and supply energy to muscle cells in vertebrates., The name creatine is derived from the Greek kreas (flesh)., The enzyme creatine kinase adds a phosphate to creatine (see |FRAME: CREATINE-KINASE-RXN|), generating, |FRAME: CREATINE-P|. The energy stored in the creatine-phosphate bond can be reused when creatine phosphate, reacts with ADP to regenerate ATP. , In fast-twitch skeletal muscles, a large pool of creatine-phosphate is available for immediate regeneration of ATP, hydrolyzed during short periods of intense work. Because of the high cytosolic creatine kinase activity in these, muscles, the creatine kinase reaction remains in a near-equilibrium state, keeping ADP and ATP almost constant,, and buffering the cytosolic phosphorylation potential that is crucial for proper functioning of cellular ATPases, |CITS: [10893433]|., Creatine is found in the blood, brain, and muscle of many organisms. , Creatinine is a breakdown product of creatine phosphate in muscle, and is usually produced at a fairly constant rate, by the body in a nonenzymatic process. Creatinine is not reabsorbed, and is mainly filtered by the kidney and, excreted in the urine., Both creatine and creatinine can be used by microorganisms as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [Tsuru77]|., At least three different routes by which different microbes degrade creatinine have been discovered, |CITS: [10893433]|., About This Pathway, A second metabolic pathway for the degradation of creatinine was discovered in |FRAME: ORG-5940| |CITS: [Yamada85a]|, and later detected in several organisms, including |FRAME:TAX-286|, |FRAME:TAX-1696|, |FRAME:TAX-475|, Micrococcus,|FRAME:TAX-1663|, |FRAME:TAX-1485| and |FRAME:TAX-41273| |CITS: [1510564][10893433]|., In this pathway, creatinine is not hydrolyzed back to creatine. Instead, it is deaminated to N-methylhydantoin, releasing an amonia molecule, by the action of creatinine deaminase (also known as creatinine iminohydrolase). , In all organisms studied so far, a single enzyme shares both creatinine deaminase and cytosine deaminase, |CITS: [10893433]|., N-methylhydantoin is then hydrolyzed to N-carbamoylsarcosine, by the action of N-methylhydantoin amidohydrolase, at the expense of one ATP molecule |CITS: [3827889]|. N-carbamoylsarcosine is deaminated further to sarcosine by N-carbamoylsarcosine amidohydrolase, releasing a second ammonia molecule., In the last step of this pathway, which is shared with |FRAME: CRNFORCAT-PWY|, sarcosine is hydrolyzed to glycine and formaldehyde, by either sarcosine dehydrogenase or sarcosine oxidase., All of the enzyme involved in this pathway are highly inducible when the bacteria grow on creatinine as the main source, of nitrogen, and in some cases, carbon., Many organisms, including Bacillus, |FRAME:TAX-1716|, |FRAME:TAX-237|, |FRAME:TAX-561| and |FRAME:TAX-583| as well as some fungi (including Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus bacillisporous) were reported to be able to catalyze only the first step of this pathway, accumulating N-methylhydantoin. Apparently, the reason for this wide distribution is the fact that the enzyme catalyzing this reaction,, creatinine deiminase, is the abundant enzyme cytosine deaminase |CITS: [Kim87]|. Since most of these organisms lack the enzymes that catalyze subsequent steps, this first step may be considered a side effect of cytosine deaminase rather than a true degradation pathway |CITS: [10893433]|., Since mammals do not have a creatininase function, creatinine is absorberd in the kidneys and released into urine. As a result, measuring the level of creatinine in the blood and urine provides an accurate measure of renal function. Assays for measuring creatinine concentration based on the enzymes that participate in this pathway have been developed |CITS: [Siedel88][8611752]|.

Summary: General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway: , Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes have been involved in a variety of biological processes: inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161],[16114093]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Isopimaric acid, an pimarane-type DRA, is one of the principal resin acids |CITS:[17082986],[11269960]|. This compound has been shown to have antimicrobial properties when used against multidrug-resistant and EMRSA strains of |FRAME:TAX-1280| |CITS:[16114093]|. Moreover, isopimaric acid was demonstrated to inhibit strongly spore germination of the ascomycete Ophiostoma ips (a parasitic fungus closely associated with bark-boring beetle) |CITS:[KOPPER05]|. The formation of this acid involves the formation of the pimarane skeleton via cyclization of the diterpenoid precursor |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This cyclization occurs via the formation of the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-4750| and is followed by the stepwise oxidation of the C18 methyl group of the derived olefin |FRAME:CPD-8699|. Several abietadiene synthases have been identified, which can produce a variety of other olefins including |FRAME:CPD-8699| |CITS:[8798524],[15310829],[16497345]|. The mechanism of oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-8699| to |FRAME:CPD-8729| resembles that of the oxidation of |FRAME:CPD1F-128| to |FRAME:CPD1F-132| and that |FRAME:CPD1F-132| to |FRAME:CPD1F-95| (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|) in which a single multifunctional enzyme (ent-kaurene oxidase) catalyze the consecutive oxidation steps. No single enzyme has been found to date that could catalyze all three conversion steps from |FRAME:CPD-8699| to |FRAME:CPD-8729|, however, one enzyme from |FRAME:TAX-3352| (loblolly pine) could catalyze the two oxidation steps between |FRAME:CPD-8726| and |FRAME:CPD-8729| |CITS:[15911762]|. This same enzyme was additionally shown to be involved in the formation of other diterpene resin acids (such as |FRAME:CPD-8725|, |FRAME:CPD-8708| and |FRAME:CPD-8712|) |CITS:[15911762]|. To date, however, no enzyme catalyzing the first step of oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-8699| to |FRAME:CPD-8726| has been identified.

Summary: General Background, Disproportionation is a process in which a reactant is both oxidized and reduced in the same chemical reaction, forming two separate compounds. The disproportionation of |FRAME: S2O3|, an important step in sulfur transformation in aquatic systems, was discovered in 1987 |CITS: [Bak87]|. Thiosulfate-disproportionating bacteria are numerically significant, and have been detected in high numbers in several environments, including freshwater, mud, and marine sediments (see |FRAME:PWY-5277|)., Several microorganisms have also been shown to grow by the disproportionation of elemental sulfur |CITS: [16348835]|. This observation was initially surprising, because under standard conditions the reaction is endergonic with G'° = 40.9 kJ. However, the removal of sulfide, which occurs in the presence of sulfide scavengers such as oxidized metals (for example iron and manganese oxides) makes the process energetically favorable |CITS: [15028874]|., About This Pathway, The first organisms that were shown to disproportionate sulfur were anaerobic (see |FRAME: P203-PWY|) |CITS:[16348835][9435068]|. However, the thermoacidophilic chemolithotrophic sulfur-metabolizing archaeons of the genus, |FRAME: TAX-12914| can obtain energy through the aerobic disproportionation of elemental sulfur to |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME:HS|., The initial enzyme in the aerobic sulfur oxidation pathway of |FRAME: TAX-12914| is a soluble, cytoplasmic sulfur oxygenase reductase (SOR) |CITS: [2493451]|. The SOR catalyzes the oxygen-dependent disproportionation of elemental sulfur leading to |FRAME: HS|, |FRAME: SO3|, and |FRAME: S2O3| as reaction products, although the latter is likely the result of a chemical reaction between sulfite and sulfur |CITS: [2493451]|. Sulfur acts simultaneously as electron donor and electron acceptor, as no external electron donor or cofactor, not even glutathione, is required., SORs have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-2283| and from |FRAME: TAX-146920| |CITS: [2493451][12664265]|, and found to be very large complexes (an icosatetramer in the case of |FRAME: TAX-2283|) composed of a single type of subunit |CITS: [1569862]|. The monomers assemble to create a large hollow sphere enclosing a positively charged, nanocompartment. Apolar channels provide access for linear sulfur compounds. The active sites, accessible from inside the sphere, contain a cysteine persulfide and a low-potential mononuclear non-heme iron ligated by a 2-His-1-carboxylate facial triad. the iron is likely the site of both sulfur reduction and sulfur oxidation |CITS: [16484493]|.

Summary: Benzene is a highly toxic industrial compound with a broad range of industrial uses. It is one of the top 20 production volume chemicals in the United States, with an annual production of almost 9 million metric tons. In addition to being a component of petroleum-based fuels, benzene is often used as a raw material for the manufacture of other chemicals, rubbers, lubricants, dyes, detergents, drugs, and pesticides. Benzene is among the most prevalent organic contaminants in groundwater and is a major concern due to its toxicity and relatively high solubility |CITS: [12558180]|., Many soil bacteria, notably Pseudomonas species, are able to catabolize a wide variety of natural and man-made aromatic compounds. The catabolism of aromatic compounds under aerobic conditions by these bacteria generally requires the formation of dihydroxy aromatic intermediates. The initial dihydroxylation reaction is carried out by ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase enzymes that incorporate both atoms of molecular oxygen into the aromatic nucleus to form cis-dihydrodiols |CITS: [8344526]|., A number of dioxygenases from different strains of |FRAME: TAX-303| have been well characterized, for example those for toluene (|FRAME:CPLX-6702|), naphthalene (|FRAME:CPLX-7256|) and benzoate (|FRAME:CPLX-2541|). These enzymes are multicomponent, and consist of one or two redox proteins that transfer electrons from NADH to the terminal dioxygenase, a non-heme iron-sulfur protein that dihydroxylates the aromatic substrate |CITS: [3446181]|., |FRAME: TAX-160393| can grow on |FRAME:BENZENE| as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [167712]|. A soluble enzyme system was purified from this organism capable of coverting |FRAME:BENZENE| to |FRAME:CATECHOL|., The system was shown to be composed of a |FRAME:CPLX-7283| and a |FRAME:CPLX-7285| |CITS: [4362337]|. The catabolic plasmid pHMT112 carried by this strain was found to carry the bed gene cluster encoding both enzymes (bedC1C2BA and bedD). However, similar genes were found on the chromosome of a different strain of |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS:[3667527]|.

Glycerol is a good feedstock for butanol production because it is inexpensive and readily available, being a byproduct of biodiesel production., About this Pathway, The butanol biosynthesis pathway from glycerol, depicted here is a naturally occurring one in |FRAME: TAX-1501|, albeit a system with a low yield of butanol due to the limitations of the naturally occurring ABE fermentation mechanism. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-18905 Chlorophyll a2| is a type of chlorophyll found only in marine cyanobacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-1218| genus. It differs from the prevalent |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| (sometimes referred to as chlorophyll a1) by having a double bond at position C81 resulting in a second vinyl group at C8 (another vinyl group, at position C3, is common to both |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| and |FRAME: CPD-18905|). Thus the pigment is also referred to as 3,8-divinyl chlorophyll a. |FRAME: CPD-18905 Chlorophyll a2| has absorption and fluorescence excitation maxima in the blue part of the visible spectrum red-shifted by 8 to 10 nm compared to |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|., In 1983 an unknown red-shifted chlorophyll a derivative was described from subtropical Atlantic waters - the first description of |FRAME: CPD-18905| |CITS: [Gieskes83]|. The absorption spectrum of this new pigment was identical to that of |FRAME: CPD-18905|, which was purified previously from a mutant of |FRAME: TAX-4577| |CITS: [Bazzaz81][Bazzaz82]|., While the first observation of |FRAME: TAX-1218| was published already in 1979, the authors were not certain about the identitiy of the cells, which they isolated at a depth of 100 m and called "type II cells". The authors did suggest that the cells may not contain phycoerythrin since they contained many "greenish autofluorescing cells" . At the time, no correlation was made between the organisms and |FRAME: CPD-18905| |CITS: [Johnson79]|., Due to their tiny size, further characterization of |FRAME: TAX-1218| became possible only in 1988 with the introduction of shipboard flow cytometry equipment. The authors announceed the new genus |FRAME: TAX-1218|, and reported that it contains unusual divinyl chlorophyll forms |FRAME: CPD-18905| and |FRAME: CPD-22996| |CITS: [Chisholm88][Chisholm92]|., All photosynthetic organsims produce a divinyl intermediate in their cholorophyll biosynthesis pathway - |FRAME: DIVINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|. However, all other organisms possess the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.13|, which reduces the double bond at C81, forming the monovinyl |FRAME: MONO-VINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|, which is processed further to the different chlorophyll species. |FRAME: TAX-1218| is unique in lacking this enzyme, and thus the pathway continues with divinyl species |CITS: [15632054]|., In addition to evolving divinyl chlorophylls, |FRAME: TAX-1218| species also evolved modified D1 proteins in the action center of their photosystem II complexes that accomodate binding of the divinyl chlorophylls |CITS: [22006316]|.

Summary: Please note: This is a general detoxification pathway, where the first step can be catalyzed by many different enzymes, collectively known as glutathione transferases, or GSTs. In the first reaction, R may be an aliphatic, aromatic or heterocyclic group, and X may be a sulfate, nitrile or halide group, or simply a proton., General Background, Thiols play several major roles in the cell; they help maintain the redox balance, keeping a reduced environment (see the pathway |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY|), they fight reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS and NOS, respectively), and they are involved in the detoxification of many other toxins and stress-inducing factors., In most organisms the major thiol is the tripeptide |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly, known as GSH). GSH is active against toxins by a process that involves multiple enzymes, and in the case of eukaryotes, occurs across multiple organs., About This Pathway, In this important detoxification mechanism GSH binds to electrophilic chemicals, forming conjugates which are exported from the cell. These conjugation reactions have been demonstrated for a multitude of foreign chemicals, as well as endogenous reactive intermediates. GSH has been shown to form thioether conjugates with leukotrienes, |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, hepoxilin, |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|, hydroxyalkenals, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, |FRAME: L-DIHYDROXY-PHENYLALANINE|, |FRAME: DOPAMINE|, and |FRAME: MALEATE|, and it forms thioesters with |FRAME: CYS|, |FRAME: CO-A|, proteins, and other cellular thiols |CITS: [9755286]|. In addition, GSH also binds endogenous metals, such as copper, selenium, chromium, and zinc, via nonenzymatic reactions. , The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-5803|, a family of enzymes found mainly in the cytosol. Once formed, the |FRAME: S-Substituted-Glutathione "glutathione-S conjugates"| are metabolized by the same degradative enzymes that metabolize GSH (see |FRAME: PWY-4041|). The GSH-toxin conjugate is transported out of the cell, where it is subsequently degraded by |FRAME: HS06361-MONOMER| or |FRAME: CPLX-6042|, and dipeptidases. The breakdown products of the GSH-toxin conjugates (glutamate and glycine) are reabsorbed and can be used for GSH synthesis. The |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "L-cysteine-S-conjugate"| that is left is also transported back into the cell, where it can be metabolized in different ways. , One route is the acetylation of the amino group of the cysteinyl residue by intracellular N-acetyltransferases to form the corresponding |FRAME: Mercapturates "mercapturic acids"| (N-acetylcysteine S-conjugates). The addition of the N-acetylcysteine moiety generally increases the compound's polarity and water solubility, and converts neutral compounds to anions, facilitating their transport across cell membranes and their excretion from the organism |CITS: [4892500]|. Mercapturic acids are released into the circulation or bile |CITS: [ 1939239]|; some are eventually excreted in urine, and some may undergo further metabolism., A second route for |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "L-cysteine-S-conjugates"| is the breakage of the carbon-sulfur bond, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.13|, resulting in the formation of thiols, pyruvate and ammonia |CITS: [4024656][Field96][9045797][15627473]|. This enzymatic activity has been shown in both eukaryotes |CITS: [5627473]| and prokaryotes |CITS: [12480900]|. The thiols that are produced in this reaction are most likely oxidized to sulfonates or methylated to methylsulfinyl or methylsulfonyl derivatives., Yet additional fates for |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "L-cysteine-S-conjugates"| are possible. It has been shown that these compounds can be substrates for other enzymes, including aminotransferase and L-amino acid oxidase |CITS: [15627473]|., While this pathway has been studied in detail in eukaryotes, considerably less is known about bacteria. Recent sequencing projects of bacterial genomes have revealed the presence of numerous glutathione S-transferase genes in many microbes |CITS: [9045797][11876405]|. Biochemical evidence for the activity of such enzymes is also abundant. It has also been shown that glutathione conjugates can be metabolized to cysteine conjugates by the action of soil microorganisms, although the specific enzymes involved in the process have not been identified |CITS: [Field96]|. It seems that bacteria are more likely to continue by the cysteine-S-conjugate β-lyase route, as there are several reports for this activity in bacteria |CITS: [4024656][12480900]|.

|FRAME: 8-Methylmenaquinones 8-Methylmenaquinone| is a methylated form of menaquinone that is produced by a diverse range of microorganisms that include members of the bacterial phyla |FRAME: TAX-201174 Actinobacteria| and |FRAME: TAX-1224 Proteobacteria| as well as the archaeal phyla |FRAME: TAX-28889 Crenarchaeota| and |FRAME: TAX-28890 Euryarchaeota| |CITS: [6663282][3937542][2312688][26472620][28164386]|., The addition of methyl groups to menaquinone shifts the redox potential to more negative values |CITS: [Schmid99][19265668]|, making these derivatives good redox mediators in electron transport chains that use low-potential electron acceptors such as polysulfide or sulfite |CITS: [11856339]|., |FRAME: TAX-844| is known to produce |FRAME: CPD-9724| using the futalosine pathway, as well as |FRAME: CPD-19843| (MMK6), depending on the growth conditions. The former is involved in fumarate, nitrate and nitrite respiration, while the latter is used during growth by fumarate and polysulfide respiration |CITS: [11803015][11856339][19171117]|. Apparently MMK6 serves as the redox partner for a dedicated type of a membrane-bound fumarate reductase complex, named Mfr |CITS: [19170876]|., The enzyme responsible for the methylation of menaquinone is a class C radical SAM methyltransferase enzyme. It uses two molecules of SAM - one serves as the methyl group donor, while the other is cleaved into methionine and |FRAME: CPD-15400|, which helps drive the reaction forward., The |FRAME: G-55044| gene, which encodes the enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-844|, is located upstream of the psr locus encoding the PsrABC |FRAME: CPLX-7195 "polysulfide reductase complex"|. Orthologs (named either |FRAME: G-55044| or |FRAME: G-55045|, depending whether the organism produces menaquinone via the futalosine or cannonical pathways) were discovered in most 8-methylmenaquinon-producing organisms, with the exception of euryarchaeal species |CITS: [28164386]|.

Summary: General Background, The ability to reduce sulfur using |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| or organic substrates as electron donors is widespread among thermophiles. It is mostly found in hyperthermophilic archea living in volcanic habitats, and in mesophilic and thermophilic bacteria living in anoxic marine or brackish sediments, fresh water sediments, bovine rumen, hot water pools from solfataric fields, and volcanic hot springs |CITS: [FEMSMicRev22-353]|. Some methanogens, especially the thermophilic and hyperthermophilic members of the genera |FRAME:TAX-2319|, |FRAME:TAX-2160|, |FRAME:TAX-2179|, and |FRAME:TAX-2184| are also able to reduce elemental sulfur to |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [Stetter83]|., Some of the organisms (including members of the archaebacterial genera |FRAME:TAX-2260|, |FRAME:TAX-2270|, Pyrodictum, |FRAME:TAX-12914|, |FRAME:TAX-12914|, |FRAME:TAX-41674| and |FRAME:TAX-2276|) are able to use |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| as the sole energy source. These organisms must couple sulfur reduction to ADP phosphorylation. The majority of sulfur reducers, however, grow organotrophically, and can utilize complex substrates such as proteins. Since some of these organisms excrete organic products such as |FRAME: ACET| or |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|, the metabolic significance of sulfur reduction in them is less clear, |CITS: [Schauder93]|., Elemental sulfur is not a good substrate for enzymatic reactions because its solubility in water is very low (5 μg/L at 25 °) |CITS: [Boulegue78]|. One mechanism that solves the problem is the conversion of the sulfur ring to a more soluble sulfur intemediate (sometimes referred to as activated sulfur) prior to reduction |CITS:[16346781][Zoephel88][Schauder93]|. This mechanism has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-844|, in which the soluble compound has been shown to be |FRAME: Polysulfides| |CITS: [Klimmek91]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5364|)., A second possibility is the physical attachment of the microbes to the elemental sulfur, resulting in a direct conversion of sulfur to sulfide. Such physical attachment has been shown to be important during aerobic sulfur oxidation by |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS:[16349107][16535613]|. In addition, a recently purified |FRAME: CPLX-7193| from the acidophilic hyperthermophile |FRAME: TAX-2283| was shown to oxidize elemental sulfur in vitro without the need for |FRAME: HS| |CITS: [12949162]|. Since polysulfides are unstable at low pH, it is possible that |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| is the actual substrate for acidophilic organisms. With the exception of a few organisms, it is still not clear which of these two possible mechanisms is used by the different sulfur reducers., About This Pathway, Elemental sulfur, while having little solubility, is readily converted to polysulfide in aqueous solutions containing sulfide. The sulfur ring is cleaved by a nucleophilic attack of the sulfide, forming a linear polysulfide, as shown in the equation:, |FRAME:RXN-8380|, Evidence gathered from experiments with several different bacteria and archaea suggested that a sulfur solubilization step is involved in the reduction of elemental sulfur. For example, sulfur reduction by membrane fractions of |FRAME: TAX-65553| was facilitated by the addition of sulfide to the medium |CITS: [Zoephel88]|, and polysulfides were involved in sulfur reduction by |FRAME: TAX-876| |CITS: [Cammack84]|., A study about the role of polysulfides in sulfur reduction by the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2261| found that the organism does not need to be in direct contact with the sulfur to metabolize it, and that polysulfides serve as substrates for sulfur reduction |CITS: [16348181]|. A cytoplasmic |FRAME:CPLX-7194| was isolated from this organism that catalyzed the reduction of polysulfide to |FRAME: HS| with NADPH as the electron accpetor |CITS: [7961401]|., In some strains of sulfate reducing bacteria, the sulfur reductase appears to be cytochrome c3. Purified cytochromes from |FRAME: TAX-876| strain Norway 4 and another sulfate-reducing strain were able to reduce colloidal sulfur to |FRAME: HS| in vitro |CITS: [229785]|., Perhaps the best characterized system is found in |FRAME: TAX-844|, where it has been shown that the main substrate for sulfur reduction is polysulfides |CITS: [Klimmek91]|. A reductase that was originally purified from this bacterium as sulfur reductase |CITS: [Schroeder88]| was eventually renamed to |FRAME: CPLX-7195| |CITS: [1597189]|, and the genes encoding it were cloned and sequenced. This enzyme is a membrane-bound molybdoenzyme, which oxidizes |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| with electrons obtained from either a hydrogenase or a formate dehydrogenase, through a methyl-menaquinone-6 electron carrier |CITS: [11856339]|., It should be noted that in addition to this |FRAME: CPLX-7195|, |FRAME: TAX-844| appears to have another sulfur/polysulfide reductase, as mutants lacking this enzyme were still able to grow by the reduction of either elemental sulfur or polysulfides, although the growth yield was about 25% of that obtained by the wild type |CITS: [Ringel96]|.

Names: acyl-[acyl-carrier protein] thioesterase pathway // acyl-ACP thioesterase pathway // acyl-[acp] thioesterase pathway
Summary: Acyl-[acyl-carrier protein] thioesterases (acyl-[acp] thioesterases) terminate the process of de novo fatty acid biosynthesis by releasing free fatty acids from acyl-[acyl-carrier proteins] (see |FRAME:FASYN-ELONG-PWY|)., In plants, fatty acid biosynthesis occurs in the plastid and thus requires plastid-localized acyl-[acp] thioesterases. The main products of acyl-[acp] thioesterase are |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| (C18:1) and to a lesser extent |FRAME: PALMITATE| (C16:0) in the vegetative tissues of all plants. The released free fatty acids are re-esterified to coenzyme A in the plastid envelope and exported out of plastid., There are two isoforms of acyl-[acp] thioesterase in plants - FatA and FatB. Substrate specificity of these isoforms determines the chain length and level of saturated fatty acids. The highest activity of FatA is with |FRAME: Oleoyl-ACPs "oleoyl-[acp]"|. FatA has very low activities towards other acyl-[acp]s when compared with |FRAME: Oleoyl-ACPs "oleoyl-[acp]"|. FatB has highest activity with |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"|. It also has significant high activity with |FRAME: Oleoyl-ACPs "oleoyl-[acp]"|, followed by |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| and |FRAME: Palmitoleoyl-ACPs "palmitoleoyl-[acp]"|. Kinetics studies of FatA and FatB indicate that their substrate specificities with different acyl-[acp]s come from the Kcat values, rather than from Km, as the Km values of the two isoforms with different substrates are similar, in the micromolar order. Domain swapping of FatA and FatB indicates the N-terminus of the isoforms determines their substrate specificities |CITS: [12061798]|., Plants that predominantly accumulate medium-chain length saturated fatty acids in their seeds have evolved specialized FatB and/or FatA thioesterases |CITS: [11337402]|. For example, coconut, in which |FRAME: DODECANOATE| (12:0) is the predominant seed oil fatty acid, has a corresponding medium-chain acyl-[acp] thioesterase activity.

Summary: |FRAME: Xanthan Xanthan| is an exopolysaccharide produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-339| and related species. It was approved for use in foods in 1968 and is a common food additive, used primarily as a thickener due to its ability to increase the viscosity of liquids., The polymer is composed of repeating pentasaccharide units with the structure of a β-1,4-linked D-glucose backbone with trisaccharide side chains composed of mannose-(β-1,4)-glucuronic acid-(β-1,2)-mannose attached to, alternate glucose residues in the backbone by α-1,3 linkages |CITS: [1212669]|., The terminal repeat unit is anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane by an undecaprenyldiphosphate lipid carrier, and assembly of the repeating unit occurs while anchored. Acetyl and pyruvyl residues are often added at the C6 position of the mannose units, with the pyruvate forming an acetal structure. , The biosynthetic pathway by which xanthan is produced involves several steps |CITS: [7683019]|: , (1) assembly of pentasaccharide subunits attached to an inner-membrane polyprenol phosphate carrier, (2) addition of acetyl and pyruvate groups, (3) polymerization of the pentasaccharide repeating units and secretion of xanthan., The genes encoding the proteins of xanthan biosynthesis are located in the gum gene cluster, which encompasses a 14 kb region. Most of the genes have been characterized by mutation |CITS: [7683019][9537354]|. Five genes, |FRAME: G-12289|, |FRAME: G-12290|, |FRAME: G-12291|, |FRAME: G-12292| and |FRAME: G-12293|, are responsible for assmembly of the pentasaccharide. Two acetyltransferases, encoded by |FRAME: G-12294| and |FRAME: G-12295|, can acetylate the C6 carbon of the inner and outer mannose residue, respectively. Alternatively, the C6 position of the outer (but not inner) mannose can be pyruvylated by |FRAME: G-12296|., The final assembly of the polymer involves the translocation of the mature pentasaccharide unit from the cytoplasm to the periplasm, probably catalyzed by gumJ gene product, polymerization, potentially catalyzed by the gumE gene product, and export via the outer membrane, potentially catalyzed by a complex formed by the products of gumB and gumC |CITS: [9537354][18304669]|. However, the function of the enzymes involved in polymerization and export has not been verified experimentally yet.

The lignan |FRAME:CPD-17595| is a typical component of heartwood in angiosperm trees |CITS:[Erdtman79]| that serves as long-term protectant against pathogen attacks and significantly contributes to the robustness, hence lifespan, of the trees |CITS:[20371107]|. In addition, yatein is a key intermediate in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-8959| and its derivatives (see |FRAME: PWY-7749|), which are important precursors for anti-cancer drugs such as |FRAME:CPD-16754|, |FRAME:CPD-16755| and |FRAME:CPD-17609| |CITS:[Umezawa03][15378293]|. Lignans such as |FRAME:CPD-8912| and |FRAME:CPD-17592| have also been reported to exhibit antiradical and antioxidant properties and may have a potential as natural nutraceuticals |CITS:[Yen12]|., The biosynthetic steps from |FRAME:CPD-8912| to |FRAME:CPD-17595| have been elucidated in |FRAME: TAX-48027|, a plant rich in |FRAME:CPD-8912| and |FRAME:CPD-8958| |CITS:[Suzuki02]|, by feeding radio-labeled lignans to young shoots |CITS:[12956064]|. The results propmpted a suggestion for a pathway consisting of the following steps:, 5-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-8912| to form |FRAME:CPD-17592|,, O-dimethylation at positions C-4 and C-5 to generate |FRAME:CPD-17594| via |FRAME:CPD-17593| , methylenedioxy bridge formation at C3' and C4', giving rise to |FRAME:CPD-17595|., The first O-methylation step of the pathway, the 5-O-methylation of |FRAME:CPD-17592| forming |FRAME:CPD-17593|, is catalyzed by a thujaplicatin 5-O-methyltransferase that has been isolated, cloned, purified and characterized| |CITS:[Ragamustari13]|. The second O-methylation has been detected in the crude protein fraction of various organs (root, stem) from |FRAME: TAX-48027|, but the encoding gene remains to be identified |CITS:[Ragamustari13]|., It should be noted that a fully elucidated, very different pathway for |FRAME:CPD-17595| biosynthesis has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-93608|, and is described in |FRAME: PWY-7748|.

Summary: General Background, Many organisms produce large complex polymers that contain |FRAME: Uronates "uronic acids"|. A few examples include |FRAME: Pectin pectin|, an important component of plant cell walls that contains |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, and glycosaminoglycans produced by animals, which include |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: Hyaluronan|, |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| etc., The bacterial degradation pathways for these polymers usually invovle an intial attack on the polymer that breaks it into short oligosaccharides. Two main types of enzymes that perform this task are the hydrolases and the endolyases. While hydrolases produce oligosaccharides that contain sugar residues similar to those in the polymer, lyases produce oligosaccharides that have a 4-5 unsaturated uronic acid at their non-reducing end. This is typically followed by the action of exolyases or hydrolases that cleave the oligosaccharides, resulting in the production of unstable unsaturated mono uronic acid monomers. Two forms of unsaturated uronic acids are formed, depending on the stereochemistry of the original acid - |FRAME: CPD-17705| and |FRAME: CPD-13122|. The degradation of many polymers, including gellan, rhamnogalacturan, pectin, heparin, heparan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, hyaluronan and chondroitin results in formation the latter. |FRAME: CPD-13122| is unstable and the ring opens spontaneously, forming the keto acid |FRAME: CPD-37|. This pathway describes the degradation of that intermediate to metabolites of central metabolism., About This Pathway, The pathway, which was first studied in detail in the pectin degrader |FRAME: TAX-556|, begins with the ring opening of xxx, forming |FRAME: CPD-37| (DKI). While this reaction can occur spontaneously, it was shown to be catalyzed by a dedicated enzyme |CITS: [27185956]|. The pathway proceeds by the isomerization of DKI to |FRAME: CPD-343| (DKII). The kduI gene encoding the isomerase has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-556| |CITS: [1766386]|, but that enzyme has not been characterized. Earlier work characterized this enzyme in a pseudomonad |CITS: [13986017]|. |FRAME: CPD-343| is reduced to the common metabolite |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE|, a compound that is also an intermediate in |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|. |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| is phosphorylated and then cleaved by an aldolase encoded by the kdgA gene, producing the central metabolites |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|., The same pathway has also been characterized from the heparin/hyaluronan-degradating bacterium |FRAME: TAX-211110| |CITS: [25605731]|. Two of the enzymes (|FRAME: EC-5.3.1.17| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.127|) have been characterized in detail from this organism. While their actions are identical to those of the |FRAME: TAX-556| enzymes, they share very little sequence similarity and possess different structures, suggesting parallel evolution. The |FRAME: G-14833| and |FRAME: G-12012| genes are found in enterococci and clostridia, while the |FRAME: G-43933| and |FRAME: G-43934| genes are much less common and found primarily in streptococci |CITS: [25605731]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| the aldolase encoded by gene eda is involved in the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|., However, in |FRAME: TAX-556| this enzyme does not appear to be involved in |FRAME: GLUCONATE| catabolism and no product of the edd gene that encodes the |FRAME: PGLUCONDEHYDRAT-MONOMER| could be detected in various species of |FRAME:TAX-551|. These observations question the existence of the Entner-Doudoroff pathway in these organisms (|CITS: [8145647][8905080]|. , Most of the enzymes in this pathway are controlled by kdgR a transcriptional regulator that is induced by |FRAME: 2-DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-D-GLUCONATE| |CITS: [1840643] [1874406]|. A comparative genomics analysis of the kdgR regulon in eight enterobacteria including |FRAME: TAX-198628| and |FRAME: TAX-554| and two members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-662|, yielded a metabolic map of pectin and pectin-derivative degradation in these organisms |CITS: [15528647]|.

General Background, Plants must confront many different dangerous xenobiotic compounds in their environments. Often, plant enzymes modify these compounds to change their reactivity and/or subcellular localization in order to render them less toxic |CITS: [20626660]|. Glycosylation, glutathione conjugation, sulfonylation, and other modifications have been observed in many plant species and their role in detoxification has been compared to xenobiotic modifications that take place in the liver |CITS: [7894495]|. Sometimes, multiple modifications may be introduced sequentially, such as the glycosylation followed by malonylation depicted in this pathway |CITS: [6303788][1832837][20626660][11598135]|., About This Pathway, Naphthols are phenolic xenobiotic compounds that may be encountered in the soil by plants. Studies on tobacco cultured cells indicate that naphthols are harmful. Not surprisingly, tobacco, as well as several other plant species, including Arabidopsis thaliana, |FRAME:TAX-3880|, and |FRAME:TAX-4530| (rice) modify naphthols forming compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-13685| |CITS:[TAGUCHI03][15860007 ][20626660]|. , In this pathway, glucosyl moieties are first introduced by glucosyltransferases. When plants are grown in liquid media, glucosylated naphthols are excreted into the solution by some plant species, including Arabidopsis and tobacco |CITS: [20626660]|. However, malonyltransferases, such as two enzymes identified in Arabidopsis (|FRAME: AT5G39050-MONOMER PMaT1| and |FRAME: AT3G29670-MONOMER PMaT2|) and one in tobacco can further modify the glucosylated naphthols to produce malonylated glucosides . In contrast to the glucosides, these doubly modified compounds appear to be retained within plants, presumably within the vacuole |CITS: [20626660]|. The compounds present in this pathway represent a subset of the products that can be formed by |FRAME: AT5G39050-MONOMER PMaT1| and |FRAME: AT3G29670-MONOMER PMaT2| in vitro. Further work will be required to understand the biologically relevant substrates of these enzymes and to gain a better understanding of how both glycosylation and subsequent malonylation of compounds contribute to plant defense against both xenobiotics and endogenously produced harmful compounds |CITS: [20626660]|.

Names: Kdo transfer to lipid IV<sub>A</sub> (four Kdo residues)
Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage., Bacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-810| genus contain a genus-specific epitope that consists of the trisccharide α-Kdo-(2->8)-α-Kdo-(2->4)-α-Kdo (in the form of |FRAME: CPD-12281|) |CITS: [7686488][7515346]|. , The third Kdo unit in this epitope was shown to be attached by the same enzyme that attaches the other two units. The |FRAME: G-11884| gene of |FRAME: TAX-83558| strain TW-183 that encodes this enzyme has been cloned and expressed in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1718|, which lacks any LPS biosynthetic background. The host bacterium produced |FRAME: CPD-12281|, confirming that the enzyme acts as a trifunctional glycosyltransferase |CITS: [8748024]|., When the |FRAME: G-11886| of |FRAME: TAX-331636| was cloned and expressed in a rough mutant of |FRAME:TAX-562|,, the LPS produced by the mutant was shown to contain two additional products - |FRAME: CPD-27358| and |FRAME: CPD-12285|. Thus this enzyme enables the formation of at least five different bonds |CITS: [7744029]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-9776 Cocaine| is a rare |FRAME: Tropane-Alkaloids "tropane alkaloid"| principally produced by members of the |FRAME: TAX-22118| family. The coca crop comprises four closely related varieties classified into two species (Amazonian and Huanuco varieties within |FRAME: TAX-289672|, and Colombian and Trujillo varieties within |FRAME: TAX-1862640|). Genomic studies suggest that all four varieties originated from |FRAME: TAX-2303035|, which has been domesticated multiple times. A domestication event in northwestern South America led to the Colombian and Trujillo coca varieties, a later domestication event in southeastern Peru led to the Huanuco variety, and a third domestication event in the western Amazon basin likely led to the Amazonian variety |CITS: [32979264]|., The coca plant has been cultivated for over 8000 years and is the most culturally significant pharmaceutical plant in South America. Currently, over 5 million South Americans chew the leaves for their mild stimulant and medicinal effects |CITS: [16480174]| ., Cocaine was first purified in 1855 by the German chemist Friedrich Gaedcke, who named it erythroxyline |CITS: [Gaedcke55]|. An improved purificatioin protocol was soon published by Albert Niemann, who renamed it cocaine |CITS: [Niemann60]|. The compound was first synthesized (from |FRAME: TROPINONE|) and its structure was reported in 1898 (in |CITS: [11699882]|)., In the 1880s cocaine was used in eye, nose, and throat surgeries as a local anesthetic and for its ability to constrict blood vessels and limit bleeding. Coca leaves were also used as an ingredient in beverages, such as coca wine and coca cola (the Coca-Cola company began using decocainized leaves in 1906)., However, cocaine is the most powerful addictive stimulant of the nervous system due to its affinity for dopamine receptors and its uphorigenic properties. Its effects were described in 1884 by Sigmund Freud, who got addicted to the drug (in |CITS: [21467292]|). In the US, the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 introduced a national labeling requirement for cocaine and cocaine-containing products, and the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914 set up a regulatory and licensing regime. Serious restrictions on cocaine manufactures were introduced in 1922 by the Jones—Miller Act., Due to its adictive properties, many of the therapeutic applications of cocaine have been replaced by safer drugs. Today cocaine is used worldwide as an illegal drug. Three-quarters of the world's annual yield of cocaine are produced in Colombia, from locally grown coca as well as coca imported from Peru and Bolivia., About This Pathway, For many years the cocaine biosynthesis pathway was hypothesized based on feeding experiments with different precursors |CITS: [2236285][Leete91][Leete88]| |CITS: [Leete91][8835455][11699882]|. Identification of the enzymes involved was not complete until 2022 |CITS: [36376019]|., An early common intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-9779|, has been found for the biosynthesis of cocaine and many tropane alkaloids such as |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE|, |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE|, and |FRAME: CPD-8001| |CITS: [32745157][33908526]|. The compound was shown to be the product of spontaneous condensation between |FRAME: CPD-9778| and |FRAME: CPD-7994|. The former was shown in the |FRAME: CPD-8001|-producer |FRAME: TAX-33113| to be produced by a type III polyketide synthase |CITS: [30538251]|, while the latter is produced by a common pathway that has been studied in the early 90s |CITS: [MCLAUCHLAN93][16653064][8038607][17283012]|., The enzymes catalyzing the last two steps in the pathway were discovered next. The biosynthesis of most tropane alkaloids involves a tropinone-reduction step. In species of the |FRAME: TAX-4070|, which produce compounds such as |FRAME: ATROPINE| and |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE|, this reaction is known to be catalyzed by enzymes of the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.206| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.236|). However, a 2012 study has reported that in |FRAME: TAX-289672| this step is catalyzed by an unrelated enzyme that belongs to the aldo-keto reductase family |CITS: [22665766]|., The last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.334|, catalyzes the esterification of |FRAME: CPD-9777| with benzoate. The enzyme, which belongs to the family of BAHD acyltransferases, was discovered in 2015 |CITS: [25406120]|., The remaining two enzymes were not discovered until 2022. The detection of |FRAME: CPD-9774| by in vivo labeling studies 30 years earlier suggested that it is a pathway intermediate, and led to the proposal of a pathway in which O-methylation occurs before the oxidation that results in ring closure |CITS: [Leete91]|. However, despite considerable efforts, no methyltransferase that could catalyze the methylation of |FRAME: CPD-9779| was discovered., A 2022 study found that oxidation actually occurs before methylation |CITS: [36376019]|. The study identified both the oxidase (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.194|) and the methyltransferase (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.403|), and by doing so concluded the identification of the pathway's enzymes.

Names: palmitate biosynthesis III (type II fatty acid synthase, NADPH-dependent enoyl-[acp] reductase)
Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also, determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]|, and protein modification, where fatty acyl moieties of proteins modify their location and function, |CITS: [10446384]|., |FRAME: PALMITATE Palmitate| is one of the most common saturated fatty acids found in animals and plants., It was discovered by Edmond Fremy in 1840 in saponified palm oil, of which it is a major component, and hence its name., Palmitate is synthesized by stepwise condensation of C2 units to a growing acyl chain. Each elongation cycle results in the addition of two carbons to the acyl chain, and consists of four separate reactions. The first step is the condensation of a C2 unit with the nascent [acp]-bound acyl, forming a |FRAME: B-KETOACYL-ACP| and releasing CO2. This step is followed by reduction to |FRAME: OH-ACYL-ACP|, dehydration to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-ACP|, and a final reduction to form the elongated fatty acid-[acp]. This chain of event repeats itself several times, until the final product, |FRAME:Palmitoyl-ACPs|, is formed., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II., The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|)., The pathway catalyzed by the type I systems is available at |FRAME: PWY-5994|., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|., The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., Unlike the type I system that accepts |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of the two-carbon units, the type II systems accept only |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|. The final product of the pathway is |FRAME:Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl group bound to the acyl-carrier protein"|. It is released from the [acp] moiety and converted to a free acid or a CoA-derivative., The difference between this pathway and the one described at |FRAME: PWY-5971| is the replacement of the NADH-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.9| with the NADPH-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.104|. Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-837|, only have NADPH-dependent enzymes |CITS: [29400320]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-2261| is a strict anaerobic archaeon, capable of utilizing pyruvate, sugars and, complex organic compounds as carbon and energy sources., It is a facultative sulfur-reducing species that is able to grow in the absence of sulfur by fermentation, of peptides, carbohydrates, and pyruvate., |FRAME: TAX-2261| employs a modified glycolytic pathway for the catabolism of sugars, as shown in, the pathway |FRAME: P341-PWY| |CITS:[8830684][9119024]|., Pyruvate, formed during glycolysis, is converted to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| by a |FRAME: CPLX-7001|, rather than the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex that is common in most eubacteria and eukaryotes., |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| is converted to |FRAME: ACET| in a single step,, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7000| (in most other organisms, this conversion is catalyzed, in two steps, via |FRAME: ACETYL-P|). , A similar pathway leading from pyruvate to acetate has also been described in the human parasite, |FRAME: TAX-5759| |CITS: [13076]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14143 Ribostamycin| is an aminoglucoside antibiotic of the neomycin group, which is produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-80859 "Streptomyces ribosidificus (previously known as Streptomyces thermoflavus)"|. The antibiotic was described in 1970 |CITS: [5521353]| and its structure was reported three years later |CITS: [4792382]|. While ribostamycin is a potent antibiotic on its own |CITS: [779802]|, it is also an intermediate in the biosynthetic pathways of several related antibiotics, such as |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin| |CITS: [924894]| and |FRAME: CPD-14140 butirocin| |CITS: [81827]|., About This Pathway, For information about the pathway leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-14125|, please see |FRAME: PWY-7014|., |FRAME: CPD-14125 Paromamine| is modified by the |FRAME: G-15007|/|FRAME: G-15008| oxidase/aminotransferase system, producing |FRAME: CPD-14137| |CITS: [21983602]|. Homologs of these genes are found in organisms that produce several aminoglycoside antibiotics, including the |FRAME: CPD-14140|-producer |FRAME: TAX-1397| and the |FRAME: Kanamycins kanamycin|-producer |FRAME: TAX-1967|., The genes responsible for the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-14137| to |FRAME: CPD-14143| are conserved among a smaller group of organisms, which includes producers of |FRAME: CPD-14140 butirosin|, |FRAME: Neomycins neomycin|, |FRAME: CPD-14143|, |FRAME: CPD-14177|, and |FRAME: Lividomycins lividomycin|. Four such genes have been identified, and all four genes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [17482823]|. All possible combinations of the four enzymes were examined, and the results showed that only two of these genes were necessary for conversion of |FRAME: CPD-14137| to |FRAME: CPD-14143|. The |FRAME: G-15040| gene encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-17254| that utilizes |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to produce |FRAME: CPD-14178|, while the |FRAME: G-15041| gene encodes a phosphatase that produces the final product |CITS: [17482823]|.

|FRAME: CPD-14755 Aureobasidin A| is an antifungal antibiotic which is produced by a certain strain (BP-1938) of the black yeast |FRAME: TAX-5580|. This fungus belongs to the phylum Ascomycetes and is known for colonizing surfaces of plants and buildings |CITS:[Desphande92]| but due to its high stress tolerance is considered a polyextremotolerant organism and can also inhabit extreme environments with high salinity, acidity, basicity, tropical and polar areas, soils and water, polluted environments and synthetic polymers (summarized in |CITS:[24984952]|). Noteworthy is furthermore the use of Aureobasidium pullulans in the biological control of postharvest pathogens, for instance against Penicillium expansum in pear |CITS:[17390846]| and against Monilinia laxa in apple and peach by excreting an alkaline serine protease |CITS:[22225984]|. , Various strains of Aureobasidium pullulans produce valuable metabolites such as the exo-polysaccharide pullulan which has been widely used in the food and wood product industries and has recently successfully employed as biomolecular nanoparticle for the controlled release of pharmaceuticals |CITS:[23294062]| and drug and gene targeting |CITS:[25843851]|. The cyclic depsipeptide |FRAME: CPD-14755| (this pathway) has been first isolated and structural elucidated from the strain R-106 of Aureobasidium pullulans |CITS:[1938614] [1938613]| and shown to have a high antifungal activity against Candida albicans and other fungal human pathogens whereas displaying a high tolerance and low toxicity in animals |CITS:[8226319]|. The biological properties of |FRAME: CPD-14755| initiated a number of biotechnological approaches to modify the compound in order to expand its rather narrow target spectrum (e.g. |CITS:[8784430]|). |FRAME: CPD-14755 Aureobasidin A| has been demonstrated to be an very efficient inhibitor of the inositol phosphoylceramide synthase in Candida and Saccharomyces |CITS:[19047657] [19210614]| involved in the making of sphingolipids (see |FRAME:SPHINGOLIPID-SYN-PWY|), which represent essential components of plasma membranes. For this reason, |FRAME: CPD-14755| is considered a potential candidate for targeting this critical enzyme as a nontoxic therapeutic agent in the development of efficacious antifungal treatments |CITS:[15578972]|., Complex peptides such as |FRAME: CPD-14755| are synthesized in fungi by multi-domain enzymes, such as non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) (reviewed in |CITS:[12828367]| which also provide access to the chemoenzymatic production of desired new peptides by manipulating NRPSs through genetic engineering of the various domains |CITS:[16524919]|. The isolation and bioinformatics analysis of the gene aba1 encoding for the NRPS aureobasidin A synthetase in Aureobasidium pullulans revealed that aba1 is comprised of 9 modules with adenylation (A), condensation (C), carrier protein (ACP) and termination/cyclization (T/C) domains |CITS:[19084058]|. , The order of the domains in aba1 encoding for the aureobasidin A synthetase was deduced from the structure of |FRAME: CPD-14755| |CITS:[19084058]| where eight amino acids and one hydroxyl acid were stringed together in a sequential arrangement as described for type A NPRS complexes |CITS:[16524919]|. The specificity of six of the nine A-domains was matched in agreement to the relevant specificity-conferring code for adenylation domains |CITS:[10421756] [10712928]|. The order of the modules was also corroborated by the presence of methylation domains in modules where methylation of the respective amino acid residues is expected. The hydroxylation of |FRAME:VAL| in module 9 is proposed to occur post assembly by a not yet identified hydroxylase. Interestingly, eight of the nine modules (except for the |FRAME:CPD-17912| activating first module) shared an unusual high sequence similarity which is unprecedented in fungal NRPS genes. The molecular function of the aba1 encoded aureobasidin A synthetase could be demonstrated by knocking out aba1 using hygromycin disruption cassettes which completely abolished the production of |FRAME: CPD-14755| |CITS:[19084058]|., Note from curator:, The structure of |FRAME: CPD-14755| (this pathway) differs from the structure of another |FRAME:CPD-14755|, which is also present in the database. The latter is supported by chemical databases but lacks the N-methyl and hydroxyl groups on amino acid residues which have been reported as structural components for this compound from the literature (see for example |CITS:[1938614] [8784430] [19047675] [19084058]|).

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., About This Pathway, There are two types of IAA conjugates: ester and amide conjugates. The ester conjugates are formed with sugars or polyols through an oxygen bridge, whereas the amide conjugates are formed with amino acids or polypeptides through an amide bond. The content of conjugates varies among different plants. The majority of IAA conjugates in |FRAME: TAX-4577| endosperm are ester conjugates, whereas |FRAME: TAX-3702| leaves contain mainly amide conjugates. IAA conjugates play important roles in IAA homeostasis. They could serve as either intermediates for further degradation, or storage forms for the free IAA. Both ester and amide conjugates have been reported to be converted back to free IAA by hydrolysis., The biosynthetic pathway of IAA conjugates was best studied in maize endosperm. The first reaction of the pathway, which is energetically unfavorable, is coupled with the next energetically favorable reaction to drive the pathway. Thus maize kernels contain small amounts conjugates of IAA and glucose. The IAA and myo-inositol conjugate can be further glycosylated as shown here.

Names: oligomeric urushiol biosynthesis // urushiol biosynthesis // lacquer biosynthesis
Summary: |FRAME: Urushiol Urushiols| are a class of compounds found in the sap of plants of the family |FRAME: TAX-4011|, especially members of the |FRAME: TAX-43852| genus. (e.g., poison oak, poison ivy, poison sumac). The urushiols consist of a catechol substituted with an alkyl chain that has 15 or 17 carbon atoms that may be saturated or unsaturated. Most plants have a mixture of several compounds, and the exact composition varies depending on the plant souce, Urushiols cause an allergic skin rash on contact, with the likelihood and severity of allergic reaction dependent on the degree of unsaturation of the alkyl chain., Urushiol is an oleoresin. After injury to the plant it leaks to the surface where it contacts oxygen. The oxidation and polymerization of urushiol in the tree's sap in the presence of moisture allows it to form a hard lacquer, which is used to produce traditional Chinese and Japanese lacquerware. The name comes from kiurushi, the Japanese name for the lacquer produced in East Asia from the sap of |FRAME: TAX-4013| (the Lacquer Tree)., The ancient lacquerware art from Japan is world famous for the long lasting, tough and brilliant film used as coating material. The plant exudates, which contain a mixture of urushiols, glycoproteins and saccharides, are collected from artificial wounds of the tree. The fresh exudates contain nearly 70% monomeric urushiols. The glycoproteins in the exudate are copper-containing enzymes like peroxidases, laccases and stellacyanin |CITS: [12121769]|., The unsaturated hydrocarbon chains of the laquer tree urushiols consist of mono-enes, di-enes, and tri-enes at the 3 or 4 position of catechol.  Although several synthetic analogues are available, authentic kiurushi is desired as it provides an environment friendly method for coating technologies |CITS: [UYAMA06]|., The natural polymerization catalyst of urushiol is the laccase enzyme |CITS: [NAGASE04]| which acts during natural drying of the exudate. This enzyme was discovered in 1883 and has since been found to play a variety of roles, mostly in the biosynthesis and degradation of lignin and in pigment formation and detoxification |CITS: [12121769]|. Laccases are found in fungi and higher plants, where they are are encoded by multigene families and have divergent roles. The laccase-catalyzed reaction with urushiol has been performed in vitro done with pyrocatechols |CITS: [KUMANOTANI03]|. Urushiol-quinone participation in the oxidative polymerization and cross-linking of the sap has also been shown |CITS: [KATO68]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, The thiamine biosynthesis pathway illustrated here has been most extensively studied in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| and the plant |FRAME: ORG-5993|., |FRAME: THIAMINE-P "Thiamine phosphate"| is formed by the coupling of two moieties, the pyrimidine |FRAME:AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP| and the thiazole |FRAME: THZ-P|, which are produced by two different pathways. In eukaryotes |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| is first dephosphorylated into|FRAME: THIAMINE|, which is diphosphorylated to |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|, the activive form of thiamine., The occurrence of thiamine triphosphate in plants has also been demonstrated; however the physiological function of that compound remains to be shown |CITS:[12943234]|., While many of the enzymes involved in eukaryotic thiamine biosynthesis have been identified, most of the enzymes have not been extensively characterized at a biochemical level. Moreover, several steps in the pathway require further clarification. For example, the source of the sulfur in thiazole has not been identified, and the gene encoding the putative TMP phosphatase has not been discovered., The subcellular compartmentalization of thiamine biosynthesis is also a subject of on-going investigation. The Arabidopsis proteins TH1, ThiC, and TH1 all localize to the chloroplasts |CITS:[18048325][18332905][17174261][11575719]|, but THI1 can also localize to the mitochondria |CITS:[11575719]|. The downstream TPK1 and TPK2 enzymes are both cytosolic in Arabidopsis |CITS:[17611796]|, suggesting that intermediates in the vitamin B1 biosynthesis pathway may need to be transported out of organelles for |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| synthesis to be completed. In addition,, because TPP is used as a cofactor for enzymes present in different organelles, TPP transporters likely exist as well |CITS:[17611796]|.

Summary: |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is a secondary messenger molecule used in signal transduction and lipid signaling in eukaryotic cells., It mediates the biological response of a large number of hormones and neurotransmitters in target cells by regulating calcium release from intracellular stores., |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is synthesized by hydrolysis of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| (PIP2), a phospholipid that is located in the plasma membrane, by the action of phospholipase C, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6351|., Once formed, the levels of |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| are tightly regulated by two mechanisms., In the first mechanism the compound is dephosphorylated to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-BISPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [6285891][6095097]|, initiating a pathway that recycles the inositol moiety to the plasma membrane as posphatidylinositols (see |FRAME: PWY-6363|)., In the second mechanism, which is described here, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is phosphorylated by inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate 3-kinase to |FRAME: CPD-506|. This compound has been suggested to have roles in controlling calcium homeostasis, transferring calcium between intracellular stores, and/or regulating calcium entry across the plasma membrane |CITS: [1659392]|. It may also play a role in regulating cross-talk between the calcium and other signaling pathways. A |FRAME: CPD-506|-binding protein has been identified that can stimulate the GTPase activity of the ras and rap small GTP binding proteins |CITS: [7637787][9038348]|., In fungi and in plants |FRAME: CPD-506| is phosphorylated further to |FRAME: CPD-1107| and eventually |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [2550825][2548474]|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6361|., However, in mammals |FRAME: CPD-506| is cleaved to |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [3010126]|, and synthesis of |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| proceeds from there, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6362|., |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| also acts as a link between the degree and duration of receptor-dependent phospholipase C activation (expressed as levels of |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| and thus |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE|) and the generation of other second messenger compounds such as |FRAME: INOSITOL-1456-TETRAKISPHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: CPD-178| (see |FRAME: PWY-6366| and |FRAME: PWY-6365|).

Summary: Some organisms utilize organic substrates (such as fatty acids, alcohols, esters, as well as waxes, alkenes, and methylated compounds) that are metabolized via |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|. These organisms need to find a way to convert |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, a 2-carbon compound, to a 4-carbon compound that could feed their anaplerotic reactions (reactions that form metabolic intermediates for biosynthesis). , A common solution to the problem is the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, a modified version of the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"| that bypasses those steps in the cycle that lead to a loss of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Acetyl-CoA enters the cycle at two steps, and since no carbon escapes it in the form of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, the output is the 4-carbon compound succinate., However, many bacteria are known to not contain |FRAME:EC-4.1.3.1|, the key enzyme of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|. These organisms employ alternative pathways to satisfy this requirement. One such pathway is the |FRAME: PWY-5741|, which was originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1063|, but is present in bacteria from different clades., Another solution, described here, operates in many species of the |FRAME: TAX-183963| |CITS: [21252347]|. These organisms are known to accumulate substantial amounts of polyhydroxyalkanoate such as |FRAME: Poly-Hydroxybutyrate "poly-β-hydroxybutyrate"| during bloom conditions |CITS: [16348261]|. The |FRAME: PWY-6728| is likely to be used during starvation in the process of converting these storage compounds to biosynthetic intermediates., In this pathway one molecule of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| is initially transformed into |FRAME: GLT| through reactions of the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| and |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|. L-glutamate is rearranged to |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| with subsequent elimination of ammonia to yield mesaconate. The latter compound is activated to mesaconyl-CoA by CoA transfer, hydrated to β-methylmalyl-CoA, and split into propionyl-CoA and |FRAME: GLYOX|. Propionyl-CoA carboxylation leads to methylmalonyl-CoA and subsequently to the TCA cycle intermediate succinyl-CoA, which closes the cycle, whereas glyoxylate condensation with another |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| molecule yields the final assimilation product |FRAME: MAL|, which exits the pathway and is used to replenish the biosynthetic metabolite pool., All of enzymes of the pathway were demonstrated in extracts of acetate-grown |FRAME: TAX-2238| cells. Because the affinity of |FRAME: MONOMER-16255| for methylaspartate is very low, a functioning methylaspartate cycle is expected to require high intracellular glutamate concentration. Indeed, cytoplasmic glutamate concentration in acetate-grown |FRAME: TAX-2238| cells is ~35 mM. This is not unexpected, since glutamate is a well-known osmolyte used by many Halobacteria |CITS: [21252347]|.

Summary: This arginine catabolic pathway has been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS:[3897201]|. The pathway is essentially identical to an anabolic pathway that is used by many bacteria for the biosynthesis of putrescine (see  |FRAME:PWY-40| |CITS:[4908781]|. Even though the main catabolic arginine pathway of |FRAME: TAX-83333| is the succinyltransferase pathway (|FRAME:AST-PWY|), this pathway provides an alternative route, and is used under certain growth conditions. , Interestingly, unlike |FRAME: TAX-83333|, wild-type |FRAME:TAX-562| strains are unable to use |FRAME:ARG| as a carbon source, even though they can use it as a nitrogen source |CITS:[3534538]|., |FRAME: TAX-83333| has two forms of the enzyme arginine decarboxylase: a constitutive biosynthetic form, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10959| gene, and an inducible catabolic form, encoded by the |FRAME:EG11501| gene. When the catabolic form is not expressed, the pathway operates only in an anabolic manner, catalyzing the biosynthesis of |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, which is used by the bacteria either directly or as a precursor for the biosynthesis of other polyamines (see |FRAME: PWY-40| and |FRAME:POLYAMSYN-PWY|). However, when the cells are grown in an arginine-rich medium, especially if the medium is acidic and conditions are semi-anaerobic, the catabolic arginine decarboxylase is expressed, and the pathway operates in a catabolic manner, feeding |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| via |FRAME:4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| and |FRAME:SUC| into the |FRAME:TCA| |CITS:[3157043]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Jasmonates Jasmonates| (JA) are an important class of compounds, related to |FRAME:CPD-734|, found throughout the plant kingdom as well as in fungi |CITS:[17513307]|. They participate in a number of biological processes including resistance to herbivores and some pathogens, protection against ozone, senescence, and reproductive development (reviewed in |CITS:[19025383][17513307]|)., Many different jasmonate precursors and jasmonate derivatives have biological activity, including |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Amino-Acid-Conjugates "jasmonoyl-amino acid conjugates"|. Different species may have a different array of JA-amino acid conjugates, and the biological activity of each compound may differ between species. For example, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonyl-L-isoleucine"| (JA-Ile) has been shown to have biological activity in a number of different plants, including |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS:[15258265][18247047]|, |FRAME:TAX-49451| |CITS:[17273867][17085687]|, |FRAME: TAX-384659| |CITS:[18812165]|, |FRAME: TAX-4513| (barley) |CITS:[9315685]|, |FRAME: TAX-4081| (tomato) |CITS:[18458331]|, |FRAME: TAX-4530| (rice) |CITS:[ 9013895]|, and others., In |FRAME: TAX-3702|, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmoonyl-L-isoleucine"| promotes the interaction between the COI1 protein (Coronatine-insensitive protein 1) and the TIFY10A (JAZ1) repressor protein. In this manner, JA-Ile is believed to help destabilize the JAZ1 repressor and thereby promote JA-responsive transcription |CITS:[17637677]|. COI1 and JAZ1 homologs have been found in other plants, such as tomato, where they also bind in a JA-Ile-dependent manner |CITS:[18458331]|, indicating that JA-Ile might have a similar function in other plant species. However, this is not a universal phenomenon. For example, a treatment of 100 uM JA-Ile fails to stimulate JA-responsive emissions of volatile sesquiterpenes in |FRAME: TAX-467333|, a weed commonly found in Japan |CITS:[TAMOGAMI07]|. Other differences in biological activity have been observed across species for many other conjugates including |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-ACCs "jasmonoyl-1-aminocyclopropane-1 carboxylate"| (JA-ACC), |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Leucines "jasmonoyl-L-leucine"| (JA-leucine), and |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Valines "jasmoonyl-L-valine"| (JA-valine). , Jasmonates are found in nature in two isomeric forms, which can have very different biological effects. For example, the biologically active form of |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"| is |FRAME: CPD-11259|, while |FRAME: CPD-11232| does not promote JAZ1/COI1 binding in vitro |CITS: [19349968]|. Initial studies actually suggested that |FRAME: CPD-11232| was a biologically active phytohormone |CITS: [SEMBDER93][17291501]|, but it is now believed that this was due to impure preparations that contained small amounts of |FRAME: CPD-11259|., In |FRAME: TAX-3702| no biological function has been identified yet for |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Leucines "jasmonoyl-L-leucine"|, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Valines "jasmonoyl-L-valine"|, |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Phenylalanines "jasmonoyl-L-phenylalanline"|, and |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-ACCs "jasmonoyl-1-aminocyclopropane-1 carboxylate"|, even though there is evidence that all of these compounds exist in this plant |CITS:[15258265]|. It is unclear whether these are storage forms of JA or catabolic intermediates., Another important phytohormone, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA), can be conjugated with several amino acids, as shown in the |FRAME:PWY-6219| pathway. Some of these compounds, such as |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP|, are targeted for further breakdown |CITS:[9733548]| while others, such as |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ALA|, may serve as storage forms. A family of amidohydrolases can release free active |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| from some of these storage IAA conjugates |CITS:[7792259][10072397]|. To date, no corresponding JA-amidohydrolases have been identified in plants, even though such an enzyme has been detected in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-45133| |CITS:[9141491]|. Further work is required to determine the metabolic and functional fate of the "inactive" JA-amino acid conjugates identified in |FRAME: TAX-3702|., So far only one JA-amino acid conjugate synthetase, encoded by |FRAME: AT2G46370|, has been discovered in |FRAME: TAX-3702|. In vitro the enzyme can catalyze the addition of many different amino acids to jasmonate |CITS: [15258265][17291501][18247047]|. However, in a |FRAME: AT2G46370| mutant of |FRAME: TAX-3702| only the level of |FRAME: Jasmonoyl-Isoleucines "jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine"| is reduced, suggesting that other enzymes must be responsible for the production of other JA-amino acid conjugates in this plant |CITS: [15258265]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: NICOTINE Nicotine| is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-4093|) |CITS: [Schmeltz77]|, where it functions as a defense compound. In the plant tissue nicotine is mostly present in the |FRAME: NICOTINE| isomeric form |CITS: [Armstrong98]|, although tobacco smoke contains up to 10% of |FRAME: R-NICOTINE|, probably due to racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|). Nicotine is the major toxic component in tobacco waste and its degradation is of interest in the bioremediation field. The chemical or biocatalytic transformation of nicotine into useful compounds is of commercial interest (in |CITS: [22466953]|)., The pathway shown here is a novel variant of the two well studied pathways of bacterial nicotine degradation. The initial reactions are those of the |FRAME: P181-PWY "pyridine pathway"| characterized from |FRAME: TAX-29320| while the later part of the pathway is similar to the |FRAME: PWY-6993 "pyrrolidine pathway"| described from |FRAME: TAX-286| species. The chimeric pathway has been named the VPP (variant of the pyridine and pyrrolidine) pathway of nicotine degradation., The two pathway segments are connected by |FRAME: EC-1.4.98.M1|, followed by an as yet uncharacterized transformation from |FRAME: CPD-17782| to |FRAME: CPD-14096|.
