Summary: General Background, Marine organisms, including bacteria, algae and invertebrates, produce many organobromine compounds. Over 2,200 of those, with a wide range of biological properties, have been reported by 2017. Some brominated compounds, such as |FRAME: PBDEs "polybrominated diphenyl ethers"| (BDEs) in their hydroxylated and methoxylated forms, are found across all trophic levels in marine biota, from cyanobacteria and macroalgae to whales and seabirds. In some marine sponges within the |FRAME: TAX-190525| family BDEs can exceed 10% of the sponge tissue by dry weight |CITS: [Unson94][Becerro04]|., Other compounds, such as the brominated biphenyl |FRAME: CPD-20552|, the brominated bipyrrole |FRAME: CPD-20553|, and the hybrid |FRAME: CPD-20554|, have been shown to be synthesized by several species of |FRAME: TAX-53246|, a marine γ-proteobacterial genus often associated with eukaryotic hosts |CITS: [4380876][Andersen74][12543647]|., To find the genes encoding the biosynthesis of brominated compounds, the genomes of two |FRAME: TAX-53246| species, |FRAME: TAX-1315281| and |FRAME: TAX-1353533|, were sequenced, and the genomes were searched for homologs of two genes known to be involved in the formation of chlorinated pyrroles - |FRAME: G-55300| and |FRAME: G-55299| (based on the assumption that a similar mechanism may operate in the formation of chlorinated and brominated pyrroles). The search led to the identification of a brominated marine pyrroles/phenols (bmp) biosynthetic gene cluster in both bacteria |CITS: [24974229]|., Cloning of the bmp1-8 genes and their expression in |FRAME: TAX-562| led to production of many typical brominated compounds, including brominated phenols, pyrroles, biphenyls, bipyrroles and hydbrid phenyl-pyrrole molecules. By expressing the bmp cluster with individual gene deletions it was possible to delinetate the function of the individual enzymes, and to show that the cluster encodes all of the enzymes that are necessary for production of brominated phenols, brominated pyrroles, and their derivatives |CITS: [24974229]|., About This Pathway, Most of the biosynthesis of brominated pyrroles occurs while the substrate is attached to the dedicated peptidyl-carrier protein Bmp1. The pathway begins when an |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.53|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55301| gene, activates |FRAME: PRO| and attaches it as a thioester on the phosphopantetheinyl arm of |FRAME: Holo-Bmp1|. Tandem four-electron oxidation of the attached prolyl residue, which is catalyzed by the flavoprotein |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.14| (Bmp3) yields a pyrrolyl 2-carboxylate residue. This is followed by triple bromination by the FAD-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.57| (Bmp2). The fully brominated compound is released from the peptidyl-carrier protein by its C-terminal thioesterase domain, and is decarboxylated by Bmp8, forming |FRAME: CPD-20566| |CITS: [24974229]|., In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-910454|, the synthesis of brominated pyrroles ends at |FRAME: CPD-20566|. Other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1353533|, |FRAME: TAX-1315281|, and |FRAME: TAX-717774|, which possess the |FRAME: G-55297| gene encoding |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18|, are also able to produce the dipyrrole |FRAME: CPD-20553|. In addition, organisms that have the genes required for production of both brominated pyrroles and brominated phenols (see |FRAME: PWY-7929|) as well as |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.M18|, also produce hybrid compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-20554| (see |FRAME: PWY-7932|) |CITS: [24974229]|.

Summary: General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives. These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|. The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two broad categories - oxidative and reductive. In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-5935| was isolated from a petrochemical-contaminated soil and water sample by enrichment culture. The organism can use |FRAME: CPD-9168| as sole carbon, nitrogen, and energy source, and is not able to utilize 3-nitrobenzoate, nitrophenols, or |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| |CITS: [11034277]|. Early characterization of |FRAME: CPD-9168| degradation in this organism showed that the pathway was reductive (as ammonia was released), and that , |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| is an intermediate, unlike previously reported |FRAME: CPD-9168|-degeradation pathways from other organisms, in which |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| was an intermediate (see |FRAME: PWY-5648|). , This initial work also identified |FRAME: 2-AMINO-3-3-OXOPROP-2-ENYL-BUT-2-ENEDI| as the direct product of ring cleavage |CITS: [11034277]|., The gene cluster that encodes the enzymes of this pathway has been cloned and sequenced |CITS: [12620844]|. Sequence analysis revealed that two of the genes, |FRAME: G-10161| and |FRAME: G-10162|, encode novel homologs of the eukaryotic enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-7478| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13360|, which participate in eukaryotic |FRAME:TRP| degradation (see the pathway |FRAME: TRYPTOPHAN-DEGRADATION-1|). These two enzymes have been purifed and their activity verified |CITS: [12620844]|. The other genes in this cluster were highly homologous to genes that are involved in degradation of |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL| by |FRAME: TAX-874293| (see |FRAME: PWY-5637|), and thus the pathway was predicted to continue by processing of |FRAME: 2-AMINOMUCONATE_SEMIALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| via |FRAME: CPD-14447| |CITS: [12620844]|., The enzymes catalyzing the first two reactions in the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-7477| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13358|, have also been purified and characterized |CITS: [17277060]|. Attraction of the organism to |FRAME: CPD-9168| has been linked to a chemoreceptor encoded by the nbaY gene, which is also found on the same gene cluster |CITS: [17277060]|., The proteobacterium |FRAME: ORG-5996| apparently possesses both this pathway and a pathway that proceeds via |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5648|) |CITS: [17213670]|.

Summary: The filamentous fungus Penicillium chrysogenum, producer of the antibiotic |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G|, has been exploited for a long time as a valuable source of bioactive metabolites |CITS:[22865068] [23662444]|. Secondary metabolites produced by the fungal genus Penicillium, for instance the diketopiperazine (DKP) alkaloid |CITS:[Martins07] [23955505]| |FRAME:CPD-17381| and intermediates of the |FRAME:PWY-7605| have been found as contaminants on food crops |CITS:[16348301]| and recognized as potentially health-threatening for the known neurotoxicity of |FRAME:CPD-17381| |CITS:[16345552] [613945]|. In addition, properties such as antibacterial |CITS:[16309319]| and bacteriostatic activities against Gram-positive bacteria |CITS:[2231314]|, and inhibition of mammalian cytochrome P450's |CITS:[11559041] [16019806]| have been reported and are of considerable interest for the pharmaceutical industry. , |FRAME:CPD-17381 Roquefortine C| was first isolated and reported as a neurotoxic compound from Penicillium roquefortine |CITS:[956545]| but has shown since then to be wide-spread within the genus of Penicillium |CITS:[Frisvad04]|. Interestingly, |FRAME:CPD-17381| and intermediates were also biosynthesized from Penicillium chrysogenum and Penicillium expansum strains in a near zero-gravity environment as demonstrated on board the Mir space station |CITS:[12526198]|. The occurrence of other intermediates of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17380|, |FRAME:CPD-17378| and |FRAME:CPD-17379| |CITS:[23776469]| has also been verified in various Penicillium species |CITS:[14520967]| which indicates a possible role of the respective pathways for competitive fitness of the invading fungus and outlines probable biosynthetic routes towards |FRAME:CPD-17381| |CITS:[16195849]| . , Although |FRAME:CPD-17381| is best known from Penicillium roquefortine no genes and enzymes of the |FRAME:PWY-7605| have been reported from this organism. However, the sequencing of the Penicillium chrysogenum genome |CITS:[18820685]| provided the platform for in-depth bioinformatics analysis, molecular biology and biochemical approaches which allowed the elucidation of the |FRAME:PWY-7605| and closely related pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-7607|, |FRAME:PWY-7608|; summarized in |FRAME:PWY-7609|). It has been shown that the biosynthetic gene cluster (roq) is responsible for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17381| and descendants of this pathway. Bioinformatics studies revealed the structure of the roq cluster consisting of 7 genes and corresponding putative functions based on sequence homology with characterized enzymes |CITS:[22118684]|. , The first step of the pathway is catalyzed by a non-ribosomal cyclodipeptide synthetase (NRCPS) encoded by roqA, which contains two modules each consisting of an activation (A), thiolation (T), and condensation (C) domain |CITS:[22118684]|. In contrast to other NRPS and PKS post-translational activation through phosphopantetheinylation appears not to be required for |FRAME:PWY-7605| |CITS:[18558918]|. The molecular function as histidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine synthetase utilizing the amino acids |FRAME:TRP| and |FRAME:HIS| and yielding |FRAME:CPD-17378| was elucidated by a combination of gene knock-out, metabolite profiling and gene expression data analysis |CITS:[22118684] [23776469]|. The order of the following steps is still not verified and may occur either way, i.e. prenylation before oxidation or vice versa. The reverse prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-17378| to form |FRAME:CPD-17380| as well as yielding |FRAME:CPD-17381| by reverse prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-17379| at the indole moiety C3 position is carried out by roqD which encodes for the histidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine prenyltransferase and the dehydrohistidyltryptophanyldiketopiperazine prenyltransferase, respectively |CITS:[22118684] [23776469]|. RoqR encoding for a multifunctional cytochrome P450 roquefortine oxidoreductase realized the reduction at the histidinyl moiety of |FRAME:CPD-17378| forming |FRAME:CPD-17379| and of |FRAME:CPD-17380| yielding |FRAME:CPD-17381|, respectively |CITS:[22118684] [23776469]|.

Summary: General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids)., The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also forming a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., About This Pathway, Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir (|FRAME: TAX-46611|) oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes are involved in a variety of biological processes, including inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Abietic acid, an abietane-type DRA, is one of the principal resin acids |CITS:[17082986],[11269960]|. The formation of this acid involves the formation of the abietane skeleton via cyclization of the diterpenoid precursor |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This cyclization occurs via the formation of the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-4750| and is followed by the stepwise oxidation of the C18 methyl group of the derived olefin |FRAME:--ABIETADIENE|. Several abietadiene synthases have been identified, which can produce a variety of other olefins such as |FRAME:CPD-8695| or |FRAME:CPD-8696| |CITS:[8798524],[15310829],[16497345]|., The mechanism of oxidation of |FRAME:--ABIETADIENE| to |FRAME:CPD-8694| resembles that of the oxidation of |FRAME:CPD1F-128| to |FRAME:CPD1F-132| (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|). However, while the later is catalyzed by a single multifunctional enzyme (|FRAME: MONOMER-11800|), the conversion from |FRAME:--ABIETADIENE| to |FRAME:CPD-8694| appears to be performed by several enzymes., Two microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes that hydroxylate |FRAME: --ABIETADIENE| to |FRAME: CPD-8691| and |FRAME: CPD-8691| to |FRAME: CPD-8692|, respectively, have been reported from |FRAME: TAX-46611| (grand fur) and |FRAME: TAX-3339| (lodgepole pine) |CITS:[8311462][12232380]|. A gene encoding the second enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-12739|, has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-3352| (loblolly pine) |CITS: [15911762]|. The recombinant enzyme catalyzed the oxidation of multiple diterpene alcohol and aldehydes, including levopimaradienol, isopimara-7,15-dienol, isopimara-7,15-dienal, dehydroabietadienol, and dehydroabietadienal, but was not able to oxidize |FRAME: --ABIETADIENE|., |FRAME: CPD-8692| is unstable, and spontaneously loses a water molecule to become |FRAME: CPD-8693|. The final reaction of the pathway, the oxidation of the aldehyde to |FRAME: CPD-8694| has been reported to be catalyzed by different enzymes in different organisms. An oxygen-independent |FRAME: MONOMER-14869| has been reported from |FRAME: TAX-46611| |CITS: [8311462]|, while in |FRAME: TAX-3352| this conversion may be catalyzed by the same oxygen-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-12739| that catalyzes the hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-8691| |CITS: [15911762]|.

General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1718| synthesizes the rare, bicyclic C50 carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-19254|, a compound that is responsible for its yellow pigmentation. Although this is the predominant carotenoid, a number of other caroteoids have also been identified in this organism |CITS: [11511870]|. They are derived from two precursors, |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| and its isomer |FRAME: CPD-4211|, which are in turn derived from the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|. From there the carotenogenesis pathway proceeds through |FRAME: PWY-5123|, |FRAME: PWY-5120| and |FRAME: PWY-5942| to the pathway shown here. , About This Pathway, The metabolic intermediates involved in the conversion of the acyclic C40 carotene |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to the bicyclic, hydroxylated C50 carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-19254| have not been completely characterized, as indicated by the triple arrows in this pathway diagram. Several reports suggest that two of the intermediates are |FRAME: CPD-19285| and |FRAME: CPD-19251| |CITS: [11432736][11511870][22963379][24270893][25181035]|., CrtEb (not shown here) is a lycopene elongase that catalyzes the elongation (diprenylation) of C40 |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to acyclic C50 carotenoids by the sequential addition of C5 isoprenoid units. The likely C5 donor is |FRAME: CPD-4211|. A deletion of crtEb results in lycopene accumulation |CITS: [22963379]| suggesting that CrtEb catalyzes the first step in the pathway shown here. There is agreement in the literature that the C45 intermediate |FRAME: CPD-19285| and the C50 intermediate |FRAME: CPD-19251| are formed by successive prenylation reactions catalyzed by CrtEb, with each prenylation followed by a hydroxylation catalyzed by an as yet unidentified cellular hydroxylase(s) |CITS: [11432736][11511870][20802040][22963379]|. It has been suggested that hydroxylation is necessary to stabilize the prenylated intermediates formed by CrtEb |CITS: [11432736]|., A |FRAME: CPLX18HP-79| complex comprised of CrtYe and CrtYf functions as a C50 carotenoid ε-cyclase in this pathway |CITS: [20802040][11432736]|. Finally, mutant studies suggest that |FRAME: G18NG-10193-MONOMER "CrtX"| is a carotenoid glucosyltransferase that catalyzes the di-glucosylation at the hydroxyl groups of |FRAME: CPD-19254| to |FRAME: CPD-19267|, although the identity of the glucose carrier was not reported |CITS: [24270893]|.

Summary: Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., Each of these can be utilized by bacteria as a total source of carbon and energy., Sorbitol is one of several acyclic polyols or sugar alcohols found in higher plants |CITS:[BIELESKI82]|. In Rosaceae plants, sorbitol is the main photoassimilate produced in the leaves from which it is translocated to sink tissues |CITS:[WEBB62][BIELESKI85]|. Sorbitol synthesis shares a common hexose phosphate pool with sucrose synthesis, and it was recently shown in apple that synthesis pathways are not independent from one another |CITS:[ZHOU02]| as, |FRAME:MONOMER-11709| was shown to be inhibited by |FRAME:D-SORBITOL-6-P|, an intermediate in sorbitol biosynthesis. , D-sorbitol degradation is common in prokaryotes. For example, |FRAME: TAX-1423| can utilize it as a sole carbon source via the gut operon (glucitol-utilizing transporter), consisting of a transporter and an NAD+-dependent glucitol dehydrogenase |CITS: [6402486][12897001]|., The pathway also occurs in plants, as translocated sorbitol is 'unloaded' in fruit tissues and eventually converted to fructose. In plants that use sorbitol as the main product of photosynthesis D-sorbitol dehydrogenase is a key enzyme, supplying carbon during fruit development., The pathway can also occur in mammals. D-sorbitol can be produced from glucose by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.21|, when glucose concentration is very high, leading to saturation of hexokinase. While not common, the pathway operates in uncontrolled diabetics, directing the D-sorbitol that is formed back to glycolysis |CITS: [15919781]|.

Summary: Betaines are quarternary ammonium derivatives of amino acids produced by plants and marine algae that can serve as osmoprotectants. |FRAME: CPD-821|, known as stachydrine or N,N-dimethyl L-proline, can be used by |FRAME: TAX-382| as a carbon and nitrogen source and as an osmoprotectant |CITS: [Goldmann91]|. In the absence of osmotic stress, |FRAME: TAX-382| can degrade |FRAME: CPD-821|, whereas |FRAME: CPD-821| degradation in osmotically stressed cells is strongly reduced, resulting in accumulation of the osmoprotectant |CITS: [ArchMic151-143]|., |FRAME: CPD-821| (stachydrine) is proposed to undergo two sequential demethylations, the first demethylation produces |FRAME: CPD-904| (monomethyl L-proline) and the subsequent demethylation produces |FRAME: PRO|, which then enters general metabolism |CITS: [Goldmann94][10689197][9758825]|, or is further catabolized as shown in the pathway link |CITS: [24520058]|. The degradation of |FRAME: CPD-821| is similar to |FRAME: BETAINE| degradation (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-3661|), which also involves two sequential demethylations and produces monomethyl glycine |CITS: [3290197]|. The initial demethylation of |FRAME: CPD-821| is proposed to be catalyzed by a Rieske type iron-sulfur monooxygenase system, similar to those involved in aromatic hydrocarbon degradation |CITS: [10689197]|. The second demethylation step is proposed to be catalyzed by an enzyme showing homology to oxidoreductase flavoproteins |CITS: [9758825]|., The stc2, stc3, and stc4 genes, which appear to encode the monooxygenase system that catalyzes the initial demethylation of |FRAME: CPD-821|, are intermingled with the nodulation and nitrogen fixation function on the symbiotic plasmid, pSym |CITS: [GOLDMANN94]|. The stc2, stc3, and stc4 genes appear to have a functional role in nodulation, as stc- mutants exhibited delayed and reduced nodulations |CITS: [GOLDMANN94]|. Summary: General background, The amino acid glutamine is a constituent of proteins and a nitrogen donor for many biosynthetic reactions, including the biosynthesis of amino acids, purines, pyrimidines, glucosamime and carbamoyl phosphate. Phylogenetic analysis of glutamine synthetase genes has suggested that they are among the oldest functioning genes in the history of evolution |CITS: [8096645]|. In microorganisms and plants, glutamine synthetase (also known as GS) has a role in ammonia assimilation in combination with glutamate synthase (glutamine: α-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, or GOGAT) as indicated by the pathway links and pathways |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-3282|). This is known as the GS/GOGAT pathway |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|. , About this pathway, Three types of glutamine synthetases have been described, differing in number of subunits. The active site residues of all three types are conserved. , Glutamine synthetase type I is found mostly in bacteria and archaea, including |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-90371| (reviewed in |CITS: [11585846]|). It is a well-studied homododecamer built from two back-to-back hexameric rings., Glutamine synthetase type II is found mostly in eukaryotes and some soil bacteria, but it has also been described in the halophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2252| |CITS: [17020556][16884924]|. It is a homooctamer., Glutamine synthetase type III has been described in anaerobic bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-246199|) and cyanobacteria, and is generally a homohexamer |CITS: [16237031]|.

In this alternative glycogen and starch-degrading pathway, linear α(1,4) glycans are broken down to |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.2.13| |CITS: [7766642][9187252][10446355][15110094]|. While this activity has been well characterized in red algae and fungi, it may also be present in mammals, where the product, |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE|, is converted to |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-GLUCITOL| by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.263| |CITS: [9022716]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| has been found in fungi, red algae, Escherichia coli C600 and rat liver tissue |CITS: [Baute91][9022716][10036159][9880813]|. It acts as an antioxidant |CITS: [11842320]|, an antibiotic |CITS: [22977551]|, and a precursor of several other antibiotics |CITS: [10446355]|., In some red algae and fungi |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| is further metabolized to the secondary metabolites |FRAME: CPD-9432|, |FRAME: CPD-9433| and |FRAME: CPD-9435| |CITS: [Baute87][Baute91][Baute93][Broberg96][10036159]|., |FRAME: CPD-9433 "Ascopyrone P"| was first prepared as a pyrolysis product of amylopectin, amylose and cellulose |CITS: [Shafizadeh78]|. It was shown to possess an antimicrobial activity |CITS: [12234354][Baute93]|., |FRAME: CPD-9435 Microthecin| was discovered by Naito et al. in 1979 in the culture medium of the fungus |FRAME: TAX-152785| and was named after the genus name |CITS: [Naito79]|. It is also found in red algae, and shows antimicrobial activity |CITS: [Baute84][Baute86][Baute87a][Broberg96][10036159]||., |FRAME: CPD-9433 "Ascopyrone P"| is generated from |FRAME: 15-ANHYDRO-D-FRUCTOSE| in two steps. |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.111|, first generates the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-9432|, which is then tautomerized by |FRAME: EC-5.3.2.7|, forming |FRAME: CPD-9433| |CITS: [15110094]|. |FRAME: CPD-9435 Microthecin|, on the other hand, is generated by a single enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.110|, which catalyzes both the generation of |FRAME: CPD-9432| and its conversion to |FRAME: CPD-9435| |CITS: [15716041]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Phosphonates| are quite abundant in nature, primarily as components of phosphonolipids, where |FRAME: CPD-1106| is analogous to ethanolamine phosphate as the constituent of phospholipids. In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics |CITS: [7765831]|. Phosphonates contain a direct carbon-phosphorus (C-P) bond in place of the more familiar carbon-oxygen-phosphorus bond, which makes their degradation challenging., Bacteria have evolved many different mechanisms for cleaving the carbon-phosphorus bond. Enzymes that have been described include the following:, • |FRAME: EG10719-MONOMER "Carbon-phosphorus lyase"|, a widespread but poorly characterized enzyme. See |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|., • Hydrolytic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.1| (phosphonatase, see |FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY|), |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.2| (shown in pathway |FRAME: P483-PWY|)., • Dioxygenases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.78|, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7447|., Data suggest that additional pathways for phosphonate degradation may exist (in |CITS: [21543322]|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-22922| is a naturally occurring organophosphonate that can be degraded to |FRAME: BETAINE| and organic phosphate by two enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80632| and |FRAME: G-80633| genes. The genes, which were identified in more than 350 bacterial genomes, encode functional homologues of a pair of enzymes (|FRAME: G-17966 PhnY| and |FRAME: G-17967 PhnZ|) that degrade |FRAME: CPD-1106| (see |FRAME: PWY-7447|) |CITS: [30789718]|., The |FRAME: G-80632| gene encodes an iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenase. This type of enzymes couples reduction of dioxygen to the oxidative decarboxylation of |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to form |FRAME: SUC| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. This reaction generates an Fe(IV)oxo (ferryl) intermediate that (in most cases) extracts two electrons from the primary substrate to balance the complete four-electron reduction of O2. Most of the members of this family are hydroxylases like TmpA, which adds a hydroxyl group with (R) stereospecificity., The product of TmpA, |FRAME: CPD-22923|, is oxidized by TmpB, which activates dioxygen for carbon—phosphorus bond-cleavage, forming |FRAME: BETAINE| and |FRAME: Pi| |CITS: [30789718]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Despite the fact that cobamides containing phenolic lower ligand bases comprise about 16% of the total cobamides isolated from gut microbiome of humans |CITS: [18469256]|, not much information is available about the organisms that produce them. One organism that is known to produce both |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108| as lower ligand bases of biologically active cobamides is the homoacetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2378| |CITS: [3350008][Stupperich89]|. Another such organism is |FRAME: TAX-1122947|, which, when grown in lactate-amended, B12-free medium, produces both phenolylcobamide and 4-methylphenolylcobamide |CITS: [24463969]|., Unlike other common cobamide lower ligand bases, |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108| cannot establish a coordination bond with the cobalt ion of the ring. The lack of this coordination bond limits the use of these cofactors to enzymes that use cobamide coenzymes in their base-off conformation |CITS: [Stupperich89a]|, This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20844|.The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the phenolic lower ligand bases (both |FRAME: PHENOL| and |FRAME: CPD-108|) are activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.55|, a heterodimeric enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-44074| and |FRAME: G-44075| genes |CITS: [21696461]|, by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphoribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) to form the cobamide. The last two enzymes that operate in this pathway are believed to be the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis., Enzymes of |FRAME: TAX-2378| appear to have a preference for the phenolyl cobamides. The addition of benzimidazoles to cultures results in a decrease in growth rate when grown on |FRAME: METOH|, |FRAME: CPD-20857|, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| plus |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, or |FRAME: BETAINE| |CITS: [23417488]|.

|FRAME: CPD-19188 "Polyethylene terephthalate"| (PET) is the most common thermoplastic polymer resin of the polyester family and is used in fibers for clothing, containers for liquids and foods, thermoforming for manufacturing, and in combination with glass fiber for engineering resins. In the context of textile applications, PET is referred to by its common name, polyester., PET, which consists of polymerized units of the monomer |FRAME: CPD-19187|, is the fourth-most-produced polymer, surpassed only by polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC). About 56 million tons of PET, were produced in 2013 alone. PET is chemically inert, making its accumulation in the environment a global concern., Degradation of PET is limited to a few fungal and bacterial species. A number of cutinases, lipases, and esterases active on PET have been identified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-169388|, |FRAME: TAX-5541|, |FRAME: TAX-5062|, |FRAME: TAX-300|, and |FRAME: TAX-2021| |CITS: [21076908]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1547922|, isolated from sediment at a PET bottle recycling site, was shown to use PET as its major energy and carbon source. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it is accumulated at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant. In addition to its osmoprotectant activity, glycine betaine is also a potent protectant against mutagenic compounds |CITS: [12730887][15802867]| and radiation-induced damage |CITS: [12841603]|., Glycine betaine can either be taken up directly from the environment, or synthesized. A common biosynthesis pathway for glycine betaine is from choline, utilizing a two-step pathway with betaine aldehyde as intermediate. This pathway is conserved in bacteria and plants, but shows divergence in the enzymes involved. Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive bacteria and higher plants all use |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8|, to catalyze the conversion of betaine aldehyde to glycine betaine. The choline-to-betaine aldehyde reaction, however, is divergent: Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-287|, and |FRAME: TAX-382| utilize |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.1| (see |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|), Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, use an alcohol dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.1) (see |FRAME: PWY-3722|), while high plants use |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.7| (see |FRAME: PWY1F-353|)., Certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1677| and |FRAME: TAX-1665|, as well as the fungus |FRAME: TAX-109805|, use yet another enzyme to catalyze this conversion: they use a soluble choline oxidase that catalyzes both steps (see |FRAME: PWY-3721|). , There exists at least one more variation for the synthesis of glycine betaine, which is found in several halotolerant bacteria. The pathway was found in |FRAME: TAX-1052| and several other organisms, which synthesize glycine betaine from glycine through a series of methylation reactions |CITS: [10896953]| (this pathway). However, since methylation reactions are expensive (due to the cost of regenerating S-adenosylmethionine), this pathway is less common., About This Pathway, Several organisms have been shown to synthesize glycine betaine from glycine through a series of methylation reactions. These include |FRAME:TAX-1850|, |FRAME:TAX-1052|, |FRAME:TAX-72020|, and |FRAME: TAX-39664|. , The enzymes performing the methylation reactions have been characterized in some of these organisms. Even though the pathway is conserved, there are differences among the different organisms concerning the specificity of the enzymes., In |FRAME: TAX-1850| and |FRAME: TAX-1052| the pathway involves two enzymes - the first two reactions are catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.156| (GSMT), while the second and third reactions are catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.157| (SDMT) (the middle reaction can be catalyzed by either of these enzymes) |CITS: [10896953][11319079]|., In |FRAME:TAX-72020| the first two reactions are also catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.156| (GSMT), but the thrid reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.161|, which can accept only |FRAME: DIMETHYL-GLYCINE| |CITS: [12466265]|., On the other hand, in |FRAME: TAX-39664| all three reactions are catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.162| |CITS: [17098399]|., It has been shown that |FRAME: TAX-1850| possesses two pathways for glycine betaine synthesis - the de novo pathway (this pathway) and a pathway of choline oxidation |CITS: [11685374]|.

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, Most microorganisms are able to detoxify arsenic species by pumping them out of the cell. This cytoplasmic detoxification system involves the arsC-encoded cytoplasmic arsenate reductase, which reduces |FRAME: ARSENATE| to |FRAME: CPD-763|, and an efficient arsenite efflux pump (such as the ArsAB arsenite-transporting ATPase, and ArsB arsenite:proton antiporter, or the Arc3 permease) |CITS: [12165430]|., ArsC cytoplasmic arsenate reductases are found widely in microbes |CITS: [15691908]|. Even though they were all named ArsC, they belong to several different clades, some of which share no sequence similarity, indicating parallel evolution |CITS: [15691908]|., Many bacterial species have been shown to possess a thioredoxin-dependent arsenate reductase (|FRAME: EC-1.20.4.4|). Most of the thioredoxin-linked ArsC arsenate reductases are from low G+C Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [ 1409657][8003493][11698660]|, but these enzymes have also been found in the ars operons of the Gram-negative proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [9802012]| and |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [10788346]|. In addition, a gene encoding a thioredoxin-dependent enzyme has been found in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2234|, although it has not been characterized biochemically yet.

Summary: Under anaerobic conditions the photosynthetic protist |FRAME: TAX-3039| performs a process known as wax ester fermentation, during which a storage polymer, |FRAME: Paramylon|, is degraded into glucose, which is then used to produce fatty acids and fatty alcohols. Those are condensed into wax esters that are stored inside the cells until oxygen is available again. While the wax esters are composed of saturated fatty acids and alcohols ranging from C10 to C17, the predominant ones were |FRAME: CPD-7836| and |FRAME: CPD-7875| |CITS: [Inui83]|., The fatty acids produced during this process are synthesized in the mitochondria by a malonyl-CoA-independent de novo fatty acid synthetic system different from the two canonical systems that operate in the cytosol and mitochondria of most eukaryotes. Acetyl-CoA is used as the C2 donor, resulting in a pathway that is the reverse of the |FRAME: FAO-PWY "fatty acid β-oxidation"| pathway |CITS: [38041972]|. The acetyl-CoA-dependent pathway allows net fermentative ATP synthesis from glucose, because acetyl-CoA is condensed without prior ATP-dependent carboxylation to malonyl-CoA. The pathway can start with either acetyl-CoA, in which case even-numbered fatty acids are produced, or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, leading to production of odd-numbered fatty acids |CITS: [24241313]|. The pathway shown here only shows the production of even-numbered fatty acids., The pathway was first reported in 1984 by Inui et al, who proposed that the enzymes involved are those used for β-oxidation, with the exception of |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.38|, which is used instead of acyl-CoA dehydrogenases (such as |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.7|), which were thought at the time to catalyze a unidirectional reaction in the oxidative direction |CITS: [6146525]|., However, later research concluded that the pathway is a complete reversal of the β-oxidation pathway. Inactivation of |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.38| (TER1) did not affect wax ester synthesis |CITS: [30328102][30650145]|. On the other hand, silencing of |FRAME: G-124898|, one of seven genes encoding acyl-CoA dehydrogenase isozymes, led to a significant decrease in anaerobic wax ester production |CITS: [38041972]|. The authors proposed a model in which electrons originating from NADH are delivered by |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.2| (complex I) to |FRAME: Rhodoquinones rhodoquinone| (RQ), which has a lower redox potential than ubiquinone. Rhodoquinol, in turn, reduces |FRAME: Etf ETF| (electron transfer protein), the electron donor for acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. The model was confirmed by experiments that involved inhibition of complex I by |FRAME: CPD-5741| (a specific complex I inhibitor) and silencing the rquA gene, which is involved in RQ synthesis. Both cases resulted in a significant decrease in anaerobic wax ester synthesis |CITS: [30328102]|., The electron donor to the pathway (either directly to |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.35|, or indirectly as described above, is NADH. However, the main form of reducing power generated during wax ester fermentation is NADPH, which is formed by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.51| (PNO). The conversion from NADPH to NADH is perfromed by |FRAME: EC-1.6.1.3| (NNT1). Silencing that gene resulted in a 25% decrease in wax esters and a significant drop in viability |CITS: [34738635]|.

General Background, Xanthohumol is the principal prenylflavonoid found in the cones (female inflorescences) of |FRAME:TAX-3486|, an important crop known as hop, widely used in the brewing of beer. A simple prenylated chalcone, xanthohumol, along with other prenylated chalcones have attracted attention as cancer chemopreventive agents, while |FRAME: CPD-9440|, an isomerization product of |FRAME:CPD-7120| also found in beer, has been reported as the most potent phytoestrogen to date (for review, see |CITS:[16076101]|). For an extensive review of xanthohumol and other prenylflavonoids, see |CITS:[15231405]|. The sequence of reaction leading to the formation of xanthohumol from naringenin chalcone is unclear. However, the detection of desmethylxanthohumol in hops suggests that naringenin chalcone is first prenylated for form desmethylxanthohumol which would subsequently be methylated at the 6'-hydroxyl group to form xanthohumol as shown in this pathway. The question remains open., Enzymes of This Pathway, The first enzyme that has been reported in this pathway is |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.74|. This enzyme catalyzes the successive condensation of three malonyl-CoA molecules onto p-coumaroyl-CoA to form naringenin chalcone. It would appear that, in vitro at least, a certain amount of intermediates are also released as |FRAME:CPD-6955| and |FRAME:CPD-6956| were detected |CITS:[15170123]|. The enzyme was also able to use isovaleryl-CoA as substrate, showing its possible involvement in |FRAME:PWY-5132|., The next enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.136|, is also involved in the biosynthesis of bitter acids |CITS: [22166201][25564559]|.

Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxinitriles. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks, cyanogenic glycosides are cleaved releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN|, which serves as the first line of chemical defense.,  |FRAME: TAX-4558| possesses two cyanogenic β-glucosidases that hydrolyze the cyanogenic glucosides into the glucoside and aglycone |CITS: [9536065]|.

|FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| is a nucleotide-sugar that is used as biosynthetic precursor of L-galactosyl residues in polysaccharides and oligosaccharides in plants |CITS:[15134748],[14991405]|.  The L-galactosyl residues of cell wall polysaccharides, as well as those of glycoproteins only represent relatively minor components of those compounds, which helps explain the relative scarcity of information available concerning their biosynthesis. Importantly, |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| is also used in |FRAME:PWY-882| in plants.  , The key enzyme for the conversion of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| is the bifunctional |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.18| (GME) which catalyzes the dual epimerization of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| into both |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-7078| |CITS:[12954627][16413588]|.

The C50-carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-20670| was originally isolated from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1270|, at the time known as Sarcina lutea. It was independently characterized from |FRAME: TAX-41986| (then known as Flavobacterium dehydrogenans) and named dehydrogenans-P439 |CITS: [6035068][5806304]|. The two compounds were shown to be identical in 1967 |CITS: [6032832]|., An analysis of the carotenoids produced by |FRAME: TAX-1270| demonstrated that in addition to a large amount of |FRAME: CPD-20670|, the bacterium also produces smaller amounts of the mono- and di-glucosides |CITS: [20802040]|., Upon the sequencing of the |FRAME: TAX-1270| genome, a gene cluster resmbling those found in other C50 carotenoid-producing bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-370437| and |FRAME: TAX-196627|, was identified. Based on sequence similarity, the |FRAME: G-58159| gene was predicted to encode |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.149|, the |FRAME: G-58160| and |FRAME: G-58161| genes were predicted to encode the two subunits of |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.M10|, and the |FRAME: G-58162| gene was predicted to encode |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.M35|. The cluster also included the genes required for the production of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| |CITS: [20802040]|., When the full cluster (with the exception of the |FRAME: G-58162| gene) was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, the host produced a small amount of |FRAME: CPD-20670|. The reason for the low yield was traced to inefficient production of |FRAME: CPD1F-114|. When the |FRAME: G-58159|, |FRAME: G-58160|, and |FRAME: G-58161| genes were expressed in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-562| that was engineered to produce and accumulate large amounts of |FRAME: CPD1F-114|, 98% of the lycopene were converted to |FRAME: CPD-20670|., Upon the addition of the |FRAME: G-58162| gene, the recombinant host also produced small amounts of |FRAME: CPD-20672| and |FRAME: CPD-20673|, completing the pathway |CITS: [20802040]|.

Summary: Chlorogenic acids (CGA) are involved in producing the bitter effect of coffee, as a property of their decomposition in phenolic compounds during roasting. CGA mainly include caffeoyl-quinic acids (CQA), dicaffeoyl-quinic acids (diCQA) |CITS: [12861362]| and feruloyl-quinic acids (FQA). Chlorogenic acid (5-CQA) is one of the major soluble phenolic compounds that are accumulated in the green beans of coffee. Other hydroxycinnamoyl quinic acids (HQAs), is accumulated in particular in green beans of the cultivated species |FRAME: TAX-49390| |CITS: [17333503]|. Biosynthesis of 5-CQA can be catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 enzymes, from Arabidopsis. But only one of them hydroxylates the chlorogenic acid precursor p-coumaroyl quinate. CYP98A35 appears to be the first C3'H capable of metabolizing p-coumaroyl quinate and p-coumaroyl shikimate with the same efficiency. The results indicated that HQA biosynthesis and accumulation occurred mainly in the shoot tip and in the phloem of the vascular bundles. The biosynthetic activity of chlorogenic acids was clearly reduced in ripening and ripe seeds, especially in |FRAME: TAX-49390| |CITS: [18069248]|. TheCGA biosynthesis pathway is is described at |FRAME: PWY-6039|. , About this pathway: , Dietary antioxidants from plant sources are usually phenolics. Chlorogenic acid (CGA) has high bioavailability and it is hydrolyzed to caffeic acid. The degradation is done by microbial enzymes found in |FRAME: TAX-5061|, |FRAME: TAX-13373| and |FRAME: TAX-470|. The antioxidant capacity is enhanced by its availability to multiple mechanisms that are involved in scavenging of free-radicals, such as metal-ion chelation and inhibition of free-radical forming enzymes. CGA releasing enzymes are of immense interest in industrial applications |CITS: [17630312]| to help the release of aromatic compounds found in agricultural by-products like apple marc and coffee pulp.

Summary: General Background, The mycotoxin |FRAME: CPD-16726| is a polyketide metabolite produced by molds including species of |FRAME: TAX-5052|, |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-33202|. Its presence in food is a health risk to humans and animals due to its known immunological, neurological and gastrointestinal effects. Patulin is the main mycotoxin contaminating apples. Along with several other mycotoxins, including the |FRAME: Aflatoxins "aflatoxins"|, levels of |FRAME: CPD-16726| in food are regulated in many countries (reviewed in |CITS: [22069602]|)., The genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-16726| biosynthetic enzymes are clustered and the functions of some of them have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-5073| species, and |FRAME: CPD-16726| producing strains of |FRAME: TAX-5057|, as shown here. Other genes in the cluster are involved in transport and regulation (reviewed in |CITS: [22069602]|). It has been shown that |FRAME: MN+2| is required for |FRAME: CPD-16726| biosynthesis and exerts its effect at the level of transcription |CITS: [3518892]|., About This Pathway, In species of |FRAME: TAX-5073| early radiotracer studies demonstrated the incorporation of |FRAME: ACET| and the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-637| (6-methylsalicylic acid) to |FRAME: CPD-16726| |CITS: [13672977][5013816]|. The utilization of the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-112| (m-cresol), |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZYL-ALCOHOL| (m-hydroxybenzyl alcohol), |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZALDEHYDE|, |FRAME: CPD-16722| and |FRAME: CPD-16721|, and the para-hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-112| were shown |CITS: [SCOTTAI73]|. More recently, a putative |FRAME: CPD-16726| biosynthetic pathway has been proposed based on additional biochemical and mutant studies (|CITS: [24334092][19383676]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22069602]|). The latter portion of the pathway remains highly speculative, however, and awaits future research., The initial step in the pathway is the condensation of one |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| unit and three |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| units to form |FRAME: CPD-637| catalyzed by the polyketide synthase 6-methylsalicylic acid synthase encoded by gene patK. The |FRAME: CPD-637| is then decarboxylated to |FRAME: CPD-112| in a reaction catalyzed by 6-methylsalicylic acid decarboxylase encoded by gene patG |CITS: [24334092]|., In the |FRAME: CPD-16726| forming pathway |FRAME: CPD-112| undergoes methyl group hydroxylation to form |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZYL-ALCOHOL| catalyzed by the monooxygenase CYP169C3 encoded by gene patH. The |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZYL-ALCOHOL| is then further hydroxylated to |FRAME: CPD-16721| in a reaction catalyzed by the monooxygenase CYP619C2 encoded by gene patI (|CITS: [19383676]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22069602]|)., Although |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZALDEHYDE| is currently not thought to be a precursor of |FRAME: CPD-16726|, this compound and its corresponding acid |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYBENZOATE| are metabolites |CITS: [SCOTTAI73]|. The conversion of |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYBENZOATE| by a |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenase was suggested by |CITS: [241643]|., |FRAME: CPD-16722 "Gentisaldehyde"| is thought to be a |FRAME: CPD-16726| precursor. The formation of |FRAME: CPD-633| from |FRAME: CPD-16722| is suggested by the accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-633| in |FRAME: CPD-16726|-negative mutants |CITS: [418806]|., As discussed in |CITS: [19383676]|, the potential hydroxylation of |FRAME: 3-OH-BENZALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: CPD-16722| as part of the |FRAME: CPD-16726| pathway remains uncertain. This reaction is shown in |CITS: [19383676]| but is absent in |CITS: [22069602]| and is not shown here., The |FRAME: CPD-112| can also undergo para-hydroxylation catalyzed by PatI to form |FRAME: CPD-16720|l. This compound has been identified as a co-metabolite of |FRAME: CPD-16726|, but |FRAME: CPD-16720| is not an intermediate in |FRAME: CPD-16726| biosynthesis |CITS: [5013816][SCOTTAI73]|., The characterization of |FRAME: CPD-16726|-negative mutants has allowed identification of the |FRAME: CPD-16723|, |FRAME: CPD-16724|, |FRAME: CPD-16725| (isopatulin), and |FRAME: CPD-16727| intermediates |CITS: [418806][SEKIGUCHIJ79][508294][43192][6881967]|. This led to the proposed epoxidation reactions that convert |FRAME: CPD-16722| to |FRAME: CPD-16723|, and |FRAME: CPD-16721| to |FRAME: CPD-16724| (|CITS: [19383676]| and reviewed in |CITS: [22069602]|). A |FRAME: CPD-16721| epoxidase activity was found in crude extracts of |FRAME: TAX-5078 "Penicillium griseofulvum (previously known as Penicillium patulum)"| that produced |FRAME: CPD-16724| which was further converted to |FRAME: CPD-16725| by the extract (neopatulin synthase activity) |CITS: [2605253]|.

|FRAME: SCOPOLETIN Scopoletin| (7-hydroxy-6-methoxy coumarin) is a hydroxycoumarin. It is found in a number of plant species including Arabidopsis, cassava, sweet potato, sunflower, cotton and tobacco |CITS: [19004461], [18547395]|. Scopoletin is thought to be involved in plant defense responses. In tobacco, accumulation of scopoletin was shown to strongly correlate with tobacco mosaic virus-induced localized acquired resistance |CITS: [12060240]|., In addition, |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN| serves as a precursor for the production of the siderophores |FRAME: CPD-21613| and |FRAME: CPD-21615 sideretin| |CITS: [29581584]|. Root exudation of phenylpropanoid-derived coumarins has been shown to be required for efficient iron uptake, especially under alkaline conditions. Mutations of the oxoglutarate-dependent oxidase |FRAME: AT3G13610|, involved in |FRAME: SCOPOLETIN| biosynthesis, and the ABC-type transporter PDR9, involved in coumarin export, result in severe symptoms of iron deficiency when iron is supplied in an insoluble form |CITS: [23735511][24015802][24246380][25058345]|., Scopoletin was indicated to have many pharmacological effects as well, such as antidepressant |CITS: [20599906]|, anti-arthritic |CITS: [21078410]|, anti-gastro-esophageal inflammatory |CITS: [21163341]|, potential in ameliorate insulin resistance |CITS: [20886413]|, and potential in treatment of hypertriglyceridemia |CITS: [17786283]|. In addition, it was also shown to have antitermite activity |CITS: [20563628]|., The biosynthesis pathway leading to scopoletin in plants is still largely unclear. Genetic and biochemical evidence in Arabidopsis supports that, in this plant, scopoletin is derived from feruloyl-CoA, not ferulate |CITS: [18547395]| as previously thought. A 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase is responsible for the ortho-hydroxylation of feruloyl-CoA, an important branch point from lignin biosynthesis. Ortho-hydroxylation of the feruloyl-CoA aromatic ring is followed by trans-cis isomerization of the side chain, and subsequent lactonization to close the ring and yield scopoletin. The mechanism of the E-Z isomerization step in the biosynthesis of coumarins varies between genera or even species, for being either light-dependent photoisomerization or light-independent enzyme catalyzed isomerization |CITS: [19004461]|. It is not clear what mechanism is involved in the above depicted scopoletin biosynthesis pathway in Arabidopsis. , In cassava, where scopoletin and its glycoside derivative appear to be involved in significant crop losses due to Post-harvest Physiological Deterioration (PPD), some detailed experiments performed with isotopic intermediates have shed light on the reactions comprising this |FRAME: PWY-7186 biosynthetic pathway| in |FRAME: TAX-3983| |CITS: [19004461]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipopolysaccharides that comprise all three regions are called |FRAME: Smooth-Form-LPS "smooth (S)-form LPS"|, while LPS lacking the O-antigen are named |FRAME: LOS "rough (R)-form LPS"| or lipooligosaccharide (LOS)., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. The core oligosaccharide is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., In most bacteria studied to date the core region is composed of ~10 sugars. The core oligosaccharides are conceptually divided further into two regions: inner core and outer core. The inner core is more conserved and contains |FRAME: KDO| (Kdo). In many bacterial species (but not |FRAME: TAX-837|) the inner core contains |FRAME: CPD-21358| (Hep) residues. The inner core oligosaccharide plays a critical role in essential barrier function of the outer membrane. The outer core is usually composed of hexoses and provides an attachment site for O-antigen., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-837| synthesizes two different types of lipopolysaccharides, which have been named O-LPS and A-LPS. Numerous studies have shown that both structures share the lipid A and core oligosaccharide structures, and differ only in their O antigens, which are referred to as O antigen and A antigen, respectively (see |FRAME: PWY-8228|). While the structure of the O antigen is known, there is still controversey regarding the structure of the A antigen, as rather different structures have been reported |CITS: [25733619][28972686]|., It should be noted that while the polysaccharides are divided into two groups based on the O antigen, additional variability is present in both the lipid A moiety (as described in |FRAME: PWY-8247| and the core moiety (as described here). For simplicity, all of the structures shown here are based on a single lipid A form (|FRAME: CPD-24240 "penta-acylated, bis-phosphorylated"|)., As of 2021, the structure of the inner core of the |FRAME: TAX-837| LPS has been studied at a minimal level |CITS: [16367871]|, but the outer core has been reported in detail |CITS: [19525343][25733619]|. This part of the core contains a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| molecule that is attached to a |FRAME: KDO| (Kdo) residue via a phosphoester. An unusuall |FRAME: CPD-24225 α-D-allosaminyl"| residue is attached to the other end of the glycerol molecule, while the central carbon of the glycerol is attached to a long chain of α-D-mannopyranose residues connected by (1->3) linkages. The mannose chain has been divided into two sections: the first section contains either three or four mannosyl residues, and is considered part of the minimal outer core, while the second section, which was named the "cap", includes three to five additional mannosyl residue and is the site of the O antigen attachment. The last two mannosyl residues in the first section are modified by |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| |CITS: [19525343]|., Becasue the first section can contain either three or four mannosyl residues, two type of outer cores can be observed in LPS isolated from this organism, adding to the significant variability of the |FRAME: TAX-837| LPS., It has been shown that the same O-antigen ligase, encoded by the |FRAME: HMPREF1322_RS00350| gene, is responsible for the attachment of both types the O and A antigens |CITS: [18263730][19525343]|. However, the two antigens are attached at different positions - the O antigen is attached at position O-3 of the terminal cap mannose |CITS: [19525343]|, while the A antigen is attached at position O-4 of one of the non-terminal cap mannoses |CITS: [25733619]|.

Flavonoids are a highly diverse class of plant secondary metabolites (with over 9000 compounds identified so far, |CITS: [16137727]|) synthesized by the phenylpropanoid pathway. They exhibit a wide range of biological functions in higher plants. They are involved in UV protection, flower coloration, and antimicrobial defense |CITS: [11130659]|., They also exhibit antioxidant and anticancer properties |CITS: [12224601][18645020]|., Chrysoeriol is a flavonoid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties |CITS: [16450301]|. Chrysoeriol has, also been shown to function as a signal molecule and induce the transcription of nodulation (nod) genes in, |FRAME:TAX-382| |CITS: [16667231]|.

Summary: General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn this variant of the TCA cycle converts one molecule of acetyl-CoA into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, reduces a total of four molecules of either |FRAME: NAD|, |FRAME: NADP|, or |FRAME: Quinones quinone| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively, and phosphorylates one molecule of nucleotide diphosphate (ADP or GDP) to nucleotide triphosphate (ATP or GTP)., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that transport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The name of the TCA (short for tricarboxylic acid) cycle is derived from the fact that the first step in the pathway is attachment of acetyl-coA to |FRAME: CIT|, an acid with three carboxylate groups. The pathway is also known as the citric acid cycle, and as the Szent-Gyorgyi-Krebs cycle (or just the Krebs cycle), named after the scientists who described it., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|., About This Pathway, One of the main differences between the eukaryotic TCA cycles (described in this pathway and in |FRAME: PWY66-398|) and the |FRAME: TCA "prokaryotic pathway"| is that the latter contains an alternative route between |FRAME: MAL| and |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.4|. That enzyme is found in some bacteria, but is absent from most eukaryotes, in which the reaction is catalyzed only by the |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37 "NAD+-dependent malate dehydrogenase, EC 1.1.1.37"|., Another difference concerns the enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase. Most prokaryotes possess only an NADP+-dependent form (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.42|), which supports both respiration via the TCA cycle and glutamate biosynthesis for anabolic reactions. Eukaryotes, on the other hand, have two types of the enzyme - an NADP+-dependent forms (EC 1.1.1.42) and NAD+-dependent forms (EC 1.1.1.41). It has been shown that the NADP+-dependent enzymes are involved primarily in glutamate biosynthesis, while the NAD+-dependent enzymes are those involved in the TCA cycle |CITS: [2198251]|., It should be noted that while rare, NAD+-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenases are also found in bacteria that lack the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate bypass"|, and thus are missing the enzyme |FRAME: ISOCIT-CLEAV-RXN "isocitrate lyase"| |CITS: [15653464]|. Examples for prokaryotes that contain an NAD-dependent enzyme include |FRAME: TAX-930| |CITS: [12204383]| and |FRAME: TAX-542| |CITS: [22117777]|., The only difference between this pathway, found in plants and fungi, and |FRAME: PWY66-398|, which is found in animals, is the step between |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: SUC|. While plants and fungi only use |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.5|, animals also use |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.4|.

Summary: General Background, Sterols are isoprenoid-derived molecules that have essential functions in eukaryotes. In vertebrates |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| is by far the major sterol, whereas a mixture of various sterols is present in higher plants, including |FRAME: CPD-4143| (usually predominant), |FRAME: CPD-4162|, |FRAME: CPD-707|, |FRAME: CPD-4127|, |FRAME: CPD-4161| and |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. Sterols are present in three forms: free sterols (the major form with a free 3β-hydroxyl), steryl esters, and steryl glucosides., Free sterols are integral components of the membrane lipid bilayer and thus interact with some molecular species of, phosphoglycero(sphingo) lipids. The extent of this interaction plays a functional role in the regulation of membrane fluidity and permeability. Sterols have also been shown to play important roles in embryonic development of vertebrates and the formation of membrane microdomains (rafts), which may constitute signaling centers for multiple pathways |CITS:[11278759]|., Finally, sterols are precursors of compounds with a high physiological activity such as brassinosteroids, an important class of plant hormones involved in growth and development |CITS: [8602526]|, ecdysteroids in invertebrates |CITS:[7791536]| and plants |CITS:[Coriot93]|, and antheridiol and oogoniols, sexual pheromones of aquatic fungi belonging to, the saprolegniale class |CITS:[1913877]|., In plants:, The plant sterol biosynthesis pathway is essentially linear until reaching 24-methylene lophenol, with a bifurcation downstream of this compound that results in two main pathways leading to 24-methyl- and 24-ethyl-sterols. The simplicity of this pathway is essentially due to i) the relatively high substrate specificity of most enzymes from the postsqualene segment of the biosynthetic chain and ii) to the channeling of substrates/products through microdomains of the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS:[15377227]|., A number of minor sterols have been detected suggesting that in addition to the main sterol biosynthesis pathway depicted here a number of side pathways exist. Those compounds remain largely undetected until sterol biosynthesis inhibitors are used or genes encoding various enzymes of the biosynthesis pathways are mutated. Our knowledge of the sterol biosynthesis pathway in plants results largely from the study of Arabidopsis thaliana mutants and through detecting the accumulated intermediates and/or functional complementation of the mutant phenotypes with wild type genes., Key Notes on the Enzymes:, i) Of the many enzymes involved in the sterol biosynthesis pathway, very few have been purified to homogeneity. Nonetheless many genes encoding those proteins have been cloned in |FRAME:TAX-3701| and have been expressed in heterologous systems where the substrate specificity of the corresponding enzymes has been assessed (see individual comments on particular enzymes)., ii) One of the major rate-limiting steps of this pathway is the C-24 methylation of |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL| catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.41| (SMT1)., iii) |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.154| (OBT14DM; CYP51) from |FRAME:TAX-4577| (corn) has been described as a major potential herbicide target.

Summary: The traditional |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathway"| joins the |FRAME:OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY| to glycolysis., While basic carbon metabolic pathways such as the Entner-Doudoroff pathway are rather conserved within eukaryotes and eubacteria, archaebacteria have proved to be unexpectedly diverse., The central metabolic pathways of carbohydrate catabolism found in these organisms exhibit a high variability, and include modifications to the ED pathway, as well as to the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway (glycolysis)., The classical Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathway of bacteria (and some eukaryotes) (|FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY|) starts with the phosphorylation of either glucose or its oxidized derivative gluconate. There are two "flavors" of ED-like pathways in archaea that do not follow this route., One variation is found in halophilic archaea (and some bacteria), in which 2-keto-3-deoxygluconate (KDG) is phosphorylated to KDPG by KDG kinase, rather than the general conversion of glucose into glucose 6-phosphate (see |FRAME: PWY-2221|)., The second variation is found in the thermophiles |FRAME:TAX-2284|,|FRAME:TAX-2302| and |FRAME:TAX-2270|, in which the activation via phosphorylation occurs only at the level of glycerate. Utilization of this modified pathway has a cost: there appears to be no net generation of ATP by the non-phosphorylating ED pathway |CITS: [12921536][6440533]|., Not all of the proteins that participate in this pathway have been purified from archaea. Some of the steps were deduced from biochemical assays performed with cell extracts. Budgen and Danson |CITS: [Budgen86]| found that cell extracts of Thermplasma acidophilum produced glycerate-2-phosphate rather than the more common glycerate-3-phosphate. In addition, there was no phosphoglycerate mutase activity. As a result, it was determined that in this organism glyecrate, is phosphorylated to 2-phosphoglycerate. Based on this data, this conversion has been proposed to occur in |FRAME:TAX-2284| as well |CITS: [2497944]|., Overall, the modified ED pathway in these organisms can be summarized as:, glucose --> 2 pyruvates + 2 NADPH, with no net ATP gain. There are two potential explanations for this: one possibility is that efficient cofactor reoxidation (either by oxidative phosphorylation, or by sulfur respiration) makes substrate level phosphorylation not important. The other possibility is that this modified ED pathway is reversible, and could be used as an alternative gluconeogenesis route (reviewed in |CITS: [ 9119021]|).
