Summary: |FRAME:CPD-13080 Solasodine| also referred to as tomatidenol is the main steroidal alkaloid aglycone in Solanum melongena from which the steroidal glycoalkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-13081 solasodine 3-O-β-D-glucoside|, |FRAME:CPD-18738 solasodine 3-O-β-D-galactoside| and others are formed in unripe fruits |CITS:[DeWaal60] [Bajaj79]|. Together with the steroidal saponins (melongosides), which are derivatives of e.g. |FRAME:CPD-15437 diosgenin| and accumulate in the roots |CITS:[Kintia85a] [Kintia85b]|, they form the bulk of steroidal glycosides found in this plant. Solanum melongena is able to synthesize both steroidal saponins and glycoalkaloids and has therefore been a suitable subject for studying the respective pathways |CITS:[Heftmann83] [Tschesche80]|. In comparison to the high variety and number of steroidal saponins in plants the glycoalkaloids show less diversity and are scarcer in nature |CITS:[Hostettmann95]| which make the Solaneceae the best resource for this type of steroidal glycosides as shown in analyses of various Solanum tuberosum cultivars |CITS:[18616273]| and other members of the Solaneceae family |CITS:[17265223]|. , The bioactivities of steroidal saponins and glycoalkaloids have been extensively investigated in the Solaneceae family |CITS:[12913278]|. The compound class of steroidal glycosides are considered toxic for humans in which toxicity depends on the aglycone type and attached sugar moieties |CITS:[Maga94]|. Numerous studies have been carried out to assess the risk they may pose to human food safety and nutrition |CITS:[Valkonen96] [Friedman97]| (see also |FRAME:PWY18C3-3 α-tomatine biosynthesis|). In addition, steroidal glycoalkaloids have been shown to inhibit pre-implantation embryo development |CITS:[15581508]|. On the other side steroidal glycoalkaloids have been considered as mother compounds for novel cancer drugs |CITS:[22460423]| because of their ability to efficiently induce apoptosis and cell cycle arrest |CITS:[15670922]|. This is one of the reasons to investigate and maximize the yield of steroidal alkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-13080 solasodine| for medicinal purposes |CITS:[Loc14] [Ravindran15]|. |FRAME:CPD-13080 Solasodine| and its glucosylated derivative |FRAME:CPD-13081 solasodine 3-O-β-D-glucoside| may also act as phytoalexins and are increasingly formed when plants are attacked by pathogens such as Fusarium oxysporum. The mode of action in such cases is the inhibition of hyphae formation in the fungus |CITS:[23229144]|. The many facets of steroidal glycoalkaloids and respective aglycones with respect to their antimicrobial, anticancer, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory properties have been addressed in various reviews |CITS:[21401040]|., The glycosylation of |FRAME:CPD-13080 solasodine| is carried out by glycosyltransferases from a variety of plant species. Glycosyltransferases which modify sterols have been in the focus of research for a long time because of the important role sterols play as structural (membranes) and functional (signaling molecules, hormones, defense) components in developmental and growth processes |CITS:[21468635] [16669774]|. Bioinformatics and genetic analyses allowed to document specific domains in glycosyltransferases and sterol glycosyltransferases in particular which makes the identification of newly detected enzymes and their possible molecular function significantly more efficient |CITS:[10521532] [12538870]|., |FRAME:CPD-13080 Solasodine| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-2 solasodine biosynthesis|) is glycosylated in various species of the Solaneceae family. A solasodine 3-O-glucosyltransferase has been observed in protein extracts from leaves of eggplant (Solanum melongena) seedlings |CITS:[Paczkowski94]|. It could be demonstrated that the partially purified solasodine 3-O-glucosyltransferase was able to glucosylate the 3-O-position of |FRAME:CPD-13080 solasodine| forming |FRAME:CPD-13081 solasodine 3-O-β-D-glucoside| |CITS:[8957283] [9241353]|. It appears that the solasodine 3-O-glucosyltransferase also glucosylated spirostane-type sapogenins which resulted in the discussion whether or not the glucosylation of steroidal alkaloids such as |FRAME:CPD-13080 solasodine| and |FRAME:CPD-15437 diosgenin|, the precursor for steroidal sapogenins, is carried out by a single enzyme or separate enzymes. Studies to this effect yielded ambiguous results and remain to be resolved |CITS:[8957283] [9241353] [Paczkowski98] [11672729]|. Although the importance of certain amino acid residues has been revealed for the full catalytic activity of the Solanum melongena solasodine 3-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[12833182]| only partial isolated DNA sequences from Solanum melongena have been associated with the solasodine 3-O-glucosyltransferase activity and the gene still remains to be identified and functionally characterized |CITS:[15821879]|. However, the solasodine 3-O-glycosyltransferase encoded by GT4A from Solanum aculeatissimum has been cloned, recombinant expressed and functionally characterized |CITS:[15821879] [17204296]|., The galactosylation of |FRAME:CPD-13080 solasodine| to form |FRAME:CPD-18738 solasodine 3-O-β-D-galactoside| has been observed in Solanum lycopersicum where the GAME1 codes for a tomatidine 3-O-galactosyltransferase but shows comparable activities towards |FRAME:CPD-13080 solasodine| |CITS:[Zimowski98]|. The question whether or not the SGT1 encoded glycosyltransferase in Solanum tuberosum glucosylates or galactosylates steroidal alkaloids was for some time a matter of debate |CITS:[9076990]|. It was later shown that the SGT1 encoded protein was much more active with |FRAME:CPD-14553 UDP-α-D-galactose| than with |FRAME:CPD-12575 UDP-α-D-glucose| hence acting as galactosyltransferase rather than glucosyltransferase |CITS:[McCue05] [17204296]|.

Note that the quinolone compound in this pathway and those in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6660| exist in tautomeric forms (as indicated on their respective compound display pages). The forms shown on this page were suggested to be predominant in the physiological pH range (see |CITS: [20738404]|], Fig. 2). However, in some publications and databases they are shown in the non-physiological tautomeric form (reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|)., General Background, Microorganisms, plants and animals produce many types of quinolone compounds. Bacteria produce a variety of 2-alkylquinolones that have antimicrobial properties. Chemically synthesized quinolone antibiotics that contain a 3-carboxy group, such as |FRAME: CPD-12843|, are well known. The opportunistic human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287| produces a family of 4-hydroxy-2-alkylquinolines one of which is the |FRAME:TAX-286| quinolone signal molecule (PQS) (see |FRAME: CPD-12838|) |CITS: [14739337]|. In addition to its function in quorum sensing and biofilm production, PQS may also function in iron scavenging and in formation of membrane vesicles (|CITS: [18630345] [16872396] [17254955]| and in |CITS: [19788310]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6660| and |FRAME: PWY-6662|)., Another quinolone produced by |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: TAX-57975| is |FRAME: 4-hydroxy-2-1H-quinolone| (also named 4-hydroxy-2-quinolone, DHQ) that lacks a 2-alkyl group |CITS: [17655503]|. This extracellular metabolite is of unknown function, although it was shown to inhibit the viability of cultured mouse lung epithelial MLE-12 cells. This observation is relevant to the colonization of the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients by |FRAME: TAX-287| biofilms (|CITS: [18728009]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| utilized in this pathway may be derived from the phnAB and trpEG encoded anthranilate synthases found in |FRAME: TAX-287| (in |CITS: [17655503]|) (see below). |FRAME: TAX-57975| appears to lack phnAB homologs |CITS: [18539738]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-287| the first step in this pathway is the activation of |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| to its |FRAME: CO-A| derivative by an anthranilate CoA ligase encoded by pqsA |CITS: [17655503]|. The presence of pqsA within the pqsABCDE operon suggested its specific function in activating |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| for quinolone biosynthesis, distinguishing it from the catabolic enzyme for growth on aromatic substrates |CITS: [18083812]|. , DHQ formation involves the PqsD-catalyzed condensation of |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZOYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| (or |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|). PqsD forms an acyl-enzyme intermediate with |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZOYL-COA|, which then reacts with |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| (or |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|, not shown) to produce a short-lived product that spontaneously undergo intramolecular cyclization to form DHQ |CITS: [18728009]|., In |FRAME: TAX-287| the biosynthesis of DHQ, as well as PQS and other alkylquinolones, involves genes of the pqsABCDE operon. Adjacent to this operon is the phnAB operon encoding a second anthranilate synthase, an alternative to trpE and trpG in this organism, that also produces the |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| precursor for this pathway. Also adjacent is gene pqsR which encodes a LysR-type transcriptional regulator of both operons |CITS: [2153661]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20738404]|.

Summary: The isoflavonoid glycosides in legumes have conserved patterns of glycosylations, the monosaccharides and dissacharides are usually β-glucopyranosides. Dissacharides among the isoflavonoid glucosides are known to occur less frequently. Nevertheless, unusual isoflavone glycosides are reported every year, for example the uncommon sugar β-apiofuranose has been found a s a monosaccharid invariably O-linked to C-4' of the isoflavone aglycone or as a terminal sugar of various disaccharids |CITS: [VEITCH06]|. , The biosynthesis of legume isoflavonoid glycosides is poorly understood. A few isoflavonoid-specific , glucotransferases have been cloned providing some insight into the mechanism of isoflavonoid production , in legumes. In |FRAME: TAX-106130|, an isoflavonoid β-glucosidase called dalcochinase had been , isolated and cloned |CITS: [17998137]|. This enzyme hydrolyzes the rotenoid glycoside , |FRAME: CPD-9677| |CITS: [16814564]|. Dalcochinase has also been shown to carry out reverse , hydrolysis of saccharides in the presence of excess sugars.

Summary: Brassinosteroids are steroidal hormones that regulate the growth and development of plants. Brassinosteroids are C<sub>27</sub>, C<sub>28</sub> and C<sub>29</sub> steroids depending on their C-24 alkyl substituents. More than 50 free, naturally occurring brassinosteroids have been identified in plants, of which brassinolide (BL) is the most biologically active C<sub>28</sub>, and together with its C<sub>28</sub> congeners, is distributed widely in the plant kingdom |CITS:[15012241]|. The biosynthesis pathway of brassinolide was initially elucidated using cultured |FRAME:TAX-4058| cells. Extensive metabolic studies suggested parallel-branched brassinolide pathways, namely the early and late C-6 oxidation pathways |CITS:[14502988]|. It has proposed that the late C-6 oxidation pathway plays a predominant role in the light, whereas the early C-6 oxidation pathway is dominant in the dark |CITS: [10982435]|. Recent studies suggest that there is a crosstalk between these parallel pathways, implying that they are not totally autonomous. The operation of an early C-22 oxidation branch of the brassinosteroid biosynthetic pathway has also been demonstrated (see |FRAME:PWY-2582|) |CITS:[12376657]|. Thus, brassinosteroid biosynthesis pathways are highly networked. The identification of |FRAME:TAX-3701| mutants defective in enzymes of the various branches of the brassinosteroids biosynthesis pathway has been instrumental in the elucidation of the many steps of the biosynthesis of those compounds., Those mutants often display a dwarf phenotype. Although the current evidence indicates that both the early and late C-6 oxidation pathways are common in the plant kingdom, as seen in plants such as rice, pea and zinnia |CITS:[11161013],[12223591],[12445121]|, it appears that in tomato and tobacco the late C-6 oxidation pathway is predominant as endogenous brassinosteroids of these species comprise only members of this branch |CITS:[11551544],[10631252],[9990098]|., A putative brassinosteroid receptor has been described: BRI1 |CITS: [11268216]|., As of 2021, several reactions steps (the C-6 oxidation step of |FRAME: CPD-710|, C-2 hydroxylation, and the oxidation/reduction of oxygen functionality at C-3) remain unelucidated |CITS: [30363110]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10231| is a precursor of the antibiotic |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B| and other ansamycin class and mitomycin class antibiotics (in |CITS: [11278540]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5984|). It provides the mC7N unit of these antibiotics (a six-carbon ring, usually aromatic or quinoid, with an extra carbon and a nitrogen in meta arrangement) |CITS: [KIM96]|. Its proposed biosynthetic pathway is shown here |CITS: [12207504] [12207505] [11804477] [15128242]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|. This pathway, referred to as the aminoshikimate pathway, is a novel variation of the shikimate pathway |CITS: [12207505]| (see pathway |FRAME: ARO-PWY|). As shown in the first pathway link, this pathway begins with the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10224| from |FRAME: CPD-12575|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CPD-10231| biosynthetic pathway was shown to be related to the shikimate pathway (see pathway |FRAME: ARO-PWY|) by incorporation of the amino analogs of shikimate pathway intermediates |FRAME: CPD-10228|, |FRAME: CPD-10229| and |FRAME: CPD-10230| in cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-33910| |CITS: [Kim96]|. However, the terminal enzyme 3-amino-5-hydroxybenzoate synthase has no parallel in the shikimate pathway. Its product, |FRAME: CPD-10231|, has been shown to be the starter unit for the rifamycin polyketide synthase (in |CITS: [9497318]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5984|)., The amino group of |FRAME: CPD-10228| was originally thought to be derived from transamination of |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| to |FRAME: CPD-10227| by |FRAME: GLN| |CITS: [KIM96]|, but later work suggested that |FRAME: CPD-10227| may result from fragmentation of |FRAME: CPD-10226| by a transketolase |CITS: [11804477] [12207504]| and in |CITS: [15128242]|. The source of the nitrogen atom in this pathway is likely to be |FRAME: CPD-10224| |CITS: [12207504]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5978|). The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10225| to |FRAME: CPD-10226| is labeled as hypothetical because it may be catalyzed by an as yet unidentified isomerase outside of the rif gene cluster (in |CITS: [12207505]|). , The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10228| to |FRAME: CPD-10229| and of |FRAME: CPD-10229| to |FRAME: CPD-10230| via cyclization and dehydration are predicted to be catalyzed by the products of genes rifG and rifJ, respectively. These genes have been shown to be essential for |FRAME: CPD-10231| biosynthesis |CITS: [11278540]|. The product of gene rifK was proposed to function twice in the pathway, as a transaminase in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-10224| and as a synthase in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-10231| (reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|)., Although this pathway has been referred to as the aminoshikimate pathway, |FRAME: CPD-21874| is not produced in this pathway. Even though the compound is produced in small amounts in |FRAME: TAX-33910| by the |FRAME: G-62986| gene product, |FRAME: MONOMER-20729|, which competes with RifK for its substrate, its role in the organism is not known |CITS: [15128242]|.

The |FRAME: G-58184| and |FRAME: G-58185| genes, which encode the enzymes of this pathway, belong to an unidentified bacterium. The genes were isolated from an envireonmental DNA sample extracted from soil. A cosmid library prepared from the DNA was used to screen for antibacterial activity, and the substances responsible for the observed activities were identified., |FRAME: TAX-562| cells expressing the two genes produced the isonitrile compound |FRAME: CPD-20765| that had antibacterial activity against the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [16206308]|., |FRAME: G-58184 IsnA| was found to be an |FRAME: MONOMER-20396|. It was the first isonitrile synthase enzyme to be described, and as such, not much was known about its mechanism at the time. Using 15N-L-tryptophan it was shown that the nitrogen of the isonitrile group originates in the |FRAME: TRP| |CITS: [16206308]|. Surprisingly, a later study has shown that the carbon atom of the isonitrile group comes from the carbonyl group of |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| |CITS: [16217820]|., Further study of IsnA's mechanism was hampered by difficulties in producing a recombinant enzyme. The mechanism was thus studied with orthologous enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-56108|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58189| and |FRAME: G-58190| genes |CITS: [28212039]|. The authors were able to verify that the product of the enzyme is |FRAME: CPD-20766|, and suggested a mechanism, according to which the reaction starts with the formation of an imine intermediate composed of the two substrates, followed by loss of the phosphate group and formation of a β-keto imine and enol-keto automerization. This is followed by a C-C bond cleavage, releasing |FRAME: ACETOL|, and a retro aldol type reaction that forms the final product and releases |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| |CITS: [28212039]|., |FRAME: G-58185 IsnB| shows the highest sequence identity to Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases, and catalyzes a hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-20766|, followed by decarboxylation and dehydration that lead to desaturation of the product, forming |FRAME: CPD-20765| |CITS: [16206308][28212039]|., IsnB is stereoselective, forming a trans product. A homologous enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-56108|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58188| gene, catalyzes a similar reaction, but forms a cis product |CITS: [24180436]|.|

Summary: Fluorescent pseudomonads such as |FRAME: TAX-303| and |FRAME: TAX-294| can catabolize lysine and other amino acids as a sole carbon and nitrogen source, giving them the ability to grow in the rhizosphere of plants where amino acids are part of the root exudates. These soil bacteria are believed to promote the growth and health of crop plants (in |CITS: [11679348][15150230][16237033]|). , |FRAME: TAX-303| can catabolize |FRAME: LYS| via the |FRAME: 5-AMINOPENTANOATE| (δ-aminovalerate) (AMV) pathway to |FRAME: GLUTARATE| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5280|). However, some strains also catabolize |FRAME: CPD-219| via a different pathway, as shown here. This pathway involves a lysine racemase that converts |FRAME: LYS| to |FRAME: CPD-219|, which is then converted to cyclic, six-carbon intermediates (|CITS: [5128165]| and in |CITS: [914858][15561717][16237033]|). This pathway is also known as the α-aminoadipate (|FRAME: CPD-468|) (AMA) pathway, and some of the enzymes, as well as a transporter, may be encoded on the OCT plasmid (|CITS: [8234494]| and in |CITS: [16237033]|). , Two enzymes that act on D-lysine have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-160488|. One is a D-lysine aminotransferase encoded by the amaC gene (PP3590), and the other is a D-lysine oxidase, encoded by the amaD gene (PP3596). Mutant and biochemical studies suggested that AmaD plays a major role, while AmaC has a minor, as yet undefined role, in lysine catabolism |CITS: [17259313]|. Earlier evidence for this conversion derived from induction studies |CITS: [4359655]|, radiolabeling experiments |CITS: [5554291]|, and trapping of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE| as an o-aminobenzaldehyde adduct |CITS: [8234494]|. , The cyclic intermediate substrate |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE| forms spontaneously and exists in equilibrium with its open chain form |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE| |CITS: [4285660][Rodwell71][1909881][10772957]|. It is converted to |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.1| and then to the last cyclic intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-7682|, by |FRAME: EC-1.5.3.7|. Next, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.31|, catalyzes the essentially irreversible NAD-dependent oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-7682|, or |FRAME: ALLYSINE| (the open chain form of |FRAME: CPD-7682|,) to |FRAME: CPD-468| |CITS: [16237033]|., The last three steps of the pathway were described in 2019. An aminotransferase converts |FRAME: CPD-468| to |FRAME: 2K-ADIPATE|, which is converted by oxidative decarboxylation to |FRAME: R-2-HYDROXYGLUTARATE|. The final reaction in the pathway is dehydrogenation to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS: [31064836]|., |FRAME: LYS| catabolism in |FRAME: TAX-286| varies as to species and strain. |FRAME: TAX-287| does not use the δ-aminovalerate (AMV) pathway. It was proposed to catabolizes |FRAME: LYS| via decarboxylation, to |FRAME: CADAVERINE| (in |CITS: [16237033]|) (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY0-461|)., Fungi and mammals have also been shown to degrade |FRAME: CPD-219| or |FRAME: LYS| to |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE|. In |FRAME: TAX-1541393|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| formed from |FRAME: LYS| is a biosynthetic precursor of indolizidine alkaloids. In mammals, the predominant pathway for |FRAME: LYS| degradation is via |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: LYSINE-DEG1-PWY|). However, the pipecolate pathway via |FRAME: CPD-219| or |FRAME: LYS| is predominant in mammalian brain (|CITS: [1259753]| in |CITS: [10772957]| and reviewed in |CITS: [1909881]|). More recently though, the existence of this pathway has been questioned in studies using L-[α-15N]lysine or L-[ε-15N]lysine in human fibroblasts |CITS: [19932104]|.

Names: Escherichia coli serotype O:15 O antigen biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, This O antigen has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-57706| O:35 |CITS: [8821392]| and |FRAME: TAX-2067424| |CITS: [21167479]| (it was also reported erroneously from |FRAME: TAX-59203| |CITS: [2447898]|, but that organism is now known to produce an O antigen based on the |FRAME: CPD-23856| |CITS: [21167479]|)., The O antigen gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2067424| was sequenced in 2005 and found to contain nine open reading frames. The cluster includes all three genes required for biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15644| (see |FRAME: PWY-7330|), two glycosyltransferases, O antigen flippase and polymerase, a gene similar to the |FRAME: EG11525| gene of |FRAME: TAX-83333|, which encodes a putative transposase, and a truncated non-functional gene named wbuC |CITS: [15695667]|.

Names: ubiquinol-7 biosynthesis (early decarboxylation) // ubiquinone-7 biosynthesis (prokaryotic) // ubiquinol-7 biosynthesis (prokaryotic)
Summary: General Background, Ubiquinone (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|, which feeds isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9717 Ubiquinone-7| (Q-7) is not common in bacteria. The only bacterium that was found to use Q-7, as its main quinone is the phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6034| |CITS:[13673033][Takamiya75]|. Other species were reported to contain small amounts of Q-7 in addition to their major form of ubiquinone. For example, 10% of the ubiquinone in |FRAME:TAX-562| was found to be Q-7 |CITS: [4861596]|. Small amounts of Q-7 were also reported in |FRAME: TAX-303|, |FRAME: TAX-294|, |FRAME: TAX-86179|, |FRAME: TAX-296| and |FRAME: TAX-339| |CITS: [4886765][5797102][5420949]| (note that Q-9 is the major ubiquinone in Pseudomonas species, though they often produce smaller amounts of Q-6, Q-7 and Q-8)., Q-7 is much more common in yeast. Many strains of |FRAME: TAX-5475|, |FRAME: TAX-4919| and |FRAME: TAX-604195| form Q-7 (see |FRAME: PWY-5873|).

Gram-negative bacteria reutilize most of the products of peptidoglycan turnover, and the complete degradation of muropeptides to its component amino acids, shown here, constitutes only a minor pathway |CITS: [2858468]|., Most of the |FRAME: L-ALA-GAMMA-D-GLU-DAP "murein tripeptide"| is utilized by |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.45| (|FRAME: EG12440-MONOMER "Mpl"|) to form the peptidoglycan biosynthesis intermediate |FRAME: UDP-AAGM-DIAMINOHEPTANEDIOATE|, as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1261| and |FRAME: PWY-7883| |CITS: [18535144]|.

Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, This D-xylose degradation pathway, which belongs to the second type of pentose sugar degradation pathways, involves reduction of |FRAME: D-Xylose| to produce |FRAME: XYLITOL|, which is degraded as shown in pathway |FRAME: LARABITOLUTIL-PWY|., Several forms of enzymes capable of catalyzing this reaction have been described, differing in their substrate and cosubstrate specificity., Deletion analysis studies concluded that in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5061| the first step is catalyzed by three different enzymes: a reductase encoded by the |FRAME: G-12470| gene, which has a preferred specificity for |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and two reductases with a preference for |FRAME: D-Xylose|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10035| and |FRAME: G-107617| genes |CITS: [33666344]|. , Similar enzymes have been characterized from many additional species. Most xylose reductases utilize NADPH as the cosubstrate of the reaction. A few D-xylose reductases have been reported to be active in the presence of both NADPH and NADH as a cofactor, such as those from |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [15746370]|, |FRAME: TAX-2315449| |CITS: [9307017][10661866]|, |FRAME: TAX-4924| |CITS: [3921014]|, and from the thermophilic fungus |FRAME: TAX-209285| |CITS: [12653995][30621365]|. However, even these enzymes prefer NADPH to NADH. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-5480| is a rare example of an enzyme that prefers NADH |CITS: [14532079]|., In |FRAME: TAX-51453| the enzyme has a much wider substrate specificity and has been classified as |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.21|. That enzyme also catalyzes the first step in |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| degradation (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5515|) and |FRAME: D-Galactose| degradation (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6693|) |CITS: [21212945]|.

General Background, The common anthocyanins found in roses are based on the simple structure , of cyanidin 3,5-diglucoside. This anthocyanin is obviously potent enough to provide the wide spectrum of , colors found in roses. Like the anthocyanidin 3-glucoside in other plants (compare |FRAME:PWY-5125|, , |FRAME:PWY-5153|; see also |FRAME:PWY-7262|) the anthocyanidin 3,5-diglucoside constitutes the first stable anthocyanin in roses and , contributes to its solubility in the vacuole |CITS: [Heller94]| |CITS: [11960739]|. The pathway described , here is unique to the rose family., About This Pathway, The formation of cyanidin 3,5-diglucoside in roses is catalyzed by a distinctive , enzyme that is able to glucosylate both the flavonoid A-ring 5-O-position and the 3-O-position of the flavonoid , C-ring. In contrast to the two single glucosyltransferases involved in the generation of anthocyanin 3,5-diglucoside , in other plants this enzyme possesses both catalytic activities and also changes the order of glucosylation , |CITS: [15944692]|. The first intermediate in this pathway is the unstable anthocyanidin-5-O-glucoside which , is subsequently further glucosylated to form the stable cyanidin 3,5-diglucoside., So far the enzyme catalyzing this reaction sequence has not been found in other plants and molecular , phylogenetic analysis indicates a significant difference to other anthocyanidin 3- and 5-O-glucosylatransferase , subfamily members. It has been proposed that the anthocyanidin 5,3-O-glucosyltransferase encoded by , the gene GT1 evolved independently of the typical enzymes involved in anthocyanin pigment metabolism , |CITS: [15944692]|.

Names: adenine and adenosine salvage V // adenosine nucleosides salvage V
Summary: The distinction between nucleoside degradation and recycling is not always straight forward., However, salvage pathways start with the nucleoside or free base forms (such as |FRAME: ADENINE|) and lead to the formation of the nucleotide forms, while degradation pathways usually start with the nucleotide form (e.g. |FRAME: AMP|) and end with compounds that lead to production of energy and provision of nitrogen and carbon, such as |FRAME: URATE|., This salvage pathway describes a route by which the organisms recycle the free base |FRAME: ADENINE| (which is often transported into the organism) leading to the production of guanosine nucleotides. A key enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: CPLX0-322|, whicht catalyzes the direct phosphorylation of |FRAME: INOSINE| and |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME:IMP| and |FRAME:GMP|, respectively. This enzyme has been observed only in some bacterial species.

General Background, Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., The mannitol cycle has been described in |FRAME: TAX-2870| (brown algae) and in protozoan parasite members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-5800|. In brown algae |FRAME: MANNITOL| is one of the two main carbon storage compounds (the other is |FRAME: CPD-3602 laminaran|). Depending on the species, mannitol can represent up to 20-30% of the dry weight. In addition, it also serves as an osmoprotectant and an antioxidant., The mannitol cycle also operates in oocysts of the apicomplexan parasites |FRAME: TAX-5802|, |FRAME: TAX-5811| and |FRAME: TAX-5807|, where mannitol serves as the main source of energy for sporulating oocysts. It comprises approximately 25% of the dry weight of unsporulated oocysts and is reduced to 3% by the completion of sporulation |CITS: [15463215][2538747][1487375][9309770][9461622][10219290][11780835]|., The parasite |FRAME: TAX-5802| causes coccidiosis (an intestinal disease) and poses an economic problem in the poultry industry. Inhibitors of enzymes in the cycle are of interest because the animal hosts do not biosynthesize or degrade |FRAME: MANNITOL|., The mannitol cycle has also been proposed to occur in some |FRAME: TAX-4751| |CITS: [6782999] [15251212]|, but its presence in fungi is controversial |CITS: [3141571][17092745][20136633]|., The mannitol cycle in parasites appears to be regulated in part by a protein inhibitor of the key enzyme mannitol-1-phosphate dehydrogenase in order to prevent a futile cycle of |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| utilization., About This Pathway, |FRAME: MANNITOL| is formed in the mannitol cycle from |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P "fructose 6-phosphate"| in two enzymatic steps: the direct reduction of |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P "fructose 6-phosphate"| into |FRAME: MANNITOL-1P|, and the hydrolysis of the phosphoric ester of the latter to produce |FRAME: MANNITOL|., This route for mannitol formation is also found in other organisms, including some bacteria, fungi, and red micro- and macroalgae., |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P "Fructose 6-phosphate"| is provided either from |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis|, or, in photosynthetic organisms such as brown algae, from the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|., The first reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.17|. This enzyme has been studied as a target for drug development |CITS: [11780835]|., The second reaction, which is irreversible in vivo, is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.22|, producing |FRAME: MANNITOL|, which is then stored for later use., The second half of the cycle involves the conversion of mannitol back to fructose 6-phosphate. The process starts with |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.67|, which produces |FRAME: FRU|, and continues by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.4|, which produces |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|. , |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P "Fructose 6-phosphate"| may enter glycolysis to produce |FRAME: ATP| via conversion to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| catalyzed by a unique pyrophosphate-dependent phosphofructokinase found in protozoa and plants |CITS: [1331784]|. |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| could also enter gluconeogenesis. Re-entry of |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| into the mannitol cycle would create a futile cycle and evidence suggests that mechanisms exist to prevent this, including the inhibition of mannitol-1-phosphate dehydrogenase by a dedicated protein inhibitor |CITS: [9309770]|., Evidence that the cycle proceeds in one direction only is based on the apparent lack of a mannitol kinase and higher Km values for the dehydrogenase enzymes in the reverse direction than in the forward direction |CITS: [2538747]|.

The formation of |FRAME:CPD-17688| (this pathway) is one out of four degradation pathways of |FRAME:CPD-693| (ABA) known to be involved in the cellular homeostasis of this phytohormone which is mainly biosynthesized via the de novo pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-695|) in plants. Besides the |FRAME:PWY-7642| two other pathways remove |FRAME:CPD-693| irreversibly from the equilibrium in the cell, i.e. |FRAME:PWY-5271| and |FRAME:PWY-7640| whereas the fourth, i.e. |FRAME:PWY-5272| produces |FRAME:CPD-7727| which can, when required, be readily converted back to |FRAME:CPD-693| |CITS:[Schwartz10] [Zaharia05] [14671016]|. |FRAME:CPD-693 Abscisic acid| is involved in the regulation of a wide scope of physiological activities in plants such as seed germination, embryo development, growth and responses to endogenous and environmental stimuli |CITS:[Nambara10] [Endo14]|., |FRAME:CPD-17688| has been found in a variety of plant families across the Magnoliophyta as a metabolite of |FRAME:CPD-693|, for instance in Xanthium strumarium (Asteraceae) |CITS:[Boyer86]|, Solanum lycopersicum (Solanaceae) |CITS:[24232333]|, Hordeum vulgare (Poaceae) |CITS:[Meyer88]|, Nigella damascena (Ranunculaceae) |CITS:[Lehmann83]|, Chelidonium majus (Papaveraceae) |CITS:[Lehmann83a]|, Vicia faba (Fabaceae) |CITS:[Lehmann89]|, and Brassica napus (Brassicaceae) |CITS:[14503817]|., In vitro biochemical assays and in vivo experiments have often been carried out with racemic mixtures of (+)-ABA, the natural occurring plant hormone, and (-)-ABA, the synthetic enantiomer. Both enantiomers were accepted by plants and showed physiological activity with the natural occurring (+)-ABA being more efficient than its (-)-enantiomer. In contrast, neither the (+)- nor the (-)-enantiomer of |FRAME:CPD-17688| exhibited appreciable bioactivities indicating that 7'-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-693| rendered the plant hormone inactive (e.g. |CITS:[Gusta92]|). The activity of an abscisic acid 7'-hydroxylase has been observed in cell suspensions of Bromus inermis |CITS:[Hampson92]| and Zea mays |CITS:[12232311]|. It could be demonstrated that the stereochemistry of the products, i.e. either (+)- or (-)-|FRAME:CPD-17688| remained unchanged when fed with the respective (+)- and (-)-enantiomer of ABA. However, the catalyzing enzymes remain to be further characterized and no gene encoding the abscisic acid 7'-hydroxylase has been identified yet. Summary: |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| is the universal precursor for the synthesis of the 4'-phosphopantetheine moiety of |FRAME:CO-A| and |FRAME: ACP "acyl carrier protein"|. Only plants and microorganisms (including some eukaryotic microbes, such as |FRAME: TAX-4932|) can synthesize pantothenate de novo - animals require a dietary supplement. The enzymes of this pathway are therefore considered to be antimicrobial drug targets., The starting compound for pantothenate biosynthesis, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, is derived from the |FRAME: VALSYN-PWY| pathway. The first committed step in the pathway is the transfer of a methyl group to 2-keto-isovalerate by |FRAME: 3-METHYL-2-OXOBUT-OHCH3XFER-CPLX|. The product of this reaction, |FRAME: 2-DEHYDROPANTOATE|, is subsequently reduced by |FRAME: 2-DEHYDROPANTOATE-REDUCT-MONOMER| to |FRAME: L-PANTOATE|. , The next steps, as found in bacteria/eukaryotes, consist of the ATP hydrolysis-dependent condensation of R-pantoate with |FRAME: B-ALANINE| to form |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE|, followed by the phosphorylation of the latter to |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE|. While archaea are known to produce |FRAME:CO-A|, and archaeal genomes harbor homologs for most of the enzymes involved in this pathway, homologs of the bacterial/eukaryotic pantothenate synthetase and pantothenate kinase, which catalyze these last two steps, are missing. The puzzle has been solved with the discovery of two new enzymes - |FRAME: MONOMER-15970| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15971|. Apparently, the order of these two steps (condensation and phosphorylation) has been reversed in archaea |CITS: [19666462]|. , The two enzymes have been purified and characterized, and their activities verified. Homologs of both genes are widely distributed among the archaea, suggesting that this is the predominant pathway for 4'-phosphopantothenate biosynthesis in the archaea |CITS: [19666462]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: PWY-101 "aerobic photosynthesis pathway"| generates two main products: proton motive force (which is translated to ATP production by ATP synthase) and NADPH. When the ATP supply drops and the level of NADPH rises, plant chloroplasts and cyanobacteria can shift to an alternative pathway that bypasses photosystem II, called "cyclic electron flow"., In this pathway the electrons generated by |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.12 "photosystem I"| are transferred to ferredoxin, just like they are in regular photosynthesis. However, instead of transferring those electrons to |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|, which results in NADPH production, the ferredoxin transfers the electrons to the NDH-1 complex, which returns them to the |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone| pool. Plastoquinol delivers the elelctrons to |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.6| (known better as the cytochrome b6f complex), which generates proton motive force due to the Q-cycle and transfers the electrons to |FRAME: Plastocyanins plastocyanin|. Plastocyanin delivers the electron back to |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.12 "photosystem I"|, closing the cycle., The truncated cycle bypasses NADPH production, but generates ATP due to the proton motive force generated by |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.6|.

Summary: General Background, Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are a class of bacterial storage compounds that accumulate inside cells in the form of inclusion bodies (granules) when carbon sources are oversupply. PHAs may accumulate to levels of up to 90% of cellular dry weight and can provide the bacterium with a source of carbon and energy during periods of nutritional deprivation. These polyesters are of industrial interest due to their biodegradability to water-soluble products, and their ability to be synthesized from renewable resources (in |CITS: [18706425]| and in |CITS: [11457823]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19270094]|). There is evidence that archaea may also synthesize PHAs (in |CITS: [19648370]|)., PHAs are generally classified as short-chain-length (monomers contain 3-5 carbon atoms) (this pathway) or medium-chain-length (monomers contain 6-14 carbon atoms) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6657|) (in |CITS: [11425728] [19925642]|). The chain length may vary depending on organism and culture conditions. Many 3-hydroxyacids have been identified as constituents of PHA polymers and the theoretical number of copolymers is high. |FRAME: Poly-Hydroxybutyrate| (PHB) is the most abundant storage compound in bacteria. PHB and its copolymer with |FRAME: CPD-12765| have been commercialized. Considerable progress has also been made in elucidating the molecular architecture of intracellular PHA granules and identifying them as complex subcellular organelles (in |CITS: [16511073]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19270094]|)., PHA polymerases (synthases) are the key enzymes of PHA biosynthesis. They catalyze the stereoselective, covalent linkage of |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| thioesters in a transesterification reaction with concomitant release of |FRAME: CO-A| (in |CITS: [19925642]|). All PHA polymerases share a conserved active site |FRAME: CYS| residue to which the growing polymer is attached. The mechanism of PHA polymerase initiation, elongation and termination of the polymer has not yet been elucidated and no structural data are available. However, evidence suggests that these enzymes may dimerize when substrate is provided, with one subunit attached to the growing polymer chain and the other binding a new substrate molecule (reviewed in |CITS: [19275166] [19270094]| and in detail in |CITS: [17263145]|)., Enzymes that degrade PHAs can be of two types, those that are secreted and act extracellularly, or those that act intracellularly. They may be specific for either short-chain-length PHAs (EC 3.1.1.75) or medium-chain-length PHAs (EC 3.1.1.76) and catalyze their hydrolysis to monomeric, or oligomeric hydroxyalkanoates (see |FRAME: MONOMER-15977|, |FRAME: CPLX-8171| and |FRAME: MONOMER-15978|). Intracellular enzymes degrade PHAs for direct utilization, while extracellularly secreted enzymes may act on PHAs that are released from dead bacterial cells (in |CITS: [16511073]| and in |CITS: [18706425]|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Poly-Hydroxybutyrate| (PHB), a homopolymer of |FRAME: CPD-335|, is a storage material, produced by a variety of bacteria in response to environmental stress. The presence of PHB in bacteria was first recognized by Lemoigne in 1926 |CITS: [Lemoigne26]|, and has since been identified in bacteria from diverse phylogenetic groups, including proteobacteria, actinobacteria, firmicutes and cyanobacteria |CITS:[4594739][16175209][16004452][15793618][17116969][16614903][16440119]|. The level of accumulation and the molecular weight of the PHB produced vary among bacterial species |CITS: [2670936]|., The PHB biosynthetic pathway includes only three enzymes. |FRAME:CPLX-7355| catalyzes, the reversible condensation of two |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| molecules to |FRAME: ACETOACETYL-COA|. Acetoacetyl-CoA is subsequently reduced to |FRAME:CPD-650| by |FRAME:CPLX-7356|,, and PHB is then produced by the polymerization of |FRAME:CPD-650| via the action of |FRAME:CPLX-7357|. It is believed that the synthase enzyme remains covalently linked to the polymer chain during chain growth |CITS: [10099235]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates, formed by certain plants from any one of eight amino acids, namely, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, phenylalanine, methionine, tyrosine and tryptophan. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified |CITS: [18458837]|. Much of, the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine. , Glucosinolates are found prominently in the order |FRAME: TAX-3700|, which includes cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, broccoli, and the model plant Arabidopsis, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are hydrolyzed by the plant to compounds that are toxic to herbivores, and play an important role in plant defense. The hydrolysis of is catalyzed by |FRAME: AT5G26000-MONOMER "myrosinases"| (b-thioglucoside glucohydrolase, |FRAME: RXN-8134 "EC 3.2.1.147"| ), enzymes that are physically segregated from glucosinolates within the intact plant in specialized ''myrosin'' cells, and are brought into contact by tissue damage |CITS: [Bones96]|., The products of the myrosinase reaction are unstable aglycons, |FRAME: THIOHYDROXIMATE-O-SULFATES "thiohydroximate-O-sulfates"|, that decompose to different types of products, depending on the chemical nature of the side chain of the parent glucosinolate and the conditions of hydrolysis. Products include nitriles, isothiocyanates, thiocyanates, oxazolidine-2-thiones, and epithionitriles., Glucosinolates with an aliphatic side chain are generally hydrolyzed to yield isothiocyanates at a neutral pH. However, acidic pH or the presence of |FRAME:FE+2| ions favors the production of nitriles |CITS: [Gil80]|., In some plants, additional proteins are involved in glucosinolate hydrolysis. For example, it has been shown that the presence of an epithiospecifier protein (ESP) results in conversion of thiohydroximate-O-sulfates to bioactive nitriles or epithionitriles |CITS: [11752388]|. If the parent glucosinolate possessed a terminal alkene group, epithionitriles are formed (by transfer of the sulfur atom from the basic glucosinolate backbone to the terminal alkene residue of the side chain), whereas other glucosinolates are converted to simple nitriles. The protein appears to have no catalytic activity in the absence of myrosinase |CITS: [Daxenbichler68][4130022][MacLeod85][11752388][15845404]|. In the absence of ESP, as in some Capparales species, isothiocynates are the only breakdown products |CITS: [11752388]|., About this pathway : The hydrolysis products of glucosinolates are methylated to volatile sulfur compounds by five distinct isoforms of thiol methyltransferases (TMT) in |FRAME: TAX-3712|. The produced sulfur volatiles play a role in anti-insect and anti-pathogen activities. The expression pattern of TMT's in cabbage correlated with the glucosinolate accumulation. These TMT's possess the methyltransferase signature in their sequence but had distinct functions from them |CITS: [12369626]|.

Summary: Tetrapyrroles are compounds whose molecules have four rings of the pyrrole type, generally linked together by single-atom bridges between the alpha positions of the five-membered pyrrole rings. Tetrapyrroles function as a metal-binding cofactor in many important enzymes, proteins and pigments, such as heme, chlorophyll, cobalamine (vitamin B12), siroheme, and cofator F430., The biosynthesis of all of these cofactors start in a similar manner, with the production of the intermediate |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|. This intermediate is an important branch point: its methylation directs it toward siroheme, cobalamin or cofactor F430 synthesis, while decarboxylation directs it toward the synthesis of heme and chlorophyll |CITS: [14633982]|., The tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway shown here, which starts with glutamate, is found in plants, many bacteria (including |FRAME:TAX-562|), and the archaea. A second tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway, which is found in animals, fungi, certain protozoans, and members of the α-proteobacteria, starts with glycine and succinyl-coA (see, |FRAME:PWY-5189|). Interestingly, both pathways are present in the chloroplast-containing protozoan |FRAME: TAX-3039|., Regardless whether the starting point is glycine or glutamate, both pathways converge at the intermediate |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| and proceed through the important intermediate |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, which is a major branch point that leads to biosynthesis of different tetrapyrrole compounds, such as the corrinoid cobalamine (vitamin B<sub>12</sub>) (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P381-PWY|), the methanogenic coenzyme F<sub>430</sub> (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|),  |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|, and heme D.

Summary: General Background, Polyunsaturated |FRAME: Long-Chain-Fatty-Acids "long-chain fatty acids"| (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear., These compounds are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturatedare very long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. , Polyunsaturated very long chain fatty acids are also found in mammals. In humans |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| are precursors of the regulatory molecules eicosanoids, which are involved in many cellular functions including vascular permeability, inflammation, regulation of immune system, blood clotting, neurotransmission and cholesterol metabolism., |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Eicosapentaenoate| (EPA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains five cis double bonds, one of which is located at the third carbon from the omega end, which makes it an omega-3 fatty acid. EPA is produced by microalgae and is common in fish who eat the algae, although the fish can not produce it. It is also produced by mosses and ferns, but is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. EPA is also produced by some marine bacteria, mostly those adapted to low temperatures and high pressures, via a completely different pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7050|) |CITS: [10220156]|., About This Pathway, The most common |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| biosynthetic pathway is the 6-desaturase/Δ6-elongase pathway, in which |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| is first desaturated by a 6-desaturase to yield |FRAME: CPD-12653|, followed by a Δ6-elongation to produce |FRAME: CPD-8121| and a second desaturation by a 5-desaturase to form |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (see for example |FRAME: PWY-6958|). However, some of the organisms that produce |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| lack a 6-desaturase and utilize an alternative pathway that includes a Δ9 elongase and an 8-desaturase, as described in this pathway |CITS: [10328826]|., The Δ8 pathway has been described in the ciliated protozoan |FRAME: TAX-5908| |CITS: [5961271]|, in the soil amoebae |FRAME: TAX-5756| |CITS: [4309952]|, in euglenoid species |CITS: [14216427]| and in the microalga |FRAME: TAX-561169| |CITS: [17291553]|. Flavonoids are widely distributed in the plant kingdom. Flavonoids are a highly diverse class of plant secondary metabolites (with about 9000 compounds identified so far |CITS: [16137727]|) derived from the phenylpropanoid pathway. Based on core structures and chemical modifications flavonoids are classified as chalcones, aurones, flavonols, flavones, flavanones, isoflavones and anthocyanins. Flavonoids serve as pigments (red and purple anthocyanin pigments), act as signals for pollinators and other organisms, participate in plant hormone signaling, facilitate pollen-tube growth, protect plants from UV-B radiation, and function as phytoalexins |CITS: [11130659]|, |CITS: [10924197]|, |CITS: [11402179]|. , Flavone and flavonol-O-glycosides make up one of the largest classes of flavonoid constituents with over 2000 known structures. Although |FRAME:GLC| |CITS:[5058406]| and |FRAME:CPD0-1112| |CITS:[1939145]| are the most frequent O-glycoside conjugates found on flavones and flavonols, the presence of arabinose, xylose, and glucuronic acid has also been reported. The formation of |FRAME:CPD-14825| from |FRAME:LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCOSIDE| catalyzed by a flavonoid 1,6-glucosyltransferase isolated from cultured cells of |FRAME:TAX-4058| |CITS:[19561332]| |CITS:[17940060]| further extends the structural complexity of luteolin glycosides occurring in plants. , |FRAME:5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE Luteolin| and glycosidic derivatives thereof belong to the more common flavones found in plants. Several potential functions have been ascribed to luteolin and its glycosides. In humans these compounds have been shown to exhibit anti-oxidant |CITS: [15543940]|, |CITS: [16732514]|, and anti-inflammatory activities |CITS: [17977562]|.

General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|), and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, In this pathway, which has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, methylglyoxal is reduced to lactaldehyde by the enzyme methylglyoxal reductase |CITS: [SaikusaAgBioChem51-1893]|. |FRAME: LACTALD| is then reduced to |FRAME:L-LACTATE| which is finally converted to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and joins the pool of central metobolites |CITS: [2663129]|., Methylglyoxal reductases have been characterized in bacteria |CITS: [SaikusaAgBioChem51-1893]| and fungi |CITS:[3896793][3276516]|. Some of the enzymes are NADP-linked, while others are NAD-linked., Two variants of this pathway have been entered in MetaCyc to reflect the different biochemistry of the last enzyme, L-lactate dehydrogenase. The |FRAME: TAX-83333| enzyme encoded by gene |FRAME: EG11963| uses an unidentified electron acceptor (see |FRAME:PWY-5459|), while the |FRAME: TAX-4932| enzyme uses an |FRAME: Cytochromes-C-Oxidized| (see |FRAME:PWY-5458|)., |FRAME:MGLDLCTANA-PWY| is a similar pathway based on methylglyoxal reductases that are specific for the D form of lactaldehyde.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-1437824| is a facultatively anaerobic β-proteobacterium that can utilize acyclic, monocyclic and bicyclic monoterpenes, including |FRAME: Limonenes limonene|, as sole carbon source under oxic as well as anoxic conditions |CITS: [24952578]|., The genes responsible for the degradation of these compounds are located in a 70 kb genomic island. A collection of 72 transposon mutants unable to grow on limonene identified several involved genes. , The first step in the pathway is a ring hydroxylation catalyzed by a heterodimeric enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-58816| and |FRAME: G-58817| genes (ctm stands for cyclic terpene metabolism). Although not yet verified, the natural electron acceptor for the enzyme is likely a heterodimeric |FRAME: Etf "electron transfer flavoprotein"| (ETF). The hydroxyl group added by CmtAB is oxidized by two additional enzymes to a carboxylate via an aldehyde intermediate, yielding |FRAME: CPD-12443| |CITS: [24952578]|., The subsequent degradation of |FRAME: CPD-12443| is very similar to the |FRAME: P321-PWY "anaerobic degradation of benzoate"|. Before the ring could be cleaved, the compound is activated by ligation to coenzyme CoA. Once activated, a hydratase, a dehydrogenase and a hydrolase acts sequentially to cleave the ring, resulting in |FRAME: 4-Isopropenyl-Pimelyl-CoA| |CITS: [24952578]|., As of 2018, the final steps of the pathway have not been characterized.

Summary: General Background, Flavonole such as quercetin and its glycosidic derivatives (this pathway) and kaempferol/kaempferol glycoside (compare |FRAME:PWY-5320|) are the major flavonoids found in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [10514319]| |CITS: [16939316]|. Metabolic mutants of Arabidopsis were found to express a different profile of flavonols emphasizing the value of metabolic profiling for the exploration of the underlying pathways |CITS: [Graham98]|. , The occurrence of the two main flavonols kaempferol and quercetin is predominant in different tissues. Quercetin appears to be the main flavonoid in seeds and kaempferol is more prominent in flowers of Arabidopsis |CITS: [9112784][8528278]|. Beside the glycosylated monomeric flavonols, dimers and oligomers of flavonols have been identified in Arabidopsis which again accumulate in a spatially and temporally controlled manner that is dependent of seed development and maturation of seeds |CITS: [16395586]|., The biological function of flavonoids including flavonols such as UV-protection, defense and resistance against biological and non-biological agents and interacting with plant hormones |CITS: [11960739]| has been investigated in depth. However, flavonols also have a significant impact on human health as that they are an important component of the daily diet. Flavonols are involved in the prevention of cancer and cardiovascular diseases that have attracted researchers to reveal the causal molecular principles |CITS: [16176136][16097445]|., About This Pathway, Glycosylation is one of the most widespread modifications of plant secondary metabolites that can alter properties and functions of the modified compound. 120 putative UDP-glucose: glycosyltransferases alone have been predicted from the genome of Arabidopsis but for only a few their molecular function has been verified experimentally |CITS: [16214386]|. , The metabolic steps that generate glycosides of quercetin are catalyzed by enzymes that express broader substrate specificity and usually accept kaempferol and/or isorhamnetin to a comparable degree. In general, flavonols are preferred over flavones and flavanones |CITS: [14697269]| |CITS: [12900416]| matching the flavonoid composition found in Arabidopsis., The glycosyltransferases acting in Arabidopsis thaliana have been demonstrated to preferentially transport sugars to the 3-OH and 7-OH position of the C and the A-ring of the flavonol, respectively. The enzymes catalyzing the 3-O and 7-O--glucosylation have been purified from Arabidopsis |CITS: [Kim06]| |CITS: [16794327]| |CITS: [14697269]|. Quercetin and kaempferol-3-rhamnoside are the most abundant flavonols reported and the corresponding enzymes have been purified and characterized via a functional genomic approach just recently |CITS: [12900416]|. The quercetin biosynthesis as displayed reflects the currently known enzymatic steps and the results of metabolic profiling |CITS: [16939316][16395586]| but some of the enzymes catalyzing the formation of e.g. quercetin-3,5-diglucoside remain to be characterized.The identification of the flavonol 7-O-rhamnosyltransferase responsible for the formation of major kaempferol and quercetin glycosides in |FRAME:TAX-3701| has been achieved by utilizing transcriptome expression analysis. The molecular function of the flavonol 7-O-rhamnosyltransferase (UGT89C1) was confirmed through T-DNA mutants knocked out for the UGT89C1 in which rhamnosylated flavonols could not be found in the metabolic profile. In addition, the recombinant expressed GST-fusion protein demonstrated the very specific 7-rhamnosylation for flavonol mono- and diglucosides |CITS:[17314094]|. The enzymes catalyzing the steps leading to the generation of the precursor compounds |FRAME:CPD-14849| and |FRAME:CPD-14820| have not yet been identified and remain to be shown.

General Background, |FRAME: Sulfofucose| is an unusual modified sugar originally reported from the glycolipids of algae from the order Fucaceae, which are distributed across the North Atlantic Ocean |CITS: [1016655]|. it was later reported in an N-linked glycan produced by |FRAME: TAX-2303|, a thermoacidophilic archaeon that does not have a cell wall or an S-layer |CITS: [22692048]|., About This Pathway, An organism capable of degrading |FRAME: Sulfofucose sulfofucose| was isolated in 2023 from an inner-Melbourne creekside market garden. The genome sequence was originally submitted under the strain name |FRAME: TAX-1675788| strain merri 1-1_RES21-00831_2. However, in a manuscript published in 2025 the authors defined it as a new species, which they named |FRAME: ORG-57130| sp. nov. strain merri. The name is based on its isolation from the banks of Merri Creek, which runs through the lands of the indigenous Wurundjeri people |CITS: [40823846]|., Proteomics and metabolomics analysis revealed a sulfofucolytic variant of the Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathway, in which sulfofucose is converted to |FRAME: CPD-11799|, which is further degraded to pyruvate and sulfite |CITS: [40823846]|. The pathway is very similar to the |FRAME: CPD-10247| degradation pathway characterized from |FRAME: ORG-6286| (see |FRAME: PWY-7722|) |CITS: [40823846]|., While a gene encoding |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.97|, the last reaction in this pathway, has not been found, genes encoding the enzymes involved in downstream processing, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6616|, were present, and metabolomic analysis revealed the accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-11799| as an intracellular metabolite during growth on |FRAME: Sulfofucose|, suggesting the presence of this activity in the organism |CITS: [40823846]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A "Chlorophyll a"| (Chla) and |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B| (Chlb) are light harvesting pigments that function to capture photons and transfer them to the reaction centers of the photosystems. Chla and Chlb share the same structure except for the side chain at C-7, which is a methyl group in Chla and a formyl group in Chlb. Whereas the biosynthesis of Chla has been widely reported (see |FRAME:PWY-5086| and |FRAME:PWY-5064|), that of Chlb has been more elusive., Although it has long been known that |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| appears before |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B| when chlorophyll synthesis begins, little was known of the formation of the formyl group of Chlb. The discovery of |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.122| (CAO) showed that this enzyme was sufficient for the transition of a- to b-type chlorophyll pigments. The enzyme was originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-3052|, where mutants lacking in |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLL-B| biosynthesis were generated, and the gene responsible for the phenotype was isolated |CITS: [9770552]|. Subsequent work showed that the homologous |FRAME:AT1G44446| gene from |FRAME: ORG-5993| is required for chlorophyll b synthesis in that organism |CITS: [10468639][10758481]|., In many organisms Chlb can be reduced back back to Chla, forming a cyclic pathway for the interconversion of the two types of chlorophyll molecules, as a response to changing light conditions |CITS:[8576141][16228557]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5068|). However, while the cycle operates in other |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|-producing cyanobacteria that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-1222| and |FRAME: TAX-1214| genera, it does not occur in |FRAME: TAX-1218| |CITS: [31392311]|., All of the |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|-producing organisms possess the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.13|, which reduces the double bond at position C81, and thus converts divinyl compoundsto monovinyl ones (such as |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|). However, members of the |FRAME: TAX-1218| genus do not have theat enzyme, and thus produce divinyl compounds, such as |FRAME: CPD-22996| |CITS: [15632054]|.

Summary: |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE Phenylacetate| is a major intermediate in bacterial degradation of many aromatic compounds |CITS: [11260461]|. Microbes can oxidize phenylacetate under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see also |FRAME: PWY0-321|), and the first step in both pathways is the same - the activition of phenylacetate to |FRAME: CPD-207| by a |FRAME: MONOMER-12132 "phenylacetate-CoA ligase"|., Although aerobic oxidation of phenylacetate requires molecular oxygen, anaerobic oxidation does not.  Anaerobic oxidation of phenylacetate by |FRAME:TAX-59405| can be divided into two parts.  In the first part of the pathway, phenylacetate is oxidized to benzoyl-CoA via phenylacetyl-CoA and phenylglyoxylate, and in the second part of the pathway, benzoyl-CoA, a common intermediate in anaerobic aromatic degradation, is oxidized via a central pathway.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: D-APIOSE| is a unique branched-chain pentose found principally in plants. It is a key component of structurally complex cell wall polysaccharides such as |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| (RG-II) in the cell walls of higher plants and in apigalacturonan in the cell walls of aquatic monocots, and is a building block of a large number of naturally occurring secondary metabolites., The name "apiose" is derived from the flavonoid glycoside |FRAME: 7-O-BETA-D-APIOFURANOSYL-12-BETA-D-GLU apiin|, from which it was first obtained |CITS: [Vongerichten01]|. Apiin itself is named after parsley (|FRAME: TAX-4043|), which at the time was known as Apium petroselinum |CITS: [26848180]|., About This Pathway, The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway were found by first identifying genes encoding D-apiose-specific substrate binding proteins (SBPs), since SBPs, which are components of certain types of transporters, are often clustered with catabolic genes that metabolize the compound the SBPs bind to., This pathway has been characterized using enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-218491| and |FRAME: TAX-558270| and is predicted to be present in 176 bacterial species. The pathway's product, |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, is an intermediate in the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Phosphonates| are quite abundant in nature, primarily as components of phosphonolipids, where |FRAME: CPD-1106| is analogous to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE| as the constituent of phospholipids. In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics |CITS: [7765831]|. Phosphonates contain a direct carbon-phosphorus (C-P) bond in place of the more familiar carbon-oxygen-phosphorus bond, which makes their degradation challenging., Bacteria have evolved many different mechanisms for cleaving the carbon-phosphorus bond. Enzymes that have been described include the following:, 1. |FRAME: EG10719-MONOMER "Carbon-phosphorus lyase"|, a widespread but poorly characterized enzyme. See |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|., 2. Hydrolytic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.1| (phosphonatase, see |FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY|), |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.2| (shown in pathway |FRAME: P483-PWY|)., 3. Dioxygenases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.78|, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7447|., Data suggest that additional pathways for phosphonate degradation may exist (in |CITS: [21543322]|). , About This Pathway, This pathway was studied in |FRAME: TAX-29497|, though the genes involved are present in many bacterial strains. The distinguishing enzyme of this pathway is |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.33| (PbfA), an enzyme with narrow substrate specificity that acts only on |FRAME: CPD-16526|. The reaction catalyzed by the enzyme releases ammonia and generates |FRAME: CPD-551|, which can be then hydrolyzed by PhnX.

Summary: Note: click twice on the More Detail button at the top of the page to see the enzymes involved in this pathway., General Background, The thyroid hormones |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| (T4) and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| (T3) are essential for normal vertebrate metabolism, growth and development. These |FRAME: CPD-387|-containing molecules are biosynthesized in the thyroid gland, the function of which is to concentrate environmentally scarce |FRAME: CPD-387| in order to make it available for thyroid hormone biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-387| insufficiency in the diet remains a public health problem in some parts of the world (reviewed in |CITS: [19196800]|). Various human disorders of thyroid metabolism are characterized by hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, goiter, and cretinism (a syndrome resulting from hypothyroidism during development (in |CITS: [VOET04]|). These phenotypes have many possible causes including mutations in receptors, transporters, proteins involved in the pathway and its regulation, developmental defects, inflamation, autoimmune reactions, drug side effects, diet, or deficiency of other hormones. Also see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6241| and |FRAME: PWY-6260|., About This Pathway, The thyroid hormones |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| are regulated at many levels. In addition to deoidination (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6260|), other routes of thyroid hormone metabolism have been described and metabolically active metabolites have been identified. These routes are shown here for |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE|, although other iodothyronines can be similarly metabolized. In some cases however, the enzymes involved in formation of these metabolites have not been characterized (reviewed in |CITS: [18279024]|)., Glucuronidation, or sulfoconjugation of iodothyronines has been shown to occur. Glucuronidation of |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| or |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| is catalyzed by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases and is a major pathway. It may involve the phenolic hydroxyl group to form ether glucuronides, or the carboxyl group to form ester glucuronides |CITS: [17875670]|. Glucuronidation aids hormone excretion in bile. Sulfoconjugation by various tissue sulfotransferases, such as |FRAME: CPLX-7858|, can promote hormone degradation by deiodinases in the liver. Alternatively, hormone recycling can occur via reverse reactions catalyzed by tissue sulfatases, intestinal bacterial sulfatases, or intestinal bacterial β-glucuronidases (|CITS: [8070342]| and reviewed in |CITS: [18279024]| and |CITS: [16131336]|). , Small amounts of |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| may also be transaminated, or oxidatively deaminated, at the alanine side chain to yield |FRAME: CPD-11403| (tetrac) or |FRAME: CPD-11404| (triac). Oxidative deamination possibly by kidney L-amino acid oxidase appears more likely, although this remains to be demonstrated (in |CITS: [16131336]| and in |CITS: [8070342]|). |FRAME: CPD-11403| and |FRAME: CPD-11404| may be conjugated to form glucuronides. Depending upon species, ether glucuronides or ester glucuronides of these metabolites may form by conjugation of the phenolic hydroxyl group, or carboxyl group respectively |CITS: [8070342]|., |FRAME: L-THYROXINE| and |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE| may also be sequentially deiodinated (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-6260|). Decarboxylation at the alanine side chain to |FRAME: CPD-11405| (T1AM) and |FRAME: CPD-11406| (T0AM), respectively, may occur (reviewed in |CITS: [18279024]|). The decarboxylation reaction is possibly catalyzed by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (in |CITS: [18279024] [16131336] [15146179]|). However, the specific enzymes involved in these conversions remain to be shown. See MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-6688|., Cleavage of the ether link of the thyronine nucleus has also been suggested to be a mode of degradation (not shown). This reaction produces diiodotyrosine from the inner ring, and the outer ring phenolic iodine is removed. Peroxidases can catalyze this reaction (reviewed in |CITS: [16131336]|).
