Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Arabinogalactan Arabinogalactans| (AG) are biopolymers consisting mostly of arabinose and galactose residues. Two main classes of arabinogalactans are found in nature: |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans "plant arabinogalactan"| and |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "microbial arabinogalactan"|. Plant arabinogalactans are widely spread throughout the plant kingdom. They are associated with the |FRAME: Pectin pectin| cell-wall component by physical bonds, and some of them are covalently linked to the complex pectin molecule as neutral side chains |CITS: [Ebringerova05]|. Plant AGs occur in two structurally different forms described as |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-I "type I"| and |FRAME: Plant-Arabinogalactans-II "type II"|., AG type II, also known as arabino-3,6-galactan, is more widespread than the AG type I. The common structural feature of AG type II is a backbone of β-1,3-galactan, which is often substituted at O6 with side chains of β-1,6-galactan decorated further with arabinofuranose, and less frequently with fucopyranose, rhamnopyranose, and (methyl) glucuronate. Type II AGs from acacia, larch and wheat flour were reported to also contain small amounts of β-arabinopyranose |CITS: [Aspinall58][Groman94][8137369][20971454]|., Type II AG in cell walls of dicots and cereals is often linked to proteins (known as arabinogalactan proteins or AGPs) by a β-(1,4) linkage from the reducing end galactosyl residue to a 4-hydroxyproline residue in the protein. The arabinogalactan proteins are often attached to the plasma membrane by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor |CITS: [11337397][15322080]|., AG type II, along with |FRAME: Galactomannans galactomannans| and |FRAME: CELLULOSE cellulose|, comprises the predominating polysaccharides of green arabica coffee beans|CITS: [11217967]|., AG type II occurs asa minor, water-soluble component in softwoods. It is very abundant in the wood of larch trees (members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-3325|) - certain parts of the western larch (|FRAME: TAX-3327|) contain up to 35% AG |CITS: [Whistler93]|. However, larch AG type II is located in the lumen of the tracheids and ray cells, and is thus not a cell-wall component and by definition, not part of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| of these trees., The glycan structure shown here is adapted from |CITS: [24966860]|., About This Pathway, Three enzymes are expected to participate in the degradation of the arabinogalactan backbone - |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.181|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.145|, and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.23|. The endogalactanases break the chain into shorter fragments, which are then digested from their ends by the exogalactanases and β-galactosidases. The latter also plays an important role in releasing terminal galactose residues from the galactan side chains., So far very few endo-β-1,3-galactanases have been isolated and characterized. The best studied enzyme is from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-38945|, which belongs to the GH16 family of glycosyl hydrolases |CITS: [21653698]|. More is known about endo-β-1,3-galactanases. An earlier work described such an enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-5061|, but no sequence information is available for that enzyme |CITS: [7805066]|. Several other microbial exo-β-1,3-galactanases were shown to degrade the β-1,3-galactan backbone of AGP glycans |CITS: [15866877][17090926][16672498][19809200]|. These enzymes, which belong to the GH43 family, degrade β-1,3-linked galactose residues regardless of the substitution by side chains. All of these enzymes are capable of releasing the β-1,6-side chains of type II arabinogalactans by hydrolyzing the β-1,3-linkages in the main chain adjacent to the branching point., Enzymes that are required for the degradation of the side chains include |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.164|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.M17|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.55|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.31|, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.51|,and |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.40|., Several microbial endo-β-1,6-galactanases that hydrolyze the β-1,6-galactan side chains of AGP glycans have been characterized from the fungi |FRAME: TAX-5547|, |FRAME: TAX-5507| and |FRAME: TAX-5141| and the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-33903| |CITS: [14565843][17351093][18310439][20932514]|. All of these enzymes have increased activity on de-arabinosylated substrates, and have been classified in the GH30 family |CITS: [20932833]|. Exo-β-1,6-galactanases are much less studied. An enzyme with robust activity, which also has exo-β-1,3-galactanase activity, has been described from radish (|FRAME: TAX-3726|) |CITS: [15980190]|., In higher plants an α-arabinofuranosidase that belongs to the GH3 family is believed to participate in the degradation of AGP glycans. One such enzyme, named RsAraf1, was isolated from radish seeds |CITS: [16831850]|. A different type of α-arabinofuranosidase (|FRAME: MONOMER-20548 NcAraf1|), classified in the GH54 family, has been described from |FRAME: TAX-5141|. That enzyme has a broad substrate specificity toward AGPs, pectic arabinan, and arabinoxylan. Produced as a recombinant protein in the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4922|, the enzyme demonstrated α-arabinofuranosidase activity with both α-1,3- and α-1,5-linked arabinofuranose |CITS: [20932514]|., Two microbial enzymes were shown to cleave and release the glucuronate residues from AG glycans. One of these β-glucuronidases (NcGlcAase) was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-5141| and the other (|FRAME: MONOMER-20549 AnGlcAase|) was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-5061| |CITS: [18377882]|. The two enzymes are very similar to each other, but have different catalytic properties. The former has similar efficiency cleaving unsubstituted β-glucuronate and 4-methylated β-glucuronate, while the latter has much higher activity with the non-methylated species. Both enzymes belong in in family GH79., The rhamnose residues in AG glycans have been shown to be released by the action of a GH78 |FRAME: MONOMER-20550 "α-L-rhamnosidase"| from |FRAME: TAX-33903| (SaRha78A) |CITS: [23486481][23291751]|., Less in known about the enzymes that remove the fucose residues from AG glycans. A commercial preparation of an α-1,2-fucosidase from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-43353| (PROzyme product GK80170) was used to cleave α-1,2-fucose from AGP glycans |CITS: [20194500]|, but this activity has not been characterized.

Nepetelactones are iridoids produced by some plants to repel insects. Compounds of this class are responsible for the psychoactive effects plants belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-39172|, such as catnip, have on cats |CITS: [30531909]|. They have also been shown to function as sex pheromones by |FRAME: TAX-27482 "aphids"| |CITS: [8733613]|. Currently, four nepetelactone stereoisomers |FRAME: CPD-22360|, |FRAME: CPD-15029|, |FRAME: CPD-22365|, and |FRAME: CPD-22364| have been observed in |FRAME: TAX-39172|. |CITS: [30531909]|, The first enzyme found to be involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15030| was |FRAME: MONOMER-20521| in |FRAME: TAX-4058|. |CITS: [23172143]|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.122| reduces |FRAME:CPD-9978 | to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-22362|. At the time of its discovery, it was proposed that the intermediate would spontaneously cyclize into |FRAME: CPD-15029|. However, it was later determined that a family of nepetalactol-related short-chain reductase enzymes specific to |FRAME: TAX-39172| were able to catalyze the subsequent steps of biosynthesis for |FRAME: CPD-15029| and |FRAME: CPD-22360|. |CITS: [30531909]|

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Pyrrolomycins Pyrrolomycins| are a group of polyhalogenated metabolites produced by |FRAME: TAX-1883| species whose structures include a dichloro-pyrrole moiety linked to a halogenated-hydroxyphenyl ring via a one-carbon bridge. Some of those compounds contain a 3-nitropyrrole moiety. This family of compounds includes |FRAME: CPD-24066|, |FRAME: CPD-24071|, |FRAME: CPD-24067|, |FRAME: CPD-24074|, |FRAME: CPD-24076|, |FRAME: CPD-24068|, |FRAME: CPD-24069|, |FRAME: CPD-24073|, |FRAME: CPD-24075|, and |FRAME: CPD-24070| |CITS: [15730262][16441063]|., |FRAME: CPD-24070 Dioxapyrrolomycin|, which was originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-67302|, is considered the principal component of pyrrolomycins |CITS: [3570973]|, and many of the observed pyrrolomycins are considered to be either intermediates or shunt products of the dioxapyrrolomycin biosynthetic pathway. Dioxapyrrolomycin has anthelmintic |CITS: [1500366]| and neuropeptide-activity modulatory |CITS: [1712007]| properties. Another member of the family, |FRAME: CPD-24071|, has been reported to exhibit immunomodulatory activity |CITS: [6501096]|. Pyrrolomycins have also been shown to have a strong antistaphylococcal biofilm activity |CITS: [18082373][20234952]| and to act as potent protonophores |CITS: [31405863]|. Despite their powerful biologically activity, natural pyrrolomycins are not suitable as drugs due to their high cytotoxicity. Several efforts are underway to modify pyrrolomycins to become less cytotoxic |CITS: [24914855][26690095][27565555][32486200]|., About This Pathway, Experiments with labeled isotopes suggest that the pyrrole ring is derived from |FRAME: PRO| and the phenyl moiety is derived from condensation of three acetate units, and that the methylenedioxy bridge of |FRAME: CPD-24070| is derived from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|. The nitrate group appears to be derived from nitrogen fixation |CITS: [16441063][18986197]|., The pyrrolomycin biosynthetic gene clusters have been cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-76728| and |FRAME: TAX-428401| in 2007 |CITS: [17158935]|. Pyrrolomycins are similar in their structure to |FRAME: CPD-17024|, a polyketide metabolite with antimicrobial activity produced by several |FRAME: TAX-286| species |CITS: [10094695]|. The clusters contain several genes that are highly similar to the genes involved in |FRAME: PWY-7930|, suggesting that the early steps of the pathway, leading to the formation of , are similar for the two compounds., The later steps of the pathway are less well understood. |FRAME: CPD-24067 "Pyrrolomycin C"| is formed by further halogenation. Two candidates for this halogenase, pyr16 and pyr17, are present in the cluster. It is likely that one of those genes envodes this halogenase, while the other encodes the halogenase that introduces a third chlorine atom into the pyrrole ring to produce |FRAME: CPD-24074|., The exact mechanism for the formation of the nitrated pyrrolomycins is not known. However, the clusters contain genes (pyr18 and pyr19) encoding the two components of an assimilatory nitrate reductase, suggesting that nitrite may be involved. The pyr4 and pyr5 genes encode a putative 2-oxoglutarate ferredoxin oxidoreductase, potentially providing the ferredoxin that is required by the nitrate reductase |CITS: [10094695]|. The pyr2 and pyr21 genes encode putative monooxygenases and might play a role in the introduction of a nitro group into the pyrrolomycin skeleton. The first nitrated pyrrolomycin to be formed is most likely |FRAME: CPD-24068| |CITS: [16441063]|., The |FRAME: G-81007| gene encodes a methyltransferase, and has been proposed to O-methylate |FRAME: CPD-24068| to form |FRAME: CPD-24069| |CITS: [16441063][17158935]|. The last reaction that is required for formation of |FRAME: CPD-24070| is the oxidative cyclization of the aryl methoxyl group to produce the methylenedioxy bridge. This type of reaction has been demonstrated in other pathways to involve a cytochrome P450-dependent oxidation (see for example |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.68|). The only candidate for encoding the cytochrome P450 enzyme in the cluster is the |FRAME: G-81006| gene |CITS: [17158935]|.

The |FRAME: CPD-6954|, |FRAME: CPD-6955|, |FRAME: CPD-8636| and |FRAME: CPD-8647| (raspberry ketone) are some of the aromatic compounds of raspberry that have been studied extensively |CITS: [10835233]|. Several kinds of polyketide synthases have been identified in Rubus including, chalcone synthase (CHS), benzalactone synthase (BAS) and stilbene synthase (STS) |CITS: [12226219]|. The messenger RNAs (mRNAs) of eukaryotes from yeasts to mammals, as well as most eukaryotic viruses, possess a 5' cap structure consisting of a 7-methyl guanosine (m7G) linked via an inverted 5'5' triphosphate bridge to the initiating nucleoside of the transcript |CITS: [1194288][9275164][12154373]|., The inverted m7G structure, also known as cap0, marks transcription start sites and has multiple effects on gene expression, including enhancement of RNA stability, splicing, nucleocytoplasmic transport and translation initiation, as facilitated by interactions with nuclear and cytoplasmic cap binding proteins |CITS: [8069914][9628920][14967145][10872469][18678651]|., The cap structure is formed cotranscriptionally by the sequential action of three enzymes. The first step is the hydrolysis of the 5'-triphosphate terminus of a nascent pre-mRNA to a diphosphate, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.33| (often referred to as RNA triphosphatase). The diphosphate RNA end is capped with GMP by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.50|, to yield a GpppNpNp- structure, also known as capG, and finally capG is methylated by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.56| to yield a cap0 structure., While in some cases (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-10245|) a multifunctional polypeptide contains all three active sites, in other cases (e.g. fungi) each function is catalyzed by a different polypeptide., In many eukaryotes the small nuclear (sn) RNAs involved in splicing also receive cotranscriptional cap0. However, following the formation of cap0 they are modified further by hypermethylation of m7G, forming m2,2,7G (trimethylguanosine or TMG), a reaction catalyzed in the cytoplasm by trimethylguanosine synthase 1 (Tgs1)., In higher eukaryotes, including insects, vertebrates and their viruses, further modification of mRNAs and snRNAs 5' ends involves the 2'-O-ribose methylation of the first transcribed nucleotide, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.57|. The structure that includes a cap0 and the 2'-O-ribose methylation is called cap1. In about 50% of the mRNAs the second nucleotide is also methylated at the same position by a different enzyme, forming cap2 |CITS: [21310715]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22651 "Roxarsone"| and |FRAME: CPD-24364 nitarsone| are aromatic arsenicals that have been used worldwide as a feed additive for farm animals (particularly poultry). Roxarsone has been used for prevention of coccidiosis, a protozoan disease caused in poultry by coccidian protozoa of the |FRAME: TAX-5800| genus, and nitarsone was used to prevent histomoniasis (blackhead disease, which is caused by the protozoan |FRAME: TAX-135588|). Both compounds have the added benefit of enhanced growth. In 2010 nearly 90% of all broiler chickens in the U.S. were estimated to be treated with roxarsone |CITS: [27735790]|. Roxarsone is excreted from chickens as a mixture of unaltered and partially metabolized species. When the chicken litter is used as a fertilizer or moved into landfills, roxarsone and its metabolites are broken down to inorganic arsenic, and the resulting inorganic |FRAME: ARSENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-763| can be taken up by crop plants or enter the groundwater |CITS: [24461427]|. In addition, the use of these compounds was found to increase inorganic and methylated arsenic species concentrations in poultry meat, resulting in a source of arsenic exposure for consumers |CITS: [22897610][23259671][23694900][26320952][27735789]|. Roxarsone and nitarsone are no longer used either in member countries of the European Union or in the United States, but are still in use as animal feed supplements in other countries |CITS: [23694900]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-22651 "Roxarsone"| and |FRAME: CPD-24364 nitarsone| exist as pentavalent and trivalent species under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, respectively. Accordingly, the aerobic degradation of these compounds, which is described here, begins with the pentavalent species, while the anaerobic degradation pathway starts with the trivalent species (see |FRAME: PWY-8262|)., Aerobic degradation of roxarsone was reported for the soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2516874| |CITS: [30703681]| and for the legume symbiont |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [31682413]|., The main transformation of |FRAME: CPD-22651| and |FRAME: CPD-22662| by |FRAME: TAX-382| is the reduction of their nitro groups, resulting in their conversion to the corresponding aromatic amines |FRAME: CPD-24374| and |FRAME: CPD-22663|, respectively. The arsenic in these species is subsequently reduced, producing trivalent |FRAME: CPD-24365| and |FRAME: CPD-24366|, which are much more toxic compared to the corresponding pentavalent species., These highly toxic compounds are exported from the cell into the environment. It has been proposed that they serve as an antibiotic to enhance the competitive advantage of the degrading organism in contaminated sites |CITS: [31682413]|. Some other species such as |FRAME: TAX-1501233| can degrade these trivalent compounds by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.M19|, liberating |FRAME: CPD0-2040| |CITS: [21272184]|., The nitroreduction of the pentavalent aromatic arsenicals by |FRAME: TAX-382| was shown to be catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G-81185| gene. The gene was identified based on its similarity to genes such as |FRAME: EG12656| ((modulator of drug activity B)) from |FRAME: TAX-562|, which were reported to have nitroreductase activity such as the activation of the bioreductive prodrugs |FRAME: CPD0-2575| (CB1954) and |FRAME: CPD0-2628 PR-104A| |CITS: [23399641][23399641]|. Purified recombinant MdaB from |FRAME: TAX-382| required FAD, NADPH, and an additional reducing factor such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| or |FRAME: CPD-24379| (TCEP) for nitroreductase activity with |FRAME: CPD-22651| and |FRAME: CPD-22662|. |CITS: [31682413]|. The other organism known to transform |FRAME: CPD-22651|, |FRAME: TAX-2516874|, possesses multiple mdaB genes, suggesting that that organism may possess a similar pathway |CITS: [31682413]|., As of 2021, the identity of the enzyme that reduces the pentavalent arsenic compoudns to trivalent is not known. As for the transporter that exports the trivalent products out of the cell, it has been proposed that it may be encoded by the arsK gene. |FRAME: TAX-382| carries an arsRK operon in pSymB, one of its two megaplasmids |CITS: [11481431]|. ArsK from |FRAME: TAX-1315272| was shown to be an arsenic efflux pump that confers resistance to |FRAME: CPD-763|, |FRAME: ANTIMONITE|, |FRAME: CPD-24334|, and |FRAME: CPD-22656| |CITS: [30315082]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-57081| belongs to enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) group, which has been recognized as a common cause of foodborne outbreaks |CITS: [10487636]|. |FRAME: ORG-57081| is one of the most prevalent ETEC pathogens associated with foodborne outbreaks in many countries, including Korea |CITS: [23800632]|, Japan |CITS: [24270144]|, and the USA.|CITS: [15109427]|., The structure of the |FRAME: CPD-24157| and the sequence of its O antigen biosynthetic cluster were reported in 2015 |CITS: [26232763]|. The repeat unit differs from that of |FRAME: ORG-57079| only in the presence of a side-chain glucose residue. Correspondingly, the O antigen biosynthesis gene clusters of the two organisms are very similar. Both clusters share the genes involved in |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| biosynthesis, four glycosyltransferase, an O antigen repeat unit flippase, and an O antigen polymerase, and the first seven genes, including four glycosyltransferase genes, share 96-100% DNA and protein identities. However, the the 3'-end of the O169 cluster contains three insertion sequence (IS) elements and an additional gene encoding a glycosyltransferase that is responsible for adding the glucosyl side-chain residue |CITS: [11598067][15774901][26232763]|.

Summary: General Background, Natural, pigmented |FRAME: CPD-12873|-containing compounds are produced by a variety of Gram-negative and Gram-positive eubacteria. Phenazines possess broad-spectrum antibiotic activity, although their mode(s) of action is not completely understood. Phenazines have important physiological effects on the producing organism as well as on host organisms. Phenazines can be simple, or complex including isoprenylated, or carbohydrate-containing derivatives. In addition to bacteria, the archaeal genus |FRAME:TAX-2207| produces an unusual, membrane-bound phenazine, |FRAME: CPD-7323|, that is used as an electron carrier in methanogenesis (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5207|), although its biosynthetic route is unknown. The major product of the phenazine biosynthesis pathway is |FRAME: CPD-9522|, although |FRAME: CPD-12872| and unsubstituted |FRAME: CPD-12873| are also produced |CITS: [19053436][20008172][20352425][19658148]|., Fluorescent pseudomonads such as |FRAME: ORG-5929|, |FRAME: TAX-1038921 "Pseudomonas chlororaphis aureofaciens 30-84 (previously named P. aureofaciens 30-84)"| |CITS: [11114932]| and |FRAME: TAX-287| are the best studied phenazine producers. These organisms typically biosynthesize two or more phenazines, although |FRAME: ORG-5929| produces only |FRAME: CPD-9522|. This compound may be modified by methylation, transamidation, decarboxylation, or hydroxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-5776|) by the products of linked, or unlinked genes., Phenazine production by fluorescent pseudomonads makes them interesting as biological control agents to combat fungal plant pathogens in the soil. Although the physiological role of phenazines within these organisms is uncertain, they appear to give them a competitive advantage in the environment. The phenazine |FRAME: CPD-12847| is a virulence factor for |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: CPD-9522| has been shown to be involved in |FRAME: ORG-5929| phytotoxicity. Reviewed in |CITS: [16719720]| and |CITS: [15008629]|., About This Pathway, The early part of this pathway is based on |CITS: [19053436]|, while the later part is based on information from |CITS: [23897464]|. This pathway originates from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, which is a branch point for the biosynthesis of may aromatic primary and secondary metabolite. , Early work showed that the phenazine ring structure is essentially formed by the condensation of two molecules of |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, with the ring nitrogen derived from the amide nitrogen of |FRAME: GLN|. Phenazine biosynthetic genes were later cloned and found to constitute an operon phzABCDEFG encoding biosynthetic enzymes, regulatory proteins and phenazine modification enzymes in |FRAME: ORG-5929| and |FRAME: TAX-1038921| |CITS: [11114932]|. In |FRAME: TAX-208964| this operon was found to be present in two copies |CITS: [11591691]|. However, gene nomenclature differs among species. The phzC gene encodes |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.54|, the first step in |FRAME: CHORISMATE| biosynthesis. This enzyme redirects primary metabolic intermediates into the biosynthesis of phenazines |CITS: [9573209][8586283][11591691]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16719720]|., In the first reaction of the pathway, PhzE converts |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to |FRAME: CPD-9517| |CITS: [11562236]|. This compound is converted by PhzD to |FRAME: CPD-9518| |CITS: [11562236][12741825]|, and the latter is converted by the PhzF isomerase to |FRAME: CPD-9521| |CITS: [15545603] [15449932]|. This compound is dimerized by head-to-tail condensation to form the first tricyclic intermediate, which is converted by |FRAME: G-12422| (Pseudomonads contain two genes, phzA and phzB, which are duplicates, but only the latter catalyzes the reaction) resulting in |FRAME: CPD-12990|. This unstable intermediate undergoes a rapid, apparently spontaneous, oxidative decarboxylation, producing |FRAME:CPD-19105| |CITS: [19053436]|., The rest of the pathway is catalyzed by the FMN-dependent oxidase |FRAME: CPLX-8210| (PhzG). Despite decades of work in this field, these last reactions were completely defined only in 2016 |CITS: [23897464]|, although it has been speculated earlier that |FRAME: CPD-12874|, the reduced form of |FRAME: CPD-9522|, may be the core pathway end product, upon which phenazine modifying enzymes act (reviewed in |CITS: [19658148]| and in |CITS: [16719720]|)., The later part of the pathway is a mixture of PhzG-catalyzed reactions and spontaeous tautomerization and decarboxylation reactions, resulting in three parallel branches leading to different products |CITS: [23897464]|. When PhzG, which is an oxidase, acts directly on the product of PhzA/B, it produces |FRAME: CPD-19103|, which is also a substrate for the enzyme. A second round of catalysis produces |FRAME: CPD-19104|, which spontaneously converts to |FRAME: CPD-12988|, the reduced form of |FRAME: CPD-12872|., However, the PhzA/B product can also undergo a spontaneous decarboxylation, producing |FRAME: CPD-19105|, which is also a substrate for PhzG. When the enzyme acts on this compound, it produces |FRAME: CPD-19106|, which spontaneously rearranges to form |FRAME: CPD-12874|, the reduced form of |FRAME: CPD-9522|., Finally, the product of the spontaneous decarboxylation, |FRAME: CPD-19105|, can undego tautomerization to form |FRAME: CPD-19108|. This compound is also a subject for spontaneous decarboxylation, forming |FRAME: , CPD-19109|, the reduced form of |FRAME: CPD-12873|., While in theory all three products of the pathway can undergo spontaneous oxidation in the presence of oxygen, forming |FRAME: CPD-12872|, |FRAME: CPD-9522|, and |FRAME: CPD-12873|, in actuality it appears that it is the reduced forms that are subject to enzymatic modifications |CITS: [23897464]|., In fluorescent pseudomonads phenazine biosynthesis is regulated by quorum sensing and the GacA/S, two-component signal transduction system. Phenazine production is also influenced by the amount, and quality of carbon and nitrogen sources in the environment. Reviewed in |CITS: [16719720]|.

Summary: Phospholipids are the major structural components of biological membranes. Some phospholipids , (i.e. phosphatidylinositol) also serve as important lipid-signaling molecules.  In plants, phospholipids , predominate extra-chloroplast membranes including the plasma membrane, mitochondria membrane, , endoplasmic reticulum, and microsomal membrane, with phosphatidylcholine and , phosphatidylethanolamine being the major constituents. On the other hand, glycolipids predominate , chloroplast envolope and thylakoid membranes. Phosphatidylglycerol is the only phospholipid found in , chloroplast thylakoids, and is critical for the structural and functional integrity of the thylakoid , membranes. , Phospholipids are mostly synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. Once synthesized, , they are transported to other phospholipid containing membranes. However, genetic and biochemical evidence has , demonstrated that phosphatidylglycerol can be synthesized in the plastids |CITS: [16774646]|. In addition, , mitochondria also contain enzymes for phospholipid synthesis, thus we cannot rule out the possibility , that phospholipids can be synthesized there.

|FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| are major components of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage) in animals., They are both |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| polymers composed of repeating disaccharide units,  each containing |FRAME: CPD-12557|  linked by a (1,3) or (1,4) linkage to a uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-12521| or |FRAME: CPD-12515|, with extensive N and O-sulfation. Sulfation occurs to various degrees at position 2 of uronic acid and at positions 4 or 6, or both, of galactosamine. In addition, the amino group of galactosamine is acetylated, Many microorganisms have enzymes that enable them to degrade glycosaminoglycans |CITS: [7654407]|. This ability is particularly important for soil bacteria, which may depend on connective tissues in animal carcasses as a nutrient source., There are several steps in the degradation process. It starts with the cleavage of the polymer into smaller fragments, initially tetra- and hexasaccharides, but ultimately disaccharides. The process continues with the removal of the sulfate groups, and ends with the final degradation of the disaccharides into individual sugars, a step that has not been characterized yet. , The lyases that break the polymer to smaller fragments are classified based on the position of cleavage as either endo-lyases or exo-lyases. The endolytic enzyme can produce products of several sizes, although the final product tends to be disaccharides. The exo-lyases cleave dissaccharide molecules from the non-reducing end of the polymer chain |CITS: [9083041]|. Some lyases, known as chondroitinase AC, can act only on |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A| and |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C| (that contain |FRAME: CPD-12521|), some, known as chondroitinase B, can act only on |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| (that contains |FRAME: CPD-12515|), and some, known as condroitinase ABC, can act on both |CITS: [10618199][9083041]|., The lyases act by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disacchrides. , Chondroitin ABC lyases may help in the regeneration of spinal cord injuries that were thought for a long time to be incurable. Injection of chondroitinase ABC at sites of central nervous system injury, where a glial scar develops, removes the GAG components of ECM chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and attenuates the inhibitory effects to axon growth |CITS: [11948352][11948352][11948332]|., The removal of the sulfate groups is catalyzed by specialized sulfatases that can remove the sulfate groups at either the 4 or 6 positions. The sulfatases have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-585| but the genes that encode them have not been identified |CITS: [5647268]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The O antigen of group A |FRAME: TAX-590| strains corresponds to serogroup O2 and is produced by a Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O-antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., The first step in Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways is the addition of a sugar phosphate residue to |FRAME: CPD-9646| (Und-P) to form the undecaprenyl diphosphate-linked sugar. Most O antigens found in |FRAME: TAX-590| species start with GlcNAc or GalNAc and their biosynthesis is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). However, the |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigens belonging to serogroups O2 (A), O4 (B), O8 (C2C3), O9 (D1), O9,46 (D2), O9,46,27 (D3), O3,10 (E1-E3), and O1,3,19 (E4) form a distinct set that is characterized by having a Gal residue as the first sugar of the O unit., The enzyme responsible for the initiation of these pathways is |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.6| (WbaP, previously called RfbP |CITS: [9004408]|). The use of Gal as initial sugar appeared in |FRAME: TAX-590| after its divergence from |FRAME: TAX-561|, but the eight Gal-initiated O antigens have grown to be very important in this species |CITS: [23874940]|., The only structural difference between the A and D1 O antigens is the presence of the dideoxyhexose paratose in place of tyvelose |CITS: [13526677][4587616][6179619]|, which is a result of a mutation in |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.10|, which prevents conversion of |FRAME: CDP-36-DIDEOXY-D-MANNOSE| to |FRAME: CPD-9698| |CITS: [4808896]|. , The full O antigen biosynthesis cluster was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-54388| and analyzed by restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) |CITS: [2447059]|. The cluster was later fully sequenced |CITS: [23874940]|. It is similar to the D1 gene cluster, but as expected, it contains a frame shift mutation that generated a stop codon reducing |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.10|, to 5 residues. Some group A members have a triplication of one segment, which led to an increased copy number of the wbaV gene and generated a wbaU::wzx chimeric gene at the recombination site for the triplication |CITS: [23874940]|. Group A strains have arisen from D1 very recently, as there are only a small number of group A serovars reported, and all still contain the non-functional tyv gene |CITS: [23874940]|., Following the completion of the synthesis of a repeat unit, the flippase Wzx flips the full molecule to the other side of the membrane, where the Wzy polymerase transfers additional repeat units from their anchor to a single elongating molecule. The Wzz protein ensures termination of the polymerization once the correct chain length has been achieved., |FRAME: TAX-590| strains belonging to group A contain the wzyB gene, which encodes a polymerase that links the repeat units by an α(1,2) linkage between the galactose and the mannose residues [α-D-Gal-(1→2)-α-D-Man] |CITS: [23874940]|.

The |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| that is formed during L-carnitine degradation was shown to be converted to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE| (TMA), which is transferred to the liver, where it is converted to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| (TMAO) by liver flavin containing enzymes such as |FRAME: HS00223| (see |FRAME: PWY-8292|). While multiple community members could convert |FRAME: CARNITINE| to |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| (see |FRAME: CARNMET-PWY|), only a single Clostridiales bacterium, |FRAME: TAX-1776384|, was able to convert |FRAME: GAMMA-BUTYROBETAINE| to |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE|. Experiments confirmed the presence of the pathway in these organisms |CITS: [34949826]|.

Summary: The Cfr methyltransferase confers combined resistance to five classes of antibiotics that bind to the peptidyl transferase center of bacterial ribosomes by catalyzing methylation of the C-8 position of 23S rRNA nucleotide A2503., These five different classes of antibiotics include phenicols, lincosamides, oxazolidinones, pleuromutilins, and streptogramin A antibiotics |CITS: [16801432]|. These include the entirely synthetic oxazolidinone antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-19629|, an important therapeutic option and often the last line of defense in the treatment of infections caused by MRSA |CITS: [17555436]|., It is also known that Cfr expression confers resistance to the 16-membered macrolides |FRAME: CPD-15942| and |FRAME: CPD-13983| |CITS: [18299405]|. Thus, the Cfr-mediated resistance functions in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and includes important antimicrobial agents that are currently used in human and/or veterinary medicine., The |FRAME: G-14551| gene was originally detected on the pSCFS1 plasmid from |FRAME: TAX-1296| |CITS: [10952608]|, The gene encodes a methyltransferase that catalyzes the methylation of the C-8 carbon of adenosine at position 2503 of 23S rRNA |CITS: [16091044][19144912]|., Some bacteria already have one methyltransferase (RlmN) that methylates adenosine 2503 at the 2 position (see |FRAME: RXN-11586 "EC 2.1.1.192, 23S rRNA (adenine<sup>2503</sup>-C<sup>2</sup>)-methyltransferase"|). Cfr can methylate either unmodified residues, or ones that have already been methylated at position 2 by RlmN., The mechanism of action has been studied in detail and is distinctly different from that of typical |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases. Due to the inertness of the C8 position, the enzyme utilizes radical chemistry and utilizes two SAM molecules, one as the methyl group donor, and the second as the source of the |FRAME: CPD-15400| (a similar mechanism is used by |FRAME: EG12401 RlmN|). A methyl group is first transferred to an internal L-cysteine residue of Cfr (C338) in a typical S<sub>N</sub>2 displacement reaction. A hydrogen atom is abstracted from the Cys-appended methyl group via a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical derived from the second SAM molecule, forming a methylene radical. Subsequent attack of the methylene radical on the C8 carbon atom of the substrate generates a transient cross-linked intermediate between the methylated cysteine and the adenine in the RNA substrate. The intermediate is resolved by an unidentified residue of the enzyme (in RlmN it is C118) |CITS:[21415317][23088750][23861844][23644479][24806349][26253978][27081063]|.

Names: Kdo transfer to lipid IVA (P. gingivalis)
Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor lipid IVA in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. The donor of Kdo units is its activated form, |FRAME: CMP-KDO|., Many organisms have monofunctional enzymes that catalyze one of these steps. |FRAME: TAX-562| has a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes the addition of two Kdo units with different glycosidic linkages., Kdo-containing lipid IVA molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD0-1676 "Tetramethylammonium hydroxide"| is a reagent used in the fabrication of electronic chips, and treatment of wastewater contaminated with it is a problem for manufacturers |CITS: [Tanaka94]|. It has been shown that certain methanogens are able to degrade |FRAME: CPD-7679| anaerobically, producing |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: AMMONIUM|. One such organism, |FRAME: TAX-117561|, has been isolated |CITS:[Tanaka94]|., The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., The enzymes responsible for this pathway were isolated from |FRAME: TAX-117561| and found to consist of two methyltransferases (MtqA and MtqB) and a 22-kDa corrinoid protein (MtqC) (the naomenclature MTQ stands for Methyl Transferase Quarternary amine) |CITS: [9732435]|., MtqA is a 40 kDa protein exibiting MT2 activity. Its N-terminal amino acid sequence revealed similarity to MT2 isoenzymes found in |FRAME: TAX-2208| and particularly to |FRAME:MONOMER-12205| (65%). MtqB is a 50 kDa protein with MT1 activity. Its N-terminal amino acid sequence has no homology to other MT1 proteins. The corrinoid protein was bound to the MT2 enzyme in cell extracts. After separating the two proteins using a Mono Q column they were not able to reconstitute tetramethylammonium:coenzyme M methyltransferase activity when added to MT1. Prior to separation, though, combining the fractions that contained MT1 and MT2/corrinoid protein resulted in |FRAME: Me-CoM| formation from |FRAME:CPD-7679| and |FRAME:CoM|. Activity also required the addition of ATP and Ti(III) citrate |CITS: [9732435]|.

Summary: 2,3-butanediol is a compound of commercial interest, mostly as an antifreeze agent due to to its low freezing point |CITS: [Magee87]|. One of its well known applications is the formation of methyl ethyl ketone, by dehydration, which can be used as a liquid fuel additive |CITS: [11234948]|., Many bacterial species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2-3-butanediol"| via several intermediate compounds,, including |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|, |FRAME: ACETOIN|, and |FRAME: DIACETYL|. Not all species carry the process all the way through - some may stop earlier, accumulating some of the intermediates. , Of particular importance is the production of |FRAME: DIACETYL|, an important flavor metabolite in dairy products, wine and beer |CITS: [2198252][15454314]|., The metabolic function of 2,3-butanediol is not well understood, although it may play a role in preventing intracellular, acidification by changing the metabolism from acid production to the formation of a neutral compound, |CITS: [6298028]|.  In addition, the pathway might participate in regulation of the NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio, in the bacteria |CITS: [8444801]|., In this pathway |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is produced by substrate level phosphorylation, is converted to |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-5243| (also known as α-ALS). 2-acetolactate is an unstable intermediate, and  in the presence of oxygen it can undergo a spontaneous decarboxylation, producing |FRAME: DIACETYL| that is converted to acetoin by the activity of the dual-function enzyme acetoin (diacetyl) reductase (see below)., Under anaerobic conditions  |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE| is converted directly to acetoin by a decarboxylation step catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-5262| (α-ALD), and production of diacetyl is bypassed., The relative activities of α-ALS and α-ALD in specific strains determine the fluxes and concentrations of the different intermediates in these organisms., The two enzyme activities diacetyl reductase and acetoin reductase were initially reported to be catalyzed by two different enzymes |CITS: [13211662]|, and two different EC numbers were issued based on that observation (|FRAME: ACETOINDEHYDROG-RXN "EC 1.1.1.5"| and |FRAME: RR-BUTANEDIOL-DEHYDROGENASE-RXN "EC 1.1.1.4|). However, later research indicated that in most bacteria both activities are catalyzed by the same enzyme, for which the name diacetyl(acetoin) reductase was suggested |CITS: [5540507][4350968][2040298][10647818]|. Moreover, the enzyme appears to have a much wider substrate range than orignally believed, and it has been suggested to rename it L-glycol dehydrogenase |CITS: [2040298]|., This pathway includes multiple decarboxylation reactions, generating |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., This CO<sub>2</sub> is the source of the  "eyes", or holes that certain cheeses, such as Swiss cheese, develop during maturation.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.1|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.1|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.4.2| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., Thiamine biosynthesis in bacteria is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| (see |FRAME: PWY-6893|)., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the last part of the thiamine biosynthesis pathway - the coupling of the two moieties of thiamine, forming |FRAME: THIAMINE-P|, and its phosphorylation to the biologically active form, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. , Although it is not absolutely clear at this time, it is possible that the key enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: BSU38290-MONOMER|, acts in vivo on different substrates in different organisms (see |FRAME: PWY-6894|). This pathway describes the process as documented in |FRAME: TAX-1423|. It is also predicted to occur in haloarchaea |CITS: [25348237]|.

Summary: Toluene is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic compounds can be degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus |FRAME:TAX-286| and closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward bioremediation of environmental pollutants by metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|)., Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various species that involve different initial monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these pathways converge in the formation of 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound is a substrate for ring cleavage enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission pathway, resulting in the formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-3-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-2-OH-PWY|). , The chromosome of |FRAME:TAX-303| F1 contains a gene cluster encoding enzymes that allow this organism to grow on toluene and related compounds as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [2670929], [1916282], [8063106]|. Other strains of P. putida may contain plasmid-encoded genes for toluene degradation (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|). The inducible toluene dioxygenase enzyme hydroxylates toluene to its dihydrodiol derivative by incorporating both atoms of an oxygen molecule into the aromatic nucleus. The dihydroxylated derivative is dehydrogenated to a catechol. Ring fission of the catechol 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) is catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase to produce cis,cis-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate. This compound is hydrolyzed to 2-oxopent-4-enoate, or its tautomeric dienol form cis-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate. This tautomerization occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|. It is not known which tautomeric form is produced by the hydrolase, and which form is used by the hydratase of P. putida F1 in this pathway. However, it has been suggested that the |FRAME:TAX-303| mt-2 hydratase, encoded by the TOL plasmid pWW0, uses the dienol form as a substrate |CITS: [2681159]|, and there is evidence that the |FRAME:TAX-562| hydratase also uses the dienol form as substrate, producing a ketonized intermediate in the reaction mechanism |CITS: [9492273]|. The products of the pathway are pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and acetaldehyde, which may be converted by acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, a central metabolite |CITS: [8063106]|.

Many bacterial species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2-3-butanediol"| via several intermediate compounds, including |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|, |FRAME: ACETOIN|, and |FRAME: DIACETYL|. There are three isomeric forms of 2,3-butanediol (BD ) - |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|, |FRAME: CPD-346| and |FRAME: CPD-12004|, and two isomeric forms of acetoin - |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: CPD-255|. |FRAME: CPD-346| is formed only from |FRAME: CPD-255|., Not all species carry the process all the way through - some may stop earlier, accumulating some of the intermediates. Thus this pathway only describes the production of |FRAME: CPD-346| from |FRAME: CPD-255|, and the pathway leading to the production of |FRAME: CPD-255| is described in |FRAME: PWY-6389|., The metabolic function of 2,3-butanediol is not yet known, although it may play a role in preventing intracellular acidification by changing the metabolism from acid production to the formation of a neutral compound |CITS: [6298028]|. In addition, the pathway might participate in regulation of the NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio in the bacteria |CITS: [8444801]|., The conversion of acetoin to 2,3-butanediol, which is reversible, is performed by the enzyme acetoin reductase (AR), also known as 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenase (BDH)., 4 types of AR activities have been identified, differing in their stereo-specificity for both the substrate and the product |CITS: [Ui84]|. The production of |FRAME: CPD-346| is catalyzed by enzymes that are often referred to as L-BDH. Such enzymes have been characterized from several organisms, including |FRAME: CPLX-5283| from |FRAME: TAX-548| and |FRAME: CPLX-5281| from |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [2040298][11577733]|.

Summary: General Background, Plants produce a number of non-standard amino acids that are not incorporated into proteins, including |FRAME: CPD-13644| |CITS: [11354600][12720365][21917546]|. Although some of these amino acids participate in primary metabolism, others may play a role in plant defense by directly causing harm to the attacking pathogen or herbivore or by making nitrogen less available to it (see refs in |CITS: [21917546]|). Elevated levels of |FRAME: CPD-13644| are produced in response to attack by several different insects, as well as the volatile phytohormone |FRAME: Methyl-Jasmonates methyl jasmonate| (MeJA) in Arabidopsis, and this compound can be detected in phloem exudates. |FRAME: CPD-13644| appears to act as a defense compound against phloem-feeding herbivores in |FRAME: ORG-5993| where its effects may be both direct and indirect |CITS: [21917546]|., |FRAME: CPD-13644| has been detected in a number of different plants, including 25 ecotypes of |FRAME: ORG-5993|. Within its larger taxonomic family, the |FRAME:TAX-3700|, this compound was also detected in Arabidopsis shokei, Arabidopsis suecica, Capsella rubella and Boechera stricta but it was not found in at least nine other related species that were tested including |FRAME:TAX-3712|, Camelina sativa, and, Thellungiella salsuginea |CITS: [21917546]|. However, |FRAME: CPD-13644| has been reported to exist in a number of other non-Brassicaceae plant species including Corydalis ochotensis, Asplenium, nidus, Bistorta bistortoides and in the seeds of legumes such as |FRAME:TAX-3880|, but its presence in other species, including several grasses, remains controversial |CITS: [11809451][LIPSON96][21917546]|. Outside of plants, |FRAME: CPD-13644| has been detected in mushrooms and in sea cucumber, but it is unclear how this non-standard amino acid is produced in these organisms |CITS: [FINDLAY84][OGAWA87]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-13644| can be produced from at least three different amino acids, namely, proline, arginine, and glutamate, based on radiotracer studies. It is likely that these are first transformed into the non-standard amino acid |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| before they are acetylated by NATA1 |CITS: [21917546]|. , Up-regulation of the flux through this pathway in |FRAME: ORG-5993| appears to be regulated, at least in part, through changes in NATA1 transcript levels since stimuli such as MeJA and insect herbivory appear to cause increased levels of NATA1 expression followed by increased levels of |FRAME: CPD-13644|. There is evidence that |FRAME: CPD-13644| must also be broken down in Arabidopsis, but the catabolic pathway has not been uncovered to date |CITS: [21917546]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, A study of enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) in the UK has found that the most common serogroups were E. coli O145, |FRAME: ORG-57097| and |FRAME: ORG-57097| |CITS: [23893920]|., A study of the O antigen from |FRAME: ORG-57097| has found that it consists of β-(1→2)-linked tetrasaccharide repeat units that contain the unusual monosaccharide |FRAME: CPD-24436| (DQui4N(S3HOBut)) |CITS: [18457569]|., In addition to determining the structure of the O antigen, the authors sequenced the O antigen biosynthesis gene cluster of the organism. The cluster was found to contain 13 open reading frames. Five genes (rmlA, rmlB, rmlC, rmlD, and vioA) that encode the enzymes required for biosynthesis of the building blocks |FRAME: DTDP-RHAMNOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-472| (a precursor for Qui4N(S3HOBut)); a gene encoding |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.26|; three genes encoding glycosyltransferases, and a wzx and wzy genes encoding a repeat unit flippase and O antigen polymerase. The other two genes showed a similarity to acetyltransferase and hydratase genes, respectively, and were suggested to be responsible for the synthesis and transfer of the 3-hydroxybutanoyl group to Qui4N |CITS: [18457569]|. While the authors have functionally assigned all genes, they have not characterized any of them biochemically., It should be noted that while the glucosamine residue was found acetylated at the O6 position, it is not clear whether this acetylation takes place early on, as shown here, or whether it occurs later in the pathway. No gene encoding this acetyltransferase is present in the O antigen biosynthetic cluster. Acetylation of O antigens is often catalyzed by enzymes encoded elsewhere in the genome, and sometimes occurs in the periplasm, following the export of the complete repeat unit, or even the assembly of the O antigen polymer.

General Background, |FRAME:MALONATE Malonate| is found in small amounts in plants |CITS: [13013230]| and is produced by some bacteria |CITS: [786256]|. Most of the malonate in the environment, however, comes from industrial production. The dimethyl and diethyl forms, in particularly, are produced at more than 12,000 tons per year (1995) |CITS: [11902724]|., Several strains of bacteria are able to utilize malonate as sole source of carbon and energy. The key reaction in the pathway is the decarboxylation of malonate to acetate. Malonate is a rather inert compound, and its decarboxylation under physiological conditions requires an activation step, in which malonate forms a thioester derivative., Two types of malonate decarboxylases have been described. The first type (described here), which has been characterized in the anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-57040|, is |FRAME: EC-7.2.4.4|, an enzyme complex that also functions as a Na+-translocating pump. In this enzyme the carboxylate group is first transferred to a biotin carrier protein that shuttles it to the membrane-bound decarboxylase subunit (see |FRAME: PWY-6060|)., The second type (described in |FRAME: PWY-5794|) is |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.88|, a cytosolic enzyme copmplex that releases the carboxylate group directly to the cytosol |CITS: [10561613]|., About This Pathway, Unlike the |FRAME: CPLX-7677| from |FRAME: TAX-573|, the |FRAME: CPLX-7676| from |FRAME: TAX-57040| comprises water-soluble cytoplasmic and membrane components that are not assembled into a single enzyme complex |CITS: [1628643]|., Prior to decarboxylation, malonate needs to be activated by binding to an acyl-carrier protein [acp] subunit, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10903| gene. There are several steps that need to take place prior to this activation reaction., First, the [acp] subunit needs to be pre-activated by binding a unique |FRAME: 2-5-TRIPHOSPHORIBOSYL-3-DEPHOSPHO-| cofactor, which is also used by the citrate lyase enzyme complex (see |FRAME: PWY-5796|). Following this pre-activation, the [acp] subunit binds an acetyl group in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.35| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-10884| gene), forming |FRAME: Malonate-Decarboxylases-Acetyl-Form|. Finally, this acetylated form can exchange the acetyl group for malonate in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.187| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-10885| gene)., Once activated and bound to the [acp] subunit as |FRAME: Malonate-Decarboxylases-Malonyl-Form|, the malonyl group becomes the substrate for the |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.10| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-10886| and |FRAME: G-10887| genes), which transfers a carboxylate moiety group from the bound-malonyl group to a biotin-carrier protein, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10902| gene. The carboxylated biotin-carrier protein travels to |FRAME: MONOMER-14257|, the membrane bound component of the malonate decarboxylase complex, which releases the carboxyl group. The enzyme couples this exergonic reaction to Na+ ion pumping across the membrane, building up a gradient. After transfering the carboxylate group to the biotin-carrier protein, the [acp] subunit returns to its acetylated form, and is ready to bind a new malonate molecule. Thus, the enzyme catalyzes a continous turnover of |FRAME: MALONATE| to |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [11902724]|., An operon that encodes all of the components that are involved in this pathway has been sequenced |CITS: [9128730]|., The overall process is described by |FRAME: EC-7.2.4.4|:, |FRAME: RXN-9774|

Natural rubber is an important raw material in an enormous number of products. The backbone of natural rubber comprises a (cis)-1,4-polyisoprene with two or three trans-isoprene units at the ω-terminus, formed by the sequential condensation of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) units in cis configuration onto a short all-trans prenyl diphosphate. It is very similar in structure to |FRAME: DOLICHOL dolichols|, but the chain length is much longer (C>1500)., Natural rubber is produced from latex - a material that makes up the cytoplasmic content of the latecifers or latex vessels of |FRAME: TAX-3981| (the Brazilian rubber tree) |CITS: [17545224]|. Although over 2000 plant species capable of producing rubber have been identified, only a few synthesize the high molecular weight rubber that is required for the production of high quality rubber products, and natural rubber is currently produced commercially only from |FRAME: TAX-3981|. Potential alternative sources are the Russian rubber-producing dandelion (|FRAME: TAX-333970|), which was cultivated in the former Soviet Union during World War II to satisfy the demand for natural rubber |CITS: [22504822]|, and guayule (|FRAME: TAX-35935|), a xerophytic perennial shrub that produces high quality natural rubber and is endemic to the Chihuahuan desert |CITS: [29116401][33513965]|., Rubber biosynthesis is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.20|. The enzyme is localized at the surface of cytosolic vesicles known as rubber particles, and biosynthesis is initiated through the binding of an allylic pyrophosphate primer, such as |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| |CITS: [Tanaka01][14622254][18799172]|., The source of IPP are the isoprenoid pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-922| and |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|). Although conventionally the cytoplasmic |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| was considered to be the source of IPP for the biosynthesis of rubber, some studies suggest that the plastidic |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| may provide an alternative means of generating IPP for rubber synthesis |CITS: [15010614]|., In 2003 two cDNAs encoding cis-prenyltransferases, sharing 88% of the predicted amino acid sequence of their products, were isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3981| and named |FRAME: G-54973| and |FRAME: G-54976| |CITS: [14622254]|. Expression of |FRAME: G-54973| is restricted to the latex, while that of |FRAME: G-54976| has been observed in various tissues |CITS: [25017153]|., Upon addition of fresh rubber particles from |FRAME: TAX-3981|, purified recombinant |FRAME: G-54976| was shown to catalyze |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| incorporation and form a rubber polymer of 3,00015,000 isoprene units |CITS: [14622254]|., The activity of |FRAME: G-54973| was demonstrated only in 2016, when it was discovered that activity requires formation of a complex with two other proteins - a rubber elongation factor (|FRAME: G-54974|), and the HRT1-REF bridging protein (|FRAME: G-54975|). |FRAME: G-54975| appears to act as a bridge, bringing the other two components together. Activity of the complex was demonstrated by using a cell-free translation-coupled system with detergent-washed rubber particles. This system enabled de novo synthesis of natural rubber in vitro, providing the first direct evidence that |FRAME: G-54973| participates in rubber biosynthesis |CITS: [27790974]|., Rubber biosynthesis by |FRAME: TAX-35935| (guayule), The desire to reduce the environmental cost of rubber production, the need for pesticides for growing clonal |FRAME: TAX-3981| plantations in non-native environments, and increasing labor costs for Hevea rubber production motivate efforts to use alternative crops for rubber production. Guayule has major advantages over Hevea since it can be cultivated broadly across temperate and arid climates and it produces high molecular weight natural rubber suitable for use in the manufacture of tires. In addition, harvesting of biomass and rubber extraction are easily mechanized. The one significant disadvantage of guayule is the fact that rubber is produced only under cold temperature in the winter months., Four guayule genes - three cis-prenyltransferases (CPs) and one CPT-binding protein that can form complexes with any of the CPTs, have been identified in guayule, and one of the CPTs was shown to be predominantly expressed in stem and induced by cold-stress, suggesting involvement in rubber biosynthesis |CITS: [30858856]|. Transcriptome analysis of rubber biosynthesis in guayule has identified several new enzymes potentially involved in the biosynthesis of rubber as well as transcription factors specifically expressed in rubber-producing tissues |CITS: [30755179]|. However, as of 2022 the pathway for rubber biosynthesis in guayule is not fully understood.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-942 Dibenzothiophene| (DBT) is one of many organic sulfur compounds found in crude oil. The consumption of petroleum products that contain such compounds is a source of environmental pollution, resulting in release of |FRAME: SULFUR-DIOXIDE| into the environment. This pollution may be reduced by the reduction or removal of organic sulfur compounds from petroleum products in a process known as the desulfurization of crude oil. DBT has been used as a model aromatic sulfur compound for the investigation of biological desulfurization systems and the solation and characterization of bacteria that possess the ability to degrade organic sulfur compounds., |FRAME: TAX-334542| is a Gram-positive soil bacterium that was originally isolated from coal deposits. Under sulfur-limiting conditions strain IGTS8 is able to selectively remove sulfur from organosulfur compounds and incorporate the sulfur into its biomass. It can utilize dibenzothiophene (DBT) as a sole sulfur source, utilizing a 4-step, 3-enzyme pathway. The pathway stops at |FRAME: CPD-946| and releases the sulfur in the form of |FRAME: SO3| that is assimilated into the cell |CITS: [8467997][7961424][9308179]|. Similar genes have been found in several other organisms |CITS:[1575493][10068795][11229891][16233084][11682191][12226734][16310728][24470304][25627402]|. A full dsz operon isolated from oil contaminated soil metagenome was expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, conferring the ability to use DBT as the only sulfur source on the recombinant host |CITS: [31600862]|., Two of the enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-493| and |FRAME: G-494| genes, are FMN-dependent monooxygenases. DszC produces an oxidized FMN, while DszA produces the unusual cofactor |FRAME: CPD-22329|, which reacts spontaneously with NADH to form FMN. The FMN cofactors produced by the two enzymes are reduced back to their active form by the action of |FRAME: G-80417 DszD|, an NADH-dependent FMN-reductase |CITS: [ 12831898][15538557]|., The desulfurization occurs without breaking any carbon-carbon bonds, leaving the 'fuel value' of the substrate intact.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The enterobacterial common antigen (ECA) is an outer membrane glycolipid common to all members of the Enterobacteriaceae., The carbohydrate portion of the ECA consists of heteropolysaccharide chains that contain repeats of a trisaccharide unit composed of |FRAME: CPD-12541|, |FRAME: CPD-15664| and |FRAME:CPD-15611| (also known as 4-acetamido-4,6-dideoxy-α-D-galactose or 4-acetamido-α-D-fucose) |CITS: [2166030]|., This pathway describes the synthesis of the |FRAME:TDP-FUC4NAC| monosaccharide, which is synthesized in its activated form |FRAME: TDP-FUC4NAC|. Like many other dTDP-activated deoxysugars, it is formed from |FRAME: GLC-1-P|. Following activation to |FRAME: DTDP-D-GLUCOSE|, the activated sugar is transaminated by the |FRAME: EG11456| gene product and acetylated by the |FRAME: EG11455| gene product |CITS: [2166030]|.

However, |FRAME:CPD-10072| accumulation was not observed experimentally., The former compound, |FRAME: CPD-10065|, is metabolized by |FRAME: MONOMER-13973| and, |FRAME: MONOMER-13974| to |FRAME: CPD-10066|, which is completely mineralized by, β-oxidation |CITS: [10832640]|.
