Summary: This short pathway describes an intermediary step in the pathway of menaquinone biosynthesis, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.74|. This enzyme condenses two components - |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE|, whose production is described in the pathways of |FRAME: DHNA-Biosynthesis|, and |FRAME: TRANS-POLYISOPRENYL-PP|, whose length varies among different taxa, and is determined by the specificity of the polyprenyl diphosphate synthase., This particular pathway describes the step in organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD-21305|., |FRAME: CPD-9726 MK-4| is present in photosystem I (PSI) of the cyanobacteria |FRAME: TAX-33072| and |FRAME: TAX-32049| |CITS: [15955532][15681848]|, in |FRAME: TAX-2836| (diatoms) |CITS: [18302929]| and in the primitive red alga |FRAME: TAX-2771|. It is also synthesized by the intraerythrocytic stages of |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [21036171]|.

General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms., Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (this pathway), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., About This Pathway, Certain microbes make olefinic long-chain hydrocarbons, generally C25 to C33, that contain a double bond near the middle of the chain. This class of compounds has been described both in Gram-positive bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-1270| |CITS: [6039357][6039356]| and |FRAME: TAX-43663| |CITS: [19168653]|, and in Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-40324| |CITS: [Suen88]|. One such compound, |FRAME: CPD-14238| (C31:9), has been reported from multiple members of the |FRAME: TAX-22| genus |CITS: [Nichols95][Tamaoka98][20418444]|. , The source of these hydrocarbons has been shown by carbon-14 labeling studies to derive from fatty acids |CITS: [5781029]|. The process by which these olefins are synthesized, which was initially described in 1929 |CITS: [16744199]|, is known as head-to-head hydrocarbon biosynthesis and involves the coupling of the head (C1) and the α-carbon (C2) of two fatty acids |CITS: [5785213][4390164]|. This type of reaction is known as a non-decarboxylative Claisen condensation |CITS: [ Claisen81]|., A set of four |FRAME: TAX-40324| genes involved in the pathway has been reported in patent applications filed by researchers from the LS9 company |CITS: [Friedman08]|, and was subsequently studied in |FRAME: TAX-1270| |CITS: [20038703]|, |FRAME: TAX-211586| |CITS: [20418444]|, and |FRAME: TAX-339| |CITS: [21266575][28029240][28223313]|., The key reaction in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.20| (OleA), which condenses C8-C16 fatty acyl groups via a non-decarboxylative Claisen condensation reaction to form a β-keto acid (3-oxo acid). If the β-keto acid is not quickly reduced by OleD, it spontaneously decarboxylates in aqueous solution to a ketone |CITS: [20418444]|. However, if OleD (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.412|) is present, it catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reduction of the β-keto acid intermediate to produce a β-hydroxy acid that is significantly more stable than the β-keto acid |CITS: [21958090]|. The next enzyme, |FRAME: EC-6.1.3.1|(OleC), reacts with the product of OleD to generate a thermally labile β-lactone, and is the first β-lactone synthetase to be described |CITS: [28029240]|. While The β-lactone can undergo a spontaneous decarboxylation to an olefin in vitro, the reaction is catalyzed in vivo by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.114| (OleB) |CITS: [28029240]|., The OleB, OleC, and OleD proteins form a multiprotein complex |CITS: [28223313]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-17304 "Okenone"| is a red carotenoid pigment. Structurally this ketocarotenoid has a χ-ring at one end and an open chain ψ-end that is methoxylated at the C-1' position and contains a keto group at the C-4' position. It is found in some purple sulfur bacterial members of the family |FRAME: TAX-1046|. These photosynthetic organisms reside in illuminated anoxic zones of aquatic habitats. Purple sulfur bacteria are anaerobic or microaerophilic, oxidizing |FRAME: HS| to produce granules of |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| (elemental sulfur) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5274|). The light absorption properties of |FRAME: CPD-17304| allow these bacteria to exist in deeper water layers. In addition to its role in bacterial ecology, |FRAME: CPD-17304| also becomes an important geochemical biomarker via its diagenesis product |FRAME: CPD-17311|, which is found in ancient rock formations ( |CITS: [BROCKSJJ05]| and in |CITS: [21921032][22070388]|., |FRAME: TAX-572262| is a purple sulfur bacterium that synthesizes |FRAME: CPD-17304| as its only carotenoid when grown anoxically under chlorophototrophic conditions. A gene cluster encoding the enzymes for |FRAME: CPD-17304| biosynthesis (genes crtE, crtB, crtI, crtC, crtU and crtY and an unlinked gene crtF) was identified and analyzed. The biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-17304| was elucidated based on heterologous expression of recombinant enzymes in carotenoid-producing hosts, followed by carotenoid analysis |CITS: [21921032][22070388]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway CrtY was shown to catalyze the cyclization of one ψ-end of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| producing the β-ring of |FRAME: CPD1F-126|. The CrtC hydratase hydrates the double bond of the ψ-end group of |FRAME: CPD1F-126| producing |FRAME: CPD-11446|. CruO is a unique C-4/4' ketolase required for |FRAME: CPD-17304| biosynthesis that introduces a keto group at the C-4' position of |FRAME: CPD-11446|. CrtF is an O-methyltransferase that further modifies the ψ-end group by transfer of a methyl group to the hydroxyl formed by CrtC, producing the methoxy group of |FRAME: CPD-17302|. Finally, the β-ring of |FRAME: CPD-17302| is converted to a χ-ring and the molecule is further desaturated by the carotene desaturase/methyltransferase CrtU to produce |FRAME: CPD-17304|. The key enzymes of the pathway are CrtY and CrtU |CITS: [21921032][22070388]|., In addition, a putative |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE|-dependent pathway for |FRAME: CPD-17307| biosynthesis involving genes crtC, cruS and crtF was also proposed (not shown), based on the demonstration of these enzymatic functions in Escherichia coli. However, no physiological evidence for the pathway could be found in either |FRAME: TAX-572262| or |FRAME: TAX-244573|. The novel gene cruS was shown to encode a unique 2-ketolase/3,4-desaturase that could participate in the hypothetical pathway |CITS: [21921032]|.

Summary: This pathway is found in several sulfur-oxidizing organisms, including the facultative chemolithotroph |FRAME: TAX-921| and the acidophilic thiobacilli, as well as in some heterotrophic bacteria |CITS: [27573649]|. Acidithiobacilii are prominent bacteria that catalyse the oxidation of inorganic sulfur compounds under acidic conditions (pH 1 to 3) and ambient temperatures. Important members include the Acidithiobacillus and Acidiphilium spp., which can grow chemolithoautotrophically with sulfide, elemental sulfur, thiosulfate or polythionates |CITS: [9828441][10758854]|., Earlier work by Sugio et al concluded that |FRAME: TAX-920| possesses a sulfur dioxygenase capable of using |FRAME: HS| as substrate |CITS: [3667519][Sugio89][16348640]|. However, in a later study conducted by Rohwerder and Sand |CITS: [12855721]| it was shown that cell-free systems from several members of the |FRAME: TAX-119977| and |FRAME: TAX-522| oxidized sulfide only via |FRAME: CPD-11281| (GSSH), a non-enzymic reaction product from |FRAME:OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE| (GSSG) and |FRAME: HS|., The enzyme that oxidizes the sulfur, the periplasmic |FRAME:CPLX-7137|, cannot accept either elemental sulfur or |FRAME: HS|, and is specific for  the sulfane sulfur of monoorganylpolysulfanes (RS<sub>n</sub>H, where n>1),, and predominantly persulfides (where n=2), which is oxidized to sulfite in the presence of molecular oxygen and water., Organic persulfides such as |FRAME: CPD-11281| could not be replaced by other sulfane-sulfur-containing compounds (thiosulfate, polythionates, bisorganylpolysulfanes or monoarylthiosulfonates) as sulfur donor., These results provided a new interpretation for the earliest results of Sugio et al.(1989). The assay in Sugio's work required 8 mM of glutathione for activity, and is likely to have contained |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE| due to autoxidation |CITS: [12855721]|., Much later work has demonstrated how the pathway also involves another sulfide-oxidizing enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.8.5.4|(see |FRAME:P222-PWY|). That enzyme forms polysulfides. However, the polysulfides react with glutathione to produce GSSH, which is then metabolized by  |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.18|. Rhodanese activity speeds up the reaction between the polysulfides and glutathione |CITS: [27573649]|., The product of the sulfur dioxygenase activity was shown to be |FRAME:SO3|, which is subsequently oxidized to |FRAME:SULFATE| |CITS: [5142118][Nakamura95][deJong2000]|. Alternatively, sulfite can react spontaneously with polysulfides to generate |FRAME: S2O3| |CITS: [27573649]|., For a discussion of elemental sulfur oxidation by this system, see |FRAME:SULFUROX-PWY|.

Summary: The product of the |FRAME: AT4G26850| gene (named for Vitamin C defficiency) has been originally classified as GDP-L-galactose phosphorylase. However, the term was misleading for several reasons. First, the enzyme can accept |FRAME: GDP-D-GLUCOSE| just as efficiently as |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE|. Secondly, multiple sugar 1-phosphates, such as |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P|, |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, and |FRAME: GALACTOSE-1P|, are actually better guanylyl acceptors than phosphate. Thus the enzyme is better described as |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.69| |CITS: [17485667][17877701]|., When acting on |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE|, the enzyme's activity leads to formation of |FRAME: CPDQT-4|, which is intermediate in the main |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis pathway in plants (see |FRAME: PWY-882|). The gualylyltransferase activity allows the enzyme to utilize |FRAME: GLC-1-P| and |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P| as phosphate sources., |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis usually starts with |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|, which can be produced from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| in several steps as described in |FRAME: PWY-5659|. However, due to the |FRAME: AT4G26850| enzyme |FRAME: CPDQT-4| can be formed in different ways using the so called |FRAME: PWY4FS-12| and |FRAME: PWY4FS-13|, bypassing the need for |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| production from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|. The importance of VTC2 is clear since Arabidopsis double mutants of |FRAME: AT4G26850|/|FRAME: AT5G55120| are seedling lethal (they can be rescued by supplementation with L-galactose; |FRAME: AT5G55120| is a minor form of the enzyme with similar activity but considerably lower expression) |CITS:[17877701]|., The VTC2 cycle incorporates two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.69| (VTC2) and |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.18| (GME). GME can restore |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|, thus enabling VTC2 to continue to produce |FRAME: CPDQT-4| |CITS: [17485667]|., The |FRAME: PWY4FS-13| takes into account the activity of VTC2 with the very abundant |FRAME: GLC-1-P| (derived from photosynthesis) as the guanylyl acceptor, driving production of |FRAME: CPDQT-4| and thus L-ascorbate production. The product of such a reaction, |FRAME: GDP-D-GLUCOSE|, strongly inhibits |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.18|. Thus the authors speculated that another enzyme, a putative GDP-D-mannose 2"-epimerase, catalyzes its conversion to |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. The conversion of the "toxic" |FRAME: GDP-D-GLUCOSE| by the extended VTC2 cycle makes the extended pathway more favorable than the original |FRAME: PWY4FS-12| (reviewed in |CITS:[17950389]|).

General Background, Betalains are water-soluble, chromo-alkaloid pigments that replace the , anthocyanins in most families of the Caryophyllales order |CITS: [16212790]|. Except for the families , Caryophyllaceae and Molluginacea the two subclasses of betalains, i.e. betacyanins and betaxanthins , dominate that order and provide violet and yellow cues to flowers, fruits and vegetative tissues, respectively , |CITS: [12620337]| |CITS: [16669781]|. Betaxanthins have also been shown to emit green fluorescence which creates contrasting flower color patterns and might serve as signal or guide for pollinators |CITS:[16163341]|. The mutual exclusion of betalains and anthocyanins makes this compound class a useful chemotaxonomic criterion to differentiate families within the Caryophyllales order |CITS: [13831375]|. It appears that both pigment pathways may originate from common ancestors as an anthocyanin like regulator, i.e. MYB1 was identified in Beta vulgaris being able to up- or downregulate betalain biosynthesis |CITS:[25436858]|. The MYB1 in Beta vulgaris has been discussed as being acquired at the time when both pigment pathways were splitting up and is regarded an exciting example for an transcription factor being co-opted out of an existing anthocyanin pathway to regulate the very different betalain pathway instead |CITS:[25547597] [Gerritsen15]|., Those pigments have also been identified in a restricted number of basidiomycetes such as in the genera , Amanita and Hygrocybe. No betacyanin pigments have been found in those fungi but the biosynthesis of , several betaxanthin compounds along with other derivatives of betalamic acid such as muscaflavin and , muscapurpurin has been established |CITS: [MUELLER97A]|. However, their physiological role in fungi , remains completely unknown |CITS: [12620337]|., The term 'betalain' had been coined by Wohlpart and Mabry |CITS: [16656788]| to point out the derivation , of these pigments from betalamic acid. Although similar in function to the anthocyanins, betalains are , structural diverse compounds biosynthesized in a different way. , Betalains are induced after pathogenic attacks and wounding |CITS: [STEDDOM03]| and are biosynthetically , influenced by light through competing pathways |CITS: [ENDRESS84]|. Betalains are compounds that have , found use as colorants in the food industry, the horticultural sector or the agroscience industry |CITS: [11087483]| , |CITS: [Stintzing00]|. , Recently, they have been considered as potential antioxidants which effectuated intensified corresponding research , addressing certain oxidative stress-related disorders in humans |CITS: [11714300]| |CITS: [12405794]| |CITS: [12868496]|., About This Pathway, The central intermediate for both betacyanin (|FRAME:PWY-5399|) and betaxanthin , biosynthesis (|FRAME:PWY-5404|, |FRAME:PWY-5403|, |FRAME:PWY-5426|) is betalamic acid which derives , from 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (DOPA) |CITS:[20467875]|. The key-enzyme, i.e. the extradiol ring-opening DOPA-4,5-dioxygenase (DODA) catalyzes the formation of 4,5-seco-DOPA in plants which is, in a consecutive reaction, spontaneously converted to the chromophore betalamic acid |CITS: [14730069]|. The common or sugar beet Beta vulgaris is one of the oldest known and richest sources of betalain |CITS:[Keller36]| and was used to identify and biochemically characterize the 4,5-DOPA dioxygenase extradiol encoded by the gene DODA |CITS:[22270561]|. In fungi this enzyme also catalyzes the 2,3-extradiol cleavage of DOPA that produces muscaflavin, indicating a case of convergent evolution of this enzyme |CITS: [Mueller97]| |CITS: [MUELLER97A]|., DOPA may be synthesized through two different pathways from L-tyrosine involving either a bifunctional , tyrosinase |CITS: [Steiner99]| or a tyrosine hydroxylase that requires pteridin cofactors for its activity, the , latter representing a new enzyme reported for this reaction |CITS: [Yamamoto01]|.

Summary: |FRAME: HEME_O "Heme o"| and |FRAME: HEME_A "heme a"| are key compounds of the aerobic respiration in mitochondria and bacteria and used for the dioxygen reduction site of the heme-copper terminal oxidases (e.g. |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.9| and |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.3|). |FRAME: Heme-b "Heme b"| (protoheme IX), the product of the initial heme biosynthetic pathways, is preferred as an electron-accepting heme and used as the dioxygen reduction site only in microaerobic cytochrome bb3 and cbb3 terminal oxidases., Both |FRAME: HEME_O| and |FRAME: HEME_A| carry a 17-hydroxyethylfarnesyl group at position 2 of pyrrole ring A. They differ only in a formyl group at position 8 of pyrrole ring D that is found in |FRAME: HEME_A|., Like in |FRAME: Cytochromes-B "b-type cytochromes"|, heme a is often attached to the apoprotein through a coordinate bond between the heme iron and a conserved amino acid side-chain. All known heme a-containing oxidases belong to the hemecopper superfamily of terminal oxidases |CITS: [808315]|., |FRAME: HEME_A "Heme a"| is derived from |FRAME: Heme-b| by two integral-membrane enzymes that were initially identified in bacteria, and later found in eukaryotes. The first step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.141|, consists of the addition of a farnesyl tail to the vinyl group on pyrrole ring A. This enzyme is well characterized., The second reaction, catalyzed by heme a synthase, is less well understood. The enzyme oxidizes the methyl substituent on pyrrole ring D to an aldehyde, apparently by two successive hydroxylation. The first hydroxylation forms |FRAME: Heme_I|, the second hydroxylation results in an unstable dihydroxymethyl group, which spontaneously decomposes into a formyl group and a water molecule. However, while heme a synthase is strictly dependent on molecular oxygen, the source of the oxygen atom in |FRAME: HEME_A| was shown not to be molecular oxygen. It may be derived from water, but this has not been proven, and the mechanism for such a reaction is not understood |CITS: [15236569]|. In addition, it is still unknown how electrons enter the bacterial enzyme (both a thioredoxin-like protein and menaquinol have been suggested). For a review see |CITS: [22484221]|.

General Backround, Polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME:SPERMINE|), a group of positively charged small molecules present in virtually in all living organisms, have been implicated in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [4873311][3157043][2185470][1409623]|., Although polyamines are clearly necessary for optimal cell growth, a surplus of polyamines can cause inhibition of growth and protein synthesis |CITS: [8223591]|, and thus a balance is desired between the production and breakdown of polyamines., Several metabolic pathways for the degradation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| are known., About This Pathway, This eukaryotic pathway, which involves acetylated intermediates, was discovered in mammalian brain |CITS: [4156831]|., This pathway starts with the acetylation of putrescine, followed by oxidative deamination, through |FRAME: CPD-30|, to |FRAME: CPD-35|, and subsequent transformation to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|. |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| is then fed to the GABA shunt (see |FRAME:GLUDEG-I-PWY|), by which it is degraded to succinate, and transferred to the |FRAME: TCA|., In contrast to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, which is a substrate of diamine oxidase, |FRAME: CPD-569| is deaminated by monoamine oxidase.

Summary: Bupropion is a drug in the amino ketone class that was developed for use as an antidepressant , |CITS: [22628], [6804243], [6406469]|. It is marketed as bupropion hydrochloride under the brand name Wellbutrin , (GlaxoSmithKline). Its exact mechanism of action as an antidepressant is unknown. Bupropion has also been , found to be useful in smoking cessation therapy, particularly in combination with nicotine replacement therapy and , behavioral therapy |CITS: [9378846]| (and reviewed in |CITS: [12911050]|). It is marketed for smoking cessation , therapy as bupropion hydrochloride, sustained-release formulation, under the brand name Zyban , (GlaxoSmithKline). It can block the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain and may be a brain , nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist, suggesting its use in smoking cessation therapy , (reviewed in |CITS: [12911050]|). , In humans given an oral dose of bupropion, radioimmunoassay indicated rapid absorption and appearance of the , drug in plasma. Plasma levels fall as the drug is extensively metabolized in the liver. Approximately 80% of a dose , of bupropion is excreted as metabolites in urine, with less than 1% excreted as unchanged bupropion , |CITS: [6804243], [6406469]|. Bupropion is metabolized to basic and acidic metabolites in humans. Major basic , metabolites include hydroxybupropion, and the amino alcohol isomers threohydrobupropion and , erythrohydrobupropion. Two acidic metabolites, m-chlorobenzoic acid and m-chlorohippuric acid, , have also been identified |CITS: [6406469], [3931955], [3107223]|. Differences in bupropion metabolism between , humans and animals have been described. Humans given an oral dose of 14C-bupropion excreted , relatively more basic metabolites than rats, which excreted predominantly acidic metabolites. Human plasma , contained relatively more hydroxybupropion than bupropion, while the opposite was true for rat plasma , |CITS: [3107223]|., Hydroxybupropion is the main physiologically active metabolite in humans |CITS: [3931955], [15081921]|. The , involvement of the cytochrome P450 isoform 2B6 in this hydroxylation reaction has been shown |CITS: [10997944], , [11454731]|. The formation of threohydrobupropion and erythrohydrobupropion involves modification of the , aminoketone bupropion to amino alcohols by ketone reduction |CITS: [15081921]|. The concentration of , erythrohydrobupropion in human plasma is low compared to that of the threohydrobupropion isomer , |CITS: [15081921]|. Glucuronide conjugates of threohydrobupropion and erythrohydrobupropion have been , identified |CITS: [6406469], [3107223]|. In humans given an oral dose of 14C-bupropion, an average , of 13% of the dose was excreted in urine as these glucuronides |CITS: [3107223]|., The formation of m-chlorobenzoic acid involves side chain cleavage, converting basic bupropion to an , acidic metabolite. In humans given an oral dose of 14C-bupropion, only 0.3% of the dose was , excreted in urine as m-chlorobenzoic acid |CITS: [3107223]|. This metabolite is inactive |CITS: [8830063]|. , m-Chlorohippuric acid is the glycine conjugate of m-chlorobenzoic acid. In humans given an oral , dose of 14C-bupropion, 22% of the dose was excreted in urine as m-chlorohippuric acid , |CITS: [3107223]|.

Summary: General Background, The inorganic sulfur compound |FRAME: S2O3| contains two sulfur atoms: a sulfone-sulfur (oxidation state +V), and a sulfane-sulfur (oxidation state -I). At low pH thiosulfate decomposes spontaneously to |FRAME: SO3| and elemental sulfur, |CITS: [4552952]|. At neutral pH the compound is relatively stable, but several types of bacteria can catalyze its disproportionation in a process in which thiosulfate serves as both an electron donor and an electron acceptor. , Several types of enzymes have been described that are able to catalyze the disproportionation of thiosulfate. These enzymes have been differentiated based on the nature of the electron donor: some enzymes require thiols for this purpose, some utilize cytochrome c3, which receives the electrons from molecular hydrogen via a hydrogenase, some accept the electrons from the quinone pool, and some have only been active in vitro when coupled to cyanide. These four classes of enzymes are described in the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5277|, |FRAME:PWY-5352|, |FRAME: PWY-7813|, and |FRAME:PWY-5350|, respectively., About This Pathway, Thiosulfate sulfurtransferase is more often referred to by the name rhodanese, from the German word for thiocyanate, "rhodanid". The enzyme catalyzes the transfer of a sulfur atom from suitable sulfur donors to nucleophilic sulfur acceptors. The original description of rhodanese, purified from bovine mitochondria, used thiosulfate and cyanide for this purpose., Rhodanese is a widespread enzyme, and has been detected in many major phyla, both prokaryotic and eukaryotic |CITS: [6357923]|., Despite its ubiquity, the physiological role of rhodanese has not yet been established unambiguously. It has been suggested that rhodanese is involved in detoxification of cyanide in both mammals |CITS: [3073057][10762072]| and bacteria |CITS: [18685272]|. It has also been proposed that rhodanese, using the dithiol |FRAME:CPD-296| as the sulfur acceptor, may act as a sulfur insertase involved in the formation of iron-sulfur clusters in proteins such as ferredoxin |CITS: [6430704][2983992]|., Rhodanese performs the reaction by a double displacement formal mechanism. The crystal structure of rhodanese from |FRAME: TAX-354| has been determined at 1.8 Å, and the study revealed that the active form of the enzyme contains a persulfide, where a sulfur is attached to the active cysteine residue |CITS: [10788330]|., Monothiols such as glutathione have been reported to be poor substrates for rhodanese |CITS: [14086740][5333153][10735872]|. However, more recent work has suggested that at least some rhodanese enzymes utilize glutathione as their major sulfur receipient |CITS: [37237993]|., The distinction between thiosulfate reductase and rhodanese is not always straight forward. For example, Aird et al purified an enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-471| that could catalyze either reaction under different conditions |CITS: [3480285]|.

General Background, Most pathogenic bacteria have an absolute requirement for iron, which is scarce within their host environment. In vertebrates the majority of the iron is found in the form of heme. Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. In general, the bacteria express outer membrane proteins that bind heme compounds, extract heme from them, and transport the heme into the cell, where it is degraded to release the iron |CITS: [1425573][7783623][9157245]|. The most common heme-degradation systems utilize heme oxygenase enzymes that degrade heme to yield iron, carbon monoxide, and biliverdin., Several forms of bacterial heme oxygenases are known, and they are described in the various heme degradation pathways in MetaCyc. The enzymes consume three molecules of oxygen and a total of seven electron equivalents to break the tetrapyrrole ring and liberate the iron. However, while some enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), others produce different unusual isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| (|FRAME: PWY-7844|), |FRAME: CPD-18928| (|FRAME: PWY-7843|), |FRAME: CPD-19710| (|FRAME: PWY-7846|), |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| (|FRAME: PWY-7847|) and |FRAME: CPD-19716| and |FRAME: CPD-19715| (|FRAME: PWY-7848|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-287| possesses two heme oxygenase enzymes. The enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-54979| gene produces |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), and the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-54978| gene produces the unusual isomers |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714|., The |FRAME: G-54978| gene, which is part of a five-gene operon (pigA-E), is under the control of the global iron regulator Fur (ferric uptake regulator) and is only expressed under iron-limiting conditions |CITS: [10564483]|. The unusual production of |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| was shown to be due to a rotated positioning of the heme substrate in the active site pocket |CITS: [12475329][15122889]|. The fate of these products is currently unknown.

Summary: General Background, Linamarin is a cyanogenic glucoside found in the following plant families: Compositae, Euphorbiaceae, Linaceae, Papaveraceae and Fabaceae. The hydrolysis or cyanogensis of linamarin as well as other cyanogenic glycosides, releases hydrogen cyanide (HCN). HCN is highly toxic. It plays an important role in protecting plants from pathogen attacks. In addition to its role in defense, HCN has been proposed to be involved in seed germination of a few , species. The toxic effects from feeding on linamarin or other cyanogenic glycoside-containg plants by animals and human beings have also been broadly reported. , About This Pathway, Converting linamarin to hydrogen cyanide involves two steps: deglucosylation of linamarin (EC 3.2.1.21) and cleavage of acetone cyanohydrin (EC 4.1.2.37). The first reaction is catalyzed by a β-glucosidase, linamarase. It is generally assumed to be the rate-limiting step. The second reaction, breakdown acetone cyanohydrin, can occur both enzymatically catalyzed by a hydroxynitrile lyase and spontaneously at temperatures above 35 oC or at pH above 4.0.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamin diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamin-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamin is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., Thiamin biosynthesis is composed of the separate formation of the pyrimidine and thiazole moieties, which are subsequently coupled to form |FRAME: THIAMINE-P| (see |FRAME: PWY-6894|)., About This Pathway, This pathway describes only the synthesis of the thiazole moiety of thiamin. Different variations of this pathway exist, this particular pathway describes a pathway that was studied in |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-90371|. , The biosynthesis of the thiazole moiety is complex. In |FRAME:TAX-562| it involves six proteins, the products of the |FRAME: G1|, |FRAME: EG11587|, |FRAME: EG11589|, |FRAME: EG11590|, |FRAME: G6238|, and |FRAME: G7325| genes. , The process begins when |FRAME: CPLX0-248 IscS|, a protein that is also involved in the biosynthesis of iron-sulfur clusters, catalyzes the transfer of a sulfur atom from cysteine to |FRAME:Sulfur-Carrier-Proteins-ThiI|, generating a |FRAME: Sulfurylated-ThiI|., In a parallel route, the |FRAME: ThiF-Proteins "ThiF protein"| activates |FRAME: Thi-S| by adenylation of its carboxy terminus, generating |FRAME:Adenylated-ThiS-Proteins|. In a second reaction, which may also be catalyzed by ThiF, the sulfur from |FRAME: Sulfurylated-ThiI| is transferred to ThiS, generating |FRAME: ThiS-CoASH-proteins|., The final reaction of this pathway, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: THIG-MONOMER| protein, requires three inputs: |FRAME: ThiS-CoASH-proteins|, |FRAME: DEOXYXYLULOSE-5P| and |FRAME: CPD-12279|., |FRAME: CPD-12279| is formed in |FRAME:TAX-562| from |FRAME: TYR| by |FRAME: THIH-MONOMER| (ThiH), which forms a complex with |FRAME: THIG-MONOMER| |CITS:[9632726][11438688][16388576]|. , For many years the products of this reaction was assumed to be |FRAME: THZ| (thiazole). However, recent work performed with the thiazole synthase from |FRAME: TAX-1423| has shown that the actual product is the thiazole tautomer |FRAME: CPD-13575| |CITS: [19216519]|. While in Bacillus a dedicated |FRAME: BSU11660-MONOMER| converts this product into a different tautomer (|FRAME: CPD-13576|), most of the proteobacteria lack the tautomerase.

Summary: Microcins are a class of gene-encoded low-molecular-mass antibacterial peptides secreted by bacteria. They are ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified. Microcins produced by commensal |FRAME: TAX-562| strains target and eliminate enteric pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-28901| at nanomolar concentrations |CITS: [17827970]|. , Microcin C, originally named microcin 7 |CITS: [6370248][2861788]| and often referred to as microcin C7, is a heptapeptide produced by |FRAME: TAX-562| with an N-formylated methionine and a C-terminal phosphoramidate linkage to adenosine, modified with an aminopropyl moiety |CITS: [7559516]|., Microcin C is exported from producing cells through a major facilitator superfamily efflux pump encoded by the |FRAME: G-124166| gene. It is imported by target cells via the |FRAME: ABC-41-CPLX "inner membrane transporter YejABEF"|, which recognizes the peptide part of the microcin |CITS: [17873039][21855353]|. Following import, the peptide is cleaved by non-specific peptidases, releasing |FRAME: CPD-25930|, a toxic |FRAME: CPD0-915| mimic that targets |FRAME: EC-6.1.1.12|, inhibiting protein synthesis |CITS: [16574659]|., The genes encoding biosynthesis of microcin C7 are located on the single-copy plasmid pMccC7 (previously named pRYC7 |CITS: [6370248][3536876]|. The |FRAME: CPD-25924 "microcin C7 precursor peptide"| is encoded by the 21-bp mccA gene, the shortest bacterial gene known |CITS: [8183363]|., Most of the activities during the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD0-1129| are catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-85398|. Despite its relatively small size (39 kDa), the enzyme catalyzes a remarkable posttranslational modification of the MccA heptapeptide., MccB starts its reaction with the adenylation of MccA's C-terminal |FRAME: ASN|. The resulting MccA-adenylate undergoes intramolecular rearrangement, during which AMP is expelled by the carboxamido nitrogen of Asn, forming a peptidyl-succinimide intermediate. Next, MccB catalyzes a aecond adenylation - a very unusual adenylation of the succinimide in which the succinimidyl nitrogen attacks the α-phosphate of a second ATP molecule. This links the AMP moiety to the peptide terminus through an N-P bond. The succinimide ring is then hydrolyzed, yielding a peptidyl-aspartyl-N-P-adenosine group |CITS: [19494832]|., Unlike normal acyl-adenylate complexes, which are hydrolytically labile, the phosphoramidate-linked analogue of the aspartic acyl-adenylate is resistant to hydrolysis, and results in the eventual toxic inhibition of aspartyl-tRNA synthetase and protein synthesis in competing bacteria |CITS: [19494832]|., The transformations catalyzed by MccB are followed with aminopropylation, which proceeds in two sequential steps. In the first step, MccD uses |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as a donor in a sulfur to oxygen 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl group transfer. In the second step MccE catalyzes a decarboxylation reaction |CITS: [19168611][ 25026542]|., MccE is a bifunctional fusion protein. While the N-terminal domain participates in biosynthesis as described above, the C-terminal domain is involved in protection. Unwanted processing of intact microcin can result in formation of the active |FRAME: CPD-25930| witihin the producing cell and self-toxicity. In order to protect the producing cell from the toxic affects, the processed compound is acetylated at the amino group by the C-terminal domain of the |FRAME: G-124164 "MccE protein"|, resulting in its inactivation |CITS: [20159968][21507941]|.

Summary: The rates of oxidation and reduction of NAD and NADH must be balanced for the continuation of both catabolism and, anabolism. NADH, produced in the cytosol during glycolysis, need to be oxidized to NAD+., The net NADH oxidation process in the cell occurs primarily via mitochondrial respiration. However, NADH , cannot traverse the inner mitochondrial membrane |CITS: [16661409]|. Therefore, cytosolic reducing equivalents must, be transferred to the mitochondria through metabolite shuttles that operate between the two compartments., One such shuttle is the |FRAME: PWY-6118| (G3P shuttle). , This shuttle involves the combined actions of a |FRAME: CPLX-7723| (EC 1.1.1.8) and a FAD-dependent, |FRAME: CPLX-7724| (EC 1.1.5.3)., The cytosolic enzyme consumes NADH during the conversion of |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| to, |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|, which can pass through the permeable mitochondrial outer membrane., |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| is then reoxidized to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| at the outer surface of the, inner mitochondrial membrane by the mitochondrial FAD-dependent enzyme, which donates the electrons to the, mitochondrial quinone pool. The |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| is subsequently channeled back to, the cytosol., The shuttle operates in yeast |CITS: [9171333][9559543]|, animals and plants |CITS: [16415206]|.

Summary: Acylsugars such as acylglucose |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| and acylsucrose metabolites (this pathway and summarized in |FRAME:PWY18C3-12 superpathway of acylsucrose biosynthesis (cultivated tomato)|) are produced in glandular trichomes of and confined to plants of the Solanaceae family |CITS:[2652002]|. Acylsugars have been demonstrated to act as broad-spectrum insecticides |CITS:[Maluf10] [Leckie12]|, interact with phytohormones to fend off aphids and whiteflies |CITS:[21068365]|, and interfere with feeding behaviors of the peach aphid |CITS:[Rodriguez93]| and larvae from major pests (beet armyworm, corn earworm) of cultivated tomatoes |CITS:[Juvic94]|. Remarkably, acylsugars are also often first food for pest larvae which then emit distinctive volatiles allowing predators of those larvae to locate their prey |CITS:[21518882]|. In addition, acylsugars have commercial value as unobjectionable additives to food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical products |CITS:[Hill99]|., Specific glandular trichomes found in the nightshade family have been the focus of research for some time because of their ability to produce and excrete specialized metabolites involved in defense and signaling pathways |CITS:[3138948] [16664099]|. The wide occurrence and diversity of acylsucrose and acylglucose compounds is typifying for the genus Solanum |CITS:[20113441]| and has promoted the elucidation of underlying pathways and genes |CITS:[Leckie14]| by generating ingression lines with species possessing acylsugars of unique acylation patterns |CITS:[24772058]|. The broad variability of acylated sucrose is particularly obvious in wild species of Solanum (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)| and |FRAME:PWY18C3-16 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum habrochaites)|) and appears to be associated with geographical locations |CITS:[Shapiro94] [23054567]|. The high variability of acyl groups on either the pyranose or furanose moiety of the |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold appears to result from the biosyntheses of branched-chain amino acid pathways that give rise to the respective acyl-donors |CITS:[2318213] [12687369] [18931142] [25986128]|. , The catalyzing enzymes for the versatile decoration of acylsucrose metabolites found in the Solaneceae family are BAHD acyltransferases |CITS:[16616872]| which have undergone structural changes resulting in genetic variations which accept and process various acyl groups of varying length as suitable substrates at specific ring positions |CITS:[25862303]| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-10 triacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|). The formation of monoacylated sucrose metabolites (this pathway) is the first step in the biosynthetic path towards tri- and tetraacyl sucroses (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-11 tetraacylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum)|) usually found in cultivated tomatoes |CITS:[24772058]|. , A functional genomics approach was used to identify genes encoding for potential acyltransferases of the BAHD family in Solanum lycopersicum and Solanum pennellii. Metabolic profiling of RNAi silenced Solanum lycopersicum plants indicated the gene ASAT1 (Solyc12g006330) as the acyltransferase involved in the first acylation step because no acylsucrose intermediates usually decorated with up to four acyl-groups have been detected in those RNAi silenced plants |CITS:[26715757]|. The use of transformed (RNAi) Solanum lycopersicum plants and biochemical assays confirmed that ASAT1 encoded for an acyltransferase that catalyzed the first acylation of |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| with a variety of acyl-CoA's. It was shown that ASAT1 of Solanum lycopersicum and its ortholog in Solanum pennellii was able to monoacylate |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| at the 4-position of the pyranose ring with |FRAME:ISOBUTYRYL-COA isobutanoyl-CoA| to form |FRAME:CPD-19017 sucrose-4-isobutanoate|, with |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA isovaleryl-CoA| forming |FRAME:CPD-19018 sucrose-4-isovalerate|, with |FRAME:2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA 2-methylbutanoyl-CoA| generating |FRAME:CPD-19019 sucrose-4-(2-methyl)butanoate|, using |FRAME:CPD-10267 decanoyl-CoA| to form |FRAME:CPD-19020 sucrose-4-decanoate| and finally utilizing |FRAME:LAUROYLCOA-CPD lauroyl-CoA| to form |FRAME:CPD-19021 sucrose mono-4-lauroate|. The latter, i.e. |FRAME:LAUROYLCOA-CPD lauroyl-CoA| was also found to inhibit the acylation reaction with increasing substrate concentration |CITS:[26715757]|.

The fungal genus Fusarium combines many species which colonize more than 100 species of plants as either pathogens or endophytes and are known to cause health threatening infections in animals and humans (Leslie06). More than 50 families of secondary metabolites have been found to be produced from Fusarium species |CITS[Desjardins06] [Glenn07]|, amongst them the polyketide-derived |FRAME:CPD-18031| which can be produced by a number of species across the Fusarium genus |CITS:[8899996]|. |FRAME:CPD-18031 Fusaric acid| and congeners have been associated with many plant related diseases and negative physiological incidents such as wilting and leaf chlorosis in banana |CITS:[ 24282097] [23922960]| and tomato |CITS:[Capasso96]|, general phytotoxicity in cotton |CITS:[20955724] [Gaumann57]| and inducing programmed cell death in tobacco |CITS:[23838885]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-18031| has been reported to inhibit the |FRAME:CPD-18045| (DAPG) production which is the main compound contributing to the antimicrobial activity of the biocontrol strain Pseudomonas fluorescens |CITS:[11976092]|. It also was found to inhibit dopamine-β-hydroxylase causing hypotensive effects in animals |CITS:[5811396]| which appears to be mediated via brain alteration and pineal neurotransmitter interference |CITS:[7542129]|. , On the other side, |FRAME:CPD-18031| has also been linked to useful pharmacological properties (summarized in |CITS:[10465344]|) such as exhibiting acanthamoebicidal |CITS:[22864988]|, antioomycete |CITS:[17927749]| and antimycobacterial activities |CITS:[21811925]|. At nontoxic concentration |FRAME:CPD-18031| was also shown to inhibit the germination of the angiosperm parasite Orobanche ramose, hence acting in a biocontrol capacity |CITS:[16673942]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-18031| exhibits cytotoxicity towards various human cancer cell lines |CITS:[8476229]| and inhibits the HIV-1 transactivator protein tat indicating a therapeutic potential for the treatment of HIV-1 dementia |CITS:[22698778]|., Taken together, |FRAME:CPD-18031| has been regarded as an structural interesting and potentially useful compound but the elucidation of the pathway is still incomplete and not fully understood. Early feeding experiments indicated the involvement of |FRAME:ACET| |CITS:[Hill66]| which was later corroborated by feeding experiments with double labeled |FRAME:ACET|, |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME:GLN| |CITS:[21495723]|, basically pointing out the pathway to |FRAME:CPD-18031| as displayed above. The latter experiments indicated that a polyketide synthase was responsible for forming a |FRAME:CPD-18035|, which was fused to |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| mostly originating from the |FRAME:PWY-5690| via |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| and that the required nitrogen for building the N-substituted benzene ring of |FRAME:CPD-18031| stems from |FRAME:GLN| which was supported by the respective high insertion rate |CITS:[21495723]|., The sequencing of genomes from Fusarium species, e.g. Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[23825955]| allowed the identification of polyketide synthases (PKSs) and corresponding biogenetic clusters involved in |FRAME:PWY-7672|. The fusaric acid synthase encoded by FUB1 was identified and characterized by single gene deletion in Fusarium fujikurai |CITS:[24389666]|, Fusarium verticillioides |CITS:[22652150]| and Fusarium oxysporum |CITS:[25372119]| and shown to be indispensable for the production of |FRAME:CPD-18031|. Five genes had been reported to form the gene cluster in Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[24389666]| and Fusarium verticillioides |CITS:[22652150]| which was later extended to twelve genes by approach of comparative and functional genomics and microarray expression analysis |CITS:[25372119]|. Only two genes, i.e. FUB1 encoding the fusaric acid synthase and FUB4 encoding for an amino acid hydrolase had been shown to be required for biosynthesizing |FRAME:CPD-18031| in Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[24389666]| but the later analysis demonstrated the requirement of more FUB genes for an fully functional |FRAME:CPD-18031| biosynthetic pathway |CITS:[25372119]|., Interestingly, the pathway and its genes could only be induced under nitrogen-sufficient conditions and was regulated by the GATA transcription regulator AreB and the pH regulator PacC. Full expression of |FRAME:PWY-7672| genes also required the involvement of the fungal-specific velvet complex (Vel1, Lae1) |CITS:[24389666]|. Three more |FRAME:CPD-18031| related compounds have been found in Fusarium species, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18032|, |FRAME:CPD-18033| and |FRAME:CPD-18034| which have been shown to be formed enzymatically but which encoding genes do not belong to the biosynthetic cluster of |FRAME:PWY-7672| |CITS:[24389666]|. It should be pointed out that the specific precursor(s), intermediate(s) and the reaction order and respective mechanisms of the pathway forming |FRAME:CPD-18031| are still largely unknown, under ongoing investigation and remain to be elucidated.

|FRAME:CPD-14960 Kaempferide triglycoside| had been isolated as a constitutive compound in |FRAME:TAX-3570| and its chemical structure determined |CITS:[11314958]|. This flavonol glycoside was reported to be a major metabolite in the |FRAME:TAX-5506| resistant cultivars of |FRAME:TAX-3569| and shown to exhibit antifungal activities |CITS:[Curir05]| |CITS:[11314958]|. Dianthi (Fod) |CITS:[11314958]|. The activation of the pathway after the pathogen attack is probably due to the elicitable flavonoid 4'-O-methyltransferase which is involved in the metabolic sequence by producing |FRAME:CPD-7252|, an important precursor |CITS:[12899699]|. Because of the constitutive nature of |FRAME:CPD-14960| it was first thought that it represents a phytoanticipin however the escalated biosynthesis after |FRAME:TAX-5506| attack classifies it more as a phytoalexin-like compound |CITS:[Curir05]|. General Background, The TCA pathway is a catabolic pathway of mostly aerobic respiration that generates both energy and reducing power. In addition, it is also the first step in generating precursors for biosynthesis. The pathway is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]| as well as some anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [3049083][11131021]|., The typical input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, an activated form of |FRAME: ACET| that is generated by the degradation of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. A common source of acetyl-coA is |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is generated by |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| and converted to acetyl-CoA by the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|., In every turn of this variant of the TCA cycle one molecule of acetyl-CoA is converted into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, four molecules of either |FRAME: NAD|, |FRAME: NADP|, or |FRAME: Quinones quinone| are converted to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively, and one molecule of nucleotide diphosphate (ADP or GDP) is phosphorylated to nucleotide triphosphate (ATP or GTP)., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation. In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that transport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., The |FRAME: TCA| is a common variation of the pathway that occurs in many bacteria and archaea. While the pathway is most common in heterotrophic bacteria and archaea, there is evidence for its presence in some facultatively autotrophic archaea when growing under heterotrophic conditions. There are a few small differences between this common prokaryotic version of the cycle and the version found in most eukaryotes (see |FRAME: PWY-5690|).One difference is that while in most eukaryotes the conversion of |FRAME: MAL| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| is catalyzed only by the NAD-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.37|, some prokaryotes that employ this variation of the TCA cycle possess the alternative quinone-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.4|, and this is seen in the C. trachomatis |FRAME: PWY-8560|., Some organisms possess a truncated version of the TCA cycle, known as the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate cycle"|, that converts |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| to biosynthetic intermediates without the loss of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS:[6378912][3333001][3332993]|. However, this type of truncated TCA cycle is not that same as the version seen in C. trachomatis., About this C. trachomatis Pathway, The complete genome sequence of |FRAME: TAX-272561| indicated that Chlamydia likely have a partial (or truncated) TCA cycle because three canonical TCA cycle genes, citrate synthase (gltA), aconitase (acn) and isocitrate dehydrogenase (icd), appeared to be missing |CITS: [9784136]|. Because of these missing genes, the truncated TCA cycle of Chlamydia starts at |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| and ends with |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, which can feed a gluconeogenesis pathway or be converted to |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| and feed into glycolysis. |FRAME:ACETYL-COA Acetyl-CoA| does not appear to feed into the Chlamydial truncated TCA cycle, and the main input apears to be |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| which is proposed to be generated from |FRAME: GLT| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1| |CITS: [10411734][15213176][27997721][31681215]|., C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular parasitic bacterium with different developmental stages made up of the near-metabolically inert, nonreplicative elementary body (EB) and the metabolically active replicative reticulate body (RB) found only within infected host cells. It was considered an "energy parasite" that couldn't generate it's own ATP, instead relying on uptake of ATP from the host cell |CITS: [2030670][9973346]|. Although Chlamydia does use host-generated ATP, it can generate it's own ATP, as shown through gene expression and proteomics studies, with different expression of central metabolic reactions occurring in RBs compared to EBs |CITS: [10411734][12730178][26871455]|. , Conversion between the different developmental stages appears to be regulated by an Rsb phospho-regulatory pathway that interacts with |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to sense environmental conditions |CITS: [31637787]|.

Summary: General Background, Deoxyribonucleotides are synthesised de novo at the diphosphate level through reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group of the corresponding ribonucleotides (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|). This reduction is mediated by the key enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|., The de novo synthesis of ribonucleotides is very expensive, and organisms have adapted to salvage potential precursors from their environment. Since nucleotides can not be imported into the cell due to the negative charge of the phosphate groups, salvage is limited to free bases and nucleosides. , Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. It has been shown that in quiescent or terminally differentiated mammalian cells, resting in the G0 phase, ribonucleotide reductase is not produced due to a block during transcription and the cells rely on salvage for deoxyribonucleotides for DNA repair |CITS: [3044582][1696835]|. Similarly, the salvage pathway is the sole provider of deoxyribonucleotides to be used in DNA repair or mitochondrial DNA replication in G1 cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|., The deoxyribonucleosides enter through the cell membrane by facilitated diffusion via a low affinity, high capacity, non-concentrative nucleoside carrier protein with a wide specificity, possessed by almost all animal cells |CITS: [3048401]|. The next step in the salvage pathway is the phosphorylation of the nucleosides to monophosphates. Once phosphorylation occurs, the nucleotides are trapped intracellularly due to their negative charge., About This Pathway, As shown in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7199|, the deoxyribonucleosides are imported into the cell and phosphorylated by deoxyribonucleoside kinases at the 5' position. The monophosphates are then phosphorylated further to form the triphosphates that are required for DNA synthesis, as described in this pathway. , |FRAME: TMP| is phosphorylated to the diphosphate form by a specific |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.9 "dTMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.9)"|, while |FRAME: DCMP| is phosphorylated in eukaryotes by the |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.14 "bifunctional UMP/CMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.14)"| and in prokaryotes by a dedicated |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.25 "(d)CMP kinase (EC 2.7.4.25)"|., Both diphosphates, |FRAME: DUDP| and |FRAME: DCDP|, are phosphorylated to the triphosphate forms by the broad-substrate range |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.6 "nucleoside-diphosphate kinase (EC 2.7.4.6)"|.

Summary: Malonyl glucosides have been frequently overlooked due to their lability and inadequate isolation procedures. Numerous , N-and O-malonyl conjugates have been reported in different plant species, including isoflavones, isoflavanones and , isoflavonoids but also xenobiotics, D-amino acids and the ethylene precursor 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid. , The latter are considered to be detoxification products |CITS: [6497385]|, whereas the former may serve as pools for , the release of free aglycons. Released isoflavones can be either incorporated into the biosynthetic pathway of phytoalexins, or act as phytoanticipins |CITS: [11730862]|. , The finding that isoflavone conjugates are sometimes constitutively present in considerable amounts in legumes , |CITS: [Graham91]|, support such a possible role as preformed toxins (phytoanticipins)., Glucosides and malonyl glucosides of isoflavones, such as biochanin A and formononetin and further metabolic derivatives , (e.g. cicerin, medicarpin) are exclusively located in the vacuole |CITS: [Mackenbrock92]|and it has been speculated, that , acylation of these compounds could precede and facilitate their transport through the tonoplast |CITS: [6639051]|.

Summary: General Background, Leucodelphinidin is a colorless intermediate in the biosynthesis of the corresponding colored anthocyanin delphinidin 3-O-glucoside and derivatives thereof (|FRAME:PWY-5153|) |CITS: [12828368][14719829]|. Leucoanthocyanidins in general are compounds at a branch-point embedded in that metabolic sequence and represent an important regulatory point to feed a range of flavonoid subclasses of diverse biological properties |CITS: [11402179]|., The occurrence of delphinidin-type pigments in the plant kingdom has been found widespread, namely in plant families such as Gentianacea, Geraniacea, |FRAME:TAX-4747| and Solanacea |CITS: [ANDERSEN06]|. , Special attention to explore the underlying pathways has been paid to the genus Petunia which is a widely-cultivated , flowering plant with a broad range of flower colors |CITS: [SINK84]| |CITS: [WIERING84]| |CITS: [15587706]|. Leucodelphinidin which has a trihydroxylated B-ring gives rise to anthocyanins adding blue colors to a broad variety of plants |CITS: [11287230]|., About This Pathway, The dihydroflavonol central to leucodelphinidin biosynthesis and the delphinidin derived anthocyanins is dihydromyricetin. The complete, trifold hydroxylation of the flavonoid B-ring to form dihydromyricetin can be catalyzed via various intermediates, such as dihydrokaempferol, dihydroquercetin and eriodictyol. , The most important enzyme involved in the B-ring hydroxylation is the flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylase |CITS: [8232589]| , |CITS: [10476065]| |CITS: [10567704]|. The enzyme may successively hydroxylate naringenin and dihydrokaempferol , at the 3' and 5'-position to form 5,7,3',4',5'-pentahydroxyflavanone and dihyromyricetin, respectively. However, , intermediate substrates already hydroxylated at the 3'-position such as dihydroquercetin and eriodictyol are also accepted by the enzyme for 5'-hydroxylation and may constitute a prerequisite for this step |CITS: [10476065]|. It has been demonstrated that a cytochrome b5, presumably involved in the regulation of the flavonoid 3',5'-hydroxylase activity is necessary for the full color development of 3',5'-hydroxylated pigments |CITS: [9892710]|. Other factors, namely copigments such as phenolic acids |CITS: [12452676]|, flavones and flavonols |CITS: [11164576]| are also involved in the stability and increase of color intensity., The flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase and the flavanone 3β-hydroxylase are modifying enzymes of this pathway which either specifically hydroxylate the B-ring 3'-position |CITS: [10504566]| or catalyze the conversion of flavanones to dihydroflavonols |CITS: [Forkmann80]| |CITS: [2154946]|. Although experimental evidence on the conversion of pentahydroxyflavanone to dihydromyrcetin is still missing the reaction is believed to occur |CITS: [8232589]| |CITS: [10567704]| |CITS: [11287230]|., The discernible step in the biosynthetic route towards leucoanthocyanidins is the stereospecific reduction of (2R,3R)-dihydroflavonols carried out by dihydroflavonol 4-reductase (DFR). The enzyme generally exhibits a pronounced substrate specificity which determines a visible pattern of anthocyanins, catechins and proanthocyanidins indicative for certain species |CITS: [12435592]|. However, other species such as |FRAME:TAX-101596| possess DFR's that are able to use a broad varieties of substrates including the three dihydroflavonols |CITS: [3293532]|.

Summary: The indole-diterpene mycotoxin |FRAME:CPD-17202| is produced by epichloid fungi, i.e. the symbiotic fungus Epichloe festucae and asexual endophytic fungi of the form genus Neotyphodium which infect cool-season grasses such as the important forage perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne) |CITS:[11495800]|. |FRAME:CPD-17202 Lolitrem B| is a tremorgenic compound |CITS:[3912307]| that causes the so-called ryegrass staggers in sheep and cattle |CITS:[22913513] [23721156] [22913546]|. The intoxicating impact of |FRAME:CPD-17202| has been shown on the cellular level as interference with K(+) and Ca(2+) channels |CITS:[23134178] [21300077]| but the entire scope of |FRAME:CPD-17202| implications remains to be demonstrated., , However, as symbionts of the grasses those mycotoxins primarily confer bioprotective and psychoactive properties which deter insects and mammalian herbivores and consequently benefit their host plants |CITS:[Schardl09] [24233445]|. Fungal secondary metabolites have influenced the human society significantly as pharmaceuticals and/or facilitator for research on pathogenic interactions with plants and animals |CITS:[18973828]| and are even involved in signaling pathways |CITS:[20507448]| and regulation of developmental processes |CITS:[18280128]|. The epichloid fungi produced anti-herbivore alkaloids including the indole-diterpenoid |FRAME:CPD-17202| display a broad range of chemotypic diversity which may reflect adaption to special environmental circumstances and defense response to herbivores |CITS:[Schardl12] [18262778]| emphasizing the dynamics and structural variation of alkaloids biosynthesized in such species |CITS:[23468653]|., , Research on |FRAME:PWY-7572| revealed the existence of three biosynthetic gene clusters involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-17202| |CITS:[15991026] [16765617] [19181837]|. Some of the genes in those clusters have been shown to be functional orthologues of genes involved in the biosynthesis of the neurotoxic mycotoxin |FRAME:CPD-16744| and derivatives (see |FRAME:PWY-7493|) |CITS:[12884010] [17428785]|. The molecular function of genes from all three lolitrem (ltm) clusters uniquely involved in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17202| have been determined through mutant analysis and heterologous expression of Epichloe festuca genes in the host Penicillium paxilli |CITS:[22750140]|. The entrance compound into the |FRAME:PWY-7572| is |FRAME:CPD-16741| (see |FRAME:PWY-7492|) which is sequentially transformed to |FRAME:CPD-17196| by a series of oxygenations. It was shown that the various cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases encoded by LtmQ, LtmP, LtmJ and LtmK as well as the prenyltransferases encoded by LtmE and LtmF are multifunctional and catalyze a variety of substrates within the metabolic grid of |FRAME:PWY-7572|. The display of the above pathway represents one of various possibilities. Although the oxygenation of substrates catalyzed by monooxygenases encoded by LtmK and LtmJ follows the prenylation by enzymes encoded by LtmF and LtmE, respectively the general order of the intermediates remains to be verified and different metabolic outcomes appear possible in dependence of the versatility of the involved enzymes |CITS:[22750140]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD0-1385 "Perchlorate"| has been detected in numerous ground and surface waters, and has been added to the drinking water Candidate Contaminant List in the United States. Its toxicity primarily results from the fact that it inhibits thyroid hormone output by inhibiting the uptake of iodide by the thyroid gland., Perchlorate-reducing bacteria use the highly oxidized perchlorate ion as the sole electron acceptor for oxidation of organic matter |CITS: [11471705][11487102]|. The reduction of perchlorate occurs in a two-step reaction: |FRAME: CPD0-1385| reduction to |FRAME: CHLORITE| |CITS: [14717455]|, followed by the decomposition of the latter to |FRAME: CL-| ions and |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [14723936]|. The second step is one of the rare occasions where molecular oxygen is formed in a metabolic reaction [other examples include |FRAME: PWY-101 "photosynthesis"|, the detoxification of reactive oxygen species (see for example |FRAME: DETOX1-PWY|), and potentially the reaction catalyzed by "nitric oxide lyase" (see |FRAME: PWY-6523|)]., The two enzymes that catalyze perchlorate reduction, |FRAME: CPLX-8079| and |FRAME: CPLX-8078|, are periplasmic, and have been purified from several organisms |CITS: [16030201][19361444]|. Electron transport from the bacterial inner membrane to the soluble periplasmic perchlorate reductase is mediated by soluble c cytochromes |CITS: [20015627]|, while additional c cytochromes present in the periplasm appear to serve as electron donors for the terminal oxidase |CITS: [19233956]|., The oxygen that is produced in the process is believed to be used by either terminal oxidases or by monooxygenases that attack hydrocarbons, enabling the organisms to use oxygen-requiring enzymes under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [14735323]|., Perchlorate and chlorate reduction has also been observed in the archaea. However, in those organisms chlorite is not enzymatically split into chloride and oxygen. Instead, it is eliminated by an interplay of abiotic and biotic redox reactions involving sulfur compounds |CITS: [23559251]|.

Summary: The primary nitrogen assimilation routes in photosynthetic eukaryotes and prokaryotes are nitrogen fixation, nitrate assimilation, and ammonia assimilation., Ammonia is liberated by photorespiration, protein and amino acid metabolism, and the breakdown of nitrogen transport compounds. The rate of ammonia generation during photorespiration is about 10 times the rate of nitrate assimilation., The ammonia released from photorespiration is immediately re-assimilated via the ammonia assimilation cycle. The net result of this cycle is the conversion of one molecule of ammonia to one molecule of glutamate at the expense of one ATP molecule., The pathway includes two steps catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-4585 "glutamine synthetase"| (GS) and |FRAME: MONOMER-7421 "glutamate synthase"| (also known as glutamine oxoglutarate aminotansferase or GOGAT), and thus is often referred to as the GS/GOGAT pathway. Two types of GOGAT are known in photosynthetic organisms - NADH-dependent, and ferredoxin-dependent. NADH-GOGAT is found in the nucleus of vascular plants, fungi, and diatoms. The ferredoxin-dependent enzyme is only found in Cyanobacteria and photosynthetic eukaryotes. Plants possess both enzymes., An NADPH-dependent version of GOGAT is found in non-photosynthetic bacteria and archaea (see |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY|).

General Background, Tetrathionate is a common sulfur compound, present in most soils (except for very humid regions). Since it is unstable, and would not be expected to persist in soils, its occurrence suggests that it is contantly generated by the chemical or biological oxidation of thiosulfate |CITS: [Starkey50]|., The ability to respire tetrathionate is rather widespread in bacteria |CITS: [Barbosa98]|. It is found among the sulfate reducing bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-872| and |FRAME:TAX-1562| |CITS: [14908011]|, but also in various non-sulfate reducing bacteria, including several genera of the enterobacteriaceae (|FRAME:TAX-590|, |FRAME:TAX-583|, |FRAME:TAX-544| and |FRAME:TAX-635| |CITS: [16747675][Richard77][3299028]|), |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [3094300]|, |FRAME: TAX-24| |CITS: [5726148]|, |FRAME: TAX-670| |CITS: [5784207]| and others. The ability of bacteria to respire tetrathionate is exploited in clinical diagnostics and classification |CITS: [16747675][3094300]|., About This Pathway, When incubated under anaerobic conditions, two strains of |FRAME: TAX-920| produced |FRAME:HS| from tetrathionate at pH 1.5. After 12 hours of incubation under anaerobic conditions, tetrathionate decomposed, while sulfide and trithionate were formed. Thiosulfate and sulfite were not detected. The cells were also able to produce hydrogen sulfide from elemental sulfur., Based on these findings, the authors proposed that |FRAME: HS| is produced at pH 1.5 from tetrathionate by |FRAME: TAX-920| strain NASF-1 via a two-step reaction. In the first step tetrathionate is decomposed by tetrathionate-decomposing enzyme to give trithionate and elemental sulfur. In the second step the elemental sulfur is reduced by sulfur reductase using electrons from an unknown donor to give |FRAME:HS|. Molecular hydrogen was a suitable electron donor for the reduction of elemental sulfur |CITS: [16232841]|.

General Background, The proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: GLY| can biosynthesized via several different pathways. The main pathway in most organisms is the production of glycine from |FRAME:SER| via |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|. Eukaryotic organisms have both a cytosolic enzyme (SHMT2) and a mitochondrial enzyme (SHMT1) (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-PWY|). The two isoforms were reported to work in opposite directions depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [9398220]|., A less well described glycine production pathway is acheived by the operation of the |FRAME: CPLX-7302| in reverse (see |FRAME: GLYCINE-SYN2-PWY|)., In a third pathway glycine is formed from |FRAME: GLYOX|, a product of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-ALA-PWY|)., And finally, glycine can also be formed from |FRAME:THR| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.48| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-THR-PWY|)., About This Pathway, It has been recognized since 1969 that many organisms possess an L-threonine aldolase that catalyzes the interconversion of |FRAME:THR| and |FRAME:GLY| |CITS: [5353532]|. The enzyme is widespread in nature and has been shown to exist in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes |CITS:[5438301][9151955][9228760][9346293][9464392][9692922][17172352]|., In yeast the enzyme is important for the synthesis of cellular glycine |CITS: [9163906]|. In bacteria, despite the enzyme's wide distribution, its physiological significance is not certain. Experiments with |FRAME: TAX-562| mutants suggested that the threonine aldolase is not a major source of cellular glycine in wild-type bacteria, but catalyzes an alternative pathway for cellular glycine when |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, is inactive |CITS: [9692922]|.

Summary: Cyanobacteria are unusual among prokaryotes in possessing two distinct membrane systems: the thylakoid, containing an electron transfer chain capable of both respiratory and photosynthetic functions, and the cytoplasmic membrane., In |FRAME: TAX-1148| plastoquinone is the electron acceptor from either |FRAME: CPLX-7610| or any of several dehydrogenase complexes (ferredoxin-plastoquinone oxidoreductase NDH-1L, NADH-quinone oxidoreductase NDH-2, |FRAME: CPLX2PN3-58|), which are linked to the oxidation of NADPH, NADH, or succinate. Electrons are transferred directly from plastoquinone to a |FRAME: CPLX2PN3-1| (Cyd), encoded by cydAB |CITS: [11876651]|, or via cytochrome b6f complex and the soluble redox carriers to either PSI or an aa3-type cytochrome c oxidase complex |CITS: [9922162]|., A third terminal oxidase, known as the alternative respiratory terminal oxidase, is believed to be a cytochrome bo-type quinol oxidase. Unlike the other two oxidases, which are located in both the thylakoid and the cytoplasmic membranes, this oxidase is located only in the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [9922162]|., A fourth terminal oxidase, the plastoquinol terminal oxidase (PTOX), which is present in some cyanobacterial strains, is not present in |FRAME: TAX-1148| |CITS: [21056542]|.
