Summary: General Background, Saffron, prepared from the stigmas of |FRAME: TAX-82528|, is characterized by its color, bitter taste and fragrance. All three attributes of this extremely expensive spice are due in large part to products of the degradation of the carotenoid |FRAME:CPD1F-130|. The color is mainly due to a number of carotenoid glycosides derived from |FRAME:CPD-8662| (this pathway). In contrast, |FRAME:CPD-8668| is largely responsible for the bitter taste of this spice, whereas |FRAME:CPD-8669| is at the main constituent of its aroma (see |FRAME:PWY-5397|). Crocetin is an insoluble aglycone compound, which, through sequential glucosylation, is converted to the soluble |FRAME:CPD-8666|. It is this carotenoid dye that gives food a rich golden-yellow hue. Crocetin can be converted by saffron cell suspension cultures into several glycosyl esters, which, in addition to those shown on the pathway diagram, include esters of the rare trisaccharide |FRAME: CPD-26405| (β-D-glucopyranosyl-(1->2)-[β-D-glucopyranosyl-(1->6)]-β-D-glucose) in the compounds |FRAME:CPD-8687|, |FRAME:CPD-8688| and |FRAME:CPD-8689| |CITS:[COTE00B]|. Finally, although this pathway only present the most common all-trans compounds, cis isomers have also been identified |CITS:[16448211],[COTE00b]|. In vivo, |FRAME:CPD-8666| is the most abundant pigment found in the stigma of saffron and the fruit of Gardenia jasmonoides |CITS:[16448211] [Pfister96]|., |FRAME: CPD-8666 Crocin-1| is the compound primarily responsible for the golden yellow-orange color of the stigma of saffron flowers. Its content in ethanol extracts of |FRAME: TAX-82528| flowers has been reported to be around 20% |CITS: [Sugiura95]|. However, the content of crocin varies significantly among saffron populations and reports very from 0.8% to 32.4% |CITS: [Lage09][26012879]|. Crocin is largely absent from petal extracts |CITS: [16979327]|., Together with other components of saffron stigmas (|FRAME: CPD-8669|, |FRAME: CPD-8662|, and |FRAME: CPD-8668|) |FRAME: CPD-8666| has antidepressant properties |CITS: [Hosseinzadeh04][24401376][19787421][25484177][26468466][29068592]|. Crocin-1 acts via inhibition of dopamine and norepinephrine uptake |CITS: [9518580][18496783][Ettehadi13][29136602][32495180]|., |FRAME: CPD-8666 Crocin-1| appears to reduce the COVID-19-related cytokine cascade and downregulate angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) gene expression, and in silico studies suggested that it could have inhibitory actions on the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein |CITS: [34312610]|., Enzymes of the pathway:, Several enzymes have been identified that catalyze the glucosylation of crocetin. The only one, however, that has been cloned is the |FRAME:TAX-82528| |FRAME:MONOMER-12719| |CITS:[15605174]|. This enzyme was shown to catalyze the glucosylation of crocetin. Although the exact nature of the products formed by this enzyme remain to be unequivocally confirmed, the enzyme was shown to catalyze specifically the glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-8662|, |FRAME:CPD-8663| and |FRAME:CPD-8664| |CITS:[15605174]|. It is currently believed that more than one glucosyltransferase catalyze the glucosylation of crocetin |CITS:[COTE00]|., Two UDP-glucose: crocetin glucosyltransferases identified and characterized from cell cultures of Gardenia jasminoides were able to sequentially glucosylate the aglycon |FRAME:CPD-8662| and all the subsequent mono- and diglucosylated intermediates to the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-8666|. It was demonstrated that the crocetin glucosyltransferase UGT75L6 glucosylated the free carboxyl groups of |FRAME:CPD-8662| and monoglucosylated and gentiobioside intermediates while the crocetin ester glucosyltransferase UGT94E5 catalyzed the β1 to β6 glucosylation of the intermediates generating the corresponding gentio- and digentiobosyl ester of |FRAME:CPD-8662| |CITS:[22569263]|.

Pyrazines are monocyclic aromatic rings with two nitrogen atoms in para position. While most of the pyrazines are anthropogenic, many substituted pyrazines are produced naturally and are widely distributed in plants, animals and microorganisms. In addition, substituted pyrazines form spontaneously upon heating of many types of foods, such as beef, products, toasted barley, cocoa, coffee, peanuts, popcorn, potato chips, rye crisp bread and roasted filberts as well as in fresh foods like tomatoes, peas, green bell peppers, asparagus, kohlrabi and dairy products |CITS: [Maga73]|., In general, very little is known about the degradation of pyrazines. Various bacterial strains are able to use alkyl-substituted pyrazines as a sole carbon and energy source. Several of them were shown to hydroxylate the pyrazine ring at a free ring position, while others oxidize an alkyl group to form the corresponding alcohol or carboxylic acid |CITS: [16461697][17120096][19957079]|., |FRAME: CPD-15901| (TTMP) is a pyrazine compound that is produced by different bacteria and plants |CITS: [14458746][10843553][21480771][22334234]|. It is one of the most important active ingredients of the Chinese herb |FRAME: TAX-49555|, which is widely used for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases. , Unlike other modified pyrazines, TTMP cannot be degraded via initial hydroxylation to form hydroxypyrazine, since each of the ring carbons carries a substituent. Instead, it was proposed that the ring is cleaved already in the initial step of its degradation |CITS: [19957079]|., The degradation pathway of TTMP has been studied with the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1072366|, a strain known to use it as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [23563941]|. The genes involved in the process, which are all induced by TTMP, are located in a single locus, and the enzymes catalyzing the first three reactions have been characterized in detail. The first enzyme (encoded by |FRAME: G-17824|, |FRAME: G-17825|, and |FRAME: G-17828|) is a flavin-containing dioxygenase that catalyzes the ring cleavage, comcomitant with the introduction of two oxygen atoms. The second enzyme (|FRAME: G-17826|) hydrolyzes the product, releasing an |FRAME: ACETAMIDE| molecule. The third enzyme (|FRAME: G-17827|) is a hydrogenase that reduces a keto group in the remaining product., The later steps of the pathway have not been characterized, but are believed to be catalyzed by the remaining two ORFs in the same locus and to involve a |FRAME: CPD-15905| intermediate |CITS: [23563941]|.

General Background, Thiols are compounds that play a major role in the detoxification of stress-inducing factors. Pathogenic bacteria live in a particularly hostile environment, in which the host deliberately generates toxins, including reactive oxygen species, to destroy the invading organism. Thus thiols are particularly important for the survival of these organisms. While |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE glutathione| is the major low-molecular-weight thiol in eukaryotic organisms, Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive bacteria, it is not universal |CITS: [417060]|. In some organisms other thiols have taken its role, including |FRAME: CoM coenzyme M|, |FRAME: TRYPANOTHIONE trypanothione|, ergothioneine, |FRAME: CPD1G-2 mycothiol|, and the ovothiols. , The small thiol |FRAME: CPD8J2-3 bacillithiol| has been discovered in a variety of Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1299|, |FRAME:TAX-1392|, |FRAME:TAX-1280|, and |FRAME:TAX-1423| |CITS: [19578333]|. Genes similar to those of the B. subtilis biosynthetic pathway were also discovered in the δ-proteobacterium |FRAME:TAX-34| and the halophilic alkalithermophile |FRAME:TAX-375929| |CITS: [20308541]|., About This Pathway, A pathway for the biosynthesis of bacillithiol was proposed based on parallels to the |FRAME: PWY1G-0 mycothiol biosynthesis| pathway, and candidate enzymes were identified by bioinformatic analysis. The function of the first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: BSU22460-MONOMER L-malate glycosyltransferase|, was confirmed by assays of the purified protein and its mutant phenotype. Two acetylases with partially redundant function catalyze the second reaction, deacetylation of |FRAME: CPD8J2-1 GlcNAc-Mal|. The last enzyme of the pathway, a cysteine-adding enzyme, was identified by its mutant phenotype |CITS: [20308541]|.

Summary: Phosphatidate (PA) is a central metabolite for the biosynthesis of triacylglycerols and major phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphatidylinositol (PI), the latter being synthesized through the metabolization of PA via the CDP-diacylglycerol pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5667|) |CITS:[20332534]|. Phosphatidate is known to be synthesized in yeast |CITS:[10049376] [9401016]| and mammals |CITS:[9370313]| by two pathways, one pathway takes the route via |FRAME:GLYCEROL-3P| (G3P) and the other pathway produces phosphatidate through |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| (DHAP). , The impact of phosphatidate on the regulation of phospholipid biosynthesis has been under investigation for some time. It could be demonstrated that the transcriptional regulation of gene expression in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is subject to the content of phosphatidate in the cell which controls the biochemistry of enzymes active in the synthesis of phospholipids |CITS:[21275641]|. The formation of diacylglycerol (DAG), a precursor for triacylglycerol (TAG) and phospholipid biosynthesis, is catalyzed both by the triacylglycerol lipase TGL4 |CITS:[16135509]| and phosphatidate phosphatase PAH1 |CITS:[2542283]|, the former catalyzing the degradation of TAG and the latter forming DAG by dephosphorylation of phosphatidate (PA). Both enzymes are regulated in their activity through a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK1/CDC28) which phosphorylates both enzymes resulting in the activation of TGL4 and inactivation of PAH1 indicating their control of the flux in the DAG/TAG pathway, the gateway to phospholipids synthesis |CITS:[19150427] [22910056]|. , In the G3P pathway |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| is reduced to |FRAME:GLYCEROL-3P| which is catalyzed by the NAD-dependent glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase encoded in yeast by GPD1 |CITS:[1499720]|. |FRAME:GLYCEROL-3P Glycerol-3-phosphate| is then the substrate for the two enzymes expressing dual glycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase/dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase activity, i.e. SCT1p and GPT2p |CITS:[11544256]| which results in the formation of an lyso-phosphatidate. In the DHAP branch the latter enzymes also catalyze the esterification of |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| with a fatty acid forming a lyso-glycerone phosphate which is subsequently reduced by the 1-acyl dihydroxyacetone phosphate reductase encoded by AYR1 |CITS:[10617610]| yielding the corresponding lyso-phosphatidate. In the last step of the pathway lyso-phosphatidate undergoes another acylation which forms the key product for phospholipid biosynthesis, i.e. phosphatidate. Because of the central metabolic position of phosphatidate it is not unexpected that many of the lyso-phospholipid acyltransferases accept lyso-phosphatidate, e.g. |FRAME:L-1-LYSOPHOSPHATIDATE| as substrate and re-esterify it to the corresponding phosphatidate molecular species, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-8268| with varying efficiency. Besides the triacylglycerol lipases TGL4p |CITS:[16135509] [16267052] [20332534]| and TGL5p |CITS:[16135509] [20016004]| which also demonstrated oleoyl-CoA:lysophosphatidate acyltransferase (LPAT) activity the major LPATs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae are SLC1p |CITS:[8408076] [1767529]| and LOA1p |CITS:[22090344]| which have both a dual location at the endoplasmatic reticulum and lipid droplets in the yeast cell.

Summary: The biphenyl |FRAME:CPD-14666| (this pathway) and various dibenzofurans have been found to be the major phytoalexins of economically important pome fruit trees like apple, pear, cherry, peach, plum and apricot |CITS:[22563359]|. Those phytoalexins are formed upon the attack of pathogens and seem to be restricted to a subfamily of the Rosaceae, i.e. the Maloideae. This plant family not only includes above mentioned fruit crops but also highly valuated ornamental plants such as rowan (Sorbus spp.), rose (Rosa spp.), hawthorn (Crataegus spp.) |CITS:[Kokubun95] [22377689]|, Photinia glabra |CITS:[Widyastuti92]| and Eriobotrya japonica |CITS:[Watanabe82]| as well as other family members with inherent medicinal properties such as the Asian Rhaphiolepsis umbellate |CITS:[Watanabe90a]|. The most fatal diseases in apple, pears and other pome fruit trees are scab, caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis, and fire blight induced by the bacterium Erwinia amylovora |CITS:[Vanneste00]|. Considering the worldwide production of apples (80 million tons) and pears (25 million tons) |CITS:[FAO15]| the economic loss caused by those pathogens can be devastating |CITS:[Carisse02]|., The biphenyl |FRAME:CPD-14666| was first isolated from the heartwood of Sorbus aucuparia |CITS:[Erdtman63]| and has ever since become the favorite subject to investigate the |FRAME:PWY-7739| and dibenzofuran formation |CITS:[20961041]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-14666| is usually initiated by pathogenic attacks which cause the enhanced expression of the catalyzing enzymes |CITS:[Huttner11]|. The pathway starts with the formation of |FRAME:CPD-8991| by condensation with |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| and the unusual starter unit |FRAME:BENZOYLCOA| catalyzed by the |FRAME:CPLX-8546| |CITS:[14595561] [17109150] [19699497]|. The following steps in the pathway, a O-methylation followed by a 4-hydroxylation and another O-methylation have been elucidated by feeding experiments in pathogen-elicited Sorbus aucuparia cell cultures |CITS:[24074553]|. , The two separate O-methylations are carried out by the 3,5-dihydroxybiphenyl O-methyltransferase (OMT1) and the noraucuparin O-methyltransferase (OMT2), where the former produces |FRAME:CPD-18574|, the substrate for the subsequent 4-hydroxylation, and the latter methoxylated |FRAME:CPD-18575| to form the final product of the pathway |FRAME:CPD-14666| |CITS:[26017378]|. The intermediary 4-hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-18574| to yield |FRAME:CPD-18575| is catalyzed by the 3-hydroxy-5-methoxybiphenyl 4-hydroxylase (CYP736A107) in Sorbus aucuparia and by two homologs from Malus domestica cv. Golden Delicious and Malus domestica cv. Holsteiner Cox |CITS:[25862456]|. All three enzymes belong to the cytochrome P450 group of CYP736A which is one of the 59 CYP families that constitute 1% of all protein-coding genes |CITS:[21443632] [Nelson08]|. The localization of the biphenyl synthase (BIP1) to plasmodesmata |CITS:[Reckwell14]|, the O-methyltransferases (OMT1 and OMT2) to the cytoplasm |CITS:[26017378]| and the 4-hydroxylase to ER |CITS:[25862456]| brings all catalyzing enzyme into close proximity to each other which has prompted the notion of a metabolon functioning in the |FRAME:PWY-7739| |CITS:[25862456]|.

Summary: General Background, The rifamycins are members of the ansamycin family of antibiotics. |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B| is produced as an end product by the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-33910 "Amycolatopsis mediterranei (previously known as Streptomyces mediterranei and Nocardia mediterranei)"|. Rifamycin production is controlled by a single gene cluster containing structural, resistance, export and regulatory genes |CITS: [9512878]|. |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B| is less potent as an antibiotic than its precursor |FRAME: CPD-10236|, which has been used clinically. Many analogs of rifamycin have been produced, with rifampicin being widely used to treat mycobacterial infections. Due to the rapid development of resistance to rifampicin, it is used in combination with other agents such as |FRAME: ISONIAZIDE|, or other analogs such as rifabutine can be used (reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|). Rifamycins inhibit DNA-dependent RNA synthesis by binding tightly to prokaryotic DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. The mechanism of rifampicin inhibition has been studied in detail |CITS: [11290327]|. The majority of mutations leading to resistance are found in the RNA polymerase β subunit, although other mechanisms including impeded uptake and antibiotic modification are known. Autoresistance of |FRAME: TAX-33910| is due to the insensitivity of its DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to the antibiotic it produces. A rifamycin export protein, the product of gene rifP has been identified and is thought to prevent the accumulation of rifamycin within the cell |CITS: [17351715]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [15700959]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-10231| is a precursor of the antibiotic |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B| and other ansamycin class and mitomycin class antibiotics (in |CITS: [11278540]|). It provides the mC7N unit of these antibiotics (a six-carbon ring, usually aromatic or quinoid, with an extra carbon and a nitrogen in meta arrangement) |CITS: [Kim96]|. |FRAME: CPD-10224 Kanosamine| has been proposed to be the source of the nitrogen atom for |FRAME: CPD-10231| |CITS: [12207504] [12207505]|. , The |FRAME: CPLX-9376| utilizes |FRAME: CPD-10231| as a starter unit, followed by ten rounds of C2 chain extension using two |FRAME: ACET| and eight |FRAME: PROPIONATE| units derived from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| to form an undecaketide (in |CITS: [15791687] [12623077] [16089423]|). In this pathway diagram the biosynthesis of the polyketide chain is shown in an abbreviated form. The individual chain extension steps are illustrated and described in |CITS: [11352749] [15700959]|., |FRAME: CPD-10241 Proansamycin X| undergoes a series of complex post-polyketide synthase modification reactions to finally produce |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B|. First, formation of a double bond at position 7,8 of the second ring (this reaction is attributed in some papers to RifT; however, a study that used complementation of a rifT mutant concluded that the enzyme is not involed directly in rifamycin B biosynthesis |CITS: [20726561]|) and hydroxylation of C-34α by an unknown enzyme form |FRAME: CPD-10243|. This is followed by a very complex oxygenation catalyzed by the cytochrome P-450 enzyme |FRAME: G-58871| that generates |FRAME: CPD-10239| |CITS: [16079331]|. Three additional modifications transform this compound into |FRAME: CPD-10236| |CITS: [12623077][15791687]|., The hydroquinone |FRAME: CPD-10236| is spontaneously oxidized to the quinone |FRAME: CPD-21864| by ambient O2, and this transformation is dramatically accelerated by the presence of divalent metal ions. It is possible that an enzyme catalyzes this reaction in vivo |CITS: [29904078]|., In the next step |FRAME: CPLX-9377|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10784| and |FRAME: G-58870| genes, forms |FRAME: CPD-21865|, which is oxidized by another cytochrome P-450 enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58872| gene, to |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-O|. The last reaction is this pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-O| to |FRAME: RIFAMYCIN-B|, occurs spontaneously in the presence of NADPH |CITS: [29904078]|.

Sterols are essential lipids which exist in free and esterified forms in all eukaryotic cells. Only the free amphiphilic sterols are incorporated into membranes whereas steryl esters are of hydrophobic nature (|CITS:[16916618]|) and accumulate in lipid droplets (LD) which serve as storage bodies for neutral lipids in Saccharomyces cells (reviewed in |CITS:[10998572]|). Although steryl ester biosynthesis and lipid body formation appear as important but not essential processes in yeast (|CITS:[11741946]|) a strict control is exercised to maintain the required amount of free sterols (|CITS:[19111628] [3307928]|)., Consequently, steryl ester storage and mobilization is considered significant in sterol homeostasis for the biosynthesis and distribution of the various sterols in yeast such as |FRAME:LANOSTEROL| (see |FRAME:PWY-6132|), |FRAME:ZYMOSTEROL| (see |FRAME:PWY-6074|) and the main sterol |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL| (see |FRAME:PWY-6075|) (|CITS:[18258205] [19111628] [11111085]|). A lack of steryl esters in a quadruple mutant deficient in triacylglycerol synthases (DGA1, LRO1) and ARE1 and 2, the acyl-CoA:sterol acyltransferases in yeast, strongly interfered with the squalene epoxidase ERG1, located upstream of the |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL| biosynthetic route causing reduced incorporation of |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL| into yeast plasma membranes (|CITS:[15155725]|)., An interesting phenomenon has been observed when yeast grows under heme-limiting/anaerobic conditions. Various pairs of isoenzymes involved in the sterol:steryl ester interconversion pathway, such as the steryl ester hydrolases YEH1 and YEH2 and the acyl-CoA:sterol acyltransferases ARE1 and ARE2 behave differently in terms of enzyme and transcriptional activity which may explain the existence of seemingly redundant proteins. , Under heme-deficient conditions YEH1 was identified as the only steryl ester hydrolase being active under these conditions (|CITS:[15713625]|). The data also indicate a transcriptional control of YEH1 through ROX3, a component of the complex that regulates RNA polymerase II |CITS:[16835446]|. In addition, under conditions of heme-deficiency the acyl-CoA:sterol acyltransferase (ASAT) ARE1 is transcriptionally up-regulated which is regulated by ROX1p in the ARE1 promoter region. Hence, ARE1p is the hypoxic form of the ASAT's which is induced by heme depletion. On the other side ARE2p is the normoxic form of the ASAT's which is induced under aerobic conditions |CITS:[11786267]|. Moreover, ARE1 and ARE2 contribute differentially to the steryl ester formation in the sterol biosynthetic pathway with ARE2p predominantly esterifying |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL| and ARE1p carrying out the esterification of sterol precursors of the pathway such as |FRAME:ZYMOSTEROL| and |FRAME:LANOSTEROL| (|CITS:[8650549] [8798656] [10672016] [11489845]|). Overall a differentially regulated activity of both the steryl ester hydrolases and the ASAT's by the heme status of the cell highlights the adaptability of the pathway and individual impact of the isoenzymes under varying conditions.

Aminoacylation of glycerophospholipids is prevalent among Gram-positive bacteria, but rare among Gram-negatives. One case of such modification if the addition of one and two glycine residues to lipid A in |FRAME: TAX-666| strains., The process involves three proteins encoded by the |FRAME: FY484_RS07925|, |FRAME: FY484_RS07920| and |FRAME: FY484_RS07915| genes. ElmF is a small glycine-carrier protein that is acylated with a glycyl residue by the |FRAME: FY484_RS07925-MONOMER| encoded by |FRAME: FY484_RS07925|. ElmG is a transferase that transfers the glycyl residue from the carrier protein to the hexa-acylated lipid A |CITS: [22589301]|., All three proteins are predicted to be soluble and contain no signal peptides required for secretion across the inner membrane. The authors proposed that glycine addition occurs on the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane., Addition of amine-containing substituents such as glycine reduces the net negative charge of the bacterial surface and confers resistance towards cationic antimicrobial peptides. |FRAME: TAX-666| strains that express this system are highly resistant to |FRAME: CPD-19297|. Deletion of |FRAME: FY484_RS07915| resulted in nearly a 100-fold decrease in polymyxin resistance compared with wild-type levels |CITS: [22589301]|.

Summary: All polyketide synthases, fatty-acid synthases and non-ribosomal peptide synthases require post-translational modification of their constituent acyl-carrier-protein (ACP) domains to become catalytically active. The inactive apo-proteins are converted into their active holo-forms by transfer of the |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| moiety of |FRAME: CO-A| to the side chain hydroxy group of a conserved serine residue in each ACP domain. The activation is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.7|, Found only in some bacteria, a dedicated enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.14|, catalyzes the removal of the 4-phosphopantetheinyl moiety from holo-ACP. The enzyme from |FRAME:TAX-562| has been characterized, and found not to be essential for growth. Its physiological role is still unknown |CITS: [16107329]|.

Summary: General Background, C-glycosides are widespread in the plant kingdom and have been shown to occur in at least 20 families of angiosperms |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. Moreover, they have also been found in insects and microbes |CITS:[17404902]| and are attributed to a broad range of biological activities. They act as antioxidants |CITS:[Ramarathnam89]| |CITS:[1824129]|, show antimicrobial activity |CITS:[16651765]|, facilitate mycorrhizal symbioses |CITS:[12026171]|, screen and protect from UV |CITS:[Les90]| and are valuable agents in preventing lipoprotein oxidation |CITS:[Kim2005]| and cancer development |CITS:[11172671]| in humans. , C-glycosideflavonoids represent the largest group of C-glycosides and are especially dominant in cereals such as maize, wheat and rice |CITS:[17404902]| |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. The special attachment of the aglycone directly to the C1 of the pyranose ring of a sugar confers high structural stability to the C-glycosides which even withstand acidic treatment., About This Pathway, The pathway has been shown to proceed via 2-hydroxyflavanone precursors |CITS:[Kerscher87]| |CITS:[Kerscher88]|. This first committed reaction of the pathway is catalyzed by a cytochrome P-450 enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.162|, which hydoxylates the corresponding flavanones |CITS:[20647377]|. The C-glycosyltransferase only acts on the open form of the 2-hydroxyflavanones, i.e. dibenzoylmethane tautomers, which are subsequently glycosylated in either the 6C or 8C position of the A ring |CITS:[19411659]| |CITS:[Kerscher88]|. In vitro experiments showed that upon acidic treatment the 2-hydroxyflavanone glucosides were dehydrated to the corresponding flavones forming a mixture of 6C and 8C-glycosylflavones. However, in planta experiments demonstrated the existence of a C-glycosylflavanone dehydratase which preferentially catalyzed the formation of 6C-glycosylflavones |CITS:[19411659]|., C-glycosylflavones extracted from rice revealed a pattern of |FRAME:GLC| attached to 6C and |FRAME:CPD-12049| attached to 8C of the A-ring |CITS:[Besson85]| whereas in wheat the pattern was |FRAME:GLC| in 6C and |FRAME:BETA-D-XYLOSE| in the 8C position |CITS:[16494903]|. To date the characterized C-glycosyltransferases only act on |FRAME: CPD-12575| in vitro |CITS:[19411659]| and the question whether or not one or more C-glycosyltransferases are involved in the pathway remains to be shown. Besides |FRAME:CPD-15083| and |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN| various other C-glycosylflavones in cereals are produced from either |FRAME:NARINGENIN-CMPD| (see |FRAME:PWY-6602|) or |FRAME:CPD-6991| (see |FRAME:PWY-7189|)., A different route that produces |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN| directly from |FRAME: 5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE| has been found in |FRAME: TAX-55190| |CITS: [25479084]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8340|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-9436 Isoprene| is a volatile compound produced by many plants. The yearly production of isoprene emissions by vegetation is around 600 million tonnes (with half of it coming from tropical broadleaf trees), making it about a third of all hydrocarbons released into the atmosphere |CITS: [Guenther06]|., Isoprene is incorporated into cell membranes in response to heat stress, and its stabilizing effect confers some tolerance to heat spikes. Its emission increases dramatically with temperature and maximizes at around 40 °C. Thus, it is thought that isoprene protects plants against heat stress |CITS: [17921528]|. It also confers some resistance to reactive oxygen species |CITS: [19183288]|., Isoprene is a common structural motif in biological polymers, although those compounds (|FRAME: Polyisoprenoids isoprenoids|) are not derived from isoprene, but instead are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4211| and its isomer |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|., Isoprene is used to produce a diverse range of industrial products including a wide variety of specialty elastomers used in surgical gloves, motor mounts and fittings, rubber bands, golf balls, and shoes. It is also used as a component of Styrene-isoprene-styrene block copolymers that form an essential part of most hot-melt pressure-sensitive adhesive formulations, and of cis-polyisoprene or synthetic rubber, which is used in tire manufacturing |CITS: [Whited2010]|., About This Pathway, The production of isoprene by engineered bacteria from renewable feedstocks offers the opportunity to deliver a sustainable manufacturing process to supply isoprene for its many current uses., This biosynthetic pathway, expressed in |FRAME: TAX-511693|, has been developed by Genencor |CITS: [Whited2010]|. The pathway relies on supply of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| from the native glycolysis pathway. The immediate precursor to |FRAME: CPD-9436|, |FRAME: CPD-4211|, which can be produced by two potential pathways - the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway) and the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (MEP pathway), is produced here by the mevalonate pathway, which does not exist natively in |FRAME: TAX-562|., The MVA pathway was cloned as two synthetic operons - the upper part of the pathway, consisting of the conversion of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: MEVALONATE|, and the lower part of the pathway, producing |FRAME: CPD-4211| from |FRAME: MEVALONATE|. The last part of the engineered pathway consists of a cloned plant |FRAME: MONOMER-14888|., The first synthetic operon, encoding enzymes of the upper pathway, consists of two genes from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1351|. The |FRAME: EF_RS06585| gene encodes a bifunctional protein that catalyzes both the first and third enzymatic steps in the pathway. The |FRAME: EF_RS06580| gene encodes the enzyme that catalyzes the second enzymatic step. The combined action of both enzymes produces one molecule of |FRAME: MEVALONATE| from three molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|., The second synthetic operon, encoding the enzymes of the lower MVA pathway, consists of four genes from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|. In addition, this operon includes the gene encoding |FRAME: CPLX-8756| from the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-192952|, since the archaeal enzyme is free of the feedback inhibition that characterizes the homologous eukaryotic and bacterial enzymes. All of these genes have been integrated into the |FRAME: TAX-562| chromosome., The last part of the pathway consists of the gene encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-14888| in the tree |FRAME: TAX-43335|, which was found to produce a higher titer than the only other isoprene synthase for which sequence is available at as of 2013, from the Asian vine kudzu (|FRAME: TAX-132459|). The gene was introduced to the host bacterium on a second plasmid., The pathway described here produced a titer of approximately 30 g/L in 40 h of fermentation. By adding a constitutively expressed |FRAME: G6397| gene from |FRAME: TAX-511145|, to compensate for the low activity of the enzyme in the |FRAME: TAX-511693| host strain, the titer increased to greater than 60 g/L, with a cell productivity of 0.85 g isoprene/g dry cell weight |CITS: [Cervin09]|.

Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|). Analogs for these pathways are also found in the metabolism of deoxyhexoses such as |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-fucoses| (see |FRAME: PWY-6714| and |FRAME: PWY-8318|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Free |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| rarely exists in the nature (though it has been found in the core of coniferous trees |CITS: [Pingman57]|). However, it is widely distributed as a component of complex nonstarch polysaccharides in plant cell walls, including many plants common in the human diet such as maize, wheat, rye, rice, sugar beets, and plant gums, and in bacterial polysaccharides. Free arabinose is formed during the degradation of complex polymers, as in |FRAME: PWY-6790|, |FRAME: PWY-8006|, and |FRAME: PWY-6813|., The earlier steps of this pathway have been characterized from multiple bacterial species, as they are common to all three routes of the third type of pathways (as described above). The last two steps, which are specific for this route, were characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-863372| |CITS: [30655589]|.

|FRAME: CPD-17560 2,4-Dinitroanisole| (DNAN) is an insensitive munition ingredient that is increasingly used in explosive formulations as a replacement for |FRAME: CPD-9138| (TNT). Insensitive munitions have a high detonation temperature and enhanced resistance to shocks, and are thus expected to reduce accidental explosions. While DNAN is less sensitive, some of its technical properties compare favorably with those of TNT and make it advantageous for the manufacturing of explosives |CITS: [Davies06]|., DNAN has been reported to undergo microbial transformation to |FRAME: CPD-17563| under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [21566358][20855103][20855103][23280483][25460743]| and to |FRAME: CPD-17562| under aerobic conditions |CITS: [21881912]|. A study of the toxicity of |FRAME: CPD-17560| and its two metabolites has found that they are toxic to some bacteria (specifically methanogens) |CITS: [24041820]|, as well as to earthworms, algae, and plants |CITS: [24021166]|., In a later study, the complete mineralization of DNAN has been observed in |FRAME: TAX-1517491|, an organism isolated from a sludge sample obtained from the Holston Army Ammunition Plant, based on its ability to grow with DNAN as the sole carbon, nitrogen, and energy source |CITS: [25281383]|. The organism was found to have a novel ether hydrolase enzyme that converts DNAN to |FRAME: CPD-8179|. The latter is completely degraded in a pathway whose first part is well understood (see |FRAME: PWY-7627|)., Unlike other o-demethylases, which require oxygen and an electron donor (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.15|, |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.31| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.32|) or tetrahydrofolate (e.g. |FRAME: MONOMER-15113|), the |FRAME: CPLX-8963| from |FRAME: TAX-1517491| is not oxygen-dependent and does not require any cofactors, and provides robust biodegradation of DNAN suitable for waste treatment or biodegradation applications |CITS: [25281383]|.

General Background, The tocopherols (|FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL|, |FRAME: BETA-TOCOPHEROL|, |FRAME: GAMA-TOCOPHEROL| and |FRAME: DELTA-TOCOPHEROL|) and their corresponding tocotrienols are synthesized by plants and have vitamin E antixoidant activity (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-1422|). They differ in the number and location of methyl groups on the chromanol ring. The naturally occurring form of |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| is (2R,4'R,8'R)-α-tocopherol (synonym (R,R,R)-α-tocopherol). Synthetic α-tocopherols are a racemic mixture of eight different R and S stereoisomers. Only the 2R forms are recognized as meeting human requirements. Reviewed in |CITS: [17628169]|., The in vivo function of vitamin E is to scavenge peroxyl radicals via its phenolic (chromanol) hydroxyl group, thus protecting lipids against free radical-catalyzed peroxidation. The tocopheryl radical formed can then be reduced by reductants such as |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). Other major products of |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| oxidation include α-tocopherylquinone and epoxy-α-tocopherols. The metabolites α-tocopheronic acid and its lactone, known as the Simon metabolites, are generally believed to be artefacts. In addition to these oxidation products, the other major class of tocopherol metabolites is the carboxyethyl-hydroxychromans (this pathway). These metabolites are produced in significant amounts in response to excess vitamin E ingestion. Reviewed in |CITS: [17628169] [17306359]| and |CITS: [17561088]|., Vitamin E is fat-soluble and its utilization requires intestinal fat absorption mechanisms. It is secreted from the intestine into the lymphatic system in chylomicrons which subsequently enter the plasma. Lipolysis of these chylomicrons can result in delivery of vitamin E to tissues, transfer to high-density lipoproteins (and subsequently to other lipoproteins via the phospholipid exchange protein), or retention in chylomicron remnants. These remnants are taken up by the liver. Natural (R,R,R)-α-tocopherol and synthetic 2R-α-tocopherols are then preferentially secreted from the liver into plasma as a result of the specificity of the α-tocopherol transfer protein. This protein, along with the metabolism of excess vitamin E in the liver and excretion into urine and bile, mediate the supply of |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| in plasma and tissues. Reviewed in |CITS: [17628169]| and |CITS: [17439363]|. , About This Pathway, In the pathway shown here, the triple arrows represent a series of proposed reactions of |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| and |FRAME: GAMA-TOCOPHEROL| metabolism. The compounds shown here, |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL|, |FRAME: CPD-11960|, |FRAME: CPD-11961| and |FRAME: CPD-11962|, have been identified in vivo, although most of the proposed intermediates have only been identified in vitro using cultured cell lines, with results varying as to cell line studied |CITS: [11997390] [15671218] [19819327]|, in |CITS: [15753130]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17628169] [17306359]|. The proposed reactions include: dehydrogenation of |FRAME: CPD-11960| to a carboxylate (13'-carboxy-α-tocopherol) by an unidentified microsomal enzyme(s) probably via an aldehyde intermediate (in |CITS: [19819327]| and in |CITS: [15753130]|); conversion of the carboxylate to an acyl-CoA ester; four cycles of β-oxidation resulting in side chain shortening, producing |FRAME: CPD-11961| |CITS: [19819327]|; and an additional cycle of |FRAME: CPD-11961| β-oxidation, producing |FRAME: CPD-11962| (see pathway |FRAME: FAO-PWY|)., More recently, in vivo studies of intracellular compartmentalization in this pathway suggest that the initial β-oxidation steps in |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| degradation are localized in peroxisomes, while the final steps are localized in mitochondria |CITS: [19819327]|. In the pathway shown here, evidence suggests that the ω hydroxylation of |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| is likely catalyzed by the products of genes CYP3A4 |CITS: [11061988]| or |FRAME: HS02675| |CITS: [17284776]|. This alcohol must then be dehydrogenated to a carboxylate, probably via an aldehyde intermediate, by enzymes found in the cytoplasm and endoplasmic reticulum. Based on analogy with the intracellular trafficking and degradation of a 2-methyl-branched fatty acids such as |FRAME: PRISTANATE|, the carboxylate would then be activated to an acyl-CoA ester and undergo β-oxidation. The two initial cycles of β-oxidation would occur in peroxisomes, which contain enzymes highly active toward medium and long chain branched chain acyl-CoA substrates. The final three cycles of β-oxidation would occur in mitochondria. However, exclusively mitochondrial β-oxidation was not ruled out |CITS: [19819327]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17628169]| and |CITS: [17439363]|., Most of the |FRAME: CPD-11962| metabolites produced undergo conjugation before excretion in urine or bile, by unknown excretion mechanisms. Conjugation occurs via sulfation by as yet unidentified sulfotransferases, or by glucuronidation by as yet unidentified UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (not shown). In addition, |FRAME: ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| and |FRAME: GAMA-TOCOPHEROL| can be directly excreted into bile. The metabolite |FRAME: CPD-11962| itself has been shown to promote natriuresis (urinary sodium excretion) and have anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory activities. Reviewed in |CITS: [17628169]| and |CITS: [17306359]|.

Summary: General Background, The acid sugar |FRAME: KDO| (known as Kdo for ketodeoxyoctonate) is a component of bacterial |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) and of the |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan II"| (RG-II) pectin fraction of the primary cell walls of most higher plants, including dicots, monocots and gymnosperms |CITS:[York85][7958328][shin97][9779594]|., The number of Kdo units in bacterial polysaccharides vary, depending on the species, but the majority of Gram-negative bacteria contain at least one Kdo molecule in their LPS., To date, the specific contribution of Kdo to RG-II function in plants remains largely unknown. , Kdo needs to be activated prior to its incorporation into the polymers. This activation occurs through the unusual coupling of Kdo to the monophosphonucleotide CMP |CITS:[11050325]|., About This Pathway, Despite incorporating Kdo into very different macromolecules, the Kdo biosynthesis and activation pathway is almost completely conserved between plants and bacteria |CITS: [23974348]|. , The pathway starts with the isomerization of |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| to |FRAME: ARABINOSE-5P|, followed by its conversion to |FRAME: KDO-8P| (KDOP), which is catalyzed by a family of enzymes called |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.55|| (KDOPS). The bacterial KDOPSs have been grouped in two classes, and plant KDOPSs belong to a third class |CITS:[15070398]|., In the next step the phosphate group is removed from |FRAME: KDO-8P|, generating Kdo. This is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.45|. It should be noted that the plant enzyme responsible for this dephosphorylation has not been identified yet., The last step of the pathway is the activation of Kdo to |FRAME: CMP-KDO|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.38|.

Summary: The phytopathogenic fungus Alternaria brassicicola is known to produce a wide spectrum of secondary metabolites, amongst them phytotoxins such as the anti-bacterial isocyanide antibiotic |FRAME:CPD-16853| |CITS:[Gloer88]| and phytoalexins such as |FRAME:CPD-16850| |CITS:[19223049]|. Many of the Alternaria phytotoxins attack plasma membranes causing electrolyte loss, hence compromising the physiological function of vital organelles such as mitochondria |CITS:[Otani95]|. Alternaria brassicicola causes black spot disease in cruciferous vegetables which can lead to crop losses between 20 to 80% worldwide |CITS:[Nowicki12]|. The ascomycetous fungus also produces compounds, i.e. brassicicene which are similar to the fusicoccins produced in another group of ascomycetes (see |FRAME:PWY-6659|). Besides |FRAME:CPD-16830| (this pathway) five more brassicicene have been identified so far (|FRAME:CPD-16831|, |FRAME:CPD-16832|, |FRAME:CPD-16833|, |FRAME:CPD-16834|, and |FRAME:CPD-16835|) |CITS:[MacKinnon99]| with more brassicicenes being discovered and characterized. Although the exact physiological function in the fungus and probable drug properties of brassicicenes are not very well known first studies have shown seed dormancy breaking activities in plants and necrotic/apoptotic activities in mammalian cells |CITS:[24689212]|., More than 55.000 isoprenoid structures have been found in nature highlighting the numerous possible decorations of the core skeleton formed by isoprene units |CITS:[12013278] [17412950]|. The biosynthesis of the fusicoccane diterpenoid |FRAME:CPD-16830| is carried out by an biosynthetic gene cluster identified in Alternaria |CITS:[19097780]|. Although not all steps in the pathway have been characterized the basic reaction sequence and corresponding gene products have been established. The first committed step of the pathway is catalyzed by the fusicoccadiene synthase forming the intermediate |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| from |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| with either |FRAME:DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| or |FRAME:CPD-4211| as allyl donors elongating the carbon chain and the subsequent cyclization reaction to form |FRAME:CPD-12805| |CITS:[19097780]|. The following hydroxylation of the C-8 and C-15 position is carried out by cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases which generate |FRAME:CPD-16827| |CITS:[19700326]|. The introduction of the 3-hydroxylgroup to |FRAME:CPD-16827| is catalyzed by a dioxygenase which, in coproduction with a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase produces |FRAME:CPD-16828|. Interestingly, the same enzyme is also involved in fusicoccin biosynthesis but promotes a different reaction there |CITS:[21299202]|. The last enzyme characterized so far is a methyltransferase which may catalyze the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16829|, however where exactly in the pathway the C-16 methylation occurs remains to be verified |CITS:[19097780]|.

Male fertility in |FRAME:TAX-4101| has been found to be linked to the formation of specific flavonols that only occur and accumulate in the gametophyte of the plant |CITS:[12244218]|. The flavonol diglycosides |FRAME:CPD-15105| and |FRAME:CPD-15106| are the only flavonoids found in wild-type |FRAME:TAX-4102| pollen |CITS:[Zerback89]| |CITS:[7630971]|. Conditional male fertility (CMF) observed in plants with suppressed chalcone synthase gene expression describes a condition where viable pollen are formed but are unable to germinate and start tube growth. The anthers of such plants are devoid of the flavonol diglycosides found in wild-type plants |CITS:[Taylor92]|. The arrested development can be rescued by adding external flavonols, i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-90| and |FRAME:CPD-520| which restores the normal development of the pollen |CITS:[12231878]|. The biochemical complementation overcomes the self-cross blockage in the pollen and is working at very low, micromolar concentrations of the flavonols |CITS:[11607312]|. , Two enzyme activities have been found which in a sequential manner glycosylate the aglycones to form the corresponding flavonol-3-O-glucosylgalactoside. The flavonol 3-O-galactosyltransferase (F3GalTase) catalyzing the formation of flavonol 3-O-galactosides has been identified in |FRAME:TAX-4101| pollen, cloned and recombinant expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. The recombinant F3GalTase shows remarkable high catalytic activities in both the forward and reverse direction and comes close to virtual catalytic perfection |CITS:[10567367]|. It had been previously shown that F3GalTase precedes the glucosylation step which completes the flavonol-3-O-glucosylgalactoside biosynthesis in pollen. The flavonol 3-O-galactoside-2"-O-glucosyltransferase (F2"GT) only acts on either |FRAME:CPD-7260| (this pathway) or |FRAME:CPD-13509| (see |FRAME:PWY-7192|) producing the flavonol glucosylgalactoside which have been shown to accumulate in the pollen cytoplasm |CITS:[7630971]|., Based upon the experimental data a model for the reproductive role of the pollen-specific flavonol glucosylgalctoside biosynthesis was suggested |CITS:[7630971]| |CITS:[Taylor98]|. It was proposed that the flavonol aglycone formation is compartmentally separated from the flavonol glucosylgalactoside biosynthesis. The flavonol aglycones are produced in the tapetum and internalized through an unknown mechanism in the pollen where they are glycosylated to form the flavonol glucosylgalactoside. Through this process the polar, chemical active and smaller molecules are converted to bulkier, chemical less active and more water-soluble molecules. Either the flavonol galactosyltransferase |CITS:[Taylor98]| and/or the flavonol 3-galactoside glucosyltransferase |CITS:[7630971]| are associated in a way with the pollen membrane to further the uptake of the flavonol aglycones. The flavonol glucosylgalctosides are then formed and accumulate in the pollen cytoplasm. The dual activity of the |FRAME:MONOMER-17892| might be responsible to maintain an enzymatically controlled pool of pollen reproduction active flavonols and pollen reproduction inactive flavonol diglycosides. However, this model does not solve the findings that neither flavonol aglycones (the active principle) nor flavonol 3-O-galactosides can be found in wild-type |FRAME:TAX-4101| pollen. It cannot be ruled out at this point that despite of the lack of experimental evidence the flavonol glucosylgalactosides are the active components for pollen fertility or trigger an unknown signal to initiate this process. Hence, further research is necessary to resolve the remaining problems.

Summary: In the anaerobic respiratory chain formed by NADH dehydrogenase and nitrate reductase the transfer of electrons from NADH to nitrate is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane (|CITS: [4385809], [5996] [776172]| and see |CITS: [9230919]|)., E. coli K-12 contains two NADH dehydrogenases - NDH-II (shown in this pathway) which does not contribute to the proton gradient and energy conserving NDH-I; both enzymes appear to be involved in anaerobic nitrate respiration |CITS: [7565112], [9063459]|. Nitrate respiration with NADH is only slightly affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II suggesting that NDH-II is used preferentially in nitrate respiration |CITS: [9063459]|., E. coli K-12 also contains two energy conserving (H+/e- = 1) nitrate reductases. Expression of nitrate reductase A (NRA) occurs in response to high levels of nitrate in the environment whereas expression of nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is not dependent on nitrate levels or anaerobiosis (|CITS: [10464201]| and see |CITS: [7747940]|)., Quinones are the obligate redox carriers during anaerobic nitrate respiration; the concentration of menaquinone increases in cells grown anaerobically with nitrate while the concentration of ubiquinone decreases (as compared with cells grown aerobically) |CITS: [195602]|. Nitrate reductase A can use both ubiquinol (shown in this pathway) and menaquinol as electron donors |CITS: [2204318], [1444716]|. In anaerobic growth with nitrate the major quinone is demethylmenaquinone (DMK) |CITS: [2849923]|; an E. coli strain containing only demethylmenaquinone is unable to grow with nitrate as terminal reductase |CITS: [1444716]|.

Summary: Note: this pathway has not been completely elucidated. The pathway shown here was proposed based on the analysis of mutants |CITS: [22221333]|. It will be updated as more information becomes available., General Background, Hopanoids are a diverse group of functionalized pentacyclic triterpenoids (also referred to as bacteriohopanepolyols) that are produced by some Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. Studies suggest that they function in maintaining membrane integrity and permeability, although they may have other undiscovered functions |CITS:[19592593][21873238][22221333]|. Hopanoids are known as molecular fossils because their hopane hydrocarbon skeletons are preserved in ancient sedimentary rocks and can serve as biomarkers for microbial metabolic evolution. Recent analyses suggest that hopanoids may also serve as biomarkers of cellular processes in present-day organisms. Genetic studies and bioinformatic analysis of the genes involved in hopanoid biosynthesis can potentially predict the phylogenetic distribution of these compounds (in |CITS: [22221333]| and in |CITS: [20421508]|)., The Gram-negative, purple non-sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1076| produces three classes of hopanoids: C30 hopanoids and |FRAME: CPD-11533| (a gammacerane-type triterpenoid); C35 hopanoids containing a polyhydroxylated side chain that may or may not have a terminal amino group; and C-2 methylated C30 hopanoids, C-2 methylated C35 hopanoids, and the C-2 methylated |FRAME: CPD-14517| |CITS: [22221333]|. , A hopanoid biosynthesis gene cluster has been identified and studied in |FRAME: TAX-1076| |CITS: [19592593][20421508][21873238][22221333]|. |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.17|, product of the |FRAME: G-15236| gene, has been biochemically characterized in this organism |CITS: [8305486]| and several other bacteria, particularly |FRAME: TAX-405212| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8508|). A squalene-tetrahymanol cyclase has been purified from the protist |FRAME: TAX-5911| (|CITS: [1892870]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21531832]|)., In addition, a gene required for C-3 methylation of hopanoids encoded by hpnR has been identified in the aerobic methanotroph |FRAME: TAX-243233| by phenotypic analysis of an hpnR deletion mutant. It was postulated that hpnR encodes a radical AdoMet protein, possibly containing a B-12 binding domain. However, the gene was not surrounded by other hopanoid biosynthesis genes on the chromosome. Homologs of hpnR were identified in a limited number of other species including aerobic acetic acid bacteria, a few other methanotrophs, and some species of |FRAME: TAX-32008|, |FRAME: TAX-1883| and |FRAME: TAX-407| |CITS: [22826256]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with the synthesis of |FRAME: SQUALENE| from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. This conversion, which is catalyzed in eukaryotes in a single step catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.21|, is catalyzed in most bacteria by three enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-44272|, |FRAME: G-44273| and |FRAME: G-44274| genes, which are located in the hopanoid biosynthesis gene cluster |CITS: [26258173]|., The rest of the pathway shown here was determined by analysis of certain deletion mutants created in the hopanoid biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-395960| and complementation studies of these mutants. Compounds present in total lipid extracts of the mutants were separated, derivatized (except |FRAME: HOPAN-22-OL|), and identified by high-temperature gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and/or liquid-chromatography-mass spectrometry |CITS: [22221333]|., Deletion of |FRAME: G-15236| resulted in loss of hopanoid production and extreme sensitivity to bile salts, suggesting that some hopanoids play a role in enhancing membrane integrity |CITS: [20421508][19592593]|. Deletion of hpnH resulted in production of only |FRAME: HOP-2229-ENE| (diploptene), |FRAME: HOPAN-22-OL| (diplopterol) and |FRAME: CPD-11533|. The ΔhpnH mutant was partially resistant to growth in the presence of bile salts, growing slower than wild-type. Thus, the production of C35 hopanoids is needed for full membrane integrity. Deletion of hpnG resulted in loss of |FRAME: CPD-14519| and |FRAME: CPD-14521| as well as accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-14522|. The latter compund has been shown to be an intermediate in hopanoid side chain biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-272630| |CITS: [-8]|. The compounds |FRAME: CPD-14523| and |FRAME: CPD-14524| are proposed intermediates in the pathway |CITS: [22221333]|. , Deletion of hpnO resulted in loss of |FRAME: CPD-14521| production, but not |FRAME: CPD-14519|. Production of the former compound was restored by re-introduction of the gene. It was annotated as a putative ornithine: oxo-acid aminotransferase and its function was also inferred by bioinformatic analysis. The putative intermediates |FRAME: CPD-14523| and |FRAME: CPD-14524| were not detected in this mutant, although ribosyl-hopane lactone was detected which is a possible oxidation artifact. The ΔhpnO mutant was able to grow in the presence of bile salts, suggesting that addition of an amino group to the polar head group does not enhance membrane integrity |CITS: [22221333]|., HpnP was annotated as a putative B-12 binding radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) protein |CITS: [20421508][22221333]| (and see |CITS: [22097883]|). This is reflected in the reaction equations shown here using |FRAME: CPD-9037| as the methyl group donor. Deletion of gene hpnP resulted in loss of production of C-2 methylated hopanoids, which could be restored by re-introduction of the gene. The ΔhpnP mutant was able to grow in the presence of bile salts, suggesting that C-2 methylation does not enhance membrane integrity |CITS: [20421508]|., HpnN (not shown) was characterized as a hopanoid-associated RND transporter. Phenotypic analyses of mutants suggested that it is involved in intracellular movement of hopanoids from the inner to the outer membrane |CITS: [21873238][22221333]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ALGINATE Alginate| is a major component of the cell walls of |FRAME: TAX-2870| (brown algae), and can make up to 45% of the total algal material. It is a linear polysaccharide of (1-4)-linked |FRAME: CPD-15205|, with variable amounts of its C-5 epimer |FRAME: CPD-15204| |CITS: [Schmidt26]|. The |FRAME: CPD-15205| (M) and |FRAME: CPD-15204| (G) residues are arranged in homopolymeric regions of M and G blocks, interspaced with regions of alternating structure (MG blocks). The physicochemical properties of alginate depend on both the overall M to G ratio and the relative proportions of the three block types in the chain. G block-rich alginate forms a high-strength gel in presence of divalent cations such as calcium, and is found in more rigid parts of the alga. Alginates rich in M or MG blocks are more flexible. The composition varies among species, and within an organism according to the nature and the age of the tissues as well as to the season and to the growing area. Depending on its composition, alginate can absorb 200-300 times its own weight in water, forming a viscous gum., Historically, alginate extracted from seaweed has had a wide variety of uses. Its unique physical properties enable it to be used as a stabilizer, viscosifier, and gelling agent in the food and beverage, paper and printing, biomaterials,, and pharmaceutical industries |CITS:[9283015][9393029][11018131][12149954][16183570][20581859][25300542]|. Commercial varieties of alginate are extracted from several species, including the giant kelp |FRAME: TAX-35122|, |FRAME: TAX-52969|, and various types of |FRAME: TAX-33637|., The alginates formed by brown algae are non-acetylated. An acetylated form of alginate is produced by bacteria that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-286| and |FRAME: TAX-352| genera. The higher the degree of O-acetylation, the higher the viscosity and pseudoplastic rheology of the alginate |CITS: [Skjak-Braek88]|. The biological function of alginates differs between the two genera. In |FRAME: TAX-286| alginate is associated with biofilms, promoting bacterial adherence to target cell walls |CITS: [3155514]|. Alginate production is a major contributing factor in chronic pulmonary infections by |FRAME: TAX-287|, the causative agent of cystic fibrosis |CITS: [3155514]|. Most strains of |FRAME: TAX-287| do not produce alginate, although alginate is always produced in the lung of CF pateints. it is believed that alginate encapsulation protects the infecting bacterial cells from phagocytosis, as well as from antibiotic therapy. , In |FRAME: TAX-352| alginate is a structural element in the wall of the cyst, a desiccation-resistant capsule that is formed under adverse environmental conditions |CITS: [16912921]|., About This Pathway, The main difference between algal and bacterial alginate biosynthesis lies in the length of the polysaccaharide and the fact that bacterial alginates are acetylated., Generally, the alginate biosynthesis pathway can be divided into four different stages: synthesis of precursor substrate, polymerization and cytoplasmic membrane transfer, periplasmic transfer and modification, and export through the outer membrane., Twelve of the proteins required for the biosynthesis of alginate in |FRAME: TAX-287| are are encoded by the algD operon (|FRAME: G-10982| |FRAME: G-43910| |FRAME: G-43911| |FRAME: G-43914| |FRAME: G-43916| |FRAME: G-43912| |FRAME: G-43915| |FRAME: G-43913| |FRAME: G-43920| |FRAME: G-43918| |FRAME: G-43919| |FRAME: G-10182|), while another protein, |FRAME: G-43921 AlgC|, is encoded elsewhere |CITS: [7686997][21991261]|., The precursor substrate, |FRAME: CPD-1828|, is formed from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-14396| (|FRAME: G-10982|) |CITS: [2470755]| (the production of |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| from central metabolism precursors is described in |FRAME: PWY-5659|)., |FRAME: CPD-1828| is polymerized into a polymannuronate chain by the inner membrane glycosyltransferase, |FRAME: G-43910 Alg8|, with some involvement of |FRAME: G-43911 Alg44|. Alg8 has multiple transmembrane domains and a large cytoplasmic glycosyltransferase domain and forms the catalytic subunit of the polymerase |CITS: [18524915]|, while Alg44 has a single transmembrane domain separating a cytoplasmic |FRAME: C-DI-GMP|-binding domain and a large C-terminal periplasmic domain, and is thought to endoe a regulatory subunit |CITS: [16797016][17645452][18524915]|., Upon polymerization, the nascent polymannuronate chain is proposed to be translocated across the periplasm by a periplasmic scaffold composed of |FRAME: G-43912 AlgG|, |FRAME: G-43913 AlgL|, |FRAME: G-43914 AlgK|, |FRAME: G-43915 AlgX|, and |FRAME: G-43916 AlgE| |CITS: [9457868][12581364][15489449][16177314][20097812]|. The complex pans the entire bacterial envelope fraction |CITS: [23335756]|. , The proteins that form the scaffold have well-understood functions beside contributing to the integrity of the periplasmic scaffold. AlgG is an epimerase that acts on the |FRAME: CPD-15205| residues in the nascent chain (see below); AlgL serves as an alginate-degrading enzyme |CITS: [16177314][15901714]|; AlgE forms an electropositive β-barrel pore in the outer membrane through which the nascent alginate is secreted out of the cell |CITS: [7521870][20097812][21778407]|; AlgK, which is attached to the outer membrane with a lipid moiety, contributes to the correct localization of the AlgE porin |CITS: [20159471]|; and AlgX is an O-acetylase (see below) |CITS: [15489449][16376476][21713511]|. All of these proteins are essential for alginate secretion |CITS: [8550492][9457868][15489449]|. , During the secretion process, while in the periplasm, the nascent alginate chain is modified in two ways. First, |FRAME: CPD-15205| residues are selectively O-acetylated at O2' and/or O3' positions by the action of |FRAME: G-43920 AlgI|, |FRAME: G-43918 AlgJ|, |FRAME: G-43919 AlgF| and |FRAME: G-43915 AlgX| |CITS:[8636017][12003941]|. Second, some |FRAME: CPD-15205| residue are converted into |FRAME: CPD-15204| by |FRAME: G-43912 AlgG|, an epimerase that is a component of the proposed periplasmic scaffold |CITS: [5368261][5150892][8144447][12581364]|.

|FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., In high concentrations, it causes death in humans and animals because of its corrosive effects, while smaller amounts can cause various pathological disorders, including hyperoxaluria, calcium oxalate stones, pyridoxine deficiency, and even renal failure., In oxalate-accumulating plants, calcium oxalate crystal accumulation occurs in specialized idioblast cells. The crystals are thought to deter herbivore feeding |CITS: [16514014]| and may also serve a role in regulating free calcium levels |CITS: [15862089]|., |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.8|, the key enzyme in this pathway, was originally reported from extracts of seeds from peas |CITS: [13705596][16655888]| and eventually also from lupin, pumpkin and wheat germ |CITS: [4288975]|., The |FRAME: AT3G48990| gene that encodes the enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-3702| was discovered many years later.  Assays with several carboxylic and fatty acids yielded very low activity, indicating that the enzyme is highly specific for |FRAME: OXALATE|. Two mutant strains were shown to have three-fold higher levels of oxalate compared with the wild type and to have reduced and delayed germination, indicating that the enzyme is required in Arabidopsis for oxalate degradation |CITS: [22447686]|., Studies of the orthologous enzyme from yeast suggested that the enzyme catalyzes the first step in an oxalate degradation pathway. Since no other oxalate degrading enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.2|, or |FRAME: EC-1.2.3.4|, have been found in yeast, the AAE3-dependent pathway of oxalate degradation may be the sole pathway of degrading |FRAME: OXALATE| to CO<sub>2</sub> in yeast |CITS: [24291261]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In |FRAME: TAX-810| additional Kdo units are added by a (2->8) or (2->4) linkages (see |FRAME: PWY-6467|). The actual donor of Kdo units is its activated form, |FRAME: CMP-KDO|., Many organisms have monofunctional enzymes that catalyze one of these steps. |FRAME: TAX-562| has a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes the addition of two Kdo units with different glycosidic linkages., Kdo-containing |FRAME: LIPID-IV-A| molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety., There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are also synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

Summary: Background, There is a growing need to find renewable biologically produced compounds as replacements for petroleum-based fuels. Due to the branched and ringed structures found in their hydrocarbon chain, isoprenoid compounds have great potential to serve as biofuels. The branching improves the cetane number and the C15 isoprenoid bisabolane has a cetane number of 52. The cetane number is a unit that measures the combustion attributes of diesel with a value between 40-60 being optimal |CITS: [MURLEY]|. Bisabolane can be produced commercially via a hybrid method, a microbial process is used to generate bisabolene which is then chemically reduced to bisabolane |CITS: [21952217]|., Like other isoprenoid based biofuels, bisabolene is derived from the C5 precursors, isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and dimethyl alleyl diphosphate (DMAPP). These two compounds are derived from two distinct pathways: the |FRAME: PWY-922| (MVA) and the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (MEP), also known as deoxyxylulose pathway.The MVA pathway is more energetically favorable than the MEP pathway as it generates protons which can be used to generate ATP, and does not require an input of ATP per se |CITS: [MURLEY]|., About this Pathway, The |FRAME: PWY-922| and |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| in |FRAME: TAX-4932| and E.coli respectively, have been deregulated to overexpress the relevant isoprenoid precursors |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP "Isopentenyl diphosphate| (IPP) and |FRAME: CPD-4211| (DMAPP) |CITS: [22895337]|. These are precursors to E,E farnesyl diphosphate which is converted to bisabolene via |FRAME: MONOMER-12817|, a flux controlling enzyme that was originally identified in |FRAME: TAX-46611 | |CITS: [9618485]|. The gene for |FRAME: MONOMER-12817| has been engineered into both |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-4932| for the synthetic production of bisabolene |CITS: [22895337]|.

Glutamate synthase (glutamine-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, GOGAT) is an important enzyme involved in ammonia (nitrogen) assimilation., Many plants, including Arabidopsis, have both NADH-dependent and ferredoxin-dependent GOGAT enzymes. The ferredoxin-dependent GOGAT is the predominant form found in Arabidopsis. Ferredoxin-dependent enzymes are also found in |FRAME: TAX-1117|, such as |FRAME: TAX-1148| |CITS: [7727752]|., There are two genes in Arabidopsis encoding Fd-GOGAT. |FRAME: AT5G04140| is primarily expressed in the leaves and its expression is induced by light and sucrose, whereas GLU2 is preferentially expressed in roots. |FRAME: AT5G04140| plays a major role in assimilating the large amount of ammonia released from photorespiration and is also involved in primary nitrogen assimilation in leaves. GLU2 may be involved in primary nitrogen assimilation in roots |CITS:[SOMERVILLE80][9057836][9596633]|.

Summary: Background, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| is a linear polysaccharide found in all animal tissues. It occurs as a proteoglycan in which two or three heparan sulfate chains are attached to cell surface or extracellular matrix proteins, known as "core proteins". |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| binds to diverse protein ligands (known as heparin-binding proteins) and regulates a wide variety of biological activities, including developmental processes, cell adhesion and motility, angiogenesis, blood coagulation and tumour metastasis., The molecule is built of |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| chains attached to specific serine residues in a core protein. The chains are composed of a simple sugar backbone that is modified to different degrees depending on the cellular conditions. The backbone is built of several types of disaccharide building units with different sulfation patterns and can accomodate over 1,000,000 different sequences built up of up to 200 disaccharide units |CITS: [11102866]|., The disaccharide building units are composed of a hexose sugar and a uronic acid. The most common repeating unit, which makes up around 50% of the total disaccharide units in heparan sulfate, is composed of |FRAME: CPD-12521| linked to |FRAME: CPD-12541|. In other units |FRAME: CPD-12521| may be substituted by |FRAME: CPD-12515| or its sulfated form |FRAME: CPD-12518|, and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| may be sulfated to |FRAME: N-sulfo-D-glucosamine|, |FRAME: CPD-12533|, |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-3-N-disulfate| or |FRAME:Heparan-Glc-N-3-6-trisulfate|., |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate "Heparan sulfate"| chains comprise three different types of domains: S-domains that contain contiguous N-sulfated residues, unmodified N-acetyl-rich regions, and mixed transition zones between the S-domains and the unmodified segments. Only the S-domains have binding capacities for growth factors and other proteins |CITS: [11489926]|. The structure of |FRAME: HEPARIN| is very similar, but its chains are not organized into distinct sulfated and non-sulfated domains |CITS: [15047699]|., The synthesis of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| takes place in the Golgi apparatus, with the exception of the first reaction, the attachemnt of xylose to the core protein, which takes place within the endoplasmic reticulum., About This Pathway, The synthesis of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| begins with the formation of a tetrasaccharide linkage region on the core protein, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|. Once the linkage region is synthesized, a key reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME: HS08719| and |FRAME: HS00333|, adds an |FRAME: CPD-12541| residue to the linkage region tetrasaccharide. This addition is a molecular switch that prevents the synthesis of |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| or |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| on the linkage region., The chain is then elongated by the |FRAME: CPLX-8112|, a bifunctional protein composed of |FRAME: HS00012| and |FRAME: HS07726| units, that can add both |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12541| in an alternating manner to the nascent chain. Once the basic backbone is synthesized, many enzymes alter the structure., A key enzyme is the bifunctional |FRAME: HS01001-MONOMER "heparan sulfate N-deacetylase/N-sulfotransferase"| (4 isoforms are encoded by |FRAME: HS01001|, |FRAME: HS09410|, |FRAME: HS09011| and |FRAME: HS06527|). The enzyme removes the acetyl groups from |FRAME: Heparan-NAc-Glc| residues in what would become S-regions, and sulfates the free NH2 groups, resulting in |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-D-GlcNS|., |FRAME: HS11947-MONOMER "Heparosan-N-sulfate-glucuronate 5-epimerase"| (|FRAME: HS11947|) converts |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues to |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues. |FRAME: ENSG00000153936-MONOMER "[Heparan sulfate]-uronosyl-2-O-sulfotransferase 1"| (|FRAME: HS07933|), which interacts with |FRAME: HS11947|, transfers a sulfate group to the C2 position of the |FRAME: CPD-12515| residues., Finally, a set of 3-O-sulfotransferases and 6-O-sulfotransferases act on the |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-D-GlcNS| residues, resulting in formation of the bi-sulfated forms |FRAME: Heparan-sulfate-3-N-disulfate|, |FRAME: Heparan-GlcN-6-N-bisulfate| and the triple-sulfated |FRAME: Heparan-Glc-N-3-6-trisulfate| residues.

The fungi belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-68776| are unique group of fungi, commonly called the "bird's nest fungi" due to their appearance resembling tiny bird's nests filled with eggs. In 1966 a new species of the genus was described from the Canadian Rockies and named |FRAME: TAX-380658| |CITS: [Brodie66]|. In the following year a Masters thesis published at the University of Alberta reported that the organism produced substance with antibiotic activity. The antibiotic, which was named "cyathin", inhibited the growth of several Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [Olchowecki67]|. Further research published in 1971 reported that "|FRAME: Cyathins cyathin|" is a complex of multiple compounds, seven of which were isolated at the time: |FRAME: CPD-26073|, |FRAME: CPD-26040|, |FRAME: CPD-26090|, |FRAME: CPD-26091|, |FRAME: CPD-26074|, |FRAME: CPD-26082|, and |FRAME: CPD-26087| |CITS: [5156938]|., Since that time many more members of the |FRAME: Cyathins cyathin| family have been discovered in multiple species of |FRAME: TAX-68776|, some of which showing interesting biological activities. For example |FRAME: CPD-26078| was found to have a strong anticancer activity |CITS: [26871659]|, and several compounds from |FRAME: TAX-380649| display significant acetylcholinesterase inhibitory effect |CITS: [34700067]|., Studies in the late 1970s concluded that |FRAME: CPD-26030| is a common initially-formed intermediate during the biosynthesis of cyathins and the related erinacines |CITS: [Ayer79]|, and this conclusion was confirmed in 2001 with the isolation of the compound from the erinacine-producing basidiomycete |FRAME: TAX-91752| |CITS: [Kenmoku01]|. The terpene cyclase that catalyzes the formation of this compound was discovered in 2017, along with the erinacine biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS: [28371074]|. Subsequent cloning and expression of the genes in the Ascomycota host |FRAME: TAX-5062| enabled the elucidation of the full biosynthetic pathway leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-26042| and |FRAME: CPD-26040| |CITS: [31535864]|., Following the generation of |FRAME: CPD-26030|, the pathway continues with three successive hydroxylations carried out by three different cytochrome P450 enzymes, forming |FRAME: CPD-26039|. The hydroxyl group at C14 could be either oxidized to an oxo group, leading to production of cyathins, or glycosylated with a xylosyl sugar, leading to production of erinacines |CITS: [31535864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8408|).

Summary: Fatty acids are often found in the cell in the activated form of an acyl-coA. Acyl-CoAs are used in the biosynthesis of many cellular products and components. In plants they are involved in the biosynthesis of membrane lipids, seed storage lipids, |FRAME: Wax-Esters wax|, |FRAME: Cutins cutins| and |FRAME: Suberins suberin|., Intracellular membranes are generally barriers for acyl-CoAs, preventing their movement within the cell. To circumvent this limitation, fatty acids are transported in their free form, and converted to acyl-CoAs while crossing the membrane by the enzymes acyl-CoA synthetases (ACS). These enzymes catalyze the esterification of fatty acids into the CoA thioesters concomitant with transport. In plant cells, ACS activity has been detected in plastids, oil bodies, peroxisomes, mitochondria, and the ER., The activated fatty-CoAs can be hydrolyzed back to free acids (see |FRAME: PWY-5148|)., The Arabidopsis genome contains nine functional genes encoding long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase - |FRAME: AT2G47240|, |FRAME: AT1G49430|, |FRAME: AT1G64400|, |FRAME: AT4G23850|, |FRAME: AT4G11030|, |FRAME: AT3G05970|, |FRAME: AT5G27600|, |FRAME: AT2G04350| and |FRAME: AT1G77590| |CITS: [12177484]|. Genetic and biochemical evidence have sorted the physiological roles of some of them., The plastidial |FRAME: AT1G77590| contributes to the activation of de novo synthesized fatty acids during their exporting from the chloroplast |CITS: [12177483]|. |FRAME: AT3G05970| and |FRAME: AT5G27600| are peroxisome-localized and are involved in fatty acids β-oxidation (|FRAME: PWY-5136|) in the peroxisome |CITS: [12366803]|. |FRAME: AT1G49430| is required for |FRAME: PWY-321|, where it was shown to activate the cutin monomer |FRAME: 16-HYDROXYPALMITATE| |CITS: [14973169]|.
