Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, The pathway depicted here involves a one-step direct condensation of |FRAME: CHOLINE| with CDP-diacylglycerol to form phosphatidylcholine by the bacterial enzyme phosphatidylcholine synthase (EC 2.7.8.24)., This pathway is found in bacteria that interact with eukaryotic cells. |FRAME: CHOLINE| is obtained from the eukaryotic host and the biosynthesis of bacterial phosphatidylcholine is necessary for successful symbiosis. Both this pathway and pathway |FRAME: PWY-6825| are present in |FRAME: TAX-358| and |FRAME: TAX-382|. The pathway shown here is the preferred pathway in |FRAME: TAX-235|, |FRAME: TAX-446| and |FRAME: TAX-287|. It may be a minor pathway in |FRAME: TAX-375| |CITS: [17993534]| (reviewed in |CITS:[20656373][12848422][14663079]|)., In the human and animal pathogens |FRAME: TAX-235|, |FRAME: TAX-446|, |FRAME: TAX-447 "Fluoribacter bozemanae (previously known as Legionella bozemanae)"| and |FRAME: TAX-139| and the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-358|, phosphatidylcholine synthesized by this pathway appears to be a virulence determinant |CITS: [16484204][16882035][17979985][14766917][18978052][20437057]|.

The conversion of |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| to |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| is part of the systemic acquired resistance (SAR) in plants. Plant defense is based on the interaction between pathogen and host on the molecular level, often referred to as gene-for-gene interaction |CITS:[2088175]| which elicits a response such as ion flux changes, increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) or the release/production of |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate|, nitric oxide and increased expression of pathogen related (PR) genes |CITS:[11459065]|. The hydroxybenzoate |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| has been recognized as a stress hormone that functions as a signal in the SAR pathway in plants |CITS:[7858199]|. It has been proposed to be involved in the activation of plant defensive actions at both the infection as well as distal, uninfected sites, hence acting systemically |CITS:[Dempsey99]|. Plants attacked by pathogens often accumulate high amounts of |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| |CITS:[17746925]|. |FRAME:CPD-110 Salicylate| can be metabolized in plants in various ways and may occur as a methylated |CITS:[Shulaev97] [9489012]| (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-22 methylsalicylate biosynthesis|) or glucose conjugated compound |CITS:[12297650]| (compare also with |FRAME:PWY18C3-21 phenylpropanoid volatiles glycoconjugation (tomato)|)., The expression of pathogen related (PR) genes in tobacco when infected with the tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) is similar to PR gene expressions after treatment with exogenous |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| |CITS:[18631626]|. At the same time levels of |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| rise up in response to pathogen invasion |CITS:[Shulaev97] [Seskar98]|. Aside from pathogen infections systemic acquired resistance (SAR) has been reported to be induced by a number of chemicals such as the above mentioned |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| but also the synthetic compound |FRAME:CPD-19219 acibenzolar-S-methyl| |CITS:[8758979 ] [Ishii99]| and at least for local resistance |FRAME:CPD-19222 2,2,2,2'-tetra-fluoroacetophenone| |CITS:[20687805] [19131332]|. The former is widely used in agriculture because of its low toxicological impact on plants compared to commercially used pesticides |CITS:[Friedrich96] [8624439]|. , The plant immune system is fine-tuned to attacks of pathogens and may respond directly or indirectly in various ways, for instance in form of a hypersensitive response (HR) |CITS:[17108957]|. There are still many open questions regarding the SAR immune response in plants but a clearer picture of the process has been obtained over the last years (reviewed in |CITS:[7858199] [Vidhyasekaran15]|). Although |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| has been reported to be involved in many developmental processes in plants including thermogenesis |CITS:[17834449]| and stresses of biotic or abiotic nature the main focus of research was upon its role in plant immune responses and respective signaling pathways. The mechanism through which |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| operates in the SAR immune response appears to be via |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate|, which functions as a mobile signal in the phloem |CITS:[17916738]| and is re-converted to |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| at the target issues by the action of the methylsalicylate esterase. The released |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| then initiates the SAR response and induces the expression of NPR genes |CITS:[15337097]|. The latter, particularly NPR1 might be induced via redox changes |CITS:[12837250]| and has also been shown to interact with other NPR genes |CITS:[22785561] [22699612]|. However, not all immune responses in plants are upregulated in the same way. Some defense related pathways are responsive to |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| but independent of NPR1 |CITS:[19820324] [21535470]|. Consequently, |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| may not act as an receptor in the traditional sense but through many targets in various developmental processes related to biochemistry, physiology and pathology in plants and animals (|CITS:[14673096] [25584724]| and summarized in |CITS:[27303403]|). , The purified methylsalicylate esterase from Nicotiana tabacum (SABP2) |CITS:[12223676]| was studied with respect to local and systemic resistance against the tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) |CITS:[14673096]|. Biochemical and structural research of the protein revealed the high affinity towards |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| which allows the regulation of the enzyme at distal, unaffected tissues. The catalytic triad characteristic for the α/β hydrolase superfamily (Ser-81, His-238, and Asp-210) was present in SABP2 with Ser-81 being determined as essential for esterase activity |CITS:[15668381]|. The SABP2 encoded protein was shown to also catalyze the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-19219 acibenzolar-S-methyl| to |FRAME:CPD-19221 acibenzolar|. Interestingly, SABP2 silenced plants treated with |FRAME:CPD-19219 acibenzolar-S-methyl| (ASM) were unable to induce the expression of pathogenesis related (PR) genes, especially PR-1 whereas the same plants treated with the esterase product, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-19221 acibenzolar| elicit a SAR response. This indicates that the SABP2 encoded methylsalicylate esterase does not act as receptor in the SAR immune response but rather as a biochemical mediator in the SAR signaling pathway |CITS:[20621100]|. In contrast to tobacco which has very low concentrations of |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| in non-induced tissues, potato (Solanum tuberosum) contains naturally rather high amounts of |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| |CITS:[Coquoz95]|. Nevertheless, the methylsalicyl esterase (MES1) characterized from potato exhibited not only comparable biochemical properties but also, via its catalyzed reaction to form |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| from |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate|, elicited corresponding immune responses in this plant. In general, silencing of MES1 in Solanum tuberosum resulted in a different SAR, increased the level of |FRAME:CPD-6442 methylsalicylate| at induced leaves under concurrent decreased levels of |FRAME:CPD-110 salicylate| at distal, untreated tissues and diminished the expression of pathogen-related (PR) genes, e.g. PR-1 |CITS:[20687805]|.

In this eukaryotic route of aspartate degradation, aspartate is converted to malate as part of the reversible malate-aspartate shuttle.  This pathway spans the mitochondrial and cytoplasmic spaces, transferring reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane.  It is one of several shuttle mechanisms used to transfer electrons from cytosolic NADH produced by glycolysis into the mitochondrion, because NADH itself cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.  Inside the mitochondrion, NADH can be oxidized by the electron transport chain to produce ATP.  , In the cytosolic reactions of this shuttle shown here, oxaloacetate produced by transamination of aspartate is reduced to malate by electrons from NADH.  Malate is transported into the mitochondrial matrix via the malate-α-ketoglutarate carrier.  There, malate is oxidized by NAD<sup>+</sup> back to oxaloacetate, forming NADH.  Mitochondrial oxaloacetate (which also does not readily cross the inner mitochondrial membrane) is transaminated to aspartate, which can be transported back to the cytosol via the glutamate-aspartate carrier.  In the cytosol, oxaloacetate is regenerated by transamination of aspartate.  Because this shuttle is reversible, electrons from NADH are brought into the mitochondrion when the NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio is higher in the cytosol than in the mitochondrial matrix.  The malate-aspartate shuttle yields approximately 3 molecules of ATP per molecule of cytosolic NADH |CITS: [VOET04]|.    , In mammals, this shuttle is found in liver, heart and kidney.  The malate-aspartate shuttle may be present in fungi |CITS: [14622413]|.  In plants, however, a malate/oxaloacetate shuttle has been described |CITS: [14671011]|., The first reaction shown here, on its own, serves as an aspartate degradation pathway (see pathway |FRAME: ASPARTATE-DEG1-PWY|).  The reaction is reversible and can also function in aspartate biosynthesis (see pathway |FRAME: ASPARTATESYN-PWY|).

Names: succinate to cytochrome bo quinol oxidase (cyanobacteria, cytoplamic membrane) // aerobic respiration (alternative oxidase)
Summary: General Background, Cyanobacteria are able to conduct both photosynthesis and respiration and have evolved a electron transport pathways that operate under both conditions. Another important electron transfer pathway these organisms must operate is cyclic electron flow, which allows them to generate proton motive force without producing reducing power. An additional requirement the organisms face is the ability to dissipate excess electron flow, which could happen when light and environmental conditions change rapidly., Like most cyanobacterial species, |FRAME: TAX-84588| possesses two membrane systems: the cytoplasmic membrane and a series of internal thylakoid membranes. The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes, as does a resipratory electron chain, while an additional respiratory electron transfer chain is localized in the cytoplasmic membrane., The only electron-transfer quinone found in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone| (PQ), which is shared among the photosynthetic light reactions and the respiratory electron chain. Three other components - |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76|, the small copper protein |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER|, are also shared between the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transfer chains., It has been shown that the major electron source for the respiratory pathways is |FRAME: SUC|, which feeds into |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-18| (SDH), an enzyme complex that contributes to the proton gradient |CITS: [11418566]|. It is less clear whether the organisms utilize NADPH or NADH as an electron source. Two types of NAD(P)H dehydrogenase-like enzymes are present - NDH-1, of which several different complexes are present |CITS: [1907569]| and |FRAME: TX72_RS01490-MONOMER NDH-2| |CITS: [11418566]|. An emerging understanding of these enzymes suggests that NDH-1 complexes are only involved in cyclic electron flow |CITS: [30573545][32060291]|, and questions the role of NDH-2 enzymes in respiration as well |CITS: [10383967][30847494]|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes a cytoplasmic electron transfer chain that transfers electrons from |FRAME: SUC| to oxygen. The chain includes the |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-18|, |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone|, and |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-26|., Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) is a part of the respiratory chain of cyanobacteria. It appears to be located both in the thylakoid membrane, where it is interwoven with photosynthetic processes, and in the cytoplasmic membrane. Studies in |FRAME: TAX-1148| have shown that succinate dehydrogenase has a major effect on the plastoquinone (PQ) redox poise, as mutants lacking this enzyme showed a much more oxidized PQ pool. The electron donation capacity of succinate dehydrogenase was found to be an order of magnitude larger than that of the type I and II NAD(P)H dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX1YI0-20| and |FRAME: TX72_RS01490-MONOMER|), indicating that in that organism succinate dehydrogenase is the main respiratory electron transfer pathway into the PQ pool |CITS: [11418566]|., The electrons from SDH are transferred to PQ, which diffuses through the cytoplasmic membrane. Most of the cyanobacterial terminal oxidases are located only in the thylakoid membrane |CITS: [11466301][12543932][15548742][19577535]|. The only oxidase that was found in the cytoplasmic membrane is |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-26| (ARTO) |CITS: [12543932][16400685][17288559]|. , Like the cytochrome aa3-type cytochrome c oxidase, ARTO complexes appear to be members of the heme-copper superfamily. Members of this family reduce molecular oxygen to water and couple electron transfer with the pumping of protons, leading to ATP production. However, the alternative respiratory terminal oxidases are not typical cytochrome c oxidases because they lack the binding site for the binuclear center CuA in subunit II and a Mg2+ binding site in subunit I |CITS: [9922162]| and show very low, perhaps negligible, activity in the standard in vitro assays of oxidation of reduced horse heart cytochrome c |CITS: [Schmetterer94]|, so the function of this enzyme is currently uncertain., The ARTO of |FRAME: TAX-1148|, which is located only in the cytoplasmic membrane, was originally described as a cytochrome bo-type quinol oxidase |CITS: [9922162]|. Later results, however, have suggested that in vivo, it can oxidize cytochrome c6 |CITS: [11583851]|., The presence of ATP synthase in the membrane supports the presence of a proton gradient across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [12543932]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Strigolactones Strigolactones| are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi., The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635 "Gossypium hirsutum (cotton)"| infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels |CITS: [17780042]|., Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| |CITS: [Hauck92]|, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| |CITS: [Mueler92]| and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) |CITS: [Yokota98]|., The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis |CITS: [15944687]|., The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone |CITS: [Mosse73]|., Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interaction between the fungi and the roots., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14657 Orobanchol| is a strigolactone compound originally isolated from the root exudates of red clover (|FRAME: TAX-57577|) based on its ability to stimulate germination of |FRAME: TAX-36748| seeds |CITS: [Yokota98]|. It has been later detected in the root exudates of numerous plants, including Fabaceae, Solanaceae, a few Gymnosperm species, and rice. , The genuine structure of orobanchol was established in 2011 |CITS: [21899364]|. Based on the structure, all strigolactones have been divided into two subgroups - the orobanchol-type and strigol-type, which differ in their C-ring configuration., Orobanchol is produced from |FRAME: CPD-14651| in two routes - either directly, or via a |FRAME: CPD-28128| intermediate |CITS: [32064317][35222492]|. The enzymes catalyzing the indirect route have been characterized from several plants, including rice (|FRAME: TAX-4530|) |CITS: [25344813][29479714]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-9 Ubiquinone-9| (Q-9) is the major quinone of several large families of aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, including the the γ-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-135621| |CITS:[13869492][13673033] [14429752][4886765 ]| and the phototrophic α-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-41295| |CITS:[13673033][5727384][Sasaki79]|. Pseudomonads are known to have ubiquinones exclusively |CITS: [6774977]| (while Q-9 is their major form, they often produce smaller amounts of Q-6, Q-7 and Q-8). Members of the |FRAME: TAX-41295| family, on the other hand, were reported to also produce menaquinones, such as MK-9 |CITS: [5727384]|., Q-9 is also common in fungi and animals. For discussion of its biosynthesis in eukaryotic organisms, see |FRAME: PWY-5871|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, also known as vitamin C, fulfils multiple essential roles in both plants and animals., Being a strong reducing agent, it functions as an antioxidant and a redox buffer. It is also a cofactor for several enzymes, which are involved in many important pathways, including collagen hydroxylation, carnitine biosynthesis, norepinephrine biosynthesis, and hormone and tyrosine metabolism., In plants L-ascorbate is also implicated in defense against pathogens and in control of plant growth and development., A significant proportion of a plant's ascorbate is found in the apoplast (the aqueous solution permeating the cell walls) |CITS: [15608627]|., Under aerobic conditions L-ascorbate is oxidized in cells to |FRAME: CPD-13907 dehydroascorbate| (via the radical |FRAME: CPD-318|), which can be recycled back to ascorbate by the |FRAME: PWY-2261|. However, once formed, dehydroascorbate can be further broken down in vivo by irreversible reactions, escaping the |FRAME: PWY-2261|., Several pathways for the irreversible catabolism of ascorbate have been described. Facultatively aerobic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-573| degrade L-ascorbate by different pathways under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6961| and |FRAME: PWY0-301|). The anaerobic pathway begins with phosphorylation of ascorbate (mediated by a PTS-type transporter), while the aerobic pathway proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-334|. Both pathways produce |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a centeral metabolite that is fed into the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [18708499]|., Plants from the |FRAME: TAX-3602| family (e.g. grapes) metabolize ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-13059| and |FRAME: L-IDONATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6704|). The tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 1-4 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 4 and 5 |CITS: [Loewus99][16567629]|. , The geraniaceous plant |FRAME: TAX-1417776| metabolizes ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| and |FRAME: OXALATE| via a different pathway, with |FRAME: L-THREONATE|, rather than L-idonate, as an intermediate (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6960|). In this case the tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 3-6 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 2 and 3 |CITS:[Loewus99][15862089]|. Grapes are also known to accumulate |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [DeBolt04]|, and thus may be using both pathways to generate tartrate., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TARTRATE| is found in many plants, particularly in grapes, bananas and tamarinds. It is the principle acid found in wine, contributing important aspects to the taste, mouthfeel and aging potential of wine. , The pathway leading from ascorbate to tartrate in grapes has been deduced from radiotracer studies and shown to proceed via |FRAME: L-IDONATE| |CITS: [16567629]|. Radiotracer studies showed that the tartrate skeleton was derived from carbons 1-4 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 4 and 5 |CITS: [16659212][Loewus99][16567629]|. This pathway appears to occur only in grape and other vitaceous plants |CITS:[16663792][Malipiero87]|., At this time only one enzyme of the pathway has been identified from grapevine. The NAD-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-16192| catalyzes reversible conversion of |FRAME: L-IDONATE| and |FRAME: 5-DEHYDROGLUCONATE|. A deletion of the L-idonate 5-dehydrogenase gene was found in a non-tartrate-forming grape species that accumulates excess level of L-ascorbate |CITS: [16567629]|, indicating a possible way to manipulate grapes for desired high vitamin C content. The subsequent reaction, C4/C5 cleavage of 5-keto-D-gluconate, involves an unknown hydrolase |CITS: [Saito97]|.

Summary: Many bacterial species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: ACETOIN| and |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2,3-butanediol"| via, |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|., There are three isomeric forms of 2,3-butanediol (BD ) - |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|, |FRAME: CPD-346| and |FRAME: CPD-12004|, and two isomeric forms of acetoin - |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: CPD-255|., Acetoin reductases (AR, also known as 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenases or BDH) catalyze a reversible reaction between 2,3-butanediol and acetoin, as well as the irreversible reduction of |FRAME: DIACETYL|. Four types of AR enzymes have been identified, differing in substrate specificity; an R-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: CPD-12004|, an S-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: CPD-12004|, an S-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: CPD-346|, and an R-acetoin reductase forming |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| |CITS: [Ui84]|., The |FRAME: G-6713| gene of |FRAME: TAX-573| was cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and shown to catalyze the reversible formation of |FRAME: CPD-10353| from |FRAME: CPD-12004|, as well as the production of |FRAME: CPD-255| from |FRAME: DIACETYL| |CITS: [Ui97]|. , In a subsequent study, the enzyme was introduced into |FRAME:TAX-562| for its diacetyl reductase activity, along with the, acetoin reductase from |FRAME: TAX-1718|, which converts |FRAME: CPD-255| to |FRAME: CPD-346| |CITS: [15548307]|. Summary: |FRAME: CPD-11752 "Rebeccamycin"| is a secondary metabolite isolated from cultures of the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-68170| in 1985 (it is named after the daughter of the scientist who isolated the compound) |CITS: [Nettleton85]|. |FRAME: CPD-11752 "Rebeccamycin"| consists of a halogenated indolocarbazole chromophore to which is attached a 4-0-methylglucose via an N-glycosidic linkage |CITS: [3204382]|. , Indolocarbazole compounds from natural sources are often powerful inhibitors of protein kinases or DNA topoisomerases. For example, |FRAME: STAUROSPORINE| is the strongest inhibitor of phospholipid-Ca2+-dependent protein kinase (protein kinase C), with an IC50 of only 2.7 nM., |FRAME: CPD-11752 "Rebeccamycin"| intercalates into the DNA and is an inhibitor of topoisomerase I. It stabilizes the covalent topoisomerase I-DNA intermediate (the cleavable complex) resulting in increased DNA strand breaks |CITS: [10052965]|. It inhibits DNA topoisomerase I with an IC50 of 1.75 μM in vitro, and inhibits the growth of human lung adenocarcinoma cells with a GI50 of 6.0 μg/ml in vivo |CITS: [3112080]|. DNA topoisomerases are important in cell proliferation, so specific inhibitors are promising candidates for antitumor drugs |CITS: [12619684]|., Biosynthetic studies using isotope-labeled precursors indicated that the indolocarbazole structure is derived from, two molecules of tryptophan |CITS: [3204382]|., The first rebeccamycin-related gene to be identified was |FRAME: G-11518| (then called ngt), encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-15083| |CITS: [10866221]|. Using the |FRAME: G-11518| gene as a probe it was possibole to clone the full rebeccamycin biosynthetic gene cluster, which included 18 open reading frames |CITS: [11983340]|. Based on sequence analysis and database searches the authors proposed a pathway, which involved eight enzymes. A refinement of the pathway was provided by generating mutants sefective in each of these genes |CITS: [12619684]|., Due to the medical importance of |FRAME: CPD-11752|, which also serves as a model compound for indolcarbazole alkaloids biosynthesis, there has been interest in its biosynthesis. All of the enzymes involved in the pathway have been characterized to a certain extent: |FRAME: G-11518| |CITS: [10866221][16575939]|, |FRAME: G-11519| and |FRAME: G-11526| |CITS: [15743914][16784243][17876823]|, |FRAME: G-11521| |CITS: [16313168][16417354][25837855]|, |FRAME: G-11520| |CITS: [15743957][16313168][25837855]|, |FRAME: G-11522| |CITS: [16967980][17873060][18007056][19035832]|, |FRAME: G-11523| |CITS: [17705392]| and |FRAME: G-11525| |CITS: [16575939][18502766]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| (Chla) and |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B| (Chlb) are light harvesting pigments that function to capture photons and transfer them to the reaction centers. Chla and Chlb share the same structure except for the side chain at C-7 which is a methyl group in Chla and a formyl group in Chlb., Whereas the biosynthesis of Chla has been widely reported (see |FRAME:PWY-5086| and |FRAME:PWY-5064|), that of Chlb has been more elusive., Although it has long been known that |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| appears before |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B| when chlorophyll synthesis begins, little was known of the formation of the formyl group of Chlb. The discovery of the |FRAME: AT1G44446-MONOMER| (CAO) showed that this enzyme was sufficient for the transition of a- to b-type chlorophyll pigments., The enzyme was originally discovered in |FRAME: TAX-3052|, where mutants lacking in |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLL-B| biosynthesis were generated, and the gene responsible for the phenotype was isolated |CITS: [9770552]|., Subsequent work showed that the homologous |FRAME:AT1G44446| gene from |FRAME: ORG-5993| is required for chlorophyll b synthesis in that organism |CITS:[10758481][10468639]|., The reduction of Chlb back to Chla (and its hydrolysis to chlorophyllide a) is not as well characterized, although strongly supported by observations. The process has been demonstrated in vitro in etioplasts and etioplast membranes preparations from several organisms |CITS: [8215395][8071325][8576141][8954166][9857045]|., The compound |FRAME: CPD-7016| was identified as an intermediate in the reduction reaction and it was found that the reduction of |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B| to |FRAME: CPD-7016| proceeded with NADPH as reductant while the next step, reduction of |FRAME: CPD-7016| to |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, required reduced ferredoxin |CITS: [9857045]|. This fact indicated that two enzymes, |FRAME: MONOMER-13499| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13500|, contribute to the overall reaction |CITS: [16228557]|., These combined findings suggest the existence of a cyclic pathway for the interconversion of the two types of chlorophyll molecules, as a response to changing light conditions |CITS:[8576141][16228557]|.

Licorice, the root and rhizome of the genus |FRAME:TAX-46347|, has been used for centuries both in eastern and western medicine to treat a variety of illnesses. It is known for its wide-ranging therapeutic properties, including relief of rheumatic and other pain, and its healing effect on gastric ulcers. The roots contain a number of secondary metabolites including coumarins, flavonoids, isoflavonoids etc. Echinatin, a compound isolated from the licorice (roots and rhizomes of |FRAME:TAX-46348|), is a typical example of a small group of chalcone derivatives called retrochalcones. In chalcones and retrochalcones the O-substitution patterns of the A- and B-rings are reversed. Echinatin has been shown to disturb the mitochondrial energy transfer reactions and membrane permeability in the isolated rat liver mitochondria |CITS: [6221118]|. Echinatin, isolated from the roots of Glycyrrhiza inflata, also showed antimicrobial activity |CITS: [9621457]|.

|FRAME: Polyunsaturated-fatty-acids "Polyunsaturated fatty acids"| (PUFAs) can be oxygenated either enzymatically or in free radical-mediated reactions into hundreds of oxygenated species including regio- and stereo-isomers of mono- and poly-hydroxy-, hydroperoxy-, epoxy- and oxo-fatty acids, prostanoids, isoprostanes, and leukotrienes, which act as mediators of cellular processes. The best-studied classes of these oxygenated mediators are the |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (sometimes spelled eicosanoids), whose name is derived from the ancient Greek word eikosi, which means twenty, to signify the 20 carbons in the |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived compounds (though the term is often used to include metabolites of 18- and 22-carbon PUFAs). , This pathway describes how the C<sub>20</sub> PUFA |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) is liberated from |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine|, one of the common glycerophopholipids in the cell, and how it is converted to some of the common icosanoids.

The genes encoding these enzymes are located in a cluster encoding multiple pheonol-induced proteins |CITS: [11004186 ]|. 4-hydroxybenzoate is then activated to a CoA thioester, which is reduced to benzoyl-CoA |CITS: [9490068]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They are grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. As a consequence, little is known about the biosynthesis of glucosinolates derived from other amino acids., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates are very similar to those involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases its chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

General Background, |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans Glucuronoxylans| are a component of |FRAME: Hemicelluloses|. They are linear polymers of β-D-xylopyranosyl units linked by (1→4) glycosidic bonds, with many of the xylose units substituted with 2, 3 or 2,3-linked glucuronate residues. Many of the D-glucuronosyl units are methylated at position 4. Angiosperm (hardwood) glucuronoxylans also have a high rate of substitution (70-80%) by acetyl groups, at position 2 and/or 3 of the β-D-xylopyranosyl., |FRAME: Glucuronoarabinoxylans Glucuronoarabinoxylans| (GAX) is a hemicellulose component typically found in softwood. GAX-type polymers are located in the non-endospermic tissues of cereal grains such as in wheat, corn, and rice bran |CITS: [8401598]|. GAX has the same xylan backbone as in |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans glucuronoxylans|, with about one in ten β-D-xylopyranosyl residues substituted by α-L-arabinofuranose at position 3. Unlike glucuronoxylans, the glucuronate residues in GAX polymers can be methylated, but not acetylated |CITS: [15944805]|. GAX contains some xylopyranose units that are doubly substituted by both 4-O-methylglucuronate and α-L-arabinofuranose |CITS: [Ebringerova05]|. Some of the arabinofuranose side chains in GAX are further substitued by either a β-D-xylopyranose attached by a (1→2) linkage or by a second arabinofuranose attached by a (1→3) linkage., GAX fractions isolated from wheat bran were feruloylated |CITS: [Schooneveld-Bergmans99]|., It should be noted that a different hemicellulose component, |FRAME: Arabinoglucuronoxylans arabinoglucuronoxylan|, (AGX) has a very similar structure. However, GAX-type polymers consist of |FRAME: Arabinoxylan| backbone, which contains about ten times more α-L-arabinofuranose side chains than glucuronate ones, while AGX-type polymers are based on |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans| back bone, with a lower ratio of arabinose to glucuronate residues |CITS: [Ebringerova05]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Glucuronoxylans Glucuronoxylans| are known to be degraded by a large number of fungal and bacterial species. Degradation of the backbone is catalyzes by multiple types of enzymes. |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.8|, cleaves the xylan backbone into smaller oligosaccharides, which can then be degraded further to xylose by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.37|. The enzymes isolated so far differ in their specificity toward the xylan polymer. While some cut randomly between unsubstituted xylose residues, the activity of others strongly depends on the substituents on the xylose residues neighboring the attacked residues |CITS: [Fujimoto95][27280644][Kormelink93]|. An example is |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.136| from |FRAME: TAX-224308|, which has high activity towards feruloylated arabinoxylans |CITS: [16666240]|., Arabinose residues can be removed by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.55|, and by arabinoxylan arabinofuranohydrolases. Many such enzymes have been isolated, and were found to differ strongly in substrate specificity. For example, an arabinofuranosidase purified from |FRAME: TAX-5061| was able to release only terminal α-1,3-linked arabinose residues |CITS: [7763988]| whereas a similar enzyme from the same organism (named arabinofuranosidase B) was able to release terminal α-1,2-, α-1,3- and α-1,5-linked arabinose residues |CITS: [Beldman93]|. Unlike the arabinofuranosidases, which are general arabinose-releasing enzymes, arabinoxylan arabinofuranohydrolase (AXH) is specifically involved in arabinoxylan degradation. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-105351| was not able to release arabinose from pectin or pectin-derived oligosaccharides, and was highly specific for arabinose residues linked to xylan |CITS: [Kormelink91]|. The enzyme is also not able to release arabinose from xylose residues adjacent to glucuronate-substituted xylose residues, or to remove arabinobiose side chains |CITS: [9691451][9691450]|., Finally, glucuronate residues and their 4-O-methyl ethers can be removed from the xylan backbone by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.131|. The enzyme is active mainly on small xylooligomers and therefore is dependent on the action of endoxylanases |CITS: [40][93]|.

Summary: Many bacteria, including species of |FRAME:TAX-352|, |FRAME:TAX-48736| and numerous species of, |FRAME:TAX-286|, possess genes for the degradation of aromatic compounds, through the meta pathway |CITS: [4325686][6853447][1732207][1856161][12732969]|., These genes are often found on plasmids, such as the TOL plasmids, that contain all of the genes, required for the complete degradation of |FRAME:TOLUENE|, xylene, |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE| and, other aromatic compounds to TCA cycle intermediates., The degradative pathway consists of two parts: an "upper pathway" that converts the compounds to, their carboxylic acid derivatives (see |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-5428|, and |FRAME: PWY-5429|), and a "lower pathway" that converts the (substituted) benzoic acids to, TCA cycle intermediates via |FRAME: CATECHOL| (this pathway)., The lower pathway, also known as the meta cleavage pathway, is induced by benzoic acids,, or by upper pathway substrates |CITS: [1176436]|., The most comprehensively studied meta-cleavage pathway is that of the TOL plasmid pWWO,, which encodes a toluene degradation pathway in |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [2183008]|., |FRAME: CATECHOL| is an intermediate in the degradation of many different aromatic compounds, in addition to |FRAME:BENZOATE|, such as |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE|, |FRAME:CPD-110|, and, |FRAME: PHENOL|. In addition, substituted catechols are intermediates in the catabolism of methylated, and chlorinated derivatives of these compounds., The aromatic ring of |FRAME:CATECHOL| is cleaved in a position adjacent to the two hydroxyls by the, enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-2841|., The product of this cleavage, |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD|, is metabolized in one of two routes., In one route it is hydrolyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-12763|, generating the important intermediate, |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| in a single step., In the second route, |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD| is dehydrogenated by |FRAME:CPLX-7245|, to the enol-form of 4-oxalocrotonate, which is then isomerized by |FRAME:CPLX-7237| to the keto-form,, and decarboxylated by |FRAME:CPLX-7239|., The later is in a tight complex with the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7240|. Its product,, |FRAME:CPD-6761|, is an unstable tautomer of |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE|. This product is transferred, to |FRAME: CPLX-7240| within the complex., Thus, the two variants, which separated at |FRAME:HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD|, join again at, |FRAME:OXOPENTENOATE| (or its tautomer |FRAME:CPD-6761|), which is then metabolized to, pyruvate and acetaldehyde (and eventually, acetyl-coA) by successive action of the enzymes, |FRAME:CPLX-7240|, |FRAME:MONOMER-11384| and |FRAME:MONOMER-11388|., While may organisms possess these genes on plasmids, other have integrated very similar genes, into their chromosomes, where they have aquired little mutation. For example, strains TW3 and 4NT, of |FRAME:TAX-303| have been shown to express similar but chromosomally-encoded, enzymes which catalyze the same pathway |CITS: [8357257][8245826][9555884]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the biosynthesis of several compounds that are derived from the central metabolite |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, an intermediate of the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|, including the amino acids |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: LYS|, |FRAME: THR|, and |FRAME: MET|, as well as the main methyl-group carrier |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| and the proton/electron carrier |FRAME: NAD|. The specific pathways shown here are those used by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|., The pathway starts by the reversible transamination of |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.1|, providing a link between carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID Oxaloacetate|, which is consumed in this pathway, is replenished from the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|, by |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|, and in some bacteria also by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31| |CITS: [Gottschalk1986]|., To start |FRAME: NAD| biosynthesis, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is oxidized by |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.16|, the first enzyme dedicated to de novo |FRAME: NAD| biosynthesis in some bacteria. The enzyme can use either |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| or |FRAME: FUM| as electron acceptor, enabling it to function under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions |CITS: [11863440]|. |FRAME: NAD| biosynthesis proceeds via |FRAME: QUINOLINATE|, |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE|, and |FRAME: DEAMIDO-NAD|, which is aminated to |FRAME: NAD| (see pathway |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|), |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| can also by converted in two steps to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, where the pathway branches further. One branch leads toward |FRAME: LYS| biosynthesis, while the other continues towards the biosynthesis of |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| |CITS: [14929228]|., Because the conversion of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| is common to many downstream biosynthetic pathways, |FRAME: TAX-562| has three different enzymes that initialize it (|FRAME: ASPKINIHOMOSERDEHYDROGI-CPLX "aspartate kinase I"|, |FRAME: ASPKINIIHOMOSERDEHYDROGII-CPLX "aspartate kinase II"|, and |FRAME: ASPKINIII-CPLX "aspartate kinase III"|), which are controlled by the available supply of |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET| and |FRAME: LYS|, respectively |CITS: [4148765]|., The L-lysine pathway shown here belongs to the diaminopimelate (DAP) group of Lysine pathways, and is known as the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|, as it involves succinylated intermediates., The rest of the |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| is converted to |FRAME: HOMO-SER| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.3|. Once again, |FRAME: TAX-562| has two different enzymes catalyzing this reaction, which are controlled by the availability of |FRAME: THR| and |FRAME: MET|, respectively |CITS: [4551091][4889171]|., |FRAME: HOMO-SER| can be isomerized to |FRAME: THR| in two steps that involved phosphorylation and de-phosphorylation |CITS: [11368768]|, or alternatively can lead to the formation of |FRAME: MET| in a 4-step pathway. , For |FRAME: MET| biosynthesis, homoserine is first activated by O-succinylation, and the product is combined with |FRAME: CYS| to form cystathionine. This compound is cleaved to homocysteine, which is subsequently methylated to produce methionine. The last reaction is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-562| by two different enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13| and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14|. Both enzymes use |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N| as the methyl donor. However, the former requires cobalamin (vitamin B12), while the latter does not |CITS: [1339288]|., Once |FRAME: MET| is formed, a single enzyme, the ATP-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.6|, can convert it to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| |CITS: [6251075]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-11473 Astaxanthin| (3,3'-dihydroxy-4,4'-diketo-β,β-carotene) is the red ketocarotenoid pigment that is famous for giving the orange-red color to the flesh of wild salmon and other fish |CITS:[9491309]|., The pigment, which is synthesized by bacteria and plants, is ingested by the animals through their feed and accumulates in their skin, muscle, exoskeleton and gonads. , In the aquatic environment, |FRAME: CPD-11473| (AX) is produced by microalgae and bacteria which are consumed by zooplankton, insects or crustaceans, to be finally ingested by fish. Farmed fish and crustaceans which do not have access to the natural sources of AX have their feed supplemented with synthetic AX. |FRAME:CPD-7851 Canthaxanthin|, an intermediate in the biosynthesis AX, is also used as a synthetic supplement for the pigmentation of farmed fish although AX is usually preferred due its higher color intensity |CITS: [Storebakken92]|. AX is also deposited in the muscles more efficiently in some species |CITS:[torrisen89][10554206][buttle01]|., In addition to its role as a pigment, AX has many other important functions particularly in fish reproduction. It is involved in acceleration of sexual maturity, increase in fertilization and egg survival, and better embryo development of fish |CITS:[putnam91]|. AX is mostly known for its antioxidant properties, which have been reported to surpass even those of |FRAME:CPD1F-129| or |FRAME:ALPHA-TOCOPHEROL| |CITS:[miki91]|. These properties have led to the initiation of a number of pre-clinical trials aiming to test the effectiveness of AX as an anticancer drug, its prevention of cardiovascular drugs or as a booster of the immune system (for more information, please see the recent review by |CITS:[16431409]|). , The biosynthesis of astaxanthin occurs in a number of bacteria (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-188916| and |FRAME: TAX-44155|), fungi (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-264483|) and a few unicellular algae (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-44745|) |CITS:[goodwin80][16001255][16431409]|. In plants, astaxanthin is found mostly in members of the |FRAME: TAX-46984| genus where it accumulates in the flowers. Very few other plants produce this compound., |FRAME: CPD-11473 Astaxanthin| presents three stereochemical isomers: two enantiomers (|FRAME:CPD-7847| and |FRAME:CPD-7957|) and a meso form (|FRAME:CPD-7958|). The 3S,3'S form is the most abundant in nature, while synthetic astaxanthin consists of a racemic mixture of all three forms. Finally, astaxanthin can be found associated with a variety of other compounds: esterified in one or both of the hydroxyl groups with fatty acids (e.g. palmitic, oleic, estearic or linoleic), bound to proteins (carotenoproteins), or bound to lipoproteins (carotenolipoproteins)., About This Pathway, The conversion of |FRAME: CPD1F-129| into astaxanthin occurs via a series of 3-hydroxylation and 4-ketolation steps. Although the pathway outline remains similar between species, the nature of the enzymes catalyzing the hydroxylation and ketolation steps vary tremendously. Some species use distinct hydroxylases or ketolases, while others, like the fungus |FRAME: TAX-264483|, have bifunctional enzymes |CITS:[16416328],[16455271]|., Some hydroxylases, like the |FRAME: G-11387|-encoded enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-549| |CITS:[8764486]| or |FRAME: TAX-44155| |CITS:[7592436]|, accept substrates with keto groups, while others, such as the cyanobacterial hydroxylases, are not able to accept |FRAME:CPD-7850| and |FRAME:CPD-7851| as substrates |CITS:[11367579]|., Similarly, some cyanobacterial ketolases, such as |FRAME: G-9542| from |FRAME: TAX-63737|, introduces 4-keto groups into the 3-hydroxylated |FRAME:CPD1F-130|, while others, such as |FRAME: G-9546| from the same organism, cannot |CITS:[15269553]|., In fact, the displayed pathway shows several routes, some of which are shared by various organisms and others which are species specific. Although cyanobacteria are listed in the pathway, they cannot produce |FRAME:CPD-7847| |CITS:[18987067]| but share reaction sequences catalyzed by enzymes such as β-carotene ketolase (crtO) and β-carotene hydroxylase (crtR) which, however, show no sequence homology to related bacterial or plant enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7638|). Similar to the deviant biosynthesis of xanthophylls in cyanobacteria is also the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-7847| in flowering plants (see below) where both sequence similarity of catalyzing enzymes and reaction mechanisms differ significantly from their bacterial, fungal and algal counterparts (see |FRAME:PWY-7636|)., This pathway in Plants, At the time of this review, the exact sequence of biochemical steps leading to the formation of astaxanthin in |FRAME: TAX-46984| plants has not been fully elucidated. The pathway presented here shows two branches, one with early hydroxylation on C3 and C3', the other with early addition of a keto group on C4 and C4'. These branches transit via the intermediate production of |FRAME:CPD-7851|, |FRAME:CPD-7849| and |FRAME:CPD-7852|. It has been postulated that the biosynthetic pathway in plants might differ from the one represented in this diagram (for a complete putative metabolic route, see |CITS:[15659105]| and |CITS:[16455271]|). A peculiarity of the plant pathway conists in the mechanism of formation of the C4 keto groups. In bacteria and green algae, the addition of the carbonyl by β-carotene 4-ketolases, both in vitro and in vivo, proceeds without the release of any intermediates |CITS:[8764486],[7750556],[9523693],[7733978],[7592436]|. In contrast, the |FRAME: TAX-46984| genes leading to the formation of the 4-keto-β-ring would proceed via a dual enzymatic 4-hydroxylation/3,4-desaturation, which is followed by the ketolation of the 4- and 4'-ionone rings and the subsequent 3- and 3'-ring hydroxylation forming the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-7847| (see |FRAME:PWY-7636|).

Avenacins are triterpene glucosides which act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents conferring resistance against soil-borne pathogens and influencing the development of close neighbors |CITS:[10536024] [16995908]|. There are four avenacins known, the ones acylated with |FRAME:CPD-402| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7463|), i.e. |FRAME:CPD-10678| and |FRAME:CPD-16597| and the ones acylated with |FRAME:BENZOATE| (see also |FRAME:PWY-7468|), i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16599| and |FRAME:CPD-16598|, all of them exclusively found only in roots |CITS:[Crombie86a]|; more specifically in the vacuoles of the root epidermal cells |CITS:[18203919]|. The occurrence of the phytoalexic avenacins appears to be restricted to the genus Avena which is an expression of a highly specialized defense biochemistry |CITS:[Hostettmann95]|. In general, triterpenes are valued compounds with a wide range of commercial applications and because of that in the focus of metabolic engineering. One of the major goals is to re-introduce lost traits of resistance into cultivated crops |CITS:[22639586]|. , |FRAME:CPD-10678 Avenacin A-1| (this pathway) is the most abundant avenacin found in Avena. The unusual property for a saponin of a bright fluorescence under UV-illumination due to the acylation with |FRAME:CPD-402| has been used to identify and isolate sodium-azide generated mutants and corresponding genes involved in |FRAME:CPD-10678| biosynthesis |CITS:[10536024] [20557911]|. As a general rule genes in plant biochemical pathways, unlike bacterial biochemical pathways, have been regarded as unlinked. However, the avenacin biosynthesis appears to be carried out by an avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster which implies a high degree of coordination regarding avenacin synthesis, transport and sequestration, all of which must be precisely orchestrated in time and space between different cell organelles and compartments |CITS:[21876149] [15148404] [21443624] [20040536]|. , The first committed step into the |FRAME:CPD-10678| biosynthesis is the cyclization of |FRAME:EPOXYSQUALENE| to form |FRAME:CPD-6948| catalyzed by the Avena oxidosqualene cyclase encoded by SAD1 (saponin-deficient = SAD) |CITS:[11606766]|. The following step(s) of hydroxylation and epoxidation of |FRAME:CPD-6948| to yield the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-16622| via two possible routes is carried out by a cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase (CYP51H10) encoded by SAD2. This enzyme belongs to a subgroup of cytochrome P450's which are known to function as 14α-sterol demethylases. However, through neofunctionalization CYP51H10 (SAD2) has been evolved and gained a different catalytic property. SAD2 is a component of the avenacin genetic cluster |CITS:[17124172] [22687421] [23940321]|. , The enzymes and the exact position within the avenacin biosynthetic sequence of the glycosylation steps of |FRAME:CPD-10678| are mostly unknown. However, two genes SAD3 and SAD4 have been identified which are able to glucosylate |FRAME:CPD-16625| and add the 1->4 linked |FRAME:GLC|. Mutants deficient in SAD3 and 4 form incompletely glucosylted avenacins (|FRAME:CPD-16626|) which causes a phenotype of stunted roots with a decreased number of root hairs. While SAD3 is a member of the avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster SAD4 is unlinked and might have other biochemical functions in Avena |CITS:[18203919]|. Nevertheless, the correct and complete glucosylation of the avenacin skeleton is very important for its biological activity as phytoalexin. It has been shown that incomplete glucosylated avenacins are less toxic, hence less efficient in warding off microbial attacks |CITS:[7824933]| and fungi which possess the ability to de-glucosylate avenacins are more successful to invade Avena plants |CITS:[Osbourn91]|., The last step in the direct pathway of |FRAME:CPD-10678| biosynthesis is the acylation of |FRAME:CPD-16623| with |FRAME:CPD-402| which is provided through the acyl-donor |FRAME:CPD-16600| (see |FRAME:PWY-7463|). |FRAME:CPD-16623 Des-acyl avenacin A| is also the cross point that leads to |FRAME:CPD-16599| (see |FRAME:PWY-7474|) and |FRAME:CPD-16624| (see |FRAME:PWY-7475|). The enzyme is a serine carboxypeptidase-like (SCPL) protein (SCPL1) encoded by SAD7, also a member of the avenacin genetic cluster, which catalyzes the final conversion of |FRAME:CPD-16623| to |FRAME:CPD-10678| |CITS:[19684243]|.

Names: coenzyme M biosynthesis II // CoM biosynthesis II
Summary: General Background, 400 million tons of methane are produced each year through methanogenesis, a process in which methanogenic archaea anaerobically reduce acetate or single carbon compounds to methane |CITS: [11830598]|., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| (CoM; 2-mercaptoethanesulfonic acid) plays a key role in methanogenesis as the terminal methyl carrier. In the terminal step of methanogenesis, the methylated form of CoM is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-664 "methyl-coenzyme M reductase"|, forming methane and a |FRAME: CPD-1282| (CoB-S-S-CoM), which is reduced in a key energy yielding step (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|) |CITS: [12102556]|., Initially, CoM was thought to be only present in methanogenic archaea. However, several eubacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-78245| and |FRAME:TAX-1829| strain B276 have been shown to possess CoM, which they use in |FRAME: PWY-5534| |CITS: [10411892][10762269]|., About This Pathway, The first posulation of a biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CoM| was based on studying the labeling patterns of CoM purified from the three methanogens |FRAME: TAX-2162|, |FRAME: ORG-5913|, and a methanogenic bacterium similar to |FRAME: TAX-83816| |CITS: [white85]|, and is described in |FRAME: P261-PWY|., However, some methanogens, such as the euryarchaeon |FRAME: TAX-2214|, have no homologues of the first three enzymes in that pathway. Instead, these organisms produce the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-380| from |FRAME: 3-P-SERINE| in two steps, via |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| |CITS: [19761441]|., The enzyme catalyzing the last reaction in the pathway was discovered only in 2019 |CITS: [30932481]|.

General Background, |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL Erythritol| is a four-carbon polyol that is produced by microorganisms as an osmoprotectant, and occurs naturally in small quantities in mushrooms, fruits such as pears, grapes, and watermelons, and in fermented foods. , Erythritol is used as a natural sweetener in the food and pharmaceutical industries. It exhibits about 70% of the relative sweetness of sucrose, and was approved as low calorie sweetener by the FDA in 2001. The majority of erythritol (ca. 90%) is not metabolized in the human body and is excreted into urine within 48 h after oral intake, resulting in an extremely low energy value (0.2 - 0.4 kcal/g) |CITS: [28954540]|., Erythritol is produced on an industrial scale through the fermentation of sugars by some yeasts, such as |FRAME: TAX-64607| sp., |CITS: [28954540]|. As of 2018, the world production of erythritol was about 60000 ton/year |CITS: [32095676]|., About This Pathway, The wine lactic acid bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1247| metabolizes glucose using the |FRAME: P122-PWY| pathway. In addition to the common products (|FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ACET|, and |FRAME: Lactate|) the organism also produces |FRAME: ERYTHRITOL| and |FRAME: GLYCEROL| |CITS: [Peynaud64][16348738]|. The production of erythritol occurs anaerobically and is almost absent under aerobic conditions. Under anaerobic conditions the rate of erythritol production represented 37% of the rate of glucose consumption |CITS: [8391532]|., During growth on glucose under anaerobic conditions, the high NADPH/NADP ratio inhibits glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase. Accumulated glucose 6-phosphate is isomerized into fructose 6-phosphate, which is later cleaved into acetylphosphate and erythrose-4-phosphate. The cleavage might be a nonspecific reaction catalyzed by the same phosphoketolase which splits xylulose 5-phosphate under aerobic growth conditions. Erythrose 4-phosphate is reduced to erythritol 4-phosphate, which enables the regeneration of NADP. The last step is erythritol 4-phosphate dephosphorylation to erythritol |CITS: [28954540]|.

Summary: Archaeal tRNA contains |FRAME: CPD-13057| (often referred to as G*), a 7-deazaguanosine modified nucleoside unique to Archaea |CITS: [7683667]|. Archaeosine is found in the majority of archaeal tRNAs specifically at position 15 of the dihydrouridine loop (D-loop) |CITS: [2470031]|, a position not modified in either eukaryotic or bacterial tRNA., The presence of the positively charged formamidine group of archaeosine and its location at the interface of the D-loop/T-stem in the tertiary structure of the tRNA are thought to be important in structural stabilization of the tRNA through electrostatic interactions with the anionic phosphates |CITS: [7683667]|. This is assumed to be a critical role in thermophiles, protecting tRNA from thermal denaturation., The pathway leading to production of the intermediate |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is common to the archaea and bacteria, and is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6703|., While in bacteria |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is converted to |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| prior to incorporation in tRNA (see |FRAME: PWY-6700|), in archaea |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is incorporated directly by the archaeal |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.48|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12503| gene |CITS: [20129918]|., Once incorporated, the enzyme archaeosine synthase catalyzes the direct addition of an ammonia group to the nitrile of |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, a previously unknown amidinotransferase chemistry, generating |FRAME: CPD-13057| within the tRNA |CITS: [20129918]|., In Euryarchaeota the enzyme is encoded by the |FRAME: G-12502| gene, which generates the ammonia from, glutamine or asparagine hydrolysis (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.97|). However, many Crenarchaeota that produce |FRAME: CPD-13057| do not have the |FRAME: G-12502| gene, and instead contain the |FRAME: G-55183| gene (which is very similar to the bacterial |FRAME: G7452| gene) |CITS: [22032275]|, whose product catalyzes a similar activity to ArcS. However, QueF-L cannot use glutamine and requires ammonia as the amino group donor |CITS: [28383498][27802572]|.

|FRAME: CPD-15322 L-Homophenylalanine| is a nonproteinogenic amino acid. It is similar to |FRAME: PHE|, but its side chain is extended by one carbon., Biosynthetic studies using radiolabeled precursors indicated that |FRAME: CPD-15322| exists as an intermediate during |FRAME: GLUCOTROPEOLIN| biosynthesis |CITS: [5658141]|., |FRAME: CPD-15322| residues are also found in |FRAME: Anabaenopeptins anabaenopeptin|, a protease inhibitor depsipeptide produced by some cyanobacteria including |FRAME: TAX-46234| |CITS: [20338518]|., |FRAME: CPD-15322 L-Homophenylalanine| is a useful chiral building block for the synthesis of several pharmaceutical drugs, such as |FRAME: HS08412-MONOMER "angiotensin-converting enzyme"| (ACE) inhibitors and the proteasome inhibitor |FRAME: CPD-15327|, which is used for treating multiple myeloma |CITS: [9577953][17591945]|. The majority of ACE inhibitors, including |FRAME: CPD0-2065|, |FRAME: CPD-15328| and |FRAME: CPD-15329|, contain a common |FRAME: CPD-15322| core in their structures., A pathway leading to the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15322| from |FRAME: PHE| has been reported from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-63737| |CITS: [23354699]|. The enzymes that paprticipate in the pathway include an aminotransferase whose identity has not been studied that catalyzes the first and last steps, and three enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-16016|, |FRAME: G-16018| and |FRAME: G-16017| genes. These three enzymes catalyze a biochemical transformation that is homologous to the process of |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| convertsion to |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| during |FRAME: LEUSYN-PWY|., An |FRAME:TAX-562| strain harboring hphABCD-expressing plasmids was able to produce |FRAME: CPD-15322| from |FRAME: PHE|. After optimization of the expression a yield to 630 mg/liter was obtained |CITS: [23354699]|.

The pentitols |FRAME: RIBITOL| and |FRAME: CPD-355| are common in nature, while the pentitols |FRAME: XYLITOL| and |FRAME: L-ARABITOL| are rare or absent., Pentitols and other neutral polyols can be taken up by bacteria and serve as a carbon and energy source. Gram-negative bacteria and Actinobacteria import the polyol intact, convert them into a keto sugar by a polyol hydrogenase, and then phosphorylate the keto sugar and metabolize it via the pentose phosphate or glycolytic pathways (this pathway). Some Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1582| |CITS: [118163]| and |FRAME:TAX-33945| |CITS: [12467497]|, transport polyols into the cell using a phosphotransferase system, resulting in their phosphoylation. The polyol phosphates are then oxidized by polyol phosphate dehydrogenases (see |FRAME: PWY-8394|). , Several species of enteric bacteria have been shown to have naturally occurring ribitol degradation pathways as indicated here. Approximately 85% of |FRAME:TAX-570| strains and 10% of |FRAME:TAX-562| strains can degrade ribitol and D-arabitol (|FRAME:TAX-562| K-12 and B strains do not utilize these compounds) (|CITS: [COLISAL] [1097416]| and in |CITS: [9639934]|). The genes form an operon encoding an NAD-dependent dehydrogenase, and ATP-dependent kinase, and a specific H+ symporter, controlled by a repressor. D-ribulose is the inducer in |FRAME:TAX-570| (|CITS: [9639934]|), and ribitol is the inducer in |FRAME:TAX-562| C |CITS: [350825]|. However, the gene encoding ribulose-phosphate-3-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.1), rpe, is not part of the operon. Its function in this pathway has been inferred from its presence in enteric bacteria (in |CITS: [9639934]|). , In this pathway, |FRAME: RIBITOL| is transported into the cell, converted to the ketopentose |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE|, and then phosphorylated to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, which enters the pentose phosphate pathway., Examples of other pentitol degradation pathways are |FRAME: DARABITOLUTIL-PWY| and |FRAME: LARABITOLUTIL-PWY|.

Summary: The common ice plant (Mesembryanthemum crystallinum), a member of the Aizoaceae family in the order Caryophyllales has been studied with focus on its unique phenylpropanoid metabolism. The Caryophyllales often substitute the chromophoric anthocyanins with betacyanins as fruit and flowers pigments (see for instance |FRAME:PWY-5399|) |CITS:[Mabry80]|. Under high intensity irradiation and exposure to UV a variety of methylated and glucosylated flavonol conjugates and feruloylglucose accumulate in bladder cells of young and epidermal cells of mature leaves |CITS:[10570827] [Ibdah02]|. The ice plant has also received attention due to the chemopreventive effects of Mesembryanthemum plant extracts on colon carcinogenesis in animal cancer tests |CITS:[Ibtissem12]|. , Utilizing a cDNA library obtained from irradiated leaves of Mesembryanthemum crystallinum a multi-specific O-methyltransferase has been identified and characterized which probably contributes in vivo to the observed diversity of methylated phenylpropanoids. The penylpropanoid and flavonoid O-methyltransferase (PFOMT) has been shown to specifically methylate the meta-position of aromatic vicinal dihydroxy groups covering a broad range of phenylpropanoids from cinnamic acids and respective CoA and glucosylated derivatives to a number of flavonoids including flavonols, flavones and flavanones which maintained the structure of vicinal dihydroxy groups |CITS:[12941960]|. , The PFOMT belongs to the class I of OMT's which are characterized by cation (Mg2+) dependence and high substrate specificity, properties which are shared throughout the OMT's of this class between animals and plants |CITS:[11459845]|. In order to elaborate on the deviating catalytic behavior of the ice plant O-methyltransferase the PFOMT has been crystallized and studied in more detail using site-directed mutagenesis and in silico docking experiments. This research revealed the structure of the N-terminus and a variable loop near the C-terminus as the probable reason for the substrate promiscuity of PFOMT. The importance of the N-terminus for regiospecificity and catalytic properties of plant O-methyltransferase had already been reported |CITS:[15013769]|. Only small changes in these two regions (N- and C-terminus) transformed the broad substrate specificity of the PFOMT into the narrow substrate specificity of a CCoAOMT |CITS:[18342334]|.

Names: A series fagopyritols biosynthesis // fagopyritol A1 biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Fagopyritols are galactosyl cyclitols found primarily in seeds of buckwheat (|FRAME:TAX-3617|). Whereas maturing embryos of many plant seeds accumulate |FRAME:CPD-1099|, |FRAME:CPD-170| and |FRAME:CPD-8065| (in addition to sucrose) as the predominant soluble sugars, maturing embryos of buckwheat seeds accumulate fagopyritols. These compounds are grouped into two main series: A and B, which differ from the positioning of the O-α-D-galactopyranosyl linkage to |FRAME:CPD-8052| [(1->3) for A series, (1->2) for B series]. The first fagopyritol of the A series is termed |FRAME:CPD-8257|. The subsequent di- and tri-galactopyranosyl-fagopyritols (A2 and A3) result from the addition of galactosyl units linked in (1->6)-O-α-D-galactopyranosyl to fagopyritol A1. Fagopyritols of the A series have only been detected so far in the seeds of bluckwheat |CITS:[HORBOWICZ05],[11284502]| whereas fagopyritols of the B series have been detected in several other species (mostly fagopyritol B1). Fagopyritols have attracted attention as they are structurally similar to a galactosamine derivative of D-chiro-inositol, a putative insulin mediator, and may be useful in the treatment of non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and polycystic ovary syndrome (for references, see the introduction of |CITS:[11093720]|)., Key Notes on the enzymes: Crude extracts from immature embryos harvested 20 days after pollination or from buckwheat bran prepared from mature dry seeds did not show any fagopyritol synthase activity using galactinol as galactosyl donor. The same experiments was successful in producing |FRAME:CPD-8253| using UDP-galactose instead of galactinol, suggesting that fagopyritol synthases might be homologous to galactinol synthases (GolS). Using conserved oligonucleotide sequences of GolS, two fagopyritol synthases genes (|FRAME:G-9730| and |FRAME:G-9731|) were identified from cDNA libraries of buckwheat developing seeds harvested 20-25 days after pollination. The enzymes catalyze the formation of fagopyritol A1 and B1 but not the subsequent compounds in the series |CITS:[UEDA05]|. To date no enzyme has been identified that can catalyze the formation of fagopyritols A2, B2, A3 or B3.

Macrolide antibiotics are therapeutically important agents that are effective inhibitors of bacterial protein biosynthesis. They bind to the large 50S ribosomal subunit at or near the peptidyl transferase center and block the elongation of the peptide chain., |FRAME: OLEANDOMYCIN Oleandomycin| is a clinically important 14-membered macrolide antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1890|. It contains a macrolactone ring (|FRAME: CPD-13827|) modified by the attachment of two cyclic sugars, |FRAME: Oleandrose| and |FRAME: CPD-13780|. Oleandomycin differs from |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycins| by an exocyclic epoxide at C8, a unique feature not found in any other known polyoxo macrolide |CITS: [16405329]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6971|)., Once produced (see |FRAME: PWY-6971|), |FRAME: OLEANDOMYCIN| could harm its producer. To protect the host against the antibiotic, oleadomycin is inactivated in the cell by two intracellular glycosyltransferases, encoded by |FRAME: G-14862| and |FRAME: G-14861|, which add a glucose molecule to the 2'-OH group of the desosamine moiety |CITS:[1530845][8244027]|. While |FRAME: G-14862| is highly specific, |FRAME: G-14861| can inactivate several other macrolide antibiotics |CITS: [9680207][17376874]|., Once the inactive antibiotic is secreted out of the cell, it is reactivated by an extracellular glucosidase (encoded by |FRAME: G-14863|) that removes the glucose |CITS: [8200337][9680207]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylate"| is an aromatic compound that is is common throughout the plant kingdom and is also found in some bacteria., Several bacterial genera utilize salicylate as a building block for low-molecular-weight organic Fe3+ chelators (siderophores), such as |FRAME: CPD-9991| in |FRAME: TAX-632| and |FRAME: TAX-630|, |FRAME: Pyochelin| in |FRAME: TAX-287|, and |FRAME: CPD-12068 "mycobactin"| in |FRAME: TAX-1773|., In bacteria |FRAME: CPD-110| is derived from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| in two steps, via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, as described in this pathway., Salicylate is also important in plants, where it induces flowering and is involved in resistance against pathogen infection through the systematic acquired resistance mechanism |CITS: [15283665][12873532]|. Plants can synthesize salicylate in two different pathways that differ trom the pathway used by bacteria. See |FRAME:PWY-8321| and |FRAME: PWY-981|).

Summary: General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms. Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7027|), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., About This Pathway, Alkanes are produced in multiple organisms - for example, in the |FRAME: PWY-282 "production of plant cuticular waxes"| |CITS: [18251711]|, as |FRAME: PWY-7035 "insect pheromones"| |CITS: [7937826][10406089]|, in green algae |CITS: [1898004][15630516]|, in fungi |CITS: [18957585]| and in bacteria |CITS:[ 6025301][15170379]|, especially cyanobacteria, which produce mostly |FRAME: CPD-7946| and |FRAME: HEPTADECANE-CPD| |CITS:[17731762][McInnes80][12495426]|. In fact, all cyanobacterial membranes contain alkanes and/or alkenes of 1519 carbons at concentrations similar to that of chlorophyll., The alkanes are typically produced from long-chain and very-long chain (20-34) fatty acids that are produced from the "standard" C16 and C18 fatty acids by specialized fatty acid synthases, known as elongases (see |FRAME: PWY-5080|). These fatty acids are converted to alkanes in three steps - activation of the fatty acid by an |FRAME: ACP "acyl-carrier-protein"| or |FRAME: CO-A|, reduction of the activated fatty acid to an aldehyde, and decarbonylation of the aldehyde, resulting in an alkane that is one carbon short of the original fatty acid |CITS: [3343228][1608940][12467640]|., Since most fatty acids have an even number of carbons (fatty acids are synthesized by the addition of two carbon units), the resulting alkanes have an odd number of carbons., Recently the genes that are responsible for alkane biosynthesis in cyanobacteria, which also involve decarbonylation, have been identified and cloned from several strains of cyanobacteria |CITS: [20061450][20671186]|. , While long-chain activated fatty acids can be generated in cyanobacteria de novo (via the elongase complex),it has been shown that they can also be generated from free fatty acids (provided either externally or by lipid degradation) by the action of |FRAME: MONOMER-17302| |CITS: [20061450]|., The conversion of the activated fatty acids to alkanes is catalyzed by two enzymes, the products of the |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1594| and |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1593| genes, which encode an |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1594-MONOMER| and an |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1593-MONOMER|, respectively. These two genes are located next to each other on the chromosomes of most strains that were studied, and appear to form an operon. In |FRAME: TAX-1140| the two genes reside in an operon with a third gene, accA, which encodes the α subunit of the carboxyl transferase component of acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Extracts of |FRAME:TAX-562| expressing the two genes contained substantial quantities of odd-chain alkanes and alkenes. The two proteins interact with each other via electrostatic interactions |CITS: [31601165]|., |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1593-MONOMER "Aldehyde decarbonylase"| was originally thought to produce |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| like the enzymes from higher plants and green algae. However, the most recent studies showed that the actual product of the cyanobacterial enzyme is |FRAME: FORMATE| |CITS: [21341652]|. There was some controversy regarding the actual reaction. While some researcher found that the enzyme requires oxygen |CITS: [21671322][21462983]|, others reported that the enzyme is much more active anaerobically |CITS: [22074177]|. However, additional work verified that the enzyme is indeed an oxygenase |CITS: [22947199]|., A mutant of |FRAME: TAX-1148| that does not produce alkanes exhibited enhanced cyclic electron flow, in which electrons from photosystem I (PSI) were returned to the |FRAME: Plastoquinols plastoquinone| pool, resulting in a slower growth rate |CITS: [26459862]|.
