Summary: General Background, The fungi |FRAME: TAX-51453 "Trichoderma reesei (previously known as Hypocrea jecorina)"|, |FRAME: TAX-5061| and |FRAME: TAX-162425| have been shown to catabolize |FRAME: GALACTOSE| by two pathways, the Leloir pathway (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6317|) and a second pathway that involves a series of reductive and oxidative steps. In the oxidoreductive pathway, |FRAME: GALACTOSE| is converted to |FRAME: BETA-D-FRUCTOSE| by multiple |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent reduction reactions and |FRAME: NAD|-dependent oxidation reactions via the intermediates |FRAME: GALACTITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-13036|, and |FRAME: SORBITOL|. A previously missing enzyme in the pathway, L-xylo-3-hexulose reductase, was identified which provides the activity that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13036| to |FRAME: SORBITOL| |CITS: [22654107]|., The first three reactions of this second pathway have been experimentally established in |FRAME: TAX-5061| and |FRAME: TAX-51453|, and the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-13036| has been identified in vitro using recombinant lad1 from |FRAME: TAX-51453| and recombinant ladB from |FRAME: TAX-380704| |CITS: [22155165][22654107]|. However in |FRAME: TAX-162425| mutant analysis suggested that |FRAME: CPD-9569| is a pathway intermediate and its catabolism involves a hexokinase step. The catabolism of |FRAME: GALACTOSE| also represents part of the catabolism of the galactose-containing disaccharide |FRAME: Alpha-lactose|, as well as galactose-containing, plant-derived |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| and |FRAME: Pectin "pectin"| (reviewed in |CITS: [19723296] [21212945]|)., In |FRAME: TAX-5061|, |FRAME: GALACTOSE| reduction to |FRAME: GALACTITOL| is catalyzed by D-xylose reductase (aldose reductase) encoded by xyrA. However, unlike |FRAME: TAX-51453| and |FRAME: TAX-162425| in which Lad1 is used in the oxidation of both |FRAME: GALACTITOL| and |FRAME: L-ARABITOL|, in |FRAME: TAX-5061| LadB functions as a specific galactitol-3-dehydrogenase that is not involved in pentose metabolism. LadA functions as an L-arabitol dehydrogenase in this organism |CITS: [22155165][22245674]|. The gene encoding sorbitol dehydrogenase sdhA in |FRAME: TAX-5061| has also been identified, cloned and its product characterized |CITS: [22245674]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-51453| can catabolize |FRAME: GALACTOSE| by both the Leloir pathway (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6317|) and this second, reductive pathway in which |FRAME: GALACTOSE| is reduced to |FRAME: GALACTITOL| by an aldose reductase encoded by gene xyl1. This enzyme is also operative in the initial reduction step in the |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-25028| catabolic pathways in this organism (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5515| and |FRAME: PWY-5516|). In the second step |FRAME: GALACTITOL| has been shown in vitro to be oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-13036| by the product of gene lad1, which also oxidizes |FRAME: L-ARABITOL| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5515|) |CITS: [15128296] [17924946] [14763977]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-51453| the third step is catalyzed by L-xylo-3-hexulose reductase encoded by gene lxr4 and in |FRAME: TAX-5061| by gene xhrA. Deletion mutants lacking these genes did not grow on |FRAME: GALACTITOL| and showed reduced growth on |FRAME: GALACTOSE|. The product of gene lxr4 was shown to specifically catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13036| to |FRAME: SORBITOL| |CITS: [22654107]|. In the fourth step the product of |FRAME: TAX-51453| gene xdh1 has been shown to utilize |FRAME: SORBITOL| as well as |FRAME: XYLITOL| |CITS: [14555469]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-162425| there is also evidence for this second pathway, but differences from |FRAME: TAX-51453| might exist. In |FRAME: TAX-162425| mutant analysis suggested that |FRAME: CPD-9569| was an intermediate of this pathway |CITS: [14624333]|. The catabolism of |FRAME: CPD-9569| is known to occur by reduction to |FRAME: SORBITOL|, oxidation of |FRAME: SORBITOL| to |FRAME: FRU|, and phosphorylation of |FRAME: FRU| to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| which enters glycolysis (reviewed in |CITS: [21212945]|)., In contrast, in |FRAME: TAX-5061| |FRAME: GALACTOSE| is primarily catabolized through the oxidoreductive pathway shown here, rather than through the Leloir pathway |CITS: [22155165][22654107]|., The physiological importance of this pathway may also differ between fungi. In |FRAME: TAX-162425| the pathway can fully compensate for loss of the Leloir pathway, but in |FRAME: TAX-51453| it cannot and inactivation of the Leloir pathway results in impairment of growth on |FRAME: GALACTOSE| (reviewed in |CITS: [19723296] [21212945]|).

General Background, Purine bases consist of a six-membered and a five-membered nitrogen-containing rings fused together. There are four purine bases, namely |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE| and |FRAME: XANTHINE|. Purine nucleotides may be synthesized de novo from simpler precursors, or they may be derived from exogenous purine nucleosides and bases by the salvage pathways., In |FRAME:TAX-562|, the salvage pathways collect exogenous, preformed bases and nucleosides for nucleotide synthesis, reutilize bases and nucleosides produced endogenously from nucleotide turnover, and make available the pentose moieties of exogenous nucleosides as sources of carbon. When free bases or nucleosides present in the growth medium are salvaged, the contribution from the de novo pathways to nucleotide synthesis is greatly suppressed. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: XANTHOSINE Xanthosine| is converted to |FRAME: XANTHINE| by |FRAME: XANTHOSINEPHOSPHORY-CPLX|, one of the two purine nucleoside phosphorylases (PNPs) in |FRAME:TAX-562|, encoded by the |FRAME: G85| gene |CITS: [7559336][15808857]|. This enzyme does not cleave or synthesize adenosine and deoxyadenosine but catalyzes the phosphorolysis of |FRAME: XANTHOSINE|, |FRAME: INOSINE| and |FRAME: GUANOSINE| with comparable efficiency., |FRAME: XANTHINE Xanthine| is converted to |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| by |FRAME: GPT-CPLX|, a purine salvage enzyme which converts either xanthine or guanine to |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| or |FRAME: GMP|, respectively |CITS: [6305942][3886014]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10806 4-Hydroxy-2-nonenal| is a highly reactive neurotoxic product of lipid peroxidation that is implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. It reacts with and modifies different macromolecules including proteins, DNA, RNA and lipids, inducing toxic effects that are eventually involved in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology |CITS: [9258256][9596412][22114878]|. The level of free and protein-bound |FRAME: CPD-10806| is significantly higher in the brain and cerebrospinal fluid of AD patients in comparison with age matched controls |CITS: [9109537]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-10806 4-Hydroxy-2-nonenal| is detoxified in mammalian cerebrum by a glutathione (GSH) dependent pathway |CITS: [9109537][9258256][9596412][12460747][12578224]|., The pathway starts with the conjugation of 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal with GSH, a step that can be catalyzed by many different enzymes, collectively known as glutathione transferases, or GSTs. Once formed, the GSH conjugate is metabolized by the same degradative enzymes that metabolize GSH (see |FRAME: PWY-4041|). The GSH conjugate is transported out of the cell, where it is subsequently degraded by |FRAME: HS06361-MONOMER| or |FRAME: CPLX-6042|, and dipeptidases. The breakdown products (glutamate and glycine) are reabsorbed and can be used for GSH synthesis. The |FRAME:CPD-14706| that is left is also transported back into the cell, where it is acetylated by intracellular N-acetyltransferases to form the mercapturic acid |FRAME: CPD-14707|., The addition of the N-acetylcysteine moiety generally increases the compound's polarity and water solubility, and converts neutral compounds to anions, facilitating their transport across cell membranes and their excretion from the organism |CITS: [4892500]|. Mercapturic acids are released into the circulation or bile |CITS: [ 1939239]|; some are eventually excreted in urine, and some may undergo further metabolism.

In addition to common polyamines, thermophiles (from both bacteria and archaea) contain two types of unusual polyamines as major polyamines. One type consists of long linear polyamines such as |FRAME: CPD-13491| and |FRAME: CPD-22711|, and the other consists of branched polyamines such as |FRAME: CPD-16925|], |FRAME: CPD-13493|, and |FRAME: CPD-17107|, Several polyamine synthases that can form long linear polyamine were isolated from |FRAME: TAX-54248| and |FRAME: TAX-13773| and their susbtrate range was characterized. The |FRAME: MONOMER-21055| from |FRAME: TAX-54248| synthesized several long-chain polyamines with high activity using the same mechanism that is used by a wide range of organisms to synthesize common polyamines, in which the aminopropyl residue derives from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE| (decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine) |CITS: [19822146]|., Phylogenetic analysis of crenarchaeal polyamine synthases showed that they can be divided into two subtypes. Subtype I contains polyamine synthases which mainly synthesize triamines, while Subtype II contains polyamine synthases which mainly synthesize tetramines or longer polyamines., |FRAME: TAX-54248| has two synthases - |FRAME: MONOMER-21056|, which belongs to the first subyupe, and |FRAME: MONOMER-21055|, which belongs to subtype II. |FRAME: MONOMER-21056 "Polyamine aminopropyltransferase 1"| primarily synthesizes |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|, which is extended by |FRAME: MONOMER-21055| to form |FRAME: CPD-10689| and longer polyamines |CITS: [19822146]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-18540 Thiocoraline| is a thiodepsipeptide antitumor compound produced by two actinomycetes (|FRAME: ORG-6291| and |FRAME: TAX-349725|) that were isolated from two marine invertebrates (a soft coral and a mollusc) found at the Indian Ocean coast of Mozambique |CITS: [9360617][9360618 ]|. It belongs to the family of quinomycin-type antibiotics, which are C2-symmetric cyclic depsipeptides with a pair of intercalative chromophores that show potent antibacterial, anticancer and antiviral activities. The quinomycin-type antibiotics have been divided into two groups based on whether they contain |FRAME: CPD-18533| or |FRAME: CPD-18534| chromophores. |FRAME: CPD-18540 Thiocoraline|, like |FRAME: CPD-18542|, belongs to the group that contains |FRAME: CPD-18533|., All of the quinomycin-type antibiotics have potent DNA binding affinities at a level between nM and mM with different sequence selectivities. Reflecting these distinct affinities, quinomycin antibiotics show different inhibitory activities against various enzymes, such as DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase and topoisomerase |CITS: [16408310]|. Most of them are toxic to mammalian cells and cannot be used as drugs., |FRAME: CPD-18540 Thiocoraline| possesses a strong antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive microorganisms. It binds to supercoiled DNA and was shown to have a potent cytotoxic activity against P-388, A-549 and MEL-28 cell lines |CITS: [9360617]| as well as LoVo and SW620 human colon cancer cell lines, due to inhibiton of DNA elongation by DNA polymerase alpha |CITS: [10362104]|., About This Pathway, Each of the two symmetrical halves of the |FRAME: CPD-18540| core structure is constituted by 3-hydroxyquinaldyl-D-cysteinyl-glycyl-N-methyl-L-cysteinyl-N,S-dimethyl-L-cysteine. The halves are linked together through thioester bonds between the first D-Cys residue of one half and the last N,S-dimethyl-L-Cys residue of the other, half, and by one disulfide cross-bridge., The pathway could be roughly divided into the assembly of the |FRAME: CPD-18533| chromophore (described in |FRAME: PWY-7733|) and the assembly of the peptide backbone, which is carried out by non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPS), A study involving cloning and mutating adenylation domains of non-ribosomal peptide synthases in the |FRAME: TAX-349725| genome identified several involved genes and led to the sequencing of the full thiocoraline biosynthetic gene cluster. Cloning and expression of the full cluster in |FRAME: TAX-1916| and |FRAME: TAX-1888| resulted in |FRAME: CPD-18540| production |CITS: [16408310]|., Based on sequence analysis and similarity to clusters encoding the biosynthesis of other quinomycin-type antibiotics a pathway has been proposed. , The pathway leading to synthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-18533| chromophore is described in |FRAME: PWY-7733|. Next, the chromophore is activated by its adenylation. Since the gene cluster lacks an aryl-carrier protein, which would normally be required for loading the chromophore to the non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) modules, this function is presumed to be provided either by a peptidyl-carrier protein encoded by |FRAME: G-44308| or by the acyl-carrier protein that normally participates in fatty acid biosynthesis, as is the case for some related compounds |CITS: [15569690]|., Once loaded with the chromophore, the carrier transfers it to a D-cysteine residue that is already bound to the |FRAME: MONOMER-19607| |CITS: [16408310]|. TioR adds a |FRAME: GLY| residue and transfers the product to the |FRAME: MONOMER-19608|., According to the proposed scenario, for each nascent chain TioS receives from the |FRAME: MONOMER-19607| it activates two |FRAME: CYS| residues by adenylation and condenses them with the 3-hydroxyquinaldyl-D-cysteinyl-glycyl moiety, concomitant with N-methylation of the cysteine residues |CITS: [16408310]|. In addition, later work has shown that the PCP domain binds an S-methyl-L-cysteine residue, which has been pre-methylated by the TioN |FRAME: MONOMER-21311| |CITS: [25409494]|. That cysteine is also attached to the nascent chain., Once two such chains are loaded on the enzyme, the C terminal TE domain, which is proposed to possess a cyclorelease activity, is responsible for homodimerization of the two chains, releasing the cyclic octapeptide core structure |FRAME: CPD-18558| |CITS: [16408310]|., One additional transformation is required for formation of the final compound. A thiol oxidase catalyzes the formation of a sulfide bridge between the two non-S-methylated cysteines. The identity of the gene encoding this enzyme is still not known.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10016 Tacrolimus| (FK506), |FRAME: CPD-18261| (FK520), and |FRAME: CPD-14676| are related macrocyclic polyketides that are produced by |FRAME: TAX-83656|, |FRAME: TAX-132248|, and |FRAME: TAX-1912|, respectively. Ascomycin was isolated in the early sixties in a study of the antifungal activity of |FRAME: TAX-132248| |CITS: [14040785]|. Its structure and immunomodulatory properties were established more than 20 years later |CITS: [2461926]|., The three compounds are potent immunosuppressants that prevent T-cell proliferation. |FRAME: CPD-10016 Tacrolimus| and |FRAME: CPD-18261| bind to the receptor macrophilin-12 (FKBP-12) |CITS: [7678431]| forming a complex that blocks the calcium-dependent signal transduction cascade mediated by calcineurin. Calcineurin is a phsphatase that is responsible for activating nuclear factor of activated T-cells (NF-AT), a T cell transcriptional regulatory factor. As a consequence of the macrolide-FKBP-12 complex formation, the synthesis and release of Th1- (T helper 1) and Th2- (T helper 2) type cytokines, and other inflammatory mediators from T-cells and mast cells are blocked and the expression of signals essential for the activation of inflammatory T-lymphocytes is inhibited., Ascomycin and several of its derivatives, such as |FRAME: CPD-26194|, |FRAME: CPD-26192|, and |FRAME: CPD-26193|, are of considerable interest as therapeutics in both metastatic and inflammatory diseases, and are studied particularly as anti-inflammatory compounds for the treatment of skin diseases |CITS: [11496246][11298538][Paul05]|., About This Pathway, The three polyketides are formed by a hybrid polyketide synthase/non-ribosomal peptide synthase (PKS/NRPS) pathway that involves three polyketides synthases (encoded by the |FRAME: G-124287|, |FRAME: G-124288|, and |FRAME: G-124289| genes), which together contain 11 modules and 53 domains, one non-ribosomal peptide synthase (encoded by the |FRAME: G-124290| gene) that contains 4 domains, and additional enzymes, responsible for both the generation of building blocks and the tailoring of the final product., The |FRAME: CPD-18261| biosynthetic gene cluster was isolated and sequenced in 2000, and found to contain 22 genes |CITS: [10863099]|. The pathway starts with the unusual starter unit |FRAME: CPD-26185|. While this compound was known to be derived from |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| |CITS: [Paiva93][Wallace94][9315087][11241621]|, later research has shown that it is formed from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| via the action of |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.13|, followed by a reduction |CITS: [21383123]|. The starter unit is loaded by the loading module of the FkbB PKS and reduced further by the enoyl reductase (ER) domain of this module. Each of the other 10 domains of the three ployketide synthases extends the product using either a |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, a |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA|, or |FRAME: 2-Methoxymalonyl-ACP| extender unit. The final product of FkbA is handed over to the |FRAME: CPLX-85426|, which activates and attaches an |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE|, and presumably also catalyzes the release of the product and its cyclization into |FRAME: CPD-26183|., The released cyclic product undergoes a few additional modifications: a cytochrome P450 encoded by the |FRAME: G-124291| gene catalyzes hydroxylation of the C9 position, and potentially the further oxidation of the hydroxyl group to an oxo group (although the second activity has not been demonstrated) |CITS: [8752344]|. The second oxidation reaction was originally ascribed to the product of the |FRAME: G-124284| gene |CITS: [10863099]|, but that enzyme was later found to be a |FRAME: MONOMER-124284| |CITS: [21383123]|. Finally, a methyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124292| gene catalyzes the methylation of the hydroxyl on carbon-31, forming |FRAME: CPD-18261| |CITS: [8752344]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Phytobilins Phytobilins| are tetrapyrrole molecules that are synthesized by plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Major classes of phytobilins are:, 1. |FRAME: Phycobilins Phycobilins|, which are the chromophores of |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins| |CITS: [16663825]| and some algal phytochromes |CITS: [8616213]|, 2. |FRAME: Phytochromobilins Phytochromobilins|, which are the chromophores of higher plants |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| |CITS: [1634523][7744741]|., |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins Phycobiliproteins| are light-harvesting accessory pigments of cyanobacteria, red algae and cryptophytes, and |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| are photoreversible light signal-transducing pigments of plants, some algae, and some cyanobacteria., One of the major phycobiliproteins in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: Phycoerythrins phycoerythrin|, which is also found in the chloroplasts of red algae, glaucophytes and some cryptomonads. One of the chromophores which are always attached to phycoerythrin is |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins phycoerythrobilin|, a red light absorbing pigment that belongs to the |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|. It is found in |FRAME: TAX-1117| and in the chloroplasts of |FRAME: TAX-2763 rhodophytes|, |FRAME: TAX-38254 glaucocystophytes|, and some |FRAME: TAX-3027 cryptomonads|., |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins Phycoerythrobiln| is covalently linked to both subunits of |FRAME: Phycoerythrins phycoerythrin| by a thioether bond to conserved cysteine resudues at position 84. In addition, in some Rhodophytes and oceanic cyanobacteria, phycoerythrobilin also functions as the chromophore of another phycobiliprotein, |FRAME: R-Phycocyanins R-Phycocyanin|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathways for the production of the four cyanobacterial |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-3702| pathway for |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| biosynthesis, have been elucidated. These five chromophores share a common precursor, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, which is the product of heme macrocycle cleavage by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18| |CITS: [9744099]|. |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is subsequently reduced by one of several possible ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases., In most cyanobacteria |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| is converted to |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN| in two steps, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13950| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13952|, encoded by the genes |FRAME: G-10652| and |FRAME: G-10653|, respectively |CITS: [11283349]|. |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN| is converted to its isomer |FRAME: CPD-17223| either spontaneously or by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|., There are two stereoisomers of phycoerythrobilin, |FRAME: CPD-17223| and |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN|. While |FRAME: CPD-17223| is the major pigment that is released from phycobiliproteins by methanolysis |CITS: [1634523]|, only |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN| is produced initially |CITS: [11283349]|, with the second isomer produced either spontaneously or by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|., An alternative pathway occurs in |FRAME: TAX-1218| species infected by certain cyanophages, see |FRAME: PWY-7580| |CITS: [18356052]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-21471 Pederin| is an exremely toxic compound produced by endosymbiotic bacteria of female beetles that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-347426| and |FRAME: TAX-747091| genera. The toxin is present in the hemolymph of the beetles, making up approximately 0.025% of the insect's weight, and serves as a chemical weapon against predators., The active substance from the |FRAME: TAX-347426| beetles was first reported by Netolitzky in 1918 |CITS: [Netolitzky19]|. It was isolated in 1953 by Pavan and Bo, who collected 25 million |FRAME: TAX-347427| beetles for the task (and also named it) |CITS: [Pavan52][Pavan53]|. The structure was elucidated in 1965 |CITS: [Cardani65]|, with slight modifications and stereochemistry added a few years later |CITS: [Matsumoto68][Furusaki68]|. Two related compounds, |FRAME: CPD-22182| |CITS: [Quilico61]| and |FRAME: CPD-22183| |CITS: [Cardani67]|, were also identified and have a similar physiological effect, though to a lesser extent., |FRAME: CPD-21471 Pederin| is not transferred to people by biting or stinging; it is transferred when the beetle is crushed and its hemolymph contacts the skin. When contact with skin occurs, pederin causes an acute skin condition known as dermatitis linearis. The beetles are widespread, and outbreaks of dermatitis linearis have been observed in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, South America, North America and Australia., |FRAME: CPD-21471 Pederin| is one of the most potent non-proteinaceous substances ever isolated. When injected intravenously, it is more potent than the cobra venom. It induces an acute, necrotic reaction by inhibiting protein synthesis |CITS: [Tiboni68]|, leading to arrest of DNA synthesis and cell death |CITS: [20236196]|. The toxin binds irreversibly to the ribosome, preventing translation of mRNA |CITS: [768741][Vazquez82]|. In addition, pederin has a strong vesicant activity, causing severe blistering., The reaction to pederin is delayed 12–48 h post-exposure |CITS: [18946579][24082222][23561606]|. Subsequent scarring and hyperpigmentation are common |CITS: [5764196][18946579]|., Similar compounds have been reported from endosymbiotic bacteria of marine sponges (the mycalamides, onnamides, theopederins, and icadamides), as well as from free-living cyanobacteria (|FRAME: CPD-22184|). The pederin family includes several candidates for anticancer drug development |CITS: [15787465]|., About This Pathway, A linkage between pederin biosynthesis and symbiotic bacteria has been suspected based on studied that exposed the beetles to several antibiotics, showing that induction of pederin accumulation depends on the antibiotic's spectrum of efficaciousness |CITS: [11166312]|. Sequencing of the 16S rDNA gene of the bacterial symbionts of |FRAME: ORG-6364| beetles showed that they are closely related to |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [11886773]|., Since the structure of pederin, as well early labeling studies |CITS: [Cardani73]|, indicated that it is a polyketide product synthesized by a type I polyketide synthase (PKS), a search for genes encoding such enzymes was conducted by PCR-amplification from total DNA isolated from beetles of several |FRAME: TAX-347426| genera. PKS-encoding genes were found only in individuals that contained pederin, suggesting that the genes belong to the pederin cluster |CITS: [12381784]|. Sequencing of the region revealed two large genes encoding hybrid type I polyketide synthase (PKS)/nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) enzymes (|FRAME: G-63074| and pedH), as well as several tailoring enzymes. A subsequent study identified a second region that contained as additiona PKS gene, |FRAME: G-63077|, which encodes the first four modules of the pederin PKS system |CITS: [14695518]|. Following the discovery of a homologous gene cluster in the bacterial endosymbiont of the marine sponge |FRAME: TAX-37505|, which produces onnamides and theopederins, a third cluster was discovered in the |FRAME: TAX-176282|, which contained genes involved in the β-branching process (an "HMGS cassette") |CITS: [15520376]|., The pederin structure contains an unusual exomethylene bond branching off the C-4 position, which is formed by a β-branching process. Such processes have been characterized in several other ployketide products, and are known to comprise the addition of a two-carbon unit to the β-carbonyl of the nascent polyketide chain and subsequent modifications. The process is typically catalyzed by enzymes encoded by an "HMGS cassette" of genes (named after |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10|, the first β-branching enzyme to be described). The core enzymes of the HMGS cassette are a dedicated FAS-like acyl-carrier protein that loads a malonyl moiety from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, a mutated acyltransferase that lost the ability to catalyze formation of C-C bonds and functions as a decarboxylase, converting the malonyl moiety to an acetyl moiety, and a homolog of |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10 "EC 2.3.3.10"| that transfers the acetyl moiety from the acyl-carrier protein to the β carbonyl of the target, forming the β-branch branch., HMGS cassettes have been shown to install methyl branch points in |FRAME: CPD-21467|, |FRAME: Curacins curacin|, |FRAME: Jamaicamides jamaicamide|, and |FRAME: Pseudomonic-Acids mupirocin|. Based on sequence orthology, |FRAME: G-63080| encodes the acyl-carrier protein, |FRAME: G-63079| encodes the decarboxylase, and |FRAME: G-63078| encodes a homolog of |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10 "EC 2.3.3.10"|. In addition, the cassette includes the |FRAME: G-63081| gene which encodes an enoyl-CoA dehydratase homolog, which likely removes the hydroxyl group at the β-branch. The remaining decarboxylation and isomerization of the double bond may be catalyzed by the PedI PKS, as described below., According to the current model the pathway starts when the GCN5-related N-acetyltransferase (GNAT) domain located at the N-terminus of the |FRAME: MONOMER-20817| loads an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA. The next three modules of PedI extend the polyketide skeleton by three malonyl units. As the pederin PKSs belong to the "trans-AT" class of PKS, members of which do not contain any acyltransferase (AT) domains, they are not capable of loading the malonyl extender units directly from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|. This function is provided by the |FRAME: MONOMER-20815|, which provides the malonyl extender unit to all of the pederin PKSs |CITS: [12381784][27003309]|., PedI also adds a methyl group by SAM-dependent methylation |CITS: [14695518]|., During the extension by PedI the β-branch is formed as described above. The two crotonase-like domains in PedI are likely involved in converting the methyl group formed in the process to an exomethylene group |CITS: [12381784]|., The intermediate is then transferred to the |FRAME: MONOMER-20814|, which adds a |FRAME: GLY| moiety, followed by extension by four malonyl units. A methyltransferase domain in module 4 catalyzes the two successive methylations of the same carbon atom, introducing a gem dimethyl group. An unusual setup of two dehydratase domains in module 5 catalyzes the closure of the dimethylated tetrahydropyrane ring, most likely via dehydration and subsequent Michael addition of the C-11 hydroxyl group |CITS: [12381784]|., Downstream of |FRAME: G-63074| is the pedH gene, which encodes another hybrid NRPS/PKS enzyme. PedH should theoretically further elongate the pederin-type intermediate generated by PedF and release a compound that has an extended structure, which could be cleaved to generate the |FRAME: CPD-21471| molecule. Alternatively, pederin could be cleaved directly from PedF. It is currently not known which of these two scenarios actually takes place |CITS: [12381784]|., The PedF PKS forms ae |FRAME: CPD-22181| which undergoes two hydroxylations and four methylations to become pederin. While genes encoding a hydroxylase (pedB) and three O-methyltransferases (pedA, pedE, and pedO) have been found in the pederin gene clusters, the exact reaction associated with these enzymes, and the order in which they act, are still not known, and thus these transformations have not been included in this pathway.

General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis, (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|),, and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is, highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for, a review)., There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes, that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase, enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal, dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, Methylglyoxal dehydrogenases catalyze the direct oxidation of methylglyoxal to pyruvate., The first enzyme that was shown to catalyze this reaction was partially purified from sheep liver, |CITS: [4383524]|. That enzyme was able to utilize both NAD and NADP, and was not specific, for methylglyoxal. However, later work suggested that this enzyme might have been a mixture of two, different enzymes - one specific for NAD and the other for NADP. Such two enzymes were purified, from goat liver, and were shown to be of exactly the same size - 42 kDa |CITS: [7107625]|., NAD-specific enzymes have also been detected in microorganisms. Higgins and Turner, reported that cell extracts of |FRAME: ORG-5972| catalyzed the direct oxidation of methylglyoxal to, pyruvate by an enzyme which they named |FRAME: MONOMER-12919|. The specific activity of the, extracts was 35 nmoles/mg protein per min, and was maximal at pH 7.9. , The enzyme was inducible by growth on |FRAME:1-AMINO-PROPAN-2-OL|, and the Km of the enzyme, was 30 μM |CITS: [4390194]|., Another such enzyme has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [Rhee87]|., This pathway is probably not present in yeast or higher plants |CITS: [2663129]|.

Summary: Photosynthesis is a process in which energy from sunlight is harvested and used to fix |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| into carbohydrates., Photosynthesis occurrs in bacteria, algae, phytoplankton and higher plants. During photosynthesis the solar energy is trapped by light-harvesting complexes, and used to split a donor molecule, generating high potential electrons that are channeled to NADP<sup>+</sup>, forming NADPH, which can be used to reduce |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|., In oxygenic photosynthesis the donor molecule is water, resulting in the release of molecular |FRAME:OXYGEN-MOLECULE|. Some bacteria perform anoxygenic photosynthesis, in which different donor molecules are used for production of high potential electrons. An example are phototrophic sufur bacteria, which use sulfide, releasing molecular sulfur as a by-product., Photosynthesis is divided into two general subprocesses: the "light reactions" and the "dark reactions". The light reactions comprise the trapping of sunlight, the production of |FRAME:NADPH| and ATP, and the release of molecular |FRAME:OXYGEN-MOLECULE| (see |FRAME:PWY-101|)., The dark reactions, better known as the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|, comprise of the use of NADPH and ATP to fix |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE | and produce carbohydrates |CITS: [MatthewsvanHoldeII]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|). Analogs of these pathways are also found in the metabolism of deoxyhexoses such as |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-fucoses| (see |FRAME: RHAMCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|). The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]|.
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|). The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimnberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]|.
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: D-Xylose|, which can serve as a total source of carbon and energy for |FRAME: TAX-511145|, enters the cell either through a low-affinity, proton-motive force-driven or a high-affinity, ATP-driven (ABC) transport system, so it is not phosphorylated during entry. Once inside the cell, an isomerase converts it to |FRAME:D-XYLULOSE| and subsequently a kinase converts it to |FRAME:XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|. Hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy.

While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]|, it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|., The most common mechanism for retreiving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination,, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves, the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid., In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|)., In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central, metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich, pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the, corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde., Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced, (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols",, or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids ("fusel acids")  |CITS: [15933030]|., This pathway illustrates the Ehrlich pathway for |FRAME: VAL|, one of the three protein-building, branched chain amino acids (BCAAs) (along with |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME: ILE|)., While most other eukaryotes (as well as many prokaryotes) catabolize |FRAME: VAL| through a, succession of acyl-coA derivatives to metabolites that can enter the TCA cycle, (see |FRAME: VALDEG-PWY|), providing the organism with carbon as well as nitrogen,, yeast are not able to use |FRAME:VAL| as a carbon source, and process it through the Ehrlich pathway, to |FRAME:ISOBUTANOL| |CITS: [8277258]|., Initial work performed by Ehrlich and others suggested that the catabolism of |FRAME:VAL| in, |FRAME: TAX-4932| begins by transamination using |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| (similar to the, first step of the pathway found in other eukaryotes), and continues with decarboxylation producing, |FRAME:CPD-7000| that is further reduced to |FRAME:ISOBUTANOL| |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|., Later work by Dickinson et al suggests that the product of |FRAME: VAL| transamination,, |FRAME:2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, can be decarboxylated by any isozyme of pyruvate decarboxylase, |CITS: [8325383][9748245][10989420]|. Mutants lacking all three pyruvate decarboxylase isozymes, were still able to use valine as a nitrogen source, but produced no |FRAME:ISOBUTANOL|, |CITS: [9748245]|., In |FRAME: TAX-1358|, on the other hand, the decarboxylation of |FRAME:2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| to, |FRAME:CPD-7000| is catalyzed by an enzyme highly specific for |FRAME:2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, |CITS: [15358422]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13455 "Justicidin B"| is an arylnaphthalene lignan that has been used traditionally by native Taiwaneseas a fish killing agent. It was first identified as the active ingredient in the |FRAME: TAX-4190| plant in 1965 |CITS: [Munakata65]| and the correct structure was reported soon after |CITS: [Govindachari67]|., The compound was subsequently reported from other |FRAME: TAX-4185| and |FRAME: TAX-23513| species |CITS: [Okigawa70][Nukul87]| and is now known to be produced by several plant families, especially |FRAME: TAX-4190|, |FRAME: TAX-58880 Phyllanthus|, |FRAME: TAX-266078| and |FRAME: TAX-4005| species |CITS: [11809070][19323270][27347906]|., There is growing interest in |FRAME: CPD-13455| and synthetic derivatives due to their application in cancer chemotherapy and other pharmacological effects |CITS: [11809070][27347906]|. The compound exhibits a wide array of biological properties that range from piscicidal to antifungal, antiviral and antibacterial activities. It shows strong cytotoxicity on the chronic myeloid leukemia cells |CITS: [16872135]| and strong activity against the parasite Trypanosoma brucei. In addition |FRAME: CPD-13455| is a potent bone resorption inhibitor, and has been used as a lead compound for the design of new antirheumatic drugs |CITS: [16872135 ]|., About This Pathway, Calli and hairy roots of |FRAME: TAX-35941| accumulate the |FRAME: CPD-13455| as a major constituent |CITS: [16872135]|. The pathway begins with the formation of |FRAME: CPD-18761| from |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL|. Whether |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.7|, or |FRAME: EC-1.10.3.2|, function in the oxidation of monolignols to radicals has been under active evaluation for many years |CITS: [13657039][17812228][Sterjiades93][9914531]|. Both peroxidases and laccases were shown to catalyze the oxidation of |FRAME: CONIFERYL-ALCOHOL| to a radical in vitro |CITS: [16027971][25626739]|., Most lignans are optically active as a result of a stereo-specific linkage that builds the various dimers. The unique protein that mediates the regio- and stereospecificity of bimolecular phenoxy radical coupling to generate oligomeric lignans and polymeric lignins is not an enzyme The protein, which was named 'dirigent protein' (DP) serves only to bind and orientate the coniferyl alcohol-derived free radicals |CITS: [8994027][10859176][16023845]|. It could be demonstrated that dirigent proteins form a multigene family in plants |CITS: [12359517]|, and their function is not limited to the formation of lignans but also includes other biosyntheses of various phenolics employing corresponding radicals., Two distinct enzyme classes of pinoresinol/lariciresinol reductases (PLR) have been identified. These enzymes are bifunctional and catalyze the enantioselective reduction of |FRAME: CPD-20974| and |FRAME: CPD-20973| towards |FRAME: CPD-8910|, as discovered in Forsythia |CITS: [8910615]|. , While the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-35941| can act on both enantiomers of both compounds, it displays a unique enantiospecificty, prefering |FRAME: CPD-8905| in the first step and |FRAME: CPD-8908| in the second step |CITS: [17257599]|., The next step in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.331|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-20975|. The enzyme has been studied in detail in |FRAME: TAX-35933| and |FRAME: TAX-55183| |CITS: [2037574][11278426][15653677][16493463]|., The enzymes catalyzing the last steps of |FRAME: CPD-13455| biosynthesis have not been identified yet |CITS: [17257599]|.

General Background, Thiols play several major roles in the cell; they help maintain the redox balance, keeping a reduced environment (see the pathway |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY|), they fight reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and they are involved in the detoxification of many other toxins and stress-inducing factors., In most aerobic organisms the major thiol is the tripeptide |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly, known as GSH). The intracellular concentration of GSH ranges from 0.5-10 mM. Most of the non-protein cysteine is stored in the form of GSH, since free |FRAME: CYS| auto-oxidizes rapidly to |FRAME: L-CYSTINE|, producing potentially toxic oxygen radicals |CITS: [11544348]|., In the process of reducing other molecules (such as peroxides) two molecules of GSH are condensed into a single molecule of the oxidized form |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE| (see |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY|). In eukaryotes this reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme glutathione peroxidase (for example, see |FRAME: CPLX-5881|). Glutathione-dependent peroxidases have been discovered in several prokaryotes as well |CITS: [11399772] [12606554]|. The disulfide is reduced back to GSH by the action of |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE-REDUCT-NADPH-CPLX|. Most of the glutathione pool is kept in the reduced form. In |FRAME:TAX-562|, the ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione is 200:1 |CITS: [11544348]|., GSH is active against toxins by a process that involves multiple enzymes, and in the case of eukaryotes, occurs across multiple organs. Toxins are conjugated to GSH by a dedicated enzyme, resulting in a cysteine-toxin conjugate (this occurs in the liver in eukaryotes). The conjugate is acetylated (in the kidney), and cleaved, resulting in a part of the glutatione molecule and a mercapturate form of the toxin, which is excreted out of the cell (see |FRAME: PWY-4061|) |CITS: [8145281]|., In addition, low molecular weight thiols have been found to be involved in a few other cellular process, including DNA synthesis |CITS: [1970635]| and formaldehyde reduction (see |FRAME: PWY-1801| |CITS: [Patel98]|., While GSH is the major thiol in eukaryotic organisms, Gram negative bacteria and the majority of Gram positive bacteria, it is not universal. In some organisms other thiols have taken its role, including |FRAME: CoM|, |FRAME: TRYPANOTHIONE|, |FRAME: Ergothioneine|, |FRAME: CPD1G-2| and |FRAME: CPD-17028|., About This Pathway, In mammals, the intracellular synthesis of glutathione and its utilization are linked by the γ-glutamyl cycle, which is composed of six enzyme-catalyzed reactions. The first two reactions are responsible for GSH biosynthesis - in the first step, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-16|, an amide linkage is formed between |FRAME:CYS| and |FRAME: GLT|., |FRAME: CPLX-5961| then catalyzes the reaction between |FRAME:GLY| and the cysteine carboxyl of the |FRAME: L-GAMMA-GLUTAMYLCYSTEINE| dipeptide to form GSH., The second part of the pathway consists of glutathione degradation, and occurs outside of the cell. The enzymes that catalyze its breakdown are |FRAME: CPLX-6041| and different dipeptidases, which are membrane-bound proteins located predominantly on the apical surface of epithelial tissues in mammals. |FRAME: CPLX-6041| is the only enzyme that can remove the γ-glutamyl moiety from GSH under physiological conditions, while the dipeptidases (EC 3.4.11.2) remove the glycyl moiety. The breakdown products (glutamate, glycine, and cysteine) can be reabsorbed into the cell and used for additional GSH synthesis (by EC 6.3.22 and EC 6.3.2.3) |CITS: [9027][9755286]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7670 "Dimethyl sulfide"| (DMS) is a major contributor to the total sulfur emissions to the atmosphere from land and the ocean. In marine, estuarine, and salt marsh systems, the main source of DMS is the degradation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|. There are two main routes for DMSP degradation, leading to formation of either |FRAME: CPD-7670| or |FRAME: CPD-7672|. Other sources for DMS include the reduction of |FRAME: DMSO| and the degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids., DMS, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere, and is considered the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to sulfuric and methanesulfonic acids, which attract water and promote cloud formation and thus influence the climate |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, up to 90% of the DMS in the ocean is degraded biologically |CITS: [Kiene90]|., DMS is toxic, and attempts to isolate in pure culture DMS-degrading organisms that can use it as the sole carbon and energy source have been often unsuccessful due to this toxicity. However, several organisms capable of degerading DMS have been isolated over the years. Aerobic bacterial DMS oxidation has been demonstrated in organisms from a few taxonomic domains, including Thiobacillus sp. strain MS1 |CITS: [Sivela80]|, |FRAME: ORG-5989| |CITS: [Kanagawa82], [Kanagawa86][2930168][Tanji89][Gould92]|, |FRAME: ORG-6053| |CITS: [1872604][8285684]|, |FRAME: ORG-6050| |CITS: [Debont81]|, |FRAME: ORG-6052| |CITS:[3767349][Suylen86][Suylen87] [Smith88a]|, |FRAME: ORG-6060| |CITS: [1575493][Omori95]|, |FRAME: ORG-6062| |CITS: [Omori95]|, |FRAME: ORG-6061| |CITS: [9345770]|, and |FRAME: ORG-6066| |CITS: [12835925]| and |FRAME:TAX-392484||CITS:[16535680][17322322]|. Anaerobic degradation of DMS has been documented by methanogens |CITS: [11073950]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5258|) and by sulfate-reducing bacteria |CITS: [8074524]|., About This Pathway, The preferred sulfur sources for most bacteria are |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: SULFATE|. In the absence of these, many types of bacteria are able to utilize organosulfur compounds as alternative sulfur source (the process has been named the sulfate starvation response). Several types of bacteria are able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) as their sole sulfur source. These include |FRAME: ORG-6060| |CITS: [1575493][Omori95]|, |FRAME: ORG-6062| |CITS: [Omori95]|, |FRAME: ORG-6061| |CITS: [9345770]|, and |FRAME: ORG-6066| |CITS: [12835925]|., In these organisms DMS is oxidized via |FRAME: DMSO| (DMSO) and |FRAME: CPD-10437| to |FRAME: CPD-3746|,, which can be oxidized to |FRAME: SO3|. Sulfite can be oxidized to sulfate in several pathways (see |FRAME: Sulfite-Oxidation|)., The first two steps of the pathway, leading to |FRAME: CPD-10437|, are catalyzed by the same enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.245|. The genes encoding the enzyme have been cloned from |FRAME: ORG-6061| and found to be very similar to the genes encoding |FRAME: CPLX-7253|, a multicomponent enzyme containing six different polypeptides |CITS: [9345770]|., |FRAME: CPD-10437 "Dimethyl sulfone"| is oxidized by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.35|, which has been characterized from |FRAME: ORG-6066| and |FRAME: TAX-205922| |CITS: [15661012][27392454]|. The product, |FRAME: CPD-15551|, is unstable in the presence of dioxygen and reduced FMN, and spontaneously oxidize to |FRAME: CPD-3746|, which is oxidized further to |FRAME: SO3| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.34|. Both enzymes are |FRAME: FMNH2|-dependent, and are controlled by the SfnR transcription regulator, which regulates genes that are activated by sulfate stravation |CITS:[12835925][15661012]|., A PTS trasport system for organosulfur compounds has been shown to be essential for |FRAME: CPD-10437| utilization, by |FRAME: ORG-6066| |CITS: [17711452]|.

Summary: Halogenated phenols, such as |FRAME: CPD-10866|, |FRAME: CPD-10868| and |FRAME: CPD-10870|,, are widely used as broad spectrum biocides, which are released into the environment, as free compounds or sodium salts., Halophenols pose a serious environmental risk because of their acute toxicity and relative resistence to chemical and, biological degradation |CITS: [678009]|., Several organisms are able to metabolize chlorophenols. Some of them, such as |FRAME: TAX-65741| |CITS: [678009]|,, |FRAME: ORG-6093| |CITS: [16535177]| and |FRAME: ORG-6092| |CITS: [7576526]|, are able to grow on chlorophenols as, their sole source of carbon and energy., The metabolism of chlorophenols usually starts with hydroxylation of the chlorophenol to a chlorocatechol (a less common, pathway involves transformation to hydroquinones - see |FRAME: MONOMER-14674|)., While no specialized enzyme for the chlorophenol hydroxylation has been described, it has been shown that the, broad spectrum |FRAME: CPLX-7811| enzymes of both fungi and bacteria are often able to metabolize substituted, phenols, including chlorophenols |CITS: [569150][8269923][7851397][9797289][12396129][14600239][17425111]|., The chlorocatechols that are formed are usually degraded by modified ortho-cleavage pathways |CITS: [678009]|,, although organisms that utilize modified meta-cleavage pathways have been described |CITS: [16535738]|.

|FRAME: Camphor Camphor| is a bicyclic monoterpene with a characteristic pungent odor and taste. Two enantiomers occur naturally - |FRAME: CPD-862|, the predominant natural isomer, and |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR|. Camphor is produced by several trees, including the camphor tree (|FRAME: TAX-13429|) as well as hundreds of other plants, including |FRAME: TAX-38868| (garden sage), |FRAME: TAX-39367| (rosemary), |FRAME: TAX-39169| (lavender), |FRAME: TAX-35608| (sweet wormwood), and |FRAME: TAX-13328| |CITS: [5532413][ 32619737][35921521]|. Camphor can be synthesized chemically from |FRAME: CPD-4892|, which is obtained from oil of turpentine., Camphor is metabolized by some soil bacteria, depending on the species, via either 5-exo |CITS: [LeGall63]| or 6-endo hydroxy camphor |CITS: [Chapman66]|. These pathways have been termed, respectively, the 2,5- and 2,6-hydroxylating systems |CITS: [806252]|., |FRAME: ORG-5941|, which carries the linear 533 kb CAM plasmid |CITS: [23524667]|, can grow on both |FRAME: CPD-862| and |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| as its sole carbon source, due to the presence of enantiomer-specific Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenases that handle the different enantiomorphs |CITS: [8515237]|. The organism utilizes the 2,5 pathway, and the pathway for |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| degradation is described here |CITS: [BRADSHAW59][4351810][6848481][8515237]|. A similar pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-862| is described in |FRAME: P601-PWY|., The cleavage of the bicyclic ring of camphor involves the participation of three unrelated monooxygenases, one dehydrogenase and one CoA ester synthetase. The camphor hydroxylase, P-450<sub>CAM</sub>, became a primary prototype for P-450 monooxygenases |CITS: [3011733]|. , The CAM plasmid appears to contain the information for all the enzymes that are required to convert camphor to |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| |CITS: [4351810]|. However, the enzymes involved in the later steps of the pathway have not been discovered yet.

General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway: , Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes have been involved in a variety of biological processes: inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Neoabietic acid, an abietane-type DRA, is one of the principal resin acids |CITS:[17082986],[11269960]|. Neoabietic acid purified from rosin shows a strong dose-related cytotoxicity when tested on human polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMN cells) and human gingival fibroblasts |CITS:[9335345]|. This effect was inhibited by increased zinc concentrations. In addition, neoabietic acid (CTCM189) was shown to act as an inhibitor of the autoimmune reaction in murine EAE neoabietic acid (CTCM189) as an inhibitor of the autoimmune reaction in murine EAE |CITS:[Saxena04]|. This compound isomerizes mostly to abietic acid (82%) and some palustric acid (13%) |CITS:[Loeblich57]|. The formation of this acid involves the formation of the abietane skeleton via cyclization of the diterpenoid precursor |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This cyclization occurs via the formation of the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-4750| and is followed by the stepwise oxidation of the C18 methyl group of the derived olefin |FRAME:CPD-8696|. Several levopimaradiene/abietadiene synthases have been identified, which, in addition to |FRAME:--ABIETADIENE| and |FRAME:CPD-8695|, can produce a variety of other olefins including |FRAME:CPD-8696| |CITS:[8798524],[15310829],[16497345]|. The mechanism of oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-8696| to |FRAME:CPD-8712| is thought to resembles that of the oxidation of |FRAME:CPD1F-128| to |FRAME:CPD1F-132| and that |FRAME:CPD1F-132| to |FRAME:CPD1F-95| (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|) in which a single multifunctional enzyme (ent-kaurene oxidase) catalyze the consecutive oxidation steps. An enzyme catalyzing those steps remains to be identified.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8718 Taxol| (paclitaxel) is a highly effective anticancer drug extensively used in the treament of various carcinomas, melanomas and sarcomas |CITS: [11707604]|. Taxol was first isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew tree (|FRAME: TAX-46220|). Limited supply prompted intensive research efforts to find alternate sources including isolation from renewable foliage tissues. Currently, biosynthesis in tissue culture systems from renewable plantation-grown Taxus species, along with semi synthesis of taxol and its analogs from advanced taxane diterpenoid metabolites, remain the main source for this potent chemotherapeutic agent |CITS: [8621577]|. , The total number of naturally occurring taxoid drugs now stand at 350. The study of these compounds led to the discovery of novel structures and the preparation of new derivatives with improved biological properties (second generation taxoid drugs) |CITS: [11707604]|. However, total synthesis is not yet a commercially viable option, and limited supply from the plant source inhibits wider application of the drug. The increasing demand for improved biological production requires an understanding of the biosynthetic pathways leading to taxol and related taxoids., Current research aims at the up-regulation of the taxol biosynthetic pathway by over expression of selected genes in Taxus or other suitable hosts |CITS: [12089320]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7392|)., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-8718| starts with the cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| to form the basic taxane body, followed by multiple oxygenations (mostly carried out by cytochrome P450 enzymes) and 4 CoA-dependent acylations of the core structure, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: BACCATIN-III|., Additional steps are required to form the C-13 side chain, which is appended to |FRAME: BACCATIN-III|. Two additional steps are required to form taxol |CITS: [Croteau06]|., The C13-side chain is considered functionally important as it significantly contributes to the anticancer properties of taxol through binding to the microtubule surface which subsequently inhibits cell proliferation |CITS:[Malik11]|., The genes encoding the pathway's enzymes have been cloned and some of them have been characterized with regard to their role in functionalizing the taxane core and 13C-side chain. Working with surrogate substrates such as |FRAME:CPD-13925|, a supposedly dead end product in heartwood but structurally closely related to complex taxol intermediates, have helped to identify many of the enzymes |CITS:[15178487][15157877][Croteau06][16137660][25899320][28878800][31113367][ 30665359][37897038][38271490]|. , The order of oxygenation is not known, and it is likely that the taxol pathway is not a linear sequence but rather a branched and anastomosed network of side steps and common cross points that produce not only taxol but other toxoids as well |CITS:[Croteau06]|. In this pathway diagram we show one possible scenario, but it is likely that this sequence of events is not correct.

Summary: The biosynthesis of several important metabolites involves the consumption of |FRAME: MET| through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), in a reaction that releases |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA)., These metabilites include polyamines (see |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME:BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-1303|), |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|), and bacterial auto-inducers (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration is tightly regulated through the methionine salvage cycle, where MTA is recycled through a series of reactions back to |FRAME: MET|., The methionine salvage pathway, also called the Yang cycle, is present with some variations in all types of organisms |CITS: [19946895]| (|FRAME: TAX-562| is a notorious exception). It has been partially characterized from a number of organisms, including bacteria |CITS:[8227039][7852397][8694776][9880484][11371200]|, plants |CITS: [Baur72][Murr75][Kushad83][Miyazaki87]|, yeast |CITS: [3906034]|, protozoal parasites |CITS: [8585735][ 11443076]| and rat |CITS: [7007366][7068632][7852397]|. The pathway was best studied in the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-573|., While most of the pathway is conserved among all organisms, several variants exist that differ in the initial steps of the pathway, between |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) and |FRAME: CPD-1063| (MTRP). These variants, describing bacteria and plants, higher eukaryotes, and protozoa, are described by several pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|., This metabolic differences in the early steps of the methionine salvage pathway are being exploited for developing new drugs targeted against pathogenic microorganisms |CITS: [2854458][2153115][1929327]|., Several variants of the methionine salvage cycle are available in MetaCyc. The pathway shown here operates in bacteria and plants and includes polyamine biosynthesis., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here depicts the formation of MTA by the production of the polyamine |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, although MTA is also formed during the biosynthesis of other polyamines., Unlike in higher eukaryotes, where the recycling of MTA to methionine starts with phosphorolytic cleavage by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.28| to yield |FRAME: CPD-444|, in most bacteria and plants this conversion is achieved by the action of two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.16| and |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.100|, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-560| |CITS: [8694776][10574451]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6754|)., Once |FRAME: CPD-444| is formed, it is recycled back to L-methionine in 6 steps, comprising an isomerase, a dehydratase, an enolase, a phosphatase, an oxygenase, and a transaminase. The last enzyme, a glutamine-dependent transaminase, produces the byproduct |FRAME: 2-KETO-GLUTARAMATE|, which is believed to be toxic. Thus an additional enzyme, an ω-amidase that converts the latter to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, is also considered a part of the pathway |CITS: [24837359]|., A few notes of interest about the enzymes of this pathway, At least in some strains, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: EC-5.3.2.5|, is a one of the few members of the RubisCO protein family |CITS: [17352497]|., The reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|, can occur non-enzymatically in the presence of air. It is yet unknown whether the non-enzymatic reaction occurs in vivo |CITS: [7852397]|., If the enzyme that usually catalyzes this reaction binds a Ni2+ instead of Fe2+, it catalyzes a different reaction (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.53|), forming a shunt of the methionine salvage pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5389|) |CITS:[7852397] [9880484][11371200]|. While the purpose of this shunt is yet unknown, it has been suggested that it may provide a mechanism for regulating |FRAME: MET| levels in vivo |CITS: [11371200]|., In some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-571|, the reactions catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.3.2.5| (MtnW) and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.87| (MtnX) are catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.77| (MtnC).

Summary: Flavonoids constitute an important group of plant secondary metabolites. Over 10,000 flavonoids have been , described in the literature |CITS: [17587669]|. Flavonoids are known for their diverse bioactivities. They act as , antioxidants, plant defense agent, anticancer agent etc. The structural diversity of flavonoids is attributed , to acylation, glycosylation and methylation of their hydroxyl groups. O-methylation of flavonoids results in , a reduction of their reactivity and an increase in their antimicrobial activity, whereas glycosylation increases their , solubility and stability |CITS: [18817819]|. O-methylation of flavonoids is catalyzed by O-methyltransferases (OMTs). , They transfer the methyl group from S-adenosyl-l-methionine to specific hydroxyl groups of flavonoids. Plant , OMTs are highly regioselective, i. e. each one transfers the methyl group to a specific hydroxyl group in a flavonoid |CITS: [18817819]|., The 3'-O-methyltransferase specifically O-methylating the B-ring 3'- position of flavonoids and 3-position of phenylpropanoids has been isolated from |FRAME:TAX-36749| and heterologously expressed and partially purified in E.coli. With respect to substrate specificity the two OMT homologs identified in |FRAME:TAX-36749| were both unique in the sense that they accepted phenylpropanoids and flavonoids alike, however expressed a clear preference for flavonoids over phenylpropanoids. It was proposed that these methyltransferases are more ancient or adapted to the living conditions of |FRAME:TAX-36749| as other methyltransferases have lost the capability to catalyze both compound classes |CITS:[9514654]|.

Summary: General Background, Vitamin B12 (also known as adenosylcobalamin or |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|) was discovered in the 1920s after Minot and Murphy reported that they could cure the symptoms of pernicious anaemia by feeding patients with crude liver extract |CITS: [Minot26]| (they received the Nobel prize in 1934 for this discovery). The unknown factor has been isolated and subsequently crystallized in 1948 |CITS:[Lester48][Rickes48]|, and was given the name vitamin B12 and, as it was shown to contain a cobalt ion, cobalamin |CITS: [12195810]|. , Vitamin B12 is one of the most structurally complex small molecules made in Nature. It contains a contracted porphinoid ring (called a corrin ring) with a cobalt ion ligated at its center and further held in place by a lower axial base (a dimethylbenzimidazole) and an upper methyl or adenosyl group. Its biosynthesis is similarly complex, and requires more than thirty genes. It's biosynthesis is confined to only some bacteria and archaea |CITS: [11935176]|., Two main pathways are known for |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthesis - an aerobic pathway (this pathway) and an anaerobic pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5507|). The main differences between these pathways are the timing of the |FRAME: CO+2| ion insertion and the ring-contraction mechanism (for more about ring contraction, see |CITS: [16592942]|). |FRAME: CO+2| is inserted early on in the anaerobic pathway, and rather late in the aerobic pathway., The two different routes then merge at |FRAME: CPD-689|, and the later part of the pathway is identical, or at least very similar., About This Pathway, The best characterized aerobic |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| biosynthetic pathway is that of the aerobic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-43306|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| starts with the biosynthesis of the tetrapyrrole intermediate |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, which is a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of several important compounds, such as |FRAME: Hemes heme| and |FRAME: Chlorophylls chlorophyl|. |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III "Uroporphyrinogen III| is converted to a corrin ring by a complex process that involves (among other things) the attachment of eight methyl groups, all derived from |FRAME:S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM). During the process the ring contracts via bonding of carbons C-1 and C-19 to each other, eliminating carbon C-20 from the ring. Both the C-20 carbon and the added C-20 methyl group are lost in the form of |FRAME: ACET|., The intermediates formed prior to the formation of the corrin ring are called precorrins. The precorrins are numbered corresponding to the number of methyl groups that have been already introduced. If two different intermediates have the same number of methyl groups, they are also labeled by A or B (as in |FRAME:CPD-675|). If there is still some uncertainty about an intermediate, it is given a temporary designation of X or Y., The first committed step in this pathway is the addition of a methyl group to carbon C-20 of the tetrapyrrole ring to give |FRAME: CPD-642|. This intermediate, which contains three additional methyl groups (compared with |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|), is oxidized by |FRAME:MONOMER-84|, using molecular oxygen, to |FRAME:CPD-643|, an intermediate that has been described as "spring-loaded for contraction" |CITS: [12195810]|., This intermediate, which has a hydroxy group at carbon C-20, forms a lactone between carbons C-1 and C-2. However, the ring is not contracted until the next enzyme (another methyltransferase) adds a methyl group to carbon C-17., At this point the ring contracts, forming the next intermediate, |FRAME:CPD-651|., Following the addition of four more methyl groups (at positions C-11, C-1, C-5 and C-15) and the release of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, the final precorrin intermediate, |FRAME:CPD-686|, is formed. This intermediate is the substrate for the enzyme |FRAME:MONOMER-115|, which finally converts it to a true corrin ring compound, |FRAME:CPD-687|., This corrin ring intermediate still requires an extensive modification. Successive amidation reactions transfer two amide groups from two |FRAME: GLN| molecules to the carboxy groups a and c, resulting in |FRAME:CPD-689|, and a |FRAME: CO+2| ion is inserted into the ring by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-327|, forming |FRAME: CPD-689| - the point where the early-insertion and late-insertion pathways combine., The rest of the pathway is described in |FRAME: PWY-5509| and |FRAME: P381-PWY|.

The only unsaturated fatty acids found in |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247|, comprise about one-half the fatty acid content of the organism. The proportion of unsaturated fatty acids is known to increase in |FRAME:TAX-562| with lower growth temperature, a phenomenon found in most organisms that provides a mechanism for adjusting the lipid phase transition of the membrane phospholipids to differing temperatures., |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| is the only enzyme that can catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-9245| to |FRAME: CPD-9247|, and is believed to play a major role in the thermal regulation of fatty acid composition of the membrane phospholipids of |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [6988423]|. |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| is one of three β-ketoacyl-ACP synthases (KAS) in |FRAME:TAX-562|: |FRAME: FABB-CPLX|, |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| and |FRAME: CPLX0-252|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG12606| and |FRAME: EG10277|, respectively., It has been shown that |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| is more active at low temperatures (relative to the overall rate of fatty acid synthesis) than at high temperatures |CITS: [7002930]|. This relative increase results in the production of |FRAME: CPD-9247| rather than |FRAME: CPD-9245|. Furthermore, because the former (but not the later) can be incorporated into both positions of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|, the synthesis of diunsaturated phospholipids occurs and the thermotrophic phase transition of the membrane phospholipids is lowered |CITS: [6988423]|., Some plant species such as |FRAME: TAX-48545| and |FRAME: TAX-73871| (Doxantha unguis-cati L.) produce relatively high levels of |FRAME: CPD-9245| and |FRAME: CPD-9247| in their seed oils |CITS: [CHISHOLMMJ60][CHISHOLMMJ65]|. The plastidal synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9247| from |FRAME: CPD-9245| via KASII is thought to be similar to that of the |FRAME:TAX-562| pathway (in |CITS: [20943853]|). KAS II enzymes (EC 2.3.1.179) have been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-3708| |CITS: [11442062]| and |FRAME: TAX-3562| |CITS: [6756317]|, and a |FRAME: NADH|-dependent enoyl-ACP reductase (EC 1.3.1.9) has been characterized in these and several other plant species |CITS: [6756317][1912503][7075600 ][7125663]|.
