Summary: |FRAME: DAIDZEIN Daidzein| is an isoflavone present in a number of plants and herbs, including the Thai Kwao Krua (|FRAME: ORG-6203 "Pueraria mirifica"|), the Japanese Kudzu (|FRAME: TAX-3893|), and soybean (|FRAME: TAX-3847|). It is found in all soy products like tofu and textured vegetable protein. Much of the daidzein is found in planta in the form of its 7-O-glucosylated form, |FRAME: CPD-3424|. Upon ingestion, |FRAME: CPD-3424| is restored to |FRAME: DAIDZEIN| by the glucosidases of the intestinal bacteria |CITS: [9875509 ]|. Daidzein is then degraded further, producing several compounds including |FRAME: CPD-14115|., Many soy isoflavonoids have estrogenic activity, which gave them the name phytoestrogens. |FRAME: CPD-14115| has the highest estrogenic activity among all soy isoflavonoids, and is studied as a potential drug for the prevention of several sex hormone-dependent diseases, including prostate cancer and several bone and skin diseases, as well as for reducing the severity and frequency of hot flashes in menopaused women |CITS: [12468591][15247126][16963248][20484552][21934634][21988617][21992596]|., The conversion of |FRAME: DAIDZEIN| to |FRAME: CPD-14115| has been noted in several intestinal bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-239760 Eggerthella strain Julong 732"| |CITS: [17109177][19304836]|, |FRAME: TAX-394340| |CITS: [19502755]|, |FRAME: ORG-6201| |CITS: [20639368]| and |FRAME: TAX-84108| strains |CITS:[22113864][22179235]|. , The main three enzymes that participate in the conversion of |FRAME: DAIDZEIN| to |FRAME: CPD-14115| were partially characterized from |FRAME: ORG-6201| |CITS: [20639368][22286043]|. This was followed by the identification of a dihydrodaidzein racemase from the same organism that was reported to be essential for the pathway |CITS: [22582059]|., Reports about the stereospecificity of the enzymes involved have been quite controversial. However, the first study of a fully purified daidzein reductase has shown that the enzyme produces only the (R enantiomer |FRAME: CPD-24413| |CITS: [29699942]|. While characterization of an unpurified dihydrodaidzein reductase from |FRAME: TAX-239760 Eggerthella strain Julong 732"| suggested that the enzyme produces exclusively the |FRAME: CPD-14114| stereomer |CITS:[19304836]|, a later study by the same authors has reported that only the |FRAME: CPD-24423| enantiomer can be converted to |FRAME: CPD-14115| |CITS: [ 20515029]|. The same study also suggested that the pathway proceeds only via |FRAME: CPD-12609|. This apparent conflict is resolved by the finding that a dihydrodaidzein racemase is essential for the pathway |CITS: [22582059]|. Indeed, incubation of all four enzymes (all enzymes were purified recombinant proteins from |FRAME: ORG-6201| cloned with a His6 tag and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|) with |FRAME: DAIDZEIN| resulted in formation of |FRAME: CPD-14115| with a yield of 90% |CITS: [22582059]|., .

The yellow color of flavonols is caused by 6- and/or 8-hydroxylation at the aromatic A-ring of the core flavonoid skeleton |CITS:[Harborne67]| and reported to be of physiological importance as honey guides in reproductive flower biology (discussed in |FRAME:PWY-7157|) |CITS:[5050486] [Daumer58] [Eisner02]|. The 8-hydroxy and 8-methoxy derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-520|, i.e. |FRAME:334578-HEXAHYDROXYFLAVONE| and |FRAME:33457-PENTAHYDROXY-8-METHOXYFLAVON| (corniculatusin), respectively are not uncommon and have been found in plant families such as Asteraceae |CITS:[Harborne78]|, Fabaceae |CITS:[Harborne81]| and Ericaceae and Papaveraceae for which they are considered taxonomic markers |CITS:[Harborne69]|. , The 7-glucosylated |FRAME:CPD-520|, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16762| has been studied with focus on its contribution to the evolution of honey guides in Chrysanthemum segetum |CITS:[Geissman57] [Harborne81]|, whereas 8-hydroxy and 8-methoxy substituted |FRAME:CPD-520| have been especially researched with respect to their involvement in the ontogeny of flowers in Lotus corniculatus |CITS:[Jay86]|. The latter is an intriguing example about specific tissue distribution of flavonols which accumulate as aglycones, for instance |FRAME:CPD-520|, |FRAME:CPD1F-90| and |FRAME:CPD-8004| in the leaves whereas the corresponding 8-methoxy derivatives are present in flower petals of Lotus corniculatus |CITS:[Jay78]|. , The respective 8-hydroxylation and 8-methoxylation of |FRAME:CPD-520| towards |FRAME:33457-PENTAHYDROXY-8-METHOXYFLAVON| via |FRAME:334578-HEXAHYDROXYFLAVONE| is catalyzed by region-specific hydroxylases and O-methyltransferases. The flavonoid 8-O-hydroxylase catalyzing the formation of 8-hydroxylated flavonols has been characterized as a novel |FRAME:NADPH|/|FRAME:FAD| dependent hydroxylase which does not completely match all the properties of typical Cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases. The 8-hydroxylase accepts only |FRAME:CPD-520| and |FRAME:5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE| (see |FRAME:RXN-15524|) forming the corresponding |FRAME:334578-HEXAHYDROXYFLAVONE gossypetin| and |FRAME:CPD-16763|, respectively |CITS:[16678869]|. The following 8-methoxylation has been observed in Lotus corniculatus where the position-specific O-methyltransferase accepts only |FRAME:334578-HEXAHYDROXYFLAVONE gossypetin| and |FRAME:CPD-14867| (see |FRAME:RXN-15525|) to yield |FRAME:33457-PENTAHYDROXY-8-METHOXYFLAVON| (corniculatusin) and |FRAME:CPD-16764| accordingly |CITS:[4076180]|. |FRAME:334578-HEXAHYDROXYFLAVONE Gossypetin| is also the branchpoint towards its 7-glucoside formed in the pathway. The gossypetin 7-O-glucosyltransferase has been characterized in petals of Chrysanthemum segetum where the formed |FRAME:CPD-16762| confers and intensifies the yellow color of the petals. |FRAME:CPD-16762 Gossypetin 7-O-glucoside| is restricted to areas of yellow coloration and can be found in certain Chrysanthemum species only in the yellow stripes of the inner petals |CITS:[9167271]|.

The legume-specific pterocarpans medicarpin and maackiain have been originally thought not to be converted into malonylglucosides but to exist exclusively as de novo formed aglycones. However, medicarpin- (MeGM) and maackiain 3-O-glucoside-6''-O-malonate (MaGM) have been isolated as constitutive metabolites of chickpea cell cultures |CITS: [Weidemann91]| |CITS: [Barz89]| |CITS: [Barz92]| and are also found in chickpea plants but only after elicitation |CITS: [Weidemann91]|., In addition, trifolirhizin (maackiain-3-O-glucoside), maackiain- and and medicarpin malonyl glucosides together with afrormosin malonyl glucoside have been established as constitutive compounds in red clover |CITS: [McMurchy84]| |CITS: [11413204]| and alfalfa |CITS: [Kessmann90]|, respectively., Upon elicitation not only the aglycones medicarpin and maackiain increased in cell cultures of chickpea but a delayed and significant higher amount of their conjugates also occurred. The accumulation of maackiain and medicarpin conjugates was especially noticeable when a first burst in aglycone accumulation has passed |CITS: [Weidemann91]|., The pterocarpan malonyl glucosides are found predominantly in vacuoles |CITS: [Mackenbrock92]| whereas the de novo cytoplasmatic synthesized aglycones (medicarpin, maackiain) are often excreted. This has been discussed as a metabolic channeling preventing aglycone conjugation and reflecting a tight regulation of pools |CITS: [Barz92]| spatially separated in cytoplasm (pterocarpan aglycones) and vacuoles (pterocarpan conjugates)., All enzymes necessary to catalyze the conversion of the aglycones to the conjugated metabolites exist and function in chickpea, and their activities upon elicitation have been measured |CITS: [Daniel88]|. The enzymes catalyzing the formation of the pterocarpan malonylglucosides were highly induced at lower elicitor level. Increasing elicitation caused a strong repression of those enzymes but increased the activities of the enzymes involved in the catabolism of the malonylglucosides towards the aglycones |CITS: [Barz92]| |CITS: [11413204]|., Experiments with the phenylalanine-ammonia-lyase (PAL) specific inhibitor AOPP (α-amino-β-phenylpropionic acid) under elicitor conditions resulted in the channeling of formononetin released from the corresponding alonylglucosides , into the biosynthetic route of medicarpin/maackiain formation underlining the regulatory importance of this pathway |CITS: [Barz89]|., The isoflavone conjugate cycle is discussed as an anapleurotic sequence for legumes, when a high demand for phytoalexin formation exists and the de novo biosynthesis is delayed because of insufficient amounts of early precursors. It has also been argued that the conjugation prevents the excessive formation of medicarpin in alfalfa, which inhibits nodulation through its phytotoxity to |FRAME:TAX-379| species |CITS: [Kessmann90]|., Research in leguminous plants has revealed the existence of the conjugate interconversion for many intermediates involved in the biosynthesis of phytoalexins. Glucosides and/or malonylglucosides of isoflavones (daidzein, genistein, biochanin A, formononetin), isoflavanones (cicerin, homoferreirin) and pterocarpans (medicarpin, maackiain) have been isolated along with other conjugates of phenolic secondary metabolites |CITS: [Kessmann90]| indicating that the pathway in general may function as an metabolic puffer system.

Summary: General background, The violet pigment |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| is produced by |FRAME: TAX-536| and some other Gram-negative bacteria including those shown above. Its biosynthetic precursor is two molecules of |FRAME: TRP| (note that this stoichiometry is not shown in the pathway diagram displayed here due to its branching nature). Like |FRAME: CPD-11752| and |FRAME: STAUROSPORINE|, |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| is a member of the bisindole class of natural products (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6324| and |FRAME: PWY-6346|). Its in vivo function remains unclear, but it may protect the organism against ultraviolet irradiation. |FRAME: VIOLACEIN Violacein| and its derivatives are of interest in the development of antibacterial, antitrypanosomal, antiulcer and anticancer drugs (reviewed in |CITS: [21779844][21253897][19389622][27288924]|)., The |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| biosynthetic pathway is mostly well understood. The pathway shown here is based on the review by |CITS: [21779844]|, which updates some earlier conclusions of others |CITS: [11075927][16874749][17176066][ASAMIZU07][20012278]|. Please note that the product of |FRAME: G-15141 VioB| is very labile and has not been isolated. The structure shown here has not been verified experimentally. , The gene cluster vioABCDE encodes the biosynthetic enzymes involved in the pathway |CITS: [16874749]|. They are regulated by acylhomoserine lactone-mediated quorum sensing |CITS: [20944413]|. |FRAME: G-15140 VioA| and |FRAME: G-15141 VioB| have been determined to be functionally equivalent to |FRAME: G-11520 RebO| and |FRAME: G-11521 RebD| respectively in the |FRAME: PWY-6324| pathway, and |FRAME: G-11591 StaO| and |FRAME: G-11590 StaD| in the |FRAME: PWY-6346| pathway (reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|)., There have been numerous reports about the synthetic production of |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| |CITS: [25592762][27288924][34584039][35810697]|., About This Pathway, The carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen skeleton of |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| is entirely derived from two molecules of |FRAME: TRP| and the oxygen atoms are derived from |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| (|CITS: [17176066]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|). The first enzyme in the pathway, VioA, functions as a flavin-dependent L-amino acid oxidase that catalyzes the production of two molecules of |FRAME: CPD-11890| (IPA imine) from two molecules of |FRAME: TRP| (in |CITS: [17925955][17176066]|). This reaction is also found in antibiotic biosynthesis pathways |FRAME: PWY-6346| and |FRAME: PWY-6345|, in |FRAME: TAX-201174|., The key reactions in the pathway convert |FRAME: CPD-11890| to |FRAME: CPD-14320| and are catalyzed by the second and third enzymes |FRAME: G-15141 VioB| and |FRAME: CPLX-8473|. The product of VioB, which is the substrate for |FRAME: CPLX-8473|, remains speculative, since it is too labile to be isolated (reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|). , |FRAME: G-15141 VioB| is a heme |FRAME: FE+2|-containing enzyme. It catalyzes a reaction that converts |FRAME: CPD-11890| to a short-lived, dimeric intermediate that results from C-C bond formation between the β-carbon atoms of two |FRAME: CPD-11890| molecules. Possible structures and structural transitions for this dimeric intermediate have been proposed (shown and reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|). VioB has high amino acid sequence homology with |FRAME: G-11521 RebD| and |FRAME: G-11590 StaD| in the |FRAME: PWY-6324| and |FRAME: PWY-6346| pathways, respectively |CITS: [17176066]|. , The short-lived dimeric intermediate undergoes deamination and decarboxylation via cyclopropane ring formation. |FRAME: CPLX-8473| has been proposed to catalyze these transitions as well as the unique 1,2-shift of the indole ring seen in its product |FRAME: CPD-14320| (|CITS: [17925955]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|). |FRAME: CPLX-8473| is an interesting enzyme that has few sequence homologies, and no cofactor requirement has been found |CITS: [17176066]|. The crystal structure of |FRAME: CPLX-8473| has been determined |CITS: [18171677][18171675]|., In the absence of |FRAME: CPLX-8473| the short-lived dimeric intermediate formed from |FRAME: CPD-11890| by VioB may undergo deamination and spontaneous aromatization to produce |FRAME: CPD-11786|, without the 1,2-shift of the indole ring (in |CITS: [18171677]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|). In pathway |FRAME: PWY-6346|, |FRAME: CPD-11786| synthesis is catalyzed by StaD, and in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6345| by NokB., VioD catalyzes a hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-14320| to yield the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-14319|. VioC then hydroxylates the 2-position of the opposite indole ring of |FRAME: CPD-14319| to produce |FRAME: CPD-14324|. In the absence of VioD, VioC can oxidize |FRAME: CPD-14320| to |FRAME: CPD-14323|. Both VioC and VioD were shown to be |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent and flavin-dependent oxygenases. The final reaction in the main pathway that produces |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| occurs via nonenzymatic (spontaneous) autooxidation and decarboxylation. The metabolite |FRAME: CPD-14318| can be produced similarly (|CITS: [17925955]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|). , In contrast to compounds |FRAME: CPD-14320| and |FRAME: CPD-14319| which are true, but labile intermediates of the pathway, compounds |FRAME: CPD-14322| and |FRAME: CPD-14321| are considered to be artifacts. They are generated from |FRAME: CPD-14320| and |FRAME: CPD-14319| in the absence of VioC via non-enzymatic (spontaneous) autooxidation and decarboxylation |CITS: [17925955]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|., As noted above, a unique feature of |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| biosynthesis is the indole shift mediated by |FRAME: CPLX-8473| that generates |FRAME: CPD-14320| (as compared with no indole shift in |FRAME: CPD-11786|). This shift does not occur during |FRAME: PWY-6324| or |FRAME: PWY-6346| and a |FRAME: CPLX-8473| homolog is lacking in those gene clusters. Another feature of the pathway is the combination of enzymatically catalyzed reactions and nonenzymatic (spontaneous) autooxidation and decarboxylation reactions. A third feature is that oxygen is incorporated into |FRAME: VIOLACEIN| via VioD and VioC, as well as a final nonenzymatic step (reviewed in |CITS: [21779844]|).

General Background, Polyamines are found in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes and are necessary for normal cellular physiology. Examples include the standard polyamines |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME: SPERMINE|. Several independent pathways have been identified for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|. In pathway |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE| (decarboxylated |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|) donates an aminopropyl group to |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| to form |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| in a reaction catalyzed by spermidine synthase. In contrast, in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6559| |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| donates a carboxyaminopropyl group to |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| to form |FRAME: CPD-10012| in a reaction catalyzed by carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase. Then, decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-10012| catalyzed by carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine decarboxylase produces |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| |CITS: [19196710]| and in |CITS: [20194510]|. The pathway shown here has been proposed in hyperthermophilic bacteria and archaea based on genetic and functional analyses and involves |FRAME: CPD-13489| as the key intermediate |CITS: [20675472][15983049]| (see below)., About This Pathway, Gene disruption experiments and functional analysis of recombinantly expressed enzymes have suggested that the extremely thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-300852| utilizes only the unique |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthesis pathway shown here. Similar studies suggested that the hyperthermophilic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-69014| utilizes mainly this pathway, but also pathway |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| (and linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-40|) to a lesser extent. Both pathways utilize TK0147 as agmatine aminopropyltransferase (spermidine synthase) and TK0882 as aminopropylagmatine ureohydrolase (agmatinase). Because both organisms lack a homolog of ornithine decarboxylase (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-46|), |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| appears to be synthesized only from |FRAME: ARG| |CITS: [15983049][20675472]|., In this pathway |FRAME: ARG| is decarboxylated to |FRAME: AGMATHINE| (which is also a precursor of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| utilized in pathways |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6559|). |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINAMINE| (decarboxylated |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|) donates an aminopropyl group to |FRAME: AGMATHINE| to form |FRAME: CPD-13489| which then undergoes hydrolysis to produce |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|. Although S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (EC 4.1.1.50) is not curated here, unpublished functional studies have confirmed its identity as SpeD2 (TTHA1457)) in |FRAME: TAX-300852| (in |CITS: [20417109]|)., In |FRAME: TAX-300852| the product |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| is also a key intermediate in the synthesis of unique, long chain or branched polyamines which may be important for life at high temperatures. Examples of these unique polyamines include |FRAME: CPD-13491|, |FRAME: CPD-13492| and |FRAME: CPD-13493| (in |CITS: [20417109]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21318868]|). These polyamines have also been suggested to be a chemotaxonomic marker in bacterial systematics (reviewed in |CITS: [1524675]|, also see |CITS: [15747232][14673752]| and other papers by these authors). See |FRAME: PWY-8114| and |FRAME: PWY-8115|.

Summary: General Background, The term ''indirect defense" is used to describe a defense mechanism used by certain plants, in which herbivore damage induces the emission of volatile organic compounds that attract natural enemies of the herbivores |CITS:[7753779][11251117]|. One of the plants that employ indirect defense is maize. After herbivory by lepidopteran larvae, maize releases a mixture of volatiles that is highly attractive to females of various parasitic wasp species including the braconid wasp |FRAME: TAX-93006| |CITS: [17829213]|., The volatile oil mixture is complex, and contains a large number of mono- and sesquiterpenes, lipoxygenase pathway, products, and indole. However, herbivore attack on the inbred line B73 induces a group of volatiles that includes only |FRAME:CPD-8239|, |FRAME: CPD-13396|, and seven additional sesquiterpene hydrocarbons in a fixed relative proportion |CITS: [16418295]|. Bergamotenes are sesquiterpenoids that are components of volatile oils from a number of plants. They function as insect repellents in some plants, although they may also function as attractants for certain organisms. There are several isomers of bergamotene, including |FRAME: CPD-8849|, |FRAME: CPD-11287|, |FRAME:CPD-13396| and |FRAME: CPD-13402|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: G-9837|, a gene similar to terpene synthases, was isolated from a maize ESTs library |CITS:[16418295]| and shown to be responsible for the synthesis of the comnpounds in the volatile oil mixture. The gene was introduced into |FRAME: TAX-3702| for analysis of the mixture of sesquiterpenes produced by it's product, and the recombinant enzyme was shown to utilize |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and produce mainly |FRAME:CPD-8239| and |FRAME: CPD-13396| |CITS:[16418295]|., Another gene encoding a sesquiterpene synthase, |FRAME: G-11317|, was cloned from lavender (|FRAME: TAX-39329|) leaves and flowers. The enzyme transformed farnesyl diphosphate mainly to |FRAME: CPD-13396| (74% of all products), and represented the first reported |FRAME: MONOMER-14818| |CITS: [17662687]|., A hexane extract from flowers of |FRAME: TAX-39329| confirmed the presence of |FRAME: CPD-13396|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHITIN| is the second most abundant biologically produced polymer (|FRAME: CELLULOSE| is the most abundant). It is a linear homopolymer of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| residues linked by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Note that in this pathway the final product |FRAME: CHITIN| is shown using its polymeric name in the chitin synthase polymerization reaction. |FRAME: CHITIN| exists is several crystalline forms termed α, β and γ |FRAME: CHITIN|. The most abundant form is α |FRAME: CHITIN|, which forms microfibrils arranged in an antiparallel manner resulting in high tensile strength. |FRAME: Chitosan|, which is partially deacetylated |FRAME: CHITIN|, is also found naturally. Both |FRAME: CHITIN| and |FRAME: Chitosan| are of interest in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries (reviewed in |CITS: [21700357]|)., |FRAME: CHITIN| is synthesized by some or all members of several lower eukaryote groups including fungi |CITS: [21700357]|, arthropods |CITS: [21700357]|, protists |CITS: [21775209 ][16400183]|, sponges |CITS: [17285638]|, coelenterates |CITS: [1345775,]| nematodes |CITS: [16098962]| and molluscs |CITS: [18083970]|. It has also been reported in algae (in chlorovirus CVK2-infected |FRAME:TAX-3071| |CITS: [12429521]|). Among prokaryotes, |FRAME: CHITIN| oligomers linked to fatty acids are secreted by some rhizobia during nodulation |CITS: [8146173]|. |FRAME: CHITIN| biosynthesis is best characterized in fungi and insects, which have conserved cellular machinery for |FRAME: CHITIN| biosynthesis. Linear |FRAME: CHITIN| chains are secreted into the extracellular matrix where microfibrils are assembled and organized. Chitin is well known as a component of insect cuticles, and is a structural polysaccharide in fungal cell walls (reviewed in |CITS: [21700357]| and |CITS: [KRAMER05]|)., As an essential component of fungal cell walls, |FRAME: CHITIN| biosynthesis during the cell cycle is highly regulated. Because chitin is absent in vertebrates and it appears to have a role in immune responses, its biosynthesis remains of interest as a drug target for fungal and other chitin-containing parasites (reviewed in |CITS: [20561815]|)., About This Pathway, The overall |FRAME: CHITIN| biosynthetic pathway in fungi and insects is highly conserved. The sugar source is |FRAME: GLC|, or its storage compounds |FRAME: Glycogens|, or |FRAME: TREHALOSE|. In insects |FRAME: GLC| may be derived from fat body glycogen via |FRAME: TREHALOSE|. Glycogen phosphorylase produces |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, which is converted to |FRAME: TREHALOSE|. In insects, |FRAME: TREHALOSE| enters the hemolymph (insect blood) and serves as an extracellular source of sugar. Trehalase, which is found in many insect tissues, hydrolyzes |FRAME: TREHALOSE| to produce intracellular |FRAME: GLC|. |FRAME: GLC| is converted to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| by the two cytosolic, glycolytic enzymes hexokinase (glucokinase) and glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (reviewed in |CITS: [21700357][KRAMER05][19725772]|. The spontaneous conversions of |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE| to its epimer |FRAME: GLC| and |FRAME: ALPHA-GLC-6-P| to its epimer |FRAME: GLC-6-P| are indicated here. , The pathway then branches off from glycolysis toward amino sugar biosynthesis, and glutamine:fructose-6-p aminotransferase is considered to be the first committed and rate-limiting step of amino sugar biosynthesis |CITS: [11716769][21700357][KRAMER05]|. This segment of the pathway involves amination, acetyl group transfer and isomerization steps. The |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| intermediate can also be supplied by chitin degradation reactions as shown in the pathway link. , The next reaction leads to formation of the activated sugar |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|. This activated sugar also participates in the eukaryotic N-linked glycosylation pathway (see pathway |FRAME: MANNOSYL-CHITO-DOLICHOL-BIOSYNTHESIS|). The final step in |FRAME: CHITIN| biosynthesis utilizes |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| in a polymerization reaction to form |FRAME: CHITIN|, catalyzed by chitin synthase. The chitin synthase reaction occurs in specialized microdomains of the plasma membrane. Chitin synthase is an integral membrane protein complex that polymerizes and extrudes chitin., Important pathway enzymes include glutamine:fructose-6-p amidotransferase which appears to be rate-limiting, and chitin synthase which is the key enzyme of the pathway and the only enzyme specifically associated with chitin biosynthesis (reviewed in |CITS: [21700357]| and |CITS: [KRAMER05]|). , Chitin synthase encoding genes of fungi may be found in multiple copies and are divided into two families based on amino acid sequence motifs. Each family contains several classes. The yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| contains three chitin synthase genes, CHS1, CHS2 and CHS3 which have different roles in the life cycle, with CHS3 producing most of the |FRAME: CHITIN| in this organism including the lateral cell wall (reviewed in |CITS: [21700357]|). In insects, only two chitin synthase encoding genes have been identified to date and are divided into class A and class B. Their enzyme products are specialized in formation of the cuticle and gut lining (peritrophic membranes). During the growth and development of both organisms, pathway enzymes are regulated at the transcriptional, posttranscriptional and intracellular localization levels (reviewed in |CITS: [21700357]| and |CITS: [KRAMER05]|)., |FRAME: CHITIN| can be degraded enzymatically by chitin deacetylases (EC 3.5.1.41) to produce |FRAME: Chitosan| (see |FRAME: MONOMER-16910|). Chitin deacetylases are found in fungi, some insects, and marine bacteria (reviewed in |CITS: [20161969]|). In the fungus |FRAME: TAX-290576| secreted chitin deacetylase may function in partial deacetylation of the cell wall chitin of fungal hyphae during colonization of plant tissue. This partial deacetylation may confer resistance to plant chitinases, which hydrolyze chitosan only poorly (in |CITS: [16878976]|).

Summary: Assessing more than 80 accessions of the wild tomato Solanum habrochaites revealed a great diversity of the acylation pattern in accumulated acylsucroses in this species as well as a noticeable association between geographic location and acylation |CITS:[23054567]|. Acylsugars such as acylglucose |CITS:[King86] [King88] [11607435] [Leckie13]| and acylsucrose metabolites (this pathway) are produced in glandular trichomes of and confined to plants of the Solanaceae family |CITS:[2652002]|. It has been shown that acylsucrose dominates both in the cultivated tomato Solanum lycopersicum and in the wild species Solanum habrochaites |CITS:[Shapiro94] [21098679]|. There are a few types of glandular trichomes, e.g. type I, IV or VI which have been found in the Solanaceae family and associated with the biosynthesis of acylsugars |CITS:[21098679]| which are produced in those epidermal protuberances and exudate onto leaf or stem surfaces |CITS:[Severson85]|. The biochemistry in these appendices is highly dynamic which has been considered a reason for the observed diversity of specialized metabolites produced in trichomes |CITS:[22563774]|., The physiological role of acylsugars is still under investigation but already broad-spectrum insecticidal properties for acylsugars have been reported |CITS:[Hawthorne92] [18807203] [Maluf10] [Leckie12]| which are based on phytohormone interactions |CITS:[21068365]|, interfering with feeding behavior of pests |CITS:[Rodriguez93] [Juvic94] [Liedl95]| and even alerting predators of feeding pest larvae to their presence on plants, for instance Nicotiana species |CITS:[21518882]|. Mutant plants with altered trichomes due to silenced genes were unable to produce trichome specific metabolites and exhibited a significant lower resistance against insect herbivores |CITS:[20668059]|. Various acylsugars have also been used commercially as safe additives in the food, cosmetics and pharmaceutical industries |CITS:[Hill99]|., The wild tomato species Solanum habrochaites expresses the highest diversity of acylation patterns on the |FRAME:SUCROSE sucrose| scaffold but also Solanum pennellii deviates from the acylation pattern observed in cultivated species of tomato (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-15 acylsucrose biosynthesis (Solanum pennellii)|). In fact, in Solanum habrochaites the furanose moiety was either not acylated (northern accessions), contained a single short (C4-C5) or long acyl (C10-C12) chain or even accommodated two short acyl chains (southern accessions). The reason for the high variability of acylsucroses in the species is the existence of various ASAT3-like |CITS:[25862303]| and ASAT4-like |CITS:[23054567]| sequences which encode for acyltransferases with different substrate specificities in various accession lines of Solanum habrochaites. For the ASAT3 genes two different groups had been identified and labeled with either a 'P' (pyranose ring acylation) or an 'F' (furanose ring acylation) extension. The ASAT3-F and/or P genes of four Solanum habrochaites accessions, i.e. LA1777, LA1731, LA2861 and LA2098 have been cloned and recombinant expressed in E. coli and subjected to biochemical assays. The catalytic activities of the ASAT3 genes generally follow their gene cluster affiliation in the phylogenetic tree but can also exhibit double activities to catalyze two subsequent reactions, e.g. ASAT3 genes from the accessions LA2098 and LA1777 of Solanum habrochaites |CITS:[25862303]|., The situation is similar for ASAT4-like genes found in Solanum habrochaites accessions LA1777, LA1731 and LA2098. The possession of an ASAT4 gene encoding a functional acetyltransferase divides C-2 bearing acylsugars in southern areas (supercluster 1) from the C-2 lacking acylsugars from accession in northern areas of Peru and Ecuador (supercluster 2). It appears that ASAT4 became non-functional in the northern species which resulted in the production of non-acetylated acylsugars in those Solanum habrochaites accessions |CITS:[23054567]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Polymyxins "Polymyxins"| are a class of antibiotics that are active against Gram-negative bacteria. They are produced by species of |FRAME: TAX-44249|, including |FRAME: TAX-1406| and |FRAME: TAX-59841|. A number of unique polymyxins have been characterized from different strains of |FRAME: TAX-1406| (see |FRAME: CPD-16444|, |FRAME: CPD0-1277|, |FRAME: CPD-16462|, |FRAME: CPD-16463| and |FRAME: CPD-13158|). |FRAME: ORG-6251| produces |FRAME: CPD-16461| |CITS: [12569104]|. Polymyxins consist of ten amino acids with a characteristic polycationic heptapeptide ring and a linear tripeptide with an attached N-terminal fatty acid moiety. They differ in the identity of the fatty acid moiety and in amino acids at positions 3, 6 and 7 |CITS: [22195566]|., Polymyxins were biochemically characterized several decades ago. More recently, genes involved in their biosynthesis have been isolated and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-349520| that synthesizes |FRAME: CPD-16444| |CITS: [19304848]| and from |FRAME: ORG-6250| that synthesizes stereochemical variants of |FRAME: CPD0-1277| and |FRAME: CPD-16462| |CITS: [22195566]|., Polymyxins B and E were used clinically several decades ago, but due to their toxic side effects they were later replaced by other antibiotics. Currently polymyxins remain in use in topical ointments, but due to the problem of multidrug-resistant bacteria, they have also been used for severe infections. There is interest in synthesizing new polymyxin derivatives with reduced toxicity |CITS: [23412346][24105917]|., The activity of polymyxins against Gram-negative bacteria is due to their interaction with lipopolysaccharide and disruption of both the outer and inner membranes. The development of resistance to polymyxins via lipopolysaccharide modification has been reported (see pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1338|)., Polymyxins are biosynthesized by nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs). These large, polyfunctional proteins are organized into modules. Each module consists of independent catalytic and carrier domains that participate in polypeptide chain synthesis (reviewed in |CITS: [10631508][19636447][20153164]|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-16444 "Polymyxin A"| was shown to be produced by |FRAME: TAX-349520|. The gene cluster encoding the |FRAME: CPLX-8811| complex was predicted computationally during whole genome sequencing of this organism. It consisted of pmxA, pmxB, pmxC, pmxD and pmxE. Genes |FRAME: G-17936|, |FRAME: G-17937| and |FRAME: G-17935| encode |FRAME: CPLX-8811|, while pmxC and pmxD encode possible membrane transporters. The PmxE protein comprises five modules, PmxA four modules and PmxB a single module. The order of modules for amino acid assembly was suggested to be PmxE-PmxA-PmxB (see |FRAME: CPLX-8811|) |CITS: [19304848][20851896]|., Experimentally, the production of |FRAME: CPD-16444| in culture supernatants of |FRAME: TAX-349520| was demonstrated using LC/MS. The identity of the gene cluster was confirmed by construction and characterization of a |FRAME: G-17935| insertion mutant strain that did not produce |FRAME: CPD-16444| and lacked antibiotic activity against |FRAME: TAX-562| in a bioassay. When the gene cluster was heterologously expressed in an engineered strain of |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: CPD-16444| was produced upon addition of |FRAME: CPD-470| (L-2,4-diaminobutyrate) to the growth medium |CITS: [19304848]|. The requirement for addition of |FRAME: CPD-470| was later eliminated by further strain engineering |CITS: [22467510]|., The timing and mechanism of attachment of the 6-methyloctanoyl moiety has not been firmly established. No genes that could account for fatty acid attachment have been found adjacent to the polymyxin gene clusters in sequenced |FRAME: TAX-1406| strains. However, it was noted that module 1 of PmxE in P. polymyxa PKB1 contains an N-terminal condensation domain that shows similarity to starter condensation domains that attach lipids to amino acids in other lipopeptides |CITS: [22195566]|. Studies of surfactin, an NRPS-synthesized lipopeptide antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-1423|, showed that the mechanism of lipid transfer during the initial step of surfactin biosynthesis by surfactin synthetase involves the transfer of a |FRAME: CO-A|-activated fatty acid to the enzyme-bound amino acid |CITS: [20797616]|. In addition, early studies of polymyxin E biosynthesis in a cell-free system suggested that the initial thioesterified |FRAME: CPD-470| is acylated via a fatty acyl-coenzyme A |CITS: [3861608]|. An acyl-coenzyme A synthetase would activate the fatty acid |CITS: [20797616]|., The timing and mechanism of peptide cyclization has also not been established. However, the thioesterase domains of some NRPSs have been shown to act as cyclization catalysts |CITS: [11401555]|.

Polyamines are important for cell growth and are believed to be involved in many processes including, DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis, as well as membrane integrity and resistance to stress, to name a few. , Cadaverine and aminopropylcadaverine are alternative polyamines that can at least partially substitute for, purtrescine and spermidine, the primary polyamines found in |FRAME:TAX-562|. Summary: General Background, One of the most striking physiological differences between the Archaea and other organisms is the structure of their, membrane lipids. The most exclusive feature of archaeal phospholipids is their |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE|, backbone, which is an enantiomer of the |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| used by bacteria and eukaryotic organisms. It has been suggested that Archaea and Bacteria were differentiated by the occurrence of cells enclosed by membranes of phospholipids with |FRAME: SN-GLYCEROL-1-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| as a backbone, respectively |CITS: [9419225]|., Other features that are unique to archaeal phospholipids include side chains that are derivatives of isoprenoid alcohols rather than fatty acids, which are linked by ether linkages (rather than ester linkages) to the glycerophosphate backbone |CITS: [358256]|. The isoprenoids are usually modified by saturation of the double bonds - a modification that is believed to increase the ability of the lipids to survive the extreme conditions that archaea often face. Another unique feature is the occurrence of bipolar lipids with a tetraether core, which are present in significant numbers in archaeal species., In contrast to these differences, most of the polar head groups of archaeal phospholipids are similar to those found in the other kingdoms - |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| and |FRAME: CHOLINE| |CITS: [17347520]|., The major polar lipids of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-145262| are L-serine, ethanolamine, or myo-inositol-containing di- and, tetraether type phospholipids and phosphoglycolipids, and gentiobiose-containing di- and tetraether type glycolipids., Examples of non-glycosylated lipids include |FRAME: CPD-10741 "archaetidylserine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11919 "archaetidylethanolamine"|, |FRAME: CPD-11918 "archaetidylinositol"| and |FRAME: CPD-11920 "archaetidylglycerol"|., About This Pathway, Many archaea contain inositol lipids |CITS: [Koga93][18515030]|. As a matter of fact, the only Archaea known to not possess inositol lipids are members of the Methanococcales, Methanomicrobiales, and Halobacteriales |CITS: [18515030]|. Membrane phospholipids in many archaea are composed solely of inositol phospholipids. In |FRAME: TAX-145262|, inositol lipids are the most predominant polar lipids |CITS:[3611047][3611039][Morii93]|., Archaetidylinositol has been shown to be essential for glycolipid biosynthesis in Archaea |CITS: [17416653]|., The pathway leading to the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10740 "CDP-archaeol"| is described in |FRAME: PWY-6349|., CDP is replaced with |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-15156|., This enzyme is homologous to the eukaryotic |FRAME: YPR113W-MONOMER|, but unlike the eukaryotic enzyme that utilizes |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|, the substrate for the archaeal enzyme was found to be |FRAME: 1-L-MYO-INOSITOL-1-P| |CITS: [19740749]|., An extensive BLAST search identified possible archaeal |FRAME: MONOMER-15156|-encoding candidates based on their similarity to the gene encoding |FRAME: YPR113W-MONOMER| of the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [16243780]|., When the candidate gene from |FRAME: TAX-145262| was cloned and expressed in E .coli, the host cells showed |FRAME: MONOMER-15156| activity, confirming the prediction |CITS: [19740749]|., |FRAME: CPD-11917 "Archaetidylinositol phosphate"| was converted by the membrane fraction of |FRAME: TAX-145262| cell homogenate to |FRAME: CPD-11918 "archaetidylinositol"|, indicating the presenceof a phasphatase. That enzyme has not been characterized yet |CITS: [19740749]|., |FRAME: MONOMER-15156 "Archaetidylinositol phosphate synthase"| activity was also found in the extremely thermophilic archaeaon |FRAME: TAX-2261|, and homologous genes encoding the enzyme were found in two other hyperthermophilic Crenarchaeota, |FRAME: TAX-2287| and |FRAME: TAX-56636| |CITS: [19740749]|.

In plants, the major site for fatty acid biosynthesis is plastids. However it is known that mitochondria of eukaryotes are also capable of de novo fatty acid biosynthesis. For example, synthesis of fatty acyl-ACP from labeled malonate was detected in isolated mitochondria from pea |CITS: [10671542]|, and from Neurospora |CITS: [2137086]|., The plant mitochondrial pathway differs from the |FRAME: PWY-4381 "plastidic pathway"|. First, in the mitochondrial pathway, malonate, not acetyl-CoA, is the sole precursor of fatty acids, although the source of malonate is still poorly understood |CITS: [10671542]|. Second, malonyl-ACP serves as both the primer and donor substrates for de novo fatty acid synthesis |CITS: [14660674]|. Third, there is only one condensing enzyme involved in the mitochondrial pathway. In contrast to the three condensing enzymes in the plastids, KASIII, KASI and KASII, where each carry out the initial condensation, elongation from C4 to C16, and the elongation from C16 to C18 reactions, respectively, the mitochondrial condensing enzyme carries out both the priming and all the elongating reactions |CITS: [14660674]|. , The biological role of the mitochondrial pathway is not entirely clear. One role is to provide octanoyl-ACP for the |FRAME: PWY0-501 "biosynthesis of lipoate"|, an important sulfur-containing cofactor of a number of enzymes such as glycine decarboxylase complex and pyruvate dehydrogenase |CITS: [10671542]|. Another role is likely to provide fatty acyl chains for the |FRAME: PWY-5269 "synthesis of cardiolipin"|, a lipid unique to mitochondrial membranes |CITS: [Li-Beisson2010]|. , The pathway does not appear to operate in grasses (Poaceae) |CITS: [12972648]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Bryostatins bryostatins| are a family of structurally related macrolide compounds originally found in the bryozoan |FRAME: TAX-10212|. The |FRAME: TAX-10205| are marine colonial filter-feeders, with each member (polypide) enclosed in a separate unit (zooecium)., |FRAME: CPD-21475 "Bryostatin 1"|, the first member to have its structure reported, was identified from samples collected from the California coast. The authors noted its anticancer activity, which they described as "remarkable" |CITS: [Pettit82]|. Other samples, collected in the Gulf of Mexico, the Gulf of California, and other locations, afforded other members. Currently 20 members of the bryostatin family are known |CITS: [Pettit91]|., In 1990 it was suggested that the bryostatins may be produced by endosymbiotic bacteria |CITS: [Anthoni90]|. The presence of such endosymbionts was confirmed in 1997, and sequencing of the small-subunit rRNA gene has shown that they belong to a new genus within the γ-proteobacteria. They were named |FRAME: TAX-62101| |CITS: [9361448]|. The bacteria cannot be cultivated outside the host; however, the discovery of genes encoding polyketide synthases in the bacterial DNA provided proof for a bacterial origin of the bryostatins |CITS: [11571152]|., Most, but not all, of the bryostatins pharmacological effects are attributed to their interaction with the |FRAME: Diacyl-sn-Glycerols diacylglycerol| binding site of the C-1, C-19 and C-26 regulatory domain of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.13| |CITS: [20971628]|. In addition, bryostatins can function as very potent immunostimulants (in |CITS: [24033119]|). More than 30 clinical trials have been conducted with |FRAME: CPD-21475| in monotherapy or in combination with clinically used cytotoxic drugs, testing its efficacy against different tumor types such as sarcoma, melanoma, ovaria, cervical, neck and head carcinoma, esophageal, gastric, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma, as well as a variety of leukemias, e.g., chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkins lymphoma, or multiple myeloma. However, phase II studies of |FRAME: CPD-21475| have failed to demonstrate any clinically meaningful activity, and bryostatin has not progressed to phase III clinical trials as a cancer treatment |CITS: [Newman12]|., On the other hand, |FRAME: CPD-21475| has been shown to reverse synaptic loss and facilitate synaptic maturation in animal models of Alzheimer's disease, Fragile X, stroke, and other neurological disorders. Advanced Alzheimer patients treated with bryostatin demonstrated return of major functions such as swallowing, vocalization, and word recognition, and in 2017 Phase II clinical trials started with |FRAME: CPD-21475| as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's disease |CITS: [28482641]|., About This Pathway, The first step towards understanding the bryostatins biosynthesis pathway was the cloning of a large DNA region from |FRAME: TAX-62101| encoding several type I modular polyketide synthases (PKSs) and the sequencing of the first gene, |FRAME: G-63066| |CITS: [15556005]|. The full sequence of the bryostatin biosynthetic cluster was obtained in 2007, revealing the presence of five modular PKS genes (|FRAME: G-63066|, |FRAME: G-63067|, |FRAME: G-63068|, |FRAME: G-63069|, and the cryptic bryX), a discrete acyltransferase (|FRAME: G-63073|), a malonyl-[acp] decarboxylase (|FRAME: G-63070|), a hydroxy-methyl-glutaryl CoA synthase homolog (|FRAME: G-63064|), and a methyltransferase (bryS) |CITS: [17253852]|. The genome of |FRAME: TAX-62101| was sequenced in 2016, revealing the identity of two more genes that were predicted to encode pathway enzymes - |FRAME: G-63072| and |FRAME: G-63065| |CITS: [27590822]|., The bryostatin polyketide synthases (PKSs) belong to the "trans-AT" class of PKS, members of which do not contain any acyltransferase (AT) domains and are thus not capable of loading the malonyl extender units directly from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|. This function is provided by the |FRAME: MONOMER-20813|, which provides the malonyl extender unit to all of the bryostatin PKSs |CITS: [17253852]|., According to the proposed pathway, biosynthesis starts with |FRAME: G3P| or a similar glycolysis intermediate, which is bound to the loading module of the |FRAME: MONOMER-20806| and converted to a D-lactyl starter unit. This unit is then extended by the next three domains of BryA to form a tetraketide, at which point the first β-branch is formed (see below). The next four modules (M4-7) come from the |FRAME: MONOMER-20807|, extending the chain from 9 to 17 carbons. In addition, the methyltransferase (MT) domain of BryB introduces the first characteristic gem-dimethyl group. At the end of the extension by BryB, a second β-branch is introduced. The next enzme, |FRAME: MONOMER-20808|, also contains four modules (M8-11), and extends the chain to 25 carbons. The first module of BryC contains an unusual domain which has been named a pyran synthase (PS) domain. This domain is believed to catalyze the formation of the tetrahydropyran ring found in bryostatin. Module 9 also contains an MT domain, and introduces the second gem-dimethyl group. The last PKS, |FRAME: MONOMER-20809|, contains only a single KS domain and extends the chain to 27 carbons. The molecule is then cyclyzed by forming a bond from C-1 to C-25 and released from BryD. Two five-carbon pyran rings form by the condensation of a keto and a hydroxyl group from C-19 to C-23 and C-5 to C-9. The enzyme responsible for the cyclization could be the NRPS condensation domain in BryD together with the adjacent KS domain, or may be catalyzed by the TE domain pf BryX |CITS: [17253852]|, It should be noted that the biosynthesis of bryostatins involves an unusual polyketide β-branching process, which comprises the addition of a two-carbon unit to the β-carbonyl of the nascent polyketide chain and subsequent modifications. The process is typically catalyzed by enzymes encoded by an "HMGS cassette" of genes (named after |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10|, the first β-branching enzyme to be described). The core enzymes of the HMGS cassette are a dedicated FAS-like acyl-carrier protein that loads a malonyl moiety from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, a mutated acyltransferase that lost the ability to catalyze formation of C-C bonds and functions as a decarboxylase, converting the malonyl moiety to an acetyl moiety, and a homolog of |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10 "EC 2.3.3.10"| that transfers the acetyl moiety from the acyl-carrier protein to the β carbonyl of the target, forming the β-branch branch., HMGS cassettes have been shown to install methyl branch points in |FRAME: CPD-21467|, |FRAME: Curacins curacin|, |FRAME: Jamaicamides jamaicamide|, and |FRAME: Pseudomonic-Acids mupirocin|. |FRAME: G-63064 BryR|, a homolog of |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10 "EC 2.3.3.10"|, has been implicated in β-branching at C13 and C21 of the core ring system. It's activity requires that the acetyl group is provided by the |FRAME: MONOMER-20812|. The acetylated form of BryU is generated by |FRAME: G-63070 BryQ|, a decarboxylative ketosynthase in which a Cys residue in the active site has been replaced by a Ser, preventing the enzyme from catalyzing the formation of C-C bonds |CITS: [21035732][29779653]|. Following the incorporation of the acetyl unit at the β position; a dehydration catalyzed by |FRAME: G-63065 BryT| results in formation of a double bond. This is followed by O-methylation, catalyzed by MT domains in the BryA and BryB PKSs. The β-branching process is finalized by isomerization of the double bond, most likely by an ER-like domain within BryB module-4 |CITS: [29779653]|. The β-branching process is repeated twice, forming two vinyl methylester moieties, both of which are situated at key sites of interaction with bryostatin's biological target, protein kinase C |CITS: [25808573][26859836]|.

Flavonoids are highly diverse class of plant plant polyphenols (with about 9000 compounds have been , identified so far |CITS: [16137727]| that impart much of the color and flavor of fruits and vegetables. , They exhibit a wide range of biological functions in higher plants such as UV protection, flower coloration, , and antimicrobial a activity |CITS: [11130659]|. They also exhibit antioxidant and anticancer properties |CITS: [12224601]| |CITS: [18645020]|., Flavan-3-ols, sometime referred to simply as flavanols, represent an important classs of flavonoids. They are the building blocks of condensed tannins, and exhibit numerous potentially benefical medicinal properties. They show antioxidant and free radical scavenging |CITS: [14733505]|, anticarcinogenic |CITS: [11448533]| and cardioprotective properties. It has recently been shown that epicatechin present in dark chocolate has the potential to promote cardiovascular health in humans ., The most common flavan-3-ols belong to one of two sterioisofoms - either |FRAME: CPD-10359 "(2R,3S)-flavan-3-ols"| (2,3-trans-flavan-3-ols) or |FRAME: CPD-10414 "(2R,3R)-flavan-3-ols"| (2,3-cis-flavan-3-ols).|FRAME: EC-1.3.1.77| converts anthocyanidins to their corresponding 2,3-cis-flavan-3-ols.

Summary: |FRAME: VAL| is one of the three main branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), along with |FRAME: LEU|, and |FRAME: ILE|., The catabolic pathways of the BCAAs can be divided into two sequential series of reactions, referred to, as the common pathway and the distal pathway., The common pathway includes the enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-6941|, |FRAME: CPLX8J2-279|, and, |FRAME: CPLX-6942|. These three enzymes catalyze the conversion of all three BCAAs to their, respective acyl-CoA derivatives, (|FRAME:METHACRYLYL-COA|, |FRAME:3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA|, and |FRAME: CPD-1083|, for |FRAME:VAL|, |FRAME:LEU|, and |FRAME:ILE|, respectively), though the intermediates formed, by these enzymes are different for the different amino acids., The distal parts of the pathway are completely different for the three BCAAs, and comprise enzymes, specific for each amino acid |CITS: [773366]|., The catabolism of |FRAME: VAL| involves its conversion via |FRAME:2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| to, |FRAME:ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, which is desaturated to form the α,β-unsaturated, thioester |FRAME:METHACRYLYL-COA|. Hydration to |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, and thioester hydrolysis forms the diffusible and transportable compound, |FRAME:3-HYDROXY-ISOBUTYRATE|., Finally, this β-hydroxy acid is oxidized to |FRAME:CH3-MALONATE-S-ALD|, and thioesterified to form |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA|., The pathway is widely distributed and has been demonstrated in bacteria |CITS: [4957438][5030618]|,, fungi, cilliates |CITS: [13457352]|, higher plants |CITS: [Gerbling88][15280033]| and animals, |CITS: [13233241][13398382][8824301]|. A few exceptions are |FRAME: TAX-83333|, which does not possess, a |FRAME: CPLX8J2-279|, and |FRAME: TAX-4932|, which cannot use |FRAME: VAL| as a carbon source,, and degrades it into |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL| (see |FRAME:PWY-5057|)., In eukaryotic organisms the pathway spans both the cytoplasmic and mitochondrial, compartments, as the first reaction takes place in the cytoplasm, while its product,, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, is transported into the mitochondria, where the rest of the pathway, occurs.

|FRAME: CPD-26970 "Oxetanocin A"| is a nucleoside analog isolated from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1404|. It is an unusual nucleoside, where an adenine moiety is attached to position 2 of an oxetane ring, which is further modified by hydroxymethyl groups at positions 3 and 4 |CITS: [3025147]|. The compound was found to have a potent antiviral, anti-tumor, and antimicrobial activities due to its ability to inhibit DNA polymerases |CITS: [3025147][28346939][2787618]|., The genes encoding the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-26970| were found on a 51.5-kb plasmid, pOXT1 |CITS: [ 10227144]|. Its biosynthesis from |FRAME: DAMP| involves the cobalamin (Cbl)-dependent radical SAM enzyme OxsB and the phosphohydrolase OxsA |CITS: [28346939]|. OxsB/OxsA complex formation is crucial for the ring contraction reaction |CITS: [33560833]|., The pathway includes an oxidation of the oxetane aldehyde that is produced by OxsB to the corresponding alcohol. This oxidation is catalyzed by a nonspecific dehydrogenase from the general cellular pool |CITS: [33560833]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for O antigen synthesis are often present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The lipid A-core oligosaccharide and the O-antigens are synthesized in the cytoplasm, exported to the periplasm, and combined by the |FRAME: BAB_RS18990-MONOMER|, forming lipopolysaccharides (LPS) attached to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane. The LPS are then transferred from the inner membrane to the outer membrane and through it, remaining attached to outer leaflet of the outer membrane |CITS: [36806059]|., In |FRAME: TAX-234| lipopolysaccharides the O-antigen polymer is attached to the lipid A-core moiety by a β(1→4) linkage between the reducing-end |FRAME: CPD-15695| residue of the O-antigen and a terminal glucosyl residue in the branched core component |CITS: [23261780]|., In Brucella the system responsible for transporting lipopolysaccharides from the inner membrane to the outer membrane consists of six Lpt proteins - LptB, LptF, LptG, LptC, LptA, and LptE. Together these proteins form a transenvelope bridge that transports LPS from the inner membrane, across the periplasm to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane., LptB2FG is an ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter which, together with LptC, extracts the lipid A-core oligosaccharide from the inner membrane. LptA is a periplasmic protein that acts as a bridge between the inner membrane and the outer membrane. LptE is an outer membrane protein that functions to anchor the oligosaccharide at the cell surface.The Lpt system acts downstream from |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.6|, which is responsible for flipping the lipid A-core structure across the inner membrane.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: S2O3 Thiosulfate| is a relatively stable environmentally abundant sulfur compound of intermediate oxidation state. Several pathways of thiosulfate oxidation are known. The two best understood pathways are the direct oxidation of thiosulfate to sulfate, catalyzed by the |FRAME:CPLX-882|, and the indirect oxidation of thiosulfate through polythionate intermediates, the main of which is |FRAME:CPD-14| (see |FRAME:THIOSULFOX-PWY|)., Two versions of the direct oxidation pathway are known. A number of facultatively chemo- or photolithotrophic organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-82367| or |FRAME: TAX-35806|, which possess the SoxCD proteins, oxidize a single molecule of thiosulfate to two molecules of sulfate (this pathway). Organisms that lack the SoxCD proteins utilize a different route, in which one molecule of thiosulfate is converted into only one molecule of sulfate while the other sulfur atom is added to inorganic sulfur globules that are deposited either in the periplasmic space or outside the cells (see |FRAME: PWY-6677|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-82367| is a Gram-negative, neutrophilic, facultatively lithoautotrophic bacterium that is able to grow with thiosulfate as an energy source using the first type of pathway. The organism posseses a periplasmic enzyme complex known as the |FRAME: CPLX-882| (for sulfur oxidation) that is able to oxidize thiosulfate to sulfate with no intermediates |CITS:[10940005]|., The sox gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-82367| comprises at least two transcriptional units with 15 genes., Seven of these genes, soxXYZABCD, encode 4 proteins which can be combined in vitro to reconstitute an active Sox enzyme complex. The four proteins encoded by these seven genes are |FRAME:CPLX-7149|, |FRAME:CPLX-881|, |FRAME:SOXBDENIT-MONOMER|, and |FRAME:CPLX-7150|. , |FRAME:CPLX-7149| is a heterodimeric c-type cytochrome; |FRAME:CPLX-881| is a heterodimeric protein that binds thiosulfate covalently. |FRAME:SOXBDENIT-MONOMER| is a monomer that contains two manganese atoms |CITS: [9260941]|. |FRAME:CPLX-7150| is an α2β2 heterotetramer composed of two, units each of SoxC, a molybdenum cofactor-containing subunit, and SoxD, a diheme c-type, cytochrome |CITS: [10795683]|., An in vitro reconstituted Sox system mediates not only |FRAME: S2O3|, but also |FRAME: SO3|-,, |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur|-, and |FRAME: HS|-dependent cytochrome c reduction |CITS: [9260941][11443084]|. , While thiosulfate oxidation yields eight electrons, sulfite oxidation follows the following equation,, and yields only 2 electrons per mol substrate:, |FRAME:SO3| + |FRAME:WATER| = |FRAME:SULFATE| + 2|FRAME:E-| + 2|FRAME:PROTON|, Sulfite oxidation does not require the presence of the SoxCD protein., The overall reaction of thiosulfate oxidation is:, |FRAME: S2O3| + 5 |FRAME:WATER| = 2 |FRAME:SULFATE| + 8|FRAME:E-| + 11|FRAME:PROTON|, A model for the mechanism of the Sox system in |FRAME: TAX-82367| has been proposed |CITS: [11425697]|., According to this model, the first step is the |FRAME: CPLX-7149|-mediated binding of thiosulfate or sulfite to a cysteine residue of |FRAME: SOXYDENIT-MONOMER|. When thiosulfate binds, a |FRAME: SoxY-Thiocysteine-Sulfate| is formed, which is then hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16064|, liberating a sulfate, and forming a |FRAME: SoxY-S-Thiocysteine|. At the time, it was suggested that the pathway proceeds as follows: |FRAME: CPLX-7150| would successively oxidize the outer sulfur atom, using three water molecules and forming |FRAME: SoxZY-Cysteine-Sulfate|. The second sulfate group would then be hydrolyzed by |FRAME: SOXBDENIT-MONOMER|, bringing the cysteine residue of |FRAME:SOXYDENIT-MONOMER| to its initial condition. However, several years later it was shown that the pathway proceeds via different intermediates: Following the first release of sulfate, a second |FRAME: S2O3| is added by SoxXA, forming |FRAME: SoxY-Thiocysteine-S-Sulfate|. It is this molecule that serves as a substrate for |FRAME: SOXBDENIT-MONOMER|, which hydrolyzes it to release a second |FRAME: SULFATE| molecule, forming |FRAME: SoxY-S-S-Thiocysteine| that is oxidized by |FRAME: CPLX-7151| to |FRAME: SoxY-Thiocysteine-Sulfate|, closing the cycle |CITS: [28257465]|., It should be noted that many sulfur oxidizers do not contain SoxCD and have a so-called truncated Sox system. For complete oxidation to sulfate, truncated Sox systems interact with cytoplasmic sulfur oxidation systems such as the one described in |FRAME: PWY-8573| |CITS: [36367491][37627615]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-28161 Neosartorin| is a yellow pigment that was originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-36630| (then known as Neosartorya fischeri) |CITS: [Proksa98]|. It was later isolated from several different fungal species such as |FRAME: TAX-340412| and was found to possess substantial antibacterial activity against several Gram-positive bacteria including methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| (MRSA) |CITS: [Ola14][27941865]|., The compound is a xanthone dimer made of two different monomeric units |CITS: [Proksa98][Ola14]|. A biosynthetic gene cluster encoding its biosynthesis was reported in 2018 from |FRAME: TAX-340412| |CITS: [30394754]|., Like other fungal xanthone compounds, biosynthesis starts with a polyketide synthase (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.336|) and proceeds via the common intermediate anthraquinone |FRAME: CPD-8215| (see |FRAME: CPD-8215|). As described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-8609|, emodin is converted to |FRAME: CPD-28149|, which is thought to be a common precursor for the fungal xanthones |CITS: [30746079]|., The two monomeric units, |FRAME: CPD-28190| and |FRAME: CPD-28191|, are both synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-28149|, by the same set of enzymes. An intial split in the pathway, which is a result of the exact ring bond that is cleaved by the dioxygenase NsrF, leads to to two alternate pathway, producing |FRAME: CPD-28189| and |FRAME: CPD-28191|. Acetylation of the former produces |FRAME: CPD-28190|, which is coupled to |FRAME: CPD-28191| by the P450 monooxygenase MsrP |CITS: [30394754]|.

|FRAME: CPD-15213 Mycocyclosin| is a diketopiperazine secondary metabolite produced by |FRAME: TAX-1773| and discovered in 2009 |CITS: [19416919]|., The |FRAME: G185E-6494| gene, which encodes |FRAME: G185E-6494-MONOMER|, was shown to be essential for |FRAME: TAX-1773| viability, suggesting that mycocyclosin has a vital (although undetermined at this time) cellular role in the organism's survival |CITS: [18818197]|., The biosynthesis of mycocyclosin starts with an initial condensation of two molecules of |FRAME: Charged-TYR-tRNAs| to generate the cyclodipeptide |FRAME: CPD-15209|, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: TYRS-CPLX| |CITS: [19430487][20852636]|., Subsequent oxidative coupling of the tyrosine aromatic rings is catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme |FRAME: G185E-6494-MONOMER| (CYP121), which generates a 3,3'-dityrosine-type biaryl cross-link to complete the bicyclic framework of |FRAME: CPD-15213| |CITS:[18818197][19416919]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Gallotanins Gallotannins| belong to the 'complex' galloylglucose group of hydrolysable tannins, which are built by addition of further galloyl residues to |FRAME: 12346-PENTAKIS-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUC| (see |FRAME:PWY-5475|). Gallotannins are characterized by meta-depside group, i.e. the esterification with another molecule of |FRAME: 1-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| at the meta-position of a galloyl residue., The gallotannins found in |FRAME: TAX-255348| (Staghorn sumac) vary from gallotannins found in other plants, e.g. |FRAME: TAX-35924| |CITS: [6652813]| in that the C1 and C6 positions of the glucose core remain free of depside attachments |CITS: [16153405]| indicating a deviant set of enzymes in those plants. Hydrolyzable tannins are widely distributed among plants but differ with regard to gallotannins (more restricted occurence) and ellagitannins (broad occurence) |CITS: [Haddock82]|., Gallotannins have also been used in human health care for their anti-cancer and apoptosis-inducing properties |CITS: [11142343][15889414]| as well as their radical scavenging activities that marks gallotannins as potent antioxidants |CITS: [10641736]|., About This Pathway, The experimental data clearly indicate that the impressive number of gallotannins is produced following one general reaction type. The question whether there are one (or few) unspecific enzyme(s) or many specific enzymes involved in the gallotannin biosynthesis has been answered in favor of the latter by the isolation, purification and characterization of 5 different enzymes |CITS: [Niemetz00]|. Those enzymes catalyze the progressive galloylation of pentagalloylglucose towards penta-, hexa- and heptagalloylglucoses and even higher substituted galloylglucoses |CITS: [ 2148866]|. Although the enzymes itself are not very specific towards their substrates it was found on the basis of calculated catalytic efficiency that each of them had a preferred substrate (and major product) and therefore operates along a mainstream metabolic sequence |CITS: [16153405]|., The five galloyltransferases identified in sumac (also called galloyltransferase A to E) have been demonstrated to catalyze the 4- and 2-O-acylation of 1,2,3,4,6-pentagalloylglucose towards more substituted gallotannins such as 4-O-digalloyl-1,2,3,6-tetra-O-galloyl-β-D-glucose and 2,4-di-O-digalloyl-1,3,6-tri-O-galloyl-β-D-glucose (galloyltransferase A) |CITS: [Niemetz99]| - left site of the pathway or the 3-O-acylation of 1,2,3,4,6-pentagalloylglucose to form the gallotannins 3-O-digalloyl-1,2,4,6-tetra-O-galloyl-β-D-glucose (galloyltransferase C) - middle part of the pathway |CITS: [Niemetz98]|. , Two other galloyltransferases, i.e. galloyltransferase B |CITS: [11672728]| and galloyltransferase D |CITS: [12430027]| then further galloylates 3-O-digalloyl-1,2,4,6-tetra-O-galloyl-β-D-glucose to form 3-O-trigalloyl-1,2,4,6-tetra-O-galloyl-β-D-glucose |CITS: [11672728]|. The enzyme affording the conversion of 2-O-digalloyl-1,3,4,6-tetra-O-galloylglucose to 2,4-di-O-digalloyl-1,3,6-tri-O-galloylglucose and 2,3-di-O-digalloyl-1,4,6-tri-O-galloylglucose (galloyltransferase E) - right site of the pathway |CITS: [12430027]| completes the metabolic grid forming the various heptagalloylglucoses in sumac.

Summary: |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP) is an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS: [17068264]|., DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh, sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|., Two main routes are known for DMSP degradation, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-7670| and, |FRAME: CPD-7672|, respectively. |FRAME: CPD-7670|, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely, between the ocean and the atmosphere, and is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere., DMS influences climate because it is oxidized in the troposphere to sulfuric and methanesulfonic acids,, which attract water and promote cloud formation |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, most of the DMS in the, oceanic environment is degraded biologically (see |FRAME: PWY-6047|)., The second product of DMSP degradation, |FRAME: CPD-7672|, can be processed in either of two ways:, it can be cleaved to |FRAME: CPD-7671| and |FRAME: ACRYLATE|, or it can be demethylated further, to form |FRAME: CPD-7673| |CITS:[16347732][16348607]|., In a study of marine bacteria in coastal seawater fifteen strains that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-2433|, group were isolated from seawater and characterized with respect to their ability to transform organic and, inorganic sulfur compounds. All of the isolates were able to degrade DMSP to DMS by the cleavage, pathway. In addition, five of the isolates also produced methanethiol, indicating that both the cleavage, and demethylation pathways for DMSP occurred in the same organisms |CITS: [10473380]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Ketomemicins ketomemicins| are carbonyl-methylene-containing pseudotripeptides that have been reported from three actinobacterial species - |FRAME: TAX-219305|, |FRAME: TAX-1223523|, and |FRAME: TAX-369723| |CITS: [27023439][27289319][28097768]|. Their biological role is not known, as they do not exhibit antibacterial properties., The discovery of the ketomemicins followed the characterization of |FRAME: CPLX-85493| (Pgm1), which catalyzes amide bond formation between a non-proteinogenic amino acid and ribosomally supplied oligopeptides during |FRAME: Pheganomycins pheganomycin| biosynthesis (|CITS: [25402768]|). A search for orthologs of the ligase identified multiple candidates. In the three organisms |FRAME: TAX-219305|, |FRAME: TAX-1223523|, and |FRAME: TAX-369723| the ortholog was found in conserved genes clusters that contain six genes. To probe the functions of those genes, they were heterologously expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1916| |CITS: [27023439]|., Upon expressing the cluster from |FRAME: TAX-1223523|, the host produced multiple new products that were identidied as |FRAME: CPD-27246| through |FRAME: CPD-27248|. The cluster from |FRAME: TAX-219305| resulted in production of |FRAME: CPD-27249|, and that from |FRAME: TAX-369723| produced |FRAME: CPD-27250|. As the original strains did not produce these compounds, the biosynthetic gene clusters in them were silent under the conditions employed |CITS: [ 27023439]|.

Summary: |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines 7-Deazapurines"| are compounds that contain pyrrolopyrimidine functional groups (similar to purines, but lacking one of the nitrogens in the pentameric ring). These compounds form a structurally diverse class of nucleoside analogues that often possess antibiotic, antineoplastic, or antiviral activities., Various species of Streptomyces produce 7-deazapurine nucleoside antibiotics, such as |FRAME: CPD-13056|, |FRAME: CPD-13052|, |FRAME: CPD-13054|, and |FRAME: CPD-13055|., An important |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines 7-deazapurine"| compound is |FRAME: CPD-13053|, a modified nucleoside that is present in certain tRNAs in bacteria and most eukaryotes (with the exception of mycoplasmas and yeast) but not in the archaea |CITS: [ 12697167]|. The pathway describing the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13053| can be found at |FRAME: PWY-6700|., The biosynthesis of all 7-deazapurines proceeds via the common intermediate |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, which is produced in four steps from the nucleotide |FRAME:GTP|. The pathway starts with the conversion of GTP to |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3| by |FRAME: FOLE-CPLX|, an enzyme that is also involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: THF|. |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3| is converted to |FRAME: CPD0-1699| by the action of |FRAME: G7431-MONOMER| (|FRAME: G7431|). This intermediate is converted to |FRAME: CPD-13043| by an unusual transformation catalyzed by |FRAME: BSU13740-MONOMER| (|FRAME: BSU13740|), a member of the radical SAM enzyme superfamily. , Finally, the carboxylate moiety of the latter is converted subsequently to a nitrile in an ATP-dependent reaction, in which ammonia serves as the nitrogen source, catalyzed by |FRAME: BSU13720-MONOMER| (|FRAME: BSU13720|), generating the final product, |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| |CITS: [19354300]|.

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN Enterobactin| is a catecholate siderophore produced almost exclusively by enterobacteria, |CITS:[4908639][4908541][3067977]|, although it has been reported in some Streptomyces species |CITS:[11267771]|., It is a cyclic compound made of three units of 2,3-dihydroxybenzoylserine joined in a cyclic structure by lactone linkages (only the δ-cis isomer of the ferric chelate is biologically active). Not only the cyclic molecule, but also the biosynthetic precursor 2,3-dihydroxy-N-benzoylserine and its linear dimer and trimer condensation products are able to transport iron into enterobacteria |CITS: [2139424][1831634]|., |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN Enterobactin| not only is used by the oorganisms that produce it but also serves as an, exosiderophore for many bacteria that are unable to synthesize it, such as |FRAME: TAX-287|, in a strategy of siderophore, piracy |CITS: [26431675]|., About This Pathway, Enterobactin is synthesized under iron-deficient conditions and excreted into the environment where it binds Fe(III) with high affinity and specificity. The ferrisiderophore complexes are taken up into the cell by specific transport components., Enterobactin synthesis is divided into two parts:, 1) the conversion of |FRAME: CHORISMATE| to |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, 2) the synthesis of enterobactin from |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| and |FRAME:SER|., The second part of the pathway can be summarized in a single reactiom (|FRAME: EC-6.3.2.14|):, |FRAME:ENTMULTI-RXN|, However, it is a rather complex process catalyzed by the different components of the non-ribosomal peptide synthase |FRAME: ENTMULTI-CPLX|. The process starts with the activation of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.71|, encoded by |FRAME:EG10263| |CITS: [2531000]| in the following reaction, |FRAME: DHBAMPLIG-RXN|, The product is transferred onto the aryl-carrier protein (ArCP) domain of the entB bi-functional protein |CITS: [2139796][9214294]|, where it is attached to the free thiol group of its cofactor, |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P|. The cofactor attachment is catalyzed by the |FRAME: ENTD-MONOMER| protein (EntD)., |FRAME: SER| is activated in a similar manner by the four-domain protein |FRAME: ENTF-PANT EntF|, and then bound to the peptidyl-carrier protein domain of this protein. , A different domain of EntF catalyzes the condensation of the activated serine and the activated 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate |CITS: [9485415][1826089]|, and then transfers the |FRAME: N-23-DIHYDROXYBENZOYL-L-SERINE| to the fourth domain of EntF, named the Te domain, which is responsible for the trimerization of three such moieties and the release of the trilactone |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN| |CITS: [10375542]|.

Synthesis of nitrogen-containing biomolecules requires nitrogen in a reduced form., Plants and various fungi and bacteria are able to utilize |FRAME: NITRATE| and |FRAME: NITRITE| from the environment by reducing these nitrogen oxides to ammonium ions, which are readily metabolized into organic molecules., |FRAME:EC-1.7.1.3 "Assimilatory nitrate reductase"| passes a pair of electrons from the donor molecule NAD(P)H to |FRAME: NITRATE| through a series of enzyme prosthetic groups, which can include |FRAME:FAD|, |FRAME: MONOMER-13439|, and a |FRAME: CPD-15870|, reducing nitrate to |FRAME: NITRITE| |CITS: [4388959]|., The nitrite produced is then reduced to ammonium through the action of |FRAME:EC-1.7.1.15 "assimilatory nitrite reductase"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-9620| gene. Nitrite reductase accepts six electrons from three equivalents of NAD(P)H and transfers them via bound |FRAME: FAD|, an |FRAME: CPD-7|, and |FRAME: SIROHEME| to nitrite |CITS: [4154942][6457037]|., The ammonium formed is incorporated into glutamate and glutamine by the enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.4| and |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.2| (glutamine synthase). Glutamate and glutamine serve as precursors for many other nitrogenous compounds |CITS: [157059]|.
