Summary: |FRAME: CPD-16637 Elloramycin| is |FRAME: Anthracyclines| antitumour drug and antibiotic. This group of compounds is defined by the presence of a four fused-ring aromatic system, based on a 7,8,9,10-tetrahydro-5,12-naphthacenequinone framework,, which usually occurs as a glycoside with a deoxy(amino)sugar., Elloramycin is produced by |FRAME: TAX-47716| Tu2353, and was found to possess a weak activity against a variety of Gram-positive bacteria (especially streptomycetes) and against stem cells of L-1210 leukemia |CITS: [3840789]|., The aglycon of elloramycin closely resembles |FRAME: CPD-15533| but has an additional C-12a-O-methyl group and, in contrast to tetracenomycin C, the C-8 hydroxyl group is not methylated but glycosylated with a permethylated L-rhamnose residue., The genes encoding ellaromycin biosynthesis are located in multiple clusters. One large cluster contains the genes responsible for the biosynthesis of the aglycone, a glycosyltransferase, and the methyltransferases that modify the deoxysugar, while a second cluster contains the genes required for biosynthesis of L-rhamnose., Early work isolated a cosmid (16F4) that contained the first cluster |CITS: [8529875]| and characterized the glycosyltransferase (|FRAME: G-18057|) |CITS:[10937435][11306350]|, the three methyltransferases that modify the deoxysugar (|FRAME: G-18054|, |FRAME: G-18055| and |FRAME: G-18056|) |CITS: [11376004]|, two oxygenases and a cyclase |CITS: [11325225]|., In a subsequent study the rest of the cosmid was sequenced, identifying a total of 17 genes involved in elloramycin biosynthesis, and the missing genes were assigned functions based on their similarity to the homologous genes from the |FRAME: CPD-15533|-producer |FRAME: TAX-1907| |CITS: [18310024]|. The four genes required for the biosynthesis of the L-rhamnose were identified elsewhere in the chromosome |CITS: [18310024]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-14436| (NAGGN) is a modified dipeptide that functions in bacterial osmoregulation. This compound was first identified in osmotically stressed |FRAME: TAX-382 "Sinorhizobium meliloti (previously known as Rhizobium meliloti)"| |CITS: [2768187]| and later reported in a few species of |FRAME:TAX-286| and marine bacteria. However, the genes encoding its biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-266834| were found to be highly conserved in diverse bacteria including halophiles, mesophiles, and both plant and animal pathogens |CITS: [20571117]|., In addition to NAGGN, a number of other bacterially produced low molecular weight organic osmolytes (compatible solutes) are produced and accumulated by bacteria in response elevated osmolarity in the environment. They include sugars, polyols, amino acids and their derivatives, quaternary amines and their sulfonium analogs, and sulfate esters (in |CITS: [20571117]|). For example see pathways |FRAME: P101-PWY|, |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-3722| and |FRAME: Trehalose-biosynthesis|., About This Pathway, Two contiguous orfs SMb20481 and SMb20482 were identified as encoding the enzymes of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-266834| |CITS: [20571117]|. These orfs are located on the pSymB replicon, one of two megaplasmids found in this organism along with a circular chromosome |CITS: [11474104]|. DNA sequence analysis showed that SMb20481 and SMb20482 are contiguous orfs separated by only one base pair. Five genes putatively encoding four components of a dipeptide ABC transporter and a transcriptional regulator were found 122 base pairs upstream of SMb20481, along with a divergently transcribed putative transcriptional regulator at the 3' end. Both SMb20481 and SMb20482 were found to be osmotically induced |CITS: [20571117]|., Orf SMb20481 was previously named asnO due to the similarity of its product with that of |FRAME:TAX-1423| AsnO that is involved in pathway |FRAME: ASPARAGINE-BIOSYNTHESIS|. However, it was found that the SMb20481 product did not appear to be involved in that pathway |CITS: [11389771]|. As shown here it was found to be involved in the biosynthesis of NAGGN. Orf SMb20482 was named ngg and was predicted to be bifunctional, with both N-acetylating and peptide bond-forming activities. The N-terminal domain is conserved in N-acetyltransferases, and the C-terminal domain is conserved in cyanophycin synthases |CITS: [20571117]| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8482|). Evidence suggested that Ngg catalyzes formation of the dipeptide |FRAME: CPD-14437| (NAGG) in a reaction involving nonribosomal peptide bond synthesis., In the first step of the pathway Ngg was suggested to catalyze both N-acetylation of one |FRAME: GLN| residue and formation of a peptide bond between this residue and a second |FRAME: GLN| residue to produce the dipeptide intermediate NAGG. In a second step, AsnO catalyzes the transfer of the amide nitrogen of a free |FRAME: GLN| molecule to the second |FRAME: GLN| residue of NAGG to produce NAGGN. This pathway was supported by studies in which strains carrying mutations in ngg or asnO were used in combination with NMR analyses of their products produced under salt-stress conditions. The intermediate NAGG and the final product NAGGN were identified. The asnO mutation was also shown to be deleterious for growth of the organism at high osmolarity |CITS: [20571117]|.

Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|). Analogs for these pathways are also found in the metabolism of deoxyhexoses such as |FRAME: L-rhamnose| and |FRAME: L-fucoses| (see |FRAME: PWY-6714| and |FRAME: PWY-8318|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Arabinoses Arabinose| is an aldopentose - a monosaccharide containing five carbon atoms. Unlike many other aldoses, which are more abundant in nature as the "D"-form, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE| is far more common in nature than |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|. Both forms can be degraded by microorganisms. , The earlier steps of this pathway have been characterized from multiple bacterial species, as they are common to all three routes of the third type of pathways. The last two steps, which are specific for this route, were characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-863372| |CITS: [30655589]|.

Summary: Note: this is a proposed pathway based mainly on stable isotope labeling and mass spectrometry studies |CITS: [21455182]|. The reactions need to be confirmed by enzymological studies. The pathway will be updated in MetaCyc as new information becomes available., General Background, Twenty-two amino acids are naturally incorporated into polypeptides, twenty via the universal genetic code and two (|FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: CPD-3321|) via unique mechanisms (|CITS: [20417644]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21550296]|). The twenty-second amino acid, |FRAME: CPD-3321|, is found in methyltransferases that initiate methanogenesis in |FRAME: TAX-2207| species. This amino acid is incorporated into polypeptides under the direction of an amber UAG stop codon that serves as a sense codon during translation. Incorporation requires the pylT gene, which encodes an unusual tRNA with a CUA anticodon, and the pylS gene, which encodes an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase that charges the pylT-derived tRNA with |FRAME: CPD-3321| (see |FRAME: MONOMER-15529|, EC 6.1.1.26) (reviewed in |CITS: [21550296][21796749][21455167]|). See enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-7101|, |FRAME: CPLX-7102| and |FRAME: CPLX-7100|., |FRAME: CPD-3321| was first identified in 2002 in the active site of MtmB (|FRAME: CPLX-7101|) from the methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2208| |CITS: [12029132][12029131]|. More recently, genetic and biochemical studies have resulted in a proposal for its complete biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [21455182]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-3321| and its incorporation into proteins is encoded in the pylTSBCD gene cluster found in archaea belonging to the family |FRAME: TAX-2206|. Although confirmatory enzymological studies of purified biosynthetic enzymes PylB, PylC and PylD remain to be done, recombinant PylB has been expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, purified and its crystal structure has been determined |CITS: [22095926]|., About This Pathway, Although details of the enzymatic reactions in this pathway are not yet available, it has been demonstrated that |FRAME: CPD-3321| is biosynthesized enzymatically from two molecules of |FRAME: LYS|. To elucidate the pathway, the pylTSBCD gene cluster from |FRAME: TAX-2214| and the mtmB gene from |FRAME: TAX-2208| were expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| grown with |FRAME: LYS| radiolabeled in all of its carbon and nitrogen atoms. This demonstrated that |FRAME: CPD-3321| is biosynthesized from two molecules of |FRAME: LYS|, with elimination of a nitrogen atom (|CITS: [21455182]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21455167]|)., Recombinant PylB has been expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, purified, and its crystal structure determined. The identification of |FRAME: CPD-14086| in the active site cavity suggested that this is indeed its product |CITS: [22095926]|. Although the activities of the PylC and PylD enzymes have not yet been fully characterized, homology data and alternative substrate studies suggested the PylC-catalyzed ligase and PylD-catalyzed oxidation reactions shown in this pathway., Early work has suggested that the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-14093| to |FRAME: CPD-3321| occurrs in two step, via |FRAME: CPD-14098|. However, studies of a cloned and purified PylD enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-269797| suggest that the reaction proceeds with no intermediates, and requires only an NAD+ cofactor |CITS: [23720358]|. , Pyrrolysine biosynthesis is of interest in metabolic engineering studies aimed at incorporating modified amino acid residues into proteins. This was demonstrated by the incorporation of |FRAME: CPD-14090| (desmethylpyrrolysine) into proteins using |FRAME: LYS| and |FRAME: CPD-217| as precursors (|CITS: [21455182][21525873][21670250]|. Summary: |FRAME: Lipoarabinomannans Lipoarabinomannan| (LAM) and |FRAME: Lipomannans lipomannan| (LM) are lipoglycans found anchored in the plasma membrane of |FRAME: TAX-1763| species via a phosphatidyl-myo-inositol moiety |CITS: [9218490][20560059]|. Holes in the cell envelope poles, which have been described as kettle holes, allow the surface exposure of plasma membrane anchored LAM |CITS: [1871433][9451020]|., Lipomannans and lipoarabinomannans are biosynthesized by extending the phosphatidylinositol mannoside |FRAME: Phosphatidyl-myo-inositol-Man-6-acyl-Man "2-O-(6-O-acyl-α-D-mannosyl)-6-O-(α-D-mannosyl)-1-phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol"| (AcPIM2). That structure is extended by a linear α-1,6-linked mannan backbone made up of 20-25 mannopyranose residues. Different acyl groups, including |FRAME: PALMITATE|, |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|, |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-18581|, are attached to the glycerol and inositol residues. Most of the backbone residues are elaborated by single α-1,2-linked mannopyranose units., Lipomannan is converted to lipoarabinomannan by the attachment of a single large branched D-arabinan structure, very similar to that found in |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "mycobacterial arabinogalactan"|. The arabinan is attached to single mannose residue in the α-1,6-D-mannan backbone. The major LAM glycoforms contain about 50 arabinofuranose residues |CITS: [29443974]|., Some of the lipoarabinomannan glycoforms are capped at their non-reducing arabinan termini. A common cap, described from |FRAME: TAX-1764|, |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1769|, |FRAME: TAX-1781|, |FRAME: TAX-1789|, and |FRAME: TAX-1768|, consists of one to three α-1,2-linked mannopyranose residues attached by an α-1,5 linkage to the terminal arabinofuranose residue and is known as ManLAM |CITS: [29443974]|., The capping has been found to be catalyzed by two enzymes: the mannosyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-5824| gene catalyzes the transfer of the first mannosyl residue of the cap |CITS: [16704981]|, while the mannosyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-6391| gene catalyzes the transfer of one or two additional residues |CITS: [19004785]|., Note that the chain lengths shown in this diagram have been significantly shortened. The actual molecule contains about 110 glycosyl residues. In addition, some modifications found in LAM such as succinylation of some arabinofuranose residues are not shown.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-10896| (2,4,5-T) is an herbicide that is used extensively in many countries for weed control. It was developed in the late 1940s and was widely used in the agricultural industry until being phased out, starting in the late 1970s, due to toxicity concerns. Agent Orange, a defoliant used by the U.S. in the Vietnam War, was equal parts 2,4,5-T and |FRAME: CPD-9009|., Due to slow co-oxidative metabolism by natural microflora, 2,4,5-T is not easily biodegradable and persists in the environmentfor long periods. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-252970 "Burkholderia phenoliruptrix (previously known as Burkholderia cepacia ACll00 and Pseudomonas cepacia ACll00)"| |CITS: [15612618]|), which was isolated from a chemostat after several months of selection on 2,4,5-T, is capable of utilizing it as a sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [7125648]|., The pathway employed by this organism has been studied extensively, and all the enzymes have been characterized., With the exception of |FRAME: CPLX-7815|, all the genes that encode the enzymes have been isolated |CITS:[3224825], [7538273][8955624][9721310]|., The pathway starts with a hydroxylation that releases glyoxylate and generates a trichlorophenol |CITS: [7527626], [16535134]|. Two of the chorines are then removed by |FRAME: MONOMER-14674|, which also converts the phenol to, a hydroquinone, which is chemically reduced by FADH2 or NADH to a hydroquinol |CITS: [11410285][12700257]|. The last chlorine is removed by a dedicated dechlorinase, resulting in a |FRAME: HYDROXYBENZOQUINONE| |CITS: [9721310]|. This intermediate is converted in two steps to |FRAME: CPD-294|, which is reduced to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, a common intermediate in aromatic compounds degradation |CITS: [8900023]|, which is degraded into central metabolism compounds.

It also serves as a cofactor for all three nitric-oxide synthases (NOS) |FRAME: CPLX-6585|, |FRAME: CPLX-6581|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6582| (see |FRAME: PWY-4983|)., In addition, |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN| has been proposed to be involved in proliferation of murine erythrocyte cells |CITS: [2762302]|, promotion of neurotransmitter release in the brain |CITS: [1680529]| and regulation of human melanogenesis |CITS: [8128228]|. Deffciency causes severe neurological disorders characterized by hyperphenylalaninaemia and monoamine neurotransmitter deffciency, and is also implicated in Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease and depression (|CITS: [11592814][10727395]|., |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN Tetrahydrobiopterin| is present in probably every cell or tissue of higher animals |CITS: [10727395]|. On the other hand, most bacteria, fungi and plants do not synthesize tetrahydrobiopterin., However, tetrahydrobiopterin was found in glycosylated forms in some groups of bacteria including cyanobacteria |CITS: [11113566]| and the anaerobic photosynthetic |FRAME:TAX-1091| species |CITS: [9468332]|, and have been reported in several types of fungi |CITS: [7899493][21852350]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN Tetrahydrobiopterin| is formed de novo from GTP via a sequence of three enzymatic steps. The pathway involves two intermediates, |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P3| and |FRAME: 6-PYRUVOYL-5678-TETRAHYDROPTERIN|, which have been isolated, although they are rather unstable. The three enzymes of the pathway, |FRAME: ENZRXN-14275|, |FRAME: CPLX-7492| and |FRAME: CPLX-7494|, are required and sufficient., In mammals the |FRAME: CPLX-7494| enzyme produces |FRAME: CPD-14053|, as described here. In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1097| the enzyme produces |FRAME: CPD-14054| (see |FRAME: PWY-6983|) |CITS: [10333495]|.

General Background, Most microorganisms capable of osmotic adaptation accumulate compatible solutes in response to increases in the levels of salts or sugars in the environment. |FRAME: 2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE| (MG) is a compatible solute that is very common in organisms living near or at the highest growth temperatures for life |CITS: [17061210]|. It has been detected in thermophilic bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-29549|, |FRAME: TAX-274|, |FRAME: TAX-28237| and |FRAME: TAX-49319| |CITS: [8824608][16535053][10357003]|, and in the hyperthermophilic archaea of the genera |FRAME:TAX-2260|,|FRAME:TAX-2263|, Palaeococcus, Aeropyrum, and in some strains of |FRAME:TAX-2233| |CITS:[16535556][9758772]|., Even though MG is usually found in hyperthermophilic organisms, low levels have also been identified in red algae |CITS: [Karsten03]| and in mesophilic bacteria |CITS: [15205409]|., Physiological studies were conducted with several organisms, and showed that MG behaves like a typical solute, accumulating concomitantly with increasing levels of NaCl in the growth medium |CITS: [12220406]|. It is the primary osmolyte in many archaea, including |FRAME: TAX-2261|, |FRAME: TAX-53953|, |FRAME: TAX-2265|, |FRAME: TAX-2264|, and |FRAME: TAX-49900|, and also in the thermophilic and slightly halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29549|., In addition to protection against osmotic pressure, MG was shown to protect proteins against thermal denaturation |CITS: [16535713]|., About This Pathway, The mesophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-29549|, like most organisms that produce |FRAME: 2-O-ALPHA-MANNOSYL-D-GLYCERATE|, can do so in a two-step route, converting |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| into the intermediate |FRAME:ALPHA-D-MANNOSYL-3-PHOSPHOGLYCERATE|, followed by removal of the phosphate to generate MG (see |FRAME: PWY-5656|). However, unlike most other organisms, this bacterium possesses a second route for converting, GDP-mannose to MG. This route consists of a single step, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7485| |CITS: [10585410]|., The two routes appear to be utilized in response to different environmental trigers. While the two-step route is used in response to osmotic stress, the single-step route is selectively stimulated by heat stress |CITS: [14701859]|.

General Background, A unique combination of hydrogenases has been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-119072|, a thermophilic Gram-positive bacteria. These enzymes work in concert to generate |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| from reducing equivalents generated during fermentation of glucose to acetate, ethanol and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and couples |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production with energy conservation., About this Pathway, A membrane bound [NiFe] hydrogenase and a cytoplasmic heterotrimeric [Fe] only hydrogenase perform in synchrony to evolve |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| from |FRAME: PROTON| in |FRAME: TAX-119072|. The [Fe] only hydrogenase is an |FRAME:CPLX-8255|., The [NiFe] hydrogenase is ferredoxin dependent, 6 subunit enzyme with a the high level of identity to the 6 subunits of |FRAME: CPLX-7206| from the methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2208| |CITS: [15256587]|. Adjacent to the ech operon, |FRAME: TAX-119072| has a gene cluster designated hyp, encoding all the proteins required for the biosynthesis of [NiFe] centres |CITS: [15256587]|. , Membrane bound hydrogenases use electrons derived from reduced ferredoxins to catalyze the reduction of |FRAME: PROTON|. This is coupled to energy conservation via electron transport phosphorylation |CITS: [15168611]| and these enzymes have been designated energy-converting [NiFe] hydrogenases (Ech) |CITS: [11524134]|. |FRAME: TAX-2261|has a similar membrane bound (Mbh) hydrogenase, that couples |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolution with proton respiration and ATP synthesis and it has been proposed that a similar mechanism may operate with the Ech hydrogenase of |FRAME: TAX-119072| during |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production |CITS: [12792025]|. The six conserved subunits that make up the core of the Ech hydrogenases share sequence similarity with the catalytic core subunits of NADH:quinone oxidoreductase (complex I), which pumps protons across the inner membrane of mitochondria or the plasma membrane of many bacteria |CITS: [16645307]|. , |FRAME: TAX-119072| uses the enzymes of the |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY| pathway to convert glucose to pyruvate, generating ATP and NADH. Pyruvate is then oxidized to acetyl CoA and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| using the |FRAME: PWY-6758| pathway, thus generating reduced ferredoxin via |FRAME: CPLX-1868| |CITS: [15256587]|.

Summary: General Background, The formation of the free hydroxycinnamic acids such as caffeate, ferulate and , sinapate has long been thought to derive through a series of hydroxylation and methylation reactions at the , phenolic ring of cinnamic acid (|FRAME:PWY-2181|) |CITS: [BAUCHER98]|. However, intensive research , directed towards the biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids has led to a significant change of the layout and , interconnectivity of this central pathway (|FRAME:PWY-361|) giving rise to the biosynthesis of a vast variety , of major secondary metabolites such as flavonoids, lignins, lignans, stilbenes and aurones |CITS: [LEWIS99]| , |CITS: [11960740]| |CITS: [14503002]|. , The discovery of new enzymes involved in the metabolic sequence of phenyplpropanoids caused the revision , of the pathway generating ferulate and sinapate (this pathway) which constitute precursors for e.g. hydroxycinnamic , esters (|FRAME:PWY-3301|) the main secondary metabolites found in the mustard family |CITS: [8972602]|., About This Pathway, The main stream in the phenylpropanoid pathway has been demonstrated to , lead from p-coumarate to the various monolignols via coumaroyl-CoA and coniferyl aldehyde as the main , branching intermediates (|FRAME:PWY-361|). The phenylpropanoid 3-hydroxylation resulting in the formation , of 3,4-hydroxylated phenylpropanoids and their further metabolization has been shown to involve , hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA esters as substrates |CITS: [11429408]| |CITS: [11967091]| |CITS: [12381722]| , |CITS: [15161961]| whereas 5-hydroxylation and 5-methylation occur on the level of hydroxycinnamaldehydes , and/or hydroxycinnamyl alcohols |CITS: [10468559]| |CITS: [10430877]|., The formation of the free phenylpropanoid acids ferulate and sinapate is catalyzed via the oxidation of the , corresponding cinnamaldehydes as proposed earlier |CITS: [10468559]|. The gene (REF1) encoding the , enzyme catalyzing the reaction, i.e. cinnamaldehyde dehydrogenase was characterized in Arabidopsis thaliana , |CITS: [14729911]| and shown to possess both coniferyl aldehyde- and sinapyl aldehyde dehydrogenase activity. , This enzymatic activity has been found earlier in bacteria where coniferyl aldehyde was converted to ferulate , |CITS: [9721273]|.

The flavan-3,4-diols and the flavan-3-ols (catechins) are the monomeric building units which constitute the oligo- or polymeric proanthocyanidins forming one of the larger subgroups of flavonoids |CITS:[11402179]|. In the tea plant (Camellia sinensis) catechins are the predominant secondary compounds accounting for 70-80% of the polyphenols. Catechins are classified into galloylated and nongalloylated compounds in which the former often esterify with |FRAME:CPD-183| in the 3-position of the C-ring. The major galloylated catechin is |FRAME:CPD-15291| which amounts to about three-fourths of all catechins detected in tea |CITS:[19140075] [20189205]|. It has been found that catechins and other polyphenols are high in younger leaves and lower in stems and roots which coincides with the gene expression involved in phenylpropanoid and flavonoids pathways and appears to be regulated by both anabolic and catabolic events |CITS:[23646127]|. Moreover, at the subcellular level catechins are mainly detected in the chloroplasts of mesophyll cells and in cell walls of the vessels |CITS:[19831398]|., Catechins and especially |FRAME:CPD-15291| are linked to many health-promoting effects such as antioxidant activity, exhibiting antimutagenic, anticarcenogenic and antibacterial potential as well as being effective agents for body weight control and promising therapeutic properties for Parkinson disease |CITS:[9759559] [20370896]|. It also appears that in this respect galloylated catechins are more effective than nongalloylated catechins |CITS:[16470636]|. In addition, catechins have been considered as effective defence compounds against pathogen or herbivore attacks and as such assume an important ecological function in a plants life |CITS:[15877931]|. , Despite significant efforts to unravel the biosynthetic routes of proanthocyanins some of the underlying mechanism are still unsolved and require further research |CITS:[15720617]|. The finding that |FRAME:CPD-183| was esterified with epigallocatechin and epicatechin to form the galloylated catechins was first shown in tea shoots utilizing radioactive precursors |CITS:[Saijo83]|. However, it was shown later that not |FRAME:CPD-183| was the immediate precursor for galloylated catechin biosynthesis but |FRAME:1-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| (reviewed in |CITS:[16153405]|) which had already been demonstrated for the biosynthesis of hydrolyzable tannins (see |FRAME:PWY-5475|) where the formation of |FRAME:1-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| represents the first committed step of the pathway |CITS:[Gross82] [Gross83]|. , This reaction, the formation of |FRAME:1-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| catalyzed by the gallate 1-β-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[24412325]| is also the first step of the galloylated catechin biosynthesis. The second step of the pathway is carried out by a epicatechin:1-O-galloyl-β-D-glucose O-galloyltransferase which catalyzes the galloylation of |FRAME:CPD-7630| (EC) and |FRAME:CPD-10411| (EGC) to yield |FRAME:CPD-16530| (ECG) and |FRAME:CPD-15291| (EGCG), respectively |CITS:[23132863]|. The formation of |FRAME:CPD-16531| (GCG) which has been detected in processed tea leaves is most likely the result of a temperature dependent epimerization of |FRAME:CPD-15291| occurring during green tea production |CITS:[18361498]| and has not been observed in in vitro experiments |CITS:[23132863]|.

Summary: The degradative pathway of |FRAME:TOLUENE| in |FRAME: ORG-5948| consists of two parts:, an upper pathway that converts toluene and xylene to their carboxylic acid derivatives, (this pathway, and see also |FRAME: PWY-5428| and |FRAME: PWY-5429|),, and a lower pathway that converts the (substituted) benzoic acids to Krebs cycle intermediates, (see |FRAME: PWY-5430|)., In the upper pathway, the methyl side chain of toluene is subjected to several progressive oxidations, to carboxylic acid, followed by an oxygenative cleavage of the aromatic ring., The upper pathway is induced by toluene, xylenes, and their alcohol derivatives. The , lower pathway is induced by benzoic acids, or by upper pathway substrates |CITS: [1176436]|., In |FRAME: ORG-5948|, the TOL plasmid pWW0 encodes all the enzymes responsible for the degradation, of toluene and xylene. The genes encoding these enzymes are organized into two operons,, the upper operon, which contains the first three enzymes in the pathway, and the meta operon,, which contains the genes responsible for the degradation of benzoates and toluates., In addition, some strains have integrated very similar genes in their chromosomes, where they have, aquired little mutation. For example, strains TW3 and 4NT have been shown to , express similar but chromosomally-encoded enzymes which catalyze the same pathway, |CITS: [8357257][8245826][9555884]|.

Summary: Phospholipases hydrolyze phospholipids, and are ubiquitous in all organisms. In plants, at least four types of phospholipases have been reported including phospholipase A1 (PLA1), phospholipase A2 (PLA2), phospholipase C (PLC), and phospholipase D (PLD). PLAs are directly implicated in the removal of unusual fatty acids from phospholipids for their integration into triacylglycerol. PLAs are also involved in plant signal transduction, such as responding to auxin stimulation of growth, pathogen and elicitor (reviewed in |CITS: [15130548]|)., PLCs hydrolyze phosphotidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to inositol 1,4,5-triphosphate and diacylglycerol, and are thus important in secondary messenger pathways |CITS: [11377433]|. Broad physiological activities have been postulated for PLDs, including plant responses to abscisic acid, ethylene, wounding, pathogen elicitation, seed germination, water loss, and nodulation |CITS: [11706190]|., PLA1 and PLA2 specifically hydrolyze the sn-1 and sn-2 acyl ester bond of phospholipids, respectively. In addition to PLA, phospholipase B (PLB) sequentially removes both sn-1 and sn-2 acyl groups of phospholipids.

Summary: |FRAME: CHLORAMPHENICOL Chloramphenicol| is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome. It is active against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, including many multiply drug-resistant strains. Chloramphenicol is produced by several Gram-positive soil actinomycetes, but its biosynthesis has been analyzed mostly in |FRAME: TAX-953739| |CITS: [8688636]|., Early studies of the chloramphenicol biosynthetic pathway suggested that it is derived from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, a common precursor for aromatic primary and secondary metaboiltes, and identified several early intermediates of the pathway such as |FRAME: CPD-13483|. Mutants analysis has shown that the genes encoding |FRAME: CHLORAMPHENICOL| biosynthesis are located in a cluster |CITS: [3464692][3475271]|., Initial analysis identifed 12 genes in the cluster |CITS: [11495989][11577160]|, but subsequent studies revealed additional ones |CITS: [14702400][25267678]|., The main part of the pathway is well understood. The first reaction, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.85|, is not unique to chloramphenicol biosynthesis, as it is also found in |FRAME: PWY-6543|, a primary metabolism pathway leading to |FRAME: PWY-6614|. However, |FRAME: TAX-54571| has two sets of genes that can catalyze it, with the |FRAME: G-58846| gene product dedicated to chloramphenicol biosynthesis |CITS: [11495989]|., The next three reactions, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.67|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.120| and a non-specific aminotransferase, produce |FRAME: CPD-13483| in a pathway that parallels |FRAME: TYRSYN "L-tyrosine biosynthesis"| |CITS: [11577160]|. This intermediate is then adenylated by the |FRAME: MONOMER-20703| and transferred to its peptidyl-carrier domain, where it is β-hydroxylated by |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.65| (|FRAME: G-58850|) |CITS: [20713732]|. Following the hydroxylation, the compound is relased from the NRPS in a reductive reaction, forming free |FRAME: CPD-21795| |CITS: [25564306]|. It is also possible that CmlP releases the product in the form of an aldehyde, which is then reduced by an as-yet unidentified reductase., The next step in the pathway is the least understood. It involves the transfer of a dicholoroacetyl moiety, most likely from |FRAME: CPD-21788|. Several genes involved in the process have been found, including a halogenase (cmlS) and an AMP-ligase (cmlK). Disruption of these genes leads to formation of |FRAME: CPD-21797|, a chloramphenicol analogue in which a propanoyl group replaces the dichloroacetyl substituent. However, the pathway certainly involves additional enzymes that have not been identified yet |CITS: [14702400][20080101]|. The |FRAME: G-58851| gene is proposed to encode the transferase., The last reaction of the pathway is the 6-electron oxidation of the amine group, forming the nitro group found in |FRAME: CHLORAMPHENICOL|. This reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.99.67| (|FRAME: G-58845|). The enzyme, whose active site contains a diiron cluster ligated by three histidine and four glutamate residues, has been studied extensively |CITS: [24347692][25564306][28823151]|., Resistance to |FRAME: CHLORAMPHENICOL| is achieved by acetylation of the 3-hydroxyl group of the antibiotic by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.28| |CITS: [5335032]|. The 3-hydroxyl of the antibiotic is buried in the interface with the ribosome through direct hydrogen bonding as well as van der Waals interactions with the RNA phosphosugar backbone, and thus the acetylation of this group is disruptive of chloramphenico-ribosome binding. This acetylation has also been proposed to be utilized by the producing organisms as a self-resistance mechanism |CITS: [11814778]|.

Summary: Inositol is the generic name for 1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is the physiologically most common stereoisomer and is distributed abundantly (but not universally) throughout the biological system., |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is an essential polyol in eukaryotes, where its phospholipid derivative |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols phosphatidylinositol| (PI) is an important constituent of phospholipid membranes. PI is also cleaved by phospholipase C to generate inositol phosphate (IP) and diacyglycerol, both of which are central cell signalling molecules., A pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| was initially characterized in |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [5905122][5905123][4328832]|, which can grow on |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| as its sole carbon source |CITS: [13129279][13130520]|., The pathway has been subsequently shown to exist in multiple bacterial species, as well as the yeast |FRAME: TAX-54550| |CITS: [4351258]|., More recent studies in |FRAME: TAX-1423| have identified multiple genes required for inositol catabolism. The iol divergon includes the operons iolABCDEFGHIJ and iolRS |CITS: [9226270]|, and the iolT gene |CITS: [11807058]|. Detailed studies in |FRAME: TAX-1423| have uncovered one inconsistency between the pathway in that organism and the one reported from |FRAME: TAX-548|. The third step in the original pathway, the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-1133| to |FRAME: CPD-827|, is carried out in |FRAME: TAX-1423| two steps - a hydrolysis to |FRAME: CPD-15127|, followed by isomerization to |FRAME: CPD-827| |CITS: [18310071]|. However, since the genome of |FRAME: TAX-548| contains a gene homologous to the isomerase (Uniprot ID G0E259), it is possible that the early report was incorrect., This pathway of myo-inositol degradation appears to be important in root nodule colonization and competition in rhizobial symbiotes |CITS: [9802033][11497462][11274120]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (ascorbic acid, vitamin C) is a reducing agent and antioxidant biosynthesized by plants, eukaryotic algae, some bacteria and many, but not all vertebrates.|FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it. These species rely on mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy. |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and animal feed industries. Reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|., In photosynthesizing plants and eukaryotic algae |FRAME: ASCORBATE| has roles in metabolism, electron transport, the cell cycle and responses to pathogens and abiotic stress. When coupled with its redox system, the ascorbate/glutathione cycle, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| can effectively regulate cellular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| levels (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-2261|) |CITS: [18460785]|. Interestingly, |FRAME: TAX-1117| do not possess any of the known enzymes for ascorbate biosynthesis, and minimize photo-oxidative stress using alternative mechanisms, such as peroxiredoxins, catalases and glutathione peroxidases, suggesting that the use of ascorbate evolved after the endosymbiotic acquisition of a cyanobacterial ancestor by a non-photosynthetic eukaryote |CITS: [23109712][25768426]|., Ascorbate Biosynthesis in Plants, Four different pathways for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| have been described in plants., • The first plant pathway was suggested in 1998 by Wheeler et al |CITS: [9620799]|. The pathway starts from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| and proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-Galactopyranose| and |FRAME: CPD-330| (see |FRAME: PWY-882|)., • A second pathway, known as the L-gulose pathway, also starts with |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. However, that pathway proceeds via the key intermediates |FRAME: L-gulopyranose| and |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS:[12954627]| (see |FRAME: PWY4FS-11|)., • A third pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-3747| (strawberry). In that pathway |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is formed from |FRAME: CPD-330|, as in the first pathway. However, the pathway starts from |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE|, and proceeds via |FRAME: CPD0-1083| |CITS:[13363799][12524550]|. Tracer and feeding studies have also shown conversion of |FRAME: CPD-23305| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [Loewus63]|. (see |FRAME: PWY-8143|)., • A fourth pathway suggested that |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| can also be channeled towards the production of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: EC-1.13.99.1|, based on the effect of overexpressing the |FRAME: AT4G26260| gene. According to that proposal, |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is reduced to |FRAME: L-GULONATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| via |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| |CITS: [14976233]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8142|)., About This Pathway, Back in 1953 Isherwood et al described conversion of |FRAME: CPD-23305| to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| in |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [13036892][13126085]|. Radiotracer |CITS: [14466265]| and biochemical evidence |CITS: [13363799]| suggested the enzymatic reduction of derivatives of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| to |FRAME: CPD0-1083| by plant extracts., A 1999 study that looked at the biosynthesis of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| in |FRAME: TAX-3702| by incubation with a range of potential biosynthetic precursors, analogs, and inhibitors confirmed that administration of |FRAME: CPD-23305| to cultured cells substantially increases their |FRAME: ASCORBATE| content |CITS: [10517845]|., Additional evidence for the existence of this pathway came with the demonstration that overexpression of |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.365|, from |FRAME: TAX-3747| (strawberry) in |FRAME: TAX-3702| plants results in increased levels of |FRAME: ASCORBATE| |CITS: [12524550]|., This pathway utilizes sugars provided by the breakdown of cell walls to form |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. The degradation of pectin releases |FRAME: CPD-23305|, which is converted into |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| by methyl esterase. This is supported by the observation that the high |FRAME: ASCORBATE| content found in tomato introgression lines IL124 compared with the parental M82 seems to be due to a higher expression of a pectinesterase and two polygalacturonases |CITS: [20691085]|., This pathway seems to be active mainly during fruit ripening in some species. In tomato, |FRAME: ASCORBATE| synthesis in immature green fruit is enhanced only by the supply of |FRAME: L-Galactose|, whereas in red ripened fruits by feeding with either L-galactose and |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| |CITS: [21984649]|.

General Background, The ripe cones of the hop (|FRAME:TAX-3486|) plant are covered with glandular hairs containing a mixture of essential oil and |FRAME: BITTER-ACIDS "bitter acids"|. These compounds are commercially important. In addition to their great importantce for the beer brewing industry, having a major effect on the final aroma and taste of beer, they also have antimicrobial, antifungal and antifeedant activities |CITS:[mizobuchi85a]|., The bitter acids that are synthesized by the hop fall into two types: the |FRAME: ALPHA-ACIDS "α acids"|, which contain two prenyl side chains, and the |FRAME: BETA-ACIDS "β acids"|, which contain three such chains. The former group is of particular importance for the brewing industry as they are transformed during the brewing process into |FRAME: Iso-Alpha-Bitter-Acids "iso-α bitter acids"|, such as |FRAME:CPD-7116| and |FRAME:CPD-7115|, which contribute to the bitter taste of beer |CITS:[15953717]|., About This Pathway, The pathway described here shows the biosynthesis of the α acid |FRAME: CPD-7106| and the β acid |FRAME: CPD-7110|. The first commited step of the pathway, leading to the formation of the 2-acyl-phloroglucinol derivative |FRAME: 3-METHYL-1-246-TRIHYDROXYPHENYLBUTAN|, is catalyzed by the chalcone synthase-like enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.156|, using |FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA| as the starter molecule. The |FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA| was shown to be derived from |FRAME: ISOVALERATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-20124|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-55017| gene |CITS: [23300257]|., The next steps consist of prenylations catalyzed by two different prenyltransferases |CITS: [22166201][25564559]|. The prenyl moieties are provided by |FRAME: CPD-4211| that predominantly originates from the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY|, although a small fraction has been shown to derive from the |FRAME:PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| |CITS:[10406953]|. Following an initial prenylation at position 4 by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.136|, a second prenylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.137|, adds a second prenyl side chain at position 6. If the same enzyme adds a third prenyl chain at position 6, |FRAME: CPD-7110| is formed. If, instead, a monooxygenation occurs, |FRAME: CPD-7106| is formed. Since the identity of the oxygenase is not known yet, this last step of the pathway is not well understood.

General Background, Pyrimidine nucleotides can be catabolized through three different pathways. The best characterized is the reductive pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6430| and |FRAME: PWY-3982|), in which the pyrimidine nucleotides are reduced to |FRAME:Beta-amino-acids|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. The pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms |CITS:[13428755][13416173][16655478][16656066][10656811]|. The oxidative pathway (this pathway) is only found in a few bacterial species and has not been characterized nearly as well. In it uracil is converted to |FRAME: UREA| and |FRAME: MALONATE| via |FRAME: BARBITURATE| |CITS: [12981104][14955523]|. A third pathway, known as the Rut pathway, was discovered much later in |FRAME: TAX-562| and other bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY0-1471|) |CITS: [16540542]|. That pathway starts by ring opening of the pyrimidine nucleotide, and forms |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| from uracil, with concomitant production of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|., About This Pathway, The oxidative pathway has been studied mostly in the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-36822| and |FRAME: TAX-1833| |CITS: [14955523][13687768][11748240]|, but has also been reported in some other unidentified Gram-positive strains |CITS:[12981104][14927671]| and in |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [Patel87]|. These organisms can use uracil as the sole source of either carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [14927671]| or nitrogen alone |CITS: [Patel87]|., In this pathway pyrimidine bases are first oxidized to barbiturate derivatives by |FRAME: MONOMER-15395|, and those derivatives are further hydrolyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7999| (EC 3.5.2.1) and |FRAME: MONOMER-15397| (EC 3.5.1.95) to |FRAME: UREA| and |FRAME: MALONATE| derivatives., Initial studies of this pathway were carried out with crude enzyme preparations |CITS: [12981104][14955523][14927671]| and predicted the presence of only two enzymes, proposing that barbiturase catalyzes the hydrolysis of barbiturate to malonate and urea.. The third enzyme was discovered only when barbiturase was purified and its reaction carefully characterized |CITS: [11485332]|. It was shown that barbiturase catalyzes the amidohydrolysis of barbituate to |FRAME: CPD-7299|, and another enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15397|, catalyzes the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-7299| to |FRAME: UREA| and |FRAME: MALONATE|., The only enzyme of this pathway that has been purified and characterized biochemically is |FRAME: CPLX-7999|, a zinc amidohydrolase. The gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned |CITS:[11485332][11748240]|, and iIdentical genes have been found in members of the genera |FRAME: TAX-53457|, |FRAME: TAX-1839|, |FRAME: TAX-44260|, |FRAME: TAX-547|, |FRAME: TAX-374| and |FRAME: TAX-1663|, suggesting that the oxidative pathway is probably present in these organisms |CITS: [17555842]|.

General Background, The compound eyes of insects are composed of long hexagonal units called ommatidia. An ommatidium contains a cluster of photoreceptor cells surrounded by support cells and pigment cells. In most insects each ommatidium is innervated by one axon and thus provides the brain with one picture element. The number of ommatidia in the eye ranges from just a handful to around 30,000, depending on the species. , Most of the inner portion of the ommatidium is composed of 6 to 9 long and thin photoreceptor cells (abbreviated "R cells") that contain the visual pigments. The portion of the R cells at the central axis of the ommatidium collectively form a a transparent tube that serves as a light guide, called the rhabdom. In certain flies, the rhabdom has separated into seven independent rhabdomeres. In these organisms each ommatidium contains seven axons leading from it, rather than a single one., Not all photoreceptor cells in insects express the same type of visual pigments. Different versions of |FRAME: Rhodopsins rhodopsins| are known to exist in insects, and three different chromophores have been reported - |FRAME: CPD-881|, |FRAME: CPD-14328| and |FRAME: CPD-14329| |CITS: [8001586][Seki98]|. Most of the insect visual pigments use the (3R)-3-hydroxyretinal enantiomer, but members of the higher Diptera, the |FRAME: TAX-480117|, have been shown to synthesize and use the (3S)-3-hydroxyretinal enantiomer as chromophore |CITS: [Seki98]|., In the case of the house fly, |FRAME: TAX-7370| (3000 ommatidia) or the fruit fly, |FRAME: TAX-7227| (800 ommatidia), each of the ommatidia contains eight photoreceptors, named R1 through R8. The R1-R6 cells contain a blue/green-sensitive rhodopsin Rh1 that confers response to UV light |CITS: [3087059][3617517]|. The R7 and R8 cells express different types of rhodopsin - R7 cells express either Rh3 or Rh4, which are sensitive to UV (345 nm and 375 nm, respectively) |CITS: [2953598][2437266][2952772][1403087]|, while R8 cells express either Rh5 or Rh6, which absorb blue and green light |CITS: [8982159][9165115][9109375][10594055]|. While it is well established that Rh1 rhodopsin is associated with a |FRAME: CPD-14328| chromophore, it is still not known which chromophores are used by the other types. It has been shown that at least in |FRAME: G-15150| mutants, Rh4 rhodopsin binds |FRAME: CPD-14329| |CITS: [16464863]|., This pathway has been defined using a generic form of the chromophore, without defining a specific enantiomer., About This Pathway, The visual cycle of insects is simpler that those found in higher eukaryotes. As a matter of fact, until recently it has been thought that no such cycle exists; however, recent information suggests that a visual cycle does exist in insect eyes |CITS: [20045323]|, Similar to vertebrate rhodopsins, the absorption of a photon at 490 nm by rhodopsin Rh1 causes the bound |FRAME: CPD-14328| chromophore to change its conformation to an all-trans form. However, unlike the unstable vertebrate |FRAME: Metarhodopsins-II metarhodopsin| that hydrolyzes into an opsin and |FRAME: RETINAL|, the Rh1 metarhodopsin is stable. Most of it is converted back to active rhodopsin by absorption of a second photon, this time at 570 nm. This is the reason that until recently it has been thought that insects lack a visual cycle |CITS: [Hardie86][3780740][8446607][8639666]|., However, a visual cycle has been demonstrated for |FRAME: TAX-7227| |CITS: [20045325]|. It has been known for some time that a small proportion of the inactivated rhodopsin molecules are internalized and degraded in a light-dependent manner |CITS: [11086989][11086990][14963491][14769922][16213818]|. This visual cycle enables the flies to regenerate the chromophores of the recycled rhodopsin molecules. Inactivation of enzymes that are involved in the cycle results in progressive light-dependent loss of rhodopsin and retinal degradation |CITS: [20045325][22399771]|., According to this pathway, the all-trans form of the chromophore can be transferred from metarhodopsin to the |FRAME: MONOMER-17367|. The retinal is then reduced to retinol by the |FRAME: G-15147|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17368|, followed by isomerization to a cis conformation, catalyzed by an as-yet unidentified isomerase. Next, the chromophore is oxidized back to retinal by the |FRAME: G-15148|-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-17369|, and transferred back to opsin, forming a fully active rhodopsin |CITS: [22399771]|.

General Background, The predominant circulating pyrimidine in humans is |FRAME: URIDINE| |CITS: [8155674][16769123]|. Among different species, including man, its plasma level is strictly maintained at 3-5 μM, a concentration higher than that of other nucleosides |CITS: [7877593]|., |FRAME: URIDINE Uridine|, produced de novo in the liver and kedney, is circulated to other organs, where it serves as an important precursor of pyrimidine salvage pathways |CITS: [35970][6323418][3966913][8650301][11782482]|., Cells maintain uridine concentration by balancing its input, its salvage, and its catabolism.The main enzyme responsible for uridine catabolism is |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "uridine phosphorylase"|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "Uridine phosphorylase"| breaks down |FRAME: URIDINE| to the free base |FRAME: URACIL| and to |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P|., |FRAME: URACIL Uracil| is catabolized to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| in a process considered to be restricted to the liver (see |FRAME: PWY-3982|) |CITS: [13535735][10354618][16098809]|, while |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P| is converted into |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP), which is used in the salvage synthesis of purine nucleotides |CITS: [6277907][7546322]|., Since the phosphorylase is not capable of cleaving |FRAME: CYTIDINE|, this nucleoside must be deaminated to uridine before it can be used by the cell., While the overall metabolic outcome of this pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: CYTIDINE| to |FRAME: URACIL|, is identical to that achieved by salvage pathways, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6556| and |FRAME: PWY-7195|, this pathway is known to function as a catabolic pathway., Catabolic nucleoside degradation is also found in bacteria. The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| can use both naturally occurring pyrimidine ribonucleosides (|FRAME: CYTIDINE| and |FRAME: URIDINE|) as total sources of carbon and energy. The amino nitrogen of |FRAME: CYTIDINE| (but not the ring-nitrogen of uracil) can serve as a total nitrogen source for |FRAME: TAX-562| over its entire temperature range of growth. At room temperature, the ring nitrogen becomes available as a total nitrogen source via a |FRAME: PWY0-1471 "uracil degradation pathway"| encoded by genes in the rut operon |CITS: [16540542]|. |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P|, after being converted to |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P| by |FRAME: PPENTOMUT-MONOMER|, enters central metabolism through the nonoxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway., Plants and yeast do not have |FRAME: HS00053-MONOMER "uridine phosphorylase"|, and thus can not utilize this pathway.

Polyphosphates are linear polymers containing a few to several hundred residues of orthophosphate linked by energy-rich phosphoanhydride bonds. They occur in representatives of all kingdoms of living organisms., One major role of polyphsphates is as a storage form for phosphate. When phosphate is abundant, organisms can form polyphosphate from ATP by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.1|. When conditions change and posphate becomes limiting, phosphate can be liberated from the polymers with no expenditure of energy by |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.11|., In addition to serving as a phosphorus and energy source, polyphosphates have been shown to be involved in other processes |CITS: [16232585]|, including:,
, • Regulation of the levels of ATP and other nucleotide and nucleoside-containing coenzymes.
, • Participation in the regulation of homeostasis and storage of inorganic cations and other positively charged solutes in an osmotically inert form.
, • Formation of channels across the membrane.
, • Participation in the formation and functions of cell surface structures.
, • Control of gene activity.
, • Regulation of activities of the enzymes and enzyme assemblies involved in the metabolism of nucleic acids and other acid biopolymers, In humans polyphosphates also play a key role in blood coagulation. Produced and released by platelets, they activate |FRAME: Factor-XII "factor XII"|, which is essential for blood clot formation |CITS: [15308650][20005807]|.

|FRAME: CPD-3745 Isethionate| (2-hydroxyethanesulfonate) is found at high concentrations in several terrestrial and, marine environments. Concentration of about 200 mM were measured in red algae |CITS: [Barrow93][15545063]| and the squid giant axon |CITS: [16589435]|. An extremely high concentration of 2M was found in the sticky secretion that covers the silk orb web of an araneoid spider |CITS: [16574806]|. Lower concentrations of |FRAME: CPD-3745| are found in mammalian tissues |CITS: [6291329]| and urine |CITS: [6066118]|., Aerobic and anaerobic respirations and fermentations of isethionate have been reported in bacteria |CITS: [197072][12471498][19933343]|., Kondo et al |CITS: [197072]| isolated an unidentified bacterium that was able to grow on either |FRAME: TAURINE| or |FRAME: CPD-3745|. A cell free extract from this organism oxidized isethionate in two steps; an initial dehydrogenation to, |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| (with the consumption of oxygen), followed by desulfonation, leading to formation of |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: ACET|. , The enzyme responsible for isethionate oxidation, |FRAME: MONOMER-6042| (IDH) was partially purified, and was, found to be particulate in nature, and to require an FAD cofactor. A solubilized preparation obtained by extraction with buffer of low ionic strength had oxidizing activities against isethionate and n-butanol. The enzyme was inhibited by thiol and carbonyl reagents. The solubilized enzyme preparation was unstable, preventing complete purification |CITS: [197072]|. , Isethionate dehydrogenase activity was also demonstrated in |FRAME: ORG-5923|, although that enzyme was not purified. IDH was located in the particulate fraction, oxidized isethionate to sulfoacetaldehyde with cytochrome c as electron acceptor, and correlated with the expression of a 62 kDa protein |CITS: [15073291]|.

Summary: The C15 isoprenoid farnesenes are a group of closely related sesquiterpenoids that occur as α- and β- isomers. , The α-farnesene can exist in four isomeric forms, |FRAME: CPD-8764|, (E,Z), (Z,Z), and , |FRAME: CPD-9338|, of these, the most abundant one is (E,E)-α-farnesene. Summary: General Background, Cell-cell communication in bacteria is accomplished through the exchange of extracellular signalling molecules called autoinducers. This process, termed quorum sensing, allows bacterial populations to coordinate gene expression as a function of cell density. Many processes benefit from community cooperation, including bioluminescence, virulence factor expression, antibiotic production and biofilm development., Autoinducer systems depend on two main components - the autoinducer and its receptor, which also functions as an autoinducer-dependent transcriptional regulator that binds DNA immediately upstream of the genes that are controlled., Autoinducer systems have been implicated in regulation of various systems. For example, |FRAME: G-11135|/luxR of |FRAME: TAX-668| regulate bioluminescence, luxM/luxN of |FRAME: TAX-669| regulate bioluminescence and polyhydroxybutyrate biosynthesis, |FRAME: G-11138|/lasR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates virulence factors, |FRAME: G-11136|/rhlR of |FRAME: TAX-287| regulates rhamnolipid synthesis as well as virulence factors, and |FRAME: G-11137|/TraR of |FRAME: TAX-358| regulates plasmid conjugal transfer |CITS: [8905097]|., Several types of autoinducers are known. Gram-negative bacteria typically use |FRAME: Acyl-homoserine-lactones "acyl-homoserine lactones"|, known as type AI-1, as their autoinducers. The first autoinducer to be discovered was |FRAME: CPD-10780|, an AI-1 type compound from |FRAME: TAX-668| |CITS: [7236614]|. Many variants of AI-1 type inducers exist, differing from each other in the composition of the acyl moiety. Although polymethylated kaempferols have not been found in trichomes of wild and cultivated tomatoes their widespread occurrence in the plant kingdom is well documented |CITS:[11130659]|. Nevertheless, apart from the tomato secretory (type 1/4) and storage (type 6) glands various |FRAME:CPD1F-90| metabolites have been detected in other parts of tomatoes as well |CITS:[16896233]| |CITS:[21343428]|. |FRAME:CPD1F-90 Kaempferol| and its numerous derivatives are present in many edible or medicinal plants being appreciated for their positive impact on long term health in humans due to their valuable pharmacological properties |CITS:[21428901]|. In addition, flavonols such as |FRAME:CPD1F-90| and derivatives play important roles in the biology of plants, for example during various developmental stages (pollen germination) |CITS:[12083465]| |CITS:[10567367]| or in plant defense |CITS:[11314958]|. , This pathway displays the catalytic breadth by which three myricetin ortho-methyltransferases (MOMT's) isolated and characterized from |FRAME:TAX-62890| and |FRAME:TAX-4081| |CITS:[21343428]| |CITS:[22711283]| utilize other substrates than |FRAME:MYRICETIN| (see |FRAME:PWY-7160|), i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-90| catalyzing the formation of polymethylated kaempferols (compare also |FRAME:PWY-7161|). MOMT3 characterized from both |FRAME:TAX-62890| and |FRAME:TAX-4081| was dubbed as 3-methyltransferase. MOMT3 catalyzed the formation of |FRAME:CPD-14950| and |FRAME:CPD-14952| with likewise high efficiency |CITS:[22711283]|. From tissues of |FRAME:TAX-3570| a very specific 4'-O-methyltransferase was characterized which only worked with flavonoids having a sole hydroxyl group in the 4'-position of the B-ring. Consequently |FRAME:CPD1F-90| turned out to be the best substrate for the |FRAME:TAX-3569| 4'-O-methyltransferase which is probably involved in a phytoalexin pathway producing |FRAME:CPD-14960| |CITS:[12899699]|.

Summary: General Background, The major pathway for fatty acid degradation in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans is fatty acid β-oxidation. Mammalian cells contain two β-oxidation systems, one in the mitochondria and one in the peroxisomes (see |FRAME: PWY66-391|) |CITS: [180535]|. Common saturated and unsaturated fatty acids are overwhelmingly metabolized by the mitochondrial system, whereas most other substrates of β-oxidation (e.g. very long-chain fatty acids, dicarboxylic acids, |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins|, hydroxylated 5-β-cholestanoic acids, and |FRAME: PRISTANATE|) are partially degraded in peroxisomes |CITS: [1998729][1892883]|., A major difference between the two systems lies in the structure of the enzymes. In animal mitochondria, after initial metabolism of long chain acyl-CoAs by membrane-bound enzymes, medium and short chain acyl-CoAs are metabolized in the matrix by separate soluble enzymes. In contrast, animal peroxisomes contain multifunctional proteins (MFPs) that catalyze multiple steps of the pathway. Mammals contain two distinct MFPs (|FRAME: HS03720| and |FRAME: HS05792|), which form (S)- and (R)-stereospecific intermediates, respectively (reviewed in |CITS: [17028011][17434787][20558530][20195903]|)., Another difference between the two systems lies in the step that converts |FRAME: ACYL-COA an acyl-CoA| to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA a trans-2-enoyl-CoA|. In mitochondria this reaction is catalyzed by one of the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases (|FRAME: EC-1.3.8.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.7|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.8|, or |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.9|). The electrons removed by the oxidation pass through the respiratory chain to oxygen, generating water as the final product. In peroxisomes this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.6|, where the electrons pass directly to oxygen and produce |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE hydrogen peroxide|, which is immediately cleaved by peroxisomal catalase (reviewed in |CITS: [11755682][17028011][20558530][21683154]|)., In the case of 2-methyl branched fatty acids, initial reports suggested that β-oxidation can take place in either the peroxisome or the mitochondria. For example, it was reported that both peroxisomes and mitochondria efficiently catalyze the β-oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-23622| |CITS: [1837026]|. A sudy of 2-methyl fatty acids β-oxidation by rat liver mitochondria found that medium-chain 2-methyl fatty acids were the best substrates |CITS: [7639525]|. , About This Pathway, Short- and medium-chain fatty acids and fatty acyl-CoAs, including 2-methylated ones, can enter the mitochondria on their own. Long-chain fatty-acyl CoAs enter the mitochondria via the |FRAME: PWY-6111|. Free Short- and medium-chain fatty acids that enter the mitochondria are esterified with CoA by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.2| |CITS: [7639525]|., There are five different acyl-CoA dehydrogenases in the mitochondria, differing by their substrate specificity. However, |FRAME: CPLX-8484| was the only enzyme that showed activity with 2-methylated medium- and long-chain substrates |CITS: [7639525]|. Short-chain substrates are dehydrogenated by |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.5| |CITS: [6874697][2112956]|., The rest of the activities of the β-oxidation cycle on medium- and long-chain substrates (|FRAME: EC-4.2.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.35|, and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.16|) are catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-9531| (TOC) |CITS: [7639525]|., However, the TOC complex is inactive with short-chain substrates. The matrix enoyl-Coa dehydratase (|FRAME: HS05132|) is assumed to catalyze the formation of short-chain enoyl-CoA, as it has been shown to act on metabolites of valproate (see |FRAME: PWY-8182|) |CITS: [1988037]|. A short-chain 3-hydroxy-2-methylacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (|FRAME: HS01071|) has been identified and purified from rat liver |CITS: [7639524]| and later purified from bovine liver |CITS: [12696021]|. The last step of the cycle, the thiolytic cleavage of short-chain 2-methyl-3-oxoacyl-CoAs is catalyzed by the mitochondrial |FRAME: CPLX-7837| (|FRAME: HS09539|) |CITS: [ 7173255]|., Measuring mitochondrial respiration using either 2-methyl fatty acids or straight chain fatty acids as substrates, it was found that the best branched substrate was |FRAME: CPD-23623| (respiration rate was 70% that acheived with decanoate). Short-chain fatty acids such as |FRAME: CPD-7076| were processed, though at a lower rate. Feeding the mitochondria with |FRAME: CPD-23626| resulted in no respiration, indicating that a fatty acid:CoA ligase must act inside the organelle. It was concluded that 2-methyl fatty acids that are activated intra-mitochondrially are effectively degraded by β-oxidation |CITS: [7639525]|.

Names: volatile esters biosynthesis (during fruit ripening) // ethylene-stimulated fruit ester biosynthesis
Summary: The plant hormone ethylene plays an important role in the fruit ripening stages of climacteric fruits. It triggers the formation of complex sets of flavor and aroma volatiles at specific stages of fruit ripening |CITS: [9177311]|. In kiwi fruits, volatile esters are formed by the action of acyltransferases belonging to BAHD (benzyl alcohol-acetyl-, anthocyanin-O-hydroxy-cinnamoyl-, anthranilate-N-hydroxycinnamoyl/benzoyl-, deacetyl-vindoline) superfamily. The BAHD proteins use Coenzyme A (CoA)-thioesters as acyl donors, and one sub group of alcohol acyltransferases produce volatile esters that are associated with fruity aroma. The alcohol acylation of ripening specific acyltransferases was molecularly analyzed |CITS: [21450321]|. , The fruit ester profiles of the kiwifruit cultivars reach peak levels at the soft end of their eating firmness stage |CITS: [9177311]|. Methylsulfanyl alkanoate and benzoate esters are part of the volatile profiles of kiwifruit |CITS: [20189207]|. |FRAME: ETOH| is the major alcohol detected in kiwi cultivars and nearly 50% of volatile esters are ethyl esters. , About this pathway, The changes of volatile profiles in response to ethylene is well researched, and the above pathway documents the volatile ester formation during specific fruit ripening stages. The substrate preferences of several alcohol acyltransferases (AAT) of kiwifruit was analyzed and found to be variable. AT16 possessed benzoyl-CoA:alcohol O-acyltransferase activity and AT9 catalyzed mostly acetyl-CoA- and propanoyl-CoA- alcohol O-acyltransferase activities. Although ethanol is the main alcohol in ripe kiwifruit, AT16 and AT9 were more reactive in vitro with |FRAME: BUTANOL| than with |FRAME: ETOH| |CITS: [21450321]|.

General Background, Polyketide (exclusive of fatty acids) represent a large group of natural products, i.e. secondary metabolites that are widespread in fungi, bacteria and plants |CITS: [BIRCH68]| |CITS: [SCHRODER99]| |CITS: [12946402]|. Polyketides are often involved as intermediates in the formation of a vast variety of secondary metabolites with mixed biosynthetic origin. Polyketide such as chalcone and 6'-deoxychalcone are precursors in the biosynthesis of thousands of biologically important compounds functioning as pigments, anti-pathogens (phytoalexins), UV protectants, signals for the interaction with microorganisms and mediators of fertility |CITS: [10426943]| |CITS: [SCHRODER97]|., The entry enzymes of the biosynthesis of polyketides in plants are the polyketide synthases producing the general backbone of compounds who give rise to a large array of natural products representing an amazing degree of structural diversity. The chalcone synthase (CHS) and stilbene synthase (STS) are the most well-known plant polyketide synthases, however there exists a growing superfamily of related proteins referred to as CHS/STS-type proteins |CITS: [SCHRODER99]|. Depending on the specific polyketide synthase involved very diverse compound classes evolve such as chalcones (|FRAME: PWY1F-FLAVSYN|),stilbenes |CITS: [10426943]|, stilbenecarboxylates |CITS: [12620338]|, benzalacetone |CITS: [12226219]|, pyrone |CITS: [ECKERMANN98]|, C-methylated chalcone |CITS: [SHEN00]| and acridone alkaloids |CITS: [8148006]| |CITS: [7727746]|., The formation of polyketides resembles the biosynthesis of fatty acids but is different in various aspects. In contrast to , fatty acid synthases (FAS) plant polyketide synthases (PKS) are relatively small homodimeric enzymes, which do not use , the acyl carrier protein (ACP) as activating agent but utilize acyl-CoA esters directly as substrates |CITS: [SHEN00]| , |CITS: [BIRCH68]|. Although the synthesis of chalcone usually does not involve modifications by other proteins the chalcone derivatives reduced at a specific position in the synthesized aromatic ring are frequently found in plants increasing the structural variability of derivatives |CITS: [SCHRODER97]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-11557 Aloenin| is a bitter glucoside isolated from the plant |FRAME: TAX-45385| that was reported to have an inhibitory activity for the gastric juice secretion of rats |CITS: [Suga72]|, on n rat mast cell degranulation |CITS: [Nakagomi87]|, and on on carrageenan-induced rat-paw inflammatory edema |CITS: [Yamamoto91]|. It was also shown to have potent peroxyl radical-scavenging activities and moderate inhibitory active on β-secretase |CITS: [17184120]|., |FRAME: CPD-11557 Aloenin| is a hexaketide, and its skeleton is formed by a polyketide synthase |CITS: [19348024]|. Cyclization of the initial polyketide skeleton forms a 2-pyrone structure. Biosynthesis continues with O-methylation of the cyclized intermediate and attachment of a glucose molecule |CITS: [Takayuki78]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, A limited number of species of Gram-negative bacteria, all in the family |FRAME: TAX-543|, utilize unusual sugars, derivatives of 3,6-dideoxyhexose, as |FRAME: O-Antigens| of their lipopolysaccharides. These sugars are the dominant antigenic determinants in the membranes of these organisms., Out of the eight possible stereoisomers of 3,6-dideoxyhexoses, only five have been identified in nature. These are |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: CPD-9396|, |FRAME: L-Colitose|, |FRAME: CPD-9399| and |FRAME: CPD-9395|. All five 3,6-dideoxyhexoses have been found in different serovars of |FRAME: TAX-633|, while other genera possess only some of them. For example, |FRAME: TAX-90371| group B contains |FRAME: CPD-9394|, type A contains |FRAME: CPD-9399| and type D contains |FRAME: CPD-9395| |CITS: [8071227]|., These sugars are synthesized via a complex series of enzymatic reactions starting, in most cases, from |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE|, derived from |FRAME: GLC-1-P| (for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9391|, see |FRAME: PWY-5740|)., In a reaction catalyzed by the NAD+-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7584|, |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-658|, which is then converted to the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-1078| in two consecutive enzymatic reactions, mediated by two components of the |FRAME: CPLX-7585| enzyme complex. The first component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13781| (E1), a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| (PMP)-linked iron-sulfur-containing catalyst, while the second, component is |FRAME: MONOMER-13782| (E3), a [2Fe-2S]-containing flavoprotein., The product of this complex, |FRAME: CPD-1078|, is the parent to four different 3,6-dideoxyhexoses., |FRAME:CPD-9701| is produced by the successive action of two enzymes: |FRAME:MONOMER-13784| inverts the configuration at C-5, while |FRAME: MONOMER-13785| catalyzes stereospecific reduction at C-4, yielding CDP-ascarylose |CITS: [Thorson93]|., |FRAME: CDP-ABEQUOSE| and |FRAME: CDP-36-DIDEOXY-D-MANNOSE| are both created in a single step, catalyzed by the related enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13793| and |FRAME: CPLX-7587|, both of which transfer 2 electrons from NAD(P)H to the keto group of |FRAME: CPD-1078|, but differ in the formation of the resulting product |CITS:[2793832][9538012]|., |FRAME: CPD-9698| is produced from |FRAME: CDP-36-DIDEOXY-D-MANNOSE| in a single reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-13795| |CITS: [2793833]|.

Names: wax esters biosynthesis I // jojoba wax biosynthesis // liquid seed wax biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Wax esters are composed of aliphatic alcohols and acids that have been condensed to form an ester bond. Both the fatty acid and alcohol components usually comprise medium- to long-chain (C12—C18) or very-long-chain (C20 and longer) carbon chains. The wax esters have diverse biological functions in bacteria, insects, mammals, and terrestrial plants and are also important substrates for a variety of industrial applications. , In plants, wax esters are mostly found in the cuticles coating the primary shoot surfaces, but they also accumulate to high concentrations in the seed oils of a few plant species, including jojoba (|FRAME: TAX-3999|), a desert shrub that is the major commercial source of these compounds. , Jojoba seeds contain wax composed of esters of long-chain fatty acids (18:1, 20:1, 22:1) and long-chain alcohols |CITS: [10712527]|. The waxes are produced in developing embryos during seed formation. The commercial interest in cultivating this plant for industrial and pharmaceutical use of its wax has lead to the identification of the biosynthetic pathways and some genes have been cloned. Transgenic technology has enabled the engineering of these genes into other plants with promising results. Several U.S patents exists for the enzymes of this pathway, given their potential use in industry |CITS: [8742713]|., About This Pathway, The pathway is carried forward by an |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.84| (FAR) and |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.75| (WS). FAR carries out the reduction of fatty acyl-CoA to a fatty alcohol by a four-electron transfer |CITS: [10712526]|. The reaction proceeds through an aldehyde intermediate that is not released from the active site., Co-expression of the enzyme complement of jojoba KCS, FAR and WS in transgenic Arabidopsis plants resulted in the production of large amounts of wax in the seeds |CITS: [LASSNER99]|.

Galena (PbS) is the most abundant of the lead minerals and can be found in a variety of environments. Galena is most commonly found in lead sulfide veins, scattered in igneous and sedimentary rocks. It is often found in association with silver minerals, and is commonly present in lead and silver mines. Kingma and Silver |CITS: [KINGMA80]| have shown that when iron-oxidizing bacteria, |FRAME:TAX-920|, grew in a solution containing insoluble galena, 20.2 g of lead were converted into the lead sulfate, anglesite., Bang et al |CITS: [BANG95]| argue that the growth of |FRAME: TAX-920|, in the presence of galena, can cause both direct bacterial and indirect chemical leaching of lead. However, they suggest an active involvement of metabolic enzymes in the oxidation., Drobner et al |CITS: [1510552]| have isolated a novel strain called |FRAME: TAX-171865|, an aerobic, rod-shaped, mesophilic, chemolithoautotrophic bacteria, which oxidizes galena for growth, forming anglesite (PbSO<sub>4</sub>).  , It can also oxidize H<SUB>2</SUB>S and H<SUB>2</SUB>, but unlike |FRAME: TAX-920| it does not oxidize ferrous iron.  |FRAME: TAX-171865| is not closely related to other |FRAME:TAX-919| strains (such as |FRAME: TAX-920|,|FRAME: TAX-364030|) as shown by DNA-DNA hybridization.  This strain contains ubiquinone 8 (CoQ<sub>8</sub>) as its main quinone, and is more resitant against ions of cadmium and molybdenum as compared to |FRAME: TAX-920|.   , Despite these early observations, there is currently little knowledge about the oxidation of galena, and no information is available about specific enzymes involved in this process., It should be noted that the reverse of this pathway, the biological reduction of anglesite to galena, has also been described |CITS: [12153311]|.

Summary: General Background, Androgens are steroid hormones that stimulate or control the development and maintenance of male characteristics in vertebrates, including the activity of the accessory male sex organs and development of male secondary sex characteristics, by binding to androgen receptors. Androgens are also produced by females, and are the precursors to estrogens. Present in lower concentrations than in males, androgens contribute to libido and sexual arousal in females., Important androgens include |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, |FRAME: 17-BETA-HYDROXY-5ALPHA-ANDROSTAN-3-O| (DHT) and |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE androstenedione|. |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE Testosterone| is the major androgen in adult males, while DHT plays a crucial role in utero, causing differentiation of the penis, scrotum and prostate. In adulthood DHT contributes to balding, prostate growth, and sebaceous gland activity. Unlike |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, which is synthesized mainly in the testes (but also in ovary and the adrenal glands), DHT is synthesized within target cells, such as in the prostate or skin., 11-oxygenated C19 steroids (11-oxyandrogens) have been long identified and recognized as major androgens in teleost fishes. Much more recently it has been discovered that they are also produced in humans, and play an important role in several disorders such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and premature adrenarche |CITS: [29742491]|., About This Pathway, This pathway starts with the conversion of the inactive C21 steroid hormone precursor |FRAME: PREGNENOLONE| to the androgens |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE androstenedione| and |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE|, as also described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY66-378|., The synthesis of all 11-oxyandrogens relies on the adrenal enzyme cytochrome P450 |FRAME: HS08547-MONOMER| (|FRAME: HS08547|).
