Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for O antigen synthesis are often present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The LPS of |FRAME: TAX-234| shows very low endotoxicity, indicating poor detection by innate immunity. It is considered one of the virulence factors that allow the pathogen to escape early detection by the host immune system |CITS: [15694858][17637846]|. In 1932, Wilson and Miles proposed the presence of two different O antigens in |FRAME: TAX-234| species, which they named A and M |CITS: [Wilson32]|. It was suggested that the A form is found in |FRAME: TAX-235|, while the M form is found in |FRAME: TAX-29459| |CITS: [3300712]|, but it is now known that some strains (that belong to the A+M+ serotype) can produce a lipopolysaccharide that contains both epitopes |CITS: [ 2457599][ 2479655][9125584][9801349]|., The |FRAME: TAX-234| O antigens consist of an unbranched linear homopolyrner of |FRAME: CPD-24443 "N-formyl-perosaminyl"| (Rha4NFo) residues |CITS: [3300712]| that is attached at the reducing end to (Man)2-N-acetyl-D-quinovosaminyl chain, which is in turn attached to a lipid anchor (an undercaprenyl diphopsphate during biosynthesis, and lipid A in the mature lipopolysaccharide). The A form consists predominantly of α[1→2]-linked Rha4NFo monomers, while in the M form every fifth residue is linked in α[1→3] linkage |CITS: [3111502][3442684][3582676]|., The presence of a repeating pentasaccharide in the M-form antigen has led to the suggestion that this polymer is synthesized by the assembly of preformed oligosaccharide repeating units |CITS: [3442684]|. However, sequencing of the wbk O antigen gene cluster in |FRAME: TAX-29459| showed that it contains |FRAME: BAB_RS18520| and |FRAME: BAB_RS18515| genes, which are typical to the ABC-type biosynthetic pathway, in which the O antigen is synthesized to completion in the cytoplasm and then exported to the periplasm via an ABC-type transporter |CITS: [11081580]|., Most of the genes involved in LPS biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-234| are clustered in the wbk and wbo genetic regions. Wbk is the major genetic region and contains genes encoding for enzymes necessary for |FRAME: N-formyl-D-perosamine| synthesis (|FRAME: BAB_RS18530|, |FRAME: BAB_RS18525|, and |FRAME: G-107455|), two O antigen glycosyltransferases (wbkA and wbkE), an ABC transporter (|FRAME: BAB_RS18520| and |FRAME: BAB_RS18515|), a polyisoprenyl-phosphate N-acetylhexosamine-1-phosphate transferase (|FRAME: BAB_RS18470|) and at least one enzyme necessary for the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-15647| (|FRAME: BAB_RS18465|) |CITS: [11081580][19439075]|. The wbo region contains the wboA and wboB genes, which encode glycosyltransferases involved in O antigen biosynthesis |CITS: [18648644]|.

Although |FRAME:CPD-14493| did not accumulate in the leaf epidermis of Catharanthus roseus its 28-monooxygenase (CYP716AL1) was shown in in vitro and in vivo experiments through co-expression with the lupeol synthase from Arabidopsis in yeast to catalyze the stepwise oxidation of |FRAME:CPD-90| to yield |FRAME:CPD-14493| |CITS: [22837051]|. , Besides the multifunctional |FRAME:TAX-3877| lupeol 28-oxidase another cytochrome P450-dependent oxidase (CYP716A15) has been identified in |FRAME:TAX-29760| through coexpression analysis and shown to catalyze the same series of oxidations on C-28 of the lupeol core structure to form |FRAME:CPD-14493| |CITS:[22039103]|. Such multifunctional cytochrome P450's functionalizing substrate backbones with a series of oxidative steps have also been reported in the formation of another triterpenoid, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14483| (see |FRAME:PWY-7066|) where β-amyrin 11-oxidase (CYP88D6) and 11-oxo-β-amyrin 30-oxidase (CYP72A154) have been shown to carry out a sequential two (on C-11) and three-step substrate oxidation (on C-30), respectively |CITS:[18779566]| |CITS:[22128119]|.

Summary: Diamondoids are a series of saturated hydrocarbons whose structure can be superimposed on the diamond lattice. The simplest of the diamondoids is adamantane (from the Greek word for diamond), a tricyclic C10H16 isomer. Adamantane was first discovered and isolated from a Czechoslovakian petroleum in 1933. The unique structure of adamantane is reflected in its highly unusual physical and chemical properties. The carbon skeleton of adamantane comprises a small cage structure. Because of this, adamantane and diamondoids in general are commonly known as cage hydrocarbons., |FRAME: CPD-743 Adamantanone| is a derivative of adamantane (a 2 hydroxy-adamantane)., While no organism has been shown today to be able to grow on adamantane derivatives as a sole carbon source, |FRAME:TAX-303| ATCC 17453 (CAM) cells, which carry the camphor degradative plasmid CAM, are able to break down adamantane and |FRAME: CPD-743| after the camphor degradation enzymes have been induced by growing on camphor., |FRAME:TAX-303| ATCC 17453 can oxidize |FRAME: CPD-743| via two routes, utilizing two of the camphor degradation enzymes. The two routes differ only in the order of action of the two enzymes. The resulting product from both routes is, |FRAME: CPD-746|, which accumulates in the cells. Since |FRAME: CPD-746| is not broken any further, the adamantanone pathway represents only a partial oxidation pathway |CITS: [6696444][1510672][3944058][4288652][672627]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13962 Daunorubicin| is |FRAME: Anthracyclines| antibiotic produced by some strains of |FRAME: TAX-1950| and other streptomycetes. This group of antibiotics is defined by the presence of a four fused-ring aromatic system, based on a 7,8,9,10-tetrahydro-5,12-naphthacenequinone framework, which usually occurs as a glycoside with a deoxy(amino)sugar |CITS: [11851469]|., The anthracyclines intercalate between base pairs of the DNA/RNA strand, inhibit topoisomerase II enzymes, and prevent DNA replication. They are among the most effective anticancer treatments ever developed and are effective against more types of cancer than any other class of chemotherapeutic agents., |FRAME: CPD-13962 Daunorubicin| was discovered in the 1960s |CITS: [14142092]|, and was widely used as as antitumor drug. However, by 1967 it was recognized that it could produce fatal cardiac toxicity, and today synthetic analogs of the natural antibiotic are used., About This Pathway, The polyketide framework of |FRAME: CPD-13962| is made from |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| as the starter unit and nine |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender units while bound to an acyl-carrier protein which is part of the |FRAME: CPLX-8735| |CITS: [7828855][7928998]|. Following condensation of these units, a reductase and an aromatase modify the structure to form |FRAME: CPD-15771|, which is then hydroxylated to form |FRAME: CPD-15738|, the first free and stable intermediate. Further modifications, including O-methylation, formation of a fourth ring, and a reduction, result in formation of |FRAME: CPD-15720|, an intermediate that is common in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-13962 | and |FRAME: Aclacinomycins aclacinomycins| |CITS:[8360627][7836284][8655529]|., Hydroxylation at position C11 generates |FRAME: CPD-13972| |CITS: [7961477]|, which is glycosylated with the unusual deoxyaminosugar |FRAME: CPD-13971| |CITS: [7592454][10631513]|, forming |FRAME: CPD-15730|. The next modification is the removal of the methoxycarboxylate moiety, which occurs in two steps: first, a methylesterase removes the methoxy group, and next the carboxylate group is eliminated (it is still not known if the latter occurs spontaneously or enzymatically) |CITS: [9098063]|. A second methyltransferase converts the product to |FRAME: CPD-15733| |CITS: [8509343][9098063]|. The last enzyme of the pathway is a hydroxylase (DoxA) that catalyzes a hydroxylation of the C13 carbon, followed by oxidation of the hydroxyl group to a keto group, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-13962|., There exists the possibility of a split in the last part of the pathway with the reaction sequence of 13-hydroxylating |FRAME:CPD-15732| and the following ketolation at the same position of |FRAME:CPD-15736| to produce |FRAME:CPD-15734| by the |FRAME:G-17683| encoded cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. The latter compound is being considered a natural substrate for the subsequent C-4 methoxylation by the |FRAME:G-17684| encoded 4-O-methyltransferase forming |FRAME:CPD-13962| |CITS:[15273252]|. It seems noteworthy to mention that current kinetic data favor a flux via the 4-methoxy pathway over the 4-hydroxy side step pathway, i.e. methylation of the C-4 position occurs prior to hydroxylation/ketolation at C-13 (Walczak). Nevertheless, the rather broad substrate specificity of |FRAME:G-17683| and |FRAME:G-17684| encoded enzymes enable also this loop in the pathway and requires further elucidation |CITS: [9098063] [9864343] [15273252]|., Only in the strain |FRAME: TAX-55158| DoxA catalyzes one additional hydroxylation of the C14 carbon, converting |FRAME: CPD-13962| to |FRAME: CPD-13973| (see |FRAME: PWY-7355|) |CITS: [11851469]|.

Background, There is growing need to find renewable biologically produced compounds as replacements for petroleum-based fuels. Due to the branched and ringed structures found in their hydrocarbon chain, isoprenoid compounds have the potential to be used as biofuels. The branching improves the cetane number (a measurement of the combustion quality) of fuel mixtures |CITS: [MURLEY]|. The C15 isoprenoid compound farnesol is a putative biodiesel with a cetane number that falls withing the expected range for petroleum diesel., Biodiesel has both disadvantages and advantages compared to petroleum diesel. The disadvantages include biodiesel having poorer cold weather characteristics, producing higher nitrous oxide emissions and a greater ability to oxidize. The advantages include biodiesel being derived from a renewable source, having a lower sulfur content and hence lower oxidized sulfur emissions, increased lubricity and lower carbon monoxide emissions., Isoprenoid compounds are derived from isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and dimethyl alleyl diphosphate (DMAPP). These two compounds can be derived from two distinct pathways: the |FRAME: PWY-922| (MVA) and the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (MEP), also known as deoxyxylulose pathway. The MVA pathway is more energetically favorable than the MEP pathway as it generates protons which can be used to generate ATP, and does not require an input of ATP per se |CITS: [Murley]|., About this Pathway, |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP "Isopentenyl diphosphate| (IPP) and |FRAME: CPD-4211| (DMAPP) are both derived from either the MVA or MEP pathways |CITS: [18303110]|. These compounds are precursors to E,E farnesyl diphosphate, an intermediate in the putative biodiesel farnesol biosynthesis |CITS: [16484724]|. , A soluble form of phosphatase capable of converting farnesyl diphosphate (FPP) to E,E-farnesol was identified in |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS: [16484724]|. The purified FPP phosphatase is a truncated form of alkaline phosphatase |CITS: [16484724]|., FPP can also be converted to farnesane, another valuable diesel fuel, but this does not occur naturally in a biological system.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ergothioneine Ergothioneine| (EGT) is a histidine derivative with a thiol group attached to the C2 atom of the imidazole ring and a trimethylated amine. EGT was initially isolated in 1909 by Tanret from |FRAME: TAX-5111| (ergot), the fungal infection of rye grain |CITS: [Tanret09]|, and its structure was determined within two years |CITS: [Barger11]|. It has been reported only from certain fungi, actinomycetales bacteria and cyanobacteria |CITS: [13376573][13405916][Pfeiffer11]|. The function of EGT in the microbial cells is not well understood, even though it is believed that EGT may protect cells from oxidative stress |CITS: [Garay56][2172707][22001064]|., The most significant difference between EGT and other biological thiols is the instability of the EGT disulfide under physiological conditions. Unlike other small thiols such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, EGT is stable in its reduced form in aerated aqueous solutions and does not form the disulfide |CITS: [15730267]|. Another significant difference is that EGT exists predominantly as the |FRAME: Ergothioneine-Thione "thione form"| at physiological pH |CITS: [22001064]|., Although EGT is not synthesized by non-fungal eukaryotes, animals and plants acquire EGT from the environment through a specific transporter, ETT/OCTN1 |CITS: [15795384]|. It has been shown that the human body absorbs it from dietary sources and concentrates it in specific tissues or cells such as liver, kidney, central nervous system, and red blood cells |CITS: [2172707]|. Both hyperactivity and deficiency of the OCTN1 transporter exert negative effects on human cells |CITS: [15795384][19136526]|. The precise function of ergothioneine in human tissue is also uncertain |CITS: [17616140]|., About This Pathway, Early studies of the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Ergothioneine|, carried out with cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-5141|, demonstrated that it generated from |FRAME: HIS|, |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME:MET|, and the presence of several intermediates, namely |FRAME: CPD-15280| and |FRAME: CPD-15277| |CITS: [5484456][4276459]|., Additional work revealed a gene cluster responsible for |FRAME: Ergothioneine| biosynthesis in the genomes of mycobacteria |CITS: [20420449]|. In mycobacteria 5 enzymatic steps are involved, catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-15982| |CITS: [16262797]|, |FRAME: G-15978|, |FRAME: G-15979|, |FRAME: G-15980| and |FRAME: G-15981| genes |CITS: [20420449]|. The genes were cloned from |FRAME: TAX-1772| and were all purified and used for in vitro characterization |CITS: [20420449][26149121]|. The genes have also been identified in |FRAME: TAX-83332| and egtD has been characterized from that organism as well |CITS: [26229105]|., Analysis of the distribution of |FRAME: G-15979| and |FRAME: G-15978| suggests that ergothioneine biosynthesis is a common trait among actinobacteria, cyanobacteria, pezizomycotina, and basidiomycota, and also occurs in numerous bacteroidetes and α-, β-, γ- and δ-proteobacteria. This wide distribution suggests that ergothioneine may have fundamental physiological importance |CITS: [20420449]|., In fungi the EgtB and EgtD homologs are fused into a single protein |CITS: [22209968]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7550|).

Summary: General Background, Anthocyanins are produced in two distinguished sets of reactions, the first , one (early-stage) leading to the first stable anthocyanidin, i.e. anthocyanidin-3-O-glucosides (|FRAME:PWY-5125|) , and the second one (late-stage) comprising further modification of those compounds such as glycosylation, acylation , and methylation (this pathway). These late-stage reactions are concerned with fine adjustment for a variety of floral , color which is diverse and less understood than the steps involved in the early-stage reactions |CITS: [10066805]| |CITS: [10845463]|., The decoration of pelargonidin (this pathway) is typical for a variety of plants such as |FRAME:TAX-48386|, , |FRAME:TAX-76714|,|FRAME:TAX-39879| |CITS: [10066805]| and |FRAME:TAX-101596| |CITS: [12481098]|. , Many of the above mentioned plants are characterized by anthocyanins that are intermediately 5-O-glucosylated. , About This Pathway, All the modifications of the anthocyanidin-3-O-glucosides contribute to the stability , of the anthocyanins and/or the refinement of the colors which appear in flowers and fruits. The 5-O-glucosylation , of anthocyanidin-3-O-glucosides, catalyzed by the anthocyanin 5-O-glucosyltransferase (5-GT) does not significantly , change the color of anthocyanins but is important for further modification of anthocyanin molecules |CITS: [11905966]| , |CITS: [10066805]|. It has been discussed that these modifications increase the stability and color variation towards , purple hues by inter- and intramolecular stacking of the anthocyanins with polyphenols |CITS: [BROUILLARD94]|., A significant contribution to intensification of color and color shift towards blue is accomplished by aromatic , acylation with hydroxycinnamic acids of the anthocyanin molecules due to a bathochromic shift. The enzyme , catalyzing this step, anthocyanin 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-acyltransferase has been characterized in |FRAME:TAX-48386| , |CITS: [FUJIWARA98]| |CITS: [10845463]|. The exact metabolic succession of aromatic acylation (C-ring 3-position, , A-ring 5-position) of the anthocyanin glucosides (mono-, diglucoside) is not known and may depend on the species involved , (compare |FRAME:PWY-5268| and |FRAME:PWY-5307|)., The other type of acylation that commonly contributes to furnish anthocyanins and many other secondary metabolites, , i.e. aliphatic acylation, such as malonylation is thought to enhance pigment solubility in water, protect the anthocyanins , from enzymatic degradation and facilitates the uptake of anthocyanins into vacuoles |CITS: [Heller94]|. The malonylation , of anthocyanins, for instance catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-malonyltransferase |CITS: [12481098]| , generally occurs under strict regiocontrol during the late stage of their biosynthesis., Other modifications of the anthocyanins involve further glycosylations catalyzed by anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-rhamnosyltransferase , |CITS: [KAMSTEEG80]| and anthocyanidin 3-O-rutinoside-5-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS: [751641]|. Rhamnosylation , appears to be a frequent step altering the structure of compounds and the nucleoside has been shown to be produced , in plants, e.g. in red campion |CITS: [680134]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Pyrethrins Pyrethrins| are natural insecticides extracted from the seed cases of |FRAME: TAX-118510|, and are considered the most important natural pesticides economically., The chemical structure of pyrethrins inspired the production of a variety of synthetic insecticides called |FRAME: Pyrethroids pyrethroids|, such as |FRAME: CPD-22549|, |FRAME: CPD-22550|, and |FRAME: CPD-22551|. Pyrethrins are more environmentally friendly, less toxic, and less stable than the synthetic commercial pyrethroids, which are toxic to fish and other non-target organisms |CITS: [Haya89]|., |FRAME: CPD-13655 "Pyrethrin I"| is an ester with a chrysanthemoyl (an acid bearing a cyclopropane ring) moiety and a pyrethrolone (alcohol) moiety. |FRAME: CPD-14456 "Pyrethrin II"| is closely related, but one of its methyl groups is oxidized to a carboxymethyl group., About This Pathway, The first dedicated step in the pathway is an intermolecular cyclopropanation reaction of two |FRAME: CPD-4211| molecules, linked in head-to-middle linkage, to form |FRAME: CPD-9445| |CITS: [11287653]|. The enzyme responsible for this step, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-14698| gene, is bifunctional and also catalyzes the dephosphorylation of the product, forming |FRAME: CPD-22540| |CITS: [25378387]|. In seedlings, radio tracer evidence supports a non-mevalonate origin of the |FRAME: CPD-4211| |CITS: [15964038]|, whereas in flowers it is likely derived from mevalonate |CITS: [13882441]|. Two oxidoreductases, encoded by |FRAME: G-80477| and |FRAME: G-80478|, catalyze sequential oxidation reactions to |FRAME: CPD-22541| and |FRAME: CPD-13662|, respectively |CITS: [29122986]|. The acid is then activated by a CoA ligase to form |FRAME: CPD-14450|., The |FRAME: CPD-13661| moiety is most likely formed from linolenate via the oxylipin pathway, which also gives rise to the plant hormone |FRAME: CPD-734|. However, most of the steps leading to pyrethrolone biosynthesis are still unknown |CITS: [15964038]|., The final event is the transfer of the chrysanthemoyl group from the CoA-thioester to |FRAME: CPD-13661|. The reaction is catalyzed by a GDSL lipase-like protein encoded by the |FRAME: G-15211| gene |CITS: [22385412]|.

General Background, The biosynthesis of phytoalexins is one of the major defensive systems of higher plants. Capsidiol is the major phytoalexin produced by inoculation of green pepper and tobacco with pathogenic fungi. Capsidiol is a bicyclic dihydroxylated sesquiterpene which prevents the germination and growth of several fungal species., Key note on the enzymes: Capsidiol biosynthesis is regulated by the expression of two key enzymes: 5-epi-aristolochene synthase (EAS) catalyses the cyclisation of farnesyl diphosphate to the bicyclic intermediate 5-epi-aristolochene and is responsible for the diversion of farnesyl diphosphate from the mevalonate pathway toward antimicrobial compound biosynthesis. The regio- and stereospecific hydroxylation of 5-epi-aristolochene at positions C-1 and C-3 to capsidiol is mediated by the 5-epi-aristolochene dihydroxylase (EAH) |CITS: [11556809]|. Investigation of the intermediate monohydroxylated compounds suggest that the preferred order of hydroxylation by EAH is C-1 followed by C-3 |CITS: [15522862]|.

General Background, Bacteria often accumulates choline, since it can easily be converted to glycine betaine, a common osmoprotectant, in bacteria |CITS: [LeRudulier84]|., Many organisms can also catabolize glycine betaine, and can thus use choline as a sole source for both carbon, and nitrogen |CITS: [3290197] [6406829]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3661|)., While the conversion of choline to glycine betaine for the purpose of accumulating the latter as an osmoprotectant is, considered biosynthetic (see |FRAME:BETSYN-PWY|, |FRAME:PWY-3722|, and |FRAME:PWY1F-353|), , the conversion of choline to glycine betaine for the purpose of further catabolism should be considered as a choline, degradation pathway. Two such pathways have been demonstrated: Certain Gram-negative bacteria, such as Synrhizobium meliloti degrade choline to glycine betaine using a combination of two different dehydrogenases, (see |FRAME:CHOLINE-BETAINE-ANA-PWY|), while certain Gram-positive bacteria, as well as certain fungi, achieve, this by the activity of a single enzyme, choline oxidase (this pathway)., About This Pathway, The choline ester choline-O-sulfate is widespread in nature and plays an important role in the microbial, transformation of sulfur in the soil |CITS: [8318261]|. It is synthesized by a variety of plants, lichens, algae, fungi,, and by several bacterial species in a reaction catalyzed by sulfur transferases that use, 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate (PAPS) and choline as their substrates |CITS: [14399663][871964], [12232402]|., Choline-O-sulfate serves in the detoxification of sulfate. In addition, it has been identified as a potent, osmoprotectant in several bacterial species and the osmotolerant and xerotolerant fungus Penicillium, fellutanum |CITS: [7814329][Hanson91][8278383][9925583]|. , Choline-O-sulfate has been shown to accumulated as an osmolyte in some bacteria (such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, and B. subtilis) that have been subjected to an osmotic stress. However, these bacteria are not able to, catabolize this compound (neither can they catabolize glycine betaine) |CITS: [Hanson91][9925583]|. , Unlike these organisms, some bacteria, such as Synrhizobium meliloti and |FRAME:TAX-287|, , can degrade choline-O-sulfate to choline, which is , then converted to glycine betaine and catabolized further into ammonia and pyruvate. The key enzyme for this, process is choline sulfatase, encoded by the betC gene |CITS: [4196744][9736747]|., As a result, these organisms can utilize choline sulfate as the sole carbon, nitrogen and sulfur source for growth, |CITS: [9736747][9141699]|.

Summary: The cleavage of the s-triazine ring is an important step in the mineralization and complete removal of s-triazine compounds from the environment. Several pathways for the degradation of s-triazines (such as |FRAME: ATRAZINE|, |FRAME: CPD-7398| and |FRAME: CPD-7403|) converge at |FRAME:CYANURIC-ACID| |CITS: [6762212][6477516]|, which can be used as the sole source of nitrogen by bacteria and fungi |CITS: [Cook81]|., |FRAME:CYANURIC-ACID Cyanuric acid| degradation starts with a ring-cleaving hydrolysis by |FRAME: EC-3.5.2.15| (AtzD), which forms |FRAME: CPD-21687|. In the |FRAME: PWY-8025 "canonical cyanurate degradation pathway"| the product of |FRAME: CYANURIC-ACID| ring fission, |FRAME: CPD-21687|, is acted on by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.131|, a protein complex encoded by the |FRAME: G-10309| and |FRAME: G-58806| genes. However, some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-216596|, do not possess that enzyme. Instead, these organisms utilize |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.84|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58807| gene |CITS: [16640791][21897878]|., |FRAME: CPD-21687| is unstable, and in the absence of |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.131|, it decarboxylates spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-809|. In two successive hydrolyzation steps, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.84|, and |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.54|, |FRAME: CPD-809| is degraded to |FRAME: CARBAMATE|, which decoposes spontaneously to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|.

|FRAME: CPD-22651 "Roxarsone"| is an aromatic arsenical that was first synthesized in 1923. It has been used commercially since 1944 for prevention of coccidiosis in chickens and other farm animals. In 2010 nearly 90% of all broiler chickens in the U.S. were estimated to be treated with roxarsone |CITS: [27735790]|. Roxarsone is excreted from chickens as a mixture of unaltered and partially metabolized species. When the chicken litter is used as a fertilizer or moved into landfills, roxarsone and its metabolites are broken down to inorganic arsenic, and the resulting inorganic |FRAME: ARSENATE| and |FRAME: CPD-763| can be taken up by crop plants or enter the groundwater. In the U.S roxarsone production ceased in 2011. However, it is still produced and used in other countries., |FRAME: CPD-22651 "Roxarsone V"|, the pentavalent form of the compound, is not toxic to bacteria, but the reduced trivalent species |FRAME: CPD-22656| is highly toxic |CITS: [24359149]|. An enzyme that can oxidize |FRAME: CPD-22656| to |FRAME: CPD-22651| was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-160488|. The enzyme was reported to function as an organoarsenical oxidase that detoxifies trivalent methylated and aromatic arsenicals by oxidation to pentavalent species, and was shown to confer resistance to trivalent forms of the herbicide |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| and the poultry growth promoter |FRAME: CPD-22656| |CITS: [25732202]|., A later study of |FRAME: TAX-160488| has shown that the presence of the arsH genes strengthens the organism's tolerance and relieves the oxidative stress caused by both inorganic As(V) and As(III). Expression of the genes in |FRAME: TAX-562| suggested that ArsH has an additional effect on arsenic resistance by mediating reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) produced in vivo upon exposure to the oxyanion, potentially by generating FMNH2 to fuel ROS-quenching activities |CITS: [32202357]|.

General Background, Polyunsaturated long- and very-long-chain fatty acids (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear. While PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants and are not synthesized by animals, they are also produced by a narrow group of predominately marine γ-proteobacteria, which includes (among others) species of the |FRAME: TAX-22|, |FRAME: TAX-657|, |FRAME: TAX-58050|, |FRAME: TAX-28228| and |FRAME: TAX-662| genera |CITS: [4197274][Johns77][16347037][16535638][11777566][12594015]|. Since these organisms are associated with growth in low temperatures and often high pressure, it has been suggested that PUFA synthesis by these organisms is an important adaptation for countering the effects of elevated hydrostatic pressure and low temperature on membrane fluidity or phase. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that in strains that have been analysed, PUFA synthesis is temperature-dependent and, for deep-sea isolates, pressure-dependent |CITS: [10671446]|., |FRAME: CPD-10244 Docosahexaenoate| (DHA) is a 22 carbon long chain polyunsaturated fatty acid with 6 methylene interrupted cis-double bonds |CITS: [15292371]|. It is an n-3 (ω-3) fatty acid (defined according to the location of the last double bond at the methyl end). It is synthesized de novo in several microalgae and some fungi, and is also produced by some marine bacteria |CITS: [10220156]|. The pathways used by microalgae and bacteria are completely different. In the aerobic pathway used in microalgae, saturated fatty acids synthesized by fatty acid synthase are desaturated and elongated to PUFAs in many enzymatic reactions, some of which oxygen-requiring. In the anaerobic pathway utilized by bacteria, PUFAs are anaerobically synthesized from acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA by PUFA synthases., About this Pathway, Even though the exact mechanism of the bacterial PUFA synthases has not been defined, it is well documented that these complexes are encoded by four or five genes |CITS: [9274025][11104010]|, which have been designated pfaEABCD |CITS: [12055309]|. The genetic structure of the PUFA biosynthetic genes consists of a four-gene operon that includes pfaABCD, while pfaE, which encodes the phosphopantetheinyl transferase required for catalytic activation of acyl carrier protein domains, may be found elsewhere in the genome |CITS: [21105981]|., PUFA synthases capable of synthesizing |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) were found in several marine bacteria including |FRAME: TAX-314092| |CITS: [11452122][8729138]| and |FRAME: TAX-298386| |CITS: [12055309]|. A synthase responsible for synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) was identified in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-90736| |CITS: [16988784]|, and a synthase capable of producing |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| was identified in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-365033| |CITS: [25263707]|., Genes encoding four of the subunits of a |FRAME: CPLX-8944| were first identified in the |FRAME: CPD-10244|-producing marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1202962| based on their similarity to genes encoding an eicosapentaenoate synthase in |FRAME: TAX-314092| |CITS: [Tanaka99]|., A fifth gene (|FRAME: G-43752|), encoding the missing 4'-phosphopantetheinyl transferase subunit, was identified several years later |CITS: [16988784]|. All five genes were then cloned and expressed together in an |FRAME: TAX-562| host, and analysis of the fatty acids produced by the recombinant host showed that up to 5% of the total fatty acids was |FRAME: CPD-10244|, confirming the synthase activity |CITS: [16988784]|.

General Background, Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight |CITS: [Overmann92]|., Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10-30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics., The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C31 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-132-methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates |CITS: [16245042]|., Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported., In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-82 and C-121 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-82 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. , Despite the fact that most research has focused on |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, most of the green sulfur bacteria growing in stratified lakes contain |FRAME:CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| |CITS: [vanGemerden95]|. An example for such an organism is |FRAME: TAX-1098|., About This Pathway, The pathways leading to |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| diverge from that for |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| and |FRAME: CPD-9067| after |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| is formed., The pathway starts with the removal of the C-132-methylcarboxyl moiety, forming |FRAME: CPD-18841| |CITS: [21550979]|., Two radical-SAM (S-adenosyl-lmethionine) oxidative methyltransferases, |FRAME: G-44408 BchR| and |FRAME: G-44409 BchQ|, add methyl groups to the C-121 ethyl and C-82 methyl carbons, respectively |CITS: [17586634]|. The latter can add a second methyl group at the same position. These four different forms (non-methylated, mono-methylated, di-methylated and tri-methylated) serve as substrates to the hydratases BchV (most of them can also serve as substrate for BchF, a homologous enzyme that is primarily involved in |FRAME: PWY-5526|). These enzymes hydrate the C-31 carbon, converting the vinyl group to the 1-hydroxyethyl group that is necessary for the aggregation of the chlorophyll molecules inside the chlorosomes. The hydroxyl group produces a chiral center. Experiments looking at the stereo-specificity of the two enzymes were inconclusive, as different results were obtained in vivo and in vitro. However, it was shown that in the absence of BshF the bacteria produced higher ratios of (S) epimers to (R) epimers |CITS: [26331578]|., The last step in the pathway is the attachment of the farnesyl tail, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44411 "BchK synthase"|, which is specific for bacteriochlorophyll c, d and e |CITS: [12029054]|.

Summary: In this pathway |FRAME:GLT| is deaminated by an NAD-linked dehydrogenase, forming, |FRAME:AMMONIA| and |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, which is then fed to the |FRAME:TCA|., The pathway is found in microbes and plants., The deamination of |FRAME: GLT| is a key reaction not only in the degradation of |FRAME: GLT|,, but also in the degradation of several other amino acids.  |FRAME:ARG|, |FRAME:GLN|, |FRAME:HIS|,, and |FRAME:PRO| are all converted to |FRAME:GLT| during their catabolism |CITS[3289795]|., The enzymes catalyzing the deamination of |FRAME: GLT| are the ubiquitous glutamate dehydrogenases, (GDHs). , GDHs catalyze a reversible reaction, and are involved in both the anabolic function of, glutamate biosynthesis and the catabolic function of glutamate utilization, depending on the organism, and the conditions.  In some organisms, a single enzyme can catalyze both functions under different, physiological conditions., Most of the prokaryotic enzymes can use either NAD+ (EC 1.4.1.2) or NADP+ (EC 1.4.1.4), |CITS:[4147773]|. Although the NADP+-specific enzymes are capable of catalyzing a reversible reaction,, they are believed to take part only in the anabolic reactions of glutamate biosynthesis, and thus , included in |FRAME: GLUTSYNIII-PWY|., In yeast cells the amino group of glutamate and the amide group of glutamine are the source, of nitrogen for all other macromolecules |CITS: [1975578]|. In order to provide ammonia for the synthesis, of glutamine during growth on glutamate-yielding nitrogen sources, cells degrade glutamate into ammonia., The main pathway for |FRAME: TAX-4932| glutamate degradation is catalyzed by the NAD-dependent, glutamate dehydrogenase encoded by GDH2 |CITS:[1975578]|., Plants have multiple forms of GDH enzymes. NAD(H)-specific enzymes are localized in the mitochondria,, while NADP(H)-specific enzymes are associated with the chloroplasts |CITS: [Srivastava87][9112779]|. , Under severe carbon shortage conditions, plants convert |FRAME: GLT| to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, via this pathway, also known as the GDH shunt. |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| then enters the, |FRAME: TCA| and carbon metabolism.  Plant mutants lacking this capability have inhibited, growth, especially under stress when carbon metabolism is in intense demand |CITS: [8643469]|. , The GDH shunt, together with the ammonia assimilation cycle (see |FRAME: PWY-3282|), play important, role in the maintenance of carbon and nitrogen balance in plants.  The GDH shunt is also thought to play, a role in maintaining the internal glutamate concentration which is remarkably constant in Arabidopsis, leaves., some organisms posses a glutamate dehydrogenase that can utilize both NAD and NADP as a cofactor., these enzyme are described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-5766|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THR| is an indispensable amino acid. It is degraded by a complex network of pathways and regulatory signals |CITS: [9871012]|., Two of the major routes for the degradation of L-threonine are known to occur both in mammals and in microorganisms., In the first route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREDEHYDCAT-CPLX| (EC 4.3.1.19) to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, which is rapidly and irreversibly converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5437|). A biosynthetic version of this enzyme has also been reported in certain anaerobic bacteria (see |FRAME:ILEUSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [13405870]|., In the second route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREODEHYD-CPLX| (EC 1.1.1.103) to form |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT|, which is mainly cleaved by |FRAME: AKBLIG-CPLX|, forming glycine and acetyl-CoA (see |FRAME:THREONINE-DEG2-PWY|). In the absence of the latter activity |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT| is spontaneously converted to |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|, which is further metabolized into |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| (see |FRAME: THRDLCTCAT-PWY|)., A third route has been demonstrated in several bacteria and fungi. This route is based on the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7266| (EC 4.1.2.5), which cleaves threonine directly into |FRAME:GLY| and |FRAME:ACETALD| (see |FRAME:PWY-5436|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: THREODEHYD-CPLX| catalyzes the oxidation of threonine by NAD+ to |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT|, which is typically converted by |FRAME:AKBLIG-CPLX| into glycine and acetyl-CoA (see |FRAME:THREONINE-DEG2-PWY|)., However, in certain bacteria, and in mammals when the ratio acetyl-CoA/CoA increases in nutritional deprivation (e.g., in diabetes) |FRAME:AKBLIG-CPLX| activity is lacking or is deminished, and |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT| is instead converted non-enzymatically to |FRAME: AMINO-ACETONE|., Aminoacetone, like many other endogenous (e.g., |FRAME: METHYLAMINE|) and xenobiotic (e.g., |FRAME:BENZYLAMINE|) amines, is oxidized by dioxygen in a reaction catalyzed by amine oxidases, a group of poorly understood Cu-dependent enzymes. In mammals amine oxidases can be either plasma circulating or membrane bound., The reaction yields an aldehyde, |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and |FRAME:AMMONIA| ions |CITS: [6833209][8920635]|. With aminoacetone as the substrate, the product is the cytotoxic and genotoxic |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL|, which is detoxified into |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, as described in |FRAME:PWY-5386|. This pathway has been reported as the main route of threonine degradation in |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [355220]|., In mammals this pathway spans the cytoplasmic and mitochondrial compartments. The first reaction occurs in the cytosol, but aminoacetone moves into the mitochondrial compartment, where the remaining reactions occur., While this pathway occurs in mammals |CITS:[6437452]|, it plays only a minor role in humans |CITS: [10780944]|, potentially due to the fact that the human |FRAME:THREODEHYD-CPLX| is an expressed pseudogene |CITS: [12361482]|.

Summary: Terpenoids constitute the largest group of specialized metabolites across the various kingdoms of life. Over 50.000 terpenoid compounds have been identified to date and a wealth of diverse structures discovered. This structural diversity is due to numerous terpenoid cyclases which have been shown to synthesize compounds with multiple chiral centers which give rise to the observed broad range of terpenoids in terms of structural arrangements and bioactivity |CITS:[16895335] [22907771]|. However, sesterterpenoids, i.e. terpenoids formed by a homologous series of five isoprene units (C25) are scarcely found in nature and the elucidation of respective structures |CITS:[Qureshi80]| and biosynthetic pathways is still at an early stage |CITS:[Crews85] [23385977]|., |FRAME:CPD-18556 Stellatic acid| |CITS:[ 15612624]| and |FRAME:CPD-16664| (see |FRAME:PWY-7720|) |CITS:[23324037]| are two sesterterpenoids which have been found to be produced by Aspergillus and Emericella species. The identified gene in Aspergillus stellatus, i.e. Stl-SS was shown to have two fused domains, a prenyltransferase (PT) and a terpene cyclase (TC) domain and was characterized by both heterologous expression in the system Aspergillus oryzae and by in vitro incubation of the recombinant expressed Stl-SS purified from E. coli. The prenyltransferase (PT) part catalyzes the production of |FRAME:ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| from both |FRAME:CPD-4211| and |FRAME:DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| via |FRAME:GERANYL-PP|, |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. The terpene cyclase (TC) domain of the fusion protein realized the subsequent cyclization of |FRAME:ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| yielding |FRAME:CPD-18553|. In contrast to |FRAME:MONOMER-19519| the Stl-SS encoded protein employs the terminal |FRAME:CPD-4211|-group of |FRAME:ALL-TRANS-PENTAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE| and in doing so creates the unique 11-6-5 fused tricyclic scaffold of the |FRAME:CPD-18556| |CITS:[26351860]|., The identification of the sesterterpene synthase (Stl-SS) in the genome of Aspergillus stellatus (perfect state Emericella variecolor) allowed detection of a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase gene (Stl-450) in the flanking regions of the Stl-SS gene. It could be shown by coexpression with the Stl-SS gene in the expression system of Aspergillus oryzae that the Stl-450 encoded monooxygenase catalyzed three successive oxidations on C-20 of |FRAME:CPD-18553| to form |FRAME:CPD-18556| via |FRAME:CPD-18554| and |FRAME:CPD-18555| |CITS:[26351860]| similar to the reaction sequence observed in the |FRAME:PWY-5195| catalyzed by the |FRAME:MONOMER-12185|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9720| (MK-9) is found in many bacterial species from different phyla. While it has not been observed in aerobic or facultatively aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, it has been described as the major quinone in several obligate anaerobic Gram-negatives and in many Gram-positive bacteria., Gram-negative bacteria that contain MK-9 as their major or sole quinone include |FRAME: TAX-28123| |CITS: [6102980]|, |FRAME: TAX-28114| |CITS: [Martius64]| and |FRAME: TAX-28118| |CITS: [Shah83]|. It has also been reported as a minor components of many other Bacteroides species |CITS: [6102980] [Shah83]|, as well as of several phototrophic bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1079|, |FRAME: TAX-1082| and |FRAME: TAX-1083| |CITS: [5727384]|., Among the Gram-positive bacteria, MK-9 is mostly found in |FRAME: TAX-201174|, as the main quinone of most firmicutes is |FRAME: CPD-9718|. However, some firmicutes, including |FRAME: TAX-1467| |CITS: [119033]|, |FRAME: TAX-1618| |CITS: [Collins81]| and several |FRAME: TAX-1301| strains |CITS: [118232]| have been reported to contain MK-9 as their main quinone., Actinobacteria that produce MK-9 include many species from different genera, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-1696|, |FRAME: TAX-2034|, |FRAME: TAX-1269|, and many more |CITS: [479832][6102980][13971217]|., In addition, most of the |FRAME: TAX-1762|, including the important strains |FRAME: TAX-1773|, |FRAME: TAX-1772|, |FRAME: TAX-1771| and |FRAME: TAX-1765|, produce MK-9 as a secondary quinone (their main form is the partially desaturated MK-9(H2)) |CITS: [894261]|., A few enzymes involved in this pathway, including |FRAME:CPLX-7591| and |FRAME:MONOMER-13819|, have been purified from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1270| that produced MK-9 |CITS:[1748647][7275947]|.

General Background, Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. In the environment, iron is mostly found in two different oxidation states: II and III. Fe(II) is the thermodynamically favored state at low pH and reducing conditions, while Fe(III) is favored at high pH and oxic conditions. In oxic environments iron forms various oxide and hydroxide compounds; iron(II,III) oxides (such as magnetite, Fe3O4) and iron(III) oxides (such as hematite, Fe2O3) are most common. Under anoxic conditions the soluble |FRAME: FE+2| species is the most common. In certain environments Fe(III) can also be found in soluble form, coupled to stabilizing ligands., Oxidation of ferrous iron (Fe(II)) by microbes is an important component of the iron geochemical cycle. Bacterial iron oxidation is well documented under anaerobic conditions (see for example |FRAME: PWY-8554|), or under aerobic, acidic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6692|). Even though iron is oxidized spontaneously and rapidly in the presence of oxygen, many bacterial species have been found to oxidize Fe(II) at neutral pH |CITS: [20565252][32071158][33328652]|., About This Pathway, Members of the purple and green bacteria perform a process known as phototrophic Fe(II) oxidation or photoferrotrophy, in which electrons obtained from oxidation of extracellular iron are used in anoxygenic photosynthetic carbon fixation. , Purple phototrophic bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1060| perform anoxygenic photosynthesis where, following photon absorption by bacteriochlorophyll and carotenoid pigments in dedicated light harvesting (LH) complexes, excitation energy is passed to the special pair bacteriochlorophylls in the reaction center (RC). Subsequently, a cyclic electron flow between the RC, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c generates a transmembrane proton gradient that is used to power ATP synthesis. More specifically, electrons are transferred from NADH to the membrane quinone pool by complex 1. Cytochrome bc1 complex III) transfers the electrons from the membrane quinol pool to cytochrome c2, generating proton-motive force. Cytochrome c2 delivers the electrons to the RC, which cycles them back to the quinone pool at the expense of absorbed photons. The final output of the system is the generated proton motive force, which is used to generate ATP |CITS: [18197174]|. The purple bacteria use reverse electron flow to endergonically reduce NADP+ to NADPH by quinols., |FRAME: TAX-371731| is a freshwater purple nonsulfur bacterium isolated from a pond in Germany |CITS: [7811087]| that couples Fe(II)-oxidation with anoxygenic photosynthesis. A three-gene operon (the foxEYZ operon) was found to confer enhanced light-dependent Fe(II) oxidation activity when expressed in the genetically tractable relative |FRAME: TAX-272942| |CITS: [17189371]|., The iron-oxidizing activity was found to be conferred by the product of the |FRAME: G-124843| gene, which encodes a c-type cytochrome. Expression of |FRAME: G-124843| alone conferred significant light-dependent Fe(II) oxidation activity on SB1003, though coexpression with |FRAME: G-124844| and foxZ increased the oxidation activity. The exact roles of these two proteins is not known, though FoxY contains the redox cofactor |FRAME: PQQ| and FoxZ appears to have a transport function |CITS: [17189371]|. It is assumed that FoxY is the redox partner of FoxE, though this hypothesis has not been verified., FoxE has been crystallized, and a prelimiary structure confirmed that the protein contains two heme molecules per monomer |CITS: [22949206]|. A more detailed study of the FoxE structure found that it is a homotrimer with two hemes and a disulfide bridge per monomer |CITS: [28760394]|. The two hemes of each monomer are hexacoordinated by histidine and methionine and have different reduction potentials |CITS: [22661703]|., Unlike all other proteins that have been shown to oxidize Fe(II), which are extracellular, FoxE appears to be periplasmic. This location of the oxidase inside the cell poses a problem for the organism - the removal of Fe(III) before it precipitates as insoluble minerals. It has been proposed that the trimeric structure of the enzyme and the 37 Å distance between hemes II (the heme responsible for iron oxidation) of different monomers ensure the segregation of the iron oxidation reaction from the electron transfer reaction to the partner mediating the delivery of electrons to the cyclic electron transfer chain. A slow transfer of the electron from heme II to heme I will allow the ferric hydroxide product to diffuse away before another oxidation event takes place.

Summary: Many organisms can synthesize guanosine nucleotides de novo. In that route |FRAME: GMP| (GMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| (XMP) , which is converted to GMP by the action of |FRAME: GMP-SYN-CPLX|, an enzyme that can use either glutamine or ammonia as substrate (see |FRAME: PWY-6125|). Note that the free base |FRAME: GUANINE| or the ribonucleoside |FRAME: GUANOSINE| are not produced via the de novo pathway., Many organisms also use salvage enzymes to obtain purine bases and nucleosides and convert them to the corresponding nucleotides. The pathway described here is used by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms for this purpose., For example, all parasitic protozoa (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|, |FRAME: TAX-5810|, |FRAME: TAX-38568|, |FRAME: TAX-5690|) lack the ability to synthesize purine nucleotides de novoand use this salvage pathway to convert purine bases and nucleosides obtained from their hosts to the corresponding nucleotides |CITS: [3920982][6316234]|. After their uptake by specific transporters |CITS: [ 7443300][ 10743614]| the purine nucleosides are first hydrolyzed to ribose and a base by nucleoside hydrolases. The bases are then converted to the concomitant nucleotides by |FRAME: GPT-CPLX|, which utilizes |FRAME: PRPP| to convert the free base to the mononucleotide |FRAME: GMP|., Nucleoside hydrolases from parasites are attractive drug targets against parasitic protozoa since no such activity has been reported thus far in mammalian cells |CITS: [6396514]|., The pathway has also been described in green plants |CITS: [GURANOWSKI79]|., Other routes from |FRAME: GUANOSINE| to |FRAME: GMP| are described in |FRAME: PWY-6620| and |FRAME: PWY-6618|.

General Background, |FRAME: CARNOSINE "Carnosine"| is a dipeptide found in abundance in the skeletal muscle and brain of many vertebrates and some invertebrates |CITS: [20097752]|. It was originally isolated by Gulewitsch and Amiradzibi over 100 years ago from Liebig's meat extract, the first-ever peptide isolated from animal tissue., Carnosine is the best-known representative of a series of imidazole dipeptides such as |FRAME: CPD-12185|, |FRAME: CPD-401| and |FRAME: CPD-12186|. In 1938, Bate Smith realized that the pK value of carnosine (6.9) made it an ideal buffer at physiological pH and demonstrated that 40% of the buffer capacity of fast twitch muscle fibers is due to carnosine and other dipeptides |CITS: [16994977]|. , Subsequent experiments have shown that carnosine can also serve as an antioxidant |CITS: [3362866]|, metal chelating agent |CITS: [6243942]|, neuromodulator |CITS: [10501633]| and suppressor of human cell senescence |CITS: [19041712]|. An allelic variant of |FRAME: CPLX66-419| that resulted in increased enzyme activity and an association with susceptibility for diabetic nephropathy, suggested that L-carnosine may also be a protective factor in diabetic patients |CITS: [17601992]|. However, the molecular mechanism of carnosine activity remains a mystery., About this Pathway, |FRAME: CARNOSINE "Carnosine"| is synthesized from |FRAME: B-ALANINE| and |FRAME: HIS| in an ATP dependent reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-491| |CITS: [20097752]|. |FRAME: B-ALANINE| is synthesized in the liver, primarily via |FRAME: PWY-3982|. In mammals, β-alanine is not incorporated into proteins and much of the cellular pool of β-alanine is incorporated into carnosine. The rest is degraded via |FRAME: BETA-ALA-DEGRADATION-I-PWY|., The concentration of β alanine is the rate limiting factor in carnosine biosynthesis. Dietary supplementation of β alanine has been shown to increase the concentration of carnosine in muscles and attenuate fatigue in athletes |CITS: [17690198]||CITS: [16868650]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHOLINE Choline| is a quaternary ammonium compound and a fundamental metabolite for eukaryotic organisms, forming the head group of important phospholipids such as |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| |CITS: [12215503]|., Choline is also the precursor for the neurotransmitter |FRAME: ACETYLCHOLINE|, and serves as a precursor for the formation of the important osmoprotectant |FRAME: BETAINE| (see |FRAME:PWY1F-353| for an example) ., Most plants synthesize choline, since phosphatidylcholine accounts for 40 to 60% of lipids in non-plastid plant membranes |CITS: [12215503]|. Animals cannot synthesize |FRAME: CHOLINE|, which must be consumed through the diet, making it a vitamin. It is usually grouped within the B-complex vitamins. Most microbes are not able to produce choline, although many have transporters for its uptake., About This Pathway, The first step in choline biosynthesis is the direct decarboxylation of serine to ethanolamine |CITS: [11461929]|, which is catalyzed by a serine decarboxylase unique to plants |CITS: [14634155]|. Ethanolamine is widely recognized as the entrance compound to choline biosynthesis., The pathway variant displayed (nucleotide pathway) represents the biosynthetic route as found in diverse plant families., The synthesis of choline from ethanolamine may take place at three parallel pathways, where three consecutive N-methylation steps are carried out either on free-bases |CITS: [PRUDHOMME92A]|, phospho-bases |CITS: [10799484]|, , phosphatidyl-bases |CITS: [11481443]| or a mixture of the latter |CITS: [Datko88a][Datko88b][Hitz81]|. , The synthesis of intermediates on both the phospho-base and phosphatidyl-base level includes the nucleotide pathway via CDP-phosphoaminoalcohol and the methylation pathway. However, it has been pointed out that the synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine is characterized by a high degree of interaction and furcation on the various levels of arising intermediates. Consequently, it has been assumed that the reactions embedded in the nucleotide, and methylation pathways may be two characteristics of one overall phosphoaminoalcohol pathway for the formation of , phosphatidylcholine in plants |CITS: [Kinney93]|., The release of choline from the different pathway levels is also species-specific. Phosphocholine can either be directly dephosphorylated to release choline as observed in spinach |CITS: [12232019]| or incorporated into phosphatidylcholine with the subsequent release of choline, as in tobacco |CITS: [10806254]|. The latter reaction has been shown to be specifically catalyzed by phospholipase D (|FRAME:LIPASYN-PWY|) in castor bean |CITS: [8051126]|. Although a well-defined physiological role of phospholipase D (PLD) still await further research, progress has been made to assign some members of the heterogeneous family of PLD's to distinct cellular functions |CITS: [Wang99]|. The remaining enzymes involved in this pathway, phosphoaminoalcohol cytidylyltransferase and CDP-aminoalcohol phosphotransferase, cover a broader spectrum of substrates. This may be beneficial to process the heterogeneous mixture of possible substrates but it also indicates that the pathway flux is probably controlled more upstream |CITS: [Kinney93]|.

Summary: General Background, Cyanobacteria are able to conduct both photosynthesis and respiration and have evolved a electron transport pathways that operate under both conditions. Another important electron transfer pathway these organisms must operate is cyclic electron flow, which allows them to generate proton motive force without producing reducing power. An additional requirement the organisms face is the ability to dissipate excess electron flow, which could happen when light and environmental conditions change rapidly., Like most cyanobacterial species, |FRAME: TAX-84588| possesses two membrane systems: the cytoplasmic membrane and a series of internal thylakoid membranes. The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes, as does a resipratory electron chain, while an additional respiratory electron transfer chain is localized in the cytoplasmic membrane., The only electron-transfer quinone found in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone| (PQ), which is shared among the photosynthetic light reactions and the respiratory electron chain. Three other components - |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76|, the small copper protein |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER|, are also shared between the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transfer chains., It has been shown that the major electron source for the respiratory pathways is |FRAME: SUC|, which feeds into |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-18| (SDH), an enzyme complex that contributes to the proton gradient |CITS: [11418566]|. It is less clear whether the organisms utilize NADPH or NADH as an electron source. Two types of NAD(P)H dehydrogenase-like enzymes are present - NDH-1, of which several different complexes are present |CITS: [1907569]| and |FRAME: TX72_RS01490-MONOMER NDH-2| |CITS: [11418566]|. An emerging understanding of these enzymes suggests that NDH-1 complexes are only involved in cyclic electron flow |CITS: [30573545][32060291]|, and questions the role of NDH-2 enzymes in respiration as well |CITS: [10383967][30847494]|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the transfer of electrons from succinate to oxygen in a chain that includes |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-18| (SDH), |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone|, |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76|, |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-27|., The electrons from SDH are transferred to PQ, which diffuses through the membrane and can deliver the electrons to different components, depending on the needs of the organsim. The electrons can be transferred directly to a |FRAME: TX72_RS04385-MONOMER| |CITS: [19067963][Mackey08]| (see |FRAME: PWY1YI0-7|), to an alternative |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-26 "cytochrome bo-type quinol oxidase"| |CITS: [9922162]| (see |FRAME: PWY1YI0-8|), or to the |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76| as shown here., From the |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-76| the electrons are transferred to |FRAME: CPLX1YI0-27| by either |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER| (as shown in |FRAME: PWY1YI0-3|) or, under copper limitation, by |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER|, as shown here |CITS: [22749908]|. In cyanobacteria, |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER| and |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER| are able to replace each other as redox carriers in the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transport chains, with the synthesis of one or another protein being regulated by the copper concentration in the culture medium |CITS: [1326543][10050775][14660567]|., Despite their intrinsic different conformations, |FRAME: TX72_RS07525-MONOMER| and |FRAME: TX72_RS07520-MONOMER| share a number of similar physicochemical and structural features that allow them to interact with the same redox partners with equivalent kinetic efficiency and replace each other inside the cells |CITS: [7547859][11013249]|.

Summary: Above-ground epidermal surfaces of vascular plants are covered by a lipophilic layer known as the cuticle. Plant cuticles are composed of cutin (|FRAME: PWY-321|) and cuticular wax. , The major components of cuticular wax are very long chain fatty acids (chain length is greater than 18 carbon) and very long chain fatty acid derived aldehydes, alkanes, secondary alcohols, ketones, primary alcohols, and wax esters. The composition of cuticular wax varies among species and even within species in different tissues and at different developmental stages.

The eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5A (eIF-5A), which is present in all eukaryotic cells, must be activated by post translational modification before it can participate in the initiation of protein synthesis. , The modification involves the addition of a |FRAME: BUTYLAMINE| residue (derived from |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|) to a highly conserved lysine in the eIF-5A protein |CITS: [11278418]|. This results in the formation of an unusual amino acid called |FRAME: CPD-9974|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9974| occurs exclusively within the eIF-5A precursor, and is catalyzed by two enzymatic steps, |FRAME: MONOMER-13914| (DHS) and |FRAME: HS05318-MONOMER| (DOHH) |CITS: [10542236]|. , The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9974| is found in all eukaryotes and the DHS and DOHH enzymes are highly conserved, indicating that the fundamental cellular function of elF5A is maintained from plants to mammals. DHS enzymes have been isolated and characterized from several animals and plants. The second enzyme (DOHH) has been charaterized from mammals, and homologs were identified in the |FRAME: TAX-3701| and |FRAME: TAX-4527| genomes., In tomato there is an increase in the abundance of DHS mRNA as well as elf5A mRNA in senescing flowers and fruits and in environmentally stressed leaves, suggesting that this enzyme plays a role in programmed cell death |CITS: [11278418]|. The antisense suppression of deoxyhypusine synthase in tomato dealys fruit softening and alters growth and development |CITS: [15951486]|., The strict substrate specificity for hypusine modification provides possible drug targeting of these enzymes, particularly in aberrant cell proliferation |CITS: [17476569]|.

Subsequent oxidative rearrangement results in formation of the 6,6-bicyclic quinolone |FRAME: CPD-25947| (see |FRAME: PWY-7705|)., Multiple prenylations of C7 of the phenolic ring, combined with hydration, yield the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-25971|, which can either rearrange to form the chromene-containing |FRAME: CPD-25969| and |FRAME: CPD-25970| |CITS: [16321026]|, or hydrate spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-25944| |CITS: [23659680]|., An epoxidase acts on the latter, forming |FRAME: CPD-25942|, which can be converted into multiple compounds. |FRAME: MONOMER-124185 PenJ| can convert it to |FRAME: CPD-25956|; |FRAME: MONOMER-124184 PenF| can convert it to |FRAME: CPD-25957|, which is processed into |FRAME: CPD-25958| and |FRAME: CPD-25966| that contain the gem-dimethyl pyran ring |CITS: [17191681][11210117]| (this pathway); and |FRAME: MONOMER-124181 AsqC| can convert it into a compound that is rearranged into |FRAME: CPD-18303| and |FRAME: CPD-18304|, which contain a fused cyclopropane-tetrahydrofuran unit |CITS: [17036148]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8388|).

Acridone alkaloids are found mainly in |FRAME: TAX-23513| and to lesser extent in |FRAME: TAX-16739| and Simarubaceae. , The core of these alkaloids 1,3-dihydroxyacridone is formed by the condensation of the starter substrate |FRAME: N-METHYLANTHRANILOYL-COA| with 3 units of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|. This gets modified by prenylation and cyclization reactions to form complex acridones |CITS: [17988223]|. Several acridone alkaloids have been tested and classified as potential chemopreventive agents |CITS: [12706869]|.

General Background, Plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-40553| family have been valued both for flavor and medicinal purposes throughout the world., The domestic Alliums (such as onion, garlic, chives and leek) contain high concentrations of organic sulfur compounds especially in their bulbs and leaves. These compounds consist mostly of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| such as |FRAME: CPD-9269|, |FRAME: CPD-9307|, and |FRAME: CPD-9277|, as well as γ-glutamyl peptides (together these compounds make up over 70% of the total sulfur in garlic |CITS: [ Lawson96]|)., These compounds, which are found in the cytoplasm, are produced constitutively. The S-alkyl cysteine S-oxides are substrates for the alliinase enzymes (|FRAME: EC-4.4.1.4|), which convert them to |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|. However, the enzymes are kept in vacuoles, and are thus sequestered from their substrates |CITS: [Lancaster81][19463015]|. Only when the tissue is injured, the alliinase enzymes are released from the vaculoes and interact with their substrates, producing |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|., |CITS: [16010345]|. Once formed, S-alkylsulfenates are very active and tend to condense spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-17425 thiosulfinates| |CITS: [21905712]|. Depending on the Allium species, and under differing conditions, the thiosulfinates can decompose to form additional sulfur constituents including diallyl, methyl allyl, and diethyl mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, and hexasulfides, vinyldithiins, and (E)- and (Z)-ajoene |CITS: [16010345]|., In some species, dedicated enzymes commonly known as "lachrymatory-factor synthases" act on the S-alkylsulfenates rapidly, before they condense, producing volatile compounds that cause the eyes of animals to tear (lachrymatory factors) - a further defense mechanism against herbivory., About This Pathway, Even though |FRAME: TAX-46142| is a non-Allium herbaceous perennial of the order |FRAME: TAX-3524|, it has similar chemistry to that found in the |FRAME: TAX-40553|. The plant is indigenous to the Amazon rainforest and tropical areas of Central and South America, the Caribbean, and sub-Saharan Africa, and has a long history of use in herbal medicine., Several organosulfur small molecules have been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-46142|, including |FRAME: CPD-12486|, |FRAME: CPD-12487|, |FRAME: CPD-17423| and |FRAME: CPD-9305| |CITS: [11684199][12423888]|., Roots of |FRAME: TAX-46142| contain roots four cysteine S-oxide derivatives, which upon maceration are converted to thiosulfinates by an |FRAME: CPLX-8953 alliinase| enzyme, in a similar fashion to the formation of thiosulfinates in |FRAME: TAX-40553| plants. The cysteine S-oxide derivatives that serve as alliinase substrates are odorless and kept separated from the enzyme by storage in different compartments. In addition, |FRAME: TAX-46142| possesses a lachrymatory-factor synthase, and produces the lachrymatory factor |FRAME: CPD-12490| upon tissue injury., The |FRAME: CPLX-8953 alliinase| enzyme has been purified from roots of |FRAME: TAX-46142| and found to act on two substrates - |FRAME: CPD-12486| and |FRAME: CPD-17423|, resulting in production of |FRAME: CPD-12491| and |FRAME: CPD-17424|, respectively |CITS: [19789290]|., |FRAME: CPD-12491 Phenylmethanesulfenate|, in turn, is converted into |FRAME: CPD-12490|, a novel potent lacrimating factor, by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-8955| (sometimes called lachrymatory-factor synthase). In the absence of the enzyme, |FRAME: CPD-12491| condenses spontaneously with other S-alkylsulfenates, forming |FRAME: CPD-12487| and other thiosulfinates |CITS: [19692535][21840558]|., Despite the similarity, the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-46142| are rather different from those of |FRAME: TAX-40553|, being large, heteromeric complexes.

Summary: Higher alcohols, such as |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL|, possess several beneficial characteristics, such as a low hygroscopicity, vapor pressure and corrosivity, full compatibility with existing engines and pipelines, and a high energy density., |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL Isobutanol| is produced biologically as a by-product of yeast fermentation. While most other eukaryotes (as well as many prokaryotes) catabolize |FRAME: VAL| through a succession of acyl-coA derivatives to metabolites that can enter the TCA cycle (see |FRAME: VALDEG-PWY|), providing the organism with carbon as well as nitrogen, yeast are not able to use |FRAME:VAL| as a carbon source, and process it through the |FRAME: PWY-5057 "Ehrlich pathway"| to |FRAME:ISOBUTANOL| |CITS: [8277258]|. In this pathway, the nitrogen is removed, creating the 2-oxo acid |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, which is metabolized to isobutanol via |FRAME: CPD-7000|., Since the use of L-valine as a feed-stock would be cost prohibitive for industrial scale isobutanol production, the common strategy to engineer common microbial hosts such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: TAX-1718| and |FRAME: TAX-4932| for the production of isobutanol is to combine the last two reactions of the Ehrlich pathway with the pathway for |FRAME: VALSYN-PWY "valine biosynthesis"| from pyruvate via the mutual intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| |CITS: [Donaldson10][21161324][22008938]|., The two reactions from the Ehrlich pathway are usually catalyzed by a broad range 2-ketoacid decarboxylase (encoded by |FRAME: G-10082|) from |FRAME: TAX-1358| and an alcohol dehydrogenase from either |FRAME: TAX-4932|, |FRAME: TAX-1718|, |FRAME: TAX-562| or |FRAME: TAX-1358| (encoded by |FRAME: YMR303C|, adhA, |FRAME: G7564| and adhA, respectively) |CITS: [18172501][19609521][20376637][21441331][21533914]|., In order to increase the isobutanol yield in the engineered organisms, it is essential to increase the pyruvate pool by knocking out enzymes that compete for the pyruvate, such as |FRAME: EG10031|, |FRAME: G592|, |FRAME: EG10330| and |FRAME: EG10331|, |FRAME: EG10325|, |FRAME: EG20173| and |FRAME:EG10701| (encoding alcohol dehydrogenase, D-lactate dehydrogenase, fumarate reductase, transcriptional regulator FNR, phosphate acetyltransferase, and pyruvate formate lyase, respectively) |CITS: [18172501]|.

Summary: The most abundant type of O glycosylation in proteins is the GalNAc-type, where |FRAME: CPD-3604| is linked to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues in the protein chain by an α-glycosidic linkage. In most cases other sugars are added to this galactosamine residue, resulting in glycosidic chains of variable lengths. Among O-GalNAc glycosylated proteins, mucins are the most ubiquitous. That type of glycosylation is described in other pathways, such as |FRAME: PWY-7433| and |FRAME: PWY-7435|., However, it has been subsequently found that in all eukaryotic systems |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues of some proteins are also modified with a β-linked |FRAME: CPD-12541| |CITS: [6421821]| that is not elongated to more complex structures |CITS: [8953283]|., This type of glycosylation is ubiquitous and abundant on nuclear and cytoskeletal proteins of virtually all eukaryotes, including protozoans |CITS: [2128647][7876162]| and fungi |CITS: [Machida94]|. More than 400 proteins are known to be modified in this manner, including RNA polymerase II and its transcription factors, nuclear pore proteins, viral proteins, cytoskeletal proteins, tumor suppressor proteins, and oncoproteins |CITS: [19277546 ]|., The O-[N-acetyl]-glucosylation is highly dynamic, with turnover rates much higher than those of the the protein backbones |CITS: [2000378][1371281][8639509]|. In addition, the glucosylation is often associated with phosphorylation, and sometimes the phosphate groups and the NAcGlc groups occupy the same hydroxyl groups |CITS: [8486697][7642555][10924527]|. These observations lead to the conclusion that O-[N-acetyl]-glucosylation serves a regulatory role, controlling protein phosphorylation and protein multimerization |CITS: [Hart95][8597237]|. Glycosylation generally promotes the associations with other proteins, while phosphorylation favor disassociation., The modified proteins, which are involved in regulation processes of the cell, can exhibit reciprocal O-GlcNAc glycosylation and phosphorylation during the cell cycle, cell stimulation, and/or cell growth |CITS: [8953283][9242909]|. Glycosylation appears to be involved in mediating cytoskeletal assembly and organization |CITS: [8344946][8647865]|., The enzyme that attaches the |FRAME: CPD-12541| moiety to the proteins is |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.255|. Deletion of the |FRAME: HS07403| gene that encodes it is lethal |CITS: [1533623][9083067]|., The N-acetylglucosamine residues are not extended into longer structures, and are removed from the modified proteins by |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.169|. While there may be multiple proteins that catalyze this activity, it has been well documented as one of the activities of the |FRAME: HS03036-MONOMER| |CITS: [11148210][11788610]|.
