Summary: Socrates's death by hemlock poisoning is a well-known historical event. Hemlock poison is the name given to the monocyclic alkaloids produced by the highly poisonous |FRAME: TAX-13447 "Conium maculatum (hemlock)"|, a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the |FRAME: TAX-4037| family that is native to Europe and the Mediterranean region., The hemlock poisons are toxic to animals that ingest the seeds, vegetative or flowering parts of the plant. These piperidinic alkaloids produce neuromuscular blockage that could lead to death |CITS: [Reynolds05]|. The cytotoxicity is irreversible and the chronic symptoms can be seen in pregnant animals, with the fetuses showing malformation of organs |CITS: [Lopez99]|. The structure of the alkaloid determines the degree of teratogenicity (fetal malformation). The larger side chains of the propyl group and partial unsaturation appears to increase toxicit, as |FRAME:CPD-9424| is more toxic than |FRAME:CPD-9425| |CITS:[Lopez99]|., In addition to |FRAME: TAX-13447| these alkaloids are also reported from other plants such as |FRAME: TAX-25641|. In hemlock, eight piperidine alkaloids have been identified, |FRAME: CPD-9425|, |FRAME: CPD-9426|, N,N-dimethylconiine, |FRAME: CPD-9424|, conhydrinone, pseudoconhydrine, and N-methylpseudoconhydrine. Of those, |FRAME: CPD-9424| and |FRAME: CPD-9425| are the most abundant and most toxic ones |CITS: [Roberts75]|. The alkaloid content varies with development stage of the plant, seeds and leaves have high concentration of them, while younger plants have a lower content of alkaloids., These alkaloids are built from eight acetate units from the metabolic pool of the plant, forming a polyketoacid which cyclizes to form |FRAME: CPD-9424| which represents the parent alkaloid |CITS: [Roberts77]|. The formation of the main alkaloids in |FRAME:TAX-13446|, i.e. |FRAME: CPD-9424| and |FRAME: CPD-9425| had been shown to proceed via the intermediates 5-ketooctanoic acid and 5-ketooctanal (|CITS:[5422776]| |CITS:[Leete72]|) and the corresponding transaminase(s) had been partially purified and biochemically characterized |CITS:[Roberts71]| |CITS:[Roberts77]| |CITS:[Roberts78]|., However, the biosynthesis of other alkaloids which had been identified in Conium maculatum still requires further research and no enzymes for this pathways have been reported to date. Based on experimental data biosynthetic routes to form |FRAME:CPD-14511| via its intermediate |FRAME:CPD-14512| and |FRAME:CPD-14514| via |FRAME:CPD-14516| has been proposed by Leete (|CITS:[Leete72]|. Hence, |FRAME:CPD-9424| provides a common node for all |FRAME:TAX-13446| alkaloids. |FRAME:CPD-14511 γ-Conhydrine| is thought to be catalyzed by oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-9424| and later reduction to |FRAME:CPD-14511| |CITS:[Roberts75]|. The bioformation of |FRAME:CPD-14514| has been proposed to proceed through tautomerization of the C-N double bond creating an allylic C5 which is than hydroxylated (see |FRAME:CPD-14516|) and subsequently reduced |CITS:[Leete67]|. In connection with this it is interesting to note that in dependence on environmental stimuli alkaloid patterns in |FRAME:TAX-13446| may shift favoring the production of |FRAME:CPD-14511| and |FRAME:CPD-14514| |CITS:[Leete67]|.

Sesame seed has been an important oil-seed for centuries and was long since connected to health issues in ancient China and India |CITS:[Namiki95]| |CITS:[Moazzami06]|. The health promoting properties of Sesame seeds have been attributed to a range of lignans which typify the genus of |FRAME:TAX-4181| (see |FRAME:PWY-5469|) and include structures, e.g. the oxygen bridge between benzene and furofuran rings (|FRAME:CPD-8928|, |FRAME:CPD-8927|) which have not been found in any other lignans. About one third of all the lignans present in |FRAME:TAX-4181| are glucosides of |FRAME:CPD-14837| and |FRAME:CPD-8927| which have been reported to help against cognitive deficits |CITS:[19721225]|, exhibit anti-inflammatory effects and are therefore useful agents against Alzheimer's disease |CITS:[16842873]| and prevented or delayed neuronal cell death through antioxidant properties |CITS:[Lee05]|. It also had been shown that lignans of |FRAME:CPD-8922| and derivatives are important precursors to mammalian lignans, e.g. enterodiol and enterolactone |CITS:[19537732]| which are biotransformed by intestinal microbiota and may be involved in the protection against hormone-related diseases such as breast cancer |CITS:[16549449]|. , All the |FRAME:TAX-4181| lignan glucosides depicted in the pathway have been identified in this genus and a few other species |CITS:[Katsuzaki94]| |CITS:[16448160]| |CITS:[Parmar97]|. The general sequence of |FRAME:PWY-5469| had been established previously (e.g. |CITS:[Kato98]|). The first committed step towards the biosynthesis of sesamin derivative glucosides is the formation of the precursor |FRAME:CPD-14837| which either may derive from |FRAME:CPD-8922| |CITS:[Suzuki07a]| or via |FRAME:CPD-8928| |CITS:[Fukuda86]|. At present no enzymes have been reported for either route. The following 2-O-glucosylation of |FRAME:CPD-14837| is carried out by a lignan glucosyltransferase forming |FRAME:CPD-14838| (UGT71A8, UGT71A9, UGT71A10) and the |FRAME:CPD-14839| (UGT94D1) |CITS:[18248594]|. The flavonoid 1,6-glucosyltransferase characterized from |FRAME:TAX-4058| had the catalytic capability to sequentially 1,6-glucosylate |FRAME:CPD-14838| to form |FRAME:CPD-14841| via |FRAME:CPD-14839| |CITS:[19561332]|. The glucosyltransferase catalyzing the β-1,2-glucosylation of either |FRAME:CPD-14838| or |FRAME:CPD-14839| to form (+)-sesaminol triglucoside, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-14840| remains to be characterized.

Summary: Sanguinarine and macarpine belong to a subgroup of benzylisoquinoline alkaloids known as benzophenanthridines that are derived from (S)-reticuline via (S)-scoulerine. While several benzylisoquinoline-producing species are known to accumulate sanguinarine, the best-studied organisms include Eschscholzia californica (California poppy), Papaver somniferum (opium poppy) and Sanguinaria canadensis, or (bloodroot), due to the red pigmentation of the roots of this plant as a result of sanguinarine accumulation. In cell suspension cultures of these plants, sanguinarine biosynthesis is inducible with the addition of fungal elicitors. Many of the enzymes involved in the sanguinarine/macarpine biosynthesic pathway were identified and characterized using elicited plant cell cultures. The toxicity of sanguinarine and related alkaloids suggests that they are involved in plant defense against herbivores and microbes. Sanguinarine also exhibits anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, and anti-microbial effects that are useful to humans. It has been widely used in toothpastes and mouth washes due to its anti-microbial activity., Various enzymes from different plants catalyzing the the formation of the methylenedioxy bridge of |FRAME:S-SCOULERINE|, |FRAME:S-CHEILANTHIFOLINE| (this pathway) and |FRAME:S-TETRAHYDROCOLUMBAMINE| (see |FRAME:PWY-3901|) |CITS:[17250743] [21094631]| also catalyze the formation of |FRAME:S-TETRAHYDROBERBERINE| which was once discussed as an possible intermediate towards |FRAME:S-STYLOPINE|. However, this assumption could not be corroborated |CITS:[Bauer91]| and it remains an open question whether or not |FRAME:S-TETRAHYDROBERBERINE| is part of a metabolic side-step towards |FRAME:S-STYLOPINE| or branch point towards other plant alkaloids.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7172 "Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol"| (THC) is the main psychoactive substance found in the cannabis plant. In 1988 it was found that the pharmacological actions of THC result from its binding to two receptors - the cannabinoid receptors CB1, located mainly in the central nervous system, and CB2, mainly present in cells of the immune system. Both receptors belong to the superfamily of membrane-bound G-protein-coupled receptors |CITS: [9336020]|., As THC is not a naturally occurring substance in the mammalian body, the existence of a specific receptor for THC implied that there should be endogenous molecules for these existing receptors (endocanabinoids). The first such molecule, |FRAME: CPD-7598| (N-arachidonoyl ethanolamine), was isolated by the Israeli scientist Raphael Mechoulam in 1992 |CITS: [1470919]|. Since then four more endocanabinoids have been reported - |FRAME: CPD-12600|, |FRAME: CPD-22217| (noladin ether), |FRAME: CPD-22218|, and |FRAME: CPD-22219| |CITS: [17227440]|., Binding of endocannabinoids (or cannabinoids) to cannabinoid receptors results in a decrease in the intracellular level of |FRAME: CAMP| and activation of |FRAME: EC-2.7.11.24|, through the coupled Gi/o proteins. In addition, the activation of cannabinoid receptors modulates ion channels through Gi/o proteins, leading to the activation of A-type and inward-rectifyier potassium channels and the inhibition of N-type and P/Q-type calcium channels |CITS: [19126434]|., |FRAME: CPD-7598 Anandamide| is a fatty acid amide composed of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| coupled to |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE| through an amide linkage |CITS: [7990962][19126434]|. Unlike THC, anandamide breaks down very quickly in the body, and thus does not produce the same psychoactive effect as THC., It is synthesized in areas of the brain that are important in memory and higher-thought processes. Synthesis is highest in the hippocampus, followed by the thalamus, cortex, as well as striatum, and lowest in the cerebellum, pons, and medulla |CITS: [8022836]|. |FRAME: CPD-7598 Anandamide| and other |FRAME: N-Acylethanolamines ethanolamides| are present in the maternal milk and were reported to be critical for milk ingestion and therefore the survival of the newborn., About This Pathway, Unlike classical neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, endocannabinoids are not stored in vesicles in the cell, and are produced on demand from membrane phospholipids. The main phospholipid precursor of |FRAME: CPD-7598| is, |FRAME: N-arachidonoyl-PE "N-arachidonoyl phosphatidylethanolamine"| (NAPE), which is produced from |FRAME: 1-arachidonoyl-PC "1-arachidonoyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine"| by an N-acyltransferase enzyme |CITS: [12052034]|., Several reports were made about a Ca2+-dependent, membrane-associated N-acyltransferase that catalyzes this reaction |CITS: [8656287][9006968]|. However, as of 2019 that enzyme has not been purified and the gene encoding it has not been cloned. In 2007 a different enzyme catalyzing this activity was identified from rat, and later from mouse and humans. Unlike the previously reported enzyme, this enzyme was soluble and not dependent on Ca2+ concentrations. The enzyme did not show selectivity with respect to the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of the |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| as an acyl donor |CITS: [17158102]|., It was soon found that the enzyme (now known as |FRAME: HS15623|) is a member of a family of related proteins, previously known as HRAS-like suppressors since they were reported to negatively regulate the activity of oncogene Ras. The other members of the family, |FRAME: HS13232|, |FRAME: HS13475|, |FRAME: HS11053|, and |FRAME: HS05758|, were shown to possess similar activities |CITS: [19047760][19615464][21880860]|. Based on this discovery, it was suggested to rename these enzymes to phospholipase A/acyltransferase-1 through 5 (PLA/AT-1–5)., While these enzymes catalyzed the transfer of an acyl group from both sn-1 and sn-2 positions of phosphatidylcholine to the amino group of phosphatidylethanolamine, as described in this pathway, they also possess the activities of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.32|, of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.4|, and of an O-acyltransferase that transfers an acyl group from a glycerophospholipid to the hydroxyl group of a lysophospholipid |CITS: [19000777]|., Several different routes have been described for the release of |FRAME: CPD-7598| from its phospholipid precursor, consisting of one, two, or three steps., The direct route consists of a single reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.54|, whose activities were found to be highest in the brain, kidney, and testis. The enzyme, which belongs to the metallo-beta-lactamase family, contains |FRAME: ZN+2| and is activated by |FRAME: MG+2| or |FRAME: CA+2|. While it is very specific for N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines, it does not discriminate among them based on the chain-length of the N-acyl moiety |CITS: [16527816]|., The second route, which consists of two steps, has been proposed based on the detection of N-acyl-lysophosphatidylethanolamine in homogenates of rat heart, rat brain and dog brain |CITS: [6308001][6726229][10428468]|, and the fact that radiolabelled N-acyl-lysophosphatidylethanolamine was hydrolysed to |FRAME: N-Acylethanolamines "N-acylethanolamines"| by the microsomal preparations of rat heart and dog brain |CITS: [6308001][6726229]|. In this route NAPE is first hydrolyzed to N-acyl-lysophosphatidylethanolamine and a free fatty acid by a |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.4| (PLA2) or a similar enzyme, followed by the action of |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.39| (lysophospholipase D) |CITS: [6726229]|. The pathway was confirmed in a study that demonstrated the predicted enzymatic activities both in vivo and in vitro. Several PLA-2 enzymes (including groups IB, IIA and V of the secretory PLA2s) demonstrated the activity, with the most active one being |FRAME: HS10199| |CITS: [14998370]|. A second enzyme that catalyzes this cleavage was shown to be |FRAME: HS02085|, a lysophospholipase/phospholipase B that selectively hydrolyzes N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines and lyso N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines |CITS: [16818490]|. The second activity in this route was confirmed for |FRAME: HS06258| |CITS: [14998370]|., The third route starts like the second one, with the hydrolysis of NAPE to N-acyl-lysophosphatidylethanolamine and a free fatty acid by PLA2 or |FRAME: HS02085|, but continues with the removal of the second sn acyl group, also catalyzed by |FRAME: HS02085| |CITS: [16818490]|. The resulting glycerophospho-N-(acyl)eathanolamine is then converted to |FRAME: CPD-7598| by the action of |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.46| (|FRAME: HS00157|) |CITS: [18227059]|., Even though all three routes have been verified to operate in vivo, it appears that different N-acyleathanolamines are synthesized in vivo by different routes dependent on the identity of their acyl chains |CITS: [18227059]|.

Summary: General Background, The mold |FRAME: TAX-746128| produces the meroterpenoid |FRAME: CPD0-1436| |CITS: [16561815][14809278]|, which irreversibly binds to and inhibits |FRAME: HS03371-MONOMER| (MetAP2, |FRAME: EC-3.4.11.18 "EC 3.4.11.18"|) and has been studied for its anti-angiogenic properties |CITS: [9177176][17678422]|. |FRAME: CPD0-1436 Fumagillin| also has pharmaceutical potential for the treatment of microsporidiosis, and is the only effective chemical treatment currently available for honey bee nosemiasis, which is caused by parasitic fungi from the |FRAME: TAX-6029| phylum |CITS: [12075057][24621007]|. See also |CITS: [31861936]|., The compound is structurally composed of a highly oxygenated cyclohexane-containing terpenoid (|FRAME: CPD-26043|) that is esterified with a decatetraenedioic acid. |FRAME: CPD-26043 Fumigallol| is derived from the sesquiterpene |FRAME: CPD-13402|, which has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-746128| |CITS: [Nozoe76]|., The gene cluster encoding |FRAME: CPD0-1436| biosynthesis was identified based on the presence of a polyketide synthase gene (since the decatetraenedioic acid moirty was predicted to be produced by a reduced polyketide pathway) and two genes encoding methionine aminopeptidases, which provide a self-resistance mechanism against the effects of |FRAME: CPD0-1436| |CITS: [23488861]|. The cluster was later shown to be a part of a region that contains the genetic machinery for three natural products (|FRAME: Fumitremorgins fumitremorgin|, |FRAME: CPD0-1436|, and |FRAME: CPD-26054|), with the genes encoding fumagillin and pseurotin biosynthesis physically intertwined in a single supercluster |CITS: [24082142]|., About This Pathway, The pathway starts with the terpene cyclase |FRAME: G-124247|, which is a member of the UbiA family. Despite its low similarity to other members of the family, the cyclase was shown to act on |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, forming |FRAME: CPD-13402| |CITS: [23488861]|. The next enzyme of the pathway is a multifunctional cytochrome P450 encoded by the |FRAME: G-124251| gene, which catalyzes a very complex transformation, comprising hydroxylation, bicyclic ring-opening, and two epoxidations, generating the sesquiterpenoid core skeleton of |FRAME: CPD0-1436| |CITS: [24568283]|. The combined action of a second oxygenase and a methyltranferase adds a methoxy group at C6, and a ketoreductase converts the oxo group at C5 to a hydroxyl group, forming |FRAME: CPD-26043|., In a parallel branch, the |FRAME: MONOMER-124252| condenses acetyl-CoA with 5 molecules of malonyl-CoA, forming the decatetraenedioate side chain, which remains bound to the synthase. An acyltransferase transfers the chain to the 5-hydroxy group of |FRAME: CPD-26043|, forming |FRAME: CPD-26044|. The final step of the pathway is catalyzed by a third oxygenase, which cleaves the side chain at C10'-C11' and further oxidizes of the aldehyde intermediate into |FRAME: CPD0-1436| |CITS: [24568283]|.

|FRAME: DIHYDROPTERIN-CH2OH-PP| (6-hydroxymethyl-dihydropterin diphosphate) is the pterin precursor for the biosynthesis of several important cofactors, including |FRAME:THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate|, |FRAME: CPD-10763| and |FRAME: CPD-10764|., The compound is always synthesized from GTP, but the enzymes involved may differ among organisms., This pathway variant has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-810|, obligate intracellular bacteria that cause a wide variety of infectious diseases in humans and animals. Unlike other intracellular bacteria that salvage |FRAME:THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| or its precursors from their hosts, many Chlamydia species have retained the ability to synthesize folate., While the |FRAME: PWY-6147 "cannonical pathway"|, which is found in most bactreria and in eukaryotes, starts with |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.16|, the Chlamydial pathway variant starts with |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.25|, an enzyme that usually functions in flavin biosynthesis |CITS: [25006229]|., The product is then isomerized to |FRAME: DIHYDRONEOPTERIN-P| by a unique Chlamydial isomerase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-34499| gene. In most organisms this enzyme only catalyzes |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.24|. However, in |FRAME: TAX-810| the enzyme has evolved to afford the additional activity seen in this pathway |CITS: [25006229]|., The last two steps are identical to the cannonical pathway - the resulting |FRAME: DIHYDRO-NEO-PTERIN| is converted to |FRAME: AMINO-OH-HYDROXYMETHYL-DIHYDROPTERIDINE| by |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.25|, and the last reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.6.3|, which in |FRAME: TAX-810| is a bifunctional enzyme that also catalyzes |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.15|., The unusual pathway is probably a result of a loss of the |FRAME: EG11375| and |FRAME: G-10191| genes, which encode the enzymes that catalyze the first two steps in the cannonical pathway, and the evolution of other enzymes to fulfill the missing roles.

The |FRAME: Cyanopeptolins cyanopeptolins| are a class of cyclic peptides produced by cyanobacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-1125|, |FRAME: TAX-54304|, and |FRAME: TAX-1163| genera. They are formed by nonribosomal peptides synthases (NRPSs). The cyanopeptolins usually consist of a six-residue peptide that is formed into a ring by a beta-lactone bridge (and are thus depsipeptides). The first position is usually |FRAME: THR|, which links to one or two residues via an ester bound on the beta-hydroxyl group. In some cases the threonine unit is substituted by a hydroxy methyl proline unit and the ring-closing ester bond is formed with this hydroxy group. The third position is always either |FRAME: CPD-26950| (Ahp) or a derivative of it. All other positions are highly variable., |FRAME: CPD-26950| has also been reported from other organisms, such as the myxobacterium |FRAME: TAX-52| |CITS: [24171398]| and the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1963| |CITS: [30087936]|., The enzymes responsible for formation of |FRAME: CPD-26950| were discovered in the myxobacterium |FRAME: TAX-52|, which produces crocapeptins, which have a cyanopeptolin-like skeleton containing |FRAME: CPD-26950| |CITS: [24171398]|., Two enzymes were shown to convert an |FRAME: PRO| residue to |FRAME: CPD-26950|. The first enzyme is a cytochrome P450 that hydroxylates the proline residue at position 5. The second enzyme is an isomerase that rearranges the structure to form |FRAME: CPD-26950| |CITS: [24171398]|

Summary: |FRAME: CHORISMATE Chorismate| is an important intermediate that leads to the biosyntrhesis of several essential metabolites,, including the aromatic amino acids |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|, vitamins E and K, ubiquinone and certain siderophores |CITS: [4200844][2279393]|., In this pathway, which is often referred to as the shikimate pathway, chorismate is synthesized from the central metabolite |FRAME:ERYTHROSE-4P|. , The pathway is found in prokaryotes (mostly bacteria) and several eukaryotes, including ascomycete fungi, apicomplexans, plants and algae |CITS: [16963634]|. The presence of the pathway in many parasites and pathogens, but not in metazoa, makes it a prime drug target |CITS: [17348836]|. The broad-spectrum systemic herbicide |FRAME: CPD0-1308|, which is used to kill weeds (known best under the tradename Roundup) is an inhibitor of the enzyme |FRAME: 2.5.1.19-RXN "5-enolpyruvylshikimate-3-phosphate synthase"| (EC 2.5.1.19), which catalyzes a reaction in the pathway (the condensation of |FRAME: SHIKIMATE-5P| and |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to form |FRAME: 3-ENOLPYRUVYL-SHIKIMATE-5P|)., The organization and structure of the shikimate pathway enzymes varies between taxonomic groups |CITS: [2824247]|, with a differential distribution of fused genes. In most prokaryotes the seven shikimate pathway enzymes are encoded as separate polypeptides. The plant enzymes (which are nucleus encoded, but assumed to function within the plastid) are also encoded as separate polypeptides, with the exception of AroD and AroE that have fused to a single bifunctional polypeptide., In contrast, all fungi, as well as the apicomplexan |FRAME: TAX-5811|, possess a pentafunctional supergene which includes conserved domains homologous to the genes (in fusion order) AroB, AroA, AroL/K, AroD, and AroE |CITS:[2825635][14711585]|., In |FRAME: TAX-562|, the first reaction in the pathway is catalyzed by three separate enzymes, each of which is subject to feedback inhibition by one of the three amino acids that are synthesized from chorismate - |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|., The enzyme subject to regulation by tryptophan (encoded by |FRAME: EG10080|) cannot be inhibited more than 60 percent, ensuring that sufficient enzymatic activity is present to permit synthesis of the other four metabolites synthesized from chorismate even in the presence of all three amino acids |CITS: [Pittard04]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "Hapalindole-type alkaloids"| are a group of hybrid isoprenoid-indole alkaloids produced solely by members of Subsection V of the cyanobacteria, such as the |FRAME: TAX-1190| and |FRAME: TAX-162985| species. These compounds often have antibacterial, antimycotic, or antialgal activities., Since the initial isolation of |FRAME: CPD-20793| in 1984 |CITS: [Moore84]|, more than 80 members of this family have been isolated |CITS: [Moore87][Smitka92][Park92][Stratmann94][17315959][19371071]|. All of these compounds have an isonitrile- or isothiocyanate-containing indole alkaloid skeleton, with a cyclized isoprene unit. The major classes of the hapalindole-type molecules are the |FRAME: Hapalindoles hapalindoles|, the |FRAME: Fischerindoles fischerindoles|, the |FRAME: Welwitindolinones welwitindolinones|, and the |FRAME: Ambiguines ambiguines|, which differ in their core structure., The first biosynthetic pathway for a hapalindole-type alkaloid was reported from |FRAME: TAX-230521|, which was the only axenic cyanobacterial hapalindole-type-molecule producer available at the time. The genome of the organism was sequenced, and searches for putative genes encoding isonitrile synthase and prenyltransferase have identified a cluster of 32 protein-coding genes involved in ambiguine biosynthesis. This discovery was made by two different labs, which named the genes in the cluster amb and fam, respectively |CITS: [24180436][26629885]|., In addition to genes unique to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "hapalindole-type alkaloids"|, the cluster contains homologs of the trpA-E genes, which are responsible for |FRAME: TRP| biosynthesis, as well as five dedicated genes for |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, |FRAME: CPD-4211|, and |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| biosynthesis., The first committed step in the pathway is the addition of an isonitrile function to |FRAME: TRP|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.25| |CITS: [16206308]|. The enzyme is known to use |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-20766| |CITS: [16217820]|. The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.11|, which catalyzes an Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent monooxygenation at C-3 of the substrate, followed by decarboxylation and dehydration to form a cis C-C double bond |CITS: [24180436][28212039]|. The third enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.146|, catalyzes geranylation of the intermediate, forming the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-20795| |CITS: [26629885]|., This intermediate is the last common intermediate in the synthesis of the different hapalindole-type alkaloids, as different organisms possess different cyclases that form different core structures while acting on it. When orthologous gene clusters were sequenced from two fischerindole-producing strains - |FRAME: TAX-83542| (the fim cluster) and |FRAME: TAX-1930929| (the fis cluster), it was found that the two strains possess a new cyclase-encoding gene not found in other, non fischerindole-producing strains. Analysis of this enzyme (encoded by the |FRAME: G-58197| and |FRAME: G-58196| genes) showed that it forms |FRAME: CPD-20797|, which is likely to serve as the starting compound for formation of all other 12-epi-fischerindoles |CITS: [28288107]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-7957| and |FRAME: PWY-7959|.

|FRAME:TAX-1148| is an cyanobacterium which is known to accumulate carotenoid pigments such as |FRAME:CPD-7850| |CITS:[Bramley85]|, |FRAME:CPD1F-130| and the myxoxanthophyll |FRAME:CPD-17672| |CITS:[11479383]| but not the ketocarotinoid |FRAME:CPD-7847| known to be produced in various bacteria, algae (see |FRAME:PWY-5288|) and very few species of the plant genus Adonis (see |FRAME:PWY-7636|) |CITS:[18987067]|. Although the genome of |FRAME:TAX-1148| has been sequenced |CITS:[8905231]| only a limited number of the genes involved in the biosynthesis of various carotinoids in Synechocystis have been characterized to date (summarized in |CITS:[17643187]|)., Amongst them are two genes encoding for enzymes connected to the formation of xanthophylls and myxoxanthophylls. The β-carotene 4-monoketolase encoded by crtO was shown to exhibit asymmetric β-carotene monoketolase activity forming |FRAME:CPD-7850| from |FRAME:CPD1F-129|. It could be demonstrated that the crtO encoded enzyme catalyzed a completely different reaction as observed for other bacterial, fungal, algal or higher plant β-carotene ketolases which have been associated with oxygen dependent dioxygenases (see also |FRAME:PWY-5288| and |FRAME:PWY-7636|) |CITS:[9092504] [23220023]|. The other crucial enzyme in the pathway, commonly regarded as catalyzing its rate-limiting step(s), is the β-carotene hydroxylase encoded by crtR. The enzyme expressed in transformed |FRAME:CPD1F-129|-producing E. coli produced mainly |FRAME:CPD1F-130| and considerably less |FRAME:CPD-7409| indicating a symmetrical action of the crtR encoded enzyme on both 3- and 3'-positions of the β-ionone rings |CITS:[9664719] [10618204]|. In addition, it could be demonstrated in crtR deletion experiments that the crtR encoded β-carotene hydroxylase also 3'-hydroxylated |FRAME:CPD-7850| forming |FRAME:CPD-7861| which accumulated in the wild-type but not in the crtR-deficient mutant |CITS:[11479383]|. Both crtO and crtR from |FRAME:TAX-1148| did not have any homology with related ketolases and hydroxylases from bacteria and plants |CITS:[17415558] [21673887]| and seem to have originated evolutionary from different ancestor proteins |CITS:[9092504] [9664719]|. , In contrary to other cyanobacteria the β-carotene hydroxylase of |FRAME:TAX-1148| (crtR) was multifunctional and also involved in the biosynthesis of myxoxanthophylls |CITS:[18708496]|. The myxoxanthophylls in cyanobacteria of even the same genus can be very different with regard to the associated sugar moiety. For example, the myxoxanthophyll in |FRAME:TAX-32049| is |FRAME:CPD-11450| with fucoside as the attached sugar (see |FRAME:PWY-6279|) whereas the myxoxanthophyll found in the very closely related |FRAME:TAX-1148| is |FRAME:CPD-17672|, which sugar moiety is a 2,4-dimethylated fucoside |CITS:[11479383]|. A crtR deficient Synechocystis mutant (Δcrtr) accumulated in addition to |FRAME:CPD1F-129| and |FRAME:CPD-7850| also |FRAME:CPD-17673| which only occurs in minor amounts in the wild-type and is considered an intermediate to be 3-hydroxylated by crtR to form |FRAME:CPD-17672|, the major myxoxanthophyll in |FRAME:TAX-1148| |CITS:[10431816] [11479383]|.

General Background, Betaxanthins represent a subclass of betalains, the nitrogen-containing compounds , that replace the anthocyanins in the order of Caryophyllales and some higher fungi |CITS: [12620337]| |CITS: [16212790]|. , These pigments are biosynthesized by the condensation of betalamic acid (|FRAME:PWY-5394|) and amino acids/amines , forming a Schiff-base that causes the yellow to orange colors (λ max 470-486 nm) |CITS: [Christinet04]|., Pigments such as anthocyanins and carotenoids are important ecological means to attract pollinators. It could be , demonstrated that betalains are equally developed pigments to fill out this physiological function. Betaxanthins are , able to fluoresce by absorbing blue light and emitting green light |CITS: [16177911]|. That implies a complex , light-filtering system to create a contrasting fluorescent pattern as violet betacyanins absorb those emitted wavelengths , of the yellow betaxanthins. Those findings about fluorescent flowers have been discussed as a new possibility for , pollinator perception |CITS: [16163341]|., About This Pathway, This pathway demonstrates the formation of betaxanthins such as portulacaxanthin II , and dopaxanthin by means of non-enzymatic condensation from the amino acids L-tyrosine and L-DOPA, respectively. , Tyrosinases have been described as capable to use those betaxanthins |CITS: [16277424]| as substrates for further , metabolization. , From those results, an alternative pathway has been proposed for the formation of betanidin which involves a tyrosinase , activity that converts dopaxanthin into dopaxanthinquinone. Dopaxanthinquinone is than spontaneously cyclisized into , betanidin |CITS: [15805475]|. A similar approach has been undertaken to delineate alternative metabolism for the , formation of 2-descarboxy-betanidin (compare |FRAME:PWY-5439|) by acting of those tyrosinases on the amine-derived , intermediates such as dopamine-betaxanthin to produce the corresponding quinone |CITS: [15968512]|. This article , also describes miraxanthin III (tyramine as amine moiety) as an alternative substrate for the tyrosinase to form , dopamine-betaxanthin, usually derived from the precursor dopamine.

General Background, Diverse structures of anthocyanins significantly contribute to flower color, an , important floricultural trait in ornamental plants. The 3-O-glucosylated anthocyanins represent the first stable , molecules which are further decorated through glycosylation, acylation and methylation involved in fine adjustment , and color variation and stabilization |CITS: [Heller94]|. , Antocyanidins often occur as sophoroside, i.e. a diglucoside that consists of glucose attached to the , 2''-O-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of anthocyanidins. Such sophoroside, frequently acylated and , methylated, are widely found in such plant families as Lamiacea |CITS: [11557083]|, Convolvulaceae , |CITS: [15577190]| |CITS: [1367882]| |CITS: [7763602]| |CITS: [7492373]| |CITS: [16045946]| and Ranunculacea , |CITS: [8722091]| |CITS: [12031427]|. The anthocyanidin that confers the bright blue color to |FRAME:TAX-35883| , (a member of the Convolvulacea) is a sophoroside that forms a complex with several caffeoyl residues, known , as |FRAME:CPD-7840| (HBA). Reddish-brown flowers of dusky mutants of |FRAME:TAX-35883| contain , |FRAME:CPD-7841| (WBA) representing the most favorite flower hue for Japanese floriculturists |CITS: [15842621]|. , Anthocyanidin sophoroside and their derivatives have been demonstrated to exhibit a strong inhibition of , maltase when subjected to an α-glucosidase (AGH) inhibitory assay. Acylation of the anthocyanidin , sophoroside increased the inhibitory action substantially |CITS: [11308352]|. Acylation as a promoting agent , has also been shown for the antimutagenicity effect against |FRAME:TAX-90371| TA 98 caused , by anthocyanidin sophoroside |CITS: [10227139]| |CITS: [11515552]|. Although anthocyanidin sophoroside , and derivatives are induced by UV-B (290-320 nm) and act as protectants UV-A irradiation (320-400 nm) , produces a down regulation of those anthocyanins implying complex interactions between UVA and UVB , responses that remain to be addressed |CITS: [11421075]|., About This Pathway, The crucial step in the formation of anthocyanidin sophoroside as precursors for , HBA and WBA in Ipomoea is catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside 2-O''-glucosyltransferase (3GGT). , The enzyme adds glucose to anthocyanidin 3-glucosides at the 2''-O-position of the glucose moiety , forming the corresponding sophorosides. Although the enzyme accepts all three major anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside, , anthocyanidin 3,5-diglucoside are not suitable substrates for the 3GGT |CITS: [15842621]|., The reddish-brown hue of the flowers (WBA) in mutants of Ipomoea is based on pelargonidin- based anthocyanins , whereas the blue flower color (HBA) in this plant has been synthesized from cyanidin-based anthocyanins. It has , been found that all the mutants are deficient in a gene that encodes flavonoid 3'-hydroxylase (compare |FRAME:PWY1F-823|), , involved in the earlier steps towards the biosynthesis of anthocyanins |CITS: [14581624]|.

Summary: Organosulfonate compounds are found in the environment as both natural products and xenobiotics.  They are catabolized by microorganisms that utilize the carbon and sulfur moieties.  Aliphatic C<sub>3</sub> sulfonates are widespread natural products found in the environment and are derived from microbial, plant and animal sources.  The bacterial catabolism of C<sub>3</sub> sulfonates such as |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| (racemic sulfolactate), |FRAME: CPD-380|, and |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| has been studied.  The work has focused on the catabolism of the carbon moiety, the fate of the sulfonate group, and the transport systems necessary for organosulfonates to cross the cell membrane.  Bioinformatics analyses have shown a diversity in pathways of sulfonate degradation in bacteria from both marine and terrestrial environments (in |CITS: [20007648]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16341843]|)., To date, three desulfonation pathways have been proposed for the degradation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| including:, (1) |FRAME: PWY-6616|: direct desulfonation of |FRAME: CPD-367| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-8144|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-12191| and |FRAME: G-12192| genes. |FRAME: CPD-11799| is isomerized to |FRAME: CPD-367| via |FRAME: CPD-380| by two dehydrogenases of opposite stereochemistry, encoded by |FRAME: G-12189| and |FRAME: G-12190|., (2) |FRAME: PWY-6637|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), followed by decarboxylation of sulfopyruvate to |FRAME: SULFOACETALDEHYDE| by the |FRAME: CPLX-8153| encoded by the |FRAME: G-12226| and |FRAME: G-12227| genes, desulfonation to acetyl phosphate by |FRAME: G-12229|, and conversion of acetyl phosphate to acetyl-CoA., (3) |FRAME: PWY-6638|: oxidation of |FRAME: RS-3-Sulfolactate| to |FRAME: CPD-380| by |FRAME: MONOMER-15905| (|FRAME: G-12225|), transamination of |FRAME: CPD-380| to |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE|, and desulfonation of |FRAME: L-CYSTEATE| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| by the product of  the |FRAME: G-12230| gene., In all of these pathways the |FRAME: HSO3| or |FRAME: SO3| produced by the desulfonation reaction is proposed to be transported through the cell membrane and oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE| by a periplasmic enzyme, possibly the product of the |FRAME: G-9517|/|FRAME: G-9518| genes in some organisms |CITS: [19581363][20150239] [16341843]|., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-89187| both the second and third pathways occur and function simultaneously, as depicted by this superpathway |CITS: [19581363]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-575 Cyclohexane-1-carboxylate| is formed by oxidative microbial degradation of n-alkylcycloparaffins and anaerobic degradation of benzoate. It also occurs in nature as a functional group in more complex compounds (e.g. polyketide antibiotics from Streptomyces species). Several pathways for its degradation, both aerobic and anaerobic, have been described., The first anaerobic degradation pathway was described from |FRAME: TAX-1076|, in which the compound is degraded via |FRAME: CPD-558| and modified β-oxidation steps that yield three acetyl-CoA molecules and one CO2 molecule |CITS: [10781543]| (see |FRAME: PWY-301|). |FRAME: TAX-1076| is capable of rapid growth (doubling time of 7-8 h) on |FRAME: CPD-575| under oxic or photosynthetic conditions. The compound was initially believed to be an intermediate in anaerobic benzoate degradation |CITS: [ 5807211][5370288]|, but later research has shown that it is funneled into the anaerobic benzoate degradation pathway at the level of |FRAME:CPD-533|., Two enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-814| and |FRAME: G-816| genes, participate in this side pathway. The first one is a CoA ligase that activates |FRAME: CPD-575| into a CoA ester at the expense of ATP hydrolysis |CITS: [8572887][9177244]|. The second enzyme is a dehydrogenase that insets a double bond at the 1(2) position of the ring |CITS: [10781543]|., This pathway is rather rare. A more common anaerobic pathway is |FRAME: PWY-8485|.

Penicillium species have been exploited by the pharmaceutical industry for a long time as a source of bioactive metabolites such as Penicillium chrysogenum which is a well-known producer of the antibiotic |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| |CITS:[22865068] [23662444]|. Secondary metabolites of the diketopiperazine (DKP) alkaloid class |CITS:[Martins07] [23955505]| produced by the fungal genus Penicillium in pathways such as |FRAME:PWY-7605|, |FRAME:PWY-7607| and |FRAME:PWY-7608| (this pathway - see also |FRAME:PWY-7609|) frequently contaminate food and forage plants and are considered harmful because of the known neurotoxicity of, for instance |FRAME:CPD-17381| |CITS:[16345552] [613945]|. Moreover, |FRAME:CPD-17394| has been found to inhibit cell proliferation and arrests the cell cycle in the M phase of human Jurkat cells presumably by inhibiting tubulin polymerization indicating a potential as cell-cycle specific drug |CITS:[15276324]|. In addition, an epimer of |FRAME:CPD-17394|, i.e. epi-neoxalin was usable as chemotaxonomic marker in Penicillium tulipae |CITS:[Overy06]|. , |FRAME:CPD-17394 Neoxaline| and |FRAME:CPD-17393| were identified in Penicillium chrysogenum |CITS:[24225953]| but the compounds are probably not restricted to the genus. It appears that |FRAME:CPD-17394| is wider distributed in the fungal Aspergillaceae family. The compound has also been reported from a culture broth of Aspergillus japonicas and shown to exhibit a weak stimulation of the central nervous system in mice |CITS:[500498]|. , The sequencing of the Penicillium chrysogenum genome |CITS:[18820685]| provided the platform for in-depth bioinformatics analysis, molecular biology and biochemical approaches which allowed the elucidation of the |FRAME:PWY-7608| (this pathway) and closely related pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-7605|, |FRAME:PWY-7607|). It has been shown that the biosynthetic gene cluster (roq) is responsible for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17394|. Bioinformatics studies revealed the structure of the roq cluster consisting of 7 genes and corresponding putative functions based on sequence homology with characterized enzymes |CITS:[22118684]|. , The pathway descending from the |FRAME:PWY-7607| via |FRAME:CPD-17392| with |FRAME:CPD-17394| as the final product is catalyzed by two enzymes, the roquefortine/glandoline O-methyltransferase (roqN) which also operates in the |FRAME:PWY-7607| and a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase encoded by roqO which also is multifunctional and is involved in oxygenation reactions in |FRAME:PWY-7607| and the conversion of the novel intermediate |FRAME:CPD-17393| to |FRAME:CPD-17394|. The molecular function of the former enzyme roquefortine/glandoline O-methyltransferase has been shown through RNAi silencing |CITS:[22118684]| and a combination of gene knock-out, metabolite profiling and gene expression data analysis |CITS:[23776469] [24225953]|. The latter enzyme, i.e. cytochrome P450 glandicoline/roquefortine monooxygenase catalyzed in this pathway the hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17393| at C-9 followed by the cleavage of C-9 and N-14 and the subsequent formation of a bond between C-2 and N-11 forming |FRAME:CPD-17394| |CITS:[24225953]|.

Names: penicillin G and penicillin V biosynthesis
Summary: |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G Penicillin G| also known as benzylpenicillin is a hydrophobic β-lactam antibiotic |CITS:[13622762] [23228980]| which is mainly produced by filamentous fungi of the Aspergillaceae genus Penicillium |CITS:[1815263]| but has also been observed in the genus Aspergillus from the same family |CITS:[18942174]|. It has been generally regarded as indispensable in the treatment against gram-negative bacteria, for instance Treponema pallidum, the agent causing the sexual-transmissible disease syphilis |CITS:[25387188] [23228980]| and is listed on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines which contains medications required in every elementary health system |CITS:[WHO15]|. , The sequence of reactions that convert |FRAME:ISOPENICILLIN-N| (see |FRAME:PWY-5629|) to |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| is bifurcated. One branch is leading from |FRAME:ISOPENICILLIN-N| directly to |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| while the other branch forms |FRAME:6-AMINOPENICILLANATE| as intermediate towards |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G|. In both cases |FRAME:CPD-207| is the activated acyl which attaches the |FRAME:PHENYLACETATE| side chain to either |FRAME:ISOPENICILLIN-N| or |FRAME:6-AMINOPENICILLANATE|. Remarkably all the required reactions are catalyzed by one multifunctional protein characterized from both Penicillium chrysogenum |CITS:[2829713] [2110531] [8384123] [2555269] [2120195] [8396910] [8224864] [8344300]| and Aspergillus nidulans |CITS:[12709055] [2110531] [2166227] [2120195]|, which acts as isopenicillin-N acyltransferase for the direct catalysis of |FRAME:ISOPENICILLIN-N| to |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| or as amidopenicillin N amidohydrolase forming the pathway intermediate |FRAME:6-AMINOPENICILLANATE| and 6-aminopenicillate acyltransferase catalyzing the subsequent acylation to yield |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G|. The gene (penDE) encoding this protein has been shown to be associated with an penicillin biosynthetic cluster |CITS:[2129535]|. , In addition, the penDE encoded protein also functioned as penicillin G amidase cleaving off |FRAME:PHENYLACETATE| and thus forming |FRAME:6-AMINOPENICILLANATE| and as an penicillin G transacylase by reversibly exchanging side chains such as |FRAME:PHENYLACETATE| of |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| with |FRAME:CPD-10902| in |FRAME:CPD-9196| and vice versa |CITS:[8344300]|. The molecular structure and maturing of the penDE encoded protein has been investigated in detail and crucial amino acid residues like Ser309 identified |CITS:[8082826] [20223213]|. The enzyme is situated in peroxisomes as indicated by the microbody targeting motif and shown by using mutants lacking the microbody targeting signal. In these mutants the enzyme was not located in the peroxisomes and unable to produce |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| |CITS:[1581347]|., As mentioned before |FRAME:CPD-207| is the activated acyl donor attaching the |FRAME:PHENYLACETATE| side chain to |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G|. The gene encoding for the respective phenylacetyl-CoA ligase (phI) generating |FRAME:CPD-207| from |FRAME:PHENYLACETATE| was identified in Penicillium chrysogenum and shown not to be a part of the |FRAME:PENICILLIN-G| cluster |CITS:[2129535]|. Interestingly, the phenylacetyl-CoA ligase encoded by phl is located to peroxisomes which prompted the suggestion that the also peroxisomal located isopenicillin N acyltransferase (penDE) form a functional complex with phenylacetyl-CoA ligase (phl) in the |FRAME:PWY-7716| |CITS:[16321143]|. This notion requires an active transport of precursors into the peroxisomes which has been addressed in various studies |CITS:[23053082] [25436576] [22160272]| and is a characteristic feature of specialized metabolite biosynthesis |CITS:[25709603]|.

|FRAME: CPD-16768 Mycosamine| (3-amino, 3-6 dideoxy D-mannose) is the amino sugar present in polyene macrolide antibiotics, represented by |FRAME: Candicidins|, |FRAME: CPD-17211|, |FRAME: CPD-17212| and |FRAME: CPD-17213|. Mycosamine plays a critical role in conferring the antifungal properties exhibited by polyene antibiotics |CITS: [9380018][16045354]|., Mycosamine is synthesized in a GDP-activated form from the primary metabolite |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| in three steps. In the first step, which is common to several modified sugars, |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| is dehydrated to |FRAME: GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE|, which becomes |FRAME: CPD-17205| in the second step through a 3,4-isomerization. The product then undergoes a transamination to form |FRAME: CPD-17206|., While genes encoding the first and last enzymes of the pathway have been found in the biosynthetic clusters of all relevant organisms, no gene that encodes an enzyme that would catalyze the second step, GDP-4-dehydro-6-deoxy-mannose-3,4-isomerase, has been discovered yet.

Summary: The concept of a plant wound hormone was first proposed in 1892 |CITS: [Wiesner92]|. The wound hormone is a compound that stimulates cell division near a trauma site to form a protective callus and to heal the damaged tissue. A quantitative assay for measuring the activity of the wound hormone was developed in 1927, measuring renewal of the parenchymous lining of the seed chambers of immature bean pods |CITS: [Wehnelt27]|., An active compound responsible for this activity was detected in 1937 and named traumatin for the Greek word trauma (wound) |CITS: [English37][17751236][16653492]|. However, two years later the authors reported that the compound is a dicarboxylic acid and renamed it accordingly as |FRAME: CPD-25932 "traumatic acid"| |CITS: [17791417]|., With the discovery of |FRAME: 12-OXO-TRANS-10-DODECENOATE| in 1979 it was realized that the latter is the actual natural wound hormone, and that |FRAME: CPD-25932| is formed non-enzymatically by its oxidation in the presence of oxygen |CITS: [16660762]|., |FRAME: 12-OXO-TRANS-10-DODECENOATE Traumatin| is an oxidation product of polyunsaturated fatty acids in plant tissues, formed by the combined action of lipoxygenases and hydroperoxide lyases. Lipoxygenases (LOX) are ubiquitous enzymes in eukaryotes. Depending on the positional specificities, they are further classified as 9-LOX and 13-LOX, converting poly unsaturated fatty acids to 9-hydroperoxides and 13-hydroperoxides, respectively. In plants, most reported LOXs are 13-LOXs, which is important in the biosynthesis of the plant hormone jasmonic acid (see |FRAME:PWY-735|). , The hydroperoxide intermediates can be converted to aldehydes and oxoacids by hydroperoxide lyases (HPL). HPLs are divided into two groups, 9-HPL and 13-HPL, depending on their substrate preferences, either being 9-hydroperoxides, or 13-hydroperoxides. 13-HPL activity has been detected in many plants. The |FRAME: CPLX-1383| encoded by the |FRAME: G-1082| gene was shown to act on products of both LOX9 and LOX13, forming |FRAME: 12-OXO-CIS-9-DODECENOATE|, which is subsequently converted to |FRAME: 12-OXO-TRANS-10-DODECENOATE| (though the final conversion step has not been described). , |FRAME: 12-OXO-CIS-9-DODECENOATE| was shown to be converted to |FRAME: CPD-19335| via |FRAME: RXN-23334| |CITS: [9727603]|, although a non-enzymatic mechanism was also proposed |CITS: [11027649]|., In addition, the aldehydes and alcohols produced by 13-HPL are often responsible for the flavors or odors of plants, for example the odor of cucumbers. , One of the products of 13-HPL, |FRAME: CIS-3-HEXENOL|, is converted in a single reaction to |FRAME: CPD-12846|, the major volatile released upon mechanical wounding of the leaves of |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [17163881]|.

General Background, The cyanopeptolins are a class of cyclic peptides produced by cyanobacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-1125|, |FRAME: TAX-54304|, and |FRAME: TAX-1163| genera. They are formed by nonribosomal peptides synthases (NRPSs)., The |FRAME: Cyanopeptolins cyanopeptolins| usually consist of a six-residue peptide that is formed into a ring by a beta-lactone bridge (and are thus depsipeptides). The first position is usually |FRAME: THR|, which links to one or two residues via an ester bound on the beta-hydroxyl group. In some cases the threonine unit is substituted by a hydroxy methyl proline unit and the ring-closing ester bond is formed with this hydroxy group. The third position is always either |FRAME: CPD-26950| (Ahp) or a derivative of it. All other positions are highly variable., A side chain of variable length is attached via the amino group of the threonine unit. Two major types of side chains are common: one consisting of one or two amino acids and an aliphatic fatty acid from formic to octanoic acid, and one with a glyceric acid unit at the N-terminus |CITS: [16774586]|., Most cyanopeptolins are serine protease inhibitors, and are likely produced as a defense against predation. They can be neurotoxic towards vertebrates |CITS: [20405925][24561424][29949853]|., The first cyanopeptolins, cyanopeptolins A-D, were first isolated from |FRAME: TAX-267872| in 1993 |CITS: [8244882]|. Since then cyanopeptolin-type peptides have been isolated from a wide variety of cyanobacteria. Due to a lack of an accepted classification system, the peptides have been given many different names, including micropeptins |CITS: [19260658]|, aeruginopeptins |CITS: [11501278]|; nostopeptins |CITS: [Okino97]|, nostocyclin |CITS: [Kaya96]|, oscillapeptins |CITS: [Itou99]|, and somamides |CITS: [11421730]|., The |FRAME: Micropeptins micropeptins| were first described in 1993, when micropeptins A and B were isolated from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1126|. Both compounds were found to be inhibitors of plasmin and trypsin |CITS: [Okino93]|. The NRPS genes for cyanopeptolin biosynthesis (mcn/oci) in |FRAME: TAX-59625|, |FRAME: TAX-267872|, |FRAME: TAX-449447|, and |FRAME: TAX-329558| were cloned and sequenced |CITS: [17464052][17921284][18192279][18534010]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-26960 "Micropeptin K139"| is a micropeptin that was isolated from |FRAME: CPD-26960|. It consists of the hetadepsipeptide hexanoic acid-Asp-Thr-Arg-Ahp-Ile-N-MeTyr-Ile. The gene cluster involved in its biosynthesis was cloned and sequenced. The |FRAME: G-124572|-|FRAME: G-124573|-|FRAME: G-124574|-|FRAME: G-124575| genes, which encode the NRPSs, are organized as an operon of 26 kb. McnA and McnB have one module each, specific for |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: THR|, respectively. McnC contains four modules (specific for |FRAME: ARG|, |FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: ILE|, and |FRAME: TYR|, with the last one including an N-methyltransferase (MT) domain, and McnE has one module specific for |FRAME: ILE|, as well as a thioesterase (TE) domain |CITS: [21212071]|., As shown later in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-52|, the biosynthesis of cyanopeptolins involves the initial incorporation of |FRAME: PRO|, followed by its hydroxylation by a cytochrome P450 enzyme, and rearrangment of the hydroxylated acid to form |FRAME: CPD-26950| |CITS: [24171398]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8497|). As this information was not yet available when the micropeptin K139 biosynthetic gene cluster was characterized, there has been no discussion of the relevant enzymes, nor was there any discussion of the enzyme(s) responsible for attaching the hexanoate tail.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of, polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl, diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme., Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the, polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a, preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone, molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length., However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain, length., Quinones containing chains of 8 prenyl units are found in all kingdoms of life. They are particularly, common among the |FRAME: TAX-2157| (in the form of menaquinone-8) and the |FRAME: TAX-543|., For a review detailing the distribution of polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|., In |FRAME: TAX-83333| the initial addition of two isoprenyl units to form |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is, catalyzed by |FRAME: FPPSYN-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10508|., Additional isoprenoid units are added sequentially to a maximal length of 8 units by, |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10017|.

Summary: General Background, The major pathway for fatty acid degradation in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans is fatty acid β-oxidation. However, pathways for fatty acid α-oxidation and ω-oxidation have also been characterized in plants and animals (see MetaCyc pathways under |FRAME: Fatty-Acid-Degradation Fatty Acids Degradation|). A mammalian peroxisomal fatty acid α-oxidation pathway for 2-hydroxylated, even numbred, straight chain (unbranched) fatty acids is shown here |CITS: [15644336]|. A variant of this pathway for β-methyl branched (3-methyl branched) fatty acids is shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-387 fatty acid α-oxidation II| (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]| and in |CITS: [17956236]|)., 2-Hydroxylated, even numbered. straight chain fatty acids are found in a subset of mammalian sphingolipids where they are present as the N-acyl chain of ceramide (reviewed in |CITS: [20026285]|). A fatty acid 2-hydroxylase encoded by gene |FRAME: HS02454 FA2H| was recently identified as a catalyzing this C-2 hydroxylation. This hydroxylase has also been suggested to catalyze the initial step of straight chain fatty acid α-oxidation. Although the substrate specificity of this fatty acid 2-hydroxylase has not been extensively studied, it has been shown to hydroxylate the straight chain (unbranched) long (or very long) chain fatty acids that are found in mammalian sphingolipids (|CITS: [15337768][15863841][15644336][21708296][22517924][20519515]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17956236][20026285]|)., An ortholog of the lyase encoded by gene |FRAME: HS05516 HACL1| was identified in |FRAME:TAX-6239| suggesting that this peroxisomal α-oxidation pathway may also be present in invertebrates |CITS: [10468558]|., About This Pathway, In the first step of this fatty acid α-oxidation pathway, a straight chain fatty acid is 2-hydroxylated by the product of gene |FRAME: HS02454 FA2H| which stereospecifically produces the (R)-2-hydroxy enantiomer |CITS: [22517924]|. The subsequent ligase and lyase enzymes can accept both R and S enantiomers of their substrates |CITS: [10191284]|. It is not yet clear whether unsaturated fatty acids are good substrates for the fatty acid 2-hydroxylase (in |CITS: [20519515]|). The 2-hydroxylated fatty acid is then activated to its |FRAME: CO-A coenzyme A| (CoA) derivative. The exact acyl CoA synthetase(s) involved remain unclear. Following import into the peroxisome, the peroxisomal lyase encoded by gene |FRAME: HS05516 HACL1| cleaves the 2-hydroxy-fatty-acyl-CoA to produce a fatty aldehyde that has been shortened by one carbon unit (an n-1 aldehyde) and |FRAME: FORMYL-COA formyl-CoA| |CITS: [9276483]|., Further metabolism of the aldehyde proceeds as in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-387 fatty acid α-oxidation II| |CITS: [15644336]|. A peroxisomal aldehyde dehydrogenase reaction oxidizes the aldehyde to its corresponding fatty acid. No gene(s) has yet been identified that encodes this aldehyde dehydrogenase, although |FRAME: HS01061| (FALDH) has been suggested |CITS: [9662422][17510064]|. Following production of the shortened fatty acid by α-oxidation, it is again activated to its CoA ester. It remains to be established which isoform(s) of ASCL or ACSVL catalyzes this reaction (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|)., The shortened fatty acyl-CoA derivative produced in peroxisomes, or a fatty acyl-CoA that was taken up into peroxisomes from the cytosol, can also undergo limited peroxisomal β-oxidation |CITS: [9469587][15644336]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5136|). Three types of fatty acids are known to undergo limited peroxisomal β-oxidation: |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids|; |FRAME: 2-Me-Branched-234-Sat-FA| (eg. |FRAME: PRISTANATE|); and the bile acid synthesis intermediates |FRAME: CPD-1834| and |FRAME: CPD-1836| (reviewed in |CITS: [20558530]|). The products can be shuttled into mitochondria and undergo further rounds of β-oxidation by either carnitine-dependent or carnitine-independent routes. These routes are tissue-dependent (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|) (see pathway |FRAME: FAO-PWY|)., The various mechanisms of peroxisomal import and export of metabolites involved in this pathway are also under investigation and include the porin encoded by PXMP2, as well as carrier proteins such as that encoded by SLC25A17 (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-9 Ubiquinone-9| (Q-9) has been reported in different types of eukaryotic organisms. It is the only quinone found in many animals, including the common mammals mouse (|FRAME: TAX-10090|) and rat (|FRAME: TAX-10116|), the fish |FRAME: TAX-283036| (walleye), the worm |FRAME: TAX-6239| |CITS: [17482885]|, and certain insects, such as the house fly (|FRAME: TAX-7370|) and the cabbage white butterfly |FRAME: TAX-64459| |CITS: [13673033]|., Q-9 is also synthesized by several fungal species. It has been found in the |FRAME: TAX-5204| species |FRAME: TAX-200324|, |FRAME:TAX-336994| and |FRAME:TAX-198662| |CITS: [Sugiyama88]|, and the |FRAME:TAX-4890| species |FRAME: TAX-4903| |CITS: [13673033]| and |FRAME: TAX-4952| |CITS: [3983092]|. A recent study of the distribution of quinones in fungi belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-5042|, |FRAME: TAX-33183|, and related genera, found that organisms belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-5086| and |FRAME: TAX-5104|, as well as members of the |FRAME: TAX-34384| family, contain Q-9 |CITS: [10768477]|., In addition, Q-9 is common in plants. In general, the most common ubiquinones in plants are Q-9 and Q-10. |FRAME: TAX-4530| |CITS: [20421194]|, |FRAME:TAX-3702| |CITS:[12437513][15784989]| and most algae, including at least green algae (|FRAME: TAX-34125|) and brown algae |CITS: [13673033]|, produce Q-9., For discussion of prokaryotic |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-9| biosynthesis, see |FRAME: PWY-5856|.

Summary: General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic formaldehyde is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms. In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central intermediate., It has been suggested that the formaldehyde concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph would rise to 100mM in less than 1 minute if formaldehyde consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by unrelated or distantly related genes. , About This Pathway, Perhaps the best characterized is the pathway involving |FRAME:CPLX-3381| (GSH-FDH) and |FRAME:CPLX-3404| (FGH). GSH-FDH enzymes are a well studied class of the alcohol dehydrogenase protein family (class III ADH ), |CITS: [ 1872853]| that have been discovered in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Unlike many alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes, GSH-FDH do not exhibit appreciable activity with short aliphatic alcohols. Instead, GSH-FDH enzymes catalyze the NAD-dependent oxidation of long-chain alcohols or hydroxylated fatty acids., Specifically, |FRAME:S-HYDROXYMETHYLGLUTATHIONE| (HMGSH), an adduct formed spontaneously by glutathione (GSH) and formaldehyde (HCHO) , is both the preferred in vitro and presumed in vivo substrate for GSHFDH enzymes., Even though it is formed spontaneously, in certain bacteria |FRAME: S-HYDROXYMETHYLGLUTATHIONE| production is accelerated by a dedicated enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-3403| |CITS: [8631716][8892832][11173978][12904537][7798140][12196016]|.

The occurrence of 7-polyacylated anthocyanins as the main pigments inducing blue color(s) in flowers has been reported from various plant families |CITS:[19554240]|. Many of them are delphinidin derivatives which have been found in the Campanulaceae family, for instance |FRAME:CPD-16561| (see |FRAME:PWY-7458|) |CITS:[Kondo90] [7763601]|. The formation of this pigment, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16561| is different from the anthocyanin 3,5-glucoside derivatives, for instance found in the Gentianaceae family (see |FRAME:PWY-5307|) where |FRAME:CPD-7965| fulfills the same function as |FRAME:CPD-16561| in conferring blue flower colors to this species |CITS:[Goto82]|., The formation of 7-polyacylated cyanidins (this pathway) has its beginning with |FRAME:CPD-15005| which has been formed as a crucial compound before |CITS:[20971893] [22673029]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7256|). The progression of the |FRAME:PWY-7464| has been elucidated by enzymes isolated from sepals of Delphinium grandiflorum assayed with cyanidin 3,7-diglucoside derivative intermediates deduced from the delphinidin 3-rutinoside 7-diglucosides of the |FRAME:PWY-7458|., The noteworthiness of this pathway is the utilization of one acyl-glucose donor, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15283| by both glucosyltransferases and acetyltransferases which further furnish the cyanidin 7-O-side chain. The donor provides both glucosyl- and p-hydroxybenzoyl groups and in doing so serves as a zwitter donor in the |FRAME:PWY-7464| |CITS:[24179131]|. The two acylation steps in the pathway, i.e. the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-15005| to |FRAME:CPD-16602| and |FRAME:CPD-16603| to |FRAME:CPD-16604| have been demonstrated in crude extracts from sepals of Delphinium grandiflorum. Although the cDNA (SCPL2) for the acyl-glucose dependent anthocyanin glucoside(s) acyltransferase was obtained the expression in an recombinant organism failed but its molecular function could be confirmed in vivo in white Delphinium varieties where the gene was absent |CITS:[24179131]|. Two cDNA's encoding for the acyl-glucose dependent anthocyanin 7-O-(6-O-(p-hydroxybenzoyl)-glucoside) glucosyltransferase catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-16602| to |FRAME:CPD-16603| were also isolated, expressed in E. coli and biochemically identified. Both, glucosyltransferase and acyltransferase were localized to the vacuole which coincides with the localization of |FRAME:CPD-16561| |CITS:[24179131]| and the occurrence of other enzymes of the pathway |CITS:[20971893] [22673029]|.

Summary: General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmospheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5265|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the peptidoglycan found in most Gram-negative bacteria, as well as some Gram-positive bacteria. The pathway starts at the cytoplasm, where in six steps the peptidoglycan precursor |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| is synthesized. This precursor is then attached to the memberane acceptor |FRAME:CPD-9646|, generating a molecule known as |FRAME: Lipid-I "lipid I"|., Another transferase then adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding the complete monomeric unit known as |FRAME:NAcMur-Peptide-NAcGlc-Undecaprenols "lipid II"|., This final lipid intermediate is transferred by the MurJ flippase through the membrane. The peptidoglycan monomers are then polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide crosslinks |CITS: [11320055]|. While some of these enzymes are mono-functional, a group of bifunctional proteins possessing both glycosyltransferase and transpeptidase activity plays a major role in this process in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. These bifunctional proteins are known as |FRAME: Class-A-PBPs "Class A Penicillin-binding Proteins"| (PBPs) |CITS: [9791115]|., Peptide crosslinks form between different parts of the peptides depending on the organism. For example, in Mycobacteria and in |FRAME:TAX-562| most links form between the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide to the amino group at the D-center of |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (residue 3) of an adjacent peptide of a second glycan chain (as in |FRAME:TAX-562|). The crosslinking reaction is catalyzed by transpeptidases and involves the cleavage of the D-alanyl-D-alanine bond of the donor peptide, providing the energy to drive the reaction. As a result, the peptides in the peptidoglycan polymers are one or two amino acids shorter than the peptides in the monomers., The transpeptidases include either the bifunctional protein described above (|FRAME: Class-A-PBPs "Class A PBPs"|) or monofunctional proteins, known as |FRAME: Class-B-PBPs "Class B PBPs"|., About the variability of peptidoglycan composition, Peptidoglycan is the only cell wall polymer common to both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, as well as cyanobacteria. The composition and structure of peptidoglycan is rather constant among Gram-negative bacteria., Significant variability is found among Gram-positive bacteria, and is discussed in |FRAME: PWY-5265|.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, The conversion of |FRAME:Me-CoM| to |FRAME: CH4|, which is the final step in the methanogenesis process, involves the reduction of the |FRAME: CoM|-bound methyl group to |FRAME:CH4|. This step is catalyzed by methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR), a key enzyme that is found in all methanogens |CITS: [9782487][16260307]|. Two forms of MCR exist. While MCR-I (encoded by the mcrBDCGA operon, see |FRAME: CPLX-664| for an example) is present in all methanogens, isoenzyme MCR-II (encoded by the mrtBDGA operon, see |FRAME:CPLX-668| for an example) is additionally present in members of the |FRAME: TAX-183939| and the |FRAME: TAX-183925| only |CITS: [2269306]|., Both operons encode additional proteins (McrC and McrD, and mrtD, respectively), whose function is unknown. However, they may be involved in post-translational modification of the α subunit, which contains 4 methylated residues and one thiolated glycine |CITS: [9367957]|., Purified MCR protein contains 2 moles of |FRAME:CPD-7425|, |FRAME: CoM|, and |FRAME:CPD-1281| each |CITS: [6954513][3106338][3094527]|. The enzyme is inactive when purified and resumes activity only when the |FRAME:NI| atom at the center of the |FRAME:CPD-7425| cofactor is reduced to the Ni(I) oxidation state |CITS: [3094527]|. During the reaction, the enzyme forms |FRAME:CPD-1282|, a disulfide of the CoM and CoB coenzymes. This disulfide is then oxidized back to the active forms of the coenzymes by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-321| (see |FRAME:PWY-5207|) |CITS: [ArchMicro155-483][Ferry93][9782487]|.
