Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Opines Opines| are a large family of low molecular weight compounds. The vast majority of opines are secondary amine derivatives resulting from the reduction of the imine formed by condensation of an amino acid with either a keto acid or a sugar. Opines from the |FRAME: CPD-308| family are formed when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| serves as the keto substrate in the condensation reaction, while those of the |FRAME: CPD-309| family are formed when |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is involved in the condensation reaction. Opines of the |FRAME: CPD-15773| and |FRAME: CPD-26410| families are formed by the condensation of an amino acid with a sugar., A small, separate class of opines is the |FRAME: Agrocinopines agrocinopines|, which are sugar-phosphodiesters (e.g., |FRAME: CPD-15774|, which is a phosphodiester of sucrose and L-arabinose)., While opines are found in marine invertebrates, fungi, higher plants and mammals, they are most commonly found in plant crown gall tumors or hairy root tumors, where they are produced by bacteria of the genera |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379|, respectively. Biosynthesis of opines in crown gall tumors is performed by enzymes encoded by genes contained in T-DNA (transfer DNA), which is part of the Ti plasmid (in |FRAME: TAX-357|) or Ri plasmid (in |FRAME: TAX-379|). The plasmids are inserted by the bacteria into the plant genome, where they are integrated and expressed. Those opines are used by the bacteria as energy, carbon and nitrogen sources. Each strain of |FRAME: TAX-357| and |FRAME: TAX-379| induces and catabolizes a specific set of opines, determined by the specific Ti or Ri plasmid they possess. Over 30 different opines have been described., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-25248 "Deoxyfructosyl-L-glutamine"| can be formed by the non-enzymatic reaction of the aldehyde group of |FRAME: CPD-15374| with the amino group of |FRAME: GLN| (the Maillard reaction), followed by a spontaneous isomerization of the sugar, referred to as an Amadori rearrangement |CITS: [2675036]|. However, it has been shown that the reaction is catalyzed by an enzyme during the biosynthesis of some opine compounds in crown gall tumors., The location of genes involved was determined by site directed insertions and deletions in the TR region of the octopine Ti plasmid, pTiB6Tra |CITS: [Ellis84]|. Three enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124421|, |FRAME: G-124422| and |FRAME: G-124423| genes, were shown to be required to catalyze formation of |FRAME: CPD-25248|, its reduction to |FRAME: CPD-15773|, and its further conversion to |FRAME: CPD-26409|, respectively |CITS: [16453491]|., The |FRAME: G-124421| and |FRAME: G-124422| genes are divergently transcribed and all the cis-acting elements that modulate the strength, tissue and developmental specificity, and induction of their expression are found within the regulatory region between the two mas transcription units |CITS: [10628843]|., The plant |FRAME: TAX-4097| contains three Agrobacterium-derived T-DNA sequences inherited from its paternal ancestor |FRAME: TAX-4098|s. One of these loci carries an intact copy of the |FRAME: G-124421| gene, encoding an active mannopine synthase. The gene is expressed at very low levels in |FRAME: TAX-4098| and in most |FRAME: TAX-4097| cultivars, but some cultivars show high expression levels, with detectable levels of |FRAME: CPD-25248| in their roots |CITS: [27125327]|.

One of the most important food plants in the world is rice (Orza sativa). It is the staple food for half of the world's population and the principal food crop in the lower-income countries |CITS:[Seck12]|. The plant family Poaceae is considered the main food resource for human diet and three members of that family, i.e. wheat, rice and corn provide 60% of the calories required by humans worldwide |CITS:[Bennett10]|. Because of this impact on human society rice has been thoroughly researched, showing that during the process of rice domestication the genome was shaped through numerous artificial and natural selections and introgressions. The two cultivars of Oryza sativa, i.e. indica and japonica are thought to have diverged about 200.000 years ago, before domestication began, and have developed some different traits |CITS:[23545218]| which also may explain some divergences in the biochemistry of those cultivars |CITS:[17456599]|. Rice (Oryza sativa) is capable of producing a broad scope of about 15 different types of antimicrobial compounds in response to pathogenic attacks, for instance by the rice blast fungus |FRAME:TAX-318829| |CITS:[16956633] [20615111]|. Oryzalexine, like all the other phytoalexins are formed through bicyclyzation of |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| catalyzed by copalyl/labdadienyl diphosphate synthases (CPS) |CITS:[15341631] [15542489]| and further rearrangements/cyclization via kaurene synthase like (KSL) proteins (see |FRAME:PWY-2981|) |CITS:[17141283]|., Oryza sativa has become popular in the emerging theme of genetic clusters |CITS:[20921179]| which have been reported to be common amongst microbes |CITS:[18216259]| but are rather rare in plants |CITS:[19662496]|. The formation of the rice diterpenoid phytoalexins and allelochemicals, including oryzalexine D and E (this pathway) and oryzalexine A, B and C (see |FRAME:PWY-7489|) originate from biosynthetic gene clusters on chromosome 2 and 4 |CITS:[19662496]|. Oryzalexine have been found in rice induced by UV-irradiation and shown to inhibit the spore germination of the blast fungus Pyricularia oryzae |CITS:[Kato93] [Kato94]|., The |FRAME:PWY-7478| pathway may proceed via different routes which remain to be verified. Most of the enzymes characterized in rice and involved in the biosynthesis of the various diterpenoid phytoalexins have been codon optimized, N-terminally modified for bacterial expression and introduced to an modular metabolic engineered system in E. coli |CITS:[17480080]|. The cytochrome P450 dependent diterpene olefin hydroxylase encoded by KOL4 (also referred to as CYP701A8) was shown to hydroxylate the C3α-position of |FRAME:CPD-4753| to form |FRAME:CPD-16610| and, but with considerably less efficiency, accept |FRAME:CPD-16627| forming |FRAME:CPD-16612| in the process |CITS:[22247270] [23795884]|. The intermediate |FRAME:CPD-16610| is substrate for two cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases which either hydroxylate at the C9β-position to form |FRAME:CPD-16611| or catalyze the hydroxylation of the C7β-position yielding |FRAME:CPD-16612|. The former reaction is carried out by |FRAME:MONOMER-18618| and the latter by |FRAME:MONOMER-18617| which are multifunctional oxidases also been able to hydroxylate |FRAME:CPD-4753| to form the elusive |FRAME:CPD-16627| in the possible secondary route towards |FRAME:CPD-16612| |CITS:[22215681] [23795884]|.

|FRAME: CPD-7075 Hesperidin| is an abundant citrus flavanone glycoside. Its name is derived from the Hesperides nymphs of Greek mythology. The compound has a significant impact on fruit production and processing, contributing to the cloudiness and bitterness of juices., Several different glycosidase activities have been described for hesperidin deglycosylation. |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.40|, can remove the terminal α-L-rhamnose residue from the compound. Once the rhamnose is removed, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.21|, can remove the terminal β-D-glucose residue. In addition, |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.168|, can remove the rutinose disaccharide as a single unit (diglycosylation)., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-512565| was shown to posses both EC 3.2.1.168 and EC 3.2.1.40 |CITS: [26549237][Baglioni22]|. However, the activity of the former is 3-4 orders of magnitude higher than the latter. In addition, EC 3.2.1.168 is an extracellular enzyme, able to digest externally avaliable 7-O-rutinosylated flavanones. The |FRAME: CPD-12733| that is liberated by this activity is imported into the cell by a dedicated ABC-type transporter, where it is hydrolyzed by EC 3.2.1.40 into its consituent monosaccharide. The enzyme were found in multiple |FRAME: TAX-1865| strains |CITS: [Baglioni22]|.

|FRAME: CPD-19876| is a four-carbon acid sugar that can be used by some bacteria as the sole carbon source., The pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-19876| was found by a bioinformatic analysis of genes clustered with a D-threonate-binding protein (SBP), which is a part of a TRAP (tripartite ATP-independent permease) transporter for the compound |CITS: [25540822]|., Following import into the cell, |FRAME: CPD-19876| is phosphorylated to form |FRAME: CPD-19879| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.219|. The enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: STM0162| gene, is one of the first members of a large family of enzymes, known as DUF (domain of unknown function) 1537, to which a function has been assigned |CITS: [27402745]|., Following phosphorylation, the compound is dehygrogenated at position 3 by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.408|. This dehydrogenase, with has some similarity to |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.262|, catalyzes a dehydrogenation, generating an unstable product that undergoes a decarboxylation to yield the central metabolite |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| |CITS: [27402745]|.

Names: cell-surface glycoconjugate-linked phosphocholine biosynthesis // Kennedy pathway
Summary: |FRAME: CHOLINE Choline| is a quaternary ammonium compound and a fundamental metabolite for eukaryotic organisms, forming the head group of important phospholipids such as |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| |CITS: [12215503]|., Bacteria do not possess the |FRAME: PWY3O-450 "eukaryote-like CDP-choline-dependent pathway"| for phosphatidylcholine synthesis, but it is now well-documented that a wide range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative species that colonize mucosal tissue utilize a pathway very similar to the eukaryotic pathway as a means to decorate cell wall glycoconjugates with phosphocholine. While the addition of phosphocholine to these glycoconjugates is not as common as acetylation or methylation, it has far more potent biological consequences due to the multiple interactions between phosphocholine and host proteins, which are important at all stages of the infection process by pathogens |CITS: [23911414]|. , These phosphocholine glycoconjugate modifications are found on various surface structures depending on the species. Examples include |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides| (|FRAME: TAX-727|) |CITS: [10632893]|, pili (|FRAME: TAX-487| and |FRAME: TAX-485|) |CITS: [9712776]|, |FRAME: Lipoteichoic-Acids "lipoteichoic acid"| (|FRAME: TAX-1313|) |CITS: [10200966]|, a 43-kDa surface protein (|FRAME: TAX-287|) |CITS: [9712776]|, and surface components of diverse commensal oral species |CITS: [11598029]|., The first two enzyme activities in the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.32|, and |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.15|, are essentially identical to those of the eukaryotic pathway. These enzymes are encoded by homologues of the eukaryotic genes (|FRAME: G-44724| and |FRAME: G-44725|, respectively) that have been detected in many species that colonize mucosal tissue., The third and last enzyme, diphosphonucleoside choline phosphotransferase, catalyzes the transfer of the phosphoclholine moiety to a cell surface glycoconjugate. The gene encoding this enzyme has not been definitively identified in many of these organisms |CITS: [23911414]|, but is proposed to be |FRAME: G-43708| in |FRAME: TAX-727| |CITS: [10632893]| and |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [10200966]|.

Summary: The 2-keto acid |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is a common intermediate in the degradation of organic acids., For example, both |FRAME: THR| and |FRAME: MET| are catabolized  into |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|, (see |FRAME:THREOCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: METHIONINE-DEG1-PWY|)., |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be further metabolized to at least three possible products: |FRAME: 2-Aminobutyrate|,, |FRAME:CPD-3564|, or by oxidative decarboxylation, |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|., The oxidative decarboxylation of 2-keto acids such as |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, to their acyl coenzyme A (acyl-CoA) derivatives is a key reaction of intermediary metabolism in virtually all, organisms and is catalyzed by two types of |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| (TPP)-, containing enzymes., Most aerobic organisms contain large, multienzyme complexes which function as 2-keto acid, dehydrogenases., These contain |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID| and |FRAME: FLAVIN| as prosthetic groups, use |FRAME: NAD|, as an electron acceptor, and have been extensively studied (see |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|,, |FRAME: PWY-5046| and |FRAME: PWY-5084|). Apparently, no such dehydrogenase is specific for, |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|. Rather, other dehydrogenases are able to accept it as a substrate., this has been shown for mammalian |FRAME:PYRUVDEHYD-PWY| and |FRAME:PWY-5046|, |CITS: [3718468]|., Anaerobic organisms, as well as some aerobic archaebacteria, utilize enzymes from a different family,, 2-keto acid oxidoreductases, to carry out the same reaction. That pathway is described in, |FRAME:2OXOBUTYRATECAT-PWY|., |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| is further metabolized to succinyl-CoA, a tricarboxylic acid cycle substrate,, via the |FRAME:PROPIONMET-PWY|., The mouse and human genes encoding |FRAME: CPLX-5205| (epimerase) have been identified, |CITS: [14651853][11481338]|. cDNAs encoding |FRAME:MONOMER-8610| have, also been cloned from mouse |CITS: [1978672]| and human |CITS: [2567699]| sources.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of several important metabolites involves the consumption of |FRAME: MET| through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), in a reaction that releases |FRAME:5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA). , These metabilites include polyamines (see |FRAME: ARGSPECAT-PWY|, |FRAME:BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY0-1303|), |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| (see |FRAME: ETHYL-PWY|), and bacterial auto-inducers (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration is tightly regulated. Several pathways that recycle MTA back to |FRAME: MET| have been described., The pathway shown here, also known as the universal methionine salvage pathway, is present with some variations in almost all eukaryotes and some bacteria |CITS: [19946895]|. It has been partially characterized from a number of organisms, including bacteria |CITS:[8227039][7852397][8694776][9880484][11371200]|, plants |CITS: [Baur72][Murr75][Kushad83][Miyazaki87]|, yeast |CITS: [3906034]|, protozoal parasites |CITS: [8585735][ 11443076]| and rat |CITS: [7007366][7068632][7852397]|. The pathway was best studied in the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-573|., A limiting factor to the distribution of this pathway is that it contains an oxygen-requiring step (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|), and is thus present only in aerobic organisms. Alternative pathways exist in anaerobic organisms and are described in |FRAME: PWY-7174| and |FRAME: PWY-8132|., While most of the pathway is conserved among the different organisms that possess it, several variants exist that differ in the initial steps of the pathway, between |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) and |FRAME: CPD-1063| (MTRP). These variants, describing bacteria and plants, higher eukaryotes, and protozoa, are described by several pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|. The metabolic differences in the early steps of the methionine salvage pathway are being exploited for developing new drugs targeted against pathogenic microorganisms that utilize the MTA nucleosidase-MTR kinase pathway |CITS: [2854458][2153115][1929327]|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the conserved part of the methionine salvage cycle, starting with |FRAME: CPD-444|. In 6 steps, comprising an isomerase, a dehydratase, an enolase, a phosphatase, an oxygenase, and a transaminase, |FRAME: CPD-444| is converted to |FRAME: MET| |CITS: [19946895]|. The last enzyme, a glutamine-dependent transaminase, produces the byproduct |FRAME: 2-KETO-GLUTARAMATE|, which is believed to be toxic. Thus an additional enzyme, an ω-amidase that converts the latter to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|, is also considered a part of the pathway |CITS: [24837359]|., A few notes of interest about the enzymes of this pathway, At least in some strains, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: EC-5.3.2.5|, is a member of the RubisCO protein family |CITS: [17352497]|., The reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54|, can occur non-enzymatically in the presence of air |CITS: [7852397]|. It is yet unknown whether the non-enzymatic reaction occurs in vivo |CITS: [7852397]|., If the enzyme that usually catalyzes |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.54| binds a Ni2+ instead of Fe2+, it catalyzes a different reaction (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.53|), forming a shunt of the methionine salvage pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5389|) |CITS: [11371200][9880484][7852397]|. The purpose of this off-pathway reaction is yet unknown; it may, however, provide a mechanism for regulating |FRAME: MET| levels in vivo |CITS: [11371200]|., In some organisms the reactions catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.3.2.5| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.87| are catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.77| (MtnC).

Names: α-solanine/α-chaconine biosynthesis // solanine/chaconine biosynthesis // steroidal glycoalkaloid biosynthesis // SGA biosynthesis
Summary: The potato steroidal glycoalkaloids (SGAs) are toxic secondary metabolites found in potatoes (|FRAME: TAX-4113|) and other Solanaceous members like tomato and eggplant |CITS: [Ripperger98][17157337]|. These compounds were shown to have antifungal activity against the potato dry rot pathogen |FRAME: TAX-185651| |CITS: [Li22]|., |FRAME:CPD-9214 "α-Chaconine"| and |FRAME:CPD-9211| represent the major SGAs in potato |CITS: [17701426]| and are found to be especially high in flowers and tuber sprouts |CITS:[Ginzberg09]|. The average content of SGAs in green potato peel was reported to be more than 2g/kg, with the |FRAME: CPD-9214| content about 1.8 times higher than that of |FRAME: CPD-9211| |CITS: [Li22]|. SGAs have a bitter taste and their total content should not exceed 20mg/100g fresh weight. This is one of the reasons that controlling tuber sprouting is of high priority for potato breeders worldwide |CITS:[24100410]|., Tuber phelloderm or the layers directly below the tuber skin is the main SGA-producing tissue in potato. Symptoms of SGA poisoning include gastrointestinal disorders, hallucinations, partial paralysis, convulsions, and coma and death |CITS: [17701426]|. At the cellular level they exhibit strong lytic properties and inhibit acetylcholine-esterase activity. Cooking does not destroy the SGA's and varieties that contain low levels of SGA are bred. The biosynthetic pathway has not been completely worked out and possible positive roles these compounds may play in antifungal and wounding response are being studied. Wounding in potato activates the sterol and SGA synthesis |CITS: [17701426]|. , The efforts to characterize the solanine 3-O-galactosyltransferase encoded by SGT1 had been dominated by resolving the question whether or not the SGT1 encoded protein catalyzed the glucosylation, the galactosylation or both reactions of |FRAME:CPD-9217|. While at first glucosyltransferase activity was observed in vitro in potato tubers |CITS:[Stapleton91]| and phelloderm |CITS:[9076990]| with partially purified protein, it was later shown that the SGT1 encoded protein was much more active with |FRAME:CPD-14553| than with |FRAME:CPD-12575| hence acting as galactosyltransferase rather than glucosyltransferase. This was demonstrated in vivo through antisense mutants of Solanum tuberosum devoid of SGT1 which accumulated |FRAME:CPD-9214| and produced much less |FRAME:CPD-9211| and in vitro using recombinant SGT1 proteins. It was shown that |FRAME:CPD-9217| was mainly galactosylated and only marginally glucosylated but also that |FRAME:CPD-13080| and |FRAME:CPD-17697| were galactosylated with even higher efficiency forming |FRAME:CPD-18738| and |FRAME:CPD-18641|, respectively. That indicates that the SGT1 encoded protein also acted on other steroidal alkaloids further upstream the steroidal glycoside pathway(s) (see |FRAME:PWY18C3-4|) |CITS:[McCue05] [17204296]|. , The recently described GAME25, characterized in both tomato and potato, potentially extends the biosynthetic sequence beyond the formation of |FRAME:CPD-9214| and |FRAME:CPD-9211| towards |FRAME:CPD-22280|. GAME25 belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family and has been demonstrated to exhibit dual activities, one as 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and the other as Δ5,4 isomerase. The GAME25 catalyzed reaction is however just one out of three reactions that convert unsaturated steroidal alkaloids (SG) towards saturated SGs. However, saturated SGAs such as |FRAME:CPD-22280| have not been observed in cultivated potato, but they have been found in wild species. Although potato has a functional GAME25 encoding protein, the following reactions producing |FRAME:CPD-22280| might have been lost during the domestication process. Characterizing the whole reaction sequence must therefore carried out in wild Solanum species |CITS:[29784829]|.

General Background, Isoflavones comprise a class of plant secondary metabolites related to the flavonoids. They are produced almost exclusively by the members of the family Fabaceae. Many of them act as phytoestrogens in mammals., Coumestrol is a coumestan isoflavone found in many leguminous plants. It has been shown to accumulate to significant levels in mycorrhizal roots. It has also been shown to stimulate growth of hyphae in Gigaspora margarita |CITS: [Morandi84]|, |CITS: [Morandi92]| . Coumestrol can inhibit enzymes involved in steroid hormone formation and metabolism in humans and can thus play an important role in delaying the development of hormone-dependent cancers |CITS: [11165023]|., About This Pathway , Feeding experiments using mung bean root cell cultures indicated that daidzein and dihydrodaidzein are both good precursors of coumestrol |CITS: [Berlin72]|. In an earlier study, 2'-hydroxydaidzein (2',4',7-trihydroxyisoflavone) was shown incorporated into coumestrol and 2'-hydroxydaidzein was proposed being an important intermediate in coumestrol biosynthesis |CITS: [Dewick70]|. In a later study, competitive feeding experiment using daidzein plus 2'-hydroxydaidzein clearly indicated that daidzein was a much better precursor and that the route via 2'-hydroxydaidzein was most likely a minor pathway |CITS: [Berlin72]|. The proposed major route for coumestrol biosynthesis in mung bean consists of a dihydrodaidzein 2'-hydroxylation step, followed by cyclization and oxidation to give rise to coumestrol. , The proposed pathway was based on preliminary radio tracer studies in the early 70's. Since then there was no further literature about the biosynthesis pathway of coumestrol.

General Background, Sulfur is an essential nutrient for all life forms. Plants, fungi, and many bacteria reduce inorganic sulfate to sulfide to cover their need for the element. Before the sulfur can be assimilated into biosynthetic pathways it needs to be reduced to |FRAME:HS|., Pathways catalyzing the reduction of sulfate to sulfide for the purpose of incorporation into newly synthesized molecules are called pathways of assimilatory sulfate reduction. In addition, certain organisms can use sulfate as an alternative electron acceptor in the absence of oxygen. Pathways of sulfate reduction for the purpose of energy production are called pathways of dissimilatory sulfate reduction., The reduction of sulfate to sulfite requires two electrons at a standard redox potential (E0') of -516 mV, which is too high for physiological electron carriers |CITS: [860983]|. The problem is solved by the activation of the sulfate, by forming a mixed anhydride between phosphate and sulfate as in |FRAME:APS| (APS) or |FRAME:PAPS| (PAPS). This linkage lowers the potential to E0' = -60 mV, which is easilly covered by thiols or pyrimidine nucleotides |CITS: [14627706]|., About This Pathway, As described above, the initial step in sulfate reduction is its activation to |FRAME: APS| (APS), which is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: AT3G22890-MONOMER| (ATP sulfurylase). In plants, as well as certain bacteria (such as |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [10939523]|), APS can be reduced to sulfite directly, without phosphorylation to PAPS., In enteric bacteria, cyanobacteria, and yeast, on the other hand, APS is phophorylated to PAPS, and only the latter is reduced to sulfite (see |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) |CITS: [11940598]|., Two types of enzymes are known to catalyze the direct reduction of APS to sulfite - a |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: 1.8.4.9-RXN "EC 1.8.4.9"|) |CITS: [8917600][8917599][10939523]|, and a |FRAME: Thioredoxin thioredoxin|-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: RXN-12019 "EC 1.8.4.10"|) |CITS: [10464198]|., The former enzyme is included in the pathway |FRAME: SULFMETII-PWY|, while the latter enzyme is described in |FRAME: PWY-6683| (this pathway)., In both pathways sulfite is reduced to sulfide by the action of |FRAME:CPLX-1285| |CITS: [11488606]|. Again, two types of enzymes are known - a ferredoxin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: SULFITE-REDUCTASE-FERREDOXIN-RXN "EC 1.8.7.1"|) and an NADPH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: SULFITE-REDUCT-RXN "EC 1.8.1.2"|). Most bacteria utilze NADPH as the electron donor., The sulfide is incorporated into |FRAME: CYS|, and later into |FRAME: MET| (see |FRAME: CYSTSYN-PWY|).

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran|, marketed under the trade name Furadan, is one of the most toxic broad-spectrum and systemic N-methyl carbamate pesticides, which is used extensively as insecticide, nematicide and acaricide for agricultural, domestic and industrial purposes. The chemical is highly toxic to mammals, birds, and honeybees, and has a moderate to high toxicity to most aquatic organisms |CITS: [32593003]|. |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran| is an endocrine disruptor and a probable reproduction/development intoxicant. It is an inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.7|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.8| |CITS: [18706518]|., |FRAME: CPD-24209 Carbofuran| has been banned in Canada and the European Union for many years. It was banned in the US in 2009 after the U.S. Supreme Court denied a counter petition by FMC and several corn grower associations., Despite its considerable toxicity, |FRAME: CPD-24209| is still used in some countries with a wide variety of field crops including potatoes, corn and soybeans. In addition, according to several journalistic investigations illegally smuggled |FRAME: CPD-24209| is used on marijuana grown illegally on public land in California, and |FRAME: CPD-24209|-contaminated marijuana appears to be the main source of marijuana consumed in states where it hasn't been legalized. In East Africa |FRAME: CPD-24209| is used by farmers to poison lions., Diverse carbofuran-degrading bacteria have been described, including members of the genera Pseudomonas, Flavobacterium, Achromobacter, Sphingomonas, Novosphingobium, and Paracoccus. However, most of these organisms are only capable of hydrolyzing |FRAME: CPD-24209| to |FRAME: CPD-24214|. Only sphingomonads are able to proceed by fully degrading |FRAME: CPD-24214| |CITS: [ 29884759]|., About This Pathway, Two types of carbofuran hydrolases, Mcd and CfdJ, have been reported. Mcd was purified from |FRAME: TAX-104199| |CITS: [ 2661544]|. Homologs of |FRAME: G-107481| were detected in phylogenetically diverse carbofuran-degrading isolates, but not in the sphingomonads |CITS: [Parekh95]|. The |FRAME: G-107480| gene, which was reported from |FRAME: TAX-1478134| |CITS: [26159535]|, is a close homolog of the cehA gene of |FRAME: TAX-168685|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.137|., One of the intermediates of this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-24218|, was reported already in 2004 during degradation of carbofuran by |FRAME: TAX-227154| |CITS: [15080638]|. However, the full pathway was proposed much later, based on a study of |FRAME: TAX-1478134| that used mutants with diminished or abolished capacity to degrade carbofuran, based on the identified intermediates |CITS: [ 24931307]|., Most of the genes involved in carbofuran degradation appear to be located in the cfd operon, which contains 8 open reading frames. The |FRAME: G-107478| gene encodes a putative mono-oxygenase, and insertions in the gene abolished mineralization of carbofuran. The mutant accumulated |FRAME: CPD-24214| and did not produce any of the downstream metabolites, suggesting that CfdC directly attacks carbofuran phenol. The authors proposed that the hydroxylation results in the opening the furan ring |CITS: [ 24931307]|. The product of the |FRAME: G-107479| gene, a dioxygenase, appears to catalyze the ring cleavage step. The authors identified two potential candidates (encoded by cfdD and cfdF, respectively) for catalyzing the last step, but the identity of the actual enzyme catalyzing that step, as well as other pathway holes, has not been identified as of 2021 |CITS: [ 24931307]|., It should be noted that during the degradation, several strains, such as |FRAME: TAX-227154| and |FRAME: TAX-1478134|, produce several red metabolites, which are presumed to be shunt products. One of those was identified in 2006 as |FRAME: CPD-24548| |CITS: [Park06]|.|

Summary: General Background, Sialic acids are a family of polyhydroxylated α-keto acids that contain nine carbon atoms. Most sialic acids are derivatives of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, or |FRAME: CPD-21259| (KDN). |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is the most common sialic acid in mammals (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6138|), while KDN is abundant in lower vertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Their core structures can be modified at the hydroxyl groups, lactonized, or hydroxylated at the acetamido group, generating many derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-262| is a derivative of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6144|). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Sialic acids are found mainly in vertebrates and a few higher invertebrates (ascidians and echinoderms). These acidic sugars are usually the terminal sugar residue in the glycan chains of vertebrate glycoconjugates (mostly glycoproteins and glycolipids, but also proteoglycans and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors). They function in mediating cellular recognition and adhesion events for many important processes such as development, the immune and inflammatory responses, and oncogenesis. Sialic acid occurs rarely in invertebrates. Endogenous sialylation has been shown to occur in |FRAME: TAX-7215|, but details of sialic acid biosynthesis in this organism remain to be determined |CITS: [18568399]|. However, it is possible the sialic acids might be biosynthesized by other eukaryotes in a species and/or life cycle-dependent manner. In |CITS: [7841794]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Most bacteria do not biosynthesize sialic acids, but some pathogenic, or symbiotic bacteria biosynthesize sialic acids as a means of evading a host's immune system (this pathway). The sialic acid is displayed on the bacterial cell surface (in capsular polysaccharides) in order to mimic mammalian cells. Pathogens that biosynthesize sialic acids include |FRAME: TAX-487|, |FRAME: TAX-1392869| and |FRAME: TAX-197|. In addition, the human gut symbiont |FRAME: TAX-818| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-21259| |CITS: [18804026]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Whether or not archaea contain sialic acids remains to be determined. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Other sialic acid-like sugars biosynthesized by bacteria include the nonulosonic acids |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [16751642]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|) and legionaminic acid (see pathway class |FRAME: CMP-Legionaminate-Biosynthesis|) |CITS: [18275154]|., Protists are thought to lack the ability to biosynthesize sialic acids although more genome data are needed to confirm this. Sialic acids have been thought to be absent in plants but some studies raise the possibility |CITS: [18258224]|. Fungi appear to lack any known sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, although strain-specific, or novel pathways could exist. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Also see |FRAME: PWY-6145|., About This Pathway, In both pathogenic bacteria (this pathway) and animals (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6138|) |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| biosynthesis begins with the conversion of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC|. This reaction involves both an inversion of stereochemistry at C-2 of the sugar moiety and hydrolysis of the glycosidic phosphate bond. However, in animals |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE| is then phosphorylated to its 6-phosphate derivative and condensation with |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| then forms |FRAME: N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE-9P|. After dephosphorylation to |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, |FRAME: CTP| is used to generate the activated form of sialic acid, |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE|. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., In contrast to the animal pathway, in this bacterial pathway |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE| is not phosphorylated, but is converted to |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| directly by condensation with |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|. This is followed by formation of the activated form |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE|. This step is similar to the bacterial and plant biosynthesis of Kdo (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-1269| and |FRAME: PWY-1269|). This |FRAME: CMP| activated form is the sialic acid donor for glycoconjugates. Bacterial polysialyltransferases utilize the |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| in the synthesis of capsular polysialic acid, a virulence factor |CITS: [12578835]|. Sialic acid analogs are of interest in the development of antibacterial drugs. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Interestingly, this pathway also appears to occur in the nonpathogenic |FRAME: TAX-203119| although the function of sialic acid in this organism is not known |CITS: [17602221]|.

General Background, Lipoxins belong to the eicosanoid family, have a distinct conjugated tetraene structure and are generated from |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|. These lipid derived mediators play an important role in the cessation of the inflammatory response. |FRAME: CPD66-53| (ATL) mediates cellular responses and control leukocyte trafficking in vivo by activating the G protein-coupled receptor ALX |CITS:[16968948]|., |FRAME: CPD-524 Aspirin| has well known anti-inflammatory and antipyretic functions. It also has an anti-clotting function through the inhibition of thromboxane synthesis. It is often prescribed long-term, at low doses, to help prevent heart attacks, strokes, and blood clot formation in high risk patients. Aspirin may also prevent the occurrence of certain types of cancer., About this Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-22263| is formed when |FRAME: HS01115| (COX2) is irreversibly acetylated by |FRAME: CPD-524|. Statins produce the same effect via S-nitrosylation of COX-2 |CITS: [21071715]|., The 15-epi lipoxins have similar biological activity to lipoxins.15-epi lipoxin biosynthesis is also, triggered by the cytochrome P450 enzymes and this may play a role in the generation of 15-epi lipoxins in the, absence of aspirin |CITS: [21071715]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycolysis, which was first studied as a pathway for the utilization of glucose, is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, the other two being the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| and the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. Glycolysis is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces six of the 13 precursor metabolites that are the starting materials for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules (the six compounds are |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:G3P|, |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). Glycolysis can be found, if at least in part, in almost all organisms., Even though glycolysis is often described starting with glucose, other hexoses (e.g. fructose) can also serve as input (as its name implies - glycose is a general term for simple sugars)., Glycolysis has evolved to fulfill two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) being an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism), it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy., This switching of direction is possible because all but two of the enzymatic reactions comprising glycolysis are reversible, and the conversions catalyzed by the two exceptions are rendered functionally reversible by other enzymes (|FRAME:F16B-CPLX "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase"| and |FRAME:PEPSYNTH-CPLX|) that catalyze different irreversible reactions flowing in the opposite direction., About This Pathway, The standard glycolysis pathway (|FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS|) depicts the sugar input into the pathway as glucose. However, the glycolysis pathway is utilized for the degradation of many different types of sugars., This partial depiction of the glycolysis pathway is used with substrates other than glucose, such as |FRAME: D-Allose|,, |FRAME: CPD-9569| , |FRAME: MANNITOL| , |FRAME: SORBITOL| , |FRAME: MANNOSE| and |FRAME: SUCROSE|,, which are processed into |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|., D-fructose 6-phosphate enters glycolysis and is processed to the end product pyruvate, which is often fermented, further into fermentation products such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: Lactate| and |FRAME: ACET|.

Summary: Under anaerobic growth conditions L-aspartate can be used as both a substrate for nitrogen assimilation and for growth by fumarate respiration |CITS: [33754467]|. L-aspartate is transported into the cell by the C4-dicarboxylate transporters DcuA and DcuB mediating an L-aspartate:succinate exchange reaction |CITS: [7961398][33754467]|. L-aspartate is then metabolized by aspA-encoded |FRAME: ASPARTASE-CPLX aspartase| to produce ammonium and fumarate; ammonium is further metabolized by |FRAME: GLUTAMINESYN-OLIGOMER| and the |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY GOGAT| pathway to produce L-glutamine and L-glutamate, while fumarate functions as the terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic electron transport chains (see |CITS: [6387427][9230919]|)., In this manner L-aspartate is able to satisfy all the major cellular requirements for nitrogen and to support growth by anaerobic fumarate respiration. Unlike the parental wild-type strain, ΔaspA single mutants and ΔdcuAΔdcuB double mutants are unable to grow anaerobically in minimal medium with L-asparate + glycerol |CITS: [33754467]|. The capacity for L-aspartate metabolism is important for the fitness of |FRAME: TAX-562| in the mammalian intestine |CITS: [33754467]|., This pathway also functions during aerobic growth when L-aspartate is used as a substrate for nitrogen assimilation (see |FRAME: PWY-8291|).

Background, |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| plays an important osmoprotectant role in mammals, protects from several other forms of cellular stress and functions as a methyl group donor |CITS: [20346934]|. Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negatives is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as KDO, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: CPD-22402| in sequential steps, with different KDO units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In some cases a third Kdo residue is added to the second one., In |FRAME: TAX-160488| two molecules of |FRAME: DODECANOATE| are incorporated into the distal unit of lipid A by two homologues of the |FRAME: TAX-562| acyltransferase LpxL. Further modifications result in 4 different variants- |FRAME: CPD-22413|, |FRAME: CPD-22414|, |FRAME: CPD-22411|, and |FRAME: CPD-22412| |CITS: [28557109]|.

Summary: Fatty acid biosynthesis in eukaryotic organisms is carried out in independent, dual cellular locations, the cytosol with fatty acid synthase (FAS) complexes (FAS I type) synthesizing fatty acids |CITS:[6137188] [16950653]| (for example |FRAME:PWY-5994|) and the mitochondria where monofunctional enzymes encoded in the yeast nucleus catalyze the various steps of fatty acid biosynthesis (FAS II type) |CITS:[19028688] [9187370]|. The latter resembles the bacterial FAS II system (see |FRAME:PWY0-501|, |FRAME:PWY0-1275|) but except for |FRAME:CPD-195|, the precursor for |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| |CITS:[9218413]|, the functions of other final products made by the pathway remain unclear and require further research |CITS:[19028688]|., It has been speculated that the main purpose of mitochondrial fatty acid biosynthesis lies in the maintenance of mitochondria |CITS:[11509667]| and respiration |CITS:[16246072]| which is closely connected to |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| biosynthesis and incorporation |CITS:[9037098] [9218413] [18779316]| but may also contribute fatty acids as constituent of mitochondrial phospholipid membranes |CITS:[Schneider95]|. In addition, novel links have been proposed to exist between mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis and RNA processing where products from the mitochondrial FAS II pathway are required for RNase P activity in yeast which in turn is controlled by positive feedback mechanisms |CITS:[18779316] [19686777]|., The mitochondrial fatty acid biosynthesis involves an initiation sequence (see |FRAME: PWY66-429|) and an elongation sequence that involves four enzymes and produces an acyl-[acyl carrier protein] (acyl-[acp]). In each cycle the acyl-[acp] product is condensed with |FRAME:MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"| formed in the initiation pathway, resulting in its elongation by two carbons. The cycle is repeated three times until |FRAME: Octanoyl-ACPs "octanoyl-[acp]"| is formed |CITS:[18779316]|., The last enzyme of the initiation pathway (|FRAME: YER061C|), which produces |FRAME:Acetoacetyl-ACPs "acetoacetyl-[acp]"|, participates in both initiation and elongation, as the reaction it catalyzes is also the first of the 4 elongation steps - the condensation of a substrate with |FRAME:MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"|. The subsequent reduction to |FRAME:Beta-3-hydroxybutyryl-ACPs| by the 3-oxoacyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] reductase (|FRAME: YKL055C|) |CITS:[9388293] [14562095]| is followed by the dehydration reaction that produces |FRAME:Crotonyl-ACPs| |CITS:[15387819]|. The enzyme catalyzing the dehydration (|FRAME: G3O-31118|) differs from the prior enzymes in the pathway by a lack of homology to the corresponding prokaryotic enzyme. The enoyl-[acyl-carrier-protein] reductase (|FRAME: G3O-29006|) catalyzes the formation of the end product of the first cycle, |FRAME:Butanoyl-ACPs butanoyl-[acp]|. This enzyme also shows no obvious homology to its bacterial counterpart |CITS:[11509667][12614607]|. , The cycle repeats itself until |FRAME: Octanoyl-ACPs "octanoyl-[acp]"| is produced. This product serves as the precursor for |FRAME:LIPOIC-ACID| biosynthesis (see  |FRAME:PWY-7382|.

Theobromine is the immediate precursor of caffeine biosynthesis in caffeine accumulating plants such as coffee and tea plants. However theobromine plants accumulate theobromine instead of caffeine as the major purine alkaloid. The biosynthetic pathway of theobromine is similar to the major pathway of caffeine biosynthesis |FRAME: PWY-5037|, except that conversion of theobromine to caffeine is very slow or blocked in these plants |CITS: [Koyama03][Ashihara98][Fujimori90][Ashihara87]|., In cocoa, the major sites of theobromine biosynthesis are the young pericarp and cotyledons of fruits |CITS: [15128023]|. In addition to fruits, significant amount of theobromine is also detected in young leaves. Theobromine level falls markedly when the leaves fully developed |CITS: [Koyama03]|. Theobromine may play a role in protecting the young plant tissues against predators such as insect larvae. No enzyme information is avaible.

Summary: General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic formaldehyde is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms. In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central intermediate. It has been suggested that the formaldehyde concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph would rise to 100mM in less than 1 minute if formaldehyde consumption stopped |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for formaldehyde detoxification are known in bacteria, encoded by unrelated or distantly related genes. , About This Pathway, This cyclic pathway for the oxidation of formaldehyde exists in methylotrophs that possess the ribulose-monophosphate (RuMP) pathway for formaldehyde assimilation (see |FRAME: PWY-1861|) |CITS: [1909921][ 6768606][353476]|. The pathway involves several enzymes that are used by the RuMP cycle, namely |FRAME:CPLX-3443| (HPS) and |FRAME: CPLX-3445| |CITS: [10658669]|., Unlike the RuMP cycle, there is no net fixation of formaldehyde in this pathway due to the release of a CO2 molecule. Rather, the organisms use this pathway to generate reducing power in the form of NADH and NADPH., Most obligate methanotrophs do not employ this pathway, and instead use a linear pathway for formaldehyde oxidation using formaldehyde dehydrogenase (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|). The organisms that do use this pathway fall into three groups: Gram-negative obligate methylotrohps, Gram-positive facultative methylotrophs, and thermotollerant Bacillus spp. |CITS: [12351229][1909921]|., Recently it has been shown that these enzymes are also present in heterotrophs such as B. subtilis, and that they play a role in formaldehyde detoxification in these organisms |CITS: [10572115][14532071]|. However, it does not seem that the oxidation pathway is used in the heterotrophs. 14C labeled formaldehyde was incorporated into cellular material, indicating that it was the RuMP assimilative pathway which took place |CITS: [14532071]|.

Summary: Citrus-based cosmetic products occupy an important place in fragrance related industrial products. One of the main aroma contributing agents is a sesquiterpene called |FRAME: CPD-7989|, which is easily isolated from valencia oranges. It is also present in a number of other plant species. The biosynthesis of this sesquiterpene is facilitated by occurrence of the enzyme valencene synthase |CITS: [15464152]|. |FRAME: CPD-7989| has also been isolated from fungi., In grapes, anthers have been found to be the floral structures that produce high amounts of sesquiterpenes, indicative of their role in pollination via release of floral scent volatiles |CITS: [19359488]|. The volatiles accumulate in anthers during the prebloom period differing significantly from flower scent volatiles that accumulate during bloom, mainly attributed to other floral parts such as petals. The localization of the terpene synthase and its products in the anther presents a new way of studying the biology of scent formation and its use in the natural biology as pollinator attractant.

Because the citrate molecule is very stable, it has to be activated by forming a thioester bond with the enzyme before cleavage can take place., The enzyme is a complex of three subunits (in a 6:6:6 configuration), one of them a dedicated acyl carrier protein (acp)., The acp protein is synthesized in an apo form, and is converted to its holo form by the covalent binding of the prosthetic group |FRAME: 2-5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-3-DEPHOSPHO-COA| to a serine residue. This prosthetic group is very unusual and the only other enzyme known to use it is |FRAME: CPLX-7660 "malonate decarboxylase"|., The synthesis and attachment of the prosthetic group are catalyzed by two different enzymes. The first step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.52| is the formation of an unusual α-1,2-glycosidic linkage between ATP and dephospho-CoA, forming the prosthetic group and releaing adenine |CITS: [10924139]|. In the second step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.61|, the group is transferred to the apo-[acp] protein, generating the holo-[acp] form |CITS: [11948157]|., The holo form is still not active - in order to be fully active, the prosthetic group needs to be acetylated. The most common enzyme performing the acetylation is |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.22|, which uses |FRAME: ACET| as the donor |CITS: [4365579]|. A different enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.49|, that uses |FRAME: S-ACETYLPHOSPHOPANTETHEINE| as the acetyl donor, has been characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [4741546]|., Another enzyme that modulates the activity of |FRAME:EC-4.1.3.6 "citrate lyase"| has been reported in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-28068|. That enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.1.2.16|, converts the active acetyl form back into the inactive thiol form by removal of its acetyl groups |CITS:[7460909]|.

Summary: Heme (protoheme, heme b) is an iron-containing prosthetic group found in many essential proteins including cytochromes and heme-containing globins. It is a porphyrin member of the cyclic tetrapyrroles., It is biosynthesized as protoheme, but different derivatives of protoheme can be formed that differ in modifications to the porphyrin ring, including how it is bound to the protein, such as |FRAME: HEME_O|, |FRAME: HEME_A|, |FRAME: HEME_C|, and |FRAME: HEME_D|., This superpathway shows the two routes of synthesis found in the facultative anaerobe |FRAME:TAX-562|. Under aerobic conditions, the transition from |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN| is catalyzed by the oxygen -dependent |FRAME: COPROGENOXI-MONOMER| (EC 1.3.3.3). However, when oxygen is not available, the organism is still able to catalyze this transition, using the readical-SAM enzyme |FRAME: HEMN-MONOMER| (EC 1.3.99.22), which can catalyze the transition without the need for molecular oxygen. This enzyme, which contains an iron-sulfur cluster, is able to break SAM into |FRAME: MET| and a 5'-deoxyadenosineyl radical. This radical can attack |FRAME: COPROPORPHYRINOGEN_III| and bring about the conversion to |FRAME: PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN|., This enzyme is found in many bacteria, but does not appear to be present in archaea or eukarya (the only reference for the enzyme in a eukaryote is in the organism |FRAME: TAX-5911|, but this finding is based on sequence analysis alone, and has not been verified biochemically)., Important branch points within this pathway lead to biosynthesis of other important compounds such as vitamin B12 (cobalamin) (see |FRAME: P381-PWY|), |FRAME: CPD-7425| (see |FRAME: PWY-5196|), |FRAME: SIROHEME| (see |FRAME: PWY-5194|), heme D biosynthesis, and bacteriochlorophyll (see |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|).

Summary: General Background, 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes convert 2-oxo acids to the corresponding acyl-CoA derivatives and produce NADH and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an irreversible reaction., Five members of this family are known at present, including the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| (PDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| (OGDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| (BCDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27 - this pathway| (GDHC), and the |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190| (ADHC). They all function at strategic points in (usually aerobic) catabolic pathways and are subject to stringent control |CITS: [9655933]|., With the exception of GDHC, the 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes share a common structure. They consist of three main components, namely a 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3)., In Gram-positive bacteria and mitochondria, the E1 component is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, while in Gram-negative bacteria it is made of a single type of subunit., In all cases described so far, many copies of each subunit assemble to form the full complex. For example, the |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| comprises 24, 24, and 12 units of the E1, E2, and E3 components, respectively., The core of the complex is made of either 24 (Gram-negative bacteria) or 60 (mitochondria) E2 units, which contain the lipoyl active site in the form of lipoyllysine, as well as binding sites for the other two subunits. E1, which contains a |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| cofactor, catalyzes the binding of the 2-oxo acid to the lipoyl group of E2, which then transfers an acyl group (the nature of the acyl group depends on the particular enzyme) to |FRAME: CO-A|, forming an acyl-CoA. During this transfer, the lipoyl group is reduced to dihydrolipoyl. E3 then transfers the protons to NAD, forming NADH and restoring the dihydrolipoyllysine group back to lipoyllysine., Cryoelectron microscopy of PDHC from |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS:[12411477]| and ox kidney |CITS: [11752427]| has revealed that the E2 inner core is surrounded by an outer shell of E1 and E3 components, with the lipoyl domains confined to the annular space between them where they must make successive journeys between the three types of active sites (E1-E3), which are physically far apart |CITS: [12795594]|., About This Pathway, In eukaryotes the mitochondrial glycine cleavage complex (glycine decarboxylase complex) is a loosely-associated multienzyme complex that catalyzes the oxidative cleavage of glycine to carbon dioxide, ammonia, and a methylene group, in a multistep reaction (in |CITS: [15791207]|). The complete reaction of the complex can be described by the following reaction:, |FRAME: GCVMULTI-RXN|, The methylene group, carried by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF|, enters cellular one-carbon metabolism. The complex participates in several processes, as described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-2201|, |FRAME: 1CMET2-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-181|. In mammals, it is the primary pathway for glycine catabolism |CITS: [6402507]|., The glycine cleavage complex is composed of four different proteins: the P-protein (|FRAME: EC-1.4.4.2|); the T-protein (|FRAME: EC-2.1.2.10|); the L-protein (|FRAME: EC-1.8.1.4|); and the H-protein (lipoyl-carrier protein, a non-enzyme that contains a lipoyl group that interacts successively with the three other components of the complex during the enzymatic reactions., The L-protein (also known as the E3 component) also participates in the |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|, the |FRAME: PWY-5084|, and the |FRAME: PWY-5046| multienzyme systems., In plants, this complex is known as the |FRAME: GLYCINEDECARBOXYLASE| complex and functions in |FRAME: PWY-181 photorespiration|. Its components from the mitochondria of |FRAME:TAX-3888| (pea) leaf have been extensively studied |CITS: [3080433]| and reviewed in |CITS: [11286922]|. In vertebrates, the components of the |FRAME: CPLX-7302| from |FRAME:TAX-9031| (chicken) have been well studied |CITS: [1993704][1526969][1993703]|. , The glycine cleavage complex is also present in bacteria |CITS: [11495998]|. The |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate"| that is formed by the complex can be channeled to the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "reductive acetyl coenzyme A pathway"|, producing acetyl-CoA and leading to substrate-level phosphorylation. In addition, components of the glycine cleavage complex have been characterized in archaea including the T-protein from |FRAME:TAX-53953| |CITS: [15272174]| and the L-protein from halophilic archaebacteria |CITS: [6426463] [8655478]| (although the role of the L-protein in glycine metabolism in halophiles is unclear |CITS: [8655478]|). In yeast, studies have been done on the regulation of genes encoding components of the glycine cleavage complex |CITS: [12702322]|., In humans, non-ketotic hyperglycinemia results from deficiency-causing mutations in the genes encoding P-protein, or T-protein. This autosomal recessively inherited disorder results in accumulation of large amounts of glycine in body fluids such as plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, causing severe neurological symptoms |CITS: [16450403]| and in |CITS: [16051266]|. Mutations in gene DLD that encodes L-protein can result in lipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency, a disease with multiple physiological symptoms and significant morbidity |CITS: [9934985]|., Crystal structures of the components of the glycine cleavage complex have been determined from plant, animal, and bacterial sources. References include: P-protein |CITS: [15791207]|, T-protein |CITS: [15272174] [16051266]|, L-protein |CITS: [10806386]|, and H-protein |CITS: [10806386]|. , The reactions of the glycine cleavage complex are reversible, and also provide a route for glycine biosynthesis (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: GLYCINE-SYN2-PWY|).

Degradation of |FRAME: Citronellols| has been studied in some members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-286|. In early work, |FRAME: TAX-53408| was shown to utilize |FRAME: Citronellols| and related compounds as a sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [14445211]|. In contrast, |FRAME: TAX-160488| was unable to grow on |FRAME: Citronellols| or |FRAME: Citronellates| and lacks the atu gene cluster (see below) |CITS: [16820476]|., Based on mutant analysis, degradation of the related acyclic monoterpenol |FRAME: GERANIOL| in |FRAME: TAX-53408| and |FRAME: TAX-287| has been suggested to occur in separate steps, independent from |FRAME: Citronellols| oxidation (cited as unpublished data in |CITS: [20490788]|). However |FRAME: GERANIOL| degradation (not shown) converges with the |FRAME: PWY-6670| pathway at |FRAME: CPD-1827|., About This Pathway, This pathway has been functionally divided into four phases. Phase one is the upper acyclic terpene utilization pathway that results in |FRAME: CO-A| activation of |FRAME: Citronellates|. Phase two is the lower acyclic terpene utilization pathway in which the β-methyl group is removed in several steps, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-12897| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (as shown in the pathway link to |FRAME: PWY-6672|). These reactions are catalyzed by enzymes encoded in the atuABCDEFGH gene cluster (see below). Phase three involves two rounds of β-oxidation converting |FRAME: CPD-12897| to |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA|. Phase four involves further metabolism of |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA| via the |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY| pathway to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, as shown in the pathway link from |FRAME: PWY-6672| and in the subsequent pathway link to |FRAME: ACETOACETATE-DEG-PWY|. Phase four enzymes are encoded by the leucine/isovalerate utilization gene cluster liuABCDE which allows utilization of both |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME: ISOVALERATE| after its conversion to |FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA| (reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]|)., As shown in the pathway link, the initial step involves oxidation of |FRAME: Citronellols| first to its corresponding aldehyde |FRAME: Citronellals| and then to an acid |FRAME: Citronellates|, followed by activation via formation of its |FRAME: CO-A| ester. |FRAME: CPD-12896| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1827| by the dehydrogenase AtuD. However, the β-methyl group of this compound must be removed before the β-oxidation steps can occur. Geranyl-CoA carboxylase is a key enzyme in the conversion of the β-methyl group to an acetate group that is then removed by double bond hydration (probably catalyzed by the putative hydratase AtuE |CITS: [19597963]|) and lyase cleavage, as shown in this pathway., Regarding the lyase cleavage step, the product of gene liuE has been proposed to be a bifunctional hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA lyase (EC 4.1.3.4) / 3-hydroxy-3-isohexenylglutaryl-CoA lyase (EC 4.1.3.26) that participates in both this acyclic monoterpene degradation pathway and in the |FRAME: LEU| (and |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|) degradation pathway |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY|). A mutant in liuE was unable to utilize |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|, or acyclic terpenes. Purified recombinant LiuE showed both activities in vitro in an indirect, coupled enzyme assay |CITS: [19597963]|. However, an in vivo role for the LiuE-associated 3-hydroxy-3-isohexenylglutaryl-CoA lyase activity has been questioned based on several lines of evidence. A separate, as yet unidentified enzyme (possibly the atuA gene product) was hypothesized to have this function (reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]|)., Two rounds of β-oxidation follow and the resulting |FRAME: 3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA| is thought to be degraded via the |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY| pathway as shown in the pathway link. Note that in the β-oxidation steps it is uncertain whether the enzymes used are the same as those used for fatty acids, or whether enzymes specific for methyl-branched substrates are used (therefore, partial EC numbers are shown here). Overall, one molecule of |FRAME: Citronellols| yields six molecules of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, and two molecules of carbon dioxide (as |FRAME: HCO3|) are fixed during the four phases of this pathway. In |CITS: [16000717]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]| and in |CITS: [12658511]|., The acyclic terpene utilization (atuABCDEFGH) gene cluster is highly similar in |FRAME: TAX-53408| and |FRAME: TAX-287|. Highly similar gene clusters are also found in |FRAME: TAX-300| and |FRAME: TAX-220664| and |FRAME: TAX-205922|, although |FRAME: TAX-220664| lacks atuG and atuH and is unable to utilize |FRAME: GERANIOL|. Evidence suggests that the genes are regulated by atuR and they are not expressed during growth on unrelated substrates, or substrates of the |FRAME: LEU-DEG2-PWY| pathway. In addition, other genes involved in acyclic monoterpene utilization include exaA encoding a PQQ-dependent ethanol dehydrogenase, aceA encoding isocitrate lyase, mqoB encoding malate:quinone oxidoreductase, and moeA2 which is necessary for molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis. Notably, it appears that utilization of |FRAME: GERANIOL|, but not |FRAME: Citronellols|, is molybdenum-dependent which suggests that oxidation of |FRAME: GERANIOL| and |FRAME: Citronellols| requires different enzymes (reviewed in |CITS: [20490788]|).

Summary: General Background, Curcuminoids are a class of diarylheptanoid secondary metabolites produced in turmeric (|FRAME:TAX-136217|) and other related plant species. These yellow pigment compounds appear to offer numerous health benefits based on their anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-tumor, and anti-amyloid properties |CITS: [16413584][15974909][15863007][18370854]|. The rhizome of tumeric has been used both for medicine and as a source of spices for cooking, particularly in Asian societies |CITS: [16081279]|. The biosynthesis of three of the most prominent curcuminoids, |FRAME: CPD-6602|, |FRAME: CPD-12187|, and |FRAME: CPD-12188| is described in this pathway., About This Pathway, Curcuminoid biosynthesis has been a topic of research for many years. Radiotracer studies have suggested several potential routes for curcuminoid synthesis |CITS: [ROUGHLEY73][18603793]| and complementary research on type III polyketide synthases in several species has provided further insights into potential curcuminoid biosynthetic mechanisms |CITS: [Schroeder97][11129580][16496097]|. In general, these studies suggested that two phenylpropanoid units derived from phenylalanine condense to form the curcumin scaffold. A set of labeling experiments suggested that cinnamate (and likely cinnamoyl-CoA) was the primary source of a putative curcumin skeleton intermediate that lacks any functional modifications on either ring (referred to as bisdeshydroxybisdesmethoxycurcumin in |CITS: [18603793]|) (see upstream pathway |FRAME: PWY1F-467|). The discovery and characterization of four enzymes involved in this pathway, DKS, and CURS1, 2, and 3, led to the proposal that |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| and |FRAME: FERULOYL-COA| are the starter CoA ester substrates used by these enzymes. The hydroxy and methoxy groups are introduced as part of the starter substrates in the first and second condensation reactions to produce a modified diketide intermediate and the final curcuminoid products |CITS: [19622354][19258320]|. The diketide-CoA esters form a β-keto acid intermediate prior to the addition of the second CoA ester |CITS: [19258320]|., Regulation of curcuminoid biosynthesis will require further study, but a few hints have emerged from the characterization of these enzymes. DCS, the first enzyme in the pathway, appears to be subject to allosteric regulation. Because both DCS and the downstream CURS enzymes use feruloyl-CoA as a substrate, it may be important to ensure that not all of this compound is consumed by DCS. In comparison to the CURS enzymes, the homotropic activation of DCS may cause a relatively greater decrease in activity in response to reduced levels of feruloyl-CoA and thus promote an adequate flow of both the diketide-CoA esters and feruloyl-CoA to the downstream enzymes |CITS: [19258320]|. In addition, differential control of the three CURS (polyketide synthases) may help to account for differences in the levels and distribution of curcuminoids found within different organs and cultivars of tumeric. Although these enzymes are similar in sequence, they fall into two groups, with CURS1 and CURS2 showing similarities in substrate preference and transcript expression patterns that differ from CURS3 |CITS: [19622354][19258320]|., Based on the medicinal importance of these compounds and other structurally related compounds found in other plant species, research on curcuminoid biosynthesis continues.
