General Background, |FRAME: THR| is an indispensable amino acid and is degraded by two major degradative pathways in vertebrates. In most vertebrates, the degradation of L-threonine occurs through a two-step pathway, |FRAME: THREONINE-DEG2-PWY|, involving the enzymes L-threonine 3-dehydrogenase and |FRAME: HS01980-MONOMER|, where threonine is converted to |FRAME: GLY| via the formation of |FRAME: AMINO-OXOBUT| |CITS: [7028754]||CITS: [728468]||CITS: [12097150]|. , However, while functional L-threonine 3-dehydrogenase has been cloned in many mammals including, goat, pig and mouse, the human enzyme, |FRAME: ENSG00000154316-MONOMER|, has been shown to be a nonfunctional product of a pseudogene |CITS: [7827500]||CITS: [3888978]||CITS: [12361482]|. , About This Pathway, In the first step of this two step pathway, |FRAME: THR| is deaminated to |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-392| |CITS: [18342636]|. In the second step, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-7050| |CITS: [3718468]|. The pathway can then proceed via |FRAME: PROPIONMET-PWY|.

General Background, Organohalogen compounds are produced naturally by biological and nonbiological processes. They are also produced by the chemical industry and are widely used. Some organohalogens can be completely degraded by microorganisms. Several of the enzymes involved in organic haloacid degradation have been characterized and their mechanisms studied. Such studies have applications in the production of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals as well as in environmental remediation |CITS: [18499064][23568428]|., About This Pathway, The soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-306678| was shown to grow on |FRAME: CPD-15408| as sole carbon source. Mass spectrometric monitoring of cell-free extracts from |FRAME: CPD-15408|-grown cells showed that |FRAME: CPD-15408| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-15409| in a |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent manner. These data also suggested that the product |FRAME: CPD-15409| is hydrolytically dehalogenated to |FRAME: D-LACTATE| (D-lactate) by |FRAME: MONOMER-18422| and that |FRAME: D-LACTATE| is probably further metabolized to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| by |FRAME: DLACTDEHYDROGFAD-MONOMER| |CITS: [15781461]|., Two major |FRAME: CPD-15408|-inducible proteins were detected in |FRAME: CPD-15408| grown cells. One of them was identified as |FRAME: MONOMER-18421| and its encoding gene was cloned, expressed in E. coli, purified and characterized. It was shown to catalyze the asymmetric |FRAME: NADPH|-dependent reduction of the carbon-carbon double bond in |FRAME: CPD-15408| to produce |FRAME: CPD-15409| |CITS: [15781461]|., A second pathway for |FRAME: CPD-15408| degradation may also exist in |FRAME: TAX-306678|. This organism contains a homolog of the |FRAME: MONOMER-18423| that has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-66693| (|CITS: [20656877]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21307570]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7428|).

|FRAME: CPD-11776 "Camptothecin"| (CPT) is a monoterpene indole alkaloid that was isolated from the Chinese happy tree, |FRAME: TAX-16922|. This compound has drawn considerable interest among drug researchers as it was shown to possess anti-tumor activity. In fact, it has been called one of the most promising anticancer drugs of the 21st century. The richest source of |FRAME: CPD-11776| is |FRAME: TAX-159386|, a tree native to Indo-malaysia and Indo-china, that is also distributed in some parts of Assam, Burma, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Thailand. In addition to |FRAME: CPD-11776|, several modified camptothecinoids have been deteced in |FRAME: TAX-159386|, including |FRAME: CPD-21274|, |FRAME: CPD-21273|, |FRAME: CPD-21275|, and |FRAME: CPD-21276| |CITS: [18596662]|. Since no viable synthetic synthesis of the compound is available, the tree is being subjected to extensive harvesting and is now endangered., |FRAME: CPD-21277 Irinotecan| and |FRAME: CPD-21278| are water-soluble semi-synthetic analogues of |FRAME: CPD-11776| that are FDA approved for treatment of colorectal and ovarian cancers., The exact mechanism of anti-cancerous activity has been pinpointed to |FRAME: CPD-11776| being an inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-5.6.2.2 "topoisomerase 1"|. |FRAME: CPD-11776 "Camptothecin"| inhibits religation of the nicked DNA strands by reversibly binding to the cleavable complex, preventing the binding of DNA polymerase and creating a double strand break. Subsequent downstream events are fatal to the cell |CITS: [19476377]|., |FRAME: CPD-11776 "Camptothecin"| is derived biosynthetically from |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: SECOLOGANIN-CPD| via the precursor |FRAME: STRICTOSIDINE|. The first committed intermediate of the pathway is |FRAME: CPD-11775|, but it is still not clear whether it is formed enzymatically or spontaneously |CITS: [19709698]|. , While the last three steps of the pathway also remain speculative, there is evidence for both intermediate compounds (|FRAME: CPD-15042| and |FRAME:CPD-15043|) in |FRAME: TAX-157934|. Moreover, in this species, genetic suppression of the upstream enzymes leads to a decrease in the levels of these intermediates. It has been suggested that the enzymatic steps between |FRAME: CPD-11775| and |FRAME: CPD-11776| are catalyzed by cytochrome P-450 enzymes |CITS: [22035094]|. Nevertheless, the complex steps and the enzymes involved in these steps have not yet been identified |CITS: [22652243]|. , A few studies have attempted to identify the |FRAME: TAX-159386| genes that are involved in |FRAME: PWY-6326| |CITS: [27432874][29270891]|. However, no genes are known for the latter part of the pathway, which is shown here.

Powerful antidepressant activity and other pharmocological properties are displayed by compounds from |FRAME:TAX-65561| (St. John's wort). Previously it was thought that |FRAME:CPD-9562| (see |FRAME:PWY-5780|) was responsibile for this actvity but it has been confirmed that the actual active ingredient is |FRAME: CPD-9635|. In addition to |FRAME:CPD-9635|, its homolog |FRAME:CPD-14533|, which is found in the genus |FRAME:TAX-55962|, also posseses similar pharmacological properties |CITS:[11263672]|. While the concentration of |FRAME:CPD-9635| is 10 times higher than |FRAME:CPD-14533| in |FRAME:TAX-65561| |CITS:[17226474]|, the reverse ratio was reported in |FRAME:TAX-55963| |CITS:[15652570]|., |FRAME:CPD-9635 Hyperforin| is a bicyclic polyprenylated acylphloroglucinol derivative |CITS: [16973193]|. It consists of a mixture of interconverting tautomers, and is very unstable when exposed to light and oxygen. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-9635| is not well understood. Enzymatic formation of the hyperforin skeleton is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.156|, a polyketide synthase that also participates in bitter acids biosynthesis in hops. The enzyme utilizes |FRAME:ISOBUTYRYL-COA| and 3 molecules of |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| to form the acylphologlucinol skeleton |CITS: [15649510]|. The five isoprenoid moieties are supplied by the MEP pathway. Electrophilic substitution of the unsubstituted hyperforin nucleus involves 2 |FRAME:CPD-4211| units and one |FRAME:GERANYL-PP| molecule, and the ring closure is finally achieved by a third |FRAME:CPD-4211|. The sequence of these steps is yet to be characterized. The bioformation of |FRAME:CPD-14533| is carried out in the same fashion but utilizes |FRAME:ISOVALERYL-COA| instead of |FRAME:ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, which results in a |FRAME:3-METHYL-1-246-TRIHYDROXYPHENYLBUTAN| skeleton. , Recently, the biosynthetic origin of |FRAME:CPD-9635| and |FRAME:CPD-14533| has been investigated in more detail. According to this research branched-chain amino acids are involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-9635| and |FRAME:CPD-14533|. Using radioactive tracer molecules, |FRAME:VAL| and |FRAME:ILE| have been demonstrated as precursors for for |FRAME:CPD-9635| and |FRAME:CPD-14533|, repsectively |CITS:[17307206]|., |FRAME:CPD-9635 Hyperforin| and |FRAME:CPD-14533| have been thought to be biosynthesized in the dark glands of the leaves but recent research has shown that hyperforin essentially accumulates in the translucent glands of the leaves indicating a similar biosynthetic site and production modus as monoterpene biosynthesis |CITS:[17468113]|. |FRAME:CPD-9635 Hyperforin| and |FRAME:CPD-14533| may serve as defense agents.

General Background, Every year malaria affects 300-500 million people worldwide, accounting for about 2 million fatal infections. The disease is caused by the protozoan |FRAME: TAX-5833|, which is transmitted by mosquitoes of the genus |FRAME: TAX-7164 Anopheles| |CITS: [10371589]|. , A tea made of |FRAME: TAX-35608| (a type of wormwood native to Asia) has been a traditional Chinese malaria medicine for millenia. The first active ingredient found in the tree was |FRAME: CPD-7561|, in 1972. The discovery was part of a military research project conducted by the Chinese military, aiming to aid the North Vietnamese army in the war againt the United States. As such, the discovery was not published at the time. Professor Youyou Tu, who was a principle investigator, managed to purify |FRAME: CPD-7561| from |FRAME: TAX-35608| in 1971, resulting in 100% inhibition of the Plasmodium parasite in a mouse model. The compound has been used successfully in several thousand malaria patients in China before it was described in the Western literature |CITS: [3887571]|., Other active ingredients were also identified in the plant, including |FRAME: CPD-21877|, which was described already in 1973 |CITS: [Jeremic73][4833346][4833347]|. , |FRAME: CPD-7561 Artemisinin| is one of the most potent antimalarial drugs |CITS: [2255584][12709893]|. Artemsinin and its derivatives are particularly effective in treatments of multidrug-resistant malaria, replacing other drugs of natural sources that have become ineffective |CITS: [9037139]|. In addition, artemisinin also shows antiviral activity and has been successfully tested as a treatment against hepatitis B virus (HBV) |CITS: [16122816]|. Dihydroartemisinin has recently been reported to possess angiogenic activity. The advantage of artemisinin and derivatives lies in their proven low toxicity, which makes the compounds useful for the chemotherapeutic treatment of human diseases such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) |CITS: [16075280]|., |FRAME: TAX-35608| is the only plant that contains artemisinin in an amount (0.01-0.8% dry weight) that allows commercial exploitation. However, on a global scale the yield of artemisinin extracted from |FRAME: TAX-35608| cannot accommodate the demand. Research had focused on improving the production of the drug in |FRAME: TAX-35608| cell lines or breeding of high artemisinin yielding plants, as well as understanding the pathway to allow recombinant production |CITS: [12709893]|., About This Pathway, The sesquiterpene lactone artemisinin derives from |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| (FDP), a ubiquitous precursor for the formation of olefinic sesquiterpene skeletons. The biosynthesis of sesquiterpenes starts with the cyclization of FDP catalyzed by sequiterpene synthases, which can lead to a remarkable diversity of cyclic sesquiterpenes |CITS: [McCarvay95]|., , The first committed step in the pathway is the cyclization of |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| to form |FRAME:CPD-7554|. The enzyme catalyzing that reaction (|FRAME: EC-4.2.3.24|) has been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-35608|, cloned and biochemically characterized |CITS:[10626375][11185551][11289612][11032404][15797234]|., The other steps of the pathway are less well characterized. However, the metabolic sequence leading from |FRAME:CPD-7554| to |FRAME:CPD-7561| has been identified based upon the analysis of intermediates and corresponding enzyme activities |CITS: [15678372]|. |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.114|, a cytochrome P-450 (|FRAME: G-9424|), converts |FRAME:CPD-7554| to |FRAME:CPD-7556| |CITS: [16458889]|. The enzyme further oxidizes |FRAME:CPD-7556| to |FRAME:CPD-7557| and is able to convert the aldehyde to |FRAME:CPD-13248|, which is converted non-enzymatically to |FRAME: CPD-21877|. Arteannuin-B was found to act synergistically with |FRAME: CPD-7561| against a chloroquine-resistant strain of |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [23289055]|. In addition, the cytoxicity of |FRAME: CPD-21877| was found to be ten times higher than that of |FRAME: CPD-7561| against 8 different cancer cells |CITS: [21831619]|., In order to proceed towards |FRAME: CPD-7561|, |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.92| (|FRAME: G-14993|) diverts |FRAME:CPD-7557| from the oxygenase by reducing the Δ11(13) double bond, forming |FRAME:CPD-7558| |CITS: [15678372][Covello08][18495659]|. This compound still serves as a substrate for |FRAME: G-9424|, which oxidizes it to |FRAME:CPD-7559| |CITS: [18495659]|. The final steps, forming |FRAME:CPD-7561| from |FRAME:CPD-7559|, occur non-enzymatically in the presence of oxygen, and are most likely photochemical conversions |CITS: [10096851][10479327]|.

Names: toluene degradation to 2-hydroxypentadienoate I (via o-cresol) // toluene degradation via 2-hydroxytoluene
Summary: Toluene is widely used as an industrial additive and solvent. Toluene and related aromatic , compounds can be degraded by bacteria, and have been studied in the metabolically versatile genus , |FRAME:TAX-286| and closely related genera. These studies have been directed toward , bioremediation of environmental pollutants by metabolic engineering, and the development of syntrophic bacterial , consortia (reviewed in |CITS: [15492931]|). Aerobic pathways of toluene degradation have been identified in various , species that involve different initial monooxygenase, or hydroxylating dioxygenase reactions. Several of these , pathways converge in the formation of 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) |CITS: [1892384]|. This compound , is a substrate for ring cleavage enzymes, the products of which are metabolized via a common meta fission , pathway, resulting in the formation of compounds of central metabolism (see this pathway and MetaCyc , pathways |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-3-OH-PWY| and |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-DIOL-PWY|). , A degradative plasmid, TOM, containing an operon for the inducible toluene ortho-monooxygenase pathway , has been identified in Burkholderia cepacia G4. The operon, tomA012345, encodes toluene , ortho-monooxygenase and catechol 2,3-dioxygenase, which allow this organism to grow on toluene and , related compounds as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [7538275]|, and in |CITS: [11751810]|. This pathway , for toluene degradation via 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) in Burkholderia cepacia , (Pseudomonas cepacia) is shown here. In this pathway, toluene is sequentially hydroxylated by the toluene , ortho-monooxygenase system. The first hydroxylation is at the ortho position yielding , o-cresol (2-hydroxytoluene) as an intermediate, and the second is at the meta position yielding 2,3-dihydroxytoluene (3-methylcatechol) |CITS: [7578004]|. , Ring fission of 2,3-dihydroxytoluene is catalyzed by catechol 2,3-dioxygenase to produce , cis,cis-2-hydroxy-6-oxohepta-2,4-dienoate. This compound is hydrolyzed to 2-oxopent-4-enoate, , or its tautomeric dienol form cis-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate. This tautomerization occurs spontaneously , in aqueous solution |CITS: [15301547]|. It is not known which tautomeric form is produced by the hydrolase, and , which form is used by the hydratase of B. cepacia in this pathway. However, it has been suggested that the , |FRAME:TAX-303| hydratase uses the dienol form as a substrate |CITS: [2681159]|, and there is evidence , that the |FRAME:TAX-562| hydratase also uses the dienol form as substrate, producing a ketonized , intermediate in the reaction mechanism |CITS: [9492273]|. The last two reactions are labeled as hypothetical , because these enzymes and their products were not directly demonstrated in this organism. However, their , existence in B. cepacia is inferred by work in Pseudomonas |CITS: [8063106]|. The products of the , pathway are pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and acetaldehyde, which may be converted by acylating , aldehyde dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, a central metabolite |CITS: [8063106], [8419288]|.

General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, Many organisms detoxify |FRAME: ARSENATE| using a glutaredoxin-dependent arsenate reductase (see |FRAME: PWY-4621|) or the thioredoxin-dependent arsenate reductase (|FRAME: PWY-8101|). The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1718| does not possess glutaredoxin. This organism has one thioredoxin-dependent enzyme (encoded by the ArsC1' gene), and two mycothiol-dependent enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G18NG-9817| and |FRAME: G18NG-11093| genes |CITS: [19286650][22032722]|., It has been shown that |FRAME: CPD1G-2| can reduce arsenate to |FRAME: CPD-763| on its own. However, the reaction is greatly accelerated in the presence of arsenate reductase proteins and |FRAME: G18NG-10412-MONOMER "mycoredoxin"|. The entire process has been reconstituted in vitro and a model has been proposed., The two arsenate reductase enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G18NG-9817| and |FRAME: G18NG-11093| catalyze the formation of a |FRAME: CPD-12152|. A thiolate at the active site of the enzyme activates arsenate, facilitating its transfer to |FRAME: CPD1G-2|., In the next step |FRAME: G18NG-10412-MONOMER "mycoredoxin"| reduces the thiol-arseno bond of the conjugate and forms arsenite and |FRAME: Mycothiol-mycoredoxin-mixed-disulfides|. Finally, a second glutathion molecule releases the mycoredoxin, forming |FRAME: MYCOTHIONE|. The later is restored to mycothiol by the action of |FRAME: CPLX-7991| |CITS: [19286650]|.

Names: succinate to cytochrome bd oxidase electron transfer
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| respiratory chain formed by succinate dehydrogenase and cytochrome bd oxidase the transfer of electrons from succinate to cytochrome bd oxidase is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force (pmf) across the cytoplasmic membrane. Succinate dehydrogenase does not contribute to the generation of proton potential (see |CITS: [18930017]|); cytochrome bd oxidase translocates 1 H+/e- by means of an oriented redox loop |CITS: [1850294]|., Cytochrome bd oxidase is expressed under oxygen-limiting conditions |CITS: [2172211], [8576043]| unlike cytochrome bo oxidase which is expressed when oxygen levels are high |CITS: [6365921]|. E. coli K-12 also contains a second bd-type cytochrome not shown in this pathway (|FRAME: APP-UBIOX-CPLX| - encoded by the appBC genes). The physiological role of cytochrome bd-II is uncertain although it is able to generate PMF via a mechanism similar to cytochrome bd-I |CITS: [21987791]|. The expression of succinate dehydrogenase is maximal during aerobic growth; repression under anaerobiosis is mediated by the global regulators ArcA and Fnr (reviewed in |CITS: [7855430]|). Electron transport from succinate to oxygen is dependent on the presence of ubiquinone (Q8) |CITS: [195602]|.

Names: nicotinate riboside salvage pathway I // nicotinic acid riboside salvage pathway I
Summary: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) is an essential cofactor for cellular redox reactions and energy , metabolism.  NAD also has been shown to be an important substrate in a variety of biological processes, , including transcriptional regulation, DNA repair, calcium-dependent signaling pathways, , calorie-restriction-mediated life-span extension and age-associated diseases , |CITS: [12736687],[12648681]|. NAD appears to affect these processes by regulating the Sir2p family of , NAD-dependent deacetylases (Sirtuins) |CITS: [12648681]|. , There are a number of pathways for NAD biosynthesis.  In yeast and most other organisms, the two major , pathways are de novo synthesis of NAD (the de novo pathway) and regeneration of NAD from its , nicotinamide degradation products (the NAD salvage pathway) |CITS: [12972620], [12648681]|. NAD is , synthesized de novo from tryptophan via kynurenine |CITS: [12972620]|. In this pathway tryptophan is , converted to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NAMN) in 6 enzymatic steps (catalyzed by Bna1-2p, and , Bna4-7p) and one non-enzymatic step |CITS: [12972620]|. At NAMN the de novo pathway converges with , the NAD salvage pathway and the last two steps to NAD are shared |CITS: [12972620], [12648681]|. In , the yeast NAD salvage pathway, the vitamin precursors nicotinamide and nicotinic acid are converted to , NAMN, the point of convergence with the de novo pathway |CITS: [12648681]|.  The steps from nicotinic , acid to NAD were elucidated by Preiss and Handler and are sometimes referred to as the Preiss-Handler , pathway |CITS: [13416279], [13563526]|. Yeast can also import extracellular nicotinic acid into the cell by , the permease Tna1p and then convert it into NAD via the Preiss-Handler pathway |CITS: [12648681]|., There are four additional pathways for synthesizing NAD in yeast: two salvage pathways from the vitamin , precursor nicotinamide riboside (NR) and two salvage pathways from nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) , |CITS: [15137942], [17482543], [17914902]|. Three of these salvage pathways converge first with the NAD , salvage pathway and then with the de novo pathway, while the fourth, the NR salvage pathway I, is , independent of both of these pathways. In the NR salvage pathway I, NR is phosphorylated to , nicotinamide mononucleotide by the kinase Nrk1p, and then adenylated to NAD by Nma1p or Nma2p , |CITS: [15137942]|. Bacteria such as Haemophilus influenza that lack the enzymes of the de novo and , Preiss-Handler pathway can synthesize NAD from NR and nicotinamide mononucleotide as well , |CITS: [15137942]|. Humans also appear to have this NR salvage pathway |CITS: [15137942]|. Yeast have , a second NR salvage pathway (NR salvage pathway II) that is independent of Nrk1p; in NR salvage , pathway II NR is split into a ribosyl product and nicotinamide, which is subsequently converted to NAD , via enzymes of the NAD salvage pathway and de novo pathway |CITS: [17482543]|. The initial steps in , the two NaR salvage pathways are similar to those of the NR salvage pathways and are catalyzed by the , same enzymes; Nrk1p catalyzes the first step in the NR and NaR salvage pathways I and Urh1p and , Pnp1p catalyze the first steps of the NR and NaR salvage pathways II |CITS: [17914902]|.

Hinokiresinol is structurally the simplest norlignan and regarded as being produced in one of the first steps in norlignans biosynthesis. Norlignans are natural occurring phenolic compounds with a diphenylpentane core skeleton being formed from a phenylpropane (C6C3) and an phenylethane unit (C6C2) which are linked via a C7-C8' bond and constitute the basic norlignan [C6-C3(C2)-C6] carbon scaffold as seen in |FRAME:CPD-17602| and |FRAME:CPD-17603| |CITS:[Umezawa11] [Suzuki07] [Suzuki02]|. Norlignans are found together with lignans (see |FRAME:PWY-7629|, |FRAME:PWY-7631|, |FRAME:PWY-7630|) as typical compounds in heartwood of coniferous trees |CITS:[2833712] [Ward99]|. It is worth noting that two enantiomers of hinokiresinol have been identified in plants, the trans or (E)-isomer, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17603| in the heartwood of conifers, for instance Cryptomeria japonica |CITS:[Yamada88] [16884819]|, Metasequoia glyptostroboides |CITS:[21226514]|, Chamaecyparis obtusa |CITS:[Takaku01]|, Chamaecyparis formosensis |CITS:[19003728]| and Libocedrus yateensis |CITS:[Erdtman79]|. The accumulation of |FRAME:CPD-17603| in the transition zone between sap- and heartwood has been used as biomarker to differentiate between the otherwise undistinguishable wood zones |CITS:[Yoshida06] [18232669]| and is in general increasingly formed in response to fungal attacks and other stress |CITS:[Imai05]|. In contrast, its geometrical isomer cis or |FRAME:CPD-17602| occurs in the dicotyledonous legume (Pueraria lobata - Kudzu) |CITS:[Nohara93]| and in monocotyledonous plants such as Anemarrhena asphodeloides |CITS:[17260262]| and Asparagus officinalis |CITS:[Suzuki01]|., Norlignans, with |FRAME:CPD-17602| as one of the most common representative of the compound class, are known for their wide spectrum of physiological and pharmacological activities. Besides functioning as phytoalexins in Asparagus |CITS:[Takasugi93]| and Cryptomeria |CITS:[Yamada88]|, |FRAME:CPD-17602| has been observed to inhibit angiogenic response |CITS:[14646178]|, expresses estrogen-like activities |CITS:[10726863]|, acts as antioxidant and prevents abnormal fatty deposits in arteries |CITS:[18087806]|, shows antifungal |CITS:[10563936] [14561517]| and anti-inflammatory |CITS:[20091263]| activities and also inhibited enzymes such as hyaluronidase |CITS:[17260262]|, testosterone 5α-reductase |CITS:[11379787]|, cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase |CITS:[6280885] [Nikaido81]|, β-hexosaminidase |CITS:[17051467]| and LTB4 binding receptors |CITS:[10364852]|. On the other hand |FRAME:CPD-17603| has been reported to possess estrogen-like activity |CITS:[10726863]|, was effective against protozoa such as Leishmania and Plasmodium |CITS:[9358645]|, and exhibited moderate antimalarial |CITS:[16392829]| and free radical scavenging activities |CITS:[23287539]|., The elucidation of the |FRAME:PWY-7632| is still in progress and the reaction mechanism and involved enzymatic activities under further investigation |CITS:[Umezawa15]|. Feeding experiments confirmed |FRAME:COUMARYL-ALCOHOL| and |FRAME:P-COUMAROYL-COA| as precursors |CITS:[Suzuki01]| forming |FRAME:CPD-17610| as an intermediate towards the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17602| catalyzed by the enzymatic activity of the (Z)-hinokiresinol synthase (Z-HRS) in Asparagus officinalis without the participation of any cofactor |CITS:[12122678]|. The HRS from Asparagus was later cloned and shown to consist of two subunits, i.e. HRSα and HRSβ which have been individually and in combination assayed for the formation of hinokiresinol. It could be shown that the formation of pure |FRAME:CPD-17602| is only carried out by the heterodimeric Z-HRS with the subunit composition HRSα/HRSβ whereas the dimerization of either (HRSα)2 or (HRSβ)2 (E-HRSs) results in the formation of the steroisomer |FRAME:CPD-17603| |CITS:[18093914]|. In addition to the control of cis/trans isomerism the subunit composition has also been shown to determine enantioisomerism. This was demonstrated by combining the subunits HRSα and HRSβ either to the heterodimer (HRSα/HRSβ) or the two possible homodimers (HRSα/HRSα or HRSβ/HRSβ). Whereas the former combination results in the formation of optical pure |FRAME:CPD-17604| (as found naturally in Asparagus), the latter combinations yielded |FRAME:CPD-17606| as major and |FRAME:CPD-17607| as minor product demonstrating the enantiospecific activity of the subunit(s) composition |CITS:[20165801]|. The natural formation of |FRAME:CPD-17603| was detected in a cultured cell suspension obtained from stems of Cryptomeria japonica and the respective enzyme coined (E)-hinokiresinol synthase (E-HRS) |CITS:[15599432]|.

Summary: |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE Tryptamine| is an important molecule in eukaryotes. In mammals, |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| is an endogenous neuroactive metabolite of |FRAME: TRP|, with behavioral, physiological and pharmacological effects |CITS: [8098507]|. In plants, |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| is a merging point of primary and secondary metabolism. Tryptamine, which is derived from tryptophan by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.105|, provides the indole unit of monoterpenoid-indole and derived alkaloids, many of which are psychoactive |CITS: [8868227][9490777]|., Tryptophan decarboxylase has been cloned from |FRAME: TAX-4058| and overexpressed in |FRAME: TAX-4097|, resulting in high tryptamine levels and resistance to whitefly |CITS: [12228625]|., The pathway from |FRAME: TRP| to |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| via |FRAME: TRYPTAMINE| is widely spread in plants and fungi |CITS: [8868227]|, but little information is available about tryptamine in bacterial metabolism., Mitoma and Udenfriend |CITS: [14423022]| demonstrated that strains of |FRAME:TAX-1351| possess tryptophan decarboxylase activity, transforming tryptophan to tryptamine. However, since their enzyme preparation also had tyrosine and phenylalanine decarboxylase activity, and taking into account the very high Km that enzyme had for tryptophan (13 mM) , they were not sure whether tryptophan decarboxylation in that organism was a result of a distinct enzyme or a secondary activity of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.28|. , Perley and Stowe |CITS: [4960870]| demonstrated production of tryptamine from tryptophan in |FRAME:TAX-1396|, strain KVT. The enzyme required pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor, and had an optimum pH of 8.0. Buki et al |CITS: [4036551]| isolated and partially purified a tryptophan decarboxylase from another Bacillus strain. , Nakazawa et al detected an aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase in several bacterial species that was highly active against tryptophan, forming tryptamine |CITS: [4441405][Nakazawa77]|. The highest activity was detected in several |FRAME: TAX-1269| species. The decarboxylase was produced constitutively, but was repressed by high concentrations of tryptamine., It has been suggested that the soil bacterium |FRAME:TAX-192|, which lives in association with the roots of grasses and cereals, possesses a pathway for the production of IAA from tryptophan via tryptamine |CITS: [Hartmann83][11129057]|. The organism was able to convert tryptamine, which was added to the growth medium, to IAA, but no enzyme has been identified.

This is followed by a transamination to |FRAME: CPD-13781|, and finally acetylation to |FRAME: CPD-15598| |CITS: [17941826]|., The three enzymes encoded by |FRAME: G-17645|, |FRAME: G-17646| and |FRAME: G-17647| were cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified to homogeneity and characterized |CITS: [17941826]|.

Summary: General Background, Ecdysteroid is a generic name for a class of multifunctional, polyhydroxylated steroid hormones that are found in arthropods, plants and fungi. In members of the phylum |FRAME: TAX-6656| ecdysteroid hormones control embryonic and larval development, molting (moulting, ecdysis) and metamorphosis. |FRAME: CPD-276 "20-Hydroxyecdysone"| is considered to be the major active molting hormone and is derived from the pro-hormone |FRAME: ECDYSONE|. The biosynthesis, storage, hormonal regulation, secretion, and metabolism of ecdysteroids have been studied in insects and crustaceans (reviewed in |CITS: [22687472][22017307][20837145][19669094][19796154][19771554][18680437][18222403][15026169][15844229][11729094]|) (also see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7300|). Ecdysteroids can undergo activation and inactivation reactions that are catalyzed by the enzymes shown here (see below)., In decapod crustaceans ecdysteroid inactivation can occur by their conversion to highly polar conjugates which are excreted in urine. Levels of the conjugates vary during the molting cycle. Apolar conjugates of ecdysteroids are formed primarily in the hepatopancreas are eliminated in the feces (|CITS: [1601260]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20837145]|)., About This Pathway, Ecdysteroid inactivation by phosphorylation and activation by dephosphorylation:, In insects, ecdysteroids that are synthesized in the ovary and egg are required for early embryonic development, before differentiation of the prothoracic gland (molting gland) where they are synthesized during molting. The ecdysteroid |FRAME: CPD-276| is the active form of the molting hormone |FRAME: ECDYSONE|. In the eggs of |FRAME: TAX-7091|i, |FRAME: CPD-276| was shown to originate both from dephosphorylation of physiologically inactive ecdysteroid phosphates in yolk granules, and from de novo synthesis from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| (|CITS: [15738639]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19524123]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7300|)., Most of the free ecdysteroids synthesized in the insect ovary are converted to physiologically inactive ecdysteroid 22-phosphates by |FRAME: MONOMER-18146|. These ecdysteroid 22-phosphates are transferred to eggs and then converted to free ecdysteroids by |FRAME: MONOMER-18151| during early embryonic development |CITS: [12721294][16899460]|., Ecdysone inactivation by ecdysone oxidase and 3-dehydroecdysone 3α-reductase:, The conversion of |FRAME: ECDYSONE| to |FRAME: CPD-331| and subsequently to |FRAME: CPD-15607| by |FRAME: MONOMER-16688| and |FRAME: MONOMER-18158| is a major route of ecdysone inactivation in insects. The latter reduction reaction is physiologically irreversible. Functional characterization of the enzymes involved may lead to development of new methods for the biological control of insect pests (in |CITS: [22215981][10861234]|)., 20-hydroxyecdysone inactivation by CYP18A1:, Ecdysteroid 26-hydroxylase encoded by |FRAME: G-17671| is a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that catalyzes the 26-hydroxylation of the insect molting hormone |FRAME: CPD-276| to form a |FRAME: CPD-15601| intermediate, and the subsequent oxidation of the 26-hydroxyl group to the 26-carboxylic acid |FRAME: CPD-15602| via a 26-aldehyde intermediate in a multi-step reaction that inactivates the hormone. It is a key enzyme of ecdysteroid hormone metabolism because both increases and decreases in the levels of circulating active ecdysteroid hormones coordinate molting and metamorphosis |CITS: [21145504][20932968]|.

General Background, |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE Testosterone| is a steroid hormone found in mammals, reptiles, birds, and other vertebrates. It is the principal male sex hormone. In mammals, testosterone is primarily secreted in the testes of males and the ovaries of females, although small amounts are also secreted by the adrenal glands., Like many other steroid hormones, |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| is found in the environment, and can be used by certain microorganisms as the sole carbon and energy source. Both aerobic and anaerobic pathways for testosterone degradation have been described. For the aerobic pathway, see |FRAME: PWY-6943|., About This Pathway, The γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-465721| can degrade androgens anaerobically through an oxygenase-independent pathway that has been named the 2,3-seco pathway since it involves cleaving of the C2-C3 bond of the A ring |CITS: [20413554][21725000][23458847]|. Different steroids appear to be degraded by different pathways that lead to a common part, which is described in |FRAME: PWY-8152|, In this anaerobic pathway |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| is first transformed to |FRAME: CPD-23372| by |FRAME: EC-1.3.99.4|, which is then reduced to produce |FRAME: CPD-23373|. Oxidation of the the hydroxy group at C-17 by 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase forms |FRAME: CPD-23354|, which is degraded by the 2,3-seco pathway as shown in |FRAME: PWY-8152| |CITS: [23458847]|., It should be noted that the order in which enzymes act results in different intermediates in the pathway. It has been shown that 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase can act on many different intermediates in the pathway. Since the enzyme can act on a later intermediate than |FRAME: CPD-23373|, many of the pathway's intermediates can be formed with either a 17-oxo group or a 17β-hydroxy group, and both types have been detected., For example, if the bifunctional molybdoenzyme (AtcABC), which adds an oxo group at position C-1 |CITS: [26872041]| acts before 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, this pathway may join the 2,3-seco pathway at the level of |FRAME: CPD-23375| rather than |FRAME: CPD-23354|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| are complex cofators that are required for the enzymatic activity of many enzymes, which can be divided into three broad classes: isomerases, methyltransferases, and dehalogenases. , Active forms of |FRAME: Cobamides cobamides| contain upper (Coβ) and lower (Coα) ligands. The upper ligands of active cofactors are either 5'-deoxyadenosyl or methyl groups. Much more variability exists with the lower ligand bases, where 16 different compounds have been described (as of 2017), including |FRAME: BENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: CPD-18320|, |FRAME: CPD-18321|, |FRAME: CPD-18497|, |FRAME: CPD-18495|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|, |FRAME: ADENINE|, |FRAME: CPD-18323|, |FRAME: GUANINE|, |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CPD-108|, |FRAME: CPD-5723|, |FRAME: CPD-20865|, |FRAME: CPD-20864|, and |FRAME: CPD-20885|. The best known cobamides, the |FRAME: Cobalamins cobalamins|, contain |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| as the lower ligand by definition. Cobamides with different lower ligands may not be functionally equivalent as cofactors for cobamide-dependent enzymes |CITS: [14351147][13796808][13796809][21696461][22923412][23417488][24055007]|., Enzymes that catalyze isomerase reactions generally require adenosylcobamides, the cofactor form in which the upper ligand is a 5'-deoxyadenosyl group. Enzyme that catalyze methyltransfer reactions usually require methylcobamides. The methyl group is donated to the substrate during catalysis, and is regenerated by a methyl donor. The cobamide form used by the reductive dehalogenases is still not known., About This Pathway, Cobamides containing the purines |FRAME: ADENINE| and |FRAME: CPD-18323| as the lower ligand bases (known as |FRAME: CPD-20858 "pseudo-vitamin B12"| and |FRAME: CPD-20859 "factor A"|, respectively, before the identity of their lower ligand bases was discovered |CITS: [13159915][Dion54]|) have been reported from multiple organisms. |FRAME: CPD-17189 "Pseudo-adenosyl cobamide"| has been reported as the predominant cobamide in |FRAME: TAX-1494| |CITS: [1315276][10940017]|, in |FRAME: TAX-1598| |CITS: [17888910][24055007]|, in some methanogenic archaea, including all methanococcales |CITS: [Stupperich88]|, and in some cyanobacteria |CITS: [10552882][17147452][17616007][20086323]|. It serves as a cofactor of |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.7| |CITS: [4297225]| and |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.1| |CITS: [1315276]|. Both cobamides were shown to be produced by |FRAME: TAX-28901| when grown anaerobically |CITS: [10648108]|. It has been shown that all three corrinoid-dependent enzymes of |FRAME: TAX-28901| can use |FRAME: CPD-20858| |CITS: [17981976]|., It has been shown that when incorporated into enzymes, these cofactors operate in the "base-off" conformation, meaning that one of the protein's amino acids displaces the the Co-coordinating lower ligand base |CITS: [Fieber02]|., This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-17189|, better known as pseudocobalamin.The pathway starts with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of adenosylcobamides with different lower ligand bases. Prior to its attachment, the lower ligand base is activated by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.21| (CobT) by the transfer of a phosphoribose moiety from nicotinate mononucleotide or a related compound to form an α-glycosidic linkage. The phosphoribosylated base is subsequently attached to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.26| (CobS), and the phosphate group is removed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.73| (CobC) to form the cobamide. The enzymes that operate in this pathway are the same enzymes that are involved in adenosylcobalamin biosynthesis. Studies of the specificity of these enzymes have suggested that the nature of the lower ligand is controlled by metabolic factors |CITS: [11441022]| as well as by the specificity of CobT |CITS: [24055007]|. CobT from |FRAME: TAX-1598| appears to be specific for |FRAME: ADENINE| |CITS: [24055007]|.

Summary: |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE "4-Aminobenzoate"| is an important metabolic intermediate, leading to the biosynthesis of various products such as |FRAME: All-Folates folates|, |FRAME: Ubiquinones ubiquinone| (in eukaryotes), and various bacterial antibiotics (e.g. |FRAME: Candicidins|)., Most organisms produce |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| using the PabA/PabB and PabC enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-6543| and |FRAME: PWY-8276|). However, some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-813|, |FRAME: TAX-915|, and |FRAME: TAX-1613|, are capable of synthesizing |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| de novo and yet to not have the pabABC genes., A study of |FRAME: TAX-272561| has found that |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE| is produced by a suicide enzyme that converts its own active-site tyrosine(s) to |FRAME: P-AMINO-BENZOATE|. The enzyme, which contains a |FRAME: CPD-13142| cofactor, reuires oxygen and an electron donor, but does not requires free |FRAME: TYR| or any other substrate |CITS: [32967910]|.

There have been several reports conccerning the fatty acid composition of the Brucella lipid A, which often contradicted each other. A 1990 study reported that the main fatty acid was C16:0, followed by 3-OH-C16:0 and 3-OH-C14:0 . Other fatty acids, including 3-OH C12:0, C18:0, 3-OH-C18:0, 3-OH-C13:0, and C17:0, were present in lower amounts. That study also reported the presence of significant (but not quantified) amounts of 27-OH C88:0 |CITS: [2113907]|. This very long fatty acids is found in most bacterial species belonging to the alpha-2 subgroup of the Proteobacteria |CITS: [1854635]|., A 1994 study has found that amide-linked acids included either two 3-OH-C16:0 molecules + one 3-OH-C14:0 + one 3-OH-C12:0, or two 3-OH-C16:0 molecules and 2 3-OH-C12:0. There were also three ester-linked acids, all of them C16:0. That study also reported the presence of either mono- or diphosphorylated lipid A molecules |CITS: [Qureshi94]|., The next study, from 2006, reported the presence of mainly hepta-acylated species in Brucella species |CITS: [16556309]|. This was contrasted by a 2017 study that found mainly hexa-acylated and penta-acylated species |CITS: [28924631]|. The 2017 study also reported the presence of a diphosphoethanolamine residue. However, in |FRAME: TAX-235| the lptA gene, which encodes phosphoethanolamine transferase, has a deletion of a thymine in position 774 that results in a truncated protein lacking the amino acids related to the enzymatic activity |CITS: [29375522]|.

Fucose is a hexose deoxy sugar. It received its name from the brown algae genus |FRAME: TAX-3011|, from which it was first decribed. The alga was named because of its dark redish color, as one of the meanings of the Latin word fucus is "red paint"., Fucose is a common sugar, found in N-linked glycans on the mammalian, insect and plant cell surface, in many bacterial glycans, and in other biomolecules. Most of the fucose found in biology is in the |FRAME: L-fucoses "L conformation"|, and the use of |FRAME: D-Fucoses| is rather rare (for example in some |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolide glycosides"|)., |FRAME: L-fucoses| can be used by some organisms as a total source of carbon and energy. It has been shown to be metabolized via three separate pathways - |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-8444|, and |FRAME: PWY-8318|., In this pathway, which was described only in strictly anaerobic bacteria, L-fucose is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-24866| and then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-33|. This product is subsequently dehydrated to |FRAME: DEHYDFUC-CPD|. Up to this point the pathway is very similar to |FRAME: PWY-8318|. However, the two pathways diverge at this point. In this pathway an aldolase splits |FRAME: DEHYDFUC-CPD| into |FRAME: LACTALD| and pyruvate. The aldolase was characterized from the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-103892| |CITS: [31914410]|., In |FRAME: TAX-103892| |FRAME: LACTALD| is reduced to |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.77|, as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1315|. The gene encoding the reductase is located in a cluster together with the |FRAME: G-124411|, |FRAME: G-124410|, |FRAME: G-124409|, and |FRAME: G-124408| genes, which encodes the enzymes of this pathway |CITS: [31914410]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12974 Dehydrophos|, originally designated A53868, is a phosponate-containing natrual product produced by |FRAME: TAX-67320| that exhibits broad spectrum antibiotic activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria., The chemical structure of dehydrophos contains a vinyl aminophosphonate moiety linked to a |FRAME: GLY|-|FRAME: LEU| dipeptide |CITS: [17990255]|. Unlike other known phosphonates, dehydrophos contains a methyl ester of the phosphonoate group |CITS: [20876132]|. Both the phosphonate monomethyl ester and the vinyl phosphonate moiety are important for bacteriocidal activity of the natural product |CITS: [20871915]|., The minimal contiguous gene cluster for dehydrophos biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-67320| has been identified |CITS: [20416511]|. The first three steps in the pathway are shared with the pathways for |FRAME: PWY-5757| and |FRAME: PWY-6322|, up to the stage of |FRAME: CPD-9466| (2-HEP) |CITS: [18544530]|. The remaining steps were proposed based on sequence homology of the gene products to other enzymes of known function and on the observation of accumulated intermediates in pathway mutants |CITS: [20416511]|. Later work used purified recombinant protein to clarify the activities associated with the later steps of the pathway |CITS: [23776232]|.

|FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE Nitric oxide| (NO) plays an important role in cell signaling in the nervous system, and is implicated in synaptic plasticity. A function for nitric oxide in signal transduction was established by the demonstration that NO that is generated by endothelial cells relaxes vascular smooth muscle, in part, through the activation of guanylate cyclase |CITS: [2873150]|., NO is synthesized from arginine by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.39 "nitric oxide synthase"| (NOS), generating |FRAME:L-CITRULLINE| as a by-product (see |FRAME: PWY-4983|)., It was soon found that |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| also affects proteins directly by a process known as S-nitrosylation, a post-translational protein modification during which |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| attacks specific cysteine residues in proteins, forming an S-nitrosothiol (SNO) group. , S-Nitrosylation is ubiquitous in biology, and is found in all phylogenetic Kingdoms |CITS: [22539721][21893250]|. It is considered an ancient mechanism of redox-based signalling that has evolved on primordial Earth prior to the accumulation of oxygen in the atmosphere |CITS: [11572774][17524376]|. The first protein whose activity was shown to be regulated by S-nitrosylation in this fashion was the NMDA-type glutamate receptor in the brain |CITS: [1376999][8394509]|. However, within a decade the number of reported substrates for S-nitrosylation has grown to well over a hundred |CITS: [11572774]|., S-nitrosylation is regulated precisely in time and space |CITS: [12727142][11752656][14527267][11907582][11796706]|. The temporal and spatial regulation of the process within and between proteins confer specificity to NO-derived effects |CITS: [15688001]|., Specific enzymatic mechanisms that function primarily in protein S-nitrosylation have not yet been described. However, several enzymes are known to promote S-nitrosylation. For example, |FRAME: EC-1.15.1.1| (SOD) catalyzes the S-nitrosylation of haemoglobin by NO in solution |CITS: [10430889]| or by |FRAME: S-NITROSOGLUTATHIONE| (GSNO) |CITS: [Romeo03]|., The source of the nitroso group is not always directly NO. It can also be nitrite, other NOx species (higher NO oxides), metal-NO complexes, or various SNOs like |FRAME: S-NITROSOGLUTATHIONE|. For example, a principal source of the NO group in mammalian S-nitroso-haemoglobin under physiological conditions is the heme iron-nitrosyl species (FeNO) that is formed from NO |CITS: [12524454]|., The removal of S-nitrosylation is termed denitrosylation, and proceeds via |FRAME: S-NITROSOGLUTATHIONE|. It has been demonstrated that nitrosylated proteins are in a cellular equilibrium with the latter, which is based on the transfer of NO groups between the two |CITS: [11524431]|., A dedicated enzyme, previously known as |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.284|, was shown to be conserved in all organisms and to catalyze the reduction of |FRAME: S-NITROSOGLUTATHIONE| to |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE| (via |FRAME: CPD-19217|), with concomitant release of |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| or |FRAME: AMMONIUM| |CITS: [9531510][11260719]|.

Summary: The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-101510| can use |FRAME: PHTHALATE| as its sole carbon source. Phthalate catabolism is encoded the pad gene clusters. Two such clusters are present in the organism, each on a different plasmid (plasmids pRHL1 and pRHL2)., The pad and pat gene products are only detected in phthalate-grown cells as shown in proteomic analysis |CITS: [15937168]|. The study demonstrated that phthalate is catabolized by a branched beta-ketoadipate pathway. The |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| branch proceeds via |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY| and the two branches converge at |FRAME: 3-OXOADIPATE-ENOL-LACTONE| |CITS: [15937168]|.

|FRAME:CPD-17134 Bassianin| is an hexaketide with an 2-pyridone core and a representative example of highly reduced (HR) polyketides known for their structural complexity and broad range of biological activities |CITS:[19636450] [11548049]|. It has been identified and structurally elucidated as one of the yellow pigments in the fungal genus Beauveria |CITS:[McInnes74] [Wat77]| and is very similar to the closely related |FRAME:CPD-17122| (see |FRAME:PWY-7561|) but differs in chain length and methylation pattern. , The genus Beauveria was amongst the first discovered entomopathogenic fungi which caused the white muscardine disease in the domesticated silk worm (Bombyx mori) with devastating consequences for the European silkworm industry in the 18th century (summarized in |CITS:[Rehner05]|. The pathogenic principle of Beauveria bassiana is based on the production of mycotoxins and toxic proteins which upon secretion affect numerous insects |CITS:[15209284] [20674578]|. In turn, these entomopathogenic properties also furthered the development of biological pest control with Beauveria bassiana as a cost-effective mycoinsecticide which prompted the sequencing of the genome of Beauveria bassiana and laid the foundation for exploring potential biosynthetic secondary metabolite pathways and toxic protein production |CITS:[22761991]|. It has been shown that |FRAME:CPD-17134| inhibits membrane ATPase activity in erythrocytes causing varying degrees of cell lysis |CITS:[Jeffs97]| and displays general neuritogenic activities |CITS:[21448865]|., |FRAME:CPD-17134 Bassianin| has been found several decades ago in Beauveria tenella |CITS:[McInnes74]| but the original strain is not available anymore and thought to be extinct |CITS:[21899331]|. However, |FRAME:CPD-17133| which differs from |FRAME:CPD-17134| by one less methyl group has been found in certain strains of Beauveria bassiana and the corresponding biosynthetic gene cluster for |FRAME:CPD-17134| production identified. The gene cluster is very similar to the |FRAME:CPD-17122| gene cluster (see |FRAME:PWY-7561|) and consists like this of 4 genes, named DmbS, DmbC, DmbA and DmbB with overall identities to the respective genes in the |FRAME:CPD-17123| gene cluster between 80 and 100% |CITS:[Heneghan11]|. , DmbS, the gene encoding the desmethylbassianin synthetase, a polyketide synthase-nonribosomal peptide synthetase (PKS-NRPS), has the same domain organization with domain identities between 80 and 97% as TenS, the corresponding tenellin synthetase. It could also be confirmed that the enoyl reductase domain in DmbS is inoperative and that only in cooperation with the respective trans enoyl reductase encoded by DmbC the first product of the |FRAME:CPD-17133| pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17131| could be produced |CITS:[Heneghan11] [21899331]|. When coexpressing DmbS and DmbC from the |FRAME:CPD-17133| gene cluster together with TenA and TenB from the |FRAME:CPD-17122| gene cluster in the fungal host Aspergillus oryzae the final product |FRAME:CPD-17133| was found to be generated |CITS:[21899331]|. Systematic domain swapping between TenS and DmbS allowed the determination of the programming part of the PKS-NRPS's. It could be shown that two domains of the PKS part were decisive in programming chain length and methylation pattern. The C-methylation domain (CMeT) was found responsible for the number and positions of methyl-groups in the chain and the chain length was exclusively determined by the β-keto reduction (KR) domain |CITS:[21899331]|. The NRPS has no programming function for the final product and is responsible for the aminoacylation and release (for further reading see |CITS:[17581644] [18804170] [17369821] [20111804]|)., In addition, the chimaeric gene TenS(ΔKR:dmbS-KR) coexpressed with DmbC or TenC in Aspergillus oryzae generated |FRAME:CPD-17132| the first expected intermediate in the |FRAME:CPD-17134| biosynthetic pathway. In extension of this experiment the additional coexpression with the cytochrome P450 dependent oxigenases TenA and TenB from the |FRAME:CPD-17122| gene cluster led to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17134|. As mentioned above |FRAME:CPD-17134| is considered an extinct compound which resurrection was therefore classified as 'Lazarus metabolite' demonstrating the potential of combinatorial biosynthesis |CITS:[21899331]|.

Summary: Background, |FRAME: CPD-7901| is an aliphatic methyl ketone that is naturally occurring in plants, where it can play a role as both a pheromone and insecticide |CITS: [14560395]|. The methyl ketone biosynthetic pathway was characterized in tomato plants, specifically |FRAME: TAX-62890|, from which two key genes (|FRAME: G-12180| and |FRAME: G-12179|) were identified that were required for methyl ketone synthesis from fatty acid intermediates |CITS: [20605911]|. |FRAME: G-12180| is purported to hydrolyze a β-ketoacyl ACP to generate a β-keto acid, and |FRAME: G-12179| may decarboxylate the β-keto acid to a methyl ketone (see |FRAME: PWY-6585|)., Being a reduced aliphatic compound, methyl ketones may have relevance as a biofuel, and recently |FRAME:TAX-562| has been metabolically engineered to overproduce methyl ketones with application to biofuel production |CITS: [22038610]|. , About this Pathway, To successfully create this synthetic pathway akin to a truncated form of the |FRAME: FAO-PWY| pathway in |FRAME:TAX-562|, two key genes of this pathway, fadE and fadA were deleted. The reaction catalyzed by fadE was reconstituted by cloning the gene for acyl-CoA oxidase from |FRAME: TAX-1270|. This was done to replace membrane associated fadE with a highly soluble enzyme and |FRAME: TAX-1270| acyl-Co oxidase has homology to a high activity acyl coA oxidase from |FRAME: TAX-37931|. The fadA gene was knocked out to push the pathway towards β-keto acid production. The genes fadB and fadM were overexpressed to optimize methyl ketone biosynthesis.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 Salicylate| is a key phenolic compound biosynthesized by many plants and some microorganisms. It is a member of an important anti-inflammatory drug class used widely in human medicine. In microorganisms |FRAME: CPD-110| is a biosynthetic precursor of secondary metabolites and siderophores, and a regulator of antibiotic efflux |CITS: [15837391]|. In plants |FRAME: CPD-110| may be converted by glucosylation, esterification, or methylation to physiologically active derivatives |CITS: [11607533]|. The source of the name |FRAME: CPD-110| (salicylic acid) comes from the name of the willow tree, |FRAME:TAX-40685|, from whose bark it can be obtained., For examples of salicylate biosynthetic pathways, see |FRAME: PWY-6408|, |FRAME: PWY-6407|, |FRAME: PWY-6406|, |FRAME: PWY-981|, |FRAME: PWY-6621|, |FRAME: PWY-6624| and |FRAME: PWY-4203| |CITS: [20020317]|., In bacteria, |FRAME: CPD-110| can be degraded through several pathways including oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6183|), oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-633| followed by aromatic ring cleavage (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6224|), direct fission of |FRAME: CPD-110| (see |FRAME: CPLX-8159|), and degradation after CoA derivative formation). |FRAME: CPD-110| is also an intermediate in |FRAME: PWY-5427|., In yeast, earlier work on |FRAME: TAX-5554| showed |FRAME: CPD-110| oxidation to |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [7364712] [6539772]|. In a more recent report using |FRAME: ORG-6162| a novel pathway of |FRAME: CPD-110| degradation via |FRAME: PHENOL| was elucidated (pathway |FRAME: PWY-6636|) |CITS: [20020317]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway |FRAME: CPD-110|, which is also an intermediate in the degradation of |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE|,, is degraded via |FRAME: CATECHOL|, a common intermediate in the degradation of many aromatic compounds,, including |FRAME:BENZOATE|, |FRAME: BENZENE| and |FRAME:PHENOL|., Catechol can be subject to either intradiol cleavage by a |FRAME: CPLX-2842| (the ortho cleavage pathway), or extradiol cleavage by a |FRAME: CPLX-2841| (the meta cleavage pathway)., This pathway has been demonstrated in both bacteria |CITS:[14321380][10197990][17172348]| and fungi |CITS: [6539772]|.

Summary: |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-XYLANS "β-1,3-D-xylan"| is a polysaccharide composed of β-1,3-linked |FRAME: BETA-D-XYLOSE| residues. This polysaccharide was first found in the siphonous green seaweed |FRAME: TAX-148944| as a water-insoluble and alkaline-soluble component of cell walls |CITS: [Mackie59]|. It was subsequently found in cell walls of some red (|FRAME: TAX-2784| and |FRAME: TAX-31346|) and green (|FRAME: TAX-76312|, |FRAME: TAX-3128| and |FRAME: TAX-170436|) algae |CITS: [13852998][Fukushi86][Yamagaki96][12860427]|. It has not been detected in cell walls of land plants, which contain |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan| instead., Analysis of |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-XYLANS "β-1,3-D-xylan"| from the siphonous green alga |FRAME: TAX-177073| showed that it is a linear heteropolysaccharide also containing glucose residues linked by β(1,3) linkages as well as some xylose residues linked by β(1,4) linkages. Both of these are thought to be located within the β-1,3-xylose chain and linked via covalent bonds |CITS: [16891637]|., |FRAME: 13-BETA-D-XYLANS "β-1,3-D-xylan"| can be degraded by several organisms, mostly marine bacteria and fungi. The first enzyme to attack the polymer is |FRAME: MONOMER-16528|, an enzyme that randomly hydrolyzes the (1→3)-β-D-glycosidic linkages within the polymer, producing short oligosaccharides ranging from |FRAME: CPD-13290| to |FRAME: CPD-13292|., A |FRAME: MONOMER-16528| has been purified to homogeneity from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-247155| |CITS: [10635569]|. The enzyme consists of a β-(1,3)-xylan binding module and a glycosyl hydrolase family 26 module, and hydrolyzes β-1,3-xylan to produce mainly |FRAME: CPD-13291| and |FRAME: CPD-13290| |CITS: [10635569]|. It does not act on |FRAME: CPD-13290|, |FRAME: CPD-13210|, |FRAME: 1-4-beta-Xylan|, |FRAME: 1-3-beta-D-Glucans|, or |FRAME: Carboxymethylcellulose| |CITS: [10742274]|. Similar enzymes have been purified from the same organism |CITS: [15743273][15272180]| as well as from |FRAME: TAX-118970| |CITS: [11948152][12501421][16061225]|., The next enzyme to act is |FRAME: CPLX-8286|, a protein that attacks the ends of the oligosaccharides and removes xylosyl residues. This enzyme has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-98227| |CITS: [17993567]|.

Under aerobic conditions, |FRAME:TAX-562| is able to utilize D-malate as the sole source of carbon for growth.  D-malate is transported into the cell by the proton motive force-dependent dicarboxylate transporter |FRAME: DCTA-MONOMER "DctA"|.  A D-malate-specific enzyme, |FRAME: G6986-MONOMER|, decarboxylates D-malate to pyruvate while reducing NAD<sup>+</sup>.  Pyruvate then enters central metabolism via |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|.  |CITS: [stern66][17088549][20233924]|, Under anaerobic conditions, fermentation of pyruvate via pyruvate-formate lyase and the pathway of |FRAME: FERMENTATION-PWY| is theoretically feasible, but that route does not produce enough ATP to compensate for the loss of ATP by utilization of the proton motive force during D-malate transport.  Thus, D-malate alone is unable to support growth as the sole source of carbon under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [20233924]|.

Summary: Flavonoids (C15 compounds consisting of two aromatic rings linked by a C3 unit) are a highly diverse class of , plant secondary metabolites (with about 9000 compounds have been identified so far |CITS: [16137727]|). , They are involved in a wide range of biological processes in higher plants such as UV protection, flower coloration, , and antimicrobial defense |CITS: [11130659]|. They also have antioxidant and anticancer properties , |CITS: [12224601]| |CITS: [18645020]|., Flavones, Flavones are a class of flavonoids synthesized directly from flavanones. Flavone formation in various tissues in a wide range of higher and lower plant species is catalyzed by a flavone synthase belong to the plant cytochrome P450 superfamily |CITS: [18645020]|. The flavones can be classified into several subgroups based on (i) hydroxylation, (ii) O-methylation, (iii) C-methylation, (iv) isoprenylation, or (v) methylenedioxy substitutions. , Isovitexin is 6-C-glucosylated apigenin (6-C-glucosylapigenin). Further glycosilation of isovitexin at the 7-hydroxyl position with glucose or xylose has also been reported. In some cases the 2"-O-position of the 6-C-glucose of isovitexin is further glycosylated., Biochemical investigations and genetic research on genetic lines of Silene latifolia (formerly referred to as Silene pratensis) have been shown that some of the loci responsible for glycosylation processes in the plant are differentially expressed in dependence on the ontogenetic stage in the development of the plant. There are two genes responsible for the expression of isovitexin 2''-O-arabinosyltransferases, i.e. glA and D6a, the latter only expressed at early ontogenetic stages in the cotyledons |CITS:[Heinsbroek79]| and also two loci for isovitexin 7-O-galactosyltransferases which are expressed at different developmental stages and in different plant organs, i.e. 07g in cotyledons and Xgal in petals |CITS:[VanBrederode83] [Steyns86a]| indicating the activation of different proteins with similar catalytic and physico-chemical properties in dependence on external and/or internal signals |CITS:[Steyns83] [STEYNS84]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE Testosterone| is a steroid hormone found in mammals, reptiles, birds, and other vertebrates. It is the principal male sex hormone. In mammals, testosterone is primarily secreted in the testes of males and the ovaries of females, although small amounts are also secreted by the adrenal glands., |FRAME: ANDROSTERONE Androsterone| is a steroid hormone with weak androgenic activity that is synthesized from the adrenal hormone |FRAME: 3-BETA-HYDROXYANDROST-5-EN-17-ONE| by the enzyme |FRAME: 1.3.99.5-RXN "steroid 5α-reductase"|. Androsterone is well known in many animal species, and is also found in some plants |CITS: [16044944]|., Like many other steroid hormones, both |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| and |FRAME: ANDROSTERONE| are found in the environment, and can be used by certain microorganisms as the sole carbon and energy source., One of these organisms is |FRAME: TAX-285|, a Gram-negative bacterium that can grow using certain C19 and C21 steroids. Another well-studied testosterone-degrading organism is |FRAME: TAX-43767 "Rhodococcus equi (previously known as Nocardia restrictus)"|., About This Pathway, Degradation of testosterone in |FRAME: TAX-285| is initiated by dehydrogenation of the 17β-hydroxyl group to |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8373|. The degradation of androsterone is initiated by transformation to the same intermediate, which has to be catalyzed by two enzymes - |FRAME: CPLX-8376| and |FRAME: MONOMER-16925|., The pathway downstream from |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| was proposed already in 1968 based on analysis of the compounds produced in culture of testosterone-grown |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [Coulter68]|. , |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE "Androst-4-en-3,17-dione"| undergoes Δ1-dehydrogenation followed by a 9α-hydroxylation to produce |FRAME: CPD-13680|, an unstable compound that rearranges spontaneously to form |FRAME: CPD-13708|, a structure that misses the B ring., The opening of the A ring is achieved by the successive actions of a hydroxylase that hydroxylates the C4 position and a meta-cleavage dioxygenase that opens the ring |CITS: [11739769]|. A hydrolase (|FRAME: G185E-7847|) then breaks the product into two parts - |FRAME: CPD-13711| (which still contains the intact C and D rings) and |FRAME: CPD-13712| |CITS: [12676694][16151114]|. The latter is believed to be processed by three enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-14747|, |FRAME: G-14748| and |FRAME: G-14749|, into |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [16151114]|., The degradation of the last two steroid rings, starting with |FRAME: CPD-13711|, was shown to begin with the removal of the side chain in the form of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by one β-oxidation cycle |CITS:[Lee67][Miclo90][Miclo92]| in a process that involves the |FRAME: G185E-7838| and |FRAME: G-14760| genes |CITS: [21901092][23146019]|. However, the complete pathway was described only in 2017 |CITS: [28377529]|. This part of the pathway is catalyzed by the, KstR2-regulated genes. The 5-member D ring is first hydrolyzed by an enoyl-CoA hydratase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7827| gene, followed by hydrolysis of the 6-member C ring by a hydrolase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-7828| and |FRAME: G185E-7829| genes |CITS: [29581275]|. Following another round of β-oxidation, which results in the release of another |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, the remaining product is split into |FRAME: SUC-COA| and |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [28377529]|.

Names: methanol and methylamine oxidation to formaldehyde // methylotrophy
Summary: General Background, Methylotrophs are organisms that are capable of growing on single carbon (C1) compounds, like methanol. These organisms can derive all their energy and carbon needs from reduced molecules that have no C-C bond. Methylotrophy is found only in a few prokaryotic and eukaryotic microorganisms. , While prokaryotic methylotrophs are capable of growing on a variety of C1 compounds (see |FRAME:PWY-1641| and |FRAME:PWY-1701|), eukaryotic methylotrophs can grow only on |FRAME:METOH|., Methylotrophic eukaryotes include only a few species of yeast that belong to the Pichia and Candida genera. They include |FRAME: TAX-5477|, |FRAME: TAX-36026|, |FRAME: TAX-870730 "Ogataea angusta (previously known as Hansenula polymorpha)"|, |FRAME: TAX-1156966| and |FRAME: TAX-4922| (see |FRAME: PWY-5506|)., The key enzyme in the oxidation of methanol in methylotrophic bacteria is methanol dehydrogenase (MDH). Different bacterial strains use different types of MDH. Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria have a periplasmic |FRAME: CPLX-3264| that contain a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ) cofactor (see |FRAME: PWY-1701|). Thermophilic methylotrophic Bacili such as |FRAME: TAX-1471| use an |FRAME: CPLX-8059| (see |FRAME: PWY-6510|), while Gram-positive bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1814|, |FRAME: TAX-1777| MB19, |FRAME: TAX-1829| LMD 89.129 and |FRAME: TAX-1833| DSM 1069 possess nicotinoprotein methanol dehydrogenases with a bound NAD(P) cofactor that use an unknown electron acceptor for reduction of their bound cofactor and can use the artificial electron acceptor |FRAME: CPD-12424| in vitro |CITS:[1995642][8385013][8449887]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6509|)., The formaldehyde that is formed is a branch point, as it can be channeled into either an assimilatory pathway that provides the cells with carbon for biosynthesis (see |FRAME:P185-PWY|), or a dissimilatory pathway that provides the cells with energy (see |FRAME: PWY-1801|)., About This Pathway, Gram-negative methylotrophic bacteria are aerobic bacteria that utilize one-carbon compounds more reduced than formate as sources of carbon and energy, and assimilate formaldehyde as a major source of cellular carbon |CITS [8801441]|. , Methylotrophic bacteria utilize a variety of different one-carbon compounds including methane (see |FRAME: PWY-1641|), methanol, methylated amines, halomethanes and methylated compounds containing sulfur. , Methanol from both endogenous (methane oxidation) or exogenous sources is oxidized to formaldehyde by a periplasmic methanol dehydrogenase (MDH) in Gram-negative methylotrophs |CITS [3020939]|. Electrons are transferred from MDH to an atypical cytochrome cL, which in turn is oxidized by a typical class I cytochrome c (cH). The two cytochromes are periplasmic as well., Methylamine is oxidized by several species of methylotrophic bacteria by a methylamine dehydrogenase (MADH). , With the exception of the genus |FRAME:TAX-16|, which uses a c type cytochrome as an electron acceptor, , MADHs use blue copper proteins (usually amicyanins) as electron acceptors, which are encoded by a gene located in the same operon that encodes the subunits of the MADH itself |CITS [8021187]|., The product of these two reactions, formaldehyde, is transported into the cytosol, where it is either oxidized to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, or assimilated (see formaldehyde assimilation and formaldehyde oxidation pathways).

Summary: |FRAME: Camphor Camphor| is a bicyclic monoterpene with a characteristic pungent odor and taste. Two enantiomers occur naturally - |FRAME: CPD-862|, the predominant natural isomer, and |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR|. Camphor is produced by several trees, including the camphor tree (|FRAME: TAX-13429|) as well as hundreds of other plants, including |FRAME: TAX-38868| (garden sage), |FRAME: TAX-39367| (rosemary), |FRAME: TAX-39169| (lavender), |FRAME: TAX-35608| (sweet wormwood), and |FRAME: TAX-13328| |CITS: [5532413][ 32619737][35921521]|. Camphor can be synthesized chemically from |FRAME: CPD-4892|, which is obtained from oil of turpentine., Camphor is metabolized by some soil bacteria, depending on the species, via either 5-exo |CITS: [LeGall63]| or 6-endo hydroxy camphor |CITS: [Chapman66]|. These pathways have been termed, respectively, the 2,5- and 2,6-hydroxylating systems |CITS: [806252]|., |FRAME: ORG-5941|, which carries the linear 533 kb CAM plasmid |CITS: [23524667]|, can grow on both |FRAME: CPD-862| and |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| as its sole carbon source, due to the presence of enantiomer-specific Baeyer-Villiger monooxygenases that handle the different enantiomorphs |CITS: [8515237]|. The organism utilizes the 2,5 pathway, and the pathway for |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| degradation is described here |CITS: [BRADSHAW59][4351810][6848481][8515237]|. A similar pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-862| is described in |FRAME: P601-PWY|., The cleavage of the bicyclic ring of camphor involves the participation of three unrelated monooxygenases, one dehydrogenase and one CoA ester synthetase. The camphor hydroxylase, P-450<sub>CAM</sub>, became a primary prototype for P-450 monooxygenases |CITS: [3011733]|. , The CAM plasmid appears to contain the information for all the enzymes that are required to convert camphor to |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| |CITS: [4351810]|. However, the enzymes involved in the later steps of the pathway have not been discovered yet.

Names: methane oxidation to methanol I // methanotrophy
Summary: Methanotrophic bacteria, or methanotrophs, are a part of a physiological group of bacteria known as methylotrophs., Methanotrophic bacteria are unique in their ability to utilize |FRAME: CH4| as a sole carbon and energy source., A defining characteristic of all methanotrophs is the use of the enzyme methane monooxygenases (MMO) to catalyze the oxidation of methane to |FRAME: METOH|. Methane monooxygenases is oxygen-dependent and requires reducing equivalents to activate the oxygen. The oxygen molecule is split during catalysis, with one atom reduced to water and the other incorporated into methane to produce methanol. Methanol is subsequently oxidized to formaldehyde, which can be assimilated to provide carbon, or further oxidized to CO2 in a reaction that generates energy., MMOs exhibit a striking lack of substrate specificity, resulting in the metabolism of a very large number of compounds including xenobiotic chemicals such as small, unactivated alkanes and halogenated hydrocarbon solvents |CITS: [78039848]|., Methanotrophs are divided into two phylogenetic groups. Type I methanotrophs include γ-Proteobacteria, of the genera |FRAME: TAX-413|, |FRAME: TAX-39773|, |FRAME: TAX-429|, |FRAME: TAX-416|, |FRAME: TAX-73778| and |FRAME: TAX-54115|. These bacteria possess bundles of intracytoplasmic membranes, contain predominantly 16-carbon, fatty acids and assimilate formaldehyde produced from the oxidation of methane by the |FRAME: PWY-1861 "ribulose monophosphate cycle"|.The type II methanotrophs contained the closely related α-Proteobacteria genera |FRAME: TAX-133| and |FRAME: TAX-425|. These organisms have intracytoplasmic membranes arranged around the periphery of the cell, contain predominantly 18-carbon fatty acids in their membranes and assimilate formaldehyde into cell carbon using the |FRAME: PWY-1622 "serine cycle"| |CITS: [7857800][8801441]|., All methanotrophs express a membrane-bound particulate MMO (pMMO), which contains copper and apparently uses a quinol as the electron donor (see |FRAME: PWY-6742|). A few species of methanotrophic bacteria produce a second, soluble form of MMO (sMMO) that does not contain copper. , Initially it was thought that sMMOs were confined to the type II genera |FRAME: TAX-425| and |FRAME: TAX-133| and the type I methanotroph |FRAME: TAX-243233|. However, sMMOs have been found in additional type I organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-595536| |CITS: [2542319]|, the marine |FRAME: TAX-81932| |CITS: [9836428]| and |FRAME: TAX-416| strains such as |FRAME: TAX-90656| |CITS: [10583965]|., sMMO is a cytosolic multi-component enzyme that utilizes NAD(P)H as the electron donor. The hydroxylase component of the enzyme contains two dinuclear iron active sites |CITS: [15544][572296]|., Differential expression of the two enzyme systems is regulated by the availability of copper ions. When the copper, to biomass ratio is low, sMMO activity is observed, whereas pMMO is expressed at high copper to biomass ratios |CITS: [Prior85]|., Even though the reaction of methane oxidation requires oxygen, the pathway has been demonstrated in a bacterium that lives under anaerobic conditions. This organism, |FRAME:TAX-671143|, generates the required oxygen as a by-product of nitrite reduction |CITS: [20336137]|.
