Summary: This superpathway integrates some of the fundumental components of energy metabolism, starting with a hexose sugar and ending with |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and several forms of highly reducing metabolites that can be used for ATP generation., The first component in the superpathway is the |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS gycolysis| pathway. Glycolysis is essential under all conditions of growth because it produces many of the key precursor metabolites that are essential for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules. Due to its importance, glycolysis can be found in almost all organisms., Glycolysis fulfills two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) it can produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules by running in the reverse direction., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy. The glycolysis pathway used in this superpathway is the well characterized glycolysis pathway of the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| growing with |FRAME: D-Glucose| as a source of carbon and energy (glucose is phosphorylated by the phosphotransferase system that import it into the cell, and thus the pathway starts with |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|)., The final product of glycolysis, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, is converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| by the action of the |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"|. This is a key reaction of central metabolism, as it links the substrate-level phosphorylation glycolysis pathway with the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, which accepts the input of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|., The |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX|, which in |FRAME:TAX-562| consists of 24 E1 subunits, 24 E2 subunits, and 12 E3 subunits, catalyzes three reactions that constitute a cycle, which is described in the pathway |FRAME: PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|.  The three reactions can be summarized by the reaction, |FRAME:PYRUVDEH-RXN|., The product of the complex, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, feeds into the TCA cycle, a catabolic pathway that generates energy and reducing power as well as precursors for biosynthesis. The TCA cycle is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]|., Even though |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| is shown in this superpathway as a product of the glycolysis pathway, it is also generated by the degradation of fats and proteins and by the fermentation of many metabolites.., In every turn the TCA cycle converts one molecule of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, reduces a total of four molecules of either |FRAME: NAD|, |FRAME: NADP|, or |FRAME: Quinones quinone| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively, and phosphorylates one molecule of GDP to GTP., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., Finally, this superpathway includes the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, which bypasses those steps in the TCA cycle that lead to a loss of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, eliminating the loss of carbon. The glyoxylate cycle operates in bacteria and some eukaryotic organisms. In |FRAME:TAX-562| the bypass is active when growth on 2 carbon compounds requires conservation of 4 carbon TCA intermediates, and is repressed during growth on glucose |CITS: [6378912][6389540][6329757][2512996]|. In plants the cycle is invovled in the metabolism of storage oils during germination of seeds |CITS:[Brownleade97]|. The cycle also operates in developing eggs of nematodes, where it converts triacylglycerols to carbohydrates |CITS: [627278]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Vernolates Vernolate| (vernolic acid) is an unusual fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain that contains a cis double bond at position 9 and an epoxy group at positions 12-13. This unusual fatty acid is found in high concentration (from 60 up to 75%) in seed oils of several |FRAME: TAX-4210| genera, including |FRAME: TAX-13695 Stokesia|, |FRAME: TAX-13753|, and |FRAME: TAX-13464| |CITS: [Gunstone54][7033990]|, as well as certain |FRAME: TAX-3977| species such as |FRAME: TAX-54672| |CITS: [Kleiman65]| and |FRAME: TAX-1441922| |CITS: [Spitzer96]|. Small amount of |FRAME: Vernolates| and related epoxy fatty acids are also found in |FRAME: TAX-4498| (white oat) |CITS: [18707115][Doehlert10]|., Epoxy fatty acids are valuable products and are widely used as plastisizers. The ability of the epoxy group to crosslink makes vernolate-containing oils useful in adhesives and coating materials such as paint |CITS: [Perdue86]|. It can also be used as a precursor of monomeric components of nylon-11 and nylon-12 |CITS: [Ayorinde89][Ayorinde97]|., Several types of enzymes have been reported to catalyze the synthesis of |FRAME: Vernolates| from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|., In |FRAME: TAX-72611| a fatty acid desaturase-like enzyme is responsible for the epoxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-6014|) |CITS: [9572738]|. In the plant |FRAME: TAX-54672| two different enzymes have been described - a peroxygenase that can epoxidize free |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| to generate |FRAME: Vernolates| |CITS: [8267615][21784965]| (this pathway), and a cytochrome P450 enzyme (see |FRAME: PWY-7634|)., About This Pathway, The enzyme that is responsible for the epoxidation in oat is |FRAME: MONOMER-16854|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-14679| gene |CITS: [21784965]|. The enzyme uses hydroperoxy fatty acids as the oxygen donor, and prefers hydroperoxy-trienoic acids over hydroperoxydienoic acids. These hydroperoxy fatty acids are produced by lipoxygenases, such as those encoded by the |FRAME: G-14678| and |FRAME: G-14675| genes., The preferred substrate for the peroxygenase is oleate, although the enzyme can accept a wide range of unsaturated fatty acids with cis double bonds as substrates. |FRAME: G-14679| uses only free fatty acids or fatty acid methyl esters as substrates, and does not act on phospholipids or acyl-CoAs |CITS: [21784965]|., When incubated with |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| as the sole substrate, and with the product of the |FRAME: G-14675| gene, which produces |FRAME: CPD-8677| from |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, the enzyme produced a mixture of |FRAME: Vernolates| and |FRAME: CPD-13636|, indicating it can epoxidize both the 9,10 and the 12,13 positions |CITS: [21784965]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lankacidins "lankacidins"| are a class of unique 17-membered carbocyclic polyketide natural products isolated from Streptomyces spp. that show promising antimicrobial activity. , |FRAME: CPD-27267 "Lankacidin C"| was originally isolated in 1960 from |FRAME: TAX-68280| under the name lankacidin |CITS: [Gaumann60]|. It was subsequently isolated from multiple other species such as |FRAME: TAX-146922| |CITS: [Sakamoto62]| and Streptomyces sp. 6642-GC |CITS: [5796585]|, sometimes under the name bundlin A., In 1971 a group of related antibiotics, which included lankacidin C, was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-885435| (previously named strain T-2636). These compounds, which were referred to as "T-2636 antibiotics", have been studied extensively. The antibiotics were found to be active against a number of organisms, particularly Gram-positive bacteria, including many strains that are resistant to macrolide antibiotics |CITS: [5541329][5541328][5541330][4833376][1212749][4792112][4792113][1126865][240790]|. X-ray crystallographic analysis revealed that lankacidin C and |FRAME: CPD-27278| (a 14-membered macrolide antibiotic also produced by |FRAME: TAX-885435|) inhibit peptide formation synergistically by binding to neighboring sites in the large bacterial ribosomal subunit |CITS: [20080686][21282615]|. In addition, the lankacidins were shown to have considerable antitumor activity against certain cell line models |CITS: [4801122][1148][27718573]|. |FRAME: CPD-27267 "Lankacidin C"| is currently used in veterinary medicine., About This Pathway, In 1994 it was found that the genes encoding the biosynthesis of the lankacidin-group antibiotics reside on the linear plasmid pSLA2-L |CITS: [7844039]|. Sequencing of the region suggested that biosynthesis of the lankacidin skeleton is mediated by one nonribosomal peptide synthase/polyketide synthase (PKS/NRPS) hybrid (LkcA) and three PKSs (LkcC, LkcF, and LkcG) |CITS: [10767533]|. A starter glycine molecule is extended first by a lactoyl unit (|CITS: [25160004]|) and then by eight malonyl-[acp] molecules |CITS: [ 18057700]|. The methyl groups at C-2, C-4, C-10, and C-16 are added by C-methylation from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| |CITS: [Uramoto78]|., Two different cyclization events occur during the pathway: the formation of the δ-lactone ring and the final cyclization of the macrolide. It has been shown that the δ-lactone ring is formed by the thioesterase domain of LkcG while the product is still attached to the PKS. Following its removal from the PKS machinary, the molecule is cyclyzed by an |FRAME: MONOMER-124699 "amide oxidase/macrocyclase"| (LkcE) that converts the linear amide intermediate to an imide, which is then attacked by C2 to form the C2-C18 linkage |CITS: [15734652][18057700][21953738]|., While eight malonyl-[acp] units are added during the formation of the lankacidin skeleton, only 5 ketosynthase modules are available. Two theories have been proposed to explain this discrepancy: according to the first, the LkcC PKS acts four times before handing the nascent chain over to the LkcF, which adds two more molecues and transfers the product to LkcG, the last PKS in the process. This proposal was supported by the fact that a gene fusion of lkcF and lkcG produced lankacidin at a similar level to the parent strain |CITS: [18057700]|. However, this model does not support the predicted specificites of the individual KS domains. A second model (shown here) suggests the both LkcC and LkcF act iteratively in the sequence LkcC-LkcF-LkcC-LkcF-LkcC-LkcG., The first intermediate that is not tethered to a polyketide that has been isolated is |FRAME: CPD-27273| |CITS: [15734652]|. This intermediate contains an acetyl group, but as of 2024 it is still not known when the acetyl group is added and by which enzyme. That acetyl group appears to be removed in the last reaction of the pathway, but the identity of the enzyme that removes it is also unknown.

Summary: Brassinosteroids (BRs) are steroidal hormones that regulate the growth and development of plants. The most abundant and widely occurring BRs are C28 steroids, and among them, brassinolide (BL) is the most biologically active one. The biosynthesis pathway of BL was initially elucidated by extensive metabolic studies which suggested parallel-branched pathways, namely the early and late C-6 oxidation pathways (|FRAME: PWY-699|).  In all plant species examined to date, the 6-deoxo intermediates are predominant indicating that the late C-6 oxidation branch is the main route. Following the identification and biochemical characterization of CYP P450s involved in BR biosynthesis, an early C-22 oxidation branch (|FRAME: PWY-2582|) was proposed which was indicated to be the dominant route leading to BL biosynthesis. More recently, a new shortcut via C-23 hydroxylation following C-22 oxidation was demonstrated (|FRAME: PWY-2582|). Additional modifications (for example, lactonization) of the intermediates have also been reported |CITS: [18685225]|. The BL biosynthesis pathway may be best represented as a grid where substantial interconnections between the different proposed routes exist |CITS: [17138693], [12529536]|.

Summary: Formononetin, a 4'-methoxylated isoflavone, is a crucial precursor to many isoflavonoids found in a, number of plant species. Over 1600 of these secondary metabolites have been identified in plants., Isoflavonoids are found primarily within the Leguminosae family, but over 200 instances of isoflavonoids, in a total of 48 different plant families have been reported |CITS: [17390003]|., In plants, isoflavonoids are best know for their role in plant defense and stress responses, but they are, also involved in the regulation of mutualistic interactions with bacteria, |CITS: [DAKORA96]|, allelopathy |CITS: [12897458]| and may have other functions., Moreover, isoflavonoids impact many other types of organisms,, including bacteria, fungi, insects, humans, and other animals, |CITS: [DAKORA96][15377220][11471948]|., Notably, many studies have explored the anti-carcinogenic,, phtyoestrogenic, and other properties of these compounds that are relevant to human, health |CITS: [15547735][15377220]|., Formononetin can be produced from 2-hydroxyisoflavanone via at least two different pathways, |CITS: [12610212][11006341]|. Subsequent hydroxylations of the B ring of formononetin, lead to the production of two different groups of pterocarpans. Hydroxylation at the 3' position, shunts formononetin toward the production of maackiain and pisatin, while hydroxylation at the, 2' position leads to medicarpin biosynthesis. These three defense compounds, which accumulate, preferentially in particular species, are often called phytoalexins, a term now broadly used to, describe protective metabolites that are induced and accumulate in response to biological attacks, against plants |CITS: [DAKORA96]|. , Formononetin, like many other isoflavonoids, can also be glucosylated, and then further modified, by acylation. Ononin, formed by the addition of glucose to the 7' hydroxyl group on the A ring, of formononetin has biological activity, for example, in allelopathy |CITS: [12897458]|., But, it may also be an intermediate storage form that can be liberated through the activity of, beta-glucosidases induced by signals such as elevated methyl jasmonate levels |CITS: [17971436]|., The addition of a malonyl group to ononin might be required for it to enter the, vacuole |CITS: [6639051]| for long term storage where it can be accessed when, pterocarpan production is elicited., Therefore, the formononetin conjugate interconversion pathway likely provides an important source, of reserve storage forms of formononetin that feed into the medicarpin and maackiain biosynthesis, pathways.

In plants proline can be synthesized from either glutamate [|FRAME: PROSYN-PWY|] or ornithine, [|FRAME: PWY-3341|]. In addition to the route from ornithine to proline described in [|FRAME: PWY-3341|], (via |FRAME:L-GLUTAMATE_GAMMA-SEMIALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE|),, an additional route is believed to exist, as depicted in here., In this alternative ornithine route, the α-amino group of ornithine is lost, (opposed to the, δ-amino group in the other route), giving rise to |FRAME: 5-AMINO-2-OXOPENTANOATE|, which is, then converted to proline via |FRAME: DELTA1-PYRROLINE_2-CARBOXYLATE|., This existence of this pathway is supported by radio tracer experiments. No information is available, about the enzymes or genes of this pathway in plants.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-883 6-Caprolactam| is a man-made compound that is used as a precursor for the synthesis of |FRAME: Nylon-6 nylon-6|. Nylon-6 is produced by a process of ring cleavage polymerization of caprolactam. In this process caprolactam molecules are heated in the presence of water. A spontaneous reaction converts some of the cyclic caprolactam molecules to the linear |FRAME: CPD-884| form, which is the basic monomeric unit of nylon-6. Remaining caprolactam molecules then react with 6-aminohexanoate in a polymeric manner, producing polymers containing more than 100 units., Due to the large quantities of nylon-6 produced annually, |FRAME: CPD-883| is one of the most heavily used chemical intermediates in industrial manufacturing. In addition, the polymerization process generates several by-products, including oligomers of |FRAME:CPD-884|, and particularly linear and cyclic dimer forms. As a result, vast quantities of 6-caprolactam and other by-products are being produced as contaminants of waste water in the plants. 6-Caprolactam is highly soluble and occurs in high concentrations in this waste water. Caprolactam has been shown to be toxic in humans, where heavy exposure can lead to dermatitis, fever, and seizures. It is also mutagenic, inducing DNA damage and causing chromosomal aberrations |CITS: [2811921][2811930]|, and is also toxic to bacteria above certain concentrations., Waste water containing 6-caprolactam can be adequately treated by combining it with domestic sewage, or by the addition of phosphates. Microbial degradation of 6-caprolactam in activated sludge has been demonstrated as early as 1967 |CITS: [Iizuka67][5371808]|. |FRAME:TAX-287| MCM B-407 was isolated from activated sludge used to treat waste from a factory producing nylon-6, and is able to remove 6-caprolactam aerobically with simultaneous reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) |CITS: [9688819]|. Other organisms that degrade caprolactam aerobically include several unidentified |FRAME:TAX-286| strains, |FRAME:TAX-303|, |FRAME: TAX-511|, |FRAME:TAX-1670|,, |FRAME: TAX-1421| and |FRAME:TAX-1829| |CITS: [Baxi2001]|. Recently researchers were able to isolate a |FRAME:TAX-136097| strain that degrades 6-caprolactam unaerobically, using it as a substrate for denitrification |CITS: [15137443]|., It was shown that naturally-occuring conjugative plasmids control the ability of five different |FRAME:TAX-286| strains isolated from rectifiers of chemical plants to grow on 6-caprolactam |CITS: [3724565]|. Similar plasmids conferred this ability on |FRAME:TAX-303| strains BS836 |CITS: [1287407]| and MCM-408 |CITS: [Kulkarni98a]|. However, as of now, the enzymes catalyzing the first two degradation steps have not been isolated, and little information is available about them., More information is known about enzymes that are involved in the degradation of 6-aminohexanoate oligomers. In |FRAME: TAX-37931| the plasmid encoded genes |FRAME: G-4043| and |FRAME: G-4044| encode two enzymes which degrade  the cyclic dimer and small linear oligomers of 6-aminohexanoate, respectively |CITS: [7400094]|. A third gene on this plasmid, |FRAME: G-4041|, encodes a third enzyme, an endo 6-aminohexanoate oligomer hydrolase, which degrades larger 6-aminohexanoate oligomers by a different mechanism |CITS: [8285701]|. Similar plasmids have been isolated from |FRAME:TAX-286| strains |CITS: [2722746][8515236]|. The |FRAME: G-58249| and |FRAME: G-58250| genes, which encode enzymes that catalyze further degradation into |FRAME: ADIPATE|, have been located on the chromosome |CITS: [29188330]|., It should be mentioned that some fungi are able to degrade intact nylon-6, a plastic which was considered to be non-degradable. The fungus |FRAME: TAX-5331| is able to use nylon-6 as the sole nitrogen source under submerged cultivation conditions. After 40 days of exposure to the fungus, the fibers began to disintegrate |CITS: [Kzran2004]|. In another study,  a nylon-degrading enzyme found in the extracellular medium of a ligninolytic culture of a white rot fungus was able to partially degrade nylon-6 fibers |CITS: [9546174]|.

Summary: The mycotoxins |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587| are intermediates in the biosynthesis of the B-group and G-group aflatoxins, which constitute the major groups of naturally occurring aflatoxins. The production of aflatoxins by some strains of several |FRAME:TAX-5052| species has been extensively studied. However many species, including the model organism |FRAME: TAX-162425 "Emericella nidulans (previously known as Aspergullus nidulans)"|, produce only |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| as a final product (in |CITS: [18486503]|). |FRAME: TAX-5067| produces both B- and G-group aflatoxins from |FRAME: STERIGMATOCYSTIN| and |FRAME: CPD-4587|, while |FRAME: TAX-5059| produces only B-group aflatoxins. The biological role of these mycotoxins in fungi remains unclear (in |CITS: [17620135] [18246345]| and, reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|)., Aflatoxins are highly toxic and carcinogenic crop contaminants that create major economic and public health problems worldwide. Much research has been focused on identifying compounds that inhibit aflatoxin biosynthesis. |FRAME: CPD-4592| is metabolized by mammalian liver cytochrome P450 enzymes to a mutagenic epoxide that covalently binds to DNA. Its genotoxic mechanism of action has been studied in yeast |CITS: [8968101] [9771940]|. Other species, such as |FRAME: TAX-5062| and |FRAME:TAX-41058|, are unable to produce aflatoxins and are used in food fermentation |CITS: [17665189]|., Most of the aflatoxin biosynthetic genes are clustered in Aspergilli and are positively regulated by gene aflR (in |CITS: [17620135] [16448506] [16108793] [15094053] [7618880] [16535712]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]| and |CITS: [15006741]|). The enzyme reactions and biosynthetic intermediates in the aflatoxin biosynthetic pathway have been reviewed |CITS: [15022028]|., For detailed pathway comments, click on the subpathways listed below. Overall, the aflatoxin biosynthesis pathway, contains several cytochrome P450 monooxygenase-catalyzed steps that mediate the major skeletal rearrangements, (in |CITS: [11996570]|). Monooxygenases are involved in both the biosynthesis and degradation of toxic compounds, (in |CITS: [10618248]|). The pathway is costly in its consumption of |FRAME: NADPH| and appears to be, dependent on the energy status of the organism. A key desaturation step of the bisfuran ring occurs during the, conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10175| to |FRAME: CPD-10176|. This desaturation is a branch point that separates, the biosynthesis of aflatoxins B1 and G1 from aflatoxins B2 and, G2. The production of |FRAME: CPD-4592| from |FRAME: CPD-7157| and |FRAME: CPD-10177| from, |FRAME: CPD-4588| remarkably appears to involve multiple transformations catalyzed by a single, cytochrome P-450 enzyme |CITS: [11996570]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15022028]|. Aflatoxins are excreted from, mycelia and their biosynthetic intermediates accumulate in cells. No aflatoxin export system has yet been, identified. The biochemistry of the pathway has been reviewed in detail in |CITS: [15022028]|. Strains of, |FRAME: TAX-5059| are thought to produce only aflatoxins B1 and B2, while strains, of |FRAME: TAX-5067| produce all four major aflatoxins (B1, B2, G1 and, G2).

Names: L-isoleucine degradation III (oxidative Stickland reaction) // L-isoleucine fermentation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, The branched-chain amino acids serve most often as substrates for the oxidative branch of the Stickland reactions, as indicated by formation of branched-chain fatty acids shorter by one carbon compared to the original amino acids (|FRAME: LEU| is an exception, as it participates in both branches)., As described above, the amino acid is first transaminated to a 2-oxoacid, which is oxidatively decarboxylated to an acyl-CoA, shutlling the electrons to ferredoxin. The acyl-CoA is hydrolyzed, and the free carboxylic acid is the final product., Already in 1948 it was shown that cell suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-1509| and related clostridia converted |FRAME: VAL| to |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE|, |FRAME: LEU| to |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|, and |FRAME: ILE| to |FRAME: CPD-7076| |CITS: [Cohen-Bazire48]|, results that were reproduced by multiple researchers over the years |CITS: [678022]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-8183| and |FRAME: PWY-8185|).

Summary: General Background, Hydrolyzable tannins (HT), divided in the two subclasses |FRAME: Gallotanins gallotannins| (see |FRAME:PWY-5477|) and |FRAME: Ellagitannins ellagitannins| (see |FRAME:PWY-5476|) are derivatives of |FRAME: 12346-PENTAKIS-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUC| |CITS: [NIEMETZ00]|. The category 'hydrolyzable tannins' is based on the classical definition of Freudenberg |CITS: [FREUDENBERG20]| who distinguished condensed tannins (also referred to as proanthocyanins; flavonoid origin) and hydrolyzable tannins (esters of gallic acid with typically β-D-glucose). That class of compounds belongs to the more general 'plant polyphenols' (synonym vegetable tannins) which have been intensively studied in the last few decades (reviewed in |CITS: [HASLAM89][15206456][HASLAM98]|)., The name 'tannin' derived from the pronounced property of these compounds to precipitate proteins which has been used over the centuries for the tannery procedure to produce endurable leather from raw hides. Beside that, hydrolyzable tannins have many antimicrobial, antioxidant and antitumor properties used in human health care |CITS: [8991956]| and apply the varying amount of astringency as food components/phytonutrients |CITS: [14519822]|. Hydrolyzable tannins are widely distributed among plants but differ with regard to gallotannins (more restricted occurence) and ellagitannins (broad occurence) |CITS: [HADDOCK82]|., Hydrolyzable tannins and corresponding enzymes have been localized to the walls of leaf mesophyll cells, vitiating the former hypothesis of 'tannin vacuoles' as major sites for HT formation and deposition. The biogenesis of hydrolyzable tannins also followed a discernible seasonal pattern with galloylglucoses being formed in spring, a peak of ellagitannin biosynthesis observed in summer and tannin degradation taking place in fall |CITS: [11423141]|., The mono- to penta-substituted esters being generated on the biogenetic way towards pentagalloylglucose are also referred to as 'simple' galloylglucoses in contrast to the 'complex' galloylglucoses produced as the result of further galloylation of pentagalloylglucose |CITS: [16153405]|. However, that categorization does not indicate the tanning potential of the associated compounds., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis towards pentagalloylglucose displays a high specificity with a defined metabolic sequence. The first step is the formation of |FRAME: 1-O-GALLOYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSE| from gallic acid catalyzed by the UDPG-dependent gallate-1-β-glucosyltransferase |CITS: [Gross83]|. This compound does not only function as the common acyl acceptor throughout the pentagalloylglucose biosynthetic pathway but exerts in addition a dual role as acyl donor indicating the characteristic of an energy-rich 'activated' compound |CITS: [Gross83a]|., The further galloylation follows the metabolic sequence 1,6-digalloylglucose mediated by β-glucogallin O-galloyltransferase |CITS: [Schmidt87]|, 1,2,6-trigalloylglucose formed by the enzyme β-glucogallin dikisgalloylglucose O-galloyltransferase |CITS: [Gross91]|, 1,2,3,6-tetragalloylglucose being catalyzed by β-glucogallin trikisgalloylglucose O-galloyltransferase |CITS: [Hagenah93]| and finally 1,2,3,4,6-pentagalloylglucose that is formed by β-glucogallin tetrakisgalloylglucose O-galloyltransferase |CITS: [2757399]|., The formation of 1,2,6-trigalloylglucose can also be catalyzed by an enzyme, i.e. l,6-di-O-galloylglucose: 1,6-di-O-galloylglucose 2-O-galloyltransferase that has been isolated and characterized in |FRAME:TAX-255348| |CITS: [Denzel91]|. This reaction gives rise to a alternative route, using only the substrate 1,6-digalloylglucose instead of the usual β-glucogallin, therefore defined as 'disproportionation'.

Names: cytochrome c biogenesis (system III type) // cytochrome c biogenesis
Summary: General background, C-type cytochromes (cytC) are electron-transfer proteins that have one or more |FRAME: HEME_C| groups. They are characterized by the covalent attachment of the heme to the polypeptide chain via two (or rarely one) thioether bonds formed between thiol groups of cysteine residues and vinyl groups of a |FRAME: PROTOHEME| molecule. The two cysteine residues almost always occur in the amino-acid sequence CXXCH |CITS: [10647174]|., C-type cytochromes possess a wide range of properties and function in a large number of different redox processes. In general, the differences in c-type cytochromes among bacteria are much larger than those among animal species. The use of the term term "c-type cytochromes" was introduced to distinguish this family of diverse proteins from the well-characterized mitochondrial protein, which is often referred to as "cytochrome c"., Bacterial c-type cytochromes function in the electron transport chains of bacteria with many different types of energy metabolism, including phototrophs, methylotrophs, denitrifiers, sulfate reducers and the nitrogen-fixers. , The biogenesis of c-type cytochromes involves covalent attachment of |FRAME: PROTOHEME| to two cysteines at a conserved CXXCH sequence in the apocytochrome. The histidine residue acts as an axial ligand to the heme iron., Three unique cytochrome c assembly pathways, known as systems I, II, and III, have ben described. This pathway describes system III, which is found in the mitochondria of fungi, vertebrates, invertebrates, and sme protozoa., About This Pathway, System III of cytochrome c biogenesis is found exclusively in mitochondria of many organisms, including fungi, vertebrates, invertebrates, some protozoan (such as |FRAME: TAX-418103 Plasmodium| and |FRAME: TAX-5782|), and some primitive chlorophytes such as |FRAME: TAX-3066| and |FRAME: TAX-3052| |CITS: [19721088]|., In system III heme attachment is catalyzed by the holocytochrome c synthase (|FRAME: HS00120|), which is also necessary for the import of apocytochrome c from the cytosol into the mitochondrial intermembrane space. The enzyme, which is located in this space (bound to inner membrane), receives the heme group from |FRAME: EC-4.98.1.1| (|FRAME: HS00891|), which is located inside the mitochondrion, and attaches it to the apocytochrome., Studies in yeast have shown that the only other protein that is necessary for this activity is Cyc2, a flavoprotein that has been proposed as a redox component that reduces either the heme-iron or the cysteines of the CXXCH motif of the apocytochrome. However, the exact mechanism(s) involved in maintaining the apocytochrome c cysteines in reduced state is still unknown for system III |CITS: [19721088]|.

The fungal genus Fusarium is well known for producing structural diverse secondary metabolites. Off those polyketides and polyketide-derived metabolites represent the largest compound group which is reflected by the numerous polyketide synthases (PKSs) and non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) found in the respective genomes |CITS:[16278459]|. Fungal secondary metabolites are often produced by biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS:[16322742]| and PKSs and NRPSs are the initiating enzymes which give rise to a remarkable structural diversity of the produced compounds |CITS:[21102597] [Tkacz00]|. The main pigments found in Fusarium species are naphtoquinones |CITS:[16240659] [9564730]| such as |FRAME:CPD-18180| and congeners as well as |FRAME:CPD-18207| (see |FRAME:PWY-7692|) |CITS:[19400779]| which are known to provide the red coloration to the fruiting bodies (perithecium) of the fungi. Although similar in structure and biosynthetic sequence |FRAME:CPD-18207| and |FRAME:CPD-18180| are mutually exclusive and are formed under different pH conditions |CITS:[Studt14]|. The biological importance of pigments is not well understood but pigments are generally considered as protective compounds against irradiation and virulence (summarized in |CITS:[11837241]|) which biosynthesis is boosted in response to endogenous and exogenous stress |CITS:[16240659] [24036343]|., |FRAME:CPD-18180 Fusarubin| was first characterized from Fusarium javanicum and was therefore named oxyjavanicin |CITS:[21066111]| but was later re-designated |FRAME:CPD-18180| |CITS:[Ruelius50]|. Comparing gene cluster involved in the biosynthesis of perithecial pigments revealed differences between certain species such as Fusarium solani |CITS:[17886180]| reflected by a small difference in the metabolite profile |CITS:[Kurobane78]| and Fusarium fujikuroi (this pathway). However, it appears that the initial step of the |FRAME:CPD-18187| biosynthetic sequence follows the same reaction mechanism of the catalyzing polyketide synthase producing the same product, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18181| as shown for Fusarium fujikuroi |CITS:[22492438]| and Nectria haematococca, the sexual form of Fusarium solani |CITS:[22633689]|. Many of the intermediates of the |FRAME:PWY-7689| such as |FRAME:CPD-18187|, |FRAME:CPD-18188|, |FRAME:CPD-18191| and |FRAME:CPD-18189| had been identified previously in Fusarium species |CITS:[Steyn79] [Tatum85] [Tatum87] [Tatum87a] [2001980]| but a biosynthetic sequence has only be proposed recently |CITS:[22492438]|., The first committed reaction of the Fusarium fujikuroi |FRAME:CPD-18180| pathway is catalyzed by a polyketide synthase (PKS) encoded by fsr1 producing |FRAME:CPD-18181| via the heptaketide |FRAME:CPD-18195| from one |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and six |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| starter units |CITS:[22492438]|. The polyketide synthase encoded by PKS1 catalyzes the same reaction in Nectria haematococca |CITS:[22633689]|. The domain organization of the fsr1 and PKS1 encoded protein containing a reductase (R) domain instead of the more common thioester/Claisen cyclase (TE/CLC) domain allows to release the product as an aldehyde. The following steps which decorate |FRAME:CPD-18181| with methyl and hydroxyl groups are carried out by a multifunctional O-methyltransferase and a multifunctional FAD-dependent monooxygenase encoded by fsr2 and fsr3, respectively, which give rise to the main |FRAME:CPD-18180|-like compounds such as the main product |FRAME:CPD-18187| and congeners such as |FRAME:CPD-18188|, |FRAME:CPD-18191| and |FRAME:CPD-18189|. The molecular function of the involved enzymes has been demonstrated by a combination of single and multiple gene deletions and corresponding metabolite profiling |CITS:[22492438]|. , The regulation of the expression of genes involved in |FRAME:PWY-7689| is complex and depends on various factors such as low nitrogen as required for the production of gibberellins in this fungus |CITS:[Bruckner91]| and acidic conditions |CITS:[22492438]|, but also on protein activities of the cAMP-signalling network |CITS:[23469152]|. It appears that the pathway control and regulation of the red pigment |FRAME:CPD-18180| biosynthesis is multilayered similar to the |FRAME:PWY-7692| and remains to be further elucidated.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8950 "Cornusiin E"| is a dimeric |FRAME: Ellagitannins ellagitannin| that has been found to accumulate in, leaves of |FRAME:TAX-29775|. The underlying pathway was identified based on the purification and characterization of enzymes isolated from this plant. In general, ellagitannins are frequently found in many plant families |CITS: [Haddock82]| which distinguish them from the rather restricted occurrence of gallotannins. In addition, the progressive oxidative succession in the biogenesis of hydrolysable tannins (gallotannin - ellagitannin - dehydroellagitannin - transformed dehydroellagitannin) seems to correspond to evolutionary routes in plants |CITS: [11130661]|., Ellagitannins are formed from pentagalloylglucose through oxidative reactions which yield |FRAME: CPD-17774| (HHDP) oieties, the typical constituents of ellagitannins. Due to the many possible linking sites for HHDP ellagitannins display a , plethora of structures which elucidation is still far from complete hampering the recognition of structural principles and their biogenetic relationship |CITS: [16153405]|., Ellagitannins have been found to operate efficiently as chemotherapeutic agents exhibiting antitumor |CITS: [10230625][10800466]| as well as radical-scavenging and anti-oxidative properties |CITS: [2664829]|., About This Pathway, The oxidative steps from pentagalloylglucose to the dimeric cornusiin E via the monomeric ellagiotannin tellimagrandin II are catalyzed by two enzymes that belong to the group of p-diphenol: O2-oxidoreductases (EC 1.10.3.2) also known as 'laccases'. The enzyme of the first oxidative step, i.e. pentagalloylglucose: O2 oxidoreductase catalyzes the sterespecific phenolic coupling to produce the (S)-stereoconfiguration as observed in tellimagrandin II |CITS: [Niemetz01]| |CITS: [12620341]| which seems to be executed independently from 'dirigent proteins'. , The final oxidative step forming cornusiin E from two molecules of tellimagrandin II was catalyzed by tellimagrandin II: O2 oxidoreductase |CITS: [12946409]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SIROHEME Siroheme| is an iron-containing isobacteriochlorin, a modified tetrapyrrole similar in structure to both heme and chlorophyll that was discovered in 1973 |CITS: [4583265]|. Siroheme is covalently coupled to an iron-sulfur cluster ([FeS]) to form an electronically integrated metallo-cofactor for delivering electrons to substrate., Siroheme is found as a prosthetic group of several enzymes, including sulfite and nitrite reductases, which catalyze the six-electron reductions of sulfite to sulfide and nitrite to ammonia, respectively., Assimilatory sulfite reductases (see |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME:SULFITE-REDUCT-ENZRXN|) are found in bacteria, fungi and plants but not in animals, while dissimilatory sulfite reductases are found in diverse sulfate-reducing eubacteria (see |FRAME: TAX-879| |FRAME:CPLX-266|) and some species of thermophilic archaebacteria (see |FRAME: TAX-2234| |FRAME: CPLX-7178|) |CITS: [8994874]|., Siroheme is also an intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-17059| in denitrifying bacteria, and in an alternative |FRAME: Heme-b| biosynthesis pathway found in many archaea and sulfate reducing bacteria |CITS: [21969545]|., About This Pathway, Siroheme biosynthesis starts by the same route as other tetrapyrroles, the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| (see |FRAME:Tetrapyrrole-Biosynthesis "tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathways"|). |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III "Uroporphyrinogen-III"| is an important branch point: its methylation directs it toward siroheme, cobalamin or factor F430 synthesis, while decarboxylation directs it toward, the synthesis of chlorophyl and heme |CITS: [14633982]|., For siroheme synthesis, successive methylation at positions 2 and 7 forms |FRAME: CPD-9038| and |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| (also known as dihydrosirohydrochlorin), respectively |CITS: [2407558]|. The enzyme that catalyzes the two methylation reactions, uroporphyrin III methyltransferase, requires |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| as a methyl donor, and has been characterized from several sources including bacteria |CITS: [1906874][2546914]|, archaea |CITS: [1856165]|, and higher plants |CITS: [8953249]|. , To complete the synthesis of siroheme, |FRAME: DIHYDROSIROHYDROCHLORIN| is oxidized to |FRAME: SIROHYDROCHLORIN| and then chelated with ferrous iron. The first three intermediates are also intermediates in cobalamine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-5507|), and thus the committed step in the pathway is the ultimate one, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.99.1.4|., There are many variations of the enzymes catalyzing this pathway. In some bacteria (for example in the Gram-positive |FRAME: TAX-1423|) the transformation of |FRAME: UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III| into |FRAME:SIROHEME| is catalyzed by three separate enzymes (uroporphyrin III methyltransferase, dihydrosirohydrochlorin dehydrogenase and sirohydrochlorin ferrochelatase) |CITS: [12408752][10217486]|. In other organisms, such as the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|, the last two reactions are catalyzed by a single bifunctional enzyme |CITS: [11980703]|. Yet in other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, a single trifunctional enzyme (|FRAME:SIROHEMESYN-CPLX|) catalyzes all four reactions |CITS: [7945210]|., Organisms that use siroheme for |FRAME: Heme-d1| biosynthesis often have very different enzymes for synthesizing siroheme. For example, in P. denitrificans the nirE gene, which is located in the heme d1 biosynthetic cluster, encodes the methyltransferase that catalyzes the first step, and a different ferrocheletase (Pdne_2332) that is not related to the cheletases mentioned above catalyzes the last step (the identity of the dehydrogenase is still not known in these organisms) |CITS: [24673795]|.

Names: hydrogen to dimethyl sulfoxide electron transfer // hydrogen to DMSO electron transfer
Summary: In the respiratory chain fromed by hydrogenase and dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) reductase the transfer of electrons from hydrogen to DMSO is coupled to the generation of a proton motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane. Electron flow from H(2) to DMSO results in the formation of a proton gradient in whole cells and membrane vesicles of E. coli HB101; proton translocation is blocked by the uncoupler carbonyl cyanide p-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone (CCPP) and by the quinone analog 2-n-heptyl-4-hydroxy-quinoline-N-oxide (HOQNO) |CITS: [2989249]|., E. coli K-12 contains two membrane bound, H(2) uptake hydrogenases - hydrogenase 2 (shown in this pathway) and |FRAME: FORMHYDROGI-CPLX "hydrogenase 1"|. Hydrogenase 2 is a standard O2 sensitive hydrogenase and is the major hydrogenase during anaerobic respiration with hydrogen and fumarate |CITS: [3905769] [11506918]| while hydrogenase 1 is an O2 tolerant hydrogenase whose physiological function is not yet clearly defined (see for example |CITS: [24715724][23260654]|., Hydrogenase 2 is presumed to be an energy conserving enzyme (see |CITS: [9230919]|). H2-dependent reduction of the quinol analogs, menadione and ubiquinone-1, in E. coli spheroplasts is coupled to a protonophore-sensitive, proton translocation with H+/2e- stoichiometry of approx. 2 |CITS: [6249272]|. , DMSO reductase functions under anaerobic conditions and in the absence of nitrate (a preferred electron acceptor) |CITS: [2544558]|. DMSO reductase does not contribute to proton potential |CITS: [9063459]| (and see review by |CITS: [18930017]|). Menaquinone is the major redox mediator during anaerobic respiration with DMSO as the electron acceptor and H(2) as the electron donor |CITS: [2204318][1444716]|.

General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, Several fungi, including |FRAME: TAX-5005| |CITS: [Lilly56]|, |FRAME: TAX-5476| |CITS: [7768790]| and |FRAME: TAX-4924| |CITS: [10849789]|, have been reported to be able to grow on |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE| as the sole sugar carbon source., In the fungal pathway the sugar is transported into the cell and subsequently converted to |FRAME: CPD-355| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.21|. Two different enzymes that can metabolize |FRAME: CPD-355| have been identified in fungi: |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.250|, which produces |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE|, and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.11|, which produces |FRAME: D-XYLULOSE|. |FRAME: TAX-4924| possesses only the former, encoded by the |FRAME: G-107616| gene |CITS: [7483848]|. It has been proposed that in this organism |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE| is phosphorylated into |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, which enters the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| |CITS: [27400037]|., In other organisms, it is possible that |FRAME: CPD-355| is processed via the |FRAME: DARABITOLUTIL-PWY| pathway, which produces |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, providing a different entry point into the pentose phosphate pathway.

Summary: Fusicoccin compounds are phytotoxins produced by the fungus |FRAME: TAX-1214568| which is a parasite on plants like peaches and apples. This toxin is a very powerful activator of plasma membrane H+-ATPase and causes irreversible stomatal opening. Infection with this fungus results in rapid acidification of the plant cell wall, causing the stomata to open permanently, leading to death by dehydration |CITS: [20633238 ]|. Fusicoccin A has been assayed as a potential anti-cancer drug and has shown to selectively induce apoptosis in tumor cells after interferon-alpha priming |CITS: [ 20153922]|. In sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus L.) cultured cells, fusicoccin has been shown to induce a set of stress responses |CITS: [20630615]|., The pathway has not yet completely elucidated but a general picture, depicted here, has emerged and is supported by the functional annotation of various genes encoding enzymes catalyzing key reactions in the pathway. The participating genes are part of a biosynthetic gene cluster for the biosynthesis of fusicoccins. The first committed step in the pathway is carried out by a unique chimeric enzyme, fusicoccadiene synthase, possessing two catalytic properties, i.e. geranylgeranyl-, and fusicocca-2,10(14)-diene synthase which converts |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| in two sequential reactions to |FRAME:CPD-12805| via |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP| |CITS:[1730612]|. A |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| dependent dioxygenase catalyzes the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16837| from |FRAME:CPD-16827| which is subsequently reduced to |FRAME:CPD-16838| by a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase |CITS:[21299202]|. The steps leading to |FRAME:CPD-16827| from |FRAME:CPD-12805| have not yet been corroborated but there are indications that they may follow the same reaction sequence as described in |FRAME:PWY-7517| |CITS:[21299202]|. The last identified reaction in the |FRAME:PWY-6659| is the prenylation of |FRAME:CPD-16839| which will produce |FRAME:CPD-12804|, a presumed intermediate in the biosynthetic route towards |FRAME:CPD-12803|. This prenyltransferase is unique because it represents the first to catalyze the prenylation of a sugar moiety hydroxyl group |CITS:[22287087]|.

Names: all-trans-nonaprenyl diphosphate biosynthesis II // solanesyl diphosphate biosynthesis // solanesyl pyrophosphate biosynthesis
Summary: Isoprenoids are among the most diverse and widely distributed natural compounds. They include both essential products (sterols, quinones, prenylated proteins, chlorophylls) and secondary metabolites (plant terpenoids and hormones) |CITS: [15024605]|., In this pathway |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| and multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain of nine units, known as |FRAME: CPD-21340| or solanesyl diphosphate., In most organisms, the enzyme that adds the isoprenyl units to form |FRAME: CPD-21340| prefers |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5805|. However, the enzymes found in |FRAME: TAX-3702| were shown to prefer |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| |CITS: [12437513]|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific synthase. Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones. However, the enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone, molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., Quinones with nine isoprenyl units in the side chains are very common. They are the predominant form of plastoquinones, found in green plants and cyanobacteria, and are the major quinones in some large Gram-negative and Gram-positive genera, including the Pseudomonads and the Streptococci. Nine-isoprenyl quinones are also found in many animals, including the rat., |FRAME: ORG-5993| possesses two alleles of solanesyl diphosphate synthases - |FRAME: AT1G17050| supplies the precursor of the plastoquinone side-chain, while |FRAME: AT1G78510| contributes to the biosynthesis of the ubiquinone side-chain |CITS: [15784989]|.

Summary: Flavonoids are highly diverse class of plant secondary metabolites (with about 9000 compounds have been identified so far |CITS: [16137727]|)  synthesized by the phenylpropanoid pathway. They exhibit a wide range of biological functions in higher plants such as UV protection, flower coloration, and antimicrobial activity |CITS: [11130659]|. They also exhibit antioxidant and anticancer properties |CITS: [12224601]| |CITS: [18645020]|., Flavones, Flavones are a class of flavonoid synthesized from flavanones as the direct biosynthetical precursor. Flavone formation in various tissues of a wide range of higher and lower plant species is catalyzed by the flavone synthase belong to the plant cytochrome P450 superfamily |CITS: [18645020]|. The flavones can be classified into several subgroups based on (i) hydroxylation, (ii) O-methylation, (iii) C-methylation, (iv) isoprenylation, or (v) methylenedioxy substitutions. Vitexin and its derivatives are 8-O-glycosylated flavones naturally occur in wide range of plants.

General Background, The indoleamine |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is a vertebrate hormone secreted by the pineal gland. It is involved in regulation of circadian and seasonal rhythms. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| also has immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. In addition to the pineal gland it is synthesized in many vertebrate cells and tissues (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|). It is ubiquitously present in cells and body fluids due to its amphiphilic properties that allow it to cross membranes. Mitochondria have the highest intracellular concentration of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| |CITS: [15981996]|. Its functional groups allow both specific receptor binding and a role in oxidation chemistry. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also found in invertebrates |CITS: [12662344]|, protozoa |CITS: [12899443]|, plants |CITS: [11485009]|, fungi |CITS: [12662344]| and bacteria |CITS: [9181522]| although its function in many cases remains incompletely defined. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also used as a human dietary supplement. In vertebrates, endogenous or ingested |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is catabolized several ways in different tissues (see below and pathways |FRAME: PWY-6398| and |FRAME: PWY-6399|). Reviewed in |CITS: [16219483] [18344019]|., The enzymatic pathways of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| degradation are shown in this pathway and pathways |FRAME: PWY-6398| and |FRAME: PWY-6399|. Melatonin can also be degraded by nonenzymatic pathways involving melatonin radical species, reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, or ultraviolet B radiation. It can also be degraded by nonenzymatic reactions involving oxoferryl hemoglobin, or hemin. These nonenzymatic reactions are not shown here, but are shown in |CITS: [18344019] [18155917] [17198536] [16793870]|., About This Pathway, This oxidative pathway of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| degradation involves cleavage of the pyrrole ring of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| to the 5-methoxylated kynuramine |FRAME: CPD-12022| (AFMK). It has been demonstrated in human neutrophils |CITS: [16148002]| and cultured human keratinocytes in vitro |CITS: [16793870]|. It is also the dominant pathway of pineal |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| degradation in the mammalian brain and central nervous system |CITS: [4814344] [16219483]|. , |FRAME: CPD-12022| can be formed from |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| enzymatically by several enzymes including myeloperoxidase |CITS: [16148002] [15636586]| and |FRAME: HS05502-MONOMER| (in a peroxidase-like reaction with hydrogen peroxide as co-substrate) |CITS: [15636586]|. More recently, rat liver microsomal and mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzymes have also been implicated in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12022| and 2-hydroxymelatonin |CITS: [18717775]|. The involvement of mitochondrial cytochrome C in the conversion of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-12022| via hydroxylated intermediates has also been suggested |CITS: [15981996]|., |FRAME: CPD-12022| can also be formed nonenzymatically in reactions involving oxyferryl-hemoglobin, hemin, ultraviolet B radiation, reactive oxygen species, or reactive nitrogen species (not shown). Many other melatonin metabolites, such as cyclic-3-hydroxymelatonin and 2-hydroxymelatonin can also be formed in such nonenzymatic reactions |CITS: [16793870] [18155917]| (not shown). In fact, the number of ways in which |FRAME: CPD-12022| can be formed is remarkable., The deformylation of |FRAME: CPD-12022| to |FRAME: CPD-12023| can occur enzymatically via formamidase |CITS: [4814344]|. Catalase has also been shown to catalyze this reaction in vitro (|CITS: [11121726]| and reviewed in |CITS: [10899700] [19573038]|). The reaction can also occur nonenzymatically as a result of ultraviolet irradiation. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| and its metabolites |FRAME: CPD-12022| and |FRAME: CPD-12023| have antioxidant activity |CITS: [16217125]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [18344019] [18155917] [19573038]|., |FRAME: CPD-12022| has been identified in many different organisms, from protozoa to plants and metazoa. However, in the lower taxa it is likely formed by nonenzymatic reaction(s). The metabolite |FRAME: CPD-12023| can also undergo various nonenzymatic reactions (not shown) (reviewed in |CITS: [17198536]|).

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-16782 Chelerythrine| belongs to the large and diverse group of benzylisoquinoline alkaloids (BIAs) for which about 2500 compound structures have been reported so far |CITS:[18251710]|. Many of them exhibit pharmacological activities which have been exploited in folk medicine for centuries. Modern science and technological progress have allowed the stepwise elucidation of structures, underlying pathways and pharmaceutical properties and opened up opportunities for biology platforms to produce the valuable BIAs in microbial systems (reviewed in |CITS:[23385146]|. Benzylisoquinoline alkaloids such as |FRAME:SANGUINARINE|, |FRAME:CPD-16782|, |FRAME:CPD-9893| and |FRAME:CPD-7848| have been found mostly in four plant families, i.e. Papaveraceae, Ranunculaceae, Berberidaceae, and Menispermaceae |CITS:[18251710]| and there in dependence on the species in varying amounts in roots, aerial parts, capsules and seeds |CITS:[20600683] [21094631] [23313486]|., |FRAME:CPD-16782 Chelerythrine| has been shown to express a broad range of antimicrobial, immunomodulating and anticancer properties and especially holds promise as agent in immune therapies for certain carcinomas, for example prostate cancer |CITS:[16936897] [16964588]|. Benzophenanthridines including |FRAME:CPD-16782| are induced upon biotic and abiotic stress as well as endogenous signals such as jasmonates |CITS:[18309269] [24248920]|. Due to the stress-inducible behavior and high cytotoxicity numerous BIAs play a key role in the protective system of plants and serve as phytoalexins in the defense against microbes and herbivore attacks. In order to protect their own living cells from the cytotoxic effects |CITS:[Matile84]| alkaloids are either compartmented within the cell |CITS:[Wink98]| or converted to less toxic compounds in biochemical reactions. , The pathway sequence of |FRAME:CPD-16782| biosynthesis is very similar to the last part of the biosynthesis of the related benzophenanthridine alkaloid |FRAME:SANGUINARINE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5287|) and employs the same set of enzymes exhibiting dual activities. Starting from |FRAME:S-N-METHYLCANADINE| (see |FRAME:PWY-7138|) the methylcanadine 14-monooxygenase catalyzes the formation of |FRAME:ALLOCRYPTOPINE| |CITS:[Rueffer87] [23313486]| which subsequently is hydroxylated by a Cytochrome P450 dependent 6-hydroxylase and spontaneously converted to its dihydro derivative, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16781| |CITS:[Tanahashi90] [22421633]|. The last step in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-16781| is catalyzed by a dihydrobenzophenanthridine oxidase |CITS:[1444440]|. The formed |FRAME:CPD-16782| as well as |FRAME:SANGUINARINE| are however excreted in the cell-wall to function as phytoalexins and to prevent self-poisoning of the producing cell. After reaching a certain threshold the benzophenanthridine alkaloids are re-imported in the cell and detoxified through the action of a sanguinarine/chelerythrine reductase |CITS:[17080644] [20378534]|.

Summary: General Background, Some bacteria living in anoxic environments are able to ferment amino acids to |FRAME: AMMONIA|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: ACET| and short chain fatty acids., Proteins are initially hydrolysed by exogenous proteases to small peptides and single amino acids, which are then taken up by the bacteria and degraded internally., Acetogenic organisms use the |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| for the synthesis of |FRAME: ACET|, while the so called "syntrophic" bacteria oxidize the short chain fatty acids to |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, provided methanogenic archaea in the environment keep the partial pressure of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| at very low values (see |FRAME:METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., At least one pathway is known for the fermentation of every one of the 20 protein-buildng amino acids. In the case of |FRAME: GLT|, at least five such pathways are known |CITS: [11759672]|., About This Pathway, Different methylaspartate pathways are used to ferment glutamate into different end compounds. The pathway has been first described in a closely related group of soil clostridia. In this variety of the pathway |FRAME:GLT| is degraded into |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID|. It is different from another pathway of glutamate fermentation which is found in clostridia living within animals (see |FRAME: P162-PWY|). Although the final products from both pathways are the same (|FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: AMMONIUM|, and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|), they can be discerned by the different labeling patterns of the product |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID| when, [14C]-glutamate is used as a substrate |CITS: [4813895]|., The stoichiometry of the overall pathway is approximated as follows |CITS: [LENGELER99]|:, 5 glutamate + 6 H2O + 2 H+ = 5 NH4+ +, 5 CO2 + 6 acetate + 2 butanoate + 2 H2, and the free energy is ΔGo' = -59 KJ per mol glutamate., In the methylaspartate pathway, the linear carbon chain of |FRAME: GLT| is rearranged into the branched carbon skeleton of |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE|, facilitating the subsequent elimination of |FRAME: AMMONIA| since the β-H is now activated by the adjacent carboxyl group. |FRAME:MESACONATE| is then hydrated to |FRAME:S-CITRAMALATE|, which is subsequently cleaved to |FRAME:ACET| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|. |FRAME:PYRUVATE| undergoes oxidative decarboxlyation to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: FERREDOXIN-MONOMER|. Some of the |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| is converted to |FRAME:ACET| while the rest is converted to |FRAME:BUTYRIC_ACID|. The |FRAME: FERREDOXIN-MONOMER| is reoxidized during the synthesis of |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| from 2 molecules of |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| |CITS: [LENGELER99] [Gottschalk1986]|., The methylaspartate pathway has also been demonstrated in enterobacteriaceae, including |FRAME: TAX-35703|, |FRAME: TAX-546| and |FRAME: TAX-582| |CITS: [9385136]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipoarabinomannans Lipoarabinomannan| (LAM) is a lipoglycan that comprises a major component of the cell envelope of all mycobacteria.It is based on a mannan skeleton and carries a large branched arabinan chain, similar to those found in |FRAME: Mycobacterial-Arabinogalactans "mycobacterial arabinogalactan"|., The non-reducing termini of the arabinogalactan chains in LAM are often capped by a structure that is species-specific. Several species, including |FRAME: TAX-1773|, produce mannoside caps made of one to three α-(1→2) linked mannopyranose residues that may be further substituted with an α-(1→4)-linked methylthio-D-xylose (MTX) residue |CITS: [16608340]|. This sugar was the first thiosugar described from a bacterial polysaccharide |CITS: [22575989]|., The biosynthesis of the MTX capping motif is encoded by a five-gene cluster, which includes two glycosyltransferases, |FRAME: G185E-4672 MtxS| and |FRAME: G185E-4674 MtxT|, that are responsible for the production of |FRAME: CPD185E-68| and the transfer of MTX to the mannoside caps of LAM, respectively |CITS: [28075556]|., The pathway begins with |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE|, a ubiquitous byproduct of |FRAME: BSUBPOLYAMSYN-PWY "spermidine biosynthesis"|. Following its phosphorylation and activation by an as-yet unidentified nucleotide, the modified sugar is transferred to |FRAME: CPD-11994|, which serves as a membrane anchor, from which it is transferred to LAM by the glycosyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-4674| gene |CITS: [28075556]|

General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives. These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|. The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two broad categories - oxidative and reductive., In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or di-oxygenase enzymes (as in this pathway). In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, A new |FRAME: TAX-316| strain, named |FRAME: ORG-6281|, that is capable of using |FRAME: CPD-18106| as the sole source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy, was isolated from soil contaminated with chloronitrobenzenes. When grown on |FRAME: CPD-18106| the organism released chloride and nitrite into the medium. This was the first organism known to be able to grow on |FRAME: CPD-18106| |CITS: [15742150]|., In a preliminary study of the organism a DNA fragment encoding a polypeptide homologous to the α-subunit of ring-hydroxylating dioxygenases was isolated |CITS: [15742150]|. This fragment was used as a probe in a subsequent study and enabled the isolation of a 16.2-kb DNA contig that contained 19 complete open reading frames |CITS: [21602392]|., The cluster included four genes encoding a novel |FRAME: EC-1.14.12.23|, which is responsible for converting |FRAME: CPD-18106| to |FRAME: CPD-9151|, as well as genes encoding enzymes involved in |FRAME: PWY-6089 "3-chlorocatechol degradation"|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, Since the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| is a very complex process, many organisms possess various salvage pathways that enable them to rescue thiamine fragments obtained from the environment. This pathway describes the salvage of base-degraded thiamine compounds, and starts with |FRAME: CPD-13577|, a compound that is generated by base-mediated degradation of the thiazolium moiety of thiamine |CITS: [17618314]|., |FRAME: CPD-13577 "Formylaminopyrimidine"| is transported into the cell and deformylated by |FRAME: MONOMER-16806| (|FRAME: G-14641|). The resulting |FRAME: CPD-13578| is converted to |FRAME: HMP| (HMP) by |FRAME: BSU11650-MONOMER "4-amino-5-aminomethyl-2-methylpyrimidine hydrolase"| (TenA, thiaminase II). The salvaged HMP is then phosphorylated to form |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP|, which is incorporated into the de novo thiamine biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [18054064]|., In |FRAME:TAX-4932| the trifunctional fusion protein THI20p is also able to hydrolyze |FRAME:CPD-13578| to form |FRAME:HMP| in this salvage pathway. The enzyme which exhibits HMP/HMP-P kinase and thiaminase II activity was a puzzle for a long time as it apparently fuses |FRAME:THIAMINE| biosynthetic and degradation activities in one enzyme. However, those activities, encoded by several monomers in bacteria, fit well in the |FRAME:THIAMINE| salvage pathway as they hydrolyze |FRAME:THIAMINE| and similar compounds, e.g. |FRAME:CPD-13578| to |FRAME:HMP| which is immediately phosphorylated by the HMP/HMP-P kinase activity of the same protein |CITS:[15967475] [18028398] [21904031]|. , The key enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: BSU11650-MONOMER|, was considered a thiamine degradation enzyme for a long time after its discovery |CITS: [13243520]|, since it is able to catalyze the hydrolysis of thiamine to its thiazole and pyrimidine components. Its true nature as a salvage enzyme was revealed only five decades later |CITS: [17618314]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: CPD2B4Q-2 "core oligosaccharide"| of |FRAME: TAX-234| species (which includes both smooth [|FRAME: TAX-235|, |FRAME: TAX-29459|, |FRAME: TAX-29461|] and rough [|FRAME: TAX-236|] biotypes) possesses a branched structure - one branch serves as an anchor for the O antigen, while a lateral branch carries a mannose residue and four glucosamine residues |CITS: [26867577][34335551]|. This unique structure acts as a shield against innate immunity recognition, hampering the recognition by complement, antimicrobial peptides and pathogen recognition receptor complex TLR4-MD2 |CITS: [22589715]|., As of 2021, four glycosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: BAB_RS18990|, |FRAME: BAB_RS17610|, |FRAME: BAB_RS23165|, and |FRAME: BAB_RS20495| genes, are known be involved in its biosynthesis. The exact order in which the residues are added, as well as the exact functions of the WadB and WadD enzymes, have not been determined, and the pathway shown here combines current available data with speculation about the order of events and assumptions about the role of these two enzymes. The reader is advised that as more information becomes availble, some changes to this pathway may be required., The wadA gene encodes the enzyme linking the second Kdo residue and glucose, wadC encodes a mannosyltransferase acting on the first Kdo, and WadB and WadD are glucosaminyltransferases involved in the assembly of the GlcN branch |CITS: [12761107][22589715][24927935][30319590]|.

|FRAME: Astragalosides Astragalosides| are triterpenoid saponins produced by some species of |FRAME: TAX-20400|, the largest genus of |FRAME: TAX-3803| family, such as |FRAME: TAX-649199|. The compounds are the main active ingredients in "Huang-Qi", a traditional Chinese medicine |CITS: [30210687]|., Some astragalosides, particularly |FRAME: CPD-26859|, have been shown to have neuroprotective, hepatoprotective, anticancer, and antidiabetic activities |CITS: [19122295][24980548][26125738][32089240][32197276][33098932]|. The low yield and intermittent supply of astragalosides from natural or cultivated sources, and their complex chemical synthesis, drive interest in the biosynthetic pathway., The |FRAME: Astragalosides astragalosides| are derived by glycosylation of |FRAME: CPD-26858|, which is derived from |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL| in a process that has not been defined as of 2024., Several glycosyltranferases involved in the biosynthesis of astragalosides have been identified from |FRAME: TAX-119829| , catalyzing 3-O-glycosylation, 6-O-glycoylosylation, 25-O-glycosylation, and 2'-O-glucosylation |CITS: [34894044][ 36529909][36815054]|.
