Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes and are determinants of intracellular communication, in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]|, and fatty acyl moieties of proteins that modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid (FAS) biosynthesis mechanisms, named type I and type II. The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes, as well as some Gram-positive bacteria such as the mycobacteria. The mammalian and bacterial systems consist of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two multifunctional proteins, α and β, arranged in an α6β6 complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|)., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., A major difference between the two pathways is that the type I systems accept |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of two-carbon units, while the type II systems accept |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|. Pathways catalyzed by type II systems are described by |FRAME: PWY-5971|, |FRAME: PWY66-430|, and |FRAME: PWY-7388|., About This Pathway, Mammalian |FRAME: CPLX-7628| enzymes are homodimers whose gigantic subunits (about 240 kDa) are encoded by a single gene |CITS: [700134]|. Each subunit is multifunctional protein, whose main function is to catalyze the synthesis of |FRAME: PALMITATE| from |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| in the presence of NADPH., The two subunits are arranged in a head to tail fashion, and each subunit contains, in addition to an acyl-carrier-protein (acp) domain, additional domains that catalyze 7 different catalytic activities. The enzymes from lower fungi consist of two multifunctional proteins, α and β, arranged in an α6β6 complex. Five of the seven enzymatic activities reside in the β subunit, while the remaining two activities and the acyl-carrier protein domain are in the α subunit., The process is initiated by the sequential transfer of a primer substrate, usually an acetyl moiety, from CoA thioester form, first to the nucleophilic serine residue of the acyltransferase domain, then to the phosphopantetheine thiol of the acyl-carrier protein (ACP) domain, and finally to the active site cysteine residue of the β-ketoacyl synthase domain (see |FRAME: PWY-5966-1|). , In the next step the chain extender substrate, a malonyl moiety, is transferred from its CoA thioester form via the nucleophilic serine residue of the acyltransferase domain to the phosphopantetheine thiol. Formation of a new C-C bond, by condensation of the acetyl and malonyl moieties, is coupled with an energetically favorable decarboxylation. The 3-oxoacyl condensation product is then reduced to a saturated acyl moiety through the sequential action of a 3-oxoacyl reductase, (3R)-3-hydroxyacyl dehydratase, and enoyl reductase, and the newly formed saturated acyl moiety is translocated back to the active site cysteine residue, in a reaction catalyzed by the β-ketoacyl synthase domain., The phosphopantetheine thiol of the ACP domain is then reloaded with a new malonyl moiety, and another round takes place. After completion of seven cycles of chain extension, when the acyl group has reached 16 carbon atoms, the saturated acyl moiety is released from the phosphopantetheine thiol through the action of the chain-terminating thioesterase domain. Although small amounts of |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| are sometimes formed through the actions of FAS, the process generally stops at 16 carbons and |FRAME: PALMITATE| is released from the ACP moiety |CITS: [16477801]|., A general description of the reactions catalyzed by the mammalian |FRAME: CPLX-7628| complex is provided by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.85|:, |FRAME:FATTY-ACID-SYNTHASE-RXN|, The sum of reactions catalyzed by the yeast enzyme is described by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.86|:, |FRAME: FATTY-ACYL-COA-SYNTHASE-RXN|, |FRAME: PALMITATE Palmitate| is one of the most common saturated fatty acids found. It was discovered by Edmond Fremy in 1840 in saponified palm oil, of which it is a major component, hence its name., |FRAME: Insulins Insulin|, |FRAME: LIOTHYRONINE|, glucocorticoids, and |FRAME: D-Glucose| induce de novo lipogenesis, while C20 PUFAs (polyunsaturated fatty acids), glucagon, and |FRAME: L-EPINEPHRINE| suppress it |CITS: [7831398]|

Names: L-leucine degradation V (oxidative Stickland reaction) // L-leucine fermentation
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, The branched-chain amino acids serve most often as substrates for the oxidative branch of the Stickland reactions, as indicated by formation of branched-chain fatty acids shorter by one carbon compared to the original amino acids (|FRAME: LEU| is an exception, as it participates in both branches)., Already in 1948 it was shown that cell suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-1509| and related clostridia converted |FRAME: VAL| to |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE|, |FRAME: LEU| to |FRAME: ISOVALERATE|, and |FRAME: ILE| to |FRAME: CPD-7076| |CITS: [Cohen-Bazire48]|, results that were reproduced by multiple researchers over the years |CITS: [678022]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-8183| and |FRAME: PWY-8184|)., As mentioned above, |FRAME: LEU| is one of the few amino acids that can be fermented in both the reductive and oxidative branch. The reductive pathway is described in |FRAME: PWY-7767|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-7901| is an aliphatic methyl ketone that is naturally occurring in plants, where it can play a role as both a pheromone and insecticide |CITS: [14560395]|. The methyl ketone biosynthetic pathway was characterized in tomato plants, specifically |FRAME: TAX-62890|, from which two key genes ShMKS1 and ShMKS2 were identified that were required for methyl ketone synthesis from fatty acid intermediates |CITS: [20605911]|. ShMKS1 is purported to hydrolyze a β-ketoacyl ACP to generate a β-keto acid, and ShMKS2 may decarboxylate the β-keto acid to a methyl ketone. More specifically, ShMKS2 and ShMKS1, heterologously expressed in E. coli and shown to work in sequence produced a variety of 2-methylketones such as |FRAME:CPD-7901|, |FRAME:2-UNDECANONE| and |FRAME:CPD-7898| |CITS:[15772286] [20605911] [19801397]|. , The (C7- C15) methylketones are natural insecticides/pesticides and the biochemical pathways underlying the production of these toxins have been studied in tomato plants |CITS: [15772286]|. |FRAME: TAX-62890| accumulates methyl ketones in specific glandular trichomes and these cause mortality to insect pests such as the spider mites. Methyl ketones (MK) are abundantly present in the wild species Lycospersicum hirsutum (synonym Solanum habrochaites) and in significant lower concentrations in the domesticated species Solanum lycopersicum |CITS:[15772286]| which has prompted research that made those species the subject of breeding experiments to isolate the respective genes and improve the defense mechanism in the cultivated varieties |CITS: [10737735]|. Interspecific populations derived from crosses of wild and cultivated tomato species were used and experiments were carried out to analyze the morphological basis for accumulation of MK's in certain types of trichomes as well as to study the chemical composition of the methylketones. The wild-type species had larger numbers of Type VI glandular trichomes on the leaf surfaces where methylketones accumulated. The cultivated species had fewer such trichomes and almost no accumulation of MK's of chain length C7 -C15. , With application to biofuel production, this pathway has recently been engineered into E.coli to overproduce saturated and monounsaturated C11- C15 methyl ketones, see |FRAME: PWY-7007| |CITS: [22038610]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, also known as vitamin C, fulfils multiple essential roles in both plants and animals., Being a strong reducing agent, it functions as an antioxidant and a redox buffer. It is also a cofactor for several enzymes, which are involved in many important pathways, including collagen hydroxylation, carnitine biosynthesis, norepinephrine biosynthesis, and hormone and tyrosine metabolism., In plants L-ascorbate is also implicated in defense against pathogens and in control of plant growth and development., A significant proportion of a plant's ascorbate is found in the apoplast (the aqueous solution permeating the cell walls) |CITS: [15608627]|., Under aerobic conditions L-ascorbate is oxidized in cells to |FRAME: CPD-13907 dehydroascorbate| (via the radical |FRAME: CPD-318|), which can be recycled back to ascorbate by the |FRAME: PWY-2261|. However, once formed, dehydroascorbate can be further broken down in vivo by irreversible reactions, escaping the |FRAME: PWY-2261|., Several pathways for the irreversible catabolism of ascorbate have been described. Facultatively aerobic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-573| degrade L-ascorbate by different pathways under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6961| and |FRAME: PWY0-301|). The anaerobic pathway begins with phosphorylation of ascorbate (mediated by a PTS-type transporter), while the aerobic pathway proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-334|. Both pathways produce |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a centeral metabolite that is fed into the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [18708499]|., Plants from the |FRAME: TAX-3602| family (e.g. grapes) metabolize ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-13059| and |FRAME: L-IDONATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6704|). The tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 1-4 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 4 and 5 |CITS: [Loewus99][16567629]|. , The geraniaceous plant |FRAME: TAX-1417776| metabolizes ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| and |FRAME: OXALATE| via a different pathway, with |FRAME: L-THREONATE|, rather than L-idonate, as an intermediate (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6960|). In this case the tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 3-6 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 2 and 3 |CITS:[Loewus99][15862089]|. Grapes are also known to accumulate |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [DeBolt04]|, and thus may be using both pathways to generate tartrate., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TARTRATE| is found in many plants, particularly in grapes, bananas and tamarinds. It is the principle acid found in wine, contributing important aspects to the taste, mouthfeel and aging potential of wine. , |FRAME: TAX-1417776| accumulates |FRAME: TARTRATE| |CITS: [Stafford61]| which it produces from |FRAME: ASCORBATE| with concomitant production of |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [16658623]|. Radio-tracer studies have shown that |FRAME: TARTRATE| is produced from |FRAME: L-THREONATE|, which is derived from carbons 3-6 of ascorbate, indicating cleavage between C2 and C3 carbons of ascorbate (unlike the |FRAME:PWY-6704 "alternative pathway"| found in grapes, where theronate is derived from carbons 1-4 of ascorbate, cleaved between C4 and C5). , The pathway is believed to exist in many plant families |CITS: [16660361]|. While the existence of the pathway has been documented for quite a long time, it has been poorly understood until recent times., A study of ascorbate degradation by cultured cells of |FRAME: ORG-6200| revealed that the pathway, which is extracellular, proceeds via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-13914|, |FRAME: CPD-13910|, and |FRAME: CPD-13911| |CITS: [15608627]|. While the pathway can proceed non-enzymatically, it was shown that several steps are enzymatically catalyzed, including the initial oxidation of L-ascorbate, the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13910| to |FRAME: CPD-13911|, and the hydrolysis of |FRAME: CPD-13911| to |FRAME: L-THREONATE| and |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [15608627]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD0-1074 "Aminomethylphosphonate"| (AMPA) is a phosphonate that can be metabolized by a wide variety of microorganisms. It is the primary degradation product of |FRAME: CPD0-1308| (N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine), the most commonly used broad-spectrum systemic herbicide in the world, and glyphosate degradation is the primary source of AMPA in the environment |CITS: [26187493]|., AMPA has no significant toxicity in acute, subchronic and chronic animal studies, nor any genotoxicity, teratogenicity or carcinogenicity |CITS: [10854122]|. AMPA was found to inhibit proliferation and promote apoptosis in cancer cells, but not in normal cells |CITS: [23983455][26006246]|., AMPA is imported into bacterial cells by an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transport system consisting of a periplasmic, binding protein for phosphonates (encoded by |FRAME: EG10714| in |FRAME: TAX-562|), an ATP-binding polypeptide (|FRAME: EG10713|), and a membrane-spanning transporter polypeptide (|FRAME: EG11283 phnE|). Once inside the cell, AMPA is processed by the C-P lyase enzyme system, which includes 10 different polypeptides ((|FRAME: EG10716|, |FRAME: EG10717|, |FRAME: EG10718|, |FRAME: EG10719|, |FRAME: EG10720|, |FRAME: EG10721|, |FRAME: EG10722|, |FRAME: EG10723|, |FRAME: EG10724|, and |FRAME: EG10725|) |CITS: [24600043]|., In the case of 1-aminoalkylphosphonates such as AMPA, the pathway begins with N-acetylation, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.280| |CITS: [23056305]|. The combined action of four enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.37|, |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.63|, |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.55|, transfer the phosphonate phosphorus to a ribose that originates in ATP, generating |FRAME: RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE|., A number of bacterial species have been shown to be able to use AMPA as a phosphate source, including |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [23056305]|, |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [9882650]|, Arthrobacter sp.GLP-1 |CITS: [2439330]|, |FRAME: TAX-37927| ATCC 13752 |CITS: [16347639]|, |FRAME: TAX-1404|, and several |FRAME: TAX-286| sp., including 4ASW and |FRAME: TAX-272915| |CITS: [Quinn89]|, and Pseudomonas sp. strain LBr |CITS: [3223761]|. Among 133 environmental bacterial strains isolated from soils, 55 were able to use AMPA as a phosphate source |CITS: [7632402]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:S-ALLANTOIN "(S)-(+)-allantoin"| is a common product of purine degradation. Allantoin is rich in nitrogen, and many organisms are able to degrade and recycle it. Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1458|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, do so under aerobic conditions, while others such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: ORG-5985| and |FRAME: TAX-587| do so only anaerobically., Allantoin degradation is not limited to bacteria. Ureide-transporting plants convert fixed nitrogen in their roots to |FRAME:S-ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|, which are then transported to upper parts of the plant, where they are degraded to release the nitrogen. In addition, some fungi and animals also degrade allantoin., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-64|, comprises the hydrolysis of the internal amide bond of |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN|, forming |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| |CITS: [786256]|. This enzyme turned out to be common to all organisms that can degrade allantoin, and is the first step in all allantoin degradation pathways., |FRAME: ALLANTOATE "Allantoate"| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1091| via one of two routes. In the first route the nitrogen is liberated in a single step in the form of |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: ALLANTOICASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.4"|), while in the other route it is liberated in the form of |FRAME: AMMONIA| in two steps, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD0-2298| (starting with |FRAME: ALLANTOATE-DEIMINASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.9"|)., The next step in the pathway is the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-1091| to |FRAME: GLYOX|. Similarly, this conversion can proceed with the liberation of either |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-LYASE-RXN "EC 4.3.2.3"|) or |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-HYDROLASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.19"|)., Several combinations of these routes have been documented. Some organisms possess pathways that produce solely |FRAME: UREA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5694|), some produce only |FRAME: AMMONIA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5692|), and some produce both (see |FRAME: PWY-5705|). In addition, some anaerobic organisms can degrade allantoin to |FRAME: CPD-389| instead of |FRAME: GLYOX| (see |FRAME: PWY0-41|)., About This Pathway, Complete degradation of |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| to |FRAME: GLYOX| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|, without the production of |FRAME: UREA|, has been demonstrated in vitro with purified proteins from |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [19935661]|. The reactions occur in the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [16661891][20038185]|., There has been an ongoing debate which route is used by the soy bean plant |FRAME: TAX-3847|. Early reports found that different cultivars were utilizing different routes |CITS:[16664492][16664133][16665292][16666035][10944160]|. , Specifically, |CITS: [16666035]| found that the pathway in this organism proceeds without production of |FRAME: UREA|. It should be noted that a later study questioned this statement, suggesting that the previous investigations may have been misled by side effects of the enzyme inhibitor used. That study proposed that both cultivars are utilizing the same degradation pathway, in which the route from |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| to |FRAME: CPD-1091| involves the production of |FRAME: AMMONIA|, while the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-1091| to |FRAME: GLYOX| was carried out by EC 4.3.2.3,, resulting in production of |FRAME: UREA| |CITS: [15020640]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5705|).
Level 2: Amide, amidine, amine, and polyamine degradation

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-12572 Tricin| is a flavonoid typically distributed in sedges, palms, and grasses, including cereal crops such as rice (|FRAME: TAX-4530|), wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|), barley (|FRAME: TAX-4513|), maize (|FRAME: TAX-4577|), and sorghum (|FRAME: TAX-4558|) |CITS: [Zhou10]|. It is found mostly as O-linked conjugates that serve as allelochemicals |CITS: [20730995]| and insect deterrents |CITS: [Ling07]|. |FRAME: CPD-12572 Tricin| is also found as a flavonoid monomer in monocot lignin, representing the first non-monolignol monomer involved in lignification |CITS: [25667313]|. Tricin is considered a major candidate to be developed as a nutraceutical because of its antioxidant |CITS: [17350657]|, anticancer |CITS: [17089164]|, anti-inflammatory |CITS: [22705359]|, and cardiovascular-protective properties |CITS: [20006366]|., |FRAME: CPD-12572 Tricin| is produced in rice from the flavanone |FRAME: NARINGENIN-CMPD|, which is converted into the flavone |FRAME: CPD-431|. Two enzymatically distinct flavone synthases occur in plants - the soluble Fe2+/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.5|, and the cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.76|. It has been shown that only the latter contributes to tricin formation, forming |CITS: [26082402]|., |FRAME: CPD-431| is hydroxylated at the C-3' position, followed by methylation of the hydroxyl group to form |FRAME: 574-TRIHYDROXY-3-METHOXYFLAVONE|. The main enzyme responsible for the hydroxylation is the cytochrmome P-450 |FRAME: G-58315|, as a mutation in this gene results in complete absence of |FRAME: CPD-12572| derivatives |CITS: [26082402]|. The methylation can be catalyzed by a number of O-methyltransferases, such as |FRAME: G-58316| |CITS: [26082402]| and |FRAME: G-58318| |CITS: [17943312]|. |FRAME: G-58315| then catalyzes an additional hydroxylation, this time at position 5', forming |FRAME: CPD-12571|, which is methylated to |FRAME: CPD-12572| |CITS: [26082402]|., Note that |FRAME: CPD-12572| can also be formed from |FRAME: CPD-12570| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.175|, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6631|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, Since the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| is a very complex process, many organisms possess various salvage pathways thart enable them to rescue thiamine fragments obtained from the environment. This pathway describes the salvage of two thiamine-degradation compounds, |FRAME: THZ| and |FRAME: HMP| (HMP)., The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-8351| (|FRAME: BSU38300|), an enzyme that phosphorylates the degradation product |FRAME: THZ|, turning it into the phosphorylated form that it a part of the de novo biosynthetic pathway., HMP is processed by |FRAME: BSU11710-MONOMER| (|FRAME: BSU11710|), a bifunctional enzyme that also takes part in the biosynthetic pathway. The enzyme phosphorylates HMP into |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYL-PYR-P|, already an intermediate of the biosynthetic pathway, and continues to add another phosphate, resulting in |FRAME: AMINO-HYDROXYMETHYL-METHYLPYRIMIDINE-PP|, the other substrate of |FRAME: BSU38290-MONOMER|., The rest of the pathway is identical to the biosynthetic pathway: |FRAME: BSU38290-MONOMER| catalyzes the coupling of the thiazole and pyrimidine moieties, while |FRAME: BSU05900-MONOMER| adds another phosphate group, generating the active form |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|.

The evolutionary ancient concept of utilizing the bioactivation of cyanogenic glucosides to deter predators belongs to the most effective defense principles plants have developed over time. More than 3000 species from 130 plant families have developed the ability to biosynthesize about 70 different cyanogenic glucosides for the purpose of fending off herbivores |CITS:[9431670]| |CITS:[Seigler98]| |CITS:[22404468]|. In addition, the bioactivation of cyanogenic glucosides has also been found to serve as N-storage in non-cyanogenic compounds and alternative source for amino acid synthesis (see |FRAME:ASPSYNII-PWY|) |CITS:[Lieberei85]|., Cyanogenesis, the release of |FRAME:HCN| from cyanogenic glucosides after tissue disruption takes place in the leaves where most of the cyanogens reside. According to the 'linustatin pathway' |CITS:[16665975]| the cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesized in the seed must be transported to the vacuoles in the leaves. Because of the existence of monosaccharide β-glucosidases in the apoplastic space cyanogens are transported as disaccharides which are not hydrolyzed by those β-glucosidases |CITS:[Selmar91]| |CITS:[Selmar93]| |CITS: [16665288]|. For this reason |FRAME:LINAMARIN| (valine derived) and |FRAME:CPD-14594| co-occur in plants forming a functioning unit of transport vehicle and executing molecule |CITS:[16665975]|. A similar relationship exists between |FRAME:CPD-10277| (isoleucine derived) and |FRAME:CPD-14596| where |FRAME:CPD-14596| represents the protected transport form and |FRAME:CPD-14596| the |FRAME:HCN| releasing cyanogen |CITS:[Selmar93]|., However, similar to |FRAME:PWY-7091| in |FRAME:TAX-3981| the formed |FRAME:HCN| is re-fixed by a β-cyanoalanine synthase (see |FRAME:ASPSYNII-PWY|), hence converted to non-cyanogenic compounds. The enzymes involved in the cyanogenesis of |FRAME:CPD-14596|, i.e. β-diglucosidase |CITS:[3936419]|, β-glucosidase |CITS:[16665288]| |CITS:[3936419]| and (S)-hydroxynitrile lyases |CITS:[Selmar89]| have all been identified and biochemically characterized.

Summary: The |FRAME:PWY-7711| pathway describes the biosynthetic sequence that all trichothecenes, except for |FRAME:CPD-18430| and |FRAME:CPD-18439|, have in common. The biosynthetic steps that form |FRAME:CPD-18411| are core pathway reactions towards the generation of |FRAME:CPD-18416| (see |FRAME:PWY-7730|) and |FRAME:CPD-18421| (see |FRAME:PWY-7712|) and are also part of the |FRAME:PWY-7713| which branches out from intermediates of both |FRAME:PWY-7712| and |FRAME:PWY-7730|. The genes TRI5 encoding for the trichodiene synthase and TRI4 coding for a multifunctional trichodiene oxygenase characterized from species of Trichoderma are also listed in the pathway. Although both Trichoderma species, i.e. Trichoderma arundinaceum and Trichoderma brevicompactum do not produce the above mentioned trichothecenes but |FRAME:CPD-18430| and |FRAME:CPD-18439| instead, the catalyzing enzymes and genes have been associated with the early reactions to avoid redundancy and highlight the shared part of the pathway. While the TRI5 encoded trichodiene synthase carries out the exact reaction of the Fusarium TRI5 protein |CITS:[Gallo04] [23454546] [21145409]| the TRI4 encoded protein catalyzes only three out of the four oxidation steps performed by the homolog Fusarium TRI4 enzyme, producing |FRAME:CPD-18383| from which the |FRAME:PWY-7714|) branches off |CITS:[21642405]|., Trichothecene are sequiterpenoids characterized by a varying pattern of oxygen and ester groups on a core tricyclic skeleton bearing an epoxide function which is commonly referred to as 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene (EPT) structure |CITS:[Grove07]|. More than 200 trichothecene have been identified from various genera of fungi and classified into four groups according to the substitution pattern on the basic EPT core |CITS:[Ueno80] [Betina89]|. The biosyntheses of the various trichothecenes have been mostly elucidated by feeding experiments and mutants blocking a specific reaction in the pathway |CITS:[22069741] [17827683]|. Trichothecene are considered mycotoxins which are phytotoxic |CITS:[22295175]|, contaminate food and animal feed, have been reported to cause vomiting, skin dermatitis, and hemorrhagic lesions |CITS:[3158480] [8246841]| and interfere with complex developmental processes |CITS:[23667578]|. Fusarium species are the causative agents of the Fusarium head blight (FHB), a devastating disease that worldwide affects barley, maize, rice, wheat and causes the loss of tens of millions of dollars every year |CITS:[23078349] [16277434] [Alexander09] [8246841]|. The toxicity of trichothecene is based upon the 12,13-epoxide which not only must be present but also present in the right configuration as demonstrated by using two 12,13-epoxide isomers |CITS:[Colvin86]|. In addition, Fusarium species are adaptive and able to develop new trichothecene such as |FRAME:CPD-18599| which has been shown together with its deacylated derivative to inhibit protein synthesis in rice |CITS:[25403493]|., The biosynthetic cluster for trichothecene biosynthesis (TRI) has been studied mostly in Fusarium species |CITS:[14998528]| where most of the genes appear to be coordinately expressed and regulated |CITS:[12080147]|. In contrast to the well-established biosynthesis of trichothecenes, the regulation of the respective TRI genes is much less understood. It is known that various regulative genes are present in the trichothecene biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS:[14998528] [12650935] [19843228]| which consists of three separate clusters |CITS:[17827683]|. Genes such as TRI6, TRI10 and TRI14 |CITS:[16277434] [11679358] [21691790]|, the velvet gene Ve1 |CITS:[22013911]| as well as endogenous factors such a pH |CITS:[21691790] [20169482] [21126599]| play a role in regulation, induction and pathogenicity of trichothecene biosynthesis. , The biosynthetic reactions and the respective catalyzing enzymes from |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| to |FRAME:CPD-18411| have been studied in much detail. The first committed step in the |FRAME:PWY-7711| is catalyzed in Fusarium by the trichodiene synthase |CITS:[3800398]| to form |FRAME:TRICHODIENE-CPD| which is subsequently oxidized in four positions, i.e. C-2, C-12,13, C-11 and C-3 to yield |FRAME:CPD-18384| |CITS:[7651333] [16917519] [17188234]|. The following acetylation of the spontaneously formed |FRAME:CPD-18409| catalyzed by the isotrichodermol 3-acetyltransferase (TRI101) is regarded a key reaction in the pathway and essentially involved in the self-defense mechanism to protect Fusarium against its own toxin because the C-3 acetylated intermediate is far less toxic than its C-3 hydroxylated precursor |CITS:[9430709] [9762900] [17923480] [10583973] [11122517]|. The TRI11 encoded isotrichodermin 15-hydroxylase catalyzes the late hydroxylation step in the pathway forming |FRAME:CPD-18410| |CITS:[9435078] [7651333] [16535589]| and the final reaction resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18411| is carried out by the trichothecene 15-O-acetyltransferase (TRI3) which reaction mechanism was elucidated by the crystallization and following investigation of the three-dimensional structure of the Tri3 encoded protein |CITS:[8593041] [19319932] [18776660]|.

|FRAME: Methyleneureas Methyleneureas| are condensation products of urea and formaldehyde that are used in large amounts as resins, binders, and insulating materials for industrial applications. In addition, short-chain methyleneureas are widely utilized as slow-release nitrogen fertilizerss on professional turf, in greenhouses, on lawns, and for general gardening and landscaping. , The degree of polymerization depends on the ratio of urea to formaldehyde during the condensation process. The short chain length products used as fertilizers [such as |FRAME: METHYLENEDIUREA| (MDU), |FRAME: CPD-28007| (DMTU), and |FRAME: CPD-28008| (TMTU)] are formed when the ratio is between 1.2-1.5 to 1., The short-chain methyleneureas are degraded by bacteria via hydrolysis, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.141|. The enzyme has been isolated from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-529| |CITS: [Jahns97]|, |FRAME: TAX-82633| |CITS: [Jahns00]|, and |FRAME: TAX-362| |CITS: [Koivunen03]|. However, as of 2025 the gene(s) encoding the enzyme are still not known.

Gray mold is a disease caused by the necrotrophic fungus |FRAME: TAX-40559|. Several economically important crops and ornamental plants are affected by this disease. Two major phytotoxins are secreted by this filamentous fungus after infection; the sesquiterpene |FRAME: CPD-11442| and the polyketide boticinic acid. These phytotoxins, along with reactive oxygen species, induce oxidative bursts in the host cells, killing the cells. This is followed by a range of fungal degrading exoenzymes that prepare the host tissue for ingestion by the fungus |CITS: [17986079]|. In grapes the infection can cause (under specific climatic conditions) the disease "la pourritude noble", otherwise known as 'noble rot'., This pathway describes the production of |FRAME: CPD-11442|. In microbes, the genes involved in terpene biosynthesis are often present in clusters |CITS: [19035644]|. The BcBot2 gene of |FRAME: TAX-40559| is part of cluster that contains five genes, and has been shown to encode a sesquiterpene synthase that produces |FRAME: CPD-11441|, a precursor of |FRAME: CPD-11442| |CITS: [19035644]|., The virulence factors of |FRAME: TAX-40559| are shared with other phytopathogens |CITS: [17986079]|.

Summary: General Background, Arginine biosynthesis is notable for its complexity and variability at the genetic level, and by its connection with several other pathways, such as pyrimidine and polyamine biosynthesis, and certain degradative pathways. The initial steps of the arginine biosynthetic pathways proceed via N-acetylated intermediates. The presumed reason for this is that the acetylation prevents the spontaneous cyclization of glutamate derivatives, which leads to proline biosynthesis, thus keeping the two pathways separate |CITS: [12633501]|. A variation of the pathway found in some archaebacteria and hyperthermophilic bacteria utilizes a dedicated carrier protein to protect the intermediates instead of acetylation., Several alternative arginine biosynthetic pathways have evolved in bacteria:, In |FRAME:ARGSYN-PWY|, which is not very common, the key intermediate |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG) is formed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.1|. A second key intermediate downstream, |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE|, is hydrolyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.16|, releasing acetate, and forming the arginine precursor |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|., In |FRAME:ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|), which is found in most of the prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbes investigated up to now, the two reactions mentioned above are linked: the acetyl group which is removed from |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is recycled onto glutamate, regenerating |FRAME:ACETYL-GLU| (NAG)., This recycling is performed by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.35|. This pathway is considered more evolved, since the overall reaction is energetically more favorable |CITS: [3534538]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-5154| is found in several eubacteria. While in the two pathways mentioned above |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is deacetylate to |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, which is subsequently transcarbamoylated to form |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|, in this variant |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is not deacetylated. Instead, it is, transcarbamoylated directly by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.1.3.9|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-7224|. The enzyme |FRAME:ACETYLORNDEACET-CPLX| can accept |FRAME: CPD-7224| as a substrate, and deacetylates it into |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| |CITS: [16585758]|., The variant |FRAME: PWY-7400|, which has been described in the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2285|, involves early intermediates that are protected not by acetylation but by a carrier protein (the LysW |FRAME: LysW|), which participates in the biosynthesis of both |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: LEU| in these organsims |CITS: [23434852]|., About This Pathway, This linear variant of the arginine biosynthesis pathway has been reported from the Enterobacteriaceae |CITS: [3534538]|, the |FRAME:TAX-641| |CITS: [10692366]|, and the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME:TAX-34| |CITS: [ 9829957]|. The pathway was also described in the archaeon |FRAME:TAX-2287| |CITS: [vandecasteele90]|, but in most likelihood that organism possesses a different variant of the pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7400|)., In this pathway glutamate is acetylated to N-acetyl-glutamate (NAG) by the enzyme NAG synthase, encoded by the argA gene. The acetyl donor for this reaction is acetyl-CoA. NAG is then converted in several enzymatic steps to N-acetyl-ornithine. The acetyl group is removed in the form of acetate by the enzyme acetylornithine deacetylase, encoded by the argE gene. Ornithine is then combined with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline, which is converted in two steps to L-arginine.

Summary: General Background, The transition element molybdenum (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. This molybdenum cofactor (moco) consists of a unique tricyclic pterin compound (molybdopterin) containing a Mo-binding and -coordinating dithiolene group. Moco finally binds to diverse apoproteins and confers activity to the resulting holoproteins ubiquitously involved in essential redox reactions in the global C-, N-, and S-cycles |CITS: [11848841]| |CITS: [16307306]|., Although molybdenum enzymes are found in all organism kingdoms only four enzymes have been reported in plants so far |CITS: [12147719]|. However, the importance of those enzymes is highlighted by the fact that unavailability of Mo, hence failure to complement the apoproteins with moco is lethal for the organism. Moco enzymes in plants are subdivided into two classes, |FRAME:CPLX-7198| |CITS: [3393528]| and |FRAME:CPLX-7196| |CITS: [11598126]| originating from the dioxo-form of moco and |FRAME:CPLX-6985| |CITS: [14726515]| and |FRAME:CPLX-7097| |CITS: [11050171]| that require, the addition of a terminal inorganic sulfur to the Mo center (sulfo-form of moco) for enzymatic activity., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of moco has been investigated in detail in bacteria, e.g. |CITS: [7836363][8514783][8514782][1587808][14761975]|. The group of R.R. Mendel (TU Braunschweig) has considerably contributed to the corresponding research in plants, and their results have been summarized in several excellent reviews |CITS: [16669776][16784786][12147719][16234918][9421926]|., About This Pathway, Plant enzymes such as aldehyde oxidase (AO) and xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH) depend on the sulfo-form of molybdenum cofactor (moco). The so called maturation of moco involves the addition of sulfur to the Mo center. In eukaryotes this reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.9| (e.g. the plant ABA3) |CITS: [11553608][15561708]|. This enzyme is a two-domain protein. The N-terminal ABA3-NifS domain generates an enzyme-bound persulfide intermediate whereas the C-terminal domain is probably involved in recognizing target enzymes and posttranslational activation of ABA3 |CITS: [11553608]|. , Prokaryotes do not have such an enzyme. In prokaryotes MoCo first binds to a chaperone before it is sulfurylated by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.7|. See for example |FRAME: PWY-8164| and |FRAME: PWY-8165|.

Summary: General Background, There are several alternative pathways for the degradation of trehalose., Depending on the organism, trehalose may enter the cell either through a permease, in which case it remains, unmodified, or it may be transported by a phosphotransferase system (PTS), resulting in the phoshorylated, trehalose-6-phosphate form., Degradation then proceeds by different mechanisms: , Unmodified trehalose may be degraded by a hydrolyzing trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|), or it may be split, by the action of a trehalose phosphorylase (see |FRAME: PWY-2722| and |FRAME: PWY-2723|)., Likewise, trehalose-6-phosphate may be either hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase, (see |FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) or it could be attacked by a trehalose-6-phosphate phosphorylase, (see |FRAME: PWY-2721|)., In insects, trehalose is produced from fat body glycogen and is released into the hemolymph. In many insects, trehalose serves as an extracellular source of sugar via the action of trehalase, an enzyme widely distributed in insect tissues (reviewed in |CITS: [KRAMER05][19725772]|)., About This Pathway, Trehalase enzymes hydrolyze a molecule of |FRAME: TREHALOSE| into two molecules of glucose. , |FRAME: TAX-83333| can grow with trehalose as the sole carbon source, and employs different pathways, for its degradation under different osmolarity conditions. Under high osmotic conditions external, trehalose is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: TREHALAPERI-MONOMER| (TreA) |CITS: [2820965]|., The resulting glucose molecules are then transported back into the cytoplasm through the glucose PTS, |CITS: [1825082]| (see |FRAME: PWY0-1466|)., A second trehalase, the |FRAME: TREHALACYTO-MONOMER| (TreF), is active during the transition, period between high and low osmolarity. As the cells are shifting their metabolism to adjust to low, osmolarity, TreF removes the internal pool of trehalose. The relatively low enzymatic activity of TreF is, low enough not to compromise the biosynthesis of trehalose during high osmolarity, yet is sufficient to, degrade the accumulated trehalose after the return to normal conditions, when no more biosynthesis, occurrs |CITS: [8892826]|., This trehalose degradation pathway is also used by the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|., This organism also has a cytoplasmic and a periplasmic trehalase enzymes |CITS:[8444853]|., Nth1p, the cytoplasmic enzyme, is required for the hydrolysis of intracellular trehalose,, while Ath1p, the periplasmic enzyme, hydrolyzes extracellular trehalose |CITS: [15128531]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Vitamins-B6 "Vitamin B6"| is an important cofactor of many enzymes. While the active form of the vitamin is |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, it occurs in several forms within organisms. There are three free forms, |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE|, |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL| (|FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| is the form given as vitamin B6 supplement) and three phosphorylated forms (|FRAME:PYRIDOXINE-5P|, |FRAME:PYRIDOXAMINE-5P| and |FRAME:PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|), all of which can be interconverted. A seventh form, |FRAME:CPD-1112|, is excreted in urine., Some bacteria can use the different forms of vitamin B6 as a sole source for carbon and nitrogen. Two different but related degradation pathways have been described (|FRAME: PWY-5499| and |FRAME: PWY-8384|) |CITS: [ 21004555][13610871][Burg70]|., About This Pathway, In the pathway shown here, which was originally discovered in |FRAME: ORG-57114| and |FRAME: ORG-6357|, |FRAME:PYRIDOXINE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-383|. This compound oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-25922| either directly or via |FRAME: CPD-9028| |CITS: [13610871][3533936][3771565]| ., The aromatic ring of |FRAME: CPD-25922| is cleaved by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.241|, forming |FRAME: 2-HYDROXYMETHYL-3-ACETAMIDOMETHYLENE| (referred to as "compound B" in the original publications |CITS: [4306031]|. The last pathway enzyme that has been characterized is |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.66|, which hydrolyzes compound B, releasing acetate, ammonia, and CO2, and forming |FRAME: 2-HYDROXYMETHYL-4-OXOBUTANOATE| |CITS: [3972793]|., As of 2022, none of the genes encoding these enzymes have been identified, and the final steps of the pathway have not been elucidated.

Summary: Acidithiobacilli are prominent bacteria that catalyze the oxidation of inorganic sulfur compounds under acidic conditions (pH 1 to 3) and ambient temperatures. |FRAME: TAX-920| is a member of this family, which obtains energy via the oxidation of iron as well as sulfur, and is often found in pyrite deposits. , |FRAME: TAX-920| is an important industrial microorganism, involved in bioleaching of copper ores and the biooxidation of gold-containing ores |CITS: [Rawlings2001]|. The organism can oxidize sulfur compounds under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, using either molecular oxygen or |FRAME: FE+3| ions as electron acceptors, respectively |CITS: [FEMSMicroLett41-1]|. Despite much research, the oxidation pathway of elemental sulfur has not been clearly elucidated yet, and the pathway described here is still considered tentative., Working with |FRAME: TAX-920|, |FRAME: TAX-930| and |FRAME: TAX-76588|, Rohwerer and Sand proposed a model for the oxidation of elemental sulfur and free sulfide by these organisms |CITS: [12855721]|. , According to this model, the process begins with a series of spontaneous reactions, in which extracellular elemental sulfur and hydrogen sulfide are activated by thiol groups of specific membrane proteins (for simplification, in the pathways shown here the thiol groups are represented by the simple thiols |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| and |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE|) and transported into the periplasm as persulfide sulfane sulfur with the general formula GS<sub>n</sub>H (such as |FRAME: CPD-11281|). , These persulfide molecules are subject to two types of reactions: a non-enzymic sulfur reduction that generates |FRAME: HS| , and an enzymic sulfur oxidation that produces |FRAME: SO3| ., The |FRAME: HS| that is formed by the first reaction is recycled back to persulfide sulfane compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-11281|. It is first oxidized back to elemental sulfur by a |FRAME:CPLX-7905| (see |FRAME:P222-PWY|), and the elemental sulfur reacts with organic thiols to form the persulfides |CITS: [15618623]|. This process keeps the sulfur from precipitating in the periplasm. This model has been reviewd in |CITS: [15877814]|., The |FRAME: SO3| formed by the enzymic oxidation reaction is further oxidized to |FRAME: SULFATE|. Two systems have been reported to carry out the oxidation to |FRAME: SO3| and |FRAME: SULFATE| in |FRAME: TAX-920|., In one system, which has also been reported in other sulfur oxidizers, the persulfides are oxidized to |FRAME: SO3| by a |FRAME: CPLX-7904|, followed by further oxidation to |FRAME: SULFATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-7140| (see |FRAME: SULFUROX-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5276|)., The second system, reported only in |FRAME: TAX-920|, includes a |FRAME:CPLX-921| and a |FRAME:CPLX-922|, which operate under anaerobic conditions, and utilize |FRAME: FE+3| as an electron acceptor exclusively |CITS: [3667519][3345075]| (see |FRAME:FESULFOX-PWY|).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE Plastoquinones| (PQ) are benzoquinone electron carriers that can function as acceptor/donor for either one or two electrons. They are analogs of |FRAME: Ubiquinones "ubiquinones"| (Coenzyme Q), with two methyl groups substituting the methoxy groups found in Q. The fully reduced form is called |FRAME: Plastoquinols|., Plastoquinones are found in the chloroplasts of higher plants, red, brown and green algae, and in cyanobacteria, and are important members of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, where they carry electrons from |FRAME: CPLX490-3506| to the |FRAME: CPLX-9022|. Plastoquinones also serve as a membrane-associated two-electron carriers in other respiratory electron transport chains. In fact, it has been shown that in cyanobacteria essentially all electron transport through unbound quinones proceeds via PQ in cyanobacterial thylakoids. Apart from PQ the only quinone found in thylakoids is |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1), which is associated with PS I |CITS: [Vermaas01]|., Plastoquinones also serve as cofactors involved in the desaturation of |FRAME: CPD-12321| in the synthesis of carotenoids (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|)., Plastoquinone was isolated originally in 1946 from alfalfa, but was not identified at the time. It was rediscovered in 1959 and its structure was described in the same year (see |CITS: [7022156]|)., About This Pathway, The pathway for the biosynthesis of plastoquinone in plants starts with |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE|. |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE| is a branching point in the formation of plastoquinones and |FRAME: Vitamin-E tocopherols|. The committed step in plastoquinone biosynthesis is condensation of |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE| and |FRAME: CPD-21340|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-3784|., A different enzyme (|FRAME: AT2G18950-MONOMER|) catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE| with |FRAME: PHYTYL-PYROPHOSPHATE|, the committed step for biosynthesis of tocopherols (see |FRAME: PWY-1422|)., The plastoquinone biosynthesis in cyanobacteria is different than that of plants (see |FRAME: PWY-6978|).

Summary: Plant volatiles contribute to aroma, flavor and scents of plants., |CITS: [16469917]|. They are produced by the terminal branches of primary metabolic pathways. A single , reaction and enzyme can convert a primary metabolite into a volatile compound. , |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: CPD-7035| are two such aroma volatiles derived from phenylalanine , |CITS: [16698923]|. Both compounds have pleasant fruity, floral smells and are major contributors of scent in , many flowers. |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| is the major scent volatile of hyacinth and lilac. , |FRAME: CPD-7035| is the major aroma volatile associated with roses |CITS: [17644147]|. In tomato, , both these compounds are a big impact on the fruit's flavor and the rapid interconversion of , |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| to |FRAME: CPD-7035| in vivo has been demonstrated , |CITS: [16698923]|. They also act as powerful insect attractants and each attracts different sets of , pollinating and predatory insects. , While the biosynthetic route of |FRAME:CPD-7035| production via |FRAME:PHENYLETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME:PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| has experimental support |CITS:[16698923]| |CITS:[16766535]| |CITS:[17928708]| the proposed route via |FRAME:CPD-13031| so far lacks identified enzymes and genes in the Solanecea or other plants. However, a corresponding protein converting |FRAME:PHE| into |FRAME:CPD-13031| has been identified and characterized in |FRAME:TAX-3701| |CITS:[10799553]| and the formation of |FRAME:CPD-13031| has also been reported in rose |CITS:[Hayashi04]|. In addition the fast conversion of |FRAME:PHENYLACETALDOXIME| into |FRAME:CPD-7035| was observed in rose petals emphasizing the possible occurrence of this metabolic pathway in plants |CITS:[17928708]|., , Despite the multiple roles these compounds play, little is known about their biosynthesis in plants. In , yeast, |FRAME: CPD-7035| is produced from phenylalanine via phenylpyruvate and |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| , |CITS: [17928708]|. In petunia and tomato, the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-7035| appears to have evolved , into distinct pathways. The tomato enzymes catalyze the simple conversion of phenylalanine to , |FRAME: PHENYLETHYLAMINE|, whereas the petunia enzyme is a complex one and catalyzes the , efficient coupling of phenylalanine decarboxylation to oxidation, generating |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE|, , |FRAME: AMMONIA|, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in , stoichiometric amounts |CITS: [16766535]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipid-A "Lipid A"| is the hydrophobic anchor of the outer membrane lipopolysaccharide of Gram-negative bacteria . Free lipid A does not exist as such in cells. It is normally found glycosylated with two KDO (3-deoxy-D-manno-octulosonic acid) residues and acylated with laurate and myristate residues. , In |FRAME:TAX-562|, if the organism is subjected to cold shock or grown at low temperatures, the laurate residue is replaced by palmitoleate. Myristate is subsequently added, resulting in a distinct cold adapted form of KDO2-lipid A |CITS: [ColiSalII][8662613][2203778][9099672][10092655]|., A PagP homodimer can catalyze palmitate transfer from a phospholipid (sn-1 position) to lipid A or to a lipid A precursor (N-linked hydroxymyristate on the proximal unit) |CITS: [11013210]|. The catalytic site localizes to the exterior of the outer membrane, indicating that enzyme activity may require outer membrane problems that result in mislocalization of palmitate-donor phospholipids from the interior face to the exterior face of the outer membrane |CITS: [12357033]|.

Anthocyanins can be divided in two groups, the common 3-hydroxyanthocyanins which bear a hydroxyl group at the 3-position of the C-ring and the rare 3-deoxyanthocyanidins which are lacking this hydroxyl group. 3-Deoxyanthocyanidins are found mostly in mosses and ferns and have been reported in higher plants especially in the New World angiosperm families |FRAME:TAX-26122| and |FRAME:TAX-24079| |CITS:[Harborne66]| and some members of the |FRAME:TAX-4479| such as maize, sorghum and sugarcane |CITS:[Styles75]|. In the highly developed |FRAME:TAX-26122| species the 3-deoxyanthocyanidins are mostly involved in providing orange-red to scarlet flower colors which have been discussed as attractants for bird pollinators |CITS:[Harborne66]|. In addition, they are known to be induced as phytoalexins in response to pathogenic attacks in apple and sorghum |CITS:[12667486]|., The occurrence of the 3-deoxyanthocyanidins |FRAME:CPD-7096| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-11945| has been reported from petals of |FRAME:TAX-189007| |CITS:[Stich88]| |CITS:[Winefield05]| and silk tissue of maize |CITS:[Halbwirth03]|. The structures of the flavan 4-ols have been questioned and a retrodihydrochalcone structure (|FRAME:CPD-15275|) proposed instead |CITS:[Khalil12]|. It has been classified as an UGT88 enzyme, a phylogenetic clade which involves |FRAME:MONOMER-12113| (see |FRAME:PWY-5160|) |CITS:[15944692]| and |FRAME:MONOMER-12697| (see |FRAME:PWY-1901|) |CITS:[16832053]|.

General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, The first committed step of carotenoid biosynthesis is that of the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12321| from, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This conversion is in fact a two-step reaction catalyzed by the enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-14934|., Phytoene is then isomerized to |FRAME: PHYTOENE| and undergoes a series of desaturation reactions. The number of these reactions depends on the species and the enzyme. Some enzyme stop after two steps, some catalyze three steps, and some continue with a fourth step, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:CPD1F-114| (see |FRAME:PWY-5942|)., This pathway represents organisms that convert |FRAME: PHYTOENE| to |FRAME: NEUROSPORENE|, such as the purple non-sulfur bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1061| and |FRAME: TAX-1063| that produce |FRAME: CPD-11468| (see |FRAME: PWY-6286|). This conversion proceeds via the intermediates |FRAME:CPD-7408| and |FRAME:CPD1F-98|., The desaturation steps use all-trans compounds.

Various lines of evidence suggest that the |FRAME: YAL060W| gene product catalyzes the first step in 2,3-butanediol degradation, the oxidation of 2,3-butanediol to acetoin |CITS: [10938079]|. The enzyme was purified and shown to catalyze the NADH-dependent, reversible conversion of |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL| and |FRAME: CPD-12004| to |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: CPD-255|, respectively, with a clear preference for |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|. , Mutants with a disrupted |FRAME: YAL060W| gene can still grow on 2,3-butanediol as the sole carbon and energy source, indicating that there are other enzymes that can metabolize 2,3-butanediol |CITS: [10938079]|. That enzyme also preferentially oxidized the hydroxyl group in the (R) configuration., How acetoin is further degraded in S. cerevisiae is not yet known. Many prokaryotes have a multienzyme, complex, |FRAME: CPLX-7659|, that is similar to pyruvate dehdrogenase and transforms acetoin, into |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which can enter the glyoxylate and TCA, cycles |CITS: [11306064]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6028|).

Summary: General Background, Sulfate is one of the most common electron acceptors for anaerobic respiration. Sulfate-reducing organisms are ubiquitous in anaerobic environments such as soil, sediments, marine and freshwaters, and the mouth and gut of many animals |CITS: [16388601]|. , Sulfate-reducers contribute greatly to the global cycling of carbon and sulfur, mostly in marine habitats, where the sulfate concentration is high. It is estimated that dissimilatory sulfate reduction is responsible for up to 50% of carbon remineralization in marine environments |CITS: [9389475]|., Dissimilatory sulfate-reducing prokaryotes are a heterogenous group of bacteria and archaea consisting of diverse phyla such as Archaeoglobi |CITS: [11265481]|, Proteobacteria |CITS: [8572886]|, Firmicutes |CITS:[3395110]|, Nitrospirae |CITS: [11541228]| and others that can use sulfate as a terminal electron acceptor. During the process, sulfate is ultimately reduced to |FRAME: HS| through the intermediates |FRAME: APS| (APS) and |FRAME: SO3|., The reduction of sulfate to sulfite requires two electrons at a standard redox potential (E0') of -516 mV, which is too high for physiological electron carriers |CITS: [860983]|. This problem is solved by the formation of a mixed anhydride between the sulfate and phosphate, as in |FRAME:APS| (APS). This linkage lowers the potential to E0' = -60 mV, which is easilly negotiateded by biological reductants |CITS: [14627706]|., About This Pathway, All steps of sulfate reduction occur in the cytoplasm, implying that sulfate must be transported across the cytoplasmic membrane into the cell. Sulfate is activated with ATP in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-7176|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: APS| (APS) and pyrophosphate., This enzyme has an unfavorable equilibrium (Keq ~ 10-7 M) in the direction of APS formation, and it has been postulated that the reaction is driven by the hydrolysis of PPi by a ubiquitous inorganic pyrophosphatase |CITS: [2821345]| and the favorable adenylylsulfate reductase reaction which consumes the product., The next step is the reduction of APS to sulfite and AMP, which is catalyzed by |FRAME:CPLX-7177|, for which the natural electron donor is not known. , The last enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME:CPLX-7178| catalyzes the six-electron reduction of sulfite to sulfide, the main energy-conserving step in sulfate respiration. Dissimilatory sulfite reductases (DSRs) are present in all studied organisms capable of reducing sulfite to sulfide during anaerobic respiration. All DSR enzymes contain |FRAME: SIROHEME| and [4Fe-4S] prosthetic centers, and they are classified according to their spectroscopic properties in four major groups which are: desulfoviridins (found in all |FRAME:TAX-872| strains |CITS:[5128167]|), desulfurubidins (discovered in a mutant, |FRAME: TAX-876| strain unable to synthethize desulfoviridin |CITS: [4717523]|), desulfofuscidin (discovered in |FRAME: TAX-1741| |CITS: [6826522]|), and P582 (found in members of the |FRAME:TAX-1562| genus |CITS: [4745421]|)., The subunit structure was initially described as α2β2. Following the discovery of a third subunit, an α2β2γ2 structure was proposed for, some organisms including |FRAME: TAX-881|, |FRAME: TAX-879|, |FRAME: TAX-876| |CITS: [1555572]| and |FRAME: ORG-5878| |CITS: [11160104]|. However, it is now accepted that the |FRAME: DsrC-sulfur-carrier-proteins "DsrC sulfur carrier protein"| is not a subunit of the sufite reductase, but rather a protein with which it interacts |CITS: [18829451]|., An early proposal for the process of sulfite reduction suggested that DsrAB persulfurates the |FRAME: DsrC-sulfur-carrier-proteins "DsrC sulfur carrier protein"| at one of its two conserved cysteine residues. Following the dissociation of DsrC from the sulfite reductase, the persulfide is reduced by the second conserved cysteine, resulting in the release of |FRAME: HS| and the formation of an intramolecular disulfide in DsrC, which could be regenerated to a disulfide form by the DsrMKJOP transmembrane complex (a membrane complex with disulfide/thiol reductase activity) |CITS: [18829451][20952577]|. However, this mechanism is now deemed incorrect. Later work has shown that DsrAB uses the two electrons it receives from its unknown physiological partner to reduce the sulfur in |FRAME: SO3| to an S(II) intermediate, which forms (together with two cysteine residues of DsrC) a trisulfide., The last step in the pathway is catalyzed by DsrK, an iron-sulfur protein that is related to the cytoplasmic catalytic subunit |FRAME:G-390 HdrD| of membrane-bound |FRAME: CPLX-321 "heterodisulfide reductases"| from methanogenic archaea. DsrK is the catalytic subunit of the |FRAME: CPLX-8188|, and acts as a disulfide reductase on DsrC that contains a trisulfide bridge, releasing |FRAME: HS| and restoing DsrC to its reduced state, using the membrane quinone pool as the electron source |CITS: [9695921][20952577][26680199]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SUCROSE Sucrose| is the major product of photosynthesis in most plants and is known to be essential for their growth, development, carbon storage, signal transduction and stress protection |CITS: [11005202]|., Sucrose is also found in cyanobacteria, and the ability to synthesize sucrose is a widespread feature of these organisms |CITS: [21054739]|. In addition, sucrose is produced by many nonphotosynthetic aerobic methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria |CITS: [1055047][12656177][14529181][23808151][23865613]|., In photosynthetic organisms, the product of photosynthetic carbon fixation (|FRAME: GAP|) is transported from the chloroplast into the cytoplasm, where it is transformed to hexose phosphate by enzymes of the |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis| pathway. In plants, these hexose phosphates are used to synthesize sucrose, the form in which most fixed organic carbon is translocated from photosynthetic tissue to non-photosynthetic organs. Sucrose also provides substrates for plant storage glycosides such as |FRAME: Starch starch| and |FRAME: Fructans fructans|. Storage glycosides, including sucrose, are mobilized and utilized during seed germination and plant growth., In marine and freshwater cyanobacteria, sucrose fulfils a different role. It is often synthesized in response to salt or temperature stress and seems to maintain the osmotic balance and to stabilize protein and membrane structure and function |CITS: [Reed86][7854254]|. Methanotrophic and methanol-utilizing bacteria also synthesize sucrose as a secondary osmotic compound, along with the major compatible solute |FRAME: ECTOINE|., About This Pathway, Sucrose synthesis is performed by generating the phosphorylated form, |FRAME: SUCROSE-6P| (the "F" indicates that the phosphate group is attached to the furanose moiety), followed by dephosphorylation. The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.14|, which condenses |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| with |FRAME: CPD-12575|. The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.24|, which hydrolyzes |FRAME: SUCROSE-6P| to |FRAME: SUCROSE|. In nonphotosynthetic bacteria the two functions are catalyzed by a single bifunctional enzyme |CITS: [23865613]|., A similar pathway occurs in photosynthetic organisms. However, in those organisms both precursors originate from biosynthetic-derived carbon (see |FRAME: SUCSYN-PWY|).

General Background, The violet to red betacyanins (e.g. |FRAME:PWY-5399|) are a subclass of the betalains (see |FRAME:PWY-5394|) and occur almost exclusively in the order of |FRAME: TAX-3524| |CITS: [12620337][16212790][16669781]|. While the biosyntheses of betacyanins and the closely related betaxanthins (e.g. |FRAME:PWY-5404|) are well studied, almost nothing is known about the degradative metabolization of those compounds. , About This Pathway, Soboleva and coworkers |CITS: [17435]| first described the enzymatically caused discoloration and breakdown of betacyanins in |FRAME: TAX-161934| (garden beet) under uptake of oxygen. Since then some progress has been made to identify and characterize the enzyme with special focus on its substrate specificity |CITS: [SHIH81][ELLIOTT83]|., The assumption that a peroxidase may be involved in the catabolic oxidation of betacyanins has been corroborated by studying the reaction in |FRAME:TAX-4442|. The peroxidase was found to oxidize both betanidin and its glucosidic derivative betanin. For the betanin oxidation the peroxidase catalyzed a reaction that yielded a intermediate cyclo-DOPA 5-O-β-D-glucoside dimer, and several oxidized cyclo-DOPA 5-O-β-D-glucoside polymers and betalamic acid |CITS: [ELLIOTT83][MARTINEZPERRA97]|., The peroxidative oxidation of the aglycon betanidin led to the formation of betanidin quinone. The enzymatic reaction involved was to produce the betanidin radical intermediate which subsequently, by further nonenzymatic dismutation, generated betanidin quinone and betanidin. However, the further catabolism of betanidin quinone or its association with interconnecting pathways remains to be studied in more detail. The peroxidase has been classified as a class III peroxidase located in the vacuole. The much lower efficiency of the peroxidase towards betacyanin glucosides and the known vacuolar localization of β-glucosidases were discussed as interactions of both enzymes indicating a metabolic role of this peroxidase(s) in the metabolization of betacyanins |CITS: [11513711]|.

Summary: The first purine nucleotide that is synthesized de novo is |FRAME: IMP IMP|. IMP is converted to |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| by the enzyme |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCCINATE-SYN-DIMER|, and the latter is converted to the first adenosine nucleotide, |FRAME: AMP| (AMP), by the action of |FRAME:AMPSYN-ENZRXN|., AMP is phosphorylated to ADP and subsequently to ATP. While the first reaction is catalyzed by the dedicated enzyme, |FRAME: ADENYL-KIN-MONOMER|, reactions that convert ADP to ATP are numerous and found in multiple pathways, including fueling pathways such as anaerobic respiration, TCA-aerobic respiration, fermentation, and glycolysis. However, a major source for this conversion is the |FRAME: CPLX490-3510 ATP synthase| complex, which is membrane bound and utilizes the proton gradient across membranes to phosphorylate ADP. This is the reaction depicted in this pathway., ADP can also be converted to the deoxy form |FRAME: DADP dADP|. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this conversion is catalyzed by either |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTI-CPLX| or |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTII-CPLX|, which differ by the type of thioredoxin-like enzyme they utilize as the electron donor. dADP is further phosphorylated to the DNA building block |FRAME: DATP dATP| by the broad-substrate range enzyme |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX|., A few organisms, including the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562|, also possess the enzyme |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-TRIP-REDUCT-CPLX|, which can reduce nucleotide triphosphates to their 2'-deoxy forms., In bacterial systems genetic studies indicate that the majority of de novo purine biosynthetic genes are unlinked but may act as a single unit of regulation controlled by the `purR' repressor protein |CITS:[2404765]|.

Summary: Many bacterial species can ferment |FRAME:PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2,3-butanediol"| via several intermediate compounds, including |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|, |FRAME: DIACETYL| and |FRAME: ACETOIN|. Not all species carry the process all the way from pyruvate to 2,3-butanediol - some may stop earlier, accumulating some of the intermediates., There are two isomeric forms of acetoin - |FRAME: CPD-10353| and |FRAME: CPD-255|, and three isomeric forms of 2,3-butanediol (BD ) - |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|, |FRAME: CPD-346| and |FRAME: CPD-12004|. Different organisms produce different forms, or different combinations of the different forms. This pathway describes the production of |FRAME: CPD-12004| from |FRAME: CPD-255|., The conversion of acetoin to 2,3-butanediol, which is reversible, is performed by the enzyme acetoin reductase (AR), also known as 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenase (BDH)., 4 types of AR activities have been identified, differing in the substrate and product stereo-specificity. One of the enzymes shown to be able to catalyze the production of |FRAME: CPD-12004| from |FRAME: CPD-255| is the |FRAME: YAL060W|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX3O-79| of |FRAME: TAX-4932|. The enzyme can also accept |FRAME: CPD-10353|, which it converts to |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|. , The conversion of acetoin to 2,3-butanediol is desired in wine making, since the former imparts an unfavorable flavor, while the later is neutral in this respect |CITS: [19329666]|., The metabolic function of 2,3-butanediol is not yet known, although it may play a role in preventing intracellular, acidification by changing the metabolism from acid production to the formation of a neutral compound, |CITS: [6298028]|.  In addition, the pathway might participate in regulation of the NADH/NAD<sup>+</sup> ratio, in the organism |CITS: [8444801]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-21760 Coptisine| is an isoquinoline alkaloid that was originally isolated from rhizome of |FRAME: TAX-3442|. It was later described from several other |FRAME: TAX-3441| species, as well as from |FRAME: TAX-3469| (opium poppy) |CITS: [13710637]| and |FRAME: TAX-71251| (greater celandine). The dried rhizomes of |FRAME: TAX-261450| have been widely used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries for the purposes of heat clearing, dampness drying, fire draining, and detoxification. Over 100 patented drugs have been produced from |FRAME: TAX-261450| in China., |FRAME: CPD-21760 Coptisine| has extensive pharmacological actions including antibacterial, hypoglycemic, anti-tumorigenic, and gastric-mucous membrane protection |CITS: [11725963][16635741][18330249][17804078]|. In addition, coptisine was reported to exert antidepressant effects as a potent type A monoamine oxidase inhibitor |CITS: [11833714]|., The pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-21760| biosynthesis has not been fully characterized in coptisine-producing plants, although data from other plant species suggests a plausible pathway. , Like many other benzylisoquinoline alkaloids, including the protoberberine, benzophenanthridine, and morphinan alkaloids, the pathway towards |FRAME: CPD-21760| passes through the central intermediate |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| (for its biosynthesis, see |FRAME: PWY-3581|). |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| is converted to |FRAME: S-SCOULERINE| by |FRAME: EC-1.21.3.3|, also known as berberine bridge enzyme, or BBE |CITS: [8972604][16728404]|., The conversion of |FRAME: S-SCOULERINE| to |FRAME: CPD-21760| continues with the formation of two methylenedioxy bridges by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.65| (CFS) and |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.64| (SPS), which are members of the CYP719 family, forming |FRAME: S-STYLOPINE|. CFS and SPS have been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3467| |CITS: [18854999][21094631]| and |FRAME: TAX-54796| |CITS: [21094631]| and characterized. Curiously, in a recent publication reporting a comprehensive transcriptome study of |FRAME: TAX-261450| and |FRAME: TAX-261448| no homologs for CFS and SPS were found |CITS: [29915609]|., Subsequent oxidation of |FRAME: S-STYLOPINE| by |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.8| (STOX) yields |FRAME: CPD-21760|, as has been demonstrated by expressing the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-3442| in |FRAME: TAX-3467| |CITS: [Matsushima12]|.
