Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN "Biotin"| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation, and transcarboxylation reactions involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism |CITS: [8676868]|. Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|., Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria, and certain archaea and fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. The biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail in bacteria. Sequencing analysis and some experimental evidence suggests that the steps in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|., About This Pathway, Biotin consists of two fused heterocyclic rings and a |FRAME: VALERATE| side chain, derived from a |FRAME: CPD-205|-like structure. The early steps of the pathway are responsible for the synthesis of the precursor pimelate moiety, and are described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6578|. The late steps of the pathway, which are responsible for forming the two rings in the structure of biotin, are described here., The first step in this part of the pathway involves the unusual use of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| as an amino-group donor, a reaction catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-3702| by the bifunctional enzyme |FRAME: G-12146| |CITS: [40028677]|. Note that the enzyme catalyzing this transamination use different donors in different organisms (|FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| by the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: LYS| by the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-1423|). Although it hasn't been proven yet, it is thought that other plant enzymes have similar substrate preference to the |FRAME: TAX-3702| enzyme., The bifunctional enzyme also catalyzes the next reaction, the carboxylation of |FRAME: DIAMINONONANOATE| |FRAME: EC-6.3.3.3 "EC 6.3.3.3"|. This activity, which is responsible for the first ring closure, is a unique carboxylation reaction that does not require biotin as a prosthetic group |CITS: [4921568]|., The ultimate step in the pathway is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.1.6|. This enzyme inserts a sulfur atom between C6 and C9 of dethiobiotin in a |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent reaction. A |FRAME: CPD-6| of the enzyme is the source of the sulfur atom. Consistent with its proposed role as the sulfur donor, degradation of the [2Fe-2S] cluster |CITS: [14967042]| as well as exchange of sulfur atoms between the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] clusters |CITS: [16533066]| is observed during turnover of the enzyme |CITS: [8680961][9428635][11706201][12714594]|.

General Background, C-glycosides are widespread in the plant kingdom and have been shown to occur in at least 20 families of angiosperms |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. Moreover, they have also been found in insects and microbes |CITS:[17404902]| and are attributed to a broad range of biological activities. They act as antioxidants |CITS:[Ramarathnam89][1824129]|, show antimicrobial activity |CITS:[16651765]|, facilitate mycorrhizal symbioses |CITS:[12026171]|, screen and protect from UV |CITS:[Les90]| and are valuable agents in preventing lipoprotein oxidation |CITS:[Kim2005]| and cancer development |CITS:[11172671]| in humans. , C-glycosideflavonoids represent the largest group of C-glycosides and are especially dominant in cereals such as maize, wheat and rice |CITS:[17404902]| |CITS:[Harborne93a]|. The special attachment of the aglycone directly to the C1 of the pyranose ring of a sugar confers high structural stability to the C-glycosides which even withstand acidic treatment., |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN Isoorientin| is a C-glycoside flavone identified in a number of plants that possesses strong antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and anti-obesity properties. The compound was first reported (under the name homoorientin) from |FRAME: TAX-448966| (rooibos tea) in 1962 |CITS: [14457727]|., |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN Isoorientin| was reported to be one of the major phenolic compounds present in silk extracts of corn inbreds tested for resistance to |FRAME: TAX-5518| |CITS: [Reid92]|, and was also shown to be active against larvae of the corn earworm (|FRAME: TAX-7113|), an important pest of corn |CITS: [Elliger80]|., More recently the compound has been generating interest due to its multiple pharmacological activities. Plants rich in isoorientin have demonstrated strong ameliorative properties against complications such as hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance |CITS: [15666535][18254247][22948221][26961674][ 27261613]|. A detailed review on the compound's pharmacological effects has been published in 2020 |CITS: [32407953]|., The compound was first designated as 6-C-galactosyl-luteolin |CITS: [Snook94]| but was later reported to be 6-C-glucosyl-luteolin, common name isoorientin |CITS: [Widstrom98]|., About This Pathway, The first C-glucosyltransferases (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.360|) to be identified were those involved in the biosynthesis of C-glycosylflavone in rice (|FRAME: TAX-4530|) |CITS: [19411659]|. Those enzymes act on the open-chain form of 2-hydroxyflavanone produced by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.162|, followed by enzymatic dehydration (see |FRAME: PWY-7188|) |CITS: [20647377][21443631]|. Thus, in cereals, C-glycosylflavones are generated by C-glycosylation before the flavone skeleton is complete. The same pathway was also described from buckwheat (|FRAME: TAX-3617|) |CITS: [25142187]|., However, earlier data about the formation of |FRAME: ISOORIENTIN| in corn (|FRAME: TAX-4577|) has suggested a different pathway, in which the compound os formed directly from |FRAME: 5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE| |CITS: [15220389]|., An enzyme that catalyzes the direct C-hglucosylation of |FRAME: 5734-TETRAHYDROXYFLAVONE|, as well as |FRAME: CPD-431|, was identified in 2015 from Japanese gentian (|FRAME: TAX-55190|) |CITS: [25479084]|. The enzyme provides a second pathway for production of C6-glucosulated flavones, which mediates direct C-glucosylation of the flavone skeleton.

Summary: General Background, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) can occur via two distinct routes: the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"| (MVA pathway, such as this pathway) and the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (MEP pathway). In the former, IPP is synthesized from the condensation of three acetyl-CoA molecules; in contrast, in the MEP pathway IPP is synthesized via the condensation of pyruvate and D-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate., For many years, the MVA pathway was considered to be the sole source of IPP in all living organisms, until several inconsistencies led to the discovery of the MEP pathway in bacteria and plants. The MEP pathway is present in most eubacteria, in unicellular green algae, in the chloroplasts of phototrophic organisms and in some unicellular eukaryotes related to photosynthetic phyla, such as the Plasmodium parasites. , The mevalonate pathway is found in animals, fungi, the cytoplasm of phototrophic organisms, archaea, and some, eubacteria. A considerable variability exists among archaea, and at least four different variants of the MVA pathway have been described from that kingdom. The |FRAME: PWY-922 "eukaryotic variant"| is rare in archaea, but occurs in members of the order |FRAME: TAX-2281|, such as |FRAME: TAX-2287| |CITS: [23378249]|. While most archaea posses a variant now known as the |FRAME: PWY-8125 "archaeal pathway"| |CITS: [30224495]|, a |FRAME: PWY-6174 "third variant"| has been described from halophilic archaea such as |FRAME: TAX-2246| |CITS: [24375100]| (that pathway was also found in the eubacterium |FRAME: TAX-120962| |CITS: [24327557]|), and a |FRAME: PWY-7524 "fourth variant"| has been described from archaea of the order |FRAME: TAX-2301| |CITS: [24755225][25636853]|., About This Pathway, Early work with the methanogen |FRAME: TAX-2190| suggested that the archaeal mevalonate pathway is somewhat different from the eukaryotic/bacterial pathway. Initially it was not realized that multiple variants of the pathway exist among different archaeal taxonomic clades, leading to some confusion regarding the nature of the pathway in different archaeons., The key enzyme of this pathway is |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.99|, which is only present in the halophilic variant of the archaeal mevalonate pathway. The |FRAME: G-27169| that encodes it was discovered in the |FRAME: TAX-2246| genome based on low-homology (~30% amino acid identity) with |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.33| from |FRAME: TAX-1282| |CITS: [24375100]|. Most archaea utilize two enzymes to achive this transformation, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8125|., Curiously, this key enzyme is also present in members of the eubacterial |FRAME: TAX-200795 Chloroflexi| phylum. Those organisms possess the enzymes of both this halophilic variant of the archaeal pathway and the eukaryotic/eubacterial pathway, resulting in a bifurcated mevalonate pathway |CITS: [24327557][31268677]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Peptidoglycans Peptidoglycan|, the bacterial bag-shaped envelope, is best described as a fisherman net. The net is made of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads consisting of alternating |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (GlcNAc) and |FRAME: CPD-19950| (MurNAc) sugars, which are held together by small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., Gram-negative bacteria recycle a very large proportion of the peptidoglycan polymer during normal growth in a process termed cell wall recycling. For example, the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| recycles about half of its cell wall within one generation |CITS: [18535144][23163477]|., During this process anhydromuropeptides (mainly |FRAME: CPD0-1080|), which are steadily released during growth by lytic transglycosylases and endopeptidases, are imported back into the cytoplasm by the |FRAME: EG12183|-encoded |FRAME: AMPG-MONOMER|., Once inside the cytoplasm, the anhydromuropeptides are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.28| (|FRAME: EG10041|), |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.52| (|FRAME: G6567|) and |FRAME: EC-3.4.17.13| (|FRAME: G6621|), yielding |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, |FRAME: CPD0-882|, |FRAME: L-ALA-GAMMA-D-GLU-DAP| and |FRAME: D-ALANINE| |CITS: [ 3891732]|., |FRAME: CPD0-882| is phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.170| (|FRAME: G6880|) and then converted into |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.126| (|FRAME: G7263|). This is a branch point, as this compound could be directed either for further degradation (see pathways of |FRAME: N-Acetylglucosamine-Degradation|) or for recycling into new peptidoglycan monomers, as described in this pathway |CITS: [15901686][15983044]|., The final product of this pathway, |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYLMURAMATE|, is one of the precursors for peptidoglycan biosynthesis., The tripeptide |FRAME: L-ALA-GAMMA-D-GLU-DAP|, which is generated by |FRAME: EC-3.4.17.13|, can be degraded further, as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1546|. However, the vast majority is recycled by muropeptide ligase (|FRAME: EG12440|). This enzyme is a dedicated recycling enzyme that attaches the recovered Ala-Glu-DAP tripeptide to |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYLMURAMATE|, thereby substituting three amino acid ligases of the peptidoglycan de novo biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [8808921]|., Although exogenously provided |FRAME: CPD0-882| can be taken up by |FRAME:TAX-562|, it can not serve as the sole source of carbon for growth, suggesting that it may be toxic to the cell |CITS: [16452451]|.

Summary: General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (such as bettles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway:, Oleoresin turpentine is composed of a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes. Many monoterpene synthases can produce a single product but often will produce a variety of monoterpenes of which a few are produced preferentially |CITS:[12176064],[16684230],[15310829],[10562434]| (for additional information concerning monoterpenes, see |FRAME:PWY-3041|). Conifer monoterpenes produce mainly acyclic and cyclic olefins as product, which is consistent with the measured constituents of turpentine, in which oxygenated monoterpenes only represent trace components. The volatile monoterpene constituents of conifer oleoresin is involved in a variety of roles in bark boring bettle (the most destructive agent of conferous forests worldwide |CITS:[berryman72]|) chemical ecology: host recognition and selection; pheromone signaling and tritrophic level interactions (interactions between the tree, beetle and parasitoids; for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). Resin monoterpenes are toxic to the bark beetles; however, they provide the insect with olfactory cues that it uses to locate its target host. Many bark beetles use monoterpene volatiles to synthesize aggregation pheromones (produced by pioneer-beetle to attract other insects to initiate aggregation and colonization). The pheromones |FRAME:CPD-8832|, |FRAME:CPD-8833|, |FRAME:CPD-8834| and |FRAME:CPD-8835| are derived from |FRAME:CPD-8754|, |FRAME:CPD-4892| and |FRAME:CPD-4888| |CITS:[11337413]|. The function of these hormones as aggregation or aggregation inhibition pheromones is dependent on the species and potentially their geographical location. Several enzymes have been identified from different coniferous species which can produce monoterpenes in a variety of mixtures in vitro., Compared to monoterpenes, fewer sesquiterpene synthases from conifers have been identified and studied to date. Generally, the longer chain of |FRAME:FARNESYL-PP| compared to that of |FRAME:GERANYL-PP|, and the additional double bond, allows for a greater diversity of products being formed by those enzymes. Two coniferous enzymes |FRAME:ENZRXN-13510| and |FRAME:ENZRXN-13583| from Grand Fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) produces each in excess of 30 different sesquiterpenes olefins. In contrast, |FRAME:MONOMER-12817| catalyzes only the synthesis of |FRAME:CPD-8738| |CITS:[9618485]|. Importantly, this compound has been shown to be converted by methyl-jasmonate-induced suspension cell cultures of Grand Fir into |FRAME:CPD-8836|, a sesquiterpene derivative structurally similar to the insect |FRAME:CPD-8838| |CITS:[9618485]|, and can disrupt insect reproduction and/or larval development |CITS:[11337413]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. It is closely related to |FRAME: TAX-562|, and while was given its own genus in the 40s, sequence-based phylogeny suggests that the genus may have to be re-incorporated into |FRAME: TAX-562|., The Shigella serotypes were named B/D/F/S for variations found in the four species |FRAME: TAX-621|, |FRAME: TAX-622|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, and |FRAME: TAX-624|, respectively |CITS: [18422615]|., The structure of the O antigen repeat unit of |FRAME: ORG-57079| was first reported in 1975 |CITS: [165891]| and revised in 2005 |CITS: [15774901]|. The O antigen biosynthetic gene cluster was sequenced and reported in 2002 |CITS: [11598067]|. The cluster contains genes involved in |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| biosynthesis, four glycosyltransferase, an O antigen repeat unit flippase, and an O antigen polymerase |CITS: [11598067]|., Similar repeat units are produced by |FRAME: ORG-57080| and |FRAME: ORG-57082|, which contain an additional ribofuranose residue |CITS: [15774901][27710814]|, and by |FRAME: ORG-57081|, which contains an additional galactosyl residue |CITS: [26232763]|.

|FRAME: HYDROXYNAPHTHOQUINONE Juglone|, first isolated from the walnut tree over 150 years ago |CITS: [Vogel56]|, is a brown naphtoquinone pigment found in black walnut, pecan and other plants in the |FRAME: TAX-16714| family., Juglone is toxic, and when released from the roots of black walnut trees causes growth retardation or even death of susceptible plants |CITS: [25240266]|. In studies testing the relative toxicity of some low molecular weight quinones to a broad range of organisms juglone was consistently among the two most toxic compounds (together with |FRAME: CPD-4461|) |CITS: [17270232]|. Despite its toxicity, juglone has been used in hair and wool dyes., |FRAME: HYDROXYNAPHTHOQUINONE Juglone| also possesses antiviral, antibacterial and antifungal properties |CITS: [16271620][18565285][23163769]|, as well as anticancer activity |CITS:[19555768][22266044][23181283]|., A bacterium able to metabolize |FRAME: HYDROXYNAPHTHOQUINONE|, |FRAME: ORG-6333|, was isolated from garden soil under the leafy canopy of a walnut tree. Two intermediates, |FRAME: CPD-275| and |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, were isolated from its cultures. The latter was shown to undergo meta-cleavge, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7480| |CITS: [Rettenmaier83]|., An investigation of the enzymes involved in juglone degradation identified two enzymes with juglone 3-hydroxylase activity and an NADH-dependent enzyme that reduces the hydroxylated product to |FRAME: CPD-19246| |CITS: [4041238]|.

Summary: The degradative pathway of toluene in |FRAME:TAX-303| consists of two parts: an upper pathway that converts toluene and xylene to their carboxylic acid derivatives, and a lower pathway that converts the the (substituted) benzoic acids to Krebs cycle intermediates. In the upper pathway, the methyl side chain of toluene is subjected to several progressive oxidations to carboxylic acid, followed by an oxygenative cleavage of the aromatic ring. The upper pathway is induced by toluene, xylenes, and their alcohol derivatives. The lower pathway is induced by benzoic acids, or by upper pathway substrates., In |FRAME:TAX-303|, the TOL plasmid pWW0 encodes all the enzymes responsible for the degradation of toluene and xylene. The genes encoding these enzymes are organized into two operons: the upper operon, which contains the three enzymes involved in the upper pathway, and the meta operon, which contains the genes responsible, for the degradation of benzoates and toluates via the lower pathway., Some strains have integrated very similar genes in their chromosomes, where they have aquired little mutation. For example, strains TW3 and 4NT have been shown to express similar but chromosomally-encoded enzymes which catalyze the same pathway as that encoded by the TOL plasmid |CITS: [8357257][8245826][9555884]|.

Furan-containing fatty acids are generated in large amounts in algae, but they are also produced by plants and microorganisms. Fish and other marine organisms as well as mammals consume these acids in their food and incorporate them into phospholipids and cholesterol esters. They are catabolized to dibasic urofuran acids, which are excreted in the urine., Furan-containing fatty acids react readily with peroxyl radicals to generate dioxoenes. Their radical-scavenging ability may contribute to the protective properties of fish and fish oil diets against mortality from heart disease |CITS: [Okada90][8996648][16296395]|., The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1063| contains the 19 carbon furan-containing fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-18205| in its phospholipids. This unusual fatty acid is derived from |FRAME: CPD-9247| via the methyl-branched fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-18204| |CITS: [25092314]|., |FRAME: CPD-18205| was discovered in phospholipids isolated from a |FRAME: TAX-1063| mutant lacking an antisigma factor, ChrR, that has increased transcription of genes that are normally activated in the presence of the reactive oxygen species singlet oxygen (1O2), a byproduct of photosynthesis. This observation supports the suggestion that furan-containing fatty acids serve a role in detoxifying reactive oxygen species., The pathway intermediate |FRAME: CPD-18204| is produced from |FRAME: CPD-9247| by the action of a single enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44114| gene, which has a significant amino acid similarity to bacterial cyclopropane fatty acid synthase. This S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylase converts the 18 carbon cis unsaturated fatty acyl chain to a 19 carbon methylated trans unsaturated fatty acyl chain., The |FRAME: G-44115| gene, implicated in catalyzing the second step, is located in an operon that is controlled by ChrR. Inactivation of the gene abolished production of |FRAME: CPD-18205|, but did not affect |FRAME: CPD-18204| production, suggesting that the gene product is involved in the conversion of the latter to the former. It is still not known if other enzymes are involved in this transformation |CITS: [25092314]|.

Acute inflammation is a beneficial response to injury and infection that involves neutrophils, eosinophils, and M1-polarized macrophages, which produce bioactive molecules such as leukotrienes and prostaglandins. If successful, this response leads to clearance of invading organisms, tissue repair, and regeneration. The pro-inflammatory response eventually transitions to the pro-resolution phase of inflammation, during which M2-polarized macrophages produce potent molecules collectively known as |FRAME: SPMs "specialized pro-resolving mediators"| (SPMs). The SPMs include |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|-derived |FRAME: Lipoxins lipoxins|, |FRAME: Resolvins resolvins|, which are derived from either |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (EPA) or |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA), and the DHA-derived |FRAME: protectins protectins| and |FRAME: Maresins maresins|., Protectins are a class of SPMs made from |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA). |FRAME: CPD-24703 "Protectin D1"| was the first identified member of this class. It was originally named "neuroprotectin D1", based on its neuroprotective bioactivity in brain ischemia reperfusion (BIR) and oxidatively stressed retina pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, as well as its ability to protect cells from oxidative stress-induced apoptosis. It was also shown to upregulate the stimulation of the anti-apoptotic protein, Bcl-2, and decrease the level of pro-apoptotic protein, Bax, in ARPE-19 cells during oxidative stress |CITS: [15912889][19018037]|. Another member of this family, |FRAME: CPD-24692| (an isomer of |FRAME: CPD-24703|), was found to inhibit inflammation associated with cyclooxygenase (COX) activities, reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation, and influenza virus replication |CITS: [19818771][32956736]|.  There are also protectin sulfido-conjugates, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8355|., The pathway starts with the action of a lipoxygenase on |FRAME: CPD-10244| (DHA) to form |FRAME: CPD66-80|. Careful studies have shown that while all three lipoxygenases (|FRAME: EC-1.13.11.34|, |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.31| and |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.33|) can catalyze this reaction, |FRAME: HS03167-MONOMER| is the most efficient of the three |CITS: [34029049]|., Both |FRAME: HS03167-MONOMER| and |FRAME: HS08621-MONOMER| can act on |FRAME: CPD66-80|, forming  four products: |FRAME: CPD-25482|, |FRAME: CPD-25503|, 11,17S-diHDHA, and 16,17S-diHDHA. However, the reticulocyte isozyme of |FRAME: HS08621-MONOMER| was far more active. The epithelial 15-lipoxygenase-2 [h15-LOX-2] isozyme did not react with |FRAME: CPD66-80| at all |CITS: [34029049]|., Formation of |FRAME: CPD-24703| requires a hydrolase, which has not been identified as of 2022. |FRAME: CPD-24692 "Protectin DX"| is formed via reduction by |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.12| |CITS: [34029049]|.

In humans, |FRAME: PHE| is an indispensable amino acid, which may either be used for protein synthesis or be converted to the nonessential amino acid |FRAME: TYR|, the precursor for catecholamine and thyroid hormone synthesis. |FRAME: TYR| is not considered indispensable, despite being an essential component of body proteins, because it can be synthesized from |FRAME: PHE| |CITS:[4265522][1093910]|., |FRAME: EC-1.14.16.1|, is responsible for the irreversible oxidation of the essential amino acid |FRAME: PHE| to |FRAME: TYR| in animals. The enzyme is found mostly in the liver |CITS: [4004813]| and in the kidney |CITS: [10655515]|, and its subcellular location is the cytoplasm. The enzyme, whose active form is tetrameric, requires the binding of L-phenylalanine to the regulatory domain in order to promote phosphorylation of Ser16, followed by a conformational change, which allows the formation of active tetramers from inactive precursor dimers. Once the active tetrameric form of the enzyme has been produced, |FRAME: PHE| and the cofactor |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN| can bind to the active site domain initiating catalysis., In addition, |FRAME: CPLX-7067| is tightly coupled to |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.96|, the key enzyme that is responsible for the recycling of the cofactor |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN|. It has been shown that |FRAME: CPLX-7068| increases the rate of |FRAME: CPLX-7067| 7-fold, and converts the product |FRAME: CPD-5881| to |FRAME: 78-dihydrobiopterins| by dehydration,, which is further reduced to |FRAME: TETRA-H-BIOPTERIN| in the presence of NADH by |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.34|.

A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The O antigen of group D3 |FRAME: TAX-590| strains is produced by a Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway. The basic repeat unit of O antigens from D group strains contains a |FRAME: CPD-9395| dideoxysugar |CITS: [14479760][14324537][ 4380946][5327479][5326096]|. The O antigen of group D3 |FRAME: TAX-590| strains corresponds to serogroups O9, O27, and O46. The ancestral D form is believed to be group D3. The use of Gal as initial sugar appeared in |FRAME: TAX-590| after its divergence from |FRAME: TAX-561|, but the eight Gal-initiated O antigens have grown to be very important in this species |CITS: [23874940]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O-antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes. The D3 gene cluster has an ortholog of the wbaU gene of group D1, which accounts for the α(1→4) Man-Rha linkage, but no additional gene encoding a β(1-4) form. Screening the genome for an ortholog of the wbaO gene, which encodes such an enzyme in group D2 and E1 strains, did not identify a candidate |CITS: [9473060]|., Following the completion of the synthesis of a repeat unit, the flippase Wzx flips the full molecule to the other side of the membrane, where the Wzy polymerase transfers additional repeat units from their anchor to a single elongating molecule. The Wzz protein ensures termination of the polimerization once the correct chain length has been achieved., |FRAME: TAX-590| strains belonging to Group D3 contain a |FRAME: G-80956| polymerase that links the repeat units by an α(1,6) linkage between the galactose and the mannose residues [α-D-Gal-(1→6)-α/β-D-Man]. The enzyme has no sequence similarity to the |FRAME: G-80955| polymerase which is found in groups D2 and E, even though it confers the same linkage |CITS: [9473060]|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell., Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions., Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these, compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or, NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of , NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while, the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation,, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and, transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases, |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo , pathway, and the salvage pathway., In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from aspartate, (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with tryptophan, (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, This pathway is an NAD salvage pathway which proceeds via the intermediate |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_RIBOSE| (nicotinamide riboside, (N-ribosylnicotinamide, or NR). While the presence of this pathway has been suggested for several organisms, including |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-272131|, |FRAME:TAX-1358|, |FRAME:TAX-727|, |FRAME: TAX-730|, |FRAME: TAX-714|, and |FRAME:TAX-747| |CITS: [12446641]|, it is of particular importance to |FRAME:TAX-727| and other V-factor-dependent members of the |FRAME:TAX-745| family. These organisms lack the enzymes necessary for the de novo synthesis of NAD, as well as most of the enzymes for the more common NAD salvage pathway, and therefore require exogenous NAD supply in the form of one of the V-factor compounds, which include, NADP, NAD, NMN, and NR. However, only the non-phosphorylated V factor, NR, can be transported across the inner, membrane into the cytoplasm, where it can be converted to NAD and NADP |CITS: [12446641]|. Thus this pathway, is critical for these organisms |CITS: [1694467]|. For additional information about V-factor-dependent bacteria, look at the pathway |FRAME: NAD-BIOSYNTHESIS-III|., Since NAD+, which is obtained from extracellular sources, is highly polar, it has to be hydrolyzed before it can be transported across the cytoplasmic membrane for final uptake. A key enzyme in this pathway is the periplasmic NadN protein, encoded by the nadN gene (ushA in |FRAME:TAX-562|). It has been shown that NadN has two activities: firstly, it hydrolyzes NAD+ to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), and secondly, it hydrolyzes NMN to nicotinamide riboside (NR) |CITS: [11395461]|. After NAD+ is transported into the periplasmic space it is hydrolyzed into NMN and AMP by the NAD-nucleotidase activity of NadN. NMN is then hydrolyzed to NR and pyrophosphate, and the nicotinamide riboside thus formed is transported across the inner membrane into the cytoplasm, where it is it is converted back to NMN, and eventually, to NAD+., The identity of the NR transporter has not been confirmed experimentally, but it is suggested that it is encoded by the pnuC gene, although earlier work with the PnuC protein of |FRAME:TAX-28901| serovar Typhimurium suggested that it encodes the transport of NMN |CITS: [6216244][11395461]|., NADP+ is recycled in the same manner, following dephosphorylation to NAD+. In |FRAME: TAX-727|, this dephosphorylation is performed by the outer membrane glycoprotein e (P4), encoded by the hel gene., While the pathway is predicted to be present in |FRAME:TAX-543|, it probably serves a minor role compared to de novo biosynthesis and the main NAD salvage cycle (|FRAME: PYRIDNUCSAL-PWY|). Some of the enzymatic activities associated with this pathway have been described in |FRAME:TAX-543| as early as 1951 |CITS: [14907738]|, but it was only recently that the genes responsible for them were identified. Surprisingly, several activities were found to be functions of the multifunctional protein NadR, which was initially believed to have a role in regulation only |CITS: [10464228][12446641]|.

PHAs are a microbially produced class of polyesters that can serve as renewable plastics, see |FRAME: PWY1-3|. However, microbial production of PHAs is a costly affair, and engineering microbes to produce hydroxyalkanoates is significantly cheaper. Furthermore, hydroxyalkanoates are small molecules which can be secreted into the extracellular millieu as opposed to PHAs which accumulate intracellularly as insoluble granules |CITS: [23333586]|. , While |FRAME: CPD-335| monomer units can be synthesized by depolymerization of microbially synthesized poly-(R)-3-hydroxybutyric acid (PHB), due to stereospecific constraints the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-1843| from PHB is not possible |CITS: [19304817]|. Summary: General Background, Bile (or gall) is a dark green to yellowish brown fluid, produced by the liver of most vertebrates, that aids the digestion of lipids in the small intestine. In humans bile is produced continuously by the liver and stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. After eating, the bile is discharged into the the first section of the small intestine (the duodenum)., The main active ingredient (about 0.7%) of the bile is bile acids., Bile acids are classified into primary and secondary. The primary bile acids |FRAME: CHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-15189| are synthesized from |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| by a series of oxidative transformations in the liver. They are further modified by attachemnt of a glycine or taurine molecule, forming |FRAME: GLYCOCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: GLYCOCHENODEOXYCHOLIC_ACID|, |FRAME: CPD-3743|, and |FRAME: CPD-7283| (see |FRAME: PWY-6061|)., The bacterially-produced secondary bile acids affect host physiology in multiple ways. Some of them are ligands for the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), the liver X receptor (LXR), the G proteincoupled receptor TGR5, and the vitamin D receptor, and have been shown to trigger signaling cascades |CITS: [12016314][17823458][18670431]|. |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE Deoxycholate| production has been shown to have a positive affect by limiting the outgrowth of the enteric pathogen |FRAME: TAX-1496| |CITS: [25337874]|, while on the other hand |FRAME: DEOXYCHOLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7235| have been implicated as causative agents in colon carcinogenesis |CITS: [4427390][1255778]|., |FRAME: CPD-10534 Ursodeoxycholate| (UDCA) is a bile acid that makes up a small percentage (< 5%) of the biliary pool in most healthy mammals. In most mammals it is a secondary bile acid, produced from primary bile acids by the action of intestinal bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-7588|). It is an important ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine, and has verified therapeutic benefits for the treatment of several ailments including cholestatic liver disease |CITS: [74722][7372061][7051912][16530513][17185355]| and colon cancer |CITS: [7923119][12839936][14747693]|., About This Pathway, The principal actions of gut bacteria on bile acids are C24 amide hydrolysis and 7-dehydroxylation. , C24 amide hydrolysis is catalyzed by bile acid hydrolases that remove the glycine and taurine conjugants. Bile acid hydrolases are members of the choloylglycine hydrolase family. They are widespread among both Gram-negative and Gram-positive intestinal bacteria and have a wide range of substrate specificities |CITS: [1429446]|. A hydrolase that acts on |FRAME: CPD-18799| has been described from |FRAME: TAX-821| |CITS: [2628421]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8135|)., The 7-dehydroxylation process is less common, and is found in some species of anaerobic intestinal bacteria. The process is rather complex and consists of an oxidative part, a dehydration, and a reductive part. The enzymes involved are encoded by the bile acid-inducible (bai) operons., Gene products involved in the pathway may vary depending upon the bile acid substrate. The products of the |FRAME: G-44404| and |FRAME: G-44405| genes are specific for the degradation of the 7β-hydroxy bile acid |FRAME: CPD-10534| (reviewed in |CITS: [16299351]|). The degradation of the more common 7α-hydroxy bile acids is described in |FRAME: PWY-7754|., In |FRAME: TAX-29347| the oxidative part of the pathway begins with active transport of a bile acid across the bacterial membrane, which is mediated by the product of the baiG gene, a H+-dependent primary bile acid transporter |CITS: [8955384]|. The bile acid is activated by ligation to |FRAME: CO-A| in an |FRAME: ATP|-dependent manner by the product of |FRAME: G-139| |CITS: [1551828]|. The 3α-hydroxy group of the bile acid-CoA thioester is oxidized by either of the products of the three genes |FRAME: G-140|, |FRAME: G-141| and |FRAME: G-142|, which can utilize |FRAME: NAD| or |FRAME: NADP| and are specific for bile acid-CoA conjugates. A double bond is inserted between C-4 and C-5 by the product of |FRAME: G-44404|, one of the 7β-specific enzymes |CITS: [7766153][23836456]|., There is some uncertainty regarding at which stage the intermediates remain as CoA-esters. Earlier models suggested that CoA-esters serve as substrates for most of the downstream enzymes. However, based on substrate preference of the enzymes in the later part of the pathway, it is currently believed that |FRAME: G-18017 BaiF|, a CoA-transferase, acts after |FRAME: G-12042 BaiCD|, and that the intermediates for the rest of the pathway are free bile acids rather than CoA-esters |CITS: [16299351][31092280]|., The next reaction is the rate-limiting and irreversible dehydration of the 7β-hydroxyl group, which is catalyzed by the second 7β-specific enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.M3| (|FRAME: G-44405 BaiI)|, resulting in the introduction of a second double bond at C-6 |CITS: [8808760][26650892]|. The pathway continues by a series of three reductions, the first two of which catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.114| (|FRAME: G-58251 BaiN)| |CITS: [29217478]|, and the last one likely by the |FRAME: MONOMER-21157| |FRAME: G-80673 BaiO| |CITS: [31092280]|.

Summary: General Background, This pathway depicts the degradation of purine nucleotides to purine nucleosides, purine bases, and |FRAME: URATE|. Further degradation is shown in the pathway llink. Purine degradation plays an important role in nitrogen metabolism in most organisms. The pathway in vertebrates is discussed below. Fungi, bacteria and archaea can utilize some of the intermediates in this pathway and the linked pathway as sole sources of nitrogen, or nitrogen and carbon (|CITS: [19060149][11344136][8376322]| and reviewed in |CITS: [786256]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| exogenous purine nucleosides and purine bases are converted to nucleotides via salvage pathways. Although all of the enzymes of the pathway shown here are present in this organism, aerobic purine degradation is incomplete and does not progress past |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| or |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| formation, and this catabolism does not suffice as a source of nitrogen under aerobic growth conditions |CITS: [10986234]|. However, |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN| can be degraded anaerobically |CITS: [10601204]|. See pathways |FRAME: PWY0-1296|, |FRAME: PWY-7179| and |FRAME: PWY0-41|., The pathways of biosynthesis and degradation of mammalian purine and pyrimidine bases, nucleosides and nucleotides were elucidated in the 1950s and 1960s. Much work in the 1970s and 1980s focused on inborn errors of purine metabolism, although the regulation of purine nucleotide synthesis and the metabolism of purine bases and nucleosides were also studied. More recent work on purine and pyrimidine metabolism using genomics, proteiomics and metabolomics is likely to impact several areas of clinical research including studies of a possible role for high levels of soluble urate in cardiovascular diseases; the development of purine and pyrimidine analogs for the chemotherapy of cancer and autoimmune diseases as well for antiviral and antiparasitic drugs; and the development of urate-lowering drugs for the treatment of gout. Reviewed in |CITS: [18600501]| and |CITS: [16176880]|., About This Pathway, In mammals both purine ribonucleotide and purine deoxyribonucleotide monophosphates are degraded similarly using a final common pathway. The degradation reactions of purine ribonucleotide monophosphates are shown here as in |CITS: [6262603] [17520339] [1576959]| and |CITS: [11150394]|. Purine degradation in higher plants is very similar. However, plants contain an enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-11783| (EC 3.5.4.15) that is not present in vertebrates |CITS: [14725335]|. The plant pathway is shown in |FRAME: PWY-5044|., Related pathways of eukaryotic purine de novo biosynthesis and purine salvage (reutilization) are shown in pathways |FRAME: PWY-841|, |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY| and |FRAME: SALVPURINE2-PWY|. Rodent studues have demonstrated the catabolism of dietary purines by epithelial cells lining the gastrointestinal tract. These cells coexpress key purine catabolic enzymes |CITS: [1918135]| ., The first step in degradation involves hydrolysis of purine ribonucleotides to ribonucleosides by 5'-nucleotidase (EC 3.1.3.5). As stated in |CITS: [6262603]| this step can also be catalyzed by non-specific phosphatases such as EC 3.1.3.2 (not shown). |FRAME: AMP| is deaminated to |FRAME: IMP| (EC 3.5.4.6). Ribonucleosides are converted to purine bases and |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P| by phosphorolysis catalyzed by purine nucleoside phosphorylase (EC 2.4.2.1). |FRAME: ADENOSINE| is deaminated to |FRAME: INOSINE| (EC 3.5.4.4), and |FRAME: GUANINE| is deaminated to |FRAME: XANTHINE| (EC 3.5.4.3). |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE| is converted to |FRAME: XANTHINE|, which is then converted to |FRAME: URATE| by the same enzyme, xanthine oxidoreductase (xanthine dehydrogenase EC 1.17.1.4, xanthine oxidase EC 1.17.3.2). This is the rate-limiting enzyme in the pathway. Reviewed in |CITS: [6262603] [18513323]| and |CITS: [19436671]|)., Also shown in this pathway is the degradation of |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: GMP| from |FRAME: IMP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-841|). |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| degradation is included in some pathway diagrams |CITS: [1576959] [VOET04]|. |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| has been shown to be a substrate for 5'-nucleotidase EC 3.1.3.5 (reviewed in |CITS: [15963349]|). |FRAME: XANTHOSINE|, in addition to |FRAME: GUANOSINE| and |FRAME: INOSINE|, is also a substrate for phosphorolysis by purine nucleoside phosphorylase EC 2.4.2.1 |CITS: [12180982]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15218545]|. Unlike the prokaryotic |FRAME: DEOD-CPLX|, |FRAME: ADENOSINE| is not a natural substrate for mammalian |FRAME: CPLX-6181| (in |CITS: [12180982]|)., The end product of purine catabolism depends upon the taxon of the organism in question. |FRAME: URATE| is the end product in humans, hominoid primates (i.e. chimpanzees, gorillas), new world monkeys, birds and reptiles. Higher primates contain a mutational inactivation of the liver enzyme uricase and cannot produce |FRAME: ALLANTOIN|. |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| is produced in non-primate mammals and old world monkeys, which produce uricase (see linked pathway |FRAME: PWY-5691|). Other organisms can also produce and further catabolize |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| (see the pathway link in |FRAME: PWY-5691| and subsequent links). In |CITS: [18649082]| and in |CITS: [15919000]|., In humans, |FRAME: URATE| in blood enters the kidney but most is reabsorbed by a renal |FRAME: URATE| reabsorption system. Only approximately 10% is excreted. Kidney |FRAME: URATE| transporting systems are still under investigation. Both |FRAME: URATE| and |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| are found in the urine of species that produce them (reviewed in |CITS: [15919000]|)., Abnormalities of the human pathway occur as a result of enzyme deficiencies, enzyme overactivities, and increased turnover of nucleic acids due to certain disorders. Conditions resulting in increased degradation of |FRAME: ATP|, or decreased synthesis of |FRAME: ATP|, also affect purine nucleotide degradation. After purine nucleotide dephosphorylation, the salvage (reutilization) reactions may be a major regulatory mechanism (reviewed in |CITS: [6262603]|) (see pathways |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY| and |FRAME: SALVPURINE2-PWY|). The enzymes of the pathway occur in a variety of mammalian tissues. In mice the highest levels of purine catabolic enzymes have been found in the proximal small intestine |CITS: [8226898]|.

General Background, The patellamides are a class of ribosomal peptide natural products (RiPPs) characterized from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1216|, a symbiont of the tunicate |FRAME: TAX-13110|. They are further classified as |FRAME: Cyanobactins cyanobactins|, which are RiPPs produced by cyanobacteria. |FRAME: CPD-22770 "Patellamide A"| and |FRAME: CPD-22772| have antimicrobial and cytotoxic properties |CITS: [2724305]|., |FRAME: CPD-22770 "Patellamide A"| and |FRAME: CPD-22772| comprise eight-residue macrocycles produced from the same substrate peptide, which is encoded by the patE gene. The two patellamides are produced from a different regions of the peptide. Despite their different amino acid composition, both compounds contain two thiazoles and two oxazolines, as well as two D-amino acids |CITS: [15988766][15883371][25460274]|., While the patellamide biosynthesis pathway is the best studied among the cyanobactins, all cyanobactins are produced by a similar mechanism., About This Pathway, In 2005 |FRAME: TAX-1216| cells were purified from whole |FRAME: TAX-13110|, and the genome was sequenced and assembled. Searching the genome sequence for all eight possible peptides that could lead to the formation of |FRAME: CPD-22770| identified the patE gene, which was found to also contain the sequence required for synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-22772|. The gene was located in a cluster that included genes encoding other enzymes involved in the patellamide biosynthesis pathway. Expression of the full cluster in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in production of |FRAME: CPD-22770| |CITS: [15883371]|., The PatE peptide contains 71 amino acids, the first 37 of which act as a leader sequence essential for processing. Each of the 8-amino acids core peptides is flanked by an N-terminal five-residue protease signature and a C-terminal macrocyclization signature. The first transformation of the peptide is performed by the |FRAME: G-80601 "PatD heterocyclase"|. That enzyme catalyzes the formation of a bond between the side chain oxygen of certain |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues, as well as the side chain sulfur of certain |FRAME: CYS| residues, and the preceeding amide bond at the expense of ATP, forming oxazoline, methyloxazoline, and thiazoline heterocycles, respectively |CITS: [20210311][22522320][26167873][30912640]|., The modified core peptides are cleaved from the precursor protein by two proteases. One protease, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80603| gene, cleaves the N-terminal leader peptide, releasing the core peptide still bound to the downstream amino acids. The second protease, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80602| gene, cleaves the C-terminal segment, generating an octapeptide. PatG is a multifunctional protein. In addition to the cleavage, it also catalyzes the cyclization of the peptide, as well as the oxidation of the thiazoline rings to thiazole rings |CITS: [19166292][27841750][29779651]|., The last steps in the pathway are the epimerizations of two of the amino acids from L to D. As of 2020, the enzymes involved in these modifications have not been identified.

General Background, |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE| is the universal precursor for the synthesis of the 4'-phosphopantetheine moiety of coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein. Only plants and microorganisms can synthesize pantothenate de novo. In contrast to the bacterial biosynthesis of pantothenate, which have been extensively studied (see |FRAME:PANTO-PWY|), plant pathways for pantothenate formation are still not well understood., Although in most plants and bacteria pantoate:β-alanine ligase catalyzes the formation of pantothenate from pantoate and β-alanine, another route of synthesis has been described in |FRAME: TAX-3562| where pantothenate can be formed using pantolactone in place of pantoate |CITS:[julliard94][raman04]|., Only one of the pathway's enzymes has been purified: |FRAME: MONOMER-9482|. This enzyme was shown to be predominantly located in the chloroplast stroma, suggesting that the formation of pantothenate via pantoyl lactone might be plastidic whereas pantoate-dependent pantothenate biosynthesis might be restricted to the cytosol |CITS:[julliard94]|.

General Background, In gram-positive bacteria, the ε-amino group of L-lysine in the pentapeptide stem of peptidoglycan precursors is often replaced by amino acid chains of various lengths and compositions., During the cross-linking of the peptide stems of nascent chains of peptidoglycan these amino acids form cross bridges, between L-Lys3 of one glycan thread and D-Ala4 of another thread |CITS: [4568761]|., In enterococci, streptococci, and staphylococci, the enzymes that add the bridge amino acids are membrane-associated, and act on late peptidoglycan precursors that are already linked to the undecaprenyl-phosphate lipid carrier |CITS: [5218655]|., Two types of enzymes catalyze the addition of the cross-bridge amino acids. |FRAME: GLY| and L-amino acids are added by a special type of non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) that use charged aminoacyl tRNAs as substrates. D-amino acids, on the other hand, are added in tRNA-independent reactions |CITS: [4248526][4262567]|., About This Pathway, The peptide chains of the model lactic acid bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1358| are cross-linked via a single |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| residue. The bridge is formed by a D,D-transpeptidase between the |FRAME: D-ALANINE| in position 4 of one peptide and the |FRAME: CPD-3633| of the second peptide |CITS: [16816203][4568761]|. |FRAME: CPD-302| is transferred to the peptidoglycan precursors by an |FRAME: MONOMER-15487 "aspartate ligase"| which ligates the β-carboxylate group of |FRAME: CPD-302| to the ε-amino group of |FRAME:LYS| |CITS: [17083466]|. The ligase was partially purified and the amino acid sequence was used to identify the |FRAME: G-11868| gene that encodes it |CITS: [16510449]|. The gene was cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| as a His-tag fusion protein, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity., In the final mature |FRAME: TAX-1358| peptidoglycan about 75% of the side chain and crossbridge |FRAME:CPD-302| residues are amidated into |FRAME: CPD-3633| |CITS: [16816203]|. The amidation of of |FRAME: CPD-302| occurs after its incorporation into the peptidoglycan. The |FRAME: G-11898| gene encoding the amidase has been identified. A mutant of |FRAME: TAX-1360| defective in |FRAME: G-11898| was constructed, and found to lack any |FRAME: CPD-3633| in its peptidoglycan |CITS: [19329637]|., A single |FRAME: CPD-3633| cross-bridge has also been reported for |FRAME: TAX-1352| |CITS: [8611145]|., In certain strains of |FRAME: TAX-1352| a metallo-D,D-carboxypeptidase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11903| gene, cleaves the second |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue from the pentapeptide of the cytoplasmic precursor of peptidoglycan, forming a tetrapeptide and abolishing activity of the D,D-transpeptidase that usually forms the cross bridges. In these strains an L,D-transpeptidase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11907| gene, forms alternative cross bridges between the |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of one peptide and the |FRAME: CPD-3633| of a second peptide (see |FRAME: PWY-6470|).

Summary: Avenacins are triterpene glucosides which act as phytoalexins and allelopathic agents conferring resistance against soil-borne pathogens and influencing the development of close neighbors |CITS:[10536024] [16995908]|. The occurrence of the phytoalexic avenacins appears to be restricted to the genus Avena which is an expression of a highly specialized defense biochemistry |CITS:[Hostettmann95]|. In general, triterpenes are valued compounds with a wide range of commercial applications and because of that in the focus of metabolic engineering. One of the major goals is to re-introduce lost traits of resistance into cultivated crops |CITS:[22639586]|., As a general rule genes in plant biochemical pathways, unlike bacterial biochemical pathways, have been regarded as unlinked. However, the avenacin biosynthesis appears to be carried out by an avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster which implies a high degree of coordination regarding avenacin synthesis, transport and sequestration, all of which must be precisely orchestrated in time and space between different cell organelles and compartments |CITS:[21876149] [15148404] [21443624] [20040536]|., The formation of |FRAME:CPD-12630| (this pathway) as acyl-donor is critical for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-16599| (see |FRAME:PWY-7474|) and the other |FRAME:BENZOATE| acylated avenacin, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16598| |CITS: [Crombie86a]|. It has been demonstrated that the C-21 acylation of the avenacin skeleton is pivotal for the biological activity of this antimicrobial agent |CITS:[20835386]|. , The glucosylation of |FRAME:BENZOATE| is catalyzed by two glucosyltransferases, SAD10 (UGT74H5) and UGT74H6 which are capable to glucosylate both |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME:BENZOATE|. SAD10 appears to be included in the avenacin biosynthetic gene cluster but UGT74H6, although catalyzing the same reaction, albeit with lower efficiency, may have other or additional biochemical functions in Avena |CITS:[23258535]|. Co-expression of three SAD gens, i.e. SAD9 (anthranilate N-methyltransferase), SAD10 (N-methylanthranilate glucosyltransferase) and SAD7 (des-acyl avenacin A acyltransferase) demonstrated that those SAD genes are involved in consecutive steps of the acylation of avenacin and that a loss of any of them resulted in enhanced disease susceptibility of the respective mutant |CITS:[23532069]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8215 Emodin| is a secondary metabolite produced by fungi and plants. It has been documented in at least 17 plant families, 28 genera and 94 species, but is most abundant in three plant families: Fabaceae (Cassia spp.), Polygonaceae (Rheum , Rumex and Polygonum spp.) and Rhamnaceae (Rhamnus and Ventilago spp.) |CITS: [Izhaki02]|., |FRAME: CPD-8215 Emodin| is a plant defense compound and has a deterrent effect on a large spectrum of organisms from invertebrates to vertebrates |CITS: [Trial79]|. , |FRAME: CPD-8215 Emodin| and its derivatives has been widely used from ancient times as laxatives. When ingested by mammals, emodin glycosides, which are the most common form in plants, are carried unabsorbed to the large intestine, where they are metabolized to the active aglycones by intestinal bacterial flora. The aglycone exerts its laxative effect by damaging epithelial cells, which leads directly and indirectly to changes in absorption, secretion and motility. Emodin also inhibits the ion transport (Cl--channels) across colon cells, contributing to the laxative effect |CITS: [10456676]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-8215 Emodin| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of many natural products. Its biosynthesis was sudied in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-33178|, which produces the emodin-derived |FRAME: CPD-14536|. The |FRAME: G-80810| gene, encoding the polyketide synthase |FRAME: CPLX-9519|, was the first gene to be identified, in a study of gene expression associated with |FRAME: CPD-14536| production |CITS: [12536215]|. This was followed by characterization of the |FRAME: G-80809| gene product, which encodes |FRAME: MONOMER-21292| |CITS: [19549600]|. Using available seqence information, a large gene cluster encoding emdin and geodin biosynthesis was subsequently identified in |FRAME: TAX-33178|. The cluster was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-162425|, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-14536| production |CITS: [24009710]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "Glycosaminoglycans"| (also known as mucopolysaccharides) are long unbranched polysaccharides consisting of a repeating disaccharide unit that consists of an N-acetyl-hexosamine, and a hexose or hexuronic acid, either or both of which are often sulfated., Members of the glycosaminoglycan family vary in the type of hexosamine, hexose or hexuronic acid, unit they contain and the degree of its sulfation (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-12521|, |FRAME: CPD-12515|, galactose, |FRAME: CPD-12541|, |FRAME:CPD-12557|, |FRAME: CPD-12527|, |FRAME: CPD-12516| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|). , Glycosaminoglycans are an important component of connective tissues. Important glycosaminoglycans include |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates|, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN| and |FRAME: Hyaluronan|., Many of the glycosaminoglycans are covalently linked to proteins, resulting in |FRAME: Proteoglycans proteoglycans|. Common glycosaminoglycans such as |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate|, |FRAME: HEPARIN|, |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| and |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| are actually synthesized on the protein chain. This pathway describes the initial reactions that are common to the synthesis of these glycosaminoglycans. All of these glycosaminoglycans are attached via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the "glycosaminoglycan-protein linkage region". This tetrasaccharide is formed by sequential stepwise additions of the sugar residues to specific core proteins., The first step in the process is the attachment of a D-xylose group to specific |FRAME:SER| residues in the core protein. The attachment sites have the consensus sequence |FRAME:SER|-|FRAME:GLY|/|FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|-X-|FRAME:GLY|. The enzymes catalyzing this reaction are known as xylotransferases (|FRAME: HS02509| and |FRAME: HS00371|) and utilize |FRAME: UDP-D-XYLOSE| as the sourse of the sugar., The two subsequent additions of galactose units (from |FRAME: CPD-14553|) are catalyzed by |FRAME: HS00459| and |FRAME: HS10991|, respectively, and the final |FRAME: CPD-12521| residue is transferred from |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| by one of the three isoforms of galactosylgalactosylxylosylprotein 3-β-glucuronosyltransferase (|FRAME: HS03272|, |FRAME: HS03557| and |FRAME: HS07624|)., The fifth residue that is added (not described in this pathway) determines the nature of the glycosaminoglycan that would be synthesized from the linkage region. Addition of |FRAME: CPD-12541| results in synthesis of |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| or |FRAME: HEPARIN|, while addition of |FRAME:CPD-12557| results in synthesis of |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| or |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate|., The synthesis of |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycans"| takes place in the Golgi apparatus, and all of the proteins that participate in this pathway are type II membrane proteins, embedded in the Golgi membrane |CITS: [12512855]|.

Aurones are a subclass of flavonoids derived from the |FRAME: PWY-361| pathway. In legumes the chalcone synthase forms 6-deoxy |FRAME: CPD-3041| as a diverging set of secondary metabolites. The molecule |FRAME: CPD-3041| is metabolized to |FRAME:CPD-3061| via chalcone isomerase, a precursor molecule to a range of 5 deoxy |FRAME:CPD-8485|, flavonols and |FRAME: ISOFLAVONE|. However, the route for |FRAME: PWY-1901| deviates from these other products as they are directly synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-3041| |CITS: [19571306]|. Aurones are implicated in flower pigmentation |CITS: [11073455]|, |CITS: [11418122]|, and in defense responses. For humans they are important as anticancer, anti-diabetic and antibacterial agents. , |FRAME: CPD-12037 Hispidol| was isolated from Soya hispida along with |FRAME: ISOFLAVONE| and isoflavone glucosides |CITS: [FARKAS68]|. |FRAME: CPD-12037 Hispidol| and its glucosides are elicited in response to yeast elicitor or methyl jasmonate (MeJa) treatments. Their role in plant defense and as antifungal agents has been demonstrated. |FRAME: CPD-12037 Hispidol| has been hypothesized as being formed as a result of spillover of precursor molecule |FRAME:CPD-3041| from the |FRAME: PWY-361|, thus balancing the upstream and downstream activities of the |FRAME: PWY-361| |CITS: [19571306]|. The peroxidase enzymes are implicated as the catalyzing agents for |FRAME: CPD-12037|. However, the presence and accumulation of these enzymes in the roots where |FRAME: CPD-12037| does not accumulate may indicate that the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12037| may be only one of the functions of these enzymes |CITS: [19571306]|., The pathway depicted above is based on experimental findings with three peroxidases in Medicago truncatula, i.e. PRX1, PRX2 and PRX3 upregulated in response to treatment with yeast elicitor (YE). Metabolic profiling after induction with YE had shown the accumulation of |FRAME:CPD-12037| and its corresponding 4-O-β-D-glucoside indicating a potential involvement of the three PRXs in the formation of those aurones |CITS:[19571306]|. In vitro assays with recombinant PRX1, PRX2 and PRX3 and the starting substrate |FRAME:CPD-3041| resulted, in dependence of experimental conditions, in the formation of either |FRAME:CPD-12037| catalyzed by PRX1 and PRX2 or |FRAME:CPD-12038| when PRX3 was tested. The same result for the three PRXs was obtained when |FRAME:CPD-7391| was used as substrate, i.e. the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17481| by PRX1 and 2 and the yield of |FRAME:CPD-17482| by PRX3. , Although the reactions and reaction products between starting substrates |FRAME:CPD-3041| and |FRAME:CPD-7391| and the respective final products |FRAME:CPD-12037| and |FRAME:CPD-12038| are hypothetical the reaction sequence is supported by findings in other studies. The formation of |FRAME:CPD-12037| from |FRAME:CPD-3041| in Cicer arietinum |CITS: [Wilson76]| and Glycine max |CITS:[Wong66]| including the identification of various intermediates was reported to be the result of the catalytic action of a dioxygenase which utilized hydrogen peroxide and oxygen to initiate the formation of intermediates which then were converted to the final product, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-12037| via a non-enzymatic radical chain mechanism. In addition, the intermediate compounds |FRAME:CPD-12033| and |FRAME:CPD-12036| of the above biosynthetic sequence had been previously identified in Glycine max as intermediates towards the formation of |FRAME:CPD-12037| from |FRAME:CPD-3041| |CITS:[Wong67]|. , The reaction mechanism of PRX1 and PRX2 in Medicago truncatula was proposed to involve the enzymatic formation of a specific neutral phenoxy radical |CITS:[Altwicker67]| from |FRAME:CPD-3041| that is further converted into |FRAME:CPD-12037| by non-enzymatic steps of self-arrangements, intramolecular addition, cleavage and dehydration. However, the reaction sequence and the respective intermediates of the |FRAME:PWY-6401| remain to be elucidated. The obtained main product of the reaction(s), i.e. |FRAME:CPD-12037| and |FRAME:CPD-17481| by PRX1 and PRX2 in contrast to |FRAME:CPD-12038| and |FRAME:CPD-17482| formed by PRX3 has been explained by the varying optimal pH conditions for each enzyme which cause the diversion of the pathway at the potential common intermediate |FRAME:CPD-12032| or its corresponding 4'-O-β-D-glucoside even though these reaction steps are propsed to be non-enzymatical. However, the products |FRAME:CPD-12038| and |FRAME:CPD-17482| have not been detected in Medicago and are therefore considered arteficial products of the in vitro reaction |CITS:[Farag14]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-355| (D-arabinitol), is found in the capsular polysaccharide (CPS) of |FRAME: TAX-1313| serotypes and may be a virulence factor in this human pathogen (in |CITS: [22328666]|). |FRAME: CPD-355| is also produced by many fungi, including pathogenic yeasts |CITS: [7024306]|., About This Pathway, This pathway was elucidated by sequentially carrying out each enzymatic step in a single reaction mixture, starting with the substrate |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|. Peaks appearing at different times were identified by comparison with standard compounds using capillary electrophoresis. Reaction products were purified by HPLC and analyzed by electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. The compound produced by Abp2 was also analyzed by GLC and its structure was determined by NMR spectroscopy. These data defined the activities of Abp1 and Abp2 as a D-xylulose-5-phosphate cytidylyltransferase and a CDP-D-xylulose reductase, respectively |CITS: [22328666]|., The starting compound, |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, is part of the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY| and is produced by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.1|. The gene encoding this enzyme is present on the |FRAME: TAX-1313| chromosome (in |CITS: [22328666]|).

General background, |FRAME:9-CIS11-TRANS-OCTADECADIENOATE 9-cis-11-trans-Octadecadienoate| and |FRAME:CPD-15704| belong to the compound family of positional and geometric isomers of |FRAME:LINOLEIC_ACID| (9-cis, 12-cis-octadecadienoate) known as conjugated linoleic acids (CLAs). The odd numbered conjugated |FRAME:9-CIS11-TRANS-OCTADECADIENOATE| (rumenic acid) and its even numbered conjugated isomer are found in dairy products and meat and arise through microbial conversion of |FRAME:LINOLEIC_ACID| in ruminant animals |CITS:[15522764]|. As component of human nutrition CLAs have been thoroughly researched and reported in animal studies to convey numerous beneficial properties. Amongst others CLAs have been associated with anticancer, anti-arteriosclerosis, immune strengthening and body fat reduction traits |CITS:[Banni98] [12055356]| but are also connected to studies with detrimental effects (reviewed in |CITS:[15522764]|)., , |FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- and/or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291| and |FRAME:PWY-7292|) |CITS:[12697341] [14523547] [8685242]|., The degradation of the cis, trans-unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME:9-CIS11-TRANS-OCTADECADIENOATE| in |FRAME:TAX-4930| (this pathway) has been investigated by monitoring the formation of polyhydroxyalkanoates (see |FRAME:PWY-6657|) |CITS:[16040271]|. The commonly used method to study the degradation of unsaturated fatty acids in yeast such as observing clearing zones around colonies growing on media which provide those fatty acids as sole carbon source had been shown to be limited in detecting certain intermediates in the |FRAME:9-CIS11-TRANS-OCTADECADIENOATE| degradation pathway |CITS:[11566445]|. The formation of polymers from polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) had been originally developed for commercial purposes by producing protein-based polymers and elastomers as part of the efforts to produce renewable and biodegradable raw materials |CITS:[10209132] [9634754]|. However, it rapidly became apparent that the polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) polymerization method also represented a powerful tool to follow carbon fluxes, monitor substrate specificities, detect and engineer new metabolic routes and analyze quantity and quality of unusual fatty acid degradation intermediates in a variety of organisms |CITS:[9634754] [11679353] [10571864] [18657232]|. , About the pathway, By introducing a bacterial PHA synthase from Pseudomonads modified for yeast peroxisomal targeting which polymerizes the various 3-hydroxy-acyl-CoA species generated in the β-oxidation cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-7288|) it is now possible to determine the composition and amount of the substrates and intermediates in a range from 5 to 16 carbons in length |CITS:[16347790] [11679353]|. The degradation of |FRAME:9-CIS11-TRANS-OCTADECADIENOATE| following the fatty acid activation to form the respective CoA derivative occurs in a pathway which combines one auxiliary enzyme with core-enzymes of the β-oxidation cycle. Utilizing yeast single and double mutants, i.e. Δeci1, Δsps19, Δdci1, Δeci1Δdci1, Δeci1Δsps19 and Δdci1Δsps19 evaluating the quantity and monomer composition of the synthesized PHA the pathway sequences degrading |FRAME:9-CIS11-TRANS-OCTADECADIENOATE| could be determined |CITS:[16040271]|., , There are four potential pathways which can be considered in the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15683|, one of them employing only Δ3-Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) whereas the other three depend at one point or another on the participation of Δ3,5,Δ2,4-dienoyl-CoA isomerase (DCI1). The isomerase-dependent pathway (this pathway) produces the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-15690| which is a unique marker for the pathway as it is not generated by β-oxidation of endogenous yeast fatty acids. In addition the increase or decrease in the amount of this 12:1 monomer by analyzing the various mutants indicated what auxiliary enzymes are involved in the pathway and excluded the participation of Δ3,5,Δ2,4-dienoyl-CoA isomerase (DCI1) |CITS:[16040271]|. The first part of the pathways is catalyzed by the β-oxidation enzymes POX1 |CITS: [2189786] [11431484]|, the multifunctional enzyme FOX2 |CITS:[1551874] [10497229] [16574148]| and the 3-keto-thiolase (POT1) |CITS:[7754706] [9402066] [7812714]| up to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15688|. At this point the pathway employs Δ3-Δ2-enoyl-CoA isomerase (ECI1) |CITS:[9837886] [9813046]| to direct further degradation and also to convert |FRAME:CPD-15692| to |FRAME: T2-DECENOYL-COA| which is an eligible substrate for the core β-oxidation cycle.
