Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, Deoxysugars are found in nature as constituents of plant, fungi, and bacteria, where they serve as ligands for cell-cell interactions. The 3,6-dideoxyhexoses are specifically found in the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) component of several Gram-negative bacteria, as part of the O-antigen region of the LPS., There are five naturally occurring simple 3,6-dideoxyhexoses, four of which (|FRAME: CPD-9399|, |FRAME: CPD-9394|, |FRAME: CPD-9395|, and |FRAME: CPD-9396|) are derived from |FRAME: CDP-D-GLUCOSE| and one (|FRAME: CPD-9388|) from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|. In addition, modified compounds exists, such as the two branched 3,6-dideoxyhexoses (|FRAME: CPD-9397| and |FRAME: CPD-9398|) found in |FRAME: TAX-629 Yersinia| species., Organisms that were found to contain |FRAME: CPD-9388| in their O-antigens include the cholera-inducing strain |FRAME: TAX-45888| |CITS: [9163895]|, |FRAME: TAX-373045| |CITS: [14400435][10960113]|, several types of |FRAME:TAX-590|, such as |FRAME: TAX-29473| |CITS:[13660308][7687601][9228739][10960113]|, |FRAME: TAX-633|, |FRAME: TAX-126385| |CITS: [17559819]| and marine bacteria of the |FRAME:TAX-53246| genus, such as, |FRAME: TAX-43659| |CITS: [11423109]|., The biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-9391| was studied in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-633| |CITS:[12733868][15610039]|. |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9391| in three steps. First, two successive dehydration reactions generate |FRAME:GDP-4-DEHYDRO-6-DEOXY-D-MANNOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-9392|, respectively, with the later step being catalyzed by a unique bifunctional |FRAME: PYRIDOXAMINE-5P|-dependent enzyme |CITS: [15610039]|. |FRAME: CPD-9392| is then reduced to |FRAME: CPD-9391| by |FRAME: CPLX-7540|, an enzyme that catalyzes both C-5 epimerization and C-4 reduction |CITS: [15610039]|.

|FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE Phosphatidylcholine|, a major membrane lipid in eukaryotes, can be produced in Saccharomyces cerevisiae in two pathways |CITS:[12627972]|, the CDP-choline biosynthetic route via |FRAME:CHOLINE| (see |FRAME:PWY3O-450|) |CITS:[20503434]| and the triple methylation pathway via |FRAME:ETHANOL-AMINE| (see |FRAME:PWY-6825|) |CITS:[2198947]|. It is also known that both yeast and mammals can deacylate |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| to form |FRAME:L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| |CITS:[11078727]|. Saccharomyces cerevisiae employs a pathway which recycles |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| (this pathway), contributes to the homeostasis of membrane lipids, and provides a compound that can cover the complete demand for phosphor in the cell |CITS:[16172116] [19841481]|. In addition, excess |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| can be avoided which has been reported to be intrinsically toxic to the secretory function of the yeast Golgi apparatus |CITS:[11294911]|., Two enzymes are involved in the resynthesis of |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|, a phosphatidyl phospholipase B (NTE1) which catalyzes two successive deacylations at both sn-2 and sn-1 of |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| yielding |FRAME:L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| and the concomitant release of 2 fatty acids |CITS:[15044461] [15611060]| and a glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase (GDE1) catalyzing the cleavage of |FRAME:L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| releasing |FRAME:CHOLINE| and |FRAME:GLYCEROL-3P| in the process |CITS:[16141200]|. |FRAME:CHOLINE| can be reintroduced to the CDP-choline pathway and used to regenerate |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|. , It is remarkable that NTE1p specifically accepts only |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| which has been generated through the CDP-choline pathway. NTE1p is also the only phospholipase producing intracellular |FRAME:L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| |CITS:[16781190]| and interacts with SEC14, an essential protein for phosphatidylinositol (PI)/phosphatidylcholine (PC) traffic, in regulating the phosphatidylcholine flux in the cell |CITS:[15044461] [15611060] [9252414]|. There are two types of phospholipases in yeast which can metabolize |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|, the phospholipase D |CITS:[9642212]| and the phospholipase B encoded by NTE1 |CITS: [15044461]|. The product of the NTE1p catalysis, i.e. |FRAME:L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| is the substrate for the glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase encoded by GDE1 |CITS:[16141200]| which catalyzes the last step in this resynthesis cycle of |FRAME:PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|. The gene GDE1 has been associated with EC 3.1.4.46 but EC 3.1.4.2 also shows the catalysis of |FRAME:L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| to |FRAME:CHOLINE|. Both designations have been approved by authors working on this enzyme (personal communication Christopher McMaster, September 2013). Both enzymes have not been purified to homogeneity but their molecular functions have been validated by null mutations of the respective genes.

General Background, In contrast to the |FRAME: METOH| utilization/assimilation pathways of methylotrophic bacteria (for example see pathways |FRAME: PWY-1701| and |FRAME: PWY-6966|), strains of |FRAME: TAX-1718| utilize the pathway shown here to metabolize the growth inhibiting and toxic compounds |FRAME: METOH|, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: FORMATE| |CITS: [22767548][24014532][24065717]|., |FRAME: TAX-196627| cannot grow on |FRAME: METOH| as a sole carbon source, and it does not possess any known |FRAME: METOH| assimilation pathways. However, this organism was shown to metabolize |FRAME: METOH| in stationary growth phase in minimal medium containing |FRAME: D-Glucose| and various concentrations of |FRAME: METOH|. The growth rate decreased with increasing |FRAME: METOH| concentration. Radiotracer experiments using 13C-methanol showed that |FRAME: METOH| is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. Thus, this organism possesses an endogenous pathway for the conversion of |FRAME: METOH| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. |FRAME: METOH "Methanol"| derived from renewable carbon sources is of interest for the production of chemicals. Elucidation of this pathway raises the possibility of engineering this industrially important bacterium into a methylotroph |CITS: [24014532]|., About This Pathway, Studies suggested that the |FRAME: ZN+2|-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase AdhA is primarily responsible for the initial oxidation of |FRAME: METOH| to |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|. An adhA null mutant showed a 62% reduction in the rate of |FRAME: METOH| consumption. Mutant analysis showed that |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| is further oxidized to |FRAME: FORMATE| predominantly by the FadH (AdhE) and Ald dehydrogenases (also see pathway |FRAME: PWY1G-170|). Finally, |FRAME: FORMATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| by formate dehydrogenase FdhF. As expected, |FRAME: METOH| catabolism is subject to carbon catabolite repression by |FRAME: D-Glucose|, and catabolism is dependent on the transcriptional regulator RamA. RamA is essential for the expression of genes adhA and ald |CITS: [24014532]|.

Names: superpathway of sterol biosynthesis in diatoms
Summary: General Background, Sterols are isoprenoid-derived molecules that have essential functions in eukaryotes. In vertebrates |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| is by far the major sterol, whereas a mixture of various sterols is present in higher plants, including |FRAME: CPD-4143| (usually predominant), |FRAME: CPD-4162|, |FRAME: CPD-707|, |FRAME: CPD-4127|, |FRAME: CPD-4161| and |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|. Sterols are present in three forms: free sterols (the major form with a free 3β-hydroxyl), steryl esters, and steryl glucosides., Free sterols are integral components of the membrane lipid bilayer and thus interact with some molecular species of, phosphoglycero(sphingo) lipids. The extent of this interaction plays a functional role in the regulation of membrane fluidity and permeability. Sterols have also been shown to play important roles in embryonic development of vertebrates and the formation of membrane microdomains (rafts), which may constitute signaling centers for multiple pathways |CITS:[11278759]|., Finally, sterols are precursors of compounds with a high physiological activity such as brassinosteroids, an important class of plant hormones involved in growth and development |CITS: [8602526]|, ecdysteroids in invertebrates |CITS:[7791536]| and plants |CITS:[Coriot93]|, and antheridiol and oogoniols, sexual pheromones of aquatic fungi belonging to, the saprolegniale class |CITS:[1913877]|., About This Pathway, Diatoms possess sterols that are typical for both plants and animals |CITS: [Rampen09]|. For example, the bloom-forming species |FRAME: TAX-267567| and |FRAME: TAX-29204| synthesize |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL| and |FRAME: DESMOSTEROL-CPD|, which are typical for animals; |FRAME: CPD-8134| and |FRAME: CPD-706|, which are typical for plants; |FRAME: CPD-22095|, commonly found in algae; and |FRAME: CPD-24178|, which is often found in marine invertebrates |CITS: [32144288]|., Molecular studies in the diatom |FRAME: TAX-2850| suggested the existence of a mixed plant and fungal pathway, but that proposal was questioned due to the fact that diatoms do not produce |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL|, the typical fungal sterol |CITS: [24996048]|. The complete biosynthetic pathway of sterols in |FRAME: TAX-267567| and |FRAME: TAX-29204| was reported in a study that involved transcriptomics, labelling methods, and GC-MS profiling |CITS: [32144288]|., Like the pathways in in plants and algae, sterol biosynthesis starts in diatoms with |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL|, which is derived from |FRAME: MEVALONATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-922|)., This superpathway describes the biosynthesis of all sterols synthesized by the diatoms. As soon as it starts it splits into two main branches - one for cholesterol, and othe rleads to the rest of the sterols., The diatom cholesterol biosynthesis pathway is almost identical to the pathway characterized from the rhodophyte |FRAME: TAX-2769| (see |FRAME: PWY-8191|). The two pathways share the the beginning and the end portions. However, they differ in the section between |FRAME: 4-METHYL-824-CHOLESTADIENOL| and |FRAME: 5-ALPHA-CHOLESTA-724-DIEN-3-BETA-OL|, which in the diatom involves a |FRAME: ZYMOSTEROL| intermediate and enzymes usually found in animals and fungi |CITS: [32144288]|., A large part of the pathway leading to the rest of the sterols is similar to the pathway found in plants (see |FRAME: PWY-2541|). Both diatoms and plants form |FRAME: CPD-8134| (also called Δ22-dihydrobrassicasterol) using the same enzymatic steps., A split point in both the plant pathway and the diatom pathway is |FRAME: CPD-4101|, which can be either oxygenated, leading to |FRAME: CPD-8134|, or methylated. In plants, |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.143|, forms |FRAME: CPD-4124|, leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-4143| and |FRAME: CPD-4162|. However, the methylase in diatoms forms |FRAME: CPD-24186|, leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-22095| and |FRAME: CPD-24178| |CITS: [32144288]|.

Summary: General Background, The superpathway of anthocyanin biosynthesis that originates from pelargonidin 3-O-glucoside comprises the formation of compounds such as salvianin, anthocyanidin sophoroside and pelargondin conjugates. Those anthocyanins contribute to the wide variation of flower colors in various species being likewise attractive for pollinating insects and floriculturists., Salvianin, the predominant anthocyanin causing the scarlet flower coloration of |FRAME:TAX-180675| has two malonyl groups linked to the 4" and 6"-hydroxyl groups of the 5-glucosyl moiety |CITS: [11809447][Kondo89]|. , Its biosynthesis represents a species-specific variety of the decoration of pelargonin that involves glucosylation , and aromatic and aliphatic acylation to increase stability, solubility and color variation of the chromophoric anthocyanins |CITS: [10066805][10845463][Heller94]|., Anthocyanins are produced in two distinguished sets of reactions, the first one (early-stage) leading to the first stable anthocyanidin, i.e. anthocyanidin-3-O-glucosides and the second one (late-stage) comprising further modification of those compounds such as glycosylation, acylation and methylation. These late-stage reactions are concerned with fine adjustment for a variety of floral color which is diverse and less understood than the steps involved in the early-stage reactions |CITS: [10066805]| |CITS: [10845463]|. The decoration of pelargonidin is typical for a variety of plants such as |FRAME:TAX-48386|, |FRAME:TAX-76714|, |FRAME:TAX-39879| |CITS: [10066805]| and |FRAME:TAX-101596| |CITS: [12481098]|. Many of the above mentioned plants are characterized by anthocyanins that are intermediately 5-O-glucosylated. , Anthocyanidins often occur as sophoroside, i.e. a diglucoside that consists of glucose attached to the 2''-O-position of the 3-O-glucose moiety of anthocyanidins. The anthocyanidin that confers the bright blue color to |FRAME:TAX-35883| (a member of the Convolvulacea) is a sophoroside that forms a complex with several caffeoyl residues, known as |FRAME:CPD-7841| (HBA). Reddish-brown flowers of dusky mutants of |FRAME:TAX-35883| contain |FRAME:CPD-7840| (WBA) representing the most favorite flower hue for Japanese floriculturists |CITS: [15842621]|. , About This Pathway, Salvianin: Pelargonidin 3-O-β-D-glucoside represents the starting compound that is stepwise converted into bisdemalonylsalvianin, the precursor for the aliphatic acylation with malonyl-CoA. Those reactions involve 5-O-glucosylation |CITS: [10066805]| and 3-aromatic acylation with caffeic acid |CITS: [Fujiwara98]| |CITS: [10845463]| which may proceed via two parallel pathway branches. Bisdemalonylsalvianin is further malonylated twice on its 5-O-glucosidic moiety which is carried out by two different regio-specific malonyltransferases |CITS: [11598135]| |CITS: [15165190]|., Pelargonidin conjugates: The 5-O-glucosylation of anthocyanidin-3-O-glucosides, catalyzed by the anthocyanin 5-O-glucosyltransferase (5-GT) does not significantly change the color of anthocyanins but is important for further modification of anthocyanin molecules |CITS: [11905966][10066805]|. A significant contribution to intensification of color and color shift towards blue is accomplished by aromatic acylation with hydroxycinnamic acids of the anthocyanin molecules due to a bathochromic shift. The enzyme catalyzing this step, anthocyanin 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-acyltransferase has been characterized in |FRAME:TAX-48386| |CITS: [Fujiwara98]| |CITS: [10845463]|. The exact metabolic succession of aromatic acylation (C-ring 3-position, A-ring 5-position) of the anthocyanin glucosides (mono-, diglucoside) is not known and may depend on the species involved. The malonylation of anthocyanins, for instance catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-malonyltransferase |CITS: [12481098]| generally occurs under strict regiocontrol during the late stage of their biosynthesis. Other modifications of the anthocyanins involve further glycosylations catalyzed by anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside-6"-O-rhamnosyltransferase |CITS: [Kamsteeg80]| and anthocyanidin 3-O-rutinoside-5-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS: [751641]|., Anthocyanin sophoroside: The crucial step in the formation of anthocyanidin sophoroside as precursors for HBA and WBA in Ipomoea is catalyzed by the anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside 2-O''-glucosyltransferase (3GGT). , The enzyme adds glucose to anthocyanidin 3-glucosides at the 2''-O-position of the glucose moiety forming the corresponding sophorosides. Although the enzyme accepts all three major anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside, anthocyanidin 3,5-diglucoside are not suitable substrates for the 3GGT |CITS: [15842621]|.

General information on carotenoids: , Carotenoids with cyclic ends are integral constituents of plants, algae and cyanobacteria photosynthetic reaction , centers |CITS:[GOODWIN80],[YOUNG93]|. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although , they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A. These isoprenoids pigments are lipid-soluble and are , involved in a variety of functions including: protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of , excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments; light-harvest for photosynthesis; the prominent lutein, as well as , zeaxanthin, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring , agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal; , finally they are precursors for the plant growth hormone abscisic acid and vitamin A (for a succinct review of the , applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|)., Most of the |FRAME: carotenoids carotenoids| are C40 isoprenoids, consisting of eight isoprene units, and are commonly biosynthesized in plants, algae, fungi, and bacteria. The C40 carotenoids can be divided in two major groups: |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|. Carotenes are linear or cyclized hydrocarbons such as |FRAME: CPD1F-114 lycopene|, |FRAME: CPD1F-118| and |FRAME: CPD1F-129 β-carotene|. Xanthophylls are oxygenated derivatives (epoxy, keto or hydroxyl groups) of carotenes; for example: |FRAME: CPD1F-119| and |FRAME: CPD1F-130|. The carotenoid composition varies from species to species; in plants, the concentration and composition of xanthophylls are affected by light intensity and the accumulation of specific carotenoids in fruit and flower chromoplasts is a highly, developmentally regulated process |CITS:[12232210],[8485401]|. Important carotenoids variations are observed during fruit ripening (for review, see |CITS:[10205893]|). Higher plant chloroplasts typically accumulate |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, |FRAME: CPD1F-129 β-carotene|, |FRAME: CPD1F-133| and |FRAME: CPD1F-135| in the thylakoid membrane-bound photosystems |CITS:[1885603],[RYBERG93]|. |FRAME: CPD1F-129 β-Carotene| is generally found in the reaction center where it plays a critical photoprotective role by quenching triplet chlorophyll and singlet oxygen, and can undergo rapid degradation during photooxidation |CITS:[YOUNG93B]|. Adjacent to the reaction centers, in the core complex proteins, |FRAME: CPD1F-129 β-carotene| and |FRAME: CPD1F-119| can be found |CITS:[1885603],[8444169]|., Finally, the surrounding antenna complexes contain xanthophylls (|FRAME: CPD1F-119|, |FRAME: CPD1F-133| and |FRAME: CPD1F-135 neoxanthin|) |CITS:[1885603],[8444169]|. In the chromoplasts of ripening fruits and flower petals, and in the chloroplasts of senescing leaves, the carotenoids are found in membranes or in oil bodies or other structures within the stroma., General information on paprika carotenoids: , Capsanthin and capsorubin are two disctinctive xanthophylls unique to the |FRAME:TAX-4071| family. They contain , a 'cyclopentane' ring (cyclo- = ring; -pent- = five carbons; -ane = single bonds). These xanthophylls are , responsible for the bright red colors of ripe peppers. The major red color in paprika (|FRAME:TAX-4072|, , pepper) comes from the carotenoids capsanthin and capsorubin, while the yellow-orange color is from , beta-carotene and violaxanthin |CITS:[reeves87]|. Capsanthin which represents one of the major carotenoid in ripe , pepper fruits, contributes up to 60% of the total carotenoids. Capsanthin and capsorubin increase proportionally , with increased fruit maturation; capsanthin is the more stable of the two |CITS:[kanner77]|. Both capsanthin and , capsorubin have demonstrated significant antioxidant activity. A recent study found that capsanthin's , radical-scavenging action was as strong as that of β-carotene, lutein, and zeaxanthin. In addition, it was , shown to be more resistant to decomposition, and retained its antioxidant properties longer than the other , carotenoids. About 70 - 80% of the capsanthin was found to be 'esterified' with various fatty acids; these esterified , xanthophylls were also determined to have antioxidant properties |CITS:[matsufuji98]|., Capsanthin and capsorubin

Summary: The homeostasis of glycerophospholipids constitutes an indispensable element for buildup, maintenance and component dynamics of cell membranes in all organisms. The many different phospholipid molecular species found in yeast basically vary in their composition of fatty acids esterified to the sn-1 and sn-2 position of a phosphorylated |FRAME:GLYCEROL| and a head group which can either be a |FRAME:CHOLINE|, |FRAME:ETHANOL-AMINE|, |FRAME:SER|, |FRAME:MYO-INOSITOL| or the one phospholipid without a head group, i.e. phosphatidate (for example |FRAME:CPD-8291|) |CITS:[14321173] [22345606]|. After the de novo synthesis of phospholipids in the Kennedy pathway (see |FRAME:TRIGLSYN-PWY|, |FRAME:PWY3O-450|) glycerophospholipids can be degraded (see |FRAME:LIPAS-PWY|) and remodeled (this pathway; see also |FRAME:PWY-7416| and |FRAME:PWY-7417|). The latter has been proposed by William E.M. Lands |CITS:[14413818]| who describes in the eponymous 'Lands cycle' a de-acylation-re-acylation process of phospholipids typically characterized by saturated acyl chains at the sn-1 and unsaturated acyl chains at the sn-2 position |CITS:[7871882]|., This remodeling process starts with the de-acylation at the sn-2 position of phospholipids catalyzed by phospholipases (e.g. phospholipase A2) generating the corresponding lyso-phospholipids. The resulting lyso-phospholipids represent the substrates for acyl-CoA dependent lyso-phospholipid acyltransferases or phospholipid transacylases which can re-acylate the sn-2 position. Generally, the Lands cycle constitutes an exchange of fatty acids at the sn-2 position which is an substantial factor in the maintenance of the homeostasis of phospholipids |CITS:[17010666]|. This de- and re-acylation process translates into many physiological functions, for example increasing membrane fluidity through a higher percentage of unsaturated acyl chains, re-esterification of exogenous lyso-phospholipids |CITS:[17726007]|, buffering excess toxic fatty acids |CITS:[22090344] [19608739]| and maintenance of the intrinsic membrane curvature necessary to preserve membrane integrity |CITS:[16339082] [31173]|., In the phosphatidylethanolamine remodeling pathway the de-acylation of |FRAME:CPD-8355| is catalyzed by the phospholipase A2 activity of the triacylglycerol lipase TGL4p |CITS:[16135509] [16267052] [20332534]| whereas the re-acylation of |FRAME:L-1-GLYCEROPHOSPHORYLETHANOL-AMINE| is carried out by the acyl-CoA dependent lyso-phosphatidylethanolamine acyltransferase (ALE1p) |CITS:[17652094] [17726007] [17996202]|. However, the remodeling of |FRAME:CPD-8355| can also be achieved by the enzymatic action of the phospholipases B, i.e PLB1p and PLB2p |CITS:[8051052] [10231538] [10497163] [15588231]| in cooperation with the glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase encoded by GDE1 |CITS:[16141200]| channeling |FRAME:ETHANOL-AMINE| into the Kennedy pathway of phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis (see |FRAME:PWY4FS-6|) which in turn may resupply |FRAME:CPD-8355| or other molecular acyl phosphatidylethanolamine species to the remodeling pathway.

|FRAME:CPD-9539 Calycosin| and its 7-O-glucoside |FRAME:CPD-17611| are isoflavonoids found in herbs used particularly in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) |CITS:[Thwe12]|. The dried roots of |FRAME: TAX-119829| referred to as Radix astragali are especially high in both |FRAME:CPD-9539| and |FRAME:CPD-17611| |CITS:[12198969] [15752625]| and considered the most bioactive compounds in this Chinese drug |CITS:[12735475]|. This is reflected by the market prices where roots with the highest isoflavone content are also the most expensive ones |CITS:[12166972]|. The various pharmaceutical properties of |FRAME:CPD-9539| and |FRAME:CPD-17611| have been employed as antiperspirant, immunostimulant, dietary supplement for women with menopausal irregularities, in cancer therapy |CITS:[16569074] [9657051]| and as protector of endothelial cells from hypoxia-induced barrier impairment |CITS:[14637172]|., Although also occurring in non-leguminous taxa isoflavonoids such as |FRAME:CPD-9539| and |FRAME:CPD-17611| are typical compounds found predominantly in legumes |CITS:[17904596]|. The pathway towards |FRAME:CPD-17611| branches out from the |FRAME:PWY-2464| at the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-9539|. It could be shown in expression analyses that the genes coding for enzymes involved in the making of |FRAME:CPD-17611| can be traced back as far as to the |FRAME:PWY1F-467| (phenylalanine ammonia lyase - PAL) |CITS:[18583351]|, via |FRAME:PWY1F-FLAVSYN| (chalcone reductase - CHR) |CITS:[21647549]|, |FRAME:PWY-2002| (chalcone isomerase - CHI), |FRAME:PWY-2321| (isoflavone O-methyltransferase - IOMT) and |FRAME:PWY-2464| (isoflavone 3'-hydroxylase - I3'H) |CITS:[17253088]|. The latter, i.e. isoflavone 3'-hydroxylase (I3'H) was shown to be induced in the same way as the calycosin 7-O-glucosyltransferase (UCGT) in Astralagus mongholicus by low temperature stress |CITS:[17253088]| and UV-irradiation |CITS:[21438882]|. Interestingly, |FRAME:CPD-17611| accumulates both in roots and leaves of Astralagus mongholicus although the gene is rarely expressed in roots indicating that the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17611| takes place in the leaves. The transportation of |FRAME:CPD-17611| could be demonstrated in phloem exudate supporting the hypothesis that after the biosynthesis in the leaves |FRAME:CPD-17611| was transported to the roots of Astragalus mongholicus, and is deposited in the vacuole of the cells |CITS:[17253088]|. The deposition of |FRAME:CPD-17611| in the vacuole is in accordance to the observation that in this organelle secondary metabolites are less prone to interfere with metabolism or act as toxins |CITS:[16006598]|.

Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the second segment - the attachemnt of Kdo residues to the intermediate lipid IV<sub>A</sub>., Many bacterial species produce lipid A molecules that contain |FRAME: CPD-24440|. This modification has been shown to dampen the host immune response and increase resistance to antimicrobial peptides., A partial list of such organisms include |FRAME: TAX-1079| and |FRAME: TAX-1076| |CITS: [1125951][1000526]|, |FRAME: TAX-293| |CITS: [Wilkinson78]|, |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [6811780]|, |FRAME: TAX-40137| |CITS: [2719525]|, |FRAME: TAX-197| |CITS: [1987154]|, |FRAME: TAX-529| |CITS: [ 9691452]|, |FRAME: TAX-234| |CITS: [Qureshi94]|, |FRAME: TAX-28104| |CITS: [15030481]|, |FRAME: TAX-920|, |FRAME: TAX-173|, and |FRAME: TAX-446| |CITS: [15044494]|, |FRAME: TAX-29448| |CITS: [20087912]|, |FRAME: TAX-7| |CITS: [22456102]|, and |FRAME: TAX-300193| |CITS: [28409238]|., This sugar is produced from |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, which is converted by two enzymes, a dehydrogenase (|FRAME: G-107456|) and an aminotransferase (|FRAME: G-107457|), to |FRAME: CPD-24442|. That compound is subsequently acylated and deacetylated, resulting in acylated 2,3-diamino-2,3-dideoxy-D-glucopyranose |CITS: [15044494]|.

General Background, Cyanobacterial lipids consist of glycerolipids with a C18 fatty acid esterified at position sn-1 and a C16 fatty acid esterified at position sn-2 |CITS: [Sato82]|., The cyanobacteria have been classified into four groups according to the distribution of the fatty acids in their glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|. , Strains in Group 1 are characterized by the presence of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (|FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9245|) at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively., Strains in Group 2 contain the tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| at the sn-1 position and the mono-unsaturated C16 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-9245| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 3 have a different tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid (|FRAME: CPD-8117|) at the sn-1 position and the saturated C16 acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 4 are similar to strains in Group 3 except that they have, in addition, the tri-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| and the tetra-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: CPD-12653| at the sn-1 position., |FRAME: CPD-8117| (GLA), found in Group 3, is a polyunsaturated (18:3) ω-6 fatty acid (the 6 refers to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid)., In addition to cyanobacteria, certain other organisms can produce substantial amounts of |FRAME: CPD-8117|, including some plants |CITS:[11170598][16718484]| and filamentous fungi |CITS:[11112411][10570972]|. In the plant kingdom, |FRAME: CPD-8117| is only found in a few higher plants (including black currants, evening primrose, borage and hemp), and is usually found exclusively in the seeds., GLA is of major importance in animal cells, being the precursor for the synthesis of several Δ6-desaturated fatty acids, such as |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7592|). Unlike its precursor, GLA is not an essential fatty acid for animals, since almost all animals possess a Δ6 desaturase enzyme., About This Pathway, In cyanobacteria |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is formed bound to an acyl-carrier protein, part of the fatty acid synthase complex. Stearate is transfered to the sn-1 position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.15| |CITS: [16039611]|., As described above, glycerolipids from all cyanobacteria contain unsturated C18 fatty acids in the sn-1 position, but differ in the degree and nature of unsaturation. The desaturation occurs only after |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| has been incorporated into the glycerol backbone, and is catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes known as acyl-lipid desaturases., The first desaturation occurs at position 9, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS15040|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS15040-MONOMER| |CITS: [7929259]|. This is followed by desaturation at position 12, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10130|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS10130-MONOMER| |CITS: [2118597]|. A third desaturation occurs at position 6, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.46|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10796| gene |CITS: [16328883]|.

Summary: The ABH histo-blood antigen system, The ABH histo-blood group system (sometimes referred to as ABO) was originally defined in terms of the antigenic substances occurring on red blood cells |CITS: [Landsteiner00][Landsteiner40]|. However, substances exhibiting similar serological specificities also occur in various mucous bodily fluids (such as saliva and milk), mostly as glycoproteins |CITS: [16747710][Morgan44]|., The ABH and the related Lewis blood group determinants are formed from |FRAME: Blood-Group-Antigen-Precursor "precursor disaccharides"| that decorate glycosphingolipids or protein glycans by concerted actions of several glycosyltransferases., There are differences between the ABH antigens found in red blood cells (RBCs) and those found in bodily fluids. The ABH-antigens in the RBC membrane are N-linked to glycoproteins (Band 3) and sphingolipids |CITS: [6799656]|, while those in fluids are O-linked to glycoproteins by O-glycosidic linkage to |FRAME: SER| or |FRAME: THR| residues of the peptide chains |CITS: [Wu88a]|. In addtion, in red blood cells both glycoproteins and glycosphingolipids contain only the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 precursor"| |CITS: [729592]| while in the fluids both |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1"| and |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2"| precursors are used |CITS: [6156588]| (see also |FRAME: PWY-7831|)., A key reaction in this pathway is the formation of |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen| on the surface of the epithelial cells and in mucosal secretions by fucosylation of the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 precursor"| at the 2 position. The main enzyme that catalyzes this reaction in secretions and on epithelial cells is encoded by the |FRAME: HS11104| gene. The gene has a dominant allele (known as the Se gene) and a recessive non-functional allele (known as the se gene). In red blood cells, on the other hand, the parallel reaction is catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: HS10855| gene., Additional glycosyltransferases can modify the H type 1 structure. The |FRAME: HS10887 "A-glycosyltransferase"| and |FRAME: G-54960 "B-glycosyltransferase"| of the ABO system add either an N-acetylgalactosamine or a galactose in an α(1,3) linkage, forming |FRAME: Type-1-A-antigen| and |FRAME: Type-1-B-antigen|, respectively., A bifunctional α(1,3)/(1,4)fucosyltransferase, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249| gene, can add a fucose residue to the non-terminal sugar of the precursor disaccharide, generating the assorted Lewis antigens shown here., The Lewis antigen system, The Lewis blood group antigens, discovered in 1946, are biosynthetically and structurally related carbohydrate structures used as markers of cell differentiation and embryonic development, based on fucosylation carried by a number of fucosyltransferases. The system is named after Mrs. H. D. G. Lewis, in whose serum the first member of the family was discovered |CITS: [20995492]|. However, the presence of the Lewis antigens is not limited to erytrocytes, and they are found in different tissues and organs., A key enzyme in the formation of some Lewis antigens is a fucosyltransferases, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10249| gene. The enzyme is bifunctional and can fucosylate both the 3 and 4 positions of the penultimate sugar in the precursor disaccharide. The gene, also known as the Lewis gene, has a dominant allele (which was named Le) and a recessive non-functional allele (known as le)., The Lewis antigens shown in this pathway are components of exocrine epithelial secretions, but are also adsorbed onto the surface of erythrocytes following their biosynthesis. The two main components of the system are the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a antigen"| (Lea) and the |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b antigen"| (Leb). The former is generated directly from the |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 blood group antigen precursor disaccharide"| by the action of the |FRAME: HS10249| fucosyltransferase, which adds a fucose residue to the non-terminal galactosyl residue of the disaccharide precursor. In people that have the Le and se alleles, this is the only Lewis antigen present in secretions. However, in people that also have the Se allele of |FRAME: HS11104| and thus produce |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen|, the |FRAME: HS10249| enzyme also acts on the latter, producing an |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Leb antigen"|., Since |FRAME: HS11104| is also responsible for the presence of soluble A, B and H antigens in bodily fluids, the lack of a functional |FRAME: HS11104| has an effect on both blood group systems: individuals lacking the enzyme produce the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lea antigen"| rather than the |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Leb antigen"|, and they do not have A, B or H antigens in their bodily fluids |CITS: [6156588]|., Even though the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lea"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Leb"| antigens are present on the red blood cell surface, they are not synthesized in the erythrocyte precursor cells but are secondarily acquired from the plasma in which the red cells circulate |CITS: [13244653][13381985]|. They are synthesized on glycosphingolipids and carried in the plasma by high and low-density lipoproteins |CITS: [5778002]|. In bodily fluids, on the other hand, these antigens are found on glycoproteins., The |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis a epitope"| (SLea) was discovered in 1979 with the use of a monoclonal antibody |CITS: [94699]|. While the antigen is believed to play an important role during embryogenesis |CITS: [6381330]|, in adults only low amounts of the antigen are present on normal epithelial cells |CITS: [6751528][6381289]|., When the selectin family of adhesion molecules was described, it was found that SLea, along with the |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x antigen"|, is a ligand for E-selectin., Higher expression of the SLea antigen in adults is strongly associated with cancer. It was found in high amounts on the surface of human pancreatic, colon and gastric cancer cell lines |CITS: [7142214][6188455]| and in human adenocarcinomas of the colon, stomach, pancreas and gall-bladder |CITS: [94699][6751528][2910493]|., The expression of the antigen has been linked to tumor progression. A gradual increase in SLea was found in colon and rectum during neoplastic transformation and progression |CITS: [2863413]|, and its presence was restricted to tumorigenic and invasive human urothelial cell lines |CITS: [8900435]|. The antigen is responsible for adhesion of colon,, pancreas, urinary bladder and gastric cancer cells to endothelium via its interaction with selectin E |CITS: [1716885][7687590][7678075][8900435][9578490]|., The expression level of the SLea antigen is used as a prognostic factor for colorectal carcinoma, and is associated with high incidence of recurrence and the length of survival time |CITS: [8273774][7697593][9303355]|., In a similar process, the α(1,3) fucosylation of the N-acetylglucosaminyl residue of |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R| leads to formation of several other Lewis-type antigens, including the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x epitope"| (also known as SSEA-1, for stage-specific embryonic antigen 1 |CITS: [281705]|), |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y epitope"|, and the |FRAME: sLea-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x epitope"| (see |FRAME: PWY-7831|)., ABH and Lewis epitopes in Helicobacter pylori, The human pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| synthesizes fucosylated oligosaccharides (see |FRAME: PWY-7833|). Most strains are able to synthesize type 2-based blood group antigens such as |FRAME: Type-2-H-Antigen "H type 2"|, |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y"| |CITS: [9398905][8890213]|, some can synthesize |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x"| |CITS: [10632700]|, and a small population also expresses the type 1 based blood group antigens |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "H type 1"| |CITS: [23828675]|, |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a|, and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| |CITS: [9565568][10992504][18436591][22160312]|. Several roles have been proposed for the presence of these antigen in the bacterium, including mucosal adhesion, immune evasion, permiting the bacteria to escape from the host immune respons, and autoantibody induction |CITS: [18279843]|.

Summary: Background, In this pathway chorismate is synthesized from |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE|. The pathway is found in prokaryotes (both bacteria and archaea) and several eukaryotes, including ascomycete fungi, apicomplexans, plants and algae |CITS: [16963634]|. However, its starting point, |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE|, can be synthesized in different routes. In most microorganisms it is synthesized from |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| (see |FRAME: PWY-6164|), but the methanogens of the |FRAME: TAX-28890| phylum utilize an alternative route |CITS: [15182204]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6160|). , |FRAME: CHORISMATE "Chorismate"| is an intermediate in the synthesis of the three aromatic amino acids: |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. These amino acids serve as substrates in other pathways for secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, flavonoids, lignin, coumarin, indole derivatives and other phenolic compounds |CITS: [22296303]|. , |FRAME: SHIKIMATE "Shikimate"| is an important intermediate in the chorismate biosynthetic pathway. It was first isolated from Japanese star anise. Shikimate is used for the production of some antiviral drugs used to halt the spread of the flu virus, but as a biosynthetic intermediate, it is usually not found in high concentrations in organisms. Shikimate can be easily harvested from the needles of several species of pine trees, and biosynthetic pathways in |FRAME:TAX-562| have been enhanced to obtain sufficient amounts of the metabolite for commercial use. , About this Pathway, The first enzyme in this section of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.10|, dehydrates |FRAME: DEHYDROQUINATE| to |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE|, which is subsequently reduced to |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.25| (or in some organisms also by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.282|). The next enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.71|, was shown in |FRAME: TAX-1423| to form a complex with the bifunctional |FRAME: CPLX-1101| (|FRAME: BSU29750|). The complex may serve as a regulatory unit |CITS: [170268] [BSUB225]|., |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.19|, catalyzes the penultimate step in chorismate biosynthesis. The synthase is activated by ammonium ions and exhibits allosteric behavior. |FRAME: CPD0-1308 Glyphosate| acts as a competitive inhibitor with respect to |FRAME: PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| and as a partial uncompetitive inhibitor with respect to |FRAME: SHIKIMATE-5P| |CITS: [3111378] [7744055][7589547]|., The last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.5|, catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: 3-ENOLPYRUVYL-SHIKIMATE-5P| into |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, the key branch-point intermediate in aromatic biosynthesis.

Summary: The three aromatic amino acids tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine are all derived from a common , precursor chorismate. In tyrosine and phenylalanine biosynthesis, chorismate is first converted to an , intermediate prephenate.  There are two possible routes to synthesize phenylalanine or tyrosine from , the intermediate prephenate: 1) via arogenate by the activity of prephenate aminotransferase, illustrated , here, or 2) via phenylpyruvate by the activity of prephenate dehydratase for phenylalanine synthesis, or , via hydroxyphenylpyruvate by the activity of prephenate dehydrogenase for tyrosine synthesis., The latter route has been confirmed in many microorganisms , including E.coli and yeast. In fact, the two alternative routes have been reported co-exist in , microorganisms. However, compiling evidence suggests that many plants may only employ the , arogenate route for phenylalanine and tyrosine synthesis. There is so far no sound evidence support the , other route in plants.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8846| (TMTT) is a volatile homoterpene implicated in attracting pollinators or defending against heribivores in many plant species including |FRAME: TAX-3884 "Phaseolus lunatus (lima bean)"|, |FRAME: ORG-5993|, and |FRAME: TAX-4081 Solanum lycopersicum (tomato)"| |CITS: [18842097][21088219][10952311][16786318][11710601]|. In some cases, this volatile compound can participate in tritrophic interactions. For example, in |FRAME: ORG-5993| leaf damage by the specialist herbivore pest |FRAME: TAX-64459| can lead to |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| production which then attracts the parasitoid wasp |FRAME: TAX-32392| to feed on |FRAME: TAX-64459| larvae and to reduce herbivore-induced damage |CITS: [11710601]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP GGPP| isoprenoid precursor to this pathway is first acted on by a terpene synthase to form |FRAME: CPD-8848|. |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| is synthesized next through the activity of a cytochrome p450 monooxygenase, but, the exact mechanism of enzyme action is still being investigated. For instance, it is possible that |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1|, a p450 enzyme from Arabidopsis, may promote the direct transformation of |FRAME: CPD-8848| to |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| with the concomittant release of |FRAME: CPD-8847| as depicted in this pathway diagram. However, this reaction is labeled a "hypothetical" because the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8847| has not been detected in yeast overexpressing |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1|. It is also possible that a two-step conversion may occur that includes the formation of intermediate C-18 compound |FRAME: CPD-12898|, but this intermediate has also not been observed in yeast studies using |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| nor did it act as a good substrate for that enzyme |CITS: [21088219]|. However, |FRAME: CPD-12898| has been detected to exist in numerous plant species such as Commiphora parvifolia and Salvia hierosolymitana , |CITS:[20335939][19935471]|. Several researchers have examined this |FRAME: CPD-8848| to |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| chemical conversion in different plants (see refs in |CITS: [21088219]|), but further work will be required to clarify the exact manner in which the final step of this pathway is executed. , Several lines of evidence suggest that multiple layers of regulation contribute to the control of |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| and the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| . For example, |FRAME: AT1G61120-MONOMER GES| and |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| both have increased transcript levels in response to treatment with a fungal peptide elicitor |CITS: [21088219]|. Also, interestingly, mutants that lack |FRAME: AT3G25180-MONOMER CYP82G1| fail to make |FRAME: CPD-8846 TMTT| but do not accumulate its precursor |FRAME: CPD-8848| suggesting that some sort of feedback inhibition may control the flux into this pathway |CITS: [21088219]|. In addition, TMTT production depends, in an unknown way, on the jasmonate-signalling associated F-box protein COI1 |CITS: [21088219]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-14 "Tetrathionate"| is one of the most important intermediates in dissimilatory sulfur oxidation and can itself be utilized as a sole energy source by some sulfur-oxidizing microorganisms., Among the organisms reported to oxidize tetrathionate are obligate chemolithoautotrophs such as |FRAME: TAX-929|, |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [26665]|, |FRAME: TAX-930|, and |FRAME: TAX-152475| |CITS: [11931180]|, facultative chemolithoautotrophs such as |FRAME: TAX-76588| and |FRAME: TAX-47959|, and obligate heterotrophs |CITS: [10508936]|., Unlike thiosulfate oxidation, tetrathionate oxidation is not coupled to a c-type cytochrome, but is likely to be linked to a b-type cytochrome, possibly via |FRAME: Ubiquinones| |CITS:[ArchMicro160-87]|., In a study of the oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds by |FRAME: TAX-76588|, |FRAME: CPD-14| was formed as an, intermediate during |FRAME: HS| oxidation. It was found that during anaerobic incubation of the cell suspensions, the tetrathionate was stoichiometrically converted to |FRAME: S2O3|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and some form of sulfur. KOH consumption assay revealed that two moles of H+ were released per mol of tetrathionate metabolized |CITS: [Meulenberg92]|. These results suggest that tetrathionate metabolism is initiated by a cleavage reaction according to the equation:, |FRAME: RXN-10852|, Tetrathionate hydrolases play a significant role in tetrathionate oxidation and are believed to catalyze the initial step in the oxidative dissimilation when sulfur-oxidizing bacteria are grown on tetrathionate., Such enzymes have been purified and characterized from several acidophilic chemolithoautotrophic bacteria belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-119977| |CITS:[Tano96][deJong97][14717695]| and |FRAME: TAX-76588| |CITS: [9057831]|. A |FRAME: CPLX-7906| from |FRAME: TAX-920| has been purified and sequenced, and the gene encoding it has been cloned |CITS: [17904676]|. The enzyme is induced by growth on tetrathionate, and is not expressed during growth on iron., In |FRAME: TAX-920| tetrathionate is produced from two molecules of |FRAME: S2O3| by the action of |FRAME: CPLX-7152| (TQO) |CITS: [15178473]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5303|)., The |FRAME: S2O3| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur| that are produced by tetrathionate hydrolase are eventually converted to sulfate (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6677| and |FRAME: SULFUROX-PWY|) |CITS: [28873420]|.

Summary: General Background, Polyunsaturated long- and very-long-chain fatty acids (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear., These compounds are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturated very long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. , |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Eicosapentaenoate| (EPA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains five cis double bonds, one of which is located at the third carbon from the omega end, which makes it an omega-3 fatty acid. EPA is produced by microalgae and is common in fish who eat the algae, although the fish can not produce it. It is also produced by fungi, mosses and ferns, but is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. EPA is also produced by some marine bacteria, mostly those adapted to low temperatures and high pressures, via a completely different pathway |CITS: [10220156]|., About this Pathway, Some fungi possess an ω3-desaturase that can desaturate n-6 PUFAs into the corresponding n-3 PUFA |CITS: [14651475]|.These enzymes can catalyze the direct conversion of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID arachidonate| to |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE eicosapentaenoate| |CITS: [15538555]|., The filamentous fungus, |FRAME: TAX-64518 Mortierella alpina| is a prolific producer of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID arachidonate| (see |FRAME: PWY-5353|) |CITS: [SHIMIZU]|. An ω3-desaturase gene was cloned from this organism and shown to catalyze the direct conversion of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID arachidonate| to |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE eicosapentaenoate| |CITS: [15538555]|. It was not reported whether the fatty acids substrates are in the form of coenzyme A esters or attached to glycerolipids.

Homogalacturonan (HGA) is a linear chain of 1,4-linked a-D-galacturonic acid residues in which some of the carboxyl groups are methyl esterified. HGA accounts for up to 60% of the pectin found in primary cell walls of all plants., To synthesize HGA, UDP-galacturonate is formed from UDP-glucuronate in the cytosol. UDP- galacturonate is then transported into the Golgi by a proposed UDP- galacturonate:UMP antiporter. The galacturonate residue is transferred onto a growing HGA chain. Some of the newly added galacturonate residues are methyl esterifed at the C-6 carboxyl group. Vesicles containing the newly synthesized HGA are targeted to and fuse with the plasmamembrane thereby releasing the HGA into the exocellular space for subsequent incorporation into the wall.

|FRAME: ECTOINE Ectoine| is a natural compound found in high concentrations in some halophilic microorganisms. It is a compatible solute, helping the organisms survive extreme osmotic stress by acting as an osmolyte. Along with |FRAME: BETAINE|, it is one of the two predominant compatible solutes in halophilic bacteria |CITS: [16176595]|., Ectoine was discovered in the halophilic γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1052| (at the time identified only as a species of |FRAME: TAX-1051|, hence the name ectoine) |CITS: [3838936]|, but is now known to be synthesized by a wide range of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. |FRAME: ECTOINE Ectoine| has commercial uses as an enzyme stabilizer and as a cell protectant in skin and health care applications, and is produced in an industrial process using the halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2746| as a producer strain., Ectoine levels are highly regulated according to external salt levels. In addition to a biosynthetic pathway in which ecotine is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: P101-PWY|), organisms employ a dedicated ectoine degradation pathway (described here) in which ectoine is degraded back to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|. Even though the pathway was studied in the halophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2746|, genome comparisons suggest that the ectoine degradation pathway exists predominantly in non-halophilic bacteria unable to synthesize ectoine |CITS: [20849449]|., The degradation of |FRAME: ECTOINE| begins with a dedicated hydrolase (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.44|) that converts it to |FRAME: CPD-19757|, followed by deacetylation to |FRAME: CPD-470|. Two more enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.76| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.M5|, complete the degradation to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|. In ectoine producers such as |FRAME: TAX-2746|, |FRAME: CPD-470| can either be degraded further to |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| or re-enter the ectoine synthesis pathway, forming a cycle of ectoine synthesis and degradation.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain. Recent, findings suggest that GABA has a role as a signal molecule in plants as well |CITS: [15003233]|. In animals and plants GABA is produced by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: GLUTDECARBOX-RXN "glutamate decarboxylase"|., The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|. Diiferent variants of both enzymes are known. The amino-group acceptor for the transamination can be either |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|) or |FRAME:PYRUVATE| (e.g. in the plant |FRAME: ORG-5862| |CITS: [Vancauwenberghe02]|). Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+., The action of glutamate decarboxylase, γ-aminobutyrate aminotransferase and succinate semialdehyde, dehydrogenase, combined, defines a short pathway known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. , While there is no evidence for a special role for GABA in bacteria, the capabillity to degrade it exists in many strains. GABA is present in the environment as a product of plant and animal tissue decay, and many bacteria can synthesize GABA as an intermediate in the degradation of putrescine (see |FRAME: Putrescine-Degradation "putrescine degradation"|). , The first indication for a bacterial pathway for GABA degradation was found in |FRAME: TAX-294|, |CITS:[13654294][13654295]|. While some organisms, like |FRAME: TAX-294|, can grow on GABA as the sole carbon and nitrogen source, others, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, can grow on it only as a nitrogen source |CITS: [8951816][12123465]|., About This Pathway, This variant of the pathway includes a |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent 4-aminobutyrate transaminase and an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase., This combination of enzymes has been documented in bacteria and animals and in some plants., The transaminase found in animals and bacteria utilizes |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (e.g. in mammalian brain |CITS: [13044808]|). While this form of enzyme appears to be a minor form in plants, studies of ripening tomatoes have shown that in this plant |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent activity is significantly higher (4200 times) than |FRAME:PYRUVATE|-dependent activity |CITS: [18713763]|., Regarding the hydrogenase, NAD-specific variant have been studied from many bacteria, fungi, plants and animals |CITS: [6995433][18713763][3190233]|.

Summary: General Background, 6-methoxymellein (6MM), an isocoumarin, is a rare phytoalexin produced in carrots upon infection with pathogenic microorganisms. This compound also accumulates in response to treatment with certain elicitors such as ethylene |CITS: [LAFUENTE96]|, buthionine sulfoximine, Cu2+ |CITS: [12231796]|, oligogalacturonides |CITS: [2806265]| and 2-chloroethylphosphonic acid |CITS: [KUROSAKI89]|., The biosynthetic formation of 6-methoxymellein proceed via the immediate polyketide precursor 6-hydroxymellein (6HM). , Those compounds have been found to affect mitotic activities and cell viability in carrot cell cultures upon increased , concentration. The observation that 6MM is more toxic than 6HM |CITS: [MARINELLI96]| fits in the former finding that, 6MM is readily degraded to 6HM or glucosylated as part of the detoxification metabolism in carrots |CITS: [KUROSAKI84]|. , About This Pathway, 6-methoxymellein is produced via the acetate-malonate pathway evoking the catalytic activities of two inducible enzymes, 6-hydroxymellein synthase synthase and 6-hydroxymellein-O-methyltransferase. Although genes of the pathway remain to be isolated the 6HM synthase has been thoroughly investigated and characterized (|CITS: [2806265]|, and thereafter). , The formation of 6-hydroxymellein is carried out by the 6HM synthase, a multifunctional polyketide enzyme |CITS: [8424647][1879555]|. The fully active enzyme (homodimer) catalyzes 2 reactions; the condensation of 1 acetyl-CoA and , 4 malonyl-CoA forms the pentaketamethylene chain and the NADPH dependent ketoreduction at the triketide intermediate , stage finalizes the formation of the dihydroisocoumarin skeleton |CITS: [2806265]|. Both identical monomer subunits are , aligned in a head-to-tail direction to form two complete reaction centers |CITS: [12423879]|. The monomers contain , functional domains of the ketoreduction and acyl condensation, but only the condensation reaction is functional in the , dissected monomer |CITS: [7639527]|. , In absence of NADPH or when the active homodimer is dissected into monomeric subunits triacetic acid lactone is liberated as a derailment product. The interruption of the keto-reducing reaction prevents the further condensation of malonyl-CoA producing the triketide product instead of 6 HM |CITS: [2806265]| |CITS: [8638933]|., The terminal step in the biosynthesis of 6-methoxymellein is catalyzed by an O-methyltransferase specific for the hydroxyl , moiety at the 6-position of isocoumarin |CITS: [KUROSAKI88]|. Besides 6 HM the only other substrate tested and accepted by the enzyme was 3,4-dehydro-6-hydroxymellein forming the corresponding 6-methoxy derivative.

General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-2208| is one of the few methanogenic species that are capable of methylotrophic methanogenesis, and can grow on various methyl-containing substrates such as |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME: METOH|, methylthiols and methylamines as a sole energy source., The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., Methyl transfer from |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE| to |FRAME: CoM| was reconstituted in vitro using three |FRAME: TAX-2208| proteins, which included a |FRAME:MONOMER-12211| MtbC, |FRAME:MONOMER-12205| (the isoform of MT2 specific for methanogenesis from methylamines), and |FRAME: CPLX-7102|., |FRAME:MONOMER-12211|, which binds 1.0 mol of corrinoid cofactor/mol of 24-kDa polypeptide, copurified with |FRAME:MONOMER-12205|. This complex was used to assay and purify the |FRAME: CPLX-7102|, MtbB1. MtbB1 is a 230-kDa protein composed of 51-kDa subunits. An MtbB1:MtbC ratio of 1 was optimal for coenzyme M methylation, with |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE|., Purified MtbB1, MtbC, and MtbA were the sole protein requirements for in vitro dimethylamine:coenzyme M methyl transfer. |FRAME: CPD-15212 Pulcherrimin| is a red extracellular pigment formed by a number of species of bacteria and some species of yeast after growth in media enriched in iron(III). It is an iron chelate of |FRAME: CPD-15211|, a hydroxamic acid derivative of the cyclic dipeptide |FRAME: CPD-15210| (|CITS: [16589308]| and references therein)., Pulcherrimin was first identified as a red pigment produced by the yeast |FRAME: TAX-27326 "Candida pulcherrima (also known as Torula pulcherrima or Torula rubefaciens and later renamed Metschnikowia pulcherrima|) |CITS: [Beijerinck08][16559644]|. It is formed via a nonenzymic reaction between |FRAME: CPD-15211| and iron(III) in the extracellular medium |CITS: [20690619]|., It has been suggested by Beijerinck that the production of the pigment is a defense reaction of the organism against a harmful effect of an excess of iron present in the medium |CITS: [Beijerinck08]|. This was supported by the observation that all strongly pigmented cells of |FRAME: TAX-27326| are non-viable |CITS: [ROBERTS]|., It was noted early on that pulcherrimin can also be produced by spore-forming bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [16589308][4968608]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is the second most abundant biologically produced polymer (|FRAME: CELLULOSE| is the most abundant). |FRAME: CHITIN "Chitin"| is found in the cell walls of fungi, yeast and green algae, as well as the exoskeletons of crustaceans (including planktonic types) and insects. In the marine environment |FRAME: CHITIN| is an abundant polysaccharide that is a source of carbon and nitrogen for marine organisms. Its degradation by several genera of marine chitinolytic bacteria is part of the cycling of nutrients in ocean water In addition to ocean water, chitinase genes have been identified in bacteria from freshwater and saline lakes, estuaries, and soil. The ability to degrade chitin appears to be limited to the Proteobacteria, Bactriodetes, Actinobacteria and Firmicutes (in |CITS: [17933912]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21607543]|). Some bacterial species have been shown to contain multiple chitinase genes to efficiently utilize different forms of |FRAME: CHITIN| and some of its by-products |CITS: [16535505]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CHITIN| catabolic pathway has been studied in species of the genus |FRAME: TAX-662| |CITS: [1761533][11850417][17933912][19553519]|. The proposed pathway shown here for |FRAME: TAX-666| and |FRAME: TAX-29494| involves a core set of genes that appear to be conserved in members of the family |FRAME: TAX-641|. The predicted gene functions are based on a combination of biochemical evidence in |FRAME: TAX-662| species, microarray expression data, experimental evidence, and bioinformatic predictions |CITS: [17933912]|. Overall, |FRAME: CHITIN| utilization is a highly complex process that has been divided into several stages (sensing, attachment, extracellular degradation, uptake and catabolism) and involves many genes |CITS: [14699052][14983042]|., The overall pathway spans the extracellular space, periplasm, and cytosol. This pathway shows the reactions that can occur in the cytosol, as proposed and summarized in |CITS: [17933912]|. The reactions occurring in the extracellular space and periplasm are described in pathway |FRAME: PWY-6902| as indicated by the pathway link. Transport of compounds from the periplasm into the cytosol is also indicated here. Click on the PTS transport links for transport figures., As described in the summary for pathway |FRAME: PWY-6902|, partially deacetylated chitooligosaccharides such as GlcNAc-GlcN (|FRAME: CPD-12274|) may also be deacetylated in the extracellular space or periplasm to form (GlcN)2 (|FRAME: CPD-13545|). This compound can undergo PTS transport from the periplasm into the cytosol with concomitant phosphorylation to |FRAME: CPD-15993| as shown in the transport reaction link |CITS: [17933912][14983042]|., In the cytosol |FRAME: CHITOBIOSE| is ultimately converted into two molecules of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| via the combined action of |FRAME: MONOMER-16878| which produces |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-1-P| and |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| |CITS: [10913116]|; N-acetylglucosamine -1-phosphate mutase which produces |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| |CITS: [14699052][17933912]|; and an ATP-dependent kinase specific for |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| (EC 2.7.1.59, |FRAME: MONOMER-16883|) |CITS: [1761533]|. The |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| generated by these enzymes, or by PTSGlcNAc transport, is ultimately converted into |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| via the combined action of |FRAME: CPLX-8363| |CITS: [8987551][9301118]| and |FRAME: MONOMER-16884| |CITS: [14983042][1761533]|. |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| enters central metabolism., After chitobiase cleavage of |FRAME: CPD-15993| which produces |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| and |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| |CITS: [14983042][17933912]|, and phosphorylation of the |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.8| |CITS: [11850417]|, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P| enters the final reaction in the pathway |CITS: [17933912]|., Overall, |FRAME: CHITIN| is degraded to monomers which are channeled into central metabolism as |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: AMMONIUM|) (|CITS: [17933912]| and reviewed in |CITS: [21607543]|)., The regulation of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| catabolism in |FRAME: TAX-666| is also relevant to its pathogenic mechanism in humans due to the presence of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| residues in glycosaminoglycans, glycoproteins and glycolipids. This regulation appears to be more complex than originally thought |CITS: [21488982]|. In a transcriptional regulation study, analysis of microarray expression data suggested the involvement of two gene clusters. In addition to the gene cluster encoding β-N-acetylglucosaminidase, the N-acetylglucosamine-specific transporter, N-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate deacetylase and glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase, which is under negative control by the |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine| specific repressor nagC, a second gene cluster is also involved in coordinate regulation, which is under positive control by nagC |CITS: [21488982]|.

Next to water, tea is the most consumed beverage worldwide. In the year 2000 the annual production of tea on about 2.3 million hectare exceeded 3 mill tons per year. About 75 percent of the worldwide tea production is black tea (fermented); about 23 percent is green tea (non-fermented); and about 2 percent is oolong tea (semi-fermented). The tropical to subtropical plant |FRAME:TAX-4442| represents the source of all non-herbal teas. Over millennia various cultivars have been bred to best accommodate the three mainstream teas which are distinguished by the length and procedure of fermentation |CITS:[Bliss03]|. , The typical tea aroma of black, green or oolong tea is formed during the fermentation process when complex mixtures of volatile aroma compounds are liberated |CITS:[Sanderson73]|. More than 600 volatiles have been described which define the aroma of fermented black and semi-fermented oolong tea |CITS:[Teranishi95]|. Many of those compounds providing the tea with its particular character are glycosidically bound aliphatic and mono- and sesquiterpene alcohols. The aroma forming alcohols in tea mostly occur as alcohol disaccharides |CITS:[ Matsumura97]| |CITS:[11087494]|. It has been found that β-primeverosides are 3-fold more abundant in tea plants than any other glucoside indicating that β-primeverosides are the major components for floral tea aroma formation |CITS:[11308343]|. Most of the various alcohols responsible for the aroma of tea, e.g. |FRAME: Linalools|, |FRAME:GERANIOL|, |FRAME:BENZYL-ALCOHOL|, |FRAME:CPD-7035| and |FRAME:CPD-6481| have been identified in Camilla sinensis as either β-primeveroside or acuminoside and β-vicianoside |CITS:[11087494]| |CITS:[7522061]| |CITS:[8704326]| |CITS:[7763947]| |CITS:[8987857]| |CITS:[11324911]| |CITS:[Yamada67]|., The cleavage of the glucosidic tea aroma precursors is catalyzed by a special diglucosidase, i.e. β-primeverosidase which almost exclusively hydrolyzes the glucosidic bond between aglycon and disaccharide but does not attack intra-glycosidic bonds between sugars |CITS:[Guo95]| |CITS:[11826969]|. β-Primeverosidases have been identified and biochemically characterized from all three teas of different fermentation, i.e. green tea |FRAME:TAX-542762| (cultivar Yabukita) |CITS:[Guo95]| |CITS:[12481100]|, oolong tea |FRAME:TAX-542762| (cultivar Shuixian) |CITS:[Ogawa97]| and black tea |FRAME:TAX-261999| (Assam) |CITS:[Ijima98]|. All three β-primeverosidases are very similar to each other with regard to molecular weight and catalytic properties and only show minor differences on the molecular level which was proposed to be due to posttranslational modifications |CITS:[12481100]|. Further research is on the way to characterize the molecular basics and catalytic mechanism of the β-primeverosidase in more detail |CITS:[18256510]| |CITS:[Han06]|., However, aroma formation through alcoholic aglycon liberation catalyzed by β-primeverosidases is just a useful by-product of a natural process humans use to their advantage. In the life of the tea plant the discharge of those various alcohols which are known to possess antimicrobial, antifungal |CITS:[9218354]| and insect-repellent properties |CITS:[11960742]| |CITS:[10517823]| is part of the defense mechanisms triggered by predator attacks which cause the damage of plant tissues (see also cyanogenesis, e.g. |FRAME:PWY-7089|).

General Background, |FRAME: Phytobilins Phytobilins| are tetrapyrrole molecules that are synthesized by plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Major classes of phytobilins are:, 1. |FRAME: Phycobilins Phycobilins|, which are the chromophores of |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins| |CITS: [16663825]| and some algal phytochromes |CITS: [8616213]|, 2. |FRAME: Phytochromobilins Phytochromobilins|, which are the chromophores of higher plants |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| |CITS: [1634523][7744741]|., |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins Phycobiliproteins| are light-harvesting accessory pigments of cyanobacteria, red algae and cryptophytes, and |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| are photoreversible light signal-transducing pigments of plants, some algae, and some cyanobacteria., One of the major phycobilins in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilin|. Phycobiliproteins from all marine cyanobacteria adapted to oceanic waters, including |FRAME: TAX-1129|, |FRAME: TAX-263510|, and |FRAME: TAX-1205|, are particularly rich in |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilin|, probably making it the most abundant phycobilin in the ocean. This chromophore absorbs blue-green light efficiently, with maximal absorption at 495 nm, a wavelength range prevailing in open oceanic subsurface waters and which is only poorly absorbed by |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|., A trichromatic |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilin|-containing phycobiliprotein has been described from |FRAME: TAX-84588|. That protein, |FRAME: R-Phycocyanins-V "R-phycocyanins-V"|, contains one |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilin| attached to the α subunit at αCis84, one |FRAME: Phycocyanobilins phycocyanobilin| attached to the β subunit at βCis82, and one |FRAME: Phycoerythrobilins phycoerythrobilin| attached to the β subunit at βCis153 |CITS: [19182270]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathways for the production of the four cyanobacterial |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-3702| pathway for |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| biosynthesis, have been elucidated. These five chromophores share a common precursor, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, which is the product of heme macrocycle cleavage by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18|. |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is subsequently reduced by one of several possible ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases., |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is converted to |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN| in two steps, catalyzed by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-13950| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13952|, encoded by the genes |FRAME: G-10652| and |FRAME: G-10653|, respectively |CITS: [11283349]|. |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOERYTHROBILIN| is converted to its isomer |FRAME: CPD-17223| either spontaneously or by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|. , Free |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilin| does not seem to exist. It has been shown that the bifunctionall |FRAME: MONOMER-18985| catalyzes the attachment of free |FRAME: CPD-17223| to the α subunit of |FRAME: R-Phycocyanins-V "R-phycocyanin V"| followed by its isomerization to |FRAME: Phycourobilins phycourobilin| |CITS: [19182270]|.

|FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., Fungi are believed to utilize oxalate in lignin degradation, nutrient availability, pathogenesis, and competition. There is good correlation between pathogenesis, virulence, and oxalate secretion., Solubility of soil nutrients is achieved by soil-living species, when cations freed by oxalate diffusing in clay layers increases the effective solubility of Al and Fe. Oxalate retained in hyphal mats of mycorrhizal species increases phosphate and sulfate availability. The formation of calcium oxalate crystals provides a reservoir of calcium in the ecosystem. The ability of oxalate to bind divalent cations permits detoxification of copper, particularly evident in wood preserved with copper salts. In addition, oxalate plays a unique role in lignocellulose degradation by wood-rotting basidiomycetes, acting as a low molecular mass agent initiating decay. In white-rot fungi oxalate also acts as a potential electron donor for lignin-peroxidase catalyzed reduction and chelates manganese, allowing the dissolution of Mn3+ from the manganese-enzyme complex and thus stimulating extracellular manganese peroxidase activity |CITS: [Dutton96]|., In fungi and in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1423|, oxalate can be metabolized by |FRAME: CPLX-8225|, a manganese-containing cupin family protein that generates |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an O<sub>2</sub>-dependent reaction |CITS: [11546787]|., The best characterized enzymes are from the white-rot wood-decaying fungus |FRAME: TAX-38945| |CITS: [1748632]|, the mold |FRAME: TAX-5061| |CITS: [5729956]| and the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [12056897]|.
