Summary: |FRAME:TAX-266| can utilize |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| as sole carbon source for aerobic growth., Studies showed that |FRAME: GLYOX| is the first product of glycolate utilization, and that the enzyme responsible for glyoxylate oxidation, |FRAME: MONOMER-15940|, was inducibly formed on transfer of the organism to glycolate-containing media |CITS: [14342490]|., In the early 60s a key intermediate in glyoxylate utilization was reported to be |FRAME: CPD-655| |CITS: [14194868][16749162]|. Enzymes catalyzing both its synthesis from glyoxylate and glycine (|FRAME: MONOMER-15946|) and its conversion into |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| (|FRAME: MONOMER-15938|) were reported to be induced during growth of |FRAME: ORG-6165| on glycolate as well as other substrates yielding glyoxylate. Based on this intermediate the pathway was named the β-hydroxyaspartate pathway. , However, in 2003 an enzyme similar to the described |FRAME: MONOMER-15946| was purified to homogeneity from the related organism |FRAME: ORG-6166| |CITS: [12835921]|. Characterization of the purified enzyme revealed that unlike the enzyme reported earlier, it was strictly D-specific as to the α-position of the substrate. The enzyme accepted both the threo and erythro forms at the β-position, although |FRAME: CPD-12739| is a far better substrate than |FRAME: CPD-12738| (about 100 fold)., Further insight into the pathway was obtained in 2019, with the discovery of an operon encoding all of the pathway's enzymes in |FRAME: ORG-57124|. The operon consisted of four structural genes and a putative transcriptional regulator, which were named bhcABCD and bhcR, respectively. The bhcABCD genes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were characterized |CITS: [31723261]|., BhcA is a PLP-dependent aminotransferase that transaminates |FRAME: GLYOX| into |FRAME: GLY| using |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| as the preferred amino group donor. BhcB functions as |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.184|. BhcC is an |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.41|, the key enzyme of the pathway that catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: GLYOX| and |FRAME: GLY| into |FRAME: CPD-12739|, and BchD is a |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.29|. Overall, the pathway converts two molecules of |FRAME: GLYOX| (C2) into |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| (C4) without the loss of carbon as CO2, consuming just one reducing equivalent (NADH) and regenerating the catalytic amino donor (|FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|), making it one of the most efficient glyoxylate assimilation pathways described so far |CITS: [31723261]|., The bhc gene cluster is widespread among the |FRAME: TAX-356| and |FRAME: TAX-204455| orders of the Alphaproteobacteria, and is also found in several gammaproteobacterial orders. Most of these species were isolated from marine habitats. In addition, 94% of the isolates that were found to carry the bhc gene cluster also encode glycolate oxidase in their genomes, enabling them to oxidize glycolate, which is common in the marine environment.

General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, The opportunistic pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287| can coexpress two distinct forms of lipopolysaccharides, known as the A-band and the B-band. The A-band, also known as the common antigen, is found in all strains, and consists primarily of a trisaccharide repeating unit of |FRAME: CPD-13829| |CITS: [Arsenault91]|. The B-band, which is the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen| of the organism, shows significant variability, and its composition defines the many immunologically distinct serotypes of |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [19710102]|., The serotype-specific O antigen (B-band) is a heteropolymer composed of repeats of two-to-five sugar residues., One of the components of the O-antigen of P. aeruginosa O6 is |FRAME: CPD-15665|. Formation of this compound in |FRAME: TAX-287| starts with |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, and requires two proteins, encoded by the |FRAME: G-17654| and |FRAME: G-10027| genes |CITS: [10627048][18065759]|., |FRAME: G-17654 WbpO| is a member of the sugar-nucleotide dehydrogenase family, which also includes |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.22| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.132|. Members of this enzyme family catalyse the NAD+-dependent 2-fold oxidation of an alcohol to an acid without the release of an aldehyde intermediate. WbpO is able to use both NAD+ and NADP+ with only a small difference in activity |CITS: [10931835]|., |FRAME: G-10027 WbpP| is an NAD+-binding SDR enzyme that functions as a 4-epimerase. It is a group 3 UDP-hexose 4-epimerase, meaning that it has a strong preference for N-acetylated substrates |CITS: [10747995]|. It was initially thought that |FRAME: G-10027| acts first |CITS: [10747995]|, but later shown that |FRAME: G-17654| acts before |FRAME: G-10027| |CITS: [18065759]|., |FRAME: CPD-15639| is also used by |FRAME: TAX-90370| as the main building block for a capsular polysaccharide coat known as the Vi antigen, which is important for virulence and is the basis of a current glycoconjugate vaccine. The Vi antigen backbone is composed of poly-α-(1→4)-linked N-acetylgalactosaminuronate, modified with O-acetyl residue at C-3 |CITS: [34896394]|.

Summary: This anaplerotic pathway replenishes the intermediates of the TCA cycle., |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.31| (PEPC), is an enzyme often associated with photosynthesis in C4 plants such as |FRAME: TAX-4577| (see |FRAME: PWY-241|). However, in C3 plants, such as |FRAME: TAX-3702|, this enzyme plays a role in several processes such as replenishing depleted |FRAME: PWY-5690 TCA cycle| compounds that have been used for nitrogen assimilation or other tasks |CITS: [17894783][20202167]|., The enzyme, which is the major anaplerotic source for the replenishement of TCA cycle intermediates, achieves this function by enabling the fixation of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| into |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|. Since the enzyme accepts only |FRAME: HCO3| molecules, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| needs to be converted to |FRAME: HCO3| by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7750| |CITS: [10515911]|., The pathway also plays an important part in some autotrophic bacteria and archaea such as the thermophilic methanogenic archaeon |FRAME: TAX-145262|. The organism is an autotrophic anaerobe that can grow on a gas mixture of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| as its carbon and energy sources, respectively. It possesses two oxaloacetate-synthesizing enzymes, |FRAME: CPLX-7747| and |FRAME: CPLX-7743| |CITS: [9478969]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-25411 Malbrancheamide| is a complex halogenated indole alkaloid produced by the terrestrial fungus |FRAME: TAX-78605|, which was isolated from bat detritus collected in a cave in Mexico |CITS: [Martinez-Luis06]| and by the marine fungus |FRAME: TAX-465706|, which was isolated from a marine invertebrate |CITS: [21682275]|. The compound contains a characteristic bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core., The malbrancheamides belong to a diverse family of biologically active prenylated indole alkaloids isolated mainly from various |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| species of fungi that are characterized by the presence of the unique bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core ring system. All of these compounds are derived from |FRAME: TRP|, a cyclic amino acid (|FRAME: PRO|, |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| or a derivative of one of those compounds), and one or two isoprene units. In addition to their structural diversity, members of this family have been attributed a variety of bioactivities, including (but not limited to) insecticidal, cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial properties., The bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane-containing compounds can be divided into two sub-categories: the |FRAME: 2-5-Diketopiperazines "diketopiperazines"| (DKPs) and the monoketopiperazines (MKPs). DKPs include the |FRAME: Stephacidins stephacidins|, |FRAME: Brevianamides brevianamides|, and |FRAME: Notoamides notoamides|, while MKPs include the |FRAME: Paraherquamides paraherquamides|, |FRAME: Asperparalines asperparalines|, |FRAME: Marcfortines marcfortines|, |FRAME: Chrysogenamides chrysogenamides|, and |FRAME: Malbrancheamides malbrancheamides|., |FRAME: CPD-25411 Malbrancheamide| was identified during a search for calmodulin antagonists, and several later studies have confirmed its significant vasorelaxant effect |CITS: [20939762][25643751]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of malbrancheamide begins with the condensation of |FRAME: PRO| and |FRAME: TRP| by the non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) |FRAME: G-107668 MalG|, generating a cyclo-L-tryptophan-L-proline analog. The NRPSs involved in the biosynthesis of MKPs and DKPs differ: in DKP-producing systems, the NRPS contains a terminal condensation domain, responsible for production of the DKP compound |FRAME: CPD-15265| (cyclo-L-Trp-L-Pro). In MKP-producers the NRPS terminal domain is a reductase that catalyzes off-loading of a reduced Pro-Trp compound leading to a monoketopiperazine intermediate such as |FRAME: CPD-25421| |CITS: [20722388][23213353]|., The tryptophanyl subunit of the dipeptide is subsequently prenylated in a reverse manner, and the product undergoes spontaneous oxidation, forming a |FRAME: CPD-25425 "prenylated zwitterion compound"|. The pathway proceeds with the action of the bifunctional MalC, which first reduces the zwitterion compound, then catalyzes an intramolecular [4+2] Diels-Alder reaction that forms the bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core |CITS: [23213353][31548667]|. The involvement of an intramolecular [4+2] Diels-Alder reaction in the formation of the bicyclo[2.2.2]diazaoctane core was proposed already in 1970 |CITS: [Porter70]|, but the responsible enzyme was identified only in 2019 |CITS: [31548667]|, The last steps in the pathway are catalyzed by a flavin-dependent halogenase that successively adds two chloride groups |CITS: [28777910]|., In |FRAME: TAX-465706|, but not in |FRAME: TAX-78605|, |FRAME: CPD-25411| is modified further into |FRAME: CPD-25420| |CITS: [21682275]|.

Names: indole-3-acetate degradation I // indole-3-acetic acid degradation I
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN "Indole-3-acetate"| (IAA) is the main auxin hormone in plants, controlling many important physiological processes including cell enlargement and division, tissue differentiation, and responses to light and gravity. Many bacterial species have evolved the ability to produce IAA, and can thus interfere with any of these processes by input of IAA into the plant, directing its physiological responses in a way advantagious to the bacteria. While some IAA-producing bacteria are considered pathogens (e.g. |FRAME:TAX-358|), others, such as |FRAME:TAX-375|, have a beneficial effect |CITS: [KANESHIRO83]|., In addition to IAA synthesis, some bacterial species are able to catabolize IAA. This phenomenon was recognized as early as 1958, and over the years many isolates were reported to have this capability |CITS: [13541474][tsubokura61][Libbert69][5370530][Mino70] [1856182][7592320][15870323]|., Studies with |FRAME: ORG-6229| showed that |FRAME: CATECHOL| is formed, and the involvement of the |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.1 cat| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.24 pca| genes suggested that the catechol is further processed via the |FRAME:CATECHOL-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY "β-ketoadipate pathway"| |CITS: [18205812]|., About This Pathway, An 8994-bp DNA fragment from the chromosome of |FRAME: ORG-6229| was shown to confer the ability to utilize IAA upon |FRAME: TAX-160488|, an organism that does not have that ability naturally. That locus, named iac (for indole 3-acetate catabolism), contains ten genes |CITS: [18205812][23881445]|. Copies of this gene cluster have been found in members of the Alphaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, and Actinobacteria., Gene inactivation studies indicated that the pathway starts with a monooxygenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-17618| gene, which hydroxylates |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN|, forming |FRAME: CPD-15555|. The next enzyme is also a monooxygenase, and forms |FRAME: DIOXINDOLE-3-ACETATE| |CITS: [23881445]| (that enzyme was originally attributed to the |FRAME: G-17619| gene, but was later shown to be heteromeric, with the other subunit encoded by the |FRAME: G-63050| gene |CITS: [27795307]|)., The next enzyme in the pathway is a dioxygenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-80473| and |FRAME: G-80474| genes (|FRAME: G-80475| and |FRAME: G-80476| may encode the reductase component for this enzyme). In addition, presence of the iacI gene accelerates IAA degradation and prevents catechol accumulation, suggesting that it too is involved in the pathway |CITS: [27795307]|. While the final product of the pathway is |FRAME: CATECHOL|, the exact transformation from |FRAME: DIOXINDOLE-3-ACETATE| to |FRAME: CATECHOL| is still unknown., Some differences in the pathway were noticed in a study of the plant-growth-promoting rhizobacterium |FRAME: TAX-398527|. In this organism the iac cluster contains several additional genes, including several transporters. It was found that |FRAME: DIOXINDOLE-3-ACETATE|, the second intermediate of the pathway, is exported out of the cells, and continued processing requires a dedicated transporter, encoded by the iacT1 gene, that imports the compound back into the cell. A putative tautomerase encoded by the iacY gene is also involved in the import process |CITS: [27795307]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-22802 "Microcin B17"| (MccB17) is a linear azol(in)e-containing peptide (LAP) that functions as a narrow-spectrum bactericidal peptide. The peptide, which is produced by |FRAME: TAX-562| strains that carry the pMccB17 plasmid, targets DNA gyrase, and is produced by bacteria to inhibit the growth of similar bacterial strains |CITS: [3086495][1846808][21904817]|. It is active mostly against Enterobacteriaceae and some Pseudomonas species, due to its limited ability to enter cells of other genera., MccB17 was the first compound discovered from the thiazole/oxazole-modified microcins family and from the linear azole-containing peptides. The name microcin indicates a small size (<10 kDa), unlike the larger colicins., About the Pathway, The genes encoding production of the peptide are present on plasmid pMccB17 |CITS: [2993228]|. The precursor peptide is encoded by the mcbA gene and has the amino acid sequence MELKASEFGV VLSVDALKLS RQSPLGVGIG GGGGGGGGGS CGGQGGGCGG CSNGCSGGNG GSGGSGSHI, which comprises a 26-amino-acid leader sequence and a 43-amino-acid glycine-rich core peptide. All four |FRAME: CYS| and four of the six |FRAME: SER| residues in the core peptide are modified by |FRAME: EC-6.2.2.2|, to azoline residues, which are further oxidized to azole rings by |FRAME: EC-1.3.3.16|. These modifications are catalyzed by a octomeric synthetase comprising four copies of |FRAME: G-80604 McbB| (a substrate recognition module), two copies of |FRAME: G-80606 McbC| (an azoline dehydrogenase module), and two copies of |FRAME: G-80605 McbD| (an azoline synthase module) |CITS: [30661981]|., Heterocycles are introduced sequentially from the N terminus to the C terminus of the McbA precursor peptide, with each one being fully formed before the next. Reduced azoline cycles have never been observed during MccB17 biosynthesis, suggesting tight coupling of the two reactions |CITS: [9662507][10200165]|., Following generation of the azole rings the leader peptide is removed by the endogenous heterodimeric metallopeptidase |FRAME: 76890-MONOMER TldD|/|FRAME: 107410-MONOMER PmbA|, which is encoded on the |FRAME: TAX-562| chromosome |CITS: [2082149][12029038][28943336]|. The remaining 43-amino-acid modified core peptide is exported to the periplasm by a two-component ABC transporter, encoded by the |FRAME: G-80607|/|FRAME: G-80608| genes in the mccb17 cluster on the plasmid |CITS: [3049078]|., Microcin B17 is imported into target cells by two membrane proteins - the outer membrane protein OmpF and the plasma membrane protein SmbA. Once inside the cells, the peptide inhibits DNA gyrase and triggers double strand breaks in DNA.

Summary: The citrulline degradation pathway is widely distributed among prokaryotic organisms, often associated with the degradation of arginine into citrulline (see |FRAME: ARGDEGRAD-PWY|), it has been detected in lactic bacteria |CITS: [10359490][10733246][15939575]|, bacilli |CITS: [4436643][690081]|, |FRAME:TAX-286| spp. |CITS: [6438064][3129535]|, |FRAME:TAX-642| spp. |CITS: [6303241]|, clostridia |CITS: [12999794][5335895]|, |FRAME:TAX-2093| spp. |CITS: [5911610][126306][6438064][3806049]|, streptococci |CITS: [2843090]|, |FRAME:TAX-2132| spp. |CITS: [Igwebe78]|, Spirochaeta spp. |CITS: [977548]|, halobacteria |CITS: [5903088]|, and cyanobacteria |CITS: [100070]|., In addition, the pathway is also present in some primitive eukaryotic protozoans, including |FRAME: TAX-5722| |CITS: [6312311]|, |FRAME: TAX-56690| |CITS: [7866382]|, |FRAME: TAX-28002| |CITS: [12706792]|, and |FRAME: TAX-5741|, in which it plays a significant role in energy metabolism, providing a route for anaerobic substrate level phosphorylation |CITS: [2228433]|. , The enzymes of this pathway, as well as arginine deiminase, have also been found in |FRAME: ORG-5993|, and it was, shown that |FRAME:TAX-3701| chloroplasts can metabolize arginine and citrulline all the way to CO2., However, since |FRAME:TAX-3701| rarely encounters exogenous citrulline, it is thought that in this organism the pathway may serve as a means for extracting nitrogen from endogenous sources |CITS: [8278506]|. The ornithine carbamoyltransferase (OTC) has been identified from a T-DNA-tagged mutant of |FRAME:TAX-3701| and has been shown to be encoded by a gene that overlaps with another, unrelated gene (AUL1), one of the rare cases of gene convergence observed in Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [10561504]|. Ornithine carbamoyltransferase has also been cloned from other plant sources such as |FRAME:TAX-3888| |CITS: [8914525]| and |FRAME:TAX-28957| |CITS: [10987149]| |CITS: [11575720]|., Bacteria that employ this pathway use the enzyme ornithine carbamoyltransferase to convert |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| to |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P|. The later is then broken into |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an ATP-forming reaction, catalyzed by the enzyme carbamate kinase, providing the bacteria with energy, carbon and nitrogen., While this pathway is a subset of the arginine deiminase pathway, some of the organisms that employ it lack the enzyme arginine deiminase (for example, |FRAME: TAX-1247| |CITS: [15939575]|), and thus are not able to utilize arginine, making this a distinct pathway.

Reactions of pathway: RXN-13570 // HAONITRO-RXN // AMONITRO-RXN // RXN-12130 // NITRITE-REDUCTASE-CYTOCHROME-RXN // NITRIC-OXIDE-REDUCTASE-RXN
Summary: Nitrifier denitrification is a pathway found in autotrophic ammonia oxidizers as well as many methane oxidizing bacteria. In this pathway, which was first described in 1972 |CITS: [5073730]|, |FRAME: AMMONIA| is oxidized to |FRAME: NITRITE|, which is consequently reduced via |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| and |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE| to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [8580647][Wrage01]|. Not all of the |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE| is converted to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE|. Unlike respiratory denitrification, most characterized nitrifier denitrification pathways terminate with the production of |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, which is a potent greenhouse gas |CITS: [22103535][22103534]|. The pathway is thought to contribute as much, and perhaps more, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE| to the atmosphere as heterotrophic denitrification in terrestrial |CITS: [Webster96]| and marine |CITS:[Dore98]| ecosystems., In addition, the pathway shown here also shows the production of |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| by |FRAME: CPLX-1321|, a well-documented secondary activity of this protein |CITS: [497235]|., This pathway should not be confused with the combined effect of |FRAME: AMMOXID-PWY "ammonia oxidation to nitrite"| (carried out by ammonia oxidizers), followed by |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY "regular denitrification"| performed by heterotrophic organisms under anaerobic conditions. Nitrifier denitrification, also known as aerobic denitrification, occurs under fully oxic to hypoxic conditions (despite technically being classified as anaerobic respiration, since O<sub>2</sub> does not serve as the terminal electron acceptor). The process is especially active during limiting O<sub>2</sub> conditions and high nitrite concentrations., The pathway has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-914| and |FRAME: TAX-35798| spp., both of which are known to reduce |FRAME: NITRITE| and release substantial quantities of |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE| |CITS: [Dundee01][16423010]|, as well as in methane oxidizing bacteria |CITS: [21682764][22103534]|. In the latter organisms, |FRAME: CPLX-3222 "methane monooxygenase"| catalyzes the first step - oxidation of ammonia to hydroxylamine., The second step of the pathway appears to be catalyzed in both organisms by hydroxylamine dehydrogenase, and the third step is catalyzed in ammonia oxidizers by the |FRAME: CPLX-8527 "NirK nitrite reductase"|. In some methane oxidizers, such as |FRAME: TAX-414|, there are no known NO-producing (NirK and NirS) nitrite reductases in the genome. It has been suggested that in these organisms a C-terminal truncated hydroxylamine dehydrogenase may be involved in the reduction of nitrite to nitric oxide |CITS: [18650926]|, or alternatively, that this reaction is catalyzed by reversely operating hydroxylamine dehydrogenase |CITS: [21682764]|., The 4th step is likely catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8528 cNOR|, and in addition by |FRAME: CPLX-8529 sNOR| in ammonia-oxidizers and by |FRAME: CPLX-8523| in methane oxidizers. Little information is available regarding the ultimate step (reduction to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE|) in these organisms., Several proposals have been made regarding the physiological role of the pathway, including (1) the conservation of O<sub>2</sub> under microaerophilic conditions for ammonia oxidation, by using alrternative electron acceptors for other steps (2) the removal of the large amounts of toxic nitrite formed by ammonia oxidation and (3) the decrease in competition for O<sub>2</sub> with aerobic nitrite oxidizers through the removal of |FRAME: NITRITE| |CITS: [16346787]|. However, it is usually accepted that the main role of the pathway is to remove intracellular nitrite to prevent its toxicity.

Summary: Galactarate is a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid analog of D-galactose. |FRAME:TAX-562| can use both, diacid sugars galactarate and D-glucarate as the sole source of carbon for growth. The initial step in the, degradation of galactarate is its dehydration to 5-keto-4-deoxy-Dglucarate by, |FRAME: GALACTARDEHYDRA-MONOMER|. The subsequent steps in this pathway, cleavage of, 5-keto-4-deoxy-Dglucarate into pyruvate and tartronate semialdehyde by |FRAME: CPLX0-7615|, reduction, of tartronate semialdehyde to D-glycerate by |FRAME: TSA-REDUCT-MONOMER|, and phosphorylation of, D-glycerate to form 2-phosphoglycerate by |FRAME: GKI-MONOMER|, are shared with the, |FRAME: GLUCARDEG-PWY| pathway., Review: Mandrand-Berthelot, M.-A., Condemine, G., and Hugouvieux-Cotte-Pattat, N., EcoSal Module 3.4.2, |CITS: [ecosal]|

Names: spermine and spermidine degradation II // polyamine degradation II // polyamine terminal catabolic pathway
Summary: General Background, Polyamines are widespread in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, with spermine, spermidine, and putrescine being the most abundant ones. Polyamines play important roles in cell growth and differentiation, in response to abiotic stress such as potassium deficiency, osmotic shock, drought and salt stress, and in plant-pathogen interactions. , In plants, polyamines can be degraded via two routes, the so-called terminal catabolic pathway and the back-conversion pathway. In both cases, H2O2 was produced as a by-product. In the |FRAME: PWY-6440 "terminal catabolic pathway"| plant apoplastic polyamine oxidases (PAOs) oxidize spermine and spermidine to |FRAME: CPD-313|, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the corresponding aminoaldehydes. These compounds cannot be converted directly to other polyamines. Therefore, this route is referred to as the terminal catabolic pathway |CITS: [16406305]|. In the |FRAME: PWY-6441 "back-conversion pathway"|, polyamines are interconverted. The peroxisome-localized PAOs oxidize spermine to spermidine, and consequently oxidize spermidine to putrescine |CITS: [18583528]|. Putrescine can be further degraded by putrescine oxidase (see |FRAME: PWY-2|)., About This Pathway, The terminal catabolic pathway has only been found in monocots. PAOs involved in this route have been characterized in maize, barley, millet, and oat |CITS: [1366693]|. The association of these PAOs with cell walls suggested they could play specific roles in apoplastic processes such as cell wall maturation and lignification, wound healing, and cell wall reinforcement during pathogen invasion. |FRAME: CPD-313 "Propane-1,3-diamine"| formed from either spermine or spermidine, is a precursor in |FRAME: PWY-3981|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Methanofurans Methanofurans| are a group of related carbon-carrier cofactors involved in the first step of the methanogenic reduction of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|). Methanofurans react with |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to form the carbamate N-carboxymethanofuran, which is reduced to |FRAME: Formyl-methanofurans| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.12|., In addition, the cofactor also participates at a later stage of all methanogenesis pathways. These pathways converge at the compound |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|; the latter process involves methanofuran (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|)., Methanofuran is also used by methylotrophic bacteria as a coenzyme to oxidize formaldehyde to formate |CITS: [9651254][11532013]|., Methanofurans are the only cofactors known to contain a furan moiety, although furans have been identified in polyketides and fatty acid derived natural products, and are often formed during the heating or oxidation of carbohydrates |CITS: [12013276]|., The chemical structure of methanofuran varies among different methanogens. At this time (2014) five variants have been characterized:, |FRAME: CPD-17181| (from |FRAME: TAX-145262|) |CITS: [1517208]|, |FRAME:CPD-7628| (from |FRAME: TAX-2208|) |CITS: [2883935]|, |FRAME:CPD-7629| (from |FRAME: TAX-2173|) |CITS: [3170480]|, |FRAME: methanofuran-d| (from |FRAME: TAX-2190|) |CITS: [25203397]| and |FRAME: CPD-17182| (from |FRAME: TAX-39152|, |FRAME: TAX-2187| and |FRAME: TAX-155863|) |CITS: [25203397]|., All methanofurans contain the basic core structure of 4-[N-γ-L-glutamyl-γ-L-glutamyl)-p-(β-aminoethyl)phenoxymethyl]-2-(aminomethyl)furan, but with different attached side chains., About This Pathway, For many years the pathway leading to the biosynthesis of methanofuran was poorly understood. An initial pathway was proposed based on isotope incorporation patterns and observed intermediates, but was rather inaccurate |CITS: [White87][3166985][1517208][16349232]|. Isotope incorporation data also showed that the |FRAME:TYRAMINE| moiety is produced from |FRAME:TYR|, and let to the identification of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.25| from |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [15715981]|., The early part of the pathway was established almost 20 years later, when the route leading to synthesis of the 5-(aminomethyl)-3-furanmethanol moiety of methanofuran was described, along with the associated genes |CITS: [24977328]|. This was closely followed by discovery of |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.24| |CITS: [25211225]|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.31| |CITS: [26100040]| and |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.131| |CITS: [26100040]|.

Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towrds complete mineralization., About This Pathway, This pathway shares several steps with the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6609|. However, the salvage pathway starts with the free base |FRAME: ADENINE| (which is often transported into the organism) and ends with the nucleotide |FRAME: IMP|, leading to biosynthesis of nucleotides, while this degradation pathway starts with the nucleotide form (|FRAME: AMP|) and ends with |FRAME: URATE|, which in most organisms is degraded further, providing the organism with carbon, nitrogen and energy., A key enzyme in this pathway is adenosine deaminase, which converts |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: INOSINE|. This has been shown to be the main form of adenosine degradation by the fungi |FRAME: TAX-36642| |CITS: [7551735]| and |FRAME:TAX-293373| |CITS: [15812856]|., Xanthine degradation to allantoin has been observed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, but this degradation does not progress past allantoin or allantoate and this catabolism does not suffice as a source of nitrogen under aerobic growth conditions |CITS: [10986234]|.

General Background, There are several alternative pathways for the degradation of trehalose., Depending on the organism, trehalose may enter the cell either through a permease, in which case it, remains unmodified, or it may be transported by a phosphotransferase system (PTS), resulting in the, phoshorylated trehalose-6-phosphate form., Degradation then proceeds by different mechanisms: , Unmodified trehalose may be degraded by a hydrolyzing trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|), or it may, be split by the action of a trehalose phosphorylase (see|FRAME: PWY-2722| and |FRAME: PWY-2723|)., Likewise, trehalose-6-phosphate may be either hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase, (see |FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) or it could be attacked by a trehalose-6-phosphate phosphorylase, (see |FRAME: PWY-2721|). , About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1358| degrades phosphorylated trehalose by the action of an inorganic phosphate-dependent, |FRAME: MONOMER-5861| (TrePP) |CITS: [11553642]|., Trehalose enters the cell by a transport reaction through a trehalose PTS, which phosphorylates it into, trehalose-6-phosphate. , TrePP then catalyzes the reversible conversion of trehalose 6-phosphate into |FRAME: CPD-448|, and |FRAME:GLC-6-P| |CITS: [11553642]|. |FRAME: CPD-448| is then converted to, |FRAME:GLC-6-P| by a β-specific phosphoglucomutase (β-PGM), and the two , β-glucose 6-phosphate molecules enter glycolysis |CITS: [11571154]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-25183 "Rosmarinic acid"| (RA) is an ester of |FRAME: CAFFEATE| and |FRAME: CPD-6982|. It is widely spread in species of the |FRAME: TAX-4136| and |FRAME: TAX-21571| |CITS: [12482446]| and also occurs in some lower plants such as ferns and hornworts |CITS: [TAKEDA90]| |CITS: [12721853]|. It was first isolated in 1958 from rosemary (|FRAME: TAX-39367|), which is the source of its name. The 3'-O-β-glucoside of RA (|FRAME:CPD-7018|) has been identified in the hornwort |FRAME: TAX-41834| |CITS: [16133208]|, where it accumulates up to 1% of the cell dry weight. Other rosmarinic acid derivatives of biological importance are |FRAME: CPD-26619 "lithospermic acid"|, a conjugate of rosmarinic acid and caffeic acid, and |FRAME: CPD-26620 "lithospermic acid B", which is a dimer of rosmarinic acid |CITS: [12482446]|., Rosmarinic acid is used in foods or beverages as a flavoring, in cosmetics, and as a dietary supplement. Its biosynthesis has been studied extensively |CITS: [11943155]|., About This Pathway, The first report about the biosynthetic route of rosmarinic acid was published in 1970 |CITS: [5484678]| demonstrating the involvement of two aromatic amino acids, L-tyrosine and L-phenylalanine in the biogenesis of rosmarinate. Since then the entire pathway has been elucidated, mostly in |FRAME: TAX-4142| (|FRAME: TAX-4136|) including most of the involved enzymatic steps |CITS: [PETERSEN93]| |CITS: [PETERSEN93]|., Coumaroyl-CoA is one of the essential components being used for the assembly of rosmarinic acid. It is derived from , L-phenylalanine in three well characterized enzymatic steps in plants catalyzed by L-phenylalanine-ammonia-lyase , (PAL), cinnamic acid 4-hydroxylase (C4H) and 4-coumaric acid-CoA ligase (4CL) (compare |FRAME:PWY1F-467|). , Some of those enzymes have been purified from lower plants like hornworts as well |CITS: 12721853[]| indicating that the general biosynthetic route of rosmarinic acid seems to be identical in higher and lower plants., The other metabolic branch contributing to the biosynthesis of RA originates from L-tyrosine resulting in the formation of 4-hydroxyphenyllactate (4HPL). The two moieties of the parallel pathways are connected by rosmarinic acid synthase (RAS) catalyzing a transesterification reaction |CITS: [PETERSEN88]| |CITS: [PETERSEN91]|. The RAS accepted caffeoyl-CoA and 3,4-dihydroxyphenyllactic acid (DHPL) resulting in the formation of rosmarinic acid. It should be noted that only the R(+)-stereoisomer of 3,4-dihydroxyphenyllactic acid is accepted by the RAS. On the other side 4-coumaroyl-CoA and either DHPL or its monohydroxylated isomer, 4-hydroxyphenyllactic acid (PHPL) was converted to their corresponding coumaroyl-hydroxyphenyllactates. The enzymatic capability of RAS and the precedent enzyme hydroxypuruvate reductase |CITS: [HAUSLER91]| |CITS: [15284489]| to accept different substrates (mono- or dihydroxylated forms of phenyllactates/phenylacetates) prompted the proposition for a potential second biosynthetic route for RA (|FRAME:PWY-5049|)., The last steps in this pathway are catalyzed by two cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenases introducing hydroxyl groups to the 3- and 3'-position of 4-coumaroyl-4'-hydroxyphenyllactate |CITS: [PETERSEN97]| |CITS: [11943155]|. Whereas the 3-hydroxylation of this hydroxycinnamic acid ester has been established the 3'-hydroxylation has yet to be fully characterized.

Summary: Catechol can be degraded via either of two routes: the meta cleavage pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5430|), or the ortho-cleavage pathway (this pathway). When degraded by this pathway, catechol is cleaved between the two ring hydroxyls by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-2842| forming |FRAME:CIS-CIS-MUCONATE|, which is then further metabolyzed in three steps to the important intermediate |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE|., |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE| is a convergence point of the two branches of the β-ketoadipate pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-5431|); one of the branches is this pathway, while the other one starts with protocatechuate (see |FRAME:PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|. Once β-Ketoadipate is formed, it is converted to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA., The pathway is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi, even though its organization and regulation vary among species |CITS:[15421941][8905091][3941043][16885292]|. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-303| the genes that encode the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of this pathway are clustered into two distinct groups |CITS: [761399]|, while in |FRAME: TAX-471| they are arranged in a single cluster induced by protocatechuate |CITS: [7961399]|., In |FRAME: TAX-303| the enzymes involved in β-ketoadipate degradation (|FRAME:CPLX-2722|, and |FRAME:CPLX-7260|) are inducible by |FRAME:3-KETO-ADIPATE| |CITS: [5916393]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Organophosphonates| are organic compounds containing C-PO(OH)2 or C-PO(OR)2 groups (where R can be either an alkyl or an aryl group). Phosphonates are quite common among different organisms, including both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. They occur primarily as components of phosphonolipids (|FRAME: CPD-1106| is a common phosphonate constituent of phospholipids, analogous to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE|). In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics., Many bacterial species can utilize organophosphonates as the sole source of phosphorous |CITS: [16245012]|. Breaking the C-P bond, which is much more stable than the C-O-P phosphoester bonds of phosphates, requires special enzymes |CITS: [7765831]|., The utilization of |FRAME: CPD0-1068|, the most common organophosphonate, has been studied in detail and several different pathways have been described., About This Pathway, The pathway begins with a nucleophilic attack of |FRAME: CPD0-1068| on the anomeric carbon of ATP to form adenine and |FRAME: CPD0-2479|, a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.37|, an enzyme complex composed of four polypeptides encoded by the |FRAME: EG10716|, |FRAME: EG10717|, |FRAME: EG10718| and |FRAME: EG10721| genes., The pathway continues by phosphohydrolysis of pyrophosphate (catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.63|) to form |FRAME: CPD0-2480|, the substrate of the enzyme that actually cleaves the C-P bond. The cleavage, performed by |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1| in a SAM-requiring radical-based reaction, produces |FRAME: CPD0-2463| and |FRAME: CH4| |CITS: [22089136]|., The obesrvation of methane production by C-P lyase has explained why vast sections of the aerobic ocean are supersaturated with methane |CITS: [Karl08][22936780]|., In the majority of organophosphonate-degrading bacteria the cyclic phosphate is cleaved by |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.55| to form |FRAME: RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [19366688]|. In a small number of organisms a different enzyme produced |FRAME: CPD-15317| (see |FRAME: PWY-7399|).

General Background, Curcumin and other curcuminoids are plant secondary metabolites produced by |FRAME:TAX-136217| (turmeric) (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-6432|). Curcumin is the main yellow pigment of turmeric which is used as a spice and a pigment. In addition, curcumin has a range of medicinal properties including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and analgesic. Curcumin metabolism has been studied in humans and rodents and the production of reduced dihydro-, tetrahydro-, hexahydro- and octahydrocurcumin derivatives has been identified, with tetrahydrocurcumin and hexahydrocurcumin being the major products. These reduced curcumin derivatives may then be conjugated to form glucuronides, sulfates, or mixed glucuronides/sulfates. However, the mammalian enzymes and their encoding genes responsible for production of the reduced curcumin derivatives have not been identified. Tetrahydrocurcumin has been shown to have more potent antioxidative activity than curcumin (in |CITS: [21467222]| and reviewed in |CITS: [17569222]|)., Intestinal microorganisms have also been shown to metabolize curcumin. Curcumin metabolizing microorganisms were found in samples of human feces and the organism with the highest curcumin converting activity was isolated, cultured and identified as |FRAME:TAX-562|. High curcumin converting activity was also identified in |FRAME:TAX-562| K-12 substr. DH10B whose genome sequence has been determined. The curcumin metabolizing enzyme was purified from extracts of this organism and used to identify its encoding gene. Following gene cloning and overexpression, the recombinant enzyme was purified and characterized. The results showed that |FRAME:TAX-562| gene yncB (annotated as predicted oxidoreductase, Zn-dependent and NAD(P)-binding) encoded the curcumin-converting enzyme and it was renamed curA |CITS: [21467222]|., About This Pathway , The purified product of |FRAME:TAX-562| gene curA was shown to catalyze the NADPH-dependent, sequential reduction of curcumin first to the stable intermediate dihydrocurcumin, and then to the final end product tetrahydrocurcumin. These compounds were identified by mass spectrometry techniques. How curcumin enters the |FRAME:TAX-562| cell and the fate of tetrahydrocurcumin in |FRAME:TAX-562| is not yet known. However, the optimum culture conditions for curcumin-converting enzyme formation in |FRAME:TAX-562| K-12 substr. DH10B included the use of 0.03% curcumin as the sole carbon source and 0.3% yeast extract as nitrogen source, suggesting further metabolism of curcumin under these conditions. It has also been speculated that tetrahydrocurcumin produced by human or animal gut microorganisms may be used for various activities in the body |CITS: [21467222]|.

Summary: De novo synthesis of cobamides requires a great deal of genetic information, which is only found in some prokaryotes., Many bacterial species do not have the full genetic information required for de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, but can synthesize cobalamin when supplied with |FRAME: COBINAMIDE|, a stable cobamide that is not a true intermediate of the de novo pathway |CITS: [14351147][8770581]|., In order to process |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, it has to be converted into a real intermediate of the pathway. In most bacteria this is done by the attachment of the upper ligand 5'-deoxyadenosine to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE|, followed by phosphorylation to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P|, an intermediate of the de novo biosynthetic pathway (see |FRAME: COBALSYN-PWY|)., Archaebacteria utilze a different salvage pathway, where |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| is first converted to |FRAME: CPD-691| by |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.90| (CbiZ). |FRAME: CPD-691 " Adenosylcobyrate"| is then converted to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P| by the action of |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.10| (CbiB) |CITS: [14990804]|., Archaea possess several enzymes that are non-orthologous replacements for the bacterial genes. For example, the archaeal |FRAME: G-11341| catalyzes the same reaction as the bacterial |FRAME: G-10054| |CITS: [16547066]|, and the archaeal |FRAME: G-11343| replaces the bacterial |FRAME: G-502| and |FRAME: G-10056| |CITS: [12486068]|., Some archaea carry the |FRAME: G-11342| gene, which encodes a fusion of the genes |FRAME: G-11339| and |FRAME: G-11341| |CITS: [16740929]|., There are many bacterial species that carry the genes of the archaeal salvage pathway. It is believed that the origin of the genes is archaeal, and that the bacterial genes were acquired by horizontal gene transfer |CITS: [18808385]|

|FRAME: D-ALANINE| is a key component of peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall and is an important component of the dissolved organic matter (DOM) pool of seawater. It represents 44% and 21-40% of total dissolved alanine in deep waters of the eastern Arctic ocean and North Atlantic waters, respectively |CITS: [Dittmar01][Perez03]|., |FRAME: TAX-562716|, isolated from a marine sediment |CITS: [19301066]|, can kill a variety of Gram-positive bacteria with diverse peptidoglycan chemotypes and utilize the released peptidoglycan-derived |FRAME: D-ALANINE| and |FRAME: D-GLT| for growth |CITS: [31941905]|. The organism can grow with 50 mM glucose and 2 mM |FRAME: D-ALANINE|, and the growth increases with the concentration of |FRAME: D-ALANINE| up to 20 mM, at which point it becomes inhibitory |CITS: [34818098]|., The organism catabolizes |FRAME: D-ALANINE| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.21|. The enzyme showed high activities toward |FRAME: D-ALANINE| using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| as the amino group acceptor, but almost no activity toward |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| |CITS: [34818098]|. Over-expression of the gene in its native host allowed the organism to grow at concentration of |FRAME: D-ALANINE| up to 50 mM. The products of the enzyme are |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which can be processed via glycolysis, and a D-amino acid, most likely |FRAME: D-GLT|, which can be used for peptidoglycan biosynthesis |CITS: [34818098]|., Bioinformatic analyses showed that homologs of the enzyme are prevalent in genomes of marine bacteria and metagenomes, especially in seawater samples, and that the predominant group that possesses the gene is the |FRAME: TAX-1236| |CITS: [34818098]|.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine nucleotides can be catabolized through three different pathways. The best characterized is the reductive pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6430| and |FRAME: PWY-3982|), in which the pyrimidine nucleotides are reduced to |FRAME: Beta-amino-acids|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. The pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms |CITS: [13428755][13416173][16655478][16656066][10656811]|. The oxidative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6426|) is only found in a few bacterial species and has not been characterized nearly as well. In it, uracil is converted to |FRAME: UREA| and |FRAME: MALONATE| via |FRAME: BARBITURATE| |CITS: [12981104][14955523]|. A third pathway, known as the Rut pathway, was discovered much later in |FRAME: TAX-562| and other bacteria and is described here., About This Pathway, |FRAME:TAX-562| is able to utilize pyrimidine nucleosides and bases as the sole source of nitrogen at room temperature. This novel pathway for pyrimidine degradation was discovered by a combination of functional and comparative genomics techniques including high-throughput microarray and phenotype analysis |CITS: [16540542]|., In the presence of a flavin reductase, |FRAME: G6523-MONOMER| catalyzes the first step in this pathway, the ring opening of uracil at the C4 carbonyl by a novel flavin hydroperoxide-catalyzed mechanism |CITS: [20369853][20400551][28661684][32066967]|. |FRAME: G6522-MONOMER Ureidoacrylate amidohydrolase| then hydrolyzes |FRAME: CPD0-2331 3-ureidoacrylate|, yielding carbamate and 3-aminoacrylate. In a spontaneous reaction, carbamate decomposes into one molecule each of |FRAME: AMMONIA| and CO2. 3-Aminoacrylate can then hydrolyze either spontaneously or enzymatically, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX0-8589|, to |FRAME: MALONATE-S-ALD| and a second molecule of ammonia. 3-Oxopropanoate appears to be toxic and can not be utilized further. The compound may be detoxified by one of two malonic semialdehyde reductases to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE|, which is then excreted into the medium. The toxicity of 3-oxopropanoate appears to limit growth on pyrimidines as the sole source of nitrogen., Enzymes that are encoded by the rut operon of |FRAME: TAX-562|, but are not essential for degradation of uracil in vitro, may catalyze one or more of the spontaneous reactions of this pathway |CITS: [20400551][33839153]|., Reviews: |CITS: [16595627][17555842]|

Summary:
General Background, Pentose sugars, including |FRAME: D-Xylose|, |FRAME: L-ARABINOSE|, and |FRAME: D-ARABINOSE|, are metabolized through three main types of pathways., The first type, common in bacteria, uses isomerases, kinases, and epimerases to yield |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which feeds into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: ARABCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|, and |FRAME: DARABCAT-PWY|)., In the second type of pathways, which involves reductases and dehydrogenases and is found mainly in yeast and fungi, pentoses are converted into a sugar alcohol, which is then converted to |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| or |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, feeding into the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| (see |FRAME: PWY-5515|, |FRAME: PWY-5516|, and |FRAME: PWY-8334|)., The third type is partially analogous to the archaeal |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY "non-phosphorylative Entner-Doudoroff pathway variant"|, and has been sub-classified into three routes. All routes share the early steps, in which the pentoses are converted into 2-dehydro-3-deoxypentonate (KDP, either |FRAME: CPD-1134| or |FRAME: 2-DH-3-DO-D-ARABINONATE| depending on the initial sugar) through the participation of aldose 1-dehydrogenases, lactonases, and acid-sugar dehydratases. The next steps are route-dependent:, In Route I the KDP intermediate is cleaved through an aldolase reaction to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLYCOLALDEHYDE|. The D-xylose degradation variant of this route was first described by A. Stephen Dahms, and thus the pathway is known as the Dahms pathway |CITS: [4423285]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7295| and |FRAME: PWY-7294|).
, In Route II the KDP intermediate is converted into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| via |FRAME: CPD-654|. The general scheme for this route has been proposed by Weimberg, and is thus known as the Weimberg pathway |CITS: [13783864]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5517|, |FRAME: PWY-6760|, |FRAME: PWY-8020|, and |FRAME: PWY-5519|).
, In Route III the KDP intermediate is oxidized into |FRAME: 5-OH-2-4-DIOXOPENTANOATE|, which is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8329|, |FRAME: PWY-8330|, and |FRAME: PWY-8331|)., About This Pathway, This pathway is analogous to the oxidative pentose catabolic pathways proposed for the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-192| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5517|). In this pathway |FRAME: CPD-25028| was shown to be exclusively degraded to the tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (α-ketoglutarate)., Enzymes biochemically characterized include |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.424| |CITS: [15342590][28854683]|, |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.68| |CITS: [28854683]|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.82| |CITS: [19584053]|, |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.141| |CITS: [18448118]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.26|, that converts |FRAME: CPD-654| (2-ketoglutarate semialdehyde) to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| |CITS: [16835232]|., The oxidation product of the first enzyme (|FRAME: D-XYLONO-14-LACTONE|) can undergo spontaneous lactone ring opening. However, the hydrolysis of the lactone is accelerated by the lactonase |CITS: [22709678][25073011][28854683]|., Characterization of this pathway provided the first validation for |FRAME: D-Xylose| degradation in archaea |CITS: [19584053]|. For the comparable L-arabinose degradation pathway, see |FRAME: PWY-5517|.

A variety of aromatic compounds, including catechol and protocatechuate, can be degraded via the β-ketoadipate pathway, which is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi, even though its organization and regulation vary among species |CITS: [8905091]|., Once β-ketoadipate is formed, it is converted to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. In |FRAME: TAX-303|, the enzymes involved in β-ketoadipate degradation (β-ketoadipate:succinyl-CoA transferase, and β-ketoadipyl CoA thiolase) are inducible by β-ketoadipate |CITS: [5916393]|. , The genes that encode the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of this pathway in |FRAME: TAX-303| are clustered into two distinct groups: pcaIJ |CITS: [8376330]| are separate from pcaRKF |CITS: [761399]|, while in |FRAME: TAX-471| the genes are arranged in a single cluster (pcaIJFBDKCHG), which is, induced by protocatechuate (as reported in |CITS: [7961399]|).

General Background, Please see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6632| for a background summary of the degradation of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) and related methylxanthines., About This Pathway, Bacteria have not been reported to demethylate |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| to |FRAME: CPD-12479| (1,3-dimethylxanthine), a reaction found in |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|-degrading fungi and plants (reviewed in |CITS: [14977550]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6552|). However, it has been shown that |FRAME: ORG-6144| was able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| as sole carbon and nitrogen source, in addition to |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 3-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: 1-7-DIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: 7-METHYLXANTHINE|. |FRAME: CPD-12479| and |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| were metabolized to |FRAME: XANTHINE| via N-demethylation |CITS: [19447909]|., |FRAME: CPD-12479 Theophylline| and its |FRAME: 3-METHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-9025| derivatives were also metabolized by oxidation to |FRAME: CPD-14118|, |FRAME: CPD-12489|, and |FRAME: CPD-14119|, respectively via an as yet uncharacterized reaction(s). These compounds did not appear to be further metabolized |CITS: [19447909]|., Growth of |FRAME: ORG-6144| on either |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE|, |FRAME: CPD-12479|, or the N-demethylated metabolites of |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| resulted in coexpression of enzymes involved in the N-demethylation pathways of both |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12479| |CITS: [19447909]|. More recently, genes encoding enzymes that degrade both |FRAME: 1-3-7-TRIMETHYLXANTHINE| and |FRAME: CPD-12479| have been cloned and their products characterized, as shown here |CITS: [22328667][20966097]|.

Fatty acids are often found in the cell in the activated form of an acyl-coA (see |FRAME: PWY-5143|). Acyl-CoAs are used in the biosynthesis of many cellular products and components. In plants they are involved in the biosynthesis of membrane lipids, seed storage lipids, |FRAME: Wax-Esters wax|, |FRAME: Cutins cutins| and |FRAME: Suberins|., Acyl-CoA thioesterase hydrolyzes fatty acyl-CoAs to free fatty acids. In eukaryotes, the enzyme activity has been detected in the cytosol, ER, mitochondrion and peroxisome. In prokaryotes, the enzymes activity is localized in the periplasm and cytosol. In prokaryotes acyl-CoA thiesterases are involved in catabolism, supporting growth on fatty acids or conjugated fatty acid as the sole source of carbon |CITS: [18702504]|., The physiological roles of acyl-CoA thioesterase in eukaryotic organisms remain unclear. Works in animal and yeast shed some preliminary clue about the involvement of the enzyme in fatty acid oxidation. |FRAME: AT1G01710| is the first cloned plant acyl-CoA thioesterase |CITS: [14660652]|. The gene is highly expressed in mature tissues rather than in germinating seedlings where fatty acid beta-oxidation predominantly occurs. It indicates the role of |FRAME: AT1G01710| is not linked to fatty acid oxidation.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium Selenium| is an essential micronutrient for many organisms (see |FRAME: PWY0-901| and |FRAME: PWY-6281|) but has not yet been proven to be an essential micronutrient for land plants |CITS: [11683552][16307305]|. There is evidence, however, of |FRAME: TAX-3055| proteins that contains a |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| residue suggesting that algal species might also require |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [17105189][12110581]|., The health requirement of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for humans and animals can be met by crops and forage plants that contain selenocompounds. Among the oilseed crops |FRAME: TAX-4232| was shown to be a good source for this micronutrient |CITS: [15012198]|. In addition, there is evidence that certain seleno-compounds, including |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE|, have anti-carcinogenic properties |CITS: [14748935]|., Despite its importance as a micronutrient, higher concentrations of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| are toxic to humans, other animals, and plants largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064][12753978][16661781]|., In general, plants take up both |FRAME: SELENATE| and |FRAME: SELENITE| from soil. A series of |FRAME: PWY-6932 reduction steps| converts |FRAME: SELENATE| to |FRAME: SE-2| / |FRAME: CPD-678| and this is assimilated into the seleno-amino acids |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| and |FRAME: SELENOMETHIONINE| |CITS: [19309459]|., In Se accumulator plants, these seleno-amino acids may be modified to create organic seleno-compounds for storage. Seasonal weeds like |FRAME: TAX-3575| and |FRAME: TAX-83445| along with perennial weeds like |FRAME: TAX-41550| employ this strategy and accumulate high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| |CITS: [19800657]|. Se accumulation can help to protect plants against attacks by prairie dogs, insects, and fungi (see refs in |CITS: [21628258]|)., Other plants, like |FRAME: ORG-5993| generate seleno-compounds as well, but rather than storing them, they transform them into less toxic volatile compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-12005| (DMSe) that can then be released from the plants |CITS: [10759525]|. This process is also called phytovolatilization |CITS: [19656903]|., While these strategies directly benefit the plants that employ them, they can also be put to use for the phytoremediation of seleniferous soils that contain dangerously high amounts of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium|. Numerous insights into endogenous seleno-compound metabolism in plants have been gained through efforts to engineer plants that show improved selenium phytoremediation abilities |CITS: [15005814][19800657][19893365][17445958][10759525]|., About this pathway, Selenocysteine formation likely parallels the cysteine biosynthetic pathway in plants, and may use many of the same enzymes.The first step in cysteine biosynthesis involes a serine acetyltransferase (SAT). While there is definite evidence of enzymes capable of producing O-acetyl-L-serine in Arabidopsis and many other plant species, these enzymes have not yet been explicitly linked to selenium metabolism in planta. In fact, when SAT activity is compared across different |FRAME:TAX-20400| species that accumulate vastly different levels of selenium, no correlation is detected |CITS: [ 15941393]|. Selenocysteine formation is likely to be catalyzed by O-acetyl-L-serine (thiol) lyase (OAS-TL) enzymes and selenocysteine production in the presence of O-acteyl-serine has been measured in a number of plants including including |FRAME:TAX-3888| (pea), clover, and several Astralagus species |CITS: [NG78]|. This activity could be competitively inhibited by sulfur, and conversely, cysteine biosynthesis could be competetively inhibited by selenium, arguing that these reactions are catalyzed by the same enzymes |CITS: [NG78]|. Direct evidence for OAS-TL-based production of selenocysteine has only been demonstrated in the bacteria |FRAME:TAX-266| to date |CITS: [14692]|, but it is likely that plant OAS-TLs catalyze this reaction, too., |FRAME: CPD-13717| production probably depends on the activity of the cystathionine synthase enzymes that play a comparable role in sulfate metabolism. Over-expression of an Arabidopsis |FRAME: AT3G01120| enzyme in |FRAME:TAX-3707| appears to increase flux through this pathway and leads to higher levels of volatile selenium compound production |CITS: [14618405]|., Evidence for activity of the next enzyme in the pathway, β-(seleno)cystathionine lyase can be detected in plant extracts from several species including selenium non-accumulators, such as spinach (see |FRAME: MONOMER-16912| ), pea and Se accumulators, such as |FRAME:TAX-20406|. As seen for many other enzymes in this pathway, it is active with both the sulfur and selenium analogs |CITS: [MCCLUSKEY86]|., The final step toward selenomethionine biosynthesis could be catalyzed by at least three different types of enzymes if the proteins involved in |FRAME: PWY-702| also participate in selenomethionine (Se-Met) metabolism. For instance, E.coli has both cobalamin-dependent (2.1.1.13) and cobalamin-independent enzymes (|FRAME: RXN-12730 2.1.1.14|) that can catalyze the formation of Se-Met |CITS: [11078203]|. No cobalamin-independent candidates have been found in Arabidopsis. On the other hand, it does have three cobalamin-independent methionine synthases (see |FRAME: RXN-12730 2.1.14|) which could also potentially accept selenohomocysteine, but their role in seleno-amino acid biosynthesis has not yet been tested |CITS: [15024005]|. , These seleno-amino acids can be misincorporated during protein synthesis. To prevent this, selenium accumulating or hyperaccumulating plants typically transform them into non-coding seleno-amino acids, such as Se-methylselenocysteine or other related compounds. Non-accumulating plants employ a different strategy and further metabolize these seleno-amino acids into the production of volatile compounds that can be released into the atmosphere |CITS: [16307305]|.

General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| anaerobic respiratory chain formed by formate dehydrogenase and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) reductase the transfer of electrons from formate to TMAO is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [7000002], [9274019]|., TMAO reductase does not contribute to proton potential (see review by |CITS: [18930017]|); formate dehydrogenase N contributes to the generation of proton potential (H+/e- = 1) by means of a redox loop mechanism |CITS: [11884747]| . Menaquinone (shown here) or demethylmenaquinone serves as the redox mediator during anaerobic respiration with TMAO |CITS: [2204318], [1444716]|., E. coli K-12 contains two respiratory formate dehydrogenases. Formate dehydrogenase N is induced by anaerobiosis and the presence of nitrate |CITS: [12923080], [2168848]|. Formate dehydrogenase O (FdhO) is expressed aerobically and may be important during aerobic to anaerobic transition |CITS: [8522521]|. , In addition to the inducible TMAO reductase encoded by torCA (shown here), E. coli K-12 contains a second TMAO reductase encoded by |FRAME:G7022|. TorZ has low constitutive expression and is not induced by TMAO or dimethyl sulfoxide |CITS: [11004177]|. TorAC is an inducible TMAO reductase and is expressed in both anaerobic and aerobic conditions |CITS: [17850256]|., Many early studies on anaerobic TMAO respiration were done using E. coli K-10 |CITS: [7031034], [393699]|.

Summary: General Background, A subclass of icosanoids, the C20 prostanoids comprise of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and prostacyclins. They are all lipid compounds derived from the ω6 essential fatty acid |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|. Every prostanoid contains 20 carbon atoms, with an internal carbon ring structure., Prostaglandins are messenger molecules produced de novo by most tissues and organs, that act in an autocrine or paracrine fashion to mediate both homeostatic and inflammatory reactions. The name prostaglandin derives from the fact that initially it was thought to be present mainly in prostate secretions. E. J. Corey completed the first total syntheses of prostaglandins E2 and F2 in 1969., About this Pathway, Cell trauma, cytokines, growth factors or other stimuli activate phospholipase A2 (PLA2). There are many isoforms of PLA2 in the cell but the key player appears to be type IV cytosolic PLA2 which is translocated to the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [11729303]|. This causes the release of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| from cell membrane phospholipids. , The prostaglandin G/H synthases (cyclooxygenases) catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| to |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2| in two steps. First, two |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| molecules form two peroxide linkages and a 5-carbon ring is created near the middle of the fatty acid chain, forming an unstable intermediate prostaglandin G. Next, a single oxygen is shed from one of the peroxide linkages to form |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|. All prostanoids originate from |FRAME: PROSTAGLANDIN-H2|. , The effect of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) on the synthesis of prostaglandins was discovered by J. R. Vane in 1971. Aspirin, the quintessential NSAID exerts its effects can affect the activities of both |FRAME: HS01815-MONOMER "COX-1"| and |FRAME: HS01115-MONOMER "COX-2"|. However, its primary mode of action is the irreversible acetylation of COX-2 which loses the ability to generate prostaglandin intermediates but retains oxygenase activity. Statins mediate S-nitrosylation of COX-2 which has the same effect as aspirin mediated acetylation |CITS: [2107175]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, The elongation of |FRAME: MET| starts with its transamination to form a 2-oxo acid (as described in |FRAME: PWY-1186|). The 2-oxo acid is then extended by one methyl group by a condensation with acetyl-CoA, followed by an isomerization reaction and an oxidative decarboxylation reaction. The newly formed 2-oxo acid can be transaminated to homomethionine or undergo further cycles of condensation, isomerization and oxidative decarboxylation to form di, tri, tetra, penta, and hexahomomethionines. Mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, and hexahomomethionines all serve as precursors for aliphatic glucosinolates biosynthesis |CITS: [17369439][16669764]|., This side chain elongation cycle resembles the reaction sequence of |FRAME:LEUSYN-PWY|. Correspondingly, some enzymes of leucine biosynthesis also function in methionine chain elongation and vice versa |CITS: [18162591][19597944][19674406]|.

Summary: General Background, Deoxyribonucleotides are synthesised de novo at the diphosphate level through reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group of the corresponding ribonucleotides (see |FRAME:PWY-7220| and |FRAME:PWY-7222|). This reduction is mediated by the key enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|., The de novo synthesis of ribonucleotides is very expensive, and organisms have adapted to salvage potential precursors from their environment. Since nucleotides can not be imported into the cell due to the negative charge of the phosphate groups, salvage is limited to free bases and nucleosides. , Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. It has been shown that in quiescent or terminally differentiated mammalian cells, resting in the G0 phase, ribonucleotide reductase is not produced due to a block during transcription and the cells rely on salvage for deoxyribonucleotides for DNA repair |CITS: [3044582][1696835]|. Similarly, the salvage pathway is the sole provider of deoxyribonucleotides to be used in DNA repair or mitochondrial DNA replication in G1 cells., The deoxyribonucleosides enter through the cell membrane by facilitated diffusion via a low affinity, high capacity, non-concentrative nucleoside carrier protein with a wide specificity, possessed by almost all animal cells |CITS: [3048401]|. The next step in the salvage pathway is the phosphorylation of the nucleosides to monophosphates. Once phosphorylation occurs, the nucleotides are trapped intracellularly due to their negative charge., About This Pathway, The salvage of purine deoxynucleosides to deoxynucleotides is common, but not universal. For example, the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| does not have the enzymes that phosphorylate purine deoxynucleosides to deoxynucleoside monophopsphates, and thus is not able to utilize this salvage pathway., Mammalian cells contain four principal nucleoside kinase salvage enzymes, namely deoxycytidine kinase (|FRAME: HS08100|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.74 "EC 2.7.1.74"|), thymidine kinases 1 and 2 (|FRAME: HS09657| and |FRAME: HS09420|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.21 "EC 2.7.1.21"|), and deoxyguanosine kinase (|FRAME: HS03819|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.113 "EC 2.7.1.113"|). In addition, adenosine kinase (|FRAME: HS08097|, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.20 "EC 2.7.1.20"|) should also be considered a deoxyribonucleoside salvage enzyme, because it is can phosphorylate |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE|, although with much lower efficiency that the other enzymes |CITS: [7494863]|., The phosphorylation of purine deoxyribonucleosides in mammalian cells is mediated predominantly by two of these enzymes, the cytosolic deoxycytidine kinase (|FRAME: HS08100|) and the mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase (|FRAME: HS03819|). The |FRAME: CPLX-8620| is responsible for phosphorylation of purine deoxyribonucleosides in the mitochondrial matrix. It phosphorylate |FRAME: DEOXYGUANOSINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYINOSINE| with high affinity (Km < 25 μM) and |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE| with lower affinity (Km > 60 μM) |CITS: [6295492]|., Despite of its name, |FRAME: CPLX-8618| catalyzes the phosphorylation of not only |FRAME: DEOXYCYTIDINE| but also |FRAME: DEOXYADENOSINE| and |FRAME: DEOXYGUANOSINE| |CITS: [3030413][7494863]|., The enzyme can utilize either ATP or UTP as phosphoryl donors, and based on comparison of in vitro kinetic data of |FRAME: CPD-15099| phosphorylation by both compounds it has been suggested that UTP is the in vivo relevant donor |CITS: [2021937][1406603]|., While there do not appear to exist dedicated enzymes that catalyze the phosphorylation of deoxyribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates to the diphosphate form, the enzymes that catalyze the phosphorylation of ribonucleoside monophosphates, namely adenylate kinase (|FRAME: EC-2.7.4.3 "EC 2.7.4.3"|) and guanylate kinase (|FRAME: EC-2.7.4.8 "EC 2.7.4.8"|), appear to also catalyze the reaction with the deoxynucleotides in all species studied so far |CITS: [11008000]|., Once the diphosphate forms are generated, they are phosphorylated to the triphosphate forms by the broad-substrate range |FRAME: EC-2.7.4.6 "nucleoside-diphosphate kinase (EC 2.7.4.6)"| |CITS: [1659321][12009894]|.

Summary: General Background, α-Dystroglycan (DG) is a highly glycosylated basement membrane receptor involved in a variety of physiological, processes, including maintenance of the skeletal muscle-cell membrane integrity and establishment of the structure and function of the central nervous system. The protein is composed of a cell surface α subunit and a transmembrane β subunit |CITS: [8325873]|, and acts as a receptor for laminin-G domain-containing extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, such as laminin, agrin, perlecan, and neurexin |CITS: [16410545]|., α-Dystroglycan also serves as a cellular receptor and entry site for most Old World arenaviruses, including the highly pathogenic Lassa virus (LASV) and Clade C New Word arenaviruses |CITS: [9851928][17360738]|., α-Dystroglycan is heavily glycosylated, including N-glycosylation, mucin-type O-glycosylation, and O-mannosylation. The latter consists of an extensively modified |FRAME: bGalNAc-13-bGlucNAc-14-Man-R "M3-type core"| and is responsible for the binding of laminin-G ligands |CITS: [20044576]|. Mutations that affect the O-mannosylation of α-dystroglycan lead to reduced ligand binding and result in congenital disorders termed dystroglycanopathies. Notable is Walker-Warburg syndrome (WWS), a severe muscular dystrophy with malformations of the eyes and brain, associated with defective binding of α-dystroglycan to its ligands, such as laminin. Other mutations result in Fukuyama CMD, Muscle-Eye-Brain disease (MEB), and certain types of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy |CITS: [2140558]|., The entire glycan structure of the modified core M3 was found to be [β-glucuronosyl-(1→3)-α-xylosyl-(1→3)]n-β-glucuronosyl-(1→4)-[β-D-xylosyl-(1→4)-(ribitol-5-phosphate)2-3-N-acetyl-β-D-galactosaminyl-(1→3)-N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminyl-(1→4)-6-phospho-α-D-mannosyl)]-Ser/Thr-[protein]. A rare tandem |FRAME: CPD-372| moiety extends from the terminal GalNAc residue of the core M3 glycan to a GlcA/Xyl unit, which serves as a primer for a βGlcA(1→3)αXyl(1→3) polysaccharide chain |CITS: [14699049][22223806][23929950][25279697][25279699][26923585]|. It is the polysaccharide moiety that is responsible for the binding of extracellular matrix ligands |CITS: [20044576]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of this O-mannosyl glycan is initiated by the transfer of mannose to an L-serine or L-threonine via |FRAME: HS05428|/|FRAME: HS00268| in the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [14699049]|. The phosphorylated core M3 unit is then formed by the combined action of |FRAME: HS14042|, |FRAME: HS08750|, and |FRAME: G66-30734| in the endoplasmic reticulum |CITS: [23929950]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7979|)., The pathway continues with the addition of the two |FRAME: CPD-372| units, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: HS02944| and |FRAME: HS17614|, respectively, in the Golgi |CITS: [26923585]|., The ultimate purpose of this glycan is the polymeric repeat of the [β-glucuronosyl-(1→3)-α-xylosyl-(1→3)] disaccharide at the non-reducing end, which is essential for binding the extracellular matrix ligands. This polymer is synthesized by the paralogous |FRAME: HS05762| and |FRAME: HS09299| proteins. Each of these bifunctional enzymes can add both xylosyl and glucuronosyl residues |CITS: [25138275]|. Mass spectrum suggests the presence of at least 13 Xyl/GlcA repeats, which are sufficient for laminin binding |CITS: [24132234]|. However, in order for the LARGE enzymes to act, they require a [β-glucuronosyl-(1→4)-β-xylosyl-(1→4)] primer unit, which they are not able to form themseleves. This primer unit is synthesized by the action of dedicated glucuronosyltransferase and xylosyltransferase, encoded by the |FRAME: HS10821| and |FRAME: HS04237| genes |CITS: [25279699][27733679]|.
