Summary: General Background, The complete, oxidative tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle plays a central role in the energy metabolism of aerobic organisms (see for example |FRAME: TCA|). In most autotrophic bacteria and anaerobic archaea, the TCA cycle operates in a reductive, biosynthetic direction (see for example |FRAME: P23-PWY|). , Incomplete reductive TCA cycles have also been identified in some organisms, including obligate autotrophs and methanotrophs. Although the genes encoding |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105|, are absent or not expressed, these incomplete cycles can still convert pyruvate to necessary biosynthetic intermediates in response to anaerobic, or microaerophilic growth conditions (reviewed in |CITS: [15449607]|)., Methanogens (anaerobic archaea) lack the ability to perform a complete oxidative or reductive TCA cycle, and biosynthetic intermediates are proposed to be synthesized by incomplete cycles (in |CITS: [15595725]|). Most methanogens use the incomplete reductive TCA cycle for biosynthesis of intermediates (in |CITS: [3922956]|). An incomplete reductive TCA cycle has been shown in the methanogen |FRAME: TAX-2203| using 13C labeling and NMR, although no enzyme assays were provided |CITS: [6619097]|. It has also been shown in |FRAME: TAX-145262| by radiolabeled succinate incorporation studies |CITS: [29586]|., About This Pathway, Enzymes of an incomplete reductive TCA cycle shown here have been experimentally demonstrated in the autotrophic methanogen |FRAME: TAX-39152| |CITS: [3667534]|. The aetyl-CoA entering this pathway may be biosynthesized by the acetyl-CoA pathway of autotrophic carbon dioxide fixation (see |FRAME: CODH-PWY|) |CITS: [11607093] [3133359]|, or it may be biosynthesized from acetate when this facultative autotroph is grown on acetate (see, |FRAME: PWY0-1313|) |CITS: [3667534]|. Acetyl-CoA is converted to pyruvate by |FRAME: CPLX-7031|, and pyruvate is converted to the necessary biosynthetic intermediates |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|, |FRAME: SUC-COA|, and |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|. The latter is a precursor of |FRAME:GLT|, as indicated by the pathway link., It should be noted that some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-145262|, predicted to have an incomplete TCA cycle, might eventually be shown to contain complete cycles. In such cases other gene products would provide t he missing enzyme activity (|CITS: [14568143]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [10390638]|).

Summary: General Background, Phytate (phytic acid) is the most abundant myo-inositol phosphate (hexakisphosphate) in plant cells. Phytate serves as a storage form of myo-inositol, phosphate and mineral nutrients for utilization during seed germination and seedling growth. It is deposited within single-membrane storage organelles referred to as protein bodies and is usually present as mixed complexes with minerals (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+, Zn2+) known as phytin |CITS:[11590064],[8744268]|. Up to 80% of the total seed phosphorus is stored in phytin |CITS:[15700415]|. Although phytate is found in large quantities in seeds, it is also present in other plant tissues and organs such as pollen, roots, tuber and turions (for review see |CITS:[14568069]|). The potential of phytate to form very stable complexes with mineral and proteins confers upon this molecule its notorious antinutritional properties. Humans and monogastric animals lack the hydrolytic phytases in their digestive tract. Therefore, the high concentrations of phytate in food grains and its ability to chelate mineral cations compromise mineral absorption. Undigested phytate in animal waste also contributes to eutrophication and environmental phosphorus pollution |CITS:[11590064],[11906835]|. The degradation of phytate is achieved by a group of enzymes called phytases which have been mostly studied in microorganisms and plants. Phytases belong to a special class of phosphomonoesterases and are capable of initiating the stepwise release of phosphate from phytate. Phytases are used to reduce the level of phosphate pollution in areas of intensive animal production. Addition of adequate amounts of microbial phytases in animal feed improves the utilization of phosphate from phytate, allowing for a reduction in inorganic phosphate supplementation in the diets for simple-stomached animals. As a result, the fecal phosphate excretion of these animals may be reduced by up to 50%. Finally, phytases can improve the nutritional value of plant-based foods (especially grains) by increasing the availability of the minerals chelated in phytin., This Pathway in Plants: The degradation of phytate into myo-inositol phosphate intermediates and, finally, myo-inositol, is performed by phytases which catalyze the removal of all the phosphate residues of the phytate molecule in a sequential order. Each myo-inositol intermediate is released from the enzyme and may become a substrate for further hydrolysis |CITS:[12405789]|. To date two main types of phytases have been described: 3-phytases (myo-inositol hexakisphosphate 3-phosphorylase, EC 3.1.3.8) and 4-phytases (myo-inositol hexakisphosphate 6-phosphorylase, EC 3.1.3.26), which lead to the production of , Ins(1,2,4,5,6)P5 and Ins(1,2,3,5,6)P5, respectively, from phytate. The main phytate degradation route elucidated in legumes, cereals, |FRAME:TAX-4932| and |FRAME:TAX-286|, then, goes from the conversion of either of these two compounds to Ins(1,2,5,6)P4, Ins(1,2,6)P3 and Ins(1,2)P2 |CITS:[12405789]|. A minor route proceeds through the dephosphorylation of Ins(1,2,3,5,6)P5 to Ins(1,2,3,6)P4. This minor branch results from lesser activities from the same enzymes involved in the catalysis of the reaction of the main branch, rather than that of the activity of a different set of enzymes |CITS:[12405789],[10879469]|., Note on Inositol Phosphates: Inositol phosphates containing the (1,2,3)-trisphosphate cluster are iron-binding antioxidants |CITS:[9034232],[spiers95]|, and Ins(1,2,3,6)P4 has a structure that is moderately effective in opening calcium channels |CITS:[9160166],[8141257]|. In addition, Ins(1,2,6)P3 has anti-inflammatory and antisecretory properties |CITS:[claxon90]|.

General Background, Ternatins are a group of 15 polyacetylated delphinidin glucosides that confer , blue color to the petals of butterfly pea (|FRAME:TAX-43366|). The general structure of ternatins consists , of malonylated delphinidin 3,3',5'-triglucosides having 3',5'-side chains with alternating D-glucose and , p-coumaric acid units of varying lengths |CITS: [8991946]| |CITS: [12482461]|. , Ternatins are categorized into three major groups, the A, B and D series that are characterized by either , two D-glucose attached to the 3' and 5' position of the B-ring (A-series), a D-glucose and an acylated , (p-coumaric acid) glucose chain (B-series) or two acylated glucose units (D-series) affixed to this position , |CITS: [9834153]|. The variation of flower color depends on the chemical composition of the involved , anthocyanins. Blue flower color changes to red-purple flowers in the Labiatae (compare |FRAME:PWY-5284|, , |FRAME:PWY-5268|) when the backbone structure (peonidin to pelargonidin) and the length of acylated , glucoside chains change. Similar to this blue flower color of butterfly-pea changes to other hues, such as , mauve and white because of the lack of ternatins that contain acylated glucose units and an overall decreased , content of anthocyanins |CITS: [14568080]|., There is some confusion in the literature with regard to the general compound name since ternatin is also , commonly used to refer to a flavone (|FRAME:CPD-7954|) that has been isolated from Egletes viscosa , of the sunflower family |CITS: [8588867]| in contrast to the same named anthocyanidin compound (this pathway) , isolated from species of the bean family., Ternatins are usually very stable in aqueous solutions. Because of this stability the flower pigment is traditionally , utilized in Southeast Asia as food colorant |CITS: [9834153]| |CITS: [8991946]|., About This Pathway, The simplest ternatin is |FRAME: CPD-7864|, which is the starting point for the formation of more complex ternatins, such as |FRAME:CPD-7865| and its intermediates (see |FRAME:PWY-7280|). Ternatin A1 is formed through a series of acylation (four steps) and glucosylation (four steps) starting with the acylation with p-coumaric acid of ternatin C5 |CITS: [9834153]|. However, the actual sequence and corresponding enzymes of this pathway remain to be characterized., It has been proposed that the biosynthesis of ternatin C5 may occur by acylation with malonic acid of preternatin C5. , Preternatins are triglucosylated delphinidins bearing no alphatic or aromatic acyl groups |CITS: [9834153]|. , However, it could be shown that the malonation of delphinidin 3-O-glucoside catalyzed by the , anthocyanidin 3-O-glucoside-6''-O-malonyltransferase (3MAT) precedes the 3' and 5'-O-glucosylation of the , B-ring |CITS: [16887235]| |CITS: [KAZUMA04]|. Other 3MAT's isolated from species of the Compositae |CITS: [12481098]| |CITS: [SUZUKI03]| have been shown to have high affinities for delphinidin 3-O-glucoside although their malonylated products are not found in this species., Glucosylation is catalyzed by a single enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-12402|. It activity has first been shown in extracts |CITS: [KAZUMA04]| and the enzyme was eventually purified |CITS: [17668234]|., This enzyme catalyzes two successive reactions: the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-7862| to |FRAME: CPD-7870|, followed by the conversion of the later to |FRAME: CPD-7864|, by transferring two glucosyl groups in a stepwise manner.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ILE| is almost always synthesized from |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|. In the most common pathway, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is generated from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| via |FRAME: THR| (see |FRAME:PWY-3001|). The key enzyme in that pathway is |FRAME:THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10493| gene., In addition to the standard pathway, microorganisms have developed several alternative pathways for |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis. |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be synthesized from |FRAME: GLT| via |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5103|) |CITS: [4550817]|, from |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (this pathway) |CITS: [4607875][4808901][15292141]|, and from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| by carboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-5104|) |CITS: [5800441][1212197][Eikmanns83a]|). In addition, there are several reports that under anaerobic conditions some anaerobic bacteria can carboxylate |FRAME: CPD-7076| to |FRAME: ILE| via |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5108|) |CITS: [5813342][6726176][6440485 ]|., About This Pathway, The pathway desribed here was originally proposed in the spirochaete |FRAME: TAX-173| in 1974 |CITS: [4808901]|. Using isotope labeling data, it was shown that the pathway, which was named "the pyruvate pathway", started with the condensation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE| to form citramalate. At the time it wasn't clear whether the product of this initial reaction is |FRAME: CPD-31| or its stereoisomer, |FRAME:S-CITRAMALATE|. As a result, two plausible routes were proposed, depending on the stereoisomer formed. The route starting with |FRAME:S-CITRAMALATE| would proceed via |FRAME:L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE|, while the route starting with |FRAME: CPD-31| would proceed in a manner very similar to the pathway of |FRAME:LEUSYN-PWY|. Both routes were proposed to combine at |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, the key intermediate which is formed directly from |FRAME: THR| in the more common |FRAME: ILE| biosynthetic pathway (|FRAME:ILEUSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [4808901]|., Subsequent work has confirmed the presence of the pyruvate pathway in other |FRAME:TAX-171| strains |CITS: [6404889]| as well as in many species of archaea |CITS: [Eikmanns83][Ekiel84]|, but did not determine the exact route employed by the organisms. In 1999 an |FRAME: CPLX-7022| was purified from |FRAME: TAX-2190|, and shown to catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-31| |CITS: [9864346]|. In 2004 a similar enzyme was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-189518|. These authors were also able to show that |FRAME: 2-METHYLMALEATE| is the substrate for the following reaction. By cloning and overexpressing the enzymes |FRAME:CPLX-7020 | and |FRAME: CPLX-7021|, which catalyze the comparable steps in |FRAME: LEU| biosynthesis (see |FRAME: LEUSYN-PWY|), the authors were able to demonstrate the conversion of |FRAME: 2-METHYLMALEATE| to |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|, confirming that this is indeed the route, employed by |FRAME:TAX-171| strains for |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis. Despite the sharing of several enzymes between the biosynthetic pathways of |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME: ILE| in these organisms, these pathways are not co-regulated, due to the difference in the enzymes catalyzing the first reaction. |FRAME:CPLX-7019| expression is not regulated by |FRAME: LEU|, but is sensitive to |FRAME: ILE| concentrations |CITS: [15292141]|., Even though the pathway has not been characterized as well in archaebacteria, the presence and nature of several key enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-2190| suggests that this is most likely the |FRAME: ILE| biosynthestic pathway employed by methanogens |CITS: [15292141][17449626]|. The pathway has been subsequently detected in non-methanogenic archaea |CITS: [17400748]| as well as in the Delta-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-35554| |CITS: [18245290]|. The CimA protein from |FRAME: TAX-35554| constituted the first characterized member of a phylogenetically distinct clade of citramalate synthases. Based on the distribution of homologs of that protein, the pathway has been predicted to have a much wider occurrence than previously thought, and may exist in Delta-proteobacteria, Alpha-proteobacteria, Cyanobacteria, Deinococci, Clostridia, Actinobacteria, Sphingobacteria, Chlorobia, and the Chloroflex, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-183968| class of the archaea |CITS: [18245290]|.

Summary: General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , In order to avoid self-intoxication cyanogenic glucosides are stored in the vacuole. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks they come in contact with activating enzymes (specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases) that reside in the cytoplasm or apoplastic space of the cells, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN| that serves as the first line of chemical defense |CITS:[16667728][Ganjewala10]|., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1042 Dhurrin| is a cyanogenic glucoside produced by seedlings of |FRAME:TAX-4558| |CITS: [11312134] [10585420]|. The biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: CPD-1042| was shown to involve |FRAME: TYR|, |FRAME: CPD-267|, and (4-hydroxyphenyl)acetaldehyde oxime as early intermediates |CITS: [468842]|. A study with a microsomal preparation obtained from etiolated seedlings of sorghum has shown that the pathway produces initially the (E)-isomer of (4-hydroxyphenyl)acetaldehyde oxime, which is converted to the (Z) isomer |CITS: [2684955]|., The conversion of |FRAME: TYR| to |FRAME: CPD-2205| is catalyzed by a cytochrome P-450 enzyme, |FRAME: G-452| |CITS: [16668136][7937883]|. The activity involves two successive N-hydroxylation reactions, producing |FRAME: CPD-7070| as an intermediate |CITS: [7876084]|. A second cytochrome P-450, |FRAME: G-453|, then converts the (E) isomer to the (Z) isomer, and converts it in two steps to |FRAME: CPD-648| |CITS: [9414567][26361733]|, which is glucosylated to form |FRAME: CPD-1042| |CITS: [10585420]|.

Summary: The lipoxygenase-catalyzed conversion of polyenoic fatty acids, specifically linoleate and linolenate in , plants, and the subsequent reactions are collectively called the lipoxygenase pathway. The , lipoxygenase pathway plays an important role in plant defense and giving plants the special , "fresh green" odor. , Lipoxygenases (LOX) are ubiquitous enzymes in eukaryotes. Depending on the positional specificities, , they are further classified as 9-LOX and 13-LOX, converting polyunsaturated fatty acids to , 9-hydroperoxides (9-HOPD and 9-HPOT) and 13-hydroperoxides (13-HPOD and 13-HPOT), respectively. , The hydroperoxide intermediates are further metabolized by enzymes such as allene oxide synthase , (AOS), hydroperoxide lyase (HPL), and divinyl ether synthase (DES), all belonging to the CYP74 family. , Depending on the substrate preferences, being either a 9-hydroperoxide or 13-hydroperoxide, these , enzymes are divided into 9- or 13-AOS, 9- or 13-HPL, and 9- or 13-DES. 13-AOS is ubiquitous to plants, , it leads to the biosynthesis of the plant hormone and signaling molecule jasmonic acid. Similarly, , 13-HPL activity has been detected in many plants. It leads to the biosynthesis of the regulatory , molecule traumatin (12-oxo-trans-10-dodecenoate).  In addition, the aldehydes and alcohols , produced by 13-HPL give the unique flavors and tastes to plants, such as the cucumber odor. On the , other hand, 9-AOS and 9-HPL have only been detected in a few plants. The 9-AOS product alpha-ketols , may be involved in plant development control |CITS: [16960383]|. The 9-HPL derived aldehydes are known as , defense compounds |CITS: [16116284]|. The DES activities have also only been detected in a few plants. , Divinyl ethers such as colneleic acid and colnelenic acid, derived from DES act as antimicrobials |CITS: [11060314]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The structure of the repeat unit of O antigens isolated from |FRAME: TAX-2162915| was reported in 2009. It is very similar to the |FRAME: CPD-24104|, differing only in the substitution of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine for D-glucose |CITS: [19040662]|., The O antigen gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2162915| was cloned and sequenced along with the cluster of |FRAME: TAX-2067430|. The two clusters were found to be very similar, sharing 98.6% overall DNA identity |CITS: [19040662]|. , The product of the |FRAME: G-81043| gene shares 31-35% identities to many rhamnosyltransferases and was proposed to encode the glycosyltransferase that forms the α-L-Rha-(1→4)-α-D-Glc linkage |CITS: [19040662]|. The product of the |FRAME: G-81044| gene shares 45% identity to |FRAME: G-27214 WbwC| of |FRAME: TAX-2072453|, which is a galactosyltransferase responsible for the β-D-Gal-(1→3)-β-D-GalNAc linkage in its O antigen. As the same linkage is present in the antigens of O107 and O117 strains, the same function was assigned to |FRAME: G-81044| |CITS: [19040662]|., The function of the other two glycosyltransferases remained unknown until 2012, when it was shown that the genes named wclY encode a GlcNAc-transferase and a glucosyltransferase in |FRAME: TAX-2162915| and |FRAME: TAX-2067430|, respectively, even though they differ by only three residues |CITS: [Wang12]|. That left the last gene, |FRAME: G-81046|, as the only candidate for encoding the β-(1,3)-GalNAc-transferase., As in all other Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways, the Wzx flippase flips the completed O-unit across the inner membrane from the cytoplasm to the periplasm, where the O-units are linked together by the Wzy polymerase. In the case of the |FRAME: CPD-24103|, the repeat units are linked in an α(1,4) linkage.

Summary: |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| (also known as geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, or GGPP) is a, crucial compound involved in the biosynthesis of a variety of terpenes and terpenoids, including, central compounds such as ubiquinones and menaquinones., In plants, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of essentail, compounds such as chlorophylls, carotenoids, tocopherols, plastoquinones, and gibberellins, |CITS:[12427975]|, as well as a variety of secondary metabolites., In addition, GGPP is also used in posttranslational modifications of proteins (geranylgeranylation) which, is important for membrane adhesion as well as the function of some proteins |CITS:[11500541][16183844]|., GGPP is synthesized from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| either by dedicated enzymes,, such as the |FRAME: YPL069C-MONOMER| of |FRAME: TAX-4932|, or by the action of polyprenyl, transferases such as the |FRAME: MONOMER-13766| from |FRAME: TAX-1061| or, |FRAME: CPLX0-7426| from |FRAME: TAX-83333|., It should be noted that the building blocks for |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, are synthesized in different organisms by different pathways. While most eukaryotes and some, bacteria use the |FRAME: PWY-922|, most bacteria, as well as green algae utilize the, |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (as described in the two superpathways |FRAME: PWY-5910| and, |FRAME: PWY-5121|)., In plants, GGPP is synthesized using both routes - in the cytosol using the |FRAME: PWY-922|,, and in the plastids using the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|., This superpathway describes the production of GGPP via the |FRAME:PWY-922|., In plants, cytosolic GGPP is mainly used in the geranylgeranylation of proteins.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In |FRAME: TAX-810| additional Kdo units are added by a (2->8) or (2->4) linkages (see |FRAME: PWY-6467|). The actual donor of Kdo units is its activated form, |FRAME: CMP-KDO|., Kdo-containing |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA| molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety., LPS are produced by all Gram-negative bacteria, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-909932| and |FRAME: TAX-53433|, which belong to the firmicutes phylum, suggesting that an ancient LPS-containing diderm cell envelope was present in the ancestor of the Firmicutes |CITS: [27580370]|. There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are also synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, Methylated thiols such as |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) and |FRAME: CPD-7672| can serve as methylotrophic methanogenic precursors |CITS: [16347202][10224009]|. These compounds are generated in nature by many different processes, such as the degradation of |FRAME:MET|, the reduction of |FRAME:DMSO|, the anaerobic degradation of methoxylated aromatics, anoxygenic photosynthesis by some phototrophs, and the demethylation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN|, a common algae osmolite |CITS: [11073950]|., Most |FRAME: TAX-2207| species are able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-7670| and |FRAME: CPD-7672|, although, some species, such as |FRAME: TAX-2208|, can only do so when grown on |FRAME:ACET| (but not, |FRAME:METOH|)., The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., Unlike similar systems for |FRAME:CoM| methylation by |FRAME:METOH| and different methylamines, the enzymatic complex that methylates |FRAME:CoM| with methylated thiols consists of only two types of peptides. The MtsA peptide catalyzes both methyltransferase activities, which are catalyzed in the other systems by two different methyltransferase, MT1 and MT2 |CITS: [11073950]|. , The second peptide, MtsB, is a corrinoid protein, similar to the one found in the other systems. Earler studies suggested that one corrinoid cofactor is bound per MtsA:MtsB pair, and six to seven such pairs coprise a 480 kDa complex |CITS: [8335638][8282704]|. However, later work suggested that MtsA forms dimers in solution |CITS: [11073950]|.

Summary: General Background, Bacteria and plants often accumulates |FRAME: CHOLINE|, since it can easily be converted to |FRAME: BETAINE|, a common osmoprotectant |CITS: [LeRudulier84]|., Many organisms can also use choline as a sole source for both carbon and nitrogen by catabolizing it via |FRAME: BETAINE| |CITS: [3290197][6406829]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3661|)., While the conversion of choline to glycine betaine for the purpose of accumulating the latter as an osmoprotectant is, considered biosynthetic (see |FRAME:BETSYN-PWY|, |FRAME:PWY-3722|, and |FRAME:PWY1F-353|), the conversion of choline to glycine betaine for the purpose of further catabolism should be considered as a choline degradation pathway. Two such pathways have been demonstrated: Certain Gram-negative bacteria such as Synrhizobium meliloti, as well as some plants, degrade choline to glycine betaine using a combination of two different dehydrogenases (this pathway), while certain Gram-positive bacteria, as well as certain fungi, achieve this by the activity of a single enzyme, choline oxidase (see |FRAME: PWY-3721|)., About This Pathway, The conversion of choline to glycine betaine in this pathway is performed by the action of two dehydrogenases. Choline dehydrogenase converts choline to betaine aldehyde, while betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase converts the aldehyde to glycine betaine. , It has been proposed that choline degradation in R. meliloti can be used as a mechanism for osmoregulation., When the bacteria grow at normal osmolarity conditions, they degrade choline, using it as a carbon and nitrogen, source. However, under inhibiting osmotical conditions, enzyme activities that lead to glycine betaine, degradation decrease, while enzyme activities that convert choline to glycine betaine either remain constant, or increase. In this way, a high concentration of glycine betaine can be maintained in osmotically stressed cells, |CITS: [3290197]|., Similarly, while |FRAME:TAX-287| catabolizes both choline and glycine betaine under low osmolarity, conditions, it accumulates the latter under high osmolarity, presumably by down regulating the enzyme glycine betaine, transmethylase, which converts glycine betaine to N,N-dimethylglycine (DMG), while, maintaining the activity of the enzymes of this pathway |CITS: [12107149]|., In the plant |FRAME: TAX-4513| the formation and accumulation of glycine betaine via choline degradation was studied under salt and low temperature stress conditions |CITS: [21769646]|. GB accumulation increased under salt stress. The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16786| (CMO) which converts choline to |FRAME: BETAINE| with |FRAME: NADPH| as the co-factor. In barley, interestingly, this enzyme's localization is restricted to perioxisomes whereas in spinach and other higher plants it is localized in the chloroplast. Plant choline degradation pathways differ from bacterial pathways primarily due to the cellular localization of the two enzymes |CITS: [18429940]|. This in turn determines how and when the enzymes are regulated under stress conditions and during recycling of compounds. Expression pattern of the two enzymes, CMO and betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase (BADH), varied; CMO was abundant in leaves and BADH was abundant in awn and florets |CITS: [7888620]|. As many plants do not synthesis GB, studies are underway to find out how and where this compound is produced, transported and degraded |CITS: [21793308][17924116]| so effective bioengineering strategies can be worked out.

Summary: Nitrification, the oxidation of |FRAME: AMMONIA| to |FRAME: NITRATE| by microorganisms, is a key process in the global nitrogen cycle, resulting in nitrogen loss from ecosystems, eutrophication of surface and ground waters, and the production of atmospherically active trace gases. For many years it has been thought that no one organism is capable of carrying out the whole process, with ammonia oxidizers limited to the conversion of ammonia to |FRAME: NITRITE| and nitrite oxidizers confined to the oxidation of nitrite to nitrate. However, that paradigm has been proven unfounded with the isolation of organisms capable of the full oxidation of ammonia to nirtate |CITS: [26610024][26610025]|., The "classical" ammonia-oxidizing bacteria are chemolithoautotrophs that utilize the process to generate sufficient energy for growth and maintenance reactions, including the reductive fixation of carbon dioxide. However, other organisms are able to oxidize ammonia to nitrite, including some marine archaea |CITS: [16177789][16894176][19794413]|, methane-oxidizing bacteria |CITS: [18650926][21682764]| and some heterotrophic bacteria |CITS:[6721486][2782877][2181927]|. The key difference between heterotrophic and autotrophic ammonia oxidation is that heterotrophic ammonia oxidation usually does not generate energy. It has been suggested that in these bacteria nitrification is used as a sink for excess reducing power generated by oxidative metabolism |CITS: [Robertson88][8253206]|. , Autotrophic ammonia oxidizing bacteria include the genera |FRAME: TAX-35798|, |FRAME: TAX-914| and |FRAME: TAX-1227| (the best studied ammonia oxidizing organism is |FRAME: TAX-915|). All of these organisms possess the genes encoding the two essential enzymes, ammonia monooxygenase (AMO) and hydroxylamine oxidoreductase (HAO). , The 4 electrons released in the oxidation of |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| by HAO are channeled throgh an electron transfer chain to the quinone pool |CITS:[4372235][9808046]|. The nature of the electron transfer chain appears to differ among different types of organisms. The hypothesized chain in |FRAME: TAX-915| is described in |FRAME: PWY-7082| |CITS: [11807563][12209257][11004450]|., Many heterotrophic bacteria also possess genes encoding AMO and HAO activities. However, the enzymes found in these organisms can be very different from the ones found in the chemolithoautotrophs. While the second step of the pathway (the oxidation of hydroxylamine to nitrite) is catalyzed in autotrophs only by a complex hexameric |FRAME: CPLX-1321|, which is composed of three octaheme cytochrome c monomers (haoA) cross-linked between a tyrosine residue and the active site heme c group of the neighboring monomer, other types of enzymes have been reported from heterotrophs. HAOs consisting of a small (20 kDa) periplasmic monomer containing ferric iron that is non-heme and non iron-sulfur have been reported from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-266| |CITS: [8253206][8920986]| and a |FRAME:TAX-286| Sp. |CITS: [9082922]|. An HAO isolated from |FRAME: ORG-5975| was reported to be a homo-dimer of 68 kDa subunits that contains no detectable cofactors |CITS: [9049019]|. In addition, some heterotrophs lack the enzyme, but are still able to oxidize ammonia by other routes, as demonstrated in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-2242| |CITS: [8674977]|., Many organisms couple ammonia oxidation to |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY "denitrification"|. This has been shown for both heterotrophs |CITS: [2181927][8253206][9765887]| and autotrophs |CITS:[Bock95][15583163]|. In this process the nitrite produced by ammonia oxidation is reduced to nitric oxide, nitrous oxide, and possibly to nitrogen gas. For more information, see |FRAME: PWY-7084|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9009| (2,4-D ) is a common herbicide that is particularly toxic to broad leafed plants., It is used principally for the control of broad leaf weeds in cereal crops, including wheat, maize, rice and sorghum, as well as, in grassland and turf areas. It is also widely used in mixtures with other herbicides to provide weed control in forestry,, orchards and non-crop areas, and for the control of aquatic weeds., 2,4-D is the major weed control used in the US for wheat, and was the third most used pesticide in the early to mid, 1990s in the US. It has been classified as a WHO Class II 'moderately hazardous' pesticide., Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-264198|, can use |FRAME: CPD-9009| as the sole sources for carbon and energy, |CITS: [6257648]|. Other strains that degrade 2,4-D have been reported, including |FRAME: TAX-244562| |CITS: [12089027]|,, |FRAME: TAX-69003| |CITS: [8779585]|, and |FRAME: TAX-80866| |CITS: [11572451]|., Genes encoding |FRAME: CPD-9009| degradation are often located on conjugative plasmids |CITS:[6257648][7646006]|., One such plasmid, pJP4 from |FRAME: TAX-264198|, has been studied extensively and become a model system, for 2,4-D degradation. The genes on this plasmid are organized in three clusters. One cluster includes the, |FRAME: G-10972| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-14384|., The two other operons, named tfdI (or simply tfd) and tfdII, are very similar to each, other, and each encodes the same set of five enzymes, although not at the same order. Some differences in the function, and regulation of the proteins encoded by the two clusters have been reported |CITS: [16597983][14676989]|., The enzymes encoded by pJP4 catalyze the overall conversion of 2,4-D to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|., |FRAME: MONOMER-14384|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10972|, cleaves the ether bond of |FRAME: CPD-9009| and, produces |FRAME: 24-DICHLOROPHENOL| in a |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|-dependent reaction., The chlorophenol is a substrate for the two chlorophenol hydroxylases encoded by the |FRAME: G-10973| and, |FRAME: G-10974| genes, which transform it to |FRAME: 35-DICHLOROCATECHOL|. While both TfdB enzymes, are active during growth on 2,4-D, TfdB(I) plays the major role |CITS: [16597983]|. |FRAME: 35-DICHLOROCATECHOL|, is then converted to |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE| by the enzyme encoded by the rest of the tfd genes, (see |FRAME: PWY-6084|). Further metabolism of this common intermediate to tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, is encoded by chromosomal genes. , The enzymes described in this pathway also catalyze the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-10614| (MCPA) (see, |FRAME: PWY-6086|).

Summary: Glycerophospholipids are the fundamental building blocks of eukaryotic and bacterial membranes. The primary glycerophospholipids found in bacteria are |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE phosphatidylethanolamine| (PE), |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol| (PG), and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN cardiolipin| (CL). In addition, many bacterial species produce various additional lipids such as |FRAME: SPHINGOLIPIDS sphingolipids|, sterol-like lipids (|FRAME: Hopanoids hopanoids|), |FRAME: 1-Phosphatidyl-2-O-D-Ala-Glycerol|, |FRAME: 3-PHOSPHATIDYL-3-O-L-LYSYLGLYCEROL| or methylated PE derivatives like |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| (which is the major phospholipid in eukaryotes)., Bacteria remodel their membrane lipid composition in response to environmental challenges by modifying the lipid head group or fatty acid composition to maintain optimal membrane function. In addition, some bacteria degrade their phospholipids in response to phosphate limitation, replacing them with phosphate-free lipids such as ornithine lipids and, glycolipids., In addition to providing the membrane matrix, phospholipids are also involved in synthesizing several types of surface molecules. The phosphoethanolamine head groups of phosphatidylethanolamine are transferred and attached to the , lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core sugars and to periplasmic membrane-derived oligosaccharides (MDO). The head group of phosphatidylglycerol is used for modifying various lipoproteins and MDO. The entire molecule is used in the , synthesis of cardiolipin |CITS: [2404013]|.

Summary: General Background, When grown with non-limiting phosphate concentrations, the cell walls of many |FRAME: TAX-1239| contain |FRAME: Teichoic-Acid "teichoic acids"|. While the structure of teichoic acids differ among different species, and sometimes multiple types are found within a single cell, all of them contain large amount of phosphates., In addition to the teichoic acids, the cell walls of certain organisms contain a different kind of polymers that do not contain phosphate, but contain a large amount of uronate. The first polymer of this type was isolated from the walls of |FRAME: TAX-1402| 6346, and owing to the high content of uronate was named teichuronic acid |CITS: [13789369]|., Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1270| and |FRAME: TAX-384602|, which do not produce teichoic acids, do produce teichuronic acids. Like teichoic acids, teichuronic acids are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. , Different species produce different types of teichuronic acids. One type found in some Bacillus species contains equal proportions of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine| and |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| |CITS: [6263243]|. The one from |FRAME: TAX-1270| contains equal proportions of |FRAME: Glucopyranose| and |FRAME: ManNAcA| |CITS: [13942446][4648861][1268881]|. Yet other forms are known, for example from Bacillus subtilis AHU 1031 |CITS: [6426958]| and Bacillus subtilis AHU 1219 |CITS: [2492228]|., It was subsequently found that organisms that produce teichoic acids replace their wall teichoic acids with teichuronic acids when grown under phosphate limitation |CITS: [4975313][Ellwood72][4570613]|. The synthesis of teichuronic acid in these organisms is accompanied by the degradation of teichoic acid and the reutilization of the liberated phosphate for other processes |CITS: [104966]|., About This Pathway, The structure of the teichuronic acid produced by |FRAME: TAX-1402|, |FRAME: TAX-224308|, and |FRAME: TAX-655816| was originally described simply as a polymer of the disaccharide [α-D-glucuronosyl-(1→3)-α-N-acetyl-D-galactosaminyl-(1→4)] |CITS: [808222]|. However, a more thorough study has shown that the repeating unit is [β-D-glucuronosyl-(1→4)-β-D-glucuronosyl-(1→3)-N-acetyl-α-D-galactosaminyl-(1→6)-N-acetyl-α-D-galactosaminyl-(1→4)] |CITS: [6263243]|. The polymer is synthesized while attached to a linker unit composed of an N-acetyl-D-galactosamine residue connected in α configuration to a diphospho-undecaprenyl membrane anchor., Extension of the repeating unit is carried out by three glycosyltransferases, which add a second N-acetyl-D-galactosamine residue and two D-glucuronosyl residues. This is followed by the action of a transporter that flips the lipid-linked oligosaccharide subunit from the inner to the outer membrane surface, where the blocks are subsequently polymerized. Polymerization involves the transfer of the oligosaccharide subunits from their membrane anchor to the reducing end of the nascent polysaccharide, while the latter remains bound to its own membrane anchor. This direction of chain extension is the same as that found in peptidoglycan biosynthesis |CITS: [7022154]|., The last step is the transfer of the polymeric chain from its lipid anchor to peptidoglycan. Like teichoic acids, teichuronic acids are linked to the 6-hydroxyl of a muramate residue via a phosphodiester bond from the reducing sugar of the polysaccharide |CITS: [5419740]|. The reaction is believed to be catalyzed by the same promiscuous enzymes that catalyze the transfer of teichoic acids, which are members of the LCP (LytR-Cps2A-Psr) family |CITS: [21964069]|., An eight gene operon, named tuaABCDEFGH, encodes all the enzymes that are required for the polymerization of teichuronic acid as well as for the synthesis of one of its precursors, |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE|. The operon belongs, to the Pho regulon, and its transcription is turned on by phosphate limitation |CITS: [10048024][10627039]|.

Summary: Like many other bacterial pathogens, pathogenic species of the |FRAME: TAX-1762| synthesize and secrete specialized, iron chelators known as siderophores, which they take up after the compounds complex ferric iron. The mycobactins were the first siderophores to be recognized and characterized. Their history began in 1912 with the discovery that |FRAME: TAX-1770|, which had previously not been cultivable, could be grown with the aid of a substance derived from other mycobacteria |CITS: [Twort12]|. The importance of this discovery was noted only 30 years later, by researchers at the laboratories of Imperial Chemical Industries, Ltd who eventually managed to purify the factor from |FRAME: TAX-1771| and named it mycobactin |CITS: [18112287][13115341]|. In 1965 mycobactin was purified from |FRAME: TAX-1773|, and found to differ from the compound isolated previously. Thus the compound isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1771| was renamed |FRAME: CPD-12072|, while the compound from |FRAME: TAX-1773| was named |FRAME: CPD-12068| |CITS: [16749098]|. Eventually many more varieties of mycobactin were characterized from multiple species of Mycobacterium., Following the discovery of the membrane-associated |FRAME: CPD-12072| and |FRAME: CPD-12068|, |FRAME: TAX-1773| was reported to also produce water-soluble siderophores, which were given the names exochelins |CITS: [240908][7761471][24684595]| or carboxymycobactins |CITS: [Lane95][Lane98]|. Later studies have shown that mycobactins and carboxymycobactins (exochelins) are highly related in their core structures and vary mainly in their fatty acid substituents. The lipid-soluble mycobactins have long-chain (C18-21) saturated or monounsaturated acyl chains on the first lysine residue, whereas the water soluble carboxymycobactins have a shorter (C5-9) sidechain that terminates with a carboxylic acid or methyl ester. It has been suggested that the carboxymycobactins pass ferric ions to the membrane-associated mycobactins on their way into the mycobacterial cell |CITS: [ 8666910]|., Based on the structure of mycobactin, certain enzymatic functions involved in its biosynthesis could be predicted. A search for the |FRAME: TAX-1773| genome for such enzymes resulted in the identification of the mbt-1 cluster, which contains 10 genes |CITS: [9634230][9831524]|. Several of cluster's genes encode non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs) (|FRAME: G185E-6609|, |FRAME: G185E-6606|, |FRAME: G185E-6605|), some encode polyketide synthases (PKSs) (|FRAME: G185E-6608|, |FRAME: G185E-6607|), and some encode other functions. A putative biosynthetic pathway was peroposed based on the predicted gene functions, according to which the biosynthesis involves assembly of the mycobactin backbone by a hybrid NRPS)/PKS megasynthase, followed by tailoring of the backbone by N6 acylation of the central L-Lys residue and subsequent N6-hydroxylation of the central N6-acyl-L-Lys and the terminal caprolactam |CITS: [983152]|. Testing of the proposal was hindered by the inability to heterologously produce soluble megasynthase components. However, it was later found that the |FRAME: G185E-6603| gene product helps the production of solubility of the NRPS enzymes. Coexpression of MbtH with these enzyme resulted in production of soluble NRPSs, enabling their biochemical characterization and resulting in modification of the original proposed pathway |CITS: [22447909]|., The last step of the pathway, demethylation of the β-methyl oxazoline ring, has not been characterized as of 2021.

Summary: Background, Amidst concerns of global warming and dwindling natural resources, there is a concerted effort to to come up with renewable sources of fuel via microbial pathways. To enhance microbial production of relevant compounds, metabolic engineering is increasingly performed which increases product yields and endows microorganisms with the ability to synthesize compounds they would not naturally produce |CITS: [23233208]|. , Ethylene glycol is an important chemical commonly used as anti-freeze and coolant in vehicles. It is commercially produced from fossil fuels. This pathway was genetically engineered in E.coli for the production of |FRAME: GLYCOL| from |FRAME: CPD-15377 "D-xylose"|., About this Pathway, This engineered pathway consists of four steps. The gene encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-13208| from |FRAME: TAX-190650| was cloned into E.coli. The natural conversion of D-xylose to D-xylulose in E.coli was blocked by mutation of the D-xylose isomerase gene |CITS: [23233208]|. To prevent carbon shuttling via the conversion of glycoaldehyde to glycolate, the aldehyde dehydrogenase gene was also disrupted |CITS: [23233208]|. Ethylene glycol production was not optimal and D-xylonate accumulation occurred. The authors are further optimizing their studies to improve ethylene glycol synthesis |CITS: [23233208]|.

General Background, Carnitine was first discovered in 1905 in muscle extracts, and its name is derived from the Latin word for flesh, Carnis |CITS: [11183736]|. In 1962 it was found that the physiological enantiomer is |FRAME: CARNITINE|, and since then the widespread distribution of L-carnitine has been established in higher and lower eukaryotes (including plants) and many microorganisms |CITS: [9706218]|. In eukaryotes, among other roles, it is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The physiological role of carnitine in bacteria is still unknown |CITS: [9037756]|. , |FRAME: D-CARNITINE| is a much rarer form. However, some bacterial species are capable of metabolizing it as well. Several mechanisms for the metabolism of D-carnitine have been discovered. |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-303| can convert D-carnitine to L-carnitine by the action of carnitine racemase |CITS: [7815937][Monnich95]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7472|). |FRAME:TAX-357| has |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.254|, a dedicated enzyme that acts only on D-carnitine, converting it to 3-dehydrocarnitine (see |FRAME: PWY-7471|), while |FRAME:TAX-471| has a monooxygenase that can accept both L- and D-carnitine as substrates |CITS: [9214773]| (see |FRAME: PWY-3641|)., About This Pathway, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.254| is an enzyme that is specific for D-carnitine and produces |FRAME: 3-DE-H-CARNITINE|. The enzyme has been characterized from two |FRAME:TAX-357| species independently by two groups |CITS: [9214773][9003445]|. , It took many years to decipher the latter part of the pathway. Earlier reports from multiple organisms found that |FRAME: 3-DE-H-CARNITINE| is broken down to |FRAME: BETAINE|, though the exact steps were not clear |CITS:[14296565][Lindstedt67][5438040]|. A 2009 study has identified two gene clusters in |FRAME: TAX-287| that appeared involved in the pathway, and characterized some of the genes, although the crucial components (|FRAME: G1FZ6-5512| and |FRAME: G1FZ6-5514|) were not characterized at the time, and the proposed pathway turned out to be incorrect |CITS: [19406895]|. The final clarification of the pathway was provided only in 2014, with the proper characterization of these two enzymes |CITS: [24240508]|. , While that pathway was studied in |FRAME: TAX-287|, the pathway's enzymes were subsequently characterized also from |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [30670548]|. Homologs of both |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.317|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.2.33|, are present in the genomes of Agrobacterium species such as |FRAME: TAX-176299|.

Summary: General Background, Some bacteria living in anoxic environments are able to ferment amino acids to |FRAME: AMMONIA|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: ACET| and short chain fatty acids., Proteins are initially hydrolysed by exogenous proteases to small peptides and single amino acids, which are then taken up by the bacteria and degraded internally., Acetogenic organisms use the |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| for the synthesis of |FRAME: ACET|, while the so called "syntrophic" bacteria oxidize the short chain fatty acids to |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, provided methanogenic archaea in the environment keep the partial pressure of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| at very low value (see |FRAME:METHANOGENESIS-PWY|)., At least one pathway is known for the fermentation of every one of the 20 protein-building amino acids. In the case of |FRAME: GLT|, at least five such pathways are known |CITS: [11759672]|., About This Pathway, Different methylaspartate pathways are used to ferment glutamate into different end compounds. This pathway has been first described in two members of the |FRAME: TAX-31977| - |FRAME: TAX-81464| and |FRAME: ORG-6019| |CITS: [NANNINGA87][11759672]|. In this pathway variant |FRAME:GLT| is degraded into |FRAME: PROPIONATE|., In the methylaspartate pathways, the linear carbon chain of |FRAME: GLT| is rearranged into the branched carbon skeleton of |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE|, facilitating the subsequent elimination of |FRAME: AMMONIA| since the β-H is now activated by the adjacent carboxyl group. |FRAME:MESACONATE| is then hydrated to |FRAME:S-CITRAMALATE|, which is subsequently cleaved to |FRAME:ACET| and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|. A carboxyl group, originating from |FRAME:D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| is then added to the |FRAME:PYRUVATE| by a transcarboxylase,, generating |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|. |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID| is converted by a partial reverse |FRAME: TCA|, resulting in |FRAME: SUC|, which then accepts a Co-A factor from |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA|, generating |FRAME: PROPIONATE|. The |FRAME:SUC-COA| which is formed is used to regenerate |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA|, via a reversed |FRAME: PROPIONMET-PWY| |CITS: [11759672]|.

Summary: General Background, 400 million tons of methane are produced each year through methanogenesis, a process in which methanogenic archaea anaerobically reduce acetate or single carbon compounds to methane |CITS: [11830598]|., |FRAME: CoM "Coenzyme M"| (CoM; 2-mercaptoethanesulfonic acid) plays a key role in methanogenesis as the terminal methyl carrier. In the terminal step of methanogenesis, the methylated form of CoM is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-664 "methyl-coenzyme M reductase"|, forming methane and a |FRAME: CPD-1282| (CoB-S-S-CoM), which is reduced in a key energy yielding step (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|) |CITS: [12102556]|., Initially, CoM was thought to be only present in methanogenic archaea. However, several eubacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-78245| and |FRAME:TAX-1829| strain B276 have been shown to possess CoM, which they use in |FRAME: PWY-5534 "propylene degradation"| |CITS: [10411892][10762269]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of CoM was postulated based on studying the labeling patterns of CoM purified from three different methanogens (|FRAME: TAX-2162|, |FRAME: ORG-5913|, and a methanogenic bacterium similar to |FRAME: TAX-83816|) grown on stable isotope-labeled acetates, sulfolactate, and sulfite |CITS: [white85]|. These studies suggested that the first step in CoM biosynthesis is the reaction of phosphoenolpyruvate with sulfite to produce sulfolactate, which is then oxidized to sulfopyruvate |CITS: [white85]|. Sulfopyruvate is then converted to sulfoacetaldehyde by |FRAME: CPLX-2003| |CITS: [10940029]|., Sulfoacetaldehyde is subsequently converted to CoM. The transformation has been studied for a long time |CITS: [White85][white86]|, and the enzyme responsible for it was discovered only in 2019 |CITS: [30932481]|., The proposed biosynthetic pathway of CoM has been shown to be similar in three methanogenic bacteria, |FRAME: TAX-2162|, |FRAME: ORG-5913|, and rumen isolate 10-16B. An alternative pathway that appears to function in members of the orders |FRAME: TAX-94695| and |FRAME: TAX-2191| is described in |FRAME: PWY-6643|.

In the |FRAME: CPD-16932| biosynthetic gene cluster of this organism three tandem ORFs, ORF33, ORF34 and ORF35 catalyze the formation of the |FRAME: CPD-16935| moiety of |FRAME: CPD-16932|. Other ORFs in the cluster encode a large type I polyketide synthetase |CITS: 15844935|. |FRAME: CPD-16935 "2-Amino-3-hydroxycyclopent-2-enone"| (an enol tautomer of |FRAME: CPD-16936|) is a C5N unit that is present in many members of the manumycin antibiotic family as well as in other bioactive metabolites. In |FRAME: CPD-16932| the amino group of |FRAME: CPD-16935| is amide-bonded to the polyketide-derived polyenoic acid component, whereas in |FRAME: MOENOMYCIN| it is amide-bonded to |FRAME: Hexuronates| group |CITS: [20394362][15844935][NAKAGAWAA85]|., About This Pathway, In the first reaction |FRAME: GLY| is condensed with |FRAME: SUC-COA| which produces |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE|, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-18786| encoded by ORF34. |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE "5-Aminolevulinate"| is also an intermediate in tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in some species of |FRAME: TAX-1883| |CITS: [16816183]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5189|). In the next reaction an |FRAME: ATP|-dependent |FRAME: MONOMER-18787| encoded by ORF35 catalyzes the ligation of |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| to |FRAME: CO-A| producing |FRAME: CPD-16937|. The latter compound is unstable and can either undergo spontaneous intramolecular cyclization to produce the off-pathway shunt product |FRAME: CPD-16938|, or be converted enzymatically to |FRAME: CPD-16935| by the cyclase activity of the ORF34 product |CITS: [20394362]|., The reaction link shows a condensation step catalyzed by the |FRAME: MONOMER-18788| product of ORF33 that is proposed to incorporate |FRAME: CPD-16935| into the polyketide chain of |FRAME: CPD-16932| which constitutes the final chain termination step. This reaction was experimentally demonstrated using the synthetic partial polyenoate scaffold |FRAME: CPD-16939| which was derived from the structure of |FRAME: CPD-16932| |CITS: [20394362]|., Recombinant proteins encoded by ORF33, ORF34 and ORF35 were overexpressed in Escherichia coli, purified and biochemically characterized. In addition, the entire |FRAME: CPD-16935| biosynthetic pathway was reconstituted in vitro. The three enzymes were incubated with |FRAME: MG+2|, |FRAME: ATP|, |FRAME: CO-A|, |FRAME: GLY| and |FRAME: SUC-COA| (or |FRAME: 5-AMINO-LEVULINATE|) and |FRAME: CPD-16939|. The reaction product |FRAME: CPD-16941| was identified by LC-MS. Gel filtration chromatography demonstrated that none of the three enzymes formed complexes, indicating freely diffusible intermediates |CITS: [20394362]|.

Summary: General Background, Blood glucose levels in mammals are maintained during fasting by utilization of liver glycogen stores. When this reserve is depleted, glucose must be generated from non-sugar carbon substrates in the process known as gluconeogenesis |CITS: [Salway]|. Most of the reactions in the process are the exact reversal of |FRAME: ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY "glycolysis"| reactions. However, the three reactions of glycolysis catalyzed by |FRAME: HS02935-MONOMER|/|FRAME: HS08136-MONOMER "hexokinase"|, |FRAME: HS00894-MONOMER "phosphofructokinase"| and |FRAME: HS00906-MONOMER "pyruvate kinase"| that occur with a free energy change are circumvented during gluconeogenesis by using different enzymes., Gluconeogenesis in mammals is perfomed primarily in the liver and to a lesser extent in the kidney cortex and intestine. The pathway is considered to start with pyruvate. The liver utilizes mainly lactate (|FRAME: EC-1.1.1.27|) and alanine (|FRAME: EC-2.6.1.2|) as the pyruvate source |CITS: [458501]|. Glycerol can also function as a gluconeogenic precursor, entering the pathway at the level of dihydroxyacetone phosphate (|FRAME: EC-2.7.1.30| and |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.8|)., Lactate is formed in skeletal muscle cells during anaerobic glycolysis |CITS: [14960150]|. It is converted to pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase. The conversion of glucose to lactate and back to glucose is referred to as the Cori cycle |CITS: [5355347][10484349]|., In humans, gluconeogenesis occurs during periods of fasting or rigorous exercise. As carbohydrates are limited under these circumstances, it is often associated with ketosis. Hepatic gluconeogenesis is tightly regulated by the opposing actions of insulin and glucagon |CITS: [19450513]|. , About this Pathway , In mammals gluconeogenesis is initiated in the mitochondria with the carboxylation of pyruvate to form oxaloacetate. This reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: HS10697-MONOMER "pyruvate carboxylase"| and requires 1 molecule of ATP |CITS: [13840551]|. The enzyme is stimulated by high levels of acetyl coA produced by β oxidation of fatty acids and inhibited by high levels of ADP |CITS: [9597748]|., Most of the remaining steps of gluconeogenesis occur in the cytosol. Since oxaloacetate cannot leave the mitochondria, two enzymes, |FRAME: HS07366-MONOMER| and |FRAME: CPLX-7322|, form part of a shuttle to transport oxaloacetate from the mitochondria to the cytosol. Oxaloacetate is first reduced to malate in an NADH-dependent reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: HS07366-MONOMER|. Malate is transported into the cytosol and oxidized back to oxaloacetate by |FRAME: CPLX-7322| |CITS: [6849808]|., The cytosolic |FRAME: HS04751-MONOMER "phosphoenolpyruvate decarboxylase"| decarboxylates and phosphorylates oxaloacetate to form phosphoenolpyruvate at the expense of 1 mole of GTP |CITS: [6304730]|. The next steps are akin to reverse glycolysis, with the exception of the rate limiting step of gluconeogenesis, the conversion of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate, which is catalyzed by the gluconeogenic enzyme |FRAME: HS09189-MONOMER "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase" | |CITS: [8387495]|., The final step of gluconeogenesis occurs in the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum, where glucose-6-phosphate is hydrolyzed to glucose by |FRAME: HS05538-MONOMER| |CITS: [12093795]|. Glucose transporters in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane then shuttle glucose into the cytoplasm |CITS: [8211187]|. Since many tissues (for example, skeletal muscle) lack glucose-6-phosphatase, in these tissues gluconeogenesis is utilized for the synthesis of glycogen rather than free glucose.

Summary: |FRAME: DL-12-Propanediol "1,2-Propanediol"| (1,2-PDO) occurs in two stereoisomers - |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| and |FRAME: CPD-8891|. Both forms are produced by certain organisms. For example, during the catabolism of 6-deoxyhexoses |CITS: [Suzuki68][16346466]| or during the fermentation of glucose via |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [Tran-Din85][Cameron86]|. , 1,2-PDO is a bulk industrial chemical with a global demand of around 1.36 million tons/year |CITS: [Shelley07]|. It is widely used in the production of unsaturated polyester resin and as a nontoxic replacement of ethylene glycol in de-icer and antifreeze products. Current commercial production of 1,2-PDO is mainly by a synthetic process that results in a racemic mixture., Several efforts have been made to produce 1,2-PDO in culture. The highest titers reported as of 2014 are of 4.5 g/L from glucose |CITS: [11101319]| and 5.6 g/L from glycerol |CITS: [21404260]|, using the methylglyoxal pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5453|). Since |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| is highly cytotoxic, a pathway that would circumvent its formation is desirable., This synthetic pathway describes the stereospecific microbial conversion of lactate into 1,2-PDO that eliminates the need for production of |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| |CITS: [25007409]|. The pathway was constructed in an |FRAME: TAX-562| host that was modified to disable the utilization of lactate by inactivating the |FRAME: EG11963| and |FRAME: EG10231| genes (which encode (R)- and (S)-lactate dehydrogenases, respectively), as well as the production of D-lactate, by inactivating the |FRAME: G592| gene. This was necessary to ensure the enantiomeric purity of the bioconversion product, by eliminating endogenous sources of lactate. Another modification was the deletion of the |FRAME: EG10031| gene, which encodes a fermentative enzyme leading to ethanol production., The first step in the pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: Lactate| to |FRAME: Lactoyl-CoAs|, is carried out by the broad substrate range CoA-transferase form |FRAME: TAX-907|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-34517| gene., The second step, the reduction of |FRAME: Lactoyl-CoAs| to |FRAME: Lactaldehydes|, has not been documented in biology. However, it was found that the |FRAME: STM2051-MONOMER| encoded by the |FRAME: STM2051| gene from |FRAME: TAX-28901| was able to catalyze this transformation with both stereomers of lactoyl-CoA., The final step could theoretically be catalyzed by a number of native alcohol dehydrogenases of |FRAME: TAX-562|. However, it was found that the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G6190| gene is best suited for acting on both stereomers. Overexpression of the gene cloned on a plasmid with a Ptac promoter significantly improved the initial growth rate for the |FRAME: D-LACTATE| bioconversion culture and improved the titer and yield for both bioconversions. At 72 hours, a total of 19.6 mM and 21.9 mM 1,2-PDO were accumulated from |FRAME: D-LACTATE| or |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, which corresponds to 35.3% and 39.4% molar yield, respectively. It has been shown that the products retain the stereoscopic configuration of the starting material |CITS: [25007409]|.

Summary: General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , In order to avoid self-intoxication cyanogenic glucosides are stored in the vacuole. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks they come in contact with activating enzymes (specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases) that reside in the cytoplasm or apoplastic space of the cells, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN| that serves as the first line of chemical defense |CITS:[16667728][Ganjewala10]|., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1125 "(R)-Amygdalin"| is a phenylalanine-derived cyanogenic diglucoside. It accumulates in seeds of rosaceous stone fruits such as bitter almonds, apricots, cherries, peaches and plums, and is responsible for the bitterness in the seeds |CITS: [18192442]|., Because of the high amounts of amygdalin in seeds, it was suggested that it may serve as a storage form for reduced nitrogen. Studies have shown that upon seed germination, amygdalin is metabolized to form hydrogen cyanide, which is detoxified into the amino acids |FRAME: ASN| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to provide nitrogen and carbonyl compounds for the developing seedlings |CITS: [16652959][12232341]|., To find the cytochrome P450 enzymes that are involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-553| and |FRAME: CPD-1125|, the |FRAME: TAX-102107| genome was searched for members of the CYP79 and CYP71 families. Candidate genes were heterologously coexpressed with yeast cytochrome P450 reductase in microsomes of |FRAME: TAX-4932|. When incubated with |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MONOMER-20058 CYP79D16| produced the corresponding aldoxime (a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-13031| and |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDOXIME|), while |FRAME: MONOMER-20057 CYP71AN24| converted the aldoxime to |FRAME: CPD-12702| |CITS: [25015725]|.

Systemic acquired resistance (SAR) is an immune response induced in the distal parts of plants following defense activation in local tissue. Following local infection, mobile signals are generated and transported to other parts of the plant, leading to activation of long-lasting protection against a broad spectrum of microbial pathogens. |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylic acid"| is required for both SAR and local defense responses, but is unlikely to function as the mobile signal. |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| is also known to be a critical regulator of inducible plant immunity, but was also deemed unlikely to be the mobile signal |CITS: [23221596]|., Among the genes that have been found to play important roles in plant defense responses are |FRAME: AT2G13810|, |FRAME: GQT-4892|, and |FRAME: AT1G19250|. While it has been known for some time that |FRAME: AT2G13810| encodes an aminotransferase that acts on |FRAME: LYS| |CITS: [14729919]|, it was shown only in 2016 that its product, |FRAME: 2-KETO-6-AMINO-CAPROATE|, is converted to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-CARBOXYLATE|, which serves as the substrate for the product of the |FRAME: GQT-4892| gene, producing |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| |CITS: [27758894]|., |FRAME: AT1G19250| encodes a monooxygenase that is required for both local resistance and systemic acquired resistance (SAR) |CITS: [16531493][16856982][16778014]|. It was proposed that |FRAME: AT1G19250| is involved in the synthesis of a defense signal molecule that is derived from |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| |CITS: [27758894]|. In 2018 it was shown that this molecule is |FRAME: CPD-22664| |CITS: [29576453]|., The pathway is positively regulated by |FRAME: L-PIPECOLATE| and by the immune regulators EDS1 and PAD4 at the transcriptional level |CITS: [29576453]|.

Summary: |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID Stearate| is a saturated fatty acid that occurs in many animal and vegetable fats and oils. It is an important constituent of milk fats, lard, and cocoa and shea butters. Stearate was first described by Michel Eugene Chevreul in 1823, and its name comes from Greek for "hard fat", reflecting the fact that stearate forms a waxy solid |CITS: [16477801]|., In animals and fungi the precursor of stearate, |FRAME: PALMITATE|, is produced by the |FRAME: CPLX-7628| (FAS) complex, which is found in the cytoplasm (see |FRAME: PWY-5994|). Further elongation, starting with stearate, is performed in animals mainly in the ER by several membrane-bound enzymes. The enzymatic steps involved in the elongation process are principally the same as those carried out by FAS. However, the four principal successive steps of the elongation are performed by individual proteins, which may be physically associated |CITS:[4379659][16564093]|., Prior to elongation, |FRAME: PALMITATE| is activated to |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA| by |FRAME: HS07766-MONOMER| or a similar isozyme. The activated form is the substrate for the key enzyme of the pathway, the condensing enzyme, or elongase, which determines the rate of fatty acid elongation. Six distinct fatty acid elongase (Elovl) subtypes are present in the mouse, rat, and human genomes. However, only two of them, |FRAME: HS00873| and |FRAME: HS10142|, are taking part in the elongation of |FRAME: PALMITYL-COA| to |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| in the ER., Several attempts that have been made to purify the enzymes involved in the microsomal elongation process were largely unsuccessful, owing to the hydrophobic properties of the proteins |CITS: [16564093]|. One exception was the partial purification of |FRAME: MONOMER-14114| from rat liver microsomes |CITS: [500661]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it is accumulated at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant. In addition to its osmoprotectant activity, glycine betaine is also a potent protectant against mutagenic compounds |CITS: [12730887][15802867]| and radiation-induced damage |CITS: [12841603]|., |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| can either be taken up directly from the environment, or synthesized. A common biosynthesis pathway for glycine betaine is from |FRAME: CHOLINE|, utilizing a two-step pathway with |FRAME: BETAINE_ALDEHYDE| as intermediate. This pathway is conserved in bacteria and plants, but shows divergence in the enzymes involved. Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive bacteria and higher plants all use |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8|, to catalyze the conversion of betaine aldehyde to glycine betaine. The choline-to-betaine aldehyde reaction, however, is divergent: Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-287|, and |FRAME: TAX-382| utilize |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.1| (see |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|), Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, use an alcohol dehydrogenase (see |FRAME: PWY-3722|), while high plants use |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.7| (see |FRAME: PWY1F-353|)., Certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1677| and |FRAME: TAX-1665|, as well as the fungus |FRAME: TAX-109805|, use yet another enzyme to catalyze this conversion: they use a soluble |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.17|, that catalyzes both steps (see |FRAME: PWY-3721|). , There exists at least one more variation for the synthesis of glycine betaine, which is found in several halotolerant bacteria. The pathway was found in |FRAME: TAX-1052| and several other organisms, which synthesize glycine betaine from glycine through a series of methylation reactions |CITS: [10896953]| (this pathway). However, since methylation reactions are expensive (due to the cost of regenerating S-adenosylmethionine), this pathway is less common., About This Pathway, Glycine betain biosynthesis in plants differs from that in bacteria and animal. Plants convert choline to betaine aldehyde by the activity of choline monooxygenase, a Rieske type iron-sulfur-containing enzyme, whereas bacteria and animals catalyze this reaction utilizing either choline dehydrogenase or choline oxidase., The two enzymes of this pathway have been characterized in plants including spinach and sugar beet. |FRAME:TAX-3701| is generally considered a non-glycine betaine accumulating plant |CITS: [12192001]|, yet data suggests the endogenous glycine betaine level can be induced by cold acclimation and water stress |CITS: [11378169]|.
