Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized, route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Recently an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|., The pathway, which branches at chorismate, follows a different route, including the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-10477|, an unusual nucleoside derivative consisting of inosine and o-substituted benzoate moieties. Several genes that encode enzymes in this pathways have been identified by mutagenesis |CITS: [18801996]| and most enzymes have been characterized |CITS: [19420717][19602440][23763543][24083939]|.

Summary: Mangroves are intertidal plants in the tropical and subtropical regions. In accordance with their occupation of a unique habitat, they have special morphological modifications and produce several kinds of unique secondary metabolites. Mangrove plants comprise a heterogeneous group of independently derived lineages that are defined ecologically by their location in tidal zones and physiologically by their ability to withstand high salt concentrations or low soil aeration |CITS: [18820760]|.Extracts of these plants are used in folklore medicine |CITS: [17803686]|. The diverse skeletons of triterpenoids, such as |FRAME: GERMANICOL| (an oleanane), |FRAME: CPD-10667| (an oleanane), |FRAME: CPD-6948| (an oleanane) and |FRAME: CPD-90| (a lupane) are biosynthesized by various oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs).To date, very little is known about the OSC's of mangroves |CITS: [17617700]|. The physiological function of these triterpenoids in the plants is also poorly understood. It is believed that |FRAME: CPD-10667|, identified in |FRAME: TAX-40031|, may function as a chemical defense molecule because it exhibits insecticidal activity. The presence of multifunctional OSCs in mangrove has been considered to represent a transistional state before their evolution to product-specific OSC |CITS: [17078982]|., About This Pathway, We have used a separate pathway to display the triterpenoid biosynthesis in mangrove species as some of the unique triterpenoids like |FRAME: CPD-10667| and |FRAME: GERMANICOL| have been characterized from these species, along with the usual triterpenoids such as |FRAME: CPD-6948| and |FRAME: CPD-90|. This pathway delineates the evolutionary significance of monofunctional and multi-functional OSC's present the species of mangrove which throws light on the adaptation to salt tolerance in different mangrove species |CITS: [18820760]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1095 Acacetin|, the 4'-O-methylated derivative of |FRAME: CPD-431| |CITS: [Wollenweber94]| and its glycosides |CITS: [WILLIAMS94]| have been found in a number of species across various plant families, most prominently in the asteracea and leguminosae. , Acacetin has been employed as folk medicine for a long time displaying manifold pharmaceutical activities. Acacetin has been demonstrated to impair the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids| (potent biological regulators) by inhibiting the cyclooxygenase involved in the process |CITS: [10514305]|. Acacetin also interferes with human cytochrom P450s |CITS: [10781868]| and xanthine oxidase |CITS: [16450295]|, expresses antimycobacterial activity, cytotoxicity |CITS: [15202555]|, antimutagenic activity |CITS: [14586095]|, and acts as superoxide scavenger and antioxidant |CITS: [2170243]|. Most importantly, acacetin is able to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis |CITS: [15246561]| and is widely used in the research of and remedy for various cancers such as melanogenesis |CITS: [15577216]|, prostate cancer |CITS: [15637089]| and gastric carcinoma |CITS: [15686411]|., About This Pathway, The 4'-O-methylation of apigenin to produce acacetin has been demonstrated in cell-free extracts of |FRAME:TAX-35938| |CITS: [Kuroki81]|, a plant where - following germination - the accumulation of acacetin and related glycosidic derivatives has been observed. In contrast to the widespread 3'- and 5'-methylation of the flavonoid B-ring the 4'-O-methylation is relatively scarce and the knowledge about the catalyzing enzyme(s) is rather limited |CITS: [Heller94]|. In addition, the formation of |FRAME:CPD-1095| from |FRAME:CPD-431| could also be demonstrated in in vitro assays with a flavonoid 4'-O-methyltransferase isolated and purified from |FRAME:TAX-3570| |CITS:[12899699]|., Similar to the formation of acacetin (this pathway) the biosynthesis of ponciretin (|FRAME:PWY-5118|) is also catalyzed by a 4'-O-methyltransferase with a somewhat lower specificity towards accepted substrates. In contrast to the methyltransferase involved in ponciretin biosynthesis the 4'-O-methyltransferase forming acacetin clearly prefers apigenin over naringenin |CITS: [Kuroki81]| |CITS: [15961179]|. In order to determine in what respects those enzymes differ further research needs to be done.

General Background, This background summary covers this pathway and related pathways |FRAME: PWY-7008|, |FRAME: PWY-7009| and |FRAME: PWY-7010|. These pathways were studied in |FRAME: TAX-46680|, or a regulatory mutant of |FRAME: TAX-46680| designated Prp, as described below., Pathway |FRAME: PWY-7008|: |FRAME: CPD-946| has been used as a volatile fungicide (in |CITS: [8449871]|) and is a product of |FRAME: PWY-681| (in |CITS: [9305879]|). |FRAME: TAX-46680 "Pseudomonas nitroreducens (previously known as Pseudomonas azelaica HBP1 or Pseudomonas sp. strain HBP1)"| was able to grow on |FRAME: CPD-946| as sole source of carbon and energy via a pathway involving ortho hydroxylation by a soluble, |FRAME: NADH|-dependent monooxygenase (HbpA), ring cleavage of the hydroxylated product at the meta position by a dioxygenase (HbpC), and hydrolysis of the meta cleavage product by a hydrolase (HbpD) to produce |FRAME: BENZOATE| and the common aromatic intermediate |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (which has an enol tautomeric form |FRAME: CPD-6761|). The latter two compounds were further metabolized as shown in the pathway links. The last two reactions of this pathway are shared with pathway |FRAME: PWY5F9-12| (|CITS: [3214154][8449871]| and in |CITS: [10629187]|)., Pathway |FRAME: PWY-7009|: |FRAME: TAX-46680| was also able to grow on |FRAME: CPD-14144| as sole source of carbon and energy via enzymes HbpA, HbpC and HbpD, producing the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-927|, |FRAME: CPD-928|, |FRAME: CPD-110|, and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (|CITS: [3214154][8449871]| and in |CITS: [10629187]|). The latter two reactions are shared with pathway |FRAME: P662-PWY|. In addition, HbpA was also shown to hydroxylate |FRAME: CPD-927| to |FRAME: CPD-14164|, with subsequent metabolism via these enzymes to |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, |FRAME: PYROGALLOL| and |FRAME: CPD-13339| (2-hydroxymuconate), as shown here. However, the route via |FRAME: CPD-14164| was suggested to be a minor one |CITS: [8449871]|., Pathway |FRAME: PWY-7010|: A regulatory mutant of |FRAME: TAX-46680|, designated Prp, (Pseudomonas sp. strain HBP1 Prp, or Pseudomonas azelaica HBP1 Prp) was isolated by growth on |FRAME: CPD-14147|. It was able to use this compound as a sole source of carbon and energy. |FRAME: CPD-14147| did not support growth of wild-type |FRAME: TAX-46680|. The same enzymes that catalyze |FRAME: PWY-7008| (HbpA, HbpC and HbpD) also appeared to catalyze |FRAME: CPD-14147| degradation. The HbpA monooxygenase was induced by |FRAME: CPD-14147| in the mutant, but not in the wild-type strain. In addition, a small amount of the first two enzymes were constitutively produced. Pathway intermediates of |FRAME: CPD-14147| degradation were identified as |FRAME: CPD0-2477| (the hydroxylation product), |FRAME: CPD-14149| (the meta-cleavage product), and hydrolase products |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (butyrate) and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|. However, it was noted that the pathway enzymes had higher affinities for the substrates of pathway |FRAME: PWY-7008| |CITS: [8481010]|., This pathway: The |FRAME: TAX-46680| Prp regulatory mutant also utilized enzymes HbpA, HbpC and HbpD to degrade |FRAME: CPD-14150| (o-cumenol) as the sole source of carbon and energy, with the corresponding intermediates |FRAME: CPD-14151|, |FRAME: CPD-1008|, |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|. |FRAME: CPD-14150| is used in industry and is a potential pollutant |CITS: [7811094]|., These pathways are an example of the generally broad specificity of enzymes functioning in meta-cleavage pathways |CITS: [8481010]|. The |FRAME: TAX-46680| genes hbpA hbpC and hbpD encoding the three enzymes used in these pathways have been characterized. A regulatory gene hbpR was also identified and characterized as a member of the XylR/DmpR subclass of the NtrC family of transcriptional activators. The third reaction is catalyzed by HbpC, a hydrolase that cleaves the meta-cleavage product to |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (which has an enol tautomeric form |FRAME: CPD-6761|). The further metabolism of |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| was not reported |CITS: [7811094]|. |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| is degraded to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| which enters the |FRAME: TCA|, as shown in the pathway link (in |CITS: [10629187]|).

Summary: General Background, 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes convert 2-oxo acids to the corresponding acyl-CoA derivatives and produce NADH and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| in an irreversible reaction., Five members of this family are known at present, including the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| (PDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| (OGDHC), the |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| (BCDHC - this pathway), the |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| (GDHC), and the |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.190| (ADHC). They all function at strategic points in (usually aerobic) catabolic pathways and are subject to stringent control |CITS: [9655933]|., With the exception of GDHC, the 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complexes share a common structure. They consist of three main components, namely a 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3)., In Gram-positive bacteria and mitochondria, the E1 component is a heterodimer composed of two subunits, while in Gram-negative bacteria it is made of a single type of subunit., In all cases described so far, many copies of each subunit assemble to form the full complex. For example, the |FRAME: TAX-83333| |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| comprises 24, 24, and 12 units of the E1, E2, and E3 components, respectively., The core of the complex is made of either 24 (Gram-negative bacteria) or 60 (mitochondria) E2 units, which contain the lipoyl active site in the form of lipoyllysine, as well as binding sites for the other two subunits. E1, which contains a |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE| cofactor, catalyzes the binding of the 2-oxo acid to the lipoyl group of E2, which then transfers an acyl group (the nature of the acyl group depends on the particular enzyme) to |FRAME: CO-A|, forming an acyl-CoA. During this transfer, the lipoyl group is reduced to dihydrolipoyl. E3 then transfers the protons to NAD, forming NADH and restoring the dihydrolipoyllysine group back to lipoyllysine.., Cryoelectron microscopy of PDHC from |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS:[12411477]| and ox kidney |CITS: [11752427]| has revealed that the E2 inner core is surrounded by an outer shell of E1 and E3 components, with the lipoyl domains confined to the annular space between them where they must make successive journeys between the three types of active sites (E1-E3), which are physically far apart |CITS: [12795594]|., About This Pathway, In the pathway illustrated here |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, a transamination product of |FRAME: VAL|, is used as an example for the 2-oxo acid substrate of the branched-chain dehydrogenase complex (BCDHC). This reaction is summarized by the EC entry 1.2.1.25, |FRAME: 1.2.1.25-RXN|. , BCDHC can also recognize |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| and |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| (which are the transamination products of |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME: ILE|, respectively), and plays a key role in the degradation of |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, and |FRAME: ILE|., Many Gram-positive bacteria, such as the bacilli, staphylococci, and streptomycetes, produce odd- and even-carbon-number branched-chain fatty acids (for example, in |FRAME: TAX-1423| 95% of the total fatty acids are branched |CITS: [4392505][1886522]|). The most common starter molecules for branched-chain fatty acids biosynthesis are the products of the branched-chain 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase system (|FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA|, |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, and |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|) |CITS: [ 3142877]|.

Summary: While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]|, it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|., The most common mechanism for retrieving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination,, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves, the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid., In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|)., In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central, metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich, pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the, corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde., Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced, (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols",, or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids (fusel acids) |CITS: [15933030]|., |FRAME: LEU| is one of the three protein-building branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), along with, |FRAME: VAL| and |FRAME: ILE|., The metabolism of BCAA in yeast is different than in other eukaryotes. While most other eukaryotes, (as well as many prokaryotes) catabolize |FRAME: LEU| through a succession of acyl-coA derivatives, to metabolites that can enter the TCA cycle (see |FRAME:LEU-DEG2-PWY|), providing the organism, with carbon as well as nitrogen, yeast are not able to use, |FRAME:LEU| as a carbon source, and process it through the Ehtlich pathway to |FRAME:CPD-7032|, |CITS: [9341119]|., Initial work performed by Ehrlich and others suggested that the catabolism of |FRAME:LEU| in, |FRAME: TAX-4932| first involves transamination using |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| (similar to the, first step of the pathway found in other eukaryotes), but continues with decarboxylation of the keto acid, to produce an aldehyde that is then reduced to |FRAME:CPD-7032| |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. Later work, by Dickinson et al suggests that the product of |FRAME: LEU| transamination,, |FRAME:2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE|, is decarboxylated by a pyruvate decarboxylase-like enzyme encoded, by the THI3 gene |CITS: [9341119][12499363]|. Mutants lacking this enzyme were not able to grow in, ethanol minimal medium with leucine as a sole nitrogen source |CITS: [9341119]|. The mutants, were able to grow in glucose minimal medium with leucine as the sole nitrogen source, but produced, very little |FRAME: CPD-7032| (since some |FRAME: CPD-7032| was still formed, the authors speculate, that there is at least one other decarboxylase that is involved in the decarboxylation of, |FRAME:2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE| and the formation of |FRAME: CPD-7032| |CITS: [9341119]|.

|FRAME: ITACONATE Itaconate| is an unsaturated acid with conjugated double bonds and two carboxyl groups. The acid was discovered in 1837 |CITS: [Baup37]|, and was named |FRAME: ITACONATE| as an anagram of |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE|, from which it was first derived by Crasso in 1840 |CITS: [Turner41]|., Because of its unique structure and characteristics, itaconate and its ester are useful materials for the bioindustry. It is used for the synthesis of fiber, resin, plastic, rubber, paints, surfactant, ion-exchange resins and lubricant |CITS: [17451943]|., |FRAME: ITACONATE Itaconate| inhibits |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.1|, the key enzyme of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS "glyoxylate shunt"|, which is essential for bacterial growth under specific conditions |CITS: [17593]|. Its production by mammalian macrophages can inhibit the growth of pathogenic bacteria and is considered an immune defense |CITS: [23610393]|., The production of |FRAME: ITACONATE| by fungi was first observed in |FRAME: TAX-36638| in 1929 |CITS: [Kinoshita31]|, but was studied the most in the organism |FRAME: TAX-33178| |CITS: [16747058] [13438853][13438855][13911957][8227940]|, which is also used for the industrial production of |FRAME: ITACONATE| |CITS:[11548996][12146646][17451943][17697977]|. , A pathway for the microbial production of |FRAME: ITACONATE| via direct decarboxylation of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediate |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE| was proposed already in 1957 |CITS: [13438853][ 13438855]|, and was later verified when the gene encoding the responsible enzyme, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.6|, was identified in |FRAME: TAX-33178| |CITS: [16233265]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5750|)., Studies of |FRAME: ITACONATE| production in the smut fungus |FRAME: TAX-5270| revelaed that in this organism itaconate is synthesized by a different pathway variant. Upon export of |FRAME: CIS-ACONITATE| from the mitochondrion to the cytosol, which is mediated by |FRAME: G-58773|, it is converted to |FRAME: CPD-225| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.3.7| (encoded by the |FRAME: G-58772| gene). |FRAME: TAX-5270| possesses a different decarboxylase that acts only on the trans form of the substrate, forming |FRAME: ITACONATE|. The latter can be secreted across the plasma membrane out of the cell, or could be oxidized further into |FRAME: CPD-21502| |CITS: [26639528][27750034]|.

Names: superpathway of coenzyme A biosynthesis III (mammals) // CoA biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CO-A "Coenzyme A"| is a crucial cofactor in all living organisms. It functions as an acyl carrier and carbonyl-activating group in numerous central biochemical transformations, including the |FRAME: PWY66-398| and fatty acid metabolism |CITS: [16415216]|. It is estimated that about 4% of all known enzymes require CoA as an obligate cofactor |CITS: [11153265]|. While many organisms are capable of de novo CoA biosynthesis from |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE| and |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| via |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| (vitamin B5), animals and some pathogenic microbes require exogenous |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| for CoA synthesis. In mammals, a deficiency of vitamin B5 can cause many systemic consequences such as impaired motor response, depressed heme synthesis and altered growth. Levels of CoA can also be affected by metabolic stress such as starvation, alcoholism, diabetes and some cancers |CITS: [1746161]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: CO-A| from |FRAME: PANTOTHENATE| is an essential universal pathway in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Despite significant variations in the sequence of individual enzymatic components, the overall topology of CoA biosynthesis appears to be preserved in all taxons. In mammals, it consists of five enzymatic steps. In the first step, the pantothenate kinases phosphorylate pantothenate to |FRAME: 4-P-PANTOTHENATE|, and are feedback inhibited by CoA itself, accounting for the primary regulatory mechanism of CoA biosynthesis.The addition of |FRAME: CYS| results in the formation of |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE| in an ATP dependent reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-497| |CITS: [11923312]|. This is in contrast to the E. coli ortholog which utilizes CTP for the reaction |CITS: [11278255]|., Next, |FRAME: CPLX66-498| mediates the decarboxylation of |FRAME: R-4-PHOSPHOPANTOTHENOYL-L-CYSTEINE| to |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| |CITS: [15581364]|. In the last two steps of the pathway, |FRAME: HS00931-MONOMER| converts 4'-phosphopantetheine to CoA |CITS: [11994049]|.The conservation of this pathway in biological systems, allowed the efficient use of comparative genome analysis to visualize the mosaic of conserved genes and reveal previously uncharacterized genes in the human CoA biosynthetic pathway |CITS: [15014152]|. The first two enzymes of the pathway are present in all eukaryotes but are consistently fused in many bacteria and archaea. In contrast, a fusion event for the last two enzymes in the pathway occurred in mammals and flies, but not in plants, fungi or prokaryotes.

|FRAME: N-EE-PIPEROYL-PIPERIDINE Piperine| is an alkaloid that gives the pungent flavor of black pepper (Piper nigrum) and related species. Piperine in diet can stimulate the digestive enzymes of pancreas and enhance the digestive capacity. It has also been documented to enhance the bioavailability of a number of therapeutic drugs. Although non-genotoxic, piperine has been found to have anti-mutagenic and anti-tumor influences (see a recent review |CITS: [17987447]|)., The biosynthetic pathway of piperine is still not comletely understood. The first enzyme to be reported is the last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.145|, which was originally reported in 1990 |CITS: [Geisler90]|, although the gene encoding it was identified only in 2021 |CITS: [33833371]|., The two substrates of this enzyme are |FRAME: PIPERIDINE| and |FRAME: EE-PIPEROYL-COA|. While it is still not known how the former is produced (although data suggests it is derived from |FRAME: LYS|), two enzymes involved in the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-26163| to |FRAME: EE-PIPEROYL-COA| via |FRAME: CPD-26162| have been described. The first enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-124270|, is a cytochrome P450 |CITS: [33435446]|, while the latter is a CoA-ligase with similarity to a peroxisomal acyl-coenzyme A synthetase from |FRAME: TAX-3702| |CITS: [31837062]|., |FRAME: CPD-26163 Feruperare| is believed to be generated from |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| by a C2 extension, but the enzymes involved have not been identified yet.

Names: aloin biosynthesis // octoketide biosynthesis // barbaloin biosynthesis
Summary: Several |FRAME: TAX-25641| species contain a bitter compound called aloin or barbaloin in their exudates. Unlike the aloe bitters |FRAME: CPD-11557|, |FRAME: CPD-11558| and |FRAME: CPD-11558 aloeresin|, which are medicinal compounds used in wound healing and skin lightening applications, the anthroquinone aloin has been tradionally known for its use as a bittering agent in beverages and for its laxative effects |CITS: [17853381][18470597]| (The FAO removed it from the safe list of compounds for laxatives in 2002.), However, in recent years several medical properties were reported for aloin, including antagonizing stimulated ischemia/reperfusion-induced damage and inflammatory response in cardiomyocytes |CITS: [33502605]|, deceleration of the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma |CITS: [3472005]|, alleviation of pathological cardiac hypertrophy |CITS: [34801516]|], regulation of matrix metabolism and apoptosis in human nucleus pulposus cells |CITS: [35035490]|, inhibition of proteolytic and deubiquitinating activity of papain like protease (PLpro) of SARS-CoV-2 |CITS: [35140265]|,  inhibitory effects of aloin on lipopolysaccharide-induced severe inflammatory responses |CITS: [35023793]|, prevention of ulcerative colitis in mice |CITS: [33839199][36075180]|. Aloin appears to often act via activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 defense pathway |CITS: [33410857][33502605]| or by inhibition of PI3K/Akt/NF-κB signaling |CITS: [33096361]|., The latex is produced in aloe vascular cells just under the epidermis of the leaves. The younger leaves have higher concentration of anthroquinones like aloin. The compound is found in higher concentration in the leaf lamina compared with the middle of the leaf, and at the top of the leaf compared with the bottom, indicating a protective function |CITS: [12624988]|., Aloin is yellow brown in color. It occurs as a natural mixture of two diasteoromers with very similar properties - |FRAME: CPD-11590| (barbaloin) and |FRAME: CPD-26379| (isobarbaloin) |CITS: [17373434]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-15477 Salvigenin| is a flavonoid found in sweet basil (|FRAME: TAX-39350|) and numerous other plant species |CITS: [20804824][ 21893325][22923679]|. Flavonoids are found throughout the plant kingdom where they play diverse and important physiological roles |CITS: [21880658]|. Many of these structurally diverse compounds also have an impact on human health and the enzymes involved in their production are attractive candidates for metabolic engineering |CITS: [21732240]|. Notably, |FRAME: CPD-15477| has neuroprotective effects, likely due to its antioxidant activity |CITS: [22899171]|., Flavone metabolism in basil appears to occur in complex manner. While |FRAME: CPD-431| appears to be a general precursor of this pathway multiple routes with varying orders of hydroxylation and methylation seem to be involved in the production of |FRAME: CPD-15477| |CITS: [23184958]|. A similar pattern is found in the downstream |FRAME: PWY-7298| pathway |CITS: [23747095]|. Both of these pathways take place in the peltate trichomes on basil leaves |CITS:[23184958][GRAYER96]|., The pathway has been delineated based on the experimental approach of integrating biochemical, metabolic and transcript data which provide insights into substrate preferences for the various O-methyltransferases and metabolite fluxes within the metabolic network of |FRAME:PWY-7325|. The occurrence and availability of accumulating intermediates (|FRAME:CPD-15486|, |FRAME:CPD-15631|, |FRAME:CPD-15632|, |FRAME:CPD-16765| and |FRAME:CPD-15477|) and key compounds such as |FRAME:CPD-431| and |FRAME:CPD-15630| obtained from metabolite profiles in connection with substrate affinities of 7-O (FOMT1+2), 6-O (FOMT4+6), and 4'-O-methyltransferases (FOMT3+5) directs the order of the metabolite decoration with methyl and hydroxyl groups in this pathway and indicates the most favorable biosynthetic route |CITS:[22923679]|.

Names: L-homomethionine biosynthesis // L-methionine chain elongation pathway
Summary: Homomethionine is a non-protein amino acid. Homomethionine is synthesized from methionine via chain elongation. Transamination of methionine first forms a 2-oxo acid. The 2-oxo acid is then extended by one methyl group by a condensation reaction, an isomerization reaction, and a oxidative decarboxylation reaction. The newly formed 2-oxo acid can be transaminated to homomethionine or undergo further cycles of condensation, isomerization and oxidative decarboxylation to form di, tri, tetra, penta, and hexahomomethionines. Mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, and hexahomomethionines are precursors for aliphatic glucosinolates biosynthesis in Arabidopsis. , The cytosolic recycled methionine (|FRAME: PWY-5041|), not the plastid-located de novo synthesized methionine, is believed to be the substrate for methionine chain elongation and glucosinolate biosynthesis |CITS: [17056707]|. This is based on two observations: first, the first enzyme in the chain elongation pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.88| (|FRAME: AT3G19710|), is cytosolic. Second, the gene expressions of |FRAME: AT3G19710| and the two cytosolic methionine synthases, which are involved in the SAM cycle, are strongly co-regulated.

Summary: The L-serine degradation pathway consists of a single enzymatic reaction, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|. Most enzymes that catalyze this reaction are |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|-dependent, but some enzymes contain an iron-sulfur cluster instead |CITS: [8236444]|. The reaction catalyzed by both types of enzymes involves the initial elimination of water to form the enamine intermediate |FRAME: 2-AMINOACRYLATE|. This intermediate is very unstable. It tautomerizes immediately and spontaneously to the imine form |FRAME: CPD-16015|, which is then non-enzymatically hydrolyzed to form pyruvate and free ammonium., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562| two of the three serine deaminases are known to be expressed only in the absence of glucose. Although only one of the three primary serine deaminases has been shown to be expressed solely under anaerobic conditions, all three enzymes rely on catalytically critical iron-sulfur clusters that are oxygen sensitive,, suggesting that this pathway can only work in the absence of oxygen. This concept is bolstered by the fact that the bifunctional |FRAME: THREDEHYDCAT-CPLX "threonine/serine deaminase"| (TdcB) is also expressed only in the absence of oxygen |CITS: [4882014]|.

Names: nitrate reduction IV (dissimilatory) // dissimilatory nitrate reduction // nitrate respiration // respiratory ammonification
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Many bacteria are able to respire in the absence of oxygen by utilizing alternative electron acceptors., Due to the low redox potential of the nitrate/nitrite pair, nitrate is one of the preferred alternative electron, acceptors. , Bacterial anaerobic nitrate respiration can proceed along two different pathways. One pathway is the, denitrification process, in which nitrate is sequentially reduced through nitrite, nitric oxide, nitrous, oxide, and finally to dinitrogen (see |FRAME: DENITRIFICATION-PWY|)., In the second pathway, nitrate is first reduced to nitrite and the latter is subsequently converted in a, six-electron reduction step to ammonia, which is secreted from the cell., This six-electron reduction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: CPLX-7502|, a periplasmic hexaheme, c-type cytochrome |CITS: [7309757][3002798][2833168]|. These enzymes are different from, the assimilatory nitrite reductases in several ways, including their induction by nitrate under anaerobic, conditions |CITS: [4405508]| and the fact that they are not suppressed by the presence of ammonium, |CITS: [5726295]|., This pathway variant is curated for |FRAME: TAX-668|, which uses the cytochrome c-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.9.6.1| |CITS: [13412117]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NICOTINE Nicotine| is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-4093|) |CITS: [Schmeltz77]|, where it functions as a defense compound. In the plant tissue nicotine is mostly present in the |FRAME: NICOTINE| isomeric form |CITS: [Armstrong98]|, although tobacco smoke contains up to 10% of |FRAME: R-NICOTINE|, probably due to racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|)., Nicotine is composed of a pyridine ring joined with an N-methylpyrrolidine ring. The pyridine ring is derived from an intermediate in NAD biosynthesis, most likely |FRAME: NIACINE| |CITS: [Dawson56]|. The pyrrolidine ring is derived from |FRAME: CPD-7994|, a common intermediate for the tropane alkaloids that is derived from |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| |CITS: [Leete67]|., Somewhat surprisingly, the condensation of the two rings to form nicotine is largely uncharacterized at this time. A pathway has been proposed based on several observations, for example, that a hydrogen is lost from C-6 of nicotinate when it is incorporated into nicotine, while all the other hydrogens remain intact |CITS: [Friesen90]|. However, the individual steps in the pathway have not been characterized, and no enzymes have been purified. A generic "nicotine synthase" activity was detected in a crude enzyme preparation from |FRAME: TAX-4097| supplemented with |FRAME: NIACINE| and N-methyl-delta1-pyrrolinium chloride |CITS: [Friesen90]|., Once formed, nicotine may be demethylated to |FRAME: CPD-2748| by a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase. Nornicotine formation in tobacco is undesired because it serves as a precursor of the carcinogen N'-nitrosonornicotine during the curing and processing of tobacco |CITS: [16192354]|.

Names: dimethylsulfoniopropanoate biosynthesis I (Wollastonia) // DMSP biosynthesis // dimethylsulfoniopropionate biosynthesis I (Wollastonia)
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|, is also the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]|. It was first identified in 1948 in the red alga |FRAME: TAX-1261582| |CITS: [18101461]|, and is found in the highest concentrations in |FRAME: TAX-2864| (dinoflagellates) and |FRAME: TAX-2608131| (haptophytes). However, DMSP is produced by many more organisms including diatoms, green algae, some higher plants like |FRAME: TAX-4547| (sugarcane) and the coastal angiosperms |FRAME: TAX-15853| and |FRAME: TAX-101473|, bacteria, and some coral species |CITS: [31231779]|., Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS: [17068264]|., Biological degradation of DMSP is the main source for |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) in the marine environment |CITS: [12450799]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6046|). The degradation of DMSP to DMS and subsequent exchange of DMS across the ocean-atmosphere boundary is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. The flux of DMS from the ocean to the atmosphere is estimated at about 1.5 x 10(13) g of sulfur annually. Once in the atmosphere, DMS plays a major part in cloud formation and potentially in climate regulation., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway for DMSP in the green plant |FRAME: TAX-101473| starts with the methylation of L-methionine to |FRAME: CPD-397| |CITS: [8029347]| by the cytosolic enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7667|, and continues with conversion to |FRAME: CPD-10472| via a coupled transamination-decarboxylation reaction |CITS: [12223879]|., The participation of |FRAME: CPD-10472| as a pathway intermediate was verified |CITS: [7659747]|. The aldehyde is transported to the chloroplast where it is oxidized to DMSP by a dehydrogenase related to plant betaine aldehyde dehydrogenases |CITS: [12226341]|.

Summary: General Backround, The polyamines (the most common of which are |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|, |FRAME:SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME:SPERMINE|) are a group of positively charged organic polycations that are involved in many biological processes, including binding to nucleic acids, stabilizing membranes, and stimulating several enzymes |CITS: [3157043][4873311][1409623][2185470]|. While it is clear that polyamines are essential for normal cell growth, we still do not fully, understand their specific molecular functions in vivo |CITS:[3157043]|. |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| and |FRAME:SPERMIDINE| are found in all life forms, and |FRAME:SPERMINE| is found mostly in eukaryotes., |FRAME:PUTRESCINE Putrescine| can be formed either directly from |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| by ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) (see |FRAME:PWY-46|) or indirectly from |FRAME:ARG| by arginine decarboxylase (ADC) (see |FRAME:PWY-40| and |FRAME:PWY-43|). While the ODC pathway was considered the only mammalian pathway for polyamine biosynthesis, recently the presence of the ADC pathway in mammals has been demonstrated |CITS:[11804860], [14738999]|. In higher plants the presence of both pathways has been known for some time |CITS: [11537482]|., In bacteria, both pathways are common, and are often found side by side in the same organism |CITS:[3157043]|., About This Pathway, There are two flavors of the ADC pathway. In both cases |FRAME:ARG| is first converted to |FRAME:AGMATHINE| by a biosynthetic arginine decarboxylase. However, in enterobacteria and mycobacteria |FRAME:AGMATHINE| is converted directly to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| by the enzyme |FRAME:AGMATIN-CPLX| (see |FRAME:PWY-40|), while in higher plants, |FRAME:TAX-286| spp., |FRAME:TAX-642| spp., and lactic bacteria, |FRAME:AGMATHINE| is first hydrolyzed by |FRAME:CPLX-31| into |FRAME:CPD-597| and |FRAME:AMMONIA|, and |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| is formed by removal of the ureido group from |FRAME:CPD-597| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-39|., It should be mentioned that it has been suggested that in |FRAME: TAX-287| this pathway can operate in a catabolic manner |CITS:[6768836][3534538][11673419]|, catalyzing the degradation of |FRAME:ARG| through |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| into succinate, supplying the bacteria with carbon and nitrogen (see |FRAME:ARGDEG-III-PWY|)., Since the main catabolic arginine pathway in these bacteria is the succinyltransferase pathway (see |FRAME:AST-PWY|), there is still some debate whether this is a true arginine degradation pathway. However, it is agreed that the last two steps of the pathway are used for catabolic |FRAME:AGMATHINE| degradation |CITS:[12634339]|.

Summary: |FRAME: DMSO "Dimethyl sulfoxide"| (DMSO) is naturally present in significant amounts (1-200 nM) in ocean surface waters, probably originating from marine phytoplankton |CITS: [Andreae80]|. In addition, DMSO is widely used in various industries since it dissolves many organic and inorganic substances. In Japan alone a total of 5000 tons of DMSO is produced per year for use in various industries. Much of the DMSO accumulates in wastewater, where it has toxic effects on many organisms |CITS: [16233269]|. , DMSO-reducing capacity is widespread among aerobic and anaerobic bacteria, plants, and animals |CITS:[14148434 ][900930]|. Some organisms, including |FRAME: ORG-6050| and |FRAME: ORG-6051|, are able to utilize DMSO aerobically as the sole source of carbon, by the use of an |FRAME: MONOMER-14226| |CITS:[DeBont81][16233269]|. A similar organism, |FRAME: ORG-6052|, could do the same using an NADPH-dependent enzyme |CITS: [3767349][Suylen86]|., Other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-64091| and |FRAME: TAX-83333|, can not utilze DMSO as a carbon source, but are able to utilize it as as an alternative terminal electron acceptor (in the absence of nitrate), using the complex |FRAME: DIMESULFREDUCT-CPLX| |CITS:[414686][2546920][12899636][15716436]| (see |FRAME: PWY0-1356|).

Summary: |FRAME: ILE| is one of the three main branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), along with |FRAME: LEU| and |FRAME:VAL|. The catabolic pathways of the BCAAs can be divided into two sequential series of reactions, referred to, as the common pathway and the distal pathway., The common pathway includes the enzymes |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.42|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25|, and |FRAME: EC-1.3.8.5|. These three enzymes catalyze the conversion of all three BCAAs to their respective acyl-CoA derivatives (|FRAME:METHACRYLYL-COA|, |FRAME:3-METHYL-CROTONYL-COA|, and |FRAME: CPD-1083| for |FRAME:VAL|, |FRAME:LEU|, and |FRAME:ILE|, respectively), though the intermediates formed by these enzymes are different for the different amino acids. The distal parts of the pathways are completely different for the three BCAAs, and comprise enzymes specific for each amino acid |CITS: [773366]|., This |FRAME: ILE| degradation pathway is wide spread, and is found in many microorganisms, higher plants, and animals (including mammals)., The catabolism of |FRAME: ILE| begins with its transamination to |FRAME:2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE|, followed by oxidative decarboxylation to |FRAME:2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|. |FRAME:2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA| then undergoes a four-step β oxidation process, involving dehydrogenation to  |FRAME: CPD-1083|, hydration to |FRAME:2-METHYL-3-HYDROXY-BUTYRYL-COA|, dehydrogenation to |FRAME: 2-METHYL-ACETO-ACETYL-COA|, and finally a thioester hydrolysis forming |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA| |CITS: [4150713]|.

β-Alanine is a naturally occurring β-amino acid found in animals, plants |CITS: [5762452]| and , microorganisms.  It differs from L-alanine (an α-amino acid) in the position of the amino group on the , β carbon, rather than the α carbon.  In the pathway shown here, β-alanine is converted to , malonate semialdehyde by transamination of α-ketoglutarate (2-oxoglutarate) to L-glutamate in , an α-ketoglutarate-dependent reaction.  Malonate semialdehyde is then converted to acetyl-CoA , and CO<sub>2</sub> by oxidative decarboxylation., β-Alanine is synthesized in the liver, primarily by the degradation of uracil.  Unlike L-alanine, β-alanine is , not incorporated into proteins.  In mammals, much of the cellular pool of β-alanine is incorporated into the, dipeptide carnosine (β-alanyl-L-histidine).  There is considerable research interest in the possible role of , β-alanine and carnosine as neurotransmitters.  The inhibitory neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyrate , (GABA) is also a substrate for liver transaminases, as indicated in the EC 2.6.1.19 reaction.  β-Alanine can , also be transaminated by a pyruvate-dependent enzyme in liver |CITS: [10447691]|.  These data and other aspects , of mammalian β-amino acid metabolism and biochemistry are reviewed in |CITS: [3090932]|.  , Malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase from rat liver has been purified and characterized as the , methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase involved in valine degradation.  The authors found it to be identical , to the malonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase involved in β-alanine degradation |CITS: [2768248]|.  They found , that the production of acetyl-CoA in the presence of malonate semialdehyde, and propionyl-CoA in the presence of, methylmalonate-semialdehyde, was stoichiometric with the amount of CoA added.  No detectable malonyl-CoA or , methylmalonyl-CoA was produced.  The authors noted that this enzyme is unique among aldehyde , dehydrogenases in its CoA dependency.  They proposed that the formation of a CoA ester allows energy , conservation during aldehyde oxidation |CITS: [8356911] [1527093]|., A microbial pathway for β-alanine degradation in |FRAME:TAX-294| is described in MetaCyc , pathway β-alanine degradation II.

Summary: General Background, The distinction between nucleoside degradation and salvage is not always straight forward., A general rule is that degradation pathways start with the nucleotide or nucleoside forms and convert them to simpler forms, eventually leading to complete mineralization, while salvage pathways start with either the nucleoside or the free base form, and convert those to the nucleotide forms., Nucleotide recycling is achieved by a combination of both types - a nucleotide is partially degraded via a degradation pathway, but the products are shuttled into a salvage pathway rather then towards complete mineralization., About This Pathway, Type III RubisCO enzymes, capable of fixing |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| into |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|, are commonly found in archaea. The importance of carbon fixation in these organisms has been unclear, though, since there seemed to be no obvious way for the organisms to replenish the substrate for these enzymes., The enzyme that generates |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| in organisms that contain the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|, |FRAME:PRKSYN-MONOMER|, is missing from almost all archaea., A new route for the synthesis of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| has been discovered in some archaea, which involves an isomerization reaction from |FRAME:RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.29|. The pathway has been named the pentose bisphosphate pathway., In the hyperthermophile |FRAME: TAX-311400| it was shown that |FRAME:RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE| is produced from nucleotides by the enzyme |FRAME:MONOMER-13274| |CITS: [17303759]|. Thus it seems that in archaea the RubisCO enzyme's major role is not carbon fixation, but the degradation of nucleotides and nucleosides |CITS: [17303759][25822915]|. This pathway provides an altrernative way for the conversion of pentose sugars to 3-carbon precursors, which is facilitated in most bacteria and in eukaryotes by the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway"| (which is absent in these archaea)., Nucleotide degradation is carried out by the type III Rubisco enzyme (|FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39|) and two other enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.57| and |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.29|. AMP phosphorylase releases the base of the nucleotide and replaces it with a phosphate group to generate |FRAME: RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE|. The isomerase converts this compound to |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2|, and RubisCO catalyzes its carboxylative cleavage, generating two molecules of |FRAME: G3P|, which are directed towards glycolysis or gluconeogenesis |CITS: [17303759]|., Nucleosides are fed into the pathway by the combined action of dedicated phosphorylases (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.1|, |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.15|, |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.3|) that release the bases, generating |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P|, followed by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.212|, which generates |FRAME: RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE| |CITS: [25822915]|., Some of the enzymes of the pathway, including the type III RubisCO, are present in a wide range of archaea, including most members of the Archaeoglobales, Lokiarchaeota, Methanomicrobiales, Methanosarcinales, and Thermococcales, as well as some members in Desulfurococcales, Halobacteriales, Methanococcales, and most, Thermofilum species in Thermoproteales |CITS: [36434094]|. In addition, it has been reported that metagenomic analysis suggested the presence of these genes in a number of bacterial species |CITS: [27137126]|.

Summary: Carboxydotrophs are aerobic chemolithoautotrophic bacteria that are able to grow with CO as sole source of both carbon and energy. The oxidation of approximately six equivalents of CO to CO<sub>2</sub> provides the energy necessary to reductively fix one CO<sub>2</sub> molecule., The carboxydotrophs are taxonomically diverse, and include α, β, and γ-proteobacteria, firmicutes, and actinobacteria. It has been estimated that the carboxydotrophs remove about 2x10<sup>8</sup> metric tons of CO from the atmosphere annually, helping maintain a lower atmospheric concentration of this toxic gas |CITS: [16345624][    16345821 ]|., The key enzyme in this process is the |FRAME: EC-1.2.5.3|, or CODH. Two types of carbon monoxide hydrogenases are known - |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.4|, which is found in methanogens, sulfate reducers and purple sulfur bacteria, and the aerobic enzyme, which is found in the carboxydotrophs., The aerobic enzyme consists of a dimer of heterotrimers. Each heterotrimer is composed of an iron-sulfur protein that carries two types of [2Fe-2S] clusters, a flavoprotein that contains a noncovalently bound FAD cofactor, and a molybdoprotein that harbors the active site of the enzyme |CITS: [10430865]|. The active site contains a molybdopterin cytosine dinucleotide (MCD) cofactor, and a μ-sulfido ligand bridges the molybdenum atom to a copper atom |CITS: [12475995]|.

Summary: General Background, The antibiotic |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| is an aminoacyl nucleoside antibiotic produced by |FRAME: TAX-132473|. Other nucleoside antibiotics produced by other species of |FRAME:TAX-1883| include the peptidyl nucleosides mildiomycin and the polyoxins (in |CITS: [8576156] [18412191] [1156577]|). |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| is active against Gram-positive bacteria, protists and mammalian cells. In research, it is known to inhibit translation and has been used in cell-free systems to elucidate the mechanism of protein synthesis (in |CITS: [8576156]|). It acts as a structural analog of an aminoacyl-tRNA (in |CITS: [12166644]|). The |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| biosynthetic pathway in |FRAME: TAX-132473| also appears to provide this organism with a defense against the toxic effects of puromycin and some of its biosynthetic intermediates. This is done by inactivation, via N-acetylation, export from the cell, and hydrolysis by an extracellular enzyme to yield the biologically active product (in |CITS: [8576156] [8226694] [7916693]|). The gene cluster for |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-132473| has been cloned, expressed in heterologous hosts, and its transcripts characterized |CITS: [1537349] [7916693] [8576156]|. Its expression may be translationally regulated, |CITS: [9468310]|., About This Pathway, This proposed pathway is an updated version of the pathway for |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| biosynthesis that was proposed in |CITS: [8576156]|. It was later revised in |CITS: [10438762] [15556612]| and |CITS: [16513119]| as shown here. However, remaining questions include the actual substrates for the |FRAME: G-10675| and |FRAME: G-10674| gene products (see |CITS: [15556612] [16513119]|), making this pathway subject to future revision. The pathway takes into account early radiolabeling studies that showed |FRAME: ADENOSINE| as a precursor, as well as the necessity for production of nontoxic, acetylated intermediates. |FRAME: ADENOSINE| was proposed to enter the pathway through |FRAME: ATP|, becuase puromycin biosynthesis is initiated during growth. The enzyme products of genes pur4 and pur5 have not yet been experimentally characterized. Based on amino acid sequence analysis, the pur4 gene product was predicted to be an aminotransferase catalyzing the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10076| to |FRAME: CPD-10100|. The pur5 gene product was likewise predicted to be a |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent N-methyltransferase catalyzing the two consecutive reactions that convert |FRAME: CPD-10082| to |FRAME: CPD-10083| to |FRAME: CPD-10088| |CITS: [8576156]|. These compounds had earlier been found in purified samples of puromycin and were proposed to be biosynthetic intermediates. The compound |FRAME: CPD-10091| would be secreted from the cell and N-hydrolyzed extracellularly by the product of gene |FRAME: G-10679| to yield |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| |CITS: [8576156]|. The product of the gene pur8 may be involved in active efflux of |FRAME: CPD-10091| and |FRAME: PUROMYCIN| |CITS: [7916693]|.

Summary: General Background, Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-78245| and |FRAME: TAX-1829|, are capable of aerobic growth using aliphatic alkenes (such as |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|, |FRAME: PROPENE| and |FRAME: CPD-19063|) as source of carbon and energy., In these organisms the alkenes are oxidized to epoxides (also known as epoxyalkanes) by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7450|, a large complex similar to the aromatic monooxygenases such as |FRAME:CPLX-2181|. Epoxides contain an oxirane ring making them highly reactive electrophilic molecules, and are thus quite toxic to the cells. Depending on the organism, the epoxides are processed in several ways. Some organisms use glutathione and the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.34| to attack and open the oxirane ring |CITS: [10715003]|. Other organisms have been shown to use the unusual cofactor |FRAME:CoM| |CITS: [10411892]|, yet others use epoxide hydrolases |CITS: [25576605]|. The products of these reactions are then catabolized to central metabolites |CITS: [11352719]|., About This Pathway, Some bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-196162|, |FRAME: TAX-931627|, and |FRAME: TAX-78245|, can utilize the C2 alkenes |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD|, |FRAME: VINYL-CHLORIDE|, and |FRAME: CPD-19022| as growth substrates |CITS: [12450841][12949106][17948782]| (it should be noted that some strains, such as |FRAME: TAX-212767| and |FRAME: TAX-212768| can grow on |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| but not on |FRAME: VINYL-CHLORIDE| |CITS: [14532060]|)., Like the degradation pathways of all other aliphatic alkenes, the pathway starts with the action of a monooxygenase on the alkenes, generating the respective epoxides. The next step has been shown to be conjugation of the epoxide with |FRAME: CoM|, in parallel to the pathway of |FRAME: PWY-5534| |CITS: [12949106][14532060]|., The rest of the pathway has not been characterized as well. Based on sequence analysis of additional genes found in a cluster that also contained the genes encoding the monooxygenase and coenzyme M transferase of |FRAME: TAX-196162| (the cluster is located on a large linear plasmid, named pNOCA01), a tentative initial pathway has been suggested |CITS: [15599705]|. The propsoed pathway was later refined using results from peptide mass fingerprinting experiments performed with the same organism, which identified seven proteins that were expressed in response to incubation with either |FRAME: ETHYLENE-CMPD| or |FRAME: VINYL-CHLORIDE| |CITS: [17483267]|. In addition to subunits of the monooxygenase and the epoxyalkane:coenzyme M transferase, these peptides included a putative dual-function alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase and a protein with 53% amino acid identity to the |FRAME: CPLX-4822| of |FRAME: TAX-78245|. By analogy to the propene degradation pathway, the pathway shown here, which incorporates both of these enzymes, has been proposed |CITS: [17483267]|., The propsoed pathway results in production of |FRAME: MALONATE|. In theory, malonate could be converted to the central metabolite acetyl-CoA in two steps, known to be catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.3|:, |FRAME: MALONATE-COA-TRANSFERASE-RXN|, |FRAME: MALONYL-COA-DECARBOXYLASE-RXN|

General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, Methylated thiols such as |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) and |FRAME: CPD-7672| can serve as methylotrophic methanogenic precursors |CITS: [16347202][10224009]|. These compounds are generated in nature by many different processes, such as the degradation of |FRAME:MET|, the reduction of |FRAME:DMSO|, the anaerobic degradation of methoxylated aromatics, anoxygenic photosynthesis by some phototrophs, and the demethylation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN|, a common algae osmolite |CITS: [11073950]|., Most |FRAME: TAX-2207| species are able to utilize |FRAME: CPD-7670| and |FRAME: CPD-7672|, although some species, such as |FRAME: TAX-2208|, can only do so when grown on |FRAME:ACET| (but not |FRAME:METOH|)., The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., Unlike similar systems for |FRAME:CoM| methylation by |FRAME:METOH| and different methylamines, the enzymatic complex that methylates |FRAME:CoM| with methylated thiols consists of only two types of peptides. The MtsA peptide catalyzes the two methyltransferase activities that are catalyzed in the other systems by two different methyltransferase, MT1 and MT2 |CITS: [11073950]|. The second peptide, MtsB, is a corrinoid protein, similar to the one found in the other systems. Earler studies suggested that one corrinoid cofactor is bound per MtsA:MtsB pair, and six to seven such pairs comprise a 480 kDa complex |CITS: [8335638][8282704]|. However, later work suggested that MtsA forms dimers in solution |CITS: [11073950]|.

Summary: Cresols (meta-, ortho-, para-) are phenolic compounds commonly found in fuel processing activities such as coal gasification, and the fractionation of coal, tar, and petroleum. Cresols are commonly used in disinfectants, surfactants, and wood preservatives, and are intermediates in the manufacture of pesticides and resins., Despite their similarity, the different isomers of cresol are degraded through different pathways. The anaerobic degradation of the different isomers of cresol have been studied in several microorganisms. Under nitrite-reducing conditions, m-cresol appears to be degraded by a methyl group oxidation mechanism. In methanogens and sulfate-reducing bacteria, the methyl group is not oxidized, but is para-carboxylated and subsequently emethylated and dehydroxylated to yield benzoic acid |CITS: [LONDRY97]|., The aerobic degradation of cresols in microbes also proceeds via several distinct mechanisms. In Pseudomonas NCIB 9869, the degradation of the cresols is catalyzed by a series of enzymes of broad substrate specificity |CITS: [4330964]|. This involves an initial hydroxylation by an NADH-dependent hydroxylase to yield an alcohol |CITS: [743215]|, which is subsequently oxidized to form an aldehyde then an acid (benzoate) |CITS: [743216]|. Benzoate can then be oxidized to form either gentisate or protocatechuate by two distinct hydroxylases. In |FRAME:TAX-303|, m-cresol is degraded not by the gentisate pathway, but by the catechol meta cleavage pathway |CITS: [1123316]|.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, This superpathway combines the pathways for methanogenesis from several of the main energy sources for methanogens, including |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, |FRAME: ACET|, |FRAME: METHYLAMINE|, |FRAME: DIMETHYLAMINE| and |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE|.

Summary: General Background, Six pathways are now recognized in bacteria, most algae, fungi and higher plants for the biosynthesis of lysine. They are divided into two groups - the diaminopimelate (DAP) pathways, and the |FRAME:CPD-468| pathways., In the pathways that belong to the DAP group, lysine is produced from aspartate (along with methionine, threonine and isoleucine). All of the DAP group pathways share the upper segments, which include the four steps required for conversion of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|. They also share the last step, which is the conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (D,L-DAP, or meso-DAP) to lysine., However, these pathways differ in the routes leading from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|. The four variations include:, (I) the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|), which involves succinylated intermediates. In this route |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is coverted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in four enzymatic steps., (II) the acetylase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2941|), which involves acetylated intermediates. This route also involves four enzymatic steps for the conversion of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|., (III) the dehydrogenase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2942|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in a single enzymatic step. , (IV) the diaminopimelate-aminotransferase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5097|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in two steps., In addition to lysine, all of the pathways in this group also produce |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is an important metabolite on its own (for example, as a constituent of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan)., The two other pathways belong to the |FRAME: CPD-468| group. They are found in organisms that have no requirement for |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, as it is not a component of their cell walls. These pathways also share the first segments, leading to the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-468| (α-aminoadipate)., However, in yeast and fungi, as well as |FRAME: TAX-3038|, the pathway continues with the key enzyme |FRAME: YBR115C-MONOMER|, leading to the intermediate |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see |FRAME: LYSINE-AMINOAD-PWY|), while in prokaryotes the pathway continues in a path similar to bacterial arginine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., Most of the bacteria that have been investigated in detail appear to utilize only one of these pathways |CITS: [1906065]|. A few exceptions include |FRAME: TAX-44252|, in which variants (II) and (III) seem to coexist |CITS: [BARTLETT85]|, and |FRAME: TAX-1718|, in which variant (I) and (III) coexist |CITS: [1906065]|., Lysine is one of the 10 essential amino acids that mammals are unable to synthesize, and must therefore acquire in their diets., About This Pathway, The succinylase variant is the most common bacterial lysine biosynthesis pathway. It is found in many, different types of bacteria., In this pathway, a succinate moiety is added to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|,, followed by an amino group, to form N-succinyl-L,L-DAP., The succinate is then removed, and an epimerase converts the resulting L,L-DAP, to meso-DAP. This pathway has been experimentally verified in several Gram-negative bacteria, including, |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: TAX-71421|, |FRAME: TAX-1718|, |FRAME: TAX-210| and |FRAME: TAX-1773|,, and genes specific for this pathway have been identified in many other organisms.

Summary: This pathway describes the degradation of |FRAME: MANNOSE| in organisms that transport it into the cell in its unphosphorylated form. The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.7|, phosphorylates the mannose to |FRAME: CPD-15979|, which is then converted to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| by |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.8|. |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P D-fructofuranose 6-phosphate| can be fed into glycolysis, thus feeding into the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy. However, the activity of the enzymes is low inplants.

Photosynthetic membranes, such as plant chloroplast membranes, need a certain amount of anionic lipids for their proper function. These anionic lipids can be either phospholipids such as |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol| or sulfolipids such as |FRAME: SULFOQUINOVOSYLDIACYLGLYCEROL sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol| (SQDG)., SQDG is also classified as |FRAME: Glycolipids|. However the characteristic structure of SQDG is the unique head group constituent |FRAME: CPD-10247|, which is a derivative of glucose where 6-hydroxy is replaced by sulfonate |CITS: [15012227]|., SQDG is synthesized from |FRAME: UDP-SULFOQUINOVOSE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.M2|. The presence of a possible sulfoquinovose nucleotide in algal extracts was suggested already in 1963 |CITS: [Shibuya63]|, but its existence was confirmed only in 1995, by its accumulation in an |FRAME: G-44027| mutant |CITS: [7592762]|., Insight into this pathway was provided with the discovery of a four genes cluster (sqdA, sqdB, sqdC, and sqdD) encoding sulfolipid biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-1063| |CITS: [1400200][1551852]|. It has been shown that |FRAME: G-44027| encodes |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.M2| |CITS: [7592762]|. Out of these four genes, only |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_0578| has homologues in cyanobacteria. However, a gene next to it in the genome of the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1140|, |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_0579|, was shown to encode the cyanobacterial sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol synthase |CITS: [10629209]|., The cyanobacterial |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_0578| gene was used to isolate a cDNA for the orthologous |FRAME: TAX-3702| |FRAME: G-741| gene |CITS: [9465123]|, which was subsequently shown to encode |FRAME: EC-3.13.1.1| |CITS: [11073956]|., The synthesis of SQDG is not crucial under normal growth condition. It only becomes important when phosphate is limited |CITS: [9465123]|. Under such conditions, the increase of SQDG levels compensates for the decrease in phospholipids and ensures a constant proportion of anionic lipids in chloroplast membranes |CITS:[14675442]|. In the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1140| the concentration of SQDG increased by 90% upon exposure to phosphate stress |CITS: [31487556]|., While the general scheme of the pathway is understood, there are still some unanswered questions |CITS: [17334828]|. The mechanism of SQDG assembly in bacteria like |FRAME: TAX-1063| remains unclear, as the function of the essential genes sqdA and sqdC is still unknown. Disruption of sqdC led to the accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-17933|, suggesting it may be an intermediate in the pathway in that organism |CITS: [9143325]|. In addition, the SQD1 enzyme of |FRAME: TAX-3702| was found to form a complex with |FRAME: EC-1.4.7.1 "ferredoxin-dependent glutamate synthase"|, and the significance of this finding is also not understood |CITS: [15752726]|.
