Summary: General Background, Green sulfur bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-191412|) and green flimentous bacteria (|FRAME: TAX-1106|) contain chlorosomes - large organelles that are believed to be the most efficient light-harvesting antennae in nature |CITS: [20130996][Saga10]|. Green sulfur bacteria can grow at light intensities that are too low to support growth of any other phototroph, up to a million times lower light than normal sunlight |CITS: [Overmann92]|., Chlorosomes contain about 1,500 bacteriochlorophyll molecules per reaction center. They are filled with 10-30 rod-shaped elements which are oriented parallel to the long axis of the chlorosomes and have a diameter of 10 nm. Each rod consists of a tubular bilayer formed by self-organization of the antenna bacteriochlorophyll molecules. Unlike all other known photosynthetic antenna, in which the chlorophyll molecules are bound to proteins, chlorosomes do not contain accessory proteins. The chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyll pigments are able to self-aggregate due to their unique chemical characteristics., The bacteriochlorophylls found in chlorosomes are either |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| or |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"|, depending on the species. They all possess a hydroxyl group at the C31 position that allows them to chelate the Mg atom of a neighboring molecule and to interact with the C13-oxo carbonyl group of another neighboring pigment molecule, affording the self-aggregation |CITS: [16121276][19435848][22210764]|. In addition, all of these bacteriochlorophylls lack C-132-methylcarboxyl side chains, which are found in all other (bacterio)chlorophylls but would interfere with the ability to form aggregates |CITS: [16245042]|., Despite of their names, |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| are actually chlorins rather than bacteriochlorins. All three are usually found with an unsaturated farnesyl tail rather than phytyl tails |CITS: [2350541][Borrego99]|, although exceptions have been reported., In chlorosomes of |FRAME: TAX-191412| (but not |FRAME: TAX-1106| |CITS: [Risch79][3442679]|) all three types of bacteriochlorophyll appear in several forms with different degrees of methylation at the C-82 and C-121 carbons |CITS: [12656478][14610639]|. The variety in methylation is depicted in the structure shown here by the R groups. In general, pimgents produced by cultures grown at lower light intensities are more highly methylated at the C-82 position than pigments produced by cells of the same organism grown at higher light intensities. Different methylation states result in different aggregation properties and light absorbance of the chlorosome, and thus methylation is used as an adaptation to altering envireonmental conditions. , |FRAME: CPD-9092 "Bacteriochlorophyll c"| is more efficient than |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| at limiting red and near-infrared light intensities. Thus the latter is more commonly found in shallow lakes, while the former is found at deeper water., About This Pathway, The pathways leading to |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"|, |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| and |FRAME: CPD-9094 "bacteriochlorophyll e"| diverge from that for |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| and |FRAME: CPD-9067| after |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| is formed., The pathway starts with the removal of the C-132-methylcarboxyl moiety, forming |FRAME: CPD-18841| |CITS: [21550979]|., Two radical-SAM (S-adenosyl-lmethionine) oxidative methyltransferases, |FRAME: G-44408 BchR| and |FRAME: G-44409 BchQ|, add methyl groups to the C-121 ethyl and C-82 methyl carbons, respectively |CITS: [17586634]|. The latter can add a second methyl group at the same position. These four different forms (non-methylated, mono-methylated, di-methylated and tri-methylated) serve as substrates to the hydratases BchV (most of them can also serve as substrate for BchF, a homologous enzyme that is primarily involved in |FRAME: PWY-5526|). These enzymes hydrate the C-31 carbon, converting the vinyl group to the 1-hydroxyethyl group that is necessary for the aggregation of the chlorophyll molecules inside the chlorosomes. The hydroxyl group produces a chiral center. Experiments looking at the stereo-specificity of the two enzymes were inconclusive, as different results were obtained in vivo and in vitro. However, it was shown that in the absence of BshF the bacteria produced higher ratios of (S) epimers to (R) epimers |CITS: [26331578]|., At this point the pathways for |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| and |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"| diverge. The only difference between the two is the presence of a methyl group at the C20 methine bridge position in the former. Thus, the next step in |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| biosynthesis is C20 methylation, which is catalyzed by a methyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-44417| gene |CITS: [15090495]|., Interestingly, a copy of the |FRAME: G-44417| gene was found in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1098| that produces only |FRAME: CPD-9093 "bacteriochlorophyll d"|. However, the gene contained a frameshift mutation that inactivated it. A spontaneous mutant of this strain that produces |FRAME: CPD-9092 "bacteriochlorophyll c"| has a second frameshift mutation that restores the correct reading frame |CITS: [15090495]|. It has been suggested that activation/inactivation of the gene may be an adaptation mechanism for changing environments |CITS: [15292118]|., The last step in the pathway is the attachment of the farnesyl tail, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44411 "BchK synthase"|, which is specific for bacteriochlorophyll c, d and e |CITS: [12029054]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.39|, commonly referred to as ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase or RubisCO, is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both the carboxylation and oxygenation of |FRAME: D-RIBULOSE-15-P2| (RuBP). The carboxylation process is generally known as CO2 fixation (see |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|) whereas the oxygenation process is known as photorespiration (this pathway)., The two substrates (CO2 and O2) are competitive with regard to RubisCO, so that an increase in CO2 concentration inhibits oxygenation and vice versa |CITS:[Bowyer97]|. An important factor influencing the rate of oxygenation is temperature, as photorespiration is enhanced by high temperature. The reasons for this are twofold: (i) as temperatures increase the solubility of CO2 diminishes more rapidly than that of O2 and (ii) the specificity factor (Ω) of RubisCO (which represents a measure of the relative specificity for CO2) decreases with increasing temperatures between 7°C and 35°C., While the carboxylation reaction results in two molecules of |FRAME:G3P|, which are processed in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|, the oxygenation reaction forms one molecule of |FRAME:G3P| and one molecule of |FRAME:CPD-67| (2PG). The latter cannot be used in the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY| and, instead, is salvaged in the photorespiration pathway. , While photorespiration is essential for the viability of all organisms that perform oxygenic photosynthesis, including cyanobacteria and C3 plants, at ambient CO2 conditions |CITS: [18957552][26994478]|, the photorespiratory cycle results in carbon, nitrogen and energy losses, and, unlike true respiration, does not produce ATP or reducing power. As a matter of fact, despite its name photorespiration does not involve neither light nor respiration., About This Pathway, The main features of the photorespiration pathway include: (i) the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-67| into |FRAME: GLY|; (ii) the processing of two glycines into |FRAME: SER|, CO2 and ammonia; and (iii) the conversion of |FRAME: SER| into |FRAME: G3P|, which is directed towards CO2 fixation via the |FRAME:CALVIN-PWY|., The first step of the pathway involves the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:CPD-67|, which not only recycles phosphate but also prevents accumulation of this compound, which is a potent inhibitor of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.1|. The next step is the oxidation of |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| to |FRAME:GLYOX|. In plants |FRAME:GLYCOLLATE| is exported to the cytoplasm where it is oxidized in the peroxisomes to |FRAME:GLYOX| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.15|. The |FRAME:HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| generated during this step is detoxified by catalases (see |FRAME:DETOX1-PWY|; |CITS: [15012254]|) in the peroxisome. This step is catalyzed by a different enzyme in chlorophytes and cyanobacteria (see |FRAME: PWY-8363| and |FRAME: PWY-8363|)., Glyoxylate is converted into |FRAME:GLY| by two different enzymes: |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45| and |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.4|. One of the glycine molecues is converted by |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27|, to CO2, ammonia, and a single carbon that is transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate|. The methylene group is then transferred to the second glycine molecule by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, forming |FRAME: SER|. , The serine molecue feeds back into |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.45|, closing a cycle. The main carbon molecule produced by this cycle is |FRAME:OH-PYR|, which is reduced into |FRAME:GLYCERATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.29|. The pathway ends with the phosphorylation of glycerate to |FRAME:G3P|, which re-enters the Calvin cycle. The phosphorylation is performed by different enzymes in cyanobacteria vs. other photosynthetic organisms., The outcome of photorespiration in photosynthetic cells is loss of carbon via CO2 release, as well as loss of energy, yet the pathway is essential at atmospheric concentrations of CO2. The biological function of photorespiration is not clear. One possibility is that photorespiration is necessary under conditions of high light intensity and low CO2 concentration to dissipate excess ATP and NADPH from the photosynthesis light reactions, and prevent damage to the photosynthetic apparatus |CITS: [11299007]|. Another explanation is that the pathway is necessary for the assimilation of nitrate |CITS: [15272076]|., Engineering tobacco plants by intorducing into the chloroplasts synthetic glycolate metabolic pathways that are thought to be more efficient than the native pathway and blocking glycolate export from the chloroplast resulted in improved photosynthetic quantum yield by 20-40% |CITS: [30606819]|.

Summary: |FRAME: PRPP "5-Phospho-α-D-ribose 1-diphosphate"| (PRPP) is an important metabolite required in the biosynthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, the amino acids |FRAME: HIS| and |FRAME: TRP|, and the cofactors NAD and NADP. It is utilized in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: THMPT| in certain archaeal species and in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD1G-1531 "mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex"| in |FRAME: TAX-1773|., PRPP was discovered in the mid-1950s while searching for an enzyme that converted |FRAME: OROTATE| to |FRAME: UMP| |CITS: [14392173][13525411]|., The enzyme catalyzing the synthesis of PRPP, |FRAME: EC-2.7.6.1|, is ubiquitous among free-living organisms. So far, only certain obligate intracellular parasites such as some |FRAME: TAX-810| and |FRAME: TAX-780| species are known to lack the gene encoding it. Mammals contain three PRPP synthase-encoding genes, the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| contains five, and the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| contains five genes as well |CITS: [28031352]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-15671| is a constituent of O-Antigen or capsule polysaccharides in a number of pathogenic bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-287| serotypes O4 and O11, |FRAME: TAX-1280| serotypes 5 and 8, |FRAME: TAX-1313|, capsule type 4 and |FRAME:TAX-562| O4, O26 and O17. The organisms that have been studied the most are |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [19710102]|., Like all other O-antigen sugars, |FRAME: CPD-15671| is synthesized in an activated form - |FRAME: CPD-15644|. Three genes have been shown to encode all the necessary functions to modify |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| to |FRAME: CPD-15644|, and were named |FRAME: G-17655|, |FRAME: G-17656| and |FRAME: G-17657| in |FRAME: ORG-6236| |CITS: [7528730]|. The orthologous genes are known in |FRAME:TAX-562| as fnlA, fnlB and fnlC, and in |FRAME: TAX-1280| as capE, capF and capG., The |FRAME: G-17655| gene encodes a |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.115|. Unlike the related enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.135| (encoded by |FRAME: G-17659|), this enzyme alters the stereo configuration of the bond at position C5, resulting in an arabino structure |FRAME: CPD-10750|., The |FRAME: G-17656| gene encodes a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both the C3-epimerization of the WbjB product (to a lyxo structure) and the reduction of the C4 ketone to an alcohol |CITS: [15778500]|. The enzyme does not have a specific preference for either NADH or NADPH |CITS: [12464616]|., The last enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-17657|, catalyzes a C2 epimerization, generating |FRAME: CPD-15644| |CITS: [12464616]|.

Summary: |FRAME: GLYCEROL Glycerol| uptake in bacteria is mediated by the glycerol diffusion facilitator, an integral membrane protein catalyzing the rapid equilibration of concentration gradients of glycerol across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8436953]|. Intracellular glycerol is converted to |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by the enzyme glycerol kinase that uses ATP as phosphoryl donor. |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P "Glycerol-3-P"| is not a substrate of the glycerol diffusion facilitator and thus remains in the cell, where it is further metabolized. As a result, the driving force for the uptake of glycerol is generated by the phosphorylation of glycerol by glycerol kinase |CITS: [9162046]|. , While |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| can not leave the cytoplasm, it can be imported into the cell by the GlpT transporter, a member of the major facilitator superfamily, that couples the import of glycerol-3-P into the cytoplasm to the export of inorganic phosphates from the cytoplasm to the periplasm |CITS: [3522583][12893936]|. , In addition, |FRAME:TAX-562| K12 possesses two systems the salvage of |FRAME: Glycerophosphodiesters "glycerophosphoryl diesters"|, the Glp system and the Ugp system. , In the Glp system, the |FRAME: EG10399| gene encodes a periplasmic glycerophosphoryl diester phosphodiesterase (periplasmic GDP) which hydrolyzes deacylated phospholipids to an alcohol and |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| . The latter is then transported into the cell by the GlpT transporter. Periplasmic GDP is specific for the glycerophospho- moiety of the substrate, while the alcohol can be any one of several alcohols. This provides the cell with the capability of channeling a wide variety of glycerophosphodiesters into the glpQT-encoded dissimilatory system., In the Ugp system the diesters are hydrolyzed during transport at the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane to |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| and an alcohol by a cytoplasmic GDP, an enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: EG11050| gene. , The Ugp system is induced when the cells are starved for inorganic phospate, which is generates phosphate by the system |CITS: [1851953]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| can be further metabolized to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| by either of two membrane-bound enzymes, depending on the growth conditions. The presumed role of this process is the salvage of glycerol and glycerol phosphates generated by the breakdown of phospholipids and triacylglycerol. Under aerobic conditions, a homodimeric aerobic |FRAME: AERGLYC3PDEHYDROG-CPLX "glycerol-3-P dehydrogenase"| (encoded by the |FRAME: EG10394| gene) is produced, which can accept either oxygen or nitrate as the electron acceptor |CITS: [340460]|. , Under anaerobic conditions, a different |FRAME: ANGLYC3PDEHYDROG-CPLX "glycerol-3-P dehydrogenase"| is preferentially expressed. This tri-heteromeric protein complex, which is encoded by the glpACB operon, channels the electrons from |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| to either fumarate or nitrate |CITS: [3286606]|.

Summary: |FRAME: L-rhamnose| is a deoxy-hexose sugar commonly found in plants as a part of complex pectin polysaccharides and in many bacteria as a common component of the cell wall. Many microorganisms including the |FRAME: TAX-543| and |FRAME: TAX-82115| are capable of utilizing |FRAME: L-rhamnose| as a carbon source |CITS: [13888945]|., Enteric bacteria possess a canonical phosphorylated catabolic pathway for L-rhamnose, as described in this pathway |CITS: [6373710]|., It should be noted that in |FRAME: TAX-82115| the genes encoding the pathway's enzymes are present on a plasmid, and although they encode proteins with similar function, the sequence similarity to the enterobacterial enzymes is rather low |CITS: [Oresnik98]|. It is also possible that the order of events in the pathway is different among |FRAME: TAX-543| and |FRAME: TAX-82115| |CITS: [18156270][23708135]|., Other pathways that do not involved phosphorylation also exist (see |FRAME: PWY-6713| and |FRAME: PWY-6714|)., In this pathway an isomerase (|FRAME: EC-5.3.1.14|) and subsequent kinase (|FRAME: EC-2.7.1.5|) convert |FRAME: L-rhamnose| to |FRAME: RHAMNULOSE-1P|, which is cleaved by a specific aldolase (|FRAME: EC-4.1.2.19|) into |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| (an intermediate of glycolysis, which thereby enters central metabolism), and |FRAME: LACTALD|., L-rhamnose exists in solution mostly in a pyranose form. Because the isomerase has a preference for the β form of rhamnopyranose, a dedicated maturotase enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: EG11865| (rhaU in |FRAME: TAX-384|) converts the α anomers to the β form |CITS: [15060078][15876375][18156270]|. The isomerase bind the pyranose form, cleaves the ring to generate a linear form, and, following isomerization, releases the linear |FRAME: CPD-16566|, which quickly cyclyzes to form |FRAME: CPD-16567|, the stable form in solution., Two pathways can be used for degradation of |FRAME: LACTALD|. Aerobically, it is converted via |FRAME: L-LACTATE| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, also an intermediate of glycolysis (see |FRAME: PWY0-1317|). Anaerobically, |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.77| is induced and converts lactaldehyde into |FRAME: PROPANE-1-2-DIOL| (see |FRAME: PWY0-1315|), which, in |FRAME:TAX-562|, is secreted into the medium., In many bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-200795 Chloroflexi|, |FRAME: TAX-186817|, and |FRAME: TAX-28211|, |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.19| (named RhaE in |FRAME: TAX-82115|) and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.22| (named RhaW in |FRAME: TAX-82115|) are fused into a single bifunctional enzyme |CITS: [24391637]|., The related sugar |FRAME: L-fucoses| is metabolized by an analogous series of reactions (see |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|), producing the same end products. See also |FRAME: FUC-RHAMCAT-PWY|.

The mycotoxin |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| has been first isolated from Penicillium cyclopium |CITS:[5636916]| but has also been found in a number of Aspergillus species (see |FRAME:PWY-7555|) |CITS:[22069533]|. The toxicity of |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| and its joined occurrence with aflatoxin (see |FRAME:PWY-5961|) has been a long-standing concern for the safety of human food |CITS:[108598]| and livestock feed |CITS:[23604830]|. However, certain strains of Aspergillus oryzae which are known to produce |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| have been extensively and for a long time used for the production of fermented food indicating that the industry regards the employment of Aspergillus oryzae species as safe |CITS:[18820080]|. It is believed that Aspergillus oryzae has been domesticated for several thousand years and represents an descendant of Aspergillus flavus, a fungi known for the production of its many, often toxic secondary metabolites |CITS:[19081651]|., The decoding of fungal genomes have been added a new scope of investigating secondary metabolism in fungi and allowed the comparison of the discovered gene clusters involved in the making of mycotoxins |CITS:[24960201]|. The biosynthesis of |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| can be found in both the notorius Aspergillus flavus and the as safe declared Aspergillus oryzae strains |CITS:[22069533]|. In general, besides |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| Aspergillus oryzae does not produce secondary metabolites but has most of the gene clusters which however seem to have been inactivated during the evolution of the species. The comparison of the cyclopiazonate gene cluster in |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE|-producing and nonproducing Aspergillus oryzae strains revealed truncated versions of involved genes which renders the cluster metabolically inert, shown for instance for the cyclo-acetoacetyl-L-tryptophan synthetase (CpaA) |CITS:[18854220]|. , On the other side the comparison between |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE|-producing and nonproducing Aspergillus oryzae strains additional genes have been detected which have been lost in Aspergillus flavus and |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE|-nonproducing Aspergillus oryzae strains. The gene CpaH encoding for a cytochrome P450 dependent monooxygenase has been identified in an |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE|-producing strain of Aspergillus oryzae and shown to catalyze the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17093| from |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE|. The former is significantly less toxic than |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| which indicates the detoxifying properties of CpaH. It has also been suggested that |FRAME:CPD-17093| is the final pathway product of Aspergillus oryzae strains which do produce |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| reflecting the domestication of those strains by producing less toxic compounds |CITS:[ 21608094]|.

Similar to |FRAME:CPD-17992| (see |FRAME:PWY-7669|) |FRAME:CPD-17995| is a Fusarium heterosporum produced hybrid compound with a polyketide and an condensed amino acid moiety |CITS:[17707105]| forming an 2,4-pyrrolidinedione ring system which is commonly referred to as tetramic acid |CITS:[18334299] [Royles95]|. , Polyketide synthases (PKS) and non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS) often form mega-complex proteins which catalyze the biosynthesis of fungal hybrid secondary metabolites |CITS:[18804170]|. It could be shown that the two modules (PKS and NRPS) communicate with each other to ensure the correct formation of polyketide-peptide hybrid products |CITS:[25436464]|. Iterative type I polyketide synthases (IPKSs) which belong to the highly reducing PKSs (HR-PKSs) |CITS:[22938194]| and are composed of various enzymatically active domains including an enoylreductase (ER) domain (within the PKS or as an stand-alone protein) |CITS:[22733743]| are key for the formation of a wide array of polyketide moieties and shown to significantly contribute to the vast structural diversity of secondary compounds produced by fungal PKS-NRPS hybrids |CITS:[23225733] [Fisch13]|. The metabolic potential of the ascomycete Fusarium for producing such compounds is emphasized by the identification of 52 PKS and 52 NRPS orthology groups in the genus of which most remain to be explored |CITS:[25543026]|. , Searching the sequenced genome of Fusarium heterosporum ATCC 74349 for polyketide synthase (PKS) and polyketide synthase (PKS)-non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) hybrids with homology to the |FRAME:CPLX-8893| (see |FRAME:PWY-7535| resulted in the identification of the PKS-NRPS gene fsdS and the biosynthetic gene cluster for the |FRAME:PWY-7670| (fds) |CITS:[23614392]|. However, it was pointed out that |FRAME:CPD-17995| is probably not an natural final product as no co-expression of the other genes (except for the putative trans-enoyl reductase fsdC) of the cluster by native promotors was observed |CITS:[23614392]|. Employing native regulators has become an useful tool for overexpressing cryptic or silenced pathways and shown to work for many secondary metabolic clusters in fungi |CITS:[25226362]|. The fusaridione A synthetase fsd1 had been associated before with the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17992| |CITS:[15724180]| but targeted knocking out of genes in the cluster and metabolic profiling of the resultant mutants confirmed the role of fsd1 in the pathway producing |FRAME:CPD-17995|. In addition, pyrophosphate exchange assays carried out with the heterologously expressed and purified adenylation (A) domain of the NRPS pointed out the strong preference of |FRAME:TYR| which is a component of the structure of |FRAME:CPD-17995| and thus further supported the molecular role of the fsdS encoded PKS-NRPS in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17995| |CITS:[23614392]|. , The release and cyclization mechanism of the ACP-product (see |FRAME:PWY-7669|) has been shown to occur via a Dieckmann cyclization catalyzed by the C-terminal reductive (R) domain of the NRPS which is a Dieckmann cyclase and not a reductase |CITS:[18652469] [25621700]| and produces the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17995| |CITS:[23614392]|. However, the resulting |FRAME:CPD-17995| appears to be unstable and spontaneously converts to its more stable open-ring form, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17996| |CITS:[23614392]|.

Summary: The denitrifying bacterium |FRAME: TAX-76114| can utilize |FRAME: CPD-10596| under anoxic conditions., A degradation pathway similar to the |FRAME: ETHYLBENZENE| degradation pathway found in this bacterium, (see |FRAME: PWY-481|) has been suggested |CITS: [18539747]|., The pathway starts with an initial hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-10596| to |FRAME: CPD-10597|, followed by, dehydrogenation to |FRAME: CPD-10598|. These intermediates have been confirmed., The later steps in the pathway have not been verified biochemically, but are predicted to include carboxylation and, thiolytic cleavage yielding |FRAME: CPD-201|, which is channeled into the central anaerobic, |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| pathway (see |FRAME: CENTBENZCOA-PWY|)., Formation of |FRAME: CPD-10598|, as well as intermediates of the |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| degradation pathway, were confirmed by gas chromatographic-mass spectrometric analysis., The enzymes involved in the pathway are believed to be encoded in a single large operon ( approximately 15 kb)., Among them are a p-cresol methylhydroxylase-like protein (encoded by |FRAME: G-10958| and |FRAME: G-10959|),, proposed to be a |FRAME: CPLX-7692|, two predicted alcohol dehydrogenases (encoded by |FRAME: G-10960| and, |FRAME: G-10969|), a biotin-dependent carboxylase (encoded by |FRAME: G-10961|, |FRAME: G-10962| and, |FRAME: G-10963|), an acetoacetyl-CoA synthetase-like protein (|FRAME: G-10964|) and a thiolase (|FRAME: G-10965|)., None of these enzymes has been verified biochemically at the moment. However, expression of these proteins was shown, to be upregulated in cells adapted to anaerobic growth with |FRAME: CPD-10596| and |FRAME: CPD-10598|, |CITS: [18539747]|.

The antibiotic |FRAME: NOCARDICIN-A| is a member of the monocyclic, monolactam class of β-lactam antibiotics and is resistant to β-lactamase enzymes |CITS: [956036][993130][412823][412824][338567][591460]|. It is produced by the actinomycetes |FRAME: TAX-53432| and |FRAME: TAX-40567| |CITS: [6833153]| (it has been suggested that the former should be reclassified under |FRAME: TAX-40566|) and shows moderate antibiotic activity against a broad spectrum of Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [6751815][6849819][6416840][3287105]|., Organisms that produce |FRAME: NOCARDICIN-A| also produce other nocardicins (|FRAME: CPD-19210|, |FRAME: CPD-9415|, |FRAME: CPD-19211|, |FRAME: NOCARDICIN-E|, |FRAME: CPD-9417| and |FRAME: CPD-9418|), although nocardicin A is the major metabolite and the most active., Most of the pathway for |FRAME: NOCARDICIN-A| biosynthesis has been elucidated. The biosynthetic gene cluster has been characterized, and includes genes encoding enzymes, regulatory proteins and antibiotic resistance proteins |CITS: [15271351] [15629944]|., Like |FRAME: ISOPENICILLIN-N|, |FRAME: NOCARDICIN-A| has a tripeptide core of non-ribosomal origin. The nocardicin A gene cluster encodes two non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPSs), |FRAME: G-44609 NocA| and |FRAME: G-44610 NocB|, that were shown to encode five modules, producing the pentapeptide precursor |FRAME: CPD-19202, |. Three of the modules, 1,2, and 4, require the presence of the small MbtH-type protein encoded by the nocI gene |CITS: [23330869]|. , This precursor is cleaved by a trypsin-like protease, yielding the tripeptide core |FRAME: CPD-9418|, the earliest β-lactam-containing intermediate in the pathway |CITS: [Townsend88]|. The organisms contain five trypsin-like genes in the genome. While digestion by the native proteases has not been shown yet, digestion of the pentapeptide precursor using commercial trypsin resulted in the expected cleavage at the C-terminus of the L-arginine residue |CITS: [23330869]|., The enzymes involved in the late steps of nocardicin A biosynthesis have been purified and characterized, including |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.38| |CITS: [Wilson88][9804844]|, |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.14| |CITS: [Wilson88][15252031]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.43| |CITS: [12105888][15629944]|.

|FRAME: CPD-16666 Cyclooctatin| is a diterpene that was isolated from the growth medium of the actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-67327| as part of a program designed to find microorganism-produced inhibitors of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.5|. It is competitive with that enzyme's substrate, and the inhibition constant (Ki) is 4.8 x 10 μM |CITS: [1335449]|., Cyclooctatin is characterized by a unique tricyclic 5-8-5 fused ring system, and is produced from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| in three steps. The first step, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.146| (CotB2), produces the typical skeleton comprising the three rings. The following two steps consist of simple hydroxylations at C5 and C18, catalyzed by two cytochrome P450 enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-18052| and |FRAME: G-18053| genes, respectively |CITS: [19635410]|., The three genes, as well as the cotB1 gene, which encodes geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase, reside in a single operon. When the four genes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-1888|, the recombinant host produced |FRAME: CPD-16666| |CITS: [19635410]|.

In heterotrophic organisms carotenoids protect against singlet oxygen as well as against peroxy radicals. Members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-13687|, which belongs to the α-proteobacteria, produce yellow or orange pigmentation |CITS: [2111872]|. Certain strains form carotenoids such as hydroxylated |FRAME: CPD1F-129| derivatives and corresponding glycosides |CITS:[2254247][1946693]|. The cellular functions for the glycoside moieties of carotenoids have not yet been identified but are suspected to influence membrane rigidity, fluidity, and stability, especially under harsh conditions |CITS: [8529834][16199557]|., The unusual carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-17491| was initially identified from the radiotolerant bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1123267| |CITS: [19557030]|. Astaxanthin dirhamnoside has a unique structure in which a rhamnose moiety is attached to each β-ionone ring. Similarly, the major carotenoid produced by |FRAME: TAX-1355329|, a strain isolated from a river in Daejon City, South Korea, has a similar structure with two deoxysugar moieties at each of the β-ionone rings (the exact identity of the deoxysugars has not been described) |CITS: [25193422]|., Two gene clusters encoding astaxanthin dideoxyglycoside biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-1355329| have been identified. The first cluster comprises the crtYIBZ genes (see |FRAME: PWY-5288|), while the other cluster contains the crtYX genes, with crtX encoding the putative rhamnosyltranferase |CITS: [25193422]|. Since |FRAME: CPD-353| is not commercially available, it was impossible to test the activity in vitro. However, it was shown that the enzyme could not accept |FRAME: CPD-13118| or |FRAME: CPD-12575| |CITS: [25193422]|.

Summary: Glucosylation of cytokinins is a well recognized modification that is thought to play an important role in hormonal homeostasis. Several types of cytokinins conjugation exist which render cytokinins inactive: O-xylosylation, O-glucosylation, and N-glucosylation. Zeatin-O-glucoside occurs in all plants examined and is thought to be important in transport |CITS:[LETHAM94]|, storage |CITS:[LETHAM94]|, and protection against zeatin oxidases |CITS:[4214594], [ARMSTRONG94]|. These suggested role are supported by the findings that O-glucosylation is reversible (these conjugates can be converted back into active cytokinins by β-glucosidases |CITS: [8235622]|), and the O-glucosides are resistant to cleavage of the N6-side chain by cytokinin oxidases |CITS: [12721786]|. To date a number of genes encoding UDP-O-glucosyltransferases have been characterized in several plants. The genetic manipulation leading to controlled expression of those enzymes should allow a more precise assessment of the function of O-glucosylated cytokinins in regulating growth and development |CITS:[9874810]|.

Summary: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are lipophilic small molecules (< 300 Da) that are characterized by their high vapor pressures and low boiling points. They play important biological roles such as signaling molecules that enable communication over long-distances. They are also known to facilitate cross-kingdom interactions., The rhizobacterium |FRAME: TAX-682634| emitts over 100 different VOCs that have been shown to inhibit plant, and fungal growth |CITS: [17601806][17180381][20339320]|. The main VOC produced by this organsim is |FRAME: CPD-22334 Sodorifen|, a polymethylated hydrocarbon with an unusual bicyclo[3.2.1]octadiene skeleton |CITS: [20155769]|., A a 4.6 kb gene cluster involved in |FRAME: CPD-22334| biosynthesis has been identified. The cluster contains four genes, two of which were homologs of genes that participate in the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY "methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| (|FRAME: EC-5.3.3.2| (sodA), and |FRAME: EC-2.2.1.7| (sodB) |CITS: [27231241]|., Sequence analysis indicated that the remaining two genes, |FRAME: G-80419| and |FRAME: G-80418|, encode a C-methyltransferase and a terpene cyclase. Expression of the two genes in |FRAME: TAX-562| additionally harboring a plasmid encoding three MEP-pathway associated enzymes led to the production of minute amounts of |FRAME: CPD-22334| and its isomers |CITS: [28408760]|., In vivo and in vitro characterizations of |FRAME: G-80419 SodC| showed that it not only functions as a SAM-dependent C-methyltransferase that methylates |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, but also possesses a cyclization activity, forming the phosphorylated intermediate |FRAME: CPD-22335|. The terpene cyclase encoded by |FRAME: G-80418| the final bicyclic compound |FRAME: CPD-22334| |CITS: [30133268]|., The sodorifen biosynthetic gene cluster of Serratia plymuthica WS3236 was used for direct pathway cloning, leading to almost exclusive high-level sodorifen production in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [30732610]|

Summary: The strictly anaerobic δ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-316277| is able to ferment |FRAME: BENZOATE| and |FRAME: CROTONATE| in the presence and in the absence of a hydrogen-consuming partner. When a suitable partner is present, the reducing equivalents that are formed during the fermentation process can be released as hydrogen gas or formate, which are readily consumed by the synthrophic partner for CO<sub>2</sub> or sulfate reduction |CITS: [18707608]|., However, when the organism grows in pure culture, the release of reducing equivalents as H<sub>2</sub> or formate is not thermodynamically favorable. The organism solves the problem by fermenting the substrates to |FRAME: ACET| with the concomitant production of the unusual metabolite |FRAME: CPD-575|, which is excreted from the cell (see also |FRAME: PWY-7401|). Thus, the redox equivalents produced during oxidation of |FRAME: BENZOATE| or |FRAME: CROTONATE| to |FRAME: ACET| are recycled via the production of |FRAME: CPD-575|. The formation of |FRAME: CPD-575| is a unique fermentation process that has been described so far only in |FRAME: TAX-316277| |CITS:[18707608] [11282627]|., In the case of |FRAME: BENZOATE| fermentation, benzoate is first activated to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, which is then converted to acetate by the enzymes of the |FRAME: CENTBENZCOA-PWY "anaerobic benzoyl-CoA degradation pathway"|. However, the first intermediate in this pathway, |FRAME: CYCLOHEXA-15-DIENE-1-CARBONYL-COA|, acts as a branching point. While some of it is fermented to acetate, the rest is reduced in two steps to |FRAME: CPD-577|, which is converted by an as-yet unidentified enzyme to |FRAME: CPD-575|. Summary: Conidia, the asexual spores of fungi, are often heavily pigmented, which has been ascribed to conferring strength, impermeability and UV-protection to the cell walls of the conidia |CITS:[2283502]|. In addition, structurally similar but differently folded products from the shared intermediary hepta- (|FRAME:CPD-18240|) and nona-polyketides (|FRAME:CPD-18209|) of those pathways, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18256| and |FRAME:CPD-18257|, have been reported in the literature for various species of |FRAME: TAX-5052| |CITS:[Watanabe98]|, |FRAME: TAX-5073| |CITS:[Lai91] [10479334] [10870185]|, and |FRAME: TAX-5506| |CITS:[19170495]|. , The formation of |FRAME:CPD-18256| was first reported in |FRAME: TAX-162425| |CITS:[Watanabe98]|. The gene sequence of the responsible polyketide synthase (wA) was later revised, revealing that the generation of |FRAME:CPD-18256| was the result of the enzyme lacking a C-terminus part. The full-length enzyme catalyzes formation of the true intermediate of the |FRAME:PWY-7695| pathway, which is |FRAME:CPD-18255| |CITS:[Watanabe99]|. Research on the domains of the wA-encoded |FRAME: MONOMER-19447| identified the missing amino acid residues that caused the wA encoded protein to act as citreoisocoumerin synthase, and confirmed that the C-terminal thioester (TE) domain in that enzyme actually functioned as a Claisen cyclase |CITS:[11251292]|. The latter domain is known to be involved in the structuring of the polyketide chain, hence defining the metabolic direction of the emerging polyketide intermediate |CITS:[17581644]|. , |FRAME:CPD-18257 Bikisocoumarin| as a product was obtained after reconstructing the active site of the nonaketide pre-bikaverin synthase (bik1) |CITS:[12409099]| from |FRAME: TAX-5127| |CITS:[18072779]|. It could be demonstrated that the structurally altered |FRAME:MONOMER-19414| (see also |CITS:[22377171]|) formed |FRAME:CPD-18257| via the differently folded nonaketide |FRAME:CPD-18266| because the protein was unable to catalyze the cyclization of all the rings |CITS:[18072779]|. , The redirection of |FRAME:PWY-7692| and |FRAME:PWY-7695| towards isocoumarin had also been demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-5518| utilizing an alternate medium. This medium contained low amounts of nitrogen and was able to change the metabolic direction of the above mentioned pathways towards the isocoumarins |FRAME:CPD-18257| and |FRAME:CPD-18256|, respectively. This change was influenced by the nitrogen supply and nitrogen source as well as pH conditions of the medium. Under nitrogen starvation conditions and low pH both |FRAME:CPD-18257| and |FRAME:CPD-18256| were produced indicating a much more complex regulation modus of the pathway(s) than originally assumed |CITS:[22713716]|.

In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-83333| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426| or the human |FRAME: CPLX-7582|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme. Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length. However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain length. For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|.

Summary: General Background, Thiols such as glutathione play several major roles in the cell, including maintainance of the redox, balance, fighting reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and the detoxification of many other toxins and, stress-inducing factors (see |FRAME: PWY-4061|)., In most organisms the major thiol is the tripeptide |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly,, known as GSH), whose intracellular concentration ranges from 0.5-10 mM (see |FRAME: PWY-4041|). , Most of the glutathione pool is kept in its reduced form. The functionality of GSH largely depends on, its being in a reduced form., About This Pathway, One of the main roles of glutathione in the cell is the reduction of other molecules, such as peroxides, or protein-disulfide groups. In this pathway the process is represnted by |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.12|:, |FRAME:1.11.1.12-RXN|, and by |FRAME: EC-1.11.1.9|:, |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE-PEROXIDASE-RXN|, In the process two molecules of GSH are condensed into a single molecule of the oxidized form,, |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE|., In eukaryotes this oxidation reaction is often catalyzed by enzymes belonging to the glutathione, peroxidase family., It was believed that glutathione-dependent peroxidases are not present in prokaryotic organisms, but, recently some glutathione-dependent peroxidases have been discovered in bacteria |CITS: [12606554]|., The glutathione disulfide is reduced back to GSH by the action of |FRAME: EC-1.8.1.7|, Another redox cycle involving glutathione is described in |FRAME: GLUT-REDOX-PWY|.

Summary: Background, Many bacterial species have the ability to oxidize |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE "carbon-monoxide"| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [1644755]|. Phototrophic bacteria exhibit aspects of both aerobic and anaerobic systems. Under anaerobic conditions, some of these organisms utilize CO as the sole energy source and couple the oxidation of CO to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| with proton reduction to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [6688413]| |CITS: [6687360]|. Organisms known to utilize this reaction include the Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1085|, and |FRAME: TAX-28068|, and the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-129958|. , About This Pathway, The purple phototrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1085| expresses a CO-oxidizing, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|-evolving enzymatic system during anaerobic growth in the presence of CO |CITS: [17123462]|. The system consists of two main enzymes - |FRAME: CPLX-8269| (CODH), which is encoded by the cooFSCTJ operon, and |FRAME: CPLX-8271|, encoded by the cooMKLXUH operon |CITS: [8892819][20400563]|., In addition, the |FRAME: MONOMER-16455 "CooF protein"|, which is encoded in the CDOH operon, is a 22kDa hydrophobic ferredoxin type Fe-S protein that shuttles the electrons generated by the dehydrogenase to the hydrogenase, and is essential for the activity of CODH |CITS: [17123462]|. , CODH is a membrane bound enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of CO to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| producing two electrons |CITS: [8892819]|. It is an α2 homodimer with five metal clusters. Each subunit contains an unusual Ni2Fe4S4 cluster (known as the |FRAME: C-Clusters|) and |FRAME: CPD-7| (the B-cluster). Another Fe4S4 cluster (the D-cluster) is located at the interface of the two subunits near the protein surface. CO oxidation occurs at the C-cluster and electrons travel through the B and D-clusters to the CooF protein, which passes the electrons, possibly via intermediate electron carriers, to the membrane bound |FRAME: CPLX-8271|, which consumes the electrons by reducing two protons to form |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [2498285]|., The activity of the whole pathway is regulated at the transcription level by the CO sensing transcription factor |FRAME: CPLX-8272| |CITS: [15598507]|, and is inhibited in the presence of |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [2498285]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| (phytate, phytic acid) is one of the most prevalent forms of phosphorylated inositols in the eukaryotic cell, with a total concentration of 15-100 μM |CITS:[3426614][1684044][8435066]|. It's cellular distribution is not completely known - some of it is soluble, some is "wall-papered" around membranes, while some is bound to proteins |CITS: [9838040]|. In plant seeds, large amount of phytate are complexed with cations and deposited as globular inclusions in membrane-bound storage bodies |CITS: [15700415]|., The compound has been proposed to have a number of signaling roles, including regulation of insulin exocytosis |CITS: [9114007]|, regulation of nuclear mRNA export |CITS:[10390371][10683435]|, binding of the clathrin assembly proteins AP2 and AP3 |CITS: [1849645][1371119]|, inhibition of clathrin cage assembly |CITS: [7814377][7829485]|, and inhibition of serine and threonine protein phosphatases that are thought to regulate L-type Ca2+ channels |CITS: [9334307]|., About This Pathway, In plant cells phytate serves as a storage form of myo-inositol, phosphate and mineral nutrients for utilization during seed germination and seedling growth. It is deposited within single-membrane storage organelles referred to as protein bodies and is usually present as mixed complexes with different cations, including |FRAME: K+|, |FRAME: MG+2|, |FRAME: CA+2|, |FRAME: FE+2|, and |FRAME: ZN+2|, known as phytin |CITS:[11590064][8744268]|., Although phytin only makes up about 1% of the seed weight, it may contain up to 80% of the total seed phosphorus |CITS:[15700415]|. Phytate is also present in other plant tissues and organs such as pollen, roots, tuber and turions in smaller quantities |CITS:[14568069]|. , One phytate biosynthetic pathway found in plants proceeds from |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (produced by phospholipase C) as described in |FRAME: PWY-6361| by a series of successive phosphorylations carried out by only two enzymes, |FRAME: AT5G07370-MONOMER| and |FRAME: AT5G61760-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: AT5G07370| and |FRAME: AT5G61760|, respectively. The ultimate product of these phosphorylation reactions is |FRAME: CPD-1107|, which is phophorylated to to |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| by another kinase, |FRAME: AT5G42810-MONOMER| (|FRAME: AT5G42810|)., A second, indirect pathway, has been suggested to occur via |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE|. The pathway is indirect because |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| itself is produced from |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6364|). However, once formed, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| can be phosphorylated by |FRAME: AT5G16760-MONOMER| (|FRAME: AT5G16760|), an enzyme that does not recognize |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| as substrate |CITS: [14568069]|. The products of |FRAME: AT5G16760| are then phosphorylated further by the same enzymes used in |FRAME: PWY-6361|.

General Background, Natural essential oils contain monoterpenes as one of their major constituents. The oil accumulates in glands found in leaves, petals and trichomes. |FRAME: GERANIOL "Geraniol"| is an acyclic monoterpene alcohol that is found in the essential oils of many plant species, including nutmeg, |FRAME: TAX-94328| (ginger) |CITS: [11743782 ]|, |FRAME: TAX-39350| (basil) |CITS: [14657409]|, rosemary, sage, cardamom, grapefruit, and |FRAME: TAX-66014| (lemon grass) |CITS: [17230350]|. It is one of the three terpene compounds principally responsible for muscat aroma, and is emitted from flowers of many plant species with an intense rose scent. |FRAME: GERANIOL Geraniol| makes up to 86-98% of the essential oil in leaves of the camphor tree (|FRAME: TAX-192326|) |CITS: [15680985]|., |FRAME: GERANIOL "Geraniol"| has cancer antiproliferative properties due to its inhibitory effect on polyamine metabolism. It is known to decreases the activity of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.17|, a key polyamine biosynthesis enzyme that is enhanced during cancer growth |CITS: [Carnesecchi01]|., About This Pathway, A single-step pathway from |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| to |FRAME: GERANIOL|, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.7.11|, has been known for many years and documented in many plants |CITS: [17187833]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5829|)., This alternative pathway, where the process is catalyzed by two different enzymes, has been described from |FRAME: TAX-128735| in 2015 |CITS: [ 26138978]|. The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.68|, a Nudix hydrolase localized in the cytoplasm. The enzyme produces a |FRAME: CPD-13243| intermediate, which must be dephosphorylated by a different enzyme, which has not been characterized yet., Since |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| originating from the |FRAME: PWY-7560 "MEP pathway"| is synthesized in plastids, the authors hypothesized that it may be exported from plastids to the cytoplasm, or may be produced in the cytoplasm by a cytosolic |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.1| (GPP synthase) |CITS: [26138978]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycolysis, which was first studied as a pathway for the utilization of glucose, is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, the other two being the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| and the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. Glycolysis is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces six of the 13 precursor metabolites that are the starting materials for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules (the six compounds are |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:G3P|, |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). Glycolysis can be found, if at least in part, in almost all organisms., Even though glycolysis is often described starting with glucose, other hexoses (e.g. fructose) can also serve as input (as its name implies - glycose is a general term for simple sugars)., Glycolysis has evolved to fulfill two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) being an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism), it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy., This switching of direction is possible because all but two of the enzymatic reactions comprising glycolysis are reversible, and the conversions catalyzed by the two exceptions are rendered functionally reversible by other enzymes (|FRAME:F16B-CPLX "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase"| and |FRAME:PEPSYNTH-CPLX|) that catalyze different irreversible reactions flowing in the opposite direction., About This Pathway, The difference between this pathway and the one described in |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS| is that glucose is phosphorylated not by a PTS transporter but intracellularly by |FRAME:CPLX-4241|. This reaction can be catalyzed by a general |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.1 "hexokinase"| (EC 2.7.1.1) |CITS: [ArchMicr161-460] [9075622]|, but some organisms have a highly specific |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.2 "glucokinase"| (EC 2.7.1.2) |CITS: [14553940]|., In mammals, glycolysis always begins with the phosphorylation of glucose by hexokinase to form glucose 6-phosphate |CITS: [1637300]|. This ensures that the intracellular glucose concentration is kept low and promotes the continuous transport of glucose into the cell. In mammalian liver this reaction is carried out by glucokinase, an isozyme of hexokinase which has a much lower affinity (high Km) for glucose so it is effective only when glucose is abundant |CITS: [3902008]|. Its role is to provide glucose 6-phosphate for the synthesis of glycogen., Glucose 6-phosphate is then isomerized to fructose 6-phosphate in a reversible reaction whose direction is driven by the concentration of fructose 6-phosphate |CITS: [12573240]|. A second phosphorylation event converts fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6 bisphosphate in a rate limiting irreversible step |CITS: [16742819]|. The formation of two charged groups prevents the diffusion of substrates out of the cell. This six-carbon sugar is then cleaved into two three-carbon sugars that are interconvertible |CITS: [999838]|. , Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate enters the second stage of the pathway that results in the production of 4 ATP and 2 NADH molecules with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH |CITS: [6188151][BERG02]|. The two substrate-level phosphorylation steps that produce ATP are catalyzed by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase respectively, and are important regulatory points in the glycolytic pathway |CITS: [BERG02]|., Glycolysis from internal glucose is also found in many prokaryotes. For example, |FRAME: TAX-2336| is a hyperthermophilic anaerobic eubacterium that can utilize various sugars or complex organic substrates as carbon and energy sources. With glucose as a substrate, |FRAME: TAX-2336| produces lactate, acetate, carbon dioxide and hydrogen as the main fermentation products (see |FRAME: PWY-5100|)., The organism has a highly specific |FRAME:CPLX-4241| and a periplasmic, high-affinity glucose-binding protein, suggesting the use of an ATP-binding casette (ABC) transporter for glucose entry into the cell |CITS: [12427944]|. The rest of the pathway occurs via the conventional Embden-Meyerhof pathway |CITS: [ArchMicr161-460][8791626][9075622][2318202]|.

Summary: Fucose is a hexose deoxy sugar. It received its name from the brown algae genus |FRAME: TAX-3011|, from which it was first decribed. The alga was named because of its dark redish color, as one of the meanings of the Latin word fucus is "red paint"., Fucose is a common sugar, found in N-linked glycans on the mammalian, insect and plant cell surface, in many bacterial glycans, and in other biomolecules. Most of the fucose found in biology is in the |FRAME: L-fucoses "L conformation"|, and the use of |FRAME: D-Fucoses| is rather rare (for example in some |FRAME: Cardenolide-Glycosides "cardenolide glycosides"|)., |FRAME: L-fucoses| can be used by some organisms as a total source of carbon and energy. It has been shown to be metabolized via three separate pathways - |FRAME: FUCCAT-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-8444|, and |FRAME: PWY-8318|., In this pathway L-fucose is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-24866| and then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-33|. This product is subsequently dehydrated to |FRAME: DEHYDFUC-CPD| and then oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-13044|, which is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: L-LACTATE|. The pathway was originally described from pig liver |CITS: [457669]|, and was later described in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-340| |CITS: [17144652]|. The identity of the last two of the pathway's enzymes was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-87883| in 2013 |CITS: [23214453]|.

Leukotriene B4 (LTB4) is a very potent chemoattractant, while LTC4 stimulates bronchial constriction in asthmatics. Enzymes in this biosynthetic pathway are also targets for cardiovascular therapies. Additional regulatory proteins are also candidate drug targets, such as the 5-lipoxygenase activating protein (FLAP), which has been linked to increased risk for myocardial infarction and stroke |CITS: [14770184]|., https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/

Summary: |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP "All-trans-geranylgeranyl diphosphate"| (also known as geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, or GGPP) is a crucial compound involved in the biosynthesis of a variety of terpenes and terpenoids, including central compounds such as ubiquinones and menaquinones., In plants, |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP| is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of essentail compounds such as chlorophylls, carotenoids, tocopherols, plastoquinones, and gibberellins |CITS:[12427975]|, as well as a variety of secondary metabolites., In addition, GGPP is also used in posttranslational modifications of proteins (geranylgeranylation) which is important for membrane adhesion as well as the function of some proteins |CITS:[11500541][16183844]|., GGPP is synthesized from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| either by dedicated enzymes, such as the |FRAME: YPL069C-MONOMER| of |FRAME: TAX-4932|, or by the action of polyprenyl transferases such as the |FRAME: MONOMER-13766| from |FRAME: TAX-1061| or |FRAME: CPLX0-7426| from |FRAME: TAX-83333|. It should be noted that the building blocks for |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| are synthesized in different organisms by different pathways. While most eukaryotes and some, bacteria use the |FRAME: PWY-922|, most bacteria, as well as green algae utilize the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| (as described in the two superpathways |FRAME: PWY-5910| and |FRAME: PWY-5121|)., In plants, GGPP is synthesized using both routes - in the cytosol using the |FRAME: PWY-922|, and in the plastids using the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|.

Summary: Peptidoglycan is best described as a fisherman's net, with each cell of the mesh defined by two segments of parallel, glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks, which allow the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|. These peptide crosslinks are usually composed of two petapeptides, each attached in one end to one of the glycan segment and extending towards (but no reaching) the other one. The two pentapeptides can form a crosslink with each other in more than one way., The composition and structure of peptidoglycan varies among different bacterial species, but in generals consists of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues. The pentapeptide is bound through its N terminus to the carboxyl group of muramate., The petapeptide is formed through the action of soluble enzymes that couple ATP-hydrolysis to the ligation of the amino acid monomers. This ATP-dependent coupling of amino acid monomers and elongating peptides by soluble enzymes is very unusual, as oligopeptides are usually formed either by ribosomes or by |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases "nonribosomal peptide synthases"|. A similar mechanism is also found in the |FRAME: GLUTATHIONESYN-PWY "biosynthesis of glutathione"|., The pentapeptide, which contains alternating L and D amino acids, reveals considerable variation among species, with the greatest variation found in the third position. This pathway describes the biosynthesis of the |FRAME: UDP-NAcMur-Peptides "UDP-N-acetylmuramoyl-pentapeptide"| found in most of the Gram-negative organisms and some Gram-positive organisms, which contains |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| is the third position., This pathway variant, characterized from |FRAME: TAX-347|, is found in bacteria that lack |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.3|. It differs from the more common variant (|FRAME: PWY-6387|) by the fact that |FRAME: GLT|, rather than |FRAME: D-GLT|, is incorporated into the nascent peptide, in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.53| (MurD2). The L-glutamyl residue is then converted to D-glutamyl within the peptide by |FRAME: EC-5.1.1.23| (MurL) |CITS: [28294606]|., Organisms that are predicted to use this pathway variant belong mostly to the γ proteobacteria, including the genera Xanthomonas, Xylella, Stenotrophomonas, Dyella, Frateuria, Rhodanobacter, Pseudoxanthomonas, and Lysobacter. In addition, orthologs of |FRAME: G-58177| were found in several rare actinobacteria such as the genera Micromonospora, Actinoplanes, Verrucosispora, and Salinispora, and in a few strains belonging to α proteobacteria, including the genera Devosia, Pelagibacterium, and Parvularcula |CITS: [28294606]|.

General Background, Some cyanobacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-103690|, grow as chains of cells (filaments) that, under nitrogen deprivation, contain two cell types: vegetative cells that fix CO2 through oxygenic photosynthesis and heterocysts that fix N2. The heterocysts are surrounded by a thick wall that protects the oxygen-sensitive nitrogenase from the oxygen produced during photosynthesis. The heterocysts provide the vegetative cells with fixed nitrogen, and the vegetative cells provide the heterocysts with reduced carbon, mainly in the form of sucrose, through intercellular molecular transfer |CITS: [25784700]|. , The fixed nitrogen is stored in the heterocysts in the form of |FRAME: Cyanophycin|, a high-molecular weight copolymer composed of an |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| backbone and |FRAME: ARG| side groups, with typical size of 25-100 kDa. The arginine moieties are linked to the β-carboxyl group of each aspartate by their α-amino group (see |FRAME: PWY-7052|)., When the bacteria need the nitrogen stored in |FRAME: Cyanophycin|, the dipeptidase |FRAME: SGL_RS08655-MONOMER| (CphB) catalyzes the specific hydrolysis of the polymer to produce |FRAME: CPD-14415| dipeptides |CITS: [10429200]|. The dipeptides are transferred to the adjacent vegetative cells, where they are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-9523| producing |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| and |FRAME: ARG|, which serve as nitrogen sources for the vegetative cells |CITS: [24550502]|., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-103690| |FRAME: ARG| can be converted to |FRAME: PRO| by a single dual-function enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-80824| gene. The N-terminal part of this enzyme functions as an arginine dihydrolase, and the C-terminal part is an ornithine cyclodeaminase. With both activites combined, this enzyme can convert |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: PRO|, liberating three molecules of ammonium. |CITS: [30636068]|., The |FRAME: PRO| that is formed is further converted to |FRAME: GLT| as described in |FRAME: PROUT-PWY|.

Summary: For description of the regular peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway in Gram-positive bacteria, please see |FRAME: PWY-5265|., Two main classes of drugs that are used to treat severe infections due to Gram-positive bacteria, the β-lactams and the glycopeptides antibiotics, are targeting this pathway. The mechanism of glycopeptides activity and resistance are described in the pathways of |FRAME: Vancomycin-Resistnace|., The β-lactams are the first and still the most frequently used class of antibacterial agents. The structure of these compounds contain a D,D linkage that is very similar to the D-Ala-D-Ala bond in the peptidoglycan pentapeptide. The D,D-transpeptidase catalytic domains of the penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) that are responsible for cross-linking the peptidoglycan threads (see |FRAME: MONOMER-15471| for an example) recognize this strucutre and bind the β-lactam antibiotics in an irreversible manner, resulting in inactivation of the enzymes., β-Lactam resistance in pathogenic bacteria is due to production of low-affinity PBPs (for example, methicillin resistance in |FRAME: TAX-1280| caused by the |FRAME: MONOMER-15469| protein, and ampicillin resistance in enterococci which results from the |FRAME: MONOMER-15537| protein), drug detoxification by production of β-lactamases, and decreased permeability. Recently a new mechanism for resistance has been described., In some strains, such as the case of |FRAME: TAX-1352| D344M512, resistance is a result of a complete bypass of the D,D transpeptidases by an |FRAME: MONOMER-15534 "L,D transpeptidase"| |CITS: [10748168]|., The regular cross-links in Enterococci are formed between the |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue at position 4 of one peptide and the |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| which are attached to the |FRAME:LYS| at position 3 of a second peptide (see |FRAME: PWY-6461|). The D,D-transpeptidase that catalyzes this linkage requires an intact D-Ala-D-Ala bond in the first peptide. This bond is hydrolyzed, providing the energy to drive the reaction., It has been shown that in the resistant strain a VanY-type |FRAME: CPLX-8039 "carboxypeptidase"| is constitutively active |CITS: [20025663]|. This carboxypeptidase, which is resistant to glycopeptide antibiotics such as vancomycin, removes the terminal |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residue from all pentapeptides, resulting in peptidoglycan precursors that exclusively include a tetrapeptide. These precursors are not a substrate for the D,D-transpeptidases, but form an excellent substrate for the |FRAME: MONOMER-15534 "L,D-transpeptidase"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-11907| gene, which catalyzes the formation of cross-links between |FRAME: LYS| of the first peptide and the |FRAME: CPD-302| or |FRAME: CPD-3633| residue of the second peptide |CITS:[16144833][16647082]|., The L,D-transpeptidase is present β-lactam-sensitive strains of |FRAME: TAX-1352|, but is usually inactive due to lack of its substrate - the tetrapeptide form of the peptidoglycan precursor, |FRAME: CPD-12258|. A mutated two-component regulatory system (DdcRS) in the resistant strains is responsible for the activation of the |FRAME: CPLX-8039|, which prepares the substrates for the transpeptidase |CITS: [20025663]|., By "by-passing" the D,D-transpeptidases the enzyme confers resistance towards most β-lactam antibiotics on the organism |CITS: [10748168]|. The enzyme was thought to be completely insensitive to β-lactam antibiotics, but recently it has been shown that it is very sensitive to |FRAME: CPD-9231|, a β-lactam of the carbapenem class |CITS: [17646161]|. The discovery indicated that the spectrum of activity of β-lactams is not restricted to transpeptidases of the DD-specificity, as previously thought.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Gangliosides "Gangliosides"| are molecules composed of |FRAME: Glycosphingolipids| (|FRAME: Ceramides| and |FRAME: Oligosaccharides|) with one or more sialic acids (usually |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) linked to the sugar chain. They are components of the cell plasma membrane that modulate cell signal transduction events, and appear to concentrate in lipid rafts., The name ganglioside is derived from the ganglion cells of the brain, from which the first gangliosides were isolated by the German scientist Ernst Klenk in 1942 |CITS: [Klenk42]|. Indeed, gangliosides dominate the composition of the glycocalyces of most of the cells of the vertebrate nervous system. Although gangliosides with various glycan structures are found in every vertebrate tissue, they are markedly more abundant in the nervous system, where each cell has on average about 10 million cell surface gangliosides |CITS: [27261254]|., Variations in the sialoglycan and lipid components of the gangliosides result in hundreds of distinct ganglioside structures with a variety of functions that range from regulating receptor tyrosine kinases to directing cell-cell communication, cell-substrate interaction, adhesion, and protein targeting |CITS: [17991443]|. Mammalian brain gangliosides, however, are dominated by only four types of gangliosides - |FRAME: CPD-7188 "ganglioside GM1a|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1a "ganglioside GD1a"|, |FRAME: Ganglioside-GD1b "ganglioside GD1b"| and |FRAME: Ganglioside-GT1b "ganglioside GT1b"| |CITS: [22735313]|. The ceramide lipid components of brain gangliosides are dominated by a single fatty acid (|FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|) attached to one of two sphingoid bases, |FRAME: SPHINGOSINE| and |FRAME: CPD-19684| |CITS: [21113547]|., While many non-human mammals synthesize gangliosides that contain two types of sialic acids - |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| and |FRAME: CPD-273|, mammalian brain gangliosides almost exclusively carry the former., Like other glycosphingolipids, gangliosides are biosynthesized stepwise by a series of glycosyltransferases that use nucleotide sugar donors to first glucosylate ceramide and then elongate the saccharide chain .|FRAME: Lactosyl-Ceramides Lactosylceramide|, a product of the second glycosylation step in the biosynthesis of many glycosphingolipids, is an important branching point, being a common precursor for the synthesis of the four major classes of glycosphingolipids: the |FRAME: Ganglio-Series-GSLs "ganglio series"|, the |FRAME: Globo-Series-GSLs "globo series"|, the |FRAME: Lacto-Series-GSLs "lacto series"|, and the |FRAME: Neolacto-Series-GSLs "neolacto series"| |CITS: [10320813]|., The ceramide lipid of glycosphingolipids is embedded in the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane, with the glycan extending 2-2.5 nm outward, perpendicular to the plane of the lipid bilayer |CITS: [19056784]|. What makes gangliosides different from other glycosphingolipids is the incorporation of sialic acids. With a mean Pka value of around 2.6, sialic acids are more acidic than the majority of carboxylic acids and negatively charged at most physiological pH values., About Arthro-Series Glycosphingolipids, The first glycosphingolipids characterized from arthropods were reported from two closely related dipteran species: the green-bottle fly |FRAME: TAX-65466|, and the blowfly |FRAME: TAX-7373|. They were found to contain glucosylceramide and mannosyl-glucosylceramide |CITS: [7142125][3988759]|. Additional studies, largely in the same species, clarified that arthropods form an arthro-series of glycosphingolipids, which derived from a β-Man-(1→4)-β-D-Glc-ceramide core, which was termed |FRAME: Mactosyl-Ceramides "mactosylceramide"| (MacSer) |CITS: [7130143][3967656][3988759][2768250][2351669][2384087][2391351][1889407]|. The new invertebrate-specific arthro-series was found to be conserved in both nematodes and insects, and many more forms with increasing complexity and oligosaccharide length were subsequently described, all of which extensions of the MacCer core., The pathway of arthro-series glycosphingolipids biosynthesis was described in detail from |FRAME: TAX-7227| |CITS: [20816215]|. Certain modifications have been observed, that are not conserved among all organisms (e.g. modification of GlcNAc residues with phosphatidylethanolamine or with phosphocholine.), The ceramide backbone composition also differs between invertebrates and mammals. Whereas mammalian sphingoid bases are usually C18, insect sphingoid bases are generally C14 and C16 and are amide-linked to shorter fatty acid chains |CITS: [26395456]|. In many arthropods the ceramide contains a phosphoethanolamine |CITS: [31067435]|, while in nematodes the ceramide tends to contain a phosphocholine group |CITS: [8231660]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-10224 Kanosamine| (3-amino-3-deoxy-D-glucose) is an antibiotic produced as an end product by |FRAME: TAX-1396| |CITS: [8702302]| and other bacteria |CITS: [7429991][3569498]|. |FRAME: CPD-10223| is an intermediate in |FRAME: CPD-4821| biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-1967| |CITS: [15313224]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7000|). |FRAME: CPD-10224 Kanosamine| and |FRAME: CPD-10223| are also intermediates in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10231| (AHBA) |CITS: [12207505]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5979|), which is a precursor of the ansamycin and mitomycin classes of antibiotics (in |CITS: [11278540]|) (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5984|)., Early work using |FRAME: TAX-1408 "Bacillus pumilus (previously known as Bacillus aminoglucosidicus)"| provided experimental evidence for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10224| via |FRAME: CPD-12575|, although the genes involved were not identified |CITS: [5708625]|. Subsequent work using |FRAME: TAX-33910| provided further evidence for the |FRAME: CPD-12575| pathway (this pathway). It has also been proposed that the kab genes of |FRAME: TAX-1396| are involved in |FRAME: CPD-10224| biosynthesis, although the pathway was not determined |CITS: [19098220]|. More recently, an alternate route for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10224| has been described in |FRAME: TAX-224308|, in which |FRAME: CPD-10224| is derived from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| rather than |FRAME: CPD-12575| |CITS: [23586652]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY8J2-22|)., About This Pathway, This is a proposed pathway for |FRAME: CPD-10224| biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-33910| |CITS: [12207504] [12207505]|. Evidence suggests that |FRAME: CPD-10224| is the source of the nitrogen atom in the |FRAME: CPD-10231| biosynthetic pathway (aminoshikimate pathway) |CITS: [12207504] [12207505]| as indicated in the pathway link. This is in contrast to the original proposal that the nitrogen atom was derived from transamination of |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P| to |FRAME: CPD-10227| by |FRAME: GLN| |CITS: [KIM96]|. Preliminary studies using recombinant enzymes coexpressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| suggested that the products of genes rifK and rifL may form a complex, jointly converting |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: CPD-10223| through a |FRAME: CPD-10220| intermediate (see comment listed as reference 25 in |CITS: [12207505]|). These reactions produce |FRAME: NADH| and use |FRAME: GLN| as a nitrogen source for |FRAME: CPD-10224| |CITS: [12207505]|. The product of gene |FRAME: G-58869| has been predicted to encode a UDP-kanosamine phosphatase that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-10223| to |FRAME: CPD-10224|. The |FRAME: G-10752| and |FRAME: G-58869| genes have been shown to be essential for |FRAME: CPD-10231| biosynthesis |CITS: [11278540]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [21081954]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, At least four alternative routes have been reported in plants. , The pathway depicted here depends on an initial N-methylation with phospho-base phosphoethanolamine, and followed by two downstream N-methylations on phosphatidyl-bases, phosphatidyl-N-methylethanolamine and phosphatidyl-N-dimethylethanolamine. In plants, phosphatidyl-N-methylethanolamine is believed to be derived from CDP-methylethanolamine, whereas in animals, it is a direct methylation product from phosphatidylethanolamine |CITS: [438165]|., Radio tracer experiments with crude cell extracts suggested such a pathway in soybean and carrot |CITS: [16666464]|.
