Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MIMOSINE|, β-(3-hydroxy-4-pyridon-1-yl)-L-alanine, is a non-protein amino acid found in the legume species |FRAME: TAX-76306| and |FRAME: TAX-3866|. It acts as an iron chelator and blocks the mammalian cell cycle at the G1/S phase. Mimosine suppresses the synthesis of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3a (eIF3a or eIF p170) and, subsequently, retards the translation of α-tubulin |CITS: [Dong04]| and ribonucleotide reductase |CITS: [12972576]|. Chelation of zinc by mimosine is also suggested to affect the function of zinc finger transcription factors, which impede the transcription of cytoplasmic serine hydroxymethyltransferase (cSHMT), an essential enzyme for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis |CITS: [15531579]|., It has been suggested that |FRAME: MIMOSINE| is inolved in defense from viral or bacterial infections |CITS: [7975217]|. Another possibility is that mimosine may serve as a reservoir of carbon and nitrogen for survival and growth in nutrient-limiting soil environments |CITS: [16349454]|., |FRAME: TAX-3866| is wide-spread in tropical and subtropical agricultural systems and provides a ready source of protein for livestock. Ruminants from Australia and India are unable to metabolize |FRAME: MIMOSINE| to non-toxic components, but ruminants in Hawaii and Indonesia can consume diets rich in Leucaena without showing any ill effects, due to rapid bacterial degradation of |FRAME: MIMOSINE| in the rumen |CITS: [Megarrity83][Allison92][7871781][7900214][7665380][Pandey07]|. Rumen fluid from Hawaiian goats has been successfully transferred to Australian ruminants to overcome the toxicity of |FRAME: TAX-3866| |CITS: [3790013]|., About This Pathway, Mimosine-degrading enzymes have been reported from the seedling extracts of both |FRAME: TAX-76306| |CITS: [Suda60]| and |FRAME: TAX-3866| |CITS: [Smith66]|, as well as from some bacteria that can degrade mimosine and utilize it as carbon and nitrogen source |CITS: [16349454][11467724][23462928][35908235]|. The enzymes were reported to degrade mimosine to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-4H-PYRID-4-ONE|, pyruvate and ammonia, supporting the theory that mimosine can serve as a storage compound for carbon and nitrogen in the plants., The mimosine-degrading enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-3866| was studied in 2014 and found to be a carbon-nitrogen lyase |CITS: [24351687][26843166]|. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-76306| was characterized in 2019 |CITS: [31368041]|. The enzyme is believed to have evolved from |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.13| by gene duplication., Studies of the mimosine-degrading bacterium |FRAME: TAX-147233| uncovered the pathway for the degradation of the intermediate |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-4H-PYRID-4-ONE|. The pathway consists of a para-cleavage dioxygenase and a deformylase, whose combined action results in degradation to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and |FRAME: AMMONIUM| |CITS: [15968058][17390132][20138776]|. It was also suggested that carboxylation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE| to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| by |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.1|, is also part of the pathway |CITS: [18493742]|.

More than 3000 plant species representing 130 families have been reported to contain cyanogenic glucosides, which form one of the most effective constitutive chemical defense compound class produced in plants |CITS:[9431670]|. Herbivore attacks cause the disintegration of tissues which in turn liberates |FRAME:HCN| from the vacuole-stored cyanogenic glucosides now no longer separated from their activating enzymes, i.e. specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases |CITS:[Ganjewala10]|. This process is called cyanogenesis and comprises the sequential release of the glycogen component and |FRAME:HCN|, the latter either spontaneously dissociating from the aglycon or its release being enzymatically accelerated by α-hydroxynitrile lyases |CITS:[16667728]| |CITS:[Ballhorn11]|., |FRAME:HCN Hydrogen cyanide| affects cellular respiration and needs to be under tight control in both cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis and degradation. In biosynthesis this is achieved by forming a metabolon of participating enzymes (membrane-bound and soluble), in doing so increasing catalytic efficiency which significantly lowers the danger of releasing harmful metabolic intermediates |CITS:[17706731]|. Cyanogenesis is also a controlled process which only takes place when plants are injured. In undamaged plants the non-toxic cyanogenic compounds are stored in the vacuole and kept spatially apart from their hydrolyzing enzymes |CITS:[22404468]|. , The plant β-glucosidases catalyzing the cleavage of the glucosidic bonds are usually very selective and specialized for the cyanogenic glucosides present in the host plant. The hydrolysis of cyanogenic disaccharides can be catalyzed either by two sequential reactions releasing monosaccharides (for example see |FRAME:PWY-6011|) or a simultaneous mechanism catalyzed by a disaccharide-specific glucosidase which liberates disaccharides in the process (this pathway). The vicianin hydrolase catalyzing the cleavage of the β-glycosidic bond between |FRAME:CPD-12702| and |FRAME:VICIANOSE| without acting on inter-glycosidic bonds of |FRAME:R-VICIANIN| |CITS:[16665903]| |CITS:[17548373]| is one out of only three characterized dissacharide-specific glucosidases to date. The other two are the β-primeverosidase from tea plants |CITS:[12481100]| and the furcatin hydrolase from |FRAME:TAX-237940| |CITS:[14976214]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7113|). In another fern (|FRAME:TAX-218620|) where |FRAME:R-VICIANIN| is the only cyanogenic glucoside the (R)-mandelonitrile lyase involved in |FRAME:PWY-7093| was purified and biochemically characterized. It was shown that the fern (R)-mandelonitrile lyase did not share common properties with the (R)-mandelonitrile lyase found in Rosacea despite the fact that they utilize the same enantiomeric substrate, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-12702| |CITS:[12228664]|.

A common type of terminal alkyne biosynthesis pathways involves three proteins: a dedicated acyl-carrier protein, a ligase that ligates the substrate to the carrier protein, and a desaturase that introduces first a a double bond, then a triple bond at the terminus of the substrate molecule, while attached to the carrier protein., The first carrier protein-dependent pathway for terminal alkyne formation was descrbied from the marine cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1155739|, which produces |FRAME: CPD-17693|. The genes encoding the three proteins in that organism, which are located in an operon, were named jamABC |CITS: [25531891]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7641|)., Subsequent studies have shown that homologs of the three genes are widespread in bacteria, including cyanobacteria,, proteobacteria, actinobacteria, and planctomycetes |CITS: [26441143]|., Such a homologous cluster was characterized from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2426|, which is a cellulose-degrading symbiont of |FRAME: TAX-457830|, a mollusc often referred to as "shipworm" (even though it is not a worm)., The gene cluster, named ttuABC, encodes the ligase, desaturase, and carrier protein, respectively. Biochecmical analysis has shown that while TtuA can act on a number of medium-length chain fatty acids, the TtuB desaturase is much more selective, acting only on |FRAME: CPD-3617| |CITS: [26441143]|., Unlike |FRAME: G-43926 JamB|, which requires that its substrates are loaded onto the JamC acyl-carrier protein, TtuB appears to have some activity (at a much lower level) with other [acp] proteins., |FRAME: CPD-23303 9-Decynoate| is likely an intermediate in the formation of another compound, though the identity of that compound is still not known |CITS: [26441143]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NAPHTHALENE Naphthalene| is the simplest fused polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon, and is abundant in soils., Several bacterial species are able to grow on naphthalene as the sole cource of carbon and energy |CITS:[4423716][10433976][10620687]|. At least two pathways for naphthalene degradation exist - an aerobic pathway and an anaerobic pathway. This pathway describes the aerobic process., Naphthalene is catabolized through |FRAME: CIS-12-DIHYDRONAPHTHALENE-12-DIOL|, |FRAME: SALICYLALDEHYDE|, and |FRAME: CPD-110|. The latter is converted into either |FRAME: CATECHOL|, which is then degraded by either the meta or the ortho cleavage pathways to TCA cycle intermediates |CITS: [1245462]|, or to |FRAME: CPD-633|, which is degraded by a different pathway to TCA cycle intermediates |CITS: [9573207]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6183| and |FRAME: PWY-6224|, respectively)., Several different models have been proposed for this pathway, due to the difficulty working with the unstable intermediate |FRAME:NAPHTHALENE-12-DIOL|, which is rapidly and spontaneously oxidized in water to |FRAME:CPD-4895|. The pathway presented here reflects the results of a careful analysis performed by Eaton and Chapman |CITS: [1447127]|., The genes encoding the enzymes required for the catabolism of naphthalene are often carried on plasmids, such as the NAH plasmids |CITS: [6259498][6277849][6278499]|. However, some organisms, such as |FRAME: ORG-5978|, carry these genes on their chromosome |CITS: [10433976]|. Transcription of the genes in this operon is regulated by a salicylate-dependent transcription regulator (such as NahR for the operon located on the NAH plasmid) |CITS: [3028396], [3007442]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms. As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions. The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane. In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-11968 "Alcaligin"| is a dihydroxamate siderophore that was originally identifed in the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-85698| (then known as Alcaligenes denitrificans)" |CITS: [Nishio88]|. Alcaligin was subsequently identified as the siderophore of the important pathogens |FRAME: TAX-520| and |FRAME: TAX-518|, previously known as bordetellin |CITS: [7860593]|., The |FRAME: G-11643| gene, which encodes the first enzyme in the pathway, was the first to be identified, by complementation of a |FRAME: TAX-518| transposon mutant defective in alcaligin biosynthesis |CITS: [8566764]|. The gene was found to be homologous to the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: G-9026| gene, which is involved in |FRAME: AEROBACTINSYN-PWY|, and to encode an |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.252| |CITS: [9266668]|. Another study has reported that the substrate for the enzyme, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, is produced by decarboxylation of |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.17| |CITS: [8550442]|., Two additional genes, |FRAME: G-11644| and |FRAME: G-11646|, were discovered next to |FRAME: G-11643| |CITS: [9266668]|. These genes were homologous to the aerobactin biosynthetic genes |FRAME: G-9027| and |FRAME: G-9028|, respectively. The three genes form an operon whose transcription is regulated by iron |CITS: [9266668]|. An identical operon was found in the genome of the related |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [8759851]|., Subsequent work revealed three additional genes in the operon. Two tightly linked open reading frames, alcD and |FRAME: G-11645|, follow |FRAME: G-11646|, and a third gene, alcR, which encodes a transcriptional regulator, ends the operon |CITS: [9473041][9473040]|., The roles of alkD and |FRAME: G-11645| are not well understood, but a recent review proposed that alcE, which shows significant similarity to Rieske dioxygenases such as naphthalene dioxygenase, may catalyze the hydroxylation of |FRAME: CPD-11964|, yielding |FRAME: CPD-11971| |CITS: [15719346]|.

Electron flow from D-lactate dehydrogenase to ubiquinone is not electrogenic |CITS: [3013300]|; cytochrome bo oxidase translocates 2 protons per electron (H+/e- = 2) through its action as a proton pump and through a redox loop mechanism |CITS: [1850294]|.

Summary: Formaldehyde produced from the oxidation of methane and methanol by methanotrophic bacteria is assimilated to form intermediates of the central metabolic routes that are subsequently used for biosynthesis of cell material |CITS: [353476][6768606][1909921]|., The two known pathways used by methanotrophic bacteria for the synthesis of multicarbon compounds from formaldehyde are both cyclic. In the serine pathway 2 molecules of formaldehyde and 1 molecule of carbon dioxide are utilized in each cycle forming a three-carbon intermediate (see |FRAME:PWY-1622|), while in the RuMP cycle 3 molecules of formaldehyde are assimilated forming a three-carbon intermediate of central metabolism |CITS:[353476][6768606][6295363][2110811][1909921]|., In the latter pathway, all cellular carbon is assimilated at the oxidation level of formaldehyde., The RuMP pathway was first described by Quayle and his colleagues |CITS: [14342526][6030306][4377654]|., Although it is cyclic in nature, it is displayed above as a linear segment, to make it simpler to follow. It is best decribed as consisting of three main parts - fixation, cleavage and rearrangement., Two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.43| and |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.27|, are unique to this pathway and were initially believed to be unique to the metabolism of one-carbon compounds by methanotrophs and some other methylotrophs that do not utilize methane. However, it was later shown that these enzymes are also present in heterotrophs such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, where they play a role in formaldehyde detoxification |CITS: [10572115][14532071]|. Thus, it is now accepted that the RuMP Cycle is a widespread prokaryotic pathway involved in either formaldehyde fixation or formaldehyde detoxification., I. Fixation, In the first part, |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| (RuMP) are condensed by |FRAME: CPLX-3441| (HPS) to form |FRAME: CPD-26| (HuMP), which in turn is converted to |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| (FMP) by |FRAME: CPLX-3445| (HPI). These two enzymes are the only enzymes which are unique to organisms that employ this pathway. This part of the pathway is displayed above as a stand alone segment. By the assimilation of three formaldehyde molecules, three molecules of FMP are created., The enzymes which participate in the other two parts of the pathway are members of other pathways, such as the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY|, and are not unique to organisms utilizing the RuMP pathway., II. Cleavage, In the second part, some of the FMP is cleaved to 3-carbon compounds. There are two routes: in the first route (displayed above) FMP is phosphorylated by 6-phosphofructokinase (EC 2.7.1.11) to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (FDP), which is then cleaved by fructose-bisphosphate aldolase (EC 4.1.2.13) to dihydroxy acetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate., In the second route FMP is first isomerized to glucose 6-phosphate (GMP) by glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (EC 5.3.1.9). GMP is dehydrogenated first to D-glucono-1,5-lactone 6-phosphate by glucose-6-phosphate 1-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.49), and then to 6-phospho-gluconate by 6-phosphogluconolactonase (EC 3.1.1.31). 6-phospho-gluconate is then converted to 2-keto-3-deoxy-6-phospho-D-gluconate (KDPG) by phosphogluconate dehydratase (EC 4.2.1.12), and, KDPG is cleaved into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and pyruvate by KDPG aldolase (EC 4.1.2.14)., The pyruvate or DHAP which are formed are then channeled to biosysnthesis. For every three molecules of formaldehyde that are condensed, one molecule of FMP is cleaved, and thus one molecule of pyruvate or DHAP is routed to biosynthesis., III. Rearrangement, The last step is a rearrangement step, in which the RuMP molecules are regenerated. There are several possible routes. For example, the GAP which is left from the cleaved FMP can react with one of the other two FMP molecules to form xylulose-5-phosphate (XuMP) and erythrose-4-phosphate (EMP)., This reaction is catalyzed by a transketolase (EC 2.2.1.1). EMP then reacts with the third FMP to form septulose-7-phosphate (SMP) and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (GAP). This reaction is catalyzed by a transaldolase (EC 2.2.1.2). These two compounds are the substrate for another aldolase (also 2.2.1.2), which generates XuMP and a ribose-5-phosphate (RiMP). The net result of these rearrangements reactions are two XuMP and a RiMP, all of which are then converted back to RuMP by ribulose-phosphate 3-epimerase (EC 5.1.3.1) and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase (EC 5.3.1.6), thus closing the cycle.

Summary: General Background, Mycolic acids are the hallmark of the cell envelope of |FRAME: TAX-1773| and related species and genera. They comprise a homologous series of C60-C90 (2R)-alkyl-(3R)-hydroxy very long-chain fatty acids, and are found as either esters of |FRAME: Arabinogalactan| or as free lipids in the form of trehalose dimycolate (TDM). Both forms contribute to forming the two leaflets of the mycobacterial outer membrane, also called the mycomembrane, which protects the organism from antibiotics and the host's immune system |CITS: [15653820][17555433][15353567]|., There is a significant variability in the structure of mycolic acids among different species. Acids from |FRAME: TAX-1716| species contain 22-38 carbon atoms, |FRAME: TAX-697025| and |FRAME: TAX-697025| spp. contain 30-36, |FRAME: TAX-37914| spp. contain 34-38, |FRAME: TAX-1827| spp. contain 34-52 in, |FRAME: TAX-1817| spp. contain 46-60, |FRAME: TAX-2053 Gordonia| spp. contain 46-66, |FRAME: TAX-2060| spp. contain 64-78 , |FRAME: TAX-1763| spp. contain 60-90, and |FRAME: TAX-286801| spp. contain up to 100 carbon atoms |CITS: [24374164]|., The acids are formed by a Claisen-type condensation of two components - the meromycolic chain and a fatty acid., Several structural classes of mycolic acids exist. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the most apolar ones, known as α-mycolic acids, contain 74-80 carbon atoms (out of which 22-26 carbons are located in the fatty acid moiety and the rest on the mero-chain) and generally two double bonds (that can be in either cis- or trans-configuration) or two cis-cyclopropyl groups located in the meromycolic chain. The cyclopropane rings are believed to protect the organism from oxidative stress |CITS: [15653820]|. α-Mycolic acids usually comprise more than 70 percent of the total mycolic acids in the cell., Other classes are defined by additional oxygen functions located in the distal part of the meromycolic chain, and include keto-, methoxy-, wax ester-, epoxy-, and hydroxy-types. In |FRAME: TAX-1773| the oxygenated mycolic acids (keto-, methoxy-, and hydroxy-types) contain ~84-88 carbon atoms, and are thus four to six carbons longer than the α-mycolic acids from the same strains., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of mycolic acids could be divided conceptually into three parts: the biosynthesis of the fatty acid moiety, the biosynthesis of the mero-acid moiety, and the condensation of both parts., Mycobacteria are quite unique in having two fatty acid synthase systems - FAS-I, a multidomain, multifunctional fatty acid synthase similar to those found in yeast and mammals, and FAS-II, a system consisting of several soluble enzymes that is similar to that found in bacteria and plants., The pathway towards mycolic acids starts with the action of the FAS-I system, which has a bimodal distribution of products - forming C14/C16 long-chain acyl-CoAs and C24/26 very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs. The C24/26 very-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs are modified only by carboxylation at the C2 position, at which point they are ready for condensation with meromycolic acids to form mycolic acids. The C14/C16 products serve as starter molecules for the FAS-II system, which continues elongation to form meromycolic acids., A key enzyme is |FRAME: G185E-4666 FabH|, which acts as a link between the FAS-I and FAS-II systems, catalyzing the condensation of the FAS-I-derived C14/C16 acyl-CoAs with malonyl-[acpM]. The enzyme is most active with |FRAME: LAUROYLCOA-CPD|., During elongation by the FAS-II system, continuous introduction of 2-carbon units upstream of the the double bond at position 3 results in its "migration" farther from the carboxylate (to positions 5, 7, 9 etc). Isomerases (encoded by echA10 and echA11) act at two stages of the pathway, introducing double bonds into the compounds. One isomerase acts on |FRAME: trans-delta2-behenoyl-ACPs|, forming |FRAME: cis-delta3-behenoyl-ACPs|, and another on |FRAME: trans-D2-cis-D15-gheddoyl-ACPs|, forming |FRAME: cis-cis-D3-15-C34-2-ACPs|. The action of the second isomerase results in a branch in the pathway, where some of the acids continue with an additional double bond, while others continue without it. Both continue to be elongated by the FAS-II system. However, all of the acids that escaped isomeization at the C35 level undergo an isomerization at the level of C40., Following completion of the elongation process, the acids are modified by several additional enzymes that introduce methoxy groups and convert double bonds to cyclopropyl groups (including |FRAME: G185E-4788|, |FRAME: G185E-4787|, |FRAME: G185E-4786|, |FRAME: G185E-4785|, |FRAME: G185E-4597|, |FRAME: G185E-4635|). The final modified acids, as well as the final product of the FAS-I system, are then transferred from their [acp] and CoA carriers (respectively) to a polyketide enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G185E-8096| gene, which catalyzes their condensation into a mycolic acid |CITS: [14695899][15042094]|., Additional enzymes catalyze the conjugation of the mycolic acids first to |FRAME: CPD1G-69| and subsequently to |FRAME: TREHALOSE-6P|. Following the removal of the phosphate, the free mycolic acid is exported to the periplasm, where it is attached to arabinogalactan in the cell wall, or to a second mycolic acid, forming a dimycolate.

Names: L-asparagine biosynthesis III (tRNA-dependent) // L-asparaginyl-tRNA<sup>asn</sup> biosynthesis via transamidation
Summary: |FRAME: ASN|, one of the 21 co-translationally inserted amino acids that make up proteins, is known to be synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| in an ATP-dependent amidation reaction., Two mechanistically distinct asparagine synthetases are known. |FRAME: EC-6.3.1.1|, encoded by the |FRAME: EG10091| gene, utilizes ammonia as amide donor (see |FRAME: ASPARAGINESYN-PWY|), whereas |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.4|, encoded by the |FRAME: EG10092| gene or related genes) works with glutamine (see |FRAME: ASPARAGINE-BIOSYNTHESIS|). These enzymes are present in organisms of all domains, the major one being the latter., For some time these enzymes were assumed to be the sole biosynthetic route to |FRAME: ASN|. However, some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-274| and |FRAME: TAX-1299|, lack these enzymes; instead they employ a tRNA-dependent transamidation mechanism for conversion of |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| to |FRAME: ASN| |CITS: [9789001]|., Two routes of |FRAME: Charged-ASN-tRNAs| synthesis are present in these organisms: one is the canonical |FRAME: CPLX-7621|, encoded by |FRAME: G-10743|. The second is a tRNA-dependent two-step pathway, which is described here. In the first step a |FRAME: MONOMER-14054| generates the misacylated |FRAME: L-aspartyl-tRNAAsn| species, and in the second step it is amidated to the correctly charged |FRAME: Charged-ASN-tRNAs| by the heterotrimeric |FRAME: EC-6.3.5.6|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10736|, |FRAME: G-10737| and |FRAME: G-10738| genes, with glutamine serving as the amide donor., It has been shown that at least in |FRAME: TAX-274| and |FRAME: TAX-1299| this pathway synthesizes the cells entire supply of |FRAME: ASN|. It was also suggested that the pathway occurs in many bacteria as the sole synthetic route to this essential amino acid |CITS: [11880622]|.

Betaines are quarternary ammonium derivatives of amino acids produced by plants and marine algae that can serve as osmoprotectants. |FRAME: CPD-821|, known as stachydrine or N,N-dimethyl L-proline, can be used by some organisms as a carbon and nitrogen source., An aerobic degradation pathway for |FRAME: CPD-821| has been described early on (see |FRAME: P561-PWY|) |CITS: [Goldmann91]|. In that pathway the two methyl groups are removed by oxidative demethylases in reactions that require molecular oxygen. An anaerobic pathway, which is shown here, was established much later, in 2019., |FRAME: TAX-1736| strains are known to utilize quaternary amines, including |FRAME: BETAINE|, |FRAME: CHOLINE| |CITS: [16345842]|, and |FRAME: CPD-821| |CITS: [31341018]|. During growth on the latter the organism demethylates it to |FRAME: CPD-904|, which accumulates in the growth medium and is not degraded further. The demethylation is calayzed by a system of three proteins - |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.388| (MtpB), |FRAME: MtqC-corrinoid-proteins| (MtqC), and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.389| (MtqA), all of which are highly enriched in cells grown on |FRAME: CPD-821|. The methyl group, which is transferred to tetrahydrofolate, is then processed by the enzymes of the |FRAME: CODH-PWY "Wood–Ljungdahl pathway"|., Unlike most such systems, where the three components are encoded by genes that reside in the same operon, the components of the proline betaine—tetrahydrofolate methyltransferase systems are encoded in three separate parts of the chromosome |CITS: [31341018]|.

Summary: The sequence of reactions in the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway may vary.  This superpathway gives an, overview of three possible routes of cholesterol biosynthesis.  These routes exist because reduction of the, carbon 24,25 double bond on the hydrocarbon side chain of the sterol ring structure by sterol, Δ<sup>24</sup>-reductase can occur at multiple points in the pathway, giving rise to different, intermediates.  These intermediates, with or without a double bond in the hydrocarbon side chain, can serve, as substrates for the other enzymes in the pathway.  However, there is evidence that the preferred point of, carbon 24,25 double bond reduction is directly after the isomerization of zymosterol |CITS: [9291139]|, as shown, in pathway |FRAME: PWY66-341|. General Background, |FRAME: Xyloglucan Xyloglucan| is the major component of the |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| in dicotyledon type I cell walls. The cross-linking between xyloglucan chains is a major factor in the stability of the three-dimensional matrix between adjacent cellulose microfibrils |CITS: [Whitney95]|., Xyloglucan has a backbone of β-1,4-linked cellotetraose units, which are substituted in C-6 by α-D-xylosyl residues at two or three of the first four glucosyl residues (but not the residue closest to the reducing end) |CITS: [8252539]|. Some of the xylosyl residues are subsequently further substituted by (1,2)-β-D-galactosyl residues at the second and/or third xylose residue and by (1,2)-α-L-fucose at the galactosyl unit of the third xylose residue |CITS:[12837954] [17011813]|. , A common terminology uses G for basic non-substituted glucosyl units within a xylosylglycan, X for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, L for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose and β-D-galactose, and F for glucose residues substituted by α-D-xylose, β-D-galactose and α-L-fucose |CITS:[Fry93]|.Using this terminology, most xylosylglucans consist of repeating heptasaccharide XXXG units as well further modified XXLG, XLXG, and XLLG units., About This Pathway, Some organisms have the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.151|, that cleaves the xyloglucan backbone at the location of the unsubstituted glycosyl moiety. The final product of these enzymes is an assortment of oligosaccharides that refelct the basic building blocks of xyloglucan. Such enzymes have been characterized from the fungi |FRAME: TAX-5053| |CITS: [9884411]|, |FRAME: TAX-34381| |CITS: [15541296]| and |FRAME: TAX-5061| |CITS: [18072936]|. The action of |FRAME: MONOMER-16611| releases the galactosyl residues, converting all of these oligosaccharides to |FRAME: CPD-13375|. This heptasaccharide can be hydrolyzed further by |FRAME: CPLX-8293| to |FRAME: CPD0-1202| and |FRAME: GLC| |CITS: [4019436]|.

Summary: |FRAME:CPD-17052 Gliotoxin| is the prototype compound of epipolythiodioxopiperazines (ETPs), a class of secondary metabolites produced only in fungi |CITS:[15817772] [24816491] [18272357]|. Research on the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-17052| has been carried out predominantly in Aspergillus fumigatus which was one of the first sequenced members of his genus |CITS:[16372009]|. Because of the severe impact of this pathogenic fungus causing invasive aspergillosis with a high mortality rate in immunocompromised humans |CITS:[2410548] [2461370] [15618207]| Aspergillus fumigatus and its metabolic arsenal of secondary metabolites has been in the focus of research for a long time |CITS:[10194462] [17544368]|. |FRAME:CPD-17052 Gliotoxin| has been reported to possess antiviral |CITS:[14254440]|, antibacterial |CITS:[9304400]|, and immunosuppressive |CITS:[7510665]| properties and caused in in vitro experiments apoptotic and necrotic cell death |CITS:[7535293]|. , The proposed role of |FRAME:CPD-17052| as a virulence factor has not been without controversy. While some researchers have contested the importance of |FRAME:CPD-17052| for the virulence of Aspergillus fumigatus |CITS:[16757745] [16956378]| others have supported the notion of |FRAME:CPD-17052| being essential for Aspergillus virulence |CITS:[17601876] [22094977]|. It appears that |FRAME:CPD-17052| is indeed an virulence factor which, however, only becomes apparent in certain virulence models |CITS:[18608908] [17030582] [18199036]|. The characteristic structural feature of epipolythiodioxopiperazines (ETPs) such as |FRAME:CPD-17052| is an internal transannular disulfide bridge |CITS:[22575049]| which has been attributed to confer toxicity by conjugation with thiol-containing proteins |CITS:[7539267] [19608453]| or the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) |CITS:[2461370] [2461370] [15817772] [20495914]|., The discovery of the gliotoxin (gli) biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS:[15979823]| comprising of 13 genes significantly accelerated the elucidation of the respective molecular function of those genes. Genes of the cluster such as GliA and GliZ have been determined to be involved in |FRAME:CPD-17052| transport |CITS:[24847038]| and transcriptional regulation |CITS:[17030582]|, respectively. The vast majority of the genes however encode for biosynthetic genes characterized in detail only recently. The nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NPRS) encoded by GliP catalyzed the committed reaction of the pathway, i.e. the formation of the dipeptide |FRAME:CPD-17043| |CITS:[17154540]|. Knocking down GliP resulted in the elimination of |FRAME:PWY-7533| and coincided with the downregulation of the genes in the gli cluster indicating that |FRAME:CPD-17052| regulates its own biosynthesis |CITS:[16757745]|. The introduction of the transannular disulfide bridge is a complex part of the pathway and includes the hydroxylation of |FRAME:CPD-17043| encoded by GliC to produce the bishydroxylated |FRAME:CPD-17045| |CITS:[21749092] [23434416]| which allows the double insertion of sulfur via |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| addition yielding |FRAME:CPD-17046| encoded by GliG |CITS:[21513890] [21749092]| followed by the subsequent shortening of the |FRAME:GLUTATHIONE| side chains encoded by GliK, GliJ |CITS:[24039048]| and Glil |CITS:[22936680]| finally resulting in the reduced |FRAME:CPD-17049|. The latter is very reactive causing cell and protein damage by forming thioconjugates with susceptible proteins and is detoxified through a specific oxidoreductase encoded by GliT forming |FRAME:CPD-17050| |CITS:[20593880] [24446392]|. , GliT is also considered a contributing factor for selfresistance against autointoxication by |FRAME:CPD-17052| although the mode of action, oxidation of reactive thiols |CITS:[20593880]| versus GliT mediated secretion pathway for |FRAME:CPD-17052| |CITS:[ 20548963]| is still under disputation. Summary: General Background, The ABH and the related Lewis blood group determinants are formed from |FRAME: Blood-Group-Antigen-Precursor "precursor disaccharides"| that decorate glycosphingolipids or protein glycans by concerted actions of several glycosyltransferases., The ABH histo-blood group system (sometimes referred to as ABO) was originally defined in terms of the antigenic substances occurring on red blood cells |CITS: [Landsteiner00][Landsteiner40]|. However, substances exhibiting similar serological specificities also occur in various mucous bodily fluids (such as saliva and milk), mostly as glycoproteins |CITS: [16747710][Morgan44]|., The Lewis blood group antigens, discovered in 1946, are biosynthetically and structurally related carbohydrate structures used as markers of cell differentiation and embryonic development, based on fucosylation carried by a number of fucosyltransferases. The system is named after Mrs. H. D. G. Lewis, in whose serum the first member of the family was discovered |CITS: [20995492]|. However, the presence of the Lewis antigens is not limited to erythrocytes, and they are found in different tissues and organs., Remarkably, some human pathogenic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-210| expresses complex carbohydrate epitopes on their lipopolysaccharides (LPS) that are structurally identical to the histo-blood group antigens produced by mammals, including a wide variety of structures belonging to the Lewis blood group system and their precursors., Not all strains of |FRAME: TAX-210| produce all of these antigens. However, most strains (80-90%) are able to synthesize the type 2-based blood group antigens |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y"| |CITS: [9398905][8890213]|. Some strains were found to synthesize |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x"| |CITS: [10632700]|, and a smaller population also expresses the type 1 based blood group antigens |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "H type 1"| |CITS: [23828675]|, |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a|, and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| |CITS: [9565568][10992504][18436591][22160312]|., Several roles have been proposed for the presence of these antigen in the bacterium, including attachment to epithelial cells, evasion of the host immune response, and autoantibody induction |CITS:[11286193][18279843]|., About This Pathway, The synthesis of the Lewis antigens requires several types of fucosyltransferases, including an α-(1,2)-fucosyltransferase (for |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "H type 1"| and |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y"| antigens), an α-(1,3)-fucosyltransferase (for |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"|, |FRAME: Antigen-Ley "Lewis y"|, and |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x"|), and an α-(1,4)-fucosyltransferase (for |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a| and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"|)., The genomes of |FRAME: TAX-210| contain two paralogous genes, termed |FRAME: HP_RS01865| and |FRAME: HP_RS03210|, encoding α-(1,3)/(1,4)-fucosyltransferases, and a single gene, |FRAME: HP_RS00480|, encoding an α-(1,2)-fucosyltransferase., Expression of the three fut genes is regulated via slipped-strand mispairing in intragenic polyC tract regions, resulting in alternate reading frames and an on/off switch. A perfect translation frameshift cassette resembling that of the |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG10245| gene is present |CITS: [10096092][10496917]|., FutA and FutB contain a C-terminal heptad repeat region, consisting of a variable number of DD/NLRV/INY tandem repeats. These vriations correlate to polymer sizes of O-antigen units recognized for Lewis x glycosylation - each heptad repeat corresponds to one N-acetyl-β-lactosamine unit in the O-antigen polysaccharide |CITS: [16477004]|., Characterization of the products of the futA and futB genes from several strains has shown that they differ among the strains - some have strictly α-(1,3)-fucosyltransferase activity |CITS: [9261149][9261148][16800635]|, some have strictly α-(1,4)-fucosyltransferase activity |CITS: [16000696]|, and some are bifunctional α-(1,3)/(1,4)-fucosyltransferases, like the mammalian |FRAME: HS10249| enzyme |CITS: [10998067][10671538][16407247]|., Characterization of the α-(1,2)-fucosyltransferase revealed that the bacterial enzyme differs in his substrate range from the mammalian enzymes. It is active on |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"| antigens, but not on the |FRAME: B-Gal-14-NacGlc-R "type 2 disaccharide precursor"|, suggesting that the Lewis y antigen may be produced in |FRAME: TAX-210| in a different path that in mammals, via the |FRAME: CPD-8594 "Lewis x"| antigen |CITS: [10096092][10589734]|. Similarly, the |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| antigen is formed from the |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a"| antigen |CITS: [10998067]|., In addition, the enzyme had high activity with |FRAME: beta-Gal-13-beta-GlcNac-R "type 1 disacchride precursor"| and with |FRAME: Lewis-a-epitope "Lewis a"| antigen, producing |FRAME: Type-1-H-Antigen "H type 1"| antigen and |FRAME: Antigen-Leb "Lewis b"| antigens, respectively |CITS: [10589734]|., An α-2,3-sialyltransferase, required for the production of |FRAME: sLex-Antigen "sialyl-Lewis x"|, has been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-56877|, the only non-pylori gastric Helicobacter species isolated from humans |CITS: [22408169]|.

The Gram-positive, soil-inhabiting, filamentous bacteria of the genus |FRAME: TAX-1883| use a number of chemical compounds, including |FRAME: Gamma-Butyrolactones "γ-butyrolactones"|, |FRAME: MMFs "methylenomycin furans"|, |FRAME: CPD-19905|, and |FRAME: Butenolides "γ-butenolides"|, as chemical signaling molecules or microbial hormones, which, together with their specific receptors, regulate morphological and/or physiological differentiation |CITS: [2268871]|. At least 60% of |FRAME: TAX-1883| species appear to produce γ-butyrolactones, although (as of 2011), only a small number of them have been characterized |CITS: [21090718]|., Based on their structures, these γ-butyrolactones have been classified into three types: the |FRAME: A-factor-type-lactones "A-factor type"|, the |FRAME: Virginiae-butanolides "virginiae butanolide (VB) type"|, and the |FRAME: IM-2-type-lactones "IM-2 type"|, all of which share the cyclic butanolide skeleton |CITS: [14523609][19778723]|., The VB-type compounds were originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1961|, where they control |FRAME: CPD-19910 virginiamycin| production. They contain a 6-α-hydroxy group |CITS: [3108224][3145258][2621168]|. Several forms have been reported that differ in their fatty tail. The differences results from incorporation of different 3-oxo-fatty-acyl-[acp] compounds by the first commited enzyme in their biosynthesis, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.277|., Each γ-butyrolactone can interact with a specific receptor |CITS: [7592371]|, which in turns binds to the promoter region of a transcriptional activator. When the concentration of the γ-butyrolactone reaches a critical threshold, it binds to receptor molecule, resulting in its dissociation from the promoter and production of the transcription activator, which then activates the transcription of a number of genes required for secondary metabolism and morphological differentiation |CITS: [24367152]|., Two possible routes for the biosynthesis of γ-butyrolactones have been proposed. One route, which involves |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.113|,  has been shown to be the main route in |FRAME: TAX-1911| during |FRAME: PWY-7878| and is likely to also operate in |FRAME: TAX-1902| during |FRAME: PWY-7882|. However, it appears that the second type of pathway operates in |FRAME: TAX-1961|, as the presence of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-19938|, which is only produced via the second route, has been documented |CITS: [Sakuda93]|, and since these organisms contain the |FRAME: G-55096| gene, which is not found in |FRAME: TAX-1911| or |FRAME: TAX-1902| |CITS: [18034227]|., The biosynthesis of all γ-butyrolactones is believed to proceed from 3-oxo-fatty-acyl-[acp] molecules, which are intermediates of fatty acid biosynthesis, and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, an intermediate of glycolysis. The two molecules are condensed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.277|, forming an ester |CITS: [17277085]|. The next step is believed to be spontaneous dehydration forming a butenolide skeleton, followed by dephosphorylation by an unknown enzyme  |CITS: [Sakuda93]|. BarS2 is presumably responsible for the next reaction step, producing 6-oxo forms of the butanolides. Finally, the oxo group is reduced to a hydroxyl group by |FRAME: G-55093 BarS1| to give the final products |CITS: [12193632]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylic acid"| (salicylate; SA) is an aromatic compound commonly found throughout the plant kingdom that is also found in some bacteria., In plants |FRAME: CPD-110| affects numerous biological and physiological processes, including plant defense (via the systematic acquired resistance system |CITS: [15283665][12873532]|), allelopathy, flowering, and stomatal movement |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|. Given its important signaling role, plants often chemically modify |FRAME: CPD-110| by attaching glycosyl, methyl, or other groups to |FRAME: CPD-110| to alters its activity, volatility, or other properties |CITS [PIERPOINT94][SCHULZ93]|. In particular, |FRAME: CPD-12628| (SAG) is believed to be more water-soluble than |FRAME: CPD-110|, thus enabling it enter the vacuole more easily via an ABC transporter or a H+-antiporter |CITS: [15032822][15871031]|. This process may serve to prevent plants from being over-exposed to active SA and/or may enable the storage of this important signaling compound |CITS: [18248508]|. Notably, in some species, enzymes that perform this glucosylation are up-regulated as levels of |FRAME: CPD-110| rise |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|., About This Pathway, A number of plant species have been shown to catalyze the formation of |FRAME: CPD-12628| (SAG), such as |FRAME: TAX-4097 (tobacco)"| |CITS: [15871031]|, |FRAME: TAX-3689| (poplar) species and hybrids, |CITS: [20177744][17599371]|, |FRAME:TAX-3708| |CITS: [19449088]|, and |FRAME: TAX-4530| (rice) |CITS: [12228500]|., |FRAME: CPD-12628 SAG| may be further modified to produce additional salicylate glucosides that differ between species. For example, |FRAME:CPD-12663| is made by |FRAME: ORG-5993| (see |FRAME: PWY-6621|) |CITS: [18248508]|.

General Background, Benzoxazinoids were identified in the early 1960s as secondary metabolites of the grasses (including the major agricultural crops maize (|FRAME: TAX-4577|), wheat (|FRAME: TAX-4565|), and rye (|FRAME: TAX-4550|)) that function as natural pesticides and exhibit allelopathic properties |CITS:[BARNES87][10804466]|. Benzoxazinoids are synthesized in two subfamilies of the |FRAME: TAX-4479| and sporadically in single species of the dicots |CITS: [19577780]|. They play an important role in defense against pests such as insects, pathogenic fungi and bacteria |CITS:[niemeyer88]|. The most common benzoxazinoids are |FRAME: CPD-6365| and |FRAME: CPD-6366|., Since the aglycone benzoxazinoids are autotoxic, they are stored in glucosylated forms that have reduced chemical reactivity |CITS: [10804466]|. The glucosides are stored in the vacuoles |CITS:[12239364]|. This allows the plants to store the toxic compounds in anticipation of pathogen attacks, prompting the suggestion to name these compounds "phytoanticipins". , For the synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13811|, please see |FRAME: PWY-6949|., About This Pathway, While |FRAME: CPD-6365| is the main benzoxazinoid in some plants, including barley, in most other benzoxazinoid-producing plants, such as maize, |FRAME: CPD-13811| is further converted to |FRAME: CPD-6562| |CITS: [19577780]| by a two-step hydroxylation/methylation at position C7, catalyzed by |FRAME: G-7822| and |FRAME: G-14794|, respectively |CITS:[18192444]|., In addition, |FRAME: CPD-6562| has been reported to be further methylated in maize into |FRAME: CPD-6561| |CITS:[12359519]|. |FRAME: CPD-6561| is relatively lipophilic amongst benzoxazinoid glucosides, a property that may affect its absorption by pathogens at the site of interaction |CITS:[12359519]|. A number of defense reaction elicitors (chitin and chitosan fragments, heavy metal ions such as copper and jasmonic acid) have been shown to lead to the production of HDMBOA-glucoside in wheat, maize and Job's Tears plants |CITS:[11314951][12359519]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Glucosinolates "Glucosinolates"| are secondary metabolites found in 16 plant families, including agriculturally important crop plants of the |FRAME: TAX-3700| such as cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, and broccoli, as well as the model plant |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and are responsible for the typical sharp taste and odor of these plants., The glucosinolates are substituted β-thioglucoside N-hydroxysulfates that are formed from any one of eight amino acids, namely, |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: VAL|, |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: ILE|, |FRAME: PHE|, |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: TYR| and |FRAME: TRP|. Over 115 naturally occurring glucosinolates have been identified. Much of the diversity amongst glucosinolates arises from the addition of different sized alkyl groups to the side chain of the amino acids, principally valine, phenylalanine and methionine |CITS: [18458837]|. They have been grouped into aliphatic, aromatic, and indolic types, depending on whether they are derived from methionine, phenylalanine and tyrosine, or tryptophan. Indolylmethyl glucosinolates are found mainly in leaves. For a review, see |CITS: [12049923]|., It should be noted that the anomeric configuration of the glucosinolates is presented in the literature in an inconsistent manner, sometimes as (E)-isomers and sometimes as (Z)-isomers. However, it is now accepted that while the early oxime is in (E)-configuration, the configuration is converted to (Z) by the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.43|, or |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.45|, and remains as such., Glucosinolates are stored in the vacuole and come into contact with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147| (myrosinase) upon breakage of the cell. Myrosinase de-glucosylates the glucosinolates, resulting in formation of nitriles, isothiocyanates and thiocyanates. The precise product that is formed depends on the glucosinolate and whether an epithiospecifier protein is present. , The breakdown products give the typical sharp taste and odor to many of the members of brassicaceae that are eaten, such as raddish and mustard. Arabidopsis has been shown to accumulate at least 23 different glucosinolates in both seeds and leaves., About This Pathway, Most of our knowledge on glucosinolate metabolism came from studies in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, which accumulates over 30 different glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated |FRAME: MET| (ranging from |FRAME: HOMOMETHIONINE| to |FRAME: CPDQT-277|), |FRAME: TRP|, and |FRAME: PHE|. The majority of those are the aliphatic glucosinolates derived from chain-elongated methionine., The early part of the biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of glucosinolates is very similar to that of the pathways involved in cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis. The pathways begin with an amino acid N-monooxygenase, which is invariably a cytochrome P450 of the CYP79 family. The enzyme catalyzes the multistep conversion of the parent amino acid (or in some cases a chain-elongated form) into the corresponding oxime, the key intermediate of both glucosinolates and cyanogenic glucosides biosynthesis |CITS: [11133994][12464638][12609033]|., In glucosinolate synthesis, the oxime is converted into a glutathione conjugate by the action of different P450 enzymes that belong to the CYP83 family |CITS: [11553739][12970475][26361733]|. Most of the glutathione moiety is cleaved off by peptidases, leaving a thiohydroximate |CITS: [19483696]|, which is subsequently decorated with a sugar |CITS: [15584955]| and a sulfate group |CITS: [15358770]|, completing the glucosinolate core structure., The side chain is subsequently modified by different tailoring enzymes, resulting in the large variety of different glucosinolates.

Summary: General Background, Organophosphonates are compounds that contain a carbon-phosphorus bond which provides chemical and biochemical stability. They are synthesized as secondary metabolites in a variety of prokaryotes and lower eukaryotes and are part of the global phosphorus cycle. Soil bacteria can utilize phosphonates as a source of phosphorus, and in some cases carbon and nitrogen (in |CITS: [16981709][19191873]|)., The carbon-phosphorus bond can be cleaved by several bacterial enzymes such as carbon-phosphorus lyase, a widespread but poorly characterized enzyme (in |CITS: [21341651]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16245012]|), or the hydrolytic enzymes |FRAME: CPLX-1201| (phosphonatase), |FRAME: CPLX-8313|, or by the phosphonoacetate hydrolases shown in this pathway. Data suggest that additional pathways for phosphonate degradation have yet to be discovered (in |CITS: [21543322]|). , About This Pathway, |FRAME: ORG-5930| can grow on |FRAME:CPD-764| as a sole carbon, energy and phosphorus source (in |CITS: [9300819]|). The enzyme that catalyzes this reaction, |FRAME:CPLX-402|, represents a fourth route of organophosphate metabolism in microbes, in addition to the three other enzymes mentioned above |CITS: [8529644] [9300819][12697754]|., This pathway also represents a continuation of pathway |FRAME: PWY-6832| in |FRAME: TAX-266834| as shown by the pathway link |CITS: [21543322]|.

General Background, |FRAME: HISTAMINE| is a biologically active diamine with important roles in animals. In mammals it is involved in the immune response, gastric secretion, neurotransmission and cell growth. |FRAME: HISTAMINE| metabolism includes its biosynthesis, degradation, storage, secretion and receptor interaction. Most current anti-histamine drugs interfere with cellular receptor interaction (reviewed in |CITS: [15612036] [18377770]|). The transport and compartmentalization of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| in relevant cell types is an important area about which little is currently known |CITS: [16648665]|. In some mammalian cells, histamine and polyamine metabolism may be interrelated (reviewed in |CITS: [16364195]|). See MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-6173|., About This Pathway, In animals, |FRAME: HISTAMINE| released from |FRAME: HISTAMINE|-producing cells can be inactivated several ways in order to terminate its effects on the receptors of target cells. In mammals it can be inactivated by |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent methylation, or oxidized to |FRAME: IMIDAZOLE_ACETALDEHYDE|. The relative contributions of the enzymes catalyzing these two reactions differs among tissues and among organisms (in |CITS: [11566133]|). In invertebrates such as the marine mollusk |FRAME: TAX-6500|, or the horseshoe crab Limulus polyphemus, |FRAME: HISTAMINE| can be γ-glutamylated |CITS: [6125565] [12160879]|. These |FRAME: HISTAMINE| metabolizing enzymes can control the levels of released |FRAME: HISTAMINE|., The metabolic fate of the product of diamine oxidase, |FRAME: IMIDAZOLE_ACETALDEHYDE|, is unclear. It may be metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLEACETATE|, as shown. |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLEACETATE| was found to be a |FRAME: HISTAMINE| metabolite in the horseshoe crab |CITS: [12160879]|. |FRAME: N-METHYL-HISTAMINE| may be similarly metabolized by diamine, or monoamine oxidase and alcohol dehydrogenase (reviewed in |CITS: [16364195]|). Transport of |FRAME: HISTAMINE| and |FRAME: N-METHYL-HISTAMINE| into cells via organic cation transporters has been suggested to be involved in the inactivation system (reviewed in |CITS: [16364195] [12102747] [16648665]|). In |FRAME: TAX-6500|, |FRAME: HISTAMINE| functions as a neurotransitter in the central nervous system. γ-Glutamylation is thought to be a means of inactivation of neuronally released |FRAME: HISTAMINE|. The subsequent metablic fate of this dipeptide was not reported |CITS: [6125565]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-20532 "Cyclosporin A"| is a non-ribosomal cyclic peptide synthesized by the insect-pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-29910|. The fungus was isolated in 1969 by Dr. H. P. Frey, an employee of Sandoz Pharmaceutical Corporation (now Novartis), from a soil sample taken during a vacation in Hardanger Vidda, Norway. Similar compounds were also identified in another fungus, |FRAME: TAX-301100|, which was collected at about the same time in Wisconsin, USA |CITS: [Borel95]|. It was named cyclosporin as it was a cyclical peptide derived from spores., |FRAME: CPD-20532 "Cyclosporin A"| was first characterized as an antifungal compound. However, it was soon found to selectively inhibit both the ability of the mammalian immune system to reject foreign tissues, as in transplantation, and to prevent chronic immune-mediated inflammation, as in autoimmunity. Since it is largely free of the life-threatening side-effects of previously-used immunosupressants, it revolutionized the field of transplantation. It is the active agent in the immunosuppressant drugs, Sandimmune® and Neoral®, both manufactured by Sandoz., The role of the compound in the native organism is still not clear. The target of the compound was determined as, cyclophilins, which exhibit a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase activity, and it was hypothesized that the compound has antifungal or anti-insect activities by inhibiting cyclophilin activity |CITS: [27130487]|. Later it was reported that the major cyclosporin-binding protein in the hemolymph of a moth was lipophorin, a major insect lipoprotein |CITS: [Vilcinskas97]|., The cyclosporins were initially isolated as a mixture based on their antifungal activity, which was found to be quite low. However, their immunosupressant activity was discovered by Sandoz in 1971 |CITS: [Borel95][8575558][23331048]|. The two components of the mixture, |FRAME: CPD-20532| and |FRAME: CPD-26318|, were separated, and the structure of the main compound, |FRAME: CPD-20532|, was reported in 1976 |CITS: [950308][931750][893116]|. Many similar compounds were also identified, all of which cyclic peptides of 11 amino acids, seldom differing by more than two amino acids |CITS: [Dreyfuss76][3725752][3076967]|. Chemical synthesis was reported in 1986 |CITS: [3546034][3725755]|, resulting in the synthesis of thousands of semisynthetic or fully synthetic analogs., The cyclosporins are produced in a pathway that involves a 1.7 MDa non-ribosomal peptide synthase |CITS: [1820050][1637876][1644193][8300618]|. The biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-29910| was identified in 2013 |CITS: [23818858]| and a biosynthetic pathway has been proposed |CITS: [30279281]|., About This Pathway, The structure of |FRAME: CPD-20532| strongly suggested a non-ribosomal biosynthesis mechanism |CITS: [Zocher84]|., Early attempts to characterize the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cyclosporins first led to the enrichment of an enzyme fraction that was able to activate all 11 amino acids that participate in cyclosporin A biosynthesis via aminoadenylation. However, total synthesis of cyclosporin A was not observed, and instead the system produced the diketopiperazine cycle-(D-Ala-MeLeu), representing a partial sequence of cyclosporin A |CITS: [3955013]|., In vitro synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-20532| was later obtained using partially purified cyclosporin synthase fractions. Replacement of |FRAME: CPD0-1942| in the reaction mixture by L-alanine, L-threonine, L-valine, or L-norvaline yielded the naturally occurring cyclosporins B, C, D, and G |CITS: [3693349][2759908]|., 72-fold purification of the enzyme was reported in 1990, resulting in near homogeneous preparation. The enzyme was reported incorrectly as having a mass of 800 kDa |CITS: [2358465]|. However, that value was corrected to 1.4 MDa in 1992 |CITS: [1644193]|. When the |FRAME: G-124405| gene, which encodes the enzyme, was cloned in 1994, it was found that the mass of the enzyme is almost 1.7 MDa, making the gene the largest genomic ORF described at the time (45.8 kb) |CITS: [8001164]|., Analysis of the SimA protein indicated that the NRPS contains 11 modules responsible for sequential uptake of substrates and chain elongation. In addition to the core condensation-adenylation-thiolation (C-A-T) domains present in each module, eight modules contain an additional N-methylation (NM) domain. The last module ends with a terminal condensation domain that is responsible for the cyclization of the final product |CITS: [8001164][30279281]|., Beside SimA, the cyclosporin biosynthetic gene cluster also encodes the enzymes necessary to produce one of its precursors - |FRAME: CPD-26317| (2-Bmt) |CITS: [23818858]|. This unusual amino acid is produced via a polyketide pathway, utilizing acetyl-CoA, malonyl-CoA, NADPH, and S-adenosylmethionine |CITS: [8253730][8679598]|. The |FRAME: G-124396|, |FRAME: G-124397|, and |FRAME: G-124398| genes encode a polyketide synthase, a cytochrome P450, and an aminotransferase, respectively, which participate in the production of |FRAME: CPD-26317| (2-Bmt) |CITS: [30279281]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8441|).

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-26787| is a carbapenem antibiotic originally isolated from |FRAME: TAX-47716| in 1976. It was reported to exhibit a broad-spectrum of antibacterial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and to be an extremely potent inhibitor of a number of β-lactamases. At the time, the structure was not reported, though it was claimed that it contained a sulfur atom |CITS: [950324]|. The structure, along with that of |FRAME: CPD-26804| (then known as MM 13902), was reported in 1977, though the stereochemistry was not specified. The full structures of |FRAME: CPD-26787|, |FRAME: CPD-26804| and |FRAME: CPD-26795|, including the stereochemistry, were reported in 1979 |CITS: [468716]|. The family of these compounds was named |FRAME: Olivanic-acids "olivanic acids"| |CITS: [Brown77] [468715]|. A potentially identical compound was isolated also from |FRAME: TAX-66891| |CITS: [924900]|. , |FRAME: CPD-26787| was shown to be the major |FRAME: Carbapenems carbapenem| produced by |FRAME: TAX-67274| ATCC 11009, and the gene cluster encoding its biosynthesis was identified in that organism. A pathway has been proposed, and the function of most genes was validated by generation of mutants. Many of the enzymes are similar to those involved in |FRAME: PWY-8481|. The major differences that distinguish |FRAME: CPD-26787| from |FRAME: CPD-26780| are the syn-relationship across C-5 and C-6 and the sulfonation. Putative enzymes responsible for the epimerization (|FRAME: G-124533 Cmm17|) and sulfonation (|FRAME: G-124529 CmmSu|) have been proposed |CITS: [24420617]|.

Summary: The first purine nucleotide that is synthesized de novo is |FRAME: IMP| (IMP)., IMP is converted to |FRAME: XANTHOSINE-5-PHOSPHATE| (XMP) by the enzyme |FRAME: IMP-DEHYDROG-CPLX|,, and the later is converted to the first guanosine nucleotide, |FRAME: GMP| (GMP), by the action of, |FRAME: GMP-SYN-CPLX|, an enzyme that can use either glutamine or ammonia as substrate., GMP is then converted to |FRAME: GDP| (GDP) and subsequently to |FRAME: GTP| (GTP) by the enzymes, |FRAME: GUANYL-KIN-CPLX| and |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX|, respectively., In |FRAME:TAX-562| both GDP and GTP can be converted to the deoxy forms of the nucleotide. GTP is converted to |FRAME: DGTP|, (dGTP) by the uncommon enzyme |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-TRIP-REDUCT-CPLX|, while GDP can be converted to |FRAME: DGDP| (dGDP) by either |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTI-CPLX| or |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTII-CPLX|., Finally, |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX| can also convert dGDP to dGTP., In bacterial systems genetic studies indicate that the majority of de novo purine biosynthetic genes are unlinked but may act as a single unit of regulation controlled by the `purR' repressor protein |CITS: [2404765]|.

This pathway has been reported for some Gram positive bacteria that can degrade L-tyrosine via 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetate (homoprotocatechuate), rather than 2,5-dihydroxyphenylacetate (homogentisate), to pyruvate and succinate, as shown by the pathway link |CITS: [931949] [20216]|. The homogentisate pathway of tyrosine degradation is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: TYRFUMCAT-PWY|., Another variation of tyrosine degradation has been shown in the Gram positive bacterium |FRAME:TAX-1817| sp. 239 which can degrade L-tyrosine to homogentisate via p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, p-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde, and, p-hydroxyphenylacetate. This organism degraded D- and L-phenylalanine similarly, via the corresponding non-hydroxylated compounds |CITS: [DEBOER88]|. There is also evidence that the yeast |FRAME:TAX-4952| can degrade tyrosine to homogentisate through these intermediates |CITS: [11472920]|.

Summary: General Background, Teichoic acids were first reported in 1958 |CITS: [Armstrong58]|, after being discovered serendipitously as "contaminants" in bacterial extracts from |FRAME: TAX-1590| |CITS: [2662967]|. As they make up a significant portion of the cell walls (about 60% in |FRAME: TAX-1423|) |CITS: [13684313]|, they were named based on the Greek word teikhos, which means a fortification wall., The teichoic acids are found in a wide range of Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [5411858][2496299]|. They include a diverse family of cell surface glycopolymers containing up to 60 phosphodiester-linked repeat units. There are two main types: the lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the plasma membrane and extend from the cell surface into the peptidoglycan layer |CITS: [406922]|, and the wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently attached to peptidoglycan and extend through and beyond the cell wall. Five types of lipoteichoic acids |CITS: [24819367]| and four types of wall teichoic acids |CITS: [24024634]| have been described so far., The best characterized wall teichoic acids are those from |FRAME: TAX-224308| and |FRAME: TAX-655816|, in which the polymeric units are |FRAME: TEICHOICACID-PWY "glycerol phosphate"| and |FRAME: PWY-7815 "ribitol phosphate"|, respectively |CITS: [13684313]|. In both cases, the repeating units are joined together by phosphodiester linkages, and are anchored via 1-3 glycerol phosphate units to a N-acetyl-β-D-mannosaminyl-(1→4)-N-acetyl-α-D-glucosamine disaccharide. The glycerol and ribitol units of the polysaccharides are modified with D-alanine esters and/or monosaccharides such as glucose or N-acetylglucosamine |CITS: [13684313][4321415]|. The anomeric phosphate of the linkage unit is covalently attached to peptidoglycan (PG) via a phosphodiester bond to the C6 hydroxyl of N-acetylmuramate., It should be noted that strain 168 also possesses a |FRAME: PWY-7819 "minor form of wall teichoic acid"| that is comprised of poly(glucosyl N-acetylgalactosamine 1-phosphate) |CITS: [4202940]|. , Teichoic acids serve several roles in the cell. They serve as reservoirs of phosphates that can be mobilized when phosphate becomes limiting |CITS: [104966]|. Being anionic, they are scavengers of cations (in particular Mg2+), and may create a pH gradient across the wall by sequestering the protons expelled through the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: [8396121]|. In addition, lipoteichoic acids are the main source of the hydrophobicity of the cell envelope |CITS: [6337099]|, and may contribute to its adhesiveness. Teichoic acids are also immunogenic, and can be considered the Gram-positive equivalent of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides |CITS: [46620]|., About This Pathway, The main form of the wall teichoic acids in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| and |FRAME: TAX-1280| is a poly(ribitol phosphate) polymer. This polymer is composed of about 40 repeating units, and is linked to the peptidoglycan moiety by the highly conserved linkage unit (in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| there is a single glycerol phosphate residue in the linkage unit, while in |FRAME: TAX-1280| there are two). The repeating ribitol phosphate units are decorated by monosacharides (|FRAME: GLC| in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| and |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-GLUCOSAMINE| in |FRAME: TAX-1280|) and |FRAME: D-ALANINE| residues., The biosynthetic process can be divided into several main steps: first, the linkage unit is synthesized, attached to an undecaprenol lipid carrier. Next, the polymeric chain is added, one unit at a time, and is decorated with monosaccharides. The polymer is subsequently translocated across the cytoplasmic membrane by an ABC transporter, D-alanylated, and ultimately cross-linked to the cell wall peptidoglycan, upon which the liberated undecaoprenyl carrier is recycled. A more detailed description follows:, The first step of the pathway in |FRAME: TAX-655816 "Bacillus subtilis W23"| is the attachment of an N-acetyl-glocasamine molecule to the lipid carrier |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-P|, by the action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33 "EC 2.7.8.33"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44667| gene. The N-acetyl-glucosamine has to be activated, in the form of |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| (for more information on the acivation of this donor molecule see the pathway |FRAME: UDPNAGSYN-PWY|)., Next, an activated |FRAME: UDP-MANNAC| unit is added by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.187 "EC 2.4.1.187"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44661| gene, to generate an N-acetyl-mannosaminyl-β-(1->4)-N-acetyl-glucosamine disaccharide, attached to the lipid., UDP-N-acetyl-mannosamine is synthesized from UDP-N-acetyl-glocasamine by |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.14 "EC 5.1.3.14, UDP-N-acetylglucosamine 2-epimerase"|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44666| gene. The last step in the synthesis of the linkage unit is the addition of a single glycerol phosphate unit, which is performed by the product of |FRAME: G-44662| |CITS: [21035733]|. The glycerol-phosphate unit has to be activated as well, in the form of |FRAME: CPD-606|, which is generated from |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.39|, the product of the |FRAME: G-44668| gene., Once the linkage unit is ready, |FRAME: MONOMER-19964|, encoded by |FRAME: G-44664|, adds a single |FRAME: CPD-372| unit. A second enzyme, encoded by |FRAME: G-44665|, adds additional ribitol phosphate units until the chain has achieved its final length. |FRAME: CPD-372| is formed from |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| by the action of the products of the |FRAME: G-44670| and |FRAME: G-44669| genes |CITS: [11882717]|., The ribitol phosphate units are modified by |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.53|, encoded by |FRAME: G-44674|, which attaches β-D-glucosyl residues at the C-2 hydroxyl groups., Following glycosylation, the lipid-anchored polymer is exported via the membrane to the external side by a dedicated ABC-type transporter encoded by the |FRAME: G-44699| and |FRAME: G-44700| genes |CITS: [21280653]|. At that location the polymer is modified further by D-alanylation of the ribitol units at the C-4 hydroxyl groups, which is carried by a complex system encoded by the dltABCD operon |CITS: [27134729]|. , Finally, the complete teichoic acid is hooked through its linkage unit on the C-6 of a MurNAc residue of a growing peptidoglycan chain in a transfer reaction catalyzed by any of three members of the LCP (LytR-CpsA-Psr) protein family (|FRAME: G-44698|, |FRAME: G-44697|, and |FRAME: G-44696|), releasing the undecaprenyl anchor |CITS:[21964069]|., The tar genes that encode the pathway's enzymes are located in a chromosomal region that spans less than 50 kb |CITS: [11882717]|. Mutations that disrupt the biosynthesis of wall teichoic acids result in a morphological change of the cell from rod shape to a sphere shape, and were initially known as rod mutations. The mutants are compromised and can grow only under a narrow range of conditions, they manifest increased sensitivity to temperature and certain buffer components, and tend to aggregate in culture. Mutants lacking both LTA and WTA are non-viable |CITS: [19229300]|.

Summary: This pathway of cysteine biosynthesis is a two-step conversion of |FRAME: SER| to |FRAME: CYS| via |FRAME: ACETYLSERINE|. The pathway has been documented in bacteria |CITS: [Kredich96]|, archaea |CITS: [10613873]| and plants |CITS: [10940562]|., In the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-83333| both pathway steps are regulated. The first step is subject to very strong feedback inhibition by the final product, |FRAME: CYS|. The second step is regulated at the genetic level with both |FRAME: ACSERLYA-ENZRXN| isozymes being under the positive control of the cysteine-responsive |FRAME: PC00040|. , |FRAME: TAX-511145| and |FRAME: TAX-90371| produce two cysteine synthase isoenzymes (|FRAME: ACSERLYA-CPLX| and |FRAME: ACSERLYB-CPLX|). |FRAME: ACSERLYB-CPLX| is preferentially used for the biosynthesis of L-cysteine during anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: [6754864]| and is able to utilize thiosulfate instead of sulfide to produce S-sulfo-L-cysteine |CITS: [6373737]|., Only one of the isoenzymes (the |FRAME: EG10192|-encoded |FRAME: ACSERLYA-CPLX|) forms a complex with |FRAME: CPLX0-237|. CysK is also the only one of the two cysteine synthases that is required for cell viability on cysteine-free medium., In higher plants |FRAME:CPLX-1323| (SAT) and |FRAME:CPLX-1326| (OAS-TL) can form a similar enzyme complex, which is thought to play an important role in regulation., Within the complex SAT activity is higher and OAS-TL activity is lower than the respective free forms., When the complex dissociates, SAT becomes inactive and OAS-TL becomes more active., The formation of the complex is regulated by the concentration of |FRAME: ACETYLSERINE| (OAS), and |FRAME: HS|, where OAS triggers the dissociation of the complex and sulfide counteracts the effect of OAS., Both pathway steps are reversible, and genetic and proteomic data suggest that the cysteine synthases may actually act as a sulfur scavenging system during sulfur starvation, stripping sulfur off of |FRAME: CYS| and generating any number of variant amino acids in the process |CITS: [Kredich96]|.

The product of the |FRAME: AT4G26850| gene (named for Vitamin C defficiency) has been originally classified as GDP-L-galactose phosphorylase. However, the term was misleading for several reasons. First, the enzyme can accept |FRAME: GDP-D-GLUCOSE| just as efficiently as |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE|. Secondly, multiple sugar 1-phosphates, such as |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P|, |FRAME: GLC-1-P|, and |FRAME: GALACTOSE-1P|, are actually better guanylyl acceptors than phosphate. Although the name was retained, a much more accurate definition of the enzyme is now provided in the modified Enzyme Commission description of |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.69| |CITS: [17485667][17877701]|., When acting on |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE|, the enzyme's activity leads to formation of |FRAME: CPDQT-4|, which is intermediate in the main |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis pathway in plants (see |FRAME: PWY-882|). The gualylyltransferase activity allows the enzyme to utilize |FRAME: GLC-1-P| and |FRAME: MANNOSE-1P| as phosphate sources., |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis usually starts with |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|, which can be produced from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate| in several steps as described in |FRAME: PWY-5659|. However, due to the |FRAME: AT4G26850| enzyme |FRAME: CPDQT-4| can be formed in different ways using the so called |FRAME: PWY4FS-12| and |FRAME: PWY4FS-13|, bypassing the need for |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE| production from |FRAME: D-glucopyranose-6-phosphate|. The importance of this enzyme is clear since Arabidopsis double mutants of |FRAME: AT4G26850|/|FRAME: AT5G55120| are seedling lethal (they can be rescued by supplementation with L-galactose; |FRAME: AT5G55120| is a minor form of the enzyme with similar activity but considerably lower expression) |CITS:[17877701]|., The VTC2 cycle incorporates two enzymes - |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.69| (VTC2) and |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.18| (GME). GME can restore |FRAME: GDP-L-GALACTOSE| from |FRAME: GDP-MANNOSE|, thus enabling VTC2 to continue to produce |FRAME: CPDQT-4| |CITS: [17485667]|., See |FRAME: PWY4FS-13| for a more complex interaction of |FRAME: AT4G26850| with additional enzymes |CITS:[17950389]|.

The petal color of rose hybrids of the cultivar 'Charleston' are characterized by a color change from yellow to red shortly after the opening of the flower |CITS:[Hennayake06]|. This change of color is caused by the enzymatic activities of anthocyanin specific glucosyltransferases forming anthocyanidin glucosides. While in most cultivated roses the anthocyanidin diglucoside |FRAME:CPD-7138| accumulates |CITS:[15944692]| (see |FRAME:PWY-5160|) other cultivars, i.e. |FRAME:TAX-128735| cv 'Charleston' and some wild roses accumulate |FRAME:CPD1F-766| instead |CITS: [Mikanagi95]|. , It has been shown that both in isolated petals of different developmental stages and suspension cultures of the cultivar 'Charleston' the |FRAME:MONOMER-18002| is highly active in the late stage of anthocyanin biosynthesis accumulating preferably |FRAME:CPD1F-766| |CITS:[Hennayake06]|. Activity of |FRAME:MONOMER-12113| |CITS: [15944692]| cannot be found and the smaller amount of |FRAME:CPD-7138| produced in the petals is catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-18001| |CITS: [Hennayake07]|. Form petals of the rose cultivar "Ehigasa' accumulating both |FRAME:CPD1F-766| and |FRAME:CPD-7138| a cyanidin 3-O-glucosyltransferase was isolated and characterized which accepted all three major anthocyanins, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-591|, |FRAME:PELARGONIDIN-CMPD| and |FRAME:CPD-7090| |CITS:[Fukuchi-Mizutani11]|.

Summary: Glutathion plays an important role in cellular redox control and detoxification of heavy metals, electrophilic xenobiotics, and toxic side products of normal metabolism. The detoxification process starts with the formation of |FRAME: S-Substituted-Glutathione "glutathione-S-conjugates"| in the cytosol, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.18|. The subsequent degradation of these conjugates may occur in either the cytosol or the vacuole., In |FRAME: TAX-3702|, the degradation routes are different in the two subcellular locations. In the vacuole, the initial step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.13|, which removes the N-terminal glutamate residue, similar to the pathway found in animals |CITS: [17561001]|. In the cytosol, however, the process starts with removal of the C-terminal glycine by |FRAME: EC-3.4.17.25| |CITS: [12620355][18522943]|, a process that has not been been reported from animals. The identity of the dipeptidase(s) that act next to remove the γ-glutamyl residue has not been reported, although this activity may be catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.13|., A similar forked pathway has also been reported from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|, although both routes appear to be associated with the vacuole. Following conjugation to glutathione, the xenobiotic is exported to the vacuole, where either the glycine residue is removed by the vacuolar serine carboxypeptidases |FRAME: G3O-29093-MONOMER| (|FRAME: G3O-29093|) and |FRAME: YMR297W-MONOMER| (|FRAME: YMR297W|), or is catabolized by the action of the vacuole-membrane-bound γ-glutamyltransferase encoded by the |FRAME: YLR299W| gene |CITS: [19897216]|., A yeast triple mutant, lacking functional |FRAME: G3O-29093|, |FRAME: YMR297W|, and |FRAME: YLR299W|, completely lost the ability to metabolize |FRAME: CPD-21160|. The expression of the Arabidopsis phytochelatin synthase |FRAME: AT5G44070| in the triple knockout mutant could restore this ability, resulted in the turnover of |FRAME: CPD-21160| to |FRAME: CPD-21164|, as observed in plants |CITS: [19897216]|., Both routes lead to a common intermediate, |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "L-cysteine-S-conjugate"|. Less is known about further degradation of this intermediate. In animals Cys-S-conjugates are acetylated by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.80|, to form N-acetyl-Cys-S-conjugates, known as |FRAME: Mercapturates mercapturates|. However, this activity has not been detected in plants. Instead, plants appear to catalyze the malonylation of the Cys-S-conjugates |CITS: [18522943]|. Although no genes have been correlated with this activity yet, potential candidates include a group of largely uncharacterized malonyltransferases that have been reported |CITS: [Benichou95]|., A second, minor, route for |FRAME: S-Substituted-L-Cysteines "L-cysteine-S-conjugate"| degradation has been described from Arabidopsis cell culture. A small portion of the Cys-S-conjugates was converted to thiols by |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.13| , followed by the action of an unknown methyltransferase to form methyl thiolethers |CITS: [18522943]|.
