Summary: General Background, At the time of this review, 136 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1, |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and, seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity., Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which, possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3,, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is, the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while, GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana., GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is, the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to, promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and, GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and GA4, enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have, either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95|, and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic, ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs, whereas, GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are, called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be, metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed., It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that, leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis., Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as, well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are:, i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of, bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring, stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme production (α-amylases) in, germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers, (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves, and citrus fruits., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the, synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|,, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis, can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). During active growth, the plant will maintain giberellin, homeostasis by metabolizing most gibberellins by rapid hydroxylation to inactive conjugates. Active, |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed in the, disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen produces large, amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Inactive conjugates might be stored or translocated, via the phloem and xylem before their release (activation) at the proper time and in the proper tissue., About This Pathway, GA12, the first true gibberellin is synthesized in plastids (see |FRAME:PWY-5034|). It is, then further oxidized in the cytosol to a wide range of gibberellins. Depending on the sequence of, hydroxylation at the 3β- and 13-positions, parallel pathways branch from GA12 to the, C19-GAs, the number and prevalence of these branch pathways varying from species to, species. The presence of the non 3, 13-hydroxylation branch pathway (also known as late, 3, 13-hydroxylation), a pathway originating from GA12 and leading to the hydroxylated, C19 GA4 has been demonstrated in many species including rice, wheat and, Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[15075394],[16160850],[2236013]|., Enzymes: The reactions of this pathway are catalyzed by 2-oxoglutarate-dependent, dioxygenases. The first enzyme, gibberellin 20-oxidase, catalyzes the removal of C-20, thereby forming, the C19-skeleton in GA4. This enzyme performs the sequential oxidation of, C-20 to the alcohol and aldehyde, followed by the removal of the C atom through formation of the 4,, 10-lactone ring. The alcohol intermediate (GA15) must be in its open lactone form (free, alcohol) to be catalyzed by the enzyme. It is however extracted from plants in its closed δ-lactone, form (|FRAME:CPD-6971|) which is no longer oxidized by GA20-oxidases. Although it is not certain, whether this form occurs naturally in planta or is an artifact of the extraction procedure, it is, interesting to note that spinach cell-free extracts contain an enzyme able to catalyze the conversion of, the δ-lactone form to its free alcohol form |CITS:[WARD97]|. Additional oxidation reactions leading, to the formation of growth-active GAs such as GA4 are performed by gibberellin 3-oxidases, which, depending on the species, are varyingly regiospecific |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|.

Summary: This superpathway integrates the common prokaryotic TCA cycle with the glyoxylate shunt, a variation that bypasses the steps of the TCA cycle in which carbon is lost in the form of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., The |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| is a catabolic pathway that generates energy and reducing power as well as precursors for biosynthesis. The TCA cycle is very common, and a variation of it exists in practically all aerobic living organisms |CITS: [16746397][16746585][16747930]|., The input to the cycle is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which is produced by the |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase complex"| from pyruvate, the product of the ubiquitous glycolysis pathway, but is also generated by the degradation of fats and proteins and by the fermentation of many feedstocks., In every turn the TCA cycle converts one molecule of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| into two |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| molecules, reduces a total of four molecules of either |FRAME: NAD|, |FRAME: NADP|, or |FRAME: Quinones quinone| to |FRAME: NADH|, |FRAME: NADPH| and |FRAME: Reduced-Quinones quinol|, respectively, and phosphorylates one molecule of GDP to GTP., The reduced molecules of NADH/NADPH/quinol that are formed by the TCA cycle serve as electron donors for oxidative phosphorylation (see for example |FRAME: PWY-3781|). In that process the electrons flow to a terminal acceptor, powering on their way proton pumps that trasport protons across the cytoplasmic or mitochondrial membranes, generating a proton motive force (PMF). As the protons return to their original location, they power ATPase enzymes that phosphorylate ADP molecules to ATP. The total energy gained from the complete breakdown of one molecule of glucose by glycolysis, the TCA cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation equals about 30 ATP molecules in eukaryotes., This superpathway also includes the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, which bypasses those steps in the TCA cycle that lead to a loss of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, eliminating the loss of carbon. The glyoxylate cycle operates in bacteria and some eukaryotic organisms. In |FRAME:TAX-562| the bypass is active when growth on 2 carbon compounds requires conservation of 4 carbon TCA intermediates, and is repressed during growth on glucose |CITS: [6378912][6389540][6329757][2512996]|. In plants the cycle is invovled in the metabolism of storage oils during germination of seeds |CITS:[Brownleade97]|. The cycle also operates in developing eggs of nematodes, where it converts triacylglycerols to carbohydrates |CITS: [627278]|.

Summary: General Background, Glycolysis, which was first studied as a pathway for the utilization of glucose, is one of the major pathways of central metabolism, the other two being the |FRAME:PENTOSE-P-PWY| and the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"|. Glycolysis is essential under all conditions of growth, because it produces six of the 13 precursor metabolites that are the starting materials for the biosynthesis of building blocks for macromolecules and other needed small molecules (the six compounds are |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|, |FRAME:G3P|, |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|, and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). Glycolysis can be found, if at least in part, in almost all organisms., Even though glycolysis is often described starting with glucose, other hexoses (e.g. fructose) can also serve as input (as its name implies - glycose is a general term for simple sugars)., Glycolysis has evolved to fulfill two essential functions:, i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and, ii) being an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism), it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules., Because various degradation pathways feed into glycolysis at many different points, glycolysis or portions of it run in the forward or reverse direction, depending on the carbon source being utilized, in order to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites and energy., This switching of direction is possible because all but two of the enzymatic reactions comprising glycolysis are reversible, and the conversions catalyzed by the two exceptions are rendered functionally reversible by other enzymes (|FRAME:F16B-CPLX "fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase"| and |FRAME:PEPSYNTH-CPLX|) that catalyze different irreversible reactions flowing in the opposite direction., About This Pathway, While this pathway appears to operate at some capacity in all mammals, it has been shown to play a key role in the metabolism of the naked mole-rat (|FRAME: TAX-10181|) under low oxygen conditions. Subterranean mammals that inhabit confined spaces are subjected to an atmosphere low in O2 and high in CO2 |CITS: [28428423][34424519]|. Naked mole-rats tolerate hours of extreme hypoxia and survive 18 minutes of total oxygen deprivation (anoxia) without apparent injury. During anoxia, the naked mole-rat switches to anaerobic metabolism fueled by fructose, which is actively accumulated and metabolized to lactate in the brain via a glycolysis pathway. In addition, the naked mole-rat heart is entirely capable of using fructose as a primary metabolic fuel |CITS: [28428423]|., Glucose-driven glycolytic respiration is inhibited during hypoxia due to the accumulation of lactate, since |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.11|, a rate-limiting step in the pathway, is subject to feedback inhibition via allosteric binding of ATP, citrate and lactate |CITS: [14073034][6228716][17666012]|. Fructose-driven glycolytic respiration, which doesn't involve this enzyme, avoids this feedback inhibition. , While both fructose and sucrose (which is cleaved to fructose and glucose) are increased in the naked mole-rat tissues during anoxia, the source of these sugars is unknown |CITS: [28428423]|. Dietary intake cannot explain the steep rise of sucrose within 10 min of hypoxia exposure, and de novo synthesis of sucrose in mammalian tissue has never been reported, making the origin of the observed sucrose an intriguing finding |CITS: [34424520]|., Fructose is used by many mammals, including whales and other cetaceans, in utero. In fetuses of ewes and pigs fructose is the primary sugar in blood, allantoic fluid, and amniotic fluid |CITS: [13320379]|. In humans, a switch to fructose metabolism under hypoxic stress has been associated with cancer malignancy, metabolic syndrome, and heart failure |CITS: [20647326][20086073][22922366][26083752]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HSCN Thiocyanate| is a major constituent of waste water from coal gasification factories. |FRAME: CPD-13584 Cyanide|, a by-product of coal gasification, is converted to thiocyanate by the addition of sulfur because thiocyanate is less toxic than cyanide. The resulting thiocyanate is then treated by activated sludge, where it is degraded by microorganisms |CITS: [1577754]|. Thiocyanate is also produced as a result of plant decomposition by the hydrolysis of cellular |FRAME: Glucosinolates glucosinolates| (thioglucosides) by glucosidase |CITS:[9573140]|., Microorganisms are known to use thiocyanate as a source of nitrogen, sulfur, carbon, energy, or some combination thereof. Some strains of the autotrophic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-931| |CITS: [7545513]|, as well as the sulfur-oxidizing alkaliphilic bacteria of the genus |FRAME:TAX-106633| |CITS: [11157213]| were shown to use thiocyanate as the sole source of carbon and energy. On the other hand, some organisms, including soil bacteria |CITS: [8000536]|, alkaliphiles belonging to the γ subdivision of |FRAME:TAX-1224| in the group |FRAME:TAX-2745| |CITS: [11157213]|, and the methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-47958| |CITS: [9446686]| can use thiocyanate only as a nitrogen source and require alternative carbon and energy sources., These observations suggest that two distinct pathways are involved in microbial thiocyanate degradation. In one pathway, which is known as the "cyanate pathway", thiocyanate is hydrolyzed by cleavage of the CS bond to form |FRAME: CPD-69| and a sulfur compound (see |FRAME: P581-PWY|) |CITS: [Youatt54][8000536][7698442][32094184]|. In the other pathway (named the "carbonyl sulfide pathway") thiocyanate is hydrolyzed by cleavage of the nitrile bond (triple N-C) forming |FRAME: CARBONYL-SULFIDE|, which is subsequenstly hydrolyzed to sulfide and carbon dioxide |CITS: [1577754][9573140]| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, The carbonyl sulfide pathway was studied primarily in the chemolithoautotroph |FRAME: ORG-5988| |CITS: [1577754][ 9573140][23406161]|, although this pathway was also described in |FRAME: TAX-381308|, a moderately halophilic chemolithoautotrophic sulfur-oxidizing γ-proteobacterium isolated from hypersaline lakes |CITS: [17216167]|., The initial enzyme, |FRAME: EC-3.5.5.8|, was purified from |FRAME: ORG-5988| and partially characterized |CITS: [1577754]|. The enzyme, which is induced by growth with thiocyanate, has strong homologies to nitrile hydratases |CITS: [9573140]|. The second enzyme in the pathway is |FRAME: EC-3.13.1.7|, which resembles members of the β-class carbonic anhydrase |CITS: [23406161]|., The fate of the sulfide which is produced in this pathway is different in different bacteria. In general, it is oxidized to one or more of the following: thiosulfate, tetrathionate, and sulfate |CITS: [8000536][7698442]|.

In the degradation pathway shown here, |FRAME: MET| is first metabolized to|FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM), a compound that mediates most biological methylations. In the second reaction, the S-methyl group is transferred to other acceptors in a transmethylation step. The product, |FRAME: ADENOSYL-HOMO-CYS|, is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| and |FRAME: ADENOSINE|., |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is a branch point. In rats and humans approximately half of the homocysteine formed is remethylated back to methionine via two salvage pathways, one involving |FRAME: MONOMER-9225| (EC 2.1.1.13), and the other involving |FRAME:CPLX-5601| (EC 2.1.1.5) (see |FRAME:ADENOSYLHOMOCYSCAT-PWY|)., The remainder of the homocysteine is degraded further. The first step is the condensation with serine to form |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE|. |FRAME:CPLX-5163| catalyzes cleavage of the C-γ-S bond of |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE|, yielding |FRAME:CYS|, |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| and |FRAME:AMMONIA| in a transsulfuration reaction (see |FRAME:HOMOCYSDEGR-PWY|) |CITS: [3309559][15539209]|.

General Background, Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are fatty acid that have 13 or more carbon atoms and contain more than one double bond in their backbone. Mammals require PUFAs, and most can convert certain PUFAs to other forms, but all mammals depend on certain PUFAs in their diet. Those are called essential fatty acids, and are classified as either ω3 or ω6 fatty acids, depending on the distance of the last double bond from the end of the molecule., PUFAs are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturated long chain fatty acids as common constituents of their lipids. They are produced by many algae, lower ukaryotes, mosses and ferns, where they are found in all major glycerol lipids and represent major constituents of membranes |CITS: [16728405]|. They are also produced by some marine bacteria that are adapted to cold temperatures and high pressure., |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID "Arachidonate"| (arachidonic acid) is a polyunsaturated ω-6 fatty acid with a 20-carbon chain and four cis-double bonds. It is produced de novo at high levels by mosses, by some lower eukaryotes (e.g. Euglena), and by some marine bacteria adapted to low temperatures and high pressures., About this Pathway, The most common mammalian |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| synthesis pathway is the |FRAME: PWY-7592 "6-desaturase/Δ6-elongase pathway"|, in which |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| is first desaturated by a 6-desaturase to yield |FRAME: CPD-8117|, followed by a Δ6-elongation to produce |FRAME: CPD-8120| and a second desaturation by a 5-desaturase to form |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID|. Some organisms that produce |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| lack a 6-desaturase and utilize an alternative pathway that includes an 8-desaturase |CITS: [10328826]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7601|)., An alternative pathway that involves a Δ8 desaturation step has also been described in rat and human testis (|CITS: [588579][459715]|. This discovery was surprising, since mammals are not known to possess an 8-desaturase. Later work has reported that the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: HS05918| gene, which was believed to catalyze only Δ6 desaturation, is also capable of catalyzing Δ8 desaturation when acting on the substrates |FRAME: CPD-12647| and |FRAME: CPD-12646| |CITS: [19202133]|. The pathway described here is suggested to be an alternate pathway for |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| biosynthesis based on the novel activity. In this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-18| is first elongated to |FRAME: CPD-12646| by the elongase complex, followed by a Δ8 desaturation catalyzed by |FRAME: HS05918| and a Δ5 desaturation catalyzed by |FRAME: HS07617|.

General Background, The name trehalose was introduced in 1858 to describe a main constituent of shells that are secreted by various, insects on tree leaves in the middle east. These shells were often dried and used as a sweetening agents, and are, believed to be related to the biblical Manna, the food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness, of Arabia. One variety of these shells, produced by the beetles Larinus maculatus and Larinus nidificans, was called "trehala manna", and the sugar extracted from it was named trehalique glucose, or trehalose, |CITS: [12065209]|. , In fact, trehalose is a disaccharide that is ubiquitous in the biosphere. It consists of two subunits, of glucose bound by an α:1-1 linkage (α-D-glucopyranosil α-D-glucopyranoside) and is thus, nonreducing. Trehalose has been isolated and characterized from many prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms, , including bacteria, yeast, plants, insects, and mammals |CITS: [11081789]| (and original references described therein). , In addition to being nonreducing, trehalose possesses several unique properties, including high hydrophilicity,, chemical stability, nonhygroscopic glass formation, and no internal hydrogen bond formation. , The combination of these features explains the principal role of trehalose as a stress metabolite., In prokaryotic organisms, trehalose can be used as an external carbon source |CITS: [7651129]|, a compatible solute, (in cyanobacteria and photosynthetic bacteria) |CITS: [8480996]|, a stress protector |CITS: [8391102]|, and a, structural component (part of the cord factor in mycobacteria) |CITS: [8075141]|., In yeast and filamentous fungi, the main roles of trehalose are as a carbohydrate storage |CITS: [6325857]| and as, a stress protector |CITS: [7887593]|., The enzymes for trehalose metabolism are present in higher animals, but their precise role is not well understood, |CITS: [11081789]|., About This Pathway, While |FRAME: CPD-12575| is the most common substrate for the biosynthesis of trehalose in yeast cells, it is not the sole donor. An |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE|-dependent trehalose synthase has been identified in mutant strains of, |FRAME: TAX-4932| lacking |FRAME: CPD-12575|-dependent trehalose synthase activity |CITS: [2532070]|. , Studies have shown that the two activities correspond to different proteins. While there are similarities between the two synthases (the apparent Km values for the respective nucleotide are similar, and Mg2+ is required by both), they were clearly different in respect to activation by ATP Mg. Trehalose accumulation in these mutants was detected only in cells grown on weakly repressive carbon sources such as maltose and galactose or during the transition phase from fermentable to non-fermentable growth on glucose |CITS: [ 9133641]|., |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE|-dependent trehalose 6-phosphate synthase activity is also known from |FRAME: TAX-1772| and |FRAME: TAX-1773|. The enzyme from the former was reported to be capable of utilizing all five nucleoside diphosphate glucose derivatives (ADP-D-glucose, CDP-D-glucose, GDP-D-glucose, TDP-D-glucose, and, UDP-D-glucose) as glucosyl donors |CITS: [Lapp71][8842710][12473104]|. The enzyme from the latter can use both |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| and |FRAME: CPD-12575|, but has higher activity with |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE|, which is believed to be the main substrate in vivo |CITS: [25277548]|.

Summary:
General Background, |FRAME: CPD-7670 "Dimethyl sulfide"| (DMS) is a major contributor to the total sulfur emissions to the atmosphere from land and the ocean. In marine, estuarine, and salt marsh systems, the main source of DMS is the degradation of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP), an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|. There are two main routes for DMSP degradation, leading to formation of either |FRAME: CPD-7670| or |FRAME: CPD-7672|. Other sources for DMS include the reduction of |FRAME: DMSO| and the degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids., DMS, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere, and is considered the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to sulfuric and methanesulfonic acids, which attract water and promote cloud formation and thus influence the climate |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, up to 90% of the DMS in the ocean is degraded biologically |CITS: [Kiene90]|., DMS is toxic, and attempts to isolate in pure culture DMS-degrading organisms that can use it as the sole carbon and energy source have been often unsuccessful due to this toxicity. However, several organisms capable of degerading DMS have been isolated over the years. Aerobic bacterial DMS oxidation has been demonstrated in organisms from a few taxonomic domains, including Thiobacillus sp. strain MS1 |CITS: [Sivela80]|, |FRAME: ORG-5989| |CITS: [Kanagawa82], [Kanagawa86][2930168][Tanji89][Gould92]|, |FRAME: ORG-6053| |CITS: [1872604][8285684]|, |FRAME: ORG-6050| |CITS: [Debont81]|, |FRAME: ORG-6052| |CITS:[3767349][Suylen86][Suylen87] [Smith88a]|, |FRAME: ORG-6060| |CITS: [1575493][Omori95]|, |FRAME: ORG-6062| |CITS: [Omori95]|, |FRAME: ORG-6061| |CITS: [9345770]|, and |FRAME: ORG-6066| |CITS: [12835925]| and |FRAME:TAX-392484||CITS:[16535680][17322322]|. Anaerobic degradation of DMS has been documented by methanogens |CITS: [11073950]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5258|) and by sulfate-reducing bacteria |CITS: [8074524]|., About This Pathway, Some purple phototrophic bacteria, such as the non-sulfur bacterium |FRAME: TAX-35806| and the sulfur bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6059|, can grow photoautotrophically with |FRAME: CPD-7670| (DMS) as the sole electron donor |CITS: [16347425][10460885]|., During this process, |FRAME:CPLX-7668| catalyzes the oxidation of DMS to |FRAME: DMSO| (DMSO) in the periplasm, transferring the electrons to |FRAME: Oxidized-cytochromes-c2|, which transfers them to the bacteriochlorophyll special pair (P870+) of the photochemical reaction center (RC) |CITS: [12067345]|.,
The enzyme has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-35806| and found to be a heterotrimeric complex |CITS: [8706745][12067345]|. The large subunit, which belongs to the DMSO reductase family, binds a |FRAME: CPD-582| cofator., In |FRAME: ORG-6059| no DMS oxidation occurs under anoxic/light conditions |CITS: [10460885]|.

Summary: General Background, Wighteone and luteone are complex prenylated isoflavones frequently found within the , tribe Phaseolae of the legume family |CITS: [Ingham90]|. Their isomers isowighteone and lupiwighteone as well , as phaseoluteone have also been isolated from various legume plants |CITS: [WOODWARD79]| |CITS: [STOBIECKI99]|. , Monoprenylated isoflavones are both involved in defense mechanisms against pathogens |CITS: [ABE87]| and nod , gene induction |CITS: [GAGNON98]|., Prenylated isoflavones such as wighteone and luteone along with the prenylated isoflavanone kievitone have been , observed to be more active against pathogens then their non-prenylated analogues (dalbergioidin, genistein, 2'-hydroxygenistein). , It has been proposed that the greater lipid-solubility of the prenylated compounds may improve their efficiency , |CITS: [ONeill83]|. Interestingly, monoprenylated isoflavones have been characterized as pre-infectional antifungal , agent in the genus |FRAME:TAX-3869| |CITS: [HARBORNE76]| |CITS: [GAGNON97]| which is different from other , phytoalexins which accumulate post-infectional in response to pathogens |CITS: [GAGNON97]|. , About This Pathway, The hydroxylation of genistein is carried out by the isoflavone-2'-hydroxylase (I2'H). , However, the enzyme(s) isolated from different species have demonstrated various substrate preferences. While I2'H , does not hydroxylate genistein in chickpea |CITS: [Hinderer87]| |CITS: [Clemens93]| the 2'-hydroxylation is carried out, in soybean |CITS: [3956488]| and licorice |CITS: [9790908]|. The intermediate 2'-hydroxygenistein is a branch point , leading to the biosynthesis of prenylated isoflavanones such as dalbergioidin and kievitone (|FRAME:PWY-4681|)., |FRAME:TAX-3870| possesses the enzymatic ability to monoprenylate genistein and its 2'-hydroxyl derivative. The , enzyme activity is strongly increased upon wounding but the enzyme does not respond to elicitors |CITS: [Schroeder79]|. , However, the question of how the mixture of isomers is obtained remains to be investigated.

These reactions are shown here after the SpnL reaction |CITS: [21544146]|., General Background, |FRAME: Spinosyns Spinosyns| are glycosylated macrolides produced by the actinomycete |FRAME: TAX-60894|. These polyketide secondary metabolites consist of a tetracyclic lactone scaffold (aglycone) with attached tri-O-methyl-L-rhamnose and |FRAME: D-Forosamine| sugars. Spinosyns have been shown to have insecticidal activity, and the sugar moieties are required for this activity. There is considerable interest in engineering spinosyn analogs to improve their insecticidal activity., |FRAME: TAX-60894| fermentatively produces a mixture of approximately 85% |FRAME: CPD-13385| and 15% |FRAME: CPD-13386| collectively referred to as spinosad (|FRAME: CPD-13386| differs only by the presence of a methyl group at C-6) (reviewed in |CITS: [19082588]|). Spinosyns J, H and K vary in methylation of the rhamnosyl group |CITS: [18704529]|. |FRAME: CPD-13385| is an active ingredient of several commercial insecticides that are effective and environmentally benign |CITS: [11695182]|. Other minor spinosyns with different methylation patterns and lower insecticidal activity can also be produced (|CITS: [10805578]| and in |CITS: [17190446]|). The non-enzymatic total synthesis of spinosyn A has also been accomplished |CITS: [15173590]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [20150928]| and |CITS: [19082588]|., The spinosyn biosynthetic genes are clustered in the |FRAME: TAX-60894| genome although the genes involved in L-rhamnose biosynthesis are located in three other regions of the genome, unlinked to the spinosyn gene cluster |CITS: [11358695][11544225]|. The L-rhamnose biosynthetic genes are required for both spinosyn and cell wall biosynthesis |CITS: [11544225]|. Another class of spinosyns, butenyl-spinosyns (pogonins), are produced by |FRAME: TAX-333966| and contain butenyl substitution at C-21 |CITS: [16179985]|., About This Pathway, Overall, |FRAME: CPD-13385| biosynthesis begins with the activities of ten modules of a predicted type I polyketide synthase (PKS) encoded by |FRAME: G-107796|-|FRAME: G-107800| that effect chain assembly, cyclization and release (|CITS: [17190446]| and reviewed in |CITS: [16895337]|). The PKS is thought to utilize |FRAME: Methylmalonyl-CoA| and |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| precursors to form the polyketide. The SpnA loading module has flexible substrate specificity and can use either |FRAME: Methylmalonyl-CoA| or |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|. Use of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| results in |FRAME: CPD-25536|, which is methylated at C-21, whereas use of |FRAME: Methylmalonyl-CoA| gives |FRAME: CPD-13385| that has an ethyl moiety at C-21 |CITS: [17190446]|. The released macrolactone ring is then modified by several tailoring enzymes (reviewed in |CITS: [20150928]| and |CITS: [19082588]|). The biosynthetic pathways for the L-rhamnose and D-forosamine glycosyl moieties that are added are shown in the pathway links to |FRAME: DTDPRHAMSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6808|., The order of tailoring reactions for |FRAME: CPD-13385| (and |FRAME: CPD-13386|) has been established by several in vitro studies. The polyketide macrocycle is oxidized at the C-15 hydroxyl group by SpnJ to form a keto-intermediate. A 1,4-dehydration reaction between C-11 and C-12 catalyzed by SpnM forms a double bond. This allows SpnF to catalyze a [4+2] cycloaddition reaction that resembles a Diels-Alder cycloaddition. Glycosyltransferase SpnG catalyzes rhamnosylation at the C-9 hydroxyl group |CITS: [21544146]|. This O-glycosylation reaction controls the biosynthetic maturation of spinosyns. The crystal structure of this key enzyme has been determined |CITS: [22283226]|., The rhamnosyl moiety is sequentially methylated by SpnI, SpnK and SpnH, producing the permethylated rhamnosyl tricyclic spinosyn pseudoglycone |CITS: [20158237]|. SpnL catalyzes the final ring closure between C-3 and C-14. Glycosyltransferase SpnP transfers the D-forosaminyl moiety to the C-17 hydroxyl group (in |CITS: [22283226]|). As noted above, it remains unclear whether the rhamnose methylation steps occur before or after SpnL action, although they were shown occur after SpnG action |CITS: [20158237]|. These reactions are shown here after the SpnL reaction |CITS: [21544146]|., Expression of the genes in |FRAME: TAX-1888| along with overexpressing of the polyketide synthase genes by the use of a constitutive promoter resulted in increased production of 70 mg/L |CITS: [34584996]|.

Inositol is the generic name for |FRAME: Inositols "1,2,3,4,5,6-cyclohexanehexol"|. Epimerization of the six hydroxyl groups results in nine stereoisomers. |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is the physiologically most common stereoisomer and is distributed abundantly (but not universally) throughout the biological system., |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "myo-Inositol"| is an essential polyol in eukaryotes, where its phospholipid derivative |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols phosphatidylinositol| (PI) is an important constituent of phospholipid membranes. PI is also cleaved by phospholipase C to generate inositol phosphate (IP) and diacyglycerol, both of which are central cell signalling molecules. |FRAME: CPD-12857 "L,L-di-myo-inositol 1,3'-phosphate"| (also known as di-myo-inositol phosphate, or DIP) is the most widespread organic solute in microorganisms adapted to hot environments., A pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| was initially characterized in |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [5905122][5905123][4328832]|, and subsequently shown to exist in multiple bacterial species, as well as the yeast |FRAME: TAX-54550| |CITS: [4351258]|. That pathway, which has been studied in detail in |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [18310071]|, is described in the pathway |FRAME: P562-PWY|., The marine hyperthermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2336| possesses a different pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| |CITS: [23441918]|. Only the first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-17948| (|FRAME: G-15941|), is identical to the pathway found in |FRAME: TAX-548| and |FRAME: TAX-1423|. The rest of the pathway, which is catalyzed by the products of the |FRAME: G-15942|, |FRAME: G-15943| and |FRAME: G-15944| genes, proceeds via dehydrogenation to |FRAME: CPD-15236|, hydration to |FRAME: CPD-14806|, and an epimerization to |FRAME: D-TAGATURONATE| |CITS: [23441918]|. This is followed by a second epimerization to |FRAME: FRUCTURONATE|, catalyzed by the product of the |FRAME: G-15945| gene |CITS: [22925190]|. While the first four genes form an operon and are specific for inositol degradation, the |FRAME: G-15945| gene has been shown to also be involved in the hexuronate catabolic netwrok of |FRAME: TAX-2336|, which enables the organism to degrade |FRAME: Pectin pectin| |CITS: [22925190]|.

Summary: General Background, Hydrolyzable tannins (HT), divided in the two subclasses gallotannins (see |FRAME:PWY-5477|) and ellagitannins (see |FRAME:PWY-5476|) are derivatives of pentagalloylglucose (1,2,3,4,6-penta-O-galloyl-β-D-glucopyranose) |CITS: [Niemetz00]|. The category 'hydrolyzable tannins' is based on the classical definition of Freudenberg |CITS: [Freudenberg20]| who distinguished condensed tannins (also referred to as proanthocyanins; flavonoid origin) and hydrolysable tannins (esters of gallic acid with typically β-D-glucose). That class of compounds belongs to the more general 'plant polyphenols' (synonym vegetable tannins) which have been intensively studied in the last few decades (reviewed in |CITS: [Haslam89]| |CITS: [15206456]| |CITS: [Haslam98]|. , The name 'tannin' derived from the pronounced property of these compounds to precipitate proteins which has been used over the centuries for the tannery procedure to produce endurable leather from raw hides. Beside that, hydrolyzable tannins have many antimicrobial, antioxidant and antitumor properties used in human health care |CITS: [8991956]| and apply the varying amount of astringency as food components/phytonutrients |CITS: [14519822]|. Hydrolyzable tannins are widely distributed among plants but differ with regard to gallotannins (more restricted occurence) and ellagitannins (broad occurence) |CITS: [Haddock82]|., The mono- to penta-substituted esters being generated on the biogenetic way towards pentagalloylglucose are also referred to as 'simple' galloylglucoses in contrast to the 'complex' galloylglucoses produced as the result of further galloylation of pentagalloylglucose |CITS: [16153405]|. However, that categorization does not indicate the tanning potential of the associated compounds., About This Pathway, Pentagalloylglucose, The biosynthesis towards pentagalloylglucose displays a high specificity with a defined metabolic sequence. The first step is the formation of β-glucogallin (1-O-galloyl-β-D-glucopyranose) from gallic acid catalyzed by the UDPG-dependent gallate-1-β-glucosyltransferase |CITS: [Gross82][Gross83]|. This compound does not only function as the common acyl acceptor throughout the pentagalloylglucose biosynthetic pathway but exerts in addition a dual role as acyl donor indicating the characteristic of an energy-rich 'activated' compound |CITS: [Gross83a]|., The further galloylation follows the metabolic sequence 1,6-digalloylglucose |CITS: [Schmidt87]|, 1,2,6-trigalloylglucose |CITS: [Gross91]|, 1,2,3,6-tetragalloylglucose |CITS: [Hagenah93]| and finally 1,2,3,4,6-pentagalloylglucose |CITS: [2757399]|. The formation of 1,2,6-trigalloylglucose may also occur using an alternative route |CITS: [Denzel91]|. , Ellagitannins, The oxidative steps from pentagalloylglucose to the dimeric cornusiin E via the monomeric ellagiotannin tellimagrandin II are catalyzed by two enzymes that belong to the group of p-diphenol: O2-oxidoreductases (EC 1.10.3.2) also known as 'laccases' |CITS: [Niemetz01]| |CITS: [12620341]| |CITS: [14599517]|. The enzymes catalyzes the sterespecific phenolic coupling to produce the (S)-stereoconfiguration as observed in tellimagrandin II and cornusiin E, respectively., Gallotannins, The experimental data clearly indicate that the impressive number of gallotannins is produced following one general reaction type. Five enzymes catalyze the progressive galloylation of pentagalloylglucose towards penta-, hexa- and heptagalloylglucoses and even higher substituted galloylglucoses |CITS: [Niemetz00][2148866]|. Although the enzymes are not very specific towards their substrates it was found on the basis of calculated catalytic efficiency that each of them had a preferred substrate (and major product) and therefore operates along a mainstream metabolic sequence |CITS: [16153405]|. Those five galloyltransferases identified in sumac (also called galloyltransferase A to E) have been demonstrated to catalyze the various heptagalloylglucoses in this plant |CITS: [Niemetz99][Niemetz98][11672728][12430027]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD0-1627 "6-Diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine"| (DON) is the best-studied broadly active |FRAME: GLN| antagonist, and is used extensively as an inhibitor of enzymes that act on |FRAME: GLN|, such as |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.2|., The compound was originally described as a tumor-inhibitory antibiotic produced by an unidentified Streptomyces species isolated from Peruvian soil |CITS: [24544086]|. In the same year it was also reported from |FRAME: TAX-66896| as a component of the tripeptide |FRAME: CPD-24748| |CITS: [13425456][5883414]|., The compound was tested as a chemotherapeutic agent in several clinical studies |CITS: [26425550][27489275][27560860][28759224][28454342]|, but was never approved due to its toxicity |CITS: [30181331]|. It is gaining renewed attention due to the recognition of the importance of glutaminolysis in cancer cells |CITS: [30181331][31699883]|., The diazo group is a rare functional group that is present in some natural products, such as |FRAME: CPD-24753|, |FRAME: CPD-24760|, the |FRAME: Kinamycins kinamycins|, and the |FRAME: Lomaiviticins lomaiviticins|. , The complete biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: CPD-24748| in |FRAME: TAX-66896|, including the production of |FRAME: CPD0-1627| from |FRAME: LYS|, has been reported |CITS: [33624374]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8293|)., About This Pathway, This pathway has been elucidated as a part of the biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: CPD-24748| by |FRAME: TAX-66896| |CITS: [33624374]|., To identify the gene cluster the researchers started with known sequences of the enzymes involved in production of |FRAME: NITRITE| from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-8295|), which have been characterized previously in a study of |FRAME: PWY-8296| |CITS: [26689788][30120394]|. Matching genes were found in both |FRAME: TAX-58347| and |FRAME: TAX-66896|, leading to the discovery of the full cluster. In |FRAME: TAX-58347| all the genes are clustered at a single locus, while in |FRAME: TAX-66896| the genes are divided into two clusters, with the azpE, azpD, and azpR genes located away from the main azp cluster |CITS: [33624374]|., To characterize the enzymes, each of the |FRAME: TAX-66896| genes was inactivated separately, and the resulting changes in metabolites were measured. When possible, the genes were clone dand expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified. Two of the three enzymes that participate in this pathway, |FRAME: G-107496 AzpK| and |FRAME: G-107498 AzpL|, showed no homology to any characterized protein. In addition, recombinant AzpL could not be produced, and recombinant AzpK did not show activity in vitro. However, multiple experiments, including heterologous production in |FRAME: TAX-1888|, permitted the functional assignemnt of these two proteins |CITS: [33624374]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Quinolizidine-Alkaloids "Quinolizidine alkaloids"| (QAs) are a class of alkaloids containing a |FRAME: CPD-28042| core that accumulate in a variety of leguminous plants. They are notoriously present in cultivated lupins (Lupinus spp.), where their presence complicates the use of the valuable, high-protein beans due to their toxic properties and bitter taste |CITS: [35302146]|., QAs can be bicyclic (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-28034| and |FRAME: CPD-28035|), tricyclic (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-28036| and |FRAME: CPD-28037|), or tetracyclic (e.g. |FRAME: CPD-28027| and |FRAME: CPD-28038|). In addition, there are a number of irregular QAs with divergent structural features, such as |FRAME: CPD-28041|. Typically, genistoid legumes accumulate mixtures of QAs belonging to several different sub-classes. For example, lupins accumulate bicyclic, tricyclic and tetracyclic QAs |CITS: [35302146]|., The biosynthesis of QAs is poorly characterized. The pathway is believed to occur in the chloroplast |CITS: [7389917][16662483]|. With the exception of some irregular QAs, the backbone of all QAs is derived from |FRAME: LYS| |CITS: [Schutte65a][Schutte65][Nowacki77][Golebiewski84]|. Lysine is believed to be converted via |FRAME: CADAVERINE| to |FRAME: CPD-11764|. In the current proposed pathway, three molecules of |FRAME: LYS|, modified into three molecules of |FRAME: CPD-11764|, are integrated into each molecule of tetracyclic quinolizidine alkaloid |CITS: [35302146]|. The pathway shown here represents the best hypothesis as of 2025 |CITS: [35302146]|., In some leguminous species, the final products of quinolizidine alkaloids biosynthesis (as well as their storage forms) are esterified forms, usually of acetic acid, tiglic acid, p-coumaric acid, or ferulic acid. The tigloyl esters of quinolizidine alkaloids are found as the major forms in some Lupinus plants including |FRAME: TAX-3870| and |FRAME: TAX-3874|.

Asparagine is the first amino acid discovered in plants, where it is the major nitrogen transport and storage compound. In plants, asparagine is metabolized in two routes, via asparaginase (|FRAME:ASPARAGINE-DEG1-PWY|) or via asparagine aminotransferase (this pathway). Studies in pea suggested that the predominant route differs in different tissues. The asparaginase pathway predominates in seeds, whereas the aminotransferase pathway predominates in leaves |CITS: [Ireland81]|., In the asparagine aminotransferase pathway, the product 2-oxosuccinamate could either be reduced to 2-hydroxysuccinamate or deaminated to oxaloacetate. 2-oxosuccinamate deaminase activity was co-detected with asparagine aminotransferase in soybean leaves |CITS: [Streeter77]|. Whereas, feeding experiment using pea leaves showed a high amount of 2- hydroxysuccinamate formed from asparagines |CITS: [Lloyd78]|. It is not clear which path is more relevant and the consequent reactions that further metabolize 2-hydroxysuccinamate |CITS: [6407397]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The enterpathogenic strain |FRAME: TAX-1450177| is one of the most common atypical EPEC strains and is associated with infantile diarrhea, one of the major causes of illness and death among children in developing countries |CITS: [Taylor55][5320784][4612325][2863319][1404557][8455192][8904439][10481102]|. Strains that belong to serogroup O:128 were divided into several subgroups designated O128ab; O128ac, and O128ad |CITS: [Ewing10]|. The subgroups differ in enterotoxin production |CITS: [3880728][3552998]| and have small differences in their O antigens that are mostly due to different acetylation patterns |CITS: [18237721]|., The structure of the |FRAME: CPD-24113| was reported in 1995 |CITS: [8556736]| and the O antigen biosynthesis cluster was sequenced in 2003 |CITS: [14550554]|. The cluster contains genes encoding the enzymes necessary for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13118|, an O antigen repeat unit flippase, an O antigen polymerase, and four glycosyltransferases. By using sequence analysis it was possible to assign functions for all four glycosyltransferases. The |FRAME: G-81062| gene, which encodes a fucosyltranferase, was cloned and the activity of the purified recombinant protein was verified in vitro |CITS: [14550554]|. That enzyme received further characterization in a later study |CITS: [18078329]|., The gene cluster contains a gene (wbsI) that encodes an acetyltransferase. At the time the cluster was sequenced it was noted that WbsI is likely an O-acetyltransferase that is responsible for the acetylation of the |FRAME: CPD-24114|, though the precise location of the acetylation has not been determined at that time |CITS: [14550554]|. A 2008 publication reported that 1H NMR spectrum analysis revealed the presence of acetyl groups distributed over two positions that differed among O:128ab and O:128 ac strains, although the positions were not identified |CITS: [18237721]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the core oligosaccharide, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., The composition of the O-antigen varies among different strains, but in general it consists of repeating oligosaccharide subunits made up of three to five sugars. At least 20 different sugars are known to occur, and many of these sugars are unique dideoxyhexoses that are rarely found elsewhere in nature. The variations in sugar content of the O-antigens contribute to the wide variety of antigenic types between species and even strains of Gram-negative bacteria., Gram-positive bacteria and Archaea do not have a lipopolysaccharide. Instead they possess the S-layer (surface layer) as a component of the cell envelope |CITS: [11742749][1938891]|. The S-layer is composed of a single layer of identical proteins or glycoproteins that form a two-dimensional, monomolecular crystalline array |CITS:[7934867]|. Structurally, S-layer glycoproteins from Gram-positive bacteria resemble the O-antigens of Gram-negative organisms, and often contain similar modified sugar building blocks |CITS: [11741945]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-12575| is a widespread compound with housekeeping roles, but it also acts as a precursor for the synthesis of specific sugar residues used by some bacterial species for incorporation in polysaccharides such as the repeat unit of their O-antigen or S-layer glycoproteins., The |FRAME: G-17652| gene encodes a dehydrogenase that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE|. This is a housekeeping gene in organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD0-1099|, such as |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME:TAX-28901|, since |FRAME: CPD-14488| is a component of |FRAME: CPD0-1099|. However, |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| is also used by some Gram-negative bacteria as one of the sugars of their O-antigen |CITS: [14670712]| and by some Gram-positive bacteria for their polysaccharide capsule |CITS: [8463246]|., |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| can be converted by an epimerase to |FRAME: UDP-D-GALACTURONATE| |CITS: [13584369]|. |FRAME: CPD-12523| is also found in the O-antigens and capsule polysaccharides of some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-1162729|, |FRAME: TAX-45888| and |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [7534644][14559113][13426189]|. The epimerase is encoded by the |FRAME: G-17651| gene, which was first characterized from |FRAME: TAX-1313| |CITS: [10027985]|., In a parallel route, |FRAME: CPD-12575| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-14553| by an epimerase encoded by the |FRAME: G-4662| gene. |FRAME: ALPHA-D-GALACTOSE| is a common component of bacterial O-antigens. |FRAME: CPD-14553| is used not only for the O-antigen, but also for synthesis of essential structures such as LPS core. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THR| is an indispensable amino acid. It is degraded by a complex network of pathways and regulatory signals |CITS: [9871012]|., Two of the major routes for the degradation of L-threonine are known to occur both in mammals and in microorganisms., In the first route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREDEHYDCAT-CPLX| (EC 4.3.1.19) to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, which is rapidly and irreversibly converted to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME: FORMATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5437|). A biosynthetic version of this enzyme has also been reported in certain anaerobic bacteria (see |FRAME:ILEUSYN-PWY|) |CITS: [13405870]|., In the second route threonine is catabolized by |FRAME:THREODEHYD-CPLX| (EC 1.1.1.103) to form |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT|, which is mainly cleaved by |FRAME: AKBLIG-CPLX|, forming glycine and acetyl-CoA (see |FRAME:THREONINE-DEG2-PWY|). In the absence of the later activity |FRAME:AMINO-OXOBUT| is spontaneously converted to |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|, which is further metabolized into |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| (see |FRAME: THRDLCTCAT-PWY|)., A third route has been demonstrated in several bacteria and fungi. This route is based on the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7266| (EC 4.1.2.5), which cleaves threonine directly into |FRAME:GLY| and |FRAME:ACETALD| (see |FRAME:PWY-5436|)., About This Pathway, Enteric bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-90371| have been shown to possess two types of, threonine dehydratases - a catabolic enzyme, which is induced by threonine, and a constitutively-produced biosynthetic enzyme |CITS: [13405870]|. Both enzymes, which are PLP-dependent, dehydrate |FRAME:THR| to the enamine intermediate |FRAME: CPD-15056|. This intermediate is very unstable, and tautomerizes immediately and spontaneously to the imine form |FRAME: CPD-16013|, which is then non-enzymatically hydrolyzed to form |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| and free ammonium., While the biosynthetic enzyme is involved in |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis, the catabolic enzyme participates in the degradation of threonine to propionate, in a pathway that generates ATP, and enables the bacteria to utilize threonine as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [4370904]|., The conversion of |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| to |FRAME:PROPIONATE| was demonstrated as early as 1963 in |FRAME: TAX-1553| |CITS: [Tokushige63]|. The identity of the enzymes that cleave |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| to |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME:FORMATE| was discovered much later, in |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS: [9484901]|. Both of these enzymes, |FRAME:PYRUVFORMLY-CPLX| and |FRAME:KETOBUTFORMLY-ENZRXN|, are expressed only under anaerobic conditions, and both utilze a glycyl radical as part of their catalytic mechanism |CITS:[9767563]|. Once |FRAME:PROPIONYL-COA| is formed, it is processed via |FRAME:PROPIONYL-P| to |FRAME: PROPIONATE|, in a reaction sequence that produces ATP., The enzymes in this pathway are able to process |FRAME:SER| as well, with |FRAME:PYRUVATE| as the final product |CITS: [9871012]|.

In this manner L-aspartate is able to satisfy all the major cellular requirements for nitrogen including amino acids, nucleotides and amino sugars |CITS: [33012071]|. This pathway is the main route for nitrogen assimilation when |FRAME: TAX-562| is cultured aerobically with glycerol and L-aspartate |CITS: [33012071]|. , This pathway also functions during anaerobic growth when L-aspartate is used to provide both nitrogen for growth and fumarate for respiration |CITS: [33754467]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8294|).

Summary: |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| are major components of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage) in animals., They are both |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycan"| polymers composed of repeating disaccharide units,  each containing |FRAME: CPD-12557|  linked by a (1,3) or (1,4) linkage to a uronic acid, |FRAME: CPD-12521| or |FRAME: CPD-12515|, with extensive N and O-sulfation. Sulfation occurs to various degrees at position 2 of uronic acid and at positions 4 or 6, or both, of galactosamine. In addition, the amino group of galactosamine is acetylated, Many microorganisms have enzymes that enable them to degrade glycosaminoglycans |CITS: [7654407]|. This ability is particularly important for soil bacteria, which may depend on connective tissues in animal carcasses as a nutrient source., There are several steps in the degradation process. It starts with the cleavage of the polymer into smaller fragments, initially tetra- and hexasaccharides, but ultimately disaccharides. The process continues with the removal of the sulfate groups, and ends with the final degradation of the disaccharides into individual sugars, a step that has not been characterized yet. , The lyases that break the polymer to smaller fragments are classified based on the position of cleavage as either endo-lyases or exo-lyases. The endolytic enzyme can produce products of several sizes, although the final product tends to be disaccharides. The exo-lyases cleave dissaccharide molecules from the non-reducing end of the polymer chain |CITS: [9083041]|. Some lyases, known as chondroitinase AC, can act only on |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-A| and |FRAME: Chondroitin-Sulfate-C| (that contain |FRAME: CPD-12521|), some, known as chondroitinase B, can act only on |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| (that contains |FRAME: CPD-12515|), and some, known as condroitinase ABC, can act on both |CITS: [10618199][9083041]|., The lyases act by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexosamine linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting disacchrides. , Chondroitin ABC lyases may help in the regeneration of spinal cord injuries that were thought for a long time to be incurable. Injection of chondroitinase ABC at sites of central nervous system injury, where a glial scar develops, removes the GAG components of ECM chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and attenuates the inhibitory effects to axon growth |CITS: [11948352][11948352][11948332]|., The removal of the sulfate groups is catalyzed by specialized sulfatases that can remove the sulfate groups at either the 4 or 6 positions. The sulfatases have been purified from |FRAME: TAX-585| but the genes that encode them have not been identified |CITS: [5647268]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Camphor Camphor| is a bicyclic monoterpene with a characteristic pungent odor and taste. Two enantiomers occur naturally - |FRAME: CPD-862|, the predominant natural isomer, and |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR|. Camphor is produced by several trees, including the camphor tree (|FRAME: TAX-13429|) as well as hundreds of other plants, including |FRAME: TAX-38868| (garden sage), |FRAME: TAX-39367| (rosemary), |FRAME: TAX-39169| (lavender), |FRAME: TAX-35608| (sweet wormwood), and |FRAME: TAX-13328| |CITS: [5532413][ 32619737][35921521]|. A study of enzymes from the camphor tree found multiple terpene synthases, two that lead to production of |FRAME: CPD-862| and one that leads to production of |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| |CITS: [36696798]|., Camphor can be synthesized chemically, as an racemic mixture of the two enantiomers, from |FRAME: CPD-4892|, which is obtained from oil of turpentine. Today most camphor is synthetic. It has a wide range of uses, including as a plasticizer for modified celluloses in lacquers, varnishes, and plastics; as a moth repellente; and as a preservative in cosmetics and embalming fluids. It is also used in medicine as an ingredient in topical creams and ointments to treat itching, irritation, and joint pain. Although it is found in essential oils used in perfumery (such as those of lavender), it significantly diminishes the quality of these oils and reduces their market value. Oils that contain elevated camphor content are usually used as insect repellents and for other non-perfumery uses |CITS: [12112282]|., Even though camphor has been traditionally used in foods and medicines, it is toxic to humans and is especially dangerous to young children. Contact can lead to skin and eye irritation. Ingestion of camphor can cause irritability, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and cardiopulmonary arrest |CITS: [7773898][31223380][38022187][39096231]|. Camphorated oil was removed from the US market in the 1980s due to accidental poisonings., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-862| is one of the major components of the volatile oil of sage (|FRAME: TAX-38868|), where it appears to function as a phytotoxin inhibiting the growth of competing grasses. Immature sage leaves synthesize and accumulate camphor most rapidly, and the camphor content of the leaves increases as they expand |CITS: [16661761]|., The first proposal for a pathway for |FRAME: CPD-862| biosynthesis suggested that |FRAME: CPD-461| was converted to |FRAME: CPD-1903|, which was then dehydrogenated to camphor |CITS: [10906]|. Subsequent studies showed that a cyclic pyrophosphate intermediate was involved |CITS: [921300]| and that the preferred precursor was |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|, rather than |FRAME: CPD-461| |CITS: [42356]|, leading to the pathway described here., The first pathway enzyme to be partially purifed and characterized was |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.198|, which catalyzes the last step in the pathway |CITS: [677891]|. The enzyme was later cloned from |FRAME: TAX-1196215| |CITS: [23058847]| and from |FRAME: TAX-13429| |CITS: [33243711]|., The first enzyme discovery was followed by a partial purification of |FRAME: MONOMER-17128| |CITS: [42357]| and |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.8| |CITS: [42356]|. The latter was cloned from sage in 1998 |CITS: [9614092]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-6991|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, Even though NAD molecules are not consumed during oxidation reactions, they have a relatively short half-life. For example, in |FRAME:TAX-562| the NAD+ half-life is 90 minutes. Once enzymatically degraded, the pyrimidine moiety of the molecule can be recouped via the NAD salvage cycles. This pathway is used for two purposes: it recycles the internally degraded NAD products |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE| (also known as nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN) and |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE|, and it is used for the assimilation of exogenous NAD+., Since the NAD+ molecule is highly polar, it has to be hydrolyzed before it can be transported across the cytoplasmic membrane for final uptake. It does seem to be able to penetrate the external membrane, though, as the enzymes that break it down are found in the periplasm |CITS: [2841298]|. NAD+ is first hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.22|, into |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE| (NMN), which can be hydrolyzed further to |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| by |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.14|. Both enzymes are periplasmic. It should be noted that even though the activity of |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.14|. has been reported from a few organisms several decades ago |CITS: [4342726][457634]|, the identity of the enzyme has not been reported., Both NMN and nicotinamide can be transported across the inner membrane into the cytoplasm. Once there, |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| is converted via |FRAME: NIACINE| to |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE|, at which point the pathway merges with the de novo biosynthesis pathway, and continues to NAD via |FRAME: DEAMIDO-NAD| (deamido-NAD)., There are several flavors of the salvage pathway found in different organisms, and even within the same organism. The one described above contains 6 reaction steps, and is often referred to as the PNC VI pathway, for Pyridine Nucleotide Cycling. However, there are also a four-step cycle (|FRAME: PWY-7761|) and a five-step cycle (|FRAME: PWY3O-4107|), termed PNC IV and V, respectively |CITS: [220211][6445894]|., PNC IV is the major intracellular recycling pathway in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [7021549]|, while PNC VI is the major cycle of |FRAME:TAX-90371| |CITS: [6445894]| and yeast |CITS:[12062417][11884393]|.

Summary: General Background, The indoleamine |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is a vertebrate hormone secreted by the pineal gland. It is involved in regulation of circadian and seasonal rhythms. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| also has immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. In addition to the pineal gland it is synthesized in many vertebrate cells and tissues (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6030|). It is ubiquitously present in cells and body fluids due to its amphiphilic properties that allow it to cross membranes. Mitochondria have the highest intracellular concentration of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| |CITS: [15981996]|. Its functional groups allow both specific receptor binding and a role in oxidation chemistry. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also found in invertebrates |CITS: [12662344]|, protozoa |CITS: [12899443]|, plants |CITS: [11485009]|, fungi |CITS: [12662344]| and bacteria |CITS: [9181522]| although its function in many cases remains incompletely defined. |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is also used as a human dietary supplement. In vertebrates, endogenous or ingested |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| is catabolized several ways in different tissues (see below and pathways |FRAME: PWY-6398| and |FRAME: PWY-6400|). Reviewed in |CITS: [16219483] [18344019]|., The enzymatic pathways of |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| degradation are shown in this pathway and pathways |FRAME: PWY-6398| and |FRAME: PWY-6400|. Melatonin can also be degraded by nonenzymatic pathways involving melatonin radical species, reactive oxygen species, reactive nitrogen species, or ultraviolet B radiation. It can also be degraded by nonenzymatic reactions involving oxoferryl hemoglobin, or hemin. These nonenzymatic reactions are not shown here, but are shown in |CITS: [18344019] [18155917] [17198536] [16793870]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-5-METHOXY-TRYPTAMINE| can be degraded by by deacetylation to |FRAME: CPD-12018|, followed by oxidative deamination by monoamine oxidase A to |FRAME: CPD-12019| and subsequent dehydrogenation of this compound by an aldehyde dehydrogenase to the acid |FRAME: CPD-12020|. |FRAME: CPD-12019| may also be reduced to the alchohol |FRAME: CPD-12021| by an alcohol dehydrogenase. Bioactive derivatives of this alcohol such as its O-acetyl derivative |CITS: [7396831]|, or the β-carboline pinoline, can also be formed in some tissues (in |CITS: [18344019]|) (not shown). This pathway has been demonstrated in the non-mammalian vertebrate eye, pineal gland, brain and skin |CITS: [7530349] [1782560] [2492661] [8812361]|. It has also been shown in mammalian skin |CITS: [16217127] [15677341]|. Deacetylation is also a minor pathway in mammalian liver (in |CITS: [8436983]|). In addition, some of these metabolites have been found in protozoa, algae and yeast (in |CITS: [18344019]|).

Summary: General Background, The pentavalent organic arsenical |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE| (MMAV) is currently used as an herbicide on cotton fields or for postemergence control of crabgrass and other turf weeds in the United States |CITS: [28936873]|. |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE "Methylarsonate| has been shown to be reduced by bacteria, producing the highly toxic |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| (MMAIII) |CITS: [21272184]|., |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE "Methylarsonous acid"| is also generated in vivo by methylation of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, which is carried out by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.137| (see |FRAME: PWY-8266|). The enzyme, which is named ArsM in prokaryotic and eukaryotic microbes and AS3MT in animals, can catalyze one to three methylations of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and its initial product is |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| |CITS: [16102566]|., It has been proposed that organisms produced |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| as a primitive antibiotic before the atmosphere became oxidizing. In today's oxidizing atmosphere the compound is oxidized spontaneously to the relatively nontoxic |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE|. However, even today some soil organisms have been shown to reduce |FRAME: METHYLARSONATE| back to |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, continually regenerating the toxic species |CITS: [21272184]|., Organisms have developed several ways to cope with the toxicity of |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, including its export, oxidation, and cleavage of the carbon-arsenic bond., About This Pathway, The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-197| possesses the |FRAME: G-80528| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-21008 "trivalent organoarsenicals efflux protein"|. The gene was originally shown to confer resistance to cells exposed to |FRAME: CPD-22651|, bit was later shown to transport only the trivalent forms of several organoarsenicals, including |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE|, |FRAME: CPD-22656|, |FRAME: CPD-24364|, |FRAME: CPD-24366|, and |FRAME: CPD1G01-9|. It cannot transport pentavalent forms |CITS: [26234817]|., ArsP is unrelated to other ars operon permeases and is the smallest, with only 315 residues. It is predicted to have only 8 transmembrane segments, compared with 10 in Acr3 and 12 in ArsB transporters. A vicinal cysteine pair, Cys65 and Cys67, is present in a highly conserved motif (TPFCSCSXXP) in the middle of predicted TM2 and is predicted to participate in the transport reaction |CITS: [26234817]|.

General Background, |FRAME: LIPOIC-ACID "Lipoate"| is an organosulfur compound that contains a ditholane ring, which is a cyclic disulfide., Lipoate is used as an essential cofactor by many enzyme systems involved in oxidative metabolism, including |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.105| |CITS: [814874][6794598][8444795]|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25| |CITS: [2188967]|, and |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.27| |CITS: [1655709][8444795]|., Each of these enzyme complexes is composed of multiple copies of three enzymes: a substrate-specific, decarboxylase-dehydrogenase (E1), a dihydrolipoamide acyltransferase (E2), specific for each type of complex, and a dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (E3). , The (E2) proteins have a dedicated lipoyl domain. In order for the complex to be active, lipoate must be attached to the lipoyl domain by an amide linkage between its carboxylate moiety and a specific lysine residue in the enzyme |CITS: [8444795]|., E1 catalyzes a reaction in which the substrate is attached to the lipoate cofactor and decarboxylated. During this reaction, the lipoate cofactor is reduced to dihydriolipoate., E2 then catalyzes an acyl transfer step, in which the product of the reaction is released. Finally, E3 catalyzes the oxidation of the dihydrolipoyl cofactor back to lipoyl form, with NAD being the ultimate electron acceptor |CITS: [2188967]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of lipoate is unusual, and shares the same mechanism as the biosynthesis of biotin., The precursor |FRAME: CPD-195| molecule is first attached to a specific |FRAME: LYS| residue within the lipoyl domain, and is then converted to lipoate., The first enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME:EG11591-MONOMER|, transfers the octanoate moiety from, |FRAME: Octanoyl-ACPs "octanoate-[acp]"| molecule to a specific lysyl residue in lipoate-dependent enzymes, resulting in |FRAME: Octanoylated-domains|, and regenerating the acyl-carrier protein in the process |CITS: [8002607], [14700636]|. |FRAME:EG11591-MONOMER|-mediated attachment of octanoate to the apo-domain probably does, not occur unless the octanoate is bound to an acyl-carrier protein. , The next enzyme in the pathway, |FRAME:CPLX0-782|, catalyzes the conversion of the octanoyl side chain to an active lipoyl, generating a fully active lipoylated domain., The enzyme is an iron-sulfur protein that requires S-adenosyl-L-methionine (AdoMet) |CITS: [8444795][11106496]|., An electron which originates from the [4Fe-4S] cluster of the enzyme serves to split at least two, molecules of AdoMet into a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical and methionine |CITS: [11834738]|., The radical then abstracts a hydrogen from a C-H bond of thew octanoyl side chain, becoming, 5'-adenosine in the process. , The newly-formed unstable octanoyl radical then reacts directly with the Fe-S center of the enzyme., Two sulfur atoms from the center enter the structure of the octanoyl side chain, producing lipoyl, which, dissociates from the enzyme along with excess iron, leaving it with a [2Fe-2S] center., Thus, in this unusual reaction, the iron-sulfur center of the enzyme is not just a catalytic accelerator, but, also a substrate, donating the two sulfur atoms |CITS: [11153271]|. , It should be noted that although this process has been well documented in vitro |CITS: [11106496]|,, there is still a possibility that there exists another sulfur donor in vivo, and that the Fe-S center, acts as sulfur donor only in the absence of this natural donor |CITS: [11395404]|., It has been suggested that the conversion of octanoylated-domains to lipoylated ones described, in this pathway may be a type of a repair pathway, activated only if the other lipoate, biosynthetic pathways are malfunctioning |CITS: [14700636]|., Other routes for lipoate incorporation involve the lipoyl-protein ligase LplA, which utilizes either lipoate, or octanoate imported from outside the cell (see |FRAME: PWY0-522| and Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Lignins "Lignin"| is the most abundant aromatic compound in nature, and its mineralization is an important step in the terrestrial, carbon cycle. Lignin is broken down to various biaryl and monoaryl compounds such as |FRAME: BIPHENYL|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|., Complex lignin is resistant to bacterial enzymes. Its degradation is initiated by white rot fungi, which secrete extracellular degradation enzymes such as |FRAME: MONOMER-14338 "lignin peroxidase"|, |FRAME: MONOMER-14335 "manganese peroxidase"|, and |FRAME: MONOMER-14334 "laccase"| |CITS: [8246842]|. The resulting low-molecular-weight lignin can be further degraded and mineralized by bacteria |CITS: [1785937]|., |FRAME: TAX-502559| is able to grow on many of these compounds as the sole sources of carbon and energy. It degrades lignin-derived compounds possessing guaiacyl (4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl) and syringyl (4-hydroxy-3,5-dimethoxyphenyl) moieties to |FRAME: VANILLATE| and |FRAME: CPD-8486|, respectively, and is able to completely mineralize these two compounds as described in the |FRAME: PWY-6338| and |FRAME: PWY-6339| pathways., About This Pathway, |FRAME: VANILLIN "Vanillin"| and |FRAME: VANILLATE| are important intermediate metabolites of lignin-derived aromatic compounds., |FRAME: TAX-502559| converts |FRAME: VANILLIN| to |FRAME: VANILLATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.67| (encoded by |FRAME: G-11556|) |CITS: [17928721]|., |FRAME: VANILLATE "Vanillate"| is converted in |FRAME: TAX-502559| to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| by the tetrahydrofolate-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.341|, encoded by |FRAME: G-11548| |CITS: [9501423]|., The methyl-carrier |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"|, which is formed by this reaction, can transfer the methyl group to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is used for |FRAME: MET| biosynthesis, or to other folates, in which case it can be used for guanosine nucleotide biosynthesis via |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| and |FRAME: IMP| |CITS: [27634497]|., |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE "Protocatechuate"| is degraded by this organism into central metabolism intermediates using the meta cleavage pathway, as described in |FRAME: P184-PWY| |CITS: [4143957]|.
