Summary: The metabolic versatility of |FRAME:TAX-286| strains is well illustrated by the catabolism of, |FRAME: ARG|. |FRAME: TAX-287| has at least 4 different pathways for this purpose, including, the arginine deiminase pathway (|FRAME:ARGDEGRAD-PWY|), the arginine succinyltransferase, pathway (|FRAME:AST-PWY|), the arginine decarboxylase pathway (|FRAME:ARGDEG-III-PWY|), and the arginine:pyruvate transaminase pathway (this pathway), It should be noted that |FRAME: TAX-303| has a slightly modified version of this , pathway, in which the first reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-11561|, (|FRAME: ARGDEG-IV-PWY|) |CITS: [5570437][237915]|., This |FRAME: TAX-287| pathway was thought to consist of a different starting reactions. Prior to the, discovery of the |FRAME: CPLX-7541| it was believed that the pathway started with the conversion, of |FRAME: ARG| to |FRAME: CPD-220|, performed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-6900|, followed by, the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-220| to |FRAME: CPD-824| by |FRAME: RXN-7563|., However, a more recent study discovered the genes encoding both a |FRAME: CPLX-7541| and a, |FRAME: MONOMER-13584|, leading to a proposal to modify the pathway |CITS: [17416670]|., The rest of the pathway is identical to the |FRAME: TAX-303| arginine-oxidase based pathway, (|FRAME: ARGDEG-IV-PWY|):  |FRAME: CPD-824| is further degraded into |FRAME: CPD-825|,, |FRAME: CPD-592|, and |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| by the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-11559|,, |FRAME: MONOMER-11560|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6898|, respectively |CITS: [6423769][237915]|., The pathway is very similar to the |FRAME: ARG| degradation pathway of |FRAME: TAX-1911|, (see |FRAME: ARGDEG-V-PWY|) |CITS: [5570437]|.

Antimony (Sb, Latin name stibium) is a silvery, lustrous gray metalloid that occurs in the Earth's crust at 0.2 parts per million. It is found in two oxidation states: Sb(III) and Sb(V). The predominant ore mineral is stibnite (Sb<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>). , During commercial processing of Sb the sulfide ore is often converted by roasting to an Sb(III) oxide, Sb<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, which is volatile. The oxide is recovered by evaporation, and Sb is isolated from the oxide by a carbothermal reduction. Approximately 48% of produced Sb is used for flame retardants, 33% for lead-acid batteries, and 8% for plastics. Elevated environmental levels of Sb have been reported at industrial sites for processing Sb-containing products |CITS: [Meharg95]| and at antimony, arsenic and lead mine sites |CITS: [Duller97][Hamilton00]|., Antimony and many of its compounds (particularly antimony trioxide) are toxic, and the effects of Sb poisoning are similar to arsenic poisoning (though antimony is less toxic than arsenic). Human exposure to low levels of Sb through ingestion and inhalation has caused severe health effects. Methylation converts inorganic Sb into volatile methylated Sb, influencing the environmental mobility, toxicity and bioaccumulation of the element. Methylated Sb species have been found in various environments |CITS: [Andreae81][Andreae84][Dodd96][Craig99]|, suggesting that the methylation of Sb is a relatively common occurrence, and there have been numerous reports of biological Sb methylation |CITS: [Gurleyuk98][Jenkins98][Andrewes99][Andrewes99b][Craig99b][Andrewes01][11999616][12209260][16307070]|. , A study with the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-103690| has shown that the enzyme responsible for Sb methylation is |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.137| (ArsM). Both arsenic and antimony belong to the pnictogen group in the periodic table. Like arsenic, Sb(III) reacts spontaneously with thiols such as glutathione to form a triglutathione compound. This compound binds to the ArsM enzyme, during which the three glutathione moieties are replaced by the thiols of three L-cysteine residues. The electrophilic methyl group of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| is transferred to Sb(III), forming intermediate methylantimony(IV), which is then reduced to methylantimony(III) with electrons supplied by thioredoxin. The process repeats, forming dimethylated and trimethylated forms. The observed ratio of |FRAME: CPD-27737|/|FRAME: CPD-27738|/|FRAME: CPD-27728| was 6/90/4, and the second methylation step appeared to be the rate-limiting step |CITS: [38180751]|.

Summary: Since the first report of the structure of |FRAME: TAX-210| LPS, which was purified from |FRAME: TAX-102618 "strain NCTC 11637"| |CITS: [8652593]|, numerous genetic, biochemical, and structural studies have been conducted to elucidate the LPS biosynthetic pathway and to further characterize the structure of the LPS of this bacterium., The genes known to be involved in LPS biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-210| are scattered over the whole genome, unlike the case for most other Gram-negative bacteria, making it more difficult to study the pathway in this organism., Attempts to produce knockout mutants of the |FRAME: HP_RS01375| gene (encoding heptosyltransferase I) were unsuccessful, suggesting that the minimal LPS structure in |FRAME: TAX-210| might require at least one heptose in addition to lipid A and Kdo. This is in contrast to |FRAME: TAX-562|, where the minimal LPS structure only requires the lipid A and the Kdo domains for viability |CITS: [12045108]|., While most of |FRAME: TAX-210| enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of lipid A and O-antigen have been identified and characterized, the enzymes responsible for the biosynthesis of the core region of LPS remain to be identified., Despite earlier work, which suggested a branched structure, it is now documented that the LPS core region of |FRAME: TAX-85962| is linear |CITS: [21903201]|. A 2017 study reported that the |FRAME: TAX-210| core-oligosaccharide domain is a short conserved hexasaccharide (Glc-Gal-D,D-Hep-LD-Hep-LD-Hep-KDO) decorated with the |FRAME: CPD2DNV-41 "O-antigen domain"| encompassing a conserved trisaccharide (-D,D-Hep-Fuc-GlcNAc-) and variable glucan, heptan and Lewis antigens |CITS: [28306723]|.

General Background, |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| are dinucleotides containing one |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| base and one |FRAME: ADENINE| base. Each nucleotide is connected to a ribose sugar at position 1, and the two riboses are connected at their 5 position via a diphosphate. The only difference between the two is that in NADP there is an additional phosphate group at the 2' position of the ribose that carries the adenine moiety., These molecules are biological carriers of reductive equivalents (i.e. high potential electrons). Most of the time they function as cosubstrates, and in some cases they function as |FRAME: Cofactors cofactors|. They are often referred to by the obsolete term "coenzymes"., The most common function of |FRAME: NAD| is to accept two electrons and a proton (a hydride ion) from a substrate that is being oxidized. This reduction converts |FRAME: NAD| to |FRAME: NADH|, the reduced form. NADH then diffuses or is transported to a terminal oxidase, where the electrons are passed on, regenerating the oxidized form., |FRAME: NADPH|, on the other hand, is mostly involved in biosynthetic reactions, where it serves as an electron donor. NADPH is formed by reduction of |FRAME: NADP|, which occurs by different mechanisms in different types of organisms. In photosynthetic organisms |FRAME: NADP| is reduced by |FRAME: CPLX-84|. In heterotrophic organisms it is reduced by central metabolism processes such as the pentose phosphate pathway (see |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY|)., About This Pathway, Cells have dedicated pathway for production of NAD. The conversion of NAD to NADP is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.23|, one of the key enzymes regulating the balance of NAD(H) and NADP(H)., NAD kinase was discovered in 1950 by Arthur Kornberg, who partially purified it from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [Kornberg50a]|. It was later found in organisms from all kingdoms, from bacteria to mammals. The gene encoding the enzyme was identified in 2000., All characterized NAD kinases show homomultimer (homodimer, homotetramer, homohexamer, or homooctamer) structures. However, they have been divided into three classes based on the following criteria: NAD kinases from Gram-positive bacteria and archaea phosphorylate both NAD+ and NADH and can utilize both ATP and polyphosphate as the phosphoryl donor |CITS: [Murata80][11006082]|; NAD kinases from eukaryotes can also phosphorylate both NAD+ and NADH, but utilize only ATP; NAD kinases from Gram-negative bacteria phosphorylate only NAD+ and can use only ATP |CITS: [18391451]|. Another enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.86|, is specific to NADH and has only been found in fungi and plants |CITS: [4335000][12912900]|., In organisms that contain a single gene encoding the enzyme, a mutation is lethal. However, some organisms, such as the plant |FRAME: ORG-5993| and the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|, possess multiple genes that encode different isozymes |CITS: [15247403][15978040]|., Structure-function relationships in NAD kinases from archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes have been reviewed |CITS: [16842123] [18391451] [19430699]|.

The phenylcoumaran linkage accounts for 3-10 % of the total intermonomer linkages in lignin |CITS: [16332110]|, and the phenylcoumaran-type dimer, |FRAME: CPD-17075| (DCA) is one of the major dilignols generated in lignifying xylem |CITS: [20554692]|., A bacterial catabolic pathway of DCA was proposed in |FRAME: TAX-13689| TMY1009 |CITS: [Habu88]|. Several mutant strains were created and shown to accumulated several compounds including |FRAME: CPD-17077| (DCA-C), |FRAME: CPD-17080| (DCA-S), |FRAME: CPD-17081|, |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID|, and |FRAME: VANILLATE|. Based on these observations, the first step in the pathway was proposed to be the oxidation of the alcohol group at the γ-carbon of the B-ring side chain of DCA into the carboxyl group., Several lignostilbene α,β-dioxygenase isozymes from |FRAME: TAX-13689| were reported to be involved in the lytic oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-17080 DCA-S| to |FRAME: CPD-17081| and |FRAME: VANILLIN| |CITS: [7763880][9339561]|., The pathway was further studied in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-627192|, which is capable of degrading various lignin-derived biaryls including β-aryl ethers, biphenyls, diarylpropanes, and phenylcoumarans, as well as monoaryls such as |FRAME: CPD-17106|, |FRAME: VANILLIN|, and |FRAME: FERULIC-ACID| as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: [24916011]|., Intermediate metabolites generated during the incubation of DCA with cell extracts of SYK-6 were identified by HPLC and negative ESI-MS analysis, and afforded a proposal for the full pathway, as depicted here., Candidate genes encoding the first two steps of the pathway were cloned and expressed in recombinant hosts. The first step is the oxidation of the alcohol group of the B-ring side chain to an aldehyde, and the second step is the further oxidation of the aldehyde group into a carboxylate. It was shown that both steps can be catalyzed by multiple enzymes. In this MetaCyc pathway only the enzymes with the highest activity are shown |CITS: [24916011]|. The next step was shown to be catalyzed by a pair of enantioselective quinone-dependent enzymes. The two enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-44490| and |FRAME: G-44489| genes, oxidize the alcohol group of the A-ring side chain to a carboxyl group, and transfer the electrons to the electron transfer chain. They are strictly specific for |FRAME: CPD-18963| and |FRAME: CPD-17077|, respectively |CITS: [26362985]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, and |FRAME: CPD-10335|). Non-oxygenic bacteria possess a related pigment called bacteriochlorophyll, which also exists in several variants (|FRAME:CPD-9067|, |FRAME:CPD-9091|,, |FRAME:CPD-9092|, |FRAME:CPD-9093|, |FRAME:CPD-9094| and |FRAME:CPD-9095|). This pathway describes the formation of |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|, an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of all chlorophylls., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| is discussed in detail in the pathway |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN|. The only difference between that pathway and the one described here is the very last step, the reduction of |FRAME: MONO-VINYL-PROTOCHLOROPHYLLIDE-A| to form |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|. , While in |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN| this step is catalyzed by the light-dependent enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.33|, in this pathway it is catalyzed by the light-independent |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.7|. The enzyme is commonly known as DPOR, for "dark protochlorophyllide reductase"., The two pathways are not mutually exclusive. The light-independent pathway, which occurs in most aerobic photosynthetic organisms with the exception of angiosperms |CITS: [14743862]|, exists alongside the |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-SYN "light-dependent chlorophyllide a biosynthetic pathway"| in the majority of those species. Many of the steps of this pathway have been described through genetic analysis of bacterial, photosynthetic algae, and non-angiosperm land plant mutants and in vitro reconstitution of individual reactions (reviewed in |CITS:[9442890][12242396][beale99][14617630][14743862]|)., Anaerobic phototrophic bacteria possess a very similar pathway. However, the cyclase found in these organisms does not require molecular oxygen. A variant of the pathway found in anaerobic bacteria is described in |FRAME:PWY-5531|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE "Androst-4-ene-3,17-dione"| (androstenedione) is a key intermediate of microbial steroid metabolism. It is a naturally occurring steroid hormone produced in the gonad or ovary, and an immediate precursor of |FRAME: TESTOSTERONE| in males and |FRAME: CPD-352| and |FRAME: ESTRONE| in females |CITS: [18329874]|. , The compound was first isolated in 1931 from a male policeman's urine and named androsterone (andro = male, ster = sterol, one = ketone) |CITS: [Butenandt34]|. The chemical structure of androsterone was reported soon after |CITS: [Ruzicka34]|., An aerobic pathway for the degradation of |FRAME: ANDROST4ENE| was proposed already in 1968 based on analysis of the compounds produced in culture of testosterone-grown |FRAME: TAX-285| |CITS: [Coulter68]|. That pathway is described in |FRAME: PWY-6944|., The study of anaerobic steroids degradation proceeded much later, and as of 2020 many of the enzymes involved have not been characterized. However, significant work was conducted with the testosterone-degrading γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-465721| and the cholesterol-degrading β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-157592|, leading to the elucidation of the pathway shown here., About This Pathway, The Gram-negative β-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-157592|, which is capable of using either nitrate or oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor, was reported to mineralize cholesterol to carbon dioxide under anoxic conditions |CITS: [9094222][12892131]|. Several studies have uncovered most of the steps of the pathway, which employs a composite repertoire of more than 40 genes, some known from the aerobic degradation pathway and some unique genes that are required to circumvent oxygenase-dependent reactions., Steroids degradation pathways involve two main processes - the elimination of the side-chain, and the opening of the steroid rings. In the anaerobic pathway side chain degradation depends on aldolytic C-C bond cleavages that involve specific acyl-CoA synthetases/dehydrogenases and promiscuous enoyl-CoA hydratases, aldolases and aldehyde dehydrogenases |CITS: [28940833][29374035]|., Degradation of the A and B rings of the sterol core is different between the aerobic and anaerobic pathways, and depends on unique enzymes found only in anaerobic steroid degraders. Following the hydrolytic cleavage of the A ring, the process again involves CoA-ester intermediates. However, the degradation of the remaining C and D rings is highly similar in aerobic and anaerobic bacteria |CITS: [28940833]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Linalools Linalool| (3,7-dimethyl-1,6-octadien-3-ol), also spelt linalool) is an acyclic monoterpene alcohol with a pleasant fragrance associated with a diverse array of plants |CITS: [7522061][RAGUSO]|. It is found in lavender, bergamot, jasmine, basil, rosemary, sage, star-anise, cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, coriander, cardamom, ginger, black pepper and mandarin, and is one of the three terpene compounds principally responsible for Muscat aroma., Linalool is a primary compound in floral scent research. Both enantiomeric forms, |FRAME: CPD-8996| and |FRAME: CPD-8997|, occur in nature., Linalool is involved as an attractant in plant interactions with pollinators, herbivores and parasitoids |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. It has also been shown to be induced by artificial wounding and by jasmonic acid |CITS: [17440821]|. The de novo synthesis of linalool has been demonstrated in floral tissues |CITS: [17440821]|, barks and roots |CITS: [RAGUSO]|. Junipers, dicots and monocots emit linalool along with other monoterpenoids |CITS: [RAGUSO]|., Even though fungi typically do not produce monoterpenes, the de novo synthesis of linalool was demonstrate in some fungi, including the wine yeast strain, Saccharomyces cerevisiae M522, in the absence of grape derived precursors |CITS: [15668008]|., Recently, it has been demonstrated that linalool is a potent precursor for an advanced biofuel. It can be chemically converted to 1-methyl-cyclopent-2-enol and isobutylene. Dehydration of the alcohol gives rise to methylcyclopentadiene dimers which can be converted into a high density fuel |CITS: [21488169]|., About this Pathway, This pathway naturally occurs in the plant |FRAME: TAX-36903|, which produces a variety of terpenoids, with |FRAME: CPD-8997| being a predominant one., |FRAME: CPLX-8656 "GPP synthase"| (GPPS) catalyzes the synthesis of the C10 monoterpene geranyl diphosphate (GPP) from the C5 compounds isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate |CITS: [11848932]|. A cDNA encoding the small subunit of the enzyme was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-36903| and shown to have 45% amino acid sequence identity to the |FRAME: TAX-34256| GPPS small subunit (GPPS.SSU) |CITS: [15031409]|. When the |FRAME: TAX-36903| small subunit was coexpressed with the large subunit of GPPS from |FRAME: TAX-34256|, it demonstrated geranyl diphosphate synthase activity in vitro |CITS: [15031409]|. The gene encoding the large subunit of the enzyme has not yet been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-36903|., |FRAME: CPD-8997| is produced in a single step from geranylpyrophosphate (GPP) by the monomeric enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.25| (LIS) |CITS: [7864636]|. LIS activity is detected only in floral tissues of the plant., The pathway was engineered in |FRAME: TAX-4932| to promote the production of |FRAME: CPD-8997| for commercial purposes. The HMG genes were mutated in |FRAME: TAX-4932| to increase flux through the |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"|, giving rise to a higher yield of the precursor |FRAME: GERANYL-PP|. The |FRAME: TAX-36903| Lis gene was simultaneously introduced to produce |FRAME: MONOMER-13464| which led to enhanced synthesis of |FRAME: CPD-8997| in yeast |CITS: [20675444]|.

Summary: The ability to degrade aromatic compounds, such as |FRAME: BENZOATE|, either aerobically or anaerobically, is common among microorgnisms., Aerobic |FRAME: BENZOATE| degradation takes different paths in different organisms. While some microorganisms degrade |FRAME: BENZOATE| via |FRAME:BENZOYLCOA| |CITS:[8335640][11222587][11306574][12399500]|, similarly to the first step in anaerobic |FRAME: BENZOATE| degradation (see |FRAME:PWY-283|), other organisms, such as some strains of |FRAME: TAX-303|, degrade |FRAME: BENZOATE| via |FRAME: CATECHOL| |CITS: [4418209]|., The exact pathway from |FRAME: BENZOATE| to |FRAME: CATECHOL| was discovered in 1971 by Reiner, who showed that in |FRAME: TAX-106590| |FRAME: BENZOATE| is first converted to |FRAME: CPD-290| by a dioxygenase |CITS:[4326771][4399343]|. |FRAME: CPD-290| is then reduced to |FRAME: CATECHOL| by a dehydrogenase, which he managed to purify |CITS: [4341530]|., In |FRAME: TAX-106590| the genes encoding the enzymes for benzoate degradation are chromosomal. In many strains these genes are carried on plasmids, which also encode the genes for toluene and xylene degradation, such has the TOL plasmid pWW0 of |FRAME: TAX-303|. The genes of the "upper pathway", which converts toluene and xylene to their carboxylic acid derivatives (see |FRAME:TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY|), are encoded by one operon, while the genes encoding the "lower pathway", converting the (substituted) benzoic acids to TCA cycle intermediates, are encoded by a second operon., Some Pseudomonmas strains have integrated the plasmid-born genes in their chromosomes, where they have acquired little mutation. For example, |FRAME: ORG-5960| and |FRAME: ORG-5973| have been shown to express similar but chromosomally-encoded enzymes that catalyze the same pathways |CITS: [8357257][8245826][9555884]|.

Summary: General Background, Tetrahydrofolate (vitamin B9) and its derivatives, commonly termed folates, are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis., Folates also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine, play a role in histidine catabolism |CITS: [11001804]|, and in plants are also involved in photorespiration, amino acid metabolism and chloroplastic protein biosynthesis |CITS: [11960743]| |CITS: [12644692]|., Folates are abundant in green leaves, and folic acid was initially isolated from a large amount (four tons) of spinach leaves. The name folate is derived from the Latin folium (leaf) |CITS: [3067148]|., Folates are modified by the addition of glutamate moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail. The polyglutamylated forms are usually preferred by the enzymes that use folates since the turnover rate of those compounds is markedly increased |CITS: [9190084][SCOTT00][KIRK94]|. In addition, in eukaryotic cells the glutamylated forms of folate facilitate the retention of the vitamin within the cell and its subcellular compartments |CITS: [1916088]|., |FRAME: THF| (H4PteGlu1) is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. Members of the family differ in the oxidation state of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions (see |FRAME: PWY-2201|), and the number of conjugated glutamate residues (see |FRAME: PWY-2161|)., About This Pathway, While plants and many microorganisms can synthesize folate coenzymes by the de novo synthesis pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6612|), many of them are also capable of salvaging folate from different varieties, such as the 5,10-methenyl form, or the 5- or 10-formyl forms. This pathway describes the conversion of pre-existing |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate"| and |FRAME:FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| to |FRAME: THF-GLU-N "tetrahydrofolate"|., As vertebrates are not able to synthesize folate in vivo, they are absolutely dependent on nutritional sources, making folate a vitamin. Food folates exist mainly as the polyglutamylated forms |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"| and |FRAME:FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (formyl-H4PteGlun) |CITS: [405403]|. The polyglutamyl folates are first hydrolyzed to monoglutamate forms by |FRAME: HS06361-MONOMER|, and subsequently metabolized into |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF|. More about that process is found at the pathway |FRAME: PWY-2161B|., Insufficient supply of the vitamin in vertebrates leads to anemia in adults, and has been shown to cause neural tube malformation in human embryos |CITS: [11744531]|. In addition, folate defficiency has been linked to a number of other birth defects, several types of cancer, dementia, affective disorders, Down's syndrom, and serious conditions affecting pregnancy outcome (for a review, see |CITS: [11001804]|).

Mycothiol (MSH) is the major low-molecular weight thiol in mycobacteria and some other Actinomycetales, (see the pathway |FRAME: PWY1G-0| for more information)., Mycothiol mirrors glutathione (GSH) in its redox biochemistry. When it is oxidized by peroxide, it forms, a disulfide, known as mycothione (MSSM). In order to maintain a reducing intracellular environment, and, to keep the pool of mycothiol in its active form, the disulfide, needs to be converted back to the reduced form of MSH. This is performed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-5741|,, encoded by the mtr gene |CITS: [Patel98]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Organophosphonates| are organic compounds containing C-PO(OH)2 or C-PO(OR)2 groups (where R can be either an alkyl or an aryl group). Phosphonates are quite common among different organisms, including both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. They occur primarily as components of phosphonolipids (|FRAME: CPD-1106| is a common phosphonate constituent of phospholipids, analogous to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-ETHANOLAMINE|). In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics., Many bacterial species can utilize organophosphonates as the sole source of phosphorous |CITS: [16245012]|. Breaking the C-P bond, which is much more stable than the C-O-P phosphoester bonds of phosphates, requires special enzymes |CITS: [7765831]|., The utilization of |FRAME: CPD0-1068|, the most common organophosphonate, has been studied in detail and several different pathways have been described., About This Pathway, The pathway begins with a nucleophilic attack of |FRAME: CPD0-1068| on the anomeric carbon of ATP to form adenine and |FRAME: CPD0-2479|, a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.37|, an enzyme complex composed of four polypeptides encoded by the |FRAME: EG10716|, |FRAME: EG10717|, |FRAME: EG10718| and |FRAME: EG10721| genes., The pathway continues by phosphohydrolysis of pyrophosphate (catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.6.1.63|) to form |FRAME: CPD0-2480|, the substrate of the enzyme that actually cleaves the C-P bond. The cleavage, performed by |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1| in a SAM-requiring radical-based reaction, produces |FRAME: CPD0-2463| and |FRAME: CH4| |CITS: [22089136]|. The obesrvation of methane production by C-P lyase has explained why vast sections of the aerobic ocean are supersaturated with methane |CITS: [Karl08][22936780]|., In most organophosphonate-degrading organisms the cyclic phosphate bond is cleaved by the |FRAME: EG10725|-encoded |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.55| to form |FRAME: RIBOSE-15-BISPHOSPHATE|, as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1533| |CITS: [19366688]|. However, in a few organisms, including the highly virulent and multi-drug resistant, human gut pathogen |FRAME: TAX-272563|, a different enzyme (encoded by the |FRAME: G-17809| gene) catalyzes two successive phosphohydrolase reactions to produce |FRAME: CPD-15317| |CITS: [24147537]|.

Names: indole-3-acetate degradation II // indole-3-acetic acid degradation II
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN "Indole-3-acetate"| (IAA) is the main auxin hormone in plants, controlling many important physiological processes including cell enlargement and division, tissue differentiation, and responses to light and gravity. Many bacterial species have evolved the ability to produce IAA, and can thus interfere with any of these processes by input of IAA into the plant, directing its physiological responses in a way advantagious to the bacteria. While some IAA-producing bacteria are considered pathogens (e.g. |FRAME:TAX-358|), others, such as |FRAME:TAX-375|, have a beneficial effect |CITS: [KANESHIRO83]|., In addition to IAA synthesis, some bacterial species are able to catabolize IAA. This phenomenon was recognized as early as 1958, and over the years many isolates were reported to have this capability |CITS: [13541474][tsubokura61][Libbert69][5370530][Mino70] [1856182][7592320][15870323]|., About This Pathway, Several strains of |FRAME: TAX-375| were shown to catabolize IAA to |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| in the presence of oxygen, and a degradation pathway has been proposed |CITS: [1856182][7592320]|. Initial research speculated that the indole ring is broken at the beginning of the pathway by an enzyme similar to |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.11|, generating o-formaminobenzoylacetate |CITS: [tsubokura61][1856182]|. However, later work by Jensen et al |CITS: [7592320]| ruled out that option, and supported the pathway described above. While some of the intermediates of this pathway have been identified by several methods, including MS-mass spectroscopy, UV spectroscopy, and high-performance liquid chromatography-MS |CITS: [7592320][Olesen96]|, only a few of the enzymes have been characterized, and none of the corresponding genes are known |CITS: [Olesen96]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Quinomycins "Quinomycin-type antibiotics"| are C2-symmetric cyclic depsipeptides with a pair of intercalative chromophores that show potent antibacterial, anticancer and antiviral activities. These antibiotics have potent DNA binding affinities at a level between nM and mM with different sequence selectivities. Reflecting these distinct affinities, quinomycin antibiotics show different inhibitory activities against various enzymes, such as DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, reverse transcriptase and topoisomerase |CITS: [16408310]|., |FRAME: CPD-18530 "Echinomycin"| was first isolated from fermentation cultures of |FRAME: TAX-67293| |CITS: [Corbaz57]|, and later isolated again and characterized from several other Streptomyces strains |CITS: [Bhatia63][6696407][3817656][19194935]|. It has significant activity against Gram positive bacteria |CITS: [14040383]| as well as antitumor properties |CITS: [Katagiri61][14282372]|. Four phase I clinical trial were initiated with |FRAME: CPD-18530|, but were hampered by significant toxic effects involving the gastrointestinal tract |CITS: [3910610]|., |FRAME: CPD-18541 "Triostin A"| was originally isolated in 1961 |CITS: [14037700]|. It also has antitumor properties and was found to bind to nucleic acid purine base derivatives in a stereospecific and sequence-specific manner |CITS: [697806][6386526][3271447][11097063]|. |FRAME: CPD-18541 "Triostin A"| is very similar to |FRAME: CPD-18530|, differing only in the nature of the linkage between two N-methylcysteine residues. While |FRAME: CPD-18541| has a simple disulfide bridge, the linkage in |FRAME: CPD-18530| contains a thioacetal bond. It has been shown that |FRAME: CPD-18541| is the direct precursor of |FRAME: CPD-18530| |CITS: [6662807][16799553]|. , About This Pathway, The pathway could be roughly divided into the assembly of the |FRAME: CPD-18534| chromophore (described in |FRAME: PWY-7734|) and the assembly of the peptide backbone, which is carried out by non-ribosomal peptide synthases (NRPS). Early experiments have shown that all amino acid constituents of the echinomycin peptide backbone (|FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, |FRAME: CYS| and |FRAME: VAL|), as well as |FRAME: TRP|, are actively incorporated into echinomycin |CITS: [6488099]|. It was later shown that the |FRAME: CPD-18534| chromophore is activated by adelylation prior to its loading to the NRPS |CITS: [2354149]|. Several of the proteins involved were isolated and partially sequenced, and the partial amino acid sequence was used to identify the genes encoding them |CITS: [15569690]|. Eventually the full |FRAME: CPD-18530| biosynthetic gene cluster was isolated from the |FRAME: TAX-324833| linear plasmid and sequenced. Sequence analysis revealed the presence of eight genes involved in |FRAME: CPD-18534| biosynthesis, five gene involved in the peptide backbone formation and modification, and a single gene conferring resistance |CITS: [16799553]|., The pathway leading to synthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-18534| chromophore is described in |FRAME: PWY-7734|. Next, the chromophore is activated by its adenylation. Since the echinomycin biosynthetic cluster lacks an aryl-carrier protein, which would normally be required for loading the chromophore to the non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) modules, this function is provided by |FRAME: MONOMER-19598 FabC|, the acyl-carrier protein that normally participates in fatty acid biosynthesis |CITS: [15569690]|. Once loaded with the chromophore, the ACP transfers it to a D-serine residue that is already bound to the |FRAME: MONOMER-19597| |CITS: [15569690]|. TrsJ adds an |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| residue and transfers the product to |FRAME: MONOMER-19599|. This large protein (originally described as two separate proteins in |CITS: [15569690]|) adds an |FRAME: CYS| and an |FRAME: VAL| residues, N-methylates both residues, and catalyzes the ligation of the carboxylate end of one tetrapeptide product with the hydroxyl group of the serine residue of a second tetrapeptide, forming a large linear octapeptide chain. The cycloesterase activity of the thioesterase domain catalyzes the formation of a bond between the C-terminal carboxylate and the other serine residue, forming the cyclic octapeptide core structure |CITS: [16799553][18721753]|., A |FRAME: MONOMER-19600| encoded by the |FRAME: G-44302| gene catalyzes the formation of a disulfide bridge between the two |FRAME: CYS| residues, forming |FRAME: CPD-18541| |CITS: [16799553][23856054]|., The last reaction in the pathway, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44305| gene product, is the conversion of the disulfide bond into a thioacetal group, forming |FRAME: CPD-18530| |CITS: [24302672]|.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, This pathway covers the anaerobic oxidation of |FRAME: Me-CoM| to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|. It should be noted that most of the enzymes in this pathway catalyze reversible reactions, and operate in different directions in the two branchs of the pathway., One of the differences between the methanogens and other methylotrophic bacteria is that the methanogens often have modified versions of the |FRAME: THMPT| cofactor and its derivatives. This pathway describes the process in organisms that produce only |FRAME: THMPT|. Some methanogens that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-94695| and |FRAME: TAX-2182| orders possess the cofactor |FRAME: CPD-8|, which is generated from |FRAME: THMPT| by the addition of a glutamate residue |CITS: [6698019]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|). Members of the genus |FRAME: TAX-2195| contain |FRAME: CPD-24457 tatiopterin|, which is different from |FRAME: CPD-8| in having an additional aspartate in the side chain of the molecule, and in not having the 7-methyl group in the pterin moiety |CITS: [2105296]|.

The |FRAME: CPLX-7207| catalyzes the first reaction, which deaminates |FRAME: 2-AMINOBENZENESULFONATE|. |FRAME: 3SC23OALCAL-MONOMER| catalyzes a second reaction, which produces a sulfo-aldehyde intermediate. Finally, this intermediates spontaneously hydrolyzes to |FRAME: CPD-13339| and |FRAME:SO3|., The |FRAME: CPLX-7207| can also desulfonate both |FRAME:4-TOLUENESULFONATE| and |FRAME:BENZENESULFONATE| |CITS: [8075807] [9990724] [8002948]|.

|FRAME: DIPYRROMETHANE Dipyrromethane| is an active-site cofactor unique to |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.61|. The cofactor is elongated by the stepwise addition of four molecules of |FRAME: PORPHOBILINOGEN| through several intermediates (|FRAME: Hydroxymethylbilane-Synthase-ES ES|, |FRAME: Hydroxymethylbilane-Synthase-ES2 ES2| and |FRAME: Hydroxymethylbilane-Synthase-ES3 ES3|), generating an enzyme bound hexapyrrole (|FRAME: Hydroxymethylbilane-Synthase-ES4 ES4|). The final product, |FRAME: HYDROXYMETHYLBILANE|, is released from by a hydrolytic reaction that generates the holo-deaminase with the cofactor still resident at the active site., The dipyrromethane cofactor is not found as a free compound. It arises from |FRAME: HYDROXYMETHYLBILANE| in a process that starts with the C-alkylation of an internal L-cysteine residue (Cys-261 in |FRAME: TAX-562|) of the apo-deaminase by reaction with the 1-hydroxymethyl group of |FRAME: HYDROXYMETHYLBILANE|. This alkylation does not generate the cofactor but the |FRAME: Hydroxymethylbilane-Synthase-ES2 ES2| intermediate. Thus the cofactor is generated only after the enzyme has added two more pyrrole units to form the hexapyrrole, followed by release of |FRAME: HYDROXYMETHYLBILANE| |CITS: [8687374]|., The nucleotide sequences of genes encoding the deaminases from bacterial, plant and animal sources show considerable conservation in the deduced protein sequences, suggesting that all deaminases employ a similar mechanism to generate the cofactor |CITS: [8687374]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Ergothioneine Ergothioneine| (EGT) is a histidine derivative with a thiol group attached to the C2 atom of the imidazole ring and a trimethylated amine. EGT was initially isolated in 1909 by Tanret from |FRAME: TAX-5111| (ergot), the fungal infection of rye grain |CITS: [Tanret09]|, and its structure was determined within two years |CITS: [Barger11]|. It has been reported only from certain fungi, actinomycetales bacteria and cyanobacteria |CITS: [13376573][13405916][Pfeiffer11]|. The function of EGT in the microbial cells is not well understood, even though it is believed that EGT may protect cells from oxidative stress |CITS: [Garay56][2172707][22001064]|., The most significant difference between EGT and other biological thiols is the instability of the EGT disulfide under physiological conditions. Unlike other small thiols such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, EGT is stable in its reduced form in aerated aqueous solutions and does not form the disulfide |CITS: [15730267]|. Another significant difference is that EGT exists predominantly as the |FRAME: Ergothioneine-Thione "thione form"| at physiological pH |CITS: [22001064]|., Although EGT is not synthesized by non-fungal eukaryotes, animals and plants acquire EGT from the environment through a specific transporter, ETT/OCTN1 |CITS: [15795384]|. It has been shown that the human body absorbs it from dietary sources and concentrates it in specific tissues or cells such as liver, kidney, central nervous system, and red blood cells |CITS: [2172707]|. Both hyperactivity and deficiency of the OCTN1 transporter exert negative effects on human cells |CITS: [15795384][19136526]|. The precise function of ergothioneine in human tissue is also uncertain |CITS: [17616140]|., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME: Ergothioneine| in fungi has been studied mostly in |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [13654346][13862898][5438052][4276459]| and in |FRAME: TAX-5111| |CITS: [13382810][13403896][13522637]|., Biosynthesis starts with the triple methylation of |FRAME: HIS| via a S-adenosyl methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferase to |FRAME: CPD-15280| (histidine betaine). The next step in the pathway requires O2 and Fe2+ for the sulfoxidation of hercynine to |FRAME: CPD-15277| |CITS: [5484456][4276459]|. Finally, a pyridoxal phosphate-requiring enzyme converts |FRAME: CPD-15277| to EGT., The bacterial pathway differs from the eukaryotic pathway, and includes two additional enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7255|)., TThe first eukaryotic |FRAME: Ergothioneine| (EGT) biosynthetic gene was identified in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5141| by its similarity to bacterial EGT biosynthetic genes |CITS: [24828577]|. The |FRAME: G-34553| gene encodes a multidomain protein: The N-terminal domain encodes a SAM-dependent methyltransferase with homology to |FRAME: G-15978| from |FRAME: TAX-1772| (27% identity), and the C-terminal domain encodes a sulfatase with homology to the |FRAME: TAX-1772| |FRAME: G-15979|. The C-terminal domain contains the iron binding motif (HX3HXE) that is also present in |FRAME: G-15979| |CITS: [24828577]|., The second gene, |FRAME: G-34554|, was identified in |FRAME: TAX-4896| a few years later |CITS: [24828577]|.

Summary: |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID Stearate| is a saturated fatty acid that occurs in many animal and vegetable fats and oils. It is an important constituent of milk fats, lard, and cocoa and shea butters. Stearate was first described by Michel Eugene Chevreul in 1823, and its name comes from Greek for "hard fat", reflecting the fact that stearate forms a waxy solid |CITS: [16477801]|., De novo plant fatty acid synthesis occurs primarily in plastids and chloroplasts (it was shown that at least in Arabidopsis fatty acid synthesis also occurs in the mitochondria). The process involves a series of reactions catalyzed by fatty acid synthase (FAS) complexes that provoke the condensation of |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| and |FRAME: ACYL-ACP| (see |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY|)., In animals the last [acp]-bound intermediate appears to be |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs "palmitoyl-[acp]"|, and elongation to |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| proceeds via CoA-bound intermediates in the ER (see |FRAME: PWY-5972|). In bacteria and plants elongation to stearate appears to continue via [acp]-bound intermediates, and |FRAME: Stearoyl-ACPs "stearoyl-[acp]"| has been detected in many species |CITS: [4831331]|. , The difference between this pathway and the one described at |FRAME: PWY-5989| is the replacement of the NADH-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.9| with the NADPH-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.104|. Some organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-837|, only have NADPH-dependent enzymes |CITS: [29400320]|.

Summary: General Background, Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated derivative, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) are two of the most important coenzymes in redox reactions in the cell. Generally, NAD is involved in catabolic reactions, while NADP is involved in anabolic reactions. Because of the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring, the oxidized forms of these compounds are often depicted as NAD+ and NADP+, respectively., Most oxidation reactions in cells are accomplished by the removal of hydrogen atoms. In reactions where NAD or NADP participate, two hydrogen atoms are typically removed from the substrate. During the reduction of NAD+ (or NADP+) the molecule acquires two electrons and one proton, while the second proton is released into the medium. Thus a typical reaction involving NAD is in the form:, NAD+ + 2H -> NADH + H+, Additional roles for NAD in the cell have been suggested, including involvement in transcriptional regulation, longevity, and age-associated diseases. In yeast, it has been shown that NAD affects longevity and transcriptional silencing through the regulation of the Sir2p family of NAD-dependent deacetylases |CITS: [12648681][14724176]|., NAD is synthesised via two major pathways in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems; the de novo pathway, and the salvage pathway. In the prokaryotic de novo pathway, the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, while in eukaryotes the de novo pathway starts with |FRAME: TRP| (|FRAME:NADSYN-PWY|)., About This Pathway, As a general rule, most prokaryotes utilize the aspartate de novo pathway, in which the nicotinate moiety of NAD is synthesized from aspartate |CITS: [11153263]|, while in eukaryotes, the de novo pathway starts with tryptophan |CITS: [12062417]| (|FRAME: NADSYN-PWY|)., The first attempt to elucidate a prokaryotic pathway to NAD was reported by Ortega and Brown in 1960 |CITS: [13731310]|. They implicated (incorrectly) glycerol and a dicarboxylic acid as precursors in the synthesis of the pyridine ring of NAD in |FRAME:TAX-562|. Subsequent work by Chandler et al. |CITS: [4321550]| established that |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is the dicarboxylic acid precursor. Suzuki et al., in 1973, established that the three carbon precursor is |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| (DHAP) and not glycerol |CITS: [4351074]|., In addition, Andreoli et al demonstrated that quinolinate was a key intermediate in this pathway |CITS: [14013029]|. Eventually it became clear that quinolinate is indeed a precursor, not only in this pathway, but in all known NAD biosynthetic pathways., The difference between this pathway and the one depicted in |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY| is only in the first step. Thermophilic bacteria and some archaea were found to have |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.21|, instead of the oxygen-dependent |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.16| (NadB). In case of anaerobes, this enzyme enables NAD biosynthesis under anaerobic conditions |CITS: [12496312][16731057]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ubiquinones Ubiquinone| (also known as coenzyme Q) is an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in membranes. In eukaryotes ubiquinone is found mostly within the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it functions in respiratory electron transport, transferring two electrons from either complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) or complex II (succinate-ubiquinone reductase) to complex III (bc1 complex). The quinone nucleus of ubiquinone is derived directly from |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, while the isoprenoid subunits of the polyisoprenoid tail are synthesized via either a |FRAME: MEP-Pathways ""methylerythritol phosphate pathway"| or a |FRAME: Mevalonate-Pathways "mevalonate pathway"|, which feed isoprene units into the |FRAME: Polyprenyl-Biosynthesis| pathways., The number of isoprenoid subunits in the ubiquinone side chain vary in different species. For example, |FRAME: TAX-4932| has 6 such subunits, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has 8, rat and mouse have 9, and |FRAME: TAX-9606| has 10. The ubiquinones are often named according to the number of carbons in the side chain (e.g. ubi-30) or the number of isoprenoid subunits (e.g. Q-10)., Following addition of the polyprenyl tail, the product (4-hydroxy-3-polyprenylbenzoate), is processed by decarboxylation, multiple hydroxylations, and multiple methylations. It has been thought that in all prokaryotes decarboxylation preceeds hydroxylation and methylation, while in eukaryotes hydroxylation and methylation preceed decarboxylation, and thus the two variants were known as the prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathways, respectively |CITS: [Shepherd96]|. However, more recent findings suggest that some ubiquinone forming bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-340|, may also produce it via a eukaryotic-like pathway |CITS: [30681910]|, and so we refer to the two general pathway variants as the early decarboxylation and late decarboxylation pathways, respectively. It should be noted that variations of the canonical ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways continue to be reported (e.g.the pathways in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [ 37716914]| and in mammals |CITS: [38425362]|)., The ubiquinone biosynthesis pathways have been elucidated primarily by the use of mutant strains that accumulate pathway intermediates; in many organisms some of the pathway's enzymes have not been biochemically characterized., About This Pathway, |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-10 Ubiquinone-10| (Q-10) is the main quinone in many eukaryotic organisms, including humans., Lower eukaryotes that were reported to contain Q-10 include the mold |FRAME: TAX-5141| |CITS: [13673033]|, the fission yeast |FRAME: TAX-4896| |CITS:[9133618][14519123]|, many species of smut fungi from the genus |FRAME: TAX-5269| and related species, such as |FRAME: TAX-5276| and |FRAME: TAX-13290| |CITS: [Sugiyama88]|, and fungi belonging to the orders |FRAME: TAX-33183| and |FRAME: TAX-5042| |CITS: [10768477]|., Higher eukaryotes that are known to synthesize Q-10 include green plants, such as |FRAME: TAX-3562| (spinach), |FRAME: TAX-3879| (alfalfa), |FRAME: TAX-4113| (potato) and |FRAME: TAX-4577| (corn) |CITS: [13673033]|, insects, such as the Lepitopteran |FRAME: TAX-470732|, the hawk-moth |FRAME: TAX-40104| and the Cleopteran |FRAME: TAX-41138| |CITS: [13713121]|, amphibians (such as the bull frog |FRAME: TAX-8400|) |CITS: [13673033]|, birds (such as the chicken |FRAME: TAX-9031|) |CITS: [13673033]|, and mammals, including |FRAME: TAX-9913| (cow), |FRAME: TAX-9940| (sheep),, |FRAME: TAX-9823| (pig) and humans |CITS: [13673033]|., In animals, biosynthesis of coenzyme Q is attributed to ten different proteins, with six of them, COQ3, COQ4, COQ5, COQ6, COQ7 and COQ9, forming a |FRAME: CPLX66-1898| (a metabolon)., Some of the enzymes involved in the eukaryotic pathway were characterized only in 2024. Somewhat unexpectedly, one of the last enzymes of the pathway, |FRAME: ENSG00000167186-MONOMER|, was found to act only on the oxidized quinone form, suggesting that the earlier quinol intermediates must be oxidized before the pathway can continue |CITS: [38425362]|., For the biosynthesis of Q-10 in prokaryotes, see |FRAME: PWY-5857|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ASCORBATE|, also known as vitamin C, fulfils multiple essential roles in both plants and animals., Being a strong reducing agent, it functions as an antioxidant and a redox buffer. It is also a cofactor for several enzymes, which are involved in many important pathways, including collagen hydroxylation, carnitine biosynthesis, norepinephrine biosynthesis, and hormone and tyrosine metabolism., In plants L-ascorbate is also implicated in defense against pathogens and in control of plant growth and development., A significant proportion of a plant's ascorbate is found in the apoplast (the aqueous solution permeating the cell walls) |CITS: [15608627]|., Under aerobic conditions L-ascorbate is oxidized in cells to |FRAME: CPD-13907 dehydroascorbate| (via the radical |FRAME: CPD-318|), which can be recycled back to ascorbate by the |FRAME: PWY-2261|. However, once formed, dehydroascorbate can be further broken down in vivo by irreversible reactions, escaping the |FRAME: PWY-2261|., Several pathways for the irreversible catabolism of ascorbate have been described. Facultatively aerobic bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-573| degrade L-ascorbate by different pathways under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (see |FRAME: PWY-6961| and |FRAME: PWY0-301|). The anaerobic pathway begins with phosphorylation of ascorbate (mediated by a PTS-type transporter), while the aerobic pathway proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-334|. Both pathways produce |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, a centeral metabolite that is fed into the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [18708499]|., Plants from the |FRAME: TAX-3602| family (e.g. grapes) metabolize ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| via the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-13059| and |FRAME: L-IDONATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6704|). The tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 1-4 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 4 and 5 |CITS: [Loewus99][16567629]|. , The geraniaceous plant |FRAME: TAX-1417776| metabolizes ascorbate to |FRAME: TARTRATE| and |FRAME: OXALATE| via a different pathway, with |FRAME: L-THREONATE|, rather than L-idonate, as an intermediate (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6960|). In this case the tartrate skeleton is derived from carbons 3-6 of L-ascorbate, indicating a cleavage between carbons 2 and 3 |CITS:[Loewus99][15862089]|. Grapes are also known to accumulate |FRAME: OXALATE| |CITS: [DeBolt04]|, and thus may be using both pathways to generate tartrate., About This Pathway, |FRAME:TAX-562| is able to utilize |FRAME: ASCORBATE| (vitamin C) as the sole source of carbon under anaerobic, conditions |CITS: [11741871]|., The ula regulon encodes all of the proteins involved in this pathway and is formed by two operons, |FRAME: G7855| and ulaA-F. |FRAME: G7855| encodes an |FRAME: CPLX0-7848|, and ulaA-F encodes the three components of the |FRAME: EIISGA| (|FRAME: SGAT-MONOMER|, |FRAME: YJFT-MONOMER|, and |FRAME: YJFU-MONOMER|) and three catabolic enzymes (UlaDEF)., L-ascorbate is imported and converted to |FRAME: L-ASCORBATE-6-PHOSPHATE| by the |FRAME: EIISGA| |CITS: [12644495]|. The intracellular L-ascorbate-6-phosphate is subsequently metabolized by UlaG, UlaD, UlaE and UlaF to D-|FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, which can enter central metabolism via the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway |CITS: [11741871]|. , Expression of the ula regulon is regulated by the L-ascorbate 6-phosphate-binding repressor UlaR and by cAMP-CRP |CITS: [14996803][18844374]|., Under aerobic conditions an additional operon, yiaK-S, is required to catabolize L-ascorbate (see |FRAME: PWY-6961|).

Summary: The transition element |FRAME: MO molybdenum| (Mo) has been long known as an essential micronutrient across the kingdoms of plants, animals, fungi and bacteria. However, molybdate itself is catalytically inactive and, with the exception of bacterial nitrogenase, needs to be activated through complexation by a special cofactor. There are several molybdenum cofactors, including |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT), |FRAME: CPD-582| (MGD), |FRAME: CPD-23445|, or others |CITS: [1587808]|., The chemical nature and biosynthesis of molybdenum cofactors have been investigated in detail in bacteria |CITS: [7836363][8514783][8514782][1587808][14761975]| and plants |CITS: [16669776][16784786][12147719][16234918][9421926]|. All of the cofactors are synthesized from |FRAME: CPD-4| (MPT). The MPT structure is conserved in all organisms and it has been demonstrated that its biosynthesis is preserved in bacteria and plants alike. It is produced from |FRAME: GTP| via |FRAME: PRECURSOR-Z| in two steps catalyzed by |FRAME: AT1G01290-MONOMER| and |FRAME: CPLX-7191| |CITS: [7890743]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6823|). The variability of the molybdenum cofactors found in bacteria is achieved by the attachment of GMP, AMP, IMP, or CMP to the phosphate group of MPT., In |FRAME: TAX-562|, both |FRAME: CPD-582| and |FRAME: CPD-23445| are present. The mocA gene product |FRAME: G7496-MONOMER| catalyzes the transfer of the cytosine nucleotide from CTP, releasing the β- and γ-phosphates of CTP as pyrophosphate and forming |FRAME: CPD-23445| |CITS: [19542235]|., Two enzymes that utilize this cofactor have been identified in |FRAME:TAX-562| - |FRAME: CPLX0-7805| |CITS: [19368556]| and two xanthine dehydrogenases - the |FRAME: CPLX0-761| encoded by |FRAME: G7485|, |FRAME: G7486| and |FRAME: G7487|, and the putative xanthine dehydrogenase |FRAME: G7500-MONOMER| |CITS: [19542235]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-12847 Pyocyanin| was first observed as a blue-pigmented phenazine compound present in infected wounds, and was shown in 1882 to be produced by the opportunistic human pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287|. It is the principal phenazine compound produced by the organism and is believed to provide it with a competitive growth advantage and to be a virulence factor in diseases such as cystic fibrosis., |FRAME: CPD-12847 Pyocyanin| was the first natural organic molecule shown to undergo one-electron reduction |CITS: [Michaelis31]|. As a result it exists in three states: |FRAME: CPD-27131| (blue), |FRAME: CPD-12848| (red), and |FRAME: CPD-12847| (colorless). Oxidized pyocyanincan be reduced nonenzymatically by NAD(P)H to the reduced form, which interacts with a second molecule of the oxidized form to form the radical. , |FRAME: RXN-24550|

, |FRAME: RXN-24551|, The radical then reacts with molecular oxygen, forming the reactive oxygen species |FRAME: SUPER-OXIDE|, depleting cellular antioxidants |CITS: [24307284]|., |FRAME: RXN-24552|, Pyocyanin has a broad spectrum of toxicity, and also poisons cells by oxidizing iron-sulfur clusters, short-circuiting electron transfer, covalently modifying proteins, and intercalating into DNA |CITS: [28174304]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-12847 Pyocyanin| is biosynthesized from the common phenazine precursor |FRAME: CPD-9522| as indicated by the pathway link (in |CITS: [17253782]| and in |CITS: [18416536]|). The conversion of |FRAME: CPD-9522| to |FRAME: CPD-12847| is proposed to occur in a two-step conversion via the reactive, unstable intermediate |FRAME: CPD-12869|, catalyzed by the products of genes phzM and phzS. Both steps appeared to require the formation of at least a transient complex between the dimeric PhzM and PhzS. Evidence suggested that the complex contained equimolar amounts of PhzM and PhzS, although a stable complex could not be isolated. PhzM alone had no methylation activity toward |FRAME: CPD-9522|, but |FRAME: CPD-12847| was produced in the presence of PhzS and |FRAME: NADH|. Formation of a complex between PhzM and PhzS would presumably prevent release of |FRAME: CPD-12869|. PhzM is a putative |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE|-dependent N-methyltransferase and PhzS is a putative flavin-dependent aromatic hydroxylase (in |CITS: [17253782]| and in |CITS: [18416536]|)., PhzS has also been shown to act directly on |FRAME: CPD-9522| to produce |FRAME: CPD-18561|, but this compound was not a precursor for |FRAME: CPD-12847| and therefore PhzM must act before PhzS (in |CITS: [17253782]|). |FRAME: CPD-12869| was shown in earlier work to be an intermediate in biosynthesis of the phenazine |FRAME: CPD-10379| (in |CITS: [18416536]|).

Summary: Adenosine nucleotides can be synthesized de novo. In that route |FRAME: AMP| (AMP) is synthesized via |FRAME: IMP| (IMP) and |FRAME: ADENYLOSUCC| , which is converted to AMP by the action of, |FRAME: ASL-MONOMER| (see |FRAME: PWY-6126|). Note that the free base |FRAME: ADENINE| or the ribonucleoside |FRAME: ADENOSINE| are not produced via the de novo pathway., Many organisms can also recycle adenosine nucleotides by a combination of degradation and salvage pathways. The degradation pathways are responsible for the conversion of the nucleotides to the nucleoside (|FRAME: ADENOSINE|) and free base form (|FRAME: ADENINE|), and further degradation to compounds that can be catabolized to basic building blocks (for example, see |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|)., However, both |FRAME: ADENOSINE| and |FRAME: ADENINE| can be salvaged by certain enzymes, and be converted back to nucleotide form., The enzyme |FRAME: DEOD-CPLX "purine phosphorylase (DeoD)"| (EC 2.4.2.1) cleaves |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: ADENINE| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-1P|, while a second enzyme, such as |FRAME: ADENPRIBOSYLTRAN-CPLX|, can utilize |FRAME: PRPP| to convert the free base to the mononucleotide |FRAME: AMP|., Other routes from |FRAME: ADENOSINE| to |FRAME: AMP| are described in |FRAME: PWY-6605| and |FRAME: PWY-6619|., Either of these routes enables the organism to salvage the degradation products of adenosine nucleotides, and recycle them back to nucleotide form.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13015| (MGG) is a compatible solute identified in the slightly thermophilic species |FRAME: TAX-28237| (optimum growth temperature of 55 to 60°C), a member of the order Thermotogales. Under optimum growth conditions MGG is the major solute in this organism. It plays a role during low-level osmotic adaptation only, whereas α-glutamate and, to a lesser extent, L-proline are used for osmoprotection under salt stress |CITS: [17521333]|., |FRAME: CPD-13015| is a derivative of |FRAME: CPD-9190|, identified in the free form in |FRAME: TAX-556|, in the marine cyanobacteria |FRAME: TAX-1219| and |FRAME: TAX-32049|, and in the thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-309805| (see |FRAME: PWY-5662| and |FRAME: PWY-6685|)., The pathways for MGG biosynthesis have been studied in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-69499|, which appears to possess two alternative pathways. In one of the pathways, mannosylglucosylglycerate is produced from |FRAME: G3P| and |FRAME: CPD-12575| by three enzymes, encoded by |FRAME:G-12444|, |FRAME: G-12436| and |FRAME: G-12440| (see |FRAME: PWY-6686|). In the second pathway, which is described here, MGG is produced from |FRAME: GLYCERATE| and |FRAME: ADP-D-GLUCOSE| by two enzymes, encoded by |FRAME: G-12442| and |FRAME: G-12445| |CITS: [20061481]|., About This Pathway, The two genes that encode the enzymes of this pathway, |FRAME: G-12442| and |FRAME: G-12445|, were cloned from |FRAME: TAX-69499| and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. While the |FRAME: G-12442| gene produced an active recombinant protein that could be purified, mggS had no detectable expression in |FRAME:TAX-562|. Attepmts to purify the native protein also failed. Instead, the homologous gene from |FRAME: TAX-2336| (|FRAME: G-12445 TM1230|) was cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. While this protein also proved difficult to purify, it was possible to characterize its activity in cell extracts prepared from the recombinant host., Activity assays carried out with purified Ggs and MggS-containing |FRAME:TAX-562| cell extracts showed synthesis of MGG.

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., The pyrimidine nucleotide de novo biosynthetic pathway derives in part from the central metabolic precursors |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, a precursor of pyrimidine ribonucleotides, is derived from oxaloacetate, which is generated in the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here illustrates a route in which the pyrimidine ribonucleotides |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are converted to the deoxyribonucleotides |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: DUTP|, which are subsequently modified to other deoxyribonucleotides, including the thymine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate |FRAME: TTP|. , While most organisms utilize a different route (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|), this pathway is found in bacteria that possess two specialized enzymes - |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.2 "ribonucleoside-triphosphate reductase (EC 1.17.4.2)"|, an enzyme that can reduce nucleoside triphosphates to their respective deoxynucleoside triphosphates (most organism posses |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "EC 1.17.4.1"|, which can only accept nucleoside diphosphates), and |FRAME: EC-3.5.4.13 "dCTP deaminase (EC 3.5.4.13)"|, an enzyme that can deaminate |FRAME: DCTP| to |FRAME: DUMP|., In this pathway the deoxyribonucleotide |FRAME: DUTP| is formed in two ways - by the direct reduction of |FRAME: UTP|, and by the deamination of |FRAME: DCTP|, which is formed from |FRAME: CTP| either directly by |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-TRIP-REDUCT-CPLX|, or in two steps, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7184|., Once formed, |FRAME: DUTP| is dephosphorylated to |FRAME: DUMP|. Deamination of |FRAME: DCTP| is the major route for de novo formation of |FRAME: DUMP| in aerobically-growing |FRAME:TAX-562|. It supplies 70-80% of total |FRAME: DUMP| |CITS: [17651436]|., Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by |FRAME: THYMIDYLATESYN-CPLX| (EC 2.1.1.45)., The enzyme only accepts the mono-phosphorylated form |FRAME: DUMP|. Thus, the first deoxyuridine nucleotide that is formed in this route, , |FRAME: DUTP|, needs to be converted to the monophosphate form by the removal of a diphosphate group, resulting in |FRAME: DUMP|., Once |FRAME: TMP| is formed, two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: DTMPKI-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: NUCLEOSIDE-DIP-KIN-CPLX|.

Summary: The phosphorylated inositol compounds described in this superpathway can be divided into two major groups - the phospholipids phosphatidyl inositols, and the cyclitols inositol phosphates., The most prominent stereomer of inositol in nature is |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL|. The inositol molecule has six hydroxyl groups, and each of these can be replaced by a single or double (pyro) phosphate group, resulting in a very large number of different forms of phosphorylated inositols., Phosphatidyl-inositol phosphates, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL| can combine with |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL| to form the glycerophospholipid |FRAME: L-1-phosphatidyl-inositols|, which serves as a a minor component in the cytosolic side of eukaryotic cell membranes. The most common fatty acids of phosphatidyl-inositol are |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| in the SN1 position and |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| in the SN2 position. , When the inositol within the phospholipid is phosphorylated, the resulting phosphatidylinositol phosphate is called |FRAME: Phosphoinositides|. Phosphoinositides can be phosphorylated at any of the 3', 4', or 5' positions on the inositol headgroup, generating a set of seven unique stereoisomers that have specific biological functions (see |FRAME: PWY-6352|)., The phosphoinositides are membrane-bound lipids that function as structural components of membranes, as well as regulators of many cellular processes in eukaryotes, including vesicle-mediated membrane trafficking, cell wall integrity, and actin cytoskeleton organization. Different forms of phosphoinositides are associated with different membranes., |FRAME: CPD-1108 "Phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate"| is the major form in the Golgi apparatus, where it plays a role in the vesicular trafficking of secretory proteins from the Golgi to the plasma membrane. , |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| is the major form found at the plasma membrane and is involved in the regulation of actin cytoskeleton organization, as well as cell wall integrity, and heat shock response pathways., |FRAME: CPD-177 "Phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate"| is found predominantly at endosomal membranes and in multivesicular bodies (MVB), where it plays a role in endosomal and vacuolar membrane trafficking. , |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH "Phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate"| is found on vacuolar membranes where it plays an important role in the MVB sorting pathway., |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-34-BISPH "Phosphatidyl-1D-myo-inositol 3,4-bisphosphate"| is used in as a secondary messenger, involved in the regulation of cellular events including growth, differentiation, vesicular sorting, glucose transport and platelet aggregation |CITS:[9599410][11485317]|., Inositol phosphates, The phospholipid |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| can be hydrolyzed by the phospholipase C enzymes to form the extremely important secondary messanger compound |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6351|). In addition to its role as a second messenger, |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| is the starting point of several complex pathways that produce many different forms of phosphorylated inositols., |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-4-5-TRISPHOSPHATE| can be phosphorylated, either in a direct route (see |FRAME: PWY-6361|) or via |FRAME: INOSITOL-1-3-4-TRIPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6362|), to the fully phosphorylated form |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE|, also known as phytate. One of the intermediates of this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1107|, is used to synthesize two other important secondary messengers - |FRAME: INOSITOL-1456-TETRAKISPHOSPHATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6366|) and |FRAME: CPD-178| (see |FRAME: PWY-6365|)., Phosphorylation does not end at |FRAME: MI-HEXAKISPHOSPHATE| - this molecule is phosphorylated further by modification of one or more of the phosphates to pyrophosphates (see |FRAME: PWY-6369|)., Even though not part of this pathway, the timely degration of these compounds is also a crucial part of their metabolism. More about it is available in |FRAME: PWY-6368|.

General Background, The metal chelating agents |FRAME: CPD-10188| and |FRAME: EDTA| are aminopolycarboxylic acids. They, are widely used industrially and can be found in natural waters and wastewaters. Copper-nitrilotriacetate and, ferric-nitrilotriacetate complexes have been shown to be carcinogenic |CITS: [10087332] [17487455]| . Bacterial, strains that can degrade these compounds have been reported and are of interest as biodegradation, agents. Because these compounds occur in the environment mostly as metal ion complexes, the, influence of metal ion type on the degradation process is also of interest (reviewed in |CITS: [16233066]|)., Bacterial strains capable of degrading |FRAME: CPD-10188| and |FRAME: EDTA| have been isolated. Earlier work, identified a pseudomonad that could aerobically degrade nitrilotriacetate and its metal ion, complexes |CITS: [4362331] [1155932] [655711]|. More recently, nitrilotriacetate degradation in, |FRAME: TAX-83263 "Aminobacter aminovorans (previously named Chelobacter heintzii ATCC 29600)"|, a Gram-negative, obligately aerobic bacterium, has been well studied. The two key enzymes in aerobic |FRAME: CPD-10188| degradation are a monooxygenase and a membrane-bound dehydrogenase (in |CITS: [17404695]| and reviewed, in |CITS: [16233066]| and |CITS: [11152941]|). These enzymes are only expressed when cells are grown on, |FRAME: CPD-10188| or |FRAME: CPD-10189| |CITS: [UETZ93]|. In addition, a bacterial strain that can degrade, |FRAME: CPD-10188| anaerobically under denitrifying conditions has been isolated. It was described as a, member of the gamma subgroup of the Proteobacteria and it utilized a nitrilotriacetate dehydrogenase, |CITS: [1368140] [8250558]|. Interestingly, a thermotolerant yeast, |FRAME:TAX-4911| IMB3, was, shown to be capable of using either |FRAME: CPD-10188| or |FRAME: CPD-10189| as a sole source of nitrogen, for growth, and both nitrilotriacetate monooxygenase and iminodiacetate dehydrogenase enzyme activities, were found in cell extracts of this yeast |CITS: [11785972]|., About This Pathway, The mechanism of transport of |FRAME: CPD-10188|, or its metal ion complexes into bacterial cells remains to be, investigated. After oxidation and dehydrogenation, the products of the pathway, |FRAME: GLYOX| and, |FRAME: GLY|, undergo mineralization through as yet undefined steps (reviewed in |CITS: [16233066]|). The, dehydrogenase was shown to be an integral membrane protein, with its activity linked to the respiratory chain, |CITS: [UETZ93]|.

Summary: General Background, In plants, the protein levels in seeds influence seed survival in natural settings and help determine the seeds' nutritional value and processing properties when they are grown for human and animal consumption. A large fraction of this protein content may be derived from the remobilization of nitrogen from proteins in senescing leaves |CITS: [11244107][16690166][17244043]|. This nitrogen can be transported in the form of amino acids, prinicipally glutamine, through the phloem. Improving the efficiency of this process could lead to the production of seed-based crops with higher protein levels |CITS: [20202167]|., One of the enzymes in this pathway, pyruvate, orthodiphosphate dikinase (PPDK), plays a prominent role in photosynthesis in C4 plants such as |FRAME: TAX-4577 "Zea mays (maize)"|, yet it is also expressed in C3 plants, such as |FRAME: ORG-5993|. This pathway may help to explain the physiological function of PPDK in C3 plants |CITS: [20202167]|. Interestingly, in all plant species studied to date, both a cytosolic and a chloroplastic isoform of the PPDK enzyme are generated from alternative promoters upstream of the same chromosomal locus. Over-expression of the cytosolic form of this enzyme in Arabidopsis during senescence can lead to an increase in seed weight and seed nitrogen content indicating that this form of the enzyme may be important for nitrogen remobilization |CITS: [20202167]|. , About This Pathway, Portions of this pathway likely occurs in several subcellular compartments, notably, the cytosol, mitochondria, and chloroplast. The pyruvate that initally feeds into this pathway may be derived from the deamination of some amino acids, such as threonine, glycine, serine, alanine, and cysteine. , Starting with pyruvate, after the sequential activities of cytosolic PPDK and PEP carboxylase, the |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| (OAA) produced can flow into the |FRAME: PWY-5690 TCA cycle| in the mitochondria where it can be converted to citrate. The citrate may be metabolized in the mitochondria or the cytosol by aconitase. The subsequent transformation of |FRAME: THREO-DS-ISO-CITRATE isocitrate| into |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| can be catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLXQT-51| in the mitochondria |CITS: [16527867]| or by |FRAME: AT1G65930-MONOMER| in the cytosol |CITS: [20199623][20202167]|., In the chloroplast, this |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| carbon skeleton can then be transformed into a nitrogen-transporting amino acid by the activities of glutamate synthase and glutamine synthase. The resulting |FRAME: GLN| can then be exported to seeds through the phloem |CITS: [20202167]|.

Isopropylamine is used as a solvent and as a raw material in manufacturing various chemicals., The compound occurs as a constituent of the herbicides |FRAME: ATRAZINE| and |FRAME: CPD-9378|,, from which it is liberated during microbial degradation., Until recently no information was available about the fate of |FRAME: ISOPROPYLAMINE| in the, environment. , An early study with an isopropylamine-utilizing Mycobacterium convolutum suggested, that degradation is initiated by an inducible amine dehydrogenase that yields ammonium and acetone, as the first intermediate |CITS: [1176433]|. However, this was not corroborated by additional studies., |FRAME: TAX-159091| was isolated based on its ability to grow with |FRAME: ISOPROPYLAMINE| and, |FRAME: CPD-9374| as its sole carbon source |CITS: [11976110]|., The genes involved in the pathway were identified by transposon mutagenesis., Isopropylamine from the environment is transported into the cytoplasm of |FRAME: TAX-159091| by a, putative permease, encoded by the ipuG gene, and is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9372| by, the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-13561|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10332| gene, in a reaction that, consumes ATP., |FRAME: CPD-9372| is then subjected to stereospecific monooxygenation by a hypothetical, four-component |FRAME: CPLX-7534| encoded by the ipuABDE genes, generating, |FRAME: CPD-9373|. Enzymatic hydrolysis by a hydrolase, IpuF, liberates |FRAME: CPD-9374|, and regenerates |FRAME:GLT| |CITS: [11976110]|., The next part of the pathway is less well documented. It is proposed that |FRAME: CPD-9374| is, converted to an aldehyde - either|FRAME: CPD-9375| or|FRAME: CPD-665|, which is then, oxidized by eother of two aldehyde dehydrogenases, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10338| and, |FRAME: G-10339| genes, to |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| or |FRAME: PROPIONATE|, respectively.
