Summary: The flavoenzyme EncM, characterized from |FRAME: TAX-115828|, catalyzes the peroxyflavin-independent oxygenation-dehydrogenation dual oxidation of a highly reactive poly-β-ketone during the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-12319|., The enzyme relies on an FAD cofactor covalently bound to the His78 side chain to perform this oxidation, which triggers a complex Favorskii-rearrangement of the carbon backbone and several cyclization reactions that ultimately afford the, non-aromatic multicyclic core of enterocin., Structural and mechanistic investigation of EncM revealed that the cofactor attached to His78 at resting state is |FRAME: CPD-22328|. A reduced FAD attached to this residue reacts with oxygen by a single-electron transfer (SET) mechanism to give a peroxide, which then loses water to give the flavin-N5-oxide |CITS: [24162851][26067765]|. This stable superoxidized flavin is reduced into |FRAME: FADH2| during substrate turnover, but is restored by reacting with molecular oxygen., EncM features two distinct active sites for substrate binding and O2 activation at the si-side and re-side of the flavin cofactor, respectively |CITS: [25619330][29686059]|. Binding of the O2 molecule lowers the activation energy barrier for bond formation at N5., The flavin-N5-oxide cofactor has also been reported from the catabolic enzymes |FRAME: G6523 RutA| (involved in uracil catabolism of |FRAME: TAX-562|) |CITS: [28661684]| and |FRAME: G-494 DszA| (from |FRAME: CPD-942| catabolism of |FRAME: TAX-334542|) |CITS: [ 27120486]|, although on those cases the cofactor is proposed to be a product arising from the oxidation of FAD by postulated reactive peroxyacid-intermediates, rather than as an oxygenating species |CITS: [30165331]|.

Background, Monoterpenes are a diverse group of naturally occurring volatile compounds with a 10 carbon backbone produced by plants and animals. The majority are unsaturated acyclic, monocyclic or bicyclic and derived from geranyl diphosphate |CITS: [20663876]|, see |FRAME: PWY-3041|. When they are oxygenated to form alcohols, ketones, and carboxylic acids, they are called monoterpenoids. The monoterpenes are a source of atmospheric nonmethane hydrocarbons that are a major constitutent of the global carbon cycle. , The aerobic degradation of monoterpenes has been characterized in |FRAME: TAX-286| species. The monoterpene mineralization pathway described here is an anaerobic one, unique to the organism |FRAME: TAX-75697|, a denitrifying proteobacterium |CITS: [10877798]|. It results in the complete mineralization of monoterpenes to carbon dioxide, although the part of the pathway downstream of |FRAME: CPD-7618| has not been characterized |CITS: [9704110]|. , About this Pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-8287 "Linalool dehydratase-isomerase"| catalyzes the first two reactions of the pathway, the hydration of |FRAME: CPD-4888| to |FRAME: CPD-8997| and the isomerization of the latter compound to |FRAME: GERANIOL| |CITS: [22286981]|. The enzyme is only active under anaerobic conditions. The oxidation of |FRAME: GERANIOL| to |FRAME: CPD-7618| is catalyzed by the sequential activity of first |FRAME: CPLX-8577| followed by |FRAME: MONOMER-17745|, see also |FRAME: PWY-6678|. Geranate was also synthesized by |FRAME: TAX-75697| when grown on α-phellandrene, limonene, or α-pinene |CITS: [10877798]|., The ability of anaerobic microorganisms to degrade monoterpenes could be used to in the food industry, and facilitate the reduction of nonmethane hydrocarbon release into the atmosphere |CITS: [8526489]|.

Summary: De novo biosynthesis of purines starts with the synthesis of |FRAME: IMP|, which can be converted to all, other purines., In bacteria and archaea |FRAME:IMP| is synthesized from |FRAME: 5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-5-AMINOIMIDAZOLE| in 6 steps, while in eukarya the first two steps are replaced by a single reaction (see |FRAME: PWY-6124|)., In bacteria the last two steps are catalyzed by a single multifunctional enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: EG10795| gene (see |FRAME: PWY-6123|)., In archaea, on the other hand, the last two steps are catalyzes by two different enzymes. The penultimate step is catalyzed by the archaeal PurP enzyme, which is format-dependent and does not require folate |CITS: [9150241]| and the last step is catalyzed by PurO. No homology exists between PurH and either PurO or PurP |CITS: [15623504]|.

Summary: Several viridans streptococci, such as |FRAME: TAX-1303|, are able to enter the bloodstream, through dental caries and cause several serious infections, including endocarditis, brain abscesses and,, in immunocompromised patients, septicaemia |CITS:[885611][10692836][10509480]|., The exact mechanisms by which these organisms proliferate in vivo are unknown., One of the potential sources of fermentable carbohydrate are host-derived sialic acids such as, |FRAME:N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, which is present in serum, and can be liberated from, glycoproteins and other sialoglyoconjugates via the action of sialidases |CITS:[2199505][10707943]|., Several species of the viridans streptococci, including |FRAME: TAX-46125|, |FRAME: TAX-1328|,, |FRAME: TAX-76860|, |FRAME: TAX-1302|, |FRAME: TAX-1338|, |FRAME: TAX-28037|,, |FRAME: TAX-1303| and |FRAME: TAX-1305| are able to utilize |FRAME:N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| as, a sole carbon source, independently of sialidase production |CITS: [8906124]|. , The major end products of N-acetylneuraminate metabolism in these organisms are, |FRAME: FORMATE|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: ETOH|. , A transport system for |FRAME:N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| was characterized in |FRAME: TAX-1303|, |CITS: [10509480]|. This system followed typical Michaelis-Menten kinetics, with a Km of 21.0 μM, and a Vmax of 2.65 nmoles/min/mg of dry cell mass., The pathway for the degradation of |FRAME:N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| has been studied in viridans, streptococci, and its first part is essentially identical to the pathway found in |FRAME: TAX-83333|, (see |FRAME:GLCMANNANAUT-PWY|)., The first step of the pathway consists of splitting of |FRAME:N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| into, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, catalyzed by the enzyme, |FRAME:CPLX-7365|., |FRAME: N-ACETYL-BETA-D-MANNOSAMINE| is then phosphorylated to, |FRAME:N-ACETYL-D-MANNOSAMINE-6P|. Next the acetyl group is removed (by |FRAME:CPLX-7366|),, followed by removal of the ammoium group (by |FRAME:CPLX-7367|), resulting in formation of, |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P|, which enters glycolysis for substrate level phosphorylation., In oral streptococci the end product of glycolysis, |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, can be fermented into either, |FRAME:L-LACTATE| or to |FRAME: FORMATE|, |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: ETOH|. , When grown on |FRAME:N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| no lactate is produced, and only the later, three products are observed |CITS: [8906124]|.

Summary: This super-pathway provides an overview of the complexity and interconnectivity of gibberellins biosynthesis. It is important to note that a given species shown here may not synthesize all the gibberellins presented. To know which gibberellins are found in a specfic species, refer to the subpathways given below., General Background, At the time of this review, 136 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity., Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana. GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and GA4 enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|) are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed. It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis., Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). During active growth, the plant will maintain giberellin homeostasis by metabolizing most gibberellins by rapid hydroxylation to inactive conjugates. Active |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed in the disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen produces large amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Inactive conjugates might be stored or translocated via the phloem and xylem before their release (activation) at the proper time and in the proper tissue.

Summary: General Background, Cyanobacterial lipids consist of glycerolipids with a C18 fatty acid esterified at position sn-1 and a C16 fatty acid esterified at position sn-2 |CITS: [Sato82]|., The cyanobacteria have been classified into four groups according to the distribution of the fatty acids in their glycerolipids |CITS: [16689682]|. , Strains in Group 1 are characterized by the presence of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (|FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| and |FRAME: CPD-9245|) at the sn-1 and sn-2 positions, respectively., Strains in Group 2 contain the tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| at the sn-1 position and the mono-unsaturated C16 fatty acid |FRAME: CPD-9245| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 3 have a different tri-unsaturated C18 fatty acid (|FRAME: CPD-8117|) at the sn-1 position and the saturated C16 acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| at the sn-2 position., Strains in Group 4 are similar to strains in Group 3 except that they have, in addition, the tri-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| and the tetra-unsaturated C18 acid |FRAME: CPD-12653| at the sn-1 position., |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID "α-Linolenate"| (often referred to as simply linolenate), which is produced by members of groups 2 and 4, is an ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (18:3) , the 3 referring to the position of the first double bond from the methyl end of the fatty acid., It is also produced by plants, and is found in many seed oils, especially those of rapeseed (canola), soybeans, walnuts, flaxseed (Linseed), perilla, chia and hemp. It is not limited to seeds, and is also common in the lipids that are found in thylakoid membranes in the green leaves of broadleaf plants and in red algae |CITS:[414660]|., |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID "α-Linolenate"| is an essential fatty acid for animals, and is considered an essential dietary requirement for all mammals., About This Pathway, In cyanobacteria |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| is formed bound to an acyl-carrier protein, part of the fatty acid synthase complex. Stearate is transfered to the sn-1 position of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.15| |CITS: [16039611]|., As described above, glycerolipids from all cyanobacteria contain unsturated C18 fatty acids in the sn-1 position, but differ in the degree and nature of unsaturation. The desaturation occurs only after |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| has been incorporated into the glycerol backbone, and is catalyzed by membrane-bound enzymes known as acyl-lipid desaturases., The first desaturation occurs at position 9, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS15040|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS15040-MONOMER| |CITS: [7929259]|. This is followed by desaturation at position 12, catalyzed by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10130|-encoded |FRAME: SGL_RS10130-MONOMER| |CITS: [2118597]|. A third desaturation at position 15, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.19.36|, encoded by the |FRAME: SGL_RS10825| gene, produces |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| |CITS: [7524725]|.

Summary: Microorganisms such as |FRAME: TAX-546| or |FRAME: TAX-573| are able to grow anaerobically on glycerol as the sole carbon and energy source. In the absence of an external oxidant, glycerol is fermented by a dismutation process involving two pathways (see |FRAME: GOLPDLCAT-PWY|)., In one of these pathways, originally discovered in |FRAME:TAX-573| ATCC 8724, glycerol is dehydrated by the |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|-dependent |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.30|, to form |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL| |CITS: [5882686]|, which is reduced to the major fermentation product |FRAME: CPD-347| (PDO) by the NADH-linked |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.202| |CITS: [13791444]|. At least in some organisms this conversion occurs in a specialized bacterial compartment called the metabolosome, perhaps due to the toxicity of |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL| |CITS: [18469107]|. |FRAME: CPD-347| is not metabolized further, and is excreted by the cells into the medium., The enzymes of this pathway are encoded by the dha regulon, the expression of which is induced when dihydroxyacetone or glycerol is present., Some other species utilize the same pathways, although the regulation may be different. For example, |FRAME: TAX-1580| and |FRAME: TAX-1581| express glycerol dehydratase and 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase during cofermentation of glycerol and other carbon sources, such as glucose, fructose, ribose and lactate |CITS: [1622279]|. These strains cannot grow on glycerol alone, and the dha regulon does not require glycerol for induction., PDO has become a commercially important chemical, due to the recent development of a new polyester called poly(propylene terephtalate), with unique properties for the fiber industry. The |FRAME:TAX-570| enzymes glycerol dehydratase and 1,3-propanediol dehydrogenase are used in engineered strains of |FRAME:TAX-562| for the commerciall production of PDO (see |FRAME: PWY-7385|)., The intermediate |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL| was independently described as an antimicrobial compound produced by the probiotic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1598|, and was named reuterin |CITS: [3245697]|. It was later shown to be identical to |FRAME: HYDROXYPROPANAL| |CITS: [Chung89]|. Reuterin has been shown to be bioactive against bacteria, viruses and fungi |CITS: [9798141][10090245][12577589][17997816][25087026]|. Reuterin induces oxidative stress in cells, most likely by modifying thiol groups in proteins and small molecules |CITS: [20150236]|.

Summary: Glucosylation of cytokinins is a well recognized modification that is thought to play an important role in hormonal homeostasis. Several types of cytokinins conjugation exist which render cytokinins inactive: O-xylosylation, O-glucosylation, and N-glucosylation. When plants are subjected to high levels of cytokinin application, the major conjugate that forms is the 7-N-glucoside (see |FRAME:PWY-2881|) |CITS: [15342621]|. Moreover, unlike O-glucosides, the glucosylation of which is reversible through the action of glucosidases, 7-N- and 9-N-glucosides are resistant to glucosidases |CITS: [8235622]|. This, taken with N-glucosides accumulation in plant subjected to high doses of cytokinins, has led to the suggestion that N-glucosylation is involved in detoxification |CITS: [15342621]|. It is not yet known whether glucosylation at position 9-N plays a specific role or whether it is merely a byproduct of the 7-N-glucosylation.

Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes and are determinants of intracellular communication, in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]|, and fatty acyl moieties of proteins that modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid (FAS) biosynthesis mechanisms. The type I system is found in mammals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex, (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|)., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|., The best studied pathway is that of |FRAME: TAX-83333|, from which all the enzymes have been purified and crystalized. In plants fatty acid synthesis occurs mainly in plastids of leaf mesophyll cells, seeds, and oil-accumulating fruits. Although most of the synthesis occurrs in plastids, it has been shown that mitochondria are also capable of synthesizing fatty acids |CITS: [14660674]|., Fatty acid biosynthesis starts with an initiation sequence that produces |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs|, an activated molecule that is used for subsequent elongation reactions, which ultimately produce the final fatty acid products. This pathway describes only the initiation sequence, subsequent elongation reactions are described in the pathways |FRAME: FASYN-ELONG-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-5971| and |FRAME: PWY0-862|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-83333| has several different routes in which it can produce acetoacetyl-ACP, and this pathway describes the major route. In it, one |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| molecule is converted to |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|, which is then activated to |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP| that is condensed with a second |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| molecule to form |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs|., The first enzyme in this pathway, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|, is the controlling point for the flux of carbon into lipids. It is a biotin-containing multi-enzyme complex with two activities, |FRAME: BIOTIN-CARBOXYL-CPLX| and |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLTRANSFER-CPLX|, catalyzing two half reactions that combined condense |FRAME: HCO3| with |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to yield |FRAME: MALONYL-COA|. Further discussion of this enzyme is available in the pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1264|., In plants this reaction is catalyzed by the plastidic heteromeric |FRAME: CPLX-6282|. A second, homomeric form of the enzyme is cytosolic and is involved in very-long-chain fatty acid biosynthesis and synthesis of flavonoids., The |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| is next attached to |FRAME: ACP| by the enzyme |FRAME: MALONYL-COA-ACP-TRANSACYL-MONOMER|., The last step of the pathway, the condensation of a second |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP malonyl-[acp]|, is carried out by the condensing enzyme β-ketoacyl-ACP synthase (KAS)., |FRAME: TAX-83333|, as well as most plants, has three β-ketoacyl-ACP synthases: |FRAME: FABB-CPLX|, |FRAME: 3-OXOACYL-ACP-SYNTHII-CPLX| and |FRAME: CPLX0-252|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10274|, |FRAME: EG12606| and |FRAME: EG10277|, respectively. |FRAME: CPLX0-252| is the key enzyme in the initiation of fatty acids biosynthesis. It selectively catalyzes the formation of acetoacetyl-ACP and specifically uses CoA thioesters rather, than acyl-ACP as the primer. The products tend to be shorter than the products of KASI and II, which are involved primarily in elongation reactions. Unlike the other two enzymes, KASIII cannot participate in the terminal elongation steps of fatty acid biosynthesis |CITS: [15952903]|., It should be noted that in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-208964|, a different enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15300| gene, catalyzes the condensation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| with |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP malonyl-[acp]| |CITS: [22753059]|., KASIII is inhibited by long-chain acyl-ACPs, indicating a role in feedback regulation of fatty acid synthesis. Since it catalyzes the first condensation step in fatty acid synthesis, it is able to control the rate of fatty acid initiation., The substrate specificity of |FRAME: CPLX0-252| is a major determining factor in membrane fatty acid composition of an organism. In |FRAME: TAX-562| the enzyme is highly selective for acetyl-CoA, and thus only straight-chain fatty acids are produced in this organism. In many gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, the enzyme prefers branched-chain acyl-CoA substrates derived from amino acid metabolism, leading to the production of primarily iso- and anteisobranched fatty acids |CITS:[10629181]|., Other potential routes for fatty acid biosynthesis initiation in |FRAME: TAX-83333| are described in |FRAME: PWY-5966| and |FRAME: PWY-5965|.

General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, Methane production from methanol was first observed in |FRAME: TAX-2207| by Stadtman and Barker |CITS: [14824081]|. , |FRAME: TAX-2208| is a methanogenic archeon that can grow on |FRAME: ACET| and various one-carbon compounds such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METHYLAMINE|, and |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE|, as well as |FRAME: METOH|, as a sole energy source., Growth on |FRAME: METOH| has been reported both in the presence and absence of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|; when hydrogen is not available, the reduction equivalents needed in methanogenesis are derived from disproportion of the methanol, leading to the the oxidation of quarter of the methanol to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [6786216 ]|., The pathways for methanogenesis from methylated C1 compounds follow a similar route. Methyl transfer from the electron acceptor to |FRAME: CoM| is carried out by enzyme systems composed of three polypeptides: a protein that binds a corrinoid prosthetic group |CITS: [9654068]|, and two methyltransferases, named MT1 and MT2. MT1 and the corrinoid protein form a tight heterodimeric complex. When the substrate binds to this complex, MT1 catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from the substrate to the corrinoid group. MT2 then transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid to , |FRAME: CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|. Individual MT1 and corrinoid-binding proteins are highly specific for their respective substrate, and exhibit little or no activity with similar substrates |CITS: [6615129][9195968][9006042][9654067][10852929]|., The conversion of |FRAME: METOH| to |FRAME:Me-CoM| is catalyzed by a methanol-specific MT1/MT2 system. The genes encoding the MT1/MT2 system in |FRAME: TAX-2208| have been cloned and sequenced. The MT1/corrinoid protein complex consists of the 49 kDa methyltransferase protein MtaB and the 24 kDa corrinoid-binding protein MtaC, encoded by the |FRAME: G-381| and |FRAME: G-82| genes, which are found in an operon |CITS: [9363780][9654068]|., MtaB catalyzes the transfer of the methyl group from methanol to the corrinoid group bound to MtaC |CITS: [9057830]|. It has been shown that MtaC can be subtituted by free cob(I)alamin |CITS: [10215883]|. MtaA, also known as methyltransferase 2, is encoded by the |FRAME: G-382| gene |CITS: [8654414 ]|, which is not closely linked to the mtaCB operon. This methyltransferase transfers the methyl group from the corrinoid group to |FRAME:CoM| |CITS:[6438059]|, generating |FRAME:Me-CoM| which is disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, as discussed above.

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, Arsenite can enter the yeast cell by several mechanisms., Yeast has two phosphate-uptake systems that complement each other: the high-affinity transporters (|FRAME: G3O-32702| and PHO89) and the low-affinity transporters |FRAME: G3O-29349| and PHO90. Both systems have been shown to allow the pentavalent |FRAME: ARSENATE| to enter the cells |CITS: [8598055][22628173]|., The hexose permeases (encoded by HXT genes) have been shown to catalyze the majority of the transport of the trivalent metalloid |FRAME: CPD-24315| into the cell |CITS: [14966117]|, and have been suggested as an entry point for |FRAME: CPD0-2040| as well |CITS: [27105594]|. However, the main entry point of trivalent arsenite under low-osmolarity conditions is via the |FRAME: CPLX3O-10933|. Like the |FRAME: TAX-562| glycerol facilitator |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF|, Fps1p also mediates influx of the trivalent metalloids |FRAME: CPD0-2040| and |FRAME: CPD0-2039|. This effect is only observed under low-osmolarity conditions, when the channel is open |CITS: [11442837]|., |FRAME: TAX-4932| has two independent transport systems for the removal of AsIII from the cytosol. |FRAME: G3O-34321| is a plasma membrane transporter that extrudes arsenite from the cells. |FRAME: G3O-29733|, a member of the ABC transporter superfamily, catalyzes the ATP-driven uptake of As(III) into the vacuole, also producing resistance to arsenite. Vacuolar accumulation requires a reductant such as glutathione, suggesting that the substrate is the glutathione conjugate, |FRAME: CPD-22658|. Disruption of either the |FRAME: G3O-34321| or |FRAME: G3O-29733| gene results in sensitivity to |FRAME: CPD-763| and disruption of both genes produces additive hypersensitivity |CITS: [10220408]|., In 2018 it was shown that the MTQ2-TRM112 complex, which is known as a methyltransferase that methylates a glutamine residue on the SUP45 subunit (eRF1) of the translation release factor ERF1-ERF3 complex, also displays SAM-dependent methyltransferase activity toward both |FRAME: CPD0-2040| and |FRAME: METHYLARSONITE| |CITS: [29846136]|.

|FRAME: NEDD8 "NEDD8 proteins"| (neural-precursor-cell expressed developmentally down-regulated protein 8) are small |FRAME: Ubiquitins ubiquitin|-like proteins that are covalently conjugated to a limited number of cellular proteins in a manner analogous to |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitination|. The attachment of NEDD8 to proteins is known as neddylation., Like ubiquitin, the NEDD8 proteins end with two glycine residues. |FRAME: NEDD8-activating-proteins-E1 "An [E1 NEDD8-activating enzyme]"|, which is a heterodimer composed of |FRAME: HS08411| and |FRAME: HS07200| subunits, activates NEDD8 in an ATP-dependent reaction by forming a high-energy thioester intermediate between NEDD8 and one of its cysteine residues |CITS: [14690597]|. The activated NEDD8 is subsequently transferred to a cysteine residue of |FRAME: NEDD8-carrier-proteins-E2| (such as the human |FRAME: HS05432| and UBE2F |CITS: [19250909]|), and is eventually conjugated to a lysine residue of specific substrates in the presence of the appropriate E3 transferase |CITS: [9694792][10207026]|., The primary known substrates of NEDD8 modification are the |FRAME: Cullins cullin| subunits of some forms of |FRAME: EC-2.3.2.27| that are not able to bind a protein substrate directly. These E3 proteins form a complex with a cullin protein and a substrate recognition subunit (SRS), and often include an adaptor that links the SRS to the complex. The complexes are known as CRLs for Cullin-RING ubiquitin Ligases (although technically they are not ligases). Within the CRL complexes, the |FRAME: Cullins cullin| protein serves as a scaffold that connects the E3 trransferase and the adapter/substrate-binding protein sub-complex |CITS: [15688063]|. However, the complex is not active until a conserved lysine residue of the cullin protein is neddylated |CITS: [10781063][10713156][15021886]|., CRLs comprise the largest known category of ubiquitin ligases, and regulate an extensive number of dynamic cellular processes, including multiple aspects of the cell cycle, transcription, signal transduction, and development |CITS: [18282298]|. By controling the activity of the CRLs, neddylation helps regulate these processes., In the absence of NEDD8, the cullin protein binds the CAND1 protein, which prevents the cullin from binding the |FRAME: HS03694| adapter protein and form a functional complex |CITS: [12504026][15537541]|. The binding of NEDD8 to a C-terminal lysine residue results in a conformation change, dissociating CAND1 and enabling the formation of an active complex |CITS: [12504025]|., Several proteases, including the human UCHL1, UCHL3, USP21, COP9 , and NEDP1 proteins, can remove NEDD8 from its protein conjugates.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| is a non-standard amino acid that is not normally incorporated into proteins during protein synthesis. Citrulline was first isolated from |FRAME:TAX-3653| (watermelon) in 1914 |CITS: [Koga14]|. It was re-isolated in 1930, at which time its chemical formula was determined and it was named (after the Latin name of the watermelon) |CITS: [Wada30]|., Free citrulline is formed mainly by catabolism of amino acids in the small intestine, as an intermediate in the conversion of ammonia to urea in the |FRAME:PWY-4984|, and as a by-product during the production of nitric oxide (see |FRAME:PWY-4983|). In addition, citrulline is also formed by modification of arginine residues in proteins (see |FRAME: PWY-4921|)., About This Pathway, Most of the |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| circulating in the blood of mammals comes from |FRAME: GLN| conversion in enterocytes, the intetsinal absorptive cells found in the mucosa of the small intestine. Several other amino acids can also act as citrulline precursors, including |FRAME: GLT|, |FRAME: PRO|, and |FRAME: ARG|. In rats, 28% of these metabolized amino acids are converted into |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|., Two |FRAME: GLT| molecules are required for the synthesis of each |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| molecule, only one of which can be substituted by another amino acid., The |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| that is formed in the intestinal mucosa enters the blood stream, and reaches the kidneys, where it is converted into |FRAME: ARG| (see |FRAME:PWY-5004|). In adults, this citrulline to arginine conversion provides the body's full arginine requirements |CITS:[16082501]|. About 83% of the citrulline released from the intestine is metabolized by the kidneys |CITS:[7325229]|, and the rest is converted to |FRAME: ARG| that is used for |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| production within other tissues (in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.39|, which regenerates |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE|)., In newborn mammals, which have a much larger need for |FRAME: ARG|, |FRAME: PRO| is the main source of |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| synthesis in the gut |CITS:[10329997]|. In addition, in new borns conversion of citrulline to arginine is not limited to the kidneys, and occurs in the intestinal mucosa as well., Inhibition of intestinal citrulline synthesis causes severe growth retardation |CITS:[4083357]|.

Summary: The |FRAME: Erinacines erinacines| are a family of diterpenes based on a cyathane skeleton and modified with a xylose sugar. Many of these compounds demonstrate unique biological activities such as potent stimulating activity for nerve-growth-factor synthesis |CITS: [Kawagishi94][Kawagishi96][Kawagishi96b][11193408]| and agonistic activity towards the κ opioid receptor |CITS: [9918390]|., Studies in the late 1970s concluded that the initially-formed intermediate during erinacines biosynthesis is |FRAME: CPD-26030| |CITS: [Ayer79]|, and this conclusion was confirmed in 2001 with the isolation of the compound from the erinacine-producing basidiomycete |FRAME: TAX-91752| |CITS: [Kenmoku01]|. The terpene cyclase that catalyzes the formation of this compound was discovered in 2017, along with the erinacine biosynthetic gene cluster |CITS: [28371074]|. Subsequent cloning and expression of the genes in the Ascomycota host |FRAME: TAX-5062| enabled the elucidation of the full biosynthetic pathway leading to production of |FRAME: CPD-26042| |CITS: [31535864]|., Following the generation of |FRAME: CPD-26030|, the pathway continues with three successive hydroxylations carried out by three different cytochrome P450 enzymes, forming |FRAME: CPD-26039|. The actions of an acetyltransferase (|FRAME: G-124259 EriL|) and a xyloxyltransferase (|FRAME: G-124260 EriJ|) result in production of |FRAME: CPD-26042| |CITS: [31535864]|. The glycosylation of C14 is a branch point in the production of erinacines and cyathins. Xyloxylation by EriJ leads to erinacine production. Alternatively, the hydroxyl group at C14 could be oxidized to an oxo group, leading to production of cyathins (see |FRAME: PWY-8409|)., Later steps in the pathway were clarified later by expressing different genes in |FRAME: TAX-4932|. An |FRAME: MONOMER-124263| (EriM) converts |FRAME: CPD-26042| to |FRAME: CPD-26056|. The formation of the aldehyde group promotes a series of non-enzaymatic rearrangements, resulting in formation of several products, including |FRAME: CPD-26058|, |FRAME: CPD-26055|, and |FRAME: CPD-26067|. Several NADP(H)-dependent reductases catalyzed formation of additional unnatural erincines in the yeast host, such as |FRAME: CPD-26135|, though their in vivo activities have not been defined yet |CITS: [34589407]|.

General Background, Thousands of nonsteroidal triterpenes have been identified and, in spite of their elusive functions,, the ubiquity of these compounds among higher plants implies that they are essential., Lupeol is a pentacyclic triterpene present in plants but not fungi and animals. Lupeol displays, anti-inflammatory properties when administered to rats, yet, unlike other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory, drugs, had no antinociceptive, anti-pyretic and ulcerogenic actions |CITS:[11378285]|. Lupeol was also, reported to be involved in apoptosis |CITS:[14719056]|. , Key Notes on the Enzymes: , Lupeol is synthesized by oxidosqualene cyclases from oxidosqualene. These enzymes catalyze, the cyclization, rearrangement and deprotonation of oxidosqualene to simultaneously form a variety, of triterpene compounds in varying amounts. The first lupeol synthase identified from, |FRAME: ORG-5993| was thus shown to catalyze the formation of -not only- lupeol but |FRAME:CPD-6951|,, |FRAME:CPD-6948|, |FRAME:GERMANICOL|, |FRAME:CPD-6949| and |FRAME:CPD-6950|, |CITS:[10930257]|.

Summary: Mycinamicins are macrolide antibiotics produced by the actinomycete |FRAME: TAX-28040| that have shown impressive activities against a spectrum of Gram-positive strains, especially some antibiotic-resistant human pathogens |CITS: [7410205][7275814][7275809][7332707][7142027][6833134][4008346][4030500][1761425][1548179]|., They are composed of a 16-membered macrolactone ring and two sugars, |FRAME: CPD-13780| and |FRAME: Mycinopyranose mycinose|, at the C-5 and C-21 positions, respectively., Wild-type |FRAME: TAX-28040| mainly produces |FRAME: CPD-15940|, |FRAME: CPD-13822|, |FRAME: CPD-13821| and |FRAME: CPD-13824| |CITS: [7410205]|, whereas a high producing industrial strain produces |FRAME: CPD-15940| and |FRAME: CPD-13822| as its two major products |CITS: [9841223]|., Early genetic work with |FRAME: TAX-28040| identified two genes that confer resistance to the antibiotics, both of which putatively encode 23S rRNA methyltranferases. One of the genes is myrA, which, when tested on |FRAME: TAX-1916|, conferred strong resistance to mycinamicin and |FRAME: TYLOSIN|, but not to |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycin| or |FRAME: CPD-15942|. The other is myrB, which, when tested on |FRAME: TAX-146923|, conferred resistance to all macrolide, lincosamide and streptogramine B antibiotics |CITS: [8163173]|. In the course of cloning the resistance genes, it was found that they are located in a large cluster of mycinamicin biosynthesis genes |CITS: [8163162]|. The cluster has been sequenced in its entirety |CITS: [Inouye95][12583909]|, and the genes and their products were studied, most of them at the biochemical level, to confirm the pathway shown here., The pathway, which resembles that of |FRAME: TYLOSIN|, starts with a very large ployketide synthase complex that condenses 3 molecules of |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| and 5 molecules of |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| to form |FRAME: CPD-15934|, the macrolide aglycone that contains one hydroxyl group at C5. A glycosyltransferase (|FRAME: G-17863|) transfers a D-desosamin sugar from |FRAME: CPD-13776| to the hydroxyl group |CITS: [15612702]|. A cytochrome P450 enzyme (|FRAME: G-17864|) converts the methyl group at C21 to a methoxy group |CITS: [18804032]|, to which a |FRAME: CPD-15941| sugar is attached by a second glycosyltransferase (|FRAME: G-17865|). Two methyltranferases (|FRAME: G-17866| and |FRAME: G-17867|) add methyl groups to the latter sugar, converting it sequentially to |FRAME: javose| and |FRAME: Mycinose| |CITS: [19415708][20158522]|., The last enzyme in the pathway is a second cytochrome P450, encoded by |FRAME: G-17868|, which catalyzes both C12-C13 epoxidation and C14 hydroxylation. When the enzyme catalyzes epoxidation of |FRAME: CPD-13821|, it forms one of the final products, |FRAME: CPD-15940|. When catalyzing hydroxylation of the same compound, it forms an intermediate which it then epoxidates to form the other final product, |FRAME: CPD-13822| |CITS: [7808395][18804032][22547618][22952225]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-110 "Salicylic acid"| (salicylate; SA) is an aromatic compound commonly found throughout the plant kingdom that is also found in some bacteria., In plants |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| affects numerous biological and physiological processes, including plant defense (via the systematic acquired resistance system |CITS: [15283665][12873532]|), allelopathy, flowering, and stomatal movement |CITS: [SCHULZ93]|. Given its important signaling role, plants often chemically modify |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| by attaching glycosyl, methyl, or other groups to |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| to alters its activity, volatility, or other properties |CITS [PIERPOINT94][SCHULZ93]|. One of the potential glucose-conjugates |FRAME: CPD-12629| (SGE), has been detected in a number of plant species, including |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [18248508]|, |FRAME: TAX-4097|, |FRAME: TAX-4075|, and Thlaspi goesingense|CITS: [15734913]|. The specific biological role of |FRAME: CPD-12629 SGE| is still under investigation. Unlike the other SA glucose, |FRAME: CPD-12628| (SAG), SGE is not expected to be a more water soluable form of the compound, and there is evidence that it is not accepted by the vacuolar transporters that require a negative charge |CITS: [15032822][15871031]|. SGE may serve as a high energy intermediate form of |FRAME: CPD-110 SA| that can be used in additional biochemical pathways, or, it may be another storage form of this important signaling compound |CITS: [18248508]|. , About This Pathway, The formation of |FRAME: CPD-12629 SGE| has been demonstrated in vitro using glucosyltransferases in several plant species, including |FRAME: TAX-35883| |CITS: [17692286]|, |FRAME: TAX-4097| |CITS: [10593966]|, and |FRAME: ORG-5993| |CITS: [18248508]|. In general, the enzymes from these organisms do not have high substrate specificity which may be a beneficial trait that allows the enzymes to detoxify numerous potential xenobiotics.

Summary: The genes necessary for histidine biosynthesis have been identified in many bacteria, fungi, plants,, and archaea. The pathway in all of these organisms is identical, with small differences in some of, the enzymes used. Histidine is an essential amino acid, and is not synthesized by mammals., A few differences between different organisms concern whether the enzymes are mono- or bifunctional. One such case is the enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.15|. Some organisms, including  |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: TAX-90371| and |FRAME: TAX-727|, have a bifunctional enzyme, with the C-terminal domain exhibiting |FRAME:IMIDPHOSDEHYD-ENZRXN| (EC 4.2.1.19) activity. These enzymes belong to the DDDD phosphohydrolase/phosphotransferase superfamily. Other organisms have separate monofunctional enzymes catalyzing these two reactions. Monofunctional histidinol-phosphate phosphatases belong to either the PHP (polymerase and histidinol phosphatase) superfamily, as in the case of |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: TAX-4932| and |FRAME: TAX-300852| |CITS: [14993698]|, or to the DDDD superfamily, as in the case of the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-342948| NA1 |CITS: [18223080]|., Another such case concerns the conversion of |FRAME:PHOSPHORIBULOSYL-FORMIMINO-AICAR-P| (BBM III) to |FRAME:D-ERYTHRO-IMIDAZOLE-GLYCEROL-P| (IGP) and |FRAME:AICAR| (AICAR), which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.3.2.10|. This process requires two catalytic functions, including the transfer of an amide from |FRAME: GLN| and a cyclization reaction. In prokaryotes, these two catalytic activities are encoded by two genes whose products form a complex. In yeast and plants, this conversion is catalyzed by a single bifunctional enzyme., In all organisms operating the pathway, the enzyme catalyzing the first step is feedback-inhibited  by |FRAME: HIS|. In plants, the entire pathway is located inside the chloroplast |CITS: [16547652]|.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain of 11 prenyl units in trans form. This product should not be confused with |FRAME: UNDECAPRENYL-DIPHOSPHATE|, which serves an entirely different role in the cell, and whose biosynthesis is described in |FRAME: PWY-5785|., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme. Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones. The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length. However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain length. For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|.

Names: [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster biosynthesis (bacterial IscS system) // [Fe-S] cluster biosynthesis // [2Fe-2S] cluster biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, |FRAME: FeS-Centers "Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters"| are cofators of |FRAME: FeS-Proteins "iron-sulfur proteins"| and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein., Several cluster types have been described, including |FRAME: CPD-6|, |FRAME: CPD-23|, |FRAME: 3FE-4S| and |FRAME: CPD-7|. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as |FRAME: CPD0-1098|, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular |FRAME: CPD-6| are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons., Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called |FRAME: Ferredoxins ferredoxins|. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. , In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, Fe-S clusters are also known to participate in, the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes, and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression |CITS: [16466637]|., The biosynthesis of Fe-S clusters in a living cell is a highly evolved process, requiring the assistance of complex assemblies of proteins. At present, three different biogenesis systems have been identified. The ISC (iron-sulfur cluster) system, which is present in α-, β-, and γ-proteobacteria as well as in mitochondria of eukaryotes, the SUF (sulfur mobilization) system, which is found in a wide range of bacteria (including cyanobacteria), archaea, and plastids of plants, and the NIF (nitrogen fixation) system, which is used in the synthesis of nitrogenase, but also occurs in nondiazotrophic ε-proteobacteria., It should be noted that the mitochondrial ISC system comprises more proteins than in bacteria, but the underlying mechanistic principles are analogous. This pathway describes the bacterial ISC system., About This Pathway, Multiple pathways have been proposed over the years, differing in the order and nature of events. The pathway shown here is based on recent work (such as |CITS: [36121382][39870763]|) and may contradict earlier reports., All three systems have in common two key proteins - |FRAME: L-Cysteine-Desulfurases| (|FRAME: G7325 IscS|/|FRAME: HS01304|, |FRAME: G6906 SufS| or NifS) and |FRAME: Iron-Sulfur-Cluster-Scaffold-Proteins "a scaffold protein"| (|FRAME: G7324 IscU|, SufU or NifU)., The IscS L-cysteine desulfurase is a |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|-dependent homodimeric enzyme that converts the amino-acid |FRAME: CYS| to |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|, liberating a sulfur atom that is covalently bound as a persulfide at a conserved Cys residue of the enzyme., The IcsU scaffold protein, which also contains Cys residues, serves as a platform for the assembly of Fe-S clusters. The scaffold protein exists in equilibrium between two conformational states: a more structured state (S) and a partially disordered state (D) |CITS: [12909018][14688265][19492851]|. , Other proteins that are essential for the IscS pathway are ferredoxin (Fdx or FDX2) and ferredoxin reductase (FdxR or FDXR). , The process begins with the binding of a single Fe2+ ion by the scaffold protein IscU |CITS: [32131593][36121382]|. The protein frataxin (|FRAME: EG11653 CyaY| in bacteria, |FRAME: G3O-29519| in yeast, FXN in humans) was found to contribute to iron transfer, and may act as a metallochaperone, but its weak iron binding activity and other observations suggest that its main role may be to maintain iron homeostasis under oxidative stress |CITS: [20956517][19932164][20522547]|. Another candidate for iron delivery is |FRAME: EG12132|, which has a strong binding activity for mononuclear iron, and has been shown to provide iron to the scaffold protein |FRAME: G7324 IscU| in the presence of |FRAME: G7325 IscS| and L-cysteine |CITS: [14720122][15828873][16877383]|., Next, two iron-bound IscU monomers bind to an IscS dimer, forming a tetrameric structure. Sulfur atoms are transferred by the desulfurase from L-cysteine to a receptor cysteine side chain of the scaffold proteins, forming persulfides |CITS: [11577100]|. The persulfide binds to the iron center, forming an iron-persulfide intermediate. Ferredoxin (Fdx) reduces the persulfide in IscU into a sulfide ion, leading to formation of a [1Fe-1S] precursor cluster. The four electrons, which are derived from NADPH, are transferred to Fdx by |FRAME: EC-1.18.1.2|. The iron center in the [1Fe-1S] precursor cluster is in the +2 redox state., The IscU monomers that carry the [1Fe-1S] cluster are released from the tetrameric complex by exchange with un-modified iron-bound IscU monomers. The released monomers dimerize in a process that results in the merging of the two [1Fe-1S] precursor clusters into a single [2Fe-2S] cluster bridging the two monomer. The fusion of two [1Fe-1S] precursors into the [2Fe-2S] cluster does not involve electron transfer, resulting in an unstable super-reduced form ([2Fe-2S]0), which is subsequently oxidized to the normal [2Fe-2S]2+ state with Fdx acting as the electron acceptor. The [2Fe-2S] cluster migrates onto one subunit of the dimer, resulting in dissociation of the second monomer, leaving one of the IscU monomers carrying the cluster and the other one in an apo state |CITS: [39870763]|., The mechanism described above may also apply to the mitochondrial eukaryotic system. However, as of 2025 this has not been confirmed., At this point the complex is ready to transfer its [2Fe-2S] cluster to a receipient protein. In |FRAME: TAX-562| this process involves the chaperone proteins |FRAME: EG12130 HscA| and |FRAME: EG12131 HscB| (the former is an ATPase with a bound ATP molecule), that form a complex with the scaffold protein. When a suitable acceptor protein approaches the complex one or two of its thiol groups attack the cluster's iron atoms, liberating one or two of the scaffold protein cluster ligands and leading to a conformational change in HscB that activates the ATPase activity of HscA. Cleavage of the bound ATP leads to an additional conformational change that results in a fundumental change |CITS: [11053447][15485839]|. A binding site on the ligand binding domain of the chaperone protein opens up and binds the scaffold protein in its disordered state. The conversion of the scaffold protein to its disordered state releases both the 2Fe-2S cluster, which is transferred to the acceptor protein, and HscB., About [4Fe-4S] clusters biosynthesis, While less is known about the synthesis of [4Fe-4S] clusters, it seems that they are formed on the same scaffold proteins that are used for [2Fe-2S] clusters synthesis. These proteins are dimeric, and since a [2Fe-2S] cluster is formed within a single subunit, a dimeric scaffold protein can form two such clusters. Some evidence suggests that [4Fe-4S] clusters are formed at the subunit interface, involving two electron reductive coupling of the two adjacent [2Fe-2S] clusters |CITS: [19021507]|., The |FRAME: G7748 NfuA| protein has been proposed to be an intermediate [4Fe-4S] cluster carrier or chaperone for clusters assembled on |FRAME: G7324 IscU| |CITS: [18339629]| or act as a scaffold protein itself in some species |CITS: [15031412][15361144]|. The presence of |FRAME: EG12130| and |FRAME: EG12131| had no effect on the rate of [4Fe-4S] cluster transfer from |FRAME: G7324| to apo aconitase, suggesting different conformations for the [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] cluster-bound forms of |FRAME: G7324 IscU|, with only the former having the ability to interact productively with |FRAME: EG12130 HscA| |CITS: [17506526]|.

Summary: Suberin is a polymeric plant cell wall constituent mainly found in the epidermal tissues of underground plant parts. Suberin consists of two domains, a polyaromatic and a polyaliphatic domain. The polyaromatics are predominately located within the primary cell wall, and the polyaliphatics are located between the primary cell wall and the plasmalemma. The two domains are supposed to be cross-linked. The exact qualitative and quantitative composition of suberin monomers varies in different species. The major monomers found in the potato tuber polyaliphatics are ω-hydroxyacids (mainly |FRAME: 18-HYDROXYOLEATE|) and α,ω-diacids (mainly |FRAME: OCTADEC-9-ENE-118-DIOIC-ACID|). The monomers of the polyaromatics are hydroxycinnamic acids and derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-440| is a major aromatic monomer found in suberized potato tubers. In addition to the aromatics and aliphatics components, glycerol has been reported a major suberin component. The role of glycerol is proposed to interlink aliphatic monomers, and possibly also to link polyaliphatics to polyaromatics, during suberin polymer assembly |CITS: [17259262]|. The polymerization step of aromatic monomers has been shown to involve a peroxidase reaction.  , Note that the biosynthesis of suberin aliphatic monomers shares the same upstream reactions with |FRAME: PWY-321|, and the biosynthesis of the aromatic monomers shares the same upstream reactions with |FRAME: PWY-361 "lignin biosynthesis"|. Although both suberin and cutin contain aliphatic monomers, suberin differs from cutin by the chain length of aliphatic monomers, which can range from C16 to C32 (cutin only contains C16-C18). , The pathway depicted here represents the biosynthesis of the major suberin monomers, namely |FRAME: 18-HYDROXYOLEATE|, |FRAME: OCTADEC-9-ENE-118-DIOIC-ACID|, and |FRAME: CPD-440|, characterized in potato, as well as very long chain aliphatic monomers found in many plants. It also shows the production of |FRAME: 16-HYDROXYPALMITATE|, a precursor of an important component of aromatic suberin in Arabidopsis  |CITS:[19759341][    19846769]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is an essential trace element for many (but not all) organisms. For example mammals require selenium, but some protists, such as |FRAME:TAX-5691|, do not |CITS: [19279205]|. The green alga |FRAME: TAX-3055| contains selenoproteins, but land plants and yeast do not |CITS: [12110581]|. The best studied biological form of |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is the amino acid |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| (sec). Examples for selenoproteins include |FRAME: EC-1.12.98.1|, |FRAME: EC-1.12.98.3|, |FRAME: EC-1.12.2.1| and |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.12|. For more selenoproteins see MetaCyc pages for |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| and |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE|, which contain links to enzymes for which |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is functionally important. |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| is also present in selenonucleosides that have been identified in bacterial tRNAs (reviewed in |CITS: [19344749]|)., In |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| the thiol group of |FRAME: CYS| is replaced by a selenol group. |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| is considered to be the 21st genetically encoded amino acid because it is co-translationally inserted into nacent polypeptide chains at an in-frame UGA nonsnense codon in the mRNA. This is done by a decoding mechanism that involves a selenocysteine insertion sequence (SECIS) element in the mRNA and coordinated interactions between RNA-protein complexes. A model for the role of these cytoplasmic and nuclear supramolecular complex interactions in |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| biosynthesis has been proposed |CITS: [16508009]|. The function of |FRAME: L-SELENOCYSTEINE| in proteins remains to be completely defined, although its occurrence in the active site of some redox-active enzymes suggests a role in their catalytic mechanism. There are two known pathways for selenocysteine biosynthesis. One is found in bacteria (see pathway |FRAME: PWY0-901|) and the other is found in archaea and eukaryotes (this pathway), which has interesting phylogenetic implications (reviewed in |CITS: [19344749]|)., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here is found in some archaea and eukaryotes, with the best studied organisms being certain methanogens and mammals |CITS: [17194211]|. It is an indirect tRNA-dependent pathway for amino acid biosynthesis in which the amino acid is synthesized on its tRNA. A non-cognate amino acid is first attached to the tRNA and is then converted to the cognate amino acid by tRNA-dependent modifying enzymes. Summary: General Background, Lactic acid fermentation is a process by which sugars such as glucose, fructose, and sucrose are converted into cellular energy and the metabolic byproduct lactate. It occurs in many bacteria and anaerobic lower eukaryotes, as well as in animal cells, such as muscle cells, in the absence of oxygen., In homolactic fermentation the only product is |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, and thus one molecule of glucose is ultimately converted to two such molecules., The lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are a group of Gram positive bacteria that produce lactate as the major end product of the fermentation of carbohydrates. The LAB were divided early on into two main groups, depending on their fermentation products. One group included those bacteria that convert carbohydrates essentially into lactate, while the other group included those producing, in addition, substantial quantities of volatile acids and carbon dioxide |CITS: [Orla-Jensen19]|., A few years after this initial classification was established the terms homo- and hetero-fermentative, respectively, were proposed for the two groups |CITS: [Kluyver24]|., It should be noted that at least some organisms are capable of shifting from one mode of fermentation to the other depending on oxygen or nutrient availability |CITS: [108249]|., About This Pathway, In homolactic fermentation sugars are metabolized via the Embden-Myerhof glycolytic pathway to pyruvate, which is then converted to lactate., Sugars can enter bacterial cells in two different mechanisms. In most homofermentative strains sugars are transported by a sugar phosphotransferase system (PTS) that phosphorylates the sugar during transport. |FRAME: GLC| is phosphorylated to |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, while |FRAME:FRU| is usually phosphorylated to |FRAME:FRU1P| (although some, PTSs were reported to generate |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| |CITS: [8246840][8550437][10627040]|)., The second mechanism involves the transport of sugars via a permease, in which case they are not phophorylated., All sugars are then activated to |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| through different routes, depending on the nature of the sugar and on the way it enters the cell. Intracellular fructose (that entered by a permease) is phosphorylated first to fructose-6-phosphate, then to fructose-1,6-biphosphate., Intracellular glucose (that entered by a permease) is first phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate, isomerized to fructose-6-phosphate, and finally phosphorylated to fructose-1,6-biphosphate |CITS: [16741753]|., Fructose-6-phosphate and fructose-1-phosphate (that entered via a PTS) are both phosphorylated to fructose-1,6-biphosphate by |FRAME: CPLX-7324| and |FRAME:MONOMER-13047|, respectively, and glucose-6-phosphate (that entered via a PTS) is isomerized to fructose-6-phosphate, and finally phosphorylated to fructose-1,6-biphosphate., The common product, fructose-1,6-biphosphate, is processed via the Embden-Meyerhof (EM) pathway to pyruvate, which is then converted to lactate, the the sole end-product of homolactic fermentation |CITS: [8550437]|. Fructose-1,6-biphosphate is an important regulator of the pathway, being a positive effector of |FRAME:CPLX-7323| |CITS: [Thompson87]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Pacidamycins pacidamycins| are a family of uridyl-peptide antibiotics. The first 7 compounds (pacidamycin 1-7) were discovered in a strain of |FRAME: TAX-116188| isolated from a soil sample collected at Offenburg, Germany. When discovered, the compounds were reported to exhibit highly specific activity only against |FRAME: TAX-287|, though a high level of resistance developed quite quickly |CITS: [2498263]|. Analysis of their structures has shown that the pacidamycins are composed of a pseudopeptide backbone (which contains 2S,3S-diaminobutanoate) linked by a unique exocyclic enamide to an atypical 3'-deoxyuridine nucleoside. They differ mostly in their terminal amino acid residues |CITS: [2498264]|. Additional pacidamycins (D, 4N and 5T) were reported in 2000 from a different strain |CITS: [11217807]|., The pacidamycins were reported to inhibit |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.13| (mraY) |CITS: [10557368][16789873]|. Dihydropacidamycins, produced synthetically by hydrogenation of the C(4') exocyclic olefin, were reported to have antimicrobial activity similar to that of the natural products, while being effective against additional Gram-negative pathogens |CITS: [11456620][12951115]|., About This Pathway, The pacidamycin gene cluster was identified twice (independently) in 2010 |CITS: [20665770][20826445]|. The cluster consists of several highly dissociated non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) domains and modules, which many of the proteins consisting of only a single domain. An initial pathway has been proposed at the time |CITS: [20826445]|, and has been revised within a year to reflect additional information about the participating enzymes |CITS: [21417270]|., A set of nine enzymes was shown to be sufficient for assembly of tetrapeptide pacidamycins such as |FRAME: CPD-27221| |CITS: [21417270]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8527|). The enzyme required for addition of the fifth amino acid, PacB, was identified shortly after |CITS: [21746899]|. Another study from the same year unveiled how the dehydroaminonucleoside component |FRAME: CPD-27224| is formed from |FRAME: URIDINE| by three enzymes |CITS: [21861518]|., The formation of last remaining component, |FRAME: CPD-27226|, from |FRAME: THR| was discovered only in 2024, as described in |FRAME: PWY-8526| |CITS: [38456538]|.

Summary: General Background, The dinucleotides NAD and NADP are ubiquitous electron carriers and coenzymes that participate in almost every metabolic pathway in the cell |CITS: [Moat87][16714307]|. The biosynthesis of NAD in plants is achieved via two major routes - a de novo biosynthesis (see |FRAME:PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|) and a salvage pathway (this pathway). The salvage pathway shown here summarizes the various routes of degradation and salvage of pyridine compounds that have been reported from plants |CITS: [4306794]|. Depending on the plant species investigated and/or environmental conditions, this cycle may involve a varying number of steps |CITS: [Wagner86b][Zheng04][15837705][Ashihara05]|. , The pyridine nucleotide cycling pathway ensures the homeostatic replenishment of NAD when the coenzyme has been involved in NAD consuming reactions. The pathway is fairly similar to the bacterial variant (|FRAME:PYRIDNUCSAL-PWY|) with the exception that some enzymes, e.g. NMN amidohydrolase, NAD synthase (NH3-dependent) have not been identified in plants, and that plants are capable of by-passing enzymes under certain conditions, hence conferring a broader adaptability |CITS: [16714307]|. , About This Pathway, The anaplerotic enzyme of the pyridine nucleotide cycle is |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.19| (QPRtase) (|FRAME:PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY|) forming |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE| (nicotinate mononucleotide, NaMN) which may be considered as the start compound of this cycle |CITS: [Wagner84]| |CITS: [11198422]|. From there two different routes can be taken to produce |FRAME: NIACINE| (vitamin B3), an important intermediate that gives rise to several secondary metabolites, e.g. trigonelline (|FRAME:PWY-5110|). , An enzyme catalyzing a direct conversion of |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE| to nicotinate, |FRAME: EC-3.2.2.M4|, has been partially purified from tobacco. However, the existence of that enzyme has not been proven., Another route that comprises several enzymatic steps, including the formation of the main intermediates nicotinate adenine dinucleotide (NaAD), NAD, nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) and nicotinamide, has been confirmed. The enzyme that catalyzes the final step of the formation of nicotinate from nicotinamide, |FRAME: EC-3.5.1.19|, has been identified in several plants |CITS: [Wagner86b][13790768][Ashihara05][15837705]|. The reverse conversion, from |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| to |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.12|, has not been detected in plants |CITS: [Hunt04][15837705]|., The final step, closing the cycle by converting |FRAME: NIACINE| to |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE| (NaMN), is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.21| |CITS: [Wagner86][16658750]|. This enzyme expresses a high affinity towards |FRAME: NIACINE|. Unlike the enzyme from animals, the plant enzyme does not accept nicotinamide |CITS: [Wagner86b]|., The pathway displays two additional routes that can be taken (1) from |FRAME: NICOTINAMIDE_NUCLEOTIDE| to |FRAME: NIACINAMIDE| and (2) from |FRAME: NIACINE| to |FRAME: NICOTINATE_NUCLEOTIDE|, that proceed via a nucleotide riboside intermediate. The nucleoside ribosides, as well as some of the associated enzyme activities, have been found in plants |CITS: [16714307][Hunt04][15837705][Polya75][6295388]|, but the enzymes remain to be further characterized.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: HIS| can be catabolized by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms in two principal routes., The main difference between these two routes is the first step, which is performed by either, a |FRAME: CPLX-6925| (as in this pathway) or a histidine transaminase (|FRAME: HISTDEG-PWY| and, |FRAME: PWY-5031|)., At least three different flavors of |FRAME: CPLX-6925|-based pathways have been found so far., All proceed in a similar manner up to the intermediate |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE|., Three steps, catalyzed by distinct enzymes, lead to this intermediate., In the first step |FRAME: HIS| is split into |FRAME: UROCANATE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA| by, a |FRAME: CPLX-6925| |CITS: [14367318][12980948]|; Next |FRAME: UROCANATE|, is converted to |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| by |FRAME: CPLX-981|, |CITS: [13587518][13821933]|; and finally, |FRAME: 4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| is converted to, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| by |FRAME: HUTIBACSU-MONOMER| |CITS: [13587518], [13739526]|., In all three flavors |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is further degraded to |FRAME: GLT|., However, the mechanism of |FRAME: GLT| production is different in the three pathways. , In several Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-90371|,, |FRAME: TAX-573|, |FRAME: TAX-548| and |FRAME: TAX-1423|, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE|, is split into |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: FORMAMIDE| |CITS: [14367318]|; the latter compound, does not appear to be metabolized further (|FRAME: HISDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [13416179]|. , In fluorescent Pseudomonads, including |FRAME: TAX-303|, |FRAME: TAX-294| and |FRAME: TAX-287|,, |FRAME: N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE| is first hydrolyzed to |FRAME: AMMONIA| and , |FRAME: CPD-600|, which in turn is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLT| and |FRAME: FORMATE|, (|FRAME: PWY-5028|) |CITS: [13211593][4290562]|; the |FRAME: FORMATE| can serve as, a source of single carbon compounds |CITS: [13563517]|. , Finally, in the livers of mammals |FRAME: GLT| is generated by the transfer of the formimino group to, |FRAME: THF| (|FRAME: PWY-5030|). |FRAME: THF| is metabolized further, transferring, the formyl moiety to the pool of single carbon compounds |CITS: [13672973]|., About This Pathway, Urocanic acid was first isolated in 1874 by the chemist M. Jaffe from the urine of a dog, hence the name, (latin: urina = urine, and |FRAME:TAX-9611| = dog) |CITS: [7944380]|., Unfortunately the dog escaped before Jaffe was able identify the structure., The identity and structure of the substance was eventually revealed in 1912 by Hunter, who was the first, to suggest that it is an intermediate in the catabolism of |FRAME: HIS| |CITS: [Hunter12]|., Edlbacher identified the locus of histidine degradation as the liver of various animals, and named the, enzyme that degrades |FRAME: HIS| to |FRAME: GLT| "histidase" |CITS: [Edlbacher26][Edlbacher30]|., In 1930 Kauffmann and Mislowitzer defined histidase more correctly, as the enzyme that converts, |FRAME: HIS| to |FRAME: UROCANATE| |CITS: [Kauffmann30]|., After a lengthy debate concerning the nature of the third intermediate, it was finally, shown conclusively that it is |FRAME:N-FORMIMINO-L-GLUTAMATE | by Borek and Waelsch, |CITS: [13117923]|. Finally, Revel and Magasanik discovered an additional intermediate, and, suggested that it is |FRAME:4-IMIDAZOLONE-5-PROPIONATE| |CITS: [13587518]|. This suggestion, was confirmed with the isolation of the substance |CITS: [13804907]|, thus establishing the pathway., This pathway has been demonstrated in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria,, including |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [14367318]|, |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS: [4899017][4930059]|,, |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [6321433]| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [Magasanik71]|., The pathway is subject to a strong catabolite repression, preventing bacteria from using |FRAME: HIS|, as a nitrogen source if |FRAME: GLC| or |FRAME: SUC| are present in the growth medium, |CITS: [4990471]|. Summary: General Background, The uronic acid |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is an aldose sugar containing a carboxyl group. It is the main monomeric constituent of pectin (see |FRAME: Pectin|), a heteropolymer present the cell walls of dicotyledonous plants. In pectin the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| monomers are in the α-pyranose form connected through a 1,4 linkage to form long chains. Homogalacturonan (see |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl|) is the simplest form of pectin. Other forms are rhamnogalacturonan-I, rhamnogalacturonan-II and xylogalacturonan (see |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan|) (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-1081| |FRAME: PWY-1061| |FRAME: PWY-5980|). In natural pectin the majority of the carboxyl groups of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| are methyl esters. Some plants also contain acetylated galacturonate residues. Non-esterified carboxyl groups may be linked through divalent cations such as |FRAME: MG+2| or |FRAME: CA+2|, causing pectin to form a gel., The complete biodegradation of pectin requires a variety of enzymes including hydrolases for polygalacturonan, rhamnogalacturonans and xylogalacturonan; lyases for pectin, pectate (see |FRAME: PECTATE|) and rhamnogalacturonan; and pectin methylesterases and acetyl esterases. Saprophytic and phytopathogenic fungi and bacteria can produce variety of extracellular and intracellular enzymes that degrade pectin and its homogalacturonan, rhamnogalacturonan and xylogalacturonan derivatives. In |CITS: [19618506]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19159926] [REIGNAULT08] [8905080]|., Pectin is used in the animal feed industry and in the food industry as a gelling agent. In ruminants, bacterial and fungal enzymes in the digestive tract aid its digestion. There is commercial interest in pectin-degrading enzymes to convert the pectin-rich by-products from citrus peel and sugar beet processing to higher value material. Pectinolytic enzymes such as esterases, hydrolases and lyases, are also used in other industries that require the processing of pectin. Reviewed in |CITS: [19159926]|., |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is an important carbon source for microorganisms that catabolize plant material. Bacterial pathways for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation have been described. |FRAME:TAX-562| uses the isomerase pathway (see |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|). |FRAME: TAX-358| and |FRAME: TAX-80866| use an oxidative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6486|). A different pathway for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation has been described for eukaryotic filamentous fungi which appears to be evolutionarily conserved in the fungal subphylum |FRAME:TAX-147538| which includes |FRAME: TAX-5061|, |FRAME: TAX-162425 Emericella nidulans (previously known as Aspergillus nidulans)"| and |FRAME: TAX-51453|. In |CITS: [18768163]| and reviewed in |CITS: [19159926]| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, In this fungal pathway the degradation of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| occurs via L-compounds |CITS: [18768163]|. The first step is reductive. In |FRAME: TAX-5061| a reversible reaction catalyzed by a reductase that can utilize |FRAME: NADH| or |FRAME: NADPH| converts |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| to |FRAME: CPD0-1083|. This reductase is the product of gene GAAA in |FRAME: TAX-5061|, with an ortholog GAR2 in |FRAME: TAX-51453|. It is co-expressed in |FRAME: TAX-5061| along with GAAB encoding a L-galactonate dehydratase, and GAAC and GAAD encoding the putative aldolase and L-glyceraldehyde reductase, respectively. These genes are evolutionarily conserved in pectin-degrading filamentous fungi |CITS: [18768163]|. However, a previously identified enzyme encoded by GAR1 in |FRAME: TAX-51453| that only uses |FRAME: NADPH| may also participate this pathway |CITS: [16101307]|. It showed no nucleotide sequence similarity with GAAA |CITS: [18768163]|., The second step is a dehydration, followed by a reversible aldolase splitting of |FRAME: CPD-12349| to produce |FRAME: L-GLYCERALDEHYDE| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is utilized in many pathways. |FRAME: L-GLYCERALDEHYDE| is reduced to |FRAME: GLYCEROL|, which can be catabolized as indicated in the pathway link |CITS: [2033381]|. In |FRAME: TAX-51453| the product of gene gld1 was shown to catalyze this reaction and was |FRAME: NADPH|-specific making it a likely candidate for this pathway. Overall, it appears that the two physiologically unidirectional enzymes drive the pathway forward. Reviewed in |CITS: [19159926]|.
