Summary: Polyamine hydroxycinnamic acid conjugates (polyamine phenylpropanoid conjugates) belong to the larger group of hydroxycinnamic acid amides. Polyamine conjugates have been identified in flowers of many plant species. Their exact role has not been proved. They may offer pollen grains protection against environmental stresses such as UV irradiation as well as pathogen attack. The accumulation of polyamine conjugates in pollen has also been associated with fertility. Dihydroxyferuloyl-sinapoyl spermidine is the predominant polyamine conjugate found in Arabidopsis flowers buds |CITS: [19077165]|. The biosynthetic pathway leading to this spermidine conjugate has only been proposed recently. Biochemical and genetic data demonstrated the involvement of a spermidine hydroxycinnamoyl transferase (SHT), an O-methyltransferase (TSM1), and a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (CYP98A8). Similar gene expression profiles were found for SHT, TSM1 and CYP98A8.

Summary: General Background, All land animals and plants are protected by a functional barrier between the organism and the environment. In mammals the permeability barrier is localized in the stratum corneum, the outermost cellular layer of the epidermis. This barrier protects the organisms against water loss and the infiltration of pathogens and toxins., The stratum corneum is composed of terminally differentiated keratinocytes (called corneocytes), which are dead flattened cells packed with keratin filaments. The corneocytes are embedded in a matrix of extracellular lipid lamellae, consisting mainly of ceramides, free fatty acids, and cholesterol., 12 types of free ceramides and 3 types of protein-bound ceramides have been characterized from the human stratum corneum, 4 of which are |FRAME: Linoleate-Acylceramides acylceramides| |CITS: [23954553]|. Acylceramides are epidermis-specific ceramide species that consist of |FRAME: Ceramides| ester linked to |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|. The chain-length of the fatty acid within the ceramide moiety is extremely long (C28–C36), making acylceramides some of the most hydrophobic lipids in mammalian bodies |CITS: [28248318]|., Acylceramides are also important as precursors of protein-bound ceramides, which connect the lipid lamellae and the corneocytes. After the removal of |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID|, the exposed ω-hydroxyl group of acylceramide is covalently bound to corneocyte proteins, forming a corneocyte lipid envelope |CITS: [20937905]|. Both acylceramides, and protein-bound ceramides are important in epidermal barrier formation., Defects in acylceramide biosynthesis result in ichthyosis, a cutaneous disorder accompanied by dry, thickened, and scaly skin., About This Pathway, Acylceramide biosynthesis requires |FRAME: Ultra-long-chain-fatty-acids "ultra-long-chain fatty acids"| (ULCFAs), which have a chain length of C28 or longer. The synthesis of ULCFAs has not been characterized well, but they appear to be formed by the same machinery that produces |FRAME: Very-long-chain-fatty-acids "very-long-chain fatty acids"| (VLCFAs), which is located in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) |CITS: [1378993]|. The elongation process is catalyzed by a membrane-bound enzyme complex known as the elongase |CITS: [10907783]|. This complex catalyzes the sequential additions of C2 moieties from |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to preformed C18 acyl groups derived from the de novo fatty acid biosynthesis pathway. Each elongation cycle is composed of 4 reactions: condensation of |FRAME: ACYL-COA| and |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to form |FRAME: 3-KETOACYL-COA|, reduction to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXYACYL-COA|, dehydration to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA|, and a final reduction to yield a chain-elongated fatty acyl-CoA |CITS: [16564093][16950653]|., Multple cycles of the elongase system result in extension of the C18 acyl groups up to C36 (see |FRAME: PWY-7036| and |FRAME: PWY-8041|)., The next step in the acylceramide biosynthesis pathway is the ω-hydroxylation (hydroxylation of the carbon furthest from of the carboxyl end) of the ultra-long fatty acids. Because the hydroxylase (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.177|), encoded by the |FRAME: HS10422| gene, only acts on free acids and is inactive with acyl-CoAs, the CoA moiety needs to be removed by a hydrolase prior to the hydroxylation, and is added again following the hydroxylation |CITS: [26056268]|. The enzyme that ligates the ω-hydroxylated acids to CoA appears to be encoded by the |FRAME: HS09515| gene |CITS: [15653672]|., The pathway continues by formation of |FRAME: Omega-OH-UCL-Ceramides|. There are six ceramide synthases in mammals. However, only one of them, |FRAME: ENSG00000154227-MONOMER "ceramide synthase 3"| (CerS3), can accepts ultra-long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs |CITS: [20222015]|. The enzyme is found mainly in skin and testis |CITS: [16753040][18308723]|, and is highly expressed in keratinocytes, where it localizes at the interface between the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum |CITS: [23754960]|. CerS3 is able to synthesize ceramides containing α-hydroxy (2-hydroxy) fatty acids |CITS: [18541923]|, which are abundant in the skin |CITS: [5489545][9284103]|., In the next step the |FRAME: Omega-OH-UCL-Ceramides "ultra-long-chain ω-hydroxyceramides"| are esterified with |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.296| (encoded by the |FRAME: HS11482| gene). The transacylase catalyzes the transfer of a linoleoyl moiety from linoleate-containing triglycerides to the ω-hydroxyl group of the ceramide, forming a mature acylceramide |CITS: [28248318]|., Next, |FRAME: ENSG00000179477-MONOMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: HS11390| gene, acts on the linoleate portion of the acylceramides |CITS: [18329855]|, introducing a hydroperoxy group. The product is then processed by |FRAME: ENSG00000179148-MONOMER|, forming an epoxylated product |CITS: [21558561]|. It has been suggested that the formation of the epoxy group is required for efficient hydrolysis of the linoleate group,regenerating the free ω-hydroxyl group at the final location. This hydrolysis, coupled with transfer to glutamine residues of membrane proteins, is catalyzed by |FRAME: HS01767-MONOMER|, facilitating the synthesis of the corneocytes lipid envelope and the establishment of the skin barrier |CITS: [10411887]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additional reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-28446| can ferment |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| via both the reductive and oxidative branches of the Stickland reasction. Both branches result in ATP synthesis |CITS: [ABB12-165]|. Both pathways begin with transamination of |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| by |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: GLT|. |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| is regenerated by NAD-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-7238|, producing one equivalent of NADH., In the reductive route |FRAME:PYRUVATE| is reduced to |FRAME:D-LACTATE|, which is subsequently reduced to |FRAME: PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: D-LACTOYL-COA|. The latter is dehydrated to |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.54| |CITS: [4055736] [1597194][11784332][12603323]|. |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.95|, reduces |FRAME: ACRYLYL-COA| to |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, consuming one equivalent of reducing power |CITS: [6586495][1953298]|., Finally, |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| is converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which can be used to generate ATP via |FRAME: ACETYL-P| and |FRAME: ACET|, as described in |FRAME: PWY0-1312|. , The oxidative branch of |FRAME:L-ALPHA-ALANINE| is described in |FRAME: PWY-8189|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Pseudomonic-Acids "Pseudomonic acids"| are polyketide antibiotics produced by |FRAME: ORG-6360| |CITS: [5003547]|. The antibiotic mupirocin is a mixture of four pseudomonic acids: |FRAME: CPD0-2581| (about 90%), |FRAME: CPD-21448| (about 8%), |FRAME: CPD-18977| (<2%), and |FRAME: CPD-21449| (<2%)., Mupirocin inhibits bacterial |FRAME: EC-6.1.1.5|, blocking formation of |FRAME: Charged-ILE-tRNAs "L-isoleucyl-[tRNAIle]"| and ultimately protein synthesis |CITS: [365175][ 659331]|. Mupirocin is used as a topical treatment for bacterial skin infections such as impetigo or folliculitis, and is also used to treat nose infections of methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) |CITS: [6135884][3924877][3098541]|. , The main component of mupirocin, |FRAME: CPD0-2581|, consists of a C17 polyketide-derived substructure (|FRAME: CPD-21453|) esterified by |FRAME: CPD-21101|. The other components are very similar, with only minor modifications., The 74-kb mupirocin biosynthetic gene cluster was identified by transposon mutagenesis |CITS: [Whatling95]| and subsequently analyzed by DNA sequencing, gene knockouts and complementation studies |CITS: [12770824]|. The cluster encodes six modular multifunctional proteins involved in polyketide and fatty acid biosynthesis and 29 single function tailoring enzymes., About This Pathway, The mupirocin polyketide synthases (PKSs), encoded by the |FRAME: G-58730| and |FRAME: G-58731| genes, belong to the "trans-AT" class and do not contain any acyltransferase (AT) domains. This function is provided in trans by a dedicated enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-58735| gene |CITS: [12770824]|. Synthesis begins with transfer of an activated starter unit (believed to be an acetyl unit) from MmpC to an acyl-carrier protein domain of MmpD. Four malonyl extender units are then condensed by MmpD, which also performs two α-methylation reactions before transferring the product to MmpA. This PKS adds two more malonyl extender units, forming the C17 precursor to |FRAME: CPD-21450|., Next, following hydroxylation by the FMN-dependent oxygenase |FRAME: G-58736 MupA|, a group of 5 proteins, encoded by the |FRAME: G-58743|, |FRAME: G-58732|, |FRAME: G-58733|, |FRAME: G-58734|, and macpC genes, introduces a 15-methyl β-branch into the structure |CITS: [18465759]|. , This is a branching point in the pathway. The oxidoreductase domain of the multifunctional |FRAME: G-58737 MmpE| protein introduces a epoxide at position 10,11 of some of the molecules, targeting them towards formation of |FRAME: CPD-21448| and eventually |FRAME: CPD0-2581|. However, some of the molecules escape the epoxidation and continue to form |FRAME: CPD-18977| |CITS: [24625190]|., A reaction catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-58738| cyclase rearranges the molecule, forming the tetrahydropyran ring found in |FRAME: CPD-21450| |CITS: [16039529]|. Up to this point the compound was still attached to MmpA, but in the next step it is transferred to |FRAME: G-58729 MmpB|, a large multi-domain iterative Type I fatty acid synthase. This enzyme forms the |FRAME: CPD-21101| moiety of mupirocin by extending a |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| starter unit by three malonate condensations (as the enoyl reductase domain of MnpB is non-functional, the reaction likely involves an additional enoyl reductase) |CITS: [12770824]|. Upon receiving the |FRAME: CPD-21450| moiety from |FRAME: G-58731 MppA| MmpB attaches it to the |FRAME: CPD-21101| moiety |CITS: [24625190]|, and its thioesterase domain releases the product, which is either |FRAME: CPD-21448| or |FRAME: CPD-21464|, depending on the branch of the pathway, from the PKS machinaryl |CITS: [12770824]|., The released product does not remain free for long, as it is immediately ligated to the acyl-carrier protein mAcpE by |FRAME: G-58739 MupU| |CITS: [16039529]|. Once attached to the [acp], the C-7 hydroxyl is oxidized to a ketone.by the cytochrome P-450 |FRAME: G-58744 MupO| |CITS: [21336932][24625190][28181382]|. Following the oxidation, the product is released from its carrier protein once more, this time by |FRAME: G-58740 MupV|, generating the free |FRAME: CPD-21469|/|FRAME: CPD-21470| |CITS: [28181382]|. A dehydratase encoded by the |FRAME: G-58745| gene generates |FRAME: CPD-21463|/|FRAME: CPD-21465|, and two more transformations, catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-58741 MupC| dehydrogenase and |FRAME: G-58742 MupF| reductase generate the final products, |FRAME: CPD0-2581| and |FRAME: CPD-18977|, respectively |CITS: [17383964][Scott11][24625190]|., |FRAME: ORG-6360| is resistant to mupirocin due to the presence of two genes that encode a mupirocin-resistant |FRAME: EC-6.1.1.5|. One is a resistant form of ileS |CITS: [7929087]|, while the other is the mupM gene, which is present in the mupirocin biosynthesis cluster |CITS: [12770824]|. The genes are only 29% identical to each other and are evolutionarily distinct |CITS: [12672810]|.

Names: ansatrienin biosynthesis // mycotrienin biosynthesis // trienomycin biosynthesis
Summary: The polyketide antibiotics |FRAME: CPD-21971|/|FRAME: CPD-21972| were discovered in 1981 from |FRAME: TAX-68264| under the names mycotrienin I and mycotrienin II |CITS: [Weber81]|. The same compounds were reported one year later from |FRAME: TAX-42684| under their currently used names |CITS: [7161186]|. Those compound defined a new family of, the |FRAME: Ansamycins ansamycin| class that was named |FRAME: Ansatrienins ansatrienins| or mycotrienins. , The unique structures of members of this family are characterized by three conjugated double bonds in the 21-membered macrolactam ring, and a side chain attached to the C-11 hydroxyl group of the ansa ring via a D-alanyl moiety |CITS: [Damberg82]|. Feeding experiments confirmed the incorporation of |FRAME: CPD-10231|, the starter unit used in the biosynthesis of all ansamycins. Additional members of this family were discovered in related organisms, including the |FRAME: Trienomycins trienomycins| |CITS: [3840155][2991181]| and the |FRAME: Thiazinotrienomycins thiazinotrienomycins| |CITS: [7622432]|. The ansatrienins exhibit potent activity against fungi and yeasts, as well as cytotoxicity and limited antibacterial activity., A 20 kb DNA region from the biosynthetic gene cluster encoding ansatrienin biosynthesis in |FRAME: TAX-42684| was identified using known sequences for two genes: the |FRAME: G-10753| gene from |FRAME: TAX-33910|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.144|, an enzyme involved in synthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-10231| starter unit (see |FRAME: PWY-5979|), and the |FRAME: G-63041| gene of |FRAME: TAX-42684|, which encodes |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.120|, an enzyme involved in synthesis of the |FRAME: CPD-575| side chain (see |FRAME: PWY-8044|). However, that sequence was incomplete |CITS: [10103039]|., In a later work, the complete biosynthetic gene cluster encoding ansatrienin biosynthesis was cloned from |FRAME: TAX-67297|. The 90 kb cluster contained 32 open reading frames, encoding all of the enzymes required for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-10231|, the |FRAME: CPD-21977| polyketide backbone, the |FRAME: CPD-575| side chain, an amide synthase, and four tailoring genes, including a methyltransferase |CITS: [21948600]|., According to the proposed pathway, a polyketide complex encoded by the |FRAME: G-63022|-|FRAME: G-63026| genes extends the starter unit to an octaketide intermediate, which is removed from the complex in a process that involves intramolecular lactonization by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.M78|. The macrolactam ring is then methylated at position O3, followed by the addition of a D-alanine moiety at position O11, a process catalyzed by a non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) protein. The last step is the acylation of the D-alanyl moiety by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.dp|. This enzyme is promiscuous and can act on several donors such as |FRAME: CPD-533|, |FRAME: CPD-17494|, |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|, |FRAME: CPD-1083|, and |FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA|, resulting in the formation of ansatrienins with different side chains.

General Background, A proteobacterium identified as |FRAME: TAX-170622| was isolated from soil and shown to grow on the carboxyl group-substituted 2-aminophenol |FRAME: CPD-14129|. The complete degradation pathway for this compound was elucidated. This pathway is different from other known pathways for the degradation of |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL| or its derivatives |CITS: [12444975][17090920]|., In contrast to the pathway shown here, the compound |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL| (an intermediate of pathway |FRAME: PWY-5637|) is degraded by some |FRAME: TAX-286| species via a 1.6-dioxygenase that opens the ring by meta cleavage to form |FRAME: 2-AMINOMUCONATE_SEMIALDEHYDE|. This is followed by dehydrogenation, deamination, and decarboxylation steps to form |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6210|). This route was termed the modified meta-cleavage pathway for 2-aminophenols |CITS: [17090920]|., Other meta cleavage pathways for the degradation of aminophenol derivatives that differ from the pathway shown here include: degradation of the methyl-derived aminophenol |FRAME: CPD-9147| which is an intermediate of |FRAME: PWY-5644|; degradation of the chloro-derived aminophenol |FRAME: CPD-9158| an intermediate of |FRAME: PWY-5645|; and degradation of the carboxy-derived aminophenol |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| an intermediate of |FRAME: PWY-5647|. Other comparisons include the two well known meta cleavage pathways for |FRAME: CATECHOL| which involve a 2,3-dioxygenase step followed by either a hydrolase step (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5415|), or a dehydrogenase step (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5420|). These pathways have been characterized in some |FRAME: TAX-1224| and |FRAME: TAX-201174|., About This Pathway, In contrast to the other pathways described above, |FRAME: CPD-14129| was shown to be metabolized by |FRAME: TAX-170622| via meta cleavage (adjacent to the hydroxyl and amino groups) by a 2,3-dioxygenase to form |FRAME: CPD-14131|. It was noted that in vitro, |FRAME: CPD-14131| is chemically unstable and can undergo spontaneous cyclization (|FRAME: RXN-13143|) |CITS: [19594622][15265044]|. |FRAME: CPD-14131| is deaminated to produce |FRAME: CPD-87|, an unstable intermediate that is proposed to undergo nonenzymatic decarboxylation to form |FRAME: HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD||CITS: [19594622][17090920]|., |FRAME: HYDROXYMUCONATE-SALD| is further metabolized by dehydrogenation to |FRAME: CPD-13339| (2-hydroxymuconate), tautomerization from enol to keto form (|FRAME: CPD-246|), and decarboxylation to |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, an important common intermediate in aromatic degradation. These last three steps leading to |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| are also found in pathways |FRAME: PWY-5419| and |FRAME: PWY-6336| |CITS: [17090920]|., Enzymes of the |FRAME: CPD-14129| pathway have been purified and characterized as shown here and in the pathway link |CITS: [17090920][15265044][14733932][19594622][12444975]|. The |FRAME: MONOMER-17214| that catalyzes the last reaction shown here appears to form a high molecular weight complex with the next enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: MONOMER-17215| shown in the pathway link. The two enzymes co-purified |CITS: [17090920]|. Similar complexes between these two enzymes have been found in other species (see |FRAME: CPLX-7822| (AmnE) and |FRAME: CPLX-7239| (XylI))., A |FRAME: TAX-170622| gene cluster containing genes ahdA, ahdB, a regulatory gene ahdR |CITS: [14733932]|, and a fragment of ahdF encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-17215| has been characterized |CITS: [19594622]|.

Flavonol triglucosides and their coumaryl ester derivatives have been found to constitute the main flavonoids in pea (|FRAME:TAX-3888|). Etiolated pea plants contain mainly |FRAME:CPD1F-90| triglucosides (see |FRAME:PWY-5348|) whereas in light-grown pea plants |FRAME:CPD-520| triglucosides (this pathway) are more abundant. The flavonol triglucosides are distributed in different organs of the pea plant, |FRAME:CPD1F-90| triglucosides occur in leaves and stems and |FRAME:CPD-520| triglucosides dominate in leaves, petioles and tendrils |CITS:[Furuya65]|., Only the flavonol triglucosides and their acylated derivatives accumulate in vivo, however the intermediates of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-437| and |FRAME: CPD-14849|, have been detected in in vitro experiments |CITS:[160697]|. The physiological role of the flavonol triglucosides and acylated derivatives in |FRAME:TAX-3888| is still largly unknown. However, the flavonol (acyl)triglucosides have been found to inhibit the indole acetic acid oxidase indicating its possible involvement in IAA metabolism and photomorphogenetic growth processes |CITS:[13896010]|. It also could be demonstrated that the compounds are somehow associated with chlorophyll content, specific leaf mass, photosynthetic rate and stomatal frequency |CITS:[16665658]| |CITS:[16663526]|., The formation of the |FRAME:CPD-520| mono-, di- and triglucoside had been demonstrated in crude cell extracts of |FRAME:TAX-3888| |CITS:[160697]|. Three similar yet different glucosyltransferases catalyzing the sequential (1->2) glucosylation of the aglycone have been isolated, partially purified and biochemically characterized |CITS:[6462109]|. The glucosyltransferases are distinguished by substrate specificity, physico-chemical properties and kinetic parameter. The flavonol glucosyltransferase catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD1F-437| from |FRAME:CPD-520| only accepts the aglycone but not any glucosylated flavonols. The second step in the pathway catalyzed by flavonol 3-glucoside 2"-glucosyltransferase yielding |FRAME: CPD-14849| does not act on the aglycone or the flavonol diglucoside. The final reaction generating |FRAME:CPD-14850| is realized by a flavonol diglucoside 2"-glucosyltransferase which invariably only accepts the flavonol 3-O-glucosyl (1->2)-glucosides |CITS:[6462109]|. Although preliminary experiments have shown the formation of quercetin coumaryltriglucoside |CITS:[145116]| (compare |FRAME:PWY-5348|) the responsible enzymatic activity still remains to be shown and is therefore not included in the depicted pathway.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The basic repeat unit of the O antigen isolated from O:6,7 serotype strains consists of four mannose residues and one N-acetylglucosamine residue and is described by |FRAME: CPD-23762|. Several modifications exist, including |FRAME: CPD-24025|, |FRAME: CPD-24023|, and |FRAME: CPD-23763|. However, the modifications do not affect the serotype |CITS: [3378232][2453206][2476213][23848592]|., The O:6,7 repeat unit is similar to the |FRAME: CPD-23771|, differing by having one additional mannosyl residue at the non-reducing end. The gene cluster that encodes the biosynthesis of the O:6,7 repeat unit has been cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-115981| in 1992 |CITS: [1373435][1383393]|, and is very similar to that of O:6,14 strains, with the addition of the |FRAME: G-80988| gene |CITS: [23848592]|., Even though the pathway contains four mannosyltransfer reactions, the cluster contains only three genes encoding mannosyltransferases (|FRAME: G-80988|, |FRAME: G-80989|, and |FRAME: G-80990|). The function of |FRAME: G-80989| and |FRAME: G-80990| has been proposed based on a study of E. coli O:77, which produces an O antigen identical to that of Salmonella O:6,14 strains. WbaD was proposed to be the transferase responsible for the β-D-Man-(1→3)-D-GlcNAc linkage, while WbaC was assigned the successive catalysis of the next two mannosyltransfer reactions |CITS: [17600060]|. That leaves WbaB to catalyze the final mannosyltransfer reaction |CITS: [23848592]| (in figure S1).

Summary: The glycolysis pathway represented here is also known as the 'Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway'. First identified in yeast cells and mammalian tissue, it is now also seen as the 'central' metabolic pathway in plants, and can be found, if at least in part, in all organisms. Glycolysis has evolved as a catabolic anaerobic pathway that fulfills two essential functions: i) it oxidizes hexoses to generate |FRAME:ATP|, reductants and |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, and ii) it is an amphibolic pathway (pathway that involves both catabolism and anabolism) because it can reversibly produce hexoses from various low-molecular weight molecules. The ultimate purpose of the pathway is to convert carbon in its reduced form in storage carbohydrates (e.g. |FRAME: Glycogens glycogen|, |FRAME:Starch| and simpler carbohydrates such as |FRAME:SUCROSE|, |FRAME:D-Glucose| and |FRAME:D-Galactose|). In plants, glycolysis is the predominant pathway fueling respiration (see |FRAME:TCA|) because, unlike animal mitochondria, plant mitochondria rarely respire fatty acids. In plants, this pathway occurs in two different subcellular locations: the cytosol and plastids, which are the sites of |FRAME:PWY-621| and |FRAME: PWY-6724|, respectively. Whereas the plastidic glycolysis pathway (see |FRAME:GLYCOLYSIS|) is identical to the conventional microbial glycolysis, the cytosolic pathway (i.e. this pathway) is slightly modified. These pathways can interact with one another though the action of highly selective transporters present in the inner plastid envelope |CITS:[Emes93]|. In chloroplasts in the dark, as well as in plastids of non-photosynthetic tissues, the primary function of |FRAME:GLYCOLYSIS| is the degradation of |FRAME:Starch| to generate carbon skeletons, reductants and ATP for anabolic pathways such as that of |FRAME:PWY-4381| via |FRAME:PYRUVDEHYD-PWY|. In the cytosol, the same products are generated from the degradation of |FRAME:SUCROSE|., The pathway starts with |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, which is made available from a variety of sources (in the plant plastids, it results from |FRAME: PWY-6724|). The first committed step of glycolysis is the reversible conversion of |FRAME:GLC-6-P| into |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| by an hexose phosphate isomerase, which changes the pyranose configuration of glucose into the furanose configuration of fructose. The second step is catalyzed by a phosphofructokinase in the presence of |FRAME:ATP|; this step is irreversible (in the cytosol of plants, see |FRAME:PWY-621|, an alternative enzyme uses |FRAME:PPI| instead of ATP). The third step is catalyzed by an aldolase which cleaves |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE| into interconvertable (they are keto-enol tautomers) two three-carbon fragments: |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|. The interconversion of these tautomers is facilitated by a triose phosphate isomerase. The following reaction, which adds one phosphate residue to |FRAME:GAP| to form |FRAME:DPG|, is freely reversible and requires |FRAME:NAD| and |FRAME:Pi|. The next step releases one molecule of ATP during the conversion of |FRAME:DPG| into |FRAME:G3P| by a Mg2+-dependent glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate kinase. The next step requires little energy change and leads to the reversible transfer of a phosphate group from the 3- to the 2-hydroxyl group of glycerate, leading to the formation of |FRAME:2-PG|. The removal of a molecule of water by an enolase in the presence of Mg2+ converts |FRAME:2-PG| into |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE|. The final step of glycolysis involves the ketolization of |FRAME:PHOSPHO-ENOL-PYRUVATE| to |FRAME:PYRUVATE| by a pyruvate kinase, leading to the release of a molecule of ATP., In the cytosol, there are two alternative reactions to the plastidic pathway: EC 2.7.1.90 and EC 1.2.1.9. The former represents an alternative to EC 2.7.1.11; this reaction utilizes |FRAME:PPI| rather than ATP to convert |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-6P| to |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE|. The plant cytosol lacks soluble inorganic alkaline pyrophosphatases (PPiases) and, consequently, contains higher concentrations of |FRAME:PPI| (up to 0.3 mM |CITS:[WEINER87]|). It has been proposed that the utilization of pyrophosphate rather than that of ATP in glycolysis is favored under nutritional Pi deprivation or oxygen deficiency |CITS:[DAVIES93],[15012287]|. The latter reaction, EC 1.2.1.9, provides a bypass between |FRAME:GAP| and |FRAME:G3P|, which allows for their conversion without phosphorylation by a non-phosphorylating glyceraldehyde 3-P dehydrogenase |CITS:[15012287],[16927206]|. This reaction produces |FRAME:NADPH| but not |FRAME:ATP|., The overall process, which requires the initial investment of one molecule of ATP to produce |FRAME:FRUCTOSE-16-DIPHOSPHATE|, yields four molecules of ATP and two molecules of |FRAME:NADH| for every molecule of hexose fed to the system. The fate of the final product of glycolysis, |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, depends on the state of the oxygen supply and can be consumed, for example, by the |FRAME:TCA| via the formation |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| in aerobic conditions, or degraded to ethanol or lactate under anaerobic conditions (see |FRAME:PWY-3801|).

Summary: The phytohormone family of auxins regulates many plant biological processes including cell division, elongation,, differentiation, root initiation, tropic responses, flowering, fruit ripening, and senescence |CITS:[15749753]|. , |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN "Indole-3-acetic acid"| (IAA) is the most abundant natural plant auxin., In addition to de novo synthesis, IAA can be released from its conjugates. In maize, hydrolysis of IAA ester conjugates provides the major source of free IAA during seed germination and early seedling growth. IAA-myo-inositol-galactose is hydrolyzed to IAA-myo-inositol at the seed scutellum., IAA-myo-inositol can be hydrolyzed to IAA within the seed or transported to shoots where it is hydrolyzed to free IAA. Hydrolysis of IAA-glucose esters including indole-3-acetyl-β-1-D-glucose and its isomers has also been detected in endosperm.

Summary: |FRAME: ACRYLATE "Acrylate"| is a product of |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| (DMSP) and |FRAME: ACRYLONITRILE| degradation (see |FRAME: PWY-6046| and |FRAME: P344-PWY|). Some organisms are able to utilize acrylate as sole carbon source., |FRAME: TAX-645472| is a marine bacterium isolated from the phylloplane of the macroalga |FRAME: TAX-3118| that can grow on both |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN| or |FRAME: ACRYLATE| as sole carbon source |CITS: [19807777]|., The genes involved in DMSP and acrylate catabolism by this organism have been identified, and found to be located in a single cluster., Different combinations of the genes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| that was fed labeled acrylate and DMSP. NMR and HPLC analyses were used to trace the metabolites, and a pathway for the degradation of these compounds has been proposed |CITS: [19807777]|., |FRAME: ACRYLATE "Acrylate"| is converted to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| via a CoA transferase encoded by |FRAME: G-11631| and a hydratase encoded by |FRAME: G-11632|. |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| is predicted to be catabolized by an alcohol dehydrogenase encoded by |FRAME: G-11633| to |FRAME: MALONATE-S-ALD|, which is converted by an aldehyde dehydrogenase encoded by |FRAME: G-11634| to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| was also found to induce of the transcription of the ddd and acu genes., It should be noted that it is not known whether the |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: MALONATE-S-ALD| intermediates of this pathway exist in their free form (as shown here) or as CoA-activated forms, since the experiments were not conducted with purified enzymes.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Flavonoids Flavonoids| are secondary metabolites formed from phenylpropanoid and fatty acid derivatives and have important functions, acting as UV-B protectors |CITS:[11724379]|, attractors of pollinators and seed dispersers, insect feeding attractors, anti-feedants, signal molecules in legume-rhizobium bacteria interactions |CITS:[3738520]|, and , fungicides (for more information, see |FRAME: PWY1F-FLAVSYN|)., Flavonoids have also received a lot of attention due to their effect on human health. They are useful for the treatment of several human pathologies |CITS: [8597679][9442297][11130659][11287230][19475406]|. However, the widespread use of pharmaceutical flavonoids is currently limited by inefficiencies in both their chemical synthesis and extraction from natural plant sources. As a result, the microbial production of flavonoids has emerged as a potential alternative method for flavonoid production., About This Pathway, In plants flavonoids are derived from |FRAME: PHE| (see |FRAME: PWY1F-467|). In that pathway, |FRAME: COUMARATE| is formed from |FRAME: PHE| in two steps, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.25| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.91|, which is a cytochorme P450 hydroxylase. Since the functional expression of plant P450 enzymes is always hard in bacterial systems due to their requirement for anchorage on endoplasmic reticulum and redox partners, this engineered pathway (described in |CITS: [21320631]|) starts with the enzyme |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.23|, which converts |FRAME: TYR| to |FRAME: COUMARATE| in a single step. The enzyme selected is from the red yeast |FRAME: TAX-5535|, since it has a high activity with L-tyrosine |CITS: [17204442]|. In addition, the pathway was constructed in L-tyrosine overproducing strains of |FRAME: TAX-562|, to ensure an abundant supply of starting material., The enzyme chosen to catalyze the second step of the pathway (|FRAME: EC-6.2.1.12|), is a well-characterized enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-4043| (parsley) |CITS: [921295][3169018]|, selected based on its proven efficacy in similar applications |CITS: [17468269][18333619]|., The enzymes catalyzing the last steps (|FRAME: EC-2.3.1.74| and |FRAME: EC-5.5.1.6|) are from |FRAME: TAX-4102| and |FRAME: TAX-3879| (alfalfa), respectively. Both of these enzymes have been used successfully in similar applications |CITS: [17468269][18333619][19475406]|., One of the difficulties of this pathway is the fact that the first enzyme (|FRAME: EC-4.3.1.23|) is severely inhibited when the downstream enzymes are present, presumably due to the accumulation of a downstream intermediate(s). This inhibition can be prevented by expressing the downstream enzymes by very strong constitutive promoters. Under those conditions the pathway produced a titer of 136 mg/l of |FRAME: COUMARATE| and 29 mg/l of |FRAME: Naringenin| |CITS: [21320631]|.

Alanine is an essential component of protein (as L-alanine) and peptidoglycan (as a roughly 3:1 mix of D- and L-alanine)., Only about a tenth of total alanine synthesized is incorporated into peptidoglycan., At least three pathways (|FRAME: ALANINE-VALINESYN-PWY|, |FRAME: ALANINE-SYN2-PWY|, and |FRAME: PWY0-1021|) are known for production of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE|. The specific contribution of |FRAME: ALANINE-VALINESYN-PWY| to overall alanine production in the cell remains unclear, given that it consists of a series of reversible reactions involved in other physiological processes, and alanine auxotrophs based on this pathway have not been generated.

|FRAME: Agarans Agarans| and |FRAME: Agaroses agaroses| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the Rhodophyta (red algae), mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, and species from the |FRAME: TAX-31444| and |FRAME: TAX-33664| genera., The basic units of |FRAME: Agarans agarans|  are repeats of β -1,3 linked D-galactose and α-1,4- linked L-galactose units, which are substituted by sulfate. Different types of agarans have sulfate groups at different positions (depicted as R3 in the structure) ( |CITS: [1367970]|. , In |FRAME: Agaroses agaroses| the α-1,4- linked galactose units are modified by having a 3,6-anhydro bridge. These bridges are responsible for the gelation that is typical to these compounds, by forming a double helix during the process., Many types of marine bacteria are known to degrade agarose. Two types of endohysdrolases - |FRAME: 3.2.1.81-RXN "EC 3.2.1.81, β agarase"| and |FRAME: 3.2.1.158-RXN "EC 3.2.1.158, α-agarase"|, are known to hydrolase the β and α linkages, producing |FRAME: Neoagaro-oligosaccharides "neoagaro-oligossaccharides"| and |FRAME: Agaro-oligosaccharides "agaro-oligosaccharides|, respectively., This pathway describes the activity of β-agarases. These enzymes have been characterized from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-47913| and |FRAME: TAX-63186|. The enzymes are endo-hydrolases, and can break the agarose backbones to short oligosaccharides. The oligosaccharides that are formed are degraded further by enzymes such as |FRAME: 3.2.1.159-RXN "EC 3.2.1.159, α-neoagaro-oligosaccharide hydrolase"|, generating a mixture of |FRAME:D-Galactose|, |FRAME:CPD-13430| and |FRAME:CPD-13431|.

Summary: Some of the most prevalent fatty acids in lipid storage tissues, such as |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, contain cis-double bonds on even-numbered carbons. When such fatty acids are processed by the first enzyme of the core β-oxidation pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-7064| (see |FRAME: PWY-5136|), they are converted into |FRAME: 2-trans-4-cis-dienoyl-CoAs|. This intermediate cannot proceed directly through the core β-oxidation pathway, and must be processed via either of two alternative routes., In the first route |FRAME: 2-trans-4-cis-dienoyl-CoAs| enters the so called reductase/isomerase pathway, which involves the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-12061| and |FRAME: CPLX-7065|. In this route the dienoyl-CoA is converted to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA|, which can be processed further by the core β-oxidation pathway., Alternatively, |FRAME: 2-trans-4-cis-dienoyl-CoAs| can be converted to |FRAME: Cis-2-enoyl-CoAs| through one more cycle of core beta-oxidation pathway. A cis-2-enoyl-CoA cannot be completely degraded via the core β-oxidation pathway since its hydratation yields |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| which is not a substrate for |FRAME:ENZRXN-12592|. Thus, the D-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA enters the so called epimerase pathway that involves converting, |FRAME: D-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| to |FRAME: L-3-HYDROXYACYL-COA| by |FRAME: ENZRXN-12606|. Alternatively, this conversion can be performed by two stereo-specific enoyl-CoA hydratases. The L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA then returns to the core β-oxidation pathway for complete degradation., The |FRAME:EC-5.3.3.8 "enoyl-CoA isomerase"| and |FRAME: EC-5.1.2.3 "3-hydroxyacyl-CoA epimerase"| activities, together with two enzyme activities also found in the core β-oxidation pathway, namely |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.17 "2-enoyl-CoA hydratase"| and |FRAME:EC-1.1.1.35 "3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase"|, are attributed to a single multifunctional protein (MFP)., Studies in |FRAME: TAX-3659| cotyledon suggested the epimerase pathway is much more effective than the reductase/isomerase pathway |CITS: [1879422]|, whereas studies in |FRAME: ORG-5993| indicated that both pathways have a similar contribution |CITS: [11080293]|.

Benzene is a highly toxic industrial compound with a broad range of industrial uses. It is one of the top 20 production volume chemicals in the United States, with an annual production of almost 9 million metric tons. In addition to being a component of petroleum-based fuels, benzene is often used as a raw material for the manufacture of other chemicals, rubbers, lubricants, dyes, detergents, drugs, and pesticides. Benzene is among the most prevalent organic contaminants in groundwater and is a major concern due to its toxicity and relatively high solubility |CITS: [12558180]|., Many soil bacteria, notably Pseudomonas species, are able to catabolize a wide variety of natural and man-made aromatic compounds. Several diiron monooxygenases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.236|, were reported to transform benzene to phenol |CITS: [8206853]|. To verify this ability, several such enzymes were cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|. Addition of |FRAME: BENZENE| to the medium resulted in successive hydroxylations. The |FRAME: CPLX-2181| from |FRAME: ORG-5936| was shown to produce |FRAME: PHENOL|, |FRAME: CATECHOL|, and |FRAME: PYROGALLOL| in succession. The enzyme hydroxylated |FRAME: BENZENE| and |FRAME: PHENOL| at rates comparable to its activity with |FRAME: TOLUENE|, though the rate of |FRAME: CATECHOL| hydroxylation was 5 times lower |CITS: [15240250]|.

Several organisms possess enzymes that can catalyze the NAD-dependent reversible oxidation of |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2,3-butanediol"| to |FRAME: ACETOIN|. However, three stereoisomers of 2,3-butanediol exist - |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|, |FRAME: CPD-346| and |FRAME: CPD-12004|, and different organisms have preferences for different isomers., The enzyme that catalyzes the reversible reaction between acetoin and 2,3-butanediol is acetoin reductase (AR, also known as 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenase, or BDH). Four types of AR activites have been described, differing in their stereo-specificity for both the substrate and the product |CITS: [Ui84]|. The enzymes that can catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-346| to |FRAME: CPD-255| are often referred to as L-BDH. Such enzymes have been characterized from several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [13837186][2040298]|, |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [11577733]| and |FRAME: TAX-1422| |CITS: [8879540]|., The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-1718| belongs to the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family. The gene encoding it has been cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the enzyme has been purified and characterized |CITS: [11577733]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-1092 Styrene| is a toxic compound used in large amounts by the chemical industry and released into the environment, causing pollution. Styrene contamination of the environment can occur by various routes, including factory wastewater, evaporation, and the pyrolysis of polystyrene |CITS: [Fu92]|., Microorganisms able to degrade styrene are not widespread in nature |CITS: [Warhurst94]|. The isolation of pure cultures degrading styrene was first reported by Shirai and Hisatsuka only in 1979 |CITS: [Shirai79]|., Two main routes of aerobic styrene breakdown have been proposed: the first involves oxidation of the lateral chain to |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| (shown here), and the second involves initial oxidation of the aromatic nucleus |CITS: [Warhurst94a]|., About This Pathway, The key enzyme in this pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-8380|, a flavin adenine dinucleotide-dependent monooxygenase that oxidizez |FRAME: CPD-1092| to |FRAME: CPD-13773| (styrene oxide). Recombinant |FRAME: CPLX-8380| was shown to catalyze the formation of the enantiomer |FRAME: CPD-13773| with an enantiomeric excess of more than 99% |CITS: [9603811]|., The other two enzymes are involved in isomerization of the latter to |FRAME: PHENYLACETALDEHYDE| and oxidation to |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE| |CITS: [2339888]|. The pathway was first proposed based on enzyme activities in cell extracts from several bacterial strains isolated from soil |CITS: [2339888]|., The genes encoding these enzymes cluster in a single a region of the chromosome of several strains, including |FRAME: ORG-6192| |CITS: [9172343]| and |FRAME: TAX-69328| |CITS: [9603811]|.

Summary: In recent years the destruction of the ozone layer due to the action of halogen radicals and its negative effects on earth has occupied scientific and popular imagination. Methyl halides from biogenic emissions are the main transporters of halogen radicals from the atmosphere to stratosphere. Of the halides, |FRAME: CPD-845| is the most abundant and is released from specific fungi and plants and by the burning of biomass. |FRAME: CPD-12221|, which was extensively used as a soil fumigant and is known to strongly deplete stratospheric ozone, has been prohibited in recent times, but is produced by some marine organisms. |FRAME: CPD-7676| has lesser half life that |FRAME: CPD-845| and |FRAME: CPD-12221| but is known to affect the formation of marine aerosol formation and cloud condensation nuclei |CITS: [10508052]|. , The anthropogenic, marine and terrestrial biogenic sources of halides are known |CITS: [11791711][10508052]|, but the mechanisms of biosynthesis are poorly understood. The enzymes involved are halide ion methyltransferase (HMT) and halide/thiol methyltransferase (HTMT). Several flowering plant families are involved in the formation of methyl halides |CITS: [2371563] [ 7721844]|.

Summary: Background, Biomass is gaining increasing attention as a renewable energy source due to environmental and energy concerns |CITS: [17942358]|. |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL Isobutanol| and |FRAME: BUTANOL| are biomass products that have many advantages compared to |FRAME: ETOH| as a substitute for gasoline because of their hydrophobicity and higher energy content., |FRAME: BUTANOL| is produced naturally by the Gram-positive strict anaerobe |FRAME: TAX-1488| |CITS: [16346258]| . However, the concomitant synthesis of the byproducts |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID|, |FRAME: ACETONE| and |FRAME: ETOH| makes |FRAME: BUTANOL| production difficult to control experimentally |CITS: [3540574]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6594|). Furthermore, |FRAME: TAX-1488| is a slow growing organism that is not as well understood as some other microorganisms, making it an arduous task to optimize in vivo |FRAME: BUTANOL| production |CITS: [17942358]|. Thus, in recent years the Clostridia butanol pathway has been engineered into hosts such as |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-4932|. While many optimizations have been successfully introduced in |FRAME: TAX-562|, reaching productions similar to those obtained in Clostridia (see |FRAME: PWY-6883|), results were less successful in yeast., About this Pathway, This pathway was designed to enable yeast to convert proteins (which are abundantly present as final waste of lignocellulose processing) to |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL|. Yeast is known to naturally produce |FRAME: ISOBUTANOL| as a by-product of |FRAME: VAL| fermentation, and that ability has been already used for commercial purposes (see |FRAME: PWY-7111|). , This pathway operates in wild type |FRAME: TAX-4932|, which is assumed to possess all of the required enzymes. When grown on |FRAME: GLY|, both alcohols were produced, although at low concentrations |CITS: [23642236]|. However, the production of higher alcohols starting with purified glycine is not economically sustainable. In order to make this pathway attractive, further work is required to construct a yeast that redirects sugars to glycine production, and to improve the alcohol yield., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.4.3.19|, has been reported in |FRAME: TAX-4932|, although the identity of the gene encoding it is not know yet |CITS: [15851099]|. Summary: General Background, Anaerobic ammonia oxidation (Anammox) is a biological process in which |FRAME: NITRITE| is used as the electron acceptor in the conversion of ammonium to dinitrogen gas and water. The overall reaction is exergonic, and thus could provide a small amount of energy for growth. Despite that, the reaction has not been observed for most of the 20th century, and it was widely accepted that ammonium can not be oxidized in anaerobic environments., In 1977 Broda published a theoretical paper describing the potential for the existence of chemolithotrophic bacteria able to oxidize ammonia to dinitrogen gas with nitrate as electron acceptor |CITS: [ 930125]|. Some time after the publication it was observed that ammonium was disappearing from a denitrifying fluidized bed reactor treating ammonium-rich effluent in the Netherlands |CITS: [mulder95]|. Ammonium loss was associated with nitrate consumption and concomitant gas production. It was soon shown that the process was biologicaly mediated |CITS: [7747947]|., Studies of Anammox using 15N labeled compounds |CITS: [vandegraaf97]| suggested that |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| and |FRAME: HYDRAZINE| are intermediates in the reaction. It was also shown that |FRAME: NITRITE|, rather than nitrate, was the preferred electron acceptor. It was suggested that hydroxylamine and ammonium are combined to yield hydrazine, which is subsequently oxidized to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [9453157]|. The process is strictly anaerobic, and is inhibited by high concentrations of nitrite, oxygen, and phosphates |CITS: [10388731]|., In 1999 Strous et al |CITS: [10440372]| identified the unculturable organisms responsible for the Anammox process, as a novel deep-branching Planctmycete. This first-discovered Anammox bacterium was provisionally named, |FRAME: TAX-174632| |CITS: [11404106]|. Following that discovery, new genera of Anommox Plactomycetes were discovered in different environments, including a marine species in the Black Sea (|FRAME: TAX-237368|) |CITS: [12686999]|. Anammox was found to contribute up to 50% of marine dinitrogen production |CITS: [15355175]|., These organisms are very difficult to grow, and divide only once in two weeks at maximum rate |CITS: [15487931]|., Anammox bacteria have a complex ultrastructure, with three compartments named the paryphoplasm, the riboplasm and the anammoxosome |CITS: [19682260]|. The anammoxosome, which makes up about 30-60% of the cell volume |CITS: [11404106]| is the site of anammox catabolism. It is surrounded by a very dense membrane composed almost exclusively of linearly concatenated cyclobutane-containing lipids called |FRAME: Ladderanes ladderanes| |CITS: [15098544][19376084]|., Anammox presents significant potential for the treatment of ammonium-rich waste water. It is projected that the application of Anammox to nitrogen removal from such water would lead to a reduction of operational costs of up to 90% |CITS: [11404106]|., About This Pathway, The exact pathway of anaerobic ammonium oxidation has been unclear for some time. Early proposals suggested that |FRAME:NITRITE| is converted to |FRAME: HYDROXYLAMINE| (either directly or via |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|), and the latter is converted to |FRAME: HYDRAZINE| |CITS:[10820012][18515490]|., However, the turnover of neither hydroxylamine nor hydrazine was demonstrated under physiological conditions, and it has been suggested that the previous observations could have been an experimental artifact resulting from the administration of hydroxylamine. In addition, a candidate gene coding for hydroxylamine reductase making nitrite could not be found in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-174633| |CITS: [16598256]|. Instead, the genome revealed the presence of genes encoding a cd1 nitrite reductase (NirS), which catalyzes the reduction of nitrite to |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|., This prompted the proposal for a different pathway, in which |FRAME:NITRITE| is converted to |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| by a |FRAME: CPLX-7982|. The |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE| is then condensed with |FRAME: AMMONIA| to form |FRAME: HYDRAZINE| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.7|. Finally, |FRAME: HYDRAZINE| is oxidized to |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| in a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.7.2.8| |CITS: [16598256][19558586]|., During the process protons are generated at the anammoxosome side of the membrane, and consumed at the cytoplasmic side, thus generating a proton motive force across the membrane |CITS: [11404106][15355175][19862513]|. A dedicated ATP synthase has been discovered in the anammoxosome proteome |CITS: [19558586]|., Subsequent experiments supported the second proposed pathway, which involves |FRAME: NITRIC-OXIDE|. By supplying metabolizing cells with unlabeled hydrazine and ammonium together with 15N-nitrite, it was shown that hydrazine is turned over during ammonium and nitrite conversion. The role of NO as an intermediate was established by a combination of inhibition studies and fluorescent labeling of the cells. In addition, NO and ammonium served as the direct, substrates for hydrazine synthesis |CITS: [21964329]|.

Summary: General Background, Polyunsaturated long- and very-long-chain fatty acids (of 20-22 carbons) accumulate in many algae, mosses and ferns. They are found in all major glycerol lipids of these organisms and represent major constituents of membranes, although their function is not clear., These compounds are not commonly found in higher plants, which typically produce saturated and mono-unsaturatedare very long chain fatty acids as common constituents of the plant cuticle. , Polyunsaturated very long chain fatty acids are also found in mammals. For example, in humans |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| (20:4Δ5,8,11,14) and |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE| (20:5Δ5,8,11,14,17) are precursors of the regulatory molecules |FRAME: Icosanoids icosanoids|, which are involved in many cellular functions including vascular permeability, inflammation, regulation of immune system, blood clotting, neurotransmission and cholesterol metabolism., |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Icosapentaenoate| (EPA) is a polyunsaturated fatty acid that contains five cis double bonds, one of which is located at the third carbon from the omega end, which makes it an omega-3 fatty acid. EPA is produced by microalgae and is common in fish who eat the algae, although the fish can not produce it. It is also produced by mosses and ferns, but is not usually found in higher plants, although trace amounts have been identified in |FRAME: TAX-46147|. EPA is also produced by some marine bacteria, mostly those adapted to low temperatures and high pressures, via a completely different pathway |CITS: [10220156]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7050|)., About This pathway, While humans can not synthesize EPA de novo, they are able to convert the essential fatty acid |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| to EPA. Humans require either |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| or EPA to produce |FRAME: CPD-10244|, a primary structural component of the human brain cerebral cortex, sperm, testicles and retina. , The biosynthesis of polyunsaturated fatty acids in animals and most fungi occurs when the compounds are activated as coenzyme A esters. Once |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| is activated to |FRAME: LINOLENOYL-COA|, the common mammalian pathway for |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE Icosapentaenoate| biosynthesis involves a Δ6 desaturation, elongation by the elongase complex, and a second desaturation at the 5th position (see |FRAME: PWY-7049|. , An alternative pathway that involves a Δ8 desaturation step has also been described in rat and human testis (|CITS: [588579][459715]|. This discovery was surprising, since mammals are not known to possess an 8-desaturase. Later work has reported that the enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: HS05918| gene, which was believed to catalyze only Δ6 desaturation, is also capable of catalyzing Δ8 desaturation when acting on the substrates |FRAME: CPD-12647| and |FRAME: CPD-12646| |CITS: [19202133]|. The pathway described here is suggested to be an alternate pathway for |FRAME: 5Z8Z11Z14Z17Z-EICOSAPENTAENOATE icosapentaenoate| biosynthesis based on the novel activity. In this pathway, |FRAME: LINOLENOYL-COA| is first elongated to |FRAME: CPD-12647| by the elongase complex, followed by a Δ8 desaturation catalyzed by |FRAME: HS05918| and a Δ5 desaturation catalyzed by |FRAME: HS07617|.

Summary: D-Glucuronate (glucuronate) can be metabolized by two different pathways in animals.  It is a precursor for , ascorbate (vitamin C) biosynthesis in animals that can synthesize this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME:PWY3DJ-35471|).  , It can also be converted to the pentose L-xylulose in all animal species studied.  This pathway is variously , known as the pentose pathway, glucuronic acid oxidation pathway (reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|), or the , glucuronate/xylulose pathway (|CITS: [SALWAY04]|).  The two pathways share the D-glucuronate reductase step , which forms L-gulonate., D-Glucuronate is formed from hydrolysis of UDP-D-glucuronate by a membrane-bound enzyme(s) of the , endoplasmic reticulum, probably UDP-glucuronidase(s) (reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|. The ultimate precursor , of UDP-D-glucuronate is D-glucose (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-4821|).  The , pathway for D-glucuronate formation from D-glucose may also involve β-D-glucuronide conjugates , as precursors (in |CITS: [16585534]|).  Non-glucuronidable xenobiotics stimulate glucuronate formation , from UDP-glucuronate, possibly by an as yet uncharacterized effect on UDP-glucuronidases , (reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|). , In this pathway, L-gulonate is oxidized to 3-keto-L-gulonate and then decarboxylated to L-xylulose, which , is then reduced to xylitol. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE "Thiamine diphosphate"|, also known as vitamin B1, is known to play a fundamental role in energy metabolism. It is an essential cofactor for a variety of enzymes such as |FRAME: TRANSKETOI-CPLX transketolase|, |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX "pyruvate dehydrogenase"|, |FRAME: CPLX3O-118 "pyruvate decarboxylase"|, and |FRAME: CPLX66-42 "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS:[15326535]|. Its discovery followed from the original early research on the anti-beriberi factor found in rice bran. Beriberi, a neurological disease, was particularly prevalent in Asia, where the refining of rice resulted in the removal of the thiamine-containing husk |CITS: [Begley96]|., Thiamine is synthesized de novo by microorganisms, plants and some lower eukaryotes (e.g. |FRAME: TAX-5820|), but not by higher eukaryotes, which must obtain it through their diet., About This Pathway, The active form of thiamine is |FRAME: THIAMINE-PYROPHOSPHATE|. The non-phosphorylated form |FRAME: THIAMINE| is not produced as an intermediate in the de novo biosynthetic route in bacteria, but is found in the environment as a degradation product., Many bacteria possess transporters that allow them to import thiamine, and salvage pathways that regenerate the active form. One such pathway, which is described here, consists of two successive phosphorylation reactions |CITS: [15150256]|., The first step is catalyzed by |FRAME: THIKIN-MONOMER| (|FRAME: G6566|), a dedicated thiamine salvage enzyme, while the second reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: THI-P-KIN-MONOMER| (|FRAME: G6234|), which also participates in , the de novo biosynthesis of thiamine diphosphate., The ThiK kinase was discovered in and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS:[6284709][15150256]|. Orthologs of thiK have so far only been found in the γ proteobacteria.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The |FRAME: CPD-23778| and the |FRAME: CPD-23896| are almost identical. They differ only by the presence of an O-acetyl group at position 2 of ~80% of the β-Galf residues of the Salmonella glycan. As expected, the O antigen gene clusters of the two organisms are closely related. The gene encoding the acetyltransferase is not present in the cluster of the salmonella strains and is most likely encoded by a bacteriophage and acts following the assembly of the repeat unit |CITS: [20501518]|., The case of the |FRAME: CPD-23778| is unusual, in that the sequence of the gene cluster that encodes its biosynthetic enzymes was reported five years before the repeat unit structure was determined |CITS: [17056694][20501518]|., Sequencing of the clusters revealed the presence of 4 genes encoding glycosyltransferases, as expected. The genes were named |FRAME: G-80982|, |FRAME: G-80983|, |FRAME: G-80984|, and |FRAME: G-80985|. The first three genes are predicted to encode glycosyltransferase that belong to the GT4 family of retaining glycosyltransferases, while |FRAME: G-80985| has been predicted to encode a GT2 family member, which is likely to be an inverting glycosyltransferase., Unfortunately, none of the enzymes has been characterized biochemically. The only functional prediction available is for |FRAME: G-80985|, which has been predicted to encode a galactofuranosyltransferase. Since it is an inverting enzyme, it likely catalyzes the first galactofyranosyltransfer reaction of the pathway., The sequences of the other three genes are sufficiently unique that it is not possible to predict which of the transfer reactions is associated with which enzyme. It should also be noted that one of the remaining three reactions involves an inverting reaction, suggesting that one of the three enzymes has been misclassified as a member of the GT4 family. For the sake of inclusion in this pathway, we have attached these enzymes randomly to the remaining three transfer reactions; it is almost certain that these functional asignments are not correct.

Summary: General Background, Six pathways are now recognized in bacteria, most algae, fungi and higher plants for the biosynthesis of lysine. They are divided into two groups - the diaminopimelate (DAP) pathways, and the |FRAME:CPD-468| pathways., In the pathways that belong to the DAP group, lysine is produced from aspartate (along with methionine, threonine and isoleucine). All of the DAP group pathways share the upper segments, which include the four steps required for conversion of L-aspartate to |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE|. They also share the last step, which is the conversion of the intermediate |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (D,L-DAP, or meso-DAP) to lysine., However, these pathways differ in the routes leading from |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|. The four variations include:, (I) the succinylase variant (see |FRAME: DAPLYSINESYN-PWY|), which involves succinylated intermediates. In this route |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is coverted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in four enzymatic steps., (II) the acetylase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2941|), which involves acetylated intermediates. This route also involves four enzymatic steps for the conversion of |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|., (III) the dehydrogenase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-2942|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in a single enzymatic step. , (IV) the diaminopimelate-aminotransferase variant (see |FRAME: PWY-5097|), in which |FRAME: DELTA1-PIPERIDEINE-2-6-DICARBOXYLATE| is converted to |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| in two steps., In addition to lysine, all of the pathways in this group also produce |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, which is an important metabolite on its own (for example, as a constituent of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan)., The two other pathways belong to the |FRAME: CPD-468| group. They are found in organisms that have no requirement for |FRAME:MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE|, as it is not a component of their cell walls. These pathways also share the first segments, leading to the synthesis of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD-468| (α-aminoadipate)., However, in yeast and fungi, as well as |FRAME: TAX-3038|, the pathway continues with the key enzyme |FRAME: YBR115C-MONOMER|, leading to the intermediate |FRAME: SACCHAROPINE| (see |FRAME: LYSINE-AMINOAD-PWY|), while in prokaryotes the pathway continues in a path similar to bacterial arginine biosynthesis (see |FRAME: PWY-3081|)., Most of the bacteria that have been investigated in detail appear to utilize only one of these pathways |CITS: [1906065]|. Summary: General Background, The major site for fatty acid β-oxidation in animal cells is the mitochondrion, although partial β-oxidation has also been shown to occur in peroxisomes. Although the same sequential cleavage chemistry is used in both organelles, the gene products utilized are different. In contrast, in plant cells the major sites for fatty acid β-oxidation are the peroxisome and the glyoxysome (a specialized peroxisome found only in germinating seeds). The mitochondrion is also active, but is most likely responsible only for degradation of branched-chain fatty acids (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5136 fatty acid β-oxidation II (peroxisome)|). In most fungi β-oxidation is a peroxisomal process., Another species difference lies in the structure of the enzymes. In animal mitochondria, after initial metabolism of long chain acyl-CoAs by membrane-bound enzymes, medium and short chain acyl-CoAs are metabolized in the matrix by separate soluble enzymes. In contrast, plant and animal peroxisomes and plant glyoxysomes contain multifunctional proteins (MFPs) that catalyze multiple steps of the pathway. Plant MFPs appear to have S stereospecificity, whereas the fungal counterparts are R stereospecific. Mammals contain two distinct MFPs, one with S and the other with R stereospecificity (reviewed in |CITS: [17434787][17028011][20558530][20195903]|)., The main biochemical difference between the animal mitochondrial and bacterial β-oxidation pathway (see |FRAME: FAO-PWY fatty acid β-oxidation I|) and the plant and animal peroxisomal counterpart lies in the first step, which converts |FRAME: ACYL-COA an acyl-CoA| to |FRAME: TRANS-D2-ENOYL-COA a trans-2-enoyl-CoA|. In bacteria or animal mitochondria, this reaction is catalyzed by acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. The electrons removed by the oxidation pass through the respiratory chain to oxygen, generating water as the final product. In plant and animal peroxisomes, this reaction is catalyzed by acyl-CoA oxidase. The electrons pass directly to oxygen and produce |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE hydrogen peroxide|, which is immediately cleaved by peroxisomal catalase (reviewed in |CITS: [20558530][21683154][11755682][17028011]|)., About This Pathway, In β-oxidation an acyl-CoA chain is cleaved between carbons 2 and 3 producing a chain-shortened acyl-CoA, and either acetyl-CoA or propionyl-CoA, depending upon substrate structure. The peroxisomal β-oxidation cycle comprises four activities: acyl-CoA oxidase, enoyl-CoA hydratase, 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, and 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase. The main intermediates produced in the pathway are 2E-enoyl-CoA (trans-2-enoyl-CoA), a chiral 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA, and 3-ketoacyl-CoA., Humans and other mammals utilize peroxisomal β-oxidation in the metabolism of a variety of compounds including α-methyl branched fatty acids (eg. |FRAME: PRISTANATE pristanate|), bile acid intermediates, saturated and unsaturated fatty acids (very long chain, long chain and medium chain), dicarboxylic fatty acids, xenobiotics, epoxy-fatty acids, polyenoic acids, and eicosanoids. The enzymes utilized in this pathway may differ depending upon the chain length, substituents, and chain structure of the acyl-CoA substrate. If an initial acyl-CoA substrate contains a 2R-methyl branch, it must be converted to the 2S configuration by |FRAME: HS01416-MONOMER| (|FRAME: 5.1.99.4-RXN "EC 5.1.99.4"|) encoded by gene AMACR before desaturation by acyl-CoA oxidase (see pathway |FRAME: PWY66-387 fatty acid α-oxidation II|) (reviewed in |CITS: [20558530][21683154][17028011]|)., The mammalian |FRAME: FAD FAD|-dependent acyl-CoA oxidases ACOX1, ACOX2 and ACOX3 catalyze the initial desaturation step of the peroxisomal β-oxidation cycle by introducing a 2-trans bond in the acyl-CoA substrate. The |FRAME: FADH2 FADH2| produced is reoxidized by |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE oxygen|. The three acyl-CoA oxidases differ in substrate specificity, biochemical properties and tissue distribution. ACOX3 is highly expressed in rat liver, but not in humans |CITS: [8387517]|., Multifunctional proteins (MFPs) are involved in the second and third steps of peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation. Mammals contain two distinct MFPs, one with S and the other with R stereospecificity. The mammalian trans-2-enoyl-CoA (2E-enoyl-CoA) hydratase activity of MFP-1 (the product of human gene |FRAME: HS03720 EHHADH|) stereospecifically produces 3S-hydroxyacyl-CoAs, whereas that of MFP-2 (the product of human gene |FRAME: HS05792 HSD17B4|) stereospecifically produces 3R-hydroxyacyl-CoAs. If a substrate contains a 2-methyl branch (eg. |FRAME: PRISTANATE pristanate|) MFP-1 produces the 3S,2S isomer of 3-hydroxy-2-methylacyl-CoA, whereas MFP-2 produces the 3R,2R isomer. The 3S,2S isomer can be converted to the 3S,2R-isomer via |FRAME: HS01416-MONOMER| |CITS: [9230115][22864515]|. The 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activities of MFP-1 and MFP-2 oxidize the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoAs to 3-ketoacyl-CoAs. The MFP-1 dehydrogenase activity utilizes only the 3S isomer of straight chain hydroxyacyl-CoAs. In the case of 2-methyl branched chain substrates, MFP-1 cannot utilize the 3S,2S isomer produced by its hydratase activity, but it can utilize the 3S,2R isomer produced by |FRAME: HS01416-MONOMER|. MFP-2 can utilize the R (or 3R,2R) isomer produced by its hydratase activity (reviewed in |CITS: [16766224]|)., The fourth step involves the thiolytic cleavage of a 3-oxoacyl-CoA to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA acetyl-CoA| and an acyl-CoA that has been shortened by two carbon atoms (n-2). It can be catalyzed by enzymes encoded by either gene ACAA1 or gene SCPx. The latter enzyme participates in the cleavage of substrates containing 2-methyl branches such as |FRAME: PRISTANATE pristanate|, or bile acid intermidiates (reviewed in |CITS: [17028011]|)., After several rounds of peroxisomal β-oxidation the products are shuttled into mitochondria and undergo further rounds of β-oxidation by either carnitine-dependent or carnitine-independent routes. These routes are tissue-dependent (reviewed in |CITS: [21683154]|) (see pathway |FRAME: FAO-PWY fatty acid β-oxidation I|).
