Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine nucleotides can be catabolized through three different pathways. The best characterized is the reductive pathway (this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-3982|) in which the pyrimidine nucleotides are reduced to |FRAME:Beta-amino-acids|, |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|. The pathway is found in mammals, plants, some fungi and microorganisms |CITS:[13428755][13416173][16655478][16656066][10656811]|. The oxidative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6426|) is only found in a few bacterial species and has not been characterized nearly as well. In it uracil is converted to |FRAME: UREA| and |FRAME: MALONATE| via |FRAME: BARBITURATE| |CITS: [12981104][14955523]|. A third pathway, known as the Rut pathway, was discovered much later in |FRAME: TAX-562| and other bacteria (see |FRAME: PWY0-1471|) |CITS: [16540542]|. That pathway starts with opening of the pyrimidine ring, and forms |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE| from uracil, with concomitant production of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME: AMMONIA|., About This Pathway, Some bacterial species are known to catabolize pyrimidines via a reductive pathway leading to the production of β-amino acids. The reductive pathway has been observed in various microorganisms including |FRAME: ORG-6124| |CITS: [13416173][13416174]|, |FRAME: TAX-12917| |CITS: [4986615]|, |FRAME: TAX-37762| |CITS: [3553866]|, |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [1903745]|, |FRAME: TAX-329| |CITS: [ 7710277]|, |FRAME: TAX-316| |CITS: [Xu92]|, |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [11759049]|, |FRAME: TAX-292| |CITS: [West97]|, |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS: [3926948]| and |FRAME: TAX-51101| |CITS: [12670488]|. , The reductive pathway of thymine is essentially the same in mammalian tissues |CITS: [12981074][13428755]|. The product of the pathway, |FRAME: CPD-471|, is is a non-protein amino acid |CITS: [4841987]|. The stereoisomer of this compound, |FRAME: CPD-466|, is produced via the degradation of |FRAME: VAL| (see |FRAME: VALDEG-PWY|). While the (S) isomer is reabsorbed into the plasma, the (R) isomer is eliminated in urine |CITS: [4841987][6945923]|., The pathway proceeds in three sequential enzymatic steps. The first enzyme is |FRAME: MONOMER-15398| (EC 1.3.1.2), which catalyzes the reversible reduction of both |FRAME:URACIL| and |FRAME: THYMINE| to |FRAME: DI-H-URACIL| and |FRAME: DIHYDRO-THYMINE|, respectively. The second enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-15399| (EC 3.5.2.2) performs reversible hydrolytic ring-opening of |FRAME: DI-H-URACIL| and |FRAME: DIHYDRO-THYMINE| to |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-ISOBUTYRATE|, respectively. Finally, |FRAME: MONOMER-15400| (EC 3.5.1.6) catalyzes the irreversible hydrolysis of |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-PROPIONATE| and |FRAME: 3-UREIDO-ISOBUTYRATE| to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| and |FRAME: 3-AMINO-ISOBUTYRATE|, respectively, in a reaction that produces ammonium and carbon dioxide.

Higher eukaryotes produce |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| from |FRAME: TYR|, as described in this pathway. In addition,, the pathway is found in some lower eukaryotes that lack |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.40|, which allows for |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| synthesis directly from |FRAME: CHORISMATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5755|)., Since |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is a precursor of ubiquinone, the pathway is essential for higher eukaryotes (yeast do have an alternative ubiquinone pathway that does not require |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate|, see |FRAME: PWY-7230|)., Considering the importance of this pathway, it is surprising how little attention it received. Most of the enzymes that participate in the pathway have not been characterized very well., A pathway for the conversion of |FRAME: TYR| to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| was proposed already in 1960, based on urinary excretion studies on animals administered with various phenolic acids and the incorporation of radiolabeled phenolic acids into ubiquinone by rat liver and yeast |CITS: [Booth60]|. Based on those results, it was suggested that |FRAME: TYR| is converted to |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE|, which is then modified to |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYPHENYLLACTATE| and |FRAME: COUMARATE| |CITS: [Booth60]|. These results were confirmed by additional work performed with rat |CITS: [14081946][14253463][6369767]|., The later part of the pathway, starting with |FRAME: COUMARATE|, has not been studied much in animals. In plants it has been shown that |FRAME: COUMARATE| is converted to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| either directly (see |FRAME: PWY-6431|) or via CoA derivatives such as |FRAME: P-COUMAROYL-COA| and |FRAME: CPD-201|  (see |FRAME: PWY-6435|). Experiments with yeast have shown that the last intermediate is |FRAME: 4-HYDROXYBENZALDEHYDE|, which is oxidized to |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.64| |CITS: [27693056]|.

|FRAME: CPD-397| (SMM) is synthesized from |FRAME: MET| by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.12| (MMT), an enzyme unique to plants. SMM has been hypothesized to be an essential methyl donor or a transportable form of sulfur, although these roles remain to be tested., The SMM cycle has been hypothesized to rectify overshoots in the conversion of free methionine required for protein biosynthesis to |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) in the SAM cycle (|FRAME: PWY-5041|) by providing a way to convert the methionine moiety locked up in adenosylmethionine back to free methionine. Alternatively, the SMM cycle has been hypothesized to regulate the cellular SAM level, hence the methylation ratio., Characterization of an Arabidopsis MMT knock-out mutant, which has a significant higher level of SAM content and unaltered free methionine pool, indicates the SMM cycle contributes to regulation of cellular methylation ratio rather than preventing depletion of free methionine., The SMM cycle operates throughout the plant, and consumes half of the adenosylmethionine produced in Arabidopsis leaves.

Summary: Hydroxycinnamic acid serotonin amides belong to the larger group of N-hydroxycinnamic acid amides (HCAAs). HCAAs are synthesized by the condensation of hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA thioesters and aromatic amines. The hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA thioesters include cinnamoyl-CoA, p-coumaroyl-CoA, caffeoyl-CoA, feruloyl-CoA and sinapoyl-CoA. The aromatic amines include tyramine, octopamine, tryptamine, serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline. The biosynthesis of HCAAs of serotonin is catalyzed by serotonin N-hydroxycinnamoyltransferase. Serotonin amides have only been reported in rice, pepper, and a few other plants. They have been reported to be antioxidants. Their role in plants is not clear.

Summary: General Background, Polyamines are widespread in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, with |FRAME: SPERMINE|, |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, and |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| being the most abundant ones. Polyamines play important roles in cell growth and differentiation, in responses to abiotic stress such as potassium deficiency, osmotic shock, drought and salt stress, and in plant-pathogen interactions. , In plants, polyamines can be degraded via two routes, the so-called terminal catabolic pathway and the back-conversion pathway. In both cases, H2O2 was produced as a by-product. In the |FRAME: PWY-6440 "terminal catabolic pathway"| plant apoplastic polyamine oxidases (PAOs) oxidize spermine and spermidine to |FRAME: CPD-313|, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| and the corresponding aminoaldehydes. These compounds cannot be converted directly to other polyamines. Therefore, this route is referred to as the terminal catabolic pathway |CITS: [16406305]|. In the |FRAME: PWY-6441 "back-conversion pathway"|, polyamines are interconverted. The peroxisome-localized PAOs oxidize spermine to spermidine, and consequently oxidize spermidine to putrescine |CITS: [18583528]|. Putrescine can be further degraded by putrescine oxidase (see |FRAME: PWY-2|)., About This Pathway, In the back-conversion pathway, unlike in mammals where acetyl-derivatives of spermine and spemidine are the best substrates of PAOs, the plant PAOs characterized so far act much better on spermine and/or spermidine than their acetyl-derivatives |CITS: [18583528], [18703589], [16778015]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram-negative bacteria, is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides, and is the first sugar added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA"|., Many species, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, add two Kdo sugars with a single Kdo bifunctional transferase (see |FRAME: KDOSYN-PWY|), whereas others, including members of |FRAME: TAX-724| and |FRAME: TAX-22|, add a single Kdo that is then phosphorylated by a separate enzyme at its 4-OH position, the same site at which the second Kdo residue is attached in |FRAME:TAX-562| |CITS: [9047308]|., Kdo-containing |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA"| molecules are intermediates; further acylation reactions are needed to produce the final Kdo(n)-Lipid A moiety. There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are also synthesized in plants |CITS: [21709257][16935939]|.

Summary: Isoflavonoids comprise a large group of secondary metabolites involved in plant-pathogen and plant-animal chemical warfare. These compounds are also involved in establishing the symbiotic relationship between legumes and rhizobial bacteria. Isoflavonoids are restrictive distributed in the plant kingdom, being mostly biosynthesized in plants of the subfamily Papilionoideae of the Leguminosae., Much of the interest in these secondary metabolites is based upon the finding that isoflavones and related compounds can act as estrogens in humans. Consequently, those compounds have now been termed phytoestrogens. In view of  their perceived chemopreventive activities against hormone-dependent cancers, cardiovascular disease, and postmenopausal ailments, isoflavonoids are considered as major targets for metabolic engineering.

Summary: Background, Purine nucleotides participate in many aspects of cellular metabolism including the structure of DNA and RNA, serving as enzyme cofactors, functioning in cellular signaling, acting as phosphate group donors, and generating cellular energy |CITS: [18365665]|. Maintenance of the proper balance of intracellular pools of purine nucleotides is critical to normal function |CITS: [18712276]|. This occurs through a combination of |FRAME: PWY-841| and purine salvage |CITS: [23575936]|. The de novo purine biosynthesis is more energy consuming than the purine salvage pathway. The two pathways converge at |FRAME: IMP|., About this Pathway, The salvage pathway utilizes |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE|, |FRAME: ADENINE| or |FRAME: GUANINE| to synthesize purine nucleotides. When there is sufficient hypoxanthine for cell growth, the salvage pathway is preferentially used for purine nucleotide biosynthesis. The regulatory capacity of this pathway is significantly less than |FRAME: PWY-841| and has a lesser effect upon growth rate. Therefore, tissues that have inherently limited biosynthetic capacity rely upon the purine salvage pathway or obtain purines from other tissues |CITS: [23575936]|., A deficiency of the purine salvage enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-7955|, leads to hyperuricemia, a condition where blood levels of uric acid are abnormally high, and a disorder called Lesch-Nyhan disease |CITS: [1301916]|. Mutations in the PRPS1 gene that give rise to overactivity of |FRAME: CPLX66-360|, the enzyme that delivers purine precursors to the pathway, result in a similar hyperuricemic metabolic disorder |CITS: [16176880]|. Hyperuricemia can also lead to debilitating inflammatory arthritis, called gout.

Summary: Thiaminase II activity has been observed in bacteria |CITS:[15709744]| and fungi, more specifically in cell free extracts of |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS:[3305065]| but its physiological role remained unresolved for a long time. In bacteria a thiamine salvage pathway has been reported in which the key enzyme thiaminase II (TenA) catalyzed the hydrolysis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| and thiamine analogs to form |FRAME:HMP|. The latter represents a precursor for the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| and its phosphorylated derivatives (see |FRAME:PWY-6899|) |CITS:[17618314] [17637774]|., |FRAME:TAX-4932| employs an enzyme, i.e. THI20p which is characterized by unique properties, namely the display of both |FRAME:THIAMINE| biosynthetic and degradation activities in one fusion protein. THI20 encodes a trifunctional protein which exhibits HMP kinase (EC 2.7.1.49) and HMP-P kinase (EC 2.7.4.7) from a dimeric structure of the N-terminal domain and thiaminase II activity (EC 3.5.99.2) from a dimeric structure of the C-terminal domain linked together through a loop and a short helix |CITS:[15967475] [21904031]|. Utilizing various mutant strains of yeast devoid of one or more activities of the trifunctional enzyme it could be shown that the thiaminase II activity was not required for the de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME:THIAMINE| but was rather involved in the salvage of |FRAME:THIAMINE| |CITS:[18028398]|. The |FRAME:THIAMINE| degrading capacity of thiaminase II had been demonstrated in yeast |CITS:[15967475]| (this pathway) but THI20p was also able to hydrolyze |FRAME:THIAMINE| analogs such as |FRAME:CPD-13578| (see |FRAME:PWY-6899|) or |FRAME:CPD-15776| and |FRAME:CPD-15777| (see |FRAME:PWY-7357|) |CITS:[18028398]|. , It is known that yeast can take up both |FRAME:HMP| and |FRAME:THZ| from its environment |CITS:[4591128] [3027234] [2407290]| indicating that the trifunctional HMP/HMP-P kinase and thiaminase II can handle both endogenous and exogenous degradation products of |FRAME:THIAMINE|. Thiaminase II had been demonstrated to significantly increase activity after the addition of |FRAME:ATP|. This finding and the observation that |FRAME:HMP|, the direct product of the thiaminase II catalysis, is a strong inhibitor of that reaction implies the immediate phosphorylation by the HMP/HMP-P kinase activities of the same enzyme and strongly indicates that the physiological role of THI20 lies in the salvage pathway(s) of |FRAME:THIAMINE| |CITS:[18028398]|.

General Background, There are several alternative pathways for the degradation of trehalose. Depending on the organism and the particular environmental conditions, trehalose may be broken down outside of the cytoplasm, enter the cell either through a permease, in which case it remains unmodified, or it may be transported by a phosphotransferase system (PTS), resulting in the phosphorylated trehalose-6-phosphate form. Degradation can proceed by different mechanisms: Unmodified trehalose may be degraded by a hydrolyzing trehalase (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182| and |FRAME: PWY0-1466|), or it may be split by the action of a trehalose phosphorylase (see |FRAME: PWY-2722| and |FRAME: PWY-2723|). Likewise, trehalose-6-phosphate may be either hydrolyzed by trehalose-6-phosphate hydrolase (see |FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) or it could be attacked by a trehalose-6-phosphate phosphorylase (see |FRAME: PWY-2721|)., About This Pathway, Trehalase enzymes of the GH37 family of glycoside hydrolases hydrolyze a molecule of |FRAME: TREHALOSE| into two molecules of glucose with inversion of the anomeric configuration. , |FRAME:TAX-562| can grow with trehalose as the sole carbon source, and employs different pathways for its degradation under different osmolarity conditions. Under conditions of high osmolarity, the PTS pathway for uptake of trehalose (|FRAME: TREDEGLOW-PWY|) is blocked. The |FRAME: TREHALAPERI-MONOMER| (TreA) provides the cell the ability to utilize trehalose under those conditions |CITS: [2671658]|. External trehalose is hydrolyzed by TreA into two molecules of glucose |CITS: [2820965]|, which are then transported into the cytoplasm through the glucose PTS |CITS: [1825082]|., TreA also has a second function: under high osmotic conditions, the bacterium synthesizes large amounts of trehalose to be used as an osmoprotectant. TreA recycles trehalose molecules that leak from the cytoplasm into the periplasm |CITS: [3131312]|., Another pathway that utilizes a cytoplasmic trehalase is active during the transition period between high and low osmolarity (see |FRAME: PWY0-1182|).

Summary: General Background, Pyrimidine and purine nucleoside triphosphates are the activated precursors of DNA and RNA. The pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: DCTP| and |FRAME: TTP| are incorporated into DNA while the ribonucleoside triphosphates |FRAME: CTP| and |FRAME: UTP| are incorporated into RNA. In addition, their diphosphates form activated derivatives of other molecules, such as |FRAME: CPD-12575|, |FRAME: CMP-KDO| and |FRAME: DTDP-D-FUCOSE|, for use in biosynthesis of polysaccharides, glycoproteins and phospholipids |CITS: [9576794][12369616][16024685][16669783]|., In addition to de novo biosynthesis, salvage pathways reutilize exogenous free bases and nucleosides and some of the resulting pyrimidine nucleotides can enter the de novo biosynthesis pathways (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|, |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7199|). The de novo biosynthetic pathways consume relatively large amounts of high energy phosphate and reducing power, and thus organisms prefer to use salvage pathways when possible. However, the de novo biosynthetic pathways are necessary when exogenous precursors are limiting. In order to conserve resources, the de novo pathways are regulated both by allosteric enzymes and at the gene expression level., These essential, evolutionarily conserved biosynthetic and salvage pathways are found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes., About This Pathway, While de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotides starts with |FRAME: UMP| (see |FRAME: PWY-7184|, some organisms utilize this salvage pathway to generate |FRAME: TTP| from |FRAME: CTP|., The key enzyme of the pathway is |FRAME: CPLX-8624| (dCMP deaminase) (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.12 "EC 3.5.4.12"|). This allosteric enzyme, which is found in Gram-positive bacteria, fungi and metazoa, catalyzes the deamination of |FRAME: DCMP| to form |FRAME: DUMP|, thus providing the nucleotide substrate for |FRAME: HS11096-MONOMER "thymidylate synthase"| (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "EC 2.1.1.45"|)., While another allosteric enzyme, |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase (EC 1.17.4.1)"| (RNR), plays an essential role in the de novo biosynthesis of all four dNTPs required for DNA synthesis, dCMP deaminase is specifically involved in the production of dTTP. The enzyme is allosterically activated by dCTP and inhibited by dTTP, and is thus regulated by the ratio of dCTP to dTTP in the cell |CITS: [22927644]|. Both dCTP and dTTP appear to bind a single allosteric site located far from the active site, and Mg2+ is involved in their binding |CITS: [7138806]|., The actual reduction of a ribonucleotide to a deoxyribonucleotide (CDP to dCDP in this case) is catalyzed by the rate-limiting |FRAME: EC-1.17.4.1 "EC 1.17.4.1, ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase"|. This enzyme, which plays a central role in DNA replication and repair, can perform the reduction of only the diphosphate form of ribonucleosides., Formation of the DNA-specific end product |FRAME: TTP| requires reductive methylation of |FRAME: DUMP| to |FRAME: TMP| by |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF| catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.45 "thymidylate synthase"| (EC 2.1.1.45)., Once |FRAME: TMP| is formed, two phosphorylations follow to form |FRAME: TTP|. The first step is catalyzed by the highly specific |FRAME: HS11626-MONOMER|, while the second step is catalyzed by the broad substrate range enzyme |FRAME: CPLX66-1052|.

Summary: General Background, While the amino acid |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| is not involved, directly in protein synthesis, it is an important intermediate in many metabolic pathways, such as, the |FRAME:PWY-4984| and the biosynthesis of several compounds, including arginine, (see |FRAME:ARGSYN-PWY| and |FRAME:ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|), proline (see |FRAME:PWY-3341|, and |FRAME:PWY-4981|), and putrescine (|FRAME:PWY-46|), which leads to the biosynthesis of other, polyamines and pyrimidines. It is also involved in |FRAME: PWY-6818|., This pathway documents the synthesis of |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE| from |FRAME:GLT| via, N-acetylated intermediates. The presumed reason for the acetylation is that it prevents the, spontaneous cyclization of glutamate derivatives, which leads to proline biosynthesis (see, |FRAME:PROSYN-PWY|), thus keeping the pathways leading to arginine and proline separate, (|CITS: [12633501]| and references therein). , Two alternative pathways have evolved, which differ in the way the key intermediate, |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU| (NAG) is formed, and in the way the acetyl group is removed from another, intermediate, |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE|., In this pathway, which is less common, NAG is formed by NAG synthase, and, |FRAME:N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is hydrolyzed by the enzyme acetylornithine deacetylase,, forming |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| and |FRAME: ACET|., In the other pathway (see |FRAME:ARGSYNBSUB-PWY|), which is found in most of the prokaryotic and, eukaryotic microbes investigated up to now, the two reactions are linked: the acetyl group which is, removed from |FRAME: N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE| is recycled onto |FRAME: GLT|, regenerating, |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU| (NAG). , About This Pathway, This ornithine biosynthesis pathway has been found in the |FRAME:TAX-543|, |FRAME: TAX-83333| and |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS: [3534538]|,, the |FRAME: TAX-641| |CITS: [10692366]|, the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-34|, |CITS: [ 9829957]|, and the archaeon |FRAME: TAX-2287| |CITS: [vandecasteele90]|., In it |FRAME: GLT| is acetylated to NAG by the enzyme, |FRAME:N-ACETYLTRANSFER-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10063| gene., The acetyl donor for this reaction is |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. , NAG is then converted in several enzymatic steps to |FRAME: N-ALPHA-ACETYLORNITHINE|., The acetyl group is removed in the form of |FRAME: ACET| by the enzyme, |FRAME:ACETYLORNDEACET-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME:EG11286| gene, resulting in, |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|.

Summary: General Background, The common |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| pathway, used by most organisms for the catabolism of glucose and related sugars, can be regarded as both an energy-producing catabolic pathway and an anabolic pathway, producing |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which can be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|. While |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| can be fed to the TCA cycle for further energy production, it is also used as a biosynthestic precursor for many types of biomolecules (e.g. fatty acids). However, glycolysis is unable to produce 5-carbon sugars such as D-ribose, which are essential for the biosynthesis of DNA and RNA, neither can it form the 4-carbon sugar |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, a precursor of aromatic amino acids and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, or the 7-carbon sugar |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, a precursor for |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|., The |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| is an alternative way of oxidizing glucose that is targeted at anabolic reactions. The pathway fulfills two anabolic roles: it produces NADPH, making it a major source of reducing equivalents for biosynthetic reactions, and it produces C4, C5, and C7 sugars |CITS: [13129245][13174590][14790817][14285485]|., About This Pathway, The pentose phosphate pathway is an important member of central metabolism, as it supplies three of the 13 precursor metabolites (compounds needed for the biosyntheses): |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|, |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|. For convenience, the pentose phosphate pathway is commonly divided into its preliminary |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative portion"| and the subsequent |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative portion"|., The unidirectional oxidative branch fulfills two roles of the pathway - it produces a pentose sugar (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|) from the hexose |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, and it produces two equivalents of NADPH in the process., The non-oxidative branch of composed of a series of rearrangements catalyzed by an isomerase, an epimerase, a transketolase, and a transaldolase, involving a C3 compound (|FRAME: GAP|), a C4 compound (|FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|), C5 compounds (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|), a C6 compound (|FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|), and a C7 compound (|FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|). Unlike the oxidative branch, the non-oxidative branch is fully reversible, allowing for different molecules to enter the pathway at different stages and be transformed to any other intermediate in this branch. No energy or reducing power is produced by the non-oxidative branch - it's sole purpose is carbon rearrangements. It should be noted that due to its reversibility, the non-oxidative branch also participates in the catabolism of pentoses (see |FRAME: XYLCAT-PWY|)., In prokaryotes and animals the pentose phosphate pathway takes place in the cytosol, the same location as glycolysis. In plants, the oxidative part of the pathway also takes place in plastids |CITS: [Foster93]|.

Summary: General Background, Carbon tetrachloride (CT) is a toxic and carcinogenic compound which is primarily used as a chemical intermediate in the production of the refrigerants, |FRAME: CPD-8224| and |FRAME:CPD-8223|. Freon 11 and 12 are also used as solvents, in plastic and resin production, as foam blowing agents and previously as aerosol propellants. CT has also been used as a grain fumigant, but this use was banned by the EPA in 1985. In 2000 alone, the United States exported approximately 32 billion lbs worldwide of CT |CITS: [ROC11]|. Improper disposal of CT resulted in widespread contamination of soils and groundwater., Fully halogenated compounds such as CT are resistant to aerobic degradation and are relatively stable under aerobic conditions. However, under anaerobic conditions CT can be degraded by bacterial enzymes or compounds in several different pathways. Carbon tetrachloride degradation has been documented in many environments, including methanogenic |CITS: [Egli90]|, acetogenic |CITS: [3145712][Egli90]|, sulfate reducing |CITS: [3145712][Egli90]|, iron reducing |CITS: [8285682][7926693]|, and nitrate reducing |CITS: [6859850]| conditions. In all of these cases, CT appears to be cometabolized, that is, the reaction is a fortuitous modification of the substrate by enzymes or cofactors that would normally catalyze other reactions. The bacteria derive no benefit from cometabolic reactions., About This Pathway, In many organisms the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-842| results in the accumulation of less chlorinated methanes (see |FRAME:PWY-5370|). However, less than 50% of the CT is actually converted into these compounds |CITS: [2001359]|., Labeling studies indicated that in the case of |FRAME: TAX-33952| the main product was actually |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [3145712]|. Similar results were obtained with additional CT-degrading organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-2296| and |FRAME: TAX-145262| |CITS: [Egli90]|., Further research revealed that a second pathway exists that converts CT to |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| via |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE| and |FRAME: FORMATE| |CITS: [2001359]|. The first step, which is common to both pathways, is the cometabolic reaction between CT and a |FRAME:CPLX-1|, an important protein of the |FRAME:CODH-PWY|. During this reaction a |FRAME:CPD-8214| is formed |CITS: [2001359]|. This radical is either protonated to form |FRAME:CPD-843|, as depicted in the |FRAME:PWY-5370| pathway, or alternatively it could eliminate a chloride and become a |FRAME:CPD-8225| |CITS: [2001359]|. The carbene is unstable, and is hydrolyzed into |FRAME:HCL| and either |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE| or |FRAME:FORMATE| |CITS: [2001359]|, depending on the number of water molecules involved. This finding was supported by further research, which demonstrated that |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE| was generated during CT degradation in an electrolytic model system |CITS: [Criddle91]|, during in vitro reaction with vitamin B12 |CITS:[Chiu96]|, and by living cultures of |FRAME: TAX-38313| strain BrY |CITS:[Workman97]|. Hasham and Freedman showed that |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| accounted for up to 30% of the CT degraded by a culture of |FRAME: TAX-33952|, and that conversion to |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE| was the predominant pathway in formation of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| |CITS: [10508086]|., |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE "Carbon monoxide"| is rapidly oxidized into |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| by the enzyme, |FRAME:EC-1.2.7.4|, working in reverse direction (in the |FRAME:CODH-PWY| this enzyme catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:CARBON-MONOXIDE|, which provides the carbonyl group of acetyl-coA)., Similarly, the formate that is formed can also be converted into |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-1241|, another enzyme of the |FRAME:CODH-PWY|.

Summary: General Background, Cyanogenic glycosides are phytotoxic secondary metabolites found in several thousand plant species including a number of agriculturally important crops such as cassava, sorghum, flax and lotus. Chemically they are β-glycosides of α-hydroxynitriles. They are derived from amino acids, including tyrosine, phenylalanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, and cyclopentenyl-glycine. Generally, a particular cyanogenic glycoside occurs only in one or two plant families, and conversely, only one or two cyanogenic glycosides are present in a given plant. , In order to avoid self-intoxication cyanogenic glucosides are stored in the vacuole. Under pathogen or herbivore attacks they come in contact with activating enzymes (specific β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases) that reside in the cytoplasm or apoplastic space of the cells, releasing toxic |FRAME: HCN| that serves as the first line of chemical defense |CITS:[16667728][Ganjewala10]|., While the most studied pathway of cyanogenic glucoside biosynthesis is that for |FRAME: CPD-1042|, all cyanogenic glycosides are synthesized from amino acids by conserved mechanisms, and the pathways only differ in the specificity of the enzymes involved. The pathways involve two cytochrome P450s and a glucosyltransferase. The first step, the conversion of the amino acid to an oxime, is catalyzed by a membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belongs to the CYP79 family. This is the rate-limiting step of the pathway, and the substrate preference of this enzyme is the major factor determining the content of different cyanogenic glucosides accumulated in a given species., The next step, the conversion of the aldoxime into a hydroxynitrile by dehydration and C-hydroxylation is catalyzed by a different membrane-bound multifunctional cytochrome P450 that belong to the CYP71 family. The substrate for the dehydration reaction is the (Z) isomer of the oxime, while the isomer produced by the CYP79 enzyme is known tio be the (E) isomer. While the two isomers do reach equilibrium without catalysis, the reaction is very slow and early observations indicated that the isomerization is catalyzed in vivo by an enzyme |CITS: [2684955]|. The identity of that enzyme responsible for the isomerization was revealed only in 2015, when it was shown to be one of the enzymatic activities of CYP71 enzymes |CITS: [26361733]|. Thus CYP71 enzymes are trifunctional, catalyzing isomerization, dehydration and C-hydroxylation., The last part of the pathway is catalyzed by soluble UDP-sugar glycosyltransferases that glycosylate the hydroxynitriles into cyanogenic glycosides., About This Pathway, |FRAME: LINAMARIN Linamarin| and |FRAME: CPD-10277| have a broader distribution in the plant kingdom than most cyanogenic glycosides. They have been reported in five plant families, and co-exist in lotus, flax and cassava (|FRAME: TAX-3983|), the most important tropical root crop., Over-dose eating of cyanogenic glycoside-containing plants by animals and humans can be lethal. The high linamarin content in cassava hinders its direct consumption. It is thus highly desired to reduce the linamarin level possibly by metabolic engineering., Studies using seedlings indicated that linamarin is synthesized in the cotyledons and transported to the other tissues in cassava. In |FRAME:TAX-34305|, linamarin and lotaustralin (derived from isoleucine) are synthesized and stored in young growing tissues like seedlings, apical leaves and stems. They are not transported to other tissues. Roots and dry seeds contain no detectable cyanogenic glucosides.

Summary: |FRAME: SQUALENE Squalene| is a naturally occurring polyprenyl compound primarily known for its key role as an intermediate in sterol biosynthesis. The name originates from the scientific name for the shark (|FRAME: TAX-7796| spp.), since shark liver oil is considered the richest source of squalene. However, squalene is abundant in many plant oils, including olive oil, palm oil, wheat-germ oil, amaranth oil, and rice bran oil., Squalene is structurally similar to |FRAME: CPD1F-129|, and is produced in two steps from two molecules of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| which are joined and reduced by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.21|. After its biosynthesis, squalene can be transported to other areas of the body for incorporation into tissues (in humans, about 60 percent of dietary squalene is absorbed and transported in serum to be distributed ubiquitously in different tissues, with the greatest, concentration in the skin |CITS: [9988781]|) or it can be further metabolized by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.17|, generating |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE|., The fate of |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| varies in different organisms. In animals and fungi it is substrate for |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.7|, an enzyme that generates |FRAME: LANOSTEROL|, a main gateway for the synthesis of all other sterols in these organisms, including cholesterol (see |FRAME: PWY66-341|). In plants |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| is processed by |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.8|, which generates |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL|. This compound is then converted to many different sterol compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-2541|)., Squalene and its derivatives appear to be very common in the Archaea.  A study of the lipid composition of the thermophilic chemolithotroph |FRAME: TAX-145262| showed that squalene was the major component of the non-polar lipids |CITS: [691077]|. Another study of the neutral lipids of nine species of methanogens found that squalene and/or hydrosqualene derivatives were the predominant components in eight of them |CITS: [458874]|., Sterol biosynthesis by eubacteria is very rare. However, steroid precursors including |FRAME: LANOSTEROL| and |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL| were isolated from several prokaryotes, including |FRAME: TAX-41| |CITS: [12519197]|, |FRAME: TAX-54| |CITS: [Kohl83]|, |FRAME: TAX-114| |CITS: [14660793]| and |FRAME: TAX-51353| |CITS: [10802170]|., Genes encoding the enzymes |FRAME: MONOMER-14485| and |FRAME: MONOMER-14484| have been cloned from |FRAME: TAX-414|, which produces several modified lanosterol products (see |FRAME: PWY-8026|) |CITS: [17928701]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-7994 1-Methylpyrrolinium|, derived from |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, is a major branch-point metabolite in alkaloid metabolism. The medicinal tropane alkaloids |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE| and |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE|, as well as the non-tropane alkaloid |FRAME: NICOTINE|, are derived from this intermediate. The fore-mentioned alkaloids generally accumulate in roots of solanaceous plants.  Putrescine methyltransferase is the first committed enzyme specific to the biosynthesis of these alkaloids. It diverts the metabolism of putrescine from polyamine synthesis to alkaloid synthesis.

Names: polymyxin resistance // L-Ara4N-modified lipid A biosynthesis // 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose-modified lipid A biosynthesis
Summary: |FRAME: Polymyxins Polymyxins| are antibiotics with a general structure consisting of a cyclic peptide with a long hydrophobic tail. , They are produced by the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME:TAX-1406| and are selectively toxic for Gram-negative bacteria due to their specificity for the lipopolysaccharide molecules that exist within many Gram-negative outer membranes. Polymyxins disrupt the structure of the bacterial cell membrane by interacting with its phospholipids, and specifically with lipid A. Lipid A is negatively charged due to two phosphate groups, and the cationic polymyxin readily binds to it and induces cell death by permeabilizing the bacterial membrane., Some Gram-negative bacteria, specifically Salmonella typhimurium and |FRAME:TAX-562|, can become resistant to polymyxin by the modification of  their lipid A structure via the attachment of 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinopyranose (L-Ara4N) groups to one or more phosphate groups |CITS: [17686460][18467098][19076233][19767429][ 21114395]|. This addition causes an absolute increase in lipid A charge, thus lowering the affinity of positively charged polymyxins |CITS: [18187325]|., The modification of lipid A with 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinopyranose (L-Ara4N) was first found in mutants of |FRAME:TAX-562| that are resistant to polymyxin |CITS: [7565089][11535605]|. However, the pathway for the synthesis of L-Ara4N and its transport and attachment to lipid A has been studied mostly in Salmonella., The pathway is well understood up to the formation of |FRAME: CPD0-888| (UDP-Ara4FN). All steps up to this intermediate occur in the cytoplasm. UDP-Ara4FN is deformylated and transferred from the inner to the outer bacterial membrane by mechanisms that are not fully understood, although ArnE(PmrM) and ArnF(PmrL) may have a role in the transportation of UDP-Ara4FN across the bacterial inner membrane |CITS: [17928292]|. Once in the periplasm, LAra4N is transferred to lipid A by ArnT(PmrK) |CITS: [15939024][12045108][16226890]| ., The pathway is regulated by the |FRAME: PWY0-1482| (pmrA/pmrB). |FRAME: EG11615| is a response regulator that in its phosphorylated form can activate the genes that encode the proteins described in this pathway. Activation occurs either directly by Fe3+ ions |CITS: [11051552]|, or by a second two component system, the |FRAME: PWY0-1458|, which is activated by low Mg2+ concentration |CITS: [9371451]|. , The two systems are linked in Salmonella by the polymyxin resistance protein, |FRAME: G7172-MONOMER PmrD|. The PhoP-activated PmrD protects the phosphorylated response regulator PmrA from dephosphorylation, and promotes the transcription of PmrA-activated genes responsible for polymyxin resistance |CITS: [10775270]|. In E. coli PmrD does not protect the phosphorylated |FRAME: EG11615|. This may be the reason why E. coli fails to activate the pathway under low Mg2+ concentrations |CITS: [10373459]|.

Several different enzymes convert |FRAME: LYS| to |FRAME: ALLYSINE|, as shown in MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-5298|, |FRAME: PWY-5314| and |FRAME: PWY-5324|. , In this pathway, |FRAME: LYS| is converted to |FRAME: ALLYSINE| by |FRAME: CPLX-7145|. |FRAME: ALLYSINE| is subsequently cyclized by spontaneous intramolecular dehydration to |FRAME: CPD-7682| |CITS: [5722275][4088080][10965037]|. , This enzymatic activity has been shown in the γ-proteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-255 "Flavobacterium lutescens IFO3084 (previously known as Achromobacter liquidum)"| |CITS: [4088080]| and in the actinomycete |FRAME:TAX-1901|., Further catabolism of |FRAME: CPD-468| in |FRAME: TAX-255| has not been described although in some other γ-proteobacteria it is catabolized to glutarate (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5283|)., Iin |FRAME:TAX-1901| |FRAME: CPD-468| is a precursor of β-lactam antibiotics and is a substrate for |FRAME: MONOMER-13331| (see |FRAME: PWY-5629|) |CITS: [9355735]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: BIOTIN| is a water soluble, heterocyclic cofactor for a small number of enzymes, that facilitate the transfer of CO2 during carboxylation, decarboxylation and transcarboxylation reactions , involved in fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism |CITS: [SHELLHAMMER90][11706201][15012185]|. , The biotin-requiring enzymes identified so far (including |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX|,, |FRAME: CPLX66-17|, |FRAME: CPLX-5203|, and |FRAME: CPLX-6001|) play essential roles in cell metabolism, |CITS: [8676868]|. , Biotin may also have functions in metabolism other than its mere catalytic role as an enzyme cofactor. It has been, shown that biotin also carries out non-catalytic functions in the expression of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, in |FRAME:TAX-3701| biotin-auxotroph mutants, by modulating and regulating gene expression |CITS: [12644697]|. , Biotin biosynthesis is found in plants, bacteria and certain fungi. Although animals and most fungi cannot synthesize their own biotin, a daily intake is required for normal growth and development |CITS: [11322938]|. , The biotin biosynthetic pathway has been explored in detail in bacteria (|FRAME: PWY0-1507|). The , ongoing success in sequencing whole genomes from other organisms has provided evidence that the general steps , in bacterial biotin synthesis are conserved in plants |CITS: [11322938]|. , About This Pathway, The classic models for microbial biotin biosynthesis are |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-1423| and |FRAME: TAX-1421|, but recently detailed analysis of biotin biosynthetic genes was done with several other bacteria., There is much variation in the organization of the genes involved: In some cases all of the bio genes, are organized within a single transcription unit (such as in |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [8763940]|, and |FRAME: TAX-381| |CITS: [11320134]|), while in other cases the genes are organized in multiple operons, sometimes at different locations in the chromosome., Some organisms even lack some of the genes - for example, |FRAME: TAX-1718| seems to lack the bioC, bioH and bioF genes |CITS: [8161820]|., There are two documented differences between the biosynthetic pathways of |FRAME: TAX-562| (|FRAME: BIOTIN-BIOSYNTHESIS-PWY|) and |FRAME: TAX-1423| (|FRAME: PWY-5005|)., The first one concerns the synthesis of |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE|. While most Gram-negative bacteria synthesize it from |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP "malonyl-[acp]"| as described in |FRAME: PWY-6519|, Bacilli are believed to generate it from |FRAME: CPD-558|, which is derived from |FRAME:CPD-205|. These two reactions are catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-10705| and |FRAME: G-10706| gene products |CITS:[12658511]|., In addition, the amino donor for the conversion of |FRAME: 8-AMINO-7-OXONONANOATE| to |FRAME: DIAMINONONANOATE| is |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| in |FRAME: TAX-562| and |FRAME: LYS| in |FRAME: TAX-1423|., While the exact pathway leading to |FRAME: CPD-205| formation is still unknown, it has been shown that the fatty acid biosynthesis system is involved in pimelate production, as |FRAME: CPD-6901|, an inhibitor of the key fatty acid elongation enzyme FabF, markedly decreased biotin production in a wild type |FRAME: TAX-1423|, whereas a strain having a cerulenin-resistant FabF mutant produced more biotin |CITS: [28196402]|.

Hordatines are antifungal compounds found to be highly abundant in young barley seedlings. The accumulation of hordatines reaches its maximum level within the first 3-6 days after seed germination |CITS: [12582168]|. Although hordatines seem to be confined to the genus |FRAME:TAX-4512|, structurally related compounds such as |FRAME: CPD-12236| and |FRAME: CPD-12237| were found in wheat |CITS: [10993146], [12843649]|., Hordatines are directly derived from hydroxycinnamoylagmatines. The first step of hordatine biosynthesis is a condensation reaction of a hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA with agmatine. The enzyme catalyzing this reaction, agmatine coumaroyltransferase (ACT), has been purified from barley, and its cDNA cloned |CITS: [12582168]|. Among varies hydroxycinnamoyl-CoAs, in vitro assays of ACT indicated that the enzyme had the highest activity for coumaroyl-CoA. The oxidative dimerization mechanism which yields hordatines from hydroxycinnamoylagmatines is not known. It was indicated that the process could be achieved in the presence of hydrogen peroxide and a horseradish peroxidase, as referenced in |CITS: [12582168]|.

Summary: This is one of only two aromatic-ring-cleavage pathways, found in |FRAME:TAX-562| (for the second one, see |FRAME: PWY0-321|)., That |FRAME:TAX-562| can degrade aromatic acids suggests a, wider natural distribution for |FRAME:TAX-562| than the anaerobic environment, of the animal gut.  |CITS: [6345502]| In the utilization of aromatic, acids as a carbon and energy source, |FRAME:TAX-562| employs a branched, meta-cleavage pathway for the degradation of 3-phenylpropionate and, 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl)propionate.  Degradation of these two compounds, ultimately yields succinate, acetaldehyde and pyruvate.  Acetaldehyde is , further metabolized to yield acetyl-CoA. The pathway, has eight known steps, which makes it among the longest catabolic, sequences in |FRAME:TAX-562|.  |CITS: [3531186] [8399388] [9098055]|

|FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| is the most oxidized two-carbon compound. It is made in high concentrations by some plants and fungi and can reach high micromolar concentrations in soil. Oxalate is toxic to mammals but is metabolized by many bacteria and plants by various pathways., The homoacetogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1525| can split one molecule of |FRAME: OXALATE| into two molecules of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, which feed into the |FRAME: CODH-PWY|, in a single enzymatic step. During growth on |FRAME: OXALATE|, |FRAME: TAX-1525|  produces 1 mol of |FRAME: ACET| and 6 mol of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| for every 4 mols of oxalate |CITS: [14769464]|., The protein responsible for this conversion is |FRAME: CPLX-8221|, a member of the 2-oxoacid:ferredoxin oxidoreductase family |CITS: [20956531]|. Unlike all other members known at the time of its discovery, it does not use coenzyme A as a substrate. The enzyme transfers its reducing equivalents to a broad range of electron acceptors, including ferredoxin and the nickel-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-1302 "carbon monoxide dehydrogenase"|.

General Background, Gentiodelphin, i.e. delphinidin 3-O-glucosyl-5-O-caffeoylglucoside-3'-O-caffeoylglucoside , found in the genus Gentiana is a unusual stable anthocyanin conferring deep blue flower colors to this species , |CITS: [GOTO82]|. The stability of this compound has been proposed as an effect of the intramolecular stacking , of acyl residues attached to the opposite sides of the A and B-ring sandwiching the corresponding anthocyanidin , |CITS: [YOSHIDA91]|. The anthocyanidins are self-assembled into chiral supramolecular complexes that have , been proposed to contribute to biological functions such as UV protection and specific color variations to attract , insects for pollination |CITS: [16385618]|., Research on mono-deacyl derivatives of gentiodelphin, i.e. albireodelphin (acetylated in the A-ring 5-O-glucoside) , and mono-deacylgentiodelphin (acytelated in the B-ring 3'-O-glucoside) revealed that the positioning of , the caffeoyl residues is vital to stability and coloration of the anthocyanidin. The caffeoyl residue attached to , the 3'-O-glucoside of the B-ring contributed more stability through intramolecular stacking and more , color development to gentiodelphin than the caffeoyl residue on the A-ring |CITS: [10846752]|., About This Pathway, The first committed step in the gentiodelphin biosynthesis is the 5-O-glucosylation , of delphinidin 3-O-glucoside. The enzyme has been characterized from |FRAME:TAX-48386| , |CITS: [10066805]| but the activity of the anthocyanin 5-O-glucosyltransferase (5-GT) has also been reported , (unpublished results) in crude extracts of |FRAME:TAX-55190| |CITS: [9363752]|. Anthocyanin 5-O-glucosyltransferase activity was reported from |FRAME:TAX-55190| petal extracts, the cDNA cloned and recombinant expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. The catalytic properties of the recombinant enzyme indicate |FRAME:CPD-7117| as the preferred substrate and its in vivo activity was also confirmed in transgenic tobacco catalyzing the 5-O-glucosylation of the endogenous |FRAME: CPD-15001| yielding |FRAME: CPD-15002| which is not occurring naturally in this plant |CITS:[18375606]|., The next steps that further decorate delphinidin 3,5-glucoside with caffeic acid and glucose are proposed to , constitute a metabolic grid in the biosynthetic route towards gentiodelphin. Both possible routes, i.e. 3'-O-glucosylation , followed by the aromatic 5-O-acylation or vice versa are displayed and thought to be present in Gentiana , |CITS: [9881162]| |CITS: [12857844]|. The glucosyltransferases involved in the biosynthesis of gentiodelphin are , highly position specific and follow a defined order which is the 3-O-glucosylation followed by the , 5-O-glucosylation and the subsequent 3'-O-glucosylation of the delphinidin backbone , |CITS: [12857844]|. Although the function of the anthocyanin 3'-O-glucosyltransferase characterized , in |FRAME:TAX-43366| (compare |FRAME:PWY-5295|) |CITS: [Kazuma04]| is very similar to the 3'GT , involved in the biosynthesis of gentiodelphin (this pathway) there are differences, i.e. substrate preference , between those enzymes with regard to the occurrence of acyl groups in the anthocyanidin molecule. , The aromatic acylation with two caffeoyl residues also exhibits strict substrate specificity. The 5-aromatic , acyltransferase |CITS: [9363752]| |CITS: [9881162]| can only acylate the 5-O-glucoside but not the , 3, 7 or 3' positions of anthocyanins. This enzyme has been located to the cytosol of the outer epidermal , cells of petals |CITS: [9881162]| which coincides with the location of the 3'-O-glucosyltransferase , whose activity has been only found in petals but not in sepals of |FRAME:TAX-55190| |CITS: [12857844]|. , The aromatic 3'-acyltransferase shaping the final structure of gentiodelphin has not yet been identified and , remains to be characterized., Addendum, The final step in the gentiodelphin biosynthesis, i.e. the acetylation of the 3'-position of the B-ring has been described in an US patent |CITS:[Tanaka11]|. It has been published that |FRAME:MONOMER-12014| |CITS:[9881162]| characterized as a 5-acyltransferase is also able to acylate the 3'-position at the B-ring of anthocyanins but no further experimental results have been provided |CITS:[Mizutani06]|.

Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) catalyzes the degradation of phenylalanine to tyrosine. The enzyme was reported in human, animal and some microbes. Deficiency of PAH in human is related to the metabolic disorder phenylketonuria. It is only very recent, through a phylogenetic and biochemical study, PAH was shown to present in nonflowering plants |CITS: [20959559]|. Still, there is no evidence for its presence in flowering plants |CITS: [20959559], [18245455]|. The cofactor for human PAH is tetrahydrobiopterin |CITS: [10727395]| which however does not exist in plants. In vitro assay of recombinant PAH from chlamydomonas or moss showed highest enzyme activity with 10-formyltetrahydrofolate. Thus 10-formyltetrahydrofolate is very likely to be the in vivo cofactor in plants |CITS: [20959559]|. PAH reaction converts the cofactor 10-formyltetrahydrofolate to 10-formyltetrahydrofolate-4a-carbinolamine which needs to be recycled back to 10-formyltetrahydrofolate. Similar to the human pathway (see |FRAME: PHENYLALANINE-DEG1-PWY|), the cofactor regeneration in plants needs pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase (PCD) and q-dihydropterin reductase (qDHPR). Plant PCD has been identified [18245455], but qDHPR remains to be unknown in plants. The qDHPR reaction seems unlikely to be mediated by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR, EC 1.5.1.3) because PAH and PCD are both plastidial yet DHFR is in mitochondria |CITS: [21275646]|.

General Background, This background summary covers this pathway and related pathways |FRAME: PWY-7009|, |FRAME: PWY-7010| and |FRAME: PWY-7011|. These pathways were studied in |FRAME: TAX-46680|, or a regulatory mutant of |FRAME: TAX-46680| designated Prp, as described below., This pathway: |FRAME: CPD-946| has been used as a volatile fungicide (in |CITS: [8449871]|) and is a product of |FRAME: PWY-681| (in |CITS: [9305879]|). |FRAME: TAX-46680 "Pseudomonas nitroreducens (previously known as Pseudomonas azelaica HBP1 or Pseudomonas sp. strain HBP1)"| was able to grow on |FRAME: CPD-946| as a sole source of carbon and energy via a pathway involving ortho hydroxylation by a soluble, |FRAME: NADH|-dependent monooxygenase (HbpA), ring cleavage of the hydroxylated product at the meta position by a dioxygenase (HbpC), and hydrolysis of the meta cleavage product by a hydrolase (HbpD) to produce |FRAME: BENZOATE| and the common aromatic intermediate |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (which has an enol tautomeric form |FRAME: CPD-6761|). The latter two compounds were further metabolized as shown in the pathway links. The last two reactions of this pathway are shared with pathway |FRAME: PWY5F9-12| (|CITS: [3214154][8449871]| and in |CITS: [10629187]|)., Pathway |FRAME: PWY-7009|: |FRAME: TAX-46680| was also able to grow on |FRAME: CPD-14144| as a sole source of carbon and energy via enzymes HbpA, HbpC and HbpD, producing the intermediates |FRAME: CPD-927|, |FRAME: CPD-928|, |FRAME: CPD-110|, and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (|CITS: [3214154][8449871]| and in |CITS: [10629187]|). The latter two reactions are shared with pathway |FRAME: P662-PWY|. In addition, HbpA was also shown to hydroxylate |FRAME: CPD-927| to |FRAME: CPD-14164|, with subsequent metabolism via these enzymes to |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|, |FRAME: PYROGALLOL| and |FRAME: CPD-13339| (2-hydroxymuconate), as shown here. However, the route via |FRAME: CPD-14164| was suggested to be a minor one |CITS: [8449871]|., Pathway |FRAME: PWY-7010|: A regulatory mutant of |FRAME: TAX-46680|, designated Prp, (Pseudomonas sp. strain HBP1 Prp, or Pseudomonas azelaica HBP1 Prp) was isolated by growth on |FRAME: CPD-14147|. It was able to use this compound as a sole source of carbon and energy. |FRAME: CPD-14147| did not support growth of wild-type |FRAME: TAX-46680|. The same enzymes that catalyze |FRAME: PWY-7008| (HbpA, HbpC and HbpD) also appeared to catalyze |FRAME: CPD-14147| degradation. The HbpA monooxygenase was induced by |FRAME: CPD-14147| in the mutant, but not in the wild-type strain. In addition, a small amount of the first two enzymes were constitutively produced. Pathway intermediates of |FRAME: CPD-14147| degradation were identified as |FRAME: CPD0-2477| (the hydroxylation product), |FRAME: CPD-14149| (the meta-cleavage product), and hydrolase products |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| (butyrate) and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|. However, it was noted that the pathway enzymes had higher affinities for the substrates of pathway |FRAME: PWY-7008| |CITS: [8481010]|., Pathway |FRAME: PWY-7011|: The |FRAME: TAX-46680| Prp regulatory mutant also utilized enzymes HbpA, HbpC and HbpD to degrade |FRAME: CPD-14150| (o-cumenol) as the sole source of carbon and energy, with the corresponding intermediates |FRAME: CPD-14151|, |FRAME: CPD-1008|, |FRAME: ISOBUTYRATE| and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE|. |FRAME: CPD-14150| is used in industry and is a potential pollutant |CITS: [7811094]|., These pathways are an example of the generally broad specificity of enzymes functioning in meta-cleavage pathways |CITS: [8481010]|. The |FRAME: TAX-46680| genes hbpA hbpC and hbpD encoding the three enzymes used in these pathways have been characterized. A regulatory gene hbpR was also identified and characterized as a member of the XylR/DmpR subclass of the NtrC family of transcriptional activators. Gene hbpR was shown to be necessary for transcriptional activation of these genes |CITS: [10629187][11114926][11495995]|., About This Pathway, The first reaction of this pathway is catalyzed by a |FRAME: TAX-46680| monooxygenase HbpA that has been designated as EC 1.14.13.44 |CITS: [3214154]|. The second reaction is catalyzed by HbpB, a meta-cleaving dioxygenase. The third reaction is catalyzed by HbpC, a hydrolase that cleaves the meta-cleavage product to |FRAME: BENZOATE| and |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| (which has an enol tautomeric form |FRAME: CPD-6761|) |CITS: [3214154]|. |FRAME: BENZOATE| is further degraded by benzoate 1,2-dioxygenase to |FRAME: CATECHOL|, as shown in the pathway link. |FRAME: CATECHOL| is metabolized in the well characterized lower meta-cleavage pathway (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-5415| and |FRAME: PWY-5420|). |FRAME: OXOPENTENOATE| is degraded to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| which enters the |FRAME: TCA|, as shown in the pathway link (in |CITS: [10629187]|).

|FRAME: CPD-18070 Rosamicin| is a 16-member macrolide antibiotic produced by the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-47874|., It is an important antibiotic that has clinical efficacy and broad-spectrum antibacterial activity. It's activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria is equal to or superior to that of |FRAME: Erythromycins erythromycin| |CITS: [4486485][4647834][4840436]|., New modifications of the antibiotic result in additional activities, including efficacy against Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) |CITS: [19408026][24064918][25047182]|., It has been assumed that two different cytochrome P-450 enzymes participate in the synthesis of rosamicin. Based on this assumption, a PCR product was amplified from |FRAME: TAX-47874| DNA using degenerate primers designed based on sequences of P-450 cytochromes implicated in biosynthesis of several 16-member macrolides. The PCR product was used as a probe to isolate a cosmid containing a cluster of genes involved in rosamicin biosynthesis |CITS: [23274670]|., The cluster included two genes encoding cytochrome P-450 enzymes, which were named |FRAME: G-44064| and |FRAME: G-44065|. The genes were similar to |FRAME: G-17887| (71% identity), which is involved in |FRAME: PWY-7415|, and |FRAME: G-14857| (48% identity), which is involved in |FRAME: PWY-6971|, respectively. Mutants disrupted in either of the cytochrome P-450 genes were generated, and analysis of the intermediates they accumulated suggested several options for the pathway. The pathway from |FRAME: CPD-18072| to |FRAME: CPD-18070| was studied further by expression of the enzymes in |FRAME: TAX-562| using a bacterial P-450 expression system, and the results supported the pathway described here |CITS: [23274670]|. , The complete nucleotide sequence of the rosamicin biosynthetic gene cluster in a different organism, |FRAME: TAX-47853|, was published in a patent application |CITS: [Farnet03]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Organophosphonates Phosphonates| are quite abundant in nature, primarily as components of phosphonolipids, where |FRAME: CPD-1106| is analogous to ethanolamine phosphate as the constituent of phospholipids. In addition, phosphonates are constituents of polysaccharides, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and several antibiotics |CITS: [7765831]|. Phosphonates contain a direct carbon-phosphorus (C-P) bond in place of the more familiar carbon-oxygen-phosphorus bond, which makes their degradation challenging., Bacteria have evolved many different mechanisms for cleaving the carbon-phosphorus bond. Enzymes that have been described include the following:, 1. |FRAME: EG10719-MONOMER "Carbon-phosphorus lyase"|, a widespread but poorly characterized enzyme. See |FRAME: EC-4.7.1.1|., 2. Hydrolytic enzymes such as |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.1| (phosphonatase, see |FRAME: PHOSPHONOTASE-PWY|), |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.3|, and |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.2| (shown in pathway |FRAME: P483-PWY|)., 3. Dioxygenases, such as |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.78|, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY-7447|., Data suggest that additional pathways for phosphonate degradation may exist (in |CITS: [21543322]|). , About This Pathway, The phosphonotase pathway has a narrow substrate specificity, as it acts only on a phosphonates that contain a substitution on the α carbon which can be converted to an aldehyde. The pathway acts primarily on |FRAME:CPD-1106|, which is the most common naturally occurring phosphonate. The pathway consists of only two steps - |FRAME:CPD-1106| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-551| by |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.37|, and phosphonoacetaldehyde is subsequently converted to |FRAME: ACETALD| and inorganic phosphate by |FRAME: EC-3.11.1.1| |CITS: [7592415]|., The C-P bond cleavage involves the formation of an aldolase-like imine of phosphonoacetaldehyde with an active site, lysine on phosphonatase, leading to destabilization of the C-P bond and allowing for its hydrolytic cleavage, Enzymes carrying out both steps have been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-1396| |CITS: [3132206][1605625][15109258]|, |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS: [7592415]| and |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [6406228][2504289][8394813]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8179 2,4-Dinitrophenol| has been used during the first world war by the French in the manufacture of munitions. Later it was also used as a dye, wood preserver, herbicide and photographic developer., |FRAME: CPD-8179 2,4-Dinitrophenol| is a well known protonophore (an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation) by preventing the uptake of inorganic phosphate molecules into the mitochondria |CITS: [18910739][4388239][5799112]|. At lower concentrations this property causes a significant increase in the basal metabolic rate, and as aresult, a rapid weight loss, which prompted its use as weight loss drug. However, severe side effects have resulted in its labelling as "extremely dangerous and not fit for human consumption" by the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act of 1938. The UK Food Standard Agency issued a warning in 2003, labelling it as "not fit for human consumption" as well. Despite this, |FRAME: CPD-8179| is still marketed as a weight loss drug, mainly over the internet |CITS: [21739343]|., |FRAME: CPD-17566 "2,4,6-Trinitrophenol"| (picric acid) and its ammonium or potassium salts (picrates) were also used as explosives during the first and second world wars. It is also used in the production of |FRAME: ANILINE|, one of the most important starting materials in chemical synthesis. As a consequence they have been found as pollutants in ground water at former production and military sites, and in waste streams of current aniline production sites. Studies have shown that like many other nitroaromatic compounds, |FRAME: CPD-17566| is acutely toxic |CITS: [1404487]|., About This Pathway, A number of organisms that utilize |FRAME: CPD-8179| as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen have been described |CITS: [13235894][Gundersen56][16348203][24196208][13093710]|. Lenke et al have shown that two strains of |FRAME: TAX-1833| liberated stoichiometric amounts of nitrite during the degradation |CITS: [1444407]|. It was also shown , In 1999 it was reported that both |FRAME: CPD-8179| are |FRAME: CPD-17566| are degraded via hydride-Meisenheimer complexes, which eventually lose a nitrite molecule |CITS: [10103224][9973345]|. It was initially thought that the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of these complexes utilize NADPH as the hydride source. However, the identification of the enzyme from the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6275| showed that the immediate hydride donor is |FRAME: Factor-420|, which in turn is reduced by NADPH by the action of |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.40| |CITS: [10217752]|., A subsequent study showed that the hydride-Meisenheimer complex formed from |FRAME: CPD-8179| is also the dinitration product of the hydride-Meisenheimer complex formed from |FRAME: CPD-17566|, demonstrating that the catabolism of both compounds converge |CITS: [11995829]|., A novel high throughput differential display method was used to identify a gene cluster in the bacterium |FRAME: ORG-6273| that is involved in |FRAME: CPD-8179| degradation |CITS: [11595177]|. Further characterization of the enzymes identified the |FRAME: G-43866| and |FRAME: G-43867| genes, which encode two hydride transferases, the npdG gene, which encodes the NADPH-dependent F420 reductase, and a fourth gene, named |FRAME: G-43868|, which acts on the hydride-Meisenheimer complex formed from |FRAME: CPD-17566|, converting it to (at the time) an unknown product |CITS: [11882715]|., Further clarification of the pathway was provided with the identification of additional enzymes from |FRAME: ORG-6275| |CITS: [15128543]|. It was shown that the successive action of both hydride transferases results in formation of the |FRAME: CPD-17570 "aci-nitro form"| of the dihydride-Meisenheimer complex formed from |FRAME: CPD-17566|. A nitrite-eliminating enzyme acts on this compound, catalyzing the removal of the nitro group at position 6 and forming the hydride-Meisenheimer complex formed from |FRAME: CPD-8179|. This compound is acted on by |FRAME: G-43867|, forming a dihydride complex that is protonated to form |FRAME: CPD-17568|. A hydrolase, encoded by |FRAME: G-43869|, cleaves the ring, forming |FRAME: CPD-17571|., The |FRAME: CPD-17570 "aci-nitro form"| of the dihydride-Meisenheimer complex formed from |FRAME: CPD-17566| can spontaneously convert to the |FRAME: CPD-17572 "nitro-form"| tautomer, which is not a substrate for the nitrite-eliminating enzyme. The function of the |FRAME: G-43868|-encoded tautomerase is presumably to convert this form back to the aci-nitro form of this complex, ensuring that no dead-end compounds are formed., The later part of the pathway, responsible for the complete mineralization of |FRAME: CPD-17571|, is still not known.

Summary: |FRAME: TAX-1488| is a Gram-positive anaerobe of commercial importance, capable of fermenting a variety of sugars to solvents and acids. During acidogenesis |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| are produced, while solventogenesis yields |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ACETONE|, and |FRAME: BUTANOL|. The production of acetone, and butanol by |FRAME: TAX-1488| was a thriving industrial process, but lost its importance since the fermentation could no longer compete economically with the chemical synthesis of solvents from petroleum., In continuous culture, |FRAME: TAX-1488| can be maintained in three different stable metabolic states |CITS: [Girbal95]|: acidogenic - production of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| when grown at neutral pH on glucose (see |FRAME: PWY-6590|), solventogenic - production of |FRAME: ACETONE|, |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH| when grown at low pH on glucose (|FRAME: PWY-6594|), and alcohologenic - formation of |FRAME: BUTANOL| and |FRAME: ETOH| but not |FRAME: ACETONE| when grown at neutral pH under conditions of high NAD(P)H availability. Despite numerous physiological studies, it is still unclear how the metabolic switch from acid to solvent production is regulated at the molecular level |CITS: [10191392]|., Once this metabolic transition has been initiated, most of the excreted acids are taken up and converted into solvents, The pathway from |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is a major carbon metabolism channel and in |FRAME: TAX-1488| contains the branch points to solventogenesis and acidogenesis. , The three key intermediates are |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA |, and |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA|. |FRAME:ACETYL-COA Acetyl-CoA| is a branching point for the production of |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: ETOH|.  |FRAME:ACETOACETYL-COA Acetoacetyl-CoA| is the branching point for |FRAME: ACETONE| production, and |FRAME: BUTYRYL-COA| is the branching point for |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| and |FRAME: BUTANOL| production., For more information about the pathways leading to fermentation of individual compounds, please look at the respective sub-pathways - |FRAME: PWY-6587|, |FRAME: P142-PWY|, |FRAME: CENTFERM-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-6583| and |FRAME: PWY-6588|.

Unlike the cycle, that pathway does not require, ATP to drive the reaction. However, the K<sub>m</sub> of |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.4| for ammonium is much higher than the, that of |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.13|., In |FRAME: TAX-562| these two ammonium-to-glutamate pathways are regulated so as to operate under different environmental circumstances. The ATP-independent pathway functions when ammonia is abundant; the ATP-driven pathway functions when concentrations of ammonia are low.  The ATP-independent pathway offers significant energy savings because when functioning, the ATP-driven pathway utilizes over 10 percent of the cell's total expenditure of ATP., If complex sources of nitrogen are available, |FRAME: GLT| can be synthesized from |FRAME: ARG| (|FRAME: AST-PWY|) or |FRAME: PRO| (|FRAME: PROUT-PWY|) or from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| by transamination of the amino group from |FRAME: ARG| or |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|. , The complexity of glutamate biosynthesis reflects the quantitatively central role that this amino acid plays in metabolism. Summary: Trichothecene are sequiterpenoids characterized by a varying pattern of oxygen and ester groups on a core tricyclic skeleton bearing an epoxide function which is commonly referred to as 12,13-epoxytrichothec-9-ene (EPT) structure |CITS:[Grove07]|. More than 200 trichothecene have been identified from various genera of fungi and classified into four groups according to the substitution pattern on the basic EPT core |CITS:[Ueno80] [Betina89]|. In general, type A trichothecene carry either a hydroxyl group on C-8 (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18505|), an ester at C-8 (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18416| - see |FRAME:PWY-7730|) or bear no oxygen at this position (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18439| and |FRAME:CPD-18430| - this pathway). Trichothecene of type B carry a carbonyl group (keto) on that C-8 position, for instance in |FRAME:CPD-18427| (see |FRAME:PWY-7713|) and |FRAME:CPD-18421| (see |FRAME:PWY-7712|). Trichothecenes of type C have an additional epoxide function (C7/C8) on the core structure, as exemplified in |FRAME:CPD-18597| and finally type D trichothecenes possess an additional ring which has been formed by connecting the C-4 and the C-15 position (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-18598|) |CITS:[22069741]|., The biosyntheses of the various trichothecenes have been mostly elucidated by feeding experiments and mutants blocking a specific reaction in the pathway |CITS:[22069741] [17827683]|. Trichothecene are considered mycotoxins which are phytotoxic |CITS:[22295175]|, contaminate food and animal feed, have been reported to cause vomiting, skin dermatitis, and hemorrhagic lesions |CITS:[3158480] [8246841]| and interfere with complex developmental processes |CITS:[23667578]|. Fusarium species are the causative agents of the Fusarium head blight (FHB), a devastating disease that worldwide affects barley, maize, rice, wheat and causes the loss of tens of millions of dollars every year |CITS:[23078349] [16277434] [Alexander09] [8246841]|. The toxicity of trichothecene is based upon the 12,13-epoxide which not only must be present but also present in the right configuration as demonstrated by using two 12,13-epoxide isomers |CITS:[Colvin86]|., Fusarium species can be grouped into certain chemotypes. The two main chemotypes are associated with species which either produce |FRAME:CPD-18421| or |FRAME:CPD-18427| |CITS:[Miller91]|, the former being further divided into an |FRAME:CPD-18419| (3-ADON) and an |FRAME:CPD-18420| (15-ADON) chemotype |CITS:[21216300]|. It has been demonstrated that the genetic difference between |FRAME:CPD-18421| and |FRAME:CPD-18427| chemotypes lies in the functionality of two genes, i.e. TRI13 coding for a trichothecene 4-hydroxylase and TRI7 encoding for a trichothecene 4-acetyltransferase. Both genes are present but nonfunctional in |FRAME:CPD-18421|-producing Fusarium chemotypes |CITS:[11352533] [11976083]|., The |FRAME:PWY-7711| describes the biosynthetic sequence that all trichothecenes, except for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18430| and |FRAME:CPD-18439|, have in common. The biosynthetic steps that form |FRAME:CPD-18411| are core pathway reactions towards the generation of |FRAME:CPD-18416| (see |FRAME:PWY-7730|) and |FRAME:CPD-18421| (see |FRAME:PWY-7712|) and are also part of the |FRAME:PWY-7713| which branches out from intermediates of both |FRAME:PWY-7712| and |FRAME:PWY-7730|. The first committed step in the |FRAME:PWY-7711| is catalyzed in Fusarium by the trichodiene synthase |CITS:[3800398]| to form |FRAME:TRICHODIENE-CPD| which is subsequently oxidized in four positions, i.e. C-2, C-12,13, C-11 and C-3 to yield |FRAME:CPD-18384| |CITS:[7651333] [16917519] [17188234]|. The further reaction sequence comprises 3-acylation by the isotrichodermol 3-acetyltransferase (TRI101), regarded a key reaction in the pathway and essentially involved in the self-defense mechanism to protect Fusarium against its own toxin because the C-3 acetylated intermediate is far less toxic than its C-3 hydroxylated precursor |CITS:[9430709] [9762900] [17923480] [10583973] [11122517]|. The isotrichodermin 15-hydroxylase (TRI11) |CITS:[9435078] [7651333] [16535589]| and the trichothecene 15-O-acetyltransferase (TRI3) |CITS:[8593041] [19319932] [18776660]| catalyze the remaining steps to generate |FRAME:CPD-18411|. , The first pathway to branch off from the core reactions of the various trichothecenes biosyntheses is |FRAME:PWY-7714| which can be found in various Trichoderma species. The multifunctional trichodiene hydroxylase (TRI4) of Trichoderma carries out only three out of the four oxidations catalyzed by the Fusarium TRI4 encoded protein, producing |FRAME:CPD-18383| from which the |FRAME:PWY-7714|) branches off |CITS:[21642405]|. Further details on reactions and catalyzing enzymes of this pathway can be checked in the respective |FRAME:PWY-7714|. Two other pathways, i.e. |FRAME:PWY-7712| and |FRAME:PWY-7730| bifurcate at |FRAME:CPD-18411|, the last commonly shared intermediate of all but one (|FRAME:PWY-7714|) trichothecenes. The type B trichothecene |FRAME:CPD-18427| can be accessed via two pathways, the |FRAME:PWY-7712| where two genes, i.e. TRI13 coding for a trichothecene 4-hydroxylase |CITS:[11976083] [12135578]| and TRI7 encoding for a trichothecene 4-acetyltransferase |CITS:[11425709] [11976083]| of certain strains from Fusarium graminearum are functional and catalyze the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-18423|, and |FRAME:PWY-7730| where the TRI1 encoded trichothecene 7,8-dihydroxylase leads to the same intermediate. Finally, the pathway towards |FRAME:CPD-18416| has been mostly observed in Fusarium sporotrichoides. Although equipped with similar gene sets various enzymes of the same TRI encoding genes display different substrate specificities. For example, the previously mentioned TRI13 |CITS:[12135578]| and TRI7 |CITS:[11352533]| genes which encode proteins that connect |FRAME:PWY-7712| with |FRAME:PWY-7713|, attack the same position (C-4) but on different substrates (|FRAME:CPD-18411|, |FRAME:CPD-18412|). Further details on reactions, enzymes and comments are references in the respective trichothecene pathways.

Summary: |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD Oleate| (18:1Δ9) is the most commonly found mono-unsaturated fatty acids in plant oils. However a number of other mono-unsaturated fatty acid species are naturally accumulated in some plants. The seed oil of |FRAME: TAX-42439| (meadowfoam) has high content of Δ5 unsaturated C20 and C22 fatty acids, with |FRAME: CPD-17310| (20:1Δ5) accounting for 60% of the total fatty acids. The high content of |FRAME: CPD-17310| makes the meadowfoam seed oil desirable for use in cosmetics, surfactants and lubricants. , The biosynthesis of |FRAME: PWY-5361| in |FRAME: TAX-42439| has several novel features. Firstly, the elongation step, which is catalyzed by saturated fatty acid-specific FAE1, starts with |FRAME: PALMITATE| (16:0) instead of |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| (18:0) or |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| (18:1). The latter two serve as the initial substrates for very long chain fatty acids biosynthesis in most plant species |CITS: [16661496]|., Secondly, the Δ5 double bond is introduced by an acyl-CoA desaturase |CITS: [7294800][10982439]|. Acyl-CoA desaturation is the major route of monounsaturated fatty acid synthesis in animals and fungi, but is rarely found in plants, which usually use either an acyl-[acp] desaturase or an acyl-lipid desaturase (which act on fatty acids bound to coenzyme A or glycerol lipids, respectively, as substrates).

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: L-rhamnose| is a 6-deoxy-aldohexose that occurs in nature. Some fungi and bacteria posess an |FRAME: L-rhamnose| degradation pathway that involves non-phosphorylated intermediates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6713|), analogous to the |FRAME: NPGLUCAT-PWY|. Pathway |FRAME: PWY-6713| is in contrast to the known bacterial |FRAME: L-rhamnose| degradation pathway which involves phosphorylated intermediates (see |FRAME: RHAMCAT-PWY|). Genes encoding enzymes of pathway |FRAME: PWY-6713| in |FRAME: TAX-322104 "Scheffersomyces stipitis CBS 6054 (previously known as Pichia stipitis)"|, |FRAME: TAX-284592| and |FRAME: TAX-354| have been cloned, expressed and their products functionally characterized., Phylogenetic studies of the fungal and bacterial 2-keto-3-deoxy-L-rhamnoate aldolases (L-KDR aldolases) suggested that they are unerelated evolutionarily. Their respective non-phosphorylative |FRAME: L-rhamnose| degradation pathways appear to have evolved independently and are the result of convergent evolution (in |CITS: [18505728]| and in |CITS: [19187228]|). In |FRAME: TAX-314266|, a variation of this non-phosphorylative pathway was demonstrated in which |FRAME: DEHYDRO-3-DEOXY-L-RHAMNONATE| is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-13044|, followed by hydrolysis of this compound to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: L-LACTATE| (L-lactate) |CITS: [19187228]| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, The first reaction in this pathway shows the spontaneous conversion of the pyranose ring form of |FRAME: L-rhamnose| to its furanose ring form |FRAME: L-RHAMNOFURANOSE| (the α and β anomers of each form are not specified here). This reaction is shown because the reaction that follows is catalyzed by L-rhamnose 1-dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.173) which specifies |FRAME: L-RHAMNOFURANOSE| as a substrate and |FRAME: L-RHAMNONO-14-LACTONE| (L-rhamnono-γ-lactone) as a product. As noted in |CITS: [4335867]|, a δ-lactone (1,5-lactone) would be produced by a pyranose ring form)., In |FRAME: TAX-314266| the first three enzymatic reactions are shared with pathway |FRAME: PWY-6713|, but the last two reactions of the pathway were shown to be catalyzed by L-2-keto-3-deoxyrhamnoate 4-dehydrogenase and L-2,4-diketo-3-deoxyrhamnoate hydrolase encoded by genes lra5 and lra6, respectively. |FRAME: PYRUVATE| and |FRAME: L-LACTATE| (L-lactate) are the end products of this variant and |FRAME: LACTALD| is not produced |CITS: [19187228]|.
