Summary: |FRAME: GFP "Green fluorescent proteins"| (GFPs) are proteins that exhibit bright green fluorescence when exposed to light in the blue to ultraviolet range. GFPs form a part of the bioluminesence systems of many marine organisms, and the first such protein, from the jellyfish |FRAME: TAX-6100|, was described already in 1962 |CITS: [13911999]|., Some other species, including non-bioluminesent species, encode homologs of GFP. Many |FRAME: TAX-6101| species exhibit bright fluorescent colors, and while the most common color is green, other colors are also found |CITS: [Catala59][Mazel95]|. The fluorescence in these species is assumed to provide protection from strong solar radiation |CITS: [Kawaguti44]|. A different function has been proposed for organisms living in deeper habitats - the conversion of blue light into a longer wavelength that is more suitable for photosynthesis by the algal endosymbionts |CITS: [28313957]|., In a 1999 study genes encoding remote homologs of the |FRAME: G-55175| gene of |FRAME: TAX-6100| were cloned from six non-bioluminescent reef corals and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and the recombinant proteins were purified. Despite a low overall identity with GFP (26-30%), all of the proteins fluoresced, and two of them (from |FRAME: TAX-105401| and |FRAME: TAX-86599| species) were found to fluoresce at the yellow and red wavelengths, respectively |CITS: [10504696]|. It is now recognized that the family of GFP-like proteins includes |FRAME: GFP "green fluorescent proteins"| (GFP), |FRAME: PWY-8514 "red fluorescent proteins"| (RFP), |FRAME: YFP-Chromophore "yellow fluorescent proteins"| (YFP), |FRAME: CFP-Chromophore "cyan fluorescent proteins"| (CFP) and |FRAME: BCP-Chromophore "purple-blue non-fluorescent chromoproteins"| (CP) |CITS: [18648549]|., All of these proteins share the same β-can fold first observed in GFP, but most are not associated with bioluminescence. While the fluorophores of previously-described GFPs are formed autocatalitically from  the three amino acids Ser/Thr-Tyr-Gly, later identified proteins have significant variability in the first position, containing Gln, Lys, His, or Asn |CITS: [10504696][12271129]|., When the chemical form of the fully mature red DsRed-type chromophore was elucidated, it was found that it contains an acylimine extension to the two-ring π-system of the GFP-like chromophore, resulting from dehydrogenation of the Gln residue at the C<sub>α</sub>-N main chain bond |CITS: [11050230][11101896][11209050]| and reviewed in |CITS: [20666493]|. Note that the pathway shown here describes a somewhat simplified version of the process., Due to the slow maturation of the fluorescence, and the presence of the intermediate chromophore stage during which much of the fluorescence emission occurs in the green spectral region, the application of the wild type DsRed in cell biology studies is severely compromised. However, variants of the protein in which these problems have been addressed have been developed |CITS: [11753367][15556986][17704916]|. Variants with altered spectral properties have also been developed |CITS: [ 18203801]|, Several closely related red fluorescent proteins have been isolated following the discovery of DsRed |CITS: [10981720][11682051][12185250][12909624][15876379]|.

General Background, |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it is accumulated at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant. In addition to its osmoprotectant activity, glycine betaine is also a potent protectant against mutagenic compounds |CITS: [12730887][15802867]| and radiation-induced damage |CITS: [12841603]|., |FRAME: BETAINE "Glycine betaine"| can either be taken up directly from the environment, or synthesized. A common biosynthesis pathway for glycine betaine is from |FRAME: CHOLINE|, utilizing a two-step pathway with |FRAME: BETAINE_ALDEHYDE| as intermediate. This pathway is conserved in bacteria and plants, but shows divergence in the enzymes involved. Gram-negative bacteria, Gram-positive bacteria and higher plants all use |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.8|, to catalyze the conversion of betaine aldehyde to glycine betaine. The choline-to-betaine aldehyde reaction, however, is divergent: Gram-negative bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-287|, and |FRAME: TAX-382| utilize |FRAME: EC-1.1.99.1| (see |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|), Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, use an alcohol dehydrogenase (see |FRAME: PWY-3722|), while high plants use |FRAME: EC-1.14.15.7| (see |FRAME: PWY1F-353|)., Certain Gram-positive bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-1677| and |FRAME: TAX-1665|, as well as the fungus |FRAME: TAX-109805|, use yet another enzyme to catalyze this conversion: they use a soluble |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.17|, that catalyzes both steps (see |FRAME: PWY-3721|). , There exists at least one more variation for the synthesis of glycine betaine, which is found in several halotolerant bacteria. The pathway was found in |FRAME: TAX-1052| and several other organisms, which synthesize glycine betaine from glycine through a series of methylation reactions |CITS: [10896953]| (this pathway). However, since methylation reactions are expensive (due to the cost of regenerating S-adenosylmethionine), this pathway is less common., General Background, Glycine betaine (N,N,N-trimethylglycine) is a very efficient osmolyte found in a wide range of bacteria and plants, where it is accumulated at high cytoplasmic concentrations in response to osmotic stress, to act as an osmoprotectant. In addition to its osmoprotectant activity, glycine betaine is also a potent protectant against mutagenic compounds |CITS: [12730887][15802867]| and radiation-induced damage |CITS: [12841603]|., Glycine betaine can either be taken up directly from the environment, or synthesized. Common biosynthesis pathways for glycine betaine start with either choline (see |FRAME: BETSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-3722| and |FRAME: PWY1F-353|) or glycine (see |FRAME: P541-PWY|)., Glycine betaine synthesis from glycine, which was originally described in several halotolerant bacteria, involves a series of methylation reactions |CITS: [10896953]|. However, since methylation reactions are expensive (due to the cost of regenerating S-adenosylmethionine), this pathway is far less common., About This Pathway, Synthesis of glycine betaine from exogenously provided choline or betaine aldehyde confers considerable osmotic, stress tolerance to Bacillus subtilis in high-osmolarity media |CITS: [8071213]|. The production of glycine, betaine is performed in two steps, through the intermediate betaine aldehyde., The genes required for the synthesis of glycine betaine from choline in B. subtilis were cloned by, complementation of an |FRAME:TAX-562| betBA mutant. While the gbsA gene, encoding a betaine aldehyde, dehydrogenase, is similar to other betaine aldehyde dehydrogenases from bacteria and plants, and gsbB, gene is similar to type III alcohol dehydrogenases |CITS: [8752328]|. , The gbsBA operon is not stimulated by high osmolarity alone - maximal expression is obtained, by the combination of high osmolarity and the presence of choline |CITS: [8752328]|., The GbsA betaine aldehyde dehydrogenase was purified, and found to be highly tolerant to high salt concentrations, , as well as to molar concentrations of glycine betaine. These two facts ensure that B. subtilis can produce high, levels of the compatible solute glycine betaine under conditions of high osmolarity stress |CITS: [9297465]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., The genes specific for O antigen synthesis are often present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., About This Pathway, The lipid A-core oligosaccharide and the O-antigens are synthesized in the cytoplasm, exported to the periplasm, and combined by the |FRAME: HP_RS05105-MONOMER|, forming lipopolysaccharides (LPS) attached to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane. The LPS are then transferred from the inner membrane to the outer membrane and through it, remaining attached to outer leaflet of the outer membrane., In |FRAME: TAX-210| the system responsible for transporting lipopolysaccharides from the inner membrane to the outer membrane is the |FRAME: CPLX2DNV-1202|, which consists of seven Lpt proteins - LptA through LptG. Together these proteins form a transenvelope bridge that transports LPS from the inner membrane, across the periplasm to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane |CITS: [22919621]|., LptB2FG is an ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) transporter which, together with LptC, extracts the lipid A-core oligosaccharide from the inner membrane. LptA is a periplasmic protein that acts as a bridge between the inner membrane and the outer membrane. LptE is an outer membrane protein that functions to anchor the oligosaccharide at the cell surface, and LptD forms a channel in the outer membrane. The Lpt system acts downstream from |FRAME: EC-7.5.2.6|, which is responsible for flipping the lipid A-core structure across the inner membrane |CITS: [22919621]|.

|FRAME: CPD-10201 Homofuraneol | (2-ethyl-4-hydroxy-5-methyl-3(2H)-furanone, also known as HEMF) is the characteristic component of soy sauce and miso due to its strong, sweet, and caramel-like aroma |CITS: [17602655][22463595]|. Although a small amount of HEMF has been detected in cheese |CITS: [Milo97]| and beer |CITS: [16159184]|, it is best known from soy sauce |CITS: [Nunomura76]| and miso |CITS: [Sugawara91]|., In addition to its distinct aroma characteristics, HEMF possesses strong antioxidant properties, and has anticarcinogenic effects |CITS: [1551105]| and anticataract effects |CITS: [9836421][9972235]|., The only enzyme that has been shown to be specific for |FRAME: CPD-10201| biosynthesis is |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.105|. Several pathways have been suggested, but only the pathway shown here has been reporduced in vitro |CITS: [27865643]|., Earlier work using stable isotopes showed that the skeleton of the five-membered ring and the methyl group of the side chain originate from ribose, while the ethyl group is derived from a D-glucose metabolite, presumably |FRAME: ACETALD| |CITS: [17284850]|. The formation of HEMF was confirmed when |FRAME: ACETALD| and a cell-free extract from yeast were added to a medium containing amino-carbonyl reactants |CITS: [17284850]|. The involvement of |FRAME: ACETALD| as a precursor was also supported by the finding that deletion of the |FRAME: YOL086C| gene of |FRAME: TAX-4932|, associated with acetaldehyde accumulation, results in high-level HEMF production. Deletion of the ADH1 gene in |FRAME: TAX-4956|, the dominant strain of yeast found during soy sauce fermentation, also promotes HEMF production |CITS: [25362059]|., |FRAME: D-Ribose| and |FRAME: GLY| can react in a Maillard reaction to produce |FRAME: CPD-10204|. Once formed, |FRAME: CPD-10204| can react with |FRAME: ACETALD| by a Knoevenagel condensation to form |FRAME: CPD-10206|., When purified |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.105|, from |FRAME: TAX-4932| was assayed using HEMF-G medium (200 mM |FRAME: GLY|, 200 mM |FRAME: D-Ribose|, 7.3 mM KH2PO4, 20 mM MgSO4, and 0.5% w/v yeast extract, pH 6.0), |FRAME: ACETALD|, and NADPH, all three products were detected - |FRAME: CPD-10204|, |FRAME: CPD-10206|, and |FRAME: CPD-10201| |CITS: [27865643]|.

Summary: Cresols (|FRAME: CPD-109|, |FRAME: CPD-112| and |FRAME: CPD-108|, also known as ortho-, meta-, and para-cresol) are phenolic compounds commonly found in fuel processing activities such as coal gasification, and the fractionation of coal, tar, and petroleum. Cresols are commonly used in disinfectants, surfactants, and wood preservatives, and are intermediates in the manufacture of pesticides and resins., Despite their similarity, the different isomers of cresol are degraded through different pathways, and in some cases, the same isomer can be degraded by more than one pathway., |FRAME: CPD-112| (m-cresol) is degraded by several Pseudomonas species by oxidation of the methyl group in the meta position (see |FRAME: M-CRESOL-DEGRADATION-PWY|). The linear product, a methylated from of |FRAME: CPD-1070|, is hydrolyzed into pyruvate, which enters central metabolism, and |FRAME: 2-METHYLMALEATE|, which is converted to |FRAME: CPD-31| |CITS: [5124802]|.

Summary: |FRAME: BERBERINE Berberine|, a benzylisoquinoline alkaloid, is derived from tyrosine. Berberine is naturally produced in rhizomes of members of the |FRAME: TAX-22774| and |FRAME: TAX-3441| genera, and has long been used in clinical anitibacterial treatments. The first committed step in berberine synthesis from the intermediate |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.21.3.3|, also known as the berberine bridge enzyme or BBE. BBE is a major branch-point enzyme in benzylisoquinoline alkaloid biosynthesis, since |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| is a common intermediate in the biosynthesis of many compounds, including berberine, sanguinarine, macarpine, codeine, and morphine., BBE catalyzes the conversion of the N-methyl group of |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| into the berberine bridge carbon. The reaction involves the oxidation of the N-methyl group followed by ring closure |CITS: [Steffens85]|. The reaction is unique in nature and cannot be achieved by synthetic methods., All of the enzymes of the berberine biosynthesis pathway depicted here are specific for the (S)-enantiomers of their substrates., Like many other alkaloids, the cell type-specific localization of berberine biosynthesis and accumulation are temporally and spatially separated. In |FRAME: TAX-150094| it was shown that the transcripts of nine berberine biosynthetic genes were restricted to the pericycle and adjacent cortical cells of roots, and protoderm of leaf primodia, whereas berberine accumulation is restricted to endodermal cells of roots and pith and cortex of rhizomes |CITS: [15722473]|. , At the subcellular level, as shown in |FRAME: TAX-22774| and |FRAME: TAX-3441| species, all enzymes of the pathway are present in specific vesicles |CITS: [Galneder88]|. It is proposed that the vesicles containing the enzymes (and the end product berberine) are eventually fused with the central vacuole |CITS: [12430014]|. All of the berberine biosynthetic genes are observed co-expressed in |FRAME: TAX-3442| cultured cells and in roots, which suggests that the expression of these genes is co-regulated |CITS: [12732624]|.

Summary: Numerous species of the genus |FRAME: TAX-71950| produce psychotropically active natural products that change perception profoundly when ingested (these species are commonly known as magic mushrooms) |CITS: [21956378]|. The major constituent in these mushrooms is |FRAME: CPD-20576|, which acts as a pro-drug. Upon oral ingestion, |FRAME: CPD-20576| is rapidly dephosphorylated to generate |FRAME: CPD-20617|, the actual psychotropic agent. |FRAME: CPD-20617 Psilocin| primarily acts as a partial agonist on the 5HT2A receptor in the human central nervous system |CITS: [14615876][14761703]|., The structure of |FRAME: CPD-20576| was first reported in 1959 |CITS: [Hofmann59]|, followed by the structures of intermediates in the pathway |CITS: [5684732]|. A potential pathway was suggested in 1968, based on 14C and 3H radiotracer labeling |CITS: [5689110]|. However, when the enzymes that participate in the pathway were discovered 49 years later, it was found that the order of transformations differs from the original propoal |CITS: [28763571]|., A bioinformatic search of the genomes of |FRAME: TAX-181762| and |FRAME: TAX-93625| (two |FRAME: CPD-20576| producers) for gene clusters that encode a methyltransferase, a hydroxylase, and a kinase, has identified a locus in each genome, that also included a putative decarboxylase gene. The genes were named |FRAME: G-58125|, |FRAME: G-58123|, |FRAME: G-58124|, and |FRAME: G-58122|, respectively |CITS: [28763571]|. A mixture of in vitro and in vivo assays has shown that the order of actions (starting with |FRAME: TRP|) is decarboxylation, hydroxylation, phosphorylation, and methylation. In addition, it was found that the pathway can also start with |FRAME: CPD-20578|. The source for this compound is not known, but it has been shown that it is not produced from |FRAME: TRP| by |FRAME: G-58123 PsiH| |CITS: [28763571]|.

Summary: The reduction of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to one-carbon units is essential for the anabolism of Clostridia. In the case of |FRAME: TAX-1534|, CO<sub>2</sub> was shown to be the predominant precursor of one-carbon units |CITS: [6051580][5645529]|., The process is mediated by two key enzymes. The indirect CO<sub>2</sub> reduction via reductive carboxylation of |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| to |FRAME: PYRUVATE| is catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-62|. The pyruvate is cleaved into acetyl-CoA and |FRAME: FORMATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-7078|. The formate thus formed enters the anabolic pathways by incorporation into the one-carbon carrier |FRAME:THF|, generating |FRAME:10-FORMYL-THF|, a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-1261| |CITS:[11947600][4340563]|., It should be noted that while in this pathway |FRAME:CPLX-7078| provides an anabolic function, in other organisms, such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, the enzyme has a pure catabolic function in the fermentation of pyruvate to acetate (see |FRAME: PWY-5485|).

Nopaline and octopine are opines derived from arginine. They are biosynthesized in the cells of plant crown gall , tumors. These tumors are caused by infection with the plant pathogen |FRAME:TAX-358|. The , enzymes for both the biosynthesis and degradation/utilization of opines are encoded by the tumor-inducing Ti , plasmids found in A. tumefaciens. This host-pathogen interaction has an interesting mechanism. , A. tumefaciens infects wounded plants in response to chemical signals released by plant cells. Infection , by this organism involves products of the vir genes encoded by a Ti plasmid. These gene products cause , the transfer of oncogenic fragments of DNA (T-DNA) from the Ti plasmid into the nucleus of host plant cells, where , they become integrated into the host genome. , In plant cells, the T-DNA onc genes express plant hormones causing neoplastic growth. Genes encoding , opine synthases (ops genes such as nos encoding nopaline synthase and ocs encoding , octopine synthase) are also expressed and direct the biosynthesis of opines (|FRAME: 1.5.1.11-RXN "EC 1.5.1.11"| and |FRAME: 1.5.1.19-RXN "1.5.1.19"| reactions in the reverse direction). These synthases are soluble, NAD(P)H-dependent dehydrogenases |CITS: [8045881]| (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-7351|). Opines produced in the plant tumor cells are secreted into the environment, enter the bacteria via opine permeases, and induce their catabolism by opine-specific enzymes. Opines therefore provide a source of carbon, nitrogen and energy for A. tumefaciens inside the plant tumor cells (in |CITS: [16195384], [9791116], [9244272]|, and reviewed in |CITS: [10869063]|). , The proteins required for uptake and catabolism of nopaline and octopine are organized into operons in , the noc region of a nopaline-type Ti plasmid, or the occ region of an octopine-type Ti , plasmid |CITS: [11877409], [9791116], [8288543]|. The enzymatic degradation of nopaline to arginine , and α-ketoglutarate by nopaline oxidase is shown here. Nopaline oxidase is a membrane-bound opine , oxidase that does not require an added cofactor when assayed in crude preparations. However, it was postulated , by sequence analysis to require a cofactor such as FAD, FMN, or NAD(P)H. Therefore, the electron acceptor(s) , for this reaction remains to be identified in this organism |CITS: [8045881]|. Clicking on the pathway link shows the , conversion of arginine to proline and then glutamate in A. tumefaciens , |CITS: [8045881], [8981973], [8606160]|. A similar degradation of octopine to arginine and pyruvate by octopine , oxidase in this organism is shown in MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: OCTOPINEDEG-PWY|.

Summary: Background, Unicellular green algae can utilize molecular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| in the dark to drive cellular metabolism, or evolve |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| in the light with electrons derived from the photosynthetic oxidation of water |CITS: [11706159]|. |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| is produced anaerobically when mitochondrial respiration is inhibited, and this permits electron flow through the electron transport chain with the concommitant generation of ATP |CITS: [11102662]|. , Molecular oxygen suppresses expression of the genes associated with |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production and also inhibits the hydrogenase enzyme, hence under aerobic conditions, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| is not evolved |CITS: [16143840]|. A prior anaerobic incubation of the algae in the dark can remove this inhibition and induces expression of a [FeFe] hydrogenase. A subsequent illumination then drives |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolution for a short period of time, till the release of photosynthetic |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE| inhibits the process. Photosystem II (PSII) mediates the light driven reaction of splitting water molecules into |FRAME: PROTON| and |FRAME: OXYGEN-MOLECULE|., About This Pathway, During eukaryotic photosynthesis, electron transport is driven by photons captured by the antenna proteins LHCII/LHCI bound to PSII and PSI respectively. Linear photosynthetic electron transport originating from water oxidation, proceeds via PSII, cytochrome b6-f and PSI to the chloroplast ferredoxin |CITS: [21605544]|. Ferredoxin can pass electrons to several further acceptors. Under aerobic conditions, most of the electrons are used to reduce NADP+ to NADPH by ferredoxin-NADP+ reductase (FNR). The NADPH is then consumed by reductive |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| assimilation in the |FRAME: CALVIN-PWY|., The catalytic site, also known as the "hydrogen cluster" (HC) of [FeFe] hydrogenase accepts electrons from reduced ferredoxin |CITS: [10631256]|. The HC generates molecular |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| utilizing protons as a sink for these high potential-energy electrons |CITS: [17721788]|., Under conditions that inhibit photosynthesis and generate anoxia, |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production naturally occurs. This requires a fully active PSI for electron transfer to ferredoxin. PSII activity is partially inhibited by a block in turnover of the D1 protein causing a reduction in photosynthetic oxygen evolution |CITS: [11006346]|. However, PSII still retains a low level of water oxidation activity, which can feed some electrons into the electron transport chain. When the level of oxygen evolved by PSII drops below respiratory consumption, the cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and express the hydrogenase., The majority of the electrons required for |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| evolution during anoxia come from the redox equivalents of fermentative metabolism. These are supplied into the electron transport chain by an NAD(P)H-plastoquinone-oxidoreductase through non-photochemical PQ reduction. Prior aerobic PSII activity is crucial for build up of the starch and protein required for this. , During prolonged fermentative metabolism in |FRAME: TAX-3055|, formate and ethanol are generated. This creates alternate sources for reduced ferredoxin, which feeds directly into |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production at the level of the [FeFe] hydrogenase.

Summary: Vanilla as a flavoring agent is a global favorite and its worldwide consumption is estimated to be over 2000 tonnes |CITS: [12423881]|. Natural vanilla is obtained from beans of the vanilla orchid |FRAME: TAX-51239| and the major flavor compound is |FRAME: VANILLIN| (4-hydroxy-3-methoxy-benzaldehyde). The characteristic flavor develops only after 'curing' the beans, a process that lasts several months and involves several hydrolytic enzymes |CITS: [12423881]|., Vanillin is shown to accumulate in special secretory tissue composed of closely packed unicellular hairs located in the three gaps between placentas along the central fruit cavity |CITS: [JOEL03]|. The flavor substances including vanillin are present as glycosides in the mature green bean, the glycosylation prevents reactivity |CITS: [DIGNUM01]|. , Despite extensive literature documenting the formation of benzoic acids and aldehydes from the |FRAME: PWY-361| pathway, there is still considerable debate about the nature of vanilla biosynthesis |CITS: [15118832]|. There are two major views regarding the phenylpropanoid precursors that are converted to |FRAME: VANILLIN|. The |FRAME: PWY-6343 "'ferulate pathway'"| proposal suggests that the aromatic ring on the C6-C3 compound undergoes hydroxylation and methylation to give ferulic acid which undergoes chain shortening to vanillin. Summary: Fumiquinazoline are mycotoxins of a peptidyl alkaloid group which derives from the cyclization of the nonproteinogenic aryl β-amino acid |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| with two or more proteinogenic amino aicid residues |CITS:[18663394]|. Consequently, research on fumiquinazolins in Aspergillus fumigatus, one of the most pathogenic fungi in humans |CITS:[10194462]|, has been carried out to understand the scope and importance of secondary metabolites produced in this fungus. Fumiquinazoline have been also found interesting from a pharmacological standpoint as those compounds have been reported to possess antibacterial |CITS:[15646377]|, antifungal |CITS:[10840958]| and anti-tumor |CITS:[Han07]| properties., In spite of this background, the biological importance and involvement of this wide-spread Aspergillus compound class in the metabolism of the fungus still remains unknown and needs to be demonstrated. General Background, Xanthones are yellow pigments of phenolic origin restricted in occurrence to only a few families of higher plants and some fungi and lichens. The majority of xanthones is rarely glucosylated and has been found in basically two families of higher plants, the Clusiaceae (syn. Guttiferae) and |FRAME:TAX-21472| |CITS: [Hostettmann89][Bennett89]|. However, xanthones also appear sporadically throughout the remainder of the plant kingdom. Xanthone-C-glucosides, such as mangiferin are the exception with a much wider distribution among plants and also arising in ferns and fungi |CITS: [Hostettmann89]|., Xanthones can be classified based on their oxygenation, prenylation and glucosylation pattern. The majority of xanthones, isolated so far are of the tetraoxygenated-type which have been intensively studied in plants of the Guttiferae and, |FRAME:TAX-21472| but are reported from 12 other plant families as well |CITS: [11190384]|. The restricted biosynthesis of, xanthones and their plant-specific substitution pattern has been employed as a useful marker for systematic purposes,, i.e. comparing the phyletic order of genera within the Guttiferae |CITS: [Da Mate Rezente73]|and chemotaxonomic differentiation between plant families |CITS: [Sultanbawa80]|., Xanthones posses a number of remarkable pharmacological traits and bioactivities (summarized in |CITS: [11190384]|) and, have been used as, e.g. cardiovascular protective agents |CITS: [15179447]| and antitumor promotors |CITS: [10397461]|. Tetrahydroxylated xanthones can be induced by phytopathogens |CITS: [12391565]| and accumulate in calli and cell suspension upon treatment with plant hormones and supplements, such as naphtaleneacetic acid (NAA) in combination with kinetin |CITS: [DIAS00]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14997 "Hyperxanthone E"| is a prenylated xanthone phytoalexin produced by |FRAME: TAX-55963| |CITS: [22992510]|. The compound is formed from |FRAME: CPD-6884| by prenylation, carried out by |FRAME: MONOMER-124402|, followed by formation of a pyran ring |CITS: [26343621]|.

C-glycosylflavanones are widely present as secondary metabolites in plants. The sugars are attached directly to the flavonoid skeleton. This makes such flavonoids resistant to acid hydrolysis. The accumulation of C-glycosylflavones has been used by taxonomists in chemosystematics studies of certain families like Compositae |CITS:[VALANT-VETSCHERA85]|., C-glycosyl flavones have been isolated from a number of plant sources; flavoayamenin and luteoayamenin from petals of Iris nertshinskia, and swertisin and swertiajaponin |CITS: [HIROSE81]|. In cereals, the C-glycosylflavones are involved in several important physiological functions including plant defense and are also valuable as nutritive components |CITS: [20647377]|. These phytocompounds have been shown to have several useful metabolic benefits as antioxidants, in cereals they are usually localized in the bran which is not consumed, therefore to metabolically engineer these useful compounds into the endosperm tissue (the consumed portion) it is necessary to know the biochemical machinery underlying the biosynthesis of these compounds |CITS: [19411659]|. , C-glycosylation is suggested to occur much earlier than O-glycosylation of flavonoid biosynthesis, in which the O-glycosylation occurs only at the terminal stages. In cereals the C-glycosylation is carried out in concert by the CGT and a dehydratase which act on the 2-hydroxyflavonones. This is an alternate route for the production of flavonoid metabolites |CITS: [19411659]|., Co-expression of the rice |FRAME: MONOMER-15865| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.360| in yeast resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-20015|, but not of the dehydrated flavone C-conjugates |FRAME: VITEXIN| and |FRAME: ISOVITEXIN|, indicating that the dehydration-cyclization reaction does not proceed spontaneously in vivo |CITS: [23246521]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: N-Acylethanolamines N-acylethanolamines| are a class of endogenous bioactive lipid molecules formed by the linkage of an acyl group to the nitrogen atom of |FRAME: ETHANOL-AMINE|. These compounds exert a variety of biological actions through their interactions with various receptors., |FRAME: CPD-20399 "Palmitoyl ethanolamide"| (PEA) was first isolated in 1957 from soy, peanuts, and egg yolk and described as the active ingredient in egg yolk that confers anti-allergic and anti-inflammatory properties |CITS: [Kuehl57]|. At that time egg yolks were routinely prescribed as a preventative against convalescent rheumatic fever and other Streptococcal infections |CITS: [13211905][13539486][13826312][13810795]|., During the subsequent years the compound was consistently found in mammalian brain, liver, and muscle tissue, and its anti-inflammatory action was demonstrated in a classical anti-inflammatory model, the carrageen-induced edema model |CITS: [5699335][4729458]|, leading to its marketing in the late 60s as a medication against influenza and the common cold under the brand name Impulsin. The efficacy of this indication was verified by multiple clinical trials |CITS: [902351][392005]|., Insight into PEA's mode of action began with the work of the Nobel laureate Rita Levi-Montalcini, the discoverer of the Nerve Growth Factor (NGF), who found that PEA is a natural modulator of hyperactive mast cells, counteracting the pro-inflammatory actions of NGF |CITS: [7505999][8931279][Hesselink13]|. Since then PEA has been found to be effective in a number of animal models for inflammation, neuroinflammation, neurotoxicity, and chronic pain., PEA is now known to have affinity for several receptors, including the orphan cannabinoid receptors GPR55 and GPR119, the vanilloid receptor TRPV1, and the nuclear peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-α (PPAR-α) |CITS: [15963531][18602217][19615459][22972997]|., Considering it was first isolated from soy, it is not surprising that PEA is produced not only by animals but also by plants |CITS: [10444099][15234550][16054175][22673881]|. Although its function in plants is still unknown, it appears to be synthesized in all organisms by very similar pathways |CITS: [24397856]|. , About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-20399 "Palmitoyl ethanolamide"| is synthesized from palmitate (C16:0), the most common fatty acid in animals and a product of the fatty acid synthase. Synthesis takes place in membranes of various cell types and involves several partly parallel pathways. This pathway describes only the main route. The parallel routes are similar to those described for the biosynthesis of the related N-acylethanolamine |FRAME: CPD-7598| (see |FRAME: PWY-8051|)., The main phospholipid precursor of PEA is |FRAME: N-Palmitoyl-PE "N-palmitoyl phosphatidylethanolamine"|, which is produced from |FRAME: CPD-17523 "1-palmitoyl-2-acyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine"| by an N-acyltransferase enzyme |CITS: [12052034]|. Several reports were made about a Ca2+-dependent, membrane-associated N-acyltransferase that catalyzes this reaction |CITS: [8656287][9006968]|. However, as of 2019 that enzyme has not been purified and the gene encoding it has not been cloned. In 2007 a different enzyme catalyzing this activity was identified from rat, and later from mouse and humans. Unlike the previously reported enzyme, this enzyme was soluble and not dependent on Ca2+ concentrations. The enzyme did not show selectivity with respect to the sn-1 and sn-2 positions of the |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE phosphatidylcholine| as an acyl donor |CITS: [17158102]|., It was soon found that the enzyme (now known as |FRAME: HS15623|) is a member of a family of related proteins, previously known as HRAS-like suppressors since they were reported to negatively regulate the activity of oncogene Ras. The other members of the family, |FRAME: HS13232|, |FRAME: HS13475|, |FRAME: HS11053|, and |FRAME: HS05758|, were shown to possess similar activities |CITS: [19047760][19615464][21880860]|. Based on this discovery, it was suggested to rename these enzymes to phospholipase A/acyltransferase-1 through 5 (PLA/AT-1–5)., While these enzymes catalyzed the transfer of an acyl group from both sn-1 and sn-2 positions of phosphatidylcholine to the amino group of phosphatidylethanolamine, as described in this pathway, they also possess the activities of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.32|, of |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.4|, and of an O-acyltransferase that transfers an acyl group from a glycerophospholipid to the hydroxyl group of a lysophospholipid |CITS: [19000777]|., Several different routes have been described for the release of PEA from its phospholipid precursor, consisting of one, two, or three steps. In this pathway, only the direct route, which consists of a single reaction, is described., The reaction is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-3.1.4.54|, whose activities were found to be highest in the brain, kidney, and testis. The enzyme, which belongs to the metallo-beta-lactamase family, contains |FRAME: ZN+2| and is activated by |FRAME: MG+2| or |FRAME: CA+2|. While it is very specific for N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines, it does not discriminate among them based on the chain-length of the N-acyl moiety |CITS: [16527816]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway menaquinone is synthesized from chorismate via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|. In a series of reactions, |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE| is converted to the two-ring compound |FRAME: DIHYDROXYNAPHTHOATE| via several intermediates that include |FRAME: O-SUCCINYLBENZOATE|. At this point a prenyltransferase enzyme attaches a polyprenyl tail to form |FRAME: Demethylmenaquinones|, which can be converted to |FRAME: Menaquinones| by a, dedicated methylase., Demethylmenaquinones with a side chain of 8 isoprenyl units (DMK-8) have been detected mainly in facultatively anaerobic Gram-negative bacteria, mostly belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-91347| order (|FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, |FRAME: TAX-554|, |FRAME: TAX-584|, and |FRAME: TAX-585|) |CITS:[11945333][4886765][4900998][4100202][4148761]|, but also outside that group, as in the case of |FRAME: TAX-644| |CITS: [4886765]|. However, DMK-8 has also been reported from the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1351| |CITS: [14321383][118232 ][11722738]|., Interestingly, most of these organisms produce not only DMK-8 but also |FRAME: UBIQUINONE-8| and |FRAME: CPD-9728|. Since their redox potential is different, each of these electron transfer agents appear to be best suited for specific growth conditions, and having all three maximizes the ability of the organism to adjust to available substrates. It has been suggested that DMK-8 is used for nitrate and |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O| (TMAO) respiration |CITS: [2849923]|, but its role in nitrate respiration has been contested |CITS: [2204318][1444716][7601837]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: TAX-1511| and other |FRAME: TAX-1485| species can utilize certain combinations of amino acids for growth using Stickland reactions. Stickland reactions, named after their discoverer, L. H. Stickland |CITS: [16745572] [16745669]|, are fermentations of amino acid pairs in which one amino acid is oxidized and the other one is reduced., The oxidative branch of some amino acids leads to formation of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, but produces 4 reducing equivalents per amino acid. These reducing equivalents are consumed by the reduction of other amino acids via the reducing branch, maintaining a balanced redox potential in the cell (reviewed in |CITS: [13140081][6791576]|)., Both branches begin with the transamination of the amino acid to its corresponding 2-oxo-acid in a reaction that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: GLT|. Coupled to |FRAME: EC-1.4.1.2|, this transformation generates one NADH molecule |CITS: [5697992][6791576]|. In the case of |FRAME: SER|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET|, and |FRAME: CYS|, alternative mechanisms exist, involving |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.17|, |FRAME: EC-4.3.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.11| |CITS: [8344301][24303205]|., Following this first step the two branches separate. In the oxidative pathway, the formed 2-oxo acid gets oxidized by ferredoxin with the formation of a CoA thioester and the release of CO2 in a reaction catalyzed by enzymes encoded by vorCBA or iorBA (e.g. |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.7|) |CITS: [8206994][8550513][26170002]|. The CoA thioester is then cleaved. If the pathway leads to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA|, ATP can be generated, as shown in pathway |FRAME: PWY0-1312| |CITS: [13140081][13840823][2844725][2719475]|., In the reductive branch the 2-oxo acid is reduced to a 2-hydroxy acid at the expense of NADH |CITS: [12603323][15634349][16957230]|. Though there are several variations, in general the 2-hydroxy acid is dehydrated to an enoate in a complex reaction that involves CoA intermediates |CITS: [11967068][15654892]|. Reduction of the enoate to a carboxylic acid consumes additinal reducing equivalents., Initially it was thought that the only purpose of the reductive branch was consumption of the reducing equivalents that are formed by the oxidative branch |CITS: [6354130]|. However, recent findings suggest that some oxidoreductases of the reductive branch are bifurcating, directing the electrons derived from NADH not only to the enoyl-CoA substrate but also to ferredoxin. Electron transfer from the reduced ferredoxin to NAD+ catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-7.2.1.2| (Rnf complex) generates a primary electrochemical potential across the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in proton motive force generation |CITS: [24045950][30828322]|., It should be noted that variations on this general scheme are common, such as the reduction of |FRAME: PRO|, the degradation of |FRAME: ARG| via ornithine, and both the reduction and oxidation of |FRAME: GLY|., About This Pathway, It has been well documented that aromatic amino acids can serve as electron acceptors in the reductive branch of the Stickland reaction. In 1970 Moss et al reported that when suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-1509| were incubated with |FRAME: PHE|, the end product was |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE|. In addition, the study reported that |FRAME: CPD-674| was formed as an intermediate |CITS: [5437307]|. A study from 1976 confirmed that |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE| was the final product, and also reported the formation of |FRAME: CPD-5921| |CITS: [1275638]|., Trying to find the physiological role of an enoate reducatase they had previously characterized from Clostridial species, Bühler et al showed that incubation of |FRAME: TAX-1509| with |FRAME: PHE|, as well as |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE|, |FRAME: CPD-5921|, and |FRAME: CPD-674|, resulted in formation of |FRAME: 3-PHENYLPROPIONATE|, thus delineating for the first time the pathway shown here. According to their proposed pathway, the aromatic amino acid is converted to its 3-propanoate derivative via transamination to a 2-oxoacid, reduction to a 2R-hydroxyacid, dehydration to an enoate, and finally reduction of the double bond to form the 3-propanoate derivative |CITS: [7353645][7084457]|., The dehydration step is the most energetically-demanding step in the pathway, owing to the poor acidity of the β-hydrogen. The reaction requires activation of the substrate by coenzyme A, followed by a dehydration reaction that involves the formation of a highly reactive ketyl radical that helps to acidify the β-hydrogen |CITS: [18337824]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negatives is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In some cases a third Kdo residue is added to the second one., In |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: DODECANOATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7836| fatty acids are incorporated into the distal unit of lipid A. |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.241|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10464|, is a Kdo-dependent lauroyltransferase. |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.243|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10614|, functions after laurate has been added to Kdo2-lipid IVA |CITS: [8662613] [2203778] [9099672]|. However, a great variability exists in the nature of fatty acids incorporated by these enzymes from different species, and often even within the same species.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chlorophylls Chlorophyll| is a green photosynthetic pigment found in photosynthetic plants, algae, and bacteria. Its name is derived from ancient Greek: chloros = green and phyllon = leaf. Chlorophyll absorbs mostly in the blue and, to a lesser extent, red portions of the electromagnetic spectrum, hence its intense green color. There are several variants of chlorophyll (|FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A|, |FRAME: CPD-10334|, |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-B|, |FRAME: CPD-10336|, |FRAME: CPD-10337|, and |FRAME: CPD-10335|). Non-oxygenic bacteria possess a related pigment called bacteriochlorophyll, which also exists in several variants (|FRAME:CPD-9067|, |FRAME:CPD-9091|,, |FRAME:CPD-9092|, |FRAME:CPD-9093|, |FRAME:CPD-9094| and |FRAME:CPD-9095|). This pathway describes the formation of |FRAME:CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|, an important intermediate in the biosynthesis of all chlorophylls and bacteriochlorophylls., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathway of bacteriochlorophylls begins with the condensation of eight molecules of |FRAME:5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| to form |FRAME:UROPORPHYRINOGEN-III|, the first cyclic tetrapyrrole compound in the pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5188|). This compound is then sequentially converted to |FRAME:PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX|, which is the, branch-point intermediate to hemes and chlorophylls., The incorporation of |FRAME: MG+2| into |FRAME:PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX| occurs at the next step, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:MG-PROTOPORPHYRIN| (MgP). A methyl transferase converts MgP into |FRAME:MG-PROTOPORPHYRIN-MONOMETHYL-ESTER| (MgPMME), which is the substrate for a cyclase that creates a fifth ring (ring E), a common feature of all chlorophylls. In anaerobic phototrophs the cyclase is a hydratase, incorporating, an oxygen atom from a water molecule, by a complex process catalyzed by the cobalamin-dpendent, enzyme |FRAME:MONOMER-13265|., The ultimate step of this pathway is the reduction of protochlorophyllide to chlorophyllide. In this pathway, which is found in anoxygenic phototrophs, this final reduction is carried by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.3.7.7|, permitting the organisms to synthesize bacteriochlorophyll in the dark., This biosynthetic pathway, which occurs in all anaerobic photosynthetic organisms, has been described through genetic analysis of bacterial mutants and in vitro reconstitution of individual reactions |CITS:[9442890][beale99][14617630][17370354]|., Aerobic phototrophs possess a very similar pathway. One important exception is that the cyclase found in these organisms uses molecular oxygen as the oxygen source. A variant of the pathway found in aerobic phototrophs is described in |FRAME: PWY-7159|.

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., IAA (indole-3-acetic acid), one of the most common active forms of the phytohormone auxin, is often, present in conjugated forms. Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. Meanwhile, conjugated forms of auxin play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., About This Pathway, The degradation pathway in broad bean (|FRAME: ORG-5992|) differs from that in |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen). Following oxidation of |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| at the C2 position, |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| is further metabolized by hydroxylation and glucosylation instead of being hydrolyzed to |FRAME: 2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETIC-ACID|. From the seedling feeding experiment it was suggested that reaction 1 through 3 occurs in both cotyledons and roots, whereas reaction 4 occurs only in the cotyledons. The end product, |FRAME: 3-O-BETA-GLUCOSYL-2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETYL-| is transported from the cotyledons to the roots. No enzyme or gene information is available for the pathway.

|FRAME: CPD-9937 "Diphenylamine"| (DPA) is a naturally occurring compound acting as an antihyperglycemic agent in onions and tea leaves |CITS: [6512531]|., DPA has been widely used as a precursor of dyes, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and photographic chemicals and as a stabilizer for explosives |CITS: [14505701]|. It is a common contaminant at munitions-contaminated sites and |FRAME: ANILINE| manufacturing sites, and is potentially hazardous to aquatic organisms |CITS: [8521780]|., Bacteria able to use DPA as the growth substrate have been reported |CITS:[7066552][9353218][14505701]|., The strains |FRAME: TAX-622617| and |FRAME: TAX-622618| were isolated in an enrichments culture, and can use DPA as a carbon, nitrogen and energy source |CITS: [19251893]|., The genes involved in DPA degradation have been cloned from |FRAME: TAX-622617| and characterized. The key enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-8083|, was shown to convert DPA to stoichiometric amounts of |FRAME: ANILINE| and |FRAME: CATECHOL|. The |FRAME: ANILINE| that is formed is also converted to catechol (see |FRAME: PWY-6533|), and the catechol is degraded to TCA cycle intermediates by a common route (see |FRAME: PWY-5415|) |CITS: [19251893]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: SS-DIMETHYL-BETA-PROPIOTHETIN "Dimethylsulfoniopropionate"| (DMSP) is an osmolyte of many marine algae and certain plants |CITS: [15181109]|. Marine phytoplankton synthesize DMSP not only as an osmolyte, but also as a predator deterrent and an antioxidant |CITS: [17068264]|. DMSP is readily degraded in a variety of biological systems, including bacterial cultures, salt marsh sediments, and seawater samples containing algae and zooplankton |CITS: [16347732]|., Two main routes are known for DMSP degradation, one leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-7670| (as described in this pathway and in |FRAME: PWY-6046|) and the other leading to formation of |FRAME: CPD-7672| (see |FRAME: PWY-6052|)., |FRAME: CPD-7670 "Dimethylsulfide"|, which is very volatile, is exchanged freely between the ocean and the atmosphere,, and is the main natural source of sulfur to the atmosphere. Once in the troposphere, DMS is oxidized to sulfuric and methanesulfonic acids, which attract water and promote cloud formation |CITS: [Charlson87]|. However, most of the DMS in the oceanic environment is degraded biologically (see |FRAME: PWY-6047|)., About This Pathway, The traditional pathway for DMSP cleavage by |FRAME: MONOMER-14221| is described in |FRAME: PWY-6046|. In that pathway, DMSP is cleaved directly to DMS and |FRAME: ACRYLATE| by |FRAME: MONOMER-14241|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10872| gene. However, a different enzyme that degrades DMSP to DMS was identified from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-400668| |CITS: [17272727]|., The |FRAME: G-10871| gene encodes a CoA transferase, suggesting that in this organism DMSP is activated to a CoA derivative prior to its cleavage. The authors proposed that the |FRAME: CPD-10473| thioester may be catabolized by one or more steps to |FRAME: CPD-7670| plus |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-PROPIONATE|. Such a pathway would explain the observations that some bacteria that degrade DMSP to DMS accumulated 3-hydroxypropionate rather than acrylate |CITS: [11425733]|. A detailed mechanism for the enzyme's action has been proposed |CITS: [25140443]| (see |FRAME: G-10871 DddD|)., Homologs of the |FRAME: G-10871| gene were found in several other marine bacteria, as well as in the plant-associated bacteria |FRAME: TAX-339670| and |FRAME: TAX-394|. The ability of all of these strains to produce DMS while catabolizing DMSP was confirmed |CITS: [17272727]|., It should be noted that some DMS-emitting bacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-89187|, do not possess homologs of either |FRAME: G-10871| or |FRAME: G-10872|, and thus are likely to utilize a third alternative pathway |CITS: [18237308]|.

Summary: |FRAME: GLYCOL "Ethylene glycol"| is commonly used as a coolant, as a deicing fluid, and to produce plastics such as |FRAME: CPD-19188| (PET). Eethylene glycol readily partitions into the aqueous phase, resulting in high mobility and rapid dispersion through the biosphere. Although the toxicity is low |CITS: [11302583]|, acute exposure can result in kidney and brain damage and possibly teratogenesis., Aerobic degradation of |FRAME: GLYCOL| is well documented |CITS: [4568254][620072][Shieh98][11302583][14703144]|. The compound is partially oxidized to |FRAME: GLYOX| via |FRAME: GLYCOLLATE|, and is further degraded in the usual glyoxylate degradative pathways., Anaerobic degradation (either methanogenic or via |FRAME: ACETALD|) has also been reported, although not as well characterized |CITS: [6614903][19132327]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Radical-AdoMet-Enzymes "Radical-SAM (S-adenosyl-L-methionine) enzymes"|, often referred to as radical-AdoMet enzymes, catalyze various types of reactions utilizing the radical generated by the cleavage of an |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (AdoMet or SAM) molecule. The reaction starts when an electron supplied by a flavodoxin domain is transferred to an iron-sulfur cluster, shifting the cluster to its most reduced state (for example, [4Fe–4S]1+). The electron is then transferred to a bound |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| molecule that interacts with the FeS cluster, resulting in its reductive cleavage to a |FRAME: CPD-15400| and |FRAME: MET|. The reactive 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from the substrate, prompting the actual reaction to start. In the process the radical is converted to |FRAME: CH33ADO|., Accumulation of |FRAME: CH33ADO| leads to defects in growth and metabolism |CITS: [19328201]|. On the other hand, elimination via export constitutes a loss of valuable organic carbon and nitrogen., About This Pathway, The bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1085| and |FRAME: TAX-1076| possess three genes (|FRAME: G-15516|, |FRAME: G-15512| and |FRAME: G-80668|) that encode enzymes that catalyze the initial steps of methionine salvage pathways from |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE|. Those pathways proceed via |FRAME: CPD-23221| as the key product, with |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| produced as a side product |CITS: [29133429]| (see |FRAME: PWY-8132|)., In vitro studies of these enzymes indicated that they may also function in |FRAME: CH33ADO| metabolism. To investigate this possibility, individual deletions of the three genes were constructed in |FRAME: TAX-1085|. All three mutants accumulated |FRAME: CH33ADO| extracellularly to a level twofold higher than that of the wild-type strain. Plasmid-based gene complementation of each respective gene deletion strain with the relevant gene restored |FRAME: CH33ADO| abundance to wild-type level. Thus the three enzymes participate in an oxygen-independent dual-purpose metabolic pathway that can degrade both |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| and |FRAME: CH33ADO| |CITS: [31950558]|., Labeling of |FRAME: CH33ADO| with tritium identified the products of the Ald2 aldolase as |FRAME: ACETALD| and |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|. Further confirmation of the proposed enzyme activites was achieved by production of purified recombinant proteins and in vitro characterization |CITS: [31950558]|.

Most of the pathway is shared between yeast and other organisms whose plasma membranes are composed predominantly of other types of sterols, (e.g. |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|)., This superpathway describes the complete pathway for the synthesis of |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| from the central metabolite |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|. Mutations in the genes encoding these enzymes and others in the pathway, as well as alterations in the expression levels of the pathway constituents, can lead to antifungal drug resistance |CITS: [11815273]|., Even though the pathway is very common in fungi, it is not universally present; for example, |FRAME: TAX-4754| plasma, membranes lack ergosterol |CITS:[12531182]|.

General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, Desferrioxamines are a group of nonpeptide hydroxamate siderophores that are produced by many |FRAME: TAX-1883| species. Several forms are known, and one member of this group, |FRAME: CPD-3764|, is marketed under the name Desferal for the treatment of iron overload in humans |CITS: [14011640][14113899]|., Studies of the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-3764| in |FRAME: TAX-28893| have shown that the first step is the decarboxylation of |FRAME: LYS| to yield |FRAME: CADAVERINE| |CITS: [Schupp87]|. A DNA fragment that complemented a mutant defective in this step has been isolated, and eventually a partial sequence was obtained, which contained the promoter region and two genes, which were named |FRAME: SCO2782| and |FRAME: SCO2783| |CITS: [2841191][8501033]|., Following the sequencing of the |FRAME: TAX-100226| genome a cluster of four genes has been identified and proposed to be responsible for desferrioxamine biosynthesis |CITS: [12000953]|. Unlike |FRAME: TAX-28893|, this organism produces |FRAME: CPD-11957| as its major siderophore, along witrh smaller amounts of |FRAME: CPD-11956|. However, it is likely that very similar pathways lead to the synthesis of the various desferrioxamines, A plausible pathway for the complete synthesis has been proposed on the basis of comparative sequence analysis and biochemical evidence |CITS: [15600304]|. Based on the proposed pathway, which is described here, |FRAME: G-11638| encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-15209| that produces |FRAME: CPD-11953|. The |FRAME: TAX-100226| |FRAME: SCO2784| gene encodes a |FRAME: SCO2784-MONOMER| that can use |FRAME: SUC-COA| to acylate |FRAME: CPD-11953|, forming |FRAME: CPD-11955|. It is assumed that the desC products of |FRAME: TAX-28893| and other organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD-3764| have a relaxed substrate specificity that permits them to accept either |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| or |FRAME: SUC-COA|, thus producing two different types of hydroxamates |CITS: [15600304]|., The last enzyme in the pathway, encoded by |FRAME: SCO2785|, catalyzes the oligomerization of two |FRAME: CPD-11955| molecule with one |FRAME: CPD-11959| to produce |FRAME: CPD-3764|., Mutants of |FRAME: G-11637| and |FRAME: G-11638| were not able to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-3764|. Production of the siderophore was restored by complementation with the cloned genes |CITS: [2841192]|. The last two enzymes have not been characterized from |FRAME: TAX-28893|., Transcriptional regulation of the desferrioxamine gene cluster is mediated by binding of the Fe(II)-dependent repressor DmdR1 to an iron box in the promoter of the |FRAME: G-11637| gene |CITS:[8501033][12801423]|.

Summary: Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| and |FRAME: GLT| are the most abundant neurotransmitters in mammalian brain. While |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter, |FRAME: GLT| is an excitatory neurotransmitter. Both are key mediators of synaptic plasticity and neuroendocrine function |CITS: [15571623]|. , Disturbances in the homeostasis of GABA in the brain are implicated in the development of epilepsy, depression, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's chorea, Alzheimer's disease, and Stiff-Man syndrome |CITS: [15571623]|. , The |FRAME: GLUDEG-I-PWY| serves two functions, it can mediate both the catabolism of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| and channels |FRAME: GLT| to the |FRAME: PWY66-398|, bypassing two steps of that cycle |CITS: [OLSEN]|., About this Pathway, This pathway forms a closed loop whose function is the production and conservation of the supply of GABA in the central nervous system across a variety of neural cells. The first step is the transamination of |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| formed in the |FRAME: PWY66-398|, to |FRAME: GLT| by the mitochondrial glutamate dehydrogenases |CITS: [8207021]|. In the next step, the cytosolic glutamate decarboxylases |FRAME: CPLX-6887 "GAD67"| and |FRAME: CPLX-6889 "GAD65"| catalyze the decarboxylation of |FRAME: GLT| to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| |CITS: [9816471]|. , GABA then enters the mitochondrion, where the two mitochondrial enzymes are located |CITS: [15003233]|. |FRAME: CPLX-6886| catalyzes the conversion of GABA to |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD| |CITS: [15528998]|. To conserve the available supply of GABA, this transamination only occurs when |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| is present to accept the amino group removed from GABA, reforming |FRAME: GLT| |CITS: [13044808]|. , The last enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-6888| catalyzes the irreversible oxidation of |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD| to |FRAME: SUC| |CITS: [12208142]|. The latter compound reenters the |FRAME: PWY66-398| and GABA can be resynthesized from |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|. , Epileptic convulsions can be controlled by administering drug inhibitors of |FRAME: CPLX-6886|. One such drug which is used in the treatment of some types of epilepsy is |FRAME:VIGABATRIN| |CITS:[8156960]|.

Summary: |FRAME: PICOLINATE Picolinate| is a C-2-carboxylated pyridine derivate that is generated from physiological metabolism in mammalian and microbial cells |CITS: [8840783]|., |FRAME: PICOLINATE Picolinate| is formed spontaneously from |FRAME: 2-AMINOMUCONATE_SEMIALDEHYDE|, an intermediate in the microbial degradation of |FRAME: 2-AMINOPHENOL|, |FRAME: CATECHOL|, and |FRAME: BENZENE-NO2| |CITS: [8368838][24124510][Asano14]|. It is also formed as a dead-end metabolite of |FRAME: TRP| degradation by mammals |CITS: [9291104][26820800][26970015]|, which excrete it through urine or sweat., |FRAME: PICOLINATE Picolinate| was found to be toxic to mammalian cells, enhancing seizure activity in mice and inducing cell death via apoptosis |CITS: [11758936][26497245][27907839][26995730]|. However, it is degraded by many different bacterial species |CITS: [14089438][4792924][Siegmund90][Kiener93][8840783][19042125][Kutanovas16][28917103][30692170][31160400]|., A |FRAME: PICOLINATE|-degrading strain of |FRAME: TAX-511| was isolated from municipal wastewater. Initially only the first intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-22505|, was detected |CITS: [28243718]|. A subsequent study has shown that the |FRAME: G-80470| gene (then called maiA), which encodes |FRAME: EC-5.2.1.1|, is essential for |FRAME: PICOLINATE| degradation |CITS: [29802182]|. Soon after the next intermediate, |FRAME: CPD-22506|, has been positively identified using a library of transposon mutants that lost the ability to grow on |FRAME: CPD-22505|. Sequencing of the mutated gene has resulted in the identification of the |FRAME: G-80466| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-20938| |CITS: [30692170]|., Further analysis has found that the |FRAME: G-80466| gene is located in a gene cluster consisting of 12 genes, including one regulatory gene (picR) and eleven catabolic genes. Thorough characterization has shown that the cluster contains all of the genes necessary to encode the catabolism of |FRAME: PICOLINATE| to |FRAME: MALEATE|. An exception is the |FRAME: G-80470| gene, which is located elsewhere in the genome |CITS: [31160400]|., Orthologous pic gene clusters were found in other α-, β-, and γ-Proteobacteria, with most clusters occurring in species that belong to the order |FRAME: TAX-80840|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ORNITHINE-LIPIDS "Ornithine lipids"| are amino acid-containing acyl-oxyacyl lipids |CITS: [19703488]|. They are found in the membranes of many Gram-negative bacteria and in some Gram-positive bacteria, but have not been detected in archaea and eukaryotes. Ornithine lipids have been identified in the α-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-382| |CITS: [12139618]| and |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [17921310]|, the β-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-292| |CITS: [9695908]| |FRAME: TAX-520| |CITS: [6315433]|, the γ-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [3030307]|, some Pseudomonas species |CITS: [3409887][21535098]|, the Gram-positive actinobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [2118941]|, and |FRAME: TAX-986 "Flavobacterium johnsoniae (previously known as Cytophaga johnsonae)"| |CITS: [2914878]|. However, other bacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| do not appear to contain ornithine lipids., The presence of ornithine lipids depends upon the growth conditions. They are almost absent if wild-type |FRAME: TAX-382| is grown on complex medium, but can comprise up to 8% of total membrane lipids when phosphorus is growth limiting (in |CITS: [15341653]|). Little is known about the function of these non-phosphorus lipids. It has been shown that under certain growth conditions, ornithine lipids are important for optimal steady-state amounts of some c-type cytochromes in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [16856942]|. Ornithine lipids are also important for growth during acid and temperature stress in |FRAME: TAX-398| |CITS: [21205018]|, and depletion of the lipids results in an increase in the speed of crown gall tumor formation in plants infected with |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [ 22958119]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [19703488][12848422]|., About This Pathway, Ornithine lipids are biosynthesized in two steps. In the first step the N-acyltransferase product of gene olsB catalyzes the transfer of the 3-hydroxy fatty acyl group from an acyl carrier protein to the α-amino group of |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| forming an amide linkage to produce |FRAME: LYSO-ORNITHINE-LIPIDS|. The configuration of the asymmetric carbon of the 3-hydroxy fatty acids of several bacterial ornithine lipids was determined to be D (R) |CITS: [10030549]|. In the second step the O-acyltransferase product of gene olsA catalyzes the transfer of a fatty acyl group from an acyl carrier protein to the hydroxy group of |FRAME: LYSO-ORNITHINE-LIPIDS| forming an ester linkage to produce |FRAME: ORNITHINE-LIPIDS| (reviewed in |CITS: [19703488]|)., In |FRAME: TAX-266834| the olsB and olsA genes are separated on the chromosome, although in many other bacteria they form an olsBA operon |CITS: [15341653]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1061| the olsB and olsA functional homologs of the |FRAME: TAX-266834| genes were identified by interspecies complementation studies. OlsA and OlsB deficient mutants were unable to form ornithine lipids. It was shown that under certain growth conditions, ornithine lipids are important for optimal steady-state amounts of some c-type cytochromes in |FRAME: TAX-1061| |CITS: [16856942]|. Mutant analysis also showed that OlsA is a bifunctional enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-1061| that catalyzes both ornithine lipid and glycerophospholipid biosynthesis |CITS: [17921310]|., It has been found that in |FRAME: TAX-287| the homologous olsB and olsA genes are highly induced under phosphate limiting conditions and ornithine lipids are the primary membrane lipids produced. Analysis of an olsA mutant showed that it was required for ornithine lipid production. The data also suggested that ornithine lipids are not required for antimicrobial peptide resistance or virulence in |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [21535098]|., Many bacterial species possess a single |FRAME: G-34498| gene that encodes a bifunctional ornithine lipid synthase that catalyses both reactions. OlsF is not related to OlsA and OlsB. Homologs of OlsF are widely distributed among γ-, δ-, and ε-proteobacteria and in the CFB (Cytophaga-Flavobacterium-Bacteroidetes) group of bacteria, including some important pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-666| and |FRAME: TAX-573|. About 50% of the sequenced bacterial species have either the olsBA genes or the olsF gene., Ornithine lipids in which the ester linked fatty acyl group is hydroxylated at the 2-position have also been identified, for example in species of |FRAME: TAX-237|and |FRAME: TAX-398|. These lipids may contribute to symbiosis and acid tolerance in that organism. The hydroxylation is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.11.58| (|FRAME: G-55117|) |CITS: [16353552][21205018]|. Other modifications incude methylation of the δ-amino group of ornithine, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.344| (|FRAME: G-55116|) |CITS: [25925947]|, and hydroxylation of the amide-linked fatty acyl moiety and the ornithine moiety, which are catalyzed by hydroxylases encoded by the olsD and olsE genes, respectively |CITS: [21707055][21205018][22958119]|. The exact location of wither of these hydroxylations has not been determined yet.

Summary: General Background, Sphingolipids are ubiquitous components of eukaryotic cells. They are composed of a long-chain base (amino alcohol), an amide linked fatty acyl chain, and a polar head. The predominant long-chain bases in plants are C18 amino alcohols, with sphinganine, 4-hydroxysphinganine, and 4-hydroxy-8-sphingenine being the prevalent long-chain bases. The prevalent long-chain base of many mammalian sphingolipids, sphingosine (4-sphingenine), is found only in trace amounts in plants. The predominant fatty acyl chains in plants are alpha-hydroxy fatty acids, with saturated C22 to C26 hydroxy fatty acyl chains, especially 2-hydroxylignoceric acid, are the most common ones., Ceramide (without a polar head group), glucosylceramide, and derivatives of inositolphosphorylceramide are the predominant plant sphingolipids. Sphingomyelin, which has phosphocholine as the polar head group and is the major phosphosphingolipid in animals, has not been detected in plants. On the other hand, yeast contains exclusively inositolphosphorylceramides., Species- and tissue-specific diversity of the long-chain base and fatty acyl chain exists in plant glucosylceramides. In general, seed glucosylceramides are enriched with dihydroxy long-chain bases and C16 to C20 saturated hydroxy fatty acids. In contrast, leaves are enriched with trihydroxy long-chain bases and very long-chain (C20 to C26) saturated and monoenoic hydroxy fatty acids. Monoenoic hydroxyl fatty acids are predominantly found in glucosylceramides from cold hardy crops and Arabidopsis., It is estimated that sphingolipids account for up to 10% of total lipids in plants. Glucosylceramide is the major sphingolipid. It is a significant lipid component of the plant cell plasma and tonoplast. While our knowledge of sphingolipid functions are mainly learned from studies in mammals and yeast, plant sphingolipids are thought to serve as membrane structural components and signal molecules., About This Pathway, Two mechanisms were shown for ceramide formation via condensation of a fatty acyl group with the amino group of a long chain base. One utilizes acyl-CoAs and is catalyzed by sphinganine N-acyltransferase, the other uses free fatty acids by ceramide synthase. The sphinganine N-acyltransferase route is most likely the major route in plants. The relative activity of sphinganine N-acyltransferase using acyl-CoA of varying chain length from 16 to 24 carbons parallel the distribution , of fatty acyl chains in glucosylceramides from different plant sources |CITS: [Lynch00]|. It suggests that sphinganine N-acyltransferase plays a key role in determining the respective acyl chain composition of naturally occurring plant glucosylceramides., Although hydroxylation of the long chain base can occur with free sphinganine, hydroxylation and desaturation of long chain bases, as well as alpha-hydroxylation of fatty acyl chains, occur primarily after the formation of ceramides.
