Summary: General Background, The bacterial bag-shaped envelope (sacculus) can resist turgor pressures of 2-5 atmpspheres in Gram-negative bacteria, and up to 20 atm in Gram-positive bacteria., This remarkable tensile strength, combined with elasticity, is achieved by the structure of the cell wall's main component, peptidoglycan (also known as "basal structure", "mucopeptide", "glycopeptide", "glycosaminopeptide" and "murein"). Peptidoglycan is found on the outside of the cytoplasmic membrane of almost all eubacteria, and is unique to these organisms., Peptidoglycan can be described as a fisherman's net. The mesh of the net is made of two segments of parallel, rather inextensible glycan threads, held together by two small elastic peptide crosslinks allowing the net to expand or shrink |CITS: [10532377]|., The glycan moiety of the peptidoglycan is remarkably uniform among all bacteria, and is made up of alternating β-1,4-linked N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetyl muramate residues, with an average chain length (in different organisms) of 10 to 65 disaccharide units (although it is about 5000 in |FRAME: TAX-1423|). The peptide moiety is less uniform, as described in |FRAME: PWY-5265|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the biosynthesis of peptidoglycan in Mycobacteria. The Mycobacterial peptidoglycan is similar to that found in |FRAME:TAX-562|, with one main difference: the membrane acceptor portion of the molecule is the unusual |FRAME: CPD-11994|, instead of the much more common |FRAME:CPD-9646|., As in other bacteria, the peptidoglycan monomer precursor |FRAME:UDP-NAcMur-Peptides| is produced in the cytoplasm by six enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-6387|). This molecule is then attached to |FRAME: CPD-11994| by a transferase encoded by |FRAME: G185E-6364|, generating |FRAME:CPD-11997|, also known as lipid I., A second transferase, encoded by |FRAME: G185E-6361|, then adds |FRAME:UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, yielding lipid II, which carries the full monomer unit, |FRAME: CPD-11998|., This final lipid intermediate is transferred by an as yet unknown mechanism through the membrane, and the peptidoglycan monomers are then polymerized on the outside surface by glycosyltransferases, which form the linear glycan chains, and transpeptidases, which catalyze the formation of peptide cross-links |CITS: [11320055]|. , Most of the cross-links in Mycobacteria are between the the carboxyl group of the penultimate |FRAME: D-ALANINE| (residue 4) of one peptide to the amino group at the D-center of |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| (residue 3) of an adjacent peptide of a second glycan chain (as in |FRAME:TAX-562|). The reaction is catalyzed by D-D transpeptidases also known as |FRAME: Penicillin-Binding-Proteins "penicillin-binding proteins"| (PBPs), and involves the cleavage of the D-alanyl-D-alanine bond of the donor peptide, providing the energy to drive the reaction., However, about third of the linkages are between the carboxyl group at the L-center of a |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| of one chain and the amino group at the D-center of the |FRAME: MESO-DIAMINOPIMELATE| of another peptide side chain, resulting in an L,D-cross-link |CITS: [4210702 ]|. In stationary phase bacteria up to 80% of the cross-links were in the L,D form |CITS:[18408028]|. The |FRAME: G185E-4233-MONOMER| has been identified as the product of the |FRAME: G185E-4233| gene |CITS: [18408028]|. The prevalance of L,D cross-links enables the bacteria to resist β-lactam antiobiotics.

General Background, Glucosinolates are 1-thio-β-D-glucosides. They are found prominently in the order Capparales, which include cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, broccoli, and the model plant Arabidopsis. Many glucosinolate-producing plants have typical sharp taste and odor that are caused by their glucosinolates. , The glucosinolates play an important role in plant defense. Upon herbivore attack glucosinolates are hydrolyzed and broken down to toxic compounds in a process that starts with the action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147 "EC 3.2.1.147, myrosinase|. The myrosinases are S-glycosidases that remove the sugar moiety from glucosinolates, leaving unstable thiohydroximate-O-sulfate products that undergo spontaneous hydrolysis to form |FRAME: ISOTHIOCYANATES isothiocyanates|. The resulting isothiocyantaes are bioactive, and have been shown to have antimicrobial and insecticidal activities., In the presence of specific plant proteins, some glucosinolate hydrolysis products are diverted away from isothiocyanate. |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5 "Nitrile-specifier proteins (NSPs, EC 4.8.1.5)"| are known to catalyze the formation of nitriles. |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.6 "Epithiospecifier proteins (ESPs, EC 4.8.1.6)"| are responsible for the formation either nitriles or epithionitriles, depending on the structure of the parent glucosinolate (see |FRAME: PWY-5267|), and |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.7 "thiocyanate-forming proteins (TFPs, EC 4.8.1.7)"| are known to catalyze the formation of thiocyanates |CITS: [17139450]|., In contrast to isothiocyanates, the ecological roles of nitriles and thiocyanates formed by the NSP/ESP/TFP proteins are still unclear. They are thought to be involved in defense responses against insect herbivores rather than against pathogens (reviewed in |CITS: [Burow09]|)., About This Pathway , The production of organic thiocyanate upon glucosinolate hydrolysis is restricted to only a few plant species. Besides, only a few glucosinolates, namely |FRAME: 2-PROPENYL-GLUCOSINOLATE|, |FRAME: GLUCOTROPEOLIN| and |FRAME: CPDQT-281| can be converted to organic thiocyanate |CITS: [912594]|. In |FRAME: TAX-33125|, |FRAME: GLUCOTROPEOLIN| is the major, if not only, glucosinolate found in the above-ground plant organs. Upon tissue damage, it is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: BENZYL-ISOTHIOCYANATE|, |FRAME: CPD-65| and |FRAME: PHENYLACETONITRILE|. The formation of the isothiocyanate from the benzylglucosinolate aglycone is spontaneous, whereas the formation of the thiocyanate and nitrile compounds requires the presence of a dedicated protein, known as |FRAME: G-12435| (|FRAME: EC-4.8.1.7|). The gene encoding the enzyme has been cloned from |FRAME: TAX-33125| and found to share 63-68% amino acid sequence identity with known epithiospecifier proteins (ESPs) |CITS: [17139450]|. , The |FRAME: TAX-33125| TFP has a wide substrate range, and acts on substrate not encountered in its native host. When acting on other substrates in vitro the ebzyme had the activities of |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5| and |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.6|, forming simple nitriles and epithionitriles, respectively |CITS: [17139450]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-17940 Holomycin| is |FRAME: Dithiopyrrolones| antibiotic isolated from multiple genera of bacteria. It was discovered in 1959, the third dithiopyrrolone antibiotic to be discovered following |FRAME: CPD-17938| and |FRAME: CPD-17934| (the latter is a methylated form of holomycin)., |FRAME: CPD-17940 Holomycin| was originally isolated from a strain of |FRAME: TAX-1911| (and named at the time "desmethyl-thiolutin") |CITS: [Ettlinger59]|, and later identifed in the important industrial strain and |FRAME: CPD-9261| producer |FRAME: TAX-1901| |CITS: [468729]|. Production is not limited to actinomycettes, since holomycin has also been been reported from the marine Gram-negative bacteria |FRAME: TAX-265726| |CITS: [21339958]| and fish-gut pathogen |FRAME: TAX-29486| |CITS: [23572522]|. Both |FRAME: CPD-17934| and |FRAME: CPD-17940| display bacteriostatic activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [24542052][12374383]|. They appear to inhibit RNA synthesis and are active against rifamycin-resistant strains |CITS: [4597739][11158751]|., Although |FRAME: CPD-17940| had been known for a long time, its biosynthesis was poorly understood until 2010, after the genome of |FRAME: TAX-1901| became available. Based on the structure of |FRAME: CPD-17940|, it was hypothesized that two cysteine residues serve as its building blocks following activation by |FRAME: Non-ribosomal-peptide-synthetases| (NRPS). A search for cysteine-specific NRPSs uncovered the gene cluster encoding holomycin biosynthesis |CITS: [21041678]|., The gene cluster contains a single module NRPS (|FRAME: G-44108|) with a condensation/cyclization (Cy) domain, an adenylation (A) domain predicted to activate cysteine, and a thiolation (T) domain. In addition, four flavin-dependent oxidoreductases (|FRAME: G-44109|, |FRAME: G-44107|, |FRAME: G-44112| and |FRAME: G-44113|), an acyl transferase (|FRAME: G-44030|), and a standalone thioesterase (|FRAME: G-44111|) were also found in the gene cluster. While some of the gene functions illustrated in this pathway have been supported biochemically, others were assigned based on the sequence of the encoded enzymes., Expression of the whole holomycin cluster in |FRAME: TAX-1888| and |FRAME: TAX-1902| resulted in production of holomycin by the recombinant host |CITS: [Huang11][23147422]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13619 Pentalenolactone| is a widely occurring sesquiterpenoid antibiotic produced by some |FRAME: TAX-1883| strains. |FRAME: CPD-13619 Pentalenolactone| is a specific irreversible inhibitor of the glycolytic enzyme NAD-dependent glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH, |FRAME: GAPOXNPHOSPHN-RXN "EC 1.2.1.12"|) |CITS:[361434][7034785][3736593]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6915|)., The soli bacterium |FRAME:TAX-33903| does not produce |FRAME: CPD-13619|, but possesses a biosynthetic gene cluster that is very similar to those found in |FRAME: CPD-13619|-producing organisms. In addition, the organism produces the shunt metabolite |FRAME: CPDMETA-13643|. By cloning the genes from the cluster and expressing them in |FRAME:TAX-562|, it was found that the organism diverts from the |FRAME: CPD-13619|-biosynthetic pathway at |FRAME: CPD-13625| and continues with a different branch leading to production of |FRAME: CPDMETA-13642| |CITS: [19485417]|. , About This Pathway, The committed step in the biosynthesis of pentalenolactone and its derivatives is the cyclization of |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| to the triquinane sesquiterpene |FRAME: CPD-1763|, a reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16846| |CITS: [Cane84]|., Large (13 kb) biosynthetic gene clusters that were sequenced from several of the |FRAME: CPD-13619|-producing organisms were shown to encode all of the enzymes that are required for synthesis. The related cluster in |FRAME: TAX-33903| encodes all the enzymes required for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPDMETA-13642| |CITS: [19485417]|., The pathways are identical up to the point of |FRAME: CPD-13625|. In pentalenolactone-producing organisms a dedicated monooxygenase converts this intermediate to |FRAME: CPD-13621|. However, the orthologous enzyme from |FRAME:TAX-33903|, encoded by |FRAME: GMETA-14676|, produces |FRAME: CPD-13623|. The next enzyme in the pathway, encoded by |FRAME: GMETA-14677|, catalyzes the conversion of this intermediate to |FRAME: CPD-13638| and |FRAME: CPD-13624|. The latter is unstable, and seems to spontaneously rearrange to |FRAME: CPDMETA-13642| |CITS: [21250661]|.

Summary: General Background, All polyketide synthases, fatty-acid synthases and non-ribosomal peptide synthases require post-translational activation of their constituent apo acyl-carrier-protein (ACP) domains to become catalytically active. The inactive apo-proteins are converted into their active holo-forms by transfer of the |FRAME: PANTETHEINE-P| moiety of |FRAME: CO-A| to the side chain hydroxy group of a conserved serine residue in each ACP domain., About this Pathway, The mammalian cytosolic |FRAME: HS14278-MONOMER| is involved in the post-translational modification of several apoproteins, including the acyl carrier protein domains of both cytosolic and mitochondrial fatty acid synthases, |FRAME: CPLX66-394|, |FRAME: CPLX66-445| and |FRAME: CPLX66-446| |CITS: [18022563]|. In yeast, three different enzymes catalyze the activation of different ACP proteins.

Names: ketolysis // ketone body metabolism // ketone body degradation
Summary: Ketone bodies are carbonyl compounds produced as water-soluble byproducts when fatty acids are broken down for energy in the liver (ketogenesis). There are only three endogenous ketone bodies: |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE|, |FRAME: CPD-335|, and |FRAME: ACETONE|. Ketone bodies are mostly synthesized in liver mitochondria, but are exported from hepatocytes for circulation to metabolizing tissues. Heart, skeletal muscle under exertion, and brain under starvation conditions use ketone bodies as a major energy source |CITS: [14769483]|., This pathway describes the conversion of the ketone bodies to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, which feeds into the TCA cycle. Ketone bodies are more efficient energy storage molecules than glucose, and ketone body degradation results in lower production of reactive oxygen species and less mitochondrial stress |CITS: [15048898]|. , Varous tissues internalize ketone bodies using a number of different monocarboxylate transporters from two distinct families. The SLC16 monocarboxylate family of transporters (MCT1-14) comprises twelve transmembrane domain containing proteins that transport lactate, pyruvate and ketone bodies by a proton-coupled mechanism |CITS: [18668440]|. |FRAME: HS08049| (MCT1) is present in non-neuronal cells including liver, heart, endothelial cells of cerebral microvasculature and astrocytes. MCT2 is expressed in heart and is the predominant monocarboxylate transporter in neurons. MCT4 appears to be specific for astrocytes |CITS: [15953344]|. The second family includes the sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter (SMCT1, SLC5A8), which is specifically expressed in neurons and transports lactate and ketone bodies |CITS: [16805814]|. , Three processes control ketolysis: the process of adipocyte lipolysis is controlled by |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.79| (|FRAME: HS01328|); the entry of fatty acids into mitochondria is controlled by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.21| (|FRAME: HS03286|), which is inhibited by |FRAME: MALONYL-COA malonyl-CoA|; and the rate-limiting enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.3.3.10| (|FRAME: HS03634|) is controlled at the transcriptional and post-translational levels |CITS: [14769483]|., There is some evidence that increased utilizaton of ketone bodies as fuel may reduce oxidative stress and loss of neurons in animal models of neurodegenerative disorders including Parkinson's diseases and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). In MPTP (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine) treated mice exhibiting dopaminergic neuron loss and movement disorders, infusion of |FRAME: CPD-335 (R)-3-hydroxybutanoate| ameliorated these effects by improving mitochondrial respiration and ATP production |CITS: [12975474]|. Mice transgencially altered to develop ALS (SOD1-G93A) treated with |FRAME: CPD-335 (R)-3-hydroxybutanoate| as well as a ketogenic diet, exhibited less motor neuron cell loss and resistance to rotenone induced neurotoxicity |CITS: [16584562]|. Both caloric restriction and a high-fat, low carbohydrates (ketogenic) diet are being investigated as means to reduce oxidative damage to neurons |CITS: [18845187]|.

Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, The key enzyme in the salvage of the pyrimidine nucleobase |FRAME: URACIL| is (|FRAME: EC-2.4.2.9 "uracil phosphoribosyltransferase (EC 2.4.2.9)"| (UPRT), which transfers a phosphoribosyl group from |FRAME: PRPP| (PRPP) to uracil, generating |FRAME: UMP| in a single step. The enzyme is found in archaea, bacteria, lower eukaryotes and plants |CITS: [16660311][216696][2189783][8856065][11773618][14658380]|. This pathway was shown to be the major route for uracil salvage in potato tubers |CITS: [12244448]|., Mammals lack the enzyme, and thereby are unable to perform the one-step salvage of uracil |CITS: [15685165]| and are limited to recycling pyrimidine nucleosides via uridine kinases (see |FRAME: PWY-7193|)., Some archaea, bacteria and lower eukaryotes that possess the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7932| (|FRAME: EC-3.5.4.1 "EC 3.5.4.1"|) are also able to salvage exogenously supplied |FRAME: CYTOSINE| by converting it to |FRAME: URACIL| (see |FRAME: PWY-7194|)., Once the nucleobases are converted to |FRAME: UMP|, it can be phosphorylated to form the RNA building blocks |FRAME: UTP| and |FRAME: CTP| by the enzymes that participate in the de novo biosynthetic pathway, as described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7176|.

General Background, |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine "N-acetyl-D-galactosamine"| (GalNAc, Aga) and |FRAME: GALACTOSAMINE| (GalN, Gam) are amino sugars that are found in cellular structures of both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. For example GalNAc is a component of the major cell surface carbohydrates of |FRAME: TAX-197| |CITS: [15509570]|, and GalN is a component of the lipopolysaccharide of |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [21999536]|. GalNAc is found in the carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes |CITS: [18694827]|. It is also found in eukaryotic glycosaminoglycans (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-6572|, |FRAME: PWY-6573| and |FRAME: PWY-6576|)., Some proteobacteria such as |FRAME: TAX-562| B and C strains and |FRAME:TAX-562| EC3132 can utilize GalNAc or GalN as carbon and nitrogen sources |CITS: [10931310]|. Species of |FRAME: TAX-22| can grow on GalNAc as sole carbon and energy source |CITS: [20836887]|. Utilization is controlled by the AgaR regulon. Other proteobacteria, such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, strains of |FRAME: TAX-573| and |FRAME: TAX-571|, and |FRAME: TAX-99287| cannot utilize these compounds |CITS: [10931310][20836887][22711537]|., About This Pathway, The catabolic pathways of |FRAME: N-acetyl-D-galactosamine "N-acetyl-D-galactosamine"| and |FRAME: GALACTOSAMINE| in |FRAME: TAX-562| were proposed from bioinformatic analysis of the aga/gam regulon in |FRAME: TAX-83333| and later from studies using |FRAME: TAX-498388|, since it was found that the K-12 strain has a 2.3 Kb deletion leading to the loss and truncation of genes that are needed for the utilization of these substrates |CITS: [10931310]|., Bioinformatic analyses have also shown that different proteobacteria utilize different phosphorylation routes to produce |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| or |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE|, while some of the downstream reactions are shared |CITS: [22711537][20836887]|. In some organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-22| species GalNAc enters the cell via a predicted outer membrane porin (OMP) and a predicted inner membrane permease encoded by agaP and is then phosphorylated by the product of agaK (see |FRAME: PWY-7077|). In contrast, in GalNAc and GalN utilizing |FRAME:TAX-562| strains, two specific PTS systems are respectively used to transport these compounds into the cell with concomitant phosphorylation, as described in this pathway |CITS: [22711537][23634833]|., In |FRAME: TAX-22| species, after phosphorylation of GalNAc by the novel kinase product of agaK, |FRAME: N-ACETYL-D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| is deacetylated to |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| by the novel deacetylase AgaA-II which is non-orthologous to |FRAME:TAX-562| AgaA. The deaminase/isomerase product of AgaS then converts |FRAME: D-GALACTOSAMINE-6-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: L-TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE|. The kinase product of agaZ is predicted to convert |FRAME: L-TAGATOSE-6-PHOSPHATE| to |FRAME: TAGATOSE-1-6-DIPHOSPHATE|. The latter compound was proposed to be cleaved to glycolytic intermediates by the non-committed class II fructose-bisphosphate aldolase present in |FRAME: TAX-22| species |CITS: [22711537]|., Conserved gene agaS was found in all proteobacterial genomes examined by |CITS: [22711537]|. In the |FRAME:TAX-562| C strain |FRAME: TAX-481805| the function of gene agaS was experimentally validated by mutant analysis to be the main D-galactosamine-6-phosphate isomerase in the the GalNAc utilization pathway in that organism |CITS: [22711537]|.

General Background, |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE "A phosphatidylcholine"| is |FRAME: Phosphoglycerides| composed of a |FRAME: GLYCEROL| backbone esterified to |FRAME: PHOSPHORYL-CHOLINE| and two |FRAME: Fatty-Acids "fatty acids"|. Phosphatidylcholine is a major component of eukaryotic cell membranes, in which it accounts for 40-60% of total phospholipids. It is also found in an estimated 10-15% of bacterial taxa, and especially in bacterial symbionts and pathogens of eukaryotes., Phosphatidylcholine is often referred to by the name lecithin, obtained from ancient Greek for egg yolk (lekithos), from which it was originally isolated. There are two variations of the molecular structure, since either an end carbon or a middle carbon of the glycerol can be attached to the phosphocholine., The phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic pathways vary among different organisms, and many variants have been described (see |FRAME: PhosphatidylcholineBiosynthesis|). At least four alternative routes have been reported from plants, and additional routes were reported from animals, yeast and bacteria., About This Pathway, The pathway depicted here involves bacterial |FRAME: ACYL-COA "acyl-CoA"|-dependent acyltransferases that catalyze the two-step acylation of |FRAME: L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| |CITS: [24329598]|., Although the most common membrane lipids found in bacteria are |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE|, |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE|, and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN|, some bacteria contain typical eukaryotic phospholipids such as |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|. The presence of such phospholipids in these bacteria often correlates with a symbiotic or pathogenic lifestyle. This pathway was discovered in the plant pathogen |FRAME: TAX-340| and is described here |CITS: [24329598]|., In |FRAME: TAX-340| mutant and radiotracer studies have excluded the two predominant bacterial pathways for production of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| (see 5 and 6 above). Feeding experiments suggested a novel yeast-like pathway for synthesis of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| involving the addition of two acyl chains to |FRAME: L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE|. The organism was able to produce |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| in the presence of |FRAME: 2-Lysophosphatidylcholines| or |FRAME: L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE| |CITS: [24329598]|., Heterologous expression studies identified two acyltransferases in |FRAME: TAX-340| encoded by genes |FRAME: G-18039| and |FRAME: G-18040| that catalyze the acylation of a |FRAME: 2-Lysophosphatidylcholines| to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE|. Both acylations were shown to be |FRAME: ACYL-COA "acyl-CoA"|-dependent. The identity of the first enzyme in the pathway remains to be determined. The data suggest the existence of |FRAME: L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE|-dependent biosynthesis of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYLCHOLINE| in bacteria |CITS: [24329598]|.

Names: formate to dimethyl sulfoxide electron transfer
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, In the |FRAME: TAX-562| respiratory chain formed by formate dehydrogenase and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) reductase the transfer of electrons from formate to DMSO is coupled to the generation of a proton-motive force across, the cytoplasmic membrane., Two electrons are transferred from the formate oxidation site to the DMSO reduction site by a menaquinone pool. Neither formate dehydrogenase nor DMSO reductase catalyse vectorial proton translocation however, the reduction of DMSO and many other amine-N-oxides and methyl-sulfoxides, including trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), contributes two protons to the proton-motive force. , Two of |FRAME:TAX-562|'s formate dehydrogenases, N and O, catalyse the oxidation of formate. Expression of formate dehydrogenase N (Fdh-N) is induced by anaerobiosis and the presence of nitrate |CITS: [12923080], [2168848]| whereas aerobic conditions, and to a lesser extent nitrate under anaerobic conditions, induce expression of formate dehydrogenase O (Fdh-O) |CITS: [8522521]|. , DMSO reductase is functionally similar to the TMAO reductases (see |FRAME: G7022-MONOMER|), but genetically distinct |CITS: [2832366]|. This enzyme functions under anaerobic conditions and in the absence of nitrate (a preferred electron acceptor) |CITS: [2544558]|. DMSO is the preferred substrate for this enzyme |CITS: [3280546]|.

Summary: Please note: to see this pathway properly, please click the "More Detail" button until the compound structures and enzyme names show up., The various folate coenzymes are essential cofactors that facilitate the transfer of one-carbon units from donor molecules into important biosynthetic pathways leading to methionine, purine, and pyrimidine biosynthesis. They also mediate the interconversion of serine and glycine (|FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|), and play a role in histidine catabolism |CITS: [11001804]|. , Tetrahydrofolate (tetrahydropteroylmonoglutamate, H4PteGlu1, THF), is merely the parent structure of this large family of coenzymes. The folate coenzymes differ in the oxidation state of the pteridine ring, the character of the one-carbon substituent at the N5 and N10 positions, and the number of glutamic acid moieties conjugated one to another via a series of γ-glutamyl links to form an oligo-γ-glutamyl tail (see the pathway, |FRAME: PWY-2161B| for more information on this subject)., There are numerous enzymes that convert the folates from one form to another, and the important ones are included in this pathway., Important folate coenzymes include the mono- and polyglutamylated forms of |FRAME: THF-GLU-N "tetrahydrofolate"| (H4PteGlun), |FRAME: N5-Formyl-THF-Glu-N "N5-formyl tetrahydrofolate"| (5-formyl-H4PteGlun), |FRAME: FORMYL-THF-GLU-N "N10-formyl tetrahydrofolate"| (10-formyl-H4PteGlun), |FRAME: 5-10-METHENYL-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methenyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (5,10-methenyl-H4PteGlun), |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N "5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate"| (5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun), and |FRAME: 5-METHYL-THF-GLU-N "5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate"| (5-methyl-H4PteGlun)., Folate cofactors are particularly important in the methylotrophs - the bacteria that can utilize C1 (single carbon)compounds as their sole carbon and energy source. In the methylotroph |FRAME: TAX-272630|, formaldehyde that enters the cytoplasm condenses with one of the two pterin cofactors, |FRAME: THF-GLU-N "tetrahydrofolate"| or |FRAME:THMPT| (H4MPT), and forms the respective methylene derivative (see the pathway |FRAME: PWY-1722|). , The reaction of formaledehyde with THF is spontaneous |CITS: [5954363][14645276]|, and produces 5,10-methylene-THF, which can be metabolized in two ways: it can enter the serine cycle (see |FRAME: PWY-1622|), where the carbon is used for biosysnthesis, or it may be oxidized via 5,10-methenyl-THF to 10-formyl-THF. 10-formyl-THF can be eventually converted back to THF, releasing formate which is oxidized to CO2 (see |FRAME: PWY-1881|), |CITS: [11889483][10215859][12123819]|. This route is completely reversible, and can flow in both directions; as described above it catalyzes the oxidation of formaldehyde to formate. However, in the other direction, it catalyzes the conversion of formate (which accumulates through the pathway |FRAME: PWY-1723|) to methylene-tetrahydrofolate, which feeds the serine cycle, a formaldehyde assimilation cycle (|FRAME: PWY-1622|)., Vertebrates are not able to synthesize folates, and are completely dependent on folates in their diet. Dietary folates exist mainly as poly and mono-glutamylated 5-methyl-THF and formyl-THF |CITS: [405403]|. Polyglutamyl folates in food are hydrolyzed to folylmonoglutamates by |FRAME: EC-3.4.19.9|), and metabolized within the enterocyte into 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1., This monoglutamyl folate is the main form of the vitamin in the plasma |CITS: [13906633][2736319]|, and is transported to peripheral tissues. In the tissues it is demethylated by vitamin B12-dependent |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13|, to monoglutamyl tetrahydrofolate (H4PteGlu1). This H4PteGlu1 form is the preferred substrate of |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.17|, which conjugates glutamate moieties to generate oligo-γ-glutamyl H4PteGlu., The predominant product of this reaction is the hexaglutamyl-HPteGlu form |CITS: [3828323]|., The conversion of 5- methyl-H44PteGlu1 into H44PteGlu1 by vitamin B12- dependent methionine synthase is thus responsible for the conversion of extracellular 5-methyl-H4PteGlu1 from dietary sources into the form that can be used in the biosynthetic pathways |CITS: [3266075]|., In erythrocites folate is largely present in the forms of 5- methyl-H44PteGlun and formyl-H44PteGlun, mostly containing five or six glutamate residues |CITS: [10833329][1247496]|., However, the active forms of folate required for nucleotide synthesis are 10-formyl-H4PteGlun and 5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun., 5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun is also required by |FRAME: EC-1.5.1.53|, in the biosynthesis of methionine. Thus, 5,10-methylene-H4PteGlun is at the branch point of three important pathways |CITS: [3266075]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN Cardiolipin| is an anionic membrane phospholipid. Along with |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol|, the anionic lipids are important for the biogenesis and function of membranes. Cardiolipin is present in the plasma membrane of bacteria and in the mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes., A main difference exists between bacterial and eukaryotic cardiolipin biosynthesis; In bacteria cardiolipin is formed by the condensation of two molecules of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol|, while in eukaryotes it is formed from one molecule of |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL CDP-diacylglycerol|  and one molecule of |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol|.

|FRAME: CPD-9936 Magnoflorine| is an aporphine-type of isoquinoline alkaloid. It was shown to have anti-oxidant activity against the oxidation of low density lipoprotein (LDL) |CITS: [17973202]|. Our knowledge of magnoflorine biosynthesis came mainly from a study in |FRAME: TAX-3442| |CITS: [18230623]|. Magnoflorine is derived from |FRAME: S-RETICULINE| via an intramolecular C-C phenol-coupling reaction, catalyzed by a novel cytochrome P450, CYP80G2. This C-C phenol-coupling reaction is analogous to the conversion of (R)-reticuline to salutaridine in |FRAME: PWY-5270|. In cultured |FRAME: TAX-3442| cells, berberine is a major alkaloid, and magnoflorine is produced at moderate level.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on. Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Much later an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate, which proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-10477|, has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|. Initial analysis of sequenced genomes suggested that the pathway might be present in a variety of organisms |CITS: [19557031]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6262|). Further analysis revealed that the newly discovered pathway may not be identical among all of these organisms. It appears that in some organisms |FRAME: CPD-13324| is converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-10484| (see |FRAME: PWY-7371|), while in others this transformation occurrs via |FRAME: CPD-10477| (as shown in this pathway)., In both pathways |FRAME: CHORISMATE| is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-16467| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-16550| (|FRAME: G-11332|), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-13324| in a complex reaction catalyzed by a radical Ado-Met enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-17947| |CITS: [24083939]|., In the pathway shown here |FRAME: CPD-13324| is deaminated by 6-aminodeoxyfutalosine amidohydrolase (|FRAME: G-17733|) to form |FRAME: CPD-10477|, which is then hydrolyzed by the |FRAME: G-10895| gene product to form |FRAME: CPD-10484|. The later part of the pathway is identical in both pathway variants. The last intermediate shown here is |FRAME: CPD-11420|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD0-920 Indolmycin| is an antibacterial drug produced by both terrestrial and marine bacteria that exhibits potent antibacterial activity against human pathogens such as |FRAME: TAX-210| |CITS: [11502514]| and mupirocin-, methicillin-resistant |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [15243028]|. Indolmycin, discovered in 1960 |CITS: [14421508]|, is a structural analog of |FRAME: TRP| and competitively inhibits the bacterial |FRAME: EC-6.1.1.2| |CITS: [786633]|. Organisms that produce indolmycin are resistant to it due to the presence of a resistant tryptophan--tRNA ligase |CITS: [19546369]|., Indolmycin has not been tested in humans, although it has been proposed to be tested as a topical treatment for staphylococcal infections., The indolmycin structure contains an oxazolinone ring in its core, making it of interest to synthetic chemists, and over the years several total synthetic routes have been reported |CITS: [5729561][Takeda80][Dirlam86][Akita90][Witty96][Shue96][11767081][Sutou08]|., Early studies of the indolmycin biosynthetic pathway established that |FRAME: TRP|, |FRAME: ARG|, and |FRAME: MET| are precursors and that |FRAME: CPD-398| and |FRAME: CPD-18934| are pathway intermediates |CITS: [Hornemann69][5095271][Zee75]|. Additional work has demonstrated the activity of two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.99|, and |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.47|, in cell-free extracts of |FRAME: TAX-1911| |CITS: [809439]|., A siginificant progress in the understanding of the pathway arrived in 2015. A gene cluster encoding indolmycin biosynthesis was identified in |FRAME: TAX-1911| based on the inclusion of a gene encoding tryptophan--tRNA ligase, and sequenced |CITS: [25730866]|., Indolmycin is synthesized from two precursors, |FRAME: CPD-18935| and |FRAME: CPD-18934|, which are derived from |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: TRP|, respectively. The enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-44481| gene catalyzes amide bond formation between these two precursors, followed by subsequent cyclization to form the oxazolinone ring. The cyclization reaction can fomr two different products - either |FRAME: CPD-18940|, or a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-18933| and |FRAME: CPD-18938|. Both |FRAME: CPD-18940| and |FRAME: CPD-18933| contain the characteristic oxazolinone heterocycle. The presence of the "gatekeeper" multitasking protein |FRAME: G-44482 Ind6| ensures that |FRAME: CPD-18933| is produced as the dominant product. Interestingly, Ind6 also has a chaperone-like activity earlier in the pathway, forming a complex with Ind5, which is involved in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-18935|. Finally, a methyltransferase encoded by |FRAME: G-44480| forms |FRAME: CPD0-920| |CITS: [25730866]|.

Summary: General Background, Plants belonging to the |FRAME: TAX-40553| family have been valued both for flavor and medicinal purposes throughout the world., The domestic Alliums (such as onion, garlic, chives and leek) contain high concentrations of organic sulfur compounds especially in their bulbs and leaves. These compounds consist mostly of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| such as |FRAME: CPD-9269|, |FRAME: CPD-9307|, and |FRAME: CPD-9277|, as well as γ-glutamyl peptides (together these compounds make up over 70% of the total sulfur in garlic |CITS: [ Lawson96]|)., These compounds, which are found in the cytoplasm, are produced constitutively. The S-alkyl cysteine S-oxides are substrates for the alliinase enzymes (|FRAME: EC-4.4.1.4|), which convert them to |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|. However, the enzymes are kept in vacuoles, and are thus sequestered from their substrates |CITS: [Lancaster81][19463015]|. Only when the tissue is injured, the alliinase enzymes are released from the vaculoes and interact with their substrates, producing |FRAME: Alkyl-Sulfenates S-alkylsulfenates|., |CITS: [16010345]|. Once formed, S-alkylsulfenates are very active and tend to condense spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-17425 thiosulfinates| |CITS: [21905712]|. Depending on the Allium species, and under differing conditions, the thiosulfinates can decompose to form additional sulfur constituents including diallyl, methyl allyl, and diethyl mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, and hexasulfides, vinyldithiins, and (E)- and (Z)-ajoene |CITS: [16010345]|., In some species, dedicated enzymes commonly known as "lachrymatory-factor synthases" act on the S-alkylsulfenates rapidly, before they condense, producing volatile compounds that cause the eyes of animals to tear (lachrymatory factors) - a further defense mechanism against herbivory., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-9280 Ethiin| is a minor |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxide"| found in most members of the domesticated |FRAME: TAX-40553|. Its presence has been suggested already in 1968, although not verified at the time |CITS: [5715558]|. In 1997 it was shown that feeding |FRAME: CPD-10467| to onion root cultures resulted in production of |FRAME: CPD-9280| |CITS: [Prince97]|. The final proof was provided by utilization of a new sensitive method for detection of |FRAME: S-Alkyl-L-Cysteine-S-Oxides "S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides"| |CITS: [10691652][16010345]|. Since |FRAME: CPD-9280| accounts for less than 4% of the total S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides, it probably does not contribute significantly to the aroma formation of common Allium species |CITS: [10691652]|., The path leading to |FRAME: CPD-9280| biosynthesis is still speculative. Two possible routes that may coexist have been suggested - one from serine and allyl thiol (shown here), and the other from γ glutamyl peptides |CITS: [15652575][16010345]|., Like other S-alkyl-L-cysteine S-oxides, |FRAME: CPD-9280| is a substrate for the allinase enzyme |CITS: [9799098]|. Sequestration of the enzyme and substrate to the vacuoles and cell cytoplasm, respectively, prevents interaction in undisturbed tissue. However, upon tissue injury the enzyme and substrate come into contact and |FRAME: CPD-9280| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-9311|, which condenses spontaneously with other S-alkylsulfenates to form thiosulfinate compounds |CITS: [16010345]|.

Summary: General Background, Phenylphenalenones are polycyclic aromatic diarylheptanoids. Several specific compounds within this class have been shown to be involved in plant defense, particularly in the |FRAME: TAX-54924| and |FRAME: TAX-4637| families of species, |CITS: [16496097]|. In addition, |FRAME: CPD-12201| and |FRAME: CPD-12209|, two compounds produced by this pathway, were recently shown to have leishmanicidal activity against human protozoal parasites from the genus Leishmania that cause a diseases known as leishmaniasis that can affect more than 12 million people annually |CITS: [15105102]|., About This Pathway, Radiotracer experiments have been performed to elucidate the compounds and reactions that give rise to phenylphenalenones |CITS: [Holscher95][11129580][HOLSCHER96][BAZAN78]| and have shown that a diarylheptanoid is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of these secondary metabolites. The specific details of many steps in the pathway have not been firmly established, but there is strong support for the idea that the pathway is derived from phenylpropanoid biosynthesis |CITS: [16496097]|. The putative pathway depicted in this diagram is also based on evidence from the characterization of a |FRAME: MONOMER-15420| from |FRAME: TAX-95970| that likely catalyzes one or more of the first few steps required for the formation of the diarylheptanoid intermediate. There is stronger experimental support for the assignment of PKS1 to the first reaction and additional work will be required to determine whether it can also catalyze the second condensation reaction or whether another enzyme performs this function |CITS: [16496097]|. , The last few steps in the pathway are also hypothetical and more than one set of reactions have been proposed immediately upstream of anigorufone production. The steps shown in the diagram appear to be more likely based on a biomimetic synthesis that involves an interamolecular Diels-Alder reaction |CITS: [BAZAN78]|, but another set of hypothetical reactions (|FRAME: RXN-11249 "(1)"| and |FRAME: RXN-11250 "(2)"|) remains a formal possibility |CITS: [10703053]|.

General Background, |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is produced in small amounts during glycolysis (via |FRAME:DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE|), fatty acid metabolism (via |FRAME:ACETONE|), and protein metabolism (via |FRAME:AMINO-ACETONE|). |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL "Methylglyoxal"| is highly toxic, most likely as a result of its interaction with protein side chains (see |CITS: [10597025]| for a review). There are several pathways for the detoxification of methylglyoxal, based on different enzymes that are able to convert methylglyoxal to less toxic compounds. These enzymes include glyoxalase enzymes, methylglyoxal reductases, aldose reductases, aldehyde reductases and methylglyoxal dehydrogenases., About This Pathway, The glyoxalase system is probably the most common pathway that catalyzes the conversion of methylglyoxal to a less toxic product. In this pathway, |FRAME:METHYL-GLYOXAL| is converted to |FRAME:D-LACTATE|.., The glyoxalase system is probably the most common pathway that catalyzes the conversion of methylglyoxal to a less toxic product. In this pathway, |FRAME:METHYL-GLYOXAL| is converted to |FRAME:D-LACTATE|., In many organisms this coversion occurs via the intermediate |FRAME:S-LACTOYL-GLUTATHIONE| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.4.1.5|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.2.6|, known as glyoxalase I an II, respectively. However, a different version of the enzymes, which depends on |FRAME: CPD8J2-3| rather than |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE|, has been discoevered in organisms that produce |FRAME: CPD8J2-3| such as |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [24330391]|., The first enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU38370| gene, isomerizes the hemithioacetal that is formed non-enzymatically from |FRAME: METHYL-GLYOXAL| and |FRAME:CPD8J2-3| to |FRAME:CPD8J2-29|. The second enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: BSU32660| gene, hydrolyzes the thioester to |FRAME:D-LACTATE|, regenerating bacillithiol in the process., Production of the intermediate |FRAME: CPD8J2-29| leads to activation of the KhtSTU K+ efflux pump, resulting in cytoplasmic acidification. This acidification is both necessary and sufficient for maximal protection from methylglyoxal |CITS: [ 24330391]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Strigolactones Strigolactones| are plant hormones that stimulate the branching and growth of symbiotic arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, but inhibit plant shoot branching. They promote the probability of establishment of a symbiotic association between the plant and the fungi., The first strigolactone (|FRAME: CPD-14655|) was described from |FRAME: TAX-3635 "Gossypium hirsutum (cotton)"| infected by the root parasitic weeds |FRAME: TAX-4169| (witchweed) (hence the name). It has been shown that the seeds of the parasites germinated only if they were exposed to stimulant molecules present in the root exudate of the host. Although the nature of strigol was not understood at the time, it was observed that it was active at hormonal levels |CITS: [17780042]|., Discovery of additional strigolactones from other plants followed, such as |FRAME: CPD-14659| from |FRAME: TAX-4558| |CITS: [Hauck92]|, |FRAME: CPD-14660| from |FRAME: TAX-3917| |CITS: [Mueler92]| and |FRAME: CPD-14657| from |FRAME: TAX-57577| (red clover) |CITS: [Yokota98]|., The real purpose of strigolactones, which was understood 40 years after the discovery of strigol, is to promote the formation of symbiotic associations known as arbuscular mycorrhiza, which consist of close interaction between the plants roots and |FRAME: TAX-214504| fungi |CITS: [15944706][16574693]|. Arbuscular mycorrhiza, which are found in more than 80% of higher plant species, are one of the most ancient symbioses of land plants. The fungi acquire and deliver nutrients to the plants, which in return provide the fungi with carbohydrates produced by photosynthesis |CITS: [15944687]|., The lactones induce extensive hyphal branching in germinating spores of the fungi, which increases the chance of contact with the root and subsequently infecting it. The branching phenomenon has been known for more than 30 years before the identity of the chemical signal that promotes it has been traced to strigolactone |CITS: [Mosse73]|., Since strigolactones are very labile and active at concentrations as low as picomolar, they are active only in close proximity to potential host roots, ensuring successful interaction between the fungi and the roots., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14651| is a central intermediate in the biosynthesis of most strigolactones., Although the involvement of several dioxygenases in the pathway has been found earlier, full understanding of the early steps in the pathway leading to strigolactones biosynthesis was obtained only in 2012 |CITS: [22422982]|. The first committed step is catalyzed by a |FRAME: MONOMER-17611|, which converts the all-trans version of β-carotene to |FRAME: CPD-14646|. A dioxygenase, encoded by the |FRAME: AT2G44990| gene, cleaves this molecule between the 10' and 9' positions, producing |FRAME: CPD-14647| (and releasing |FRAME: CPD-7204|)., The key enzyme of the pathway, encoded by the |FRAME: AT4G32810| gene, catalyzes a complex reaction that involves the incorporation of two oxygen molecules and complete rearrangement, resulting in |FRAME: CPD-14649|, a precursor of strigolactones that already contains some of the important structural features |CITS: [22422982]|., In the last step of this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-14649| is converted into |FRAME: CPD-14651| by cytochrome P450 711A1 (known as MAX1 in Arabidopsis), which catalyzes three sucessive oxidations, first introducing a hydroxyl at position 19, then converting it to an oxo group and eventually to a carboxylate |CITS: [25425668]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-23962 Allopregnanolone| is a neuroactive steroid which is a steroid that is able to regulate neural functions. It is derived from |FRAME: PROGESTERONE| and is synthesized within the nervous tissue |CITS: [24121112]| ., Contrary to |FRAME: PROGESTERONE| and its first metabolite dihydroprogesterone (|FRAME: CPD-293|), |FRAME: CPD-23962| is able to interact with GABA-A receptor and not with the classical progesterone receptor |CITS: [8883217]|., About This Pathway, This pathway consists in a two step reduction of |FRAME: PROGESTERONE|. In the first step |FRAME: PROGESTERONE| is reduced to its first metabolite dihydroprogesterone by the enzyme 5α-reductase. The second step, in which dihydroprogesterone is reduced to |FRAME: CPD-23962|, is catalyzed by enzymes showing a 3α-hydroxysteroid oxidoreductase activity. In humans there are four isoforms: |FRAME: HS10741|, |FRAME: HS07754|, |FRAME: HS03054|, |FRAME: HS10739|. These isoforms display broad specificity for steroid substrates and hence their physiological role in steroid metabolism is influenced by their tissue distribution |CITS: [10998348]|. |FRAME: HS07754| is the most implicated in |FRAME: CPD-23962| formation |CITS: [12943710]|., The back-oxidation of |FRAME: CPD-23962| to |FRAME: CPD-293| is catalyzed by a NAD-dependent 3α-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase |FRAME: HS01113| |CITS: [11294878]|.

Significantly more antibacterial than antifungal antibiotics have been identified which can be used in efficacious therapeutic treatments. For this reason the elucidation of echinocandins as agents attacking fungal cell walls has been a breakthrough in the field of antifungal chemotherapy |CITS:[17047411] [19724014]|. Echinocandins represent a family of fungal cyclic lipo-hexapeptides characterized by their fungicidal and fungistatic properties against ascomycetes of the genera Candida and Aspergillus, respectively |CITS:[25156669]|. In the face of increasing invasive fungal infections in intensive care units (IUC) |CITS:[19952319]| echinocandins have been successfully used in treatments against invasive candidiasis |CITS:[22412055]|. , The application of echinocandins for human treatments was somewhat hindered by their hemolytic properties which led to the development of semisynthetic derivatives of |FRAME:CPD-17711| (ECB) and close relatives such as |FRAME:CPD-17738| |CITS:[23688303]|. However, the preliminary requirement for the substitution of the |FRAME:LINOLEIC_ACID| side chain, which had been shown to play a role in the toxicity of |FRAME:CPD-17711| |CITS:[7650681]|, was to be able to produce |FRAME:CPD-17775| |CITS:[3063167] [Cockshott01]| which then can be reacylated to produce semisynthetic derivatives such as |FRAME:CPD-17734| |CITS:[6389460] [2708131]| and |FRAME:CPD-17735| |CITS:[10639364] [17266452]| exhibiting significantly reduced hemolysis while retaining the bioactivity of the original compounds., Echinocandin B deacylase activity had been observed in whole cells of the gram-positive bacterium Actinoplanes utahensis |CITS:[2708131]|. Purification of the native and recombinant expressed enzyme enabled to determine catalytic and physico-chemical properties which revealed a rather broad substrate specificity not only for |FRAME:CPD-17711| (see |FRAME:PWY-7650|) but also for other 6-membered and more complex cyclic peptides |CITS:[Kreuzman00]|. The echinocandin B decaylase from Actinoplanes utahensis also cleaved various semisynthetic ECB derivatives, bacterial lipo-peptides such as |FRAME:CPD-13365|, daptomycin and derivatives thereof (e.g. |FRAME:CPD-12251|) |CITS:[Kreuzman00]| as well as |FRAME:CAPSAICIN| |CITS:[Romano11]| which indicated its potential as pharmaceutical biocatalyst. For biotechnological applications the suitability of the echinocandin B deacylase was shown by overexpressing the enzyme (multiple gene copies) in both native and heterologous hosts which tripled the yield of |FRAME:CPD-17775| |CITS:[23220968]| as the valuable starting material for semisynthetic fungicides |CITS:[9451830]|.

Summary: Mycosporines and mycosporine-like amino acids such as |FRAME: CPD-18778| are small molecules that absorb UV radiation in the wavelength range 310-365 nm. They are synthesized by cyanobacteria, fungi, algae, and vertebrates that live in areas with strong sunlight exposure, and are used as sunscreen, protecting the organisms from the damaging radiation |CITS: [9586224][11826269][11826269][17286572][25965179]|., These compounds are involved in many other biological processes as well, and were discovered and named for mediating light-induced fungal sporulation |CITS: [5972212]|. However, their role as sunscreen is well documented, and |FRAME: CPD-18778| is even used in a commercial formulation used in skin care and cosmetic products, known as Helioguard 365. All of these compounds consist of a cyclohexenone core to whoch one or two amino acids are attached through imine linkages., A gene cluster encoding the enzymes that are involved in shinorine biosynthesis was originally observed in the sea anemone |FRAME: TAX-45351| (reported at the time as encoding shikimate pathway enzymes of bacterial origin) |CITS: [18268342]|. Homologs were found in genomes of dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria, and fungi, and the gene cluster was studied in detail from the cyanobacteria |FRAME: TAX-63737| and |FRAME: TAX-264691| |CITS: [20813918]|., The entire 6.5-kb shinorine biosynthetic gene cluster of |FRAME: TAX-264691| was cloned, and its introduction into |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in |FRAME: CPD-18778| production. The individual enzymes that participate in this pathway were expressed recombinantly and their activities characterized. It was shown that the first enzyme is the pathway is |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.152|, which acts on |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, a key metabolite produced by the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY|. Following a spontaneous dehydration to |FRAME: CPD-18773| and enzymatic methylation, |FRAME: GLY| and |FRAME: SER| are added by two very different ATP-dependent enzymes - the former a member of the ATP grasp family, and the latter a non-ribosomal peptide synthase |CITS: [20813918]|., It should be noted that knocking out |FRAME: EC-4.2.3.152| did not halt |FRAME: CPD-18778| production in |FRAME: TAX-264691|, indicating that an altarnative pathway operates in the organism |CITS: [22278966]|.

Summary: General Background, Methanogenesis, the biological production of |FRAME: CH4|, is an anaerobic respiration process carried out by the methanogens, a group of microorganisms belonging to the Archaea domain. These organisms account for most of the biogenic methane production, which is estimated at 5x1014 g of methane per year., Methanogenic pathways utilize a small group of fermentation products formed by other anaerobes as electron donors and acceptors. Typical electron donors are |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, |FRAME: FORMATE|, and one of several alcohols, such as |FRAME: ETOH|, |FRAME: ISO-PROPANOL|, |FRAME: CPD-326|, or |FRAME: CPD-7032|. Typical electron acceptors are C-1 substrates (carbon-containing compounds that lack carbon-carbon bonds) such as |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME: METOH|, and several different methylamines and methylsulfides., |FRAME: ACET Acetate| is a special methanogenic substrate, as it serves as both the electron donor and the electron acceptor after being split into two parts (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|). Most of the |FRAME:CH4| in nature originates from |FRAME:ACET|., Four main types of methanogenic pathways have been characterized: the pathway from H2 and CO2 (see |FRAME: METHANOGENESIS-PWY|), the aceticlastic pathway from acetate (see |FRAME: METH-ACETATE-PWY|), methanogenesis from methylated compounds, and methanogenesis from methoxylated aromatic compounds (see |FRAME: PWY-8304|). All pathways involve the transfer of a methyl group from the terminal acceptor to |FRAME: CoM|, forming |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|: One in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5209|), providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|) |CITS: [Keltjens93][15882413]|., Methanogenic pathways do not afford substrate level phosphorylation. Moreover, in the aceticlastic pathway an ATP molecule is spent for acetyl-CoA formation. Instead, ATP is formed by a chemiosmotic mechanism. The |FRAME: CPD-1282|, which is produced during methane formation (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|), is restored into |FRAME: CPD-1281| and |FRAME: CoM| by the action of two membrane-bound dehydrogenases (|FRAME: CPLX-7105| and |FRAME: CPLX-7104|), both of which translocate protons across the memberane (see |FRAME: PWY-5207|). The translocation results in a proton gradient that energizes ATP synthase enzymes., About This Pathway, The process of methanogenesis from |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| starts with activation of the |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE| by the unique cofactor |FRAME:Methanofurans|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:Formyl-methanofurans|. The formyl group is then transferred to another cofactor, |FRAME:THMPT|. A succession of transformations, catalyzed by |FRAME:CPLX-601|, |FRAME:CPLX-622|, and finally |FRAME:CPLX-641|, which depends on the methanogenic cofactor |FRAME:Factor-420|, results in the formation of |FRAME:METHYL-THMPT|. The methyl group is then transferred by, |FRAME:CPLX-643| to |FRAME: CoM|, resulting in |FRAME:Me-CoM|, which is then disproportionated into |FRAME: CH4| and |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, as described above., Since only one in four |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules is oxidized to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|, providing the six electrons that are required for the reduction of the other three |FRAME:Me-CoM| molecules to |FRAME: CH4|, the net reaction is conversion of |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| to |FRAME:CH4| (see |FRAME: METHFORM-PWY|).

Summary: The enterobacterial common antigen (ECA) is an outer membrane glycolipid shared by all members of the |FRAME: TAX-543| and is restricted to this family. A notable exception is |FRAME: TAX-556|, which does not produce ECA |CITS: [3078744]|., ECA was discovered in 1962 in antisera against |FRAME: TAX-2100498|, and originally named "Kunin antigen" |CITS: [Kunin62]|. It is located in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane, and is a glycophospholipid built up by an aminosugar heteropolymer linked to an L-glycerophosphatidyl residue., The carbohydrate portion consists of |FRAME: CPD-12541|, |FRAME: CPD-23559| and |FRAME: CPD-15611| arranged into →3-α-D-Fuc4NAc-(1→4)-β-D-ManNAcA-(1→4)-α-D-GlcNAc-(1→ trisaccharide repeat units |CITS: [658050][Lugowski83]|. In addition, the 6 position of the GlcNAc residues in the trisaccharide repeat units are nonstoichiometrically O-acetylated |CITS: [16936038]|. These repeating units are concatenated into longer linear heteropolysaccharide chains |CITS: [2166030]|., The ECA trisaccharide repeat unit is assembled on the cytosolic face of the cytoplasmic membrane as an undecaprenyldiphosphate-linked intermediate (lipid III). However, the Wzy-catalyzed polymerization of repeat units to form linear polysaccharide chains occurs on the periplasmic face of the membrane. This requires the translocation of lipid III to the periplasmic face of the membrane, which is mediated by a flippase encoded by the wzxE gene |CITS: [7698674]|., Polymerization is followed by the transfer of polysaccharide chains from the lipid carrier to either an as yet unidentified acceptor to yield phosphoglyceride-linked chains or to the core region of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharides|. ECA linked to phosphoglycerides is known as |FRAME: CPD-21605 ECAPG| and ECA linked to the core region of |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides| is known as |FRAME: CPD0-2294 ECALPS| |CITS: [352696][3078744]|. Both of those forms are translocated, by different mechanisms, to the outer membrane. A third form is |FRAME: CPD0-2646 ECACYC|, a cyclic water-soluble polymer that contains only ECA trisaccharide repeat units and is found in the periplasm |CITS: [6498860][8039177][11297429][12618464]|., In the case of |FRAME: CPD-21605 ECAPG|, each polysaccharide chain is covalently linked to diacylglycerolphosphate via a glycosidic linkage between the potential reducing terminal GlcNAc residue and the phosphate residue of the aglycone |CITS: [9592122]|. The phosphoglyceride aglycone anchors the ECA chains to the outer membrane |CITS: [6154038][7021535]|. The number of repeats units in each chain varies within the organism and among organisms. For example, in |FRAME: TAX-83333| the chains range from 1 to 14 repeat units |CITS: [10515954]|.

General Background, Ponciretin, the 4'-O-methyl derivate of naringenin occurs in plants where its , antifungal activity may be involved in the defense against pathogenic attacks. The modification of compounds , via O-methylation occurs frequently in nature and is thought to increase their lipophilicity being associated , with potentially higher antimicrobial activities |CITS: [Middleton94]|. In contrast to the likewise frequent , glycosylation that also modifies compounds O-methylation appears to be far more specific in plants |CITS: [9484457]|., Besides antimicrobial properties, ponciretin has also been reported to possess anti-allergenic capacities , |CITS: [15678369]| and efficiently inhibits growth and activity of the gastritis and peptic ulcer disease causing , bacteria |FRAME:TAX-210| in humans |CITS: [10454900]| |CITS: [10328566]|., About This Pathway, The enzyme has been characterized in vitro to be regiospecific for naringenin , to form ponciretin. However, other substrates such as the isoflavones daidzein and genistein as well as quercetin , (dihydroflavone) and apigenin (flavone) were also converted to their 4'-O-methyl derivatives with varying but rather , high turnover rates. The fact that ponciretin has not been found in soybean indicates that more likely daidzein , represents the in vivo substrate in this plant |CITS: [15961179]|. , In contrast to that the enzyme involved in the 4'-O-methylation of daidzein to form formononetin (|FRAME:PWY-2321|) , and genistein to produce biochanin-A (|FRAME:PWY-2083|) does not accept naringenin |CITS: [4452353]| , |CITS: [11006341]| indicating that the enzymes involved are different. Another 4'-O-methyltransferase purified from , |FRAME:TAX-46348| involved in the formation of formonoetin is even more specific and does not convert , daidzein or flavanone but only 2,7,4'-trihydroxyisoflavanone |CITS: [12610212]|. Yet another 4'-O-methyltransferase , isolated recently from |FRAME:TAX-4058| very specifically methylated homoeriodictyol (3'-O-methyl-eriodictyol) , in vitro and was discussed with regard to the substrate substitution pattern preferred for the subsequent , enzymes involved in the flavonoid biosynthetic route |CITS: [15110688]|., The 4'-O-methyltransferase forming ponciretin (this pathway) seems to be very similar to the one involved in the , biosynthesis of acacetin, the 4'-O-methyl derivate of apigenin (|FRAME:PWY-5119|). However, this enzyme expresses , a pronounced specificity towards apigenin and converted naringenin with only half the efficiency compared to apigenin , |CITS: [KUROKI81]|. The current lack of relevant data requires the further investigation of those enzymes to determine , their in vivo relationship across different species.

The accumulation of hydroxylated cinnamate conjugates which built up an impressive array of compounds in higher plants is well known and documented |CITS:[2690858]|. Hydroxycinnamates can form esters with a broad variety of carboxylic acids, for instance with |FRAME:TARTRATE| |CITS:[Scarpati58]| (this pathway), |FRAME:D-GLUCARATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-6673| and |FRAME:PWY-7461|) and |FRAME:GLUCONATE| |CITS:[Strack86]|. The main hydroxycinnamate dicarboxylate ester found in spinach is |FRAME:CPD-16579| which is the result of the somewhat unusual esterification of |FRAME:MESO-TARTRATE| with |FRAME:COUMARATE| |CITS:[Tadera71]|., The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-16579| has been elucidated in Spinacea oleracea from crude leave extracts. The pathway consists of two reactions which, originating from |FRAME:MESO-TARTRATE| successively confer acyl and acetyl moieties to the C-3 and C-2 position of |FRAME:MESO-TARTRATE|. The first step is the addition of |FRAME:COUMARATE| catalyzed by the meso-tartrate p-coumaroyltransferase which uses the acyl-glucose donor |FRAME:CPD-8674| to yield |FRAME:CPD-16578|. In the second step an acetyl-group is appended to |FRAME:CPD-16578| utilizing the acetyl-donor |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| which is catalyzed by a trans-coutarateacetyltransferase and yields the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-16579| |CITS:[Strack87b]|.

Summary: General Background, The common |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis| pathway, used by most organisms for the catabolism of glucose and related sugars, can be regarded as both an energy-producing catabolic pathway and an anabolic pathway, producing |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which can be converted to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.104|. While |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| can be fed to the TCA cycle for further energy production, it is also used as a biosynthestic precursor for many types of biomolecules (e.g. fatty acids). However, glycolysis is unable to produce 5-carbon sugars such as D-ribose, which are essential for the biosynthesis of DNA and RNA, neither can it form the 4-carbon sugar |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|, a precursor of aromatic amino acids and |FRAME: PYRIDOXAL_PHOSPHATE|, or the 7-carbon sugar |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, a precursor for |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|., The |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"| is an alternative way of oxidizing glucose that is targeted at anabolic reactions. The pathway fulfills two anabolic roles: it produces NADPH, making it a major source of reducing equivalents for biosynthetic reactions, and it produces C4, C5, and C7 sugars |CITS: [13129245][13174590][14790817][14285485]|., About This Pathway, The pentose phosphate pathway is an important member of central metabolism, as it supplies three of the 13 precursor metabolites (compounds needed for the biosyntheses): |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|, |FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|, and |FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|. For convenience, the pentose phosphate pathway is commonly divided into its preliminary |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "oxidative portion"| and the subsequent |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY "non-oxidative portion"|., The unidirectional oxidative branch fulfills two roles of the pathway - it produces a pentose sugar (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|) from the hexose |FRAME: GLC-6-P|, and it produces two equivalents of NADPH in the process., The non-oxidative branch of composed of a series of rearrangements catalyzed by an isomerase, an epimerase, a transketolase, and a transaldolase, involving a C3 compound (|FRAME: GAP|), a C4 compound (|FRAME: ERYTHROSE-4P|), C5 compounds (|FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P|, |FRAME: XYLULOSE-5-PHOSPHATE|, and |FRAME: RIBOSE-5P|), a C6 compound (|FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P|), and a C7 compound (|FRAME: D-SEDOHEPTULOSE-7-P|). Unlike the oxidative branch, the non-oxidative branch is fully reversible, allowing for different molecules to enter the pathway at different stages and be transformed to any other intermediate in this branch. No energy or reducing power is produced by the non-oxidative branch - it's sole purpose is carbon rearrangements., In prokaryotes and animals the pentose phosphate pathway takes place in the cytosol, the same location as glycolysis. In plants, the oxidative part of the pathway also takes place in plastids |CITS: [Foster93]|.
