Summary: This superpathway integrates the conversion of the amino acids |FRAME: ARG| and |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| to the polyamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, its subsequent degradation to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE|, and finally the conversion of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC|, which is fed into the TCA cycle., |FRAME: TAX-83333| has two forms of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.19|: a constitutive biosynthetic form, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10959| gene, and an inducible catabolic form encoded by the |FRAME:EG11501| gene. When the cells are grown in an arginine-rich medium, especially if the medium is acidic and conditions are semi-anaerobic, the catabolic arginine decarboxylase is expressed, and |FRAME: ARG| is converted to |FRAME:PUTRESCINE| in two steps via |FRAME: AGMATHINE|., Similarly, |FRAME: TAX-562| encodes two versions of |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.17|: a constitutively expressed biosynthetic enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: EG10961| gene, and an inducible degradative enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: EG10964 speF| gene |CITS:[3157043] [1939141]|. Under conditions of |FRAME: L-ORNITHINE| degradation, the catabolic enzyme is expressed and produces |FRAME:PUTRESCINE|., When |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is produced by either of these degradative enzymes, it can be degraded further to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| and eventually |FRAME:SUC|, which is fed into the |FRAME:TCA "TCA cycle"| |CITS:[3157043]|., There are two routes in which |FRAME: TAX-562| can degrade |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|:, In one route, which is described in |FRAME: PUTDEG-PWY|, |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| is transaminated with |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to generate |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, which is then oxidized to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA). GABA can be further degraded into |FRAME: SUC| as described in |FRAME: 4AMINOBUTMETAB-PWY| pathway., In a second pathway, which is described in |FRAME: PWY0-1221|, |FRAME:PUTRESCINE | is first γ-glutamylated at the expense of an ATP molecule. The resulting |FRAME: GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-PUTRESCINE| is oxidized to |FRAME:GAMMA-GLUTAMYL-GAMMA-AMINOBUTYRALDEH|, which is then dehydrogenated into |FRAME: CPD-9000|. In the last step, the γ-glutamyl group is removed by hydrolysis, generating |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| |CITS: [15590624]|., It has been suggested that the former pathway is dedicated to the degradation of intracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, while the latter is dedicated to the degradation of extracellular |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|. However, the most significant, difference between these two pathways is the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| in the latter route. One possible explanation for this is the fact that the intermediate fromed in the former pathway, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRALDEHYDE|, is unstable and tends to form the cyclic form |FRAME: CPD-6124| nonenzymatically. It is possible that the γ-glutamylation of |FRAME: PUTRESCINE| facilitates its catabolism by preventing this cyclization |CITS: [15590624]|., The last part of this superpathway is the degradation of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC|. The most common path for GABA degradation involves transamination to |FRAME:SUCC-S-ALD|, followed by oxidation to |FRAME: SUC|, and is known as the "GABA shunt", since it can channel glutamate into the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"|, bypassing two steps of that cycle. Different variants of the second enzyme, succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase, were shown to possess different cofactor requirement, for either NAD+, NADP+, or NAD(P)+.

General Background, The earliest report of alkylglycerols was made in 1909, from lipids isolated from starfish |CITS: [16742127]|. The name plasmalogen was coined in 1924 by Feulgen and Voit to describe an unknown compound that produced an aldehyde (which they called "plasmal") that they observed in plasma after acid treatment |CITS: [Feulgen24]|. It took nearly 40 years to establish the exact structure of the plasmalogens |CITS: [13416288][13499384][13576152][Marinetti59][Warner63]|., |FRAME: Plasmalogens Plasmalogens| are a unique class of membrane glycerophospholipids that represent up to 20% of the total phospholipid mass in humans and other mammals (between 1/2 and 2/3 of the ethanolamine phospholipids are plasmalogens |CITS: [11275267]|). They contain a fatty alcohol with a vinyl-ether bond at the sn-1 position, and an ester-linked fatty acids at the sn-2 position of the glycerol backbone. In mammals, the sn-1 position is typically derived from C16:0, C18:0, or C18:1 fatty alcohols while the sn-2 position is most commonly occupied by the polyunsaturated fatty acids |FRAME: ARACHIDONIC_ACID| or |FRAME: CPD-10244|. The most common head groups present in mammalian plasmalogens are ethanolamine (designated |FRAME: Alkyl-enyl-acyl-gly-P-EtOH-amines plasmenylethalomines|) or choline (designated |FRAME: PLASMENYLCHOLINE plasmenylcholines|), although inositol, serine and threonine have been observed., Both alkyl and alk-1-enyl phospholipids appear to serve as important structurally-stable lipid components of membranes, since the ether linkage can impede the hydrolysis of the acyl moiety at the sn-2 position by phospholipase A2 |CITS: [Snyder85]|., Interestingly, plasmalogens are widely found in anaerobic bacteria, invertebrates, and vertebrates, but are absent from aerobic and facultative aerobic bacteria, and most fungi and plants. This distribution suggests that they appeared, disappeared, and then reappeared during evolution, an explanation that is supported by major differences in their biosynthesis between anaerobic bacteria and animals |CITS: [22627108]|., About This Pathway, Membrane plasmalogen composition is tightly controlled by synthesis, remodeling, signaling induced hydrolysis and degradation. The first reaction in the degradation pathway shown here is the hydrolysis at sn-2, which occurs through receptor mediated stimulation of a phospholipase A2 (PLA2) that is calcium independent, plasmalogen selective and tissue specific |CITS: [21382416]|., Degradation proceeds in several possible routes, depending on the enzymes that act. Phospholipase C hydrolyzes the bond between phosphate and the glycerol backbone, while phospholipase D hydrolyzes the bond between phosphate and the head group. Alternatively, |FRAME: EC-3.3.2.2|, which is specific for the sn-2-deacylated (lyso) form of plasmalogen, catalyzes the hydrolytic cleavage of the vinyl ether bond, forming |FRAME: Fatty-Aldehydes| and |FRAME: L-1-GLYCEROPHOSPHORYLETHANOL-AMINE| or |FRAME: L-1-GLYCERO-PHOSPHORYLCHOLINE|. The latter can be re-acylated to form the corresponding diacyl phosphoglycerol, and the fatty aldehyde can be oxidized to a fatty acid or reduced to a fatty alcohol. Lysoplasmalogenase activity in tissues inversely correlates to plasmalogen levels, being lowest in brain and heart, and highest in liver and small intestinal mucosa and may also be important in regulating tissue plasmalogen levels |CITS: [21515882]|.

|FRAME: TAX-588858| can grow on |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINATE| as its sole source of carbon and nitrogen. The necessary functions for importing and degrading |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINATE| into central metabolism intermediates are encoded by 6 genes in a single opron, named dgaABCDEF. Expression is controled by an RpoN-dependent activator designated dgaR, and is induced by D-Glucosaminate |CITS: [23836865]|. Introduction of the full operon into |FRAME:TAX-562| strains BL21, DH5α and JM101, which are unable to utilize |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINATE|, allowed them to grow on D-glucosaminate minimal medium |CITS: [23836865]|., The first four genes encode a mannose family PTS permease that imports |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINATE| into the cell. A dedicated aldolase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-17632| gene, cleaves the latter to |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which are fed into central metabolism |CITS: [23836865]|., Glucose inhibits D-glucosaminate utilization via the glucose-specific PTS, which inhibits transcription of dgaABCDEF by diverting P~HPr to prevent phosphorylation of the activator DgaR, thereby blocking its activation., Bacterial genomes that possess the dga locus are mostly found within members of the |FRAME:TAX-543|. However, the locus is also found in some members of the genera |FRAME:TAX-1350| and |FRAME:TAX-1578| (in the phylum |FRAME:TAX-1239|), in one Actinobacterium, and in one β-proteobacterium |CITS: [23836865]|.

The bacterium |FRAME: TAX-2148|, which lacks cell walls, contains two major membrane lipids, |FRAME: 12-DIACYL-3-O-ALPHA-D-GLUCOPYRANOSYL "α-monoglucosyldiacylglycerol"| and |FRAME: 12-DIACYL-3-O-ALPHA-D-GLUCOPYRANOSYL1 "α-diglucosyldiacylglycerol"|. The latter, but not the former, is a major component of the bilayer membrane |CITS: [1533160]|., Maintaining proper ratio between the two lipids is crucial for the maintenance of phase equilibria close to a potential bilayer-nonbilayer transition and a nearly constant spontaneous curvature for the membrane bilayer lipid mixture |CITS: [10220338]|., A two-step pathway produces both lipids. The first enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.337|, transfers a glucose moiety from |FRAME: CPD-12575| to |FRAME: DIACYLGLYCEROL| membrane acceptor, forming |FRAME: 12-DIACYL-3-O-ALPHA-D-GLUCOPYRANOSYL "α-monoglucosyldiacylglycerol"| |CITS: [8995384][9368025][11294844][12911309]|. Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of almost all Gram-negative bacteria. While they are protecting the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems., Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Due to the complexity of the pathway leading to lipid A biosynthesis, we have broken the pathway into several shorter segments. This pathway describes the first segment, up to the intermediate lipid IV<sub>A</sub>., In many bacterial species lipid A consists of two |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE| units decorated with four to six acyl chains and one or two phosphate groups. Four β hydroxy acyl chains, 10 to 18 carbons in length, are attached directly to the glucosamine sugars at positions N-2 and O-3 (and N'-2 and O'-3, respectively), while two additional acyl chains are often attached to the β hydroxy group of two of the four β hydroxy acyl chains. The phosphate groups are attached at position O-1, O'-4, or both., This pathway includes the steps that lie between |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE| and the immediate lipid A precursor |FRAME: Lipid-IVA|. Most of the genes encoding the enzymes involved in this pathway are highly conserved. However, note that many bacterial species produce lipid A molecules that contain |FRAME: CPD-24440| instead of |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE| (see |FRAME: PWY2B4Q-4|)., LPS are produced by all Gram-negative bacteria, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-909932| and |FRAME: TAX-53433|, which belong to the firmicutes phylum, suggesting that an ancient LPS-containing diderm cell envelope was present in the ancestor of the Firmicutes |CITS: [27580370]|. There is some evidence that lipid A or its precursors are also synthesized in plants |CITS: [16935939][21709257]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME:ALLANTOIN "Allantoin"| is a common product of purine degradation. Allantoin is rich in nitrogen, and many organisms are able to degrade and recycle it., Some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1458|, |FRAME: TAX-80866| and |FRAME: TAX-264198|, do so under aerobic conditions, while others such as |FRAME: TAX-83333|, |FRAME: ORG-5985| and |FRAME: TAX-587| do so only anaerobically., Allantoin degradation is not limited to bacteria. Ureide-transporting plants convert fixed nitrogen in their, roots to |FRAME:ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|, which are then transported to upper parts, of the plant, where they are degraded to release the nitrogen. In addition, some fungi and animals also, degrade allantoin., The first step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-64|, comprises the hydrolysis of the internal amide bond of |FRAME: S-ALLANTOIN|, forming |FRAME: ALLANTOATE| |CITS: [786256]|. This enzyme turned out to be common to all organisms that can degrade allantoin, and is the first step in all allantoin degradation pathways., |FRAME: ALLANTOATE "Allantoate"| is converted to |FRAME: CPD-1091| via one of two routes. In the first route the nitrogen is liberated in a single step in the form of |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: ALLANTOICASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.4"|), while in the other route it is liberated in the form of |FRAME: AMMONIA| in two steps, via the intermediate |FRAME: CPD0-2298| (starting with |FRAME: ALLANTOATE-DEIMINASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.9"|)., The next step in the pathway is the conversion of |FRAME:CPD-1091| to |FRAME: GLYOX|. Similarly, this conversion can proceed with the liberation of either |FRAME: UREA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-LYASE-RXN "EC 4.3.2.3"|) or |FRAME: AMMONIA| (|FRAME: UREIDOGLYCOLATE-HYDROLASE-RXN "EC 3.5.3.19"|)., Several combinations of these routes have been documented. Some organisms possess pathways that produce solely |FRAME: UREA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5694|), some produce only |FRAME: AMMONIA| (see |FRAME: PWY-5692|), and some produce both (see |FRAME: PWY-5705|). In addition, some anaerobic organisms can degrade allantoin to |FRAME: CPD-389| instead of |FRAME: GLYOX| (see |FRAME: PWY0-41|)., About This Pathway, Some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-83333|, are able to utilize allantoin as a sole nitrogen source under anaerobic conditions. , In this pathway, |FRAME: CPD-1091| is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-389| by the enzyme |FRAME: G6286-MONOMER|., This enzyme was postulated to be present in |FRAME: ORG-5985| |CITS: [13779743][13924343]|,, |FRAME: ORG-5863| and |FRAME: TAX-83333| |CITS: [5328936]|, and was eventually purified from, |FRAME: ORG-5863| |CITS: [4399430]|., The |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme has not been purified yet, but its activity was measured in a cell extract, (175 mU/mg) and the gene encoding it mapped |CITS: [10601204]|., |FRAME: CPD-389| is then converted into |FRAME: OXAMATE| and |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| by the, enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-13524|. This activity has been measured in |FRAME: ORG-5985|, |CITS: [14102876]|., It has been suggested that |FRAME: CARBAMOYL-P| is further metabolized to, |FRAME:CARBON-DIOXIDE|, |FRAME:AMMONIA| and ATP |CITS: [10601204]|, although an enzyme, that catalyzes the reaction in this direction is yet to be described.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-23315 "1-tuberculosinyladenosine"| (1-TbAd) is a membrane permeable terpene nucleoside produced by many pathogenic mycobacterial species that acts as an antacid, neutralizing the acidic pH of host cell vacuoles and exerting a lysomotrophic effect on phagolysosomes. The compound is an abundant natural product in |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [24516143][31427817]|., In |FRAME: TAX-83332|, 1-TbAd is synthesized via the sequential acion of the Rv3377c and Rv3378c gene products. In the first step of the pathway a |FRAME: G185E-7653-MONOMER| transforms the linear isoprenoid molecule, geranylgeranyl disphosphate to form tuberculosinyl diphosphate |CITS: [15719101]|. Rv3378c then catalyses the condensation of adenosine and tuberculosinyl diphosphate to produce 1-TbAd |CITS: [24516143]|. Expression of Rv3377c and Rv3378c in |FRAME: TAX-1768| confers a growth advantage in media at pH 5.4 - 5.1 when compared to the non-1-TbAd producing wild-type |CITS: [31427817]|., Tuberculosinyl diphosphate has the halimane skeleton, which is very rare in prokaryotes. Halimanes are a group, of bicyclophytanes, diterpenes that have been originally characterized from the shrubs |FRAME: ORG-6043| and |FRAME: TAX-335161| |CITS: [11838978]|, although similar compounds have been subsequently found not only in other plants, but also in animals, such as the Okinawa sponge |FRAME: TAX-279581| |CITS: [1611691][15750645]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| (16:1Δ9) is a common unsaturated fatty acid, found in bacteria, fungi |CITS: [8294460]|, plants |CITS: [7548115]| and animals |CITS:[14321753] [6030882]|. It comprises from 10% to 65% of the seed oil of several plants., |FRAME: CPD-9245 Palmitoleate| can be formed directly from the saturated fatty acid |FRAME: PALMITATE| by the action of Δ9 desaturase enzymes. Such enzymes have been reported from cyanobacteria |CITS: [7929259][10937442][16689682][17385315]|, fungi |CITS: [2674136][12055292]|, higher plants |CITS: [12208502][8861937]|, , fish |CITS: [11170264]| and mammals |CITS: [16443825]|., Desaturase enzyme do not operate on a free acid substrate. Three types of desaturases are known, that act on acyl-CoA, acyl-[acp], and acyl-lipid conjugates, respectively., In many bacteria and some plants |FRAME: CPD-9245| is derived from |FRAME: Palmitoyl-ACPs|, as shown in this pathway |CITS: [9154992]|. In mammals the enzyme acts only on CoA-derivatives |CITS: [16443825]|, while in some plants and cyanobacteria the desaturase acts on fatty acids embedded within the structure of lipids |CITS: [7929259]| (see |FRAME: PWY-7589|)., For an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-9245|, found in the bacterium |FRAME:TAX-562|, see |FRAME: PWY-6282|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Jasmonates jasmonates| are a group of important phytohormones, structurally similar to animal |FRAME: Prostaglandins prostaglandins| and ubiquitous in the plant kingdom. Many forms exist, based on the structure of |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| (jasmonic acid, JA). The jasmonates act as regulatory molecules in many developmental processes that include fertility, sex determination, root elongation and fruit ripening. They are also potent signals activating plant defenses against pathogens, herbivory, wounding and abiotic stress., The jasmonate regulation system includes the COI1 receptor protein and several JAZ (JAsmonate ZIM domain) repressors, which, in the absence of jasmonate, are bound to the MYC2 transcription factors, preventing transcription. In the presence of active jasmonate molecules, COI1 interacts with the JAZ repressors, causing their |FRAME: PWY-7511 ubiquitylation|. The ubiquitylated repressors are targeted for proteasome degradation, releasing the MYC2 transcription factors and activating transcription |CITS: [19716757]|., Only two of the four stereoisomers of jasmonate occur naturally: |FRAME: CPD-731| and |FRAME: CPD-734| |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. These two forms are present in equilibrium within cells and can interconvert spontaneously through epimerization |CITS: [8074303][19349968]|. The exact ratio of these stereoisomers within a cell has not been conclusively determined, and it may vary based on species, cell type, and physiological state. But, in the systems tested so far, |FRAME: CPD-734| is found at higher levels than |FRAME: CPD-731| |CITS:[19349968]|. The biological activity of these stereoisomers can be quite different |CITS: [8074303]|. In addition, enzymes involved in JA metabolism may have different preferences for the different stereoisomers |CITS: [17291501]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: Jasmonic-Acids "Jasmonate"| biosynthesis starts with the conversion of |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID| to |FRAME: CPD-729| (OPDA) in the chloroplast, by sequential actions of |FRAME: EC-1.13.11.12| (LOX), |FRAME: EC-4.2.1.92| (AOS) and |FRAME: EC-5.3.99.6| (AOC). Once formed, OPDA needs to be transported from the chloroplast into the peroxisome, where it is reduced by |FRAME: EC-1.3.1.42| to give rise to |FRAME: CPD-730| (OPC8). OPC8 is attached to coenzyme A and undergoes three cycles of β oxidation, resulting in shortening of the octanoate side chain by six carbons. The steps of β oxidation are catalyzed by three core enzymes acyl-CoA oxidase (|FRAME: AT4G16760|), multifunctional protein containing 2-trans-enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activities (|FRAME: AT4G29010|), and 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (|FRAME: AT2G33150|). At the end of β oxidation, |FRAME: CPD-11529| is hydrolyzed to form free |FRAME: CPD-731|, which spontaneously epimerizes to form |FRAME: CPD-734|.

Summary: General Background, The plant hormone |FRAME: INDOLE_ACETATE_AUXIN| (IAA) can be inactivated via multiple mechanisms, A common mechanism involves in non-decarboxylative oxidation. |FRAME: TAX-4577| readily oxidizes free IAA (|FRAME: PWY-1961|) whereas |FRAME: TAX-47664| (hybrid aspen) oxidizes |FRAME: INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP| (IAA-asp) (|FRAME: PWY-1962|). |FRAME: TAX-3702| oxidizes both free IAA and IAA-asp (|FRAME: PWY-2021|)., Other inactivation mechanisms involve direct glycosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1741|), hydroxylation followed by O-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-1981|, |FRAME: PWY-5811|), N-glucosylation (|FRAME: PWY-5797|), and conjugation with different amino acids (|FRAME: PWY-6219|), which could be followed by further hydroxylation (|FRAME: PWY-5788|)., IAA (indole-3-acetic acid), one of the most common active forms of the phytohormone auxin, is often, present in conjugated forms. Free IAA is involved in regulating many aspects of plant growth from embryogenesis to root and shoot development and reproduction. Meanwhile, conjugated forms of auxin play varied roles: some still have biological activity, others serve as inactive storage forms, and some appear to be permanently inactivated |CITS:[15749753]|., About This Pathway, A number of different IAA metabolites have been isolated in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, including |FRAME:INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ALA|, |FRAME:INDOLE-3-ACETYL-LEU|, |FRAME:INDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP|, |FRAME:INDOLE-3-ACETYL-GLU|, |FRAME:2-OXINDOLE-3-ACETYL-ASP|, and |FRAME:CPD-1102| (rev in |CITS:[15749753]|). New conjugated forms of IAA continue to be identified through improved isolation and verification technologies, including |FRAME: CPD-9583| (6-OH-IAA-Val) and |FRAME: CPD-9584| (6-OH-IAA-Phe), which were identified using LC-ESI-MS/MS techniques |CITS:[17548096]|. Radiotracer labeling studies indicate that 6-OH-IAA-Val and 6-OH-IAA-Phe can be generated using deuterated forms of |FRAME: CPD-9577| and |FRAME: CPD-9582| respectively, whereas they do not seem to arise from a 6-hydroxy-IAA precursor |CITS:[17548096]|, ., Neither |FRAME: CPD-9577| nor |FRAME: CPD-9582| have been isolated from |FRAME: TAX-3702| to date, though there is some evidence for the presence of these compounds in mosses and liverworts |CITS:[ 10562246]|. Moreover some GH3 family members from Arabidopsis can synthesis IAA-Val and/or IAA-Phe in vitro |CITS:[ 15659623]|, and a recombinant IAA-amide hydrolase from Arabidopsis, |FRAME: AT3G02875|, can act on IAA-Phe and IAA-Val |CITS:[7792599]|. Additional conjugates of these compounds, namely |FRAME: CPD-9596| and |FRAME:CPD-9595|, were also generated during the radiotracing studies. These IAA metabolites have not been encountered in |FRAME: TAX-3702| plants yet, either, but will be investigated in the future. , Neither 6-OH-IAA-Val nor 6-OH-IAA-phenylalanine show auxin activity in root elongation assays in |FRAME: TAX-3702| seedlings, suggesting that they are inactive products of auxin catabolism |CITS:[17548096]|. Subsequent modifications to these molecules are likely |CITS:[17548096]| and need to be characterized.

|FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "Hapalindole-type alkaloids"| are a group of hybrid isoprenoid-indole alkaloids produced solely by members of Subsection V of the cyanobacteria, such as the |FRAME: TAX-1190| and |FRAME: TAX-162985| species. These compounds often have antibacterial, antimycotic, or antialgal activities., Since the initial isolation of |FRAME: CPD-20793| in 1984 |CITS: [Moore84]|, more than 80 members of this family have been isolated |CITS: [Moore87][Smitka92][Park92][Stratmann94][17315959][19371071]|. All of these compounds have an isonitrile- or isothiocyanate-containing indole alkaloid skeleton, with a cyclized isoprene unit. The major classes of the hapalindole-type molecules are the |FRAME: Hapalindoles hapalindoles|, the |FRAME: Fischerindoles fischerindoles|, the |FRAME: Welwitindolinones welwitindolinones|, and the |FRAME: Ambiguines ambiguines|, which differ in their core structure., The first biosynthetic pathway for a hapalindole-type alkaloid was reported for |FRAME: CPD-20794|, a compound produced by |FRAME: TAX-230521|, which was the only axenic cyanobacterial hapalindole-type-molecule producer available at the time. The genome of the organism was sequenced, and searches for putative genes encoding isonitrile synthase and prenyltransferase have identified a cluster of 32 protein-coding genes involved in ambiguine biosynthesis. This discovery was made by two different labs, which named the genes in the cluster amb and fam, respectively |CITS: [24180436][26629885]|., In addition to genes unique to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: Hapalindoles-Types "hapalindole-type alkaloids"|, the cluster contains homologs of the trpA-E genes, which are responsible for |FRAME: TRP| biosynthesis, as well as five dedicated genes for |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, |FRAME: CPD-4211|, and |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| biosynthesis., The first committed step in the pathway is the addition of an isonitrile function to |FRAME: TRP|, which is catalyzed in |FRAME: TAX-230521| by two paralougous enzymes encoded by the |FRAME: G-58189| and |FRAME: G-58190| genes. Both genes are homologous to the |FRAME: G-58184| gene, which has been shown to encode an |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.25| |CITS: [16206308]|. The enzyme is known to use |FRAME: TRP| and |FRAME: RIBULOSE-5P| to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-20766| |CITS: [16217820]|. The second step is catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.14.20.11|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-58188| gene. This enzyme catalyzes an Fe2+, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent monooxygenation at C-3 of the substrate, followed by decarboxylation and dehydration to form a cis C-C double bond |CITS: [24180436][28212039]|. The third enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.146|, catalyzes geranylation of the intermediate, forming the key intermediate |FRAME: CPD-20795| |CITS: [26629885]|., This intermediate is the last common intermediate in the synthesis of the different hapalindole-type alkaloids, as different organisms possess different cyclases that form different core structures while acting on it. The cyclase encoded by the |FRAME: G-58192| gene of |FRAME: TAX-230521| is thermostable and forms |FRAME: CPD-20794|, which serves as the starting compound for formation of all other 12-epi-hapalindoles |CITS: [26629885]|. Summary: General Background, |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| (farnesyl pyrophosphate, FPP) is a crucial compound involved in the, biosynthesis of a variety of terpenoids including sesquiterpenoids and sterols., Moreover, FPP is also used in posttranslational modifications of proteins (farnesylation) which is, believed to act as a membrane attachment device., The biosynthesis of FPP is largely thought to occur in the cytosol where sesquiterpenoids and sterols, are produced. This cytosolic FPP is synthesized from the condensation of |FRAME: CPD-4211|, (dimethylallyl pyrophosphate, DMAPP) and two molecules of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, (isopentenyl pyrophosphate, IPP) originating from the |FRAME:PWY-922| |CITS:[16179482][11289612]|., In plants FPP is found not only in the cytosol, but also in plastids and mitochondria |CITS:[14630967], [16179482]|) where IPP and DMAPP may originate from the |FRAME:NONMEVIPP-PWY|, instead of the mevalonate pathway., The synthesis of FPP is the result of two head-to-tail condensation reactions: first, |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| (geranyl pyrophosphate, GPP) is formed from the condensation of DMAPP, and IPP; then another IPP molecule is added to form FPP.

Summary: Flavonoids belong to one of the best studied secondary metabolite classes because of the important roles they play in a plants life and the beneficiary effects they have on human health. The functions of the widely-distributed flavonoids are variegated and often distinct from each other within the plant kingdom reaching from pigmentation, pollinator attraction and UV screen to acting as signaling molecules between species, regulatory and hormonal functions and defense |CITS:[11130659]| |CITS:[20921162]|. Flavonoids exhibit antioxidant, antiallergenic, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer and neuropharmacological activities |CITS:[17935117]| |CITS:[19075837]| which have been extensively exploited for long-term health benefits in humans., The vast structural diversity of flavonoids (~9000 compounds) can be attributed to modifications of the flavonoid core skeleton by e.g. glycolysation, acylation, methylation, prenylation and hydroxylation |CITS:[16137727]| |CITS:[12946402]|. Glycosylation not only contributes to the variety and complexity of flavonoids but also enhances their water solubility and consequently improves their chemical stability, metabolic availability and bioactivity |CITS:[10973093]|. Glycosyltransferases which attach additional sugar groups to existing sugar moieties of glucosides are less frequently reported in the literature despite the fact that the resulting compounds have been shown to further increase water solubility |CITS:[14644434]| and participate in the modification of physiological traits like color |CITS:[15842621]| and taste (see |FRAME:PWY-5094|)., The formation of quercetin gentiotetroside is based on the catalytic activity of a flavonol 1,6-glucosyltransferase which sequentially elongates the glucosidic side-chain of |FRAME:CPD1F-437| by 1,6-addition of |FRAME:GLC| to the respective terminal |FRAME:GLC| of the growing gentioside (this pathway), |FRAME:CPD-14838| (see |FRAME:PWY-7139|) and |FRAME:CPD-6622| (see |FRAME:PWY-4421|). The flavonol 1,6-glucosyltransferase (UGT3) did not express activity towards aglycones but accepted other monoglucosylated flavonols such as |FRAME:CPD-14843| and |FRAME:CPD1F-453|, the flavone glucosides |FRAME: APIGENIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCOSIDE| and |FRAME: LUTEOLIN-7-O-BETA-D-GLUCOSIDE| and the flavanone glucoside |FRAME:CPD-3421| forming the corresponding gentiobiosides with varying catalytic efficiency |CITS:[19561332]| |CITS:[17940060]|. However, phenolic gentiosides have not yet been identified in |FRAME:TAX-4058| and the in vivo activity of UGT3 remains to be shown.

Summary: Many species that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-213115| order can grow in the absence of sulfate on |FRAME: Lactate| as sole energy source when in syntrophic association with H2 consuming methanogenic archaea, which keep the H2 partial pressure low and drive the pathway forward |CITS: [879775][16345708][16346421][Conrad86]|. A study in which |FRAME: TAX-58180| was grown in chemostats under respiratory and syntrophic conditions with the methanogenic partners |FRAME: TAX-39152| or |FRAME: TAX-2203| has found that not only hydrogen but also formate is exchanged between the organisms |CITS: [23264581]|., Cell suspensions of |FRAME: TAX-881| were found to catalyze, in the absence of sulfate, the complete conversion of one mol of lactate to one mol of acetate, one mol of CO2, and two mol of H2. The pathway results in production of one mol of ATP by substrate level phosphorylation |CITS: [6127735]|. The organism can use |FRAME: D-LACTATE| or |FRAME: L-LACTATE| equally with the same efficiency |CITS: [26167158]|., The pathway starts in the cytoplasm with lactate dehydrogenases specific for either |FRAME: D-LACTATE| or |FRAME: L-LACTATE|, which produce |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. These enzymes are different from lactate dehydrogenase characterized from organisms such as |FRAME: TAX-562|. They are dimeric, contain iron-sulfur clusters, and are believed to interact with cytochromes |CITS: [7275946][26167158]|., Pyruvate is decarboxylated oxidatively by |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.1| (better known as pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase or PFRO). One of the reaction's products, acetyl-CoA, is phosphrylated and converted to acetate in a reaction that yields ATP. The second product, CO2, diffuses to the periplasm, where it is reduced to formate by the periplasmic formate dehydrogenases. While the organisms contain 3 different formate dehydrogenase, the molybdenum-containing |FRAME: CPLX-9763| appears to be the main form that participates in lactate fermentation. The third product of PFOR is reduced ferredoxin. The electrons from ferredoxin travel along an electron chain not shown here, which includes the |FRAME: QmoABC "Qmo electron transfer complex"|, membrane menaquinone, and the |FRAME: CPLX-9771 "Qrc complex"|, and eventually reach |FRAME: Cytochromes-c3 "cytochrome c3"|, which is the most widespread c-type cytochrome in |FRAME: TAX-194924| species. The cytochrome transfers the elctrons to a hydrogene that form moleculr hydrogen |CITS: [23974031]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8816 "γ-Resorcylate"| and |FRAME: CPD-623| occur in nature as secondary metabolites in plants and fungi |CITS: [18427109][19795855]|. , A bacterial strain that could use |FRAME: CPD-623| as the sole source of carbon (|FRAME: ORG-5953|) was originally isolated by enrichment culture in 1976. The degradation pathway was shown to proceed via |FRAME: CPD-8130|, |FRAME: CPD-294| and |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which is degraded to acetyl-CoA via the |FRAME: PWY-2361| pathway |CITS: [1280][942589]|., The same pathway was subsequently documented in |FRAME: TAX-267998| |CITS: [17158677]|, |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [16963551]| and |FRAME: TAX-101510| |CITS: [26319878]|. While the pathway's intermediates are shared within all of these organisms, variability occurs in the enzymes that catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-623| to |FRAME: CPD-8130|. In |FRAME: TAX-267998| the reaction is catalyzed by a two-component FADH2-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.14.27|), in |FRAME: TAX-1718| it is catalyzed by a single-component NADPH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.219|), and in |FRAME: TAX-101510| it is catalyzed by a single-component NADH-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-1.14.13.220|)., About This Pathway, The industrial value of |FRAME: CPD-8816|, which is an important intermediate in the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, and agricultural chemicals |CITS: [14858847][4801686]|, and the fact that the reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.103|, is reversible, resulted in interest in this enzyme, which in vivo functions in the degradation of |FRAME: CPD-8816|., Thermophilic enzymes are particularly desired for industrial catalysis, and such an enzyme was found in the thermophilic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-267998| |CITS: [15466039]|., The gene encoding the enzyme, |FRAME: G-44491|, was found in a cluster that includes enzymes known to participate in |FRAME: CPD-623| degradation |CITS: [15466039]|. The region was sequenced in its entirety, and the complement of enzymes identified suggested the usual resorcinol degradation pathway that has been characterized before, with a single exception. The cluster contains genes encoding for two components of |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.27|, which is markedly different from other enzymes known to catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-623| to |FRAME: CPD-8130|. This enzyme system includes an oxygenase component (encoded by |FRAME: G-44496|) that utilizes reduced FAD, provided by a dedicated NADH-FAD reductase, which is encoded by the graD gene that is also present in the cluster |CITS: [17158677]|.

Summary: General Background, The proteinogenic amino acid |FRAME: GLY| can biosynthesized via several different pathways. The main pathway in most organisms is the production of glycine from |FRAME:SER| via |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|. Eukaryotic organisms have both a cytosolic enzyme (SHMT2) and a mitochondrial enzyme (SHMT1) (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-PWY|). The two isoforms were reported to work in opposite directions depending on the culture conditions |CITS: [9398220]|., A less well described glycine production pathway is acheived by the operation of the |FRAME: CPLX-7302| in reverse (see |FRAME: GLYCINE-SYN2-PWY|)., In a third pathway glycine is formed from |FRAME: GLYOX|, a product of the |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS|, by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-2.6.1.44| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-ALA-PWY|)., And finally, glycine can also be formed from |FRAME:THR| by the action of |FRAME: EC-4.1.2.48| (see |FRAME: GLYSYN-THR-PWY|)., About This Pathway, This single reaction pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-2.1.2.1|, is the major pathway for biosynthesis of |FRAME: GLY| in many organisms. In eukaryotes and bacteria the enzyme catalyzes the reversible transfer of Cβ of |FRAME: SER| to |FRAME: THF-GLU-N|, forming |FRAME: GLY| and |FRAME: METHYLENE-THF-GLU-N|, the latter functioning as a carrier of C1 units. In methanogens and several other archaea |FRAME: THF-GLU-N tetrahydrofolate| is replaced by |FRAME: THMPT|. , The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-2190| was produced recombinantly in |FRAME: TAX-562| and purified. The enzyme was found to be homodimeric. When assayed in vitro the enzyme was active with |FRAME: THMPT|. Activity with tetrahydrofolate was 450-fold less efficient |CITS: [12902326]|.

Selenium is an essential trace element that is crucial for the normal development of bacteria and animals. High concentrations of selenium are however toxic, largely because transporters and enzymes involved in sulfur and sulfo-compound metabolism can often erroneously substitute |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| for sulfur and can misincorporate seleno-amino acids into proteins |CITS: [21913064]|. In humans the safety threshold between acute selenium poisoning (>400 μg/day) and selenium deficiency (<40 μg/day) is very narrow. , The natural forms of selenium include |FRAME: SELENATE| [Se(VI)], |FRAME: SELENITE| [Se(IV)], |FRAME: Elemental-selenium| [Se(0)], and |FRAME: SE-2| [Se(-II)]. Selenite is the most toxic, while elemental selenium is insoluble and is generally considered to be non-toxic |CITS: [25631289]|. However, selenium rarely occurs in its elemental state in nature. , |FRAME: SELENATE Selenate| can be used by some bacterial species as a respiratory terminal electron acceptor to support anaerobic growth. The key enzyme for this process is selenate reductase, which reduces selenate to selenite. Two such enzymes have been described - a periplasmic |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.9|, which receives its electrons from s soluble cytochrome c, and |FRAME: EC-1.97.1.14|, which is a membrane-bound enzyme that receives its electrons directly from the membrane quinone pool. Both enzymes are molybdoenzymes, though the former is a type II molybdoenzyme, while the latter is a type I., One of the best studied type II enzymes is from the Gram-negative betaproteobacterium |FRAME: TAX-33058|, which has been isolated from seleniferous waters of the Joaquin Valley, CA, USA |CITS: [8427805]|. The enzyme has been purified and characterized |CITS: [9295321][20388716]|., The product, |FRAME: SELENITE|, is presumed to be reduced in the cytoplasm, forming intracellular selenium nanospheres that are ultimately secreted into the surrounding medium along with a protein factor (SefA) which is believed to stabilize the formation of the selenium nanospheres before secretion |CITS: [ 23176461]|.

This ethanol degradation pathway begins with conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde by the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) |FRAME: HS05414-MONOMER "Microsomal Ethanol Oxidising System"| (MEOS), also known as cytochrome P-450 2E1 |CITS: [SALWAYJG2002]|. The resulting acetaldehyde leaves the ER to the cytoplasm and then passes into the mitochondrial compartment where it is converted to acetate (by |FRAME: CPLX66-81|). Should acetate be activated to acetyl-CoA within the liver, it would not be oxidized by the Krebs cycle because of the prevailing high ratio of NADH + H / NAD+ within the liver mitochondrial matrix. Consequently, acetate leaves the mitochondrial compartment and the hepatocyte to be metabolized by extra-hepatic tissues |CITS: [SALWAYJG2002]|. Extrahepatic tissues take up acetate where it is converted to acetyl-CoA |CITS: [11420176]|., Four distinct human ethanol degradation pathways have been described - three oxidative pathways and one nonoxidative pathway. All oxidative pathways mediate the oxidation of ethanol to acetaldehye which is then oxidized to acetate for subsequent extra-hepatic activation to acetyl-CoA |CITS: [11420176]|.  Oxidative pathways are differentiated based on the enzyme/mechanism by which ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde. The present pathway utilizes the endoplasmic reticulum MEOS, also known as cytochrome P-450 2E1, with the other two oxidative pathways utilizing cytoplasmic alcohol dehydrogenase (|FRAME: PWY66-21|) and peroxisomal catalase (|FRAME: PWY66-162|), respectively. The nonoxidative pathway is less well characterized but produces fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEEs) as primary end products |CITS: [12456329]|., Oxidative and nonoxidative pathways have been demonstrated in a range of tissues including gastric, pancreatic, hepatic and lung. Inhibition of oxidative ethanol degradation pathways raises both hepatic and pancreatic FAEE levels demonstrating that oxidative and nonoxidative pathways are alternative metabolically linked pathways. Pancreatic ethanol metabolism occurs predominantly by the nonoxidative pathway but oxidative routes to acetaldehyde have also been demonstrated in the pancreas - the cytochrome P450 2E1 and alcohol dehydrogenase pathways |CITS: [12870777]|. , Ethanol metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver and the resulting oxidative metabolite acetaldehyde is thought to play a role in alcohol induced liver injury. Additionally, there is now solid evidence that FAEEs also play a role in alcoholic pancreatitis |CITS:[12065293]|.  Blood and organ levels of FAEEs are raised by ethanol consumption with the highest concentration observed in the pancreas. FAEE generation from ethanol is greater in the pancreas than in any other organ suggesting that the pancreatic pathway contributes to raised blood and organ FAEE levels |CITS: [12065293]|. , Under conditions of acute ethanol consumption, the majority of ethanol is degraded by the hepatic oxidative pathways predominantly the alcohol dehydrogenase mediated pathway. However, under conditions of chronic ethanol consumption, hepatic MEOS activity and nonoxidative pathways are induced and quantitatively make a greater contribution to ethanol catabolism. The stimulatory effect of ethanol on Cytochrome P450 2E1 levels results in increased oxygen consumption, production of excess free radicals and increased metabolism of ethanol, vitamin A and testosterone - the chronic effects of which contribute to depletion of antioxidative activity.  Antioxidative deficiency (glutathione, vitamin E, phosphatidylcholine) , and excess free radicals are believed to subsequently contribute to the progression of alcoholic liver disease |CITS: [12901271]|. , Polymorphic loci for genes encoding enzymes of ethanol degradation pathways have been identified and resulting variant isoenzymes characterized and found to exhibit distinct kinetic properties. Indeed, genetically determined differences in ethanol metabolism may, in part, account for the variability of individual susceptibility to the physical complications of alcohol abuse |CITS: [3519419]|.

Summary: General Background, Biotin-dependent carboxylases constitute a group of enzymes with many common features in structure and mechanism |CITS: [Wood77]|. These enzymes are involved in various metabolic reactions such as lipogenesis, gluconeogenesis, and amino acid metabolism. Another group of bioin-dependent enzymes are the decarboxylases mediating sodium transport |CITS: [2896195]| (for an example, see |FRAME: CPLX-7676| from |FRAME: TAX-57040|)., The different biotin-dependent enzymes have different architectures in different organisms. For example, eukaryotic acetyl-CoA carboxylases (|FRAME: EC-6.4.1.2 "EC 6.4.1.2"|) contain three functional modules in one large polypeptide (biotin carboxylase/biotin-carboxyl-carrier protein/carboxyltransferase), eukaryotic propionyl-CoA-carboxylases and bifunctional acetyl/propionyl-CoA carboxylases of Mycobacteria are composed of a coupled biotin carboxylase/biotin-carboxyl-carrier protein polypeptide and separate carboxyltransferase proteins, while all the subunits of |FRAME:TAX-562| acetyl-CoA carboxylase exist as single proteins (|FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLTRANSFER-CPLX|, |FRAME: BIOTIN-CARBOXYL-CPLX|, and |FRAME: BCCP-MONOMER|) |CITS: [8102604][7909542][8772169]|., About This Pathway, The enzyme |FRAME:ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX| is one of the key enzymes in the biosynthesis of fatty acids (see |FRAME: FASYN-INITIAL-PWY|). In |FRAME: TAX-562| the enzyme exists as a complex composed of two catalytic units and one carrier protein, encoded by four different genes. The catalytic units are |FRAME:BIOTIN-CARBOXYL-CPLX| (BC), a homodimer encoded by the |FRAME: EG10276| gene, and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLMULTI-CPLX| (ACCT), an α2β2 tetramer, encoded by the |FRAME:EG11647| and |FRAME: EG10217| genes. The carrier protein is the |FRAME:BCCP-CPLX "biotin carboxyl carrier protein"| (BCCP), a homodimer encoded by the |FRAME:EG10275| gene., The BCCP monomer is biotinylated by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.15|. Following dimerization of the biotinylated monomers, |FRAME: EC-6.3.4.14|, catalyzes the carboxylation by |FRAME: HCO3| of the biotin molecules, forming, a carboxybiotinylated BCCP. This form of the carrier protein in turn is the substrate for |FRAME: EC-6.4.1.2|, which transfers the carboxy group to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| and the regeneration of biotinylated BCCP dimer. Both biotinylation and carboxylation of the carrier protein require ATP, while the last step, transfer of the carboxy group to |FRAME: ACETYL-COA|, does not |CITS: [15749055]|., It should be noted that eukaryotes have a large single polypeptide (|FRAME: EC-6.4.1.2|) that includes the carrier protein, the biotin carboxylase, and the acetyl-CoA carboxytransferase activities, and thus calayzes the following transformation as a single reaction:, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA-CARBOXYLTRANSFER-RXN|

Summary: General Background, Glycogen, a branched polymer of glucose, is a storage molecule whose accumulation is under rigorous control in many cells. Glycogen metabolism increases in response to a wide variety of environmental stresses, including heat stress or exposure to sodium chloride, hydrogen peroxide, copper sulfate, high levels of ethanol, or weak organic acids, such as sorbate or benzoate. Glycogen metabolism also increases in response to conditions of nutrient starvation, such as limited nitrogen, carbon, phosphorous, or sulfur, and during diauxic growth on glucose |CITS:[11152943]|., Glycogen is highly branched. It is formed of small chains of 8 to 12 glucose molecules linked together by α (1->4) bonds (these short linear chains are also called maltodextrins) that are in turn linked to each other by α (1->6) bonds, known as branch linkages., About This Pathway, In this pathway, common in fungi and animals, glycogen is degradeby two enzyme systems working in tandem - |FRAME: CPLX-7568| and |FRAME: YPR184W-MONOMER| (encoded in |FRAME: TAX-4932| by |FRAME: YPR160W| and |FRAME: YPR184W|, respectively |CITS: [11152943]|). Glycogen phosphorylase progressively releases |FRAME: GLC-1-P| from the linear α-(1,4)-glucosidic bonds |CITS:[2657401][1092346]|, but is not able to break bonds that are close to α(1,6)-branch linkages, leaving tails of 4 α-1,4-linked residues next to branching points |CITS:[11152943]|. The highly-branched, short-chained product formed by exhaustive hydrolysis by the glycogen phosphorylase has been named |FRAME: CPD0-971|, since it is the limit of what this enzyme is able to achieve on its own., The branches are resolved by the dual-functional |FRAME: YPR184W-MONOMER|, which eliminates branch points in a two-step process. The first step is the transfer of a maltotriosyl (or maltosyl) unit from a branch to the non-reducing end of an adjacent α-1,4-glucosyl chain, resulting in formation of |FRAME: Truncated-Limit-Dextrins|, catalyzed by the |FRAME:ENZRXN-14616| activity (|FRAME: EC-2.4.1.25 "EC 2.4.1.25"|) of the enzyme. This is followed by the hydrolysis of the residual α-1,6-linked glucose residue by the |FRAME:ENZRXN-14615| activity (|FRAME: EC-3.2.1.33 "EC 3.2.1.33"|) |CITS:[11094287]|. Once all the branches are removed, the polymer becomes |FRAME:CPD0-1027|, and |FRAME:CPLX-7568| can resume its activity, resulting in complete breakdown to |FRAME:GLC-1-P| units |CITS:[11152943]|., Another enzyme that can act on the |FRAME:CPD0-1027 "debranched limit dextrin"| is |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.3|, which, unlike the phosphorylase, produces non-phosphorylated |FRAME: GLC| residues., Note that many bacteria species possess a different debranching enzyme (encoded by the |FRAME: EG10381| gene) that is able to remove |FRAME: MALTOTETRAOSE| chains from the |FRAME: CPD0-971|, enabling the removal of the four-residue side-branches that are linked to the main chain by an α-1-6 linkage in a single step, as described in |FRAME: GLYCOCAT-PWY|., In the last step of the pathway |FRAME:GLC-1-P| is converted to |FRAME:GLC-6-P|, which can enter |FRAME: GLYCOLYSIS glycolysis|.

Summary: Background, There is renewed interest in lignocellulosic biomass as a renewable feedstock for the production of |FRAME: ETOH| and other chemicals as result of increasing fuel costs and limited resources for fossil fuels |CITS: [16672461]|. |FRAME: ETOH "Ethanol"| production from lignocellulose is not a straightforward process. |FRAME: CELLULOSE "Cellulose"| and |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| form a complex with |FRAME: Lignins "lignin"| and need to be liberated first by delignification. |FRAME: CELLULOSE "Cellulose"| and |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| then need to be depolymerized to release free sugars such as |FRAME: Glucose "glucose"| and |FRAME: CPD-25028 "xylose"|. These mixed hexose and pentose sugars then require fermentation to produce |FRAME: ETOH| |CITS: [9246788]|., With the release of |FRAME: CELLULOSE| and |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| from delignification, low acid concentrations will hydrolyze |FRAME: Hemicelluloses| into monomeric sugars, while fungal cellulases are required to hydrolyze |FRAME: CELLULOSE| to glucose in a process called saccharification |CITS: [16209550]|. Fermentation of glucose to ethanol is also carried out by fungal cellulases which function optimally at 50°C and pH 5.0 |CITS: [10514249]|. The component pentose sugar of hemicellulose, xylose is not easily converted to ethanol by any organism but can be converted to lactate by lactic acid bacteria using the |FRAME: P122-PWY| pathway |CITS: [1660563]|. |FRAME: Lactate "Lactate"| can be used as a source of lactic acid polymers to create biodegradeable plastics |CITS: [15269531]|. The conversion of xylose to lactate by lactic acid bacteria has limitations industrially as two of the five carbons in the pentose are converted to |FRAME: ACET| |CITS: [11800488]|. , About this Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-1398| is a Gram-positive thermophilic bacterial strain that can grow and ferment at pH 5.0 and temperatures of 60°C, conditions optimal for the hydrolysis of cellulose by fungal cellulases |CITS: [15269531]|. While the type strain, |FRAME: TAX-1121088|, is not able to grow on xylose, three other strains, including |FRAME: TAX-345219|, were able to convert both glucose and xylose to lactate |CITS: [16672461]|. The conversion of xylose to lactate in these organisms utilizes the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY|, unlike in other lactic acid bacteria which utilize the |FRAME: P122-PWY| pathway |CITS: [1660563]|. , It should be noted that while |FRAME: TAX-1398| is thermophilic, and fungal cellulases function optimally at 50°C, one of the enzymes in this pathway |FRAME: CPLX-8356| is thermolabile, and is rendered non-functional at 55°C |CITS: [7462149]|.

Glycerol uptake in |FRAME: TAX-1351| and related organisms occurs through an energy-independent diffusion facilitator (GlpF). Once inside the cell, glycerol can be dissimilated by two pathways, described by |FRAME: PWY-8508| and |FRAME: GLYCEROLMETAB-PWY|., In this pathway |FRAME: GLYCEROL| is phosphorylated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.1.30| (GlpK) to yield |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P|. GlpK activity is inhibited by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and activated by phosphorylation through the general phosphotransferase system (PTS) component Hpr protein |CITS: [17158705]|., The |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| formed is subsequently oxidized to |FRAME: DIHYDROXY-ACETONE-PHOSPHATE| by |FRAME: EC-1.1.3.21| (GlpO). This enzyme uses molecular oxygen as an electron sink and leads to the formation of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE|. As a result, this pathway only operates under aerobic conditions., Exogenous catalase increases the aerobic growth of |FRAME: TAX-1351| on glycerol, indicating that |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| can accumulate to growth-inhibiting concentrations under these conditions |CITS: [19828491]|., In |FRAME: TAX-1351| the |FRAME: EF_RS09230|, |FRAME: EF_RS09240| and |FRAME: EF_RS09235| genes are located in a single operon.

This ethanol degradation pathway begins with conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde by |FRAME: CPLX66-101 "cytosolic alcohol dehydrogenase"|. The resulting acetaldehyde passes into the mitochondrial compartment where it is converted to acetate (by |FRAME: CPLX66-81|). Should acetate be activated to acetyl-CoA within the liver, it would not be oxidized by the Krebs cycle because of the prevailing high ratio of NADH + H / NAD+ within the liver mitochondrial matrix. Consequently, acetate leaves the mitochondrial compartment and the hepatocyte to be metabolised by extra-hepatic tissues |CITS: [SALWAYJG2002]|. Extrahepatic tissues take up acetate where it is converted to acetyl-CoA |CITS: [11420176]|., Four distinct human ethanol degradation pathways have been described - three oxidative pathways and one nonoxidative pathway. All oxidative pathways mediate the oxidation of ethanol to acetaldehye which is then oxidized to acetate for subsequent extra-hepatic activation to acetyl-CoA |CITS: [11420176]|. Oxidative pathways are differentiated based on the enzyme/mechanism by which ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde. The present pathway utilizes cytoplasmic alcohol , dehydrogenase with the other two oxidative pathways utilizing endoplasmic reticulum Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS) (|FRAME: PWY66-161|) and peroxisomal catalase (|FRAME: PWY66-162|), respectively. MEOS is also known as Cytochrome P450 2E1. The nonoxidative pathway is less well characterized but produces fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEEs) as primary end products |CITS: [12456329]|.  , Oxidative and nonoxidative pathways have been demonstrated in a range of tissues including gastric, pancreatic, hepatic and lung. Inhibition of oxidative ethanol degradation pathways raises both hepatic and pancreatic FAEE levels demonstrating that oxidative and nonoxidative pathways are alternative metabolically linked pathways. Pancreatic ethanol metabolism occurs predominantly by the nonoxidative pathway but oxidative routes to acetaldehyde have also been demonstrated in the pancreas - the cytochrome P450 2E1 and alcohol dehydrogenase pathways |CITS: [12870777]|. , Ethanol metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver and the resulting oxidative metabolite acetaldehyde is thought to play a role in alcohol induced liver injury.  Additionally, there is now solid evidence that FAEEs also play a role in alcoholic pancreatitis |CITS:[12065293]|.  Blood and organ levels of FAEEs are raised by ethanol consumption with the highest concentration observed in the pancreas. FAEE generation from ethanol is greater in the pancreas than in any other organ suggesting that the pancreatic pathway contributes to raised blood and organ FAEE levels |CITS: [12065293]|. , Under conditions of acute ethanol consumption, the majority of ethanol is degraded by the hepatic oxidative pathways predominantly the alcohol dehydrogenase mediated pathway.  However, under conditions of chronic ethanol consumption, hepatic MEOS activity and nonoxidative pathways are induced and quantitatively make a greater contribution to ethanol catabolism.  The stimulatory effect of ethanol on Cytochrome P450 2E1 levels results in increased oxygen consumption, production of excess free radicals and increased metabolism of ethanol, vitamin A and testosterone - the chronic effects of which contribute to depletion of antioxidative activity.  Antioxidative deficiency (glutathione, vitamin E, phosphatidylcholine) , and excess free radicals are believed to subsequently contribute to the progression of alcoholic liver disease |CITS: [12901271]|. , Polymorphic loci for genes encoding enzymes of ethanol degradation pathways have been identified and resulting variant isoenzymes characterized and found to exhibit distinct kinetic properties. Indeed, genetically determined differences in ethanol metabolism may, in part, account for the variability of individual susceptibility to the physical complications of alcohol abuse |CITS: [3519419]|.

Summary: Ketone bodies are carbonyl compounds produced as water-soluble byproducts when fatty acids are broken down for energy in the liver (ketogenesis). There are only three endogenous ketone bodies: |FRAME: 3-KETOBUTYRATE|, |FRAME: CPD-335|, and |FRAME: ACETONE|. Ketogenesis occurs primarily in the mitochondrial matrix of liver cells and is important for providing metabolic fuel for peripheral tissues, especially cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle under exertion. The brain normally uses only glucose as its energy source, but during starvation or glucose dysregulation ketone bodies serve as its primary fuel as fatty-acids can not pass the blood-brain barrier. Ketogenesis is the last step of lipid energy metabolism, a superpathway linking dietary lipids and adipose triglycerides to the TCA cycle and the respiratory chain. This pathway has three highly regulated control points, adipocyte lipolysis, mitochondrial fatty acid entry, and HMGCoA synthase |CITS: [14769483]|, Acetoacetate is formed in three reactions: condensation of two molecules of acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA tranferase working in the reverse direction from its function as the final step in beta oxidation |CITS: [17371050]|; condensation of acetoacetyl-CoA with a third acetyl-CoA by HMG-CoA synthase |CITS: [10031425]|; and degradation of HMG-CoA to acetoacetate by HMG-CoA lyase |CITS: [8027038]|. Acetoacetate, a β-keto acid, undergoes spontaneous decarboxylation to acetone. , The liver releases acetoacetate and D-3-hydroxybutyrate from mitochondria, via |FRAME: ENSG00000155380-MONOMER monocarboxylate transporter 1|, into the bloodstream for distribution to peripheral tissues and brain where ketone body utilization occurs |CITS: [18668440]|. In a potentially life-threatening complication of diabetes mellitus (ketoacidosis) accumulation of these acids can lower blood pH beyond the normal buffering capacity and reduces the ability of hemoglobin to bind oxygen |CITS: [20491249]|. Also when acetoacetate is produced faster than it can be metabolized, a buildup of acetone results, giving the breath of diabetics with poorly controlled glucose levels a characteristic sweet smell |CITS: [9727714]|., Under normal conditions the acetyl-CoA starting material for ketogenesis is generated by beta-oxidation of fatty acids derived from triacylglycerols (TAG) which are metabolized in adipose tissue under the control of |FRAME: HS01328-MONOMER hormone-sensitive lipase| |CITS: [12364542]|. This is balanced with |FRAME: GLUCONEO-PWY gluconeogenesis I|, by directing |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID oxaloacetate| out of mitochondria to the cytosol so that acetyl-CoA flux is shifted away from the |FRAME: PWY-5690 TCA cycle variation III (eukaryotic)|, which requires oxaloacetate, and towards ketogenesis |CITS: [1196305]|. During starvation when TAG stores are reduced, certain amino acids can enter the ketogenesis pathway at different points; |FRAME: ILE L-isoleucine| (at acetyl-CoA), |FRAME: PHE L-phenylalanine| and |FRAME: TYR L-tyrosine| (at acetoacetyl-CoA), |FRAME: LEU L-leucine| (at HMG-CoA) and |FRAME: LYS L-lysine| and |FRAME: TRP L-tryptophan| (at acetoacetate).

Summary: The germicidins are a group of natural products produced by Streptomyces species. The first report of germicidin was published in 1993, when it was observed that spores of |FRAME: TAX-1938| released a compound during germination, resulting in inhibition of germination by other spores |CITS: [8360109]|. Four germicidin homologs were reported in 2011 from |FRAME: TAX-100226| |CITS: [21792209]|, followed by reports of additional members of this class from different Streptomyces species |CITS: [21506215][Li13][27507632][29400957][31284448][34272496]|., The spore germination effect of germicidin A is reversible. In addition to inhibiting spore germination, the compound was also found to inhibit hyphal elongation in |FRAME: TAX-100226| |CITS: [21792209]|., The core structure of the gemicidins is produced by a type III polyketide synthase that shows a strong preference toward acyl-carrier protein-bound starter units. The enzyme has a broad substrate range, and can accept different starter and extender units, though it has a clear preference for branched substrates |CITS: [17105255][22480290]|.

Background, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| and |FRAME: GLT| are the most abundant neurotransmitters in mammalian brain, and the |FRAME: GLUDEG-I-PWY "GABA shunt"| is a well known mammalian pathway that mediates the catabolism of |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| and channels |FRAME: GLT| to the |FRAME: PWY66-398|, bypassing two steps of that cycle |CITS: [OLSEN]|. However, the pathway has also been described to occur in plants |CITS: [18155636]| and in bacteria that lack an efficient route between 2-oxoglutarate and succinate in their ricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. For example, the pathway was shown to operate in a sucA mutant of |FRAME: TAX-375| |CITS: [10781553]|., The pathway shown here was described from the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-1148|., About this Pathway, The |FRAME: 2OXOGLUTARATEDEH-RXN "2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex"|, a key member of the "standard" TCA cycle that converts |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| to |FRAME: SUC-COA|, is absent, or not expressed, in many organisms, including obligately autotrophic and methanotrophic bacteria and archaea |CITS: [15449607]| as well as mycobacteria |CITS: [16045627]|. Most cyanobacteria also lack a gene encoding the enzyme |CITS: [4963789][15449607][21282404]|., The absence of this enzyme could theoretically result in incomplete oxidative or reductive TCA cycles that supply biosynthetic intermediates in response to growth conditions (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: P42-PWY|). However, in some cases other enzymes substitute for the missing activity and complete the cycle. For example, some archaea and the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-210| possess the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.2.7.3| (see |FRAME: REDCITCYC|) |CITS: [10091606]|. , In many cyanobacterial species, including |FRAME: TAX-1148|, the role of the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex is replaced by two enzymes, |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.71| and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.79 "EC 1.2.1.79, succinate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase"|, whose combined activities convert 2-oxoglutarate to succinate (see |FRAME: P105-PWY|) |CITS: [22174252]|., However, it was found that |FRAME: TAX-1148| also operates the GABA shunt, providing an alternative route between 2-oxoglutarate and succinate. Furthermore, it was estimated that the shunt contributes 60% of the flux betweeen these metabolites |CITS: [24989231]|.

Summary: Glutamine is the amino group donor for many cellular biosynthetic reactions and serves as a storage reservoir of ammonia, playing an important role in nitrogen metabolism.  In bacteria and archaea |CITS: [9202379]|, glutamine can be converted to glutamate by the reversible, NADPH-utilizing glutamate synthase, (also known as GOGAT for glutamine: α-oxoglutarate aminotransferase).  In eukaryotes and bacteria, glutamine is also converted to glutamate by glutaminase (see pathway |FRAME: GLUTAMINDEG-PWY|) |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986] [VOET04]|., In plants and cyanobacteria, a NADH-dependent glutamate synthase (EC 1.4.1.14) and a ferredoxin-dependent glutamate synthase (EC 1.4.7.1) are found (in |CITS: [10898944]|).  A plant-like NADH-dependent glutamate synthase has been urified from the yeast |FRAME:TAX-4932| |CITS: [7836314]| (see pathways |FRAME: GLUGLNSYN-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-4341|).

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-12185 "Homocarnosine"| is a dipeptide found in abundance in mammalian brain and muscle. In human brain, it is synthesized in both glial cells and subclasses of GABAergic neurons, and its concentration is 100 times higher than that of |FRAME: CARNOSINE|. Organisms have developed mechanisms for defence against oxygen induced damage in their adaptation to living in an aerobic environment. , Reactive oxygen species damage DNA, lipids and proteins, and have been implicated in ageing, cancer and many other diseases. Homocarnosine has been shown to protect against oxidative stress in mammalian brain and muscle, two tissues that have the most active oxidative metabolism |CITS: [3362866]|., Homocarnosine may also be an inhibitory neuromodulator |CITS: [9851440]|. The anti-epileptic drug |FRAME:VIGABATRIN| increases both homocarnosine and GABA concentrations, by inhibiting the activity of |FRAME: CPLX-6886| |CITS:[8156960]|. Epileptic patients given vigabatrin had better seizure control and higher mean homocarnosine levels |CITS: [9851440]|., About this Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-12185 "Homocarnosine"| is synthesized from |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| and |FRAME: HIS| in an ATP dependent reaction catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX66-491| |CITS: [20097752]|. |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in mammalian brain. It is a key mediator of synaptic plasticity and neuroendocrine function |CITS: [15571623]|. Disturbances in the homeostasis of GABA in the brain are implicated in the development of epilepsy, depression, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's chorea, Alzheimer's disease, and Stiff-Man syndrome |CITS: [15571623]|. |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE "GABA"| participates in the |FRAME: GLUDEG-I-PWY| and is degraded via |FRAME: PWY-6535|.

General Background, The uronic acid |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is an aldose sugar containing a carboxyl group. It is the main monomeric constituent of |FRAME: Pectin pectin|, a heteropolymer present in the cell walls of dicotyledonous plants. In pectin the |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| monomers are in the α-pyranose form connected through a 1,4 linkage to form long chains. |FRAME: 1-4-alpha-D-galacturonosyl "Homogalacturonan"| is the simplest form of pectin. Other forms are |FRAME: Rhamnogalacturonans-I "rhamnogalacturonan-I"|, |FRAME: CPD-14581 "rhamnogalacturonan-II"| and |FRAME: Xylogalacturonan xylogalacturonan| (see pathways |FRAME: PWY-1081|, |FRAME: PWY-1061|, and |FRAME: PWY-5980|). In natural pectin the majority of the carboxyl groups of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| are methylated. Some plants also contain acetylated galacturonate residues. Non-esterified carboxyl groups may be linked through divalent cations such as |FRAME: MG+2| or |FRAME: CA+2|, causing pectin to form a gel., |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| is an important carbon source for microorganisms that catabolize plant material. Bacterial pathways for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation have been described. |FRAME:TAX-562| uses the isomerase pathway (see |FRAME: GALACTUROCAT-PWY|). |FRAME: TAX-358| and |FRAME: TAX-80866| use an oxidative pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-6486|). Other bacteria use a different variant of the oxidative pathway (this pathway). A different pathway for |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| degradation has been described for eukaryotic filamentous fungi. That pathway is evolutionarily conserved in the fungal subphylum |FRAME:TAX-147538|, which includes |FRAME: TAX-5061|, |FRAME: TAX-162425| and |FRAME: TAX-51453| |CITS: [18768163][19159926]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6491|)., About This Pathway, Both oxidative pathways begin with the oxidation of |FRAME: D-GALACTURONATE| by the inducible |FRAME: EC-1.1.1.203| to |FRAME: CPD-17138| |CITS: [19060141][19921179]|. The lactone was initially thought to hydrolyze only by a spontaneous reaction |CITS: [2471][19897761]|. Later |FRAME: EC-5.4.1.4| was found, an enzyme that converts |FRAME: CPD-17138| to the 1,4-lactone, as described in |FRAME: PWY-6486|. However, the isomerase, as well as the enzyme that processes its products, are not found in genomes of members of the |FRAME: TAX-135621|, |FRAME: TAX-119060|, and |FRAME: TAX-80864|. Instead, these organisms have dedicated enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124194| and |FRAME: G-124195| genes, that hydrolyze the 1,5-lactones directly to a linear product as shown here |CITS: [30249705]|., With the help of three additional enzymes, two dehydratases and a dehydrogenase, the pathway proceeds to |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-6497|), which can be metabolized via the |FRAME: TCA "TCA cycle"| or used in many other pathways.

General Background, |FRAME: Camphor Camphor| is a bicyclic monoterpene with a characteristic pungent odor and taste. Two enantiomers occur naturally - |FRAME: CPD-862|, the predominant natural isomer, and |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR|. Camphor is produced by several trees, including the camphor tree (|FRAME: TAX-13429|) as well as hundreds of other plants, including |FRAME: TAX-38868| (garden sage), |FRAME: TAX-39367| (rosemary), |FRAME: TAX-39169| (lavender), |FRAME: TAX-35608| (sweet wormwood), and |FRAME: TAX-13328| |CITS: [5532413][ 32619737][35921521]|. A study of enzymes from the camphor tree found multiple terpene synthases, two that lead to production of |FRAME: CPD-862| and one that leads to production of |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| |CITS: [36696798]|., Camphor can be synthesized chemically, as an racemic mixture of the two enantiomers, from |FRAME: CPD-4892|, which is obtained from oil of turpentine. Today most camphor is synthetic. It has a wide range of uses, including as a plasticizer for modified celluloses in lacquers, varnishes, and plastics; as a moth repellente; and as a preservative in cosmetics and embalming fluids. It is also used in medicine as an ingredient in topical creams and ointments to treat itching, irritation, and joint pain. Although it is found in essential oils used in perfumery (such as those of lavender), it significantly diminishes the quality of these oils and reduces their market value. Oils that contain elevated camphor content are usually used as insect repellents and for other non-perfumery uses |CITS: [12112282]|., Even though camphor has been traditionally used in foods and medicines, it is toxic to humans and is especially dangerous to young children. Contact can lead to skin and eye irritation. Ingestion of camphor can cause irritability, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and cardiopulmonary arrest |CITS: [7773898][31223380][38022187][39096231]|. Camphorated oil was removed from the US market in the 1980s due to accidental poisonings., About This Pathway, Tansy (|FRAME: TAX-128002|) produces |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| along with |FRAME: CPD-13996| as its major essential-oil components |CITS: [4552632]|. , A |FRAME: MONOMER-17129| enzyme that produced |FRAME: S-CAMPHOR| from |FRAME: CPD-1908| has been partially purified from this plant |CITS: [Croteau80]|., Tracer isotope studies have shown that tansy leaves catalyze the cyclization of |FRAME: GERANYL-PP| to |FRAME: --bornyl-diphosphate| and the hydrolysis of the latter to |FRAME: CPD-1908| |CITS: [3997807][3970524]|. The labeling pattern was identical to that observed previously for the (+) isomer using enzymes from sage (see |FRAME: PWY-6990|), suggesting the same mechanism of cyclization, but of opposite enantiospecificity, operates in tansy |CITS: [3970524]|., See also |FRAME: PWY-6990|.

Summary: |FRAME: POLYVINYL-ALCOHOL "Polyvinyl alcohol"| (PVA) is a water-soluble synthetic polymer that is used in paper and textile mills and in copolymers as a biodegradable segment. PVA is the only xenobiotic carbon-chain polymer that is known to be biodegradable at high molecular weights |CITS: [16804170]|. The pathway for its degradation has been studied in several organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-41276| |CITS: [820265]|, |FRAME: ORG-6128| |CITS: [Matsumura99]|, |FRAME: ORG-6127| |CITS:[16347841][10746768]| and |FRAME: TAX-292913| |CITS: [15817792]|., The major route of |FRAME: POLYVINYL-ALCOHOL| degradation involves its importation into the periplasm, where it is oxidized by |FRAME: MONOMER-15497| to |FRAME: Oxidized-Polyvinyl-Alcohol|, which is then hydrolyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8028|, releasing acetate monomers., A |FRAME: POLYVINYL-ALCOHOL-OXIDASE-RXN "PVA oxidase"| enzyme has also been reported n earlier works |CITS:[16346065][16346711]|. However, it is not clear whether this enzyme actually exists., PVA dehydrogenase enzymes have been purified from several organisms including |FRAME: TAX-292913|, and all appear to be quinohaemoprotein that contain |FRAME: PQQ| |CITS: [Hatanaka95]|. The enzymes show a somewhat broad substrate specificity with 1, 3-diols, although PVA is the most favorable substrate., The genes encoding these enzymes have been cloned from several organisms |CITS: [16804170][8782398][10746768][15817792]|. In addition, the gene encoding the native cytochrome c from |FRAME: TAX-292913| has been cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. The recombinant cytochrome c was fully reduced by PVA when coupled with a catalytic amount of the recombinant PVA dehydrogenase, suggesting that the cytochrome c is the physiological primary electron acceptor for the enzyme and that PVA dehydrogenation is linked with the respiratory chain in |FRAME: TAX-292913| |CITS: [18343342]|., In |FRAME: TAX-292913| the genes encoding |FRAME: CPLX-8028| (|FRAME: G-11879|), |FRAME: MONOMER-15497| (|FRAME: G-11878|) and cytochrome c (cytC) are located in a single operon on a megaplasmid. The operon is constitutively expressed, although expression is enhanced by PVA |CITS: [18214469]|.
