Summary: General Background, The essential ribonucleoside triphosphates (|FRAME:UTP| and |FRAME:CTP|) can be synthesized either de novo (see |FRAME: PWY0-162|) or by utilizing free pyrimidine bases (|FRAME: URACIL| and |FRAME: CYTOSINE|) or their nucleosides (|FRAME: URIDINE| and |FRAME: CYTIDINE|) by importing them from the environment. Both free bases and nucleosides can be imported into the cell by specialized transporters |CITS:[8982282][22616996][22857534]|. On the other hand, nucleotides (which are phosphorylated) can not be imported due to their negative charge, and thus can not be salvaged from the environment., Salvage is very important for many types of organisms and cells. Studies with the plant |FRAME: TAX-3702| showed that uracil salvage is necessary for early development |CITS: [19563437]| and that uridine salvage plays a crucial role in photoassimilate allocation and partioning |CITS: [21828290]|. The inability to salvage uracil caused a light-dependent dramatic pale-green to albino phenotype, dwarfism and the inability to produce viable progeny in loss-of-function mutants |CITS: [19563437]|. In mammals it is generally accepted that only the liver and kidney maintain de novo pyrimidine and purine synthesis, and supply other tissues and organs, including the brain, with pyrimidine nucleosides (mainly uridine) and purine nucleosides and bases for nucleotide synthesis |CITS: [11782482][15772079][16769123]|. , Any of the pyrimidine bases and pyrimidine nucleosides can in theory serve as a total source of pyrimidine for ribonucleoside triphosphates biosynthesis (and subsequently for deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates synthesis). It is well documented that yeast prefer to salvage nucleobases, while animals prefer the salvage of nucleosides., About This Pathway, In this pathway, the pyrimidine nucleoside |FRAME: CYTIDINE| is first deaminated by |FRAME: CPLX-8106| to |FRAME: URIDINE| |CITS: [10024464][10469156]|, which is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: AT2G36310-MONOMER| to free the pyrimidine base |FRAME: URACIL| by removal of the sugar ribose group |CITS: [19293370]|., The resulting uracil base can be salvaged to form a pyrimidine nucleotide (see |FRAME: PWY-7183| and |FRAME: PWY-7193|). Alternatively, uracil can be degraded to |FRAME: B-ALANINE| by releasing NH3 and CO2 in a three step reductive pathway (|FRAME: PWY-3982|). β-Alanine is a precursor of pentothenate and coenzyme A., The overall metabolic outcome of this pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: CYTIDINE| to |FRAME: URACIL|, can also be achieved by a different pathway, as described in |FRAME: PWY-7195|., Mammals do not have the enzyme |FRAME: AT2G36310-MONOMER| and thus can not salvage uridine by this pathway. Instead they utilize a nucleoside kinase-based pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-7183|).

Aurones are plant flavonoids that provide yellow color to the flowers of some popular ornamental plants. Their structures lack the typical flavonoid skeleton, but they are biosynthetically directly derived from chalcones, the pivotal precursor of all flavonoids. |CITS: [11668535 ]| The higher efficiency in forming the 6-glucosides of aurones compared to their orresponding aglycones suggested a possibility that the chalcone-4-glucosides may be the real substrate for aurone biosynthesis in the flower. |CITS: [11164594]|. That has been demonstrated in |FRAME:TAX-4151| by isolating a chalcone 4'-O-glucosyltransferase that catalyzes the formation of tetra- and pentahydroxychalcone 4'-O-glucosides. Those 4'-O-glucoside intermediates have been converted into their corresponding aurone 6-O-glucosides by aureusidin synthase that preferred the glucosylated chalcones over their aglycones. This enzyme has been shown to be localized in the cytoplasm |CITS: [16832053]|., Interestingly, the aureusidin synthase, a polyphenol oxidase (PPO) that catalyzes the conversion of the tetra- and pentahydroxychalcone to the corresponding aurones aureusidin and bracteatin, respectively has been located in the vacuole lumen |CITS: [16367960]| which is in contrast to all other plant PPO's which have been found associated with plastids |CITS: [VAUGHN88]|. This finding is discussed as conformation for the enzymes molecular characteristics such, as the low optimum pH for catalytic activity and the sugars attached to the molecule |CITS: [16367960]|., Taken together it has been proposed that the 4'-glucosylation of chalcones takes place in the cytoplasm. The chalcone 4'-glucosides are transported to the vacuole where the final conversion to the corresponding aurones is catalyzed. The competition between several pathways (anthocyanin, flavone and aurone biosynthesis) that must share the supply of chalcones has been demonstrated in transgenic Torenia hybrida plants containing both the chalcone 4'-glucosyltransferase and aureusidin synthase from |FRAME:TAX-4151| resulting in increased aurone production when anthocyanin formation was simultaneously downregulated by RNA interference |CITS: [16832053]|.

General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms. Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7027|), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., The alkene hydrocarbon |FRAME: CPD-14266| is the major constituent in the sex pheromone produced by the females of several insects, including the house fly, |FRAME: TAX-7370| |CITS: [5120874]|, the spider |FRAME: TAX-1184414| |CITS: [20462911]|, and the ant |FRAME: TAX-72781| |CITS: [18319215]|. This compound, which functions as a short range attractant and stimulant to males, is produced from a fatty acid by a pathway that involves decarbonylation |CITS: [7937826]|., About This Pathway, Alkanes are produced in multiple organisms - for example, in the |FRAME: PWY-282 "production of plant cuticular waxes"| |CITS: [18251711]|, as insect pheromones |CITS: [7937826][10406089]|, in green algae |CITS: [1898004][15630516]|, in fungi |CITS: [18957585]| and in bacteria |CITS:[ 6025301][15170379]|, especially cyanobacteria, which produce mostly |FRAME: CPD-7946| and |FRAME: HEPTADECANE-CPD| |CITS:[17731762][McInnes80][12495426]|., The alkanes are typically produced from long-chain and very-long chain (20-34) fatty acids that are produced from the "standard" C16 and C18 fatty acids by specialized fatty acid synthase systems, known as elongases (see |FRAME: PWY-5080|). These fatty acids are converted to alkanes in three steps - activation of the fatty acid by an |FRAME: ACP "acyl-carrier-protein"| or |FRAME: CO-A|, reduction of the activated fatty acid to an aldehyde, and decarbonylation of the aldehyde, resulting in an alkane that is one carbon short of the original fatty acid |CITS: [3343228][1608940][12467640]|., Since most fatty acids have an even number of carbons (fatty acids are synthesized by the addition of two carbon units), the resulting alkanes have an odd number of carbons., In the pathway described here, the monounsaturated fatty acid |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD| (in its activated form |FRAME: OLEOYL-COA|), which is produced by the fatty acid synthase complex, is elongated via three cycles of the elongase system to |FRAME: CPD-15363| (gondoyl-CoA), |FRAME: CPD-14293| (erucoyl-CoA), and |FRAME: CPD-14269|, respectively. |FRAME: CPD-14269| is then reduced to an aldehyde, and decarbonylated to form |FRAME: CPD-14266|., Incubation of |FRAME: CPD-14268| with microsomes from |FRAME: TAX-7370| (house fly) gave equal amounts of |FRAME: CPD-14266| and CO2. Incubation of |FRAME: CPD-14269| with the microsomal preparations in the presence of NADPH and O2 gave almost equal amounts of |FRAME: CPD-14267| and |FRAME: CPD-14266|. The aldehyde was efficiently converted to |FRAME: CPD-14266| only in the presence of both NADPH and O2 |CITS: [7937826]|. Thus, the mechanism for hydrocarbon biosynthesis in the housefly is similar to that reported for algae, plants, and animals in that a fatty acid is activated to an acyl-CoA, reduced to the corresponding fatty aldehyde, and decarbonylated to an alkane., Unlike the aldehyde decarbonylase of higher plants and green algae, which produce carbon monoxide, and those from cyanobacteria, which produce formate, the insect enzyme produces carbon dioxide. The reaction was inhibited by an antibody to cytochrome P450 reductase, suggesting that the insect aldehyde decarbonylase is a cytochrome P450 enzyme |CITS: [7937826]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria. This pathway incorporates generic reactions that do not specify the number of isoprene units in the side chain.

Summary: Glycerophospholipids are the fundamental building blocks of eukaryotic and bacterial membranes. The primary glycerophospholipids found in bacteria are |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-ETHANOLAMINE phosphatidylethanolamine| (PE), |FRAME: L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL phosphatidylglycerol| (PG), and |FRAME: CARDIOLIPIN cardiolipin| (CL). Cardiolipin is a diphosphatidylglycerol, composed of two |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE phosphatidate| molecules covalently linked to a molecule of glycerol at positions 1 and 3. It is an abundant anionic lipid in bacteria and in eukaryotes , where it is exclusively present in the inner mitochondrial membrane., Cardiolipin was first isolated from beef heart |CITS: [Pangborn42]|, hence its name. Many enzymes involved in energy metabolism interact with cardiolipin. |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.9|, also known as Complex IV, requires two associated cardiolipin molecules in order to maintain its full enzymatic function |CITS: [8389748]|. |FRAME: EC-7.1.1.8| (cytochrome bc1, Complex III) also needs cardiolipin to maintain its quaternary structure and functional role |CITS: [10413476]|. |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2| (Complex V) binds four molecules of cardiolipin |CITS: [2147180]|., The metabolic pathways and enzymes involved in biosynthesis of the major phospholipids (PE, PG and CL) are well conserved in bacteria and have been studied extensively. Biosynthesis starts with a two-step acylation of |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| via |FRAME: ACYL-SN-GLYCEROL-3P lysophosphatidate| (LPA) to |FRAME: L-PHOSPHATIDATE phosphatidate| (PA). Two different systems catalyze this process: the PlsB/PlsC system, and the the PlsX/PlsY/PlsC system. PA is then converted to the central precursor of all phospholipids, |FRAME: CDPDIACYLGLYCEROL CDP-diacylglycerol| by |FRAME: EC-2.7.7.41|., The combined action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.8|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.1.65| produces PE, the most abundant zwitterionic membrane lipid., The combined action of |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.5|, and |FRAME: EC-3.1.3.27| produces PG, a negatively charged lipid., Various CL synthesis pathways have been described. In most bacteria it is formed by a reversible transesterification, reaction of two PG molecules, catalyzed by |FRAME: CARDIOLIPSYN-MONOMER|/|FRAME: G6406-MONOMER|. Some bacteria possess |FRAME: G6551-MONOMER|, which condenses one molecule of PE and one molecule of PG. Yet actinobacteria and some proteobacteria use |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.41|, which condenses CDP-DAG and PG.

Even though the the involved genes were functionally characterized only in |FRAME: TAX-62977|, the gene clusters share 75% identity, suggesting the enzymes are similar in both organisms., The cluster contains genes encoding enzymes for |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| biosynthesis, three non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (|FRAME: E5A72_RS01990|, |FRAME: E5A72_RS01985|, |FRAME: E5A72_RS01980|), and additional genes. The three non-ribosomal peptide synthases combine two molecules of |FRAME: 2-3-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| and two molecules of |FRAME: SER| to form |FRAME: CPD-26852| attached to |FRAME: E5A72_RS01980-MONOMER|. The C-terminal C domain of that protein catalyzes the release of the bound intermediate by nucleophilic attack of |FRAME: CPD-26851|, resulting in the formation of |FRAME: CPD-26845| |CITS: [23456955]|.

Summary: In this pathway homocysteine is condensed with serine to form |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE| in an, irreversible reaction, catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-5162|., The enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-5163| then cleaves of the C-γ-S bond of |FRAME:L-CYSTATHIONINE|, yielding |FRAME:CYS|, |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| and |FRAME:AMMONIA| in a transsulfuration reaction (reviewed in |CITS: [3309559], [15539209]|). |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be degraded further into TCA cycle intermediates (see |FRAME: PWY-5130|)., This is part of the most common |FRAME: MET| degradation pathway in mammals (see |FRAME:PWY-5328|). Under normal metabolic conditions, essentially all of the sulfur derived from methionine degradation is transferred to cysteine before the sulfur atom is oxidized and excreted (reviewed in |CITS: [15189131]|)., The amino acid |FRAME: CYS| has important roles in protein structure and function, including the catalytic activity of some enzymes.  It is also a component of |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| and |FRAME:Thioredoxin|, which maintain a reducing environment inside the cell., In animals, cysteine derives its carbon and nitrogen from |FRAME: SER|, and its sulfur from |FRAME: MET| (reviewed in |CITS: [3309559]|).

Summary: The primary nitrogen assimilation routes in photosynthetic eukaryotes and prokaryotes are |FRAME: Nitrogen-Fixation "nitrogen fixation"|, |FRAME: PWY-381 "nitrate assimilation"|, and ammonia assimilation., Ammonia is liberated by |FRAME: PWY-181|, protein and amino acid metabolism, and the breakdown of nitrogen transport compounds. The rate of ammonia generation during photorespiration is about 10 times the rate of nitrate assimilation., The ammonia released from photorespiration is immediately re-assimilated via the ammonia assimilation cycle. The net result of this cycle is the conversion of one molecule of ammonia to one molecule of glutamate at the expense of one ATP molecule., The pathway includes two steps catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-4585 "glutamine synthetase"| (GS) and |FRAME: MONOMER-7421 "glutamate synthase"| (also known as glutamine oxoglutarate aminotansferase or GOGAT), and thus is often referred to as the GS/GOGAT pathway. Two types of GOGAT are known in photosynthetic organisms - NADH-dependent, and ferredoxin-dependent. NADH-GOGAT is found in the nucleus of vascular plants, fungi, and diatoms. The ferredoxin-dependent enzyme is only found in Cyanobacteria and photosynthetic eukaryotes (see |FRAME: PWY-6964|). , An NADPH-dependent version of GOGAT is found in non-photosynthetic bacteria and archaea (see |FRAME: AMMASSIM-PWY|).

Summary: General Background, While the jury is still out about whether Napoleon Bonaparte died of arsenic poisoning or cancer |CITS: [367316][6750413]|, it is agreed by all that arsenic is a potent toxicant. Indeed, the results of exposure to high arsenic concentration in drinking water in West Bengal, India, and Bangladesh are considered by some to be the worst public health disaster in recent history |CITS: [15276412]|. The form of arsenic influences the type and severity of toxicity. Arsenate (AsV) is a structural analog of phosphate, and inhibits phosphorylation processes. For example, ADP-arsenate spontaneously hydrolyzes, resulting in uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation |CITS: [518594]|, while arsenite (AsIII) has a very high affinity for thiol groups, and thus binds to and inhibits many key enzymes that have thiol groups in their active sites. In addition, inorganic arsenic is a potent carcinogen |CITS: [12505313]|., Arsenic exists in two oxidation states, AsIII and AsV. In aerobic environments most of the inorganic arsenic is found as AsV, and in neutral pH the common species is |FRAME: ARSENATE|. Most (but not all) of the inorganic AsIII in neutral pH exists as the non-charged species |FRAME: CPD0-2040|., Both AsV and AsIII compounds can enter the cell. |FRAME: ARSENATE Arsenate| is chemically similar to phosphate, and enters the cell via the phosphate transport systems, such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| |FRAME: PITA-MONOMER| and |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX| systems. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenious acid"| is a polyol similar to glycerol, and can enter cells via bidirectional channels that allow water and small uncharged molecules like glycerol to pass through (such as |FRAME: EG10396 GlpF| of |FRAME: TAX-562| and aquaglyceroporins). The absorption rate of |FRAME: ARSENATE| is much lower than that of |FRAME: CPD0-2040|, and the role of phosphate transporters in the uptake of arsenic appears to be limited. For example, bacterial periplasmic phosphate-binding proteins discriminate phosphate over |FRAME: CPD0-2040| more than 500- to 850-fold (up to 4500-fold in the extremely arsenic-resistance species |FRAME: TAX-1118153|) |CITS: [32435915]|. , Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes reduce intracellular arsenate to arsenite. However, prokaryotes and single-cell eukaryotes can pump arsenite out of the cell by using a dedicated pump (such as the |FRAME: G3O-34321-MONOMER Acr3| or |FRAME: CPLX-7 ArsB|), multicellular organisms require other means of getting rid of the metal. Certain mammals, including humans, methylate arsenite to several methylated forms that are oxidized to non-toxic methylated As(V) forms and excreted from the organism in the urine., About This Pathway, Arsenic compounds can enter the plant cell by similar mechanisms to those observed in other organisms. Since |FRAME: ARSENATE| is chemically similar to phosphate, it enters most cells via phosphate transporters such as the |FRAME: MONOMER-21678|. |FRAME: CPD0-2040 "Arsenous acid"|, the neutral form of |FRAME: CPD-763|, can enter the cell via aquaglyceroproteins such as |FRAME: MONOMER-21673| in |FRAME: TAX-3702| or |FRAME: MONOMER-21679| in rice |CITS: [16572174][19029297]|., Once inside cells, |FRAME: ARSENATE| is reduced to the more txoic |FRAME: CPD-763| by |FRAME: EC-1.20.4.1|. There has been some controversy about the identity of the gene encoding the enzyme in plants. The |FRAME: TAX-3702| genome, as well as the genomes of several other plants, contain homologs of the yeast |FRAME: G3O-34320| gene (such as atACR2), and these genes were claimed to encode the plant arsenate reductase |CITS: [16507083][16766666][17388894]|. There were several indications that the gene functions as an arsenate reductase - for example, it was able to complement an |FRAME: TAX-562| arsenate reductase mutant, and an AtACR2 knockout line showed no arsenate reductase activity |CITS: [15834011]| and displayed a strong As(V)-sensitive phenotype |CITS: [16567632]|., However, in 2012 it was shown that knocking out ACR2 does not affect arsenic redox status in |FRAME: TAX-3702|, and it was suggested that the gene does not encode a functional arsenate reductase |CITS: [22879969]|. A different gene, |FRAME: AT2G21045|, was discovered in 2014, and appeared to encode an active enzyme |CITS: [25464340][25099865][28695678]|. When expressed in an |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: EG12237| mutant, the gene complemented the mutation, resulting in a similar As(V) resistance to the wild type strain |CITS: [25099865]|., Unlike mammals, plants do not have an |FRAME: EC-2.1.1.137|, and arsenite must be exported. In contrast to yeast, mammals, and many microorganisms in which arsenic species form complexes with glutatione, in plants detoxification of arsenic has been shown to mainly depend on |FRAME: Poly-Gamma-Glutamylcysteine-Glycines phytochelatins| (PCs) |CITS: [10368185][16313638][20192735][20130102]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6745|). Vacuolar transporters such as |FRAME: AT1G30400-MONOMER| (|FRAME: AT1G30400|) have been shown to export the arsenite-phytochelatin complexes into the vacuoles, where presumably the complex is broken down, leaving the arsenic inside the vacuole while the phytochelatin is exported back into the cytoplasm., An additional route for arsenite export has been reported in some plants such as rice that have dedicated silicon transporters. The |FRAME: G-107426| gene encodes an active efflux transporter, driven by the proton gradient across the plasma membrane. While the transporter's physiological role is to transport silicon out of root cells so that it could be translocated to the xylem, it is also transporting arsenite outside the cell |CITS: [17625566][18626020]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Quinolones Quinolone| alkaloids are found in diverse types of organisms and exhibit a variety of biological activities, including antibacterial, antimalarial, antiviral and antitumor activities |CITS: [19442143][22365088]|., TThe quinolone compound |FRAME:CPD-18297| was isolated from the ascomycete |FRAME: TAX-60134| in 1953. At that time it was reported to have no antibiotic activity against a number of organisms, with the exception of some activity against |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [13032073]|. It was later observed in other fungi species including |FRAME: TAX-60167| |CITS:[Luckner62][Luckner80]|, |FRAME: TAX-293373| |CITS:[5487865]|, and |FRAME: TAX-36656| |CITS: [Taniguchi70]|. Despite the early reports, the compound was reported to exhibit strong antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive bacteria and inhibition of the growth of rice seedlings |CITS: [Taniguchi70]|., Organisms that produce |FRAME:CPD-18297| were found to also produce |FRAME: Benzodiazepine-Alkaloids "benzodiazepine alkaloids"| |CITS: [11947032][5823102]|, and the backbone of quinolones such as |FRAME:CPD-18297|, |FRAME:CPD-18303|, and |FRAME:CPD-18304| has been proposed to be formed via benzodiazepinediones |CITS:[Smith69][17036148]|., The benzodiazepinediones originate from the condensation of |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and an amino acid |CITS:[Luckner62]|, carried out by nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) (summarized in |CITS:[23659680]|). The NRPS |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.40|, which produces |FRAME:CPD-15014| from |FRAME:ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME:PHE|, was initially partially purified from |FRAME: TAX-60167| |CITS:[2995633][Gerlach85]|, and later purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-162425| |CITS: [25251934]|., The following steps |CITS:[11947032] [15121720]| are catalyzed by the |FRAME: G-44196|-encoded dioxygenase that performs a complex transformation consisting of two oxidation reactions, a desaturation that produces a double bond, and a monooxygenation of the double bond that forms an epoxide |CITS:[25251934]|., The epoxidation reaction provides the condition for the rearrangement of the 6,7-bicyclic |FRAME: Benzodiazepines benzodiazepine| structure into the 6,6-bicyclic |FRAME: Quinolones quinolone| structure, a reaction catalyzed by a cyclopenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124168| gene |CITS:[30026518]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MET| (Met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in protein biosynthesis, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines. In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., Some bacteria can synthesize methionine using organic sulfur through transsulfuration of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE| with |FRAME: CYS| to form |FRAME: L-CYSTATHIONINE|. Cystathionine is then cleaved to |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is methylated to methionine (this pathway) |CITS: [3309561]|. Plants use a modification of this pathway, where |FRAME: O-PHOSPHO-L-HOMOSERINE|, instead of |FRAME: O-SUCCINYL-L-HOMOSERINE|, is the intermediate converting homoserine to cystathionine (see |FRAME: PWY-702|)., Other bacteria, as well as yeast and fungi, can use a different route in which they directly assimilate inorganic sulfur by a sulfhydrylation (see |FRAME:HSERMETANA-PWY|). In that route |FRAME: HS|, the final product of microbial sulfate reduction (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|) reacts with O-acetylated homoserine, with replacement of the acetyl group by sulfide to form |FRAME: HOMO-CYS|, which is once again methylated to methionine (see |FRAME: PWY-5344|)., Most methanogenic archaea utilize yet a different pathway. While these organisms also use |FRAME: HS| as the sulfur source, the other precursor for |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| production is |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE|, produced from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-7977|)., Methylation of |FRAME: HOMO-CYS| is catalyzed by either a cobalamin-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.13 "EC 2.1.1.13"|) or a cobalamin-independent enzyme (|FRAME: EC-2.1.1.14 "EC 2.1.1.14"|), depending upon the species or growth conditions |CITS: [9409150][12948640]|., About This Pathway, While many organisms seem to contain both routes for methionine biosynthesis, in |FRAME:TAX-562| and other enteric bacteria only the transsulfuration pathway is used (Greene, R.C. in |CITS: [COLISAL]| pp. 542-560). Published evidence for these pathways includes gene identification; complementation of known mutants; analysis of mutant phenotypes; and gene cloning, expression, and enzyme activity assays., The presence of |FRAME: EC-2.5.1.49| was considered indicative of the presence of a direct sulfhydrylation pathway., Note that all bacterial methionine biosynthetic pathways involve acylated homoserine. However, the O-acyl group is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast, and most Gram-positive bacteria (see |FRAME: HSERMETANA-PWY|) but a succinyl group in enteric bacteria and some other Gram-negative bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-287| and |FRAME:TAX-303| (this pathway) (|CITS: [10482527][3309561][9409150]|).

The monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and the xylene isomers , (o-, m-, and p-), collectively know as BTEX, are some of the most water-soluble , constituents of gasoline and are toxic. Consequently, BTEX compounds pose a particular threat to human, health and the environment because once released into the environment, they can migrate readily wtih , water, and eventually contaminate drinking water supplies. BTEX compounds have become prevalent soil, and groundwater contaminants as a result of leaking underground storage tanks, and improper handling , and disposal of gasoline., Aromatic compounds are important growth substrates for microorganisms. Initially, it was believed that, these compounds could only be degraded under aerobic conditions, i.e., in the presence of molecular, oxygen. Aerobic degradation of aromatic compounds is characterized by the use of molecular oxygen,, which is used in the initial oxidative attack of the aromatic compound, and subsequently in the, cleavage of the aromatic ring structure |CITS: [1368147]|. Thus, by definition, degradation of aromatic , compounds under anaerobic conditions, i.e., in the absence of molecular oxygen, requires a, completely different strategy. BTEX compounds were initially believed to be, recalcitrant to anaerobic degradation due to the resonance stability of their aromatic ring structure, and their lack of any reactive functional groups. However, beginning around 1990, microbiological , research began to demonstrate that particular microorganisms can anaerobically degrade such aromatic, compounds. Since then several bacterial pure cultures have been isolated that can anaerobically , degrade BTEX compounds. Several denitrifying bacteria, which belong to the β-subclass of , proteobacteria |CITS: [2244785][10515931][8590677][7710331][9172330]|, and one sulfate-reducing , bacterium, which belongs to the δ-subclass of proteobacteria |CITS: [10049854]| have been isolated, that can degrade m-xylene under anaerobic conditions. , The initial steps of anaerobic m-xylene degradation were elucidated in |FRAME:TAX-12960| sp. , strain T, a denitrifying bacterium capable of anaerobically degrading m-xylene to carbon dioxide, and water. The initial reactions of anaerobic m-xylene , degradation are analogous to those of anaerobic toluene degradation, |CITS: [10515931][8706665][9006019]|. In fact, the same enzyme, benzylsuccinate synthase/, (3-methylbenzyl)succinate synthase, catalyzes the first step of anaerobic degradation of toluene and , m-xylene |CITS: [11698363]|. It is interesting to note that all of the m-xylene-degrading, bacteria isolated thus far can also degrade toluene, but the reverse is not true |CITS: [HEIDER99]| . Only, some of the toluene-degrading bacteria can degrade m-xylene as well. , The last step shown in this pathway, (3-methylphenyl)itaconyl-CoA to 3-methylbenzoyl-CoA is postulated to be comprised of three , individual reactions (see the analogous reactions in the anaerobic toluene degradation pathway). , However, the intermediates of these three reactions have yet to be demonstrated.

General Background, |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOADENOSINE| (MTA) is a side product in the biosynthesis of several important compounds., An important case is polyamine synthesis, where |FRAME: MET| is consumed through the utilization of |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| (SAM) in a reaction that releases MTA (see the pathway |FRAME:POLYAMINSYN3-PWY|). MTA is a strong inhibitor of polyamine biosynthesis and transmethylation reactions, and its concentration needs to be tightly regulated., Another example is found in the pathogen |FRAME: TAX-287|, where MTA is a by product in the synthesis of the autoinducer compounds |FRAME: CPD-10783| and |FRAME: CPD-10784| (see |FRAME: PWY-6157|)., To ensure that the pathways that produce MTA as a byproduct are not blocked, the organism must remove this compound. The most common way of achieving it is through the |FRAME: PWY-4361 "methionine salvage"| pathway, in which MTA is recycled through a series of reactions back to AMP and |FRAME: MET|., While the methionine salvage pathway is widely conserved, its initial steps, converting MTA to |FRAME:CPD-444|, differ among microorganisms and plants (such as the bacteria |FRAME: TAX-573| |CITS: [8694776]| and |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [12022921]|), protozoans (such as |FRAME: TAX-5741| and |FRAME: TAX-5833| |CITS: [2854458]|) and mammalian cells. The different routes employed by these organisms are described in the different pathways under |FRAME: Methylthioadenosine-Degradation|., About This Pathway, In the pathogenic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-287| MTA is converted in two steps to |FRAME: CPD-444|, via deamination to |FRAME: 5-METHYLTHIOINOSINE| followed by phosphorolysis to hypoxanthine and |FRAME: CPD-444|. This pathway also exists in some archaea such as |FRAME: TAX-2190| |CITS: [24375099]| and in |FRAME: TAX-5833|, where |FRAME: MONOMER-16357| catalyzes the first reaction and |FRAME: CPLX-8258| (PNP) catalyzes the second reaction |CITS: [15576366]|. |FRAME: TAX-5833| is not capable of synthesizing purine de novo and relies on purine salvage. |FRAME: HYPOXANTHINE Hypoxanthine|, which is formed in this pathway, has been reported to be the major purine precursor for purine salvage in this organism |CITS: [11707439]|., In mammalian cells, MTA is transformed to MTRP in one step by |FRAME:CPLX-1163|, yielding adenine and MTRP (see |FRAME: PWY-6756|). Theis metabolic difference is being exploited for developing new drugs targeted against pathogenic organisms that utilize the MTA nucleosidase-MTR kinase pathway |CITS: [2854458][2153115][1929327]|.

Summary: Tropane alkaloids are found mostly in plants that belong to the |FRAME: TAX-4070| family. They include the medicinal alkaloids |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE| and |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE| that act on mammalian nervous systems. The alkaloids have very complex structures. The commercial natural sources of the alkaloids are plants in the genera of |FRAME: TAX-195735|, |FRAME: TAX-221161|, and |FRAME: TAX-4074|., The pathway has been studied in detail, and currently all of the enzymes involved have been discovered., There are two tropinone reductases, which catalyze the stereo-specific reduction of tropinone and give rise to separate alkaloid groups, encoded by |FRAME: G-10563| and |FRAME: G-10566| |CITS: [16653065]|. The medicinal alkaloids |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE| and |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE| are derived from |FRAME: TROPINE|, the product of tropinone reductase I (|FRAME: G-10563|), while the calystegines, a family of non-medicinal nortropane alkaloids, are derived from |FRAME: PSEUDOTROPINE|, the product of tropinone reductase II (|FRAME: G-10566|) (see |FRAME: PWY-5318|)., |FRAME: TROPINE Tropine| condenses with the phenylalanine-derived |FRAME: CPD-24928| to form |FRAME: CPD-7996| |CITS: [ 31705812]|, which is converted to |FRAME: L-HYOSCYAMINE|, and subsequently to |FRAME: SCOPOLAMINE| via |FRAME: CPD-2202|.  , Enzymes catalyzing different steps of scopolamine biosynthesis, specifically, the tropinone reductase and hyoscyamine 6-hydroxylase, were detected in different cell compartments and cell types, suggesting that the pathway intermediates are transported, crossing different compartments and cell types |CITS: [10635114]|.

tRNAs are the molecular adapters that carry amino acids and enable the synthesis of proteins based on mRNAs transcribed from protein-coding genes. The active form of tRNA is generated by a combination of nuclease-based processing, the modification of select nucleosides, and finally charging with an amino acid via the |FRAME: TRNA-CHARGING-PWY|., The processing of tRNA in |FRAME: TAX-2157| and |FRAME: TAX-2759| involves the splicing of introns by a mechanism that involves three protein enzymes (unlike mRNA splicing, which is RNA catalyzed). While there are some examples of tRNA intron splicing in prokaryotes, that process occurs via the so called "primitive" autocatalytic mechanism and does not involve dedicated enzymes., Much of the knowledge about tRNA intron splicing comes from the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932|. The S. cerevisiae genome contains 272 tRNA genes of which 59, encoding ten different tRNAs, contain introns. These introns are 14-60 bases in length, and all interrupt the anticodon loop immediately 3' to the anticodon |CITS: [6096826]|. It has been estimated that ~500 000 molecules of tRNA are spliced per generation in yeast |CITS: [15684411]|., Splicing of the introns from the precursor tRNA is accomplished through the action of a site-specific |FRAME: CPLX-8216|, a |FRAME: G3O-31543-MONOMER|, and a |FRAME: G3O-33500-MONOMER|. The tRNA splicing endonuclease, a complex of four different subunits, cleaves pre-tRNA at the 5' and 3' splice sites to release the intron. The products of this cleavage are an intron and two tRNA half-molecules, one bearing a 2',3' cyclic phosphate terminus and the other bearing a 5'-OH terminus |CITS: [6186398]|. tRNA ligase covalently joins the two half-molecules through a complex series of ATP-dependent reactions |CITS: [3277966][8428919][8428918]|. After ligation, a 2' phosphate remains at the splice junction and is removed by a specific |FRAME: G3O-33500-MONOMER| |CITS: [9148937]|., During the process of tRNA splicing |FRAME: CPD-9007| is formed as a by-product. This compound is recycled back to |FRAME: ADENOSINE_DIPHOSPHATE_RIBOSE| by the action of two enzymes - |FRAME: YGR247W-MONOMER| and |FRAME: G3O-29003-MONOMER| |CITS: [10734185][15684411]|/

Summary: General Background, Fusidane-type antibiotics are a group of fungi-derived 29-nor-protostane triterpenoid antibiotics that are characterized by a Z-configured double bond between C17 and C20, a C21 carboxylic acid, and a 16-O acetyl group in the protostadienol framework. All of the fusidane-type antibiotics exhibit potent bacteriostatic activity against Gram-positive bacteria, targeting elongation factor G (EF-G) to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis |CITS: [4900137][16489743][19833919]|. Since they are the only known clinically used antibiotics that target EF-G, they have little cross-resistance with other commonly used antibiotics |CITS: [4900137][4945809][24336183]|., |FRAME: CPD0-1606 "Fusidic acid"| was first isolated in 1958 from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-41833| under the name ramycin |CITS: [13525656]|. It was isolated again in 1960 from the fungus |FRAME: TAX-475927| (at the time known as Fusidium coccineum) by a group of scientists from the Danish firm Leo Pharmaceutical Products, who named it fusidic acid. Its accurate stereo configuration was reported in 1964 |CITS: [5855867]|, and in the following year it was recognized that ramycin and fusidic acid are identical |CITS: [14287421]|. The compound has been used clinically since 1962 for the treatment of both topical and systemic infections caused by |FRAME: TAX-1280| |CITS: [13899435][13996455][5425879]|, though it is not approved for marketing in the United States., The gene cluster encoding the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD0-1606| was identified in the sequenced genome of the fungus |FRAME: TAX-749674| in 2019 and found the contain eight genes |CITS: [30972287]|. Since the first six reactions are conserved in the biosynthesis of fusidane-type antibiotics, the enzymes catalyzing the first six reactions are similar (37%-65% identity) to the previously characterized enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-330879|, which are involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13284| |CITS: [29158519]|., About This Pathway, The pathway begins with |FRAME: EC-5.4.99.32|, which converts the common precursor |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE| to |FRAME: CPD-13283|. Next, a cytochrome P450 encoded by |FRAME: G-124773| catalyzes three successive oxidations of the C-4β methyl group, resulting in a carboxylate at that position., The pathway continues with hydroxylation at position 16, catalyzed by a second P450 enzyme (encoded by |FRAME: G-124774|), acetylation of the new hydroxyl group by the acetyltransferase |FRAME: G-124775 FusD|, and introduction of a second carboxylate at position C20, which is catalyzed by a third P450 enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-124776|., At this point, a hydrogenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124777| gene oxidizes the 3β-ol group to a carbonyl group, which triggers decarboxylation of the 4β carboxylate, forming |FRAME: CPD-27370|. Thus the FusB4 and FusC2 enzymes form a system that removes one methyl group from the C-4 position of the 4,4-dimethylated steroid substrate. This system acts preferentially on the 4β-methyl group, which is similar to the bacterial enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.246|, and differs from the animal/fungal enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.9|, and the plant enzymes |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.10| and |FRAME: EC-1.14.18.11|. In those systems that act on the 4α carbon, the remaining methyl group isomerizes from β to α configuration, enabling the enzymes to remove the second methyl group. However, in fusidane-type antibiotics, the remaining 4α methyl is unlikely to change configuration, and thus the compounds retain one methyl group at that position., The pathway is completeted by the action of two more enzymes. A fourth P450 enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124779| gene, introduces a hydroxyl group at position 11, and a hydrogenase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124780| reduces the carbonyl group at position 3 to an α-hydroxyl group |CITS: [30972287]|.

Summary: |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE α-Cyclopiazonate| has been first isolated and characterized as mycotoxin from Penicillium cyclopium |CITS:[5636916]| but has also been found in a number of Aspergillus species. Special interest has been paid to this mycotoxin because of its joint occurrence with aflatoxin (see |FRAME:PWY-5961|) |CITS:[108598]| contaminating agricultural products such as corn and peanuts |CITS:[11665730]| and causing the so called 'Turkey X' disease in livestock when feed is infested |CITS:[23604830]|. It appears that the close neighborhood of the aflatoxin gene cluster and cyclopiazonate gene cluster, which has been found in the genome of Aspergillus flavus, may provide an explanation for that phenomenon |CITS:[19038354]|. |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE α-Cyclopiazonate| is also known as a nanomolar inhibitor of the sarcoplasmic Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) |CITS:[2530215]| obstructing the corresponding calcium pump |CITS:[17259168]| by means of blocking key residues near the ATP binding site |CITS:[19289472]|., The biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| is a short, three step pathway in which a decorated 2,5-pyrrolidinedione (also referred to as tetramate) ring system is generated. The tetramate ring structure represents a well-known pharmacophore element which has been attributed with a broad variety of biological activities |CITS:[18334299]|. , The first step of the pathway is carried out by a hybrid polyketide (PKS)-nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) which is organized in cooperating modules that form the assumed intermediate |FRAME: Acetoacetyl-ACPs| from |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| attached to |FRAME:ACP| (PKS activity) and tethered to the PKS-NRPS module which, after adding |FRAME:TRP| is cyclized and released as the three ring structured |FRAME:CPD-17072| (NRPS activity). The activity of this PKS-NRPS enzyme has been shown in Penicillium cyclopium |CITS:[McGrath77]|. In addition, the corresponding genes in Aspergillus flavus, i.e. CpaS |CITS:[19663400] [19410456]| and CpaA in Aspergillus oryzae |CITS:[18854220]| have been identified, heterologously expressed and the two PKS-NRPS's biochemically characterized. , In the subsequent reaction the formed |FRAME:CPD-17072| is prenylated by a cyclo-acetoacetyl-L-tryptophan dimethylallyltransferase encoded by CpaD which gives rise to |FRAME:BETA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| |CITS:[19877600]|. The last step of the |FRAME:PWY-7555| is carried out by a |FRAME:FAD| dependent β-cyclopiazonate oxidocyclase (CpaO) which realizes both the dehydrogenation reaction (forming a double bond) and subsequent cyclization generating the five ring structure of |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE|. The enzymatic activity of CpaO has been investigated in Penicillium cyclopium |CITS:[5143339] [5143340] [4731971]| and Aspergillus oryzae |CITS:[21608094]|. Although |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| is the final product in most fungal |FRAME:ALPHA-CYCLOPIAZONATE| producers it appears to be the next to last intermediate of an longer pathway in Aspergillus oryzae (see |FRAME:PWY-7558|) |CITS:[21608094]|.

Organophosphates are a major class of synthetic compounds that have been used extensively as insecticides, fungicides, and herbicides. These compounds, being potent cholinesterase inhibitors (see |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.7| and |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.8|) are extremely toxic to most animals including humans (in which LD50 is 5 to 10 mg/kg), and may cause death by inducing respiratory failure., All organophosphates are susceptible to hydrolysis, resulting in the release of an ionic phosphorus-containing moiety, most often an ionic dialkyl phosphate, an arylphosphonate, or a sulfur analog of these. Examples include |FRAME:CPD-8974| (DMTP), |FRAME:DIETHYLTHIOPHOSPHATE| (DETP) and |FRAME:DIETHYLPHOSPHATE| (DEP), which are the degradation products of |FRAME:CPD-8973|, |FRAME:PARATHION| and |FRAME:PARAOXON|, respectively., Several studies have demonstrated that microorganisms are capable of degrading these phosphorus-containing comopounds, and even utilizing them as the sole source of phosphorus |CITS:[1254803][727784][16345521]|. In addition, several mixed cultures were shown to degrade |FRAME:DIETHYLTHIOPHOSPHATE| |CITS:[16347763][16987656]|, but the exact nature of this degradation pathway is not known yet., |FRAME: TAX-80866| is one of the organisms investigated by Cook et al that can grow with DMTP, DEP and DETP as sole sources of phosphorus |CITS: [16345521]|. Recently, the |FRAME:CPLX-7319| enzyme responsible for catalyzing these reactions has been isolated from this organism and characterized |CITS: [12514034]|. , Even though the reaction has not been thouroughly characterized, it is believed that ethanol is the product of cleavage of the alkoxy groups of DEP, based on previous studies with an enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-548| |CITS: [168197]|. Surprisingly |FRAME: TAX-80866| is not able to utilize DEP as the sole carbon source even though it is capable of growing on ethanol. The authors suggest that the discrepancy may result from the amount of the enzyme being too low to satisfy the cells carbon demand |CITS: [16345521]|.

Summary: |FRAME: Ubiquitins Ubiquitin| is a small (76-amino-acids), highly-conserved (almost invariant from yeast to man) regulatory protein that is ubiquitously expressed in eukaryotes., Many proteins are modified post-translationally by the covalent attachment of one or more ubiquitin monomers, a process known as ubiquitination or ubiquitylation., Protein ubiquitination has many functions: it can signal for degradation of the modified protein via the proteasome |CITS: [11917093]|, alter the protein's cellular location |CITS: [17218518]|, affect it's activity, and promote or prevent interactions with other proteins |CITS: [12860974]|. The different fates of the proteins are determined by the pattern of ubiquitylation, as described below., The ubiquitination process is carried out by an enzymatic cascade that includes |FRAME: Ubiquitin-activating-proteins-E1|, |FRAME: Ubiquitin-carrier-proteins-E2|, and sometimes |FRAME: E3-ubiquitin-carrier-proteins|, as described in this pathway. These enzymes first catalyze the formation of an isopeptide bond between the glycine at the C terminus of ubiquitin and usually a lysine residue in the target, leading to monoubiquitination. Monoubiquitination can occur at a defined residue, such as Lys164 in proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) |CITS: [12226657]|, or it might be confined to a domain, as in the transcription factor p53 |CITS: [17369817]|. In some cases, such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), multiple lysine residues become modified with one ubiquitin each during multimonoubiquitination |CITS: [12717448]|., Modification of the N-terminus or one of the seven lysine residues of a ubiquitin attached to a protein leads to formation of polymeric chains. These chains can as short as two ubiquitin molecules or as long as more than ten ubiquitin melocules. In some cases the same residue is modified in all ubiquitins during elongation, forming homogenous ubiquitin chains, while in other cases different linkages alternate at succeeding positions of the chain (for example, in NF-κB signaling or protein trafficking) |CITS: [21113135][19948006][20833710][21455173]|., In addition, sometimes a single ubiquitin is modified with multiple molecules, forming branched chains whose function is unknown. In general, all possible linkages have been detected in cells |CITS: [12872131][19345192]|.,  It is assumed that in Homo sapiens there are about 10 E1 enzymes, 70 E2 enzymes, and several hundred E3 enzymes, distributed into two main groups based on the mechanism and the occurrence of intermediates.

Summary: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), a prevalent form of auxin, is an important phytohormone that affects many aspects of plant, development throughout the whole plant life cycle. IAA also plays a crucial role in allowing plants to respond to the biotic and, abiotic stimuli they encounter |CITS: [15749753]|. IAA is subject to a number of biochemical modifications that regulate its, activity and allow plants to fine tune their levels of active auxin |CITS: [15749753]|., IAA can be conjugated to a number of amino acids through the activity of enzymes with structural similarity to the, firefly luciferase family of adenylate forming enzymes |CITS: [15659623]|. Some of these amino acid modications can be, reversed through the activity of amido hydrolases |CITS:[7792259][10072397]|, suggesting that some compounds,, such as IAA-alanine and IAA-leucine, are storage forms of auxin that can be metabolized, to contribute to the pool of free auxin |CITS: [15659623]|. Other IAA-amino acid conjugates, such as IAA-aspartate,, are targeted for further breakdown (|CITS:[9733548]| (see |FRAME:PWY-2021|) and act as intermediates in IAA catabolic, pathways. , Given the importance of auxin homeostatic maintenance, the transcripts encoding several IAA-amido synthetases are, up-regulated in response to applications of free auxin (rev in |CITS:[15659623]|). , Together with an array of other IAA-based modification pathways (see |FRAME:PWY-1782|),, IAA-amino acid conjugation appears to play a vital role in regulating the active levels of a potent phytohormone.

Summary: Background, The synthesis of |FRAME: Fatty-acid-methyl-esters "fatty acid methyl esters"| (FAMEs) and |FRAME: Long-Chain-Acyl-Ethyl-Esters "fatty acid ethyl esters"| (FAEEs) by transesterification of long chain fatty acids from plant oil triacylglycerols (TAGs) with methanol and ethanol, respectively, produces biodiesel that can be used as a petroleum-based diesel substitute |CITS: [16946248]|. The use of biodiesel has many positive ecological aspects, however, there are numerous limitations and drawbacks to its production on a technical scale. These include:, 1) Production depending on the availability of sufficient vegetable oil feedstock., 2) Vegetable oils used contain TAGs which cannot be used directly and have to be transesterified, this is cost intensive and energy consuming., 3) The production of FAMEs requires methanol which is currently produced from natural gas, thus FAME-based biodiesel is not truly a renewable product. , About this Pathway, This pathway for the biosynthesis of FAEEs was metabolically engineered in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [16946248]|. The |FRAME: TAX-542| |FRAME: CPLX-8341| and |FRAME: CPLX-8344| enzymes were cloned to aerobically generate ethanol, and |FRAME:ACIAD0832-MONOMER| (WS/DGAT) from |FRAME: TAX-62977| was cloned to transesterify the acyl moieties of fatty acyl-CoA thioesters in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [16946248]|. Cells were cultivated aerobically with glucose and oleic acid.

Summary: General Background, Fungi including the well-studied yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| and yeast |FRAME: TAX-28985| are known to use the arginase pathway for |FRAME: ARG| degradation (see pathway |FRAME: ARG-PRO-PWY|). However, a new (hypothetical) alternative arginase-independent pathway that links |FRAME: ARG| catabolism to |FRAME: SUC| has been proposed in |FRAME: TAX-28985|, a yeast that is genetically diverged from |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [24912400]|. , The enzyme specific to this alternative arginine degradation pathway in yeast is guanidinobutyrase. In |FRAME: TAX-28985| it was shown to be encoded by locus KLLA0F27995g which was renamed gene KlGBU1. Although this enzyme allowed the organism to grow on medium containing |FRAME: CPD-592| as sole nitrogen source, the physiological significance of the pathway is unclear. Orthologs of gene KlGBU1 were identified in a variety of fungal genomes including two strains of |FRAME: TAX-4932|, EC1118 and VIN7 |CITS: [24912400]|., About This Pathway, This pathway is similar to the |FRAME: TAX-286| pathway (see |FRAME: PWY-5742|) except that the cofactors of some of the reactions in the yeast pathway have not been defined., The role of gene KlGBU1 was demonstrated both in vivo and in vitro. Deletion of the arginase gene in |FRAME: TAX-28985| did not completely abolish growth on |FRAME: ARG| as a sole nitrogen source, suggesting the operation of an alternative pathway. Evidence for the alternative pathway was derived from transcriptome analysis, isotope-based flux analysis, and enzyme activity assays of cell extracts. In an arginase-negative strain of |FRAME: TAX-28985|, |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| was identified as a key intermediate in |FRAME: ARG| catabolism |CITS: [24912400]|., Data suggested that in the first reaction |FRAME: ARG| is reversibly transaminated to |FRAME: CPD-824| by one or more of the constitutively expressed transaminases in this organism. |FRAME: CPD-824 "2-Ketoarginine"| is decarboxylated to |FRAME: CPD-825| which is then oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-592|, coincident with transcriptional up-regulation of locus KLLA0E02707g, which is highly similar to |FRAME: TAX-4932| gene ARO10 encoding a TPP-dependent |FRAME: CPLX3O-71| with broad substrate specificity. Although |FRAME: CPD-824| is not a known substrate of such decarboxylases in fungi, |FRAME: MONOMER-13584| is known in |FRAME: TAX-286| species. |FRAME: CPD-592 "Guanidinobutyrate"| is then converted to |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| (GABA) by the gene KlGBU1-encoded ureohydrolase which mobilizes nitrogen by release of |FRAME: UREA| |CITS: [24912400]|. , As shown in the pathway link, the last two reactions convert |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUC| which enters the TCA cycle. A 4-aminobutanoate transaminase converts |FRAME: 4-AMINO-BUTYRATE| to |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD|. This enzyme is likely encoded by the transcriptionally upregulated KLLAF20548g locus which shows sequence similarity with |FRAME: TAX-4932| |FRAME: CPLX-8091| |CITS: [24912400]|.

Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons out of the cell., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons inside the cell, or produce them outside the cell, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, Arsenic is ubiquitous in the environment, and is present in four oxidation states: 0 (elemental), -3 (arsine), +3 (arsenite) and +5 (arsenate). The two soluble forms of arsenic, arsenite and arsenate, are toxic to biological systems, with arsenite considered 100 times more toxic., Since arsenate is far less toxic than arsenite, the oxidation of arsenite can be considered a detoxification process. However, the oxidation of As(III) to As(V), when coupled to the reduction of oxygen or nitrate, is an exergonic process, and it has been suggested that at least some bacteria may derive energy out of this process |CITS: [15178476]|., Since the first report of bacterial arsenite oxidation |CITS: [Green18]|, several arsenite-oxidizing bacteria have been isolated from various environments including gold mines |CITS: [10618208]|, sewage |CITS: [10837]|, hyper-saline lake |CITS: [12324322]|, soil |CITS: [Osborne76]|, cattle dip fluid |CITS: [Green18][13229843]|, geothermal springs |CITS: [Salmassi02]| and arsenic-contaminated ground water |CITS: [10406083]|., Both chemolithoautotrophic and heterotrophic arsenite-oxidizing bacteria have been identified, including strains of |FRAME: TAX-76588| |CITS: [Leblanc95]|, |FRAME: TAX-920| |CITS: [Leblanc95]|, |FRAME: TAX-204773| |CITS: [12486049]|, |FRAME: TAX-511| |CITS: [1331097]|, |FRAME: TAX-106590| |CITS: [7219219]|, |FRAME: TAX-47420| |CITS: [15178476]|, and |FRAME: TAX-286| |CITS: [7219219]|, as well as the thermophiles |FRAME: TAX-271| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [11642444]|., The most common arsenite oxidase is encoded by the |FRAME: G-8323| and |FRAME: G-8324| genes (AioAB). The enzyme was first purified from |FRAME: TAX-511| in 1992 |CITS: [1331097]|, and was further charaqcterized from different As(III) oxidizers, such as |FRAME: TAX-204773| and |FRAME: TAX-1125847| |CITS: [10618208][12486049][28496149][28801050]|. Homologs of the genes encoding AioAB have been found in phylogenetically diverse strains including members of α-,β-,γ-Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Aquificae, Bacteroidetes, Chlorobi, Chloroflexi, Crenarchaeota, Deinococcus-Thermus, Firmicutes and Nitrospira |CITS: [24507904]|., AioBA is a heterotetramer consisting of a large catalytic subunit (AioA) and a small subunit (AioB) located on the periplasmic surface of the inner membrane. AioA is divided into four domains, in which domain I contains a bound [3Fe-4S] cluster and a Rieske subunit and domains II-IV contain bound molybdenum |CITS: [11250197]|. AioB contains a Rieske [2Fe-2S] domain |CITS: [11250197]|. During the initial purification of the enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-511| it was reported that it can transfer the electrons to either an azurin or a c-type cytochrome |CITS: [1331097]|. The activity with azurin was classified as |FRAME: EC-1.20.9.1|, while activity with c-type cytochrome was classified as |FRAME: EC-1.20.2.1|. Subsequent work with the enzymes from |FRAME: TAX-375569| and |FRAME: TAX-1125847| identified only a c-type cytochrome as the dedicated electron acceptor |CITS: [15178476][17306216][23891971]|., In this pathway arsenite transfers two electrons to the [3Fe-4S] center of AioA. The electrons are then passed one at a time to the [2Fe-2S] center of the Rieske (AioB) subunit, from which they are taken up simultaneously by the c-type cytochrome. Finally, an aa3 cytochrome oxidase acts as a terminal electron, accepting the electrons at the CuA site. A total of four electrons are required to reduce O2 to H2O, in a process that results in the release of 4 protons, generating a proton-motive force |CITS: [15178476]|., Disruption of the gene encoding the cytochrome c550 in |FRAME: TAX-1315272| did not completely block bacterial As(III) oxidation, leading to the discovery of a novel protein involved in As(III) oxidation electron transport, which was named |FRAME: MONOMER-21714 AioE| |CITS: [28128323]|. The protein (Uniprot accession I6R3V7) has been originally annotated as an FAD-dependent pyridine nucleotide-disulfide oxidoreductase. The redox potential gradient is AioBA > AioE > CytC550, leading to the suggestion that AioE functions as the direct electron acceptor for AioAB. Deletion of aioE resulted in a null As(III) oxidation phenotype and decreased the production of NADH |CITS: [28128323]|. The authors reported that AioE belongs to the TrkA family, and speculated that because of that AioE may reduce NAD+ to NADH and H+ in addition to transfering electrons to the cytochrome, due to the presence of an NAD(P)-binding domain |CITS: [28128323]|. AioE is not included in this pathway due to insufficient information tregarding its role.

Summary: The depicted super-pathway combines the sub-pathways |FRAME:PWY-7150| and |FRAME:PWY-7151| which describe the biosynthetic route of polymethylated |FRAME:CPD-520| and |FRAME:CPD-14866| glucosides which represent the final products accumulating in |FRAME:TAX-36749| |CITS:[Collins81a]|. The formation of the polymethylated flavonol glucosides are carried out in a coordinated and highly ordained sequence of methylation, hydroxylation and glucosylation. Catalytic data obtained from in vitro experiments characterizing the involved enzymes of the pathway established a methylation sequence of |FRAME:CPD-520| - |FRAME:3457-TETRAHYDROXY-3-METHOXYFLAVONE| - |FRAME:345-TRIHYDROXY-37-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE| - |FRAME:CPD-10510| |CITS:[De82]| |CITS:[3994393]| |CITS:[3415239]|. The final products of the polymethylated |FRAME:CPD-520| glucoside biosynthesis are catalyzed by a sequence of a position-specific 2'-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[16663104]| |CITS:[Latchinian87]| |CITS:[6236078]| followed by a 3'-O-specific methyltransferase |CITS:[9002616]| |CITS:[9747535]|., |FRAME:345-TRIHYDROXY-37-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE 3,7-Dimethylquercetin| is the main metabolite from which the |FRAME:CPD-14866| derived glucoside series branches off. The first committed step of this pathway is the 6-hydroxylation of partial methylated quercetins such as |FRAME:345-TRIHYDROXY-37-DIMETHOXYFLAVONE| and |FRAME:CPD-10510| |CITS:[11068865]| |CITS:[15596008]|. A series of 3'-, (|CITS: [DE82]| |CITS:[3994393]|) 6, (|CITS: [DE82]| |CITS:[3994393]|) and 4'-O-specific methyltransferases (|CITS:[3994393]| |CITS:[3994394]|) lead to |FRAME:CPD-14856| and |FRAME:CPD-14861| which in turn is the starting metabolite to produce |FRAME:CPD-14863| and |FRAME:CPD-14864| in either a catalytic sequence of 3'-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[16663104]| |CITS:[Latchinian87]| |CITS:[6236078]| followed by a 2'-O-specific methyltransferase |CITS:[Khouri87]| or a metabolic sequence that proceeds vice versa. , All of the enzymes characterized in the pathway are highly substrate- and position-specific catalyzing only the corresponding A-, and B-ring positions of their mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, or pentamethylated precursor flavonols., The final six polymethylated glucosides of the pathway could be localized in the cell walls of leaf epidermal and mesophyll cells utilizing immunofluorescence |CITS:[Lamoureux86]| |CITS:[Brisson86]|, immunogold labeling |CITS:[Marchand87]| and electron microscope observations |CITS:[Charest86]|. The highly coordinated and stepwise sequence of methylation, hydroxylation and glucosylation of the pathway as well as the location of final products prompted the proposal of a multienzyme system. This multienzyme complex is localized at the ER where the pathway is executed and from which vesicles transport and eventually excrete the final products into or near the cell wall |CITS:[Ibrahim87]|. , Note regarding the numbering of the B-ring, The usual consecutive numeration of the C-atoms of the B-ring is clockwise, starting on the C-atom connected to the side-chain. The 3'- and 5'-position are similar as they are both in meta-position to the side-chain. However, when the 2'-position is substituted the 3'-position is often designated as 5'-position in the literature. In order to maintain consistency and to avoid confusion all compounds and enzymes of the pathway are depicted and named according to the consecutive, clockwise numeration of the B-ring whether or not the 2'-position is substituted, i.e. 3' is not replaced by 5' in neither structure nor naming.

Ternatins are a group of 15 polyacetylated delphinidin glucosides that confer blue color to the petals of butterfly pea (|FRAME:TAX-43366|). The general structure of ternatins consists of malonylated delphinidin 3,3',5'-triglucosides having 3',5'-side chains with alternating D-glucose and p-coumaric acid units of varying lengths |CITS: [8991946]| |CITS:[12482461]|. , Ternatins are categorized into three major groups, the A, B and D series that are characterized by either two D-glucose attached to the 3' and 5' position of the B-ring (A-series), a D-glucose and an acylated (p-coumaric acid) glucose chain (B-series) or two acylated glucose units (D-series) affixed to this position |CITS: [9834153]|. The variation of flower color depends on the chemical composition of the involved anthocyanins |CITS:[20054474]|. The blue flower color of butterfly-pea changes to other hues, such as mauve and white because of the lack of ternatins that contain acylated glucose units and an overall decreased content of anthocyanins |CITS:[14568080]|., The simplest ternatin is |FRAME: CPD-7864| (see |FRAME:PWY-5295|), which is the starting point for the formation of more complex ternatins, such as |FRAME:CPD-15371| (this pathway) and the most complex |FRAME:CPD-7865| and its intermediates. |FRAME:CPD-15371 Ternatin C3| is an intermediate towards the formation of |FRAME:CPD-7865| which is formed through a series of acylation and glucosylation steps, however, the actual sequence and corresponding enzymes of this pathway remain to be characterized., The enzyme catalyzing the acylation of |FRAME: CPD-7864| to form |FRAME:CPD-15371| has been purified and cloned from petals of |FRAME:TAX-43366| and shown to belong to the class of serine carboxypeptide like acyltransferases utilizing |FRAME:CPD-8674| as acyl donor |CITS:[Noda06] [Noda07]|.

The biotrophic fungus Epichloe festucae produces a number of alkaloidal bioprotective metabolites (for example see |FRAME:PWY-7572|) which confer protection against insect and mammalian herbivory to their host plants, i.e. cool-seasoned grasses such as species from ryegrass (Lolium) and fescue (Festuca) |CITS:[11495800]|. Improved technologies in genomics and metabolomics permit the quantification of fungal metabolites in their host plants which significantly improves the elucidation of plant and fungal metabolic interplays |CITS:[22351180]|. A unique and structural unusual compound produced by Epichloe is |FRAME:CPD-17338| , an pyrrolopyrazine alkaloid, which is a very strong insect deterrent |CITS:[22913513]|, particularly effective against larvae and adults of Argentine stem weevil (Listronotus bonariensis) |CITS:[Rowan86] [24263837] [Rowan93] [Lane00]| and taxonomically the most prevalent bioprotective agent of the Epichloe genus |CITS:[18707456]|. In addition, |FRAME:CPD-17338| was also reported to effect the reticulum motility of sheep |CITS:[19231961]|. , In general, anti-herbivore alkaloids display a broad range of chemotypic diversity which may reflect adaption to special environmental circumstances and defense response to herbivores |CITS:[Schardl12]|. This emphasizes the dynamics and structural variation of alkaloids biosynthesized in such species |CITS:[23850071]| which may be further diversified by interspecific hybridization |CITS:[25065688]|. It has been shown that alkaloidal metabolites become more potent at higher trophic levels (aphids and aphid predators) by accumulating both |FRAME:CPD-17338| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-17202| (see |FRAME:PWY-7572|) |CITS:[24233445]|. , It has been experimentally verified that the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17338| is catalyzed by the action of a single multifunctional nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) encoded by perA |CITS:[16091042]|. The gene perA is widely distributed in the strains of sexual Epichloe and asexual Neotyphodium species but not all of them are capable of biosynthesizing |FRAME:CPD-17338| |CITS:[Scott07]|. The gene perA reveals a two modular structure where module 1 activates and binds |FRAME:L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| and module 2 does the same with |FRAME:ARG|. The condensation domain forms the peptide bonds between |FRAME:L-DELTA1-PYRROLINE_5-CARBOXYLATE| and |FRAME:ARG| , the latter being methylated by the methylation domain of module 2. Finally the reductase domain carries out reduction, cyclization and release of the peramine iminium ion which, in a last step, is probably spontaneously oxidized and rearranged to form the final product of the pathway, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-17338| |CITS:[16091042]|.

Summary: In this pathway multiple units of |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (IPP) undergo a series of, polymerizations to form a polyisoprenoid chain., The sequential addition of isoprenyl units to |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is performed by polyprenyl, diphosphate synthase enzymes such as the |FRAME:TAX-562| enzyme |FRAME: CPLX0-7426|., Additional isoprenoid units are added to a maximal length that is determined by the specific enzyme., Most organisms generate polyprenyl chains of predominantly one length. Once completed, the, polyprenyl chain is incorporated into other molecules, such as quinones., The enzyme that attaches the polyprenyl chain to the quinone precursor molecule does not have a, preference towards a particular length. Thus, the length of the polyprenyl chain in the mature quinone, molecule is determined by the predominant polyprenyl diphosphate synthase enzyme of the organism., In most organisms there is one type of a predominant quinone, with a specific polyprenyl chain length., However, most organisms also have minor amounts of quinones with a different polyprenyl chain, length. For a review detailing the polyprenyl chain length in different bacteria, see |CITS: [7022156]|., Long chain menaquinones, such as |FRAME: CPD-9723|, |FRAME: CPD-9722| and |FRAME: CPD-9721|, are not common, but have been documented in several bacterial species, belonging to the, |FRAME: TAX-171552| and |FRAME: TAX-85023| families |CITS: [6102980][7462123][2223612]|.

|FRAME: CPD-8912|General Background, |FRAME: CPD-8959 Podophyllotoxin| is an aryltetralin lignan that has been attracted a lot of attention because of its use in anticancer treatments. Podophyllotoxin is highly toxic and for that reason of limited medicinal use on its own. However it is used as a starting marerial in the production of semi-synthetic derivatives such as |FRAME: CPD-16754| and |FRAME: CPD-16755|, which are used in cancer therapy (reviewed in |CITS: [15302526]|). The mode of action of these drugs is based on interactions with DNA/topoisomerase II complexes, causing DNA double-strand breaks that are followed by cell arrest in the G2-phase |CITS: [9615861]|., Although podophyllotoxin and its congeners are found in various families of higher plants such as Berberidaceae, Polygalaceae, Apiaceae, Linaceae, Labiaceae and Fabaceae, the compound does not accumulate to an exploitable level. The only plants that produce usable amounts of podophyllotoxin are |FRAME: TAX-93608| (Indian Podophyllum) , and |FRAME:TAX-35933| (American Podophyllum), whose podophyllotoxin content is 4.3 and 0.25% of dry weight, respectively |CITS: [15302526]|. , Since the chemical synthesis of podophyllotoxin is not economic at this time, the substance is still isolated from wild growing Podophyllum species. Unfortunately the heavy use of these plants in the past has placed them on the list of endangered species |CITS: [AIRI97]| and alternative ways of establishing cell and organ cultures are now intensively investigated |CITS: [11330705][KUHLMANN02][Fuss03]|., Attempts to boost the production of podophyllotoxin by adding synthetic or natural elicitors such as |FRAME: CPD-18752| (a synthetic 6-ethyl indanoyl isoleucine conjugate) and |FRAME: CPD-18753| |CITS: [16136333]| and |FRAME: CPD1F-2| |CITS: [15818489]| have been of moderate success, but have proven useful for the elucidation of the underlying pathways., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of podophyllotoxin is not completely known. Although the late steps in the biosynthesis have been corroborated with enzymatic data the early steps are not well understood. The research of Sakakibara and coworkers |CITS: [12956064]| points to the lignan |FRAME: CPD-17595| as intermediate. A pathway that starts with |FRAME: CPD-8912| and forms yatein in four steps has been proposed |CITS: [12956064]|. Even though the enzymes catalyzing those reactions remain to be characterized, the identification of the presumed intermediates in planta supports the pathway (e.g. |CITS: [SUZUKI02]|)., |FRAME: CPD-8912 "(-)-Matairesinol"| has been established as direct precursor for podophyllotoxin, and |FRAME: CPD-17595| was shown to be effectively converted to podophyllotoxin |CITS: [BROOMHEAD91]|. (-)-Matairesinol is formed through a series of reactions that start with the stereospecific coupling of coniferyl alcohol (see |FRAME:PWY-5466|) |CITS: [12355164]|., The first established enzyme involved in the late steps of the formation of podophyllotoxin derivatives is |FRAME: MONOMER-13010| (DOP6H). The enzyme, a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase, specifically 6-hydroxylates |FRAME: CPD-8958| to |FRAME: CPD-8960|, indicating that the formation of |FRAME: CPD-8962| does not proceed via podophyllotoxin |CITS: [11800394]|. Podophyllotoxin, which is also formed from deoxypodophyllotoxin, requires a 7-hydroxylase that has not been described yet |CITS: [VANUDEN95]|., A second enzyme identified in the biosynthetic route for |FRAME: CPD-8962| is |FRAME: MONOMER-13011| |CITS: [12943762]|. The resulting β-peltatin-A methylether is most likely hydroxylated at position 6 to form 6-methylpodophyllotoxin., An alternative pathway has been proposed that involves the formation of 7'-hydroxymatairesinol, which is efficiently metabolized into 5-methoxypodophyllotoxin |CITS: [11130663]| but the actual enzymes involved in this pathway still, need to be identified.

|FRAME: CPD-27856 Sporandol| is a binaphthalene compound produced by the mold |FRAME: TAX-108922|. It was identified in 1997 based on its antiparasitic activity. The compound was active against a variety of parasites in living mice, including the endoparasite (fluke) |FRAME: TAX-6192| and the ectoparasite |FRAME: TAX-72496|. There were no signs of gross toxicity to the mouse when a daily dose of 620 mg/kg was administered for six straight days, indicating that the compound is less toxic than other binaphthalene antparasiticides |CITS: [Tsipouras97]|., The enzymes involved in sporandol biosynthesis were identified and studied in 2020 |CITS: [32227858]|. The first enzyme of the pathway, |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.335|, is a polyketide synthase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124975| gene. Like several polyketide synthases involved in similar functions, SpoP lacks a fused thioesterase domain that mediates product release. This function is predicted to be provided by a thioesterase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124976| gene., The released product, a carboxylate, is decarboxylated, presumably spontaneously, forming |FRAME: CPD-27853|. This intermediate is methylated at the O6 position by a methyltranferase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124977| gene, forming |FRAME: CPD-27869|., In the final step of the pathway two molecules of |FRAME: CPD-27869| are linked by a 7,7' linkage, forming |FRAME: CPD-27856|. This reaction requires the participation of two proteins - a laccase encoded by the |FRAME: G-124978| gene and a fasciclin protein encoded by |FRAME: G-124979| |CITS: [32227858]|.

The degradative pathway of |FRAME:TOLUENE| in |FRAME: ORG-5948| consists of two parts:, an upper pathway that converts toluene and xylene to their carboxylic acid derivatives, (this pathway, and see also |FRAME: TOLUENE-DEG-CATECHOL-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5429|),, and a lower pathway that converts the (substituted) benzoic acids to Krebs cycle intermediates, (see |FRAME: PWY-5430|)., In the upper pathway, the methyl side chain of toluene is subjected to several progressive oxidations, to carboxylic acid, followed by an oxygenative cleavage of the aromatic ring., The upper pathway is induced by toluene, xylenes, and their alcohol derivatives. The , lower pathway is induced by benzoic acids, or by upper pathway substrates |CITS: [1176436]|., In |FRAME: ORG-5948|, the TOL plasmid pWW0 encodes all the enzymes responsible for the degradation, of toluene and xylene. The genes encoding these enzymes are organized into two operons,, the upper operon, which contains the first three enzymes in the pathway, and the meta operon,, which contains the genes responsible for the degradation of benzoates and toluates., In addition, some strains have integrated very similar genes in their chromosomes, where they have, aquired little mutation. For example, strains TW3 and 4NT have been shown to , express similar but chromosomally-encoded enzymes which catalyze the same pathway, |CITS: [8357257][8245826][9555884]|.
