Summary: Most organisms that are able to disproportionate elemental sulfur (|FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur|), (see |FRAME:P203-PWY|) and |FRAME: S2O3| (see |FRAME:PWY-5277|) are sulfate reducers., For example, see |FRAME:PWY-5306| for the sulfur metabolism of the sulfate reducer and thiosulfate-, disproportionating bacterium |FRAME: TAX-63561|., However, the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-65555|, which can disproportionate, both elemental sulfur and |FRAME: S2O3|, is not able to reduce sulfate |CITS: [9435068]|., The sulfur metabolism of this organism was studied using cell-free extracts |CITS: [12889609]|., The products of both disproportionation reactions were |FRAME: HS| and |FRAME: SO3|. While sulfide, was not used further, sulfite was further oxidized to sulfate. Two distinct pathways for the, oxidation of sulfite were identified: one pathway involves |FRAME: MONOMER-12414| and, |FRAME:MONOMER-12415| (see |FRAME:PWY-5278|), and can be described as the reversion of the, initial steps of the dissimilatory sulfate reduction pathway (see |FRAME:DISSULFRED-PWY|)., The second pathway is the direct oxidation of sulfite to sulfate by |FRAME: MONOMER-12412|, (see |FRAME:PWY-5276|). , Thiosulfate reductase, which cleaves thiosulfate into sulfite and sulfide, was only present in cell-free, extracts from thiosulfate disproportionating culture., The presence of the uncouplers |FRAME:CPD-7975| (HQNO) and |FRAME:CPD-7970| (CCCP), in growing cultures had negative effects on both thiosulfate and sulfur disproportionation |CITS: [12889609]|.

Summary: Bacterial formation of 3-ketoglycosides from disaccharides was first described and studied in 1960 |CITS: [13799610][13799611]|. The production of |FRAME: 3-KETOLACTOSE| has been considered characteristic of |FRAME:TAX-357| biovar 1 strains |CITS: [7581688]|, although |FRAME:TAX-13687| species have also been, reported to produce this compound as well |CITS: [Sakane95]|. , One of the enzymes involved in the pathway, |FRAME: CPLX-9689|, has been studied in the 1960s., The enzyme, which catalyzes the formation of |FRAME: 3-KETOLACTOSE| from |FRAME: Alpha-lactose| and |FRAME: CPD-384| from |FRAME: SUCROSE|, has been purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [5726844]|., A much later study has identified the genes that encode what appears to be a homologous enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-155892| |CITS: [20190087]|., The second enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-6107|, is less well characterized. |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.218|, an enzyme hydrolyzing α-3-ketoglucosides, including as |FRAME: CPD-384|, has been purified from A. tumefaciens but found to be inactive with |FRAME: 3-KETOLACTOSE| |CITS: [5438043]|. However, activity was demonstrated in particle-free extracts of several A. tumefaciens strains grown on lactose, including |FRAME: TAX-359| and A. radiobacter M2/1 (this strain has later been included in |FRAME: TAX-358|), and the enzyme was partially purified from the latter |CITS: [23194588]|. , While |FRAME: GLC| was identified as a reaction product, the authors were unable to identify |FRAME: CPD-1242|. , Conversion of |FRAME: CPD-1242| to |FRAME: GALACTOSE| remains a hypothetical reaction, and is based on the homologous reaction in the sucrose degradation pathway of |FRAME: TAX-358| (see |FRAME: SUCROSEUTIL2-PWY|), where |FRAME: 3-Dehydro-D-Glucopyranose| is converted to |FRAME: ALPHA-GLUCOSE|., Two |FRAME: MONOMER-6110| enzymes have been partially purified and characterized from |FRAME: TAX-358| |CITS: [4144143]|. , Further catabolism of glucose in |FRAME: TAX-358| was found to be oxidative, involving the |FRAME: ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY "Entner-Doudoroff pathway"| and |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY "pentose phosphate pathway"|, as well as the |FRAME: TCA| and |FRAME: GLYOXYLATE-BYPASS| |CITS: [4745418]|.

Summary: At the time of this review, 136 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1, |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and, seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity., Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which, possess the highest biological activity. These include the three gibberellins mentioned in this pathway, GA3, GA5, and GA6, as well as , GA1, GA4, and GA7. GA3 (gibberellic acid) has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. , GA3 is used commercially to, promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth. In |FRAME:TAX-4520|, GA5 and, GA6 have been shown to enhance flowering, whilst GA1 and, GA4 enhanced stem elongation |CITS:[12475622]|., GA1 is, the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while, GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have, either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95|, and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). The fifth ring is a lactone ring. GAs containing a, tetracyclic ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-95|) are called C20-GAs,, whereas GAs containing a pentacyclic 20-nor-ent-gibberellane structure (|FRAME: CPD1F-134|), are called C19-GAs. C20-GAs do not usually have biological activity but can, be metabolized to active C19-GAs (note that not all C19-GAs are bioactive)., Gibberellins are believed to be synthesized in young tissues of the shoot and also the developing seed., It is uncertain whether young root tissues also produce gibberellins. There is also some evidence that, leaves may be the source of some biosynthesis.Active gibberellins show many physiological effects,, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the, physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating, cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption, of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme, production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction, of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and, vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Certain commercial chemicals which are used to stunt growth do so in part because they block the, synthesis of gibberellins. Some of these chemicals are |FRAME:CPD-6966|, |FRAME: AMO-1618|,, |FRAME:CPD-6968|, |FRAME: CPD-4022| and |FRAME:CPD-6970| (more inhibitors of GA biosynthesis, can be found in |CITS:[SPONSEL04]|). During active growth, the plant will maintain gibberellin, homeostasis by metabolizing most gibberellins by rapid hydroxylation to inactive conjugates., Active |FRAME:GIBBERELLIN| is degraded much slower which helps to explain the symptoms observed, in the disease bakanae caused by the rice pathogen |FRAME:TAX-5127|. This pathogen produces, large amounts of GA3 which it secretes. Inactive conjugates might be stored or, translocated via the phloem and xylem before their release (activation) at the proper time and in the, proper tissue., About This Pathway, GA3, GA5, and GA6 appear to be derived from, GA20, a compound synthesized in the |FRAME: PWY-5035 early 13-hydroxylation pathway|. The presence of this pathway variant has been demonstrated in many species including maize, rice, pea and, Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS:[10557253],[11117879],[9154988],[7630935]|. So far, however, there is no evidence that these gibberellins exist in |FRAME: TAX-3208| or green algae |CITS: [JOHRI08][18930434][ANTEROLA08]|, however there is evidence that gibberellins present in this pathway, including GA3, exist in ferns and gymnosperms |CITS: [KAMIENSKA76B][16736188]|.

Summary: General Background, Nitroaromatic compounds such as nitrophenols, nitrotoluenes and nitrobenzoates, are used in the, synthesis of pesticides, plasticizers, dyes, pharmaceuticals, and explosives., These compounds are contaminants of waste waters, rivers and groundwater, and of the atmosphere, |CITS: [Leuenberger88]|. In most cases nitroaromatic compounds are highly toxic to living organisms,, and several of them have been listed as priority pollutants by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Despite their toxicity, these compounds can be degraded by several microorganisms. These degradation, pathways almost always start with the removal or replacement of the nitro group |CITS: [7765729]|., The mechanisms in which bacteria are able to remove the nitro group can be divided into two, broad categories - oxidative and reductive., In oxidative pathways the nitro group is released in the form of nitrite, usually catalyzed by a mono- or, di-oxygenase enzymes. For examples, see |FRAME: PWY-5641| and, |FRAME: 4-Nitrotoluene-Degradation|. In reductive pathways the nitro group is reduced via, a nitroso intermediate to a hydroxylamino group, and sometime further to an amino group, and is, released in the form of ammonia. For examples see |FRAME: PWY-5644| and |FRAME: PWY-2381|., About This Pathway, Dinitrotoluenes are intermediates in the production of the explosive |FRAME: CPD-9138| (TNT) and, precursors of |FRAME:CPD-9139| used in the manufacture of polyurethane foams., Both |FRAME:CPD-9132| and |FRAME: CPD-9133| are produced in large quantities, and are widely, distributed in contaminated groundwater and soil., Both exhibit acute toxicity and low level carcinogenicity. The 14-day LC50 for guppy, (|FRAME: TAX-8081|) of |FRAME:CPD-9132| is 69 μM and that of |FRAME: CPD-9133| is 98, μM, indicating aquatic toxicity at low concentrations |CITS: [10397821]|. Both isomers are listed as, U.S. EPA priority pollutants |CITS: [Callahan79]|., Bacterial degradation of |FRAME: CPD-9133| have been reported multiple time |CITS:[10397821], [10788393][17633643]|., A few strains were shown to be able to grow with |FRAME: CPD-9133| as the sole source of carbon,, nitrogen, and energy |CITS:[10788393]|. These organisms, |FRAME: ORG-5882| and, |FRAME: ORG-5909|, degrade the compound in a pathway that hasn't been completely defined yet., However, the initial steps in this pathway were determined. , |FRAME: CPD-9133| was converted to |FRAME: CPD-9142| by a dioxygenation reaction accompanied, by the release of |FRAME:NITRITE|. |FRAME: CPD-9142| was the substrate for extradiol ring cleavage, yielding |FRAME: CPD-9143|, which was converted to |FRAME: CPD-9144|., These organisms were used in a fluidized-bed biofilm reactor to remove |FRAME:CPD-9132| and, |FRAME: CPD-9133| simultaneously from contaminated water |CITS: [Lendenmann98][10397821]|.

General Background, |FRAME: Phytobilins Phytobilins| are tetrapyrrole molecules that are synthesized by plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Major classes of phytobilins are:, 1. |FRAME: Phycobilins Phycobilins|, which are the chromophores of |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins| |CITS: [16663825]| and some algal phytochromes |CITS: [8616213]|, 2. |FRAME: Phytochromobilins Phytochromobilins|, which are the chromophores of higher plants |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| |CITS: [1634523][7744741]|., |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins Phycobiliproteins| are light-harvesting accessory pigments of cyanobacteria, red algae and cryptophytes, and |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochromes| are photoreversible light signal-transducing pigments of plants, some algae, and some cyanobacteria., One of the major class of phycobiliproteins in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: Phycoerythrocyanins phycoerythrocyanin|, which contains the violet chromophore |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins phycoviolobilin|, covalently linked by a thioether bond to a cysteine residue. |FRAME: Phycoerythrocyanins Phycoerythrocyanin| occurs mainly in heterocystous cyanobacteria, and has not been found together with |FRAME: Phycoerythrins phycoerythrin| |CITS: [Bryant82]|., It has a characteristic magenta color, and an absorption maximum around 570 nm, with a shoulder at 595 nm. , Like other |FRAME: Phycobiliproteins phycobiliproteins|, |FRAME: Phycoerythrocyanins phycoerythrocyanin| is composed of two different subunits that form either trimers [(αβ)3] or hexamers [(αβ)6]., The α chain (encoded by the pecA gene) contains one molecule of |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins phycoviolobilin|, which is covalently attached at Cys-84, and the β subunit (encoded by the pecB gene) contains two molecules of the blue chromophore |FRAME: Phycocyanobilins phycocyanobilin|, which are covalently attached at Cys-84 and -155, respectively., About This Pathway, The biosynthetic pathways for the production of the four cyanobacterial |FRAME: Phycobilins phycobilins|, as well as the |FRAME: TAX-3702| pathway for |FRAME: Phytochromobilins phytochromobilin| biosynthesis, have been elucidated. These five chromophores share a common precursor, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|, which is the product of heme macrocycle cleavage by |FRAME: EC-1.14.14.18|. |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is subsequently reduced by one of several possible ferredoxin-dependent bilin reductases., |FRAME: BILIVERDINE "Biliverdin-IX-α"| is converted to |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN| by a single enzyme, |FRAME: MONOMER-13954|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10655| gene |CITS: [11283349]|. |FRAME: 3Z-PHYCOCYANOBILIN| is converted to its isomer |FRAME: CPD-17222| either spontaneously or by a distinct bilin isomerase |CITS: [1939256]|. , Free |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins phycoviolobilin| does not seem to exist. It has been shown that the bifunctional |FRAME: CPLX-8936| catalyzes the attachment of free |FRAME: CPD-17222| to the α subunit of |FRAME: Phycoerythrocyanins phycoerythrocyanin| (PecA) followed by its isomerization to |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins phycoviolobilin| |CITS: [7759546][10708746][11591166][19182270]|. |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins Phycoviolobilin| is formed in a |FRAME: 15-Z-alpha-Phycoerythrocyanins " (15Z)"| isomeric configuration. Upon absorbing light at 570 nm it is coverted to a |FRAME: 15-E-alpha-Phycoerythrocyanins "(15E)"| form. The 15Z form is restored when the excited 15E isomer emits a photon at 500 nm |CITS: [Zhao95]|., The entire pathway for the biosynthesis of a His-tagged holo-α subunit of a cyanobacterial phycoerythrocyanin carrying a |FRAME: Phycoviolobilins phycoviolobilin| chromophore was successfully reconstituted in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [19182270]|.

Summary: Mycoplasmas (also known as mollicutes ) are the smallest free living microorganisms,, and have the smallest genome among this group. For example, the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-272634|, has a genome size of ~800 kb., Because of the small genome, mollicutes do not have an extensive range of metabolic activities., As a matter of fact, they lack a complete tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and have no quinones and cytochromes,, making oxidative phosphorylation impossible |CITS: [1402786][9439886]|., Glucose, fructose and mannitol are transported by the PTS system into the cell and further degraded, by an Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas (EMP) glycolytic pathway to |FRAME: PYRUVATE|., All enzymes required for this pathway have been identified in these organisms., In addition, mollicutes also have the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-2022|, which in most organisms links, the glycolysis pathway with the TCA cycle., However, due to the absence of oxidative phosphorylation, pyruvate can be further metabolized, by only two alternative routes: either to |FRAME: L-LACTATE| by |FRAME:MONOMER-601|, or to, |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| by the |FRAME:CPLX-2022|, in which case it is further, metabolized to |FRAME:ACET| by |FRAME:MONOMER-602| and |FRAME:MONOMER-603|, |CITS: [8948633]|.

Summary: General Background, Rotenoid compounds are a class of plant secondary metabolites that derive from isoflavones. They are commonly found in leguminous species, but also occur in other families, such as the Iridiceae (see refs in |CITS: [11711058]|). These compounds play a role in plant interactions with insects |CITS: [Birch85]|. But, they have also been extracted for use by humans. |FRAME: CPD-5741|, perhaps the most commonly known member of the family, has a long history of use as a fish poison |CITS: [Leonard39]|, and it is also the major bioactive component of a commerically available insecticide |CITS: [16332203]|. Rotenone is also used in scientific experiments due to its ability to interfere with the electron transport chain |CITS: [4295606]| and it can also interfere with tubulin self-assembly |CITS: [568944]|. Other studies suggest that rotenone can promote Parkinson's Disease |CITS: [18155613]|. However, several rotenoids also have medicinal qualities. For example, amorphigenin |CITS: [8350086]|, |FRAME: CPD-12163|, and alpha-toxicarol |CITS: [14765285], [17125241]| seem to have anti-tumor effects., About This Pathway, The steps leading up to the formation of rot-2'-enonate, the common precursor to |FRAME: CPD-5741|, |FRAME: CPD-12163|, and a number of other rotenoids, have been characterized through an extensive series of radiotracer studies in |FRAME:TAX-56063| and |FRAME:TAX-48131|, though it seems likely that this pathway or a similar pathway will exist in other species that produce rotenoids, such as |FRAME: TAX-1157238| |CITS: [11711058]|. The skeleton of rot-2'-enonate is formed from |FRAME: PHE| and then progresses through various stages of flavanone and isoflavone biosynthesis before undergoing the rotenoid-specific prenylation and cyclization steps depicted in this pathway |CITS: [11711058]|.

Labdane diterpenes are an important class of compounds produced by many plants with wide ranging biological activities. They have been isolated from alga and from a number of plants including the Brazilian medicinal plant, Renealmia exaltata |CITS:[11520240]|, in Afromomum sceptrum K. Schum (Zingiberaceae) etc |CITS: [12009324 ]|. In 2006, for the first time ent-labdanes were chemically synthesized |CITS: [17971756]|.  , Labdane diterpenoids find use as precursor molecules in perfume manufacture. They give off a strong smell of ambergris, which is a product of sperm whale metabolism and a starting material for many perfumes. The odor is due to the oxidation of the main component, amberin, a triterpene |CITS: [VIAD82]|. Labdane diterpenes from Croton oblongifolius are potential drug targets as cytotoxic agents in human tumor cell lines |CITS: [11198816 ]|, |CITS: [12624826]|. The labdane diterpenes isolated from alga are also potent antibacterial agents, similarly labdane diterpenes isolated from Plectranthus ornatus show moderate antimicrobial activity against Candida species and gram negative and gram positive bacteria |CITS: [12398532]|. , The chemical structures of labdane diterpenes have a characteristic skeleton with a basic bicyclic structure and an additional C6 skeleton with or without an oxygen atom. Most of the research has been concentrated on the metabolism of ent kaurene which is an hydrocarbon precursor of gibberellin (GA), in contrast biosynthesis of labdane type with the oxygen atom in the skeleton are not well understood. The above pathway depicts the key biosynthetic step which leads to the formation of labdane diterpenes with oxygen atom, from the plant |FRAME: TAX-191224| which produces resins rich in these compounds and labdanum |CITS: [20595348]|.

Summary: Propionate can have broad negative effects on the bacterial cell functions, including cytosol acidification,, dissipation of the proton motive force, disruption of CoA homeostasis, and, in some cases,, inhibition of the key TCA enzymes aconitase and citrate synthase due to formation of |FRAME: CPD-622|., For these reasons propionate is sometimes used as a preservative in foods., However, some bacteria are able to degrade propionate, and even use it the sole carbon source. Out, of all the propionate degradation pathways, the 2-methylcitric acid cycle is the most widely destributed., In this pathway, the Cα methylene group of propionate is oxidized to a keto group yielding, |FRAME:PYRUVATE|, a common precursor for biosynthesis and energy production., The pathway, which was discovered in fungi |CITS: [Tabuchi74]| was best characterized in, |FRAME: TAX-90371| |CITS:[10482501][11294638]| (see |FRAME: PWY0-42|)., In that organism the pathway begins with the activation of |FRAME: PROPIONATE| to, |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| by |FRAME: MONOMER-62|, followed by the synthesis of, |FRAME: CPD-622| from |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| and |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|, catalyzed, by |FRAME: MONOMER-63|. |FRAME: CPD-622| is then dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-1136| by, |FRAME: MONOMER-64|, followed by rehydration to |FRAME: CPD-618| (catalyzed by, |FRAME: MONOMER-65| and |FRAME: MONOMER-13618|) and cleavage of the later into, |FRAME:PYRUVATE| and |FRAME:SUC|, performed by |FRAME: CPLX-7556|. , As mentioned above, pyruvate is a common precursor for biosynthesis and energy production., Oxaloacetate may be regenerated from succinate via the |FRAME:TCA| |CITS: [10482501]|., About This Pathway, A key reaction in the |FRAME: TAX-90371| pathway catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-622| to, |FRAME: CPD-1136|. This reaction is catalyzed by the |FRAME: MONOMER-64| enzyme, encoded by, the |FRAME: G-10383| gene. Some organisms do not have this enzyme, and thus utilize a different, variant of the pathway. These organism use a combination of two enzymes, encoded by the, |FRAME: G-10386| and |FRAME: G-10387| enzymes |CITS:[11495997][14702315]|. Characterization of, the proteins revealed that the |FRAME: G-10386| gene product is a |FRAME: MONOMER-13619|, , while the |FRAME: G-10387| gene product is an isomerase that catalyzes the transfer between, |FRAME: CPD-9421| and |FRAME: CPD-1136|. Since both proteins are required for the pathway to, proceed, the dehydratase must produce a stereoisomer of 2-methylaconitate that is not a substrate for, the aconitate hydratase enzyme, which catalyzes the next step, and thus this stereoisomer must be, converted by |FRAME: CPLX-7555| to the different form |CITS: [17567742]|., The Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-106590| possesses both a prpD gene and the acnD, (called acnM in that organism) and prpF genes. However, it was shown by gene, inactivation that while the prpD gene was dispensible, the latter two genes were required for growth, on propionate, suggesting that the organism is utilizing this variant of the pathway |CITS: [11495997]|., In addition, |FRAME: TAX-106590|, like several other organisms, lack the prpE gene. It is assumed that, in these organisms |FRAME:MONOMER-13637| is responsible for propionate activation |CITS:[11495997]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-13835 Pikromycin| (also known as picromycin) is an antibiotic macrolide produced by several strains of Streptomyces bacteria, the most well documented of which is |FRAME: TAX-54571|. It is the first macrolide antobiotic to have been isolated |CITS: [Brockmann51]|. While pikromycin is not a clinically useful antibiotic, the enzymes involved in its biosynthesis can be used in combination with enzymes from other organisms to synthesize novel antibiotic ketolide compounds., The pikromycin biosynthetic pathway was elucidated about five decades after its discovery, when the biosynthetic gene cluster encoding its synthesis was cloned and sequenced from |FRAME: TAX-54571| |CITS: [9770448]|. The cluster contains 18 discreet genes that can be divided into five separate loci: a polyketide synthase (PKS, pikA), a desosamine biosynthesis locus (des), a cytochrome P450 hydroxylase (pikC), a transcriptional activator (pikD), and a resistance locus (pikR)., The pikA gene locus encodes five polypeptides (|FRAME: G-17908|, |FRAME: G-17909|, |FRAME: G-17910|, |FRAME: G-17911| and |FRAME: G-17907|) that together encode a type I modular polyketide synthase. The first four polypeptides consist of a single loading module and six PKS elongation modules. While the first two polypeptides contain two elongation modules each, |FRAME: G-17910| and |FRAME: G-17911| contain only a single elongation module each |CITS: [10713461]|. The fifth polypeptide, PikAV, is a type II thioesterase. In vitro characterization of this enzyme suggests that it functions to remove aberrantly decarboxylated extender units from PKS ACP domains, preventing blockage of the PKS assembly line |CITS: [12368286]|., The pikromycin PKS is unique from other known PKS systems due to its capacity to efficiently generate two distinct macrolactone products. Early termination of polyketide biosynthesis at the |FRAME: G-17910| level results in production of the 12-membered ring macrolactone |FRAME: CPD-13831| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-7422|), while continued elongation through |FRAME: G-17911| results in the synthesis of the 14-membered ring macrolactone |FRAME: CPD-15995| |CITS: [10421766][12031664][12733905]|., Both macrolactones are glycosylated at the C5 position with the deoxyamino sugar |FRAME: CPD-13780|, via the activity of the |FRAME: G-17903|-encoded glycosyltransferase, generating |FRAME: CPD-13830| and |FRAME: CPD-13834|, respectively., Following glycosylation, both compounds are either singly or doubly hydroxylated by the same |FRAME: G-17902|-encoded cytochrome P450 hydroxylase to yield several antibiotic compounds |CITS: [9873687][16825192]|. In the case of the 12-membered ring macrolide, the products are |FRAME: CPD-13832|, |FRAME: CPD-13833|, and |FRAME: CPD-15998| |CITS: [11720530]|. In the case of the 14-membered ring macrolide, the products include |FRAME: CPD-13835|, |FRAME: CPD-15997|, and |FRAME: CPD-15996| |CITS: [16724858]|., The unique substrate flexibility of the tailoring enzymes of the picromycin biosynthesis pathway make them a promising tool for the generation of novel macrolide antibiotic compounds |CITS: [19027305]|.

Summary: The key enzyme of this pathway is apyrase (|FRAME: EC-3.6.1.5|)., Apyrases are active against both di- and triphosphate nucleotides (NDPs and NTPs) and hydrolyze NTPs to nucleotide monophosphates (NMPs) in two distinct successive phosphate-releasing steps, with NDPs as intermediates., They are widely distributed in eukaryotic cells from yeast |CITS: [10409709]| to mammals |CITS: [9556635]|, but similar enzymes have also been reported in bacteria |CITS: [15576788]|. They differ from ATPases, which specifically hydrolyze ATP, by hydrolyzing both ATP and ADP (although the relative rates of ATP and ADP hydrolysis differ depending on the species) |CITS: [8611638]|., Apyrases can be divided into ecto-apyrases, in which the catalytic domain is outside the cell |CITS: [7721538]|, and endo-apyrases, with the catalytic site inside the cell |CITS: [8611638]|. Ecto-apyrases participate in neurotransmission, blood platelet aggregation, and pressure regulation. Endo-apyrases are involved in protein glycosylation and sugar level control and in regulation of membrane integrity. , Apyrases are well studied in lower |CITS: [8703025][10409709][12686557]| and higher eukaryotes |CITS: [9364474][11985621][15122917][16752921]|, and less so in plants |CITS: [8579614][Steinebrunner00][17434987]|. They appear to be absent from bacteria and archaea., Apyrases are involved in many functions, and the pathway may be utilized in different capacities depending on specific cases., One case that has been studied involves protein and lipid glycosylation within the Golgi apparatus. NDP-sugars are synthesized in the cytosol and translocated into the Golgi lumen via specific membrane carriers. After transfer of sugar residues to proteins and lipids by galactosyltransferases, the resulting NDPs is likely hydrolyzed by the apyrases to NMPs. In this way, the NDPs, which are highly inhibitory to galactosyltransferases, do not accumulate in the lumen of the Golgi apparatus. The NMPs then exit the Golgi lumen by exchange with new cytosolic NDP-sugars via an anti-porter |CITS: [9204706][10409709]|.

General Background, Four types of aromatic compounds degradation pathways are thought to occur in different types of bacteria: , Aerobic organisms take advantage of the availability of molecular oxygen, and use oxygenases that introduce hydroxyl groups, and cleave the aromatic ring. These pathways usually lead to a few central intermediates such as |FRAME: CATECHOL|,, |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, and |FRAME: CPD-633| (see |FRAME: PWY-6079|)., Facultative aerobes utilize two types of pathways, depending on the availability of oxygen., When oxygen is present, these organisms use the so-called "hybrid" type of aerobic metabolism for some aromatic compounds, including |FRAME: BENZOATE|, |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: PHENYLACETATE|., These pathways use |FRAME: CO-A| to activate and form thioesters of the substrates, followed by an oxygenase/reductase step to dearomatize (but not cleave) the ring. Cleavage of the dearomatized ring does not require oxygen (see |FRAME: PWY-6077|)., Under anaerobic conditions, facultative aerobes and phototrophs use a reductive aromatic metabolism., The aromatic compounds are activated by |FRAME: CO-A| to an active intermediate that can be transformed to important, central intermediate such as |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|. Reduction of the aromatic ring of |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA|, is catalyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-883| and is driven by the hydrolysis of 2 ATP molecules (see, |FRAME: 2AMINOBENZDEG-PWY|)., Strict anaerobes utilize a completely different and not well characterized benzoyl-coenzyme A reductase that does not utilize ATP |CITS: [18378589]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: TAX-420246| degrades |FRAME:TRP| to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| via the intermediates |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| and |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE|. While |FRAME:TRP| degradation via |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE| is well documented in eukaryotes (although via a different pathway, as documented in pathway |FRAME: TRYPTOPHAN-DEGRADATION-1|), this is an unusual route for bacteria |CITS: [19942660]|., The key enzyme of the pathway, which converts |FRAME: ANTHRANILATE| to |FRAME: 3-HYDROXY-ANTHRANILATE|, is |FRAME: MONOMER-15633|. The gene encoding the protein has been cloned, expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562| and purified, and was shown to be an FAD-dependent hydroxylase. The |FRAME: G-12003| gene that encodes the enzyme is found in a cluster that also contains two additional genes that encode a riboflavin kinase/FMN adenylyltransferase and an FAD reductase, which together provide FAD for the hydroxylase |CITS: [19942660]|.

Summary: All cyanobacterial membranes contain alkanes and/or alkenes of 1519 carbons at concentrations similar to that of chlorophyll. The most common alkanes observed are |FRAME: CPD-7946| and |FRAME: HEPTADECANE-CPD| |CITS:[17731762][McInnes80][12495426]|. These alkanes are prduced from fatty acids in three steps - activation of the fatty acid by an |FRAME: ACP "acyl-carrier-protein"|, reduction of the activated fatty acid to an aldehyde, and decarbonylation of the aldehyde, resulting in an alkane that is one carbon short of the original fatty acids. Since most fatty acids have an even number of carbons (fatty acids are synthesized by the addition of two carbon units), the resulting alkanes have an odd number of carbons., It should be noted that alkanes are produced in other organisms as well - for example, in the |FRAME: PWY-282 "production of plant cuticular waxes"| |CITS: [18251711]|, as |FRAME: PWY-7035 "insect pheromones"| |CITS: [7937826][10406089]|, in green algae |CITS: [1898004][15630516]|, in fungi |CITS: [18957585]| and in bacteria other than cyanobacteria |CITS:[ 6025301][15170379]|. The final step in the synthesis of n-hydrocarbons in animals and higher plants is thought to involve enzymatic decarbonylation of aldehydes to the corresponding alkanes |CITS: [3343228][1608940][12467640]|., The genes that are responsible for alkane biosynthesis in cyanobacteria, which also involve decarbonylation, have been identified and cloned from several strains of cyanobacteria |CITS: [20061450][20671186]|. , While long-chain activated fatty acids can be generated in cyanobacteria de novo (via the elongase complex),it has been shown that they can also be generated from free fatty acids (provided either externally or by lipid degradation) by the action of |FRAME: MONOMER-17302| |CITS: [20061450]|., The conversion of the activated fatty acids to alkanes is catalyzed by two enzymes, the products of the |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1594| and |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1593| genes, which encode an |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1594-MONOMER| and an |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1593-MONOMER|, respectively., These two genes are located next to each other on the chromosomes of most strains that were studied, and appear to form an operon. In |FRAME: TAX-1140| the two genes reside in an operon with a third gene, accA, which encodes the α subunit of the carboxyl transferase component of acetyl-CoA carboxylase., Extracts of |FRAME:TAX-562| expressing the two genes contained substantial quantities of odd-chain alkanes and alkenes., |FRAME: SYNPCC7942_1593-MONOMER "Aldehyde decarbonylase"| was originally thought to produce |FRAME: CARBON-MONOXIDE| like the enzymes from higher plants and green algae. However, the most recent studies showed that the actual product of the cyanobacterial enzyme is |FRAME: FORMATE| |CITS: [21341652]|. There was some controversy regarding the actual reaction. While some researchers found that the enzyme requires oxygen |CITS: [21671322][21462983]|, others reported that the enzyme is much more active anaerobically |CITS: [22074177]|. However, additional work verified that the enzyme is indeed an oxygenase |CITS: [22947199]|., A mutant of |FRAME: TAX-1148| that does not produce alkanes exhibited enhanced cyclic electron flow, in which electrons from photosystem I (PSI) were returned to the |FRAME: Plastoquinols plastoquinone| pool, resulting in a slower growth rate |CITS: [26459862]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid) is a member of the diverse sialic acid family of α-keto sugars. Members of this family mediate or modulate many cellular interactions in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. , Many pathogenic organisms can display, bind, or catabolize sialic acids, helping them to evade host immune responses and invade cells |CITS: [19282391]|. Bacteria incorporate sialic acid-like derivatives into virulence-associated cell surface glycoconjugates which may include lipopolysaccharide (LPS), capsular polysaccharide, pili and flagella. These nonulosonate derivatives are unique to microorganisms and may show configurational differences as compared with sialic acid. , |FRAME: CPD-13166| is a nonulosonate derivative that shows the same D-glycero-D-galacto absolute configuration as sialic acid (|FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) |CITS: [19282391]|. It was first identified in 1994 as a component of |FRAME: TAX-66976| LPS |CITS: [8168511]|. Its correct stereochemistry was determined in 2001 |CITS: [11383892]|. |FRAME: TAX-66976| is the causative agent of Legionnaires' disease, an often fatal pneumonia that was first recognized in a large outbreak at an American Legion convention in Philadelphia in 1976., Legionaminic acid derivatives have also been found in the O-antigens of |FRAME:TAX-294| |CITS: [8593624]|, Vibrio alginolyticus |CITS: [1707620]|, Vibrio salmonicida |CITS: [8766209]|, and Acinetobacter baumannii |CITS: [9428717]|., The gastrointestinal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-195| was shown to have novel |FRAME: CPD-13166| derivatives O-linked to serine/threonine residues of flagellin, and genes critical to |FRAME: CPD-13167| biosynthesis were identified |CITS: [17371878]|. The complete biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-13167| has been elucidated in the gastrointestinal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-192222| (see |FRAME: PWY-6749|)., About This Pathway, In |FRAME: TAX-446|, the active form of legionaminic acid, |FRAME: CPD-13167|, is produced from |FRAME: CPD-14248| by the action of three enzymes, encoded by the |FRAME: G-15418|, |FRAME: G-15417|, and |FRAME: G-15416| genes |CITS: [18275154]|. These genes are homologous to known sialic acid biosynthetic genes from |FRAME: TAX-487| and |FRAME: TAX-1392869| (see |FRAME: PWY-6139|)., The |FRAME: G-15416| gene encodes a hydrolyzing |FRAME: MONOMER-17728| that converts |FRAME: CPD-14248| into |FRAME: CPD-13165| and UDP. Despite the similarity to the genes from other organisms, the enzyme is specific for its substrate and cannot accept |FRAME: UDP-N-ACETYL-D-GLUCOSAMINE|, indicating it is not involved in the biosynthesis of sialic acid. The |FRAME: G-15417| gene encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-17729| that condenses 2,4-diacetamido-2,4,6-trideoxymannose with phosphoenolpyruvate, and the |FRAME: G-15418| gene encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-17730| that generates the activated form of legionaminic acid used in lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis., Together, the three enzymes constitute a pathway that converts a UDP-linked bacillosamine derivative into a CMP-linked legionaminic acid derivative |CITS: [18275154]|.

Summary: While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]| it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|. The most common mechanism for retreiving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid. In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|). In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde. Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols", or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids ("fusel acids")  |CITS: [15933030]|., Although |FRAME: MET| is not an aromatic amino acid, many similariies are found between its degradation and the degradation of aromatic amino acids in |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [15933030]|. Cultures grown with either |FRAME: MET|, |FRAME: PHE| or |FRAME: LEU| all induced the same decarboxylase, and in all cases the culture medium contained not only the fusel alcohol derived from the amino acid that was added to the medium, but also the fusel alcohols which are derived from the other two amino acids. These data suggest that the same broad specificity enzymes were involved in all cases, and that the induced enzymes compete with biosynthetic pathways for the fate of other amino acids, not included in the synthetic medium |CITS: [15933030]|, Following the transamination of |FRAME: MET| to |FRAME:CPD-479|, the 2-oxo acid is converted to |FRAME:CPD-7036| and eventually |FRAME:CPD-7037|, which is excreted from the cell |CITS: [15933030]|., The first step can be catalyzed by either of |FRAME: TAX-4932| two aromatic amino acid transaminases, |FRAME: YGL202W-MONOMER| and |FRAME: YHR137W-MONOMER|. |FRAME: MET| has been shown to be a substrate for both enzymes. In both cases, the amino acceptor was |FRAME: PHENYL-PYRUVATE| (but not |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE|)  |CITS: [9491082][9491083]|., Once transaminated, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated by the |FRAME:CPLX3O-71|, encoded by the |FRAME: YDR380W| gene, whose transcription increased 15-fold when |FRAME:MET| replaced |FRAME: AMMONIA| as the culture's nitrogen source |CITS: [15933030]|., The last step of this pathway has not been investigated, but it is likely similar to the comparable step in the degradation of other amino acids, such as |FRAME: PHE| and |FRAME: TRP|, which can be performed by any of the yeast alcohol dehydrogenases |CITS: [12499363]|.

Male fertility in |FRAME:TAX-4101| has been found to be linked to the formation of specific flavonols that only occur and accumulate in the gametophyte of the plant |CITS:[12244218]|. The flavonol diglycosides |FRAME:CPD-15105| and |FRAME:CPD-15106| are the only flavonoids found in wild-type |FRAME:TAX-4102| pollen |CITS:[Zerback89]| |CITS:[7630971]|. Conditional male fertility (CMF) observed in plants with suppressed chalcone synthase gene expression describes a condition where viable pollen are formed but are unable to germinate and start tube growth. The anthers of such plants are devoid of the flavonol diglycosides found in wild-type plants |CITS:[Taylor92]|. The arrested development can be rescued by adding external flavonols, i.e. |FRAME:CPD1F-90| and |FRAME:CPD-520| which restores the normal development of the pollen |CITS:[12231878]|. The biochemical complementation overcomes the self-cross blockage in the pollen and is working at very low, micromolar concentrations of the flavonols |CITS:[11607312]|. , Two enzyme activities have been found which in a sequential manner glycosylate the aglycones to form the corresponding flavonol-3-O-glucosylgalactoside. The flavonol 3-O-galactosyltransferase (F3GalTase) catalyzing the formation of flavonol 3-O-galactosides has been identified in |FRAME:TAX-4101| pollen, cloned and recombinant expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|. The recombinant F3GalTase shows remarkable high catalytic activities in both the forward and reverse direction and comes close to virtual catalytic perfection |CITS:[10567367]|. It had been previously shown that F3GalTase precedes the glucosylation step which completes the flavonol-3-O-glucosylgalactoside biosynthesis in pollen. The flavonol 3-O-galactoside-2"-O-glucosyltransferase (F2"GT) only acts on either |FRAME:CPD-13509| (this pathway) or |FRAME:CPD-7260| (see |FRAME:PWY-7191|) producing the flavonol glucosylgalactoside which have been shown to accumulate in the pollen cytoplasm |CITS:[7630971]|., Based upon the experimental data a model for the reproductive role of the pollen-specific flavonol glucosylgalctoside biosynthesis was suggested |CITS:[7630971]| |CITS:[Taylor98]|. It was proposed that the flavonol aglycone formation is compartmentally separated from the flavonol glucosylgalactoside biosynthesis. The flavonol aglycones are produced in the tapetum and internalized through an unknown mechanism in the pollen where they are glycosylated to form the flavonol glucosylgalactoside. Through this process the polar, chemical active and smaller molecules are converted to bulkier, chemical less active and more water-soluble molecules. Either the flavonol galactosyltransferase |CITS:[Taylor98]| and/or the flavonol 3-galactoside glucosyltransferase |CITS:[7630971]| are associated in a way with the pollen membrane to further the uptake of the flavonol aglycones. The flavonol glucosylgalctosides are then formed and accumulate in the pollen cytoplasm. The dual activity of the |FRAME:MONOMER-17892| might be responsible to maintain an enzymatically controlled pool of pollen reproduction active flavonols and pollen reproduction inactive flavonol diglycosides. However, this model does not solve the findings that neither flavonol aglycones (the active principle) nor flavonol 3-O-galactosides can be found in wild-type |FRAME:TAX-4101| pollen. It cannot be ruled out at this point that despite of the lack of experimental evidence the flavonol glucosylgalactosides are the active components for pollen fertility or trigger an unknown signal to initiate this process. Hence, further research is necessary to resolve the remaining problems.

Summary: General Background, Glucosyltransferases as one subclass of glycosyltransferases are involved in the glucosylation , of a broad variety of secondary plant metabolites, amongst them monolignols involved in the metabolic sequence of lignin , biosynthesis |CITS: [Ibrahim77]| |CITS: [Foerster99]|. Modifying enzymes such as the multigene family of glucosyltransferases , contribute to the plasticity of metabolism where corresponding products are either involved in a particular biosynthetic route , or may act as gateways into different metabolic pathways |CITS: [11042211]| |CITS: [10973093]|., The presence and significance to lignification of glucosylated cinnamyl alcohols in the cambium of woody plants were emphasized , several decades ago by Freudenberg |CITS: [Freudenberg63]| |CITS: [5593877]|. Although , glucosyltransferases in general may cover a broad substrate spectrum it has been demonstrated that certain glucosyltransferases , exhibit a rather strict specificity towards their substrates |CITS: [4731963]| |CITS: [11430981]| |CITS: [15907484]|., Extensive research has revised the view about how the metabolic sequence for lignin formation proceeds in plants. It appears , that the interconversion of lignin precursors may occur at varied points along the lignification pathway, along a preferred , metabolic route, but most probably not at the phenylpropanoid acid stage |CITS: [11960740]| |CITS: [14503002]|. Furthermore, , the ratio of guaiacyl to syringyl units can be modified at the level of CoA esters |CITS: [GRIMMIG99]|, cinnamyl aldehydes , |CITS: [10430877]|, cinnamyl alcohols |CITS: [14709025]| and monolignol glucosides |CITS: [MATSUI96]|. However, it is , still a matter of debate whether and to what extent monomeric alcohol and aldehyde glucosides are involved in the in vivo , lignin biosynthesis |CITS: [11430981]| |CITS: [15986215]| and more research is needed to address this issue., The CAGT activity obtained from seasonal harvests of cambium and developing xylem appeared synchronously with resumption , of cambial cell-division activity and is, as its product coniferin, completely undetectable in dormant tissues |CITS: [Savidge98]| , |CITS: [Foerster99]|. This link between cambial and enzymatic activity still remains to be demonstrated for the enzymatic , counterpart of this pathway, the coniferin specific β-glucosidase |CITS: [7765617]| |CITS: [7724669]| |CITS: [10412914]| , which liberates the aglycones and makes them available for the final assembly of lignin. The turnover of coniferin in pine , seedlings has been measured with a half life in the order of 60 to 120 hr, but a quantitative correlation between coniferin , turnover and lignification could not be established |CITS: [27355]|., Coniferin accumulation appears to be under hormonal control. The metabolization of exogenous coniferin in dependence on , hormone supplements has been demonstrated in cell cultures of |FRAME:TAX-3348| cambium |CITS: [Savidge89]|. A , combination of auxin-cytokinin in the media quickly abolished exogenous applied coniferin whereas the control experiment , (auxin and cytokinin alone) had no such effect. It was discussed that a defined ratio of auxin to cytokinin promotes coniferin , hydrolysis as demonstrated in various plant tissues |CITS: [HOSEL82]| and that the varying ratio of this plant hormones , throughout the cambial region may be the regulative principle for the observed spatial and temporal phenomenon of , accumulation or disappearance of coniferin |CITS: [Savidge89]|. Proof for the significance of exogenous and endogenous , signals on the biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids and their derivatives is also the recently published accumulation of coniferin , and syringin upon light induction in roots of Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [15144378]|. The reported coniferin , accumulation is the result of a high-irradiance response (HIR) demonstrating the involvement of primary photoreceptors , such as phytochrome and cryptochrome. , About This Pathway, The most prominent monolignol glucoside accumulating in a variety of plants is the , 4-O-β-D-glucopyranoside of trans-coniferyl alcohol, i.e. coniferin. The enzyme catalyzing the formation of , coniferin has been purified from different plant sources |CITS: [10853]| and appears to be most active in developing , xylem of gymnosperms |CITS: [6210530]| |CITS: [11430981]|., The UDPG:coniferyl alcohol glucosyltransferase (CAGT) also glucosylates sinapyl alcohol with high efficiency in pine , cambium |CITS: [Savidge98]| |CITS: [Foerster00]| and cell cultures of |FRAME:TAX-55182| and |FRAME:TAX-3764| spec. |CITS: [Ibrahim77]| , |CITS: [10853]|. In addition, coniferyl and sinapyl aldehydes have been converted with comparable catalytic efficiency , |CITS: [6210530]| |CITS: [11430981]| |CITS: [10853]| (|FRAME:PWY-83|). , The coniferin specific β-glucosidase (and isomers thereof) was isolated from the differentiating xylem of pines and , characterized with regard to biochemical and molecular features |CITS: [7765617]| |CITS: [7724669]| |CITS: [10412914]|. , The β-glucosidase specifically acts on coniferin and syringin and has been shown to be exclusively localized to the , differentiating xylem |CITS: [7724669]| supporting a potential role of the enzyme in the lignification process. The in vitro , finding that coniferylaldehyde glucoside can be enzymatically derive from coniferin and that the aldehyde glucoside can be , deglucosylated to yield coniferylaldehyde suggest an alternative pathway for coniferin to enter the monolignol biosynthetic , route |CITS: [15986215]|.

Summary: Phospholipids are the major structural components of biological membranes in plants, animals, and yeasts. Summary: The |FRAME: Yeast-GPI-Anchor "glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor"| is a glycolipid structure that is added posttranslationally to the C-terminus of many eukaryotic proteins (roughly 1% of all proteins encoded by eukaryotic genomes, and ~10-20% of all membrane proteins that enter the secretory pathway after being targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum). It anchors the attached protein in the outer leaflet of the cell membrane. , The GPI anchor is preassembled by enzymes attached to the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). For a full description of the GPI anchor biosynthesis in the ER see |FRAME: PWY-8601|. Following the transfer of the GPI anchor to target proteins in the ER, a post-attachment remodeling phase begins, which prompts an ER-to-Golgi transport of the GPI-anchored proteins, where they continue the modification and eventually sorted out of the Golgi to their final location |CITS: [24784135][38167496]|., The first modification process is the removal of the acyl chain linked to the 2-OH position of inositol ring, which is catalyzed by the ER-located enzyme |FRAME: EC-3.1.1.M30| |FRAME: G3O-30435| |CITS: [14734546]|. , At this point the processed GPI-anchored proteins are transported from the ER to the Golgi in vesicles formed by coat protein complex II (COPII). These vesicles bud off from the ER at specialized sites and then fuse with the Golgi apparatus. Specific proteins, including those of the p24 family, are involved in packaging GPI-anchored proteins into these vesicles |CITS: [11207371][19054390]|., The processing of the GPI anchor continues in the Golgi. The yeast GPI anchor is originally synthesized with a diacylglycerol that contains conventional C16 and C18 fatty acids. However, the lipid moiety in mature GPI-anchored proteins is exchanged to either diacylglycerol containing a C26:0 fatty acid in the sn-2 position or to ceramide. While the enzymes responsible for the exchange with ceramides have not been identified yet, the enzymes responsible for incorporation of the C26:0 fatty acid have been described. The modification process begins with the removal of the acyl chain at sn-2 by GPI-phospholipase A2 activity catalyzed by |FRAME: G3O-29355| |CITS: [17021251]|. Following the removal of the acyl group, |FRAME: G3O-30585| adds a C26 fatty acid to that position |CITS: [16597698][18036137]|.

|FRAME: Carrageenans "Carrageenans"| are sulfated polysaccharides that are extracted from sea weeds belonging to the Rhodophyta, mainly from |FRAME: TAX-2769|, Euchema and Gigartina. The basic units are repeats of alpha -1,3 linked D-galactose and beta 1,4- linked D-galactose |CITS: [1367970]|. These repeating units allow gelation due to the presence of a 3,6 - anhydro bridge on the beta 1,4- linked galactose unit giving rise to a double helix during gelation. The precursors for |FRAME: iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, enzymatically convert the 6-sulphate group on the 1-4 linked galactose to the 3,6 anhydro form. |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| is also of commercial importance and each sample of extract may contain mixtures of |FRAME:iota-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| and several variations of carrageenans |CITS: [GRIERSON84]|., Carrageenan's are used as food additives particularly for puddings, based on the property of gel formation with milk and also as stabilizing agents in flavored milk products like chocolate milk and ice cream. The non gelling |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| thickens when added to cold milk. There is an extensive use of carrageenans in meat products, particularly pet food |CITS: [8747100]|. The texture of carrageenan can be controlled by altering the concentrations of |FRAME: kappa-Carrageenan|, |FRAME:iota-Carrageenan| and |FRAME: Lambda-Carrageenan| carragenans in the gel mix |CITS: [GRIERSON84]|. , The enzyme responsible for polymerizing carrageenan, producing 3,6-anhydrous D-galactose with stochiometric release of sulphur has been identified in |FRAME: TAX-2769| |CITS: [16660358]|.

Summary: This pathway describes the late steps in the biosynthesis of adenosylcobalamin starting with |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP| - the last common intermediate used for the synthesis of cobamides with different lower ligand bases. By definition, the lower ligand base of cobalamin-type B12 vitamins is |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|., In this pathway |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE| is tethered to the corrin ring via a structure known as the nucleotide loop, which is composed from |FRAME:R-1-AMINOPROPAN-2-YL-PHOSPHATE| and |FRAME:DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|., Until 2007 it was believed that the last reaction in the biosynthesis of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN| was the linking of |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| (a product of |FRAME: DIMETHYLBENZIMIDAZOLE|) to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-GDP|, in a reaction catalyzed by cobalamine synthase. However, it has been shown that at least in |FRAME: TAX-90371| the true substrate for the enzyme is |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P|, and not |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE| |CITS: [17209023]|, and that the product of the reaction is actually |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P|. Thus, there is one more reaction in the pathway, the dephosphorylation of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P| to |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, which is catalyzed by |FRAME:MONOMER-13213|, the enzyme initially proposed to catalyze the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P| |CITS: [17209023]|., This model addresses several questions that were associated with the previous model, such as the presence of |FRAME:ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN-5-P| (which has been documented much earlier in the organism |FRAME: TAX-1752| |CITS: [4296474]|), the higher affinity of the CobS protein (and its homologs in other organisms) towards |FRAME:ALPHA-RIBAZOLE-5-P|, and the inability of |FRAME:G-10054| mutants to salvage cobyrate under aerobic conditions |CITS: [17209023]|., For more information, please see the summaries for the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5507| and |FRAME:P381-PWY|.

General Background, The pyridine nucleotide coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) play key roles as cofactors in oxidation-reduction reactions in all living cells. The nicotinamide ring functions as a prosthetic group for these reactions. Their oxidized forms are depicted here as |FRAME: NAD| and |FRAME: NADP| due to the positive charge on the nitrogen atom in the nicotinamide ring. Their reduced forms are referred to as |FRAME: NADH| and |FRAME: NADPH|. , Although they appear chemically equivalent, their metabolic roles differ. |FRAME: NAD| is generally the cofactor for energy-producing oxidation reactions, while |FRAME: NADPH| is the cofactor for reductive biosynthetic reactions. The |FRAME: OXIDATIVEPENT-PWY| is an important source of |FRAME: NADPH| |CITS: [14660605]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPLX66-456| is a cytosolic enzyme which phosphorylates |FRAME: NAD| to form |FRAME: NADP| |CITS: [11594753]|. Its activity is regulated by the redox state of the cell and is inhibited by |FRAME: NADPH|. , |FRAME: CPLX66-457| is a pyridine nucleotide transhydrogenase and an integral component of the inner mitochondrial membrane. It consists of three subunits and is part of the energy-transfer system of the respiratory chain |CITS: [10673423]|. The protein catalyzes the transfer of a hydride ion between |FRAME: NADH| and |FRAME: NADP| |CITS: [9524818]|. The transhydrogenation between NADH and NADP is coupled to respiration and ATP hydrolysis and functions as a proton pump across the membrane. , Detoxification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in mitochondria by glutathione peroxidases depends on NADPH produced by |FRAME: CPLX66-457|, for regeneration of reduced |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| from oxidized |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE| |CITS: [22634753]|.

Summary: |FRAME: NICOTINE Nicotine| is the principal alkaloid in the leaves of commercially used tobacco (|FRAME: TAX-4097| and |FRAME: TAX-4093|) |CITS: [Schmeltz77]|, where it functions as a defense compound. In the plant tissue nicotine is mostly present in the |FRAME: NICOTINE| isomeric form |CITS: [Armstrong98]|, although tobacco smoke contains up to 10% of |FRAME: R-NICOTINE|, probably due to racemization during combustion (in |CITS: [15734728]|)., Early studies of nicotine degradation by |FRAME: TAX-286| species identified several intermediates, including |FRAME: CPD-14092|, |FRAME: METHYLAMINE|, |FRAME: CPD-14094| and |FRAME: CPD-14096| |CITS:[Tabuchi55][13471069]|. The latter was predicted to be further metabolized by cleavage at the 3 position to form |FRAME: 2-5-DIHYDROXYPYRIDINE| and |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD| |CITS: [8840783]|. |FRAME: 2-5-DIHYDROXYPYRIDINE| is believed to be further degraded into the central metabolite |FRAME: FUM| via |FRAME: MALEAMATE| and |FRAME: MALEATE| |CITS: [17464070]|., The genetics of the system began to clarify upon the study of the aerobic soil bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1042876|, isolated in China, which is able to grow on nicotine as a sole source of carbon and nitrogen |CITS: [15604785]|. The genes encoding the enzymes required for nicotine degradation reside in the core genome and in a genomic island |CITS: [21914868]|. The first genes were identified by transforming an |FRAME:TAX-562| strain with a genomic library prepared from |FRAME: TAX-1042876|. Among the three reading frames identified was the |FRAME: G-14949| gene, which was shown to encode a |FRAME: MONOMER-17157| |CITS: [18203859]|, and the |FRAME: G-14948| gene, which encodes a |FRAME: MONOMER-17156| that was reported to catalyze multiple reactions, transforming |FRAME: NICOTINE| to |FRAME: CPD-14094| via |FRAME: CPD-14091| |CITS: [19060159]|. A gene encoding a second |FRAME:CPLX-8439| was subsequently discovered outside the nic cluster |CITS: [21949128]|., The last holes in the pathway were filled after the genome sequencing of |FRAME: TAX-1042876|. A second nicotine dehydrogenase, encoded by the |FRAME: G-43961| gene, was discovered, along with three genes that encode a |FRAME: CPD-23445|-dependent |FRAME: CPLX-8991| |CITS: [24204321]|., While the NicA1 protein was reported to catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-14091| to |FRAME: CPD-14094| in a single step, a study of another nicotine-degrading strain, |FRAME: TAX-879273|, revealed a different route via |FRAME: CPD-14100|, which involved two novel enzymes |CITS: [22267672]|. These two enzymes are also present in the genome of |FRAME: TAX-1042876|, and one of them, |FRAME: EC-1.4.2.3|, has been shown to be essential for nicotine degradation in this organism |CITS: [24204321]|, suggesting that the actual pathway involves all of these enzymes.

General Background, Organisms produce hydrocarbons of different types by different mechanisms., Several mechanisms have been described for the production of hydrocarbons from fatty acids or their intermediates, including synthesis of alkanes from fatty aldehydes by decarbonylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7032| and |FRAME: PWY-7033|), synthesis of long-chain olefins by head-to head condensation of fatty acids (see for example |FRAME: PWY-7027|), and production of alkenes from fatty acids by decarboxylation (see |FRAME: PWY-7026| and |FRAME: PWY-7029|)., |FRAME: 1-Alkenes 1-Alkenes| are acyclic hydrocarbons with a single carbon-carbon double bond at the very end of the molecule. Terminal olefins are similar, but may contain additional double bonds throughout the molecule. They are natural products that have important industrial applications as both fuels and chemicals. 1-Alkenes have been reported to occur in both prokaryotes eukaryotes, and are produced by several mechanisms. One such mechanism is the decarbonylation of unsaturated fatty aldehydes |CITS:[17731762][Tornabene82][3343228][Ladygina06]|. However, in some cases the alkenes are synthesized by decarboxylation of free fatty acids. Examples are |FRAME: CPD-14227| in beetles of the genus |FRAME: TAX-7069| |CITS: [Goergen90][Villaverde07]|, |FRAME: CPD-14223| and related higher unsaturated polyenes in plants such as |FRAME: TAX-4222| |CITS: [2583180][3816783]|, and C23-C33 dienes and trienes in the green microalga |FRAME: TAX-869302|., About This Pathway, This pathway describes the production of terminal olefins by decarboxylation of fatty acids. The process has been described in |FRAME: TAX-4222| (safflower) |CITS: [2583180][3816783]|, and in Gram-positive bacteria of the |FRAME: TAX-227979| genus. , Germinating safflower seedlings contain several 1-alkenes and terminal olefins, including |FRAME: CPD-14227|, |FRAME: CPD-14223|, |FRAME: CPD-14249|, |FRAME: CPD-14250| and |FRAME: CPD-14251|, which are derived from |FRAME: PALMITATE|, |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID|, |FRAME: OLEATE-CPD|, |FRAME: LINOLEIC_ACID| and |FRAME: LINOLENIC_ACID|, respectively |CITS: [Binder75][3816783]|. Analysis of several |FRAME: TAX-227979| strains showed the presence of several 1-alkenes and terminal olefins, including |FRAME: CPD-14230|, |FRAME: CPD-14233|, |FRAME: CPD-14221|, |FRAME: CPD-14222|, |FRAME: CPD-14220|, |FRAME: CPD-14235|, |FRAME: CPD-14236| and |FRAME: CPD-14237| |CITS: [21216900]|., Cell-free lysates of |FRAME: TAX-946435| converted |FRAME: ARACHIDIC_ACID| and |FRAME: STEARIC_ACID| exclusively to |FRAME: CPD-14220| and |FRAME: CPD-14223|, respectively, while in vivo bioconversion of C16 and C18 fatty acids was primarily to C19 terminal olefins, suggesting that shorter chain length fatty acids may be elongated prior to decarboxylation in vivo., The enzyme catalyzing the conversion in |FRAME: TAX-946435| is a P450 enzyme that uses |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| as its main source of electrons. In addition to decarboxylation, the enzyme also functions as a hydroxylase, forming minor amounts of hydroxy fatty acids |CITS: [21216900]|., A mechanism that explains how the enzyme can catalyze both hydroxylation and decarboxylation of its substrates has been proposed |CITS: [21216900]|. According to the model, the iron center of the P450 enzyme is oxidized by |FRAME: HYDROGEN-PEROXIDE| to the high-energy oxo-ferryl heme via the hydrogen peroxide shunt. The iron then abstracts a hydrogen atom from either the α or β position of the free fatty acid, giving rise to a carbon radical on the substrate. At this point two different reactions could take place. If the oxygen rebounds, it results in hydroxylation at the α or β position forming a hydroxy fatty acid. Alternatively, an additional proton can be abstracted from the β-position, forming water and a carbocation, which can readily decarboxylate to form the terminal olefin |CITS: [21216900]|.

General Background, The |FRAME: Depsides depside| compound |FRAME: CPD-25039| is one of the most common lichen secondary metabolites. It is often present in lichens from the families |FRAME: TAX-5198|, |FRAME: TAX-39933|, |FRAME: TAX-78060|, and |FRAME: TAX-50937|, but has also been reported from other lichen families, as well as from some mosses and higher plants |CITS: [Studzinska-Sroka17]|.., |FRAME: CPD-25039 Atranorin| was isolated in 1898 by Hesse, and has been studied extensively for its pharmacological and biological activities. It has antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria |CITS: [Toledo-Marante03][18236733][Neeraj11][ 23374132][Kosanic14][Rajan16]|, antifungal activity |CITS: [16989308]|, antiviral activity |CITS: [25793970]|, antiprotozoal activity |CITS: [21487780][ 21814840][Susithra14][32079149]|, antioxidant activity |CITS: [21138055][21111802]|, photoprotective activity |CITS: [Fernandez96][9595708][23416709][Varol15]|, and cytotoxic and antiproliferative activities. In recent years it has been reported to suppress lung cancer cell motility and tumorigenesis |CITS: [28811522]|, exert selective cytostatic and anti-invasive effects on human prostate and melanoma cancer cells |CITS: [28095330]|, comprehensively suppress hepatocellular carcinoma tumorigenesis and metastatic potential |CITS: [30974882]|, and exhibit in vitro anti-breast cancer activity through interaction with Akt activity |CITS: [32096436]|., About the Pathway, An early proposal for the biosynthetic pathway postulated |FRAME: CPD-25037| and |FRAME: CPD-25038| as intermediates |CITS: [Millanes03]|. However, we now know that the actual pathway is different, with a polyketide synthase catalyzing the formation of the rings and their condensation via an ester bond., The genes encoding atranorin biosynthesis were found by the identification of a biosynthetic gene cluster that is present exclusively in lichens producing atranorin. By expressing different combinations of genes in the plant-pathogenic fungus |FRAME: TAX-5454| it was shown that |FRAME: CPD-25039| biosynthesis requires only three genes - a non-reducing polyketide synthase (NR-PKS) that produces |FRAME: CPD-25208|, a methyltransferase, and a cytochrome P450 that forms the aldehyde group |CITS: [34154413]|., Different intermediiates were observed when different gene combinations were present in the recombinant host, indicating that the hydroxylase and methyltransferase do not act in a particular order |CITS: [34154413]|.

Summary: Please note: This pathway does not necessarily represent a single organism. Rather, it is a super-pathway, assembled from several pathways found in a variety of organisms, each producing a different stereoisomer of |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2-3-butanediol"|. The purpose of this pathway is to provide an overview of the metabolic capabilities of the ecosystem, pertaining to the biosynthesis of this compound. That said, there are indications that some organisms are indeed capable of producing all three stereoisomers., 2,3-butanediol is a compound of commercial interest, mostly as an antifreeze agent due to to its low freezing point |CITS: [Magee87]|. One of its well known applications is the formation of methyl ethyl ketone, by dehydration, which can be used as a liquid fuel additive |CITS: [11234948]|., Many bacterial species can ferment pyruvate to |FRAME: 2-3-Butanediols "2-3-butanediol"| via several intermediate compounds,, including |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE|, |FRAME: ACETOIN|, and |FRAME: DIACETYL|. Not all species carry the process all the way through - some may stop earlier, accumulating some of the intermediates. , Of particular importance is the production of |FRAME: DIACETYL|, an important flavor metabolite in dairy products, wine and beer |CITS: [2198252][15454314]|., The metabolic function of 2,3-butanediol is not well understood, although it may play a role in preventing intracellular, acidification by changing the metabolism from acid production to the formation of a neutral compound, |CITS: [6298028]|. In addition, the pathway might participate in regulation of the NADH/NAD+ ratio, in the bacteria |CITS: [8444801]|., In this pathway |FRAME: PYRUVATE|, which is produced by substrate level phosphorylation, is converted to |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-5243| (also known as α-ALS). 2-acetolactate is an unstable intermediate, and in the presence of oxygen it can undergo a spontaneous decarboxylation, producing |FRAME: DIACETYL| that is converted to acetoin by the activity of the dual-function enzyme acetoin (diacetyl) reductase (see below)., Under anaerobic conditions |FRAME: 2-ACETO-LACTATE| is converted directly to acetoin by a decarboxylation step catalyzed by the enzyme |FRAME: CPLX-5262| (α-ALD), and production of diacetyl is bypassed., Diacetyl can be converted into any of the two stereoisomers of acetoin - |FRAME: CPD-10353| or |FRAME: CPD-255|, by stereo-specific enzymes., The enzymes that catalyze the irreversible reduction of diacetyl to acetoin also catalyze the last step in the pathway - the reversible conversion of acetoin to 2,3-butanediol. These enzymes are known in the literature by several names, including acetoin reductase (AR), acetoin (diacetyl) reductase, and 2,3-butanediol dehydrogenase (BDH). Four types of AR activites have been described, differing in their stereo-specificity for both the substrate and the product:, 1. An |FRAME: CPD-12004|-forming R-acetoin reductase, 2. An |FRAME: CPD-12004|-forming S-acetoin reductase, 3. An |FRAME: CPD-346|-forming S-acetoin reductase, 4. An |FRAME: BUTANEDIOL|-forming R-acetoin reductase., Among the enzymes that have been characteized, some appear to have only one of these activities, while others have multiple activities |CITS: [Ui84]|., The two enzyme activities diacetyl reductase and acetoin reductase were initially reported to be catalyzed by two different enzymes |CITS: [13211662]|, and two different EC numbers were issued based on that observation (|FRAME: ACETOINDEHYDROG-RXN "EC 1.1.1.5"| and |FRAME: RR-BUTANEDIOL-DEHYDROGENASE-RXN "EC 1.1.1.4|). However, later research indicated that in most bacteria both activities are catalyzed by the same enzyme, for which the name diacetyl(acetoin) reductase was suggested |CITS: [5540507][4350968][2040298][10647818]|. Moreover, the enzyme appears to have a much wider substrate range than orignally believed, and it has been suggested to rename it L-glycol dehydrogenase |CITS: [2040298]|., Yeast appears to also have dedicated NADP-linked enzymes that reduce diacetyl but not acetoin |CITS: [2180695]|., This pathway includes multiple decarboxylation reactions, generating |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE|., This CO2 is the source of the "eyes", or holes that certain cheeses, such as Swiss cheese, develop during maturation.

Summary: |FRAME: s-Triazines| herbicides, such as |FRAME: ATRAZINE|, are common herbicides that have been, used over the last half century. Commercial s-triazines characteristically comprise ring carbon, atoms that contain substituents other than hydrogen. After their introduction, s-triazine compounds, were found to be poor targets for biodegradation, but more recently it was found that the environmental, half-lives for these compounds have substantially decreased. This decrease indicates that microbes have, developed new mechanisms to facilitate the degradation of s-triazine compounds., Early investigations of microbial atrazine degradation found that degradation proceeded mostly, via dealkylation of the N-alkyl substituents on the s-triazine ring, usually with no, subsequent ring cleavage. However, currently most atrazine-degrading bacteria utilize a pathway that, does involve ring cleavage. At the first stage, acyl substituents are removed from the compounds, ending, with |FRAME: CYANURIC-ACID|. At the second stage the ring is cleaved, and complete degradation, to |FRAME: CARBON-DIOXIDE| and |FRAME:AMMONIA| follows |CITS: [17114259]|., A set of nearly identical s-triazine-catabolic genes has been found worldwide in diverse bacterial, genera, and in almost all cases, the genes are present on plasmids, packaged via flanking insertion, sequence elements |CITS: [11544232][15240330]|., The genes encoding the pathway shown here were named either atz or trz, depending on, the organism. The |FRAME:MONOMER-13542|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-10313| gene, is found in, Gram-positive bacteria, and has a very wide substrate specificity |CITS: [16885454]|. The corresponding protein in, Gram-negative bacteria is |FRAME: CPLX-2201|, encoded by the |FRAME: G-124| gene, which has a, much narrower specificity - it catalyzes the hydrolytic displacement of only chloride and fluoride, substituents from the s-triazine ring |CITS: [11010866]|.

General Background, The process of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| production occurs in organisms that occupy anaerobic niches and is used as a means of disposing of excess reductant from oxidative metabolism |CITS: [20463892]|., Hydrogenases catalyze the reversible oxidation of |FRAME:HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, and have been purified from both aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms. Thus, hydrogenases can function either as a safety valve for the disposal of excess reducing equivalents by evolving |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, or utilize |FRAME: Hydrogen-Oxidation| for the generation of reducing equivalents like NADH and NADPH for anabolic metabolism. , Hydrogenases can be divided into two major groups based on the presence of Ni and Fe or Fe alone in their active sites. The role of the [FeFe] hydrogenases is to evolve |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|, while that of the [NiFe] hydrogenases is to oxidize it |CITS: [19411328]|. The [Fe] hydrogenases contain FeS clusters, while the [NiFe] hydrogenases contain Ni and FeS clusters. There is also a hydrogenase from a methanogen which does not contain any metal. Most [Fe] hydrogenases are found in anaerobic bacteria and are sensitive to irreversible inactivation by oxygen, much more so than [NiFe] hydrogenases. , About This Pathway, The formation of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| from NADH is thermodynamically unfavorable under physiological conditions |CITS: [17993531]|. Therefore, NADH oxidation is often catalyzed by an NADH:ferredoxin oxidoreductase to reduce ferredoxin, which can then donate electrons to [Fe-Fe] or [Ni-Fe] hydrogenases for the production of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE|. NAD(P)H dependent [Fe-Fe] hydrogenases have been reported and these enzymes have a high requirement for FMN |CITS: [15256587]|., The pathway described here - the NADH and ferredoxin-dependent reduction of protons to |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| by a single enzyme complex has been elucidated in the bacterium |FRAME:TAX-2336| |CITS: [19411328]|. The catalysis of such linked redox reactions by an enzyme complex has been defined as a bifurcation system., Electron bifurcation has been proposed as a type of energy conservation, in addition to substrate level phosphorylation and electron transport phosphorylation (respiration) |CITS: [18039764]|. The heterotrimeric [Fe-Fe] hydrogenase of |FRAME: TAX-2336| is a "bifurcating" enzyme, as it couples the exergonic oxidation of reduced ferredoxin to the unfavorable oxidation of NADH to produce |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [19411328]|. The enzyme, located in the cytoplasm, operates under anaerobic conditions, and is irreversibly inactivated by exposure to oxygen. , An enzyme complex that uses a similar bifurcating mechanism to link redox reactions is seen in the anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1534|. This organism ferments alcohol and acetate to butyrate, caproate and |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| |CITS: [18218779]|. A conventional [Fe-Fe] hydrogenase catalyzes the reduction of protons for the evolution of |FRAME: HYDROGEN-MOLECULE| using electrons from reduced ferredoxin. The protons are generated by the activity of a flavoprotein, the cytoplasmic enzyme complex butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase. The enzyme contains 3 FAD containing subunits and it uses NADH oxidation to couple the endergonic reduction of ferredoxin with the exergonic reduction of crotonyl-CoA |CITS: [17993531]|., |FRAME:TAX-2336| utilizes |FRAME:ANAGLYCOLYSIS-PWY| and |FRAME:ENTNER-DOUDOROFF-PWY| for glucose catabolism., NADH is generated during glycolysis via |FRAME:CPLX-1865|. Reduced ferredoxin is generated by the oxidation of |FRAME:PYRUVATE| to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| by the enzyme |FRAME:CPLX-1868|., A search of the genome database using the sequences for the three subunits of |FRAME:TAX-2336| hydrogenase has yielded 30 bacterial species that encode homologues of all three subunits of the |FRAME:TAX-2336| enzyme, indicating that these organisms may possess a similar type of bifurcating enzyme |CITS: [19411328]|.
