Summary: General Background, Rutin is a flavonol glucoside that is widespread in the plant kingdom, and has been especially found in the |FRAME:TAX-3615| and |FRAME:TAX-3803| families. Rutin has several interesting pharmacological properties (e.g. antioxidative activity) that have been exploited in human medicine and nutrition. Quercetin-3-rhamnoside and its rutinoside, i.e. rutin has been demonstrated to possess antimalarial activity |CITS: [3081917]|. Rutin was identified as one of the most active agents of an aqueous crude extract of Baccharis trimera that was shown to express strong anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties |CITS: [8693035]|. The inhibitory effect against non-enzymatic lipid peroxidation, deoxyribose degradation |CITS: [9741300]| and on lipopolysaccharide-induced NO production |CITS: [12098601]| emphasizes the biological relevance of rutin in the treatment of related human conditions. Moreover, |FRAME:RUTIN| has been shown to be a promising agent against Alzheimer's disease |CITS:[22445961]| |CITS:[22441036]|, provides resistance to biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens |CITS:[22677447]| and showed protective effect against pro-carcinogenic agents |CITS:[20399630]|., Rutin production in plants has been found to be increased under the influence of UV-B radiation. Ambient radiation was the most effective mean to elevate rutin content, especially in leaves, indicating a possible involvement into UV protection |CITS: [12147730]|. The high accumulation of |FRAME:RUTIN| in the upper epidermis of leaves in |FRAME:TAX-3616| species also supports its possible role as UV screen |CITS:[Margna90]|. Rutin content in plants also seems to be influenced by the photoperiod as it was promoted under far red (FR) conditions with no obvious changes in the overall production of phenolics |CITS: [5423471]|. , About This Pathway, This pathway mostly describes the metabolic situation found in buckwheat species and represents a branch of the phenylpropanoid biosynthesis (see also |FRAME:PWY1F-FLAVSYN|, |FRAME:PWY-3101| and |FRAME:PWY-5321|). This has been demonstrated through monitoring the differential expression of involved genes during developmental stages of buckwheat which are characterized by the accumulation of |FRAME:RUTIN| as one of the most abundant flavonol glycoside in this plant |CITS:[21872967]| |CITS:[21062042]|. The increased production of |FRAME:RUTIN| after overexpressing the flavonol-specific transcription factor AtMYB12 in |FRAME:TAX-3617| and observing the expression of genes presumably involved in |FRAME:RUTIN| biosynthesis shows that key enzymes of the phenylpropanoid and flavonoid biosynthetic pathways up to |FRAME:PWY1F-467| are channeled towards |FRAME:RUTIN| formation |CITS:[22113884]|. , An important metabolic step in this pathway is carried out by the flavonol synthase catalyzing the |FRAME:2-KETOGLUTARATE| dependent oxygenation of |FRAME:CPD-474| to form |FRAME:CPD-520|. The corresponding gene has been cloned, heterologously expressed and characterized with regard to protein structure and catalytic properties |CITS:[22563787]|. The following conversion in the pathway forming the immediate precursor for rutin, |FRAME:CPD1F-437| (isoquercetin) is realized by the flavonol 3-O-glucosyltransferase |CITS:[Suzuki05]| |CITS:[Lucci09]| (compare also |FRAME:PWY-5321|). The enzyme catalyzing the final step in the pathway, i.e. flavonol-3-O-glucoside L-rhamnosyltransferase has been partially purified from mung bean |CITS: [13864833]| and |FRAME:TAX-149691| (fava d'anta) |CITS:[Lucci09]|. The enzyme catalyzes the transfer of a rhamnosyl group from |FRAME:UDP-L-RHAMNOSE| to quercetin 3-O-glucoside forming rutin. Although dTDP-rhamnose had been considered as the primary donor |CITS: [13864833]| it has been demonstrated that UDP-L-rhamnose is the native donor for the transfer of L-rhamnose |CITS: [1898019]| |CITS: [14084592]|. , It had long been a pending question how exactly UDP-L-rhamnose was biosynthesized in plants. It is clear now that UDP-L-rhamnose can be catalyzed from UDP-D-glucose (see |FRAME:PWY-3261|) |CITS: [1898019]| |CITS: [14084592]| which is an ubiquitous activated nucleotide sugar readily available for metabolic processes in plants.

Citrate lyase is an anaerobic enzyme that catalyzes the cleavage of |FRAME: CIT| to |FRAME: ACET| and |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| |CITS: [6354265]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6038|). Because the citrate molecule is very stable, it has to be activated by forming a thioester bond with the enzyme before cleavage can take place., The enzyme is a complex of three subunits (in a 6:6:6 configuration), one of them a dedicated acyl carrier protein (acp)., The acp protein is synthesized in an apo form, and is converted to its fully active form in two steps - first, a holo form is generated by the covalent binding of the prosthetic group |FRAME: 2-5-PHOSPHORIBOSYL-3-DEPHOSPHO-COA| to a serine residue. Next, the holo form is acetylated, either by |FRAME: EC-6.2.1.22|, which uses |FRAME: ACET| as the donor, or by |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.49|, that uses |FRAME: S-ACETYLPHOSPHOPANTETHEINE| as the acetyl donor (see |FRAME: P2-PWY|)., The α subunit of the citrate lyase is |FRAME: EC-2.8.3.10|, an enzyme that catalyzes the exchange of the bound acetyl group with a citrate molecule, generating |FRAME: Citrate-Lyase-Citryl-Form| and releasing an |FRAME: ACET| molecule., The β subunit, |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.34|, catalyzes the subsequent step, cleaving the bound citryl group, releasing |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID| and regenerating |FRAME: CITRATE-LYASE|. Since the active form is regenrated, the enzyme can continuously catalyze the cleavage reaction., Genes complementary to the bacterial citrate lyase β subunit have been identified in the mouse and human genomes |CITS: [11741334]|. The physiological role of these genes in eukaryotes is not known yet., The sum of this pathway is described by |FRAME: EC-4.1.3.6|: , |FRAME: CITLY-RXN|

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| are related sulfated |FRAME: Glycosaminoglycans "glycosaminoglycans"|., |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates "Chondroitin sulfate"| is composed of alternating units of sulfated |FRAME:CPD-12557| and |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues, while in |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| the |FRAME: CPD-12521| residues have largely been converted to |FRAME: CPD-12515|. The |FRAME: CPD-12557| residues are substituted to varying degrees with sulfate linked to 4- and/or 6-hydroxyl positions, forming |FRAME: CPD-12516|, |FRAME: CPD-12565| or |FRAME: CPD-12526|, and to a lesser extent the uronic acid residues may be substituted with sulfate at the 2-hydroxyl position forming |FRAME: CPD-12527| or |FRAME:CPD-12518|., The uronic acid residues may also be substituted with sulfate at the 3-hydroxyl positions, although this substitution is quite rare., The chondroitin/dermatan chains vary in size up to a hundred or more disaccharide repeating units. Both are usually found attached to assorted core proteins as part of a proteoglycan complex. They are major components of connective tissue matrix (such as skin and cartilage), but are also found on cell surface and basement membranes and in intracellular granules of certain cells. Functions in matrix locations are mainly structural, while functions in membranes are mainly as receptors., The chondroitin/dermatan chains are actually synthesized in situ on the protein chain. They are attached to the core protein via a specific tetrasaccharide known as the "glycoaminoglycan-protein linkage region", which is formed by sequential stepwise additions of the sugar residues to specific core proteins. The synthesis of the linkage region is described in |FRAME: PWY-6557|., About This Pathway, The linkage region may be extended into mutiple kinds of glycosaminoglycans. However, the addition of an |FRAME: CPD-12557| residue prevents the formation of |FRAME: HEPARIN| or |FRAME: Heparan-Sulfate| and commits the molecule to become chondroitin or dermatan. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme chondroitin sulfate N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase. Humans have two isoforms of this enzyme, encoded by the |FRAME: HS07428| and |FRAME:HS10013| genes |CITS: [11788602][12716890][12433924]|., Once the linkage region has been formed and committed, the polymerzation of the chondroitin/dermatan chain proceeds by the alternate addition of |FRAME: CPD-12521| and |FRAME: CPD-12557| from activated precursors to the non-reducing end of the elongating chain. The addition of both residues is catalyzed by the biofunctional chondroitin sulfate synthases., Humans possess three isoforms of this bifunctional enzyme (|FRAME: HS13400|, |FRAME: HS13103| and |FRAME: HS11959|), plus an additional enzyme that can catalyze only the addition of |FRAME: CPD-12521| (|FRAME: HS12080|) |CITS:[11514575][12907687][12145278]|. It has been suggested that chondroitin polymerization is achieved by multiple combinations of the different enzymes and that each combination may play a unique role in the biosynthesis of chondroitin or dermatan sulfate |CITS:[17253960][18316376]|., Further modifications of |FRAME: Chondroitin-sulfates| and |FRAME: Dermatan-Sulfate| are described in the pathways |FRAME: PWY-6567| and |FRAME: PWY-6568|, respectively.

Summary: General Background, At the time of this review, over 130 fully characterized gibberellins (starting with GA1 |CITS:[5638147]|) have been identified in more than a hundred vascular plant species, seven bacteria and seven fungi |CITS:[SPONSEL04],[11986764]|. Of these gibberellins only a few have biological activity. Many of the GAs identified early in the history of the discovery of these hormones are the ones which possess the highest biological activity. These include GA1, GA3, GA4, GA5, GA6 and GA7. GA1 is the most active GA for stem elongation in |FRAME:TAX-4577| and |FRAME:TAX-3888|, while GA4 is the most active GA in Cucurbitaceae and in Arabidopsis thaliana. GA3 (gibberellic acid), on the other hand, has been identified in more than 40 plants and is the major GA in the fungus |FRAME:TAX-5127|. GA3 is used commercially to promote seed germination, stem elongation and fruit growth |CITS:[12475622]|., Gibberellins are diterpenes which, in higher plants, are synthesized in the plastids from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and pyruvate via the isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP). They all have either 19 or 20 carbon units grouped into either four or five ring systems (see |FRAME: CPD1F-95| and |FRAME: CPD1F-134|, respectively). , Active gibberellins show many physiological effects, each depending on the type of gibberellin present as well as the species of plant. Some of the physiological processes stimulated by gibberellins are: i) stimulation of stem elongation by stimulating cell division and elongation, ii) stimulation of bolting/flowering in response to long days, iii) interruption of seed dormancy in plants requiring stratification or light to induce germination, iv) stimulation of enzyme production (α-amylases) in germinating cereal grains for mobilization of seed reserves, v) induction of maleness in dioecious flowers (sex expression), vi) parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit development, and vii) delay of senescence in leaves and citrus fruits., Given the important roles that GAs play in plant growth and development, several levels of regulation are used to carefully control the level and types of bioactive GAs present in various tissues. Direct chemical modifications to gibberellins including oxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-102|, (|CITS: [12481092][10200325]|, et al.)), epoxidation (see |FRAME: PWY-6494|) and methylation (this pathway) |CITS: [17220201]| may be used to reduce the levels of bioactive GAs., About This Pathway, Gibberellin methylation is believed to inactivate bioactive GAs and to lead to their further catabolism |CITS: [17220201]|. The existence of this pathway is supported by the identification of two enzymes from Arabidopsis, GAMT1 and GAMT2, that can catalyze GA methylation in vitro |CITS: [17220201]|. Although no methylated forms of GA have been detected in Arabidopsis plants to date, over-expression of the enzymes reduced the levels of active GAs while a gamt1 gamt2 double mutant had elevated levels of bioactive GAs arguing that these enzymes do play a role in gibberellin metabolism in vivo. In addition, there is evidence for the existence of methylated GAs as these have been observed in at least one plant species, namely, the fern |FRAME: TAX-84615| |CITS: [12226326]|. Although gibberellins are produced by a number of fungi (for example, see |FRAME: PWY-5047|) and bacteria, there is no evidence to date of GA methyl ester formation in these species, and it may be unlikely to occur in organisms where GA does not play a role as an endogenous signaling molecule that needs to be selectively inactivated |CITS: [19560174]|., Several lines of evidence suggest that GA methyl esters are not biologically active. Importantly, direct application of exogenous GA methyl esters are not nearly as effective at inducing GA-mediated biological responses as non-methylated GAs in several plant species including Arabidopsis thaliana |CITS: [WEISS93][9701576]|. In addition, the putative GA receptor in rice, GID1, does not bind to GA methyl esters significantly |CITS: [16193045]|. On the other hand, in some assays, methyl or dimethyl-GAs appear to cause biological responses |CITS: [SMITH93][12226326]|. It is possible that specific GA methyl esters will have different biological activities in different species., The role of GA methylation in various plant processes will also depend on the tissues and organs in which this process occurs. In Arabidopsis, expression of the two GA carboxymethyl transferases is largely limited to siliques during the later stages of development indicating that methylation of GAs might play a limited role in other GA-regulated processes that occur in other organs or in different developmental stages |CITS: [17220201]|. Additional studies on different plant species will reveal if expression during seed development is a generalized trend or if this expression pattern is limited to Arabidopsis thaliana., Several other plant hormones including jasmonic acid and salicylic acid may be reversibly methylated and later demethylated to be reactivated. There is no evidence to date that GA methyl esters can be cleaved by methylesterases, but, it is interesting to note that the GID1 receptor in rice is part of the superfamily that includes the methyl salicylate and methyl jasmonate methylesterases |CITS: [17220201][16193045]|.

Summary: General Background, Chloroaromatic compounds occur in the environment in large amounts due to their release as herbicides or as byproducts, of industrial production., These compounds are stable chemically, and biological degradation capabilities have evolved only recently as a response, to their widespread availability in soil and water., Many of the degradation pathways merge at the level of chlorocatechols. Thus, in order to be able to degrade chlorobenzoates and chlorobenzenes successfully, the bacteria must, possess specific enzymes for the degradation of chlorocatechols., About This Pathway, The first bacterium that was isolated based on its ability to grow with |FRAME: CPD-3486| as the sole carbon source, was |FRAME:TAX-65741 "Pseudomonas knackmussii (then called Pseudomonas sp. strain B13)"| |CITS: [4852581]|., That study showed that |FRAME: CPD-3486| was converted by two enzymes to a mixture of |FRAME: CPD-9151|, and |FRAME: CPD-9152| |CITS:[4852581][3025183]|., The chlorinated catechols were degraded in a modified ortho cleavage pathways via |FRAME: CPD-294| to, |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which was degraded further to TCA cycle intermediates., This pathway for |FRAME: CPD-9151| degradation starts with a dioxygenase attack, resulting in |FRAME: 2-CL-MUCONATE|., The "regular" catechol 1,2 dioxygenases have little activity with chlorocatechol. Instead, chlorocatechols, are substrates to specialized enzymes that evolved for this purpose, known as "type II" enzymes., The next enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX-7704|, catalyzes a two step process, starting with the the conversion of the, chloromuconate to |FRAME: CPD-10638|, followed by its dehalogenation to |FRAME: CPD-10608| |CITS: [11443090]|., Two last steps, catalyzed by a hydrolase and a reductase, generate the common intermediate |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|., Most of the genes encoding chlorocatechol catabolism enzymes are present on plasmids. Examples include the two, tdf operons on the |FRAME: TAX-264198| plasmid pJP4 |CITS: [2981813]|, the clc operon on the, |FRAME: TAX-65741| plasmid pB13 (pWR1) |CITS: [7217013]|, and the tcb operon on the |FRAME: TAX-65067|, plasmid pP51 |CITS: [1987135]|.

The pathway of phosphatidylglycerol degradation is an example of an unique regulation mechanism for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-12824| (see |FRAME:PWY-5269|). Cardiolipin (CL) is the major anionic phospholipid in mitochondria with important functions for growth, energy-related processes and biogenesis (reviewed in |CITS:[10799718] [18725250] [23172229]|. Phosphatidylglycerol, an intermediate in the biosynthetic route to cardiolipin, is also an essential lipid in chloroplast membranes |CITS:[15538651]| but occurs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae in only small amounts. Of major interest in yeast is its role of an intermediate in the cardiolipin biosynthesis |CITS:[9614098]| but it also has been reported to play a role in the in vivo activation of enzymes involved in the generation of bioactive ceramides |CITS:[15611094]|. , The regulation of the flux of |FRAME:L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL| towards |FRAME:CPD-12824| in yeast appears to be managed through an pathway removing excessive amounts of |FRAME:L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL| by hydrolytic cleavage of this intermediary lipid. The resulting |FRAME:DIACYLGLYCEROL| and |FRAME:GLYCEROL-3P| can be reused in the mitochondria under special conditions. It had been demonstrated that Δpgc1 and the wild type have no different growth phenotypes which prompted the proposition that the pathway serves as fine adjustment for the cardiolipin biosynthesis |CITS:[18434318]|. The enzymatic activity of the PGC1 product is that of a phosphatidylglycerol phospholipase C |CITS:[18434318]| and not as a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase involved in the metabolism of glycerophosphocholine and glycerophosphoinositol as previously considered based on homology to enzymes in other organisms |CITS:[16172116]|. It was shown that the Δpgc1 mutant significantly accumulated phosphatidylglycerol in comparison to the wild type because the "removal pathway" of surplus |FRAME:L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL| catalyzed by the phosphatidylglycerol phospholipase C (PGC1) was not operating |CITS:[18434318]|. The absence of inositol amplified the accumulation effect in the Δpgc1 mutant as inositol is a negative regulator of phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthase which in turn increased the flow of |FRAME:L-1-PHOSPHATIDYL-GLYCEROL| in the cardiolipin biosynthesis |CITS:[12821656]|.

The antibiotic |FRAME: CPD-17212|, discovered in 1950, is produced by the Gram positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-316284| |CITS: [12987085]|. It is commonly used as a fungicide, primarily for infections involving the skin, mouth, esophagus, and vagina |CITS: [4919155][10796846]|., |FRAME: CPD-17212 "Nystatin A1"| is a polyene macrolide antibiotic. These compounds have 20-44 membered lactone rings containing three to eight conjugated double bonds, and interact with membrane sterols. The interaction leads to formation of polyene-sterol complexes that make the membrane permeable to water and ions, leading to cell death. Since the interaction with the fungal |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| is much stronger than with mammalian sterols such as |FRAME: CHOLESTEROL|, the antibiotic can be used against fungal infections, with side effects developing only at high concentration |CITS: [4585230][3539192]|., Like other polyene macrolides, the nystatin macrolactone ring is generated by a polyketide synthase (PKS) complex., Based on its chemical structure it can be predicted that synthesis starts with |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| and proceeds through condensation of three |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| and 15 |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender units., The nystatin biosynthesis gene cluster was identified by screening a |FRAME: TAX-316284| gene library for DNA encoding a PKS. A 125 kb region was isolated and sequenced |CITS: [10873841]|. Six of the genes, |FRAME: G-43843|, |FRAME: G-43844|, |FRAME: G-43845|, |FRAME: G-43846|, |FRAME: G-43847| and |FRAME: G-43848|, encode a very large type I PKS that produces the macrolactone ring-containing |FRAME: CPD-17499|. The cluster also contains a thioesterase (nysE), two P450 monooxygenases (|FRAME: G-43849| and |FRAME: G-43850|) and a ferredoxin that presumably interacts with them, mycosamine biosynthesis genes, including a glycosyltransferase, a regulatory region, and transporters, presumably involved in ATP-dependent efflux of nystatin |CITS: [10873841]|., The propsoed pathway, which is described here, starts with loading of the |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| starter unit onto the NysA protein, and proceeds through condensation of three |FRAME: D-METHYL-MALONYL-COA| and 15 |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| extender units by the NysB, NysC, NysI, NysJ and NysK components of the PKS complex. After cleavage of the mature polyketide chain from the PKS complex by the TE domain of NysK, the chain is cyclized to form the nystatin aglycone. The next two steps are hydroxylation and oxidation of the macrolactone ring at C-10 and C-16, respectively, which are presumably accomplished by the NysL and NysN monooxygenases. Note that it is not known which monooxygenase catalyzes which step, and the assignment of the enzymes to the specific reactions shown here was done arbitrarily. Finally, the |FRAME: CPD-16768| sugar is attached by the |FRAME: G-43851 "NysDI mycosaminyltransferase"| |CITS: [10873841]|.

Summary: Please note: This pathway does not represent a single organism. Rather, it is a superpathway, assembled from pathways found in a variety of organisms. Its purpose is to provide an overview, of the diversity of ways that organisms can biosynthesize sialic acids and their CMP-derivatives., Sialic acids are a family of polyhydroxylated α-keto acids that contain nine carbon atoms. Most sialic acids, are derivatives of |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|, or |FRAME: CPD-21259| (KDN). , |FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE| is the most common sialic acid in mammals (see pathway, |FRAME: PWY-6138|), while KDN is abundant in lower vertebrates (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Their, core structures can be modified at the hydroxyl groups, lactonized, or hydroxylated at the acetamido group,, generating many derivatives. |FRAME: CPD-262| is a derivative of |FRAME: CMP-N-ACETYL-NEURAMINATE| (see, pathway |FRAME: PWY-6144|). Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Sialic acids are found mainly in vertebrates and a few higher invertebrates (ascidians and echinoderms). These, acidic sugars are usually the terminal sugar residue in the glycan chains of vertebrate glycoconjugates (mostly, glycoproteins and glycolipids, but also proteoglycans and glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors). They function in, mediating cellular recognition and adhesion events for many important processes such as development, the immune, and inflammatory responses, and oncogenesis. Sialic acid occurs rarely in invertebrates. Endogenous sialylation, has been shown to occur in |FRAME: TAX-7215|, but details of sialic acid biosynthesis in this organism remain to, be determined |CITS: [18568399]|. However, it is possible the sialic acids might be biosynthesized by other, eukaryotes in a species and/or life cycle-dependent manner. In |CITS: [7841794]| and reviewed in, |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|., Most bacteria do not biosynthesize sialic acids, but some pathogenic, or symbiotic bacteria biosynthesize sialic, acids as a means of evading a host's immune system (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6139|). The sialic acid is, displayed on the bacterial cell surface (in capsular polysaccharides) in order to mimic mammalian cells. Pathogens, that biosynthesize sialic acids include |FRAME: TAX-487|, |FRAME: TAX-1392869| and |FRAME: TAX-197|. In, addition, the human gut symbiont |FRAME: TAX-818| has been shown to synthesize |FRAME: CPD-21259|, |CITS: [18804026]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6140|). Whether or not archaea contain sialic acids remains to be, determined. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|. Other sialic acid-like sugars biosynthesized by bacteria include the nonulosonic acids |FRAME: CPD-10754| |CITS: [16751642]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|) and legionaminic acid |CITS: [18275154]|., Protists are thought to lack the ability to biosynthesize sialic acids although more genome data are needed to confirm, this. Sialic acids have been thought to be absent in plants but some studies raise the possibility, |CITS: [18258224]|. Fungi appear to lack any known sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, although strain-specific, or, novel pathways could exist. Reviewed in |CITS: [15888312] [16897172] [18568399]| and |CITS: [11841250]|.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-21467 Bacillaene| is a polyene antibiotic obtained from |FRAME: TAX-1423| that is active against a broad spectrum of bacteria, including both Gram-negative and Gram-positive strains. The compound was discovered in 1995 and reported to have 6 unsaturated bonds, and to act as a bacteriostatic at the level of protein synthesis |CITS: [7592068]|. Bacillaene has been shown to protect |FRAME: TAX-1423| from predation by |FRAME: TAX-34| |CITS: [25002419]|. Bacillaene's rapid decomposition when exposed to light or room temperature had prevented its full structural characterization for many years. The complete structure was reported only in 2007 |CITS: [17234808]|., In 1993, when the complete genome of |FRAME: TAX-1423| was being sequenced, a large gene cluster that spans 78.5 kb (about 2% of the genome) was discovered and named pksX. It was clear that the cluster encodes a large hybrid polyketide/nonribosomal peptide synthase product, though the identity of that product was not known at the time |CITS: [8344529][9384377]|. A study of the related organism |FRAME: TAX-326423| identfied an orthologous cluster, and by transforming the cluster into a non-producer, the researchers were able to link the cluster to the production of |FRAME: CPD-21467| |CITS: [16707694]|., The polyketide/nonribosomal peptide synthases encoded by the cluster were shown to assemble as multiple copies into a single organelle-like enzymatic complex with a mass of tens to hundreds of megadaltons, which was an unprecedented finding in bacterial subcellular organization. Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The O antigen of group B |FRAME: TAX-590| strains corresponds to serogroup O4 and is produced by a Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway. Members of group B1 and group B2 form O antigens from the same repeat unit (|FRAME: CPD-23730|) and result in the same O:4 serotype. However, these two groups possess a different O-antigen polymerase. While group B1 members polymerize the repeat units by an α(1→2) linkage (as shown in this pathway), members of group B2, such as |FRAME: TAX-181736|, |FRAME: TAX-181798|, |FRAME: TAX-181797|, and |FRAME: TAX-340190|, possess an α(1→6) polymerase almost identical to that found in group D3 strains, resulting in production of an O:27 factor (see |FRAME: CPD-24012|) |CITS: [11872718][23874940]|., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O-antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes. The first such genes to be studied were those of strain LT2 |CITS: [5326096][5231414][4896188][ 2423848][2447067][3070321]|., The first step in Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways is the addition of a sugar phosphate residue to |FRAME: CPD-9646| (Und-P) to form the undecaprenyl diphosphate-linked sugar. Most O antigens found in |FRAME: TAX-590| species start with GlcNAc or GalNAc and their biosynthesis is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). However, the Salmonella O antigens belonging to serogroups O2 (A), O4 (B), O8 (C2C3), O9 (D1), O9,46 (D2), O9,46,27 (D3), O3,10 (E1E3), and O1,3,19 (E4) form a distinct set that is characterized by having a Gal residue as the first sugar of the O unit., The enzyme responsible for the initiation of these pathways is |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.6| (WbaP, previously called RfbP |CITS: [9004408]|). The use of Gal as initial sugar appeared in |FRAME: TAX-590| after its divergence from |FRAME: TAX-561|, but the eight Gal-initiated O antigens have grown to be very important in this species |CITS: [23874940]|., The gene cluster encoding the O antigen of the group B |FRAME: TAX-99287| was cloned and sequenced in 1991 |CITS: [ 1710759]|, and the functions of the genes encoding the different transferases were identified later by enzyme assay of membrane fractions from cells carrying cloned genes |CITS: [7684736]|. , Following the completion of the synthesis of a repeat unit, the flippase Wzx flips the full molecule to the other side of the membrane, where the Wzy polymerase transfers additional repeat units from their anchor to a single elongating molecule. The Wzz protein ensures termination of the polimerization once the correct chain length has been achieved., The O antigen repeat unit produced by this pathway is common to the group B1 and group B2 |FRAME: TAX-590| strains. However, organisms belonging to group B1 contain the wzyB gene which encodes a polymerase that links the repeat units by an α(1,2) linkage between the galactose and the mannose residues [α-D-Gal-(1→2)-α-D-Man], while strains in group B2 possess a wzyD3 gene, which encodes a polymerase that links the repeat units by an α(1,6) linkage between these residues, resulting in the O27 epitope. The wzyB gene of the B1 group is located outside of the main gene cluster, indicating that this group arose from B2 by gain of this gene and the subsequent loss of function of the original wzyD3 gene |CITS: [23874940]|.

Summary: General Background, Menaquinones (MK) and demethylmenaquinones (DMK) are low-molecular weight lipophilic components of the cytoplasmic membrane, found in many bacterial species. These quinones function as a reversible redox component of the electron transfer chain, mediating electron transfer between hydrogenases and cytochromes., Menaquinones have also been implicated in regulation, as they are necessary for sporulation and proper regulation of cytochrome formation in some Gram-positive bacteria |CITS: [4353869][4202999]|., Most aerobic Gram-negative bacteria contain ubiquinone as the sole quinone, while most aerobic Gram-positive bacteria contain menaquinone and/or demethylmenaquinones as the main quinone. However, most of the anaerobic bacteria, regardless whether they are Gram-negative or Gram-positive, contain menaquinone or demethylmenaquinone as their main quinones. Some facultatively anaerobic bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, contain ubiquinone, menaquinone, and demethylmenaquinone, which they use under different growth conditions |CITS: [11153266]|. The main difference between, these quinone molecules is their redox potential. For example, the redox potential for ubiquinone, demethylmenaquinone, and menaquinone has been measured as +112 mv, +36 mv, and -74 mv, respectively, in the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-729| |CITS: [187454]|., Menaquinones are considered a vitamin (vitamin K2), since they are essential for animals, mostly for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins required for blood coagulation. Animals can not synthesize menaquinones, but usually receive a sufficient amount from bacteria growing in their intestines. In the absence of menaquinone or the related compound |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1) which is synthesized in plants, animals suffer from hemorrhage |CITS: [Dam35]|. Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, The best characterized menaquinone biosynthetic pathway is that of |FRAME: TAX-83333| that synthesizes |FRAME: CPD-9728| (MK-8). MK-8 is not unique to E. coli, and is found in many different bacterial species., A study of the quinones of halophilic archaebacteria found that MK-8 was the major quinone in most species included in the study, including |FRAME: TAX-2246|, |FRAME: TAX-2250|, |FRAME: TAX-2242|, |FRAME: TAX-2248| and |FRAME: TAX-29284| |CITS: [5049648][4822788][Collins81]|., MK-8 is very common in facultatively anaerobic Gram negative bacteria, such as the enterobacteria. In addition to |FRAME: TAX-83333| it has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-546|, |FRAME: TAX-548|, |FRAME: TAX-554|, |FRAME: TAX-584|, |FRAME: TAX-585| |CITS: [4886765]| and |FRAME: TAX-615| |CITS: [Bezborodov69]|, as well as the non-eneterobacteria |FRAME: TAX-644|, |FRAME: TAX-648| |CITS: [4886765]| and |FRAME: TAX-51367| |CITS: [Collins81]|., MK-8 has not been discovered in obligate anaerobes so far., Some aerobic Gram-negative bacteria that contain MK-8 as their major quinone include the gliding bacterium |FRAME: TAX-33| |CITS: [4216336]|, and several members of the |FRAME: TAX-1297| phylum, including |FRAME: TAX-271| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [7462123][7022156]|, |FRAME: TAX-32062| and |FRAME: TAX-1299| |CITS: [Yamada77]|., Even though most Gram-positive bacteria contain |FRAME: CPD-9718| as their major quinone, a few are known to make MK-8 instead, including |FRAME: TAX-1473| |CITS: [119033]|, |FRAME: TAX-1428| |CITS: [119033]|, |FRAME: TAX-1618| |CITS: [7462123]|, |FRAME: TAX-37922| |CITS: [Collins81]|, certain |FRAME:TAX-1270| strains |CITS:[Watanuki72][Yamada76]|, and |FRAME:TAX-1373| |CITS:[Yamada76]|., MK-8 was also found as a minor component in the phototrophic bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1049| |CITS: [14240125]|, |FRAME: TAX-28068| and Rhodospirillum sp. 2761 |CITS: [5727384]|.

Menaquinone was first isolated from putrefied fish meal by McKee in 1939 |CITS: [17783315]|, and its structure resolved in 1958 |CITS: [Isler58]|., The biosynthesis of menaquinones is essentially identical to that of demethylmenaquinones, with one additional step, comprising the addition of a methyl group to the naphthoquinone ring. Many bacterial species do not have this methylase and produce demethylmenaquinone as their sole quinone |CITS: [7022156]|., All three quinones are synthesized from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, an intermediate of aromatic amino acid biosynthesis. However, the pathways of (demethyl)menaquinone synthesis diverts from that for ubiquinones early on., Most organisms synthesize their menaquinones via |FRAME: ISOCHORISMATE|, although some organisms, including |FRAME: TAX-210|, |FRAME: TAX-197|, |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274|, synthesize menaquinones in alternative pathways, via |FRAME: CPD-10477| or |FRAME: CPD-13324| |CITS: [18801996][21489995][23972005]|., Menaquinones are known to have side chains of different sizes in different organisms, and sometimes even within the same organism. The most common menaquinones contain 7, 8 and 9 isoprene units. However, menaquinones containing 4 |CITS:[413478][6048777]|, 5 |CITS: [6048777][5005959]|, 6 |CITS: [5005959][6102980][5418698][5412037]|, 10 |CITS: [6102980][7462123]|, 11 |CITS: [6102980] [7462123]|, 12 |CITS: [6102980]|, and 13 |CITS: [6102980]| isoprene units have been reported in bacteria., About This Pathway, Most bacteria appear to synthesize menaquinone from chorismate by seven enzymes in a well characterized route (see |FRAME: PWY-5838|). Much later an alternative pathway for the biosynthesis of menaquinone from chorismate, which proceeds via |FRAME: CPD-10477|, has been identified in some bacteria, including |FRAME: TAX-1902| and |FRAME: TAX-274| |CITS: [18801996]|. Initial analysis of sequenced genomes suggested that the pathway might be present in a variety of organisms |CITS: [19557031]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6262|). Further analysis revealed that the newly discovered pathway may not be identical among all of these organisms. It appears that in some organisms |FRAME: CPD-13324| is converted directly to |FRAME: CPD-10484| (as shown here), while in others this transformation occurrs via |FRAME: CPD-10477| (see |FRAME: PWY-7374|)., In both pathways |FRAME: CHORISMATE| is dehydrated to |FRAME: CPD-16467| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-16550| (|FRAME: G-12801|), followed by conversion to |FRAME: CPD-13324| in a complex reaction catalyzed by a radical Ado-Met enzyme encoded by |FRAME: G-17947| |CITS: [24083939]|. In this pathway the latter is hydrolyzed by |FRAME: MONOMER-16549 MqnB| to form |FRAME: CPD-10484|, a common intermedaite to both pathways |CITS: [21489995]|., The rest of the pathway is identical in both pathway variants. Very little is known about the biosynthesis of the other forms. , Most of the bacteria that synthesize bacteriochlorophyll are anoxygenic species that belong, to the proteobacteria. They are also known as purple bacteria, due to the color of the pigment., These species photosynthesize only under anaerobic conditions. However, bacteriochlorophylls are, also present in some groups of aerobic bacteria, such as members of the Acidiphilium genus, |CITS: [Wakao93]|. For a complete list of aerobic bacteria that contain bacteriochlorophyll,, see |CITS: [12483616]|., |FRAME:CPD-9067| functions not only as a light-harvesting pigment in antenna complexes, but also acts, as a "special pair" to drive the photosynthetic electron transfer in the reaction center., About This Pathway, The biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-9067| is a complex multienzymatic process, and involves at least, 15 steps starting at |FRAME:5-AMINO-LEVULINATE| (the first committed step)., The first half of the biosynthetic pathway (up to |FRAME:PROTOPORPHYRIN_IX|) is shared with heme, biosynthesis, while the latter half, which starts with the insertion of a |FRAME: MG+2| ion into the, porphyrin ring, is specific to |FRAME:CPD-9067|., The biosynthetic pathways of |FRAME:CPD-9067| and |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLL-A| share common, intermediates up to the synthesis of |FRAME: CHLOROPHYLLIDE-A|. Summary: This pathway of L-tyrosine degradation has been characterized in mammals, some bacteria, and the fungi |FRAME: TAX-162425| and |FRAME: TAX-746128| |CITS: [9734339] [7568087] [15262943][19028908]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15581571]| and |CITS: [11567547]|.  L-Phenylalanine degradation shares this pathway after its initial hydroxylation to L-tyrosine (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PHENYLALANINE-DEG1-PWY|).  |FRAME: TAX-162425| also degrades phenylacetate via 2-hydroxyphenylacetate to homogentisate using this pathway |CITS: [7673153]|. The pathway ends in intermediates of central metabolism, as indicated by the pathway links.  Deficiencies of enzymes in this pathway have been associated with several human genetic disorders (as indicated in the comments for the individual enzymes in this pathway).  Homogentisate is a central intermediate.  In addition to being further catabolized, it can also be a biosynthetic precursor for melanins (in |CITS: [8071207]|), and is used by higher plants in the biosynthesis of plastoquinone and tocopherols (in |CITS: [15157070]| and reviewed in |CITS: [15581571]|) (see MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: PWY-1581| and |FRAME: PWY-1422|)., This pathway does not occur in |FRAME:TAX-562| and |FRAME:TAX-590|, which cannot utilize L-tyrosine as a carbon and energy source (McFall, E. and Newman E. G. in |CITS: [COLISAL]|).  The pathway is also lacking in the yeast |FRAME:TAX-4932| which uses a limited number of carbon sources for growth, but can use most amino acids as sole nitrogen source (in |CITS: [15933030]|) (see MetaCyc pathways |FRAME: ANAPHENOXI-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-5079|). , A variation of this pathway has been reported in some Gram positive bacteria that can degrade L-tyrosine via 2,5-dihydroxyphenylacetate (homoprotocatechuate), rather than homogentisate, to pyruvate and succinate |CITS: [931949] [20216]|.  Another variation has been shown in the gram positive bacterium |FRAME:TAX-1817| sp. 239 which can degrade L-tyrosine to homogentisate via p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, p-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde, and p-hydroxyphenylacetate.  D- and L-phenylalanine were similarly degraded by this organism via the corresponding non-hydroxylated compounds |CITS: [DEBOER88]|.  There is also evidence that the yeast |FRAME:TAX-4952| can degrade tyrosine to homogentisate through these intermediates |CITS: [11472920]|.  Among the archaea, however, there is little information regarding aromatic amino acid degradation, even in the well studied hyperthermophile |FRAME:TAX-2261| (in |CITS: [15803651]|), although a preliminary pathway has been proposed |CITS: [8206994]|.

Summary: Enzymatic glycosylation of proteins and lipids is an abundant and important biological process., A great diversity of oligosaccharide structures and types of glycoconjugates is found in nature, and this diversity is the result of the actions of a large number of glycosyltransferase enzymes., Glycosyltransferases have high donor and acceptor substrate specificities, and are in general limited to catalysis of one unique glycosidic linkage. The formation of many glycosidic linkages is covered by large homologous glycosyltransferase gene families, and in many cases multiple enzyme isoforms in each family provide a degree of redundancy as well as a higher level of regulation of the glycoforms synthesized |CITS: [10580128]|. In this MetaCyc pathway we show only a representative enzyme for each type., The glycosyltrasnferase field progressed slowly for a long time due to the inherent problems associated with the isolation of these proteins, which are often large membrane proteins with overlapping activities. The introduction of the transfection cloning strategy in 1990 provided a major breakthrough, since it enables the isolation of the encoding gene without the need to purify the enzyme |CITS: [2464598][2738063]|., |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.38|, was the first mammalian glycosyltransferase that was cloned |CITS: [2419911][3014508][3134348][2502398]|. It was followed by |FRAME: EC-2.4.3.1| |CITS: [3121604]|, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.69| |CITS: [2738063]|, |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.87| |CITS: [2503516]| and |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.40| |CITS: [2104828]|. At this point it became clear that the primary sequences of glycosyltransferases that catalyze different functions were entirely different. However, once a gene encoding a new type of glycosyltransferase has been cloned, its sequence was used successfully for the discovery of other members of this gene family. For example, six additional human β-4Gal-T genes (EC 2.4.1.38) designated β4Gal-T2 to -T7 were identified and shown to be functional |CITS: [9405390][9792633][9435216][10473568]|., |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.150|, is also known as the "blood group I" enzyme. The |FRAME: Lower-case-i-Antigens "i antigen"| is found on membrane proteins in red blood cells and many other cell types as well as various body secretions of developing fetuses and newborn infants |CITS: [13767181][4971635]|, while the |FRAME: Upper-case-I-antigens "I antigen"| is found in in all adults |CITS: [13292836]|. The i antigen undergoes gradual conversion to the I antigen in newborn infants, a process dependent on expression of |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.150|. Complete conversion of the antigen is usually acheived by the age of 18 months |CITS: [6490658]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13173 Salicortin| is a phenolic glycoside (PG) that makes an important contribution to plant defense against herbivores in |FRAME: TAX-3689| and |FRAME: TAX-40685| species |CITS: [20177744][11504029]|. |FRAME: CPD-13173 Salicortin| and related compounds likely deter herbivore attack when they are hydrolyzed in insect guts, leading to the release of a potent 6-hydroxy-2-cyclohexen-on-oyl moiety similar in structure to |FRAME: CPD-13172 HCC| |CITS: [11521399]|. Phenolic glycosides, including |FRAME: CPD-13173| and |FRAME: CPD-1142| can accumulate to extremely high levels in leaves of |FRAME: TAX-3689| and |FRAME: TAX-40685| species, with exact levels of specific PGs varying based on genotype, environment, time of day, and developmental stage |CITS: [11504029][16724272][5886251]|. Interestingly, there is evidence that the creation of large amounts of these compounds may impose a metabolic cost that can negatively impact plant growth |CITS: [11504029][16411958]|, suggesting that plants must finely tune PG biosynthesis to maximize overall fitness., The pathways of PG biosynthesis, including |FRAME: CPD-13173| and |FRAME: PWY-6766 salicin| biosynthesis have been explored over many years often through the use of radioactive tracers |CITS: [16748997][ZENK67][20177744][12921436]|. Studies in different species, including |FRAME: TAX-77065| and |FRAME: TAX-3691| indicate that a number of alternative pathways for PG biosynthesis may exist between and within species suggesting that a "metabolic grid" would be a more appropriate representation of this network of connected reactions |CITS: [12921436][20177744]| that lead to the production of these ecologically-important defense compounds., About This Pathway, A breakthrough in the understanding of the pathway came with the discovery of several enzymes involved in it., Two genes encoding |FRAME: MONOMER-124403| and |FRAME: MONOMER-124404| were identified from |FRAME: TAX-3694| in 2015 |CITS: [25561400]|. Later studies identified a glucosyltransferase (|FRAME: G-124402|) that had the same expression pattern of these acyltranferases, which was shown to catalyze the glucosylation of both |FRAME: CPD-26326| and |FRAME: CPD-26330| |CITS: [31736216][35532172]|. Since inactivation of the gene abolished production of |FRAME: CPD-13173| and related compounds, it became clear that the products of the glucosyltransferase are important intermedaite in the pathway. In addittion, a |FRAME: G-124402| mutant was found to accumulate |FRAME: CPD-110|. The authors speculated that |FRAME: CPD-110| could be released from a salicinoid intermediate when |FRAME: G-124402| is blocked, suggesting that |FRAME: CPD-26326| is hydroxylated prior to glucosylation |CITS: [35532172]|.

Summary: General Background, Benzoic acid, derived from phenylalanine, is a precuror to several important benzenoid compounds, including floral scent constituents, such as |FRAME:CPD-12217|, |FRAME:CPD-6443| |FRAME:CPD-6441| |CITS:[15286288][12884048][12226525][12361714]|; the defense signaling compounds salicylic acid (SA) and its derivatives |CITS:[19400653][19820324]|, and a number of pharmacologically active compounds, such as taxol |CITS: [11095755 ]| (rev in |CITS: [16600669]|). An important step in the creation of benzoic acid is the cleavage of two carbon atoms from the 3-carbon side-chain present on trans-cinnamic acid. At least three different chain-shortening routes have been proposed in plants |CITS: [15286288]| and there is evidence that a subset of the different pathways may operate in individual species, and may differentially contribute to benzoic acid biosynthesis within each species. For example, |FRAME:TAX-4102| has at least two pathways present (this pathway and |FRAME: PWY-6444|), whereas cucumber (|FRAME:TAX-3659|) and |FRAME:TAX-49451| seem to lack the |FRAME: PWY-6444| variant |CITS: [11219576]| and |FRAME:TAX-140968| relies on a third pathway (|FRAME: PWY-6446|) that incorporates elements of the other two variants. , A greater understanding of the metabolic pathways involved in benzoic acid biosynthesis may contribute to genetic engineering efforts aimed at altering floral scents, modifying SA-based defense responses, and increasing the production of pharmaceutically important compounds |CITS: [17234289][17511599]|., Although benzoate biosynthesis has been primarily studied in plants, there is evidence that |FRAME: TAX-115828| bacteria make |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| using the early steps in the |FRAME: PWY-6443| pathway |CITS: [12502351]|., About This Pathway, Following the initial activation of trans-cinnamic acid with CoA, the next three steps of this pathway are expected to share similarities with the β-oxidation process involved in |FRAME: PWY-5136 "fatty acid metabolism"|. These reactions, from |FRAME: CINNAMOYL-COA| to |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| will likely require the sequential activities of an enoyl-CoA hydratase, a dehydrogenase, and a thiolase |CITS: [15286288]|. , |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA "Benzoyl-CoA"| can then be used to produce |FRAME: BENZOATE| through at least two different routes. In petunia, the |FRAME: MONOMER-15440 "BPBT"| enzyme that catalyzes the formation of the volatile intermediate |FRAME: CPD-6443| has been characterized |CITS: [17194766][15286288]|. |FRAME: CPD-6443 "Benzylbenzoate"| can be used to produce |FRAME: BENZOATE| through the activity of an esterase. Alternatively, a thioesterase may perform the conversion from |FRAME: BENZOYLCOA| to |FRAME: BENZOATE| in one step. , Although many of the enzymes that are predicted to participate in this pathway have not yet been cloned or characterized in plants, radiotracer studies provide strong evidence for some of the early |CITS: [11219576]| and later steps in the pathway |CITS: [11219576][19659733]|. The identification of two enzymes from petunia that work late in the pathway provide additional support |CITS: [15286288][19659733]|., Given the importance of the many compounds that can be derived from benzoic acid, it is not surprising that the biosynthesis of benzoate is regulated |CITS: [11219576]|, for example, by changes in the level of transcript expression for the BPBT and KAT1 enzymes |CITS: [15286288][19659733]|.

General Background, |FRAME: CPD-18985 Butane|, along with |FRAME: CPD-9312|, |FRAME: CPD-18984|, and |FRAME: CPD-9285|, is a gaseous n-alkane. The main sources for gaseous n-alkanes in the atmosphere are natural oil seepage and oil spills., A number of microorganisms have been isolated for their ability to use gaseous n-alkanes as a sole carbon source, including some Gram-negative strains |CITS: [Takahashi80]| and many strains belonging to the order |FRAME: TAX-2037|, such as those of the genera |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus|, |FRAME: TAX-1763|, |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, and |FRAME: TAX-1847| |CITS: [7958761][11679317]|. Most of these organisms can utilize several of these gases, but not methane. On the other hand, bacteria that can grow on methane (methanotrophs) generally do not use other alkanes as growth substrates |CITS: [1515161]|., A number of bacteria have been isolated that are capable of growth on butane |CITS: [5066104][Perry80][Takahashi80][16346339][7958761]|., About This Pathway, This butane degradation pathway, characterized from |FRAME: TAX-86174|, begins with an oxidation of a terminal carbon of |FRAME: CPD-18985| by |FRAME: EC-1.14.13.230|, forming |FRAME: BUTANOL| |CITS: [10376833]|. The enzyme has a low secondary activity of hydroxylating the sub-terminal carbon, and, at least in vitro, also forms a small amount of |FRAME: CPD-326| |CITS: [17526838][19383682]|., |FRAME: BUTANOL Butanol| is oxidized to |FRAME: BUTANAL| by two periplasmic enzymes that contain a |FRAME: PQQ| cofactor. The enzymes are not identical - one of them interacts directly with the electron transfer chain via quinones, while the other transfers its electrons to a cytochrome c |CITS: [11238982][12142403][11889098]|. Butanal is oxidized further to |FRAME: BUTYRIC_ACID| by an oxygenase that has not been characterized yet. Butanoate is degraded quickly, presumably via the fatty acid β-oxidation cycle |CITS: [10376833]|.

Summary: General Background, Vitamin C (|FRAME: ASCORBATE|), a reducing agent and antioxidant, is a cofactor in reactions catalyzed by, copper-dependent monooxygenases and iron-dependent dioxygenases. It is synthesized, in vertebrates having, this capacity, from |FRAME: GLUCURONATE|. This compound is formed through direct hydrolysis, of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| by enzyme(s) bound to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. They share many, properties with, and are most likely identical to, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases |CITS:[17222174]|., |FRAME: ASCORBATE| can be biosynthesized by plants (see |FRAME: PWY-882|), some bacteria, (see |FRAME: PWY-5521|) and many vertebrates. It is used in the pharmaceutical industry for the production, of vitamin supplements, cosmetics and therapeutic preparations. It is also used in the food, beverage and, animal feed industries. , |FRAME: ASCORBATE| is an essential vitamin in the diet of humans, non-human primates and certain other, vertebrates that cannot biosynthesize it (some fish and birds, bats and guinea pigs). These species rely on, mechanisms for efficient uptake and recycling of this vitamin (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6370|). It is taken up in the intestine, transported in plasma and delivered to tissues. Its recycling in erythrocytes has been described (reviewed in |CITS: [9405334]|). It has roles in collagen biosynthesis, as an antioxidant, as a cofactor in reactions catalyzed by some metal-dependent mono- and dioxygenases, and may be involved in cell signaling reactions and transcription factor activation. A deficiency of vitamin C leads to the disorder scurvy (reviewed in |CITS: [16516325] [17222174]|). Yeasts are known to biosynthesize D-erythroascorbate, a 5-carbon analog of ascorbate. It functions as an antioxidant, but it lacks antiscorbutic activity (prevention of scurvy) (reviewed in |CITS: [16516325]|). , About This Pathway, The mammalian liver pathway for |FRAME: ASCORBATE| biosynthesis is shown here. |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is formed from hydrolysis of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| by a membrane-bound enzyme(s) of the endoplasmic reticulum, probably UDP-glucuronidase(s) (reviewed in |CITS: [17222174]|. The ultimate precursor of |FRAME: UDP-GLUCURONATE| is D-glucose (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-4821|)., |FRAME: GLUCURONATE| is reduced to |FRAME: L-GULONATE| by a NADP+-dependent aldehyde reductase. A broad specificity lactonase then forms |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE|. The |FRAME: L-GULONO-1-4-LACTONE| is oxidized to |FRAME: ASCORBATE| by L-gulonolactone oxidase via an intermediate lactone which spontaneously isomerizes to |FRAME: ASCORBATE|. The production of hydrogen peroxide by this endoplasmic reticulum enzyme is unusual and transfer of electrons to another acceptor might occur in intact cells, as has been shown for plant homologues of this enzyme. L-Gulonolactone oxidase is deficient in humans and other animals unable to biosynthesize |FRAME: ASCORBATE| due to mutations in the gene encoding it |CITS: [8175804]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [17222174] [9405334]|).

Malonyl glucosides have been frequently overlooked due to their lability and inadequate isolation procedures. , Numerous N-and O-malonyl conjugates have been reported in different plant species, including isoflavones, isoflavanones , and isoflavonoids but also xenobiotics, D-amino acids and the ethylene precursor 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid., The latter are considered to be detoxification products |CITS: [6497385]|, , whereas the former may serve as pools for the release of free aglycons. Released isoflavones can be either incorporated , into the biosynthetic pathway of phytoalexins or act as phytoanticipins |CITS: [11730862]|., The finding that isoflavone conjugates are sometimes constitutively present in considerable amounts in legumes |CITS: [Graham91]|,, support such a possible role as preformed toxins (phytoanticipins). , Glucosides and malonyl glucosides of isoflavones, such as biochanin A and formononetin and further metabolic derivatives , (e.g. cicerin, medicarpin) are exclusively located in the vacuole |CITS: [Mackenbrock92]| and it has been speculated, that , acylation of these compounds could precede and facilitate their transport through the tonoplast |CITS: [6639051]|.

General background, |FRAME:TAX-4932| is able to grow on various carbon sources including fatty acids. Saturated fatty acids or fatty acids with trans-double bonds at even-numbered positions can be completely degraded in the β-oxidation cycle (|FRAME:PWY-7288|) |CITS:[12697341]|. However, unsaturated fatty acids with cis- or trans-double bonds at odd-numbered positions or cis-double bonds at even-numbered positions entails the involvement of so-called auxiliary enzymes (see |FRAME:PWY-7291| and |FRAME:PWY-7292|) |CITS:[12697341] [14523547] [8685242]|., The degradation of the trans-unsaturated fatty acid |FRAME:CPD-15679| in |FRAME:TAX-4930| (this pathway) has been investigated by monitoring the formation of polyhydroxyalkanoates (see |FRAME:PWY-6657|). The commonly used method to study the degradation of unsaturated fatty acids in yeast such as observing clearing zones around colonies growing on media which provide those fatty acids as sole carbon source has its limits in detecting certain intermediates |CITS:[11566445]|. The formation of polymers from polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) had been originally developed for commercial purposes by producing protein-based polymers and elastomers as part of the efforts to produce renewable and biodegradable raw materials |CITS:[10209132] [9634754]|. However, it rapidly became apparent that the polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) polymerization method also represented a powerful tool to follow carbon fluxes, monitor substrate specificities, detect and engineer new metabolic routes and analyze quantity and quality of unusual fatty acid degradation intermediates in a variety of organisms |CITS:[9634754] [11679353] [10571864] [18657232]|. , About the pathway, By introducing a bacterial PHA synthase from Pseudomonads modified for yeast peroxisomal targeting which polymerizes the various 3-hydroxy-acyl-CoA species generated in the β-oxidation cycle (see |FRAME:PWY-7288|) it is now possible to determine the composition and amount of the substrates and intermediates in a range from 5 to 16 carbons in length |CITS:[16347790] [11679353]|. The degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15679| following the fatty acid activation to form the respective CoA derivative occurs in two pathways which combine auxiliary enzymes with core-enzymes of the β-oxidation cycle. Utilizing yeast mutants, i.e. Δeci1, Δsps19 and Δdci1 and evaluating the quantity and monomer composition of the synthesized PHA the pathway sequences degrading |FRAME:CPD-15679| could be determined |CITS:[15904873]|. As mentioned above the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15679| could only be monitored via PHA polymerization to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15660| as this is the detection limit of the method |CITS:[16347790]|. , Whereas the degradation of |FRAME:CPD-15680| is done by one single pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-7337|) the breakdown of its trans-isomer , i.e. |FRAME:CPD-15679| is realized via two metabolic routes |CITS:[15904873]|. The first part of the two pathways is catalyzed by the β-oxidation enzymes POX1 |CITS: [2189786] [11431484]|, the multifunctional enzyme FOX2 |CITS:[1551874] [10497229] [16574148]| and the 3-keto-thiolase (POT1) |CITS:[7754706] [9402066] [7812714]| up to the formation of |FRAME:CPD-15661|. At this point the pathway splits up in two directions. The reductase-dependent pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-7338|) employs 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase (SPS19) |CITS:[9268358] [1738316]| to direct further degradation. The other metabolic branch, i.e. the MFE-dependent pathway (this pathway) is characterized by the action of the multifunctional enzyme (MFE) trans-2-enoyl-CoA hydratase 2/3R-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FOX2) which is name-giving for a pathway that requires no participation of auxiliary enzymes.

The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-562716| can kill a variety of Gram-positive bacteria by attacking their cell-wall peptidoglycans and can use |FRAME: D-GLT| for growth |CITS: [31941905]|. The organism can grow with as little as 50 μM |FRAME: D-GLT| as its sole carbon and nitrogen source., The organism utilizes a deamination-independent D-glutamate degradation pathway in which |FRAME: D-GLT| is acetylated to |FRAME: CPD-26441|. The acetylated product is racemized to |FRAME: ACETYL-GLU|, which is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GLT|. The latter serves as a carbon/nitrogen source for growth., The genes encoding the enzymes involved are located in a single operon whose expression is controlled by the DgcR transcriptional regulator. The key enzymes, DgcA and DgcN, occur widely in marine bacterial genomes and metagenomes, and are found in Proteobacteria (predominantly Rhodobacterales) and halophilic archaea (Halobacteria) |CITS: [36690779]|.

General Background, |FRAME: carotenoids Carotenoids| are isoprenoid pigments in the yellow to red color range. They have conjugated double bond chains of varying length with varying substituents, which determines their light absorption spectrum. They are produced by photosynthetic organisms and some non-photosynthetic fungi and bacteria. Animals, including humans, cannot synthesize carotenoids, although they are an essential source of retinoids and vitamin A., Carotenoids have diverse functions that include participation in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, serving as antioxidants, virulence factors, and modulation of membrane function. In photosynthetic organisms carotenoids provide protection against photooxidative stress through energy-dissipation of excess light absorbed by the antenna pigments as well as light-harvest. The prominent |FRAME: CPD1F-119|, as well as |FRAME: CPD1F-130|, are involved in the reduction of cataract and macular degeneration; others are exploited as coloring agents in flowers and fruits to attract pollinators (and in industry as food colorant) and agents of seed dispersal. Carotenoids serve as precursors for the plant growth hormone |FRAME: Abscisic-Acid| and |FRAME: Vitamin-A| (for a succinct review of the applications of carotenoids, see |CITS:[15012246]|). In addition, they may be cleaved to |FRAME: Apocarotenoids apocarotenoids|, whose functions include serving as a cofactor for light-sensing proteins, acting as hormones, or acting as antifungals. Carotenoids have been the subject of metabolic pathway engineering studies because microbial carotenoid production is environmentally preferable to chemical synthesis., Over 700 carotenoids have been identified. The two main structural classes of carotenoids are the |FRAME: Carotenes carotenes| and the |FRAME: Xanthophylls xanthophylls|, which are composed of hydrocarbons and oxygenated hydrocarbons, respectively. , Most carotenoids have a C40 chain length derived from the symmetric precursor |FRAME: CPD-12321| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6287|). |FRAME: CPD-12321| is derived from |FRAME: GERANYLGERANYL-PP|, which is in turn derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5120|). , Larger, C50 carotenoids also occur in nature and appear to be derived from the addition of two isoprene units to a C40 carotenoid. Biosynthetic intermediates and novel bacterial genes involved in C50 carotenoid biosynthesis have been identified and biosynthetic pathways postulated in only a few organisms (as in |CITS: [11511870][11432736][17008032][20802040][25712483]|)., Smaller, C30 carotenoids have also been found in plants and microorganisms. In microorganisms they appear to be synthesized by a distinct C30 pathway, whereas in plants they appear to result from cleavage of C40 carotenoids. |FRAME: CPD-9911| is a bacterial C30 carotenoid derived from |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|. It is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite |FRAME: CPD-9916| in |FRAME: TAX-1280| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5875|). |FRAME: CPD-9911| has also been identified in a few other bacteria |CITS: [20303609] [9297464]|., Genes encoding the enzymes of carotenoid biosynthesis have been cloned from many plants, cyanobacteria and other microorganisms (|CITS: [20582313][11511870][18535920] [17257797] [17912511][12730708]|. Extensive comparative genomics analysis of microbial carotenoid biosynthetic proteins has shown new phylogenetic and evolutionary patterns of these pigments that had not been found in previous, more limited, analyses |CITS: [20582313]|., About This Pathway, Carotenoids with cyclic ends are integral constituents of plants, algae and cyanobacteria photosynthetic reaction centers |CITS:[GOODWIN80],[YOUNG93]|. One of the major carotenoids (>15%) of the cyanobacterium |FRAME: TAX-32049| is the xanthophyll |FRAME: CPD-11462| - an aromatic dicarboxylate carotenoid |CITS: [18715035]|. This compound was assigned the structure (all-E) χ,χ-caroten-18,18'-dioate., In non-cyanobacteria the synthesis of aromatic carotenoids from |FRAME: CPD1F-129| involves a carotene desaturase/methyltransferase encoded by the crtU gene |CITS: [10395965]|. The homolog of this gene in cyanobacteria was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-32049| and named |FRAME: G-11377| |CITS: [18849428]|. This gene encodes an enzyme that acts sequentially on the two rings of |FRAME: CPD1F-129| to form |FRAME: CPD-11456| and and eventually |FRAME: CPD-11457|., Another enzyme of this pathway is encoded by the |FRAME: G-11378| gene. CruH is responsible for hydroxylation at the C-18 and C-18' positions. It first acts on one ring, producing |FRAME: CPD-11459|, and then, following further oxidation of the hydroxyl to a carboxyl, acts on the other ring to produce |FRAME: CPD-11461|., A third enzyme, which hasn't been discovered yet, catalyzes the oxidation of the hydroxyl groups to carboxylates, resulting in the final product, |FRAME: CPD-11462| |CITS: [18849428]|.

Summary: |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL Ergosterol| is a major sterol found in green algae, including |FRAME: TAX-3055| where it accounts for roughly 55% of the total sterol content found when analyzing whole cells or isolated flagella |CITS:[GEALT81]|. |FRAME:ERGOSTEROL Ergosterol| is typically found in plasma membranes where it may affect membrane flexibility and fluidity. It is unclear whether sterols also play signaling roles in green algae., The primary evidence for this pathway comes from radiotracer studies demonstrating that green algae exclusively use the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| for polyisoprenoid precursor biosynthesis |CITS: [11289606][10584331]| and from radiotracer and metabolite-based experiments demonstrating that |FRAME: TAX-3055| synthesizes ergosterol via a Δ<sup>25(27)</sup>-olefin pathway |CITS: [22591742]| distinct from the Δ<sup>24(28)</sup>-olefin pathway found in yeast and other fungi |CITS: [346585] [2654239]|. Another notable difference between this pathway and the |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL-SYN-PWY| typically found in fungi is the use of |FRAME: CYCLOARTENOL| rather than |FRAME: LANOSTEROL| as the primary backbone for |FRAME: PWY-7154| |CITS: [20333205][22591742]|., This superpathway describes the complete pathway for the synthesis of |FRAME: ERGOSTEROL| from the central metabolites, |FRAME: GAP| and |FRAME: PYRUVATE|. It includes several subpathways, including the |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY| pathway, which describes the synthesis, of the isopreoid building blocks |FRAME: CPD-4211| and |FRAME: DELTA3-ISOPENTENYL-PP|, |FRAME: PWY-5123|, which, describes the synthesis of this central intermediate, which feeds into many different metabolic routes, |FRAME: PWY-5670|,, which describes the first committed step for the synthesis of sterols, generating |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE|,, and finally the pathways for |FRAME: PWY-5174 egosterol biosynthesis| in green algae (|FRAME: TAX-3041|), and possibly, in sponges (|FRAME: TAX-6040|).

De novo synthesis of cobamides requires a great deal of genetic information, which is only found in some prokaryotes. Many bacterial species do not have the full genetic information required for de novo biosynthesis of |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, but can synthesize cobalamin when supplied with |FRAME: COBINAMIDE|, a stable cobamide that is not a true intermediate of the de novo pathway |CITS: [14351147][8770581]|., In order to process |FRAME: COBINAMIDE| to |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN|, it has to be converted into a real intermediate of the pathway. In most bacteria this is done by the attachment of the upper ligand 5'-deoxyadenosine to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE|, followed by phosphorylation to yield |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE-P|, an intermediate of the de novo biosynthetic pathway (this pathway)., Archaea as well as many bacterial species utilze a different salvage pathway, where |FRAME: ADENOSYLCOBINAMIDE| is first converted to |FRAME: CPD-691| (see |FRAME: PWY-6269|).

Of the ten existing hexitols (|FRAME: CPD-15703|, |FRAME: CPD-12811|, |FRAME: CPD-15702|, |FRAME: SORBITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-12810|, |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: CPD-15701|, |FRAME: CPD-357|, |FRAME: CPD-369| and |FRAME: GALACTITOL|) only three occur naturally - |FRAME: MANNITOL|, |FRAME: SORBITOL| (also known as D-glucitol), and |FRAME: GALACTITOL| (owing to symmetry, D- and L-galactitol are identical)., |FRAME: MANNITOL| is the most abundant polyol in nature, and is found in bacteria, fungi, algae, lichens and vascular plants. It has been reported in more than 100 species of vascular plants |CITS:[stoop96]|, and in many plants it is a major photosynthetic product and form of transportable carbohydrate comprising 10 to 60% of the soluble carbohydrates |CITS:[bieleski82]|., Mannitol is known as a 'compatible solute'. High compatible solute concentrations prevent loss of water or balance salt accumulation, while not interfering with normal metabolism. D-mannitol-producing plants exhibit a high degree of salt tolerance |CITS:[zhifang03]|., |FRAME: MANNITOL| protection also occurs at concentrations too low for significant osmotic effects. It has been suggested that sugar alcohols, because of their water-like hydroxyl groups, may mimic the structure of water and maintain an artificial sphere of hydration around macromolecules. They have also been postulated as scavengers of activated oxygen species preventing peroxidation of lipids and resulting cell damage., Mannitol synthesis in plants  occurs simultaneously with either sucrose synthesis |CITS:[rumpho83]| or with raffinose saccharide synthesis |CITS:[flora93]|. To date no plants have been found that produce only mannitol. D-mannitol biosynthesis in higher plants occurs via the isomerization of fructose-6-phosphate to mannose-6-phosphate, which is in turn converted to mannitol-1-phosphate by the NADPH-dependent mannose-6-phosphate reductase, M6PR. The final step of conversion of mannitol-1-phosphate to mannitol is irreversible. Interestingly, transgenic |FRAME:TAX-3701| plants overexpressing |FRAME:TAX-4045| M6PR were shown to produce mannitol but also a mannitol-derivative: |FRAME:CPD-6021| (GPM), one of two constituents of the industrial sweetener isomalt. Incidentally, these transgenic plants were also shown to have increased salt-tolerance without any observed phenotypical defects |CITS:[zhifang03]|.

|FRAME: Ginsenosides Ginsenosides| or panaxosides are a class of steroid glycosides and triterpene saponins found exclusively in the plant genus |FRAME: TAX-4053 "Panax (ginseng)"|. They are the principal components responsible for the pharmaceutical activities of ginseng., Ginsenosides are composed of an aglycone and sugar moieties. Based on the structure of their aglycones, ginsenosides have been categorized into three broad types; |FRAME: Protopanaxadiol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxadiol-type ginsenosides"| (PPD), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3 and 20, |FRAME: Protopanaxatriol-type-ginsenosides "protopanaxatriol-type ginsenosides"| (PPT), which contain hydroxyl groups at positions 3, 6 and 20, and |FRAME: Oleanonic-acid-type-ginsenosides "oleanonic-acid-type saponins"|., Although ginsenosides only have three kinds of aglycones, more than 60 kinds of ginsenosides have been identified by now due to the variability in the type of sugar moieties, their number, and the carbon positions they link to., The biological activity of ginsenoside increases with the decrease of the number of the sugar moieties. All of the ginsenosides found in large quantities in wild ginseng (known as major ginsenosides) are heavily glycosylated, while the more active less-glycosylated ginsenosides are found in much smalller quantities (and are commonly referred to as the, minor ginsenosides). Following oral intake of ginseng, the large low-solubility and poor-permeability major ginsenosides cannot be absorbed by the human body directly |CITS: [Su06]|, and are deglycosylated into smaller forms in the gastrointestinal tract by intestinal bacteria and/or digestive enzymes |CITS: [8923812]|., Glycosidase enzymes that can convert the major ginsenosides to minor ginsenosides are not common and are of commercial interest., |FRAME: CPD-12102| has been isolated as a minor constituent from the root of |FRAME: TAX-4054| |CITS: [14751305]|, the root of Ginseng radix |CITS: [9527441]| and the fruits of |FRAME: TAX-4054| |CITS: [8216805]|. |FRAME: CPD-12102| is a saponin with a lower amount of sugar chains. This type of ginsenosides are known to be more effective as cancer drugs |CITS: [12583159]|. |FRAME: CPD-12102| is cytoprotective, relaxing vasculature by inducing nitric oxide synthase in response to |FRAME:NITRIC-OXIDE| production |CITS: [14534150]|., The compound has been evaluated extensively as an anti cancer drug |CITS: [9527441]|. Its inhibitory effect on lung metastasis of mouse lymphoma has been demonstrated |CITS: [15733388 ]|. The antiproliferative effects of |FRAME: CPD-12102| on proteins in colon cancer cells using a proteomic approach has been demonstrated |CITS: [19352032]|., About This Pathway, Although |FRAME: CPD-12102| is a promising pharmacological agent, its industrial production is difficult. It has been synthesized mainly by acid and heat treatment of tissue, with low yields. General Background, Most pathogenic bacteria have an absolute requirement for iron, which is scarce within their host environment. In vertebrates the majority of the iron is found in the form of heme. Several heme-iron acquisition systems have been characterized from pathogenic bacteria. In general, the bacteria express outer membrane proteins that bind heme compounds, extract heme from them, and transport the heme into the cell, where it is degraded to release the iron |CITS: [1425573][7783623][9157245]|. The most common heme-degradation systems utilize heme oxygenase enzymes that degrade heme to yield iron, carbon monoxide, and biliverdin., Several forms of bacterial heme oxygenases are known, and they are described in the various heme degradation pathways in MetaCyc. The enzymes consume three molecules of oxygen and a total of seven electron equivalents to break the tetrapyrrole ring and liberate the iron. However, while some enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| like the eukaryotic enzymes (see |FRAME: PWY-7845|), others produce different unusual isomers such as |FRAME: CPD-19713| and |FRAME: CPD-19714| (|FRAME: PWY-7844|), |FRAME: CPD-18928| (|FRAME: PWY-7843|), |FRAME: CPD-19710| (|FRAME: PWY-7846|), |FRAME: CPD-15535| and |FRAME: CPD-15534| (|FRAME: PWY-7847|) and |FRAME: CPD-19716| and |FRAME: CPD-19715| (|FRAME: PWY-7848|)., About This Pathway, The first prokaryotic heme oxygenase was identified from the Gram-positive bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1717|, which is encoded by the |FRAME: G-54982| gene |CITS: [9006041][9422739]|. The first such enzyme from a Gram-negative organism, encoded by the |FRAME: G-54982|, was identified shortly after from |FRAME: TAX-487| |CITS: [10629191][11073924]|. Both of those enzymes produce |FRAME: BILIVERDINE|., In |FRAME: TAX-287| the |FRAME: G-54979| gene, which encodes a heme oxygenase, is located in an operon with the bphP gene, which encodes a bacterial |FRAME: Phytochromes phytochrome|. The product of BhpO, |FRAME: BILIVERDINE| (BV), has high affinity for the BhpO and could not be removed by gel filtration, ion exchange chromatography, or changes in solution pH. However, when purified BphOηBV was incubated with purified apo-BphP, the BV was transferred from BphO to BphP, forming a holo phytochrome. Thus, it appears that the main role of BhpO is to participate in the synthesis of the bacterial phytochrome |CITS: [15310749]|.
