Summary: General Background, |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE Plastoquinones| (PQ) are benzoquinone electron carriers that can function as acceptor/donor for either one or two electrons. They are analogs of |FRAME: Ubiquinones "ubiquinones"| (Coenzyme Q), with two methyl groups substituting the methoxy groups found in Q. The fully reduced form is called |FRAME: Plastoquinols|., Plastoquinones are found in the chloroplasts of higher plants, red, brown and green algae, and in cyanobacteria, and are important members of the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, where they carry electrons from |FRAME: CPLX490-3506| to the |FRAME: CPLX-9022|. Plastoquinones also serve as a membrane-associated two-electron carriers in other respiratory electron transport chains. In fact, it has been shown that in cyanobacteria essentially all electron transport through unbound quinones proceeds via PQ in cyanobacterial thylakoids. Apart from PQ the only quinone found in thylakoids is |FRAME: 2-METHYL-3-PHYTYL-14-NAPHTHOQUINONE| (vitamin K1), which is associated with PS I |CITS: [Vermaas01]|., Plastoquinones also serve as cofactors involved in the desaturation of |FRAME: CPD-12321| in the synthesis of carotenoids (see |FRAME: PWY-6475|)., Plastoquinone was isolated originally in 1946 from |FRAME: TAX-3879| (alfalfa), but was not identified at the time. It was rediscovered in 1959 and its structure described in the same year (see |CITS: [7022156]|)., About This Pathway, Researchers suspected for some time that the pathway for plastoquinone biosynthesis in cyanobacteria is different from that of higher plants (see |FRAME: PWY-1581|). Inactivation of the cyanobacterial |FRAME: SGL_RS15355-MONOMER|, a key enzyme in the plant pathway that catalyzes the conversion of |FRAME: P-HYDROXY-PHENYLPYRUVATE| to |FRAME: HOMOGENTISATE|, while abolishing tocopherol biosynthesis, had no effect on the synthesis of plastoquinone, suggesting that plastoquinone is synthesized in cyanobacteria by a different pathway |CITS: [12123828]|., A clue for the alternative pathway was provided with the functional characterization of the |FRAME: SGL_RS16820| gene, encoding |FRAME: SGL_RS16820-MONOMER| |CITS: [22166075]|. The gene is a functional homolog of the |FRAME: EG11370| gene, which is involved in ubiquinone biosynthesis in bacteria. Studies using labeled isotopes confirmed that |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| is a precursor of |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE-9| in |FRAME: TAX-1148|. , Subsequent studies of |FRAME: G-17958|, a homolog of |FRAME: EG11369| that produces |FRAME: 4-hydroxybenzoate| from |FRAME: CHORISMATE|, and of |FRAME: G-17959|, a homolog of |FRAME: EG11044| that catalyzes the decarboxylation of |FRAME: NONAPRENYL-4-HYDROXYBENZOATE| to |FRAME: CPD-9863|, clarified the early part of the pathway and demonstrated that it is very similar to that of prokaryotic ubiquinone biosynthesis |CITS:[24337576]|.

|FRAME: INDICAN Indican| is the β-D-glucoside of |FRAME: INDOXYL|, and is found in several plant families, the most important being Acanthaceae, Asclepiadaceae, Apocynaceae, Fabaceae, and Polygonaceae. The function of |FRAME: INDICAN| in plants is still unknown., After enzymic or chemical hydrolysis, |FRAME: INDICAN| can converted back to |FRAME: INDOXYL|, which is spontaneously oxidized (in the presence of oxygen) to |FRAME: CPD-10525|. Indigo was one of the most important dye compounds in the past, and is still an esteemed dye., The pathway from indican biosynthesis diverts from that if |FRAME: TRP| at |FRAME: INDOLE|, which is produced from, |FRAME: INDOLE-3-GLYCEROL-P| by the α subunit of tryptophan synthase. Indole is converted by dioxygenase systems (enzyme complexes that form cis-dihydrodiols) to |FRAME: CPD-10523|, which spontaneously eliminate a water molecule to form |FRAME: INDOXYL|. While dioxygenase enzymes from the plants that are konwn to produce |FRAME: CPD-10525| have not been studied yet, bacterial enzymes, such as |FRAME:CPLX-7256| from |FRAME: TAX-303|, have been used successfully for the production of |FRAME: INDICAN| in strain of |FRAME:TAX-562| engineered, to produce |FRAME: CPD-10525| |CITS: [6353574]|., In the plant, |FRAME: INDOXYL| is converted to |FRAME: INDICAN| by |FRAME: MONOMER-14292|. This enzyme has been purified from |FRAME: TAX-222567| |CITS: [10680172]| and |FRAME: TAX-96455| |CITS: [10795317]|.

Summary: General Background, Fatty acids are key building blocks for the phospholipid components of cell membranes. They are also determinants of intracellular communication in the form of lipid second messengers |CITS: [11094259]| and protein modification, where fatty acyl moieties of proteins modify their location and function |CITS: [10446384]|., There are two basic types of fatty acid biosynthesis systems, named type I and type II. The type I system is found in animals and lower eukaryotes. The mammalian system consists of a single gene product that contains all of the reaction centers required to produce a fatty acid (see |FRAME: CPLX-7628| from |FRAME: TAX-9606|), while the system of lower eukaryotes (such as yeast) consists of two genes, whose polypeptide products combine to form a multifunctional complex (see |FRAME: CPLX-7627| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|). The pathway catalyzed by the type I systems is available at |FRAME: PWY-5994|., Type II systems are found in bacteria, plants |CITS: [15952903]|, parasites of the |FRAME: TAX-5794| phylum |CITS: [17112527]| and mitochondria |CITS: [12882974][12654921]|. The reactions in these systems are catalyzed by a series of individual soluble proteins that are each encoded by a discrete gene, and the pathway intermediates are transferred between the enzymes as thioesters of |FRAME: ACP|. Unlike the type I system that accepts |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| as the source of the two-carbon units, the type II systems accept only |FRAME: MALONYL-ACP|., About This Pathway, Many Gram-positive organisms, such as the bacilli, staphylococci, and streptomycetes, produce odd- and even-carbon-number branched-chain fatty acids. Branched-chain fatty acids display a lower melting point temperature than their straight-chain equivalents, and their presence in the membrane is expected to increase its fluidity, similar to the effect of unsaturation |CITS: [26300876]|. In |FRAME: TAX-1423| 95% of the total fatty acids are branched |CITS: [4392505][1886522]|. The most common fatty acids are |FRAME: CPD-9917| (34%), |FRAME: CPD-19657| (24%), |FRAME: CPD-18175| (13%), |FRAME: CPD-23515| (12%), |FRAME: CPD-23509| (9%), and |FRAME: CPD-19660| (4%) |CITS: [28825491]|., The substrate specificity of the FabH condensing enzyme is the determining factor in the biosynthesis of branched-chain fatty acids by type II fatty acid synthases. In organisms that produce non-branched fatty acids such as |FRAME: TAX-562| FabH is specific for |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| as the starter molecule. In contrast, the FabH enzymes from organisms that produce branched-chain fatty acids, such as |FRAME: TAX-1423|, utilize branched-chain acyl-CoA primers much more efficiently than |FRAME: ACETYL-COA| (for |FRAME: TAX-1423| the ratio is 100:1) |CITS: [1886522]|. The rest of the enzymes that form the fatty acid synthase system do not have a significant degree of selectivity for either branched-chain or straight-chain fatty acids |CITS: [10629181]|., The most common starter molecules for branched-chain fatty acids are derived from the branched-chain amino acids |FRAME: LEU|, |FRAME: VAL|, and |FRAME: ILE|. An aminotransferase converts these acids to the α-keto acids |FRAME: 2K-4CH3-PENTANOATE|, |FRAME: 2-KETO-ISOVALERATE|, and |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE|, respectively. A specialized α-keto acid dehydrogenase, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.25|, is critical for generating the branched-chain acyl-CoA primers for the FabH enzymes (|FRAME: ISOVALERYL-COA|, |FRAME: ISOBUTYRYL-COA|, and |FRAME: 2-METHYL-BUTYRYL-COA|, respectively) |CITS: [ 3142877]|., The type of primer used determines the type of the branched-chain fatty acid formed. |FRAME: Anteiso-fatty-acids "Anteiso-fatty acids"|, which are derived from |FRAME: ILE|, have an odd number of carbons and are characterized by a methyl-substituent located on the antepenultimate carbon of the carboxyalkyl chain. Anteiso-fatty acids are the most prominent fatty acids of cell membranes of some bacteria, especially of the genus Bacillus. The most relevant anteiso-fatty acids in food and bacteria are |FRAME: CPD-9917| and |FRAME: CPD-23509| |CITS: [28129363]|., Unlike classic fatty acids and |FRAME: Iso-fatty-acids "iso-fatty acids"|, |FRAME: Anteiso-fatty-acids "anteiso-fatty acids"| are chiral molecules due to the stereogenic center at the carbon of the branching point. A distinct pre-dominance of (S)-anteiso-fatty acids, or even (S)-enantiopurity, has been described in bacteria |CITS: [1886522][20117788]| and also in fish |CITS: [13373794][17508720][20221853]|, dairy products |CITS: [13373794][13412644][13827622][20221853]|, mutton fat |CITS: [13018208]|, and Brussel sprouts |CITS: [26390192]|.

Summary: General Background, Polyamines are found in bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes and are necessary for normal cellular physiology. They include the diamine |FRAME: PUTRESCINE|, the triamines |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (sym-norspermidine) and |FRAME: CPD-1821| (homospermidine) and the tetraamine |FRAME: SPERMINE| (in |CITS: [20194510]| and in |CITS: [19196710]|). Links to their biosynthetic pathways can be found by clicking on these compounds links. See also |FRAME: POLYAMSYN-PWY|, |FRAME: POLYAMINSYN3-PWY| and |FRAME: PWY-6565|. In members of the genus |FRAME:TAX-662|, |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| is a major polyamine (in |CITS: [19196710]|., About This Pathway, In this pathway |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| donates a carboxyaminopropyl group to |FRAME: CPD-313| to form |FRAME: CPD-9995| in a reaction catalyzed by carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine dehydrogenase (CANSDH). Decarboxylation of |FRAME: CPD-9995| catalyzed by carboxynorspermidine/carboxyspermidine decarboxylase (CANSDC) produces |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|. |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| is also a precursor for |FRAME: CPD-313| biosynthesis from |FRAME: CPD-470| which is catalyzed by a bifunctional fusion protein L-2,4-diaminobutyrate aminotransferase/decarboxylase (DABA AT/DC) (|CITS: [3697846] [19196710]| and in |CITS: [20194510]|)., This |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE-SEMIALDEHYDE| based pathway has been experimentally demonstrated in vivo in |FRAME: TAX-666| including a branch of this pathway that leads to the biosynthesis of |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| as shown in the pathway link. Both pathways are shown together in |FRAME: PWY-6565|., Heterologous expression in |FRAME:TAX-562| of the genes encoding the enzymes in this pathway resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-313| and |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| (which are inactive polyamines in |FRAME:TAX-562|). Deletion of the gene encoding CANSDC in |FRAME: TAX-666| resulted in accumulation of |FRAME: CPD-9995|. Deletion of the genes encoding either CANSDC or CANSDH led to loss of |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| and |FRAME: SPERMIDINE|, thus identifying the gene encoding CANSDH. Interestingly, deletion of the |FRAME: TAX-666| genes encoding either CANSDH or CANSDC reduced the growth rate of planktonic cells by approximately 50% and severely reduced biofilm formation. Biofilm formation could be rescued by adding exogenous |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE|, but not |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| . The pathway did not appear to be related to the infectivity of |FRAME: TAX-666|, using a mouse model |CITS: [19196710]|. Earlier work also suggested a role for |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| in biofilm formation in |FRAME: TAX-666| |CITS: [16237027]|., Bioinformatic analysis suggested that DABA AT/DC fusion proteins and their clustering with CANSDH and CANSDC were found only in the family |FRAME: TAX-641|, giving support to their role in both |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| and |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| biosynthesis in these organisms. However, a clustered pair of CANSDH and CANSDC genes was widespread in the α-, β-, γ-, δ- and ε-proteobacteria, firmicutes and a candidate division TG-1, suggesting that the pathway for |FRAME: SPERMIDINE| biosynthesis may be more widely used. However, this conclusion could not be extended to |FRAME: NORSPERMIDINE| biosynthesis without experimental support due to the use of |FRAME: CPD-470| in other pathways (see |FRAME: P101-PWY|, |FRAME: PWY-6409| and |FRAME: PWY-761|) |CITS: [19196710]|.

Summary: Purine nucleotides participate in many aspects of cellular metabolism including the structure of DNA and RNA, serving as enzyme cofactors, functioning in cellular signaling, acting as phosphate group donors, and generating cellular energy. Maintenance of the proper balance of intracellular pools of these nucleotides is critical to normal function. This occurs through a combination of de novo biosynthesis and salvage pathways for pre-existing purine bases, nucleosides and nucleotides., The de novo biosynthetic pathway for purine nucleotides is highly conserved among organisms, but its regulation and the organization of the genes encoding the enzymes vary. This fourteen step pathway contains ten steps that branch at |FRAME: IMP| to form |FRAME: AMP| and |FRAME: GMP|, each in two steps. Regulation of the pathway has been well studied in microbes such as |FRAME:TAX-562|, |FRAME:TAX-1423| and |FRAME:TAX-4932|, but little is known about its regulation in higher eukaryotes (metazoa and plants |CITS: [8938402]|). The pathway appears to vary in archaea |CITS: [9150241]|. Some organisms, such as the mycoplasmas, do not biosynthesize purine and pyrimidine bases de novo and must rely on salvage pathways |CITS: [11737647]|. , In |FRAME: TAX-4932| regulation of the pathway occurs at both the enzyme level as shown in this pathway, and at the genetic level. For example, at the genetic level positive-acting regulatory proteins Bas1 and Pho2 and biosynthetic intermediates |FRAME: P-RIBOSYL-4-SUCCCARB-AMINOIMIDAZOLE| and/or |FRAME: AICAR| are required to derepress ADE gene expression. Summary: General Background, The detoxification of the highly toxic |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| is a major biochemical necessity for most life forms., In the case of methylotrophic bacteria, formaldehyde is not just a toxic compound, but also a central intermediate. It has been suggested that the |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| concentration in the cytoplasm of a methylotroph would rise to 100 mM in less than 1 minute if |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| consumption would stop |CITS: [11073907]|. Several different pathways for |FRAME: Formaldehyde-Oxidation| are known in bacteria, encoded by unrelated or distantly related genes. , About This Pathway, Even though |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| is almost a universal thiol, present in eukaryotes, Gram negative bacteria, and several Gram positive bacteria, there are some organisms that produce alternative thiols. The small thiol |FRAME: CPD8J2-3 bacillithiol| has been discovered in a variety of Gram-positive bacteria, including |FRAME:TAX-1299|, |FRAME:TAX-1392|, |FRAME:TAX-1280|, and |FRAME:TAX-1423| |CITS: [19578333]| (see pathway |FRAME: PWY8J2-1|). Genes similar to those of the |FRAME:TAX-1423| biosynthetic pathway were also discovered in the δ-proteobacterium |FRAME:TAX-34| and the halophilic alkalithermophile |FRAME:TAX-375929| |CITS: [20308541]|., |FRAME: CPD-20111|, which is formed spontaneously by |FRAME: CPD8J2-3| and |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE|, is oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-20112| in the presence of |FRAME: NAD| by a dedicated enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: BSU27010| gene, which is induced specifically by |FRAME: FORMALDEHYDE| |CITS: [19170879]|. The presence of the enzyme's product, |FRAME: CPD-20112|, was demonstrated in |FRAME: TAX-1471| cells grown on |FRAME: METOH|. A sudden increase in |FRAME: METOH| resulted in a comparable increase in the level of |FRAME: CPD-20112|, confirming that |FRAME: CPD8J2-3| plays a role in formaldehyde oxidation under formaldehyde stress conditions |CITS: [26303953]|., |FRAME: CPD-20112| is proposed to be hydrolyzed to |FRAME: FORMATE| and |FRAME: CPD8J2-3|. However, it is still not known whether the hydrolysis is catalyzed enzymatically.

The progress in sequencing and mining fungal genomes has revealed a significant number of biosynthetic genes which are not functional mirrored in the metabolic profile of those organisms |CITS:[16716432] [22228366] [23178386]|. Such cryptic or silent genes have been detected in Aspergillus nidulans. Amongst those genes are 27 nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) genes alone of which only 5 have been associated with a metabolic function so far |CITS:[18804170]| . Although shown to be transcriptionally regulated the trigger for activation remain obscure in most cases |CITS:[16372000]|. In general, predictions for metabolic products of fungal metabolic clusters, silent or not, are difficult to make because of the often iterative acting and intricately programmed synthases |CITS:[17581644]| and synthetases |CITS:[23307607]| which are involved in building the core of the compounds. In addition, fine tuning of gene expression levels may influence the chemical structures produced by an biosynthetic cluster as shown for the |FRAME:PWY-7561| |CITS:[21675761]|. |FRAME:CPD-17148 Aspyridone A|, the final product of the described pathway, has been found to be slightly cytotoxic |CITS:[17369821]| but its physiological function, conditions under which the compound is produced and pharmacological and toxicological properties remain to be elucidated., Utilizing an genomic-driven approach and by overexpressing the pathway-specific regulator gene ApdR the gene cluster for the formation of |FRAME:CPD-17148| and the biosynthetic active genes of that cluster were identified in Aspergillus nidulans |CITS:[17369821]|. The first step of the reaction is catalyzed by the polyketide synthase (PKS) - nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) hybrid encoded by ApdA |CITS:[17369821]|. The highly reductive (HR) polyketide synthase (PKS) module of ApdA in cooperation with the trans enoyl reductase ApdC produced the ACP-bound tetraketide |FRAME:CPD-17151| from |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| and |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| which is subsequently linked to |FRAME:TYR| and released as |FRAME:CPD-17150| by the NRPS module of ApdA. The conversion comprises a cascade of about 20 enzymatic steps catalyzed by the multidomain enzyme encoded by ApdA and the monomodular ApdC which was demonstrated by heterologous expression of both genes in the expression host Saccharomyces cerevisiae |CITS:[20828130]|. , The final conversion of |FRAME:CPD-17150| to |FRAME:CPD-17148| is catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 dependent oxidase encoded by ApdE which carries out an unique oxidative rearrangement of the 2-pyridone ring of |FRAME:CPD-17150| similar to the one catalyzed by TenA in the |FRAME:PWY-7561| |CITS:[Wasil13]|. ApdE was expressed using a unique, generally applicable plasmid system in which genes are expressed under the control of strong artificial promoters hence avoiding the difficulties of the native transcription system |CITS:[23084942]|. The preaspyridone A oxidase has a more diverse oxidation chemistry than the comparable Ten A and also produces |FRAME:CPD-17152| and a 5-dephenylated 2-pyridone. Although |FRAME:CPD-17152| had been proposed as an intermediate towards |FRAME:CPD-17149| |CITS:[17369821]| it appears that the compound is rather a shunt product and the ability to produce |FRAME:CPD-17149| is not included in the Apd gene cluster |CITS:[Wasil13]|.

Summary: Glucosinolates are 1-thio-β-D-glucosides. They are found prominently in the order Capparales, which include cabbage, mustard, oilseed rape, broccoli, and the model plant Arabidopsis. Many glucosinolate-producing plants have typical sharp taste and odor that are caused by their glucosinolates. , The glucosinolates play an important role in plant defense. Upon herbivore attack glucosinolates are hydrolyzed and broken down to toxic compounds in a process that starts with the action of |FRAME: EC-3.2.1.147 "EC 3.2.1.147, myrosinase|. The myrosinases are S-glycosidases that remove the sugar moiety from glucosinolates, leaving unstable thiohydroximate-O-sulfate products that undergo spontaneous hydrolysis to form |FRAME: ISOTHIOCYANATES isothiocyanates|. The resulting isothiocyantaes are bioactive, and have been shown to have antimicrobial and insecticidal activities., In the presence of specific plant proteins, some glucosinolate hydrolysis products are diverted away from isothiocyanate. |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.5 "Nitrile-specifier proteins (NSPs, EC 4.8.1.5)"| are known to catalyze the formation of nitriles. |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.6 "Epithiospecifier proteins (ESPs, EC 4.8.1.6)"| are responsible for the formation either nitriles or epithionitriles, depending on the structure of the parent glucosinolate (see |FRAME: PWY-5267|), and |FRAME: EC-4.8.1.7 "thiocyanate-forming proteins (TFPs, EC 4.8.1.7)"| are known to catalyze the formation of thiocyanates |CITS: [17139450]|., About This Pathway , Unlike aliphatic and aromatic glucosinolates, the immediate degradation of indole glucosinolates was considered to form only nitriles and isothiocyanates, which are degraded further into a assortment of compounds (see |FRAME: PWYQT-4476|) |CITS: [18346197]|. However, a different glucosinolate metabolism pathway that operates in intact cells results in production several unusual metabolites, as shown here. It should be noted that the reactions described in this pathway occur during normal growth, and not upon disruption of the cells by herbivore attack., The product of the |FRAME: AT2G44490| gene of |FRAME: TAX-3702| was reported to encode glucosylhydrolase that together with PEN3, an ATPbinding cassette (ABC) transporter, forms a defense system that restricts the growth of a broad spectrum of pathogens, including the nonadapted oomycete |FRAME: TAX-4787|, the adapted powdery mildews |FRAME: TAX-62715| and |FRAME: TAX-62708|, and the necrotrophic fungus |FRAME: TAX-40658| |CITS: [16293760]|., Comparison of metabolites produced by a |FRAME: AT2G44490| mutant and the wild type revealed that the mutant lost the ability to produce two compounds, identified as |FRAME: CPDQT-331| and |FRAME: CPD-8913|. In addition, the mutant line accumulated high amounts of |FRAME: 4-METHOXY-3-INDOLYLMETHYL-GLUCOSINOLATE|. These results indicated the presence of a novel glucosinolate metabolism pathway in which |FRAME: AT2G44490| acts as an atypical myrosinase. Characterization of purified |FRAME: AT2G44490| verified that it catalyzes the hydrolysis of both |FRAME: CPD-1863| and |FRAME: 4-METHOXY-3-INDOLYLMETHYL-GLUCOSINOLATE| |CITS: [19095900]|. Furthermore, by identifying a monooxygenase (|FRAME: AT5G57220|) that hydroxylates |FRAME: CPD-1863| (the first step in formation of |FRAME: 4-METHOXY-3-INDOLYLMETHYL-GLUCOSINOLATE|), it was shown that biosynthesis and cleavage of the latter are essential for plant defense |CITS: [19095900]|., The likely source of sulfur in the final metabolites was assumed to be glutathione. This has been confirmed by performing metabolite profiling of a mutant lacking |FRAME: AT4G23100|, encoding |FRAME: EC-6.3.2.2| |CITS: [19095900]|.

Names: galactolipid biosynthesis II // galactosylglyceride biosynthesis II
Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Galactolipids galactolipids| |FRAME: D-Galactosyl-12-diacyl-glycerols monogalactosyldiacylglycerol| (MGDG) and |FRAME: Galactosyl-galactosyl-diacyl-glycerols digalactosyldiacylglycerol| (DGDG) are prevalent membrane, lipids in organisms that carry out oxygenic photosynthesis, such as land plants, algae, and cyanobacteria |CITS: [Dormann01]|. MGDG and DGDG constitute about 50% and 30%, respectively, of the total lipids in the majority of photosynthetic membranes., Crystallographic analysis of photosystem complexes revealed that stoichiometric amounts of both types of galactolipids are bound in the interior of photosystem complexes |CITS: [16963124][21499260]|, and it has been shown that a galactolipid-deficient mutant of |FRAME: TAX-3702| lacks photosynthetic activity |CITS: [17940034]|., |FRAME: D-Glucosyl-12-diacyl-glycerols "1,2-diacyl-3-O-(β-D-glucopyranosyl)-sn-glycerol"| (monogalactosyldiacylglycerol, MGlcDG) is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of galactolipids. However, it also participates on its own in stress acclimation of cyanobacteria. The compound was shown to accumulate during heat stress |CITS: [15797247]|, is involved in cold acclimation |CITS: [24370445]|, and in phosphate stress adaptation |CITS: [31787233]|, and its accumulation may be linked to fatty acid desaturation |CITS: [31787233]|., About This Pathway, Despite the conservation of galactolipids in the membranes of plants and cyanobacteria, the biosynthetic pathways leading to their production differ. Plants use |FRAME: CPD-14553| and diacylglycerol as substrates for |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.46|, which transfers a galactose unit to diacylglycerol, generating |FRAME: D-Galactosyl-12-diacyl-glycerols monogalactosyldiacylglycerol| in a single reaction (see |FRAME: PWY-401|)., Cyanobacteria, on the other hand, start by producing |FRAME: D-Glucosyl-12-diacyl-glycerols monoglucosyldiacylglycerol| (GlcDG) by the transfer of a glucose unit from |FRAME: CPD-12575| to, diacylglycerol |CITS: [Sato82][16714404]|. GlcDG then undergoes epimerization to yield MGDG via the action of |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.34| |CITS: [25197079]|. The addition of a second galactose unit is carried out by a reaction identical to that carried out by plants, even though the cyanobacterial enzymes are not related to the plant enzymes |CITS: [17932115][17921339]|., While |FRAME: SGL_RS10570| (encoding |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.336|) appears to be an essential gene |CITS: [24370445]|, |FRAME: SGL_RS10580| (encoding |FRAME: EC-5.1.3.34|) mutants did possess thylakoid membranes and showed normal maximal photosynthetic activity, albeit with reduced utilization of light energy, suggesting that glucolipids may substitute for galactolipids in the thylakoid membranes |CITS: [25197079]|. Similarly, no significant differences were found between the growth curves of the wild-type and a Δ|FRAME: SGL_RS09310| (encoding |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.241|) mutant, even though the oxygen evolution rate of the mutant was reduced |CITS: [17932115]|.

Like many other hyperthermophiles isolated from marine environments, |FRAME: TAX-2336| is slightly halophilic (optimum NaCl concentration of 2.7%, wt/vol). To cope with the salinity, the organism developed biochemical strategies. The most common osmoadaptation mechanism is the accumulation of low-molecular-mass organic compounds in the cytoplasm. Interestingly, the organic solutes produced by thermophiles are often different from those used by mesophiles., The most widespread organic solute found in hyperthermophiles is |FRAME: CPD-12857| (di-myo-inositol phosphate, or DIP). In addition to DIP, |FRAME: TAX-2336| produces two additional compounds under heat stress: |FRAME: CPD-21543| (MDIP) and |FRAME: CPD-21544| (MMDIP) |CITS: [8824608][19648237]|. In cells grown under heat stress, MDIP was the major solute, accounting for 43% of the total pool. Under those conditions MMDIP and DIP accumulated to similar levels, each corresponding to 11.5% of the total pool |CITS: [19648237]|., The |FRAME: G-124303| gene, which encodes |FRAME: EC-2.4.1.361|, was found by looking for genes encoding glycosyltranferases that were common to organisms that produce MDIP.  The gene was cloned and expressed in |FRAME: TAX-562|, and found to confer MDIP synthase activity on the host |CITS: [19648237]|., The recombinant enzyme was purified and characterized. The enzyme catalyzes two reactions, initially forming MDIP, and later forming MMDIP. The optimal temperature was 95 °C, and the presence of Mg<sup>2+</sup> was required for maximal activity |CITS: [19648237]|., Homologs of |FRAME: G-124303| are found only in the genera |FRAME: TAX-2335|, |FRAME: TAX-2713|, and |FRAME: TAX-2233| |CITS: [19648237]|.

Summary: General Background, Flavanones such as naringenin, eriodictyol and pinocembrin are key intermediates in the , flavonoid biosynthetic pathway in plants towards the synthesis of flavonols, anthocyanidins and catechins |CITS: [15013767]|. , Pinobanksin, a dihydroflavonol (or flavanonol) is characterized by the absence of B-ring substitution (compare |FRAME:DIHYDROKAEMPFEROL-CMPD|, |FRAME:CPD-474|) , and has been frequently found in association with its metabolic predecessor pinocembrin and pinocembrin-7-methyl ether , (pinostrobin) in pine species such as |FRAME:TAX-3349| and |FRAME:TAX-3353| |CITS: [BOHM94]|., Flavonoids in general are valuable natural products and have been thoroughly studied with respect to their manifold functions , in plants |CITS: [11724379]| |CITS: [3738520]| and significant effect on human health |CITS: [16176136]|. Pinocembrin chalcone , has antibacterial properties |CITS: [9933997]| and pinocmebrin exhibited larvicide activities on pest insects |CITS: [2056764]|. , The flavanones naringenin and pinocembrin are central precursors of many flavonoids and branch points for various related , pathways (|FRAME:PWY1F-FLAVSYN|). That has attracted the research on the production of those compounds in microbial , systems |CITS: [16133333]| |CITS: [15932991]| |CITS: [12732539]| by employing corresponding key genes of plants in varying , assembled gene clusters. , About This Pathway, The entry enzyme into the flavonoid pathway is chalcone synthase (CHS). Chalcone synthase can , use both p-coumaroyl-CoA and cinnamoyl-CoA, giving rise to naringenin chalcone or pinocembrin chalcone, respectively , |CITS: [1536925]| |CITS: [11880657]|. Chalcone synthase is encoded in plants either as a single gene copy such as in Arabidosis , thaliana |CITS: [11557794]|, multiple gene copies as found in |FRAME:TAX-4102| |CITS: [2806915]| or as a CHS gene , family generally found in leguminous plants |CITS: [7579172]|. The question whether the observed substrate specificity , (p-coumaroyl-CoA vs cinnamoyl-CoA and other starter CoA's) is a common feature of CHS or if the multiplicity of genes in , certain plants accounts for that metabolic flexibility remains to be investigated. The formation of small amounts of pinocembrin , chalcone as a side product has even been observed with stilbene synthases (STS) |CITS: [12620343]| |CITS: [15821144]| , as has pinosylvin with chalcone synthases (CHS) |CITS: [15821144]| when cinnamoyl-CoA was provided accentuating the , close relationship of the two polyketide synthases CHS and STS |CITS: [2033084]| |CITS: [8083886]|. , The formation of pinocembrin has been observed in |FRAME:TAX-4558| as the result of the catalytic activity of chalcone , synthase forming pinocembrin chalcone and the presumably spontaneous isomerization to the corresponding flavanon , |CITS: [15821144]|. Pinocembrin has also been found as a constituent of the unsubstituted B-ring flavonoids in cell cultures of , the cactus |FRAME:TAX-223054| |CITS: [7646065]|. Pinocembrin is further metabolized to the flavanonol pinobanksin, , catalyzed by the flavanone-3β-hydroxylase introducing a hydroxyl group to the 3β-position of ring C |CITS: [15013767]|. , The 7-methylated ester of pinocembrin, i.e. pinostrobin has been isolated from honey and ginger (Boesenbergia pandurata) , |CITS: [12452678]| but the corresponding enzyme remains to be isolated and characterized.

Summary: The presence of an anaerobic respiratory chain comprising |FRAME: EC-1.9.6.1| (periplasmic nitrate reductase) and |FRAME: EC-1.1.5.3| in |FRAME: TAX-83333| is supported by studies using isogenic strains with combinations of null lesions encompassing the periplasmic and membrane associated nitrate reductases (|FRAME: NAP-CPLX Nap|, |FRAME: NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX "NRA"| and |FRAME: NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX "NRZ"|). These studies indicate that |FRAME: TAX-562| can use |FRAME: NAP-CPLX| (Nap) and |FRAME: FUMARATE-REDUCTASE| equally well in a respiratory chain with |FRAME: GLYCEROL-3P| as electron donor |CITS: [11844760]|. A strain expressing only Nap (lacking NRA and NRZ) is preferentially selected during continuous anaerobic growth with glycerol under nitrate limiting conditions |CITS: [10548536]|, Nap is preferentially expressed at low nitrate concentration - conditions under which it may be economical for the cell to reduce nitrate in the periplasm and make nitrite directly available to the energy conserving |FRAME: NRFMULTI-CPLX periplasmic nitrite reductase| |CITS: [10464201][11844760]|. Nap can accept electrons from either ubiquinol (shown in this pathway) or menaquinol, but couples more effectively to menaquinol oxidation |CITS: [9325429]|. When menaquinol serves as the electron donor, the |FRAME: EG12060 NapC| c-type cytochrome can transfer electrons directly from the membrane quinol pool to the |FRAME: EG12061 NapB| subunit of the reductase, from which they are transferred to the |FRAME: EG12067 NapA| catalytic subunit. However, when ubiquinol serves as the electron donor, the iron-sulfur proteins |FRAME: EG12064 NapG| and |FRAME: EG12062 NapH| need to catalyze the transfer of electrons from ubiquinol to NapC before they can be transferred to the reductase |CITS: [11967083]|., The pathway is predicted to function with ubiquinol as the electron source during periods of transition from aerobic conditions to anoxia, while the cells need to shift from oxygen to nitrate as the terminal acceptor, but have not yet synthesized a sufficient amount of menaquinone., Please note: due to software limitations the soluble periplasmic nitrate reductase NapAB is incorrectly depicted as a membrane protein in this pathway representation.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: Ulvan Ulvans| are cell wall matrix polysaccharides in |FRAME: TAX-3041 "green algae"| belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-3118|. They represent 8-30% of the dry weight of Ulva species., Ulvans have a complex structure that has not been completely elucidated. They are composed mainly of |FRAME: Rha3S| (Rha3S), the uronic acids |FRAME: CPD-12521| (GlcA) and |FRAME: CPD-12515| (IduA), and, in smaller amounts, |FRAME: BETA-D-XYLOSE| (Xyl) |CITS: [8901268][Quemener97]|., Studies have indicated that unlvan is likely composed from repeats of three types of disaccharides, all of which are composed of Rha3S linked to one of the other residues, giving |FRAME: CPD-17745| (GlcA- Rha3S), |FRAME: CPD-17748| (IduA-Rha3S), and |FRAME: CPD-17749| |CITS: [9468631][17458931]|. The relative proportions of the three repetiing units depend on the algal species, harvesting season, stabilization treatment, and extraction procedures |CITS: [Robic08][Robic09][Robic09a]|., About This Pathway, The marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-906888| was isolated from the feces of the gastropod |FRAME: TAX-71498| that had been fed with green algae belonging to the genus |FRAME: TAX-3118|, based on its ability to degrade |FRAME: Ulvan| |CITS: [20833882]|., Ulvan degradation starts by the action of |FRAME: MONOMER-19226| |CITS: [22009751]|. Polysaccharides lyases act by the removal of a relatively acidic C5 proton of the uronic acid (C5 is the carbon linked to the carboxylic group) followed by the elimination of the hexose linked to C4, resulting in the formation of an unsaturated C4-C5 bond on the hexuronic acid moiety of the resulting oligosaccharide. All end products of the |FRAME: MONOMER-19226| were shown to contain an [unsaturated uronic acid--rhamnose 3-sulfate] unit at the nonreducing end, with the smallest product being a disaccharide. It was shown that the enzyme can break the bond between rhamnose 3-sulfate and either glucuronate or idonurate, but not between rhamnose 3-sulfate and xylose |CITS: [22009751]|., The tetra- and disaccharides generated by the lyase are hydrolyzed by |FRAME: CPLX-8985|. That enzyme cleaves the unsaturated glucuronyl acid residue, which spontaneously rearranges from its cyclic form to a linear |FRAME: CPD-37|.enzyme is nore active with the tetrasaccharides than the disaccharides |CITS: [24407291]|.

|FRAME: CPD-13973 Doxorubicin| is an anthracycline antibiotic closely related to |FRAME: CPD-13962| that was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-55158| in 1969 |CITS: [5365804]|. It is commonly used in the treatment of a wide range of cancers, including hematological malignancies, many types of carcinoma, and soft tissue sarcomas. It has better activity against solid tumors and a higher therapeutic index than |FRAME: CPD-13962|. Both compounds are toxic and can cause fatal cardiac toxicity., Doxorubicin is formed from |FRAME: CPD-13962| by C-14 hydroxylation performed by the DoxA hydroxylase |CITS: [9864344]|. The enzyme also catalyzes the last two steps in |FRAME: PWY-7352|. However, while |FRAME: CPD-13962| is formed by many strains of |FRAME: TAX-1950|, only |FRAME: TAX-55158| is known to produce |FRAME: CPD-13973|. Biochemical characterization of DoxA from non-doxorubicin producing strains showed that the enzyme from these strains is able to catalyze the conversion of |FRAME: CPD-13962| to |FRAME: CPD-13973|, but at a very low rate |CITS: [9098063]|.

Summary: General Background, The inorganic sulfur compound |FRAME: S2O3| contains two sulfur atoms: a sulfone-sulfur (oxidation state +V), and a sulfane-sulfur (oxidation state -I). At low pH thiosulfate decomposes spontaneously to |FRAME: SO3| and elemental sulfur, |CITS: [4552952]|. At neutral pH the compound is relatively stable, but several types of bacteria can catalyze its disproportionation in a process in which thiosulfate serves as both an electron donor and an electron acceptor. , Several types of enzymes have been described that are able to catalyze the disproportionation of thiosulfate. These enzymes have been differentiated based on the nature of the electron donor: some enzymes require thiols for this purpose, some utilize cytochrome c3, which receives the electrons from molecular hydrogen via a hydrogenase, some accept the electrons from the quinone pool, and some have only been active in vitro when coupled to cyanide. These four classes of enzymes are described in the pathways |FRAME:PWY-5277|, |FRAME:PWY-5352|, |FRAME: PWY-7813|, and |FRAME:PWY-5350|, respectively., About This Pathway, Non thiol-dependent dissimilatory thiosulfate reduction is found in two unrelated groups of bacteria. One group consists of the sulfate reducing bacteria, such as |FRAME:TAX-872| and |FRAME:TAX-1562| (described in this pathway), while the other includes several genera of the enterobacteriaceae - |FRAME:TAX-590|, |FRAME:TAX-583 Proteus|, |FRAME:TAX-544|, |FRAME:TAX-82978| and |FRAME:TAX-635 Edwardsiella| |CITS: [3299028]| (described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-7813|)., In 1955 Ishimoto and Koyama reported that in the Gram-negative sulfate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-876| cytochrome c3 functions as as an electron shuttle between hydrogenase and thiosulfate reductase |CITS: [Ishimoto55]|. Two years later they were able to partially purify the thiosulfate reductase from this organism |CITS: [Ishimoto57]|., In 1969 a similar enzyme was discovered in the Gram-positive sulfate-reducing bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1565| |CITS: [5784203]|. These authors partially purifed the enzyme, and using 35S-labeled thiosulfate they were able to show that the enzyme cleaved the sulfane sulfur atom from thiosulfate and converted it to sulfide, while the inner sulfur atom remained in the form of sulfite., Unlike |FRAME: G3O-33772-MONOMER| from |FRAME: TAX-4932|, the only thiosulfate reductase enzyme purified at the time, this enzyme was not able to use thiols such as |FRAME: GLUTATHIONE| or |FRAME: CYS| as electron donors, nor was any stimulatory effect observed when these compounds were added to the standard assay. The electron donors used in the assays were either pyruvate or molecular hydrogen in the presence of a hydrogenase from |FRAME: TAX-881| |CITS: [5784203]|., A thiosulfate reductase enzyme was purified from |FRAME: TAX-881| strain Hildenborough in 1971. That enzyme catalyzed the disproportionation of thiosulfate into sulfite and sulfide in the presence of hydrogen when coupled to a hydrogenase using methyl viologen as an electron acceptor |CITS: [5573735]|. The molecular size of the enzyme was ~16 kDa, and a flavin and nucleic acid were tightly bound to it. A second |FRAME: MONOMER-12530| was purified from |FRAME: TAX-881| strain Miyazaki F by Aketagawa et al |CITS: [2993256]|. This enzyme was clearly different, as its molecular weight was 80-89 kDa, yet it catalyzed the same reaction when coupled to hydrogenase and methyl viologen. An even larger enzyme was isolated from |FRAME: TAX-879|. That enzyme, which catalyzed a similar reaction to the other proteins, was about 220 kDa |CITS: [242299]|., Kraemer and Cypionka showed that the ability to disproportionate thiosulfate was common among sulfate-reducing bacteria |CITS:[Kraemer89]|. Disproportionation of thiosulfate is associated with only a small free energy change, (ΔG'o = -22 kJ/mol) |CITS: [Kraemer89]|., Despite this, in 1987 it was shown that the disproportionation of thiosulfate can provide a bacterium with enough energy for growth |CITS: [Bak87]|. The thiosulfate-disproportioning bacterium |FRAME: TAX-63561| can grow by disproportionation of thiosulfate when small amount of acetate is present as a carbon source |CITS: [Bak87]|.

Summary: The asexual spores, i.e. conidia of fungi in the genus Fusarium are often strongly colored by the red pigments |FRAME:CPD-18245| (this pathway) and |FRAME:CPD-18207| |CITS:[18120664]| (see |FRAME:PWY-7692|) which are thought to reinforce the spores and protect them against UV-radiation |CITS:[2283502]|. Various Fusarium species infect crops such as wheat and corn, for instance Fusarium graminearum the causative agent of Fusarium head blight (FHB) |CITS:[McMullen97]| which leads to the deterioration of grain quality by disintegrating carbohydrates and proteins and accumulating mycotoxins |CITS:[8589414]|. , The red pigment |FRAME:CPD-18245| belongs to the compound group of naphthoquinones |CITS:[Samson00]| which are known to interfere with crucial biochemical processes such as phosphorylation, electron transport and superoxide production, all of which are highly significant for the normal functioning of cell metabolism |CITS:[9564730]|. A high concentration of |FRAME:CPD-18245| in wheat grains has been reported to be responsible for diseases in poultry |CITS:[11879787]|, considerably degrades egg quality in chicken |CITS:[11811917]| and makes cells more vulnerable to lipid peroxidation |CITS:[8415517]|. Besides |FRAME:CPD-18245| the pathway intermediate |FRAME:CPD-18242| |CITS:[16746350]| has been reported to be bioactive and exhibits antimycobacterial |CITS:[14987063]|, antiallergic |CITS:[9810700]| and phytotoxic |CITS:[10869195]| properties. , Polyketide synthases (PKSs) and nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) are abundantly present in the genus Fusarium |CITS:[22377171] [16196211]| and known to be involved in the biosynthesis of a plethora of fungal secondary metabolites. The gene PKS12 encoding for a minimal polyketide synthase in Fusarium graminearum |CITS:[14676319]| has been identified to belong to an biosynthetic gene cluster catalyzing the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18245|. The cluster consists of 11 genes of which 6 genes encode for proteins which are directly involved in the biosynthetic process |CITS:[15811992] [15809006]|. , The polyketide synthase (PKS12) carrying out the first step in the |FRAME:PWY-7695|) was shown to catalyze the formation of |FRAME:CPD-18255| from one |FRAME:ACETYL-COA| and six |FRAME:MALONYL-COA| starter units |CITS:[21296881]| and not |FRAME:CPD-18241| as previously assumed |CITS:[16879655]|. The intermediary heptaketide of this complex reaction, i.e. |FRAME:CPD-18240| is also substrate for the biosynthesis of |FRAME:CPD-18256| (see |FRAME:PWY-7696|) ( summary can be found in |CITS:[22713716]|). The molecular functions of the proteins catalyzing the subsequent reactions, i.e. the YWA1 dehydratase (aurZ) |CITS:[21296881]|, the nor-rubrofusarin O-methyltransferase (aurJ) |CITS:[16879655]|, and the decorating oxidases (aurF, aurO) |CITS:[16879655]| and the laccase-like protein (gip1) |CITS:[16879655]| have been demonstrated in single and double deletion mutants followed by metabolic profiling of the mutant media. , Recombinant production of |FRAME: CPD-18242| was achieved in |FRAME: TAX-4932| by expression of the |FRAME: G-44155|, |FRAME: G-44156|, and |FRAME: G-44157| genes, together with the |FRAME: TAX-746128| npgA gene encoding |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.7| |CITS: [23557488]|., The exact order of the reactions down-stream of |FRAME:CPD-18242| remains to be elucidated and may proceed via two different routes. It is possible that the aurF, aurO and gip1 encoded proteins can act on various intermediates |CITS:[21296881]|. The dimerization of compounds via laccase or laccase-like enzymes such as the gip1 encoded rubrofusarin laccase has been reported in the literature (summarized in |CITS:[15036303]|). Although transcription factors of the aurofusarin gene cluster are under investigation |CITS:[16461721]| the regulation of the pathway is mostly unknown and remains to be explored in more detail.

Names: juvenile hormone III biosynthesis II // JH III biosynthesis // methyl-10R,11-epoxy-3,7,11-trimethyl-2E,6E-dodecadienoate biosynthesis // methyl (2E,6E)-(10R)-10,11-epoxy-3,7,11-trimethyl-2,6-dodecadienoate biosynthesis
Summary: General Background, Juvenile hormones, a group of sesquiterpenoids, regulate several processes including embryonic development, metamorphosis, and reproduction in many insect species. |FRAME:CPD-8838 Juvenile hormone III| (JH III) is the most widespread juvenile hormone in insects |CITS: [15355237]|. One of the main roles of JH III is preventing metamorphosis by modulating |FRAME: ECDYSONE| action. When JH III is present, |FRAME: ECDYSONE| causes insect to repeat the most recent stage, and |FRAME: ECDYSONE| must act in the absence of JH in order for metamorphosis to be initiated. JH III is synthesized and released from the corpora allata (CA), a pair of small endocrine glands with nervous connections to the brain |CITS: [14599502]|. , The late stages of JH III biosynthesis start with |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP|, which is produced via the |FRAME: PWY-922 mevalonate pathway|. |FRAME: FARNESYL-PP| is hydrolyzed by a pyrophosphatase to |FRAME: 2-TRANS6-TRANS-FARNESOL|, then oxidized successively to |FRAME: 2-TRANS6-TRANS-FARNESAL| and |FRAME: CPD-12585| by an alcohol dehydrogenase and an aldehyde dehydrogenase, respectively., The next two step differ depending on the insect order. In Orthoptera, Dictyoptera and mosquitoes |FRAME: CPD-12585| is methylated by a SAM-dependent methyltransferase to form |FRAME: CPD-12586|, which is converted by a P450 monooxygenase to the epoxide form |FRAME: CPD-8838| |CITS: [12728004]| (see |FRAME: PWY-6575|). In Lepidoptera, on the other hand, methylation follows epoxidation (this pathway|)., Enzymes catalyzing all steps in the pathway have been cloned or characterized in insects, crustaceans or plants, including farnesyl phosphatase, farnesol and farnesal dehydrogenases and oxidases, carboxy methyltransferases, and a cytochrome P450 epoxidase |CITS: [6366103][19940247][16165084][1160503]|. Names: protective electron sinks in the thylakoid membrane (PSII to PTOX)
Summary: Cyanobacteria are able to conduct both photosynthesis and respiration, and have evolved a diverse range of electron transport pathways. An additional requirement is the ability to dissipate excess electron flow, which happens with varying light and environmental conditions., Like most cyanobacterial species, |FRAME: TAX-84588| possesses two membrane systems: the cytoplasmic membrane and a series of internal thylakoid membranes. The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes, as does a resipratory electron chain, while an additional respiratory electron transfer chainis localized in the cytoplasmic membrane., The only electron-transfer quinone found in cyanobacteria is |FRAME: PLASTOQUINONE plastoquinone| (PQ), which is shared among the photosynthetic light reactions and the respiratory electron chain. Three other components - cytochrome b6f complex, the small copper protein plastocyanin, and cytochrome c6, are also shared between the photosynthetic and respiratory electron transfer chains., As a result of the intersection between the respiratory and photosynthetic electron transport chains, the terminal oxidases in the thylakoid membrane apparently have an important role in addition to any function in respiration, namely the transfer of excess electrons generated from PSII to oxygen, preventing over-reduction of the PQ pool. Such cnditions could occur, for example, when iron concentrations are low, limiting the biosynthesis of the reaction center of photosystem I and the cytochrome b6f complex |CITS: [18241667]|., An electron transfer pathway involving a |FRAME: TX72_RS04385-MONOMER| (ptox) has been reported to be a sink for a significant fraction of photosynthetic electron transport under high irradiance |CITS: [19067963][Mackey08]|., A conflicting result was obtained by an experiment that measured the expression of 3 gene families involved with photoacclimation - the psbA gene family (encoding the photosystem II reaction center protein D1), the hli gene family (encoding the high-light inducible proteins), and |FRAME: TX72_RS04385| (encoding the |FRAME: TX72_RS04385-MONOMER|) was studied in |FRAME: TAX-84588| acclimated to either low or high light. In response to growth at higher irradiance, the organism increased expression of the psbA multigene family 5- to 60-fold). Expression of 4 hli genes increased 2- to 5-fold, whereas expression of the |FRAME: TX72_RS04385| gene decreased 3-fold. These findings suggested that the induction of psbA, resulting in synthesis of the PSII reaction center protein D1, may be critical for the acclimation of Synechococcus WH8102 to high irradiances. The low rates of ptox expression implied that the activity of the |FRAME: TX72_RS04385-MONOMER| may be limited in |FRAME: TAX-84588| under these conditions. Interstingly, expression of the ptox gene of |FRAME: TAX-59919| was induced under the same conditions |CITS: [Berg11]|.

Summary: General Background, The |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides lipopolysaccharide| (LPS) is one of the major structural and immunodominant molecules of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria. It consists of three moieties: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface. The structure of the O antigen consists of a polymer of oligosaccharide repeating units normally containing two to eight sugar residues., The presence of an O antigen is essential for survival of bacteria in their natural environment and plays a role in bacterial virulence. There is direct evidence that the loss of O antigen makes many pathogens, such as |FRAME: TAX-562|, |FRAME: TAX-623|, |FRAME: TAX-263|, and |FRAME: TAX-630|, serum sensitive or otherwise seriously impaired in virulence |CITS: [6196296][15066033][15731456][17905975][17030571]|., The synthesis and translocation of the O antigen can occur through three distinct pathways: the flippase/polymerase (Wzx/Wzy)-dependent pathway, the ABC transporter-dependent pathway, and the synthase-dependent pathway |CITS: [9791168][12045108]|. Among them, the Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway accounts for the synthesis of most heteropolysaccharides |CITS: [18289083]|., About Serotyping, Serotyping is a highly useful technique for identifying strains that vary in host range and disease spectrum, including pathogens, and is invaluable for epidemiological investigations. The Kauffmann-White-Le Minor serotyping scheme for designation of |FRAME: TAX-590| serotypes, which includes 46 O serogroups, is used by most laboratories. A serotype of |FRAME: TAX-590| is determined on the basis of O and flagellar (H) antigens. The O antigen determines the serogroup, while the H antigen completes the definition of the serovar or serotype of the isolate |CITS: [23848592]|., About This Pathway, The O antigen of groups C2 and C3 |FRAME: TAX-590| strains corresponds to serogroup O8 and is produced by a Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathway., The genes specific for |FRAME: TAX-590| O antigen synthesis are generally present as a gene cluster in the chromosome, called the O-antigen gene cluster, which maps between the galF and gnd genes., The first step in Wzx/Wzy-dependent pathways is the addition of a sugar phosphate residue to |FRAME: CPD-9646| (Und-P) to form the undecaprenyl diphosphate-linked sugar. Most O antigens found in |FRAME: TAX-590| species start with GlcNAc or GalNAc and their biosynthesis is initiated by |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.33| (WecA). However, the Salmonella O antigens belonging to serogroups O2 (A), O4 (B), O8 (C2,C3), O9 (D1), O9,46 (D2), O9,46,27 (D3), O3,10 (E1,E3), and O1,3,19 (E4) form a distinct set that is characterized by having a Gal residue as the first sugar of the O unit |CITS: [23848592]|., The enzyme responsible for the initiation of these pathways is |FRAME: EC-2.7.8.6| (WbaP, previously called RfbP |CITS: [9004408]|). The use of Gal as initial sugar appeared in |FRAME: TAX-590| after its divergence from |FRAME: TAX-561|, but the eight Gal-initiated O antigens have grown to be very important in this species |CITS: [23874940]|., The repeat unit in serogroup C2-C3 is different from that found in all other O-antigens with Gal as initial sugar. While it utilizes the same sugar residues, they are connected in a different order and contain more than one mannose residue. All of the genes in the central region of the gene cluster (wzx-wbaR-wbaL-wbaQ-wzy-wbaW-wbaZ) are unique to serogroup C2-C3 |CITS:[1722557][1379320]|., Following the completion of the synthesis of a repeat unit, the flippase Wzx flips the full molecule to the other side of the membrane, where the Wzy polymerase transfers additional repeat units from their anchor to a single elongating molecule. The Wzz protein ensures termination of the polimerization once the correct chain length has been achieved. The Wzx flippase from |FRAME: TAX-596| was found to have a strong preference for the presence of an abequose side-branch |CITS: [25837817]|., |FRAME: TAX-590| strains belonging to Group C2 contain a WzyC2 polymerase that links the repeat units by an α(1,4) linkage between the galactose and the rhamnose residues [α-D-Gal-(1→4)-β-L-Rha].

Summary: General Background, Iron is an essential trace element. In the presence of oxygen, ferrous iron is oxidized to ferric iron which forms insoluble compounds, and is thus not available to organisms., As a result, the level of physiologically available iron can drop to far below 1 μM, and become growth-limiting for bacteria. To survive, many bacteria evolved specialized transport systems called siderophores, which can complex and retract ferric iron ions., The siderophores are low molecular mass compounds, and have been generally divided into three main types: catecholate-, hydroxamate-, and carboxylate-siderophores., The siderophores, which have a very high and specific affinity for |FRAME: FE+3|, are excreted out of the cell and bind the metal extracellularly. The siderophore-metal complex is transported back into the cell through specific binding proteins present in the bacterial membrane., In Gram-negative bacteria, the binding protein transports the ferric-siderophore into the periplasm, where a second transporter transports it into the cytosol |CITS: [12196166]|., About This Pathway, |FRAME: CPD-11970 "Bisucaberin"| is a dimeric macrocylic siderophore that was initially isolated from the marine bacterium |FRAME: TAX-228| |CITS: [2962972][2962973]|. More recently the compound has been detected also in |FRAME: TAX-40269|, an important pathogen of farmed fish, including Atlantic salmon, cod and rainbow trout |CITS: [12046923]|. The structure and thermodynamics of the compound have been characterized |CITS: [11670794]|., |FRAME: CPD-11970 "Bisucaberin"| is very similar structurally to the siderophore |FRAME: CPD-11957|, which is synthesized by several |FRAME: TAX-1883| species (see |FRAME: PWY-6375|). While |FRAME: CPD-11957| is made of three molecules of |FRAME: CPD-11955| that have been condensed and cyclized, |FRAME: CPD-11970| is made of two such molecules. Thus, the biosynthetic pathway for the two siderophores only differs in the last step, which is catalyzed by the |FRAME: SCO2785|-encoded |FRAME: CPLX-7949| in |FRAME: TAX-1883|, and by the |FRAME: G-11649|-encoded enzyme in |FRAME: TAX-40269|., The gene cluster that encodes the biosynthesis and utilization of |FRAME: CPD-11970| has been identified in the |FRAME: TAX-40269| genome |CITS: [18956041]|. Biosynthesis is encoded by three genes - |FRAME: G-11647|, |FRAME: G-11648| and |FRAME: G-11649|, the later a fusion of two functions, encoding a single |FRAME: CPLX-7951| protein., The C-terminal part of the |FRAME: G-11649| gene, which encodes bisucaberin synthetase, has been cloned and expressed in |FRAME:TAX-562|, and the purified protein catalyzed the predicted activity |CITS: [18956041]|., The three biosynthetic genes are followed by five additional genes that are predicted to encode a ferric-siderophore, outer membrane receptor, a ferric-siderophore periplasmic binding protein, and 2 permease components and an ATPase component of a ferric-siderophore ABC transport system. The cluster is flanked by tranposase sequences, suggesting it may have been acquired by horizontal gene transfer |CITS: [18956041]|.

General Background, Polyketide (exclusive of fatty acids) represent a large group of natural products, i.e. secondary metabolites that are widespread in fungi, bacteria and plants |CITS: [Birch68][Schroder99][12946402]|. , Polyketides are often involved as intermediates in the formation of a vast variety of secondary metabolites with mixed , biosynthetic origin |CITS: [10426943]| |CITS: [Schroder97]|., The entry enzymes of the biosynthesis of polyketides in plants are the polyketide synthases producing the general backbone of compounds who give rise to a large array of natural products representing an amazing degree of structural diversity., The chalcone synthase (CHS) and stilbene synthase (STS) are the most well-known plant polyketide synthases, however , there exists a growing superfamily of related proteins referred to as CHS/STS-type proteins |CITS: [Schroder99]|. Depending on the specific polyketide synthase involved very diverse compound classes evolve such as chalcones (|FRAME:PWY1F-FLAVSYN|), stilbenes |CITS: [10426943]|, stilbenecarboxylates |CITS: [12620338]|, benzalacetone |CITS: [12226219]|, pyrone |CITS: [Eckermann98]|, C-methylated chalcone |CITS: [Shen00]| and acridone alkaloids |CITS: [8148006]| |CITS: [7727746]|., The formation of polyketides resembles the biosynthesis of fatty acids but is different in various aspects. In contrast to fatty acid synthases (FAS) plant polyketide synthases (PKS) are relatively small homodimeric enzymes, which do not use the acyl carrier protein (ACP) as activating agent but utilize acyl-CoA esters directly as substrates |CITS: [Shen00]| |CITS: [Birch68]|. , Although the synthesis of chalcone usually does not involve modifications by other proteins the chalcone derivatives , reduced at a specific position in the synthesized aromatic ring are frequently found in plants increasing the structural , variability of derivatives |CITS: [Schroder97]|. A number of diverse type III polyketide synthases present in various plants , have been cloned and found to produce diketides and heptaketides |CITS: [15044020]| as well as pentaketide chromones , |CITS: [15686354]|., About This Pathway, The pentaketide chromone synthase (PCS) involved in the biosynthesis of 5,7-dihydroxy-2-methylchromone represents a novel type of PKSs catalyzing five successive condensations steps with malonyl-CoA as the starter unit. The product is an aromatic pentaketide chromone. The pentaketide chromone synthase (EC 2.3.1.-) isolated from aloe (|FRAME: TAX-45385|) belongs to the CHS superfamily (PKS type III). The pentaketide chromone synthase is a plant-specific, unique enzyme taking up a central function in the biosynthesis of chromones |CITS: [15686354]|.

Summary: In the anaerobic respiratory chain formed by glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) dehydrogenase and cytochrome c peroxidase (CCP) the oxidation of sn-glycerol-3-phosphate in the cytoplasm is coupled to the reduction of H2O2 in the periplasm via the membrane menaquinone pool., CCP supports respiratory growth in anoxic glycerol medium using H2O2 as the terminal electron acceptor |CITS: [28696311]|. E. coli K-12 contains two G3P dehydrogenases, encoded by the glpABC and glpD genes. GlpABC, commonly referred to as anaerobic G3P dehydrogenase is depicted in this pathway although its involvement has not been experimentally confirmed. , CCP derives electrons directly from the quinone pool; a mutant strain which is unable to synthesize menaquinone, shows a significant reduction in H2O2 scavenging during anaerobic growth in LB medium, whilst a strain lacking both ubiquinones and menaquinones is essentially devoid of this activity |CITS: [28696311]|., The energetics of this pathway are not known.

Summary: |FRAME: CPD-463| is an unusual amino acid that is ubiquitous throughout the plant kingdom. It is a chelator of several divalent transition metals. |FRAME: CPD-13053 Queuosine| is an important |FRAME: 7-Deazapurines 7-deazapurine"| modified nucleoside that is present in certain tRNAs in bacteria and most eukaryotes (with the exception of mycoplasmas and yeast). It is not found in the archaea |CITS: [ 12697167]|. Prokaryotes can synthesize queuosine de novo by a complex biosynthetic pathway, whereas eukaryotes are unable to synthesize it, and utilize a salvage system, acquiring the |FRAME: QUEUINE| base as a nutrient factor from their diet or from intestinal microflora |CITS: [19925456 ]|., Queuosine and its derivatives occur exclusively at position 34 (the wobble position) in the anticodons of tRNAs coding for the amino acids |FRAME: HIS|, |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE|, |FRAME: ASN| and |FRAME: TYR| |CITS: [ 4550561]|. Each of these tRNAs posses the anticodon sequence GUN (positions 34-36), where N can be any nucleotide. Queuosine improves accuracy of translation |CITS: [ 2988936][11532950]|. These tRNAs of the 'Q-family' originally contain guanine in the first position of anticodon, which is post-transcriptionally modified with |FRAME: QUEUINE| by an irreversible insertion during maturation. , Beside the 7-deazaguanosine core, quenosine possesses an additional adaptation - a cyclopentendiol ring attached to an aminomethyl group at position 7. In in some mammalian species the cyclopentendiol ring is further modified by glycosylation with galactose (on |FRAME: ASP-tRNAs|) or mannose (on |FRAME: TYR-tRNAs|) at the C5'' hydroxyl (see |FRAME: 2.4.1.110-RXN "EC 2.4.1.110"|) |CITS: [190593]|. In bacteria |FRAME: ASP-tRNAs| appears to be glutamylated at the same position (see |FRAME: EG11362-MONOMER|) |CITS: [16164993]|., The first part of the pathway leading to formation of queuosine, up to the intermediate |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE|, is described in the pathway |FRAME: PWY-6703|. , |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE "PreQ0"| is a common intermediate, and is also found in the pathways leading to the biosynthesis of several 7-deazapurine antibiotics produced by Streptomyces species. Before it can be inserted into a tRNA it is converted into |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| by the enzyme |FRAME: EC-1.7.1.13| (|FRAME: G7452|). This enzyme uses 2 NADPH molecules to reduce the nitrile group of |FRAME: 7-CYANO-7-DEAZAGUANINE| to an amino group |CITS: [15767583]|. The next enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.4.2.29| (|FRAME: EG10996|) catalyzes a complex reaction in which |FRAME: 7-AMINOMETHYL-7-DEAZAGUANINE| is transferred into a target tRNA molecule, replacing the guanine base, and generating a 7-aminomethyl-7-deazaguanine nucleoside at position 34 |CITS: [8323579]|. The enzyme recognizes the anticodon region of its substrate, and only acts on tRNAs that contain a GUN sequence |CITS: [8494901]|., The third enzyme, |FRAME: EC-2.4.99.17| (|FRAME: EG10812|) transfers a ribose moiety from |FRAME: S-ADENOSYLMETHIONINE| to the tRNA, resulting in the formation of the 2,3-epoxy-4,5-dihydroxycyclopentane ring of epoxyqueuosine and releasing |FRAME: ADENINE| and |FRAME: MET| |CITS: [8347586][7849103]|. In the last step of the pathway, catalyzed by |FRAME: EC-1.17.99.6|, the eopxy bonds are reduced, generating the final queuosine residue. Two different enzymes, not related to each other, have been found to catalyze the last step, encoded by the |FRAME: G7843| and |FRAME: HP0100| genes, respectively. Some organisms possess both genes, but most contain only one form |CITS: [21502530][28128549]|.

The N-linked glycans of |FRAME: TAX-4932| can be extended with an outer chain of 50 or more α-1,6-linked mannosyl residues that is extensively decorated with short α-1,2-mannose side branches terminated in α-1,3-mannosyl residues. Some of the alpha;-1,2-linked residues are phosphorylated at position 6, and additional mannose residues are linked to them via a phosphodiester-linkage, forming branched side chains. The polysaccharide is named the yeast α-mannan |CITS: [23135325]|., This polysaccharide is a viable food source for the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-818|, a dominant member of the human large bowel microbiota. Transcriptional studies have identified three polysaccharide utilization loci (PULs) in the |FRAME: TAX-818| genome. PULs often have genes that are required for the degradation of more than one type of polysaccharide (e.g. the yeast α-mannan, the high mannose mammalian N-glycan (HMNG), and the α-mannans of other fungi) |CITS: [25567280]|., The degradation of the yeast mannan occurs in two locations. In the first stage extracellular enzymes break down the mannan into smaller fragments. The enzymes involved in this step include |FRAME: MONOMER-124351| (|FRAME: G-124349|, GH99), which liberates |FRAME: CPD-12789| from the side branches, leaving short branches consisting of a single α(1,2)-linked mannosyl residue, some constitutively-expressed α-mannosidases that can remove the remaining mannosyl residue from the backbone such as the |FRAME: MONOMER-124365| (GH92),encoded by |FRAME: G-124363|, and the endo-α-1,6-mannanases encoded by the |FRAME: G-124350| and |FRAME: G-124351| genes (GH76), which cleave the α(1,6) backbone. Since the backbone is not accessible to the endo-α1,6-mannanases until some side chains have been removed, the activity of these enzymes depends on earlier cleavage by |FRAME: MONOMER-124351| and the α-mannosidases. These extracellular endo-α-1,6-mannanases cleave infrequently, generating large oligosaccharides that minimize extracellular metabolism and loss to neighboring bacteria |CITS: [25567280]|., The fragments produced by the extracellular enzymes are imported into the cell in a mechanism siimilar to that characterized for starch degradation. The fragments first bind to a membrane-bound binding protein similar to SusD, which orients them into the porin formed by SusC-like proteins. Genes encoding SusC-like porins are present in all three PULs |CITS: [25567280]|., Once inside the periplasm, the oligosaccharides are degraded to completion by a number of enzymes. The |FRAME: MONOMER-124354| encoded by |FRAME: G-124352| removes terminal α(1,3)-linked residues, exposing the α(1,2)-linked residues they were connected to for removal by the |FRAME: MONOMER-124355| encoded by |FRAME: G-124353| (both enzymes belong to the GH92 family). The |FRAME: MONOMER-124356| encoded by |FRAME: G-124354| (GH38) removes α(1,2)-linked residues connected directly to the backbone, and also the residues that are connected via a phosphodiester-linkage. This activity exposes the phosphate group, which is removed by phosphatases encoded by the |FRAME: G-124355| and |FRAME: G-124356| genes. Once the phosphate is removed, the remaining mannosyl residue is removed by |FRAME: G-124354|., The α(1,6) backbone, now free of side branches, is cleaved into di- and trisaccharides by the α-1,6-endo-mannanases encoded by the |FRAME: G-124357| and |FRAME: G-124358| genes (GH76). The final reactions in this pathway are carried out by α-1,6-mannosidases (|FRAME: G-124359| and |FRAME: G-124360|, GH125) that break down the α(1.6) saccharides into mannose monomers, and the |FRAME: MONOMER-124363| encoded by |FRAME: G-124361| (GH92) which does the same to the |FRAME: CPD-12789| formed earlier by |FRAME: G-124349| and imported into the periplasm by the SusC-like porin |CITS: [25567280]|.

A conserved cluster of five genes is found in the genomes of pathogenic mycobacterial species, as well as other actinobacterial genera including |FRAME: TAX-1883|, |FRAME: TAX-43356|, |FRAME: TAX-1817|, and |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus|. Expression of the five genes from |FRAME: TAX-116188| in |FRAME: TAX-562| resulted in production of two isonitrile lipopeptides (INLPs) - |FRAME: CPD-24902| and its acetylated form |FRAME: CPD-24903| |CITS: [28634299]|. While the exact function of these lipopeptides is not known, it was reported that they function as virulence factors in |FRAME: TAX-1773| |CITS: [14569030][20566858]|, and a mutagenesis study in |FRAME: TAX-1781| suggested that the gene cluster plays a role in metal acquisition |CITS: [28634299]|., The assembly line starts with the activation of |FRAME: CROTONATE| by |FRAME: G-107562 ScoC| through adenylation, followed by its loading onto a dedicated acyl-carrier protein (ScoB). The free product, |FRAME: CPD-24899|, is oxidized and decarboxylated by an unusual nonheme iron(II)/2-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase (|FRAME: G-107561 ScoE|), generating the isonitrile fatty acid intermediate |FRAME: CPD-24900|. This unprecedented transformation provides a novel, second route for the formation of isonitrile groups |CITS: [ 29906336][33361191]|. Previously, the only enzymes known to produce such a group were members of the IsnA family of isonitrile synthases (|FRAME: EC-4.1.99.24|, and |FRAME: EC-4.1.99.25|)., The isonitrile product is loaded again on the ScoB acyl-carrier protein, a second activity of ScoC within this pathway. The last step of the pathway is catalyzed by the non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS) |FRAME: G-107564 ScoA|. The enzyme loads an |FRAME: LYS| molecule on a lysine-specific peptidyl-carrier domain and accepts two (R)-3-isocyanylbutanoyl moieties from ScoB, condensing them to the two amino groups of the lysine and forming the final product. A reduction domain catalyzes a 4 electron reduction that releases the product from the NRPS with a terminal alcohol group |CITS: [28634299]|.

Aromatic sulfonic acids are not common among natural products, but they are produced in large, quantities by the chemical industry. They are typically used as detergents, dyes, dispersants, ion, exchangers, optical brighteners, and pharmaceuticals., The presence of sulfonate substituents usually significantly decreases the rates of biodegradation,, and several examples of the accumulation of sulfonated aromatics in the environment have been, described. however, some organisms are capable of degrading such compounds., |FRAME: CPD-10418| is an intermediate in the catabolism of several sulfonates, including, |FRAME: CPD-10427| |CITS: [Feigel 06]| and |FRAME: CPD-10428| |CITS: [8919454]|., It has also been reported as an intermediate in the degradation of linear alkylbenzenesulfonates, such as |FRAME: CPD-10430| by |FRAME: ORG-6048| and other organisms, |CITS:[10788358][10788359][14962144][15240283]|., |FRAME: CPD-10418| thus appears to be a central intermediate for the degradation of substituted, sulfonated benzenes., It was shown that in some organisms 4-sulfocatechol is degraded in an ortho cleavage pathway, resembling the protocatechuate ortho cleavage pathway (see, |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|)., 4-sulfocatechol is first oxidized to |FRAME: CPD-10419| by specifically adapted forms of, protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenases |CITS: [8439234][8772173]|. The genes encoding these enzymes,, which have been named "type 2 protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenases", have been cloned from, |FRAME: TAX-65786| and |FRAME: ORG-6047| |CITS: [11029433][11454212]|., |FRAME: CPD-10419| is further converted in a cycloisomerization reaction to a sulfonated lactone,, again, by type 2 enzymes similar to the parallel enzymes from the protocatechuate cleavage pathway., The genes encoding these enzymes were also cloned from the same organisms |CITS: [17074892]|., The lactone is hydrolyzed to |FRAME: CPD-294| by hydrolases that are very similar to, |FRAME: MONOMER-3463| enzymes, which are involved in the meta cleavage pathway of, protocatechuate (see |FRAME: P184-PWY|) |CITS: [17660282]|., Finally, |FRAME: CPD-294| is converted by a reductase to the common intermediate, |FRAME: 3-KETO-ADIPATE|, which is degraded in a common pathway to |FRAME:ACETYL-COA|.

Summary: |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is synthesized from and degraded to |FRAME: OXALACETIC_ACID|, an intermediate of the |FRAME: TCA|, by a reversible transamination reaction with |FRAME: GLT| (for the degradation of aspartate, see |FRAME: ASPARTATE-DEG1-PWY|). This pathway is common in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and provides a link between amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism., |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID Oxaloacetate|, which is consumed in this pathway, is replenished from the |FRAME:TCA|, and from the |FRAME: CPLX-6001| reaction in both bacteria and eukaryotes, and from |FRAME: PEPCARBOX-CPLX| in some bacteria |CITS: [GOTTSCHALK1986]|., In |FRAME: TAX-83333| the |FRAME: ASPAMINOTRANS-DIMER|, encoded by the |FRAME: EG10096| gene, is the principal transaminase that catalyzes this reaction, although |FRAME: TYRB-DIMER|, which is encoded by |FRAME: EG11040|, also catalyzes it.  Null mutations in |FRAME: EG10096| do not confer aspartate auxotrophy, while null mutations in both |FRAME: EG10096| and |FRAME: EG11040| do., In addition to being a constituent of proteins, |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| is also a precursor for the biosynthesis of many other compounds including |FRAME: LYS|, |FRAME: THR|, |FRAME: MET| and |FRAME: NAD| (see |FRAME: PWY0-781|)., Approximately 27 % of |FRAME: TAX-83333| nitrogen flows through |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|.

General Background, Cytokinins have profound physiological roles in plants, e.g. promotion of cell division, release of lateral buds from apical dominance, and delay of senescence. The biological activity of cytokinins have long been studied. However, the uncertainty persists as to how different classes of cytokinins play different roles in plant development. The main form of cytokinin in plant cytoplasmic prenylated-tRNAs is cis-zeatin |CITS:[TALLER94]|. Although cis-zeatins can sometimes be found in plants in the tRNA-free form |CITS:[12228609]|, and even be the predominant form of cytokinins in the species |FRAME:TAX-3827| |CITS:[9701607]|, the physiological relevance of cis-hydroxylated cytokinins remains unclear. Indeed, in plants, it has been shown that cis-cytokinins have only low activity. The most biologically-relevant cytokinins have a trans-hydroxylated N6 side-chain. , With the uncovered existence of a zeatin cis-trans isomerase |CITS:[12231873]| came the postulate that cis-type cytokinins could contribute to the synthesis of trans-type cytokinins. This possibility is however thought to be improbable |CITS:[14726522]|. In Arabidopsis thaliana the trans-type cytokinins are synthesized in plastids from DMAPP precursors originating from the plastidic |FRAME: NONMEVIPP-PWY|. The cis-type cytokinins, on the other hand, are synthesized through prenylation of tRNA molecules in the cytosol using DMAPP precursors originating from the cytosolic |FRAME: PWY-922 "mevalonate pathway"|., About This Pathway, So far only one enzyme has been characterized for the tRNA-dependent cytokinin biosynthesis in |FRAME:TAX-3701|. The tRNA isopentenyltransferase activity of the enzyme encoded by IPT2 was demonstrated by heterologous expression of the gene in yeast |CITS:[11999372]|. To date no enzyme able to catalyze the stereo-specific hydroxylation of the isoprene side chain has been found and it is not known whether this hydroxylation step occurs after pentenylation of the tRNA adenine using DMAPP as a substrate or whether an hydroxylated analogue of DMAPP could give cis-zeatin-tRNA directly |CITS:[11999372]|.

Summary: |FRAME:ORCINOL-CPD "Orcinol"| is a natural phenolic organic compound that occurs in many species of lichens, such as |FRAME: TAX-269078|. It is also a precursor of the phenolic methyl ether |FRAME: CPD-9502|, the major scent compound of many rose varieties |CITS: [16361520]|., |FRAME:ORCINOL-CPD "Orcinol"| is also used in the production of the reddish-brown dye |FRAME: CPD-12326| and as a reagent in some chemical tests for pentoses, such as Bial's Test., Two |FRAME: TAX-303| strains, |FRAME: ORG-5951| and |FRAME: ORG-5953|, are capable of growing with |FRAME:ORCINOL-CPD| as the sole source of carbon |CITS:[1126936][1280][942589][1254564]|., 1,3-dihydroxy-derivatives of benzenoid are widespread products of plant and microbial metabolism |CITS: [1254564]|. |FRAME:CPD-616| can be rapidly and nonenzymatically oxidized to a quinone |CITS: [1126936]|., Degradation of |FRAME: ORCINOL-CPD| has also been demonstrated in the fungus |FRAME: TAX-5061|, although the exact pathway is not known |CITS: [3742332]|.
