Summary: General Background, |FRAME: ILE| is almost always synthesized from |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|. In the most, common pathway, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is generated from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE| via, |FRAME: THR| (see |FRAME:PWY-3001|)., The key enzyme in that pathway is |FRAME:THREDEHYDSYN-CPLX|, encoded by the |FRAME:EG10493| gene., In addition to the standard pathway, microorganisms have developed several alternative pathways for, |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis. |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| can be synthesized from |FRAME: GLT| via |FRAME: L-THREO-3-METHYL-ASPARTATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5103|) |CITS: [4550817]|, from |FRAME: PYRUVATE| (see |FRAME:PWY-5101|) |CITS: [4607875][4808901][15292141]|, and from |FRAME: PROPIONATE| by carboxylation (this pathway) |CITS: [5800441] [1212197][Eikmanns83a]|)., In addition, there are several reports that under anaerobic conditions some anaerobic bacteria can carboxylate, |FRAME: CPD-7076| to |FRAME: ILE| via |FRAME: 2-KETO-3-METHYL-VALERATE| (see |FRAME: PWY-5108|) |CITS: [5813342][6726176][6440485 ]|., About This Pathway, This pathway was first suggested by Buchanan, who in 1969 discovered the key enzyme,, |FRAME: CPLX-7028|, in cell extracts from the photosynthetic bacterium |FRAME: TAX-1047|, |CITS: [5800441]|., This enzyme catalyzes a ferredoxin-dependent reductive carboxylation of |FRAME: PROPIONYL-COA| to, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE|. Buchanan found that at least in |FRAME: TAX-1047| the resulting, |FRAME: 2-OXOBUTANOATE| is processed to |FRAME: ILE| by enzymes involved in the "common", |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis pathway. He was also able to show the same enzymatic activity in the non-photosynthetic, bacteria |FRAME: TAX-1501| and |FRAME: TAX-876| |CITS: [5800441]|., An independent report of the pathway in another |FRAME:TAX-1485| sp., |FRAME: TAX-1509|, has also, been published |CITS: [6726176]|., A few years later Sauer et al published a report that documented the incorporation of labeled, |FRAME:PROPIONATE| into |FRAME:ILE| by mixed cultures of rumen microorganisms |CITS:[1212197]|., These authors also found that the |FRAME:PROPIONATE| was converted to |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE |, by reductive carboxylation., A third study supporting this pathway was published in 1983 by Eikmanns et al |CITS: [Eikmanns83a]|. This study, reported that several methanogenic archaea, including |FRAME: TAX-145262|, |FRAME: TAX-39441| and |FRAME: TAX-2208|,, incorporated assimilated |FRAME:PROPIONATE| almost exclusively into |FRAME: ILE|. The process was inhibited, by several |FRAME: ILE| biosynthesis intermediates, including |FRAME:CPD-7076|, |FRAME:2-OXOBUTANOATE|, and |FRAME: ILE|.

C50 carotenoids are only produced by several restricted groups of actinobacteria (including species belonging to the bacterial genera |FRAME: TAX-1716|, |FRAME: TAX-37914|, and |FRAME: TAX-1269|) and extremely halophilic archaea. The C50 carotenoid |FRAME: CPD-18004| has been documented in several extremely halophilic archaea including |FRAME: TAX-2252|, |FRAME: TAX-2246|, and |FRAME: TAX-29282| |CITS: [5585680][5485032][4635697][Ronnekleiv95]|., An enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the pathway, the conversion of |FRAME: CPD1F-114| to |FRAME: CPD-18005|, was discovered in |FRAME: TAX-2242|. The gene encoding the enzyme was identified and named Lye for lycopene elongase |CITS: [21840984]|. The subsequent discovery of several pathway intermediates in |FRAME: TAX-29282| |CITS: [24672517]| lead to the proposal of the biosynthetic pathway shown here., Upon sequencing of the |FRAME: TAX-29282| genome, three genes (|FRAME: G-58154|, |FRAME: G-58153|, and |FRAME: G-11373|) were identified as candidates for encoding the carotenoid biosynthetic enzymes. For each gene a mutant was constructed, and the carotenoids produced by the mutants were analyzed. The deduced activities confirmed the proposed pathway |CITS: [25712483]|.

|FRAME: CPD-27928 Thienodolin| is a secondary metabolite initially isolated from |FRAME: TAX-1887| and later reported from other Streptomyces species |CITS: [Kanbe93a][22816309][25724963]|., Thienodolin, which has a thienoindole skeleton chlorinated at the 6-position of the indole ring, regulates plant growth. When applied at a concentration range of 1.2-12 μM, it promoted growth of rice seedlings, but at concentrations above 40 μM it inhibited growtrh |CITS: [Kanbe93a][Kanbe93]|. In addition it exhibits potent anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor activity through suppression of nitric oxide synthases |CITS: [22816309]|. The closely-related compound |FRAME: CPD-27944| was shown to inhibit methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) |CITS: [25724963]|., The biosynthetic cluster that encodes thienodolin biosynthesis was identified in |FRAME: TAX-1887| based on the presence of the |FRAME: G-125006| gene, which encodes a tryptophan halogenase. The function of the |FRAME: G-125006| and |FRAME: G-125012| gene products was confirmed experimentally |CITS: [24692213][27531243][30559288]|, and a pathway has been proposed based on the predicted function of other genes in the cluster |CITS: [24692213]|., Gene inactivation studies in |FRAME: TAX-710705| have suggested that some of the genes originally predicted to participate in the pathway are not essential for thienodolin biosynthesis, resulting in a modification of the proposed pathway |CITS: [26854280]|., Sulfur is introduced into |FRAME: CPD-27939| by an unknown mechanism, possibly catalyzed by the concerted action of a dehydrogenase, an isopeptidase, and a protein of unknown function encoded by the thnD, thnE, and thnF genes, which are located in the thienodolin biosynthetic gene cluster. The second C—S bond was proposed to be catalyzed by a cytochrome P450 enzyme encoded by the |FRAME: G-125014| gene. However, as of 2025, only the first two and the last steps of the pathway have been defined accurately |CITS: [26854280]|.

Summary: Triacylglycerol (TAG) degradation is critical to many plants for which lipids rather than carbohydrates are the major seed storage reserves. The breakdown of the seed storage lipid provides carbon skeletons and energy that can drive postgerminative plant growth before the plant root system and photosynthetic capacity are fully established. , TAG degradation occurs in the seed oil body where TAG is deposited and stored. The liberated free fatty acids are transported to glyoxysomes where they are converted to acetyl-CoAs via the beta oxidation pathway (|FRAME: PWY-5136|). The acetyl-CoAs are eventually converted to carbohydrates via glyoxylate cycle (|FRAME: PWY-561|). It is generally thought that the hydrolytic attack of TAG primarily occurs at the sn-1 or sn-3 positions but not the sn-2 position. Sn-2 monoacylglycerols are naturally racemized to sn-1 monoacylglycerols to be completely hydrolyzed by monoacylglycerol lipases (pg255 in |CITS: [plantbiochemistry97]|)., Despite the importance of the pathway for plants, there is still not much known about the plant enzymes and genes of the pathway, especially di- and mono-acylglycerol lipases. To date, only an Arabidopsis triacylglycerol lipase has been biochemically and genetically proven to play a role in the breakdown of seed storage TAG during seed germination., In Saccharomyces cerevisiae the degradation of TAG and phospholipids is taking place in the lipid droplets |CITS:[16916618] [22345606]| where all the tri- to monoacylglycerol lipases of yeast have been shown to be located and enzymatically active |CITS:[10515935] [16135509]|. The major TAG lipase TGL3p also exhibited DAG lipase activity in vitro |CITS:[16267052]|. The other TAG lipase of importance in yeast, i.e. TGL4 has even been demonstrated to represent a multi-functional enzyme which also acts as steryl ester hydrolase, sn-1 and sn-2 phospholipase A2 and acyl-CoA dependent lysophospholipid acyltransferase |CITS:[20332534]|. In addition, the TAG lipase TGL5 has been found to be bifunctional and furthermore catalyzes the acylation of lysophosphilipids |CITS:[20016004]| indicating that TAG lipase enzymes of yeast are likewise involved in catabolic and anabolic pathways of fatty acid metabolism. The in vivo and in vitro activity of the only monoacylglycerol lipase (MGL) in yeast encoded by YJU3 has been demonstrated in Δyju3 mutants which showed no MGL activity but could be rescued by murine monoacylglycerol lipase (mMGL). Moreover, heterologous expressed and purified YJU3 enzyme efficiently hydrolyzed both |FRAME:CPD-11690| and |FRAME:CPD0-1812| to yield |FRAME:GLYCEROL| and |FRAME:OLEATE-CPD| |CITS:[20554061]|.

Summary: General Background, The nucleotides |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) and |FRAME: GDP-TP| (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-triphosphate), referred to collectively as (p)ppGpp, have been shown to regulate gene expression during the stringent response in some bacteria. Their levels become elevated during this response and they are key indicators and regulators of it. The stringent response is a global regulatory system that operates under conditions of nutrient or energy starvation or other environmental stress. It has varying effects on gene expression and metabolism |CITS: [18039766] [18430135]|. In addition to bacteria, there is evidence that (p)ppGpp may regulate transcription by plastid-encoded RNA polymerase in plant chloroplasts |CITS: [19308923]|., Due to its role as an effector molecule in the stringent response in bacteria, (p)ppGpp has been described as a bacterial alarmone. It can contribute to the regulation of various cellular processes that are affected by nutritional stress such as growth, cell division, motility, adaptation and virulence. Its effect on the pathogenicity of some bacteria has led to the development of |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| analogs as possible antibacterial compounds |CITS: [18776539]| and new in vitro synthesis |CITS: [18789883]| and detection |CITS: [18166051]| methods for |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP|. Different bacteria have different ways of synthesizing and responding to (p)ppGpp, many of which are still being discovered. Even in the well-studied |FRAME:TAX-562| many details of |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| action remain to be elucidated. Reviewed in |CITS: [18454629] [15866041] [18359660]|., In the |FRAME:TAX-562| stringent response transcription, translation and DNA replication are affected by (p)ppGpp levels. Transcription is redirected from genes related to growth to genes involved in survival under starvation and stress conditions. The regulation of transcription by (p)ppGpp occurs at the transcription initiation stage and affects promoter use. However, the mechanism remains unclear and direct and indirect models for regulation have been proposed. It has been shown that |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| and a cofactor protein DksA bind to RNA polymerase and modulate its activity at promoters |CITS: [15294157] [15899978]|, although the exact |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| binding site(s) responsible for regulation are undefined |CITS: [18272182]|. Transcription of many σ70-dependent genes and genes dependent upon alternative sigma factors is negatively or positively regulated by |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP|. In direct models for regulation, |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| affects the RNA polymerase-promoter interaction via stabilization, or destabilization of the RNA polymerase-promoter open complex. Indirect models include changes in the availability of RNA polymerase, and a role for |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| in regulating differential binding of sigma factors to core RNA polymerase. Transcriptional alterations resulting from these mechanisms include repression of tRNA and rRNA synthesis (a key event in limiting the growth rate), induction of stress response factors, and induction of genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis and transport. Reviewed in |CITS: [16554711] [15686546] [18359660]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| the regulation of translation by (p)ppGpp involves its repression of transcription of rRNA, tRNA and ribosomal proteins, as well as its interaction with initiation factor IF2 and possibly with elongation factors. The regulation of DNA replication by (p)ppGpp in |FRAME:TAX-562| involves inhibition of the initiation step. The demonstration that the |FRAME:TAX-562| DnaG primase is inhibited by |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| in vitro also suggests inhibition of the elongation step |CITS: [19945481]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [18359660]|., In |FRAME:TAX-562| the products of genes relA and spoT have prominent roles in (p)ppGpp metabolism. This was shown by the absence of |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| in relA/spoT null mutants under stringent conditions |CITS: [2005134]|. RelA functions as a synthetase and SpoT mainly as a hydrolase, although it also has synthetase activity. Regulation of these opposing activities is critical for the ability of bacteria to respond to nutritional stress and to avoid a futile cycle of synthesis and hydrolysis of (p)ppGpp.. Homologous variants of the RelA and SpoT genes encoding Rsh proteins (Rel Spo homologs) are found in some bacteria and plants. The β- and γ-proteobacteria have proteins homologous to RelA and SpoT, while most other bacteria have a bifunctional protein designated Rel. Reviewed in |CITS: [18454629]|., Experiments have shown that regulation of (p)ppGpp levels by RelA in response to amino acid starvation occurs at the level of translation on the ribosome. Ribosome-associated RelA produces |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| in response to the presence of uncharged tRNA in the ribosomal A-site which results in a stalled ribosome. Regulation of (p)ppGpp levels by SpoT is less well understood, but involves sensing other sources of nutrient stress, such as a limitation in fatty acid synthesis |CITS: [17078815]|. SpoT also senses phosphate starvation |CITS: [17640895]| and iron limitation |CITS: [15853883]|. Reviewed in |CITS: [18454629] [16554711]|., About This Pathway, The pathway shown here for the biosynthesis and metabolism of (p)ppGpp is based upon that shown in Cashel et. al. in |CITS: [ColiSalII]| (see reference below) except as noted. Early kinetic studies established the overall pathway of |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| metabolism. The first product of the stringent response to amino acid starvation is |FRAME: GDP-TP| which is quickly converted to the more stable compound |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP|. |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| is then hydrolyzed to |FRAME: GDP| |CITS: [782536] [321933]|. A role for a kinase in converting |FRAME: ENTEROBACTIN| back to |FRAME: GTP| to complete a cycle was proposed early (in |CITS: [321933] [365225]|) and nucleoside diphosphate kinase, the product of gene ndk, was suggested as a likely candidate. This was supported by mutant studies in |FRAME:TAX-28901| serovar Typhimurium (|FRAME:TAX-90371|) although there is no direct evidence for a unique effect of Ndk on (p)ppGpp levels in |FRAME:TAX-562| or S. typhimurium (reviewed in Cashel et. al. in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|, see below)., RelA can catalyze the conversion of both |FRAME: GTP| to |FRAME: GDP-TP|, and |FRAME: GDP| to |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| with similar S0.5 values derived from the Hill equation. These values are well below the intracellular pool concentrations of |FRAME: GTP| and |FRAME: ATP|, but are similar to the intracellular pool concentration of |FRAME: GDP| |CITS: [3015258]|. Therefore |FRAME: GDP-TP| is probably the main RelA product, although both reactions are shown here (reviewed in Cashel et. al. in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|, see below). In addition to a synthetase (PSI) domain, RelA also contains an inactive hydrolase domain (in |CITS: [18454629]|). RelA is responsible for ppGpp synthesis during the stringent response to amino acid starvation., In vivo |FRAME: GDP-TP| is rapidly converted to |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| by Gpp (reviewed in |CITS: [15590778]|). It is the major route of |FRAME: GDP-TP| degradation, although minor routes via enzymes with similar activity may also exist (Cashel et. al. in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|, see below)., SpoT is a bifunctional enzyme with both a hydrolase activity and a weak synthetase activity (designated PSII) |CITS: [2005135] [8730877]|. The SpoT |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| hydrolase activity is inhibited under conditions of physiological stress and has a major role in |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| degradation. The role of the SpoT synthetase (PSII) activity is less clear. It has been proposed to have a role in maintaining the basal level of |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| during exponential growth (in |CITS: [8648647]|). SpoT also has pppGpp hydrolase activity |CITS: [365225]| and possibly pppGpp synthetase activity. The putative SpoT |FRAME: GDP-TP| synthetase activity is based on mutant phenotype. In ΔrelA/Δgpp mutants starved for glucose |FRAME: GDP-TP| accumulates which suggests phosphoryl group transfer to |FRAME: GTP| as well as |FRAME: GDP|, although the phsophoryl donor is not known (cited as unpublished data in Cashel et. al. in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|, see below). This reaction is not shown here., Reviewed in Cashel, M., D.R. Gentry, V. J. Hernandez and D. Vinella (1996) "The Stringent Response", chapter 92, pp. 1458-1496, in |CITS: [ColiSalII]|.

Summary: Most organisms have to deal with the excretion of nitrogen waste originating from protein and amino acid catabolism. In aquatic organisms the most common form of nitrogen waste is ammonia (ammonotelism), while land-dwelling organisms developed ways to convert the toxic ammonia to either |FRAME: UREA| (ureotelism) or |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"| (uricotelism). Generally, birds and saurian reptiles excrete |FRAME: URATE "uric acid"|, while the remaining species, including mammals, excrete |FRAME: UREA| |CITS:[13672961][13672962]|. Remarkably, tadpoles excrete ammonia, and shift to urea production during metamorphosis |CITS:[13672962]|., The |FRAME: UREA| is formed in the livers of mammals in a cyclic pathway which was initially named the Krebs-Henseleit cycle after its discoverers, and later became known simply as the urea cycle. This cycle was partially deduced by Krebs and Henseleit in 1932 |CITS: [Krebs32]| and was clarified in the 1940s as the roles of |FRAME: L-CITRULLINE| and |FRAME: L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE| as intermediates were understood |CITS:[3545062]|., In this cycle, amino groups donated by |FRAME:AMMONIA| and |FRAME:L-ASPARTATE| are converted to |FRAME:UREA|, while |FRAME:L-ORNITHINE|, |FRAME:L-CITRULLINE|, |FRAME:L-ARGININO-SUCCINATE|, and |FRAME:ARG| act as intermediates., Despite the generalization above, the pathway has been documented not only in mammals and amphibians, but in many other organisms as well, including birds |CITS:[4217066]|, invertebrates |CITS:[14465664][5869779]|, insects |CITS: [697760][5791517]|, plants |CITS: [13741005] [13958361]|, yeast |CITS:[11946245]|, fungi |CITS:[4996649]|, and even microorganisms |CITS:[5593971][5709377]|.

Summary: General Background, Betalains are water-soluble, chromo-alkaloid pigments that replace the anthocyanins in most families of the Caryophyllales order |CITS: [16212790]|. The two subclasses of betalains, i.e. betacyanins and betaxanthins dominate that order and provide violet and yellow hues to flowers, fruits and vegetative tissues, respectively |CITS: [12620337][16669781]|., The red to violet betacyanins are the result of the condensation of betalamic acid (|FRAME:PWY-5394|) and cyclo-DOPA to form the aglycon betanidin from which the big majority of natural betacyanins derive (compare |FRAME:PWY-5439|). The violet color of betacyanins is based on the observed shift to the corresponding absorbance maximum (λmax 534-554 nm) of the aromatic structure after that condensation |CITS: [Christinet04]|. In general, the majority of betacyanins are derived from cyclo-DOPA (|FRAME:PWY-5399|). However, there are few exceptions that have demonstrated the alternative route of betacyanins derived from the catecholamine dopamine such as 2-descarboxybetanidin and derivatives thereof |CITS: [Piattelli70][10198080]|., Amaranthin belongs to and is the eponym for a major subgroup of betacyanins (see |FRAME:PWY-5399|) that have mostly been identified in the amaranth family. Only betacyanins contain a glucose moiety that may be further furnished with other molecules such as malonylate and hydroxycinnamic acids., Betaxanthins represent another subclass of betalains. These pigments are biosynthesized by the condensation of betalamic acid (|FRAME:PWY-5394|) and amino acids/amines forming a Schiff-base that causes the yellow to orange colors (λmax 470-486 nm) |CITS: [Christinet04]|., Those pigments have also been identified in a restricted number of basidiomycetes such as in the genera Amanita and Hygrocybe. No betacyanin pigments have been found in those fungi but the biosynthesis of several betaxanthin compounds along with other derivatives of betalamic acid such as muscaflavin and muscapurpurin has been confirmed |CITS: [Mueller97a]|. However, their physiological role in fungi remains completely unknown |CITS: [12620337]|., About This Pathway, The central intermediate for both betacyanin (|FRAME:PWY-5399|) and betaxanthin biosynthesis (|FRAME:PWY-5404|, |FRAME:PWY-5403|, |FRAME:PWY-5426|) is betalamic acid which derives from 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (DOPA). The key-enzyme, i.e. the extradiol ring-opening DOPA-4,5-dioxygenase (DODA) catalyzes the formation of 4,5-seco-DOPA in plants which is, in a consecutive reaction, spontaneously converted to the chromophore betalamic acid |CITS: [14730069]|. The decisive step in both subclasses to form the corresponding betacyanin- and betaxanthin compounds is a non-enzymatic condensation of betalamic acid with either cyclo-DOPA and derivatives or amino acids/amines, respectively |CITS: [10198080]|., Betacyanin, DOPA may be synthesized through two different pathways from L-tyrosine involving either a bifunctional tyrosinase |CITS: [Steiner99]| or a tyrosine hydroxylase that requires pteridin cofactors for its activity, the latter representing a new enzyme reported for this reaction |CITS: [Yamamoto01]|., The observed diversity of betacyanin structures is due to the frequently observed acylation and glucosylation of the aglycone betanidin. The glucosylation of betanidin takes place in a regiospecific way resulting in either the production of betanin (via betanidin 5-O-glucosyltransferase) |CITS: [10504573]| or e.g. gomphrenin I (via betanidin 6-O-glucosyltransferase) |CITS: [11855654]|. One crucial intermediate in this biosynthesis is cyclo-DOPA that is also a precursor for the further furnishing of betalains. The glucosylated cyclo-DOPA is further metabolized by a rather specific UDP-glucuronic acid: cyclo-DOPA 5-glucoside glucuronosyltransferase that adds glucuronic acid to the structure thus forming amaranthin |CITS: [16247652]|., Betaxanthin, It has been demonstrated that the conjugation of a broad variety of amino acids (see |FRAME:PWY-5404|) and amino acid derivatives (e.g. 3-methoxytyramine) with betalamic acid results in the corresponding betaxanthins |CITS: [Trezzini91]|. The first enzymatic step in the pathway is the decarboxylation of aromatic amino acids such as tyrosine or DOPA to form the corresponding amines tyramine and dopamine, respectively |CITS: [7929401][12242361]|., Tyrosinases have also been described as capable to use certain betaxanthins |CITS: [16277424]| as substrates for further metabolization. From those results, an alternative pathway has been proposed for the formation of betanidin which involves a tyrosinase activity that converts dopaxanthin into dopaxanthinquinone. Dopaxanthinquinone is than spontaneously cyclisized into betanidin |CITS: [15805475]|. A similar approach has been undertaken to delineate alternative metabolism for the formation of 2-descarboxy-betanidin (compare |FRAME:PWY-5439|) by acting of those tyrosinases on the amine-derived intermediates such as dopamine-betaxanthin to produce the corresponding quinone |CITS: [15968512]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid, 5,7-diacetamido-3,5,7,9-tetradeoxy-D-glycero-D-galacto-nonulosonic acid) is part of the diverse sialic acid family of α-keto sugars. Members of this family mediate or modulate many cellular interactions in prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Many pathogenic organisms can display, bind, or catabolize sialic acids, helping them to evade host immune responses and invade cells (in |CITS: [19282391]|). , Bacteria incorporate sialic acid-like 5,7-diacetamido-3,5,7,9-tetradeoxy-nonulosonate derivatives into virulence-associated cell surface glycoconjugates which may include lipopolysaccharide (LPS), capsular polysaccharide, pili and flagella. These nonulosonate derivatives are unique to microorganisms and may show configurational differences as compared with sialic acid. |FRAME: CPD-13166| is a nonulosonate derivative that shows the same D-glycero-D-galacto absolute configuration as sialic acid (|FRAME: N-ACETYLNEURAMINATE|) (in |CITS: [19282391]|). It was first identified in 1994 as a component of |FRAME: TAX-66976| LPS |CITS: [8168511]|. Its correct stereochemistry was determined in 2001 |CITS: [11383892]|. |FRAME: TAX-66976| is the causative agent of Legionnaires' disease., The gastrointestinal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-195| was shown to have novel |FRAME: CPD-13166| derivatives O-linked to serine/threonine residues of flagellin, and genes critical to |FRAME: CPD-13167| biosynthesis were identified |CITS: [17371878]|. In the gastrointestinal pathogen |FRAME: TAX-192222| the complete biosynthetic pathway for |FRAME: CPD-13167| has been elucidated and was shown to involve genes in the |FRAME: TAX-194| flagellin glycosylation locus |CITS: [19282391]| (this pathway)., About This Pathway, The elucidation of this pathway was based on a combination of bioinformatic, comparative genomic, metabolomic, and functional analyses as discussed in |CITS: [19282391]|. Eleven recombinant enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of |FRAME: CPD-13167| (CMP-legionaminic acid) the CMP-activated form of |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid) in |FRAME: TAX-192222| were purified and characterized and a biosynthetic pathway of |FRAME: CPD-13167| was proposed. The work also provided a method for the large-scale production of |FRAME: CPD-13166| |CITS: [19282391]|. The pathway involves unique GDP-sugar intermediates, rather than the UDP-sugar intermediates found in other pathways (such as pathway |FRAME: PWY-6143|), which may provide a means of independent pathway regulation (in |CITS: [19282391]|)., In this pathway PtmF and PtmA were found to efficiently convert |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| to |FRAME: D-GLUCOSAMINE-6-P|. The isomerase PtmF was stabilized by copurification with glutaminase PtmA, and together they constituted an unfused D-glucosamine-6-phosphate synthase. The next committed step is catalyzed by a phosphoglucosamine mutase PgmL in a reversible reaction. PtmE is a nucleotidyltransferase with an absolute specificity for |FRAME: GTP| when |FRAME: GLUCOSAMINE-1P| is the substrate (this allowed large-scale purification of |FRAME: CPD-13160|). In "one pot" enzymatic reactions, PtmF, PtmA, PgmL and PtmE converted |FRAME: FRUCTOSE-6P| to |FRAME: CPD-13160|. Metabolites were purified and identified by capillary electrophoresis/mass spectrometry analysis and NMR spectroscopy |CITS: [19282391]|., Although still uncertain, the next step was proposed to involve a GlmU catalyzed acetylation of |FRAME: CPD-13160| to |FRAME: CPD-13161|. The enzyme is known to be a bifunctional glucosamine-1-phosphate N-acetyltransferase/UDP-N-acetylglucosamine pyrophosphorylase. The enzyme converted |FRAME: CPD-13160| to |FRAME: CPD-13161|, but not to completion. The authors stated that other candidate enzymes for this reaction are being screened |CITS: [19282391]|., The data and rationale used in elucidating the remaining biosynthetic route to |FRAME: CPD-13166| (legionaminic acid) are detailed in |CITS: [19282391]|. Large scale biosynthesis of this compound could be achieved using two separate "one pot" reactions converting |FRAME: CPD-13161| to |FRAME: CPD-13164|, and this product to |FRAME: CPD-13166|. LegF could efficiently catalyze production of |FRAME: CPD-13167| (CMP-legionaminic acid) |CITS: [19282391]|., The majority of this pathway's enzymes were used in an engineered legionaminate de novo biosynthesis pathway in |FRAME: TAX-562| |CITS: [27538580]|.

|FRAME: COUMARIN Coumarin|, a compound that imparts the pleasant aroma of freshly mown hay, is not present as a constituent of intact plant cells, but is produced upon cell injury, usually by the action of fungi on rotting plant material |CITS: [5665249]| (see |FRAME: PWY-5176|). , One of the intermediates in the synthesis of coumarin, |FRAME: 2-COUMARATE|, can be used by mold such as |FRAME: TAX-5073| and |FRAME: TAX-5052| to synthesize the compound |FRAME: CPD-12111| |CITS: [MURRAY82]|. Two molecules of |FRAME: CPD-12111| can spontaneously combine with formaldehyde to give |FRAME: DICOUMAROL|. Dicoumarol causes bleeding in livestock (a phenomenon known as sweet clover disease) and is a prominent member of the warfarin group of medicinal anticoagulents |CITS: [17109150]|., While |FRAME: CPD-12111| biosynthesis is usually considered a fungal metabolic process, it can also be synthesized by plants via the action of biphenyl synthase (BIS) enzymes. Two such enzymes were isloated from elicitor-treated |FRAME: TAX-36599| cells. The enzymes preferred |FRAME: CPD-12112| as a starter substrate and catalyzed a single decarboxylative condensation with |FRAME: MALONYL-COA| to give 4-hydroxycoumarin |CITS: [19757094]|.

Names: aerobic respiration III (alternative oxidase pathway) // alternative oxidase pathway
Summary: General Background, Like |FRAME: Fermentation fermentation|, respiration is a process by which electrons are passed from an electron donor to a terminal electron acceptor. However, in respiration the electrons do not pass directly from the donor to the acceptor. Instead, they pass a number of membrane-bound electron carriers that function as a transport chain, passing the electrons from one to another in steps that follow the electrochemical gradients between the electron donor and the acceptor., Each oxidized member of the electron transfer chain (which can be |FRAME: Flavoproteins|, |FRAME: ETR-Quinones|, |FRAME: Cytochromes|, or other type of electron carrier) can be reduced by the reduced form of the preceding member, and the electrons flow through the chain all the way to the terminal acceptor, which could be oxygen in the case of aerobic respiration, or another type of molecule in anaerobic respiration. , Known terminal acceptors include organic compounds (|FRAME: FUM|, |FRAME: DMSO|, or |FRAME: TRIMETHYLAMINE-N-O|), or inorganic compounds (|FRAME: NITRATE|, |FRAME: NITRITE|, |FRAME: NITROUS-OXIDE|, |FRAME: CHLORATE|, |FRAME: CPD0-1385|, |FRAME: MN+3 "oxidized manganese ions"|, |FRAME: FE+3 "ferric iron"|, gold, |FRAME: SELENATE|, |FRAME: ARSENATE|, |FRAME: SULFATE| and |FRAME: Elemental-Sulfur "elemental sulfur"|)., During the process of electron transfer, a proton gradient is formed across the membrane due to three potential processes:, 1. The use of some of the energy associated with the electron transfer for active pumping of protons across a membrane., 2. Exporting protons out of the cell during electron-to-hydrogen transfers., 3. Scalar reactions that consume protons on one side of a membrane, or produce them on the other side of the membrane, without actually moving a proton from one compartment to another., Upon passage of protons back into the cytoplasm, they drive multisubunit |FRAME: EC-7.1.2.2 "ATP synthase"| enzymes that generate ATP., About This Pathway, The alternative terminal oxidase pathway is found in the mitochondrial respiratory chain of plants (also known as the electron transport chain, or ETC), as well as some fungi and protists |CITS:[9349280][9426242][12228600][10981696][11405094]|, but is absent from animal mitochondria., Unlike the cytochrome respiratory pathway (see |FRAME:PWY-3781|), the alternative pathway is not coupled to synthesis of ATP and is not inhibited by cyanide. It is however inhibited by substituted hydroxamic acids such as |FRAME:CPD-6543| (SHAM) and |FRAME:CPD-6542|., Alternative oxidase (AOX) activity was first described as oxygen consumption in the presence of cyanide from the study of lily pollen and was later found in high levels in the thermogenic inflorescences of the unusual group of plants belonging to the family Araceae. In this family AOX allows rapid, uncoupled respiration, leading to a characteristic heating of the inflorescence |CITS:[meeuse]|. This process, also known as thermogenesis, uses the heat produced during flowering to volatize a compound that attracts pollinating insects. In other, more typical plant species, AOX activity has been proposed to be involved in response to oxidative stress |CITS:[moller01]|. There, AOX would be used to minimize the formation of reactive oxygen species by preventing the overreduction of the ETC., The pathway has drawn special interest as a target for anti-parasite therapeutics since it was shown to play a key role in the respiration of the trypanosome, better known as the causative agent of African sleeping sickness |CITS:[7581322]|. The alternative pathway branches from the cytochrome pathway in the inner mitochondrial membrane at the ubiquinone pool and passes electrons to a single terminal oxidase, the alternative oxidase. This protein reduces molecular oxygen to water in a single four-electron transfer step. The electron transport through the alternative oxidase from ubiquinone to water does not contribute to the transmembrane potential and wastes two of the three coupling sites that are part of the cytochrome pathway. Some energy production is nevertheless achieved through the phosphorylating potential of NADH dehydrogenase (|FRAME:CPLX-5263|) |CITS:[15012279]|.

Summary: General Background, |FRAME: MYO-INOSITOL "Myo-Inositol"|-containing phospholipids play an important role in the control of cellular functions within eukaryotic cells, being part of the intracellular signal transductions pathways from various regulators, including hormones, neurotransmitters, growth factors, and serum |CITS: [164246]|. When these regulators interact with their receptors in cell membranes, they induce the hydrolysis of certain |FRAME: Phosphoinositides "phosphoinositides"| to produce second messenger molecules., |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA "Phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate"| was discovered, in 1997 in mammalian fibroblasts as a source for |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate"| |CITS: [9367159]|, and is still considered the least-characterized member of the phosphoinositol family. It represents only 0.5% of the PI pool present in the cells, but its levels strongly fluctuate due to external stimuli such as TCR activation, insulin treatment, oxidative stress, and pathogen cellular invasion |CITS: [28302928]|. It is believed to play a role as a regulator of membrane trafficking |CITS: [18774718]|, and is considered as crucial for the endocytic pathway, intracellular signaling, and adaptation to stress |CITS: [28302928]|. , The best established pathway for the synthesis of |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate"| is the dephosphorylation of |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-35-BISPH|, catalyzed by a number of myotubularin-related phosphatases, such as |FRAME: HS02045| |CITS: [11676921]| and |FRAME: HS08920| |CITS: [17008356]|., Another source for the compound is the removal of the 4-phosphate group from |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA| by either of two dedicated phsphatases, encoded by |FRAME: HS14553| and |FRAME: HS15363| |CITS: [16365287]|., It has been shown that |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate"| is phosphorylated to |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA| by |FRAME: HS07693-MONOMER|, encoded by |FRAME: HS07693| |CITS: [9367159]|. However, the concentration of |FRAME: 1-PHOSPHATIDYL-1D-MYO-INOSITOL-5-PHOSPHA "phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate"| in the cell is very low (about 2% of |FRAME: CPD-1108 "phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate"|), and thus it is unlikely that its main role is as a source of |FRAME: PHOSPHATIDYL-MYO-INOSITOL-45-BISPHOSPHA| biosynthesis. However, the exact role of this compound in the cell is still unknown.

Summary: Nitrogen is frequently the limiting nutrient for growth of many crop plants. Legumes solved this problem by establishing a symbiotic relationship with bacteria from the genus |FRAME: TAX-374|, which contain the enzyme nitrogenase., Nitrogenase catalyzes the conversion of atmospheric |FRAME: NITROGEN-MOLECULE| to |FRAME: AMMONIA|, which can be used to meet the plant's metabolic nitrogen requirements (see |FRAME: N2FIX-PWY|)., The ammonia generated by the bacteria is first converted into the amino acid |FRAME:GLN| and then incorporated into |FRAME: IMP| (IMP), a purine synthesized de novo during nitrogen fixation by roots (see |FRAME: PWY-841|)., Before the fixed nitrogen can be used by the plant, it must be converted into organic forms that can be transported throughout the plant and further metabolized., There are two major forms of organic nitrogen compounds that can be transported - amides (such as |FRAME:ASN| and |FRAME:GLN|) and ureides (such as |FRAME: ALLANTOIN| and |FRAME: ALLANTOATE|)., Temperate-region legumes, such as pea, are amide exporters, while legumes of tropical origin, such as soybean, kidney bean and peanut, export nitrogen in the form of ureides. , Isotope-labeling studies performed with tropical legumes demonstrate that ammonia produced from dinitrogen reduction is rapidly converted into allantoin and allantoate |CITS: [Ohyama78]|, and that up to 95% of the nitrogen in the xylem sap in nodulated soybeans is in the form of ureides |CITS: [16662061]|.

Summary: Over 200 non-protein amino acids are present in plants. Many occur in free forms while some are detected in peptide conjugates. Many have toxic properties. The role of non-protein amino acids in plants has been proposed to  include serving as defense compounds against predators, as storage forms of carbon and nitrogen, and as detoxification products |CITS: [Wallsgrove95]|. Canavanine is a structural analog of arginine. It accumulates in many legumes, but limited strictly to the Lotoideae subdivision of Leguminosae. Canavanine can accumulate in the seeds of such plants for more than 10% of the seed dry weight, and accounts for 90% of the seed nitrogen of free amino acids. Catabolism of canavanine supports primary metabolism of the developing plants |CITS: [Rosenthal90]|. The catabolic intermediate of canavanine, canaline, is toxic, and can hinder predators of canavanine-producing plants |CITS: [Rosenthal90]|., The canavanine biosynthesis pathway is analogous to the animal Krebs-Henseleit ornithine-urea cycle |CITS: [Rosenthal82]|. Feeding experiments demonstrated the existence of enzyme activities of canaline-dependent ornithine carbamyltransferase, ureidohomoserine-dependent argininosuccinate synthetase, and canavaninosuccinate-dependent argininosuccinate lyase in Canavalia lineate |CITS: [Hwang96][Hwang96A]|. The canaline-dependent ornithine carbamyltransferase has been purified subsequently |CITS: [Lee97]|. The synthesis of ureidohomoserine is probably the rate-limiting step |CITS: [Hwang96]|. Due to the deleterious nature of canaline and its low natural abundance, it was speculated that canaline is not a significant precursor of canavanine biosynthesis |CITS: [Rosenthal90]|. Canaline may be derived from homoserine |CITS: [Rosenthal82]|. There is not yet any evidence that homoserine is converted to canaline. On the other hand, canaline reductase catalyzes the irreversible conversion of canaline to homoserine |CITS: [Rosenthal92]|., This pathway operates in chloroplasts. Feeding canaline to isolated chloroplasts yielded a 2.2-fold increase of canavanine content. Both canaline-dependent ornithine carbamyltransferase and ureidohomoserine dependent argininosuccinate synthetase were reported localized in chloroplasts |CITS: [Lee97][Hwang96]|.

Summary: |FRAME: MET| (met) is one of the proteinogenic amino acids. In addition to its role in proteins, L-methionine is required for a number of important cellular functions, including the initiation of protein synthesis, the methylation of DNA, rRNA and xenobiotics, and the biosynthesis of cysteine, phospholipids and polyamines., In all metzoa |FRAME: MET| is an essential amino acid (an indispensable amino acid that cannot be synthesized de novo) and must be supplied in the diet., Most bacteria, yeast and fungi can directly assimilate inorganic sulfur for the biosynthesis of sulfur-containing amino acids. This pathway depicts such a direct sulfhydrylation pathway for the biosynthesis of |FRAME: MET|., |FRAME:HOMO-SER| is biosynthesized from |FRAME: L-ASPARTATE|, which is synthesized from |FRAME:OXALACETIC_ACID|, a TCA cycle intermediate. Homoserine is then activated through esterification to form the O-acetyl ester. In most organisms |FRAME: HS|, the final product of sulfate reduction (see |FRAME: SO4ASSIM-PWY|), reacts with |FRAME:ACETYLSERINE| generating |FRAME: CYS| (see |FRAME:CYSTSYN-PWY|)., However, in certain organisms, including the yeast |FRAME: TAX-4932| and certain bacteria, |FRAME: HS| reacts with |FRAME:CPD-667|, replacing the acetyl group and forming |FRAME:HOMO-CYS|. Homocysteine is then methylated to |FRAME: MET| via either a cobalamin-independent enzyme or a cobalamin-dependent enzyme, depending upon the species and growth conditions |CITS: [12948640][9409150]|., The other route of microbial methionine biosynthesis involves the use of organic sulfur through transsulfuration of O-acylated homoserine with cysteine to form cystathionine (see MetaCyc pathway |FRAME: PWY-5347|). Cystathionine is then cleaved to homocysteine, and methylated to methionine |CITS: [3309561]|., Organisms for which there is evidence for the existence of a direct sulfhydrylation pathway for methionine biosynthesis include |FRAME: TAX-4932| |CITS: [9409150]|, the spirochete |FRAME: TAX-29508| |CITS: [9440513][12951250]|, |FRAME: TAX-1423| |CITS: [11832514]|, |FRAME: TAX-92706| |CITS: [7096282][7275950]|, |FRAME: TAX-1718| |CITS: [11844756]|, |FRAME: TAX-287| |CITS: [10482527]|, and |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS: [10482527]|., In most of these organisms, there is also evidence for the transsulfuration pathway, and the use of one pathway may predominate over the other. In |FRAME: TAX-83333| and other enteric bacteria, only the transsulfuration pathway is used (Greene, R.C. in |CITS: [COLISAL]| pp. 542-560)., The O-acyl group of homoserine is an acetyl group in fungi, yeast and most Gram positive bacteria, or a succinyl group in enteric bacteria, as well as |FRAME: TAX-287| and |FRAME: TAX-303| |CITS:[10482527][3309561][9409150]|.

General Background, Oleoresin (also simply termed 'resin' or 'pitch') is a viscous secretion common in coniferous trees, which is involved in the chemical and physical defense of conifers against predators (beetles and fungal pathogens). The accumulated resin is released upon tissue injury and/or produced at the site of infestation (for review, see |CITS:[11337413]|). The predator is killed, encased in resin and expelled from the bore point of entry (a process called 'pitching out'). This process has the dual function of killing and expelling the predator, but also to form a physical barrier around the wound through evaporation of the oleoresin turpentine which allows the resin acids to seal the wound |CITS:[CROTEAU85],[GIJZEN93]|. Oleoresin is composed in roughly equal parts of volatile turpentine (a mixture of monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes) and rosin (also known as diterpene resin acids). The exact composition of turpentine and rosin varies from one conifer species to the next, as well as depending on the resin-producing tissue analyzed |CITS:[11337413]|. The main constituents of these fractions have been regrouped in the following pathways: |FRAME:PWY-5424| and |FRAME:PWY-5416|., Concerning this pathway: , Diterpene resin acids (DRAs) are major constituents of conifer oleoresin. They play important roles in conifer defense against insects (e.g. bark boring beetle) and microbial pathogens. DRAs are usually classified into two main categories: abietanes and pimaranes. Abietane-type diterpenes have been known to possess a variety of biological activities, such as antibacterial |CITS:[Kobayashi88]|, cardiovascular |CITS:[11105567]|, antioxidant |CITS:[16848519]| and aldose reductase and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities |CITS:[10748716]|. DRAs of the abietane family, characterized by the perhydrophenanthrene-type tricyclic ring structure of normal absolute configuration (C10 β-methyl) with an isopropyl group at C13 of the C ring, are the principal constituents of the rosin fraction of grand fir (|FRAME:TAX-46611|) oleoresin |CITS:[11112547]|. Pimarene-type diterpenes have been involved in a variety of biological processes: inhibition of platelet formation |CITS:[8135873]|, antimicrobial activity |CITS:[9428161]|, or anti-inflammatory agents |CITS:[9428161]| (for review, see |CITS:[8135873]|)., Levopimaric acid, an abietane-type DRA, is one of the principal resin acids |CITS:[17082986],[11269960]|. Of several diterpene acids tested for their ability to inhibit the aggregation of washed rabbit platelets induced by platelet activating factor (PAF), adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and by calcium ionophore A23187, levopimaric acid was the DRA with the highest activity |CITS:[8135873]|. During gum distillation, levopimaric acid, which represents from 23 to 40% of the acid portion of commercial pine oleoresins, is completely isomerized to other resin acids (palustric, neoabietic and abietic acids) |CITS:[Loeblich55]|. The formation of this acid involves the formation of the abietane skeleton via cyclization of the diterpenoid precursor |FRAME:GERANYLGERANYL-PP|. This cyclization occurs via the formation of the intermediate |FRAME:CPD-4750| and is followed by the stepwise oxidation of the C18 methyl group of the derived olefin |FRAME:CPD-8695|. No single enzyme has been found to date that could catalyze all three conversion steps from |FRAME:CPD-8705| to |FRAME:CPD-8708|, however, one enzyme from |FRAME:TAX-3352| (loblolly pine) could catalyze the first oxidation step between |FRAME:CPD-8705| and |FRAME:CPD-8706| |CITS:[15911762]| (|FRAME:CPD-8707| could not be tested as it was unstable and |FRAME:CPD-8724| during synthesis). This same enzyme was additionally shown to be involved in the formation of other diterpene resin acids (such as |FRAME:CPD-8725|, |FRAME:CPD-8694| and |FRAME:CPD-8712|) |CITS:[15911762]|. To date, however, no enzyme catalyzing the first step of oxidation of levopimaradiene to |FRAME:CPD-8705| has been identified.

|FRAME: CPD-20950| (NMP) is a five-membered cyclic amide produced industrially and used in a variety of applications across diverse industries such as electronics, petrochemical processing, agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, industrial cleaners, paints and coatings. Although NMP shows only low acute toxicity, it produces skin and mucosal irritation and its metabolites showed teratogenic effects in rats |CITS: [19281833]|, resulting in restricted use in the European Union and Japan. Despite its toxicity, NMP is rapidly biodegraded under aerobic conditions, and is not considered a significant risk to the environment |CITS: [Akesson01]|., Early analysis of NMP biodegradation in activated sludge systems showed that the C-N bond between the nitrogen atom and the carbonyl group is cleaved |CITS: [Chow83]|. Multiple genera have been impicated in NMP degradation ,including |FRAME: TAX-469|, |FRAME: TAX-286|, |FRAME: TAX-265 Paracoccus| and |FRAME: TAX-1827 Rhodococcus| |CITS: [25768226]|. Paracoccus sp. NMD-4 was shown to use it as its sole carbon and nitrogen source |CITS: [Cai14]|., The enzymes involved in the degradation pathway were identified in |FRAME: TAX-179636|. The genes are located on a six-gene cluster, and were named nmpABCDEF. The first enzyme is a heterodimeric |FRAME: CPLX-9283|, which cleaves the C-N bond, forming |FRAME: CPD-124|. The next enzyme is an oxidase that forms |FRAME: SUCC-S-ALD|. The third and last enzyme is |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.24|, which produces |FRAME: SUC| that can enter the TCA cycle. Introduction and expression of the nmpABCD genes in |FRAME: TAX-562| enabled that organism to grow on NMP as its sole carbon source |CITS: [29030443]|., Homologous gene clusters were identified in the β-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-1572758| and |FRAME: TAX-488447| and in the α-proteobacteria |FRAME: TAX-82367| and |FRAME: TAX-147645|.

The Rapoport-Luebering glycolytic shunt, which has been documented in |FRAME: TAX-5782|, birds and mammals, generates and dephosphorylates |FRAME: 23-DIPHOSPHOGLYCERATE| (2,3-BPG) |CITS: [12124254][14829]|., The enzyme that generates 2,3-BPG is the bifunctional |FRAME: CPLX-7970|. The enzyme converts the glycolytic intermediate |FRAME: DPG| (1,3-BPG) to 2,3-BPG, and also acts as a phosphatase, converting 2,3-BPG to |FRAME: G3P| (3-PG), which then reenters the main glycolytic pathway. , During the standard glycolysis pathway 1,3-BPG is converted to 3-PG in a single step, generating an ATP molecule, and by directing 1,3-BPG to the Rapoport-Luebering shunt the cell gives up the production of this ATP molecule. However, the purpose of this shunt is the production of 2,3-BPG, which is a key regulator in the cell., First, 2,3-BPG fulfills an essential role in glycolysis by priming the |FRAME: PHOSGLYCMUTASE "phosphoglycerate mutase"| reaction that converts 3-PG to |FRAME: 2-PG| (2-PG) |CITS: [8426905]|. In addition, 2,3-BPG provides a molecular link between the turnover of phosphorylated inositol derivatives and glycolytic flux, being a regulator of key enzymes such as |FRAME: HS00936-MONOMER| |CITS: [6285891]| and |FRAME: HS09849-MONOMER| |CITS: [8769125]|., Finally, 2,3-BPG is a key regulator of oxygen release from erythrocytes, by preferentially binding to deoxyhemoglobin |CITS: [6030262][5238982]|., Recently a new enzyme activity in this pathway has been discovered |CITS: [18413611]|. 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate 3-phosphatase catalyzes the direct production of 2-PG from  2,3-BPG, bypassing |FRAME: PHOSGLYCMUTASE "phosphoglycerate mutase"|., The enzyme that catalyzes this activity, which is encoded by the |FRAME: HS03025| gene, has been previously known as |FRAME: HS03025-MONOMER|, and thus 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate 3-phosphatase is a new activity attributed to it. The enzyme from |FRAME: TAX-44689| has been characterized, and total activity in erythrocytes was equivalent to the level of the phosphatase activity of  2,3-BPG synthase/2-phosphatase |CITS: [18413611]|.

Names: Kdo-lipid A biosynthesis (Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 El Tor)
Summary: |FRAME: Lipopolysaccharides Lipopolysaccharides| (LPS) are a major component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. While they protect the membrane from certain kinds of chemical attacks, they also induce a strong response from animal immune systems. , Lipopolysaccharides can be conceptually divided into three parts: |FRAME: Lipid-A "lipid A"|, which anchors LPS into the membrane; the |FRAME: LPS-Core-Oligosaccharides "core oligosaccharide"|, which contributes to membrane stability; and the |FRAME: O-Antigens O-antigen|, which is a polysaccharide that extends away from the cell surface., Lipid A, which is common to most Gram negatives is the most toxic part and elicits the strongest immune response. Despite some variability in its structure, it is rather conserved among species. The core oligosaccharide, which contains unusual 7-carbon and 8-carbon sugars, is genus-specific, and and the O-antigen side chains vary greatly in their structure and toxicity. The polysaccharide usually contains of about 20-40 repeats of the O-antigen basic monomeric unit., |FRAME: KDO "3-Deoxy-D-manno-octulosonate"| (known as Kdo, which is an acronym for its old name ketodeoxyoctonate) is a part of the inner core of lipopolysaccharides. It is added to the lipid A precursor |FRAME: Lipid-IVA "lipid IVA| in sequential steps, with different Kdo units added by different linkages. The first unit is always added by a (2->6) glycosidic linkage and the second one by a (2->4) linkage. In some cases a third Kdo residue is added to the second one., In |FRAME: TAX-562| |FRAME: DODECANOATE| and |FRAME: CPD-7836| fatty acids are incorporated into the distal unit of lipid A. |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.241|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10464|, is a Kdo-dependent lauroyltransferase. |FRAME: EC-2.3.1.243|, encoded by |FRAME: EG10614|, functions after laurate has been added to Kdo2-lipid IVA |CITS: [8662613] [2203778] [9099672]|. However, a great variability exists in the nature of fatty acids incorporated by these enzymes from different species, and often even within the same species.

Names: saponin biosynthesis III // monodesmoside saponin biosynthesis // triterpene saponin biosynthesis III
Summary: Triterpene saponins are a structurally diverse set of compounds derived from |FRAME: EPOXYSQUALENE|., A number of these compounds have been isolated in the common herb, |FRAME:TAX-39387|, also known as Wang-Bu-Liu-Xing |CITS: [17172290], [9611829]|., In general, saponins appear to function in plant defense, but many have medicinal properties, as well. Wang-Bu-Liu-Xing has been used traditionally to treat a number of problems in China,, including amenorrhea and breast infections |CITS: [17172290], [9611829]|. Although the, pharmacological properties of the saponins in V.hispanica have not been tested, compounds with a, similar structure from other species have been used as adjuvants in vaccines |CITS: [17172290]|. , Saponins in V.hispanica are primarily derived from |FRAME: CPD-6948|, and contain either one, (monodesmoside) or two (bidesmoside) sugar chains. Though the reactions required to produce, these compounds remain largely uncharacterized, it seems that most monodesmosides arise, from the addition of glucose to the C-28 carboxyl carbon, especially on gypsogenate. In contrast,, bidesmosides, generally derived from quillaic acid, seem to undergo fucose addition at the C-28, carbon and glucuronic acid addition at the C-3 carbon. Subsequent glcosylations and other, modifications in both mono- and bidesmosides can lead to the development of complex sugar chains,, such as those found on the monodesmoside triterpene saponins known as vaccarosides A, B, C, and D, |CITS: [17172290]|. The UGT74M1 enzyme capable of carrying out the first glucosylation on, gypsogenate and other saponin aglycone substrates in vitro likely plays an important role in the, initial steps of monodesmoside triterpene saponin biosynthesis in V.hispanica.

General Background, |FRAME: SHIKIMATE "Shikimate"| is a common biosynthetic precursor of many compounds in microorganisms, higher plants, and animals (see |FRAME: ARO-PWY|). As such, it is an abundant compound in the biosphere, and occurs commonly in decaying plant matter |CITS: [14642355][8126417]|., In addition to its biosynthetic role, shikimate can be used by several microorganisms as a carbon and energy source. It is metabolized by two enzymatic reactions to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE|, a central intermediate leading to complete mineralization (see |FRAME: PROTOCATECHUATE-ORTHO-CLEAVAGE-PWY|)., Two variants of this pathway are present in MetaCyc; the difference between them lies in the enzyme that catalyzes the initial oxidation of |FRAME: SHIKIMATE|. Gram-positive bacteria use an NAD(P)-dependent enzyme while Gram-negative bacteria use a |FRAME: PQQ| (PQQ)-dependent enzyme (|FRAME: 1.1.99.25-RXN "EC 1.1.99.25"|) |CITS: [3044290]|. The former pathway is desribed in |FRAME: PWY-6419|., About This Pathway, The catabolic pathway of shikimate degradation has been documented in the Gram-negative bacterium |FRAME: TAX-62977|. This organism produces |FRAME: MONOMER-28|, an enzyme capable of using either |FRAME: QUINATE| or |FRAME: SHIKIMATE| as a substrate |CITS: [8002591][7592351][14586098]|. , While the bacterium |FRAME: TAX-442| also produces a similar enzyme |CITS: [14586099]|, it is less active toward shikimate |CITS: [15598527]|. In both organisms the enzyme is membrane-associated and requires |FRAME: PQQ| as an electron acceptor., The |FRAME: 3-DEHYDRO-SHIKIMATE| formed is dehydrated to |FRAME: 3-4-DIHYDROXYBENZOATE| by the enzyme |FRAME: MONOMER-37| |CITS: [7592351]|., The pathway is inducible by growth on quinate, shikimate, or protocatechuate |CITS: [3044290]|. In |FRAME: TAX-62977| the qui genes for quinate degradation and the pca genes for protocatechuate degradation via the β-ketoadipate pathway are organized into a large transcriptional unit |CITS: [15514110][15691962]|.

Summary: While |FRAME: TAX-4932| can utilize only a limited range of carbon sources |CITS: [1478472]|, it can obtain its nitrogen from many different sources, including most amino acids |CITS: [Large 68]|., The most common mechanism for retreiving the nitrogen from amino acids is transamination,, using |FRAME: 2-KETOGLUTARATE| or other 2-oxo acids as amino acceptors. This process leaves, the carbon skeleton of the amino acid intact, in the form of a 2-oxo acid., In a few cases the resulting 2-oxo acid can be directly fed into central metabolism (such as the case of, |FRAME: L-ALPHA-ALANINE| and its derived 2-keto acid, |FRAME: PYRUVATE|)., In most cases, though, the 2-oxo acids resulting from transamination are not intermediates of central, metabolism, and are excreted from the cells after some transformation., An important and common pathway for catabolism of amino acids by yeast is the Ehrlich, pathway |CITS: [Ehrlich07]|. In this pathway, following transamination of an amino acid into the, corresponding 2-oxo acid, the 2-oxo acid is decarboxylated to an aldehyde., Depending on the redox status of the cells |CITS: [12902239]|, the aldehydes can then be either reduced, (by alcohol dehydrogenases) to alcohols, which are called collectively "fusel alcohols",, or oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenases to organic acids ("fusel acids") |CITS: [15933030]|., This pathway illustrates the Ehrlich pathway for |FRAME: TYR|.
